Mil. 19: (bestiarum) ad res salutares (opp. recessus), id. N. D. 2, 12 fin.: accessus prohibet refugitque viriles, Ov. M. 14, 636: solisaccessus discessusque, Cic. N. D. 2, 7; of the tide, id. Div. 2, 14 fin.; of a disease, Gell. 4, 2; of soldiers: difficilis, Caes. B. Afr. 5: maritimus, from the sea: pedestris, on the land side, id. B.

accidens.full: accĭdens, entis. P. a. fr. accĭdo.— As subst. n. The accidental, nonessential quality of any thing, τὸ συμβεβηκός (opp. substantia, the Greek οὐσία): causa, tempus, locus, occasio . . . rerum sunt accidentia, the accidental or extraneous circumstances, Quint. 5, 10, 23; so 3, 6, 36; 4, 2, 130: ex accidentibus (= epithetis), id. 8, 3, 70; hence, an adjective, Macr. S. 1, 4.— An accident or chance. In gen., Dig. 35, 2, 51: per accidens, accidentally, Firm. Math. 5, 4.— In part., an unfortunate cir

accidentia.full: accĭdentĭa, ae, f. accĭdo, that which happens, a casual event, a chance: esse illam naturae accidentiam, Plin. 32, 2, 9, § 19; Tert. de Anim. 11 al.

accido1.full: ac-cīdo, cīdi, cīsum, 3, v. a. caedo, to begin to cut or to cut into [cf.: adamo, addubito, etc.); hence, so to cut a thing that it falls, to fell, to cut (as verb. finit. very rare). Lit.: accidunt arbores, tantum ut summa species earum stantium relinquatur, Caes. B. G. 6, 27, 4: accisa ornus ferro, Verg. A. 2, 626; cf.: velut accisis recrescenti stirpibus, Liv. 26, 41, 22: accisis crinibus, cut close, Tac. G. 19: ab locustis genus omne acciditur frugum, eaten up, Arnob. 1, 3.—Poet., to use up:

accido2.full: ac-cĭdo, cĭdi, no sup., 3, v. n. cado, to fall upon or down upon a thing, to reach it by falling. Lit. In gen. constr. with ad, in, local adverbs, with dat. or absol.: utinam ne accidisset abiegna ad terram trabes, Enn. ap. Auct. Her. 2, 22 (Trag. p. 281 ed. Vahl., where it is: accĕdisset, acc. to the MSS., v. Vahl. N. v.): signa de caelo ad terram, Plaut. Rud. prol. 8; so, tam crebri ad terram accidebant quam pira, id. Poen. 2, 38: trabs in humum accidens, Varr. ap. Non. 494 fin.; so, imago aet

accieo.full: ac-cĭĕo, ēre, 2, v. a., old form for accio, ire, to fetch, to bring: ego illum huc acciebo, Plaut. Mil. 3, 3, 61; dub. (Ritschl and Fleckeisen: oneratum runcinabo).

accinctus.full: accinctus, a, um, P. a. of

accingo.full: ac-cingo, nxi, nctum, 3, v. a. Lit., to gird to or on, to gird round or about (in prose, first after the Aug. per.; in poetry, a favorite word with Verg.): lateri ensem, Verg. A. 11, 489; and med., to gird one's self: accingitur ense, id. ib. 7, 640; cf.: quo (ense) fuit accinctus, Ov. M. 6, 551; so, ferro, Tac. A. 6, 2.— Transf., to arm, equip, furnish, provide: facibus pubes accingitur, Verg. A. 9, 74: gladiis accincti, Liv. 40, 13; hence: accinctus miles, an armed soldier, Tac. A. 11, 18: orn

accino.full: ac-cĭno, ĕre, v. n. cano, to sing to any thing, acc. to Diom. p. 425 P.; cf. accano.

accio.full: ac-cĭo, īvi, ītum, 4, v. a., to call or summon, to fetch (rare but class.). Lit.: cujus vos tumulti causā accicrim, Att. ap. Non. 484, 7 (Rib. Trag. Rel. p. 199): horriferis accibant vocibus Orcum, Lucr. 5, 996: tu invita mulieres, ego accivero pueros, Cic. Att. 5, 1, 3; 13, 48, 1; id. de Or. 3, 35, 141; Sall. J. 108; Liv. 2, 6; Tac. A. 1, 5 al. — Fig.: accire mortem, to kill one's self, Vell. 2, 38 fin.; Flor. 4, 2, 71: scientiam artemque haruspicum accibam, Tac. H. 2, 3; cf.: accitis quae usqu

accipio.full: ac-cĭpĭo, cēpi, ceptum, 3, v. a. (fut. perf. accepso = accepero, Pac. ap. Non. 74, 31, or Rib. Trag. Rel. 118) [capio], to accept. In gen., to take a person or thing to one's self: leno ad se accipiet hominem et aurum, will take the man and his money to himself (into his house), Plaut. Poen. 1, 1, 51. Of things received by the hand, to take, receive: cette manus vestras measque accipite, Enn. ap. Non. 85, 1 (Trag. v. 320 ed. Vahl.): ex tua accepi manu pateram, Plaut. Amph. 2, 2, 132; hence, trop

accipiter.full: accĭpĭter, tris (earlier also tĕris, Prisc. p. 695 P.), m. (f. Lucr. 4, 1006) [com. deriv. from accipio; see 2. acceptor; but cf. ὠκύπτερος, swift-winged], a general name for birds of prey, esp. those of the falcon kind, Plin. 10, 8, 9, § 21; Ter. Ph. 2, 2, 16; Lucr. 5, 107; Cic. N. D. 3, 19; Hor. Ep. 1, 16, 50 al.— In partic. The common hawk, Falco Palumbarius, Linn.; Hor. C. 1, 37, 17 sq.; Ov. M. 5, 605 sq.; Col. 8, 4, 6; 3, 8, 4 al.: sacer, because auguries were taken from it, Verg. A. 11, 72

accipitrina.full: accĭpĭtrīna, ae, f. accipiter, hawkweed, hieracium, Linn.; App. Herb. 30.

accipitro.full: accĭpĭtro, āre, 1, v. a. id., used by Laevius for lacerare, to tear, to lacerate, ap. Gell. 19, 7, 11.

accisus.full: accīsus, a, um, P. a. of accīdo.

accitio.full: accītĭo, ōnis, f. accio, a calling or summoning (late Lat.), Arn. 4, p. 134.

accitus1.full: accītus, a, um, Part. of accio.

accitus2.full: accītus, ūs, m. (only in abl. sing.) [accio], a summoning to a place, a summons, a call: magistratus accitu istius evocantur, Cic. Verr. 2, 3, 28, § 68: accitu cari genitoris, Verg. A. 1, 677.

acclamatio.full: acclāmātĭo (adc.), ōnis, f. acclamo, a calling to, an exclamation, shout. In gen.: acuta atque attenuata nimis, Auct. Her. 3, 12, 21; the calling of the shepherd, Col. 7, 3, 26; so in plur., id. 6, 2, 14.— In partic. A cry of disapprobation (so esp. in the time of the republic): ei contigit non modo ut adclamatione, sed ut convicio et maledictis impediretur, Cic. Q. Fr. 2, 3, 2; 2, 1, 2; quanto jam levior est adclamatio, C. Rabir. 18; id. de Or. 2, 83, 339 etc.; Suet. Dom. 23 al.— On the contrar

acclamito.full: acclāmĭto, āre, a false read. in Plaut. Am. 3, 2, 3, for occlamitat.

acclamo.full: ac-clāmo (adc.), āvi, ātum, 1, v. n., to raise a cry at, to shout at, to exclaim (in a friendly or hostile manner), with and without the dat.; also with the acc. of the thing called. To shout at in a hostile sense, to disapprove or blame by shouting (so partic. in the time of the republic): non metuo, ne mihi adclametis, cry out against, Cic. Brut. 73, 256; cf. id. Muren. 8; id. Piso, 65; Cic. Verr. 2, 48; id. Caecin. 28; so Sen. Ep. 47, 11; Suet. Galb. 20 al.: hostis omnibus, qui adclamassent,

acclaro.full: ac-clāro (adc.), āvi, ātum, 1, v. a., to make clear or evident, to show or make known; in the lang. of the augurs: uti tu signa nobis certa adclarassis (i. e. adclaraveris), Liv. 1, 18 fin.

acclinis.full: acclīnis, e, adj. (also adc-) [ad-CLINO], leaning on or against something, inclined to or toward (poet. and in post-Aug. prose); constr. with dat. Lit.: corpusque levabat arboris adclinis trunco, Verg. A. 10, 834; so Ov. M. 15, 737; Stat. Silv. 5, 3, 36 al.—In prose, Plin. 8, 15, 16, § 39; Just. 28, 4: crates inter se acclines, Col. 12, 15, 1.— Esp. of localities, Amm. 14, 8; 29, 5.— Trop., inclined to, disposed to (= inclinatus, propensus): acclinis falsis animus meliora recusat, Hor. S. 2, 2,

acclino.full: ac-clīno, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a., to lean on or against something (not before the Aug. period; mostly poet.). Lit.: se acclinavit in illum, Ov. M. 5, 72: latus leoni, Stat. Silv. 4, 2, 51.—Most freq. in part. pass.: acclinatus: colla acclinata, Ov. M. 10, 268; cf.: terrae acclinatus, id. ib. 14, 666: castra tumulo sunt acclinata, Liv. 44, 3, 6: maria terris, Stat. Silv. 5, 4, 5.— Trop., with se, to incline to a thing: ad causam senatus, Liv. 4, 48, 9.

acclivis.full: ac-clīvis, e, also (but much less freq.) -vus, a, um, adj. ad + clivus, up hill, mounting upwards, ascending, steep: stadium, Lucil. ap. Non. 4, 11: ea viae pars valde acclivis est, Cic. Q. Fr. 3, 1, 2, § 4; so, leniter acclivis aditus, Caes. B. G. 2, 29 al.: acclivus, Ov. M. 2, 19.
acclivis.short: ac-clīvis, e, also (but much less freq.) -vus, a, um, adj.

acclivitas.full: acclīvĭtas, ātis, f. acclivis, an ascending direction, an acclivity, ascent: pari acclivitate collis, Caes. B. G. 2, 18; so Col. 2, 4, 10.—Concr. of the rising place itself, Amm. 14, 2, 13.

acco.full: Acco, ōnis, m., a chieftain of the Senones, Caes. B. G. 6, 4; 44 al.
acco.short: Acco, ōnis, m., a chieftain of the Senones, Caes.

accognosco.full: ac-cognosco, ĕre, 3, v. a., to know or recognize perfectly, Petr. Fragm. 69 Burm.; Tert. ad Ux. 2, 6; adv. Marc. 4, 20 al.

accola.full: accŏla, ae, c. [accolo], a dweller by or near a place, a neighbor (incola, one who dwells in a place): optati cives, populares, incolae, accolae, advenae, Plaut. Aul. 3, 1, 1: pastor accola ejus loci, Liv. 1, 7, 5; 37, 53; Tac. A. 2, 68; Verg. A. 7, 729 al.: accolae Cereris, i. e. dwellers at her temple, Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 50, § 111.—In Tacitus, adj., of the tributary streams of the Tiber: Tiberim accolis fluviis orbatum, the neighboring rivers, A. 1, 79. (The Vulg. uses this word in the sense of

accolo.full: ac-cŏlo (adc.), cŏlui, cultum, 3, v. a., to dwell by or near, constr. with acc. or absol. With acc.: Histrum fluvium, Naev ap. Cic. Or. 45, 152 (Rib. Trag. Rel. p. 14): arcem, Att. ap. Non. 357, 14 (ib. p. 202): illum locum, * Cic. Rep. 6, 18 fin.: viam, Liv. 28, 13, 4: Macedoniam, id. 39, 46, 7: Pontum, Tac. H. 3, 47: Nilum, Verg. G. 4, 288; cf.: Rhenum, Tac. H. 1, 51: nives Haemi, Ov. F. 1, 390: Capitolī saxum, Verg. A. 9, 448 al.; hence, pass.: fluvius crebris oppidis accolitur, Plin. 3, 1, 3

accommodate.full: accommŏdāte, adv., v. accommodo, P. a. fin.

accommodatio.full: accommŏdātĭo, ōnis, f. accommodo, the fitting or adjusting of one thing to another. In gen.: a. verborum et sententiarum ad inventionem, Cic. Inv. 1, 7, 9.— Esp., the adapting of one's feeling or will to another's, compliance, complaisance, indulgence: ex liberalitate atque accommodatione magistratuum, Cic. Verr. 2, 3, 82, § 189.

accommodatus.full: accommŏdātus, a, um, P. a. of

accommodo.full: ac-commŏdo, āvi, ātum (better, adc.), 1, v. a., to fit or adapt one thing to another, to lay, put, or hang on (in good prose, esp. in Cic., very freq.), constr. with ad, dat., or absol. Lit.: coronam sibi ad caput, Cic. de Or. 2, 61, 250: clupeum ad dorsum, Plaut. Trin. 3, 2, 93: gladium dextrae, Lucil. ap. Cic. Tusc. 4, 21, 48; so, hastam dextrae, Sil. 5, 146: calauticam capiti, Cic. Fragm. Or. in Clod. 5; so, lateri ensem, Verg. A. 2, 393; absol.: insignia, Caes. B. G. 2, 21, 5.— In gen., to p

accommodus.full: ac-commŏdus (adc.), a, um, adj., fit, suitable (vox Verg. and poet. for adcommodatus); with dat.: valles adcommoda fraudi, Verg. A. 11, 522; so, membra bellis, Stat. S. 4, 4, 65: nox fraudi, id. Theb. 10, 192.— Also in late prose, Cod. Th. 15, 1, 41; Pall. Jul. 8, 2; Veg. 4, 2, 12 al.—Comp., sup., and adv. not found.
accommodus.short: ac-commŏdus (adc.), a, um, adj., fit, suitable (vox Verg.

accongero.full: ac-congĕro (adc.), essi, estum, 3, v. a., to bear or bring to: ego huic dona adcongessi, Plaut. Truc. 1, 2, 17.

accorporo.full: ac-corpŏro (adc.), āre, v. a. ad + corpus: aliquid alicui, to incorporate, to fit or join to (late Lat.), Amm. 16, 8, 11; Sol. 37.

accredo.full: ac-crēdo (adc.), dĭdi, dĭtum, 3, v. a. (pres. sub. adcredŭas, Plaut. Asin. 5, 2, 4), to yield one's belief to another, i. e. to believe unconditionally (rare). With dat.: quisnam istuc adcredat tibi? Plaut. Asin. 3, 3, 37: neque mi posthac quidquam adcreduas, id. ib. 5, 2, 4; so, tibi nos, Hor. Ep. 1, 15, 25.— Aliquid: facile hoc, Lucr. 3, 856. — Absol.: vix adcredens, * Cic. Att. 6, 2, 3: primo non accredidit, Nep. Dat. 3. 4.

accrementum.full: accrēmentum, i, a false read. in Plin. 9, 1, 2, for nutrimentum.

accresco.full: ac-cresco (adc.), ēvi, ētum, 3, v. n., to grow, to become larger by growth, to increase. Lit.: nobis jam paulatim adcrescere puer incipiat, Quint. 1, 2, 1; so, adcrescens imperator, Amm. 27, 6, 13: eruca, Plin. 11, 32, 37; ib. 35, 41: flumen subito, Cic. Inv. 2, 31, 97; so, nondum adcrescente unda, Tac. A. 2, 8: caespes jam pectori usque adcreverat, id. ib. 1, 19.—Part.: adcretus, in pass. sense, wrapped up, Plin. 11, 32, 37.— Of abstract subjects: valetudo decrescit, adcrescit labor, Plaut. Cur

accretio.full: accrētĭo, ōnis, f. accresco, an increasing, increment: lunam accretione et deminutione luminis ... significantem dies, Cic. Tusc. 1, 28, 68.

accua.full: Accŭa, ae, f., a town of Apulia, Liv. 24, 20, 8; dub., v. Weissenb. a. h. l.
accua.short: Accŭa, ae, f., a town of Apulia, Liv.

accubatio.full: accŭbātĭo, ōnis, f. accubo, a rare collat. form of accubitio, a lying, reclining, Cic. Off. 1, 35, 128, acc. to the MSS.

accubitalia.full: accŭbĭtālĭa, ĭum, n. id., sc. stragula, the coverings spread over the tablecouches, Trebell. Claud. 14.

accubitatio.full: accŭbĭtātĭo, ōnis, f. accubito, a reclining, lying at the table, Spart. Ver. 5; cf. accubitio.

accubitio.full: accŭbĭtĭo, ōnis, f. accubo. A lying or reclining, esp. at meals (in the Rom. manner, on the triclinium or accubitum): accubitio epularis amicorum, Cic. de Sen. 13, 45; cf. Non. 193, 30; so Cic. N. D. 1, 34, 94 (but in Off. 1, 35, 128, the MSS. give accubatio).— Concr., a couch, Lampr. Sev. 34; cf. accubitatio.

accubitorius.full: accŭbĭtōrĭus, a, um, adj. accubo, pertaining to reclining: vestimenta, Petr. 30.

accubitum.full: accŭbĭtum, i, n. id., a couch for a large number of guests to recline on at meals (while the triclinium contained only three seats), Lampr. Heliog. 19, 25 al.

accubitus.full: accŭbĭtus, ūs, m., = accubitio. A reclining at table, Stat. Ach. 1, 110 (quoted by Prisc. 863 P.); id. Theb. 1, 714; and perh. also Varr. ap. Isid. Orig. 20, 11, 19.— Per meton., a couch, Vulg. Cant. 1, 11; a place on a couch, ib. Luc. 14, 7.

accubo.full: ac-cŭbo (adc.), āre, 1, v. n., t. t. (the forms accubui and accubitum belong to accumbo), to lie near or by a thing. In gen., constr. with dat. or absol.: quoi bini castodes semper accubant, Plaut. Mil. 2, 2, 57: Furiarum maxima juxta accubat, Verg. A. 6, 606: accubantes effodiunt, Plin. 35, 6, 19, § 37.—Rarely with acc.: lectum, App. M. 5, p. 160.—Of things: nigrum nemus, Verg. G. 3, 334: cadus (vini), Hor. C. 4, 12, 18.—Also of places (for adjacere): theatrum Tarpeio monti accubans, Suet. Caes

accubuo.full: ac-cŭbŭo (better, accubio, Lachm. ad Lucr. 5, 679 fin.), adv. accubo, lying near, a word formed by Plautus to answer to assiduo (fr. sedeo), Truc. 2, 4, 68.

accudo.full: ac-cūdo, ĕre, 3, v. a., lit. to strike or stamp upon, to coin (of gold; cf. cudo); hence, metaph., to coin further, to add to a sum of money: tris minas accudere etiam possum, et triginta sient, Plaut. Merc. 2, 3, 96.

accumbo.full: ac-cumbo (adc.), cŭbui, cŭbĭtum, 3, v. n., to lay one's self down at a place; and hence, to lie somewhere. In gen. (so very rare): in via, Plaut. Most. 1, 4, 13; of one swimming: summis in undis, Manil. 5, 429.— In part. To recline at table, in the manner in which the Romans (and finally even the Roman women, Val. Max. 2, 1, 2) reclined, after luxury and effeminacy had become prevalent. While they extended the lower part of the body upon the couch (triclinium, lectus triclinaris), they supported

accumulatio.full: accŭmŭlātĭo (adc.), ōnis, f. accumulo, a heaping up, only as t. t. in the lang. of gardening, of the heaping up of earth round the roots of plants, Plin. 17, 26, 39, § 246.

accumulator.full: accŭmŭlātor (adc.), ōris, m. id., one who heaps up or accumulates: opum, Tac. A. 3, 30.

accumulo.full: ac-cŭmŭlo (adc.), āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. cumulus, to add to a heap, to heap up, accumulate, to augment by heaping up (mostly poetical). Lit. In gen.: ventorum flatu congeriem arenae accumulantium, Plin. 4, 1, 2: confertos acervatim mors accumulabat, Lucr. 6, 1263.—Absol., of heaping up money: auget, addit, adcumulat, * Cic. Agr. 2, 22, 59. (The syn. augere and addere are used of any object, although still small, in extent or number, after the increase; but adcumulare only when it becomes of conside

accurate.full: accūrāte, adv., v. accuro, P. a.

accuratio.full: accūrātĭo, ōnis, f. accuro, accuracy, exactness, carefulness (very rare): mira in inveniendis componendisque rebus, Cic. Brut. 67, 238: ad omnem accurationem = accuratissime, Veg. 1, 56, 35.

accuratus.full: accūrātus, a, um, P. a., from

accuro.full: ac-cūro (adc.), āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. (arch. accurassis = accuraveris, Plaut. Ps. 4, 1, 29; id. Pers. 3, 1, 65), to take care of, to do a thing with care. In gen. (in Plaut. and Ter. very often; more rare in the class. per., partic. in the verb. fin.; while the P. a. occurs very often in Cic., see below). With acc.: prandium alicui, Plaut. Mer. 1, 3, 25: quod facto est opus, id. Cas. 3, 3, 25: rem sobrie aut frugaliter, id. Pers. 4, 1, 1 al.: melius adcurantur, quae consilio geruntur, quam quae si

accurro.full: ac-curro (adc.), cŭcurri and curri, cursum, 3, v. n., to run to a place, to come to by running, to hasten to. Lit. constr. absol., with ad and in: expeditus facito ut sis, si inclamāro ut accurras, Cic. Att. 2, 20; 12, 18 (accucurrisse); 13, 48: cupide ad praetorem accurrit, Cic. Verr. 2, 5, 3; so Caes. B. G. 1, 22; ib. 3, 5; Sall. J. 106, 2: in Tusculanum, Cic. Att. 15, 3: ad gemitum collabentis, Tac. A. 2, 31: in castra, Caes. B. Alex. 53: in auxilium accucurrerunt, Suet. Calig. 58: ad visendu
accurro.short: ac-curro (adc.), cŭcurri and curri, cursum, 3, v.

accursus.full: accursus (adc.), ūs, m. accurro, a running or coming to: Remi, Ov. F. 2, 3, 72: comitum, Stat. Th. 6, 511: populi, Tac. A. 4, 41: subitus militum, Val. Max. 6, 8, 6: tot provinciarum, Tac. H. 4, 25 al.: civium, Sen. Hipp. 894.

accusabilis.full: accūsābĭlis, e, adj. accuso, blameworthy, reprehensible: turpitudo, Cic. Tusc. 4, 35, 75.

accusatio.full: accūsātĭo, ōnis, f. id., complaint, accusation, indictment. In abstr.: ratio judiciorum ex accusatione et defensione constat, Cic. Off. 2, 14: comparare et constituere accusationem, to bring in, Cic. Verr. 1, 1: intentare, Tac. A. 6, 4: capessere, id. ib. 4, 52: exercere, id. H. 2, 10: factitare, to pursue or urge, Cic. Brut. 34: accusatione desistere, to desist from, give up, id. Fragm. Corn. ap. Ascon.; later, demittere, Aur. Vict. 28, 2: accusationi respondere, to answer, Cic. Clu. 3.— In con

accusativus.full: accūsātīvus, a, um id., prop. belonging to an accusation, hence, in gramm. with or without casus, the accusative case, as if the defendant in a suit, Varr. L. L. 8, § 67 Müll. (in the prec. §: casus accusandi); Quint. 7, 9, 10, and all the later writers.—Hence, praepositiones accusativae, i. e. those joined with the accusative, Serv. ad Verg. A. 1, 28 al.

accusator.full: accūsātor, ōris, m. id., orig. one who calls another to account; hence, transferred to public life, an accuser, a plaintiff, esp. in a state-offence (while petitor signifies a plaintiff in private causes; yet accusator is often used for every kind of accuser, and then includes the petitor, v. accuso no. II. A.). In gen. (very freq.): accusatorem pro omni actore et petitore appello, Cic. Part. Or. 32, 110: possumus petitoris personam capere, accusatoris deponere? id. Quint. 13 fin.; cf. Quint. 6,

accusatorius.full: accūsātōrĭus, a, um, adj. accusator, pertaining to an accuser, accusatory: lex, Cic. Mur. 5: jus et mos, id. Flacc. 6, 14; artificium, id. Rosc. Am. 17, 49: animus, id. Clu. 4, 11: vox, Liv. 45, 10: spiritus, id. 2, 61: vita, Quint. 12, 7, 3: libelli, Dig. 48, 5, 17, § 1 al.—Adv.: accūsātōrĭe, in the manner of an accuser, Cic. Verr. 2, 2, 72, § 176; 2, 3, 70, § 164; Liv. 40, 12, 6.

accusatrix.full: accūsātrix, īcis, f. id., she who makes accusation against any one, a female accuser (v. accuso no. I.): tu mi accusatrix ades, Plaut. As. 3, 1, 10; so Plin. Ep. 10, 67; cf. Prisc. Op. Min. 102 Lind.

accusito.full: accūsĭto, āre, 1, v. freq. [accuso], to accuse: nil erit quod deorum ullum accusites, Plaut. Most. 3, 2, 23.

accuso.full: ac-cūso (also with ss; cf. Cassiod. 2283 P.), āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. fr. causa; cf. cludo with claudo, orig. = ad causam provocare, to call one to account, to make complaint against, to reproach, blame. In gen., of persons: si id non me accusas, tu ipse objurgandus es, if you do not call me to account for it, you yourself deserve to be reprimanded, Plaut. Trin. 1, 2, 59: quid me accusas? id. As. 1, 3, 21: meretricem hanc primum adeundam censeo, oremus, accusemus gravius, denique minitemur, we must

ace.full: Acē, ēs, f., Ἄκη, a town in Galilee, afterwards called Ptolemais or Acca, now St. Jean d'Acre, Nep. Dat. 5; Plin. 5, 19, 17, § 75.
ace.short: Acē, ēs, f., Ἄκη, a town in Galilee, afterwards called Ptolemais or Acca, now St.

acedior.full: ăcēdĭor, āri, 1, v. dep. ἀκηδία, to be morose, peevish, Vulg. Sir. 6, 26; 22, 6.

acentetus.full: ăcentētus, a, um, adj., = ἀκέντητος, without points or spots: calix, Fronto de fer. Als. 3.—Subst.: ăcentēta, ōrum, n., = ἀκέντητα, used of crystals, Plin. 37, 2, 10, § 28.
acentetus.short: ăcentētus, a, um, adj., = ἀκέντητος, without points or spots: calix, Fronto de fer.

aceo.full: ăcĕo, ui, 2, v. n. v. 2. acer, to be sour. Lit. (of wine): vinum, quod neque aceat neque muceat, Cato R. R. 148.— Fig., to be disagreeable (late Lat.): mentio pectori acet, Sid. Ep. 7, 6 a med.

acephalus.full: ăcĕphălus, i, adj., = ἀκέφαλος. Without head, without chief or leader.— Subst.: ăcĕphăli, a sect of heretics, Isid. Or. 8, 5, 66; cf. 5, 39, 39 sq.— In prosody, of a hexameter which begins with a short syllable (e. g. ἐπειδή), Vel. Long. p. 2219 P.

acer1.full: ăcer, ĕris, n. kindred with Germ. Ahorn (f. Serv. ap. Prisc. p. 698 P.), the maple-tree, Plin. 16, 15, 26, § 66 sq.— Transf., the wood of the maple-tree, maplewood, used, on account of its hardness and firmness, for writing-tablets, Plin. 33, 11, 52, § 146; Ov. Am. 1, 11, 28.

acer2.full: ācer, cris, cre, adj. (m. acris, Enn.; f. acer, Naev. and Enn.; acrus, a um, Pall.; Veg.; cf. Charis. 63 and 93 P.) [cf. ἀκίς, ἀκών, άκμή, ἄκρος, ὠκύς, ὀξύς; Sanscr. acan = dart, acus = swift; Germ. Ecke; Engl. edge, to egg; and with change of quantity, ăcus, acuo, ăceo, ăcies, ăcerbus], sharp, pointed, piercing, and the like. Prop., of the senses and things affecting them, sharp, dazzling, stinging, pungent, fine, piercing: praestans valetudine, viribus, formā, acerrimis integerrimisque sensibu

aceratus.full: ăcĕrātus, a, um, adj. acus, ĕris, mingled with chaff: lutum, Fest. p. 20, and 187 Müll.; cf. Non. 445, 14. † ăcĕrătus, a, um, adj., = ἀκέρατος, without horns: cochleae, Plin. 30, 6, 15, § 46 dub. (acc. to others, ăcērătae = ἀκήρατοι, complete).

acerbitas.full: ăcerbĭtas, ātis, f. acerbus, sharpness, sourness, harshness, the harsh taste of fruits. Prop.: fructus non laetos et uberes, sed magna acerbitate permixtos tulissem, Cic. Planc. 38, 92.—Hence, Fig., sharpness. Of moral qualities, harshness, severity, rigor, moroseness (opp. comitas, lenitas, and the like): severitatem probo, acerbitatem nullo modo, Cic. de Sen. 18: acerbitas morum immanitasque naturae, id. Phil. 12, 11; so id. Q. Fr. 1, 1, 13; Suet. Caes. 12; id. Ner. 44; cf. Brem. Nep. Dion. 6,

acerbitudo.full: ăcerbĭtūdo, ĭnis, f. id., = acerbitas, acc. to Gell. 13, 3.

acerbo.full: ăcerbo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. id. (vox Vergil.). To make harsh or bitter, to embitter; lit. and trop. (very rare): gaudia, Stat. Th. 12, 75: mortem, Val. Fl. 6, 655.— Hence in an extended sense, To augment or aggravate any thing disagreeable (cf. acuo): formidine crimen acerbat, Verg. A. 11, 407: nefas Eteoclis, Stat. Th. 3, 214.

acerbus.full: ăcerbus, a, um, adj. fr. 2. acer, like superbus fr. super, yet the short ă should be noticed, harsh to the taste, of every object which has an astringent effect upon the tongue (opp. suavis, Lucr. 4, 661 sq.). Prop.: Neptuni corpus acerbum, bitter, briny, Lucr. 2, 472; and esp. of unripe fruit, sharp, sour, harsh, and the like: uva primo est peracerba gustatu, deinde maturata dulcescit, Cic. de Sen. 15: saporum genera tredecim reperiuntur: acer, acutus, acerbus, acidus, salsus, etc., Plin. 15, 2

acerneus.full: ăcernĕus, a, um, adj. 1. ăcer, of maple (late Lat.): cancelli, Inscr. ap. Fabr. p. 745, note 513: pocula, Ven. Ep. 1 ad Greg. Pap.; cf. acernus.

acernia.full: ăcernĭa, ae, f., an unknown fish, Cassiod. Var. 2, 4.
acernia.short: ăcernĭa, ae, f., an unknown fish, Cassiod.

acernus.full: ăcernus, a, um, adj. 1. ăcer, made of maple: equus trabibus contextus acernis, Verg. A. 2, 112; 9, 87: solio, ib. 8, 178: mensa, Hor. S. 2, 8, 10; cf. Mart. 14, 90: mensae, Ov. Met. 12, 254 al.

acerosus.full: ăcĕrōsus, a, um, adj. ăcus, ĕris, full of chaff: far, mixed with chaff, Gr. αὐτόπυρος, Lucil. ap. Non. 445, 14: caenum, id. ib.; v. Fest. s. v. OBACERARE, p. 187 Müll.

acerra.full: ăcerra, ae, f. etym. unc., perh. from ăcer = maple, a casket in which was kept the incense used in sacrifices, esp. in burning the dead, an incense-box: ne sumptuosa respersio, ne longae coronae, nec acerrae praetereantur, from the XII. Tab. ap. Cic. Leg. 2, 24, 60: plenā veneratur larem, Verg. A. 5, 745; cf.: plena turis, Hor. C. 3, 8, 2; tacitā libabit acerrā, Pers. 2, 5; so also Ov. M. 13, 703; id. Pont. 4, 8, 39; Fratr. Arval. in Orell. I. L. 2270, p. 391 al. Cf. Fest. s. h. v. p. 18 Müll, w

acerrae.full: Ăcerrae, ārum, f. A town in the interior of Campania, N. E. of Naples, now Acerra, exposed to frequent inundations from the Clanius, on which it is situated; hence in Verg.: vacuis Clanius non aequus Acerris, G. 2, 225 Wagner; imitated by Silius, 8, 538.—Deriv., ăcerrāni, ōrum, m., the inhabitants of A., Liv. 27, 3, 6; Vell. 1, 14, 4; Plin. 3, 5, 9, § 63.— A town in Umbria, called, for the sake of distinction, Acerrae Vatriae, now Gerrha, Plin. 3, 14, 19, § 114.

acersecomes.full: ăcersĕcŏmēs, ae, m., = ἀκερσεκόμης, with unshorn hair; in Juv., a young man, a youth, 8, 128.
acersecomes.short: ăcersĕcŏmēs, ae, m., = ἀκερσεκόμης, with unshorn hair;

acerus.full: ăcērus, a, um, adj., = ἄκηρος, without wax: mel acerum, which flows spontaneously from the comb, Plin. 11, 15, 15, § 38 lec. dub.
acerus.short: ăcērus, a, um, adj., = ἄκηρος, without wax: mel acerum, which flows spontaneously from the comb, Plin.

acervalis.full: ăcervālis, e, adj. acervus, that is heaped up, used by Cic. in dialec. lang. for the Gr. σωρείτης, a sophism by accumulation, Div. 2, 4, 11.

acervatim.full: ăcervātim, adv. id., by heaping up or accumulation, by or in heaps. Prop.: confertos ita acervatim mors accumulabat, Lucr. 6, 1263: stercus aspergi oportere in agro, non acervatim poni, Varr. R. R. 1, 38, 1; so Col. 9, 13, 4; acervatim se de vallo praecipitaverunt, Caes. B. A. 31: cadere, Vulg. Sap. 18, 23; cf.: pulmentis acervatim, panibus aggeratim, poculis agminatim ingestis, App. M. 4, p. 146 Elm.— Fig.: i. q. summatim, crowded together, briefly, summarily: acervatim reliqua dicam, Cic, Clu.

acervatio.full: ăcervātĭo, ōnis, f. acervo, a heaping up, accumulation: saporum, Plin. 11, 53, 117.

acervo.full: ăcervo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. acervus, to form a heap, to heap or pile up, to amass (rare, not in Cic.; per. not before the Aug. period). Prop.: jam pigritiā singulos sepeliendi promiscue acervatos cumulos hominum urebant, Liv. 5, 48, 3: aggerem, Sen. Here. Fur. 1216: panicum praedensis acervatur granis, Plin. 18, 7, 10: acervantur muricum modo, they gather or collect together, id. 32, 9, 31.— Trop., to accumulate, to multiply: leges, Liv. 3, 34; Quint. 9, 3, 47; Plin. 26, 4, 10, § 21; 36, 15, 24,

acervus.full: ăcervus, i, m. v. 2. acer, a multitude of objects of the same kind, rising in a heap. Prop. A heap considered as a body: frumenti, Plaut. Ps. 1, 2, 55; cf. id. Cas. 1, 1, 38; Att. ap. Non. 192, 3: altus, Lucr. 3, 198; 1, 775: ut acervus ex sui generis granis, sic beata vita ex sui similibus partibus effici debeat, Cic. Tusc. 5, 15: acervi corporum, id. Cat. 3, 10: pecuniae, id. Agr. 2, 22: tritici, id. Ac. 2, 29: farris, Verg. G. 1, 185; thus Ovid calls Chaos: caecus acervus, M. 1, 24.— A heap c

acesco.full: ăcesco, acui, 3, v. inch. [aceo], to become sour, to turn sour: quodcumque infundis acescit, Hor. Ep. 1, 2, 54: lac, Plin. 20, 14, 53: musta, id. 7, 15, 13; id. 11, 16, 15, § 45; 11, 35, 41; Dig. 18, 1, 9, § 2 al.

acesines.full: Ăcĕsĭnēs, ae, m., = Ἀκεσίνης, a river in India, which falls into the Indus, now the Chenaub, Curt. 9, 3, 20; Mel. 3, 7, 6; Plin. 6, 20, 23 al.
acesines.short: Ăcĕsĭnēs, ae, m., = Ἀκεσίνης, a river in India, which falls into the Indus, now the Chenaub, Curt.

acesinus.full: Ăcĕsīnus, a, um, adj., pertaining to the river Acesinus in the Tauric Peninsula (Crimea): agmina, Val. Fl. 6, 69.
acesinus.short: Ăcĕsīnus, a, um, adj., pertaining to the river Acesinus in the Tauric Peninsula (Crimea): agmina, Val.

acesis.full: ăcĕsis, is f., = ἄκεσις, a sort of borax, used in medicine, Plin. 33, 5, 28, § 92.
acesis.short: ăcĕsis, is f., = ἄκεσις, a sort of borax, used in medicine, Plin.

acesta.full: Ăcesta, ae, also Acestē, es, f., = Ἄκεστα and Ἀκέστη, a town in the N. W. part of Sicily, near the coast; earlier Egesta, later Segesta, near the modern Alcamo, Verg. A. 5, 718; 9, 218; cf. Serv. ad 1, 550, and Heyne Excurs. I. ad Aen. V.— Deriv. ăcestenses, ium, m., the inhabitants of A., Cic. Verr. 2, 3, 36, § 83. — ăcestaei, the same, Plin. 3, 8, 14, § 91.
acesta.short: Ăcesta, ae, also Acestē, es, f., = Ἄκεστα and Ἀκέστη, a town in the N.

acestes.full: Ăcestēs, ae, m., a mythical king of Sicily, Verg. A. 5, 757; Ov. M. 14, 83.
acestes.short: Ăcestēs, ae, m., a mythical king of Sicily, Verg.

acetabulum.full: ăcētābŭlum, i, n. acetum, orig., a vessel for vinegar, Isid. 20 Orig. 4, 12; but in gen., Any cup-shaped vessel, Quint. 8, 6, 35; Vulg. Ex. 25, 29: acetabula argen tea, id. Num. 7, 84; as a liquid or dry measure, the fourth part of a hemina, Cato R. R. 102; Plin. 18, 7, 14; 21, 34, 109; and with jugglers, the cup or goblet with which they performed their feats, Sen. Ep. 45, 7.— In anatomy, the socket of the hip-bone, Plin. 28, 11, 49, § 179.— In zoölogy, the suckers or cavities in the arms of po

acetaria.full: ăcētārĭa, ōrum, n. id., sc. olera, that which is prepared with vinegar and oil, salad, Plin. 19, 4, 19, § 58; 20, 20, 81, § 212.

acetasco.full: ăcētasco, tāvi, 3, = acesco [id.], to become sour, App. Herb. 3.
acetasco.short: ăcētasco, tāvi, 3, = acesco [id.], to become sour, App.

aceto.full: acĕto, āre, 1, v. a., old form for agito, acc. to Paul. ex Fest. p. 23 Müll.; cf. the letter C.

acetum.full: ăcētum, i, n. orig. P. a. fr. aceo, become sour, hence sc. vinum, sour wine, wine-vinegar, or simply vinegar (acc. to Varr. L. L. 9, § 66 Müll., only in the sing.). Lit.: cum aceto pransurus est et sale, Plaut. Rud. 4, 2, 32; Verg. M. 113: acre, Hor. S. 2, 3, 117: vetus, i. e. spoiled, id. ib. 2, 2, 62: Liv. 21, 37; Cels. 2, 18; 2, 21; Vulg. Joan. 19, 29 al.: mulsum aceti, vinegarmead, v. mulsus.— Trop., of acuteness of mind, sense, wit, shrewdness, sagacity (like sal, sales, wit, witty sayings,

achaemenes.full: Ăchaemĕnēs, is, m., = Ἀχαιμένης, the ancestor of the old Persian kings, grandfather of Cyrus: dives Achaemenes, poet. for great or Asiatic wealth in gen., Hor. C. 2, 12, 21.
achaemenes.short: Ăchaemĕnēs, is, m., = Ἀχαιμένης, the ancestor of the old Persian kings, grandfather of Cyrus: dives Achaemenes, poet.

achaemenides.full: Ăchaemĕnĭdes (Ache), is, m., a companion of Ulysses, Verg. A. 3, 614; Ov. M. 14, 161.
achaemenides.short: Ăchaemĕnĭdes (Ache), is, m., a companion of Ulysses, Verg.

achaemenis.full: ăchaemĕnis, ĭdis, f., = ἀχαιμενίς, an amber-colored plant in India, used in magical arts, Plin. 24, 17, 102; 26, 4, 9; App. Herb. 56.
achaemenis.short: ăchaemĕnis, ĭdis, f., = ἀχαιμενίς, an amber-colored plant in India, used in magical arts, Plin.

achaemenius.full: Ăchaemĕnĭus, a, um, adj. Achaemenes q. v., Persian: urbes, Ov. M. 4, 212: costum, Hor. C. 3, 1, 44 al.

achaetus.full: Ăchaetus, i, m., a river of Sicily, Sil. 14, 268.
achaetus.short: Ăchaetus, i, m., a river of Sicily, Sil.

achaeus1.full: Ăchaeus, i, m. Son of Xuthus, brother of Ion, and ancestor of the Achaei. — A king of Lydia, Ov. Ib. 301.

achaeus2.full: Ăchaeus, a, um, adj., = Ἀχαιός. Belonging to Achaia; subst., an Achaean: Achaeis in finibus, Lucr. 6, 1114; Liv. 35, 13.— In gen., Grecian; subst., a Greek (v. Achaia, II.), Juv. 3, 61; Stat. Th. 2, 164; Plin. 4, 7, 14.— An inhabitant of a Greek colony on the Black Sea, Ov. Pont. 4, 10, 27.— Portus Achaeorum, the harbor before Troy, where the Greeks landed, Plin. 4, 12, 26.

achaia.full: Ăchāia or (in poets) Ăchāĭa (quadrisyl.), ae, f. Ἀχαία. The province of Achaia, in the northern part of the Peloponnesus, on the Gulf of Corinth, earlier called Aegialea (maritime country), Mel. 2, 3, 4; Plin. 4, 5, 6.—Hence, In gen. (cf. the Homeric Ἀχαιοί), for Greece, opposite to Troja: et quot Troja tulit, vetus et quot Achaia formas, Prop. 2, 21, 53; cf. Ov. M. 8, 268; id. Her. 17, 209 al.— After the destruction of Corinth by Mummius, B. C. 146, Greece proper became a Rom. prov. under the n
achaia.short: Ăchāia or (in poets) Ăchāĭa (quadrisyl.), ae, f.

achantum.full: ăchantum, i, n., a kind of frankincense, Veg. 1, 20.
achantum.short: ăchantum, i, n., a kind of frankincense, Veg.

achanum.full: ăchănum, i, n. ἀχανής, mute, stupid, Gesner, a disease of animals, Veg. 3, 2.

acharnae.full: Ăcharnae, ārum, f., a demus or borough of Attica, Stat. Th. 12, 623.—Hence, ăcharnānus, a, um, of Acharnae, Nep. Them. 1.
acharnae.short: Ăcharnae, ārum, f., a demus or borough of Attica, Stat.

acharne.full: ăcharnē, ēs, f., a sea-fish, Plin. 32. 11, 53, § 145. (Al. acarne.)
acharne.short: ăcharnē, ēs, f., a sea-fish, Plin.

acharrae.full: Ăcharrae, ārum, f., a town of Thessaly, Liv. 32, 13, 13. † ăchātēs, ae, m. and f., = ὁ ἀχάτης, the agate, so called from Achates, a river in Sicily, where it was first found, Plin. 37, 10, 55; Sil. 14, 228.
acharrae.short: Ăcharrae, ārum, f., a town of Thessaly, Liv.

achates1.full: Ăchātes, ae, m., a river in the southern part of Sicily, between Thermae and Selinus, now unknown, Plin. 3, 8, 14, § 90.
achates1.short: Ăchātes, ae, m., a river in the southern part of Sicily, between Thermae and Selinus, now unknown, Plin.

achates2.full: Ăchātes, ae, m., the armor-bearer and faithful friend of Aeneas, Verg. A. 1, 120; 174; Ov. Fast. 3, 603 al.
achates2.short: Ăchātes, ae, m., the armor-bearer and faithful friend of Aeneas, Verg.

acheloias.full: Ăchĕlōĭăs, ădis, patron. f. [Achelous], daughter of Achelous; hence (plur.), the Sirens, Ov. M. 14, 87: Parthenope, Sil. 12, 34; cf. the follg. art.

achelois.full: Ăchĕlōĭs, ĭdis, patron. f. [id.], daughter of Achelous; hence (plur.), the Sirens, Ov. M. 5, 552.

acheloius.full: Ăchĕlōĭus, a, um, adj. id.. Pertaining to the river Achelous, Verg. G. 1, 9; Ov. H. 16, 265: Callirrhoë, daughter of Achelous, id. M. 9, 413.— Aetolian: heros, i. e. Tydeus, the son of Oeneus, king of Aetolia, Stat. Th. 2, 142.

achelous.full: Ăchĕlōŭs, i, m., Ἀχελῶος. A celebrated river of Middle Greece, which, rising in Pindus, separates Aetolia from Acarnania, and empties into the Ionian Sea, now the Aspropotamo, Mel. 2, 3, 10; Plin. 4, 1, 2 al.—Hence, The river-god Achelous, Ov. M. 8, 549 sq.; 10, 8 sq.; Prop. 2, 34, 33 al.

acherini.full: Ăchĕrīni, ōrum, m., an unknown people in Sicily, Cic. Verr. 2, 3, 43.
acherini.short: Ăchĕrīni, ōrum, m., an unknown people in Sicily, Cic.

acheron.full: Ăchĕron, ntis (collat. form Acheros, Liv. 8, 24, 11; the form Acheruns, untis, see below), m., = Ἀχέρων (interpr. ὁ ἄχεα ῥέων, the stream of woe). A river in Epirus, which flows through the Lake Acherusia into the Ambracian Gulf, now Suli, Liv. 8, 24, 3; Plin. 4, 1, 1, § 4.— A fabulous river in the Lower World: illi qui fluere apud inferos dicuntur, Acheron, Cocytus, Styx, etc., Cic. N. D. 3, 17: via Tartarei quae fert Acherontis ad undas, Verg. A., 6, 295 al.—Hence, The Lower World itself: Ache

acherontia.full: Ăchĕrontĭa, ae, f., a small town of Apulia, near the frontiers of Lucania, situated on a hill, now Acerenza: celsa, Hor. C. 3, 4, 14.
acherontia.short: Ăchĕrontĭa, ae, f., a small town of Apulia, near the frontiers of Lucania, situated on a hill, now Acerenza: celsa, Hor.

acheronticus.full: Ăchĕrontĭcus, a, um, adj., belonging to the Acheron or the Lower World: stagna, Prud. Cath. 5, 127: libri, sacred books, written, according to tradition, by the Etruscan Tages, prob. relating to the Acherontian rites of the dead, Arn. adv. Gent. 2, p. 87; cf. Serv. ad Aen. 8, 398; and Müll. Etrusc. 1, p. 77.
acheronticus.short: Ăchĕrontĭcus, a, um, adj., belonging to the Acheron or the Lower World: stagna, Prud.

acheruns.full: Ăchĕruns, untis, m. v. Acheron (f., Plaut. Capt. 5, 4, 2; cf. Non. 191, 24; poet. in Cic. Tusc. 1, 16, 37; the u for o, as in Enn. and Lucr. frundes for frondes, acc. Gr. Acherunta, Lucr. 4, 170; 6, 251); a form much used by ante-class. poets, esp. by Plaut., For Acheron no. II. B.: adsum atque advenio Acherunte, poet. ap. Cic. Tusc. 1, 16, 37; Rib. Trag. Rel. p. 245; si ab Acherunte veniam, Plaut. Am. 5, 1, 26; so Lucr. 3, 37; 628 al.—And with the ending i (as in Karthagini): si neque hic neque

acherusia.full: Ăchĕrūsĭa, ae, f. Acheruns. Acherusia Palus, A lake in Epirus, through which the Acheron flows, Plin. 4, 1, 1.— A lake in Campania, between Misenum and Cumae, now Lago di Fusaro, Plin. 3, 5, 9.— A cave in Bithynia, from which Cerberus is said to have been dragged, Mel. 1, 19, 7; Plin. 6, 1, 1; the same called ăchĕrūsĭs, ĭdis, f., Val. Fl. 5, 73.

acherusius.full: Ăchĕrūsĭus (old writing Acherunsius), a, um, adj. id.. Pertaining to the Acheron in Calabria: aqua, Liv. 8, 24.— Pertaining to the Acheruns (Acheron), or the Lower World: templa, the Lower World, Enn. ap. Cic. Tusc. 1, 21, 48 (Trag. v. 107 ed. Vahl.); in Varr. L. L. 7, § 6 Müll.; and in Lucr. 1, 120; cf. Lucr. 3, 25 and 86: humor, Sil. 13, 398: vita, a life of gloom, Lucr. 3, 1024.— Pertaining to Acheron in Epirus: amnis, Just. 12, 2, 3.
acherusius.short: Ăchĕrūsĭus (old writing Acherunsius), a, um, adj.

acheta.full: āchĕta, ae, m., = ἀχέτης, ἠχέτης (sounding; pr. the chirper), the male singing cicada, Plin. 11, 26, 32, § 92.

achillas.full: Ăchillas, ae, m., the murderer of Pompey, Caes. B. C. 3, 104; 108; Luc. 8, 538.
achillas.short: Ăchillas, ae, m., the murderer of Pompey, Caes.

achillea.full: ăchillēa, ae, f., a plant, perhaps the same as achilleos, Plin. 26, 15, 90.
achillea.short: ăchillēa, ae, f., a plant, perhaps the same as achilleos, Plin.

achilleis.full: Ăchillēĭs, ĭdis, f. Achilles, a poem of Statius, of which only two books were finished, the Achilleid.

achilleos.full: ăchillēos, i, f., = Ἀχίλλειος, sc. herba, a medicinal plant, said to have been discovered by Achilles, milfoil or yarrow, Plin. 25, 5, 19; cf. achillea.

achilles.full: Ăchilles, is, m., = Ἀχιλλεύς (poet., after the manner of the Gr. Nom., Achilleus, trisyl., Inscr. Grut. 669, 6.—Gen. Achillei, quadrisyl., Hor. C. 1, 15, 34; id. Epod. 17, 14; and Achilli, as Neocli, Lacydi from Neocles, Lacydes, Plaut. Bacch. 4, 9, 14; Verg. A. 3, 87; cf. Val. Prob. 1468 P.—Acc. Achillĕa, Luc. 10, 523.—Voc. Achille, Prop. 4, 11, 40.—Abl. Achilli, Ov. Pont. 3, 3, 43), the celebrated Grecian hero in the Trojan war, distinguished for strength and beauty; son of Peleus, king of The
achilles.short: Ăchilles, is, m., = Ἀχιλλεύς (poet., after the manner of the Gr.

achillides.full: Ăchillīdes, ae, patron. m. (more correct than Achilleides), = Ἀχιλλείδης, a descendant of Achilles, Ov. H. 8, 3.

achivus.full: Ăchīvus, a, um (gen. plur. Achivom, Verg. A. 11, 266), adj. fr. Achaeus, with the Digamma, Achaefos, Achifus, Achivus, Achaean, Grecian (v. Achaia): tellus, Ov. Pont. 1, 4, 33: castra, id. H. 1, 21.—Hence, ăchīvi, the Greeks, Cic. Div. 1, 14: quidquid delirant reges plectuntur Achivi, whatever wrongs the (Grecian) kings are guilty of (before Troy) their subjects must suffer for; but it soon became a general proverb: whatever errors the great commit, the people must atone for, Hor. Ep. 1, 2, 14.

achlis.full: achlis, is, f., a wild beast of the North, which modern naturalists consider to be the same as the alces.—Acc. achlin, Plin. 8, 15, 16, § 39.
achlis.short: achlis, is, f., a wild beast of the North, which modern naturalists consider to be the same as the alces.—Acc.

acholla.full: Ăcholla, ae, f. (also Achilla), a town in Africa, in the vicinity of Thapsus, now El-Aliah, Auct. B. Afr. 33.

achor.full: ăchor, ōris, m., = ἀχώρ, the scab or scald on the head, Macer. de Ruta, 1, 12; Theod. Prisc. 1, 5.
achor.short: ăchor, ōris, m., = ἀχώρ, the scab or scald on the head, Macer.

achradina.full: Achrădīna, or Acradina, ae, f., a part of the city of Syracuse, Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 53; Liv. 25, 24, 10.
achradina.short: Achrădīna, or Acradina, ae, f., a part of the city of Syracuse, Cic.

achras.full: achras, ădis and ădos, f., = ἀχράς, a wild pear-tree, Col. 7, 9, 6; 10, 15, 250.
achras.short: achras, ădis and ădos, f., = ἀχράς, a wild pear-tree, Col.

acia.full: ăcĭa, ae, f. 1. acus, a thread for sewing, ῥάμμα, Titin. ap. Non. 3, 21 (Rib. Com. Rel. p. 115); Cels. 5, 26, 23.

acicula.full: ăcĭcŭla, ae, f. id., a small pin for a head-dress, Cod. Theod. 3, 16, 1; Inscr. Grut. 1004, 5.

acidalia.full: Ăcīdălĭa, ae, f., = Ἀκιδαλία, an epithet of Venus, perhaps from the Fountain Acidalius, in Boeotia, where the Graces, daughters of Venus, used to bathe, Verg. A. 1, 720 Serv.—Hence, ăcīdălĭus, a, um, adj., pertaining to Venus: ludit Acidalio nodo, with the girdle of Venus, Mart. 6, 13: arundo, id. 9, 14: ales, i. e. a dove, Carm. ad Pis. 79.
acidalia.short: Ăcīdălĭa, ae, f., = Ἀκιδαλία, an epithet of Venus, perhaps from the Fountain Acidalius, in Boeotia, where the Graces, daughters of Venus, used to bathe, Verg.

aciditas.full: ăcĭdĭtas, ātis, f. acidus, sourness, acidity: stomachi, Marcell. Emp. 20.

acidulus.full: ăcĭdŭlus, a, um, adj., dim. [acidus], a little sour, sourish, acidulous: sapor, Plin. 15, 15, 16, § 54: aqua, mineral water, id. 2, 103, 106, § 230; 31, 2, 5, § 9; so, fons, ib.

acidus.full: ăcĭdus, a, um, adj. aceo, sour, tart, acid. Lit.: sapor, Plin. 15, 27, 32, § 106; sorba, Verg. G. 3, 380: inula, Hor. S. 2, 2, 43: lac, Plin. 28, 9, 36, § 135: caseus, ib. 9, 34, § 132: acidissumum acetum, Plaut. Ps. 2, 4, 49.— Transf. Like acer, from taste to sound, harsh, rough, shrill: sonus acidior, Petr. 68; cf. canticum, ib. 31.— Acida creta, chalk steeped in vinegar, Mart. 6, 93.— Fig., sharp, keen, pungent: homo acidae linguae, Sen. Contr. 5, 34; cf. Quint. 6, 3, 53: quod petis, id sane

acieris.full: ăcĭēris, is f. acies, securis aerea, qua in sacrificiis utebantur sacerdotes, Paul. ex Fest. p. 10 Müll.

acies.full: ăcĭēs, ēi, f. v. 2. acer (gen. acii and acie, like dii and die, facii and facie, fr. dies, facies, Cn. Mat. ap. Gell. 9, 14; Caes. B. G. 2, 23; Sall. ap. Serv. ad Verg. G. 1, 208, or Sall. Fragm. ed. Kritz. p. 118; cf. Prisc. p. 780 P.), a sharp edge or point. Lit., of a sword, dagger, sickle, etc.: gladiorum, Plaut. Truc. 2, 6, 11: Vulg. Heb. 11, 34: securium, Cic. Verr. 2, 5, 43, § 113: falcis, Verg. G. 2, 365: hastae, Ov. M. 3, 107: ferri, Plin. 7, 15, 13.— Transf. Of the sense or faculty of

acilianus.full: Ăcīlĭānus, a, um, adj., pertaining to Acilius: annales, the annals of C. Acilius Glabrio, Liv. 25, 39; libri, id. 35, 14.
acilianus.short: Ăcīlĭānus, a, um, adj., pertaining to Acilius: annales, the annals of C.

acilius.full: Ăcīlĭus, i, m., the name of several Romans, among whom was M' Acilius Glabrio, trib. pleb., by whom the severe law de pecuniis repetundis was introduced, Cic. Verr. 1, 9 and 17.—C. Acilius Glabrio, the historian, Cic. Off. 3, 32, 115.—Hence, ăcīlĭus, a, um, adj., Acilian: lex, Cic. Verr. 1, 1.
acilius.short: Ăcīlĭus, i, m., the name of several Romans, among whom was M' Acilius Glabrio, trib.

acinaces.full: ăcīnăcēs, is, m., = ἀκινάκης, the short sabre of the Persians, Medes, and Scythians, a scimitar, Hor. C. 1, 27, 5; Curt. 3, 3, 4; 4, 15, 17 al.
acinaces.short: ăcīnăcēs, is, m., = ἀκινάκης, the short sabre of the Persians, Medes, and Scythians, a scimitar, Hor.

acinarius.full: ăcĭnārĭus, a, um, adj. acinus, pertaining to the grape: dolia, vessels for holding grapes, Varr. R. R. 1, 22, 4.

acinatius.full: ăcĭnātĭus, a, um, adj. id., prepared from grapes: vinum, made from dried grapes, Pall. 1, 6, 9; Dig. 33, 6, 9.

acinos.full: ăcĭnos, i, f., = ἄκινος, a fragrant plant, perh. wild basil, Plin. 21, 27, 101, § 174.
acinos.short: ăcĭnos, i, f., = ἄκινος, a fragrant plant, perh.

acinosus.full: ăcĭnōsus, a, um, adj. acinus, like or similar to grapes, Plin. 12, 13, 27, § 47; id. 21, 17, 68, § 109.

acinus.full: ăcĭnus, i, m., and ăcĭnum, i, n., partic. in plur. acina, orum (also ăcĭna, ae, f., Cat. 27, 4). A berry, esp. the grape, Col. 11, 2, 60; also: hederae sambucique, Plin. 15, 24, 29, § 100 sq.: cissanthemi, ib. 25, § 116: ligustri, ib. 24, 74: trychni, ib. 21, § 177.— Per meton., the stone of a berry, Cic. Sen. 15, 52.
acinus.short: ăcĭnus, i, m., and ăcĭnum, i, n., partic.

acionna.full: Acionna, ae, f., a Gallic deity, Inscr. Orell. 1955.
acionna.short: Acionna, ae, f., a Gallic deity, Inscr.

acipenser.full: ăcĭpenser, ĕris, and ăcĭpensis, is (also aquip., not accipenser), m., = ἀκκι^πησίος, a fish very highly esteemed in the age of the greatest luxury of the Romans, perh. the sturgeon, Cic. Tusc. 3, 18; id. Fin. 2, 8; Hor. S. 2, 2, 47; Ov. Hal. 132.
acipenser.short: ăcĭpenser, ĕris, and ăcĭpensis, is (also aquip., not accipenser), m., = ἀκκι^πησίος, a fish very highly esteemed in the age of the greatest luxury of the Romans, perh.

acis1.full: Ācis, ĭdis, m., = Ἆκις, a river in Sicily, which rises in Mount Aetna, and falls into the sea; now Fiume di Taci, Ov. F. 4, 468; Sil. 14, 221; Claud. Rapt. Pros. 3, 332 al.—Hence, A river-god, acc. to the myth, son of Faunus, beloved by Galatea on account of his beauty, Ov. M. 13, 750 sq.
acis1.short: Ācis, ĭdis, m., = Ἆκις, a river in Sicily, which rises in Mount Aetna, and falls into the sea;

acis2.full: Acis, ĭdis, f., one of the Cyclades, i. q. Siphnus, Plin. 4, § 66.
acis2.short: Acis, ĭdis, f., one of the Cyclades, i.

acisco.full: ăcisco, ĕre, i. q., acesco, Garg. Mart. ap. Maj. Auct. Class. 3, p. 419.

acisculus.full: ăciscŭlus, i, m. perh. ascia, and so more prop. asciculus, a little adze, Isid. Gloss.— As a surname, Quint, 6, 3, 53. † ăciscŭlārĭus, ii, m. acisculus, λατόμος (stone-cutter), Gloss.

aclassis.full: aclassis, is, f., tunica ab humeris non consuta, Paul. ex Fest. p. 20 Müll.
aclassis.short: aclassis, is, f., tunica ab humeris non consuta, Paul.

aclys.full: aclys, ўdis (better than aclis), = ἀγκυλίς (first used by Verg.), a small javelin, Verg. A. 7, 730; Sil. 33, 362 al.; cf. Non. 554, 3.
aclys.short: aclys, ўdis (better than aclis), = ἀγκυλίς (first used by Verg.), a small javelin, Verg.

acmon.full: Acmōn, ŏnis, m. A companion of Aeneas: Acmon Lyrnessius, Verg. A. 10, 128.— A companion of Diomed, Ov. M. 14, 484; acc. Acmona, ib. 497.

acmonensis.full: Acmŏnensis, e, adj., pertaining to Acmonia, a town of Phrygia, Cic. Fl. 15, 34; Plin. 5, 29, 29, § 106
acmonensis.short: Acmŏnensis, e, adj., pertaining to Acmonia, a town of Phrygia, Cic.

acmonides.full: Acmŏnĭdes, is, m., one of Vulcan's workmen, Ov. F. 4, 288.
acmonides.short: Acmŏnĭdes, is, m., one of Vulcan's workmen, Ov.

acnua.full: acnŭa or acna, ae, f. ἄκενα or ἄκαινα, a measure or piece of land, 120 feet square, Varr. R. R. 1, 10; Col. 5, 1, 5; cf. Isid. Orig. 15, 15, 5.

acoenonetus.full: ăcoenōnētus, i, m., v. the foll.

acoenonoetus.full: ăcoenŏnŏētus, i, m., = ἀκοινονόητος, one who has not common-sense, Juv. 7, 218: communi carens seusu, Schol. ad h. 1. (Herm. and Rib.; but Jahn and Mayor here read ἀκοινώνητος (in Greek letters); perh. not sharing, i. e. selfish).
acoenonoetus.short: ăcoenŏnŏētus, i, m., = ἀκοινονόητος, one who has not common-sense, Juv.

acoetis.full: ăcoetis, is, f., ἄκοιτις, a bed-fellow, a wife: Amphitryonis, Lucil. ap. Non. 26, 5.
acoetis.short: ăcoetis, is, f., ἄκοιτις, a bed-fellow, a wife: Amphitryonis, Lucil.

aconae.full: ăcŏnae, ārum, f., = ἀκόναι, pointed stones: nudae cautes, Plin. 27, 3, 3, § 10.
aconae.short: ăcŏnae, ārum, f., = ἀκόναι, pointed stones: nudae cautes, Plin.

aconiti.full: ăcŏnīti, adv., = ἀκονιτί, without labor (lit. without dust, the figure taken from the athletae, Hor. Ep. 1, 1, 51), Plin. 35, 11, 40, § 139.

aconitum.full: ăcŏnītum, i, n., = ἀκόνιτον, a poisonous plant, wolf's-bane, monk's-hood, aconite, Plin. 27, 2, 2; 6, 1, 1 fin.: aconiton, Ov. M. 7, 407.—In plur., Verg. G. 2, 152; Ov. M. 7, 419; Aus. Idyll. 12, 9, 11; Luc. 4, 322. —For a strong poison in gen., Ov. M. 1, 147; Juv. 10, 25.
aconitum.short: ăcŏnītum, i, n., = ἀκόνιτον, a poisonous plant, wolf's-bane, monk's-hood, aconite, Plin.

acontias.full: ăcontĭas, ae, m., = ἀκοντίας. A quick-darting serpent, Amm. 22, 15, 27.— In plur., ăcontĭae, ārum, = ἀκοντίαι, meteors or shooting-stars with dartlike trains, Plin. 2, 25, 22, § 89.

acontius.full: Ăcontĭus, i, m. A lover of Cydippe, Ov. Her. 20, 239, and 21, 229.— A mountain in Boeotia, Plin. 4, 7, 12.

acontizo.full: ăcontīzo, āre, v. n., = ἀκοντίζω, lit., to shoot a dart; hence, intrans. of blood, to spout or gush forth, Veg. 1, 26 and 27.

acontizomenos.full: Ăcontīzŏmĕnos, i, m., = Ἀκοντιζόμενος (struck with a dart), the title of a comedy of Naevius, see the fragment in, Rib. Com. Rel. p. 5.
acontizomenos.short: Ăcontīzŏmĕnos, i, m., = Ἀκοντιζόμενος (struck with a dart), the title of a comedy of Naevius, see the fragment in, Rib.

acopos.full: ăcŏpos, -us, i, m., or ăcōpon, -um, i, n., = ἄκοπος (removing weariness, pain, etc.). A kind of stone, perh. crystalline quartz or spar, Plin. 37, 10, 54, § 143.— f., a plant useful in childbirth, also called anagyros, id. 27, 4, 13.— Aco-pum (sc. medicamentum or unguentum), i, n., a soothing salve, Cels. 4, 31; 5, 24; Plin. 23, 8, 80; 29, 3, 13 al.
acopos.short: ăcŏpos, -us, i, m., or ăcōpon, -um, i, n., = ἄκοπος (removing weariness, pain, etc.).

acor.full: ăcor, ōris, m. aceo, a sour taste, sourness. Lit., Col. 3, 21, 5; 7, 8, 1; Plin. 11, 41, 96; 18, 11, 26; of meat, Quint. 9, 3, 27.— Fig. hortor ut jucundissimum genus vitae nonnullis interdum quasi acoribus condias, i. e. excitements, Plin. Ep. 7, 3 fin.

acorna.full: ăcorna, ae, f., = ἄκορνα, a kind of thistle, Plin. 21, 16, 56, § 95.
acorna.short: ăcorna, ae, f., = ἄκορνα, a kind of thistle, Plin.

acorus.full: ăcŏrus, i, f., and ăcŏrum, i, n., = ἄκορος and ἄκορον, an aromatic plant, conjectured by some to be our sweet-flag or calamus, Plin. 25, 13, 100, § 157 sq.; 26, 5, 15, § 28; Cels. 3, 21; 2, 23 al. In the form acoros, i, f., App. Herb. 6.
acorus.short: ăcŏrus, i, f., and ăcŏrum, i, n., = ἄκορος and ἄκορον, an aromatic plant, conjectured by some to be our sweet-flag or calamus, Plin.

acquiesco.full: ac-quĭesco (adqu.), ēvi, ētum, 3, v. n., lit., to become physically quiet, to come to physical repose; hence, in gen., to repose or rest (freq. in Cic.). Lit.: sine respirem, quaeso. Pe. Immo adquiesce, Plaut. Ep. 2, 2, 20; id. As. 2, 2, 60: vitandi caloris causā Lanuvii trīs horas acquieveram, Cic. Att. 13, 34: a lassitudine, Nep. Dat. 11, 3: somno, Curt. 9, 5, 16; cf.: gravi sopore, id. 6, 10, 6, and absol. of sleep, id. 8, 6, 3: cum aures extremum semper exspectent in eoque acquiescant, Cic.

acquiro.full: ac-quīro (adqu.), sīvi, sītum, 3, v. a. quaero, to add to, to get or acquire (in addition), with ad or dat. (freq. in Cic.). Lit.: mihi quidem ipsi, quid est quod ad vitae fructum possit acquiri? Cic. Cat. 3, 12; 2, 8: vides quam omnis gratias non modo retinendas, sed etiam acquirendas putemus, but even new favor is to be acquired, id. Att. 1, 1; Sall. J. 13, 6; and poet.: viresque adquirit eundo, and gains (ever new and greater) strength in her course, Verg. A. 4, 175.— In gen. To get, obtain,

acquisitio.full: acquīsītĭo, ōnis, f. acquiro, acquisition. In abstr., Dig. 44, 4, 4, § 31; Tert. Exh. Cast. 12.— Concr., an increase, accession, Frontin. Aquaed. 10; 69 sq.

acra.full: acra, ōrum, n., also ae, f., = ἄκρα, a promontory or headland, App. de Mundo prooem.: Acra Iapygia, a promontory in Magna Graecia, Plin. 3, 11, 16, § 100.
acra.short: acra, ōrum, n., also ae, f., = ἄκρα, a promontory or headland, App.

acrae.full: Acrae, ārum, f., = Ἄκραι. A city of Sicily, on a lofty hill near Syracuse, now Palazzolo, Liv. 24, 36; Sil. 14, 206.— A town in the Chersonesus Taurica (Crimea), Plin. 4, 12, 26, § 86.

acraephia.full: Acraephĭa, ae, f., Ἀκραιφία, a town of Boeotia, now Kardhiza, Liv. 33, 29; Plin. 4, 8, 12, § 26.
acraephia.short: Acraephĭa, ae, f., Ἀκραιφία, a town of Boeotia, now Kardhiza, Liv.

acraeus.full: Acraeus, a, um, adj., = ἀκραῖος, dwelling on the heights; an epithet of Jupiter and of Juno, whose temples stood on heights, Liv 38, 2; 32, 23.
acraeus.short: Acraeus, a, um, adj., = ἀκραῖος, dwelling on the heights;

acragas1.full: Ăcrăgās, antis, m., Ἀκράγας (acc. Gr. Acraganta, Ov. F. 4, 475), a mountain on the S. W. coast of Sicily, and a city upon it; the city was also called Agrigentum, now Girgenti, Verg. A. 3, 703; Mel. 2, 7, 16; cf. Plin. 3, 8, 14, § 89 (v. Agrigentum); the birthplace of the philosopher Empedocles, who was hence called Acragantinus, Lucr. 1, 716.

acragas2.full: Acrăgas, antis, m., a celebrated graver (caelator), Plin. 33, 12, 55, § 154.
acragas2.short: Acrăgas, antis, m., a celebrated graver (caelator), Plin.

acratophorum.full: ăcrātŏphŏrum, i, n., = ἀκρατοφόρον, a vessel (a pitcher or flask) for holding unmixed wine, Varr. R. R. 1, 8, 5; Cic. Fin. 3, 4, 15.
acratophorum.short: ăcrātŏphŏrum, i, n., = ἀκρατοφόρον, a vessel (a pitcher or flask) for holding unmixed wine, Varr.

acredo.full: ācrēdo, ĭnis, f. fr. 2. acer, as dulcedo fr. dulcis, a sharp or pungent taste, Pall. 2, 15, 19: tollere, Plin. Val. 1, 25: humorum, Theod. Prisc. 1, 16.

acredula.full: ā^crēdŭla, ae, f., the name of an unknown bird, by which Cic. translates the ὀλολυγών of Aratus, Div. 1, 8, 14; acc. to some, the thrush or the owl, Auct. Carm. Phil. 15.
acredula.short: ā^crēdŭla, ae, f., the name of an unknown bird, by which Cic.

acriae.full: Acrĭae, ārum, f., Ἀκριαί, a town of Laconia, Liv. 35, 27, 3.
acriae.short: Acrĭae, ārum, f., Ἀκριαί, a town of Laconia, Liv.

acriculus.full: ācrĭcŭlus, a, um, adj. dim. [2. acer], somewhat sharp, testy: ille acriculus senex Zeno, Cic. Tusc. 3, 17, 38 (cf. acerbus, and the passage there quoted fr. Cic. N. D. 3, 31).

acridium.full: ācridĭum, ĭi, n., another name for the scammonia, acc. to Isid. Orig. 17, 9, 64.
acridium.short: ācridĭum, ĭi, n., another name for the scammonia, acc.

acrifolium.full: ācrĭfŏlĭum, ii, n. 2. acer + folium, an unknown tree of ill omen, Auct. ap. Macr. Sat. 2, 16.

acrillae.full: Acrillae, ārum, f., a town in Sicily, on the road from Syracuse to Agrigentum, Liv. 24, 35, 8.
acrillae.short: Acrillae, ārum, f., a town in Sicily, on the road from Syracuse to Agrigentum, Liv.

acrimonia.full: ācrĭmōnĭa, ae, f. 2. acer, sharpness or pungency (so far as it has a quickening, animating power, diff. fr. acerbitas, which desig. a disagreeable sharpness). Lit., of taste: si ulcus acrimoniam brassicae ferre non poterit, the pungency, irritation, smart, Cato R. R. 157, 5: dulcis cum quadam acrimonia, Plin. 24, 14, 78, § 128; cf. sinapis, id. 18, 13, 34, § 128 al.—Of smell, Plin. 27, 13, 109, § 133.— Fig., sharpness, acrimony, austerity of character, energy of acting: animi vivacitas, Non. 73,

acrisione.full: Ācrĭsĭōnē, es, f., Ἀκρισιώνη, the daughter of Acrisius, i. e. Danaë, Verg. Cat. 11, 33.
acrisione.short: Ācrĭsĭōnē, es, f., Ἀκρισιώνη, the daughter of Acrisius, i.

acrisioneus.full: Ācrĭsĭōnēus, a, um, adj., pertaining to Acrisius: arces, i. e. Argos, Ov. M. 5, 239: muri, i. e. Ardea, built by Danaë, the daughter of Acrisius, Sil. 1, 661; so, coloni, Verg. A. 7, 410 (where some improperly refer it to Danaë).
acrisioneus.short: Ācrĭsĭōnēus, a, um, adj., pertaining to Acrisius: arces, i.

acrisioniades.full: Ācrĭsĭōnĭădes, ae, m. patron., Ἀκρισιωνιάδης, a descendant of Acrisius, i. e. Perseus, son of Danaë, Ov. M. 5, 70.

acrisius.full: Ācrĭsĭus, ii, m., Ἀκρίσιος, King of Argos, son of Abas, and father of Danaë; unintentionally killed by his grandson, Perseus, Ov. M. 4, 608 sq.; Verg. A. 7, 372; Hor. C. 3, 16, 5 al.
acrisius.short: Ācrĭsĭus, ii, m., Ἀκρίσιος, King of Argos, son of Abas, and father of Danaë;

acritas1.full: ācrĭtas, ātis, f. 2. acer, i. q. acritudo, Gell. 13, 3, 2: vis veritatis atque acritas, Att. ap. Non. 493, 14 (Rib. Trag. Rel. p. 196).

acritas2.full: Ācrītās, ae, m., Ἀκρίτας, the most southerly promontory in Messenia, now Capo di Gallo, Mel. 2, 3, 8; 2, 7, 10; Plin. 4, 5, 7, § 15.
acritas2.short: Ācrītās, ae, m., Ἀκρίτας, the most southerly promontory in Messenia, now Capo di Gallo, Mel.

acritudo.full: ācrĭtūdo, ĭnis, f. 2. acer, the quality of acer, sharpness. Lit., of a fluid, Vitr. 2, 9, 12; 8, 3, 18 sq.— Trop. Liveliness, vivacity, force: vigor et acritudo populi Romani, Gell. 10, 27: haut quisquam potis est tolerare acritudinem, Att. ap. Fest. p. 356 Müll. (Rib. Trag. Rel. p. 196). — Harshness of character: morum, App. M. 9, 224.

acro.full: acro or acrōn, ōnis, m., = ἄκρων, the extremity of a thing; so of a member of the body, Veg. 2, 28, 17; 5, 65, 2; of the stem of a plant, Apic. 4, 4.
acro.short: acro or acrōn, ōnis, m., = ἄκρων, the extremity of a thing;

acroama.full: ācrŏāmă, ătis, n., = ἀκρόαμα.— Prop., that which is heard with pleasure, a gratification to the ear; as music or reading; esp. used for entertainment at meals, with music or reading, Plin. Ep. 6, 31, 13; Suet. Vesp. 19; Petron. Fragm. Tragun. p. 297.—Hence, meton. (like the plur. in Greek), the entertainer at table, by music (a performer) or by reading (a reader); also a buffoon: cum ex Themistocle quaererctur, quod acroama aut cujus vocem lubentissime audiret, Cic. Arch. 9: nemo in convivio eju
acroama.short: ācrŏāmă, ătis, n., = ἀκρόαμα.— Prop., that which is heard with pleasure, a gratification to the ear;

acroamatarius.full: ācrŏāmătārĭus, a, um, adj. acroama, belonging to a musical or reading entertainment: SER. ACROAMAT. GRAEC., i. e. serva acroamataria Graeca, Inscr. Orell. 2885.

acroamaticus.full: ācrŏāmătĭcus, a, um, adj., read in the old edd. of Gell. 20, 5, where the MSS. give, in the same sense, acroaticus, q. v.
acroamaticus.short: ācrŏāmătĭcus, a, um, adj., read in the old edd.

acroasis.full: ācrŏāsis, is, f., = ἀκρόασις (a hearing, a listening to), the discourse delivered before an assembly, public lecture (cf. the use of contio among Eng. and collegium among Germ. scholars, for discourse, etc.): ut eas vel in acroasi audeam legere, in a public lecture, Cic. Att. 15, 17, 2: Callias acroasin fecit, Vitr. 10, 22: plurimas acroases fecit, Suet. Gram. 2 (al. ἀκροάσεις).
acroasis.short: ācrŏāsis, is, f., = ἀκρόασις (a hearing, a listening to), the discourse delivered before an assembly, public lecture (cf.

acroaticus.full: ācrŏātĭcus, a, um, adj., = ἀκροατικός, designed for hearing only, esoteric (opp. ἐξωτερικός), in the Aristotelian philosophy, acc. to the interpreters, Gell. 20, 5.
acroaticus.short: ācrŏātĭcus, a, um, adj., = ἀκροατικός, designed for hearing only, esoteric (opp.

acroceraunia.full: Ācrŏcĕraunĭa, ōrum, n. fr. ἄκρις and κεραυνός; pr. Thunder-Heights, a very rocky promontory in Epirus, running out into the Ionian Sea, now Glossa, called by the Italians Linguetta (the mountain to which it belongs was called Ceraunii montes or Ceraunia; see this art.): infamīs scopulos Acroceraunia, Hor. C. 1, 3, 20; the same in sing.: promontorium Acroceraunium, Plin. 3, 11, 15, § 97; for any dangerous place: haec tibi sint Syrtes; haec Acroceraunia vita, Ov. R. Am. 739.

acrochordon.full: ăcrŏchordon, ŏnis, f., = ἀκροχορδών, a kind of wart, Cels. 5, 28, 14.
acrochordon.short: ăcrŏchordon, ŏnis, f., = ἀκροχορδών, a kind of wart, Cels.

acrocolefium.full: acrŏcōlēfĭum, ĭi, n., = ἀκροκωλήφιον, the upper part of the foot of a swine, Veg. 6, 1, 2.
acrocolefium.short: acrŏcōlēfĭum, ĭi, n., = ἀκροκωλήφιον, the upper part of the foot of a swine, Veg.

acrocolion.full: acrŏcōlĭon, ĭi, n., = ἀκροκώλιον, i. q. acro, Cael. Aur. Acut. 1, 11; cf. Veg. 2, 47, 1.

acrocorinthus.full: Ācrŏcŏrinthus (-us), i, f., Ἀκροκόρινθος, the citadel of Corinth, situated on a height, from which the two seas could be seen, the Aegean and Ionian, Mel. 2, 3, 7; Plin. 4, 4, 5, § 11; Liv. 33, 31 fin.; 34, 50, 8; Stat. Th. 7, 106.
acrocorinthus.short: Ācrŏcŏrinthus (-us), i, f., Ἀκροκόρινθος, the citadel of Corinth, situated on a height, from which the two seas could be seen, the Aegean and Ionian, Mel.

acrocorium.full: acrŏcŏrĭum, ii, n., a kind of onion, Plin. 19, 5, 30, § 95.
acrocorium.short: acrŏcŏrĭum, ii, n., a kind of onion, Plin.

acrolithus.full: acrŏlĭthus, a, um, adj., = ἀκρόλιθος (of stone at the extremity): statuae, statues whose extremities only consisted of marble, the remainder of wood, Treb. Poll. XXX. Tyr. c. 32 (in Vitr. 2, 8, 11 written as Greek); cf. Müll. Arch. § 48, 1; Winckelm. Hist. Art. 1, 2, 17.
acrolithus.short: acrŏlĭthus, a, um, adj., = ἀκρόλιθος (of stone at the extremity): statuae, statues whose extremities only consisted of marble, the remainder of wood, Treb.

acron.full: Ācron, ōnis, m. A king of the Caeninenses, who, in the war with the Romans on account of the rape of the Sabines, was slain by Romulus, Prop. 4, 10, 7.— A Greek slain by Mezentius, Verg. A. 10, 719.— Helenius Acron, a commentator on Terence, Horace, and perh. Persius; cf. Teuffel, Rom. Lit. II. § 370.

acronius.full: Acrōnĭus lacus, a part of Lake Constance, now the Ueberlingen Lake, Mel. 3, 2, 8.
acronius.short: Acrōnĭus lacus, a part of Lake Constance, now the Ueberlingen Lake, Mel.

acronoma.full: Acrŏnŏma saxa, an unknown place in Lower Italy, Cic. Att. 13, 40, 2.
acronoma.short: Acrŏnŏma saxa, an unknown place in Lower Italy, Cic.

acropodium.full: ăcrŏpŏdĭum, i, n. ἄκρος, extreme, and πούς, foot, the pedestal of a statue, Hyg. F. 88.

acror.full: ācror, ōris, m. 2. acer, = acritudo, Fulg. Cont. Verg. init.

acrota.full: Acrŏta, ae, m., king of the Albani, brother of Romulus Silvius, Ov. M. 14, 617.
acrota.short: Acrŏta, ae, m., king of the Albani, brother of Romulus Silvius, Ov.

acroteria.full: ăcrōtērĭa, ōrum, n., = ἀκρωτήρια, the projecting or extreme part of a thing. Of a harbor, Vitr. 5, 12.— In architecture, the projecting parts of a pediment, serving as a support for figures or statues, Vitr. 3, 5, 12 sq.; cf. Müll. Arch. § 284.
acroteria.short: ăcrōtērĭa, ōrum, n., = ἀκρωτήρια, the projecting or extreme part of a thing.

acrozymus.full: acrōzȳmus, a, um, adj., = ἀκρόζυμος, slightly leavened, Isid. Or. 20, 2, 15.
acrozymus.short: acrōzȳmus, a, um, adj., = ἀκρόζυμος, slightly leavened, Isid.

acta1.full: acta, ae, f., = ἀκτή, the sea-shore, as place of resort: in acta jacebat, Cic. Verr. 2, 5, 25; so id. Cael. 15; id. Att. 14, 8; id. Fam. 9, 6; Nep. Ages. 8, 2; Verg. A. 5, 613 al. (perh. also in Verg. Cul. 13; v. Sillig. N. cr.).
acta1.short: acta, ae, f., = ἀκτή, the sea-shore, as place of resort: in acta jacebat, Cic.

acta2.full: acta, ōrum, v. ago, P. a.

actaea.full: actaea, ae, f., a strong - smelling plant, herb Christopher, Actaea spicata, Linn., Plin. 27, 7, 26, § 43.
actaea.short: actaea, ae, f., a strong - smelling plant, herb Christopher, Actaea spicata, Linn., Plin.

actaeon.full: Actaeōn, ŏnis, m., Ἀκταίων, a grandson of Cadmus, who, having seen Diana bathing naked with her nymphs, was torn to pieces by his own dogs, Ov. M. 3, 230 sq.; ib. 720; id. Tr. 2, 105; Varr. R. R. 2, 9, 9; Hyg. F. 181 al.
actaeon.short: Actaeōn, ŏnis, m., Ἀκταίων, a grandson of Cadmus, who, having seen Diana bathing naked with her nymphs, was torn to pieces by his own dogs, Ov.

actaeus.full: Actaeus, a, um, adj., Ἀκταῖος, pertaining to Attica, Attic, Athenian: in Actaeo Aracyntho, Verg. E. 2, 24 (as being on the border of Attica): arces, of Athens, Ov. M. 2, 720; fratres, i. e. Clytos and Butes, ib. 7, 681: mel Hymetti, Col. 10, 386: imbres, a rain of honey, Stat. Th. 4, 453. —Hence, subst.: Actaei, ōrum, m., the inhabitants of Attica, Nep. Thras. 2, 1.— Actaea, ae, f., a female Athenian; of Orithyia, Ov. M. 6, 711.
actaeus.short: Actaeus, a, um, adj., Ἀκταῖος, pertaining to Attica, Attic, Athenian: in Actaeo Aracyntho, Verg.

acte1.full: actē, ēs, f., = ἀκτῆ, a plant, perh. = ebulum, Plin. 26, 11, 73, § 120; Ap. Herb. 91.
acte1.short: actē, ēs, f., = ἀκτῆ, a plant, perh.

acte2.full: Actē, ēs, f., = Ἀκτή. Lit., coastland or maritime country; hence, the earlier name for Attica, the province of Middle Greece, in which Athens was situated, Plin. 4, 7, 11; Gell. 14, 6.— One of the Horae, Hyg. F. 183.— A concubine of Nero, Suet. Ner. 28; Tac. A. 13, 12; Inscr. Orell. 735; 2885.

actiacus.full: Actĭăcus, a um, adj. Actium, relating to Actium: victoria, at Actium, Suet. Aug. 18: ludi, the games which Augustus revived at Actium in honor of his victory, id. Tib. 6: Phoebus, who had a temple here, Ov. M. 13, 715: acquor, id. H. 15, 166: legiones, which had fought at Actium, Tac. A. 1, 42.

actias.full: Actĭăs, ădis, f. [Acte.] Attic, Athenian, Verg. G. 4, 463.— [Actium.] Of Actium: Cleopatra, conquered at Actium by Augustus, Stat. S. 3, 2, 120.

actinophoroe.full: actīnŏphŏroe, adj. (Gr. nom. plur.), = ἀκτινοφόροι (bearing rays), epithet of the cochloe, Plin. 32, 11, 53, § 147, v. Jan ad h. l.

actinosus.full: actīnōsus, a, um ἀκτίς; pr. full of rays, hence, glorious: ecclesia, Ambros. in Psa. 41.

actio.full: actĭo, ōnis, f. ago, a doing, performing, acting, action, act. In gen.: non modo deos spoliat motu et actione divina, sed etiam homines inertes efficit, Cic. N. D. 1, 37; 2, 16; virtutis laus omnis in actione consistit, id. Off. 1, 6; id. Fin. 5, 19, 54.—With subject. gen.: ad eas res parandas, quibus actio vitae continetur, active, practical life, id. Off. 1, 5: corporis, id. Div. 1, 32: mentis, id. N. D. 1, 17; and with object. gen.: itaque nec actio rerum illarum (the public performance of th

actito.full: actĭto, āre, v. freq. [ago], to act or be employed in, often or much (only of judicial or dramatic action): multas privatas causas, Cic. Brut. 70: tragoedias, id. Rep. 4, 35: so Tac. H. 3, 62; Suet. Galb. 3; cf. Gell. 9, 6.

actium.full: Actĭum, i, n. A promontory and town in Epirus, on the Ambracian Gulf (now La Punta), where Augustus conquered Antony and Cleopatra, 31 B. C., and, in commemoration of it, repaired the temple of Apollo, which existed there, and revived the Actian games, Mel. 2, 3, 10; Plin. 4, 1, 2, § 5; Cic. Fam. 16, 6.— A harbor in Corcyra, Cic. Att. 7, 2, 3.

actiuncula.full: actĭuncŭla, ae, f. dim. actio, a short judicial harangue, Plin. Ep. 9, 15.

actius1.full: Actĭus, a, um, adj. poet. for Actiacus, pertaining to Actium: ludi, Verg. A. 3, 280; 8, 675; 704; Hor. Ep. 1, 18, 61; Phoebus, as having a temple at Actium (v. Actium), Prop. 4, 6, 67.

actius2.full: Actĭus, i, m., a proper name, Suet. Tib. 47.
actius2.short: Actĭus, i, m., a proper name, Suet.

active.full: actīve, adv., v. the foll. art. fin.

activus.full: actīvus, a, um, adj. ago. Active: philosophia, practical (opp. to contemplativa): philosophia et contemplativa est et activa; spectat simul agitque, Sen. Ep. 95, 10: (opp. to spectativus) thesin a causa sic distinguunt, ut illa sit spectativae partis, haec activae, Quint. 3, 5, 11: (rhetorice) quia maximus ejus usus actu continetur, dicatur activa, id. 2, 18, 5.— In gramm.: verba activa, which designate transitive action (opp. neutra or intransitiva), Charis. p. 138; Diom. p. 326 P. al.—Adv.: ac

actor1.full: actor, ōris, m. id.. One who drives or moves something: pecoris actor, Ov. H. 1, 95: habenae, a slinger, Stat. Ach. 2, 419.— In gen., he who does any thing, a doer or performer (cf. ago, II.). In gen. of every kind of action: ut illum efficeret oratorem verborum actoremque rerum, Cic. de Or. 3, 15, 57 (a translation of the Homer. πρηκτῆρα ἔργων, Il. 9, 443): Cato dux, auctor, actor rerum illarum fuit, id. Sest. 28 fin.; so Caes. B. C. 1, 26; Nep. Att. 3, 2 al.— In judicial lang., one who brings

actor2.full: Actor, ŏris, m. A companion of Aeneas, Verg. A. 9, 500.— An Auruncan, ib. 12, 94; 96.—Hence, Actŏ-rĭdes, ae, patron. m., son or grandson of Actor: his son, Menoetius, Ov. F. 2, 39; his grandson, Patroclus, Ov. Tr. 1, 9, 29; id. M. 13, 273; Erithos, id. ib. 5, 79.—In plur.: Actŏrĭdae, i. e. Eurytus and Cleatus, sons of Actor, King of Phthia, id. ib. 8, 308.

actorius1.full: actōrĭus, a, um, adj., i. q. activus, Tert. An. 14.

actorius2.full: Actōrĭus, ĭi, m., a Roman name, Suet. Caes. 9 al.
actorius2.short: Actōrĭus, ĭi, m., a Roman name, Suet.

actrix.full: actrix, īcis, f. actor. A female plaintiff, Cod. Th. 7, 16, 41.— A stewardess, Inscr. Murat. 913, 6.

actualis.full: actŭālis, e, adj. id., active, practical, Macr. Somn. Scip. 2, 17.—Adv.: ac-tŭālĭter, actively, Myth. Vatic. vol. 3, p. 181 ed. Bod.

actuariolum.full: actŭārĭŏlum, i, n. dim. actuarius, a small, swift vessel impelled by oars, row-boat, barge, Cic. Att. 10, 11, 4; 16, 3, 6; 16, 6, 1.

actuarius1.full: actŭārĭus, a, um., adj. ago that which is easily moved, swift, agile: navis, a swift sailer, Caes. B. G. 5, 1; Sall. Fragm. ap. Non. 535, 1, and Sisenn. ib. 534, 33; Liv. 25, 30: navigium, Caes. B. C. 1, 27; cf.: actuariae naves sunt, quae velis simul et remis aguntur, Isid. Or. 19, 1, 24: also, abs. actŭāria, ae, f., or actŭārium, ĭi, n., the same, Cic. Att. 5, 9; cf. Gell. 10, 25: limes, a road 12 feet wide between fields, Hyg. de Lim. p. 151: canes, hunting-dogs, hounds, acc. to Vel. Long. 22

actuarius2.full: actŭārĭus, ĭi (written by some actarius, to distinguish it from the preceding, Vel. Long. 2234 P., and so found in Inscr. Grut. 260; ap. Henzen, 6284), sc. scriba, m. 2. actus, II. B. 1.. A short-hand writer, Suet. Caes. 55; Sen. Ep. 33, 9; cf. Lips. Tac. Ann. 5, 4.— One who writes out accounts, Petr. 53.
actuarius2.short: actŭārĭus, ĭi (written by some actarius, to distinguish it from the preceding, Vel.

actuose.full: actŭōse, adv., see the foll. art. fin.

actuosus.full: actŭōsus, a, um, adj. actus, full of activity, very active (with the access. idea of zeal, subjective impulse; diff. from industrius, which refers more to the means by which an object is attained, Doed. Syn. 1, 123): virtus actuosa (est), et deus vester nihil agens expers virtutis (est), Cic. N. D. 1, 40; so id. Or. 36, 125; Sen. Ep. 39.—Hence, acc. to Fest. s. v. actus, p. 15, subst., an actor or dancer.—Adv.: actŭōse, in a lively manner, with activity, Cic. de Or. 3, 26, 102.

actus1.full: actus, a, um, P. a., from ago.

actus2.full: actus, ūs, m. ago. The moving or driving of an object, impulse, motion: linguae actu, Pacuv. ap. Non. 506, 17: mellis constantior est natura ... et cunctantior actus, Lucr. 3, 192: levi admonitu, non actu, inflectit illam feram, by driving, Cic. Rep. 2, 40: fertur in abruptum magno mons inprobus actu, Verg. A. 12, 687: pila contorsit violento spiritus actu, Sen. Agam. 432; hominum aut animalium actu vehiculum adhibemus, Cael. Aurel. Tard. 1, 1.— Hence, Transf. The right of driving cattle through

actutum.full: actūtum, adv. ab actu (as astutus from astu; or with tum as enclitic, in der Handlung da, Corss. Ausspr. II. 849), id est, celeritate, Prisc. 1013 P.; so Hand, s. v. who explains: uno actu, nulla re intercedente; Lindem. de Adv. Lat. Spec. 4, p. 17, regards it as formed from an obs. vb. actuo, with the meaning cum multo actu, non segniter; cf.: ait et dicto citius placat, qs. while in the act of speaking, Verg. A. 1, 142; cf. Hor. S. 2, 2, 80; immediately, quickly, instantly (in Plaut. very ofte

acuarius.full: ăcŭārĭus, i, m. 1. acus, one who makes needles or pins, Inscr. Orell. 4139.

acula.full: ăcŭla, ae, f. dim. id., a little needle, acc. to Cledon, p. 1896: frigit fricantem corpus acula (lect. dub.), Att. Rib. Trag. Rel. p. 195.

aculeatus.full: ăcūlĕātus, a, um, adj. aculeus, furnished with stings or prickles, thorny, prickly. Lit., of animals and plants: animalia, Plin. 20, 22, 91: bruchus, Vulg. Jer. 51, 27: herbae, Plin. 24, 19, 119: ictus, a puncture made by a sting, Plin. 20, 21, 84, § 223.— Fig. Stinging, pointed, sharp: istaec ... aculeata sunt, animum fodicant, Plaut. Bacch. 1, 1, 30: litterae, Cic. Att. 14, 18, 1.— Subtle, cunning: contorta et aculeata sophismata, Cic. Ac. 2, 24.

aculeo.full: Ăcūlĕo, ōnis, m., a Roman cognomen in the gens Furia, Liv. 38, 55, 4.—C. Aculeo, a famous lawyer, friend of L. Licinius Crassus, Cic. de Or. 1, 43, 191; 2, 1, 2 al.
aculeo.short: Ăcūlĕo, ōnis, m., a Roman cognomen in the gens Furia, Liv.

aculeolus.full: ăcūlĕŏlus, i, m. dim. aculeus, a little needle or pin: aculeolos in cochleare tulit, an old reading in Mart. 8, 71, where now acu levius vix cochleare, is read.

aculeus.full: ăcūlĕus, i, m. acc. to Prisc. 618 P. dim. from 1. acus, with the gender changed, like diecula fr. dies, cf. Val. Prob. 1463 P., a sting. Lit. Of animals: apis aculeum sine clamore ferre non possumus, Cic. Tusc. 2, 22; so Plin. 11, 17, 17: neparum, Cic. Fin. 5, 15 al.—Also, the spur of fowls, Col. 8, 2, 8: locustarum, Vulg. Apoc. 9, 10.— Of plants, a spine or prickle: spinarum, Plin. 13, 9, 19: carduorum, id. 20, 23, 99.— Of an arrow or dart, the point, Liv. 38, 21, 11.— Fig., a sting. Of a sharp

acumen.full: ăcūmĕn, ĭnis, n. acuo, a point to prick or sting with; diff. fr. cacumen, which designates merely the summit or extremity of a thing, Doed. Syn. 2, 108. Lit.: tum clupei resonunt et ferri stridit acumen, Enn. ap. Prisc. p. 838 P. (Ann. v. 369 ed. Vahl.): coni, Lucr. 4, 431: nasi, id. 6, 1193 (i.e. the pointed contraction of the nose before death; cf. Bentl. ad Hor. S. 1, 3, 29): stili, Cic. de Or. 1, 33: ferrum Diana volanti abstulerat jaculo: lignum sine acumine venit, Ov. M. 8, 353; 3, 84.—Hen

acuminarius.full: ăcūmĭnārĭus, a, um, adj. acumen, good for sharpening: mola, for sharpening weapons, Schol. ad Stat. Th. 3.

acumino.full: ăcūmĭno, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. id., to make pointed, to sharpen, in verb finit.: contextum spinae acuminavit in caudam, Lact. Opif. 7, 7.—Part. perf.: telum culicis, Plin. 11, 2, 1: cornu lunae, id. 18, 35, 79: corpus, id. 11, 24, 28.

acuo.full: ăcŭo, ui, ūtum, 3, v. a. (part. fut. acuturus, not used) [cf. 2. acer], to make sharp or pointed, to sharpen, whet. Lit.: ne stridorem quidem serrae audiunt, cum acuitur, Cic. Tusc. 1, 40; so, ferrum, Verg. A. 8, 386; Hor. C. 1, 2, 21: enses, Ov. M. 15, 776: gladium, Vulg. Deut. 32, 41: sagittas, id. Jer. 51, 11.—Poet.: fulmen, Lucr. 6, 278: dentes, Hor. C. 3, 20, 10; cf. Tib. 4, 3, 3.— Trop. First, of the tongue, qs. to whet, i. e. to sharpen, exercise, improve: acuere linguam exercitatione dic

acupedius.full: acūpĕdius, dicebatur, cui praecipuum erat in currendo acumen pedum, swift of foot, Paul. ex Fest. p. 9 Müll. [qs. acer + pes; cf. Gr. ὀξύπους, ὠκύπους].
acupedius.short: acūpĕdius, dicebatur, cui praecipuum erat in currendo acumen pedum, swift of foot, Paul.

acus1.full: ăcus, ūs, f. cf. 2. acer. A needle or pin, as being pointed, both for common use and ornament:quasarcinatrix veletiam ornatrix utitur, Paul. ex Fest. p. 9 Müll. Lit.: mirabar vulnus, quod acu punctum videtur, Cic. Mil. 24.—Hence, acu pingere, to embroider, Verg. A. 9, 582; Ov. M. 6, 23; cf. Plin. 8, 48, § 191; Isid. Orig. 19, 22, 22.—Esp. a hair-pin: figat acus tortas sustineatque comas, Mart. 14, 24: foramen acūs, the eye of a needle, Vulg. Matt. 19, 24.—Also, a surgeon's needle, a probe, Cels.

acus2.full: ăcus, ĕris, n. (also, ūs, f., v. 1. acus, III.) [kindred with acus, ūs, Goth. ahana, old Norse agn, old Germ. Agana], = ἄχυρον, the husk of grain and of pulse; chaff, Cato, R. R. 54, 2; Varr. R. R. 1, 52; 57; 3, 9, 8.

acus3.full: ăcus, i, m. 1. acus, a kind of sea-fish with a pointed snout, the hornpike or gar-pike (Gr. βελόνη): acus sive belone unus piscium, etc., Plin. 9, 51, 76, § 166: et satius tenues ducere credis acos, Mart. 10, 37, 6; cf. Plin. 32, 11, 53, § 145, where belonae again occurs. (Some read una for unus in the passage from Plin., and acūs for acos in Mart., as if these forms belonged to 1. acus.)

acusilas.full: Ăcūsĭlas, ae, m. from Ἀκουσίλαος, an Argive historian, Cic. de Or. 2, 12, 53.

acutalis.full: ăcūtālis, e, adj. acutus, pointed: terminus, Front. Col. p. 132 Goes.

acutarus.full: ăcūtārus (for acutarius), a, um, adj. id., that sharpens instruments: acutarus taber, Ins. ap. Henzen. 7216.

acutatus.full: ăcūtātus, a, um, adj. id., sharpened: sagittæ, Veg. 1, 22, 4.

acute.full: ăcūte, adv., v. acuo, P. a. fin.

acutor.full: ăcūtor, ōris, m. acuo, one that sharpens, a sharpener, Not. Tir. p. 120.

acutule.full: ăcūtŭle, adv., see the foll. art. fin.

acutulus.full: ăcūtŭlus, a, um, adj. dim. [acutus], somewhat pointed, acute, or subtile: conclusiones, * Cic. N. D. 3, 7, 18: doctores, Gell. 17, 5.—Adv.: ăcūtŭle, somewhat sharply, Aug. Conf. 3, 7.

acutum.full: ăcūtum, adv., v. acuo, P. a.

acutus.full: ăcūtus, a, um, v. acuo, P. a.

acva.full: acva and acvarivs, in Inscrr. for aqua and aquarius.

acylos.full: ăcўlos, i, f., = ἄκυλος, the acorn of the holm-oak (ilex), Plin. 16, 6, 8, § 19 (cf. Hom. Od. 10, 242).
acylos.short: ăcўlos, i, f., = ἄκυλος, the acorn of the holm-oak (ilex), Plin.

acyrologia.full: ăcȳrŏlŏgĭa, ae, f., = ἀκυρολογία, in rhetoric, an impropriety of speech; e. g.: sperare for timere, Serv. ad Verg. A. 4, 419 (in pure Lat. improprium or impropria dictio is used instead of it: (quod proprietati est contrarium) id apud nos improprium, ἄκυρον apud Graecos vocatur; quale est tantum sperare dolorem; Quint. 8, 2, 3; cf. Don. ap. Lind. Corp. Gr. 1, 28; Charis. p. 242; Diom. 2, p. 444).
acyrologia.short: ăcȳrŏlŏgĭa, ae, f., = ἀκυρολογία, in rhetoric, an impropriety of speech;

ad.full: ad, prep. with acc. (from the fourth century after Christ written also at; Etrusc. suf. -a; Osc. az; Umbr. and Old Lat. ar, as in Eug. Tab., in S. C. de Bacch., as arveho for adveho; arfuerunt, arfuisse, for adfuerunt, etc.; arbiter for adbiter; so, ar me advenias, Plant. Truc. 2, 2, 17; cf. Prisc. 559 P.; Vel. Long. 2232 P.; Fabretti, Glos. Ital. col. 5) [cf. Sanscr. adhi; Goth. and Eng. at; Celt. pref. ar, as armor, i.e. ad mare; Rom. a]. As antith. to ab (as in to ex), in a progressive order

adactio.full: ădactĭo, ōnis, f. adigo, a forcing or bringing to: ad legitimam juris jurandi adactionem, to the taking of an oath, Liv. 22, 38, where just before we find: milites jurejurando adacti.

adactus1.full: ădactus, a, um, Part. of adigo.

adactus2.full: ădactus, ūs, m. adigo, a forcing or bringing to or together.—Hence, poet., of the teeth, a biting, a bite: dentis adactus, Lucr. 5, 1330.

adad.full: Adad or Adădus, i, m., name of the supreme god of the Assyrians, Macr. Sat. 1, 32.
adad.short: Adad or Adădus, i, m., name of the supreme god of the Assyrians, Macr.

adadunephros.full: adadūnĕphros = Ἀδάδου ϝεφρός (Adad's kidney), i, m. Adad, a certain precious stone, Plin. 37, 11, 71, § 186.
adadunephros.short: adadūnĕphros = Ἀδάδου ϝεφρός (Adad's kidney), i, m.

adaequatio.full: ădaequātĭo, ōnis, f. adaequo, a making equal, an adjusting, adapting, Tert. ad Nat. 1, 1; Sol. 1, where more correctly peraequatio.

adaeque.full: ăd-aeque, adv., in like manner as, equally, so (most. ante- and post-class.; not in Cic.; and in Plautus always with the negatives nemo, numquam, neque, nullus, etc., by means of which the clause acquires a compar. signif.; hence, sometimes a compar. abl., and even a pleonastic compar., is allowed): numquam, ecastor, ullo die risi adaeque, Plaut. Cas. 5, 1, 3: neque munda adaeque es, ut soles, id. Cist. 1, 1, 57; so id. Cas. 3, 5, 45; id. Capt. 5, 4, 2; id. Mil. Gl. 3, 1, 180: quo nemo adaeque a
adaeque.short: ăd-aeque, adv., in like manner as, equally, so (most.

adaequo.full: ăd-aequo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. and n. Act. To make equal to, to equalize, to level with; hence, In Cic. usually with cum (cf. aequare cum, Verg. A. 1, 193): qui cum virtute fortunam adaequavit, Cic.
