ambitiosus.full: ambĭtĭōsus, a, um, adj. ambitio. (Very rare and mostly poet.) Going round, encompassing; poet., embracing, twining round: lascivis hederis ambitiosior, Hor. C. 1, 36, 20 (cf.: undique ambientibus ramis, Curt. 4, 7, 16).—Of a river, making circuits, having many windings: Jordanes amnis ambitiosus, Plin. 5, 15, 15, § 71.— Of oratorical ornament, excessive, superfluous: vir bonus ambitiosa recidet Ornamenta, Hor. A. P. 447.— Transf. That asks for a thing fawningly; esp., that solicits the favor, go

ambitor.full: ambītor, ōris, m. ambio. Lit., a candidate (post-class.), Lampr. Alex. Sev. 28.— Trop.: aeternae laudis, Paul. Nol. Ep. 13, 16.

ambitudo.full: ambĭtūdo, ĭnis, f. 2. ambitus, period of revolution: reditūs, App. Trism. 31, p. 258.

ambitui.full: Ambitŭi, ōrum, m., a people in Galatia, Plin. 5, 32, 42, § 146.
ambitui.short: Ambitŭi, ōrum, m., a people in Galatia, Plin.

ambitus1.full: ambītus, a, um, Part. of ambio.

ambitus2.full: ambĭtus, ūs, m. ambio. Lit. A going round, a moving round about, a revolution: cum se octo ambitus ad idem caput rettulerint, Cic. Tim. 9: aquae per amoenos ambitus agros, Hor. A. P. 17 (cf. ambio, II. A.): alligata mutuo ambitu (i. e. amplexu) corpora, Petr. 132: ambitu breviore luna currit quam sol, Plin. 2, 23, 21, § 86: saeculorum, Tac. A. 6, 28: verborum (i. e. ambages), Suet. Tib. 71.— Transf. Abstr. pro concr., a circuit, circle, circumference, periphery, edge of a circular object: ambitu

ambivareti.full: Ambĭvarēti, Ambĭlarēti, or Am-blŭarēti, ōrum, m., a people of Gallia Celtica, in the neighborhood of the Ambarri, Caes. B. G. 7, 75; 7, 90.
ambivareti.short: Ambĭvarēti, Ambĭlarēti, or Am-blŭarēti, ōrum, m., a people of Gallia Celtica, in the neighborhood of the Ambarri, Caes.

ambivariti.full: Ambĭvarīti, ōrum, m., a people of Gallia Belgica, near the Meuse, in the region of the present Breda, Caes. B. G. 4, 9.
ambivariti.short: Ambĭvarīti, ōrum, m., a people of Gallia Belgica, near the Meuse, in the region of the present Breda, Caes.

ambivium.full: ambĭ-vĭum, ii, n. via, a double way, a place where two roads meet: hic in ambivio navem conscendimus palustrem, Varr. ap. Non. 451, 2.

ambivius.full: Ambĭvĭus, ii, m., L. Turpio. A very distinguished actor in the time of Terence, in most of whose pieces he acted, v. Didascal. Fab. And., Eun., Heaut., Hec., and Phorm.; cf. Cic. Sen. 14; Varr. L. L. 7, 30; Symm. Ep. 1, 25.— Ambĭvĭus, ii, m., a keeper of a restaurant, Cic. Clu. 59, 163; perh. also Col. 12, 4, 2.

ambo.full: ambō^, bae, bo, num. (nom. plur. ambo for ambae, Plaut. Merc. 2, 1, 7; acc. plur. orig. ambo, analog. to the Gr. ἄμφω, but from the adj. use of the word ambos arose; acc. ambo is found in Plaut. Am. 1, 2, 8; 5, 1, 67; id. As. 3, 3, 121; id. Curc. 5, 3, 14; id. Cist. 2, 1, 49; id. Ep. 2, 2, 19; id. Bacch. 4, 8, 19; 5, 2, 69; id. Most. 3, 2, 140; id. Rud. 3, 5, 7; Afran. ap. Charis. p. 96 P.; Cic. (who never uses ambos) Fam. 5, 8; 9, 13; Caes. (who never uses ambos) B. C. 1, 48; Verg. (who never u

ambracia.full: Ambrăcĭa, ae, f., = Ἀμβρακία, A town in the south of Epirus, upon the gulf of the same name, now Arta, Plin. 4, 1, 1, § 4; Cic. Ep. ad Brut. 6; Caes. B. C. 3, 36; Liv. 38, 4.—Hence, Ambrăcĭ-ensis, e, adj., Ambracian, Liv. 38, 43.— Subst. plur., the inhabitants of Ambracia, Liv. 38, 43.—† Ambrăcĭōtēs, ae, m., = Ἀμβρακιώτης, Ambracian; hence, vinum ... Ambraciotes (v. abrotonites), Plin. 14, 7, 9, § 76.— Ambrăcĭus, a, um, adj., Ambracian (more freq. than Ambraciensis), Ov. H. 15, 164; Plin. 4, 1,
ambracia.short: Ambrăcĭa, ae, f., = Ἀμβρακία, A town in the south of Epirus, upon the gulf of the same name, now Arta, Plin.

ambrices.full: ambrĭces: regulae, quae transversae asseribus et tegulis interponuntur, Paul. ex Fest. p. 16 Müll.
ambrices.short: ambrĭces: regulae, quae transversae asseribus et tegulis interponuntur, Paul.

ambrosia1.full: ambrŏsĭa, ae, f., = ἀμβροσία. Lit., ambrosia, the food of the gods (as nectar was their drink): non enim ambrosiā deos aut nectare laetari arbitror, Cic. Tusc. 1, 26, 65; Ov. P. 1, 10, 11: Suaviolum dulci dulcius ambrosiā, Cat. 99, 2.—Hence: orator ambrosiā alendus, prov. once in Cic., qs. a god among orators, of a distinguished orator (opp. faenum esse), Cic. de Or. 2, 57.— Also food for the steeds of the gods: equos ambrosiae suco saturos, Ov. M. 2, 120; 4, 215 (acc. to Hom. Il. 5, 368 and 369

ambrosiacus.full: ambrŏsĭăcus, a, um, adj. ambrosia, ambrosial: ambrosiaca vitis, on account of the sweetness of its grapes, Plin. 14, 3, 4, § 40.

ambrosie.full: Ambrŏsiē, ēs, or -a, ae, f., = Ἀμβροσίη, Ambrosia, daughter of Attas and Pleione, one of the Hyades, Hyg. Fab. 182 and 192; id. poët. Astr. 2, 21.
ambrosie.short: Ambrŏsiē, ēs, or -a, ae, f., = Ἀμβροσίη, Ambrosia, daughter of Attas and Pleione, one of the Hyades, Hyg.

ambrosius1.full: ambrŏsĭus, a, um, adj., = ἀμβρόσιος, immortal, divine, ambrosial (syn.: immortalis, divinus), in gen., all that pertains to the gods, and their prerogatives and endowments; hence, an epithet for every thing lovely, pleasant, sweet, etc. (in gen. only poet.): comae, Verg. A. 1, 403; so Stat. Th. 9, 731: dapes, Mart. 8, 39: suci, Sil. 7, 210; Col. 10, 408: sinus, Claud. Nupt. Hon. et Mar. 110: corpus, App. M. 8, p. 205, 26: pedes, id. ib. 11, p. 258, 39: color, id. ib. 10, p. 254, 4: nectar, Prud.
ambrosius1.short: ambrŏsĭus, a, um, adj., = ἀμβρόσιος, immortal, divine, ambrosial (syn.: immortalis, divinus), in gen., all that pertains to the gods, and their prerogatives and endowments;

ambrosius2.full: Ambrŏsĭus, i, m., a celebrated Church father of the fourth century, archbishop of Milan.
ambrosius2.short: Ambrŏsĭus, i, m., a celebrated Church father of the fourth century, archbishop of Milan.

ambrysus.full: Ambrȳsus or Ambryssos, i, f., = Ἄμβρυσος or Ἄμβρυσσος, a small town in Phocis, now Dhistomo, Liv. 32, 18; Plin. 4, 3, 4, § 8.
ambrysus.short: Ambrȳsus or Ambryssos, i, f., = Ἄμβρυσος or Ἄμβρυσσος, a small town in Phocis, now Dhistomo, Liv.

ambubaia.full: ambūbāĭa, ae, usu. in the plur., am-būbāĭae, ārum, f. from Syr. , plur. = tibia, Vulg. 1 Cor. 14, 7, a class of Syrian girls in Rome, who supported themselves by their music and immorality: ambubajarum collegia, * Hor. S. 1, 2, 1: ambubajarum ministeria, Suet. Ner. 27.—In sing., Petr. 74, 13.

ambubeia.full: ambubēĭa, ae, f., wild succory or endive, Cels. 2, 30; Plin. 20, 8, 29, § 73; cf. id. 20, 8, 29, 1 ind. 20, 30, p. 68 Sillig.
ambubeia.short: ambubēĭa, ae, f., wild succory or endive, Cels.

ambulacrum.full: ambŭlācrum, i, n. ambulo, a walk planted with trees, commonly near a house (only ante-and post-class. for the class. ambulatio), Fest. p. 18: senex Gynaeceum aedificare volt hic in suis Et balineas et ambulacrum et porticum, Plaut. Most. 3, 2, 69: longa et mollia ambulacra, * Gell. 1, 2, 2; Pall. 1, 18, 2.

ambulatilis.full: ambŭlātĭlis, e, adj. id., walking about; hence, movable, Vitr. 10, 13.

ambulatio.full: ambŭlātĭo, ōnis, f. id., a walking about, a walk (only in prose, oftenest in Cic.). Lit.: ambulationem pomeridianam conficere in Academiā, Cic. Fin. 5, 1: compitaliciae, id. Att. 2, 3: ventum est in ambulationem, id. de Or. 1, 7, 26: recta, flexuosa, Cels. 1, 2.—Of the orator on the platform: conveniet etiam ambulatio quaedam propter immodicas laudationum moras, Quint. 11, 3, 126.—Hence, Transf., concr., a walk, a place for walking, a promenade (usu. near a dwelling; either covered or open): amb

ambulatiuncula.full: ambŭlātĭuncŭla, ae, dim. f. [ambulatio], a short walk (perh. only in the foll. passages of Cic.). Lit., Cic. Fam. 2, 12. —And, Concr., a small place for walking: tecta, Cic. Att. 13, 29.

ambulator.full: ambŭlātor, ōris, m. ambulo, one that walks about, i.e., An idler, lounger: vilicus ne sit ambulator, Cato, R. R. 5, 2 (cf. id. ib. 5, 2: minus licebit ambulare); Col. 1, 8, 7.—* A pedlar, hawker: Transtiberinus, Mart. 1, 42 (not found elsewhere).

ambulatorius.full: ambŭlātōrĭus, a, um, adj. ambulator, that moves about (rare; never in Cic.); hence, Of machines which can be moved to and fro. movable: praeterea alias (so. turres) ambulatorias totidem tabulatorum confixerant, movable towers with an equal number of stories, Auct. B. Alex. 2 Moeb.; Vitr. 10, 19; Plin. 21, 14, 47, § 80.—Hence, trop., of the will, wavering, fickle, changeable: voluntas, Dig. 24, 1, 32; and of other things: actio, a cause that passes from one to another, Cod. Just. 6, 2, 22.—* Suit

ambulatrix.full: ambŭlātrix, īcis, f. ambulator, she that walks about, a female lounger, etc.: vilica ne ambulatrix siet, Cato, R. R. 143, 1.

ambulatura.full: ambŭlātūra, ae, f. ambulo, a walking, a pace, step, amble; only of horses (Fr. l'amble; Ital. ambio, ambiadura), Veg. 6, 6, 6; 6, 6, 7; 2, 5, 2.

ambulatus.full: ambŭlātus, ūs, m. id., walking: Christus scitur ambulatum dedisse contractis, i. e. power to walk, Arn. 1, p. 28.

ambulo.full: ambŭlo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. n. regarded by Doed. as a sort of dim. of ambio, but better regarded as comp. of am- and the root of βαίνω, beto, -bito, baculum = βάκπρον, vado, venio; Sanscr. gā = go; Germ. gehen; Engl. go. Curtius. Lit. In gen., to go about, to walk: cum illā neque cubat neque ambulat, Plaut. Bacch. 4, 8, 56: si non ubi sedeas locus est, est ubi ambules, id. Capt. prol. 12: quem ad modum quis ambulet, sedeat, Cic. Fin. 5, 17, 47: sedetur, ambulatur, Varr. L. L. 6, 1, p. 72 Müll.: amb

amburbale.full: amburbāle, is, n. (sc. sacrificium), i. q. amburbium, Serv. ad Verg. E. 3, 77; cf. the two foll. articles.

amburbiales.full: amburbĭāles hostiae, the victims which were led round the city of Rome, Paul. ex Fest. p. 5 Müll.
amburbiales.short: amburbĭāles hostiae, the victims which were led round the city of Rome, Paul.

amburbium.full: amb-urbĭum, ii, n. urbs, the expiatory procession round the city of Rome, at which sacrifices were offered (v. the preced.); Serv. ad Verg. E. 3, 77; Paul. ex Fest. p. 17 Müll.: lustrata urbs, cantata carmina, amburbium celebratum, ambarvalia promissa, Vop. Aur. 20 (described in Luc. 1, 592 sq.).

amburo.full: amb-ūro, ussi, ustum, 3, v. a., to burn around, to scorch (opp. exurere, to burn entirely up); also, with an extension of the idea, to burn wholly up, to consume (most freq. in part. perf.; class.). Lit. Hadrianus vivus exustus est: Verres sociorum ambustus incendio, tamen ex illā flammā periculoque evasit, Cic. Verr. 2, 1, 27: Herculis corpus ambustum, id. Sest. 68, 143: terret ambustus Phaëthon avaras spes, Hor. C. 4, 11, 25 al.—So Cicero jestingly calls the tribune of the people Munacius Plan

ambustio.full: ambustĭo, ōnis, f. amburo = ambustum, a burn: eruptionibus, ambustionibus (medetur myrteum oleum), Plin. 23, 4, 44, § 87.

ambustulatus.full: ambustŭlātus, a, um, adj. id., burned or scorched around, roasted: Teque ambustulatum obiciam magnis avibus pabulum, Plaut. Rud. 3, 4, 65.

ameci.full: ămēci and ămēcae (a different orthography for amici and amicae), Paul. ex Fest. p. 15 Müll.
ameci.short: ămēci and ămēcae (a different orthography for amici and amicae), Paul.

amelas.full: Amelas, a town in Lycia, Plin. 5, 27, 28, § 101.
amelas.short: Amelas, a town in Lycia, Plin.

amellus.full: amellus, i, m., the purple Italian starwort: Aster amellus, Linn.; Verg. G. 4, 271 (cf. Serv. ad h. 1.); Col. 9, 4, 4.
amellus.short: amellus, i, m., the purple Italian starwort: Aster amellus, Linn.;

amen.full: āmēn ; Gr. ἀμήν (eccl. Lat.). Adj., true, faithful: (tu Deus) fecisti mirabilia, cogitationes fideles, amen (Heb. = verity), Vulg. Isa. 25, 1.— Subst., truth, faith fulness: qui benedictus est, benedicetur in Deo amen, in the God of faithfulness, Vulg. Isa. 65, 16: haec dicit Amen (Gr. ὁ Αμήν), He that is True, ib. Apoc. 3, 14.— Most freq. adv. Prop., to confirm words spoken by one's self or another, So be it; Fr. Ainsi soit-il; LXX. γένοιτο, Amen: et respondebit omnis populus, Amen, Vulg. Deut.

amenanus.full: Ămĕnānus, i, m., = Ἀμένανος, a river in Sicily, at the southern declivity of Ætna, Ov. M. 15, 279.—Also adj.: ămĕnānus, a, um: Amenana flumina, Ov. F. 4, 467.
amenanus.short: Ămĕnānus, i, m., = Ἀμένανος, a river in Sicily, at the southern declivity of Ætna, Ov.

amens.full: ā-mens, mentis, adj. Lit., out of one's senses, beside one's self, senseless, mad, insane, frantic, distracted (of every kind of passionate excitement; while insanus designates one diseased in mind; and excors or vecors, one that is without mind; among the poets a favorite word with Verg. and Ov.): inceptio est amentium, haud amantium, Ter. And. 1, 3, 13: homo amentissimus atque in omnibus consiliis praeceps, Cic. Phil. 5, 13: o vecors et amens, id. Pis. 9: arma amens capio, Verg. A. 2, 314: in

amentatus.full: āmentātus, a, um, Part. of amento.

amentia.full: āmentĭa, ae, f. amens, the being out of one's senses, beside one's self, madness, insanity. Lit.: animi adfectionem lumine mentis carentem nominaverunt amentiam eandemque dementiam, Cic. Tusc. 3, 5, 10: Di monerint meliora atque amentiam averruncassint tuam, Pac. ap. Varr. L. L. 7, § 102 Müll., and in Paul. ex Fest. p. 373 Müll. (Trag. Rel. p. 90 Rib.): heu cor ira fervit caecum, amentiā rapior ferorque, Att. ap. Non. 503, 7 (Trag. Rel. p. 194 Rib.): Quor meam senectutem hujus sollicito amentiā,

amento.full: āmento, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. amentum. Lit., to furnish with a strap or thong; esp. of the javelin, to the middle of which a strap was fastened, so that it might be thrown with greater force (very rare; only twice in Cic.): hastae amentatae, Cic. Brut. 78, 271.—Trop., of discourse: amentatae hastae (i. e. apta et parata argumenta), Cic. de Or. 1, 57, 242 (so Juv. sagittae and jaculator, q. v.).—Hence, Transf., poet., to hurl or dart the javelin by means of a thong: cum jaculum parvā Libysamentavit

amentum.full: āmentum, i, n. ἅμμα, ἅπτω; v. apo, a strap or thong, esp. upon missile weapons, by means of which they were thrown with greater force (cf. amento): amenta, quibus, ut mitti possint, vinciuntur jacula sive solearum lora, Paul. ex Fest. p. 12 Müll.: epistola ad amentum deligata, Caes. B. G. 5, 48 Herz.: inserit amento digitos, Ov. M. 12, 321: amenta torquent, Verg. A. 9, 665: umor jaculorum amenta emollierat, Liv. 37, 41 al.—Rarely, a shoe-string: soleae sine amento, Plin. 34, 6, 14, § 31.

ameria.full: Ămĕrĭa, ae, f., = Ἀμερία, a very ancient town in Umbria (acc. to Cato, built before the Trojan war), now Amelia, Plin. 3, 14, 19, § 114; Cic. Rosc. Am. 7 al.—Hence, ămĕrīnus, a, um, adj., of or pertaining to Ameria: municeps, Cic. Rosc. Am. 6: corbulae, Cato, R. R. 1, 15: salix, Plin. 24, 9, 37, § 58; Verg. G. 1, 265; Col. 4, 30 al.— ămĕrīni, ōrum, m., the inhabitants of Ameria, Plin. 3, 14, 19, § 113.—ămĕrīna, ōrum, n. (sc. mala or pira), Amerian fruit, Stat. S. 1, 16, 18.
ameria.short: Ămĕrĭa, ae, f., = Ἀμερία, a very ancient town in Umbria (acc.

amerimnon.full: ămĕrimnŏn, i, n. ἀμέριμνος, caredispeller, houseleek, also called aïzoon majus, Plin. 25, 13, 102, § 160.

ames.full: ămĕs, ĭtis, prob. m. cf. amentum, a pole or fork, esp. for holding and spreading bird-nets: amites: perticae aucupales, Paul. ex Fest. p. 12 Müll.: aut amite levi rara tendit retia, * Hor. Epod. 2, 33; Pall. Sept. 12. —Also for bearing a litter or sedan: amites basternarum, Pall. Jun. 2, 3.

amestratus.full: Ămestrătus, i, f., a town on the north coast of Sicily, mentioned only by Cic. and Steph. B., now Mistretta, is prob. the same place as the Amastra of Sil. 14, 267; Cic. Verr. 3, 39, 43; Steph. B. s. v.—Hence, ămestrătīni, ōrum, m., the inhabitants of Amestratus, Cic. Verr. 3, 39, 89.
amestratus.short: Ămestrătus, i, f., a town on the north coast of Sicily, mentioned only by Cic.

amothystinatus.full: ămŏthystĭnātus, a, um, adj. qs. from amethystino, that wears a dress of the color of amethyst, i. e. violet-blue, Mart. 2, 57.

amethystinus.full: ămĕthystĭnus, a, um, adj. amethystus. Of the color of amethyst: vestes, Mart. 1, 97, 7.—Also absol.: amethystina (sc. vestimenta), * Juv. 7, 136.— Set or adorned with amethyst: trientes, Mart. 10, 49.

amethystizon.full: ămĕthystīzōn, ontis, adj., m., = ἀμεθυστίζων, resembling the amethyst in color: carbunculi, prob. our violet ruby, Plin. 37, 7, 25, § 93.
amethystizon.short: ămĕthystīzōn, ontis, adj., m., = ἀμεθυστίζων, resembling the amethyst in color: carbunculi, prob.

amethystus.full: ămĕthystus, i, f., = ἀμέθυστος. The amethyst, a precious stone of violet-blue color, Plin. 37, 9, 40, § 121 sqq.; Vulg. Exod. 28, 19; ib. Apoc. 21, 20.— A kind of vine, Col. 3, 2, 24; cf. Plin. 14, 2, 4, § 31.

ametor.full: ămētor, ŏris, comm., = ἀμήτωρ, motherless, Tert. Praescr. cap. 53.
ametor.short: ămētor, ŏris, comm., = ἀμήτωρ, motherless, Tert.

amflexus.full: amflexus, a, um, Part. [qs. from amflecto], bent or curved round: ora grandi circuitu amflexa, Mel. 3, 2, 1.

amia.full: ămĭa, ae, f., and ămĭas, ae, m., = ἀμία, the tunny, a sea-fish: (piscem) amiam vocant cujus etc., Plin. 9, 15, 19, § 49.—The form amias: acc. amian, Lucil. ap. Varr. L. L. 7, § 47 Müll.; cf. Paul. ex Fest. p. 21 ib.
amia.short: ămĭa, ae, f., and ămĭas, ae, m., = ἀμία, the tunny, a sea-fish: (piscem) amiam vocant cujus etc., Plin.

amiantus.full: ămĭantus, i, m., = ἀμίαντος (unspotted, pure), the amianth, a stone which may be separated into threads and spun, and is inconsumable by fire; asbestos, earth-flax, Plin. 36, 19, 31, § 139.
amiantus.short: ămĭantus, i, m., = ἀμίαντος (unspotted, pure), the amianth, a stone which may be separated into threads and spun, and is inconsumable by fire;

amicabilis.full: ămīcābĭlis, e, adj. amicus, friendly, amicable (post-class. and rare), Firm. Math. 5, 5.—Adv.: ămīcābĭlĭter, in a friendly manner, Jul. Epit. Nov. 63, § 211.

amicalis.full: ămīcālis, e, adj. id., friendly (postclass.): affectio, Dig. 17, 1, 10, § 7: transactio, Cod. 6, 58, 15, § 5: Deus hospitalis, amicalis, App. de Mundo, p. 75, 9.

amicarius.full: ămīcārĭus, i, m. amica, one that procures a mistress, a procurer, Diom. p. 313 P.

amicimen.full: ămĭcīmen, ĭnis, n. amicio, a garment, = amictus (only post-class.): candidum, App. M. 11, p. 261, 9: rude, id. ib. 11, p. 268, 32.

amicinum.full: amicinum, i, n., the neck of a winesack, Paul. ex Fest. p. 15 Müll. (neutr. by mistake; cf. amicinus: ἀσκοῦ στόμα, Gloss.).
amicinum.short: amicinum, i, n., the neck of a winesack, Paul.

amicio.full: ăm-ĭcĭo, ĭcui, or ixi, ictum, 4, v. a. (fut. amicibor, Plaut. Pers. 2, 5, 6; perf. only in exs. below; inf. perf. amicisse, Front.) [jacio], to throw round, to wrap about (cf. ἀμφιβάλλω); exclusively of upper garments (on the contr., induere, of clothes put or drawn on; vestire, of those for the protection or ornament of the body): se amicire or pass. amiciri, to throw round, veil one's self. Lit.: amictus epicroco, Naev. ap. Var. 7, 3, 92: palliolatim amictus, Plaut. Ps. 5, 1, 29: amicibor glor
amicio.short: ăm-ĭcĭo, ĭcui, or ixi, ictum, 4, v.

amicitia.full: ămīcĭtĭa, ae, f. (gen. sing. amicitiāï, Lucr. 3, 83; acc. amicitiem, id. 5, 1019 Lachm.; cf. Charis. p. 94 P., and Neue, Formenl. I. p. 372) [amicus], friendship (very freq. in Cic., occurring more than 200 times). Lit.: Est autem amicitia nihil aliud nisi omnium divinarum humanarumque rerum cum benevolentiā et caritate summa consensio, Cic. Am. 6: eo ego ingenio natus sum: amicitiam atque inimicitiam in frontem promptam gero, Enn. ap. Non. 129, 26: jam diu ego huic bene et hic mihi volumus, et

amicities.full: ămīcĭtĭes, ēi, f., v. the preced. art.

amico.full: ămīco, āre, v. a. amicus, to make friendly to one's self: Oeclides solitā prece numen amicat, Stat. Th. 3, 470.

amicosus.full: ămīcōsus, a, um, adj. id., rich or abounding in friends, Diom. p. 313 P.

amictorius.full: ămictōrĭus, a, um, adj. amicio, suitable for throwing about one: linteamen, Cod. Th. 8, 5, 48, § 1.—Hence, subst.: ămic-tōrĭum, i, n., a garment which is thrown about or over one, a light, loose garment, esp. of women, a scarf, a tie for the neck, Cod. Th. 8, 5, 48; Hier. ad Isa. 2, 3, v. 23.

amictus1.full: ămictus, a, um, Part. of amicio.

amictus2.full: ămictus, ūs, m. amicio, orig. a throwing about or on one of a garment; hence, The manner of dressing, fashion: amictum imitari alicujus, Cic. de Or. 2, 22, 91 (cf. Plin. Ep. 2, 3, 2): est aliquid in amictu, Quint. 11, 3, 156.— Meton., abstr. pro concr., the garment itself that is thrown about or on, any clothing, a mantle, cloak, etc.: quam (statuam) esse ejusdem, status, amictus, anulus, imago ipsa declarat, Cic. Att. 6, 1, 17: frustra jam vestes, frustra mutatur amictus, Tib. 1, 8, 13: velut a

amiculum.full: ămĭcŭlum, i, n. amicio, a garment that one throws about or on him, a mantle, cloak: amiculum genus est vestimenti, a circumjectu dictum, Paul. ex Fest. p. 28 Müll.: amicae amictus amiculo, Cic. Div. 2, 69: agreste duplex amiculum, Nep. Dat. 3, 2: cum aliquem videret minus bene vestitum, suum amiculum dedit, id. Cim. 4, 2: toga picta plerumque amiculo erat accum benti, Sall. Fragm. ap. Macr. S. 2, 9: matrem familiae tuam purpureum amiculum habe re non sines? Liv. 34, 7; 27, 4.—Trop.: novissimum h

amiculus.full: ămīcŭlus, i, m. dim. amicus, a dear friend: quid de Docimo amiculo meo? * Cic. Verr. 2, 3, 34: te nil miseret, dure, tui dulcis amiculi? Cat. 30, 2; * Hor. Ep. 1, 17, 3.—Hence, ămīcŭla, ae, f., a dear (female) friend: de amiculà rixatus, * Cic. de Or. 2, 59, 244; so Plin. Ep. 3, 9, 13; Suet. Calig. 33.

amicus1.full: ămīcus (old form ămēcus, Paul. ex Fest. p. 15 Müll.), a, um, adj. amo, friendly, kind, amicable, favorable, inclined to, liking; constr. with dat., Zumpt, Gram. § 410: animo esse amico erga aliquem, Ter. Hec. 3, 3, 29; Cic. Fam. 1, 7, 3: tribuni sunt nobis amici, id. Q. Fr. 1, 2 fin.: homo amicus nobis jam inde a puero, Ter. Ad. 3, 3, 86: Pompeium tibi valde amicum esse cognovi, Cic. Fam. 1, 8, 5; id. Att. 9, 5: amicus non magis tyranno quam tyrannidi, Nep. Dion, 3, 2; id. Att. 9: male numen ami

amicus2.full: ămīcus, i, m. from amo, as φίλος from φιλέω, and from (gen. plur. amicūm, Ter. Heaut. prol. 24). A friend; constr. with gen. or poss. adj.; v. Zumpt, Gram. § 410: est is (amicus) tamquam alter idem, Cic. Am. 21, 80 (cf. id. ib. 25, 92; id. Off. 1, 17): amicum qui intuetur, tamquam exemplar intuetur sui, id. Am. 7, 23: Non tam utilitas parta per amicum, quam amici amor ipse delectat, id. ib. 14, 51: Amicus certus in re incertā cernitur, Enn. ap. Cic. ib. 17, 64: boni improbis, improbi bonis amici

aminaeus.full: Ămīnaeus (-ē^us), a, um, adj., = Ἀμιναῖος, of or pertaining to Aminœa, a region in the country of the Piceni, distinguished for the culture of the vine: vites, Verg. G. 2, 97; so Cato, R. R. 6, 4; 7, 2; Varr. R. R. 1, 25 Schneid.; Col. 3, 2, 7; 3, 9, 3; Plin. 14, 3, 4, § 8; Pall. Febr. 9, 4; Inscr. Orell. 3678.
aminaeus.short: Ămīnaeus (-ē^us), a, um, adj., = Ἀμιναῖος, of or pertaining to Aminœa, a region in the country of the Piceni, distinguished for the culture of the vine: vites, Verg.

amisia.full: Ămīsĭa, ae. Masc., a river in Germany, now the Ems, Tac. A. 1, 60; 1, 63; 2, 23; in Plin. 4, 14, 28, § 100, and Mel. 3, 3, called ămīsĭus, ii; cf. Mann. Germ. 419. — Fem., a fortress built by the Romans upon the Ems (near the Fort Delf Zyl, in West Friesland), Tac. A. 2, 8; cf. Mann. Germ. 82.

amissibilis.full: āmissĭbĭlis, e, adj. amitto, that may be lost (only in eccl. Lat.), Aug. Trin. 5, 4; so id. ib. 15, 13 al.

amissio.full: āmissĭo, ōnis, f. id., a losing, a loss (several times in Cic., elsewh. rare): oppidorum, Cic. Pis. 17, 40: dignitatis, id. ib. 18, 43: omnium rerum, id. Fam. 4, 3: foliorum, Plin. 17, 2, 2, § 12: boni, rei, Sen. Ep. 4: duorum luminum, of (my) two eyes, Vulg. Jud. 16, 28: nullius animae, ib. Act. 27, 22; ib. Rom. 11, 15.

amissus1.full: āmissus, a, um, Part. of amitto.

amissus2.full: āmissus, ūs, m., for amissio, a loss. Siciliae, Nep. Alcib. 6, 2.
amissus2.short: āmissus, ūs, m., for amissio, a loss.

amisus.full: Ămīsus, i, f., = Ἀμισός, a town in Pontus, now Samsoon, Cic. Imp. Pomp. 8; Plin. 37, 8, 37, § 115; Mel. 1, 19.—ămīsum, i, n., Plin. 6, 2, 2, § 7. Cf. Mann. Asia Min. 2, 448 sq.—ămīsēni, ōrum, m., the inhabitants of Amisus, Plin. Ep. 10, 93.
amisus.short: Ămīsus, i, f., = Ἀμισός, a town in Pontus, now Samsoon, Cic.

amita.full: ămĭta, ae, f. cf. abba, avus, and Engl. aunt (so the mother's sister is called matertera, from mater; cf. Dig. 38, 10, 10), a father's sister, a paternal aunt, Cic. Clu. 10; Liv. 39, 11; Tac. A. 12, 64; 27, 16; Vulg. Lev. 20, 19 et saep.— Hence, Amita magna, a sister of a grandfather (avi), a great-aunt, Tac. A. 2, 27; Paul. l. c.— Amita major, an aunt of a grandfather, Paul. l. c. and Fest. s. v. Major, p. 98.— Amita maxima, an aunt of a great-grandfather, also called abamita, Paul. l. c. and F

amiternum.full: Ămĭternum, i, n. acc. to Varr. L. L. 5, 5, 12, from am- = amb- and Aternus, = Ἀμίτερνον, a very ancient town built by the Aborigines, in the Sabine country, now San Vettorino; cf. Mann. Ital. 1, 509; the birthplace of the historian Sallust.—Derivv. ămĭternīnus, a, um, adj., belonging to Amiternum, Col. 10, 422.—ămĭ-ternīni, ōrum, m. subst., its inhabitants, Varr. L. L. 5, 28, p. 11 Müll.; Liv. 28, 45, 19; Plin. 3, 12, 17, § 107.— ămĭternus, a, um, adj., poet. for Amiterninus: cohors, Verg. A. 7,

amitinum.full: Ămĭtīnum, i, n., a town in Latium, Plin. 3, 5, 9, § 68.
amitinum.short: Ămĭtīnum, i, n., a town in Latium, Plin.

amitinus.full: ămĭtīnus, a, um, adj. amita, descended from a father's sister; hence, ămĭtī-ni, ōrum, m., and ămĭtīnae, ārum, f., cousins, cousins-german, Dig. 38, 10, 1 and 10.

amitto.full: ā-mitto, mīsi, missum, 3, v. a. (amīsti, sync., = amisisti, Ter. Eun. 2, 2, 10; id. Hec. 2, 2, 9: amīssis, sync., = amiseris, Plaut. Bacch. 5, 2, 70). In gen., to send away from one's self, to dismiss (thus, anteclass., freq. in Plaut. and Ter.): quod nos dicimus dimittere, antiqui etiam dicebant amittere, Don. ad Ter. Heaut. 3, 1, 71; Att. ap. Non. 75, 32: stulte feci, qui hunc (servum) amisi, Plaut. Mil. 4, 8, 66; id. ib. 4, 5, 25; so id. ib. 4, 5, 28: quo pacto hic servos suum erum hinc amitt

ammi.full: ammi (ami) and ammium (ami-um), ii, n., = ἄμμι and ἄμμιον, ammi, an umbelliferous plant: est cumino simillimum quod Graeei vocant ami, Plin. 20, 15, 58, § 163; 20, 24, 100, § 264 Jan. (al. ammium): ammium, Scrib. Comp. 121 ext.
ammi.short: ammi (ami) and ammium (ami-um), ii, n., = ἄμμι and ἄμμιον, ammi, an umbelliferous plant: est cumino simillimum quod Graeei vocant ami, Plin.

ammianus.full: Ammĭānus Marcellīnus, i, m., a Latin historian of the 4th century. Of his work, Rerum gestarum libri XXXI., which extended from the beginning of the reign of Nerva (91 A.D.) to the death of Valens (378), the first thirteen books are lost; cf., concerning him, Bähr. Lit. Gesch. 349 sq., and Teuffel, Rom. Lit. § 421, 1-5.
ammianus.short: Ammĭānus Marcellīnus, i, m., a Latin historian of the 4th century.

ammiror.full: ammīror and ammitto, v. admiror, etc.

ammochrysus.full: ammŏchrȳsus, i, m., = ἀμμόχρυσος (gold sand), a precious stone unknown to us, perh. golden mica, Plin. 37, 11, 73, § 188.
ammochrysus.short: ammŏchrȳsus, i, m., = ἀμμόχρυσος (gold sand), a precious stone unknown to us, perh.

ammodytes.full: ammŏdўtēs, ae, m., = ἀμμοδύτης (sand-burrower), a kind of serpent in Africa, * Luc. 9, 716; Sol. 27 al.
ammodytes.short: ammŏdўtēs, ae, m., = ἀμμοδύτης (sand-burrower), a kind of serpent in Africa, * Luc.

ammon.full: Ammōn, better Hammon, ōnis, m. Egypt. Amun, = Ἄμμων, a name of Jupiler, worshipped in Africa under the form of a ram (on the present oasis Siwah). Connected with his temple was an oracle often consulted by the ancients; cf. Cat. 7, 5 sqq.; Curt. 4, 7; Luc. 9, 511 al.—Whence Ammonis cornu, a gold-colored precious stone of the shape of a ram's horn, ammonite, Plin. 37, 10, 60, § 167.—Hence, Ammōnĭăcus, a, um, belonging to Ammon (Africa, Libya): sal, Plin. 31, 7, 39, § 79; Col. 6, 17, 7; Ov. Med. F

ammoneo.full: ammŏnĕo and ammŏnī^trix, v. admoneo, etc.

ammonitrum.full: ammŏnī^trum (ham-), i, n., = ἀμμόνιτρον, natron mingled with sand, Plin. 36, 26, 26, § 194.
ammonitrum.short: ammŏnī^trum (ham-), i, n., = ἀμμόνιτρον, natron mingled with sand, Plin.

amnacum.full: amnăcum, i, n., an herbaceous plant, pellitory, Plin. 21, 30, 104, § 176.
amnacum.short: amnăcum, i, n., an herbaceous plant, pellitory, Plin.

amnenses.full: amnenses or amnēses, ium, f. amnis, towns situated near a river, Paul. ex Fest. p. 17 Müll.

amnestia.full: amnestĭa, ae, f., = ἀμνηστία (a forgetting), an amnesty, a forgiving or pardoning of a state crime: haec oblivio, quam Athenienses ἀμνηστίαν vocant, Vop. Aur. 39 (Nep. Thras. 3, 2, uses for it oblivio; cf.: venia et oblivio, Suet. Claud. 11: abolitio facti, id. Tib. 4).
amnestia.short: amnestĭa, ae, f., = ἀμνηστία (a forgetting), an amnesty, a forgiving or pardoning of a state crime: haec oblivio, quam Athenienses ἀμνηστίαν vocant, Vop.

amnicola.full: amnĭcŏla, ae, comm. amnis-colo, that dwells upon or grows by a river: salices, Ov. M. 10, 96.

amniculus.full: amnĭcŭlus, i, m. dim. amnis, a small river, rivulet, brook, Liv. 36, 22 fin.

amnicus.full: amnĭcus, a, um, adj. id., of or pertaining to a river (only post-class.): calami, Plin. 16, 36, 66, § 166: insula Metubarris amnicarum maxima, i. e. of those formed by rivers, id. 3, 25, 28, § 148: calami, id. 16, 36, 66, § 166: pisces, Sol. 37: terga, Aus. Mos. 205.

amnigena.full: amnĭgĕna, ae amnis-gigno. Born in a river: pisces, Aus. Mos. 116.— Born of a river-god: Choaspes, Val. Fl. 5, 602.

amnis.full: amnis, is, m. (fem., Plaut. Merc. 5, 2, 18; Naev. and Att. ap. Non. 191, 33; Varr. R. R. 3, 5, 9; cf. Prisc. pp. 652 and 658 P.; Rudd. I. p. 26, n. 37; Schneid. Gram. 2, 98; abl. regularly amne; but freq. amni in the poets, Verg. G. 1, 203; 3, 447; Hor. S. 1, 10, 62; Col. R. R. 10, 136; also in prose, Liv. 21, 5; 21, 27 al.; cf. Prisc. p. 766; Rhem. Pal. 1374 P.; Rudd. I. p. 85, n. 85) [qs. for apnis from Sanscr. ap = water; n. plur. āpas. Van.; v. aqua], orig., any broad and deep-flowing, rapid

amnon.full: Amnon, a river in Arabia Felix, Plin. 6, 28, 32, § 151.
amnon.short: Amnon, a river in Arabia Felix, Plin.

amo.full: ămo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. (amāsso = amavero, Plaut. Cas. 5, 4, 23; id. Curc. 4, 4, 22; id. Mil. 4, 2, 16; cf. Paul. ex Fest. p. 28 Müll.: amāsse = amavisse, Ter. Eun. 5, 1, 11: amantum = amantium, Plaut. Men. 2, 3, 4; Lucr. 4, 1077; Ov. A. A. 1, 439) [cf. Sanscr. kam = to love; ἅμα = Sanscr. sam = Germ. sammt; Engl. same, Lat. similis; with the radical notion of likeness, union], to like, to love, ἐράω, φιλέω (both in the higher and the lower sense, opp. odisse; while diligere (ἀγαπῶ) designates

amodo.full: ā-mŏdo (better, separately), adv. formed after the Greek; v. examples, from this time forward, henceforth, = ἀπὸ τούτου (only in eccl. Lat.): a modo et usque in sempiternum (Gr. ἀπὸ τοῦ νῦν), Vulg. Isa. 9, 7; so ib. ib. 59, 21: non me videbitis a modo, donec etc. (Gr. ἀπʼ ἀρτί), ib. Matt. 23, 39; so ib. ib. 26, 29; ib. Joan. 13, 19 al.; Hier. Vit. Hil. 51, p. 157 Francf.; Paul. Nol. 8, 28; cf. Hand, Turs. I. p. 286.

amoebaeus.full: ămoebaeus, a, um, adj., = ἀμοιβαῖος. alternate (pure Lat. alternus); hence, amoebaeum carmen = ᾆσμα ἀμοιβαῖον, a responsive song, Fest.; Serv. ad Verg. E. 3, 28, 59, 66 al.—Hence in metre, pes amoebaeus: ex duabus longis et totidem brevibus et longā, Diom. p. 478 P. (e. g. īncrēdĭbĭlēs; opp. antamoebaeus, q. v.).

amoebeus.full: Ămoebeus (trisyl.), ĕi, m., = Ἀμοιβεύς, a distinguished Athenian harp-player, Ov. A. A. 3, 399.
amoebeus.short: Ămoebeus (trisyl.), ĕi, m., = Ἀμοιβεύς, a distinguished Athenian harp-player, Ov.

amoenitas.full: ămoenĭtas, ātis, f. amoenus, pleas antness, delightfulness, loveliness. Lit., of places (as scenery, a garden, river, etc.; in the poets, except Plaut., rare; never in Ter., Lucr., or Hor.): nunc domus suppeditat mihi hortorum amoenitatem, Cic. Q. Fr. 3, 1, 4: fluminis, id. ib. 3, 1, 1: amoenitates orarum et litorum, id. N. D. 2, 39; so id. Leg. 2, 1; id. Rep. 2, 4; Nep. Att. 13; Col. 1, 4, 8; Flor. 2, 11, 4 al.— Metaph. Of other things (so in Plaut. and the prose-writers of the post-Aug. per.,

amoeno.full: ămoeno, āre, v. a. amoenus, late Lat. Lit., of places, to make pleasant: regio aut consita pomis aut amoenata lucis, Salv Gub. Dei, 7 med.— Trop., to please, delight: amoenare oculos, Cypr. Ep. 2, 1: amoenare felices animas, Cassiod. Ep. 2, 40 al.

amoenus.full: ămoenus, a, um, adj. amo; some comp. ἀμείνων, lovely, delightful, pleasant, charming (in gen. of objects affecting the sense of sight only; as a beautiful landscape, gar dens, rivers, pictures, etc.: amoena loca.. quod solum amorem praestentetad se amanda adliciant, Varr. ap. Isid. Orig. 14: amoena sunt loca solius voluptatis plena, Serv. ad Verg. A. 5, 734; while jucundus is used both in a phys. and mental sense; cf. Doed. Syn. III. p 36; class. in prose and poetry). Lit.: amoena salicta, Enn.

amolior.full: ā-mōlĭor, ītus, 4, v. dep., to remove a person or thing from a place (with effort or difficulty), to move or carry away: amoliri dicuntur ea, quae cum magnā difficultate et molimine summoventur et tolluntur e medio, Don. ad Ter. And. 4, 2, 24 (never in Cic. or Hor.). Lit., Att. ap. Non. 75, 31: amoliri omnia, Plaut. Ps. 3, 2, 67; so id. Most. 2, 1, 44: impedimentum omne, Sisenn. ap. Non. 73, 15: omnia e medio, Plin. 11, 10, 10, § 25: obstantia silvarum, Tac. A. 1, 50: onus, Luc. 5, 354.—Hence, a

amolitio.full: āmōlītĭo, ōnis, f. amolior, a removing, putting away: ubi infantis aliorsum dati facta ex oculis amolitiost, Gell. 12, 1, 22.

amomis.full: ămōmis, ĭdis, f., = ἀμωμίς, a plant similar to the genuine amomum, but inferior in fragrance, Plin. 12, 13, 28, § 49.
amomis.short: ămōmis, ĭdis, f., = ἀμωμίς, a plant similar to the genuine amomum, but inferior in fragrance, Plin.

amomum.full: ămōmum or -on, i, n., = ἄμωμον, an aromatic shrub, from which the Romans prepared a costly, fragrant balsam: Cissus vitiginea, Linn.; Plin. 12, 13, 28, § 43; 16, 32, 59, § 135: Assyrium vulgo nascetur amomum, Verg. E. 4, 25; so id. ib. 3, 89; Ov. P 1, 9, 52; Mart. 5, 65; Pers. 3, 104.
amomum.short: ămōmum or -on, i, n., = ἄμωμον, an aromatic shrub, from which the Romans prepared a costly, fragrant balsam: Cissus vitiginea, Linn.;

amor.full: ămor (old form ămŏs, like honos, labos, colos, etc., Plaut. Curc. 1, 2, 2; v. Neue, Formenl. I. p. 170), ōris, m. amo, love (to friends, parents, etc.; and also in a low sense; hence in gen., like amo, while caritas, like diligere, is esteem, regard, etc.; hence amor is used also of brutes, but caritas only of men; v amo init.): Amicitiae caritate et amore cernuntur. Nam cum deorum, tum parentum, patriaeque cultus, eorumque hominum, qui aut sapientiā aut opibus excellunt, ad caritatem referri so
amor.short: ămor (old form ămŏs, like honos, labos, colos, etc., Plaut.

amorabundus.full: ămōrābundus, a, um, adj. amor, loving, amorous: Laberius in Lacu Averno mulierem amantem verbo inusitatius ficto amorabundam dixit, Gell. 11, 15, 1.

amorgus.full: Ămorgus or -ŏs, i, f., = Ἀμοργός, one of the Sporades in the Ægean Sea, the birthplace of the poet Simonides; under the Roman emperors, a place for the banishment of criminals; now Amorgo, Plin. 4, 12, 23, § 70; Tac. A. 4, 30; v. Mann. Gr. 734 sq.
amorgus.short: Ămorgus or -ŏs, i, f., = Ἀμοργός, one of the Sporades in the Ægean Sea, the birthplace of the poet Simonides;

amorifer.full: ămōrĭfer, ĕra, ĕrum, adj. amor-fero, producing, or awakening love: sagittae, Ven. 6, 2, 13.

amorificus.full: ămōrĭfĭcus, a, um, adj. amor-facio, causing love, App. Herb. 123.

amosio.full: amosio: annuo, Paul. ex Fest. p. 26 Müll. (very dub.).

amotio.full: āmōtĭo, ōnis, f. amoveo, a removing, removal (rare; only twice in Cic.): doloris, Cic. Fin. 1, 11, 37; 2, 3, 9: ordinis, Dig. 47, 10, 43.

amotus.full: āmōtus, a, um, Part. of amoveo.

amoveo.full: ā-mŏvĕo, mōvi, mōtum, 2, v. a., to remove from, to put or take away, to withdraw (esp. with effort or trouble; syn.: dimoveo, abduco, averto, arceo, repello): proprie amovetur saxum de loco, Don. ad Ter. Ad. 4, 2, 14; cf.: amoveamus lapidem de ore putei, Vulg. Gen. 29, 8; v. amolior. In gen. (class.): me exinde amovit loco. Plaut. Truc. 1, 1, 64: Ubi erit empta, ut aliquo ex urbe (eam) amoveas, id. Ep. 2, 2, 94: testem hanc quom abs te amoveris, Ter. Hec. 4, 4, 72: Age, tamen ego hunc amovebo, i

ampelinus.full: ampĕlĭnus, a, um, adj., = ἀμπέλινος, of the vine, Caecil. ap. Non. 548, 15.
ampelinus.short: ampĕlĭnus, a, um, adj., = ἀμπέλινος, of the vine, Caecil.

ampelitis.full: ampĕlītis, ĭdis, f., = ἀμπελῖτις, a kind of bituminous earth, with which the vine was sprinkled in order to keep off worms, Plin. 35, 16, 56, § 194.
ampelitis.short: ampĕlītis, ĭdis, f., = ἀμπελῖτις, a kind of bituminous earth, with which the vine was sprinkled in order to keep off worms, Plin.

ampelodesmos.full: ampĕlŏdesmŏs, i, m., = ἀμπελόδεσμος, a plant used for tying up vines, Plin. 17, 23, 35, § 209.
ampelodesmos.short: ampĕlŏdesmŏs, i, m., = ἀμπελόδεσμος, a plant used for tying up vines, Plin.

ampeloleuce.full: ampĕlŏleucē, ēs, f., = ἀμπελολεύκη (white vine), the white vine, bryony: Bryonia alba, Linn.; Plin. 22, 1, 16, § 21.
ampeloleuce.short: ampĕlŏleucē, ēs, f., = ἀμπελολεύκη (white vine), the white vine, bryony: Bryonia alba, Linn.;

ampeloprason.full: ampĕloprăson, i, n., = ἀμπελόπρασον, a plant, probably field-garlic, Plin. 24, 15, 86, § 136.
ampeloprason.short: ampĕloprăson, i, n., = ἀμπελόπρασον, a plant, probably field-garlic, Plin.

ampelos1.full: ampĕlŏs, i, f., = ἄμπελος, a vine, grape-vine (used technically; in pure Lat. vitis). Ampelos agria, wild vine (in pure Lat. labrusca), Plin. 23, 1, 14, § 19.— Ampelos chironia, greasewort; in pure Lat. vitis nigra or bryonia, Plin. 23, 1, 17, § 27; 24, 4, 16, § 34.
ampelos1.short: ampĕlŏs, i, f., = ἄμπελος, a vine, grape-vine (used technically;

ampelos2.full: Ampĕlŏs, i, f. A city of Macedonia, Plin. 4, 10, 17, § 37.— A headland and town in Crete, Plin. 4, 12, 20, § 59.

ampelos3.full: Ampĕlŏs, i, m., a beautiful youth, loved by Bacchus, Ov. F. 3, 409.
ampelos3.short: Ampĕlŏs, i, m., a beautiful youth, loved by Bacchus, Ov.

ampendices.full: ampendĭces, appendages, so called by the ancients, acc. to Festus, quod circumpenderent, quos nunc appendices appellamus, Paul. ex Fest. p. 21 Müll.
ampendices.short: ampendĭces, appendages, so called by the ancients, acc.

amphemerinos.full: amphēmĕrĭnŏs, a, on, adj., = ὰμφημερινος, daily (in pure Lat. cotidianus): genus febrium, not intermittent, Plin. 28, 16, 66, § 228.
amphemerinos.short: amphēmĕrĭnŏs, a, on, adj., = ὰμφημερινος, daily (in pure Lat.

amphiaraus.full: Amphĭărāus, i, m., = Ἀμφιάραος, a distinguished Grecian seer, father of Alcmœon and Amphilochus. Knowing that he was doomed to lose his life in the Theban war, he concealed himself in his house; but his wife, Eriphyle, was prevailed upon to betray him by the offer of a golden necklace, and he was compelled by Polynices to accompany him to the war, where he was swallowed up, with his chariot, in the earth, Cic. Div. 1, 40; Ov. P. 3, 1, 52.— Derivv. Amphĭărēus (five syll.), a, um, adj., Amphiarian
amphiaraus.short: Amphĭărāus, i, m., = Ἀμφιάραος, a distinguished Grecian seer, father of Alcmœon and Amphilochus.

amphibolia.full: amphĭbŏlĭa (amphĭbŏlŏgĭa, in Charis. p. 243 P.; Diom. p. 444; Isid. Orig. 1, 33), ae, f., = ἀμφιβολία (ἀμφιβολογία); in rhet., ambiguity, double-meaning, Cic. Div. 2, 56, 116; id. Fam. 7, 32; Auct. ad Her. 2, 11; Quint. 7, 9, 1 al.

amphibolus.full: amphĭbŏlus, a, um, adj., = ἀμφίβολος, ambiguous, Mart. Cap. 5, 149.
amphibolus.short: amphĭbŏlus, a, um, adj., = ἀμφίβολος, ambiguous, Mart.

amphibrachys.full: amphĭbrăchys, ўos, m., = ἀμφίβραχυς (short before and after); in metre, the foot ˘¯˘, Quint. 9, 4, 82 (later gramm. sometimes give the word the Latin ending, amphibrachus; cf. Quint. 9, 4, 105).
amphibrachys.short: amphĭbrăchys, ўos, m., = ἀμφίβραχυς (short before and after);

amphibrevis.full: amphĭbrĕvis, is, m., for amphibrachys, Diom. p. 475 P.
amphibrevis.short: amphĭbrĕvis, is, m., for amphibrachys, Diom.

amphictyones.full: Amphictўŏnes, um (acc. Gr. -ăs; v. infra), m., = Ἀμφικτύονες, the political and religious assembly of the confederated Greek States at Thermopylœ, later at Delphi, the Amphictyons (cf. Tittm. Amphyct. Bund, Heeren Ideen, 3, 196): Thebani accusantur apud Amphictyonas, Cic. Inv. 2, 23; Quint. 5, 10, 111: decreto Amphictyonum, Tac. A. 4, 14.

amphidamas.full: Amphĭdămas, antis, m., = Ἀμφιδάμας, one of the Argonauts, son of Alĕus, from Arcadia, Hyg. Fab. 14; Val. Fl. 1, 376.
amphidamas.short: Amphĭdămas, antis, m., = Ἀμφιδάμας, one of the Argonauts, son of Alĕus, from Arcadia, Hyg.

amphilochia.full: Amphĭlŏchĭa, ae, f., = Ἀμφιλοχία, a small province in Acarnania, Cic. Pis. 40; Mann. Gr. 62 sq.—Hence, Amphĭlŏchĭ-us or Amphĭlŏchĭcus, a, um, adj., Amphilochian: Argos Amphilochium, Liv. 38, 10: Argos Amphilochicum, Plin. 4, 1, 2, § 5. —Amphĭlŏchi, ōrum, m., the inhabitants of Amphilochia, Liv. 38, 3.
amphilochia.short: Amphĭlŏchĭa, ae, f., = Ἀμφιλοχία, a small province in Acarnania, Cic.

amphilochus.full: Amphĭlŏchus, i, m., = Ἀμφίλοχος. Son of Amphiarāus, founder of Argos Amphilochium, in Epirus, Plin. 4, 1, 2, § 3. — Son of Alcmœon and Manto, who, as a seer had a temple at Oropus, in Attica, Liv. 45, 27.

amphimacrus.full: amphĭmā^crus, i, m., = ἀμφίμακρος (long before and after), an amphimacer, the poetical foot ¯˘¯ (also called Creticus), Quint. 9, 4, 81.
amphimacrus.short: amphĭmā^crus, i, m., = ἀμφίμακρος (long before and after), an amphimacer, the poetical foot ¯˘¯ (also called Creticus), Quint.

amphimallum.full: amphĭmallum, i, n., = ἀμφίμαλλον (hairy on both sides), woollen cloth, which was hairy or shaggy on both sides, Varr. L. L. 5, § 167 Müll.; Plin. 8, 48, 73, § 193.
amphimallum.short: amphĭmallum, i, n., = ἀμφίμαλλον (hairy on both sides), woollen cloth, which was hairy or shaggy on both sides, Varr.

amphimedon.full: Amphĭmĕdōn, ontis, m., = Ἀμφιμέδων, a Libyan who, while fighting for Cepheus against Perseus, was slain by the latter. Ov. M. 5, 75.
amphimedon.short: Amphĭmĕdōn, ontis, m., = Ἀμφιμέδων, a Libyan who, while fighting for Cepheus against Perseus, was slain by the latter.

amphinomus.full: Amphĭnŏmus, i, m., = Ἀμφίνομος, a youth of Catana who, with his brother Anapis, saved his parents upon his shoulders from the flames of Ætna; on account of which monuments were erected to both of them by their fellow-citizens, Sen. Ben. 3, 37; Sil. 14, 197; Val. Max. 5, 4, ext. 4.
amphinomus.short: Amphĭnŏmus, i, m., = Ἀμφίνομος, a youth of Catana who, with his brother Anapis, saved his parents upon his shoulders from the flames of Ætna;

amphion.full: Amphīon, ŏnis, m., = Ἀμφίων, son of Antiope by Jupiter, king of Thebes, and husband of Niobe; renowned for his music. by the magical power of which the stones came together for the building of the walls of Thebes, Hyg. Fab. 6 and 7; Hor. A. P. 394. He killed himself on account of grief for the loss of his children, who had been slain by the arrows of Apollo and Diana, Ov. M. 6, 221; 6, 271; 6, 402: Amphionis arces, i. e. Thebes, id. ib. 15, 427.—Whence, Amphīŏnĭus, a, um, adj., Amphionian: Amphi
amphion.short: Amphīon, ŏnis, m., = Ἀμφίων, son of Antiope by Jupiter, king of Thebes, and husband of Niobe;

amphipolis.full: Amphĭpŏlis, is, f., = Ἀμφίπολις, a distinguished city in Macedonia, now Neokhorio, Plin. 4, 10, 17, § 38; Liv. 45, 9; 45, 29.— Derivv. Amphĭpŏlītes, ae, m., = Ἀμφιπολίτης, an Amphipolitan, Varr. R. R. 1, 1.— Amphĭpŏlītānus, a, um, adj., belonging to Amphipolis, Just. 14 fin.
amphipolis.short: Amphĭpŏlis, is, f., = Ἀμφίπολις, a distinguished city in Macedonia, now Neokhorio, Plin.

amphiprostylos.full: amphĭprostȳlos, i, m., = ἀμφιπρόστυλος (with pillars before and behind), a temple which had pillars in front and rear, but not at the sides, Vitr. 3, 1.
amphiprostylos.short: amphĭprostȳlos, i, m., = ἀμφιπρόστυλος (with pillars before and behind), a temple which had pillars in front and rear, but not at the sides, Vitr.

amphisbaena.full: amphisbaena, ae, f., = ἀμφίσβαινα, a kind of serpent in Libya which can move either backwards or forwards, Plin. 8, 23, 35, § 85; Luc. 9, 719.
amphisbaena.short: amphisbaena, ae, f., = ἀμφίσβαινα, a kind of serpent in Libya which can move either backwards or forwards, Plin.

amphissa.full: Amphissa, ae, f., = Ἄμφισσα. The ancient chieftown in Locri Ozolœ, near Phocis, now Salona, Luc. 3, 172; cf. Mann. Gr. 125.— A promontory of Locri Epizephyrii, in Lower Italy; whence, Amphissi-us, a, um, adj., of Amphissa: Amphissia saxa, Ov. M. 15, 703 Riese, where Merkel reads Amphrisia, the designation of a place now unknown.

amphissus.full: Amphissus or -ŏs, i, m., son of Apollo and Dryope, builder of the town Œta, at the foot of Mt. Œta, Ov. M. 9, 356.
amphissus.short: Amphissus or -ŏs, i, m., son of Apollo and Dryope, builder of the town Œta, at the foot of Mt.

amphitane.full: amphĭtănē, ēs, f., a kind of precious stone, also called chrysocolla, perh. a magnetic pyrites, Plin. 37, 10, 54, § 147.
amphitane.short: amphĭtănē, ēs, f., a kind of precious stone, also called chrysocolla, perh.

amphitapa.full: amphĭtăpa, ae, f., = ἀμφιτάπης, a coverlet, shaggy on both sides: dormire super amphitapa bene molli, Varr. ap. Non. 540, 30; Lucil. ib.; Dig. 34, 2, 24.
amphitapa.short: amphĭtăpa, ae, f., = ἀμφιτάπης, a coverlet, shaggy on both sides: dormire super amphitapa bene molli, Varr.

amphithalamos.full: amphĭthălămŏs, i, m., = ἀμφιθάλαμος, an antechamber: quorum (cubiculorum) unum thalamos, alterum amphithalamos dicitur, Vitr. 6, 10 Rose and Müll. (al. antithalamus, a chamber opp. to the sleeping-chamber).
amphithalamos.short: amphĭthălămŏs, i, m., = ἀμφιθάλαμος, an antechamber: quorum (cubiculorum) unum thalamos, alterum amphithalamos dicitur, Vitr.

amphitheatralis.full: amphĭthĕātrālis, e, adj. amphitheatrum, of or pertaining to the amphitheatre, amphitheatrical: spectaculum, Plin. 11, 24, 28, § 84: magistri, Mart. 11, 70: pompa, Claud. Cons. Mall. Theod. 293.

amphitheatricus.full: amphĭthĕātrĭcus, a, um, adj. id., i.q. amphitheatralis: charta, made near the amphitheatre, of little value, Plin. 13, 12, 23, § 75: spectaculum, Symm. Ep. 4, 8.

amphitheatrum.full: amphĭthĕātrum, i, n., = ἀμφιθέατρον, an amphitheatre, a circular or oval building in which each successive seat, raised above the last, furnished an unobstructed view. From its shape it was sometimes called circus. In Rome it was used for public spectacles: for combats of wild beasts and of ships, but most frequently for gladiatorial shows. It was at first built of wood, but afterwards of stone, and with great splendor. The largest one, designed by Augustus, but begun by Vespasian and finished b
amphitheatrum.short: amphĭthĕātrum, i, n., = ἀμφιθέατρον, an amphitheatre, a circular or oval building in which each successive seat, raised above the last, furnished an unobstructed view.

amphitrite.full: Amphītrītē, ēs, f., = Ἀμφιτρίτη, Amphitrite, the wife of Neptune, and goddess of the Sea, Col. 10, 201; hence an appel. for the sea, Ov. M. 1, 14; Cat. 64, 11.
amphitrite.short: Amphītrītē, ēs, f., = Ἀμφιτρίτη, Amphitrite, the wife of Neptune, and goddess of the Sea, Col.

amphitryo.full: Amphī^trўo (-ŭo) or ōn, ōnis, m., = Ἀμφιτρύων. Son of Alceus and Hipponome, king of Thebes, and husband of Alcmene, Ov. M. 6, 112.—Hence, Amphī^trў-ōnĭădēs, ae, patr. m., a male descendant of Amphitryo, i. e. Hercules, Cat. 68, 112; Ov. M. 9, 140; 15, 49; Verg. A. 8, 214.— The name of a comedy of Plautus.
amphitryo.short: Amphī^trўo (-ŭo) or ōn, ōnis, m., = Ἀμφιτρύων.

amphora.full: amphŏra,, ae (gen. plur. as a measure, usually amphorūm, v infra, II.; cf. Charis. p. 41 P.), f., = ἀμφορεύς, a vessel, usually made of clay, with two handles or ears; for liquids, esp. wine, a flagon, pitcher. flask, bottle, jar, etc.; cf. Smith, Dict. Antiq. Lit.: amphoras implere, Cato, R. R. 113, 2: amphora coepit Institui, Hor. A. P. 22; so id. C. 3, 8, 11; 3, 16, 34; Petr. 34 al.— Also for holding wine: amphora vini, Vulg. 1 Reg. 1, 24; ib. Dan. 14, 2; oil: amphorae oleariae, Cato, R. R. 1

amphoralis.full: amphŏrālis, e, adj. amphora, containing the measure of an amphora: vas, Plin. 37, 2, 10, § 27.

amphorarius.full: amphŏrārĭus, a, um, adj. id., contained in the amphora: vinum, kept therein, Dig. 33, 6, 16.

amphrisius.full: Amphrīsĭus, a, um, adj., v. Amphissa, II.

amphrysus.full: Amphrȳsus or -ŏs, i, m., = Ἀμφρυσός, a small river in the Thessalian province of Phthiotis, near which Apollo fed the flocks of Admetus, Ov. M. 1, 580; 7, 229; Verg. G. 3, 2.— Derivv. Am-phrȳsĭus, a, um, adj., belonging to Amphrysus, or, poet. transf., to Apollo: vates, i. e. the Sibyl, Verg. A. 6, 398.— Am-phrȳsĭăcus, a, um, adj., the same: gramen, Stat. S. 1, 4, 105.
amphrysus.short: Amphrȳsus or -ŏs, i, m., = Ἀμφρυσός, a small river in the Thessalian province of Phthiotis, near which Apollo fed the flocks of Admetus, Ov.

amplector.full: am-plector (old form amploctor, Prisc. p. 552, 39 P.), exus, 3, v. dep. (act. form amplecto, Liv. And. Od. ap. Diom. p. 379 P.; cf. Prisc. p. 797 P.; Struve, 114.—In pass., Plaut. Mil. 2, 6, 27; Lucil. ap. Prisc. p. 791 P.). Lit., to wind or twine round a person or thing (aliquem, πλέκεσθαι ἀμφίτινα; hence with reference to the other object; cf. adimo), to surround, encompass, encircle; of living beings, to embrace (class. in prose and poetry): genua amplectens, Liv. And. Od. ap. Diom. p. 379 P.

amplexor.full: amplexor, ātus, 1, v. dep. freq. (act. form amplexo, analog to amplecto, Plaut. Poen. 5, 4, 60; Att. ap. Non. 470, 11; Lucil. ap. Prisc. p. 791 P.; Petr. 63) [amplector], to embrace, encircle (more rare than the simple verb; for the most part only anteclass., and in Cic. and eccl. Lat.). Lit.: aram amplexantes, Plaut. Rud. 3, 3, 33: tenebit praedam et amplexabitur, keep it fast, Vulg. Isa. 5, 29.—Esp., in love, at greeting, parting, etc., Plaut. Truc. 5, 33; id. Mil. 5, 40: mitto jam osculari at

amplexus1.full: amplexus, a, um, Part. of amplector.

amplexus2.full: amplexus, ūs, m. amplector, an embracing, encircling, surrounding (mostly poet. and in post-Aug. prose). In gen.: amplexu terrarum, * Lucr. 5, 319: serpentis amplexu, * Cic. Div. 1, 36: exuit amplexus, my embrace, Ov. M. 9, 52: occupat (serpens) hos morsu, longis amplexibus illos, id. ib. 3, 48: oceanus, qui orbem terrarum amplexu finit, Liv. 36, 17; so Plin. 5, 9, 9, § 48; Stat. Th. 6, 255 al.— Esp. A loving embrace, caress (mostly in plur.): cum dabit amplexus atque oscula dulcia figet, Verg.

ampliatio.full: amplĭātĭo, ōnis, f. amplio. * An extending, enlarging: addita est sacramento, Tert. Bapt. 13.— In law t. t., a deferring of the decision of the judge: ampliata est et ipsa ampliatio, Sen. Contr. 1, 3 fin.; v. Pseudo Ascon. ad Cic. Verr. p. 164 Bait.; cf. amplio, II.

amplificatio.full: amplĭfĭcātĭo, ōnis, f. amplifico, a widening; hence, An extending, enlarging, increasing (perh. only in Cic.): pecuniae, Cic. Div. 2, 14, 33: rei familiaris, id. Off. 1, 8, 25.—Trop.: honoris et gloriae, Cic. Off. 2, 12, 42.— In rhet. t. t., an exaggerated description of an object, an amplification, Auct. ad Her. 2, 30; Cic. Part. Or. 15; Quint. 2, 5, 9; 5, 10, 99; v. amplifico, II.

amplificator.full: amplĭfĭcātor, ōris, m. id., he who enlarges, an amplifier (very rare): rerum, Cic. Tusc. 5, 4, 10: MVNICIPII, Inscr. Orell. 1025: VRBIS ROMAE, Inscr. Grut. 282, 3.—Trop.: dignitatis, Cic. Fam. 10, 12.

amplificatrix.full: amplĭfĭcātrix, īcis, f. amplificator, she that enlarges or amplifies: amplificatrix veri vetustas, Pacat. Pan. Theod. 8.

amplifico.full: amplĭfĭco, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. amplusfacio, to make wide, to widen, extend, enlarge, increase (class., but mostly in prose). In gen.: ingressum domūs et atrii amplificavit, Vulg. Eccli. 50, 5: dolorem, Pac. ap. Cic. Tusc. 2, 21, 50: divitias, Cic. Rep. 3, 12: fortunam, id. Am. 16, 59: sonum, to strengthen, increase, id. N. D. 2, 57: urbem, id. Cat. 3, 1; Liv. 1, 44: rem publicam, Cic. N. D. 2, 3: civitatem, Vulg. Eccli. 50, 5.— Trop.: auctoritas amplificata, Cic. Imp. Pomp. 16: Aeduorum auctorit

amplificus.full: amplĭfĭcus, a, um, adj. id., splendid, Fronto, Or. 21, Fragm. 3, p. 259 Francof. —Hence, * adv.: amplĭfĭcē, splendidly: amplifice vestis decorata, Cat. 64, 265.

amplio.full: amplĭo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. amplus, to make wider, to extend, enlarge, increase, amplify (rare, esp. before the Aug. per.; mostly in prose). In gen.: amplianda scalpello plaga est, Cels. 7, 5: rem (familiarem), * Hor. S. 1, 4, 32: de ampliando numero, Plin. Pan. 54, 4; so Suet. Ner. 22: orbem, Luc. 3, 276: servitia, Tac. H. 2, 78: ampliato vetere Apollinis templo, Suet. Aug. 18 al.— Trop.: nomen, to render glorious, to ennoble, Mart. 8, 66: Hannibalis bellicis laudibus ampliatur virtus Scipionis

amplitudo.full: amplĭtūdo, ĭnis, f. amplus, in space, wide extent, breadth, width, amplitude, size, bulk (class., but only in prose). Lit.: membrorum, Varr. R. R. 2, 4, 3: simulacrum modicā amplitudine, Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 49: urbis, Liv. 7, 30: oppidum stadiorum LXX. amplitudine, Plin. 6, 26, 30, § 119: platanus adolescit in amplitudinem, id. 12, 1, 3, § 7: corporis, Plin. Ep. 6, 16, 3: Apollo amplitudinis et artis eximiae, Suet. Tib. 74: margaritarum, id. Caes. 47: valli, Tac. H. 4, 22: numeri, Gell. 19, 8, 12 a

ampliusculus.full: amplĭuscŭlus, a, um, adj. amplus, somewhat larger, or more magnificent: fortuna, App. Mag. p. 322, 19 Elm.—* Adv.: amplĭuscŭlē, rather more, Sid. Ep. 3, 16.

amplo.full: amplo, āre, v. a. id., old form for amplifico, to extend, enlarge; trop., to make glorious: qui causam humilem dictis amplent, Pac. ap. Non. p. 506, 26 (Trag. Rel. p. 120 Rib.).

amplus.full: amplus, a, um, adj. some regard this as a shortened form of ἀνάπλεως, = filled up, full; others, as for ambulus from amb-, rounded out, as superus from super, etc.; v. Doed. Syn. II. p. 113; but perh. it is better to form it from am- and -plus, akin to -pleo, plenus, q. v. Pott, thus pr., full all round; hence, great, large.—In space, of large extent, great, large, wide, ample, spacious (the forms amplus and amplior are very rare in the ante-class. per., and rare in all periods. Amplius is com.

ampsanctus.full: Amp-sanctus (better than Am-), i, m., a lake in Italy, highly dangerous from its pestiferous exhalations (hence, in the poets, the entrance to the infernal regions), now Le Mofete or Lago d' Ansante, Verg. A. 7, 565; Cic. Div. 1, 36; Plin. 2, 93, 95, § 208.
ampsanctus.short: Amp-sanctus (better than Am-), i, m., a lake in Italy, highly dangerous from its pestiferous exhalations (hence, in the poets, the entrance to the infernal regions), now Le Mofete or Lago d' Ansante, Verg.

ampulla.full: ampulla, ae, f. amb- and olla, as having handles on both (opposite) sides, or an irreg. dim. of amphora. A vessel for holding liquids, furnished with two handles and swelling in the middle, a flask, bottle, jar, pot, etc. (also made of leather), Plaut. Merc. 5, 2, 86; id. Pers. 1, 3, 44; Cic. Fin. 4, 12 al.—* Prob. on account of its shape, like λήκυθος, of inflated discourse, swelling words, bombast: proicit ampullas et sesquipedalia verba, * Hor. A. P. 97; cf. Cic. Att. 1, 14, and ampullor.

ampullaceus.full: ampullācĕus, a, um, adj. ampulla, in the form of a flask, big-bellied: a collo ampullacea (pira) appellant, a tankardpear, Plin. 15, 15, 16, § 55; so Col. 8, 2, 15.

ampullarius.full: ampullārĭus, i, m. id., a flask-maker, Plaut. Rud. 3, 4, 51; besides only in Inscr. Orell. 4143.

ampullor.full: ampullor, ātus, 1, v. dep. id. II., to make use of a bombastic style of discourse, = ληκυθίζω (prob. coined by Hor.): tragicā ampullatur in arte, Hor. Ep. 1, 3, 14.

amputatio.full: ampŭtātĭo, ōnis, f. amputo, a pruning, lopping off of branches, tendrils, etc. Lit.: sarmentorum, * Cic. Sen. 15.— Meton., the part that has been cut off, a cutting, Plin. 12, 25, 54, § 118.

amputo.full: am-pŭto, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a., to cut around, to cut away or off, to lop off, prune. Lit., esp. of plants: amputata id est circum putata, Paul. ex Fest. p. 24 Müll.: vitem ferro, Cic. Sen. 15: mergum, Col. 4, 15, 4: cacumen (ulmi), Plin. 16, 32, 57, § 132.— Of other things: praeceidit caulem testīsque una amputat ambo, Lucil. 7, 22 Müll.: pestiferum in corpore, Cic. Phil. 8, 5: umeros, to mutilate, Sen. Thyest. 761: ex ipso vertice capillos, Plin. Ep. 7, 27, 12: caput, Suet. Galb. 20: manus, id.

ampycides.full: Ampўcĭdes, ae, m. patr., = Ἀμπυκίδης, son of Ampycus, i. e. the seer Mopsus, Ov. M. 12, 456; 8, 316.

ampycus.full: Ampўcus, i, m., = Ἄμπυκος. A priest of Ceres, Ov. M. 5, 110 sq.— Father of the seer Mopsus, Hyg. Fab. 14; 128.

ampyx.full: Ampyx, ўcis, m., = Ἄμπυξ. One of the Lapithœ; acc. Ampyca, Ov. M. 12, 450. — One of the companions of Phineus, changed to stone by Perseus, Ov. M. 5, 184.

amsegetes.full: am-sĕgĕtes: quorum ager viam tangit, Paul. ex Fest. p. 21 Müll.
amsegetes.short: am-sĕgĕtes: quorum ager viam tangit, Paul.

amtermini.full: am-termĭni: qui circa terminos provinciae manent, Paul. ex Fest. p. 17 Müll.
amtermini.short: am-termĭni: qui circa terminos provinciae manent, Paul.

amtruo.full: amtrŭo, antrŭo, and andrŭo, āre, v. n. v. andruo, to dance around, in the Salian religious festivals: praesul ut amtruet, inde vulgus redamtruat, Lucil. ap. Fest. p. 270 Müll.
amtruo.short: amtrŭo, antrŭo, and andrŭo, āre, v.

amuletum.full: ămŭlētum, i, n. (Arab. hamalet), a sympathetic preservative against sickness, etc., φυλακτήριον, an amulet (usu. hung around the neck): veneficiorum amuleta, Plin. 29, 4, 19, § 66; so id. 30, 15, 47, § 138 al.

amulius.full: Ămūlĭus, i, m., = Ἀμούλιος, son of Procas, king in Alba, who expelled his brother Numitor, and ordered his grandsons Romulus and Remus to be thrown into the Tiber; hence, dirus, Ov. F. 4, 53; cf. Liv. 1, 3 sq.: injustus, Ov. M. 14, 772 al.
amulius.short: Ămūlĭus, i, m., = Ἀμούλιος, son of Procas, king in Alba, who expelled his brother Numitor, and ordered his grandsons Romulus and Remus to be thrown into the Tiber;

amurca.full: ămurca (better than ămurga), ae, f., = ἀμόργη (cf. Serv. ad Verg. G. 1, 194), the watery part that flows out in pressing olives, the lees or dregs of oil, Cato, R. R. 91; 101; 103; Varr. R. R. 1, 64; Col. 12, 50, 5; Plin. 15, 8, 8, § 33; Verg. G. 3, 448.
amurca.short: ămurca (better than ămurga), ae, f., = ἀμόργη (cf.

amurcarius.full: ămurcārĭus, a, um, adj. amurca, pertaining to the lees of oil (v. amurca): dolia, Cato, R. R. 10, 4.

amusia.full: ămūsĭa, ae, f., = ἀμουσία, ignorance of music, Varr. ap. Non. p. 171, 30.
amusia.short: ămūsĭa, ae, f., = ἀμουσία, ignorance of music, Varr.

amusos.full: ămūsos, i, m., = ἄμουσος, one unskilled in music, * Vitr. 1, 1 med.
amusos.short: ămūsos, i, m., = ἄμουσος, one unskilled in music, * Vitr.

amussis.full: ămussis, is, f. etym. unc.; perh. from am- and assis = axis, a plank, i. e. something flat, straight, moved about a surface in adjusting it (acc. amussim, v. Neue, Formenl. I. p. 198; abl. and plur. not used; only ante- and post-class.), a rule or level, used by carpenters, masons, etc.: amussis: tabula, quā utuntur ad saxa leviganda, Varr. ap. Non. p. 9, 17; Aus. Idyll. 16, 11; cf. Sisenn. ap. Charis. p. 178 P.; Paul. ex Fest. p. 6 Müll. —In class. Lat. in the adv. phrases, ad ămussim (also wri

amussito.full: ămussĭto, āre, v. a. amussis, to make according to rule, i. e. accurately, nicely: amussitata indoles, Plaut. Mil. 3, 1, 38 Ritschl.

amussium.full: ămussĭum, i, n. id., a horizontal wheel for denoting the direction of the wind, Vitr. 1, 6.

amyclae.full: Ămȳclae, ārum, f., = Ἀμύκλαι. A town in Laconia, in a beautiful, fertile region, the residence of Tyndarus and the birthplace of Castor and Pollux; also renowned on account of its temple and Colossus of Apollo, now Agios Kyriaki, Mart. 9, 104; Ov. M. 8, 314; cf. Mann. Graec. 616. — An unknown town in Latium, between Cajeta and Tarracina, Verg. A. 10, 564, called tacitae, as being conquered because it was forbidden to announce the approach of an enemy; cf. Serv. ad h. l.; Sil. 8, 35, and Mann. It

amyclides.full: Ămȳclīdēs, ae, m. patr., a male descendant of Amyclas, the builder of Amyclœ, i. e. Hyacinthus, Ov. M. 10, 162.

amycticus.full: ămyctĭcus, a, um, adj., = ἀμυκτικός, scratching; hence, of medical remedies, sharp, biting, Cael. Aur. Tard. 2, 6; Theod. Prisc. 2, 5.
amycticus.short: ămyctĭcus, a, um, adj., = ἀμυκτικός, scratching;

amycus.full: Ămўcus, i, m., = Ἄμυκος. Son of Neptune, king of the Bebrycians, Val. Fl. 4, 148.— A centaur slain in the contest with the Lapithœ, Ov. M. 12, 245.— A Trojan, Verg. A. 10, 704.

amygdala.full: ămygdăla, ae, f., = ἀμυγδάλη. An almond, Cato, R. R. 8, 2; Col. 6, 10, 12; Plin. 12, 9, 19, § 36.— = ἀμυγδαλῆ, an almond-tree, Col. 5, 10 fin.; Plin. 16, 26, 42, § 103.

amygdalaceus.full: ămygdălācĕus, a, um, adj. amygdala, similar to the almond-tree: folium, Plin. 26, 11, 69, § 111.

amygdaleus.full: ămygdăleus, a, um, adj. id., of an almond-tree: ramus, Pall. Insit. 157.

amygdalinus.full: ămygdălĭnus, a, um, adj. id.. Of or from almonds: oleum, Plin. 15, 7, 7, § 26.— Pruna, i. e. ingrafted on an almond-tree, Plin. 15, 13, 12, § 42.

amygdalites.full: ămygdălītes, ae, m. id., like the almond-tree, Plin. 26, 8, 44, § 70.

amygdalum.full: ămygdălum, i, n., = ἀμύγδαλον, i. q. amygdala. An almond, an almondkernel, Ov. A. A. 3, 183; Pall. 2, 15 fin.— An almond-tree, Col. Arb. 25.

amygdalus.full: ămygdălus, i, f., = ἀμύγδαλος, an almond-tree, Pall. 2, 15.
amygdalus.short: ămygdălus, i, f., = ἀμύγδαλος, an almond-tree, Pall.

amylo.full: ămўlo, āre, v. a. amylum, to mix with starch (only post-class.): jus, Apic. 7, 6: lac, Cael. Aur. Tard. 2, 13.

amylum.full: ămўlum or ămŭlum, i, n., = ἄμυλον, starch, Cato, R. R. 87; Cels. 2, 20; Plin. 18, 7, 17, § 76.
amylum.short: ămўlum or ămŭlum, i, n., = ἄμυλον, starch, Cato, R.

amymone.full: Ămȳmōnē, ēs, f., = Ἀμυμώνη. Daughter of Danăus, and grandmother of Palamedes, Hyg. Fab. 169; Prop. 3, 22, 27. — A fountain near Argos, Ov. M. 2, 240.—Hence, ămȳmōnĭus, a, um, pertaining to Amymone, Hyg. Fab. 169.

amyntas.full: Ămyntas, ae, m., = Ἀμύντας. The father of the Macedonian king Philip, Nep. Reg. 2; Just. 7, 4.—Hence, ămyntĭă-dēs, ae, m. patr., a descendant of Amyntas, i. e. Philip, Ov. Ib. 297.— Name of a shepherd, Verg. E. 3, 66.

amyntor.full: Ămyntor, ŏris, m., = Ἀμύντωρ, king of the Dolopians, and father of Phœnix, Ov. M. 8, 307; id. H. 3, 27.—Hence, ămyn-tŏrĭdes, ae, m., son of Amyntor, i. e. Phœnix, Ov. A. A. 1, 337.
amyntor.short: Ămyntor, ŏris, m., = Ἀμύντωρ, king of the Dolopians, and father of Phœnix, Ov.

amystis.full: ămystis, ĭdis, f., = ἄμυστις, the emptying of a cup at one draught, Hor. C. 1, 36, 14.
amystis.short: ămystis, ĭdis, f., = ἄμυστις, the emptying of a cup at one draught, Hor.

amythaon.full: Ămȳthāōn (also Ămĭth-), ŏnis, m., = Ἀμυθάων, a Greek, the father of Melampus, Ov. M. 15, 325.—Hence, ămўthāŏ-nĭus, a, um, of Amythaon, Verg. G. 3, 550; Prop. 2, 4, 10.
amythaon.short: Ămȳthāōn (also Ămĭth-), ŏnis, m., = Ἀμυθάων, a Greek, the father of Melampus, Ov.

an1.full: ăn, conj. [etym. very obscure; v. the various views adduced in Hand, I. p. 296, with which he seems dissatisfied; if it is connected with the Sanscr. anjas, = Germ. ander, = Engl. other, we may comp. the Engl. other and or with the Germ. oder, = or]. It introduces the second part of a disjunctive interrogation, or a phrase implying doubt, and thus unites in itself the signif. of aut and num or -ne, or, or whether (hence the clause with an is entirely parallel with that introduced by num, utrum,

an3.full: -ăn. This word appears in forsan, forsitan, and fortasse an (Att. Trag. Rel. p. 151 Rib.) or fortassan, seeming to enhance the idea of uncertainty and doubt belonging to fors, etc., and is regarded by some as the Greek conditional particle ἄν, and indeed one of these compounds, forsitan, sometimes in the Vulgate, translates ἄν; as, Joan. 4, 10; 5, 46; 8, 19; and in 3, Joan. 9, it still represents the various reading, ἄν.

anabaptismus.full: ănăbaptismus, i, m., = ἀναβαπτισμός, a second baptism, Aug. ad Psa. 38.
anabaptismus.short: ănăbaptismus, i, m., = ἀναβαπτισμός, a second baptism, Aug.

anabasis.full: ănăbăsĭs, is, f., = ἀνάβασις, a plant, horse-tail: equisetum, Linn.; Plin. 26, 7, 20, § 36; 26, 13, 83, § 133.
anabasis.short: ănăbăsĭs, is, f., = ἀνάβασις, a plant, horse-tail: equisetum, Linn.;

anabathrum.full: ănăbathrum, i. n., = ἀνάβαθρον, an elevated place for beholding public games: quae conducto pendent anabathra tigillo, tiers of benches that rest on hired beams, * Juv. 7, 46.

anabolium.full: ănăbŏlium, ii, n. ἀναβάλλω, a surgical instrument, Inscr. Orell. 1572.

anacampseros.full: ănăcampsĕrōs, ōtis, m., = ἀνακαμψέρως (love-restoring), an herb, the touch of which was said to have the power of bringing back lost love, Plin. 24, 17, 102, § 167.
anacampseros.short: ănăcampsĕrōs, ōtis, m., = ἀνακαμψέρως (love-restoring), an herb, the touch of which was said to have the power of bringing back lost love, Plin.

anaces.full: Ănăces, um, m., = Ἄνακες (v. ἄναξ, L. and S.), an epithet of the Dioscuri (Castor and Pollux), Cic. N. D. 3, 21.

anacharsis.full: Ănăcharsis, is, m., = Ἀνάχαρσις, a distinguished Scythian philosopher in the time of Solon, Cic. Tusc. 5, 32, 90; Plin. 7, 56, 57, § 209 al.
anacharsis.short: Ănăcharsis, is, m., = Ἀνάχαρσις, a distinguished Scythian philosopher in the time of Solon, Cic.

anachoresis.full: ănăchōrēsis, is or eos, f., = ἀναχώρησις, retirement, the life of an eremite, Sid. Ep. 7, 9.
anachoresis.short: ănăchōrēsis, is or eos, f., = ἀναχώρησις, retirement, the life of an eremite, Sid.

anachoreta.full: ănăchōrēta, ae, m., = ἀναχωρητής, a hermit, an eremite, recluse, anchorite, Sulp. Sev. Dial. 1, 18; Sid. Carm. 16, 97.
anachoreta.short: ănăchōrēta, ae, m., = ἀναχωρητής, a hermit, an eremite, recluse, anchorite, Sulp.

anaclinterium.full: ănăclintērĭum, i, n., = ἀνακλιντήριον, a cushion for leaning upon, Spart. Ael. Ver. 5.
anaclinterium.short: ănăclintērĭum, i, n., = ἀνακλιντήριον, a cushion for leaning upon, Spart.

anacreon.full: Ănā^crĕōn, ontis, m., = Ἀνακρέων, a distinguished lyric poet of Teos, who fl. 540 B.C., Cic. Tusc. 4, 33, 71; Hor. C. 4, 9, 9; id. Epod. 14, 10 al.—Hence, ănā^crĕōntēus, a, um, adj., Diom. p. 512 P.; ănā^crĕōn-tĭus, a, um, adj., Quint. 9, 4, 78; Gell. 19, 9; and ănā^crĕōntĭcus, a, um, adj., Fulg. Myth. 1.
anacreon.short: Ănā^crĕōn, ontis, m., = Ἀνακρέων, a distinguished lyric poet of Teos, who fl.

anactorium.full: ănactŏrĭum, i, n., = ἀνακτόριον, a plant, sword-grass, App. Herb. 78.
anactorium.short: ănactŏrĭum, i, n., = ἀνακτόριον, a plant, sword-grass, App.

anadema.full: ănădēmă, ătis, n., = ἀνάδημα, a band, a fillet, an ornament for the head: Et bene parta patrum flunt anademata, mitrae, the well-earned property of fathers is converted into head-bands, etc., * Lucr. 4, 1129; Dig. 34, 2, 27.
anadema.short: ănădēmă, ătis, n., = ἀνάδημα, a band, a fillet, an ornament for the head: Et bene parta patrum flunt anademata, mitrae, the well-earned property of fathers is converted into head-bands, etc., * Lucr.

anadiplosis.full: ănădiplōsis, is or eos, f., = ἀναδίπλωσις, the reduplication or repetition of the same word (in pure Lat., conduplicatio); as, Sequitur pulcherrimus Astur, Astur equo fidens, Verg. A. 10, 181; cf. Aquila, Rom. 32; Jul. Rufin. 7; Mart. Cap. 5, 175.
anadiplosis.short: ănădiplōsis, is or eos, f., = ἀναδίπλωσις, the reduplication or repetition of the same word (in pure Lat., conduplicatio);

anadyomene.full: Ănădўŏmĕnē, ēs, f., = ἀναδυομένη (she that emerges), an epithet of Venus emerging from the sea, a celebrated picture of the painter Apelles, Plin. 35, 10, 36, § 12.
anadyomene.short: Ănădўŏmĕnē, ēs, f., = ἀναδυομένη (she that emerges), an epithet of Venus emerging from the sea, a celebrated picture of the painter Apelles, Plin.

anagallis.full: ănăgallis, ĭdis, f., = άναγαλλίς, a plant, pimpernel or chickweed, Plin. 25, 13, 92, § 144.
anagallis.short: ănăgallis, ĭdis, f., = άναγαλλίς, a plant, pimpernel or chickweed, Plin.

anaglypticus.full: ănăglyptĭcus, a, um, adj., = ἀναγλυπτικός, carved or engraved in bas-relief: metallum, Sid. Ep. 9, 13.
anaglypticus.short: ănăglyptĭcus, a, um, adj., = ἀναγλυπτικός, carved or engraved in bas-relief: metallum, Sid.

anaglyptus.full: ănăglyptus or -phus, a, um, adj., = ἀνάγλυπτος or -φος; in sculpture, wrought or carved in bas-relief, Inscr. Orell. 3838.— Hence, subst.: ănăglypta, ōrum, n., work in bas-relief, Plin. 33, 11, 49, § 139, where the old form was anaglypha.
anaglyptus.short: ănăglyptus or -phus, a, um, adj., = ἀνάγλυπτος or -φος;

anagnia.full: Ănagnĭa, ae, f., = Ἀναγνία, a town in Latium, the chief seat of the Hernici, now Anagni, Cic. Att. 16, 8, 1; Liv. 45, 16; Plin. 34, 6, 11, § 23; cf. Mann. Ital. 1, 665.—Hence, ănagnīnus, a, um, belonging to Anagnia, Cic. Dom. 30.—Subst.: ănagnīnum, i, n., an estate near Anagnia, Cic. Att. 12, 1. —Plur.: ănagnīni, ōrum, m., its inhabitants, Cic. Phil. 2, 41; Plin. 3, 5, 9, § 63.
anagnia.short: Ănagnĭa, ae, f., = Ἀναγνία, a town in Latium, the chief seat of the Hernici, now Anagni, Cic.

anagnostes.full: ănăgnostēs, ae, m., = ἀναγνώστης, a reader, com. among the ancients an educated slave (cf. acroama): noster, Cic. Att. 1, 12, where Orell. would write it as Greek; Vatin. ap. Cic. Fam. 5, 9, 2; Nep. Att. 13, 14; Gell. 3, 19; 18, 5.
anagnostes.short: ănăgnostēs, ae, m., = ἀναγνώστης, a reader, com.

anagyros.full: ănăgȳros, i, f., = ἀνάγυρος, a strengscented, pod-bearing shrub, bean-trefoil: Anagyris foetida, Linn.; Plin. 27, 4, 13, § 30
anagyros.short: ănăgȳros, i, f., = ἀνάγυρος, a strengscented, pod-bearing shrub, bean-trefoil: Anagyris foetida, Linn.;

anaitis.full: Ănăītis, ĭdis, f., an Armenian goddess, said to be the name of Diana read backwards (Anaid), Plin. 33, 4, 24, § 84.
anaitis.short: Ănăītis, ĭdis, f., an Armenian goddess, said to be the name of Diana read backwards (Anaid), Plin.

analecta.full: ănălecta, ae, m., = ἀναλέκτης, he that collected the crumbs, etc., left after a meal, Mart. 7, 20; 14, 82.— Trop.: grammaticos habere analectas, that picked up words (said of parasites), Sen. Ep. 27.
analecta.short: ănălecta, ae, m., = ἀναλέκτης, he that collected the crumbs, etc., left after a meal, Mart.

analectris.full: ănălectris, ĭdis, f. ἀνά-λέκτρον, perh. a cushion for the shoulders, used to improve the figure, a shoulder-pad, Ov. A. A. 3, 273, where Merkel reads analeptrides; v. analeptris.

analemma.full: ănălemmă, ătis, n., = ἀνάλημμα, a sundial which showed the latitude and meridian of a place, Vitr. 9, 4.
analemma.short: ănălemmă, ătis, n., = ἀνάλημμα, a sundial which showed the latitude and meridian of a place, Vitr.

analeptris.full: ănăleptris, ĭdis, f., = ἀναληπτρίς (ἀναλαμβάνω, to hold up), a suspensory bandage, Ov. A. A. 3, 273 Merkel; v. analectris.
analeptris.short: ănăleptris, ĭdis, f., = ἀναληπτρίς (ἀναλαμβάνω, to hold up), a suspensory bandage, Ov.

analogia.full: ănălŏgĭa, ae, f., = ἀναλογία, the resemblance or agreement of several things; in gram., the analogy of language, analogy, Varr. L. L. 9, 4 al. (in Cic. Att. 6, 2, written as Greek).
analogia.short: ănălŏgĭa, ae, f., = ἀναλογία, the resemblance or agreement of several things;

analogicus.full: ănălŏgĭcus, a, um, adj. analogia, = ἀναλογικός, pertaining to analogy: in libris analogicis, Gell. 4, 16.

analogus.full: ănălŏgus, a, um, adj., = ἀνάλογος, analogous, proportionate, Varr. L. L. 10, § 37 (by Müll. written as Greek).
analogus.short: ănălŏgus, a, um, adj., = ἀνάλογος, analogous, proportionate, Varr.

anancaeum.full: ănancaeum, i, n., = ἀναγκαῖον (that must be done), a large drinking-cup, which must be drained on a wager, a brimmer or bowl, Plaut. Rud. 2, 3, 33; Varr. ap. Non. p. 547, 33 dub.
anancaeum.short: ănancaeum, i, n., = ἀναγκαῖον (that must be done), a large drinking-cup, which must be drained on a wager, a brimmer or bowl, Plaut.

anancites.full: ănancītes, ae, m., ἀν- ἄγχω, to free from distress, a name of the diamond as a remedy for sadness and trouble of mind: adamas et venena vincit et lymphationes abigit metusque vanos expellit a mente. Ob id quidam eum ananciten vocavere, Plin. 37, 4, 15, § 61 Sillig, Jan; the old reading here was anachiten.
anancites.short: ănancītes, ae, m., ἀν- ἄγχω, to free from distress, a name of the diamond as a remedy for sadness and trouble of mind: adamas et venena vincit et lymphationes abigit metusque vanos expellit a mente.

anancitis.full: ănancītis, ĭdis, f., a precious stone used in hydromancy: Anancitide in hydromantiā dicunt evocari imagines deorum, Plin. 37, 11, 73, § 192.
anancitis.short: ănancītis, ĭdis, f., a precious stone used in hydromancy: Anancitide in hydromantiā dicunt evocari imagines deorum, Plin.

anapaesticus.full: ănăpaestĭcus, a, um, adj. anapaestus, consisting of anapœsts, Sid. Ep. 4, 3; Serv. ad Verg. E. 8, 78.

anapaestus.full: ănăpaestus, a, um, adj., = ἀνάπαιστος (struck back). Pes, the metrical foot, anapœst: ˘˘¯ (i. e. a reversed dactyl), Cic. Tusc. 2, 16, 37; id. de Or. 3, 47; also absol. without pes, id. Or. 56.— ănă-paestum, i, n. (sc. carmen), a poem in anapœsts, Cic. Tusc. 3, 24, 57; id. Or. 56; Gell. praef. 20.
anapaestus.short: ănăpaestus, a, um, adj., = ἀνάπαιστος (struck back).

anapauomene.full: Ănăpauŏmĕnē, ēs, f., = ἀναπαυομένη (she that rests), a painting of the Theban Aristides, Plin. 35, 10, 36, § 99; cf. Anapauomenos.
anapauomene.short: Ănăpauŏmĕnē, ēs, f., = ἀναπαυομένη (she that rests), a painting of the Theban Aristides, Plin.

anapauomenos.full: Ănăpauŏmĕnos, i, m., = ἀναπαυόμενος (he that rests), a painting of Protogenes, which represents a satyr as leaning idly against a tree, Plin. 35, 10, 36, § 106.
anapauomenos.short: Ănăpauŏmĕnos, i, m., = ἀναπαυόμενος (he that rests), a painting of Protogenes, which represents a satyr as leaning idly against a tree, Plin.

anaphe.full: Ănăphē, ēs, f., = Ἀνάφη, an island that rose of itself (i. e. volcanic) in the Cretan Sea, now Namfi or Namfio, Ov. M. 7, 461; Plin. 2, 87, 89, § 202; Amm. 17, 7.
anaphe.short: Ănăphē, ēs, f., = Ἀνάφη, an island that rose of itself (i.

anaphora.full: ănăphŏră, ae, f., = ἀναφορά. A rising or mounting up, the rising of the stars, Plin. 7, 49, 50, § 160; Firm. Math. 3, 3. — In rhet. The bringing up or repetition of a word at the beginning of successive clauses, e. g. Cic. Verr. 2, 2, 10: Verres calumniatores apponebat, Verres adesse jubebat, Verres cognoscebat, etc., Don. p. 1773 P.; Charis. p. 250 P.; Diom. p. 440 P.— The improper reference of a word to a preceding word, e. g. Sall. C. 18, 1: conjuravere pauci, in quibus Catilina: de quā (sc.

anaphoricus.full: ănăphŏrĭcus, a, um, adj., = ἀναφορικός. In astronomy, adjusted according to the rising of the stars: horologium, Vitr. 9, 9.— In medicine, bringing up blood, spitting blood, Firm. Math. 3, 13.

anapis.full: Ănāpis, is, or -us, i, m. Brother of Amphinomus, q. v.— A river in Sicily, which empties into the bay of Syracuse, now Anapo or Fiume di Sortino, Ov. M. 5, 417; id. F. 4, 469.

anapleroticus.full: ănăplērōtĭcus, a, um, adj., = ἀναπληρωτικός, suitable for filling up, Veg. Vet. 2, 26.
anapleroticus.short: ănăplērōtĭcus, a, um, adj., = ἀναπληρωτικός, suitable for filling up, Veg.

anartes.full: Anartes, ium, or Anarti, ōrum, m., a people in Transylvania, on the Theis, Caes. B. G. 6, 25.
anartes.short: Anartes, ium, or Anarti, ōrum, m., a people in Transylvania, on the Theis, Caes.

anas1.full: ănăs, ănătis (gen. plur. anatum, Cic. N. D. 2, 48, 124; Plin. 25, 2, 3, § 6; rarely anatium, Varr. R. R. 3, 5, 14; 3, 11, 1) [kindr. with old Germ. Anut; Lith. antis; mod. Germ. Ente; perh. also with Sanscr. ātis, a waterfowl], f., the duck: greges anatium, Varr. R. R. 3, 11: anatum ova, Cic. N. D. 2, 48, 124 al.: Anas fluviatilis, wild-duck, Ov. M. 11, 773.

anas2.full: ănās, ātis, f. 3. anus, disease of old women: anatem morbum anuum dicebant, id est, vetularum sicut senium morbum senum, Paul. ex Fest, p. 29 Müll.; cf. Placid. p. 435 Mai.

anas3.full: Ănas, ae, m., a river in Spain, now Guadiana (Arab., i. e. Wadi-Ana, = river Anas), Caes. B. C. 1, 38; Plin. 3, 1, 3, § 3; 4, 22, 35, § 116; Mel. 2, 6; 3, 1; cf. Mann. Hispan. 325.
anas3.short: Ănas, ae, m., a river in Spain, now Guadiana (Arab., i.

anassum.full: Anassum, i, n., a small river in the Venetian territory, now Stella, Plin. 3, 18, 22, § 126 Hard.; Anaxum, Jan; cf. Mann. Ital. 1, 82.
anassum.short: Anassum, i, n., a small river in the Venetian territory, now Stella, Plin.

anatarius.full: ănătārĭus, a, um, adj. anas, relating to a duck: aquila, the duck-eagle, which stations itself by the water and carries off ducks: Falco haliaëtus, Linn.; Plin. 10, 3, 3, § 7.

anathema1.full: ănăthēmă, ătis, n., = ἀνάθημα, an offering, a gift, Prud. Psych. 540: in anathema oblivionis, Vulg. Judith, 16, 23.
anathema1.short: ănăthēmă, ătis, n., = ἀνάθημα, an offering, a gift, Prud.

anathema2.full: ănăthĕmă, ătis, n., = ἀνάθεμα, a later form of ἀνάθημα, used in mal. part. (eccl. Lat.), pr. an offering not to be redeemed; and of a living thing, to be put to death, doomed; hence, an accursed thing, a curse. Concr., of things: vocavit nomen loci illius Horma, id est anathema, Vulg. Num. 21, 3; ib. Jud. 1, 17; ib. Deut. 13, 16.— A curse of excommunication, anathema: anathematis injuria, Aug. Ep. 75.— Meton. (like the Heb. ). The person cursed: nec inferes quippiam ex idolo in domum tuam, ne fi
anathema2.short: ănăthĕmă, ătis, n., = ἀνάθεμα, a later form of ἀνάθημα, used in mal.

anathematizo.full: ănăthĕmătīzo, āre, v. a., = ἀναθεματίζω. Lit., to anathematize, to put under the ban: aliquem or aliquam rem, Aug. Ep. 75.— In gen., to curse, Vulg. 1 Macc. 5, 5; ib. Marc. 14, 71.— To detest: aliquid, Hier. Ep. 75.—Form ănă-thĕmo, Aug. Serm. 164; id. Temp. 3; id. Ep. 95.

anathymiasis.full: ănăthȳmĭāsis, is, f., = ἀναθυμίασις, a rising vapor, Petr. 47; Theod. Prisc. 2, 2, 1.
anathymiasis.short: ănăthȳmĭāsis, is, f., = ἀναθυμίασις, a rising vapor, Petr.

anaticula.full: ănătĭcŭla, ae, f. dim. anas. A little duck, a duckling, * Cic. Fin. 5, 15, 42.— In Plaut., a term of endearment, duckie, * As. 3, 3, 103.

anatinus.full: ănătīnus, a, um, adj. id., of or pertaining to the duck: Utinam fortunam nunc [ego] anatinam uterer, Uti quom exivissem ex aquā, arerem tamen, * Plaut. Rud. 2, 6, 49.—Hence, ănătīna, ae, f. (sc. caro), duck-flesh, duck, Petr. 56, 3.

anatocismus.full: ănătŏcismus, i, m., = ἀνατοκισμός, interest upon interest, compound interest (twice in Cic.): centesimae cum anatocismo anniversario, Cic. Att. 5, 21, 11; 5, 21, 12; Inscr. Orell. 4405.
anatocismus.short: ănătŏcismus, i, m., = ἀνατοκισμός, interest upon interest, compound interest (twice in Cic.): centesimae cum anatocismo anniversario, Cic.

anatomia.full: ănătŏmĭa or ănătŏmĭca, ae, also ănătŏmĭcē, ēs, f., = ανατομία or ἀνατομική (sc. τέχνη); in medicine, anatomy, Cael. Aur. Acut. 1, 8; Macr. S. 7, 15.—Hence, ănătŏmĭcus, i, m. (sc. medicus), an anatomist, Macr. S. 7, 13; Amm. 28, 4 fin.; Aug. Civ. Dei, 22, 24.
anatomia.short: ănătŏmĭa or ănătŏmĭca, ae, also ănătŏmĭcē, ēs, f., = ανατομία or ἀνατομική (sc.

anatonus.full: ănătŏnus, a, um, adj., = ἀνάτονος, extending upwards (opp. catatonus), Capitula, Vitr. 10, 15 fin.
anatonus.short: ănătŏnus, a, um, adj., = ἀνάτονος, extending upwards (opp.

anatresis.full: ănā^trēsis, is, f., = ἀνάτρησις, a boring through, Cael. Aur. Tard. 2, 1.
anatresis.short: ănā^trēsis, is, f., = ἀνάτρησις, a boring through, Cael.

anaudia.full: ănaudĭa, ae, f., = ἀναυδία, loss of speech, dumbness, Cael. Aur. Acut. 2, 10.
anaudia.short: ănaudĭa, ae, f., = ἀναυδία, loss of speech, dumbness, Cael.

anaurus.full: Ănaurus, i, m., = Ἄναυρος, a river in Thessaly, that rises near the foot of Pelion, Luc. 6, 370.
