G. 3, 14: malis antemnisque de nave in navem trajectis, Liv. 30, 10 Weissenb.: antemnae gemunt, * Hor. C. 1, 14, 6: Effugit hibernas demissa antemna procellas, Ov. Tr. 3, 4, 9: cornua velatarum antemnarum, the ends of the sail-yards covered with the sails, Verg. A. 3, 549.—As pars pro toto = velum: pinus ... antemnis apta ferendis, Ov. M. 13, 783.

antenor.full: Antēnor, ŏris, m., = Ἀντήνωρ. A noble Trojan, who was in favor of restoring Helen and making peace with the Greeks; after the fall of Troy, he went to Italy and founded Patavium (Padua), Serv. ad Verg. A. 1, 247; Ov. M. 13, 201; id. F. 4, 75; Liv. 1, 1.— Hence, Derivv. Antēnŏrĕus, a, um, adj., pertaining to Antenor; or, Patavian, Paduan, Mart. 1, 77; 4, 25.— Antēnŏrĭdes, ae, m., a male descendant of Antenor, Verg. A. 6, 484; also, an inhabitant of Padua, Serv. ad Verg. A. 1, 252.

antenuptialis.full: antĕ-nuptĭālis, e, adj., before marriage (only in late Lat.), Justin. Novell. 2, 1 al.
antenuptialis.short: antĕ-nuptĭālis, e, adj., before marriage (only in late Lat.), Justin.

anteoccupatio.full: anteoccŭpātio and anteoccŭpo, better separately, ante occŭpātio, etc.
anteoccupatio.short: anteoccŭpātio and anteoccŭpo, better separately, ante occŭpātio, etc.

antepaenultimus.full: antĕ-paenultĭmus (less correctly written -pēn-), a, um, adj.; in gram., pertaining to the third syllable from the end, antepenultimate, Diom. p. 425 P.; Mart. Cap. 3, p. 60 al.
antepaenultimus.short: antĕ-paenultĭmus (less correctly written -pēn-), a, um, adj.;

antepagmentum.full: antĕ-pagmentum or antĭp-, i, n. pango; in archit., every thing that is used for garnishing the exterior of a house, as the ornaments about the doors, windows, etc., Cato, R. R. 14; cf. Vitr. 4, 6; Paul. ex Fest. p. 8 Müll.; Müll. Archaeol. § 287.

anteparo.full: antĕpăro and antĕpartus, more correctly, antĕ păro, etc.
anteparo.short: antĕpăro and antĕpartus, more correctly, antĕ păro, etc.

antepassio.full: antĕ-passĭo, ōnis, f., a transl. of the Gr. προπάθεια, a presentiment of pain, suffering, etc., Hier. Ep. 97 ad Salv. 9.

antependulus.full: antĕ-pendŭlus, a, um, adj., hanging before (only late Lat.): crines, App. M. 2, p. 125, 4 Elm.; 5, p. 168, 23 Elm.
antependulus.short: antĕ-pendŭlus, a, um, adj., hanging before (only late Lat.): crines, App.

antepereo.full: antĕpĕrĕo, more correctly written antĕ pĕrĕo.
antepereo.short: antĕpĕrĕo, more correctly written antĕ pĕrĕo.

antepes.full: antĕ-pēs, pĕdis, m. * The forefoot Cic. Arat. 454.— = anteambulo, a forerunner, etc., Agroet. Orthogr. p. 2274 P. (in Juv. 7, 143, the correct read. is ante pedes, Jahn).

antepilanus.full: antĕ-pīlānus, i, m. In milit. lang. The soldiers who fought before the pilani, i. e. the hastati and the principes, Liv. 8, 8.— In Ammianus, = antesignanus, one who fought before the standards, 16, 12, 20. — Trop., a competitor, a rival, Amm. 28, 1.

antepolleo.full: antĕ-pollĕo, ēre, v. n., to be more powerful, to excel, surpass (late Lat.): alicui, App. M. 1, p. 104, 20 Elm.: toto vertice cunctos, id. ib. 7, p. 189, 35 Elm.

antepono.full: antĕ-pōno, pŏsui, pŏsĭtum, 3, v. a., to set or place before. Lit. In gen.: equitum locos sedilibus plebis, Tac. A. 15, 32: propugnacula anteposita, id. ib. 12, 56. — Esp., to set (food) before one (com., pono, as Hor. S. 1, 3, 92; Juv. 1, 141 al.): prandium pransoribus, Plaut. Men. 2, 2, 2; so id. Curc. 1, 1, 73; id. Rud. 2, 6, 25.— Trop., to prefer, give the preference to: longe Academiae illi hoc gymnasium anteponam, Cic. de Or. 1, 21 fin.: suo generi meum, id. Sull. 8, 25: amicitiam omnibus r

antepotens.full: antĕ-pŏtens, entis, adj., superior in power or fortune: voluptatibus gaudiisque antepotens, Plaut. Trin. 5, 1, 2.
antepotens.short: antĕ-pŏtens, entis, adj., superior in power or fortune: voluptatibus gaudiisque antepotens, Plaut.

antequam.full: antĕquam and antĕ quam, v. ante, II. B. 2.

anterides.full: antērĭdes, um, f., = ἀντηρίδες; in archit., counter-props set against a wall to support it, a buttress, Vitr. 10, 1.

anteridion.full: antērĭdĭon, i, dim. n., = ἀντηρίδιον, a little prop or support, Vitr. 10, 17 fin. (dub.).

anterior.full: antĕrĭor, ōris, adj. comp. [ante] (only in late Lat.), that is before, foremost: pars. Amm. 16, 8; 25, 3.—Of time, previous, former, anterior: litterae tuae, Symm. Ep. 6, 59: reges, Sulp. Sev. Hist. Sacr. 1, 52 al.— * Adv.: antĕrĭus, before, Sid. Ep. 2, 9.

anteros.full: Antĕrōs, ōtis, m., = Ἀντέρως (an opponent of Eros) An avenger of slighted love, Cic. N. D. 3, 23, 60.— A kind of amethyst, Plin. 37, 9, 40, § 123.— A slave of Atticus, Cic. Att. 9, 14, 3; 11, 1, 1.
anteros.short: Antĕrōs, ōtis, m., = Ἀντέρως (an opponent of Eros) An avenger of slighted love, Cic.

antes.full: antes, ium, m. etym. unc., perh. from ante, as before, over against, one another, rows, e. g. of vines, Verg. G. 2, 417, cf. Paul. ex. Fest. p. 16 Müll.—Also of plants, Col. 10, 376.—Of ranks of soldiers, Cato ap. Philarg. ad Verg. G. 2, 417.

antescholanus.full: antĕ-schŏlānus, i. m. schola, a kind of teacher, Petr. 81.

antescolarius.full: antescŏlārius, ii, m., same as foregoing: ANTE SCOLARIS VIRGINVM (Vestalium), Inscr. Orell. 1175.
antescolarius.short: antescŏlārius, ii, m., same as foregoing: ANTE SCOLARIS VIRGINVM (Vestalium), Inscr.

antesignanus.full: antĕ-signānus, i, m. signum, that is before the standard; hence, Lit.: antesignant (sc. milites), a chosen band of Roman soldiers who fought before the standards, and served for their defence, Caes. B. C. 1, 43; 1, 57; Liv. 22, 5; 9, 39; Varr. ap. Non. p. 553, 10.— Transf., a leader, commander: in acie Pharsalicā, Cic. Phil. 2, 29; so App. M. 4, p. 147, 12.

antesto.full: ante-sto or anti-sto, stĕti, 1, v. n., to stand before, only in a trop. signif., to excel, be superior to; with dat. or acc.; also absol., to distinguish one's self, to be distinguished: brassica, quae omnibus holeribus antistat, Cato, R. R. 156: Crotoniatae omnibus corporum viribus et dignitatibus antestiterunt, Cic. Inv. 2, 12 B. and K.: quanto antestaret eloquentia innocentiae, Nep. Arist. 1, 2 Halm: virtute ceteris, Claud, Quadrig. ap. Gell. 9, 13: aliquem, Met. Numid. ap. Gell. 12, 9: Scand

antestor.full: antestor, ātus, 1, v. dep [acc. to Corssen, Ausspr. II. p. 564, from an-, the Gr. ἀνά, as in anhelo, q. v. fin., and testor; acc. to others, from ante and testor], a word peculiar to judicial proceedings, to call up as a witness before the opening of the cause, to call as a witness (the formula was: licet antestari? and the person gave his assent by offering the tip of his ear, which the summoner touched; cf. Smith, Dict. Antiq.); so in 1 Fragm. in XII. Tab.: SI. IN. IVS. VOCAT. NI. IT. ANTESTAT

anteurbana.full: antĕurbāna, ōrum, n.: anteurbana: praedia urbi propinqua, Paul. ex Fest. p. 8 Müll.
anteurbana.short: antĕurbāna, ōrum, n.: anteurbana: praedia urbi propinqua, Paul.

antevenio.full: antē-vĕnĭo, vēni, ventum, 4, v. n., to come before, get the start of, anticipate. Lit., with dat. or acc. (cf. Rudd. II. p. 137): temport, Plaut. Trin. 4, 2, 66 (tempus, Claud. 23, 152): exercitum, Sall. J. 48, 2; so id. ib. 56, 2: consilia et insidias (hostium), to thwart, id. ib. 88, 2.—Pass.: omni tempore anteventum est, Cato ap. Non. p. 87, 17.— Trop., to exceed, surpass, excel (very rare): amor omnibus rebus antevenit, Plaut. Cas. 2, 3, 1: per virtutem nobilitatem, Sall. J. 4, 7.— Also, abs

anteventulus.full: antĕ-ventŭlus, a, um, adj. venio, coming before, hanging before, = antependulus (perh. only in App.): comae, App. M. 9, 231, 5: crines, id. Flor. 3, p. 342, 2 Elm.

anteversio.full: antĕversĭo, ōnis, f. anteverto, an anticipating, preventing: anteversio et praegressus, Amm. 21, 5 fin.

anteverto.full: antĕ-verto (archaic -vor-), ti, sum, 3, v. a. (as dep antevortar, Plaut. Bacch. 3, 5, 1), to place one's self before, to go or come before, to precede. Lit.: maerores antevortunt gaudiis, Plaut. Capt. 4, 2, 60: stella tum antevertens, tum subsequens, Cic. N. D. 2, 20, 53: itaque antevertit, id. Mil. 17.— Trop. To anticipate: miror, ubi ego huic antevorterim, * Ter. Eun. 4, 5, 12: mihi Fannius antevertit, Cic. Am. 4, 16: damnationem veneno, Tac. A. 13, 30.— To prefer, to place before: rebus aliis

antevio.full: antĕ-vĭo, āre, v. n. via, to go before, Ven. Fort. 4, 26.

antevolo.full: antĕ-vŏlo, āre, v. n., to fly before; with acc. (only post-Aug.; in Verg. A. 9, 47, and 12, 455 Rib., it is written apart, ante volo): currum, Stat. Th. 3, 427: agmen, Sil. 12, 600: Zephyros, Claud. Phoen. 21.

antevorta.full: Antĕ-vorta, ae, f. verto, the name of a goddess who reminds men of things past (opp. Postvorta), Macr. S. 1, 7 (in Ov. F. 1, 633, and Serv. ad Verg. A. 8, 336, called Porrima).

anthalium.full: anthălĭum, ii, n., = ἀνθάλιον, a kind of bulbous esculent root: Cyperus esculentus, Linn.; Plin. 21, 15, 52, § 88.
anthalium.short: anthălĭum, ii, n., = ἀνθάλιον, a kind of bulbous esculent root: Cyperus esculentus, Linn.;

anthedon1.full: anthēdon, ŏnis, f., = ἀνθηδών, a species of the medlar-tree, the Greek medlar: Mespilus tanacetifolia, Linn.; Plin. 15, 20, 22, § 84.
anthedon1.short: anthēdon, ŏnis, f., = ἀνθηδών, a species of the medlar-tree, the Greek medlar: Mespilus tanacetifolia, Linn.;

anthedon2.full: Anthēdon, ŏnis, f., = Ἀνθηδών, A town and harbor in Bœotia, opposite the island Eubœa (hence called Euboica), the birthplace of Glaucus, and noted for its great traffic in sponges, now Paleo-kastro, Ov. M. 13, 905; 7, 232; cf. Mann. Gr. 220.— Hence, Anthēdŏnĭus, a, um, adj., Anthedonic, Stat. Th. 9, 291; 9, 328.— A maritime town in Palestine, afterwards called Agrippias, Plin. 5, 13, 14, § 68.— A port on the Saronic Gulf, belonging to Argolis, Plin. 4, 5, 9, § 18.
anthedon2.short: Anthēdon, ŏnis, f., = Ἀνθηδών, A town and harbor in Bœotia, opposite the island Eubœa (hence called Euboica), the birthplace of Glaucus, and noted for its great traffic in sponges, now Paleo-kastro, Ov.

anthemis.full: anthĕmis, ĭdis, f., = ἀνθεμίς, the herb chamomile: Anthemis, Linn.; Plin. 22, 21, 26, § 53.
anthemis.short: anthĕmis, ĭdis, f., = ἀνθεμίς, the herb chamomile: Anthemis, Linn.;

anthemum.full: anthĕmum, i, n., = ἄνθεμον, an herb good for calculi, Plin. 26, 8, 55, § 9.
anthemum.short: anthĕmum, i, n., = ἄνθεμον, an herb good for calculi, Plin.

anthemus.full: Anthĕmūs, untis, f., = Ἀνθεμοῦς. A region in Macedonia, Plin. 4, 10, 17, § 36. — A town in Mesopotamia, Plin. 6, 26, 30, § 118; called also Anthĕmūsĭăs, ădis (sc. urbs), Tac. A. 6, 41.— A river of Colchis, Plin. 6, 5, 5, § 15.—Hence, Anthĕ-mūsĭus, a, um, adj., pertaining to Anthemus, Eutr. 8, 2; Amm. 14, 9.

anthemusia.full: Anthĕmūsia, ae, f., a town in Macedonia, Plin. 5, 24, 21, § 86; also called An-themus, q. v.
anthemusia.short: Anthĕmūsia, ae, f., a town in Macedonia, Plin.

anthemusa.full: Anthĕmūsa, ae, f., an old name of the island of Samos, Plin. 5, 31, 37, § 135.
anthemusa.short: Anthĕmūsa, ae, f., an old name of the island of Samos, Plin.

anthera.full: anthēra, ae, f., = ἀνθηρά (blooming), a medicine composed of flowers, Cels. 6, 11 med.; Plin. 24, 9, 42, § 69.
anthera.short: anthēra, ae, f., = ἀνθηρά (blooming), a medicine composed of flowers, Cels.

anthericos.full: anthĕrĭcos, i, m., = ἀνθέρικος, the stalk of the asphodel, Plin. 21, 17, 68, § 109; 22, 22, 32, § 67.
anthericos.short: anthĕrĭcos, i, m., = ἀνθέρικος, the stalk of the asphodel, Plin.

anthias.full: anthĭas, ae, m., = ἀνθίας, a sea-fish unknown to us, which was difficult to catch, Plin. 9, 59, 85, § 180; Ov. Hal. 45.
anthias.short: anthĭas, ae, m., = ἀνθίας, a sea-fish unknown to us, which was difficult to catch, Plin.

anthinus.full: anthĭnus, a, um, adj., = ἀνθινός, gathered from flowers: mel, Plin. 11, 14, 14, § 34.
anthinus.short: anthĭnus, a, um, adj., = ἀνθινός, gathered from flowers: mel, Plin.

anthologica.full: anthŏlŏgĭca, ōrum, n., = ἀνθολογικά, anthology, a work consisting of choice thoughts, proverbs, poems, etc., Plin. 21, 3, 9, § 13.
anthologica.short: anthŏlŏgĭca, ōrum, n., = ἀνθολογικά, anthology, a work consisting of choice thoughts, proverbs, poems, etc., Plin.

anthracinus.full: anthrăcĭnus, a, um, adj., = ἀνθρἀκινος, coal-black, Varr. ap. Non. p. 550, 5.
anthracinus.short: anthrăcĭnus, a, um, adj., = ἀνθρἀκινος, coal-black, Varr.

anthracites.full: anthrăcītes, ae, m., = ἀνθρακίτης, a kind of blood-stone, Plin. 36, 20, 38, § 148.
anthracites.short: anthrăcītes, ae, m., = ἀνθρακίτης, a kind of blood-stone, Plin.

anthracitis.full: anthrăcītis, ĭdis, f., = ἀνθρακῖτις, a kind of carbuncle, the coal-carbuncle, Plin. 37, 7, 27, § 99; in Sol. 37 fin. called an-thrăcĭas, ae, m., = ἀνθρακίας.
anthracitis.short: anthrăcītis, ĭdis, f., = ἀνθρακῖτις, a kind of carbuncle, the coal-carbuncle, Plin.

anthrax1.full: anthrax, ăcis, m., = ἄνθραξ (coal). Natural cinnabar (the color of which is like a burning coal), Vitr. 7, 8.— In medic., a virulent ulcer (in pure Lat., carbunculus), Aem. Macr. de Herb. c. de Sabina.

anthrax2.full: Anthrax. ăcis, m., = Ἄνθραξ, name of a slave, Plaut. Aul. 2, 4, 8.

anthriscus.full: anthriscus, i, f., or -um, i, n., = ἄνθρισκον, the southern chervil: Scandix australis, Linn.; Plin. 22, 22, 38, § 81; 21, 15, 52, § 89.
anthriscus.short: anthriscus, i, f., or -um, i, n., = ἄνθρισκον, the southern chervil: Scandix australis, Linn.;

anthropographos.full: anthrōpō^grăphŏs, i, m., = ἀνθρωπογράφος, portrait-painter, an epithet of the painter Dionysius, Plin. 35, 10, 37, § 113.
anthropographos.short: anthrōpō^grăphŏs, i, m., = ἀνθρωπογράφος, portrait-painter, an epithet of the painter Dionysius, Plin.

anthropolatra.full: anthrōpŏlā^tra, ae, m., = ἀνθρωπολάτρης, a man-worshipper, Cod. Just. 1, 1, 5; 1, 1, 6.
anthropolatra.short: anthrōpŏlā^tra, ae, m., = ἀνθρωπολάτρης, a man-worshipper, Cod.

anthropomorphitae.full: anthrōpŏmorphītae, ārum, m., = ἀνθρωπομορφῖται, heretics that attributed to God a human form, Aug. Haeres. ad Quod vult Deum.—Hence, anthrōpŏmor-phītĭcus, a, um, adj., professing the error of such heretics: haeresis, Isid. Orig. 8, 5.
anthropomorphitae.short: anthrōpŏmorphītae, ārum, m., = ἀνθρωπομορφῖται, heretics that attributed to God a human form, Aug.

anthropophagus.full: anthrōpŏphăgus, i, m., = ἀνθρωποφάγος, a man-eater, a cannibal, Plin. 4, 12, 26, § 88; 6, 17, 20, § 53; 6, 30, 35, § 195.
anthropophagus.short: anthrōpŏphăgus, i, m., = ἀνθρωποφάγος, a man-eater, a cannibal, Plin.

anthus.full: anthus, i, m., = ἄνθος (cf. τὸ ἄνθος = blossom, brilliancy), a small bird, prob. the yellow wagtail: Motacilla flava, Linn.; Plin. 10, 42, 57, § 116; 10, 74, 95, § 206.

anthyllion.full: anthyllĭon, ii, n., = ἀνθύλλιον, a plant, acc. to Sprengel, the Cretan pitchplant: Cressa Cretica, Linn.; Plin. 26, 8, 51, § 84 (called in Plin. 21, 99, 103, § 175, also anthyllum).
anthyllion.short: anthyllĭon, ii, n., = ἀνθύλλιον, a plant, acc.

anthyllis.full: anthyllis, ïdis, f., = ἀνθυλλίς, a plant, acc. to Sprengel, the musk-ivy: Teucrium iva, Linn.; Plin. 26, 15, 90, § 160.
anthyllis.short: anthyllis, ïdis, f., = ἀνθυλλίς, a plant, acc.

anthypophora.full: anthўpŏphŏra, ae, f., = ἀνθυποφορά, a rhetorical figure in which one anticipates the arguments of his antagonist, and refutes them, Sen. Contr. 1, 7 (in Quint. 9, 2, 106, and id. 9, 3, 87, written as Greek, Halm).
anthypophora.short: anthўpŏphŏra, ae, f., = ἀνθυποφορά, a rhetorical figure in which one anticipates the arguments of his antagonist, and refutes them, Sen.

antiae.full: antiae, ārum, f. (cf. Charis. p. 20 P.) [ante], the hair growing upon the forehead, forelock; of Apollo, App. Flor. 3, p. 342, 1; of lions, Tert. Pall. 4; of the hair of women, Paul. ex Fest. s. h. v. p. 15 Müll.

antibacchius.full: antĭbacchīus, i, adj., = ἀντιβακχεῖ ος. Pes, a poetical foot, the antibacchus or reversed Bacchius, ˘¯¯ (e. g. nĕpō tēs), Ter. Maur. p. 2414 P. (acc. to other ¯¯˘).— Versus, a verse composed of this foot, Diom. p. 513 P.; called palimbac chius by Quint. 9, 4, 82; Isid. Orig. 1, 16, p. 30 Lind.

antibasis.full: antĭbăsis (antĕb-), is, f., = ἀντίβασις (counter-basis), the hindmost small pillar at the pedestal of the ballista, Vitr. 10, 17; cf. id. 10, 15.
antibasis.short: antĭbăsis (antĕb-), is, f., = ἀντίβασις (counter-basis), the hindmost small pillar at the pedestal of the ballista, Vitr.

antiboreus.full: antĭbŏrēus, a, um, adj., = ἀντιβόρειος, turned toward the north: horologium, Vitr. 9, 9.
antiboreus.short: antĭbŏrēus, a, um, adj., = ἀντιβόρειος, turned toward the north: horologium, Vitr.

anticategoria.full: antĭcătēgŏrĭa, ae, f., = ἀντικατηγορία, a recrimination, counter-plea, Aug. 3: contra Cresc. 26; 74 fin. (in Quint. 3, 10, 4, and 7, 2, 9, written as Greek, Halm).
anticategoria.short: antĭcătēgŏrĭa, ae, f., = ἀντικατηγορία, a recrimination, counter-plea, Aug.

anticato.full: Antĭcăto, ōnis, m., the title of Cœsar's reply to Cicero's panegyric of Cato Uticensis, the title of which was Cato, Quint. 1, 5, 68; Juv. 6, 337; Gell. 4, 16; cf. Bähr, Lit. Gesch. 267 and 462; Teuffel, Rom. Lit. § 182, 7.
anticato.short: Antĭcăto, ōnis, m., the title of Cœsar's reply to Cicero's panegyric of Cato Uticensis, the title of which was Cato, Quint.

antichristus.full: Antī^christus, i, m., = Ἀντίχριστος, the Antichrist (eccl. Lat.); Vulg. 1 Joan. 2, 18; 2, 22; 4, 3; ib. 2 Joan. 7; very freq. in the Church fathers.
antichristus.short: Antī^christus, i, m., = Ἀντίχριστος, the Antichrist (eccl.

antichthones.full: antichthŏnes, um, m., = ἀντίχθονες, = antipodes (ἀντίπόδες), the antipodes Plin. 6, 22, 24, § 81; Mel. 1, 1; 1, 9.
antichthones.short: antichthŏnes, um, m., = ἀντίχθονες, = antipodes (ἀντίπόδες), the antipodes Plin.

anticipatio.full: antĭcĭpātĭo, ōnis, f. anticipo. A preconception, the innate notion of a thing formed before receiving instruction concerning it, Gr. πρόληψις (only in Cic.): deorum, Cic. N. D. 1, 16, 43: sive anticipatio sive praenotio deorum, id. ib. 1, 17, 43.— The first movements of the body before walking, Arn. 3, p. 107.— In rhet., a figure of speech, anticipation = occupatio and πρόληψις, Jul. Ruf. p. 30 Pith.

anticipo.full: antĭ-cĭpo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. ante-capio. To take before one or before the time, to anticipate something. With acc.: vigilias, Vulg. Psa. 76, 5: nos, ib. ib. 78, 8: ita est informatum anticipatumque mentibus nostris, etc., already known, innate, Cic. N. D. 1, 27, 76 (cf. anticipatio; B. and K. here reject anticipatumque): qui anticipes ejus rei molestiam, quam triduo sciturus sis, id. Att. 8, 14: anticipata via, travelled over before, Ov. M. 3, 234: mortem, Suet. Tib. 61: saeculares anticipati

anticlea.full: Anticlēa or -īa, ae, f., = Ἀντικλεία, the mother of Ulysses, Hyg. Fab. 201; App. de Deo Socr. 24, p. 55; Serv. ad Verg. A. 6, 529; in Cicero, erroneously put for the nurse of Ulysses, Euryclea, Cic. Tusc. 5, 16, 46.
anticlea.short: Anticlēa or -īa, ae, f., = Ἀντικλεία, the mother of Ulysses, Hyg.

anticus.full: antīcus, a, um, adj. ante, that is in front, foremost, Paul. ex Fest. p. 220 Müll.: antica (pars) ad meridiem, postica ad septentrionem, Varr. L. L. 7, § 7 Müll.: pars, * Cic. Tim. 10.

anticyra.full: Antĭcўra, ae, f., = Ἀντίκιρρα, Dicaearch. and Strabo; Ἀντίκυρρα, Eustath.; and Ἀντίκυρα, which the Romans followed. A town in Phocis, on a peninsula (which Pliny and Gellius erroneously call an island), on a bay of the Corinthian Gulf, now Aspra Spitia, famous for hellebore; hence much frequented by hypochondriacs, Ov. P. 4, 3, 54; Liv. 26, 26; 28, 8; 30, 18; 32, 18; Plin. 22, 25, 64, § 133; 25, 5, 21, § 52.— A town on the Sinus Maliacus, also noted for hellebore, but less famous than the forego

antidactylus.full: antĭdactўlus, a, um, adj., = ἀντιδάκτυλος: pes, a reversed dactyl, ˘˘¯ (e. g. lĕgĕrēnt), Mar. Vict. p. 2488 P.
antidactylus.short: antĭdactўlus, a, um, adj., = ἀντιδάκτυλος: pes, a reversed dactyl, ˘˘¯ (e.

antidotum.full: antĭdŏtum, i, n., and -us or -ŏs, i, f. (cf. Scrib. Larg. Comp. 99, 106, and passages cited there), = ἀντίδοτον (-ος), a counterpoison. Lit.: antidota raro, sed interdum necessaria sunt, Cels. 5, 23; Phaedr. 1, 14, 3: se antidotum daturum, Quint. 7, 2, 25; so Suet. Calig. 23; id. Ner. 34 al.: antidotus, Gell. 17, 16; Dig. 18, 1, 35.—Sometimes, in gen., an antidote, remedy, Spart. Hadr. 23.— Trop.: antidotum adversus Caesarem, Suet. Calig. 29.
antidotum.short: antĭdŏtum, i, n., and -us or -ŏs, i, f.

antigerio.full: antigerio, an ancient word for valde, Paul. ex Fest. p. 8 Müll. [perh. antegero]; cf. Quint. 1, 6, 40; 8, 3, 25.
antigerio.short: antigerio, an ancient word for valde, Paul.

antignotus.full: Antignōtus, i, m., = Ἀντίγνωτος, an artist that cast statues, Plin. 34, 8, 19, § 86.
antignotus.short: Antignōtus, i, m., = Ἀντίγνωτος, an artist that cast statues, Plin.

antigone.full: Antĭgŏnē, ēs, or Antĭgŏna, ae, f., = Ἀντιγονη. A daughter of the Theban king Œdipus, Hyg. Fab. 72: Antigones, Juv. 8, 228.— A daughter of the Trojan king Laomedon: Antigonen, Ov. M. 6, 93; Serv. ad Verg. G. 2, 320.
antigone.short: Antĭgŏnē, ēs, or Antĭgŏna, ae, f., = Ἀντιγονη.

antigonea.full: Antĭgŏnēa, ae, f., = Ἀντιγόνεια or Ἀντιγονία, the name of several towns. In Epirus, Liv. 32, 5; 43, 23.—Hence, An-tĭgŏnensis: ager, Liv. 43, 23; and An-tĭgŏnenses, ium, m., its inhabitants, Plin. 4, praef. 1, 1.— In Macedonia, Liv. 44, 10.— In Arcadia, Plin. 4, 6, 10, § 20.— In Troas, afterwards called Alexandria, Plin. 5, 30, 33, § 124.
antigonea.short: Antĭgŏnēa, ae, f., = Ἀντιγόνεια or Ἀντιγονία, the name of several towns.

antigonus.full: Antĭgŏnus, i, m., = Ἀντίγονος. The name of several kings after Alexander the Great. Antigonus I., father of Demetrius Poliorcetes, Nep. Eum. 5, 7; Cic. Off. 2, 14, 48; Just. 13.— Antigonus Gonatas, son of Demetrius Poliorcetes, Just. 17, 1; 24, 1 al.— Antigonus Doson, Liv. 40, 54; Just. 28, 3.— Of other persons. Antigonus of Cymœ, a writer on Agriculture, Varr. R. R. 1, 1, 8, Col. 1, 1, 9.— A plastic artist, Plin. 34, 8, 19, § 84.— A messenger of king Deiotarus, Cic. Deiot. 15, 41.— A Roman free

antilibanus.full: Antĭlĭbănus, i, m., = Ἀντιλίβανος, a mountain range in Phœnicia, opposite to Libanus, now Jebel esh-Shurky, Cic. Att. 2, 16; cf. Mann. Phoen. 270 sq.
antilibanus.short: Antĭlĭbănus, i, m., = Ἀντιλίβανος, a mountain range in Phœnicia, opposite to Libanus, now Jebel esh-Shurky, Cic.

antilochus.full: Antĭlŏchus, i, m., = Ἀντίλοχος, a son of Nestor, slain by Hector before Troy, Hor. C. 2, 9, 14; Ov. H. 1, 15; Juv. 10, 253.
antilochus.short: Antĭlŏchus, i, m., = Ἀντίλοχος, a son of Nestor, slain by Hector before Troy, Hor.

antimachus.full: Antĭmăchus, i, m., = Ἀντίμαχος. A Greek poet of Colophon, a contemporary of Socrates and Plato, and author of a Thebaid, Cic. Brut. 51, 191; Cat. 95, 10; Prop. 3, 32, 45.— A centaur slain by Cœneus in the contest with the Lapithœ, Ov. M. 12, 460. — A son of Ægyptus, murdered by his bride, Idæa, Hyg. Fab. 170.— A statuary, Plin. 34, 8, 19, § 86.

antimetabole.full: antĭmĕtăbŏlē, ēs, f., = ἀντιμεταβολή, a rhet. fig., a reciprocal interchange, in Auct. ad Her. 4, 28, 39, called commutatio, e. g.: non ut edam vivo, sed ut vivam edo, Isid. Orig. 2, 21, p. 81 Lind. (in Quint. 9, 3, 85, written as Greek, Halm).
antimetabole.short: antĭmĕtăbŏlē, ēs, f., = ἀντιμεταβολή, a rhet.

antinomia.full: antĭnŏmĭa, ae, f., = ἀντινομία, a contradiction between laws, Quint. 7, 7, 1; so id. 7, 10, 2; 3, 6, 45.
antinomia.short: antĭnŏmĭa, ae, f., = ἀντινομία, a contradiction between laws, Quint.

antiochea.full: Antĭŏchēa or Antĭŏchīa (like Alexandrēa, Alexandrīa, q. v.; cf. Prisc. p. 588 P., and Ochsn. Eclog. 143), ae, f., = Ἀντιόχεια, Antioch. The name of several cities. The most distinguished is that founded by Seleucus Nicator, and named after his father Antiochus; the chief town of Syria, on the Orontes, now Antakia, Just. 15, 4; Cic. Arch. 3, 4; cf. Mann. Syr. 363.— A town in Caria, on the Mœander; also called ΙΙυθόπολις, Liv. 38, 13; Plin. 5, 29, 29, § 108.— In Mesopotamia, afterwards called Edes
antiochea.short: Antĭŏchēa or Antĭŏchīa (like Alexandrēa, Alexandrīa, q.

antiochensis1.full: Antĭŏchensis, e, adj. Antiochia, of or belonging to Antiochia: plebs, Amm. 14, 7.—Hence, in plur.: Antĭŏchenses, ium, m., the inhabitants of Antiochia, Caes. B. C. 3, 102; Tac. H. 2, 80; 2, 82 al.

antiochensis2.full: Antĭŏchensis, e, adj. Antiochus, of or belonging to King Antiochus: pecunia, received from him, Val. Max. 3, 7, 1 (cf. 2. Antiochenus).

antiochenus1.full: Antĭŏchēnus, a, um, adj. Antiochia, of or belonging to Antiochia: ager, Ven. Fort. 8, 5 fin.

antiochenus2.full: Antĭŏchēnus, a, um, adj. Antiochus, of or belonging to King Antiochus: pecunia, received from him, Gell. 4, 18; 7, 19 fin. (cf. 2. Antiochensis).

antiocheus.full: Antĭŏchēus or -īus, a, um, adj., = Ἀντιόχειος, of or pertaining to the philosopher Antiochus: ista Antiochea contemnit, Cic. Ac. 2, 36, 115; id. Att. 13, 19.
antiocheus.short: Antĭŏchēus or -īus, a, um, adj., = Ἀντιόχειος, of or pertaining to the philosopher Antiochus: ista Antiochea contemnit, Cic.

antiochinus.full: Antĭŏchīnus, a, um, adj. Antiochus. Of King Antiochus Magnus: bellum, Cic. Phil. 11, 7, 17; cf. Fasti Capitol. Baiter, p. xli.— Of or pertaining to the philosopher Antiochus, the founder of the fifth Academy, Cic. Fam. 9, 8, 1.

antiochus.full: Antĭŏchus, i, m., = Ἀντίοχος. The name of several Syrian kings, among whom Antiochus Magnus was most distinguished, on account of his war with the Romans, Liv. 31, 14; 33, 13 sq. al.; Nep. Hann. 2, 7; Cic. de Or. 2, 18, 75; Cic. Verr. 1, 21; id. Sest. 27; id. Deiot. 13 al.— The name of an Academic philosopher, a teacher of Cicero and Brutus, Cic. Ac. 2, 43, 132; id. N. D. 1, 3, 6; id. Brut. 91, 315.

antiopa.full: Antĭŏpa, ae, f., = Ἀντιόπη. A daughter of Nycteus, wife of Lycus, king of Thebes, mother of Amphion and Zethus. She was bound to the neck of a bull by Dirce, whom Lycus had married, but was released by her sons, Hyg. Fab. 7.— The name of a tragedy of Pacuvius, Cic. Fin. 1, 2, 4; Pers. 1, 77.

antipater.full: Antĭpăter, tri (later form, ANTIPATRVS, Inscr. Orell. 4727), m., = Ἀντίπατρος. One of the generals and successors of Alexander the Great, the father of Cassander, Just. 11, 7; 11, 12; 13, 5 al.; Cic. Off. 2, 14, 48.— His grandson, son of Cassander, and son-in-law of Lysimachus, Just. 16, 1.— The name of several philosophers. Of a Cyrenaic, Cic. Tusc. 5, 37, 107.— Of a Stoic, Cic. Off. 3, 12, 51; id. Ac. 2, 6, 17; id. Div. 1, 3; 1, 20.— Of a contemporary of Cicero, from Tyre, Cic. Off. 2, 24, 86.

antipathes1.full: antĭpăthēs, is, f., = ἀντιπαθής (serving as remedy for suffering), a black kind of coral used as a preventive of witchcraft, Plin. 37, 10, 54, § 145.
antipathes1.short: antĭpăthēs, is, f., = ἀντιπαθής (serving as remedy for suffering), a black kind of coral used as a preventive of witchcraft, Plin.

antipathes2.full: antĭpăthĕs, is, n., = ἀντιπαθές, a charm against pain, Lael. ap. App. Mag. 30.
antipathes2.short: antĭpăthĕs, is, n., = ἀντιπαθές, a charm against pain, Lael.

antipathia.full: antĭpăthīa, ae, f., = ἀντιπάθεια, the natural aversion of two things to each other, antipathy (opp. concordia), Plin. 37, 4, 15, § 59; so id. 20, 4, 13, § 28; 24, 9, 41, § 67 al.
antipathia.short: antĭpăthīa, ae, f., = ἀντιπάθεια, the natural aversion of two things to each other, antipathy (opp.

antipatria.full: Antĭpā^trĭa, ae, f., = Ἀντιπατρία, a town in Macedonia, on the borders of Illyria, Liv. 31, 27.
antipatria.short: Antĭpā^trĭa, ae, f., = Ἀντιπατρία, a town in Macedonia, on the borders of Illyria, Liv.

antiphates.full: Antĭphătes, ae, m., = Ἀντιφάτης. A king of the Lœstrygones, who sunk the fleet of the Greeks returning from Troy with Ulysses, and devoured one of his companions, Ov. M. 14, 234 sq.; Juv. 14, 20; Sil. 8, 531.— A son of Sarpedon, slain by Turnus, Verg. A. 9, 696.

antipherna.full: antĭpherna, ōrum, n., = ἀντίφερνα, the return-present which the bridegroom brought to the bride, Cod. Just. 5, 3, 20.
antipherna.short: antĭpherna, ōrum, n., = ἀντίφερνα, the return-present which the bridegroom brought to the bride, Cod.

antiphon.full: Antĭphōn, ōntis, m., = Ἀντιφῶν. A renowned sophist of Rhamnus, a contemporary of Socrates, Cic. Brut. 12, 47; Quint. 3, 1, 11; 12, 10, 22.— The name of an interpreter of dreams, Cic. Div. 1, 20; 1, 51.

antiphrasis.full: antĭphrăsis (better written as Gr.), is, f., = αντίφρασις, the use of a word in a sense opposite to its proper meaning; as, lucus, quod minime luceat, Diom. p. 458 P.; cf. Charis. p. 247 P. al.
antiphrasis.short: antĭphrăsis (better written as Gr.), is, f., = αντίφρασις, the use of a word in a sense opposite to its proper meaning;

antipodes.full: antĭpŏdes, um, m., = ἀντίποδες, the antipodes, Lact. 3, 23; Aug. Civ. Dei, 16, 9; Serv. ad Verg. A. 6, 532; hence ironic. of banqueters who turn night to day, Sen. Ep. 122 (in Cic. Ac. 2, 39, 123, written as Greek).
antipodes.short: antĭpŏdes, um, m., = ἀντίποδες, the antipodes, Lact.

antipolis.full: Antĭpŏlis, is, f., = Ἀντίπολις. A city in Gaul, now Antibes, Plin. 3, 4, 5, § 35; Mel. 2, 5.—Hence, Antĭpŏlĭtānus, a, um, adj., of or from Antipolis: thynni, found in that region, Mart. 13, 103; cf. id. 4, 89.— An old settlement in Latium, afterwards Janiculum, Plin. 3, 5, 9, § 68.

antiptosis.full: antiptōsis, is, f., = ἀντίπτωσις, a gram. fig., the putting of one case for another, Serv. ad Verg. A. 1, 577; 2, 283; 6, 727; 10, 653; 11, 56 al.
antiptosis.short: antiptōsis, is, f., = ἀντίπτωσις, a gram.

antiquarius.full: antīquārĭus, a, um, adj. antiquus, pertaining to antiquity. Adj.: ars, the art of reading and copying ancient MSS., Hier. Ep. ad Flor. 5, 1.—Hence, Subst.: antīquārĭus, ii, m. One that is fond of or employs himself about antiquities, an antiquarian, antiquary (post-Aug.): nec quemquam adeo antiquarium puto, ut, etc., Tac. Or. 21; * Suet. Aug. 86.—Also * antī-quārĭa, ae, f., she that is fond of antiquity, a female antiquarian, Juv. 6, 454.— One that understands reading and copying ancient MSS., C

antiquatio.full: antīquātĭo, ōnis, f. antiquo; in judicial lang., an abrogating, annulling, repealing: poenarum, Cod. Th. 6, 55, 4.

antiquitas.full: antīquĭtas, ātis, f. antiquus, the quality of being antiquus, age, antiquity (class., but only in prose). In gen.: antiquitas generis, Cic. Font. 14, 31; so Nep. Milt. 1, 1: non vestra (urbs) haec est, quae gloriabatur a diebus pristinis in antiquitate suā? Vulg. Isa. 23, 7.— Spec., ancient time, antiquity. Lit.: fabulae ab ultimā antiquitate repetitae, Cic. Fin. 1, 20, 65: habet ut in aetatibus auctoritatem senectus, sic in exemplis antiquitas, id. Or. 50, 169: antiquitas dat dignitatem verbis,

antiquo.full: antīquo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. antiquus; cf.: veto, vetus. In class. Lat. only a t. t. of civil life, to leave it in its ancient state, to restore a thing to its former condition (antiquare est in modum pristinum reducere, Paul. ex Fest. p. 26 Müll.).—Hence of a bill, to reject it, not to adopt it: legem agrariam antiquari facile passus est, Cic. Off. 2, 21, 73; so Liv. 4, 58; 5, 30, 55 et saep.: Piso operam dat, ut ea rogatio antiquetur, Cic. Att. 1, 13; cf. id. ib. 1, 14; Liv. 31, 6; cf. id. 45,

antiquus.full: antīquus, a, um, adj. a diff. orthog. for anticus, from ante (of that which is before in time, while anticus denotes that which is before in space; cf. Vel. Long. p. 2223 P.), that has been or has been done before, old, ancient, former (opp. novus, that has not previously existed, new; while vetus, that has existed a long time, is opp. recens, that has not been long in existence, recent; cf. Manut. ad Cic. Fam. 11, 21; Lind. ad Plaut. Mil. 3, 1, 154, and id. Capt. 1, 2, 29; Doed. Syn. IV. p. 82

antirrhinon.full: antirrhīnon (-um), i, n., = ἀντίρρινον; also ănarrhīnon, i, n., = ἀνἀρρινον, a plant, wild lion's-mouth: Antirrhinum Orontium, Linn.: antirrhinum, Plin. 25, 10, 80, § 129 Jan; cf. App. Herb. 86.

antisagoge.full: antīsăgōgē, ēs, f., = ἀντεισαγωγή, a figure of speech by which one thing adduced is opposed to another, a counter-assertion, Mart. Cap. 5, p. 172.
antisagoge.short: antīsăgōgē, ēs, f., = ἀντεισαγωγή, a figure of speech by which one thing adduced is opposed to another, a counter-assertion, Mart.

antiscii.full: antiscĭi, ōrum, m., = ἀντίσκιο. (counter-shadows), people on the other side of the equator, whose shadows are cast in the opposite direction from ours, Amm. 22, 15 fin.

antisigma.full: antĭsigmă, ătis, n., = ἀντίσιγμα. A character, etc., which the emperor Claudius wished to introduce into Latin for ps = the Gr. ψ, Prisc. p. 558 P.; cf. Schneid. Gram. 1, 5; Wordsworth's Early Lat. p. 9.— A critical mark, etc., placed before a verse which is to be transposed, Isid. Orig. 1, 20.

antisophista.full: antĭsŏphista, ae, m., = ἀντισοφιστής, a counter-sophist, i. e. a grammarian who takes the opposite side of a question (only post-Aug.), Quint. 11, 3, 127; Suet. Tib. 11; so id. Gram. 9.
antisophista.short: antĭsŏphista, ae, m., = ἀντισοφιστής, a counter-sophist, i.

antispastus.full: antispastus, i, m., = ἀντίσπαστος (reversed), in metre (sc. pes), an antispast, a foot in verse, ˘¯¯˘, i. e. the choriambus reversed, e. g. Mĕdūllīnă, Diom. p. 478 P.; hence: antispasticum metrum, verse consisting of antispasts, id. p. 505 P.
antispastus.short: antispastus, i, m., = ἀντίσπαστος (reversed), in metre (sc.

antispodos.full: antispŏdos, i, f., = ἀντίσποδος, ashes used instead of spodium, Plin. 34, 13, 35, § 133.
antispodos.short: antispŏdos, i, f., = ἀντίσποδος, ashes used instead of spodium, Plin.

antissa.full: Antissa, ae, f., = Ἄντισσα, a town in the southern part of the island of Lesbos, now Kalas Limneonas, Liv. 45, 31; Ov. M. 15, 287; Plin. 5, 31, 39, § 89.—Hence, An-tissaei, ōrum, m., inhabitants of Antissa, Liv. 45, 31.
antissa.short: Antissa, ae, f., = Ἄντισσα, a town in the southern part of the island of Lesbos, now Kalas Limneonas, Liv.

antistatus.full: antistātus, ūs, m. v. antesto, superiority in rank: angelorum, Tert. adv. Val. 13.

antistes.full: antistĕs, ĭtis, m. and f. (fem. also antistĭta, ae, like hospita from hospes, sospita from sospes, clienta from cliens, Inscr. Orell. 2200; cf. Charis. p. 77 P.; Prisc. p. 650 P.) [antisto = antesto, q. v.; pr. adj., standing before], an overseer, president. Lit. In gen. (rare): vindemiatorum, Col. 3, 21, 6: imperii Romani, Tert. Apol. 1. —In fem., a female overseer: latrinarum, Tert. Pall. 4 fin.—Far more freq., Esp., an overseer of a temple, a high-priest: caerimoniarum et sacrorum, Cic. Dom.

antisthenes.full: Antisthĕnes, is and ae, m., = Ἀντισθένης, a pupil of Socrates, teacher of Diogenes, and founder of the Cynic philosophy: Antisthenes, Cic. N. D. 1, 13, 32; so id. de Or. 3, 17, 62.—In plur.: Antisthenae multi, Gell. 14, 1, 29.
antisthenes.short: Antisthĕnes, is and ae, m., = Ἀντισθένης, a pupil of Socrates, teacher of Diogenes, and founder of the Cynic philosophy: Antisthenes, Cic.

antistitium.full: antistĭtĭum, ii, n. antistes, the office of an antistes, the chief-priest's office, Mart. Cap. 2, p. 34.

antistrophe.full: antistrŏphē, ēs, f., = ἀντιστροφή. In the chorus of the Greek and Roman tragedy, the antistrophe answering to the strophe, Victorin. p. 2051 P.— A rhetorical figure, when several parts of a period end with the same word = conversio, q. v.; Mart. Cap. 5, p. 175; Jul. Rufin. 35, p. 211.

antithesis.full: antĭthĕsis, is, f., = ἀντίθεσις, a gram. ng., the putting of one letter for another (e. g. olli for illi, impete for impetu), Charis. p. 249 P.; Diom. p. 437 P.
antithesis.short: antĭthĕsis, is, f., = ἀντίθεσις, a gram.

antitheton.full: antĭthĕton, i, n., = ἀντίθετον, opposition, antithesis, a rhetor. fig., Cic. Or. 50, 166; Pers. 1, 85 (e. g. frigida pugnabant calidis, humentia siccis, Ov. M. 1, 19; cf. Quint. 9, 3, 81).
antitheton.short: antĭthĕton, i, n., = ἀντίθετον, opposition, antithesis, a rhetor.

antitheus.full: antĭthĕus, i, m., = ἀντίθεος (a counter-deity), one who pretends to be God, Arn. 4, p. 134.—Hence, the devil, Lact. 2, 9.
antitheus.short: antĭthĕus, i, m., = ἀντίθεος (a counter-deity), one who pretends to be God, Arn.

antium.full: Antĭum, ii, n., = Ἄντιον. An ancient town in Latium distinguished for the temple of Fortune (Hor. C. 1, 35, 1), not far from the sea-coast, now Porto d'Anzio, the birthplace of Nero, Plin. 3, 5, 9, § 27; Inscr. Orell. 1738; cf. Mann. Ital. 1, 618; Müll. Roms Campagn. 2, 271 sq.—Hence, Derivv. Antĭānus, a, um, adj., Antian: Hercules Antianus, honored at Antium, Cic. Fragm. ap. Non. p. 284, 1.— Antĭas, ātis, adj., of or belonging to Antium, Antian, Liv. 8, 14; so id. 6, 9; 8, 12 al.—So, Valerius A

antius.full: Antĭus, a, um, adj., name of a Roman gens; hence, Antia lex (by Antius Restio), against prodigality, Gell. 2, 24; Macr. S. 2, 13.
antius.short: Antĭus, a, um, adj., name of a Roman gens;

antizeugmenon.full: antizeugmĕnon, i, n., = ἀντιζεύγμενον, a grammatical figure, by which several clauses are referred to one verb, Mart. Cap. 5, p. 176.
antizeugmenon.short: antizeugmĕnon, i, n., = ἀντιζεύγμενον, a grammatical figure, by which several clauses are referred to one verb, Mart.

antlia.full: antlĭa, ae, f., = ἀντία, a machine for drawing water, worked with the foot, a pump, Mart. 9, 14, 3; * Suet. Tib. 51.
antlia.short: antlĭa, ae, f., = ἀντία, a machine for drawing water, worked with the foot, a pump, Mart.

antodice.full: Antŏdĭcē, ēs, f., one of the Danaids, Hyg. Fab. 170.
antodice.short: Antŏdĭcē, ēs, f., one of the Danaids, Hyg.

antoniaster.full: Antōnĭaster, tri, m. dim. from Antonius, as surdaster from surdus, parasitaster from parasitus; cf. Prisc. p. 628 P., a servile imitator of the orator Antonius, a petty Antony: hic noster Antoniaster, Cic. Varen. Fragm. ap. Prisc. p. 617 P.

antoninus.full: Antōnīnus, i, m. Antonius, Antonine, the name of several Roman emperors; among whom the most distinguished were Antoninus Pius and M. Aurelius Antoninus Philosophus, Inscr. Orell. 834 sq.; 856 sq. —Hence, Antōnīnĭānus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Antonine, Eutr. 8, 10; Lampr. Elag. 24 al.

antoniopolitae.full: Antōnĭŏpŏlītae, ārum, m., the inhabitants of Antoniopolis in Lydia, Plin. 5, 25, 30, § 111.
antoniopolitae.short: Antōnĭŏpŏlītae, ārum, m., the inhabitants of Antoniopolis in Lydia, Plin.

antonius.full: Antōnĭus, ii, m., name of a Roman gens. M. Antonius, Marc Antony, a distinguished triumvir, conquered by Octavianus at Actium, a mortal enemy of Cicero. — M. Antonius, a celebrated orator just before the age of Cicero; cf. Cic. Brut. 37 sq.; Ellendt, Cic. Brut. p. lxii. sq.; Bähr, Lit. Gesch. 355; Teuffel, Rom. Lit. § 139.— C. Antonius, Cicero's colleague in the consulship.— Fem.: Antōnĭa, ae, a daughter of the triumvir Antonius, Plin. 35, 10, 36, § 16.—Derivv. Antōnĭus, a, um, adj., of or perta
antonius.short: Antōnĭus, ii, m., name of a Roman gens.

antonomasia.full: antŏnŏmăsĭa, ae, f., = ἀντονομασία, a rhetorical figure, by which, instead of the name, an epithet of a person is employed (e. g. instead of Scipio, Eversor Carthaginis; instead of Achilles, Pelides; instead of Juno, Saturnia, etc.), Quint. 8, 6, 29; 8, 6, 43.
antonomasia.short: antŏnŏmăsĭa, ae, f., = ἀντονομασία, a rhetorical figure, by which, instead of the name, an epithet of a person is employed (e.

antonomasivus.full: antŏnŏmăsīvus, a, um, adj. antonomasia, pertaining to or forming an antonomasia, Serv. ad Verg. A. 2, 171; 2, 615.

antroare.full: antroare: gratias referre, to requite, Paul. ex Fest. p. 9 Müll.; cf. Kuhn in Zeitschr. für Vergl. Sprachf. 7, p. 64 sq.; Vanicek, Etym. p. 291.
antroare.short: antroare: gratias referre, to requite, Paul.

antron.full: Antrōn, ōnis, f., = Ἀντρών (Hom. Il. 2, 697), a town in Thessaly (Phthiotis), now Fano, Liv. 42, 42; 42, 67.

antrum.full: antrum, i, n., = ἄντρον, a cave, cavern, grotto (almost entirely confined to the poets). Lit.: succedere antro, Verg. E. 5, 19: subire antra, Ov. M. 1, 121: occulere se antro, Val. Fl. 8, 315: ingens, Verg. A. 6, 42: gratum, Hor. C. 1, 5, 3: gelida antra, Verg. G. 4, 509: silvestria, Ov. M. 13, 47: Dionaeo sub antro, Hor. C. 2, 1, 39: vos Caesarem Pierio recreatis antro, id. ib. 3, 4, 40: quibus antris audiar? id. ib. 3, 25, 4: harenosum Libyae Jovis antrum, Prop. 5, 1, 103: effossa antra, Mart.
antrum.short: antrum, i, n., = ἄντρον, a cave, cavern, grotto (almost entirely confined to the poets).

anubis.full: Ănūbis, is and ĭdis (acc. Anubin, Prop. 4, 10, 41: Anubim, Plin. 33, 9, 46, § 131 Jan), m., = Ἄνουβις [Egyptian], an Egyptian deity which was represented with the head of a dog (cf. Müll. Archaeol. § 408), tutelary deity of the chase: latrator Anubis, Verg. A. 8, 698; so Ov. Am. 2, 13, 11.

anularis.full: ānŭlāris, e, adj. anulus, relating to a signet-ring; hence, anulare (sc. genus coloris), a white color prepared from chalk, mixed with glass beads, such as were worn in rings, Plin. 35, 6, 30, § 48. Cf. anularius.

anularius.full: ānŭlārĭus, a, um, adj. id., of or pertaining to a signet-ring: creta = anulare (v. anularis), Vitr. 7, 14: * Scalae anulariae, a place in Rome, in the eighth district (the origin of the name is unknown), Suet. Aug. 72.—Hence, subst.: ānŭlārĭus, ii, m., a ring-maker, Cic. Ac. 2, 26, 86.

anulatus.full: ānŭlātus, a, um, P. a. id., furnished or ornamented with a ring: aures, * Plaut. Poen. 5, 2, 21: anulati pedes, fettered, App. M. 9, p. 222, 30; cf. id. ib. 9, p. 234, 15.

anulus1.full: ānŭlus (not ann-), i, m. 2. anus, like circulus from circum, not a dim., a ring, esp. for the finger, a finger-ring; and for sealing, a seal-ring, signet-ring. Lit.: ille suum anulum opposuit, Plaut. Curc. 2, 3, 76: de digito anulum Detraho, Ter. Heaut. 4, 1, 37; id. Ad. 3, 2, 49; id. Hec. 5, 3, 31 et saep.; Lucr. 1, 312; 6, 1008; 6, 1014: (Gyges) anulum detraxit, Cic. Off. 3, 9, 38: gemmatus, Liv. 1, 11; Suet. Ner. 46; id. Caes. 33; id. Tib. 73 et saep.: anulo tabulas obsignare, Plaut. Curc. 2,

anulus2.full: ānŭlus, i, m. dim. 1. anus, the posteriors, fundament, Cato, R. R. 159.

anus1.full: ānus, i, m. for as-nus; cf. Sanscr. ās, = to sit, seat one's self; ἧμαι (Dor. ἧσμαι) κάθ-ημαι, Varr.; others refer it to 2. anus, from its form, the posteriors, fundament. Lit., * Cic. Fam. 9, 22; Cels. 7, 30; Scrib. Comp. 227.— Meton., disease of the anus, piles, hemorrhoids (eccl. Lat.): quinque anos aureos facietis, i. e. representations of, Vulg. 1 Reg. 6, 5 bis; 6, 11; 6, 17.

anus2.full: ānus, i, m. related to 2. an- = ἀμφί; prim. signif. a rounding, a circular form; hence also 1. anulus; cf. Varr. L. L. 6, 8, p. 76 Müll., an iron ring for the feet, Plaut. Men. 1, 1, 9.

anus3.full: ănus, ūs (also uis, Enn. ap. Non. p. 474, 30, or Trag. v. 232 Vahl.; Ter. Heaut. 2, 3, 46; Varr. ap. Non. p. 494, 24; cf. Gell. 4, 16; Prisc. p. 718 P.; v. domus, fructus, victus), f. cf. old Germ. Ano, Ana, = great-grandfather, great-grandmother; Germ. Ahn, ancestor, an old woman (married or unmarried), a matron, old wife, old maid (sometimes in an honorable sense, but com. as a term of contempt). Lit.: tremulis anus attulit artubus lumen, Enn. ap. Cic. Div. 1, 20, 40 (Ann. v. 36 Vahl.); Plaut.

anxietas.full: anxĭĕtas, ātis, f. anxius. The quality or state of anxius, anxiety (as a per manent condition, while angor, anguish, is only momentary; cf. Hab. Syn. 108, and v. angor), Cic. Tusc. 4, 12, 27: perpetua anxie tas, Juv. 13, 211.—But sometimes = angor, temporary anguish, fear, trouble, etc.: animi, Ov. P. 1, 4, 8; Curt. 4, 13: divortii anxietate mortuus, Plin. 7, 53, 54, § 186.— Anxious care, carefulness in regard to a thing (only post-Aug.): quaerendi, judicandi, comparandi anxietas, Quint. prooem.

anxifer.full: anxĭfer, fĕra, fĕrum, adj. anxius-fero, causing or bringing anxiety (only in Cic.): curae, Cic. Div. 1, 13, 22: dolorum vertices, id. Tusc. 2, 9, 21.

anxio.full: anxĭo, āre, v. a. anxius, to make uneasy or anxious (only in late Lat.): anxiatum iri, App. M. 4, p. 155, 14: dum anxiaretur cor meum, Vulg. Psa. 60, 3: anxiatus est super me spiritus, ib. ib. 142, 4.

anxiosus.full: anxĭōsus, a, um, adj. id., full of anxiety; act., causing anxiety, pain, uneasiness, Cael. Aur. Tard. 3, 2.

anxitudo.full: anxĭtūdo, ĭnis, f. (mostly ante-class.), and anxĭĕtūdo, ĭnis, f. (post-class. for the class. anxietas) [id.], anxiety, trouble, anguish: animi, Pac. ap. Non. p. 72, 33; Att. ib. 28; 29.—Once also in Cic.: anxitudo prona ad luctum, Rep. 2, 41: macerabatur anxietudine, Aug. Conf, 9, 3: anxietudinis poena, Paul. Nol. Ep. 14.

anxius.full: anxĭus, a, um, adj. v. ango, distressed, solicitous, uneasy, troubled, anxious (as a permanent state of mind). Lit.: neque omnes anxii, qui anguntur aliquando, nec qui anxii semper anguntur, Cic. Tusc. 4, 12, 27; cf.: anxietas and angor.—But frequently momentary' anxiae aegritudines et acerbae, Cic. Tusc. 4, 15, 34: anxio animo aut sollicito esse, id. Fin. 2, 17, 55: spiritus anxius, Vulg. Bar. 3, 1: senes morosi et anxii, Cic. Sen. 18, 65: Oratio pauperis, cum anxius fuerit, Vulg. Psa. 101, 1:

anxur.full: Anxur (rarely written Anxyr, Prob. p. 1459 P.), ŭris, n. (m., Mart. 5, 1; 10, 58 al., as lying upon a mountain of the same name). An ancient town in Latium, situated not far from the sea-shore, afterwards also called Tarracina, now Terracina, Enn. ap. Fest. p. 19: Tarracina oppidum linguā Volscorum Anxur dictum, Plin. 3, 5, 9, § 59; Hor. S. 1, 5, 26; cf. Mann. Ital. 1, 626 sq. (this town had its name from a fountain in the neighborhood, Serv. ad Verg. A. 7, 799; Vitr. 27, 38.)—Hence, Derivv. Anx

anytus.full: Ănўtus, i, m., = Ἄνυτος, one of the accusers of Socrates, Hor. S. 2, 4, 3.
anytus.short: Ănўtus, i, m., = Ἄνυτος, one of the accusers of Socrates, Hor.

aoede.full: Ăoedē (trisyl.), ēs, f., one of the first four Muses, Cic. N. D. 3, 21, 54.
aoede.short: Ăoedē (trisyl.), ēs, f., one of the first four Muses, Cic.

aones.full: Āŏnes, um, m. adj., = Ἄονες, Bœotian: Aonas in montes, Verg. E. 6, 65.—Hence subst., the inhabitants of Bœotia, Serv. ad Verg. E. 6, 65.

aonia.full: Āŏnĭa, ae, f., = Ἀονία. A part of Bœotia, in which are the Aonian mountains, Mount Helicon, and the fountain Aganippe, Serv. ad Verg. E. 6, 65; 10, 12.—Also in gen. for Bœotia, Gell. 14, 6.—Hence, Derivv. āŏnĭdes, ae, m. patr., an Aonid, i. e. Bœotian; of the Theban Eteocles, Stat. Th. 9, 95.— āŏnis, ĭdis, f. patr., a Bœotian woman; hence, in the plur.: Aonides, the Muses, as dwellers by Hellcon and Aganippe (cf. Aonia), Ov. M. 5, 333; 6, 2; Juv. 7, 59.— āŏnĭus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to A

aornos.full: Ăornos, i, = Ἄορνος (without birds) or ἡ Ἄορνος λίμνη (v. Strab. 1, 26; 5, 244 sqq.). Masc., the Lake of Avernus in Campania, now Averno, Verg. A. 6, 242.— Fem. A very high, steep rock in India, Curt. 8, 11.— A place in Epirus, Plin. prooem. 4.
aornos.short: Ăornos, i, = Ἄορνος (without birds) or ἡ Ἄορνος λίμνη (v.

aous.full: Ăōus, i, m., a river of Illyria which falls into the Ionian Sea, now Vovussa or Lao, Liv. 32, 5, 10; Plin. 3, 23, 26, § 145.
aous.short: Ăōus, i, m., a river of Illyria which falls into the Ionian Sea, now Vovussa or Lao, Liv.

apage.full: ăpăgĕ, the Greek imp. ἄπαγε, used as interj., away with thee! away! begone! avaunt! etc.; or also, away with it! away! not surely! constr. with acc. (like o, ah, en, etc.) or absol., also with sis (= si vis) (only in the comic poets or in epist. style; never used by Cic.). With acc.: apage te a me, Plaut. Am. 2, 1, 32; id. Cas. 2, 8, 23; Ter. Eun. 5, 2, 65; Auct. ad Her. 4, 51, 64; Vatin. ap. Cic. Fam. 5, 10: apage istas a me sorores, Plaut. Bacch. 3, 1, 5; id. Merc. 1, 2, 33.— Absol.: Apage, no

apala.full: ăpălă (hăp-), adj. n. plur., = ἁπαλά, soft, tender, only with ova, Apic. 7, 17; Cael. Aur. Tard. 2, 7; Scrib. Comp. 104.

apamea.full: Ăpămēa or -īa, ae, f., = Ἀπάμεια. One of the most distinguished towns in Cœle-Syria, on the Orontes, in the Middle Ages, Afamiah or Famit, now Famieh, Liv. 38, 13 (where there is an allusion to the origin of the name), Cassiod. ap. Cic. Fam. 12, 12; Plin. 5, 23, 19, § 81; cf. Mann. Syr. 360.— A town in Bithynia, earlier called Myrlea, now Moudania, Plin. 5, 32, 40, § 143; cf. Mann. Asia Min. 3, 560.— A town in Phrygia the Great, now Dineir, Cic. Att. 5, 16; id. Fam. 2, 17; Plin. 5, 29, 29, § 106

aparctias.full: ăparctĭas, ae, m., = ἀπαρκτἰας, the north wind (in pure Latin, septentrio), Plin. 2, 47, 46, § 119; cf. Gell. 2, 22.
aparctias.short: ăparctĭas, ae, m., = ἀπαρκτἰας, the north wind (in pure Latin, septentrio), Plin.

aparine.full: ăpărīnē, ēs, f., = ἀπαρίνη, a plant, cleavers: Galium aparine, Linn.; Plin. 27, 5, 15, § 32.
aparine.short: ăpărīnē, ēs, f., = ἀπαρίνη, a plant, cleavers: Galium aparine, Linn.;

apathia.full: ăpăthīa, ae, f., = ἀπάθεια, freedom from passion or feeling, insensibility, the Stoic principle of morals, Stoicism, Gell. 19, 12 fin.
apathia.short: ăpăthīa, ae, f., = ἀπάθεια, freedom from passion or feeling, insensibility, the Stoic principle of morals, Stoicism, Gell.

apator.full: ăpătōr, ŏris, adj., = ἀπάτωρ, without father, Tert. Praescr. c. 53 Melchis.
apator.short: ăpătōr, ŏris, adj., = ἀπάτωρ, without father, Tert.

apaturius.full: Ăpătūrĭus, ii, m., a scene-painter of Allabanda, Vitr. 7, 5, 5.
apaturius.short: Ăpătūrĭus, ii, m., a scene-painter of Allabanda, Vitr.

apaturos.full: Ăpătūrŏs, i, n., a place on the Cimmerian Bosporus, with a temple of Venus Apaturia, Plin. 6, 6, 6, § 18.—Hence, ăpă-tūrĭa, ōrum, n., a festival of Venus Apaturia, Tert. Apol. 39.
apaturos.short: Ăpătūrŏs, i, n., a place on the Cimmerian Bosporus, with a temple of Venus Apaturia, Plin.

ape.full: ape: prohibe, compesce, Paul. ex Fest. p. 22 Müll.; v. apio.

apeliotes.full: ăpēlĭōtes, ae, m., = ἀφηλιώτης, Att., ἀπηλιώτης, the east wind (in pure Lat., subsolanus), Cat. 26, 3; Plin. 2, 47, 46, § 119.
apeliotes.short: ăpēlĭōtes, ae, m., = ἀφηλιώτης, Att., ἀπηλιώτης, the east wind (in pure Lat., subsolanus), Cat.

apella.full: Ăpella, ae, m. The name of a Roman freedman, Cic. Att. 12, 19; id. Fam. 7, 25; Planc. ap. Cic. Fam. 10, 17.— The name of a credulous Jew who lived in the time of Horace; hence, appellative for a credulous man, Hor. S. 1, 5, 100.

apelles.full: Ăpelles, is (voc. Apella, Plaut. Poen. 5, 4, 101, as if from the Doric Ἀπελλᾶς), m., = Ἀπελλῆς, a distinguished Greek painter in the time of Alexander the Great, Plin. 35, 10, 36, § 10; Cic. Brut. 18, 70; id. Off. 3, 2, 10; id. Fam. 1, 9; Prop. 4, 8, 11 al.—Hence, ăpellēus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Apelles: opus, Mart. 7, 83: tabulae, Prop. 1, 2, 22 al.

apenninicola.full: Āpennīnĭcŏla, ae, comm. Apenninus-colo, a dweller among the Apennines, Verg. A. 11, 700.

apenninigena.full: Āpennīnĭgĕna, ae, comm. Apenninus - gigno, born upon the Apennines, originating there, Ov. M. 15, 432; Claud. VI. Cons. Hon. 505.

apenninus.full: Āpennīnus (better Appennīnus, Verg. A. 12, 703 Cod. Med.; also APENINVS, Inscr. Grut. 204, 18), i, m. from the Celtic penn, mountain - summit, the mountainchain that passes through the length of Italy, the Apennines, Plin. 3, 5, 7, § 48; conspicuous for height; hence, celsus Appenninus, Hor. Epod. 16, 29: Appenninus nubifer, Ov. M. 2, 226.—Personified: gaudetque nivali Vertice se attollens pater Appenninus ad auras, Verg. A. 12, 703; cf. Mann. Ital. 1, 264 sq.

aper1.full: ăper, pri, m. cf. old Germ. Ebar; Germ. Eber; Angl.-Sax. bār = aper, verres; Engl. boar; cf. Lat. caper, with change of meaning, and the Gr. κάπρος, a wild boar. Lit., Ov. M. 8, 282; 9, 192; 10, 550; 10, 715; Verg. E. 7, 29; 10, 56; id. A. 1, 324 al.: aper Erymanthius, Cic. Tusc. 4, 22, 50: Arcadius, the Erymanthian boar slain by Her cules, Mart. 9, 104: aper de silvā, Vulg. Psa. 79, 14.—Among the Romans a delicacy, Juv. 1, 140.—Masc. form used of the female in Varr. L. L. 8, 47, p. 183 Müll., t

aper2.full: Ăper, pri, m., a Roman cognomen, Tac. Or. 2; Lampr. Commod. 2; Inscr. Grut. 692, 8.
aper2.short: Ăper, pri, m., a Roman cognomen, Tac.

aperantia.full: Ăpĕrantĭa, ae, f., = Ἀπεραντία, a small province in Thessaly, south of the Dolopians, Liv. 36, 33; 38, 3; cf. Mann. Greece, 39.—Hence, ăpĕrantĭi, ōrum, m., its inhabitants, Liv. 43, 22.
aperantia.short: Ăpĕrantĭa, ae, f., = Ἀπεραντία, a small province in Thessaly, south of the Dolopians, Liv.

aperio.full: ăpĕrĭo, ĕrŭi, ertum, 4, v. a. (fut. aperibo, Plaut. Truc. 4, 2, 50; Pompon. ap. Non. p. 506, 30) [ab-pario, to get from, take away from, i.e. to uncover, like the opp. operio, from obpario, to get for, to put upon, i. e. to cover; this is the old explanation, and is received by Corssen, Ausspr. I. p. 653; II. p. 410, and by Vanicek, p. 503], to uncover, make or lay bare. Lit.: patinas, Plaut. Ps. 3, 2, 51: apertae surae, Turp. ap. Non. p. 236, 16: apertis lateribus, Sisenn. ib. p. 236, 26: capit

aperta.full: Ăperta, a surname of Apollo: quia patente (i.e. apertā) cortinā responsa ab eo darentur, Paul. ex Fest. p. 22 Müll.
aperta.short: Ăperta, a surname of Apollo: quia patente (i.e.

apertibilis.full: ăpertĭbĭlis, e, adj. aperio, opening, aperient, med. t., Cael. Aur. Acut. 3, 3; 3, 4, where aperibilis also is read.

apertio.full: ăpertĭo, ōnis, f. id., an opening, unfolding (only ante- and post-class.). With gen.: floris, Pall. 1, 6, 4: templi, App. M. 11, p. 266, 22: oris, Vulg. Eccli. 20, 15; ib. Ephes. 6, 19.— Absol.: cum periculo introitur recenti apertione, Varr. R. R. 1, 63: apertio, the solemn opening of a temple, Serv. ad Verg. A. 4, 301.

aperto.full: ăperto, āre, v. freq. [id.], to lay bare: Quaeso, cur apertas brachium? Plaut. Men. 5, 5, 12.

apertor.full: ăpertor, ōris, m. id., he that opens, begins (cf. aperio, II. A.): baptismi, Tert. adv. Marc. 2, 3.

apertura.full: ăpertūra, ae, f. aperio (only post Aug.). An opening (abstr.), Vitr. 4, 6 fin.; Dig. 28, 5, 3.— An opening (concr.), aperture, a hole, Vitr. 5, 5; so id. 10, 9: Vulg. Amos, 4, 3; 9, 11.

apertus.full: ăpertus, a, um, P. a., from aperio.

apex.full: ăpex, ĭcis, m. etym. acc. to Serv. ad Verg. A. 10, 270, and Paul. ex Fest. p. 18 Müll., from apo, to join to, whence aptus; cf. Van. Etym. p. 33, the extreme end of a thing, the point, summit, top (syn.: cacumen, summa, fastigium, culmen, vertex); hence, Lit., the small rod at the top of the flamen's cap, wound round with wool, Serv. ad Verg. A. 2, 683; 10, 270.—Hence, Transf. (As pars pro toto.) The conical cap of the flamen, ornamented with this rod: QVEI. APICEM. INSIGNE. DIALIS. FLAMINIS. GE

apexabo.full: ăpexăbo, ōnis, m. apex, a kind of sausage (perh. only in the two foll. examples), Varr. L. L. 5, § 111 Müll.; Arn. 7, p. 229.

aphaca.full: ăphăca, ae, f., = ἀφάκη. A kind of pulse, field or chick-pea: Lathyrus aphaca, Linn.; Plin. 27, 5, 21, § 38.— A wild plant, the common dandelion: Leontodon taraxacum, Linn.; Plin. 21, 15, 52, § 89.

aphaea.full: Ăphaea, ae, f., = Ἀφαία, an epithet of Britomartis (q. v.), Verg. Cir. 303, ubi v. Wagner.
aphaea.short: Ăphaea, ae, f., = Ἀφαία, an epithet of Britomartis (q.

aphaerema.full: ăphaerĕma, ătis, n., = ἀφαίρεμα, a coarse kind of grits, Plin. 18, 11, 29, § 2.
aphaerema.short: ăphaerĕma, ătis, n., = ἀφαίρεμα, a coarse kind of grits, Plin.

aphaeresis.full: ăphaerĕsis, is, f., = ἀφαίρεσις, a gram. fig., the dropping of a letter or syllable at the beginning of a word (e. g. ruere for eruere, temnere for contemnere, etc.), Prob. p. 1438 P.; Don. p. 1772 ib.; Charis. p. 248 ib.; Serv. ad Verg. A. 1, 546; 1, 669 al.
aphaeresis.short: ăphaerĕsis, is, f., = ἀφαίρεσις, a gram.

aphareus.full: Ăphăreus (trisyl.), ĕi, m., = Ἀφαρεύς. A king of the Messenians; hence his sons Lynceus and Idas are called ăphărēïa proles, Ov. M. 8, 304.— A centaur, Ov. M. 12, 341 sq.

aphesas.full: Ăphĕsās, antos, m., = Ἀφέσας, a mountain in Peloponnesus, near Nemea, now Fouka, Stat. Th. 3, 460 (in Plin. 4, 5, 9, § 17, called Apesantus, Jan).
aphesas.short: Ăphĕsās, antos, m., = Ἀφέσας, a mountain in Peloponnesus, near Nemea, now Fouka, Stat.

aphidnae.full: Ăphidnae, ārum, f., = Ἄφιδναι, a small place in Attica, Sen. Hippol. 24.—In sing.: Aphidna, Ov. F. 5, 708; cf. Mann Gr. p. 335.
aphidnae.short: Ăphidnae, ārum, f., = Ἄφιδναι, a small place in Attica, Sen.

aphractus.full: ā^phractus, i, f., or ā^phractum, i, n., = ἄφρακτος (uncovered, sc. ναῦς, hence), a long vessel without a deck (in pure Latin, navis aperta; only in Cic.): Navigavimus tardius propter aphractorum Rhodiorum imbecillitatem, Cic. Att. 5, 13, 1: detraxit viginti ipsos dies aphractus Rhodiorum, id. ib. 6, 8, 4: aphracta Rhodiorum habebam, id. ib. 5, 11, 4; so id. ib. 5, 12, 1.
aphractus.short: ā^phractus, i, f., or ā^phractum, i, n., = ἄφρακτος (uncovered, sc.

aphrodes.full: ā^phrōdes, adj. comm., = ἀφρώδης, foamy, like foam: mecon, a wild poppy, Plin. 27, 12, 93, § 119; cf. App. Herb. 53 (in Plin. 20, 19, 79, § 207, called aphron).

aphrodisia.full: Ā^phrŏdīsĭa, ōrum, n., = Ἀφροδίσια, a festival of Venus, Plaut. Poen. 1, 1, 62; 1, 2, 44.
aphrodisia.short: Ā^phrŏdīsĭa, ōrum, n., = Ἀφροδίσια, a festival of Venus, Plaut.

aphrodisiace.full: ā^phrŏdīsĭăcē, ēs, f., = ἀφροδισιακή, a precious stone of a reddish-white color, unknown to us, Plin. 37, 10, 54, § 148.
aphrodisiace.short: ā^phrŏdīsĭăcē, ēs, f., = ἀφροδισιακή, a precious stone of a reddish-white color, unknown to us, Plin.

aphrodisias1.full: Ā^phrŏdīsĭăs, ădis, f., = Αφροδισιάς. A region in Asiatic Æolis, Liv. 37, 21; Plin. 5, 30, 32, § 122.— A town and promontory in Caria, on the Mœander, now Geira, Plin. 5, 28, 29, § 104.— An island near Gades, Plin. 4, 22, 36, § 120.— An island in the Persian Gulf, now Kaish, Plin. 6, 25, 28, § 111.

aphrodisias2.full: ā^phrŏdīsĭas = acorus, q. v.; perh. sweet-flag, calamus, App. Herb. 6.

aphrodisium.full: Ā^phrŏdīsĭum, ii, n., = Ἀφροδίσιον. A town on the coast of Latium, in the province of Lavinium, with a renowned temple of Venus, which was destroyed as early as the time of Pliny, Plin. 3, 5, 9, § 57; cf. Mann. Ital. 1, 617; Müll. Roms Camp. 2, 271.— ā^phrŏdīsĭum promontorium, a promontory in Thessaly, Plin. 31, 2, 7, § 10. — ā^phrŏdīsĭum flumen, a river in Caria, Plin. 31, 2, 7, § 10.

aphronitrum.full: ā^phrŏnī^trum, i, n., = ἀφρόνιτρον, the efflorescence of saltpetre, Plin. 31, 10, 46, § 3; Mart. 14, 58.
aphronitrum.short: ā^phrŏnī^trum, i, n., = ἀφρόνιτρον, the efflorescence of saltpetre, Plin.

aphthae.full: aphthae, ārum, f., = ἄφθαι, an eruption in the mouth, the thrush, Marc. Emp. 11 (in Cels. 6, 11, written as Greek).
aphthae.short: aphthae, ārum, f., = ἄφθαι, an eruption in the mouth, the thrush, Marc.

aphya.full: ăphўa, ae, or -ē, ēs, f., = ἀφύη, a small fish, usu. called apua, acc. to some the anchovy, Plin. 32, 11, 53, § 145; cf. id. 31, 8, 44, § 95.
aphya.short: ăphўa, ae, or -ē, ēs, f., = ἀφύη, a small fish, usu.

apia.full: Ăpĭa, ae, f., = Ἀπία, an old name of the Peloponnesus, Plin. 4, 4, 5, § 9 (v. aqua init.).
apia.short: Ăpĭa, ae, f., = Ἀπία, an old name of the Peloponnesus, Plin.

apiacus.full: ăpĭăcus, a, um, adj. apium, of or relating to parsley, similar to parsley: brassica, Cato ap. Plin. 19, 8, 41, § 136 Jan; cf. Cato, R. R. 157, 2 (others read in the first passage apianam, in the latter apia).

apianus.full: ăpĭānus, a, um, adj. apis, belonging to bees, of bees. Adj., uva, loved by bees, the muscatel, Plin. 14, 2, 4, § 3; cf. Col. 12, 39, 3; so, vitis, id. 3, 2, 17: vinum, id. 12, 47, 6.— Subst.: ăpĭāna, ae, f. (sc. herba), chamomile, App. Herb. 23.

apiarius.full: ăpĭārĭus, a, um, adj. id., relating to bees; only subst., ăpĭārĭus, ii, m., a bee-keeper, Plin. 21, 10, 31, § 56.— ăpĭ-ārĭum, ii, n., a bee-house, beehive (prob. first introd. by Columella into the written lang.; cf. Gell. 2, 20, 8), Col. 9, 5, 1; so id. 9, 3, 4; 9, 5, 6; 9, 7, 1; 9, 12, 4 al.

apiastellum.full: ăpĭastellum, i, n. The plant batrachion or herba scelerata, App. Herb. 8. — The plant bryonia, App. Herb. 66.

apiastra.full: ăpĭastra, ae, f. apis, a bird that lies in wait for bees, a bee-eater, commonly called merops (for apiaster or merops apiaster, Linn.), Serv. ad Verg. G. 4, 14.

apiastrum.full: ăpĭastrum, i, n. id.. Wild-parsley: Selinum palustre, Linn.; Plin. 21, 12, 41, § 70; cf. Col. 9, 8, 12.— Balm, a plant of which bees are fond: melissophyllon, Varr. R. R. 3, 16, 10; Plin. 21, 9, 29, § 53.

apiatus.full: ăpĭātus, a, um apium. Boiled with parsley: aqua, Theod. Prisc. 2, 2.— Like a parsley-leaf, crisped: mensa, Plin. 13, 15, 30, § 96.

apica.full: ăpīca, ae, f. (sc. ovis) [perh. ἀπεικώς, unfit, unnatural], a sheep that has no wool on the belly, Varr. R. R. 2, 2, 3; Plin. 8, 48, 75, § 198; Paul. ex Fest. p. 25 Müll.

apicatus.full: ăpĭcātus, a, um, Part., as if from apico [apex], adorned with the priest's cap: Dialis, Ov. F. 3, 397.
apicatus.short: ăpĭcātus, a, um, Part., as if from apico [apex], adorned with the priest's cap: Dialis, Ov.

apicius1.full: ăpīcĭus, a, um, adj. apis, sought by bees, liked by bees; hence, sweet, dainty, = apianus, q. v.: uvae, Cato, R. R. 24, 1; Varr. R. R. 1, 58; Plin. 14, 4, 5, § 46; Macr. S. 2, 16.—Hence, ăpīcĭum, i, n., sc. vinum, Cato, R. R. 6, 5; 7, 1; Varr. R. R. 1, 25.

apicius2.full: Ăpīcĭus, ii, m. A notorious epicure under Augustus and Tiberius, Plin. 10, 48, 68, § 133; cf. Tac. A. 4, 1.—Hence, The title of a Latin book on cookery, yet extant, in ten books, whose author is unknown, v. Bähr, Lit. Gesch. p. 521; Teuffel, Rom. Lit. § 278, 4.— Deriv.: ăpīcĭ-ānus, a, um, adj., of or pertaining to Apicius: coctura, Plin. 19, 8, 41, § 143: patina, Apic. 4, 2: condimenta, Tert. Anim. 33.

apicula.full: ăpĭcŭla, ae, f. dim. apis, a little bee, * Plaut. Curc. 1, 1, 10; Plin. 7, 21, 21, § 85; Fronto Ep. ad Ver. 8 Mai.

apiculum.full: ăpĭcŭlum: filum, quo flamines velatum apicem gerunt, Paul. ex Fest. p. 23 Müll.; cf. apex, I.
apiculum.short: ăpĭcŭlum: filum, quo flamines velatum apicem gerunt, Paul.

apidanus.full: Āpĭdănus, i, m., = Ἀπιδανός, a river in Thessaly, which, uniting with the Enipeus, flows into the Peneus, now Fersaliti, Ov. M. 1, 580; 7, 228; Luc. 6, 373; Val. Fl. 1, 357.
apidanus.short: Āpĭdănus, i, m., = Ἀπιδανός, a river in Thessaly, which, uniting with the Enipeus, flows into the Peneus, now Fersaliti, Ov.

apina.full: Ăpĭna, ae, f., a poor and small town in Apulia, Plin. 3, 11, 16, § 144.—Hence, in the plur.: ăpĭnae, prov. (as tricae, q. v.), trifles, worthless things: apinae tricaeque, Mart. 14, 1, 7; 1, 113, 2 (some regard this form as from ἀφανής, obscure, of no account).
apina.short: Ăpĭna, ae, f., a poor and small town in Apulia, Plin.

apis1.full: ăpis or -es, is, f. (nom. sing. apis, Ov. M. 13, 928; Petr. Fragm. 32, 7; Col. 9, 3, 2; 9, 12, 1.—The form apes is given in Prisc. p. 613 and 703 P., and Prob. 1470 ib. as the prevailing one, to which the dim. apicula is no objection, since fides also has fidicula.—The gen. plur. varies between -ium and -um. The form apium is found, Varr. R. R. 3, 16, 14; Liv. 4, 33, 4; 27, 23, 3; 38, 46, 5; Col. 9, 3, 3; 9, 9, 1 al.; Plin. 8, 42, 64, § 158; 11, 7, 7, § 7; 11, 11, 11, § 27; 11, 16, 16, § 46; 17,

apis2.full: Āpis, is (abl. Apide, Paul. Nol. 85), m., = Ἆπις, the ox worshipped as a god by the Egyptians, Apis, Plin. 8, 46, 71, § 184 sqq.; Ov. Am. 2, 13, 14.

apis3.full: Apis vicus, a harbor in Lake Mœotis, Plin. 5, 6, 6, § 39.
apis3.short: Apis vicus, a harbor in Lake Mœotis, Plin.

apiscor.full: ăpiscor, aptus, 3, v. dep. apo (class., but more rare than the compd. adipiscor; in the post-Aug. per. most freq. in Tac.), orig., to reach after something, in order to take, seize, or get possession of it (syn.: peto, sequor, adquiro, attingo); hence, in gen., To pursue (with effort, zeal, etc.): sine me hominem apisci, Plaut. Ep. 5, 2, 3.—And as the result of the pursuit, To take, seize upon: etenim nullo cessabant tempore apisci Ex aliis alios avidi contagia morbi, Lucr. 6, 1235.— To reach, a

apium.full: ăpĭum, ii, n. apis, parsley, esp. liked by bees; an umbelliferous plant of several species (mountain-parsley, celery, etc.), Plin. 19, 8, 37, § 123 sq. The leaves of one species (water-parsley, our celery, the Apium graveolens, Linn.), were often used by the ancients for garlands, on account of their strong fragrance, Verg. E. 6, 68 Voss., esp. in drinking-bouts: vivax, that long remains green, Hor. C. 1, 36, 16; so id. ib. 2, 7, 24; 4, 11, 3 (cf. Theoc. 3, 23); and, among the Greeks, given as a

aplanes.full: aplănēs, adj., = ἀπλανής, not moving about, standing firm, Macr. Somn. Scip. 1, 6, 9 and 11.
aplanes.short: aplănēs, adj., = ἀπλανής, not moving about, standing firm, Macr.

apluda.full: aplūda (appl-), ae, f. prob. from a and pludo or plaudo, that which is beaten off. Chaff, Plin. 18, 10, 23, § 99: non hercle apluda est hodie quam tu nequior, Naev. ap. Paul. ex Fest. p. 10 Müll. (Trag. Rel. p. 23 Rib.).— Bran: apludam edit, Auct. ap. Gell. 11, 7, 3 sq.; cf. Non. p. 69.— Acc. to some, a kind of drink: Sunt qui apludam sorbitionis liquidissimum putent genus, Paul. ex Fest. l. l.

aplustre.full: ā^plustre, is, n. (abl. aplustri, Prisc. p. 769 P.; nom. plur. aplustra, Lucr. 2, 555, and Cic. ap. Prisc. p. 769 P.; dat. heterocl. aplustris, Lucr. 4, 437), = ἄφλαστον, the curved stern of a ship, with its ornaments (ribbons, streamers, and little flags upon a pole): fluitantia quaerere aplustra, Cic. Arat. ap. Prisc. l. l. (Orell. IV. 2, p. 522): fulgent aplustria, Caes. Germ. Arat. ap. Prisc. l. l. (v. 345 Orell.); Luc. 3, 586; 3, 672: torquet aplustribus ignes, Sil. 14, 422; 10, 324 Drak.:

aplysiae.full: aplysĭae, ārum, f., = ἀπλυσίαι, an inferior kind of sponge, Plin. 9, 45, 69, § 150.
aplysiae.short: aplysĭae, ārum, f., = ἀπλυσίαι, an inferior kind of sponge, Plin.

apo.full: ăpo (or ăpio, Isid. Orig. 19, 30), ĕre, v. a. cf.: ἅπτω, apiscor, apex. To fasten, attach, join, bind, tie to (syn.: ligo, adligo, jungo, conjungo, recto): comprehendere antiqui vinculo apere dicebant, Paul. ex Fest. s. v. apex, p. 18 Müll.; cf. apex; used only in part. perf. pass. aptus (the P. a. v. infra): uteri terrae radicibus apti, fastened to the earth, Lucr. 5, 808 (Lachm., terram and apti = adepti): bracchia validis ex apta lacertis, united with the strong shoulders, id. 4, 829: gladium

apocalypsis.full: ăpŏcălypsis, is, f., = ἀποκάλυψις, a disclosing, revelation (eccl. Lat.): apocalypsim habet, Vulg. 1 Cor. 14, 26: apocalypsis Jesu Christi, ib. Apoc. 1, 1: Joannis, the Revelation, the Apocalypse, Tert. adv. Marc. 4, 5.
apocalypsis.short: ăpŏcălypsis, is, f., = ἀποκάλυψις, a disclosing, revelation (eccl.

apocarteresis.full: ăpŏcartĕrēsis, is, f., = ἀποκαρτέρησις, a voluntary starvation, Tert. Apol. 46 (in Quint. 8, 5, 23, written as Greek, Halm; cf. Cic. Tusc. 1, 34, 84).
apocarteresis.short: ăpŏcartĕrēsis, is, f., = ἀποκαρτέρησις, a voluntary starvation, Tert.

apocatastasis.full: ăpŏcătastăsis, is, f., = ἀποκατάστασις, a restoring to a former position; in astronomy, the return of the stars to their position of the preceding year, App. Ascl. 84, 6 Elm. (in Col. 3, 6, 4, written as Greek).
apocatastasis.short: ăpŏcătastăsis, is, f., = ἀποκατάστασις, a restoring to a former position;

apocatastaticus.full: ăpŏcătastătĭcus, a, um, adj., = ἀποκαταστατικός, returning: Mars, to the position of the previous year (cf. apocatastasis), Sid. Ep. 8, 11.
apocatastaticus.short: ăpŏcătastătĭcus, a, um, adj., = ἀποκαταστατικός, returning: Mars, to the position of the previous year (cf.

apocha.full: ăpŏchă, ae, f., = ἀποχή, the receipt of a creditor acknowledging the payment of a debt: apocha non alias contingit quam si pecunia soluta sit, there is no receipt till the money is paid, Dig. 46, 4, 19; 47, 2, 27; 12, 6, 67, § 3.
apocha.short: ăpŏchă, ae, f., = ἀποχή, the receipt of a creditor acknowledging the payment of a debt: apocha non alias contingit quam si pecunia soluta sit, there is no receipt till the money is paid, Dig.

apocleti.full: Ăpoclēti, ōrum, m., = ἀπόκλητοι (Select); among the Ætolians, the members of the smaller council, a select committee, Liv. 35, 34; 36, 28.

apocolocyntosis.full: ăpŏcŏlŏcyntōsis, is, f., = ἀποκολοκύντωσις, the Metamorphosis into a Pumpkin, the title of an insipid lampoon written by the philosopher Seneca upon Claudius Cæsar. who, acc. to this title, instead of being transformed to a god, is changed to a pumpkin; cf. Bähr, Lit. Gesch. pp. 469 and 470; Teuffel, Rom. Lit. § 284, 7.
apocolocyntosis.short: ăpŏcŏlŏcyntōsis, is, f., = ἀποκολοκύντωσις, the Metamorphosis into a Pumpkin, the title of an insipid lampoon written by the philosopher Seneca upon Claudius Cæsar.

apocope.full: ăpŏcŏpē, ēs, f., = ἀποκοπή, a gram. fig., the dropping of a letter or syllable at the end of a word (e. g. bonu' for bonus, do for domo), Prob. p. 1438 P.; Don. p. 1772 P.; Charis. p. 248 P.; Victor. p. 2499 P.; cf. Wagn. ad Verg. Cat. 2.
apocope.short: ăpŏcŏpē, ēs, f., = ἀποκοπή, a gram.

apocrisiarius.full: ăpocrĭsĭārĭus or ăpocrĭsārĭus, ii, m. ἀποκρινομαι, to answer; ἀπόκρισις, an answer (late Lat.), a delegate, deputy, who performs a duty in the place of another, esp. of a high Church officer, called also responsalis, Julian. Epit. 6, 26; cf. Just. Nov. 6, 2; Hon. Aug. G. Anim. 1, 185.

apocryphus.full: ăpŏcrўphus, a, um, adj., = ἀπόκρυφος (eccl. t. = spurious or uncanonical): libri, in the Church fathers, the apocryphal books incorporated with the Bible.

apocynon.full: ăpŏcўnon, i, n., = ἀπόκυνον (dog'sbane). A little bone in the left side of the venomous frog, Plin. 32, 5, 8, § 51.— A plant, dog's-bane: Aconitum lycoctonum, Linn.; Plin. 24, 11, 56, § 98.

apodicticus.full: ăpŏdīctĭcus, a, um, adj., = ἀποδεικτικός, proving clearly, demonstrative: argumentum, Gell. 17, 5, 3.
apodicticus.short: ăpŏdīctĭcus, a, um, adj., = ἀποδεικτικός, proving clearly, demonstrative: argumentum, Gell.

apodixis.full: ăpŏdīxis, is, f., = ἀπόδειξις, a conclusive proof, demonstration, = evidens prebatio, Quint. 5, 10, 7; Petr. 132, 10; Gell. 17, 5, 5 (in Quint. 5, 10, 7 al., written as Greek).
apodixis.short: ăpŏdīxis, is, f., = ἀπόδειξις, a conclusive proof, demonstration, = evidens prebatio, Quint.

apodosis.full: ăpŏdŏsis, is, f., = ἀπόδοσις, a subsequent proposition, or a clause which refers to one preceding (protasis), by which it is explained; cf. Don. ad Ter. And. 1, 5, 44.
apodosis.short: ăpŏdŏsis, is, f., = ἀπόδοσις, a subsequent proposition, or a clause which refers to one preceding (protasis), by which it is explained;

apodoti.full: Ăpŏdō^ti, ōrum, m., a people in Ætolia, Liv. 32, 34, 4.
apodoti.short: Ăpŏdō^ti, ōrum, m., a people in Ætolia, Liv.

apodyterium.full: ăpŏdȳtērĭum, ii, n., = ἀποδυτήριον, the undressing-room in a bathing-house, * Cic. ad Q. Fr. 3, 1, 1; Plin. Ep. 5, 6; Inscr. Orell. 3278.
apodyterium.short: ăpŏdȳtērĭum, ii, n., = ἀποδυτήριον, the undressing-room in a bathing-house, * Cic.

apogeus.full: ăpŏgēus, a, um, adj., = ἀπόγαιος, that comes from the land: venti, Plin. 2, 43, 44, § 114.
apogeus.short: ăpŏgēus, a, um, adj., = ἀπόγαιος, that comes from the land: venti, Plin.

apographon.full: ăpŏgrăphon, i, n., = ἀπόγραφον, a transcript, a copy: tabulae exemplar, quod apographon vocant, Plin. 35, 11, 40, § 125 (in Cic. Att. 12, 52, 3, written as Greek).
apographon.short: ăpŏgrăphon, i, n., = ἀπόγραφον, a transcript, a copy: tabulae exemplar, quod apographon vocant, Plin.

apolactizo.full: ăpŏlactīzo, āre, v. a., = ἀπολακτίζω, to thrust from one with the foot; hence, to spurn, scorn: apolactizo inimicos omnīs, * Plaut. Ep. 5, 2, 13.

apolectus.full: ăpŏlectus, i, m., = ἀπόλεκτος (picked out). A kind of tunny-fish when not a year old, Plin. 32, 11, 53, § 150.— Apolecti, pieces for salting, cut from the tunnyfish of that age (pelamis), Plin. 9, 15, 18, § 48.

apollinar.full: Ăpollĭnar, āris, n. instead of Apollinal from Apollo, like Frutinal, Supercal, Fagutal, etc., a temple dedicated to Apollo, Liv. 3, 63, 7, where Weissenb. reads Apollinarem; v. Apollinaris.

apollinaria.full: ăpollĭnārĭa, ae, f., the plant commonly called strychnos, App. Herb. 74.
apollinaria.short: ăpollĭnārĭa, ae, f., the plant commonly called strychnos, App.

apollinaris.full: Ăpollĭnāris, e, adj. Apollo, belonging or sacred to Apollo, of Apollo. Adj.: laurea, Hor. C. 4, 2, 9: Apollinarem (aedem), Liv. 3, 63, 7 Weissenb.—Hence, Ludi Apollinares, the games celebrated in honor of Apollo, annually, on the 5th of July, Liv. 25, 12; 27, 23; Cic. Att. 2, 19; id. Phil. 10, 3; Plin. 35, 10, 36, § 19 al.— Subst. ăpol-lĭnāris, is, f. (sc. herba), the herb commonly called hyoscyamus, Plin. 26, 14, 87, § 140. — A species of solanum, App. Herb. 22.

apollineus.full: Ăpollĭnĕus, a, um, adj. id., relating or belonging to Apollo (only poet.): urbs, i. e. Delos, where Apollo was born and specially honored, Ov. M. 13, 631: proles, i. e. Æsculapius, id. ib. 15, 533: mater, i. e. Latona, Stat. Th. 11, 12: vates, i. e. Orpheus, Ov. M. 11, 8: ars, both the art of soothsaying, id. Ib. 264, and that of healing, id. Tr. 3, 3, 10: cantus, id. M. 11, 155 et saep.

apollo.full: Ăpollo, ĭnis (earlier Ăpello, like hemo for homo, Paul. ex Fest. p. 22 Müll.; gen. APOLONES, Inscr. Orell. 1433, like salutes, v. salus; dat. APOLLONI, Corp. Inscr. III. 567, APOLENEI, ib. I. 167, APOLONE, Inscr. Ritschl, Epigr. Suppl. 3, p. 3; abl. APOLONE; the gen. Apollōnis etc., is often found in MSS., as in Cic. Tusc. 1, 47, 114, and even Apollŏnis is found in Plaut. Men. 5, 2, 119; Neue, Formenl. I. p. 165), m., = Ἀπόλλων, Apollo, son of Jupiter and Latona, twinbrother of Diana, and god of
apollo.short: Ăpollo, ĭnis (earlier Ăpello, like hemo for homo, Paul.

apollodorus.full: Ăpollŏdōrus, i, m., = Ἀπολλοδωρος. A distinguished rhetorician, teacher of Augustus, Suet. Aug. 89; Tac. Or. 19.— Hence, ăpollŏdōrēi, his pupils, Quint. 2, 11, 2; 3, 1, 18 al.— A distinguished grammarian of Athens, author of a work on mythology still extant, Cic. Att. 12, 23; Macr. S. 1, 13.— An Academic philosopher, Cic. N. D. 1, 34, 93.— A tyrant of Cassandrea, Cic. N. D. 3, 33, 82.

apollonia.full: Ăpollōnĭa, ae, f., = Ἀπολλωνια. The name of several celebrated towns. In Ætolia, Liv. 28, 8, 9.— In Crete, Plin. 4, 12, 20, § 59.— In Thrace, on the Pontus Euxinus, Plin. 34, 7, 18, § 39; 4, 11, 18, § 42; Mel. 2, 2.— In Macedonia, Liv. 45, 28; Plin. 4, 10, 17, § 37.— In Illyria, Cic. Phil. 11, 11; Caes. B. C. 3, 12; Plin. 3, 23, 26, § 145.— In Cyrenaica, Plin. 5, 5, 5, § 31; Mel. 1, 8 al.— Derivv. ăpol-lōnĭātes, ae, a native of Apollonia (in Crete): Diogenes Apolloniates, Cic. N. D. 1, 12, 29.—P

apollonidenses.full: Ăpollōnĭdenses, ium, m., the inhabitants of Apollonis in Lydia (between Pergamus and Sardes), Cic. Fl. 29; Plin. 5, 30, 33, § 126; Tac. A. 2, 47.
apollonidenses.short: Ăpollōnĭdenses, ium, m., the inhabitants of Apollonis in Lydia (between Pergamus and Sardes), Cic.

apollonides.full: Ăpollōnĭdes, ae, m. A ruler of Chios in the time of Alexander the Great, Curt. 4, 5.— A famous Greek graver, Plin. 37, 1, 4, § 8.— A writer in the time of Tiberius, Plin. 7, 2, 2, § 17.

apollonius.full: Ăpollōnĭus, ii, m., = Ἀπολλώνιος, a distinguished rhetorician in Rhodes, Cic. de Or. 1, 28, 126; Suet. Caes. 4.
apollonius.short: Ăpollōnĭus, ii, m., = Ἀπολλώνιος, a distinguished rhetorician in Rhodes, Cic.

apologatio.full: ăpŏlŏgātĭo, ōnis, f. from ἀπόλογος, with the Lat. ending, atio, a narration in the manner of Æsop, Quint. 5, 11, 20.

apologeticus.full: Ăpŏlŏgētĭcus, i, m., = ἀπολογητικός (suitable for defence; sc. liber), Apology, the title of a treatise by Tertullian in defence of Christianity.
apologeticus.short: Ăpŏlŏgētĭcus, i, m., = ἀπολογητικός (suitable for defence;

apologia.full: ăpŏlŏgĭa, ae, f., = ἀπολογία, a defence, apology, Hier. ap. Ruf. 2, 4; 2, 6 al. —Also, the title of a work by Apuleius of Madaura; cf. Bähr, Gesch. Rom. Lit. p. 411; Teuffel, Rom. Lit. § 362.
apologia.short: ăpŏlŏgĭa, ae, f., = ἀπολογία, a defence, apology, Hier.

apologo.full: ăpŏlŏgo, āvi, 1, v. a., = ἀπολέγω, to reject, spurn (only once in Seneca): ipse illum apologavit, Sen. Ep. 47.

apologus.full: ăpŏlŏgus, i, m., = ἀπολογος. A narrative: apologum agere, Plaut. Stich. 4, 1, 32; so id. ib. 4, 1, 38 and 64.—More freq., A fable after the manner of Æsop, an apologue' narrationes apologorum, Cic. de Or. 2, 66, 264; so id. Inv. 1, 17; Auct. ad Her. 1, 6; Quint. 6, 3, 45; Gell. 2, 29.

aponus.full: Ăpŏnus, i, m., = ἄπονος (pain-curing). A warm, medicinal fountain in the vicinity of Padua, now Bagni d' Albano: Patavinorum aquae calidae, Plin. 2, 103, 106, § 227: Aponi fons, Suet. Tib. 14: Aponi fontes, Mart. 6, 42, 4; Cassiod. Var. 2, 39; cf. Mann. Ital. 1, 91.—Hence, ăpŏ-nus, a, um, adj., Aponian: tellus, Mart. 1, 62, 3: Aponinus, dub. in Vop. Firm. Sat. c. 3.

apophasis.full: ăpŏphăsis, is, f., = ἀπόφασις (denial), rhet. fig., whereby one, as it were, answers himself, Jul. Rufin. 8.

apophlegmatismos.full: ăpŏphlegmătismos, i, m., = ἀποφλεγματισμός, a remedy for expelling phlegm, an expectorant, Cael. Aur. Tard. 1, 4; 2, 4.
apophlegmatismos.short: ăpŏphlegmătismos, i, m., = ἀποφλεγματισμός, a remedy for expelling phlegm, an expectorant, Cael.

apophoreta.full: ăpŏphŏrēta, ōrum, n., = ἀποφόρητα (to be borne away), presents which guests received at table, especially at the Saturnalia, to carry home with them, Suet. Calig. 55; id. Vesp. 19; cf. id. Aug. 75; or which candidates distributed, Symm. 2, 87 al.—Also, title of the fourteenth book of the epigrams of Martial.
apophoreta.short: ăpŏphŏrēta, ōrum, n., = ἀποφόρητα (to be borne away), presents which guests received at table, especially at the Saturnalia, to carry home with them, Suet.

apophygis.full: ăpŏphўgis, is, f., = ἀποφυγη; in archit., the curve of a column at top or bottom, the apophyge, Vitr. 4, 1; 4, 7.

apoplecticus.full: ăpŏplēctĭcus or ăpŏplēctus, a, um, adj., = ἀποπληκτικός or ἀπόπληκτος, med. t., apoplectic, Firm. Math. 3, 14, n. 8; Cael. Aur. Acut. 3, 5 al.
apoplecticus.short: ăpŏplēctĭcus or ăpŏplēctus, a, um, adj., = ἀποπληκτικός or ἀπόπληκτος, med.

apoplexia.full: ăpŏplēxĭa, ae, or -xis, is, f., = ἀποπληξια or ἀπόπληξις, med. t., apoplexy; form apoplexia, Cael. Aur. Acut. 3, 5.—Form apoplexis, Tert. Anim. 53; Firm. Math. 3, 7, n. 8.
apoplexia.short: ăpŏplēxĭa, ae, or -xis, is, f., = ἀποπληξια or ἀπόπληξις, med.

apoproegmenon.full: ăpŏprŏēgmĕnon, i, n., = ἀποπροηγμένον; in the philos, lang. of the Stoics, that which is to be rejected (opp. proegmenon): puto concedi nobis oportere, ut Graeco verbo utamur, si quando minus occurret Latinum, ne hoc ephippiis et acratophoris potius quam proëgmenis et apoproëgmenis concedatur, Cic. Fin. 3, 4, 15.

apopsis.full: ăpopsis, is, f., = ἄποψις (far-sight), an eminence that furnishes an extensive view, Fronto, Fer. Als. 3.
apopsis.short: ăpopsis, is, f., = ἄποψις (far-sight), an eminence that furnishes an extensive view, Fronto, Fer.

apor.full: apor, a form of apud, q. v.
apor.short: apor, a form of apud, q.

aporia.full: ăpŏrĭa, ae, f., = ἀπορἰα, doubt, perplexity, embarrassment, with the idea of confusion, disorder: aporia hominis in cogitatu illius, Vulg. Eccli. 27, 5 (in Cic. Att. 7, 21, 3 al., written as Greek).
aporia.short: ăpŏrĭa, ae, f., = ἀπορἰα, doubt, perplexity, embarrassment, with the idea of confusion, disorder: aporia hominis in cogitatu illius, Vulg.

aporiatio.full: ăpŏrĭātĭo, ōnis, f. aporior, vacillation of mind, uncertainty, doubt, Tert. adv. Haer. 49.

aporior.full: ăpŏrĭor, āri, v. dep., = ἀπορέω, to be in uncertainty, to doubt, vacillate (eccl. Lat.), Vulg. Isa. 59, 16; ib. Eccli. 18, 6; ib. 2 Cor. 4, 8.

aposcopeuon.full: ăposcŏpeuōn, ontis, m., = ἀποσκοπεύων (looking far off), a painting by Antiphilus, in which a satyr is represented, with his hand shading his eyes, looking at something far off, Plin. 35, 11, 40, § 138 Hard., Jan, where others read aposcopon.
aposcopeuon.short: ăposcŏpeuōn, ontis, m., = ἀποσκοπεύων (looking far off), a painting by Antiphilus, in which a satyr is represented, with his hand shading his eyes, looking at something far off, Plin.
