arne2.full: Arnē, ēs, f., = Ἄρνη, a woman who betrayed her country (the island Siphnos), and was changed into a jackdaw, Ov. M. 7, 465.
arne2.short: Arnē, ēs, f., = Ἄρνη, a woman who betrayed her country (the island Siphnos), and was changed into a jackdaw, Ov.

arnobius.full: Arnŏbĭus, ii, m. An African Church father in the time of Diocletian, c. A. D. 295. His work, Adversus Gentes, is distinguished by strength and purity of diction; cf. Teuffel, Rom. Lit. § 639, 2.— Arnŏbĭus (junior), ii, m., a theological author, c. A. D. 460, who wrote a Commentary on the Psalms; cf. Teuffel, Rom. Lit. § 462, 1.

arnoglossa.full: arnoglossa, ae, f., = ἀρνόγλωσσον, a plant, sheep's-tongue or plantain: Plantago major, Linn.; App. Herb. 1 (also called arnion; Isid., Orig. 17, 9, 50, calls it arnoglossos).
arnoglossa.short: arnoglossa, ae, f., = ἀρνόγλωσσον, a plant, sheep's-tongue or plantain: Plantago major, Linn.;

arnus.full: Arnus, i, m., = Ἄρνος, a river of Etruria, now the Arno, Plin. 3, 5, 8, § 50; Tac. A. 1, 79 al.; cf. Mann. Ital. I. 328.—Hence, Arnĭensis, e, adj., of or pertaining to the Arnus: tribus, situated on the Arnus, acc. to Liv. 6, 5, settled A. U. C. 396, most distant from Rome, as Saburana was the nearest: a Saburană usque ad Arniensem, Cic. Agr. 2, 29.
arnus.short: Arnus, i, m., = Ἄρνος, a river of Etruria, now the Arno, Plin.

aro.full: ăro, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. cf. ἀρόω = to plough, to till; ἄροτρον = aratrum; ἄροτος, ἄρουρα = arvum, = Welsh ar; ἀροτήρ = arator; armentum; Goth. arjan = to plough; O. H. Germ. aran = to ear, to plough, to till. Lit. Absol.: arare mavelim quam sic amare, Plaut. Merc. 2, 3, 21: in fundo Fodere aut arare, Ter. Heaut. 1, 1, 17: si quidem L. Quinctio Cincinnato aranti nuntiatum est etc., Cic. Sen. 16, 56: bene et tempestive arare, Cato, R. R. 61, 1; Plin. 18, 19, 49, § 174: bos est enectus arando, Hor

aroma.full: ărōma, ătis, n. (dat. and abl. plur. aromatibus, also aromatis, App. Flor. 4, 19; v. Neue, Formenl. I. p. 291), = ἄρωμα, a spice; in sing., Dig. 39, 4, 16, § 7; Prud. στεφ. 8, 72; id. Apoth. 826; in plur., spices (so only in Vulg.), Col. 12, 20, 2; Vulg. Gen. 37, 25; ib. Exod. 25, 6; ib. Marc. 16, 1; ib. Joan. 19, 40 et saepe.

aromatarius.full: ărōmătārĭus, ii, m. aroma, a dealer in spices, Inscr. Orell. 114 and 4064.

aromaticus.full: ărōmătĭcus, a, um, adj., = ἀρωματικός, composed of spice, aromatic, fragrant, Spart. Had. 19; Sedul. 5, 324.
aromaticus.short: ărōmătĭcus, a, um, adj., = ἀρωματικός, composed of spice, aromatic, fragrant, Spart.

aromatites.full: ărōmătītes, ae, m., = ἀρωματίτης. A precious stone of the smell and color of myrrh, a kind of amber, Plin. 37, 10, 54, § 145.— Aromatites vinum, aromatic wine, Plin. 14, 13, 15, § 92; 14, 16, 19, § 107.

aromatizo.full: ărōmătīzo, āre, v. n., = ἀρωματίζω, to smell of spices: aromatizans odorem dedi, Vulg. Eccli. 24, 20.

aroneus.full: Ărōnēus, a, um, adj., of or pertaining to the high-priest Aaron, Paul. Nol. 22, 27.
aroneus.short: Ărōnēus, a, um, adj., of or pertaining to the high-priest Aaron, Paul.

aros.full: ăros, i, f., also ăron or ărum, i, n., = ἄρον, wake-robin: Arum dracunculus Linn.: quod aron vocant, Plin. 19, 5, 30, § 96; and id. 24, 16, 91, § 142.
aros.short: ăros, i, f., also ăron or ărum, i, n., = ἄρον, wake-robin: Arum dracunculus Linn.: quod aron vocant, Plin.

arpi.full: Arpi, ōrum, m., a city in Apulia, earlier called Argyripa (q. v.), now Arpa, Plin. 3, 11, 16, § 104; cf. Mann. Ital. II. 82 sq.— Hence, Derivv.: Arpīnus, a, um, adj., of or from Arpi: Dasius Altinius Arpinus, Liv. 24, 45; Arpīni, ōrum, m., the inhabitants of Arpi, id. 24, 47.— Ar-pānus, a, um, adj., pertaining to Arpi, Front. Col.; Arpāni, ōrum, m., the inhabitants of Arpi, Plin. 3, 11, 16, § 103.
arpi.short: Arpi, ōrum, m., a city in Apulia, earlier called Argyripa (q.

arpinum.full: Arpīnum, i, n., a town in Latium, the birthplace of Cicero and Marius, now Arpino, Cic. Att. 2, 8; cf. Mann. Ital. I. 676.— Hence, Derivv.: Arpīnas, ātis (nom. Arpinatis, Cato ap. Prisc. p. 629 P.; cf. Ardeatis), adj., of or pertaining to Arpinum: fundus, Cic. Agr. 3, 2, 8: aquae, id. Att. 1, 16: iter, id. ib. 16, 13.—Subst.: Ar-pīnātes, ium, m., the inhabitants of Arpinum, Cic. Off. 1, 7, 21; so id. Att. 4, 7; 15, 15; so also Inscr. Orell. 571 (cf. Cic. Fam. 13, 11); Plin. 3, 5, 9, § 63: Arpina
arpinum.short: Arpīnum, i, n., a town in Latium, the birthplace of Cicero and Marius, now Arpino, Cic.

arpinus.full: Arpīnus, a, um, adj. Of or from Arpi, v. Arpi.— Of Arpinum, v. Arpinum, II. B.

arquatus.full: arquātus, a, um, adj. arquus = arcus = rainbow; v. arcus init.: morbus, the jaundice (a disease in which the skin turns to the yellow color of the rainbow), Cels. 3, 24.—Hence, subst.: arquātus, i, m., one that has the jaundice, Non. p. 425, 3: Lurida praeterea flunt, quaecumque tuentur Arquati, Lucr. 4, 332 sq.; Varr. ap. Non. p. 35, 16; Col. 7, 5, 18; and Plin. 20, 11, 44, § 115.

arquites.full: arquītes = sagittarii, bowmen, archers, Paul. ex Fest. p. 20 Müll. [arquus = ar cus].

arra.full: arra, arrabo, arralis, v. arrha, arrhabo, arrhalis.

arrectarius.full: arrectārĭus (adr-), a, um, adj. arrectus, in an erect position, erect, perpendicular; hence, arrectaria, the upright posts of a wall (opp. transversarii, cross-beams), only Vitr. 2, 8, and 7, 3.

arrenicum.full: arrĕnĭcum (arrh-, arsĕn-), i, n., = ἀρσενικόν (ἀρρενικόν), arsenic, orpiment. vitia cum chartā et arrhenico sanant, Plin. 28, 15, 60, § 214; 34, 18, 56, § 178 (Vitr. 7, 7, 7 fin. uses for it auripigmentum).
arrenicum.short: arrĕnĭcum (arrh-, arsĕn-), i, n., = ἀρσενικόν (ἀρρενικόν), arsenic, orpiment.

arrepo.full: ar-rēpo (better, adr-), repsi, reptum, 3, v. n., to creep or move slowly to or toward something, to steal softly to, lit. and trop.; constr. with ad; post-Aug. with dat. Lit.: mus aut lacerta ad columbaria, Varr. R. R. 3, 7, 3; so Plin. 35, 10, 36, § 98: rubetae adrepentes foribus, id. 11, 18, 19, § 62; Val. Max. 6, 8 fin.— Trop.: sensim atque moderate ad amicitiam adrepserat, * Cic. Verr. 2, 3, 68: leniter in spem Adrepe officiosus, * Hor. S. 2, 5, 48: qui animis muliercularum adrepit, Tac. A.

arrepticius.full: arreptīcĭus (adr-) or -tĭus (adr-), a, um, adj. arreptus, seized in mind, inspired (in eccl. Lat.). In bon. part.: ut sis dux in domo Domini super omnem virum arreptitium et prophetantem, Vulg. Jer. 29, 26.— In mal. part., raving, delirious, Aug. Civ. Dei, 2, 4 al.

arrepto.full: arrepto, āre, a false read. in Plin. 35, 10, 36, § 109, instead of obreptantibus, v. Sillig ad h. l.

arreptus.full: arreptus (adr-), a, um, P. a., from arripio.

arrha.full: arrha, ae, f., and arrhăbo (also without aspiration arra and arrăbo), ōnis, m. (the latter form ante-class.; cf. Gell. 17, 2, 21; in Cic. the word is never used), = ἀρραβών [from the Heb. from , to give security], the money given to ratify a contract, earnest-money, purchase-money, a pledge, an earnest (arrha is a part of the purchase-money, while pignus is a pledge to be restored when the contract, for security of which it is given, Las been performed, Isid. Orig. 5, 25). Lit.: arraboni has ded
arrha.short: arrha, ae, f., and arrhăbo (also without aspiration arra and arrăbo), ōnis, m.

arrhalis.full: arrhālis (arrāl-), e, adj. arrha, of a pledge: pactum, Diocl. Cod. 4, 49, 3.

arrhenogonon.full: arrhĕnŏgŏnon, i, n., = ἀρρενόγονον, a species of the plant satyrion, Plin. 26, 10, 63, § 99.
arrhenogonon.short: arrhĕnŏgŏnon, i, n., = ἀρρενόγονον, a species of the plant satyrion, Plin.

arrhetos.full: arrhētos, i, m., = ἄρρητος (unutterable), one of the Æons of Valentinus, Tert. adv. Val. 35.
arrhetos.short: arrhētos, i, m., = ἄρρητος (unutterable), one of the Æons of Valentinus, Tert.

arria.full: Arrĭa, ae, f., the wife of Pœtus, distinguished for her magnanimity, Mart. 1, 14; Plin. Ep. 3, 16; Tac. A. 16, 34.
arria.short: Arrĭa, ae, f., the wife of Pœtus, distinguished for her magnanimity, Mart.

arrideo.full: ar-rīdĕo (adr-, Lachm., B. and K., Halm, K. and H.; arr-, Fleck., Merk., Weissenb.), rīsi, rīsum, 2, v. n., to laugh at or with, to smile at or upon, especially approvingly. Lit., constr. absol. or with dat., more rarely with acc.; also pass.— Absol.: si non arriderent, dentis ut restringerent, Plaut. Capt. 3, 1, 26: oportet lenam probam arridere Quisquis veniat, blandeque alloqui, id. Truc. 2, 1, 14: cum quidam familiaris (Dionysii) jocans dixisset: huic (juveni) quidem certe vitam tuam committ

arrigo.full: ar-rĭgo (adr-, Dietsch, Halm; arr-, Fleck., Rib., Weissenb.), rexi, rectum, 3, v. a. rego, to set up, raise, erect (not used by Cic., but for it he employs erigere). Lit.: leo comas arrexit, Verg. A. 10, 726; so id. ib. 4, 280: aurīs, Plaut. Rud. 5, 2, 6; so Ter. And. 5, 4, 30; Ov. M. 15, 516; Verg. A. 2, 303 (translatio a pecudibus, Don. ad Ter. l. c.; cf. opp. demittere aures, Hor. C. 2, 13, 35): linguam, Mart. 11, 62, 10: tollit se arrectum quadrupes, Verg. A. 10, 892; so id. ib. 5, 426; 2, 2

arripio.full: ar-rĭpĭo (adr-, B. and K.; arr-, Lachm., Ritschl, Fleck., Merk., Rib., K. and H., Weissenb., Halm), rĭpŭi, reptum, 3, v. a. rapio, to seize, snatch, lay hold of, draw a person or thing to one's self (esp. with haste). In gen. Lit.: ut eum eriperet, manum arripuit mordicus: Vix foras me abripui atque effugi, Plaut. Curc. 5, 1, 7; cf. the first of the words following, formed by Plaut. after the manner of Aristophanes: Quodsemelarripides Numquampostreddonides, Pers. 4, 6, 23 Ritschl: gladium, id. C

arrisio.full: arrīsĭo (adr-), ōnis, f. arrideo, a smiling upon with approbation: alicujus adrisio, Auct. ad Her. 1, 6, 10.

arrisor.full: arrīsor (adr-), ōris, m. id., one who smiles on another, a flatterer, fawner: stultorum divitum arrosor, et (quod sequitur) adrisor, et, quod duobus his adjunctum est, derisor, Sen. Ep. 27.

arrodo.full: ar-rōdo (adr-, Kayser, Jan), rōsi, rōsum, 3, v. a., to gnaw or nibble at, to gnaw (cf.: aduro, accendo, accīdo, adedo al.). Lit.: spartum, quod asellus adrodit, Plin. 35, 11, 40, § 137: mures adrosis clipeis, etc., id. 8, 57, 82, § 221: semina adrosa, id. 11, 30, 36, § 109: sues spirantes a muribus adrosas, id. 11, 37, 85, § 213.— Trop.: ut illa ex vepreculis extracta nitedula rem publicam conaretur adrodere, * Cic. Sest. 33, 72: ecclesiasticas caulas, Sid. Ep. 7, 6.
arrodo.short: ar-rōdo (adr-, Kayser, Jan), rōsi, rōsum, 3, v.

arrogans.full: arrŏgans (adr-), antis, P. a., from arrogo.

arroganter.full: arrŏganter (adr-), adv., v. arrogo, P. a. fin.

arrogantia.full: arrŏgantia (adr-), ae, f. arrogans. An assuming, presumption, arrogance, conceitedness (syn.: superbia, insolentia, fastus): cum omnis adrogantia odiosa est, tum illa ingenii atque eloquentiae multo molestissima, Cic. Div. in Caecil. 11 fin.: P. Crassus sine adrogantiā gravis esse videbatur et sine segnitiā verecundus, id. Brut. 81, 282: illud γνῶθι σεαυτόν noli putare ad adrogantiam minuendam solum esse dictum, id. ad Q. Fr. 3, 6, 7 et saep.: Pallas tristi adrogantiā taedium sui moverat, Tac. A

arrogatio.full: arrŏgātĭo (adr-), ōnis, f. arrogo, a taking to one's self; hence, as jurid. t. t., the full adoption, in the comitia curiata in the presence of the pontifices, later of the emperor himself, of a homo sui juris in the place of a child (cf. s. v. adoptio and the authors there cited): adrogatio dicta, quia genus hoc in alienam familiam transitus per populi rogationem fit, Gell. 5, 19, 8: adrogatio dicitur, quia et is, qui adoptat rogatur, id est interrogatur, an velit eum, quem adoptaturus sit, jus

arrogator.full: arrŏgātor (adr-), ōris, m. id., he that adopts one in the place of a child (cf. arrogatio), Dig. 1, 7, 2; 1, 7, 19; 1, 7, 22; 1, 7, 40.

arrogo.full: ar-rŏgo (adr-, Fleck., B. and K., Dietsch, Halm, Weissenb.; arr-, Holder, Dinter; Keller uses both forms), āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. Jurid. and polit. t. t. To ask or inquire of one, to question: Venus haec volo adroget te, * Plaut. Rud. 5, 2, 45; cf. Dig. 1, 7, 2.—* Alicui, t. t., to add one officer to another, to associate with, place by the side of: cui consuli dictatorem adrogari haud satis decorum visum est patribus, Liv. 7, 25, 11.— To take a homo sui juris in the place of a child, to adopt (v.

arroro.full: ar-rōro (adr-), āre, v. n., to moisten, bedew: herbam vino, Marc. Emp. 34.

arrosor.full: arrōsor (adr-), ōris, m. arrodo, one who gnaws at or consumes a thing, a nibbler, consumer: stultorum divitum, Sen. Ep. 27.

arrosus.full: arrōsus (adr-), a, um, Part. of arrodo.

arrotans.full: ar-rŏtans (adr-), antis, adj. qs. Part. of arroto, āre; rota, in a winding, circular motion, turning, trop. wavering: arrotanti tactu, Sid. Ep. 6, 1.

arrotrebae.full: Arrō^trĕbae, ārum, f., a promontory in Hispania, Plin. 4, 20, 34, § 111.
arrotrebae.short: Arrō^trĕbae, ārum, f., a promontory in Hispania, Plin.

arrubium.full: Arrŭbĭum, ii, n., a town on the Danubius in Scythia Minor, Tab. Peut. Itin.
arrubium.short: Arrŭbĭum, ii, n., a town on the Danubius in Scythia Minor, Tab.

arrugia.full: arrūgĭa, ae, f. akin to runco, runcina, ὀρύσσω, ὀρύξω, to dig; cf. Corssen, Ausspr. I. p. 543; v. corrugus, a shaft and pit in a gold-mine, Plin. 33, 4, 21, § 70.

arruntius.full: Arruntĭus, ii, m., a Roman nomen. L. Arruntius, consul A.U.C. 759, Tac. A. 1, 13; 3, 11; 6, 5; prob. the same as the historian L. Arruntius, who composed a work on the Punic Wars, Sen. Ep. 114, 17 sqq.— Arruntius, a celebrated artist under Claudius Cœsar, Plin. 29, 1, 5, § 7.— Arruntius Stella, a poet, Stat. S. 1, 2; Mart. 6, 21.— Arruntius Caelius, a Latin grammarian, Diom. I. p. 307 P.; Prisc. III. p. 607 P.
arruntius.short: Arruntĭus, ii, m., a Roman nomen.

ars.full: ars, artis, f. v. arma, skill in joining something, combining, working it, etc., with the advancement of Roman culture, carried entirely beyond the sphere of the common pursuits of life, into that of artistic and scientific action, just as, on the other hand, in mental cultivation, skill is applied to morals, designating character, manner of thinking, so far as it is made known by external actions (syn.: doctrina, sollertia, calliditas, prudentia, virtus, industria, ratio, via, dolus). Skill in

arsaces.full: Arsăces, is m., = Ἀρσάκης, the first king of the Parthians, Just. 41, 5.— Derivv. Arsăcĭdae, ārum, m. (gen. plur. Arsacidūm, Luc. 10, 51), successors of Arsaces, Tac. H. 1, 40; Luc. 1, 108; 8, 217; 8, 306 al.— Arsăcĭus, a, um, adj., Arsacian, poet. for Parthian, Mart. 9, 36.
arsaces.short: Arsăces, is m., = Ἀρσάκης, the first king of the Parthians, Just.

arse verse.full: arse verse, a Tuscan-Latin incantation against fire: ARSE VERSE averte ignem significat, Paul. ex Fest. p. 18 Müll. (cf. Plin. 28, 2, 4, § 20). A pure Tuscan inscr. found at Cortona with this formula reads: ARSES. VVRSES. SETHLANL., etc., i. e. Ignem averte, Vulcane, Inscr. Orell. 1384.
arse verse.short: arse verse, a Tuscan-Latin incantation against fire: ARSE VERSE averte ignem significat, Paul.

arsella.full: arsella, ae, f., a plant, also called argemonia, q. v., App. Herb. 31.
arsella.short: arsella, ae, f., a plant, also called argemonia, q.

arsenaria.full: Arsēnārĭa, ae, f., a Roman colony in Mauretania Caesariensis, now Arzew, Plin. 5, 2, 1, § 19; it is called Arsinna in Mel. 1, 6, 1.
arsenaria.short: Arsēnārĭa, ae, f., a Roman colony in Mauretania Caesariensis, now Arzew, Plin.

arsia1.full: Arsĭa, ae, m., a small river of Istria, which became the boundary between Italy and Illyricum under Augustus; the present Arsa, Plin. 3, 26, 29, § 150; Flor. 2, 5; cf. Mann. Thrace, p. 325.
arsia1.short: Arsĭa, ae, m., a small river of Istria, which became the boundary between Italy and Illyricum under Augustus;

arsia2.full: Arsĭa Silva, ae, f., a forestin Etruria, celebrated for a battle between the Tarquinii and the Romans, Liv. 2, 7; Val. Max. 1, 8; cf. Nieb. Röm. Gesch. 1, 553.
arsia2.short: Arsĭa Silva, ae, f., a forestin Etruria, celebrated for a battle between the Tarquinii and the Romans, Liv.

arsineum.full: arsinĕum, i, n., a woman's headdress, Paul. ex Fest. p. 20 Müll.; Cato ap. Fest. p. 265 Müll.
arsineum.short: arsinĕum, i, n., a woman's headdress, Paul.

arsinoe.full: Arsĭnŏē, ēs, and Arsĭnŏa, ae, f., = Ἀρσινόη. Arsinoa, mother of the third Mercury, Cic. N. D. 3, 22, 57.— Arsinoë, daughter of Ptolemy Lagus and Berenice, wife of king Lysimachus, afterwards of her brother Ptolemy Philadelphus, Just. 17, 1; 17, 2; 24, 2.—Hence, Arsĭnŏēum, i, n., the monument erected to her by the latter, Plin. 36, 9, 14, § 68.— A daughter of Lysimachus, the first wife of Ptolemy Philadelphus; after her death worshipped as Venus Zephyritis, Plin. 34, 14, 42, § 148.— A daughter of
arsinoe.short: Arsĭnŏē, ēs, and Arsĭnŏa, ae, f., = Ἀρσινόη.

arsis.full: arsis, is, f., = ἄρσις, in metre, the elevation of the voice; opp. thesis, depression (in pure Lat., sublatio, Diom. p. 471 P.), Mart. Cap. 9, p. 328; Don. p. 1738 P.; cf. Ter. Maur. p. 2412 P., and Mar. Vict. p. 2482 P.
arsis.short: arsis, is, f., = ἄρσις, in metre, the elevation of the voice;

arsus.full: arsus, a, um, Part. of ardeo.

artaba.full: artăba, ae, f., an Egyptian dry measure = 3 1/3 Rom. modii, Rhem. Fan. Pond. 89.
artaba.short: artăba, ae, f., an Egyptian dry measure = 3 1/3 Rom.

artabanus.full: Artăbānus, i, m. A Parthian king of the family of the Arsacidœ, Just. 42, 2; Tac. A. 2, 3; 2, 58; 6, 31 sq.; 11, 8.— A general of Xerxes, Nep. Reg. 1, 5; Just. 3, 1.

artacie.full: Artăcĭē, ēs, f., = Ἀρτακίη (Hom. Od. 10, 108), a fountain in the country of the Lœstrygones, Tib. 4, 1, 60.

artatus.full: artātus (not arct-), a, um, P. a., from arto.

artaxata.full: Artaxăta, ōrum, n. (Artaxăta, ae, f., Tac. A. 2, 56), = Ἀρτάξατα, the capital of Armenia Major, on the Araxes, now Ardaschad, Juv. 2, 170.

artaxerxes.full: Artaxerxes, is, m., = Ἀρταξέρξης, the name of several Persian kings, Nep. Reg. 1, 3; Just. 3, 1; 10, 3 al.
artaxerxes.short: Artaxerxes, is, m., = Ἀρταξέρξης, the name of several Persian kings, Nep.

arte.full: artē (not arctē), adv., v. 1. artus fin.

artemis.full: Artĕmis, idis, f., = Ἄρτεμις, the Greek name of Diana, Plin. 25, 7, 36, § 73; cf. Macr. S. 1, 15; 7, 16.
artemis.short: Artĕmis, idis, f., = Ἄρτεμις, the Greek name of Diana, Plin.

artemisia.full: Artĕmĭsĭa, ae, f., = Ἄρτεμισία. Wife of King Mausolus, in Caria, to whom, after his death, she built the renowned Mausoleum, Gell. 10, 18.— artĕmĭsĭa, ae, f., the plant mugwort, Plin. 25, 7, 36, § 73; App. Herb. 10.

artemisium.full: Artĕmisĭum, ii, n., = Ἀρτεμίσιον. A promontory of the island Eubœa, Nep. Them. 3, 2 and 4.— A town in Eubœa, Plin. 4. 12, 21, § 64.

artemita.full: Artĕmĭta, ae, or Artĕmĭtē, ēs, f., = Ἀρτέμιτα. A city of Assyria or, perh. more strictly, of Babylonia, Plin. 6, 26, 30, § 117.— Another name for Rhene, one of the Echinades, Plin. 4, 12, 22, § 67.
artemita.short: Artĕmĭta, ae, or Artĕmĭtē, ēs, f., = Ἀρτέμιτα.

artemon.full: artĕmon (artĕmo, Lucil. ap. Charis. p. 99 P.), ōnis, m., = ἀρτέμων. A sail put upon the mast above the main-sail, a top-sail, Dig. 50, 16, 242; * Vulg. Act. 27, 40.— The guiding-pulley of a machine for raising weights, * Vitr. 10, 5.

arteria.full: artērĭa, ae, f. (artērĭum, i, n., v. infra), = ἀρτηρία. The windpipe: arteria ad pulmonem atque cor pertinens, Plin. 11, 37, 66, § 175; 20, 6, 22, § 49; so id. 22, 25, 66, § 136; Gell. 17, 11, 2 al.—From its internal roughness, also called arteria aspera (Gr. τραχεῖα ἀρτηρία): cum aspera arteria (sic enim a medicis appellatur) ostium habeat adjunctum linguae radicibus, Cic. N. D. 2, 54, 136; Cels. 4, 1.—And since it consists of two parts, also in the plur.: laeduntur arteriae, Auct. ad Her. 3, 1

arteriace.full: artērĭăcē, ēs, f., = ἀρτηριακή, a medicine for the windpipe, Plin. 23, 7, 71, § 136; cf. Cels. 5, 25, 17; Scrib. Comp. 74 and 75.
arteriace.short: artērĭăcē, ēs, f., = ἀρτηριακή, a medicine for the windpipe, Plin.

arteriacus.full: artērĭăcus, a, um, adj., = ἀρτηριακός, of or pertaining to the windpipe: medicamenta, that produce coughing, Cael. Aur. Tard. 2, 6.
arteriacus.short: artērĭăcus, a, um, adj., = ἀρτηριακός, of or pertaining to the windpipe: medicamenta, that produce coughing, Cael.

arteriotomia.full: artērĭŏtŏmĭa, ae, f., = ἀρτηριοτομία, an opening or incision in an artery, Cael. Aur. Tard. 1, 1 fin.
arteriotomia.short: artērĭŏtŏmĭa, ae, f., = ἀρτηριοτομία, an opening or incision in an artery, Cael.

arthriticus.full: arthrītĭcus, a, um, adj., = ἀρθριτικός, gouty, arthritic: cocus, * Cic. Fam. 9, 23.
arthriticus.short: arthrītĭcus, a, um, adj., = ἀρθριτικός, gouty, arthritic: cocus, * Cic.

arthritis.full: arthrītis, ĭdis, f., = ἀρθρῖτις, a lameness in the joints, gout (in pure Lat., articularis morbus), Vitr. 1, 6.
arthritis.short: arthrītis, ĭdis, f., = ἀρθρῖτις, a lameness in the joints, gout (in pure Lat., articularis morbus), Vitr.

articulamentum.full: artĭcŭlāmentum, i, n. articulo, the articulation of the limbs, a joint (late Lat.), Scrib. Comp. 214; 206; 263.

articularis.full: artĭcŭlāris, e, adj. articulus. Pertaining to the joints (v. articulus, I.): morbus, gout, Plin. 20, 17, 73, § 195; Suet. Galb. 21; Scrib. Comp. 101.— In gram., like the article (v. articulus, II. A. fin.): pronomen, i. e. hic, iste, Prisc. p. 938 P.; 574 P.; Serv. p. 1785 P.

articularius.full: artĭcŭlārĭus, a, um, adj. id., of or pertaining to the joints: morbus, gout, Cato, R. R. 157, 7; Plin. 23 prooem.; 22, 13, 15, § 34.

articulate.full: artĭcŭlātē, adv., v. articulo, P. a. fin.

articulatim.full: artĭcŭlātim, adv. articulatus. Joint by joint, limb by limb, piecemeal: aliquem concidere, Plaut. Ep. 3, 4, 52: membra (pueri) articulatim dividit, poët. ap. Cic. N. D. 3, 26, 67; cf. Planck, Eur. Medea, p. 102: comminuere articulatim diem, Plaut. Fragm. ap. Gell. 3, 3, 5.— Trop., of discourse, properly divided (v. articulus, II. A.); hence, clearly, distinctly, point by point: verba discernere articulatim, Lucr. 4, 555: aliquid explicare, Varr. L. L. 10, 4, 179: aliquid articulatim distincteque

articulatio.full: artĭcŭlātĭo, ōnis, f. articulo (belonging to the lang. of the vineyard). The putting forth of new joints or knots, Plin. 16, 25, 41, § 101; 17, 21, 35, § 163.— A disease of the vine at the joints of the tendrils, Plin. 17, 24, 37, § 226.

articulatus.full: artĭcŭlātus, a, um, P. a., from articulo.

articulo.full: artĭcŭlo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. articulus, lit. to divide into single members or joints; used only trop. of discourse, to utter distinctly, to articulate: hasce voces mobilis articulat verborum daedala lingua, the nimble tongue articulates, Lucr. 4, 551: verba, App. Flor. 12, p. 349, 5: sonos, Arn. 3, p. 111.—Hence, artĭcŭlātus, a, um, P.a., prop., furnished with joints; hence distinct: verba, Sol. c. 65: vox, Arn. 7, p. 217, and in gram.: articulata (vox) est, quae coartata, hoc est copulata, cum

articulosus.full: artĭcŭlōsus, a, um, adj. id., full of joints, or (of plants) full of knots (v. articulus, I.). Lit.: radix, Plin. 24, 16, 93, § 150.— Trop., of discourse (v. articulus, II. A.): vitanda concisa nimium et velut articulosa partitio, full of minute divisions and subdivisions, Quint. 4, 5, 24 (cf. just before: divisio in digitos diducta).

articulus.full: artĭcŭlus, i, m. dim. 2. artus, a small member connecting various parts of the body, a joint, knot, knuckle. Lit.: nodi corporum, qui vocantur articuli, Plin. 11, 37, 88, § 217: hominis digiti articulos habent ternos, pollex binos, id. 11, 43, 99, § 244: summus caudae articulus, id. 8, 41, 63, § 153 al.: crura sine nodis articulisque, Caes. B. G. 6, 27: ipso in articulo, quo jungitur capiti cervix, Liv. 27, 49: auxerat articulos macies, i. e. had made more joints, had made the bones visible, Ov.

artifex.full: artĭfex, fĭcis, m. ars-facio. Subst. One that is master in the liberal arts (while opifex is a master in the artes sordidae; cf. ars, I. B. 1.), an artist, artificer: illi artifices corporis simulacra ignotis nota faciebant, Cic. Fam. 5, 12: reponendarum (tegularum) nemo artifex (i. e. architectus) inire rationem potuit, Liv. 42, 3: in armamentario multis talium operum (sc. tormentorum) artificibus de industriā inclusis, id. 29, 35: ut aiunt in Graecis artificibus eos auloedos esse, qui citharoe

artificialis.full: artĭfĭcĭālis, e, adj. artificium, of or belonging to art, artificial, according to the rules of art (perh. only in Quint.): probationes, Quint. 5, 1, 1; so id. 5, 9, 1; 12, 8, 19: ratio, id. 6, 4, 4.—Once subst.: artĭfĭ-cĭālia, ium, n., things conformable to the rules of art, Quint. 1, 8, 14.—Adv.: artĭ-fĭcĭālĭter, according to art (opp. inartificialiter): se gerere, Quint. 2, 17, 42.

artificiosus.full: artĭfĭcĭōsus, a, um, adj. artificium. Act., accomplished in art, skilful, artistic (perh. found only in Cic. and Auct. ad Her.): rhetores elegantissimi atque artificiosissimi, Cic. Inv. 1, 35 fin.: quod si artificiosum est intellegere, quae sunt ex arte scripta, multo est artificiosius ipsum scribere ex arte, Auct. ad Her. 4, 4, 7: ipsius mundi natura non artificiosa solum, sed plane artifex, Cic. N. D. 2, 22, 58: Zeno naturam ita definit, ut eam dicat ignem esse artificiosum ad gignendum progre

artificium.full: artĭfĭcĭum, ii, n. artifex. In gen., the occupation of an artifex, a profession, trade, an employment, a handicraft, an art: Jam de artificiis et quaestibus, qui liberales habendi, qui sordidi sint, etc., Cic. Off. 1, 42, 150: ne opifices quidem tueri sua artificia possent, nisi, etc., id. Fin. 3, 2, 4: in artificio perquam tenui et levi (sc. scaenico), id. de Or. 1, 28, 129: sordidum ancillareque, id. Tusc. 5, 20, 58; so Tac. Or. 32; Sen. Ben. 6, 17: de hoc artificio est nobis acquisitio, * Vul

artio1.full: artĭo, īvi, ītum, 4, v. a. 1. artus, to fit close, to drive in tight (only ante-class.): surculum, Cato, R. R. 40, 3; so id. ib. 41, 2: linguam in palatum, Nov. ap. Non. p. 505, 30.

artio2.full: artĭo, īre, v. a. ars, to indue with art; only in the two foll. exs.: artitus: bonis instructus artibus, skilled in arts. Paul. ex Fest. p. 17 Müll. (cf.: centum puer artium, Hor. C. 4, 1, 15).—Hence also endowed with cunning (cf. ars, II. fin.), artful: artiti viri, Plaut. As. 3, 2, 19 in varr. lectt.

artisellium.full: artĭsellĭum, ii, n. 1. artus-sella, an arm-chair, Petr. 75, 4.

artius.full: artĭus, a, um, adj., = ἄρτιος, complete, perfect: si est artius (ut ita dicam) holocleros, quid est etc., Suet. Claud. 4.
artius.short: artĭus, a, um, adj., = ἄρτιος, complete, perfect: si est artius (ut ita dicam) holocleros, quid est etc., Suet.

arto.full: arto (not arcto), āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. 1. artus, to draw or press close together, to compress, contract (not found in Cic.). Lit.: omnia conciliatu artari possunt, * Lucr. 1, 576: libros, Mart. 1, 3, 3; Col. 12, 44, 2: vitis contineri debet vimine, non artari, Plin. 17, 23, 35, § 209: angustias eas artantibus insulis parvis, quae etc., id. 3, 6, 13, § 83.— Trop., to contract, straiten, limit, curtail: fortuna humana fingit artatque ut lubet, i. e. in angustias redigit, Plaut. Capt. 2, 2, 54 Lind.

artocopus.full: artŏcŏpus, i, m., = ἀρτοκόπος, a baker, Firm. Math. 8, 20.
artocopus.short: artŏcŏpus, i, m., = ἀρτοκόπος, a baker, Firm.

artocreas.full: artō^crĕas, ătis, n., = ἀρτόκρεας, a meat pie, Pers. 6, 50; cf. Inscr. Orell. 4937.
artocreas.short: artō^crĕas, ătis, n., = ἀρτόκρεας, a meat pie, Pers.

artolaganus.full: artŏlăgănus, i, m., = ἀρτολάγανον, a kind of bread or cake (made of meal, wine, milk, oil, lard, and pepper, Athen. 3, 28); Cic. Fam. 9, 20.
artolaganus.short: artŏlăgănus, i, m., = ἀρτολάγανον, a kind of bread or cake (made of meal, wine, milk, oil, lard, and pepper, Athen.

artopta.full: artopta, ae, m., = ἀρτόπτης. * A baker, Juv. 5, 72 Ruperti.— A vessel to bake in, a bread-pan, Plaut. Aul. 2, 9, 4; cf. Plin. 18, 11, 28, § 107.

artopticius.full: artoptīcĭus, a, um, adj. artopta, II., baked in an artopta: panis, Plin. 18, 11, 27, § 105.

artotrogus.full: Artō^trōgus, i, m. ἄρτοσ-τρώγω, bread-gnawer, the name of a parasite in Plaut. Mil.

artotyritae.full: Artŏtȳrītae, ārum, m. ἄρτοσ-τυρός, heretics who made offerings of bread and cheese, Aug. de Haeres. 25.

artuatim.full: artŭātim, adv. 2. artus, limb by limb, Firm. Math. 7, 1.

artuatus.full: artŭātus, a, um, Part. [qs. Part. of artuo, āre], torn in pieces, Firm. Math. 6, 31.

artus1.full: artus (not arctus), a, um, adj. v. arma, prop. fitted; hence, Lit., close, strait, narrow, confined, short, brief: exierunt regionibus artis, Lucr. 6, 120: claustra, id. 1, 70; so id. 3, 808: nec tamen haec ita sunt arta et astricta, ut ea laxare nequeamus, Cic. Or. 65, 220: artioribus apud populum Romanum laqueis tenebitur, Cic. Verr. 2, 1, 5: nullum vinculum ad astringendam fidem jure jurando majores artius esse voluerunt, id. Off. 3, 31, 111: compages, Verg. A. 1, 293: nexus, Ov. M. 6, 242: a

artus2.full: artus, ūs, m. id., mostly plur. (artua, n., Plaut. Men. 5, 2, 102; quoted in Non. p. 191, 12.—Hence, dat. acc. to Vel. Long. p. 2229 P. and Ter. Scaur. p. 2260 P. artibus; yet the ancient grammarians give their decision in favor of artubus, which form is also supported by the best MSS.; cf. arcus.—The singular is found only in Luc. 6, 754; Val. Fl. 4, 310, and Prisc. p. 1219 P.). Lit., a joint: molles commissurae et artus (digitorum), Cic. N. D. 2, 60, 150: suffraginum artus, Plin. 11, 45, 101,

arula.full: ārŭla, ae, f. dim. ara. A small altar: ante hosce deos erant arulae, * Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 3; Vulg. Jer. 36, 22; 36, 23 bis; Jus Papir. in Macr. S. 3, 11; Arn. 3, p. 114; Inscr. Orell. 1630.—†† Perh. the base of an altar (eccl. Lat.): quos (anulos) pones subter arulam altaris, Vulg. Exod. 27, 5; 38, 4.— Among the Campanians, the turf laid altar-like round an elm-tree, Plin. 17, 11, 15, § 77.

aruncus.full: āruncus, i, m., = ἤρυγγος (Dor. ἄρυγγος), the beard of the goat, Plin. 8, 50, 76, § 203.

arundifer.full: ărundĭfer, ărundĭnācĕus, ărundo and its derivv., v. harundifer, etc.
arundifer.short: ărundĭfer, ărundĭnācĕus, ărundo and its derivv., v.

aruns.full: Aruns, untis, m., an Etruscan name of the younger son, while the elder was called Lar or Lars [in pure Etruscan, Arnth.; Gr. Ἄρρων or Ἀρροῦνς]. A brother of Lucumo (Tarquinius Priscus), Liv. 1, 34.— A younger son of Tarquin the Proud, Liv. 1, 56; 2, 6.— A son of Porsenna, Liv. 2, 14.— An Etruscan seer, Luc. 1, 585; v. Müll. Etrusk. 1, pp. 405 and 409.
aruns.short: Aruns, untis, m., an Etruscan name of the younger son, while the elder was called Lar or Lars [in pure Etruscan, Arnth.;

arupium.full: Ărūpĭum, ii, n., = Ἀρούπεινον, Strabo, a town in Illyria, now Auersperg, Itin. Anton.—Hence, ărūpīnus, a, um, of or pertaining to Arupium: Arupinis natus in arvis, Tib. 4, 1, 110.
arupium.short: Ărūpĭum, ii, n., = Ἀρούπεινον, Strabo, a town in Illyria, now Auersperg, Itin.

arura.full: ărūra, ae, f., = ἄρουρα, a field, cornfield, Marc. Emp. 8; Vel. Long. p. 2246 P.
arura.short: ărūra, ae, f., = ἄρουρα, a field, cornfield, Marc.

aruspex.full: ăruspex and derivv., v. haruspex, etc.

arvalis.full: arvālis, e, adj. arvum, pertaining to a cultivated field; hence, Fratres Arvales, a college of twelve priests, who yearly made offerings to the field-Lares for the increase of the fruits of the field: Fratres Arvales dicti sunt, qui sacra publica faciunt propterea, ut fruges ferant arva, Varr. L. L. 5, § 85 Müll.; cf. Non. p. 560, 24 sq.; Müll. Etrusk. 2, pp. 91 and 105. Extant inscriptions show that this college of priests continued in existence until the fourth century; cf. Inscr. Orell. I. 38

arveho.full: ar-vĕho, exi, ectum, 3, v. a. (an old form for adveho, v. ad init.), to bring, to procure (only twice in Cato): arvehant ligna, Cato, R. R. 138: trapetum ubi arvectum erit, id. ib. 135, 7.

arverni.full: Arverni, ōrum, m., = Ἀρβερνοί, Plut.; Ἀρουερνοί, Strabo, a people of Gaul, in the present Auvergne, Caes. B. G. 1, 31; 1, 45; 7, 7; Luc. 1, 427; cf. Mann. Gall. p. 130.— Hence, Arvernus, a, um, adj., Arvernian: Arvernum genus (vini), Plin. 14, 1, 3, § 18.

arvina.full: arvīna, ae, f. Grease, fat, suet, lard. In gen.: pinguis, * Verg. A. 7, 627 (secundum Suetonium arvina est durum pingue, quod est inter cutem et viscus, Serv.).— Esp. Of the victim in a sacrifice (eccl. Lat.), Vulg. Exod. 29, 22; ib. Lev. 3, 15; so the dim. arvinula, * ib. ib. 8, 16.— Of a person: de latere ejus arvina dependet, Vulg. Job, 15, 27.— Greasiness, fatness, in gen., Prud. Cath. 7, 9; Sid. Ep. 8, 14.— Arvīna, a surname of the dictator A. Cornelius Cossus, Liv. 8, 38.

arvinula.full: arvīnŭla, ae, v. arvina, I. B. a.

arvix.full: arvix or harvix, ĭgis, f., = ΑΡΙΞ, with digamma ΑΡϜΙΞ, also as fem. arvi-ga (harv-), ae, a ram for offering: Aries qui etiam dicebatur Ares, veteres nostri Arviga, hinc Arvigas, Varr. L. L. 5, § 98 Lindem.: Harviga dicebatur hostia, cujus adhaerentia inspiciebantur exta, Paul. ex Fest. p. 100 Mūll. (in Don. ad Ter. Phorm. 4, 4, 28, haruga; in Vel. Long. p. 2233 P. ariuga).
arvix.short: arvix or harvix, ĭgis, f., = ΑΡΙΞ, with digamma ΑΡϜΙΞ, also as fem.

arvum.full: arvum, i, n., v. arvus, II. B.

arvus.full: arvus, a, um, adj. for aruus from aro. That has been ploughed, but not yet sown, ploughed, arable: ager, arvus et arationes ab arando, Varr. L. L. 5, § 39 Müll.: arvum, quod aratum nec dum satum est, id. R. R. 1, 29; Paul. ex Fest. p. 25 Müll.: aut arvus est ager aut consitus aut pascuus aut florens, Isid. Orig. 15, 13: Non arvus hic, sed pascuus est ager, Plaut. Truc. 1, 2, 47: agri arvi et arbusti et pascui lati atque uberes, Cic. Rep. 5, 2, 3.—Hence, Subst. arva, ae, f. (sc. terra), an arable

arx.full: arx, arcis, f. arx ab arcendo, quod is locus munitissimus rubis, a quo facillime possit hostis prohiberi, Varr. L. L. 5, § 151 Müll; cf. Serv. ad Verg. A. 1, 20; Isid. Orig. 15, 2, 32; Doed. Syn. IV. p. 428; v. arceo, a stronghold, castle, citadel, fortress, ἀκρόπολις; in Rome, the Capitolium. Lit.: arce et urbe orba sum, Enn. ap. Cic. Tusc. 3, 19, 44 (Trag. v. 114 Müll.): optumates, Corinthum quae arcem altam habetis, id. ap. ejusd. Fam. 7, 6: edicite per urbem ut omnes qui arcem astuque accolu

arytaena.full: ărўtaena or ărŭtaena, also contr. artaena, ae, f., = ἀρυταινη, a vessel for taking up liquids: arytaenam sive artaenam vas ab hauriendo sic appellabant, Paul. ex Fest. p. 21 Müll.: artaenaeque et aquales, Lucil. ap. Charis. p. 95 (1, 35 Müll.).

as.full: as, assis, m. (nom. assis, Don. ad Ter. Phorm. 1, 1, 9, and Schol. ad Pers. 2, 59; old form assārĭus, ii, m.; and in the gen. plur. assariūm, Varr. L. L. 8, § 71 Müll.; Charis. p. 58 P.) [εἷς, Dor. αἴς, Tarent. ἄς, Hinter]. In gen., unity, a unit; as a standard for different coins, weight, measure, etc. (in Vitr. 3, 1, p. 61 Rode, perfectus numerus, the perfect number, fundamental number), acc. to the duodecimal system, divided into 12 parts, or uncias, with the following particular designations

asarotum.full: ăsărōtum, i, n., = ἀσάρωτον, a floor laid in mosaic, Stat. S. 1, 3, 36; cf.: asarotos oecos (= ἀσάρωτος οἶκος), Plin. 36, 25, 60, § 184; hence, asaroticus lapillus, a little mosaic stone, Sid. Carm. 23, 56.
asarotum.short: ăsărōtum, i, n., = ἀσάρωτον, a floor laid in mosaic, Stat.

asarum.full: ăsărum, i, n., = ἄσαρον, hazelwort, wild - spikenard: Asarum Europaeum, Linn.; Plin. 12, 13, 27, § 47.
asarum.short: ăsărum, i, n., = ἄσαρον, hazelwort, wild - spikenard: Asarum Europaeum, Linn.;

asbestinum.full: asbestĭnum, i, n. (sc. linum), = ἀσβέστινον, a kind of incombustible cloth, Plin. 19, 1, 4, § 19 sqq. (written by Jan as Greek).

asbestos.full: asbestŏs, i, m. (sc. lapis), = ἄσβεστος (incombustible), a stone of an iron-gray color, found in Arcadia, differing from the common asbestos, perh. amiantus, Plin. 37, 10, 54, § 146.

asbolus.full: Asbŏlus, i, m. ἀσβόλη, soot, a black, shaggy dog of Actœon, Ov. M. 3, 218.

ascalabotes.full: ascălăbōtes, ae, m., = ἀσκαλαβώτης, a kind of lizard, in pure Lat., stellio: Lacerta gecko, Linn.; Plin. 29, 4, 28, § 90.
ascalabotes.short: ascălăbōtes, ae, m., = ἀσκαλαβώτης, a kind of lizard, in pure Lat., stellio: Lacerta gecko, Linn.;

ascalaphus.full: Ascălăphus, i, m., = Ἀσκάλαφος, a son of Acheron and Orphne, who made known to Pluto that Proserpine had eaten seven kernels of a pomegranate, on account of which he was changed by her into an illboding owl (bubo), Ov. M. 5, 539 sq.; cf. Serv. ad Verg. A. 4, 462.
ascalaphus.short: Ascălăphus, i, m., = Ἀσκάλαφος, a son of Acheron and Orphne, who made known to Pluto that Proserpine had eaten seven kernels of a pomegranate, on account of which he was changed by her into an illboding owl (bubo), Ov.

ascalia.full: ascălĭa, ae, f., = ἀσκαλία, the edible part of the artichoke, Plin. 21, 16, 57, § 97.
ascalia.short: ascălĭa, ae, f., = ἀσκαλία, the edible part of the artichoke, Plin.

ascalo.full: Ascălo, ōnis, f., = Ἀσκάλων, an important trading town in the southern part of Palestine, between Gaza and Azotus upon the sea, now Ascalon, Mel. 1, 11, 3; Plin. 5, 13, 14, § 68; cf. Mann. Palaest. 202.—Hence, adj.: Ascălōnĭus, a, um, of Ascalon: caepa, a shallot, Col. 11, 3, 57; 12, 10, 1; Plin. 19, 6, 32, § 101 sqq.
ascalo.short: Ascălo, ōnis, f., = Ἀσκάλων, an important trading town in the southern part of Palestine, between Gaza and Azotus upon the sea, now Ascalon, Mel.

ascalpo.full: a-scalpo (ads-), ĕre, v. n., to scratch at, to scratch: aurem, App. M. 6, p. 176.

ascania.full: Ascănĭa, ae, f., = Ἀσκανία, a region in Phrygia, Plin. 5, 32, 40, § 144.
ascania.short: Ascănĭa, ae, f., = Ἀσκανία, a region in Phrygia, Plin.

ascanius1.full: Ascănĭus, a, um, adj., = Ἀσκάνιος, Ascanian: lacus, in Bithynia, near Nicœa, Plin. 5, 32, 43, § 148: portus, in Troas, id. 5, 30, 32, § 121: insulae, in the Ægean Sea, over against Troas, id. 5, 31, 38, § 138.
ascanius1.short: Ascănĭus, a, um, adj., = Ἀσκάνιος, Ascanian: lacus, in Bithynia, near Nicœa, Plin.

ascanius2.full: Ascănĭus, ii, m., = Ἀσκάνιος, son of Æneas and Creüsa, king of Lavinium, and founder of Alba Longa, Verg. A. 1, 271; Liv. 1, 3; cf. Wagner ad Verg. A. l. c., and id. Exc. ad Aen. 2, n. XVII. p. 438.
ascanius2.short: Ascănĭus, ii, m., = Ἀσκάνιος, son of Æneas and Creüsa, king of Lavinium, and founder of Alba Longa, Verg.

ascaules.full: ascaules, is, m., = ἀσκαύλης, a bagpiper, Mart. 10, 3, 8 (called in Suet. Ner. 54 by the pure Lat. word, utricularius).
ascaules.short: ascaules, is, m., = ἀσκαύλης, a bagpiper, Mart.

ascendens.full: ascendens (ads-), entis, P. a., v. ascendo fin.

ascendibilis.full: ascendĭbĭlis (ads-), e, adj. ascendo, that can be ascended or climbed: semita, Pomp. ap. Schol. ad Stat. Th. 10, 841.

ascendo.full: a-scendo (ads-, Jan; ads- and as-, Müller; as-, other editors), scendi, scensum, 3, v. n. scando, to ascend, mount up, climb; and in eccl. Lat. simply to go up, to rise, to spring up, grow up (syn.: scando, conscendo, orior, surgo, prodeo). Lit. (opp. descendo; and diff. from escendo, which designates a climbing, mounting upon some high object, and involves the idea of exertion; cf. Oud. ad Caes. B. G. 7, 27; Suet. Caes. 61; Ochsn. Ecl. pp. 287 and 288; Doed. Syn. IV. pp. 60 and 61; it often int

ascensibilis.full: ascensĭbĭlis (ads-), e, adj. ascendo, that may be ascended or climbed: iter, Cael. Aur. Tard. 3, 1.

ascensio.full: ascensĭo (ads-), ōnis, f. id., an ascending, ascent (more rare than ascensus). Lit.: ad hirundininum nidum ascensionem ut faceret, Plaut. Rud. 3, 1, 7: graduum, Vitr. 9, 1, p. 208 Rode: via ascensionis, Vulg. 1 Par. 26, 16: dies ascensionis suae de terrā Aegypti, ib. Osee, 2, 15.— Trop.: quorum (oratorum) quae fuerit ascensio et quam in omnibus rebus difficilis optimi perfectio, etc., a rising, soaring, * Cic. Brut. 36, 137: ascensiones in corde suo disposuit, Vulg. Psa. 83, 6.— Meton., means of

ascensor.full: ascensor (ads-), ōris, m. id., one that ascends (eccl. Lat.). In gen.: montis Dominici, Hier. in Rufin. 1: caeli, Vulg. Deut. 33, 26.— Esp., one that mounts a horse, chariot, etc., a rider, charioteer: ut cadat ascensor ejus (equi) retro, Vulg. Gen. 49, 17: ascensor equi, ib. Amos, 2, 15: equum et ascensorem dejecit, ib. Exod. 15, 1; ib Job, 39, 18.—So absol.: ascensores (sc. equorum), Vulg. 4 Reg. 18, 23; so, asini ascensor, ib. Isa. 21, 7; cameli, ib. ib.' collidam in te currum et ascensorem e

ascensus1.full: ascensus (ads-), a, um, Part. of ascendo.

ascensus2.full: ascensus (ads-), ūs, m. ascendo, an ascending, ascent. Lit.: primos prohibere ascensu coeperunt, Caes. B. G. 5, 32: homines audaces ab ejus templi aditu atque ascensu repulisti, Cic. Dom. 21: quod hosti aditum ascensum ve difficilem praeberet, Liv. 25, 36 summi fastigia tecti Ascensu supero, Verg. A. 2, 303 ascensus muri, Vulg. 2 Esdr. 12, 36. ascensus altaris, ib. Eccli. 50, 12. adscensus siderum, a rising of the stars to our hemisphere, Plin. 29, 4, 15, § 59: ascensus aurorae, Vulg. 2 Esdr. 4,

asceteria.full: ascētērĭa, ōrum, n., = ἀσκητήρια, a place of abode for ascetics, a hermitage, Cod. Just. 1, 3, 33.
asceteria.short: ascētērĭa, ōrum, n., = ἀσκητήρια, a place of abode for ascetics, a hermitage, Cod.

ascetriae.full: ascētrĭae, ārum, f., = ἀσκήτριαι, women that have taken vows, female ascetics, Novell. Constit. Just. 123.
ascetriae.short: ascētrĭae, ārum, f., = ἀσκήτριαι, women that have taken vows, female ascetics, Novell.

ascia.full: ascĭa, ae, f. kindred with ἀξίνη, an axe, an axe for hewing wood, a carpenter's axe (syn.: securis, bipennis, ferrum). Lit.: rogum asciā ne polito, Fragm. XII. Tab. ap. Cic Leg 2, 23; Plin. 7, 56, 57, § 198: tilia ascias retundit, id 16, 40, 76, § 207: in securi et asciā aliquid deicere, Vulg. Psa. 73, 6: lignum de saltu praecidit opus manūs artificis in asciā, ib. Jer. 10, 3.—Prov.. asciam sibi in crus impingere or illidere, to cut one's own legs, Petr 74, 16; cf. App. M. 3, p. 139, 6.— Transf.

asciburgium.full: Ascĭburgĭum, ii, n., an ancient town in Gallia Belgica, on the Rhine, now Asburg (but acc. to Mann Gall. 250, now Essenberg; opp. Duisburg), Tac. G 3; id. H. 4, 33.
asciburgium.short: Ascĭburgĭum, ii, n., an ancient town in Gallia Belgica, on the Rhine, now Asburg (but acc.

ascio1.full: ascĭo, āre, v. a. ascia, II. B., to work or prepare with a trowel: calcem, Vitr. 7, 2.

ascio2.full: a-scĭo (adsc-, Rib., Halm), īvi (never ii), 4, v. a., like adopto, arrogo, etc., transf. from the sphere of civil law to common life, to receive, admit (like scio in this signif., very rare, perh. only in Verg. and Tac.; cf. ascisco): si socios sum adscire paratus, Verg. A. 12, 38: generum, id. ib. 11, 472: adsciri per adoptionem, Tac. A. 1, 3: sibi Tiberium adscivit, id. ib. 4, 57: adsciri in societatem Germanos, id. H. 4, 24: adsciri inter comites, id. ib. 4, 80: milites adscire, id. Agr. 19.
ascio2.short: a-scĭo (adsc-, Rib., Halm), īvi (never ii), 4, v.

ascisco.full: a-scisco (adsc-, Lachm., Baiter, Dietsch, Weissenb., K. and H., Halm in Tac.; asc-, Merk., Kayser, Rib., Halm in Nep.), īvi (in ante-class. and class. Lat. never ii), ītum, 3, v. a. Lit., to take or receive a thing with knowledge (and approbation), to approve, receive as true: cum jussisset populus Romanus aliquid, si id ascivissent socii populi ac Latini, etc., Cic. Balb. 8, 20: quas (leges) Latini voluerunt, asciverunt, id. ib. 8, 20, § 21: quibus (scitis) adscitis susceptisque, id. Leg. 2, 5:
ascisco.short: a-scisco (adsc-, Lachm., Baiter, Dietsch, Weissenb., K.

ascites.full: ascītes, ae, m., = ἀσκίτης (sc. ὕδρωψ), a kind of dropsy, Cael. Aur. Tard. 3, 8; Plin. Val. 3, 12 (in Cels. 3, 21, written as Greek).

ascitus1.full: ascītus (adsc-), a, um, Part. of ascisco.

ascitus2.full: ascītus (adsc-), ūs, m. ascisco, an acceptance, reception: vacuitatem doloris alii censent primum ascitum et primum declinatum dolorem, Cic. Fin. 5, 7, 18, where Madvig reads ascitam; so B. and K.

ascius.full: ascĭus, a, um, adj., = ἄσκιος (without shadow): loca, countries under the equator, Plin. 2, 73, 75, § 185.
ascius.short: ascĭus, a, um, adj., = ἄσκιος (without shadow): loca, countries under the equator, Plin.

asclepiades.full: Asclēpĭădes, ae, m., = Ἀσκληπιάδης. A distinguished physician of Prusa, in Bithynia, friend of Crassus, Cic. de Or. 1, 14, 62; Cels. 3, 4; Plin. 7, 37, 37, § 124; 26, 3, 8, § 15 sq.; Cael. Aur. Tard. 3, 8.— A blind philosopher of Eretria, Cic. Tusc. 5, 39, 113.— A Greek poet, inventor of the metre named after him metrum Asclepiadeum (e. g. Hor. C. 1, 1: Maecenas atavis edite regibus), Diom. p. 508 P.

asclepiadeus.full: Asclēpĭădēus, a, um, adj., v. Asclepiades, III.

asclepias.full: asclēpĭăs, ădis, f., = ἀσκληπιάς, the common swallowwort: Asclepias vincetoxicum, Linn.; Plin. 27, 5, 18, § 35.
asclepias.short: asclēpĭăs, ădis, f., = ἀσκληπιάς, the common swallowwort: Asclepias vincetoxicum, Linn.;

asclepiodotus.full: Asclēpĭŏdŏtus, i, m., a biographer of Diocletian, Vop. Aur. 44.
asclepiodotus.short: Asclēpĭŏdŏtus, i, m., a biographer of Diocletian, Vop.

asclepion.full: asclēpĭon, ii, n., a medicinal herb named from Æsculapius, Ἀσκληπιός, Plin. 25, 4, 11, § 30.
asclepion.short: asclēpĭon, ii, n., a medicinal herb named from Æsculapius, Ἀσκληπιός, Plin.

ascletario.full: Asclētārĭo, ōnis, m., a mathematician in the time of Domitian, Suet. Dom. 15.
ascletario.short: Asclētārĭo, ōnis, m., a mathematician in the time of Domitian, Suet.

asconius.full: Ascōnĭus, ii, m.: Q. Asconius Pedianus, a learned grammarian of Padua (c. A. D. 3-88), who devoted his studies especially to Cicero, Sallust, and Vergil, and whose valuable commentary upon five orations of Cicero is still extant; cf. Bähr, Lit. Gesch. § 260; Weich. Poet. Lat. p. 274; Teuffel, Rom. Lit. § 290.

ascopera.full: ascŏpēra, ae, f., = ἀσκοπήρα, a leathern bag or sack, Suet. Ner. 45: Imposuit abrae suae ascoperam vini, * Vulg. Judith, 10, 5.
ascopera.short: ascŏpēra, ae, f., = ἀσκοπήρα, a leathern bag or sack, Suet.

ascra.full: Ascra, ae, f., = Ἄσκρα. A village in Bœotia, near Mount Helicon, the birthplace of Hesiod, Ov. P. 4, 14, 31.—Hence, As-craeus, a, um, adj., = Ἀσκραῖος. Ascrœan: nemus, Prop. 2, 13, 4: poëta, i. e. Hesiod, id. 2, 34, 77: senex, the same, Verg. E. 6, 70.—Also subst.: Ascraeus, i, m., Hesiod, Ov. Am. 1, 15, 11.— Of or pertaining to Hesiod: carmen, i. e. rural, Verg. G. 2, 176; Col. 10, 436: boves, which Hesiod pastured, Ov. F. 6, 14.— Of Helicon, Heliconian: fontes, Prop. 2, 10, 25.

ascribo.full: a-scrībo (ads-, Baiter, Halm, Weissenb., K. and H.; as-, Kayser), psi, ptum, 3, v. a., to annex by writing, to add to a writing (syn.: annumero, addo, insero, attribuo, tribuo). In gen. Lit., constr. absol. or with dat., in with acc. or abl. Absol.: non solum illud perscribunt, quod tum prohibiti sunt, sed etiam causam ascribunt cur etc., Cic. Verr. 2, 1, 35: illud minime auguris, quod adscripsit, ob eam causam, etc., id. Div. 1, 16, 29.— With dat.: Terentia salutem tibi plurimam adscribit, Cic.

ascripticius.full: ascriptīcĭus (adscr-), a, um, adj. ascribo, II., enrolled or received in any community (as citizen, soldier, etc.): novi et adscripticii cives, * Cic. N. D. 3, 15, 39: ascripticii veluti quidam scripti dicebantur, qui supplendis legionibus ascribebantur. Hos et accensos dicebant, quod ad legionum censum essent adscripti, Paul. ex Fest. p. 14 Müll.; cf. ascriptivus: servi, slaves bound to the soil, and transferred with it from one possessor to another, Cod. 11, 47, 6.

ascriptio.full: ascriptĭo (adscr-), ōnis, f. ascribo, I., an addition in writing: declarat ipsa asc/riptio esse aliquid, Cic. Caecin. 33, 95.

ascriptivus.full: ascriptīvus (adscr-), a, um, adj. ascribo, II., enrolled as a (supernumerary) soldier (cf. ascripticius and accensus): Idem istuc aliis adscriptivis ad legionem fieri solet, Plaut. Men. 1, 3, 2; Varr. L. L. 7, § 56 Müll.

ascriptor.full: ascriptor (adscr-), ōris, m. ascribo, I., he who willingly subscribes (his name); hence, trop., he who subscribes to, agrees to, approves any thing (perh. only in the foll. exs.): ascriptores legis agrariae, Cic. Agr. 9: venalis ascriptor et subscriptor tuus, id. Dom. 19; id. Red. in Sen. 4, 9; 10, 26.

ascriptus.full: ascriptus (adscr-), a, um, Part. of ascribo.

asculum.full: Ascŭlum (Asclum, Sil. 8, 440, and Itin. Anton.), i, n., = Ἄσκουλον, more freq. Ἄσκλον. The capital of Picenum, now Ascoli, Plin. 3, 13, 18, § 111; Flor. 1, 18, 9; 1, 18, 14; cf. Mann. Ital. I. p. 492.—Hence, Ascŭlānus, a, um, adj., of Asculum, Asculanian: triumphus, Plin. 7, 43, 44, § 135. —Ascŭlāni, ōrum, m., the inhabitants of Asculum, Cic. Font. 14.— A town in Apulia, Flor. 1, 18, 9 Duker; hence, As-cŭlīnus, a, um, adj., Asculinian: ager, Front. Colon. p. 110.

ascyroides.full: ascўrŏīdĕs, is, n., = ἀσκυροειδές, a plant similar to the ascyron, Plin. 27, 5, 20, § 37.
ascyroides.short: ascўrŏīdĕs, is, n., = ἀσκυροειδές, a plant similar to the ascyron, Plin.

ascyron.full: ascўron, i, n., = ἄσκυρον, a plant, also called androsaemon, St. John's-wort, Plin. 27, 4, 10, § 26.
ascyron.short: ascўron, i, n., = ἄσκυρον, a plant, also called androsaemon, St.

asella.full: ăsella, ae, f. dim. asina, a small sheass, Ov. A. A. 3, 290.

asellio.full: Asellĭo, ōnis, m., one of the early Roman historians, Cic. Leg. 1, 2.
asellio.short: Asellĭo, ōnis, m., one of the early Roman historians, Cic.

asellulus.full: ăsellŭlus, i, m. doub. dim. [asellus], a small, young ass, Arn. 3, p. 109.

asellus.full: ăsellus, i, m. dim. asinus, a little ass, an ass's colt. Lit.: dossuarius, Varr. R. R. 2, 6 fin.: asellus onustus auro, * Cic. Att. 1, 16: tardus, Verg. G. 1, 273: lente gradiens, Ov. M. 11, 179; so id. ib. 4, 27; Hor. S. 1, 9, 20; Vulg. Num. 16, 15; ib. Joan. 12, 14 al.—Prov.: narrare fabellam surdo asello, to preach to deaf ears, Hor. Ep. 2, 1, 199 (an imitation of a Greek proverb, Ὄνῳ τις ἔλεγε μῦθον · ὁ δὲ τὰ ὦτα ἐκίνει; cf. Schmid ad Hor. l. c.).— Transf. Of a man addicted to sensuality, Ju

asemus.full: ăsēmus, a, um, adj., = ἄσημος (without sign): tunica, that has not the purple stripe, Lampr. Alex. Sev. 33 fin.
asemus.short: ăsēmus, a, um, adj., = ἄσημος (without sign): tunica, that has not the purple stripe, Lampr.

asia.full: asĭa, ae, f.; among the Taurini, rye, in pure Lat., secale, Plin. 18, 16, 40, § 141.

asiagenes.full: Ā^sĭăgĕnes, is, m., = Ἀσιαγενής, a surname of Scipio Asiaticus, Liv. 39, 44; Sid. Carm. 7, 80; cf. Gron. Obs. 4, 391 (p. 531 Frotsch.).
asiagenes.short: Ā^sĭăgĕnes, is, m., = Ἀσιαγενής, a surname of Scipio Asiaticus, Liv.

asianus.full: Ā^sĭānus, a, um, adj., = Ἀσιανός. Asiatic, belonging to the Roman province of Asia: res, Liv. 31, 2.—Hence, subst.: ā^sĭāni,ōrum, m., the inhabitants of the province of Asia, Cic. Att. 1, 17, 9; Plin. 21, 26, 98, § 171; Vulg. Act. 20, 4.— In rhet.: ā^sĭāni, orators who employ a peculiarly bombastic or redundant style (cf. Asiaticus, II.), Quint. 8 prooem. 17; 12, 10, 1; 12, 12, 16.—Hence, adv.: ā^sĭānē, in the Asiatic style: loqui, Quint. 12, 10, 17.

asiarcha.full: Ā^sĭarcha, ae, m., = Ἀσιάρχης, a high-priest, and overseer of games and theatrical exhibitions in the Roman province of Asia, Cod. Th. 15, 9, 2.
asiarcha.short: Ā^sĭarcha, ae, m., = Ἀσιάρχης, a high-priest, and overseer of games and theatrical exhibitions in the Roman province of Asia, Cod.

asiaticianus.full: Ā^sĭātĭcĭānus, a, um, adj. Asiaticus, of the Asiatic style: SCAENICI, Inscr. Orell. 2642.

asiaticus.full: Ā^sĭātĭcus, a, um, adj., = Ἀσιατικός, Asiatic. In gen.: bellum, Cic. Imp. Pomp. 7: mos, id. Or. 8, 27: creta, id. Fl. 16, 37: Graeci, id. ib. 25, 60: exercitus, Liv. 39, 6: mare, Plin. 5, 27, 28, § 102: Persica, a fruit from Asia, a kind of peach, id. 15, 12, 11, § 39; also absol.: Asiatica, Col. 10, 412: picturae genus, Plin. 35, 10, 36, § 75. — Esp. as rhet. t., Asiatic, bombaslic: genus dicendi, a bombastic style of discourse, peculiar to Asiatics, Cic. Brut. 95, 325: dictio, id. ib. 95, 325:
asiaticus.short: Ā^sĭātĭcus, a, um, adj., = Ἀσιατικός, Asiatic.

asilus.full: ăsīlus, i, m., a gad-fly, horse-fly, usu. tabanus (cf. Plin. 11, 28, 34, § 100); Gr. οἶστρος (cf. Isid. Orig. 12, 8, 15), Verg. G. 3, 147 (cf. Hom. Od. 22, 300). (Even in Seneca's time the word was antiquated; v. Sen. Ep. 58; cf. Plin. 11, 28, 34, § 100.)
asilus.short: ăsīlus, i, m., a gad-fly, horse-fly, usu.

asina.full: ăsĭna, ae, f. (dat. and abl. plur. asinabus rest only on the assertion of Prisc. p. 733 P.; Rhem Pal. 1365 P., and Phoc. p. 1707 P.: asinis, Plin. 11, 40, 95, § 233, acc. to which it should be considered as masc.; cf. Schneid. Gr. II. p. 26; Charis. p. 39, and Rudd. I. p. 50, n. 31) [asinus]. A she-ass, Varr. R. R. 2, 8, 1 and 6; so Col. 6, 37, 4; Plin. 8, 44, 69, § 171; Pall. 1, 35 fin.; Vulg. Gen. 12, 16; ib. Num. 22, 21 sqq.; ib. Matt. 21, 2; ib. Joan. 12, 15 et persaepe: molendaria, Dig. 33,

asinaeus.full: Asĭnaeus, a, um, adj., v. Asine.

asinalis.full: ăsĭnālis, e, adj. asinus, asinine, doltish, slupid (v. asinus, II.): asinali verecundiā ductus, App. M. 4, p. 153, 3 Elm.

asinarius.full: ăsĭnārĭus, a, um, adj. id., pertaining or belonging to an ass: mola, a millstone turned by an ass, Cato, R. R. 10, 4; 11, 4; so Vulg. Matt. 18, 6; ib. Marc. 9, 41. — Subst. ăsĭnārĭus, ii, m., a keeper of asses, an ass-driver, Cato, R. R. 10, 1; 11, 1, Varr. R. R. 1, 18, 1.— ăsĭnārĭa, ae, f., the title of a comedy of Plautus.—(That the Via Asinaria (Paul. ex Fest. s. v retricibus, p. 282 Müll.), a side branch of the Via Latina, and the Porta Asinaria, were named from asinus, since upon this stree

asine.full: Ăsĭnē, ēs, f., = Ἀσίνη, a town in Messenia, Plin. 4, 5, 7, § 15.—Hence, ăsĭnae-us, a, um, adj., of Asine: sinus, Plin. 4, 5, 7, § 15; cf. Mann. Gr. 546.
asine.short: Ăsĭnē, ēs, f., = Ἀσίνη, a town in Messenia, Plin.

asinianus.full: Ăsĭnĭānus, a, um, adj., v. Asinius.

asininus.full: ăsĭnīnus, a, um, adj. asinus, of or produced by an ass: stercus, Varr. R. R. 1, 38, 2: pullus, ass's foal, a young ass, id. ib. 2, 8: pilus, Plin. 8, 21, 30, § 72, where Jan reads asini: pruna asinina cognominata a vilitate, id. 15, 13, 12, § 41.

asinius.full: Ăsĭnĭus, a, um, adj., name of a Roman gens; the most celebrated was Asinius Pollio, a friend of Augustus, founder of the first library in Rome, and author of a history, now lost, of the civil war between Cœsar and Pompey, Cic. Fam. 10, 31 sq. Manut.; Vell. 2, 125; Hor. C 2, 1; Verg. E. 4; Tac. A. 4, 34; Suet. Caes. 30; id. Gram. 10; cf. Bähr, Lit. Gesch. § 192; Weich. Poët. Lat. pp. 155, 293, 327, 395; Teuffel, Röm. Lit. § 218.— Hence, ăsĭnĭānus, a, um, adj., pertaining to the gens Asinia, or to
asinius.short: Ăsĭnĭus, a, um, adj., name of a Roman gens;

asinus.full: ăsĭnus, i, m. acc. to Benfey, I. p. 123, and Hehn foll. by Curtius, an oriental word, perh. the Heb. , asina; cf. Goth. asilus; Lith. asilas; Erse, assul; Celt. asen or assen; Engl. ass; and Gr. ὄνος, which latter two forms the Lat. seems to have in combination, an ass. Lit., Cato, R. R. 10, 1; 11, 1; Varr. R. R. 2, 1, 14; 2, 6, 1 al.; Col. 6, 37, 8; 6, 7, 1 al.; Plin. 8, 43, 68, § 167 sqq. et saep.; Vulg. Gen. 12, 6; ib. Isa. 1, 3; ib. Luc. 13, 15; 14, 5 et persaepe.—Prov.: qui asinum non potes

asinusca.full: ăsĭnusca, ae, f. asinus, a kind of grape of little value, Plin. 14, 3, 4, § 42; Macr. S 2, 16.

asio.full: ăsĭo, ōnis, m., a horned owl, Plin. 10, 23, 33, § 68; 29, 6, 38, § 117 (in both these passages Jan reads axio).
asio.short: ăsĭo, ōnis, m., a horned owl, Plin.

asius.full: Ā^sĭus, a, um, v. 1. Asia, I. B. and II. B.

asmiraea.full: Asmīraea, ae, f., a district and city in Serica, Amm. 23, 6.
asmiraea.short: Asmīraea, ae, f., a district and city in Serica, Amm.

asmura.full: Asmūra, ae, f., a town in Hyrcania, Amm. 23, 6
asmura.short: Asmūra, ae, f., a town in Hyrcania, Amm.

asnaus.full: Asnaus, i, m., a mountain in Macedonia, Liv 32, 5.
asnaus.short: Asnaus, i, m., a mountain in Macedonia, Liv 32, 5.

asoi.full: Asōi, ōrum, plur m., a people of India, Plin. 6, 20, 23, § 78.
asoi.short: Asōi, ōrum, plur m., a people of India, Plin.

asomatus.full: ăsōmătus, a, um, adj., = ἀσὡματος, incorporeal, profatus, Mart. Cap. 3 init.
asomatus.short: ăsōmătus, a, um, adj., = ἀσὡματος, incorporeal, profatus, Mart.

asopiades.full: Āsōpĭădes, ae, m. patr., = Ἀσωπιάδης, grandson of Asopus, i. e. Æacus, Ov. M. 7, 484.

asopis.full: Āsōpis, ĭdis, f. (gen. Gr. Asopidos, Ov. M. 7, 616; acc. Gr Asopida, id. ib. 6, 113), = Ἀσωπίς. Daughter of Asopus, i. e. Ægina, the mother of Æacus by Jupiter, Ov. M. 6, 113; 7, 616.— His daughter Evadne, Ov. Am. 3, 6, 41.— A name of the island Eubœa (after Eubœa, the third daughter of Asopus), Plin. 4, 12, 21, § 64.— Adj. for Bœotian (v Asopus), Stat. Th. 4, 370.

asopus.full: Āsōpus (-os), i, m. (nom. Gr. Asopos, Stat. Th. 7, 315; acc. Gr. Asopon, Ov. Am. 3, 6, 33), = Ἀσωπός. A river in Bœotia; personified, the father of Ægina, Evadne, and Eubœa, and grandfather of Æacus (v. Asopis and Asopiades), Ov. Am. 3, 6, 33.— A river in Thessaly, Liv 36, 22.— In Phrygia, Plin. 5, 29, 29, § 105

asotia.full: ăsōtīa, ae, f., = ἀσωτεία, dissoluteness, sensuality, Gell. 10, 17, 3; 19, 9, 8.
asotia.short: ăsōtīa, ae, f., = ἀσωτεία, dissoluteness, sensuality, Gell.

asotus.full: ăsōtus, i, m., = ἄσωτος, a dissolute man, a debauchee (only in Cic.), Cic. Fin. 2, 7, 22; 2, 8, 23, id. N. D. 3, 31, 77.
asotus.short: ăsōtus, i, m., = ἄσωτος, a dissolute man, a debauchee (only in Cic.), Cic.

aspalathus.full: aspălăthus, i, m., = ἀσπάλαθος, a thorny shrub, whose bark and roots yielded a fragrant oil, which was used in the preparation of spiced wine (vinum aromatites), rosewood, Plin. 12, 24, 52, § 110; 15, 7, 7, § 30
aspalathus.short: aspălăthus, i, m., = ἀσπάλαθος, a thorny shrub, whose bark and roots yielded a fragrant oil, which was used in the preparation of spiced wine (vinum aromatites), rosewood, Plin.

aspalax.full: aspălax, ăcis, m., = ἀσπάλαξ, an herb now unknown, Plin. 19, 6, 31, § 99, where Jan reads spalax.
aspalax.short: aspălax, ăcis, m., = ἀσπάλαξ, an herb now unknown, Plin.

aspar.full: Aspar, ăris, m., a Numidian, Sall. J. 108, 1; 112, 1.
aspar.short: Aspar, ăris, m., a Numidian, Sall.

asparagium.full: Aspărāgĭum, ii, n., a town in Illyria, on the river Genusus, now Iskarpar, Caes. B. C. 3, 30 fin.; 3, 41; 3, 76.
asparagium.short: Aspărāgĭum, ii, n., a town in Illyria, on the river Genusus, now Iskarpar, Caes.

asparagus.full: aspărăgus (asph-, App. Herb. 84), i, m., = ἀσπάραγος (ἀσφ-). Asparagus, Cato, R. R. 6, 3; 6, 61, Col. 11, 3, 45; Plin. 19, 8, 42, § 145 sqq.; 19, 4, 19, § 54; Juv 11, 69; Suet. Aug. 87 (perh. in Varr. ap. Non. p. 550, 11, asparagos should be read instead of sparagos).— A sprout, a shoot, like asparagus, Plin. 23, 1, 17, § 24; 21, 15, 54, § 91.

aspasia.full: Aspāsĭa, ae, f., = Ἀσπασία. The accomplished friend of Socrates, afterwards wife of Pericles, Cic. Inv. 1, 31, 51; Quint. 5, 11, 27.— The mistress of the younger Cyrus, Just. 10, 2.

aspectabilis.full: aspectābĭlis (adsp-), e, adj. aspecto (perh. only in the foll. exs.). That may be seen, visible, Cic. Tim. 4: animal, id. ib. 4.— Worthy of being seen: nihil esse aspectabilius, App. Mag. p. 282, 14.

aspectamen.full: aspectāmen (adsp-), ĭnis, n. id., a look, a sight, Claud. Mam. Stat. An. 2, 12.

aspectio.full: aspectĭo (adsp-), ōnis, f. aspicio, a look, a view, Fest. s. v. spectio, p. 333 Müll.

aspecto.full: aspecto (adsp-, Ritschl; asp-, Lachmann, Fleck., Rib., B. and K., Halm), āvi, ātum, 1, v. freq. a. id., to look at attentively, with respect, desire, etc. Lit. (rare but class.): hicine est Telamon, quem aspectabant, Enn. ap. Cic. Tusc. 3, 18, 39: Quid me adspectas, stolide? Plaut. Am. 4, 2, 8: Estne ita ut tibi dixi? Adspecta et contempla, Plaut. Ep. 5, 1, 16; id. As. 5, 1, 13; id. Am. 1, 1, 114: Quid me aspectas? Quid taces? Ter Eun. 3, 5, 12: Quid me aspectas? * Cic. Planc. 42 Illum aspectari

aspectus1.full: aspectus (adsp-), a, um, Part. of aspicio

aspectus2.full: aspectus (adsp-), ūs, m. (gen. aspecti, Att. ap Non. p. 485, 21; cf. Prisc. p. 712 P.; Rudd. I. p. 103, n. 46; dat. sing. aspectu, like jussu, manu, etc., Verg. A. 6, 465; cf. Schneid Gr II. 332) [aspicio]. Act., a seeing, looking at, a look, sight. Absol.: intellegens dicendi existimator uno aspectu et praeteriens de oratore saepe judicat, Cic Brut. 54, 200: e quibus (litteris tuis) primo aspectu voluptatem cepi, quod erant a te ipso scriptae, id. Att. 7, 3, 1 hic primo aspectu inanimum quiddam

aspello.full: as-pello, ĕre (abspulsus, Fronto, Differ. Vocab. p. 473), v. a. ab-pello; cf. ab init., to drive away, remove (only ante-class.): eos, qui advorsum eunt, aspellito, Plaut. Merc. 1, 2, 5; so id. Trin. 3, 2, 46; id. Am. 3, 4, 17; Ter. Heaut. 2, 3, 20 Bentl., Fleck.— Trop.: longe a leto aspellor, Att. ap. Cic. Tusc. 2, 10, 25: metum alicui, Plaut. Capt. 3, 3, 4.

aspendios.full: aspendĭos, ii, m., = ἀσπένδιος, a kind of vine, Plin. 14, 18, 22, § 117.
aspendios.short: aspendĭos, ii, m., = ἀσπένδιος, a kind of vine, Plin.

aspendos.full: Aspendos, i, f., = Ἄσπενδος, a town built by the Argives, in Pamphylia, on the Eurymedon, now Minugat, Cic. Verr. 1, 20, 53; Mel. 1, 14, 1.—Also, Aspendum, i, n., Plin. 5, 27, 26, § 96; cf. id. 31, 7, 39, § 73.— Hence, Aspendĭus, a, um, adj., of Aspendos: Aspendii, ōrum, m., the inhabitants of Aspendos, Liv. 37, 23; Nep. Dat. 8, 2. A harper of Aspendos was distinguished in antiquity for playing with the fingers of the left hand (instead of the plectrum), and on the side of the instrument turned
aspendos.short: Aspendos, i, f., = Ἄσπενδος, a town built by the Argives, in Pamphylia, on the Eurymedon, now Minugat, Cic.

asper1.full: asper, ĕra, ĕrum, adj. (aspra = aspera, Enn. ap. App. Mag. p. 299, but Vahl. ad Enn. p. 166 reads spissa instead of aspra: aspris = asperis, Verg. A. 2, 379; aspro = aspero, Pall. Insit. 67) [etym. dub.; Doed. foll. by Hinter connects it with ἀσπαίρω, to struggle, to resist; Corssen, Ausspr. II. p. 593, regards asper (i. e. ab spe) as the proper opposite of prosper (i. e. pro spe); thus asper originally meant hopeless, desperate; v. also id. ib. II. p. 870; cf. the use of res asperae as the oppo

asper2.full: Asper, eri, m. A cognomen of L. Trebonius: L. Trebonius ... insectandis patribus, unde Aspero etiam inditum est cognomen, tribunatum gessit, Liv. 3, 65, 4. — Asper, Aspri (Prob. p. 201 Keil), m., a Latin grammarian, two of whose treatises have come down to us; v. Teuffel, Rom. Lit. § 474, 4.

asperatus.full: aspĕrātus, a, um, Part., v. aspero.

aspergo1.full: a-spergo (adsp-, Ritschl, Jan; asp-, others; in MSS. sometimes aspar-go, v. Cort. ad Luc. 1, 384, and Wagner ad Verg. G. 3, 419, and infra examples from Lucr. and Hor.; cf. 2. aspergo), ersi, ersum, 3, v. a. spargo. Aliquid (alicui rei), to scatter, strew something on something; or of liquids, to sprinkle, spatter over (syn.: adfundo, inicio; never in Ovid, but he often uses the simple spargo). Lit.: aequor Ionium glaucis aspargit virus ab undis, Lucr. 1, 719 Lachm.: Ah! adspersisti aquam, Jam r

aspergo2.full: aspergo (Merk., Müller, Strüb.; in MSS. sometimes aspargo, Lachm., Rib., e. g. Verg. A. 3, 534, acc. to Non. p. 405, 5, and Vel. Long. p. 2234 P.; v. 1. aspergo), ĭnis, f. (in the ante-class. per. com. acc. to Prisc. p. 658 P.) [1. aspergo]. A sprinkling, besprinkling (most freq. in the poets, never in Cic., who uses aspersio, q. v.): aspergo aquarum, Ov. M. 7, 108: aquae, Petr. 102, 15: (Peneus) Nubila conducit, summasque aspergine silvas Impluit, Ov. M. 1, 572: sanguis virides aspergine tinxer

asperitas.full: aspĕrĭtas, ātis, f. asper, the quality of asper, unevenness, roughness (opp. 2. levitas). Lit.: saxorum asperitates, Cic. N. D. 2, 39, 98: asperitas viarum, id. Phil. 9, 1, 2: locorum, Sall. J. 75, 2: angustiae locorumque asperitas, Liv. 32, 12 fin.; 43, 21; 44, 5 al.: linguae, Plin. 11, 37, 65, § 172: ventris, id. 11, 37, 79, § 201: squamarum, Gell. 2, 6: faucium, Plin. 30, 4, 11, § 32: animi asperitas seu potius animae, hoarseness, id. 22, 24, 51, § 111: ob asperitatem hiemis, roughness, sever

aspernabilis.full: aspernābĭlis, e, adj. aspernor, worthy of contempt, despicable (ante- and postclass.), Att. ap. Non. p. 179, 33; Gell. 16, 8, 16; 16, 11, 3; 20, 1, 10; Arn. 6, p. 203.— Comp.: aspernabilius, Aug. Mor. Manich. 8.

aspernamentum.full: aspernāmentum, i, n. id., a despising; only Tert. adv. Marc. 4, 14; id. Pud. 8.

aspernatio.full: aspernātĭo, ōnis, f. aspernor, a despising, contemning, disdain (very rare): rationis, * Cic. Tusc. 4, 14, 31: naturalis, Sen. Ep. 121 fin.: illius, * Vulg. Eccli. 22, 1.

aspernator.full: aspernātor, ōris, m. id., a despiser, contemner: divitum, Tert. adv. Marc. 4, 15.

aspernor.full: aspernor (wrongly ads-), ātus, 1, v. dep. a. [for ab-spernor, as as-pello for abpello, as-porto for ab-porto; cf. ab init.; Doed. Syn. II. p. 179, and Vanicek, p. 1182], lit., to cast off a person or thing (ab se spernari; cf. sperno and spernor); hence, to disdain, spurn, reject, despise (simply with the accessory idea of aversion = recuso, respuo, reicio, and opp. to appeto, concupisco; on the other hand, contemnere, not to fear, is opp. to metuere, timere; and despicere, not to value a thing,

aspero.full: aspĕro (aspro, Sid. Ep. 4, 8; id. Carm. 2, 418), āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. asper, to make rough, uneven. Lit. (very freq. in the poets and Tac., but not found in Cic.): asserculi asperantur, ne sint advolantibus lubrici, Col. 8, 3, 6: tum enim (apes) propter laborem asperantur ac macescunt, become rough, Varr. R. R. 3, 16, 20: cum torpent apes, nec caloribus asperantur, Pall. 7, 7, 2: (vinum myrtites) limum dysentericae passionis medicabiliter asperare, i. e. excrementa solidiora reddere, id. 3, 31, 2

aspersio.full: aspersĭo, ōnis, f. aspergo, a sprinkling upon, a sprinkling. Lit.: aspersione aquae, Cic. Leg. 2, 10, 24; Macr. S. 3, 1: sanguinis aspersio, Vulg. Heb. 12, 24; ib. 1 Pet. 1, 2: pulveris, ib. 3 Reg. 20, 28.—Of the laying on of colors: aspersio fortuita, Cic. Div. 1, 13, 23.— Trop.: ut sint in aquam aspersionis, for a water of scattering, separation, Vulg. Num. 19, 9.

aspersus1.full: aspersus (adsp-), a, um, Part. of aspergo.

aspersus2.full: aspersus (adsp-, Jan), ūs, m. aspergo, a sprinkling upon (used only in the abl., and perh. only in Plin.): calidae aquae adspersu, Plin. 8, 37, 56, § 134: insecta olei adspersu necantur, id. 11, 53, 115, § 279: aceti adspersu, id. 13, 12, 26, § 82 al.

asperugo.full: aspĕrūgo, ĭnis, f. asper, a plant with prickly leaves: Asperugo procumbens, Linn.: similis (lappaginis), sed asperioribus foliis asperugo, Plin. 26, 10, 65, § 102.

asphaltion.full: asphaltĭon, ii, n., = ἀσφάλτιον, a kind of clover with long leaves, and of the odor of asphaltum; among the Gr. μινύανθες, prob. the common bituminous clover: Psoralea bituminosa, Linn.; Plin. 21, 9, 30, § 54 (in Col. 6, 17, 2, written as Greek).
asphaltion.short: asphaltĭon, ii, n., = ἀσφάλτιον, a kind of clover with long leaves, and of the odor of asphaltum;

asphaltites.full: Asphaltītes, ae, m., = Ἀσφαλτίτης; also Asphaltites lacus, = Ἀσφαλτῖτις λίμνη, Lake Asphaltites (the Dead Sea), in Palestine, Plin. 5, 15, 15, § 71; 5, 16, 15, § 72; cf. Mann. Palaest. p. 261.

asphodelus.full: asphŏdĕlus (-ĭlus, Pall. 1, 37, 2), i, m., = ἀσφόδελος, the asphodel, a kind of lily-shaped plant with many tubercles at the root: Asphodelus ramosus, Linn.; Plin. 21, 17, 68, § 108 sqq. (acc. to Isid. Orig. 17, 9, 84, in pure Lat., albutium).

aspicio.full: a-spĭcĭo (adsp-, Jan; asp-, others except Halm, who uses both), spexi, spectum, 3, v. a. (aspexit = aspexerit, Plaut. As. 4, 1, 25), to look to or upon a person or thing, to behold, look at, see. Lit., constr. in the ante - class. per. sometimes with ad; but afterwards with the acc., with a finite clause, or absol.; in eccl. Lat., with in with acc., and super with acc. With ad: aspice ad me, Plaut. Capt. 3, 4, 38: aspicient ad me, Vulg. Zach. 12, 10: aspicere ad terram, Plaut. Cist. 4, 2, 25: ad

aspilates.full: aspīlătes, ae, m., = ἀσπιλάτης, a precious stone of Arabia, Plin. 37, 10, 54, § 146, where Jan reads aspisatis.
aspilates.short: aspīlătes, ae, m., = ἀσπιλάτης, a precious stone of Arabia, Plin.

aspiramen.full: aspīrāmen (adsp-), ĭnis, n. aspiro, a blowing, breathing; hence poet., a communicating: formae, Val. Fl. 6, 465.

aspiratio.full: aspīrātĭo (adsp-), ōnis, f. id.. In gen. Lit., a blowing or breathing to or upon: animantes adspiratione aëris sustinentur, by the blowing or breathing of the air (not by respiration, as it is commonly rendered), Cic. N. D. 2, 33, 83: ventorum, Lact. 7, 3 fin.— Trop.: superni numinis, favor, Amm. 15, 2.—Hence, Esp. Evaporation, exhalation: quae omnia fiunt et ex caeli varietate et ex disparili adspiratione terrarum, Cic. Div. 1, 36, 79; 1, 57, 130.— In gram., the enunciation of a word with an h

aspiro.full: a-spīro (adsp-, Baiter, Rib., Merk., K. and H.; asp-, Kayser, Halm, Müller), āvi, ātum, 1, v. n. and a. Neutr. To breathe or blow upon; constr. with ad, the dat., or absol.: ad quae (granaria) nulla aura umida ex propinquis locis adspiret, Varr. R. R. 1, 57: ut ne ad eum frigus adspiret, Cels. 2, 17: pulmones se contrahunt adspirantes, exhaling, Cic. N. D. 2, 55, 136: Lenius aspirans aură, Cat. 68, 64: amaracus illum Floribus et dulci adspirans complectitur umbrā, Verg. A. 1, 694: adspirant aura

aspis.full: aspis, ĭdis, f. (acc. Gr. aspida, Luc. 9, 701; plur. aspidas, Cic. N. D. 3, 19, 47) [ἀσπίς, com. shield, rarely an asp; this order of frequency is reversed in Lat.]. The asp, viper: Coluber, Linn.; Plin. 29, 4, 18, § 65: aspide ad corpus admoto, Cic. Rab. Post. 9: si scieris aspidem occulte latere uspiam, id. Fin. 2, 18, 59; Isid. Orig. 12, 4, 12.— A shield, = ἀσπίς, Just. Nov. 85 fin.

asplenum.full: asplēnum or -on, i, n., = ἄσπληνον, miltwort, spleenwort: Asplenum ceterach, Linn.: Asplenon sunt qui hemionion vocant, Plin. 27, 5, 17, § 34; in Vitr. 1, 4, written as Greek, and in Isid. Orig. 17, 9, 87, asplenos.
asplenum.short: asplēnum or -on, i, n., = ἄσπληνον, miltwort, spleenwort: Asplenum ceterach, Linn.: Asplenon sunt qui hemionion vocant, Plin.

asportatio.full: asportātĭo, ōnis, f. asporto, a carrying away: signorum, Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 49 fin.

asporto.full: as-porto abs-porto; cf. ab init., āvi, ātum, 1, v. a., to bear, carry, or take off or away (in the class. per. only in prose; cf. Wagner ad Verg. A. 2, 778).—Com., Of things: simulacrum e signo Cereris, Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 49 fin.; so id. ib. 2, 1, 20; id. Div. in Caecil. 9, 28: multa de suis rebus, id. Par. 1, 2: sua omnia Salamina, Nep. Them. 2 fin.; Liv. 2, 4; 42, 3; Vulg. 2 Reg. 12, 30.—Also, Of persons, to carry away (esp. by ship) to transport: aliquem trans mare, Plaut. Merc. 2, 3, 19: virgi

aspratilis.full: asprātĭlis, e, adj. asper, rough (late Lat. for asper): piscis, with rough scales, Plin. Val. 5; 8; 10 al.; Edict. Diocl. p. 15: terminus, of a rough, unpolished stone, Auct. Lim. p. 305 Goes.: petra, id. ib. p. 228.

aspredo.full: asprēdo, ĭnis, f. id., roughness; only in Cels. 5, 28, 2 Daremb.

aspretum.full: asprētum, i, n. id., an uneven, rough place: ad hoc saxa erant temere jacentia, ut fit in aspretis, Liv. 9, 24, 6; 27, 18; 35, 28; 36, 15; Grat. Cyn. 241.

aspritudo.full: asprĭtūdo (asperĭtūdo, App. M. 1, p. 103, 20), ĭnis, f. id., roughness: modo circa totum corpus partemve aspritudo quaedam fit, Cels. 5, 28, 15: aspritudo oculorum, id. 6, 6, 26; 7, 7, 15 Daremb. al.

aspuo.full: a-spŭo (adsp-), ĕre, v. a., to spit at or upon: a nutrice adspui, Plin. 28, 4, 7, § 39.

assabinus.full: Assabinus, i, m., a deity of the Ethiopians, Plin. 12, 19, 42, § 89.
assabinus.short: Assabinus, i, m., a deity of the Ethiopians, Plin.

assaracus.full: Assărăcus, i, m., = Ἀσσάρακος, King of Phrygia, son of Tros, brother of Ganymede and Ilus, father of Capys, and grandfather of Anchises, Ov. M. 11, 756.—Hence, Assaraci nurus, Venus, Ov. F. 4, 123: Assaraci Frater, Ganymede, a constellation (Aquarius), id. ib. 4, 943: Assaraci gens, i. e. the Romans, Verg. A. 9, 643.
assaracus.short: Assărăcus, i, m., = Ἀσσάρακος, King of Phrygia, son of Tros, brother of Ganymede and Ilus, father of Capys, and grandfather of Anchises, Ov.

assarius1.full: assārĭus, a, um, adj. asso, roasted: daps pecuina, Cato, R. R. 132, 2 Schneid.

assarius2.full: assārĭus, ii, m., v. as init.

assatura.full: assātūra, ae, f. asso, roasted meat (late Lat.), Vop. Aur. 49; Apic. 7, 5; * Vulg. 2 Reg. 6, 19.

assecla.full: assĕcla (ads-, B. and K., Jahn; ass-, Halm), ae, comm. acc. to Charis. p. 37 P. (but examples are found only in masc.) [assequor], a follower, an attendant, servant, sycophant (with the accessory idea of contempt, different from assectator; cf. Ruhnk. ad Vell. 2, 83): assentatores eorum atque adseculae, Cic. Corn. Fragm. ap. Orell. IV. 2, p. 453: legatorum adseculae, Cic. Verr. 2, 1, 25: cum adseculae suo tetrarchian dedisset, id. Div. 2, 37, 79; id. Sest. 64 fin. Orell. (ed. min.); id. Att. 6,

assectatio.full: assectātĭo (ads-), ōnis, f. assector. An (assiduous, respectful) attendance (as that of clients, etc.): in petitionibus opera atque adsectatio, Cic. Mur. 34: so Q. Cic. Petit. Cons. 9.— Observation, study: magna caeli adsectatio, Plin. 2, 20, 18, § 82.

assectator.full: assectātor (ads-), ōris, m. id., he that is in attendance upon any one (as friend, servant, client, etc.), a follower, an attendant (in a good sense, while assecla is used in a contemptuous sense). Lit.: vetus adsectator ex numero amicorum, Cic. Verr. 2, 2, 11: cum comitatu adsectatoribusque, id. Balb. 27 fin.: hujus autem rei (sc. adsectationis) tres partes sunt: una salutatorum, cum domum veniunt; altera deductorum, tertia adsectatorum, who are always in attendance upon the candidates, Q. Cic.

assector.full: as-sector (ads-, Kayser, Halm, K. and H.), ātus, 1, v. dep. a. To attend one with zeal, eagerness, etc., to accompany, follow, wait upon, be in attendance upon (esp. of the friends of candidates for office): cum aedilitatem P. Crassus peteret, eumque major natu, etiam consularis, Ser. Galba adsectaretur, * Cic. de Or. 1, 56, 239: studia adulescentulorum in suffragando, in adsectando mirifice et magna et honesta sunt, Q. Cic. Petit. Cons. 8 fin.: cum adsectaretur: Num quid vis? occupo, Hor. S. 1,

assecutor.full: assĕcūtor (ads-), ōris, m. assequor, an attendant: Cupidinis, Mart. Cap. 9, p. 306.

assedo.full: assĕdo, ōnis, m., = assessor, Non. p. 63, 23.

assefolium.full: assĕfŏlĭum, ii, n., a plant; also called, after the Gr., agrostis, App. Herb. 77.

assellor.full: as-sellor (ads-), ātus, 1, v. dep. sella, to go to stool, to void (perh. only in Veg.): multum stercoris assellatus, Veg. 2, 22, 2; 5, 44, 1; 5, 56, 1: sanguinem, id. 5, 9, 1.

assenesco.full: as-sĕnesco (ads-), ĕre, v. inch. n., to become old to any thing: Cereri, Tert. Exhort. ad Cast. 13.

assensio.full: as-sensĭo (ads-), ōnis, f. assentior, an assent, agreement, approbation, applause (esp. in rhetor. and philos. lang.; beyond this sphere assensus is more usu.): orationis genus exile nec satis populari adsensioni accommodatum, Cic. Brut. 30, 114; id. Inv. 1, 31, 51: crebrae adsensiones, multae admirationes, id. ib. 84, 290; id. Mil. 5: plurium, Sen. Ep. 7: simulata, Quint. 6, 3, 73; so Plin. Ep. 3, 4, 4; 4, 12, 6 al.—In philos. lang., an assent to the reality of sensible appearances: nunc de ads

assensor.full: assensor (ads-), ōris, m. id., he that assents to or agrees with any one: cotidie commemorabam te unum in tanto exercitu mihi fuisse adsensorem, Cic. Fam. 6, 21; Auct. ad Her. 3, 23: vindictae, Val. Max. 6, 3, 6: irae, Sen. Hippol. 1207.

assensus1.full: assensus (ads-), a, um, Part. of assentior.

assensus2.full: assensus (ads-), ūs, m. assentior, an agreement, assent, approval, approbation. In gen.: adsensu omnium dicere, Cic. N. D. 2, 2, 4: volgi adsensu et populari approbatione, id. Brut. 49, 185: omnium adsensu, Liv. 5, 9; 8, 5; 8, 4 fin.; cf. id. 3, 72: adsensu senatūs, Plin. Pan. 71: adsensum consequi agendo, id. Ep. 7, 6, 13; so Tac. A. 14, 12; 15, 22; Suet. Aug. 68; id. Tib. 45 et saep.—In the plur.: dicta Jovis pars voce probant; alii partes assensibus implent, Ov. M. 1, 245; 8, 604: hinc ingent

assentatio.full: assentātĭo (ads-), ōnis, f. assentor. A flattering assent, flattery, adulation: istaec illum perdidit adsentatio, Plaut. Bacch. 3, 3, 7: nullam in amicitiis pestem esse majorem quam adulationem, blanditiam, adsentationem, Cic. Lael. 25, 94: adsentationes, blanditiae et pejor odio amoris simulatio, Plin. Pan. 85: Graeci diuturnā servitute ad nimiam adsentationem eruditi, Cic. ad Q. Fr. 1, 1, 5: se blanditiis et adsentationibus in Asinii consuetudinem penitus immersit, id. Clu. 13: inflatus adsent

assentatiuncula.full: assentātĭuncŭla (ads-), ae, f. dim. assentatio, petty, trivial flattery: adsentatiunculae ac perjuratiunculae parasiticae, * Plaut. Stich. 1, 3, 75: non vereor, ne adsentatiunculā quādam aucupari tuam gratiam videar, * Cic. Fam. 5, 12.

assentator.full: assentātor (ads-), ōris, m. assentor, one who assents flatteringly, a flatterer (most freq. in Cic.). Lit.: semper auget adsentator id, quod is, cujus ad voluntatem loquitur, vult esse magnum, Cic. Lael. 26, 98: ita fit, ut is adsentatoribus patefaciat aures suas maxime, qui ipse sibi adsentetur et se maxime ipse delectet, id. ib. 26, 97; id. Off. 1, 14, 42; 1, 26, 91; 2, 18, 63; id. Caecin. 5, 14: Adsentatores jubet ad lucrum ire poëta Dives agris, * Hor. A. P. 420.— Trop.: non auctor, sed adse

assentatorie.full: assentātōrĭē (ads-), adv. id., in a flattering manner, fawningly: dubitare te, non adsentatorie (i. e. non tibi indulgens), sed fraterne veto, Cic. ad Q. Fr. 2, 15, 6, 3.

assentatrix.full: assentātrix (ads-), īcis, f. assentator, a female flatterer: adsentatrix scelestast, Plaut. Most. 1, 3, 100.

assentior.full: as-sentĭor (ads-, Fleck., B. and K., Halm, Weissenb.; ass-, Merk.), sensus, 4, v. dep. sentio (the act. form assentio, īre, was out of use even in the time of Varro, Varr. L. L. Fragm. ap. Gell. 2, 25, 9; cf. Spald. ad Quint. 1, 5, 55. The middle use of the word corresponds far better with its signif. than the active; for while adsentio prop. signif. only sentiendo accedere ad aliquem or aliquid, to make known one's inclination or feeling toward any object, whether in favor of or against it; the

assentor.full: assentor (ads-; v. assentior init.), ātus, 1, v. freq. [irreg. for adsensor, from assentior], lit., to join one in judgment or opinion (opp. adversor); hence, always to assent, to agree with one in every thing, to flatter (in the class. per. only in prose); with dat.: Etiam tu quoque adsentaris huice? Plaut. Am. 2, 2, 70; cf. assentatrix: (callidus adulator) etiam adversando saepe adsentetur et litigare se simulans blandiatur, etc., Cic. Lael. 26, 99; Vell. 2, 48: tibi adsentabor, Plaut. Most. 1

assequela.full: assĕquēla (ads-), ae, f. assequor, a succeeding, succession, Mar. Vict. p. 2500 P.

assequor.full: as-sĕquor (ads-, Fleck., B. and K., Halm), sĕcūtus (or sĕquutus; v. sequor), 3, v. dep., to follow one in order to come up to him, to pursue. In gen. (only ante-class. in the two foll. exs.): ne sequere, adsequere, Plaut. Fragm. ap. Varr. L. L. 6, § 73 Müll.: Adsequere, retine, Ter. Phorm. 5, 8, 89.—Far more freq., Esp., to reach one by pursuing him: sequendo pervenire ad aliquem: nec quicquam sequi, quod adsequi non queas, Cic. Off. 1, 31, 110.—Hence, to overtake, come up with a person or thing

asser.full: asser, ĕris, m. from 2. assero, quod admoveantur haereantque parietibus, Perot.; so agger from aggero. A beam, pole, stake, post, Vitr. 7, 3: Co. Sunt asseres? St. Sunt pol, Plaut. Aul. 2, 6, 8: asseres pedum XII., cuspidibus praefixi in terră defigebantur, Caes. B. C. 2, 2; Liv. 44, 5; 30, 10; 38, 5; Tac. H. 4, 30; * Vulg. Eccli. 29, 29 al.— A pole on which a litter was borne, Suet. Calig. 58; Juv. 3, 245; 7, 132.— A lath, Vitr. 4, 2.

asserculus.full: assercŭlus, i, m. dim. (assercŭ-lum, i, n., Cato) [asser] a small beam or pole, Cato, R. R. 12; 152; Col. 12, 52, 4; 8, 3, 6.
