ausus2.full: ausus, ūs, m. audeo, a hazard, attempt, Petr. 123, 184; Impp. Leo et Anthem. Cod. 1, 2, 14.

aut.full: aut, conj. [aut, Osc. auti, Umbr. ote, ute, may be a modification of autem, as at of et, the suffix -t being a relic of the demonstrative -tem, which appears in item, and is the same as -dem in quidem, and -dam in quondam, and of which the demonstrative adverbs, tam and tum, are absolute forms; the first part of these words may be compared with the Gr. αὖ (cf. αὖτε and αὐτάρ), and with the Sanscr. vā = or, with which again may be compared ve and vel; v. Corss. Ausspr. II. p. 595, and also pp. 13

autem.full: autem, conj. [v. aut init.], on the other hand, but, yet, however, nevertheless; sometimes an emphasized and (it is never found at the beginning of a clause, but after one or more words; v. fin.; like at, it joins to a preceding thought a new one, either entirely antithetical or simply different; it differs from the restricting sed in like manner with at; v. at init., and cf.: [Popilius imperator tenebat provinciam; in cujus exercitu Catonis filius tiro militabat. Cum autem Popilio videretur una

authenta.full: authenta, ae, m., = αὐθέντης, a chief prince, head, Fulg. Cont. Verg. p. 161 Muncker.
authenta.short: authenta, ae, m., = αὐθέντης, a chief prince, head, Fulg.

authenticus.full: authentĭcus, a, um, adj., = αὐθεντικός, that comes from the author, authentic, original, genuine (in the jurists and Church fathers; syn.: verus, germanus): testamentum, the original will, Dig. 29, 3, 12: tabulae, the same, ib. 10, 2, 4.—Also subst.: authentĭcum, i, n., the original writing, the original, Dig. 22, 4, 2.
authenticus.short: authentĭcus, a, um, adj., = αὐθεντικός, that comes from the author, authentic, original, genuine (in the jurists and Church fathers;

authepsa.full: authepsa, ae, f., = αὐθέψης [αὐτόσ-ἔψω, a self-cooker], a utensil for cooking (somewhat like our tea - urns): in quibus (vasis) est authepsa illa, quam tanto pretio nuper mercatus est, Cic. Rosc. Am. 46, 133: argenteae, Lampr. Elag. 19.
authepsa.short: authepsa, ae, f., = αὐθέψης [αὐτόσ-ἔψω, a self-cooker], a utensil for cooking (somewhat like our tea - urns): in quibus (vasis) est authepsa illa, quam tanto pretio nuper mercatus est, Cic.

author.full: author, authōrĭtas, etc., v. auctor, auctoritas, etc.

autochthones.full: autochthŏnes, um, m., = αὐτόχθονες, aborigines, = indigenae, App. M. 11, p. 259.
autochthones.short: autochthŏnes, um, m., = αὐτόχθονες, aborigines, = indigenae, App.

autographus.full: autŏgrăphus, a, um, adj., = αὐτόγραφος, written with one's own hand, autograph: Autographā quādam epistulā Cenavi, ait, mi Tiberi, cum īsdem, Suet. Aug. 71: litterae, id. ib. 87.—Also subst.: autŏ-grăphum, i, n., an autograph, Symm. Ep. 3, 11.
autographus.short: autŏgrăphus, a, um, adj., = αὐτόγραφος, written with one's own hand, autograph: Autographā quādam epistulā Cenavi, ait, mi Tiberi, cum īsdem, Suet.

autololes.full: Autŏlŏles, um, m., a Getulian people on the west coast of Africa, north and south of Mount Atlas, Plin. 5, 1, 1, § 9; 6, 31, 36, § 201; Luc. 4, 677; Claud. Laud. Stil. 1, 356; Sil. 3, 306; Sid. Carm. 5, 337.
autololes.short: Autŏlŏles, um, m., a Getulian people on the west coast of Africa, north and south of Mount Atlas, Plin.

autolycus.full: Autŏlўcus, i, m., = Αὐτόλυκος, son of Mercury and Chione, father of Anticlea, and maternal grandfather of Ulysses (cf. Hom. Od. 11, 85), a very dexterous robber, who could transform himself into various shapes, Ov. M. 11, 313; Serv. ad Verg. A. 2, 79; Mart. 8, 59.—Hence, meton., a thievish man: Autolyco hospiti aurum credidi, Plaut. Bacch. 2, 3, 41 Ritschl.
autolycus.short: Autŏlўcus, i, m., = Αὐτόλυκος, son of Mercury and Chione, father of Anticlea, and maternal grandfather of Ulysses (cf.

automatarius.full: autŏmătārĭus, a, um, adj. v. automatus. Of or pertaining to an automaton, automatic; hence, Subst. autŏ-mătārĭus, ii, m., a maker of automata, Inscr. Orell. 4150.— autŏmătārĭ-um, ii, n. (sc. opus), automaton-work, Dig. 30, 41 fin.

automatus.full: autŏmătus, um (os, on), adj., = αὐτόματος, self - moving, voluntary, spontaneous: plausus, Petr. 50, 1.—Hence, subst.: autŏmătŏn or -um, n, a self-moving machine, an automaton, Vitr. 9, 9; Petr. 54, 4; 140, 10; * Suet. Claud. 34 fin.
automatus.short: autŏmătus, um (os, on), adj., = αὐτόματος, self - moving, voluntary, spontaneous: plausus, Petr.

automedon.full: Autŏmĕdōn, ontis, m., = Αὐτομέσων. A son of Diores and charioteer of Achilles, Verg. A. 2, 477.—Hence, Meton. for a charioteer, in gen., Cic. Rosc. Am. 35, 98; Juv. 1, 61.

autonoe.full: Autŏnŏē, ēs. f., = Αὐτονόη. Daughter of Cadmus, wife of Aristœus, and mother of Actœon, Ov. M. 3, 720; id. Ib. 469.— Hence, Autŏnŏēĭus, a, um, adj., of cr pertaining to Autonoë: heros = Actaeon, Ov. M. 3, 198.

autopyrus.full: autŏpȳrus (-ŏs), i, m., = αὐτόπυρος, a coarse bread made of unbolted flour, Plin. 22, 25, 68, § 138; Petr. 66, 2.
autopyrus.short: autŏpȳrus (-ŏs), i, m., = αὐτόπυρος, a coarse bread made of unbolted flour, Plin.

autor.full: autor, autōrĭtas, etc., v. auctor, etc.

autumo.full: autŭmo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. n. for aitumo, as a lengthened form of aio; cf. negumo for nego; for the termination -tumo, cf. aes, aestimo, q. v., aeditumus, finitumus, and maritumus. Lit., to say aye, to affirm (mostly of questionable assertions, Ellis ad Cat. 44, 2; opp. nego, to say nay); hence, to assert, aver, say, name (chiefly anteclass.; esp. freq. in Plaut.; syn.: dico, affirmo, confirmo; used only once by Ter. and Hor., and never by Cic., Lucr., or Verg.): Ipsus sese ut neget esse eum qui s

auvona.full: Auvŏna, ae, m., a river in Britain, now the Avon, Tac. A. 12, 31; cf. Mann. Brit. p. 179.
auvona.short: Auvŏna, ae, m., a river in Britain, now the Avon, Tac.

auxiliabundus.full: auxĭlĭābundus, a, um, adj. auxilior, inclined to give help, aid, aiding, helping, App. de Deo Socr. p. 48, 10 Elm.

auxiliaris.full: auxĭlĭāris (AVXSILIARIS, Inscr. Momm. 5778), e, adj. auxilium. Bringing help or aid, aiding, helping, assisting, auxiliary (syn.: auxiliarius, opem ferens): undae, Ov. M. 1, 275: Dea (sc. Lucina), id. ib. 9, 699: numen, Luc. 6, 523: carmen, a formula of incantation in aid of Jason, Ov. M. 7, 138; cf. Plin. 28,2,4, § 21: arma (poet. periphrastically for the prose auxilia; v. infra), auxiliaries, Ov. M.6,424: aera, the cymbals, trumpets, kettles, etc., by rattling which the ancients believed that

auxiliarius.full: auxĭlĭārĭus (AVXSILIARIVS, Corp. Inscr. III. 4753), a, um, adj. id., bringing help, aiding, auxiliary (less freq. than the preceding): magis consiliarius amicus quam auxiliarius, Plaut. Truc. 2, 1, 6.—In milit. lang., With milites, equites, cohors, auxiliary troops, auxiliaries (opp. legiones): miles, Asin. ap. Cic. Fam. 10, 32 fin.: cohors, Cic. Prov. Cons. 7; Sall. J. 87, 1; Auct. B. Alex. 62; Liv. 40, 40, 13: equites, Sall. J. 46, 7.— Absol. (eccl. Lat.): assumpsit sibi auxiliarios, Vulg. Jud

auxiliatio.full: auxĭlĭātĭo, ōnis, f. auxilior, a helping, aiding, Non. p. 4, 403 dub.

auxiliator.full: auxĭlĭātor, ōris, m. id., a helper, assistant (post-Aug. and rare): litigantium, Quint. 12, 3, 2: haud inglorius, Tac. A. 6, 37: aegris auxiliator adest, Stat. S. 3, 4, 24: auxiliator tuus, Vulg. Deut. 33, 26: noster, ib. 2 Par. 32, 8: ejus, ib. Ezech. 30, 8 al.

auxiliatrix.full: auxĭlĭātrix, īcis, f. auxiliator, she that helps or aids, that which aids: gratia, Cassiod. Ep. 2, 40: sapientia, Mythogr. Vat. 2, 113 Mai.

auxiliatus.full: auxĭlĭātus, ūs, m. auxilior, a helping, aid: alituum genus videmus a pinnis tremulum petere auxiliatum, Lucr. 5, 1040.

auxilior.full: auxĭlĭor, ātus, 1, v. dep. auxilium, to give help or aid, to help, aid, assist, succor (syn.: juvo, adjuvo, opitulor, subvenio, succurro). In gen. (class. but rare; in Cic. perh. only once in his Epistt.), constr. with dat.: alicui, Plaut. Trin. 2, 2, 102: nonne id flagitiumst te aliis consilium dare, tibi non potis esse auxiliarier? Ter. Heaut. 5, 1, 50; Cic. Fam. 5, 4; Caes. B. G. 7, 50 fin.; 4, 29; Sall. J. 24, 3; Plin. 10, 8, 9, § 22; Vulg. 4 Reg. 14, 26; ib. Psa. 88, 44; ib. Heb. 2, 18: nih

auxilium.full: auxĭlĭum, ii, n. augeo, help, aid, assistance, support, succor (syn.: adjumentum, opes, praesidium, subsidium). In gen.: Fer mi auxilium, Enn. ap. Cic. Ac. 2, 28, 89: quo praesidio fretus, auxiliis quibus? Pac. ap. Non. p. 262, 32: auxilium argentarium, Plaut. Ps. 1,1, 103; id. Ep. 1, 2, 14: non habeo ad auxilium copiam, Ter. And. 2, 1, 20: navita indigus omni vitali auxilio, Lucr. 5, 224: venerunt ad auxilium, Vulg. Jud. 5, 23; ib. Isa. 10, 3 al.—Hence the phrases: auxilium esse alicui, to assi

auxilla.full: auxilla: olla parvula, a small pot, Paul. ex Fest. p. 24 Müll.; cf. olla.
auxilla.short: auxilla: olla parvula, a small pot, Paul.

auxim.full: auxim, is, it, etc., v. augeo init.

auximum.full: Auxĭmum, i, n., a town of the Piceni, now Osimo, Caes. B. C. 1, 15; Vell. 1, 15; Inscr. Orell. 3868; 3899.—Hence, Auxĭ-mātes, ium, m., the inhabitants of Auximum, Caes. B. C. 1, 13; Plin. 3, 5, 9, § 63; cf. Mann. Ital. I. p. 489 sq.
auximum.short: Auxĭmum, i, n., a town of the Piceni, now Osimo, Caes.

auxo.full: Auxo, ōnis or ūs, f., = Αὐξώ, one of the Hours, daughter of Jupiter and Themis, Hyg. Fab. 183.
auxo.short: Auxo, ōnis or ūs, f., = Αὐξώ, one of the Hours, daughter of Jupiter and Themis, Hyg.

auzea.full: Auzēa, Auzīa, or Audīa, ae, f., a place in Mauretania Caesariensis, afterwards a Roman colony: castellum semirutum, cui nomen Auzea, Tac. A. 4, 25 Halm; Itin. Ant.
auzea.short: Auzēa, Auzīa, or Audīa, ae, f., a place in Mauretania Caesariensis, afterwards a Roman colony: castellum semirutum, cui nomen Auzea, Tac.

avaricum.full: Avārĭcum, i, n., a large and fortified town of the Bituriges, in Gaul, now Bourges, in the Dép. du Cher, Caes. B. G. 7, 13; 7, 31; 7, 47.—Hence, Avārĭcensis, e, adj., of or pertaining to Avaricum: praemia, Caes. B. G. 7, 47.
avaricum.short: Avārĭcum, i, n., a large and fortified town of the Bituriges, in Gaul, now Bourges, in the Dép.

avaritia.full: ăvārĭtĭa, ae, f. avarus, a greedy desire for possessions, greediness, avarice, covetousness (opp. abstinentia, Suet. Dom. 9; periphrastically, pecuniae cupiditas, id. Vesp. 16; syn.: aviditas, cupido). Lit.: Est autem avaritia opinatio vehemens de pecuniā, quasi valde expetenda sit, inhaerens et penitus insita, Cic. Tusc. 4, 11, 26: avaritia est injuriosa appetitio alienorum, Auct. ad Her. 4, 25: avaritiam si tollere voltis, mater ejus est tollenda luxuries, Cic. de Or. 2, 40, 171: avaritia hian

avarities.full: ăvārĭtĭes, ēi, f., for avaritia, avarice: avarities et honorum caeca cupido, Lucr. 3, 59; and besides perh. only Claud. III. Cons. Hon. 185; v. Neue, Formenl. I. p. 372.
avarities.short: ăvārĭtĭes, ēi, f., for avaritia, avarice: avarities et honorum caeca cupido, Lucr.

avarus.full: ăvārus, a, um, adj. (gen. plur. fem. avarūm, Plaut. Truc. 2, 8, 9 dub.; Speng., aurum) [1. aveo, Gell. 10, 5, 13], eagerly desirous of something, esp. of possessions, avaricious, covetous, greedy (opp. largus, Quadrig. ap. Non. p. 510, 20: avarum et avidum ita discernuntur: avarum semper in reprehensione est; avidum autem malis aliquando, aliquando bonis adjungitur, Non. p. 442, 12 sq.; v. II.; syn.: avidus, cupidus, tenax, sordidus). Lit.: meretrix, Ter. Eun. 5, 4, 5, and Cat. 110, 7; cf.: Carm

aveho.full: ā-vĕho (in MSS. abvĕho; v. ab init.), vexi, vectum, 3, v. a. (avexti = avexisti, Plaut. Rud. 3, 6, 24), to carry off or away, to bear off (of chariots, ships, horses, etc.; v. veho; class., but perh. not in Cic.; syn. aufero): Pl. Rogas? Quine eam hinc avexti? La. Non avexi, Plaut. Rud. 3, 6, 24; 3, 6, 25: aliquem a patriā, id. Men. 5, 9, 56: ex Samo, id. Bacch. 4, 1, 2: Athenis, id. Mil. 2, 1, 36: domum, Liv. 45, 33, 4: in finitimas urbes, id. 5, 51, 9: in alias terras, Tac. H. 5, 3; so Suet. C

avello.full: ā-vello, velli or vulsi, vulsum or volsum, 3, v. a. (pluperf. avellerat, Curt. 5, 6, 5; perf. avulsi, Luc. 9, 764), to tear off or away, to pull or rend off (syn.: abripio, eximo). In gen. (class.): avellere tigna trabesque, to tear away planks and beams, Lucr. 6, 241: avolsaque saxa Montibus, the rocks rent from the mountains, id. 4, 141: avolsum umeris caput, Verg. A. 2, 558; so Ov. M. 3, 727; 2, 358: avolsos silices a montibus altis, Lucr. 5, 313: avolsus radicibus oculus, id. 3, 563: poma ex
avello.short: ā-vello, velli or vulsi, vulsum or volsum, 3, v.

avena.full: ăvēna, ae, f. v. 1. aveo init.; orig. nourishment. Oats; and specif., common oats, Gr. βρόμος: Avena sativa, Linn.; Verg. G. 1, 77; Col. 2, 10, 32; Hor. S. 2, 6, 84.— Wild or barren oats, a weed, Gr. αἰγίλωψ: Avena fatua, Linn.; Cato, R. R. 37, 4; Cic. Fin. 5, 30, 91; Serv. ad Verg. G. 1, 154; Plin. 18, 17, 44, § 149.— In gen. Any stem or stalk of grass or grain, a straw, etc.: (linum) tam gracili avenā. Plin. 19, 1, 1, § 5; 24, 18, 103, § 168.—Used for a shepherd's pipe, Ov. M. 8, 192.— Poet.,

avenaceus.full: ăvēnācĕus, a, um, adj. avena, of oats, oaten: farina, oatmeal, Plin. 22, 25, 67, § 137; 30, 8, 22, § 75.

avenarius.full: ăvēnārĭus, a, um, adj. id., of or pertaining to oats, Plin. 11, 26, 32, § 94.

avenio.full: Avĕnĭo (Avennĭo, Tab. Peut., and Avĕnĭon), ōnis, f., = Αὐενιὡν, a town in Gallia Narbonensis, now Avignon, Mel. 2, 5, 2; Plin. 3, 4, 5, § 36; cf. Mann. Gall. p. 94.

aventinus.full: Ăventīnus, i, m. (Sc. mons.) The Aventine, one of the seven hills of Rome, extending from the Palatine to the Cœlian Mount; until the reign of Ancus Marcius, without the city proper, Cic. Rep. 2, 18; Sen. Brev. Vit. 14; Gell. 13, 4. The origin of the name is uncertain; acc. to Liv. 1, 3, 9, it was named from Aventinus, an Alban king buried there; other etymologies are given by Varr. L. L. 5, § 43 Müll.; cf. Serv. ad Verg. A. 7, 657, where, beside the etymologies given and referred to, another is

aveo1.full: ăvĕo, ēre, v. a. from Sanscr. av, to love, to wish; to satisfy one's self, to be content, to do or fare well, to wish, desire earnestly, to long for, crave (syn.: volo, cupio): avere nihil aliud est quam cupere, Paul. ex Fest. p. 14 Müll.: ab ludis animus atque aures avent Avide exspectantes nuntium, Enn. ap. Varr. L. L. 6, § 70 (Trag. v. 70 Vahl.).—Constr. with inf., acc., and absol. With inf.: te imitari aveo, Lucr. 3, 6: Illud in his quoque te rebus cognoscere avemus, id. 2, 216: res exponere

aveo2.full: ăvĕo (or, acc. to Quint. 1, 6, 21, hă-vĕo; cf. Spald. ad l. l. and Schneid. Gr. 1, p. 185), ēre, v. n. v. 1. aveo init., to be or fare well; except once in Mamert., used only in the imper. ave, aveto, avete, and inf. avere, as a form of salutation, both at meeting and separating, like salve and χαῖρε (hence, Fest. p. 13 explains it by gaudeo). In gen., Hail! God bless thee, farewell! adieu (prob. not used by Cic.): Caesar simulatque, Have, mihi dixit, statim exposuit, i. e. had saluted me, Cael.

avernalis.full: Ăvernālis, e, adj. Avernus, of or pertaining to Lake Avernus: aquae, Hor. Epod. 5, 26: Nymphae, Ov. M. 5, 540: Naiades, Stat. S. 2, 6, 101: Sibylla, i. e. dwelling by the lake, Prop. 5, 1, 49.

avernus.full: Ăvernus, a, um, adj., = ἄορνος. Without birds: loca, where no birds can live, on account of the pestiferous exhalations, Lucr. 6, 738 sq.; 6, 818: aestus, the vapor of Avernus, id. 6, 830.—But esp. Avernus lacus or absol. Avernus, Lake Avernus, near Cumœ, Puteoli, and Baiœ, almost entirely enclosed by steep and wooded hills (now Lago Averno), whose deadly exhalations killed the birds flying over it; therefore the myth placed near it the entrance to the lower world, Plin. 3, 5, 9, § 61; Cic. Tusc

averro.full: ā-verro, verri, ĕre, v. a., to sweep or brush off or away; hence, in gen., to take away, Licin. Macer. ap. Prisc. p. 900 P.

averrunco.full: ā-verrunco, āre, v. n., a very ancient word, peculiar to the lang. of religion, to avert, remove: uti calamitates intemperiasque prohibessis, defendas averruncesque, Cato, R. R. 141, 2: di averruncent, Att. ap. Cic. Att. 9, 2, A.: quorum (prodigiorum) averruncandorum causā supplicationes senatus decrevit, Liv. 10, 23, 1; 8, 6, 11: haec procul a nobis averruncetur amentia, Arn. 1, p. 18.—So in the old Optat. form averruncassint = averruncent, Pac. ap. Varr. L. L. 7, § 102 Müll.; in Paul. ex Fest.

averruncus.full: Āverruncus, i, m. averrunco, an averting deity: avertendo Averruncare, ut deus, qui eis rebus praeest, Averruncus, Varr. L. L. 7, § 102 Müll.; cf.: In istis diis, quos placari oportet, uti mala a nobis vel a frugibus natis amoliantur, Av[er]uncus quoque habetur Robigus, Gell. 5, 12, 14 Hertz.

aversabilis.full: āversābĭlis, e, adj. aversor, that before which one is obliged to turn away, abominable: scelus, Lucr. 6, 390: foeditas, Arn. 7, p. 249.

aversatio.full: āversātĭo, ōnis, f. id., a turning of one's self away, aversion (post-Aug. and rare): tacita aversatio, Quint. 8, 3, 65: alienorum processuum, Sen. Tranq. 2 med.

aversatrix.full: āversātrīx, īcis, f. id., she that turns away from, abominates: crudelitatis, Tert. Anim. 51.

aversim.full: āversīm, adv. averto, avertedly, sidewise: lineae aversim positae, Mamert. Stat. Anim. 1, 25 dub.

aversio.full: āversĭo, ōnis, f. id.. a turning away; only in the adverb. phrases, Ex aversione, from behind: illi de praesidio insecuti ex aversione legatos jugulārunt, Auct. B. Hisp. 22 Moeb.— In the Latin of the jurists: per aversionem or aversione emere, vendere, locare, etc., to buy, sell, etc., something, with a turning away, turned away, i. e. without accurate reckoning, in the gross, by the lot, Dig. 18, 6, 4; 18, 1, 62; 14, 2, 10; 19, 2, 36; 14, 1, 1 al.— In rhet., a turning away, a figure by which th

aversor1.full: āversor, ātus, 1, v. dep. freq. [id.], to turn one's self from, to turn away (from displeasure, contempt, loathing, shame, etc.). In gen.: nulla vis tormentorum acerrimorum praetermittitur; aversari advocati et jam vix ferre posse, Cic. Clu. 63, 177: haerere homo, aversari, rubere, Cic. Verr. 2, 2, 76 fin.— Esp.: aliquem or aliquid, to turn away a person or thing from one's self, to send away, repulse, reject, refuse, decline, shun, avoid: filium (consul) aversatus, i. e. not permitting his pres

aversor2.full: āversor, ōris, m. id., a thief, pilferer, embezzler (cf. averto, I. B.): pecuniae publicae, Cic. Verr. 2, 5, 58, § 152.

aversus.full: āversus, a, um, Part. and P. a., from averto.

averta.full: āverta, ae, f., = ἀορτής, a portmanteau or saddle-bags (in pure Lat., mantica; cf. Acron. ad Hor. p. 1, 6, 106), Cod. Th. 8, 5, 47; Imp. Leo Cod. 12, 51 al.
averta.short: āverta, ae, f., = ἀορτής, a portmanteau or saddle-bags (in pure Lat., mantica;

avertarius.full: āvertārĭus, ii, m. averta (sc. equus), a horse that bears the averta, Cod. Th. 8, 5, 22, § 1.

averto.full: ā-verto (arch. -vorto; in MSS. also abverto; cf. ab init.), ti, sum, 3, v. a., to turn something away from a place, to avert, turn off, remove, etc. (opp. adverto). Lit. In gen. Constr. aliquem ab or with the simple abl.; the limit designated by in with acc. (more rarely by ad): ab saxo avortit fluctus ad litus scapham, Plaut. Rud. 1, 2, 76: Jup. Te volo, uxor, conloqui. Quor ted avortisti? Alc. Est ita ingenium meum: Inimicos semper osa sum optuerier, id. Am. 3, 2, 18: (M. Lepidus) Antonio diad

avia1.full: ăvĭa, or in late Lat., ăva, ae, f. avus, a grandmother on the father's or the mother's side: Matres duas habet et avias duas, Plaut. Truc. 4, 3, 34: anus avia, Curt. 3, 11, 25; Vulg. 2 Tim. 1, 5: avia tam paterna quam materna, Dig. 38, 10, 10: Inter avam et neptem tu mediata agas, Ven. Fort. 8, Carm. 18, 8.—Meton., a prejudice, as it were, inherited from a grandmother: dum veteres avias tibi de pulmone revello, old wives' fables, Pers. 5, 92, ubi v. Gildersleeve.
avia1.short: ăvĭa, or in late Lat., ăva, ae, f.

avia2.full: ăvĭa, ae, f., a plant, = senecio or erigeron, groundsel, Col. 6, 14, 3; 6, 14, 6; Veg. Art. Vet. 4, 14, 2; 4, 15, 4; cf. Schneid. ad h. ll.
avia2.short: ăvĭa, ae, f., a plant, = senecio or erigeron, groundsel, Col.

aviarius.full: ăvĭārĭus, a, um, adj. avis. Pertaining to birds, of birds, bird-: rete, bird-net, Varr. R. R. 3, 5, 13.—Hence, Subst. (like apiarius, etc.). ăvĭārĭus, ii, m., a bird-keeper, Col. 8, 3, 4; 8, 5, 14; 8, 11, 12 al.— ăvĭārĭum, ii, n., a place where birds are kept, an aviary, ὀρνιθών, Varr. R. R. 3, 3, 7; 3, 4, 3; 3, 5, 5; Cic. ad Q. Fr. 3, 1, 1; Col. 8, 1, 3 sq.; Plin. 10, 50, 72, § 141.—Also, the abode of wild birds in the forest: Sanguineisque inculta rubent aviaria bacis, Verg. G. 2, 430 ( = secr

avicula.full: ăvĭcŭla, ae, f. dim. avis, a small bird: aviculae nidulus, Gell. 2, 29, 2: canorae, App. M. 11, p. 260, 21.

avicularius.full: ăvĭcŭlārĭus, ii, m. avicula, = aviarius, a bird-keeper, Apic. 8, 7.

aviditas.full: ăvĭdĭtas, ātis, f. avidus, an eagerness for something (either lawful or unlawful), avidity, longing, vehement desire. In gen.: habeo senectuti magnam gratiam, quae mihi sermonis aviditatem auxit, potionis et cibi sustulit, Cic. Sen. 14, 46: aviditas legendi, id. Fin. 3, 2, 7: suscipere verbum cum omni aviditate, Vulg. Act. 17, 11: gloriae, Cic. ad Q. Fr. 1, 1, 16: pecuniae, id. Part. Or. 6, 1: rapiendi per occasionem triumphi, Liv. 31, 48, 2: imperandi, Tac. H. 1, 52: vini, Suet. Tib. 42 al.: ad

avidus.full: ăvĭdus, a, um, adj. 1. aveo, longing eagerly for something (either lawful or unlawful), desirous, eager, earnest, greedy (diff. from avarus, q. v.). In gen., constr. with gen., in with acc., dat., or absol. With gen.: cibi, Ter. Eun. 5, 4, 16: Romani semper appetentes gloriae praeter ceteras gentes atque avidi laudis, Cic. Imp. Pomp. 3, 7: festinatio victoriae avida, id. Phil. 3, 1; so, potentiae, honoris, divitiarum, Sall. J. 15, 4: avidissimus privatae gratiae, id. H. Fr. (Orat. Cottae ad Popu

avienus.full: Ăvĭēnus, i, m.: Rufus Festus Avienus, a Roman poet in the last half of the fourth century, whose most distinguished work is a Metaphrasis Periegesos Dionysii, and a metaphrase of the Phœnomena of Aratus; cf. Bähr, Lit. Gesch. pp. 128 sq. and 153; Teuffel. Rom. Lit. § 413.
avienus.short: Ăvĭēnus, i, m.: Rufus Festus Avienus, a Roman poet in the last half of the fourth century, whose most distinguished work is a Metaphrasis Periegesos Dionysii, and a metaphrase of the Phœnomena of Aratus;

avipes.full: ăvĭ-pēs, pĕdis, adj. avis, bird-footed, swift-footed: avipedis animula leporis, Serenus ap. Mart. Cap. 5, § 518 (also in Ter. Maur. p. 2415 P., and in Mar. Vict. pp. 2546 and 2595 P.).

avis.full: ăvis, is, f. (abl. sing. avi and ave; cf. Varr. L. L. 8, § 66 Müll.; Prisc. p. 765 P.; Rhem. Palaem. p. 1374 P.; Neue, Formenl. I. pp. 218, 222; in the lang. of religion, the form avi is most common; v. infra) [cf. Sanscr. vā (which may imply av), to blow (to wave); vis, a bird; Zend, vi; with which Curt. compares οἰ-ωνός, a large bird, and Benfey αἰ-ετός, an eagle]. Lit., a bird; or collect., the winged tribe: Liber captivos avis ferae consimilis est, Plaut. Capt. 1, 2, 7: videmus novis avibus

avitium.full: ăvĭtĭum, ii, n. avis, the winged race: tam pulcra ales, quae ex omni avitio longe praecellit, App. de Deo Socr. prol. p. 186 Hildebrand.

avitus1.full: ăvītus, a, um, adj. avus, of or belonging to a grandfather, coming from a grandfather, ancestral. Lit.: paternae atque avitae possessiones, Cic. Agr. 2, 30, 81: bona paterna et avita, id. Cael. 14, 34: res patrita et avita, Cic. Verr. 1, 5, 13: patrita illa et avita philosophia, id. Tusc. 1, 19, 45: avitus ac patritus mos, Varr. ap. Non. p. 161, 5: leges avitae et patritae, id. ib.: hospitium, Cic. Fam. 13, 34: divitiae, Cat. 68, 121; so, res, Hor. S. 1, 6, 79: quae (pallium, sudarium etc.) pala

avitus2.full: Ăvītus, i, m., a Roman cognomen: A. Cluentius Avitus, Cic. Clu. 5, 11 sqq.
avitus2.short: Ăvītus, i, m., a Roman cognomen: A.

avius.full: ā-vĭus, a, um, adj. via, that is out of the way, remote, out of the right way; also, untrodden, unfrequented, solitary, lonely, etc. (while devius signifies leading from the right way; and invius, having no way, pathless; in the poets and histt. freq.). Lit. Silvani lucus extra murum est avius, Plaut. Aul. 4, 6, 8: Avia Pieridum peragro loca, nullius ante Trita solo, Lucr. 1, 926: nemora avia, id. 2, 145: virgulta, Verg. G. 2, 328: montes, Hor. C. 1, 23, 2: aviis itineribus, through by-ways, Sal

avocamentum.full: āvŏcāmentum, i, n. avoco, a means of diverting from pain, trouble, etc., an alleviation, diversion, relaxation, recreation (post-Aug.): omnia mihi avocamenta exemit dolor, Plin. Ep. 8, 23, 1: admittere avocamenta, id. ib. 8, 5, 3; id. Pan. 82, 8; App. Mag. p. 498; Lact. Opif. Dei, 18; Arn. adv. Gent. 166.

avocatio.full: āvŏcātĭo, ōnis, f. id., a calling off from a thing, a diverting of the attention, diversion, interruption (very rare): avocatio a cogitandā molestiā, * Cic. Tusc. 3, 15, 33: In his, quae me sine avocatione circumstrepunt, etc., Sen. Ep. 56, 4.

avocator.full: āvŏcātor, ōris, m. id., one that calls off or away (eccl. Lat.), Tert. Carn. Christ. 5 fin.

avocatrix.full: āvŏcātrix, īcis, f. avocator, she that calls away (eccl. Lat.): veritatis, Tert. Anim. 1.

avoco.full: ā-vŏco, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. (arch. inf., AVOCARIER, C. I. L. I. p. 198), to call off or away. In gen.: partem exercitūs ad bellum, Liv. 4, 61, 3: pubem in arcem praesidio armisque obtinendam, id. 1, 6, 1: Consul ab omnibus magistratibus et comitiatum et contionem avocare potest. Messala ap. Gell. 13, 16, 1.—With dat. (for ab aliquo): nec avocare alius alii posset, si contionem habere volunt, Messala ap. Gell. 13, 16, 1.— Trop.: a rebus occultis avocare philosophiam, Cic. Ac. 1, 4, 15: ut (orator

avolo.full: ā-vŏlo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. n., to fly forth or away: per aetherias umbras, Cat. 66, 55: auspicanti pullos avolāsse, Suet. Galb. 18 fin.; Dig. 41, 1, 5.—Hence, of persons, to flee away, to go away quickly, to hasten away (opp. advolare, to flee to): experiar certe, ut hinc avolem, Cic. Att. 9, 10: avolat ipse, Verg. A. 11, 712: citatis equls avolant Romam, Liv. 1, 57, 8; 3, 61, 7 (al. advolat).—So of dying: Critoni non persuasi me hinc avolaturum, that I shall flee from this world, Cic. Tusc. 1, 43

avulsio.full: āvulsĭo (āvol-), ōnis, f. avello; in gardening, t. t., a plucking off, tearing off of the branches of a tree: Aut semine (arbores) proveniunt aut plantis radicis aut propagine aut avolsione, Plin. 17, 10, 9, § 58; 17, 13, 21, § 98.

avulsor.full: āvulsor (āvol-), ōris, m. id., one that tears off: ubi (spongeae) avolsorem sensere, Plin. 9, 45, 69, § 148.

avulsus.full: āvulsus or āvolsus, a, um, Part., v. avello.
avulsus.short: āvulsus or āvolsus, a, um, Part., v.

avunculus.full: ăvuncŭlus (AVOMCVLVS and AVONCLVS, Fabr. Gloss. p. 227, a), i, m. dim. avus; cf. Lith. avynas, uncle, a mother's brother, maternal uncle (a brother of the father, patruus). Lit. In gen., Cic. de Or. 2, 84, 341; Verg. A. 3, 343; Plin. 5, 8, 6, § 20; Vulg. Gen. 28, 2; 29, 10: uxor patrui vel avunculi, ib. Lev. 20, 10; Isid. Orig. 9, 6, 17; cf. Dig. 38, 10, 10 P.—Hence, Esp. Avunculus magnus, a grandmother's brother (aviae frater), great-uncle, Cic. Brut. 62, 222; Dig. 38, 10, 1; 38, 10, 10; Isid.

avus.full: ăvus (AVS, Inscr. Fabr. 389, also ăvŏs), i, m. kindr. with Goth. avo, grandmother; old Norse, afi, grandfather; cf. Heb. , āb, father; Chald. , ἀββᾶ; and Engl. abbot, a grandfather, grandsire. Lit.: pater, avus, proavus, abavus, atavus, tritavus, Plaut. Pers. 1, 2, 5; so Ter. Phorm. 2, 3, 48; Cic. Cael. 14, 33; id. Mur. 7; Hor. S. 1, 6, 131; Vulg. Exod. 10, 6; cf. Dig. 38, 10, 1; 38, 10, 10; Isid. Orig. 9, 5, 9; 9, 6, 23.—Also transf. to animals (cf. 1. avitus, II.), Verg. G. 4, 209.— In gen. An

axamenta.full: axāmenta, ōrum, n. axis, II. F., since they were inscribed on tables of wood, religious hymns written in Saturnian measure, which were annually sung by the Salii, Paul. ex Fest. p. 3 Müll.: axamenta: στίχοι ἐπὶ θυσιῶν?̔Ηρακλέους, Gloss.; cf. Smith, Dict. Antiq. The beginning of such a Salian hymn (in Varr. L. L. 7, § 86 Müll.) runs thus: Divom éxta cánte, Dívom Dío súpplicante.

axare.full: axāre: nominare, Paul. ex Fest. p. 8 Müll.

axe agglomerati.full: axe agglŏmĕrāti: universi stan tes, id est cohortibus aut legionibus, Paul. ex Fest. p. 25 Müll.
axe agglomerati.short: axe agglŏmĕrāti: universi stan tes, id est cohortibus aut legionibus, Paul.

axedo.full: axēdo, ŏnis, m., = axis, II. F., a board, plank, Marc. Emp. 33 fin.

axenus.full: Axĕnus, = ἄξενος (inhospitable): Axenus Pontus, an earlier name of the Pontus Euxinus, Ov. Tr. 4, 4, 55 sq.
axenus.short: Axĕnus, = ἄξενος (inhospitable): Axenus Pontus, an earlier name of the Pontus Euxinus, Ov.

axicia.full: axĭcĭa, ae, f. cf. ascia, a pair of shears, Plaut. Curc. 4, 4, 22 Fleck.

axiculus.full: axĭcŭlus (assĭc-), i, m. dim. axis. A small axle-tree, Vitr. 10, 14.— Transf. A pin, Vitr. 10, 21.— A small beam or pole, Col. 6, 19, 2.— A small board or plank, Amm. 21, 2; 16, 8.

axim.full: axim, axit = egerim, egerit, v. ago init.

axinomantia.full: axīnŏmantīa, ae, f., = ἀξινομαντεία, a kind of divination from axes, Plin. 36, 19, 34, § 142; cf. id. 30, 2, 5, § 14.
axinomantia.short: axīnŏmantīa, ae, f., = ἀξινομαντεία, a kind of divination from axes, Plin.

axioma.full: axĭōma, ătis, n., = ἀξίωμα, a principle, axiom, App. Dogm. Plat. 3; cf. Gell. 16, 8 (in pure Lat., proloquium, pronuntiatum, profatum, etc.; v. Gell. l. l.).
axioma.short: axĭōma, ătis, n., = ἀξίωμα, a principle, axiom, App.

axis.full: axis, is, m. kindred with Gr. ἄξων; Sanscr. akshas = axle, wheel; old Germ. Ahsa; mod. Germ. Achse; Engl. axle, Bopp, Gloss. p. 2, a; cf. Aufrecht, Zeitschr. für vergl. Sprachf. 8, p. 71. Lit., an axletree, about which a round body, e.g. a wheel, turns: faginus axis, Verg. G. 3, 172: axes aerii, Vulg. 3 Reg. 7, 30; 7, 33: axis versatilis, ib. Eccli. 33, 5 al.—Meton. (pars pro toto), a chariot, car, wagon, Ov. M. 2, 59; id. H. 4, 160; Sen. Herc. Oet. 1442; Sil. 16, 360 al.—Plur., Ov. M. 2, 148; 4

axites.full: axĭtes mulieres sive viri dicebantur unā agentes, Paul. ex Fest. p. 3 Müll. [ago].
axites.short: axĭtes mulieres sive viri dicebantur unā agentes, Paul.

axitiosus.full: axĭtĭōsus, a, um, adj. id., acting together, in combination; of a party: Axitiosae annonam caram e vili concinnant viris, Plaut. ap. Varr. L. L. 7, § 66 Müll.: Mulier es, uxor—Cuja vis?—Ego novi: scio axitiosam, id. ib.

axius1.full: Axĭus, ii, m., a Roman nomen: Q. Axius, a friend of Cicero's and Varro's, Cic. Att. 1, 12, 1; Varr. R. R. 3, 2, 1; Suet. Caes. 9; Gell. 7, 3, 10.
axius1.short: Axĭus, ii, m., a Roman nomen: Q.

axius2.full: Axĭus, ii, m., = ̓́Αξιος, a river in Macedonia, now the Vardar, Liv. 39, 53, 15; 44, 26, 7 and 8; 45, 29, 7 sq.; cf. Mel. 2, 3, 1; Plin. 4, 10, 17, § 34.
axius2.short: Axĭus, ii, m., = ̓́Αξιος, a river in Macedonia, now the Vardar, Liv.

axon1.full: axon, ŏnis, m., = ἄξων. A line upon the sundial, its axis, Vitr. 9, 5.— A part of the ballista, Vitr. 10, 17.— Axŏnes, um, the laws of Solon engraved on tables of wood (axibus ligneis, Gell. 2, 12; v. axis, II. F.), Amm. 16, 5.

axon2.full: Axon, ŏnis, m., a river in Caria, Plin. 5, 27, 29, § 103.
axon2.short: Axon, ŏnis, m., a river in Caria, Plin.

axona.full: Axŏna, ae, m., a river in Gaul, now the Aisne, Caes. B. G. 2, 5; Aus. Mos. 461; cf. Mann. Gall. 206.
axona.short: Axŏna, ae, m., a river in Gaul, now the Aisne, Caes.

axungia.full: axungĭa, ae, f. axis-ungo, axle-tree grease, wagon grease. Lit., Plin. 28, 9, 37, § 135; 28, 10, 43, § 156.—Hence, In gen., grease, fat, Pall. 1, 17, 3; Veg. 4, 10, 3; 4, 12, 3.

axylos.full: Axўlŏs terra ἄξυλος, a poorly wooded region in Galatia, Liv. 38, 18, 4.
axylos.short: Axўlŏs terra ἄξυλος, a poorly wooded region in Galatia, Liv.

aza.full: Aza, ae, f., a town in Armenia Minor, Plin. 6, 9, 10, § 26.
aza.short: Aza, ae, f., a town in Armenia Minor, Plin.

azali.full: Azăli, ōrum, m., = ̓́Αζαλοι, a people of Pannonia, Plin. 3, 25, 28, § 148.
azali.short: Azăli, ōrum, m., = ̓́Αζαλοι, a people of Pannonia, Plin.

azan.full: Azan, ānis, m., = ̓Αζάν; plur., Azā-nes, a people in Arcadia, Stat. Th. 4, 292.

azaniae.full: azānĭae nŭces ἀζάνω, to dry up, pine-nuts, which open while yet on the tree, Plin. 16, 26, 44, § 107.
azaniae.short: azānĭae nŭces ἀζάνω, to dry up, pine-nuts, which open while yet on the tree, Plin.

azanius.full: Azānĭus, a, um, adj., Azanian, i. e. of or belonging to a region in Aethiopia: sinus, Plin. 6, 24, 28, § 108: mare, id. 6, 28, 32, § 153.
azanius.short: Azānĭus, a, um, adj., Azanian, i.

azoni.full: azōni di, = ἄζωνοι, gods that possess no definite place in heaven (in pure Lat., communes), Serv. ad Verg. A. 12, 118; Mart. Cap. 1, p. 17.
azoni.short: azōni di, = ἄζωνοι, gods that possess no definite place in heaven (in pure Lat., communes), Serv.

azorus.full: Azōrus, i, f., = ̓́Αζωρος, a town of Thessaly, at the foot of Mount Olympus, Liv. 42, 53; 44, 2.
azorus.short: Azōrus, i, f., = ̓́Αζωρος, a town of Thessaly, at the foot of Mount Olympus, Liv.

azotus.full: Azōtus, i, f., = ̓́Αζωτος or ̓Αζωτός, a city of Palestine, near the coust, the Ashdod of Holy Scripture, and now Esdu/d, Mel. 1, 10; Plin. 5, 13, 14, § 68; in Vulg., Asedoth, Jos. 10, 40; 12, 3.
azotus.short: Azōtus, i, f., = ̓́Αζωτος or ̓Αζωτός, a city of Palestine, near the coust, the Ashdod of Holy Scripture, and now Esdu/d, Mel.

azymus.full: azȳmus (azўmon, Prud. Apoth. 421), a, um, adj., = ἄζυμος, unleavened (very freq. in Vulg.). Lit. In gen.: azymi panes, Vulg. Exod. 12, 8; ib. Jud. 6, 21: panis, Scrib. Comp. 133: lagana azyma, Vulg. Lev. 2, 4; ib. 1 Par. 23, 29; and so subst.: azȳma, ōrum, n., Vulg. Exod. 12, 15; ib. Lev. 8, 2 al.— Esp., of the Jewish feast of unleavened bread: dies festus azymorum, Vulg. Luc. 22, 1: dies azymorum, ib. Act. 12, 3; 20, 6; also absol.: Erat pascha et azyma (Gr. Ἦν τὸ πάσχα καὶ τὰ ἄζυμα), ib. Marc.

b.full: B, b, indecl. n., designates, in the Latin alphabet, the soft, labial sound as in English, unlike the Gr. beta (B, β), which approached the Engl. v in sound; v. Corss. Ausspr. I. p. 124 sqq. At the beginning of words it represents an original dv or gv, and elsewhere an original gv, p, v, or bh (v); v. Corss. Ausspr. I. pp. 134, 161. It corresponds regularly with Gr. β, but freq. also with π, and, in the middle of words, with φ; cf. brevis, βραχύς; ab, ἀπό; carbasus, κάρπασος; ambo, ἀμφί, ἄμφω; n

baal.full: Bā^al, m., indecl. (lord), a Syrian deity: Bāal, Prud. Apoth. 393: Băal, Sedul. 5, 147; Vulg. 3 Reg. 18, 19 sqq.

babae.full: băbae or păpae, interj., = βαβαί or παπαί, an exclamation of wonder and joy, odds bodkins! wonderful! strange! Form babae: huic babae! basilice te intulisti et facete, Plaut. Pers. 5, 2, 25; so id. Ps. 1, 3, 131; id. Cas. 5, 2, 26; id. Ep. 1, 1, 52; v. under II.; Petr. 37, 9.— Form papae: Ep. Cadum tibi veteris vini propino. St. Papae! Plaut. Stich. 3, 1, 24; 5, 7, 3; id. Rud. 5, 2, 33; id. Bacch. 2, 2, 29; id. Men. 5, 5, 20; Ter Eun. 2, 1, 23; 2, 2, 48; 3, 1, 26.
babae.short: băbae or păpae, interj., = βαβαί or παπαί, an exclamation of wonder and joy, odds bodkins! wonderful! strange! Form babae: huic babae! basilice te intulisti et facete, Plaut.

babba.full: Babba, ae, f., a town in Mauritania, called, as a Roman colony, Julia Campestris, Plin. 5, 1, 1, § 5.
babba.short: Babba, ae, f., a town in Mauritania, called, as a Roman colony, Julia Campestris, Plin.

babel.full: Babel, ēlis, f., the capital city of Assyria, Aug. Civ. Dei, 16, 3, 11; cf. Vulg. Gen. 11, 9.
babel.short: Babel, ēlis, f., the capital city of Assyria, Aug.

babia.full: Babĭa, ae, f., a town of Lower Italy, Plin. 14, 6, 8, § 69.
babia.short: Babĭa, ae, f., a town of Lower Italy, Plin.

babilus.full: Babilus, i, m., an astronomer of the time of Nero, Suet. Ner. 36.
babilus.short: Babilus, i, m., an astronomer of the time of Nero, Suet.

babullius.full: Babullĭus, ii, m., a rich friend of Cœsar, Cic. Att. 13, 48, 1.
babullius.short: Babullĭus, ii, m., a rich friend of Cœsar, Cic.

babulus.full: babŭlus, i, m., a babbler, fool (late Lat.), App. M 4, p. 149, 7.
babulus.short: babŭlus, i, m., a babbler, fool (late Lat.), App.

baburrus.full: baburrus, a, um, foolish, silly, Isid. Orig. 10, 31.
baburrus.short: baburrus, a, um, foolish, silly, Isid.

babylo.full: Băbўlo, ōnis, m. (prob. from Babylon, a Babylonian, foreigner), the name of a slave, Ter. Ad. 5, 7, 17 (acc. to others, a man of Oriental wealth and luxury, a nabob; cf. Bentl. ad loc.).

babylon.full: Băbўlōn, ōnis, f. (gen. Gr. Babylonos, Claud. IV. Cons. Hon. 653; acc. Gr. Babylona, Prop. 3 (4), 11, 21; Mart. 9, 76; Plin. 6, 26, 30, §§ 120 and 124), = Βαβυλών, Babylon, the ancient and renowned chief city of Babylonia, on both sides of the Euphrates, whose ruins are found at Hille, in Irak Arabi, Mel. 1, 11, 2; Plin. 6, 26, 30, § 121 sq.; Curt. 5, 6, 9; Cic. Div. 1, 23, 47; 2, 67, 139; Ov. P. 2, 4, 27; Nep. Eum. 2, 1; Vitr. 8, 3, 8; Vulg. Gen. 10, 10.— Derivv. Băbўlō-nĭa, ae, f., = Βαβυλωνία

baca.full: bāca (less correctly bacca), ae, f. acc. to Benfey, for bacsa, kindred with Sanscr. bhaksh, edere, vorare; cf. also bhaxa, food; but v. Vaniček, Etym. Wörterb. 2, p. 561, a small round fruit, a berry. Lit. In gen. (cf.: acinus, glans): virgas murteas cum bacis servare, Cato, R. R. 101; Ov. M. 11, 234: lauri, Verg. G. 1, 306: tinus, Ov. M. 10, 98: ebuli, Verg. E. 10, 27: cupressi, Plin. 16, 27, 50, § 115: platani, id. 15, 7, 7, § 29: hyssopi, id. 26, 12, 76, § 124 al.— Esp. freq. the olive: agric

bacalia.full: bācālĭa, ae. f. baca, a kind of laurel abounding in berries, Plin. 15, 30, 39, § 129.

bacalis.full: bācālis, e, adj. id., bearing berries: laurus, Plin. 17, 10, 11, § 60.

bacalusia.full: bacalusĭa, ae, f., a kind of sweetmeat, Petr. 41 init. (dub.; cf. Büchel. ad loc.).
bacalusia.short: bacalusĭa, ae, f., a kind of sweetmeat, Petr.

bacar.full: bacar, a wine-vessel similar to the bacrio, a wine-glass, Fest. p. 25; cf. Commod. p. 344.
bacar.short: bacar, a wine-vessel similar to the bacrio, a wine-glass, Fest.

bacatus.full: bācātus, a, um, Part. of a verb not otherwise in use, bāco, āre baca, II. B. 1., set or adorned with pearls, pearl- (very rare): monile, * Verg. A. 1, 655; Sil. 8, 134; Lampr. Alex. Sev. 41.

bacca.full: bacca, baccālis, etc., v. baca, bacalis, etc.

baccar.full: baccar (bacchar), ăris, n. (baccăris, is, f., Plin. 12, 12, 26, § 45), = βάκχα^ρις, a plant having a fragrant root, from which an oil was expressed; also called nardum rusticum (cf. Plin. 12, 12, 26, § 45); acc. to Sprengel it is the Celtic valerian: Valeriana Celtica. Linn.; Plin. 21, 6, 16, § 29; Verg. E. 4, 19 (baccar herba est, quae facinum depellit, Serv.); 7, 27.

baccha1.full: Baccha (old orthog. Baca; v. S. C. Bacch.; Bacca, Plaut. Aul. 3, 1, 4 Wagn.; Bacche, Ov. Tr. 4, 1, 41), ae, f., = Βάκχη; cf. also Μαινάς or Θυϊάς, a Bacchanet, a female attendant of Bacchus, who, in company with Silenus and the Satyrs, celebrated the festival of that deity with a raving madness carried even to insensibility, with an ivy crown upon her head, a fawn-skin upon her left shoulder, a staff wound with ivy in her hand, and with hair loose and flying wildly about, Plaut. Am. 2, 2, 71; id

baccha2.full: Baccha, ae, f., a kind of Spanish wine, Varr. L. L. 7, § 87 Müll.
baccha2.short: Baccha, ae, f., a kind of Spanish wine, Varr.

bacchabundus.full: bacchābundus, a, um, adj. bacchor, revelling in the manner of the Bacchantes, boisterous, noisy, ranting, raving (post-Aug. and rare; cf. bacchans): agmen, Curt. 9, 10, 27; App. Mag. p. 326, 8.

bacchaeus.full: Bacchaeus = Baccheus, v. Bacchus, II. C.

bacchanal.full: Bacchānal (old orthog. Bacānal, v. S. C. Bacch. A. V. C. 568, Wordsworth, Fragm. and Spec. p. 172: Baccānal, Plaut. Aul. 3, 1, 3), ālis, n. from Bacchus, like Fagutal, Frutinal, Lupercal, etc.; v. App. 1 to the Pref., a place devoted to Bacchus, the place where the festivals of Bacchus were celebrated: NE QVIS EORVM BACANAL HABVISE VELET, S. C. Bacch. v. 4: EA BACANALIA... IN DIEBVS X... FACIATIS VTEI DISMOTA SIENT, ib. v. 28: ad Baccas veni in Baccanal, Plaut. Aul. 3, 1, 3: aperire, id. ib. 8:

bacchanalis.full: Bacchānālis, e, adj. Bacchus, relating to Bacchus, Bacchanalian: sacra, Val. Max. 1, 3, n. 1: festum = Bacchanalia, Macr. S. 1, 4; Aur. Vict. Caes. 3.

baccharia.full: Baccharia, ae, f., the name of a lost play of Plautus, Macr. S. 2, 12.
baccharia.short: Baccharia, ae, f., the name of a lost play of Plautus, Macr.

bacchatim.full: bacchātim, adv. bacchor, in the manner of the Bacchœ or Bacchantes, in a riotous, wanton manner, App. M. 1, p. 108, 3.

bacchatio.full: bacchātĭo, ōnis, f. id.. A celebrating of the orgies of Bacchus, Hyg. Fab. 4; 8.—Hence. A revelling, raving, in the manner of the Bacchœ (rare): sileatur de nocturnis ejus baccationibus ac vigiliis, * Cic. Verr. 2, 1, 12, § 33.

baccheis.full: Bacchēĭs, ĭdis, adj. f., of or pertaining to Bacchis, the ancestor of the Corinthian Bacchiadœ; hence, poet. for Corinthian: Ephyres Baccheidos altum Culmen, i. e. Corinth, Stat. S. 2, 2, 34.

baccheius.full: Bacchēĭus, a, um, v. 1. Bacchus, II. D.

baccheus.full: Bacchēus, a, um. Of Bacchus, Bacchic; v.1. Bacchus, II. C.— Bacchantian; v.1. Baccha fin.

bacchia.full: bacchĭa, ae, f., a kind of drinking vessel, a goblet, bowl, Isid. Orig. 20, 5, 4.
bacchia.short: bacchĭa, ae, f., a kind of drinking vessel, a goblet, bowl, Isid.

bacchiadae.full: Bacchĭădae, ārum, m., = Βακχιάδαι, the Bacchiadœ, a very ancient royal family of Corinth, descended from Bacchis, one of the Heraclidœ, which, being expelled from the throne by Cypselus, wandered to Sicily, and founded Syracuse, Ov. M. 5, 407; Plin. 35, 12, 43, § 152 (cf. Aelian, V. H. 1, 19; Pausan. Corinth. p. 120; Strabo, 8, p. 260).
bacchiadae.short: Bacchĭădae, ārum, m., = Βακχιάδαι, the Bacchiadœ, a very ancient royal family of Corinth, descended from Bacchis, one of the Heraclidœ, which, being expelled from the throne by Cypselus, wandered to Sicily, and founded Syracuse, Ov.

bacchilidium.full: Bacchĭlĭdĭum (metrum) constat dimetro (troch.) hypercatalecto, ut est hoc: floribus corona texitur, Serv. Centim. p. 1819 P.
bacchilidium.short: Bacchĭlĭdĭum (metrum) constat dimetro (troch.) hypercatalecto, ut est hoc: floribus corona texitur, Serv.

bacchis.full: Bacchis, ĭdis, f., = Βακχίς. = 1. Baccha, q. v.— The name of a woman in the Hec. and Heaut. of Terence; and, in plur., Bacchides, the name of a comedy of Plautus (derived from the twin sisters, Bacchides, the chief personages of the piece): Bacchides non Bacchides, set Bacchae sunt acerrumae, Plaut. Bacch. 3, 1, 4.

bacchisonus.full: Bacchĭsŏnus, a, um, adj. Bacchussono, sounding of Bacchus, Paul. Nol. Nat. XI. S. Fel. 281 Murat.

bacchius1.full: Bacchĭus, a, um, v.1. Bacchus, II. B.

bacchius2.full: Bacchīus, a, um, v.1. Bacchus, II. E.

bacchius3.full: Bacchīus, ii, m., = Βάκχειος, a Greek proper name; esp., Bacchius Milesius, a writer on agriculture, Varr. R. R. 1, 1, 8; Col. 1, 1, 9.— (Scanned Bacchĭus.) A gladiator, Hor. S. 1, 7, 20.
bacchius3.short: Bacchīus, ii, m., = Βάκχειος, a Greek proper name;

bacchor.full: bacchor, ātus (part. pres. gen. plur. bacchantum; v. I. fin. infra), 1, v. dep. Bacchus. Lit., to celebrate the festival of Bacchus: Baccha bacchans, Plaut. Am. 2, 2, 71: saxea ut effigies bacchantis prospicit Evoe, i. e. which cries Evoe in the orgies, Cat. 64, 61; 64, 255: cum aliquo, Plin. 3, 1, 3, § 8.—Hence, P. a. as subst.: bacchan-tes, um, f., Bacchae, the Bacchantes: passis Medea capillis Bacchantum ritu, Ov.M. 7, 258; 3, 703; Curt. 8, 10, 15; gen. Bacchantium, id. 9, 10, 24.— Pass. (as

bacchus1.full: Bacchus, i, m., = Βάκχος, son of Jupiter and a Theban woman, Semele, Tib. 3, 4, 45; Ov. F. 6, 485: bis genitus (since, as Semele died before his birth, he was carried about by Jupiter in his hip until the time of his maturity), Curt. 8, 10, 12, Ov. Tr. 5, 3, 26; cf. id. M. 3, 310, and bimatris, id. ib. 4, 12; v. also Cic. Fl. 26, 60; Verg. G. 4, 521; the god of wine (as such also called Liber, the deliverer, Lyæus (λύειν), the care-dispeller; cf. Enn. ap. Charis. p. 214 P., or Trag. Rel. v. 149
bacchus1.short: Bacchus, i, m., = Βάκχος, son of Jupiter and a Theban woman, Semele, Tib.

bacchus2.full: Bacchus, i, m., a sea-fish, also called myxon, Plin. 9, 17, 28, § 61; 32, 7, 25, § 77; 32, 11, 53, § 145.
bacchus2.short: Bacchus, i, m., a sea-fish, also called myxon, Plin.

bacchylides.full: Bacchўlĭdēs, is, m., = Βακχυλίδης, a Greek lyric poet of Ceos, a nephew of Simonides, who lived about 470 B.C., Amm. 25, 4, 3.—Hence, Bacchўlĭdĭus, a, um, adj., of Bacchylides: metrum, Serv. Centim. 2, 5, p. 1819 P.
bacchylides.short: Bacchўlĭdēs, is, m., = Βακχυλίδης, a Greek lyric poet of Ceos, a nephew of Simonides, who lived about 470 B.C., Amm.

bacciballum.full: bacciballum (basioballum), i, n., a word of uncertain meaning, found only in Petr. 61.
bacciballum.short: bacciballum (basioballum), i, n., a word of uncertain meaning, found only in Petr.

baccina.full: baccīna, ae, f., a plant, also called Apollinaris, App. Herb. 22.
baccina.short: baccīna, ae, f., a plant, also called Apollinaris, App.

bacenis.full: Băcēnis (Βακέννη), a great forest in Germany; doubtless the western part of the Thuringian Forest, in Fulda, Caes. B. G. 6, 10.
bacenis.short: Băcēnis (Βακέννη), a great forest in Germany;

baceolus.full: bacĕŏlus, used by Augustus for stultus prob. from βάκηλος ὁ ἀνόητος, Hesych., acc. to Suet. Aug. 87.
baceolus.short: bacĕŏlus, used by Augustus for stultus prob.

bacifer.full: bācĭfer, fĕra, fĕrum, adj. baca-fero. Bearing berries: taxus, Plin. 16, 10, 20, § 50 (al. leg. bacas fert): hedera, Sen. Oedip. 414.— Acc. to baca, I. B., bearing olives: Pallas, Ov. Am. 2, 16, 8: Sabinus, Sil. 3, 596.

bacillum.full: băcillum, i, n. (băcillus, i, m., Isid. Orig. 20, 13, 1) dim. baculus, a small staff, a wand, Cic. Fin. 2, 11, 33; id. Div. 1, 17, 30 dub.; Varr. R. R. 1, 50, 2; Juv. 3, 28.— Esp., the wand or staff of the lictor: anteibant lictores, non cum bacillis, sed cum fascibus, Cic. Agr. 2, 34, 93.

bacis1.full: Bacis, ĭdis, m. (Βάκις, ιδος, Pausan.), a soothsayer of Bœotia, Cic. Div. 1, 18, 34.

bacis2.full: Bacis (Bacchis, Pacis), acc. Bacem, a sacred bull, worshipped at Hermonthis in Upper Egypt, Macr. S. 1, 21.

bacrio.full: bacrio, ōnis, m., a kind of vessel with a long handle, a ladle: i. q. trulla, Paul. ex Fest. p. 31 Müll.
bacrio.short: bacrio, ōnis, m., a kind of vessel with a long handle, a ladle: i.

bactra.full: Bactra, ōrum (Bactrum, i, Plin. 6, 16, 18, § 48), n., = Βάκτρα, the chief city of Bactria or Bactriana, now Balkh, Verg. G. 2, 138; Prop. 3 (4), 1, 16; 3, 11 (4, 10), 26; Hor. C. 3, 29, 28; Curt. 7, 4, 31; cf. Sil. 13, 764; Amm. 23, 6, 58.—Transf., = Bactri, the Bactrians, Verg. A. 8, 688.— Derivv. Bactri, ōrum, m., the inhabitants of Bactriana, Mel. 1, 2, 5; Varr. ap. Plin. 6, 17, 19, § 52; Plin. 6, 16, 18, § 48.— Bac-trĭa, ae. f., the country of the Bactrians, Bactria, Plin. 8, 18, 26, § 67.—

bactroperita.full: bactrŏperita, ae, m. βάκτρον, a staff—πήρα, pouch, furnished with or carrying staff and pouch; a nickname for a Cynic philosopher, Hier. Matth. 10; cf. Hor. S. 1, 3, 134; Mart. 4, 53.

bactrus.full: Bactrus (-ŏs), i, m., = Βάκτρος, a river near Bactra, now Dehas, Curt. 7, 4, 31; Luc. 3, 267; cf. Isid. Orig. 13, 21, 14; 14, 3, 30; 15, 1, 11; 9, 2, 43.
bactrus.short: Bactrus (-ŏs), i, m., = Βάκτρος, a river near Bactra, now Dehas, Curt.

bacula.full: bācŭla, ae, f. dim. baca, a small berry, Plin. 25, 8, 54, § 96; Arn. 1, p. 2; 2, p. 58; 5, p. 159.

baculum.full: băcŭlum, i, n. (băcŭlus, i, m., rare, and not before the Aug. period; Ov. M. 2, 789; id. F. 1, 177; App. M. 7, p. 194, 30; Aus. Epigr. 53; Isid. Orig. 20, 13, 1; Vulg. Gen. 38, 25; id. Psa. 22, 4; cf. bacillum), [like βάκτρον, from root ba- of βάξω, βιβάξω, βαίνω, to go = Sanscr. ga], a stick, staff, as a support in walking (class.; while scipio is a staff for ornament, and fustis a stick for beating; Doed. Syn. III. p. 266 sqq.; but later used in all these signiff.; cf. bacillum): proximus lict

badia.full: Badĭa, ae, f., a town of Hispania Baetica, now Sa. Maria de Bedoza, Val. Max. 3, 7, 1; called also Budŭa, Itin. Anton. 419.
badia.short: Badĭa, ae, f., a town of Hispania Baetica, now Sa.

badisso.full: bădisso, āre, v. n., = βαδίξω, to go, to walk, Plaut. As. 3, 3, 116 Fleck. (MSS. badizas; v. Ussing ad loc.).

baditis.full: bādītis, ĭdis, f., the name of a plant, = nymphaea, Marc. Emp. 33.
baditis.short: bādītis, ĭdis, f., the name of a plant, = nymphaea, Marc.

badius.full: bădĭus, a, um, adj., brown, chestnutcolored (rare; only of horses), Varr. ap. Non. p. 80, 2; Pal. Mart. 13, 4; Grat. Cyn. 536.
badius.short: bădĭus, a, um, adj., brown, chestnutcolored (rare;

baduhennae lucus.full: Baduhennae lūcus, a forest in the north of Germany, in Friesland (perh. now Hold Pade), Tac. A. 4, 73.
baduhennae lucus.short: Baduhennae lūcus, a forest in the north of Germany, in Friesland (perh.

baebius.full: Baebĭus, a, um, adj., the name of a Roman gens, e. g., M. Baebius, Cic. Pis. 36, 88.— Q. Baebius Tampilus, Cic. Phil. 5, 10, 27; Liv. 40, 17, 8 Drak.; v. also Val. Max. 1, 1, 12; 7, 2, 6.— G. Baebius, Sall. J. 33, 2; 34, 1.—Whence, Baebia lex de praetoribus creandis, Liv. 40, 44, 2; cf. Fest. s. v. rogat, p. 233.
baebius.short: Baebĭus, a, um, adj., the name of a Roman gens, e.

baecula.full: Baecŭla, ae, f. A small town in Spain, on the borders of Bœtica, now Baylen, Liv. 27, 18, 1; 28, 13, 16.— Another town in Spain, on the Ebro, in the territory of the Ausetani, Βαίκυλα, Ptol.—Hence, Baecŭlōnenses, ium, m., the inhabitants of Baecula, Plin. 3, 3, 4, § 23.

baeticatus.full: Baetĭcātus, a, um, adj. Baetis, clothed in Bœtican wool, Mart. 1, 97, 5.

baeticola.full: Baetĭcŏla, ae, adj. Baetis-colo, dwelling on the river Bœtis, Sil. 1, 146.

baetigena.full: Baetĭgĕna, ae, adj. Baetis-gigno, born on the Bœtis: viri, Sil. 9, 234.

baetis.full: Baetis (Bĕtis, Paul. Nol. Carm. ad Aus. 10, 236), is, m. (acc. Baetin, Plin. 3, 1, 3, § 12 (al. Baetim); Mart. 9, 62, 2; Claud. Fesc. 12, 31; Mall. Theod. 285; Claud. Laud. Stil. 2, 238: BAETEM, Inscr. Grut. 153, 4; abl. Baete, Liv. 28, 22, 1: Baeti (al. Baete), Plin. 3, 1, 3, § 13; Amm. 23, 6, 21), = Βαῖτις, a river in Southern Spain, called by the inhabitants Certis, now Guadalquivir, Liv. 28, 16, 2; Mel. 3, 1, 5; Plin. 3, 1, 3, §§ 7 and 13.— Deriv.: Baetĭcus, a, um, adj., on or belonging to t

baetulo.full: Baetŭlo, ōnis, m., a river of Hispania Tarraconensis, now the Besos, Plin. 3, 3, 4, § 22; Mel. 2, 6, 3.
baetulo.short: Baetŭlo, ōnis, m., a river of Hispania Tarraconensis, now the Besos, Plin.

baetulus.full: baetŭlus (bēt-), i, m., = βαίτυλος, a precious stone, round and of a dark color, a species of ceraunia, Plin. 37, 9, 51, § 135.
baetulus.short: baetŭlus (bēt-), i, m., = βαίτυλος, a precious stone, round and of a dark color, a species of ceraunia, Plin.

baeturia.full: Baetūrĭa, ae, f., = Βαιτουρία, Bœturia, the north-west part of Hispania Baetica, between the Bœtis and Anas, Plin. 3, 1, 3, § 13.
baeturia.short: Baetūrĭa, ae, f., = Βαιτουρία, Bœturia, the north-west part of Hispania Baetica, between the Bœtis and Anas, Plin.

bagada.full: Bagada, ae, f., a town of Ethiopia, Plin. 6, 29, 35, § 178.
bagada.short: Bagada, ae, f., a town of Ethiopia, Plin.

bagaudae.full: Bagaudae, ārum, m., a class of peasants in Gaul, who rebelled under the emperor Diocletian, and were finally conquered by Maximian, Aur. Vict. Caes. 39; Eutr. 9, 20.—Hence, Bagaudĭca rebellio, rebellion of the peasants, Eum. pro Restaur. Schol. 4.
bagaudae.short: Bagaudae, ārum, m., a class of peasants in Gaul, who rebelled under the emperor Diocletian, and were finally conquered by Maximian, Aur.

bagous.full: Băgōus, i, and Băgōas, ae, m., = Βαγῶος and Βαγώας [Persian], a eunuch at the Persian court: Bagou (gen. Gr. = Βαγώου), Plin. 13, 4, 9, § 41.—Form Bagoas, Quint. 5, 12, 21.—Hence, any guard of women, Ov. Am. 2, 2, 1.
bagous.short: Băgōus, i, and Băgōas, ae, m., = Βαγῶος and Βαγώας [Persian], a eunuch at the Persian court: Bagou (gen.

bagrada.full: Băgrăda, ae, m., = Βαγράδας, a river in Zeugitana, in Africa, near Utica, now Mejerdah, Caes. B. C. 2, 24; 2, 26; Liv. 30, 25, 4; Mel. 1, 7, 2; Plin. 5, 4, 3, § 24; 8, 14, 14, § 36; Luc. 4, 588; its frequent overflow fertilized its banks, Sil. 6, 141 sqq.
bagrada.short: Băgrăda, ae, m., = Βαγράδας, a river in Zeugitana, in Africa, near Utica, now Mejerdah, Caes.

baia.full: baia, ae, f. Copt. bai, whence βάϊς, a palm-branch, Hier. Jovin. 3, 18.

baiae.full: Bāiae (dissyl.), ārum, f., = Βαἷαι, a small town in Campania, on the coast between Cumœ and Puteoli, a favorite resort of the Romans on account of its warm baths and pleasant situation; acc. to the fable, built by one of the companions of Ulysses (Serv. ad Verg. A. 3, 441; cf. Strabo, 5, p. 376): homo durus ac priscus invectus est in eos, qui mense Aprili apud Balas essent et aquis calidis uterentur, Cic. Fragm. in Clod. 4, 1; id. Fam. 9, 12; Prop. 1, 11, 1; 1, 11, 27; 3 (4), 18, 2; Hor. C. 2, 1
baiae.short: Bāiae (dissyl.), ārum, f., = Βαἷαι, a small town in Campania, on the coast between Cumœ and Puteoli, a favorite resort of the Romans on account of its warm baths and pleasant situation;

bajulatio.full: bājŭlātĭo, ōnis, f. bajulo, = βασταγμός, a carrying of burdens, Gloss. Vet.

bajulator.full: bājŭlātor, ōris, m. id., = βαστακτής, ἀχθοφόρος, a carrier, porter, Gloss. Cyril.

bajulatorius.full: bājŭlātōrĭus, a, um, adj. bajulator, of or belonging to a carrier: sella, a sedan, Cael. Aur. Acut. 1, 11: sessio, id. ib. 1, 15, 133.

bajulo.full: bājŭlo, āre, v. a. bajulus, to carry a burden, to bear something heavy, βαστάξω (mostly ante-and post-class.): ferri proprie dicimus quae quis suo corpore bajulat, portari ea, quae quis in jumento secum ducit, agi ea, quae animalia sunt, Dig. 50, 16, 235; Non. p. 79, 9; Plaut. As. 3, 3, 70; id. Merc. 3, 1, 10: asinus bajulans sarcinas, Phaedr. 4, 1, 5; Auct. ap. Quint. 6, 1, 47; Vulg. Marc. 14, 13.— Trop.: adjectionem debiti alieni, Cod. Th. 5, 15, 3: crucem suam, Vulg. Luc. 14, 27.

bajulus.full: bājŭlus, i, m. kindr. with φέρω, fero; Engl. bear; and with Germ. Bahre, Bürde; cf. Doed. Syn. I. p. 151, and bajulo, he who bears burdens (for pay), a porter, carrier, day-laborer, βαστακτής: quod genus Graeci ἀχθοφόρους vocant, Latine bajulos appellamus, Gell. 5, 3, 1: bajulos dicebant antiqui, quos nunc dicimus operarios, Paul. ex Fest. p. 35 Müll.; Plaut. Poen. 5, 6, 17; Caecil. ap. Cic. de Or. 2, 10, 40: utrum de bonis est quaerendum, quid bajuli atque operarii, an quid homines doctissimi s

balaena.full: bālaena (bālēna), ae, f., = φάλαινα, Engl. whale (cf. Fest. p. 25, and the letter B.), a whale, Plaut. Rud. 2, 6, 61; Plin. 9, 8, 7, § 21; 9, 13, 15, § 41; 11, 40, 95, § 235; Ov. M. 2, 9; Juv. 10, 14; Aus. Mos. 144.

balaenacius.full: bālaenācĭus (bālēn-), a, um, adj. balaena, of whalebone: virga, Petr. 21, 2.

balanatus.full: bălănātus, a, um, adj. balanus, II. 3., anointed or perfumed with balsam, embalmed, Pers. 4, 37; cf. Prisc. p. 836 P.

balaninus.full: bălănĭnus, a, um, adj., = βαλάνινος, made or prepared from the fruit of the balsam (v. balanus, II. 3.): oleum, Plin. 13, 1, 2, § 8.
balaninus.short: bălănĭnus, a, um, adj., = βαλάνινος, made or prepared from the fruit of the balsam (v.

balanites.full: bălănītes, ae, m., = βαλανίτης (acornshaped), an unknown precious stone, Plin. 37, 10, 55, § 149; Isid. Orig. 16, 15, 10.
balanites.short: bălănītes, ae, m., = βαλανίτης (acornshaped), an unknown precious stone, Plin.

balanitis.full: bălănĭtis, ĭdis, f., = βαλανῖτις, skaped like an acorn: castanea, Plin. 15, 23, 25, § 93.
balanitis.short: bălănĭtis, ĭdis, f., = βαλανῖτις, skaped like an acorn: castanea, Plin.

balanus.full: bălănus, i, f. and rarely m. (masc., Plin. 13, 4, 9, § 48; 15, 23, 25, § 93; Metell. ap. Macr. S. 2, 9; cf. Rudd. I. p. 31), = βάλανος. Lit., an acorn: glans, Plin. 16, 6, 8, § 21; 17, 20, 34, § 151; 13, 4, 9, § 42.— Transf. Any fruit of similar form. A kind of large chestnut, Plin. 15, 23, 25, § 93.— The Phœnician and Cilician date, Plin. 13, 4, 9, § 48.— A nut yielding a balsam; the Arabian behen- or ben-nut: Hyperanthera semidecandra, Vahl. (called myrobalanus, Plin. 12, 21, 46, § 100; 22, 20

balatro1.full: bălā^tro, ōnis, m. 2. blatero; lit., a babbler; hence, a jester, one who makes sport, a buffoon (it seems to have desig-nated a class of actors, perh. a harlequin, jester, or something similar): mendici, mimae, balatrones, hoc genus omne, Hor. S. 1, 2, 2; Vop. Carin. 21.—Facetè, in Varr. as a designation of his friends when in dispute, Varr. R. R. 2, 5, 1 Schneid.

balatro2.full: Bălā^tro, ōnis, m. nom. prop., cognomen of Servilius, Hor. S. 2, 8, 21; 2, 8, 33; 2, 8, 40; 2, 8, 64; 2, 8, 83; cf.: in modum rustici Balatronis, Hier. Ep. 153; cf. scurra.

balatus.full: bālātus, ūs, m. balo, the bleating of sheep, Lucr. 2, 369: agni Balatum exercent, Verg. A. 9, 62; id. G. 3, 554; Ov. M. 7, 319; 7, 320; Stat. Th. 10, 46.—Also in plur., Ov. M. 7, 540.—Of the bleating of goats, Plin. 20, 14, 55, § 156; Aus. Epigr. 76, 3.

balaustium.full: bălaustĭum, ii, n., = βαλαύστιον, the flower of the wild pomegranate, Plin. 13, 19, 34, § 113; Col. 10, 297; Scrib. Comp. 85 and 112; Veg. Vet. 3, 16, 1.
balaustium.short: bălaustĭum, ii, n., = βαλαύστιον, the flower of the wild pomegranate, Plin.

balbillus.full: Balbillus, i, m., a scholar, prefect in Egypt, Sen. Q. N. 4, 2, 13; Tac. A. 13, 22; Plin. 19, 1, prooem. § 3 Jan. (al. Balbilius, Babbillus).
balbillus.short: Balbillus, i, m., a scholar, prefect in Egypt, Sen.

balbus1.full: balbus, a, um, adj. kindr. with balo; cf. Sanscr. barh, barrire, and barbarus, stammering, stuttering (opp. planus, speaking fluently, without impediment): balba, loqui non quit? τραυλίζει, does she (the loved one) stammer, can she not speak distinctly? (then he says) she lisps, Lucr. 4, 1164: Demosthenes cum ita balbus esset, ut ejus ipsius artis, cui studeret (sc. rhetoricae), primam litteram (sc. r) non posset dicere, perfecit meditando, ut nemo planius esse locutus putaretur, Cic. de Or. 1,

balbus2.full: Balbus, i, m., a Roman cognomen, Cic. Att. 8, 9, 4; id. Balb. passim; id. Cael. 11, 27; id. de Or. 3, 21, 78 al.
balbus2.short: Balbus, i, m., a Roman cognomen, Cic.

balbutio.full: balbūtĭo (-uttio), īre, v. n. and a. [balbus]. Neutr., to stammer, stutter: balbutire est cum quādam linguae haesitatione et confusione trepidare, Non. p. 80, 13; Cels. 5, 26, 31: lingua, Cod. 15, 6, 22. —Transf., of birds, not to sing clearly: merula hieme balbutit, Plin. 10, 29, 42, § 80. — Trop., to speak upon something obscurely, not distinctly or not correctly: desinant balbutire (Academici), aperteque et clarā voce audeant dicere, Cic. Tusc. 5, 26, 75; id. Div. 1, 3, 5.— Act., to stutter,

balcia.full: Balcĭa (Baltĭa), ae, f., acc. to Xenophon of Lampsacus, a large island, three days' sail from the coast of Scythia, called by Pythias Basilia, Plin. 4, 13, 27, § 95.

baliares.full: Bălĭāres (better than Bălĕāres) insulae, or absol. Bălĭāres, ĭum, f., = Βαλιαρεῖς, the Balearic Islands, Majorca and Minorca, in the Mediterranean Sea, whose inhabitants were famous slingers, Auct. B. Afr. 23; Cic. Att. 12, 2, 1; Inscr. Orell. 732; Liv. 28, 37, 4 sq.; Plin. 10, 48, 68, § 133; Mel. 2, 7, 20; Plin. 3, 5, 11, § 77; 8, 58, 83, § 226 al.— Derivv. Bă-lĭāris, e, adj., Balearic: terra, Plin. 35, 19, 59, § 202: funda, Verg. G. 1, 309: habena, Luc. 3, 710: telum, Sil. 7, 279.—Subst.: Bălĭ
baliares.short: Bălĭāres (better than Bălĕāres) insulae, or absol.

balineae.full: bălĭnĕae = balneae, v. balneum, I. B.

balinienses.full: Balinienses, ĭum, m., a name given to the Trebulani, Plin. 3, 5, 9, § 64.
balinienses.short: Balinienses, ĭum, m., a name given to the Trebulani, Plin.

baliolus.full: balĭŏlus, a, um, adj. balius = badius, dark, swarthy, chestnut-colored: amplexari baliolum (sc. Afrum), Plaut. Poen. 5, 5, 22 dub.

balista2.full: Balista (Ballista), ae, f., a mountain in Liguria, Liv. 39, 2, 7; 40, 41, 2.
balista2.short: Balista (Ballista), ae, f., a mountain in Liguria, Liv.

ballator.full: ballātor, ōris, m. ballo, a dancer: SODALES. BALLATORES. CYBELAE., Inscr. Orell. 2337.

ballematicus.full: ballēmătĭcus, a, um, adj. cf. ballo, accompanying the dance, Isid. Orig. 3, 21, 11.

ballio.full: Ballio, ōnis, m., the name of a worthless pimp in the Pseudolus of Plautus; hence, for designating any worthless man, Cic. Phil. 2, 6, 15; id. Rosc. Com. 7, 20.— Whence, Ballĭōnĭus, a, um, adj., of Ballio, Plaut. Ps. 4, 6, 2.
ballio.short: Ballio, ōnis, m., the name of a worthless pimp in the Pseudolus of Plautus;

ballista1.full: ballista (better than balista; in Gloss. also ballistra), ae, f. βάλλω, a lārge military engine, resembling a bow, stretched with cords and thongs, by which masses of stone and other missiles were thrown to a great distance; a machine for projectiles, the ballista (orig. diff. from catapulta, which was used for throwing arrows; but afterwards often interchanged with it; cf. Vitr. 10, 16-18; Veg. 4, 22): centenariae, throwing stones of a hundred pounds weight, Lucil. ap. Non. p. 555, 25: ballista

ballistarium.full: ballistārĭum (balist-), ii, n., = ballista, or the place where the ballista is worked, Plaut. Poen. 1, 1, 74 (cf. ballista fin.).
ballistarium.short: ballistārĭum (balist-), ii, n., = ballista, or the place where the ballista is worked, Plaut.

ballistarius.full: ballistārĭus (balist-; and in Gloss. ballistrārĭus), ii, m. 1. ballista. A maker of ballistœ, Dig. 50, 6, 6: COLLEGIVM BALLISTARIORVM., Inscr. Orell. 4066.— One who discharges the ballista, a slinger, Veg. Mil. 2, 2; Amm. 16, 2, 5.

ballistia.full: ballistĭa (balist-), ōrum, n. βαλλίξω, to dance, music or songs accompanying dancing, Vop. Aurel. 6, where an example of such dancing songs is given.

ballo.full: ballo, āre, v. n. βάλλω, βαλλίξω, to dance, Aug. Serm. 215 (hence, Fr. bal; Engl. ball).

ballonoti.full: Ballŏnŏti, ōrum, m., a Scythian tribe, Val. Fl. 6, 160.
ballonoti.short: Ballŏnŏti, ōrum, m., a Scythian tribe, Val.

ballote.full: ballōtē, ēs, f., = βαλλωτή, a plant, also called porrum nigrum, black horehound: Ballota nigra, Linn.; Plin. 27, 8, 30, § 54.
ballote.short: ballōtē, ēs, f., = βαλλωτή, a plant, also called porrum nigrum, black horehound: Ballota nigra, Linn.;

ballux.full: ballux (bal-), ūcis, f. Spanish, gold-sand, gold-dust, χρύσαμμος, Plin. 33, 4, 21, § 77; Just. 44, 1, 10 (less correctly paludibus); Mart. 12, 57, 9 (less correctly paludes); and Latinized ballūca (bal-), ae, f., Cod. Valent. 11, 6, 1 and 2; Cod. Th. 10, 19, 3 and 4; Veg. Vet. 1, 20, 2.

balnearis.full: balnĕārĭs, e, adj. balneum, of or pertaining to a bath (post-Aug. for the foll.): argentum, silver utensils used in baths, Dig. 34, 2, 33: jocus, Spart. Had. 17: vestis, Lampr. Alex. Sev. 42.—Subst.: balnĕā-rĭa, ĭum, n., bathing utensils, App. M. 3, p. 134, 36.

balnearius.full: balnĕārĭus (bălĭneārĭus, Inscr. Grut. 171, 8), a, um, adj. id., of or pertaining to a bath (class. for the preced.): fur, lurking about baths, Cat. 33, 1; cf. the title in Dig. 47, 17: de furibus balneariis: furtum, Dig. 1. 1. § 3: instrumentum, a bathing implement, ib. 33, 7, 17: vapores, ib. 43, 21, 3, § 6.—Subst.: balnĕārĭa, ōrum, n. plur., a place for bathing, a bathing-room, bath: nihil ei restabat praeter balnearia et ambulationem et aviarium, Cic. Q. Fr. 3, 1, 1, § 1; so id. Att. 13, 29,

balneaticum.full: balnĕātĭcum, i, n., a piece of money to be paid for a bath, bath-money; only in Schol. Juv. 2, 152; and in Vet. Gloss.: balneaticum βαλανικόν.
balneaticum.short: balnĕātĭcum, i, n., a piece of money to be paid for a bath, bath-money;

balneator.full: balnĕātor, ōris, m. (acc. to Serv. ad Verg. A. 12, 159, and Prob. p. 1452 P., gen. comm., yet v. balneatrix) [balneum], one who has the care of a bath, a bath-keeper, βαλανεύς, Plaut. Poen. 3, 3, 90; id. Truc. 2, 3, 4: balnearis, Cic. Cael. 26, 62; id. Phil. 13, 12, 26; Plin. 18, 17, 44, § 156; Dig. 3, 2, 4, § 2; ib. 19, 2, 30, § 1 al.—Facetè, of Neptune: edepol, Neptune, es balneator frigidus, Plaut. Rud. 2, 6, 43.

balneatorius.full: balnĕatōrĭus, a, um, adj. balneator, of or pertaining to a bath, = balnearius: instrumentum, Paul. Sent. 3, 6, 65; Dig. 33, 7, 17.

balneatrix.full: balnĕātrix, īcis, f. id., she who has the care of a bath, Petr. ap. Serv. ad Verg. A. 12, 159.

balneolum.full: balnĕŏlum, i, n. (plur. balnĕŏlae, ārum, f.), dim. balneum, a small bath: balneolum angustum, tenebricosum, Sen. Ep. 86, 4; Juv. 7, 4: primus balneolas suspendit, Cic. Hortens. Fragm. 69 B. and K. (ap. Non. p. 194, 13); Aug. contra Ac. 3, 4.

balneum.full: balnĕum, i. n. (in plur. usu. heterocl. balnĕae, ārum. f.; cf. Varr. L. L. 8, § 48 Müll.; since the Aug. per. sometimes bal-nĕa, ōrum, n.; cf. Dör. ad Plin. Ep. 2, 8, 2) [contr. from bălĭnĕum, also in use, and in Plaut. and post-Aug. prose predominant, = βαλανεῖον; plur. bălĭnĕae; the Lat. bal-neum stands for bad-neum, kindr. with Sanscr. root bād, lavare, se lavare; Germ. Bad; Engl. bath]. A bath, a place for bathing (the public bath, as consisting of several apartments, only in plur., Varr. L.

balo.full: bālo (bēlo, Varr. R. R. 2, 1, 7), āvi, ātum, 1, v. n. root bal = bar; Sanscr. barh, barrire; Gr. βάρβαρος; cf. βληχή, ἔβραχε; but cf. also Paul. ex Fest. p. 30 Müll., to bleat, Plaut. Bacch. 5, 2, 20; Ov. F. 4, 740; Quint. 1, 5, 72; Sil. 15, 706.—Poet.: balantes hostiae = oves, Enn. ap. Cic. Div. 1, 21 (Trag. v. 61 Vahl.): pecus balans, Juv. 13, 233; and absol. balans = ovis (so μηκάς from μηκάομαι), Lucr. 6, 1131: balantum grex, Verg. G. 1, 272; 3, 457.—Facetè, to speak of sheep: satis balasti,

balsa.full: Balsa, ae, f., a town in Lusitania, now Javira, Plin. 4, 21, 35, § 117; Mel. 3, 1, 6.
balsa.short: Balsa, ae, f., a town in Lusitania, now Javira, Plin.

balsameus.full: balsămĕus, a, um, adj. balsamum, balsamic, of balsam: unguen, Auct. Carm. Phoen. 118.

balsaminus.full: balsămĭnus, a, um, adj., = βαλσάμινος, of balsam: oleum, Plin. 23, 4, 47, § 92.
balsaminus.short: balsămĭnus, a, um, adj., = βαλσάμινος, of balsam: oleum, Plin.

balsamodes.full: balsămōdes = βαλσαμώδης, abounding in balsam: casia, Plin. 12, 19, 43, § 97.
balsamodes.short: balsămōdes = βαλσαμώδης, abounding in balsam: casia, Plin.

balsamum.full: balsămum, i, n., = βάλσαμον. A fragrant gum of the balsam-tree, balsam, Verg. G. 2, 119; Plin. 13, 1, 2, § 8 sq.: balsama olet, Mart. 3, 63; Tac. G. 45; Just. 36, 3: Vulg. Ezech. 27, 17.— The balsam-tree: Amyris opobalsamum, Linn.; Plin. 12, 25, 54, § 111; Sol. 35; Tac. H. 5, 6.

baltearius.full: baltĕārĭus, ii, m. balteus, a maker or master of sword-belts, Inscr. Orell. 3501.

balteatus.full: baltĕātus, a, um, Part., from bal-tĕo, āre, Gloss. Isid. [id.], furnished with a girdle or belt, girded, belted, Mart. Cap. 5, § 426.
balteatus.short: baltĕātus, a, um, Part., from bal-tĕo, āre, Gloss.

balteolus.full: baltĕŏlus, i, m. dim. id., a small girdle, Capitol. Max. 2, § 4.

balteus.full: baltĕus, i, m., more rare baltĕum, i, n. (in plur. baltea was generally used in the poets metri gr.; and in ante-class. prose balteum, e. g. Varr. L. L. 5, § 116 Müll.; Non. p. 194, 21; Charis. p. 59 P.) [acc. to Varr. ap. Charis. 1. 1. a Tuscan word; but cf. O. H. Germ. balz; Engl. belt] (not in Cic.). Lit., a girdle, belt; esp. a swordbelt, or the band passing over the shoulder (cf. Quint. 11, 3, 140; Dict. of Antiq.): baltea, Att. ap. Non. p. 194, 21; Varr. ib.: infelix umero cum apparuit alt
balteus.short: baltĕus, i, m., more rare baltĕum, i, n.

bambalio.full: Bambălĭo, ōnis, m. cf. βαμβάλειν, to stammer, βομβόλη; Engl. bumblebee, = Βαμβαλίων, Dio Cass. 45, 47; 46, 7 and 28: M. Fulvius, the father-in-law of Antonius, Cic. Phil. 3, 6, 16; 2, 36, 90.

bambyce.full: Bambўcē, ēs, f., = Βαμβύκη, a town in Cœlosyria, also called Hieropolis, Plin. 5, 23, 19, § 81.—Hence, adj.: Bambўcius, a, um, of or from Bambyce: pisces, Avien. Arat. 542; 646.
bambyce.short: Bambўcē, ēs, f., = Βαμβύκη, a town in Cœlosyria, also called Hieropolis, Plin.

banchus.full: banchus or bancus, i, m., a species of fish, otherwise unknown, Cael. Aur. Acut. 2, 37.
banchus.short: banchus or bancus, i, m., a species of fish, otherwise unknown, Cael.

bandusia.full: Bandŭsĭa, ae, f., a pleasant fountain near Venusia, the birthplace of Horace, celebrated by him in song, C. 3, 13, 1 sq. Ritter and Orell. ad loc. (diff. from the celebrated Digentia of the Ep. 1, 16, 12 and 104, as is shown by the Privilegium Paschalis II. anni 1103 ap. Ughell. Ital. Sacra, tom. vii. col. 30, Ven. 1721; cf. Fea and Jahn upon Hor. C. 3, 13; Capmartin de Chaupy, Découverte de la maison d'Horace t. iii. pp. 364, 518 and 537).
bandusia.short: Bandŭsĭa, ae, f., a pleasant fountain near Venusia, the birthplace of Horace, celebrated by him in song, C.

bangeni.full: Bangēni, ōrum, m., a race of Troglodytes in Ethiopia, Plin. 6, 29, 34, § 176.
bangeni.short: Bangēni, ōrum, m., a race of Troglodytes in Ethiopia, Plin.

bannanica.full: bannanica (sc. vitis), a variety of the vine, Plin. 14, 3, 4, § 37.

bantia.full: Bantĭa, ae, f., = Βαντία, a town of Apulia, in the vicinity of Venusia, on the southern declivity of the mountain, now Banzi, Liv. 27, 25, 13.—Hence, Bantīnus, a, um, adj., of or pertaining to Bantia: saltus, Hor. C. 3, 4, 15.—Bantīni, ōrum, m., the inhabitants of Bantia, Plin. 3, 11, 15, § 98.
bantia.short: Bantĭa, ae, f., = Βαντία, a town of Apulia, in the vicinity of Venusia, on the southern declivity of the mountain, now Banzi, Liv.

bapheus.full: băpheus (dissyl.), ĕi, m., = βαφεύς, a dyer, Cod. Just. 11, 7, 2 (al. baphii).
bapheus.short: băpheus (dissyl.), ĕi, m., = βαφεύς, a dyer, Cod.

baphium.full: băphīum (băphēum), ii, n., = βαφεῖον. a dye-house, Lampr. Alex. Sev. 40; Cod. Th. 10, 20, 18; Inscr. Orell. 4272.

baphyrus.full: Baphўrus, i, m., a river in Thessaly, near Mount Olympus, Liv. 44, 6, 15.
baphyrus.short: Baphўrus, i, m., a river in Thessaly, near Mount Olympus, Liv.

baptae.full: Baptae, ārum, m., = Βάπται [perh. so called from dyeing their hair; v. Meineke, Com. Fragm. I. p. 119], priests of the Thracian, afterwards Athenian, goddess Cotytto, whose festival was celebrated in a very lewd manner, Juv. 2, 92 Schol.; cf. Cotytto.

baptes.full: baptes, ae, m., an unknown precious stone, perh. colored amber, Plin. 37, 10, 55, § 149.
baptes.short: baptes, ae, m., an unknown precious stone, perh.

baptisma.full: baptisma, ătis, n., = βάπτισμα. A dipping in, dipping under, washing, ablution, Prud. Psych. 103; Apoth. 697; Vulg. Marc. 7, 4; 7, 8: mundi, i. e. the general deluge, Tert. Bapt. 8.— Esp., Christian baptism, Vulg. Eph. 4, 5; in the Church fathers very freq.—A parallel form baptismus, i, m., Cod. Th. 16, 6, 1; Vulg. Marc. 11, 30 al.—baptismum, i, n., Tert. Bapt. 15; Aug. Serm. Temp. 36; Vulg. Matt. 21, 25 al.

baptista.full: baptista, ae, m., = βαπτιστής, a baptizer, baptist, κατʼ ἐξοχήν, of John, the forerunner of Christ, Sedul. Pasch. 2, 143; Vulg. Matt. 3, 1.
baptista.short: baptista, ae, m., = βαπτιστής, a baptizer, baptist, κατʼ ἐξοχήν, of John, the forerunner of Christ, Sedul.

baptisterium.full: baptistērĭum, ii, n., = βαπτιστήριον. A place for bathing or swimming, a vessel for bathing, Plin. Ep. 5, 6, 25; 2, 17, 11; Sid. Ep. 2, 2.— In eccl. Lat., a baptistery, a baptismal font, Sid. Ep. 4, 15.

baptizatio.full: baptīzātĭo, ōnis, f. baptizo, a baptizing, Ambros. Serm. Temp. 17.

baptizator.full: baptīzātor, ōris, m. id., a baptizer (cf. baptista): Joannes, Tert. Bapt. 12; Aug. Ep. 23.

baptizo.full: baptīzo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a., = βαπτίξω, only in eccl. Lat., to baptize, Vulg. Judith, 12, 7; id. Matt. 3, 6; id. Marc. 1, 8; and Tert. Aug. Hier. al. saep.

barace.full: Barăcē, ēs, f., a seaport of India, Plin. 6, 23, 26, § 105.
barace.short: Barăcē, ēs, f., a seaport of India, Plin.

baragaza.full: Baragaza, ae, f., a town of Ethiopia, Plin. 6, 29, 34, § 175.
baragaza.short: Baragaza, ae, f., a town of Ethiopia, Plin.

baraomutae.full: Baraomutae, ārum, m., a people of India, Plin. 6, 20, 23, § 77.
baraomutae.short: Baraomutae, ārum, m., a people of India, Plin.

barathrum.full: bărā^thrum, i, n., = βάραθρον, an abyss, chasm, a deep pit, the Lower World (mostly poet; cf. vorago), Plaut. Rud. 2, 7, 12: o barathrum ubi nunc es? ut ego te usurpem lubens (words of one in despair), id. Bacch. 1, 2, 41; Lucr. 3, 966; Cat. 68, 108; 68, 117; 95, 5.—Esp., of the infernal regions: ferri in barathrum, Lucr. 6, 606: imus barathri gurges (Charybdis), Verg. A. 3, 421; 8, 245; Sil. 9, 497: poena barathri, Val. Fl. 2, 86; a pit made by art, a deep dungeon, Vitr. 10, 22, 11.— Trop.: qui
barathrum.short: bărā^thrum, i, n., = βάραθρον, an abyss, chasm, a deep pit, the Lower World (mostly poet;

barathrus.full: bărăthrus, i, a false read. for barathrum, Lucr. 3, 966; v. Lachm. ad h. 1.

barba1.full: barba, ae, f. cf. O. H. Germ. part; Germ. Bart; Engl. beard. Lit., the beard, of men: alba, Plaut. Bacch. 5, 1, 15: hirquina, id. Ps. 4, 2, 12: mollis, Lucr. 5, 673: promissa, long, Nep. Dat. 3, 1; Liv. 5, 41, 9; Tac. A. 2, 31; id. G. 31: immissa, Verg. A. 3, 593; Ov. M. 12, 351; Quint. 12, 3, 12: stiriaque inpexis induruit horrida barbis, Verg. G. 3, 366: submittere (as a sign of mourning). Suet. Caes. 67; id. Aug. 23; id. Calig. 24: prima, Juv. 8, 166: barbam tondere, Cic. Tusc. 5, 20, 58: max

barba2.full: Barba, ae, m., a Roman name, e. g. Cassius Barba, a friend of Cœsar and Antony, Cic. Phil. 13, 1, 2 sq.; id. Att. 13, 52, 1.
barba2.short: Barba, ae, m., a Roman name, e.

barbana.full: Barbāna, ae, m., a river of Illyria, Liv. 44, 31, 3.
barbana.short: Barbāna, ae, m., a river of Illyria, Liv.

barbara.full: barbăra, ae, v. barbarus, II. B. fin.

barbaria.full: barbărĭa, ae (poet., or in post-Aug. prose barbărĭes, acc. -em; so once in Cic. Brut. 74, 258), f. barbarus. Lit., a foreign country, in opposition to Greece or Rome. In gen.: a quo (philosopho) non solum Graecia et Italia, sed etiam omnis barbaria commota est, Cic. Fin. 2, 15, 49; 5, 4, 11; id. N. D. 1, 29, 81; cf.: non solum cum exercitu suo, sed etiam cum omni inmanitate barbariae bellum inferre nobis. id. Phil. 5, 13, 37; 13, 8, 18: quid tibi barbariem. gentes ab utroque jacentes Oceano nume

barbaricarius.full: barbărĭcārĭus, ii, m. barbarus, = Phrygio, a gold-weaver, an embroiderer in gold, a gilder, Cod. Just. 12, 24, 7; Cod. Th. 10, 22, 1; Inscr. Orell. 4152; Edict. Diocl. 16, 48, p. 84 Momms.; cf. Donat. ad Verg. A. 11, 777.

barbarice.full: barbărĭcē and barbărĭcum, adv., v. barbaricus fin.

barbaricus.full: barbărĭcus, a, um, adj., = βαρβαρικός [barbarus]. Foreign, strange, outlandish, barbarous, in opp. to Grecian or Roman (poet. and in post - Aug. prose). In gen.: alae, Luc. 1, 476: sermo, Amm. 18, 2, 1: pyra, Plin. 15, 15, 16, § 56: equi, Veg. 6, 7, 1.—Hence, Subst.: barbărĭcum, i, n. A foreign land (post-class.): Albis in barbarico, longe ultra Rhenum est, Eutr. 7, 8; 9, 4; Spart. Sev. 47.— Barbaricum appellatur clamor exercitus, quod eo genere barbari utantur, Paul. ex Fest. p. 31 Müll.— Esp.,

barbarismus.full: barbărismus, i, m., = βαρβαρισμός, an impropriety of speech, barbarism; esp. of pronunciation (acc. to Gell. 13, 6, 14; cf. id. 5, 20, 1, not in use before the Aug. per.; in Nigidius, instead of it, rusticus sermo), Quint. 1, 5, 5 sq.; Auct. Her. 4, 12, 17; Gell. l. l.; 5, 20, 4; Don. p. 1767 sq. P.; Charis. p. 237 sq.; id. Diom. p. 446 sq. P. al.; cf. the foll.
barbarismus.short: barbărismus, i, m., = βαρβαρισμός, an impropriety of speech, barbarism;

barbarolexis.full: barbărŏlexis, eos, f., = βαρβαρόλεξις, the perversion of the form of a word, esp. the change or in flection of a Greek word according to Latin usage (while barbarismus is the erroneous pronunciation of a Latin word), Isid. Orig. 1, 31, 2 (in Charis. p. 237 P. used as Greek).
barbarolexis.short: barbărŏlexis, eos, f., = βαρβαρόλεξις, the perversion of the form of a word, esp.

barbarum1.full: barbărum, i, n., v. barbarus, I. A.

barbarum2.full: barbărum, i, n. barbarus; in medicine, a plaster applied to raw wounds: optimum ex his (emplastris) est, quod barbarum vocatur, Cels. 5, 19, n. 1; 5. 26, n. 23; Scrib. Comp. 207 (in Scrib. Lang. Comp. l. l. barbăra, ae, f.).

barbarus.full: barbărus, a, um (gen. plur. m. barbarum, Tac. A. 14, 39; 15, 25), adj., = βάρβαρος [cf. barrio; balo, balbus; blatio]. Prop., foreign, strange, barbarous, opp. to Greek or Roman. In gen.: hospes, Plaut. Rud. 2, 7, 25: mixta facit Graiis barbara turba metum, Ov. Tr. 5, 10, 28; Hor. C. 1, 29, 6: reges, id. ib. 1, 35, 11.—Hence, in Tac., in barbarum, adverb., in the manner or according to the custom of foreigners or barbarians: civitas potens, neque in barbarum corrupta, Tac. A. 6, 42; id. H. 5, 2.

barbatia.full: Barbatĭa, ae, f., a town in Arabia, Plin. 6, 28, 32, § 146.
barbatia.short: Barbatĭa, ae, f., a town in Arabia, Plin.

barbatoria.full: barbātōrĭa, ae, f. barba, a shaving of the beard: facere, to shave the beard for the first time, Petr. 73, 6.

barbatulus.full: barbātŭlus, a, um, adj. dim. [barbatus], having a small or foppish beard: concursabant barbatuli juvenes, Cic. Att. 1, 14, 5; 1, 16, 10; Hier. Ep. 117, n. 6 and 10.— Transf. to fishes: barbatuli mulli, Cic. Par. 5, 2, 38.

barbatus.full: barbātus, a, um, adj. barba. Having a beard, bearded. Of men: dicere licebit Jovem semper barbatum, Apollinem semper imberbem, Cic. N. D. 1, 30, 83; 1, 36, 100: quos aut imberbes aut bene barbatos videtis, id. Cat. 2, 10, 22.—Poet. as a designation of age, Plaut. Cas. 2, 8, 25: equitare in harundine longā, Si quem delectet barbatum, i. e. an adult, * Hor. S. 2, 3, 249: sub Jove, sed Jove nondum barbato, i. e. in the earliest time, when Jupiter was yet young, Juv. 6, 16; 13, 56.—Hence, Meton. For

barbesco.full: barbesco, ĕre, = γενειάζω, to get a beard, Gloss. Cyril.
barbesco.short: barbesco, ĕre, = γενειάζω, to get a beard, Gloss.

barbiger.full: barbĭger, ĕra, ĕrum, adj. barba-gero, wearing a beard, bearded (only in Lucr.): capellae, Lucr. 6, 971: pecudes, id. 5, 898.

barbio.full: barbĭo, īre, 4, v. n. barba, to raise a beard (late Lat.), Theod. Prisc. p. 4, 2.

barbitium.full: barbĭtĭum, ii, n. id., = barba, the beard (perh. only in App.), App. M. 5, p. 162, 21; 11, p. 260, 40.

barbitos.full: barbĭtŏs, m. (f. in the spurious epistle of Sappho, Ov. H. 15, 8; v. infra; found only in nom., acc., and voc.; plur. barbita, n., Aus. Ep. 44). = βάρβιτον (-ος), a lyre, a lute (not before the Aug. per.): age, dic Latinum, Barbite, carmen, Hor. C. 1, 32, 4; 1, 1, 34; 3, 26, 4; Claud. Praef. ap. Nupt. Hon. et Mar. 10; Aus. Epigr. 44.— Meton., the song played upon the lute: non facit ad lacrimas barbitos ulla meas, Ov. H. 15. 8 (a spurious poem).

barbula.full: barbŭla, ae. f. dim. barba. A little beard (as worn by the young Romans; v. barba. barbatus, and barbatulus): non hac barbulā, sed illa horrida, quam in statuis antiquis videmus, * Cic. Cael. 14, 33.— Transf. to plants (cf. barba, II. A.), Plin. 27, 11, 74, § 98; 21, 8, 25, § 49.— A cognomen of Q. Aemilius, Liv 9, 20, 7.

barbus.full: barbus, i, m. barba, a barbel, a river barbel: Cyprinus barbus, Linn., Aus. Mosell. 94 and 134 (cf. barbatulus mullus, Cic. Par. 5, 2, 38, and barbati mulli, id. Att. 2, 1, 7).

barca.full: barca, ae, f., a small boat, a bark, barge (post-class.): barca est, quae cuncta navis commercia ad litus portat. Hanc navis in pelago propter nimias undas suo suscipit gremio, etc., Isid. Orig. 19, 1, 19; Paul. Nol. Carm. 21, 95.
barca.short: barca, ae, f., a small boat, a bark, barge (post-class.): barca est, quae cuncta navis commercia ad litus portat.

barcas.full: Barcas (Barca), ae, m., = Βάρκας [, a gleaming, or a gleaming sword, as an epithet of heroes; cf. Gesenius, Gesch. d. Hebr.
