Spr. und Schr, p. 229], ancestor of a distinguished family in Carthage to which Hamilcar and Hannibal belonged, hence, a surname of Hamilcar, Nep. Ham. 1, 1.— Hence, Derivv Barcīnus, a, um, adj., of Barcas, or pertaining to the family or party of Barcas: familia Barcina, Liv. 23, 13, 6: factio, id. 21, 9, 4.—Subst.: Bar-cīni, ōrum, m., the Barcini, Liv 21, 3, 3.— Poet.: Bar
barcas.short: Barcas (Barca), ae, m., = Βάρκας [, a gleaming, or a gleaming sword, as an epithet of heroes;

barce.full: Barcē, ēs, f., = Βάρκη. A town in the Libyan province Pentapolis, afterwards called Ptolemais, now Tolometa or Dolmeita (acc. to others, the ruins of Merdsjeh), Plin. 5, 5, 5, § 32.—Hence, Barcaei, ōrum, m., the inhabitants of Barce, enemies of Dido (poet. prolepsis), Verg. A. 4, 43.— The nurse of Sichœus, Verg. A. 4, 632.

barcino.full: Barcĭno or -on, ōnis, f., the present city Barcelona, in Spain, Plin. 3, 3, 4, § 22; Mel. 2, 6, 5; Aus. Ep. 24, 89; Prud. στεφ. 33.—Hence, Barcĭnōnensis, e, adj., of Barcelona: muria, Aus. Ep. 21 init.
barcino.short: Barcĭno or -on, ōnis, f., the present city Barcelona, in Spain, Plin.

bardaei.full: Bardaei, ōrum, m., an Illyrian people (in Cic. Fam. 5, 9, 2, Vardaei)—Hence, Bardăĭcus, a, um, adj., Bardœan calceus, a kind of soldier's boot, poet. for the soldiers themselves, Juv. 16, 13 (cf. Caligula)' cuculli, Capitol. Pertin. 8, 3; cf. bardocucullus.—Absol. Bardăĭcus, i, m., a soldier's boot, Mart. 4, 4. 5.
bardaei.short: Bardaei, ōrum, m., an Illyrian people (in Cic.

barditus.full: bardītus, i, m. bardus, the war-song of the Germans, Tac. G. 3 Holder ad loc.; cf. baritus.

bardocucullus.full: bardŏcŭcullus, i, m., a Gallic overcoat (cloak), with a hood or cowl, made of woollen stuff, Mart. 14, 128; 1, 54, 5, Gallien. ap. Treb. Pol. Claud. 17, 6 (in Capitol. Pertin. cucullus Bardaicus); v. Bardaïcus, s. v Bardaei fin.
bardocucullus.short: bardŏcŭcullus, i, m., a Gallic overcoat (cloak), with a hood or cowl, made of woollen stuff, Mart.

bardulis.full: Bardūlis, is, m., = Βάρδυλις, a king of Illyria, who waged war against Philip of Macedon, Cic. Off. 2, 11, 40.
bardulis.short: Bardūlis, is, m., = Βάρδυλις, a king of Illyria, who waged war against Philip of Macedon, Cic.

bardus1.full: bardus, a, um, adj [root garu-, whence also gravis; Sanscr. guruú; cf. Gr. βαρύς, βραδύς, and Lat. brutus], stupid, dull of apprehension (rare), Fest. p. 28; cf. Non. p. 10, 3 sq.; Adamant. ap. Cassiod. p. 2299 P.: stulti, stolidi, fatui, fungi, bardi, blenni, buccones, etc., Plaut. Bacch. 5, 1, 2; so id. Ep. 3, 3, 40; id. Pers. 2, 1, 2 (quoted by Non. l. l.): Zopyrus stupidum esse Socratem dixit et bardum, * Cic. Fat 5, 10: Pictor bardior, Tert. adv Herm. 36.—Sup. and adv. not in use.
bardus1.short: bardus, a, um, adj [root garu-, whence also gravis;

bardus2.full: bardus, i, m. Engl. bard; Celtic, from Wal. bar, = spirit, or Armor. bar, = distinguished, a poet and singer among the Gauls, a bard, minstrel. bardus Gallice cantor appellatur, qui virorum fortium laudes canit, a gente Bardorum, de quibus Lucanus, 1, 449; Fest. p 28; cf. Amm. 15, 9, 5 and 8.

barea1.full: Barēa, ae, f., a town in Hispania Tarraconensis, Cic. Att. 16, 4, 2; Plin. 3, 3, 4, § 19.
barea1.short: Barēa, ae, f., a town in Hispania Tarraconensis, Cic.

barea2.full: Barĕa, ae, m., a Roman cognomen, e. g. Q. Marcius Barea, consul A.U.C. 779: Barea Soranus, Tac. A. 16, 23; cf. Juv. 7, 91.
barea2.short: Barĕa, ae, m., a Roman cognomen, e.

bargullum.full: Bargullum, i, n., a town of Epirus, Liv. 29, 12, 13.
bargullum.short: Bargullum, i, n., a town of Epirus, Liv.

bargus.full: Bargus, i, m., a river of Thrace, tributary to the Ebrus, Plin. 4, 11, 18, § 50.
bargus.short: Bargus, i, m., a river of Thrace, tributary to the Ebrus, Plin.

bargusii.full: Bargūsĭi, ōrum, m., = Βαργούσιοι, Polyb., a people in Hispania Tarraconensis, near the Pyrenees, Liv. 21, 19, 7; 23, 2 al.
bargusii.short: Bargūsĭi, ōrum, m., = Βαργούσιοι, Polyb., a people in Hispania Tarraconensis, near the Pyrenees, Liv.

bargyliae.full: Bargўlĭae, ārum, f., = Βαργύλια and Βάργυλα, τά, in Strabo; Βαργυλία, ἡ, in Stephan. Byzant., a town in Caria, Liv 32, 33, 7; 33, 18, 18.—Hence, Derivv. Bargўlĭētĭcus, a, um, adj., of Bargyliœ: sinus. Liv. 37, 17, 3: campi, Plin. 5, 29, 31, § 113.—And from the parallel form Bargўlĭa, ōrum, n., = Βαργύλια, τά, Plin. 5, 29, 29, § 107.— Bargўlētae, ārum, m., the inhabitants of Bargylice, Cic. Fam. 13, 56, 2.
bargyliae.short: Bargўlĭae, ārum, f., = Βαργύλια and Βάργυλα, τά, in Strabo;

bargylus.full: Bargylus, i, m., a mountain of Phœnicia, Plin. 5, 20, 17, § 78.
bargylus.short: Bargylus, i, m., a mountain of Phœnicia, Plin.

barine.full: Barīnē, ēs, f., name of a freedwoman, Hor. C 2, 8, 2.
barine.short: Barīnē, ēs, f., name of a freedwoman, Hor.

baris.full: bāris, ĭdos, f. Egyptian, a small Egyptian row-boat, βάρις, Prop. 3 (4), 11, 44.Kuin.

baritus.full: barītus (barrītus or bardītus), ūs, m. cf. bassio and O. Germ. bar, baren, to raise the voice, the war-cry of the Germans; and in gen., battle-cry: clamor, quem baritum vocant, Veg. Mil. 3, 18: cornuti et bracati baritum civere vel maximum, Amm. 16, 12, 43; 21, 13, 15; 26, 7, 14; 31, 7, 11.—Of the battle-song: carmina, quorum relatu, quem barditum vocant, accendunt animos, Tac. G 3 Halm; v. Comm. in h. l.

barium.full: Barĭum, ii, n., = Βάριον, a town in Apulia, on the Adriatic Sea, now Bari, Mel. 2, 4, 7, Plin. 3, 11, 16, § 102; Liv. 40, 18, 8; Tac. A. 16, 9: piscosum, Hor. S. 1, 5, 97.
barium.short: Barĭum, ii, n., = Βάριον, a town in Apulia, on the Adriatic Sea, now Bari, Mel.

barnosthenes.full: Barnosthĕnes, is, m., a mountain in Laconia, east of Sparta, Liv. 35, 27, 13 (MSS. Barbosthenes, Weissenb. ad loc.); 35, 30, 9.
barnosthenes.short: Barnosthĕnes, is, m., a mountain in Laconia, east of Sparta, Liv.

baro.full: bāro, ōnis m. kindr with bardus, q. v.; cf. also Varro, varo, a simpleton, blockhead, dunce (four times in Cicero, elsewhere rare): haec cum loqueris, nos barones stupemus, tu videlicet tecum ipse rides, Cic. Fin. 2, 23, 76; so id. Div. 2, 70, 144; id. Fam. 9, 26, 3; id. Att. 5, 11, 6; Pers. 5, 138; Petr. 53, 11; 63, 7.

baroptenus.full: baroptĕnus, i, f., or barippē, ēs, f., an unknown precious stone of a black color, with white and red spots, Plin. 37, 10, 55, § 150.
baroptenus.short: baroptĕnus, i, f., or barippē, ēs, f., an unknown precious stone of a black color, with white and red spots, Plin.

barosus.full: bārōsus βάκηλος, σοβαρός, stultus, mulierosus, mollis, Gloss. Philox.
barosus.short: bārōsus βάκηλος, σοβαρός, stultus, mulierosus, mollis, Gloss.

barpana.full: Barpāna, ae, f., an island east of Corsica, Mel. 2, 7, 19; Plin. 3, 6, 12, § 81.
barpana.short: Barpāna, ae, f., an island east of Corsica, Mel.

barrinus.full: barrīnus, a, um, adj [barrus], of or belonging to an elephant, elephantine: aures, Sid. Ep. 3, 13.
barrinus.short: barrīnus, a, um, adj [barrus], of or belonging to an elephant, elephantine: aures, Sid.

barrio.full: barrĭo, īre, v. n [id.], to cry; of elephants. barrire elephantes dicuntur, sicut oves dicimus balare, utique a sono ipso vo cis: elephanti barriunt, ranae coaxant, equi hinniunt, Spart. Get 5, 5; Auct. Carm. Phil. 53; cf. Paul. ex Fest p. 30 Müll.

barritus1.full: barrītus, ūs, m. barrio, the cry of the elephant, App. Flor. 16, p. 358, 2; Veg. Mil. 3, 24; cf. Isid. Orig. under barrus.

barrus.full: Barrus, i, m., a cognomen of T, Betucius, Cic. Brut. 46, 169
barrus.short: Barrus, i, m., a cognomen of T, Betucius, Cic.

barycephalus.full: bărўcĕphălus, a, um, = βαρνκέφαλος, or bărўcus, a, um, adj [βαρύς], in archit., top-heavy, with low walls and broad roofs, Vitr. 3, 3, 5.
barycephalus.short: bărўcĕphălus, a, um, = βαρνκέφαλος, or bărўcus, a, um, adj [βαρύς], in archit., top-heavy, with low walls and broad roofs, Vitr.

barypicron.full: bărўpī^cron, ī, n., = βαρύπικρον (very bitter), a Greek epithet of wormwood: absinthium, App. Herb. 100.
barypicron.short: bărўpī^cron, ī, n., = βαρύπικρον (very bitter), a Greek epithet of wormwood: absinthium, App.

barython.full: bărўthon, ōnis, m., = βαρυθων, a plant, also called Sabina, App. Herb. 85.
barython.short: bărўthon, ōnis, m., = βαρυθων, a plant, also called Sabina, App.

barytonos.full: bărўtŏnŏs, ŏn, adj., = βαρύτονος, not accented on the last syllable, Macr. Diff. 4, 1; 5, 1 al.
barytonos.short: bărўtŏnŏs, ŏn, adj., = βαρύτονος, not accented on the last syllable, Macr.

basaboiates.full: Basaboiātes, um, m., a people of Gallia Aquitania, Plin. 4, 19, 33, § 108.
basaboiates.short: Basaboiātes, um, m., a people of Gallia Aquitania, Plin.

basaltes.full: basaltes, is, m. African, a dark and very hard species of marble in Ethiopia, Isid. Orig. 16, 5, 6; cf. Strabo, 17, p. 818.

basanites.full: băsănītes lăpis = βασανιτης (βάσανος), a touchstone, test-stone, a very hard stone, used as a test for the precious metals, for whetstones, and, in medicine, for mortars, Plin. 36, 20, 38, § 147; 36, 22, 43, § 157; Isid. Orig. 16, 4, 36.—Also basanites alone, Plin. 36, 7, 11, § 58.
basanites.short: băsănītes lăpis = βασανιτης (βάσανος), a touchstone, test-stone, a very hard stone, used as a test for the precious metals, for whetstones, and, in medicine, for mortars, Plin.

bascauda.full: bascauda, ae, f. British; whence Engl. basket; cf. Wall. basget, basgawd; and Gr βαστάζω, to carry, an article of table furniture, prob. a delicately woven mat, or dish-holder of basket-work, Juv. 12, 46; Mart. 14, 99, 1.

basella.full: băsella, ae, f dim. [basis], a small base, Pall. 1, 18, 2.

basiatio.full: bāsĭātĭo, ōnis, f [basio], a kissing; meton (abstr pro concr.), a kiss (rare; cf. osculum), *Cat. 7, 1; Mart. 7, 95, 17; 2, 23, 4.

basiator.full: bāsĭātor, ōris, m. id., a kisser, one who kisses, Mart. 11, 98, 1 sqq. (perh. not elsewhere).

basilea.full: Băsĭlēa (-īa), ae, f., the town Basel or Bāle, in Switzerland, Amm. 30, 3, 1.
basilea.short: Băsĭlēa (-īa), ae, f., the town Basel or Bāle, in Switzerland, Amm.

basilia1.full: Băsĭlīa, ōrum, n., = βασίλεια, τά (regal), the name of the books of Kings in the Bible, Tert. adv. Marc. 4, 14.
basilia1.short: Băsĭlīa, ōrum, n., = βασίλεια, τά (regal), the name of the books of Kings in the Bible, Tert.

basilia2.full: Băsĭlīa, ae, f., another name for the island Balcia, Plin. 4, 13, 27, § 95; 37, 2, 11, § 36.
basilia2.short: Băsĭlīa, ae, f., another name for the island Balcia, Plin.

basiliadae.full: Băsĭlĭădae (-lidae), ārum, m., a people of Sarmatia, Plin. 4, 12, 26, § 84; Mel. 2, 1, 4.
basiliadae.short: Băsĭlĭădae (-lidae), ārum, m., a people of Sarmatia, Plin.

basilice.full: băsĭlĭcē, adv., v. basilicus, I. A. fin.

basiliciarius.full: băsĭlĭcĭārĭus, μαλακός, ἀγοραιος, Gloss. Gr Lat.

basilicola.full: băsĭlĭcŏla, ae, f. dim. basilica, a small church, a little chapel, Paul. Nol. Ep. ad Sev 32, n. 17.

basilicus.full: băsĭlĭcus, a, um, adj., = βασιλικός, kingly, royal, princely, splendid, magnificent, = regalis (in this sense perh. only ante-class.). Adj. In gen.. basilicas edictiones atque imperiosas habet, Plaut. Capt. 4, 2, 31, id. Rud. 2, 4, 18: facinora, id. Trin. 4, 3, 23 victus, id. Pers. 1, 1, 32: status, id. Ps. 1, 5, 43.— Esp. Basilica vitis, a kind of vine among the Dyrrhachians, Plin. 14, 2, 4, § 30, Col. 3, 2, 19; 3, 2, 28; 3, 7, 1; 3, 9, 1; 3, 21, 3' uva, Isid. Orig. 17, 5, 22.— Basilica nux, Ma
basilicus.short: băsĭlĭcus, a, um, adj., = βασιλικός, kingly, royal, princely, splendid, magnificent, = regalis (in this sense perh.

basilis.full: Băsĭlis, is, m., a Greek geographer, Plin. 6, 29, 35, § 183.
basilis.short: Băsĭlis, is, m., a Greek geographer, Plin.

basilisca.full: băsĭlisca, ae, f., = βασιλίσκη, a plant, an antidote for the bite of the basilisk, also called regula, App. Herb. 128.
basilisca.short: băsĭlisca, ae, f., = βασιλίσκη, a plant, an antidote for the bite of the basilisk, also called regula, App.

basiliscus.full: băsĭliscus, i, m., = βασιλίσκος. A kind of lizard, a basilisk: Lacerta basiliscus, Linn.; Plin. 8, 21, 33, § 78 sq.; App. Herb. 128; Sol. 27, 50; Vulg. Psa. 90 (91), 13. —For the deriv. of the word from βασιλεύς (king), v. Luc. 9, 726.— A surname of Cn. Pompeius, Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 11, § 25.

basilium.full: băsĭlīum, ii, n. βασίλειον, a royal or princely ornament, Inscr. Orell. 2510; cf. Inscr. Maff. Mus. Veron. 293, 2.

basio.full: bāsĭo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. basium, to kiss, to give a kiss (poet. and rare; most freq. in Cat.; not in Plaut. or Ter.): basia multa basiare, Cat. 7, 9; 8, 18; 48, 1 sq.; Mart. 1, 94, 2; 7, 95, 7; 11, 98, 8; Petr. 18, 4; 135, 2.

basiolum.full: bāsĭŏlum, i, n. dim. id., a little kiss, Petr. 85 fin.; App. M. 10, p. 248, 35.

basis.full: băsis, is and ĕos (gen. basis, Vulg. 3 Reg. 7, 27; 7, 34: baseos, Vitr. 10, 15; acc. usu. basim, but BASEM, Inscr. Orell. 1263 al.: basidem, Ven. Fort. 8, 14; abl. usu. basi, but base, Treb. Pol. Gall. 18, 4; Inscr. Grut. 63, 3: BASIDE, ib. 16, 14; gen. plur. BASIVM, Inscr. Orell. 3272), f., = βάσις, a pedestal, foot, base. In gen.: in basi statuarum, Cic. Verr. 2, 2, 63, § 154; 2, 2, 66, § 160; 2, 4, 34, § 74; id. Phil. 9, 7, 16: quo (sc. ad sepulcrum) cum patefactus esset aditus, ad adversam b

basium.full: bāsĭum, ii, n. for sāvĭum, suavium; cf. Engl. buss; O. Germ. bus, a kiss. In gen. (rare and mostly poet.; most freq. in Cat.; not in Plaut. or Ter.): da mi basia mille, Cat. 5, 7; 5, 13; 7, 9; 16, 12; 99, 16; Mart. 2, 21, 1; 11, 98, 9; 12, 55, 9; 12, 59, 1; Petr. 21, 2, 110: impingere alicui, id. 21, 2, 31.— Esp., a kissing of the hand: jactat basia tibicen, throws kisses of the hand, Phaedr. 5, 8, 28; so Juv. 4, 117.

bassania.full: Bassānĭa, ae, f., a town in Illyria, now Elbassan, Liv. 44, 30, 7.—Hence, Bas-sānītae, ārum, m., the inhabitants of Bassania, Liv. 44, 30, 13 and 15.
bassania.short: Bassānĭa, ae, f., a town in Illyria, now Elbassan, Liv.

bassareus.full: Bassăreus, ei, m., = Βασσαρεύς [βασσάρα, a fox, fox-skin, as clothing of the Bacchantes], a title of Bacchus: candide Bassareu, * Hor C. 1, 18, 11; cf. Macr. S. 1, 18. — Derivv Bassărĭcus, a, um, adj., of Bacchus: comae, the hair of Bacchus, Prop. 3 (4), 17, 30. metrum, Mar. Vict. p. 2545 P.— Bassăris, ĭdis, f., = Βασσαρίς, a Bacchante, Pers. 1, 101 Schol.
bassareus.short: Bassăreus, ei, m., = Βασσαρεύς [βασσάρα, a fox, fox-skin, as clothing of the Bacchantes], a title of Bacchus: candide Bassareu, * Hor C.

bassus.full: Bassus, i, m., a family cognomen; e. g. A poet, a friend of Martial, Mart. 3, 76, 1 al.— Q. Caecilius Bassus, quœstor A. U. C. 695, Cic. Phil. 11, 13, 32; id. Att. 2, 9, 1; 14, 9, 3; id. Fam. 11, 1, 4; 12, 18, 1.— Lucilius Bassus, Cic. Att. 12, 5, 2.
bassus.short: Bassus, i, m., a family cognomen;

bastaga.full: bastăga or bastăgĭa, ae, f., = βασταγή [βαστάζω], a carriage of baggage (a carrying of freight upon wagons), Cod. Arcad. et Honor 12, 58, 3; Cod. Th. 8, 4, 11.
bastaga.short: bastăga or bastăgĭa, ae, f., = βασταγή [βαστάζω], a carriage of baggage (a carrying of freight upon wagons), Cod.

bastagarius.full: bastăgārĭus, ii, m. bastaga, a baggage-master, Cod. Th. 10, 20, 11; Cod. Valent. et Val. 11, 7, 4.

bastarnae.full: Bastarnae (also Basternae), ārum, m., = Βαστάρναι, a German tribe which became known to the Romans very early (in the war with Pyrrhus), whose abode extended from the sources of the Vistula to the Carpates, and from the Lower Danube to its mouth (Podolia, Galicia, Ukraine), Liv. 40, 5, 10; 40, 57, 2 sq.; 40, 58, 1 sq.; 41, 19, 4 sq.; 41, 23, 12; Plin. 4, 12, 25, § 81; Tac. A. 2, 65; id. G. 46.
bastarnae.short: Bastarnae (also Basternae), ārum, m., = Βαστάρναι, a German tribe which became known to the Romans very early (in the war with Pyrrhus), whose abode extended from the sources of the Vistula to the Carpates, and from the Lower Danube to its mouth (Pod

basterna.full: basterna, ae, f., a sedan chair or litter, enclosed on all sides, and carried by mules, Pall. 7, 2, 3; Lampr. Elag. 21; Amm. 14, 6, 16; Hier. Ep. 22 ad Eustoch. n. 16; cf. Isid. Orig. 20, 12, 5.
basterna.short: basterna, ae, f., a sedan chair or litter, enclosed on all sides, and carried by mules, Pall.

basternarius.full: basternārĭus, ii, m. basterna, a bearer of a sedan, Symm. Ep. 6, 15.

bastertini.full: Bastertīni, ōrum, m., a people of Lower Italy, Plin. 3, 11, 16, § 105.
bastertini.short: Bastertīni, ōrum, m., a people of Lower Italy, Plin.

bastetania.full: Bastētānĭa, ae, f., a district in Spain, Plin. 3, 1, 3, § 10.
bastetania.short: Bastētānĭa, ae, f., a district in Spain, Plin.

bastitani.full: Bastĭtāni, ōrum, m., the inhabitants of Basti in Spain, Plin. 3, 3, 4, § 25.
bastitani.short: Bastĭtāni, ōrum, m., the inhabitants of Basti in Spain, Plin.

bastuli.full: Bastŭli (Bascŭ-), ōrum, m., a people of Hispania Baetica, near the Strait of Gibraltar, Mel. 3, 1, 3.—Sing.: Bascŭlus, i, m., Varr. R. R. 1, 10, 4.
bastuli.short: Bastŭli (Bascŭ-), ōrum, m., a people of Hispania Baetica, near the Strait of Gibraltar, Mel.

bat1.full: băt, a comic word formed to parody the conj. at: Ps. Potin aliam rem ut cures? Cali. At. Ps. Bat. Cali. Crucior, Plaut. Ps. 1, 3, 6 Lorenz ad loc.; cf.: at enim... bat enim, id. Ep. 1, 1, 86 (95).
bat1.short: băt, a comic word formed to parody the conj.

bat2.full: băt, sonus ex ore cornicinis lituum eximentis, Charis. p. 213 P.
bat2.short: băt, sonus ex ore cornicinis lituum eximentis, Charis.

batalaria.full: bătălārĭa, ae, f., a kind of war-ship, Schol. Juv. 3, 134.
batalaria.short: bătălārĭa, ae, f., a kind of war-ship, Schol.

batavia.full: Bătāvĭa, ae, f., = Βαταούα Dio, Βαταβία Zosim, the peninsula Batavia, Holland, Pac. Pan. ad Theod. 5 (in class. per. called only Batavorum Insula, Caes. B. G. 4, 10; Plin. 4, 15, 29, § 101; Tac. A. 2, 6; id. H. 5, 23).
batavia.short: Bătāvĭa, ae, f., = Βαταούα Dio, Βαταβία Zosim, the peninsula Batavia, Holland, Pac.

batavodurum.full: Bătāvŏdūrum, i, n., a town in Holland. now Wyk by Duurstede, Tac. H. 5, 20.
batavodurum.short: Bătāvŏdūrum, i, n., a town in Holland.

batavus.full: Bătāvus, a, um, adj., pertaining to Batavia, Batavian, of Holland, Dutch: spuma, Mart. 8, 33, 20.—Hence, Batāvi, ōrum, m., = Βατάουοι, Ptol., the Batavians, Hollanders, Dutch, Tac. H. 4, 12; id. G. 29 al.: Batavorum Insula, v. Batavia.—With penult scanned short: Vangiones Bătăvīque truces, etc., Luc. 1, 431.—Sing.: Bătā-vus, i, m., one of the Batavi, Mart. 14, 176. —Collectively, Juv. 8, 51; Sil. 3, 608.
batavus.short: Bătāvus, a, um, adj., pertaining to Batavia, Batavian, of Holland, Dutch: spuma, Mart.

bateni.full: Bateni, ōrum, m., a people of Asia, on the Oxus, Plin. 6, 16, 18, § 48.
bateni.short: Bateni, ōrum, m., a people of Asia, on the Oxus, Plin.

batha.full: Batha, ae, f., a town in Ethiopia, Plin. 6, 29, 35, § 179.
batha.short: Batha, ae, f., a town in Ethiopia, Plin.

bathyllus.full: Băthyllus, i, m., = Βάθυλλος. A Samian boy, beloved by Anacreon, Hor. Epod. 14, 9; cf. Anacr. 22.— A celebrated pantomime of Alexandria, a favorite of Mœcenas, and rival of the equally celebrated Pylades, Tac. A. 1, 54 Gron.; Juv. 6, 63; Pers. 5, 123 Schol.; Sen. Q. N. 7, 32, 5; cf. Suid. s. v. ̓́Ορχησις, tom. ii. p. 720 Kust.

bathymi.full: Bathymi, ōrum, m., a people of Arabia, Plin. 6, 28, 32, § 149.
bathymi.short: Bathymi, ōrum, m., a people of Arabia, Plin.

bathynias.full: Bathynias, ae, m., a small river of Thrace, near Byzantium, Plin. 4, 11, 18, § 46.
bathynias.short: Bathynias, ae, m., a small river of Thrace, near Byzantium, Plin.

batia.full: bătĭa, ae, f., an unknown kind of fish, Plin. 32, 7, 25, § 77; 32, 11, 53, § 145.
batia.short: bătĭa, ae, f., an unknown kind of fish, Plin.

batiaca.full: bătĭăca, ae, f., a kind of drinking-cup: scaphiis, cantharis, Batiacis bibunt, Plaut. Stich. 5, 3, 11 Ritschl, Fleck. (al. batiolis).
batiaca.short: bătĭăca, ae, f., a kind of drinking-cup: scaphiis, cantharis, Batiacis bibunt, Plaut.

batillum.full: bătillum (in MSS. also vatillum), i, n. (batillus, i, m., Marc. Emp. 27). A shovel, a fire-shovel, coal-shovel, dirt or dungshovel, etc.: batilli ferrei, Plin. 33, 8, 44, § 127; 34, 11, 26, § 112; Treb. Pol. Claud. 14; Varr. R. R. 3, 6, 5.— A fire-pan, chafing-dish, fumigating-pan, incense-pan: prunae batillum, * Hor. S. 1, 5, 36 (Jahn, K. and H. vatillum).

batiola.full: bătĭŏla, ae, f., a small drinking-cup, a goblet: batiolis bibere, Plaut. Stich. 5, 4, 11 (Ritschl, batiacis): batiola aurea, id. Fragm. ap. Non. p. 545, 20.
batiola.short: bătĭŏla, ae, f., a small drinking-cup, a goblet: batiolis bibere, Plaut.

batis.full: bătis, ĭdis, f., = βατίς, a plant, seafennel, samphire: Crithmum maritimum, Linn.; Plin. 21, 15, 50, § 86; Col. 12, 7, 2; 12, 13, 2.
batis.short: bătis, ĭdis, f., = βατίς, a plant, seafennel, samphire: Crithmum maritimum, Linn.;

bato.full: Bato, ōnis, m., a leader of insurrection in Dalmatia, Ov. P. 2, 1, 46; cf.: maxima duobus Batonibus ducibus auctoritas erat, Vell. 2, 110, 4; 2, 114, 4.
bato.short: Bato, ōnis, m., a leader of insurrection in Dalmatia, Ov.

batrachion.full: bătrăchĭon, ii, n., = βατράχιον [βάτραχος = frog], a medicinal plant, also called ranunculus [rana = frog], Plin. 25, 13, 109, § 172; App. Herb. 8 and 9.
batrachion.short: bătrăchĭon, ii, n., = βατράχιον [βάτραχος = frog], a medicinal plant, also called ranunculus [rana = frog], Plin.

batrachites.full: bătrăchītes, ae, m., = βατραχίτης. a precious stone of a frog-green color, Plin. 37, 10, 55, § 149; ls id. Orig. 16, 4, 20.

batrachomyomachia.full: Bătrăchŏmўŏmăchĭa, ae, f., = Βατραχομυομαχια, The Battle of the Frogs and Mice, the title of a poem falsely attributed to Homer, Stat. S. praef.; Mart. 14, 183 lemm.
batrachomyomachia.short: Bătrăchŏmўŏmăchĭa, ae, f., = Βατραχομυομαχια, The Battle of the Frogs and Mice, the title of a poem falsely attributed to Homer, Stat.

batrachus1.full: bătrăchus, i, m., = βάτραχος, a fish, the sea-frog, Plin. 32, 11, 53, § 145.
batrachus1.short: bătrăchus, i, m., = βάτραχος, a fish, the sea-frog, Plin.

batrachus2.full: Bătrăchus, i, m., = Βάτραχος, a Greek architect at Rome in the time of Pompey the Great, Plin. 36, 5, 4, § 42.
batrachus2.short: Bătrăchus, i, m., = Βάτραχος, a Greek architect at Rome in the time of Pompey the Great, Plin.

battara.full: Battara, ae, m., a Roman whose death is mentioned by Cicero A. U. C. 700, Cic. Fam. 7, 9, 2.
battara.short: Battara, ae, m., a Roman whose death is mentioned by Cicero A.

battis.full: Battis, idis, f., = Βαττίς, the sweetheart of the poet Philetas of Cos, Ov. Tr. 1, 6, 2; id. P. 3, 1, 58 (Merkel, Bittis).
battis.short: Battis, idis, f., = Βαττίς, the sweetheart of the poet Philetas of Cos, Ov.

batton.full: Batton, ōnis, m., a Greek sculptor, Plin. 34, 8, 19, § 73.
batton.short: Batton, ōnis, m., a Greek sculptor, Plin.

battualia.full: battŭālĭa or battālia, ium, n. battuo, the fighting and fencing exercises of soldiers and gladiators: inde etiam battuatores τοὺς βασανιστὰς dici puto, Adamant. ap. Cassiod. p. 2300 P.

battuarium.full: battŭārĭum, ii, m., = κοπανιστήριον, a mortar, Gloss. Gr. Lat.
battuarium.short: battŭārĭum, ii, m., = κοπανιστήριον, a mortar, Gloss.

battuo.full: battuo (bāt-), ui, ĕre, v. a. and n. cf. Engl. beat, bat; Fr. battre; Ital. battere, to strike, beat, hit (very rare): battuit κατακόπτει, Gloss.; Naev. ap. Fulg. 562, 33; * Plaut. Cas. 2, 8, 60.—Of bruising in a mortar, Marc. Emp. Medic. c. 36.—Of pounding flesh before cooking it, Apic. 4, 2, 108; cf. Plin. 31, 9, 45, § 104.— Neutr., of fencing (like the Germ. schlagen): battuebat pugnatoriis armis, he fenced with sharp weapons (not with the foil), Suet. Calig. 54; 32.—In mal. part., Cic. Fam.

battus.full: Battus, i, m., = Βάττος. A name given to Aristotle of Thera, the founder of Cyrene, Sil. 8, 57; 17, 591; Just. 13, 7, 1.— Hence, Battĭădes, ae, m., an inhabitant of Cyrene, Sil. 2, 61; 3, 252; 17, 592; and, κατʼ ἐξοχήν, the poet Callimachus, a native of Cyrene, Cat. 65, 16; Ov. Tr. 2, 367; id. Ib. 55; id. Am. 1, 15, 13; Stat. S. 5, 3, 157.— A herdsman of Neleus, in Triphylia, near Elis, in the Peloponnesus, who, on account of his betraying a theft of Mercury, was transformed by him into the ston

batulum.full: Bătŭlum, i, n., a town in Campania, built by the Samnites, Verg. A. 7, 739 Serv.; Sil. 8, 566.
batulum.short: Bătŭlum, i, n., a town in Campania, built by the Samnites, Verg.

batus1.full: bătŭs (bătŏs), i, f., = βάτος, the blackberry-bush, App. Herb. 87; Paul. ex Fest. p. 30, 15 Müll.; esp., batos Idaea = βάτος?̓Ιδαία, the raspberry-bush, App. Herb. 87.
batus1.short: bătŭs (bătŏs), i, f., = βάτος, the blackberry-bush, App.

batus2.full: bătŭs, i, m., = βάτος; Heb. , a bath, a Hebrew measure for liquids, containing about nine gallons (eccl. Lat.), Vulg. Ezech. 45, 10 al.

baubor.full: baubor, āri, v. dep. cf. Gr. βαιΐζω; of dogs, to bark gently or moderately (cf. latrare, to bark angrily): et quom desertei baubantur in aedibus. Lucr. 5, 1071; v. the context, and Munro ad loc.

baucidias.full: Baucidiăs, ădis, f., a small island in the Gulf of Argolis, Plin. 4, 12, 19, § 56.
baucidias.short: Baucidiăs, ădis, f., a small island in the Gulf of Argolis, Plin.

baucis.full: Baucis, ĭdis, f., = Βαῦκις. The wife of Philemon, in Phrygia. She, with her husband, entertained, in a very hospitable manner, Jupiter and Mercury, who came to them in the form of men; in return for which they were changed to two sacred trees before their hut, which became a temple, Ov. M. 8, 631 sq.— Meton., an old woman, Pers. 4, 21.

baudos.full: Baudŏs, i, m., a river in Syria, Mel. 1, 12, 5.
baudos.short: Baudŏs, i, m., a river in Syria, Mel.

bauli.full: Bauli, ōrum, m., = Βαῦλοι [acc. to the fable, from βοῦς and αὐλή, since here Hercules shut up the cattle taken from Geryon; v. Serv. ad Verg. A. 6, 107; 7, 662; Symm. Ep. 1, 1, both of whom understand the original form as Boaulia], a place near Baiœ, now Bacolo, Varr. R. R. 3, 17, 5; Cic. Ac. 2, 40, 125; 2, 3, 9; id. Fam. 8, 1, 4; Plin. 3, 5, 9, § 61; 9, 55, 81, § 172; Tac. A. 14, 4; Suet. Ner. 34; Mart. 4, 63.

bauma.full: Bauma, ae, f., a town in Ethiopia, Plin 6, 29, 35, § 179.
bauma.short: Bauma, ae, f., a town in Ethiopia, Plin 6, 29, 35, § 179.

bavius.full: Băvĭus, ii, m., a stupid poet, an enemy of Virgil and Horace: qui Bavium non odit, amet tua carmina, Maevi, Verg. E. 3, 90 (pro poenā ei contingat, ut diligat Maevium pejorem poëtam. Nam Maevius et Bavius pessimi fuerunt poëtae, inimici tam Horatio quam Vergilio, Serv.; cf. id. ad Verg. G. 1, 210, where is found the attack of Bavius upon Verg. for using hordeum in the plur.; cf. also Philargyr. Verg. E. l. l., and Weich. Poët. Lat. Rel. p. 308 sq.).
bavius.short: Băvĭus, ii, m., a stupid poet, an enemy of Virgil and Horace: qui Bavium non odit, amet tua carmina, Maevi, Verg.

baxea.full: baxĕa and baxa, ae, f. πάξ?͂ ὑπόδημα εὐυπόδητον, Hesych., a kind of woven shoe worn on the comic stage and by philosophers (only ante- and post-class. and rare), Plaut. Men. 2, 3, 40; App. M. 2, p. 127, 6; 11, p. 260, 39; Flor. n. 9.—In sing., Tert. Idol. 8; Pall. 4; cf. Isid. Orig. 19, 34, 6 and 13.

baxearius.full: baxĕārĭus (baxĭ-), i, m. baxea, a maker of woven shoes: FABER SOLIARIVS BAXIARIVS, Inscr. Orell. 4085.

bazaira.full: Bazăīra, ae, f., a district of Asiatic Scythia, Curt. 8, 1, 10.
bazaira.short: Bazăīra, ae, f., a district of Asiatic Scythia, Curt.

bdellium.full: bdellĭum, ii, n. (bĕdella, ae, f., Marc. Emp. 19; cf. the letter B), = βδέλλιον, an Asiatic plant, distinguished for its fragrant gum, the vine-palm: Borassus flabelliformis, Linn.; Plin. 12, 9, 19, § 35; Isid. Orig. 17, 8, 6.— Meton., the costly gum exuding from it: Arabicum, Veg. 6, 14, 1 and 5: color bdellii, Vulg. Num. 11, 7.—Hence, as a term of endearment: tu crocinum et casia es, tu bdellium, Plaut. Curc. 1, 2, 7.

beate.full: bĕātē, adv., v. beatus fin. under beo.

beatifico.full: bĕātĭfĭco, āre, v. a. beatus-facio, to make happy, to bless (post-class.), Aug. Trin. 14, 14; Vulg. Isa. 9, 16; id. Jacob. 5, 11.

beatificus.full: bĕātĭfĭcus, a, um, adj. id., blessing, making happy (post-class.), App. Doct. Plat. 1, p. 3, 29; Aug. Conf. 2, 5.

beatitas.full: bĕātĭtas, ātis, f. beatus, the condition of the beatus, happiness, a blessed condition, blessedness, = beata vita, felicitas; a word first used by Cic.: aut ista sive beatitas, sive beatitudo dicenda sunt (utrumque omnino durum, sed usu mollienda nobis verba sunt), Cic. N. D. 1, 34, 95 (but he seems to have used neither of the two words again): apud Ciceronem beatitas et beatitudo, Quint. 8, 3, 32; so Macr. Somn. Scip. 1, 9; App. Doct. Plat. 2.—Plur., Aug. Civ. Dei, 21, 17.

beatitudo.full: bĕātĭtūdo, ĭnis, f. id., the condition of beatus, happiness, felicity, blessedness, beatitude; a word coined by Cic.; cf. beatitas, and pass. there cited. In the post-Aug. per. several times: animi, Petr. 8, 5: vitae, App. M. 6; Mamert. Grat. Act. ad Julian. 23 al.; Cod. 12, 47, 1; Vulg. Gen. 30, 13; id. Gal. 4, 15.

beatulus.full: bĕātŭlus, a, um, adj. dim. [id.], as subst., the sainted fellow (iron.), Pers. 3, 103.

beatum.full: bĕātum, i, n., v. beo, P. a. A. 3. β.

beatus.full: bĕātus, a, um, v. beo, P. a.

beber.full: bĕber, bri. m., the beaver (late Lat. for fiber), Schol. Juv. 12, 34.—Hence, bē^brī-nus, a, um, adj., of the beaver, beaver-, Schol. Juv. 2, 106.

bebra.full: bebra, ae, f., a weapon of barbarous nations, acc. to Veg. Mil. 1, 20.
bebra.short: bebra, ae, f., a weapon of barbarous nations, acc.

bebrinus.full: bebrīnus, a, um, adj. beber = fiber, a beaver, of or pertaining to a beaver: pelles, Schol. Juv. 12, 34.

bebryces1.full: Bēbrȳ^ces, cum (acc. -cas, Val. Fl. 4, 315), m., = Βέβρῦκες, a people inhabiting Bebrycia, a province of Asia Minor, afterwards called Bithynia, Plin. 5, 30, 33, § 127; Val. Fl. 4, 315.— Derivv. Bē-brȳ^cĭa, ae, f., = Βεβρυκία, the province inhabited by the Bebrycians, afterwards Bithynia, Sall. H. Fragm. ap. Serv. Verg. A. 5, 373; Val. Fl. 5, 502; y long in Avien. Perieg. 974.— Bēbryx, ȳ^cis, m., a Bebrycian, Val. Fl. 4, 315; and, κατʼ ἐξοχήν, an ancient king in Bebrycia, also called Amycus, who

bebryces2.full: Bēbrȳces, cum, m., = Βέβρῦκες [perh. of kindred origin with the preced.], a people in Gallia Narbonensis, on the Pyrenees, Sil. 3, 423 sq.— Derivv. Bēbryx, ȳcis, m., a Bebrycian; κατʼ ἐξοχήν, an ancient king of the Bebrycians, whose daughter Pyrene gave name to the mountains there, Sil. 3, 423.— Bēbrycĭus, a, um, adj., pertaining to King Bebryx, Bebrycian: aula, Sil. 3, 443: virgo, i. e. Pyrene, id. 3, 420.

beccus.full: beccus, i, m. Gallic; cf. Fr. bec; Engl. beak, a beak, bill, esp. of a cock; as a cognomen of Antonius Primus, Suet. Vit. 18.

bechicus.full: bēchĭcus, a, um, adj., = βηχικός, of or for a cough (pure Lat. tussicularis): medicamen, Cael. Aur. Acut. 1, 17, 172.
bechicus.short: bēchĭcus, a, um, adj., = βηχικός, of or for a cough (pure Lat.

bechion.full: bēchĭon, ii, n., = βήχιον, a plant good for a cough, colt'sfoot: Tussilago farfara, Linn.; Plin. 26, 6, 16, § 30.
bechion.short: bēchĭon, ii, n., = βήχιον, a plant good for a cough, colt'sfoot: Tussilago farfara, Linn.;

bechires.full: Bĕchīres, um (Bĕchīri, ōrum, Avien. Descr. Orb. 945; Bĕchēri, Mel. 1, 19, 11), m., = Βέχειρες, a Scythian people on the Pontus Euxinus; perh. kindr. with the modern Bashkirs, Plin. 6, 4, 3, § 11.

bedesis.full: Bedĕsis, is, m., a river in Gallia Cispadana, now Bedese, Plin. 3, 15, 20, § 115.
bedesis.short: Bedĕsis, is, m., a river in Gallia Cispadana, now Bedese, Plin.

bedriacum.full: Bēdrĭăcum (also Bēbrĭăcum and Bētrĭăcum), i, n., = Βητρίακον, a village in Upper Italy, between Verona and Cremona, distinguished in the civil war by two important battles between Otho, Vitellius, and the generals of Vespasian, now Cividale; form Bedriacum, Tac. H. 2, 23, 39 sq.; 2, 23, 44; 2, 23, 49; 2, 3, 15; 2, 3, 20; 2, 3, 31.—Form Bebriacum, Juv. 2, 106; Oros. 7, 8.—Form Betriacum, Suet. Oth. 9; Aur. Vict. Epit. 7, 2; Eutr. 7, 17.—Hence, Bēdrĭăcensis (Bētrĭ-), e, adj., of Bedriacum: campi,
bedriacum.short: Bēdrĭăcum (also Bēbrĭăcum and Bētrĭăcum), i, n., = Βητρίακον, a village in Upper Italy, between Verona and Cremona, distinguished in the civil war by two important battles between Otho, Vitellius, and the generals of Vespasian, now Cividale;

bee.full: bee, the sound made by a sheep, Varr. R. R. 2, 1, 7; cf. balo.
bee.short: bee, the sound made by a sheep, Varr.

beelzebub.full: Beelzĕbŭb, indecl., or Beelzĕbŭl, ūlis, m., = Βεελζεβούβ or Βεελζεβούλ, Heb. or ; in eccl. Lat. Beelzebub, the chief of evil spirits, Vulg. Luc. 11, 15; Tert. adv. Marc. 4, 26; Prud. στεφ. 2, 267.
beelzebub.short: Beelzĕbŭb, indecl., or Beelzĕbŭl, ūlis, m., = Βεελζεβούβ or Βεελζεβούλ, Heb.

begorrites.full: Begorrītes lăcus, a lake in Macedonia, now Lake of Kitrine, Liv. 42, 53, 5.
begorrites.short: Begorrītes lăcus, a lake in Macedonia, now Lake of Kitrine, Liv.

belbus.full: belbus, i, m., = hyaena, Capitol. Gord. III. 33, 1.

belenus.full: Belenus, i, m., a deity worshipped in Noricum and Aquileia, Tert. Apol. 24; id. adv. Nat. 2, 8; Capitol. Max. 22, 2; Inscr. Orell. 823; 1967.
belenus.short: Belenus, i, m., a deity worshipped in Noricum and Aquileia, Tert.

belgae.full: Belgae, ārum, m., = Βέλγαι [Balge, in Lower Germany, a low, swampy region], the Belgians, a warlike people, of German and Celtic origin, in the north of Gaul, Caes. B. G. 1, 1; 2, 4; Mel. 3, 2, 4; Tac. A. 1, 43; 3, 40; id. H. 4, 17; 4, 76 al.—In sing.: Bel-ga, ae, m., a Belgian, Luc. 1, 426; Claud. Laud. Stil. 1, 226.— Deriv.: Belgĭ-cus, a, um, adj., Belgic: esseda, Verg. G. 3, 204: color, Prop. 2 (3), 18, 26. calami, Plin. 16, 36, 65, § 161: canis, Sil. 10, 80.—Hence, Gallia Belgica, or absol.
belgae.short: Belgae, ārum, m., = Βέλγαι [Balge, in Lower Germany, a low, swampy region], the Belgians, a warlike people, of German and Celtic origin, in the north of Gaul, Caes.

belgium.full: Belgĭum. ii, n., a part of Gallia Belgica, on both sides of the Somme, including the Belloraci, Atrebates, and Ambiani, Caes. B. G. 5, 12; 5, 24; 5, 25; 8, 46.

belial.full: Belĭal, indecl. (Belĭas, ae, m.), = Heb. , Belial, a chief of the evil spirits, Prud. Psych. 714; Tert. Cult. Fem. 1, 2; Vulg. Deut. 13, 13; id. 2 Cor. 6, 15.

belion.full: belĭon, ii, n., a plant, the same as po lion, q. v., App. Herb. 58.
belion.short: belĭon, ii, n., a plant, the same as po lion, q.

bellaria.full: bellārĭa, ōrum, n., that which is used as a dessert, fruit, nuts, confectionery, sweet wine, etc.; the dessert, τράγημα, Fr. dragée [from bellus, like bellissimum, Ter. Ad. 4, 2, 51 Don., and pulchralia, Fest. p. 210], Gell. 13, 11, 7; Plaut. Truc. 2, 5, 27; Suet. Ner. 27.!*? Here the corrupted passage ap. Paul. ex Fest. p. 35 Müll. seems to belong: bellarium et bellaria res aptas bellis (epulis? acc. to Scal., or belle? Cod. Ber. and Lips. have belli) appellabant.
bellaria.short: bellārĭa, ōrum, n., that which is used as a dessert, fruit, nuts, confectionery, sweet wine, etc.;

bellator.full: bellātor, ōris (ancient form duellā-tor, Plaut. Capt. prol. 68; cf. the letter B), m. bello. A warrior, soldier (as capable of fighting, while miles signifies a soldier by profession; class.): domi bellique duellatores optimi, Plaut. Capt. prol. 68: si tu ad legionem bellator clues, at ego in culinā Ares, id. Truc. 2, 7, 54; id. Mil. 4, 2, 85; id. Trin. 3, 2, 97; id. Curc. 4, 3, 21; id. Bacch. 4, 9, 3; id. Ep. 3, 4, 56; id. Truc. 2, 7, 68; Cic. Balb. 23, 54: quis est, qui aut bellatori, aut impe

bellatorius.full: bellātōrĭus, a, um, adj. bellator, warlike, martial, useful in warlike expeditions (very rare): jumenta, Amm. 23, 5, 13: pugnax et quasi bellatorius stilus, a pugnacious, polemic style, * Plin. Ep. 7, 9, 7.

bellatrix.full: bellātrix, īcis, f. id., a female warrior; freq. in close apposition, and taking the place of an adj. (cf. bellator, II.), warlike, skilled in war, serviceable in war (mostly poet.). Lit.: Penthesilea, Verg. A. 1, 493: diva, i. e. Pallas, Ov. Tr. 1, 5, 76: Minerva, id. M. 8, 264: Roma, id. Tr. 2, 321: Hispania, Flor. 2, 6, 38: cohors, Stat. Th. 6, 262: belua, i. e. the elephant, Sil. 9, 576.— Transf., of inanim. things: carinae, Stat. Th. 7, 57: glaeba, i. e. producing warriors, Val. Fl. 7, 612:

bellatulus.full: bellātŭlus, a, um, adj. dim. [bellus] (instead of bellulus for the alliteration), pretty, neat: Bella bellatula, Plaut. Cas. 4, 4, 28.

bellax.full: bellax, ācis, adj. bello, warlike, martial: gens, Luc. 4, 406; cf. Prisc. p. 1263 P.

bellerophon.full: Bellĕrŏphōn, ontis (Bellĕrŏ-phontes, ae, Aus. Ep. 25 fin.; Serv. ad Verg. A. 5, 118; 6, 288), m., = Βελλεροφῶν, Theocr. (regularly formed Βελλεροφόντης), son of Glaucus and grandson of Sisyphus; he was sent by Prœtus, at the calumnious instigation of his wife Sthenebœa, with a letter to Iobates, in which the latter was requested to put him to death; he received from him the commission to slay the Chimæra, which he executed, riding upon the flying Pegasus, Cic. Tusc. 3, 26, 63; Hor. C. 3, 7, 15;

bellicosus.full: bellĭcōsus (duellĭc-), a, um, adj. bellicus, warlike, martial, valorous (mostly poet.; usu. of personal subjects; cf. bellicus): gentes immanes et barbarae et bellicosae, Cic. Prov. Cons. 13, 33: bellicosissimae nationes, id. Imp. Pomp. 10, 28; id. Fam. 5, 11, 3; Caes. B. G. 1, 10; 4, 1; Sall. J. 18, 12; Nep. Ham. 4, 1; Hor. C. 2. 11, 1; 3, 3, 57: provincia, Caes. B. C. 1, 85; Quint. 1, 10, 20: civitas, Suet. Gram. 1: fortissimus quisque ac bellicosissimus, Tac. G. 15. —Comp., Liv. 37, 8, 4.—Tro

bellicrepa.full: bellĭcrĕpa saltātio, an armed dance, a dancing in arms, Paul. ex Fest. p. 35 Müll. (Gr. ἐνόπλιος ὄρχησις); cf. Enn. Ann. v. 105 Vahl.
bellicrepa.short: bellĭcrĕpa saltātio, an armed dance, a dancing in arms, Paul.

bellicus.full: bellĭcus (duellĭcus), a, um, adj. bellum, of or pertaining to war, war-, military. In gen. Lit.: ars duellica, Plaut. Ep. 3, 4, 14: bellicam rem administrari majores nostri nisi auspicato noluerunt, Cic. Div. 2, 36, 76; Hor. C. 4, 3, 6; Suet. Calig. 43: disciplina, Cic. N. D. 2, 64, 161: jus, id. Off. 3, 29, 107: virtus, id. Mur. 10, 22: laus, military glory, id. Brut. 21, 84; Caes. B. G. 6, 24: laudes, Cic. Off. 1, 22, 78: gloria, Tac. A. 1, 52: caerimoniae, Liv. 1, 32, 5: certamina, Flor. 4, 1

bellienus.full: Bellĭēnus, i, m., a Roman cognomen. C. Annius Bellienus, a lieutenant of Fonteius, Cic. Font. 8, 18 (4, 8).— L. Bellienus, a friend of Pompey, Cic. Fam. 8, 15, 2: 16, 22, 2.— C. Bellienus, an advocate, Cic. Brut. 47, 175.
bellienus.short: Bellĭēnus, i, m., a Roman cognomen.

bellifer.full: bellĭfer, ĕra, ĕrum, adj. bellum-fero, making war, warlike: Italia, Claud. Eutr, 1, 429.

belliger.full: bellĭger, ĕra, ĕrum, adj. bellum-gero, waging war, warlike, martial, valiant (poet.; esp. freq. in the post-Aug. per.): gentes, Ov. Tr. 3, 11, 13: viri, Sil. 3, 124: Augustus, Claud. in Prob. et Olybr Cons. 74: Hannibal, Sil. 1, 38: numen, i.e. Mars, Stat. Achill. 1, 504: fera, i.e. the elephant used in war, Sil. 8, 261.— Of inanim things: manus, Ov A. A. 2, 672 ensis, id. M 3, 534: hasta, Mart. 5, 25: acies, Stat. Th. 12, 717: tropaea, id. ib. 10, 28: mens, Sil 3, 162: currus, id. 1, 434: axis,

belligerator.full: bellĭgĕrātor, ōris, m. belligero, a warrior, combatant (post-class. and rare): Arimaspae, Avien. Perieg. 55; Ven. Vit. Mart. 3, 370; Vulg. 1 Macc. 15, 13; 16, 4.

belligero.full: bellĭgĕro, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. (bellĭ-gĕror, āri, v. dep., Hyg. Fab. 274 fin.) [bellum-gero], to wage or carry on war, to fight (very rare): nec cauponantes bellum, sed belligerantes, Enn. ap. Cic. Off. 1, 12, 38 (Ann. v. 201 Vahl.); Poët. ap. Quint. 9, 4, 39: postquam belligerant Aetoli cum Aliis, Plaut. Capt. prol. 24; id. Truc. 2, 7, 67: excitandus nobis erit ab inferis quoniam nobis non solum cum his... sed etiam cum fortunā belligerandum fuit, * Cic. Red. Quir. 8, 19 (but ap. Cic. Font. 16,

bellio.full: bellĭo, ōnis, f., the yellow ox-eye daisy: Chrysanthemum segetum, Linn.; Plin. 21, 8, 25, § 49.
bellio.short: bellĭo, ōnis, f., the yellow ox-eye daisy: Chrysanthemum segetum, Linn.;

bellipotens.full: bellĭpŏtens, entis, adj. bellum - potens, mighty or valiant in war (poet. and rare): bellipotentes sunt magis quam sapientipotentes, Enn. ap. Cic. Div. 2, 56, 116 (Ann. v. 188 Vahl.).—Subst.: Bellipotens, i. e. Mars, Verg. A. 11, 8: diva, i. e. Pallas, Stat. Th. 2, 715; so Val. Fl. 1, 529; Claud. III. Cons. Hon. 144; id. Laus Seren. 40; Tert. cont. Jud. 9; Firm. p. 27.

bellis.full: bellis, ĭdis, f., the white daisy, ox-eye: Bellis perennis, Linn.; Plin. 26, 5, 13, § 26; App. Herb. 57.
bellis.short: bellis, ĭdis, f., the white daisy, ox-eye: Bellis perennis, Linn.;

bellisonus.full: bellĭsŏnus, a, um, adj. bellum-sono, sounding of war: flumen, Paul. Nol. Natal. S. Fel. 8, 23 fin.

bellitudo.full: bellĭtūdo, ĭnis, f. bellus, beauty, loveliness, Paul. ex Fest. p. 35 Müll.

bellius.full: Bellĭus, i, m., a shortened form of the name Duellius, Cic. Or. 45, 153; Quint. 1, 4, 15.
bellius.short: Bellĭus, i, m., a shortened form of the name Duellius, Cic.

bello.full: bello, āvi, ātum, āre, 1, v. n. bellum. Prop., to wage or carry on war, to war, to fight in war (class.; cf.: milito, proelior). Absol.: fuit proprium populi Romani longe a domo bellare, Cic. Imp. Pomp. 12, 32; 13, 36; id. Mur. 14, 32: homines bellandi cupidi, Caes. B. G. 1, 2; Nep. Ham. 3, 1; id. Hann. 2, 1: Romana arma primum Claudio principo in Mauretaniā bellavere, Plin. 5, 1, 1, § 11: verens, ne bellare perseveraret, Nep. Them. 5, 1: neque prius bellare destitit, quam, etc., id. Epam. 8, 5;

bellocassi.full: Bellocassi, ōrum (also Velocasses, ium, Caes. B. G 2, 4, and Velliocasses, Hirt. B. G. 8, 7), m., a people on the right bank of the Seine, from the mouth of the Oise to the town Le Pont de l'Arche, Caes. B. G. 7, 75

bellona.full: Bellōna (old form Duellōna; cf. Varr. L. L. 7, § 49 Müll., and the letter B), ae. f. Bellona a bello nunc, quae Duellona a duello, Varr. L. L. 5, § 73 Müll.: Ἐνυώ, Ἐριννύς, θεὰ πολεμική, Gloss., the goddess of war, sister of Mars, whose temple, built by Appius Claudius Cœcus (Inscr. Orell. 539). in the ninth district of the city, was situated not far from the Circus Maximus, Publ. Vict. Descr. Urb.—A place of assemblage for the Senate for proceedings with persons who were not allowed entrance in

bellonaria.full: bellōnārĭa, ae, f., the plant solanum, used by the priests at the festival of Bellona (v. Bellona), App. Herb. 74.
bellonaria.short: bellōnārĭa, ae, f., the plant solanum, used by the priests at the festival of Bellona (v.

bellor.full: bellor, āri, 1, dep. (collat. form of bello), to carry on war, to war, to fight (poet.): et pictis bellantur Amazones armis, Verg. A. 11, 660: et nudis bellantur equis, Sil. 2, 349; cf. Non. p. 472, 9; Prisc. 8, 4, 24, p. 796 P.

bellosus.full: bellōsus, a, um, adj. bellum, warlike: genus, Caecil. ap. Non. p. 80, 33.

bellovaci.full: Bellŏvăci, ōrum, m., = Βελλοάκοι, Strab.; Βελλούακοι, Ptol., a people in Gallia Belgica, in the modern Beauvais, Caes. B. G. 2, 4; 2, 13; 7, 59; 7, 75; Hirt. B. G. 8, 7; 8, 14; Plin. 4, 17, 31, § 106.

bellulus.full: bellŭlus, a, um, adj. dim. [bellus], pretty, fine, lovely, beautiful (ante- and post-class.); edepol haec quidem bellula est, Plaut. Mil. 4, 1, 43; id. Cas. 4, 4, 22; id. Poen. 1, 2, 134; Inscr. Murat. 1514, 3.— Adv.: bellŭlē, prettily, finely, etc., Plaut. ap. Paul. ex Fest. p. 36 Müll.; App. M. 10, p. 246, 23; 11, p. 272, 34.

bellum.full: bellum (ante-class. and poet. duel-lum), i, n. Sanscr. dva, dvi, dus; cf. Germ. zwei; Engl. two, twice; for the change from initial du- to b-, cf. bis for duis, and v. the letter B, and Varr. L. L. 5, § 73 Müll.; 7, § 49 ib., war. Form duellum: duellum, bellum, videlicet quod duabus partibus de victoriā contendentibus dimicatur. Inde est perduellis, qui pertinaciter retinet bellum, Paul. ex Fest. p. 66, 17 Müll.: bellum antea duellum vocatum eo quod duae sunt dimicantium partes ... Postea mutatā

bellus.full: bellus, a, um, adj. as if for benulus, from benus = bonus, Prisc. p. 556 P.. In gen. Of persons, pretty, handsome, charming, fine, lovely, neat, pleasant, agreeable, etc. (of persons, things, actions, etc.; most freq. in the ante-class. per. and in the poets; in Cic. mostly in his epistt.): uxor, Varr. ap. Non. p. 248, 17: nimis bella es atque amabilis, Plaut. As. 3, 3, 84; id. Rud. 2, 5, 6; Cat. 8, 16; 43, 6: puella, id. 69, 8; 78, 4; Ov. Am. 1, 9, 6; Mart. 1, 65; 2, 87: Piliae et puellae Caeci

beloacos.full: bĕlŏăcŏs or bĕlŏtŏcŏs, a plant, also called dictamnus, App. Herb. 62.
beloacos.short: bĕlŏăcŏs or bĕlŏtŏcŏs, a plant, also called dictamnus, App.

belone.full: bĕlŏnē, ēs, f., = βελόνη, a sea-fish, also called acus, hornpike, garfish, Plin. 9, 51, 76, § 166.
belone.short: bĕlŏnē, ēs, f., = βελόνη, a sea-fish, also called acus, hornpike, garfish, Plin.

belua.full: bēlŭa (not bellŭa), ae, f. (belua, dissyl., Varr. ap. Non. p. 201, 26) [perh. kindr. with θήρ, fera, as uber with οὖθαρ, and paulus with παῦρος], a beast distinguished for size or ferocity, a monster (as an elephant, lion, wild boar, whale, etc.; cf.: bestia, fera): elephanto beluarum nulla prudentior, Cic. N. D. 1, 35, 97; id. Fam. 7, 1, 3; Curt. 8, 9, 29: ea genera beluarum, quae in Rubro Mari Indiāve gignantur, Cic. N. D. 1, 35, 97: singulas stellas numeras deos, eosque beluarum nomine appell

belualis.full: bēlŭālis (bell-), e, adj. belua, bestial, brutish: educatio, Macr. S. 5, 11, 15.

beluatus.full: bēlŭātus (bell-), a, um, adj. id., ornamented or embroidered with figures of animals: tapetia, Plaut. Ps. 1, 2, 14.

beluilis.full: bēlŭīlis (bell-), e, adj. id., bestial, brutal (post-class.): beluile θηριῶδες, Gloss. Philox.: beluile saevientes, Jul. Val. Rer. Gest. Alex. M. 3, 88; 3, 55.

beluinus.full: bēlŭīnus (bell-), a, um, adj. id., brutal, bestial, animal (post-class.): voluptates, Gell. 19, 2, 2: fauces, Prud. Cath. 7, 114: pars corporis, Jul. Val. Rer. Gest. Alex. 3, 54.

belunum.full: Bēlūnum, i, n., the capital city of a people of Venetia, now Belluno, Plin. 3, 19, 23, § 110; Inscr. Orell. 69; 3549.
belunum.short: Bēlūnum, i, n., the capital city of a people of Venetia, now Belluno, Plin.

beluosus.full: bēlŭōsus (bell-), a, um, adj. id., abounding in beasts or monsters: Oceanus, * Hor. C. 4, 14, 47; so Avien. Ora Marit. 204.

belus.full: Bēlus, i, m., = Βῆλος; Heb. . An Asiatic king of a primitive age, builder of Babylon and founder of the Babylonian kingdom, Verg. A. 1, 621; 1, 729 sq.: priscus, Ov. M. 4, 213 (like Βῆλος ὁ ἀρχαῖος, Aelian. V. H. 13, 3).— An Indian deity, compared with Hercules of the Greeks, Cic. N. D. 3, 16, 42; cf. Robinson, Dict., under .— A king of Egypt, father of Danaus and Ægyptus.— Derivv. Bēlīdes, ae (for the length of the i, cf. Prisc. p. 584 P.), m., = Βηλίδης, a male descendant of Belus: Belidae fra

belutus.full: bēlūtus (bell-), a, um: bestiae similis, Paul. ex Fest. p. 34 Müll.
belutus.short: bēlūtus (bell-), a, um: bestiae similis, Paul.

beluus.full: bēlŭus (bell-), a, um, = beluinus, Gloss. Isid.

bembinadia.full: Bembinadĭa, ae, f., a district in Arcadia, Plin. 4, 6, 10, § 21.
bembinadia.short: Bembinadĭa, ae, f., a district in Arcadia, Plin.

benacus.full: Bēnācus, i, m., = Βήϝακος, Strabo: lacus, a deep and rough lake in Gallia Transpadana, near Verona, through which the Mincius (Mincio) flows, now Lago di Garda, Plin. 2, 103, 106, § 224; 9, 22, 38, § 75; and absol. Benacus, Verg. G. 2, 160; id. A. 10, 205.— Hence, Bēnācenses, ium, m., the people dwelling near Lake Benacus, Inscr. Grut. 260, 2.
benacus.short: Bēnācus, i, m., = Βήϝακος, Strabo: lacus, a deep and rough lake in Gallia Transpadana, near Verona, through which the Mincius (Mincio) flows, now Lago di Garda, Plin.

bendidius.full: Bendĭdīus, a, um, adj., = Βενδίδειος, of or pertaining to Bendis (Βένδις, the Thracian Diana or goddess of the moon): templum, Liv. 38, 41, 1.
bendidius.short: Bendĭdīus, a, um, adj., = Βενδίδειος, of or pertaining to Bendis (Βένδις, the Thracian Diana or goddess of the moon): templum, Liv.

bene.full: bĕnĕ, adv. of manner and intensity [bonus; the first vowel assimilated to the e of the foll. syllable; cf. Corss. Ausspr. 2, 366], well (comp. melius, better; sup. optime [v. bonus init.], best; often to be rendered by more specific Engl. adverbs). As adjunct of verbs. In gen. Of physical or external goodness, usefulness, ornament, and comfort: villam rusticam bene aedificatam habere expedit, Cato, R. R. 3: villam bonam beneque aedificatam, Cic. Off. 3, 13, 55: quid est agrum bene colere? Bene a

benedice.full: bĕnĕdĭcē, adv. of the adj., not in use, bĕnĕdĭcus, a, um benedico, with friendly words, kindly: ad se illicere blande ac benedice, Plaut. As. 1, 3, 54.

benedico.full: bĕnĕdīco, xi, ctum, ĕre, v. n. and a., to speak well of any one, to commend, praise. In gen., in class. Lat. always as two words, v. bene, I. B. 1.— Esp. In late and eccl. Lat. with acc. Deum, to bless, praise, or adore (Heb. ), App. Trism. fin.; Vulg. Psa. 112, 2.—Pass.: benedici Deum omni tempore condecet, Tert. Orat. 3: Deus benedicendus, App. Trism. fin.; Vulg. Gen. 24, 48; id. Jacob. 3, 9.— Rarely with dat.: benedic Domino, Vulg. Psa. 102, 1 sq.— Of men and things, to bless, consecrate, hal

benedictio.full: bĕnĕdictĭo, ōnis, f. benedico, II. (eccl. Lat.), an extolling, praising, lauding, App. Trism. p. 82, 11; Vulg. Deut. 16, 10; Tert. Test. Anim. 2.— Meton., a consecrated, sacred object: benedictio crucis = frustum sanctae crucis, Paul. Nol. Ep. 32, c. 8.— A benediction, blessing, Sulp. de Vita S. Martini, 2, 12; Vulg. Gen. 26, 29; id. Gal. 3, 14.

benedictum.full: bĕnĕdictum, v. bene, I. B. 1. g.

benefacio.full: bĕnĕfăcĭo, fēci, factum, 3, v. n., better written as two words, v. bene, I. B. 2.

benefactio.full: bĕnĕfactĭo, ōnis, f. benefacio, the performing of an act of kindness, a benefaction, Tert. c. Marc. 4, 12 fin.

benefactor.full: bĕnĕfactor, ōris, m. id., he who confers a favor, a benefaclor (late Lat.), Coripp. Laud. Anast. Quaest. 19; id. Laud. Just. 1, 314.

beneficentia.full: bĕnĕfĭcentĭa, ae, f. from beneficus, like magnificentia, munificentia, from magnificus, munificus; cf. Beier and Gernh. upon Cic. Off. 1, 7, 20, the quality of beneficus, kindness, beneficence, an honorable and kind treatment of others (opp. maleficentia, Lact. Ira Dei, 1, 1; several times in the philos. writings of Cic.; elsewh. rare): quid praestantius bonitate et beneficentiā? Cic. N.D. 1, 43, 121: beneficentia, quam eandem vel benignitatem vel liberalitatem appellari licet, id. Off. 1, 7, 20

beneficiarius.full: bĕnĕfĭcĭārĭus, a, um, adj. beneficium, pertaining to a favor. As adj. only once: res, Sen. Ep. 90, 2.— Freq. subst.: bĕnĕfĭcĭārĭi, ōrum, m.; in milit. lang., soldiers who, through the favor of their commander, were exempt from menial offices (throwing up intrenchments, procuring wood and water, foraging, etc.), free or privileged soldiers: beneficiarii dicebantur milites, qui vacabant muneris beneficio; e contrario munifices vocabantur, qui non vacabant, sed munus reipublicae faciebant, Fest. p.

beneficium.full: bĕnĕfĭcĭum (better than bĕnĭfĭcĭ-um), ii, n. beneficus. A benefaction, kindness, favor, benefit, service, εὐεργέτημα (sunt qui ita distinguunt, quaedam beneficia esse, quaedam officia, quaedam ministeria. Beneficium esse, quod alienus det: alienus est, qui potuit sine reprehensione cessare: officium esse filii, uxoris et earum personarum, quas necessitudo suscitat et ferre opem jubet: ministerium esse servi, quem condicio sua eo loco posuit, ut nihil eorum, quae praestat, imputet superiori, Sen.

beneficus.full: bĕnĕfĭcus (better than bĕnĭfĭcus), a, um, adj. bene-facio (comp. and sup. regularly formed, beneficentior, Sen. Ben. 1, 4, 5; 5, 9, 2: beneficentissimus, Cic. Lael. 14, 51; id. N. D. 2, 25, 64; ante-class. beneficissimus, Cato ap. Prisc. p. 603 P.), generous, liberal, beneficent, obliging, favorable (rare but class.): de Ptolemaeo rege optimo et beneficissimo, Cato, l. l.: beneficum esse oratione, Plaut. Ep. 1, 2, 14: ubi beneficus, si nemo alterius causā benigne facit? Cic. Leg. 1, 18, 49: in a
beneficus.short: bĕnĕfĭcus (better than bĕnĭfĭcus), a, um, adj.

beneolentia.full: bĕnĕŏlentĭa, ae, f. bene-oleo, a smelling agreeably (late Lat.), Hieron. in Dindym. Spir. Sanc. 11.

beneplaceo.full: bĕnē-plăcĕo, ŭi, ĭtum, 2, v. n., to please: alicui, Vulg. 1 Cor. 16, 2.—Hence, P. a.: bĕnēplăcĭtus, a, um, pleasing, acceptable, Vulg. Ecclus. 34, 21; Ambros. lsaac et An. 7, 57 init.—As subst.: bĕnē-plăcĭtum, i, n., good pleasure, gracious purpose, Vulg. Eph. 1, 9 et saep.

beneventum.full: Bĕnĕventum, i, n., = Βενεούεντον and Βενούεντον, Strab. [bene-ventus], a very ancient city of the Hirpini, in Samnium, now Benevento, Liv. Epit. 15; Plin. 3, 11, 16, § 105; acc. to fable (Serv. ad Verg. A. 8, 9; Sol. c. 11), founded by Diomedes; it became a flourishing Roman colony 485 A.U.C., Cic. Verr. 2, 1, 15, § 38; Hor. S. 1, 5, 71; Vell. 1, 14, 7; Plin. 32, 2, 9, § 59; called Maleventum on account of its unwholesome air, Plin. 3, 11, 16, § 105; cf. Fest. p. 340, 8 Müll.; Paul. ex Fest. p.
beneventum.short: Bĕnĕventum, i, n., = Βενεούεντον and Βενούεντον, Strab.

benevolens.full: bĕnĕ-vŏlens (in MSS. also bĕnĭvŏ-lens), entis, adj. bene-volo, wishing well, benevolent, favorable, propitious, kind, obliging (ante-class. for the class. benevolus; in Plaut. very freq.), Plaut. Ps. 2, 4, 7 and 8: ero benevolens, id. Truc. 2, 2, 61; id. Bacch. 3, 6, 24: amicus multum benevolens, id. Merc. 5, 2, 46: benevolentes inter se, id. Cist. 1, 1, 25: ite cum dis benevolentibus, id. Mil. 4, 8, 41: benevolentem cum benevolente perire, id. Ep. 1, 1, 72: sodalis, id. Bacch. 3, 3, 71 al.—Comp

benevolentia.full: bĕnĕvŏlentĭa (better than bĕnĭvŏ-lentĭa), ae, f. benevolus, good-will, benevolence, kindness, favor, friendship (diff. from amor, q.v.; in good class. prose, most freq. in Cic., esp. in Lael. and Off.): amor, ex quo amicitia nominata, princeps est ad benevolentiam conjungendam, Cic. Lael. 8, 26; id. Fam. 3, 9, 1; * Ter. Heaut. 1, 1, 63 (Fleck. sapientia): capere, movere, Cic. Off. 2, 9, 32: declarare, to express, id. Fam. 3, 12, 4: multitudinis animos ad benevolentiam allicere, id. Off. 2, 14, 4

benevolus.full: bĕnĕ-vŏlus (in MSS. and inscrr. often bĕnĭvŏlus), a, um, adj. volo, well-wishing, benevolent, kind, friendly, favorable (class. for the ante-class. benevolens, from which it borrows the comp. and sup.; cf. malevolus): erga aliquem benevolus, Plaut. Capt. 2, 2, 100: facilis benivolusque tibi, Ter. Hec. 5, 1, 33 Fleck.: benevolum efficere auditorem, Auct. Her. 1, 5, 8: benevolos auditores habere, id. ib. 1, 4, 6: ut benevolos beneque existimantes efficiamus, Cic. de Or. 2, 79, 322; Quint. 3, 7, 24

beni.full: Beni, ōrum, m., a Thracian people on the Hebrus, Plin. 4, 11, 18, § 40.
beni.short: Beni, ōrum, m., a Thracian people on the Hebrus, Plin.

benignitas.full: bĕnignĭtas, ātis, f. benignus, the quality of one benignus, an affable, kind bearing to others. Of feeling or external conduct, kindness, friendliness, courtesy, benevolence, benignity: si ad vortendum huc animum adest benignitas, Plaut. Merc. prol. 11: justitia, cui sunt adjunctae pietas, bonitas, liberalitas, benignitas, comitas, quaeque sunt generis ejusdem, Cic. Fin. 5, 23, 65: etsi me attentissimis animis summā cum benignitate auditis, id. Sest. 13, 31; id. Caecin. 3, 9; id. Dom. 14, 32; Ci

benigniter.full: bĕnignĭter, adv. (ante-class. for benigne), kindly, benignly, Titin. ap. Non. p. 510, 13; Prisc. p. 1010 P.

benignor.full: bĕnignor, āri, 1, v. dep. benignus, to rejoice, take delight (eccl. Lat.): in operibus ejus, Vulg. 3 Esd. 4, 39.

benignus.full: bĕnignus, a, um, adj. as if benigenus, from bonus genus, anal. with malignus and privignus, of a good kind or nature, beneficent, kind. Of feeling or deportment towards others, kind, good, friendly, pleasing, favorable, benignant: nam generi lenonio, Numquam ullus deus tam benignus fuit qui fuerit propitius, Plaut. Pers. 4, 4, 34: benignus et lepidus et comis, Ter. Hec. 5, 3, 39: boni et benigni, id. Phorm. 5, 2, 2: comes, benigni, faciles, suaves homines esse dicuntur, Cic. Balb. 16, 36: Apelle

benjamin.full: Benjămin, m., indecl. The young est son of the Hebrew patriarch Jacob, Aug. Civ. Dei, 17, 21; Sulp. Sev. Chron. 1, 12, 1 sqq.; Vulg. Gen. 35, 18 al.— The Jewish tribe of Benjamin, Sulp. Sev Chron. 1, 29, 5.—Hence, Benjămītae, ārum, m., the Jews of the tribe of Benjamin, Sulp. Sev. Chron. 1, 29, 5.

benna.full: benna, ae, f. (Gallic), a kind of carriage; those who sat in the same benna were called combennones, Fest. p. 27; cf. Comment. p. 347 (a wagon of wicker or basket-work is still called banne in Belgium, and benne in Switzerland).

benus.full: bĕnus, a, um, adj., v. bonus init.

beo.full: bĕo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. akin to benus, bonus, and, acc. to Fick, connected with δειδω, δεινός, to make happy, to bless (as verb. finit. rare, and mostly poet. for fortuno, beatum efficio; not in Cic.). In gen., to gladden, rejoice, refresh: hoc me beat, Plaut. Am. 2, 2, 12: foris aliquantillum etiam quod gusto, id beat, id. Capt. 1, 2, 34: ecquid beo te? does that gladden thee? Ter. Eun. 2, 2, 47.—Hence, in colloq. lang. beas or beasti, that delights me, I am rejoiced at that, Plaut. As. 2, 2,

berber.full: berber, perh. old inf., = fervere, Carm. Frat. Arv.

bercorcates.full: Bercorcātes, ium, m., a people of Gallia Aquitanica, Plin. 4, 19, 33, § 108.
bercorcates.short: Bercorcātes, ium, m., a people of Gallia Aquitanica, Plin.

berecyntus.full: Bĕrĕcyntus, i, m., = Βερέκυντος, a mountain on the banks of the river Sangarius, in Phrygia, sacred to Cybele, Serv. ad Verg. A. 6, 784; 9, 82; Schol. Cruq. ad Hor. C. 4, 1, 22.— Derivv., the adjj. Bĕrĕcyntĭus (Bĕrĕcynth-), a, um, = Βερεκύντιος. Of or pertaining to the mountain Berecyntus, Berecyntian: tractus, Plin. 5, 29, 29, § 108 (acc. to Pliny, in Caria): juga, Claud. ap. Eutr. 2, 300: mater, i. e. Cybele, Verg. A. 6, 785; Stat. Th. 4, 782; and subst.: Bĕrĕcyntia, ae, f., Verg. A. 9, 82; Ov
berecyntus.short: Bĕrĕcyntus, i, m., = Βερέκυντος, a mountain on the banks of the river Sangarius, in Phrygia, sacred to Cybele, Serv.

beregrani.full: Berē^grāni, ōrum, m., the people of Beregria, a town in Picenum, Plin. 3, 13, 18, § 111.
beregrani.short: Berē^grāni, ōrum, m., the people of Beregria, a town in Picenum, Plin.

berelides.full: Bĕrĕlĭdes, um, f., a group of small islands off the southern coast of Sardima, Plin. 3, 7, 13, § 85.
berelides.short: Bĕrĕlĭdes, um, f., a group of small islands off the southern coast of Sardima, Plin.

berenice.full: Bĕrĕnīcē (in MSS. also Bĕrŏnīcē), ēs, f., = Βερενίκη. A female name. Daughter of Ptolemy Philadelphus and Arsinoë, and wife of her own brother, Ptolemy Euergetes; her beautiful hair was placed as a constellation in heaven (Coma or Crinis Berenices), Hyg. Astr. 2, 24; cf. the poem of Catullus: de Coma Berenices, 66, 1 sqq. (Another constellation of the same name, Plin. 2, 70, 71, § 178.)—Hence, Bĕrĕnīcēus, a, um, adj., of Berenice: vertex, Cat. 66, 8.— The daughter of the Jewish king Agrippa I.,

bergae.full: Bergae, ārum, m., a people of Scythia, Mel. 3, 5, 1; 3, 6, 9.
bergae.short: Bergae, ārum, m., a people of Scythia, Mel.

bergi.full: Bergi, ōrum, m., an island in the North Sea, Plin. 4, 16, 30, § 104.
bergi.short: Bergi, ōrum, m., an island in the North Sea, Plin.

bergimus.full: Bergĭmus, i, m., a deity of the Galli Cenomani, in Upper Italy, Inscr. Orell. 1971 sq.; 2194.
bergimus.short: Bergĭmus, i, m., a deity of the Galli Cenomani, in Upper Italy, Inscr.

bergistani.full: Bergistāni or Vergistāni, ōrum, m., a community of robbers in Hispania Tarraconensis, Liv. 34, 16, 9; 34, 17, 5; 34, 21, 6.
bergistani.short: Bergistāni or Vergistāni, ōrum, m., a community of robbers in Hispania Tarraconensis, Liv.

bergomum.full: Bergŏmum, i, n., = Βέργομον, a town in Gallia Transpadana, now Bergamo, Plin. 3, 17, 21, § 124; Just. 20, 5, 8; Inscr. Orell. 65.—Hence, Bergŏmas, ātis, adj., of Bergomum: MVNICIPIVM, Inscr. Orell. 3349: RESPVBLICA, ib. 3898; and Bergomātes, ium, m., the inhabitants of Bergomum, Plin. 3, 17, 21, § 125; 34, 1, 2, § 2; Cato, Orig. 2, 4.
bergomum.short: Bergŏmum, i, n., = Βέργομον, a town in Gallia Transpadana, now Bergamo, Plin.

bernice.full: Bernīcē, es, f., v. Berenice, I. B.

beroe.full: Bĕrŏē, ēs, f., = Βερόη. The nurse of Semele, Ov. M. 3, 278; Hyg. Fab. 167.— One of the Oceanids, Verg. G. 4, 341.— The wife of Doryclus of Epirus, Verg. A. 5, 620 Wagn.

beroea.full: Bĕroea (Berrh-) (trisyl.), ae, f., = Βέροια (Βέρροια), a town in Macedonia, later called Irenopolis, north of the river Aliacmon, now Verria, Plin. 4, 10, 17, § 33; Liv. 44, 45, 2 and 5; 45, 29, 9; Cic. Pis. 36, 89. —Hence, Bĕroeaeus, i, m., a Berœan, Liv 23, 39, 3 (al. Boeotius); 42, 58, 7; and Beroeenses, ium, m., the Berœans, Plin. 5, 23, 19, § 82.
beroea.short: Bĕroea (Berrh-) (trisyl.), ae, f., = Βέροια (Βέρροια), a town in Macedonia, later called Irenopolis, north of the river Aliacmon, now Verria, Plin.

berones.full: Bērōnes, um, m., = Βήρωνες, acc. to Strab. 3, p. 238, a powerful people in Hispania Tarraconensis, Liv. Fragm. 91, lin. 213 sq.; perhaps there is a reference to these Berones in the obscure passage, Hirt. B. Alex. 53: semper enim Berones, etc. (perh. a body-guard of Berones; perh. also kindr. with the Gallic baro, acc. to the Schol. Pers. 5, 138: lingua Gallica barones vel varones dicuntur servi militum).

berosus.full: Bērōsus, i, m., = Βηρωσσός, a distinguished Babylonian astrologer of the time of Ptolemy Philadelphus, Vitr. 9, 1, (4); Sen. Q. N. 3, 29, 1; Plin. 7, 37, 37, § 123; 7, 49, 50, § 160; Tert. Apol. 19.
berosus.short: Bērōsus, i, m., = Βηρωσσός, a distinguished Babylonian astrologer of the time of Ptolemy Philadelphus, Vitr.

berresa.full: Berresa, ae, f., a town in Ethiopia, Plin. 6, 29, 50, § 180.
berresa.short: Berresa, ae, f., a town in Ethiopia, Plin.

berrice.full: Berrĭcē, ēs, f., a large island north of Europe, Plin. 4, 16, 30, § 104.
berrice.short: Berrĭcē, ēs, f., a large island north of Europe, Plin.

berula.full: berŭla, ae, f., an herb, called also cardamine, Marc. Emp. 36.
berula.short: berŭla, ae, f., an herb, called also cardamine, Marc.

beryllus.full: bēryllus (beryllus, Prud. Psych. 855; bērillus, Isid. Orig. 16, 7, 5; berul-lus, Plin. 37, 5, 20, § 76 Jan.), i, m., = βήρυλλος. A precious stone of a sea-green color, coming from India, beryl, Prop. 4 (5), 7, 9; Plin. 37, 5, 20, § 76 sqq.; Isid. Orig. l. l.; Sol. 53; Juv. 5, 37; Dig. 39, 4, 16, § 7.— Meton. for a ring with a beryl, Prop. 4 (5), 7, 9.— Beryllus aëroides, = βήρυλλος ἀεροειδής, the sapphire, Plin. l. l. § 77.

berytus.full: Bērȳtus (Bērўtus, Avien. Descr. Orb. Terr. 1080; cf. Wernsdorf poet. Lat. Min. V. p. 1103), i, f., = Βηρῦτός, a seaport town of Phœnicia, distinguished for its excellent wine; as a Roman colony, called Felix Julia, now Beirout, Plin. 5, 20, 17, § 78; Tac. H. 2, 81; Dig. 5, 15, 8; Prisc. Perieg. p. 853.—Hence, Derivv. Bērȳtĭus (Bērўtĭus, Aus. Praef. ad Syagr. 20), a, um, adj., of Berytus: vinum, Plin. 14, 7, 9, § 74: uva, id. 15, 17, 18, § 66.— Bērȳtensis, e, adj., Berytensian, of Berytus: coloni

bes.full: bes, bessis, m. (nom. bessis, Paul. ex Fest. p. 33 Müll.; Prisc. Ponder. p. 1348 P.) [be-is = binae partes assis]. Two thirds of a unit (the as); eight unciae, or twelfths (cf. as): bessis octo sunt unciae (8/12 = 2/3), triens quattuor, Paul. ex Fest. l. l. As a coin: fenus ex triente Idib. Quint. factum erat bessibus, i. e. instead of the previous monthly interest of 1/3 %, 2/3 % was now reckoned; thus, acc. to the present mode of calculating, for the year, the interest advanced from 4 % (12X1/

besa.full: Bēsā, ae, m., = Βησᾶ, an Egyptian divinity, Amm. 19, 12, 3.
besa.short: Bēsā, ae, m., = Βησᾶ, an Egyptian divinity, Amm.

besaro.full: Besaro, f., a town in Spain, Plin. 3, 1, 3, § 15.
besaro.short: Besaro, f., a town in Spain, Plin.

besbicus.full: Besbicus, i, f., a small island in the Propontis, Plin. 2, 88, 90, § 204; 5, 32, 44, § 151.
besbicus.short: Besbicus, i, f., a small island in the Propontis, Plin.

besidiae.full: Besĭdĭae, ārum, f., a town in Bruttium, perh. the present Bisignano, Liv. 30, 19, 10.
besidiae.short: Besĭdĭae, ārum, f., a town in Bruttium, perh.

bessalis.full: bessālis, e, adj. bes, comprising eight: laterculus, a tile eight inches long, Vitr. 5, 10, 2; 7, 4, 2: scutula, Mart. 8, 71, 7: clausulae, Porphyr. prooem. ad Hor. Epod.— Meton. for any thing of small value: comula, Petr. 58, 5.

bessi.full: Bessi, ōrum, m., = Βέσσοι, Strab.; Βησσοί, Herod., a savage and marauding people in the north-eastern part of Thrace, about the Hœmus mountains, and in the vicinity of the Hebrus, Veg. Mil. 2, 11; 4, 24; Plin. 4, 11, 18, § 40; Cic. Pis. 34, 84; Ov. Tr. 3, 10, 5; 4, 1, 67; Suet. Aug. 3; Isid. Orig. 9, 2, 91.—Sing.: Bessus, i, m., Inscr. Orell. 3548; 3552.—Hence, Bessĭcus, a, um, adj., of the Bessi: gens, Cic. Pis. 34, 84.

bessus.full: Bessus, i, m. A Bessian; v. Bessi. — Βῆσσος, a viceroy of Bactria, the murderer of Darius Codomannus, Curt. 5, 8, 4; 5, 9, 2; Just. 12, 5, 10.

bestia1.full: bestĭa, ae, f. perh. akin to fera and to belua, a beast (as a being without reason; opp. to man; while animal, = aliving being, includes man; bestia includes both fera, the beast as distinguished by fierceness, and belua, as distinguished by its size or ferocity; cf. Doed. Syn. 4, p. 290 sq.). Lit. In gen. (in the classical per. mostly in prose; esp. freq. in Cic., who uses it in its most extended signif., of every kind of living creature excepting man): disserens, neque in homine inesse animum

bestia2.full: Bestĭa, ae, m., a cognomen in the Calpurnian family. The consul L. Calpurnius Bestia, Sall. J. 27, 4 al.; Flor. 3, 1, 7.— The tribune of the people L. Bestia, Cic. Brut. 34, 128; id. de Or. 2, 70, 283.— Another tribune of the people, L. Bestia, a confederate of Catiline, Sall. C. 17, 3; 43, 1.
bestia2.short: Bestĭa, ae, m., a cognomen in the Calpurnian family.

bestialis.full: bestĭālis, e, adj. bestia, like a beast (post-class. and rare): villi, Prud. Cath. 7, 153.—Trop., fierce: nationes, Sid. Ep. 4, 1.

bestiarius.full: bestĭārĭus, a, um, adj. id. I. B., of or pertaining to beasts: ludus, a fight with beasts, Sen. Ep. 70, 20; 70, 22.—Usu. as subst.: bestĭārĭus, ii, m., one who fights with wild beasts in the public spectacles, a beast-fighter, θηριομάχης (persons hired, or criminals: the former with weapons, and as victors rewarded; the latter, unarmed, and sometimes bound, Vop. Aur. 37; Tert. Pud. 22): praeclara aedilitas! Unus leo, ducenti bestiarii, Cic. Sest. 64, 135: gladiatoribus et bestiariis obsedere rem

bestiola.full: bestĭŏla, ae, f. dim. bestia, a small animal, a little beast, Cic. N.D. 2, 48, 123; id. Tusc. 1, 39, 94; Varr. R. R. 1, 12, 2; Sen. Ep. 70, 17; Plin. 11, 6, 7, § 17; 18, 17, 44, § 156; 22, 25, 81, § 163; Veg. R. R. 3, 15, 10 al.

bestius.full: Bestĭus, ii, m. bestia, a rough and miserly man, otherwise unknown, Hor. Ep. 1, 15, 37; Pers. 6, 37.

beta1.full: bēta, ae (bētis, is, Ser. Samm. 54, 9), f. hence Fr. bette; Engl. beet, a vegetable, the beet: Beta vulgaris, Linn.; Plin. 19, 8, 40, § 132; 20, 8, 27, § 69; Col. 10, 254; 10, 326; 11, 3, 17 and 42; Pall. Febr. 24, 10; * Plaut. Ps. 3, 2, 26; * Cic. Fam. 7, 26, 2; cf. * Cat. 67, 21; Mart. 13, 13; 3, 47, 9; Isid. Orig. 17, 10, 15.

beta2.full: bēta, n. indecl. (beta, ae, f., Aus. Technopaegn. c. Litt. Mon. v. 13), = βῆτα, the Greek name of the second letter of the alphabet (pure Lat. be; v. B): hoc discunt omnes ante alpha et beta puellae, * Juv. 14, 209.—Hence, prov., the second in any thing (as alpha is the first), Mart. 5, 26.

betaceus.full: bētācĕus, a, um, adj. 1. beta, from or of the beet: pedes betacei, beet-roots, Varr. R. R. 1, 2, 27.—Subst.: bētācĕus, i, m. (sc. pes), beet-root (cf. Charis. pp. 24 and 128 P.; Prisc. p. 618 ib.), Apic. 3, 2; Plin. Ep. 1, 15, 2 (where others, less correctly, read Baeticae); Arn. 4, p. 133 (others, betis).

betasi.full: Betāsi, ōrum, m., a Belgian people, otherwise unknown, Plin. 4, 17, 31, § 106; Tac. H. 4, 56 and 66.
betasi.short: Betāsi, ōrum, m., a Belgian people, otherwise unknown, Plin.

bethlehem.full: Bē^thlĕhem, Bē^thleëm, Bē^th-lem, n. indecl., and Bē^thlĕhēmum, i, n., = , a town of the tribe of Judah, the birthplace of David and of Christ, now Beit el Lahm; form Bethlehem, Tert. adv. Jud. 13; Vulg. Gen. 35, 19.—Form Bethleem, Juvenc. 1, 149; 1, 153; scanned Bĕthlēēm, Prud. στεφ. 10, 737.—Form Bethlem, Prud. Cath. 7, 1; 12, 78.—Form Bethlehemum, Hier. Vit. Paulae.—Hence, Bē^thlaeus, a, um, adj., of Bethlehem, Sedul. Carm. 2, 73.— Bē^thlĕĕmĭcus, a, um, adj., of Bethlehem, Juvenc. 1, 260 dub.

betizare.full: bētīzare (or bētissare), used by Augustus for languere on account of the softness of the beet, 1. beta; cf. Cat. 67, 21: languidior tenera beta, acc. to Suet. Aug. 87 Ruhnk.
betizare.short: bētīzare (or bētissare), used by Augustus for languere on account of the softness of the beet, 1.

beto.full: bēto (baeto; in Plaut. bīto), ĕre, v. n. kindr. with vado and βαίνω, to go (with its derivatives, abito, adbito, ebito, interbito, perbito, praeterbito, rebito, bitienses, only ante-class.): in pugnam baetite, Pac. ap. Non. p. 77, 21 (Trag. Rel. v. 255 Rib.): si ire conor, prohibet betere, id. ib.; Varr. ib.: ad aliquem, Plaut. Curc. 1, 2, 52: ad portum ne bitas, id. Merc. 2, 3, 127.

betucius.full: Betucĭus, ii, m., a Roman proper name, e. g. T. Betucius Bassus, an orator of Asculum, Cic. Brut. 46. 169.
betucius.short: Betucĭus, ii, m., a Roman proper name, e.

betula.full: betŭla (also betulla), ae, f., the birch, Plin. 16, 18, 30, § 75; 16, 37, 69, § 176.
betula.short: betŭla (also betulla), ae, f., the birch, Plin.

biaeothanatus.full: bĭaeŏthănătus, a, um, adj., = βιαιοθάνατος, dying by violence, Tert. Anim. 57.
biaeothanatus.short: bĭaeŏthănătus, a, um, adj., = βιαιοθάνατος, dying by violence, Tert.

bianor.full: Bĭānor, ŏris, m. βία-ἀνήρ. A centaur slain by Theseus at the marriage festival of Pirithŏus, Ov. M. 12, 345.— An ancient hero of Mantua, Verg. E. 9, 60; acc. to Serv. in h. l. and upon A. 10, 198-200, the founder of Mantua, and identical with Ocnus.

biarchia.full: bĭarchĭa, ae, f., = βιαρχία, the office of a biarchus, a commissaryship, Cod. Const. 1, 31, 1.
biarchia.short: bĭarchĭa, ae, f., = βιαρχία, the office of a biarchus, a commissaryship, Cod.

biarchus.full: bĭarchus, i, m., = βίαρχος, a commissary, superintendent of provisions, Hier. adv. Joann. Hieros. n. 19; Imp. Leo Cod. 14, 20, 3.
biarchus.short: bĭarchus, i, m., = βίαρχος, a commissary, superintendent of provisions, Hier.

bias.full: Bĭās, antis, m., = Βίας, a Greek philosopher of Priene, one of the seven wise men of Greece, Cic. Lael. 16, 59; id. Par. 1, 1, 8; Col. 1, 1, 9; Val. Max. 7, 2, ext. 3.
bias.short: Bĭās, antis, m., = Βίας, a Greek philosopher of Priene, one of the seven wise men of Greece, Cic.

bibaculus.full: Bĭbācŭlus, i, m. bibax, a Roman cognomen; e. g. of the poet M. Furius; of the prætor L. Furius, Liv. 22, 49, 16.

bibaga.full: Bibaga, ae, f., an island near Gedrosia, Plin. 6, 21, 23, § 80.
bibaga.short: Bibaga, ae, f., an island near Gedrosia, Plin.

bibali.full: Bibali, ōrum, m., a people of Hispania Tarraconensis, Plin. 3, 3, 4, § 28.
bibali.short: Bibali, ōrum, m., a people of Hispania Tarraconensis, Plin.

bibax.full: bĭbax, ācis, adj. bibo, given to drink, Nigid. ap. Gell. 3, 12.

biberius.full: Bĭbĕrĭus Caldius Mero bibo-calidus-merum, a name given in derision to the emperor Tiberius Claudius Nero on account of his love of drink, Suet. Tib. 42.
biberius.short: Bĭbĕrĭus Caldius Mero bibo-calidus-merum, a name given in derision to the emperor Tiberius Claudius Nero on account of his love of drink, Suet.

bibesia.full: Bĭbĕsĭa, ae, f., Drinkland, a comically formed name, Plaut. Curc. 3, 74: Perediam et Bibesiam Plautus finxit suā consuetudine, cum intellegi voluit cupiditatem edendi et bibendi, Fest. p. 214, 28 Müll.; cf. Peredia.
bibesia.short: Bĭbĕsĭa, ae, f., Drinkland, a comically formed name, Plaut.

bibilis.full: bĭbĭlis, e, adj. bibo, drinkable, potable: cibus, Cael. Aur. Acut. 2, 11, 81.

bibio.full: bĭbĭo, ōnis, m. id., a small insect generated in wine, = mustio, Isid. Orig. 12, 8, 16; v. 2. bibo.— = vipio, q. v.

bibitor.full: bĭbĭtor, ōris, m. id., a drinker, toper, Sid. Ep. 1, 8.

bibitus.full: bĭbĭtus, a, um, Part., from bibo.
bibitus.short: bĭbĭtus, a, um, Part., from bibo.

biblia.full: biblĭa, ōrum, n., = Βιβλία, the Bible, eccl. Lat.; and very late, biblĭa, ae, f.
biblia.short: biblĭa, ōrum, n., = Βιβλία, the Bible, eccl.

biblinus.full: biblĭnus, a, um, adj., = βίβλινος (βύβλινος), of or made from the Egyptian papyrus: epistulae, Hier. Ep. 51, n. 1.
biblinus.short: biblĭnus, a, um, adj., = βίβλινος (βύβλινος), of or made from the Egyptian papyrus: epistulae, Hier.

bibliopola.full: biblĭŏpōla (BYBLIOPOLA, Inscr. Orell. 4154), ae, m., = βιβλιοπώλης, a bookseller (post-Aug.), Plin. Ep. 1, 2 fin.; 9, 11, 2; Mart. 4, 72; Isid. Orig. 6, 14, 1 al.

bibliotheca.full: biblĭŏthēca (also bī^blĭŏthēcē, Cic. Fam. 13, 77, 3; Inscr. Grut. 584; and BYBL-, Inscr. Orell. 40; 41; 1172), ae, f., = βιβλιοθήκη, a library; and, as in Greek and English, both a library-room and a collection of books, Fest. p. 28. The expl. of Isidorus applies to the first signif.: bibliotheca est locus, ubi reponuntur libri, βίβλος enim Graece liber, θήκη repositorium dicitur, Isid. Orig. 15, 5, 5; cf. id. ib. 18, 9, 3; 6, 3, 1. The first public library at Rome was collected by Asinius Polli

bibliothecalis.full: biblĭŏthēcālis, e, adj. bibliotheca, of or belonging to a library (post-class.): thesaurus, a repository of books, Sid. Ep. 8, 4: copia, Mart. Cap. 2, § 139.

bibliothecarius.full: biblĭŏthēcārĭus, ii, m. id., a librarian (late Lat.), M. Aurel. ap. Fronto Ep. ad M. Caes. 4, 5: bibliothecarius qui codices servat, Gloss. Isid.

bibliothecula.full: biblĭŏthēcŭla, ae, f. dim. id., a small library, a collection of books, Symm. Ep. 4, 18.

biblus.full: biblus, i, f., = βίβλος (βύβλος), the papyrus, a sort of rush that grew largely in Egypt, from the inner bark of which paper was made (poet. for the more usual papyrus): flumineae, Luc. 3, 222; cf. Plin. 13, 11, 22, § 71 sq.—Meton., paper, Sedul. 1, 6.
biblus.short: biblus, i, f., = βίβλος (βύβλος), the papyrus, a sort of rush that grew largely in Egypt, from the inner bark of which paper was made (poet.

bibo1.full: bĭbo, bĭbi (post-class. part. fut. bĭbĭtūrus, Hier. Isa. 8, 25, 8; Vulg. Matt. 20, 22; id. Act. 23, 12; Cassiod. Hist. Eccl. 1, 1; part. perf. bĭbĭtus, a, um, Cael. Aur. Chron. 4, 3, 60; Capitol. Ver. 5, 3; Aem. Mac. c. de Porro; Plin. Val. 2, 18; inf. apocop. biber, Cato, Titin., and Fannii Annal. ap. Charis. p. 99), 3, v. a. root bi; Gr. πι-, πίνω, πέπωκα; whence Lat. poto, as if from po; Sanscr. pī; Slav. piti; Lith. pota, to drink (usually from thirst, a natural want; poto, to drink from pas

bibo2.full: bĭbo, ōnis, m. 1. bibo, a tippler, drunkard, Firm. Math. 5, 4 fin.— Esp., a kind of worm bred in wine, Afran. ap. Isid. Orig. 12, 8, 16 (Com. Rel. v. 406 Rib.; al. bibiones).

bibonius.full: bĭbōnĭus, ii, m. id., πολυπότης, a hard drinker, a tippler, Vet. Gloss.

bibosus.full: bĭbōsus, a, um, adj. id., given to drinking, fond of drink, Laber. ap. Gell. 3, 12, 4; besides only in Nigidius, acc. to Gell. 3, 12, 1.

bibracte.full: Bibracte, is (abl. Bibracte, but -ti, Caes. B. G. 7, 55), n., = Φρούριον Βίβρακτα, Strabo; Αὐγουστόδουνον, Ptolem., the chief town of the Ædui, later Augustodunum, now Autun en Bourgogne, Dép. de Saōne et Loire, Caes. B. G. 1, 23; 7, 55; 7, 63; 7, 90; 8, 1; cf. Tac. A. 3, 43.—As a goddess: DEAE BIBRACTI, etc., Inscr. Orell. 1973.

bibrax.full: Bibrax, actis (Bibe, Tab. Peuting.), f., a town in Gaul, in the territory of the Remi, now Bièvre, a small place between Laon and the river Aisne, Caes. B. G. 2, 6.

bibrevis.full: bĭbrĕvis, e, adj. bis-brevis, Latin transl. of the Gr. δίβραχυς in metre, consisting of two short syllables: pes, a pyrrhic, Diom. pp. 471 and 472 P.

bibroci.full: Bibrŏci, ōrum, m., a British people, acc. to Camden, in the region of the present Bray, Caes. B. G. 5, 21.
bibroci.short: Bibrŏci, ōrum, m., a British people, acc.

bibulus1.full: bĭbŭlus, a, um, adj. 1. bibo. Lit., drinking readily, freely (poet. or in postAug. prose): bibulus Falerni, Hor. Ep. 1, 14, 34: potores, id. ib. 1, 18, 91.—More freq., Transf., of inanim. things, that sucks in or absorbs moisture: harena, sand that imbibes, drinks up moisture, Lucr. 2, 376; Verg. G. 1, 114; Ov. M. 13, 901: lapis, a stone that absorbs moisture, Verg. G. 2, 348 (qui harenarius vocatur, Serv.); Col. 3, 15, 4: litus, Ov. H. 16 (17), 139: favilla, Verg. A. 6, 227: radix, Ov. M. 14, 6

bibulus2.full: Bĭbŭlus, i, m., a proper name. L. Publicius Bibulus, a military tribune in the time of the second Punic war, Liv. 22, 53, 2.— M. (in Appian. Civ. 2, 8, Αεύκιος) Calpurnius Bibulus, a contemporary of Cœsar, consul with him A.U.C. 695, Suet. Caes. 19; 20; 49; cf. Cic. Vatin. 9, 21; id. Fam. 1, 9, 12; id. Att. 1, 17, 11; 2, 14, 1; 2, 19, 2; 6, 1, 13; 6, 8, 5.— C. Bibulus, an œdile A.U.C. 775, Tac. A. 3, 52.
bibulus2.short: Bĭbŭlus, i, m., a proper name.

bicameratus.full: bĭcămĕrātus, a, um, adj. bis-camera, with a double vault, doubly arched: cella, Hier. ad Jovin. 1, 17: ecclesia, Aug. Civ. Dei, 15, 26.—As subst.: bĭcămĕrātum, i, n., a receptacle with two compartments, Ambros. Hexaëm. 6, 9, 72.

biceps.full: bĭceps, cĭpĭtis (old form bĭcĭpes, like ancipes for anceps, acc. to Prisc. p. 754 P.; bĭcepsŏs, Varr. L. L. 5, § 50 Müll.; bĭ-căpĭtes, δικέφαλοι, Gloss. Philox.), adj. bis-caput. Having two heads, twoheaded (rare but class.): puella nata biceps, * Cic. Div. 1, 53, 121: puer, Liv. 41, 21, 12: porcus, id. 28, 11, 3: Janus, Ov. F. 1, 65; id. P. 4, 4, 23: serpens, Plin. 10, 62, 82, § 169: partus, Tac. A. 15, 47: gladius, with two edges, Vulg. Prov. 5, 4.—Poet., of mountains, with two summits: Parnas
biceps.short: bĭceps, cĭpĭtis (old form bĭcĭpes, like ancipes for anceps, acc.

bicessis.full: bĭcessis, is, m. bis-as, twenty asses, Varr. L. L. 5, § 170 Müll.; cf. as, I.

bicinium.full: bĭcĭnĭum, ii, n. bis-cano, a duet: cum duo canunt bicinium appellatur; cum multi, chorus, Isid. Orig. 6, 19, 6.

biclinium.full: biclīnĭum, ii, n. vox hibrida, from bisκλίνη; cf. Quint. 1, 5, 68, a dining-couch for two persons (only in Plaut.), Plaut. Bacch. 4, 4, 69 (3, 84); 4, 4, 102 (3, 117).

bicodulus.full: bĭcōdŭlus, a, um, adj. bis-cauda, having two tails: inlex, App. Mag. 30, p. 294, 13.

bicolor.full: bĭcŏlor, ōris (bĭcŏlōrus, a, um, Vop. Aur. 13), adj. bis-color, of two colors, twocolored (poet. or in post-Aug. prose): equus, Verg. A. 5, 566: baca, green and black, Ov. M. 8, 664: myrtus, steel-colored, id. ib. 10, 98; cf. id. ib. 11, 234; Plin. 10, 52, 74, § 144.

bicomis.full: bĭcŏmis, e, adj. bis-coma, with hair falling down on both sides, with a double mane: equus, Veg. 2, 28, 36.

bicorniger.full: Bĭcornĭger, gĕri, m. bis-corniger, two-horned, an epithet of Bacchus (v. Bacchus), Ov. H. 13, 33.

bicornis.full: bĭcornis, e bis-cornu. Adj., having two horns, two-horned (poet. or in postAug. prose): animal, Plin. 11, 46, 106, § 255: caper, Ov. M. 15, 304: fauni, id. H. 4, 49; id. F. 2, 268; 5, 99.—Poet., of a two-pronged fork: furcae, Verg. G. 1, 264; Ov. M. 8, 647: ferrum, Col. Poët. 10, 148.—Of the new moon, * Hor. C. S. 35.—Of rivers with two mouths (perh. only epith. ornans; cf. amnis init.): Rhenus, Verg. A. 8, 727: Granicus, Ov. M. 11, 763.—Of the top of Parnassus: jugum, Stat. Th. 1, 63 (cf. bicep

bicorpor.full: bĭcorpor, ŏris, adj. bis-corpus, having two bodies, double-bodied (poet. and very rare; late prose form bĭcorpŏrĕ-us, Firm. Math. 2, 12): bicorpores Gigantes, Naev. Bell.
