Pun. 2, 14 (ap. Prisc. p. 679 P.): Pallas bicorpor, Att. ap. Prisc. p. 699 P.; and so besides only in Cic. in a transl. from Sophocl. Trachin.: manus, Tusc. 2, 9, 22.

bicors.full: bĭcors, cordis, adj. bis-cor, with two hearts; trop., dissembling, false, Commod. Instr. 11, 8.

bicoxum.full: bĭcoxum bis-coxa, having two thighs, δίμηρον, Gloss. Gr. Lat.
bicoxum.short: bĭcoxum bis-coxa, having two thighs, δίμηρον, Gloss.

bicubitalis.full: bĭcŭbĭtālis, e (access. form bĭcŭbĭ-tus, a, um, App. Herb. 72), adj. bis-cubitus, of two cubits, Plin. 20, 23, 94, § 253 Sillig (Jan. bipedali).

bidens.full: bĭdens (old form duidens), entis (abl. bidenti, Lucr. 5, 209; Verg. Cir. 212; Pomp. ap. Gell. 16, 6, 7: bidente, Tib. 2, 3, 6; Verg. Cat. 8, 9; Plin. 17, 21, 35, § 159; gen. plur. bidentium, Hor. C. 3, 23, 14: bidentum, Ov. M. 15, 575), adj. bis-dens, with two teeth (not in Cic.). Adj. Lit.: amica, i.e. anus, Auct. Priap. 82: bos, Paul. ex Fest. p. 35 Müll.: hostiae, Plin. 8, 51, 77, § 206.— Transf., with two prongs, points, etc.: ancora, Plin. 7, 56, 57, § 209: forfex, Verg. Cat. 8, 9: ferrum =

bidental.full: bĭdental, ālis, n.; in the lang. of religion, a place struck by lightning, consecrated by the haruspices, and enclosed; so called from the offering, bidens, with which the lightning was propitiated (v. also puteal), Fest. p. 27; Non. p. 53, 26; cf. O. Müll. Etrusk. 2, p. 171; v. Dict. of Antiq. (perh. it is better to explain bidens here as = fulmen, from its forked form; thus Bidental = Fulminar, the temple, or the consecrated place of lightning): triste bidental Moverit incestus, * Hor. A. P. 4

bidentatio.full: bĭdentātĭo, ōnis, f. bidens, II. A., a harrowing: occatio, σκαφετός, Gloss. Gr. Lat.

bidis.full: Bidis, is, f., a small town in Sicily, north-west of Syracuse, Cic. Verr. 2, 2, 22, § 53.—Hence, Derivv. Bidinus, a, um, adj., of or pertaining to Bidis: palaestritae, Cic. Verr. 2, 2, 22, § 54.— Bi-dini, ōrum, m., the inhabitants of Bidis, Cic. Verr. 2, 2, 22, § 53; Plin. 3, 8, 14, § 91.
bidis.short: Bidis, is, f., a small town in Sicily, north-west of Syracuse, Cic.

biduus.full: bidŭus, a, um, adj. bis-dies, continuing two days, of two days; as adj. only once, with tempus, Liv. 27, 24, 3, where tempus is prob. to be omitted; v. Weissenb. ad loc. But very freq. and class. as subst.: bīdŭum, ii, n. (sc. tempus), a period or space of two days, two days: sinito biduom aut triduom consudent (oves), Cato, R. R. 96, 1: biduum supererat, Caes. B. G. 1, 23; Ter. And. 2, 6, 9; Planc. ap. Cic. Fam. 10, 17: in castra quae aberant bidui (sc. spatio), id. Att. 5, 16, 4; 5, 17, 1; cf.

biennalis.full: bĭennālis, e, adj. biennium, continuing two years, of two years: meta, Cod. Just. 5, 37, 27: pensio, Cod. Th. 11, 20, 4, § 1: culpa, ib. 12, 40, 3.

biennis.full: bĭennis, e, adj. id., of two years, lasting two years (very rare): biennis quasi duorum annorum, Beda, p. 2331 P.; Macr. S. 6, 9, 6; Serv. ad Verg. A. 4, 57; Nigid. ap. Gell. 16, 6, 13 (but in the phrase bienni spatio, Suet. Galb. 15; Plin. 2, 82, 84. § 198 Jan., bienni is the gen. of biennium).

biennium.full: bĭennĭum, ii, n. bis-annus, a period or space of two years, two years: jam biennium est, cum, etc., Plaut. Merc. 3, 1, 35: intra tempus biennii, Col. 3, 9, 6: hoc factum est ferme abhinc biennium, Plaut. Bacch. 3, 2, 4 (imitated by Ps.-Plaut. Merc. prol. 12): biennium ibi perpetuum misera illum tuli, Ter. Hec. 1, 2, 12; Caes. B. G. 1, 3; Cic. Phil. 5, 3, 7; Liv. 5, 14, 2: biennium provinciam obtinuit, Cic. Verr. 2, 3, 93, § 216; 2, 4, 30, § 67: lex usum et auctoritatem fundi jubet esse biennium,

bifarius.full: bĭfārĭus, a, um, adj. bis, after the analogy of the Gr. διφάσιος; cf.: ambifarius, trifarius, multifarius, etc., twofold, double (as adj. only post-class.): ratio, Amm. 18, 4, 3: illatio, App. Dogm. Plat. 3, p. 39, 16 dub. (al. bifariam).—Hence, adv. in two forms. bĭfārĭam (acc. fem. sc. partem), on two sides, i. e. twofold, double, in two ways, in two parts, in two places, twice, etc. (class.): ut dispertirem obsonium hic bifariam, Plaut. Aul. 2, 4, 3: annus bifariam divisus, Varr. R. R. 2, 4,

bifax.full: bĭfax, dīfax, two-faced, διπρόσωπος, Gloss. Lat. Gr. [bis-facies].

bifer.full: bĭfer, ĕra, ĕrum, adj. bis-fero. Lit., bearing fruit twice a year: arbor, malus, etc., Varr. R. R. 1, 7, 7: ficus, Col. 10, 403; 5, 10, 11; Plin. 13, 22, 41, § 121; 16, 27, 50, § 114; Suet. Aug. 76: biferique rosaria Paesti, Verg. G. 4, 119 (acc. to Serv. the rose blossomed twice in a year at Paestum).— * Transf., of twofold form: biferum Centauri corpus, a horse and man, Manil. 4, 230.

bifestus.full: bĭ-festus, a, um, adj. bis, doubly festive: dies, a twofold festival, Prud. στεφ. 12, 66.

bifidatus.full: bĭfĭdātus, a, um, adj. bifidus, cleft or divided into two parts (v. bifidus): lateribus in sese bifidatis, Plin. 13, 4, 7, § 30.

bifidus.full: bĭfĭdus, a, um, adj. bis-findo, cleft or divided into two parts (the usual form; rarer bifidatus and bifissus): bifidos relinquit Rima pedes, Ov. M. 14, 303: ridicae, Col. 4, 33, 4: lingua, Plin. 11, 37, 65, § 171: stirps, id. 17, 20, 34, § 150: cursus venarum, id. 16, 39, 76, § 195: iter, Val. Fl. 1, 570.

bifilum.full: bĭfīlum, i, n. bis-filum, a double thread, Serv. ad Verg. A. 12, 375.

bifissus.full: bĭfissus, a, um, adj. bis-findo, cleft or divided into two parts: ungulae, Sol. 52 med. (v. bifidus).

biforis.full: bĭfŏris, e (bĭfŏrus, a, um, Vitr. 4, 6 fin.), adj. bis-foris. Having two doors or folding-doors: valvae, Ov. M. 2, 4: fenestrae, id. P. 3, 3, 5.— Having two openings or holes, double: via (narium), App. Dogm. Plat. 1.—Poet.: ubi assuetis biforem dat tibia cantum, Verg. A. 9, 618 (bisonum, imparem, Serv.); Aus. Cent. Nupt. 27: biforis tumultus, Stat. Th. 4, 668.

biformatus.full: bĭ-formātus, a, um, adj. bis, doubleformed, two-shaped: non biformato impetu Centaurus (poet. for biformatus Centaurus impetu), Cic. poët. Tusc. 2, 8, 20 Kühner; v. biformis.

biformis.full: bĭformis, e, adj. bis-forma, double or two-formed, two-shaped (poet. or in postAug. prose): proles biformis Minotaurus, Verg. A. 6, 25: Scyllae, id. ib. 6, 286; Ov. M. 8, 156: Janus, id. F. 1, 89; 5, 424: (Hermaphroditus), id. M. 4, 387: pater, i. e. Chiron, id. ib. 2, 664: Nessus, id. ib. 9, 121: Hodites, id. ib. 12, 456: monstrum, id. ib. 8, 156: a Centaur, id. Am. 2, 12, 19; Claud. in Rufin. 1, 329 (cf. biformatus): Pan, Col. 10, 427: Glaucus, Claud. Rapt. Pros. 3, 12: Cecrops, Just. 2, 6, 7.

bifrons.full: bĭ-frons, ontis, adj. bis, with two foreheads, or, in a more extended sense, with two faces, an epithet of Janus, Verg. A. 7, 180; 12, 198; Gav. Bass. ap. Macr. S. 1, 9, 13.

bifurcus.full: bĭfurcus, a, um, adj. bis-furca, having two prongs or points, two-pronged: ramus, two-forked, Ov. M. 12, 442: surculi, Col. 5, 11, 3: ferramentum, id. 3, 18, 6: arbores, Plin. 16, 30, 53, § 122: valli, Liv. 33, 5, 9.— Also, subst.: bĭfurcum, i, n., a fork, Col. 3, 18, 6.—Trop., of the place where two branches start, Col. 4, 24, 10.—Of the connection of two veins upon the head of draught-cattle, Veg. 2, 40, 2; hence, sudor mihi per bifurcum volabat, over the cheeks down to the neck, Petr. 62.

bigae.full: bīgae, ārum (in plur. through the whole ante-Aug. per.; cf. Varr. L. L. 9, 39, 142; 10, 2, 165; 10, 3, 177; Serv. ad Verg. A. 2, 272; Charis. p. 20 P.; post-Aug. also in sing. bīga, ae; so Stat. S. 1, 2, 45; 3, 4, 46; id. Th. 1, 338; Sen. Herc. Oet. 1520; Plin. 34, 8, 19, § 89; 35, 11, 40, § 141; Tac. H. 1, 86; Suet. Tib. 26; Val. Max. 1, 8; Inscr. Orell. 2545; Vulg. Isa. 21, 9; v. Neue, Formenl. 1, 462; v. also trigae and quadrigae), f. for bijugae from bis-jugum, a pair of horses or (rarely) o

bigamus.full: bĭgămus, twice married [vox hibrida, bis-γαμέω]: a numero uxorum vocatus, quasi duabus maritus, Isid. Orig. 9, 7, 15; Ambros. Dignit. Sac. 4.
bigamus.short: bĭgămus, twice married [vox hibrida, bis-γαμέω]: a numero uxorum vocatus, quasi duabus maritus, Isid.

bigarius.full: bīgārius, ii, m. bigae, a driver of a pair of horses, Inscr. Murat. 621, 2.

bigatus.full: bīgātus, a, um, adj. id., having the figure of a bigae (exclusively of coin); with the figure of a bigae stamped upon it (cf. Dict. of Antiq.): argentum, Liv. 33, 23, 7; 33, 37, 11; 36, 21, 11.—Also, subst.: bīgā-tus, i, m. (sc. nummus), a silver coin with the stamp of the bigae, Plin. 33, 3, 13, § 46: nummi quadrigati et bigati a figurā caelaturae dicti, Paul. ex Fest. s. v. grave aes, p. 98 Müll.; Liv. 23, 15, 15; Tac. G. 5.

bigeminus.full: bĭgĕmĭnus, a, um, adj. bis-geminus, doubled, Poët. ap. Mar. Vict. 2572 P

bigemmis.full: bĭgemmis, e, adj. bis-gemma. * Set with two precious stones: anulus, Val. ap. Treb. Claud. 14.— Transf., of plants, having two buds, Col. 5, 5, 11.

bigener.full: bĭgĕner, ĕra, ĕrum, adj. bis-genus, like degener from de-genus, and bicorpor from bis-corpus, descended from two different races, hybrid, mongrel, Paul. ex Fest. p. 33, 14 Müll.: muli et hinni bigeneri atque insiticii, Varr. R. R. 2, 8, 1.

bigerra.full: Bigerra, ae, f., a town in Hispania Tarraconensis, in the province of the Bastitani, Liv. 24, 41, 11.
bigerra.short: Bigerra, ae, f., a town in Hispania Tarraconensis, in the province of the Bastitani, Liv.

bigerriones.full: Bĭgerrĭōnes, um (Bĭgerri, ōrum, Paul. Nol. Ep. ad Aus. 10, 246; Bĕgerri, Plin. 4, 19, 33, § 108), m., a Gallic people in Aquitania, now Bigorre, De/part. des hautes Pyre/ne/es, Caes. B. G. 3, 27.— Derivv. Bĭgerrĭcus, a, um, adj., of or pertaining to the Bigerriones: turbo, blowing from thence, Sid. Ep. 8, 12.—In fem. absol.: Bĭgerrĭca, ae, f. (sc. vestis), a warm shaggy garment, Sulp. Sev. Dial. 2, 1; Ven. de Vita S. Mart. 3, 49.— Bĭgerrĭtā-nus, a, um, adj., of the Bigerriones: patria, Aus. Ep.

bignae.full: bignae, female twins, Paul. ex Fest. p. 33, 3 Müll. [contr. from bigenae, from bisgigno].

bigradum.full: bigrădum, δίβαθμον: duos habens gradus, Gloss. Gr. Lat.
bigradum.short: bigrădum, δίβαθμον: duos habens gradus, Gloss.

bijugis.full: bĭjŭgĭs, e, adj. bis-jugum (a rare form for bijugus). Lit., yoked two together: equi, * Verg. G. 3, 91: bijugum Colla lyncum, Ov. M. 4, 24: curriculum, drawn by a pair of horses, Suet. Calig. 10.— In gen., double: uno bijuges tolli de limine fasces, i. e. two brothers, consuls from one family, Claud. Prob. et Olyb. 233.

bijugus.full: bĭjŭgus, a, um (contr. form bīgus, Manil. 5, 3; cf. also bĭjŭgis, e), adj. id., yoked two together (poet.): leones, Lucr. 2, 602; Verg. A. 10, 253: equi, Mart. 1, 13, 8: serpentes, Val. Fl. 7, 218: currus, drawn by two horses, Lucr. 5, 1299: temo, Stat. Th. 2, 723: certamen = bigarum, the contest with the bigae, Verg. A. 5, 144.— Subst.: bĭ-jŭgi, ōrum, m. (sc. equi), two horses yoked abreast: telo Admonuit bijugos, Verg. A. 10, 587; 10, 399: desiluit Turnus bijugis, i. e. from his chariot drawn

bilanx.full: bĭ-lanx, lancis, adj. bis-lanx, having two scales: libra, Mart. Cap. 2, § 180.

bilbilis.full: Bilbĭlis, is, f. A town in an elevated position in Hispania Tarraconensis, on the river Salo, the birthplace of the poet Martial, now Calatayud Vieja: Bilbilis, Mart. 10, 103, 1: Bilbilim, id. 1, 50, 3; Plin. 34, 14, 41, § 144: Bilbilin, Mart. 4, 55, 11; 10, 104, 6; 12, 18, 9.—Hence, Bilbĭlĭ-tānus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Bilbilis: aquae, a medicinal spring in the vicinity of Bilbilis, Itin. Anton.— The river Salo, near Bilbilis, now Xalon, Just. 44, 3, 13.

bilbo.full: bilbo, ĕre, v. n. onomatop., to make a noise like that of a liquid agitated in a vessel: bilbit factum est a similitudine sonitus, qui fit in vase. Naevius Bilbit amphora inquit, Paul. ex Fest. p. 34 Müll. (Com. Trag. v. 124 Rib.): bilbit βομβύζει, Gloss.

bilibra.full: bĭlībra. ae, f. bis-libra, two pounds: bilibrae farris, Liv. 4, 15, 6.

bilibralis.full: bĭlībrālis, διλιτριαῖος, weighing two pounds, Gloss. Cyril.
bilibralis.short: bĭlībrālis, διλιτριαῖος, weighing two pounds, Gloss.

bilibris.full: bĭlībris, e bilibra, of two pounds. Adj. Weighing two pounds: offae, Plin. 18, 11, 26, § 103: mullus, Mart. 3, 45, 5.— Containing two pounds: aqualis, * Plaut. Mil. 3, 2, 39: cornu, Hor. S. 2, 2, 61.— Subst., a quantity of two pounds, Veg. Vet. 3, 6, 6; 3, 6, 10; Vulg. Apoc. 6, 6.
bilibris.short: bĭlībris, e bilibra, of two pounds.

bilinguis.full: bĭlinguis, e, adj. bis - lingua, twotongued, double-tongued. Lit., having two tongues; humorously, of voluptuous persons kissing, Plaut. Ps. 5, 1, 15; cf. id. Poen. 5, 4, 65.— Transf. Tibiae, with two keys, Varr. ap. Non. p. 229, 24.— Speaking two languages: bilinguis δίγλωσσος, Gloss.: bilingues Bruttates Ennius dixit, quod Bruttii et Osce et Graece loqui soliti sint, Paul. ex Fest. p. 35 Müll.; cf. Commod. p. 350: corvinus, Canusini more bilinguis, Hor. S. 1, 10, 30: sed jam bilingues erant, p

biliosus.full: bīlĭōsus, a, um, adj. bilis. full of bile, bilious: alvus, Cels. 2, 8: sputum, id. 2, 6' biliosa reicere, Scrib. 168.—Subst.: bīlĭō-sus, i, m., a bilious person, Cels. 1, 3.— Trop., hypochondriac: biliosus, quod sit semper tristis, ab umore nigro, qui bilis vocatur, Isid. Orig. 10, 30.

bilis.full: bīlis, is (abl. bili, Plaut. Am. 2, 2, 95; Lucr. 4, 664; Cic. Tusc. 3, 5, 11; bile, Hor. C. 1, 13, 4; Petr. 124, 2; Plin. 22, 20, 23, § 49; Suet. Tib. 59; Pers. 2, 14; Juv. 13, 143; Inscr. Grut. 1040, 3), f. kindr. with galbus, gilbus; Germ. gelb. Lit., bile (the bilious fluid secreted by the liver, jecur, while fel is the vessel in which the fluid is contained): rufa, viridis, nigra, Ceis. 7, 18; Lucr. 4, 664; Cato, R. R. 156, 4; Cic. N. D. 2, 55, 137; id. Tusc. 4, 10, 23: bilem pellere, Plin.

bilix.full: bĭlix, līcis, adj. bis - licium, with a double thread, two-threaded: lorica, Verg. A. 12, 375 Heyn.; cf. trilix.

billis.full: billis apud Afros appellatur semen humanum humi profusum, Paul. ex Fest. p. 34 Müll.
billis.short: billis apud Afros appellatur semen humanum humi profusum, Paul.

bilongus.full: bĭ-longus, a, um, adj. bis, doubly long: pes, consisting of two long syllables, Mar. Vict. p. 2486 P.

bilustris.full: bĭlustris, e, adj. bis - lustrum, that lasts two lustra, i. e. ten years, of ten years' duration (very rare): bellum, Ov. Am. 2, 12, 9; so Sid. Carm. 23, 299.

bilychnis.full: bĭlychnis, e, adj. bis-lychnus, having two lights (very rare): lucerna, Petr. 30, 3; Inscr. Orell. 36, 78.

bimammius.full: bĭmammĭus, a, um, adj. bis-mamma, having two breasts; and trop., of the vine, having double clusters: vites, Plin. 14, 3, 4, § 40.

bimaris.full: bĭmăris, e, adj. bis - mare, lying between two seas. Lit., an epithet of Corinth (poet.; a favorite word of Ovid): bimarisve Corinthi Moenia, * Hor. C. 1, 7, 2; Ov. M. 5, 407: Ephyre, id. H. 12, 27: Isthmos, id. M. 7, 405; 6, 419 sq.— Trop.: morbus, of one who practises unnatural unchastity, Aus. Epigr. 131.

bimaritus.full: bĭ-mărītus, i, m. bis, the husband of two wives (a word coined by Laterensis, the accuser of Plancius): bimaritum appellas, ut verba etiam fingas, Cic. Planc. 12, 30; and besides only in Hier. adv. Jovin. 1, n. 49.

bimatris.full: bĭmātris, e, adj. bis - mater, having two mothers, poet. epithet of Bacchus (v. Bacchus init.): satumque iterum solumque bimatrem, Ov. M. 4, 12; Hyg. Fab. 167; Anthol. Lat. 1, 19, 2 (where it is scanned bīmăter).

bimatus.full: bīmātus, ūs, m. bimus, the age of two years (of animals and plants): ante bimatum, Varr. R. R. 2, 5, 17; Col. 7, 3, 6; 7, 4, 4: (polypi) ultra bimatum non vivunt, Plin. 9, 30, 48, § 89; 11, 21, 24, § 73: neque his bimatu longior vita, id. 9, 30, 48, § 93.—Of children, Vulg. Matt. 2; 16.

bimembris.full: bĭmembris, e, adj. bis - membrum, having double members: puer, half man, half beast, Juv. 13, 64; most freq. a poet. epithet of the Centaurs (half man, half horse; cf. bicorpor and biformis): Centauri bimembres, Sil. 3, 41: forma bimembris, Ov. H. 9, 99.— Subst.: bĭmembres, ium, comm., = Centauri, the Centaurs: nubigenae, * Verg. A. 8, 293 Heyn. and Jahn; Ov. M. 12, 240; 12, 494; 15, 283; Stat. Th. 12, 554.

bimenstruus.full: bĭmenstruus bis-mensis, = διμηνιαῖος, of two months, Gloss. Cyril.
bimenstruus.short: bĭmenstruus bis-mensis, = διμηνιαῖος, of two months, Gloss.

bimestris.full: bĭmestris, e (abl. regularly bimestri, Hor. C. 3, 17, 15; by poet. license, bimestre, Ov. F. 6, 158; cf. caelestis, perennis, etc.), adj. bis-mensis, of two months' duration, of two months (rare): consulatus, Planc. ap. Cic. Fam. 10, 24, 7: stipendium, Liv. 9, 43, 6: triticum, which may be reaped two months after sowing, Plin. 18, 7, 12, § 70: porcus, two months old, Hor. C. 3, 17, 15: porca, Ov. F. 6, 158.

bimeter.full: bĭmĕter, tra, trum, adj. bis-metrum, = dimeter, consisting of two metres: litterae, Sid. Ep. 9, 15: ars, id. ib. 9, 13.

bimulus.full: bīmŭlus, a, um, adj. dim. [bimus], only two years old (very rare, and only of man), Cat. 17, 13; Suet. Calig. 8 fin.

bimus.full: bīmus, a, um, adj. prob. contracted from bis-hiems, of two winters; cf. Eutych. ap. Cassiod. p. 2311 P., and Aufrecht, Zeitschrift für vergl. Sprachf. 4, p. 415, two years old, of two years, continuing two years: nuces, Cato, R. R. 17, 2; Varr. R. R. 2, 1, 13: una veterana legio, altera bima, octo tironum, Planc. ap. Cic. Fam. 10, 24, 3; so, semen, Plin. 18, 24, 54, § 195: surculi, id. 17, 14, 24, § 105: plantae, biennial, Pall. Febr. 25, 2: merum, * Hor. C. 1, 19, 15: nix, Ov. Tr. 3, 10, 16: pe

binarius.full: bīnārĭus, a, um, adj. bini, that contains or consists of two: formae, i.e. coins of the value of two gold pieces, Lampr. Alex. Sev. 39.

bingium.full: Bingĭum, ii, n., a town of Gaul, lying on the Rhine, opposite the modern Bingen, on the west bank of the Nahe, Tac. H. 4, 70; Amm. 18, 2, 4.
bingium.short: Bingĭum, ii, n., a town of Gaul, lying on the Rhine, opposite the modern Bingen, on the west bank of the Nahe, Tac.

bini.full: bīni, ae, a (in sing. only twice, Lucr. 4, 452, and 5, 877; gen. plur. always binūm, Sisenn. ap. Non. p. 80, 4; Sall. H. 3, 22 Dietsch; Plin. 31, 6, 31, § 57; Scrib. Comp. 8), num. distr. [bis]. Two by two, two to each, two each, two at a time: nam ex his praediis talenta argenti bina Statim capiebat, every year two talents, Ter. Phorm. 5, 3, 6: describebat censores binos in singulas civitates, Cic. Verr. 2, 2, 53, § 133: si unicuique bini pedes (campi) assignentur, two to each, id. Agr. 2, 31,

binio.full: bīnio, ōnis, m. bini, the number two, a deuce: jactus quisque apud lusores veteres a numero vocabatur, ut unio, binio, tri nio, quaternio, quinio, senio, Isid. Orig. 18, 65: biniones δηνάρια, Gloss. Philox.

binoctium.full: bĭnoctĭum, ii, n. bis-nox, a period or space of two nights, two nights (post-Aug and rare; perh. only in the two foll. exs.), * Tac. A. 3, 71: biduum et binoctium, Amm. 30, 1, 8.

binominis.full: bĭnōmĭnis, e, adj. bis-nomen, analog. to cognominis, from con-nomen, having two names (only in Ov. and in gen. sing.): binominis, cui geminum est nomen, ut Numa Pompilius, Tullus Hostilius, Paul. ex Fest. p. 36 Müll.: Ascanius (also called Iulus), Ov. M. 14, 609: Ister (also called Danubius), id. P. 1, 8, 11; id. Ib. 415.

binubus.full: bĭnūbus, i, m. bis-nubo, a doublymarried man (late Lat.), Cassiod. Hist. Sacr. 9, 38.

biocolyta.full: bĭŏcōlȳta, ae, m., = βιοκωλυτής, one who protects against violence, Jul. Epit. Nov. 15, 60.
biocolyta.short: bĭŏcōlȳta, ae, m., = βιοκωλυτής, one who protects against violence, Jul.

bion.full: Bĭōn (in the class. per. perh. more correctly Bio, analog. to Plato, Meno, Dio, etc.), ōnis, m., = Βίων (ὁ Βορυσθενίτης, Strab.), a very witty philosopher of the Cyrenaic school, born at Borysthenes: facetum illud Bionis, Cic. Tusc. 3, 26, 62.—Hence, Bĭōnēus, a, um, adj., Bionian, for witty, satirical, biting: hic delectatur iambis, Ille Bioneis sermonibus et sale nigro, Hor. Ep. 2, 2, 60 Orell. ad loc. (Bioneis sermonibus, lividis jocis, id est, satira, Acro).— Bion Soleus or Soleusis, a writer

biopator.full: Bĭŏpător, ŏris, f., the name of a town founded by the Trojans in Epirus, otherwise unknown, Varr. ap. Serv. ad Verg. A. 3, 349.
biopator.short: Bĭŏpător, ŏris, f., the name of a town founded by the Trojans in Epirus, otherwise unknown, Varr.

bios.full: bĭŏs, i, m., = βίος (life), a very celebrated and wholesome Greek wine, Plin. 14, 8, 10, § 77; 23, 1, 26, § 53.
bios.short: bĭŏs, i, m., = βίος (life), a very celebrated and wholesome Greek wine, Plin.

biothanatus.full: bĭŏthănătus, a, um, adj., = βιοθάνατος [βία - θάνατος], that dies a violent death, Lampr. Elag. 33; Firm. Math. 3, 14 fin.; 4, 1; Serv. ad Verg A. 4, 386.—Collat. form bĭaeŏthănătus, from βίαιοσ-θάνατος, Tert. Anim. 57.
biothanatus.short: bĭŏthănătus, a, um, adj., = βιοθάνατος [βία - θάνατος], that dies a violent death, Lampr.

bioticus.full: bĭōtĭcus, a, um, adj., = βιωτικός, of or belonging to common life, used in common life, practical: epilogi, Serv. ad Verg A. 3, 718: metrum, Mar. Vict. p. 2494 P. (in Diom. p. 470 ib. written as Greek).
bioticus.short: bĭōtĭcus, a, um, adj., = βιωτικός, of or belonging to common life, used in common life, practical: epilogi, Serv.

bipalium.full: bĭpālĭum, ii, n. bis-pala, a double mattock: solum ad bipalium defodere, Col. 11, 2, 17 Schneid. ad loc. (MSS. bĭpĕdā-lĭum; elsewhere only in abl. sing.): bipalio vertere terram, Cato, R. R. 6, 3: bipalio agrum subigere, id. ib. 45, 1; Varr. R. R. 1, 37, 5; Col. 3, 5, 3; 11, 3, 11; id. Arb. 1, 5; Plin. 17, 21, 35, § 159; 18, 26, 62, § 230.

bipalmis.full: bĭpalmis, e (access. form bĭpalmus, a, um, App. Herb. 7), adj. bis-palmus, two spans long or broad, of two spans (very rare): tabulae, Varr. R. R. 3, 7, 4: spiculum, Liv. 42, 65, 9.

bipartio.full: bĭ-partĭo (in MSS. also bĭ-pertĭo), no perf., ītum, 4, v. a. bis, to divide into two parts, to bisect (as verb. finit. very rare; more freq. in part. and adv.): ver bipartitur, is divided (in respect to weather), Col. 11, 2, 36; so, hiems bipertitur, id. 11, 2, 5 Schneid. N. cr.—Mostly part. pass.: bipartita divisio, Varr. L. L. 5, § 17 Müll.: genus bipartitum, Cic. Top. 22, 85: bipertiti Aethiopes, Plin. 5, 8, 8, § 43: ut faceres imperium bipartitum, Vulg. Ecclus. 47, 23.—Hence, bĭpartītō (bĭpe

bipatens.full: bĭpătens, entis, adj. bis-pateo, opening in two ways, open in two directions (acc. to Serv. ad Verg. A. 10, 5, used by Enn.; cf. Ann. v. 62 Vahl.; but only two exs. in Verg. are preserved): portis alii bipatentibus assunt, i.e. portis duarum valvarum, Verg. A. 2, 330 Wagn.—Of the doors of the dwellings of the gods: considunt tectis bipatentibus, Verg. A. 10, 5 (est autem sermo Ennianus tractus ab ostiis, quae ex utrāque parte aperiuntur, Serv.).

bipeda.full: bĭpĕda, ae, f. bis-pes, a tile or flagstone two feet long, for pavements (several times in Pall., elsewh. very rare), Pall. 1, 19, 1; 1, 40, 2 and 5; id. Mai, 11, 2 (twice); Inscr. Fabr. p. 511, 159 (cf. Vitr. 7, 1 fin.: tegulae bipedales).

bipedalis.full: bĭpĕdālis, e, adj. id., two feet long, broad, or thick (class. in prose and poetry): fenestrae, Cato, R. R. 14, 2: trabes, two feet thick, Caes. B. G. 4, 17: materia, id. B. C. 2, 10: sol huic (Epicuro) bipedalis fortasse videtur, * Cic. Fin. 1, 6, 20: adulescentulus bipedali minor, * Suet. Aug. 43: tegulae, Vitr. 7, 1 fin.: modulus, Hor. S. 2, 3, 309: hiatus, Plin. 16, 12, 23, § 57: latitudo, Col. 8, 3, 7.— Subst.: bĭpĕdāle, is, n., a tile or flag-stone two feet long, Inscr. Fabr. p. 500, 39.

bepedalium.full: bĕpĕdālĭum, ii, n. bipedalis, a doubtful reading for bipalium, Col. 11, 2, 17 Schneid. ad loc.; v. bipalium.

bipedaneus.full: bĭpĕdānĕus, a, um, adj. bis-pes, two feet long, wide, or thick (a rare access. form of bipedalis; most freq. in Col.): scrobs, Col. 4, 1, 2: spatia, id. 4, 30, 5: humus, id. 2, 2, 21 Gesn. and Schneid. N. cr.: latitudo, id. 5, 5, 2; 11, 2, 28: pastinatus, Plin. 17, 20, 32, § 143.

bipennifer.full: bĭpennĭfer, fĕra, fĕrum, adj. 2. bipennis-fero, bearing a two-edged axe (only in Ov.): Lycurgus, Ov. M. 4, 22; id. Tr. 5, 3, 39: Arcas, id. M. 8, 391.

bipennis1.full: bĭpennis (-pinnis), e, adj. bispenna, having two wings, two-winged (very rare): insectum, Plin. 11, 28, 33, § 96 (cf. just before, binis advolat pinnis): plumae, Varr. ap. Non. p. 79, 17.

bipennis2.full: bĭpennis, e (acc. sing. reg. bipennem, Varr. ap. Non. p. 79, 19; Verg. A. 5, 307; 11, 651; Petr. 132, 8; Juv. 6, 657; Claud. in Eutr. 1, 333; Sil. 5, 64: bipennim, only in Ov. M. 8, 766, with the var. lect. bipennem.—Abl. sing. reg. bipenni, Verg. A. 2, 479; Ov. M. 12, 611; Petr. 89, 24; Sen. Herc. Oet. 800; Claud. IV. Cons. Hon. 345; id. Rapt. Pros. 3, 79; 3, 377; Sil. 16, 264; and in prose, Plin. 8, 8, 8, § 26: bipenne, only once, Tib. 1, 6, 47) [bis-pinna]. Adj., having two edges, two-edged:

bipensilis.full: bĭ-pensĭlis, e, adj. bis, that may be suspended on two sides: forcipes, Varr. ap. Non. p. 99, 24.

bipes.full: bĭpēs (˘˘, Aus. Idyll. 11, 39; neutr. plur. bipedia, Aug. Mor. Manich. 9), pĕdis, adj. bis-pes, two-footed (mostly poet. or in post-Aug. prose): equi, Verg. G. 4, 389: mensa, Mart. 12, 32, 11: Aegyptii mures bipedes ambulant, on two feet, Plin. 10, 65, 85, § 187: alium bipedem sibi quaerit asellum, two legged ass, Juv. 9, 92: animal genus, mortale species, terrenum vel bipes differens, Quint. 5, 10, 61.— Subst., mostly contemptuously, of men: hoc ministro omnium non bipedum solum sed etiam quadr

biplex.full: biplex, duplex, διπλοῦς, double, Gloss. Gr. Lat.

biprorus.full: bĭprōrus, a, um, adj. bis-prora, of a ship, having two prows (cf Plin. 6, 22, 24, § 82): navis, Hyg. Fab. 168; and besides only id. ib. 277.

biremis.full: bĭrēmis, e, adj. bis-remus. Twooared, having two oars (rare): lembi, Liv. 24, 40 init.: scapha, * Hor. C. 3, 29, 62.— Also, Subst.: bĭrēmis, is, f., a small vessel with two oars, Luc. 10, 56; 8, 562.— Freq. in an extended signif., having two banks of oars; only subst., a galley with two banks of oars (cf. Dict. of Antiq.; first used by the Erythræans, acc. to Plin. 7, 56, 57, § 207), Cic. Verr. 2, 5, 20, § 51; 2, 5, 23, § 59; Caes. B. C. 3, 40; Tac. H. 4, 27; 5, 23; Claud. B. Gild. 369; id. Laud

birotus.full: bĭrŏtus, a, um, adj. bis-rota, twowheeled, with two wheels (post-class.): vehiculum, Non. p. 86, 30.—More freq. subst.: bĭrŏta, ae (gen. plur. birotūm, Cod. Th. 6, 29, 2, § 2; 8, 5, 9), f. (sc. raeda), a cabriolet, Cod. Th. 8, 5, 8, § 1 sqq.

birrus.full: birrus, i, m. (birrum, i, n., Aug. Serm. Divers. 49), = πυρρός (of yellow color), a cloak to keep off rain (made of silk or wool), Edict. Diocl. p. 20; cf. Salmas. Vop. Carin. 20; Burm. Anth. Lat. 2, p. 408; Cod. Th. 14, 10, 1, § 1; Schol. Juv. 8, 145; Sulp. Sev. Dial. 1, 21, 4; Claud. Epigr. 42.

bis.full: bis, adv. num. for duis, from duo; like bellum from duellum, Paul. ex Fest. p. 66 Müll.; cf. Cic. Or. 45, 153, and the letter B, twice, at two times, on two occasions, in two ways, = δίς (very freq. in prose and poetry). In gen.: inde ad nos elisa bis advolat (imago), Lucr. 4, 315; Cic. Q. Fr. 3, 8, 6; Hor. Epod. 5, 33; id. A. P. 358; 440; Verg. A. 6, 32; Ov. M. 4, 517 al.: non semel sed bis, Cic. Verr. 2, 3, 77, § 179: semel aut bis, Quint. 11, 2, 34: bis ac saepius, id. 10, 5, 7; Nep. Thras. 2

bisaccium.full: bĭsaccĭum, ii, n. bis-saccus, a double bag, saddle-bags, Petr. 31, 9.

bisaltae.full: Bīsaltae, ārum, m., = Βισάλται, a Thracian people on the Strymon, Verg. G. 3, 461; Liv. 45, 29, 7; 45, 30, 3; Plin. 4, 10, 17, § 38.—Hence the country they inhabited was called Bīsaltĭca, Liv. 45, 29, 6, or Bī-saltia, Gell. 16, 15 (Βισαλτία, Thuc.).
bisaltae.short: Bīsaltae, ārum, m., = Βισάλται, a Thracian people on the Strymon, Verg.

bisaltis.full: Bīsaltis, ĭdis, f., = Βισαλτίς, Theophane, daughter of Bisaltes, changed by Neptune into a ewe: Bisaltida (Gr. acc.), Ov. M. 6, 117; cf. Hyg. Fab. 188.
bisaltis.short: Bīsaltis, ĭdis, f., = Βισαλτίς, Theophane, daughter of Bisaltes, changed by Neptune into a ewe: Bisaltida (Gr.

bisambritae.full: Bisambritae, ārum, m., a people on the Indus, Plin. 6, 20, 23, § 78.
bisambritae.short: Bisambritae, ārum, m., a people on the Indus, Plin.

bisanthe.full: Bisanthē, ēs, f., = Βισάνθη, a town in Thrace, on the Propontis, a colony of the Samians, afterwards called Ῥαιδεστός, now Rodosto, Mel. 2, 2, 6; Plin. 4, 11, 18, § 43; Nep. Alcib. 7, 4.
bisanthe.short: Bisanthē, ēs, f., = Βισάνθη, a town in Thrace, on the Propontis, a colony of the Samians, afterwards called Ῥαιδεστός, now Rodosto, Mel.

biselliarius.full: bĭsellĭārĭus, ii, m. bisellium, one who enjoys the honor of the bisellium, Inscr. Orell. 4055.

biselliatus.full: bĭsellĭātus, ūs, m. id., the honor of a bisellium, Inscr. Orell. 4043.

bisellium.full: bĭsellĭum, ii, n. bis-sella, a richly ornamented seat of honor (so called because there was room for two persons upon it, although only one sat thereon, Varr. L. L. 5, § 128 Müll.). Such a bisellium has been found represented upon a Pompeian tomb with the inscription: C. CALVENTIO.... BISELLII. HONOR. DATVS. EST., Inscr. Orell. 4044; cf. ib. 4046; 4047; 4048.

biseta.full: bĭsēta porca dicitur. cujus a cervice setae bifariam dividuntur, etc., Paul. ex Fest. p. 33 Müll. [bis-seta].

bisextialis.full: bĭsextĭālis, e, adj. bis-sextus, containing two sextarii: olla, Marc. Emp. 15.

bisextilis.full: bĭsextĭlis, e, adj. bisextus, containing an intercalary day: annus, Isid. Orig. 6, 17, 25.

bisextus.full: bĭ-sextus (erroneously bissextus; v. bis fin.), i, m., sc. dies (bĭsextum, i, n., Censor. 20; Amm. 26, 1, 7) [bis], an intercalary day; so called, since the 24th of February = VI. Cal. Mart., was doubled: bisextus est post annos quattuor unus dies adjectus, Isid. Orig. 6, 17, 25; Dig. 50, 16, 98; 4, 4, 3, § 3; Macr. S. 1, 14; Aug. Trin. 4; Isid. Orig. 6, 17, 25-27.

bisgargitani.full: Bisgargĭtāni, ōrum, m., a people of Hispania Tarraconensis, Plin. 3, 3, 4, § 23.
bisgargitani.short: Bisgargĭtāni, ōrum, m., a people of Hispania Tarraconensis, Plin.

bisolis.full: bĭsŏlis, e, adj. bis-solea, having two (foot) soles, Edict. Diocl. p. 20.

bisomum.full: bĭsōmum, i, n. vox hibrida, from bis-σῶμα, a sarcophagus for two persons, Inscr. Orell. 8; Inscr. Rein. 20, 40; 20, 116.

bison.full: bĭson, ontis, m., = βίσων [acc. to Oppian. Cyn. 2, 155, named from the Thracian Βίστονες], a species of wild ox living in northern regions, the Urus, the humpbacked ox, bison: Bos bison, Linn.; Plin. 8, 15, 15, § 38; Sen. Hippol. 65; Mart. Spect. 23, 4; Sol. 20.

bisonus.full: bĭsŏnus, a, um, adj. bis-sono, sounding twice, Serv. ad Verg. A. 9, 618.

bispellio.full: bispellio, ōnis, m. bis-pellis, only trop., a man with two skins, a cunning man, Dig. 47, 3, 72; also written bisbel-lio, Dig. 21, 2, 31.

bissenus.full: bissēnus and bissēni, v. bis fin.

bistones.full: Bistŏnes, um, m., = Βίστονες, the Bistones, a Thracian people south of Mount Rhodope, not far from Abdera, Plin. 4, 11, 18, § 42.—In the poets, In gen., for the Thracians, Luc. 7, 569; acc. Bistonas, Val. Fl. 3, 83; Sil. 2, 76.— Derivv. Bistŏnĭus, a, um, adj., = Βιστόνιος, pertaining to the Bistones. Bistonian: plăgae. Lucr. 5, 30.— In gen., Thracian: rupes, Prop. 2 (3), 30, 36. viri, the Thracians, Ov. M. 13, 430: aqua, id. H. 2, 90: sarissae, id. P. 1, 3, 59: Minerva (as goddess of the warlike
bistones.short: Bistŏnes, um, m., = Βίστονες, the Bistones, a Thracian people south of Mount Rhodope, not far from Abdera, Plin.

bisulcilingua.full: bĭsulcĭlingua, ae, adj. bisulcuslingua, with a cloven tongue; trop., of a hypocrite, a double-tongued, deceitful person: bisulcilingua, quasi proserpens bestia, Plaut. Poen. 5, 2, 74.

bisulcus.full: bĭsulcus, a, um, adj. bis-sulcus (twofurrowed), hence, in gen., divided into two parts, two-cleft, cloven (poet. and in postAug. prose): lingua, forked, Pac. ap. Non. p. 506, 17; Ov. M. 9, 65: pedes, * Lucr. 2, 356; Ov. M. 7, 113; Plin. 11, 45, 105, § 254: ungula, a cloven hoof, id. 8, 21, 30, § 73; 10, 1, 1, § 1: cauda, id. 9, 29, 46, § 85: forcipes, id. 11, 28, 34, § 97.— Subst.: bĭsulca, ōrum, n. (sc. animalia), animals with cloven feet (opp. to the solidipedes), Plin. 11, 37, 85, § 212: corn

bisyllabus.full: bĭsyllăbus, a, um, adj. bis-syllaba, dissyllabic: sic Socer, Macer. Varr. L. L. 9, 52, 151.—Spelled bissyllăbus, Macr. Diff. 6, 8; 8, 11.

bithiae.full: Bithiae, ārum, f., the name of certain women in Scythia, said to have two pupils in each eye, Plin. 7, 2, 2, § 17.
bithiae.short: Bithiae, ārum, f., the name of certain women in Scythia, said to have two pupils in each eye, Plin.

bithynia.full: Bīthȳnĭa, ae, f., = Βιθυνία, a very fruitful province in Asia Minor, between the Propontis and the Black Sea, where the Romans carried on a considerable trade (its inhabitants were, acc. to Herod. 7, 75, Thracians, who had wandered there), now Ejalet Anadoli, Cic. Verr. 2, 5, 11, § 27; id. Agr. 2, 18, 40; id. Imp. Pomp. 2, 5; id. Fam. 13, 9, 1; 12, 13, 3; Plin. 5, 32, 43, § 148; Tac. A. 1, 74; 16, 18; Flor. 3, 5, 6 and 12; Claud. in Eutr. 2, 247; Vulg. Act. 16, 7.— Derivv. Bīthȳnĭcus, a, um, adj
bithynia.short: Bīthȳnĭa, ae, f., = Βιθυνία, a very fruitful province in Asia Minor, between the Propontis and the Black Sea, where the Romans carried on a considerable trade (its inhabitants were, acc.

bitias.full: Bĭtĭas, ae, m. A Tyrian nobleman at Dido's court, Verg. A. 1, 738.— Son of Alcanor, and a companion of Æneas, Verg. A. 9, 672; 11, 396.

bitienses.full: bītĭenses, ĭum, m. beto, those who are continually wandering about, Paul. ex Fest. p. 35 Müll.

bito2.full: Bĭto or Bĭton, ōnis, m., = Βίτων, a son of the Argive priestess Cydippe, and brother of Cleobis, distinguished for his filial affection, Cic. Tusc. 1, 47, 113; Val. Max. 5, 4, ext. 4 (cf. Herod. 1, 31).
bito2.short: Bĭto or Bĭton, ōnis, m., = Βίτων, a son of the Argive priestess Cydippe, and brother of Cleobis, distinguished for his filial affection, Cic.

bittis.full: Bittis, ĭdis, f., = Βιττίς, a woman beloved by the poet Philetas of Cos, Ov. Tr. 1, 6, 2; id. P. 3, 1, 58 Merkel (al. Battis).
bittis.short: Bittis, ĭdis, f., = Βιττίς, a woman beloved by the poet Philetas of Cos, Ov.

bituitus.full: Bituītus, i, m., a king of the Arverni, Liv. Epit. 61; Flor. 3, 2, 5; Eutr. 4, 22; Val. Max. 9, 6, 3.
bituitus.short: Bituītus, i, m., a king of the Arverni, Liv.

bitumen.full: bĭtūmen, ĭnis, n. cf. Sanscr. gatu, gum, bitumen, a kind of mineral pitch found in Palestine and Babylon, Gr. ἄτφαλτος, Plin. 35, 15, 51, § 178 sq.; Tac. H. 5, 6; 5, 17; Just. 1, 2, 7; Vitr. 2, 6; Lucr. 6, 808; Verg. G. 3, 451; Ov. M. 9, 660; 14, 792; Vitr. 8, 3, 1 sqq.: Judaicum, Veg. 1, 20, 1; 3, 56, 2; 5, 83, 3; 6, 14, 1: Apollonium, id. 6, 14, 1; Vulg. Gen. 6, 14.—For magical or religious use, Verg. E. 8, 82; Hor. Epod. 5, 82; Claud. VI. Cons. Hon. 325.

bitumineus.full: bĭtūmĭnĕus, a, um, adj. bitumen, consisting of bitumen, bituminous: vires, a poet. circumlocution for bitumen, Ov. M. 15, 350.

bitumino.full: bĭtūmĭno, āre, 1, v. a. id., to cover or impregnate with bitumen (late Lat.), Ambros. Hexaëm. 6, 9, 72; cf.: bitumino, ἀσφαλτόω, Gloss. Lab.—Hence, P. a.: bĭtū-mĭnătus, a, um, impregnated with bitumen, bituminous: aqua, Plin. 31, 6, 32, § 59.

bituminosus.full: bĭtūmĭnōsus, a, um, adj. id., abounding in bitumen, bituminous (perh. only in the two foll. exs.): terra, Vitr. 8, 3, 9: fontes, id. 8, 3, 4.

bituriges.full: Bĭtŭrĭges, um (in sing. Biturix, Luc. 1, 423), m., = Βιτούρι^γες, the Bituriges, a people in Gallia Aquitania, divided into two tribes. Bituriges Cubi, Βιτ. Κοῦβοι, Strab., the present Berry, Départ. du Cher. et de l'Indre, whose capital was Avaricum, now Bourges, Plin. 4, 19, 33, § 109; and without Cubi, Caes. B. G. 7, 5; 7, 15; Hirt. B. G. 8, 3.— Bituriges Vivisci, Βιτ. Οὐϊσκοί, Ptol., whose chief city was Burdigala, now Bordeaux, Plin. 4, 19, 33, § 108.— Sing. Biturix, one of the Bituriges, L

biuri.full: bĭūri, ōrum, m. vox hibrida, from bis-οὔρα, two-tailed, the name of rodent animals found in Campania, otherwise unknown, Plin. 30, 15, 52, § 146.

bivertex.full: bĭvertex, ĭcis, adj. bis-vertex, with two summits or peaks: Parnassus, Stat. Th. 1, 628: mons, Sid. Carm. 15, 9.

bivira.full: bĭvĭra, ae, f. bis-vir, a woman married to a second husband (opp. univira), Varr. ap. Non. p. 79, 21 sq. (Sat. Menipp. 48, 5).

bivius.full: bĭvĭus, a, um, adj. bis-via, having two ways or passages (rare; not in Cic.): fauces, Verg. A. 11, 516.—So, calles, Val. Fl. 5, 395: di, deae, worshipped at cross-roads, Inscr. Orell. 2105.—Hence, substt. bĭvĭi (sc. di), Inscr. Orell. 389; 2104.— bĭvĭum, i, n., a place with two ways, or where two ways meet. Lit.: in bivio portae, Verg. A. 9, 238: ad bivia consistere, Liv. 38, 45, 8; Plin. 6, 28, 32, § 144; Vulg. Marc. 11, 4.— Trop.: bivium nobis ad culturam dedit natura, experientiam et imitatio

bizone.full: Bizōnē, ēs, f., a town in Thrace, Mel. 2, 2, 5; Plin. 4, 11, 18, § 44.
bizone.short: Bizōnē, ēs, f., a town in Thrace, Mel.

bizya.full: Bizўa, ae, f., a town in Thrace, once the royal residence, Plin. 4, 11, 18, § 47.
bizya.short: Bizўa, ae, f., a town in Thrace, once the royal residence, Plin.

blachnon.full: blachnon (blech-), i, n., = βλῆχνον, a kind of fern (filix), Plin. 27, 9, 55, § 78.
blachnon.short: blachnon (blech-), i, n., = βλῆχνον, a kind of fern (filix), Plin.

blactero.full: blactĕro, āre, v. n. cf.: balo, blatio, to bleat, of the ram, Auct. Carm. Philom. 56.

blaesus1.full: blaesus, a, um, adj., = βλαισός, lisping, stammering, hesitating in utterance, speaking indistinctly (most freq. in poetry): blaesus, cui litterae sibilantes (s, z) molestae sunt vitioseque pronunciantur, Popm. Differ. p. 133; Ov. A. A. 3, 294; Mart. 10, 65, 10.—Of a parrot: sonus, Ov. Am. 2, 6, 24. —Hence, subst.: blaesus, i, m., one who lisps, Dig. 21, 1, 10.—Of intoxicated persons, Juv. 15, 48; cf. Ov. A. A. 1, 598.
blaesus1.short: blaesus, a, um, adj., = βλαισός, lisping, stammering, hesitating in utterance, speaking indistinctly (most freq.

blaesus2.full: Blaesus, i, m., a cognomen in the Sempronian gens, Stat. S. 2, 1, 191; Tac. A. 1, 16; 1, 18; 1, 21 al.; 6, 40.—Hence, Blaesĭānus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to a Blœsus, Mart. 8, 38, 14.
blaesus2.short: Blaesus, i, m., a cognomen in the Sempronian gens, Stat.

blanda.full: Blanda, ae. f. A maritime town in Lucania, now Maratea, Mel. 2, 4, 9; Plin. 3, 5, 10, § 72 (in Liv. 24, 20, 5, Blandae, ārum).— A small maritime town in Hispania Tarraconensis, now Blanes, Mel. 2, 6, 5 (in Plin. 3, 3, 4, § 22, Blandae, ārum).

blande.full: blandē, adv., v. blandus fin. b.

blandicella.full: blandĭcella, ōrum, n. dim., coaxing or flattering words, Paul. ex Fest. p. 35 Müll.

blandicule.full: blandĭcŭlē, adv. of an adj. not in use, blandiculus [blandus], flatteringly, soothingly, courteously: respondere, App. M. 10, p. 252.

blandidicus.full: blandĭdĭcus, a, um, adj. blandusdico, speaking soothingly, coaxingly, or kindly, Plaut. Poen. 1, 1, 10.

blandificus.full: blandĭfĭcus, a, um, adj. blandusfacio, flattering, soothing: fax, Mart. Cap. 9, § 888.

blandifluus.full: blandĭflūus, a, um, adj. blandus-fluo, flowing or diffusing itself sweetly, pleasantly: odor, Ven. Carm. 11, 10, 10.

blandiloquens.full: blandĭlŏquens, entis, adj. blandus loquor, speaking courteously, flatteringly, or soothingly, Laber. ap. Macr. S. 2, 7, 3.

blandiloquentia.full: blandĭlŏquentĭa, ae, f. blandilo quens, coaxing language, softness of expression, Enn. ap. Cic. N D. 3, 25, 65 (Trag. v. 227 Rib., or v. 305 Vahl.).

blandiloquentulus.full: blandĭlŏquentŭlus, a, um, adj. dim. [id.], speaking caressingly, fair-spoken, Plaut. Trin. 2, 1, 13.

blandiloquium.full: blandĭlŏquĭum, ii, n. blandus-loquor, soft words, flattering speech: insidiosum, Aug. Ep. ad Hier. 19, 4.

blandiloquus.full: blandĭlŏquus, a, um, adj. id., speaking smoothly or flatteringly, fair-spoken: ut blandiloqu'est! Hei mihi metuo, Plaut. Bacch. 5, 2, 54: vox, Sen. Agam. 289.

blandimentum.full: blandīmentum, i, n. blandior. flattering words, blandishment, complimentary speech, flattery (class.; most freq. in plur. and in Tac.): nec eam (virtutem) minis aut blandimentis corrupta deseret, Cic. Tusc. 5, 31, 87: pessum dedisti me blandimentis tuis, Plaut. Rud. 2, 6, 23; id. Truc. 2, 2, 63: multa igitur blandimenta plebi per id tempus ab senatu data, Liv. 2, 9, 6: captus blandimentis, Plin. Ep. 2, 19, 4: per blandimenta juvenem aggredi, Tac. A. 13, 13; 12, 64: muliebribus blandimentis infec

blandio.full: blandĭo, īre, 4 (act. collat. form of blandior), to caress, coax, court: cur ego blandirem (mulierem), App. Mag. 87, p. 328 fin.—Part. pass.: blanditusque labor molli curabitur arte, Verr. ap. Prisc. 792 P.: blandiendo duce nutrivit malum, Sen. Hippol. 135.

blandior.full: blandĭor, ītus, 4, v. dep. blandus. Prop., lit., to cling caressingly to one, to fawn upon, to flatter, soothe, caress, fondle, coax (class.). With dat.: matri interfectae infante miserabiliter blandiente, Plin. 34, 8, 19, § 88.— With inter se, Plin. 10, 37, 52, § 109.— With ut and subj.: Hannibalem pueriliter blandientem patri ut duceretur in Hispaniam, Liv. 21, 1, 4.— Absol.: cessit immanis tibi blandienti Janitor aulae Cerberus, Hor. C. 3, 11, 15: tantusque in eo vigor, et dulcis quidam bland

blanditer.full: blandĭter, adv., v. blandus fin. a.

blanditia.full: blandĭtĭa, ae (blandĭtĭes, ēi, in abl., App. M. 9, p. 230, 11), f. blandus. The quality of one blandus; a caressing, flattering, flattery (mostly in an honorable sense; cf. on the contrary, assentatio and adulatio; class in prose and poetry; most freq. in plur.). Sing.: haec meretrix meum erum blanditiā intulit in pauperiem, Plaut. Truc. 2, 7, 21: viscus merus vostra'st blanditia, id. Bacch. 1, 1, 16: in cive excelso atque homine nobili blanditiam, ostentationem, ambitionem notam esse levitatis,
blanditia.short: blandĭtĭa, ae (blandĭtĭes, ēi, in abl., App.

blanditim.full: blandītim, adv. blanditus, from blandior, in a flattering, caressing manner, Lucr. 2, 173.

blanditor.full: blandītor, ōris, m. blandior, a flatterer (late Lat.), Itin. Alex. M. 39 (90).

blanditus.full: blandītus, a, um, v. blandior, P. a.

blandulus.full: blandŭlus, a, um, adj. dim. [blandus], pleasing, charming: animula vagula, blandula, Hadrian. Carm. ap. Spart. Hadr. 25.

blandus.full: blandus, a, um, adj. for mlandus; akin to μείλιχος, mollis, mulier; Goth. milds; Engl. mild, of a smooth tongue, flattering, fawning, caressing (class and very freq.). Lit.: blanda es parum, Plaut. Cas. 3, 3, 21: nemini credo qui large blandu'st dives pauperi, id. Aul. 2, 2, 19: ut unus omnium homo te vivat numquam quisquam blandior, Ter. Hec. 5, 4, 21: scis me minime esse blandum, Cic. Att. 12, 5, 4: unum te puto minus blandum esse quam me, id. ib. 12, 3, 1: blandum amicum a vero secernere, id.

blapsigonia.full: blapsĭgŏnĭa, ae, f., = βλαψιγονία, a disease which prevents bees from breeding, Plin. 11, 19, 20, § 64.
blapsigonia.short: blapsĭgŏnĭa, ae, f., = βλαψιγονία, a disease which prevents bees from breeding, Plin.

blascon.full: Blascōn, ōnis, f., = Βλάσκων, an island off the coast of Gaul, Plin. 3, 5, 11, § 79; Avien. Or. Mar. 600.
blascon.short: Blascōn, ōnis, f., = Βλάσκων, an island off the coast of Gaul, Plin.

blasphemabilis.full: blasphēmābĭlis, e, adj. blasphemo (eccl. Lat.), that deserves reproach, censurable, Tert. Cult. Fem. 12.

blasphematio.full: blasphēmātĭo, ōnis, f. id. (eccl. Lat.), a reviling, Tert. Cult. Fem. 12.

blasphemia.full: blasphēmĭa, ae, f. (blasphēmĭ-um, ii, n., Prud. Psych. 715), = βλασφημία (eccl. Lat.), a reviling, slander, Vulg. Isa. 51, 7; towards God, blasphemy, Hier. Ep. 62, n. 2; Aug. Verb. Dom. Serm. 11; 14; 15; Vulg. 2 Par. 32, 17; id. Matt. 26, 65.

blasphemo.full: blasphēmo, āre, v. a., = βλασφημέω (eccl. Lat.), to revile, reproach, Vulg. 1 Par. 20, 7; God and divine things, to blaspheme: Christum, Prud. Apoth. 415: nomen Domini, Tert. adv. Jud. 13 fin.; Vulg. Lev. 24, 11; id. Matt. 9. 3; 26, 65.

blasphemus.full: blasphēmus, a, um, adj., = βλάσφημος (eccl. Lat.), reviling, defaming: satelles, Prud. στεφ. 1, 75; and subst., of God and divine things, blasphemer, Tert. Res Carn. 26; Hier. Ep. 9; Vulg. Lev. 24, 14 (as transl. of the Heb. ); id. 1 Tim. 1, 13.

blateas.full: blateas bullas luti ex itineribus, aut quod calceamentorum soleis eraditur appellabant, Paul. ex Fest. p. 34 Müll.
blateas.short: blateas bullas luti ex itineribus, aut quod calceamentorum soleis eraditur appellabant, Paul.

blateratio.full: blătĕrātĭo, ōnis, f. blatero, a babbling (late Lat.), Auct. Idiom. p. 576, 28 Keil.

blateratus.full: blătĕrātus, ūs, m. id., a babbling, prating (post-class.), Sid. Ep. 9, 11 fin.: canini, whining, Mart. Cap. 9, § 999.

blatero1.full: blătĕro, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. kindred with βλάξ, simple, stupid, Paul. ex Fest. p. 34 Müll.; cf. blactero. To talk idly or foolishly, to babble, prate (colloq. and mostly ante- and post-class.), Pac. ap. Fulg. p. 561, 17; Afran. ap. Non. p. 78, 32: illud memento, ne quid in primis blateres, id. ib.; Plaut. ap. Non. p. 44, 15: desine blaterare, Caecil. ap. Non. p. 79, 2: cum magno blateras clamore, furisque, * Hor. S. 2, 7, 35; Gell. 1, 15, 17: his et similibus blateratis, App. M. 4, p. 153, 18; s

blatero2.full: blătĕro, ōnis, m. 1. blatero, a babbler, prater, acc. to Gell. 1, 15 fin.

blatio.full: blătĭo, īre, v. a. kindred with blatero, to utter foolish things, to babble, prate (anteclass. and late Lat.): nugas blatis, Plaut. Am. 2, 1, 79; so id. Curc. 3, 82; id. Ep. 3, 1, 13; Tert. Pall. 2; cf. Non. p. 44, 11 sq.

blatta1.full: blatta, ae, f., an insect that shuns the light; of several kinds, the cockroach, chafer, moth, etc., Plin. 29, 6, 39, § 139; 11, 28, 34, § 99: lucifuga, Verg. G. 4, 243 (per noctem vagans, Serv.); cf. Col. 9, 7, 5; Pall. 1, 37, 4; Hor. S. 2, 3, 119; Mart. 14, 37; cf. Voss, Verg. l. l.—On account of its mean appearance: amore cecidi tamquam blatta in pelvim, Laber. ap. Non. p. 543, 27.
blatta1.short: blatta, ae, f., an insect that shuns the light;

blatta2.full: blatta, ae, f.: blatta θρόμβος αἵματος, a clot of blood, Gloss.—Hence, (Access. form blattea, Ven. Carm. 2, 3, 19.) Purple (similar in color to flowing blood; cf. Salmas. Vop. Aur. 46, and Plin. 9, 38, 62, § 135; late Lat.): purpura, quae blatta, vel oxyblatta, vel hyacinthina dicitur, Cod. Th. 4, 40, 1: serica, ib. 10, 20, 18: blattam Tyrus defert, Sid. Carm. 5, 48; Lampr. Elag. 33; Cassiod. Var. Ep. 1, 2.
blatta2.short: blatta, ae, f.: blatta θρόμβος αἵματος, a clot of blood, Gloss.—Hence, (Access.

blattarius.full: blattārĭus, a, um, adj. 1. blatta, pertaining to the moth: balnea, for moths, i. e. dark bathing-rooms (so called from the dislike of the moth to the light), Sen. Ep. 86, 7; cf. Plin. 11, 28, 34, § 99.— Subst.: blattārĭa, ae, f. (sc. herba), moth-mullein: Verbascum blattaria, Linn.; Plin. 25, 9, 60, § 108.

blatteus.full: blattĕus, a, um, adj. 2. blatta, II., purple-colored, purple: tunicae, Vop. Aur. 46, 4: pallium, id. 45, 5: funes, Eutr. 7, 9.

blattiarius.full: blattĭārĭus, ii, m. 2. blatta, II., a dyer in purple, Cod. Th. 13, 4, 2 dub.

blattifer.full: blattĭfer, ĕra, ĕrum, adj. 2. blatta, II., -fero, wearing purple, clothed in purple: senatus, Sid. Carm. Ep. 9, 16.

blaudenius.full: Blaudēnĭus, a, um, adj., of the town Blaudus (Βλαῦδος, Strab.), in Phrygia Major: Zeuxis, Cic. Q. Fr. 1, 2, 2, § 4.
blaudenius.short: Blaudēnĭus, a, um, adj., of the town Blaudus (Βλαῦδος, Strab.), in Phrygia Major: Zeuxis, Cic.

blechon.full: blēchon, ōnis, m., = βλήχων, wild pennyroyal, Plin. 20, 14, 55, § 156.
blechon.short: blēchon, ōnis, m., = βλήχων, wild pennyroyal, Plin.

blemmyae.full: Blemmўae or Blĕmўae, ārum (also Blemyes, Avien. Descr. Orb. 329; and Blemyi, ōrum, Prisc. Perieg. 209), m., = Βλέμυες, an Ethiopian people, Mel. 1, 4, 4; 1, 4, 8 fin.; Vop. Aur. 33, 4; Prob. 17; Claud Nil. 19; acc. to the fable, without head and eyes, and with the mouth in the breast, Mel. 8 fin.; Plin. 5, 8, 8, § 46; Isid. Orig. 11, 3, 17; Sol. 3, 4.
blemmyae.short: Blemmўae or Blĕmўae, ārum (also Blemyes, Avien.

blendius.full: blendĭus (in MSS. and edd. also blennĭus, corresponding more nearly to the Greek), ii, m. (blendĕa, ae, f., Plin. 1 Ind. libr. 32, 32), = βλέννος Oppian., βέλεννος Athen., an inferior kind of seafish, Plin. 32, 9, 32, § 102.

blennus.full: blennus, i, m., = βλεννός, a blockhead, dolt, simpleton: stulti, stolidi, fatui, fungi, bardi, blenni, buccones, Plaut. Bacch. 5, 1, 2; cf. Paul. ex Fest. p. 35 Müll.
blennus.short: blennus, i, m., = βλεννός, a blockhead, dolt, simpleton: stulti, stolidi, fatui, fungi, bardi, blenni, buccones, Plaut.

blepharon.full: Blĕphărōn, ōnis, m., = Βλεφάρων [eye-lids], a comic character in the Amphitruo of Plautus.
blepharon.short: Blĕphărōn, ōnis, m., = Βλεφάρων [eye-lids], a comic character in the Amphitruo of Plautus.

bliteus.full: blĭtĕus, a, um, adj. blitum, tasteless, insipid, silly, foolish, useless (ante-class.), Plaut. Truc. 4, 4, 1: belua, Laber. ap. Non. p. 80, 26.

blitum.full: blĭtum, i, n. (blĭtus, i, m., Pall. Mart. 9, 17: blitus seritur is written prob. from the corrupted or misunderstood blitūseritur, or perh. the obscure blitus eritur of the MSS.), = βλίτον, a vegetable, in itself tasteless, but used as a salad, orache, or spinach: Spinacia oleracea, Linn.; Plaut. Ps. 3, 2, 26; Varr. ap. Non. p. 550, 15; Plin. 20, 22, 93, § 252; Pall. Mart. 4, 9 fin.; Paul. ex Fest. p. 348 Müll.; Isid. Orig. 17, 10, 15.

blossius.full: Blossĭus, ii, m., a Roman proper name; esp., C. Blossius of Cumœ, a Stoic and a follower of Ti. Gracchus, Cic. Lael. 11, 37; Val. Max. 4, 7, 1; cf. Cic. Agr. 2, 34, 93.
blossius.short: Blossĭus, ii, m., a Roman proper name;

boa.full: bŏa (also bŏva in the MSS. of Pliny and Festus), ae, f. bos; cf. βουβών, a large Italian serpent: in Italiă appellatae bovae in tantam amplitudinem exeuntes ut divo Claudio principe occisae in Vaticano solidus in alvo spectatus infans, Plin. 8, 14, 14, § 37; 30, 14, 47, § 138 sq.; Sol. 2; acc. to Paul. ex Fest. p. 30 Müll., a water-serpent, so called because it milked cows, Sol. 2, 33; or because it could swallow an ox, quas boas vocant, ab eo quod tam grandes sint ut boves gluttire soleant, Hie

boarius.full: bŏārĭus (bŏvārĭus, Cic. Aem. Scaur. 11, 23), a, um, adj. bos, of or relating to neat cattle: NEGOTIANTES, Inscr. Orell. 913: forum, the cattle market at Rome (in the eighth district of the city, near the Circus Maximus): in foro bovario, Cic. Aem. Scaur. 11, 23; Paul. ex Fest. p. 30, 5 Müll.; acc. to Ov. F. 6, 478, so called from the large brazen statue of an ox placed there; cf. Plin. 34, 3, 5, § 10; Tac. A. 12, 24; acc. to fable, because Hercules fed here the herd which he took from Cacus, Pro

boatus.full: bŏātus, ūs, m. boo, a loud crying, a bellowing or roaring: praeconis, App. M. 3, p. 130, 17; Aus. Idyll. 20, 2; Mart. Cap. 2, § 98.

bocchar.full: Bocchar, ăris (in MSS. also Boc-chor, ŏris), m., a king of Mauritania at the time of the second Punic war, Liv. 29, 30, 1; cf. id. 29, 32, 1.—Hence, poet. for an African, in gen., Juv. 5, 90.

boccharum.full: Bocchărum, i, n., a town on the larger of the Balearic islands, Plin. 3, 5, 11, § 77.
boccharum.short: Bocchărum, i, n., a town on the larger of the Balearic islands, Plin.

bocchus.full: Bocchus, i, m., a king of Mauritania, father-in-law of Jugurtha, whom he gave up bound to Sulla, Sall. J. 19, 7; 80; 81; 83; 97; 101 sqq.; Vell. 2, 12, 1; Val. Max. 8, 14, 4; Flor. 3, 1, 15; Mel. 1, 5, 5; Plin. 5, 2, 1, § 19; 8, 5, 5, § 15.— A plant, so called in honor of him: Βώχ, βοτάνης εἶδος, Hesych.; Verg. Cul. 404.— A king of Mauritania, son of the former, Auct. B. Afr 25.
bocchus.short: Bocchus, i, m., a king of Mauritania, father-in-law of Jugurtha, whom he gave up bound to Sulla, Sall.

bodincus.full: Bodincus, i, m. Ligurian, = bottomless, the Ligurian name of the river Po, Plin. 3, 16, 20, § 122.

bodotria.full: Bŏdotrĭa, ae, f., = Βοδέρια, Ptol., a bay in Scotland on which the present Edinburgh is situated, now Firth of Forth, Tac. Agr. 23.
bodotria.short: Bŏdotrĭa, ae, f., = Βοδέρια, Ptol., a bay in Scotland on which the present Edinburgh is situated, now Firth of Forth, Tac.

boduognatus.full: Boduognātus, i, m., a leader of the Nervii, Caes. B. G. 2, 23.
boduognatus.short: Boduognātus, i, m., a leader of the Nervii, Caes.

boebe.full: Boebē, ēs, f., = Βοίβη. A village in the Thessalian province Pelasgiotis, on the shore of Lake Bœbeïs, Ov. M. 7, 231.— Derivv. Lacus Boebēis (Βοιβηῒς λίμνη, Hom. Il. 2, 711), Lake Bœbeïs, now Karla, Plin. 4, 8, 15, § 30; because in the neighborhood of Ossa: Ossaea, Luc. 7, 176; and because Minerva was said to have once bathed her feet in it (cf. Hesiod. Fragm. 50, Göttl. in Strab. 9, p. 640): sanctae Boebeidos undae, Prop. 2, 2, 11: pinguis, Val. Fl. 1, 449.— Boebēius, a, um, adj., Bœbeian, = Th

boeotarches.full: Boeōtarches, ae, m., = Βοιωτάρχης, one of the chief magistrates in Bœotia, a Bœotarch, Liv. 33, 27, 8; 42, 43, 7 al.
boeotarches.short: Boeōtarches, ae, m., = Βοιωτάρχης, one of the chief magistrates in Bœotia, a Bœotarch, Liv.

boeotia.full: Boeōtĭa, ae, f., = Βοιωτἰα. Bœotia, a district of Greece proper, whose capital was Thebes, the birthplace of Bacchus and Hercules, Plin. 4, 7, 12, § 25; Cic. N. D. 3, 19, 49; Ov. M. 2, 239; Mel. 2, 3, 4; acc. to fable, so called either after Apollo's cow (Βοῦς), Ov. M. 3, 13, or from Bœotus, the son of Neptune, Hyg. Fab. 186.—Its inhabitants were noted for their stupidity, Cic. Fat. 4; Nep. Alcib. 11, 3; id. Epam. 5, 2; Hor. Ep. 2, 1, 244; Liv. 42, 43 sqq.; Tert. Anim. c. 20; cf. the Comm. upon

boethius.full: Bŏēthius, ii, m.: Anicius Manlius Torquatus Severinus, a distinguished philosopher and theologian of the post-classic period under Theodoric; born about A. D. 470; beheaded in prison (A. D. 524), where he composed his most distinguished work, De consolatione philosophiae libri V.
boethius.short: Bŏēthius, ii, m.: Anicius Manlius Torquatus Severinus, a distinguished philosopher and theologian of the post-classic period under Theodoric;

boethus1.full: bŏēthus, i, m., = βοηθός, the aid or assistant of a scribe (pure Lat. adjutor), Cod. Valent. 10, 69, 4.
boethus1.short: bŏēthus, i, m., = βοηθός, the aid or assistant of a scribe (pure Lat.

boethus2.full: Bŏēthus, nom. prop. A distinguished sculptor and engraver in silver, Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 14, § 32; Plin. 33, 12, 55, §§ 154 and 155.— A Stoic philosopher, Cic. Div. 1, 8, 13; 2, 21, 47.

bogud.full: Bogud (in MSS. also Bogus; cf. Oud. ad Hirt. B. Alex. 62), ŭdis, m., son of Bocchus and king of Mauritania, captured and slain bg Agrippa B.C. 31, Cic. Fam. 10, 32, 1; Liv. Fragm. lib. 112 ap. Prisc. p. 687 P.; Auct. B. Afr. 23; Suet Caes. 54; Hirt. B. Alex. 59 and 62.—Hence, Bogŭdiāna Mauretania, that was ruled by Bogud, Plin. 5, 2, 1, § 19.

boiae.full: bŏiae, ārum, f. bos, a collar for the neck, κλοιός (orig. of leather; hence the name; but later of wood or iron), Fest. p. 29; Isid. Orig. 5, 27, 12: boia κλοιός, Gloss. Vet.: pedicae boiae, Plaut. As. 3, 2, 5: attrita boiis colla, Prud. Psych. praef. 34.—For boiam terere, v. Boii fin.

boii.full: Bŏii, ōrum, m., = Βοῖοι Polyb., Βόϊοι Strab., a people in Gallia Lugdunensis, now the Bourbonnais, Départ. de l'Allier, Caes. B. G. 1, 5; 1, 25; 1, 28; Liv. 5, 35, 2 et saep.; Plin. 4, 18, 32, § 107; 3, 15, 20, § 116; Tac. G. 28; their chief town, or, acc. to others, their country, was Boia, ae, f., Caes. B. G. 7, 14.—A part of the Boii went to Upper Italy, and occupied the region of the present Parma and Modena, Plin. 3, 17, 21, § 124; Liv. 5, 34 sqq.; 10, 26 sqq.; Front. Strat. 1, 2, 7.—Hence,
boii.short: Bŏii, ōrum, m., = Βοῖοι Polyb., Βόϊοι Strab., a people in Gallia Lugdunensis, now the Bourbonnais, Départ.

boiorix.full: Boiŏrix, ĭgis, m., a king of the Boii, Liv. 34, 46, 4.— A king of the Cimbri, Liv. Epit. 67; Flor. 3, 3.
boiorix.short: Boiŏrix, ĭgis, m., a king of the Boii, Liv.

bola.full: Bōla, ae (in Liv. 4, 49, 6 sq. Bōlae, ārum), f., = Βῶλα, a very ancient town of the Æqui, in Latium, now Poli, Verg. A. 6, 775.—Hence, Bōlānus, a, um, adj., of or pertaining to Bola: ager, Liv. 4, 49, 11.— And Bōlāni, ōrum, m., the inhabitants of Bola, Liv. 4, 49, 3; Plin. 3, 5, 9, § 69.

bolbitinus.full: Bolbitīnus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to the city of Bolbitine, now Rosetta, in Lower Egypt: ostium, the Rosetta mouth of the Nile, Plin. 5, 10, 11, § 64.—Later collat. form Bolbitĭcus, a, um: ostium, Mel. 1, 9, 9; Amm. 22, 15, 10.
bolbitinus.short: Bolbitīnus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to the city of Bolbitine, now Rosetta, in Lower Egypt: ostium, the Rosetta mouth of the Nile, Plin.

bolbiton.full: bolbĭtŏn, i, n., = βόλβιτον, the dung of cattle, Plin. 28, 17, 68, § 232.
bolbiton.short: bolbĭtŏn, i, n., = βόλβιτον, the dung of cattle, Plin.

bolbulae.full: Bolbŭlae, ārum, f., a group of small islands near Cyprus, Plin. 5, 31, 38, § 137.
bolbulae.short: Bolbŭlae, ārum, f., a group of small islands near Cyprus, Plin.

boletaria.full: bōlētārĭa, ĭum (post-class. in sing.: bōlētar, Apic. 2, 1; 5, 2; 8, 7; Treb. Claud. 17; cf. altaria), n. boletus, a vessel for mushrooms, Mart. 14, 101 lemm.— In gen., a vessel for cooking and eating in, Apic. l. l.

boletus.full: bōlētus, i, m., = βωλίτης, the best kind of mushrooms, Plin. 22, 22, 46, § 92; Plaut. Curc. 5, 2, 14; Mart. 1, 21; 14, 101; Juv. 14, 8; much valued by the Romans, Mart. 3, 60; 13, 48.—The emperor Claudius is said to have been poisoned by them, Plin. l. l.: Tac. A. 12, 67 dub.; Suet. Claud. 44; Juv. 5, 147.
boletus.short: bōlētus, i, m., = βωλίτης, the best kind of mushrooms, Plin.

bolis.full: bŏlis, ĭdis, f., = βολίς (a missile, an arrow), a fiery meteor of the form of an arrow, Plin. 2, 26, 25, § 96.
bolis.short: bŏlis, ĭdis, f., = βολίς (a missile, an arrow), a fiery meteor of the form of an arrow, Plin.

bolites.full: bŏlītes, ae, m., = βολίτης, the root of the plant lychnis, Plin. 21, 26, 98, § 171.
bolites.short: bŏlītes, ae, m., = βολίτης, the root of the plant lychnis, Plin.

boloe.full: bōloe (dissyl.), = βῶλοι (clods of earth), a kind of precious stones, Plin. 37, 10, 55, § 150.
boloe.short: bōloe (dissyl.), = βῶλοι (clods of earth), a kind of precious stones, Plin.

bolonae.full: bŏlōnae, ārum, m. from βόλος and ὠνέομαι. A draught of fishes set to sale (post-class.), Don. Ter. Eun. 2, 2, 26.— Dealers in fish, fish-mongers (postclass.), Gloss. Isid.; Arn. 2, p. 70.

bolus.full: bŏlus, i, m., = βόλος, a throw or cast (ante- and post-class.; cf. jactus). Lit. Of dice in gaming, a throw: si vis tribus bolis... Th. Quin tu in malam crucem cum bolis, cum bulbis, Plaut. Curc. 5, 2, 13: nimis lepide jecisti bolum, id. Rud. 2, 2, 30: enumerare bolos, Aus. Prof. 1, 26.— A cast of the net in fishing; and meton., the cast, i. e. the draught of fishes, the haul: bolum emere, Suet. Rhet. 1.— Trop., gain, profit, advantage; a haul, winning, piece of fortune, etc.: primumdum merces a
bolus.short: bŏlus, i, m., = βόλος, a throw or cast (ante- and post-class.;

bombax.full: bombax, interj., = βομβάξ (v. Eustath. Od. p. 1718, a), an exclamation of real or affected surprise, indeed! strange! Ca. Fur. Ba. Babae. Ps. Fugitive. Ba. Bombax, Plaut. Ps. 1, 3, 131 Lambin.

bombinator.full: bombĭnātor, ōris, m., the buzzer, hummer, of the bee, Mart. Cap. 9, § 999 Kopp. (al. bombitat ore).
bombinator.short: bombĭnātor, ōris, m., the buzzer, hummer, of the bee, Mart.

bombio.full: bombio, īre, = βομβῶ, to buzz, hum, Vet. Gloss.
bombio.short: bombio, īre, = βομβῶ, to buzz, hum, Vet.

bombito.full: bombīto, āre, v. n. bombus; cf. Gr. βομβῶ, to buzz, hum; of bees (cf.: bombio, bombitatio, bombus), Auct. Carm. Phil. 36; Mart. Cap. 9, § 999 Eyssenh.

bombizatio.full: bombĭzātĭo, ōnis, f., the buzzing of bees: est sonus apium ab ipso sonitu dictus: ut mugitus boum, hinnitus equorum, Paul. ex Fest. p. 30, 2.
bombizatio.short: bombĭzātĭo, ōnis, f., the buzzing of bees: est sonus apium ab ipso sonitu dictus: ut mugitus boum, hinnitus equorum, Paul.

bombomachides.full: Bombŏmăchĭdes (or Bumb-, Ritschl), ae, m., a name formed in ridicule of a boasting soldier, from bombus = βόμβος and μάχομαι, Plaut. Mil. 1, 1, 14.
bombomachides.short: Bombŏmăchĭdes (or Bumb-, Ritschl), ae, m., a name formed in ridicule of a boasting soldier, from bombus = βόμβος and μάχομαι, Plaut.

bombos.full: Bombŏs, i, m., = Βόμβος, a river of Cilicia, Plin. 5, 27, 22, § 93.
bombos.short: Bombŏs, i, m., = Βόμβος, a river of Cilicia, Plin.

bombus.full: bombus, i, m., = βόμβος, a hollow, deep sound, a booming, humming, buzzing: Ennius sonum pedum bombum pedum dixit, Fortun. Dial. (v. Enn. p. 183 fin. Vahl.); of bees; of a horn; of the clapping of hands: si (apes) intus faciunt bombum, Varr. R. R. 3, 16, 32: cum tuba... mugit, Et reboat raucum regio cita barbara bombum, Lucr. 4, 546: raucisonos efflabant cornua bombos, Cat. 64, 263: torva mimalloneis inplerunt cornua bombis, Pers. 1, 99 Coningt. ad loc.; Mart. Cap. 1, § 67; 2, § 197: organorum,
bombus.short: bombus, i, m., = βόμβος, a hollow, deep sound, a booming, humming, buzzing: Ennius sonum pedum bombum pedum dixit, Fortun.

bombyciae.full: bombȳcĭae hărundĭnes = βομβυκίας κάλαμος (Theophr. H. P. 4, 12), reeds suitable for flutes, βόμβυξ (v. Lid. and Scott, s. v.), Plin. 16, 36, 66, § 170.

bombycinus.full: bombȳcĭnus, a, um, adj. bombyx, of silk, silken (cf. sericus): vestis, Plin. 11, 22, 26, § 76: panniculus, Juv. 6, 260: taenia, Mart. 14, 24; Dig. 34, 2, 23, § 1.—Subst.: bombȳcĭna, ōrum, n., silk garments, Mart. 11, 50, 5; 8, 68, 7; App. M. 8, p. 214, 6.—And bombȳcĭnum, i, n., a silk texture or web, Isid. Orig. 19, 22, 13.

bombylis.full: bombȳlis, is, f., = βομβυλίς, the silkworm in its chrysalis state, Plin. 11, 22, 26, § 76.—Collat. form bombȳlĭus, ii, m., = βομβύλιος, Ambros. Hexaëm. 5, 23, 77.
bombylis.short: bombȳlis, is, f., = βομβυλίς, the silkworm in its chrysalis state, Plin.

bombyx.full: bombyx, ȳcis, m. (f., Plin. 11, 23, 27; Tert. Pall. 3), = βόμβυξ. The silk-worm, Plin. 11, 22, 25, § 75 sqq.; Mart. 8, 33, 16; Serv. ad Verg. G. 2, 121; Isid. Orig. 12, 5, 8; 19, 27, 5.— Meton. That which is made of silk, a silken garment, silk: Arabius, Arabian (the best), Prop. 2, 3, 15: Assyria bombyx, Plin. 11, 23, 27, § 78.— In gen., for any fine fibre, e. g. cotton, Plin. 19, 1, 2, § 14.

bomilcar.full: Bŏmilcar, ăris, m. A Carthaginian general, contemporary with Agathocles, Just. 22, 7, 8.— One of Hannibal's generals, Liv. 23, 41, 10; 24, 36, 7 al.— A companion of Jugurtha, afterwards guilty of rebellion, and put to death by him, Sall. J. 35; 61; 62; 70 sqq.

bomonicae.full: Bōmŏnīcae, ārum, m., = βωμονεῖκαι, the Lacedœmonian youths who allowed themselves to be whipped at the altar of Artemis Orthia, in order to gain the honor of firmness, Hyg. Fab. 261; Serv. ad Verg. A. 2, 116.
bomonicae.short: Bōmŏnīcae, ārum, m., = βωμονεῖκαι, the Lacedœmonian youths who allowed themselves to be whipped at the altar of Artemis Orthia, in order to gain the honor of firmness, Hyg.

bona.full: Bŏna Dea (Dīva), the good goddess, worshipped by the women of Rome as the goddess of chastity and fertility. No man was permitted to enter her temple; but in later times it became the resort of unchaste women, and the scene of license, Macr. S. 1, 12, 21 sqq.; Ov. A. A. 3, 244; cf. also id. ib. 3, 637; Juv. 2, 84 sq.; 6, 314. Clodius invaded this sanctuary, and is hence called by Cicero the priest of the Bona Dea, Cic. Att. 2, 4, 2; id. Har. Resp. 17, 37.
bona.short: Bŏna Dea (Dīva), the good goddess, worshipped by the women of Rome as the goddess of chastity and fertility.

bonasus.full: bŏnāsus, i, m., = βόνασος, a species of bull in Pœonia, with the hair of a horse, and with horns unfit for fighting, hence saving itself by flight, Plin. 8, 15, 16, § 40; Sol. 40; cf. Aristot. H. A. 9, 45.
bonasus.short: bŏnāsus, i, m., = βόνασος, a species of bull in Pœonia, with the hair of a horse, and with horns unfit for fighting, hence saving itself by flight, Plin.

bone.full: bŏnĕ, adv., = bene, formerly read in Lucr. 2, 7; 4, 572; 6, 998, by Gifan. after some ancient MSS.; now replaced by bene.
bone.short: bŏnĕ, adv., = bene, formerly read in Lucr.

bonifacies.full: bŏnĭfăcies, = εὐπρόσωπος, of a handsome face, Gloss. Gr. Lat.
bonifacies.short: bŏnĭfăcies, = εὐπρόσωπος, of a handsome face, Gloss.

bonifatus.full: bŏnĭfātus, = εὔμοιρος, lucky, fortunate, Gloss. Gr. Lat.

bonimoris.full: bŏnĭmōris, = καλότροπος, well-mannered, Gloss. Gr. Lat.

bonitas.full: bŏnĭtas, ātis, f. bonus, the good quality of a thing, goodness, excellence (cf. Caes. B. G. 1, 28 Herz.; class., but mostly in prose). Of concrete objects: bonitas praediorum, Cic. Rosc. Am. 7, 20: agrorum, id. Agr. 2, 16, 41; Caes. B. G. 1, 28: agri aut oppidi, Cic. Agr. 2, 28, 76: praediorum, id. Rosc. Am. 7, 20; Dig. 50, 16, 86: terrae, Lucr. 5, 1247: soli, Quint. 2, 19, 2: aquae, Phaedr. 4, 9, 8: vini, Plin. 14, 4, 6, § 55: arboris, id. 13, 9, 17, § 61: gemmarum, id. 37, 8, 37, § 116 al.: vo

bonna.full: Bonna, ae, f., a city on the Rhine, now Bonn, Tac. H. 4, 19; 4, 25; 70, 77; 5, 22; Flor. 4, 12, 26.—Hence, Bonnensis, e, adj., of Bonna: castra, Tac. H. 4, 20; 4, 62: proelium, id. ib. 4, 20.
bonna.short: Bonna, ae, f., a city on the Rhine, now Bonn, Tac.

bononia.full: Bŏnōnĭa, ae, f., = Βονωνία. A town in Gallia Cisalpina, in the neighborhood of Mutina, a Roman colony founded A. U. C. 563, Cic. Fam. 12, 5, 2; Liv. 37, 57, 7; Vell. 1, 15, 2; Sil. 8, 599; Mel. 2, 4, 2; previously a Tuscan town called Felsina, now Bologna, Plin. 3, 15, 20, § 115; Interpr. ap. Serv. ad Verg. A. 10, 198; Liv. 33, 37, 3; Amm. 20, 1, 3; 27, 8, 6.—Hence, Bŏnōnĭensis, e, adj., of or pertaining to Bononia: amnis Rhenus, Plin. 16, 36, 65, § 161; so, C. Rusticellus Bononiensis, of Bononi

bonum1.full: bŏnum, i, n., v. bonus, I. 5. and II. A. 5.

bonus.full: bŏnus (old form dŭonus, Carm. Sall. ap. Varr. L. L. 7, § 26 Müll.; cf. Paul. ex Fest. p. 67 Müll.), a, um, adj. for duonus, cf. bellum, bis, and cf. root dvi-; hence δείδω, δέος, good; comp. melior, us cf. Gr. μάλα, μᾶλλον, better; sup. optimus (optu-mus, ante-class. and often class.) [root opof ops, opes; cf. copia, apiscor], best. Attributively. As adjunct of nouns denoting persons. Vir bonus. A man morally good (καλὸς κἀγαθός): quoniam boni me viri pauperant, improbi alunt, Plaut. Poen. 5, 4,

bonum2.full: bŏnum, i, n., plur. bona; mĕlĭus, ōris, n.; optĭmum, i, n. (v. infra); of things in gen. Bonum, or plur. bona, a good, or goods in a moral and metaphysical sense, a moral good, a blessing: sunt autem hae de finibus defensae sententiae: nihil bonum nisi honestum, ut Stoici; nihil bonum nisi voluptatem, ut Epicurus; nihil bonum nisi vacuitatem doloris, ut Hieronymus... tria genera bonorum, maxima animi, secunda corporis, externa tertia, ut Peripatetici, etc., Cic. Tusc. 5, 30, 84 sq.: quid est igi

bonuscula.full: bŏnuscŭla, ōrum, n. dim. bonus, small possessions, a little estate (post-class.): de bonusculis avitis et paternis, Sid. Ep. 9, 6; Cod. Th. 10, 10, 29, § 1.

boo.full: bŏo (with the digamma bŏvo, Enn.; v. infra), āre or ĕre, v. n. from the root bo, kindr. with Sanscr. gu and the Gr. βοάω; cf. Varr. L. L. 7, § 104 Müll.; Non. p. 79, 4; acc. to Paul. ex Fest. p. 30 Müll. directly from the Gr., to cry aloud, roar (mostly ante- and post-class., and in the poets). Bŏvo, āre: clamore bovantes, Enn. ap. Varr. 1. 1. (Ann. v. 571 Vahl.).— Bŏo, ĕre: clamore et sonitu colles resonantes bount, Pac. ap. Non. 1. 1. (Trag. Rel. v. 223 Rib.; Varr. ib.; perh. in both pass. we

boopes.full: bŏōpes, is, n., = βοῶπες, a plant, pure Lat. caerefolium, App. Herb. 104.
boopes.short: bŏōpes, is, n., = βοῶπες, a plant, pure Lat.

bootes.full: Bŏōtes, ae (gen. Bootae, Ov. A. A. 2, 55; Luc. 2, 722; Juv. 5, 23; Mart. 4, 3, 5; cf. Rudd. I. p. 76, n. 48: Bootis, Hyg. Astr. 3, 24; Avien. Perieg. 364; 456; 856; Isid. Orig. 3, 70, 9: Booti, Cic. Arat. ap. Prisc. p. 706; v. 100 B. and K., and Cic. N. D. 2, 42, 110; acc. Booten, Ov. F. 5, 733; voc. Boote, id. M. 2, 176), m., = Βοώτης, the nearly stationary constellation Bootes, the Bear-keeper, = Arctophylax (q. v.; cf. also arcturus), Cic. Arat. l. l.; Verg. G. 1, 229; Ov. M. 10, 447 al.: pig

bora.full: Bora, ae, m., a mountain in Macedonia, now Nitje, Liv. 45, 19, 8 sq.
bora.short: Bora, ae, m., a mountain in Macedonia, now Nitje, Liv.

borcani.full: Borcāni, ōrum, m., a people of Apulia, Plin. 3, 11, 16, § 105.
borcani.short: Borcāni, ōrum, m., a people of Apulia, Plin.

borealis.full: bŏrĕālis, e, v. boreas, II. B.

boreas.full: bŏrĕas (borras, Prud. Psych. 847; Paul. Nol. Carm. 17, 245), ae, m., = Βορέας or Βορρᾶς. The north wind; pure Lat aquilo, Plin. 2, 47, 46, § 119: ventus Boreas, Nep. Milt. 2, 4: Boreae frigus, Verg. G. 1, 93: tellus boreā rigida spirante, id. ib. 2, 316; id. A. 3, 687: horrifer, Ov. M. 1, 65: praeceps, id. ib. 2, 185; 13, 418; 15, 471; Col. poët. 10, 288; Stat. S. 5, 1, 82.—Acc. Borean, Ov. M. 15, 471; id. F. 2, 147; Luc. 4, 61; 5, 543; 5, 705; 8, 183; 10, 289; Stat. S. 3, 2, 45; id. Th. 7, 6; M

boreotis.full: bŏrĕōtis, ĭdis, adj. f., = βορεῶτις, northern; acc. plur. boreotidas, Prisc. Perieg. 577.

boria.full: bŏrīa, ae, f., = βόρεια (northern), a kind of jasper, Plin. 37, 8, 37, § 116.
boria.short: bŏrīa, ae, f., = βόρεια (northern), a kind of jasper, Plin.

borith.full: bōrith = , a plant purifying like soap, soapwort (herbe savonnieère, Jarchi Malach. 3, 2; cf. Ges. and Robinson's Heb. Lex. under ), Vulg. Jer. 2, 22, and Mal. 3, 2.
borith.short: bōrith = , a plant purifying like soap, soapwort (herbe savonnieère, Jarchi Malach.

borrio.full: borrio (bur-), īre, 4, v. n., to swarm: in stipite formicarum nidificia borriebant, App. M. 8, p. 211, 30.

borysthenes.full: Bŏrysthĕnes, is, m., = Βορυσθένης, a large but gently-flowing river in Sarmatia, which empties into the Black Sea, now the Dnieper, Mel. 2, 1, 6; 2, 7, 2; Curt. 6, 2, 13; Plin. 4, 12, 26, § 82 sq.; Gell. 9, 4, 6.— Derivv. Bŏrysthĕnĭus, a, um, adj., pertaining to the Borysthenes: amnis, poet. circumlocution for Borysthenes, Ov. P. 4, 10, 53.— Bŏrysthĕnis, ĭdis, f., adj., = Βορυσθενίς, the same: ora, Calvus ap. Val. Prob. p. 1395 P.—And subst.: Bŏry-sthĕnis, ĭdis, f., a town on the Borysthenes, pr
borysthenes.short: Bŏrysthĕnes, is, m., = Βορυσθένης, a large but gently-flowing river in Sarmatia, which empties into the Black Sea, now the Dnieper, Mel.

bos.full: bōs, bŏvis (prob. orig. form of nom. bŏ-vis, like bovare for boare, Petr. 62, 13; cf. Varr L. L. 8, § 74 Müll., where, acc. to Cod. B., the read. should be: nunc in consuetudine aliter dicere pro Jovis Juppiter, pro Bovis Bos, pro Strus Strues.—Hence, gen. plur. bŏvĕrum, Cato, R. R. 62 Schneid. N. cr.; cf. Varr. L. L. l. l.: alios dicere Boum greges, alios Boverum; v. Juppiter, nux, rex, sus, and Schneid. Gr. 2, p. 171.— Regular gen. boum very freq.; uncontracted form bovum, Cic. Rep. 2, 9, 16 H

boscis.full: boscis, ĭdis, f., = βοσκάς, a kind of duck, Col. 8, 15, 1 (perh., acc. to the Greek, more correctly boscăs, ădis; v. Schneid. Comment. in h. l.).
boscis.short: boscis, ĭdis, f., = βοσκάς, a kind of duck, Col.

bosporus.full: Bospŏrus and Bosphŏrus (in MSS. sometimes Bosfŏrus), i, m. (fem., Sulp. Sev. Dial. 1, 26; Prop. 3, 11, 68; v. infra), = Βόσπορος and Βόσφορος (i. e. the heifer's ford, on account of Io's passage here as a heifer), the name of several straits, and particularly, Thracius, Gr. Βόσπορος Θρᾴκιος, between Thrace and Asia Minor, now the Strait or Channel of Constantinople, Varr. R. R. 2, 1, 8; Mel. 1, 1, 5; 1, 2, 2 and 6; 1, 19, 5 and 12; 2, 2, 6; 2, 7, 3; Plin. 4, 12, 24, § 76 sq.; 5, 32, 43, § 149 sq

bostar.full: Bostar, ăris, m., a Carthaginian proper name, Cic. Aem. Scaur. 2, 1 sqq.; 4, 8; Liv. 22, 22, 9 sqq.; 23, 34, 1; Sil. 3, 647.
bostar.short: Bostar, ăris, m., a Carthaginian proper name, Cic.

bostra.full: Bostra, ae, f., = Βόστρα, the capital of the Roman province of Arabia from the time of Trajan, now Bozra, Amm. 14, 8, 13. —Called Bosra, Vulg. Isa. 34, 6; id. Jer. 48, 24 al.—Hence, Bostrēnus, a, um, adj., of Bozra.—Only subst.: Bostrēnus, i, m., an inhabitant of Bozra: praetextatus, Cic. Q. Fr. 2, 12, 3; plur., Inscr. Orell. 3440.
bostra.short: Bostra, ae, f., = Βόστρα, the capital of the Roman province of Arabia from the time of Trajan, now Bozra, Amm.

bostrychites.full: bostrўchītes, ae, m., = βοστρυχίτης, a precious stone, otherwise unknown, Plin. 37, 10, 55, § 150; 37, 11, 73, § 191.
bostrychites.short: bostrўchītes, ae, m., = βοστρυχίτης, a precious stone, otherwise unknown, Plin.

bostrychus.full: bostrўchus, a, um, adj., = βόστρυχος, curled, in ringlets: crines, Firm. Math. 4, 12.
bostrychus.short: bostrўchus, a, um, adj., = βόστρυχος, curled, in ringlets: crines, Firm.

botanicum.full: bŏtănĭcum herbarium dicitur, quod ibi herbae notentur, Isid. Orig. 4, 10, 4.
botanicum.short: bŏtănĭcum herbarium dicitur, quod ibi herbae notentur, Isid.

botanismus.full: bŏtănismus, i, m., = βοτανισμός, a weeding, a pulling up of weeds, Plin. 18, 18, 47, § 169.
botanismus.short: bŏtănismus, i, m., = βοτανισμός, a weeding, a pulling up of weeds, Plin.

botellus.full: bŏtellus, i, m. dim. botulus, a small sausage (rare), Mart. 5, 78, 9; 11, 31, 13; cf. Apic. 2, 3; Sid. Ep. 8, 11.

boterdum.full: Boterdum, i, n., a town in Hispania Tarraconensis, Mart. 1, 49, 7; 12, 18, 11.
boterdum.short: Boterdum, i, n., a town in Hispania Tarraconensis, Mart.

bothynus.full: bŏthȳnus, i, m., = βόθυνος, a fiery meteor in the form of a pit: sunt bothynoe (acc. to the Gr. form = bothyni, like adelphoe, arctoe, etc.) cum velut coronā cingente introrsus ingens caeli recessus est similis effossae in orbem speluncae. Sen. Q. N. 1, 14, 1 (Haas. as Greek); App. de Mundo, pp. 58 and 64.
bothynus.short: bŏthȳnus, i, m., = βόθυνος, a fiery meteor in the form of a pit: sunt bothynoe (acc.

botrax.full: bŏtrax dicta quod ranae habeat faciem. Nam Graeci ranam βότρακα (βάτραχον?) vocant, Isid. Orig. 12, 4, 35.
botrax.short: bŏtrax dicta quod ranae habeat faciem.

botronatus.full: bō^trōnātus, ūs, m. βότρυς, an ornament for the hair of a female, in the form of a cluster of grapes, Tert. Cult. Fem. 10; Cypr. Hab. Virg. p. 98.

botruosus.full: bō^trŭōsus, a, um, adj. botrus, full of clusters (pure Lat. racemosus), App. Herb. 66; Isid. Orig. 17, 11, 8.

botryitis.full: bō^trўītis, ĭdis, f., = βοτρυῗτις and βοτρυώδης (cluster-shaped), a kind of calamine, Cels. 6, 6, n. 6; Plin. 34, 10, 22, § 101; Scrib. Comp. 24 and 220.— A precious stone in the form of a cluster of grapes, otherwise unknown, Plin. 37, 10, 55, § 150.
botryitis.short: bō^trўītis, ĭdis, f., = βοτρυῗτις and βοτρυώδης (cluster-shaped), a kind of calamine, Cels.

botryo.full: bō^trўo (bō^trĭo, Isid. Orig. 17, 5, 14), ōnis, m., a parallel form to botrys, = βοτρυών = βότρυς, a cluster of grapes, Pall. Febr. 33; id. Sept. 17; id. Nov. 12, 1; Mart. 11, 27, 4.

botryodes.full: bŏtrўōdes, is, adj., = βοτρυὠδης, in the form of a cluster of grapes: cadmea, Veg. 6 (4), 11, 1.
botryodes.short: bŏtrўōdes, is, adj., = βοτρυὠδης, in the form of a cluster of grapes: cadmea, Veg.

botryon.full: bŏtrўon, i, n., = βότρυον, a medicine prepared from excrements, Plin. 28, 4, 10, § 44.
botryon.short: bŏtrўon, i, n., = βότρυον, a medicine prepared from excrements, Plin.

botrys1.full: bō^trys, ўos, f., = βότρυς. Latinized bō^trus, i, f. (cf. Isid. Orig. 17, 5, 14), the grape, Vulg. Mic. 7, 1 (as transl. of the Heb. ).— In the Greek form botrys, a plant, also called artemisia, mugwort, Plin. 25, 7, 36, § 74; 27, 4, 11, § 28.

botrys2.full: Bō^trys, ўos, f., = Βότρυς, a town in Phœnicia, now the village of Batron, Plin. 5, 20, 17, § 78; Mel. 1, 12, 3.
botrys2.short: Bō^trys, ўos, f., = Βότρυς, a town in Phœnicia, now the village of Batron, Plin.

bottiaea.full: Bottĭaea, ae, f., = Βοττιαία, a small province in Macedonia, Liv. 26, 25, 4; whose inhabitants are called Bottiaei, = Βοττιαῖοι, Plin. 4, 11, 18, § 40 (acc. to the same in Thrace).
bottiaea.short: Bottĭaea, ae, f., = Βοττιαία, a small province in Macedonia, Liv.

botularius.full: bŏtŭlārĭus, ii, m. botulus, a sausage-maker, a dealer in sausages, Sen. Ep. 56, 3.

botulus.full: bŏtŭlus, i, m. (orig. like φύσκη and the Ital. budello, derived from the Lat.; Fr. boyau, an intestine; hence like the somewhat differently formed derivatives, Ital. boldone and boldonuccio; Fr. boudin; Engl. pudding), a sausage (very rare; acc. to Gell. 17, 7, 11, a vulgar word, used by Laber. for farcimen): botulus genus farciminis, Paul. ex Fest. p. 35 Müll.; Mart. 14, 72; Petr. 49 fin; Apic. 2, 5; Arn. 2, 73; Tert. Apol. 9. — Meton., a stomach filled with delicacies, Tert. Jejun. adv. Psych.

boudicea.full: Boudicēa or Bouducēa, ae, f., queen of the Iceni, a British tribe, Tac. A. 14, 31 sq.; id. Agr. 16 (al.: Boadicea, Boadica).
boudicea.short: Boudicēa or Bouducēa, ae, f., queen of the Iceni, a British tribe, Tac.

boustrophedon.full: boustrŏphēdŏn, adv., = βουστροφηδόν, from right to left and back again alternately, forwards and backwards, an ancient way of writing, Mar. Vict. 1, 14, 6 Gaisf. (al. boustrophen, id. p. 2499 P.).
boustrophedon.short: boustrŏphēdŏn, adv., = βουστροφηδόν, from right to left and back again alternately, forwards and backwards, an ancient way of writing, Mar.

bova2.full: bova, ae, f., a swelling of the legs: crurum tumor viae labore collectus bova appellatur, Fest. p. 25.
bova2.short: bova, ae, f., a swelling of the legs: crurum tumor viae labore collectus bova appellatur, Fest.

bovarius.full: bŏvārĭus (boār-), a, um, adj. bos, of or relating to horned cattle: arva, afterwards the site of the Forum Bovarium, Prop. 4 (5), 9, 19. Forum, the cattle-market, Varr. L. L. 5, § 146 Müll.: horam sibi octavam, dum in foro bovario inquireret, postulavit, Cic. Aem. Scaur. 11, 23; cf. Ov. F. 6, 473; Paul. ex Fest. p. 30 Müll.; Liv. 21, 62, 3; 33, 27, 4 Weissenb. ad loc.; 35, 40, 8; Val. Max. 1, 6, 5; 2, 4, 7; Plin. 34, 3, 5, § 10; Tac. A. 12, 24: lappa boaria, a kind of bur, Plin. 26, 11, 66, § 10

bovatim.full: bŏvātim, adv. id., after the manner of oxen or cows, Nigid. ap. Non. p. 40, 25 (others read boatim).

bovianum.full: Bŏvĭānum, i, n., = Βοΐᾶνον, the name of two towns in Samnium. The principal place of the Pentri, now Boiano, Cic. Clu. 69, 197; Liv. 9, 28, 2 and 3; 9, 31, 4; 10, 43, 15; in Plin. 3, 12, 17, § 107, with the appel. Vetus, to distinguish it from, Bovianum Undecumanorum, prob. a place in the neighborhood of the preceding, occupied by the veterans of the eleventh legion, Plin. l. l.—Hence, Bŏvĭānĭus, a, um, adj., of Bovianum: castra, Sil. 9, 566.—Bŏvĭā-nus, a, um, adj.: ager, Gromat. Vet. p. 259, 23
bovianum.short: Bŏvĭānum, i, n., = Βοΐᾶνον, the name of two towns in Samnium.

bovicidium.full: bŏvĭcīdĭum, ii, n. bos-caedo, a slaughtering of cattle, Sol. 1, § 10.

bovilla.full: bŏvilla, βουστασία, a cattle-stall, Vet. Gloss.

bovillae.full: Bŏvillae (Bŏbellae, Tab. Peut.; Bŏbillae, Gromat. Vet. p. 231, 11), ārum, f. (Bŏvilla, ae, f., Front. Colon. p. 103). A small but very ancient town in Latium, a colony from Alba Longa, about twelve miles from Rome, on the Appian Way, and, until some time in the Middle Ages, the first station on it; it contained the Sacrarium of the Julian gens, Tac. A. 2, 41; 15, 23; id. H. 4, 2; 4, 46; Suet. Aug. 100; Flor. 1, 11, 6; Schol. Pers. 6, 55 al.; Vell. 2, 47, 4: suburbanae, Prop. 4 (5), 1, 33. Ov. F.

bovillus.full: bŏvillus, a, um, adj., a very ancient form of the class. bubulus [bos]. Of or pertaining to oxen or cows: grex, in an old religious formula, Liv. 22, 10, 3: carnes, Theod. Prisc. 1, 7.—No comp. or sup.— Bŏvillus, a, um, = Bovillanus; v. Bovillae, I. B. 1. fin.
bovillus.short: bŏvillus, a, um, adj., a very ancient form of the class.

bovinator.full: bŏvīnātor, ōris, m. bovinor. A brawler, blusterer, reviler, acc. to the Gloss.: bovinatores θορυβοποιοί, θρύλλον ποιοῦντες ἠ ταραχήν; v. bovinor.— = tergiversator, one who seeks evasions (the figure drawn perh. from the holding back of draught cattle), Lucil. ap. Gell. 11, 7, 9; cf. Non. p. 79, 26.
