bovinor.full: bŏvīnor, āri, v. dep. bos, to bellow at, brawl, revile: bovinatur = conviciatur, Paul. ex Fest. p. 30, 12 Müll.: bovinator = conviciator, inconstans. Bovinari = conviciari, damnare, clamare, Vocab. Vet.

bovinus.full: bŏvīnus, a, um, adj., = bubulus [id.], of or pertaining to oxen or cows: medulla, Theod. Prisc. Diaeta, 15.
bovinus.short: bŏvīnus, a, um, adj., = bubulus [id.], of or pertaining to oxen or cows: medulla, Theod.

bovus.full: bovus non nisi singularem numerum capit, nam pluralem nemo dixit, Charis. p. 58 (the signif. of this word, not used elsewh., is not given by Charis.).
bovus.short: bovus non nisi singularem numerum capit, nam pluralem nemo dixit, Charis.

box.full: bōx, bōcis, m., = βώξ, βόαξ, a sea-fish, otherwise unknown, Plin. 32, 11, 53, § 145. In Paul. ex Fest. p. 30, 6 Müll. (Jan. boca), bocas: bocas = genus piscis a boando id est vocem emittendo appellatur; cf. Isid. Orig. 12, 6, 9.
box.short: bōx, bōcis, m., = βώξ, βόαξ, a sea-fish, otherwise unknown, Plin.

brabeum.full: brăbēum or -īum, i, n., = βραβεῖον, a prize in the games (late Lat.), Prud. στεφ. 5, 538; Tert. adv. Marc. 3; Vulg. 1 Cor. 9, 24.
brabeum.short: brăbēum or -īum, i, n., = βραβεῖον, a prize in the games (late Lat.), Prud.

brabeuta.full: brăbeuta, ae, m., = βραβευτής, one who presided at the public games, an umpire, one who assigned the prizes: designatores, quos Graeci βραβευτὰς appellant, artem ludicram non facere, Dig. 3, 2, 4, § 1; * Suet. Ner. 53.
brabeuta.short: brăbeuta, ae, m., = βραβευτής, one who presided at the public games, an umpire, one who assigned the prizes: designatores, quos Graeci βραβευτὰς appellant, artem ludicram non facere, Dig.

brabyla.full: brabyla, ae, f., a plant, otherwise unknown, Plin. 27, 8, 32, § 55.
brabyla.short: brabyla, ae, f., a plant, otherwise unknown, Plin.

bracae.full: brācae (not braccae), ārum (once in sing. brāca, ae, Ov. Tr. 5, 10, 34; and as access. form brāces, Edict. Diocl. p. 20), f. Germ.; Swed. brōk; Angl. -Sax. brōk; Engl. breeches; Dutch, broek, trowsers, breeches; orig. worn only by barbarians, i.e. neither Greeks nor Romans: barbara tegmina crurum, Verg. A. 11, 777; in the time of the emperors also among the Romans, Ov. Tr. 5, 7, 49: Galli bracas deposuerunt, latum clavum sumpserunt, Poët. ap. Suet. Caes. 80 al.: virgatae, Prop. 4 (5), 10, 43: br

bracari.full: Brācări, ūm, m., a tribe of Gauls in Hispania Tarraconensis, Plin. 3, 3, 4, § 28; 4, 20, 34, § 112.—Hence, † Brācărus, a, um, adj., of the Bracari: CONVENTVS, Inscr. Orell. 2165.
bracari.short: Brācări, ūm, m., a tribe of Gauls in Hispania Tarraconensis, Plin.

bracarius.full: brācārĭus, ii, m. braca, a maker of trowsers or breeches (late Lat.), Lampr. Alex. Sev. 24; Cod. Just. 10, 64, 1; Edict. Diocl. p. 20.

bracatus.full: brācātus, a, um, adj. id.. Wearing trowsers or breeches. A gen. epithet for foreign, barbarian, effeminate: sic existimatis eos hic sagatos bracatosque versari, Cic. Font. 15, 33 (11, 23): nationes, id. Fam. 9, 15, 2: miles, Prop. 3 (4), 4, 17. turba Getarum, Ov. Tr. 4, 6, 47 Jahn: Medi, Pers. 3, 53.— As a geog. designation of the land and the people beyond the Alps, = transalpinus, in distinction from togatus (q. v.): Gallia Bracata, afterwards called Gallia Narbonensis, Mel. 2, 5, 1; Plin. 3,

bracchialis.full: bracchĭālis (brāch-), e, adj. bracchium, of or belonging to the arm: nervus, Plaut. Poen. 5, 4, 99: crassitudo, the thickness of an arm, Plin. 17, 17, 27, § 123: torques, Vop. Aur. 7.—Hence, Subst.: bracchĭāle, is, n. (sc. ornamentum): argenteum, Plin. 28, 7, 23, § 82 sq.; 25, 10, 80, § 129; 32, 1, 3, § 8; and bracchĭālis, is, m. (sc. torques), Treb. Claud. 14, 5 (class. armillae); an armlet, bracelet; cf. Prisc. p. 1220 P.

bracchiatus.full: bracchĭātus (brāch-), a, um, adj. id. II. C., with boughs or branches like arms (very rare): vineae, Col. 5, 5, 9; 5, 5, 12; 5, 5, 13: arbores, Plin. 16, 30, 53, § 123.

bracchiolaris.full: bracchĭŏlāris (brāch-), e, adj. bracchiolum, II. A., pertaining to a muscle of a horse: musculi, Veg. 1, 25, 5.

bracchiolum.full: bracchĭŏlum (brāch-), i, n. dim. bracchium. A small, delicate arm: puellulae, * Cat. 61, 181.— Transf. A muscle in a horse's leg, Veg. 1, 25, 4 and 5; cf. id. 6, 1, 1; 6, 2, 2; 5, 27, 7; 5, 70, 2.— The arm of a chair or seat, Vulg. 2 Par. 9, 18.

bracchionarium.full: bracchĭŏnārĭum (brāch-), ii, n., = ψέλλιον ἀνδρός, a bracelet, Gloss. Gr. Lat. [βραχίων].
bracchionarium.short: bracchĭŏnārĭum (brāch-), ii, n., = ψέλλιον ἀνδρός, a bracelet, Gloss.

bracchium.full: bracchĭum (less correctly brāchĭ-um; gen. bracchi, Lucr. 6, 434), ii, n. perh. kindr. with Gr. βραχίων; but cf. Sanscr. bāhu; like frango, Sanscr. bhang, Bopp, Gloss. p. 239 a, the arm; particularly, Lit., the forearm, from the hand to the elbow (while lacertus is the upper arm, from the elbow to the shoulder), Lucr. 4, 830; 6, 397: bracchia et lacerti, Ov. M. 1, 501; 1, 550 sq.: subjecta lacertis bracchia, id. ib. 14, 305; Curt. 8, 9, 21; 9, 1, 29: (feminae) nudae bracchia et lacertos, Tac. G.

brace.full: bracē, ēs (acc. -em), f., a Gallic name of a particularly white kind of corn, acc. to Hard. blé blanc de Dauphiné; pure Lat. sandala, Plin. 18, 7, 11, § 62 (al. brance).

braceus.full: brācĕus, a, um, adj. bracae, pertaining to breeches: mala, Auct. Priap. 74 (others read braccica).

brachmanae.full: Brachmānae, ārum; -māni, ōrum, and -mānes, ium, m., = Βραχμᾶνες [Engl. Brahmins], the priests and learned caste of the Hindoos, the present Brahmins; form Brachmanae, Tert. Apol. 42.—Form Brachmani, Amm. 23, 6, 33; 28, 1, 13.—Gen. Brachmanūm, App. Flor. 2, n. 15 (in Plin. 6, 17, 21, § 64, mentioned as separate tribes or nations: multarum gentium cognomen Brachmanae).

brachycatalectum.full: brăchўcătălēctum (brăchў-cătălēctĭcum, Serv. Centim. p. 1817 P.), i, n. (sc. metrum), = βραχυκατάληκτον or βραχυκαταληκτικόν; in metre, a verse that wants a whole foot or half a metre, Diom. p. 501 P.

brachypota.full: brăchўpŏta, ae, m., = βραχυπότης, a small drinker, Cael. Aur. Acut. 3, 15, 120.
brachypota.short: brăchўpŏta, ae, m., = βραχυπότης, a small drinker, Cael.

brachysyllabus.full: brăchўsyllăbus, i, m. (sc. pes), = βραχυσύλλαβος (of short syllables); in metre, another name of the tribrachys, ˘˘˘, Diom. p. 475 P.; Mar. Vict. 2539 P.

bractea.full: bractĕa (also brattĕa), ae, f. perh. kindr. with βράχω, to rattle, a thin plate of metal, gold-leaf (thicker plates of metal are called laminae; cf. Isid. Orig. 16, 18, 2: bractea dicitur tenuissima lamina): aranea bratteaque auri, * Lucr. 4, 729: leni crepitabat brattea vento, Verg. A. 6, 209: inspice, quam tenuis bractea ligna tegat, Ov. A. A. 3, 232; Mart. 8, 33, 6; Plin. 33, 3, 19, § 61; cf. argenteae, id. 37, 7, 31, § 105.— Poet.: viva, the golden fleece of Spanish sheep, Mart. 9, 62, 4.— M

bractealis.full: bractĕālis, e, adj. bractea, of metallic plates: fulgor, golden, Prud. στεφ. 10, 1024.

bracteamentum.full: bractĕāmentum, i, n. id. II., glitter, splendor, Fulg. Contin. Virg. p. 140.

bractearius.full: bractĕārĭus, ii, m. bractea, a worker in gold-leaf, a gold-beater, Firm. Math. 4, 15; Inscr. Grut. 1074, 12; Inscr. Orell. 4153; 4067.—In fem.: bractĕārĭa, ae, Inscr. Don. cl. 8, n. 19; Inscr. Orell. 4153.

bracteator.full: bractĕātor, ōris, m. id., a goldbeater, Firm. Math. 8, 16; Inscr. Don. cl. 9, n. 1.

bracteatus.full: bractĕātus, a, um, adj. id., covered with gold-plate, gilt (post-Aug. for the class. aureus): sellae, Sid. Ep. 8, 8: lacunar, id. ib. 2, 10.— In gen., glistening like gold: leo, i.e. with a yellow mane, Sen. Ep. 41, 6: comae, Mart. Cap. 1, § 75.— Trop. (cf. aureus, II.). Splendid, golden: O mentis aureae dictum bracteatum! Aus. Grat. Act. ad Gratian. 8.— Shining only externally, gilded, delusive: felicitas, Sen. Ep. 115, 9.

bracteola.full: bractĕŏla, ae, f. dim. id., a thin leaf of gold, * Juv. 13, 152; so Arn. 6, p. 205; Prud. Psych. 355; id. στεφ. 12, 49.

bragae.full: Bragae, ārum, f., an island on the coast of Arabia, Plin. 6, 28, 32, § 150.
bragae.short: Bragae, ārum, f., an island on the coast of Arabia, Plin.

brana.full: Brana, ae, f., a town of Hispania Baetica, Plin. 3, 1, 3, § 15.
brana.short: Brana, ae, f., a town of Hispania Baetica, Plin.

branchiae.full: branchĭae, ārum (sing. branchia, ae, Aus. Mos. 266; Vulg. Tob. 6, 4), f., = τὰ βράγχια, the gills of fish, Col. 8, 17, 12; Plin. 9, 7, 6, § 16; 9, 18, 33, § 69.

branchidae.full: Branchĭdae, ārum, m., = Βραγχίδαι, the posterity of Branchus, a son of Apollo, hereditary priests of the temple and oracle (penetralia Branchi, Stat. Th. 8, 198) of Apollo at Miletus, Mel. 1, 17, 1; Plin. 5, 29, 31, § 112; Curt. 7, 5, 16; 7, 5, 30; Amm. 29, 1, 31.—Sing.: Branchĭdes, ae, m., a surname of Apollo, Mel. 1, 17, 1.
branchidae.short: Branchĭdae, ārum, m., = Βραγχίδαι, the posterity of Branchus, a son of Apollo, hereditary priests of the temple and oracle (penetralia Branchi, Stat.

branchos.full: branchŏs, i, m., = βράγχος, hoarseness, Cael. Aur. Tard. 2, 7, 95; cf. Isid. Orig. 4, 7, 13.
branchos.short: branchŏs, i, m., = βράγχος, hoarseness, Cael.

branchus.full: Branchus, i, m., = Βράγχος, a son of Apollo; or, according to others, of Smicrus of Delphi, inspired by Apollo with prophecy, v. Branchidae, Stat. Th. 3, 479; 8, 198 Schol.
branchus.short: Branchus, i, m., = Βράγχος, a son of Apollo;

brancosi.full: Brancosi, ōrum, m., a people of India, Plin. 6, 20, 23, § 76.
brancosi.short: Brancosi, ōrum, m., a people of India, Plin.

brasmatiae.full: brasmătĭae (access. form bras-tae, App. de Mundo, p. 65, 25), ārum, f., = οἱ βρασματίαι (sc. ἄνεμοι) or βράσται, a shaking of the earth, an earthquake: brasmatiae sunt (terrarum motus), qui terram molestius suscitantes sursum propellunt immanissimas moles, ut in Asiā Delos emersit, etc., Amm. 17, 7, 13.

brassica.full: brassĭca, ae, f., cabbage; of several varieties (much prized by the ancients, and freq. employed in medicine), Cato, R. R. 156 sq.; Col. 10, 127 sq. Schneid.; 11, 3, 23; Plin. 19, 8, 41, § 136 sq.; 20, 9, 33, § 78 sq.; Pall. Febr. 24, 7; id. Jun. 4; id. Sept. 13, 1; id. Aug. 5, 3; Veg. 3, 15, 12; Plin. Val. 4, 29; Plaut. Ps. 3, 2, 26; Prop. 4 (5), 2, 44.al. (in Cic. N. D. 2, 47, 120, perh. a gloss; v. Orell. N. cr.).—Plur.: brassĭcae, ārum, f., varieties of cabbage, Cato, R. R. 187, 3; Plin. 20,

brathy.full: brathy, ys, n., = βράθυ, the savintree (pure Lat. herba Sabina), Plin. 24, 11, 61, § 102; App. Herb. 85; Scrib. Comp. 154.
brathy.short: brathy, ys, n., = βράθυ, the savintree (pure Lat.

brattia.full: Brattia, ae, f., an island of Dalmatia, Plin. 3, 26, 30, § 152.
brattia.short: Brattia, ae, f., an island of Dalmatia, Plin.

bratus.full: bratus, i, f., a tree similar to the cypress, Plin. 12, 17, 39, § 78.
bratus.short: bratus, i, f., a tree similar to the cypress, Plin.

bratuspantium.full: Bratuspantĭum, ii, n., a town in Gallia Belgica, in the province of the Bellovaci, afterwards called Caesaromagus, Itin. Anton., now Breteuil, Caes. B. G. 2, 13.
bratuspantium.short: Bratuspantĭum, ii, n., a town in Gallia Belgica, in the province of the Bellovaci, afterwards called Caesaromagus, Itin.

brauron.full: Brauron, ōnis, m. (Braurōnia, ae, f., Mel. 2, 3, 6), = Βραυρών, a village in Attica, not far from Marathon, now Vraona, Plin. 4, 7, 11, § 24; Stat. Th. 12, 615.

bregma.full: bregma (brechma) [Indian], a defect of pepper, = abortus, Plin. 12, 7, 14, § 27.
bregma.short: bregma (brechma) [Indian], a defect of pepper, = abortus, Plin.

bregmenteni.full: Bregmentēni, ōrum, m., a people of the Troad, Plin. 5, 30, 33, § 126.
bregmenteni.short: Bregmentēni, ōrum, m., a people of the Troad, Plin.

brennus.full: Brennus, i, m., = Βρέννος, a leader of the Gauls who defeated the Romans at the river Allia, Liv. 5, 38, 3; Serv. ad Verg. A. 6, 826.—Hence, Brennĭcus, a, um, adj., of Brennus: signa, Sid. Carm. 7, 561.— A king of the Gauls who invaded Greece in the second century B.C. and attacked Delphi, Cic. Div. 1, 37, 81; Just. 24, 5 sqq.; Val. Max. 1, 1, 18; Prop. 3, 13 (4, 12), 51.
brennus.short: Brennus, i, m., = Βρέννος, a leader of the Gauls who defeated the Romans at the river Allia, Liv.

brentesia.full: Brentēsĭa, ae, m., the river Brenta, in Upper Italy, Messal. Aug. Progen. 10.— Called also Brinta, ae, m., Ven. Vit. S. Mart. 4, 677.
brentesia.short: Brentēsĭa, ae, m., the river Brenta, in Upper Italy, Messal.

brephotropheum.full: brĕphŏtrŏphēum or -īum, n., = βρεφοτροφεῖον, a foundling hospital, Cod. Just. 1, 2, 19.
brephotropheum.short: brĕphŏtrŏphēum or -īum, n., = βρεφοτροφεῖον, a foundling hospital, Cod.

brephotrophus.full: brĕphŏtrŏphus, i, m., = βρεφοτρόφος, one who brings up foundlings (v. brephotropheum), Cod. Just. 1, 3, 42, § 9.
brephotrophus.short: brĕphŏtrŏphus, i, m., = βρεφοτρόφος, one who brings up foundlings (v.

breuci.full: Breuci, ōrum, m., = Βρεῦκοι, a people in Pannonia, on the Save, Plin. 3, 25, 28, § 147; Suet. Tib. 9; Inscr. Orell. 126; 2248.
breuci.short: Breuci, ōrum, m., = Βρεῦκοι, a people in Pannonia, on the Save, Plin.

breuni.full: Breuni (erroneously Brenni), ōrum, m., a people in Rhœtia, in the Upper Valley of the Inn, and bordering upon the Genauni, in the Lower Valley of the Inn, Hor. C. 4, 14, 11; Plin. 3, 20, 24, § 136; Flor. 4, 12, 4.
breuni.short: Breuni (erroneously Brenni), ōrum, m., a people in Rhœtia, in the Upper Valley of the Inn, and bordering upon the Genauni, in the Lower Valley of the Inn, Hor.

breviarius.full: brĕvĭārĭus, a, um, adj. brevio, abridged: rationes, Dig. 33, 8, 26.—More freq. subst.: brĕvĭārĭum, ii, n., a summary, abridgment, abstract, epitome (postAug.; cf. summarium): haec quae nunc vulgo breviarium dicitur, olim, cum Latine loqueremur, summarium vocabatur, Sen. Ep. 39, 1: omnis culturae, Plin. 18, 26, 62, § 230: rationum, Suet. Galb. 12: imperii, statistical view, statistics, id. Aug. 101 (cf. id. ib. 28: rationarium imperii; and id. Calig. 16: rationes imperii): rerum omnium Romanarum,

breviatio.full: brĕvĭātĭo, ōnis, f. id., a shortening (late Lat.): dierum, Aug. Ep. ad Hesych. 18: chronicorum, Jornand. Get. praef.

breviator.full: brĕvĭātor, ōris, m. id.. * An abbreviator, epitomizer, Oros. 1, 8.—* The author of a breviarium (q. v.), Novell. 105, 2, 4.

breviculus.full: brĕvĭcŭlus, a, um, adj. dim. [brevis], somewhat short or small (rare): homo, Plaut. Merc. 3, 4, 54: pinnae, Fronto, Eloq.: grabatulus, App. M. 1, p. 107, 18.— Subst.: brĕvĭcŭlus, i, m. (sc. liber), a short writing, a summary, Cod. Just. 1, 7, tit. 44, and Cod. Th. 1, 4, tit. 17 dub.— Transf., of time: tempus, App. M. 6, p. 183, 35.

breviloquens.full: brĕvĭlŏquens, entis, adj. brevisloquor, speaking briefly, brief, Cic. Att. 7, 20, 1.

breviloquentia.full: brĕvĭlŏquentĭa, ae, f. brevis-loquentia, brevity of speech: breviloquentiam in dicendo colat, an expression of Cicero, censured by Seneca ap. Gell. 12, 2, 7.

breviloquium.full: brĕvĭlŏquĭum, ii, n. brevis-loquor, brevity in speech, Prisc. p. 754 P.; Fulg. Myth. praef. fin.; Serv. ad Verg. A. 1, 561.

breviloquus.full: brĕvĭlŏquus or -quis, = βραχυλόγος, short in speech, speaking briefty, Gloss. Lab.
breviloquus.short: brĕvĭlŏquus or -quis, = βραχυλόγος, short in speech, speaking briefty, Gloss.

brevio.full: brĕvĭo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. brevis, to shorten, abbreviate, abridge, βραχύνω brevio, Gloss. Vet. (post-Aug.; cf. Burm. Anth. Lat. 1, p. 76; most freq. in Quint.); Manil. 3, 461; 6, 431: breviare quaedam, Quint. 1, 9, 2: aliquid callide, id. 5, 13, 41 Spald. N. cr.: prolixa (in scribendo), Lact. Epit. 8, 6; Sev. Sulp. Hist. Sacr. 1, 1: breviatae horae, Paul. Nol. Carm. Nat. S. Fel. 24, 9, 13: umerorum raro decens allevatio atque contractio est. Breviatur enim cervix, Quint. 11, 3, 83: non breviat

brevis.full: brĕvis, e, adj. (abl. breve, Varr. R. R. 2, 3, 2; comp. abl. breviore, Ov. Am. 2, 17, 22) [cf. βραχύς, Fest. p. 26], short, little, of small extent, in space and time (opp. longus; in space, in good class. prose, diff. from parvus, which designates that which fills a small space in length, breadth, and thickness; while brevis is used only of length in its different directions of breadth, height, or depth; and even of a circle, as merely a line, and without reference to the space enclosed, v. inf

brevitas.full: brĕvĭtas, ātis, f. brevis, shortness. Lit., in space (cf. brevis, I.) (rare): brevitas angusti freti, the narrowness of the strait, Gell. 10, 27, 6: hominibus Gallis prae magnitudine corporum suorum brevitas nostra contemptui est, smallness of stature, Caes. B. G. 2, 30; cf.: haec habilis brevitate suā est, Ov. Am. 2, 4, 35: spatii, Caes. B. C. 1, 82, 3: crurum, Plin. 8, 34, 52, § 123: chamaeplatani coactae brevitatis, Plin. 12, 2, 6, § 13: guttarum, Vitr. 7, 8, 2.—More freq., Transf. In time, s

bria.full: brĭa, ae, f., a wine - vessel, εἶδος ἀγγείου, Gloss. Philox.; Arn. 7, p. 235; cf. Hildebr. ad App. Mag. 59 (acc. to Charis. p. 63, hebrĭa: hebria est vas vinarium, unde ebrius et ebria dicitur).
bria.short: brĭa, ae, f., a wine - vessel, εἶδος ἀγγείου, Gloss.

briareus.full: Brĭăreus (trisyl.), ei, m., = Βριαρεύς, Callim. Del. 143 (old form Βριάρεως, Hom. Il. 1, 403; v. Crus. Wb. of Prop. Names), the hundred-armed giant, also called Ægœon: centumgeminus, Verg. A. 6, 287 Serv. and Heyne; cf. id. ib. 10, 565: ferox, Luc. 4, 596 Schol.: immensus, Stat. Th. 2, 596; cf. also Ov. M. 2, 10; Claud. Laud. Stil. 1, 304: vastus, Sen. Herc. Oet. 167.—Hence, Brĭă-rēĭus, a um, adj., of or belonging to Briareus: turba, Claud. Rapt. Pros. 3, 188.

brietes.full: Brĭētes, is, m., a Greek painter, Plin. 35, 11, 40, § 123.
brietes.short: Brĭētes, is, m., a Greek painter, Plin.

brigantes1.full: brĭgantes, um, m., a species of small worm in the eyelashes, Marc. Emp. 8.
brigantes1.short: brĭgantes, um, m., a species of small worm in the eyelashes, Marc.

brigantes2.full: Brĭgantes, um (acc. Brigantas, Tac. A. 12, 32), m., the most northern and powerful people in Roman Britain, subdued by Cerialis, Tac. A. 12, 32; id. H. 3, 45; id. Agr. 17; Juv. 14, 196.—Hence, Julius Briganticus, a son of the sister of Civilis, Tac. H. 4, 70; 2, 22; 5, 21.

briganticus.full: Brĭgantĭcus, i, m., a Roman cognomen, Tac. H. 2, 22; 4, 70 (Brĕ-, Halm).
briganticus.short: Brĭgantĭcus, i, m., a Roman cognomen, Tac.

brigantium.full: Brĭgantĭum, ii, f., or Brĭgantĭa, ae, f. A town in Rhœtia, now Bregenz, Amm. 15, 4, 1 and 3; Itin. Anton.—Hence, Brĭgantīnus, a, um, adj.: lacus, the lake of Constance, Plin. 9, 17, 29, § 63 (in Mel. 3, 2, 8, Lacus Venetus).— The town of Briançon, in France, Amm. 15, 10, 7.
brigantium.short: Brĭgantĭum, ii, f., or Brĭgantĭa, ae, f.

brigiani.full: Brigĭāni, ōrum, m., an Alpine tribe in Gaul, Inscr. Trop. Aug. ap. Plin. 3, 20, 24, § 137.
brigiani.short: Brigĭāni, ōrum, m., an Alpine tribe in Gaul, Inscr.

brimo.full: Brīmo, ūs, f., = Βρῖμώ (prop. the angry one; cf. Arn. 5, p. 170), a name of Proserpine, Prop. 2, 2, 12.—Acc. Brimo, Stat. S. 2, 3, 38.

briniates.full: Brinĭātes, um, m., a Ligurian tribe south of the Po, near the modern Brignolo, Liv. 41, 19, 4.
briniates.short: Brinĭātes, um, m., a Ligurian tribe south of the Po, near the modern Brignolo, Liv.

brisa.full: brīsa, ae, f. kindr. with the Gr. βρύτεα, τά, the refuse grapes after they are pressed, grape-skins, Col. 12, 39, 2.

brisaeus.full: Brīsaeus (-sēus), i, m., = Βρισαῖος, a name of Bacchus, Macr. S. 1, 18; Mythogr. Lat. 3, 12, 2.— Transf., of the poet Attius, antiquated, Pers. 1, 76 Coningt. ad loc.
brisaeus.short: Brīsaeus (-sēus), i, m., = Βρισαῖος, a name of Bacchus, Macr.

briseis.full: Brīsēïs, ĭdos (acc. Briseïda, Prop. 2, 8, 35; Ov. A. A. 3, 189 al.: Briseïdam, Hyg. Fab. 106; voc. Brisaeï, Ov. A. A. 2, 713), f., = Βρισηΐς, Hippodamia, daughter of Brises, and slave of Achilles, from whom she was taken by Agamemnon: Varro, Sat. Men. 63, 4; Prop. 2, 22, 29; Hor. C. 2, 4, 3; Ov. Am. 2, 8, 11; id. H. 3, 137.

britanni.full: Brĭtanni, ōrum, m., the Britons, inhabitants of Great Britain, Lucr. 6, 1105; Caes. B. G. 4, 21; 5, 14; 5, 21 et saep.; Tac. Agr. 11 sq.; id. A. 14, 29; Verg. E. 1, 67; Hor. C. 1, 35, 30; 3, 4, 33; 3, 5, 3 et saep.— In sing. Britannus catenatus, Hor. Epod. 7, 7.— The inhabitants of Bretagne, or Brittany, in France, Sid. Ep. 1, 7; 9, 9.— Derivv. Brĭtannĭa (Brittānĭa in MSS. and edd. of Sol. and Mart. Cap.), ae, f., = Βρεττανία, Great Britain, in its most extended sense, consisting of Albion (Engl
britanni.short: Brĭtanni, ōrum, m., the Britons, inhabitants of Great Britain, Lucr.

britomartis.full: Brĭtŏmartis, is, f., = Βριτόμαρτις (Cretan, ΒΠΙΤΥ, rich in blessing, and ΜΑΠΤΙΣ, maiden, Sol. 11). A Cretan nymph, daughter of Jupiter and Carme, inventress of the hunting-net; when pursued by Minos, she cast herself into the sea, Verg. Cir. 285 sq.— An epithet of the Cretan Diana: ignea, Claud. III. Cons. Stil. 251: lucos Britomartis agit, id. ib. 303.
britomartis.short: Brĭtŏmartis, is, f., = Βριτόμαρτις (Cretan, ΒΠΙΤΥ, rich in blessing, and ΜΑΠΤΙΣ, maiden, Sol.

brixellum.full: Brixellum (Brixillum, Plin. 3, 15, 20, § 115; Inscr. Murat. 239), i, n., a town in Gallia Cisalpina, on the Po, between Parma and Mantua, now Brescello, Plin. 7, 49, 50, § 163; Tac. H. 2, 33; 2, 39; 2, 51; 2, 54; Suet. Oth. 9.—Hence, Brixillānus, a, um, adj., of Brixellum, Inscr. Orell. 3734.

brixentes.full: Brixentes, um, m., = Βριξάνται, a people in Rhœtia, in the modern Brixen, Plin. 3, 20, 24, § 137.
brixentes.short: Brixentes, um, m., = Βριξάνται, a people in Rhœtia, in the modern Brixen, Plin.

brixia.full: Brixia, ae, f., = Βριξία, a town in Gallia Cisalpina, now Brescia, Liv. 5, 35, 1; 32, 30, 6; Plin. 3, 19, 23, § 132; Just. 20, 5; Cat. 67, 32 (id. 33 and 34 suspicious; v. Sillig N. cr.).— Derivv. Brixĭānus, a, um, adj., of or pertaining to Brixia: Galli, Liv. 21, 25, 14: porta, Tac. H. 3, 27.—Subst.: Brixĭāni, ōrum, the Brixians, Inscr. Orell. 1971.— Brixĭensis, e, adj., of Brixia (post-class.): episcopus, Aug. Ep. 222 (id. Haeres. 41: Brixianus).
brixia.short: Brixia, ae, f., = Βριξία, a town in Gallia Cisalpina, now Brescia, Liv.

brocchitas.full: brocchĭtas, ātis, f. brochus, a projection of the teeth in animals: dentium, Plin. 11, 37, 64, § 169.

brochon.full: brŏchŏn, i, n., the gum flowing from the bdellium, Plin. 12, 9, 19, § 35.
brochon.short: brŏchŏn, i, n., the gum flowing from the bdellium, Plin.

brochus1.full: brŏchus, brocchus, broccus, or broncus, a, um, adj. root bor-; cf. voro (ante - class. and rare). Lit., of the teeth of animals, projecting: dentes, Varr. R. R. 2, 7, 3 Schneid.; 2, 9, 3.— Transf., of animals, with projecting teeth, Lucil. ap. Non. p. 25, 27 sq.; Plaut. Fragm. ap. Fest. s. v. valgos, p. 375 Müll.
brochus1.short: brŏchus, brocchus, broccus, or broncus, a, um, adj.

brochus2.full: Brŏchus, i, m., a Roman cognomen: Brochus (Brocchus), Cic. Lig. 4, 11; 11, 32 sq.
brochus2.short: Brŏchus, i, m., a Roman cognomen: Brochus (Brocchus), Cic.

brogitarus.full: Brogitărus, i, m., a Gallo - Grecian, son-in-law of King Deiotarus, to whom P. Clodius as tribune sold the office of highpriest at Pessinus and the title of king, Cic. Sest. 26, 56; id. Q. Fr. 2, 9, 2; id. Har. Resp. 26, 56.—In plur. Brogitari, to denote a class, Cic. Har. Resp. 27, 59.
brogitarus.short: Brogitărus, i, m., a Gallo - Grecian, son-in-law of King Deiotarus, to whom P.

bromatici.full: brōmătĭci, ōrum, m., those who loathe food, Isid. Orig. 5, 35, 6 [βρῶμα, edacitas, id. ib.].
bromatici.short: brōmătĭci, ōrum, m., those who loathe food, Isid.

brome.full: Brŏmē (Brŏmiē, Hyg. Fab. 182), ēs, f., a nymph who, with her sister, brought up Bacchus, Serv. ad Verg. E. 6, 15.

bromius.full: Brŏmĭus, ii (voc. Bromie, Plaut. Men. 5, 2, 82), m., = Βρόμιος (the noisy one), a surname of Bacchus (on account of the tumultuous celebration of his festivals), Enn. ap. Charis. p. 214 P.; Ov. M. 4,11; Petr. 41, 6; Luc. 5, 73; Claud. III. Cons. Hon. 132; id. IV. Cons. Hon. 132.—Hence, Adj. Brŏ-mĭālis, e, Bromian, i.e. Bacchic, Mart. Cap. 8, § 804.— Brŏmĭus, a, um, of Bacchus: Bromia auctumnitas, Varr. ap. Non. p. 71, 18 (but Lachm. ad Lucr. 5, 1006, conj. Bromii); so, remi, Claud. II. Cons. Sti

bromos.short: brŏmŏs, i, m., = βρόμος, oats, Plin.

bromosus.full: brōmōsus, a, um, adj., = βρωμώδης, stinking, fetid: caro, Cael. Aur. Acut. 2, 37: qualitas, id. Tard. 3, 2.
bromosus.short: brōmōsus, a, um, adj., = βρωμώδης, stinking, fetid: caro, Cael.

bromus.full: Brŏmus, i, m., = Βρόμος, a Centaur slain by Cœneus in the contest with the Centaurs, Ov. M. 12, 459.
bromus.short: Brŏmus, i, m., = Βρόμος, a Centaur slain by Cœneus in the contest with the Centaurs, Ov.

bronchia.full: bronchĭa, ōrum, n., = βρόγχια, the bronchial tubes, Cael. Aur. Acut. 2, 28, 147.
bronchia.short: bronchĭa, ōrum, n., = βρόγχια, the bronchial tubes, Cael.

bronte.full: Brontē, ēs, f., = Βροντή. Thunder (personified), Plin. 35, 10, 36, § 96.— As nom. propr., the name of one of the horses of the Sun, Hyg. Fab. 183.

brontea.full: brontĕa, ae, f. βροντή, the thunderstone, a precious stone, Plin. 37, 10, 55, § 150. —Also called brontia, Isid. Orig. 16, 15, 24 (MSS. bronia).

brontes.full: Brontes, ae (acc. Brontem, Stat. S. 1, 1, 4), m., = Βρόντης, a Cyclops who labored in the workshop of Vulcan, Verg. A. 8, 425; Ov. F. 4, 288; Claud. III. Cons. Hon. 193.

bronton.full: Bronton, ontis, adj., = Βροντῶν (the thunderer), an epithet of Jupiter, Inscr. Grut. 34, 5; 17, 12; Inscr. Orell. 1272.
bronton.short: Bronton, ontis, adj., = Βροντῶν (the thunderer), an epithet of Jupiter, Inscr.

broteas.full: Brŏtĕas, ae, m., = Βροτέας. One of the Lapithœ, slain by the Centaur Gryneus at the marriage festival of Perseus, Ov. M. 12, 262.— Twin-brother of Ammon, and with him slain by Phineus, Ov. M. 5, 107.— A son of Vulcan and Minerva, Ov. Ib. 515.

bruanium.full: Brŭănĭum (Brўă-), ii, n., = Βρυάνιον, a town in Macedonia, Liv. 31, 39, 5.
bruanium.short: Brŭănĭum (Brўă-), ii, n., = Βρυάνιον, a town in Macedonia, Liv.

bruchion.full: Bruchīon, ii, n., the royal residence in Alexandria, containing the palace, museum, mausoleum, etc., Amm. 22, 16, 15; Hier. Vit. St. Anton.
bruchion.short: Bruchīon, ii, n., the royal residence in Alexandria, containing the palace, museum, mausoleum, etc., Amm.

bruchus.full: brūchus, i, m., = βροῦχος or βροῦκος, a kind of locust without wings, Prud. Ham. 229; Vulg. Lev. 11, 22 al.
bruchus.short: brūchus, i, m., = βροῦχος or βροῦκος, a kind of locust without wings, Prud.

bructeri.full: Bructĕri, ōrum (gen. -terūm, Plin. Ep. 2, 7, 2), m., = Βρούκτεροι, a German people occupying the country between the Rhine, the Lippe, Ems, and Weser, Tac. G. 33; id. A. 1, 51; 1, 60; 13, 56; id. H. 4, 21; 4, 77; 5, 18; Vell. 2, 105, 1.—In sing.: Bructĕrus, i, m., Claud. IV. Cons. Hon. 451; and adj. Bructĕrus, a, um: natio, Tac. H. 4, 61.

bruma.full: brūma, ae, f. for brevima, breuma = brevissima: dicta bruma quod brevissimus tunc dies est, Varr. L. L. 6, § 8 Müll.: bruma a brevitate dierum dicta, Paul. ex Fest. p. 31 Müll.; cf. Isid. Orig. 5, 35, 6; Gesn. Claud. Rapt. Pros. 2, 106; Ruhnk. ad Ter. Phorm. 4, 4, 28. Lit., the shortest day in the year, the winter solstice, * Lucr. 5, 746; Varr. L. L. l. l.; Ter. Phorm. 4, 4, 28: circa brumam serendum non esse, Plin. 18, 24, 56, § 204 al.—Plur.: solis accessus discessusque solstitiis brumisque c

brumalis.full: brūmālis, e, adj. bruma. Of or pertaining to the winter solstice, or shortest day: dies, Cic. Div. 2, 14, 33; id. Fat. 3: polus, Varr. L. L. 9, § 24 Müll.: signum, Capricorn, Cic. de Or. 3, 45, 178: flexus, the tropic of Capricorn, Lucr. 5, 615; 5, 639: orbis, Cic. N. D. 3, 14, 37: tempus, id. ib. 2, 44, 112: circulus, Plin. 2, 70, 70, § 177: oriens, Col. 1, 6, 1; Plin. 2, 47, 46, § 119: occasus, id. l. l.: meridies, Col. 9, 5, 1: revocatio, Cic. Univ. 9: hora, the shortest (since it was the twe

brumaria.full: brūmārĭa, ae, f. (sc. herba) [bruma], a plant, also called leontopodium, App. Herb. 7.

brundisium.full: Brundĭsĭum (in many MSS., but less correctly Brundŭsĭum; cf. Suet. Caes. 34 Torrent.; Sil. 8, 576 Heins. and Drak.; Flor. 1, 20 Duker.; Luc. 2, 609 Cort.; Hor. S. 1, 5, 104 K. and H.), ii, n. (access. form Brenda, acc. to Paul. ex Fest. p. 33 Müll.: Brunda, Arn. 2, p. 50), = Βρεντέσιον or Βρεντήσιον [Βρένδον ἔλαφον, Hesych.; cf. Strab. 6, p. 432; Steph. Byz.; Isid. Orig. 15, 1, 49; from the harbor extending beyond the town like the antlers of a stag], an ancient town in Calabria, with a very con
brundisium.short: Brundĭsĭum (in many MSS., but less correctly Brundŭsĭum;

bruscum.full: bruscum, i, n., an excrescence on the maple-tree, Plin. 16, 16, 27, § 68.
bruscum.short: bruscum, i, n., an excrescence on the maple-tree, Plin.

brutesco.full: brūtesco, ĕre, v. inch. [brutus], to become brutish, rough, unreasonable (postclass.), Sid. Ep. 4, 1 fin.; Lact. 7, 12, 24; Ven. Ep. praef. carm. 6, 5.

brutianus.full: Brutĭānus, a, um, v. Bruttii, II. B., and Brutus, II. B. 2. a.

brutidius.full: Brutĭdĭus, ii, m., a Roman name; esp. Brutidius Niger, an historian of the time of Tiberius, and author of a work upon the death of Cicero, now lost, Tac. A. 3, 66; Juv. 10, 83.
brutidius.short: Brutĭdĭus, ii, m., a Roman name;

brutinus.full: Brūtīnus, a, um, v. Brutus, II. B. 2. b.

bruttii.full: Bruttĭi (in MSS. also Brutĭi, Brut-ti, and Brittĭi), ōrum, m., = Βρέττιοι Polyb., Βρούττιοι Steph., the Bruttii, the inhabitants of the southern point of Italy, Mel. 2, 4, 2; Caes. B. C. 1, 30; Liv. 22, 61, 11 al. —In sing.: Bruttĭus, ii, m., a Bruttian, collect., Liv. 31, 7, 11; Flor. 1, 18, 27; Sil. 8, 570; 11, 10.— Meton., the country of the Bruttii, Varr. R. R. 2, 1, 2: in Bruttiis, Cic. Rosc. Am. 46, 132; id. Caecin. 19, 54; Caes. B. C. 1, 30; Liv. 32, 1, 7: ex Bruttiis, id. 32, 1, 11; Gell

brutus1.full: brūtus, a, um, adj. kindr. with βα^ρύς, perh. contr. from barutus, a lengthened form of barus, like actutum, astutus, cinctutus, versutus, from actu, astus, cinctus, versus; cf. also βρῖθύς, heavy, weighty; Fr. and Engl. brute, brutal. Lit., heavy, unwieldy, immovable (rare): brutum antiqui gravem dicebant, Paul. ex Fest. p. 31 Müll.: pondus, falling down with heavy weight, Lucr. 6, 105: tellus, * Hor. C. 1, 34, 9 (cf.: terra iners, id. ib. 3, 4, 45: immota tellus, Sen. Thyest. 1020: terra sempe

brutus2.full: Brūtus, i, m., = Βροῦτος [1. brutus], a Roman cognomen. L. Junius, the relative of Tarquinius Superbus, saved by his feigned stupidity [whence the name], and the deliverer of Rome from regal dominion, Liv. 1, 56, 7 sq.; Ov. F. 2, 717; 2, 837; Verg. A. 6, 818; Cic. Tusc. 1, 37, 89 saep. After him, Brutus was the cognomen of the patrician gens Junia.— From the plebeian gens Junia, M. Junius, son of Servilia, a half-sister of Cato Uticensis by M. Brutus (not by Cæsar; v. Ellendt Cic. Brut. p. cxxvi

brya.full: brўa, ae, f., = βρυά, a shrub, also called myrice and tamarice, Plin. 13, 21, 37, § 116; 24, 9, 42, § 69.
brya.short: brўa, ae, f., = βρυά, a shrub, also called myrice and tamarice, Plin.

bryaxis.full: Brўaxis, is, m., = Βρύαξις, a Grecian sculptor, Vitr. 7, praef. § 13; Col. 1, praef. 31; Plin. 34, 7, 18, § 42; 34, 8, 19, § 73 al.
bryaxis.short: Brўaxis, is, m., = Βρύαξις, a Grecian sculptor, Vitr.

bryazon.full: Brўazon, ontis, m., a river in Bithynia, Plin. 5, 32, 43, § 148.
bryazon.short: Brўazon, ontis, m., a river in Bithynia, Plin.

bryazus.full: Brўazus, i, m., the name of a Bithynian god and of his temple, Plin. 31, 2, 18, § 23.
bryazus.short: Brўazus, i, m., the name of a Bithynian god and of his temple, Plin.

bryges.full: Bryges, um, m., a people of Macedonia, emigrants from Asia Minor, Plin. 5, 32, 41, § 145.
bryges.short: Bryges, um, m., a people of Macedonia, emigrants from Asia Minor, Plin.

bryllion.full: Bryllion, ii, n., a town in Mysia, on the Propontis, Plin. 5, 32, 40, § 144.
bryllion.short: Bryllion, ii, n., a town in Mysia, on the Propontis, Plin.

bryon.full: brўon, i, n., = βρύον. Moss; esp. the kind otherwise called sphagnos, Plin. 12, 23, 50, § 108.— The grape - formed blossom of the silver poplar, Plin. 12, 28, 61, § 132.— A plant growing upon the seashore, with leaves like lettuce, Plin. 13, 25, 49, § 137; 27, 8, 33, § 56; 32, 9, 36, § 110.

bryonia.full: brўōnĭa, ae, f., = βρυωνία, a wild vine, the bryony; of two kinds: the white, Plin. 23, 1, 16, § 24; Scrib. Comp. 59; the black, Plin. 23, 1, 17, § 27; Col. 10, 250; App. Herb. 66.
bryonia.short: brўōnĭa, ae, f., = βρυωνία, a wild vine, the bryony;

bu1.full: bu = βου, a Greek prefix, which, in composition, expresses the idea of greatness: Graeci assueti magnis et amplis rebus praeponere βου, a magnitudine scilicet bovis. Hic est, quod grandes pueri βούπαιδας appellant et mariscam ficum βούσυκον, Paul. ex Fest. p. 109 Müll.; Varr. R. R. 2, 5, 4 [cf. Engl. horse-cucumber, elephant folio, etc.].
bu1.short: bu = βου, a Greek prefix, which, in composition, expresses the idea of greatness: Graeci assueti magnis et amplis rebus praeponere βου, a magnitudine scilicet bovis.

bua.full: bua, ae, f. bu, Paul. ex Fest. s. v. im butum, p. 109 Müll., the natural sound made by infants in asking for their drink, as pappa for their food, Varr. ap. Non. p. 81, 1 sq.; cf. vinibua.

bubalinus.full: būbălīnus, a, um, adj. bubalus, pertaining to the African gazelle: laridum, Val. Imp. ap. Vop. Prob. 4.

bubalion.full: būbălĭon, ii, n., = βουβάλιον, a wild cucumber, App. Herb. 113.
bubalion.short: būbălĭon, ii, n., = βουβάλιον, a wild cucumber, App.

bubalus.full: būbălus, i, m., = βούβαλος, a kind of African stag or gazelle, Plin. 8, 15, 15, § 38; Sol. 20, 5; Vulg. Deut. 14, 5.—Hence, bū-bălus, a, um, adj., of the gazelle: caro, Vulg. 2 Reg. 6, 19; id. 1 Par. 16, 3.— The buffalo, wild-ox, = urus, Sol. 20, 5; Mart. Spect. 23, 4; this use of the word is censured by Pliny, 8, 15, 15, § 38.—Collat. form būfălus, i, m., Ven. Fort. Carm. 7, 4, 21.
bubalus.short: būbălus, i, m., = βούβαλος, a kind of African stag or gazelle, Plin.

bubassus.full: Būbassus (-ăsus), i, f., = Βύβασσος, Steph., a town in Caria, Plin. 5, 28, 29, § 104. — Derivv. Būbassĭus, a, um, adj., of Bubassus: sinus, Mel. 1, 16, 2.— Būbăsis, ĭdis, f. adj., of Bubassus, Ov. M. 9, 644.
bubassus.short: Būbassus (-ăsus), i, f., = Βύβασσος, Steph., a town in Caria, Plin.

bubastis.full: Būbastis, is, f., = Βούβαστις. A town in Egypt, on the Pelusian arm of the Nile, now Tel-Basta (i.e. Hill of Bubastis), in the vicinity of the village Benalhassar, Mel. 1, 9, 9.—Hence, Būbastītes nŏ-mŏs, Βουβαστίτης νομός, Strab., Plin. 5, 9, 9, § 49; Mel. 1, 9, 9.— The goddess Bubastis, who was worshipped there; corresponding to Diana, Ov. M. 9, 691; cf. Hdt. 2, 137; 2, 156.—Hence, Būbastius, a, um, adj., of Bubastis: sacra, Grat. Cyn. 42; gen. plur. BVBASTIVM, Inscr. Orell. 5974.

bubeium.full: Bubeium, i, n., a town in Africa, Plin. 5, 5, 5, § 37.
bubeium.short: Bubeium, i, n., a town in Africa, Plin.

bubetani.full: Bubetāni, ōrum, m., a people of Latium, Plin. 3, 5, 9, § 69.
bubetani.short: Bubetāni, ōrum, m., a people of Latium, Plin.

bubile.full: būbīle (access. form bŏvīle, unus. acc. to Varr. L. L. 8, § 54 Müll.; although used by Cato, acc. to Charis. p. 81; and by Veg. 4, 1, 3), is, n. bos, a stall for oxen: (boves) reicere in bubile, Plaut. Pers. 2, 5, 18 Ritschl; Cato, R. R. 4; Varr. R. R. 1, 13, 1; Col. 1, 6, 4; Phaedr. 2, 8, 4.

bubinare.full: bubinare (buv-) est menstruo mulierum sanguine inquinare, Paul. ex Fest. p. 32 Müll.; cf. Gloss. Isid.
bubinare.short: bubinare (buv-) est menstruo mulierum sanguine inquinare, Paul.

bubleum.full: bubleum, i, n., a kind of wine, Paul. ex Fest. 32 Müll. [Βύβλινος οῖνος, Hesiod. Op. 587 Göttl.]
bubleum.short: bubleum, i, n., a kind of wine, Paul.

bubo1.full: būbo, ōnis, m. (f. only once Verg. A. 4, 462; cf. Serv. ad loc.; Non. p. 194, 1.— Hence given erroneously by Prisc. p. 683 P. and Rhemn. Palaem. p. 1370 fin. ib. as comm.) [βύας, βῦζα], an owl, the horned owl: Strix bubo, Linn., whose cry was considered as ill-boding, Plin. 10, 12, 16, § 34; Verg. A. 4, 462: ignavus bubo, Ov. M. 5, 550: profanus, id. ib. 6, 432 (cf. id. ib. 5, 543: profana avis): funereus, id. ib. 10, 453: Stygius (since Ascalaphus, son of Acheron or Styx, was changed to an owl;

bubo2.full: bŭbo, ĕre, v. n., to cry like a bittern, Auct. Carm. Philom. 42 (al. butio).

bubon.full: Būbon, ōnis, f., = Βουβών, a town of Lycia, Plin. 5, 27, 28, § 101.
bubon.short: Būbon, ōnis, f., = Βουβών, a town of Lycia, Plin.

bubona.full: Būbōna, ae, f. bos, the protecting goddess of cattle among the Romans, Aug. Civ. Dei, 4, 34.—Hence, Būbetĭus, a, um, adj., of or for Bubona: ludi, Plin. 18, 3, 3, § 12.

bubonium.full: būbōnĭum (-on), ii, n., = βουβώνιον, a plant useful against swellings in the groin, also called aster Atticus, Plin. 27, 5, 19, § 36.
bubonium.short: būbōnĭum (-on), ii, n., = βουβώνιον, a plant useful against swellings in the groin, also called aster Atticus, Plin.

bubsequa.full: bubsĕqua (also bobsĕqua and bū-sĕqua), ae, m. bos-sequor, a neatherd, herdsman (post-class.), App. M. 8, p. 201, 13; id. Flor. 1, n. 3; Sid. Ep. 1, 6.
bubsequa.short: bubsĕqua (also bobsĕqua and bū-sĕqua), ae, m.

bubulcarius.full: bŭbulcārĭus, = βοώτης, a ploughman, Gloss. Gr. Lat. ( = bubulcus).

bubulcito.full: bŭbulcĭto, āre, v. n. (bŭbulcĭtor, āri, v. dep., Plaut.) [bubulcus], to be a herdsman, to keep, feed, or drive oxen (ante- and post-class., and very rare). Lit.: bubulcitarier, Plaut. Most. 1, 1, 50; App. Flor. n. 6, p. 343, 14.— Trop., to cry or bawl like an ox-driver, Varr. ap. Non. p. 79, 29 (Sat. Men. 52, 1).

bubulcus1.full: bŭbulcus, i, m. bos, bubulus, βοῦκος. In a restricted sense, one who ploughs with oxen, a ploughman, = arator (diff. from pastor and armentarius, a herdsman; so most freq. in the Script. rerr. rustt.), Varr. R. R. 2, prooem. § 4 sq.; Juv. 11, 151; cf. Col. 1, 6, 8; 1, 9, 2; 2, 2, 25; 2, 5, 2; 2, 12, 1 sq.; Cic. Div. 1, 27, 57; Ov. Tr. 3, 12, 30; Juv. 7, 116; 11, 151 al.— In a more general sense, a herdsman (rare, and not before the post-Aug. per.), Dig. 33, 7, 18, § 6.

bubulcus2.full: Bŭbulcus, i, m., the cognomen of several persons in the gens Junia, Liv. 9, 20, 7; 27, 6, 8; Plin. 18, 3, 3, § 10.
bubulcus2.short: Bŭbulcus, i, m., the cognomen of several persons in the gens Junia, Liv.

bubulinus.full: būbŭlīnus, a, um, adj. bos, for bubulus, of cattle, ox- (post-Aug.; only in Veg.): stercus, Veg. 1, 13, 3: fimum, id. 3, 28, 3: sevum, id. 4, 8, 2: urina, id. 4, 17.

bubulo.full: būbŭlo, āre, v. n. bubo, to cry, hoot, or screech like an owl, Auct. Carm. Phil. 37.

bubulus.full: būbŭlus, a, um, adj. bos, of or pertaining to cattle or oxen (class.): cori, thongs, straps of ox-hide, Plaut. Poen. 1, 1, 11; and humorously, cottabi, the snapping of such ox-whips (cf. cottabus), id. Trin. 4, 4, 4 Lind.; so also monimenta, for lashes, id. Stich. 1, 2, 6; and, exuviae, id. Most. 4, 1, 26: pecus, neat cattle, Varr. R. R. 2, 1, 13: armentum, Col. 1, praef. § 26: fimum, Cato, R. R. 40, 2; Liv. 38, 18, 5: utres, Plin. 6, 29, 34, § 176: lac, cow's milk, id. 11, 41, 96, § 238: caseus

buca.full: Būca, ae, f., a town in Samnium, Mel. 2, 4, 6; Plin. 3, 12, 17, § 106.—Hence, Bū-cāni, ōrum, m., the inhabitants of Buca, Inscr. Murat. 1032, 4.
buca.short: Būca, ae, f., a town in Samnium, Mel.

bucaeda.full: būcaeda, ae, m. bos-caedo, one who is whipped with thongs of ox-hide (cf. bos and bubulus), Plaut. Most. 4, 2, 1.

bucardia.full: būcardĭa, ae, f., = βουκαπδία (oxheart), an unknown precious stone, perh. a kind of turquoise, Plin. 37, 10, 55, § 150.
bucardia.short: būcardĭa, ae, f., = βουκαπδία (oxheart), an unknown precious stone, perh.

bucca.full: bucca (not buccha), ae, f. kindred with βύζω, βυκάνη; Fr. bouche. The cheek (puffed or filled out in speaking, eating, etc.; diff. from genae, the side of the face, the cheeks, and from mala, the upper part of the cheek under the eyes; v. Plin. 11, 37, 57, § 156 sqq.; mostly in plur.; class.): buccam implere, Cato ap. Gell. 2, 22, 29: sufflare buccas, Plaut. Stich. 5, 4, 42: inflare, id. ib. 5, 6, 7: rumpere buccas, to write bombast, Pers. 5, 13: sufflare buccis, Mart. 3, 17, 4.—In violent anger

buccea.full: buccĕa, ae, f. bucca, a morsel, mouthful, August. ap. Suet. Aug. 76 fin.

buccella.full: buccella, ae, f. dim. id., a small mouthful, morsel, Mart. 6, 75, 3; Apic. 7, 6; Vulg. Ruth, 2, 14: panis, Vulg. Gen. 18, 5.— Small bread divided among the poor, Cod. Th. 14, 17, 5; cf. Salmas. Vop. Aur. 35.

buccellaris.full: buccellāris, e, adj. buccellatum, farina, meal ground from biscuit, Plin. Val. 1, 6.— Subst.: buccellāre, is, n., a cooking utensil, Marc. Emp. 23 (others, bucculari, from buccula, in the same signif.).

buccellatum.full: buccellātum, i, n. buccella, soldiers' biscuit, Amm. 17, 8, 2; Vulcat. Gall. Avid. Cass. 5, 4; Spart. Pesc. Nig. 10, 4; Cod. Th. 7, 4, 6; 7, 5, 2.

buccina.full: buccĭna, buccĭnātor, buccĭno, buccĭnum, and buccĭnus, v. bucina, etc.
buccina.short: buccĭna, buccĭnātor, buccĭno, buccĭnum, and buccĭnus, v.

bucco.full: bucco, ōnis, m. amplif. [bucca, one who has distended cheeks], a babbler, blockhead, fool (very rare): bucco = garrulus, quod ceteros oris loquacitate, non sensu exsuperat, Isid. Orig. 10, 30: stulti, stolidi, fatui, fungi, bardi, blenni, buccones, Plaut. Bacch. 5, 1, 2: macci et buccones, App. Mag. p. 325, 30.

bucconiatis.full: buccŏnĭātis vītis, a species of vine in Thurium, the fruit of which is not gathered until after the first frost, Plin. 14, 3, 4, § 39.
bucconiatis.short: buccŏnĭātis vītis, a species of vine in Thurium, the fruit of which is not gathered until after the first frost, Plin.

buccula.full: buccŭla (būcŭla), ae, f. dim. bucca. A little cheek or mouth, * Suet. Galb. 4: pressa Cupidinis buccula, App. M. 6, p. 182, 17; 3, p. 137, 40; Arn. 2, p. 73.— In milit. lang. The beaver, that part of a helmet which covers the mouth and cheeks, παραγναθίς: bucculas tergere, Liv. 44, 34, 8; Juv. 10, 134; Capitol. Max. Jun. 3; Cod. Th. 10, 22, 1.— Bucculae, two cheeks, one on each side of the channel in which the arrow of the catapulta was placed, Vitr. 10, 15, 3.

buccularius.full: buccŭlārĭus, ii, m. buccula, II., the maker of beavers for helmets, Dig. 50, 6, 7 (6) dub. (Momms. bucularum structores).

bucculentus.full: buccŭlentus, a, um, adj. buccula, I., having full cheeks or a large mouth, Plaut. Merc. 3, 4, 54.

bucephalas.full: Būcĕphălas, ae (-lus, i, Paul. ex Fest. p. 32 Müll.; Būcĕphăla, Jul. Val. Rer. Gest. Alex. M. 3, 11), m., = Βουκεφάλας (Macedon. = Βουκέφαλος, that which is arked with the figure of a bullock's head—βοῦς, κεφαλή—or so called from the breadth of its forehead), the horse of Alexander the Great, Curt. 6, 5, 18; 9, 3, 23; Gell. 5, 2, 1; acc. Bucephalan, Plin. 8, 42, 64, § 154.—Hence, Būcĕphăla, ōrum, n. (or -la, ae, f., Curt. 9, 3, 23; or -īa, ae, f.; or -ē, ēs, f., Just. 12, 8, 8; or -lŏs, i, f., G

bucephalus.full: Būcĕphălus, i, m., a promontory in the Peloponnesus, Mel. 2, 3, 8; Plin. 4, 5, 9, § 18.
bucephalus.short: Būcĕphălus, i, m., a promontory in the Peloponnesus, Mel.

buceras.full: būcĕras, ătis, n., = βούκερας, a plant, otherwise called faenum Graecum, fenugreek, Plin. 24, 19, 120, § 184.
buceras.short: būcĕras, ătis, n., = βούκερας, a plant, otherwise called faenum Graecum, fenugreek, Plin.

bucerus.full: būcĕrus (būcĕrĭus, Lucr. 2, 663), a, um, adj., = βούκερως, having the horns of a bullock, ox-horned (perh. only in the foll. exs.): bucerum pecus de bubus dicimus, Paul. ex Fest. p. 32 Müll.: bucera saecla, the race of horned caltle, Lucr. 5, 864; so id. 6, 1236; imitated by Ovid: armenta, * Ov. M. 6, 395: buceriae greges, Lucr. 2, 663 (quoted by Non. p. 80, 27, and p. 208, 21).

bucetum.full: būcētum (būcīta, ōrum, n., Varr. L. L. 5, § 164 Müll.), i, n. bos, a pasture for cattle, cow-pasture (very rare), Luc. 9, 185; Gell. 11, 1, 1; Sid. Ep. 2, 2.

bucina.full: būcĭna (not buccĭna), ae, f., = βυκάνη, a crooked horn or trumpet (while tuba is usually the straight trumpet; cf. Veg. Mil. 3, 3, 5 Stewech.). Lit., a shepherd's horn, Varr. R. R. 2, 4, 20: bucina inflata, id. ib. 3, 13, 1; Col. 6, 23, 3; Prop. 4 (5), 10, 29.— Transf. A war-trumpet: bello dat signum rauca cruentum Bucina, Verg. A. 11, 475: quā bucina signum Dira dedit, id. ib. 7, 519.—In gen., as a signal employed in changing the four night-watches, and for waking the soldiers (cf. Dict. of Ant
bucina.short: būcĭna (not buccĭna), ae, f., = βυκάνη, a crooked horn or trumpet (while tuba is usually the straight trumpet;

bucinator.full: būcĭnātor (bucc-), ōris, m. bucino, one who blew the bucina, a trumpeter, Caes. B.C. 2, 35; Petr. 26, 9; Varr. L. L. 6, § 75; Dig. 50, 6, 6; Inscr. Orell. 3522.— Trop. (cf. bucina, II. D.), one who trumpets forth, blazes abroad: bucinator existimationis meae, Cic. Fil. ap. Cic. Fam. 16, 21, 2; Inscr. Orell. 3232.

bucinna.full: Bucinna, ae, f., a small island near Sicily, Plin. 3, 8, 14, § 92.
bucinna.short: Bucinna, ae, f., a small island near Sicily, Plin.

bucino.full: būcĭno (bucc-), āvi, ātum, 1, v. n. bucina, to blow the bucina, to sound or give a signal with the trumpet (mostly impers.; cf. Gr. σαλπίζειν): cum bucinatum est, Varr. R. R. 2, 4, 20: saepe declamante illo ter bucinavit, Sen. Contr. 3 praef.: bucinate in neomeniā tubā, Vulg. Psa. 81 (80), 4: Triton conchā sonaci leniter bucinat, App. M. 4, p. 157, 3; cf. bucina, II. C.

bucinum.full: būcĭnum (bucc-), i, n. id.. The sound or blast of a trumpet, Plin. 9, 33, 52, § 103; 11, 10, 10, § 20.—Hence, ad Bucinum, a quarter in Rome, Dig. 14, 4, 5, § 16. — A shell-fish used in dyeing purple, Plin. 9, 36, 61, § 129 sq.

bucinus.full: būcĭnus (bucc-), i, m. id., = bucinator, a trumpeter; of the cock, Petr. 74, 2.

bucolicus.full: būcŏlĭcus, a, um, adj., = βουκολικός, pertaining to shepherds, pastoral, bucolic. In gen.: Bucolicōn poëma, Virgil's pastoral poetry, the Bucolics, Col. 7, 10, 8; and absol.: Būcŏlĭca, ōrum, n., = τὰ Βουκολικά, Bucolics, Ov. Tr. 2, 538: Bucolica Theocriti et Vergilii, Gell. 9, 9, 4; cf. Serv. ad Verg. E.1.— Esp. Bucolice tome = βουκολικὴ τομή; in metre, the bucolic cœsura; that of an hexameter whose fourth foot is a dactyl, and ends a word (e. g. Verg. E. 3, 1: Dic mihi, Damoeta, cujum pecus? an
bucolicus.short: būcŏlĭcus, a, um, adj., = βουκολικός, pertaining to shepherds, pastoral, bucolic.

bucolium.full: Būcŏlĭum, ii, n., = Βουκόλιον, a town in Arcadia, Plin. 4, 6, 16, § 20.
bucolium.short: Būcŏlĭum, ii, n., = Βουκόλιον, a town in Arcadia, Plin.

bucranium.full: būcrānĭum, ĭi, n., = βουκράνιον, oxhead. A place of sacrifice, Inscr. Orell. 2322.— A plant like a bullock's head in shape, App. Herb. 86.

buculus.full: būcŭlus (also bōcŭlus), i, m. dim. bos, a young bullock, a steer, Col. 6, 2, 4; Front. Strat. 1, 5, 26.—More freq. and class., Subst.: būcŭla, ae, f., a young cow, a heifer, Verg. G. 1, 375; 4, 11; id. E. 8, 86. — As a work of art, Cic. Div. 1, 24, 48. The statue of a brazen cow at Athens, the work of Myron, was especially distinguished, Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 60, § 135; id. Div. 1, 24, 48; cf. Plin. 34, 8, 19, § 57.

buda.full: buda, ae, f., colloq., = ulva, Anthol. Lat. 5, 189, 2; Aug. Ep. 88, 6; Don. ad Verg. A. 2, 135.
buda.short: buda, ae, f., colloq., = ulva, Anthol.

budalia.full: Budalia, ae, f., a town of Lower Pannonia, Eutr. 9, 4.
budalia.short: Budalia, ae, f., a town of Lower Pannonia, Eutr.

budini.full: Būdīni, ōrum, m., a people of Sarmatia, Mel. 1, 9, 19; Plin. 4, 12, 26, § 88.
budini.short: Būdīni, ōrum, m., a people of Sarmatia, Mel.

bufalus.full: būfălus, i, m., = bubalus, q. v.

bufo.full: būfo, ōnis, m. root bu-; cf. 2. bubo, bos, a toad, Verg. G. 1, 184.

bugillo.full: būgillo, ōnis, m., a plant, also called ajuga reptans, Marc. Emp. 8.
bugillo.short: būgillo, ōnis, m., a plant, also called ajuga reptans, Marc.

buglossa.full: būglossa (bŭglossa, Aem. Mac. de Buglossa, 1 and 10), ae (būglossŏs, i, Plin. 25, 8, 40, § 81), f., = βούγλωσσος, oxtongue, bugloss, an herb, App. Herb. 11; Ser. Samm. 424.

bugonia.full: būgŏnĭa, ae, f., = βουγονία, the generating of bees from the putrid carcasses of cattle, the title of a work of Archelaus, Varr. R. R. 2, 5, 5.
bugonia.short: būgŏnĭa, ae, f., = βουγονία, the generating of bees from the putrid carcasses of cattle, the title of a work of Archelaus, Varr.

bulapathum.full: būlăpăthum, i, n., = βουλάπαθον, the herb patience, Plin. 20, 21, 86, § 235.
bulapathum.short: būlăpăthum, i, n., = βουλάπαθον, the herb patience, Plin.

bularchus.full: Būlarchus, i, m., = Βούλαρχος, an ancient Grecian painter, Plin. 7, 38, 39, § 126; 35, 8, 34, § 55.
bularchus.short: Būlarchus, i, m., = Βούλαρχος, an ancient Grecian painter, Plin.

bulbaceus.full: bulbācĕus, a, um, adj. 1. bulbus, that has bulbs, bulbous: hyacinthi radix, Plin. 21, 26, 97, § 170.

bulbatio.full: bulbātĭo, ōnis, f. id., a forming of bulbs, v. l. for bullatio, q. v.

bulbine.full: bulbīnē, ēs, f., = βολβίνη, a kind of bulbous plant, Plin. 20, 9, 41, § 107; 19, 5, 30, § 95.
bulbine.short: bulbīnē, ēs, f., = βολβίνη, a kind of bulbous plant, Plin.

bulbosus.full: bulbōsus, a, um, adj. 1. bulbus, bulbous: radix, Plin. 21, 21, 90, § 158; 21, 17, 62, § 102.

bulbulus.full: bulbŭlus, i, m. dim. id., a small bulb, Pall. 3, 21, 3.

bulbus1.full: bulbus (bulbŏs), i, m. βολβός. A bulb, bulbous root (tulips, hyacinths, lilies, etc.), Plin. 19, 4, 21, § 61; cf. Cels. 2, 18; Plin. 17, 20, 33, § 144; 21, 5, 11, § 24; 22, 22, 32, § 67 sq.— An onion; a garden vegetable of several kinds, among which the Megarean was the best known, Cato, R. R. 8, 2; Ov. R. Am. 797; Col. 10, 106; 4, 32, 2; Plin. 19, 5, 30, § 93; in Apic. 8, 7, and in Edict. Diocl. p. 16, called bulbus fabrilis.

bulbus2.full: Bulbus, i, m., a Roman name, Cic. Verr. 2, 2, 32, § 79.—With a play on 1. bulbus, Cic. Clu. 26, 72.
bulbus2.short: Bulbus, i, m., a Roman name, Cic.

bule.short: būlē, ēs, f., = βουλή, the (Greek) council, the senate, Plin.

buleuta.full: būleuta, ae. m., = βουλευτής, a councillor, a senātor, Plin. Ep. 10, 39 (48), 5; 10, 112 (113), 3; 10, 114 (115), 3; Spart. Sever. 17.

buleuterium.full: būleutērĭum (-on), ii, n., = βουλευτήριον, the place where the Greek senate assembled, the senate-house: in curiā Syracusis, quem locum illi buleuterium nomine appellant, Cic. Verr. 2, 2, 21, § 50: Cyzici et buleuterion vocant aedificium amplum sine ferreo clavo, etc., Plin. 36, 15, 23, § 100.
buleuterium.short: būleutērĭum (-on), ii, n., = βουλευτήριον, the place where the Greek senate assembled, the senate-house: in curiā Syracusis, quem locum illi buleuterium nomine appellant, Cic.

bulga.full: bulga, ae, f. Gallic; now bougette, a leathern knapsack, bag: bulgas Galli sacculos scorteos appellant, Paul. ex Fest. p. 35 Müll.: bulga est folliculus omnis, quam et crumenam veteres appellarunt: et est sacculus ad bracchium pendens, Lucil. ap. Non. p. 78 (Sat. 2, 16, and 6, 1); Varr. ap. Non. 78, 2 (Sat. Men. 61, 3).— Humorously, the womb, Lucil. ap. Non. p. 78, 14 (Sat. 26, 36).

bulimio.full: Būlīmĭo, ōnis, m., a Roman cognomen, Inscr. Fabr. 125, 35.
bulimio.short: Būlīmĭo, ōnis, m., a Roman cognomen, Inscr.

bulimo.full: būlīmo, āre, āvi, ātum (βουλιμιῶ), 1, v. n., to have bulimy or insatiable hunger, Pelag. Vet. 10; Theod. Prisc. 2, 29.

bulimosus.full: būlīmōsus, a, um, adj. bulimus, afflicted with insatiable hunger, Pelag. Vet. 10.

bulimus.full: būlīmus, i, m., = βούλιμος, great hunger, bulimy; hence also, weakness of the stomach, fainting, Gell. 16, 3, 9; cf. bu; Veg. 5, 34 (3, 35); 5, 37 (3, 38) (in Varr. 2, 5, 4, written as Greek).—Also written būlī-ma, ae, f., Paul. ex Fest. p. 32 Müll.
bulimus.short: būlīmus, i, m., = βούλιμος, great hunger, bulimy;

bulla.full: bulla, ae, f. root vhal-; Gr. φαλ-; cf. φαλλός, φύλλον, any object swelling up, and thus becoming round; hence, A waterbubble, bubble: ut pluvio perlucida caelo Surgere bulla solet, Ov. M. 10, 734: crassior, Mart. 8, 33, 18; Plin. 31, 2, 8, § 12; App. M. 4, p. 145, 7.—Hence, Trop., a bubble, trifle; vanity: si est homo bulla, eo magis senex, Varr. R. R. 1, 1, 1; Petr. 42, 4.— Any thing rounded by art. A boss, knob (upon a door, etc.): jussine in splendorem dari bullas has foribus nostris? Plaut.

bullatio.full: bullātĭo, ōnis, f. bullo, a bubbling, forming of pebbles, of a stone found in small detached fragments: sparsa bullatio magnetis (opp. cautes continua), Plin. 34, 14, 42, § 148 Sill. and Jan. (al. bulbatio).

bullatus.full: bullātus, a, um, adj. bulla. (Acc. to bulla, I. B.) Quickly passing; acc. to others, inflated, bombastic: nugae, Pers. 5, 19.— (Acc. to bulla, II.) Furnished with a boss or stud: cingulum, Varr. L. L. 5, § 116 Müll.—Of the heavens, studded with stars: aether, Fulg. Myth. 1, p. 24 Munck. — (Acc. to bulla, III.) Wearing a bulla about the neck: puer, Scip. Afr. ap. Macr. S. 2, 10, 7: statua, of a child, Val. Max. 3, 1, 1: heres, yet a child, Juv. 14, 5; cf. Petr. 60, 8.

bullesco.full: bullesco, ĕre, 3, v. inch. n. [bullo], to bubble, form bubbles, Ampel. 8.

bullitus.full: bullītus, ūs, m. bullio, the bubbling, gushing up of water: aquae, Vitr. 8, 3.

bullo.full: bullo, āre, and bullĭo, īvi, ītum, 4, v. n. bulla, to be in bubbling motion, to be in a state of ebullition, to bubble. Form bullo, āre: ubi bullabit vinum, ignem subducito, Cato, R. R. 105; Cels. 2, 7; 7, 4, 2; Calp. Ecl. 1, 11; Plin. 9, 7, 6, § 18; 18, 31, 74, § 317.— Form bullio, īre: bullientes fontes, Vitr. 8, 3; Cels. 5, 19, 28; Pers. 3, 34; Apic. 4, 119; 6, 212.—As v. a. in part. pass.: ammoniacum cum vino et melle mittis in ollam et bullita (sodden, i. e. half-cooked) atteres, dabisque a
bullo.short: bullo, āre, and bullĭo, īvi, ītum, 4, v.

bullula.full: bullŭla, ae, f. dim. bulla. A watery vesicle, Cels. 2, 5 fin.; 5, 28, n. 17.— A small neck-ornament (bulla), Hier. in Isa. 2, 3, 18.

bumammus.full: būmammus, a, um, adj. bu-mamma, having large breasts, of the vine, with large clusters: uva, Varr. R. R. 2, 5, 4; Macr. S. 2, 16, 7; Serv. ad Verg. G. 2, 102.

bumastus.full: būmastus, i (būmasta, ae, Edict. Diocl. p. 18), f., = βούμαστος, sc. ἄμπελος (having large breasts; cf. bumammus), a species of grape with large clusters, Verg. G. 2, 102 and Serv. ad loc.; id. Cul. 405; Col. 3, 2, 1; cf.: tument mammarum modo bumasti (acini), Plin. 14, 1, 3, § 15; 14, 3, 4, § 42.

bumelia.full: būmĕlĭa, ae, f., = βουμελία, a kind of ash-tree, Plin. 16, 13, 24, § 63.
bumelia.short: būmĕlĭa, ae, f., = βουμελία, a kind of ash-tree, Plin.

bunias.full: būnĭăs, ădis, f., = βουνιάς, a kind of Swedish turnip, Col. 10, 422; acc. buniada, Plin. 20, 4, 11, § 21.—Another kind is called būnĭon, ii, n., = βούνιον, Plin. l. l.—Hence, būnītus, a, um, adj., made from bunion: vinum, Cael. Aur. Tard. 4, 3, 52.
bunias.short: būnĭăs, ădis, f., = βουνιάς, a kind of Swedish turnip, Col.

bupaeda.full: būpaeda, ae, m. βούπαις, a huge youth, Mart. Cap. 1, § 31; 9, § 908 Kopp. (al. pubeda).

bupalus.full: Būpălus, i, m., = Βούπαλος, a statuary of Chios, who represented and exposed the deformed poet Hipponax, but in turn was severely satirized by him in his poems, Hor. Epod. 6, 14; cf. Plin. 36, 5, 4, § 11.
bupalus.short: Būpălus, i, m., = Βούπαλος, a statuary of Chios, who represented and exposed the deformed poet Hipponax, but in turn was severely satirized by him in his poems, Hor.

buphthalmos.full: būphthalmos, i, m., = βούφθαλμος. Oxeye, a plant, Plin. 25, 8, 42, § 82; Isid. Orig. 17, 9, 93.— A species of aizoon majus, houseleek, Plin. 25, 13, 102, § 160.

bupleuron.full: būpleuron, i, n., = βούπλευρον, an umbelliferous plant, hare's-ear: Bupleurum baldense, Host.; Plin. 22, 22, 35, § 77.
bupleuron.short: būpleuron, i, n., = βούπλευρον, an umbelliferous plant, hare's-ear: Bupleurum baldense, Host.;

buprestis.full: būprestis, is, f., = βούπρηστις (πρήθω, to swell up). A venomous beetle, whose sting caused a swelling in cattle, Plin. 30, 4, 10, § 30; 31, 10, 46, § 119; Veg. 5, 14, 10; 5, 77, 1; Isid. Orig. 12, 8, 5; Dig. 48, 8, 3, § 3.— A kind of vegetable, Plin. 22, 22, 36, § 78.
buprestis.short: būprestis, is, f., = βούπρηστις (πρήθω, to swell up).

bura2.full: Būra, ae, f., a town in Achaia, Plin. 4, 5, 6, § 12.
bura2.short: Būra, ae, f., a town in Achaia, Plin.

burdo.full: burdo, ōnis (collat. form burdus, i, Acron. ad Hor. C. 3, 27, 7), m., = , a mule (the offspring of a horse and she-ass, while mulus is the offspring of an ass and a mare; v. Isid. Orig. 12, 1, 61), esp. used for carrying litters, Dig. 32, 49: onus duorum burdonum, Vulg. 4 Reg. 5, 17.

burdonarius.full: burdōnārĭus, ii, m. burdo, a muledriver, Edict. Diocl. p. 19.

burdunculus.full: burduncŭlus, i, m., a plant, perh. borage, Marc. Emp. 5.
burdunculus.short: burduncŭlus, i, m., a plant, perh.

burgarii.full: burgārĭi, ōrum, m. burgus, inhabitants of a castle, defenders of the borders (late Lat.), Cod. Th. 7, 14, 1; cf. Isid. Orig. 9, 4, 28.

burgundiones.full: Burgundĭōnes, um, m., and Bur-gundĭi, ōrum, m., a tribe of Goths, divided into the East Burgundians, who dwelt between the Oder and the Vistula, and the West Burgundians, upon the upper Main. Form Burgundiones, Plin. 4, 14, 28, § 99; Mamert. I. Pan. 5 init.— Form Burgundii, Amm. 28, 5, 9 sqq.; Mamert. II. Pan. 17 init.—Sing.: Burgundĭo, ōnis, m., a Burgundian, Sid. Carm. 7, 234.—As adj.: Burgundiones equi, Veg. Vet. 6, 6, 3.
burgundiones.short: Burgundĭōnes, um, m., and Bur-gundĭi, ōrum, m., a tribe of Goths, divided into the East Burgundians, who dwelt between the Oder and the Vistula, and the West Burgundians, upon the upper Main.

burgus.full: burgus, i, m. cf. πύργος; Germ. Burg, Berg; Engl. -burg, borough, -bury, a castle, fort, fortress (post-class.): castellum parvulum, quem burgum vocant, Veg. Mil. 4, 10: crebra per limites habitacula constituta burgos vulgo vocant, Isid. Orig. 9, 2, 99; 9, 4, 28; Cod. Just. 1, 27, 2, § 4; Cod. Th. 12, 19, 2; Sid. Carm. 22.

buri.full: Buri or Burii, ōrum, m., = Βουροί, a German people in the neighborhood of the Marcomanni and Quadi, Tac. G. 43; Capitol. Anton. Phil. 22 init.
buri.short: Buri or Burii, ōrum, m., = Βουροί, a German people in the neighborhood of the Marcomanni and Quadi, Tac.

buris1.full: būris, is, m. (būra, ae, f., Varr. R. R. 1, 19, 2) [acc. to Serv. ad Verg. G. 1, 170 (cf. also Isid. Orig. 20, 14, 2), contr. from βοῦς and οὐρά, ox-tail], the curved hinder part of the plough of the ancients, the plough-beam, Varr. ap. Serv. l. l.—Acc. burim, Verg. G. 1, 170 Serv. and Voss.; Varr. R. R. 1, 19, 2.

buris2.full: Būris, is, f., a city of Achaia; acc. Burin, Ov. M. 15, 293.
buris2.short: Būris, is, f., a city of Achaia;

burius.full: burĭus, ii, m., a species of animal, otherwise unknown, Jul. Val. Rer. Gest. Alex. M. 3, 31.
burius.short: burĭus, ii, m., a species of animal, otherwise unknown, Jul.

burra.full: burra, ae, f. burrus. A small cow with a red mouth or muzzle, acc. to Fest. s. v.— A shaggy garment, Anthol. Lat. 5, 133, 5.—Hence, plur.: burrae, ārum, f., trifles, nonsense (post-class.): burras, quisquilias, ineptiasque, etc., Aus. praef. ad Latin. Pacat. 3.

burranica.full: burrānĭca pōtio id., a drink composed of milk and must, so called on account of its red color, Fest. p. 30; cf. Ov. F. 4, 780.
burranica.short: burrānĭca pōtio id., a drink composed of milk and must, so called on account of its red color, Fest.

burranicum.full: burrānĭcum, i, n. prob. formed from the preced., a kind of vessel, Paul. ex Fest. p. 36 Müll.

burrhinon.full: burrhĭnon, i, n. βοῦσ-ῥίν, a plant, oxnose, App. Herb. 86.

burricus.full: burrĭcus or būrĭcus (-chus), i, m. burrus; Fr. bourrique, a small horse, Veg. 6, 2, 2; Paul. Nol. Ep. 29; cf. Schneid. ad Varr. R. R. 2, 8, 1.

burrus1.full: burrus, a, um πυρρός, an old word, = rufus, rubens, red, Paul. ex Fest. p. 31 Müll.; cf. id. p. 36.—Collat. form byrrus, a, um, Prob. ad Juv. 3, 283.
burrus1.short: burrus, a, um πυρρός, an old word, = rufus, rubens, red, Paul.

burrus2.full: Burrus, an old form for Pyrrhus, Cic. Or. 48, 160; Quint. 1, 4, 15.
burrus2.short: Burrus, an old form for Pyrrhus, Cic.

bursaonenses.full: Bursăōnenses, ĭum, m., a people of Hispania Tarraconensis, Plin. 3, 3, 4, § 24; called Bursăvōnenses, Auct. B. Hisp. 22: Bursăōnes, um, Liv. lib. 91, Fragm. 20 Weissenb.
bursaonenses.short: Bursăōnenses, ĭum, m., a people of Hispania Tarraconensis, Plin.

buselinum.full: būsĕlīnum, i, n., = βουσέλινον, a plant, ox-parsley, Plin. 20, 12, 47, § 118.
buselinum.short: būsĕlīnum, i, n., = βουσέλινον, a plant, ox-parsley, Plin.

busiris.full: Būsīris, ĭdis and ĭdos (ĭdis, Verg. G. 3, 5; ìdos, Stat. Th. 12, 155; acc. Busiridem, Quint. 2, 7, 4; Hyg. Fab. 31; 56; Serv.ad Verg. A. 8, 300: Busirin, Ov. A. A. 1, 649; id. M. 9, 183: Busirim, Amm. 28, 1, 46), = Βούσῖρις. Masc., a king of Egypt, who sacrificed strangers, and was himself slain by Hercules, Cic. Rep. 3, 9, 15; Verg. G. 3, 5; Mythogr. Lat. 1, 65; 2, 157; Ov. Tr. 3, 11, 39; Macr. S. 3, 5, 9.— Fem., a considerable town in Lower Egypt, with a temple of Isis, now Abousir, Plin. 5, 1

bustar.full: bustar, aris, m. bustum, a place where dead bodies were burned, Charis. p. 25 P.

busticetum.full: bustĭcētum, i, n. id., post-class. for bustum, a place where dead bodies were burned, Arn. 1, p. 24; 7, p. 222.

bustirapus.full: bustĭrăpus, i, m. bustum-rapio, a robber of tombs, a term of reproach: impudice, sceleste, verbero, bustirape, furcifer, Plaut. Ps. 1, 3, 127.

bustualis.full: bustuālis, e, adj. bustum, of or pertaining to the place where dead bodies were burned, Sid. Ep. 3, 12; Prud. Cath. 9, 52.

bustuarius.full: bustŭārĭus, a, um, adj. id., of or pertaining to the place where dead bodies were burned: gladiator, that fought at a funeral pile in honor of the dead, Cic. Pis. 9, 19; Tert. Spect. 11; cf. Serv. ad Verg. A. 10, 519 (Cicero so calls Clodius, in the passage cited, on account of a tumult which he caused at the funeral ceremonies that Cicero's brother made in honor of Marius): moecha, she who prostitutes herself among tombs, Mart. 3, 93, 15: altare, upon which men were offered, Tert. Pall. 4: latr

bustum.full: bustum, i, n. buro = uro, whence also comburo; cf. burrus, red, orig. the place where the bodies of the dead were burned and buried; later also, in gen., for a tomb: bustum proprie dicitur locus, in quo mortuus est combustus et sepultus... ubi vero combustus quis tantummodo, alibi vero est sepultus, is locus ab urendo ustrina vocatur; sed modo busta sepulchra appellamus, Paul. ex Fest. p. 32 Müll.; cf. Serv. ad Verg. A. 3, 22; 11, 201; Inscr. Murat. 1514, 3. The place of burning and burying; the

buteo.full: būtĕo, ōnis, m., a kind of falcon or hawk, Plin. 10, 8, 9, § 21; 11, 49, 110, § 263; Arn. 7, p. 280; Paul. ex Fest. p. 32 Müll.; giving auguries by its flight, v. ales, II. E.
buteo.short: būtĕo, ōnis, m., a kind of falcon or hawk, Plin.

butes.full: Būtes, ae (acc. Buten, Verg. A. 5, 372; 9, 647; 11, 690 sq.; Ov. M. 7, 500), m., = Βούτης. Son of Amycus, king of the Bebrycians, slain by Dares at the tomb of Hector, Verg. A. 5, 372.— An Argonaut, son of Teleon and Zeuxippe, Hyg. Fab. 14.— Son of the Athenian Pallas, sent with Cephalus to Æacus, Ov. M. 7, 500.— An armor-bearer of Anchises, Verg. A. 9, 647 sqq.— A Trojan, Verg. A. 11, 690 sqq.

buthrotum.full: Būthrōtum, i, n. (Būthrōtŏs, i, f., Ov. M. 13, 721), = Βουθρωτόν and Βουθρωτός, a town on the coast of Epirus, now Butrinto, Caes. B. C. 3, 16; Verg. A. 3, 293 sq.; Mel. 2, 3, 10; Plin. 4, 1, 1, § 4.—Hence, Būthrōtĭus, a, um, adj., of Buthrotum: ager, causa, Cic. Att. 16, 16, A, 4: Plancus, id. ib. 15, 29, 3; and subst.: Būthrōtĭi, ōrum, m., the inhabitants of Buthrotum, id. ib. 14, 11, 2; 15, 2, 2; 16, 16, A, 4.

buthysia.full: būthўsĭa, ae, f., = βουθυσία, a sacrifice of oxen, Suet. Ner. 12 fin.
buthysia.short: būthўsĭa, ae, f., = βουθυσία, a sacrifice of oxen, Suet.

butio1.full: būtĭo, ōnis, m., a bittern, Auct. Carm. Philom. 42.
butio1.short: būtĭo, ōnis, m., a bittern, Auct.

butoa.full: Būtŏa, ae, f., a small island near Crete, Plin. 4, 12, 20, § 61.
butoa.short: Būtŏa, ae, f., a small island near Crete, Plin.

butoridas.full: Būtŏrĭdas, ae, m., = Βουτορίδης, a Greek writer on the Pyramids of Egypt, Plin. 36, 12, 17, § 79.
butoridas.short: Būtŏrĭdas, ae, m., = Βουτορίδης, a Greek writer on the Pyramids of Egypt, Plin.

butos.full: Būtŏs, i, f., = Βοῦτος, the chief city of the nomos Ptenethu in Egypt, upon the Sebennytic mouth of the Nile; containing a famous temple and oracle of Latona (Buto), Plin. 5, 10, 11, § 64.—Hence, Būtĭcus, a, um, adj., of Butos: linum, Plin. 19, 1, 2, § 14.
butos.short: Būtŏs, i, f., = Βοῦτος, the chief city of the nomos Ptenethu in Egypt, upon the Sebennytic mouth of the Nile;

butrotus.full: Butrōtus, i, m., a river of Bruttia, now the Bruciano, Liv. 29, 7, 3.
butrotus.short: Butrōtus, i, m., a river of Bruttia, now the Bruciano, Liv.

buttuti.full: buttuti, interj., Plaut. ap. Charis. p. 216 P.

butubatta.full: bŭtŭbatta = nugatoria, trifles, worthless things, Naev. ap. Paul. ex Fest. p. 36 Müll. (Com. Rel. p. 25 Rib.); Charis. 2, 16, p. 216 P.; cf. Comment. p. 351 sq.
butubatta.short: bŭtŭbatta = nugatoria, trifles, worthless things, Naev.

butuntum.full: Butuntum, i, n., a town of Calabria, now Bitonte; hence, Butuntinenses, ĭum, m., the inhabitants of Butuntum, Plin. 3, 11, 16, § 105; Front. Col. p. 111.
butuntum.short: Butuntum, i, n., a town of Calabria, now Bitonte;

butyrum.full: būtȳ^rum (ȳ, Sid. Carm. 12, 7; bŭ-tўron, Aen. Mac. Herb. c. de ruta. buturum, Edict. Diocl. p. 15), i, n., = βούτυρον [said to be a Scythian word, but prob. βοῦστυρός; Engl. butter], butter, Cels. 4, 15; 4, 18; 5, 26, 30; Col. 6, 12, 5; Plin. 11, 41, 96, § 239; 28, 9, 35, § 133 sq.

buxans.full: buxans, antis, adj. buxus, of the color of boxwood: pallor, App. M. 8, p. 211, 5; p. 180 Bip.

buxentum.full: Buxentum, i, f., = πυξοῦς, a town in Lucania, of Greek origin, colonized by the Romans after the second Punic war, Vell. 1, 15, 3; Liv. 34, 45, 2; now Policastro, Mel. 2, 4, 9; Liv. 39, 23, 3.— Derivv. Buxentīnus, a, um, adj., of Buxentum: ager, Front. Colon. p. 90.— Buxen-tĭus, a, um, adj., the same: pubes, Sil. 8, 585.
buxentum.short: Buxentum, i, f., = πυξοῦς, a town in Lucania, of Greek origin, colonized by the Romans after the second Punic war, Vell.

buxetum.full: buxētum, i, n. buxus, a plantation of boxwood, Mart. 2, 14, 15: tonsile, id. 3, 58, 3.

buxeus.full: buxĕus, a, um, adj. id.. Of or pertaining to the boxwood-tree, made of boxwood, boxwood-: luci, Sol. 52: forma, Col. 7, 8, 7: mola, Petr. 74, 5.— Of the color of boxwood: rostra (anatum), Varr. ap. Non. p. 460, 8: dentes, Mart. 2, 41, 7: anuli, perh. ironic. for spurious (on account of the paleness of boxwood), Petr. 58, 10; cf. pallor, App. M. 1, p. 110, 30: luror, id. ib. 9, p. 231, 4.

buxifer.full: buxĭfer, ĕra, ĕrum, adj. buxus-fero, bearing box-trees: Cytorus, Cat. 4, 13.

buxosus.full: buxōsus, a, um, adj. buxus, like boxwood: xylobalsamum, Plin. 12, 25, 54, § 119.

buxum.full: buxum, i, n. id., the wood of the boxtree (cf. Neue, Formenl. 1, 509; 1, 625). In gen.: torno rasile, Verg. G. 2, 449: ora buxo Pallidiora, Ov. M. 4, 134: multifori tibia buxi, id. ib. 12, 158: buxoque simillimus Pallor, id. ib. 11, 417; cf. Plin. 16, 16, 28, § 70.— Esp. of objects made of boxwood. A flute, pipe: inflati murmur buxi, Ov. M. 14, 537: terebratum per rara foramina, id. F. 6, 697; id. P. 1, 1, 45: cava buxa, Prop. 4 (5), 8, 42. ad inspirata rotari Buxa, Stat. Th. 7, 171; Sen. Agam.

buxus.full: buxus, i, f., = πύξος (cf. Prisc. p. 549, and the letter B). Lit., the pale, evergreen box-tree, Enn. ap. Phylarg. l. l.: buxus densa foliis, Ov. A. A. 3, 691: crispata, Claud. Rapt. Pros. 2, 110: horrida, id. ib. 2, 268: perpetuo virens, Ov. M. 10, 97; Plin. 16, 43, 84, § 230; for its natural history, v. Plin. 16, 16, 28, § 70 sq.— For things made of boxwood (cf. Plin. 16, 36, 66, § 172), a pipe or flute: tympana vos buxasque vocant Berecyntia. Verg. A. 9, 619 Forbig. ad loc.; Ov. M. 4, 30; Sta

buzae.full: Buzae, ārum, m., a people of India, Plin. 6, 20, 23, § 76.
buzae.short: Buzae, ārum, m., a people of India, Plin.

buzeri.full: Buzēri, ōrum, m., a people of Pontus, Mel. 1, 19, 11; Plin. 6, 4, 4, § 11.
buzeri.short: Buzēri, ōrum, m., a people of Pontus, Mel.

buzyges.full: Būzўges, ae, m., = Βουζύγης, an ancient Athenian hero, the inventor of the plough and of ploughing with oxen, = Triptolemus and Epimenides, Plin. 7, 56, 57, § 199; cf. Varr. R. R. 2, 5, 4; Aus. Ep. 22, 46; Serv. ad Verg. G. 1, 19.
buzyges.short: Būzўges, ae, m., = Βουζύγης, an ancient Athenian hero, the inventor of the plough and of ploughing with oxen, = Triptolemus and Epimenides, Plin.

byblis.full: Byblis, ĭdis, f. (voc. Bybli, Ov. M. 9, 580; 9, 651; acc. Byblida, id. ib. 9, 453; 9, 467), = Βυβλίς, a daughter of Miletus and Cyanee, who fell in love with her brother Caunus, and, being repulsed, was changed to a fountain, Ov. M. 9, 452; cf. Theocr. Id. 7, 114; acc. to Ov. A. A. 1, 283, and Hyg. Fab. 243, she hanged herself.

byblus.full: Byblus (-ŏs), i, f., = Βύβλος, a very ancient town in Phœnicia celebrated for the worship of Adonis, now Dschebail, Mel. 1, 12, 3; Plin. 5, 20, 17, § 78; Curt. 4, 1, 15.
byblus.short: Byblus (-ŏs), i, f., = Βύβλος, a very ancient town in Phœnicia celebrated for the worship of Adonis, now Dschebail, Mel.

byllis.full: Byllis or Bullis, ĭdis, f., = Βυλλίς Steph., Βουλλίς Ptol., a town in Grecian Illyria, Caes. B. C. 3, 40; Cic. Phil. 11, 11, 26.— Derivv. Bullĭdenses, Caes. B. C. 3, 12; 3, 40.— Bullien-ses, Cic. Pis. 40, 96.— Bulliōnes, Cic. Fam. 13, 42, 1 (others, Bullĭdenses).— Bulĭōnes, um, m., Plin. 3, 23, 26, § 145.— Bullīni, the inhabitants of Byllis, Liv. 44, 30, 10.
byllis.short: Byllis or Bullis, ĭdis, f., = Βυλλίς Steph., Βουλλίς Ptol., a town in Grecian Illyria, Caes.

byrsa.full: Byrsa, ae, f., = Βύρσα, the citadel of Carthage, Verg. A. 1, 367; Liv. 34, 62, 12.— Hence, adj.: Byrsĭcus, a, um, Byrsic, i.e. Carthaginian, Sid. Ep. 7, 17, 18.
byrsa.short: Byrsa, ae, f., = Βύρσα, the citadel of Carthage, Verg.

byssinus.full: byssĭnus, a, um, adj., = βύσσινος, made of byssus: linum, Plin. 19, 1, 4, § 21: vestis, App. M. 11, p. 269, 10; Isid. Orig. 19, 22, 15: opus, Dig. 39, 5, 16, § 7.—Subst.: byssĭnum, i, n. (sc. opus), a garment of byssus; trop.: vestite vos serico probitatis, byssino sanctitatis, purpură pudicitiae, Tert. Cult. Fem. 13; Vulg. 2 Par. 5, 12 al.
byssinus.short: byssĭnus, a, um, adj., = βύσσινος, made of byssus: linum, Plin.

byssus.full: byssus, i, f. (byssum, i, n., Isid. Orig. 19, 27, 4), = βύσσος [Heb. ], cotton, cotton stuff, App. M. 11, p. 258, 20; Mart. Cap. 2, § 114; Vulg. Exod. 25, 4 al. (acc. to others, a fine kind of flax, and the linen made from it; v. Liddell and Scott's Lex.).

bythos.full: Bythŏs, i, m., = βυθός (depth), one of the Æons of Valentinus, Tert. adv. Val. 7; id. adv. Haer. 49 (access. form Bythiŏs, id. adv. Val. 8).
bythos.short: Bythŏs, i, m., = βυθός (depth), one of the Æons of Valentinus, Tert.

byzacium.full: Bȳzācĭum, ii, n., = Βυσσᾶτις, a province in Africa Propria, between the river Triton and the Lesser Syrtis, Varr. R. R. 1, 44, 2; Plin. 5, 4, 3, § 24; 17, 5, 3, § 41.— Derivv. Bȳzācēnus, a, um, adj., of Byzacium: provincia, Cod. Just. 1, 27, 2; Cod. Th. 1, 27, 2.—As subst.: Bȳzācēni, ōrum, m., the inhabitants of Byzacium, Cod. Th. 11, 1, 29.— Bȳzācĭus, a, um, the same: rura, Sil. 9, 204.
byzacium.short: Bȳzācĭum, ii, n., = Βυσσᾶτις, a province in Africa Propria, between the river Triton and the Lesser Syrtis, Varr.

byzantium.full: Bȳzantĭum, ii, n., = Βυζάντιον, a city in Thrace, on the Bosphorus, opposite the Asiatic Chalcedon, later Constantinopolis, now Constantinople; among the Turks, Istamboul or Stamboul (i.e. εις τὴν πόλιν), Mel. 2, 2, 6; Plin. 4, 11, 18, § 46; 9, 15, 20, § 50 sq.; Nep. Paus. 2, 2; Liv. 38, 16, 3 sq.; Tac. A. 12, 63 sq.; id. H. 2. 83; 3, 47 al.— Derivv. Bȳzantĭus, a, um, adj., of Byzantium, Byzantine: litora, the Strait of Constantinople, Ov. Tr. 1, 10, 31: portus, Plin. 9, 15, 20, § 51.—Subst.: Bȳ
byzantium.short: Bȳzantĭum, ii, n., = Βυζάντιον, a city in Thrace, on the Bosphorus, opposite the Asiatic Chalcedon, later Constantinopolis, now Constantinople;

c.full: C, c, n. indecl., or f., the third letter of the Latin alphabet; corresponded originally in sound to the Greek Γ (which in inscrr., esp. in the Doric, was frequently written like the Latin C; v. O. Müll. Etrusk. 2, p. 295); hence the old orthography: LECIONES, MACISTRATOS, EXFOCIONT, [pu]CNANDOD, PVC[nad], CARTACINIENSI, upon the Columna rostrata, for legiones, magistratos, effugiunt, pugnando, pugnā, Carthaginiensi; and the prænomina Gaius and Gnaeus, even to the latest times, were designated b

caballa.full: căballa, ae, f. caballus, a mare, Anthol. Lat. I. p. 628 Burm.

caballarius.full: căballārĭus, i, m. id., = κέλης, ίππεύς, a rider, horseman, Gloss. Lat. Gr.: ίπποκόμος (i.e. a hostler) caballarius, Gloss. Vet.; hence, Ital. cavaliero, Fr. chevalier.

caballatio.full: căballātio, ōnis, f. id., fodder for a horse (post-class.), Cod. Th. 7, 4, 34; 12, 38, 14.

caballinus.full: căballīnus, a, um, adj. id., of or pertaining to a horse, horse. (post-Aug.): caro, Plin. 28, 20, 81, § 265. dentes, id. 30, 8, 22, § 72; flmum, id. 30, 13, 38, § 112: fons, i.e. Hippocrene, Pers. prol. 1.

caballio.full: căballĭo, ōnis, m. dim. id., a small horse, a pony: marini, perh. = hippocampi, Veg. 1, 20, 2; 6, 12, 3.

caballion.full: căballĭon, i, n., a plant, also called cynoglossa, hartstongue, spleenwort, App. Herb. 96.
caballion.short: căballĭon, i, n., a plant, also called cynoglossa, hartstongue, spleenwort, App.

caballus1.full: căballus, i, m., = καβάλλης [perh. Celtic; hence Ital. cavallo, Fr. cheval, Engl. cavalry, cavalier, etc.; cf. cob, Germ. Gaul], an inferior riding- or pack-horse, a nag (poet. and in post-Aug. prose): tardus, Lucil. ap. Non. p. 86, 15; Varr. ib.: mediā de nocte caballum Arripit, his nag, Hor. Ep. 1, 7, 88; so id. S. 1, 6, 59; 1, 6, 103; id. Ep. 1, 18, 36; Juv. 10, 60; 11, 195; Sen. Ep. 87, 8; Petr. 117, 12; Dig. 33, 7, 15: Gorgoneus, jestingly for Pegasus, Juv. 3, 118.— Prov. Optat ephippia bos

caballus2.full: Căballus, i, m., a Roman cognomen, in the pun: qui Galbam salibus tuis, et ipsum Possis vincere Sextium Caballum. Non cuicumque datum est habere nasum. Ludit qui stolidā procacitate, non est Sextius ille, sed caballus, Mart. 1, 42 fin.
caballus2.short: Căballus, i, m., a Roman cognomen, in the pun: qui Galbam salibus tuis, et ipsum Possis vincere Sextium Caballum.

cabillonum.full: Căbillōnum, i, n., = Καβυλλῖνον, a considerable town of. the Ædui in Gallia Lugdunensis, now Chalons sur Saōne, Caes. B. G. 7, 42; 7, 90.—Hence, Căbillōnen-sis, e, adj., of or belonging to Cabillonum: portus, Eum. Pan. Const. 18.
cabillonum.short: Căbillōnum, i, n., = Καβυλλῖνον, a considerable town of.

cabira.full: Cabīra, ōrum, n., = τὰ Κάβειρα, a town in Pontus, a residence of Mithridates, Eutr. 6, 8.
cabira.short: Cabīra, ōrum, n., = τὰ Κάβειρα, a town in Pontus, a residence of Mithridates, Eutr.

cabiri.full: Căbīri, ōrum, m., = Κάβειροι (v. Liddell and Scott, s.v.), the Cabiri, deities worshipped by the Pelasgi as tutelary geniì, in whose honor mysteries were celebrated at Lemnos and Samothrace; originally attendants of the great gods (dei magni and potes, Varr. L. L. 5, 10, 18); they were afterwards identified with these, and, with the Dioscuri, worshipped as guardian spirits (cf. Samothraces, s.v. Samothracia): celsa Cabirūm Delubra tenes, Att. ap. Varr. L. L. 7, § 11 Müll. (Trag. Rel. v. 526 Rib.

cabus.full: căbus, i, m., = LXX. κάβος [Heb. kab], a corn-measure, answering to the χοῖνιξ, Vulg. 4 Reg. 6, 25 Müll.

cabyle.full: Căbўlē, ēs, or -la, ae, f., a town in Thrace, Eutr. 6, 8.—Hence, Căbўlētae, ārum, m., the inhabitants of Cabyle, Plin. 4, 11, 18, § 40.
cabyle.short: Căbўlē, ēs, or -la, ae, f., a town in Thrace, Eutr.

caca.full: Cāca, ae, f., a sister of Cacus, Lact. 1, 20, 36; Serv. ad Verg. A. 8, 190.
caca.short: Cāca, ae, f., a sister of Cacus, Lact.

cacabaceus.full: cācăbācĕus (cacc-), a, um, adj. cacabus, of or pertaining to a kitchen-pot: motus, i.e. like the liquid boiling in a pot, Tert. adv. Herm. 41.

cacabatus.full: cācăbātus (cacc-), a, um, adj. id., black, sooty, besmeared like a cooking-pot: aedificia (opp. immaculata), Paul. Nol. Ep. ad Serv. 32, 9.

cacabo.full: cācăbo (⏕ Auct. Fragm. Aucup. 12), āre, v. n., to cackle; Gr. κακκαβίζω, as the natural cry of the partridge: cacabat hinc perdix, Carm. Philom. 19

cacabulus.full: cācăbŭlus (cacc-), i, m. dim. cacabus, a small cooking-pot, a pot, vessel, Tert. Apol. 13; Arn. 6, p. 200; Apic. 4, 1.

cacabus.full: cācăbus (cacc-), i, m., = κάκκαβος, a cooking-pot: vas ubi coquebant cibum, ab eo caccabum appellarunt, Varr. L. L. 5, 27, 36: aeneus, Col. 12, 46, 1: argenteus, Dig. 34, 2, 20; 33, 7, 18, § 3: novus, Col. 12, 48, 5: figuli, id. 12, 41, 2: fictilis, Scrib. Comp. 220; Stat. S. 4, 9, 45.
cacabus.short: cācăbus (cacc-), i, m., = κάκκαβος, a cooking-pot: vas ubi coquebant cibum, ab eo caccabum appellarunt, Varr.

cacalia.full: căcālĭa, ae, f., = κακαλία, a plant, called also leontice, acc. to Sprengel: Cacalia verbascifolia, Sibth.; acc. to Schneid. colt'sfoot, in pure Latin, tussilago, Plin. 25, 11, 85, § 135; 26, 6, 15, § 29.
cacalia.short: căcālĭa, ae, f., = κακαλία, a plant, called also leontice, acc.

cacaturio.full: căcātŭrĭo, īre, v. n. desid. [caco], to desire to go to stool, Mart. 11, 77.

cacemphaton.full: căcemphăton, i, n., = κακέμφατον, ill-sounding, a low or improper expression, Isid. Orig. 1, 83, 5; cf. Quint. 8, 3, 47; Serv. ad Verg. G. 2, 13.
cacemphaton.short: căcemphăton, i, n., = κακέμφατον, ill-sounding, a low or improper expression, Isid.

cachecta.full: căchecta, ae, m., = καχέκτης (in bad physical condition), one that is in a consumption; plur., Plin. 28, 9, 33, § 125; 32. 10, 39, § 117.
cachecta.short: căchecta, ae, m., = καχέκτης (in bad physical condition), one that is in a consumption;

cachecticus.full: căchectĭcus, a, um, adj., = καχεκγικός, hectic, consumptive, cachectic, Plin. 32, 10, 39, § 117.
cachecticus.short: căchectĭcus, a, um, adj., = καχεκγικός, hectic, consumptive, cachectic, Plin.

cachexia.full: căchexĭa, ae, f., = καχεξία, a consumption, wasting, cachexy, Cael. Aur. Tard. 3, 6, 80 sqq.; 4, 2, 18 (in Cels. 3, 32, as Gr.).
cachexia.short: căchexĭa, ae, f., = καχεξία, a consumption, wasting, cachexy, Cael.

cachinnabilis.full: căchinnābĭlis, e, adj. cachinno (Appuleian). Capable of laughing, laughing: homo animal cachinnabile, App. Dogm. Plat. 3, p. 33, 20.— Of or pertaining to immoderate laughter: risus, App. M. 3, p. 132, 20.

cachinnatio.full: căchinnātĭo, ōnis, f. id., a violent laughing, immoderate laughter: sine ullā suspitione nimiae suspitionis, Auct. Her. 3, 14, 25: ut si ridere concessum sit, vituperetur tamen cachinnatio, Cic. Tusc. 4, 31, 66.

cachinno1.full: căchinno, āvi, ātum, 1, v. n. like καχάζω or καγχάζω; Sanscr. kakk; and our titter, onomatop., to laugh aloud, laugh immoderately. Lit. (class. but rare): famulae furtim cachinnant, Lucr. 4, 1176; 1, 919; 2, 976: ridere convivae; cachinnare ipse Apronius, Cic. Verr. 2, 3, 25, § 62; Suet. Vesp. 5; Aur. Vict. Epit. 28.—With the acc. of that which one laughs at: exitum meum cachinnant, App. M. 3, p. 132, 25.—* Poet. (v. Liddell and Scott under καχλάζω, γέλως, γέλασμα, and Blomfield. Aesch. Prom. 90

cachinno2.full: căchinno, ōnis, m. 1. cachinno, one who laughs violently, a laugher, derider, καγχαστής, Pers. 1, 12.

cachinnosus.full: căchinnosus, a, um, adj. cachinno, given to loud laughter (late Lat.), Cael. Aur. Acut. 1, 3, 41.

cachinnus.full: căchinnus, i, m. id., a loud laugh, immoderate laughter, a laugh in derision, a jeering. Lit. (class in prose and poetry; also in plur.): tum dulces esse cachinni consuerant, Lucr. 5, 1396; so id. 5, 1402: in quo Alcibiades cachinnum dicitur sustulisse, to have set up a loud laugh, Cic.
