Fat. 5, 10; Suet. Aug. 98: tollere, Hor. A. P. 113: cachinnos irridentium commovere, Cic. Brut. 60, 216: res digna tuo cachinno, Cat. 56, 2; 31, 14; 13, 5: securus, Col. 10, 280: perversus, Ov. A. A. 3, 287: majo

cachla.full: cachla, ae, f., = κάχλα, a plant, also called buphthalmos, oxeye, Plin. 25, 8, 42, § 82.
cachla.short: cachla, ae, f., = κάχλα, a plant, also called buphthalmos, oxeye, Plin.

cachrys.full: cachrys, ўos, f., = κάχρυς (κάγχρυς). An appendage to the catkin of certain trees in autumn, a cone, Plin. 16, 8, 11, § 30; Cels. 5, 18, n. 5; admixta cachry, Plin. 22, 22, 32, § 71; 27, 13, 109, § 134.— The capsule of rosemary, Plin. 24, 11, 60, § 101. — The white kernel of the plant crethmos, Plin. 26, 8, 50, § 82.

caco.full: căco, āvi, ātum, āre, v. n. and a.,—κακάω, to go to stool, to be at stool. Neutr., Pompon. ap. Non. p. 84, 2: toto decies in anno, Cat. 23, 20; *Hor. S. 1, 8, 38; Mart. 12, 61, 10.— Act., Pompon. ap. Non. p. 84, 1 (Com. Rel. p. 209 Rib.): canes odorem mixtum cum merdis cacant, Phaedr. 4, 17, 25; Mart. 3, 89.—Also, to defile with excrement: cacata charta, Cat. 36, 1 and 20.

cacoethes.full: căcŏēthĕs, is, n., = κακόηθες, τό (bad state or habit); in medic. lang., an obstinate, malignant disease, Cels. 5, 28, n 2; Plin. 24, 3, 3, § 7.—Plur. cacoëthe = κακοήθη, τά, Plin. 22, 25, 64, § 132; 24, 10, 47, § 78. —Hence, Trop., an incurable passion for writing or scribbling: insanabile Scribendi cacoëthes, Juv. 7, 52.
cacoethes.short: căcŏēthĕs, is, n., = κακόηθες, τό (bad state or habit);

cacometer.full: căcŏmĕter or căcŏmĕtrus, a, um, adj., faulty in metre, unmetrical, Juba ap. Prisc. Mer. Ter. 58.
cacometer.short: căcŏmĕter or căcŏmĕtrus, a, um, adj., faulty in metre, unmetrical, Juba ap.

cacomnemon.full: Căcomnēmon, ŏnis, m., title of a mime of Laberius, Gell. 16, 7, 8.
cacomnemon.short: Căcomnēmon, ŏnis, m., title of a mime of Laberius, Gell.

cacophaton.full: căcŏphăton, i, n., a union of two or more disagreeable sounds which form an equivocal word or expression, cacophony, Quint. 8, 3.
cacophaton.short: căcŏphăton, i, n., a union of two or more disagreeable sounds which form an equivocal word or expression, cacophony, Quint.

cacophonia.full: căcŏphōnia, ae, f. κακόσ-φωνή, a disagreeable sound formed by the meeting of syllables or words, cacophong, Mod. Lat.

cacosyntheton.full: căcŏsynthĕton, i, n., = κακοσύνθετον; in rhet., an incorrect connection of words (as, e. g. Verg. A. 9, 610): quod male collocatum, id κακοσύνθετον Vocant, Quint. 8, 3, 59; cf. Don. p. 1771 P.; Charis. p. 243 ib.; Serv. ad Verg. l. l.; Isid. Orig. 1, 33, 12; Lucil. ap. Vel. Long. p. 2214 P.

cacozelia.full: căcŏzēlĭa, ae, f., = κακοζηλία, a bad, faulty, awkward imitation, Sen. Contr. 4, 24 fin.; id. Suas. 7; Quint. 2, 3, 9 (written as Greek, id. 8, 6, 73; cf. κακόζηλον; id. 8, 3, 56); cf. Diom. p. 446 P.
cacozelia.short: căcŏzēlĭa, ae, f., = κακοζηλία, a bad, faulty, awkward imitation, Sen.

cacozelus.full: căcŏzēlus, a, um, adj., = κακόζηλος, a bad imitator (cf. cacozelia), * Suet. Aug. 86; Ascon. Cic. Caecil. 6, 21; cf. Quint. 8, 3, 56 sqq.
cacozelus.short: căcŏzēlus, a, um, adj., = κακόζηλος, a bad imitator (cf.

cactus.full: cactus, i, m., = κάκτος, a prickly plant with edible stalks, etc., found in Sicily, Spanish artichoke: Cynara cardunculus, Linn.; Plin. 21, 16, 57, § 97.— Trop., any thing thorny, unpleasant: eradicato omni cacto et rubo subdolae familiaritatis, Tert. Pall. 2 fin.
cactus.short: cactus, i, m., = κάκτος, a prickly plant with edible stalks, etc., found in Sicily, Spanish artichoke: Cynara cardunculus, Linn.;

cacula.full: căcŭla (cacula, Plaut. Ps. Arg. 2, 13 sq.), ae, m. Sanscr. cak-, to help; cf. calon; v. Paul. ex Fest. s. h. v. p. 45 Müll.; Fest. s. v. procalare, p. 225 ib., a servant, esp. the servant of a soldier: cacula = servus militis (militaris? cf. the passage foll., from Plaut.), Fest. p. 35: cacula δοῦλος στρατιώτου, Gloss.: video caculam militarem me futurum, Plaut. Trin. 3. 2, 98; so id. Ps. Arg. 4; and perh., acc. to the MSS., also Juv. 9, 61, where Jahn reads casulis; cf. Weber, Juv. Excurs. in h

caculatum.full: căcŭlātum = servitium, servitude, Paul. ex Fest. p. 46 Müll. [cacula].

cacumen.full: căcūmen, ĭnis, n. etym. dub., the extreme end, extremity, or point of a thing; the peak, top, utmost point. Lit. (whether horizontal or perpendicular; while culmen is an extremity projecting in height; v. Doed. Syn.; in the poets freq.; in prose rare before the Aug. per.; not in Cic.): ut altis Arboribus vicina cacumina summa terantur Inter se, the extreme top, Lucr. 1, 898. —So of tree-tops: umbrosa cacumina, Verg. E. 2, 3: fracta, id. ib. 9, 9; 6, 28; id. G. 2, 29; 2, 307; Ov. M. 1, 346; 1, 55

cacumino.full: căcūmĭno, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. cacumen, to point, make pointed (prob. formed by Ovid): summas cacuminat aures, Ov. M. 3, 195: saxoque cacuminat ensem, Sid. Carm. 7, 414: ova cacuminata, Plin. 10, 52, 74, § 145: apex in conum cacuminatus, Sid. Ep. 2, 2.

cacus1.full: Cācus, i, m., = Κᾶκος, son of Vulcan, contemporary with Evander, a giant of immense physical strength, who dwelt in a cave on Mount Aventinus, and troubled the whole region around by his robberies; he robbed even Hercules of the cattle of Geryon, and was on that account slain by him, Ov. F. 1, 543 sq.; Liv. 1, 7, 5 sq.; Verg. A. 8, 190 sq., and Serv. in h. l.; Prop. 4 (5), 9, 7; 4 (5), 9, 16; Col. 1, 3, 6; Juv. 5, 125; Sol. 1, §§ 7 and 18.
cacus1.short: Cācus, i, m., = Κᾶκος, son of Vulcan, contemporary with Evander, a giant of immense physical strength, who dwelt in a cave on Mount Aventinus, and troubled the whole region around by his robberies;

cacus2.full: căcus, i, m. perh. κακός; cf. Engl. villain, rascal, as designations of a servant, a servant, Inscr. Vellerm. 7, 1, 27.

cadaver.full: cădāver, ĕris, n. cado, I. B. 2.; cf. Isid. Orig. 11, 2, 35, and the Gr. πτῶμα, from πίπτω. Lit., a dead body of man or brute, a corpse, carcass (class.). Of man: taetra cadavera, Lucr. 2, 415; 3, 719; 4, 682; 6, 1154; 6, 1273: aqua cadaveribus inquinata, Cic. Tusc. 5, 34, 97.—Freq. of the bodies of slaves, criminals, etc., Cic. Mil. 13, 33; Hor. S. 1, 8, 8; 2, 5, 85.—Of the dead bodies of those who fell in war, Caes. B. G. 7, 77; Sall. C. 61, 4; 61, 8; id. J. 101 fin.; Flor. 2, 6, 18; 3, 2, 85;

cadaverinus.full: cădāvĕrīnus, a, um, adj. cadaver, of carrion: nidores, Aug. Civ. Dei, 9, 16.— Hence, subst.: cădāvĕrīna, ae, f. (sc. caro), the flesh of a carcass, Tert. Anim. 32, 9.

cadaverosus.full: cădāvĕrōsus, a, um, adj. id., like a corpse, ghastly, cadaverous (ante- and postclass.): facies, Ter. Hec. 3, 4, 27 (sublivida, ac personata rubore et livore, Don.).—Of persons, Ambros. in Psa. 48, Serm. 16, 28.

cadi.full: Cādi, ōrum, m., a town in Phrygia, on the borders of Lydia, Prop. 4 (5), 6, 8.
cadi.short: Cādi, ōrum, m., a town in Phrygia, on the borders of Lydia, Prop.

cadialis.full: cădĭālis, e, adj. cadus, of or pertaining to a jar: resina, contained in it, Cael. Aur. Tard. 2, 7, 108.

cadivus.full: cădīvus, a, um, adj. cado (an access. form of caducus). Of fruit, falling of itself: mala, Plin. 15, 16, 18, § 59; 15, 17, 18, § 60.— In medic. lang., having the falling sickness or epilepsy, epileptic, Marc. Emp. 20.

cadmea2.full: Cadmēa, v. Cadmus, I. B. 1. b.

cadmeis.full: Cadmēïs, etc., v. Cadmus, I. B. 3.

cadmia.full: cadmī^a (cadmē^a, Paul. ex Fest. p. 47, 10 Müll.), ae, f., = καδμεία or καδμία, an ore of zinc, calamine, cadmia, Plin. 34, 1, 2, § 2; 34, 10, 22, § 100; Paul. ex Fest. l. l.; Isid. Orig. 16, 20, 2 and 11.— The dross or slag formed in a furnace, Plin. 34, 10, 22. § 100 sq.; Isid. Orig. 16, 20, 12.

cadmitis.full: cadmītis, is, f., a kind of precious stone, Plin. 37, 10, 56, § 151.
cadmitis.short: cadmītis, is, f., a kind of precious stone, Plin.

cadmus.full: Cadmus, i, m., = Κάδμος. Son of the Phœnician king Agenor, brother of Europa, husband of Harmonia, father of Polydorus, Ino, Semele, Autonoë, and Agave; founder of the Cadmea, the citadel of the Bœotian Thebes, Cic. Tusc. 1, 12, 28; id. N. D. 3. 19, 48; Ov. M. 3, 14 sq.; id. F. 1, 490; id. P. 4, 10, 55; the inventor of alphabetic writing, Plin. 7, 56, 57, § 192 sqq. (hence letters are called Cadmi filiolae atricolores, Aus. Ep. 29; and Cadmi nigellae filiae, id. ib. 21). He and his wife. Harmoni

cado.full: cădo, cĕcĭdi, cāsum, 3 (part. pres. gen. plur. cadentūm, Verg. A. 10, 674; 12, 410), v. n. cf. Sanscr. çad-, to fall away. Lit. In an extended sense, to be driven or carried by one's weight from a higher to a lower point, to fall down, be precipitated, sink down, go down, sink, fall (so mostly poet.; in prose, in place of it, the compounds decĭdo, occĭdo, excĭdo, etc.; cf. also ruo, labor; opp. surgo, sto): tum arbores in te cadent, Plaut. Men. 2, 3, 25: (aves) praecipites cadunt in terram aut i

caducarius.full: cădūcārĭus, a, um, adj. caducus, relating to property without a master: lex Julia (introduced by Augustus), Ulp. Lib. Regul. § 28.— Epileptic: homines, Aug. Vit. Beat. med.

caduceator.full: cādūcĕātor, ōris, m. caduceum. A herald, an officer sent with a flag of truce: caduceatores = legati pacem petentes. Cato caduceatori, inquit, nemo homo nocet, Paul. ex Fest. p. 47: bellantes ac dissidentes interpretum oratione sedantur, unde secundum Livium legati pacis caduceatores appellantur, Serv. ad Verg. A. 4, 242; Liv. 26, 17, 5; 31, 38, 9; 32, 32, 5; 37, 45, 4; 44, 46, 1; Curt. 3, 1, 6; 4, 2, 15 al.— A servant to a priest, Arn. 5, p. 174.

caduceatus.full: cādūcĕātus, a, um, adj. caduceus, having or bearing the herald's wand, Inscr. Grut. 927, 6.

caduceum.full: cādūcĕum, i, n. (sc. sceptrum or baculum), or cādūcĕus, i, m. (sc. scipio or baculus; which form was predominant in the class. per. is doubtful, since neither Cicero, Nepos, Livy, nor Pliny uses the word in the nom.) [kindr. with κηρύκειον, Æolic καρύκιον, —ῦ—, r changed to d, as ad = ar], a herald's staff, the token of a peaceable embassy (orig. an olive- stick, with στέμματα, which afterwards were formed into serpents, O. Müll. Archaeol. § 379, 3): caduceus pacis signum, Var. de Vita Pop. Rom.

caducifer.full: cādūcĭfer, fĕra, fĕrum, adj. caduceusfero, bearing a herald's staff, an epithet of Mercury in Ovid: Atlantiades, Ov. M. 8, 627; and absol., id. ib. 2, 708; id. F. 4, 605; 5, 449.

caducus.full: cădūcus, a, um, adj. cado. That falls or has fallen, falling, fallen (mostly poet.): bacae glandesque caducae, * Lucr. 5, 1362; cf. Dig. 50, 16, 30: glans caduca est, quae ex arbore cecidit: oleae, Cato, R. R. 23, 2: spica, that fell in mowing, Varr. R. R. 2, 2, 12: aqua, id. ib. 3, 5, 2: aquae, Ov. P. 2, 7, 39: frondes, Verg. G. 1, 368: frons, Ov. M. 7, 840; id. Tr. 3, 1, 45: folia, id. Am. 2, 16, 45: lacrimae, id. M. 6, 396: poma, Prop. 2, 32, 40: oliva, Col. 12, 52, 22: fulmen, Hor. C. 3, 4,

cadurci.full: Cădurci, ōrum, m., = Καδοῦρκοι, a people in Gallia Narbonensis, whose capital was Divona, now Cahors, Caes. B. G. 7, 4 sqq.; Plin. 4, 19, 33, § 109; 19, 1, 2, § 8; in Caes. B. G. 7, 75, with the appel. Eleutheri (perh. a division of the former people, in the present Alby).—Hence, Cădurcus, a, um, adj., of or pertaining to the Cadurci: natales, Sid. Carm. 9, 282: sedes, Aus. Prof. n. 17.—Absol.: cădurcum, i, n., a Cadurcian coverlet, a coverlet of Cadurcian linen, Juv. 7, 221; and meton., a bed o
cadurci.short: Cădurci, ōrum, m., = Καδοῦρκοι, a people in Gallia Narbonensis, whose capital was Divona, now Cahors, Caes.

cadus.full: cădus, i (gen. plur. cadūm, v. II. infra), m., = κάδος [Slav. kad, kadĭ; Serv. kada; Magyar, kád; Rouman. Kadŭ]. Lit., a large vessel for containing liquids, esp. wine; a bottle, jar, jug; mostly of earthen-ware, but sometimes of stone, Plin. 36, 22, 43, § 158; or even of metal, Verg. A. 6, 228. A wine-jar, wine-flask: cadi = vasa, quibus vina conduntur, Non. p. 544, 11: cadus erat vini: inde implevi hirneam, Plaut. Am. 1, 1, 273; so id. As. 3, 3, 34; id. Aul. 3, 6, 35; id. Mil. 3, 2, 36; 3, 2,

cadusii.full: Cădūsii (Cădūsi), ōrum, m., = Καδούσιοι, a people in Media, on the Caspian Sea (Atropatene). Mel. 1, 2, 5; Nep. Dat. 1, 2; Liv. 35, 48, 5; Just. 10, 3, 2; Curt. 4, 12, 12; Plin. 6, 16, 18, § 48.—In sing.: Cădusus, i., Avien. Descr. Orb. 910.—Cădūsĭa, ae, f., the country of the Cadusii, Plin. 6, 13, 15, § 36.
cadusii.short: Cădūsii (Cădūsi), ōrum, m., = Καδούσιοι, a people in Media, on the Caspian Sea (Atropatene).

cadytas.full: cadytas, ae, m., = καδύτας, a Syrian parasitical pl'ant, Plin. 16, 44, 92, § 244.
cadytas.short: cadytas, ae, m., = καδύτας, a Syrian parasitical pl'ant, Plin.

caecator.full: caecātor, ōris, m. caeco, prop. one who makes blind, hence, he who stops or obstructs a fountain, Paul. Nol. Carm. Nat. S. Fel. 24, 9, 618 (with ref. to Genes. 26, 15).

caeciae.full: Caeciae, ārum, f., two small islands, opposite the promontory of Spirœum, in Argolis, Plin. 4, 12, 19, § 57.
caeciae.short: Caeciae, ārum, f., two small islands, opposite the promontory of Spirœum, in Argolis, Plin.

caecias.full: caecĭas, ae, m., = καικίας, the northeast wind (acc. to more accurate nautical designation, north-east by east), Plin. 2, 47, 46, § 120 sq.; 18, 34, 77, § 334; Vitr. 1, 6; Gell. 2, 22, 24 (written as Greek, Sen. Q. N. 5, 16, 4).
caecias.short: caecĭas, ae, m., = καικίας, the northeast wind (acc.

caecigenus.full: caecĭgĕnus, a, um (caecigena τυφλογενής, Gloss. Philox.), adj. caeco-gigno, born blind, Lucr. 2, 741.

caecilia.full: caecĭlĭa, ae, f. A kind of lizard, Col. 6, 17, 1; 6, 17, 4; Veg. 4, 21, 1 (in Plin. 9, 51, 76, § 166: caecus serpens); now Ital. cecella; Sard. cicigna.— A kind of lettuce, Col. 10, 190; cf. Caecilius, II. B.

caecilianus.full: Caecĭlĭānus, i, m., v. Caecilius, II. B. 2.

caecilius.full: Caecĭlĭus, a, name of a Roman gens. C. Caecilius, Cic. Fl. 36.— Q. Caecilius Metellus, Cael. ap. Cic. Fam. 8, 8, 5; Cic. Fin. 5, 27, 82.— His son of the same name, called also Balearicus, for his triumph over the Baleares, Cic. Brut. 74, 259; Flor. 3, 8, 1.— Caia (Gaia) Caecilia, the Roman name of Tanaquil, Plin. 8, 48, 74, § 194.— Caeciliae, daughters of Q. Cœcilius Metellus the elder, Cic. Dom. 47, 123.— Caecilia, daughter of Metellus Balearicus, Cic. Div. 1, 44, 99, and 2, 40, 83.— Caecilius
caecilius.short: Caecĭlĭus, a, name of a Roman gens.

caecina1.full: Caecīna (Cēc-), ae, m., a surname in the gens Licinia, originating in Etruria (pure Etrusc. Ceicna, O. Müll. Etrusk. 1, p. 416), among whom the most celebrated is Licinius Cæcina, for whose Roman citizenship Cicero made the oration pro Caecinā, Cic. Fam. 6, 7, 1; 6, 6, 8; Suet. Caes. 75; cf. Sen. Q. N. 2, 39, 1; 2, 49, 1.—Hence, adj.: Caecīnĭānus, a, um: Caeciniana oratio, Mart. Cap. 5, § 527.
caecina1.short: Caecīna (Cēc-), ae, m., a surname in the gens Licinia, originating in Etruria (pure Etrusc.

caecina2.full: Caecīna (Cēc-), ae, m., a river in Etruria, now the Cecina, Plin. 3, 5, 8, § 50.— A town in Etruria, Mel. 2, 4, 9.
caecina2.short: Caecīna (Cēc-), ae, m., a river in Etruria, now the Cecina, Plin.

caecitas.full: caecĭtas, ātis, f. caecus, blindness. Lit. (rare but in good prose), Cic. Tusc. 5, 39, 113; 5, 38, 111; id. Fin. 5, 28, 84; Plin. 11, 37, 55, § 149; 12, 8, 18, § 34.— Trop.: furorem autem esse rati sunt mentis ad omnia caecitatem, Cic. Tusc. 3, 5, 11: in furore animi et caecitate, id. Dom. 50, 129: mentis, id. ib. 40, 105; cf.: an tibi luminis obesset caecitas plus quam libidinis, id. Har. Resp. 18, 38.

caecitudo.full: caecĭtūdo, ĭnis, f. id., blindness; plur., Opilius Aur. ap. Fest. s. v. nusciciosum, p. 173 Müll.

caeco.full: caeco, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. id., to make blind, to blind. Lit.: sol caecat, Lucr. 4, 325 (300); Paul. Nol. Carm. Nat. S. Fel. 20, 7; 20, 292: unde caecatus est (Appius Claudius), Aur. Vict. Vir. Ill. 34, 3.—Hence, in gardening: oculum, to destroy, Col. 4, 9, 2; 4, 24, 16; cf. caecus, I. C., and oculus.— Trop.: qui largitione caecarunt mentes imperitorum, Cic. Sest. 66, 139: ut (animi acies) ne caecetur erroribus, id. Tusc. 5, 13, 39: caecati libidinibus, id. ib. 1, 30, 72: cupiditate, id. Dom. 23

caecubum.full: Caecŭbum, i, n., = Καίκουβον, a marshy place in Southern Latium, near Amyclœ, distinguished for producing the most excellent kind of Roman wine, Mart. 13, 115.— Deriv.: Caecŭbus, a, um, adj., Cœcuban: ager, Col. 3, 8, 5; Plin. 2, 95, 96, § 209: agri, id. 3, 5, 9, § 60: vites, id. 17, 4, 3, § 31: vina, Hor S. 2, 8, 15.—And subst.: Caecŭbum, i, n. (sc. vinum), Cœcuban wine, Hor. C. 1, 20, 9; 1, 37, 5; id. Epod. 9, 1; 9, 36.—Plur., Hor. C. 2, 14, 25; Mart. 13, 115. (From a neglect of the vines, and
caecubum.short: Caecŭbum, i, n., = Καίκουβον, a marshy place in Southern Latium, near Amyclœ, distinguished for producing the most excellent kind of Roman wine, Mart.

caeculto.full: caeculto, āre, v. n. contr for caeculĭto, from caecus, as ausculto for ausculito, from auris, to be like one blind, to be dim-sighted: caecultare est caecos imitari, Paul. ex Fest. p. 45 Müll.: caeculto άμβλυώττω, Gloss.; Plautus: numnam mihi oculi caecultant? Paul. ex Fest. p. 62 Müll.; cf. caecutio.

caeculus.full: Caecŭlus, i, m., son of Vulcan, founder of Prœneste, Verg. A. 7, 678 sq. Serv.; Mart. Cap. 6, § 642.
caeculus.short: Caecŭlus, i, m., son of Vulcan, founder of Prœneste, Verg.

caecus1.full: caecus (not coecus; sometimes in MSS. cēcus), a, um, adj. akin to σκιά, σκότος; Sanscr. khāyā, shadow, having no light, devoid of light. Act., not seeing, blind. Lit.: Appius, qui caecus annos multos fuit, Cic. Tusc. 5, 38, 112: traditum est enim Homerum caecum fuisse, id. ib. 5, 39, 114; Lucr. 5, 839: catuli, qui jam dispecturi sunt, caeci aeque et hi qui modo nati, Cic. Fin. 4, 23, 64: si facie miserabili senis, caeci, infantis, Quint. 4, 1, 42: caecum corpus, the blind part of the body, the b

caecus2.full: Caecus, i, m.; agnomen of Appius Claudius Crassus, as being blind, Cic. Brut. 14, 55; cf. Liv. 9, 29, 11; Cic. Sen. 6, 16.

caecutio.full: caecūtĭo, īre (no perf.), v. n. from caecus, like balbutio from balbus, to be blind, to see badly (ante- and post-class.), Varr. ap. Non. p. 35, 4: omnes quodammodo caecutimus, App. Flor. n. 2: utrum oculi mihi caecutiunt, Varr. ap. Non. p. 86, 12; Mart. Cap. 1, § 3.

caedes.full: caedes, is (gen. plur. regularly caedium, Liv. 1, 13, 3; Just. 11, 13, 9; Flor. 3, 18, 14 al.; but caedum, Sil. 2, 665; 4, 353; 4, 423; 4, 796; 5, 220; 10, 233; Amm. 22, 12, 1; 29, 5, 27; cf. Prisc. p. 771 P), f. caedo. Lit. In gen., a cutting or lopping off (post-class. and rare): ligni atque frondium caedes, Gell. 19, 12, 7: capilli, qui caede cultrorum desecti, App. M. 3.— Esp. (acc. to caedo, I. B. 1.; cf. cado, I. B. 2.), a cutting down, slaughter, massacre, carnage; esp. in battle or by an

caedo.full: caedo, cĕcīdi (in MSS. freq. caecīdi, v. Neue, Formenl. 2, 460), caesum, 3, v. a. root cīd- for scid-; cf. scindo; Gr. σχίζω. Lit. In gen. To cut, hew, lop, cut down, fell, cut off, cut to pieces: caesa abiegna trabes, Enn. ap. Cic. N. D. 3, 30, 75 (Trag. v. 281 Vahl.): frondem querneam caedito, Cato, R. R. 5, 8: arbores, Cic. Div. 2, 14, 33; Ov. M. 9, 230: robur, Cic. Div. 2, 41, 86; Ov. M. 8, 769: lignum, Plaut. Merc. 2, 3. 63: silvam, Varr ap. Non. p. 272, 5; Lucr. 5, 1265; Caes. B. G. 3, 29;

caeduus.full: caeduus, a, um, adj [caedo], that can be cut without injury, fit for cutting; a t. t. of agriculture, Dig. 50, 16, 30: silva, Cato, R. R. 1 fin.; Varr. R. R. 1, 7, 9; Col. 3, 3, 1; cf. natura, Plin. 12, 19, 42, § 89: fertilitas, id. 16, 37, 68, § 175; 17, 20, 32, § 141; 17, 20, 34, § 147.
caeduus.short: caeduus, a, um, adj [caedo], that can be cut without injury, fit for cutting;

caelamen.full: caelāmen, ĭnis, n. caelo, a basso-relievo (prob. formed by Ovid; rare): clipei caelamina, Ov. M. 13, 291; App. Flor, n. 7; id. de Deo Socr. p 40, 30 Elm.

caelator.full: caelātor, ōris, m. caelo, an artisan in basso-relievo, a carver, engraver, Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 24, § 54; 2, 4, 27, § 63; Quint. 2, 21, 24: argenti caelatores, Plin. 34, 8, 19, § 85: curvus, Juv. 9, 145; Tert. Idol. 3; Inscr Grut. 583, 5 al.

caelatura.full: caelātūra, ae, f. id., the art of engraving or carving bass-reliefs in metals and ivory, engraving, celature. Lit.: caelatura, quae auro, argento, aere, ferro opera efficit: nam sculptura etiam lignum, ebur, marmor, vitrum, gemmas, praeterea quae supra dixi, complectitur, Quint. 2, 21, 8: caelatura altior, id. 2, 4, 7; Plin. 35, 12, 45, § 156.— In other substances, e. g. in clay, Plin. 35, 12, 46, § 158; cf. id. 19, 4, 19, § 53; Dig. 13, 1, 13; cf. caelo, I. B.— Meton. (abstr. pro concreto), the

caelebs.full: caelebs (not coelebs), lĭbis, adj. etym. dub., unmarried, single (whether of a bachelor or a widower) Lit.: (censores) equitum peditumque prolem describunto: caelibes esse prohibento, Cic. Leg. 3, 3, 7; Plaut. Cas. 2, 4, 11; Quint. 5, 10, 26; Suet. Galb. 5 Baumg.-Crus.: caelebs senex, Plaut. Stich. 4, 1, 37: caelebs quid agam Martiis Calendis, Hor. C. 3, 8, 1; id. S. 2, 5, 47; Ov. M. 10, 245; Mart. 12, 63; Gai Inst. 2, 286; Tac. H. 1, 13; id. A. 3, 34.— Meton.: vita, the life of a bachelor, Hor.

caeles.full: caelĕs (coel-), ĭtis, adj. caelum; v Corss. Ausspr. II. p. 210, heavenly, celestial (poet.; access. form of caelestis, but not found in nom. sing.): di caelites. Enn. ap Cic. Div. 2, 50, 104 (Trag. Rel. v. 353 Vahl.): agricolae ( = ruris dei), Tib. 2, 1, 36: Venus (opp. vulgaris), App. Mag. p. 281, 14: regna, Ov. F. 1, 236: sub caelite mensa, Paul. Nol. Carm. 24, 9 al.—Esp. freq. subst.: caelĭ-tes, the inhabitants of heaven, the gods, Enn. ap. Varr. L. L. 7, § 6 Müll. (Trag. Rel. v. 163 Rib.); P

caelestini.full: Caelestīni, ōrum, m., a people of Umbria, Plin. 3, 14, 19, § 114.
caelestini.short: Caelestīni, ōrum, m., a people of Umbria, Plin.

caelestinus1.full: caelestīnus, a, um, adj. caelum, heavenly: IOVI OPTIMO MAXIMO CAELESTINO, Inscr. Fabr. 430, 3.

caelestinus2.full: Caelestīnus, i, m., a late Roman historian, Treb. Poll. Val. Jun. 8, 1.
caelestinus2.short: Caelestīnus, i, m., a late Roman historian, Treb.

caelestis.full: caelestis (coel-), e (gen. sing. CAELESTAE, Inscr. Neapol. 2602; abl. sing. regularly, caelesti: caeleste, Ov. H. 16, 277; id. M. 15, 743; cf.: bimestris, cognominis, perennis, patruelis, etc.; gen. plur. caelestum, but caelestium, Enn. Epigr. v. 9 Vahl.; Att. ap. Cic. N. D. 3, 26, 68, or id. Trag. Rel. v. 209 Rib.; Varr. L. L. 6, § 53 Müll.; Lucr. 6, 1274; Cat. 64, 191; 64, 205; Verg. A. 7, 432; Ov. M. 1, 150), adj. caelum, pertaining to heaven or to the heavens, found in heaven, coming from he

caelibaris.full: caelĭbāris (caelĭbālis hasta, Prisc. p. 631 P.), a small spear or pin, with the point of which the bride's hair was divided into six locks, Arn. 2, 6, 7; Paul. ex Fest. p. 62, 16 Müll. (Respecting the origin of this custom, v. Ov. F, 2, 560.)

caelibatus.full: caelĭbātus (coel-), ūs, m. caelebs, celibacy, single life (severely punished by the leges Julia and Papia Poppaea; only post-Aug.), Sen. Ben. 1, 9, 4; Suet. Claud. 16; 26; id. Galb. 5; Gai Inst. 2, 144.

caelicola.full: caelĭcŏla (coel-), ae (gen. plur. caelicolūm, Enn. ap. Prisc. p. 1103 P., or Ann. v 483 Vahl.; Verg. A. 3, 21; Prud. Sym. 1, 170: caelicolarum, Juv. 13, 42), adj. caelumcolo. Dwelling in heaven, poet. designation of a deity, a god, Enn. l. l.; Verg. A. 2, 641; 6, 554; 6, 787; Ov. M. 1, 174; 8, 637; Val. Fl. 5, 111; App. de Deo Socr. 6.— A worshipper of the heavens, Cod. Th. 16, 5, 43; 16, 8, 19; Cod. Just. 1, 9; cf. Juv. 14, 97.

caelicus.full: caelĭcus (coel-), a, um, adj. caelum, = caelestis, II. B., celestial, magnificent (very rare): tecta, Stat. S.2, 3, 14; Mart. Cap 9, § 891; Paul. Nol. Nom. Christ. 64.

caelifer.full: caelĭfer (coel-), ĕra, ĕrum, adj. caelum-fero, supporting the heavens, poet. epithet of Atlas, Verg. A. 6, 796.—And of Hercules: manus, Sen. Herc. Fur. 528: laudes, extolling to heaven, Mart. Cap. 6, § 637

caelifluus.full: caelĭflŭus (coel-), a, um, adj. caelum -fluo, flowing from heaven: fontes, Paul. Nol. Nat. S. Fel. 12, 780.

caeligenus.full: caelĭgĕnus (coel-), a, um, adj. caelum-gigno, heaven-born: Victoria et Venus, Varr. L. L. 5, § 62 Müll.: stellae, App. de Mundo, p. 57, 29.

caeliger.full: caelĭger (coel-), ĕra, ĕrum, adj. caelum-gero, heaven supporting: Atlas, Avien Phaenom. 575.

caeliloquus.full: caelĭlŏquus (coel-), a, um, adj [cae lum-loquor], heavenly speaking (late Lat.), Commod. 60, 3.
caeliloquus.short: caelĭlŏquus (coel-), a, um, adj [cae lum-loquor], heavenly speaking (late Lat.), Commod.

caelimontium.full: Caelĭmontĭum (Coel-), ii, n. Caelius-mons, the second region of Rome, including the Cœlian Hill, P. Vict. Reg. Urb. R.—Hence, adj.: Caelĭmontānus (Coel-), a, um, of or pertaining to Cœlimontium: porta, Cic. Pis. 23, 55: CAMPVS, Inscr. Orell. 2617.

caelina.full: Caelīna, ae, f., a town in Venetia, Plin. 3, 19, 23, § 131.
caelina.short: Caelīna, ae, f., a town in Venetia, Plin.

caeliolus.full: Caelĭŏlus (Coel-), i, m. dim. Caelius, a part of the Cœlian Hill, Varr. L. L. 5, § 46 Müll. (in Cic. Har. Resp. 15, 32, Caelĭ-cŭlus; Mart. 12, 18, 6, Caelĭus Mĭnor)

caelipotens.full: caelĭ-pŏtens (coel-), entis, adj. m. [caelum], powerful in heaven: di, Plaut. Pers. 5, 1, 3.

caelispex.full: Caelĭspex (Coel-), ĭcis, m. Caeliusspicio, looking towards the Cœlian Hill Apollo, a place at Rome, perh. named after the statue of Apollo placed there, Sex. Ruf. and P. Vict. Reg. Urb. R.

caelitus.full: caelĭtus (coel-), adv. caelum. From heaven (late Lat. for divinitus or caelo) omnia quae caelitus mortalibus exhibentur, App. Dogm. Plat. 1, p. 8, 31; Lact. 4, 2 fin.; 4, 28; Amm. 23, 6, 34.— Transf., from the emperor, Cod. Th. 6, 32, 2; 10, 20, 16.

caelius.full: Caelĭus (Coel-), i, m. A Roman gentile name. The orator M. Caelius Rufus, for whom Cicero made an oration, and whose letters to Cicero are contained in the 8th book of the Epp. ad Famil.; Cic. Brut. 79, 273; Caes. B. C. 3, 20 sqq.; Vell. 2, 68, 1; Sen. Ira, 3, 8, 4; Quint. 10, 1, 115; v. Teuffel, Röm. Litt. § 206, 5 sqq.—Hence, Caelĭānus, a, um, adj., Cœlian: orationes, Tac. Or. 21.— L. Caelius Antipater, a distinguished historian and jurist in the time of the Gracchi, and teacher of Crassus, Ci

caelo.full: caelo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. 1. caelum. Lit., answering to the Gr. τορεύω, to engrave in relief upon metals (esp. silver) or wory, to make raised work, to carve, engrave; later also, to cast (cf. O. Müll. Archaeol. § 311 sq.; and v. Quint. 2, 21, 8, s. v. caelatura; Fest. s. v. ancaesa, p. 17; Isid. Orig. 13, 4, 1; 19, 7, 4; 20, 4, 7)' ab initio sic opus ducere, ut caelandum, non ex integro fabricandum sit, Quint. 10, 3, 18: hanc speciem Praxiteles caelavit argento, Cic. Div. 1, 36, 79: galeas aer

caelum1.full: caelum (cēlum, Serv. ad Verg. A. 1, 640), i, n. caedo, the chisel or burin of the sculptor or engraver, a graver: caelata vasa... a caelo vocata, quod est genus ferramenti, quem vulgo cilionem vocant, Isid. Orig. 20, 4, 7; Quint. 2, 21, 24; Varr. ap. Non. p. 99, 18; Stat. S. 4, 6, 26; Mart. 6, 13, 1.— Plur., Aus. Epigr. 57, 6.

caelum2.full: caelum (coelum; cf. Aelius ap. Varr. L. L. 5, § 18 Müll.; Plin. 2, 4, 3, § 9; Cic. Verr. 2, 2, 52, § 129), i, n. (old form cae-lus, i, m., Enn. ap. Non. p. 197, 9; and ap. Charis. p. 55 P.; Petr. 39, 5 sq.; 45, 3; Arn. 1, 59; cf. the foll. I. 2.; plur. caeli, only poet., Lucr. 2, 1097, caelos, cf. Serv. ad Verg. A. 1, 331; and in eccl. writers freq. for the Heb. , v. infra, cf. Caes. ap Gell. 19, 8, 3 sq., and Charis. p. 21 P., who consider the plur. in gen. as not in use, v. Rudd. I. p. 109. Fr

caelus.full: caelus, i, v. caelum init. and I. 2.

caementarius.full: caementārĭus, ii, m. caementum, a stone-cutter, a mason, a builder of walls, Hier. Ep. 53, 6; Vulg. Amos, 7, 7.

caementicius.full: caementīcĭus (-tītĭus), a, um, adj. id., of or pertaining to quarried stones, consisting of them: structurae, Vitr. 2, 4: parietes, id. 2, 8 med.: saxum unhewn, quarry-stone (opp quadratum), id. ib.

caementum.full: caementum, i, n. (access. form cae-menta, ae, f., like armenta, ae, to armentum, Enn. ap. Non. p. 196, 30, or Trag. v. 422 Vahl.; v 373 Rib.) [contr. from caedimentum, from caedo; hence Engl. cement]. A rough, unhewn stone, as it comes from the quarry, a quarry-stone, used for walls. Plur. (so most freq.), Vitr. 1, 2, 8; 7, 6, 1; Cato, R. R. 38, 3; Varr. ap. Non. p. 96, 5 al.: in eam insulam materiem, calcem, caementa, arma convexit, Cic. Mil. 27, 74; so id. Div. 2, 47, 99; id. Q. Fr. 3, 9, 7; L

caena.full: caena and its derivv., v. cena, etc.

caeneus.full: Caeneus (dissyl.), ĕos (gen., Stat. Th. 7, 644; voc. Caenĭ, Ov. M. 12, 470: Caeneu, id. ib. 12, 531), m., = Καινεύς, orig. a girl, named Cænis, Ov. M. 12, 189; 12, 195; 12, 201; 12, 470 sq., the daughter of Elatus, afterwards changed by Neptune into a boy, he was subsequently present at the Calydonian hunt. and at the contest of the Centaurs and Lapithæ, and finally was metamorphosed into a bird. Ov. M. 12, 189; 12, 459 sq.; 12, 514 sq.; Hyg. Fab. 14; acc. to Verg. he again became a female. Verg

caenina.full: Caenīna, ae, f., = Καινινη, a small but very ancient town in Latium, near Rome, now Ciano, Plin. 3, 5, 9, § 68.— Derivv Caenīnensis, e, adj., of Cœnina: SACERDOTIVM, Inscr. Grut. 436, 5.—Subst.: Caenīnenses, ium, m., the inhabitants of Cœnina, Liv. 1, 9, 8; 1, 10, 2 and 3; Ov. F. 2, 135.— Caenīnus, a, um, adj., of Cœnina: arx, Prop. 4 (5), 10, 9. Acron, king of the Cœninenses, id. 4 (5), 10, 7; nomen = Caeninenses, Liv. 1, 10, 3.
caenina.short: Caenīna, ae, f., = Καινινη, a small but very ancient town in Latium, near Rome, now Ciano, Plin.

caenis.full: Caenis, ĭdis, f. V Caeneus.— A mistress of Vespasian, Suet. Vesp. 3, 23.

caenophrurium.full: Caenophrūrĭum (-frūrĭum), i, n., a town in Thrace, on the road from Apollonia to Selymbria, now Bivados, Eutr. 9, 15; Vop. Aur. 35, 5; Lact. Mort. Pers. 6, 2.
caenophrurium.short: Caenophrūrĭum (-frūrĭum), i, n., a town in Thrace, on the road from Apollonia to Selymbria, now Bivados, Eutr.

caenositas.full: caenŏsĭtas (coen-), ătis, f [caenosus], a dirty place; only trop., Fulg. Cont. Virg. p. 156 Munk.
caenositas.short: caenŏsĭtas (coen-), ătis, f [caenosus], a dirty place;

caenosus.full: caenōsus (coen-), a, um, adj. caenum, muddy, dirty, foul, marshy (rare): lacus. Col. 7, 10, 6: gurges (i. e. Styx), Juv. 3, 266.—Comp.: caenosior liquor, Sol. 49 fin.— Trop.: impuritas, Salv. Gub. Dei, 3, 10.

caenulentus.full: caenŭlentus (coen-), a, um, adj. id., covered with mud, muddy, filthy: pedes, Tert. Pall. 4.

caenum.full: caenum (less correctly coenum), i, n. cunio, dirt, filth, mud, mire (always with access. idea of loathsomeness, diff. from limus, lutum, etc.: omnes stultos insanire, ut male olere omne caenum, Cic. Tusc. 4, 24, 54; freq. and class. in prose and poetry); prop.: pulchrum ornatum turpes mores pejus caeno collinunt, Plaut. Most. 1, 3, 133; cf. id. Poen. 1, 2, 93; 4, 2, 4; Cic. Att. 2, 21, 4; Cic. Verr. 2, 5, 68, § 173; Lucr. 6, 977; Verg. G. 4, 49; id. A. 6, 296; Ov. M. 1, 418; * Hor. S. 2, 7, 27;

caepa.full: caepa (also cēpa), ae, f., and equally freq. caepe (cēpe), is, n. (gen. caepis, Charis. p. 43 P., without voucher, but the assertion of the gram. Diom. p. 314 ib.; Prisc. p. 681 ib.; Phocae Ars, p. 1706 ib., and Serg. p. 1842 ib., that caepe is indecl., is also unsubstantiated, since the form of the gen. caepe cited by Prisc. l. l. from App. is the well-known later orthog. for caepae; v. Neue, Formenl. 1, 551; 1, 557 sq.; 1, 578; in plur. only caepae or cepae, ārum, f.; cf. Don. p. 1747 P.; Pris
caepa.short: caepa (also cēpa), ae, f., and equally freq.

caeparia.full: caepārĭa. ae, f. caepa, a disease in the privy members, Marc. Emp. 33.

caeparius1.full: caepārĭus, ii, m. id., a trader in onions. Lucil ap Non. p 201, 10.

caeparius2.full: Caepārĭus, ii, m., a Roman proper name; esp., M. Caeparius, an adherent of Catiline. Cic. Cat. 3, 6, 14; id. Fam. 9, 23. Sall. C. 46, 3.
caeparius2.short: Caepārĭus, ii, m., a Roman proper name;

caepasius.full: Caepasĭus, ii, m., a Roman proper name: esp., C. and L. Caepasius, two orators, Cic. Brut. 69. 242; id. Clu. 20, 57; Jul. Vict. Art. Rhet. 17.
caepasius.short: Caepasĭus, ii, m., a Roman proper name: esp., C.

caepina.full: caepīna (cēp-), ae (caepuila, ae, Pall. Febr. 24, 2; id. Oct. 11, 4), f. caepa; anal. to napina, porrina. rapina; lit., adj., sc. planta, a field or bed of onions, Col. 11, 3, 56 sq.

caere.full: Caere, n. indecl. (gen. Caerĭtis. f., Verg. A. 8, 597; abl. Caerēte, id. ib. 10, 183), = Καιρη Steph., Καιρέα Strab., a very ancient city of Etruria, one of the twelve; previously called Agylla, now Cervetri, Plin. 3, 5, 8, § 51; Serv. ad Verg. A. 8, 597; 10, 183; Liv 1, 60, 2.— Derivv. Caeres, ĭtis and ētis, adj., of or pertaining to Cœre, Cœritic: populus, Liv. 7, 19, 6: aquae, Val. Max. 1, 6, 9; cf. Liv. 22, 1, 10.—In plur.: Caerĭtes (Caerētes), um, m., the inhabitants of Cœre, Liv. 7, 19, 8

caerefolium.full: caerĕfŏlĭum, ii (chaerĕphyl-lum, Col. 10, 110), n. χαιρέφυλλον, whence the Fr. cerfeuil, and Germ. Kerbel, chervil, Plin. 19, 8, 54, § 170; Pall. Febr. 24, 9; id. Sept. 13, 3; App. Herb. 104.

caerimonia.full: caerĭmōnĭa (cērĭ-; scanned cĕrīmōnĭa, Prud. c. Symm. praef. 1, 5), ae, f. (collat. form caerĭmōnĭum, ii, n., Gloss. Lat. pp. 50, 69 Hild.; Inscr. Orell. 3188) [kindr. with Sanscr. root kri, = facere; cf. also creo. cerus, Ceres. strictly sacred work, divine rite; cf. Bopp, Gloss. p. 79, a; Pott, I. p. 219; Mommsen, Unterit. Dial.], the sacred. the divine, that which has reference to the Deity (in class. prose) Lit. Objectively, sacredness, sanctity (in this sense rare, and only in sing.): sancti

caerimonialis.full: caerĭmōnĭālis, e, adj. caerimonia, pertaining to religious rites, ceremonial; officia. Arn. 7, p. 237.

caerimonior.full: caerĭmōnior, āri, 1, dep. a. [id.], to treat with due ceremony, to worship, Aug. Serm. 309; Act. St. Cypr. 3.

caerimoniosus.full: caerĭmōnĭōsus, a, um. adj. id., per taining or devoted to religious rites' dies. Amm. 22, 15, 17.

caerites.full: Caerĭtes, um, v. Caere, II. A.

caeroesi.full: Caeroesi (Caeraes-), ōrum, m., a Belgian tribe, Caes. B. G. 2, 4; called Ce-rosi, Oros. 6, 7
caeroesi.short: Caeroesi (Caeraes-), ōrum, m., a Belgian tribe, Caes.

caerulans.full: caerŭlans, antis, adj. caerulus = caeruleus, dark-colored, sky-blue: Musa caerulanti peplo circumdata, i. e. astrono my, Fulg. Myth. 1.

caeruleatus.full: caerŭlĕātus, a, um, adj. caeruleus, dark-colored, dark blue, sky-blue: Plancus, i. e. of the color of a sea-god, Vell. 2, 83, 2.

caeruleus1.full: caerŭlĕus, and in poetry equally common, caerŭlus, a, um, adj. cf. cae -sius, κύανος, and Sanscr. cjamas = dark Lit., dark-colored, dark blue, dark green, cerulean, azure, κυάνεος; poet. epithet of the sky, of the sea, and other similar objects (as dark, opp. albus and marmoreus color, Lucr. 2, 771 sq., and syn. with ater, Verg. A. 3, 64; v. under II. A.). Of the sky: caeli caerula templa, Enn. ap. Cic. Div. 1, 20, 40 (Ann. v. 50 Vahl.); id. ap. Varr, L. L. 7, § 6 Müll. (Ann. v. 66 Vahl.); cf.:
caeruleus1.short: caerŭlĕus, and in poetry equally common, caerŭlus, a, um, adj.

caeruleus2.full: Caerŭlĕus, i, m., the name of an aqueduct at Rome, Plin. 36, 15, 24, § 122; Suet. Claud. 20; Front. Aquaed. 13.
caeruleus2.short: Caerŭlĕus, i, m., the name of an aqueduct at Rome, Plin.

caesa.full: caesa, ae, f. caedo (only in the milit. lang. of Veget.), a cut, Veg. Mil. 1, 12.

caesapon.full: caesăpon, i, n., a kind of lettuce, Plin. 1 ind. libr. xx. n. 25; 20, 7, 25, § 59.
caesapon.short: caesăpon, i, n., a kind of lettuce, Plin.

caesar.full: Caesar, ăris (CAESERIS, C. I. L. 4, 2308; Inscr. Orell. 4205: CAESARVS, C. I. L. 1, 696), m., = Καῖσαρ [a caeso matris utero, Plin. 7, 9, 7, § 47; cf. Non. p. 556, 32: a caesarie dictus, qui scilicet cum caesarie natus est, Fest. p. 44; cf. Comment. p. 383. Both etymm. also in Isid. Orig. 9, 3, 12, and Spart. Ael. Ver. 2. Better acc. to Doed. Syn. III. p. 17, from caesius, caeruleus, the color of the skin; cf. Rufus], a cognomen in the gens Julia. Of these the most celebrated, C.Julius Caesar, d

caesaraugusta.full: Caesăraugusta, ae, f., = Καισαραυγοῦστα, a town in Hispania Tarraconensis, on the Ebro, so called after the emperor Augustus, who colonized it; acc. to some, the native town of Prudentius, now Saragossa, Mel. 2, 6, 4; Plin. 3, 3, 4, § 24.
caesaraugusta.short: Caesăraugusta, ae, f., = Καισαραυγοῦστα, a town in Hispania Tarraconensis, on the Ebro, so called after the emperor Augustus, who colonized it;

caesarea.full: Caesărēa (-ī^a), ae, f., = Καισἀρεια. A very important town in Palestine, previously called Stratonis turris, now Kaisariyeh, Plin. 5, 13, 14, § 69; Tac. H. 2, 78; Eutr. 7, 10; Amm. 14, 8, 11.—Hence, Deriv.: Caesărĭensis, e, adj., of Cœsarea: Colonia, Dig. 50, 15, 1.—Caesărĭ-enses, ium, m., its inhabitants, Plin. 5, 29, 31, § 120; Dig. 50, 15, 8.— A town in Mauritania, earlier called Iol, now Shershell (or, acc. to others, Tniz or Tenez), Mel. 1, 6, 1; Plin. 5, 2, 1, § 20, Eutr. 7, 10.— Hence, C

caesareus.full: Caesărĕus, a, um, v. Caesar, II. C.

caesarianus.full: Caesărĭānus, a, um, v. Caesar, II. B.

caesariatus.full: caesărĭātus, a, um, adj. caesaries (very rare). Covered with hair, having long hair: caesariati comati, Fest. p. 35: miles usque caesariatus, Plaut. Mil. 3, 1, 171: Numidae equis caesariati, i. e. with helmets ornamented with horse-hair, Tert. Pall. 4.—* Trop., ornamented with foliage or leaves: terra, App. de Mundo, p. 67, 37; cf. coma.

caesariensis.full: Caesărĭensis, e, v. Caesarea, I. B. and II. B.

caesaries.full: caesărĭes, ēi, f. kindr. with Sanscr. kēsa, coma, caesaries, Bopp, Gloss. p. 85, a, a dark (acc. to Rom. taste, beautiful) head of hair, the hair (mostly poet.; only sing.). Of men (so most freq.), Plaut. Mil. 1, 2, 64: ipsa decoram Caesariem nato genitrix afflarat, Verg. A. 1, 590: nitida, id. G. 4, 337: flava, *Juv. 13, 165: pectes caesariem, *Hor. C. 1, 15, 14: umeros tegens, Ov. M. 13, 914: terrifica, id. ib. 1, 180: horrida fieri, id. ib. 10, 139: horrifica, Luc. 2, 372 et saep.—In prose: p

caesarinus.full: Caesărīnus, a, um, v. Caesar, II. A.

caesario.full: Caesărĭo, ōnis, m., = Καισαρίων, son of Cœsar by Cleopatra, put to death by the command of Augustus, Suet. Aug. 17; cf. id. Caes. 52.
caesario.short: Caesărĭo, ōnis, m., = Καισαρίων, son of Cœsar by Cleopatra, put to death by the command of Augustus, Suet.

caesena.full: Caesēna, ae, f., a town in Gallia Cispadana, now Cesena, Cic. Fam. 16, 27, 2, Plin. 3, 15, 20, § 116.—Hence, Caesēnas, ātis, adj., of Cœsena: vina, Plin. 14, 6, 8, § 67.
caesena.short: Caesēna, ae, f., a town in Gallia Cispadana, now Cesena, Cic.

caesennius.full: Caesennĭus, a, a Roman gens; esp., Caesennius Lento, an adherent of Cœsar, Cic. Phil. 12, 9, 23.— Caesennius Paetus, in Nero's time, Tac. A. 15, 6 sqq.

caesia silva.full: Caesia Silva, a forest in ancient Germany, in the western part of Westphalia, now Daemmerwald and Heserwald, on the borders of Cleves and Münster, Tac. A. 1, 50.
caesia silva.short: Caesia Silva, a forest in ancient Germany, in the western part of Westphalia, now Daemmerwald and Heserwald, on the borders of Cleves and Münster, Tac.

caesim.full: caesīm, adv. caedo, by cutting, with cuts. Lit. Of the cutting of plants by striking: major pars operis in vineā ductim potius quam caesim facienda est ... qui caesim vitem petit, etc., Col. 4, 25, 2 and 3.— T. t. of milit. lang., with the edge (opp. punctim, with the point): punctim magis quam caesim petere hostem, Liv. 22, 46, 5; cf. Veg. Mil. 1, 12; Liv. 7, 10, 9: gladio caesim percutere aliquem, Suet. Calig. 58. — Trop., of discourse, in short clauses: membratim adhuc, deinde caesim diximus,

caesio.full: caesĭo, ōnis, f. id.. A cutting, lopping, of trees. castanea fere usque in alteram caesionem perennat, Col. 4, 33, 1.— A wounding, killing, Tert. Apol. 39.

caesitas.full: caesĭtas, ātis, f. caesius, blue, blueness: oculorum, Boëth. ap. Porphyr. Dial. 2, p. 31; id. ap. Aristot. Categ. 3, p. 176.

caesitius.full: caesĭtĭus (-cĭus), a, um, adj. id., bluish, dark blue: linteolum, Plaut. Ep 2, 2, 46; cf. Doed. Syn. III. p. 17.

caesius1.full: caesĭus, a, um, adj. cf. caeruleus, bluish gray; very rare, and only of the eyes, cat-eyed: virgo caesia, Ter Heaut. 5, 5, 18; v. Don. in h. l. and Gell. 2, 26, 19: isto modo dicere licebit caesios oculos Minervae, caeruleos esse Neptuni, Cic. N. D. 1, 30, 83 (cf. in Gr. γλαυκῶπις?̓Αθήνη): caesia, Παλλάδιον, has she gray eyes? she is the impersonation of Pallas, * Lucr. 4, 1161: caesius, Ter Hec. 3, 4, 26 (glaucis oculis, quasi felis oculos habens et glaucos, Don.): hunc, judices, dico, rubrum,

caesius2.full: Caesĭus, i, m., a Roman cognomen. M. Caesius, Cic. Fam. 13, 11.— Another M. Caesius, Cic. Verr. 2, 1, 50, § 130.— P. Caesius, Cic. Balb. 22, 50.— Sex. Caesius, Cic. Fl. 28, 68.— Caesius Bassus, the friend to whom Persius addressed his sixth satire; cf. Quint. 10, 1, 96.
caesius2.short: Caesĭus, i, m., a Roman cognomen.

caeso.full: Caeso (Kaeso, v. the letter K), ōnis, m. a caeso matris utero dictus, Plin. 7, 9, 7, § 47; cf. Paul. ex Fest. p. 57 Müll.; Isid. Orig. 9, 3, 12, and v. Caesar init., a Roman cognomen in the gens Fabia, Liv. 2, 43, 2; 2, 48, 3 and 4; 3, 11, 6 sq. et saep.

caesonius.full: Caesōnĭus, a, name of a Roman gens. —So, M. Caesonius, œdile with Cicero, Cic. Att. 1, 1, 1; 1, 12, 11; Cic. Verr. 1, 10, 29. — Caesonius Paetus, consul under Nero, Tac. A. 14, 29.—Hence, Caesōnĭānus, a, um, adj., Col. 1, 4, 1.— Milonia Caesonia, mistress and afterwards wife of Caligula, Suet. Calig. 25; Juv. 6, 616.
caesonius.short: Caesōnĭus, a, name of a Roman gens.

caesor.full: caesor, ōris, m. caedo, one who hews something (post-class.): lignorum caesores, hewers of wood, Hier. Ep. 53, n. 6, after the Vulg. Deut. 29, 11: lapidum, stone-breaker, Ambros. Luc. 2, 89 fin.; Vulg. 2 Par. 24, 12; cf. Val. Prob. II. p. 1458 P

caespes.full: caespĕs (not cespes), ĭtis, m. caesus, caedo. A turf, sod as cut out: caespes est terra in modum lateris caesa cum herba, sive frutex recisus et truncus, Paul. ex Fest. p. 45 Müll.: caespes χορτόπλινθος, χορτόβωλος, πλίνθος, Gloss.: non esse arma caespites, neque glebas, * Cic. Caecin. 21, 60.— Used for altars, mounds (of tombs), for covering cottages, huts, etc., Hor. C. 1, 19, 13; Ov. Tr. 5, 5, 9; id. M. 4, 753; 7, 240; 15, 573; Verg. A. 3, 304; Tac. G. 27; id. A. 1, 62; Verg. E. 1, 69 Voss; S

caespitatores.full: caespĭtātōres suffusi equi, Serv ad Verg. A. 11, 671 dub.
caespitatores.short: caespĭtātōres suffusi equi, Serv ad Verg.

caespiticius.full: caespĭtĭcĭus, a, um, adj. caespes, made of turf (post-class.): tribunal, Vop. Prob. 10: murus, Capitol. Anton. Pius, 5.

caesposus.full: caespōsus, a, um, adj. id., abounding in turf or grass: litus, Col. 10, 130.

caestus.full: caestus (not cestus), ūs, m. (dat. plur. caestis, Varr. ap. Non. p. 492, 11) [caedo], a strap of bull's hide loaded with balls of lead or iron, wound around the hands and arms, a gauntlet, boxing-glove for pugilists (pugiles), Cic. Tusc. 2, 17, 40; Verg. A. 5, 69; 5, 379; 5, 479; Prop. 3 (4), 14, 9; Ov. F. 2, 367; Tac. A. 14, 20; Stat. Th. 6, 764; 6, 829; Val. Fl. 4, 251; Plin. 11, 37, 45, § 124; Sen. Med. 89; cf. Fest. p. 35; Dict. of Antiq.

caesullae.full: caesullae, ārum: a caesiis oculis, having gray eyes, Fest. pp. 274 and 275 Müll.
caesullae.short: caesullae, ārum: a caesiis oculis, having gray eyes, Fest.

caesum.full: caesum, i, n., v caedo fin.
caesum.short: caesum, i, n., v caedo fin.

caesura.full: caesūra, ae, f. caedo A cutting, felling, hewing, hewing off ligni, Plin. 16, 43, 84, § 230; silvae, id. 17, 20, 34, § 151— Meton. (abstr. pro concr.), that which is hewn or cut off, Plin. 8, 26, 40, § 96.— In metre, a pause in a verse, cœsura; called also incisio, Diom. p. 496 P.; Bed. Metr. p. 2368 ib.

caesuratim.full: caesūrātim, adv. caesura, with pauses in short clauses (for the class. caesim): dictio caesuratim succincta, Sid. Ep. 4, 3.

caesus1.full: caesus, a, um, Part., v. caedo.

caesus2.full: caesus, ūs, m. caedo, a cutting, a cutting off: frondium, Auct. Itin. Alex. M. p. 102 Mai

caeterus.full: caetĕrus, a, um, with its derivatives; v ceter.
caeterus.short: caetĕrus, a, um, with its derivatives;

caetra.full: caetra (better than cētra), ae, f. prob. Spanish, a short Spanish shield, Verg. A. 7, 732 Serv.; Liv. 21, 27, 5; 28, 5, 11; Plin. 11, 39, 93, § 227; Tac. Agr. 36; Suet, Calig 19; Luc. 7, 232; Sil. 3, 278; 3, 348 al.— Prov.: quis rotundam facere cetram nequeat? Varr. ap. Non. p. 82, 18.

caetratus.full: caetrātus, a, um, adj. caetra, armed with a caetra, shield-bearing ( = πελταστής): cohors, Caes. B. C. 1, 39; so Liv. 31, 36, 1: juventus, Sil. 9, 231; and subst.: caetrā-ti, ōrum, Caes. B. C. 1, 70; Liv. 31, 36, 1; 33, 4, 4 et saep.

caeus1.full: Caeus, a, um, = Ceus, v. Cea.

caia2.full: caia, ae caio, a cudgel, acc. to Isid. Orig. 18, 7, 7.
caia2.short: caia, ae caio, a cudgel, acc.

caiatio.full: cāiātĭo, ōnis, f. caio, a striking, a cudgelling or beating of children, Fulg. Cont. Virg. p. 162 Munck.

caicus.full: Căīcus (Căȳcus, Ov. M. 12, 111), i, m., = Κάικος. A river of Greater Mysia, which takes its rise on Mt. Teuthras, passes near Pergamus, and flows into the sea opposite Lesbos; now the Bakhir Tchai, Cic. Fl. 29, 72; Liv. 37, 18, 6; Mel. 1, 18, 1; Plin. 5, 30, 32, § 121; Verg. G. 4, 370; Ov. M. 2, 243; 15, 278; Luc. 3, 203.— One of the companions of Æneas, Verg. A. 1, 183; 9, 35.

caieta.full: Cāiēta, ae (and -ē, ēs), f., = Καιήτη. The nurse of Æneas, Verg. A. 7, 2; Ov. M. 14, 443.— A town and harbor in Latium, now Gaëta, Cic. de Or. 2, 6, 22; id. Imp. Pomp. 12, 33; Verg. A. 6, 900; Sil. 8, 531; Serv. ad Verg. l. l.; Aur. Vict. Orig. Rom. 10.—Hence, Cāiētānus, a, um, adj., of Caieta: villa, Val. Max. 1, 4, 5.

caio.full: cāio, āre, v. a., to beat, cudgel, Fulg. Cont. Virg.

cala.full: cāla, ae, f. κᾶλον, a piece or billet of wood: scinde, puero calam ut caleas, i. e. scinde fustes et fac focum, Lucil. ap. Serv. ad Verg. A. 6, 1 (Fragm. Inc. 139).

calabarriunculos.full: calabarriunculos dicit (Laberius) quos vulgus calabarriones, Gell. 16, 7, 6 (the signif. of these two words is unknown).
calabarriunculos.short: calabarriunculos dicit (Laberius) quos vulgus calabarriones, Gell.

calabra.full: Călābra Cūria, a Curia at the Capitol, so called from the proclamation [calare] of the calendar dates in this place by the priests (hence the gloss, ἱππών βουλή, for which should be read, ἱερῶν βουλή); cf. Varr. L. L. 5, § 13; 6, § 27 Müll.; Macr. S. 1, 15; Paul. ex Fest. s. v. curia, p. 49 Müll.; and Serv. ad Verg. A. 8, 654.
calabra.short: Călābra Cūria, a Curia at the Capitol, so called from the proclamation [calare] of the calendar dates in this place by the priests (hence the gloss, ἱππών βουλή, for which should be read, ἱερῶν βουλή);

calabria.full: Călā^brĭa, ae, f., = Καλαβρία, the country in Lower Italy from Tarentum to the promontory Iapygium, now Terra d'Otranto, Plin. 3, 11, 16, § 99; Hor. C. 1, 31, 5; Liv. 23, 34, 3; 42, 48, 7.— Derivv. Călăber, bra, um, adj., of Calabria, Calabrian: hospes, Hor. Ep. 1, 7, 14: pascua, id. Epod. 1, 27: apes, id. C. 3, 16, 33: aquae, Ov. F. 5, 162: montes, id. A. A. 3, 409: litus, Plin. 3, 26, 30, § 151: oves (of superior quality), Col. 7, 2, 3: Pierides, i. e. poems of Ennius, who was a native of Cala
calabria.short: Călā^brĭa, ae, f., = Καλαβρία, the country in Lower Italy from Tarentum to the promontory Iapygium, now Terra d'Otranto, Plin.

calabrix.full: călā^brix, īcis, f., a shrub, perh. the turkey-berry, buckthorn, used in dyeing: Rhamnus infectorius, Linn.; Plin. 17, 10, 14, § 75; Pall. Sept. 14, 3.
calabrix.short: călā^brix, īcis, f., a shrub, perh.

calacte.full: Călactē, ēs, f., = Καλὴ ἀκτή (i. e. Fair Beach), a town on the north coast of Sicily, now Caronia, Cic. Verr. 2, 3, 43, § 101; Sil. 14, 251.—Hence, Călactīnus, i, m., an inhabitant of Calacte, Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 22, § 49; id. Fam. 13, 37.—In plur.: Calactini, Cic. Verr. 2, 3, 43, § 101.

calagurris.full: Călăgurris or Călăgūris, is, f., = Καλαγοῦρις. A town in Hispania Tarraconensis, in the region of the Ilergetes, north of Osca, now Loarre, Liv. 39, 21, 8; Flor. 3, 22, 9.—Hence, Călăgurrī-tāni, its inhabitants, Caes. B. C. 1, 60; Suet. Aug. 49; acc. to Plin. 3, 3, 4, § 24, with epithet Fibularenses.— A town of the Vascones, in Spain, birthplace of Quintilian, and, acc. to some, of Prudentius, now Calahorra: Calagurritani Nassici, its inhabitants, Plin. l. l.
calagurris.short: Călăgurris or Călăgūris, is, f., = Καλαγοῦρις.

calais.full: Călăis, is (acc to Prcb. Cath 1, 40, p. 1462 P.; cf. Neue, Formenl. 1, p. 143; voc. Calai, Serv. ad Verg. A. 3, 213), m., = Κάλαϊς, the winged son of Boreas and Orithyia, and brother of Zetes, with whom he accompanied the Argonauts, Ov. M. 6, 716; Hyg. Fab. 14; 19; Val. Fl. 4, 465 sq.; Serv. ad Verg. A. 10, 350; Prop. 1, 20, 26.— The name of a youth, Hor. C. 3, 9, 14.

calamarius.full: călămārĭus, a, um, adj. calamus, pertaining to a writing-reed: theca, a pencase, Suet. Claud. 35; cf. Mart. 19, 14.

calamellus.full: călămellus, i, m. dim. id., a little reed (late Lat.), Arn. in Psa. 150.

calamentum.full: cālāmentum, i, n. cala, withered, dry wood on the vine, Col. 4, 27, 1.

calaminae.full: Călămīnae insŭlae, floating islands in Lydia, Plin. 2, 95, 96, § 209; cf. Varr. R. R. 3, 17, 4; cf. Mart. Cap. 9, § 928 Kopp ad loc.
calaminae.short: Călămīnae insŭlae, floating islands in Lydia, Plin.

calaminthe.full: călăminthē, ēs, f., = καλαμίνθη, a plant, a kind of mint, App. Herb. 70 (in Plin. 19, 10, 57, § 176 Jan. reads in zmintham; Sillig, in mentam).
calaminthe.short: călăminthē, ēs, f., = καλαμίνθη, a plant, a kind of mint, App.

calamis.full: Călămis, ĭdis, m., = Κάλαμις, a distinguished Greek sculptor and artificer in metals (about Olymp. 78), Cic. Brut. 18, 70; Quint. 12, 10, 7; Plin. 34, 7, 18, § 47; 34, 8, 19, § 71; Prop. 3 (4), 9, 10; Ov. P. 4, 1, 33.
calamis.short: Călămis, ĭdis, m., = Κάλαμις, a distinguished Greek sculptor and artificer in metals (about Olymp.

calamister.full: călămister, tri, m. (ante- and postclass.; nom. not found; also călămi-strum, i, n., Plaut. Curc. 4, 4, 21; Varr. L. L. 5, § 129 Müll.; Non. p. 546, 16; Serv. ad Verg. A. 12, 100; Isid. Orig. 20, 13, 4.—Plur.: calamistra, Varr. ap. Charis. p. 61 P.) [calamus], a hollow, tubular iron for curling the hair, a curling-iron, crisping-pin. Lit.: calamistrum quod his calfactis in cinere capillus ornatur, Varr. L. L. l. l.; Serv. l. l.; cf. Isid. Orig. l. l.; 10, 57: meum, Plaut. Curc. l. l.: calamistri

calamistratus.full: călămistrātus, a, um, adj. calamister, curled with the curling-iron, crisped, curled (of men, a reproach for effeminacy; cf. Serv. ad Verg. A. 12, 100): cinaedus, Plaut. As. 3, 3, 37: coma, Cic. Sest. 8, 18: saltator, id. post Red. in Sen. 6, 13.—Of fops: pueri cincinnatuli et calamistrati, Hier. Ep. 130, 19; so Ambros. Ep. 4, 15.

calamitas.full: călămĭtas, ātis, f. cf. in columis. Lit., loss, injury, damage, mischief, harm: sed ecca ipsa egreditur, nostri fundi calamitas (Ter. Eun. 1, 1, 34). Proprie calamitatem rustici grandinem dicunt, Don.; cf. the same on Ter Heaut. 2, 4, 15: robigo genus est vitii, quo culmi pereunt, quod a rusticanis calamitas dicitur, Serv ad Verg. G. 1, 151: postquam calamitas plures annos arvas calvitur, Pac. ap. Non. p. 192, 30; Plaut. Cas. 5, 2, 34; id. Capt. 4, 3, 4: non ut legatus populi Romani, sed ut quae

calamites.full: călămītes, ae, m., = καλαμίτης, the green frog, Plin. 32, 10, 42, § 122; so id. 32, 10, 50, § 139; 32, 7, 24, § 70.
calamites.short: călămītes, ae, m., = καλαμίτης, the green frog, Plin.

calamitose.full: călămĭtōsē, adv., v. the foll. fin.

calamitosus.full: călămĭtōsus, a, um, adj. calamitas. Act., that causes great damage or loss, ruinous, destructive. Lit.: uti (regio) bonum caelum habeat, ne calamitosum sit, Cato, R. R. 1, 2: per omnes partes provinciae te tamquam aliquam calamitosam tempestatem pestemque pervasisse, Cic. Verr. 2, 1, 38, § 96; cf. calamitas, I.: tempestas, Dig. 19, 2, 15, § 2.— Trop., destructive, disastrous, ruinous, pernicious, calamitous: acer bissimum et calamitosissimum bellum, Cic. Phil. 11, 13, 34: hoc enim ipsum, utile p

calamochnus.full: călămochnus, i, m. κάλαμοσ-χνοῦς, a kind of sea-foam; called in pure Latin adarca, Plin. 32, 10, 52, § 140.

calamus.full: călămus, i, m., = κάλαμος. Lit., a reed, cane (pure Lat. harundo; cf. canna), Plin. 16, 36, 65, § 159 sq.; 16, 21, 33, § 80; Col. 3, 15, 1; 4, 4, 1; Pall. Nov. 22, 3 al.: aromaticus (found in Syria and Arabia), sweet calamus, Col. 12, 52, 2: odoratus, Plin. 12, 22, 48, § 104; Veg. 6, 13, 3.—Also absol.: calamus, Cato, R. R. 105, 2; Plin. 13, 1, 2, § 8 sq.: Syriacus, Veg. 4, 13, 4.— Meton. For objects made of reeds (cf. harundo, and Liddell and Scott, under κάλαμος). A reed-pen (cf. Dict. of Anti

calanus.full: Călănus (Callă-), i, m., = Κάλανος, an Indian philosopher (gymnosophist) in the time of Alexander the Great, who, in old age, burned himself on a funeral pile, Cic. Tusc. 2, 22, 52; id. Div. 1, 23, 47; 1, 30, 65; Val. Max. 1, 8, ext. 10.
calanus.short: Călănus (Callă-), i, m., = Κάλανος, an Indian philosopher (gymnosophist) in the time of Alexander the Great, who, in old age, burned himself on a funeral pile, Cic.

calasis.full: calasis, a kind of tunic which the Greeks call καλάσινον: alii dicunt nodum esse tunicae muliebris, Paul. ex Fest. p. 51 Müll.
calasis.short: calasis, a kind of tunic which the Greeks call καλάσινον: alii dicunt nodum esse tunicae muliebris, Paul.

calates.full: Călătes, ae, m., a Grecian painter, Plin. 35, 10, 37, § 113.
calates.short: Călătes, ae, m., a Grecian painter, Plin.

calathiscus.full: călăthiscus, i, m., = καλαθίσκος, a small wicker basket: virgati calathisci, Cat. 64, 319; Petr. 41, 6 Burm.
calathiscus.short: călăthiscus, i, m., = καλαθίσκος, a small wicker basket: virgati calathisci, Cat.

calathus.full: călăthus, i, m., = κάλαθος. Lit., a wicker basket, a hand-basket (pure Lat. quasillum, made in the shape of a lily); acc. to diff. uses, a flower-basket, a wool-basket, a thread-basket or a fruit-basket, etc.; cf. Plin. 21, 5, 11, § 23; Vitr. 4, 1, 9; Verg. E. 2, 46; Ov. F. 4, 435: calathi Minervae, Verg. A. 7, 805; Ov. A. A. 2, 219; id. H. 9, 73; 9, 76; Juv. 2, 54; Ov. A. A. 2, 264; id. M. 12, 475.— Meton., any other vessel of similar form, of metal or wood. For milke, etc., a milk-pail, bowl,

calatia.full: Cālātĭa, ae (Cālātĭae, ārum, Plin. 3, 5, 9, § 63), f., = Καλατία, a town in Campania, on the Via Appia, between Capua and Beneventum, now Galazze, Cic. Att. 16, 8, 1; Liv. 9, 2, 2; 23, 14, 13; 27, 3, 7; Sil. 8, 542; 11, 14 sq.—Hence, Cālātīni, its inhabitants, Liv. 22, 61, 11 al.—In sing. Calatinus, cognomen of M. Atilius, Cic. Agr. 2, 24, 63; id. Sen. 17, 61.

calatina.full: călătĭna vĭŏla, f., a species of gentian, Plin. 21, 6, 14, § 27 dub. (al. calathiana, calatiana).
calatina.short: călătĭna vĭŏla, f., a species of gentian, Plin.

calatio.full: călātĭo, ōnis, f. calo, a calling, summoning, Varr. L. L. 5, § 13; cf. id. ib. 6, § 27 Müll.

calator.full: călātor, ōris, m. id.; a servant for calling, etc., a crier; hence, Lit., a servant, esp. of priests, Suet. Gram. 12; cf. Serv. ad Verg. G. 1, 268; Inscr. Orell. 2431 sqq.; so freq. in inscriptions.— In gen., any servant, attendant; cf. Paul. ex Fest. p. 38 and 225 Müll.: egomet mihi comes, calator, equus, agaso, armiger, Plaut. Merc. 5, 2, 11; id. Ps. 4, 2, 52; id. Rud. 2, 3, 5.

calatorius.full: călātōrĭus, a, um, adj. calator, relating to priests' servants, Inscr. Fabr. p. 449, n. 58.

calatus.full: călātus, a, um, Part., v. calo.

calauria.full: Călaurĭa (Călaurēa, Ov. M. 7, 384), ae, f., = Καλαύρεια or -ία, an island on the eastern coast of Argolis, now Poro, Mel. 2, 7, 10; Plin. 4, 12, 19, § 56.—Consecrated to Latona, hence, Calaurea Latois, Ov. l. l.

calautica.full: călautĭca (in many MSS. and edd. erroneously călantĭca), ae, f. of uncer.tain etym.; acc. to Beier, Cic. Clod. et Cur. 5, p. 107, perh. kindr. with καλύπτω, as auris, through the Cretan form αὖς, with οὖς, a covering for the head of women, which fell down over the shoulders (perh. a kind of veil): calautica est tegmen muliebre, quod capiti innectitur, Non. p. 537, 2 sq.: mitrae, semimitrae, calautica, etc.; cf. Mai and Orell. in h. l. (Orell. Cic. V. 2, p. 336); Cic. Fragm. Clod. et Cur. 5, 3 B.

calcaneum.full: calcānĕum, i, n. (calcānĕus, i, m., Isid. Orig. 11, 1, 14; Ambros. in Psa. 48) [calx] (a rare form for calx), the heel, Verg. M. 36: camelorum, Lampr. Elag. 20.

calcar.full: calcar, āris, n. for carcar; cf. Sanscr. kar, wound; and Lat. calx. Lit., a spur as worn on the heel: calcaria dicta, quia in calce hominis ligantur, ad stimulandos equos, Isid. Orig. 20, 16, 6 (class. in prose and poetry; esp. freq. trop.): calcari quadrupedem agitare, Plaut. As. 3, 3, 118: incendere equum calcaribus, to spur one's horse, Hirt. B. G. 8, 48; so, concitare, Liv. 2, 6, 8; Curt. 7, 4, 18: stimulare, Val. Max. 3, 2, 9: subdere equo calcaria, Liv. 2, 20, 2; Curt. 3, 13, 8; 7, 2, 4: c

calcariarius.full: calcārĭārĭus, a, um, adj. calcarius, of or pertaining to burning lime: NEGOTIANS, Inscr. Grut. 641, 1: EXONERATOR, ib. 1117, 5.

calcariensis.full: calcārĭensis, is, m. id., a limeburner, Cod. Th. 12, 1, 37.

calcarius.full: calcārĭus, a, um, adj. 2. calx, of or pertaining to lime, lime-: fornax, a limekiln, Cato, R. R. 38, 1; Plin. 17, 9, 6, § 53.— Also subst. calcārĭa, ae, f. (sc. fornax), a lime-kiln: de calcariā in carbonariam pervenire, Tert. Carn. Christ. 6.— (Sc. fodina.) A lime-quarry, Dig. 48, 19, 8, § 10.— calcārĭus, ii, m., a limeburner, Cato, R. R. 16.

calcata.full: calcāta, ae, f., an uncertain reading in Auct. B. Hisp. 16, which, acc. to the context, signifies the material for filling ditches, fascines; a marginal reading is crates; other MSS. cultatas and culcatas; v. Oud. in h.l.
calcata.short: calcāta, ae, f., an uncertain reading in Auct.

calcator.full: calcātor, ōris, m. calco, one who treads something, esp. grapes, a treader of grapes (very rare), Calp. Ecl. 4, 124: uvarum, Hier. Isa. 5, 16, n. 9.

calcatorium.full: calcātōrĭum, ii, n. id, a wine-press, Pall. 1, 18, 1 and 2; cf. Isid. Orig. 15, 6, 8.

calcatrix.full: calcātrix, īcis, f [calcator], she who treads upon something, i. e. trop despises it, she who contemns' mundi, Prud. Psych. 587.
calcatrix.short: calcātrix, īcis, f [calcator], she who treads upon something, i.

calcatura.full: calcātūra, ae, f. calco, a treading: operarum, Vitr 10, 10, 1.

calcatus1.full: calcātus, a, um, Part., v. calco

calcatus2.full: calcātus, ūs, m. calco, a treading (very rare). calcatu assiduo, Pall. Jun. 13, 17; Auct. Itin. Alex. M. 77 Mai.

calceamen.full: calcĕāmen (calcĭāmen), ĭnis, n. a collateral and rare form of calceamentum, a shoe, Plin. 19, 2, 7, § 27; 15, 8, 8, § 34.

calceamentarius.full: calcĕāmentārĭus, ii, m., = ὑποδηματάριος, caligarius, a shoemaker, Gloss. Gr. Lat.
calceamentarius.short: calcĕāmentārĭus, ii, m., = ὑποδηματάριος, caligarius, a shoemaker, Gloss.

calceamentum.full: calcĕāmentum (calcĭām-), i, n. calceo, a covering for the foot, a shoe (v. also the class. co - ordinate forms calceamen and calceatus), Cic. Tusc. 5, 32, 90; Cels. 8, 22; Suet. Aug. 73; Col. 12, 3, 1: induere, Plin. 28, 4, 7, § 38: inferre, id. 36, 17, 27, § 131; 9, 17, 30, § 65; Dig. 34, 2, 25, § 4.

calcearia.full: calcĕārĭa, ae, f [calceus], a shoe-shop, Varr. L. L. 8, 30, § 55 Müll.
calcearia.short: calcĕārĭa, ae, f [calceus], a shoe-shop, Varr.

calcearium.full: calcĕārĭum (calcĭār-), ii, n. id., lit. adj sc. argentum, money for shoes, shoemoney, Dig. 34, 1, 21; 2, 15, 8, § 14; Suet. Vesp 8.

calceator.full: calcĕātor (calcĭāt-), ōris, m. calceo, a shoemaker, Inscr Murat. 909, 12.

calceatus1.full: calcĕātus (calcĭāt-), a, um, Part., v. calceo.

calceatus2.full: calcĕātus (calcĭāt-), ūs, m. calceo, a covering for the foot, a sandal, shoe (post-Aug. for the class. calceamentum): in calceatu, Plin. 8, 57, 82, § 221; 23, 6, 59, § 110; 28, 16, 62, § 222; 11, 45, 105, § 254; Suet. Calig. 52.

calceo.full: calceo (calcio), āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. calceus, to furnish with shoes, to put on shoes, to shoe (class. in prose and poetry): calceati et vestiti, * Cic. Cael. 26, 62; Suet. Aug. 78: cothurnis, Plin. 7, 20, 19, § 83: soccis, id. 36, 5, 4, § 41: calceandi pedes, * Phaedr. 1, 14, 16; Plin. 7, 53, 54, § 181: fibrinis pellibus, id. 32, 9, 36, § 110: calceabat ipse sese, Suet. Vesp. 21 al.— Of animals (whose feet were furnished with shoes to be taken off and put on, not shod as with us): spartea quă an

calceolarius.full: calcĕŏlārĭus (calcĭŏl-), ii, m. calceolus, one who makes shoes, a shoemaker, Plaut. Aul. 3, 5, 38.

calceolus.full: calcĕŏlus, i, m. dim. calceus, a small shoe, half-boot, ὑποδημάτιον (rare), *Cic. N. D. 1, 29, 82; Memmius ap. Serv. ad Verg. A. 4, 261; Scrib. Comp. 208.

calces.full: calces, leaden bottles, Paul. ex Fest. p 46 Müll.

calceus.full: calcĕus (also calcĭus; cf. Burm. and Oud. Suet. Aug. 73, and Calig. 52), i, m. calx, a shoe, a half-boot (covering the whole foot, while soleae, sandals, covered only the lower part, Gell. 13, 22, 5; v. solea, and cf. Liddell and Scott s. v. ὑπόδημα, and Dict. of Antiq.; very freq. and class.): calcei muliebres sint an viriles, Varr. L. L. 9, § 40 Müll.; Titin. ap. Fest. s. v. mulleos, p. 142 ib. (Com. Rel. p. 128 Rib.): calcei habiles et apti ad pedem, Cic. de Or. 1, 54, 231: calcei et toga, id

calchas.full: Calchās, antis (gen. Calchae, Gell. ap. Charis. p. 50 P.; acc. Calcham, Pac. and Plaut. ib.; Calchanta, Verg. A. 2, 122; Val. Max. 8, 11, ext. 6; Stat. Achill. 1, 493; 2, 7; Calchantem, Cic. N D. 2, 3, 7; id. Div. 1, 40, 87; 2, 30, 63; abl. Calchă, Plaut. Men. 5, 1, 48; cf. Prisc. p. 702 P.; Ritschl prol. ad Plaut. Trin. p. 87), m., = Κάλχας, son of Thestor, the most distinguished seer among the Greeks before Troy, Verg. A. 2, 122; 2, 182; Ov. A. A. 2, 737.

calciarium.full: calciārium, calciātus, etc., v. calcearium, etc.

calcifraga.full: calcĭfrăga, ae, f. 2. calx-frango, an herb said to be a remedy for the stone, perh. hartstongue: Asplenium scolopendrium, Linn.; Plin. 27, 9, 51, § 75; Scrib. Comp. 150; 153; cf. Dioscorid. 3, 151.

calcitratus.full: calcĭtrātus, ūs, m. calcitro, a striking with the heel, a kicking: mulae, Plin. 8, 44, 69, § 174; cf. calcitro, I.

calcitro1.full: calcĭtro, āre, v. n. 1 calx. Lit., to strike with the heels, to kick, of animals (very rare), Plin. 30, 16, 53, § 149; cf. calcitratus.— Trop, to resist, to be stubborn or refractory: calcitrat, respuit, * Cic. Cael. 15, 36.— Prov.: calcitrare contra stimulum, to kick against the pricks, Amm. 18, 5, 1; Vulg. Act. 9, 5; 26, 14; cf. 1. calx. —* In gen., to strike convulsively with the feet, of one dying, Ov M. 12, 240.

calcitro2.full: calcĭtro, ōnis, m. 1. calcitro. One who strikes with his heels, a kicker: equus mordax, calcitro, Varr. ap. Non. p. 45, 2 (Sat. Men. 81, 3).— Of men, a boisterous fellow, a blusterer, Plaut. As. 2, 3, 11.

calcitrosus.full: calcĭtrōsus, a, um, adj. 2. calcitro, kicking, apt to kick: juvencus, Col. 2, 2, 26; Dig. 9, 1, 1; 21, 1, 4.

calco.full: calco, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. 1. calx, to tread something or upon something, to tread under foot. In gen. Lit. (very freq.; mostly poet. or in post-Aug. prose; not in Cic.)' astructos morientum acervos, Ov. M. 5, 88; 12, 391: calcata vipera, trodden upon, id. ib. 10, 23; 12, 391; 13, 804: alius manum aeger, ut pede ac vestigio Caesaris calcaretur, orabat, Tac. H. 4, 81: cineres ossaque legionum, id. ib. 5, 17: calcata lacinia togae, Suet. Calig. 35: uvam, to tread grapes, Cato, R. R. 112 fin.; Varr

calcularius.full: calcŭlārĭus, a, um, adj. calculus, of or pertaining to calculation: error, an error in reckoning, Dig. 50, 8, 8.

calculatio1.full: calcŭlātĭo, ōnis, f. calculo, a computation, calculation, reckoning, Cassiod. Ep. 1, 10; Ven. ad Syagr. Ep. 5, 6.

calculatio2.full: calcŭlātĭo, ōnis, f. calculus, calculus, gravel, stone, a disease, Cael. Aur. Tard. 5, 4, 60.

calculator.full: calcŭlātor, ōris, m. calculo, a computer, teacher of arithmetic, = λογιστής (post-Aug.), Mart. 10, 62, 4; Acron. ad Hor. S. 1, 6. 72; Isid. Orig. 1, 3, 1; cf. id. ib. 1, 10, 43.— A book-keeper, accountant, Dig. 38, 1, 7, § 5; 27, 1, 15, § 5.

calculatorius.full: calcŭlātōrĭus, a, um, adj. calculator, of or pertaining to an accountant: tabula, Schol. ad Juv. 7, 73.

calculensis.full: calcŭlensis, e, adj. calculus, of or pertaining to stones: genus purpurarum a calculo maris, Plin. 9, 37, 61, § 131.

calculo1.full: calcŭlo, āre, v. a. id., to calculate, compute, reckon (late Lat.). Lit., Prud. στεφ. 3, 131.— Trop., to consider as, to esteem, Sid. Ep. 7, 9.

calculo2.full: calcŭlo, ōnis, m. 1. calculo, a computer, accountant, Aug. Ord. 2, 12; Anthol. Lat. II. p. 268, 1.

calculosus.full: calcŭlōsus, a, um, adj. calculus. Full of small stones or pebbles, stony, pebbly, gravelly (post - Aug.): pomum, Cloat. ap. Macr. S. 2, 15, 6: loca, Col. Arb. 21: ager, id. ib. 3, 11, 7: solum, Plin. 35, 14, 49, § 170.— Afficted with calculus or stone, Cels. 7, 26, n. 2; Plin. 28, 4, 9, § 42; Scrib. Comp. 150 and 153; Veg. 2, 18.

calculus.full: calcŭlus, i, m. dim. 2. calx; cf. Paul. ex Fest. p. 46. In gen., a small stone, a pebble: conjectis in os calculis, Cic. de Or. 1, 61, 261: Demosthenes calculos linguā volvens dicere domi solebat, Quint. 11, 3, 54; Vitr. 7, 2: argilla et dumosis calculus arvis, gravel in the thorny fields, Serv. ad Verg. G. 2, 180; Plin. 4, 8, 15, § 37; 28, 9, 33, § 124.— Trop., of discourse: qui tenui venulā per calculos fluunt, Quint. 12, 10, 25.— Esp. A stone in the bladder or kidneys, the gravel, stone, Cels

calcus.full: calcus, i, v. the preced. fin.

calda.full: calda, ae, v. calidus, I. B. 1.

caldamentum.full: caldāmentum, i, n. calidus, a fermentation (late Lat.) Marc. Emp. 5.

caldariola.full: caldārĭŏla, ae, f. dim. caldaria, a small vessel for heating fluids, Schol. ad Juv. 5, 47 dub. (Jan. calvariolas).

caldarius.full: caldārĭus (călĭd-), a, um, adj. caldus = calidus, pertaining to or suitable for warming. cella, a warm bath, Plin. Ep. 5, 6, 26.— Subst. caldārĭa, ae, f. A warm bath, Marc. Emp. 25.— A pot for boiling, Vulg. 1 Reg. 2, 14; App. Herb. 59.— caldārĭum, ii, n. A hot bath, Vitr. 5, 10, 1; 8, 2, 4; Sen. Ep. 86, 11; Cels. 1, 4.— A room containing warm water for bathing, Vitr. 5, 10, 1.— Esp.: calidaria maltha, for plastering the walls in baths, Pall. 1, 41, 1: caldarium aes, that is prepared by heat or

caldius.full: Caldĭus, i, m. calda, a nickname formed from Claudius, and given to the emperor Tiberius, on account of his fondness for drink, Suet. Tib. 42; cf. Biberius and Mero.

caldor.full: caldor, ōris, m. caldus = calidus, warmth, heat (ante- and post-class.), Varr. R. R. 3, 9, 15; 1, 41, 1; 1, 55, 6; Gell. 17, 8, 10; 19, 4, 4 and 5; Arn. 7, 240.

caldus2.full: Caldus, i, m., a Roman cognomen, v. Cic. Inv 2, 9, 28.—Esp.: C. Caelius Caldus, quaestor A. U. C. 704, Cic. Fam. 2, 19 tit.
caldus2.short: Caldus, i, m., a Roman cognomen, v.

caledonia.full: Călēdŏnĭa, ae, f, also Călī- cf. Welsh celydd, a woody shelter, and Lat. celo, = Καληδονία, the province of the ancient Britons, now the Highlands in the northern part of Scotland, Tac. Agr. 10; 11; 25; 31.— Derivv. Călē-dŏnĭus, a, um, adj., Caledonian: silva, Plin. 4, 16, 30, § 102; Flor. 3, 10, 18: saltus, id. 1, 17, 3: ursus, Mart. Spect. 7: Britanni, id. 10, 44, 1; Luc. 6, 68: Oceanus, Val. Fl. 1, 8. — Călēdŏnĭcus, a, um, adj., Caledonian: angulus, Sol. 22, 1.—Călēdŏnes, um, m., a people in
caledonia.short: Călēdŏnĭa, ae, f, also Călī- cf.

calefacio.full: călĕ-făcĭo, or contr. calfăcĭo (as calidus = caldus, calidarius = caldarius, etc.), fēci, factum, 3, v. a. (in the time of Quint. the contracted form seems to have been the prevailing one, v. Quint. 1, 6, 21; also Charis. p. 220 P. gives as pass. calfio. In the poets usage varies according to the demands of the verse; e. g., cālfācì;t, Ov. F. 4, 698; cālfăcienda, id. A. A. 2, 214; cālfācti, id. Ib. 48, and călĕfēcit, Lucr. 6, 687; călēfacta, Verg. A. 12, 66; 12, 269 al. In prose writers—e. g. Qu

calefactabilis.full: călĕfactābĭlis, e, adj. calefacio, that can be warmed, made hot: ignis, Boëth. ap. Aristot. Interpr. p. 279; cf. id. ib. p. 450.

calefactio.full: călĕfactĭo, ōnis, f. id., a warming, heating (post-Aug.): balnei publici, Dig. 50, 4, 18, § 4.—In plur.: calefactiones thermarum, Dig. 50, 4, 1, § 2.

calefacto.full: călĕfacto, āre, v. freq. act. [id.], to make warm, to warm, heat (very rare; not in Cic.). Lit.: aquam, Plaut. Rud. 2, 3, 80: ahenum, * Hor. Ep. 2, 2, 169: corpora, Gell. 17, 8, 12.—* Trop.: aliquem virgis, Plaut. Cas. 2, 6, 48.

calefactorius.full: călĕfactōrĭus, a, um, adj. id., having a warming or heating power, Plin. Val. 1, 38; Theod. Prisc. de Diaeta, 10.

calefactus1.full: călĕfactus or calfactus, a, um, Part., v. calefacio.
calefactus1.short: călĕfactus or calfactus, a, um, Part., v.

calefactus2.full: călĕfactus (calfac-), ūs, m. calefacio, a warming, heating (post-Aug. and rare): faucium tumorem calfactu obiter fovere, Plin. 29, 3, 11, § 48; Lact. Opif. Dei, 14, 5.

calentum.full: Calentum (Call-), i, n., a town in Hispania Baetica, now prob. Cuzalla, Plin. 35, 14, 49, § 171.—Hence, Callenses, ium, m., the inhabitants of Calentum, Plin. 3, 1, 3, § 14.
calentum.short: Calentum (Call-), i, n., a town in Hispania Baetica, now prob.

calenum.full: Călēnum, i, and Călēnus, a, um, v. Cales.
calenum.short: Călēnum, i, and Călēnus, a, um, v.

caleo.full: călĕo, ui, 2, v. n. (part. fut. act. călĭtūrus, Ov. M. 13, 590: caleor = caleo, Caper. ap. Prisc. p. 797 P.; prob. only in reference to the impers. caletur, Plaut. Capt. 1, 1, 12; id. Truc. 1, 1, 46) [etym. dub.; cf. Gr. σκέλλω, σκληρός], to be warm or hot, to glow (object.; opp. frigere, to be cold; while aestuare, to feel, experience warmth; opp. algere, to feel cold; cf. Doed. Syn. III. p. 89). Lit.: calet aqua; eamus hinc intro ut laves, Plaut. Bacch. 1, 1, 73: sentiri hoc putat, ut calere i

cales.full: Căles, ium. f. (as sing. in acc. Calen, as if from Cale, Sil. 12, 525: Călēnum, i, n., Plin. 3, 5, 9, § 60), = Καλησία, a town in Southern Campania, celebrated for its good wine, now Calvi, Cic. Agr. 2, 35, 95; id. Phil. 12, 11, 27; id. Att. 7, 14, 1; Hor. C. 4, 12, 14; Cato, R. R. 135, 1; Verg. A. 7, 728; Sil. 8, 514.— Deriv.: Călēnus, a, um, adj., of Cales, Calenian: municipium, Cic. Fam. 9, 13, 3.—Absol., Cic. Att. 8, 3, 7: ager, Plin. 2, 103, 106, § 230: vinum, id. 14, 6, 8, § 65: prelum, Ho

calesco.full: călesco, ĕre, v. inch. n. [caleo], to grow warm or hot. Lit. (rare but class.): (vortex) suā cum Mobilitate calescit, Lucr. 6, 280: calescere vel apricatione vel igni, umbris aquisve refrigerari, Cic. Sen. 16, 57; id. N. D. 2, 55, 138: unda calescit, Ov. M. 15, 310; Curt. 4, 7, 22.— Trop., of the mind, to become excited, to glow, be inflamed; esp. with love (poet.), Ter. Eun. 1, 2, 5 Don.: quo propius nunc es, flammā propiore calesco, Ov. H. 18, 177; so id. M. 3, 372: est deus in nobis! agitante

caletes.full: Calētes, um, and Calēti, ōrum, m., a people of Belgic Gaul, Caes. B. G. 7, 75; 2, 4; Hirt. ib. 8, 7; Plin. 19, 1, 2, § 8.
caletes.short: Calētes, um, and Calēti, ōrum, m., a people of Belgic Gaul, Caes.

caletranus.full: Caletrānus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Caletra in Etruria: ager, Liv. 39, 55, 9; Plin. 3, 5, 8, § 52.
caletranus.short: Caletrānus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Caletra in Etruria: ager, Liv.

calicata.full: călĭcāta aedĭfĭcia, calce polita, plastered with lime, Paul. ex Fest. 47 Müll.; cf. decalicatum.
calicata.short: călĭcāta aedĭfĭcia, calce polita, plastered with lime, Paul.

calicellus.full: călĭcellus, i, m. dim. calix, a little cup (late Lat.), Theod. Prisc. 4, 1.

caliclarium.full: căliclārĭum, ii, n. id., ποτηριοθήκη, a place where cups stand, a cupboard, sideboard, Gloss. Gr. Lat.

caliculus.full: călĭcŭlus, i, m. dim. calix, a small cup, Cato, R. R. 108, 1; Cels. 2, 11; Plin. 9, 30, 48, § 93; Pall. Nov. 7, 11.— Esp., a little inkstand, Cassiod. Var. 11, 36.

calida.full: călĭda, ae, v. calidus, I. B. 1.

calidius.full: Călĭdĭus, a, m., the name of a Roman gens. M. Calidius, an orator, contemporary with Cicero, Cic. Brut. 79, 274 sqq.; id. Q. Fr. 1, 3, 7; 3, 2, 1; id. Fam. 8, 4, 1.— Cn. Calidius, a Roman knight, the father of a senator, plundered by Verres, Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 20, § 42.— Q. Calidius, the father of I., Cic. Verr. 1, 13, 38; 2, 3, 25, § 63.
calidius.short: Călĭdĭus, a, m., the name of a Roman gens.

calidus.full: călĭdus and caldus, a, um, adj. (contr. access. form caldus in the anteAug. per. is freq. only in Cato and Varr.; Lucr. and Cic. use only calidus; acc. to Quint. 1, 6, 19, caldus appears to have been predom. in the Aug. per., though used by Aug. poets only when demanded by the rules of prosody, as comp. caldior, Hor. S. 1, 3, 53) [caleo, like fervidus, frigidus, from ferveo, etc., aridus from areo, etc.], warm, hot. Lit.: fons luce diurnă Frigidus, et calidus nocturno tempore, Lucr. 6, 850; 6, 7
calidus.short: călĭdus and caldus, a, um, adj.

caliendrum.full: călĭendrum (călĭandrĭum, Arn. 6, p. 209), i, n. κάλλυντρον, ornament, a high head-dress, made of layers of false hair; a head-dress worn by Roman women (very rare): caliendrum κόσμιον κεφθλῆς, Gloss. Philox.; *Hor. S. 1, 8, 48 (caliendrum hoc est galericulum, Porphyr., acc. to whom it was also used by Varro; cf. Varr. Sat. Men. 95, 10); Arn. l. l.; Tert. Pall. 4.

caliga.full: călĭga, ae, f. cf. calceus, from calx, a shoe of leather, esp. that worn by the Roman soldiers (cf. Dio, 48, 12; Smith, Antiq., and Becker, Gall. III. p. 134, 2d ed.), a half-boot, a soldier's boot. Lit., *Cic. Att. 2, 3, 1; Just. 38, 10, 3; * Suet. Calig. 52; * Juv. 16, 24; Edict. Diocl. p. 241.— Meton., military service, Plin. 7, 43, 44, § 135; Sen. Brev. Vit. 17, 6; id. Ben. 5, 16, 2; Inscr. Grut. 445, 9.

caligaris.full: călĭgāris, e, adj. caliga, of or pertaining to the caliga or soldier's boot (access. form of the foll.): clavus, Plin. 9, 18, 33, § 69; 22, 22, 46, § 94: formae, Edict. Diocl. p. 23.

caligarius.full: călĭgārĭus, a, um, adj. id., of or pertaining to the soldier's boot: clavus, Plin. 34, 14, 41, § 143.—Hence, with sutor, Inscr. Grut. 649, 1.—As subst.: călĭgārĭus, ii, m., a maker of soldiers' boots, a shoemaker, Lampr. Alex. Sev. 33; Firm. Matth. 3, 12; Inscr. Spon. Misc. 220.

caligatio.full: cālīgātĭo, ōnis, f. 2. caligo, darkness, mistiness, Plin. 29, 6, 38, § 123.

caligatus.full: călĭgātus, a, um, adj. caliga, wearing soldiers' boots, booted: milites, Suet. Vit. 7 fin.; Dig. 3, 2, 2; 48, 3, 9; Inscr. Grut. 279, 3.—Of a peasant in heavy shoes, brogans, Juv. 3, 322.— Subst.: călĭgātus, i, m. (sc. miles), a common soldier, a private, = gregarius, Suet. Aug. 25; cf. Dig. 27, 1, 10.

caligineus.full: cālīgĭnĕus, a, um, adj. 1. caligo, dark, gloomy: fumus, Grat. Cyn. 56.

caliginosus.full: cālīgĭnōsus (post-class. cālīgōsus, Mart. Cap. 8, § 803; cf. Kopp. ad id. 1, § 67; Ven. Fort. Carm. 5, 4, 25), a, um, adj. id., full of mist, covered with mist, dark, obscure, gloomy (rare, but class. in prose and poetry): caelum et umidum et caliginosum, Cic. Tusc. 1, 19, 43: obscurior et quasi caliginosa stella (opp. illustris et pellucida), id. Div. 1, 57, 130: tractus, Plin. 17, 22, 35, § 171: tenebrae, Val. Max. 1, 7, ext. 1.— Trop., dark, uncertain, obscure: nox, i. e. an uncertain future,

caligo1.full: cālīgo (call-), ĭnis, f. root cal-, cover; cf.: oc-culo, clam, cella, a thick atmosphere, a mist, vapor, fog (mostly poet. or in post-Aug. prose): suffundere caelum caligine, Lucr. 6, 479; 6, 461; 6, 92: (ignis) piceă crassus caligine, Verg. G. 2, 309; cf. id. A. 9, 36; Liv. 29, 27, 7: densa caligo occaecaverat diem, id. 33, 7, 2; cf. Suet. Ner. 19: fumidam a terră exhalari caliginem, Plin. 2, 42, 42, § 111: caligo aestuosa, Col. 11, 2, 53 (for which, id. 11, 2, 57: nebulosus aestus): pruinae et

caligo2.full: cālīgo, āre, v. n. 1. caligo. To emit vapor or steam, to steam, reek: amnes aestate vaporatis, hieme frigidis nebulis caligent, Col. 1, 5, 4: aram tenui caligans vestiet umbrā, Cic. Arat. 205 (449); cf.: omnem quae nunc Mortalis hebetat visus tibi et umida circum Caligat, nubem eripiam, Verg. A. 2, 606.— Transf. To be involved in darkness, to be dark, gloomy: caligare oculos, darkness covers the eyes, Lucr. 3, 157; Verg. G. 4, 468; Stat. Th. 1, 95. — Poet.: altae caligantesque fenestrae, dizzy,

caligula.full: călĭgŭla, ae, f. dim. caliga, a small military boot; only post-class. ap. Ambros. Ep. 7, 53; Hor. S. 1, 3, 128; Schol. ad Juv. 3, 67.—Hence, As nom. propr.: Călĭgŭ-la, ae, m., a cognomen of the successor of Tiberius, since from his earliest youth he was engaged in military service; cf. Suet. Calig. 9; Tac. A. 1, 41; 1, 69; Aur. Vict. Caes. 3.

calingae.full: Calingae, ārum, m., a people of India, Plin. 6, 17, 21, § 64 sq.; 6, 20, 23, § 72; 7, 2, 2, § 30.
calingae.short: Calingae, ārum, m., a people of India, Plin.

calingii.full: Calingii, ōrum, m., a people of Arabia, Plin. 6, 28, 32, § 159.
calingii.short: Calingii, ōrum, m., a people of Arabia, Plin.

caliptra.full: caliptra, a kind of covering for the head, Paul. ex Fest. p. 47, 5 Müll. [ = καλύπτρα].
caliptra.short: caliptra, a kind of covering for the head, Paul.

calix.full: călix, ĭcis, m. root cal-, cover; cf. caligo; Germ. Kelch. A cup, goblet, a drinking-vessel: κύλιξ poculi genus, quod nos una littera immutata calicem dicimus, Macr. S. 5, 21; Plaut. Capt. 4, 4, 8; Cic. Pis. 27, 67; id. Tusc. 3, 19, 44; Tib. 2, 5, 98; Prop. 2 (3), 33, 40; Hor. S. 2, 4, 79; 2, 6, 68; 2, 8, 35; Plin. 33, prooem. 2, § 5; 36, 40, 66, § 195; Juv. 11, 145.— Meton., wine, = vinum, Cat. 27, 2; Hor. Ep. 1, 5, 19 al.— A cooking-vessel, pot, Cato, R. R. 39, 1; Varr. R. R. 1, 8, 7; id. L. L

callaecia.full: Callaecia, Callaecus, and Calla-icus, v. Gallaeci.

callais.full: callaïs, ĭdis, f., = καλλαΐς, a sea-green precious stone, the turquoise, Plin. 37, 10, 56, § 151 (in Sol. 20 called callaica).—Hence, callăĭnus, a, um, adj., turquoisecolored: lacernae, Mart. 14, 139.—Subst.: callăĭna, ae, f., a precious stone of a pale-green color, Plin. 37, 8, 33, § 110 sq.; 37, 10, 54, § 147; cf. id. 37, 10, 56, § 151.
callais.short: callaïs, ĭdis, f., = καλλαΐς, a sea-green precious stone, the turquoise, Plin.

callarias.full: callărĭas, ae, m., = καλλαρίας, a kind of codfish, Plin. 9, 17, 28, § 61; 32, 11, 53, § 146 Sillig (Jan. collyri, collyris).
callarias.short: callărĭas, ae, m., = καλλαρίας, a kind of codfish, Plin.

callens.full: callens, entis, v. calleo, P. a.

callenter.full: callenter, adv., v. calleo, P. a. fin.

calleo.full: callĕo, ēre, v. n. and a. [callum]. Neutr. Lit., to be callous, to be thickskinned (rare): plagis costae callent, Plaut. Ps. 1, 2, 4; Caecil. ap. Non. p. 258, 10: callent rure manus, Auct. Aetn. 260; Plin. 11, 37, 84, § 211.— Trop. * To be hardened, insensible, unfeeling: in illis rebus exercitatus animus callere jam debet atque omnia minoris existimare, Serv. Sulp. ap. Cic. Fam. 4, 5, 2; cf. callisco.— To be practised, to be wise by experience, to be skilful, versed in; in a pun on the literal

calliblepharum.full: callĭblĕphărum (callĭblĕphărĭ-um, Marc. Emp. 8 fin.), i, n., = καλλιβλέφαρον (sc. φάρμακον), a dye for coloring the eyebrows, Varr. ap. Non. p. 218, 22; Plin. 21, 19, 73, § 123; 23, 4, 51, § 97; 33, 6, 34, § 102. —Hence, † callĭblĕphărātus, a, um, adj., with beautiful eyelids: ostrea, Plin. 32, 6, 21, § 61.

callicia.full: callĭcĭa, ae, f., a plant that, acc. to Pythagoras, made water freeze, Plin. 24, 17, 99, § 156.
callicia.short: callĭcĭa, ae, f., a plant that, acc.

callicias.full: Callĭcĭās, ae, m., the name of a man, Plaut. Trin. 4, 2, 71.
