callicias.short: Callĭcĭās, ae, m., the name of a man, Plaut.

callicles.full: Callĭclēs, is, m., a character in the Trinummus of Plautus, Plaut. Trin. 4, 2, 114; 4, 4, 2 al.— A Grecian painter in the time of Alexander the Great, Plin. 35, 10, 37, § 114.— A Grecian statuary, Plin. 34, 8, 19, § 87.
callicles.short: Callĭclēs, is, m., a character in the Trinummus of Plautus, Plaut.

callicratidas.full: Callĭcrătĭdas, ae, m., = Καλλικρατίδας, a Spartan general, successor of Lysander, conquered and slain near the Arginusœ. Cic. Off. 1, 24, 84; 1, 30, 109.
callicratidas.short: Callĭcrătĭdas, ae, m., = Καλλικρατίδας, a Spartan general, successor of Lysander, conquered and slain near the Arginusœ.

callicula.full: Callĭcŭla, ae, f., a low mountain in Campania, not far from Casilinum, Liv. 22, 15, 3; 22, 16, 5.
callicula.short: Callĭcŭla, ae, f., a low mountain in Campania, not far from Casilinum, Liv.

callidamates.full: Callĭdămătēs, is, m., the name of a man, Plaut. Most. 5, 2, 9.
callidamates.short: Callĭdămătēs, is, m., the name of a man, Plaut.

callidemides.full: Callĭdēmĭdēs, is, m., = Καλλιδημίδης, the name of a man, Ter. Hec. 5, 3, 3.
callidemides.short: Callĭdēmĭdēs, is, m., = Καλλιδημίδης, the name of a man, Ter.

calliditas.full: callĭdĭtas, ātis, f. callidus, the being callidus, in a good or bad sense. In a good sense, shrewdness, skill, skilfulness, readiness, aptness (so several times after the Aug. period): calliditas ingenii, Nep. Eum. 1, 3; Ov. F. 3, 380; Plin. 37, 12, 74, § 195; Tac. Agr. 9; Flor. 2, 17, 15; Cic. Har. Resp. 9, 19.—Far more freq. and class., In a bad sense, cunning, craft, slyness, artfulness: scientia, quae est remota ab justitiā, calliditas potius quam sapientia est appellanda, Cic. Off. 1, 19, 6

callidromus.full: Callidrŏmus, i, m., = Καλλίδρομος, a mountain in Locris, near Thermopylœ, part of the Œta range, Liv. 36, 15 sqq.
callidromus.short: Callidrŏmus, i, m., = Καλλίδρομος, a mountain in Locris, near Thermopylœ, part of the Œta range, Liv.

callidulus.full: callĭdŭlus, a, um, adj. dim. [callidus], a little cunning or sly: fraus, Arn. 2, p. 91.

callidus.full: callĭdus, a, um, adj. calleo, that is taught wisdom by experience and practice, shrewd, expert, experienced, adroit, skilful: versutos eos appello, quorum celeriter mens versatur: callidos autem, quorum, tamquam manus opere, sic animus usu concalluit, Cic. N. D. 3, 10, 25. Ingenious, prudent, dexterous, skilful. In gen. (class.): ad suum quaestum, callidus, Plaut. As. 1, 3, 34; id. Truc. 2, 4, 62 (cf. id. ib. 2, 5, 40: omnes homines ad suum quaestum callent); id. Ps. 2, 4, 35; id. Ep. 3, 3, 47;

callifae.full: Callĭfae, ārum, f., a town in the region of the Hirpini, now Calvise, Liv. 8, 25, 4.
callifae.short: Callĭfae, ārum, f., a town in the region of the Hirpini, now Calvise, Liv.

calligonon.full: callĭgŏnon, i, n., = καλλίγονον, a plant, also called polygonon mas, Plin. 27, 12, 91, § 113 (v. Sillig N. cr.).
calligonon.short: callĭgŏnon, i, n., = καλλίγονον, a plant, also called polygonon mas, Plin.

callimachus.full: Callĭmăchus, i, m., = Καλλίμαχος. A distinguished Greek poet and grammarian of Cyrene (hence Battiades; v. Battus, I. b.) who lived in Alexandria in the reign of Ptolemy Philadelphus, B. C. 250, Quint. 10, 1, 58; Cic. Tusc. 1, 34, 84; 1, 39, 93; id. de Or. 3, 33, 32; Ov. R. Am. 759; Hor. Ep. 2, 2, 100; Prop. 2, 1, 40; Ov. P. 4, 16, 32.—Hence, Callĭmăchīus, a, um, adj.: metrum, i. e. a choriambic tetrameter and an amphibrach, Serv. Centim. p. 1823 P.— A celebrated sculptor, Plin. 34, 8, 19, § 92.

callimus.full: callĭmus, i, m., = κάλλιμος (beautiful), a kind of eagle-stone, Plin. 36, 21, 39, § 151.
callimus.short: callĭmus, i, m., = κάλλιμος (beautiful), a kind of eagle-stone, Plin.

callinicus.full: Callĭnīcŭs, i, m., = Καλλίνεικος, the name of a man, Plaut. Trin. 4, 2, 72.
callinicus.short: Callĭnīcŭs, i, m., = Καλλίνεικος, the name of a man, Plaut.

callion.full: callĭon, ii, n., = κάλλιον, a plant, called in pure Lat. vesicaria, Plin. 21, 31, 105, § 177.
callion.short: callĭon, ii, n., = κάλλιον, a plant, called in pure Lat.

callionymus.full: callĭōnўmus, i, m., = καλλιώνυμος, a sea-fish, also called uranoscopus, Plin. 32, 7, 24, § 69.
callionymus.short: callĭōnўmus, i, m., = καλλιώνυμος, a sea-fish, also called uranoscopus, Plin.

calliope.full: Callĭŏpē, ēs (Callĭŏpēa, ae, Verg. E. 4, 57; Prop. 1, 2, 28; Ov. F. 5, 80; cf. Prisc. p. 563 P.), f., = Καλλιόπη and Καλλιόπεια (fine-voiced), the chief of the Muses, goddess of Epic poetry, and, in the poets, sometimes of every other kind of poetry (e.g. the lyric, Hor. C. 3, 4, 1 sqq.; of amatory poetry, Ov. Tr. 2, 568; of rural poetry, Col. 10, 225; cf. Jahn, Trist. p. 198); the mother of Orpheus by Œagrus, Hyg. Fab. 14; acc. to Serv. ad Verg. A. 5, 864, the mother of the Sirens by Acheloüs;

callipetalon.full: callĭpĕtălon, i, n., = καλλιπέταλον, a plant, called in pure Lat. quinquefolium, App. Herb. 2.
callipetalon.short: callĭpĕtălon, i, n., = καλλιπέταλον, a plant, called in pure Lat.

callipho.full: Callĭpho, ōnis (abl. -ōne, Plaut. Ps. 1, 4, 18), m., a character in the Pseudolus of Plautus, Plaut. Ps. 1, 5, 43 et saep.

calliphon.full: Callĭphōn (-pho in all pass. of Cic. acc. to Madv. ad Cic. Fin. 2, 6, 19), ontis (dat. -ōni, Cic. Fin. 5, 8, 21; acc. -ōnem, id. Off. 3, 33, 119), m., = Καλλιφῶν, ῶντος, a Greek philosopher who considered virtue, joined with pleasure, as the highest good, Cic. Tusc. 5, 30, 85; id. Ac. 2, 42, 131; id. Fin. 2, 6, 19; 2, 11, 34; 4, 18, 50; 5, 8, 21; 5, 25, 73; Lact. 3, 7, 7; id. Epit. 33, 7.

callipides.full: Callīpĭdes (Callipp-), ae, m., = Καλλιππιδης, a Grecian runner who made no progress: quem cursitare ac ne cubiti quidem mensuram progredi proverbio Graeco notatum est, Suet. Tib. 38; cf. Cic. Att. 13, 12, 3.
callipides.short: Callīpĭdes (Callipp-), ae, m., = Καλλιππιδης, a Grecian runner who made no progress: quem cursitare ac ne cubiti quidem mensuram progredi proverbio Graeco notatum est, Suet.

callipolis.full: Callĭpŏlis, is (acc. -im or -in), f., = Καλλίπολις. A Grecian city of Calabria, now Gallipoli, Mel. 2, 4, 7.— A town on the Thracian Chersonesus, opposite Lampsacus, now Gallipoli, Liv. 31, 16, 6.— A town on the Tauric Chersonese, Liv. 36, 30, 4.

callippus.full: Callippŭs, i, m., = Κάλλιππος, the name of a man, Plaut. Trin. 4, 2, 71.
callippus.short: Callippŭs, i, m., = Κάλλιππος, the name of a man, Plaut.

callirrhoe.full: Callirrhŏē (in poets, Callĭrhŏē), ēs, f., = Καλλιρρόη (epic, Καλλιρόη). Daughter of the Acheloüs, and second wife of Alcmœon, Ov. M. 9, 414 sq.— The wife of Piranthus, and mother of Argus, Aristorides, and Triopas, Hyg. Fab. 145.— A daughter of Oceanus, wife of Chrysaor, and mother of Geryon, Hyg. praef. and Fab. 151. — A celebrated fountain at Athens, south-east of the Acropolis, Stat. Th. 12, 629, with the appell. Enneacrunos (̓Εννεάκρουνος, i. e. conducted by nine channels or pipes into the c
callirrhoe.short: Callirrhŏē (in poets, Callĭrhŏē), ēs, f., = Καλλιρρόη (epic, Καλλιρόη).

callis.full: callis, is, m. (fem., Varr. R. R. 2, 2, 10; Liv. 22, 14, 8; 31, 42, 8; 36, 15, 9; Curt. 3, 10, 10; 4, 16, 11; Amm. 30, 1, 15; 31, 10, 9; cf. Neue, Formenl. 1, p. 673) [etym. dub.; acc. to Serv. ad Verg. A. 4, 405, and Isid. Orig. 15, 16, 10, from callum; cf. Doed. Syn. IV. p. 68], a stony, uneven, narrow footway, a foot-path, a mountain-path, etc.; most freq., a path made by the treading of cattle: callis est iter pecudum inter montes angustum et tritum, a callo pecudum perduratum, Isid. Orig. l

callisco.full: callisco, ĕre, v. inch. [calleo], to become dull, insensible: aures nobis calliscerunt ad injurias, Cato ap. Non. p. 89, 27 sq. (Meyer, calliscunt, Or. Rom. Fragm. p. 118).

callisthenes.full: Callisthĕnes, is, m., = Καλλισθένης, a philosopher of Olynthus, sister's son and pupil of Aristotle, and a youthful friend of Alexander the Great; finally put to death by him for his freedom of speech, Curt. 8, 5, 13 sqq.; 8, 6, 25; 8, 8, 21; Cic. Rab. Post. 9, 23. Theophrastus bewailed his death in the work entitled Καλλισθένης ἢ περὶ πένθους, Cic. Tusc. 3, 10, 21; 5, 9, 25; cf. Sen. Q. N. 6, 23, 1 sqq.; Cic. Q. Fr. 2, 13, 4.
callisthenes.short: Callisthĕnes, is, m., = Καλλισθένης, a philosopher of Olynthus, sister's son and pupil of Aristotle, and a youthful friend of Alexander the Great;

callisto.full: Callisto, ūs (ōnis, Serv. ad. Verg. G. 1, 67), f., = Καλλιστώ, daughter of the Arcadian king Lycaon (hence, Lycaonis, Ov. F. 2, 173: virgo Tegeaea, id. ib. 2, 167: Maenalia, id. ib. 2, 192: virgo Nonacrina, id. M. 2, 409), and mother of Arcas by Jupiter; changed by Juno, on account of jealousy, into a she-bear, and then raised to the heavens by Jupiter in the form of the constellation Helice or Ursa Major, Hyg. Fab. 176; 177; Prop. 2 (3), 28, 23; Col. 11, 2, 15; Ov. F. 2, 156 sq.; cf. id. M. 2,

callistratus.full: Callistrătus, i, m., = Καλλίστρατος. A Grecian orator, Nep. Epam. 6, 1.— A Grecian statuary, Plin. 34, 8, 19, § 52.— A Grecian writer on natural history, Plin. 37, 3, 12, § 51; 37, 7, 25, § 94.

callistruthia.full: callistrūthĭa, ae (callistrūthis, ĭdis, Col. 10, 416), f. (sc. ficus), = καλλιστρούθια, a very delicate kind of figs, which sparrows were fond of [Gr. στρουθός], Col. 5, 10, 11; Plin. 15, 18, 19, § 69; pure Lat. ficus passerariae, Capitol. Albin. 11, § 2.

callithrix.full: callithrix, trĭchos, f., = καλλίθριξ (fair-haired). A plant used for coloring the hair, also called trichomanes, Plin. 26, 15, 90, § 160; 26, 14, 87, § 147; 25, 11, 86, § 135.— Plur.: callitrĭches, um, a kind of ape or monkey in Ethiopia; acc. to Lichtenstein, Simia faunus, Linn.; Plin. 8, 54, 80, § 216.

callitrichos.full: callĭtrĭchŏs, i. f., = καλλίτριχος (fair-haired), a plant, commonly called adiantum or Capillus Veneris, maidenhair, Plin. 22, 21, 30, § 62.

callon.full: Callon, ōnis, m., = Κάλλων. A statuary of Ægina, Quint. 12, 10, 7.—Plur.: Callones, i. e. people like Callon, Quint. 12, 10, 10.— A statuary of Elis, who flourished about 430 B. C., Plin. 34, 8, 19, § 49.

callositas.full: callōsĭtas, ātis, f. callosus, hardness of skin, callousness (post-class.), Scrib. Comp. 36: fistulae, Veg. 3, 27, 3.—Trop., hardness, a hardening: usus communis, Tert. Testim. Anim. 8: voluntarii erroris, id. adv. Nat. 2, 1.

callosus.full: callōsus, a, um, adj. callum, with a hard skin, hard-skinned, thick-skinned, callous (not before the Aug. per.): ulcus, Cels. 6, 3: ulcera, Plin. 26, 14, 87, § 143: venter, id. 11, 37, 79, § 203: crassior callosiorque cutis, Plin. 11, 39, 92, § 226.— In gen., solid, hard, thick: ova, * Hor. S. 2, 4, 14: acini uvae, Col. 3, 1, 5: olivae, Plin. 15, 3, 4, § 13: tactus, Pall. Sept. 17: orae (ulceris), Cels. 5, 28.

callum.full: callum, i, n. (callus, i, m., Cels. 5, 18, 36; 5, 26, 31 al.; Domit. Mars. ap. Charis. p. 55; plur. calli, Scrib. Comp. 37; 205; Suet. Aug. 80) [cf. Gr. καλάμη; Lat. culmus, culmen]. The hardened, thick skin upon animal bodies: fere res omnes aut corio sunt Aut etiam conchis aut callo aut cortice tectae, Lucr. 4, 935: calceamentum solorum callum, Cic. Tusc. 5, 32, 90: pedum, Plin. 22, 25, 60, § 127; cf. id. 9, 35, 54, § 108.—Plur., Suet. Aug. 80.—Hence, Meton. The hard flesh of certain animals:

calo1.full: călo (as a very ancient word, with its derivatives also written kălo; v. the letter K), āre, v. a. cf. Gr. καλῶ; Engl. call, to call, call out, proclaim, call together, summon, convoke; only as t. t. in reference to religious matters; v. Kalendae, and the ancient formulary in Varr. L. L. 6, § 27 Müll.; cf. Macr. S. 1, 15: calata comitia, a kind of comitia held for the purpose of consecrating a priest or a king. Of these, some were curiata, others centuriata, Laelius Felix ap. Gell. 15, 27 sq.: C
calo1.short: călo (as a very ancient word, with its derivatives also written kălo;

calo2.full: cālo, ōnis, m. κᾶλον, timber for burning or joiner's work; καίω, to burn, a servant in the army, a soldier's servant: calones militum servi dicti, qui ligneas clavas gerebant, quae Graece κᾶλα vocant, Paul. ex Fest. pp. 46 and 62 Müll.; Serv. ad Verg. A. 6, 1; cf. Non. p. 62, 16; Veg. Mil. 3, 6; Dict. of Antiq.; so Caes. B. G. 6, 36; Liv. 27, 18, 12; 30, 4, 1; Tac. H. 1, 49; 3, 20 fin.; 3, 33; Suet. Calig. 51; id. Galb. 20.—On account of their stupidity: sambucam citius caloni aptaveris alto, Pe

calocissus.full: Călŏcissus, i, m. καλός, κισσός, = beautiful ivy, the name of a cup-bearer, Mart. 9, 93, 3 Schneid.

calor1.full: călor, ōris, m. caleo; cf. Varr. ap. Non. p. 46, 22, warmth, heat, glow. Lit. In gen. (very freq. in prose and poet.): neque mihi ulla obsistet amnis nec calor; nec frigus metuo, Plaut. Merc. 5, 2, 19; so (opp. frigus) Lucr. 2, 517; 6, 371; Cic. N. D. 2, 39, 101; Verg. G. 2, 344; 4, 36; (opp. refrigeratio) Vitr. 1, 4: calor ignis, Lucr. 1, 425: solis, id. 5, 571; 6, 514: fulminis, id. 6, 234.—In plur., Cic. Off. 2, 4, 13; id. N. D. 2, 60, 151; Hor. C. 3, 24, 37 al.— Esp. Vital heat; so, vitalis,

calor2.full: Călŏr, ōris, m., a river in Samnium, now the Calore, Liv. 2, 14, 2; 25, 17, 1.
calor2.short: Călŏr, ōris, m., a river in Samnium, now the Calore, Liv.

caloratus.full: călōrātus, a, um, adj. calor (postclass. and rare). Lit., hot, heated: ferrum, Isid. 20, 16, 7 (al. coloratum): Calabria, Porphyr. ad Hor. Epod. 1, 27: dies caloratissimi, id. ad Hor. S. 1, 6, 126.— Trop., hot, incited, furious: juventutis impetus, App. M. 6, p. 182, 37: juventus, Fulg. Myth. 3, 4 fin.

calorificus.full: călōrĭfĭcus, a, um, adj. calor-facio, causing warmth, warming, heating: oleum calorificum est, Gell. 17, 8, 12.

calpar.full: calpar, aris, n. κάλπη?͂ κάλπις, a vessel for liquids, esp. for wine, a winecask, wine-pitcher, Non. p. 546, 32 sq.: calpar genus vasis fictilis, Paul. ex Fest. p. 46 Müll.— Calpar = vinum novum, quod ex dolio demitur sacrificii causā, antequam gustetur, Paul. ex Fest. p. 65 Müll.

calpe.full: Calpē, ēs, f., = Κάλπη, one of the pillars of Hercules in Hispania Baetica, now Rock of Gibraltar, Mel. 1, 5, 3; 2, 6, 8; Plin. 3, prooem. § 4; 3, 1, 3, § 7; Asin. ap. Cic. Fam. 10, 32, 1: Ibera, Sen. Herc. Oet. 1254; Luc. 1, 555; 4, 71 (abl. scanned Calpĕ, Juv. 14, 279).— Derivv. Calpētā-nus, a, um, adj., of Calpe: gurges, Avien. Progn. 1620.— Calpētĭtānus, a, um, adj., of Calpe: vada, Avien. Arat. 1023.
calpe.short: Calpē, ēs, f., = Κάλπη, one of the pillars of Hercules in Hispania Baetica, now Rock of Gibraltar, Mel.

calpurnius.full: Calpurnĭus, a, um, adj. a Calpo Numae regis filio, Fest. p. 36, the name of the very distinguished Calpurnian gens: familia, Cic. Pis. 23, 53.— Esp., as subst. Masc. C. Calpurnius Piso, prœtor B.C. 186, Liv. 39, 6, 1; 39, 30, 1 sqq.; and consul B.C. 180, id. 40, 35, 1; 40, 37, 1.— L. Calpurnius Piso, consul B.C. 112, and afterwards, B.C. 107, lieutenant of Cassius, Caes. B. G. 1, 6; 1, 12; 1, 14.— L. Calpurnius Bestia, tribune of the people B.C. 121, consul B.C. 111, and a general against Jugurt

caltha.full: caltha, ae, f. (calthum, i, n., Prud. Cath. 5, 114) [cf. Gr. χάλκανθος], a strongsmelling yellow flower, prob. our pot marigold: Calendula officinalis, Linn.; Plin. 21, 6, 15, § 28; Verg. E. 2, 50; Col. 10, 97; 10, 310.

calthula.full: calthŭla, ae, f. caltha, from its color; cf. Non. p. 548, 21, a yellow garment for women, a yellow robe, Plaut. Ep. 2, 2, 47.

calumma.full: călummă (călymm-), ătis, n., = κάλυμμα, a covering, Mart. Cap. 1, § 67.
calumma.short: călummă (călymm-), ătis, n., = κάλυμμα, a covering, Mart.

calumnia.full: călumnĭa (old form kălumnĭa; v. the letter K), ae, f. perh. for calvomnia, from calvor; cf. incīlo, trickery, artifice, chicanery, cunning device. Lit. In gen.: per obtrectatores Lentuli calumniā extracta res est, Cic. Q. Fr. 2, 2, 3: (Lucullus) inimicorum calumniā triennio tardius quam debuerat triumphavit, id. Ac. 2, 1, 3: inpediti ne triumpharent calumniā paucorum, quibus omnia honesta atque inhonesta vendere mos erat, Sall. C. 30, 4: Metellus calumniā dicendi tempus exemit, Cic. Att. 4, 3, 3

calumniator.full: călumnĭātor (kălumnĭātor; v. the foreg.), ōris, m. calumnior; mostly t. t., a contriver of tricks or artifices, a pettifogger, a perverter of law, a chicaner (sometimes, perhaps, branded on the forehead with the letter K = calumniator; cf. Voss, Arist. 1, 17; Ernest. Clav. Cic. Ind. Leg. s. v. Remmia): si calvitur et moretur et frustratur. Inde et calumniatores appellati sunt, quia per fraudem et frustrationem alios vexarent litibus, Dig. 50, 16, 223: scriptum sequi calumniatoris esse: boni judi

calumniatrix.full: călumnĭātrix, īcis, f. calumniator, she who plots against or makes false accusations, Hier. Ep. 74, 4; Dig. 37, 9, 1, §§ 14 and 16.

calumnior.full: călumnĭor (anciently kăl-; v. the letter K), ātus, 1, v. dep. act. [calumnia]. Jurid. t. t. To accuse falsely, bring false information against a person. Absol.: calumniari est falsa crimina intendere, Dig. 48, 16, 1, § 1; cf. ib. prooem.: ut hic quoque Apronio... ex miseris aratoribus calumniandi quaestus accederet, Cic. Verr. 2, 3, 15, § 38: cum aliquid habeat quod possit criminose ac suspitiose dicere, aperte ludificari et calumniari sciens non videatur, id. Rosc. Am. 20, 55: cum (defensor) ac

calumniosus.full: călumnĭōsus, a, um, adj. calumnia, full of tricks or artifices, swindling (postAug.): calumniosus est, qui sciens prudensque per fraudem negotium alicui comparat, Paul. Sent. 1, 5, 1; 1, 5, 2: accusatio, Dig. 38, 2, 14: criminationes, Arn. 1 init.— Sup., Aug. Ep. 152 fin.— Subst.: că-lumnĭōsus, i, m., a person convicted of false information, Dig. 48, 16, 3; cf. calumnia, I. B. 4.—Adv.: călumnĭōsē, artfully, by trickery, Dig. 46, 5, 7; Aug. Ep. 48. —Sup., Symm. Ep. 10, 76.

calvaria.full: calvārĭa, ae, f. calva, calvus. The skull of man, Cels. 8, 1; Vulg. 4 Reg. 9, 35: calvariae locus, id. Matt. 27, 33; of beasts: canis, Plin. 30, 6, 18, § 53: equae, asinae, Pall. 1, 35, 16.— In eccl. Lat., Calvary, the place where Jesus Christ was crucified, Tert. adv. Marc. 3, 198.

calvariola.full: calvārĭŏla, ae, f. dim. calvaria, a small cup, Schol. ad Juv. 5, 48.

calvarium.full: calvārĭum, ii, n. id., a kind of round sea-fish without scales, Enn. ap. App. Mag. p. 299, 17.

calvatus.full: calvātus, a. um, adj. calvus, made bald, bare (late Lat.): Sampson, Ambros. Ep. 9, 71.— Transf.: si vinea a vite calvata erit, Cat. ap. Plin. 17, 22, 35, § 196 Jan. (but Cato, R. R. 33, 3, calva erit; v. calvus).

calvena.full: Calvēna, ae, m. calvus, a nickname of the bald-headed Matius, a friend of Cœsar, Cic. Att. 14, 5, 1; 14, 9, 3; 16, 11, 1 (so id. ib. 14, 2, 2, the name Madarus = μαδαρός, bald).

calveo.full: calvĕo, ēre, v. n. id., to be bald, Plin. 11, 37, 47, § 130.

calvesco.full: calvesco, ĕre, v. inch. n. [calveo], to become bald (post-Aug.), Col. 6, 14, 7; Veg. 3, 4, 27; Plin. 10, 29, 41, § 78.— Transf. to plants, to grow up thin or far apart, Col. 4, 33, 3.

calvina.full: Calvīna, ae, f., the name of a notorious woman of rank, Juv. 3, 133.
calvina.short: Calvīna, ae, f., the name of a notorious woman of rank, Juv.

calvinus.full: Calvīnus, i, m., a Roman cognomen; esp., Cn. Domitius Calvinus, consul, A.U.C. 701, Cic. Q. Fr. 2, 11 (13), 2; 2, 3, 6; id. Att. 4, 17, 3; id. Fam. 16, 12, 3 al.— C. Sextius Calvinus, an eminent advocate, Cic. Brut. 34, 130; id. de Or. 2, 60, 246.
calvinus.short: Calvīnus, i, m., a Roman cognomen;

calvisius.full: Calvĭsĭus, ii, m., the name of several Romans; esp., C. Calvisius Sabinus, lieutenant of Cæsar, and afterwards prœtor in Africa, Caes. B. C. 3, 34 sq.; Cic. Phil. 3, 10, 26; cf. id. Fam. 12, 25, 1.— Calvisius Sabinus, a very rich man, Sen. Ep. 27, 4; Tac. A. 13, 21; perh. the same with Calvisius, the accuser of Agrippina, Nero's mother, Tac. A. 13, 19 sqq.—Deriv.: Calvĭsĭ-ānus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to a Calvisius, Dig. 38, 5, 3; 38, 5, 5.
calvisius.short: Calvĭsĭus, ii, m., the name of several Romans;

calvities.full: calvĭtĭes, ēi, f. calvus, baldness (a rare form for calvitium): prae calvitie, * Suet. Galb. 20; Petr. 108, 1.

calvitium.full: calvĭtĭum, ii, n. id., baldness (class.; access. form calvĭtĭes). Lit.: in luctu capillum sibi evellere, quasi calvitio maeror levaretur, * Cic. Tusc. 3, 26, 62; Plin. 11, 37, 47, § 131; Suet. Caes. 45; id. Dom. 18; Aus. Epigr. 72, 2; Tert. adv. Nat. 1, 10 fin. — Of places destitute of herbage, bareness, sterility, Col. 4, 29, 11.

calvor.full: calvor, 3, v. dep. a. (access. form cal-vo, ĕre, v. infra; calvio, Are, Serv. ad Verg. A. 1, 720). To devise tricks, use artifice, attack one with artifice, to intrigue against, to deceive (except in Sallust, only ante-class. for the class. calumnior): SI. CALVITVR. PEDEMVE. STRVIT., Fragm. XII. Tab. ap. Fest. s. v. struere, p. 313 Müll.; the same law is fragmentarily mentioned by Lucil. ap. Non. p. 7, 2, and Dig. 50, 16, 233.— In gen., to deceive, delude: me calvitur suspitio, Pac. ap. Non. p.

calvus1.full: calvus, a, um, adj. cf. O. H. Germ. chalo; Germ. kahl, bald, without hair (whether by nature or by shaving or shearing; rare; not in Lucr., Cic., Hor., or Verg.): raso capite calvus, Plaut. Am. 1, 1, 306: senex, Petr. 27; Suet. Calig. 27: moechus, id. Caes. 51; Phaedr. 2, 2, 9; 5, 3, 1; 5, 6, 1.— Subst.: calva, ae, f., the scalp without hair, Liv. 23, 24, 12; Mart. 10, 83, 12; 12, 45, 12.— Venus Calva, worshipped in a particular temple after the irruption of the Gauls (as it is pretended, becaus

calvus2.full: Calvus, i, m., a cognomen of several persons, especially of the poet and orator C. Licinius; v. Licinius.
calvus2.short: Calvus, i, m., a cognomen of several persons, especially of the poet and orator C.

calx1.full: calx, calcis, f. (m., Pers. 3, 105 dub.; Sil. 7, 696; cf. App. M. 7, p. 483 Oud.; Pers. 3, 105; Grat. Cyn. 278. Whether Lucil. ap. Charis, p. 72 P. belongs here or to 2. calx is undecided) [Sanscr. kar-, wound, kill; akin with λάξ, calcar, calceus], the heel. Lit.: calces deteris, you tread on my heels, Plaut. Merc. 5, 2, 111: quod si ipsa animi vis In capite aut umeris aut imis calcibus esse Posset, Lucr. 3, 792; 5, 136: incursare pug nis, calcibus, πὺξ καὶ λάξ, Plaut. Poen. 4, 1, 3; Ter. Eun.

calx2.full: calx, calcis, f. (m., Varr. ap. Non. p. 199, 24, and Cato, R. R. 18, 7; Plaut. Poen. 4, 2, 86; dub. Cic. Tusc. 1, 8, 15; and id. Rep. Fragm. ap. Sen. Ep. 108 fin.; cf. Rudd. I. p. 37, n. 3; later collat. form calcis, is, f., Ven. Fort. Carm. 11, 11, 10) [χάλιξ]. Liv. A small stone used in gaming, a counter (less freq. than the dim. calculus, q. v.), Plaut. Poen. 4, 2, 86; Lucil. ap. Prisc. p. 687 P.; cf. Paul. ex Fest. p. 46 Müll.— Limestone, lime, whether slaked or not, Lucr. 6, 1067; Cic. Mil.

calycadnus.full: Călўcadnus, i, m., a river and promontory of Cilicia, Amm. 14, 2, 15; 14, 8, 1; Plin. 5, 27, 22, § 92; Liv. 38, 38, 9.
calycadnus.short: Călўcadnus, i, m., a river and promontory of Cilicia, Amm.

calyculus.full: călўcŭlus, i, m. dim. calyx, a small flower-bud, the cup or calyx of a flower, Plin. 20, 19, 78, § 205; 27, 5, 20, § 37; App. M. 4, p. 143, 16.— Transf., the outer skin, hide of animals: echinorum, App. Mag. 35, p. 297, 4.

calydon.full: Călўdon, ōnis, f., = Καλυδών, a very ancient town in Ætolia (now Kurt-aga), on the river Evenus, built by a hero of the same name, Ov. M. 8, 495; the residence of Œneus, father of Meleager and Deianira, and grandfather of Diomedes, Mel. 2, 3, 10; Plin. 4, 2, 3, § 6; Ov. M. 6, 415; 8, 270 sqq.; Verg. A. 11, 270; Caes. B. C. 3, 35; Mart. 9, 49; ace. Calydonem, Plaut. Poen. prol. 72; Gr. Calydona, Verg. A. 7, 306; Ov. M. 9, 147.— Derivv. Călўdōnĭus, a, um, adj., Calydonian: sus, the Calydonian boar
calydon.short: Călўdon, ōnis, f., = Καλυδών, a very ancient town in Ætolia (now Kurt-aga), on the river Evenus, built by a hero of the same name, Ov.

calymne.full: Călymnē, ēs, f., = Κάλυμνα, an island in the Ægean Sea, not far from Rhodes, distinguished for its honey, now Kalimno, Ov. M. 8, 222; id. A. A. 2, 81.—Called Că-lymnĭa, ae, f., Mel. 2, 7, 11.
calymne.short: Călymnē, ēs, f., = Κάλυμνα, an island in the Ægean Sea, not far from Rhodes, distinguished for its honey, now Kalimno, Ov.

calypso.full: Călypso, ūs (e. g. Tib. 4, 1, 77; Plin. 3, 10, 15, § 96; Serv. ad Verg. A. 3, 171: Calypsonis, App. M. 1, p. 107; Macr. S. 5, 2, 10; acc. regularly Calypso, Ov. P. 4, 10, 13; cf. Quint. 1, 5, 63; Plin. ap. Charis. p. 102 P.; Prisc. p. 685 ib.; Rudd. I. p. 60, n. 84; but Calypsonem, Liv. And. ap. Prisc. l. l., and Calypsonem, Pac. ib., and ap. Charis. p. 47 P.; Caes. ap. Quint. 1, 5, 63; Macr. S. 5, 2, 10), f., = Καλυψώ, a nymph, daughter of Atlas (or Oceanus), who ruled in the Island Ogygia, Pli

calyx1.full: călyx, ўcis, m., = κάλυξ [καλύπτω; hence, any covering, husk, hull, shell], the bud, cup, or calyx of a flower. Lit.: narcissi, Plin. 21, 5, 12, § 25. rosae, id. 21, 4, 10, § 14; 21, 18, 73, § 121: papaveris, id. 20, 18, 76, § 198: lilii, id. 21, 5, 11, § 23.— Transf. The shell of fruits, Plin. 15, 23, 25, § 92; 15, 22, 24, § 86; 23, 4, 43, § 86. — An egg-shell, Plin. 28, 2, 4, § 19.— The covering of shell-fish, etc., the shell, Plin. 9, 31, 51, § 100, 9, 56, 82, § 174; 32, 4, 14, § 39.— A cover

calyx2.full: călyx, ўcis, f., = κάλυξ, a plant of two kinds, perh. the monk's-hood, Plin. 27, 8, 36, § 58 sq.
calyx2.short: călyx, ўcis, f., = κάλυξ, a plant of two kinds, perh.

cama.full: cama, ae, f. χαμαί = humi, a small bed near the ground, Isid. Orig. 20, 11, 2.

camarina.full: Cămărīna (in MSS. also Cămĕrī-na; cf. camera), ae, f. (acc. Gr. Camarinan, Ov. F 4, 477), = Καμάρῖνα, a city on the south-west coast of Sicily, a colony from Syracuse, now Camarana, Plin. 3, 8, 14, § 89; Serv. ad Verg. A. 3, 701; Claud. Rapt. Pros. 2, 59.

camarus.full: camarus, i, for cammarus, q. v.

cambio.full: cambio, īre, v. n. (perf. campsi, acc. to Charis. pp. 219 and 233 P., and Prisc. p. 906 ib.) [whence the Ital. and mercantile cambio, cambiare, cambiatura, etc.; Fr. change, changer, etc.; Engl. change, etc.], to exchange, barter: muto, ἀμείβομαι, Charis. l.l. (post-class. and very rare), App. Mag. p. 284; Sicul. Flacc. Cond. Agr. p. 13 Goes.

cambitas.full: cambĭtas, ātis, f. id., exchange, barter: ὰντικαταλλαγή, Gloss. Gr. Lat.

cambunii.full: Cambūnii Montes, m., a mountain range on the boundary between Thessaly and Macedonia, Liv. 42, 53, 6; 44, 2, 6.
cambunii.short: Cambūnii Montes, m., a mountain range on the boundary between Thessaly and Macedonia, Liv.

cambyses.full: Cambȳses, is, m., = Καμβύσης. The husband of Mandane, and father of the elder Cyrus, Just. 1, 4, 4.— The son and successor of the elder Cyrus, Just. 1, 9; Mel. 1, 11, 3; Val. Max. 6, 3, ext. 3; Luc. 10, 280. A river in Albania, which rises on the Caucasus and empties into the Cyrus, now Jora, Mel. 3, 5, 6; Plin. 6, 13, 15, § 39.— A river of Media, Amm. 23, 6, 40.

camela.full: cămēla, ae, f. camelus, a female camel, Treb. Claud. 14, 3.

camelae.full: cămēlae, ārum, f. γαμήλιος, pertaining to γάμος = a marriage, of or pertaining to a marriage festival: virgines, Paul. ex Fest. p. 63 Müll.

camelarius.full: cămēlārĭus, ii, m. camelus, a cameldriver, Dig. 50, 4, 18, § 11; Edict. Diocl. p. 19.

camelelasia.full: cămēlēlăsĭa, ae, f., = καμηληλασία, camel-driving, the care of the camels belonging to the State, Dig. 50, 4, 18, § 11.
camelelasia.short: cămēlēlăsĭa, ae, f., = καμηληλασία, camel-driving, the care of the camels belonging to the State, Dig.

camelinus.full: cămēlīnus, a, um, adj. camelus, of or relating to a camel, camel's-: lac, Plin. 28, 9, 33, § 123: genitale, id. 11, 49, 109, § 161: ossa, Arn. 6, p. 200.

camella.full: cămella, ae, f dim. [camera], a kind of drinking vessel, a wine-goblet, wine-cup, cup, Laber. ap. Gell. 16, 7, 9; Ov. F. 4, 779; Petr. 135, 3; 137, 10; 64, 13; cf. Pollux, id. 10, 24.

camelopardalis.full: cămēlŏpardălis, is, f. (cămēlŏ-pardălus, i, m., Capitol. Gord. III. 33; Vop. Aur 33; Vulg. Deut. 14, 5: cămēlŏ-pardus, Isid. Orig. 12, 2, 19), = καμηλοπάρδαλις, a camelopard, giraffe: Cervus camelopardalis, Linn.; Varr. L. L. 5, § 100 Müll.; cf. Plin. 8, 18, 27, § 69; Sol. 30, 19.

camelopodion.full: cămēlŏpŏdĭon, ii, n., = καμηλοπόδιον, a plant, camel's-foot, perh. horehound, App. Herb. 45.
camelopodion.short: cămēlŏpŏdĭon, ii, n., = καμηλοπόδιον, a plant, camel's-foot, perh.

camelus.full: cămēlus, i, m. (fem., Plin. 8, 18, 26, § 67; 11, 37, 62, § 164; App. M. 7, p. 194, 5; Vulg. Gen. 32, 15; Paul. Nol. Ep. 29, 2), = κάμηλος, a camel, with either one or two humps, Plin. 11, 37, 62, § 164; Varr. L. L. 5, § 100 Müll., Cic. N. D. 2, 47, 122; Liv. 37, 40, 12; Hor. Ep. 2, 1, 195; Tac. A. 15, 12; cf. camela.

camena.full: Cămēna (not Cămoena), ae, f. (old form Casmēna, acc. to Varr. L. L. 7, § 27 Müll.; Paul. ex Fest. s. v. dusmoso, p. 67 ib., and pesnis, p. 205 ib.) [root kas-, sing, whence carmen], pure Lat. (perh. Ital.) name of the Gr. Μοῦσα, a Muse (freq. in Hor., not in Lucr.), Liv. And. ap. Gell. 18, 9, 5: acceptus novem Camenis, Hor. C. S. 62: amant alterna Camenae, Verg. E. 3, 59 (cf. id. ib. 7, 19); Hor. C. 3, 4, 21; id. S. 1, 10, 45, id. Ep. 1, 19, 5, id. A. P 275; Prop. 3 (4), 10, 1; Ov M. 14, 434; 15

camera.full: cămĕra (in MSS. and editt. also că-măra; cf. Charis. p 43 P.), ae, f., = καμάρα [cf. κάμπτω = to bend, curve; Ital. camera; Germ. Kammer; Fr. chambre; Engl. chamber], a vault, an arched roof, an arch, Varr. R. R. 3, 7, 3; 3, 8, 1; Lucr. Fragm. ap. Charis. l. l.; Cic. Q. Fr. 3, 1, 1, § 1; Sall. C. 55, 4; Prop. 3 (4), 2, 10; Varr. R. R. 1, 59, 2; 3, 7, 3; Col. 4, 17, 8; 11, 3, 60: camera vitrea, covered with glass, Plin. 36, 25, 64, § 189.—In ships, Suet. Ner. 34; cf. upon the manner of building t

camerarius.full: cămĕrārĭus (cămă-), a, um, adj. camera: cucurbitae, which climb over something, climbing (opp. plebeiae, that creep upon the ground), Plin. 19, 5, 24, § 70.

cameratio.full: cămĕrātĭo, ōnis, f. camero, prop. an arching; hence, abstr. pro concr., a vault, arch, Spart. Carac. 9, 5.

cameria.full: Cămĕrĭa, ae, f., = Καμερία, a town in Latium, Liv. 1, 38, 4 (in Plin. 3, 5, 9, § 68, and Tac. A. 11, 24, Cămĕrĭum).— Deriv.: Cămĕrīnus, a, um, adj., of Camerinus: municipium, Sid. Ep. 2, 9.— As subst. Cămĕrīni, ōrum, m., the inhabitants of Cameria, Val. Max. 6, 5, n. 1. — Cămĕrīnus, i, m., a cognomen in the very distinguished gens Sulpicia, Liv. 3, 31, 8; 5, 14, 5; 29, 2 al.—Hence, for people of rank in gen., Juv. 7, 90; 8, 38.
cameria.short: Cămĕrĭa, ae, f., = Καμερία, a town in Latium, Liv.

camerinum.full: Cămĕrīnum, i, n., a town in Umbria, on the borders of Picenum, now Camerino, Cic. Att. 8, 12, B, 2; Caes. B. C. 1, 15.— Derivv. Cămers, ertis, adj., of Camerinum: ager, Cic. Sull. 19, 53.—Subst.: Cămertes, ium (Camertum, Sil. 4, 157), m., the inhabitants of Camerinum, Plin. 3, 14, 19, § 113; friends of the Romans, both in opp. to the Etruscans, and later against Hannibal, Cic. Balb. 20, 47; Liv. 9, 36, 7 and 8; 28, 45, 20.—In sing.: fulvum Camertem, Verg. A. 10, 562: laudande Camers, Sil. 8, 463
camerinum.short: Cămĕrīnum, i, n., a town in Umbria, on the borders of Picenum, now Camerino, Cic.

camero.full: cămĕro (cămă-), āre, v. a. camera, to vault or arch over, Plin. 10, 30, 50, § 97. —Trop.: cameratum elogium, constructed with art, Cassiod. Hist. Eccl. 1, 1.

cameses.full: Cămĕses, is, m., a mythic king in Italy, contemporary with Janus, Hyg. ap. Macr. S. 1, 7, 19.
cameses.short: Cămĕses, is, m., a mythic king in Italy, contemporary with Janus, Hyg.

camilla1.full: camilla or casmilla, ae, f., v. 1. camillus, II.
camilla1.short: camilla or casmilla, ae, f., v.

camilla2.full: Camilla, ae, f., a Volscian heroine, who perished in the war between Æneas and Turnus, Verg. A. 7, 803; 11, 535.
camilla2.short: Camilla, ae, f., a Volscian heroine, who perished in the war between Æneas and Turnus, Verg.

camillum2.full: camillum, i, n., in architecture = loculamentum, Vitr. 10, 15 dub. (Rode supposes scamillum, a little bench; Bald. Lex. Vitr. batillum).
camillum2.short: camillum, i, n., in architecture = loculamentum, Vitr.

camillus1.full: cămillus (also casmilus; cf. Camena and Varr. L. L. 7, § 34 Müll.), i, m. with difficulty connected with the Samothracian Kabiren-Hermes, Κάδμιλος and Κάδμος; cf. Varr. L. L. 7, 3, § 34 Müll., and Macr. S. 3, 8; perh. dim. from root of Camena; cf. carmen, a noble youth employed in the sacrifices of the Flamen Dialis, and then, gen., in religious offices, Paul. ex Fest. p. 43 Müll.: hiberno pulvere, verno luto, grandia farra Camille metes, Poët. ib. p. 93. —The same verse is given with the expl.,

camillus2.full: Cămillus, i, m., a cognomen of several persons in the gens Furia; the most distinguished of whom was M. Furius Camillus, who conquered Veii, and freed Rome from the Gauls, Liv. 5, 19, 2 sq.; Cic. Rep. 1, 3, 6.
camillus2.short: Cămillus, i, m., a cognomen of several persons in the gens Furia;

camino.full: cămīno, no perf., ātum, 1, v. a. caminus, to make like an oven or furnace (very rare; perh. only in the foll. pass.), Plin. 16, 6, 8, § 23: caminata fossura, id. 17, 11, 16, § 80.

caminus.full: cămīnus, i, m., = ἡ κάμινος [Germ. Kamin; Fr. chemine/e; Engl. chimney], a furnace. A smelting-furnace for the working of metals, a forge, Ov. M. 7, 106; Pers. 5, 10; Plin. 33, 4, 21, § 69; 35, 6, 16, § 35: crescunt (patrimonia) incude assiduā semperque ardente camino, i. e., by incessant labor, Juv. 14, 118.— Poet., the forge or smithy of Vulcan and the Cyclopes, under Ætna, Verg. A. 3, 580; 6, 630; 8, 418; Ov. F. 4, 473; Plin. 2, 106, 110, § 237.— A furnace for heating an apartment, Hor. Ep. 1

camirus.full: Cămīrus or -ŏs, i, m., = Καμειρος. Son of the fourth Hercules, brother of Jalysus and Lindus, and founder of the town named after him in Rhodes, Cic. N. D. 3, 21, 54; Mel. 2, 7, 4; Plin. 5, 31, 36, § 132. — A town on the west side of the island of Rhodes, Mel. 2, 7, 4; cf. Cic. N. D. 3, 21, 54.—Hence, Camīrenses, ium, m., the inhabitants of Camirus, Macr. S. 1, 17, 35; 1, 17, 45.

camisia.full: camĭsĭa, ae, f. Gallic; whence Ital. camicia, Fr. chemise, a linen shirt or night-gown: camisias vocari, quod in his dormimus in camis id est stratis nostris, Isid. Orig. 19, 22, 29; cf. id. ib. 19, 21, 1; Hier. Ep. Vest. Mul. 64, n. 11; Paul. ex Fest. s. v. supparus, p. 310 Müll.

cammaron.full: cammăron, i, n., = κάμμαρον, a plant, also called aconitum, Plin. 27, 3, 2, § 9.
cammaron.short: cammăron, i, n., = κάμμαρον, a plant, also called aconitum, Plin.

cammarus.full: cammărus (camărus, gammă-rus), i, m., = κάμμαρος, a sea-crab, lobster (so called from its vaulted back), Varr. R. R. 3, 11, 3; Col. 8, 15, 6; 8, 17, 4; Plin. 27, 3, 2, § 9; 31, 8, 44, § 96; Mart. 2, 43; Juv. 5, 84 al.
cammarus.short: cammărus (camărus, gammă-rus), i, m., = κάμμαρος, a sea-crab, lobster (so called from its vaulted back), Varr.

campagus.full: campăgus, i, m., a kind of boot worn by military officers (late Lat.), Treb Gall. 16; Capitol. Max. jun. c. 2; Edict. Diocl. p. 24.
campagus.short: campăgus, i, m., a kind of boot worn by military officers (late Lat.), Treb Gall.

campana1.full: campana, ae, f. Ital. campana, a bell; campanile, a belfry, a bell (late Lat.), Dig. 41, 1, 12.

campana2.full: Campāna, ae, f., v. Campania, II. A. 1.

campaneus.full: campānĕus or campānĭus, a, um, adj. campus; in the land surveyors = campestris, of or pertaining to the fields: loca, Innocent. ap. Goes. pp. 239 and 240.
campaneus.short: campānĕus or campānĭus, a, um, adj.

campania.full: Campānĭa, ae, f., = Καμπανία [campus, i. e. the plain, the level country], the very fruitful and luxurious (Cic. Agr. 2, 35, 95) province of Campania, in Middle Italy, whose chief city was Capua, now Terra di Lavoro, Mel. 2, 4, 2 and 9; Liv. 2, 52, 1; Tib. 1, 9, 33; Plin. 3, 5, 9, § 60; Flor. 1, 16, 3.— Derivv. Campānus, a, um, adj., Campanian, of Campania: ager, Cic. Agr. 1, 7, 20; 2, 32, 87; Brut. ap. Cic. Fam. 11, 20, 3: rus, Mart. 9, 61, 4: colonia, Cic. Agr. 2, 32, 85: matres, Liv. 26, 13,

campe.full: campē (Col. poët. 10, 324; 10, 366), ēs (the Lat. form of the nom. campa is not used), f., = κάμπη. * A turning, writhing: campas dicere, to seek evasions, Plaut. Truc. 5, 50.— A caterpillar, pure Lat. eruca, Col. l. l. (cf. id. 11, 3, 63, κάμπαι); Pall. 1, 35, 6 and 13.

campensis.full: Campensis campus, a surname of Isis, who had a temple on the Campus Martius, App. M. 11, p. 270, 27.
campensis.short: Campensis campus, a surname of Isis, who had a temple on the Campus Martius, App.

campester.full: campester (campestris, Cato ap. Prisc. p. 696 P.; Col. 3, 13, 8; 7, 2, 3; 3, 14, 1, is suspicious; v. Schneid. ad h. l.), tris, tre, adj. id.. Of or pertaining to a level field, even, flat, level, champaign, opp. montanus and collinus; cf. Liv. 10, 2, 5; 40, 38, 2; 40, 53, 3 al.: tria genera simplicia agrorum campestre, collinum et montanum, Varr. R. R. 1, 6, 2: campester locus, id. ib. § 6; cf.: vineae collinae et campestres, Col. 12, 21, 1: resina, Plin. 24, 6, 22, § 34: acer, id. 16, 15, 26,

campestratus.full: campestrātus, i, m., clothed with the campestre or apron, Aug. Civ. Dei, 14, 17; v. campester, II. A. 2. a.
campestratus.short: campestrātus, i, m., clothed with the campestre or apron, Aug.

campicursio.full: campĭ-cursĭo (better as two words), ōnis, f. campus, military exercise in the Campus Martius, Veg. Mil. 3, 4 (in Suet. Ner. 7, and id. Galb. 6, called decursio).
campicursio.short: campĭ-cursĭo (better as two words), ōnis, f.

campidoctor.full: campĭ-doctor (better as two words), ōris, m. id., one who drills or exercises soldiers in the Campus Martius, a drill-master, Veg. Mil. 3, 6; 3, 8; 1, 13; Lampr. Alex. Sev. 53; Amm. 15, 3, 10; Inscr. Orell. 1790; 3495.
campidoctor.short: campĭ-doctor (better as two words), ōris, m.

campigeni.full: campĭgĕni, ōrum, m. campus-gigno, well disciplined soldiers (late Lat.), Veg. Mil. 2, 7.

campsanema.full: campsanēma, ătis, n., a plant, = ros marinus, App. Herb. 79.
campsanema.short: campsanēma, ătis, n., a plant, = ros marinus, App.

campso.full: campso, āre, v. a. κάμπτω, to bend, to turn, to turn around a place, to sail by, to double: Leucatam, Enn. ap. Prisc. p. 906 P. (Ann. v. 334 Vahl.; cf. campter and flecto).

camptaules.full: camptaules, ae, m., an unknown kind of musician, Vop. Carin. 19.
camptaules.short: camptaules, ae, m., an unknown kind of musician, Vop.

campter.full: campter, ēris, m., = καμπτήρ, a bending, turning, an angle, Pac. ap. Non. p. 65, 1 (Trag. Rel. v. 48 Rib.).
campter.short: campter, ēris, m., = καμπτήρ, a bending, turning, an angle, Pac.

campus1.full: campus, i, m. cf. κῆπος, Dor. κᾶπος; perh. for scampus from σκάπτω, to dig, scabo; whence Campania, and perh. Capua; for the inserted m, cf. AAB-' λαμβάνω. In gen. Lit., of any open, level land, without reference to cultivation or use, an even, flat place, a plain, field (freq. and class.; cf.: ager, planities, aequor; opp. mons, collis, silva, etc.; cf. Doed. Syn. III. p. 8 sq.): saxum plani raptim petit aequora campi, Lucr. 3, 1015; cf. id. 5, 950: in camporum patentium aequoribus, Cic. Div. 1

campus2.full: campus, i, m., = κάμπος, a seaanimal: marini = hippocampi, Mart. 9, 43, 1.
campus2.short: campus, i, m., = κάμπος, a seaanimal: marini = hippocampi, Mart.

camulodunum.full: Camulŏdūnum, i, n., a town of the Trinobantes in Britain, the first Roman colony under Claudius, now Colchester, Tac. A. 12, 32; 14, 31; also called Camalŏdū-num, Inscr. Orell. 208: Camolŏdūnum, Itin. Anton. p. 230 Parth.; and Camal-dūnum, Plin. 2, 75, 77, § 185.
camulodunum.short: Camulŏdūnum, i, n., a town of the Trinobantes in Britain, the first Roman colony under Claudius, now Colchester, Tac.

camulus.full: Cămŭlus, i, m., a surname of Mars, Inscr. Grut. 56, 11; 40, 9.
camulus.short: Cămŭlus, i, m., a surname of Mars, Inscr.

camum.full: camum, i, n., a kind of beer, Dig. 33, 7, 12; Edict. Diocl. p. 28.
camum.short: camum, i, n., a kind of beer, Dig.

camur.full: camur, ra, rum, adj. acc. to Macr. S. 6, 4 fin., peregrinum verbum; prob. root of κάμπτω; cf.: camera, καμάρα, Non. p. 30, 8; Paul. ex Fest. p. 43 Müll.; Serv. ad Verg. G. 3, 55; nom. camur, Isid. Orig. 12, 1, 35; 15, 8, 5, crooked, turned inwards (very rare): camuris hirtae sub cornibus aures, Verg. G. 3, 55 (camuris, i. e. curvis; unde et camerae appellantur, Serv.: camuri boves sunt, qui conversa introrsus cornua habent, Philarg.): arcus, an arch, vault, Prud. στεφ. 12, 53; cf. Jan. ad Macr.

camus.full: cāmus, i, m., = κημός (Dor. καμός). A muzzle for horses (only in eccl. Lat.), Vulg. Psa. 31, 9; Ambros. Hex. 6, 3.—* Perh. a kind of collar for the neck, Non. p. 200, 16 (Trag. Rel. v. 302 Rib.).

cana.full: cana, Gr. (*κάνεον, plur. κάνεα κάνη, a wicker basket) for canistra, acc. to Paul. ex Fest. p. 45 Müll.

canaba.full: cānăba (or cannăba), ae, f. kindr. with κάναβος and κάννα; acc. to others, with καλύβη, a hovel, hut, Aug. Serm. 61, de Temp.; Inscr. Orell. 39; 4077.

canabula.full: cānăbŭla, ae, f. dim. canaba, a small hovel, Auct. Limit. p. 257 Goes.

canace.full: Cănăcē, ēs, f., = Κανάκη. Daughter of Æolus, who, living in incest with her brother Macareus, bore a son to him, and was forced by her father to kill herself, Ov. H. 11; id. Tr. 2, 384.— The name of a dog, Ov. M. 3, 217; Hyg. Fab. 181.

canacheni.full: cănăchēni, ōrum, m., a class of thieves, Arn. 6, p. 207 dub.; cf. Öhler ad h. l.
canacheni.short: cănăchēni, ōrum, m., a class of thieves, Arn.

canachus.full: Cănăchus, i, m., = Κάναχος, the name of two artists of Sicyon, Cic. Brut. 18, 70; Plin. 34, 8, 19, § 50.
canachus.short: Cănăchus, i, m., = Κάναχος, the name of two artists of Sicyon, Cic.

canae.full: Canae, ārum, f., = Κάναι, a town on the coast of Æolis, opposite Mytilene, now Kanot-Koli, Liv. 36, 45, 8; cf. Mel. 1, 18; Plin. 5, 30, 32, § 122.
canae.short: Canae, ārum, f., = Κάναι, a town on the coast of Æolis, opposite Mytilene, now Kanot-Koli, Liv.

canalicolae.full: Cănālĭcŏlae, ārum, m., poor or lazy people who used to lounge near the Forum, at a place called the Canalis, Paul. ex Fest. p. 45 Müll.
canalicolae.short: Cănālĭcŏlae, ārum, m., poor or lazy people who used to lounge near the Forum, at a place called the Canalis, Paul.

canaliculatus.full: cănālĭcŭlātus, a, um, adj. canaliculus, like a channel or pipe, channelled, Plin. 19, 7, 36, § 119; 27, 9, 55, § 78.

canaliculus.full: cănālĭcŭlus, i, m. (cănālĭcŭla, ae, f. (ante- and post-class.), Varr. R. R. 3, 5, 14; Lucil. ap. Non. p. 198, 7; Gell. 17, 11, 2; cf. canalis), dim. canalis, a small channel, pipe, or gutter. A water-channel, Vitr. 10, 14 fin.; Col. 8, 15, 6.— A channel of a triglyph, Vitr. 4, 3.— The channel or groove of a catapult, Vitr. 10, 15.— In surgery, a splint for broken bones, Cels. 8, 2 fin.

canaliensis.full: cănālĭensis, e, and cănālĭcĭus, a, um, adj. id., dug out of shafts or pits: aurum, quod puteis foditur canalicium vocant, alii canaliense, Plin. 33, 4, 21, § 68; absol. (sc. aurum), id. 33, 4, 23, § 80.
canaliensis.short: cănālĭensis, e, and cănālĭcĭus, a, um, adj.

canalis.full: cănālis, is, m. (rarely ante- and postclass., f., Cato, R. R. 18, 6; Varr. R. R. 3, 5, 2; 3, 7, 8; 3, 11, 2; Auct. Aetn. 127 and 149; cf. the dim. canaliculus, etc., Rudd. I. p. 25, n. 35) [kindr. with Sanscr. root khan, fodere, perfodere; Gr. χαίνω, χανῶ; Germ. gähnen, to yawn; or cf. canna, a pipe, reed; Fr. canale; Engl. canal; Sp. cañon]. In gen., a pipe, groove, channel, whether open or closed, esp. a water-pipe or channel, a conduit, a canal, Cato, R. R. l. l.; Varr. R. R. l. l.; Verg. G.

canarius.full: cănārĭus, a, um, adj. canis, of or pertaining to dogs, dog-: augurium, i. e. in which dogs were offered, Auct. ap. Plin. 18, 3, 3, § 14; Fest. s. v. rutilae, p. 285 Müll. (cf. Ov. F. 4, 936; Col. 10, 342 sq.; Paul. ex Fest. s. v. catularia, p. 45 Müll.): herba, a kind of grass; acc. to Sprengel, fingerformed panic: Panicum dactylon, Linn.: lappa, Plin. 24, 19, 116, § 176.— Transf. As adj. prop.: Cănārĭa insula, one of the Insulae Fortunatae in the Atlantic Ocean, so called from its large dogs, P

canaster.full: cānaster, μιξοπόλιος, half-gray, grizzled, Gloss. Gr. Lat. [canus].

canatim.full: cănātim, adv. canis, in the manner of a dog, like a dog, κυνηδόν, Nigid. ap. Non. p. 40, 26.

cancamum.full: cancămum, i, n., = κάγκαμον, an Arabian gum used for incense: Amyris Kataf, Forsk.; Plin. 12, 20, 44, § 98.
cancamum.short: cancămum, i, n., = κάγκαμον, an Arabian gum used for incense: Amyris Kataf, Forsk.;

cancellarius1.full: cancellārĭus, ii, m. cancelli; Engl. chancellor (late Lat.). A kind of porter, door-keeper, Vop. Carin. 16.— A secretary, Cassiod. Var. 11, 6.

cancellarius2.full: cancellārĭus, a, um, adj. cancelli, living or kept behind bars: turdus, Schol. Pers. 6, 24.

cancellatim.full: cancellātim, adv. cancellatus, cancello, lattice-formed, trellis-like (post-Aug.; most freq. in Plin. the elder), Plin. 7, 20, 19, § 81; 9, 33, 52, § 103; 11, 37, 79, § 201; Sid. Ep. 5, 17.

cancellatio.full: cancellātĭo, ōnis, f. cancello, in the agrimensores, the fixing of boundaries, the measuring of land, Front. Col. p. 109 Goes.; Sicul. Flacc. p. 16.

cancelli.full: cancelli, ōrum (sing. cancellus, Dig. 43, 24, 9, § 1), m. dim. 2. cancer, a lattice, enclosure, grating, grate, balustrade, bars, railings: ( = κιγκλίδες; Latini tamen cancellos non tantum fores τοῦ δικαστηρίου, sed etiam omne consaeptum appellant, Salmas. Hist. Aug. p. 483) scenici et theatri, Varr. R. R. 3, 5, 4: aenei rivorum, Col. 8, 17, 6; the bar in a court of justice, Cic. Verr 2, 3, 59, § 135: tantus ex fori cancellis plausus excitatus, the barrier in public spectacles, id. Sest. 58, 124

cancello.full: cancello, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. cancelli (post-Aug.). In gen., to make like a lattice, to lattice: solum, i. e. with vines, Col. 4, 2, 2: cancellata cutis (elephanti), Plin. 8, 10, 10, § 30; cf. cancelli: cancellato bracchiorum implexu, id. 9, 51, 74, § 164. — Esp., in the Lat. of the jurists, to strike out a writing lattice-wise (Χ), to strike or cross out, to cancel: testamentum, Dig. 28, 4, 2: chirographum, ib. 22, 3, 24: tabulae cautionesque cancellatae, ib. 47, 2, 84; 2, 14, 47, § 2; 29, 1, 1

cancellosus.full: cancellōsus, a, um, adj. cancelli, covered with bars or a railing: postes, Cassiod. Var. 5, 42.

cancer1.full: cancer, cri (gen. canceris, Lucr. 5, 616; Arn. 1, p. 30; acc. plur. canceres, Cato, R. R. 157, 3), m. (neutr. Claudius, Quadrig. ap. Prisc. p. 697 P.; Scrib. Comp. 206 and 240) [cf. καρκίνος; root kar-, to be hard; whence κάρυον, cornu], a crab, a river-crab, sea-crab. Lit., Plin. 9, 31, 51, § 97 sq.; 19, 10, 58, § 180; Pall. 1, 35, 7; Ov. M. 15, 369; Plaut. Ps. 4, 1, 45; Verg. G. 4, 48; Col. 9, 5, 6: cancer femina, Plin. 32, 10, 46, § 134; Pall. 1, 35, 7.—* Meton., hands that cling fast like th

cancer2.full: cancer, cri, m. root kar-, to bend, twist; whence corona, circus, a lattice, the radical form of cancelli, q. v., Paul. ex Fest. p. 46; cf.: inter Orci cancros, App. M. 6, p. 176, 25.

cancerasco.full: cancĕrasco, āvi, 3, v. inch. n. [cancer, III.], to become cancerous, be afflicted with a cancer, to suppurate like a cancer (post-class.; only in perf.), Plin. Val. 1, 10; App. Horb. 36; Marc. Emp. 9.—Hence, cancĕrātus, a, um, cancerous: vulnera, Plin. Val. 4, 32: ulcera, id. ib. 4, 51.

canceraticus.full: cancĕrātĭcus, a, um, adj. canceratus, v. cancero, like a cancer, cancerous: foetor, Veg. 3, 43, 1.

canceroma.full: cancĕrōma (contr. cancrōma, Veg. 6, 19, 2; Salv. adv. Avarit. 1, p. 232, and corrupted canchrēma, Veg. 3, 22, 15), ătis, n., = καρκίνωμα, a cancer, App. Herb. 19; 31.

candace.full: Candăcē, ēs, f., a queen of Meroë, Plin. 6, 29, 35, § 186; gen. is, Vulg. Act. 8, 27.
candace.short: Candăcē, ēs, f., a queen of Meroë, Plin.

candacus.full: candacus or caudacus,) a false read. in Varr. L. L. 7, § 107 Müll. ad h. l.
candacus.short: candacus or caudacus,) a false read.

candavia.full: Candāvĭa, ae, f., = Κανδαουία, a mountainous district in Illyria, Caes. B. C. 3, 11; 3, 79; Sen. Ep. 31, 8; Plin. 3, 23, 26, § 145; Cic. Att. 3, 7, 3; Luc. 6, 331.
candavia.short: Candāvĭa, ae, f., = Κανδαουία, a mountainous district in Illyria, Caes.

candefacio.full: candĕ-făcĭo, fēci, factum, 3, v. a. candeo. (Cf. candeo. I., and candidus.) To make dazzlingly white (ante- and postclass.): argentum, Gell. 6, 5, 9; and jestingly: ebur atramento candefacere, of an impossibility, Plaut. Most. 1, 3, 102; cf. atramentum.— To make glowing, to make red hot (very rare, not in Cic.): quae candefieri non possunt, Plin. 33, 3, 20, § 64: lapides candefactos, id. 34, 8, 20, § 96; 25, 10, 76, § 123; Cels. 6, 8, 1.

candela.full: candēla, ae, f. candeo; Fr. chandelle, Engl. candle; hence, a light made of wax or tallow, a wax-light, tallow-candle, taper. Lit., Varr. ap. Serv. ad Verg. A. 1, 727; Col. 2, 22, 3; as a light of the poor, diff. from lucerna, used by the rich, Mart. 14, 43.— Hence, brevis, Juv. 3, 287: ancilla lucernae, Mart. 14, 40; of peeled rushes, used in funeral processions, Plin. 16, 37, 70, § 178; Pers. 3, 103.— Meton. Fire: candelam apponere valvis, to set fire to the doors, Juv. 9, 98 (cf. id. 13, 146)

candelabrarius.full: candēlābrārius, ĭi, m. candelabrum, a maker of candlesticks or chandeliers, Inscr. Orell. 4157.

candelabrum.full: candēlābrum, i, n. (old form can-dēlāber, m., like arater for aratrum, acc. to Arn. 1, p. 36: candēlābrus, Petr. 75. 10.—Acc.: candelabrum ardentem, Caecil. Com. Fragm. 111, ap. Non. p. 202, 16) [candela]: in quo figunt candelam candelabrum appellant, Varr. ap. Serv. ad Verg. A. 2, 225; cf. id. L. L. 5, § 119 Müll.; Paul. ex Fest. p. 46 ib.; a candleslick, a branched candlestick, a chandelier, candelabrum, or also lamp-stand, light-stand, sometimes of exquisite workmanship, Cic. Verr. 2, 2, 74,

candelifera.full: Candēlĭfĕra, ae, f. candela- fero, Taper-bearer, a goddess supposed to assist at childbirth, for whom a symbolical candle or torch was lighted, Tert. ad Nat. 2, 11.

candens.full: candens, entis, Part. and P. a., v. candeo.

candentia.full: candentia, ae, f. candens, a white, clear lustre, whiteness: lunae, Vitr. 9, 2, 2.

candeo.full: candeo, ui, 2, v. n. Sanscr candami, to be light; candra, the moon; connected with caneo as ardeo with areo, to be brilliant, glittering, to shine, glitter, glisten (cf. candidus and albus; mostly poet.). Lit. Verb finit.: candet ebur soliis collucent pocula mensae, Cat. 64, 45: ubi canderet vestis, Hor. S. 2, 6, 103: stellarum turba crasso lumine candet, Manil. 1, 753. — Part. and P. a.: candens, entis, = candidus, shining. dazzling, white, bright, glowing: candens lacteus umor, the bright, mil

candesco.full: candesco, ui, 3, v. inch. n. [candeo], to become of a bright, glittering white, to begin to glisten or radiate (rare; mostly poet.): ut solet aër candescere solis ab ortu, Ov. M. 6, 49; Tib. 1, 10, 43.— To begin to glow, to grow red hot: ferrum candescit in igni, Lucr. 1, 491; Ov. M. 2, 230; Vitr. 7, 9 fin; cf. candeo fin.

candetum.full: candētum, i, n., a Gallic word signifying a space of 100 or 150 square feet, Col. 5, 1, 6; cf. Auct. Limit. p. 292 Goes.; Isid. Orig. 15, 15, 6.
candetum.short: candētum, i, n., a Gallic word signifying a space of 100 or 150 square feet, Col.

candicantia.full: candicantia, ae, a false reading in Plin. 37, 13, 76, § 200; v. Sillig ad h. l.
candicantia.short: candicantia, ae, a false reading in Plin.

candico.full: candĭco, āre, v. n. candeo, like albico, from albeo, to be whitish or white (first used by Plin. the elder), Plin. 37, 11, 73, § 189; 34, 12, 32, § 127; App. M. 5, p. 168; Scrib. Comp. 237; Mart. Cap. 1, § 70; 7, § 728; Plin. 11, 16, 16, § 51: candicans vadum, id. 3, praef. § 4: gemma, id. 37, 10, 60, § 169: cardamomum, id. 12, 13, 29, § 50: nube candicante, id. 18, 35, 82, § 356: in ficticiis (geminis) scariphatio omnis candicat, Plin. 37, 13, 76, § 200 Jan. dub.; cf. Sillig ad loc.

candidarius.full: candĭdārius pistor, a baker of white bread, Inscr. Murat. 304, 3 [candidus].
candidarius.short: candĭdārius pistor, a baker of white bread, Inscr.

candidatorius.full: candĭdātōrĭus, a, um, adj. candidatus, of or pertaining to a candidate for office: munus, Cic. Att. 1, 1, 2.

candidatus1.full: candĭdātus, a, um, adj. candidus, like albatus, atratus, from albus, ater. In adj. uses, Lit., clothed in white (only in Plaut. and in post-Aug. prose; Cic., Hor., and Plin. use albatus): aequius vos erat Candidatas venire hostiatasque, Plaut. Rud. 1, 5, 12: mastigia, id. Cas. 2, 8, 10; *Suet. Aug. 98; Prud. στεφ. 1, 67.— Trop.: farinulentā cinere sordide candidati homunculi, App. M. 9, p. 222, 33; cf. candido.— Subst. candĭdātus. i, m., a candidate for office, because clothed in a glittering wh

candidatus2.full: candĭdātus, ūs, m. id., a candidacy, Cod. Th. 6, 4, 21, § 1.

candido.full: candĭdo, āvi, 1, v. a. candidus, to make glittering or bright, to make white (eccl. Lat.): vestimenta sua, Tert. adv. Gnost. 12: albis vestibus candidari, Aug. Ep. 168.—P. a.: candĭdans, antis, brilliantly white, Isid. Orig. 14, 8, 21; cf. 1. candidatus, I. A.

candidulus.full: candĭdŭlus, a, um, adj dim. [candidus], shining white' dentes, *Cic. Tusc. 5, 16, 46: grex, Prud. Cath. 3, 157.—* Adv.: candĭdŭlē, in trop. signif. (cf. candidus fin.), candidly, sincerely, Arn. 2, p. 50.

candidus.full: candĭdus, a, um, adj. candeo, of a shining, dazzling white, white, clear, bright (opp. niger, a glistening black; while albus is a lustreless white, opp. ater, a lustreless black; cf. Serv. ad Verg. G. 3, 82; lsid. Orig. 12, 1, 51; Doed. Syn. III. p. 193 sq.) (class., and in the poets very freq.; in Cic. rare). Lit. In gen. Of shining objects, bright: stella splendens candida, Plaut. Rud. prol. 3: sidera, Lucr. 5, 1209: luna, Verg. A. 7, 8: lux clara et candida, Plaut. Am. 1, 3, 49; so, clarā lo

candifico.full: candĭfĭco, āre, v. a. candeo-facio, to make dazzlingly white, Aug. Civ. Dei, 21, 7.

candificus.full: candĭfĭcus, a, um, adj. candifico, that makes dazzlingly white: pulvisculus, tooth-powder, App. Mag. p. 277.

candor.full: candor, ōris, m. candeo, as algor from algeo, etc.. A dazzling, glossy whiteness, a clear lustre, clearness, radiance, brightness, brilliancy, splendor, glitter, etc. (class.): aetherius sol irrigat adsidue caelum candore recenti, Lucr. 5, 283; 4, 232; cf. id. 2, 322: solis candor illustrior est quam ullius ignis, Cic. N. D. 2, 15, 40: Lacteus hic nimio fulgons candore notatur, id. Arat. 249 (493): splendidissimus, id. Rep. 6, 16, 16; cf.: candore notabilis ipso (via lactea), Ov. M. 1, 169: cael

candosoccus.full: candosoccus, i, m. Gallic; in husbandry, a layer of a plant; pure Lat. mergus, Col. 5, 5, 16.

canens1.full: cānens, entis, P. a., v. caneo init.

canens3.full: Cănens, entis, f., daughter of Janus, and wife of Picus, Ov. M. 14, 333 sq.
canens3.short: Cănens, entis, f., daughter of Janus, and wife of Picus, Ov.

canentas.full: canentas (Cod. Mon. canentes), an ornament for the head, Paul ex Fest. p. 46 Müll.

caneo.full: cānĕo, ui, 2, v. n. canus, to be gray or hoary, be white (poet. or in post-Aug. prose); P. a.: cānens, entis, gray, grayish, hoary, white: temporibus geminis canebat sparsa senectus, Verg. A. 5, 416; cf. Tac. G. 31: canens senecta, Verg. A. 10, 192: canet in igne cinis, Ov. A. A. 2, 440: canens gelu, white, id. Tr. 5, 2, 66; Sil. 1, 206; pruina, id. 3, 534: canentia lilia, Ov. M. 12, 411: dum gramina canent, Verg. G. 3, 325; 2, 13: canuerint herbae, Ov. F. 3, 880; Juv. 14, 144; Ov. M. 1, 110 (cf

canephoros.full: Cănēphŏrŏs (-phŏra, ae, Plin. 34, 8, 19, § 70), f., = Κανηφόρος, ἡ (she that bears a basket, v. κανηφόρος, and cf. Hor. S. 1, 3, 10; Ov. M. 2, 711 sq.), paintings or statues of Greek artists, representing Athenian maidens, who, in the festivals of Juno, Diana, Minerva, Ceres, and Bacchus, bore different sacred utensils in wicker baskets (κάνη) on their heads; nom. sing. Canephoros (a work of Scopas), Plin. 36, 5, 4, § 25.— Nom. plur. Canephoroe = κανηφόροι (cf.: Adelphoe, arctoe, etc.), Cic. Ver

canesco.full: cānesco. ĕre, v. inch. n. [caneo]. to grow white, whiten. Lit., to become gray or hoary: pabula canescunt (sc. calore), Ov. M. 2, 212; Plin. 31, 10, 46, § 106: canescant aequora remis, Ov. H. 3, 65: canescunt tecta, id. Am. 1, 8, 52; Col. 3, 2, 12: capilli canescunt, Plin. 30, 15, 46, § 134; 7, 2, 2, § 23: in cujus (Minervae) aede ignes numquam canescunt in favillas, Sol. 22, 18.— Transf., = senescere, to grow old, Ov. M. 9, 422: eaque (quercus) canescet saeclis innumerabilibus, Cic. Leg. 1, 1,

cangi.full: Cangi, ōrum, m., = Καγγανοί, a people in the western part of Britain, Tac. A. 12, 32.
cangi.short: Cangi, ōrum, m., = Καγγανοί, a people in the western part of Britain, Tac.

cania.full: canĭa, ae, f., a kind of wild nettle, Plin. 21, 15, 55, § 92.
cania.short: canĭa, ae, f., a kind of wild nettle, Plin.

canicae.full: canĭcae, ārum, f., a kind of bran: canicae furfures de farre a cibo canum vocatae, Paul. ex Fest. p. 46 Müll.; Lucil. ap. Non. p. 88, 16 sq.
canicae.short: canĭcae, ārum, f., a kind of bran: canicae furfures de farre a cibo canum vocatae, Paul.

canicula.full: cănīcŭla, ae, f. dim. canis. A small dog or bitch, Plin. 32, 7, 26, § 79.—Hence, Trop., of a passionate, quarrelsome woman, Plaut. Curc. 5, 1, 8; Gell. 4, 20, 3.— Transf. Canis Minor, the lesser dogstar, in the mouth of the constellation Canis, q. v., Plin. 2, 47, 47, § 123; 18, 28, 68, § 268: flagrans, Hor. C. 3, 13, 9: flammans, Manil. 5, 207: rubra, Hor. S. 2, 5, 39: sitiens, Ov. A. A. 2, 231: insana, Pers. 3, 5: caniculae aestus, Hor. C. 1, 17, 17.—Trop., of Diogenes: illa canicula Diogenes,

canicularis.full: cănīcŭlāris, e, adj. canicula, II. A., of or pertaining to the dog-star (post-class.): dies, dog-days, Pall. Jul. 1 and 7; Sol. Veg. 5, 35: inclementia, Sid. Ep. 2, 2.

canidia.full: Cānĭdĭa, ae, f., a sorceress, often mentioned by Horace, Hor. Epod. 3, 8; id. S. 1, 8, 24; 2, 1, 48; 2, 8, 95; to whom Epod. 5 and 17 are addressed.
canidia.short: Cānĭdĭa, ae, f., a sorceress, often mentioned by Horace, Hor.

canidius.full: Canĭdĭus, ii, m., a Roman name; esp., P. Canidius Crassus, a general under Lepidus and Antony, put to death by Octavius, Cic. Fam. 10, 21, 4; Vell. 2, 85, 2; 2, 87, 3.
canidius.short: Canĭdĭus, ii, m., a Roman name;

canifera.full: cānĭfĕra, ae, f.: mulier, quae fert canuam, id est qualum, quod est cistae genus, Paul. ex Fest. p. 65 Müll.; v. Canephoros.
canifera.short: cānĭfĕra, ae, f.: mulier, quae fert canuam, id est qualum, quod est cistae genus, Paul.

caniformis.full: cănĭformis, e, adj. canis-forma, having the form of a dog, dog-shaped: Anubis, Prud. Apoth. 263.

caninefates.full: Caninĕfātes (Cannin-), um, m., a people dwelling upon the Batavian peninsula, Vell. 2, 105; Tac. H. 4, 15; 4, 32; 4, 56; 4, 79; 4, 85; also called Cannĕnĕfātes, Plin. 4, 15, 29, § 101; and Cannunĕfā-tes, Inscr. Orell. 96.—In sing.: dux natione Caninefas, Tac. A. 11, 18.— Adj.: Caninĕfas, ātis, of Caninefas: ala, Tac. A. 4, 73: tumultus, id. H. 4, 16: cohortes, id. ib. 4, 19 al.
caninefates.short: Caninĕfātes (Cannin-), um, m., a people dwelling upon the Batavian peninsula, Vell.

caninius.full: Cănīnĭus, a, the name of a plebeian gens at Rome. C. Caninius Rebilus, lieutenant of Cœ sar in Gaul, consul for a few hours at the end of December, A. U. C. 709; hence the jest of Cicero: Caninio consule scito neminem prandisse, Cic. Fam. 7, 30, 1; cf. id. Att. 12, 37, 4.— Caninius Rebilus, perh. a son of the preceding, notorious for his abandoned life, Sen. Ben. 2, 21, 5.— L. Caninius Gallus, accuser of Antony, afterwards his son-in-law, Cic. Fam. 1, 2, 1; 1, 4, 1; 2, 8, 3; 7, 1, 4; 9, 2, 1; Va
caninius.short: Cănīnĭus, a, the name of a plebeian gens at Rome.

caninus.full: cănīnus, a, um, adj. canis, of or pertaining to a dog, canine, dog-. Lit.: lac, Ov. Ib. 227; Plin. 29, 6, 39, § 133: pellis, Scrib. Comp. 161: stercus, Juv. 14, 64: rictus, id. 10, 271: far, spelt-bread for dogs, id. 5, 11: adeps, Plin. 29, 6, 35, § 111: fel, id. 29, 6, 38, § 117: dentes, eye-teeth, dog-teeth, Varr. R. R. 2, 7; 3; Cels. 8, 1; Plin. 11, 37, 61, § 160: scaeva canina, a favorable augury taken from meeting a dog or from his barking, Plaut. Cas. 5, 4, 4.— Subst.: canīna, ae, f. (sc.

canipa.full: cānĭpa, ae, f., = canistrum, a fruitbasket for religious uses, Frat. Arv. Marin. 3.
canipa.short: cānĭpa, ae, f., = canistrum, a fruitbasket for religious uses, Frat.

canis1.full: cănis (cănes, Plaut. Men. 5, 1, 18; id. Trin. 1, 2, 133; 1, 2, 135; Enn. ap. Varr. L. L. 7, § 32 Müll., or Ann. v. 518 Vahl.; Lucil. ap. Varr. ib.; cf. Charis. 1, 17, p. 118 P.; abl. always cane; gen. plur. canum; v. Neue, Formenl. pp. 223, 258 sq.), comm. Sanscr. cvan; Gr. κύων, κυνός; Germ. Hund; Engl. hound. Lit., a dog. In gen., v. Varr. R. R. 1, 21; 2, 9, 1 sqq.; Plin. 8, 40, 61, § 142 sqq.; Col. 7, 12, 1: tantidem quasi feta canes sine dentibus latrat, Enn. ap. Varr. L. L. 7, § 32 Müll. (A

canis2.full: Cănis, is, m., a small river tributary to the Po, Plin. 3, 16, 20, § 117.
canis2.short: Cănis, is, m., a small river tributary to the Po, Plin.

canistellum.full: cănistellum, i, n. dim. canistrum, Paul. ex Fest. s. v. cana, p. 45, 19 Müll., a bread-basket, a fruit-basket: argentea, Symm. Ep. 2, 81; 7, 76.

canistrum.full: cănistrum, i, n. cănistri, ōrum, m., Pall. Nov. 17, 1, = κάναστρα, a basket woven from reeds (κάννα), a bread-, fruit-, flower-, etc., basket (esp. for religious use in sacrifices), Cic. Att. 6, 1, 13; Tib. 1, 10, 27; Prop. 3 (4), 13, 28; 4 (5), 8, 12; Verg. A. 8, 180; id. G. 4, 280; Hor. S. 2, 6, 105; Ov. M. 2, 713; 8, 675; id. F. 2, 650; 4, 451; Col. 10, 277; Juv. 5, 74.— Canistra siccaria, baskets in which wine stood upon a table, acc. to Serv. ad Verg. A. 1, 706.

canities.full: cānĭtĭes (cānĭtĭa, Plin. 31, 7, 42, § 91; 11, 37, 64, § 169; cf. Charis. p. 41 P.), em, ē (other cases not in use), f. canus, a gray or grayish-white color, hoariness (poet. or in post-Aug. prose): lupi, Ov. M. 1, 238; folia lanatiore canitie, Plin. 21, 20, 84, § 147; 37, 11, 73, § 191: sparsa marmoris, id. 36, 7, 11, § 55.—Esp. freq. of the hair, Ov. M. 10, 425; 7, 289; Plin. 11, 37, 64, § 169; cf. id. 11, 37, 47, § 131.—Hence, Transf. (Abstr. pro concr.) Gray hair: canitiem terră atque infuso

canitudo.full: cānĭtūdo, ĭnis, f. id. (ante-class. access. form of the preced.), a gray color, hoariness: capitis, Plaut. ap. Paul. ex Fest. p. 62 Müll.—Absol., Varr. ap. Non. p. 82, 24.

canius.full: Canius, ii, m., a Roman proper name. C. Canius. a Roman of learning, Cic. Off. 3, 14, 58 sq.; id. de Or. 2, 69, 280.— Canius Rufus, a poet, Mart. 1, 61, 9; 8, 20, 1.
canius.short: Canius, ii, m., a Roman proper name.

canna.full: canna, ae, f., = κάννα, a reed, cane (less freq. than harundo), Col. 7, 9, 7; 4, 32, 3: palustris, Ov. M. 4, 298: tremulae, id. ib. 6, 326 al.— Transf., any thing made of reed. A reed-pipe, flute, Ov. M. 2, 682; 11, 171; Sil. 7, 439.— A small vessel, gondola, Juv. 5, 89; cf. Plin. 7, 2, 2, § 21; 7, 56. 57, § 206.— Canna gutturis. in later medical writers, the windpipe, Cael. Aur. Acut. 2, 16, 97; id. Tard. 2, 12, 137.
canna.short: canna, ae, f., = κάννα, a reed, cane (less freq.

cannabinus.full: cannăbĭnus, a, um, adj., = καννάβινος, of hemp, hempen: retis, Varr. R. R. 3, 5, 11: tegeticulae, id. ib. 2, 8, 2: funes, Col. 6, 2, 3; 12, 50, 8.
cannabinus.short: cannăbĭnus, a, um, adj., = καννάβινος, of hemp, hempen: retis, Varr.

cannabis.full: cannăbis, is, f., and cannăbum, i, n. kindr. with Sanscr. sana, the same, Bopp, Gloss. p. 343, a, = κάνναβις and κάνναβος, hemp; nom. cannabis, Col. 2, 10, 21; Plin. 19, 4, 22, § 63; 19, 9, 56, § 173; acc. cannabim, Varr. R. R. 1, 23, 6; abl. cannabi, Plin. 19, 2, 8, § 29: cannabe, Pers. 5, 146.— Nom. cannabum, Isid. Orig. 19, 27, 3; gen. cannabi, Isid. l. l. 2; acc. cannabum, Pall. Febr. 5; Mart. 5; Isid. l. l. 3; abl. cannabo, Varr. ap. Gell. 17, 3, 4.
cannabis.short: cannăbis, is, f., and cannăbum, i, n.

cannabius.full: cannăbĭus, a, um, adj. cannabis, of hemp: silvae, Grat. Cyn. 47.

cannae.full: Cannae, ārum, f., = Κάνναι (Κάννα, Polyb.), a village in Apulia, north of Canusium, famous for the victory of Hannibal over the Romans; it lay on the east side of the Aufidus (which is hence called Amnis Canna by Marcius vates ap. Liv. 25, 12, 5), now Canne, id. 22, 44, 1 sq. (Polyb. 3, 113); Flor. 2, 6, 15; Cic. Tusc. 1, 37, 89: Cannarum pugna, Liv. 23, 43, 4; Sil. 9, 10.—Appellative: Capuam Hannibali Cannas fuisse, a second Cannœ, Liv. 23, 45, 4; Flor. 2, 6, 21. — Deriv.: Cannensis, e, adj., o
cannae.short: Cannae, ārum, f., = Κάνναι (Κάννα, Polyb.), a village in Apulia, north of Canusium, famous for the victory of Hannibal over the Romans;

cannetum.full: cannētum, i, n. canna, a thicket of reeds, Pall. Febr. 23, 2; 24, 13; Cassiod. Var. 2, 40.

canneus.full: cannĕus, a, um, adj. id., made of reeds, reed-: tegetes, Col. 12, 50, 8 dub.

cannula.full: cannŭla, ae, f. dim. canna. A small, low reed, App. M. 4, p. 145; Mart. Cap. 2, § 224.—* (Cf. canna, II. C.) Pulmonis, the windpipe, Cael. Aur. Tard. 2, 13, 152.

cannutius.full: Cannutĭus (Cānu-), ii, m., a Roman proper name. P. Cannutius, an orator in Cicero's time, Cic. Brut. 56, 205; id. Clu. 10, 29; 18, 50; Tac. Or. 21.— Ti. Cannutius, tribune of the people A. U. C. 710, Cic. Fam. 12, 3, 2; 12, 23, 3; id. Phil. 3, 9, 23; Vell. 2, 64.
cannutius.short: Cannutĭus (Cānu-), ii, m., a Roman proper name.

cano.full: căno, cĕcĭni, cantum (ancient imp. cante = canite, Carm. Sal. ap. Varr. L. L. 7, § 37 Müll.; fut. perf. canerit = cecinerit, Lib. Augur. ap. Fest. s. v. rumentum, p. 270 ib.; perf. canui = cecini, acc. to Serv. ad Verg. G. 2, 384, predominant in concino, occino, etc.—Examples of sup. cantum and part. cantus, canturus, a, um, appear not to be in use; the trace of an earlier use is found in Paul. ex Fest. p. 46 Müll.: canta pro cantata ponebant; once canituri, Vulg. Apoc. 8, 13), 3, v. n. and a. [

canon.full: cănon, ŏnis, m. (acc. canona, Plin. 34, 8, 19, § 55; acc. plur. canonas, Aus. Ep. 136; in Cic. Fam. 16, 17, 1, used as a Greek word), = κανών [κάννα, κάνη, a reed, cane]. A marking or measuring line; hence, a rule, canon, model (cf. Lidd. and Scott, under κανών).— Esp. A wooden channel in hydraulic instruments, Vitr. 10, 13 Rod.— Under the emperors, an annual tribute, established by law, in grain, gold, silver, clothing, etc., Spart. Sev. 8; Lampr. Elag. 27.— In eccl. Lat., a catalogue of sacred

canonicarius.full: cănŏnĭcārĭus, ii, m. canon, II. B., the collector of an annual tribute, Just. Nov. Const. 30; Cassiod. Var. 6, 8; 12, 13.

canonicus.full: cănŏnĭcus, a, um, adj., = κανονικός, according to rule or measure. In music: ratio, the theory of harmony, Vitr. 1, 1; 5, 3; cf. Gell. 16, 18, 5.— In astronomy: defectiones solis, as following at regular intervals, Aug. Civ. Dei, 3, 15.—Subst.: cănŏ-nĭci, ōrum, m., theorists, Plin. 2, 17, 14, § 73; and cănŏnĭca, ōrum, n., = canonica ratio, theory: luminum, Plin. Ep. 1, 2, 12.— Of or pertaining to an annual tribute: pensitationes, Cod. Just. 12, 62, 2: equi, ib. 11, 17, 3: vestes, ib. 11, 9, 1.—
canonicus.short: cănŏnĭcus, a, um, adj., = κανονικός, according to rule or measure.

canonizo.full: cănŏnizo, āre, v. a. canon, II. C., to put into the list or catalogue of saints, to canonize, Alex. III. P.P. Ep. 3.

canopus1.full: Cănōpus, i, m., = Κάνωβος, rarely Κάνωπος; cf. Quint. 1, 5, 13. An islandtown in Lower Egypt, on the western mouth of the Nile; acc. to the fable, named after the pilot of Menelaus, who died there: Canopus (Canobus in Serv. ad Verg. G. 4, 287), Mel. 2, 7, 6; Plin. 5, 31, 34, § 128; Tac. A. 2, 60: famosus, i. e. notorious for its luxury, Juv. 15, 46; cf. id. 1, 26; 6, 84; Sen. Ep. 37, 3.— Meton., Lower Egypt; cf. Prop. 3 (4), 11, 39; Verg. G. 4, 287 Heyne.—Also the whole of Egypt, Luc. 10, 64.— D
canopus1.short: Cănōpus, i, m., = Κάνωβος, rarely Κάνωπος;

canopus2.full: Cănōpus (-pŏs), i, m., = Κάνωπος, the brightest star in the constellation Argo (visible in Southern Europe), Manil. 1, 215; Vitr. 9, 4 (7); Plin. 2, 70, 71, § 178; Luc. 8, 181 (scanned Cănŏpŭs, Mart. Cap. 7, § 808).
canopus2.short: Cănōpus (-pŏs), i, m., = Κάνωπος, the brightest star in the constellation Argo (visible in Southern Europe), Manil.

canor.full: cănor, ōris, m. cano, tune, sound, song, melody (poet. or in post-Aug. prose; rare). Lit. Of living beings, Quint. 1, 10, 22: cygni, Lucr. 4, 182; 4, 911: res est blanda canor; discant cantare puellae, Ov. A. A. 3, 315: mulcendas natus ad aures, id. M. 5, 561.— Of instruments, the tone: Martius aeris rauci canor, martial clang, Verg. G. 4, 71: lyrae, Ov. H. 16, 180.— Trop.: bella truci memorata canore, in heroic poetry, Petr. 5, 19.

canorus.full: cănōrus, a, um, adj. canor, of or pertaining to melody, melodious, harmonious, euphonious; neutr. or act. (of sound, men, animals, instruments, etc.; class. in prose and poetry). Neutr.: profluens quiddam habuit Carbo et canorum, flowing language and a melodious voice, Cic. de Or. 3, 7, 28; Tac. A. 4, 61: voce suavi et canoră, Cic. Brut. 66, 234: vox Sirenum, Ov. A. A. 3, 311; Petr. 59, 3.—As a fault in delivery, singing, sing-song, droning: sine contentione vox, nec languens, nec canora, Cic. O

cantabilis.full: cantābĭlis, e, adj. canto, worthy to be sung, Cassiod. Var. 2, 40; id. 8, 9; Vulg. Psa. 118, 54.

cantabrarius.full: cantăbrārĭus, ii, m. cantabrum, a standard-bearer on festive occasions, Cod. Th. 14, 7, 2.

cantabras.full: Cantā^bras, ae, m., a tributary of the Indus, now Tschandrabagha, Plin. 6, 20, 23, § 71 (Cantabas, Sillig).
cantabras.short: Cantā^bras, ae, m., a tributary of the Indus, now Tschandrabagha, Plin.

cantabria.full: Cantăbrĭa, ae, f., = Κανταβρία, a province in Hispania Tarraconensis, east of Asturia, in the region of the present Biscaya, Plin. 34, 14, 42, § 148; 34, 16, 47, § 158; Suet. Aug. 20; 81; id. Galb. 8; Flor. 4, 12, 48.— Derivv. Cantăber, bra, brum, adj., Cantabrian: Oceanus, Claud. Laud. Ser. 74.—Far more freq. subst.: Cantă-ber, ā^bri, and in plur.: Cantā^bri, ōrum, m., the Cantabrians, Caes. B. C. 2, 36; Mel. 3, 1, 9, § 10; Plin. 4, 20, 34, § 110 sq.; an exceedingly wild and warlike people, who
cantabria.short: Cantăbrĭa, ae, f., = Κανταβρία, a province in Hispania Tarraconensis, east of Asturia, in the region of the present Biscaya, Plin.

cantabricus.full: Cantā^brĭcus, a, um, v. Cantabria, II. B. and cantabrum, I.

cantabrum.full: cantăbrum, i, n. etym. unknown; the connection with Cantabria is a mere conjecture. A kind of bran (late Lat.), Cael. Aur. Tard. 3, 2; 4, 3; Apic. 7, 1; Schol. Juv. 5, 11 (as an explanation of far caninum); hence, cantabricus sucus, Veg. 5, 56, 3.— A kind of banner or standard under the emperors, Min. Fel. Oct. 29; Tert. Apol. 16.

cantabundus.full: cantābundus, a, um, adj. canto, singing (rare: sedeo ego cantabundus et stellas numero, Petr. 62, 4: Gallus suā disciplinā scuto projecto cantabundus (constitit), Quadrig. ap. Gell. 9, 13, 16 dub. (Hertz, cunctabundus).

cantamen.full: cantāmen, ĭnis, n. canto, III.; cf. cano, II.; cantus, II. B., and carmen; lit. a charming with words; hence, abstr. pro concr., a spell, charm, magic sentence, incantation (very rare), Prop. 4 (5), 4, 51; App. M. 2, p. 114; id. Mag. 40, p. 299: magicum, Prud. adv. Sym. 2, 176.

cantatio.full: cantātĭo, ōnis, f. canto; lit. a singing, a playing; hence, abstr. pro concr.. Music, song, mentioned by Varr. L. L. 6, 7, § 75 Müll.: animum cantationibus permulcere, App. M. 2, p. 125; Vulg. Psa. 70, 6 (but in Plaut. Stich. 5, 5, 19, the true reading is cantionem, Fleck.).—* A charm, spell, incantation, Firm. Math. 3, 6.

cantator.full: cantātor, ōris, m. id., a musician, singer, minstrel (mentioned by Varr. L. L. 8, § 57 Müll.): vetus et nobilior Ario cantator fidibus fuit, Gell. 16, 19 (transl. of the Gr. κιθαρὡδός, Herod. 1, 23 Bähr): cantator cygnus funeris ipse sui, Mart. 13, 77.

cantatrix.full: cantātrix, īcis, f. adj. cantator (postclass.). Musical, singing: choreae, Claud. B. Gild. 448.—Subst.: cantātrix, īcis, f., a female singer, Vulg. 2 Reg. 19, 35; cf. Prisc. p. 1225 P.— Using enchantments: anus, App. M. 2, p. 128, 1: aniculae, id. ib. 2, p. 123, 25.

canteci.full: Canteci, ōrum, m., a people in Sarmatia Asiatica, near Palus Maeotis, Plin. 6, 7, 7, § 22.
canteci.short: Canteci, ōrum, m., a people in Sarmatia Asiatica, near Palus Maeotis, Plin.

canteriatus.full: cantērĭātus (canth-), a, um, adj. canterius, supporied by props, underpropped: vineae, Col. 5, 4, 1.

canterinus.full: cantērīnus (canth-), a, um, adj. id., of or pertaining to a horse, horse-: ritus, like a horse, Plaut. Men. 2, 3, 44: hordeum, i. e. winter barley, Col. 2, 9, 14; 2, 10, 31; Pall. Oct. 1, 2: lapathum = rumex, Plin. 20, 21, 85, § 231.

canteriolus.full: cantērĭŏlus, i, m. dim. id., a small trellis for supporting plants, Col. 11, 3, 58.

canthara.full: Canthăra, ae, f., the name of a woman, Ter. And. 4, 4, 30; Plaut. Ep. 4, 1, 40.
canthara.short: Canthăra, ae, f., the name of a woman, Ter.

cantharias.full: canthărĭas, ae, m. κανθαρίς, a precious stone having in it the figure of a Spanish fly, Plin. 37, 11, 72, § 187.

cantharis.full: canthăris, ĭdis, f., = κανθαρίς. A genus of beetle, of several species; in pure Lat. scarabaeus parvus, Plin. 29, 4, 30, § 94; freq. used in medicine, id. 11, 35, 41, § 118; 29, 4, 30, § 93.—Esp. the (very poisonous) Spanish fly, cantharides: Meloe vesicatorius, Linn.; Cic. Tusc. 5, 40, 117; id. Fam. 9, 21, 3; Ov. Ib. 306; cf. Plin. 29, 4, 30, § 94; 11, 35, 41, § 118.— A worm injurious to the vine and rose, Pall. 1, 35, 6 and 4; cf. Plin. 18, 17, 44, § 152.

cantharites.full: canthărītes vīnum = κανθαρίτης οἶνος, a kind of wine, Plin. 14, 7, 9, § 75.
cantharites.short: canthărītes vīnum = κανθαρίτης οἶνος, a kind of wine, Plin.

cantharolethros.full: Canthărŏlĕthros, i, m., = κανθαρόλεθρος (death to beetles), a place in Thrace near Olynthus: in quo unum hoc animal exanimatur, Plin. 11, 28, 84, § 99.
cantharolethros.short: Canthărŏlĕthros, i, m., = κανθαρόλεθρος (death to beetles), a place in Thrace near Olynthus: in quo unum hoc animal exanimatur, Plin.

cantharulus.full: canthărŭlus, i, m. dim. cantharus, a small drinking-vessel, Arn. 6, p. 209.— A small candlestick, Paul. Nol. Carm. 22, 462.

cantharus.full: canthărus, i, m., = κάνθαρος. Lit., a large, wide-bellied drinking-vessel with handles, a tankard, pot (very frequent in Plaut.), Plaut. As. 5, 2, 56; id. Bacch. 1, 1, 36; id. Men. 1, 2, 64; 1, 3, 5; id. Most. 1, 4, 33; id. Ps. 4, 2, 2; 4, 4, 13; 5, 1, 34; id. Pers. 5, 2, 22; 5, 2, 40; id. Rud. 5, 2, 32; id. Stich. 5, 4, 23; 5, 4, 48; Hor. C. 1, 20, 2; id. Ep. 1, 5, 23 al.—Esp. used by Bacchus and his followers, as scyphus, by Hercules, Verg. E. 6, 17 Voss; Macr. S. 5, 21, 14; Arn. 6, 25. —Hence

cantherius.full: canthērĭus or cantērĭus, ii, m. perh. κανθήλιος, a beast of burden. A gelding, Varr. R. R. 2, 7, 15; cf. Paul. ex Fest. p. 46 Müll.; Plaut. Aul. 3, 5, 21; id. Capt. 4, 2, 34; Cic. N. D. 3, 5, 11; id. Fam. 9, 18, 4; Sen. Ep. 87, 9.— An ass, mule, Tert. Apol. 16; id. ad Nat. 1, 14.—Prov.: minime, sis, cantherium in fossam, put the hack in the ditch, when it is useless, Liv. 23, 47, 6 Weissenb. ad loc.— Meton. A man impotent through age, Plaut. Cist. 4, 2, 83.— In architecture, a spar under the roo

canthus1.full: canthus, i, m., = κάνθος; lit. the iron ring around a carriage-wheel, the tire, Quint. 1, 5, 88, where it is considered as barbarian (African or Spanish).—Hence, Meton. (pars pro toto), a wheel, Pers. 5, 71.

canthus2.full: Canthus, i, m., = Κάνθος, nom. propr., name of an Argonaut, Hyg. Fab. 14; Val. Fl. 1, 3 and 6.

canticulum.full: cantĭcŭlum, i, n. dim. canticum. * A little song, a sonnet: Zephyri, Septim. Afer. ap. Ter Maur. p. 2427 P.— A short incantation, Pomp. ap. Non. p. 482, 9.

canticum.full: cantĭcum, i, n. cantus. Lit., a song in the Roman comedy, sung by one person, and accompanied by music and dancing; a monody, solo: nosti canticum (in Demiurgo Turpilii), meministi Roscium, Cic. Fam. 9, 22, 1: agere, Liv. 7, 2, 9: desaltare, Suet. Calig. 54: histrio in cantico quodam, id. Ner. 39: Neroniana, id. Vit. 11: Atellanis notissimum canticum exorsis, id. Galb. 13.— A song, in gen.: chorus canticum Insonuit, Phaedr. 5, 7, 25: canticum repetere, id. 5, 7, 31: omne convivium obscenis canti

canticus.full: cantĭcus, a, um, adj. canto, musical: delinimenta, Macr. Somn. Scip. 2, 3.

cantilena.full: cantĭlēna, ae, f. cantillo. In anteclass. and class. lang., a song, in a disparaging sense, an old song; vulg. for silly, trite prattle, gossip: ut crebro mihi insusurret cantilenam suam, Cic. Att. 1, 19, 8: totam istam cantilenam ex hoc pendere, ut quam plurimum lucri faciant, Brut. ap. Cic. Fam. 11, 20, 2: qui non Graeci alicujus cottidianam loquacitatem sine usu, neque ex scholis cantilenam requirunt, Cic. de Or. 1, 23, 105.—Prov.: cantilenam eandem canis, = τὸ αὐτὸ ᾁδεις ᾆσμα, ever the old s

cantilenosus.full: cantĭlēnōsus, a, um, adj. cantilena, (post-class.), pertaining to song, poetic: nugae, Sid. Ep. 3, 14; 4, 1.

cantillo.full: cantillo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. dim. a. [canto], to sing low, to hum (post-class.; perh. only in App.), App. M. 4, p. 146; id. Flor. 1, p. 342, 8; 3, p. 388, 13 al.

cantio.full: cantĭo, ōnis, f. cano, lit. a singing, playing; hence meton. abstr. pro concr.. A song (rare; mostly ante-class.), Plaut. Stich. 5, 4, 25; 5, 5, 19; 5, 6, 8; Suet. Ner. 25; of birds, App. Flor. 2, p. 349, 11; Fronto ad Ver. 1 (cf. cantatio).— An incantation, charm, spell, Cato, R. R. 160: subito totam causam oblitus est, idque veneficiis et cantionibus Titiniae factum dicebat, Cic. Brut. 60, 217; App. M. 1, 10, p. 106, 27.

cantito.full: cantĭto, āvi, ātum, 1, v. freq. act. [canto; cf. Varr. L. L. 6, 7, § 75 Müll.; 8, 33, § 119], to sing or play often or repeatedly (rare): ut habeas quīcum cantites, Ter. Ad. 4, 7, 32: carmina in epulis esse cantitata a singulis convivis de clarorum virorum laudibus, Cic. Brut. 19, 75 (cf. cano, II. B.); Suet. Ner. 39: dulce cantitant aves, App. M. 6, p. 175.

cantium.full: Cantĭum, ii, n., = Κάντιον, a promontory of England, now Kent, Caes. B. G. 5, 13; 5, 22.
cantium.short: Cantĭum, ii, n., = Κάντιον, a promontory of England, now Kent, Caes.

cantiuncula.full: cantĭuncŭla, ae, f. dim. cantio, a flaitering, alluring strain: si cantiunculis (sc. Sirenum) tantus vir inretitus teneretur, Cic. Fin. 5, 18, 49.

canto.full: canto, āvi, ātum, 1, v. n. and a. [cano], freq. in form, but mostly agrees in meaning with cano. Neutr., to produce melodious sounds (by the voice or an instrument), to sound, sing, play (class. in prose and poetry; rare in Cic.). Of men: Pamphilam Cantatum provocemus, Ter. Eun. 3, 1, 53: saltare et cantare, Cic. Cat. 2, 10, 23: neque enim vocum suavitate videntur aut novitate quădam cantandi revocare eos solitae (sirenes), id. Fin. 5, 18, 49: Arcades ambo Et cantare pares, Verg. E. 7, 5; 10, 32

cantor.full: cantor, ōris, m. cano, a singer, poet. In gen.: omnibus hoc vitium est cantoribus, Hor. S. 1, 3, 1; so id. ib. 1, 3, 129; 1, 2, 3 (mutato nomine cantorem pro musico dicit, Acron.): Thamyras, Prop. 2 (3), 22, 19. cantor Apollo, Hor. A. P. 407 (cf. Apollo): (Caligula) Threx et auriga idem cantor atque saltator, Suet. Calig. 54.—In a contemptuous sense: cantor formularum, Cic. de Or. 1, 55, 236; cf. Plaut. Ps. 1, 3, 132.— And with gen. of the person (conformably to cano, II. B.), an extoller, eulog

cantrix.full: cantrix, īcis, f. cantor, a female singer, a songstress, Plaut. Trin. 2, 1, 23; Tert. adv. Marc. 3, 5.—Adj.: aves cantrices, singing, Varr. R. R. 3, 5, 14.

cantulus.full: cantŭlus, i, m. dim. cantus, a little song, Firm. Math. 3, 12.

canturio.full: cantŭrĭo, īre, v. desid. n. and a. [cano], to chirp (post-class. and rare): canturire melicam, belle diverbia dicere (vulg.: canturire belle diverbia, adicere melicam), Petr. 64, 2 N. cr.; Paul. ex Fest. s. v. dagnades, p. 68.
