carthaea.full: Carthaea, ae, f., = Καρθαία, a town on the south coast of the Cycladic island Ceos or Cea, now Poles, Plin. 4, 12, 20, § 62.— Hence, Carthēus and Carthēĭus, a, um, Carthœan, of Carthœa: arva, Ov. M. 10, 109: moenia = Carthaea, id. ib. 7, 368.
carthaea.short: Carthaea, ae, f., = Καρθαία, a town on the south coast of the Cycladic island Ceos or Cea, now Poles, Plin.

carthago1.full: Carthāgo (Karth-, and without asp. Kartāgo), ĭnis (locat. Carthagini, like Tiburi, ruri, domi, etc., Plaut. Cas. prol. 71; Cic. Agr. 2, 33, 90; Liv. 28, 26, 1 sq.; 31, 11, 7 al.; cf. Schneid. Gr. 2. p. 236; Zumpt, Gr. § 63, note), f., (prop. new town: istam urbem Carthadam Elissa dixit, quod Phoenicum ore exprimit Civitatem Novam, Sol. c. 40 (27, 10 Bip.); cf. Gesen. Gesch. d. Hebr. Spr. and Schr. pp. 228 and 229; and Robinson, Lexic. s. v. ). The city of Carthage, in Northern Africa (Gr. Καρχηδ

carthago2.full: Carthāgo (Karth-), ĭnis, f., the daughter of the fourth Hercules, Cic. N. D. 3, 16, 42.
carthago2.short: Carthāgo (Karth-), ĭnis, f., the daughter of the fourth Hercules, Cic.

cartheius.full: Carthēĭus, a, um, v. Carthaea, II.

cartibulum.full: cartĭbŭlum (-blum), i, n., a kind of oblong table of stone, standing on a pedestal: a gerendo gertibulum, unde cartibulum post dictum, Varr. L. L. 5, § 125 Müll. p. 35 sq. Bip.
cartibulum.short: cartĭbŭlum (-blum), i, n., a kind of oblong table of stone, standing on a pedestal: a gerendo gertibulum, unde cartibulum post dictum, Varr.

cartilagineus.full: cartĭlāgĭnĕus, a, um, adj. cartilago, cartilaginous, gristly, Plin. 9, 24, 40, § 78; 11, 37, 87, § 215; 19, 5, 23, § 64.

cartilaginosus.full: cartĭlāgĭnōsus, a, um, adj. id., full of cartilage, very gristly: pars, umerus, caput os, Cels. 8, 1: galbanum, Plin. 12, 25, 56, § 126.

cartilago.full: cartĭlāgo, ĭnis, f. Sanscr. kart, to spin; cf. κάρταλος, cratis, cartilage, gristle; in animals, Cels. 8, 1; Plin. 11, 37, 87, § 216; 9, 24, 40, § 78; 11, 4, 3, § 9.— Transf., in plants, a substance harder than pulp but softer than woody fibre, Plin. 15, 28, 34, § 116; 16, 36, 64, § 158.

cartismandua.full: Cartismandŭa (Cartim-), ae, f., queen of the Brigantes in Britain, Tac. A. 12, 36; 12, 40; id. H. 3, 45.
cartismandua.short: Cartismandŭa (Cartim-), ae, f., queen of the Brigantes in Britain, Tac.

caruncula.full: căruncŭla, ae, f. dim. 2. caro, a little piece of flesh, * Cic. Div. 2, 24, 52; Cels. 2, 7; 8, 4; Val. Max. 3, 7, ext. 6.

carus1.full: cārus (not chārus; in Inscrr. often kārus, Inscr. Orell. 1175; 2417 al.), a, um, adj. Sanscr. kan, to be beloved; kāru, agreeable, dear, precious, valued, esteemed (pass., freq. and class. in prose and poetry; syn.: dilectus, amatus, acceptus, gratus; opp. vilis, neglectus, contemptus; carum esse; syn. diligi); act., loving, affectionate, Verg. A. 1, 646: carum ipsum verbum est amoris, ex quo amicitiae nomen est ductum, Cic. N. D. 1, 44, 122; id. Off. 2, 8, 29; id. Fin. 3, 20, 66; 5, 10, 29: ego

carus2.full: Cārus, i, a Roman cognomen. T. Lucretius Carus, the poet; v. Lucretius.— M. Aurelius Carus, the Roman emperor, Eutr. 9, 12 al.— Another poet, Ov P. 4, 16, 7.

carventana arx.full: Carventāna arx, the citadel of Carventum near Velitrœ, in Latium, Liv. 4, 53, 9, and 55, 8.
carventana arx.short: Carventāna arx, the citadel of Carventum near Velitrœ, in Latium, Liv.

carvilius.full: Carvilius. The name of a Roman gens. Sp. Carvilius Maximus, consul B. C. 293 and 272, Liv. 10, 9, 12, and 39, 1 sq. al. — Sp. Carvilius Ruga, consul B. C. 234, the first person at Rome who divorced his wife, Cic. Sen. 4, 11; Liv. 23, 22, 4; Val. Max. 2, 1, 4; Gell. 4, 3, 2.—Hence, Carvilĭānus, a, um, adj., of Carvilius: divortium, Gell. 4, 3 in lemm.— Carvilius Pollis, Plin. 9, 11, 13, § 39; 33, 11, 51, § 144.— One of the four kings in Cantium (Kent), in the time of Julius Cœsar, Caes. B. G. 5,

caryae.full: Cărўae, ārum, f., = Καρύαι, a village in Laconia, with a temple of Diana Caryatis (now still Karyes), Liv. 34, 26, 9; 35, 27, 12. —In sing.: Cărўa, Vitr. 1, 1, 5.— Hence, Cărўātes, ium, m., the inhabitants of Caryœ, Vitr. 1, 1 bis.— Cărўā-tis, ĭdis, f., = Καρυᾶτις. An epithet of Diana, Serv. ad Verg. E. 8, 30.— Cărў-ātĭdes, the maidens of Caryœ serving in the temple of Diana, a statue of Praxiteles, Plin. 36, 5, 4, § 23.— In architecture, female figures used instead of columns in buildings, Cary
caryae.short: Cărўae, ārum, f., = Καρύαι, a village in Laconia, with a temple of Diana Caryatis (now still Karyes), Liv.

caryanda.full: Cărўanda, ae, f., a town on the coast of Caria, now Karatojan, Mel. 1, 16, 3; Plin. 5, 29, 29, § 107; 5, 31, 36, § 134.
caryanda.short: Cărўanda, ae, f., a town on the coast of Caria, now Karatojan, Mel.

caryinos.full: cărўī^nŏs, -ŏn, and -us, a, um, adj., = καρύϊνος, made from nuts: oleum, Plin. 15, 7, 7, § 28; 23, 4, 45, § 88.
caryinos.short: cărўī^nŏs, -ŏn, and -us, a, um, adj., = καρύϊνος, made from nuts: oleum, Plin.

caryites.full: cărўītes, ae, m., = καρυἱτης, a species of the plant tithymalus, Plin. 26, 8, 40, § 66.
caryites.short: cărўītes, ae, m., = καρυἱτης, a species of the plant tithymalus, Plin.

caryon.full: cărўon, ii, n., = κάρυον, a nut, Plin. 15, 22, 24, § 87.
caryon.short: cărўon, ii, n., = κάρυον, a nut, Plin.

caryota.full: cărўōta, ae (cărўōtis, ĭdis, Mart. 11, 31; Stat. S. 1, 6, 20), f., = καρυῶτις, a kind of nut-shaped date, Varr. R. R. 2, 1, 27; Plin. 15, 28, 34, § 116; 19, 5, 29, § 91; Plin. Ep. 1, 7, 6 al.; these the Romans were accustomed to send on the Saturnalia and New Year's day as a present to their friends and patrons, Mart. 8, 33, 11; 13, 27, 1.

carystos.full: Cărystŏs and -us, i, f., = Κάρυστος. A very ancient town on the south coast of Eubœa, famous for its marble, now Karysto or Castel Rosso, Mel. 2, 7, 9; Plin. 4, 12, 21, § 64; Liv. 32, 17; Tib. 3, 3, 14 al. — Derivv. Cărystēus, a, um, adj., of Carystos, Carystian: vada, Ov. F. 4, 282: marmor, Isid. Orig. 6, 11, 2; 16, 5, 15. — Cărystĭus, a, um, adj., the same: marmor, Plin. 4, 12, 21, § 64; 36, 6, 7, § 48: columellae, Plin. Ep. 5, 6, 36: LAPIDICINAE, Inscr. Orell. 2964.—In plur. subst.: Căry-stĭi

caryus.full: Cărўus, a, um, v. Caryae, II. B. 3.

casa.full: căsa, ae, f. Sanscr. khad, to cover; cf.: cassis, castrum, any simple or poorly-built house, a cottage, hut, cabin, shed, etc., Varr. R. R. 2, 10, 6; Lucr. 5, 1011; 6, 1254; Cic. Tusc. 5, 34, 97; Vitr. 2, 1; Verg. E. 2, 29; Tib. 2, 1, 24 et saep.; Cic. Fam. 16, 18, 2; a small country-house, Mart. 6, 43; Caes. B. G. 5, 43 Herz.; Veg. Mil. 2, 10.—Of babyhouses, Hor. S. 2, 3, 247.— Casae, in late Lat. meton., a country estate, a farm, Cassiod. Var. 5, 14.— Prov.: ita fugias, ne praeter casam, i. e.

casabundus.full: cāsābundus (in the best MSS. cassāb-, on account of the first long a, like cassus, caussa, Juppiter, etc.), a, um, adj. caso, ready to fall, tottering, Naev. ap. Varr. L. L. 7, § 53 Müll.; Macr. S. 5, 21, 16; cf. Paul. ex Fest. p. 48 Müll.

casarius.full: căsārĭus, a, um, adj. casa, of or belonging to a cottage; only substt., Că-sārĭus, ii, n., a dweller in a cottage, a cottager, Cod. Th. 9, 42, 7.— Căsārĭa, quae custodit casam, Paul. ex Fest. p. 48 Müll.

casca.full: Casca, ae, m., a Roman cognomen in the gens Servilia, Cic. Att. 13, 44, 3; 16, 15, 3; id. Phil. 13, 15, 31; 2, 11, 27; Suet. Caes. 82; cf. Varr. L. L. 7, § 28 Müll.
casca.short: Casca, ae, m., a Roman cognomen in the gens Servilia, Cic.

cascellius.full: Cascellĭus (Casell-), a, the name of a Roman gens, Varr. L. L. 9, § 71, p. 145 Bip.; Cic. Balb. 19, 45; id. Q. Fr. 1, 2, 2, § 5.—Esp.: A. Cascellius, a distinguished Roman lawyer in the time of Augustus, Hor. A. P. 371; Macr. S. 2, 6; Val. Max. 6, 2, 12; Dig. 1, 2, 2, § 45; Spald. ad Quint. 6, 3, 87.—Hence, Cascellianum judicium, Gai Inst. 4, 166; cf. id. ib. 4, 169.
cascellius.short: Cascellĭus (Casell-), a, the name of a Roman gens, Varr.

cascus.full: cascus, a, um, adj. cf. canus, old: cascum significat vetus: ejus origo Sabina quae usque radices in Oscam linguam egit, Varr. L. L. 7, § 28; cf. Müll. Etrusk. 1, p. 41, and v. casnar: quam prisci casci populi tenuere Latini, Enn. Ann. 24 Vahl.; cf. Cic. Tusc. 1, 12, 27; so Manil. and Papin. ap. Varr. l. l.; Att. ib.: sal, Aus. Ep. 22, 27.— Hence, * cascē, adv.: casce nimis et prisce loquens, in an old-fashioned manner, Gell. 1, 10 in lemm.

casearius.full: cāsĕārĭus, a, um, adj. caseus, pertaining to cheese, cheese-: taberna, in which cheese was smoked and kept, Dig. 8, 5, 8, § 5.

caseatus.full: cāsĕātus, a, um, adj. id., mixed with cheese: polenta, App. M. 1, p. 103, 35: montes, where much cheese was made, Hier. Ep. 66, 10.

casellula.full: căsellŭla, ae, f. dim. casa, a little hut (late Lat.), Ennod. Ep. 8, 29.

caseolus.full: cāsĕŏlus, i, m. dim. caseus, a small cheese, Verg. Copa, 17.

caseus.full: cāsĕus, i, m. (cāsĕum, i, n., Cato, R. R. 76, 3 and 4; Plaut. and Nov. ap. Non. p. 200, 9 sq.), cheese, Varr. R. R. 2, 11, 3; Col. 7, 8, 1; 12, 12 sq.; Pall Mai, 9; Plin. 11, 42, 97, § 240 sq.; Plaut. Capt. 4, 2, 72; Cic. Sen. 16, 56; Ov. F. 4, 371 al.: facere, Varr. l. l.: premere, Verg. E. 1, 35: figurare, Plin. 16, 38, 72, § 181.—As a comic term of endearment: molliculus and dulciculus caseus, Plaut. Poen. 1, 2, 157 and 179.

casia.full: căsĭa (rarely cassia, e. g. Pall. Oct. 14, 13; Veg. 6, 13, 3 and 4), ae, f., = κασία or κασσία. A tree with an aromatic bark, similar to cinnamon, prob. the wild cinnamon: Laurus cassia, Linn.; Plin. 12, 19, 42, § 85, and 12, 19, 43, § 95 sq.; Verg. G. 2, 466; Plaut. Curc. 1, 2, 6; Cels. 5, 23, 1 and 2; Scrib. Comp. 93; 125 al.— A fragrant, shrub-like plant, mexereon, also called cneoron or thymelaea, q. v., Plin. 21, 9, 29, § 53; 21, 12, 41, § 70; Verg. E. 2, 49; id. G. 2, 213; 4, 30; 4, 182; O

casignete.full: căsignētē, ēs, f., = κασιγνήτη, the name of a plant, Plin. 24, 17, 102, § 165.
casignete.short: căsignētē, ēs, f., = κασιγνήτη, the name of a plant, Plin.

casilinum.full: Căsĭlīnum, i, n., a town in Campania, on the Vulturnus, near the ancient Capua. In its place stands the present Capua, Liv. 22, 15, 3; 23, 17, 8 sq., and 19, 1 sq.; Cic. Att. 16, 8, 1; id. Phil. 2, 40, 102; Caes. B. C. 3, 21; Plin. 3, 5, 9, § 70.— Hence, Căsĭlīnenses, ium, m., the inhabitants of Casilinum, Cic. Inv. 2, 57, 171.— Căsĭlīnātes, ium, m., the same, Val. Max. 7, 6, 2.— Căsĭlīnus, a, um, adj., of Casilinum: limina, i. e. Casilini portae, Sil. 12, 426.
casilinum.short: Căsĭlīnum, i, n., a town in Campania, on the Vulturnus, near the ancient Capua.

casina.full: Căsĭna, ae, f., the name of a comedy of Plautus, from its heroine; cf. Paul. ex Fest. p. 61. Müll.
casina.short: Căsĭna, ae, f., the name of a comedy of Plautus, from its heroine;

casinum.full: Căsīnum, i, n., a town of Latium, east of Aquinium, now ruins near S. Germano: its citadel the present Monte Casino, Varr. L. L. 7, § 29, p. 86 Bip.; id. R. R. 3, 4, 2; Plin. 3, 5, 9, § 63.— Hence the adjj., Căsīnas, ātis, of Casinum: ager, Cato, R. R. 136; Cic. Agr. 2, 25, 65: fundus, id. Phil. 2, 40, 103; and absol.: in Casinati or Casinate, in the region of Casinum, Varr. R. R. 2, 3, 11; Plin. 2, 103, 106, § 227.— Căsīnus, a, um, of Casinum: Nymphae, Sil. 12, 527 dub. (others, Casini Nymphae)
casinum.short: Căsīnum, i, n., a town of Latium, east of Aquinium, now ruins near S.

casito.full: cāsĭto, āvi, āre, v. freq. [cado], to fall repeatedly, to drop down: si ex tegulā casitaverit stillicidium, Dig. 8, 2, 20, § 3 sq.

casius.full: Căsĭus mons, = Κάσιον ὄρος. A very high mountain in Syria, on the Orontes, now Jebel-Okrab, Plin. 5, 22, 18, § 80; Amm. 14, 8, 10; 22, 14, 4.— A mountain between Lower Egypt and Arabia, with a temple of Jupiter, near which Pompey was murdered, now El Kas or El Katieh, Mel. 1, 10; 3, 8, 3; Plin. 5, 12, 14, § 68.—Hence, Căsĭus, a, um, adj.: rupes, Luc. 10, 434: harenae, id. 8, 539: Juppiter, Enn. Eutr. 54 Vahl.; Plin. 5, 12, 14, § 68.

casnar1.full: casnar, in the lang. of the Osci, an old man, Varr. L. L, 7, § 29, p. 86 Bip.; Paul. ex Fest. p. 47 Müll. Here belongs the fragment of Varr. ap. Non. p. 86, 20: cum more majorum ultro carnales arripiunt, where others prefer the reading casnares; cf. Momms. Unt. Dial. p. 268 (carnales is perh. a euphonic form for casnares, from a Lat. sing. carnal = casnar, as foedesum, plusima, asa, asena = foederum, plurima, etc.; cf. the letter R).

casnar2.full: casnar, acc. to Quint. 1, 5, 8 Gallic, = assectator, attendant (Meyer, l. l. and Or. Rom. Fragm. p. 530 compares the old French, casnard, flatteur, adulateur; casnarder, aduler, idolatrer. But it is to be remarked that the best MSS. of Quint. l. l. give casami, casamo, casamum, and the like; v. Spald. and Zumpt N. cr. ad h. l.).

casperia.full: Caspĕrĭa, ae, f., an old but small town of the Sabines, now prob. Aspra, Verg. A. 7, 714; Sil. 8, 417.
casperia.short: Caspĕrĭa, ae, f., an old but small town of the Sabines, now prob.

caspium.full: Caspĭum măre, = τὸ Κάσπιον πέλαγος, the Caspian Sea, Mel. 1, 2, 1; 3, 5, 3; 3, 6, 10; Plin. 6, 11, 12, § 31; Hor. C. 2, 9, 2: pelagus, Mel. 1, 19, 13: Caspius oceanus, Plin. 6, 13, 15, § 36: Caspium aequor, id. 5, 27, 27, § 97 al.— Hence adjj., Cas-pĭus, a, um, of or belonging to the Caspian Sea, Caspian: sinus, Mel. 1, 2, 3 and 4; 3, 5, 3, 4 and 8; Plin. 2, 68, 68, § 173: litora, id. 6, 25, 29, § 112: mons, i. e. a part of Taurus, Mel. 1, 19, 13.—And as subst.: Caspĭus, ii, m. (sc. mons), Plin.
caspium.short: Caspĭum măre, = τὸ Κάσπιον πέλαγος, the Caspian Sea, Mel.

cassander.full: Cassander, dri, m., = Κάσσανδρος. A son of Antipater, and king of Macedonia after the death of Alexander the Great, Just. 15, 1 sq.; Curt. 10, 10, 9; Cic. Off. 2, 14, 48; Nep. Eum. 13, 3.—After him was named the town Cassandrea, Liv. 44, 11, 2. — A Greek astrologer, Cic. Div. 2, 42, 88.

cassandra.full: Cassandra (acc. to Quint. 1, 4, 16; cf. Alexanter; in the most ancient period written in the Etruscan manner, Cassantra), ae, f., = Κασσάνδρα, a daughter of Priam and Hecuba, who continually proclaimed the approaching evil, but was believed by no one. After the destruction of Troy she became the bondmaid of Agamemnon, and was murdered with him by Clytœmnestra, Cic. Div. 1, 39, 85; Verg. A. 2 404; 2, 246 Serv.; 3, 187; 5, 636; Ov. H. 16, 119; Hyg. Fab. 93 and 117.

cassandrea.full: Cassandrēa or -īa, ae, f., a town in Macedonia, upon the peninsula Pallene, previously called Potidœa, but rebuilt by Cassander, Liv. 28, 8, 14; 44, 11, 1 sq.; Mel. 2, 3, 1; Plin. 4, 10, 17, § 36.— Hence, Cassandrenses, ium, m., the inhabitants of Cassandrea, Liv. 44, 10, 12; Dig. 50, 15, 8.— Cassandreus (trisyl.), ei, m., = Κασσανδρεύς, of Cassandrea, a surname of the tyrant Apollodorus, who reigned there, Ov. P. 2, 9, 43.
cassandrea.short: Cassandrēa or -īa, ae, f., a town in Macedonia, upon the peninsula Pallene, previously called Potidœa, but rebuilt by Cassander, Liv.

casse.full: cassē, a false conjectural reading for the MS. cassae, Liv. 24, 26, 10 Drak.; v. Weissenb. ad loc.
casse.short: cassē, a false conjectural reading for the MS.

casses.full: casses, ium (in sing. acc. cassem, Grat. Cyn. 28; abl. casse, Ov. A. A. 3, 554; Sen. Agam. 885, p. 893 Bip.), m., a hunting-net, a snare, toil (poet.; in prose: plaga, retia), Verg. G. 3, 371; Tib. 4, 3, 17; Prop. 4 (5), 2, 33; Ov. M. 5, 579 al.— Meton., a spider's web, Verg. G. 4, 247; Mart. 3, 93, 5; Arn. 6, 202.— Trop., snares, plots: casses tendere alicui, Tib. 1, 6, 5; Ov. A. A. 3, 554.

cassi.full: Cassi, ōrum, m., a tribe of Britain, now Herts, Caes. B. G. 5, 21.
cassi.short: Cassi, ōrum, m., a tribe of Britain, now Herts, Caes.

cassianus.full: Cassĭānus, a, um, v. Cassius, B.

cassiculus.full: cassĭcŭlus, i, m. dim. casses, a small net, a cobweb, Hier. Ruf. 3, 6; cf. Paul. ex Fest. p. 48 Müll.

cassidarius.full: cassĭdārĭus, ii, m., a helmet-maker, Inscr. Orell. 4160.
cassidarius.short: cassĭdārĭus, ii, m., a helmet-maker, Inscr.

cassidile.full: cassĭdīle, is, n. dim. 1. cassis, a small bag or wallet, Vulg. Tob. 8, 2.

cassiodorus.full: Cassĭŏdōrus, i, m., Magnus Aurelius, a learned Roman, minister under Theodoric, king of the Ostrogoths, and author of several works in Latin; esp. Variarum (Epistt.), Libri XII.
cassiodorus.short: Cassĭŏdōrus, i, m., Magnus Aurelius, a learned Roman, minister under Theodoric, king of the Ostrogoths, and author of several works in Latin;

cassiope1.full: Cassĭŏpē, ēs (Cassĭŏpēa, ae, Manil. 1, 354; Cassĭĕpēa or Cassĭĕ-peia, Cic. N. D. 2, 43, 111; Hyg. Astr. 2, 10), f., = Κασσιόπη, Κασσιόπεια, and Κασσιέπεια, the proud wife of Cepheus, and mother of Andromeda, who was punished on her account; made finally a constellation, Hyg. Fab. 64; id. Astr. 2, 10; 3, 10; Prop. 1, 17, 3; Ov. M. 4, 738; Cic. l. l.

cassiope2.full: Cassĭŏpē, ēs, f., = Κασσιόπη, a town in Corcyra, now Cassopo or Cassiope, Cic. Fam. 16, 9, 1; Suet. Ner. 22; Plin. 4, 12, 19, § 52.—Called Cassĭŏpa, ae, f., Gell. 19, 1, 1.—Hence, Cassĭŏpĭcus, a, um, of Cassiope: filix, Plin. 27, 9, 55, § 80.
cassiope2.short: Cassĭŏpē, ēs, f., = Κασσιόπη, a town in Corcyra, now Cassopo or Cassiope, Cic.

cassis1.full: cassis, ĭdis (access. form cassĭda, ae, like chlamyda from chlamys, Prop. 3 (4), 11, 15; Verg. A. 11, 775; cf. Prob. II. p. 1473 P. Lind.; Charis. p. 80 P.; Prisc. p. 698 ib. Also Paul. ex Fest. p. 48, instead of cassilam, the reading should be cassidam), f. Etruscan, acc. to Isid. Orig. 18, 14, 1; cf. Müll. Etrusk. 1, p. 392; cf. Sanscr. khad, to cover, and Lat. castrum, casa, a helmet, commonly of metal (as galea was of leather, Isid. Orig. 18, 14, 1; cf. Tac. G. 6), Plaut. Trin. 3, 2, 100; Ca

cassita.full: cassīta, ae, f [1. cassis, like galerita from galerus], the crested or tufted lark: Alauda cristata, Linn.; Gell. 2, 29, 3 sqq.

cassiterides.full: Cassĭtĕrĭdes, um, f., = Κασσιτερίδες, the tin-islands, Cassiterides, now prob. the Scilly Islands, Mel. 3, 6, 2; Plin. 4, 22, 36, § 119; named from the tin found there; v. cassiterum.
cassiterides.short: Cassĭtĕrĭdes, um, f., = Κασσιτερίδες, the tin-islands, Cassiterides, now prob.

cassiterum.full: cassĭtĕrum (-ron), i, n., = κασσίτερος, orig. a mixture or alloy of lead, silver, and other metals; afterwards tin (= plumbum album), Plin. 34, 16, 47, § 156; Avien. Or. Mar. 260; cf. Charis. p. 21 P.; Diom. p. 315 ib.—Hence, cassĭtĕrĭnus, a, um, adj., = κασσιτέρινος, made of tin: lamella, Pelagon. Vet. 7.

cassius.full: Cassĭus, a old form Casseius; hence, Cassīus, and from this Cassĭus is formed; cf. Ritschl de Sepulcro Fur., the name of a Roman gens; esp. distinguished, L. Cassius Longinus Ravilla, a very severe judge; from him the Lex tabellaria Cassia proceeded, A. U. C. 617, by which the judges were obliged to vote with little tablets, Cic. Leg. 3, 16, 35; id. Sest. 48, 103; id. Brut. 25, 97; 27, 106; and Ascon. Cic. Verr. 1, 1, 10, § 30.— Hence, Cassĭānus, a, um, adj., of Cassius, Cic. Mil. 12, 32; id. Ph

cassivellaunus.full: Cassivellaunus, i, m., a British chief, defeated by Cœsar, Caes. B. G. 5, 11; 5, 18.
cassivellaunus.short: Cassivellaunus, i, m., a British chief, defeated by Cœsar, Caes.

casso1.full: casso, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. cassus (late Lat.). In gen., to bring to naught, destroy, trop., Sid. Ep. 1 fin.— In the Lat. of the jurists, to annul, make null or void, = abrogo, Cod. Th. 11, 1, 3 al.

casso2.full: casso (caso), avi, atum, 1, v. n., rare collat. form of quasso (only in Plautus), to shake, waver: ubi bacchabatur aula, cassabant cadi, Plaut. Mil. 3, 2, 41; cf. v. 37: capitibus cassantibus, id. Bacch. 2, 3, 71; cf. quasso, II.

cassus.full: cassus, a, um, adj., empty, void, hollow. Prop. (syn.: inanis, vacuus; mostly poet.). Absol.: nux, Plaut. Ps. 1, 3, 137; Hor. S. 2, 5, 36: glans, Plaut. Rud. 5, 2, 37: canna, unfruitful, Ov. F. 6, 406: granum inane cassumque, Plin. 18, 17, 45, § 161: anulus, Fab. Pict. ap. Gell. 10, 15. 6.—Subst.: palearum cassa, Sol. c. 52 fin.— Expressing that of which the subject is empty, etc., wanting, devoid of, deprived of, without. With abl.: sanguine cassa (cochlea), bloodless, Poët. ap. Cic. Div. 2, 64
cassus.short: cassus, a, um, adj., empty, void, hollow.

castabala.full: Castăbăla, ōrum, and -lum, i, n., a town of Cilicia, Plin. 5, 27, 22, § 93; Curt. 3, 7, 5.—Castăbălenses, its inhabitants, Plin. 8, 40, 61, § 143.
castabala.short: Castăbăla, ōrum, and -lum, i, n., a town of Cilicia, Plin.

castalia.full: Castălĭa, ae, f., = Κασταλία, a fountain on Parnassus, sacred to Apollo and the Muses, Liv. Andron. ap. Fest. p. 310, b Müll.; Verg. G. 3, 293; Hor. C. 3, 4, 61; Stat. Th. 1, 698.— Hence the adjj., Castă-lĭus, a, um, Castalian: fons, Plin. 4, 3, 4, § 8; Sen. Oedip. 229; cf. fontes, Stat. Th. 1, 565: arbor, the laurel, Prop. 3 (4), 3, 13. hence, umbra, Tib. 3, 1, 16: antrum, i. e. the cave of the oracle at Delphi, Ov. M. 3, 14.— Castălis, ĭdis, f., Castalian: unda, Mart. 9, 19 fin.: sorores, i. e
castalia.short: Castălĭa, ae, f., = Κασταλία, a fountain on Parnassus, sacred to Apollo and the Muses, Liv.

castana.full: Castana, ae, f., a town in Magnesia, Plin. 4, 9, 16, § 32; cf. Mel. 2, 3, 1.
castana.short: Castana, ae, f., a town in Magnesia, Plin.

castanea.full: castănĕa, ae, f., = κάστανον. The chestnut-tree, Col. 4, 33; 5, 10, 14; Pall. Febr. 25, 33; id. Nov. 7, 17; Plin. 16, 40, 78, § 212; 17, 20, 34, § 147 sq.; Verg. G. 2, 15; 2, 71.— A chestnut, Verg. E. 1, 82; 7, 53; Plin. 13, 18, 32, § 110; 15, 28, 34, § 112; cf. appos. castaneae nuces, Verg. E. 2, 52; Ov. A. A. 2, 26, 8.

castanetum.full: castănētum, i, n. castanea. a chestnut-grove, Col. 4, 30, 3; 4, 33, 3; Pall. Nov. 7, 21.

castellanus.full: castellānus, a, um, adj. castellum, of or pertaining to a fort or castle: triumphi, for the capture of a castle, * Cic. Brut. 73, 256: miles, Cod. Th. 7, 15, 2.— As subst.: castellāni, ōrum, m., the occupants of a castle, Sall. J. 92, 7; Hirt. B. Alex. 42, 3; Liv 34, 27, 2; 38, 45, 9.

castellarius.full: castellārĭus, ii, m. id., the superintendent of a reservoir, Front. Aquaed. 117; Inscr. Orell. 2899 al.

castellatim.full: castellātim, adv. id., castle-wise: dissipati, scattered about, qs. in different fortresses, i. e. in separate detachments, Liv. 7, 36, 10: grumulis imponere allium, i. e. in clusters or hills, Plin. 19, 6, 34, § 112.

castellum.full: castellum, i, n. dim. castrum, a castle, fort, citadel, fortress, stronghold, Sisenn. ap. Non. p. 514, 7; Caes. B. G. 2, 30; id. B. C. 3, 36; Cic. Phil. 5, 4, 9; id. Caecin. 7, 20; Sall. J. 54, 6; Nep. Milt. 2, 1; id. Alcib. 7, 4; Liv. 10, 46, 11; 21, 11, 10; Verg. A. 5, 440; Hor. Ep. 2, 2, 34 al.; also of a single bulwark, bastion, Caes. B. G. 1, 8; 2, 8; 7, 69; id. B. C. 3, 44; and poet. of a dwelling in an elevated position, Verg. G. 3, 475.— In mechanics, a structure in which the water of an

casteria.full: castērĭa, ae, f., a part of a ship where rowers were accustomed to rest, the rowers' room, Plaut. As. 3, 1, 10 (16); cf. Non. p. 85, 26.
casteria.short: castērĭa, ae, f., a part of a ship where rowers were accustomed to rest, the rowers' room, Plaut.

castifico.full: castĭfĭco, āre, v. a. castificus, to purify, make pure (eccl. Lat.), Tert. Pud. 19; Aug. Conf. 9, 9 al.

castificus.full: castĭfĭcus, a, um castus-facio. * Purifying: lavacrum = baptisma, Paul. Nol. Carm. 25, 188.—* Pure: mens, Sen. Hippol. 169.

castigabilis.full: castīgābĭlis, e, adj. castigo, deserving punishment: culpa, Plaut. Trin. 1, 2, 6.

castigatio.full: castīgātĭo, ōnis, f. castigo, a correcting, chastising, punishment, correction, etc. (in good prose). Lit. In gen., of blows. etc. (rare, and always with gen.: fustium, Dig. 1, 15, 3: flagellorum, ib. 48, 19, 7.— Of verbal chastisement, reproof, etc. (class. and freq.): omnis et animad. versio et castigatio contumeliā vacare debet, Cic. Off. 1, 25, 88; cf. id. ib. 1, 38, 137: admonitio frequens, interdum et castigatio, vindicta rarissima, Vell. 2, 114, 3; Quint. 1, 3, 14; 3, 8, 54: tacita, Liv.

castigator.full: castīgātor, ōris, m. castigo, one who corrects or chastises, a corrector, reprover (not in Cic.), Plaut. Trin. 1, 2, 150; 3, 1, 13: lacrimarum atque inertium querelarum, Liv. 1, 59, 4: castigator censorque minorum, * Hor. A. P. 174: tot saeculorum, Col. 8, 16, 6; cf. Sen. Ira, 1, 15, 3; Plin. Pan. 40, 1.

castigatorius.full: castīgātōrĭus, a, um, adj. castigator, after the manner of reprovers or correctors, reproving, censuring (post-Aug. and very rare): solatium, Plin. Ep. 5, 16, 10: severitas, Sid. Ep. 4, 1.

castigo.full: castīgo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. castum-ago, as purgo = purum-ago, to set right by word or deed, to correct, chastise, punish; to blame, reprove, chide, censure, find fault with (syn.: animadvertere, punire; more forcible than reprehendere and vituperare; weaker than culpare; class. in prose and poetry): pueros non verbis solum, sed etiam verberibus, Cic. Tusc. 3, 27, 64; so, verberibus, Plin. 8, 3, 3, § 6; cf. Liv. 26, 27, 8; Curt. 8, 6, 5: magnā clade, Liv. 39, 1, 4: baculo, Front. Strat. 1, 1, 3:

castimonia.full: castīmōnĭa, ae, f. (castĭmōnĭ-nium, i, n., App. M. 11. p. 266, 9; cf. castimonium ἁγνεία, Gloss. Philox.) [castus, like acrimonia, aegrimonia, etc.]. * Ingen., purity of morals, morality, Cic. Cael. 5, 11. — Esp., purity, such as is requisite for religious services (abstaining from sexual intercourse, from delicate food, etc.), purity, chastity, abstinence (rare but class.): quae sacra per summam castimoniam virorum ac mulierum fiant, eadem per istius stuprum ac flagitium esse violata, Cic. Verr

castimonialis.full: castĭmōnĭālis, e, adj. castimonia, pertaining to abstinence or continence: liquamen, Pall. Febr. 25, 12, p. 92 Bip.

castitas.full: castĭtas, ātis, f. castus, purity. In gen., purity of morals, morality (postclass.): vitae, Gell. 15, 18, 2.— Esp. Purity of body, chastity (rare but class.; syn. pudicitia): ut sentiant mulieres naturam feminarum omnem castitatem pati, * Cic. Leg. 2, 12, 29 Mos.; so * Hor. C. 3, 24, 23; Plin. 24, 9, 38, § 59; Plin. Pan. 20, 2; Tac. Agr. 4; id. A. 1, 33; Val. Max. 9, 1, 2. —Hence, person.: Castĭtas, the goddess of Chastity, = Minerva, Pall. 1, 6, 14.— Purity with regard to gain, disinterestednes

castitudo.full: castĭtūdo, ĭnis, f. id. (ante-class. access. form to castitas; cf.: bellitudo, canitudo, etc.), moral purity: antiqua, Att. ap. Non. p. 85, 11.

castor1.full: castor, ŏris, m., = κάστωρ, the castor, beaver; pure Lat. fiber: Castor fiber, Linn.; Plin. 32, 3, 13, § 26; cf. id. 8, 30, 47, § 109; Cic. ap. Isid. Orig. 12, 2, 21; Ov. Nux. 166; acc. castorem, App. M. 1, p. 106, 10: castora, Juv. 12, 34.
castor1.short: castor, ŏris, m., = κάστωρ, the castor, beaver;

castor2.full: Castor, ŏris (acc. to some gramm. Castōris, Quint. 1, 5, 60), m., = Κάστωρ. The son of the Spartan king Tyndarus and Leda, brother of Helena and Pollux, with whom, as twin star (Gemini; hence even Castores, Plin. 10, 43, 60, § 121; 35, 4, 10, § 27; 7, 22, 22, § 86; and: alter Castor, Stat. S. 4, 6, 16), he served as a guide to mariners, Varr. L. L. 5, § 58; Cic. N. D. 2, 2, 6; 3, 18, 45; Hor. Ep. 2, 1, 5; id. Epod. 17, 42; 17, 43; id. C. 4, 5, 35: gaudet equis, id. S. 2, 1, 26; cf. id. C. 1, 12,

castoreum.full: castŏrĕum, ei, n. 1. castor, castor or castoreum, a secretion of the beaver having a strong odor, Plin. 8, 30, 47, § 109; Lucr. 6, 794; Cels. 6, 7, 8; Scrib. 3.—In plur., Verg. G. 1, 59; Plin. 32, 9, 31, § 101; Nemes. C. 224.

castoreus.full: Castŏrĕus, a, um, v. 2. Castor, II. C.

castorinatus.full: castŏrīnātus, a, um, adj. 1. castor, clothed in the fur of the beaver, Sid. Ep. 5, 7.

castorinus.full: castŏrīnus, a, um, adj. id., pertaining to the beaver, beaver-: oleum, Marc. Emp. 35: pellis, Edict. Diocl. p. 23.

castra.full: castra, ōrum and ae, v. castrum.

castrametor.full: castră-mētor, āri, 1, v. n., to pitch a camp, Jornand. 4, 54 al.

castranus.full: Castrānus, a, um, adj., of Castrum Inui (v. castrum, I.): rura, Mart. 4, 60.
castranus.short: Castrānus, a, um, adj., of Castrum Inui (v.

castratio.full: castrātĭo, ōnis, f. castro. An emasculating, castration of animals, Col. 6, 26; 7, 11, 1; Pall. Mai, 7, 3; Dig. 21, 1, 38.— A pruning, Plin. 16, 40, 76, § 206.

castrator.full: castrātor, ōris, m. id., one who castrates (late Lat.), Tert. adv. Marc. 1, 1.

castratorius.full: castrātōrĭus, a, um, adj. id., of or for castration: ferramenta, Pall. 1, 4, 3.

castratura.full: castrātūra, ae, f. id.. * An emasculalion, castration of animals, Pall. Mai, 7, 2.— A pruning, cleansing of plants: siliginis, Plin. 18, 9, 20, § 86.

castrensiani.full: castrensĭāni, ōrum, m. castra, attendants of the Castrensis S. Palatii, Cod. Th. 6, 32; Cod. Just. 12, 36, 14.

castrensiarius.full: castrensĭārĭus NEGOTIATOR, a purveyor for the camp, a suttler, Inscr. Orell. 4254.
castrensiarius.short: castrensĭārĭus NEGOTIATOR, a purveyor for the camp, a suttler, Inscr.

castrensis.full: castrensis, e, adj. castra, of or per-taining to the camp, camp-: ratio ac militaris, Cic. Cael. 5, 11: arma, Prop. 3 (4), 9, 19. consilium, Liv. 44, 35, 4: triumphus, id. 7, 36, 8: corona, awarded to him who first entered the enemy's camp, acc. to Gell. 5, 6, 17; cf. Paul. ex Fest. p. 57 Müll. (also called vallaris, v. h. v.): jurisdictio, Tac. Agr. 9: ludi, Suet. Tib. 72 Oud.: jocus, id. Calig. 9: vigilia, Plin. 10, 21, 24, § 46: exsilium. sarcastically, for military service, Just. 14, 4, 14:

castricius.full: Castricius or -tius, a, um, a Roman gentile name, Cic. Verr. 2, 3, 80, § 185; id. Fl. 23, 54; id. Att. 12, 28, 3 al.—Hence, Castriciānus or -tiānus, a, um, adj., pertaining to a Castricius: negotium, Cic. Att. 12, 28, 3: nomen, id. Fl. 23, 24: mendum, id. Att. 2, 7, 5.
castricius.short: Castricius or -tius, a, um, a Roman gentile name, Cic.

castro.full: castro, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. Sanscr. çastra, knife, sword. To deprive of generative power (both of male and female), to emasculate, castrate, geld: hircum, Plaut. Merc. 2, 2, 1 and 4: agnum, Varr. R. R. 2, 2, 18: gallos, id. ib. 3, 9, 3; Curt. 6, 3, 12; Val. Max. 6, 1, 13; Suet. Dom. 7: sues, Plin. 8, 51, 77, § 208; 10, 21, 25, § 50; 11, 51, 112, § 261 al.— Transf. to plants, to prune, lop, trim, Cato, R. R. 33, 2; Plin. 17, 20, 33, § 144; 24, 8, 33, § 49.— Trop.: vina saccis, to pass through a s

castrum.full: castrum, i, n. kindred with casa, q. v.. In sing., any fortified place; a castle, fort, fortress (more rare than castellum): ei Grunium dederat in Phrygiā castrum, etc., Nep. Alcib. 9, 3; Liv. 32. 29, 4; Dig. 27, 1, 17 fin.— Esp., nom. propr. Castrum Altum or Album, in Hispania Tarraconensis, Liv. 24, 41, 3.— Castrum Inui, or simply Castrum, an ancient city of the Rutuli, near Ardea, Verg. A. 6, 775; called Castrum, Ov. M. 15, 727; Sil. 8, 359. — Castrum Novum, a city on the seacoast of Etruria,

castula.full: castŭla, ae, f., a garment used by women, a kind of petticoat, Varr. ap. Non. p. 548, 30 sq.
castula.short: castŭla, ae, f., a garment used by women, a kind of petticoat, Varr.

castulo.full: Castŭlo, ōnis, m. (Liv.), and f. (Sil.), = Καστούλων, a town in Hispania Tarraconensis, near the borders of Baetica, now the village Cazlona, Liv. 24, 41, 7; 28, 19, 2 sq.; Sil. 3, 99; 3, 391; Plin. 3, 2, 3, § 17.—Hence, Castŭlōnensis, e, adj., of Castulo: saltus, Asin. ap. Cic. Fam. 10, 31, 1; Caes. B. C. 1, 38; Liv. 22, 20, 12; and as subst.: Castŭlōnenses, ium, m., the inhabitants of Castulo, Plin. 3, 3, 4, § 25.

castus1.full: castus, a, um, adj. i. e. cas-tus, partic., kindr. to Sanscr. çludh, to cleanse; Gr. καθ-αρός; Germ. keusch, heiter; cf. the opp. in-ces-tus, impure, Bopp, Gloss. 351, 6; Pott. 1, 252. In gen., morally pure, unpolluted, spotless, guiltless, = purus, integer (gen. in respect to the person himself, while candidus signifies pure, just, in respect to other men; v. Doed. Syn. p. 196 sq.; class. in prose and poetry): castus animus purusque, Cic. Div. 1, 53, 121; cf.: vita purissima et castissima, id.

castus2.full: castus, ūs (abl. heterocl. casto, Tert. Jejun. 16; Fest. s. v. minuitur, p. 154, 6 Müll.), m. 1. castus, ante- and post-class. for castimonia, an abstinence from sensual enjoyments on religious grounds, Naev. ap. Non. p. 197, 16; Varr. ib.; Gell. 10, 15, 1; Arn. 5, p. 167.

casualis.full: cāsŭālis, e, adj. casus. Casual, fortuitous (post-class. and very rare): condicio, depending upon chance, Cod. Just. 6, 51, 1, § 7.—Adv.: cāsŭālĭter, accidentally, Sid. Ep. 9, 11; Fulg. Myth. 1, 5.— In gram., relating to or declined with cases: Casuale, ut ab equo: equum, Varr. L. L. 8, § 52, p. 116 Bip.; cf. id. ib. 10, § 18, p. 164 Bip.: formae, Prisc. p. 672 P. al.

casualiter.full: cāsŭālĭter, adv., v. casualis, I. fin.

casula.full: căsŭla, ae, f. dim. casa, a little cottage or hut, a small house, Petr. 44, 15; 46, 2; 77, 4; Juv. 11, 153.— A sepulchre = hypogeum, Petr. 111, 5.

casus1.full: cāsus (Ciceronis temporibus paulumque infra s geminabatur: cassus, etc., Quint. 1, 7, 20; cf.: causa, Juppiter al.; in inscr. also KASVS), ūs (dat. casu, Nep. Alcib. 6, 4), m. cado. Lit., a falling (acc. to cado, I. A. and C.). A falling down, etc.: stillicidi, Lucr. 1, 313: geli, id. 5, 205: nivis, Liv. 21, 35, 6: fulminum, Plin. 2, 50, 51, § 135; Ov. M. 8, 259: celsae graviore casu Decidunt turres, Hor. C. 2, 10, 10.—In plur., Lucr. 2, 231.— A fall, an overthrow, a throwing down: occumbunt mul
casus1.short: cāsus (Ciceronis temporibus paulumque infra s geminabatur: cassus, etc., Quint.

casus2.full: Cāsus, i, m., a river of Albania, that flows into the Caspian Sea, Plin. 6, 13, 15, § 39; Mel. 3, 5, 4.
casus2.short: Cāsus, i, m., a river of Albania, that flows into the Caspian Sea, Plin.

cata.full: cătă, prep., = κατά, in distrib. sense, by: faciet sacrificium super eo cata mane mane, morning by morning, Vulg. Ezech. 46, 15; cf. v. 14.

catabasis.full: cătăbăsis, is, abl. i, f., = κατάβασις, a going down, descent, the name of a ceremonial at the festival of the Magna Mater, Macr. S. 1, 21, 10.

catabathmos.full: Cătăbathmos, i, m., = Καταβαθμός, a tract of land in Libya, between Egypt and Cyrenaica, now Akabah, with a city of the same name, Sall. J. 17, 5; 19, 3; Mel. 1, 8, 1; 1, 9, 1; Plin. 5, 5, 5, § 32.
catabathmos.short: Cătăbathmos, i, m., = Καταβαθμός, a tract of land in Libya, between Egypt and Cyrenaica, now Akabah, with a city of the same name, Sall.

catabolcnses.full: cătăbŏlcnses, ium, m., a class of carriers who transport burdens by means of draught animals, a kind of muleteers, Cod. Th. 14, 3, 9; Cassiod. Var. Ep. 3, 10.
catabolcnses.short: cătăbŏlcnses, ium, m., a class of carriers who transport burdens by means of draught animals, a kind of muleteers, Cod.

catacecaumene.full: Cătăcĕcaumĕnē, ēs, f., = Κατακεκαυμένη (scorched), a region of Mysia or Mœonia, scorched by the sun, but abounding in vines.—Hence, Cătăcĕcaumĕ-nītes, ae, m., = Κατακεκαυμενίτης (sc. οἶνος), the wine of this region, Vitr. 8, 3, 12; Plin. 14, 7, 9, § 75; cf. Vitr. 2, 6.
catacecaumene.short: Cătăcĕcaumĕnē, ēs, f., = Κατακεκαυμένη (scorched), a region of Mysia or Mœonia, scorched by the sun, but abounding in vines.—Hence, Cătăcĕcaumĕ-nītes, ae, m., = Κατακεκαυμενίτης (sc.

catachana.full: cătăchāna (or -channa), ae, f., = καταχήνη, a tree inoculated with buds of different fruit-trees, M. Aurel. ap. Front. 1, p. 77.— Trop., of parodies, Spart. Had. 16, 2.
catachana.short: cătăchāna (or -channa), ae, f., = καταχήνη, a tree inoculated with buds of different fruit-trees, M.

catachresis.full: cătăchrēsis, is, f., = κατάχρησις, a rhet. figure, an improper use of a word; in pure Lat. abusio, Paul. ex Fest. p. 58 Müll.; cf. Quint. 8, 6, 34; 8, 2, 5; and Don. p. 1775 P. (where, as in Cic. Or. 27, 94, it is written as Greek).
catachresis.short: cătăchrēsis, is, f., = κατάχρησις, a rhet.

cataclista.full: cătaclīsta vestis = κατάκλειστον ίμάτιον [to be kept shut up; cf.: vestis seposita, Tib. 2, 5, 8], a splendid garment for festal occasions, a state dress, App. M. 11, p. 261, 21, p. 261 Bip.; Tert. Pall. 3.—Hence, cătaclīstĭcus, a, um, adj., of a state dress: fila, Ven. vit. S. Mart. 4 med.
cataclista.short: cătaclīsta vestis = κατάκλειστον ίμάτιον [to be kept shut up;

cataclysmos.full: cătăclysmŏs, i, m., = κατακλυσμός. A deluge, flood, inundation: Ogygi, Varr. R. R. 3, 1, 3; Hyg. Fab. 153; Tert. Apol. 40; Aug. Civ. Dei, 18, 10; Lact. 2, 20.— In medicine, a pouring of water upon a diseased member, a shower-bath, douche, Cael. Aur. Tard. 1, 1; 1, 4; 2, 3.

catacumba.full: cătăcumba, ae, f., catacombs, Inscr. Orell. 4575.

catadromus.full: cătădrŏmus, i, m., = κατάδσομος, a rope for rope-dancers, Suet. Ner. 11; cf. Plin. 8, 2, 2, § 4 sq.; Dig. 19, 1, 54.
catadromus.short: cătădrŏmus, i, m., = κατάδσομος, a rope for rope-dancers, Suet.

catadupa.full: Cătădūpa, ōrum, n., = Κατάδουπα, the celebrated cataract of the Nile, near Syene, on the borders of Egypt (cf. cataracta), now Chellal, Cic. Rep. 6, 18, 19; Macr. Somn. Scip. 2, 4, § 14.—Cătădūpi, ōrum, m., those dwelling near, Plin. 5, 9, 10, § 54; 6, 29, 35, § 178; Amm. 22, 15, 2.
catadupa.short: Cătădūpa, ōrum, n., = Κατάδουπα, the celebrated cataract of the Nile, near Syene, on the borders of Egypt (cf.

cataegis.full: cătaegis, ĭdis, f., = καταιγίς, a violent storm of wind, a hurricane, whirlwind: procellosus flatus cataegis dicitur, App. de Mundo, p. 62, 28; esp. in Pamphylia, Sen. Q. N. 5, 17, 4.
cataegis.short: cătaegis, ĭdis, f., = καταιγίς, a violent storm of wind, a hurricane, whirlwind: procellosus flatus cataegis dicitur, App.

catagelasimus.full: Cătăgĕlăsĭmus, a, um, adj., = καταγελάσιμος, serving for ridicule; subst. m., a banterer, jeerer, in a pun with Gelasimus, the name of a parasite: nolo ex Gelasimo fleri te Catagelasimum, Plaut. Stich. 4, 2, 50.
catagelasimus.short: Cătăgĕlăsĭmus, a, um, adj., = καταγελάσιμος, serving for ridicule;

catagraphus.full: cătăgrăphus, a, um, adj., = κατάγραφος. Painted, colored, depicted: Thyni, Cat. 25, 7.— Subst.: cătăgră-pha, ōrum, n., profile paintings, side views (pure Lat. obliquae imagines), Plin. 35, 8, 34, § 56.

catagusa.full: Cătăgūsa, ae, f., = κατάγουσα (bringing back), a statue of Praxiteles, representing Ceres as bringing back Proserpine to Pluto, Plin. 34, 8, 19, § 69; cf. Sil. Catal. Artif. p. 380, n. 1.
catagusa.short: Cătăgūsa, ae, f., = κατάγουσα (bringing back), a statue of Praxiteles, representing Ceres as bringing back Proserpine to Pluto, Plin.

catalauni.full: Cătălauni and Cătĕlauni, ōrum, m., a tribe in Gallia Belgica, near the mod. Chālons-sur-Marne, Eutr. 9, 13; Amm. 15, 11, 10.—Hence, Cătălaunĭcus, a, um, adj., of or at Catalauni: clades, Eum. Pan. Const. 4.
catalauni.short: Cătălauni and Cătĕlauni, ōrum, m., a tribe in Gallia Belgica, near the mod.

catalecta.full: Cătălecta, ōrum, n., = Κατάλεκτα, the title of a collection of poems ascribed to Virgil, Aus. Tech. 12; v. Wagn. Verg. IV. p. 341 sq.; Forbig. Verg. III. p. 719 sqq.
catalecta.short: Cătălecta, ōrum, n., = Κατάλεκτα, the title of a collection of poems ascribed to Virgil, Aus.

catalecticus.full: cătălēctĭcus, a, um, adj., = καταληκτικός: versus, a verse in which a syllable is wanting at the end, Prisc. p. 1216 P.— Also called cătălēctus, a, um, = κατάληκτος, Diom. p. 501 P.
catalecticus.short: cătălēctĭcus, a, um, adj., = καταληκτικός: versus, a verse in which a syllable is wanting at the end, Prisc.

catalepsis.full: cătălēpsis, is, f., = κατάληψις, a sudden attack of sickness, catalepsy (pure Lat. apprehensio or oppressio), Cael. Aur. Acut. 2, 10, 56.
catalepsis.short: cătălēpsis, is, f., = κατάληψις, a sudden attack of sickness, catalepsy (pure Lat.

catalepticus.full: cătălēptĭcus, a, um, = καταληπτικός, cataleptic, Cael. Aur. Acut. 2, 10, 74 sq.
catalepticus.short: cătălēptĭcus, a, um, = καταληπτικός, cataleptic, Cael.

catalogus.full: cătălŏgus, i, m., = κατάλογος, an enumeration (post-class.): virtutum, Hier. Ep. 83.—Esp., a list of names, a catalogue, Macr. S. 5, 15; Aus. Per. Iliad. 2.
catalogus.short: cătălŏgus, i, m., = κατάλογος, an enumeration (post-class.): virtutum, Hier.

catamitus.full: Cătămītus (-meitus), m. corrupt collat. form of Ganymedes; v. Paul. ex Fest. p. 7, 16; 44, 6 Müll., the Latin name of Ganymede, Jupiter's cup-bearer, Plaut. Men. 1, 2, 35; Lact. 1, 11, 19; App. M. 11, p. 261, 3; Prud. c. Symm. 1, 70.— Transf., as appel. = pathicus, Cic. Phil. 2, 31, 77; Aus. Epit. Her. 33, 8; App. M. 1, p. 107, 31; v. Ganymedes.

catampo.full: catampo, a kind of play, Paul. ex Fest. p. 44 Müll.
catampo.short: catampo, a kind of play, Paul.

catanance.full: cătănancē, ēs, f., = κατανάγκη, a plant used in magical love potions, Plin. 27, 8, 35, § 57.
catanance.short: cătănancē, ēs, f., = κατανάγκη, a plant used in magical love potions, Plin.

cataonia.full: Cătăŏnĭa, ae, f., = Καταονία, a province in Southern Cappadocia, Plin. 6, 3, 3, § 9; Nep. Dat. 4, 1.—Cătăŏnes, um, m., its people, Curt. 4, 12, 11.
cataonia.short: Cătăŏnĭa, ae, f., = Καταονία, a province in Southern Cappadocia, Plin.

cataphagas.full: cătăphăgas, ae, m., = καταφαγάς, a glutton, gormandizer, Petr. 39, 9.
cataphagas.short: cătăphăgas, ae, m., = καταφαγάς, a glutton, gormandizer, Petr.

cataphasis.full: cătăphăsis, is (acc. cataphasin), f., an affirmation (pure Lat. affirmatio, aientia; opp. apophasis or abnuentia), Aur. Aug. Rhet. 11; Isid. Orig. 2, 27, 3.

cataphractarius.full: cătăphractārĭus, ii, m. cataphractes, mailed, clad in mail, Lampr. Alex. Sev. 56; Decius ap. Treb. Claud. 16; cf. cataphractus.

cataphractes.full: cătăphractes or -ta, ae, m., = καταφρακτής, a coat of mail furnished with iron scales, Tac. H. 1, 79; Veg. Mil. 1, 20; acc. cataphracten, Tert. Pall. 4.
cataphractes.short: cătăphractes or -ta, ae, m., = καταφρακτής, a coat of mail furnished with iron scales, Tac.

cataphractus.full: cătăphractus, a, um, adj., = κατάφρακτος, mailed, in mail (of soldiers and their horses), Sall. ap. Non. p. 556, 16 sq. (id. H. 4, 57 Dietsch).—As subst.: cătă-phracti, ōrum, m., mailed soldiers, Sisenn. ap. Non. 1. 1.: loricatos, quos cataphractos vocant, Liv. 35, 48, 3; 37, 40, 5 al.; Prop. 3 (4), 12, 12; Serv. ad Verg. A. 11, 770; Front. Princ. Hist. 5, p. 247 Nieb.; Inscr. Orell. 804.
cataphractus.short: cătăphractus, a, um, adj., = κατάφρακτος, mailed, in mail (of soldiers and their horses), Sall.

catapirates.full: cătăpīrātes, ae, m., = καταπειρᾶτήρ, the sounding-lead, Lucil. ap. Isid. Orig. 19, 4, 10 (p. 82, 11 Gerl.).
catapirates.short: cătăpīrātes, ae, m., = καταπειρᾶτήρ, the sounding-lead, Lucil.

cataplasma.full: cătăplasma, ătis, n., Veg. 2, 14 (abl. cataplasmatibus, Veg. 3, 25; access. form cătăplasmus; only abl. sing. cataplasmo, Lucil. ap. Non. p. 311, 25, and dat. and abl. plur. cataplasmis, Cels. 7, 26, 5; 4, 4, 3; 4, 7, 2; Veg. 2, 3 b; 5, 2, 2; cf. Schneid. Gr. p. 267), = κατάπλασμα; in medicine, a poultice, plaster, cataplasm, Cels. 3, 19, and l. l.; Plin. 20, 17, 73, § 191; 36, 17, 28, § 133; Veg. 2, 14, 2.

cataplasmo.full: cătăplasmo, āre, v. a. cataplasma, to apply a poultice to: praecordia, Cael. Aur. Acut. 2, 19, 120; cf. id. Tard. 5, 1: equum, Veg. 5, 2, 2; Macer. Flor. 18, v. 723.

cataplus.full: cătăplus, i, m., = κατάπλους (the coming to shore of a fleet or ship; hence, abstr. pro concr.), the ship or fleet that comes to land: ille Puteolanus, Cic. Rab. Post. 14, 40 B. and K. dub.; Mart. 12, 74, 1; Aus. Urb. 13, 21; Sid. Ep. 6, 8; 7, 7.
cataplus.short: cătăplus, i, m., = κατάπλους (the coming to shore of a fleet or ship;

catapotium.full: cătăpŏtĭum, ii, n., = καταπότιον (that which is swallowed down); in medicine, a pill, Cels. 4, 8; Plin. 28, 1, 2, § 7; Scrib. Comp. 89; cf. id. ib. 87.
catapotium.short: cătăpŏtĭum, ii, n., = καταπότιον (that which is swallowed down);

cataprorates.full: cătăprōrātes, a false read. for catapirates.

catapulta.full: cătăpulta, ae, f., = ό καταπέλτης, a large engine of war for throwing arrows, lances, stones, etc., a catapult (cf. ballista): catapultis ballistisque per omnia tabulata dispositis, Liv. 21, 11, 7; 21, 11, 10: maximae formae, id. 26, 47, 5; Vitr. 10, 11, 1; 10, 11, 19; 10, 15 sq.; Veg. Mil. 4, 22; Naev., Lucil., Varr., and Sisenn. ap. Non. p. 552, 17 sq.; Caes. B. C. 2, 9 al.; cf. Dict. of Antiq.— Meton., like ballista, for the missile itself, Plaut. Pers. 1, 1, 28; id. Curc. 3, 24; 5, 3, 12; id
catapulta.short: cătăpulta, ae, f., = ό καταπέλτης, a large engine of war for throwing arrows, lances, stones, etc., a catapult (cf.

catapultarius.full: cătăpultārĭus, a, um, adj. catapulta, belonging to the catapult, that is thrown by it: pilum, Plaut. Curc. 5, 3, 11.

cataracta.full: cătăracta (also cătarracta), ae, f. (cătarractes, ae, m., Plin. and Sol.; v. the foll.), = ὁ καταρράκτης or καταράκτης. Lit., a waterfall, in gen.; the waterfalls of the Euphrates, Plin. 5, 24, 20, § 85.—Hence, Meton. and κατʼ ἐξοχήυ, the celebrated fall of the Nile on the southern borders of Egypt, the Cataract: novissimo catarracte, Plin. 5, 9, 10, § 54.—Acc. catarracten, Plin. 5, 9, 10, § 59; Sol. 32: pervenit ad cataractam, Vitr. 8, 2, 6.—Plur. fem.: cataractae, nobilis insigni spectaculo lo

cataractes.full: Cătăractes or Cătarrhactes, ae, m., = Καταρρακτης, a river in Pampnylia, now the Duden Su, Mel. 1, 14, 2; Plin. 5, 27, 26, § 96.
cataractes.short: Cătăractes or Cătarrhactes, ae, m., = Καταρρακτης, a river in Pampnylia, now the Duden Su, Mel.

cataractria.full: cătăractrĭa, ae, f., a word coined to designate a kind of spice, Plaut. Ps. 3, 2, 47.
cataractria.short: cătăractrĭa, ae, f., a word coined to designate a kind of spice, Plaut.

catarrhactes.full: cătarrhactes, v. cataracta init., and Cataractes init.

catarrhus.full: cătarrhus, i, m., = κατάρρους, a flowing down, the catarrh, rheum, Marc. Emp. 5; Plin. Val. 1, 2; Cael. Aur. Acut. 2, 17.
catarrhus.short: cătarrhus, i, m., = κατάρρους, a flowing down, the catarrh, rheum, Marc.

catasceua.full: cătasceua, ae, f., = κατασκευή; rhet. t. t., the confirmation of an assumption (opp. anasceua), Isid. Orig. 2, 12, 1 sq.; cf. Sulp. Vict. Inst. Or. § 3.

catascopus.full: cătascŏpus, i, m., = κατάσκοπος (exploring, spying (cătascŏpĭum, ii, n., Gell. 10, 25 fin.), = κατασκόπιον, a lookoutship, a spy-ship, a vessel sent out to reconnoitre (pure Lat. navigium speculatorium), Auct. B. Afr. 26; cf. Isid. Orig. 19, 1, 18.
catascopus.short: cătascŏpus, i, m., = κατάσκοπος (exploring, spying (cătascŏpĭum, ii, n., Gell.

catasta.full: cătasta, ae, f. κατάστασις (postAug.), a scaffold, stage, On which slaves were exposed for sale, Tib. 2, 3, 60; Pers. 6, 77 Schol.; Plin. 35, 18, 58, § 200; Suet. Gram. 13; Stat. S. 2, 1, 72.— For the public burning (of criminals, martyrs, etc.), Prud. στεφ. 1, 56; 2, 399 al.— For delivering a lecture, Rutil. 1, 393; Cypr. Ep. 28.

catastalticus.full: cătastaltĭcus, a, um, adj., = κατασταλτικός; in medicine, restraining, checking: medicamentum, Veg. 3, 22, 2; also absol. catastalticum, id. 6, 28, 2.

catastatice.full: cătastatĭcē, ēs, f., = καταστατική, a plant, called in pure Lat. scelerata, App. Herb. 8.
catastatice.short: cătastatĭcē, ēs, f., = καταστατική, a plant, called in pure Lat.

catastema.full: cătastēma, ătis, n., = κατάστημα, position, situation, condition of a star: recursu catastematis (sc. solis et siderum), at the close of a cycle, Veg. 1, 17, 5.
catastema.short: cătastēma, ătis, n., = κατάστημα, position, situation, condition of a star: recursu catastematis (sc.

catastropha.full: cătastrŏpha, ae, f., = καταστροφή (rare; cf. casus), the turning - point of an action, catastrophe, Petr. 54, 3.

catatexitechnos.full: Cătătexĭtechnŏs, i, m., = Κατατηξιτεχνος (he who enervates art by excessive polishing), an epithet of the artist Callimachus, Plin. 34, 8, 19, § 92 (in Vitr. 4, 1, Cătătechnŏs = Κατάτεχνος; cf. Sillig, Catal. Artif. pp. 123-128).
catatexitechnos.short: Cătătexĭtechnŏs, i, m., = Κατατηξιτεχνος (he who enervates art by excessive polishing), an epithet of the artist Callimachus, Plin.

catatonus.full: cătătŏnus, a, um, adj., = κατάτονος, stretching down, depressed (opp. anatonus): capitulum, Vitr. 10, 15 fin.
catatonus.short: cătătŏnus, a, um, adj., = κατάτονος, stretching down, depressed (opp.

catax.full: cătax, adj. only in nom. [cf. catena], limping, lame, Paul. ex Fest. p. 45 Müll.; Lucil. ap. Non. p. 25, 18 sq.

catechesis.full: cătēchēsis, is, f., = κατήχησις; in eccl. Lat., religious instruction, Hier. Ep. 61, 4.

catechismus.full: cătēchismus, i, m., = κατηχισμός, a book of elementary Christian instruction, a catechism, Aug. de Fide et Oper. 13.
catechismus.short: cătēchismus, i, m., = κατηχισμός, a book of elementary Christian instruction, a catechism, Aug.

catechista.full: cătēchista, ae, m., = κατηχιστής, a religious teacher, catechist, Hier. Ep. 50, 1.
catechista.short: cătēchista, ae, m., = κατηχιστής, a religious teacher, catechist, Hier.

catechizo.full: cătēchīzo (-isso), āre, v. a., = κατηχιζω, to instruct in religion, to catechise, Tert. Cor. Mil. 11; id. adv. Marc. 4, 29; id. Idol. 10.

catechumenus.full: cătēchūmĕnus, i, m., and -a, ae, f., = κατηχούμενος, η, one who is receiving elementary instruction in religion, a catechumen, Tert. Praescr. 41 et saep.—In fem., Aug. Ep. ad Euseb. 169; Ambros. Ep. 34.
catechumenus.short: cătēchūmĕnus, i, m., and -a, ae, f., = κατηχούμενος, η, one who is receiving elementary instruction in religion, a catechumen, Tert.

categoria.full: cătēgŏrĭa, ae, f., = κατηγορία (postclass.). An accusation, Hier. Ep. 82, 9; Macr. S. 7, 3 (where others write it as a Greek word).— In logic, a predicament, category or class of predicables (pure Lat. praedicamenta): Aristotelicae, Isid. Orig. 2, 26, 1; Sid. Ep. 4, 1: Aristotelica quaedam, quas appellat decem categorias, Aug. Conf. 4, 16; Serg. Expl. in Art. Don. p. 487, 25 Keil.

categoricus.full: cătēgŏrĭcus, a, um, adj., = κατηγορικός, relating to a category, categorical, Sid. Ep. 9, 9; Cassiod. de Dial. p. 513, A.
categoricus.short: cătēgŏrĭcus, a, um, adj., = κατηγορικός, relating to a category, categorical, Sid.

cateia.full: cătēia, ae, f. Celt. or Germ., a kind of spear, probably barbed, Verg. A. 7, 741; Sil. 3, 277; Val. Fl. 6, 83; Gell. 10, 25, 2; cf. Serv. ad Verg. l. l.; Isid. Orig. 18, 7, 7.

catellulus.full: cătellŭlus, dim. from catellus, acc. to Diom. p. 313 P.

catellus1.full: cătellus, i, m., and cătella, ae, f. dim. catulus, canis, a little dog, puppy, whelp. Masc., Plaut. Stich. 4, 2, 40; Varr. ap. Non. p. 94, 24; Cic. Div. 1, 46, 103 Orell. N. cr.; Val. Max. 1, 5, 3; Mart. 1, 84; Juv. 6, 551; 9, 61; and as a term of endearment, Plaut. As. 3, 3, 103; Hor. S. 2, 3, 259.— Fem., Mart. 3, 82, 19; Juv. 6, 654; and as a term of endearment: mi catella, Hier. Ep. 22, 29.
catellus1.short: cătellus, i, m., and cătella, ae, f.

catellus2.full: cătellus, i, m., and far more freq. cătella (once not contr. cătēnŭla, Paul. Nol. 26, 462), ae, f. dim. catena; cf. Prisc. p. 556 P., a small chain. Masc., in a play on the meaning of 1. catellus, Plaut. Curc. 5, 3, 13.— Fem., Cato, R. R. 135, 1; Caecil. ap. Non. p. 199, 10; Hor. Ep. 1, 17, 55; Liv. 39, 31, 19: vaginae catellis crepitant, Plin. 33, 12, 54, § 152; cf. Isid. Orig. 19, 31, 15, and Fest. p. 273, 12 Müll.
catellus2.short: cătellus, i, m., and far more freq.

catena.full: cătēna, ae, f. (once with num. distrib. as piur. tantum: trinis catenis vinctus, Caes. B. G. 1, 53) [Sanscr. kat, to fall away; cf. catax]. A wooden bracket, brace, etc., for holding two beams together, Cato, R. R. 18, 9; Vitr. 7, 3; Pall. 1, 3, 1.— A chain, Used as a fetter, shackle, etc.; usu. in plur. (syn. vincula): catenis vincire aliquem, Plaut. Men. 1, 1, 3; Ov. M. 15, 601 al.: catenas indere alicui, Plaut. Capt. 1, 2, 3: in catenas conicere aliquem, Caes. B. G. 1, 47; Liv. 29, 21, 2: cat

catenarius.full: cătēnārĭus, a, um, adj. catena, of or pertaining to a chain: canis, a dog fastened by a chain, Sen. Ira, 3, 37, 2; Petr. 72, 7.

catenatio.full: cătēnātĭo, ōnis, f [cateno; lit. a binding; hence, abstr pro concr.], a band, clamp, clincher, pin, Vitr. 2, 9; 10, 1; Petr. 34, 9.

cateno.full: cătēno, ātus, 1, v. a. catena, to chain or bind together (prob. not ante-Aug.), Col. 6, 19, 2 Schneid. N. cr.; Ven. Carm. 2, 14; cf.: cateno, πεδέω, Gloss. Vet.—More freq. in part. perf.: cătēnātus, a, um, bound with a chain, chained, fettered: Britannus, *Hor. Epod. 7, 8: janitor, Ov. Am. 1, 6, 1; Col. 1, praef. § 10; Quint. 8, 3, 69; Suet. Aug. 13; id. Tib. 64 al.: equorum linguae, Stat. Th. 4, 731.—Poet.: palaestrae (on account of their twining their limbs around one another), intertwined, St

caterva.full: căterva, ae, f., a crowd, troop, a band of men; in the sing. and plur. (class. in prose and poet.; syn.: turba, manus, agmen). In gen.: comitum, Lucr. 2, 628; cf. id. 2, 611; Verg. A. 1, 497; 11, 533; Ov. M. 12, 216: Postumius obviam cum bene magnā catervā suā venit, Cic. Mur. 33, 69; so id. de Or. 1, 40, 184; cf. Sall. C. 14, 1: catervae testium, Cic. Verr. 2, 5, 43, § 113: contra dicentium, id. Tusc. 1, 31, 77: pugilum, Suet. Calig. 18: infernae, Tib. 1, 2, 47 al.— Poet., of animals: pecudum,
caterva.short: căterva, ae, f., a crowd, troop, a band of men;

catervarius.full: cătervārĭus, a, um, adj. caterva, of or pertaining to a crowd or troop: pugiles, fighting in bands, Suet. Aug. 45 (cf.: catervae pugilum, id. Calig. 18); Inscr. Orell. 2530.

catervatim.full: cătervātim, adv. id., in companies, in troops, Lucr. 6, 1144; Verg. G. 3, 556; Sall. J. 97, 4; Liv. 23, 27, 5; 44, 41, 8; Col. 3, 19, 3; Plin. 10, 24, 35, § 72.

catharticum.full: căthartĭcum, i, n., = καθαρτικόν, a means of purifying, a cathartic, Tert. Pall. 5 fin.; Hier. in Ezech. 7, 23.
catharticum.short: căthartĭcum, i, n., = καθαρτικόν, a means of purifying, a cathartic, Tert.

cathedra.full: căthē^dra, ae, f., = καθέδρα, a chair, a stool, esp. one furnished with cushions and supports for women, an arm-chair. In gen., Hor. S. 1, 10, 91; Phaedr. 3, 8, 4; Prop. 4 (5), 5, 37; Juv. 6, 91 al.; also, a sedan chair, Juv 1, 65; 9, 52 Rup. al.; cf. Dict. of Antiq.— Esp., a teacher's or professor's chair, Juv. 7, 203; Mart. 1, 77 fin.—Hence, Meton., the office of teacher: usurpare, Aus. Prof. 10, 1; also, of a bishop: tenere, Sid. Ep. 7, 4.
cathedra.short: căthē^dra, ae, f., = καθέδρα, a chair, a stool, esp.

cathedralicius.full: căthē^drālĭcĭus, a, um, adj. cathedra, pertaining to an arm-chair: ministri, i. e. effeminate, Mart. 10, 13, 1.

cathedrarius.full: căthē^drārĭus, a, um, adj. id., of or pertaining to an arm-chair: subsellia, Dig. 33, 10, 5: servi, who carry a chair, Sid. Ep. 1, 11.— Esp., pertaining to the chair or office of a teacher: philosophi, teachers, Sen. Brev. Vit. 10, 1; cf. cathedra, II.; so, oratores, Sid. Ep. 4, 3.

catheter.full: căthĕter, ēris, m., = καθετήρ, a surgical instrument for drawing off the urine, a catheter, Cael. Aur. Tard. 2, 1, 13 al.
catheter.short: căthĕter, ēris, m., = καθετήρ, a surgical instrument for drawing off the urine, a catheter, Cael.

catheterismus.full: căthĕtērismus, i, m., = καθετηρισμός, the application of the catheter, Cael. Aur. Tard. 2, 1, 23.
catheterismus.short: căthĕtērismus, i, m., = καθετηρισμός, the application of the catheter, Cael.

cathetus.full: cathĕtus, i, f., = κάθετος (that is sunk down), a perpendicular line, a perpendicular, Vitr. 3, 3; Cod. Just. 8, 10, 12.
cathetus.short: cathĕtus, i, f., = κάθετος (that is sunk down), a perpendicular line, a perpendicular, Vitr.

catholicus.full: căthŏlĭcus (catholicus, Prud. Apoth. 70), a, um, adj., = καθολικός, universal, relating to all (post - Aug.; in Quint. 2, 13, 14 as Greek, transl. by universalis and perpetualis; cf. Cael. Aur. Acut. 1, 5, 46): catholica et summa bonitas Dei, Tert. adv. Marc. 2, 17.—Adv.: căthŏlĭcē: in medium proferre. Tert. Praescr. 26.—More freq. subst.: căthŏlĭca, ōrum. n., the universe: anne caelestes dii catholicorum dominantur? App. Trism. 39, p. 100, 13: catholica siderum, general properties, Plin. 1, epi

cati.full: Căti fons, the fountain of Catus, from which the aqua Petronia flows into the Tiber, named from a certain Catus. in whose field it was, Paul. ex Fest. p. 45 Müll.
cati.short: Căti fons, the fountain of Catus, from which the aqua Petronia flows into the Tiber, named from a certain Catus.

catia.full: Cătĭa, ae, f., the name of a woman, Hor. S. 1, 2, 95.
catia.short: Cătĭa, ae, f., the name of a woman, Hor.

catianus.full: Cătĭānus, a, um, v. Catius, II.

catiena.full: Cătĭēna, ae, f., the name of a woman, Juv. 3, 133.
catiena.short: Cătĭēna, ae, f., the name of a woman, Juv.

catienus.full: Cătĭēnus, a, a Roman cognomen, Cic. Q. Fr. 1, 2, 2, § 6.
catienus.short: Cătĭēnus, a, a Roman cognomen, Cic.

catilina.full: Cătĭlīna, ae, m. 1. catus. L. Sergius, Catiline, a Roman who was notorious for several times attempting insurrections against his country, Sall. C. 1, 1 sqq.; Cic. Cat. 1, 1 sqq.; Verg. A. 8, 668.— Appel. of a great conspirator, Juv. 14, 41; cf. Cic. Att. 4, 3, 3.—Hence, Cătĭlīnārĭus, a, um, adj., pertaining to Catiline, Catilinarian: seminarium, Cic. Cat. 2, 10, 23 Orell. N. cr.: bellum, Quint. 3, 8, 9 (Cod. Flor. Ambros. 1: Catilinae, cf. Zumpt, Suppl. ad h. l.): prodigia, Plin. 2, 51, 52, § 1

catilius.full: Cătīlĭus, a, a Roman cognomen, Cic. Fam. 5, 10, 1; Plin. Ep. 1, 22.
catilius.short: Cătīlĭus, a, a Roman cognomen, Cic.

catillamen.full: cătillāmen, ĭnis, n. catillo, junket, sweetmeat, Arn. 7, p. 230.

catillatio.full: cătillātĭo, ōnis, f. id.; lit., a licking of plates, a plundering of provinces friendly to the Roman people, Paul. ex Fest. p. 44 Müll.

catillo1.full: cătillo, ātum, āre, v. a. 1. catillus, to lick a plate, Plaut. Cas. 3, 2, 22; Auct. ap. Fulg. 563, 7.

catillo2.full: cătillo, ōnis, m. 1. catillo, a platelicker; hence, a glutton, gourmand, Lucil. ap. Macr. S. 2, 12 fin.; cf. Paul. ex Fest. p. 44 (where the best MSS. have catiliones); id. p. 90 Müll.

catillus1.full: cătillus, i, m. (plur. heterocl. catilla, ōrum, n., Petr. 50, 6; cf. Prisc. p. 556 P.; an uncontr. access. form că-tīnŭlus, Varr. ap. Charis. p. 61 ib.), dim. catinus. A small bowl, dish, or plate, Cato, R. R. 84 fin.; Asin. ap. Charis. p. 61 P.; Hor. S. 2, 4, 75; Col. 12, 57, 1; Val. Max. 4, 3, 5.— Of objects in the form of a plate. An ornament on a sword-sheath, Plin. 33, 12, 54, § 152 (catellis, Jan. and Sill.).— The upper millstone, Dig. 33, 7, 18, § 5.

catillus2.full: Cātillus (Cātĭlus, Hor. C. 1, 18, 2; Cātillus, Stat. S. 1, 3, 100; cf. on the measure Lucr. 2, p. 36 Lachm.), i, m., a son of Amphiaraus; he with his brothers Tiburtus and Coras built Tibur, Verg. A. 7, 672 Serv.; 11, 640; Sil. 8, 366; cf. Sol. c. 8.

catina.full: Cătĭna (in MSS. also Cătăna), ae (Cătănē, ēs, Sil. 14, 196), f., = Κατάνη, a town on the east coast of Sicily, at the foot of Ætna, now Catania, Mel. 2, 7, 16; Plin. 3, 8, 14, § 88; Cic. Verr. 2, 2, 75, § 185; 2, 3, 83, § 192 al.—Hence, Cătĭnensis (Cătĭnĭensis, Just. 4, 3, 4; and Cătă-nensis, Lact. 2, 4, 28), e, adj., belonging to Catina, of Catina: civitas, Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 8, § 17: pumex, Juv. 8, 16: L. Manlius Catinensis, Cic. Fam. 13, 30, 1.—In plur.: Cătĭnenses, ĭum, m., the inhabitants of

catinus.full: cătīnus, i, m. (cătīnum, i, n., Cato, R. R. 84, 1; cf. Prisc. p. 556 P.; on the contr. Charis. p. 60 ib.) [kindr. with the Siculian κάτινον, Varr. L. L. 5, § 120, p. 35 Bip.; cf. O. Müll. Etrusk. 1, p. 13; cf. also Sanscr. katina, vas fictile], a deep vessel for serving up or cooking food, a bowl, dish, pot, Varr. R. R. 1, 63, 1; id. ap. Non. p. 546, 14; Maecen. ap. Charis. p. 61 P.; Hor. S. 1, 3, 92; 1, 6, 115; 2, 2, 39; 2, 4, 77 al.—Also for melting metals, a crucible, Plin. 33, 4, 21, § 69; 3

catius.full: Cătĭus, ii, m. A Roman deity, the protector of boys, whom he made intelligent (catos), Aug. Civ. Dei, 4, 21.— An Epicurean philosopher, author of works de rerum naturā, de summo bono, etc., Cic. Fam. 15, 16, 1; Cass. ib. 15, 19; Quint. 10, 1, 124; Schol. Cruq. ad Hor. S. 2, 4, 1.—Hence, Cătĭānus, a, um, adj.: spectra, Cic. Fam. 15, 16, 1; Cass. ib. 15, 19.— A feigned name in Hor. S. 2, 4, 1 and 88.

cativolcus.full: Cativolcus, i, m., king of the Eburones, Caes. B. G. 5, 26; 6, 31.
cativolcus.short: Cativolcus, i, m., king of the Eburones, Caes.

catlaster.full: catlaster, tri, m. contr. for catulaster from catulus; cf. Charis. p. 65 P.; Prisc. p. 618 ib. and 628 ib., a boy, lad, stripling: catulaster βούπαις, πάλληξ, Gloss. Philox.; Vitr. 8, 3, 24 Schneid. (p. 242 Bip. catastros).

cato.full: Căto, ōnis, m. 1. catus, a cognomen of several celebrated Romans in the gens Porcia, Valeria, Vettia al. M. Porcius Cato the elder, distinguished as a rigid judge of morals; hence with the appel. Censorius; whose most celebrated works were the Origines and De Re Rustica, Cic. de Or. 3, 33, 135; Liv. 31, 1 sqq.; Plin. 7, 27, 28, § 100; 7, 30, 31, § 112; cf., concerning him, Bernhardy, Röm. Litt. p. 521 sq.; 650; Bähr, Lit. Gesch. p. 515; 258; 354 al.; Ellendt, Cic. Brut. p. xix.-xxv.—As appel. of

catoblepas.full: cătōblĕpas, ae, m., = κατῶβλεψ or κατωβλέπων (that looks down), a wild animal in Ethiopia, perhaps a species of buffalo, or the gnu, a species of antelope, Mel. 3, 9, 9; Plin. 8, 21, 32, § 77.
catoblepas.short: cătōblĕpas, ae, m., = κατῶβλεψ or κατωβλέπων (that looks down), a wild animal in Ethiopia, perhaps a species of buffalo, or the gnu, a species of antelope, Mel.

catocha.full: cătŏcha, ae, f., = κατοχή, a complete stupor, catalepsy, Cael. Aur. Ac. 2, 10.
catocha.short: cătŏcha, ae, f., = κατοχή, a complete stupor, catalepsy, Cael.

catochitis.full: cătŏchītis, ĭdis, f., = κατοχῖτις, an unknown precious stone found in Corsica, Plin. 37, 10, 56, § 152.
catochitis.short: cătŏchītis, ĭdis, f., = κατοχῖτις, an unknown precious stone found in Corsica, Plin.

catomidio.full: cătōmĭdĭo, āre, v. a., = κατωμίζω, to lay one over the shoulders of another, and thus to flog him; acc. to others, to strike on the shoulders, Petr. 132 init.; Spart. Had. 18.

catomitarii.full: catomitarii or catomecarii, a word of unknown signif. in Serv. ad Verg. A. 9, 329.
catomitarii.short: catomitarii or catomecarii, a word of unknown signif.

catomus.full: cătōmus, i, m. κατʼ ὤμους, the shoulders (late Lat.): catomus cervix, Gloss.: catomis caedi, Schol. Juv. 2, 142; cf. catomidio.

catonianus.full: Cătōnĭānus, a, um, v. Cato, I. B.

catonini.full: Cătōnīni, ōrum, v. Cato, II. B.

catonium.full: cătōnĭum, ii, n. κάτω, the Lower World, Laber. ap. Gell. 16, 7, 4; cf. Schol. Juv. p. 65 Cram.—Hence the play upon the word: vereor, ne in catonium Catoninos, Cic. Fam. 7, 25, 1 B. and K. (others read catomum; v. this word).

catoptritis.full: cătoptrītis, ĭdis, f., = κατοπτρῖτις, a precious stone found in Cappadocia, unknown to us, Plin. 37, 10, 56, § 152 Sill. N. cr.
catoptritis.short: cătoptrītis, ĭdis, f., = κατοπτρῖτις, a precious stone found in Cappadocia, unknown to us, Plin.

catorchites.full: cătorchītes (vīnum), = κατορχίτης οἶνος, a wine made from figs, Plin. 14, 16, 19, § 102.
catorchites.short: cătorchītes (vīnum), = κατορχίτης οἶνος, a wine made from figs, Plin.

catta.full: catta, ae, f., an unknown species of animal (acc. to Gloss. Vet. = αἴλουρος; cf. the Germ. Kater, Katze, cat), Mart. 13, 69, 1.
catta.short: catta, ae, f., an unknown species of animal (acc.

catularia.full: Cătŭlārĭa Porta, one of the gates of Rome, so called because dogs were sacrificed near it, Paul. ex Fest. p. 45 Müll.; cf. Becker, Röm. Alterth. 1, p. 178 sq.
catularia.short: Cătŭlārĭa Porta, one of the gates of Rome, so called because dogs were sacrificed near it, Paul.

catulinus1.full: cătŭlīnus, a. um, adj. catulus, of or pertaining to a little dog, dog's-: caro, Plaut. ap. Paul. ex Fest. p. 45 Müll.; and absol.: cătŭlīna, ae, f. (sc. caro), the flesh of the dog, Plin. 29, 4, 14, § 58.

catulinus2.full: Cătŭlīnus, a, um, adj., of Q. Lutatius Catulus, Plin. 34, 8, 19, § 17 Sill. N. cr.
catulinus2.short: Cătŭlīnus, a, um, adj., of Q.

catulio.full: cătŭlĭo, īre, v. n. catulus, to desire the male, of dogs, Varr. R. R. 2, 9, 11; of the she-wolf, Laber. ap. Non. p. 90, 33.

catulitio.full: cătŭlītĭo, or contr. catlītĭo, ōnis, f. catulio, a desire for the male; trop. of nature (gestiente natură semina accipere), a rustic expression, Plin. 16, 25, 39, § 94.

catullus.full: Cătullus, i, m. Q. Valerius, acc. to Plin. 37, 6, 21, § 81; C. acc. to App. Mag. 10, p. 12 Bip., a celebrated Roman writer of elegies and epigrams, born near or in Verona, 86 B. C.; Nep. Att. 12, 4; Hor. S. 1, 10, 19; Tib. 3, 6 41; Ov. Am. 3, 9, 62; Mart. 7, 99; cf. Bernhardy, Röm. Litt. p. 466 sq.; Bähr, Lit. Gesch. p. 184 sq.—Hence, Cătullĭānus, a, um, of Catullus: basia, Mart. 11, 6, 14.— Catullus Urbicarius, a mimographer of the time of Domitian, Juv. 8, 186; 12, 29; 12, 37; 13, 111.— Catull

catuloticus.full: cătūlōtĭcus, a, um, adj., = κατουλωτικός, good for healing over: medicamentum, Veg. 6, 28, 4.
catuloticus.short: cătūlōtĭcus, a, um, adj., = κατουλωτικός, good for healing over: medicamentum, Veg.

catulus1.full: cătŭlus, i, m. dim. 2. catus, the young of animals, a whelp; cf. Non. p. 457, 8 sq. In gen., of swine, Plaut. Truc. 2, 2, 13; of a panther, Lucr. 5, 1036; of a lion, Verg. G. 3, 245; Hor. C. 3, 20, 2; Ov. M. 13, 547; of a tiger, Plin. 8, 4, 5, § 10; of a cat, Phaedr. 2, 4, 24; of a wolf, Verg. A. 2, 357; of a bear, Ov. M. 13, 836; 15, 379; of a serpent, Verg. G. 3, 438 al.; cf. in gen.: catulos ferae Celent inultae, Hor. C. 3, 3, 41.— Esp., a young dog, a puppy (in this sense regarded by the anc

catulus2.full: Cătŭlus, i, m., a cognomen in the gens Lutatia; v. Lutatius.
catulus2.short: Cătŭlus, i, m., a cognomen in the gens Lutatia;

caturiges.full: Cătŭrĭges, um, m., a Ligurian tribe in Gallia Narbonensis, now De/partement des Hautes-Alpes, Caes. B. G. 1, 10; Plin. 3, 20, 24, §§ 135 and 137.
caturiges.short: Cătŭrĭges, um, m., a Ligurian tribe in Gallia Narbonensis, now De/partement des Hautes-Alpes, Caes.

catus1.full: cătus, a, um, adj. root ka-; Sanscr. ça-, to whet, sharpen; cf. cos, cautes, cuneus; Sabine, = acutus, acc. to Varr. L. L. 7, § 46, p. 90 Bip.. * Sharp to the hearing, clear-sounding, shrill (cf. acutus, 2.): jam cata signa fere sonitum dare voce parabant, Enn. ap. Varr. l. l. (Ann. 447 Vahl.). — Transf. to intellectual objects, in a good and bad sense. In a good sense, clear-sighted, intelligent, sagacious, wise, opp. stultus (in prose probably never naturalized; hence Cic., in prose, adds ut i

catus2.full: cătus, i, m., a male cat (post-class.), Pall. Mart. 9, 4; scanned, cātus, Poët. ap. Anth. Lat. 5, p. 162, 3 al.
catus2.short: cătus, i, m., a male cat (post-class.), Pall.

caucalis.full: caucălis, ĭdis, f., = καυκαλίς, an umbelliferous plant; acc. to Sprengel Caucalis orientalis, Linn.; Plin. 21, 15, 52, § 89; 22, 22, 40, § 83.
caucalis.short: caucălis, ĭdis, f., = καυκαλίς, an umbelliferous plant;

caucasigena.full: Caucăsĭgĕna, ae, m. Caucasus-gigno, born on or near the Caucasus: Alani, Sid. Ep. 4, 1.

caucasus.full: Caucăsus, i, m., = Καύκασος. The rough Caucasian chain of mountains, in.habited by wild tribes, in Asia, between the Black and Caspian Seas, Mel. 1, 15, 2; Plin. 6, 13, 15, § 37; Cic. Tusc. 2, 10, 23: inhospitalis, Hor. C. 1, 22, 7; id. Epod. 1, 12; cf. Verg. A. 4, 366; acc. Gr. Caucason, Ov. M. 8, 798; Stat. Th. 4, 394.—Hence, Caucă-sĭus, a, um, adj., pertaining to Caucasus, Caucasian: montes, Mel. 1, 19, 13; 2, 4, 8: vertex, Verg. G. 2, 440: rupes, Prop. 2, 1, 69: aves, id. 2 (3), 25, 14: volu

caucula.full: caucŭla, ae, f. dim. from the unus. cauca, v. caucus, a small dish, App. M. 5, 20, p. 62 Min. Vit. Debr.

cauculator.full: caucŭlātor, ōris, m., a reckoner, ψηφιστής, Gloss. Lat. [ = calculator].
cauculator.short: caucŭlātor, ōris, m., a reckoner, ψηφιστής, Gloss.

caucus.full: caucus, i, m., = καῦκα, a drinkingvessel, Hier. adv. Jov. 2, 14.
caucus.short: caucus, i, m., = καῦκα, a drinkingvessel, Hier.

cauda.full: cauda (also cōda, like codex, plostrum, etc., Varr. ap. Non. p. 86, 19; id. R. R. 2, 7, 5; Petr. 44, 12; Fest. p. 178, 29; Paul. ex Fest. p. 38, 17 Müll.) [etym. dub.; cf. codex], ae, f., the tail of animals, Lucr. 2, 806; 3, 658; Cic. de Or. 3, 59, 222; id. Fin. 3, 5, 18; Plin. 11, 50, 111, § 264; Varr. R. R. 2, 2, 3; 2, 5, 8.— Prov. Caudam jactare popello, to flatter, fawn upon (the figure taken from dogs), Pers. 4, 15.— Caudam trahere, to have a tail stuck on in mockery, to be made a fool of,
cauda.short: cauda (also cōda, like codex, plostrum, etc., Varr.

caudeus.full: caudĕus, a, um, adj. instead of caudĭcĕus, from caudex, of wood, wooden: cistella, Plaut. Rud. 4, 4, 65; access. form caudĕcus, a, um: caudecae cistellae ex junco, Paul. ex Fest. p. 46 Müll.

caudex1.full: caudex, ĭcis, m. (more recent orthography cōdex) [etym. dub.; cf. cauda]. The trunk of a tree, the stock, stem (rare). Caudex, Plin. 16, 30, 53, § 121; 12, 15, 34, § 67; Verg. G. 2, 30 et saep.— Codex, Ov. M. 12, 432; Col. 4, 8, 2; 5, 6, 21.— Hence, The block of wood to which one was bound for punishment: codex, Plaut. Poen. 5, 3, 39; Prop. 4 (5), 7, 44; Juv. 2, 57. — A term of reproach, block, dolt, blockhead: caudex, Ter. Heaut. 5, 1, 4; Petr. 74.— Inpartic. A block of wood split or sawn into

caudex2.full: Caudex, cis, m., a Roman cognomen: App. Claudius Caudex, consul A. U. C. 490, B. C. 264, Sen. Brev. Vit. 13, 4; Aur. Vict. 37.
caudex2.short: Caudex, cis, m., a Roman cognomen: App.

caudicalis.full: caudĭcālis, e, adj. caudex, pertaining to the trunks of trees, of wood: provincia, humorously, the employment of woodsplitting, Plaut. Ps. 1, 2, 26.

caudicarius.full: caudĭcārĭus (cōdĭc-), a, um, adj. id., of or pertaining to the trunks of trees: naves, made of rough, stout trunks of trees (cf. caudex, II.), Varr. and Sall. H. Fragm. ap. Non. p. 535, 15 sq.; Sen. Brev. Vit. 13, 4; cf. also Paul. ex Fest. p. 46 Müll.: caudicariae naves ex tabulis grossioribus factae.— Hence, patroni caudicarii, masters of such ships, Cod. Th. 14, 4, 9.—Subst.: caudĭ-cārĭi or cōdĭcārĭi, ōrum, m., those who sail on such ships (esp. those who brought the corn from Ostia to Rome),

caudiceus.full: caudĭcĕus, a, um, adj. caudex, pertaining to the trunk of a tree: lembus, Aus. Mos. 197.

caudium.full: Caudium, ii, n., a small but ancient city of Samnium, near Benevento, celebrated for the narrow mountain pass (the Furculae Caudinae) where the Roman army was shut in by the Samnites, Liv. 9, 2, 1 sq.; Cic. Off. 3, 30, 109.—Hence, Caudīnus, a, um, adj., of Caudium, Caudine: Furculae Caudinae, the Caudine Forks, now Casale di Forchia (al. Forchia d'Arpaia), Liv. 9, 2, 6; 9, 11, 3; Flor. 1, 16, 9.—The same called Furcae Caudinae, Luc. 2, 137; and Caudinae Fauces, Sil. 8, 566; Col. 10, 132: saltus,
caudium.short: Caudium, ii, n., a small but ancient city of Samnium, near Benevento, celebrated for the narrow mountain pass (the Furculae Caudinae) where the Roman army was shut in by the Samnites, Liv.

caulae.full: caulae or caullae, ārum, f. apparently contr. from cavile, Varr. L. L. 5, § 20, p. 8 Bip., from cavus; cf. Paul. ex Fest. p. 46. In gen., an opening, hole, passage (so most freq. in Lucr.), Lucr. 2, 951; 3, 707: per caulas corporis, id. 3, 255; 3, 702; 6, 839: per caulas palati, id. 4, 620; 4, 660: per caulas aetheris, id. 6, 492: intra caulas (aedis Saturni), Lex Corn. XX Quaest. 2, 41; cf.: caulae (Jani) pace clauduntur, Macr. S. 1, 9; v. Lucr. 2, p. 374 sq. Lachm. —Hence, Esp. A sheepfold or

caulares.full: Caulāres, is, m., a river of Pamphylia, Liv. 38, 15, 1.
caulares.short: Caulāres, is, m., a river of Pamphylia, Liv.

caulias.full: caulias, ae, m., = καυλίας, taken or derived from the stalk: sucus, opp. to rhizias (from the root), Plin. 19, 3, 15, § 43.
caulias.short: caulias, ae, m., = καυλίας, taken or derived from the stalk: sucus, opp.

cauliculatus.full: caulĭcŭlātus, a, um, adj. cauliculus, furnished with or having a stalk: rami, App. Herb. 90.

cauliculus.full: caulĭcŭlus or cōlĭcŭlus, i, m. dim. caulis, the small stalk or stem of a plant; form cauliculus, Cels. 2, 18; Plin. 23, 7, 63, § 119; Suet. Gram. 11; Scrib. Comp. 128; Veg. 2, 6, 2; form coliculus, Cato, R. R. 158, 1; Varr. R. R. 1, 31, 4; 1, 42, 4; Col. 11, 2, 10; 12, 7, 1; 12, 56, 1.— In architecture, a stalk or stem as an ornament on the capitals of columns, Vitr. 4, 1, 12; 7, 5, 3.

caulis.full: caulis (cōlis, Cato, R. R. 35, 2; Varr. R. R. 1, 31, 2; 1, 41, 6; Col. 5, 6, 36; id. Arb. 9, 2; also in Hor. S. 2, 4, 15, the best MSS have colis; and coles, Cels. 6, 18, 2; cf. cauliculus), is, m., = καυλός, the stalk or stem of a plant: brassicae, Cato, R. R. 157, 2: cepae, Col. 11, 3, 21 and 58: fabarum, Plin. 18, 12, 30, § 120 et saep.: dictamni, Verg. A. 12, 413.—Of the vine, the tendrils, Cato, R. R. 33, 4; Col. 4, 7, 2.—B κατʼ ἐξοχήν, a cabbage-stalk, a cabbage, colewort, Cic. N. D. 2, 47

caulodes.full: caulōdes, is, = καυλώδης, stalk-like: brassica, a kind of cabbage with large leaves, Plin. 20, 9, 33, § 79.
caulodes.short: caulōdes, is, = καυλώδης, stalk-like: brassica, a kind of cabbage with large leaves, Plin.

caulonia.full: Caulōnĭa, ae, f. (Caulon, ōnis, m., Verg. A. 3, 553; Liv. 27, 15, 8; Plin. 3, 10, 15, § 95; acc. Caulona, Ov. M. 15, 705), = Καυλωνία, a city founded by the Achœans on the east coast of Bruttium, now Castel Vetere, Mel. 2, 4, 8; Liv. 27, 12, 6 sq.; cf. Serv. ad Verg. l. l.

cauma.full: cauma, ătis, n., = καῦμα, the heat, Vulg. Job, 30, 30.
cauma.short: cauma, ătis, n., = καῦμα, the heat, Vulg.

caunus.full: Caunus or -ŏs, i, f., = Καῦνος, a very ancient town on the coast of Caria, now Kaiguez, Mel. 1, 16, 1; Plin. 5, 28, 29, § 104; Cic. Div. 2, 40, 84; acc. to the fable, built by Caunos, a son of Miletus, and brother of Byblis, Ov. M. 9, 453.— Hence the adjj., Caunĕus or -ĭus, a, um, pertaining to Caunus, of Caunus.—Subst.: Caunĕae (sc. ficus), Caunian dried figs, Cic. Div. 2, 40, 84; Cels. 5, 21; Plin. 15, 19, 21, § 83: Caunīs (for Cauneis), Col. 10, 414.—In plur.: Caunĕi or Caunĭi, ōrum, m., the
caunus.short: Caunus or -ŏs, i, f., = Καῦνος, a very ancient town on the coast of Caria, now Kaiguez, Mel.

caupo.full: caupo (also cōpo and cūpo, Charis. p. 47 P.; cf. Isid. Orig. 20, 6, 7; the form copo, Cic. Clu. 59, 163; Inscr. Orell. 4169; Inscr. Momms. 5078), ōnis, m. root cap-, to take in, receive, v. capio; cf. κάπηλος, a petty tradesman, huckster, innkeeper, Plaut. Aul. 3, 5, 35; Cic. Div. 1, 27, 51; Hor. S. 1, 1, 29 K. and H.; 1, 5, 4; Mart. 1, 57; Dig. 4, 9, 1 al.—* Trop.: sapientiae atque facundiae, Tert. Anim. 3.

caupona.full: caupōna, ae, f. (upon the form cf. Prisc. p. 684 P.) [caupo]. A female shopkeeper, huckster, a landlady, hostess (anteand post-class.), Lucil. ap. Prisc. l. l.; App. M. 1, p. 105, 23, p. 18 Bip.— A retail shop, an inn, tavern (syn. taberna), Cic. Pis. 22, 53; Hor. S. 1, 5, 51; id. Ep. 1, 11, 12; 1, 17, 8; Gell. 7, 11, 4; Plin. 9, 47, 71, § 154: cauponam exercere, to keep an inn, Just. 1, 7, 12.

cauponaria.full: caupōnārĭa, ae, f., = καπηλική, a female shopkeeper, Onom. Vet.
cauponaria.short: caupōnārĭa, ae, f., = καπηλική, a female shopkeeper, Onom.

cauponarius.full: caupōnārĭus, ii, m., = κάπηλος, a shopkeeper, Gloss. Cyr.
cauponarius.short: caupōnārĭus, ii, m., = κάπηλος, a shopkeeper, Gloss.

cauponius.full: caupōnĭus, a, um, adj. caupo, of or belonging to a retail shopkeeper, or to an innkeeper: puer, a shop or tavern boy, waiter, Plaut. Poen. 5, 5, 19: taberna, Dig. 23, 2, 43; 33, 7, 13: artes exercere, Just. 1, 7.— Subst.: caupōnĭum, ii, n., tavern furniture, Dig. 33, 7, 15 pr.

cauponor.full: caupōnor, āri, v. dep. id., to traffic or trade in any thing; trop.: bellum, Enn. ap. Cic. Off. 1, 12, 38 (Ann. v. 201 Vahl.); cf. the Gr. καπηλεύειν μάχην, Aesch. Sept. 347: verbum veritatis, Cassiod. Hist. Eccl. 4, 24.

cauponula.full: caupōnŭla, ae, f. dim. caupona, II., a small inn or tavern, * Cic. Phil. 2, 31, 77; Schol. Bobiens. Cic. Mil. p. 275 Orell. N. cr.

caupulus.full: caupŭlus, i, m., a kind of small ship, Gell. 10, 25, 5; cf. Isid. Orig. 19, 1, 25, where Lind. has caupilus.
caupulus.short: caupŭlus, i, m., a kind of small ship, Gell.

cauricrepus.full: caurīcrĕpus, a, um, adj. caurus-crepo, blown through by the north-west wind, Avien. 869.

caurinus.full: caurīnus, a, um, adj. caurus, of the north-west wind: frigus, Grat. Cyn. 296.

caurio.full: caurĭo, īre, the natural sound of the rutting panther, Auct. Philom. 50.
caurio.short: caurĭo, īre, the natural sound of the rutting panther, Auct.

caurus.full: Caurus or Cōrus, i, m. cf. Goth. skūra, the north wind, the north-west wind; form Caurus, Gell. 2, 22, 12 and 22; Lucr. 6, 135; Vitr. 1, 6, 5; Verg. G. 3, 356; form Corus, Caes. B. G. 5, 7; Sen. Q. N. 5, 16, 5; Plin. 2, 47, 46, § 110.

causa.full: causa (by Cicero, and also a little after him, caussa, Quint. 1, 7, 20; so Fast. Praenest. pp. 321, 322; Inscr. Orell. 3681; 4077; 4698 al.; in Mon. Ancyr. 3, 1 dub.), ae, f. perh. root cav- of caveo, prop. that which is defended or protected; cf. cura, that by, on account of, or through which any thing takes place or is done; a cause, reason, motive, inducement; also, in gen., an occasion, opportunity (opp. effectis, Quint. 6, 3, 66; 7, 3, 29: factis, id. 4, 2, 52; 12, 1, 36 al.; very freq. in
causa.short: causa (by Cicero, and also a little after him, caussa, Quint.

causalis.full: causālis, e, adj. causa (rare and only late Lat.). Of or pertaining to a cause, causal: ratio, Aug. Gen. 7, 23.—Subst.: Causālĭa, a work on the causes of things, Arn. 5, p. 163.— In gram.: conjunctiones. which annex a reason for what precedes (e. g. nam, enim, itaque, etc.), Charis. p. 199 P.; Diom. p. 410 ib.; Prisc. p. 16, p. 1027 ib. —Adv.: causālĭter, causally, Aug. l. l. 5 fin.; 6, 5.

causarius.full: causārĭus, a, um, adj. causa, II. D.. In medic. lang., sick, diseased, ill (not ante-Aug.): corpus, Sen. Q. N. 1 praef. § 4: partes, quibus adhibenda curatio est, id. Ep. 68, 7: dens, Marc. Emp. 12: dentes, Plin. 23, 3, 37, § 75.—Subst.: causarii vel latere vel faucibus, sick, Plin. 25, 5, 25, § 61: oculorum, Marc. Emp. 8.— In milit. lang., discharged on account of ill health, invalid, Liv. 6, 6, 14.—Hence, missio, a discharge from military service on account of sickness, a liberation from servi

causate.full: causātē, adv. from an unused adj. causatus, from causa, with good reason: causatius, Plin. praef. § 8.

causatio.full: causātĭo, ōnis, f. causa, II. C. (postclass.). A pretext, an excuse, apology, plea, Cod. Th. 3, 5, 2; Tert. ad Marc. 5, 20: aegri corporis, Gell. 20, 1, 30.— A disease: rara, Pall. 1, 4, 1.

causativus.full: causātīvus, a, um, adj. causa. Causative: vis, Mart. Cap. 7, § 731.— Of or pertaining to a lawsuit; subst.: causativum litis, the matter in dispute, the gist of the action, Mart. Cap. 5, § 472; Fortun. Art. Rhet. 1, 2; Jul. Vict. Art. Rhet. 1, 2; 3, 8.— In gram.: causativus casus = accusativus, the accusative, i. e. the arraigning case, Prisc. p. 671 P.; cf. persona, i. e. the first person, id. p. 821 ib.

causia.full: causĭa, ae, f., = καυσία, a Macedonian white hat with a broad brim, worn in Rome by the poorer people, as a protection against the sun, Plaut. Mil. 4, 4, 42; id. Pers. 1, 3, 75; Val. Max. 5, 1, 4; Mart. 14, 29.—Hence, In milit. lang., a kind of roof for the protection of besiegers, = vinea, Veg. Mil. 4, 15.
causia.short: causĭa, ae, f., = καυσία, a Macedonian white hat with a broad brim, worn in Rome by the poorer people, as a protection against the sun, Plaut.

causidicalis.full: causĭdĭcālis, e, adj. causidicus, of or pertaining to an advocate: odium et taedium, M. Aur. ap. Front. Ep. ad M. Caes. 4, 5.

causidicatio.full: causĭdĭcātĭo, ōnis, f. id., the speech of an advocate, Front. Ep. ad M. Anton. 2, p. 298.

causidicatus.full: causĭdĭcātus, ūs, m., forensic oratory, δικολογία, Gloss. Gr. Lat.
causidicatus.short: causĭdĭcātus, ūs, m., forensic oratory, δικολογία, Gloss.

causidicina.full: causĭdĭcīna, ae, f. causidicus, the office of advocate (post - class.): id habet causidicina cum ceteris metuendum, quod, etc., Amm. 30, 4, 22; Symm. Ep. 5, 75; Cod. Th. 8, 4, 30 al.
