cerebrum.full: cĕrē^brum (per tmesin: saxo cerecomminuit-brum, Enn. ap. Don. p. 1777 P., and ap. Serv. ad Verg. A. 1, 412), i, n. root kar- of κάρη, v. celsus init.; and root bharof φέρω, fero; cf. Corss. Beitr. p. 354, the brain, Plaut. Cas. 3, 5, 19; Ter. Ad. 4, 2, 32; 5, 2, 7; Verg. A. 5, 413; 9, 419; Lucr. 6, 804; Cic. Tusc. 1, 9, 19; Plin. 11, 37, 49, § 133 sq.; 33, 6, 34, § 102 et saep.— Meton., understanding, Plaut. Aul. 2, 1, 30; Hor. S. 2, 3, 75; Phaedr. 1, 7, 2; Suet. Calig. 50.—Anger, choler, Plaut.

cerellia.full: Cērellia (Caer-), ae, f., a Roman lady mentioned in the letters of Cicero, Cic. Fam. 13, 72, 1; id. Att. 12, 51, 3.
cerellia.short: Cērellia (Caer-), ae, f., a Roman lady mentioned in the letters of Cicero, Cic.

cereolus.full: cērĕŏlus, a, um, adj. dim. [cereus], of the color of wax: pruna, Col. 10, 404 (in Plin. 15, 13, 12, § 41, called cerina).

ceres.full: Cĕrēs (cf. Verg. G. 1, 96; Ov. F. 4, 615; Mart. 3, 58, 6), ĕris (gen. CERERVS, Inscr. Fabr. p. 626, 225; cf. Inscr. Orell. 1364), f. Sabini Cererem panem appellant, Serv. ad Verg. G. 1, 7; prop. the goddess of creation (cf. Serv. l. l.), from the stem cer, Sanscr. kri, to make, the daughter of Saturn and Ops, Ov. F. 6, 285, sister of Jupiter and Pluto, mother of Proserpine, goddess of agriculture, esp. of the cultivation of corn, and of the growth of fruits in gen. (cf. Cerealis); represented as

cereus1.full: cērĕus, a, um, adj. cera, waxen, of wax. Prop., Cic. N. D. 3, 12, 30: effigies, Hor. S. 1, 8, 30: imago, id. ib. 1, 8, 43; id. Epod. 17, 76; cf. id. Ep. 2, 1, 265: castra, cells of wax, honey-comb, Verg. A. 12, 589; cf. regna, waxen realms, id. G. 4, 202: simul acra, Ov. H. 6, 91.— Subst.: cē-rĕus, i, m. (sc. funis), a waxlight, wax taper, Plaut. Curc. 1, 1, 9; Cic. Off. 3, 20, 80; Sen. Ep. 122, 10; id. Brev. Vit. 20, 5; id. Tranq. 11, 7. Such waxlights were brought by clients to their patrons a

cereus2.full: cērĕus, i, m., v. 1. cereus, I. B.

ceria.full: cerĭa or cerea, ae, f., a Spanish drink, prepared from corn, = celia and cerevisia, Plin. 22, 25, 82, § 164.
ceria.short: cerĭa or cerea, ae, f., a Spanish drink, prepared from corn, = celia and cerevisia, Plin.

cerifico.full: cērĭfĭco, āvi, 1 cera - facio, lit., to make wax; hence of the purple-fish, to slime over, to prepare a slimy nest for eggs, Plin. 9, 38, 62, § 133.
cerifico.short: cērĭfĭco, āvi, 1 cera - facio, lit., to make wax;

cerillae.full: Cērillae, ārum, f., = Κηριλλοί, a small town on the sea-coast of Bruttium destroyed by Hannibal, now Cirella Vecchia, Sil. 8, 580.
cerillae.short: Cērillae, ārum, f., = Κηριλλοί, a small town on the sea-coast of Bruttium destroyed by Hannibal, now Cirella Vecchia, Sil.

cerintha.full: cērintha, ae (-ē, ēs, Plin. 21, 12, 41, § 70), f., = κηρινθη, a plant which bees are fond of, wax - flower: Cerinthe major, Linn.; Verg. G. 4, 63; Col. 9, 8, 13.

cerinthus.full: cērinthus, i, m., = κήρινθος, beebread, called also erithace or sandaraca, Plin. 11, 7, 7, § 17.
cerinthus.short: cērinthus, i, m., = κήρινθος, beebread, called also erithace or sandaraca, Plin.

cerinus.full: cērĭnus, a, um, adj., = κήρινος, waxcolored, yellow like wax: pruna. Plin. 15, 13, 12, § 41 sq.: berylli, id. 37, 5, 20, § 77.— Subst.: cērĭna, ōrum, n., a wax-colored garment, Plaut. Ep. 2, 2, 51; cf. Non. p. 548, 33.
cerinus.short: cērĭnus, a, um, adj., = κήρινος, waxcolored, yellow like wax: pruna.

ceriolarium.full: cērĭŏlārĭum, ii, or cērĭŏlāre, is, n., a candlestick for wax tapers, Inscr. Orell. 2505 sq.; 2515; Inscr. Rein. cl. 1, 273; Inscr. Orell. 4068.
ceriolarium.short: cērĭŏlārĭum, ii, or cērĭŏlāre, is, n., a candlestick for wax tapers, Inscr.

ceritis.full: cērītis, ĭdis, f., = κηρῖτις, wax-stone, a precious stone, now unknown, Plin. 37, 10, 56, § 153.
ceritis.short: cērītis, ĭdis, f., = κηρῖτις, wax-stone, a precious stone, now unknown, Plin.

cerium.full: cērĭum, ii, n., = κηρίον (v. Liddell and Scott, under the word, II.), a bad species of swelling or ulcer, Plin. 20, 2, 6, § 11; 23, 7, 63, § 119 (in Cels. 5, 28, 13, written as Greek).

cernentia.full: cernentĭa, ae. f., cernens, cerno, the sight, seeing, opp. to caecitas, Mart. Cap. 4, §§ 384 and 386.

cerno.full: cerno, crēvi, crētum (part. pass. cretus is apparently used only once: cineris bene creti, Pall. 12, 22, 3; but freq. in the compounds of cerno; for the simple part., the orig. form certus also is very rarely used: certā deinde sorte senatus consultum factum est, Liv. 36, 2, 2; v. under II. C., and cf. certus), 3, v. a. root car- for scar-, to separate; cf. κρίνω; hence, σκώρ, stercus, screo; cf. cera. To separate, sift (rare): per cribrum, Cato. R. R. 107, 1: farinam cribro, Plin. 18, 11, 29, §

cernulo.full: cernŭlo, āre, v. a. cernuo, to throw down: non vertit fortuna sed cernulat et allidit, Sen. Ep. 8, 4.

cernulus.full: cernŭlus, a, um, adj. id., turning a somersault (late Lat.), App. M. 9, p. 235, 28.

cernuo.full: cernŭo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. and n. cernuus, to throw or fall head foremost (only ante- and post-class.), Varr. ap. Non. p. 21, 8; App. M. 1, 19, p. 111, 9; Front. Princ. Hist. 5.—In dep. form: tigres cernuantur, Sol. 17: equus de industriā cernuatus, id. 45.

cernuus1.full: cernŭus, a, um, adj. root kar, v. celsus; cf. κάρηνον, cerebrum, with the face turned towards the earth, inclined forwards, stooping or bowing forwards (very rare and only poet.): cernuus dicitur proprie inclinatus, quasi quod terram cernit, Non. p. 20, 33 sq.; Lucil. ib. p. 21, 1: ejectoque incumbit cernuus armo, * Verg. A. 10, 894 (v. Serv. ad h. 1.): cernuus inflexo sonipes effuderat armo, Sil. 10, 255 sq.; Arn. 7, p. 246.—Hence, That turns a somersault; a tumbler, mountebank, κυβιστητήρ, πετ

cernuus2.full: cernŭus, i, m., a kind of shoe, acc. to Paul. ex Fest. p. 55 Müll., and Isid. Orig. 19, 34, 13.
cernuus2.short: cernŭus, i, m., a kind of shoe, acc.

cero.full: cēro, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. cera, to cover, overlay, or smear with wax, to wax: dolia, Col. 12, 52, 15.—More freq. in part. pass.: cerata tabula, Plaut. As. 4, 1, 18: tabella, * Cic. Div. in Caecil. 7, 24; cf. Dig. 32, 52: pennae, * Hor. C. 4, 2, 2: taedae, Ov. H. 7, 23: rates, id. ib. 5, 42; cf. puppes, id. R. Am. 447.

ceroferarius.full: cērōfĕrārĭus, ii, m. cera-fero, the waxlight bearer, an attendant at Christian ceremonial worship (eccl. Lat.), Isid. Orig. 7, 12, 29.

ceroliensis.full: Ceroliensis locus, a place in Rome, a part of the Carinœ, Varr. L. L. 5, § 47 Müll.
ceroliensis.short: Ceroliensis locus, a place in Rome, a part of the Carinœ, Varr.

ceroma.full: cērōma, ătis, n. (abl. plur. ceromatis, Plin. 35, 13, 47, § 168; acc. plur. ceromas, Arn. 3, 114), = κήρωμα, an ointment for wrestlers, much used in the time of the emperors, Plin. l. l.; 28, 4, 13, § 51; Mart. 4, 19; 7, 32; 14, 50.— Meton. The place for wrestling: in ceromate sedere, Sen. Brev. Vit. 12, 2; Plin. 35, 2, 2, § 5.— The ring, the combat, Plin. 29, 1, 8, § 26; Mart. 5, 65, 3 (in Plin. Val. 1, 25 fin., ceromata is perh. = canceromata, a swelling, tumor).

ceromaticus.full: cērōmătĭcus, a, um, adj., = κηρωματικός, smeared with wax-ointment: collum, Juv. 3. 68.
ceromaticus.short: cērōmătĭcus, a, um, adj., = κηρωματικός, smeared with wax-ointment: collum, Juv.

ceronia.full: cĕrōnĭa (cĕrān-), ae, f., = κερωνία, St. John's bread, Plin. 13, 8, 16, § 59.

cerosus.full: cērōsus, a, um, adj. cera, full of wax: mel, Plin. 32, 3, 13, § 27.

cerretani.full: Cerretāni, ōrum, m., an Iberian people of Hispania Tarraconensis, among the Pyrenees, Plin. 3, 3, 4, § 22; Sil. 3, 357.— Hence, Cerretānus, a, um, of the Cerretani: perna, Mart. 13, 54, 1.
cerretani.short: Cerretāni, ōrum, m., an Iberian people of Hispania Tarraconensis, among the Pyrenees, Plin.

cerreus.full: cerrĕus, a, um, adj. cerrus, of the Turkey oak: glans, Col. 9, 20, 5; Nigid. ap. Plin. 16, 6, 8, § 25: manubria, Hyg. ib. 16, 43, 84, § 230.

cerrinus.full: cerrĭnus, a, um, adj. id., of the Turkey oak: calix, Plin. 30, 10, 27, § 92.

cerritulus.full: cerrītŭlus, a, um, adj. dim. [cerritus], somewhat mad, Mart. Cap. 8, § 806.

cerritus.full: cerrītus, a, um, adj. contr. from cĕrĕbrītus, from cerebrum; cf. cerebrosus, having a crazed brain, frantic, mad: cerritus furiosus, Fest. p. 54 Müll. (rare and only poet.), Plaut. Fragm. ap. Non. p. 44, 31; id. Am. 2, 2, 144; id. Rud. 4, 3, 67; * Hor. S. 2, 3, 278.

cerrus.full: cerrus, i, f., a kind of oak, Turkey oak, Col. 7, 9, 6; Plin. 16, 5, 6, § 17; 16, 6, 8, § 19; Vitr. 2, 8; Pall. 1, 9, 3; id. Febr. 18, 3.
cerrus.short: cerrus, i, f., a kind of oak, Turkey oak, Col.

certabundus.full: certābundus, a, um, adj. 2. certo, contending, disputing, App. Mag. p. 288, 23.

certamen.full: certāmen, ĭnis, n. id., a contest, struggle, strife, whether friendly or hostile, physical or intellectual; most freq. of a pugilistic contest of any kind; but also of contention in war. A contest, struggle in games or otherwise. Lit.: videmusne apud quos eorum ludorum, qui gymnici nominantur, magnus honos sit, nullum ab iis, qui in id certamen descendant, devitari dolorem? Cic. Tusc. 2, 26, 62; cf. id. de Or. 2, 78, 317: Hac celebrata tenus sancto certamina patri, Verg. A. 5, 603; cf. Ov. M. 1,

certatim.full: certātim, adv. certatus, 2. certo, emulously, earnestly, eagerly (class. in prose and poetry): certatim de alicujus salute dicere, Cic. Sest. 34, 74; Liv. 1, 54, 3: mulieres puerique saxa et alia... certatim mittere, Sall. J. 67, 1: certatim alter alteri obstrepere, Liv. 1, 40, 6: hoc Cicero atque Asinius certatim sunt usi, * Quint. 6, 1, 21: currere, Cic. Phil. 2, 46, 118: ascendere, Liv. 26, 44, 9: exsurgere, Tac. A. 3, 65: erumpere curiā, id. ib. 12, 7: amare aliquem, * Plin. Ep. 2, 9, 5; cf.

certatio.full: certātĭo, ōnis, f. 2. certo, a contending, striving, a combat, strife, contest, etc. (in good prose, most freq. in Cic.). Lit. In gen.: jam ludi publici sint corporum certatione, cursu, etc., Cic. Leg. 2, 15, 38; cf. id. ib. 2, 9, 22; Ter. Ad. 2, 2, 4: certationes xysticorum, Suet. Aug. 45.— Esp., a military contest, a fight (very rare), Sisenn. ap. Non. p. 196, 1.— Trop.: Medea nequaquam istuc istac ibit: magna inest certatio, Enn. ap. Cic. N. D. 3, 25, 65 (Trag. Rel. v. 304 Vahl.): relinquitur

certative.full: certātīvē, adv. id., in order to stir up strife, combatively (late Lat.), Cassiod. Hist. Eccl. 1, 11.

certator.full: certātor, ōris, m. id., a disputant (rare and post-class.), Gell. 12, 10, 3; App. Dogm. Plat. p. 2.

certatus1.full: certātus, a, um, Part., from certo.
certatus1.short: certātus, a, um, Part., from certo.

certatus2.full: certātus, ūs, m. 2. certo, a contention, fight, Stat. S. 3, 1, 152.

certe.full: certē, adv., v. certus, adv. B.

certim.full: certim, adv. certus, analog. to certatim, from certatus, certainly: scire, Jul. Val. Rer. Gest. Alex. M. 1, 31.

certioro.full: certĭōro, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. certior, = certiorem facere, to inform, apprise, show (only in jurid. Lat., and most freq. used by Ulpian), Gai 2, 190; Dig. 13, 6, 5, § 8; 19, 1, 1 fin.: certioratus, ib. 29, 4, 1, § 4; 43, 29, 3, § 6.

certo1.full: certō, adv., v. certus, adv. A.

certo2.full: certo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. freq. a. cerno, to decide something by a contest (cf. cerno, II. C. b.); hence, to fight, struggle, contend, combat, implying great exertion, and usually a measuring of strength (class. in prose and poetry; most freq. in a trop. signif.; syn.: decerto, contendo). Of a physical contest of strength; mostly of battle: utrum igitur utilius Fabricio... armis cum hoste certare, an venenis? Cic. Off. 3, 22, 87: adulescentium greges Lacedaemone videmus ipsi incredibili contention

certor.full: certor, āri, v. dep. n. [collat. form of 2. certo], to strive, struggle, contend, Hyg. Fab. 273; Vulg. Ecclus. 11, 9.

certus.full: certus, a, um orig. P. a. from cerno; hence, adj., determined, resolved, fixed, settled, purposed: non dubius. (Acc. to cerno, II. D.) Certum est (mihi), it is determined, it is my (thy, his, etc.) decision, resolution, will, I am resolved, I mean, etc. (mostly ante-class.; most freq. in Plaut.); with inf.: quorum virtuti belli Fortuna pepercit, Eorundem me libertati parcere certum est, Enn. ap. Cic. Off. 1, 12, 38 (Ann. v. 206 Vahl.): certum'st hominem eludere, Plaut. Am. 1, 1, 109: tibi creder

ceruchi.full: cĕrūchi, ōrum, m., = κεροῦχοι (= κεραιοῦχοι, holding the sail-yards), ropes fastened to the sail-yards, Luc. 8, 17; 10, 495; Val. Fl. 1, 469.
ceruchi.short: cĕrūchi, ōrum, m., = κεροῦχοι (= κεραιοῦχοι, holding the sail-yards), ropes fastened to the sail-yards, Luc.

cerula.full: cērŭla, ae, f. dim. cera, a small piece of wax: miniata, a kind of crayon, Cic. Att. 15. 14, 4 (with which the Romans were accustomed to strike out exceptionable passages in books): miniatula, the same, id. ib. 16, 11, 1 (al. miniata).— Transf., = ceriolarium, a candlestick or stand for wax tapers: ARGENTEAE, Inscr. Orell. 2032.

cerus.full: cerus, in carmine Saliari intellegitur creator, Fest. s. v. matrem matutam, p. 122 Müll.—Here perhaps belongs also another passage from the Carm. Saliorum: duomis ceruses, Varr. L. L. 7, § 26 Müll.; another writing KERVS in KERI POCOLOM, an inscription on a clay vase; the word is a masc. form to the fem. Ceres, and denotes the creator; from cer = Sanscr. kri, to make; v. Ceres.
cerus.short: cerus, in carmine Saliari intellegitur creator, Fest.

cerussa.full: cērussa, ae. f., white-lead, ceruse (used by painters, and by women for making the skin white; also in medicine, and in large doses as a poison), Plin. 28, 9, 33, § 129; 34, 18, 54, § 175 sq.; Vitr. 7, 12, 1; Cels. 5, 27, 15; Plin. 28, 9, 33, § 129; 35, 6, 19, § 37; Plant. Most. 1, 3, 101; Ov. Med. Fac. 73; Mart. 10, 22, 2; Pall. Aug. 11, 3.

cerussatus.full: cērussātus, a, um, adj. cerussa, colored or painted with white-lead: buccae, Cic. Pis. 11, 25: cutis, Mart. 7, 25, 2: Sabella, id. 2, 41, 12: tabulae, Cod. Th. 11, 27, 1.

cerva.full: cerva, ae, f. cervus, a hind, Plin. 11, 37, 45, § 123 sq.; Ov. M. 6, 636; 12, 34.— Poet., for deer in gen., Ter. Phorm. prol. 7; Cat. 63, 72; Verg. A. 4, 69; Hor. C. 1, 1, 27; 3, 5, 32; Ov. M. 7, 546; 11, 772; id. A. A. 3, 670; Tib. 4, 3, 13.

cervarius.full: cervārĭus, a, um, adj. id., of or pertaining to deer: lupus, a lynx, Plin. 8, 22, 34, § 84; 11, 37, 79, § 202: venenum, an herb with which arrows were smeared, Plin. 27, 11, 76, § 101; Fest. s. v. toxicum, p. 355: cervaria ovis, quae pro cervā immolabatur (Dianae), Fest. p. 57.

cervical.full: cervīcal (cervīcāle, Cassiod. Orth. p. 2302 P.), ālis, n. cervix, a pillow or bolster, = pulvinus; sing., Mart. 14, 146; Juv. 6, 353; Petr. 56, 8; plur., Plin. Ep. 6, 16, 16; Petr. 32, 1; 78, 5; Suet. Ner. 6; Plin. 20, 20, 82, § 217; 28, 4, 12, § 47.

cervicatus.full: cervīcātus, a, um, adj. id., stiffnecked, obstinate, Vulg. Ecclus. 16, 11.

cervicositas.full: cervīcōsĭtas, ātis, f. cervicosus, stubbornness, obstinacy, Sid. Ep. 7, 9.

cervicosus.full: cervīcōsus, a, um, adj. cervix, stubborn, obstinate, Eccl. Ambros. ap. Voss. Vit. L. L. 3, 4; cf.: cervicosus αὐχενίας, Gloss. Labb.

cervicula.full: cervīcŭla, ae, f. dim. id.. A small neck, * Cic. Verr. 2, 3, 19, § 49; App. Flor. p. 348: contracta, Quint. 11, 3, 180.—* In mechanics, the neck of a hydraulic machine, Vitr. 10, 8, 2.

cervinus.full: cervīnus, a, um, adj. cervus, of or pertaining to a deer: cornu, deer's horn, Varr. R. R. 3, 9, 14; Col. 8, 5, 18 al.: pellis, Hor. Ep. 1, 2, 66: vellera, * Ov. M. 6, 592: pilus, Plin. 28, 19, 77, § 246: color equi, Pall. Mart. 13, 4: senectus, i. e. great age (because the deer was said to live to a great age; cf. Cic. Tusc. 3, 28, 69; Plin. 8, 32, 50, § 119; Aristot. H. A. 9, 6), Juv. 14, 251.— Subst.: cervīna, ae, f. (sc. caro), deer's meat, venison, Edict. Diocl. 4, 44.

cervisia.full: cervisia, cervesia, or cerevi-sia, ae, f. Gallic, beer, Plin. 22, 25, 82, § 164; Dig. 33, 6, 9; Isid. Orig. 20, 3, 17; Edict. Diocl. 2, 11.
cervisia.short: cervisia, cervesia, or cerevi-sia, ae, f.

cervix.full: cervix, īcis (gen. plur. cervicum, Cic. Or. 18, 59; Plin. 23, 2, 33, § 68: cervicium, acc. to Charis. p. 100), f. cer-vix; cf. Sanscr. s)iras, caput, and vincio, Bopp, Gloss. 348 b, the neck, including the back of the neck, the nape (in ante-Aug. prose usu. in plur.; so always in Cic. and Sall.; acc. to Varr. L. L. 8, § 14; 10, § 78 Müll.; and Quint. 8, 3, 35, Hortensius first used the sing.; it is, however, found even in Ennius and Pacuvius; v. the foll.). Sing.: caput a cervice revolsum, Enn.

cervula.full: cervŭla, ae, f. dim. cerva, a little hind, Aug. Serm. 215.

cervulus.full: cervŭlus, i, m. dim. cervus, II. B., a little chevaux-de-frise, Front. Strat. 1, 5, 2.

cervus.full: cervus (old orthogr. cervŏs; cf. Quint. 1, 7, 26), i, m. kindr. with cornu and carina, a stag, a deer, Plin. 8, 32, 50, § 112 sq.: alipedes, Lucr. 6, 765: fugax, Hor. C. 4, 6, 34; Ov. Tr. 3, 11, 11: fugientes, Hor. C. 3, 12, 11: pavidi, Ov. F. 5, 173: surgentem in cornua, Verg. A. 10, 725 al.—As a type of fleetness: vincere cervum cursu, Plaut. Poen. 3, 1, 27.— Transf. (from resemblance to the horns of a stag; cf. Varr. L. L. 5, § 117 Müll.): cervi, forked stakes. * As supports of the vine, Tert

cerycium.full: cērȳcĭum or cērȳcēum, ii, n., = κηρύκιον or κηρύκειον, a pure Greek form for caduceus, the herald's staff, Dig. 1, 8, 8; Mart. Cap. 4, § 331.
cerycium.short: cērȳcĭum or cērȳcēum, ii, n., = κηρύκιον or κηρύκειον, a pure Greek form for caduceus, the herald's staff, Dig.

ceryx.full: cērȳx, ȳcis, m., = κήρυξ, a herald, Sen. Tranq. 3, 10.
ceryx.short: cērȳx, ȳcis, m., = κήρυξ, a herald, Sen.

cespes.full: cespes, cespitator, cespito, ce-sposus, v. caespes, etc.

cessatio.full: cessātĭo, ōnis, f. cesso. A tarrying, delaying: non datur cessatio, Plaut. Poen. 4, 2, 103.—Hence, Inactivity, idling, cessation, omission, idleness: furtum cessationis quaerere, Q. Cic. Fam. 16, 26, 2: cessatio libera atque otiosa, Cic. Leg. 1, 3, 10 Orell. N. cr.: pugnae, Gell. 1, 25, 8: Epicurus nihil cessatione melius existimat... deum sic feriatum volumus cessatione torpere, etc., Cic. N. D. 1, 36, 102; 1, 37, 102.— So in jurid. lang., a punishable delay, Dig. 37, 2, 6.—And of ground, a lyi

cessator.full: cessātor, ōris, m. id., a loiterer, an idler, a dilatory person: non quo cessator esse solerem, praesertim in litteris, Cic. Fam. 9, 17, 3: de libris, Tyrannio est cessator, id. ad Q. Fr. 3, 5 (6), 6: nequam et cessator Davus, * Hor. S. 2, 7, 100; * Col. 11, 1, 16.

cessatrix.full: cessātrix, īcis, f. cessator, a (female) loiterer, idler, Tert. adv. Marc. 1, 24.

cessicius.full: cessĭcĭus (-tĭus), a, um, adj. cessus, 1. cedo; in jurid. lang., of or pertaining to giving up, ceding: tutor, Gai Inst. 1, 169 sqq.; Ulp. Lib. Reg. tit. 11, 7: tutela, Gai Inst. 1, 171.

cessim.full: cessim (cossim), adv. cesso; cf. coxim, bending or turning in; hence, also, turned backwards, backwards (mostly anteand post-class.): cum domum ab Ilio cessim revertero, Varr. ap. Non. p. 247, 26; p. 276, 9: cessim ire, Dig. 9, 2, 52, § 2; Just. 2, 12, 7: lagena orificio cessim (obliquely) dehiscente patescens, App. M. 2, p. 121, 8.

cessio.full: cessio, ōnis, f. 1. cedo; only in jurid. lang. A giving up, surrendering: abalienatio est ejus rei, quae mancipi est, aut traditio alteri nexo aut in jure cessio, Cic. Top. 5, 28; Dig. 42, 3 tit.; Gai Inst. 3, 78; v. Dict. of Antiq., de cessione bonorum.— * Diei, the approach of a term, Dig. 36, 2, 7.

cesso.full: cesso, āvi, ātum, 1, v. freq. n. and a. [1. cedo]; lit., to stand back very much; hence, to be remiss in any thing, to delay, loiter, or, in gen., to cease from, stop, give over (indicating a blamable remissness; while desinere, intermittere, requiescere do not include that idea: cessat desidiosus, requiescit fessus, Don. ad Ter. Eun. 3, 1, 15. Diff. from cunctari in this, that the latter designates inaction arising from want of resolution, but cessare that which is the result of slothfulness; c

cesticillus.full: cestĭcillus (caest-), i, m., a small ring or hoop placed upon the head to support a burden, Fest. p. 45 [dim. from cestus; cf. Commod. p. 363].
cesticillus.short: cestĭcillus (caest-), i, m., a small ring or hoop placed upon the head to support a burden, Fest.

cesticus.full: cestĭcus (caest-), a, um, adj. cestus, of a boxer's glove: ludi, Tac. A. 16, 21 dub.

cestius.full: Cestĭus, ĭi, m., the name of a Roman plebeian family. C. Cestius, Cic. Phil. 3, 10, 26.— L. Cestius Pius, a rhetorician of Smyrna, Sen. Contr. 3, prooem. p. 206, 3 al.—Hence, Cestĭānus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to L. Cestius: color, Sen. Contr. 1, 7, p. 125.
cestius.short: Cestĭus, ĭi, m., the name of a Roman plebeian family.

cestros1.full: cestros, i, f., = κέστρος, the plant betony: Betonica officinalis, Linn.; Plin. 25, 8, 46, § 84.
cestros1.short: cestros, i, f., = κέστρος, the plant betony: Betonica officinalis, Linn.;

cestros2.full: Cestrŏs, i, m., a river of Pamphylia, now Ak-su, Mel. 1, 14, 2.
cestros2.short: Cestrŏs, i, m., a river of Pamphylia, now Ak-su, Mel.

cestrosphendone.full: cestrosphendŏnē, ēs, f., = κεστροσφενδόνη, a mililary engine for hurling stones, Liv. 42, 65, 9.
cestrosphendone.short: cestrosphendŏnē, ēs, f., = κεστροσφενδόνη, a mililary engine for hurling stones, Liv.

cestrotus.full: cestrōtus, a, um, adj., = κεστρωτός, represented by means of a graver (κέστρον): cornua, Plin. 11, 37, 45, § 126.
cestrotus.short: cestrōtus, a, um, adj., = κεστρωτός, represented by means of a graver (κέστρον): cornua, Plin.

cestrum.full: cestrum (-on), i, n., = κέστρον, a graver, graving tool, used in encaustic painting, Plin. 35, 11, 41, § 149.
cestrum.short: cestrum (-on), i, n., = κέστρον, a graver, graving tool, used in encaustic painting, Plin.

cestus1.full: cestus (caest-) or -ŏs, i, m., = κεστός (lit. stitched, embroidered; hence, subst.; cf. Lidd. and Scott under κεστός), a girdle, tie, belt, girth, strap, Cato, R. R. 25 Schneid. N. cr.; Varr. R. R. 1, 8, 6.—Particularly, the girdle of Venus, Mart. 6, 138; 6, 14; 14, 206 sq.; Serv. ad Verg. A. 5, 69.

cestus2.full: cestus = caestus, a boxer's glove; v. caestus.

cetarini.full: Cētārīni (Cītār-), ōrum, m., the inhabitants of a city of Sicily, Cic. Verr. 2, 3, 43, § 103; Plin. 3, 8, 14, § 91.
cetarini.short: Cētārīni (Cītār-), ōrum, m., the inhabitants of a city of Sicily, Cic.

cetarius.full: cētārĭus, a, um, adj. cetus, of or pertaining to fish; only subst. cētārĭus, ii, m., a fish-monger, Ter. Eun. 2, 2, 26 (also in Cic. Off. 1, 42, 150); Varr. ap. Non. p. 49, 15; Col. 8, 17, 12.—Cētārĭus, title of a book of C. Matius, Col. 12, 46, 1.— cētā-rĭum, ii, n., a fish-pond, Hor. S. 2, 5, 44.— Access. form cētārĭa, ae, f.; acc. plur. cetarias, Plin. 9, 15, 19, § 49; 37, 5, 17, § 66; an uncertain form, abl. plur. cetariis, Plin. 9, 30, 48, § 91; 31, 8, 43, § 94.

cetera.full: cētĕra, cētĕro, cētĕrum, v. ceterus, II.

ceteroqui.full: cētĕrōqui or -quīn ceterus-qui (like alioqui and alioquin; v. alioqui, and cf. Hand, Turs. I. p. 235), adv., for the rest, in other respects, otherwise, = ἄλλως (rare): quem, nisi quod solum, ceteroquin recte quidam vocant Atticum, Cic. Or. 25, 83: ego ceteroqui animo aequo fero; unum vereor, ne hasta Caesaris refrixerit, id. Fam. 9, 10, 3; id. Att. 12, 3, 1; 14, 16, 1; 16, 4, 1; id. Fam. 6, 19, 1; id. N. D. 1, 22, 60; Dig. 28, 5, 35, § 3; Gell. 20, 1, 27; cf. Hand, Turs. II. pp. 44 and 42.
ceteroqui.short: cētĕrōqui or -quīn ceterus-qui (like alioqui and alioquin;

ceterus.full: cētĕrus (caet-), a, um (the nom. sing. masc. not in use; the sing., in gen., rare; in Cic. perh. only three times), adj. pronom. stem ki, and compar. ending; cf. ἕτερος, the other, that which exists besides, can be added to what is already named of a like kind with it; the other part (while reliquus is that which yet remains of an object, the rest; e. g. stipendium pendere et cetera indigna pati, and endured other indignities of the kind, Liv. 21, 20, 6. On the other hand: jam vero reliqua—not c

cethegus.full: Cĕthĕgus, i, m., a Roman cognomen in the Cornelian gens. M. Cornelius Cethegus, a distinguished orator, Cic. Sen. 14, 50; id. Brut. 15, 59 al.; to him Horace alludes in the passage: priscis memorata Catonibus atque Cethegis, Hor. Ep. 2, 2, 117; cf. id. A. P. 50.— C. Cornelius Cethegus, companion of Catiline, Cic. Cat. 3, 3, 6; Sall. C. 32, 2; 43, 2.—Prov.: Clodius accuset moechos, Catilina Cethegum, Juv. 2, 27; cf. id. 8, 231; 10, 287.
cethegus.short: Cĕthĕgus, i, m., a Roman cognomen in the Cornelian gens.

ceto.full: Cēto, ūs, f., = Κητώ. The wife of Phorcus, and mother of Medusa and the Gorgons, Luc. 9, 646.— A Nereid, honored upon the Phœnician coast, Plin. 5, 13, 14, § 69.

cetosus.full: cētōsus, a, um, adj. cetus, of or pertaining to sea-fishes: viscera, Avien. Arat. 1300.

cetus.full: cētus, i, m. (acc. to the Gr. cētŏs, n., Plin. 32, 1, 4, § 10; and hence common in the plur. cētē = κήτη, Verg. A. 5, 822; Plin. 9, 24, 40, § 78; 9, 50, 74, § 157; Sil. 7, 476), = κῆτος, any large sea-animal, a seamonster; particularly a species of whale, a shark, dog-fish, seal, dolphin, etc., Plin. l. l.; Plaut. Aul. 2, 8, 5; id. Capt. 4, 2, 72; Cels. 2, 18.— As a constellation, the Whale, Vitr. 9, 7; Manil. 1, 612.

ceu.full: ceu, adv. contr. from ce-ve, like neu and seu, from neve and sive, a particle of equality or comparison, as, like as, just as (in the ante-Aug. per., peculiar to more elevated poetry; later also in prose, in Seneca and Suet., and esp. freq. in Plin. H. N.): pars vertere terga, ceu quondam petiere rates, Verg. A. 6, 492: ceu talpae, Plin. 9, 6, 7, § 17: ceu notamus in muscis, id. 11, 48, 108, § 258; so id. 9, 37, 61, § 132; Suet. Vit. 17; Plin. 19, 12, 62, § 187.— In poet. comparisons (hence, hau

ceus.full: Cēus, a, um, v. Cea, I. B.

ceutrones.full: Ceutrones, um, m., a Gallic tribe, Caes. B. G. 5, 39.
ceutrones.short: Ceutrones, um, m., a Gallic tribe, Caes.

ceva.full: cēva or ceua, ae, f. Low Germ. Keue, a kind of small cow, Col. 6, 24, 5.

cevenna.full: Cĕvenna (also Cĕbenna and Gĕ-benna), ae, f., a mountain in Gallia, now Cevennes, Caes. B. G. 7, 8; 7, 56; Luc. 1, 434.—The same: Cebennici or Gebennici montes, Mel. 2, 5, 1; 2, 5, 6.
cevenna.short: Cĕvenna (also Cĕbenna and Gĕ-benna), ae, f., a mountain in Gallia, now Cevennes, Caes.

ceveo.full: cēveo, ēre (perf. cevi, without voucher in Prob. p. 1482 P.), v. n. Sanscr. kju, to agitate one's self; cf. quatio. To move the haunches, Plaut. Fragin. ap. Non. p. 84, 18; Juv. 2, 21; 9, 40; Mart. 3, 95, 13; cf. criso.—* Trop. (the figure taken from the wagging of the tail of a dog), to fawn, flatter, Pers. 1, 87.

ceyx.full: cēÿx, ȳcis, m., = κήϋξ, the male kingfisher (the female, halcyon), Plin. 32, 8, 27, § 86.—Personified: Cēyx, ȳcis, m., = Κήϋξ, a son of Lucifer, king of Trachis, and husband of Alcyone. Having suffered shipwreck at Delphi, he and his wife were changed to kingfishers, Ov. H. 17 (18), 81; id. M. 11, 272; 11, 544; 11, 739; Serv. ad Verg. G. 1, 399.—Acc. Gr. Cēȳca, Ov. M. 11, 727.
ceyx.short: cēÿx, ȳcis, m., = κήϋξ, the male kingfisher (the female, halcyon), Plin.

chabrias.full: Chabrĭas, ae, m., = Χαβρίας, a distinguished Athenian general; v. his life in Cornel. Nepos.
chabrias.short: Chabrĭas, ae, m., = Χαβρίας, a distinguished Athenian general;

chaere.full: chaere, interj., = χαῖρε, hail! Pers. prol. 8.

chaerea.full: Chaerĕa, ae, m. (Gr. Χαιρέας), a Roman cognomen, Ter. Eun. 2, 3, 17 al.; Cic. Rosc. Com. 1, 1; Sen. Const. Sap. 18, 3.

chaereas.full: Chaerĕas, ae, m., = Χαιρέας, a Grecian proper name. A writer on husbandry, Varr. R. R. 1, 1, 8; Col. 1, 1, 8; Plin. 20, 23, 99, § 263.— A sculptor of the time of Alexander the Great, Plin. 34, 8, 19, § 75; Vitr. 10, 13, 3.
chaereas.short: Chaerĕas, ae, m., = Χαιρέας, a Grecian proper name.

chaeronea.full: Chaerōnēa, ae, f., = Χαιρώνεια, a Bœotian town on the Cephisus, where Philip of Macedon conquered the Greeks; the birthplace of Plutarch; now the village Kaprena or Kapurna, Plin. 4, 7, 12, § 26; Liv. 35, 46, 3.
chaeronea.short: Chaerōnēa, ae, f., = Χαιρώνεια, a Bœotian town on the Cephisus, where Philip of Macedon conquered the Greeks;

chalasticamen.full: chălastĭcāmen, ĭnis, n. chalasticus, an alleviating remedy, Theod. Prisc. 2, 10.

chalasticus.full: chălastĭcus, a, um, adj., = χαλαστικός, of or pertaining to alleviating, soothing: aqua, Theod. Prisc. 1, 7 and 15: unctiones, Veg. 1, 28, 6.
chalasticus.short: chălastĭcus, a, um, adj., = χαλαστικός, of or pertaining to alleviating, soothing: aqua, Theod.

chalatorius.full: chălātōrĭus, a, um, adj. chalo, pertaining to loosing or letting down: funes, Veg. Mil. 4, 15.

chalazias.full: chălāzĭas, ae, m., = χαλαζίας [χάλαζα, hail], an unknown precious stone, of the form and color of hail, Plin. 37, 11, 73, § 189; Sol. 37, 17.
chalazias.short: chălāzĭas, ae, m., = χαλαζίας [χάλαζα, hail], an unknown precious stone, of the form and color of hail, Plin.

chalazius.full: chălāzĭus, a, um, adj. χάλαζα, hail, pertaining to hail: lapis, a precious stone, Plin. 36, 22, 43, § 157.— Subst.: chălā-zĭon, ii, n., = χαλάζιον, a pimple or small tubercle on the eyelids, Cels. 7, 7, 2, Caption: de chalazio palpebrarum (written as Greek in the text).

chalcanthum.full: chalcanthum, i, n., = χάλκανθον [χαλκόσ-ἄνθος], copperas-water; pure Lat. atramentum sutorium, Plin. 34, 12, 32, § 123.

chalcaspis.full: chalcaspis, idis, adj., = χάλκασπις, having a brazen shield, Liv. 44, 41, 2 Weissenb.; cf. aglaspis.
chalcaspis.short: chalcaspis, idis, adj., = χάλκασπις, having a brazen shield, Liv.

chalcedon.full: Chalcēdon (in MSS. also Calchē-don), ŏnis, f., = Χαλκηδών, a town in Bithynia, on the Thracian Bosporus, opposite Byzantium, Mel. 1, 19, 5; Plin. 5, 32, 43, § 149 sq.; 37, 5, 18, § 73; Liv. 42, 56, 6; acc. Gr. Chalcedona, Luc. 9, 959 al.; cf. Mann. Asia Min. 3, p. 581 sq.—Hence, Chalcēdŏnĭus, a, um, adj., of Chalcedon, Chalcedonian: Thrasymachus, Cic. de Or. 3, 32, 128: smaragdi, Plin. 37, 5, 18, § 72: harenae, Claud. in Rufin. 2, 55.—Subst.: Chalcēdŏnii, ōrum, m., the Chalcedonians, Tac. A. 12,

chalceos.full: chalcēŏs, i, f., = χάλκειος, a prickly plant, otherwise unknown, Plin. 21, 16, 56, § 94.
chalceos.short: chalcēŏs, i, f., = χάλκειος, a prickly plant, otherwise unknown, Plin.

chalcetum.full: chalcētum, i, n., an unknown medicinal plant, Plin. 26, 7, 25, § 40.
chalcetum.short: chalcētum, i, n., an unknown medicinal plant, Plin.

chalceus.full: chalcĕus, a, um, adj., = χάλκεος, brazen, of brass; only in plur. subst.: chalcea, ōrum, n., brazen things, Mart. 9, 95, 4.
chalceus.short: chalcĕus, a, um, adj., = χάλκεος, brazen, of brass;

chalcidensis.full: Chalcĭdensis, e, v. 2. Chalcis, I. B. 2.

chalcidice.full: chalcĭdĭcē, ēs, f., = χαλκιδική, a kind of lizard, = 1. chalcis, Plin. 29, 5, 32, § 102.
chalcidice.short: chalcĭdĭcē, ēs, f., = χαλκιδική, a kind of lizard, = 1.

chalcidicensis.full: Chalcĭdĭcensis, e, v. 2. Chalcis, I. B. 3.

chalcidicum.full: Chalcĭdĭcum, i, n., v. 2. Chalcis, I. B. 1. b.

chalcidicus.full: Chalcĭdĭcus, a, um, v. 2. Chalcis, I. B. 1.

chalcioecos.full: Chalcĭoecos, i, f., = Χαλκίοικος (among the Greeks, an epithet of Athene, from her temple of brass), among the Romans, a temple of Minerva, Liv. 35, 36, 9 (in Nep. Paus. 5, 2, written as Greek).
chalcioecos.short: Chalcĭoecos, i, f., = Χαλκίοικος (among the Greeks, an epithet of Athene, from her temple of brass), among the Romans, a temple of Minerva, Liv.

chalciope.full: Chalcĭŏpē, ēs, f., = Χαλκιόπη. A daughter of Æetes, sister of Medea, and wife of Phrixus, Hyg. Fab. 21; Ov. H. 16 (17), 232; Val. Fl. 6, 479.— Wife of Mnesylus, and mother of Antiphus, Hyg. Fab. 97.

chalcis1.full: chalcis, ĭdis, f., = χαλκίς. A fish of the herring kind, Col. 8, 17, 12; Plin. 9, 47, 71, § 154; 9, 51, 74, § 162.— A lizard with copper-colored spots on its back, Plin. 32, 3, 13, § 30; 32, 5, 17, § 46.

chalcis2.full: Chalcis, ĭdis or ĭdŏs, f., = Χαλκίς. Chief town of the island Eubœa, opposite to Aulis, connected by a bridge with the main land, now Egribo or Negroponte; also called Chalcis Euboica, or Chalcis Eubœœ, Col. 1, 4, 9; Luc. 5, 227; Mel. 2, 7, 9; Plin. 4, 12, 21, § 64; 11, 37, 74, § 191; Nep. Timoth. 3, 5; Vell. 1, 4, 1; gen. Gr. Chalcidos, Luc. 5, 227; acc. Gr. Chalcida, id. 2, 710.— Hence, the adjj., Chalcĭ-dĭcus, a, um, of Chalcis, in Eubœa, Chalcidian: Euripus, Cic. N. D. 3, 10, 24: creta, Varr
chalcis2.short: Chalcis, ĭdis or ĭdŏs, f., = Χαλκίς.

chalcites.full: chalcītes, ae, m., or chalcītis, ĭdis, f., = χαλκιτης or χαλκῖτις. Copperstone, copper ore, Plin. 34, 2, 2, § 2; 34, 12, 29, § 117 sq.; Cels. 6, 6, 31; 6, 7, 7.— A precious stone of a copper color, Plin. 37, 11, 73, § 191.
chalcites.short: chalcītes, ae, m., or chalcītis, ĭdis, f., = χαλκιτης or χαλκῖτις.

chalcophonos.full: chalcŏphōnŏs (chalcophthon-gŏs, Sol. 37, 22), i. f., = χαλκόφωνος or χαλκοφθογγος, a precious stone ringing like brass, Plin. 37, 10, 56, § 154.

chalcosmaragdos.full: chalcosmăragdŏs, i, f., = χαλκοσμάραγδος, an emerald with veins of brass, perh. malachite, Plin. 37, 5, 19, § 74; Sol. 15, 26.
chalcosmaragdos.short: chalcosmăragdŏs, i, f., = χαλκοσμάραγδος, an emerald with veins of brass, perh.

chalcus.full: chalcus, i, m., = χαλκός, a copper coin, the tenth (acc. to Gr. authors, the sixth or eighth) part of an obolus, Plin. 21, 34, 109, § 185.
chalcus.short: chalcus, i, m., = χαλκός, a copper coin, the tenth (acc.

chaldaei.full: Chaldaei, ōrum, m., = Χαλδαῖοι, the Chaldœans, a people of Assyria, distinguished, in an early age, for their knowledge of astronomy and astrology. Of the nation or people, Plin. 6, 28, 32, § 105; Mel. 3, 8, 5.— In gen., soothsayers, astrologers, Cic. Div. 1, 1, 2; 2, 42, 87 sq.; Val. Max. 3, 1, 2; Gell. 14, 1, 1 sqq.; sing.: Chaldaeus, a soothsayer, Cato, R. R. 5, 4; gen. plur. Chaldaeūm, Lucr. 5, 726.— Hence, Chaldaeus, a, um, adj., Chaldœan: regnum, Luc. 8, 226.— Esp., of or belonging to the
chaldaei.short: Chaldaei, ōrum, m., = Χαλδαῖοι, the Chaldœans, a people of Assyria, distinguished, in an early age, for their knowledge of astronomy and astrology.

chalo.full: chălo, no perf., ātum, 1, v. a., = χαλάω, to slacken, let down: cymbala, Vitr. 10, 13, p. 308 Bip.: culcitas, Veg. Mil. 4, 23.

chalybeius.full: chălўbēïus, a, um, adj., = χαλυβήϊος [χάλυψ], of steel, steel-: massa, Ov. F. 4, 405.
chalybeius.short: chălўbēïus, a, um, adj., = χαλυβήϊος [χάλυψ], of steel, steel-: massa, Ov.

chalybes.full: Chălўbes, um, m., = Χάλυβες. A people in Pontus, noted for their mines and their preparation of steel [chalybs, hence the name; acc. to others, on the contr., steel, χάλυψ, was named from them], Plin. 6, 4, 4, § 11; 7, 56, 57, § 197; Cat. 66, 48; Verg. G. 1, 58; id. A. 8, 421; 10, 174 al.— A tribe on the river Chalybs in Lusitania, Just. 44, 3, 9.

chalybs1.full: chălybs, ўbis, m., = χάλυψ, steel (cf. Plin. 34, 14, 41, § 142 sq.): vulnificus (because weapons were made of it), Verg. A. 8, 446; on account of its hardness: ferro durior et chalybe, Prop. 1, 16, 30; cf. Sen. Herc. Oet. 152; Sil. 1, 171; 2, 403.— Meton., the things made of it. A sword: strictus, Sen. Thyest. 364.— A horse's bit, Luc. 6, 398.— The point of an arrow, Luc. 7, 518; Val. Fl. 6, 342; Sil. 2, 107 al.— An iron rail, Luc. 6, 547.

chalybs2.full: Chălybs, ўbis, m., a river in Lusitania, Just. 44, 3, 9.
chalybs2.short: Chălybs, ўbis, m., a river in Lusitania, Just.

cham.full: Cham, m. indecl., a son of Noah, Ham, Lact. 2, 13, 5; Vulg. Gen. 9, 18 sqq.

chama1.full: chăma, ătis, n., a lynx, Plin. 8, 19, 28, § 70.
chama1.short: chăma, ătis, n., a lynx, Plin.

chamaeacte.full: chămaeactē, ēs, f., = χαμαιάκτη, dwarf elder, danewort: Sambucus ebulus, Linn.; Plin. 24, 8, 35, § 51; 26, 11, 73, § 120.
chamaeacte.short: chămaeactē, ēs, f., = χαμαιάκτη, dwarf elder, danewort: Sambucus ebulus, Linn.;

chamaecerasus.full: chămaecĕrăsus, i, f., = χαμαικερα σος, the dwarf cherry-tree: Prunus chaemaecerasus, Jacq.; Plin. 15, 25, 30, § 104.
chamaecerasus.short: chămaecĕrăsus, i, f., = χαμαικερα σος, the dwarf cherry-tree: Prunus chaemaecerasus, Jacq.;

chamaecissos.full: chămaecissŏs, i, f., = χαμαικισσος, ground-ivy: Glecoma hederacea, Linn.; Plin. 16, 34, 62, § 152; 24, 15, 84, § 135 (ā, Ser. Samm. 44, 799).— A kind of cyclaminus, Plin. 25, 9, 69, § 116.
chamaecissos.short: chămaecissŏs, i, f., = χαμαικισσος, ground-ivy: Glecoma hederacea, Linn.;

chamaecyparissos.full: chămaecўpărissŏs, i, f., = χαμαικυπάρισσος, ground-cypress, Plin. 24, 15, 86, § 136.
chamaecyparissos.short: chămaecўpărissŏs, i, f., = χαμαικυπάρισσος, ground-cypress, Plin.

chamaedaphne.short: chămaedaphnē, ēs, f., = χαμαιδάφνη, dwarf laurel, Plin.

chamaedracon.full: chămaedrăcon, ontis, m., = χαμαιδράκων, a kind of African serpent, the ground-serpent, Sol. 27, 33.
chamaedracon.short: chămaedrăcon, ontis, m., = χαμαιδράκων, a kind of African serpent, the ground-serpent, Sol.

chamaedrys.full: chămaedrys, ўos, f., = χαμαίδρυς, the plant wall-germander: Teucrium chamaedrys, Linn.; in pure Lat. trixago, Plin. 14, 16, 19, § 112; 24, 15, 80, § 130.
chamaedrys.short: chămaedrys, ўos, f., = χαμαίδρυς, the plant wall-germander: Teucrium chamaedrys, Linn.;

chamaeleon.full: chămaelĕon, ōnis and ontis, m., = χαμαιλέων. Masc., a kind of lizard that changes its color, the chameleon, Plin. 8, 33, 51, § 120; 10, 52, 73, § 143; Gell. 10, 12, 1 sq.— Masc. and fem., a plant, the carline thistle; masc., Plin. 22, 18, 21, § 45; 27, 13, 118, § 143; fem., id. 30, 4, 10, § 30.
chamaeleon.short: chămaelĕon, ōnis and ontis, m., = χαμαιλέων.

chamaeleuce.full: chămaeleucē, ēs, f., = χαμαιλεύκη, a plant, colt'sfoot, Plin. 24, 15, 85, § 135; 26, 6, 16, § 30.
chamaeleuce.short: chămaeleucē, ēs, f., = χαμαιλεύκη, a plant, colt'sfoot, Plin.

chamaelygos.full: chămaelўgŏs, i, f., = χαμαίλυγος, a plant, otherwise called verbenaca, App. Herb. 3.
chamaelygos.short: chămaelўgŏs, i, f., = χαμαίλυγος, a plant, otherwise called verbenaca, App.

chamaemelinus.full: chămaemēlĭnus, a, um, adj., = χαμαιμήλινος, of chamomile: oleum, Plin. Val. 3, 2; Theod. Prisc. p. 4, 1.
chamaemelinus.short: chămaemēlĭnus, a, um, adj., = χαμαιμήλινος, of chamomile: oleum, Plin.

chamaemelon.full: chămaemēlon, i, n., = χαμαίμηλον (lit. earth-apple, on account of the applelike smell of the blossoms), chamomile, Plin. 22, 21, 26, § 53; Pall. Jun. 10; App. Herb. 24.—Called also chămŏmilla, ae, f., Plin. Val. 3, 2; Macer. Flor. 14, v. 550.

chamaemyrsine.full: chămaemyrsīnē, ēs, f., = χαμαιμυρσίνη, dwarf myrtle, butcher's-broom, Plin. 23, 9, 83, § 165; 15, 7, 7, § 27.
chamaemyrsine.short: chămaemyrsīnē, ēs, f., = χαμαιμυρσίνη, dwarf myrtle, butcher's-broom, Plin.

chamaepeuce.full: chămaepeucē, ēs, f., = χαμαιπεύκη, the ground-larch, a plant, Plin. 24, 15, 86, § 136.
chamaepeuce.short: chămaepeucē, ēs, f., = χαμαιπεύκη, the ground-larch, a plant, Plin.

chamaepitys.full: chămaepĭtys, ўos, f., = χαμαίπιτυς, a plant, called in pure Lat. abiga, groundpine, said to have the power of producing abortion, Plin. 24, 6, 20, § 29; gen., id. 14, 16, 19, § 112; dat. chamaepityi, id. 21, 29, 103, § 175; acc. chamaepityn, id. 26, 8, 53, § 85.
chamaepitys.short: chămaepĭtys, ўos, f., = χαμαίπιτυς, a plant, called in pure Lat.

chamaeplatanus.full: chămaeplătănus, i, f., = χαμαιπλάτανος, dwarf platane, Plin. 12, 2, 6, § 13.
chamaeplatanus.short: chămaeplătănus, i, f., = χαμαιπλάτανος, dwarf platane, Plin.

chamaerepes.full: chămaerĕpes, um, f., = χαμαιρεπεῖς (creeping on the earth), the dwarf palm, Plin. 13, 4, 9, § 39.
chamaerepes.short: chămaerĕpes, um, f., = χαμαιρεπεῖς (creeping on the earth), the dwarf palm, Plin.

chamaerops.full: chămaerops, ōpis, f., = χαμαίρωψ, = chamaedrys, Plin. 24, 15, 80, § 130; App. Herb. 24; Marc. Emp. 20 (others, chamaedrops = χαμαίδρωψ).
chamaerops.short: chămaerops, ōpis, f., = χαμαίρωψ, = chamaedrys, Plin.

chamaesyce.full: chămaesȳcē, ēs, f., = χαμαισύκη, a plant, wolf's-milk, ground fig: Euphorbia chamaesyce, Linn.; Plin. 24, 15, 83, § 134; in App. Herb. 91, erroneously interchanged with chamaeacte.
chamaesyce.short: chămaesȳcē, ēs, f., = χαμαισύκη, a plant, wolf's-milk, ground fig: Euphorbia chamaesyce, Linn.;

chamaetortus.full: chămae-tortus, a, um, adj. vox hibrida, from χαμαί and tortus, that creeps on the ground, Fronto de Oratt. 2, p. 254.

chamaezelon.full: chămaezēlon, i, n., = χαμαίζηλον, a plant, called also gnaphalion, q. v., Plin. 27, 10, 61, § 88.
chamaezelon.short: chămaezēlon, i, n., = χαμαίζηλον, a plant, called also gnaphalion, q.

chamavi.full: Chămāvi, ōrum, m., = Χαμαυοί Ptolem., a German people, orig. on the north shore of the Rhine even to the Lippe; later, between the Weser and the Hercynian Forest, Tac. G. 33; 34; id. A. 13, 55; Aus. Mos. 434.
chamavi.short: Chămāvi, ōrum, m., = Χαμαυοί Ptolem., a German people, orig.

chamedyosmos.full: chămēdўosmŏs, i, f., = χαμηδύοσμος [χαμαί-ἡδύοσμος], pure Lat. ros marinus, rosemary, App. Herb. 79.
chamedyosmos.short: chămēdўosmŏs, i, f., = χαμηδύοσμος [χαμαί-ἡδύοσμος], pure Lat.

chamelaea.full: chămĕlaea, ae, f., = χαμελαία, the dwarf olive, a shrub: Cneorum tricoccon, Linn.; Plin. 24, 15, 82, § 133; 15, 7, 7, § 24; Scrib. Comp. 133; 200.
chamelaea.short: chămĕlaea, ae, f., = χαμελαία, the dwarf olive, a shrub: Cneorum tricoccon, Linn.;

chameunia.full: chămeunĭa, ae, f., = χαμευνία, a couch on the earth, Hier. Ep. 52, 3.
chameunia.short: chămeunĭa, ae, f., = χαμευνία, a couch on the earth, Hier.

chamulcus.full: chămūlcus, i, m., = χαμουλκός, a kind of machine, Amm. 17, 4, 14.
chamulcus.short: chămūlcus, i, m., = χαμουλκός, a kind of machine, Amm.

chanaan.full: Chănăān, contr. Chănān, f. indecl., the land of Canaan or Paiestine, Lact. 2, 13, 6; Vulg. Gen. 9, 22.—Form Chanan, Juvenc. 2, 129.

chane.full: chānē or channē, ēs, f., = χάνη or χάννη, a kind of sea-fish; Ital. canna: Perca cabrilla, Linn.; Ov. Hal. 108; Plin. 9, 16, 23, § 56; 32, 11, 54, § 153.
chane.short: chānē or channē, ēs, f., = χάνη or χάννη, a kind of sea-fish;

chanius.full: chanĭus pēs = Molossus, a foot consisting of three long syllables, ¯¯¯, Diom. p. 475 P.
chanius.short: chanĭus pēs = Molossus, a foot consisting of three long syllables, ¯¯¯, Diom.

chaon.full: Chāon, ŏnis, m., son of Priamus, ancestor of the Chaones, Verg. A. 3, 335 Serv.
chaon.short: Chāon, ŏnis, m., son of Priamus, ancestor of the Chaones, Verg.

chaones.full: Chāŏnes, um, m., = Χάονες, a people in the north-west part of Epirus, named after Chaon (v. the preced. art.), the Chaonians, Plin. 4, prooem. § 2; Serv. ad Verg. A. 3, 334 sq.; acc. plur. Gr. Chaonas, Claud. B. Get. 135; their country was called Chā-ŏnĭa, ae, f., Verg. A. 3, 335 Serv.; Plin. 4, prooem. § 2; Cic. Att. 6, 3, 2; Liv. 32, 5, 9. — Hence, Chāŏnĭus, a, um, adj., Chaonian; also of Epirus: campi, Verg. A. 3, 334: sinus, Ov. M. 13, 717: glans, Verg. G. 1, 8: pater, i. e. Jupiter, whose o
chaones.short: Chāŏnes, um, m., = Χάονες, a people in the north-west part of Epirus, named after Chaon (v.

chaos.full: Chăŏs or Chăus, abl. Chao (other cases not used in the class. per.; gen. Chaï, Serv. ad Verg. A. 1, 664; dat. Chaï, Prisc. p. 720 P.), n., = Χάος. The boundless, empty space; as the kingdom of darkness, the Lower World: ingens, Ov. M. 10, 30; 14, 404; id. Ib. 84: inane, id. F. 4, 600: caecum, Sen. Med. 741; Stat. Th. 12, 772; Val. Fl. 7, 402; impersonated, masc., god of the Lower World, father of Erebos and Nox, Verg. A. 4, 510 (acc. Chaos); 6, 265; Quint. 3, 7, 8; cf.: Janus... edidit hos sonos

chara.full: chara, ae, f., a root unknown to us; perh. wild cabbage, Caes. B. C. 3, 48.
chara.short: chara, ae, f., a root unknown to us;

characatus.full: chărăcātus, a, um, adj., χάραξ, provided with stakes, propped up: vineae, Col. 5, 4, 1; 5, 5, 16.
characatus.short: chărăcātus, a, um, adj., χάραξ, provided with stakes, propped up: vineae, Col.

characias.full: chărăcĭas, ae, m., = χαρακίας. Eit for making poles or stakes: calamus, a kind of reed, Plin. 16, 36, 66, § 168.— A name of a plant, wolf's-milk, Plin. 26, 8, 39, § 62; called also chărăcītes, ae, m., Plin. 26, 11, 73, § 119; 26, 14, 87, § 146.

character.full: chăracter, ēris, m., = χαρακτήρ. An instrument for branding or marking, etc.: character est ferrum coloratum, quo notae pecudibus inuruntur, χαρακτήρ autem Graece, Latine forma dicitur, Isid. Orig. 20, 16, 7.— Usu., the mark or sign burned or imprinted. Prop. (esp. upon animals): quadrupedia charactere signare, Col. 11, 2, 14; Pall. Jan. 16: characterem infigere alicui, Aug. Contr. Cresc. 1, 30.— Trop., a characteristic, mark, character, style, etc. (only ante- and postclass.): Luciliano charact

characterismos.full: chăractērismŏs (-mus), i, m., = χαρακτηρισμός characterization, the making prominent of the characteristic marks, rhet. t. t. (pure Lat. descriptio, depictio), Isid. Orig. 2, 21, 40; Porphyr. ad Hor. Ep. 1, 18, 7.
characterismos.short: chăractērismŏs (-mus), i, m., = χαρακτηρισμός characterization, the making prominent of the characteristic marks, rhet.

charadra.full: Charădra, ae, f., = Χαράδρα, a town of Epirus, Enn. Fragm. p. 166 Vahl.
charadra.short: Charădra, ae, f., = Χαράδρα, a town of Epirus, Enn.

charadrius.full: chărā^drĭus, ïi, m., = χαραδριός, a yellowish bird, Vulg. Lev. 11, 19; id. Deut. 14, 18.
charadrius.short: chărā^drĭus, ïi, m., = χαραδριός, a yellowish bird, Vulg.

charadrus.full: Chărā^drus, i, f., a town in Syria, Plin. 5, 20, 18, § 79.
charadrus.short: Chărā^drus, i, f., a town in Syria, Plin.

charax.full: Chărax, ăcis, f., = Χάραξ, a fortress in the valley of Tempe, now Carisso, Liv. 44, 6, 10.— A town on the Persian Gulf, Plin. 6, 23, 26, § 100; 6, 26, 30, § 124 sq.
charax.short: Chărax, ăcis, f., = Χάραξ, a fortress in the valley of Tempe, now Carisso, Liv.

charaxo.full: chăraxo, āre, 1, v. a., = χαράσσω, to scratch, engrave (late Lat.): ungulis genas, Prud. στεφ. 10, 557: tabulae decalogo charaxatae, Aug. Alterc. Eccl. et Synag.

charaxus.full: Chăraxus, i, m. One of the Lapithœ, Ov. M. 12, 272.— A brother of Sappho, Ov. H. 15, 117.

chares.full: Chăres, ētis, m., a Greek proper name. The Athenian general, Nep. Timoth. 3 sq.; id. Phoc. 2, 3.— A statuary of Lindos in Rhodus, the favorite pupil of Lysippus, Auct. Her. 4, 6, 9; Plin. 34, 7, 18, § 41. — A Grecian writer of Mitylene, Plin. 37, 2, 11, § 33; Gell. 5, 2, 2.
chares.short: Chăres, ētis, m., a Greek proper name.

chariclo.full: Chăriclo, ūs, f., a nymph, mother of Ocyrhoë, by the Centaur Chiron, Ov. M. 2, 636.
chariclo.short: Chăriclo, ūs, f., a nymph, mother of Ocyrhoë, by the Centaur Chiron, Ov.

charisius.full: Chărĭsĭus, ĭi, m., = Χαρίσιος. A Greek orator, imitator of Lysias, Cic. Brut. 83, 286; Quint. 10, 1, 70.— Flavius Sosipater Charisius, a Latin grammarian in the fourth Christian century.— A Roman jurist of the time of Constantine the Great.

charisma.full: chărisma, ătis, n., = χάρισμα, a gift, present, Prud. prooem. Apotheos. 11; id. στεφ. 13, 61.
charisma.short: chărisma, ătis, n., = χάρισμα, a gift, present, Prud.

charistia.full: chăristĭa (car-), ōrum, n., = χαρίστεια or χαριστήρια, an annual family repast made three days after the Parentalia, on the 20th of February; a family banquet, at which existing family feuds were settled, Ov. F. 2, 617 sq.; Val. Max. 2, 1, 8; cf. Mart. 9, 56, 1.
charistia.short: chăristĭa (car-), ōrum, n., = χαρίστεια or χαριστήρια, an annual family repast made three days after the Parentalia, on the 20th of February;

charites.full: Chărĭtes, um, f., = Χάριτες, the Charites or Graces (pure Lat. Gratiae), usu. three, Aglaia, Euphrosyne, and Thalia (cf., however, Lidd. and Scott under the word), Ov. F. 5, 219; Sen. Ben. 1, 4, 4; Plin. 36, 5, 4, § 32.—In sing. acc. Gr. Charita, one of the Graces, Plin. 35, 10, 36, § 79.
charites.short: Chărĭtes, um, f., = Χάριτες, the Charites or Graces (pure Lat.

charitonblepharon.full: chărĭtonblĕphăron, i, n., = Χαρίτων-βλέφαρον (eyelids of the Graces), a magical plant producing love, Plin. 13, 25, 52, § 142.
charitonblepharon.short: chărĭtonblĕphăron, i, n., = Χαρίτων-βλέφαρον (eyelids of the Graces), a magical plant producing love, Plin.

charmadas.full: Charmădas, ae, m., = Χαρμάδας. An Academic philosopher, pupil of Carneades, Cic. Ac. 2, 6, 16; id. de Or. 1, 11, 45; id. Tusc. 1, 24, 59; Quint. 11, 2, 26.— A Greek painter, Plin. 35, 8, 34, § 56.

charmides.full: Charmĭdes, ai or i, m., a comic person in Plaut. Trin.; hence, charmĭdātus, changed into Charmides, id. ib. 4, 2, 135; cf. decharmido.
charmides.short: Charmĭdes, ai or i, m., a comic person in Plaut.

charon.full: Chăron, ontis (ōnis, Fulg. Myth. 1), m., = Χάρων. Charon, a ferryman in the Lower World, Cic. N. D. 3, 17, 43; Verg. A. 6, 299; id. Cul. 2, 15; Sen. Herc. Fur. 771. —Hence, Chărōnēus, a, um, adj., of Charon, of the Lower World: scrobes, deep, Plin. 2, 93, 95, § 208.— A Theban, Nep. Pelop. 2, 5.

charondas.full: Chărōndas, ae, m., = Χαρώνδας, a distinguished lawgiver in Catana, Cic. Leg. 1, 22, 57; Val. Max. 6, 5, 4; Sen. Ep. 90, 5.
charondas.short: Chărōndas, ae, m., = Χαρώνδας, a distinguished lawgiver in Catana, Cic.

charta.full: charta, ae (chartus, i, m., Lucil. ap. Non. p. 196, 19). f., = ό χάρτης (cf. the letter A), a leaf of the Egyptian papyrus, paper, Plin. 13, 11, 21, § 68 sqq.; Lucr. 6, 112; 6, 114; Cic. Att. 5, 4, 4; Hor. Ep. 2, 1, 113: dentata, smooth, Cic. Q. Fr. 2, 14 (15), 1: emporitica inutilis scribendo involucris chartarum segestriumque mercibus usum praebet, Plin. 13, 12, 23, § 76: epistulares, Mart. 14, 11 in lemm.; Dig. 33, 9, 3, § 10: novae, ib. 37, 11, 4: purae, ib. 32, 1, 52, § 4: transversa, Suet.

chartaceus.full: chartācĕus, a, um, adj. charta, made of paper, paper-: codices, Dig. 32, 50.

chartarius.full: chartārĭus, a, um, adj. id., of or pertaining to paper, paper-: officinae, Plin. 18, 10, 20, § 89: calamus, App. Flor. 9.— Subst.: chartārĭus, ii, m., a papermerchant, Diom. p. 313 P.; Inscr. Orell. 4159.— chartārĭum, i, n., archives, Hier. adv. Ruf. 3, 6.

charteus.full: chartĕus, a, um, adj. charta, of or pertaining to paper, paper- (ante- and postclass.): stadium, occupation in writing, Varr. ap. Non. p. 248, 13: supellex, Aus. Ep. 10, 40: pulvis, id. Praef. ad Griph.

chartiaticum.full: chartĭātĭcum, i, n., = χαρτιατικόν, money for paper, Dig. 48, 20, 6 (others, charisticum, gift, present).
chartiaticum.short: chartĭātĭcum, i, n., = χαρτιατικόν, money for paper, Dig.

chartophylax.full: chartŏphўlax, ăcis, m., = χαρτοφύλαξ, a keeper of archives, Inscr. Grut. 587, 11.
chartophylax.short: chartŏphўlax, ăcis, m., = χαρτοφύλαξ, a keeper of archives, Inscr.

chartopola.full: chartŏpōla, ae, m., = χαρτοπώλης, a paper-merchant, Schol. Juv. 4, 27.
chartopola.short: chartŏpōla, ae, m., = χαρτοπώλης, a paper-merchant, Schol.

chartula.full: chartŭla, ae, f. dim. charta, a little paper, a small writing, a bill, * Cic. Fam. 7, 18, 2; Gai Inst. 2, 77; Fronto ad Amic. 1, 15; Cod. Th. 8, 2, 2 al.

chartularius.full: chartŭlārĭus, ii, m. chartula; in late Lat., a keeper of the archives of court, Cod. Th. 8, 1, 6 al.

charybdis.full: Chărybdis, is, f., = Χάρυβδις, a dangerous whirlpool between Italy and Sicily, opposite to Scylla, now Calofaro; personified, a monstrous female being, Mel. 2, 7, 14; Plin. 3, 8, 14, § 87: vasta, Lucr. 1, 723; Cat. 64, 156; Prop. 2 (3), 26, 54. implacata, Verg. A. 3, 420: Austro agitata, Ov. M. 8, 121: irrequieta, id. ib. 13, 730; acc. Charybdin, Hor. A. P. 145; Ov. M. 14, 75; so Cic. Phil. 2, 27, 67: Charybdim, Cic. Verr. 2, 5, 56, § 146 Zumpt N. cr.; abl. Charybdi, Hor. C. 1, 27, 19; Juv. 15,
charybdis.short: Chărybdis, is, f., = Χάρυβδις, a dangerous whirlpool between Italy and Sicily, opposite to Scylla, now Calofaro;

chasma.full: chasma, ătis, n., = χάσμα, an opening of the earth, a chasm, abyss, Sen. Q. N. 6, 9, 2; Dig. 4, 4, 11; 50, 15, 4; 18, 6, 10.— A kind of meteor: sunt chasmata, cum aliquod caeli spatium desedit et flammam velut dehiscens in abdito ostentat, Sen. Q. N. 1, 14, 1; Plin. 2, 26, 26, § 96; Serv. ad Verg. A. 9, 20.
chasma.short: chasma, ătis, n., = χάσμα, an opening of the earth, a chasm, abyss, Sen.

chasmatias.full: chasmătĭas, ae, m., = χασματίας, an earthquake which leaves chasms or openings, Amm. 17, 7, 13; App. de Mundo, 65, 25, Bip. 2, p. 264.
chasmatias.short: chasmătĭas, ae, m., = χασματίας, an earthquake which leaves chasms or openings, Amm.

chasuarii.full: Chasŭārĭi, ōrum, m., a German tribe, Tac. G. 34 Orell.; cf. Attuarii.
chasuarii.short: Chasŭārĭi, ōrum, m., a German tribe, Tac.

chatti.full: Chatti (Catti), ōrum, m., = Χάττοι, Strab., a German people in the present Hesse (which name is formed from Chatti) and Thuringia, Tac. G. 30 Rup.; 31 sq.; id. A. 1, 55 sq.; 2, 7; id. H. 4, 12; 4, 37; Plin. 4, 14, 28, § 100; Juv. 4, 147 al.—In sing.: Chatta mulier, Suet. Vit. 14.
chatti.short: Chatti (Catti), ōrum, m., = Χάττοι, Strab., a German people in the present Hesse (which name is formed from Chatti) and Thuringia, Tac.

chauci.full: Chauci (in MSS. also Chauchi, Cauci; cf. upon the signif. and orthog. of the word, Rup. Tac. G. 35; poët. Chăūci or Chăȳci, trisyl., Luc. 1, 463; Claud. ap. Eutr. 1, 379; and in sing.: Căȳco, id. Laud. Stil. 1, 225), ōrum, m., = Καῦχοι, Ptolem.; Καῦκοι, Strab., a people in Lower Germany, on the ocean, from the Ems to the Elbe, in the south to the region of Oldenburg and Bremen, divided into majores and minores, Vell. 2, 106, 1; Tac. G. 35; id. A. 2, 24; 11, 19; id. H. 4, 79; 5, 19; Suet. Claud.

chele.full: chēlē, ēs, f., = χηλή (the claws or arms of animals). * In mechanics, the claw-shaped part of the ballista, the trigger: manicula, Vitr. 10, 15 and 17.— Plur.: chēlae, ārum, f.; in astron., lit. the arms of Scorpio; but, since these extend into Libra, meton. Libra, Verg. G. 1, 33; Cic. Arat. 293; Col. 10, 56; Luc. 1, 659; Manil. 4, 203; cf. Claud. Cons. Mall. Theod. 120.
chele.short: chēlē, ēs, f., = χηλή (the claws or arms of animals).

chelidon.full: Chĕlīdon, ŏnis, f., = Χελιδών, a female client of Verres who made him her heir, Cic. Verr. 2, 1, 40, § 104; 2, 1, 52, § 137 sqq.
chelidon.short: Chĕlīdon, ŏnis, f., = Χελιδών, a female client of Verres who made him her heir, Cic.

chelidoniacus.full: chĕlīdŏnĭăcus, a, um, adj., = χελιδονιακός, pointed like a swallow's tail: gladius. Isid. Orig. 18, 6, 7.
chelidoniacus.short: chĕlīdŏnĭăcus, a, um, adj., = χελιδονιακός, pointed like a swallow's tail: gladius.

chelidoniae.full: Chĕlīdŏnĭae Insŭlae, f., = Χελιδόνεαι ?̔-δόνιαἰ Νῆσοι, the Swallow-islands, a group of three or five small, rocky islands off the Lycian coast, Liv. 33, 20, 2; Mel. 2, 7, 5.
chelidoniae.short: Chĕlīdŏnĭae Insŭlae, f., = Χελιδόνεαι ?̔-δόνιαἰ Νῆσοι, the Swallow-islands, a group of three or five small, rocky islands off the Lycian coast, Liv.

chelidonias.full: chĕlīdŏnĭas, ae, m., = χελιδονίας (pertaining to the swallow), the west wind, blowing after the 22d of Feb. (after the arrival of the swallows), Plin. 2, 47, 47, § 122.
chelidonias.short: chĕlīdŏnĭas, ae, m., = χελιδονίας (pertaining to the swallow), the west wind, blowing after the 22d of Feb.

chelidonius.full: chĕlīdŏnĭus, a, um, adj., = χελιδόνιος, pertaining to the swallow: lapilli, found in the crop of young swallows, swallow-stone, Plin. 11, 37, 79, § 203: ficus, a particular reddish species of fig, Col. 10, 415; Plin. 15, 18, 19, § 71: gemma, Plin. 37, 10, 56, § 154.— Subst.: chĕlīdŏnĭa, ae, f. (sc. herba): Chelidonium majus, Linn.; swallowwort, celandine, Plin. 25, 8, 50, §§ 89 and 90; also herba chelidoniae in Ser. Samm. 37, 699.
chelidonius.short: chĕlīdŏnĭus, a, um, adj., = χελιδόνιος, pertaining to the swallow: lapilli, found in the crop of young swallows, swallow-stone, Plin.

chelonia.full: chĕlōnĭa, ae, f., = χελωνία, a precious stone, tortoise - stone, Plin. 37, 10, 56, § 155.
chelonia.short: chĕlōnĭa, ae, f., = χελωνία, a precious stone, tortoise - stone, Plin.

chelonitis1.full: chĕlōnītis, ĭdis, f., = χελωιῖτις, a precious stone like the tortoise, Plin. 37, 10, 56, § 155; cf. Isid. Orig. 16, 15, 29.
chelonitis1.short: chĕlōnītis, ĭdis, f., = χελωιῖτις, a precious stone like the tortoise, Plin.

chelonitis2.full: Chĕlōnītis, ĭdis, f., = χελωνῖτις, an island in the Arabian Gulf, Plin. 6, 27, 32, § 151.
chelonitis2.short: Chĕlōnītis, ĭdis, f., = χελωνῖτις, an island in the Arabian Gulf, Plin.

chelonium.full: chĕlōnĭum, ii, n., = χελώνιον (lit. a tortoise-shell; hence); in mechanics, the similarly formed shield, cramp, or stay in which the axis of the crane or windlass moved, Vitr. 10, 2; 10, 4; 10, 8; 10, 15; 10, 18; 10, 21.— A plant, also called cyclaminos, App. Herb. 17.

chelydrus.full: chĕlȳ^drus, i, m., = χέλυδρος, a fetid serpent, living, for the most part, in water, Cels. 5, 27, 8; Verg. G. 3, 415; Ov. M. 7, 272; Luc. 9, 710; Sil. 3, 316; 8, 496; Prud. c. Symm. 1, 130.
chelydrus.short: chĕlȳ^drus, i, m., = χέλυδρος, a fetid serpent, living, for the most part, in water, Cels.

chelyon.full: chĕlўon, i, n., = χέλυον, the shell of the horned tortoise, Plin. 6, 29, 34, § 173; 9, 10, 12, § 38.
chelyon.short: chĕlўon, i, n., = χέλυον, the shell of the horned tortoise, Plin.

chelys.full: chĕlys, acc. chelyn, voc. chely (other cases apparently not in use), f., = χέλυς. The tortoise, Petr. Fragm. 32, 5.— As in Greek (cf. Lidd. and Scott in h. v.), a lyre or harp made of its shell, pure Lat. testudo (except Ovid, in post-Aug. poets only; most freq. in Statius): chelys, Stat. S. 1, 5, 1; 4, 4, 33; Claud. III. Cons. Hon. praef. 18; id. Cons. Mall. Theod. 313; id. IV. Cons. Hon. 123; Prud. Apoth. 455: chelyn, Ov. H. 15, 181; Stat. S. 1, 5, 11; 2, 2, 120; 4, 6, 30; 4, 8, 38; id. Th. 6,

chema.full: chēma, ae, f., = χήμη, a gaping mussel, a cockle, Plin. 32, 11, 53, § 147 Jan. (al. leg. chama).
chema.short: chēma, ae, f., = χήμη, a gaping mussel, a cockle, Plin.

cheme.full: chēmē, ēs, f., = χήμη, a measure for liquids, the third part of a mystrum, Rhem. Fan. Pond. 77.
cheme.short: chēmē, ēs, f., = χήμη, a measure for liquids, the third part of a mystrum, Rhem.

chenalopeces.full: chēnălōpĕces, um, f., = χηναλώπεκες, a species of goose or duck, Plin. 10, 22, 29, § 56.
chenalopeces.short: chēnălōpĕces, um, f., = χηναλώπεκες, a species of goose or duck, Plin.

chenerotes.full: chēnĕrōtes, um, f. (* χηνέρως), a species of small goose or duck; perh. Anas clipeata, Linn.; Plin. 10, 22, 29, § 56.

cheniscus.full: chēniscus, i, m. dim., = χηνίσκος, lit. a gosling; hence, the ornament in the form of a goose on a ship's stern, App. M. 11, p. 264, 40.

chenoboscion.full: chēnŏboscīon, ii, n., = χηνοβοσκεῖον, a pen for geese, Col. 8, 14, 1 (in Varr. 3, 10, 1, written as Greek).
chenoboscion.short: chēnŏboscīon, ii, n., = χηνοβοσκεῖον, a pen for geese, Col.

chenomyche.full: chēnŏmўchē, ēs, f., = χηνομύχη, a plant, = nyctegreton and nyctalops, Plin. 21, 11, 36, § 62.
chenomyche.short: chēnŏmўchē, ēs, f., = χηνομύχη, a plant, = nyctegreton and nyctalops, Plin.

chernites.full: chernītes, ae, m., = χερνίτης, a kind of marble resembling ivory, Plin. 36, 17, 28, § 132.
chernites.short: chernītes, ae, m., = χερνίτης, a kind of marble resembling ivory, Plin.

cherronesus.full: Cherrŏnēsus (-ŏs), or Chersŏnē-sus, i, f., = Χερρόνησος or Χερσόνησος (a peninsula; hence), Cherronesus Thracia, or absol. Cherronesus, the Thracian peninsula at the west of the Hellespont, the Chersonese, Mel. 2, 2, 7; Plin. 4, 11, 18, § 48; Cic. Agr. 2, 19, 5; id. Pis. 35, 86 B. and K.; Nep. Milt. 1, 1 sq.; Liv. 31, 16, 5. —Hence, Cherrŏnenses or Chersŏ-nenses (contr. instead of Cherronesenses), the inhabitants of the Chersonese, Just. 9, 1, 7.— Cherronesus Taurica, or absol. Cherronesus, the
cherronesus.short: Cherrŏnēsus (-ŏs), or Chersŏnē-sus, i, f., = Χερρόνησος or Χερσόνησος (a peninsula;

chersinus.full: chersĭnus, a, um, adj., = χέρσινος, living upon dry land: testudines, Plin. 9, 10, 12, § 38 (in Mart 14, 88, called chersos = χέρσος.)
chersinus.short: chersĭnus, a, um, adj., = χέρσινος, living upon dry land: testudines, Plin.

chersos.full: chersos, i, f. χέρσος, dry land, a kind of toad: feminea, Mart. 14, 88.

chersydros.full: chersȳ^dros, i, m., = χέρσυδρος, an amphibious serpent, Cels. 5, 27, 8; Luc. 9, 711; Serv. ad Verg. G. 3, 415.
chersydros.short: chersȳ^dros, i, m., = χέρσυδρος, an amphibious serpent, Cels.

cherub.full: Chĕrub, m. plur. Chĕrūbĭm (Cherubin), , plur. , the name of a rank of angels mentioned in the Old Testament, Vulg. Ezech. 9, 3; id. Gen. 3, 24; Prud. Cath. 4, 4; cf. Hier. in Ezech. 9 and 28; Isid. Orig. 7, 5, 22 sq.; 14, 3, 4; Ven. Fort. Carm. 7, 3, 131.

cherusci.full: Chē^rusci, ōrum, m., = Χηροῦσκοι. Strabo; Χερουσκοι, Dio.; Χαιρουσκοί, Ptolem.; in a more restricted sense, a German people on the south side of the Hartz Mountains; but more freq. in an extended sense, the combined German tribes, which became distinguished by their war with the Romans, living on both sides of the Weser and Lippe, Caes. B. G. 6, 10; Vell. 2, 105; 2, 117 sqq.; Tac. G. 36 Rup.; id. A. 2, 46; 1, 56 sq.; 2, 9 sq.; 12, 28 et saep.; Flor. 4, 12, 24; Claud. IV. Cons. Hon. 452; id. B. G

chesippus.full: Chesippus, i, m., a contemptuous name given by Zeno to Chrysippus, Cic. N. D. 1, 34, 93.
chesippus.short: Chesippus, i, m., a contemptuous name given by Zeno to Chrysippus, Cic.

chiliarches.full: chīlĭarchēs, ae, or chīlĭarchus, i, m., = χιλιάρχης or χιλίαρχος, a commander of 1000 soldiers, a chiliarch, Curt. 5. 2, 2. Also in gen., a head of 1000 persons, Cod. Th. 16, 10, 20, § 4.— Among the Persians, the highest officer of state next to the king, chancellor of state, Nep. Con. 3, 2.
chiliarches.short: chīlĭarchēs, ae, or chīlĭarchus, i, m., = χιλιάρχης or χιλίαρχος, a commander of 1000 soldiers, a chiliarch, Curt.

chilias.full: chīlĭăs, ădis, f., = χιλιάς, the number 1000, a chiliad, Macr. S. 1, 5.
chilias.short: chīlĭăs, ădis, f., = χιλιάς, the number 1000, a chiliad, Macr.

chiliastae.full: chīlĭastae, ārum, m., = χιλιασταί, the believers in the millennial kingdom, Aug. Civ. Dei, 20, 7.
chiliastae.short: chīlĭastae, ārum, m., = χιλιασταί, the believers in the millennial kingdom, Aug.

chiliodynama.full: chīlĭŏdўnăma, ae, f. χίλιοι-δύναμις, an unknown medicinal plant, thousand-virtues, = polemonia, q. v., Plin. 25, 6, 28, § 64.

chiliophyllon.full: chīlĭŏphyllon, i, n. χίλιοι-φύλλον, an unknown plant, thousand-leaves, App. Herb. 18.

chilius.full: Chīlĭus, ĭi, m., a Greek poet, Cic. Att. 1, 9, 2; 1. 12, 2.
chilius.short: Chīlĭus, ĭi, m., a Greek poet, Cic.

chilo1.full: Chīlo, ōnis, m., a cognomen, signifying having large lips, Fest. p. 43, 10 [χεῖλος, lip; cf. Charis. p. 78 P.; Vel. Long. p. 2234 ib.].
chilo1.short: Chīlo, ōnis, m., a cognomen, signifying having large lips, Fest.

chilo2.full: Chīlo, ōnis, m., = Χίλων or Χείλων. A Lacedœmonian, one of the seven wise men, Plin. 7, 32, 32, § 119; Aus. Sept. Sap. 6.— A Roman cognomen, Cic. Cat. 3, 6, 17.
chilo2.short: Chīlo, ōnis, m., = Χίλων or Χείλων.

chimaera.full: Chĭmaera, ae, f., = Χίμαιρα (lit. a goat), a fabulous monster in Lycia, which vomited fire; in front a lion, in the hinder part a dragon, and in the middle a goat; slain by Bellerophon, Cic. N. D. 1, 38, 108; 2, 2, 5; Lucr. 5, 903; 2, 705; Tib. 3, 4, 86; Verg. A. 6, 288; Hor. C. 1, 27, 24; 2, 17, 13; 4, 2, 16; Ov. Tr. 4, 7, 13; 2, 397; Sen. Ep. 113, 8; Hyg. Fab. 57; Serv. ad Verg. A. 5, 118; 6, 288; its figure, used to adorn a helmet, Verg. A. 7, 785.— A mountain in Lycia that sent forth flames,

chimaerifer.full: Chĭmaerĭfĕr, fĕra, fĕrum, adj. Chimaera-fero: Lycia, that produced the Chimœra (cf. Chimaera, l.), Ov. M. 6, 339.

chimerinus.full: chīmĕrĭnus, a, um, adj., = χειμέρινος, winter: tropa, Kalend. ap. Inscr. Orell. II. p. 381.
chimerinus.short: chīmĕrĭnus, a, um, adj., = χειμέρινος, winter: tropa, Kalend.

chione.full: Chĭŏnē, ēs, f., = Χιόνη. A daughter of Dœdation, mother of Autolycus by Mercury, and of the musician Philammon by Apollo, shot by Diana, Ov. M. 11, 301 sq.; Hyg. Fab. 200.— A daughter of Boreas and Orithyia, and mother of Eumolpus; hence Chīŏnĭdes, ae, = Eumolpus, Ov. P. 3, 3, 41 dub. (Merkel, Edonides).

chios.full: Chī^os (Chīus, Cic. Arat. 422), ii, f., = Χίος, an island in the Ægean Sea, on the coast of Ionia, with a capital of the same name, distinguished in ancient times for its excellent wine and marble, now Scio, or Khio, Mel. 2, 7, 4; Plin. 5, 31, 38, § 136; Hor. Ep. 1, 11, 1; 1, 11, 21; Cic. Verr. 2, 5, 48, § 127; Nep. Chabr.4 al.—Hence, Chīus (Chĭus, Avien. Arat. 251 and 1179), a, um, adj., = Χῖος, of Chios, Chian: insula, Varr. R. R. 2, prooem. § 3; also absol. Chīa, Plin. 5, 31, 38, § 136: terra

chiragra.full: chīrā^gra, ae, f., = χειράγρα, gout in the hand, Cels. 1, 9 init.: podagra et chiragra et omnis vertebrarum dolor nervorumque interquiescit, Sen. Ep. 78, 8.—Poet. collat. form chĕrā^gra, ae, f., Hor. S. 2, 7, 15; id. Ep. 1, 1, 31; Pers. 5, 58; Mart. 1, 99, 2; 9, 92, 9.
chiragra.short: chīrā^gra, ae, f., = χειράγρα, gout in the hand, Cels.

chiragricus.full: chīrā^grĭcus, a, um, = χειραγρικός, having the gout in the hand; subst.: chī-rā^grĭci, ōrum, m., Cels. 4, 24; Petr. 132, 14; rarely adj.: manus, Sid. Ep. 3, 13.
chiragricus.short: chīrā^grĭcus, a, um, = χειραγρικός, having the gout in the hand;

chiramaxium.full: chīrămaxĭum, ii, n., = χειραμάξιον, a small carriage drawn by slaves, a handwagon, Petr. 28, 4 ( = vehiculum manuale, Cael. Aur. Tard. 3, 6, 86).
chiramaxium.short: chīrămaxĭum, ii, n., = χειραμάξιον, a small carriage drawn by slaves, a handwagon, Petr.

chiridotus.full: chīrĭdōtus, a, um, adj., = χειριδωτός, furnished with sleeves, pure Lat. manuleatus or manicatus: tunica, Scip. Afr. ap. Gell. 7, 12, 5; cf. Gell. ib. § 1 sq.—Subst.: chīrĭdōtae, ārum (sc. tunicae), Capitol. Pert. 8, 2.
chiridotus.short: chīrĭdōtus, a, um, adj., = χειριδωτός, furnished with sleeves, pure Lat.

chirocmeta.full: Chīrocmēta, ōn or ōrum, n., = χειρόκμητα (lit. made by the hand), title of a book by Democritus, Plin. 24, 17, 102, § 160 (as Greek, Vitr. 9, prooem. § 14; Col. 7, 5, 17).
chirocmeta.short: Chīrocmēta, ōn or ōrum, n., = χειρόκμητα (lit.

chirographarius.full: chīrŏgrăphārĭus, a, um, adj. chirographum, pertaining to handwriting, manuscript-: creditores, who have the obligation of the debtor in his own handwriting, Dig. 42, 5, 38, § 1: pecunia, Cod. Just. 4, 2, 17: debitum, ib. 8, 27, 1.

chirographum.full: chīrŏgrăphum, i, n. (access. form * chīrŏgrăphus, i, m., sc. libellus or codex, Fulvius ap. Quint. 6, 3, 100 Spald., together with chirographum, Quint. ib. 5, 13, 8; and chīrŏgrăphon, i, n., Sid. Carm. 16, 56), = χειρόγραφον. One's own handwriting, autograph; pure Lat. manus (in good prose; freq. in Cic.): extrema pagella pupugit me tuo chirographo, Cic. Fam. 2, 13, 3; Planc. ib. 10, 21, 3; Cic. Phil. 1, 7, 16; 2, 4, 8: neque utar meo chirographo neque signo, id. Att. 2, 20, 5: imitari, id. N. D

chiron.full: Chīron (nom. Chīro, Liv. Andron. ap. Fest. s. v. ocrem, p. 181), ōnis, m., = Χείρων, one of the Centaurs, distinguished for his knowledge of plants, medicine, and divination, son of Saturn and Philyra (hence, Philyrides Chiron, Verg. G. 3, 550), the tutor of Æsculapius (Ov. M. 2, 630 sq.), Hercules, Achilles, Jason, etc.; at last translated to heaven as a constellation, Hyg. Praef. and Fab. 274; id. Astr. 2, 38; Serv. ad Verg. G. 3, 91; 3, 550; 4, 270; acc. Gr. Chirona, Ov. M. 6, 126.—As a const

chironomia.full: chīrŏnŏmī^a, ae, f., = χειρονομία, the art of moving the hands in gesturing, gesticulation: chironomia, quae est lex gestūs, Quint. 1, 11, 17.
chironomia.short: chīrŏnŏmī^a, ae, f., = χειρονομία, the art of moving the hands in gesturing, gesticulation: chironomia, quae est lex gestūs, Quint.

chironomos.full: chīrŏnŏmŏs, i, comm., and chīrŏ-nŏmōn, ontis (also Gr. untis), m., = χειρονόμος or χειρονομῶν, one who moves his hands according to the rules of art, correctly, a pantomime, Juv. 6, 63; 5, 121; Sid. Ep. 4, 7 fin.
chironomos.short: chīrŏnŏmŏs, i, comm., and chīrŏ-nŏmōn, ontis (also Gr.

chirurgia.full: chīrurgĭa, ae, f., = χειρουργία, surgery, Cels. 7 praef.; Scrib. Comp. 200; Veg. 3, 13, 1.—* Trop., a violent remedy: chirurgiae taedet, i. e. vim et arma detestor, Cic. Att. 4, 3, 3.
chirurgia.short: chīrurgĭa, ae, f., = χειρουργία, surgery, Cels.

chirurgicus.full: chīrurgĭcus, a um, adj., = χειρουργικός, surgical, chirurgical: medicina, Hyg. Fab. 274.
chirurgicus.short: chīrurgĭcus, a um, adj., = χειρουργικός, surgical, chirurgical: medicina, Hyg.

chirurgumena.full: Chīrurgūmĕna, ōn, n., = χειρουργούμενα, Surgical Operations, title of a book, Cael. Aur. Tard. 2, 12; 2, 146.
chirurgumena.short: Chīrurgūmĕna, ōn, n., = χειρουργούμενα, Surgical Operations, title of a book, Cael.

chirurgus.full: chīrurgus, i, m., χειρουργός, = a surgeon, a chirurgeon (pure Lat. medicus vulnerarius), Cels. 7 praef.; Mart. 1, 31; Scrib. Comp. 201; 209 al.; Auct. Priap. 38; Inscr. Orell. 4228 al.
chirurgus.short: chīrurgus, i, m., χειρουργός, = a surgeon, a chirurgeon (pure Lat.

chlamydatus.full: chlămўdātus, a, um, adj. chlamys, dressed in a military cloak, Plaut. Ps. 4, 2, 8; 4, 6, 39; id. Rud. 2, 2, 9 al.; * Cic. Rab. Post. 10, 27; Val. Max. 2, 6, 2 and 3.

chlamys.full: chlămys, ўdis (chlămўda, ae, as cassida = cassis, al., App. M. 10, p. 253, 31; 11, p. 269, 11; and perh. Varr. ap. Non. p. 539, 9, where, however, chlamyda may be acc. Gr. from chlamys), f., = χλαμύς, a broad, woollen upper garment worn in Greece, sometimes purple, and inwrought with gold, worn esp. by distinguished milit. characters, a Grecian military cloak, a state mantle, Plaut. Curc. 5, 2, 13; id. Ep. 3, 3, 51; id. Mil. 5, 30; id. Ps. 2, 4, 45; 4, 7, 88; Cic. Rab. Post. 10, 27; Verg. A. 5,
chlamys.short: chlămys, ўdis (chlămўda, ae, as cassida = cassis, al., App.

chloe.full: Chlŏē, ēs, f., = Χλόη, Greek female name, Hor. C. 1, 23, 1.
chloe.short: Chlŏē, ēs, f., = Χλόη, Greek female name, Hor.

chlora.full: chlora, ae, f., a medicament, Veg. 6, 28, 3.
chlora.short: chlora, ae, f., a medicament, Veg.

chloreus.full: chlōreus (dissyl.), ei, m., = χλωρεύς, a greenish bird, Plin. 10, 74, 95, § 203.
chloreus.short: chlōreus (dissyl.), ei, m., = χλωρεύς, a greenish bird, Plin.

chlorion.full: chlōrĭōn, ōnis, m., = χλωρίων, a yellow bird, the yellow thrush; acc. to Cuvier, the oriole, Plin. 10, 29, 45, § 87; 18, 29, 69, § 292.
chlorion.short: chlōrĭōn, ōnis, m., = χλωρίων, a yellow bird, the yellow thrush;

chloris.full: Chlōrĭs, ĭdis, f., = Χλῶρις (greenness) = Flora, the goddess of flowers, Ov. F. 5, 195; Lact. 1, 20, 8.— The daughter of Amphion and Niobe, wife of Neleus, Hyg. Fab. 10.— A Greek female name, Hor. C. 2, 5, 18; 3, 15, 8.
chloris.short: Chlōrĭs, ĭdis, f., = Χλῶρις (greenness) = Flora, the goddess of flowers, Ov.

chloritis.full: chlōrītis, ĭdis, f., = χλωρῖτις, a precious stone of a grass-green color, perhaps the smaragdoprasus, Plin. 37, 10, 56, § 156.
chloritis.short: chlōrītis, ĭdis, f., = χλωρῖτις, a precious stone of a grass-green color, perhaps the smaragdoprasus, Plin.

chlorus.full: Chlorus, i, m. A river of Cilicia, Plin. 5, 27, 22, § 91.— A cognomen of Sex. Pompeius, Cic. Verr. 2, 2, 8, § 23.

choaspes.full: Chŏaspes (Chŏaspis, Isid. Orig. 13, 21, 15), is, m., = Χοάσπης. A river in Susiana, distinguished for its pure water, from which the Persian kings drank, now Kerrah, Kerkhah, or Kara-su, Plin. 6, 27, 31, § 130; 31, 3, 21, § 35: regia lympha, Tib. 4, 1, 140; Curt. 5, 2, 9.—Personified, as a river-god, Val. Fl. 5, 584.— A river in India, now Kabul (acc. to others, the Attok), Curt. 8, 10, 22.

choaspitis.full: chŏaspītis (-pītes, Isid. Orig. 16, 7, 16), ĭdis, f. Choaspes, a precious stor found in the Choaspes, Plin. 37, 10, 56, § 186.

choatrae.full: Chŏātrae (Cŏātr-; al. Cŏastr-), ārum, m., a people of Lake Mœotis, Plin. 6, 7, 7, § 19; Luc. 3, 246; Val. Fl. 6, 151.

choatras.full: Chŏātras, ae, m., = Χοάτρας, a mountain in Media, Plin. 5, 27, 27, § 98.
choatras.short: Chŏātras, ae, m., = Χοάτρας, a mountain in Media, Plin.

choatres.full: Chŏātres, ae, m., = Χοάθρας, a river of Parthia, now the Adschi-Su, Amm. 23, 6, 43.
choatres.short: Chŏātres, ae, m., = Χοάθρας, a river of Parthia, now the Adschi-Su, Amm.

choenix.full: choenix, ĭcis (choenĭca, ae, Pall. Oct. 14, 5; id. Nov. 20, 1; cf. Paul. ex Fest. p. 52 Müll.), f., = χοῖνιξ, an Attic measure for grain, containing 2 sextarii, Fann. Pond. 68.

choeras.full: choerăs, ădis, f., = χοιράς, the scrofula (pure Lat. struma), Theod. Prisc. 1, 9; App. Herb. 2, n. 10.
choeras.short: choerăs, ădis, f., = χοιράς, the scrofula (pure Lat.

choerilus.full: Choerĭlus, i, m., = Χοιρίλος, a wretched Greek poet, in the train of Alexander the Great, Hor. Ep. 2, 1, 233; id. A. P. 357; Curt. 8, 5, 8; Aus. Ep. 16, 3.—After him, or another poet of the same name (cf. Hor. Ep. 2, 1, 232), is named Choerĭlīum (or -ēum) metrum, a dactylic species of verse, Serv. Centim. p. 1820 P.; Victorin. p. 2558 ib.
choerilus.short: Choerĭlus, i, m., = Χοιρίλος, a wretched Greek poet, in the train of Alexander the Great, Hor.

choerogryllus.full: choerogryllus, i, m., = χοιρόγρυλλος, a kind of hare, Vulg. Lev. 11, 5; id. Deut. 14, 7.
choerogryllus.short: choerogryllus, i, m., = χοιρόγρυλλος, a kind of hare, Vulg.

choicus.full: chŏĭcus, a, um, adj., = χοϊκός. of earth or clay: homo, Tert. adv. Val. 24; id. Anim. 40; id. Res Carn. 49.

cholas.full: cholas, ae, m., a species of emerald, Plin. 37, 5, 18, § 73.
cholas.short: cholas, ae, m., a species of emerald, Plin.

cholera.short: chŏlĕra, ae, f., = χολέρα, the jaundice, Cels.

cholericus.full: chŏlĕrĭcus, a, um, adj., = χολερικός, bilious, jaundiced, Plin. 24, 13, 72, § 116; Scrib. Comp. 256.
cholericus.short: chŏlĕrĭcus, a, um, adj., = χολερικός, bilious, jaundiced, Plin.

choliambus.full: chōlĭambus, i, m., = χωλίαμβος (the limping iambus), iambic verse, whose last foot, instead of an iambus, is a spondee or trochee, Diom. p. 503 P.
choliambus.short: chōlĭambus, i, m., = χωλίαμβος (the limping iambus), iambic verse, whose last foot, instead of an iambus, is a spondee or trochee, Diom.

choma.full: chōma, ătis, n., = χῶμα, a dam, bank, or mound (pure Lat. agger), Dig. 47, 11, 10; Cod. Th. 11, 24, 6, § 7.
choma.short: chōma, ătis, n., = χῶμα, a dam, bank, or mound (pure Lat.

chondrille.full: chondrillē (chondryllē), ēs, f., or chondrillon, i, n., = χονδρίλλη, chondrilla, Spanish succory, Plin. 21, 15, 52, § 89; 22, 22, 45, § 91.
chondrille.short: chondrillē (chondryllē), ēs, f., or chondrillon, i, n., = χονδρίλλη, chondrilla, Spanish succory, Plin.

chondris.full: chondris, is, f., a plant, a kind of horehound, resembling marjoram: Marrubium pseudodictamnus, Linn.; Plin. 25, 8, 53, § 92; 26, 8, 31, § 49.
chondris.short: chondris, is, f., a plant, a kind of horehound, resembling marjoram: Marrubium pseudodictamnus, Linn.;

chora.full: Chōra, ae, f., = Χώρα, a district of Lower Egypt, near Alexandria, Plin. 13, 4, 9, § 42; cf. id. 6, 36, 39, § 212.
chora.short: Chōra, ae, f., = Χώρα, a district of Lower Egypt, near Alexandria, Plin.

choragium.full: chŏrāgĭum, ii, n., = χορήγιον. The place where the chorus was trained and practised, Vitr. 5, 9; Inscr. Orell. 3209.— ( = χορηγία; cf. Lidd. and Scott), the preparing and bringing out of a chorus, Plaut. Capt. prol. 61; App. Mag. p. 282, 1; cf. Fest. p. 52; in plur., Val. Max. 2, 4, 6.— Hence, Transf., of any other splendid preparation or equipment, Plin. 36, 15, 24, § 115: nuptiarum, App. M. 4, p. 157, 35: funebre, id. ib. 2, p. 123, 25.—Trop.: gloriae, means of acquiring, Auct. Her. 4, 50, 63.

choragus.full: chŏrāgus, i, m., = χορηγός, he who had the care of the chorus and the supplies necessary for it, the choragus, Plaut. Pers. 1, 3, 79; id. Trin. 4, 2, 16; id. Curc. 4, 1.— Transf., he who pays the cost of a banquet, Poët. ap. Suet. Aug. 70 Ruhnk.
choragus.short: chŏrāgus, i, m., = χορηγός, he who had the care of the chorus and the supplies necessary for it, the choragus, Plaut.

choraule.full: chŏraulē, ēs, f. χοραύλη, a female flute-player, who accompanied with the flute the chorus dance, Inscr. Orell. 2610.

choraules.full: chŏraules, ae (acc. choraulen, Plin. 37, 1, 3, § 6; Petr. 52 fin.: choraulam, Suet. Ner. 54; a nom. choraula is apparently found only in the later glossaries), m., = χοραύλης, a flute-player, who accompanied with a flute the chorus dance, Mart. 5, 56, 9; 9, 78; Juv. 6, 77; Petr. 69, 5; Suet. Galb. 12 fin.; Sid. Ep. 9, 13; Inscr. Orell. 2609; cf. Diom. p. 489 P.

choraulicus.full: chŏraulĭcus, a, um, adj. choraules, of or belonging to the flute-players of the chorus: tibiae, Diom. p. 489 P.

chorda.full: chorda, ae, f., = χορδή. * An intestine, as food, Petr. 66, 7 (al. leg. cord.).— Far more freq., Catgut, a string (of a musical instrument), Cic. de Or. 3, 57, 214; id. N. D. 2, 59, 149 fin.; Lucr. 2, 412; 2, 505; Tib. 2, 5, 3; 3, 4, 70; Hor. C. 4, 9, 4; id. S. 1, 3, 8; id. A. P. 348 al.— A rope, cord, for binding a slave: tunc tibi actutum chorda tenditur, Plaut. Most. 3, 2, 55 Lorenz.

chordacista.full: chordăcista, ae, m. chorda, a player on a stringed instrument, Mart. Cap. 9, § 924.

chordapsus.full: chordapsus, i, m., = χόρδαψος, a disease of the intestines, Cael. Aur. Acut. 3, 17, 144; Theod. Prisc. 4, 8 (in Cels. 4, 14 written as Greek).
chordapsus.short: chordapsus, i, m., = χόρδαψος, a disease of the intestines, Cael.

chordus1.full: chordus (cordus, v. the letter C), a, um, adj. a very ancient word relating to husbandry, of unknown etym., lateborn, or produced late in the season: dicuntur agni chordi, qui post tempus nascuntur, Varr. R. R. 2, 1, 29; cf. Plin. 8, 47, 72, § 187; Varr. R. R. 2, 1, 19; 2, 2, 5: faenum, the second crop of hay or after-math, Cato, R. R. 5 fin.; Col. 7, 3, 21; Plin. 18, 28, 67, § 262: olus, Col. 12, 13, 2: frumenta, Paul. ex Fest. p. 65, 10.

chordus2.full: Chordus, i, m., a Roman cognomen; esp.: H. Cremutius Chordus, an historian of the times of Augustus and Tiberius, Quint. 1, 4, 25; Tac. A. 4, 34; Suet. Aug. 35; id. Calig. 16; Sen. Cons. ad Marc. 1, 2.
chordus2.short: Chordus, i, m., a Roman cognomen;

chorea.full: chŏrēa (chŏrĕa, Tib. 1, 3, 59; Prop. 2 (3), 19, 15; Verg. A. 6, 644), ae, f., = χορεία (most freq. in plur.), a dance in a ring, a dance. Sing., * Lucr. 2, 636; Verg. Cul. 19.— Plur., Tib. 1, 7, 49; Prop. 1, 3, 5; 3 (4), 10, 23; Verg. A. 9, 615; 10, 224; Hor. C. 1, 9, 16; 2, 19, 25; 4, 6, 15; Ov. M. 8, 581; 8, 746; 14, 520 et saep.— Meton., of the circular motions of the stars: choreae astricae, Varr. ap. Non. p. 451, 11; Manil. 1, 668.

chorepiscopus.full: chōrĕpiscŏpus, i, m., = χωρεπίσκοπος, a deputy of a bishop for a village, a suffragan bishop, Cod. Just. 1, 3, 42.
chorepiscopus.short: chōrĕpiscŏpus, i, m., = χωρεπίσκοπος, a deputy of a bishop for a village, a suffragan bishop, Cod.

choreus.full: chŏrēus or -īus, i, m., = χορεῖος (sc. πούς, pes), in verse, A foot, later called trochaeus,—˘, Cic. Or. 63, 212; Quint. 9, 4, 80; 9, 4, 82; 9, 4, 96; Marc. Vict. p. 2487 P.— In later metrists, for the earlier tribrachys, ˘˘˘, Diom. pp. 261 and 475 P.

choriambus.full: chŏrĭambus, i, m., = χορίαμβος, in verse, a foot composed of a choreus and an iambus,—˘˘—, Diom. p. 478 P.; Marc. Vict. p. 2490 ib. al.—Adj.: choriambum carmen, consisting of the choriambus, Aus. Ep. 10, 37.—Hence, chŏrĭambĭcus, a, um, adj., choriambic: metrum, Diom. p. 509 P.; Serv. Centim. p. 1822 ib.: versus, Sid. Ep. 9, 13.
choriambus.short: chŏrĭambus, i, m., = χορίαμβος, in verse, a foot composed of a choreus and an iambus,—˘˘—, Diom.

choricus.full: chŏrĭcus, a, um, adj., = χορικός, pertaining to the chorus: tibiae, Diom. 3, p. 489. —In metre: metrum, a kind of anapœstic verse, consisting of a hypercatalectic dipody, e. g. animus male fortis, Serv. Centim. p. 1821 P.
choricus.short: chŏrĭcus, a, um, adj., = χορικός, pertaining to the chorus: tibiae, Diom.

chorobates.full: chōrŏbătes, ae, m., = χωροβάτης. an instrument for finding the level of water, a ground-level, Vitr. 8, 5, 1 Schneid.
