chorocitharista.full: chŏrŏcĭthărista, ae, m., = χοροκιθαριστής, he who accompanied the chorus on the cithara, Suet. Dom. 4.
chorocitharista.short: chŏrŏcĭthărista, ae, m., = χοροκιθαριστής, he who accompanied the chorus on the cithara, Suet.

chorographia.full: Chōrŏgrăphĭa, ae, f., = χωρογραφία, the description of countries, geography, Lact. ad Stat. Th. 2, 44.—Esp., the title of a book of Cicero, Prisc. p. 717 P.; and of a poem of P. Terentius Varro Atacinus.
chorographia.short: Chōrŏgrăphĭa, ae, f., = χωρογραφία, the description of countries, geography, Lact.

chorographus.full: chōrŏgrăphus, i, m., = χωρογράφος, one who describes countries, a geographer, Vitr. 8, 2, 6 Schneid. (others read, instead of chorographis, chorographiis, from chorographia, q. v.).
chorographus.short: chōrŏgrăphus, i, m., = χωρογράφος, one who describes countries, a geographer, Vitr.

chortinus.full: chortĭnus, a, um, adj., = χόρτινος, of or from grass: oleum, Plin. 15, 7, 7, § 30.
chortinus.short: chortĭnus, a, um, adj., = χόρτινος, of or from grass: oleum, Plin.

chorus.full: chŏrus, i, m., = χορός [cf. Lidd. and Scott under χορός]. A dance in a ring, a choral dance, a dance, = chorea: chorus et cantus, Tib. 1, 7, 44; cf. Prop. 4 (5), 6, 70. Nympharum leves chori, Hor. C. 1, 1, 31: ferre pedem choris, id. ib. 2, 12, 17; Tib. 2, 1, 56: choros agere, Prop. 2, 3, 18: agitare, Verg. G. 4, 533: ducere, Hor. C. 1, 4, 5; 4, 7, 6: exercere, Verg. A. 1, 499: indicere, id. ib. 11, 737: instaurare, Stat. Achill. 4, 145: ostentare, id. ib. 2, 148 sq.: celebrare, Sen. Herc. Oet.

chremes.full: Chrĕmes, ētis or is, m., = Χρέμης, the name of an old miser in the Andria, Heaut., and Phormio of Terence, Cic. Fin. 1, 1, 3; id. Off. 1, 9, 30; Hor. Epod. 1, 33; gen. Chremi, Ter. And. 2, 2, 31; acc. Gr. Chremeta, Hor. S. 1, 10, 40; voc. Chreme, Ter. Phorm. 4, 1, 1; 4, 1, 11 al.: Chremes, id. Eun. 3, 3, 29; dat. Chremeti, id. Phorm. 5, 8, 37; acc. Chremen, id. ib. 1, 2, 13: Chremem, id. And. 2, 2, 24: Chremetem, id. ib. 3, 1, 14.
chremes.short: Chrĕmes, ētis or is, m., = Χρέμης, the name of an old miser in the Andria, Heaut., and Phormio of Terence, Cic.

chrestologus.full: Chrestŏlŏgus, i, m., = χρηστολόγος (well speaking, but ill working), a nickname of the emperor Pertinax, Capit. Pert. 13; Aur. Vict. Epit. 18.
chrestologus.short: Chrestŏlŏgus, i, m., = χρηστολόγος (well speaking, but ill working), a nickname of the emperor Pertinax, Capit.

chreston.full: chreston, i, n., = χρηστόν (useful), a name by which the plant cichorium was sometimes called, Plin. 20, 8, 30, § 74.
chreston.short: chreston, i, n., = χρηστόν (useful), a name by which the plant cichorium was sometimes called, Plin.

chrestus.full: Chrestus, i, m. A mutilated form for Christus, Lact. 4, 7, 5; hence, Chrestiani, instead of Christiani, was used by many; cf. Tert. Apol. 3 fin.— A Jew at Rome under the emperor Claudius, Suet. Claud. 15; v. the commentt. in h. l.— A slave or freedman of Cicero, Cic. Fam. 2, 8, 1.

chria.full: chrīa, ae, f., = χρεία, in rhetoric, a sentence proposed as a theme for rhetorical exercise, with its logical development, Quint. 1, 9, 3 sq.; 1, 9, 4 sq.; 2, 4, 26 Spald.; Sen. Ep. 33, 6; Diom. p. 289 P.
chria.short: chrīa, ae, f., = χρεία, in rhetoric, a sentence proposed as a theme for rhetorical exercise, with its logical development, Quint.

chrisma.full: chrisma, ătis, n., = χρίσμα, in eccl. Lat., an anointing, unction, Tert. Bapt. 7; id. adv. Jud. 13; Prud. Cath. 6, 128; Psych. 361 al.
chrisma.short: chrisma, ătis, n., = χρίσμα, in eccl.

christianismus.full: Christĭānismus, i, m., = Χριστιανισμός, Christianity, Tert. adv. Marc. 4, 33; Aug. Civ. Dei, 19, 23, 1; Hier. in Gal. 6, 4.
christianismus.short: Christĭānismus, i, m., = Χριστιανισμός, Christianity, Tert.

christianitas.full: Christĭānĭtas, ātis, f. Christus. Christianity, = Christianismus, Cod. Th. 16, 7, 7; 12, 1, 112.— Meton., the Christian clergy, Cod. Th. 12, 1, 123.

christianizo.full: Christĭānīzo, āre, v. n., = Χριστιανίζω, to profess Christianity, Tert. adv. Marc. 1, 21.

christianus.full: Christĭānus, a, um, adj. Christus, Christian: fides, Cod. Just. 16, 8, 18: lex, ib. 16, 8, 13: religio, ib. 9, 40, 16.—Hence, subst., a Christian, Tac. A. 15, 44; Suet. Ner. 16; Plin. Ep. 10, 97; very frequent in the Church fathers.—Absol., a Christian clergyman, Cod. Th. 5, 5, 2; 12, 1, 50.—Sup.: Christianissimus, the most Christian, Hier. Ep. 57, 12: princeps, Ambros. Ep. 1, 1.— Adv.: Christĭānē, in a Christian manner or spirit: regere, Aug. Ep. 89.

christicola.full: Christĭcŏla, ae, m. Christus-colo, a worshipper of Christ, a poet. designation for Christian, Prud. Cath. 3, 56; 8, 80; gen. plur. Christicolūm, id. contr. Symm. 2, 1002; id. στεφ. 3, 72.

christigena.full: Christĭgĕna, ae, adj. Christus-gigno, of the lineage of Christ: domus, i. e. the posterity of Ruth, Prud. Ham. 789.

christipotens.full: Christĭ-pŏtens, entis, adj. Christus, strong in Christ: juvenis, Prud. adv. Symm. 2, 709.

christus.full: Christus, i, m., = Χριστός (the Anointed, Heb. ; cf. Lact. 4, 7, 7), Christ, Tac. A. 15, 44 Rupert. ad loc.; Plin. Ep. 10, 97; and in the Church fathers very freq.
christus.short: Christus, i, m., = Χριστός (the Anointed, Heb.

chroma.full: chrōma, ătis (ătŏs, Vitr. 5, 5), n., = χρῶμα (a color), in music, a chromatic scale (a species of harmony in which the tones of the tetrachord measure two and a half tones, as a half, again a semitone, and then a tone and a half follow each other), Vitr. 5, 4, 3; cf. Dict. of Antiq. p. 645.—Hence, chrōmătĭcē, ēs, f., the science of this species of harmony, Vitr. 5, 5; and: chrō-mătĭcus, a, um, adj., chromatic: genus, the same, Macr. Somn. Scip. 2, 4 fin.

chromis.full: chrŏmis, is, m. or f., = χρόμις, a seafish: immunda, Ov. Hal. 121; Plin. 10, 70, 89, § 193: chromin, qui, etc., id. 32, 11, 54, § 153; 9, 16, 24, § 57.— Chrŏmis, nom. propr. m., of a satyr, Verg. E. 6, 13; of a Trojan, acc. Chromim, id. A. 11, 675; of a Centaur, acc. Chromin, Ov. M. 12, 333 al.

chronicus.full: chrŏnĭcus, a, um, adj., = χρονικός, pertaining to time: libri, chronicles, Gell. 17, 21, 1; so also absol.: chrŏnĭca, ōrum, n., = τὰ χρονικά, Plin. 35, 9, 35, § 58; Gell. 17, 4, 5; 17, 15, 1; and in sing.: in primo chronico, id. 17, 21, 3: morbi, chronic, lingering, Isid. Orig. 4, 7; opp. acuti morbi.— Hence the work of Caelius Aurelianus is entitled De morbis acutis et chronicis.
chronicus.short: chrŏnĭcus, a, um, adj., = χρονικός, pertaining to time: libri, chronicles, Gell.

chronius.full: chrŏnĭus, a, um, adj., = χρόνιος, chronic, Cael. Aur. Acut. 2, 28, 148; 3, 16, 135.
chronius.short: chrŏnĭus, a, um, adj., = χρόνιος, chronic, Cael.

chronographus.full: chrŏnŏgrăphus, i, m., = χρονογράφος, a chronographer, annalist, Sid. Ep. 8, 6 fin.
chronographus.short: chrŏnŏgrăphus, i, m., = χρονογράφος, a chronographer, annalist, Sid.

chrysa.full: Chrȳsa, ae, or Chrȳsē, ēs, f., = Χρύση. A town on the coast of Troas sacred to Apollo, Plin. 5, 30, 32, § 122; Mel. 1, 18; Ov. M. 13, 174 (cf. Hom. Il. 1, 390; 1, 452).— An island near Crete, Plin. 4, 12, 20, § 61.— An island of India, Mel. 3, 7, 7.
chrysa.short: Chrȳsa, ae, or Chrȳsē, ēs, f., = Χρύση.

chrysallis.full: chrȳsallis, ĭdis, f., = χρυσαλλίς, the gold-colored chrysalis, aurelia, or pupa of the butterfly, Plin. 11, 32, 37, § 112; 11, 35, 41, § 117.
chrysallis.short: chrȳsallis, ĭdis, f., = χρυσαλλίς, the gold-colored chrysalis, aurelia, or pupa of the butterfly, Plin.

chrysanthemum.full: chrȳsanthĕmum or -mon, i, n., = χρυσάνθεμον, the gold-flower, marigold, also called heliochryson, Plin. 21, 25, 96, § 168.—Access. form chrȳsanthes, Verg. Cul. 403 Sillig.
chrysanthemum.short: chrȳsanthĕmum or -mon, i, n., = χρυσάνθεμον, the gold-flower, marigold, also called heliochryson, Plin.

chrysas.full: Chrȳsas, ae, m., = Χρύσας, a river of Sicily, now Dittaino, near which is St. Asaro, Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 44, § 96 Zumpt; Sil. 14, 229.
chrysas.short: Chrȳsas, ae, m., = Χρύσας, a river of Sicily, now Dittaino, near which is St.

chryselectrum.full: chrȳsēlectrum, i, n., = χρυσήλεκτρον. Gold-colored amber, a precious stone, Plin. 37, 3, 12, § 51.— chrȳsē-lectrus, i, f., a dark-yellow precious stone, perh. amber-colored hyacinth, Plin. 37, 9, 43, § 127.

chrysendetus.full: chrȳsendĕtus, a, um, adj., = χρυσένδετος, set in gold, inlaid with gold: lances, Mart. 14, 97 inscr.—Also absol.: chrȳs-endĕta, ōrum, n. (sc. vasa), vessels inlaid with gold, Mart. 2, 43, 11; 6, 94, 2; 14, 97, 1.
chrysendetus.short: chrȳsendĕtus, a, um, adj., = χρυσένδετος, set in gold, inlaid with gold: lances, Mart.

chryses.full: Chrȳses, ae, m., = Χρύσης, a priest of Apollo, from Chryse, in Troas, the father of Astynome, on account of whose close captivity by Agamemnon, Apollo sent a pestilence upon the Grecian hosts, Hyg. Fab. 121; Ov. A. A. 2, 402.—As a title of a tragedy of Pacuvius, Cic. Or. 46, 155; id. Div. 1, 57, 131 al.—Hence, Chrȳsēïs, ĭdis, f., = Χρν σηίς, his daughter Astynome, Ov. Tr. 2, 373; id. R. Am. 469.
chryses.short: Chrȳses, ae, m., = Χρύσης, a priest of Apollo, from Chryse, in Troas, the father of Astynome, on account of whose close captivity by Agamemnon, Apollo sent a pestilence upon the Grecian hosts, Hyg.

chryseus.full: chrȳsĕus, a, um, adj., = χρύσεος, golden: basiliscus, i. e. gold - colored, App. Herb. 128.—Subst.: chrȳsĕa, ōrum, n., golden vessels, Mart. 9, 95, 4.
chryseus.short: chrȳsĕus, a, um, adj., = χρύσεος, golden: basiliscus, i.

chrysippus.full: Chrȳsippus, i, m., = Χρύσιππος. One of the most distinguished of the Stoic philosophers, from Soli, in Cilicia, a pupil of Cleanthes and Zeno, Cic. Ac. 2, 23, 73; 2, 24, 75; 2, 27, 87 al.; id. de Or. 1, 11, 50; id. Fat. 4, 7; Hor. S. 2, 3, 44; id. Ep. 1, 2, 4; Sen. Ep. 113, 18; Lact. 3, 18, 15; Pers. 6, 80. —Hence, Chrȳsippēus, a, um, adj., of Chrysippus, Cic. Ac. 2, 30, 96: sophisma, Hier. Ep. 69, 2.— A physician of Cnidus, in the time of Alexander the Great, Plin. 20, 3, 8, § 17; 20, 10, 43, §

chrysis.full: Chrȳsis, ĭdis, f., a comic person in Terence and Trabea, Cic. de Or. 2, 80, 327; id. Tusc. 4, 31, 67; Ter. And. 1, 1, 58 al.
chrysis.short: Chrȳsis, ĭdis, f., a comic person in Terence and Trabea, Cic.

chrysites.full: chrȳsītes, ae, m., = χρυσίτης. A precious stone, also called phloginos, Plin. 37, 10, 66, § 179.— Another gold-colored precious stone, Plin. 36, 22, 43, § 157.

chrysitis.full: chrȳsītis, ĭdis, f., = χρυσῖτις. Adj., gold-colored: chrysitis spuma. found in silver mines, Plin. 33, 6, 35, § 106.— Subst., a plant, also called chrysocome, q. v., Plin. 21, 8, 26, § 50; 21, 20, 85, § 148.

chrysoaspides.full: chrȳsŏaspĭdes, um, m., = χρυσοάσπιδες (bearing golden shields), a kind of soldiers under Alexander Severus, Lampr. Alex. Sev. 50.
chrysoaspides.short: chrȳsŏaspĭdes, um, m., = χρυσοάσπιδες (bearing golden shields), a kind of soldiers under Alexander Severus, Lampr.

chrysoberyllus.full: chrȳsŏbēryllus, i, m., = χρυσοβήρυλλος, chrysoberyl, Plin. 37, 5, 20, § 76.
chrysoberyllus.short: chrȳsŏbēryllus, i, m., = χρυσοβήρυλλος, chrysoberyl, Plin.

chrysocalis.full: chrȳsŏcălis, is, f., a plant, also called parthenium, App. Herb. 23.
chrysocalis.short: chrȳsŏcălis, is, f., a plant, also called parthenium, App.

chrysocanthos.full: chrȳsŏcanthos, i, f., a kind of ivy which bears gold-colored berries, App. Herb. 119; called in Plin. 16, 34, 62, § 147, chrȳ-sŏcarpus, = χρυσόκαρπος.
chrysocanthos.short: chrȳsŏcanthos, i, f., a kind of ivy which bears gold-colored berries, App.

chrysocephalos.full: chrȳsŏcĕphălŏs, i, m., = χρυσοκέφαλος, a golden basilisk, App. Herb. 128.
chrysocephalos.short: chrȳsŏcĕphălŏs, i, m., = χρυσοκέφαλος, a golden basilisk, App.

chrysococcus.full: chrȳsŏcoccus, a, um, adj., having golden grains: flos, App. Herb. 28.
chrysococcus.short: chrȳsŏcoccus, a, um, adj., having golden grains: flos, App.

chrysocolla.full: chrȳsŏcolla, ae, f., = χρυσόκολλα. Mountain - green, copper - green, borax. Natural, Plin. 33, 5, 26, § 86 sq.; Vitr. 7, 9 fin.— Made by art, Plin. 33, 5, 27, § 89 sq.— A precious stone, called also amphitane, Plin. 37, 10, 54, § 147.

chrysogonus.full: Chrȳsŏgŏnus, i, m. L. Cornelius, a freedman of Sylla.— A slave of Verres, Cic. Verr. 2, 1, 36, § 92.— A player on the cithara, Juv. 6, 74; Cic. Rosc. Am. 2, 6; cf. id. ib. 43, 124.

chrysographatus.full: chrȳsŏgrăphātus, a, um, adj. χρυσογραφης, inlaid with gold: scuta, Val. Imp. ap. Treb. Claud. 14.

chrysolachanum.full: chrȳsŏlăchănum, i, n., = χρυσολάχανον, garden orach, called also atriplex: Atriplex hortensis, Linn.; Plin. 27, 8, 43, § 66 sq.
chrysolachanum.short: chrȳsŏlăchănum, i, n., = χρυσολάχανον, garden orach, called also atriplex: Atriplex hortensis, Linn.;

chrysolampis.full: chrȳsŏlampis, ĭdis, f., = χρυσόλαμπις (gold-gleaming), a precious stone, Plin. 37, 10, 56, § 156.
chrysolampis.short: chrȳsŏlampis, ĭdis, f., = χρυσόλαμπις (gold-gleaming), a precious stone, Plin.

chrysolithos.full: chrȳsŏlĭthŏs, i, m. and f., = χρυσόλιθος, chrysolite, the topaz of the Greeks and of modern mineralogists, Plin. 37, 9, 42, § 126; Prop. 2 (3), 16, 44; Ov. M. 2, 109; Prud. Psych. 854; Isid. Orig. 16, 15, 2.

chrysomelum.full: chrȳsŏmēlum, i, n., = χρυσόμηλον (golden apple), a kind of quince, Plin. 15, 11, 10, § 37.—Hence, chrȳsŏmēlĭnus, a, um, adj.: mala, the same, Col. 5, 10, 19.
chrysomelum.short: chrȳsŏmēlum, i, n., = χρυσόμηλον (golden apple), a kind of quince, Plin.

chrysopastus.full: chrȳsŏpastus, i, m., = χρυσόπαστος, a species of our topaz, Sol. 30 fin.
chrysopastus.short: chrȳsŏpastus, i, m., = χρυσόπαστος, a species of our topaz, Sol.

chrysophrys.full: chrȳsophrys, ўos, f., = χρύσοφρυς, a sea-fish with a golden spot over each eye: Sparus aurata, Linn.; Ov. Hal. 111; Plin. 32, 11, 54, § 152.
chrysophrys.short: chrȳsophrys, ўos, f., = χρύσοφρυς, a sea-fish with a golden spot over each eye: Sparus aurata, Linn.;

chrysopis.full: chrȳsōpis, ĭdis, f., = χρυσῶπις, a precious variety of our topaz, Plin. 37, 10, 56, § 156.
chrysopis.short: chrȳsōpis, ĭdis, f., = χρυσῶπις, a precious variety of our topaz, Plin.

chrysoprasus.full: chrȳsŏprăsus, i, m., = χρυσόπρασος, the chrysoprase, a precious stone of a golden-yellow and a leek-green color, Plin. 37, 5, 20, § 77; Prud. Psych. 865; Isid. Orig. 16, 7, 7; 16, 14, 8; Ambros. in Psa. 118, Serm. 16, § 41 sq.; also called chrȳsŏ-prăsĭus lăpis, Plin. 37, 8, 34, § 113.
chrysoprasus.short: chrȳsŏprăsus, i, m., = χρυσόπρασος, the chrysoprase, a precious stone of a golden-yellow and a leek-green color, Plin.

chrysopteros.full: chrȳsoptĕrŏs, i, m., = χρυσόπτερος, a kind of jasper, Plin. 37, 8, 32, § 109; Ambros. in Psa. 118, Serm. 16, § 41 sq.
chrysopteros.short: chrȳsoptĕrŏs, i, m., = χρυσόπτερος, a kind of jasper, Plin.

chrysorrhoas.full: Chrȳsorrhŏas, ae, m., = Χρυσορρόας, the name of several rivers in Cœlesyria, in Lydia, in Bithynia, and in Pontus, Plin. 5, 18, 16, § 74; 5, 32, 43, § 148; 5, 29, 30, § 110; 6, 4, 4, § 14.
chrysorrhoas.short: Chrȳsorrhŏas, ae, m., = Χρυσορρόας, the name of several rivers in Cœlesyria, in Lydia, in Bithynia, and in Pontus, Plin.

chrysos.full: chrȳsŏs, i, m., = χρυσός, gold, Plaut. Bacch. 2, 3, 6 (in a pun with the name Chrysalus).— Chrysos melas, black ivy, App. Herb. 98.
chrysos.short: chrȳsŏs, i, m., = χρυσός, gold, Plaut.

chrysothales.full: chrȳsŏthăles, is, n., = χρυσοθαλές, a kind of aizoon or houseleek, wall-pepper, called also erithales, trithales, and isoetes, Plin. 25, 13, 102, § 160.
chrysothales.short: chrȳsŏthăles, is, n., = χρυσοθαλές, a kind of aizoon or houseleek, wall-pepper, called also erithales, trithales, and isoetes, Plin.

chthonius.full: Chthŏnĭus, i, m. A Centaur, Ov. M. 12, 441.— One of the Sparti (produced from the teeth of the dragon), Hyg. Fab. 178; Stat. Th. 2, 538.

chuni.full: Chūni and Chunni, ōrum, v. Hunni.

chus.full: chūs, ŏos, m., = χοῦς, a measure for liquids, = congius, Rhemn. Fann. Pond. 7, 70.
chus.short: chūs, ŏos, m., = χοῦς, a measure for liquids, = congius, Rhemn.

chydaeus.full: chўdaeus, a, um, adj., = χυδαῖος (abundant; hence), common: dactyli, a kind of palms, Plin. 13, 4, 9, § 46; 14, 16, 19, § 102.

chylisma.full: chȳlisma, ătis, n., = χύλισμα, the extracted juice of a plant, Scrib. Comp. 23.
chylisma.short: chȳlisma, ătis, n., = χύλισμα, the extracted juice of a plant, Scrib.

chylus.full: chȳlus, i, m., = χυλός, the extracted juice of a plant, Veg. 5, 37 and 65.
chylus.short: chȳlus, i, m., = χυλός, the extracted juice of a plant, Veg.

chymus.full: chȳmus, i, m., = χυμός (juice), the fluid of the stomach, chyle, Ser. Samm. 48, 900.
chymus.short: chȳmus, i, m., = χυμός (juice), the fluid of the stomach, chyle, Ser.

chytropus.full: chytrŏpūs, pŏdis, m., = χυτρόπους, a pot or chafing-dish with feet for coals, Vulg. Lev. 11, 35.
chytropus.short: chytrŏpūs, pŏdis, m., = χυτρόπους, a pot or chafing-dish with feet for coals, Vulg.

ciani.full: Cĭāni, ōrum, m., the inhabitants of Cios, a town in Bithynia, Liv. 31, 31, 4; 32, 21, 22 al.
ciani.short: Cĭāni, ōrum, m., the inhabitants of Cios, a town in Bithynia, Liv.

cibalis.full: cĭbālis, e, adj. cibus, pertaining to food: fistula, the œsophagus or gullet, Lact. Opif. Dei, 11, 5.

cibaria.full: cĭbārĭa, ōrum, and cĭbārĭum, ii, v. cibarius.
cibaria.short: cĭbārĭa, ōrum, and cĭbārĭum, ii, v.

cibarius.full: cĭbārĭus, a, um, adj. cibus, pertaining to or suitable for food (class.): res, Plaut. Capt. 4, 3, 1: leges, i. e. sumptuary laws, laws restraining luxury, Cato ap. Macr. S. 2, 13: uva, suitable only for eating, not for wine, Plin. 14, 3, 4, § 37; cf.: uva vilitatis cibariae, id. 14, 2, 4, § 35.— Subst.: cĭbārĭa, ōrum, n., food, nutriment, victuals, provisions, fare, ration, fodder (in the jurists a more restricted idea than alimenta, which comprises every thing necessary for sustaining life, Dig

cibatio.full: cĭbātĭo, ōnis, f. cibo, a feeding; concr., a meal, repast (post-class.), Sol. 27, 13; Cael. Aur. Tard. 1, 1, 12; 1, 4, 3.

cibatus.full: cĭbātus, ūs, m. id., concr., food, victuals, nutriment (except Pliny, only anteand post-class.), Plaut. Mil. 2, 2, 71; Varr. 1, 63, 2; 2, 4, 15; 2, 9, 8; 3, 8, 3; Lucr. 1, 1093; 6, 1126; Plin. 8, 10, 10, § 29; 8, 55, 81, § 217; 10, 61, 81, § 168; 10, 73, 93, § 199; Gell. 9, 4, 10; App. M. 1, p. 113; Sol. 25.

cibdelus.full: cibdēlus, a, um, adj., = κίβδηλος, spurious, base: fontes, impure, unhealthy, Vitr. 8, 3, 6.
cibdelus.short: cibdēlus, a, um, adj., = κίβδηλος, spurious, base: fontes, impure, unhealthy, Vitr.

cibicida.full: cĭbĭcīda, ae, m. cibus-caedo, breadwaster, bread-consumer, probably a humorous designation of a slave, Lucil. ap. Non. p. 88, 8.

cibo.full: cĭbo, no perf., ātum, 1, v. a. cibus, to give food to animals, to feed or fodder (rare): genera avium, Col. 8, 10 fin.: locustae utiles cibandis pullis, id. 8, 11, 15: draconem manu suă, Suet. Tib. 72.—In pass.: cibari, to take food, Liv. Epit. 19.— With men as objects (late Lat.), Vulg. Prov. 25, 21; id. Rom. 12, 20.

ciboria.full: cĭbōrĭa, ae, f., the Egyptian bean, App. Herb. 67.
ciboria.short: cĭbōrĭa, ae, f., the Egyptian bean, App.

ciborium.full: cĭbōrĭum. ii, n., = κιβώριον, a drinking-cup (made like the large leaves of the Egyptian bean), Hor. C. 2, 7, 22.

cibus.full: cĭbus, i, m. perh. root of capio, food for man and beast, victuals, fare, nutriment, fodder (class. in prose and poetry, both in sing. and plur.; syn.: esca, epulae; opp. potio, Cic. Fin. 1, 11, 37; cf. id. N. D. 2, 54, 136; so, cibus potusque, Tac. A. 13, 16: cibus et vinum, Cic. Div. 1, 29, 60; Juv. 10, 203: unda cibusque, Ov. M. 4, 262): cibum capere, Plaut. Trin. 4, 2, 60; Ter. Eun. 2, 3, 77: petere, id. ib. 3, 2, 38; id. Heaut. 5, 2, 25: capessere (of animals), Cic. N. D. 2, 47, 122: sumere

cibyra.full: Cĭbўra, ae, f., = Κιβυρα. A town in Magna Phrygia, on the borders of Caria, abounding in manufactures, and the seat of a Roman tribunal, now Buruz, Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 13, § 30; Liv. 38, 14 bis; and id. 38, 15, 1.— Hence, Cĭbўrāta, ae, comm., = Κιβυράτης, of Cibyra: fratres quidam, Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 13, § 30 sq.: pantherae, id. Att. 5, 21, 5.—Subst.: Cĭbўrātae, ārum, m., the inhabitants of Cibyra, Cael. ap. Cic. Fam. 8, 4, 5; 8, 9, 3; Liv. 45, 25, 13 al.— Cĭbўrātĭcus, a, um, adj., of or pertaining t

cicada.full: cĭcāda, ae, f., the cicada, tree-cricket: Cicada orni, Linn.; Plin. 11, 26, 32, § 92 sq.; Lucr. 4, 56; 5, 801; Verg. E. 2, 13; 5, 77; id. G. 3, 328; id. Cul. 151 al.—Worn as an ornament in the hair of the Athenians, Verg. Cir. 128 Sillig; cf. Lidd. and Scott, under τέττιξ.—As a symbol of summer, Ov. A. A. 1, 271; Juv. 9, 69.
cicada.short: cĭcāda, ae, f., the cicada, tree-cricket: Cicada orni, Linn.;

cicatricor.full: cĭcātrīcor, ātus, 1, v. dep. cicatrix, to be scarred over, cicatrized (late Lat.), Fest p. 65, 14 Müll.; Cael. Aur. Tard. 4, 8, 118. — Trop., Sid. Ep. 6, 7; 6, 1 fin.

cicatricosus.full: cĭcātrīcōsus, a, um, adj. id., full of scars, covered with scars: tergum, Plaut. Am. 1, 1, 290: facies, Quint. 4, 1, 61: Ira (personified), Sen. Ira, 2, 35, 5: vitis, Col. Arb. 11, 1: putatio, id. ib. 4, 27, 3.— Trop., of a writing, amended or polished here and there, Quint. 10, 4, 3; v. the context.

cicatricula.full: cĭcātrīcŭla, ae, f. dim. id., a small scar, Cels. 2, 10 fin.; 7, 7, 1.

cicatrix.full: cĭcātrix, īcis, f., a scar, cicatrice (freq. and class.). Prop., Ter. Eun. 3, 2, 29; Cic. Phil. 7, 6, 17; Quint. 5, 9, 5; 6, 1, 21; 6, 3, 100; Suet. Aug. 65 al.; Hor. S. 1, 5, 60; id. C. 1, 35, 33; Ov. M. 12, 444; id. R. Am. 623 al.: cicatrices adversae, wounds in front (therefore honorable), Cic. de Or. 2, 28, 124; Sall. H. 1, 55 Dietsch: aversa, on the back, Gell. 2, 11, 2; cf.: cicatrices adverso corpore, Cic. Verr. 2, 5, 1, § 3; Sall. J. 85, 29; Liv. 2, 23, 4: cicatricem inducere, Cels. 7, 2
cicatrix.short: cĭcātrix, īcis, f., a scar, cicatrice (freq.

ciccus.full: ciccus, i, m., = κίκκος, the thin membrane surrounding the grains of a pomegranate; hence for something unimportant, worthless, a trifle, bagatelle, Varr. L. L. 7, § 91; cf. Fest. p. 42, 10 Müll.: ciccum non interduim, I would not give a straw, Plaut. Rud. 2, 7, 22; id. ap. Varr. l. l.; cf. Aus. Idyll. praef. 13.
ciccus.short: ciccus, i, m., = κίκκος, the thin membrane surrounding the grains of a pomegranate;

cicer.full: cĭcer, ĕris, n., the chickpea: Cicer Arietinum, Linn. (used only in sing. acc. to Varr. L. L. 8, 25, 115; 9, 39, 142; 10, 3, 174); Col. 2, 10, 19; Plin. 18, 12, 32, § 124 sq.; Pall. Mart. 4; Plaut. Bacch. 4, 5, 7; Hor. S. 1, 6, 115; 2, 3, 182; id. A. P. 249; Mart. 1, 104; Pers. 5, 177; Petr. 14, 3.
cicer.short: cĭcer, ĕris, n., the chickpea: Cicer Arietinum, Linn.

cicera.full: cĭcĕra, ae, f., pulse similar to the chickpea, chickling-vetch: Lathyrus cicera, Linn.; Col. 2, 11, 1; 2, 11, 12; Pall. Mart. 6.
cicera.short: cĭcĕra, ae, f., pulse similar to the chickpea, chickling-vetch: Lathyrus cicera, Linn.;

cicercula.full: cĭcercŭla, ae, f. dim. cicera; al. cicer; v. Plin. 18, 12, 32, § 124, a kind of small chickpea, Col. 2, 10, 19; Plin. 18, 12, 32, § 124; 18, 18, 73, § 304; 22, 25, 72, § 148; Pall. Jan. 5; id. Febr. 4.

cicerculum.full: cĭcercŭlum, i, n., an African species of the pigment sinopis, Plin. 35, 6, 13, § 32.
cicerculum.short: cĭcercŭlum, i, n., an African species of the pigment sinopis, Plin.

cicero.full: Cĭcĕro, ōnis, m., = Κικέρων, a Roman cognomen in the gens Tullia. M. Tullius Cicero, the greatest of the Roman orators and writers; born on the 3d of January, 106 B.C. (648 A.U.C.), at Arpinum (hence Arpinae chartae, Mart. 10, 19, 17); assassinated, at the age of sixty-three years, by the soldiers of Antonius, 43 B.C. (711 A.U.C.): ille se profecisse sciat, cui Cicero valde placebit, Quint. 10, 1, 112; Juv. 10, 114 al.— Hence, Cĭcĕrōnĭānus, a, um, adj., Ciceronian: simplicitas, Plin. praef. § 22
cicero.short: Cĭcĕro, ōnis, m., = Κικέρων, a Roman cognomen in the gens Tullia.

ciceromastix.full: Cĭcĕrŏmastix, īgis, m. (the scourge of Cicero, a word formed after the Gr. Ὀμηρομάστιξ), a lampoon of Largius Licinius against Cicero, Gell. 17, 1, 1.

cichorium.full: cĭchŏrĭum or -on (cĭchŏrēum, * Hor. C. 1, 31, 16), ii, n., = κιχόρια (usu. κιχώριον), chiccory, succory, or endive: Cichorium intybus, etc., Linn.; Plin. 20, 8, 30, § 74 sq.; 19, 8, 39, § 129.

cici.full: cīci, indecl. n., = κῖκι, an Egyptian tree, palma Christi or castor-oil tree, also called croton: Ricinus communis, Linn.; Plin. 15, 7, 7, § 25; 16, 22, 35, § 85.

cicilendrum.full: cicilendrum and cicimandrum, i, n., feigned names for spice, Plaut. Ps. 3, 2, 42; 3, 2, 46.
cicilendrum.short: cicilendrum and cicimandrum, i, n., feigned names for spice, Plaut.

cicindela.full: cicindēla, ae, f. candela, a glowworm, Plin. 18, 26, 66, § 250; cf. Fest. p. 42, 13 Müll.

cicinnia.full: Cicinnia, θεὰ κιναίδων, Gloss. Gr. Lat.

cicinus.full: cīcĭnus, a, um, adj. cici: oleum, an aperient oil expressed from the fruit of the cici, castor-oil, Cels. 5, 24, 3; Plin. 23, 4, 41, § 83 al.

cicirrus.full: Cĭcirrus, i, m. (Κίκιρρος = ἀλεκτρυών), a nickname, Hor. S. 1, 5, 52.

cicones.full: Cĭcŏnes, um, m., = Κίκονες, a Thracian people near the Hebrus, Mel. 2, 2, 8; Plin. 4, 11, 18, § 43; Verg. G. 4, 520; Prop. 3 (4), 12, 25; Ov. M. 10, 2 al.
cicones.short: Cĭcŏnes, um, m., = Κίκονες, a Thracian people near the Hebrus, Mel.

ciconia.full: cĭcōnĭa, ae, f., a stork, Plin. 10, 23, 32, § 63; Hor. S. 2, 2, 49; Ov. M. 6, 97; Juv. 14, 74 al.; at Praeneste called conia, Plaut. Truc. 3, 2, 23.— Meton. A derisory bending of the fingers in the form of a stork's bill, Pers. 1, 58; Hier. prol. in Sophon. Ep. 125, n. 18.— An implement in the form of a T, used by rustics to measure the depth of furrows, Col. 3, 13, 11.— A transverse pole, moving upon a perpendicular post, for drawing water, etc. (syn. tolleno), Isid. Orig. 20, 15, 3.
ciconia.short: cĭcōnĭa, ae, f., a stork, Plin.

ciconinus.full: cĭcōnīnus, a, um, adj. ciconia, of the stork (late Lat.): adventus, Sid. Ep. 2, 14.

cicuma.full: cicuma, ae, f., = κικυμίς, an owl, Gloss. post Fest. p. 381, 1 Müll. (for which cecuma, in Gloss. Isid.).
cicuma.short: cicuma, ae, f., = κικυμίς, an owl, Gloss.

cicur.full: cĭcur, ŭris, adj. cf. cacula, tame (cf. mansuetus): quod a fero discretum id dicitur cicur, Varr. L. L. 7, § 91 Müll. (syn. mansuetus; opp. ferus, immanis; apparently not used after Cic.): cicurum vel ferarum bestiarum, Cic. N. D. 2, 39, 99; id. Lael. 21, 81: bestiae immanes, cicures, id. Tusc. 5, 13, 38: apes (opp. ferae), Varr. R. R. 3, 16, 19.— Trop., mild: ingenium, Auct. ap. Varr. L. L. 7, § 91 Müll.: concilium, i. e. sapiens, Pac. ap. Fest. s. v. incicorem, p. 108, 3 ib.

cicurius.full: Cĭcŭrĭus, ĭi, m. (Cĭcŭrīnus, Bip.), a cognomen in the Veturian gens [sc. a cicure], Varr. L. L. 7, § 91 Müll.

cicuro.full: cĭcŭro, āre, v. a. cicur, to tame ( = mansuefacio), Pac. ap. Varr. L. L. 7, § 91 Müll., p. 98 Bip.

cicuta1.full: cĭcūta, ae, f., the hemlock given to criminals as poison; prob. either Cicuta virosa or Conium maculatum, Linn.; Plin. 25, 13, 95, § 151; Cato, R. R. 27, 2; Lucr. 5, 897; Hor. S. 2, 1, 56 al.; plur., id. Ep. 2, 2, 53; drunk by Socrates; hence: magister sorbitio tollit quem dira cicutae, i. e. Socrates, Pers. 4, 1 sq.—To the extraordinary coldness produced by it, reference is made in Pers. 5, 145.— Meton., a pipe or flute made from the stalks of the hemlock, a shepherd's pipe, Lucr. 5, 1382; Verg
cicuta1.short: cĭcūta, ae, f., the hemlock given to criminals as poison;

cicuta2.full: Cĭcūta, ae, m., the name of a usurer in Hor. S. 2, 3, 69 and 175.
cicuta2.short: Cĭcūta, ae, m., the name of a usurer in Hor.

cicuticen.full: cĭcūtĭcen, ĭnis, m. 1. cicuta, II. and cano, a player upon a reed-pipe, Sid. Carm. 1, 15.

cidaris.full: cĭdăris, is, f. (cĭdar, aris, n., Auct. Itin. Alex. M. p. 64 Mai) [Persian; Heb. ; Gr. κίδαρις], = τιάρα ὀρθή, an ornament for the head of Persian kings, a diadem, tiara: cidarim Persae vocabant regium capitis insigne, Curt. 3, 3, 19.— The crown of the Prince of Israel (in prophetic vision), Vulg. Ezech. 21, 26.— A head-dress of the high-priest of the Jews (cf. the Talmud, ), Hier. Ep. 64, n. 3; id. in Ezech. 7, 21, 25; Lact. 4, 14, 8 (as transl. of the Heb. , Vulg. Zach. 3, 5); Vulg. Lev. 8, 9;

cieo.full: cĭĕo, cīvi, cĭtum, 2 (from the primitive form cĭo, cīre, prevailing in the compounds accio, excio, etc. (cf. Prisc. pp. 865, 905, and 908 P.), are also found: pres. cio, Mart. 4, 90, 4: cit, Verg. Cul. 201; Col. 6, 5, 1 Schneid.: cimus, Lucr. 1, 213; 5, 211: ciunt, Lact. Ep. 4 dub.: ciant, App. Flor. 2, n. 17, p. 358; Mart. Cap. 1, § 91: ciuntur, id. de Mundo, 22, p. 67), v. a. kindr. with κίω, to go; and by the addition of the causative signif. like κινέω, causative from κίω; v. 1. ci.. Lit., t
cieo.short: cĭĕo, cīvi, cĭtum, 2 (from the primitive form cĭo, cīre, prevailing in the compounds accio, excio, etc.

cignus.full: cignus, i, m., a measure, = 8 scrupuli, Plin. Val. 2, 30 and 31.
cignus.short: cignus, i, m., a measure, = 8 scrupuli, Plin.

cilibantum.full: cilibantum, i, n., a round cupboard, Varr. L. L. 5, § 121 Müll.; cf. cilliba.
cilibantum.short: cilibantum, i, n., a round cupboard, Varr.

cilicia.full: Cĭlĭcĭa, ae, f., = Κιλικία, a province in the southern part of Asia Minor, between Pamphylia and Syria, now Ejalet Itschil, Mel. 1, 2, 6; 1, 11, 2; 1, 13, 1 sq.; 2, 7, 5; Plin. 5, 27, 22, § 91; Plaut. Mil. 1, 1, 42; Cic. Imp. Pomp. 22, 64; id. Fam. 15, 1, 2 sq. al.— Hence, Cĭlix, ĭcis (abl. Cilici, Lucr. 2, 416 Lachm.; Verg. Cul. 399 al.; v. infra), adj., = Κίλιξ, Cilician: Cilici croco (of special excellence), Lucr. 2, 416; Verg. Cul. 399 Sillig; cf. Stat. S. 2, 1, 160; 3, 3, 34: Taurus, Ov. M.
cilicia.short: Cĭlĭcĭa, ae, f., = Κιλικία, a province in the southern part of Asia Minor, between Pamphylia and Syria, now Ejalet Itschil, Mel.

ciliciarius.full: cĭlĭcĭārĭus, ii, m. cilicium; v. Cilicia, II. B. β, a maker of hair coverings, Inscr. Orell. 4162.

cilicinus.full: cĭlĭcīnus, a, um, adj. id., made of hair-cloth: tentoria, Sol. 33: tunica, Hier. Vit. Hil. fin.: saga, Vulg. Exod. 26, 7.

ciliciolum.full: cĭlĭcĭŏlum, i, n. dim. cilicium, a small garment or coverlet of goats' hair, Hier. Ep. 71, 7; 108, 15.

cilicium.full: Cĭlĭcĭum, Cĭlĭcĭus, and Cĭlissa, v. Cilicia.

cilio.full: cīlĭo, ōnis, m. (a vulgar collat. form of caelum), a chisel, graver, Isid. Orig. 20, 4, 7.

cilium.full: cĭlĭum, ii, n. kindr. with Gr. κυλίς, κύλα. An eyelid, Paul. ex Fest. p. 43, 3 Müll.; Plin. 11, 39, 93, § 227; App. M. 10, p. 247, 10; Lact. Opif. Dei, 10 init.— Transf., the lower eyelid (opp. supercilium): extremum ambitum genae superioris, Plin. 11, 37, 57, § 157.

cilix.full: Cĭlix, ĭcis, v. Cilicia, II. A.

cilla.full: Cilla, ae, f., = Κίλλα, a town in Troas, distinguished for the worship of Apollo, Plin. 5, 30, 32, § 122; Sen. Troad. 227; acc. Cillan. Ov. M. 13, 174 (cf. Hom. Il. 1, 38).
cilla.short: Cilla, ae, f., = Κίλλα, a town in Troas, distinguished for the worship of Apollo, Plin.

cilliba.full: cillĭba, ae, f., = κιλλίβας, a round dining-table, Varr. L. L. 5, § 118 Müll.; Paul. ex Fest. p. 43, 9 ib.
cilliba.short: cillĭba, ae, f., = κιλλίβας, a round dining-table, Varr.

cillo1.full: cillo, ĕre, to move, put in motion (only in mal. part.), Serv. ad Verg. G. 2, 389; Isid. Orig. 20, 14, 11.
cillo1.short: cillo, ĕre, to move, put in motion (only in mal.

cillo2.full: cillo, ōnis, m. 1. cillo, = cinaedus, Pseudo ic. in Sall. 6, 18.

cilnius.full: Cilnĭus, a, um, adj. pure Etrusc. Cfelne or Cfenle, a designation of a very distinguished Etruscan gens, from which Mœcenas originated; Cilnian, Liv. 10, 3, 2; 10, 5, 13; Sil. 7, 29; Tac. A. 6, 11; Macr. S. 2, 4, 12.

cilo1.full: cilo, ōnis, m., having a prominent forehead pressed in upon the sides, Fest. p. 43, 10; cf. Charis. 1, p. 78 P.; a dim. of it, cilunculus, Arn. 3, 14.
cilo1.short: cilo, ōnis, m., having a prominent forehead pressed in upon the sides, Fest.

cilo2.full: Cīlo, ōnis, m., a Roman cognomen, Cic. Fam. 4, 12, 2.
cilo2.short: Cīlo, ōnis, m., a Roman cognomen, Cic.

cim.full: Cim, indecl. n.: nomen vici, Cels. ap. Prisc. pp. 644 and 688 P.

cimbri.full: Cimbri, ōrum, m., = Κίμβροι [Cimbri linguā Gallicā latrones dicuntur, Fest. p. 43, 7], a people of Northern Germany (in Holstein, Silesia, and Jutland); on their irruption into Italy conquered by Marius, Mel. 3, 3 fin.; Plin. 2, 67, 67, § 167; 4, 13, 27, § 94 sq.; Tac. G. 37; Caes. B. G. 1, 33; 1, 40; 2, 4; Liv. Epit. lib. 63-68; Prop. 2, 1, 24; Flor. 3, 31 sq.; Cic. Imp. Pomp. 20, 60; id. Tusc. 2, 27, 65; id. Off. 1, 12, 38.—In sing.: Cimber, bri, m., a Cimbrian, Val. Max. 2, 10, 6; cf. Quint.
cimbri.short: Cimbri, ōrum, m., = Κίμβροι [Cimbri linguā Gallicā latrones dicuntur, Fest.

cimeliarcha.full: cīmēlĭarcha, ae, m., = κειμηλιάρχης, a treasurer, keeper of treasure, Cod. Just. 7, 72, 10.
cimeliarcha.short: cīmēlĭarcha, ae, m., = κειμηλιάρχης, a treasurer, keeper of treasure, Cod.

cimeliarchium.full: cīmēlĭarchĭum, ii, n., = κειμηλιάρχιον, a place where jewels are deposited, a treasury, Cod. Just. 7, 72, 10, § 2; 11, 47, 19.
cimeliarchium.short: cīmēlĭarchĭum, ii, n., = κειμηλιάρχιον, a place where jewels are deposited, a treasury, Cod.

cimetra.full: Cimē^tra, ae, f., a town of Samnium, Liv. 10, 15, 6.
cimetra.short: Cimē^tra, ae, f., a town of Samnium, Liv.

cimex.full: cīmex, ĭcis, m. (so always acc. to Neue, Formenl. 1, p. 619 sq.; but fem., Plin. 32, 10, 47 § 136 Sillig and Jan.), a bug, Liv. Andron. ap. Fest. p. 210, 17; Varr. R. R. 1, 2 fin.; Col. 6, 18, 2; Plin. 30, 14, 45, § 131; 29, 4, 17, § 61; Veg. 2, 33, 2; 5, 14, 21; Cat. 23, 2; Petr. 98, 1; Mart. 11, 32 al.—As a term of reproach, * Hor. S. 1, 10, 78.

cimico.full: cīmĭco, āre, = κορίζω, to purify from bugs, Gloss. Gr. Lat.
cimico.short: cīmĭco, āre, = κορίζω, to purify from bugs, Gloss.

ciminus.full: Cĭmĭnus, i, m., a lake in Etruria, near Sutrium, now Lago di Vico, or di Ronciglione, with a mountain forest lying near it, Verg. A. 7, 697.—Hence, Cĭmĭnĭus, a, um, adj., Ciminian: lacus, i.e. Ciminus, Col. 8, 16, 2: silva, Liv. 9, 36, 1 sq.; 10, 24, 5; Plin. 2, 96, 98, § 211: saltus, Liv. 9, 36, 6; cf. Flor. 1, 17, 2: mons, Liv. 9, 36, 11.—As subst.: Cĭ-mĭnĭa, ae, f., the region about Lake Ciminus, Amm. 17, 7, 13.
ciminus.short: Cĭmĭnus, i, m., a lake in Etruria, near Sutrium, now Lago di Vico, or di Ronciglione, with a mountain forest lying near it, Verg.

cimmerii.full: Cimmĕrii, ōrum (gen. Cimmeriūm, Val. Fl. 3, 399; Cimmeriōn, Tib. 4, 1, 64), m., = Κιμμέριοι. A Thracian people in the present Crimea, on both sides of the Dnieper, whose chief town was Cimmerium, Mel. 1, 19, 15; Plin. 6, 6, 5, § 17; 6, 13, 14, § 35.— Hence, Adj. Cimmĕrĭus, a, um, Cimmerian: Bosporus, Plin. 4, 12, 24, § 77: litus, Ov. P. 4, 10, 1.— Cimmĕrĭcus, a, um, Cimmerian: oppida, Mel. 2, 1, 3.— A fabulous people supposed to have dwelt in caves, between Baiœ and Cumœ, Fest. p. 43, 4 sq.; cf.

cimolus.full: Cĭmōlus, i, f., = Κίμωλος, an island of the Cyclades, distinguished for its chalky soil, now Kimolo or Argentiera, Plin. 4, 12, 23, § 70; Ov. M. 7, 463.—Hence, Cĭmō-lĭus, a, um, adj., of or from Cimolus: creta (freq. used in medicine), Cels. 2, 33; Col. 6, 17, 4; Scrib. Comp. 245; Veg. 2, 29; 3, 4; cf. Plin. 35, 17, 57, § 195 sq.
cimolus.short: Cĭmōlus, i, f., = Κίμωλος, an island of the Cyclades, distinguished for its chalky soil, now Kimolo or Argentiera, Plin.

cimon.full: Cīmon (Cīmo, Val. Max. 5, 4, ext. 2), ōnis, m., = Κίμων. Father of Miltiades, Nep. Milt. 1.— A son of Miltiades, a distinguished general of the Athenians, whose life is written by Nepos, Nep. Cim. 1 sqq.; cf. also Cic. Off. 2, 18, 64; Sen. Contr. 4, 24, p. 275 sqq. Bip.; Val. Max. 5, 3, ext. 3; Just. 2, 15, 18.

cinaedias.full: cĭnaedĭas, ae, m., = κιναιδίας, a precious stone, unknown to us, said to be found in the brain of the fish cinaedus, Plin. 37, 10, 56, § 153.
cinaedias.short: cĭnaedĭas, ae, m., = κιναιδίας, a precious stone, unknown to us, said to be found in the brain of the fish cinaedus, Plin.

cinaedicus.full: cĭnaedĭcus, a, um, adj. cinaedus, 1., pertaining to one who is unchaste; immodest, lewd (ante-class.): cantio, Plaut. Stich. 5, 5, 19.—Subst. = cinaedus, Plaut. Stich. 5, 7, 1 (769); Varr. ap. Non. p. 176, 19.

cinaedulus.full: cĭnaedŭlus, i, m. dim. id., a male wanton, Scip. Afric. ap. Macr. S. 2, 10.

cinaedus1.full: cĭnaedus, i, m., = κίναιδος. He who practises unnatural lust, a sodomite, catamite, Plaut. As. 3, 3, 37; id. Aul. 3, 2, 8; id. Poen. 5, 5, 40; Scip. Afric. ap. Gell. 7, 12, 5; Cat. 16, 2; 25, 1; Petr. 21, 2; Juv. 2, 10; 14, 30 al.— Adj.: cĭnaedus, a, um, wanton, unchaste: ut decuit cinaediorem, Cat. 10, 24.—Trop., impudent, shameless: homo cinaedā fronte, Mart. 6, 39, 12.— Hence, He who performs a wanton dance, Plaut. Mil. 3, 1, 73; Lucil. ap. Non. p. 5, 31.— The name of a sea-fish, Plin. 33, 11

cinaedus2.full: cĭnaedus, a, um, v. 1. cinaedus, I. B.

cinara1.full: cĭnăra, ae, f., = κινάρα, a kind of artichoke (Cinara scolymus, Linn.), a native of the island of Cinara, Col. 10, 235; 11, 3, 14 and 28; Sen. Herc. Fur. 206.
cinara1.short: cĭnăra, ae, f., = κινάρα, a kind of artichoke (Cinara scolymus, Linn.), a native of the island of Cinara, Col.

cinara2.full: Cĭnăra, ae, f., = Κινάρα. A Greek proper name, Hor. C. 4, 1, 4 al.— An island in the Ægean Sea, now Zinara, Mel. 2, 7, 11; Plin. 4, 12, 23, § 69.

cinaris.full: cĭnăris, is, f., an unknown plant, Plin. 8, 27, 41, § 101; Sol. 19, 16.
cinaris.short: cĭnăris, is, f., an unknown plant, Plin.

cincinnalis.full: cincinnālis, e, adj. cincinnus, curled: herba, a plant, also called polytrichon, App. Herb. 51.

cincinnatulus.full: cincinnātŭlus, a, um, adj. dim. [cincinnatus], with curled hair: pueri, Hier. Ep. 130, n. 19.

cincinnatus1.full: cincinnātus, adj. cincinnus, with curled hair, having locks or ringlets of hair (as an indication of luxurious effeminacy), Plaut. Capt. 3, 4, 115: moechus, id. Mil. 3, 3, 49; id. Truc. 2, 7, 48: consul, Cic. Sest. 11, 26: ganeo, id. Red. in Sen. 5, 13; Cael. ap. Quint. 1, 5, 61.— Transf., of comets: stellae, Schol. Juv 6, 207 (in Cic. N. D. 2, 5, 14, better crinitas).

cincinnatus2.full: Cincinnātus, i, m., a cognomen of the renowned L. Qumctius, taken from the plough to the dictatorship, Liv. 3, 26, 6; 4, 13, 14 sq.; Cic. Fin. 2, 4, 12; id. Sen. 16, 56; Col. 1, praef. § 13; Plin. 18, 3, 4, § 20; Val. Max. 4, 4 al.
cincinnatus2.short: Cincinnātus, i, m., a cognomen of the renowned L.

cincinnus.full: cincinnus, i. m. kindr. with Gr. κίκιννος and Lat. cirrus; Sanscr. cicura, crinis, Bopp, Gloss. 124 a, curled hair, a lock or curl of hair, Plaut. Truc. 2, 2, 32; Varr. R. R. 1, 31, 4; Cic. Pis. 11, 25.— Trop., too artificial or elaborate oratorical ornament (cf. calamister, II.): in oratoris aut in poëtae cincinnis ac fuco offenditur, quod, etc., Cic. de Or. 2, 25, 100; Aug. ap. Suet. Aug. 86.

cinciolus.full: Cincĭŏlus, i, m. dim. Cincius, a pet name for Cincius, Cic. de Or. 2, 71, 286.

cincius.full: Cincĭus, a, um, the name of a Roman gens; hence, M. Cincius Alimentus, a tribune of the people, A.U.C. 549, whose legal enactment was called Lex Cincia De donis et muneribus (quā cavetur antiquitus, ne quis ob causam orandam pecuniam donumve accipiat, Tac. A. 11, 5); cf. Cic. Sen. 4, 10; id. de Or. 2, 71, 286; id. Att. 1, 20, 7; also: Lex muneralis, Plaut. ap. Paul. ex Fest. s. v. muneralis, p. 143 Müll.; cf. Savigny upon the Lex Cincia, etc., in his Zeitschr. für Gesch. Rechtswissenschaft IV.,
cincius.short: Cincĭus, a, um, the name of a Roman gens;

cincticulus.full: cinctĭcŭlus, i, m. dim. 2. cinctus, a little girdle, Plaut. Bacch. 3, 3, 28.

cinctor.full: cinctor, ŏris, m., = ζώστης, Gloss. Gr. Lat.

cinctorium.full: cinctōrĭum, ii, n. 2. cinctus, a swordbelt, = balteus, Mel. 2, 1, 13.— In gen., a girdle (late Lat.); trop.: et erit... fides cinctorium renum ejus, Vulg. Isa. 11, 5.

cinctura.full: cinctūra, ae, f. 2. cinctus, cingo, a nncture, a girdle (very rare), * Suet. Caes. 45; * Quint 11, 3, 139.

cinctus1.full: cinctus, a, um, Part., from cingo.
cinctus1.short: cinctus, a, um, Part., from cingo.

cinctus2.full: cinctus, ūs, m. (post-class. access. form cinctum, i, n., Scrib. Comp. 163, Isid. Orig. 19, 33, Pophyr. ad Hor. A. P. 50) [cingo]. Abstr., a girding (rare): cottidiani cinctus, Plin. 28, 6, 17, § 64; cinctus Gabinus, a manner of girding, in which the toga was tucked up, its corner being thrown over the left shoulder, was brought under the right arm round to the breast (this manner was customarily employed in religious festivals), Liv 5, 46, 2; incinctus cinctu Gabino, id. 8, 9, 9 (for which, id.

cinctutus.full: cinctūtus, a, um, adj. a lengthened form from cinctus, like astutus, actutum, versutus, etc., from astus, actus, versus, etc., girded, girt (rare; perh. only in the foll. exs.): Luperci, * Ov F 5, 101 Cethegi, i. e. the ancients (who did not, like the more effeminate men of a later time, wear the tunic ungirded), * Hor. A. P 50.

cineas.full: Cīnĕas, ae, m., = Κινέας, the friend of king Pyrrhus of Epirus, who counselled him to make peace with the Romans, he is said to have had a remarkably retentive memory, Cic. Tusc. 1, 24, 59; id. Sen. 13, 43; id. Fam 9, 25, 1; Plin. 7, 24, 24, § 88; 14, 1, 3, § 12; Sen. Contr 1, prooem. p. 65 Bip.
cineas.short: Cīnĕas, ae, m., = Κινέας, the friend of king Pyrrhus of Epirus, who counselled him to make peace with the Romans, he is said to have had a remarkably retentive memory, Cic.

cinefactus.full: cĭnĕfactus, a, um, adj. cinis-facio: at nos horrifico cinefactum te prope busto ... deflevimus, i. e. turned to ashes, Lucr. 3, 906, cf. Non. p. 93, 33 (Lachm. ad loc. makes the word = qui jam prope cineris colorem et adspectum nanctus est, but cf. Munro ad loc.).

cineraceus.full: cĭnĕrācĕus, a, um, adj. cinis, similar to ashes, ashy terra, Plin. 17, 5, 4, § 33: color, ash-colored, id. 27, 7, 27, § 44.

cinerarium.full: cĭnĕrārĭum, ii, v. cinerarius, II. B.

cinerarius.full: cĭnĕrārĭus, a, um, adj. cinis, pertaining to ashes. As adj. very rare: fines, boundaries of land bordering upon graves, Auct. Limit. p 296 Goes.— More freq. subst. cĭnĕrārĭus, ii, m., a servant who heated in glowing ashes the iron used in curling hair, a hair-curler, Varr. L. L, 5, § 129 Müll., Cat. 61, 138; Sen. Const. 14, 1; Acro ad Hor S. 1, 2, 98; Tert. ad Uxor. 2, 8.— CINERARIVM, ii, n., in tombs, the receptacle for the ashes of the dead, Inscr. Orell. 4358; 4513 al.

cineresco.full: cĭnĕresco, ĕre, v. inch. n. [id.], to turn to ashes (late Lat.), Tert. Apol. 40, Fulg. Myth. 2, 18; Cael. Aur. Tard. 5, 1, 20.

cinereus.full: cĭnĕrĕus, a, um, adj. cinis, similar to ashes, ash-colored: color, Col. 2, 2, 16; Scrib. 23; Plin. 37, 10, 68, § 183 sq.: terra, id. 35, 16, 54, § 192 uva, id. 14, 3, 4, § 42.—Hence, subst.: cĭnĕrĕum, ĕi, n., a kind of salve, Scrib. Comp. 37; cf.: collyrium spodiacum a quibusdam cinereum dicitur, id. ib. 24 init.

cinericius.full: cinĕrĭcĭus (-tĭus), a, um, adj. id., similar to ashes, like ashes: terra, Varr. R. R. 1, 9, 7.

cinerosus.full: cĭnĕrōsus, a, um, adj. id., full of ashes: mortui, App. M. 4, p. 150, 27: canities, id. ib. 7, p. 299, 41.

cinga.full: Cinga, ae, f., a small river in Hispania Tarraconensis, in the territory of the Ilergetes, now Cinca, Caes B C. 1, 48; Luc. 4, 21
cinga.short: Cinga, ae, f., a small river in Hispania Tarraconensis, in the territory of the Ilergetes, now Cinca, Caes B C.

cingetorix.full: Cingetŏrix, igis, m. A Gaul, rival of his father-in-law Indutiomarus, in respect to dominion over the Treviri, Caes B. G. 5, 3; 5, 56 al— A king of the region about Cantium, in Britain, Caes. B. G. 5, 22.

cingilia.full: Cingilia, ae, f., a town of the Vestini on the Adriatic Sea, Liv 8, 29, 13.
cingilia.short: Cingilia, ae, f., a town of the Vestini on the Adriatic Sea, Liv 8, 29, 13.

cingillum.full: cingillum, i, n. dim. cingulum, a small girdle, Petr 67, 4; Not. Tir. p 158 Grut.; cf.: cingillus, στρόφιον, ζώνιον, Gloss.

cingo.full: cingo, xi, nctum, 3, v. a. cf. Gr κυλλός, κυρτός; Lat. curvus, and clingo, Georg Curtius Griech. Etym. p. 545 sq., to go round in a circle, to surround, encompass, environ, gird, wreathe, crown, etc. (class. in prose and poetry). Prop In gen.: quid autem interius mente? Cingatur igitur corpore externo, i. e. it must be enclosed in a body, Cic. N. D 1, 11, 27: non enim coronà consessus vester cinctus est, ut solebat, id. Mil. 1, 1; cf.: judicium insolitā trepidum cinxere coronă, Luc. 1, 321; tris

cingulum1.full: cingŭlum, i, n. (access. form cin-gulus, i, m, and cingŭla, ae, f.; v. infra, cf cingulum hominum generis neutri est, nam animailum feminino genere dicimus has cingulas, Isid. Orig 20, 16, 4; Serv. ad Verg A. 9, 360) [cingo, cf. Varr. L. L. 5, § 114 Müll.]. The girdle encircling the hips, a zone, belt (mostly poet.). For persons; mostly for women. Cingulum, Varr L. L. 5, § 114 Müll.; id. ap. Non. p 47, 27; Claud. Fesc. 11, 37: cingulo, Petr. 21, 2.—More freq. in plur., cingula, Verg. A. 1, 492;

cingulum2.full: Cingŭlum, i, n., a small town in Picenum, now Cingulo, Caes. B. C. 1, 15; Cic. Att. 7, 11, 1; also Cingŭla saxa, Sil. 10, 34, its inhabitants were called Cin-gŭlāni, Plin. 3, 13, 18, § 111.—Also adj.: Cingūlānus ager, Front. Colon. p. 121 Goes.
cingulum2.short: Cingŭlum, i, n., a small town in Picenum, now Cingulo, Caes.

cinifes.full: cinifes or cĭnĭphes (cўn-), um, f., = σκνιπες or κνίπες, a kind of stinging insect (eccl. Lat.), Aug Trin. 3, 7; Hier. in Joel, 2, 25; cf. Isid. Orig. 12, 8, 14.
cinifes.short: cinifes or cĭnĭphes (cўn-), um, f., = σκνιπες or κνίπες, a kind of stinging insect (eccl.

ciniflo.full: cĭnīflo, ōnis, m. cinis-flo, or instead of cinilio, = cinerarius, a hair-curler, Hor S. 1, 2, 98; Tert. Uxor 2, 8; cf. Becker, Gallus, 2, p. 115 alt.

cinis.full: cĭnis, ĕris, m. (in sing. fem., Lucr. 4, 926; Cat. 68, 90; 101, 4; Caesar, acc. to Non. p. 198, 11; Calvus ap. Non. l. l. and ap. Charis; p. 78 p; App. M. 9, 12, p. 222; Scrib. c. 226; 230; 232; 245, Ser. c. 44; Aus. Parent 27, 3; Inscr. Orell 4479; cf. Neue, Formenl. 1, p. 657; access. form: hoc cĭnus, Gloss. Labb.; Sicul. Flacc. p. 140, 17, Agrim. p. 308, 3; p. 308, 5; cf. Lachm. ad Lucr 2, p. 190, and a nom. cĭ-ner is mentioned by Prisc. 5, p. 688: 6, p. 707) [kindr with κόνις; cf. also naucu

cinisculus.full: cĭniscŭlus, i, m. dim. cinis, a little ashes: arens, Prud. Cath. 10, 149.

cinithii.full: Cinithii, ōrum, m., a people of Africa, Tac. A. 2, 52.
cinithii.short: Cinithii, ōrum, m., a people of Africa, Tac.

cinium.full: Cinium (Civium), ii, n., a town of the island of Majorca, now Sinau, Plin. 3, 5, 11, § 77.
cinium.short: Cinium (Civium), ii, n., a town of the island of Majorca, now Sinau, Plin.

cinna.full: Cinna, ae, m., a family name of the gentes Cornelia and Helvia. L. Cornelius Cinna, consul A.U.C. 667-670; a confederate of C. Marius in the Roman civil war with Sylla, Vell. 2, 20 sq.; Flor. 3, 21; Cic. Tusc. 5, 19, 54 and 55.—Hence, appel., a Cinna, a cruel warrior: tyrannum et Cinnam appellans, Sall. H. 1, 42 Dietsch.— Hence, Cinnānus, a, um, adj., of Cinna: partes, his party, adherents, Vell. 2, 24; Nep. Att. 2, 2: rabies, Flor. 4, 2, 2: tumultus, Nep. Att. 2, 2.— Son of the preceding of the
cinna.short: Cinna, ae, m., a family name of the gentes Cornelia and Helvia.

cinnabaris.full: cinnăbăris, is, f. (cinnăbări, is, n., Sol. 25, 14 dub., and in some MSS. and edd. Plin. 33, 7, 38, § 115; cf. Neue, Formenl. 1, p. 555), = κιννάβαρι. A pigment obtained from the gum of the dragon's-blood tree, dragon's-blood, Plin. 33, 7, 39, § 117; 13, 1, 2, § 7.—Abl. cinnabari, Plin. 29, 1, 8, § 25; 29, 4, 19, § 66.— Some erroneously give this name to cinnabar, vermilion (minium), Plin. 33, 7, 38, § 115 sqq.

cinnameus.full: cĭnnămĕus, a, um, adj. cinnamum, of or from cinnamon, smelling of cinnamon: nidus, Aus. Idyll. 11, 17: odor, App. M. 8, p. 205: crines, smelling of cinnamon, id. ib. 5, p. 164.

cinnamolgos.full: cinnămolgos, i, m., a bird in Arabia (prob. = κινναμολόγος), Plin. 10, 33, 50, § 97; Sol. 33, 15.
cinnamolgos.short: cinnămolgos, i, m., a bird in Arabia (prob.

cinnamominus.full: cinnămōmĭnus, a, um, adj., = κινναμώμινος, of or from cinnamon: unguentum, Plin. 13, 1, 2, § 15.
cinnamominus.short: cinnămōmĭnus, a, um, adj., = κινναμώμινος, of or from cinnamon: unguentum, Plin.

cinnamomum.full: cinnămōmum, cinnămum, or cinnămon, i, n. (post-class. access. form cinnămus, i, m., Sol. 33, in the signif. of ll.), = κινναμωμον or κίνναμον [], cinnamon: Laurus cinnamomum, Linn. Cinnamomum, Plin. 12, 19, 42, §§ 85 and 86. —As a term of endearment: tu mihi stacte, tu cinnamomum, tu rosa, etc., Plaut. Curc. 1, 2, 8.— Cinnamum, Plin. 12, 19, 42, § 86 sq.; Ov. M. 10, 308; Mart. 4, 13, 3; Stat. S. 4, 5, 32.— Cinnamon, Prop. 3 (4), 13, 8; Luc. 10, 166.— Meton. for twigs of cinnamon; plur.: cinnama,
cinnamomum.short: cinnămōmum, cinnămum, or cinnămon, i, n.

cinnanus.full: Cinnānus, a, um, v. Cinna, I. fin.

cinnus.full: cinnus, i, m. kindr. with κυκεών, κόγχος, a mixed drink of spelt-grain and wine, Arn. 5, 174; cf. Non. p. 59, 30.

cinxia.full: Cinxia, ae. f. cingo, an appellation of Juno, as tutelary goddess of marriage, because, acc. to Paul. ex Fest., initio conjugii solutio erat cinguli, quo nova nupta erat cincta, Fest. p. 63, 9; and Arn. 3, p. 115. —Access. form cinctia, acc. to Mart. Cap. 2, § 149.

cinyphes.full: cĭnўphes, um, f. corrupted from κνῖπες, σκνῖπες, very small flies, gnats, Isid. Orig. 12, 8, 14.

cinyps.full: Cīnyps, nўpis, m., = Κίνυψ or Κίνυφος, a river flowing through a very fruitful region in Libya, between the two Syrtes, now Cinifo or Wady Khahan, Mel. 1, 7, 5; Plin. 5, 4, 4, § 27; Claud. Laud. Stil. 1, 251.— Hence, Cīnўphĭus, a, um, adj., pertaining to the Cinyps, found about the Cinyps: chelydri, Ov. M. 7, 272: hirci, Verg. G. 3, 312: tonsor, Mart. 8, 51: aristae, Claud. Eutr. 1, 405; cf. Ov P. 2, 7, 25: Macae, living near the Cinyps, Sil. 3, 275: Pelates, Ov. M. 5, 124.— In gen., Libyan, Afr
cinyps.short: Cīnyps, nўpis, m., = Κίνυψ or Κίνυφος, a river flowing through a very fruitful region in Libya, between the two Syrtes, now Cinifo or Wady Khahan, Mel.

cinyra.full: cĭnўra, ae, f., = ; Gr. κινύρα, the lyre, an instrument of ten strings, Vulg. 1 Macc. 4, 54; 13, 51.

cinyras.full: Cĭnўras (Cĭnўra, Plin. 7, 56, 57, § 195), ae, m., = Κινύρας. A king in Assyria, afterwards in Cyprus; father of Myrrha, and, by her, of Adonis, Ov. M. 10, 299 sq.; cf. Hyg. Fab. 58; 242; 270; acc. Gr. Cinyran, Ov. M. 6, 98; voc. Cinyrā, id. ib. 10, 380.—Hence, Cĭnўrēĭus, a, um, adj., Cinyrean: virgo, i. e. Myrrha, Ov. M. 10, 369; Col. 10, 172: juvenis, i. e. Adonis, Ov. M. 10, 712; so also heros, id. ib. 10, 730. — Cĭnўraeus, a, um, adj., of Cinyras: litora Cypri, Luc. 8, 716.— Cĭnў-rēus, a, um,

cios.full: Cĭŏs, i, m. A river in Bithynia, Plin. 5, 32, 40, § 144.— A town at the mouth of the river Cios, now Ghio or Ghemlio, Liv. 32, 34, 4; Mel. 1, 19, 4; Plin. l. c. v. Ciani.

cippus.full: cippus (cīpus), i, m. kindr. with scipio; cf. σκήπτω, a pale, stake, post, pillar, Lucil. ap. Fest. p. 258; and specif., A gravestone, tombstone, * Hor. S. 1, 8, 12; Pers. 1, 37; Prud. Apoth. 361; Inscr. Orell. 4524 al.— In the Agrimensores, a landmark, boundary-stone or post, Simplic. ap. Goes. p. 88.—* In milit. lang., cippi, ōrum, m., a bulwark formed of sharpened stakes, Caes. B. G. 7, 73.

cipus.full: Cīpus (Cippus), i, m., a fabled Roman prœtor, upon whose head horns grew suddenly, Ov. M. 15, 565; Plin. 11, 37, 45, § 123; Val. Max. 5, 6, 3.
cipus.short: Cīpus (Cippus), i, m., a fabled Roman prœtor, upon whose head horns grew suddenly, Ov.

circa1.full: circā, a later access. form for circum; not freq. before the Aug. per., esp. in Livy and Quintilian [acc. to Klotz, circa = circum ea; cf: antea, interea, postea, praeterea, etc.]. Adv. ( = circum, I. B.) Around, round about, all around, in the environs or neighborhood: gramen erat circa, Ov. M. 3, 411: ripaeque lacusque Responsant circa, Verg. A. 12, 757: at circa gravibus pensis affixa puella... remittat opus, Tib. 1, 3, 87: circaque quā tumor est, Cels. 5, 28, 3; 5, 28, 4: fluvius ab tergo; a

circaea.full: circaea, ae, f., = κιρκαία, a plant used as a charm, Plin. 27, 8, 38, § 60.
circaea.short: circaea, ae, f., = κιρκαία, a plant used as a charm, Plin.

circaeum.full: circaeum (-on), i, n., = κιρκαῖον, the plant also called mandragoras, Plin. 25, 13, 94, § 147.
circaeum.short: circaeum (-on), i, n., = κιρκαῖον, the plant also called mandragoras, Plin.

circaeus.full: Circaeus, a, um, pertaining to Circe; v. Circe, II.
circaeus.short: Circaeus, a, um, pertaining to Circe;

circamoerium.full: circāmoerĭum, ii, n. circa-moerus, for murus; cf. pomerium, the space about a wall, on both sides of a wall: pomerium, verbi vim solam intuentes, postmoerium interpretantur esse; est autem magis circamoerium, Liv. 1, 44, 4.

circanea.full: circānĕa, ae, f. circa, a bird so named from its circular flight, Paul. ex Fest. p. 43, 1 Müll.

circe.full: Circē, ēs (gen. Circae, Liv. And. ap. Fest. s. v. topper, p. 270; Verg. A. 3, 386: Circes, Prop. 3 (4), 12, 27. acc Circam, Plaut. Ep. 4, 2, 34 Ritschl; Cic. N D. 3, 21, 54; together with Circen, id. ib. 3, 19, 48; v. Inscr. Orell. N. cr.; abl. Circā, Hor. Epod. 17, 17; Tert. Spect. 8; cf. Charis. 1, 15, p. 46), f., = Κίρκη, the daughter of the Sun and of Perse or Perseis, sister of Æetes, a sea-nymph, distinguished for her magic arts, whose abode, after her flight from Colchis, was said to be i

circeii.full: Circēii, ōrum (abl. Circēis, Hor. S. 2, 4, 33 K. and H.), m., = Κιρκαῖον, the town of Circeii, near the promontory of the same name, in Latium; acc to the fable, named after Circe, who fled hither from Colchis (cf. the preced. art.), now Circello, Mel. 2, 4, 9; Plin. 3, 5, 9, § 56 sq.; Cic. Att. 15, 10 fin.; Liv. 1, 56, 3; distinguished for its excellent oysters, Hor S. 2, 4, 33 Heind.— Hence, Circēiensis, e, adj., of Circeii: ostreae, Plin. 32, 6, 21, § 62.—In plur.: Circēienses, lum, m., the i

circellus.full: circellus, i, m. dim. circulus, a small ring, Apic. 2, 5, Schol Juv. 6, 379.

circen.full: circen, ĭnis, n. circinus, a circle, a circular course: solis, a year, Poët. in Anth. Lat. 4, 274 (Meyer, n. 1373).

circensis.full: Circensis, e, v. Circus, II. b.

circes.full: circĕs, itis, m. circum-ire, a circle (ante- and post-class.): ut parvi circuli Anuli, sic magni dicebantur circites Ani, Varr L. L. 6, § 8 Müll.; Sid. Carm. 22, 222. —So of the circumference of the circus, Sid. Carm. 23, 381.

circinatio.full: circĭnātĭo, ōnis, f. circino (lit. the describing of a circle; hence, concrete), the circumference of a circle, a circle (a word of Vitr.): linea circinationis, Vitr. 1, 6, 6: circuli, id. 9, 7, 2; 3, 3; 10, 10 al.—Of the circular path of the planets, Vitr. 9, 4, pp. 264, 266 Bip.

circino.full: circĭno, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. circinus, to make round, to round (perh. not anteAug.): arbores, quae in orbem ramos circinant, Plin. 17, 12, 17, § 88; 16, 38, 73, § 185: circinatum tympanum, id. 18, 34, 77, § 332: folia circinatae rotunditatis, id. 16, 23, 35, § 86—Poet.: (Cyllenius) inclinat cursus, et easdem circinat auras, flies through in a circular course, * Ov. M. 2, 721: utque suos arcus per nubila circinat Iris, vaults, arches, Manil. 1, 710.

circinus.full: circĭnus, i, m.. = κίρκινος, a pair of compasses' flumen Dubis. ut circino circumductum, paene totum oppidum cingit, Caes. B. G. 1, 38: diducere, Vitr. 9, 7, 2: circino spatia dimetiri, id ib.; id. 10, 4, 1: ratio circini, Plin. 2, 15, 13, § 63.

circiter.full: circĭter, adv. and prep. circus. Adv. Of place, round about, on every side: lapidem fuisse quadratum circiter (i. e. cubical) in mediā arcā vinctum candelis quaquaversum, Cass. Hem. ap. Plin. 13, 13, 27, § 85 (cf. the passage cited under circum, I. A. 1., from Varr. R. R. 3, 10, 3).— Of time, designating nearness to a fixed point, about, near (cf. ante, post): illic noster est fortasse circiter triennium, Plaut. Mil. 2, 3, 79: circiter duobus mensibus, Varr. R. R. 3, 10, 6: diebus circiter quind

circito.full: circĭto, āre, 1, v freq. a. [for circuito, from circueo for circumeo], to frequent, make busy: omnes istae artes, quibus aut circitatur civitas aut strepit. Sen. Ep. 90, 19; cf.: circito, περινοστῶ: circitat et circat, κυκλεύει, Gloss. Labb.

circitor.full: circĭtor (or circuĭtor, Petr. 53, 10), ōris, m. for circumitor, from circumeo, lit. one who goes around, hence, A watchman (of gardens. buildings, etc.; postclass.), Auct. Priap. 16, 1, Front. Aquaed. 117; Petr. 1 1.— In milit. lang., plur., those who go the rounds and visit the posts of sentinels, patrols, Veg. Mil. 3, 8; Hier. Ep. 61, n. 7.—Sing.' CIRCITOR, Inscr. Murat. 540, 2.— A pedler, Dig. 14, 3, 5, § 4.

circitorius.full: circĭtōrĭus, a, um circitor, II., pertaining to patrols: dignitas, Cod. Th. 7, 22, 2, § 2.
circitorius.short: circĭtōrĭus, a, um circitor, II., pertaining to patrols: dignitas, Cod.

circius.full: circĭus (cercĭus, Cato ap. Gell. 2, 22, 28 sq.), ii, m. perh. from circus, on account of its circular motion, but said to be a Gallic word, a violent wind blowing in Gallia Narbonensis; to the Romans, a west-northwest wind, Plin. 2, 47, 46, § 121; Sen. Q. N. 5, 17, 5, Vitr. 1, 6, 10; Suet. Claud. 17; Favorin. ap. Gell. 2, 22, 20 sq.

circo.full: circo, āre, 1, v. a. circus. = circumeo. To go about, traverse: montem, Gromat. Vet. p. 326, 17; v. also circito fin.— To wander through: TOTAM REGIONEM, Inscr. ap. Hermes, 1, 343.

circos.full: circŏs, i, m., = κιρκος (a top), a precious stone unknown to us, Plin. 37, 10, 56, § 153.
circos.short: circŏs, i, m., = κιρκος (a top), a precious stone unknown to us, Plin.

circuitio.full: circŭĭtĭo (circŭmĭtĭo, Cic. Div. 2, 17, 40; 2, 61, 127; Liv. 3, 6, 9; Front. de Or. 3; Amm. 24, 2, 2), ōnis, f. circumeo. A going round; in milit. lang., the rounds: circuitio ac cura (vigiliarum) aedilium plebei erat. Liv. 3, 6, 9.— A circuit: muni mentum fluminis circumitione vallatum, Amm 24, 2, 2.— Trop., a circuitous mode, a circumlocution. ita aperte ipsam rem modo locutus, nil circuitione usus es, Ter. And. 1, 2, 31: quid opus est circumitione et anfractu? Cic. Div. 2, 61, 127, cf. Auct.

circuitus1.full: circŭĭtus, a, um, Part., from circumeo.
circuitus1.short: circŭĭtus, a, um, Part., from circumeo.

circuitus2.full: circŭĭtus (circŭmĭtus, Cic. N. D. 1, 12, 29; 2, 62, 155; 2, 19, 49; id. Rep. 1, 29, 45; Quint. 1, 10, 42 al.; cf. circumeo, and v. Neue, Formenl. 2, p. 737), ūs, m. circumeo (class. in prose and poetry). A going round, a circling, revolving, a revolution: solis, Cic. N. D. 2, 19, 49; cf. Plin. 2, 23, 21, § 86; Cic. Rep. 6, 12, 12: nox et dies unum circumitum orbis efflcit, id. Univ. 9 prope med.: Asiae Syriaeque circuitu Aegyptum petit, Suet. Aug. 17: mundi, Plin. 2, 5, 4, § 11.— In medic. lang.

circularis.full: circŭlāris, e, adj. circulus, circular, round (post-class.): flexus, Mart. Cap. 6, § 579; 8, § 814 init.

circulatim.full: circŭlātim, adv. circulor, circularly, in a circle (post-Aug. and rare). Prop.: pectori circulatim cerotaria apponere, Cael. Aur. Acut. 2, 29, 153; id. Tard. 1, 4, 91; Petr. 67 Gronov. (Büch circumlatum).— Fig., in circles, groups, or companies: multitudo circulatim suo quaeque more lamentata est, * Suet. Caes. 84 fin.

circulatio.full: circŭlātĭo, ōnis, f. id., a circular course, revolution: Mercurii, Vitr. 9, 1, 8.

circulator.full: circŭlātor, ōris, m. id.. A pedler: auctionum, Asin. ap. Cic. Fam. 10, 32, 3.— A mountebank, quack, Cels. 5, 27, 3; Petr 68, 6; Dig. 47, 11, 11; Sen. Ben. 6, 11, 2; App. M. 1, p. 103, 38.—Of noisy philosophers, Sen. Ep. 29, 5

circulatorius.full: circŭlātōrĭus, a, um, adj. circulator, of a mountebank, quackish (post-Aug.): jactatio, Quint. 2, 4, 15: volubilitas, id. 10, 1, 8: praestigiae, Tert. Apol. 23.

circulatrix.full: circŭlātrix, īcis, f. id., a female mountebank or stroller, Auct. Priap. 18, 1. —Adj.: lingua, of a mountebank, Mart. 10, 3, 2.

circulo.full: circŭlo, āre, v. a. (post - class. collat. form of circulor) [circulus], to make circu lar or round, App. flor. 9, p. 346, 21. circulatus gressus, Cael. Aur Tard. 1, 1: digitos. bent in, App. Mag. 89, p. 330.— Esp., to encircle, encompass: verticem varietatibus, Mart. Cap. 7, § 728: sideribus, id. 8, § 831; 4, § 333 al.; cf. Neue, Formenl. 2, p. 269.

circulor.full: circŭlor, ātus, 1, v. dep. id.. To form a circle (of men) about one's self, or to gather in a company or circle for conversation, * Cic. Brut. 54, 200: totis vero castris milites circulari et dolere, etc., Caes. B. C. 1, 64.—Hence, Of mountebanks, to collect people around one's self, Sen. Ep. 40, 3; 52, 7.

circulus.full: circŭlus, i, m. (contr. circlus, like vinclum = vinculum, Verg. G. 3, 166) [kindred with κίρκος, κύκλος, circinus], a circular figure, a circle: circulus aut orbis, qui κύκλος Graece dicitur, Cic. N. D. 2, 18, 47: muri exterior, Liv. 36, 9, 12: circulus ad speciem caelestis arcūs orbem solis ambiit, Suet. Aug. 95.— Esp. In astronomy, a circular course, orbit: stellae circulos suos orbesque conficiunt celeritate mirabili, Cic. Rep. 6, 15, 15: aequinoctialis, solstitialis, septentrionalis, Varr. L

circum.full: circum properly acc. from circus = κίρκος, adv. and prep., designates either an entire encompassing or surrounding of an object, or a proximity only partially em. bracing or comprehending it, around, about, all around, περί, ἀμφί Adv. Around, round about, all around, etc., πέριξ: furcas circum offigito, Cato, R. R. 48, 2; Varr. R. R. 3, 14, 1; Verg A 3, 230: quia (locus) vastis circum saltibus claudebatur, Tac. A. 4, 25: molli circum est ansas amplexus acantho, Verg. E. 3, 45: age tu interim Da

circumactio.full: circumactĭo, ōnis, f. circumago. Lit., a turning around, revolving (very rare): solis, Vitr. 9, 9, 15; Mart. Cap. 8, § 885.—* Trop., of discourse, a turning, turn, compass, Gell. 17, 20, 4.

circumactus1.full: circumactus, a, um, Part. and P. a., from circumago, q. v. fin.

circumactus2.full: circumactus, ūs, m. circumago, a moving or turning round (post-Aug.): assiduus caeli, Sen. Q. N. 7, 2, 2; Censor. de Die Nat. 23: corporis, Plin. 8, 30, 44, § 105; 8, 50, 76, § 201: rotarum, id. 28, 9, 37, § 141.

circumaggero.full: circum-aggĕro, no perf., ātum, 1, v. a., to heap up around (very rare): terram, Col. 5, 12, 3: fimo radices, Plin. 19, 5, 23, § 68.

circumago.full: circum-ăgo, ēgi, actum, 3, v. a. To drive or turn in a circle, turn round (most freq. since the Aug. per.; not in Cic. or Quint.): impera suovetaurilia circumagi, Cato, R. R. 141, 1.—And with two acc. (on account of circum): terram fundumque meum suovetaurilia circumagi jussi, Cato, R. R. 141, § 2: (annus) qui solstitiali circumagitur orbe, Liv. 1, 19, 6: chamaeleonis oculos ipsos circumagi totos tradunt, Plin. 11, 37, 55, § 152.—Act. in mid. sense (very rare): Aegeum pelagus summotas terras hin

circumambulo.full: circum-ambŭlo, āre, v. a., to walk around: omnes glebas, Dig. 41, 2, 3, § 1.

circumamictus.full: circum-ămictus, a, um, adj. amicio, enveloped, invested (eccl. Lat.), Vulg. Apoc. 4, 4.

circumaro.full: circum-ăro, āre, v. a., to plough around, Liv. 2, 10, 12; Plin. 18, 3, 3, § 9.

circumcaesura.full: circum-caesūra, or separate, cir-cum caesūra, ae, f., the external contour or outline ( = circumscriptio), Lucr. 3, 220; 4, 645; Arn. 3, p. 107.
circumcaesura.short: circum-caesūra, or separate, cir-cum caesūra, ae, f., the external contour or outline ( = circumscriptio), Lucr.

circumcalco.full: circum-calco (in MSS. also cir-cumculco), āre, v. a., to tread or trample upon all around: codicem, Col. 5, 6, 21; id. 5, 6, 21, § 8: terminos, Sicul. Flac. p. 6.

circumcellio.full: Circumcellĭo, ōnis, m. cella. A class of monks, who, without fixed abode, wandered about from cell to cell, Aug. in Psa. 132.— A class of heretics, Hier. Ep. 22, 15; Isid. Orig. 8, 5, 53.

circumcidaneus.full: circumcīdānĕus, a, um, adj. circumcīdo, prop., of or from cutting or paring around: mustum, wine pressed out after the ordinary pressing, when the husks and stems remaining in the press had been cut around, Cato, R. R. 23, 4; cf. Plin. 14, 20, 25, § 124 sq.; Col. 12, 36; the same, called mustum circumcisicium or circumcisitum, Varr. R. R. 1, 54, 3.

circumcido.full: circum-cīdo, cīdi, cīsum, 3, v. a. caedo, to cut around, cut, clip, trim (orig. in agriculture; syn.: amputo, reseco): ars agricolarum, quae circumcidat, amputet, erigat, etc., Cic. Fin. 5, 14, 39: gemmam acuto scalpello circumcidito... ejusdem spatii corticem circumcidito, Col. Arb. 26, 8; 12, 36: latera scrobis, id. 5, 9, 9: arbores ad medullam, Plin. 16, 39, 74, § 191: aciem, Lucr. 3, 412: caespitem gladiis, Caes. B. G. 5, 42: ungues, Cels. 7, 26, 2: volnus, Plin. 25, 5, 25, § 61: genitalia (

circumcingo.full: circum-cingo, ĕre, v. a., to enclose around, surround: quā Mons Apenninus regiones Italiae Etruriaeque circumcingit, Vitr. 2, 6, 5: eum zonā gloriae, Vulg. Ecclus. 45, 9: PORTICVS, Inscr. Orell. 4043.—In part. pres., Cels. 7, 15: telis circumcingentibus, Sil. 10, 2.

circumcirca.full: circum-circā, adv., a strengthened circum or circa, all around (cf. the Heb. , Vulg. Ezech. 40, 5; the Gr. ἀμφὶ τερί; and our round about—very rare, perh. only in the foll. exs.; and acc. to Serg. ap. Don. p. 1855 P. also in Cato): ubi erat haec defossa, occoepit scalpturire ibi ungulis circumcirca, * Plaut. Aul. 3, 4, 9: coepi regiones circumcirca prospicere, Sulp. ap. Cic. Fam. 4, 5, 4; Auct. B. Hisp. 41; App. M. 11, p. 258, 23; cf. Prisc. p. 989 sq. P.; Serg. ap. Don. 1. 1.; Hand, Turs. II. p
circumcirca.short: circum-circā, adv., a strengthened circum or circa, all around (cf.

circumcirco.full: circumcirco, āre, v. n., = circumeo, to go round: regiones, Amm. 31, 2, 23 Eyssenh.; dub. (al. circumcurrunt).

circumcise.full: circumcīsē, adv., v. circumcido, P. a. fin.

circumcisio.full: circumcīsĭo, ōnis, f. circumcido, a cutting around, circumcision, physical and moral (only in eccl. Lat.): carnis, cordis, spiritūs, Lact. 4, 17, 1 sqq.; Tert. adv. Jud. 2; 3 et saep.

circumcisorium.full: circumcīsōrĭum, ii, n. id., an instrument for cutting around, Veg. Vet. 1, 26, 2; cf. id. ib. 2, 28, 31.

circumcisura.full: circumcīsūra, ae, f. id., a cutting around: arborum, Plin. 16, 40, 79, § 219.

circumcisus.full: circumcīsus, a, um, v. circumcido, P. a.

circumclamo.full: circum-clāmo, āre, v. a., to roar around, poet. of the raging waves: ora circumclamata procellis, Sid. Carm. 2, 506.

circumclaudo.full: circum-claudo, ĕre, 3, v. a. (postclass. collat. form of circumcludo), to shut in: farinā circumclaudendus locus, Cael. Aur. Tard. 4, 7, 103.

circumcludo.full: circum-clūdo, si, sum, 3, v. a. claudo, to shut in, enclose on every side (in good class. prose): ne duobus circumcluderetur exercitibus, Caes. B. C. 3, 30; cf. * Suet. Tib. 20; Auct. B. Hisp. 6: cornua ab labris argento, to surround with a rim of silver, Caes. B. G. 6, 28 fin.; Plin. 18, 35, 78, § 344: SEPVLCRVM MACERIIS, Inscr. Orell. 4349.— Trop.: L. Catilina consiliis, laboribus, periculis meis circumclusus ac debilitatus, hemmed in, Cic. Cat. 2, 7, 14: aliquem suis praesidiis, suā diligenti

circumcola.full: circumcŏla, ae, comm. circumcolo, dwelling around: gentes, Tert. adv. Gnost. 3 fin.

circumcolo.full: circum-cŏlo, ĕre, v. a., to dwell round about or near: sinum maris, Liv. 5, 33, 10: paludem, id. 31, 41, 4; absol., Dig. 43, 12, 1; cf. ib. 43, 13, 1: Amazones circumcolunt Tanain, Amm. 22, 8, 27: insulam, id. 22, 8, 43.

circumcordialis.full: circum-cordĭālis, e, adj., around the heart (post-class.): calor, Tert. Anim. 43: sanguis, id. ib. 15.
circumcordialis.short: circum-cordĭālis, e, adj., around the heart (post-class.): calor, Tert.

circumcumulo.full: circum-cŭmŭlo, āre, 1, v. a., to heap or pile up around: exanimes circumcumulantur acervi, Stat. Th. 10, 655.

circumcurro.full: circum-curro, ĕre, v. n., to run round or about (not ante-Aug.), Vitr. 4, 6: circumcurrens linea, the periphery, Quint. 1, 10, 41.—* Trop.: eam artem (rhetoricen) circumcurrentem vocaverunt. quod in omni materiā diceret, universal, Quint. 2, 21, 7.

circumcursio.full: circumcursĭo, ōnis, f. circumcurro, a running around (late Lat.), App. M. 9, p. 222, 41.

circumcurso.full: circum-curso, āre, v. freq. a. and n., to run round about, to run about in, at, or near something (ante- and post-class.; in Cic. Fam. 7, 1, 5, more recent editt. read concursare); act.: omnia, * Plaut. Rud. 1, 4, 4: aliquam hinc illinc, * Cat. 68, 133.— Absol.: hac illac, * Ter. Heaut. 3, 2, 1: atria versari et circumcursare columnae... uti pueris videantur, Lucr. 4, 400: per omnes portas, Lact. 6, 12 (in paraphr. of Cic.).

circumdatio.full: circumdătĭo, ōnis, f. circumdo, the putting around: auri, Vulg. 1 Pet. 3, 3.

circumdo.full: circum-do, dĕdi, dătum, dăre, v. a., lit. to put, set, or place around, i. e. both to wrap around (e. g. a mantle). and also to enclose (e. g. a town with a wall; syn.: cingo, vestio, saepio, circumvallo al.), with a twofold construction (cf. Zumpt, Gr. § 418). Aliquid (alicui rei), to place something around something, to put, set around, etc. (class. in prose and poetry). With dat.: aër omnibus est rebus circumdatus appositusque, Lucr. 6, 1035: moenibus subjectos prope jam ignes circumdatosque

circumdoleo.full: circum-dŏlĕo, ēre, v. n., to suffer on every side: spiratio circumdolens; acc. to Forcellini: circum, seu undique, vel ab omni parte angens, i.e. very painful, Cael. Aur. Acut. 2, 14, 92.

circumdolo.full: circum-dŏlo, āre, v. a., to hew off around, Plin. 16, 32, 57, § 133.— Trop.: qui, tamquam bonus animi faber, vitia nostra circumdolat, Ambros. in Luc. 3, 2.

circumduco.full: circum-dūco, xi, ctum, 3, v. a. (imper. circumduce, Plaut. As. 1, 1, 83; id. Most. 3, 2, 159; id. Mil. 2, 2, 66), to lead or draw around (class.; esp. freq. in milit. lang.; in Cic. perh. only once). Prop.: circumduce exercitum, Plaut. Mil. 2, 2, 66; cf. Liv. 1, 27, 8; 8, 13, 8: miles aliquo circumducitur, Plaut. Truc. 4, 4, 21: quattuor cohortibus longiore itinere circumductis, Caes. B. G. 3, 26: alas ad latus Samnitium, Liv. 10, 29, 9: agmen per invia circa, etc., id. 21, 36, 4: pars devio sal

circumductio.full: circumductĭo, ōnis, f. circumduco. A leading or conducting around: aquarum, Vitr. 8, 6, 5 sq.: sphaerae, the circumference, Hyg. Astr. 1, 2; of a person, Cod. Th. 4, 8, 1.— Trop. * A cheating, defrauding: argenti, Plaut. Capt. 5. — The expansion of a thought, a period, only in Quint. 11, 3, 39; 9, 4, 118.

circumductor.full: circumductor, ōris, m. id., one who leads about, converts another, Tert. adv. Val. 10.

circumductum.full: circumductum, i, n. circumduco, II. B.; in rhet., a period, Quint. 9, 4, 22.

circumductus1.full: circumductus, a, um, Part., from circumduco.
circumductus1.short: circumductus, a, um, Part., from circumduco.

circumductus2.full: circumductus, ūs, m. circumduco. The circumference of a figure, Quint. 1, 10, 43.—* Motion in a circle, a revolution: orbium, Macr. Somn. Scip. 2, 1, 5.

circumeo.full: circŭm-ĕo or circŭĕŏ (v. circum, III.; Neue, Formenl. 2, p. 736 sq.), īvi or ii, circuĭtum, īre (inf. pass. circumirier, Plaut. Curc. 3, 81), v. n. and a. Prop., to go around, travel or march around, etc. (class.): sparsis Medea capillis Bacchantum ritu flagrantes circuit aras, Ov. M. 7, 258: per hortum circuit, makes a circuit, Plaut. As. 3, 3, 152; cf. Nep. Eum. 9, 2: si rectum limitem rupti torrentibus pontes inciderint, circumire cogemur, Quint. 2, 13, 16: an quasi mare omnes circumimus insu

circumequito.full: circŭm-ĕquĭto, āre, v. a., to ride round: moenia, Liv. 10, 34, 7.

circumerro.full: circŭm-erro, āre, v. n., to wander round, stroll about: neque turba lateri circumerrat, Sen. Contr. 2, 9, 7: tempora (of the revolution of Saturn in his orbit), to pass through, App. de Mundo, p. 71, 11.

circumfarcio.full: circum-farcĭo, no perf., fartus, 4, v. a., to fill up all around, to stuff, Plin. 17, 13, 21, § 98.

circumferentia.full: circumfĕrentĭa, ae, f. circumfero, a circumference (post-class.): sedilium, App. Flor. 18, p. 359; Mart. Cap. 8, § 817; Front. Expos. Form. p. 33 Goes.

circumfero.full: circum-fĕro, tŭli, lātum, ferre, v. a. to bear round, or, in gen., to move or carry round or about (class. in prose and poetry). Prop.: age circumfer mulsum, pass around, Plaut. Pers. 5, 2, 45: satiatis vino ciboque poculum... circumferetur, Liv. 26, 13, 18: circumferri vinum largius jubet, Curt. 7, 4, 7: hisce (poculis) etiam nunc in publico convivio potio circumfertur, Varr. L. L. 5, § 122 Müll.: sanguinem in pateris, Sall. C. 22, 1; Flor. 4, 1, 4 Duker: circa ea omnia templa Philippum infesto

circumfigo.full: circum-fīgo, ĕre, v. a., to fix or fasten round (very rare): columellam cuneis, Cato, R. R. 20, 1: duo scelesti circumfiguntur Christo, Tert. adv. Marc. 4, 42.

circumfingo.full: circum-fingo, ĕre, v. a., to form around: carnem alicui, Tert. Anim. 23.

circumfinio.full: circum-fīnĭo, īre, v. a., to complete a circle, to bring to an end: annum, Sol. 3.

circumfirmo.full: circum-fīrmo, āre, v. a., to fasten round: vitem, Col. 4, 17, 7.

circumflagro.full: circum-flagro, āre, v. n., to blaze or scorch all around: per immensum circumflagrantibus Austris, Avien. Arat. 274.

circumflecto.full: circum-flecto, xi, xum, 3, v. a., to bend or turn about (Verg. and post-class. writers); prop. of the charioteer in the circus; hence, transf.' longos cursus, Verg. A. 5, 131; 3, 430.— Trop.: circumflexa saecula, returning upon themselves, Claud. VI. Cons. Hon. 391: anceps labyrinthus et error circumflexus, full of windings and turnings, Prud. Apoth. 71.— In later gram. t. t., to mark with a circumflex, to pronounce as long (in Quint., instead of it, circumducere, q. v.): penultimam, Gell. 4, 7,

circumflexibilis.full: circumflexĭbĭlis, e, adj. circumflecto, provided with a circumflex accent (late Lat.), Excerpt. ex Macr. Diff. p. 235 Jan.

circumflexio.full: circumflexĭo, ōnis, f. id., a bending or winding round: obliqua circuli, Macr. Somn. Scip. 1, 12, 1.

circumflexus1.full: circumflexus, a, um, Part., from circumflecto.
circumflexus1.short: circumflexus, a, um, Part., from circumflecto.

circumflexus2.full: circumflexus, ūs, m. circumflecto, a bending round, a vault, arch: mundi, Plin. 2, 1, 1, § 1: caeli, id. 6, 34, 39, § 212.— A winding, circuit: qui (Tanais) per sinuosos labitur circumflexus, Amm. 22, 8, 27.

circumflo.full: circum-flo, āre, v. n., to blow round about; of the wind (very rare; in the class. per. only in the foll. exs.): circumflantibus Austris, Stat. Th. 11, 42.— Trop.: ab omnibus ventis invidiae circumflari, to be assailed by every blast. of envy, * Cic. Verr. 2, 3, 41, § 98.

circumfluo.full: circum-flŭo, xi, 3, v. n. and a., to flow round (class. in prose and poetry). Neutr.: in poculis repletis circumfluere quod supersit, flows over all around, Plin. 2, 65, 68, § 163; cf. Curt. 8, 8, 12.— Act.: utrumque latus circumfluit aequoris unda, Ov. M. 13, 779: Cariam circumfluunt Maeander et Orsinus, Plin. 5, 29, 29, § 108; cf.: cum aliae aquae subterfluant terras, aliae circumfluant, Sen. Q. N. 3, 30, 4; Dig. 41, 1, 30, § 2; Ov. M. 3, 74: cum (oceanus) omnis terras circumfluat, Gell. 12, 1

circumfluus.full: circumflŭus, a, um, adj. circumfluo (poet. or in post-Aug. prose). Act., flowing around, circumfluent: umor, Ov. M. 1, 30: amnis, id. ib. 15, 739: mare, Plin. 2, 66, 66, § 166.—More freq., Pass., flowed around, surrounded with water: insula, Ov. M. 15, 624: tellus Hadriaco ponto, Luc. 4, 407: Carthago pelago, Sil. 15, 220: urbs Ponto, Val. Fl. 5, 442: campi Euphrate et Tigre, * Tac. A. 6, 37: omnis circumfluo ambitu Pontus est, Amm. 22, 8, 46.— In gen., surrounded, encircled: chlamys limbo Maeon

circumfodio.full: circum-fŏdĭo, no perf., fossum, ĕre (inf. pass.: circumfodiri, Col. 5, 9, 12; cf. fodio), v. n. and a., to dig around something, dig about (agricultural t. t.). Neutr., Cato, R. R. 161. 4.— Act.: truncum, Col. 5, 6, 17: platanos, Sen. Ep 12, 2: arbores, Plin. 17, 26, 39, § 248: plantas, Pall. Febr. 20, 2.—Inf. pass.: circumfodi, Pall. Mart. 10, 19.—Part. perf. pass.: circumfosso stipite, Plin. 17, 27, 43, § 252.

circumforaneus.full: circum-fŏrānĕus, a, um, adj. forum. * Of or around the forum or market-place: aes, debts due in the forum (because the bankers' shops were at the forum), Cic. Att. 2, 1, 11.—More freq., Strolling about from market to market, that attends markets: pharmacopola, Cic. Clu. 14, 40: lanista, * Suet. Vit. 12: medicabulum, App. M. 9, p. 218, 41.— In gen., that is carried about, ambulatory, movable: domus, App. M. 4, p. 148, 29: hostiae, which are carried about for expiation (cf. circumfero, II. C.), Ap

circumforatus.full: circum-fŏrātus, a, um, Part. [foro], bored or pierced round' stipes, Plin. 17, 27, 43, § 252.

circumfossor.full: circumfossor, ōris, m. circumfodio, one who digs around something, Plin. 17, 24, 37, § 227.

circumfossura.full: circumfossūra, ae, f. id., a digging round, Plin. 17, 26, 39, § 247.

circumfractus.full: circum-fractus, a, um, Part. [frango], broken off around: turbo, broken around (sc. scopulos), Amm. 22, 8, 15: colles, precipitous, id. 29, 4, 5.

circumfremo.full: circum-frĕmo, ĕre, v. n. and a., to make a noise around something (post-Aug. and rare): nidos, of birds, Sen. Cons. ad Marc. 7, 2; Prud. Cath. 479.

circumfrico.full: circum-frĭco, āre, v. a., to rub around, to scour, Cato, R. R. 26.

circumfulcio.full: circum-fulcĭo, īre, v. a., to support, hold up around: togam, Tert. Pall. 5.

circumfulgeo.full: circum-fulgĕo, ēre, v. n., to shine around, Plin. 2, 37, 37, § 101.

circumfundo.full: circum-fundo, fūdi, fūsum, 3, v. a., lit. to pour out around, i.e. as in circumdo, either with the acc. of that which is poured, to pour around; or, with the acc. of that around which something is poured, to surround with a liquid (class. in prose and poetry). Lit. With acc. of the liquid poured (with or without dat. of the object around which): amurcam ad oleam circumfundito, Cato, R. R. 93: Tigris urbi circumfunditur, surrounds, flows round the town, Plin. 6, 27, 31, § 132.— More freq. in part

circumfusio.full: circumfūsĭo, ōnis, f. circumfundo, a pouring around (post-class.) spiritus ignei, Firm. Math. 1, 4: Oceani, id. ib. praef.

circumfusus.full: circumfūsus, a, um, Part., from circumfundo.
circumfusus.short: circumfūsus, a, um, Part., from circumfundo.

circumgarriens.full: circum-garrĭens, entis, Part. [garrio], blabbing or babbling about. falsiloquia, Claud Mam. Stat. An. 2, 9.

circumgelo.full: circum-gĕlo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a., to freeze all around corpus, Tert. Anim. 23: cortex circumgelatus, Plin. 13, 22, 40, § 120.

circumgemo.full: circum-gĕmo, ĕre, v. n., to roar around something: circumgemit ursus ovile, Hor. Epod. 16, 51.

circumgesto.full: circum-gesto, āre, v. freq. a., to bear or carry around' epistulam, * Cic. Q. Fr. 1, 2, 2, § 6; deam, App. M. 8, 213, 37.

circumglobatus.full: circum-glŏbātus, a, um, Part. [globo], rolled together, conglobated: animalia escae circumglobata, small insects, Plin. 9, 47, 71, § 154.

circumgredior.full: circum-grĕdĭor, gressus, grĕdi, v dep [gradior], to go or walk around, travel about (esp. in a hostile manner; post-Aug., several times in Tac, elsewhere rare). Absol., Tac. A. 1, 64; 2, 17; 12, 28.— With acc.: exercitum, * Sall. H. 4, 61, 21 Dietsch: terga, Tac. A. 2, 25' Syriam, Aur Vict. Caes. 21' lacunam, Amm. 16, 12, 59.
circumgredior.short: circum-grĕdĭor, gressus, grĕdi, v dep [gradior], to go or walk around, travel about (esp.

circumgressus1.full: circumgressus, a, um, Part., from circumgredior
circumgressus1.short: circumgressus, a, um, Part., from circumgredior

circumgressus2.full: circumgressus, ūs, m. circumgredior (perh. only in Amm.). * Abstr., a going about' rapidi, Amm. 22, 2, 3.— * Concr., the compass, circuit of a thing' amplissimi palus Maeotis, Amm. 22, 8, 30.
