circumhisco.full: circum-hisco, ĕre, v. n, to stare about with open mouth, Arn. 5, p 175 dub. (al. circumsciscere)

circumhumatus.full: circum-hŭmātus, a, um, Part [humo], buried around: corpora, Amm 22, 12, 8.
circumhumatus.short: circum-hŭmātus, a, um, Part [humo], buried around: corpora, Amm 22, 12, 8.

circumicio.full: circum-ĭcĭo or circum-jĭcĭo (access. form circum-jăcĭo, Liv 33, 18, 17, where more recent editt. read circumagere), jēci, jectum, 3, v. a. To cast, throw, or place around (in good class. prose)' amic tum, Varr. L. L. 5, § 132: vallum, Liv 35, 4, 6: fossam quoque et alia munimenta verticibus iis... circumjecere, id. 38, 19, 5: pars urbis, cui brevior orbis munitionis circumjectus erat, id. 36, 9, 12 miles moenibus Cremonensium castra sua, castris vallum circumjecerat, Tac H. 3, 26 vehicula, id. A

circuminicio.full: circŭm-īnĭcĭo, ĕre, v. a., to throw up all around, = circumicio: vallum, Liv. 25, 36, 5.

circuminvolvo.full: circŭm-involvo, ĕre, v. a., to involve all around, to enclose, envelop: singula puncta, Vitr. 10, 11 (al. circumvolvo).

circumjaceo.full: circum-jăcĕo, ĕre, v. n., to lie round about, border upon (rare; not in Cic.). Absol., * Cael. ap. Quint. 4, 2, 123: populi circumjacentes, surrounding, Tac. A. 2, 72. — With dat.: Lycaonia et Phrygia circumjacent Europae, Liv. 37, 54, 11: capiti et collo, App. de Deo Socr. p. 54, 33.—* Trop., in rhet.: circumjăcentĭa, ĭum, n., the context, Qumt. 9, 4, 29.

circumjectio.full: circumjectĭo, ōnis, f. circumicio. A throwing around, casting about (postclass.) manuum, Cael. Aur Acut. 1, 2, 31. —* A putting on clothing, dressing: corporis, Arn. 2, p 73

circumjectus1.full: circumjectus, a, um, Part., from circumicio
circumjectus1.short: circumjectus, a, um, Part., from circumicio

circumjectus2.full: circumjectus, ūs, m. circumicio, a casting around, a surrounding, encompassing (rare but class.): (aether) qui terram tenero circumjectu amplectitur, with soft embrace, Cic. poet N. D. 2, 25, 65 (as transl. from Euripides Καὶ γῆν πέριξ ἔχονθʼ ὑγραῖς ἐν ἀγκάλαις)' arduus, id. Rep. 2, 6, 11' rudi parietum circumjectu vox devoratur, Plin 11, 51, 112, § 270.— Meton (abstr pro concr), that which is thrown around one, as clothing, dress, Varr. L. L. 5, § 132 Müll., p 37 Bip., Tert. Pall. 5.

circumlabens.full: circum-lābens (better circum lā-bens), P a., gliding around, Luc. 6, 484.
circumlabens.short: circum-lābens (better circum lā-bens), P a., gliding around, Luc.

circumlambo.full: circum-lambo, ĕre, v. a., to lick around ora, Plin. 11, 37, 65, § 171

circumlaqueo.full: circum-lăquĕo, āre, v. a., to wind around, in tmesis cassem, Grat. Cyn 29.

circumlaticius.full: circumlātĭcĭus or -tĭus, a, um, adj. circumlatus, that may be carried around, portable carcer, Sid. Ep 2, 2 fin.

circumlatio.full: circumlātĭo, ōnis, f [id.], a carrying around (post-class.): arcae, Tert adv Marc. 4, 12; victimae, Serv ad Verg. A. 6, 229.
circumlatio.short: circumlātĭo, ōnis, f [id.], a carrying around (post-class.): arcae, Tert adv Marc.

circumlator.full: circumlātor, ōris, m. id., one who carries about (post-class.), Tert. adv Marc. 1, 19; 1, 21 fin

circumlatro.full: circum-lā^tro, āre, v. a. Prop., to bark around hominem, Sen. Cons. ad Marc. 22, 3 leonem, Amm 22, 16, 16.— Meton., of the sea (post-class.): totum hoc circumlatrat aestus, roars around, Avien. Perieg 48.— Trop., in pass.: domus circumlatratur injuriis, Symm. Ep. 8, 17 aliquem frustra occultis injuriis, Amm. 22, 12, 14: eum circumlatrantes philosophi, Lact. 2, 8, 50: circumlatrantes haeretici, Aug Ep 136.

circumlatus.full: circumlātus, a, um, Part., from circumfero
circumlatus.short: circumlātus, a, um, Part., from circumfero

circumlavo.full: circum-lăvo, āre and ĕre, v a., lit. to wash around, hence, of waters, to overflow all around (only in the foll. exs.): Aegyptus, quam Nilus circumlavat, Hyg. Fab 275: insula superjactis fluctibus circumlavitur, Sall. ap Non. p. 504, 1 (id. H. 2, 83 Dietsch).
circumlavo.short: circum-lăvo, āre and ĕre, v a., lit.

circumlevo.full: circum-lĕvo, āre, v a., to raise up all around tegmina, Cael Aur Acut. 2, 37, 194.
circumlevo.short: circum-lĕvo, āre, v a., to raise up all around tegmina, Cael Aur Acut.

circumligo.full: circum-lĭgo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. Aliquid alicui rei, to bind something to something' natam mediae circumligat hastae, * Verg. A. 11, 555' spongias hydropicis, Plin 31, 11, 47, § 128.—More freq., Aliquid aliquā re, to bind something with something, to encompass, surround: stirpem salice, Cato, R. R. 40, 2: ferrum stuppā, Liv 21, 8, 10: totas (radices) caespite, Plin. 17, 11, 16, § 86' Roscius circumligatus angui, * Cic. Div. 2, 31, 66; Plin. 28, 2, 5, § 29. —More generally: globum undis, to surro

circumlino.full: circum-lĭno, lĭtum, 3 (perf. late Lat. circumlinisti, Vulg. Ezech. 23, 40), v. a. (access. form circumlĭnĭo, īre; cf. lino; so, circumliniunt, Quint. 12, 9, 8 Spald. N. er.: circumliniri, id. 1, 11, 6: circumliniendus, Col. 6, 16, 3; 6, 17, 9). Aliquid alicui, to smear, stick, or spread all over, to besmear: vulneribus aliquid circumlinitur, Plin. 22, 23, 49, § 103: Galbanum ramis ellebori circumlitum, id. 24, 5, 13, § 22: ciroumlita taedis sulfura, Ov. M. 3, 373.—Far more freq., Aliquid aliquā

circumlitio.full: circumlĭtĭo, ōnis, f. circumlino. A smearing or spreading over, anointing: oris, Plin. 24, 7, 24, § 40.— In painting, an overlaying of color, the tint or hue given to marble by rubbing it with a mixture of oil and wax, Plin. 35, 11, 40, § 133; Sen. Ep. 86, 5; v O. Müll. Archaeol. § 310, 4.

circumlocutio.full: circumlŏcūtĭo, ōnis, f. circumloquor, circumlocution, periphrasis, = περίφρασις, * Quint. 8, 6, 61; Gell. 3, 1, 5; Arn. 6, p. 210.

circumloquor.full: circum-lŏquor, lŏcūtus, lŏqui, v. n., to make use of circumlocution or periphrasis (post-class.), Aus. Ep. 6, 7, and 146, 15.

circumlucens.full: circum-lūcens, entis, Part. [luceo], shining or glittering around; trop.: fortuna, Sen. Cons. ad Marc. 2, 5.

circumluo.full: circum-lŭo, ĕre, v. a., to flow around or wash upon (rare): Rhenus tergum ac latera circumluit, Tac. H. 4, 12: pars arcis circumluitur mari, Liv. 25, 11, 1: litora subit et circumluit pelagus, Mel. prooem. 2: (Aegeum) mare laevā Imbrum et Tenedum circumluens, Amm. 22, 8, 2.

circumlustro.full: circum-lustro, āvi, 1, v. a., to light all around; in tmesis: mundi templum, Lucr 5, 1437.— Trop., to travel over or through: populos provinciae, Cod. Th. 4, 8, 5.

circumluvio.full: circum-lŭvĭo, ōnis, f.; and cir-cumlŭvĭum, ii, n. luo, the accumulation of land by alluvion around a piece of land, alluvial land: jura circumluvionum, the right of using such land, Cic. de Or 1, 38, 173.—Form circumluvium, Paul. ex Fest. p. 64, 14 Müll., and Isid. Orig. 14, 8, 12.

circummeo.full: circum-mĕo, āvi, āre, v. a. and n., to go around: circum eam (sc. Taprobanen) isse, for circummeasse, Mel. 3, 7; Tert. Pall. 1.

circummetior.full: circum-mētĭor, īri, v. pass., to be measured around. columnae, Vitr. 4, 4, 3.

circummingo.full: circum-mingo, nxi, 3, v. a., to make water around something; aliquem, Petr. 57, 3: vestimenta, id. 62, 6.

circummitto.full: circum-mitto, mīsi, missum, 3, v. a., to send around: legationes in omnes partes, Caes. B. G. 7, 63; id. B. C. 3, 55: praecones, id B. G. 5, 51; id. B. C. 1, 12: jugo circummissus Veiens, Liv. 2, 50, 10: post montes, id. 4, 18, 4: milites, id. 29, 33, 3; 36, 14, 13: scaphas, id. 29, 25, 7.

circummulcens.full: circum-mulcens, entis, Part. [mulceo], licking gently around: linguae (serpentium), Plin. 28, 3, 6, § 30.

circummunio.full: circum-mūnĭo (old orthog. cir-cummoenĭo, Plaut. Capt. 2, 2, 4), īvi, ītum, 4, v. a., to wall up around, to fortify, secure (freq. in the histt., elsewhere rare; but in MSS. constantly confounded with circumvenire; cf. Oud. ad Caes. B. C. 1, 18; 1, 81; 1, 84; 2, 16; 3, 97; Schneid. ad Col. 5, 9, 11; 5, 10, 1): plantas caveis, Col. 5, 9, 11: oppidum, Auct. B. Afr. 79: Thapsum operibus, id. ib. 80; cf. Auct. B. Hisp. 38: aliquos ut feras, Caes. B. C. 1, 84: (hostes) vallo fossāque, id. ib. 1, 80: c

circummunitio.full: circummūnītĭo, ōnis, f. circummunio; in milit. lang., an investing of a town, circumvallation, Caes. B. C. 1, 19 fin.; Auct. B. Hisp. 38 fin.

circummuranus.full: circum-mūrānus, a, um, adj. murus, around (but beyond) the walls (perh. only in Amm.): bella, with the neighboring nations, Amm. 14, 6, 4: pericula, id. 21, 13, 2.

circumnascens.full: circum-nascens, entis, Part. [nascor], growing up around: absinthium, Plin. 2, 103, 106, § 232.

circumnavigo.full: circum-nāvĭgo, āre, v. a., to sail around, circumnavigate: sinus Oceani, Vell. 2, 106, 3.

circumnecto.full: circum-necto, no perf., nexum, ĕre, v. a., to wrap or bind around, surround, envelop (late Lat.): elephanti flammis conjectis undique circumnexi, Amm. 19, 7, 7: tenuis membrana illa perlucens, quā circumnectitur alvus, ac tegitur, Lact. Opif. Dei, 14, 2 (al. circumretitur).
circumnecto.short: circum-necto, no perf., nexum, ĕre, v.

circumnoto.full: circum-nŏto, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a., to paint or portray around: animalia vario colore, App. M. 11, p. 279, 12, p. 273 Bip.

circumobruo.full: circum-ob-rŭo, ĕre, v. a., to cover around with, wrap around, Plin. 19, 5, 26, § 83.

circumornatus.full: circum-ornātus, a, um, adj., ornamented round about, Vulg. Psa. 143, 12.
circumornatus.short: circum-ornātus, a, um, adj., ornamented round about, Vulg.

circumpadanus.full: circum-pădānus, a, um, adj., found or situate around the Po: campi, Liv. 21, 35, 8: lanae, Plin. 8, 48, 73, § 190: musta, id. 14, 20, 25, § 125.
circumpadanus.short: circum-pădānus, a, um, adj., found or situate around the Po: campi, Liv.

circumpavitus.full: circum-păvītus, a, um, Part. [pavio], beaten or trodden close around: area, Plin. 12, 14, 32, § 58.

circumpendeo.full: circum-pendeo (better written as two words), ēre, v. n., to hang around: margaritis circum pendentibus, Curt. 8, 9, 24; Ov. F. 2, 529.
circumpendeo.short: circum-pendeo (better written as two words), ēre, v.

circumpes.full: circum-pēs, pĕdis (that is round the feet). A kind of parasites (cf. antepes), Agroet. Orth. p. 2274 P.— A covering of the foot, περισκελίς, Vulg. Ecclus. 45, 10.
circumpes.short: circum-pēs, pĕdis (that is round the feet).

circumplaudo.full: circum-plaudo, ĕre, v. a., to applaud or greet on all sides by clapping the hands, Ov. Tr. 4, 2, 49.

circumplecto.full: circumplecto, ĕre (act. collat. form of circumplector; cf. Neue, Formenl. 2, p. 312), to embrace, clasp around: meum collum circumplecte, Plaut. As. 3, 3, 106: circumplectito foramina laminis, Cato, R. R. 21, 2.—Part. pass. circumplexus: turris igni, Gell. 15, 1, 6: venter, App. Dogm. Plat. 1, p. 171 sq.

circumplector.full: circum-plector, plexus, 3, v. dep. a., to clasp around, embrace, to surround, encompass (class. in prose and poetry): conjunctiones motu undique, Cic. Univ. 7 fin.: domini patrimonium quasi thesaurum draco, id. Phil. 13, 5, 12: arborem, Plin. 19, 4, 22, § 63; 13, 10, 19, § 65: pharetram auro, Verg. A. 5, 312: collem opere, to circumvallate, Caes. B. G. 7, 83: oppidum tragulis, Auct. B. Hisp. 32; Suet. Tib. 6: statuam pennis, of the eagle, id. Dom. 6; Stat. S. 1, 5, 44.— Trop.: animum, imago quae

circumplexus1.full: circumplexus, a, um, Part., v. circumplecto fin.

circumplexus2.full: circumplexus, ūs, m. circumplector, an encompassing, embracing, or folding around; only in abl. sing., Plin. 8, 11, 11, § 32; 10, 63, 83, § 174: caeli, id. 6, 34, 39, § 212.

circumplico.full: circum-plĭco, āvi, ātum, v. a. To wind, fold, or twine around: tum esset ostentum, si anguem vectis circumplicavisset, Cic. Div. 2, 28, 62: locum surculo, Gell. 17, 9, 14 (cf. id. 17, 9, 14, § 9): belua circumplicata serpentibus, Cic. Div. 1, 24, 49: puer serpentis amplexu, id. ib. 1, 36, 79.— To bend around, Lact. Opif. Dei, 12, 5.

circumplumbo.full: circum-plumbo, āre, a., to pour in lead around: modiolos, Cato, R. R. 20, 2.
circumplumbo.short: circum-plumbo, āre, a., to pour in lead around: modiolos, Cato, R.

circumpono.full: circum-pōno, pŏsui, pŏsĭtum, 3, v. a., to set, put, or place around (perh. not before the Aug. per.): ferulas, Cels. 8, 10, 1: stramenta, Plin. 17, 28, 47, § 263: armatos, * Suet. Caes. 30: piper catillis, * Hor. S. 2, 4, 75: nemus stagno, Tac. A. 14, 15; id. H. 2, 59.

circumpositio.full: circumpŏsĭtĭo, ōnis, f. circumpono, a setting or placing around (eccl. Lat.): auri, Aug. Ep. 199; Ambros. Ep. 38, 1.

circumpotatio.full: circumpōtātĭo, ōnis, f. poto, a drinking around in a funeral meal, Fragm. XII. Tab. ap. Cic. Leg. 2, 24, 60 Orell. N. cr.

circumpulso.full: circum-pulso, āre, v. a., to strike or beat around; of sounds: aures, to din, Stat. Th. 6, 228.

circumpungo.full: circum-pungo, ĕre, v. a., to prick or puncture around: clavum pedis, Cels. 5, 28, 14 (cf.: clavi circum scarificati, Plin. 22, 23, 49, § 101).

circumpurgo.full: circum-purgo, āre, v. a., to cleanse or purify around: dentem, Cels. 7, 12, 1; Ambros. Spir. Sanct. 1, 10, 113 init.

circumputo.full: circum-pŭto, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a., to measure all round: computato Oceano, Auct. Itin. Alex. M. 114.

circumquaque.full: circum-quāque, adv., on every side, all round, Auct. Orig. Gent. Rom. 17, 6.
circumquaque.short: circum-quāque, adv., on every side, all round, Auct.

circumrado.full: circum-rādo, rāsi, rāsum, ĕre, v. a., to scrape, shave, or pare around: tonsillas digito, Cels. 7, 12, n. 2: dentem, id. ib.: sarmentum circumrasum, Col. 4, 29, 14.

circumrasio.full: circumrāsĭo, ōnis, f. circumrado, a scraping or paring around: corticis, Plin. 17, 26, 39. § 246.

circumretio.full: circum-rētĭo, īvi, ītum, 4, v. a., to enclose with a net, insnare. Prop.: Martem et Venerem Vulcani esse circumretitos arte, Arn. 5, p. 186; cf. id. 4, p. 181; cf. circumnecto fin.— Trop.: aliquem, Lucr. 5, 1152: aliquem fraude, Sid. Ep. 5, 13: cum te implicatum severitate judicum, circumretitum frequentiă populi Romani esse videam, * Cic. Verr. 2, 5, 58, § 150.

circumrodo.full: circum-rōdo, di, 3, v. a., to gnaw or nibble all round. Prop.: escam, Plin. 32, 2, 5, § 12.— Trop.: dudum enim circumrodo, quod devorandum est, i. e. I have long hesitated to speak out, * Cic. Att. 4, 5, 1: qui Dente Theonino cum circumroditur, i. e. is slandered, calumniated, * Hor. Ep. 1, 18, 82.

circumrorans.full: circum-rōrans, antis, Part. [roro], sprinkling all round: aliquem, App. M. 11, p. 268, 21.

circumroto.full: circum-rŏto, āre, v. a., to turn round in a circle: caeli orbem, C. German. Fragm. 3, 9: machinas, App. M. 9, p. 222, 7.

circumsaepio.full: circum-saepĭo (-sēp-), sepsi, septum, īre, v. a., to hedge or fence round with something, to surround, enclose (not anteAug.): circumsepta loca parietibus, Col. 1, 6, 4; Dig. 41, 2, 3, § 14: stagnum aedificiis, * Suet. Ner. 31: solium circumsaeptum lapide Thrasio, on a platform of Thrasian marble, id. ib. 50: (Tarquinius) armatis corpus circumsepsit, Liv. 1, 49, 2.—Of a hostile surrounding: custodiis, Lact. 1, 14, 10: in quādam turre, Front. 1, 6, 5.—Trop.: īsdem ignibus circumsaepti, Cic. Har.

circumsaltans.full: circum-saltans, antis, Part. [salto], dancing around: chorus, Prud. adv. Symm. 1, 135.

circumscalptus.full: circum-scalptus, a, um, Part. [scalpo], scraped around: dentes, Plin. 20, 5, 15, § 32.

circumscariphicatus.full: circum-scărĭphĭcātus (circum-scărĭphātus, Plin. 30, 3, 8, § 21), a, um, Part. [scarifico], scarified around: clavi pedum, Plin. 22, 23, 49, § 101: dens, id. 30, 3, 8, § 21.

circumscindo.full: circum-scindo, ĕre, v. a., to rend, strip, or tear off around: aliquem et spoliare, Liv. 2, 55, 5.

circumscribo.full: circum-scrībo, psi, ptum, 3, v. a. Prop., to draw a line around, to circumscribe, enclose in a circle (in good prose; very freq. in Cic.): orbem, Cic. Fin. 5, 8, 23: lineas extremas umbrae, Quint. 10, 2, 7: virgulā stantem, Cic. Phil. 8, 8, 23: virgā regem, Liv. 45, 12, 5: aeneā fibulā pars auriculae latissima circumscribitur, Col. 6, 5, 4: terram surculo heliotropii, Plin. 22, 21, 29, § 60.— Trop. To draw a line as the circumference of a thing (cf. Quint. 12, 10, 5), i. e. to define, encompass,

circumscripte.full: circumscriptē, adv., v. circumscri, bo, P. a. 1. and 2.

circumscriptio.full: circumscriptĭo, ōnis, f. circumscribo. * Prop. (acc. to circumscribo, I.), an encircling, and (concrete) a circle: ex circumscriptione excedere, Cic. Phil. 8, 8, 23.— (Acc. to circumscribo, II. A.) A boundary, limit, outline, contour, circuit, compass (most freq. in Cic.): terrae situm, formam, circumscriptionem, Cic. Tusc. 1, 20, 45: aeternitas, quam nulla temporis circumscriptio metiebatur, id. N. D. 1, 9, 21: corporeae forma circumscriptionis, Arn. 2, 93; 3, 135.— In rhet. A period: verborum,

circumscriptor.full: circumscriptor, ōris, m. circumscribo. * (Acc. to circumscribo, II. C.) A defrauder, deceiver, cheat, * Cic. Cat. 2, 4, 7; * Juv. 15, 136; Sen. Exc. Contr. 6, 3; Cod. Th. 10, 10, 27, § 4.—* (Acc. to circumscribo, II. D.) He who makes void, annuls: sententiae suae, Tert. adv. Marc. 1, 27.

circumscriptorie.full: circumscriptōrĭē, adv., by fraud, deceit: agere aliquid, Lex Rom. Burg. tit. 36.
circumscriptorie.short: circumscriptōrĭē, adv., by fraud, deceit: agere aliquid, Lex Rom.

circumscriptus.full: circumscriptus, a, um, Part. and P. a., from circumscribo, q. v. fin.

circumseco.full: circum-sĕco, no perf., sectum āre, v. a., to cut or pare around: radices vitium, Cato, R. R. 114, 1: ungulas, Col. 6, 6, 4: tuberculum ferro, id. 7, 5, 13: aliquid serrulā, to saw around, * Cic. Clu. 64, 180: circumsecta aluta, Scrib. Comp. 229.—* To circumcise, of the Jews (usu. circumcido), Suet. Dom. 12.
circumseco.short: circum-sĕco, no perf., sectum āre, v.

circumsecus.full: circum-sĕcus, adv., round, round about, in the region around (only in App.): astantes, App. M. 2, p. 121, 11; 5, p. 166, 23; 11, p. 264, 33; cf. Hand, Turs. II. p. 74.
circumsecus.short: circum-sĕcus, adv., round, round about, in the region around (only in App.): astantes, App.

circumsedeo.full: circum-sĕdĕo (sĭdĕo), sēdi, sessum, 2, v. a., to sit around a person or thing, to surround. In gen., absol.: inter tot milia populi circumsedentis, App. M. 3, p. 130, 2; Sid. Ep. 3, 13.—With acc.: florentes amicorum turba circumsedet: circa eversos ingens solitudo est, Sen. Ep. 9, 9.— Esp., To encamp around in a hostile manner, to besiege, blockade, invest, encompass, beset (in Cic. and Liv. several times; elsewhere rare): qui Mutinam circumsedent, Cic. Phil. 7, 8, 21; 10, 4, 10; id. Deiot. 9, 2

circumseparo.full: circum-sēpăro, āre, to separate around: gingivas a dentibus, Cael. Aur. Tard. 2, 4, 74.
circumseparo.short: circum-sēpăro, āre, to separate around: gingivas a dentibus, Cael.

circumsero.full: circum-sĕro, ĕre, v. a., to sow, set, or plant around something: genistas alveariis, Plin. 21, 12, 42, § 72.

circumsessio.full: circumsessĭo, ōnis, f. circumsedeo, II., a hoslile encompassing, a besieging, Cic. Verr. 2, 1, 33, § 83.

circumsessus.full: circumsessus, a, um, Part., from circumsedeo.
circumsessus.short: circumsessus, a, um, Part., from circumsedeo.

circumsido.full: circum-sīdo, ĕre, v. a., to set or place one's self around in a hostile manner, to besiege (several times in Livy; elsewhere rare): Plistiam, Liv. 9, 21, 6; 36, 13, 7; 41, 19, 10; 42, 56, 5: regem urbemque Philippopolim, Tac. A. 3, 38.

circumsigno.full: circum-signo, āre, v. a., to mark around: gemmam, Col. 5, 11, 19; id. Arb. 26, 8; Pall. Jun. 5, 3.

circumsilio.full: circum-sĭlĭo, īre, v. n. salio, to spring, leap, or hop around (rare): (passer) circumsiliens modo huc, modo illuc, * Cat. 3, 9.— Trop., to leap about, surround: morborum omne genus, * Juv. 10, 218.

circumsisto.full: circum-sisto, stĕti (Caes. B. G. 3, 15 Oud. N. cr.; 4, 37; Curt. 15, 9, 10; Verg. A. 2, 559; Tac. A. 15, 15; id. H. 4, 79; cf. circumsto; rarely circumstiti, Tac. H. 3, 31), 3, v. a., to place one's self or take one's stand around a person or thing, to surround, go or stand around (class.; most freq. in the histt.; in Cic. perh. only once). With acc.: quid me circumsistitis? Plaut. Men. 5, 7, 9; so * Cat. 42, 10; Caes. B. G. 5, 7 fin.; 7, 5; id. B. C. 1, 20; id. B. G. 4, 26 Oud. N. cr.; Liv. 1,

circumsitus.full: circum-sĭtus, a, um, adj. sino, lying or situate around, neighboring: populi, Amm. 23, 6, 17, p. 358 Bip. al.

circumsocius.full: circum-sŏcĭus, a, um, adj., neighborly, in friendly neighborhood: nationes, Sext. Aur. Vict. Epit. 41.
circumsocius.short: circum-sŏcĭus, a, um, adj., neighborly, in friendly neighborhood: nationes, Sext.

circumsono.full: circum-sŏno, āre, v. n. and a. (rare but class.). Neutr., to sound, resound (with something) on every side, to be filled with any sound: locus, qui circumsonat ululatibus cantuque symphoniae, Liv. 39, 10, 7; 27, 18, 16; Vitr. 5, 8, 1; Manil. 5, 582. — Of the sound itself, to resound: dux theatri sui audiens plausum, in modum planctus, circumsonare, Flor. 4, 2, 45.— Act. To surround a thing with a sound, to make something to echo or resound, to fill everywhere with a sound: aures vocibus undique,

circumsonus.full: circum-sŏnus, a, um, adj., sounding all around. * Act., filling with sounds: turba canum, barking around, Ov. M. 4, 723.—* Pass., filled with sounds, resounding around: Thisbe avibus, Stat. Th. 7, 261.
circumsonus.short: circum-sŏnus, a, um, adj., sounding all around.

circumspectatrix.full: circum-spectātrix, īcis, f. spectator, she who looks or spies around, a spy, Plaut. Aul. 1, 1, 2: juvenum, App. Mag. 76, p. 323, 10.

circumspecte.full: circumspectē, adv., v. circumspicio, P. a. fin.

circumspectio.full: circumspectĭo, ōnis, f. circumspicio. * Prop., a looking on all sides, a looking about: singulorum, sibi horizontem facit, Macr. Somn. Scip. 1, 15, 17.— Trop., foresight, circumspection, caution (v. circumspicio, I. B.): circumspectio et accurata consideratio, Cic. Ac. 2, 11, 35; Fragm. Val. § 35: prudentiae insunt ratio, intellectus, circumspectio, Macr. Somn. Scip. 1, 8, 7.

circumspecto.full: circum-specto, āvi, ātum, āre, v. freq. a., to look about with attention, precaution, desire, etc.; to cast a look around, to search around; and with acc., to look about one's self (attentively, anxiously, etc.) after something, to look all around upon something (class.) Prop. Absol.: dum circumspecto, Plaut. Bacch. 2, 3, 45 (al.: me circumspecto): quanto se opere custodiant bestiae, ut in pastu circumspectent, Cic. N. D. 2, 49, 126: primum circumspectans tergiversari, Liv. 4, 14, 4; Plin. 8, 4,

circumspector.full: circumspector, ōris, m. circumspicio, a watcher, watchman, spy (late Lat.): septem circumspectores sedentes in excelso ad speculandum, Vulg. Ecclus. 37, 18: Deus, i. e. all-seeing, id. ib. 7, 12.

circumspectus1.full: circumspectus, a, um, v. circumspicio, P. a.

circumspectus2.full: circumspectus, ūs, m. circumspicio. Prop., a looking around eagerly, cautiously; a spying, searching around (rare but class.): cervix flexilis ad circumspectum, Plin. 11, 37, 67, § 177: (natura) circumspectum omnium nobis dedit, Sen. Ot. Sap. 5 (32), 4.— Trop.: malique In circumspectu stat sine fine sui, Ov. Tr. 4, 6, 44: ut distineret regem ab circumspectu rerum aliarum, consideration, Liv. 44, 35, 16.— Meton., a view around: facilis est circumspectus, unde exeam, quo progrediar, * Cic. Phil. 1

circumspergo.full: circum-spergo (-spargo, Apic. 8, 8, § 406; cf. aspergo), ĕre, v. a. To sprinkle, strew, or scatter something around: quaternos modios stercoris caprini, Col. 11, 2, 87: impensam talem, Apic. l. l.— To sprinkle with something all around: se purificantes aquā, Plin. 8, 1, 1, § 2.

circumspicientia.full: circumspĭcĭentĭa, ae, f. circumspicio, II. B., consideration, deliberation, Gell. 14, 2, 13.

circumspicio.full: circum-spĭcĭo, exi, ectum, 3 (perf. sync. circumspexti, Ter. Ad. 4, 5, 55; inf. sync. circumspexe, Varr. ap. Non. p. 106, 16, or Sat. Men. 82), v. n. and a. (class.). Neutr., to look about one's self, to cast a look around; or, with an obj.-clause, to observe, see, look about: circumspicedum, numquis est, Sermonem nostrum quiaucupet, see whether there is any one, Plaut. Most. 2, 2, 41; 2, 2, 43; Ter. And. 2, 2, 20; Varr. l. l.: suus conjux ubi sit circumspicit, Ov. M. 1, 605: circumspicere late,

circumstagno.full: circum-stagno, āre, v. n., to be poured forth all around: lacrimae, Tert. Pud. 22.

circumstantia.full: circumstantĭa, ae, f. circumsto (post-Aug. and rare). A standing round, a surrounding: hostium, Gell. 3, 7, 5: aquae, aëris, Sen. Q. N. 2, 7, 2 (as transl. of the Gr. ἀντιπερίστασις).—* Concr., a surrounding circle, a band, troop: angelorum, Tert. Or. 3.— Trop., the state, condition, circumstances, attribute, quality: rerum negotiorumque, Gell. 14, 1, 15; 14, 2, 2; Tert. Bapt. 17: hoc genus argumentorum sane dicamus ex circumstantiā, quia περίστασιν dicere aliter non possumus, * Quint. 5, 10, 10

circumstatio.full: circumstătĭo, ōnis, f. circumsto, a standing around; concr., a circle: militum, Gell. 7, 4, 4.

circumstipo.full: circum-stīpo or circum stīpo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a., to surround, accompany, attend (in post-Aug. poetry and rare).— Absol.: magnā circumstipante catervā, Sil. 10, 453.—Pass., Claud. Laud. Stil. 2, 356; id. VI. Cons. Hon. 595.
circumstipo.short: circum-stīpo or circum stīpo, āvi, ātum, 1, v.

circumsto.full: circum-sto, stĕti, 1, v. n. and a. (the perf. and pluperf. having the same form with those of circumsisto, and a similar meaning, it is sometimes doubtful to which verb a form belongs), to stand around in a circle, to take a station round; and, with the acc., to stand around a person or thing, to surround, encircle, encompass. Prop. (very freq. and class.). Absol.: circumstant cum ardentibus taedis, Enn ap. Cic. Ac. 2, 28, 89 (Trag. v. 51 Vahl.): circumstant lacrimis rorantes ora genasque, Lucr.

circumstrepo.full: circum-strĕpo, no perf., pĭtum, v. a. To make a noise around, to din with clamor, to cause to echo around (post-Aug.), (legatus) clamore seditiosorum circumstrepitur, Tac. H. 2, 44: fenestrae canticis circumstrepitae, App. Mag. 75, p. 322, 8; Sid. Ep. 7, 9; Manil. 1, 22.— Trop.: tothumanam vitam circumstrepentibus minis, Sen. Vit. Beat. 11, 1.— To cry or shout clamorously around (so only twice in Tac.): quidam atrociora circumstrepebant, Tac. A. 3, 36 fin.: ceteri circumstrepunt, iret in castra,

circumstridens.full: circum-strīdens, entis, Part. [strido], shrieking or gibbering around: larvae, Amm. 14, 11, 17.

circumstringo.full: circum-stringo, no perf., strictum, 3, v. a. (post-class.). * To bind about, to put on: aliquid alicui rei: habitus cervicibus circumstrictus, Tert. Pall. 1.— To tie around, to surround, clothe with: aliquid aliquā re: pallium, Tert. Pall. 5; id. Cor. Mil. 8.

circumstruo.full: circum-strŭo, no perf., ctum, 3, v. a., to build round about, surround with buildings (post-Aug. and mostly in part. pass.). Aliquid aliquā re: lacrimis arborum fores alveorum, Plin. 11, 6, 5, § 15; Col. 9, 6, 4: ripis undique circumstructis lapide, Plin. 19, 8, 48, § 163. aënum lateribus circumstructum, Dig. 19, 1, 38, § 2.— Aliquid circumstructo juxta Tiberim lacu, * Suet. Dom. 4; Col. 9, 7, 2; 9, 15, 11.

circumstupeo.full: circum-stŭpĕo, ēre, v. a., to look around with amazement, to stand amazed, Auct. Aetn. 336 dub. (al. circumstrepit).

circumsudans.full: circum-sūdans, antis, Part. [sudo], sweating on all sides: vinacea, Plin. 14, 1, 3, § 16.

circumsurgens.full: circum-surgens, entis, Part. [surgo], rising all around (post-Aug.): juga, Tac. A. 1, 64: mora, Cels. 7, 15, 6.

circumsutus.full: circum-sūtus, a, um, Part. [suo], sewed together all around (post-Aug.): linamenta, Cels. 8, 5: navigia corio, Plin. 4, 16, 30, § 104; 34, 16, 47, § 156.

circumtego.full: circum-tĕgo, ĕre, v. a., to cover round about (post-class.): corpus veste, Dict. Cret. 3, 11: arca testamenti circumtecta ex omni parte auro, Vulg. Heb. 9, 4; v. also the spurious line, Lucr. 1, 1094 Lachm. and Munro ad loc.

circumteneo.full: circum-tĕnĕo, ēre, to keep around, to possess, Vulg. 4 Esdr. 16, 40.
circumteneo.short: circum-tĕnĕo, ēre, to keep around, to possess, Vulg.

circumtentus.full: circum-tentus, a, um, Part. [tendo], bound or covered with something that is stretched or drawn around, begirt (anteand post-class.): elephanti corio, * Plaut. Mil. 2, 2, 80: vasculum linteolis, Cael. Aur. Acut. 3, 17, 174.

circumtergeo.full: circum-tergeo, ēre, v. a., to wipe around, Cato, R. R. 76, 2.

circumtermino.full: circum-termĭno, āre, 1, v. a., to bound or limit round about, Isid. Orig. 7, 8, 39.

circumtero.full: circum-tĕro, ĕre, v. a., to rub around, poet. for, to stand close around, crowd around: aliquem, Tib. 1, 2, 95.

circumtextus.full: circum-textus, a, um, Part. [texo], woven all around: velamen, Verg. A. 1, 649. —Subst.: circum-textum, i, n., a garment inwoven with purple: et quod amictui habet purpuram circum, vocant circumtextum, Varr. L. L. 5, § 132; cf. Isid. Orig. 19, 24, 10.

circumtinnio.full: circum-tinnĭo, īre, v. a., to ring or tinkle around, Varr. R. R. 3, 16, 30.

circumtollo.full: circum-tollo, ĕre, v. a., to remove on every side: corticem, Cael. Aur. Acut. 3, 4, 42.

circumtono.full: circum-tŏno, ui, 1, v. a., to thunder around; or, poet., to make a noise or clamor around: virum armis, Sil. 4, 254: aulam strepitu, id. 6, 216: montem undā, Claud. in Rufin. 1, 274.— Trop.: hunc circumtonuit gaudens Bellona cruentis (the figure taken from the clanging of the war-trumpets), Hor. S. 2, 3, 223.

circumtonsus.full: circum-tonsus, a, um, Part. [tondeo], shorn all around (rare). Prop., Varr. ap. Non. p. 179, 8; * Suet. Aug. 45: pinus, Petr. 131, 8, 3.—* Trop., of discourse: oratio circumtonsa et fucata et manu facta, elaborate, artificial, Sen. Ep. 115, 2.

circumtorqueo.full: circum-torquĕo, ēre, v. a., to twist or turn around: me retrorsum, App. M. 6, p. 186, 14.

circumtraho.full: circum-trăho, xi, ctum, 3, v. a., to draw or drag around (post-class.), Dict. Cret. 3, 15 fin; Cael. Aur. Tard. 2, 1.

circumtremo.full: circumtrĕmo (Lucr. 1, 1089), more correctly written apart, circum trĕmo.

circumtueor.full: circum-tuèŏr, ēri, v. dep. n., to look around, App. Flor. p. 341, 5.

circumtumulatus.full: circum-tŭmŭlātus, a, um, piled up around: saxa, Petr. 120, 15.
circumtumulatus.short: circum-tŭmŭlātus, a, um, piled up around: saxa, Petr.

circumundique.full: circum-undĭque, v. circum, I. A. b.

circumustus.full: circum-ustus, a, um uro, burnt around, Paul. ex Fest. p. 5, 3, Müll.
circumustus.short: circum-ustus, a, um uro, burnt around, Paul.

circumvado.full: circum-vādo, vāsi, 3, v. a., to assail or attack on every side, to encompass, beset (not ante-Aug.). Prop.: naves, Liv. 10, 2, 12: aliquem clamoribus turbidis, * Tac. A. 12, 43: redeuntem noctu, Plin. 9, 30, 48, § 92. —Pass., Amm. 20, 6, 3.— Trop., ofterror falling upon one (so only a few times in Liv.): novus terror cum ex parte utrāque circumvasisset aciem, Liv. 9, 40, 13: barbaros, id. 34, 21, 5: urbem, id. 34, 38, 6.

circumvagor.full: circum-văgor, āri, v. dep. n., to wander about, Vitr. 5, 8, 2.

circumvagus.full: circum-văgus, a, um, adj., wandering about, flowing around (very rare): oceanus, * Hor. Epod. 16, 41; cf. Auct. Pan. ad Pis. 19; Prud. Psych. 814.
circumvagus.short: circum-văgus, a, um, adj., wandering about, flowing around (very rare): oceanus, * Hor.

circumvallo.full: circum-vallo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a., to surround with a wall, to circumvallate; in milit. lang., to blockade, invest, encompass in a hostile manner (class., esp. in the histt.): circumvallare loci natura prohibebat, Caes. B. G. 7, 17; 7, 11; id. B. C. 3, 43; Liv. 10, 35, 12 and 15; 28, 3, 4, and in part. perf. pass. Caes. B. G. 7, 44 fin.; Cic. Att. 9, 12, 1; Liv. 43, 19, 9.— Trop.: tot res repente circumvallant, beset, beleaguer, Ter. Ad. 3, 2, 4.— In gen., to surround, encompass: locum duobus su

circumvectio.full: circumvectĭo, ōnis, f. circumveho (only twice in Cic.). A carrying around (of merchandise), Cic. Att. 2, 16, 4.— Solis, the circuit, revolution, Cic. Univ. 9, 26.

circumvectitor.full: circumvectĭtor, āri, 1, dep. a. [circum-vectito], to travel about, visit in succession: oppida circumvectitabor, Plaut. Rud. 4, 2, 28 Fleck.

circumvecto.full: circum-vecto, āre, v. freq. a., to carry around: Penates, Sil. 3, 291.—Hence, Esp., mid., to ride or sail around (rare): Ligurum oram, Liv. 41, 17, 7; cf. circumvectitor.—Poet., to go through, describe: +ugit irreparabile tempus, Singula dum capti circumvectamur amore, Verg. G. 3, 285 (dum speciatim cuncta describimus, Serv.).

circumvectus.full: circumvectus, a, um, Part. of circumvehor.

circumvehor.full: circum-vĕhor, vectus, 3, v. dep., to ride around (in a carriage or on horseback), to sail around (class., but not in Cic.); constr. absol. or with acc. dependent on circum: in terras orasque ultimas, Plaut. Most. 4, 3, 4: mare superum omne Graeciamque exoticam... Sumus circumvecti, id. Men. 2, 1, 13: classe Pharon, Auct. B. Alex. 14; cf. Tac. Agr. 10: classe ad Romanum agrum, Liv. 8, 26, 1: circumvectus Brundisii promunturium, id. 10, 2, 4; cf. id. 44, 28, 5: ab urbe ad aversa insulae, id. 37, 2

circumvelo.full: circum-vēlo, āre, v. a., to cover around, envelop: aurato circumvelatur amictu, Ov. M. 14, 263.

circumvenio.full: circum-vĕnĭo, vēni, ventum, 4, v. a., lit., to come around something; hence (the coming being considered as accomplished; cf. advenio and adventus, II.). Lit. In gen., to be around (a thing), to encircle, encompass, surround (rare): quibus succensis circumventi flammā exanimantur homines, Caes. B. G. 6, 16; cf.: donec ignium jactu circumveniretur, Tac. A. 15, 11; 15, 38: illum frequentia ingens circumvenit cum plausu, Petr. 92, 8: Cocytos sinu labens circumvenit atro, * Verg. A. 6, 132: omnium o

circumventio.full: circumventĭo, ōnis, f. circumvenio, II. B. 2., a circumventing, defrauding (postclass. and rare): adversarii, Dig. 4, 4, 17; Cod. Just. 2, 43, 3: innocentium, Aug. Civ. Dei, 22, 22.

circumventor.full: circumventor, ōris, m. id., a deceiver, defrauder, Lampr. Alex. Sev. 66.

circumventorius.full: circumventōrĭus, a, um, adj. circumventor, deceitful, fraudulent: obsequia, Aug. Conf. 3, 3.

circumventus.full: circumventus, a, um, Part., from circumvenio.
circumventus.short: circumventus, a, um, Part., from circumvenio.

circumversio.full: circumversĭo, ōnis, f. circumverto, a turning round, moving around, revolving (post-Aug. and rare): manus (in gesturing), * Quint. 11, 3, 105 Spald.: cursus annui, Amm. 26, 1, 11.

circumverso.full: circum-verso or circum verso (-vorso), āre, v. freq. a., to turn around (rare and only pass. in mid. sense): quaerentesque viam circumversantur, Lucr. 5, 520; 6, 200; Avien. Arat. 1528.
circumverso.short: circum-verso or circum verso (-vorso), āre, v.

circumversus.full: circum-versus, a, um, Part. [verro], brushed or swept around: locus purus, circumversus, Cato, R. R. 143, 2.

circumverto.full: circum-verto or circum verto (-vorto), ĕre, v. a., to turn around (rare; not in Cic.): citius quam rotula circumvortitur, Plaut. Pers. 3, 3, 39; cf.: rota circumvertitur axem, turns or is turned around on its axis, Ov. M. 15, 522 (Merkel, circumvolvitur): ubi circumvortor, cado, turn myself around, Plaut. Ps. 5, 1, 32; cf.: circumvertens se, turning one's self to the right side, * Suet. Vit. 2; v. the commentt. in h. l.: mancipium, to declare free, Quint. Decl. 342; v. circumago, I. B. (in Plaut
circumverto.short: circum-verto or circum verto (-vorto), ĕre, v.

circumvestio.full: circum-vestĭo, īre, v. a. To clothe or cover over (very rare): arborem, Plin. 17, 23, 35, § 208.—In a figure: aliquem amictu prudentiae, Ambros. Virg. 12, 48.—* Poet., of one who uses language to conceal his thoughts: se circumvestire dictis, to wrap himself up in words, Poët. ap. Cic. de Or. 3, 39, 158 (Trag. Rel. inc. v. 113 Rib.).

circumvincio.full: circum-vincĭo, no perf., vinctum, 4, v. a., to bind around: juncis murteta, aliquem virgis, Plaut. Rud. 3, 4, 27; Avien. Perieg. 331.

circumviso.full: circum-vīso, ĕre, v. a., to look around at, glare round upon: set angues oculis omnis circumvisere, Plaut. Am. 5, 1, 58.

circumvolitabilis.full: circumvŏlĭtābĭlis, e, adj. circumvolito, flying round: aër, Mart. Cap. 6, § 584.

circumvolito.full: circum-vŏlĭto or circum vŏlĭto, āvi, 1, v. a. and n. (mostly post-Aug.). Prop., to fly around something: lacus circumvolitavit hirundo, * Verg. G. 1, 377: thyma, * Hor. Ep. 1, 3, 21.—Absol.: circumvolitantium alitum, Tac. H. 2, 50.— In gen., of men, to rove about a place, to hover around; absol.: et circumvolitant equites, * Lucr. 2, 329; Sil. 9, 420: limina potentiorum, Col. praef. 1, § 9: agmina infestorum equitum ad conquirendas proscriptorum latebras circumvolitantia, Sen. Ira, 2, 9, 3.
circumvolito.short: circum-vŏlĭto or circum vŏlĭto, āvi, 1, v.

circumvolo.full: circum-vŏlo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. (not ante-Aug.). Prop., to fly around: turba (Harpyiae) praedam circumvolat, Verg. A. 3, 233: seu (me) mors atris circumvolat alis, Hor. S. 2, 1, 58; so Verg. A. 2, 360: caput, id. ib. 6, 866; Ov. M. 2, 719; 14, 507: sedem, Quint. 2, 6, 7: aliquem, * Suet. Aug. 97.—Pass.: nave circumvolatā ab halcyone, Plin. 10, 32, 47, § 90.— In gen., to run or hasten around: ordines exercitus, Vell. 2, 27, 2: jaculo campum, Sil. 17, 416.

circumvoluto.full: circum-vŏlūto, āre, v. a., to roll around, pass. in mid. force, Plin. 8, 17, 21, § 59.

circumvolvo.full: circum-volvo, no perf., vŏlūtum, 3, v. a., only with se or mid., to roll one's self around, to roll round, revolve, wind, or twine around (prob. not ante-Aug.): aliquid or alicui rei: magnum sol circumvolvitur annum, Verg. A. 3, 284: rota perpetuum circumvolvitur axem, Ov. M. 15, 522 Merkel: herba arboribus circumvolvens se, Plin. 16, 44, 92, § 244: serpentes circumvolutae sibi ipsae, id. 10, 62, 82, § 169; 11, 37, 88, § 217; Vitr. 10, 6, 2; Gell. 11, 9, 1.

circus.full: circus, i, m., = κίρκος [kindr. with κρίκος; Dor. κίρκος, and κορώνη; cf.: κυλινδέω, κυλλός, cirrus, curvus]. A circular line, circle, in astronomy (less freq. than circulus): quot luna circos annuo in cursu institit, Att. ap. Non. p. 20, 28: circus lacteus, the Milky Way, Macr. Somn. Scip. 1, 15, 2; cf.: candens circus, Lacteus hic notatur, Cic. Arat. 248 (492): illum incolunt locum ... erat autem is splendidissimo candore inter flammas circus elucens, id. Rep. 6, 16, 16 B. and K.: globus et ci

ciris.full: cīris, is, f., = κεῖρις, a bird (acc. to Hyg. Fab. 198, a fish = κίρρις, Etym. M.), into which Scylla, the daughter of Nisus, was changed, Ov. M. 8, 151; Verg. Cir. 488 sq.
ciris.short: cīris, is, f., = κεῖρις, a bird (acc.

cirratus.full: cirrātus, a, um, adj. cirrus. Curled, having ringlets (post-Aug.), Mart. 9, 30: feminae, Amm. 14, 6, 20.—Subst.: cir-rāti, Pers. 1, 29.— Vestes, fringed, Capitol. Pert. 8.

cirrha.full: Cirrha (Cirra), ae, f., = Κίρρα, a very ancient town in Phocis, near Delphi, devoted to Apollo, Liv. 42, 15, 5; Stat. Th. 3, 474; Luc. 3, 172; Mart, 1, 77; cf. Mel. 2, 3, 10; Plin. 4, 3, 4, § 7.—Hence, Cirrhaeus (Cirraeus), a, um, adj., of or pertaining to Cirrha, or (in post-Aug. poets freq.) to Apollo: campi, Plin. 4, 3, 4, § 7: templa, Sen. Herc. Oet. 92: Cirrhaea vates, i. e. of Delphi, Delphic, of the Pythia, Sen. Oedip. 269; cf. virgo, Stat. Th. 3, 106: Cirrhaeus vates, of Apollo, Juv. 13,
cirrha.short: Cirrha (Cirra), ae, f., = Κίρρα, a very ancient town in Phocis, near Delphi, devoted to Apollo, Liv.

cirritus.full: cirrītus, a, um, adj. cirrus, having filaments: pirum, a kind of pear, Cloat. ap. Macr. S. 2, 15, 16; cf. Not. Tir. p. 155.

cirrus.full: cirrus, i, m. (used mostly in plur.), a (natural) lock, curl, ringlet, or tuft of hair (rare): cirri, Varr. ap. Non. p. 94, 21; Mart. 10, 83.—Sing.: cirrus, Juv. 13, 165.—Also, the hair on the forehead of a horse, Veg. 2, 28, 34; 6, 2, 1.— Transf. A tuft of feathers or crest of birds, Plin. 11, 37, 44, § 122.— The arms of polypi, Plin. 9, 28, 44, § 83; 25, 7, 33, § 70; 26, 8, 37, § 58.— Filaments of plants similar to tufts of hair, Plin. 26, 7, 20, § 36; 27, 4, 9, § 25.— A fringe upon a tunic, P

cirsion.full: cirsĭon, i, n., = κίρσιον, a kind of thistle, Plin. 27, 8, 39, § 61.
cirsion.short: cirsĭon, i, n., = κίρσιον, a kind of thistle, Plin.

cirta.full: Cirta, ae, f., = Κίρτα, an important town in Numidia, now Constantine, Mel. 1, 6, 1; Plin. 5, 3, 2, § 22; Sall. J. 21, 2; 26, 1; 101, 1; 102, 1; Liv. 29, 32, 14 al.—Cirten-ses, ium, m., its inhabitants, Liv. 30, 12, 8; Tac. A. 3, 74; Dig. 22, 6, 9, § 5.
cirta.short: Cirta, ae, f., = Κίρτα, an important town in Numidia, now Constantine, Mel.

cis.full: cis, prep. pronom. stem ki-, whence -ce; Gr. ἐ-κεῖ; cf.: hic, sic, etc. (far more rare than the kindr. citra), on this side (opp. uls, ultra, and trans; cf. Varr. L. L. 5, § 83 Müll.; Liv. 5, 35, 4; 5, 33, 9 al.); with acc. In space. With verb of motion (rare): eo die cis Tiberim redeundum est, Varr. ap. Non. p. 92, 11.— With verb of rest: Oppius mons, terticeps cis lucum Exquilinum, Sacr. Argae. ap. Varr. L. L. 5, § 50 Müll.: cis Tiberim redire, Liv. 8, 14, 6: Gallia cis Rhenum perdomita, Sall.

cisalpinus.full: Cis-alpīnus, a, um, adj., lying on this side of the Alps, Cisalpine (very freq.): Gallia, Cic. Imp. Pomp. 12, 35; Caes. B. G. 6, 1: Galli, Liv. 27, 38, 6: provincia, Suet. Caes. 29.
cisalpinus.short: Cis-alpīnus, a, um, adj., lying on this side of the Alps, Cisalpine (very freq.): Gallia, Cic.

cisiarius.full: cĭsĭārĭus, ii, m. cisium. The driver of a cabriolet, Dig. 19, 2, 13.—Plur.: CISIARIEI, C. I. L. 1, 1165.— The maker of a cabriolet, Inscr. Orell. 4109; 4163.

cisium.full: cĭsĭum, ii, n., a light two-wheeled vehicle, a cabriolet (vehiculi biroti genus, Non. p. 86, 30), Cic. Phil. 2, 31, 77; id. Rosc. Am. 7, 19; Vitr. 10, 1, 6; Aus. Ep. 8, 6; gen. cisi, Verg. Cat. 8, 3 Burm.; cf. Becker, Gall. 3, p. 9; Dict. of Antiq.
cisium.short: cĭsĭum, ii, n., a light two-wheeled vehicle, a cabriolet (vehiculi biroti genus, Non.

cismontanus.full: cis-montānus, a, um, adj., situate on this side of the mountain: Aufinates, Plin. 3, 12, 17, § 106.
cismontanus.short: cis-montānus, a, um, adj., situate on this side of the mountain: Aufinates, Plin.

cisorium.full: cīsōrĭum, ii, n. caedo, a cutting instrument: ossis, Veg. 3, 22, 1.

cispellam.full: cispellam, a false read. for aspellam, Plaut. Am. 3, 4, 17.

cispius1.full: Cispĭus, a, um, a Roman gentile name; e. g. M. Cispius, Cic. post Red. in Sen. 8, 21; id. Planc. 31, 75 al.
cispius1.short: Cispĭus, a, um, a Roman gentile name;

cispius2.full: Cispĭus (also Cespĭus, old form in Varr. L. L. 5, § 50 Müll.): mons, one of the peaks of the Mons Esquilinus, now the church S. Maria Maggiore, Varr. L. L. l. l.; Gell. 15, 1, 2; Fest. p. 348, 28; p. 351, 1; Paul. ex Fest. p. 42, 11; cf. Becker, Antiq. 1, p. 534 sq.
cispius2.short: Cispĭus (also Cespĭus, old form in Varr.

cisrhenanus.full: Cis-rhēnānus, a, um, adj., situate on this side of the Rhine: Germani, Caes. B. G. 6, 2.
cisrhenanus.short: Cis-rhēnānus, a, um, adj., situate on this side of the Rhine: Germani, Caes.

cissanthemos.full: cissanthĕmŏs, i, f., = κισσάνθεμος, a plant similar to ivy, a species of cyclaminos, Plin. 25, 9, 68, § 116; 26, 15, 90, § 156.
cissanthemos.short: cissanthĕmŏs, i, f., = κισσάνθεμος, a plant similar to ivy, a species of cyclaminos, Plin.

cissaros.full: cissărŏs, i, f., or -on, i, n., the plant also called chrysanthemon, App. Herb. 17.
cissaros.short: cissărŏs, i, f., or -on, i, n., the plant also called chrysanthemon, App.

cisseus.full: Cisseus, ĕi, m., = Κισσεύς. A king of Thrace; acc. to a later myth, father of Hecuba, Verg. A. 5, 537; Hyg. Fab. 91; 911; who is on this account called Cissēïs, Verg. A. 7, 320 Serv.; 10, 705.— A companion of Turnus, acc. Cissea, Verg. A. 10, 317.

cission.full: cissĭon, ĭi, n., = κισσίον, small ivy, App. Herb. 98.
cission.short: cissĭon, ĭi, n., = κισσίον, small ivy, App.

cissis.full: Cissis, is, f., a town in Hispania Tarraconensis, Liv. 21, 60, 7 sq. Alschefski ad loc.
cissis.short: Cissis, is, f., a town in Hispania Tarraconensis, Liv.

cissitis.full: cissītis, is, f., = κισσῖτις, a precious stone of the color of ivy-leaves, Plin. 37, 11, 73, § 188.
cissitis.short: cissītis, is, f., = κισσῖτις, a precious stone of the color of ivy-leaves, Plin.

cissos.full: cissŏs, i, f., = κισσός. Ivy, Plin. 16, 34, 62, § 152.— Cissos erythranos, an ivylike plant, Plin. 24, 10, 49, § 82.* † cissўbĭum, ĭi, n., = κισσύβιον, a cup of ivy-wood, Macr. S. 5, 21, 11.

cista.full: cista, ae, f., = κίστη, a wooden box or basket, often woven of slips or twigs, used for keeping money, clothes, books, fruit, etc. In gen., Plin. 15, 17, 18, § 60; 16, 40, 77, § 209; Cic. Verr. 2, 3, 85, § 197; * Hor. Ep. 1, 17, 54; Ov. M. 2, 554; Col. 12, 54, 2; Poët. ap. Quint. 8, 3, 19; Juv. 3, 206; 6, 44; Dig. 16, 3, 1.— Esp. In mystical religious festivals, a box for holding the sacred utensils, Cat. 64, 259; Ov. A. A. 2, 609; Tib. 1, 7, 48; Val. Fl. 2, 267; App. M. 6, p. 174; 11, p. 262.—
cista.short: cista, ae, f., = κίστη, a wooden box or basket, often woven of slips or twigs, used for keeping money, clothes, books, fruit, etc.

cistella.full: cistella, ae, f. dim. cista, a small chest or box, Plaut. Cist. 3, 7; 4, 1, 3 sq.; id. Rud. 4, 4, 65 sq.; Ter. Eun. 4, 6, 15; Auct. Her. 1, 12, 21 dub. (al. sitella).

cistellaria.full: Cistellārĭa, ae, f. cistella, the title of a comedy of Plautus; cf. Varr. L. L. 7, § 64; Non. p. 63, 33.

cistellatrix.full: cistellātrix, īcis, f. id., she who has charge of the money-box (a kind of female slave), Plaut. Trin. 2, 1, 25 (253 Ritschl).

cistellula.full: cistellŭla, ae, f. dim. id., a little box or chest, Plaut. Am. 2, 2, 141 Ussing (Fleck. cistula); id. Rud. 2, 3, 60; 4, 4, 34.

cisterna.full: cisterna, ae, f. cista, a subterranean reservoir for water, a cistern, Varr. R. R. 1, 11, 2; Col. 1, 5, 2; Sen. Ep. 86, 3; Plin. 31, 3, 21, § 31; 36, 23, 52, § 173; Mart. 3, 56, 1; Tac. H. 5, 12 al.—For preserving wine, Dig. 47, 2, 21, § 5.

cisterninus.full: cisternīnus, a, um, adj. cisterna, of or pertaining to cisterns, cistern-: aqua, Col. 12, 43, 6; Cael. Aur. Tard. 5, 10; Veg. 2, 28, 18; 6, 8, 3.

cisthena.full: Cisthēna, ae, f., = Κισθήνη, a town of Æolis, Plin. 5, 30, 32, § 122; Mel. 1, 18, 2.
cisthena.short: Cisthēna, ae, f., = Κισθήνη, a town of Æolis, Plin.

cisthos.full: cisthos, i, m., = κίσθος (usu. κίστος), a shrubby plant with red blossoms, Plin. 24, 10, 48, § 81.

cistiberis.full: Cis-tĭbĕris, e, adj., = cis Tiberim, on this side of the Tiber: quinqueviri, Dig. 1, 2, 2, § 33: magistratus, Pomp. Orig. Jus. § 33 Osann.
cistiberis.short: Cis-tĭbĕris, e, adj., = cis Tiberim, on this side of the Tiber: quinqueviri, Dig.

cistifer.full: cistĭfer, ĕri, m. cista-fero, the bearer of a box or chest, Mart. 5, 17, 4.

cistophorus.full: cistŏphŏrus or -ŏs, i, m., = κιστοφόρος. The bearer of the sacred box, Inscr. Orell. 2318.— An Asiatic coin of the value of about four drachms, on which a cista was stamped, Cic. Att. 2, 6, 2; 2, 16, 4; 11, 1, 2; id. Dom. 20, 52.—Gen. plur. cistophorūm, Liv. 37, 46, 3; 39, 7, 1; Paul. ex Fest. p. 78.

cistula.full: cistŭla, ae, f. dim. cista, a little box, chest, or basket, Plaut. Am. 1, 1, 264; id. Rud. 2, 3, 58; 4, 4, 38 sq.; Mart. 4, 46, 13; App. M. 9, p. 236, 40.

citate.full: cĭtātē, adv., v. 2. cito, P. a. fin.

citatim.full: cĭtātim, adv. citatus, cito, quickly, speedily, hastily (very rare), Auct. B. Afr. 80; comp. and sup., v. 2. cito fin.

citatio.full: cĭtātĭo, ōnis, f. 2. cito. In law, the calling, proclaiming: edictorum sollemnium, Cod. Just. 1, 12, 6, § 4.— Milit. t. t., the command, Hyg. Grom. § 43, p. 91.

citatorium.full: cĭtātōrĭum, ii, n. 2. cito, a summoning before a tribunal, Cod. Th. 6, 28, 5.

citatus.full: cĭtātus, a, um, v. 2. cito, P. a.

cite.full: cĭtē, adv., v. cieo, P. a. fin.

citer.full: cĭter, tra, trum (comp. citerior; sup. citimus; most freq. in comp.; in posit. only Cato ap. Prisc. pp. 589 and 999 P.; and Afran. ap. Prisc. p. 607 ib.), adj. cis. On this side: citer agnus (ager) alligatus ad sacra erit, Cato ap. Prisc. pp. 599 and 989 P.: alter ulteriorem Galliam decernit cum Syriā, alter citeriorem, Cic. Prov. Cons. 15, 36: citerior provincia (i. e. Gallia Cisalpina), Caes. B. G. 1, 10: in Galliā citeriore, id. ib. 1, 24; Hirt. B. G. 8, 23; Suet. Caes. 56: citerior Hispania,

citeria.full: cĭtĕrĭa, ae, f., an effigy or caricature carried in procession at the games, Paul. ex Fest. p. 59, 20 Müll.; Cato ib.
citeria.short: cĭtĕrĭa, ae, f., an effigy or caricature carried in procession at the games, Paul.

cithaeron.full: Cĭthaeron (Cĭthĕron, Aus. Idyll. 11, 32), ōnis, m., = Κιθαιρών, a mountain of Bœotia, now Elatia, sacred to Bacchus and the Muses, and famous for the death of Pentheus and Actœon, Mel. 2, 3, 4; Plin. 4, 7, 12, § 25; Verg. G. 3, 43; id. A. 4, 303; Ov. M. 2, 223; 3, 702 sq.; Sen. Oedip. 930; id. Phoen. 256; Val. Fl. 5, 81 (in all these passages only in nom.).—Gen. Cithaeronis, Prop. 3 (4), 1, 43; 3 (4), 15, 25; Liv. 31, 26, 1.—Acc. Cithaeronem, Lact. 1, 22, 15; Serv. ad Verg. A. 7, 641; 10, 163; i

cithara.full: cĭthăra, ae, f., = κιθάρα, the cithara, cithern, guitar, or lute (very freq. in the poets, esp. in Hor.), Lucr. 2, 28; 4, 981; Tib. 2, 3, 12; 2, 5, 2; Verg. A. 6, 120; 9, 776; Hor. C. 1, 15, 15; 2, 12, 4; Varr. L. L. S, § 61 Müll.; id. R. R. 2, 1, 3; Auct. Her. 4, 47, 60; Plin. 7, 56, 57, § 204; Quint. 1, 10, 3; 1, 10, 10; 2, 8, 15; Tac. A. 14, 14; 15, 65 al.— Meton., the music of the cithara, or, in gen., of a stringed instrument, the art of playing on the cithara, Prop. 2 (3), 10, 10; Verg. A.
cithara.short: cĭthăra, ae, f., = κιθάρα, the cithara, cithern, guitar, or lute (very freq.

citharicen.full: cĭthărĭcen, cĭnis, m. cithara-cano; cf. tubicen, the player on the cithara (unused); cf. Varr. L. L. 8, § 61 Müll.

citharista.full: cĭthărista, ae, m., = κιθαριστής, a player on the cithara (mostly in Cic.), Cic. Phil. 5, 6, 15; id. Div. 2, 64, 133.—Esp., a statue of a player on the cithara: etiam illum Aspendium citharistam, de quo saepe audistis id quod est Graecis hominibus in proverbio, quem omnia intus canere dicebant, sustulit, i. e. he was so skilfully represented that he seemed to be playing the music inwardly, though it was unheard, Cic. Verr. 2, 1, 20, § 53 Zumpt ad loc.
citharista.short: cĭthărista, ae, m., = κιθαριστής, a player on the cithara (mostly in Cic.), Cic.

citharistria.full: cĭthăristrĭa, ae, f., = κιθαρίστρια, she who plays on the cithara, Ter. Phorm. 1, 2, 32; 1, 2, 94; Sid. Ep. 9, 13, 2; Porphyr. ad Hor. C. 1, 1.
citharistria.short: cĭthăristrĭa, ae, f., = κιθαρίστρια, she who plays on the cithara, Ter.

citharizo.full: cĭthărīzo, āre, v n., = κιθαρίζω, to play on or strike the cithara, Nep. Epam. 2, 1; Vulg. Apoc. 14, 2.
citharizo.short: cĭthărīzo, āre, v n., = κιθαρίζω, to play on or strike the cithara, Nep.

citharoedicus.full: cĭthăroedĭcus, a, um, adj., = κιθαρῳδικός, of or pertaining to the citharœdi: ars, Plin. 9, 8, 8, § 28; Suet. Ner. 40: habitus, id. ib. 25; Eutr. 7, 14: vestis, Dig. 50, 16, 127.
citharoedicus.short: cĭthăroedĭcus, a, um, adj., = κιθαρῳδικός, of or pertaining to the citharœdi: ars, Plin.

citharoedus.full: cĭthăroedus, i, m., = κιθαρῳδός, one who plays on the cithara, accompanying it with the voice (diff. from citharista by the accompanying singing), Cic. Mur. 13, 29; id. de Or. 2, 80, 325; id. Tusc. 5, 40, 116; Varr. R. R. 2, 1, 3; * Hor. A. P. 355; Quint 1, 12, 3; 4, 1, 2; 11, 3, 88; Suet. Ner. 20, 21; 20, 22; 20, 41; id. Vit. 4; id. Dom. 4 al.—In fem.: CITHAROEDA, ae, she who plays on and sings to the cithara, Inscr. Orell. 2611.— Prov.: non omnes, qui habent citharam, sunt citharoedi, Varr. R.
citharoedus.short: cĭthăroedus, i, m., = κιθαρῳδός, one who plays on the cithara, accompanying it with the voice (diff.

citime.full: cĭtĭmē, adv., and cĭtĭmus, a, um, adj, v. citer.
citime.short: cĭtĭmē, adv., and cĭtĭmus, a, um, adj, v.

citipes.full: cĭtĭ-pēs, pĕdis, adj. citus, swiftfooted, fleet: cursus, Diom, p. 472 P.

citiremis.full: cĭtĭrēmis, e, adj. citus - remus, rowed swiftly: Argo, Varr. ap. Charis. p. 94 P

citium.full: Cĭtĭum (more rare Cittĭum), i, n., = Κίτιον (Κίττιον). A seaport town in Cyprus, now Khiti, the birthplace of the Stoic Zeno, Plin. 5, 31, 35, § 130; Nep. Cim. 3, 4.—Hence, Cĭtĭēus, i, m., a Citian: Zeno, Cic. Tusc. 5, 12, 34.—In plur., Cic. Fin. 4, 20, 56.— Cĭtĭensis, is, m., the same: Zeno, Gell. 17, 21.—In plur., Dig. 50, 12, 1. — A town in Macedonia, Liv. 42, 51, 1 and 2.
citium.short: Cĭtĭum (more rare Cittĭum), i, n., = Κίτιον (Κίττιον).

citius.full: Cĭtĭus, i, m. (mons), a mountain in Macedonia, Liv. 43, 21, 7.

cito1.full: cĭtŏ, adv., v. cieo, P. a. fin.

cito2.full: cĭto, āvi, ātum (part. perf. gen. plur. citatūm, Att. ap. Non. p. 485; inf. pass. citarier, Cat. 61, 42), 1, v. freq. a. cieo. To put into quick motion, to move or drive violently or rapidly, to hurl, shake, rouse, excite, provoke, incite, stimulate, promote, etc. (mostly post-Aug. and poet.; in earlier authors usu. only in P. a.): citat hastam, Sil. 4, 583: arma, Stat. Th. 8, 124: gradum, Claud. VI. Cons. Hon. 510: urinam, Cels. 2, 19: pus, id. 5, 28, n. 13: umorem illuc, id. 4, 6: alvum, Col.

citocacium.full: citŏcăcĭum, ĭi, n., the plant chamelaea, App. Herb. 111.
citocacium.short: citŏcăcĭum, ĭi, n., the plant chamelaea, App.

citrago.full: cī^trāgo (also cĭtrĕāgo in MSS.), ĭnis, f. citrus, the citrus-plant, lemon-balm, Pall. 1, 37, 2; 5, 8, 6.
citrago.short: cī^trāgo (also cĭtrĕāgo in MSS.), ĭnis, f.

citrarius.full: cī^trārĭus, ĭi, m., a dealer in lemons, Inscr. Orell. 4811.
citrarius.short: cī^trārĭus, ĭi, m., a dealer in lemons, Inscr.

citratus1.full: cī^trātus, a, um, adj. citrus, steeped in citrus-oil: libri, Plin. 13, 13, 27, § 86.

citratus2.full: cī^trātus, a, um a late adj. form of citra, of this side, Auct. Limit. p. 298 sq.
citratus2.short: cī^trātus, a, um a late adj.

citretum.full: cī^trētum. i, n. citrus, an orchard of citrus-trees, Pall. Febr. 24, 14.

citreus.full: cī^trĕus, a. um, adj. id.. Of or pertaining to the citrus-tree: mālus, the citrustree, Opp. ap. Macr. S. 2, 15: malum, citrusapple, Cloat. ib.: mensa, of citrus-wood (which was much prized by the ancients), Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 17, § 37: sub trabe citreā, Hor. C. 4, 1, 20 Zumpt; Petr. 119, 29; Mart. 14, 89: lecti, Pers. 1, 53: oleum, Plin. 23, 4, 45, § 88.— Subst.: cĭtrĕa, ae, f., = ci-trus, Plin. 16, 26, 44, § 107.— Pertaining to the citron-tree; only subst. cĭtrĕ-um, i, n., the citron, Plin. 23, 6

citrium.full: citrĭum, ii, n., a kind of gourd, Apic. 1, 21; 4, 3.
citrium.short: citrĭum, ii, n., a kind of gourd, Apic.

citro.full: cī^trō, adv., v. citer, adv., B.

citrosus.full: cī^trōsus, a, um, adj. citrus, smelling of citrus: vestis, Naev. ap. Macr. S. 2, 15, 5 (cf. εἵματα θυώδεα, Hom. Od. 5, 264 al.; in Paul. ex Fest. p. 42, 14 Müll. erron.: citrosa vestis appellata est a similitudine citri; so also Isid. Orig. 19, 22, 20).

citrum.full: cī^trum, i, n. id., the wood of the citrus, q. v., citrus-wood, Plin. 16, 43, 84, § 231.— Meton., the household furniture, esp. tables, made of it (very costly), Cato ap. Fest. p. 242, 21 Müll.; Vell. 2, 56, 2; Mart. 9, 59, 10; 10, 98, 6; 10, 80, 2; cf. citrus, I.

citrus.full: cī^trus, i prob. a mutilation of κέδρος, cedrus. The citrus, an African tree (hence Atlantis silva, Luc. 10, 144, and Massyla robora, Stat. S. 3, 3, 94), whose very fragrant wood (v. citrum) was used in making household furniture, and was prized very highly, Plin. 13, 15, 29, § 91 sq.; 13, 16, 30, § 100; Varr R. R. 3, 2, 4; Luc. 9, 428; cf. citreus, I. and citrum.— The citrontree (also called malus Medica, Persica, etc.), Citrus Medica, Linn., whose fruit and leaves were laid between the folds o

citus.full: cĭtus, a, um, v. cieo, P. a.

civicus.full: cīvĭcus, a, um, adj. civis. Of or pertaining to citizens, civil, civic, citizens (more rare than the class. civilis, and, except in the phrase civica corona, mostly poet.): jura, Hor. Ep. 1, 3, 23: motus, id. C. 2, 1, 1: rabies, id. ib. 3, 24, 26; Flor. 3, 21, 5; cf. furor, id. 4, 2, 75: bella, Ov. P. 1, 2, 126: invidia, Sil. 8, 21: arma pro trepidis reis, i. e. defence before a tribunal, Ov. F. 1, 22.— Esp. corona civica, the civic crown, made of oak leaves (hence, civilis quercus, Verg. A. 6,

civilis1.full: cīvīlis, e, adj. civis. Of or pertaining to citizens, civil, civic (class. in prose and poetry, and very freq.): sanguine civili rem conflant, by the blood of citizens, * Lucr. 3, 70; Cic. Fam. 15, 15, 1: conjuratio, id. ib. 5, 12, 2: bellum, id. Att. 7, 13, 1; id. Imp. Pomp. 10, 28: bella, Hor. Epod. 16, 1; Luc. 1, 1: genus belli, Cic. Att. 7, 13, 1; Sall. C. 47, 2; Quint. 12, 1, 16; Flor. 3, 22, 10; 3, 23, 7: facinus, Cic. Att. 7, 13, 1.—So De Bello Civili, the title of a portion of the Commen

civilis2.full: Cīvīlis, is, m., a proper name, e. g. Julius Civilis, chief of the Batavi, Tac. H. 4, 13 sq.; abl. Civile, id. ib. 4, 35.
civilis2.short: Cīvīlis, is, m., a proper name, e.

civilitas.full: cīvīlĭtas, ātis, f. civilis. (Acc. to civilis, I. B.) The art of government, politics, only three times in Quint. as transl. of the Gr. πολιτική, 2, 15, 25; 2, 15, 33; 2, 17, 14. — (Acc. to civilis, II.) Courteousness, politeness, affability (post-Aug. and rare), Suet. Aug. 51; id. Claud. 35; Eutr. 7, 21; Lampr. Alex. Sev. 20.

civis.full: cīvis (cīves, C. I. L. 3, 966; 3337 et saep.; ceivis, S. C. Bacch. and Lex Thoria; ceus in Tab. Bant.), is, comm. (abl. usually cive: civi, Plaut. Pers. 4, 3, 6; Cic. Verr. 2, 2, 13, §§ 32 and 33 Zumpt N. cr.; id. Planc. 40, 96; 41, 97; id. Sest. 12, 29; id. Balb. 19, 43; id. Att. 7, 3, 4; 14, 11, 1; cf. Prisc. p. 766 P.; dub. Cic. Phil. 5, 19, 52) [root ki- of κεῖμαι, to lie, abide; cf. κώμη], a citizen (male or female; opp. pe regrinus, Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 35, § 77; id. Off. 1, 34, 124; Liv. 22,

civitas.full: cīvĭtas, ātis (gen. plur. civitatium, Cic. Rep. 1, 34, 51; id. Leg. 2, 4, 9; Caes. B. G. 4, 3; 5, 22; Sall. C. 40, 2; Liv. 1, 17, 4; 2, 6, 5; 33, 20, 11 Drak.; 42, 30, 6; 42, 44, 1; 45, 34, 1; Vell. 2, 42, 2; Quint. 2, 16, 4 N. cr.; Suet. Tit. 8 Oud.; Cornut. ap. Charis. p. 100 P.; cf. Varr. L. L. 8, § 66; Prisc. p. 771 P.; Neue, Formenl. 1, 268), f. civis. Abstr., the condition or privileges of a (Roman) citizen, citizenship, freedom of the city (upon its conditions, v. Zimmern, Rechtsgesch. 2,

civitatula.full: cīvĭtātŭla, ae, f. dim. civitas. Citizenship in a small city, Sen. Apocol. 9, 3. — A small city, App. M. 10, p. 238; Hier. in lsa. 8, 26, 5 sq.

clabulare.full: clābŭlāre, is, n. clabula = clavula a large, open wagon, probably with sides of wicker-work, used in transporting soldiers, Cod. Th. 6, 29, 2, § 2.—Hence, clābŭlāris (clāv-), e, and clābŭlārius, a, um, adj., of or belonging to the transport wagons: clavularis cursus facultate permissā, Amm. 20, 4, 11; Cod. Th. 8, 5, 62.

clacendix.full: clacendix, claxendix, or calcen-dix, a kind of shell-fish, Paul. ex Fest. p. 46, 16 Müll. N. cr.; Prisc. p. 655 P.
clacendix.short: clacendix, claxendix, or calcen-dix, a kind of shell-fish, Paul.

clades.full: clādes, is (gen. plur. usu. cladium, Liv. 2, 63, 7; 5, 22, 8 et saep.: cladum, Sil. 1, 41; 7, 505; 9, 353; 16, 672; Amm. 29, 1, 14; 32, 2, 1), f. kindr. with Sanscr. klath, laedere; Gr. κλάω, to break, break in pieces; cf.: per - cello, clava, gladius. Prop., a breaking, beating, dashing to pieces; hence, In gen., destruction, devastation, injury, mischief, harm, misfortune, disaster, loss, detriment, calamity (cf.: calamitas, pernicies; class. and freq.): clades calamitasque, intemperies modo i

claeon.full: Claeon, ontis, m., = Κλαίων (wailing), a fountain in Phrygia, Plin. 31, 2, 16, § 19.
claeon.short: Claeon, ontis, m., = Κλαίων (wailing), a fountain in Phrygia, Plin.

clagalopes.full: clăgălōpes, is, f., a species of eagle, = pygargus, Schol. Juv. 11, 138.
clagalopes.short: clăgălōpes, is, f., a species of eagle, = pygargus, Schol.

clam.full: clam (old access. form callim, or, acc. to Cod. Gu. 1, calam, Paul. ex Fest. p. 47, 3 Müll.) [root cal-; cf.: calix, celo, cella, occulo, caligo], adv. and prep., secretly, privately; and in the predicate after sum and fore, hidden, secret, unknown (opp. palam; except once in Caes., v. II. infra; in class. prose only used as adv.). Adv. In gen.: clamque palamque, Enn. ap. Gell. 12, 4 (247 Vahl.): ignis mortalibus clam Divisus, Att. ap. Cic. Tusc. 2, 10, 23: mea nunc facinora aperiuntur, clam qua

clamator.full: clāmātor, ōris, m. clamo, a bawler, noisy declaimer (in oratory; prob. only in the foll. exs.): ut intellegi possit, quem existimem clamatorem, quem oratorem fuisse, Cic. Brut. 49, 182; id. de Or. 3, 21, 81; Mart. 12, 26, 11 (Schneid. clamatus, i. e. vocatus); * Gell. 19, 9, 7.

clamatorius.full: clāmātōrĭus, a, um, adj. clamator, screeching, clamorous: avis = prohibitoria, a bird of bad omen, Plin. 10, 14, 17, § 37.

clamatus.full: clāmātus, ūs, m. clamo, a crying aloud, shouting, Paul. Nol. Carm. 15, 279.

clamitatio.full: clāmĭtātĭo, ōnis, f. clamito, a violent crying, clamor, noise, Plaut. Most. 1, 1, 6.

clamito.full: clāmĭto, āvi, ātum (part. pres. nom. plur. clamitantis, Varr. ap. Non. p. 356), 1, v. freq. n. and a. [clamo], to cry out violently or aloud, to bawl out, vociferate (class., esp. freq. since the Aug. per.; in Cic. only twice; not in Quint.; usu. of human beings). Neutr. (rare): ut illi clamitant, Cic. Caecin. 3, 9; of a bird: ipsum (passerem) accipiter ... vano clamitantem interficit, Phaedr. 1, 9, 7.— Act. With the words or thoughts uttered as object. With direct citation: Chremes clamitans: I

clamo.full: clāmo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. n. and a. [Sanscr. kar-, to celebrate; Gr. καλέω, κλητός; cf.: clarus, classis, nomenclator, concilium]. Neutr., to call, cry out, shout aloud, to complain with a loud voice, vociferari (class. and very freq.; mostly of human beings): populus convolat; Tumultuantur, clamant, pugnant de loco, Ter. Hec. prol. alt. 33: dic mihi, Non clamas? non insanis? id. Ad. 4, 7, 9; cf. id. ib. 5, 3, 3; id. Phorm. 4, 3, 59: clamare de pecuniā, Cic. Verr. 2, 5, 7, § 17 al.—Of a vehement b

clamor.full: clāmor (old form clāmŏs, like arbos, labos, etc., Quint. 1, 4, 13), ōris, m. clamo. A loud call, a shout, cry; of men and (poet.) of animals (very freq. in all periods and species of composition): facere clamorem, Plaut. Bacch. 4, 8, 33: tollere, id. Curc. 2, 2, 27; Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 43, § 94; id. Q. Fr. 2, 1. 3; Liv. 3, 28, 2; Quint. 5, 10, 46; Verg. A. 3, 672 al.: tollere in caelum, id. ib. 11, 745: ad aethera, id. ib. 2, 338; cf.: clamorem mittere ad sidera, Stat. Th. 12, 521: edere, Cic. Div.
clamor.short: clāmor (old form clāmŏs, like arbos, labos, etc., Quint.

clamosus.full: clāmōsus, a, um, adj. clamor (mostly post-Aug.), full of clamor or noise, i. e., Act., clamoring or bawling continually or loudly, clamorous, noisy, bawling: turbidus et clamosus altercator, Quint. 6, 4, 15: pater, Juv. 14, 191: magister, Mart. 5, 84, 2.— * Adv.: clāmōsē, clamorously: clamose ne dicamus omnia, Quint. 11, 3, 45.— Pass., filled with noise or clamor, noisy: urbs, Stat. S. 4, 4, 18: theatri turba, id. ib. 3, 5, 16: valles, id. Th. 4, 448: circus, Juv. 9, 144; Mart. 10, 53: Subura, i

clampetia.full: Clampĕtĭa, ae, f., = Λαμπέτεια, a town of the Bruttii, now Amantea, Liv. 29, 38, 1; 30, 19, 10; Mel. 2, 4, 9; the same, Clampĕtĭae, ārum, Plin. 3, 5, 10, § 72.
clampetia.short: Clampĕtĭa, ae, f., = Λαμπέτεια, a town of the Bruttii, now Amantea, Liv.

clancularius.full: clancŭlārĭus, a, um, adj. clanculum, secret, concealed, anonymous, unknown (postAug. and rare): poëta quidam, Mart. 10, 3, 5: Lydia, Tert. Pall. 4.

clanculo.full: clancŭlō, adv. (access. form of clanculum) [clam], secretly, privately (postclass.), App. M. 3, p. 133, 5; 9, p. 221, 13; 10, p. 245, 26; Macr. S. 5, 18; Amm. 21, 12, 13; August. Ep. 54.

clanculum.full: clancŭlum, adv. and prep. dim. [id.], secretly, privately (ante-class. but freq.). Adv.: aucupemus ex insidiis clanculum, Plaut. As. 5, 2, 31: abire a legione, id. Am. 1, 3, 25: noctu advenire, id. Bacch. 2, 3, 83; 3, 1, 8; id. Cas. 2, 8, 8: congerere aliquod, Ter. Eun. 2, 3, 18: mordere, id. ib. 3, 1, 21; 3, 5, 41; 3, 5, 54: agere inter se, id. Heaut. 3, 1, 63; id. Phorm. 5, 6, 33.—* Prep. with acc.: clanculum Patres, Ter. Ad. 1, 1, 27; cf. clam.

clandestinus.full: clandestīnus, a, um, adj. for clamdies-tinus; cf. matutinus; v. Corss. Ausspr. 1, p. 461 sq., secret, hidden, concealed, clandestine (class. in prose and poetry): suspitio, Plaut. Am. 1, 2, 28: nuptiae, id. Cas. 5, 3, 6: natura, Lucr. 1, 779: motus materiaï, id. 2, 127: scelere, Cic. Sull. 11, 33; cf. Liv. 42, 18, 1: introitus, Cic. Off. 2, 23, 81; cf. Suet. Ner. 48: colloquia cum hostibus, Cic. Sen. 12, 40: consilia, Crassus ap. Cic. Or. 66, 223; Caes. B. G. 7, 1; cf. Liv. 42, 24, 3: nuntiis le

clango.full: clango, no perf., ĕre, 3, v. n. kindred with crocio, glocio; cf. clamo and κλάζω, to clang, to sound, resound (rare; only in ante-class. and post-Aug. poets): crepitu clangente, Att. ap. Non. p. 463, 16: horrida clangunt signa tubae, Stat. Th. 4, 342; cf.: luctificum clangente tubā, Val. Fl. 3, 349: clangunt aquilae, Auct. Carm. Phil. 28.

clangor.full: clangor, ōris, m. clango, a sound, clang, noise (mostly poet. and in Aug. prose). Of wind instruments: tubarum, Verg. A. 2, 313; cf. id. ib. 8, 526; 11, 192; Luc. 1, 237; Sil. 2, 19; Stat. Th. 3, 651; Flor. 4, 2, 67; cf. Ov. M. 3, 707.— Of birds (in crying or flying). clangorem fundere, Cic. poët. Tusc. 2, 10, 24: tremulo clangore volare, id. poët. Div. 2, 30, 63; Ov. M. 12, 528; 13, 611: cum magno clangore volitare, Liv. 1, 34, 8; 5, 47, 4; Col. 8, 13, 2; Plin. 18, 35, 87, § 363 sq.; 10, 8, 10,

clanis.full: Clănĭs, is, m. A companion of Phineus, Ov. M. 5, 140.— A Centaur, Ov. M. 12, 379.— A river in Etruria, which falls into the Tiber, now Chiana, Sil. 8, 455; Tac. A. 1, 79.

clanius.full: Clănĭus, ii, m., a river in Campania, destructive by frequently overflowing the country around, especially the town of Acerrœ (v. Acerrae), now Lagno, Verg. G. 2, 225 Heyne; Sil. 8, 537; also called Glănis, Plin. 3, 5, 9, § 53 sq.
clanius.short: Clănĭus, ii, m., a river in Campania, destructive by frequently overflowing the country around, especially the town of Acerrœ (v.

clareo.full: clārĕo, ēre, v. n. clarus. Prop., to be clear or bright, to shine (poet.): hoc lumen candidum claret mihi, Enn. ap. Non. p. 85, 25 (Trag. Rel. v. 367 Rib.); so of stars, Cic. Arat. 5 (240); 107 (348).— Trop. To be obvious or clear, evident or manifest (poet. rare): quod in primo quoque carmine claret, which is evident also in the first canto, Lucr. 6, 937: mihi satis claret, with acc. and inf., Spart. Sev. 20, 4 Spald. and Zumpt N. cr.— Of character, to be distinguished, illustrious, famous, ren

claresco.full: clāresco, clārui, 2, v. inch. n. [clareo] (poet. or in post-Aug. prose), to become or grow bright or clear. Prop. Of the sight, to begin to shine, become visible: tecta luminibus clarescunt, Tac. A. 15, 37: clarescit dies, Sen. Herc. Fur. 123; Val. Fl. 7, 3; cf. Claud. Nupt. Hon. et Mar. 185 al.— Of the hearing, to sound clear, to become audible: clarescunt sonitus armorum, Verg. A. 2, 301: tibiae, Quint. 1, 11, 7: vox, Gabius Bassus ap. Gell. 5, 7, 2.— Trop. To become clear, manifest, evident,

clarico.full: clārĭco, āre, 1, v. n. clarus, to glow, gleam: ignes pernicitate sui claricantes, App. de Mundo, 15, p. 63.

clarificatio.full: clārĭfĭcātĭo, ōnis, f. clarifico, a glorification (eccl. Lat.): Domini, Aug. Qu. 83, 62; Cypr. Ep. 77, 2.

clarifico.full: clārĭfĭco, āre, v. a. clarus - facio, to make illustrious or famous (eccl. Lat.): nomen suum grandi aliquo facinore, Lact. 3, 18, p. 213 Bip.; so Sedul. 4, 173; 5, 8; Paul. Nol. Carm. 26, 304 al.

clarigatio.full: clārĭgātĭo, ōnis, f. clarigo, a solemn demand for redress, a religious solemnity with which the Fetialis declared war upon an enemy, in case he should refuse to give satisfaction within 33 days for injuries sustained (cf. Serv. ad Verg. A. 9, 53; 10, 14; Dict. of Antiq.), Plin. 1, epit. libr. 22, 3, p. 69 Bip.; Quint. 7, 3, 13; cf. Liv. 1, 32, 5 sq.— In gen., a fine or ransom for a transgression of limits, to be exacted of the offender by any person finding him: (Veliterni) jussi trans Tiberim h

clarigito.full: clārĭgĭto (in the MSS. clārĭcĭto), āre, v. freq. [clarigo], to recall, recollect; saecla ferarum, Lucr. 5, 947; v. Lachm. ad h. l.

clarigo.full: clārĭgo, no perf., ātum, 1, v. n. [clarus]; t. t. of the Fetiales, to proclaim war against an enemy with certain religious ceremonies (cf. Liv. 1, 32, 5 sq.; Serv. ad Verg. A. 9, 53; 10, 14; Dict. of Antiq.); Plin. 22, 2, 3, § 5; cf. clarigatio, and Lachm. ad Lucr. 5, 947.

clarisonus.full: clārĭ-sŏnus, a, um, adj. id., clearsounding, loud, distinct (poet. and rare): vox, Cat. 64, 320; 64, 125: aurae Aquilonis, Cic. Arat. 280.

clarissimatus.full: clārissĭmātus, ūs, m. clarissimus; v. clarus, II. B., the dignity of a Clarissimus (late Lat.), Cod. Th. 6, 24, 9; Amm. 21, 16, 2.

claritas1.full: clārĭtas, ātis, f. clarus, clearness, brightness, splendor (in good prose, most freq. in the post-Aug. per.). Prop. Of objects affecting the sight (so for the most part only in Pliny the elder): sidus Veneris claritatis tantae (est), ut, etc., Plin. 2, 8, 6, § 37; cf. id. 2, 8, 6, § 30; 23, 4, 41, § 84: matutina, id. 9, 35, 54, § 107: visus, id. 31, 10, 46, § 116; cf. oculorum, id. 18, 11, 29, § 114; 20, 10, 42, § 108: AD CLARITATEM (sc. oculorum), for clearness of sight (label of an ointment bo

claritas2.full: Clārĭtas Jūlia, f., the name given to the town Attuli, in Hispania Baetica, Plin. 3, 1, 3, § 12.
claritas2.short: Clārĭtas Jūlia, f., the name given to the town Attuli, in Hispania Baetica, Plin.

claritudo.full: clārĭtūdo, ĭnis, f. clarus, clearness, brightness (access. form of claritas; in lit. signif. very rare; trop. in Sall. a few times, in Tac. very freq., but not in Cic., Cæs., Quint., or Suet.). Lit. Of objects affecting the sight: fulgor et claritudo deae (sc. lunae), Tac. A. 1, 28; cf. Lact. 2, 9, 12.— * Of objects affecting the hearing: vocis, Gell. 6, 5, 1 Hertz.— Trop. (cf. claritas, II. B.), renown, celebrity, splendor, fame, reputation: inclitissima, Cato ap. Gell. 3, 7, 19; Sisenn. ap. No

claritus.full: clārĭtus, adv., = clare (a form like, antiquitus, divinitus, humanitus, etc.), acc. to Cels. ap. Charis. p. 190 P.
claritus.short: clārĭtus, adv., = clare (a form like, antiquitus, divinitus, humanitus, etc.), acc.

clarius.full: Clārĭus, a, um, v. Claros, II.

clarividus.full: clārĭvĭdus, a, um, adj. clare-video, seeing clearly, clear-sighted: sensus, Marc. Emp. 18.

claro.full: clāro, āvi, 1, v. a. clarus, to make bright or clear, to illuminate (poet. and very rare). Lit.: Juppiter excelsā clarabat sceptra columnā, showed, exhibited, Cic. poët. Div 1, 12, 21: aestatis primordia, id. Arat. 39: iter longae limite flammae, Stat. Th. 5, 286.— Trop. Mentally, to make clear, evident, to explain, illustrate, set forth: animae naturam versibus, Lucr. 3, 36: multa, id. 4, 778: obscura, App. de Deo Socr. p. 51, 15.— Morally, to make illustrious, to render famous: illum non labor

claror.full: clāror, ōris, m. id., clearness, brightness, Plaut. Most. 3, 1, 112; Ritschl ex conj. Camerar. dub.

claros.full: Clărŏs, i, f., = Κλάρος, a small town in Ionia, near Colophon, celebrated for a temple and an oracle of Apollo, now the village Zilleh, Ov M. 1, 516; cf. Tac. A. 2, 54.— Hence, Clărĭus, a, um, adj., of or pertaining to Claros, Clarian. As an epithet of Apollo: Clarii Apollinis fanum, specus, oraculum, simulacrum, Mel. 1, 17, 2; Plin. 2, 103, 106, § 232; Tac. A. 2, 54; 12, 22: deus, Ov. A. A. 2, 80; id. M. 11, 413; id. F. 1, 20.—Subst.: Clărĭus, ii, m., Apollo, Verg. A. 3, 360 Serv.; Stat. Th. 8,
claros.short: Clărŏs, i, f., = Κλάρος, a small town in Ionia, near Colophon, celebrated for a temple and an oracle of Apollo, now the village Zilleh, Ov M.

clarus.full: clārus, a, um, adj. kindr. with Germ. klar; Engl. clear; cf. clamo, clear, bright (opp. obscurus, caecus; very freq. in all periods, and in all kinds of composition). Lit. Relating to the sight, clear, bright, shining, brilliant, etc. Absol.: luce clarā et candidā, Plaut. Am. 1, 3, 49: ut mulierum famam multorum oculis lux clara custodiat, open day, Cic. Leg. 2, 15, 37; cf.: frequentissimā celebritate et clarissimā luce laetari, id. Cael. 20, 47: lumen, Lucr. 3, 1: oculorum lumina, id. 4, 825; c

classiarius.full: classĭārĭus, i, m. classis, 1. B. 2., pertaining to the navy: centurio, a captain of a ship, Tac. A. 14, 8; cf. Inscr. Orell. 3617. —More freq. as subst.: classĭārĭi, ōrum, m., marines, naval forces, Caes. B. C. 3, 100; Nep. Milt. 7, 3; id. Them. 3, 2; Tac. A. 4, 27; 12, 56; 15, 51; Suet. Tib. 62; id. Galb. 12; id. Oth. 8; id. Vesp. 8.

classicula.full: classĭcŭla, ae, f. dim. id., a little fleet, flotilla, Cic. Att. 16, 2, 4.

classicum.full: classĭcum, i, v. classicus, II. B. 1.

classicus.full: classĭcus, a, um, adj. classis, of or belonging to a classis. To a class or division of the Roman people; only transf., belonging to the first class, of the highest class: classici dicebantur non omnes qui in quinque classibus erant, sed primi tantum classis homines (opp. classem, infra), Cat. ap. Gell. 6 ($3), 13, 1; cf. Paul. ex Fest. p. 113, 12: testes classici, id. ib. p. 56, 15.— Trop., of the highest rank, classical, superior, standard: classicus adsiduusque aliquis scriptor, non proletari

classis.full: classis (old orthog. CLASIS, Column. Rostr.; v. under I. B. 2.), is (acc. sing. usu. classem; classim, Auct. B. Afr. 9, 2; abl. usu. classe; classi, Verg. A. 8, 11; Liv. 23, 41, 8; Vell. 2, 79), f. root cal-, cla-, of clamo, καλέω; prop. the people as assembled or called together, hence, After the division of the Roman people by Servius Tullius into six (or, the citizens who paid tribute alone being reckoned, into five) classes, A class, Liv. 1, 42, 5; 1, 43, 2 sq.; Cic. Rep. 2, 22, 39 sq.; Gell

clastidium.full: Clastĭdĭum, ĭi, n. A fortress in Gallia Cisalpina, near the Padus, now Chiasteggio, Cic. Tusc. 4, 22, 49; Nep. Hann. 4, 1; Liv. 21, 48, 9.— The name of a fragment of Nœvius, Varr. L. L. 7, 107; 9, 78.

claterna.full: Claterna, ae, f., a fortress in Gallia Cisalpina, near Bononia, on the river Guaderna, Cic. Fam. 12, 5, 2; id. Phil. 8, 2, 6; Plin. 3, 15, 20, § 116.
claterna.short: Claterna, ae, f., a fortress in Gallia Cisalpina, near Bononia, on the river Guaderna, Cic.

clathri.full: clāthri (in MSS. also clātri), ōrum, m. (clātra, ōrum, n., corresp. to the Greek, prob. Prop. 4 (5), 5, 74., = κλῃθπα τά, a lattice, grate (esp. to the cages of animals), Cato, R. R. 4; Col. 8, 17, 10; Hor. A. P. 473; Plin. 8, 7, 7, § 21; Claud. III. Cons. Stil. 272; Inscr. Orell. 3299.

clathro.full: clāthro (in MSS. also clātro), no perf., ātum, 1, v. a. clathri, to furnish with a grate or lattice, to set with bars (very rare), Cato, R. R. 4; Plaut. Mil. 2, 4, 26; Col. 9, 1, 4; Inscr. Grut. 207, 2.

claudaster.full: claudaster, tri, m., a little lame, Gloss.
claudaster.short: claudaster, tri, m., a little lame, Gloss.

claudeo.full: claudeo, ēre, or claudo, no perf., sum, ĕre, v. n. claudus, ground form of the more common claudico, to limp or halt, to be lame, to falter (mostly trop.). Claudeo: an ubi vos sitis, ibi consilium claudeat, Caecil. ap. Prisc. p. 889 P.— Claudo: neque ignorantia res claudit, Sall. ap. Don. ad Ter. Eun. 1, 2, 84 (id. H. 3, 61, 25 Dietsch): conjuratione claudit, id. ap. Prisc. p. 889 P. (id. H. 3, 80 ib.): claudat amor erga te meus, Front. Ep. p. 122 Nieb. — Of dub. form (yet it may be supposed tha
claudeo.short: claudeo, ēre, or claudo, no perf., sum, ĕre, v.

claudia.full: Claudĭa, ae, f. A Roman female name; v. Claudius.— A town of Noricum, Plin. 3, 24, 27, § 146.

claudialis.full: Claudĭālis, e, adj. Claudius, pertaining to the emperor Claudius, Claudian: flaminium, Tac. A. 13, 2 fin.; Inscr. Orell. 3044 al.

claudianus1.full: Claudĭānus, a, um, v. Claudius, II. B.

claudianus2.full: Claudĭānus, i, m. Claudius, a Roman poet of Alexandria, of the time of Theodosius the Great and his sons, several of whose panegyric poems are extant, Symm. Ep. 9, 13.

claudicatio.full: claudĭcātĭo, ōnis, f. claudico, a limping, Cic. N. D. 1, 30, 83; id. de Or. 2, 61, 249; Col. 6, 12, 1; Val. Max. 8, 11, ext. 3.

claudico.full: claudĭco (clōdĭco, Cic. de Or. 2, 61, 249, like Claudius and Clodius, codex and caudex, etc., v. au), āre, v. n. claudeo; like albico, candico from albeo, candeo, to limp, halt, be lame (class.). Prop.: Carvilio graviter claudicanti ex vulnere, Cic. de Or. 2, 61, 249; Ov. F. 3, 758; Col. 6, 12, 3; Suet. Aug. 80; Just. 6, 2, 6.— In Lucretius, meton., of other irregular or unbalanced motions, to waver, wabble, halt; of the lame wings of birds, Lucr. 6, 834; of the wavering of balances or scales, i

claudigo.full: claudīgo, ĭnis, f. claudus, a lameness, limping, Veg. A. Veter. 1, 26, 1.

claudiopolis.full: Claudĭŏpŏlis, is; acc. im; abl. i, f. A town in Southern Cappadocia, now Eraklia, Plin. 5, 24, 20, § 85; Amm. 14, 8, 2.— A town in Bithynia, prob. the mod. Boli or Bula, Cod. Th. 12, 1, 119.—Hence, Claudĭŏpŏlītāni, ōrum, m., the inhabitants of Claudiopolis in Bithynia, Plin. Ep. 10, 39 (48), 5; Traj. ib. 10, 40 (49), 3.

clauditas.full: claudĭtas, ātis, f. claudus, a lameness, limping (post-Aug.), Plin. 8, 43, 68, § 169; 28, 4, 7, § 35; App. Flor. 16.—In plur., Plin. 28, 4, 6, § 33.

claudius.full: Claudĭus (Clōdĭus, like claudo and clodo, codex and caudex, plostrum and plaustrum, etc.), Claudĭa, Clōdĭa, the name of two very celebrated Roman gentes (one patrician, the other plebeian; cf. Suet. Tib. 1 and 2; Verg. A. 7, 708; Liv. 2, 16, 4). Claudius; so, App. Claudius Caecus (v. Appius).— The historian Q. Claudius Quadrigarius, a contemporary of Sulla and Sisenna, Vell. 2, 9, 6; Gell. 1, 7, 9.—Called simply Claudius, Liv. 8, 19, 13; 9, 5, 2.— The emperor Claudius; in full, Tiberius Claudius
claudius.short: Claudĭus (Clōdĭus, like claudo and clodo, codex and caudex, plostrum and plaustrum, etc.), Claudĭa, Clōdĭa, the name of two very celebrated Roman gentes (one patrician, the other plebeian;

claudo1.full: claudo (* clōdo: clodunt ita (oculos), Plin. 18, 33, 76, § 330 fin.; but some refer clodo to claudeo; and more freq., although not in Cic., clūdo, as always in the compounds; v. infra), si, sum, 3, v. a. root sklu-, klu-, to shut; cf. κλείω, κλείς, clavis; O. H. Germ. scliuzu; M. H. Germ. schliessen; also claudus, clavus, to shut. To shut something that is open, to close, shut up (opp. aperire; freq. in prose and poetry). Claudo: forem cubiculi, Cic. Tusc. 5, 20, 59; cf. Quint. 10, 3, 25; and, c

claudus.full: claudus (clūdus, Plaut. Ps. 2, 2, 64; and clōdus, Arat. Act. Apost. 266), a, um, adj. root klu-; v. claudo; prop. shut in, hampered, limping, halting, lame. Prop.: sutor, Plaut. Aul. 1, 1, 34: deus, Cic. N. D. 1, 30, 83: claudus altero pede, Nep. Ages. 8, 1; Hor. Ep. 1, 17, 61: pes, id. C. 3, 2, 32: pars serpentis, Verg. A. 5. 278 al.— Prov.: iste claudus, quemadmodum aiunt, pilam, said of one who cannot make a right use of a thing, Cic. Pis. 28, 69.— Trop., wavering, crippled, imperfect, defect

clausala.full: Clausala, ae, f., a river of Illyria, now the Khiri or Drinossi, Liv. 44, 31, 3 (al. Clausula).
clausala.short: Clausala, ae, f., a river of Illyria, now the Khiri or Drinossi, Liv.

claustra.full: claustra (clostra, Cato, R. R. 13, 3; 135, 2), ōrum, n. (in sing.: claustrum, i, rare, Caes. Germ. Arat. 197; Curt. 4, 5, 21; 7, 6, 13; Petr. 89, 2, 7; Gell. 14, 6, 3; Luc. 10, 509; App. M. 4, 10, p. 146 fin.; Amm. 23, 4, 6; 26, 8, 8: clostrum, Sen.
