Ben. 7, 21, 2) [clausum, claudo], that by which any thing is shut up or closed, a lock, bar, bolt. Prop.: claves, claustra, Varr. ap. Non. p. 545, 12: claustra revellere, Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 23, § 52; Liv. 5, 21, 10: januae pandere, * Cat. 61, 76: laxar

claustralis.full: claustrālis, e id., of or pertaining to a fortress: munimen, Cassiod. Var. 11, 14.
claustralis.short: claustrālis, e id., of or pertaining to a fortress: munimen, Cassiod.

claustrarius.full: claustrārĭus, a, um claustra, pertaining to locks: artifex, a locksmith, Lampr. Elag. 12.
claustrarius.short: claustrārĭus, a, um claustra, pertaining to locks: artifex, a locksmith, Lampr.

claustritumus.full: claustrĭtŭmus, i, m. from claustrum, like aeditumus from aedes, a warden of locks, Laev. ap. Gell. 12, 105.

clausula1.full: clausŭla, ae. f. claudo. A close, conclusion, end (cf. claudo, I. B.; in good prose; most freq. in Quint.): in quo (mimo) cum clausula non invenitur, a fitting end, Cic. Cael. 27, 65: tantum bonam clausulam inpone, Sen. Ep. 77, 20; Suet. Aug. 99: epistulae, Cic. Phil. 13, 21, 47; id. Fam. 2, 4, 2: edicti, Cic. Verr. 2, 3, 14, § 35: clausulam inponere disputationi, Col. 3, 19, 3: peracti operis, id. 12, 57, 5: summae nervorum, Plin. 11, 45, 101, § 247.— Esp. In rhet., the close of a period, Cic.

clausura.full: clausūra or clūsūra, ae, f. claudo. * (Cf. claustra, I. A.) A lock, bar, bolt, Inscr. Orell. 2510.— (Cf. claustra, II. B.) A castle, fort (late Lat.), Cod. Just. 1, 27, 2, § 4; Cassiod. Var. 2, 5.

clausus1.full: clausus, a, um, Part. and P. a., from claudo.

clausus2.full: Clausus, i, m., a Sabine proper name: Attus Clausus, ancestor of the gens Claudia, Liv. 2, 16, 4; 10, 8, 6; Verg. A. 7, 707; Tac. A. 4, 9 al.
clausus2.short: Clausus, i, m., a Sabine proper name: Attus Clausus, ancestor of the gens Claudia, Liv.

clava.full: clāva, ae, f. root cel- of percello; cf. Gr. κλάω and clades. A knotty branch or stick, a staff, cudgel, club: adfer duas clavas... probas, Plaut. Rud. 3, 5, 20; Lucr. 5, 968: sternentes agmina clavā, Verg. A. 10, 318; Curt. 9, 4, 3; Ov. F. 1, 575; Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 43, § 94; Plin. 19, 1, 3, § 18; a bar, lever, Cato, R. R. 13, 1.—As a weapon for exercising, used by young men, and esp. by soldiers, a foil, Cic. Sen. 16, 58; Veg. Mil. 1, 11.—As a badge of Hercules, Prop. 4 (5) 9, 39; Ov. H. 9, 117;

clavarium.full: clāvārĭum, ii, n. id., money given to soldiers for the purchase of shoe-nails (cf. calcearium), Tac. H. 3, 50 fin.

clavator.full: clāvātor, ōris, m. clava, one who carries clubs or foils, used in military exercises, a cudgel-bearer, Plaut. Rud. 3, 5, 25; cf. Paul. ex Fest. p. 62, 9 Müll.

clavicarius.full: clāvĭcārĭus, ĭi, m. clavis, a locksmith (late Lat.), Cod. Just. 10, 64, 1.

clavicula.full: clāvĭcŭla, ae, f. dim. id. * A small key, Caes. Germ. Arat. 195.— A tendril, by which the vine clings to its props, Cic. Sen. 15, 52; id. N. D. 2, 47, 120; Col. 4, 6, 2; Plin. 23, prooem. § 5.— A bar, bolt of the door, Hyg. Grom. 55.—Hence, clāvĭcŭlārĭus, ĭi, m., a key-keeper, jailer, Firm. Math. 3, 66.

claviger1.full: clāvĭger, gĕra, gĕrum, adj., clubbearing; as an epithet of Hercules [clavagero], the club-bearer (v. clava, 1.), Ov. M. 15, 22; 15, 284; id. F 1, 544; 4, 68.—Also of the robber Periphetes: clavigera proles, Ov. M. 7, 437: clavigerum numen, Sil. 3, 14.

claviger2.full: clāvĭger, gĕri, m. clavis-gero, the key-bearer, an epithet of Janus, as the god of doors, Ov. F. 1, 228; cf. Macr S. 1, 9.

clavis.full: clāvis (clāves, acc. to Pompon. Comment. p. 459), is, f. (acc. commonly clavem, clavim, Plaut. Most. 2, 1, 78; Tib. 2, 4, 31; cf. Paul ex Fest. p. 56 Müll.; Don. p. 1750 P., Charis. p. 101 ib.; abl. clavi and clave: clavi, Varr. R. R. 1, 22 fin., App. M. 1, 14, p. 108; Dig. 48, 8, 1, § 3; Serv. ad Verg. A. 10, 252; cf. Charis. l. l.: clave, Juv. 15, 158; App. M. 9, 20, p. 226; Dig. 21, 1, 17, § 15; cf. Neue, Formenl. 1, 199) [root klu-, v. claudo], a key: clavim cedo, Plaut Most. 2, 1, 78: clave

clavo.full: clāvo, no perf., ātum, 1, v. a. clavus (rare; not ante-Aug.; mostly in part. perf.). To furnish or fasten with nails, to nail, Paul. Nol. 21, 103: clavata concha, i. e. furnished with points or prickles, Plin. 9, 36, 61, § 130.— To furnish with a purple stripe (cf. clavus, II. D.): mantilia cocco clavata, Lampr. Alex. Sev. 37: clavata auro tunica, Vop. Bonos. 15; cf. Paul. ex Fest. p. 56, 9 Müll.

clavula.full: clāvŭla (clābŭla or clāvŏla), ae, f. dim. clava, a scion, graft, Varr. R. R, 1, 40, 4; cf. Non. p. 414, 29.

clavulus.full: clāvŭlus, i, m. dim. clavus. A small nail, a tack, Cato, R. R. 21, 3; Varr. R. R. 2, 9, 15.—* A small swelling (cf. clavus, II. B.), Marc. Emp. 33.

clavus.full: clāvus, i, m. root klu-, v. claudo; prop. that which shuts or fastens. A nail, usually of metal. Lit.: offerumentas habebis pluris Quam ulla navis longa clavos, Plaut. Rud. 3, 4, 48: (leges) ad parietem fixae clavis ferreis, id. Trin. 4, 3, 32; so, clavi ferrei, Cato, R. R. 18 fin.; Caes. B. G. 3, 13; Vitr. 7, 3 al.—Sometimes of hard wood: clavis corneis occludere, Cato, R. R. 18 fin.: cornus... lignum utile, si quid cuneandum sit in ligno clavisve figendum ceu ferreis, Plin. 16, 40, 76, § 206:

clazomenae.full: Clāzŏmĕnae, ārum, f., = Κλαζομεναί, a town on the coast of Ionia, upon a peninsula of the Bay of Smyrna, now Kelisman or Vourla, Mel. 1, 17, 3; Plin. 5, 29, 31, § 117; Cic. Tusc. 1, 43, 104; Hor. S. 1, 7, 5.—Hence, Clāzŏmĕnĭus, a, um, adj., of Clazomenœ, Clazomenian: Anaxagoras, Cic. de Or. 3, 34, 138; Plin. 2, 58, 59, § 149: vinum, id. 14, 7, 9, § 73.—Clāzŏ-mĕnĭi, ōrum, the inhabitants of Clazomenœ, Liv. 38, 39, 9 al.
clazomenae.short: Clāzŏmĕnae, ārum, f., = Κλαζομεναί, a town on the coast of Ionia, upon a peninsula of the Bay of Smyrna, now Kelisman or Vourla, Mel.

cleander.full: Clĕander, dri, m., = Κλέανδρος, a favorite of the emperor Commodus, Lampr. Comm. 6, 7.
cleander.short: Clĕander, dri, m., = Κλέανδρος, a favorite of the emperor Commodus, Lampr.

cleanthes.full: Clĕanthes, is (acc. -en, Cic. N. D. 3, 2, 5; Sen. Ep. 113, 18; -em, Cic. Tusc. 2, 25, 60; id. Sen. 7, 23; voc. Cleanthe, id. Tusc. 3, 32, 77; Val. Max. 8, 7, ext. 11), m., = Κλεάνθης, a Stoic philosopher of Assos, pupil of Zeno and teacher of Chrysippus, Cic. Ac. 2, 23, 73; 2, 41, 126; id. Fat. 7, 14; id. Div. 1, 3, 6; id. Fin. 2, 21, 69; 4, 3, 7; Sen. Ep. 44, 3; 108, 10; id. Ben. 5, 14, 1; Val. Max. 8, 7, ext. 11.—Plur.: archetypos servare Cleanthas, statues of Cleanthes, Juv. 2, 7.—Hence, Clea

clearchus.full: Clĕarchus, i, m., = Κλέαρχος. A Spartan captain, Front. Strat. 4, 1.— A tyrant of Heraclea Pontica, Just. 16, 4 sq.— A philosopher of Soli, Gell. 4, 11.

clema.full: clēma, ătis, n., = κλῆμα, a plant, also called polygonon, Plin. 27, 12, 91, § 113.
clema.short: clēma, ătis, n., = κλῆμα, a plant, also called polygonon, Plin.

clematis.full: clēmătis, ĭdis, f., = κληματίς, the name of various climbing plants, as Vinca minor, Linn., etc.; Plin. 24, 10, 49, § 84; 24, 15, 88, § 138; 24, 15, 89, § 139; and 24, 15, 90, § 141.
clematis.short: clēmătis, ĭdis, f., = κληματίς, the name of various climbing plants, as Vinca minor, Linn., etc.;

clematitis.full: clēmătītis, ĭdis, f., = κληματῖτις, a creeping plant, a species of Aristolochia, called also Cretica, Plin. 25, 8, 54, § 96.
clematitis.short: clēmătītis, ĭdis, f., = κληματῖτις, a creeping plant, a species of Aristolochia, called also Cretica, Plin.

clemens1.full: clēmens, entis (abl. usu. -ti; but -te, Liv. 1, 26, 8; Laber. ap. Macr. S. 2, 7, 3), adj. etym. dub.; cf. lemures; and Germ. hold. Orig. (in the class. per. very rare), of the quiet, placid, pleasant state of the air, wind, or weather, mild, calm, soft, gentle ( = the class. placidus, quietus): undae clementi flamine pulsae, * Cat. 64, 272: clementior Auster vela vocat, Stat. Th. 5, 468: aura Favoni, Claud. Cons. Prob. Olyb. 272; cf. id. III. Cons. Hon. 165; Val. Fl. 6, 747: clementior dies, Col

clemens2.full: Clēmens, entis, m., a proper name, in later Lat. very freq.: Julius, Tac. A. 1, 23; 1, 26; 15, 73; id. H. 1, 87; 2, 12: Arretinus, id. ib. 4, 68; Suet. Dom. 11: Flavius, id. ib. 15.
clemens2.short: Clēmens, entis, m., a proper name, in later Lat.

clementia.full: clēmentĭa, ae, f. 1. clemens. A calm, tranquil state of the elements, calmness, mildness, tranquillity (like clemens in this signif. mostly post-Aug.): clementia ventorum, tranquillitas maris, App. de Deo Socr. p. 52, 1: soli caelique, Flor. 3, 3, 18; cf.: emollit gentes clementia caeli, Luc. 8, 366: aestatis, Plin. Ep. 5, 6, 5: hiemis, Col. 5, 5, 6: nascentis anni, id. 11, 3, 9: diei, id. 9, 13, 4: Nili, Stat. Th. 3, 527.— (Acc. to clemens, II. B.) Indulgent, forbearing conduct towards the erro

cleobis.full: Clĕŏbis, is, m., = Κλέοβις, son of the priesless Cydippe, brother of Bito, v. Bito; Val. Max. 5, 4, 4; Schol. ad Verg. G. 3, 132.
cleobis.short: Clĕŏbis, is, m., = Κλέοβις, son of the priesless Cydippe, brother of Bito, v.

cleobulus.full: Clĕŏbūlus, i, m., = Κλεοβουλος, of Lindus, one of the Seven Sages, Aus. Sept. Sap. 1, 16, 5.
cleobulus.short: Clĕŏbūlus, i, m., = Κλεοβουλος, of Lindus, one of the Seven Sages, Aus.

cleombrotus.full: Clĕombrŏtus, i, m. A Lacedœmonian general, Cic. Off. 1, 24, 84.— A young Academic philosopher of Ambracia, Cic. Tusc. 1, 34, 84; id. Scaur. 2, 4; Aug. Civ. Dei, 1, 22.

cleon.full: Clĕon, ōnis, = Κλέων, a Grecian proper name. An Athenian popular leader, Cic. Rep. 4, 10, 11; id. Brut. 7, 28.— A rhetorician of Halicarnassus, Nep. Lys. 3, 5.— A statuary, Plin. 34, 8, 19, § 37.— A painter, Plin. 35, 11, 40, § 140.
cleon.short: Clĕon, ōnis, = Κλέων, a Grecian proper name.

cleonae.full: Clĕōnae, ārum (Clĕōna, ae, Mel. 2, 2, 9), f., = Κλεωναί. A small town in Argolis, near Nemea, where Hercules killed the lion, now Clenia, Liv. 33, 14, 11; Ov. M. 6, 417; Plin. 4, 5, 6, § 12.—Hence, Clĕōnaeus, a, um, adj., of or pertaining to Cleonœ: ager, Liv. 33, 14, 7: leo, i. e. the Nemean lion, Luc. 4, 612; Sil. 3, 34: sidus = leo, Stat. S. 4, 28; Mart. 4, 60: stirpis, i.e. Herculeae, Stat. Th. 6, 837.— A town in Macedonia, on Mount Athos, Mel. 2, 2, 9; Plin. 4, 10, 17, § 37.

cleonia.full: clĕōnia, ae, f., = κλεωνία, the plant helenium, Theod. Prisc. 4, 1.
cleonia.short: clĕōnia, ae, f., = κλεωνία, the plant helenium, Theod.

cleonicion.full: clĕōnīcĭon, ii, n., = κλεωνίκιον, a plant, also called clinopodion, Plin. 24, 15, 87, § 137 (cleonicon, Sillig).
cleonicion.short: clĕōnīcĭon, ii, n., = κλεωνίκιον, a plant, also called clinopodion, Plin.

cleopatra.full: Clĕŏpātră (on the ā cf. Juv. 2, 109; Luc. 9, 1071; 10, 56; Stat. S. 3, 2, 120), ae, f., = Κλεοπάτρα. Queen of Egypt, and daughter of Ptolemy Auletes, notorious for her amorous intercourse with Cœsar, and afterwards with Antony; conquered at Actium by Augustus, Caes. B. C. 3, 103; 3, 107; Suet. Caes. 35; Luc. 10, 354 sqq.; Val. Fl. 4, 464; Mart. 4, 22, 2; 4, 59, 5.—Hence, Clĕŏpātrānus, a, um, adj., of or pertaining to Cleopatra: stirps, Treb. Poll. Claud. 1: uniones, id. Trig. Syr. 32.— A sister

cleophantus.full: Clĕŏphantus, i, m., = Κλεόφαντος. A physician in Rome, Cic. Clu. 16, 47; Cels. 3, 14; Plin. 20, 5, 15, § 31 al.— A painter of Corinthus, Plin. 35, 3, 5, § 15.

cleophon.full: Clĕŏphon, ontis, m., a demagogue of Athens, Cic. Rep. 4, 10, 11.
cleophon.short: Clĕŏphon, ontis, m., a demagogue of Athens, Cic.

clepo.full: clĕpo, psi, ptum (not clepi, v. Neue, Formenl. 2, 493; Madv. ad Cic. Fin. 5, 25, 74), 3, v. a. root klep- of κλέπτω, whence also clipeus; kindred with celo, cella, occul-o, clam, to steal (rare, and mostly anteclass. for furor): sacrum qui clepsit rapsitve, old form. ap. Cic. Leg. 2, 9, 22: si quis clepsit, etc., old form. ap. Liv. 22, 10, 5; Att. ap. Cic. Tusc. 2, 10, 23; id. ap. Cic. N. D. 3, 27, 68; Plaut. Ps. 1, 2, 6; Lucil. ap. Varr. L. L. 7, § 94 Müll.; Auct. ap. Cic. Rep. 4, 5, 11 (v. Non

clepsydra.full: clepsўdra, ae, f., = κλεψύδρα, an instrument for measuring time by water, similar to our sand-glasses, a water-clock, clepsydra, Sen. Ep. 24, 19; Veg. Mil. 3, 8; App. M. 3, p. 130, 19; used by speakers to measure the length of their discourse, Cic. Tusc. 2, 27, 67; Plin. Ep. 2, 11, 14; 6, 2, 5; 1, 23, 2.—Meton., the time measured by the clepsydra, and hence, petere clepsydram, to ask leave to speak; and dare clepsydram, to give leave to speak, Cic. de Or. 3, 34, 138; Mart. 6, 35; cf. aqua, II. F
clepsydra.short: clepsўdra, ae, f., = κλεψύδρα, an instrument for measuring time by water, similar to our sand-glasses, a water-clock, clepsydra, Sen.

clepsydrarius.full: clepsўdrārĭus, ii, m. clepsydra, a maker of water-clocks, Inscr. Murat. 935, 8.* † clepta, ae, m., = κλέπτης, a thief, Plaut. Truc. 1, 2, 9.

clericalis.full: clērĭcālis, e, adj. clericus, clerical, priestly (eccl. Lat.): tirocinium, Sid. Ep. 6, 7: comitatus, id. ib. 7, 2 et saep.

clericatus.full: clērĭcātus, ūs, m. id., the clerical office (eccl. Lat.), Hier. Ep. 60, n. 10; 125, n. 8 et saep.

clericus.full: clērĭcus, i, m., = κληρικός, a clergyman, priest (eccl. Lat.), Hier. Ep. 60, n. 10 al.
clericus.short: clērĭcus, i, m., = κληρικός, a clergyman, priest (eccl.

clerumenoe.full: Clērūmĕnoe, ōn, m., = Κληρούμενοι (those who draw lots), the name of a comedy of Diphilus, Lat. Sortientes, Plaut. Cas. prol. 31; cf. Rost. Plaut. Cuped. XVIII. p. 5 sq.
clerumenoe.short: Clērūmĕnoe, ōn, m., = Κληρούμενοι (those who draw lots), the name of a comedy of Diphilus, Lat.

clerus.full: clērus, i, m., = κλῆρος, the clerical order, the clergy (eccl. Lat.), Tert. Monog. 12; Prud. στεφ. 4, 78 al.
clerus.short: clērus, i, m., = κλῆρος, the clerical order, the clergy (eccl.

clibanarius.full: clībănārĭus, ii, m. clibanus, a soldier clad in mail, a cuirassier, Lampr. Alex. Sev. 56; Amm. 16, 10, 8; Eutr. 6, 7, 9.

clibanicius.full: clībănĭcĭus id.: pānis, bread baked in a clibanus, lsid. Orig. 20, 2, 15 (cf. Plin. 18, 11, 27, § 105).
clibanicius.short: clībănĭcĭus id.: pānis, bread baked in a clibanus, lsid.

clibanus.full: clībănus, i, m., = κλίβανος, an earthen or iron vessel for baking bread, broader at the bottom than at the top, Plin. 18, 11, 27, § 105; 20, 9, 39, § 99; cf. Col. 5, 10, 4; id. Arb. 19, 2; Cels. 2, 17; 3, 21 al.—As a utensil of the rich, also of silver, Petr. 35, 6.— Generally, an oven or furnace, Tert. adv. Marc. 4, 30; Sulpic. Sev. Dial. 1, 18.
clibanus.short: clībănus, i, m., = κλίβανος, an earthen or iron vessel for baking bread, broader at the bottom than at the top, Plin.

clidion.full: clīdĭon or -um, ĭi, m., = κλειδίον, the collar-bone of the tunny, Plin. 9, 15, 18, § 48.
clidion.short: clīdĭon or -um, ĭi, m., = κλειδίον, the collar-bone of the tunny, Plin.

cliduchus.full: Clīdūchus, i, m., = Κλειδοῦχος (keybearer), the name of two statues by Phidias and by Euphranor, Plin. 34, 8, 19, §§ 54 and 78.
cliduchus.short: Clīdūchus, i, m., = Κλειδοῦχος (keybearer), the name of two statues by Phidias and by Euphranor, Plin.

cliens.full: clĭens or clŭens, entis (gen. plur. usu. clientium; clientūm, Plaut. Men. 4, 2, 7; Hor. C. 3, 5, 53; Sen. Ep. 68, 9; Macr. S. 1, 2, 1), m. (comm. acc. to Charis. p. 77 P.; cf. Neue, Formenl. 1, 600, and v. clienta) [for cluens, from clueo, to hear; but acc. to Serv. ad Verg. A. 6, 609, from colens], one who hears, in relation to his protector (patronus), a client (Dion. Halic. 2, 9 and 10, pp. 83-85; cf. Nieb. Röm. Gesch. 1, p. 359 sq.; Gell. 5, 13, 2; Cato ap. Gell. 5, 13, 4; Gell. 20, 1, 40; a

clienta.full: clĭenta, ae, f. cliens, a female client, Plaut. Mil. 3, 1, 193; id. Poen. 5, 4, 12; id. Rud. 4, 1, 2; Afran. ap. Charis. p. 77 P.; * Hor. C. 2, 18, 8; Aus. Parent. 24; Pseudo Ascon. ad Cic. Verr. 2, 1, 46, § 120 Orell. N. cr.

clientela.full: clĭentēla, ae, f. id., the relation of patron and client, clientship; patronage, protection; the intimate and reciprocal duties of attachment and interest, based on the private relations in Rome between a Roman of a lower grade (plebeian or freedman) or a foreigner, and the patron chosen by him (cf. Dion. Halic. 2, 9 and 10, pp. 83- 85; Gell. 5, 13; 20, 1): Thais patri se commendavit in clientelam et fidem, * Ter. Eun. 5, 8, 9; cf.: esse in fide et clientelā. to be the client of, Cic. Rosc. Am.

clientulus.full: clĭentŭlus, i, m. dim. cliens, a small or insignificant client, Tac. Or. 37.

clima.full: clĭma, ătis (abl. plur. climatis, Firm. Math. 2, 13), n., = κλίμα (prop. the inclination, slope; hence, cf. Lidd. and Scott under κλίμα, II.), A clime, climate (late Lat.), App. Trism. p. 98, 23; Mart. Cap. 8, § 859; Tert. Anim. 49; Serv. ad Verg. G. 1, 246 (in Vitr. 1, 1, 10, used as Greek).— In gen. for region, part: clima medium ventris, Veg. Act. Vet. 1, 43, 3.— A land measure of 60 feet square, Col. 5, 1, 5.* † clīmăcis, ĭdis, f., = κλιμακίς, a small staircase or ladder, Vitr. 10, 11, 8.

climacter.full: clīmacter, ēris, m., = κλιμακτήρ (gradation), a critical epoch in human life, a climacteric (in accordance with the ancient belief, the years 7, 14, 21, 28, etc.), Plin. 7, 49, 50, § 161; Gell. 3, 10, 9; Firm. Math. 4, 14; Censor. 14 (cf. κλιμακτήρ in Lidd. and Scott).
climacter.short: clīmacter, ēris, m., = κλιμακτήρ (gradation), a critical epoch in human life, a climacteric (in accordance with the ancient belief, the years 7, 14, 21, 28, etc.), Plin.

climactericus.full: clīmactērĭcus, a, um, adj., = κλιμακτηρικός, of or pertaining to a dangerous epoch in life, climacterical: annus, Gell. 15, 7, 2; Censor. 14: tempus, Plin. Ep. 2, 20, 4; cf. Tert. Idol. 9, and climacter.* † clĭmătias, ae, m., = κλιματίας, a kind of earthquake, Amm. 17, 7, 13.
climactericus.short: clīmactērĭcus, a, um, adj., = κλιμακτηρικός, of or pertaining to a dangerous epoch in life, climacterical: annus, Gell.

climax.full: clīmax, ăcis, f., = κλῖμαξ (a ladder), a rhetorical figure, consisting in a gradual increase in force of expression, a climax (pure Lat. gradatio), Mart. Cap. 5, § 536 (in Quint. 9, 3, 54, used as Greek, and transl. by gradatio).
climax.short: clīmax, ăcis, f., = κλῖμαξ (a ladder), a rhetorical figure, consisting in a gradual increase in force of expression, a climax (pure Lat.

climax megale.full: Clīmax Mĕgălē = Κλῖμαξ μεγάλη, a narrow pass between Media and Asia Minor, Plin. 2, 26, 29, § 115.
climax megale.short: Clīmax Mĕgălē = Κλῖμαξ μεγάλη, a narrow pass between Media and Asia Minor, Plin.

clinamen.full: clīnāmen, ĭnis, n. clino; cf. clinatus, = declinatio, Gr. κλίσις, the inclination or turning aside of a thing: principiorum, Lucr. 2, 292.

clinatus.full: clīnātus, a, um, Part. [clino = κλίνω], inclined, bent, sunk (only in the foll. exs.), Cic. Arat. 53; 86 (but in Lucr. 6, 563, read inclinata; v. Lachm. ad h. l.).

clingere.full: clingĕre, cingere, Paul. ex Fest. p. 56, 13 Müll.; cf.: clingit cludit, Isid. Gloss.

clinia.full: Clīnĭa, ae, m., the name of a young man in the Heautontimorumenos of Terence, Ter. Heaut. 2, 2, 5 al.
clinia.short: Clīnĭa, ae, m., the name of a young man in the Heautontimorumenos of Terence, Ter.

clinias.full: Clīnĭas, ae, m., = Κλεινίας. The father of Alcibiades, Nep. Alcib. 1; hence, the latter is called Clīnĭădes, Ov. Ib. 635.— A Cretan, Cic. Leg. 1, 5, 15.

clinice.full: clīnĭcē, ēs, f., = κλινική (sc. τέχνη), the science of clinical medicine, praclice at the sick-bed, Plin. 29, 1, 2, § 4; 30, 11, 30, § 98.

clinicus.full: clīnĭcus, i, m., = κλινικός [κλίνη, the bed]. A physician who attends patients sick in bed, Mart. 9, 97; cf. MEDICVS, Inscr. Orell. 2983: deus, Prud. Apoth. 205.— A patient confined to his bed, Hier. Ep. 105, n. 5.— A bearer of the bier, sexton, grave-digger, Mart. 3, 93, 24 (al. archiclinico; cf. id. 1, 31).— One who was baptized when sick or infirm, Cypr. Ep. 69 fin.
clinicus.short: clīnĭcus, i, m., = κλινικός [κλίνη, the bed].

clinopale.full: clīnŏpălē, ēs, f., = κλινοπάλη, a wrestling in bed, = concubitus, Domit. ap. Suet. Dom. 22 (in Aur. Vict. Caes. 11, used as Greek).* † clīnŏpŏdĭon, ii, n., = κλινοπόδιον, a plant, wild basil, Plin. 24, 15, 87, § 137.* † clīnŏpūs, pŏdis, m., = κλινόπους, the foot of a bed, Lucil. ap. Macr. S. 6, 4.
clinopale.short: clīnŏpălē, ēs, f., = κλινοπάλη, a wrestling in bed, = concubitus, Domit.

clio.full: Clīo, ūs, f., = Κλειώ. The Muse of history: Clio Cliusque sorores, Ov. A. A. 1, 27; Hor. C. 1, 12, 2.— A daughter of Oceanus, Verg. G. 4, 341.

clipeo.full: clĭpĕo (clŭpĕo, clўpĕo), no perf., ātum, 1, v. a. clipeus, to arm or furnish with a shield (rare): clamide contortā astu clupeat bracchium, as with a shield, Pac. ap. Non. p. 87, 26 (Trag. Rel. v. 186 Rib.); Varr. L. L. 5, § 7 Müll. (Rib. Trag. Lat., Pac. 186): clipeata agmina, Verg. A. 7, 793; Sil. 8, 436: seges virorum, Ov. M. 3, 110 (transl. from Eurip. Phoen. 885).—Subst.: clĭpĕātus, i, m., one who is armed with a shield, Plaut. Curc. 3, 1, 54; cf.: frontem adversus clipeatos habebat, Liv. 4
clipeo.short: clĭpĕo (clŭpĕo, clўpĕo), no perf., ātum, 1, v.

clipeolum.full: clĭpĕŏlum (clŭp-, clўp-), i, n. dim. id., a small shield, Hyg. Fab. 139.

clipeus.full: clĭpĕus (in inscrr. and MSS. also clŭp- and clўp-), i, m. (clĭpĕum, i, n., Verg. A. 9, 709; Liv. 1, 43, 2; 34, 52, 5; 35, 10, 12; 38, 35, 5; 40, 51, 3; Licin. et Laber. ap. Non. p. 196, 22 sq. al.) [root in clepo]. The round brazen shield of Roman soldiers (diff. from scutum, which was oval, and made of wood covered with bull's hide; cf. Dict. of Antiq. p. 268 sq.), Enn. ap. Varr. L. L. 7, § 93 Müll.; id. ap. Prisc. p. 838 P. (Enn. Ann. 364 Vahl.); Plaut. Trin. 2, 4, 195; 3, 2, 93; id. Truc. 2,

clisthenes.full: Clīsthĕnes, is, m., = Κλεισθένης, a statesman and orator of Athens, Cic. Rep. 2, 1, 2; id. Leg. 2, 16, 41; id. Brut. 7, 27.
clisthenes.short: Clīsthĕnes, is, m., = Κλεισθένης, a statesman and orator of Athens, Cic.

clitae1.full: Clitae, ārum, f., a town of Macedonia, Liv. 44, 11, 4.
clitae1.short: Clitae, ārum, f., a town of Macedonia, Liv.

clitae2.full: Clitae, ārum, m., a tribe on the coast of Cilicia Trachea, Tac. A. 6, 41; 12, 55.
clitae2.short: Clitae, ārum, m., a tribe on the coast of Cilicia Trachea, Tac.

clitarchus.full: Clītarchus, i, m., = Κλείταρχος, a companion of Alexander the Great, of whose life he wrote a history, Cic. Fam. 2, 10, 3; id. Leg. 1, 2, 7; id. Brut. 11, 42; Curt. 9, 5, 21 al.
clitarchus.short: Clītarchus, i, m., = Κλείταρχος, a companion of Alexander the Great, of whose life he wrote a history, Cic.

clitellae.full: clītellae, ārum, f., a pack-saddle put upon beasts of burden, especially upon asses, a sumpter-saddle, Plaut. Most. 3, 2, 91; Cic. Fragm. ap. Quint. 5, 13, 40; Hor. S. 1, 5, 47; id. Ep. 1, 13, 8; Phaedr. 1, 15, 8.—Prov.: bovi clitellas imponere; v. bos, I.— Meton. The name of a place in Rome: clitellae dicuntur etiam locus Romae propter similitudinem, et in Viā Flaminiā loca quaedam devexa subinde et accliva, Paul. ex Fest. p. 59, 15 Müll.— An instrument of torture: est etiam tormenti genus eode
clitellae.short: clītellae, ārum, f., a pack-saddle put upon beasts of burden, especially upon asses, a sumpter-saddle, Plaut.

clitellarius.full: clītellārĭus, a, um, adj. clitellae, of or pertaining to a pack-saddle, bearing a pack-saddle: asini, Cato, R. R. 10, 1: mulus, Col. 2, 21, 3; Plaut. Most. 3, 2, 93: homines, id. ib. 3, 2, 94.

cliternini.full: Clīternīni, ōrum, m., the inhabitants of the town Cliternum, in the territory of the Æqui, Cic. Fam. 9, 22, 4; Plin. 3, 12, 17, § 106.
cliternini.short: Clīternīni, ōrum, m., the inhabitants of the town Cliternum, in the territory of the Æqui, Cic.

clitomachus.full: Clītŏmăchus, i, m., = Κλειτσμαχος, an Academic philosopher of Carthage, a disciple and follower of Carneades, Cic. Ac. 2, 4, 11 sq.; id. Tusc. 3, 22, 54; 5, 37, 107; id. de Or. 1, 11, 45; id. Or. 16, 51.
clitomachus.short: Clītŏmăchus, i, m., = Κλειτσμαχος, an Academic philosopher of Carthage, a disciple and follower of Carneades, Cic.

clitor.full: Clītor, ŏris, m., and Clītŏrĭum, ii, n., a town in Arcadia, Liv. 39, 35, 8; Plin. 4, 6, 10, § 20.—Abl. Clitori, Nov. ap. Non. p. 316, 5 (cf. Lachm. ad Lucr. 2, p. 49): Clitore, Liv. l. l.—Hence, Clītŏrĭus, a, um: fons, Ov. M. 15, 322: lacus, Plin. 31, 2, 13, § 16.
clitor.short: Clītor, ŏris, m., and Clītŏrĭum, ii, n., a town in Arcadia, Liv.

clitumnus.full: Clītumnus, i, m., a small river in Umbria, celebrated in ancient times, whose source received divine homage as Juppiter Clitumnus, now Clitunno or la Vene, Plin. Ep. 8, 8, 1; 8, 8, 5; Verg. G. 2, 146 Serv. et Heyne; Prop. 2 (3), 19, 25; Sil. 4, 547; 8, 453; Suet. Calig. 43.—Hence, Clītum-nus, a, um, adj., of Clitumnus: Clitumna novalia, Stat. S. 1, 4, 128.
clitumnus.short: Clītumnus, i, m., a small river in Umbria, celebrated in ancient times, whose source received divine homage as Juppiter Clitumnus, now Clitunno or la Vene, Plin.

clitus.full: Clītus, i, m., = Κλεῖτος, a friend of Alexander the Great, who was killed by him in a fit of drunkenness, Cic. Tusc. 4, 37, 79; Curt. 8, 1, 9 al.
clitus.short: Clītus, i, m., = Κλεῖτος, a friend of Alexander the Great, who was killed by him in a fit of drunkenness, Cic.

clivius.full: clivius, a, um, adj.: auspicia, which forbid any thing to be done, Paul. ex Fest. p. 64, 10 Müll.: avis, Plin. 10, 14, 17, § 57.
clivius.short: clivius, a, um, adj.: auspicia, which forbid any thing to be done, Paul.

clivosus.full: clīvōsus, a, um, adj. clivus, hilly, full of hills, steep (poet. or in post-Aug. prose): rus, Verg. G. 2, 212: trames, id. ib. 1, 108: loci et aridi, Col. Arb. 4, 3; opp. planus, id. R. R. 2, 16, 1: solum, Plin. 18, 24, 55, § 200: Olympus, Ov. F. 3, 415: Ida, id. Am. 1, 14, 11.— Trop.: tramite vitae, steep, difficult, Sil. 6, 120.

clivulus.full: clīvŭlus, i, m. dim. id., a little hill, Col. 6, 37, 10; App. M. 4, p. 144, 36.

clivus.full: clīvus, i, m. (plur.: clīva, ōrum, n., Cato ap. Non. p. 195, 2; Front. Limit. p. 43 Goes. dub.) [clino = κλίνω, to incline], a gently sloping height, a declivity, slope, an ascent, a hill, eminence, ascending road (class.): quā se subducere colles Incipiunt, mollique jugum demittere clivo, Verg. E. 9, 8; cf. id. G. 3, 293; Ov. M. 11, 151; 8, 191; so Plaut. As. 3, 3, 118; Ter. Ad. 4, 2, 36; Caes. B. C. 3, 46; Liv. 21, 32, 8; Hor. Ep. 1, 13, 10 et saep.—As antithet. to a plain, with the epithet ar

cloaca.full: clŏāca, ae, f. 1. cluo = purgo; cf. Gr. κλύζω, an artificial canal in Rome, constructed by Tarquinius Priscus, by which the filth was carried from the streets into the Tiber; in gen., a sewer, drain, Cic. Sest. 35, 77; id. Caecin. 13, 36; Hor. S. 2, 3, 242 al.; cf. Liv. 1, 38, 6; 1, 56, 2; 5, 55, 5; Plin. 36, 15, 24, § 104 sq.; Cassiod. Var. 3, 30; Dion. Halic. 3, 67; v. Dict. of Antiq. p. 269 sq. — Humorously, the stomach of a drunken woman, Plaut. Curc. 1, 2, 29; cf. intestini, Varr. ap. Non.

cloacalis.full: clŏācālis, e, adj. cloaca, pertaining to a cloaca (ante- and post-class.): flumen, Cato ap. Paul. ex Fest. p. 59, 18: faeculentia, Sid. Ep. 3, 13.

cloacare.full: cloācāre = inquinare, Paul. ex Fest. p. 66, 2; cf. cloaco, μολύνω, Gloss. Labb.

cloacarium.full: clŏācārĭum, ĭi, n. cloaca, the duty paid for conducting the private sewers into the public ones or for maintaining and cleansing the sewers, Dig. 30, 1, 39, § 5; 7, 1, 27, § 3; cf. Becker, Antiq. II. 2, p. 121, n. 616.

cloacula.full: clŏācŭla, ae, f. dim. cloaca, a small sewer, drain, Lampr. Elag. 17.

cloanthus.full: Clŏanthus, i, m., a companion of Æneas, Verg. A. 1, 222 al.
cloanthus.short: Clŏanthus, i, m., a companion of Æneas, Verg.

clodianus.full: Clōdĭānus, a, um, v. Claudius, II. B.

cloelius.full: Cloelĭus, Clŭĭlĭus, or Cloelĭa, name of a Roman gens: C. Cluilius, Liv. 1, 22, 4 al.—Esp.: Cloelĭa, ae, f., a Roman maiden, who, when a hostage to Porsenna, with several companions, swam back to Rome, Liv. 2, 13, 6 and 7; Verg. A. 8, 651; Piso ap. Plin. 34, 6, 13, § 29 al.
cloelius.short: Cloelĭus, Clŭĭlĭus, or Cloelĭa, name of a Roman gens: C.

clonius.full: Clŏnĭus, ĭi, m., the name of two companions of Æneas, Verg. A. 9, 574; 10, 749.* † clōnŏs, i, f., = κλών, a plant, also called batrachion or scelerata, App. Herb. 8.
clonius.short: Clŏnĭus, ĭi, m., the name of two companions of Æneas, Verg.

clonus.full: Clŏnus, i, m., a celebrated designer, Verg. A. 10, 499.
clonus.short: Clŏnus, i, m., a celebrated designer, Verg.

clostellum.full: clōstellum, i, n. dim. clostrum = claustrum, a small lock, Petr. 140, 11.

closter.full: Clōstēr, ēris, m., son of Arachne, inventor of the spindle, Plin. 7, 56, 57, § 196.
closter.short: Clōstēr, ēris, m., son of Arachne, inventor of the spindle, Plin.

clotho.full: Clōthō (apparently used only in nom. and acc.), = Κλωθώ, the spinner, among the three Parcœ, Ov. F. 6, 757; id. Ib. 241; Juv. 9, 135: ferrea, Stat. Th. 3, 556.— Trop. = vita, life: longa, Sil. 5, 404.

cluacina.full: Clŭācīna (Clŏācīna, on account of a derivation from cloaca, Lact. 1, 20), ae, f. cluo, the purifier: Cluacina Venus, so called because the Romans, after the end of the Sabine war, purified themselves in the vicinity of her statue with myrtle branches, Plin. 15, 29, 36, § 119; Liv. 3, 48, 5; Serv. ad Verg. A. 1, 720; Plaut. Curc. 4, 1, 10; Prud. Apoth. 265; Lact. 1, 20, 11; plur., Tert. Pall. 4.
cluacina.short: Clŭācīna (Clŏācīna, on account of a derivation from cloaca, Lact.

cluentius.full: Clŭentĭus, a, the name of a Roman gens, Cic. Clu. 1 sqq.; id. Brut. 78, 270 al.; Quint. 11, 1, 61; cf. Verg. A. 5, 123.
cluentius.short: Clŭentĭus, a, the name of a Roman gens, Cic.

clueo.full: clŭĕo, ēre (clŭo, ĕre, Aus. Prof. 21; Att. ap. Varr. L. L. 5, § 30 Müll.; Prud. ap. Symm. 2, 585; Symm. Ep. 1, 1; Mart. Cap. 6, § 571), v. n. and a. [root klu-; Sanscr. s)ru, hear; cf. Gr. ἀκροάομαι, κλέος; Lat. laus], like audio, 5., to hear one's self called in some way, to be named, called, spoken of, reputed, esteemed, or famed in some way, = dicor (only ante- and post-class.; most freq. in Plaut. and Lucr., but not in Ter.; mostly in mock-heroic style; cf. Lorenz ad Plaut. Ps. v. 570); with

clueor.full: clŭĕor, ēri, 2, v. dep. (collat. form of clueo, q. v.), to be named, called, reputed, esteemed: quippe ego te ni contemnam, Stratioticus homo qui cluear? Plaut. Ps. 4, 1, 13: sed hi cluentur hospitum infidissimi, Pac. ap. Non. p. 88, 3 (Trag. Rel. v. 194 Rib.); Varr. ib.

cluilius.full: Clŭĭlĭus, ii, m., = Κλοίλιος, a king of Alba, Liv. 1, 23, 4 and 7; after whom the Cluiliae fossae were named, id. 1, 23, 3; 2, 39, 5 (in Plut. Coriol. p. 227 Κλοιλεῖαι τάφροι).
cluilius.short: Clŭĭlĭus, ii, m., = Κλοίλιος, a king of Alba, Liv.

cluior.full: cluior nobilior, Gloss. Isid.; cf. praecluis.

clumae.full: clūmae, ārum, f.: folliculi hordei, Paul. ex Fest. p. 55, 13 Müll.; cf. gluma.
clumae.short: clūmae, ārum, f.: folliculi hordei, Paul.

clunaclus.full: clūnāclus culter, the sacrificial knife: vel quia clunes hostiarum dividit, vel quia ad clunes dependet, Paul. ex Fest. p. 50; 6; cf. Isid. Orig. 18, 6, 6.
clunaclus.short: clūnāclus culter, the sacrificial knife: vel quia clunes hostiarum dividit, vel quia ad clunes dependet, Paul.

clunae.full: clūnae, ārum, f., apes; so called acc. to Fest., a clunibus tritis, Paul. ex Fest. p. 55, 9 Müll.

clunalis.full: clūnālis, e, adj. clunis, pertaining to the hinder parts, hind-: pedes, Avien. Arat. 361.

cluniculus.full: clūnĭcŭlus, i, m., or -a, ae, f. dim. clunis, small hinder-parts: avium, Favorin. ap. Gell. 15, 8, 2.
cluniculus.short: clūnĭcŭlus, i, m., or -a, ae, f.

clunis.full: clūnis, is (mostly plur.; acc. clunem, Juv. 2, 21; 6, 334; Auct. Priap. 19, 2; abl. clune, Hor. S. 2, 8, 91; Juv. 11, 164; Mart. 9, 47, 6; 11, 100, 3; Plin. 10, 50, 71, § 140; 29, 6, 39, § 141; Petr. 23, 3), m. and f. (hence the grammarians vary in the designation of the gender; cf. Voss. Arist. 1, 29, p. 498; Rudd. 1, p. 25, n. 35) [Gr. κλόνις; Sanscr. s)rōni: nates, clunes, Bopp, Gloss. 358 a; cf. 1. cluo], a buttock, haunch. Masc., Plaut. Fragm. ap. Paul. ex Fest. p. 61, 17 Müll.; and in Non.

cluo1.full: clŭo = purgo, acc. to Plin. 15, 29, 36, § 119; cf. Serv. ad Verg. A. 1, 720 (where, instead of pugnare, purgare should be read).

clupea.full: clŭpĕa, ae, f., a kind of very small river-fish, Plin. 9, 15, 17, § 44.
clupea.short: clŭpĕa, ae, f., a kind of very small river-fish, Plin.

clupeae.full: Clŭpĕae (Clўp-), ārum; Clŭpĕa (Clўp-), ae (Mel. 1, 7, 2; Plin. 5, 4, 3, § 24; Flor. 2, 2, 19), f., a town and promontory in Africa propria, now Kalibia or Clybea, Caes. B. C. 2, 23; Auct. B. Afr. 3; Liv. 27, 29; 29, 32 (also called Aspis, Sil. 3, 244; Sol. 27).

clura.full: clura, ae, f., = πίθηκος, an ape, Vet. Gloss. Labb. (Gr. κολούρα).—Hence,
clura.short: clura, ae, f., = πίθηκος, an ape, Vet.

clurinus.full: clūrīnus, a, um, adj. clura, of or pertaining to apes: pecus, Plaut. Truc. 2, 2, 14; Arn. 3, p. 110; cf.: clura πίθηκος, cluria κεπκοπίθηκος, Vet. Gloss.

clusaris.full: clūsāris, e, adj. cludo = claudo, easily shutting or closing (post-class.): anguli, Hyg. ap. Goes. p. 181: portio quadrata, ib. p. 156.—Access. form * clūsārĭus, a, um: latus, Hyg. ap. Goes. p. 183.

clusilis.full: clūsĭlis, e, adj. id., easily closing: mordacesque conchae, Plin. 9, 37, 61, § 132.

clusium.full: Clūsĭum, ii, n., one of the oldest and most important towns of Etruria, the residence of Porsenna, previously called Camars or Camers, now Chiusi, Liv. 5, 33, 4 sq.; 10, 25, 11; Varr. ap. Plin. 36, 13, 19, § 91; Verg. A. 10, 167 al.; Müll. Etrusk. 1, p. 102; 1, p. 233 sq.; 2, p. 342.—Hence, Clūsīnus, a, um, adj., pertaining to Clusium, of Clusium: vulgus, Sil. 8, 480: fontes (cold baths), Hor. Ep. 1, 15, 9: far (of special whiteness and excellence), Col. 2, 6, 3: siligo, Plin. 18, 9, 20, § 87: p
clusium.short: Clūsĭum, ii, n., one of the oldest and most important towns of Etruria, the residence of Porsenna, previously called Camars or Camers, now Chiusi, Liv.

clusius.full: Clūsĭus, ii, m. cludo = claudo, a cognomen of Janus, whose temple was closed in peace (opp. Patulcius, when open during war), Ov. F. 1, 130; cf. Clusivius, Macr. S. 1, 9.

clusor.full: clūsor, ōris, m. id., one who encloses or encompasses, Sid. Ep. 8, 6.

clusus.full: clūsus, a, um, v. claudo, P. a.

clutomestoridysarchides.full: Clŭtŏmestōrĭdўsarchĭdes, ae, m., a comically formed name, Plaut. Mil. 1, 1, 14 Brix (by Lorenz written as Greek).
clutomestoridysarchides.short: Clŭtŏmestōrĭdўsarchĭdes, ae, m., a comically formed name, Plaut.

clutus.full: clŭtus = Gr. κλυτός, famous, renowned; hence, inclitus, Paul. ex Fest. p. 55, 14 Müll.

cluvia.full: Clŭvĭa, ae, f., a town of Samnium, Liv. 9, 31, 2.—Hence, Clŭvĭānus, a, um, of or pertaining to Cluvia: oppugnatio, Liv. 9, 31, 3.
cluvia.short: Clŭvĭa, ae, f., a town of Samnium, Liv.

cluvius.full: Cluvius, a, the name of a Roman gens, Cic. Rosc. Com. 14, 42; id. Fam. 13, 56, 1 sq. —Hence, Cluviāna hereditas, of a Cluvius, Cic. Att. 13, 46, 3.
cluvius.short: Cluvius, a, the name of a Roman gens, Cic.

clybatis.full: clўbătis, is, f., = κλύβατις, a plant, also called helxine: Parietaria officinalis, Linn.; App. Herb. 81.
clybatis.short: clўbătis, is, f., = κλύβατις, a plant, also called helxine: Parietaria officinalis, Linn.;

clymene.full: Clўmĕnē, ēs, f., = Κλυμένη. The wife of the Ethiopian king Merops, and mother of Phaëthon by Sol, Ov. M. 1, 756; 1, 765; 2, 37; 4, 204.—Gr. acc. Clymenen, Ov. M. 1, 756.—Hence, Clўmĕnēïus, a, um, adj., of or pertaining to Clymene: proles = Phaëthon, Ov. M. 2, 19.— Clўmĕ-nēïs, ĭdis, f., a daughter of Clymene, Albin. ad Liv. 1, 111.— One of the daughters of Oceanus, Verg. G. 4, 345.— A female servant and confidante of Helen, Ov. H. 16, 257; 17, 267; Dict. Cret. 1, 3; 5, 13.— An Amazon, Hyg. Fab. 1

clymenos.full: clўmĕnŏs, i, m., = κλύμενος, an unknown plant, Plin. 25, 7, 33, § 70.
clymenos.short: clўmĕnŏs, i, m., = κλύμενος, an unknown plant, Plin.

clymenus.full: Clўmĕnus, i, m., = Κλύμενος. A cognomen of Pluto, Ov. F. 6, 757.— A companion of Phineus, Ov. M. 5, 98.— A king of Arcadia, Hyg. Fab. 206 al.

clysmus.full: clysmus, i, m., = κλυσμός, a clyster (late Lat. for clyster), Scrib. Comp. 155; 194; 197.
clysmus.short: clysmus, i, m., = κλυσμός, a clyster (late Lat.

clyster.full: clyster (cluster, Scrib. Comp. 179), ēris (abl. clystĕre, Aem. Mac. cap. de anetho), m., = κλυστήρ. A clyster, injection (pure Lat. lotio, Cels. 2, 12), id. 7, 27; Scrib. Comp. 154; 179 al.; Plin. 25, 5, 23, § 56; Suet. Ner. 20 al.— A clyster-pipe or syringe, Suet. Claud. 44; Plin. 31, 6, 33, § 65; Dig. 9, 2, 9: oricularius, an ear-syringe, Cels. 7, 27; Cael. Aur. Tard. 2, 1.

clysterium.full: clystērĭum, ii, n., = κλυστήριον, a clyster (late Lat.), Scrib. Comp. 114; 118; Paul. ex Fest. p. 78, 13 Müll.
clysterium.short: clystērĭum, ii, n., = κλυστήριον, a clyster (late Lat.), Scrib.

clysterizo.full: clystērīzo, āre, v. a., = κλυστηρίζω, to apply a clyster (late Lat.), Cael. Aur. Acut. 3, 4; Veg. Vet. 2, 15, 5; 2, 17, 3 (in id. ib. 1, 42, clysterio is used).

clytaemnestra.full: Clўtaemnēstra (Clўtemnēstra, Liv. Andron. 11 Rib.; mutilated into Clў-temēstra, Cass. Hemin. ap. Serv. ad Verg. A. 7, 631; hence the second syllable short in Aus. Epit. Her. 1, 1, 4), ae, f., = Κλυταιμνήστρα, the daughter of Tyndarus and Leda, and sister of Helen, Castor, and Pollux; wife of Agamemnon and mother of Orestes, Iphigenia, and Electra; she, with her paramour, Aegisthus, murdered her husband on his return from Troy, and was on that account put to death by her son Orestes, Hyg. Fab. 11

clytidae.full: Clўtīdae, ārum, m., a family of haruspices at Elis, Cic. Div. 1, 41, 91.
clytidae.short: Clўtīdae, ārum, m., a family of haruspices at Elis, Cic.

clytie.full: Clўtĭē, ēs, f., = Κλυτίη, one of the daughters of Oceanus, changed to the plant heliotropium, Ov. M. 4, 206; 4, 234; 4, 256 sq.
clytie.short: Clўtĭē, ēs, f., = Κλυτίη, one of the daughters of Oceanus, changed to the plant heliotropium, Ov.

clytius.full: Clўtĭus, ĭi, m. The name of several heroes mentioned in Verg. A. 9, 774; 10, 129; 10, 325 al.— A companion of Phineus, Ov. M. 5, 140.

clytus.full: Clўtus, i, m. Son of Ægyptus, Hyg. Fab. 170.— A companion of Phineus, Ov. M. 5, 87.— A prœtor of the Acarnanians, Liv. 36, 11, 8 sq.

cnasonas.full: cnasonas acus, quibus mulieres caput scalpunt, Paul. ex Fest. p. 52, 17 Müll.
cnasonas.short: cnasonas acus, quibus mulieres caput scalpunt, Paul.

cnecus.full: cnēcus (cnīcus), i, m., = κνῆκος, safflower: Carthamus tinctorius, Linn.; Plin. 21, 15, 53, § 90; 21, 32, 107, § 184; Col. 7, 8, 1; Scrib. Comp. 135.
cnecus.short: cnēcus (cnīcus), i, m., = κνῆκος, safflower: Carthamus tinctorius, Linn.;

cnedinus.full: cnēdĭnus (cnīd-), a, um, adj., = κνήδινος, of nettles, nettle-: oleum, Plin. 15, 7, 7, § 30.
cnedinus.short: cnēdĭnus (cnīd-), a, um, adj., = κνήδινος, of nettles, nettle-: oleum, Plin.

cnemis.full: cnēmis, īdis, f., = κνημίς, a greave; fig. of the end of the verse, Mall. Theod. Metr. 4, 12.
cnemis.short: cnēmis, īdis, f., = κνημίς, a greave;

cneoron.full: cnĕōron, i, n., = κνέωρον (also cnē-stron, i, n., = κνῆστρον), a plant, also called thymelaea, mezereon: Daphne gnidium, Linn.; Plin. 13, 21, 35, § 114.
cneoron.short: cnĕōron, i, n., = κνέωρον (also cnē-stron, i, n., = κνῆστρον), a plant, also called thymelaea, mezereon: Daphne gnidium, Linn.;

cnephosus.full: cnĕphōsus, a, um, adj. κνέφας, dark, Paul. ex Fest. p. 51, 9 Müll.

cnide.full: cnīdē, ēs, f., = κνίδη, a sea-nettle; pure Lat. urtica (q. v.), a zoophyte, Plin. 32, 11, 53, § 146.
cnide.short: cnīdē, ēs, f., = κνίδη, a sea-nettle;

cnisa.full: cnīsa (cnissa), ae, f., = κνῖσα, the steam or odor of a sacrifice, Arn. 7, p. 212.
cnisa.short: cnīsa (cnissa), ae, f., = κνῖσα, the steam or odor of a sacrifice, Arn.

cnodax.full: cnōdax, ācis, m., = κνώδαξ; in mechanics, a pin, pivot, gudgeon; Fr. pivōt, boulons, Vitr. 10, 2, 11.

cnosos.full: Cnōsos, Cnōsĭus, Cnōsĭăcus, etc., v. Gnosus.

coa2.full: Cŏa, ae, f., a fictitious nickname of Clodia [from coeo; opp. Nola, from nolo], Cael. ap. Quint. 8, 6, 53.
coa2.short: Cŏa, ae, f., a fictitious nickname of Clodia [from coeo;

coaccedo.full: cŏ-accēdo, ĕre, v. n., to come to or be added besides, Plaut. Curc. 2, 3, 65.

coacervatim.full: cŏăcervātim, adv. coacervatus, from coacervo, by or in heaps: offerre aliquid, App. Flor. 2, p. 347, 7; cf. Cael. Aur. Tard. 4, 3.

coacervatio.full: cŏăcervātĭo, ōnis, f. coacervo. * A heaping together. Prop.: stratae viae, Isid. Orig. 15, 16, 7.— Trop.: actionum, Dig. 2, 1, 11.— A rhetorical figure, * Cic. Part. Or. 35, 122; * Quint. 9, 3, 53.

coacervo.full: cŏ-ăcervo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a., to heap together, heap up, collect in a mass (class., esp. in prose; most freq. in Cic.). Prop.: pecuniae coguntur et coacervantur, Cic. Agr. 2, 27, 70; cf. id. ib. 1, 5, 14: quantum (argenti, etc.) in turbā et rapinis coacervari unā in domo potuit, id. Rosc. Am. 46, 133: tantam vim emblematum, Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 24, § 54: multitudinem civium, id. ib. 2, 5, 57, § 148: cadavera, Caes. B. G. 2, 27; cf.: hostium cumulos, Liv. 22, 7, 5: armorum cumulos, id. 5, 39, 1: om

coacesco.full: cŏ-ăcesco, ăcŭi, 3, v. inch. n., to become acid or sour (rare but in good prose). Prop.: genus uvae, Varr. R. R. 1, 65, 2; cf.: ut non omne vinum, sic non omnis aetas vetustate coacescit, Cic. Sen. 18, 65; Dig. 33, 6, 9 pr.: secunda mensa in imbecillo stomacho coacescit, Cels. 1, 2: si coacuit intus cibus aut computruit, id. 4, 5 fin. — Trop (the fig. drawn from wine): quare cum integri nihil fuerit in hac gente plenā, quam valde eam putamus tot transfusionibus coacuisse? to deteriorate or becom

coacte.full: cŏactē, adv., v. cogo, P. a. fin.

coactiliarius.full: cŏactĭlĭārĭus, ii, m. coactilis, a maker of thick, fulled cloth: LANARIVS, Inscr. Orell. 4206.—Adj.: taberna, a fulling-mill, Capitol. Pert. 3; but v. coctilicius.

coactilis.full: cŏactĭlis, e, adj. coactus, cogo, made thick; hence subst.: cŏactĭlĭa, ium, n., thick, fulled cloth or felt, Dig. 34, 2, 26; cf. Edict. Diocl. p. 21.

coactim.full: cŏactim, adv. id. (of expression), concisely, briefly, Sid. Ep. 9, 16.

coactio.full: cŏactĭo, ōnis, f. cogo (post-Aug. and rare). * A collecting, calling in: coactiones argentarias factitavit, Suet. Vesp. 1. — An abridgment or epitome of a discourse, Inst. 4, 15.— A disease of animals, Veg. Art. Vet. 2, 9, 1; 2, 10, 5; 2, 15, 5.

coacto.full: cŏacto, āre, v. freq. a. id., to constrain, force (only twice in Lucr.); with inf., Lucr. 6, 1121 and 1160.

coactor.full: cŏactor, ōris, m. id.. Prop. A collector of money (from auctions, of revenues, etc.), Cato, R. R. 150, 2; Cic. Clu. 64, 180; id. Rab. Post. 11, 30; * Hor. S. 1, 6, 86; cf. Acron. and Porphyr. in h. l. and Auct. Vit. Hor. 1; Sen. Ep. 81, 2 (al. decoctor).— Coactores agminis, the rear, Tac. H. 2, 68.— ( = coactiliarius.) A fuller, Inscr. Grut. 648, 3.— Trop., one who forces to something: adjutor, et, ut ita dicam, coactor, Sen. Ep. 52, 4.

coactura.full: cŏactūra, ae, f. id.; concr., a collection, Col. 12, 50, 2.

coactus1.full: cŏactus, a, um, Part. and P. a., v. cogo.

coactus2.full: cŏactus, ūs, m. cogo, a forcing, constraint, compulsion (rare and only in abl. sing.): alterius magno coactu, * Lucr. 2, 273: coactu atque efflagitatu meo, Cic. Verr. 2, 5, 29, § 75; 2, 2, 13, § 34: civitatis, Caes. B. G. 5, 27.

coaddo.full: cŏ-addo, ĕre, v. a., to add with, add also, Cato, R. R. 40, 2; Plaut. Cas. 3, 1, 4.

coadjutor.full: cŏ-adjūtor, ōris, m., = adjutor, an assistant, Inscr. Orell. 3427.
coadjutor.short: cŏ-adjūtor, ōris, m., = adjutor, an assistant, Inscr.

coadoro.full: cŏ-ădōro, āre, v. a., to worship or adore along with (late Lat.), Ambros. Spir. Sanct. 3, 12; Cod. Just. 1, 1, 4.

coadulesco.full: cŏ-ădŭlesco, ēvi, 3, v. inch. n., to grow up along with (eccl. Lat.), Tert. Anim. 19; 16.

coadunatio.full: cŏădūnātĭo, ōnis, f. coaduno, a uniting into one, a summing up: totius calculi, Cod. Just. 5, 12, 31 fin.

coaduno.full: cŏ-ădūno, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a., to unite, add, or join together, to collect into one (postclass.), Dig. 10, 4, 7; 2, 14, 9; Aur. Vict. Vit. 1; Dict. Cret. 4, 13.

coaedifico.full: cŏ-aedĭfĭco, no perf., ātum, 1, v. a., to build up together, build upon (only in Cic.): Campum Martium, Cic. Att. 13, 33, 4: loci coaedificati an vasti, id. Part. Or. 10, 36: quarta pars (urbis), Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 53, § 119 Zumpt N. cr. (al. aedificata).

coaegresco.full: cŏ-aegresco, ĕre, 3, v. inch. n., to become sick at the same time with, Tert. Anim. 5 dub. (al. cohaerescit).

coaegroto.full: cŏ-aegrōto, āre, v. n., to be sick at the same time with, Hier. adv. Jovin. 1, 47.

coaequalis.full: cŏ-aequālis, e, adj., of equal age, coeval (post-Aug.): sinciput, Petr. 136, 1.— Subst., a comrade, companion in age, Just. 23, 4, 9; Inscr. Orell. 4407 al.—Transf., of geese, Col. 8, 14, 8.
coaequalis.short: cŏ-aequālis, e, adj., of equal age, coeval (post-Aug.): sinciput, Petr.

coaequo.full: cŏ-aequo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a., to make one thing equal or even with another, to even, level (rare but in good prose). Prop.: aream, Cato, R. R. 91 and 129: montes, Sall. C. 20, 11: pastinatum, Col. 3, 16, 1: sulcum, id. 11, 3, 48: glaebas, id. 2, 17, 4; cf. Pall. 1, 13 fin.— Trop. To make equal in worth, dignity, power, etc., to bring to the same level, place on the same footing, equalize: ad libidines injuriasque tuas omnia coaequasti, * Cic. Verr 2, 3, 41, § 95: gratiam omnium, Sall. Rep. Ord.

coaestimo.full: cŏ-aestĭmo, āre, v. a., to estimate together with: aliquid, Dig. 47, 2, 69.

coaetaneo.full: cŏaetānĕo, āre, v. n. coaetaneus, to be of the same age, Tert. Res Carn. 45.

coaetaneus.full: cŏ-aetānĕus, i, m. aetas, one of the same age; a contemporary (post-class.), App M. 8, p. 204, 5; Tert. adv. Herm. 6; Vulg. Gal. 1, 14.

coaeternus.full: cŏ-aeternus, a, um, adj., coeternal (eccl. Lat.), Tert. adv. Herm. 11; Hier. Ep. 16, n. 4 al.

coaevus.full: cŏ-aevus, a, um, adj. aevum, of the same age, coeval (eccl. Lat.), Aug. Serm. 38; id. Verb. Dom. 7; Prud. Cath. 12, 137; Vulg. Dan. 1, 10.

coaggero.full: cŏ-aggĕro, no perf., ātum, 1, v. a. * To heap together: lapides, Serv. ad Verg. A. 5, 273.—* Aliquid aliquā re, to cover by heaping upon, Col. 8, 6, 1.

coagito.full: cŏ-ăgĭto, no perf., ātum, 1, v. a., to shake together (in late medic. lang.), Apic. 2, 1; 4, 3; Marc. Emp. 8.

coagmentarius.full: cŏagmentārĭus, ii, m. coagmentum, joining together, ἁρμολόγος, Gloss. Gr. Lat.

coagmentatio.full: cŏagmentātĭo, ōnis, f. coagmento, a joining or connecting together; a connection, combination, union (several times in Cic.; elsewh. rare): corporis, Cic. Univ. 5 fin.: non dissolubilis, id. N. D. 1, 8, 20: naturae, id. ib. 2, 46, 119.—Plur., Vitr. 2, 9, 11; Plin. 36, 22, 51, § 172.

coagmento.full: cŏagmento, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. coagmentum, t. t., to join, stick, glue, cement, etc., together, to connect (in good prose; most freq. in Cic.). Prop.: opus ipsa suum eadem, quae coagmentavit, naturā dissolvit, Cic. Sen. 20, 72: nihil concretum, nihil copulatum, nihil coagmentatum, id. Tusc. 1, 29, 71; cf. id. Fin. 3, 22, 74: tubulum, Vitr. 8, 7: ancones, id. 8, 6: fissuram, Col. 4, 29, 8: allium nucleis, Plin. 19, 6, 34, § 111; Curt. 4, 7, 23.— Trop. (only in Cic. and Quint.; in the former rare

coagmentum.full: cŏagmentum, i, n. cogo, a joining together; in concr., a joint (in good prose; not in Cic.; mostly in plur.). Prop., Non. p. 42, 20 sq.; Cato, R. R. 18, 9; Plaut. Most. 3, 2, 143; Caes. B. C. 3, 105 fin.; Vitr. 2, 3, 4; 2, 8, 3; 4, 4, 4.— Trop., a joining or connecting together: syllabarum, Gell. 17, 9, 2.

coagulare.full: cŏāgŭlāre, is, n. coagulo (sc. intestinum), the colon, Veg. 8, 16, 1 al.

coagulatio.full: cŏāgŭlātĭo, ōnis, f. id., a curdling, coagulating, of a liquid (in the elder Pliny): lactis, Plin. 23, 1, 18, § 30; 28, 10, 45, § 158.

coagulo.full: cŏāgŭlo, āvi, ātum (contr. COAGLAVI, Inscr. ap. Anthol. Lat. 1177 Meyer), 1, v. a. coagulum, to cause a fluid to curdle or coagulate (mostly in the elder Pliny): lac, Plin. 12, 25, 54, § 123; 20, 14, 53, § 147: picem, id. 16, 11, 22, § 53; v. Sillig N. cr.: aquam, id. 20, 23, 97, § 259: sudorem, id. 35, 15, 52, § 186: caseum, Pall. Mai, 9, 1 al.

coagulum.full: cŏāgŭlum, i, n. cogo, a means of coagulation, a coagulum or coagulator (the curdled milk in the stomach of a sucking animal, the stomach itself, etc.), rennet or runnet, Varr. R. R. 2, 11, 4; Col. 7, 8, 1; Plin. 11, 41, 96, § 237 sq.; 23, 7, 63, § 117; Ov. M. 13, 830; 14, 274; id. F. 4, 545 al.—Meton. (causa pro effectu), the curdled milk, Plin. 28, 10, 45, § 162.— Trop., that which holds or binds together, a bond, tie (only anteand post-class. and rare): hoc (vinum) continet coagulum convivia,

coalesco.full: cŏ-ălesco, ălŭi, ălĭtum (part. perf. only in Tac. and subseq. writers; contr. form colescat, Varr. R. R. 1, 41, 2: colescere, Lucr. 6, 1068: coluerunt, id. 2, 1061 Lachm. N. cr.), v. inch. n. (most freq. since the Aug. per.; never in Cic.). To grow together with something, to unite. Prop., Lucr. 2, 1061: saxa vides solā colescere calce, id. 6, 1068: ne prius exarescat surculus quam colescat, is united, sc. with the tree into which it is inserted, Varr. R. R. 1, 41, 2: gramen, Col. 2, 18, 5: seme

coalitus1.full: cŏălĭtus, a, um, Part., from coalesco.
coalitus1.short: cŏălĭtus, a, um, Part., from coalesco.

coalitus2.full: cŏălĭtus, ūs, m. coalesco, communion, fellowship: humani generis, Arn. 4, p. 150.

coalo.full: cŏ-ălo, ĕre, v. a., to sustain or nourish together with: fetus, Hier. in Jovin. 1, 36.

coambulo.full: cŏ-ambŭlo, āre, v. n., to go with, Claud. Mam. Stat. An. 1, 3.

coangusto.full: cŏ-angusto, āvi, ātum, v. a., to bring into a narrow compass, to confine, compress, contract, enclose, hem in (rare and mostly post-Aug.). Prop.: alvos, * Varr. R. R. 3, 16, 15: quo facilius fistula claudatur vel certe coangustetur, Cels. 7, 27 fin.; Auct. B. Hisp. 5; cf. Aur. Vict. Epit. 42: aditum aedium, Dig. 19, 2, 19.—Of a city, to invest, besiege: et coangustabunt te undique, Vulg. Luc. 19, 43.— Trop., to limit, restrict: haec lex dilatata in ordinem cunctum, coangustari etiam potest, * Ci

coaptatio.full: cŏaptātĭo, ōnis, f. coapto, an accurate joining together (a word coined by Augustine for translating the Gr. ἁρμονία), Aug. Trin. 4, 2; id. Civ. Dei, 22, 24.

coapto.full: cŏ-apto, no perf., ātum, 1, v. a., to fit, join, adjust together with something (eccl. Lat.; cf. Lachm. ad Lucr. 2, pp. 135 and 248), Aug. Doctr. Christ. 1, 14; Prud. Psych. 557.

coaresco.full: cŏ-āresco, ārui, 3, v. inch. n., to dry or become dry together, Vitr. 7, 11 (al. coaluerint).

coarguo.full: cŏ-argŭo, ŭi, 3, v. a., orig., to assail a person or thing in different directions (cf. arguo init.); hence, jurid. t. t. Aliquem, to overwhelm with reasoning, refute, silence, expose; convict of guilt or crime, prove guilty (class., most freq. in Cic.; syn. convinco): Graecus testis... vinci, refelli, coargui putat esse turpissimum, Cic. Fl. 5, 11: criminibus coarguitur, Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 47, § 104: ut illum natura ipsius consuetudoque defendat, hunc autem haec cadem coarguant, id. Mil. 14, 36:

coargutio.full: cŏargūtĭo, ōnis, f. coarguo, a convicting, refutation, Hier. Ep. 41, 4.

coarmio.full: cŏarmĭo, ōnis, m. co-arma, a comrade in arms, Inscr. Orell. 2571.

coarmo.full: cŏ-armo, āvi, ātum, āre, to arm together, Cassiod. Hist. Eccl. 5, 45 al.
coarmo.short: cŏ-armo, āvi, ātum, āre, to arm together, Cassiod.

coartatio.full: cŏartātĭo (cŏarct-), ōnis, f. coarto, a drawing or crowding together (rare): laxatio aut coartatio, Vitr. 9, 9: plurium in angusto tendentium, Liv. 27, 46, 2; so, militum eo loco, Auct. B. Alex. 74 fin.

coarticulo.full: cŏ-artĭcŭlo, āre, v. a., to cause to articulate: ora mutorum, Arn. 1, p. 31.

coarto.full: cŏ-arto (cŏarcto), āvi, ātum, 1, v. a., to press together, compress, contract, confine (opp. laxo, dilato, etc.; class.). Prop.: faenum in struem, Col. 2, 19, 2; 8, 7, 2: alveum Tiberis (opp. laxo), Suet. Aug. 30: angustae fauces coartant iter, Liv. 28, 5, 8; so id. 33, 6, 7: viam, Dig. 43, 8, 2: forum, Tac. Or. 39; Front. Aquaed. 35: os et fauces sudario, to strangle one's self, Val. Max. 9, 12, 7 al.: Gnaeus in oppidis coartatus, Cic. Att. 7, 10 med.: in terra, Vulg. Exod. 14, 3.— Trop. Of tim

coassatio.full: cŏassātio (cŏax-), ōnis, f. coasso, a joining of timber (boards or planks) together; hence in concr., a boarded floor, Vitr. 6, 3, 9; 7, 1, 1 sq.—In plur., Plin. 36, 25, 62, § 186.

coasso.full: cŏasso (cŏax-), āvi, ātum, 1 co-axis, to join boards or planks together, Vitr. 7, 1, 5.
coasso.short: cŏasso (cŏax-), āvi, ātum, 1 co-axis, to join boards or planks together, Vitr.

coassumo.full: cŏ-assūmo, sumpsi, sumptum, ĕre, to assume together, Boëth. Arist. top. 6, 8.
coassumo.short: cŏ-assūmo, sumpsi, sumptum, ĕre, to assume together, Boëth.

coauctio.full: cŏauctĭo, ōnis, f. coaugeo, a joint increase, Cic. Verr. 2, 3, 82, § 189; dub. al. leg. conjectio or conjunctio.

coaxo2.full: cŏaxo, āre, v. n. the natural sound of frogs; cf. κοάξ, to croak, Suet. Aug. 94; Auct. Phil. 62; Spart. Get. 6.

cobiamachus.full: Cobiamăchus (Cobiom-), i, f., a village in Gallia Narbonensis, between Tolosa and Narbo, Cic. Font. 5, 9.
cobiamachus.short: Cobiamăchus (Cobiom-), i, f., a village in Gallia Narbonensis, between Tolosa and Narbo, Cic.

cobio.full: cobio and cobius, v. gobio and gobius.

cobion.full: cōbĭon, ii, n., = κώβιον, a species of the plant tithymalus (wolf's-milk), called also dendroides and leptophyllon, Plin. 26, 8, 45, § 71.
cobion.short: cōbĭon, ii, n., = κώβιον, a species of the plant tithymalus (wolf's-milk), called also dendroides and leptophyllon, Plin.

cocalus.full: Cōcălus, i, m., a mythic king in Sicily, who gave protection to Dœdalus when he fled from the persecution of Minos, Ov. M. 8, 261, Just. 4, 2, 2.—Hence, Cōcălĭ-des, um, f., the daughters of Cocalus, Sil. 14, 42.
cocalus.short: Cōcălus, i, m., a mythic king in Sicily, who gave protection to Dœdalus when he fled from the persecution of Minos, Ov.

cocceius.full: Coccēius, a, the name of an Italic gens. Cocceius Nerva, Hor. S. 1, 5, 28. — M. Cocceius Nerva, a celebrated lawyer under Tiberius, Tac. A. 4, 58 al.— M. Cocceius Nerva, grandson of the preceding, Inscr Orell. 1634; emperor, A.U.C. 849-851, Tac. A. 15, 72; Mart. 8, 70, 7.
cocceius.short: Coccēius, a, the name of an Italic gens.

coccinatus.full: coccĭnātus, a, um, adj. coccinus, clothed in scarlet: puerulus, Suet. Dom. 4; cf. Mart. 1, 97, 6; 5, 37, 2.

coccineus.full: coccĭnĕus, a, um, adj. coccum, scarlet-colored: pallium, Petr. 32, 2: tomentum, id. 38, 5: lacernae, Mart. 14, 131 in lemm.— Access. form coccĭnus, a, um: acini, Plin. 21, 31, 105, § 177: gausapa, Petr. 28, 4. laena, Juv. 3, 283: aluta, Mart. 2, 29, 8. — In plur subst.: coccĭna, ōrum, n., scarlet garments, Mart. 2, 39, 1; 2, 43, 8; 14, 131, 1.— In sing. subst.: coccĭnum, i, n., = coccum, Hier. in Isa. 1, 1, 18.

coccum.full: coccum, i, n., = κὀκκος (a berry, and specif.), The berry that grows upon the scarlet oak (Quercus coccifera, Linn.; acc. to modern botany a kind of insect, cochineal kermes), with which scarlet was colored, Plin. 16, 8, 12, § 32; 9, 41, 65, § 140.—Also used in medicine, Plin. 24, 4, 4, § 8 al.— Meton. Scarlet color: rubro cocco tingere, Hor. S. 2, 6, 102; Mart. 5, 23, 5: cocco fulgere, id. 10, 76, 9: sanguineum, Verg. Cir. 31; Quint. 11, 1, 31.— Scarlet garments, cloth, etc., Sil. 17, 396; Suet
coccum.short: coccum, i, n., = κὀκκος (a berry, and specif.), The berry that grows upon the scarlet oak (Quercus coccifera, Linn.;

coccygia.full: coccȳgĭa, ae, f, = κοκκυγία, a kind of sumach used in coloring, perh. Rhus cotinus, Linn.; Plin. 13, 22, 41, § 121.
coccygia.short: coccȳgĭa, ae, f, = κοκκυγία, a kind of sumach used in coloring, perh.

coccymelum.full: coccȳmēlum, i, n., = κοκκύμηλον, a plum, Cloat. ap. Macr. S. 2, 15; cf. Isid. Orig. 17, 7, 10.
coccymelum.short: coccȳmēlum, i, n., = κοκκύμηλον, a plum, Cloat.

coccyx.full: coccyx, ȳgis, m., = κόκκυξ, a cuckoo, Plin. 10, 9, 11, § 25 sq.
coccyx.short: coccyx, ȳgis, m., = κόκκυξ, a cuckoo, Plin.

cocetum.full: cocētum, i, n. perh. from κυκεών, a kind of food prepared from honey and poppies, Tert. adv. Val. 12; cf. Paul. ex Fest. p. 39, 8 Müll.

cochlacae.full: cochlacae (cocl-), ārum, f., = κόχλακες, round stones from a river, resembling snails' shells, Paul. ex Fest. p. 39, 7 Müll.
cochlacae.short: cochlacae (cocl-), ārum, f., = κόχλακες, round stones from a river, resembling snails' shells, Paul.

cochlis.full: cochlis, ĭdis, f., = κοχλίς, a precious stone like a snail-shell in form, Plin. 37, 12, 74, § 194.
cochlis.short: cochlis, ĭdis, f., = κοχλίς, a precious stone like a snail-shell in form, Plin.

cochloe.full: cochloe, ōn, m., = κόχλοι, a kind of shell-fishes with spiral shells, Plin. 32, 11, 53, § 147 Sillig N. cr.
cochloe.short: cochloe, ōn, m., = κόχλοι, a kind of shell-fishes with spiral shells, Plin.

cociator.full: cocĭātor, ōris, m., = μεταβόλος, cocio, a broker, Gloss. Vet. (prob. for cocĭōnātor).
cociator.short: cocĭātor, ōris, m., = μεταβόλος, cocio, a broker, Gloss.

cocio.full: cōcĭo or cōtĭo (coctio, Paul. ex Fest. p. 20, 12, and 51, 3 Müll. N. cr.), ōnis, m. cf. cunctor, a broker, factor; acc. to Gell. more usu. called arilator (v. h. v. and cf. Fest. p. 20), Laber ap. Gell. 16, 7, 12.

cocionatura.full: cōcĭōnātūra, ae, f. cocio, μετάπρασις, brokery, Gloss. Gr. Lat.

cocionor.full: cōcĭōnor, āri, v. dep. id., to be a broker, Quint. Decl. 12, 21 dub.

coclea.full: cō^clĕa (cō^chlĕa; cf. the letter C), ae, f. κοχλίας, ό, a snail: quom caletur cocleae in occulto latent, Plaut. Capt. 1, 1, 12; Plin. 9, 56, 82, § 173 sq.; Varr. R. R. 3, 14; Cic. Div. 2, 64, 133; Auct. Her. 4, 49, 62; Hor. S. 2, 4, 59: nudae, without shells, Plin. 29, 6, 36, § 112; an emblem of slowness, Plaut. Poen. 3, 1, 29.— In cocleam, snail-formed, spiral, Cels. 8, 10, 1; Col. 8, 17, 2; cf.: per cocleam ascendebat in cenaculum, Vulg. 3 Reg. 6, 8.— Meton. A snail-shell, Mart. 11, 18, 23.—

coclear.full: cŏclĕar (cochl-), āris (cŏclĕārĭ-um, ii, Scrib. Comp. 122; 96; Cels. 3, 22; cŏclĕāre, is, Mart. 8, 71, 10; 8, 14, 121; and coclĕārum, i, Plin. 20, 22, 89, § 242), n. coclea, of the form of a snail-shell, a spoon, Mart. l. l.; Cels. 6, 14; Plin. 28, 2, 4, § 19; Petr. 33, 6 al.—As a measure for liquids, esp. in medicine, a spoonful, = half a cheme or 1/144 of a cotyla, Rhem. Fann. Pond.; Col. 12, 21, 3; Plin. 23, 4, 38, § 76; 27, 4, 5, § 17, and the above passages with coclearium.

coclearium.full: coclĕārĭum (cochl-), ii, n. coclea. An enclosure or pen in which snails were kept and fed, Varr. R. R. 3, 12, 2; 3, 14, 1.— A spoon; v. cochlear.

cocleatim.full: coclĕātim (cochl-), adv. id., spirally, Sid. Ep. 4, 15 fin.

cocleatus.full: coclĕātus (cochl-), a, um, adj. id., spiral or screw-formed: equuleus, Pomp. ap. Non. p. 105, 15, and 182, 14: aures, Cassiod. Anim. 9.

cocleola.full: coclĕŏla (cochl-), ae, f. dim. id., a small snail, Hier. Ep. 64, n. 19; id. in Jov. 2, 6.

cocles1.full: cō^cles, ĭtis, m. for scoculus; root ska-; cf. σκιά, σκότος, and oculus (cf. Fleck. in Rhein. Mus. 8, p. 231), cognomen of a person blind with one eye, Plin. 11, 37, 55, § 150; so Enn. ap. Varr L. L. 7, § 71; Plaut. Curc. 3, 1, 23.

cocles2.full: Cō^cles, itis, m., the cognomen of a Roman, Horatius Cocles. who, in the war with Porsenna, defended a bridge alone, Liv 2, 10, 2 sq.; Cic. Off. 1, 18, 61; id. Leg. 2, 4, 10; Verg. A. 8, 650; Plin. 34, 5, 11, § 22; 36, 15, 23, § 100 al.; Prop. 3 (4), 11, 63; Sen. Ep. 120, 7.
cocles2.short: Cō^cles, itis, m., the cognomen of a Roman, Horatius Cocles.

coco.full: coco, acc. to others cocococo, the sound naturally made by the hen, clucking, Petr. 59, 2.

cocolobis.full: cŏcŏlŏbis or cŏcŏlŭbis, is, f., a Spanish name for a kind of grape.—Form -ŭbis, Col. 3, 2, 19.—Form -ŏbis, Plin. 14, 2, 4, § 30.
cocolobis.short: cŏcŏlŏbis or cŏcŏlŭbis, is, f., a Spanish name for a kind of grape.—Form -ŭbis, Col.

cocosates.full: Cocosātes, um, m., a tribe in Aquitania, Caes. B. G. 3, 27; Plin. 4, 19, 33, § 108.
cocosates.short: Cocosātes, um, m., a tribe in Aquitania, Caes.

cocta.full: cocta, ae, f., v. coquo, I. A. fin.

coctilicius.full: coctĭlĭcĭus, a, um coctilis, of or pertaining to dried wood: taberna, in which dry wood is sold, Capit. Pert. 3; others less correctly coactiliaria.
coctilicius.short: coctĭlĭcĭus, a, um coctilis, of or pertaining to dried wood: taberna, in which dry wood is sold, Capit.

coctilis.full: coctĭlis, e, adj. coquo, burned: lateres, Varr. R. R. 1, 14 fin.: laterculus, Plin. 7, 56, 57, § 193; Curt. 5, 1, 25: muri (Babylonis), built of burned bricks, Ov. M. 4, 58; cf. Curt. l. l., and Just. 1, 2, 7 (cocto latere). — Subst.: coctĭlĭa, ium, n. (sc. ligna), very dry wood, that burns without smoke (cf. acapnos), Treb. Claud. 14; cf. Dig. 32, 55, § 7.

coctio1.full: coctĭo, ōnis, f. id.. Lit., a cooking, burning: calcis, Cassiod. Var. 7, 17.— A digesting of food, Plin. 20, 9, 39, § 101.

coctivus.full: coctīvus, a, um, adj. coquo, that is easily cooked or ripens early (acc. to others, suitable for cooking): castaneae, Plin. 15, 23, 25, § 94: condimenta, used in cooking, Apic. 9, 4.

coctor.full: coctor, ōris, m. id. (more rare than coquus), a cook, Petr. 95, 8: calcis, a limeburner, Edict. Diocl. p. 19; Cod. Th. 14, 6, 1.

coctura.full: coctūra, ae, f. id., a cooking; a melting; a manner or style of cooking, Col. 11, 3, 23, p. 453 Bip.: Apiciana, Plin. 19, 8, 41, § 143; 34, 8, 20, § 96; Apic. 6, 2 al.; Pall. Nov. 1, 3.— Meton. A temperature of the air adapted to the ripening (of fruit), Plin. 14, 4, 6, § 55.— (Abstr. pro concr.) A boiling liquid, Col. 12, 20, 4; 12, 18, 7.

cocturarius.full: coctūrārĭus, ii, m., a cook, ἑψητής, Gloss. Vet.
cocturarius.short: coctūrārĭus, ii, m., a cook, ἑψητής, Gloss.

coctus.full: coctus, a, um, Part., from coquo.
coctus.short: coctus, a, um, Part., from coquo.

cocula.full: cŏcŭla (also cŏquula), ae, f. dim. coquus, a female cook, Varr. ap. Non. p. 531, 32.

coculum.full: cŏcŭlum, i, n. coquo. * A vessel for cooking, Plaut. Fragm. ap. Isid. Orig. 20, 8, 1; cf. Paul. ex Fest. p. 39, 2 Müll.— Acc. to some, small wood for cooking, Paul. ex Fest. l. l.; cf. Gloss. Isid. Plac. p. 448 Mai.

cocytus.full: Cōcȳtus (-ŏs), i, m., = Κωκυτὀς [river of lamentation, from κωκὐω, to howl, weep], a mythic river in the Lower World, Cic. Tusc. 1, 5, 10; id. N. D. 3, 17, 43; Verg. G. 3, 38; 4, 479; id. A. 6, 132; 6, 297; 6, 323; Hor. C. 2, 14, 18 al.; acc. Gr. Cocyton, Claud. Rapt. Pros. 2, 353; cf. Heyne, Verg. A. 6 Excurs. IX.— Adj.: Cōcȳtĭus, a, um, of Cocytus: aqua, Petr. 120, 69; and Cocytia aequora, Claud. in Rufin. 2, 471: virgo, i. e. Alecto, Verg. A. 7, 479.
cocytus.short: Cōcȳtus (-ŏs), i, m., = Κωκυτὀς [river of lamentation, from κωκὐω, to howl, weep], a mythic river in the Lower World, Cic.

codeta.full: Cōdēta, ae, f. coda = cauda, a place in which grew plants resembling the tails of horses. Codeta Major, a place beyond the Tiber, Paul. ex Fest. p. 58, 4; cf. ib. p. 38, 17 Müll.—Hence, Codētānus, a, um: campus, Reg. Urb. Rom. 14.— Codeta Minor, a place near the Campus Martius, Suet. Caes. 39; cf. Becker, Antiq. 1, p. 656, annot. 1414.

codicillaris.full: cōdĭcillāris, e (and cōdĭcillārius, a, um: dignitates, Cod. Th. 6, 22, 7), adj. codicilli, II. B. 1., named or appointed by the emperor's handwriting: auguratus, Lampr. Alex. Sev. 49.
codicillaris.short: cōdĭcillāris, e (and cōdĭcillārius, a, um: dignitates, Cod.

codicilli.full: cōdĭcilli, ōrum (sing. post-class. and rare in the meaning II. B. 2. infra, Cod. Just. 1, 5, 4, § 5; Cod. Th. 8, 18, 7; 16, 5, 40; Dig. 29, 7, 19; cf. ib. 50, 16, 148), m. dim. codex = caudex. Wood cut and split for burning, only in Cato, R. R. 37, 5; 130. — (Acc. to caudex, III., a writing-tablet; hence) A writing, letter, esp. a short writing, note, billet, a petition, etc.; cf. Plin. 13, 13, 27, § 89, and 33, 1, 4, § 12. In gen., Cic. Phil. 8, 10, 28; id. Fam. 6, 18, 1; 9, 26, 1; id. Q. Fr. 2

codicula.full: cōdĭcŭla, ae, f. dim. coda = cauda, a little tail, Apic. 7, 1 dub.

codomannus.full: Codomannus, i, m., cognomen of the last Persian king Darius, Just. 10, 3; 11, 6 sq.
codomannus.short: Codomannus, i, m., cognomen of the last Persian king Darius, Just.

codrio.full: Codrio or Codrion, ōnis, m., a town in Greek Illyria, Liv. 31, 27, 5.
codrio.short: Codrio or Codrion, ōnis, m., a town in Greek Illyria, Liv.

codrus.full: Cōdrus, i, m., = Κόδρος. The last Athenian king, who voluntarily devoted himself to death in order to obtain for his people victory over the Spartans, Cic. Tusc. 1, 48, 116; id. Fin. 5, 22, 62; id. N. D. 3, 19, 49; Hor. C. 3, 19, 2; Just. 2, 6, 19; Vell. 1, 2; Val. Max. 5, 6, 1.— A wretched poet, hostile to Virgil, Verg. E. 5, 11; 7, 22; Juv. 1, 2; 3, 203; 3, 208; cf. Weich. Poett. Latt. Rell.Poet. Lat. Rel. p. 402 sq.

coela.full: Coela (ōrum, n.), Euboeae, Κοῖλα τῆς Εὐβοίας, a deeply-indented maritime region in Eubœa, Liv. 31, 47, 1; Val. Max. 1, 8, 10; hence this part of Eubœa is also called Coela Euboea, Val. Max. l. l.
coela.short: Coela (ōrum, n.), Euboeae, Κοῖλα τῆς Εὐβοίας, a deeply-indented maritime region in Eubœa, Liv.

coele syria.full: Coelē Sўrĭa, or in one word Coe-lēsўrĭa, ae, f., = Κοίλη Συρἰα (lit. Hollow Syria), Cœlesyria, between Libanus and Antilibanus, Plin. 5, 20, 17, § 77; Liv. 33, 19, 8; 42, 29, 9; Curt. 4, 1, 4; cf. id. 4, 5, 9. —Called simply Coele, Mel. 1, 11, 1; Plin. 5, 12, 13, § 66; 5, 23, 19, § 81 al.; gen. COELES SYRIAE, Inscr. Fabr. 10, n. 215; acc. Coelen Syriam, Liv. 45, 11, 6.—Syria Coele, Plin. 21, 18, 72, § 120.
coele syria.short: Coelē Sўrĭa, or in one word Coe-lēsўrĭa, ae, f., = Κοίλη Συρἰα (lit.

coelectus.full: cŏ-ēlectus, a, um eligo, elected together, Vulg. 1 Pet. 5, 13.
coelectus.short: cŏ-ēlectus, a, um eligo, elected together, Vulg.

coelementatus.full: cŏ-ĕlĕmentātus, a, um, adj. elementum, composed of elements, Tert. adv. Val. 23.

coeliacus.full: coelĭăcus, a, um, adj., = κοιλιακός. Relating to the abdomen or to the stomach: dolor, pain in the stomach, Cato, R. R. 125 (in Cels. 4, 12, written as Greek).— Subst.: coelĭăca, ae, f. (sc. medicina), stomach remedy, Plin. 20, 18, 76, § 201.— Afflicted with a disease of the bowels: apes, Varr. R. R. 3, 16, 22; and subst., one diseased in the bowels, Plin. 20, 14, 53, § 148; 20, 18, 76, § 201; 28, 14, 58, § 204; 30, 7, 19, § 58; Scrib. Comp. 95 al.

coelicola.full: coelĭcŏla, coelĭcŭlus, coelĭcus, coelĭfer, coelĭgĕnus, coelĭlŏquus, etc., v. cael-.
coelicola.short: coelĭcŏla, coelĭcŭlus, coelĭcus, coelĭfer, coelĭgĕnus, coelĭlŏquus, etc., v.

coelioticus.full: coelĭōtĭcus, a, um, adj., = κοιλιωτικός, cleansing the stomach or bowels, Cael. Aur. Tard. 1, 5.
coelioticus.short: coelĭōtĭcus, a, um, adj., = κοιλιωτικός, cleansing the stomach or bowels, Cael.

coemendatus.full: cŏ-ēmendātus, a, um, Part. [emendo], amended at the same time, Arn. 2, 18 fin.

coemesis.full: coemēsis, is, f., = κοίμησις, a somniferous song, Mart. Cap. 9, p. 335 (by Kopp, § 996, written as Greek).
coemesis.short: coemēsis, is, f., = κοίμησις, a somniferous song, Mart.

coemeterium.full: coemētērĭum, ii, n., = κοιμητήριον (a sleeping - chamber; hence), a churchyard, cemetery, burying-ground (eccl. Lat.), Tert. Anim. 51 al.
coemeterium.short: coemētērĭum, ii, n., = κοιμητήριον (a sleeping - chamber;

coemo.full: cŏ-ĕmo, ēmi, emptum, 3, v. a. (cf. the contracted form, 1. como), to purchase together, to buy up (class.): aliquid, Ter. Ad. 2, 2, 17; Caes. B. G. 1, 3; Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 59, § 133; Cassius ap. Cic. Fam. 15, 19, 3; Hor. S. 1, 2, 9; Quint. 11, 1, 80; Suet. Vesp. 16 al.: coemptarum rerum pretia, id. Ner. 5; Juv. 14, 293.

coemptio.full: cŏëmptĭo, ōnis, f. coëmo, jurid. t. t. A pretended purchase of an estate which was subjected to a mock sale for the purpose of divesting it of the burden of certain sacrifices attached to it, Cic. Mur. 12, 27 Moeb.— Esp., a marriage, consisting in a mutual mock sale of the parties, by which the wife was freed from the tutela legitima and the family sacra, Gai Inst. 1, 110; 1, 113 sq.; Cic. Fl. 34, 84; id. de Or. 1, 56, 237; Varr. L. L. 6, § 43; cf. id. ap. Non. p. 531, 10 sq.; Serv. ad Verg. G.

coemptionalis.full: cŏëmptiōnālis (in MSS. also contracted cōmptiōnālis; cf. Lachm. ad Lucr. p. 135), e, adj. coëmptio, pertaining to a sham sale or a sham marriage: senex, who was made use of in such a performance (cf. Cic. Mur. 12, 27); accordingly, poor, worthless, Plaut. Bacch. 4, 9, 52.—Of a low kind of slaves, Cur. ap. Cic. Fam. 7, 29, 1.

coemptionator.full: cŏëmptĭōnātor, ōris, m. id.; jurid. t. t., one who enters into the coemptio, Gai Inst. 1, 115 sq.; 2, 98; Ulp. Sent. 11, 5 al.

coemptor.full: cŏëmptor, ōris, m. coëmo, one who purchases many things, buys up; trop.: testium, App. Mag. p. 321, 31.

coemptus.full: cŏëmptus, a, um, Part., from coëmo.
coemptus.short: cŏëmptus, a, um, Part., from coëmo.

coenobita.full: coenŏbīta, ae, m. coenobium, a cloister-brother, a monk, Hier. Ep. 22, n. 34 al.

coenobium.full: coenŏbĭum, ii, n., = κοινόβιον, a cloister, convent, Hier. Ep. 22, n. 36 al.
coenobium.short: coenŏbĭum, ii, n., = κοινόβιον, a cloister, convent, Hier.

coenomyia.full: coenŏmyia, ae, f., = κοινόμυια, the common fly, Vulg. Psa. 104, 31 al.; cf. Hier. Ep. 106 fin.
coenomyia.short: coenŏmyia, ae, f., = κοινόμυια, the common fly, Vulg.

coenon.full: coenon, i, n., = κοινόν, a kind of eyesalve, Inscr. Orell. 4234.
coenon.short: coenon, i, n., = κοινόν, a kind of eyesalve, Inscr.

coeo.full: cŏ-ĕo, īvi or ii (e. g. coierunt, Caes. B. G. 6, 22: coiere, Lucr. 6, 452; Prop. 3 (4), 24, 18; Ov. M. 4, 83 al.: cŏĭisse, Verg. A. 12, 709: coisse, Prop. 3 (4), 15, 8. Ov. F. 6, 94; Quint. 5, 9, 5; 5, 11, 35; pedants preferred conire to coire, Quint. 1, 6, 17; cf. id. 1, 5, 69, and Lachm. ad Lucr. p. 137), ĭtum, īre, v. a. and n. To go or come together, to meet, assemble, collect together (so mostly poet. or in post-Aug. prose); constr. absol., with ad aliquem, ad or in locum, more rar. in loco

coepio.full: coepĭo, coepi, coeptum, 3 (the tempp. press. only a few times in the ante-class. period, and coepturus, Liv. 30, 5, 6; 42, 47, 3; Quint. 10, 1, 46; Plin. 16, 25, 41, § 98; Suet. Calig. 46; the tempp. perff., both in act. and pass. form, very freq.; a trisyl. coëpit, Lucr. 4, 619 Lachm. N. cr.), v. a. and n. contr. from co-ăpio = apo; hence coapias for coepias in Cod. Ambros.; Plaut. Trin. 4, 3, 46; v. in the foll., and cf. Lachm. ad Lucr. 2, p. 248, lit. to lay hold of something on different sid

coepiscopatus.full: cŏ-ĕpiscŏpātus, ūs, m., an associate episcopate, Aug. Ep. 31.
coepiscopatus.short: cŏ-ĕpiscŏpātus, ūs, m., an associate episcopate, Aug.

coepiscopus.full: cŏ-ĕpiscŏpus, i, m., an associate bishop, Hier. adv. Lucif. 9; Sid. Ep. 4, 25 et saep.
coepiscopus.short: cŏ-ĕpiscŏpus, i, m., an associate bishop, Hier.

coepto.full: coepto, āvi, ātum, 1, v. freq. a. and n. coepio (mostly poet., and in Tac.; in Cic. in prose only once, apparently for a change with coepit and incipit). Act., to begin eagerly, to begin, undertake, attempt. With inf.: diffidere dictis, Lucr. 1, 267: oculi coeptant non posse tueri, id. 4, 113; 4, 405; 6, 255: contingere portus, Cic. Arat. 131: appetere ea, quae, etc., id. Fin. 5, 9, 24 (v. the passage in connection): coercere seditionem, Tac. H. 2, 29: loqui, id. ib. 3, 10; 3, 81; 5, 10: discede

coeptum.full: coeptum, i, v. coepio, I. B. fin.

coeptus1.full: coeptus, a, um, Part., from coepio.
coeptus1.short: coeptus, a, um, Part., from coepio.

coeptus2.full: coeptus, ūs, m. coepio, a beginning, undertaking (perh. only in the foll. exs.): primos suos quasi coeptus appetendi fuisse, ut, etc., * Cic. Fin. 4, 15, 41 Madv (cf.: coeptat appetere, id. ib. 5, 9, 24): dignas insumite mentes Coeptibus, * Stat. Th. 12, 644.

coepulonus.full: cŏ-ĕpŭlōnus, i, m. epulo, a fellowbanqueter or companion at a feast, Plaut. Pers. 1, 3, 20.

coepulor.full: cŏ-ĕpŭlor, āri, 1, v. dep., to feast together (late Lat.), Ambros. Ep. 19, 15.

coeranus.full: Coerănus, i, m., = Κοίρανος, a Greek Stoic philosopher, Tac. A. 14, 59.
coeranus.short: Coerănus, i, m., = Κοίρανος, a Greek Stoic philosopher, Tac.

coerceo.full: cŏ-ercĕo, cui, cĭtum, 2, v. a. arceo, to enclose something on all sides or wholly, to hold together, to surround, encompass: qui (mundus) omnia complexu suo coërcet et continet, Cic. N. D. 2, 22, 58; cf. id. ib. 2, 40, 101; Ov. M. 1, 31: quā circum Galli lorica coërcet, where the Gallic coat of mail encloses, Lucr. 6, 954; cf. of a band holding the hair together, Ov. M. 1, 477; 2, 413; Hor. C. 2, 19, 19; 1, 10, 18: est animus vitaï claustra coërcens, holding together the bands of life, Lucr. 3,

coercitio.full: cŏërcĭtĭo (in MSS. also coerctĭo, cŏërtĭo, cŏërcĭo), ōnis, f. coërceo, II., a restraining, coercing; coercion, restraint, compulsion, chastisement, punishment (not ante-Aug.). Prop.: coërcitionem inhibere, Liv. 4, 53, 7: sine coërcitione magistratus, on the part of the magistrates, id. 26, 36, 12: quo modo judex doceri potest, si desit... interpellantis coërcitio, contentio? * Quint. 9, 2, 2: servorum, Sen. Brev. Vit. 3, 2: indignamur aliquā admonitione aut coërcitione nos castigatos, id. Ira, 2

coercitor.full: cŏërcĭtor, ōris, m. coërceo, one who restrains: disciplinae militaris, an enforcer, Eutr. 7, 20; 7, 18 Bip.

coercitus.full: cŏërcĭtus, a, um, Part., from coërceo.
coercitus.short: cŏërcĭtus, a, um, Part., from coërceo.

coerro.full: cŏ-erro, āre, v. n., to go or wander about together, Dig. 1, 15, 3, § 3.

coeus.full: Coeus (dissyl. Coe-us), i, m., = Κοῖος, a Titan, father of Latona, Verg. G. 1, 279 Serv.; id. A. 4, 179; Ov. M. 6, 185; 6, 366; Prop. 3 (4), 9, 48; Val. Fl. 3, 224; Claud. Rapt. Pros. 3, 347; Tac. A. 12, 61.

coexercitatus.full: cŏ-exercĭtātus, a, um, exercised together or at the same time: artem constare ex perceptionibus consentientibus et coexercitatis ad finem vitae, Quint. 2, 17, 41 (as a transl. of the Gr. ἐγγεγυμνασμέναι καταλήψεις).
coexercitatus.short: cŏ-exercĭtātus, a, um, exercised together or at the same time: artem constare ex perceptionibus consentientibus et coexercitatis ad finem vitae, Quint.

cofanus.full: cofānus, i, m., a pelican, App. Fragm. p. 609 Oud.
cofanus.short: cofānus, i, m., a pelican, App.

cogitabilis.full: cōgĭtābĭlis, e, adj. cogito, conceivable, imaginable (post-Aug. and very rare), Sen. Ep. 58, 13: Deus, App. Mag. p. 315, 4.

cogitabundus.full: cōgĭtābundus, a, um, adj. id., thinking, thoughtful: Socrates, Gell. 2, 1, 2.

cogitamen.full: cōgĭtāmen, ĭnis, n. id., thinking, thought, Tert. Trin. 6.

cogitamentum.full: cōgĭtāmentum, i, n. id., a thought (late Lat.), Vulg. 4 Esdr. 7, 22; cf. cogitamentum, ἐνθύμημα, Gloss. Gr. Lat.

cogitata.full: cōgĭtāta, ōrum, n., v. cogito, I. b.

cogitatim.full: cōgĭtātim, adv., pro cogitate, Paul. ex Fest. p. 61, 9 Müll.

cogitatio.full: cōgĭtātĭo, ōnis, f. cogito, i. e. co-agito; cf. Varr. L. L. 6, § 43; Cic. Off. 1, 6, 19; Paul. ex Fest. p. 66, 7 Müll.. Abstr., a thinking, considering, deliberating; thought, reflection, meditation (in good prose, and very freq.). Absol.: cogitatio in se ipsā vertitur, Cic. Off. 1, 44, 156: cogitatione aliquid complecti, Quint. 11, 2, 19: subitam et fortuitam orationem commentatio et cogitatio facile vincit, Cic. de Or. 1, 33, 150; cf. Quint. 10, 6, 1 sq.: speciem dei percipere cogitatione, non

cogitato.full: cōgĭtātō, adv., v. cogito, P. a. fin.

cogitatorium.full: cōgĭtātōrĭum, ii, n. cogitatus, a receptacle of thought (late Lat.): animae caro, Tert. Res Carn. 15; id. Anim. 11.

cogitatum.full: cōgĭtātum, i, and cōgĭtāta, ōrum, n., v. cogito, I. b.
cogitatum.short: cōgĭtātum, i, and cōgĭtāta, ōrum, n., v.

cogitatus1.full: cōgĭtātus, a, um, Part., from cogito.
cogitatus1.short: cōgĭtātus, a, um, Part., from cogito.

cogitatus2.full: cōgĭtātus, ūs, m. cogito, a thinking, thought (late Lat.), App. M. 4, 5, p. 144, 22; Tert. Idol. 23; Vulg. Eccl. 9, 23 al. (but in Sen. Ep. 11, 9, cogitatus is part. pass.).

cogito.full: cōgĭto, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. contr. from cŏ-ăgito, acc. to Varr. L. L. 6, § 43 Müll.; but more prob. from con and root of aio, Sanscr. ah; cf.: nego, adagium, to pursue something in the mind (cf. agito, II.), i. e. To consider thoroughly, to ponder, to weigh, reflect upon, think (class. in prose and poetry); constr. absol., with aliquid, de aliquo, or de aliquā re, sic, ita, or a rel. -clause: cogitate cum animis vestris si quid, etc., Cato ap. Gell. 16, 1, 4; so Plaut. Most. 3, 2, 13; Ter. Ad. 3

cognatio.full: cognātĭo, ōnis, f. cognatus. Lit., blood relationship, kindred, connection by birth. Of men. Absol.: societas ... quae nata a primo satu... serpit sensim foras, cognationibus primum, tum adfinitatibus, deinde amicitiis, post vicinitatibus, tum civibus, Cic. Fin. 5, 23, 65: frater noster cognatione patruelis, id. ib. 5, 1, 1: ut quisque te maxime cognatione, adfinitate, necessitudine aliquā attingebat, Cic. Verr. 2, 2, 10, § 27: cognationem commemorare, id. ib. 2, 2, 26, § 64: cognationis jura in

cognatus.full: co-gnātus, a, um, adj. natus, nascor, sprung from the same stock, related by blood, kindred; and subst.: cognātus, i, m., and cognāta, ae, f., a blood-relation, kinsman (on either the father's or the mother's side; a more comprehensive word than agnatus, q. v.; very freq. and class.). Masc.: cognatus vester, Plaut. Poen. 5, 4, 86: propinqui atque cognati, Cic. Rosc. Am. 34, 96: amici cognatique alicujus, id. Caecin. 5, 15: cognati atque affines, id. post Red. ad Quir. 3, 6; Hor. S. 1, 9, 27 et s

cognitio.full: cognĭtĭo, ōnis, f. cognosco. In gen., a becoming acquainted with, learning to know, acquiring knowledge, knowledge as a consequence of perception or of the exercise of our mental powers, knowing, acquaintance, cognition (in good prose; esp. freq. in Cic. and Quint.). Abstr.: cognitio contemplatioque naturae, Cic. Off. 1, 43, 153: rerum occultarum, id. ib. 1, 4, 13: rerum, id. Fin. 3, 5, 17: animi, id. Tusc. 1, 29, 71: deorum, id. N. D. 2, 56, 140: urbis, id. Imp. Pomp. 14, 40: in studiis sentent

cognitionalis.full: cognĭtĭōnālis, e, adj. cognitio, II., pertaining to judicial inquiry: sententiae, Cod. Just. 7, 42, 1; 7, 45, 13.—* Adv.: co-gnĭtĭōnālĭter: introductus, by judicial investigation, Cod. Just. 7, 63, 5 fin.

cognitor.full: cognĭtor, ōris, m. cognosco, a judic. t. t. Lit., one who has made himself familiar with a case in law; hence, An advocate, attorney (acting in the name of the parties, who had previously appeared before the tribunal: cognitor est, qui litem alterius suscipit coram ab eo, cui datus est, Paul. ex Fest. p. 57, 9 Müll.; cf. Ascon. Cic. Div. in Caecil. 4, 11; Gai Inst. 4, 97; and v. advocatus), Cic. Div. in Caecil. 4, 11, Cic. Verr. 2, 2, 43, § 106 sq.; 2, 3, 34, § 78; 2, 3, 60, § 137; id. Caecin. 5

cognitorius.full: cognĭtōrĭus, a, um, adj. cognitor, pertaining to an advocate, Gai Inst. 2, 39; 2, 52; 4, 82 al.

cognitura.full: cognĭtūra, ae, f. id., the office of a fiscal agent, who looks up the debtors to the treasury; a state's attorneyship, a state agency, Gai Inst. 4, § 124; Paul. Sent. 1, 2, § 2; Suet. Vit. 2.

cognitus1.full: cognĭtus, a, um, Part. and P. a., from cognosco.

cognitus2.full: cognĭtus, ūs, m. cognosco, a becoming acquainted with, a knowing: variorum populorum, App. M. 9, p. 225.

cognobilis.full: cognōbĭlis, e, adj. id., that can be understood, intelligible (only in the two foll. exs.): libri, Gell. 20, 5, 9, as a translation of the Aristotelian ξυνετοί, and in imitation of the Catonian cognobilior cognitio, Cato ib. fin.

cognomen.full: cognōmen, ĭnis, n. co-nomen. A name added to the nomen (or name of the gens), usu. the third word in order in the full name of each citizen; sometimes followed by a fourth, the agnomen, but in the class. per. including the agnomen, a Roman surname, family name, epithet (e. g.
