Cicero, Scipio, etc., Africanus, Asiaticus, etc.; cf. Quint. 7, 3, 27; freq. and class.): T. Manlius, qui Galli torque detracto cognomen (sc. Torquati) invenit, Cic. Off. 3, 31, 112; cf. id. Fin. 1, 7, 23: duo isti T. Rosci

cognomentum.full: cognōmentum, i, n. access. form of cognomen, a surname (rare in class. prose; most freq. in Tac.; not used by Cic.; v. Madv. ad Cic. Fin. 2, 5, 15), Plaut. Mil. 4, 2, 47; id. Ps. 4, 2, 20; id. Pers. 1, 2, 8; Poët. ap. Cic. Fin. 2, 5, 15; Sall. Fragm. ap. Gell. 18, 4, 4; Messala ap. Sen. Suas. 2; Tac. A. 12, 55; 14, 27; Gell. 18, 7, 1.— (Like cognomen in poets, v. cognomen, II.) In gen., a name (partic. of inanim. things or of persons to designate a peculiar quality), Tac. A. 1, 31 Nipperd.; 2, 6

cognominatio.full: cognōmĭnātĭo, ōnis, f. access. form of cognomen, a surname, Afran. ap. Non. p. 87, 23.

cognominis.full: cognōmĭnis, e (abl. cognomine, v. the foll.; cf.: bimestris, coelestis al.), adj. cognomen, like - named, of the same name (mostly poet. or in post-Aug. prose); with gen., dat., or absol.: duae germanae meretrices cognomines, Plaut. Bacch. 1, 1, 5: cognomine Insubribus pago Haeduorum, Liv. 5, 34, 9 Weissenb. ad loc.: flumen Absarrum cum castello cognomine, Plin. 6, 4, 4, § 12: mox Asiacae cognomines flumini, id. 4, 12, 26, § 82: eorum, id. 6, 2, 2, § 5; Suet. Vit. 2: gaudet cognomine terrā, Verg

cognomino.full: cognōmĭno, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. id.. To furnish with a surname, to surname, denominate (mostly post-Aug.; only once in Cic.): amaracum Phrygium, Plin. 21, 11, 39, § 67; 21, 3, 7, § 10; * Quint. 4, 1, 2; Suet. Tib. 17.—In part. pass.: quo ex facto ipse posterique ejus Torquati sunt cognominati, Quadr. ap. Gell. 9, 13, 19; Suet. Aug. 7; Plin. 35, 10, 37, § 112; 33, 10, 17, § 133; Flor. 3, 5, 1: verba cognominata, i. e. synonyms, * Cic. Part. Or. 15, 53.— Rarely in gen., to name, call: Macedonia...

cognoscens.full: cognoscens, entis, Part. and P. a., from cognosco.

cognoscenter.full: cognoscenter, adv., v. cognosco, P. a. 1.

cognoscibilis.full: cognoscĭbĭlis, e, adj. cognosco, recognizable, discernible (late Lat.), Boëth. Arist. Anal. Post. 1, 541.—Adv.: cogno-scĭbĭlĭter, recognizably: a magnitudine creaturae cognoscibiliter poterit creator videri, Vulg. Sap. 13, 5.

cognosco.full: co-gnosco, gnōvi, gnĭtum, 3 (tempp. perff. contr. cognosti, Ter. And. 3, 4, 7: cognostis, id. Hec. prol. 8: cognoram, Cic. de Or. 1, 31, 143; Cat. 66, 26: cognoro, Cic. Att. 7, 20, 2; id. Fam. 2, 11, 2 fin.: cognorim, Cael. ap. Cic. Att. 10, 9, A, 1: cognoris, Ter. Phorm. 2, 1, 35; Lucr. 6, 534: cognorit, Ter. Eun. 5, 4, 11: cognosses, Cic. Fl. 21, 51; Cat. 91, 3: cognossent, Nep. Lys. 4 fin.: cognosse, Lucr. 1, 331; Cat. 90, 3; Ov. M. 15, 4 al.; v. Neue, Formenl. 2, 532; 2, 535), v. a. nosco. T

cogo.full: cōgo, cŏēgi, cŏactum (COGVIT = cogit, Inscr Marin Fratr Arv. p. 170), 3, v. a. contr. from co-ago, to drive together to one point, to collect, compress, crowd, bring, or urge together, to assemble, gather together (class. and very freq.; syn.: colligo, congrego) Lit. In gen. (constr. as a verb of motion with in and acc., or with adv. of direction): cogantur (oves) intro, Plaut. Bacch. 5, 2, 15; Verg. E. 3, 98; cf. pecus, id. ib. 3, 20: oves stabulis, id. ib. 6, 85: nubes in unum locum, Lucr. 6,
cogo.short: cōgo, cŏēgi, cŏactum (COGVIT = cogit, Inscr Marin Fratr Arv.

cohabitatio.full: cŏhăbĭtātĭo, ōnis, f. cohabito, a dwelling together, Aug. Ep. 137 fin.

cohabitator.full: cŏhăbĭtātor, ōris, m. id., he who dwells with any one (late Lat.), Cassiod. Var. 3, 48; Aug. Serm. 1 al.

cohabito.full: cŏ-hăbĭto, āre, v. n., to dwell together (late Lat.), Hier. Ep. 101; Aug. Ep. 12 al.

cohaerentia.full: cŏ-haerentĭa, ae, f. cohaereo, a cohering, coherence, connection (rare): mundi, * Cic. N. D. 2, 62, 155: regionum, Macr. S. 5, 15: mortis et vitae, Gell. 6, 13, 11: vocis, id. 15, 3, 6.

cohaereo.full: cŏ-haerĕo, haesi, haesum, 2, v. n., to cling together, to be united, either of that whose parts cling together, to cohere, or of that which cleaves to something else, to adhere. Of a whole as composed of parts, or of the parts of a whole, to cling together, be united, to cohere, press or crowd together. Lit. In gen.: mundus ita apte cohaeret, ut dissolvi nullo modo queat, nisi ab eodem a quo est colligatus, Cic. Univ. 5: omnia autem duo ad cohaerendum tertium aliquid anquirunt et quasi nodum vin

cohaeresco.full: cŏ-haeresco (-hēresco), si, 3, v. inch. n. [cohaereo], to hang together, cohere (very rare): atomi cohaerescunt inter se, Cic. N. D. 1, 20, 54; id. Fin. 1, 6, 17: pituita in gulā cohaerescens, Plin. 24, 15, 80, § 130; 20, 16, 64, § 172.

cohaesus.full: cŏhaesus, a, um, Part. and P. a., from cohaereo.

coheres.full: cŏ-hēres (-haeres), ēdis, comm., a coheir, fellow-heir, Cic. Verr. 2, 1, 48, § 127; id. Fam. 13, 46 init.; 7, 2, 1; Quint. 5, 14, 16.— Gen. plur. coheredum, Hor. S. 2, 5, 107: esse coheres alicui, id. ib. 2, 5, 54; Petr. 76, 2.— In the fem., Dig. 34, 9, 16.
coheres.short: cŏ-hēres (-haeres), ēdis, comm., a coheir, fellow-heir, Cic.

cohibeo.full: cŏ-hĭbĕo, ui (perf. subj. cohibessit, Lucr. 3, 444 Lachm.), ĭtum, 2, v. a. habeo. To hold together, to hold, contain, confine, embrace, comprise (class.; syn. contineo): omnes naturas ipsa (universa natura) cohibet et continet, Cic. N. D. 2, 13, 35; Lucr. 3, 441 sq.; 1, 517; 1, 536: (nubes) ut fumus constare nequirent, Nec cohibere nives gelidas et grandinis imbres, id. 6, 107: aliquid in se, id. 2, 1031; cf. Cic. Fat. 9, 19: at Scyllam caecis cohibet spelunca latebris, Verg. A. 3, 424: semen oc

cohibilis.full: cŏhĭbĭlis, e, adj. cohibeo, abridged, short, συνεχής (only trop. and very rare): oratio Herodoti, Gell. 16, 19, 1 dub.—Adv.: cŏhĭbĭlĭter; comp.: cohibilius conscribere aliquid, App. Mag. 36, p. 297, 35 Elm.: cogere fabulam, App. Flor. fin.

cohibitio.full: cŏhĭbĭtĭo, ōnis, f. cohibeo, II., a restraining, governing (post - class.): irae, Lact. de Ira Dei, 18, 3: sui, id. ib. 18, 12 (but in Cic. Verr. 2, 3, 14, § 37, the better read. is prohibitio).

cohibitus.full: cŏhĭbĭtus, Part. and P. a., from cohibeo.

cohonesto.full: cŏ-hŏnesto, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a., to honor in common or abundantly, do honor to, to honor, grace (rare, but in good prose): exsequias, Cic. Quint. 15, 50: funus laudatione pro rostris ceterisque solennibus, Tac. A. 3, 76: statuas, Cic. Verr. 2, 2, 69, § 168: aliquam, id. Fam. 13, 11, 3: MEMORIAM PVELLAE, Inscr. Orell. 5037: victoriam, Liv. 38, 47, 3: aliquid virtute, id. 25, 16, 17: patrem deorum, Arn. 5, 172: res turpes, to call by honorable names, id. 5, 187.— Meton., to palliate: defluvia capi

cohorresco.full: cŏ-horresco, horrui, 3, v. inch. n., to shudder, shake, or shiver with fear or cold: nisi cohorrescit corpus meum, Aug. ap. Suet. Tib. 21.—In perf.: quem ubi agnovi, equidem cohorrui, Cic. Rep. 6, 10, 10; id. Att. 5, 21, 12; 7, 1, 1: ex quo (sudore) cum cohorruisset, id. de Or. 3, 2, 6.

cohors.full: cŏhors (or cors; cf. Non. p. 83, 14 sq.; later aspirated orthog. of MSS. chors; cf. the letter C, and Schneid. ad Varr. R. R. 1, 13, 3), rtis, f. Sanscr. root har, rapio; cf. Gr. χορός. A place enclosed around, a court, enclosure, yard, pen, etc., esp. for cattle, poultry, etc. Cohors, Varr. R. R. 1, 13, 2 sq.; 2, 2, 9; Cato ap. Fest. p. 146, 29 Müll.; Col. 8, 3, 8; 7, 3, 8; Ov. F. 4, 704.— Cors, Varr. ap. Non. l. l.; Glaucia ap. Cic. de Or. 2, 65 fin.; Col. 2, 14, 18; Vitr. 6, 9; Mart. 3, 58, 1

cohortalinus.full: cŏhortālīnus (cort-, Paul. Nol. Ep. 22, 2), a, um, adj. cohortalis (late Lat.), pertaining to an imperial body-guard: militia, Cod. Th. 16, 5, 48; cf. ib. 6, 35, 14.

cohortalis.full: cŏhortālis (cort-), e, adj. cohors. Pertaining to a cattle or poultry-yard (freq. in Col.; elsewhere very rare): aves, Col. 1, prooem. § 27; 6, 27, 4; 8, 1, 3: gallina, id. 8, 2, 1: pullus, Cels. 2, 18: officina, Col. 8, 3, 8: ratio, id. 8, 2, 6.— Pertaining to an imperial body - guard (late Lat.): officium, Cod. Th. 12, 58, 13: condicio, ib. 16, 62, 3 al.

cohortatio.full: cŏhortātĭo, ōnis, f. cohortor, an exhorting, inciting; exhortation, encouragement (rare, but in good prose): militum, Nep. Hann. 11, 1: legionis, Caes. B. G. 2, 25: Caesaris, Auct. B. Alex. 22: ducis, Tac. A. 14, 30: judicum, Cic. Clu. 50, 138: incredibiliter me commovet tua cohortatio, id. Att. 16, 13, C, 2; so id. Fam. 1, 7, 9; id. de Or. 1, 47, 204: his cohortationibus, id. ib. 1, 61, 262.

cohortatiuncula.full: cŏhortātĭuncŭla, ae, f. dim. cohortatio, a short exhortation, Ambros. Ep. 4, 33.

cohorticula.full: cŏhortĭcŭla, ae, f. cohors, a small cohort, Cael. ap. Cic. Fam. 8, 6, 4.

cohorto.full: cŏhorto, āre, 1, v. a. (rare collat. form of cohortor), to exhort, encourage: et dicerent castra capta esse, atque hos cohortarent uti maturarent, Quadrig. ap. Non. p. 472, 19: exercitus pransus, paratus, cohortatus, Cat. ap. Gell. 15, 13, 5; v. cohortor.

cohortor.full: cŏ-hortor, ātus, 1, v. dep., to animate or encourage by forcible language, to incite, exhort, admonish. Esp., of the general before a battle, or in other milit. proceedings: cohortatus suos proelium commisit, Caes. B. G. 1, 25: acies instruenda, milites cohortandi, signum dandum, id. ib. 2, 20: exercitum ad pugnam, id. B. C. 3, 90: militem ad proelium, Quint. 12, 1, 28.— With inf., Auct. B. Alex. 21; cf. Tac. A. 12, 49.— With ut or ne: Scipionis milites cohortatur, ut, etc., Caes. B. C. 3, 82; T

cohospes.full: cŏ-hospĕs, ĭtis, m., a fellow-guest (late Lat.), Paul. Nol. Carm. 21, 385; 24, 438.
cohospes.short: cŏ-hospĕs, ĭtis, m., a fellow-guest (late Lat.), Paul.

cohospitans.full: cŏhospĭtans, antis, = cohospes, Paul. Nol. Ep. 32, 6.

cohum1.full: cohum, i, n., the strap by which the plough-beam was fastened to the yoke; so called, acc. to Paul. ex Fest. p. 39, 4, a cohibendo; cf. Varr. L. L. 5, § 135 Müll.
cohum1.short: cohum, i, n., the strap by which the plough-beam was fastened to the yoke;

cohum2.full: cŏhum poëtae caelum dixerunt a chao, ex quo putabant caelum esse formatum, Paul. ex Fest. p. 39, 5; cf. Varr. L. L. 5, § 19; Diom. p. 361 P.: vix solidum complere cohum terroribus caeli, Enn. Ann. v. 550 Vahl.
cohum2.short: cŏhum poëtae caelum dixerunt a chao, ex quo putabant caelum esse formatum, Paul.

cohumido.full: cŏ-hūmĭdo, āre, v. a., to moisten all over, to wet: genas lacrimis, App. M. 8, p. 205, 14.

coillum.full: coillum (dissyl.), i, n., = κοῖλον, the inmost part of the house, where the Lares were worshipped, Tert. Spect. 5.
coillum.short: coillum (dissyl.), i, n., = κοῖλον, the inmost part of the house, where the Lares were worshipped, Tert.

coimbibo.full: cŏ-imbĭbo, ĕre, v. a., to imbibe along with, or at the same time, Arn. 5, 178.

coinquenda.full: Cŏinquenda, ae, f., a goddess who presided over the felling of trees, Inscr. Orell. 961.
coinquenda.short: Cŏinquenda, ae, f., a goddess who presided over the felling of trees, Inscr.

coinquinatio.full: cŏinquĭnātĭo, ōnis, f. coinquino, a polluting, Vulg. Esd. 1, 6, 21; Sulp. Sev. Ep. 2, 9; 2, 19.

coinquino.full: cŏ-inquĭno (or contr. cōnquĭno, cf. Lachm. ad Lucr. 2, p. 135), āvi, ātum, 1, v. a., to defile all over, to pollute wholly, to contaminate. Prop. (rare; not in Cic.): stercore conquinatae, Col. 8, 5, 19; 8, 7, 2. — Trop. * Of infectious disease, to infect, taint: totam progeniem, Col. 7, 5, 6.—More freq., Of vices: matres coinquinari regias, Att. ap. Cic. N. D. 3, 27, 68: se crimine stupri, Val. Max. 6, 1, 6: se maximo scelere, id. 9, 7: cor vitiis, Prud. Cath. 6, 53: famam alicujus, Arn. 4, 151

coinquo.full: cŏ-inquo (cŏninquo), ĕre, 3, or cŏ-inquio, īre, 4, v. a., to cut off, cut down (belonging to econ. lang.), Trebat. ap. Serv. ad Verg. A. 11, 316; Inscr. Orell. 2270 (I. p. 390 sq.); cf.: coinquere = deputare, Paul. ex Fest. p. 64, 3, and 65, 19 Müll.
coinquo.short: cŏ-inquo (cŏninquo), ĕre, 3, or cŏ-inquio, īre, 4, v.

coitio.full: cŏĭtĭo, ōnis, f. coëo. * A coming or meeting together, a meeting: prima coitio est acerrima, Ter. Phorm. 2, 2, 32.— Esp. A uniting, banding together. In gen. (rare): societatis, Dig. 17, 2, 70.— In partic., in a bad sense, a conspiracy, plot, coalition (several times in Cic. and Liv.; elsewh. rare): suspitio coitionis, Cic. Planc. 22, 53; id. Clu. 54, 148: non factionibus modo nec per coitiones usitatas nobilibus, etc., Liv. 7, 32, 12; cf. id. 2, 35, 4; 3, 35, 9: candidatorum consularium, Cic. Q

coitus1.full: cŏĭtus, a, um, Part., from coëo.
coitus1.short: cŏĭtus, a, um, Part., from coëo.

coitus2.full: cŏĭtus, and another orthography coetus (only distinguished in signif. by use; v. infra), ūs (dat. coetu, Cat. 64, 385; 66, 37), m. coëo. In gen. Abstr., a coming or meeting together, an assembling: eos auspicio meo atque ductu primo coetu vicimus, Plaut. Am. 2, 2, 25.— Hence, Concr., an assemblage, crowd, company; in this signif. coetus alone is used: quae (opiniones) in senatu, quae in omni coetu concilioque profitendae sint, Cic. Fin. 2, 24, 77; 2, 4, 11; id. Rep. 6, 13, 13: ad divinum animoru
coitus2.short: cŏĭtus, and another orthography coetus (only distinguished in signif.

coix.full: cŏix, ĭcis, f., = κόϊξ, a kind of Ethiopian palm, Plin. 13, 4, 9, § 47 (Jan. coecas).
coix.short: cŏix, ĭcis, f., = κόϊξ, a kind of Ethiopian palm, Plin.

colaphizo.full: cŏlăphīzo, āre, v. a., = κολαφίζω, to box one's ears, Tert. adv. Marc. 5, 12.

colaphus.full: cŏlăphus, i, m., = κόλαφος, a blow with the fist, a cuff, a box on the ear: icere, Plaut. Pers. 5, 2, 65 Ritschl: ducere, Quint. 6, 3, 83.—In plur.: in cerebro colaphos abstrudere, Plaut. Rud. 4, 3, 68; cf.: infringere alicui, Ter. Ad. 2, 1, 45; Plin. 8, 36, 54, § 130: incutere alicui, Juv. 9, 5: perpeti, Plaut. Capt. 1, 1, 20; Ter. Ad. 2, 2, 37.
colaphus.short: cŏlăphus, i, m., = κόλαφος, a blow with the fist, a cuff, a box on the ear: icere, Plaut.

colatura.full: cōlātūra, ae, f. 2. colo, filtration; concr., that which has been strained, Cael. Aur. Tard. 5, 3, 55.

colatus.full: cōlātus, a, um, Part. and P. a., from 2. colo.

colax.full: Cŏlax, ăcis, m., = Κόλαξ (the Flatterer), title of comedies of Menander, Nœvius, and Plautus; cf. Ter. Eun. prol. 25 and 30.
colax.short: Cŏlax, ăcis, m., = Κόλαξ (the Flatterer), title of comedies of Menander, Nœvius, and Plautus;

colchi.full: Colchi, ōrum, v. Colchis, II. B. fin.

colchis.full: Colchĭs, ĭdis (ĭdŏs, Val. Fl. 2, 423; 5, 202), f., = Κολχίς, a province in Asia, east of the Black Sea, celebrated on account of the golden fleece and Medea; now Mingrelia; acc. Colchida, Mel. 2, 3, 6; Plin. 2, 103, 106, § 226; Val. Fl. 5, 505 al.— Hence, Colchis, ĭdis, f. adj., Colchian: gens, Val. Fl. 3, 418; and subst., a Colchian woman, κατʼ ἐξοχήν = Medea, Hor. Epod. 16, 58; Prop. 2 (3), 34, 8; Ov. M. 7, 301; 7, 348; acc. Gr. Colchida, Prop. 2 (3), 21, 11; voc. Colchĭ, Ov. R. Am. 262; abl.

coleatus.full: cōlĕātus, a, um, adj. colis = caulis, II. D., pertaining to the membrum virile: cuspis, Pompon. ap. Non. p. 470, 31 (Com. Rel. v. 69 Rib.): eculeus, id. ib. 4, 17 (Com. Rel. v. 40 ib.).

colepium.full: cōlēpĭum, ĭi, n., = κωλήπιον, a knuckle of beef or pork, Petr. 70; Veg. 5, 17, 5.
colepium.short: cōlēpĭum, ĭi, n., = κωλήπιον, a knuckle of beef or pork, Petr.

colias.full: cŏlĭas, ae, m., = κολίας, a kind of tunny-fish, Plin. 32, 11, 53, § 146.
colias.short: cŏlĭas, ae, m., = κολίας, a kind of tunny-fish, Plin.

colice.full: cōlĭcē, ēs, f., = κωλική, a remedy for the colic, Cels. 5, 25, 12; Scrib. Comp. 120 sq.
colice.short: cōlĭcē, ēs, f., = κωλική, a remedy for the colic, Cels.

colicus.full: cōlĭcus, a, um, adj., = κωλικός, pertaining to the colic; suffering from or sick with the colic, Veg. Art. Vet. 4, 28 dub.
colicus.short: cōlĭcus, a, um, adj., = κωλικός, pertaining to the colic;

coliphium.full: cōlīphĭum (in MSS. also coll-), ii, n., a kind of nourishing food for athletœ, Plaut. Pers. 1, 3, 12; Mart. 7, 67; Juv. 2, 53; cf. colepium.

collabasco.full: col-lăbasco (conl-), ĕre, v.. n., to totter or be about to fall at the same time, to waver with, etc.; trop.: si res lassa labat, itidem amici collabascunt, Plaut. Stich. 4, 1, 17.

collabefacto.full: col-lăbĕfacto (conl-), āre, v. a., to make to reel, shake, or totter (perh. only in the two foll. exs.): motu collabefactat onus, Ov. F. 1, 566.—Poet. of liquefying metals: rigorem auri, to overpower, subdue, Lucr. 1, 493; cf. collabefio.

collabefio.full: col-lăbĕfīo (conl-), factus, fiĕri, v. pass., to be made to reel or totter, to be brought to ruin (perh. only in the foll. examples): haec (mens animaeque potestas) ipso cum corpore collabefiunt, sink together, Lucr. 3, 585 (601): ut altera (navis) praefracto rostro tota collabefieret, was dashed in pieces, Caes. B. C. 2, 6.— Poet. of the melting of metals, Lucr. 4, 697 (cf. collabefacto; and labefacta, Verg. A. 8, 390).— Trop., to overthrow, supplant: a Themistocle collabefactus, Nep. Arist. 1,

collabello.full: col-lăbello (conl-), āre, 1, v. a., to form by bringing the lips together: osculum, Laber. ap. Non. p. 90, 22.

collabor.full: col-lābor (conl-), lapsus (or labsus), 3, v. dep., to fall together, to fall in ruins; esp. of buildings, to fall in, fall from age (in the ante-Aug. period very rare; not in Cic., Hor., or Quint.). Prop., Liv. 35, 9, 3: moenia subito collapsa ruinā sunt, id. 29, 18, 17; Suet. Aug. 30; id. Claud. 25; id. Calig. 21: fastigium domūs collabitur, id. Caes. 81: qui collapsā jacuere ruinā, Sil. 7, 727: succisis asseribus collapsus pons, Liv. 44, 5, 6. postquam conlapsi cineres, Verg. A. 6, 226: eodem

collaboro.full: col-lăbōro (conl-), āre, v. n., to labor with or together, Tert. Poen. 10.

collabus.full: Collăbus, i, m. con and λαβ-, λαμβάνω, a comic name, Plaut. Trin. 4, 3, 14.

collaceratus.full: col-lăcĕrātus (conl-), a, um, Part. [lacero], torn to pieces, lacerated: corpus, Tac. H. 3, 74 fin.

collacrimatio.full: col-lā^crĭmātĭo (conl-), ōnis, f. col-lacrimo, a weeping together or very much, a lamenting, Cic. de Or. 2, 45, 190.

collacrimo.full: col-lā^crĭmo (conl- and -lacrŭmo), āvi, 1, v. n. and a., to weep together or very much, to bewail, deplore (rare). Neutr.: simul omnes collacrumarunt, Plaut. ap. Gell. 1, 24, 3; Ter. And. 1, 1, 82: conplexus me senex collacrimavit, Cic. Rep. 6, 9, 9: collacrimantes suum patriaeque casum, Liv. 26, 14, 4.— Act.: histrio casum suum toties collacrimavit, Cic. Sest. 58, 123.

collactaneus.full: col-lactānĕus (conl-), a lacteo, a brother or sister nourished at the same breast, a foster-brother or sister (post-class.); masc., Gai Inst. 1, 39; Dig. 40, 2, 13; Inscr. Orell. 2281 al.; fem., Dig. 34, 4, 30, § 1 al.
collactaneus.short: col-lactānĕus (conl-), a lacteo, a brother or sister nourished at the same breast, a foster-brother or sister (post-class.);

collacteus.full: col-lactĕus (conl-), a, a foster-brother, foster-sister; masc., Hyg. Fab. 224; Inscr. Orell. 678; fem., Juv. 6, 307; Mart. Cap. 1, § 6; 2, § 111.

collacticius.full: collactīcĭus, ii, m., = collactaneus, Inscr. Afr. Renier, 509.

collaetor.full: col-laetor (conl-), āri, v. dep., to rejoice together, Tert. ldol. 14.

collapsio.full: collapsĭo (conl-), ōnis, f. collabor, a falling together, precipitation: fulminum, Jul. Firm. Err. Prof. Relig. 21.

collapsus.full: collapsus (conl-), a, um, Part., from collabor.
collapsus.short: collapsus (conl-), a, um, Part., from collabor.

collare.full: collāre (nom. sing. first in Apic. 7, 5 sq.), is (collārium, ii, acc. to Prisc. p. 590 P.), n. collum, a band or chain for the neck, a collar; abl. collari, Lucil. ap. Non. p. 36, 26; Plaut. Capt. 2, 2, 107; nom. plur. collaria, Varr. R. R. 2, 9, 15 fin.

collaris.full: collāris, e, adj. collum, pertaining to the neck: offa, Petr. 56, 8.

collatatus.full: collātātus, a, um, P. a. from collato, not in use, extended, diffuse: oratio collatata et diffusa, Cic. Or. 56, 187 dub. (al. dilatata).

collatero.full: col-lătĕro (conl-), āre, v. a. 2. latus, to admit on both sides: C vocales utrimque collaterat, Mart. Cap. 3, § 249.

collatia.full: Collātĭa, ae, f., = Κολλατία, an ancient town of the Sabines, in the vicinity of Rome, now Castellaccio, Cic. Agr. 2, 35, 96; Liv. 1, 38, 1; 1, 57, 9 al.; Ov. F. 2, 733; 2, 785.— Hence, Collātīnus, a, um, adj., of Collatia: populus, Liv. 1, 38, 2 (four times): arces, Verg. A. 6, 774 Heyne: porta, Paul. ex Fest. p. 37, 10 Müll.—Subst.: Collātīni, ōrum, m., the inhabitants of Collatia, Liv. 1, 38, 1 (diff. from a people of the same name in Apulia, Plin. 3, 11, 16, § 105); and Collātīnus, cognomen
collatia.short: Collātĭa, ae, f., = Κολλατία, an ancient town of the Sabines, in the vicinity of Rome, now Castellaccio, Cic.

collaticius.full: collātĭcĭus (conl-) or -tĭus, a, um, adj. confero, brought together, raised by contribution, mingled (post-Aug.): instrumenta, Sen. Cons. ad Marc. 10, 1: stipe, App. M. 8, p. 213, 36: myrrha, Plin. 12, 16, 35, § 69: aere, Tert. adv. Val. 12: sepultura, effected by contributions, Quint. Decl. 6, 11: PECVNIA, Inscr. Orell. 3730.

collatinus.full: Collātīnus, a, um, v. Collatia, II.

collatio.full: collātĭo (conl-), ōnis, f. confero, a bringing together, collecting. Prop., of the standards in war for battle, a hostile meeting: signorum, Cic. de Or. 1, 48, 210: centuriarum, for voting, id. ap. Ascon. in Toga Cand. p. 85, 18 Baiter: hyacinthorum et auri, Plin. 37, 9, 42, § 126.—Of money, a contribution, collection, a gratuity collected together for the emperor: stipis aut decimae, Liv. 5, 25, 5; 4, 60, 6; 6, 14, 12; Tac. G. 29; Suet. Calig. 42; id. Ner. 38; 44; id. Tit. 7; cf. Plin. Pan. 41,

collativus.full: collātīvus (conl-), a, um, adj. collatus, confero, brought or carried together, collected, combined (very rare): collativum sacrificium dicitur, quod ex collatione offertur, Paul. ex Fest. p. 37, 13 Müll.: collativum ventrem magnum et turgidum dixit Plautus (Curc. 2, 1, 16), quia in eum omnia edulia congeruntur, Paul. ex Fest. p. 58, 17 Müll.: favor, common, joint, Macr. Somn. Scip. 116: vis, Nazar. Pan. ad Const. 18 fin. — Subst.: collātīvum, n., = collatio, I., a contribution in money, Cod. Th

collator.full: collātor (conl-), ōris, m. confero. He who bears, brings, places together, a contributor, etc. (ante- and post - class.): symbolarum, Plaut. Curc. 4, 1, 13.—Trop.: salutis, Fulg. Myth. 1, 1; also, one who pays a voluntary contribution to the state, Cod. Th. 7, 6, 5.— One who compares, a comparer: et disputator, Aug. Ep. 147.

collatro.full: col-lātro (conl-), āre, v. a., to bark or yelp fiercely at; trop.: philosophiam, i.e. to inveigh against, Sen. Vit. Beat. 17, 1.

collatus1.full: collātus (conl-), a, um, Part., from confero.
collatus1.short: collātus (conl-), a, um, Part., from confero.

collatus2.full: collātus (conl-), ū s, m. confero, a bringing together (perh. only in the foll. exs.; only in the abl.). Of weapons in war, i.e. an attack: in collatu, in the affray, Auct. B. Hisp. 31.— A contributing, trop., to knowledge, teaching: alicujus collatu aliquid discere, Censor. de Die Nat. 1, 8.

collaudabilis.full: collaudābĭlis (conl-), e, adj. collaudo, worthy of praise in every respect, Prud. Ham. 694.

collaudatio.full: collaudātĭo (conl-), ōnis, f. id., warm praise (perh. only in the foll. exs.; only in the abl.): scriptoris, Cic. Inv. 2, 43, 125; Auct. Her. 2, 9, 13.

collaudator.full: collaudātor (conl-), ōris, m. id., one who praises warmly: nullo collaudatore, Aug. Con. 4, 14 fin.

collaudo.full: col-laudo (conl-), āvi, ātum, 1, v. a., to praise or commend very much, extol highly (class.): quantis laudibus Suum erum servus collaudavit, Plaut. Capt. 2, 3, 61: collegam, id. As. 3, 2, 30: alios, se, id. Truc. 2, 6, 15: filium, Ter. Ad. 3, 3, 13: ab omnibus conlaudāri, Cic. Fam. 1, 7, 5: me, * Hor. S. 1, 6, 70: collaudati milites, Caes. B. G. 5, 2; Nep. Ages. 1, 1; Liv. 1, 52, 1; Suet. Caes. 16: aliquem multum, Curt. 7, 5, 38; Stat. Th. 6, 490: magis utrumque collaudandum videri, etc., Cic.

collaxo.full: col-laxo (conl-), āre, v. a., = rarefacio, χαυνόω, to make loose or porous: omnia circum lateramina, Lucr. 6, 233; Cael. Aur. Acut. 3, 3, 20; id. Tard. 2, 1, 20.

collecta.full: collecta (conl-), ae, f. (orig. adj., sc. pecunia) [colligo]. A contribution in money: a convivā exigere, Cic. de Or. 2, 57, 233; cf. Varr. L. L. 6, 66 Müll.—* A meeting, assemblage: virginum, Hier. Ep. 108, n. 19.

collectaculum.full: collectācŭlum (conl-), i, n. id., a place of assembling, a receptacle, reservoir: aquae, Innocent. Cas. Lit. p. 230 Goes. vesicae, Cassiod. Var. 10, 30.

collectaneus.full: collectānĕus (conl-), a, um, adj. id., gathered or collected together, collectaneous (very rare): aes, Plin. 34, 9, 20, § 97: Dicta collectanea, the title of a work of Cæsar, now lost, Suet. Caes. 56 (perh. his Ἀποφθέγματα, mentioned by Cic., Fam. 9, 16, 4).—Hence, subst.: Collectānĕa, ōrum, n., the title of the collected works of Jul. Solinus.

collectarius.full: collectārĭus (conl-), ii, m. id., a money-changer, banker, cashier, Cod. Just. 4, 2, 16; Symm. Ep. 10, 49 al.

collecticius.full: collectĭcĭus (conl-), or -tĭus, a, um, adj. colligo, collected, gathered together (very rare): exercitus, gathered hastily without selection, * Cic. Fam. 7, 3, 2: ignis, fed by fuel gathered here and there, Sen. Q. N. 7, 23, 2.

collectim.full: collectim (conl-), adv. id., summarily, briefly: redigere aliquid, Claud. Mam. Stat. An. 3, 14.

collectio.full: collectĭo (conl-), ōnis, f. id.. Abstr., a collecting together. Prop.: membrorum (Absyrti), Cic. Imp. Pomp. 9, 22: spiritūs, Petr. 98: fructuum, Dig. 9, 2, 27, § 25: terrae, Paul. ex Fest. p. 96, 17 Müll.— Trop., the collecting, acquiring: amicorum (opp. detractio), Sen. Ep. 74, 25.— Esp. In rhet. lang., a summing up of things said, a short repetition, recapitulation, summary, ἀνακεφαλαίωσις, * Cic. Brut. 88, 302; Auct. Her. 1, 6, 10; Quint. 4, 4, 2.— In post-Aug. philos. lang., argumentation, r

collectivus.full: collectīvus (conl-), a, um, adj. colligo. * Collected, gathered together: umor, Sen. Q. N. 3, 7, 3.— Trop. In the rehet. lang. of Quint., pertaining to a syllogism, syllogistic, ratiocinatire: status, Quint. 3, 6, 46; 3, 6, 66: quaestio, id. 7, 1, 60.— In the lang. of grammar: nomen, a collective noun; as exercitus, populus, etc., Prisc. p. 581 P. al.

collector.full: col-lector (conl-), ōris, m., a fellow-student, Aug. Conf. 1, 17.
collector.short: col-lector (conl-), ōris, m., a fellow-student, Aug.

collectus1.full: collectus (conl-), a, um, Part. and P. a., from 1. colligo.

collectus2.full: collectus (conl-), ūs, m. 1. colligo, a collection: aquae, Lucr. 4, 414 Lachm. N. cr.; cf.: aquae pluvialis, Front. Limit. p. 43 Goes.: lapidum, Lucr. 3, 198: auri et argenti, Tert. Anim. 37.

collega.full: col-lēga (conl-), ae, m. 1. lego. Lit., one who is chosen at the same time with another: collegae, qui una lecti, Varr. L. L. 6, § 66 Müll.—Hence, Esp., a partner in office, a colleague (freq. and class.): bis una consules, collegae in censurā, Cic. Lael. 11, 39: Pericles cum haberet collegam in praeturā Sophoclem, id. Off. 1, 40, 144: in consulatu, Plin. 19, 8, 45, § 156: consulatūs, Vell. 2, 56, 4: habere, Cic. Phil. 2, 34, 85: ibi M. Marcellum, conlegam nostrum, conveni, Serv. ap. Cic. Fam. 4

collegatarius.full: col-lēgātārĭus (conl-), i, m., a person to whom is bequeathed a legacy in common with others, a collegatary, joint-legatee, Gai Inst. 2, § 199; Dig. 7, 2, 10 and 30.
collegatarius.short: col-lēgātārĭus (conl-), i, m., a person to whom is bequeathed a legacy in common with others, a collegatary, joint-legatee, Gai Inst.

collegialis.full: collēgĭālis (conl-), e, adj. collegium, collegial: FIDES, Inscr. Grut. 322, 4; Tert. Spect. 11.

collegiarius.full: collēgĭārĭus (conl-), a, um, adj. id., collegial: ministri, Tert. Spect. 11.

collegiatus.full: collēgĭātus (conl-), i, m. id., he who is with one in a society, college, corporation, etc., Cod. Just. 11, 17: De collegiatis, Cod. Th. 6, 30, 16; 7, 20, 12, § 3; so also Inscr. Orell. 3948 al.

collegium.full: collēgĭum (conl-); in inscrr. sometimes corrupted COLLEGIVS, ii, m., Inscr. Orell. 2413; 4101 al.), ii, n. collega. Abstr., the connection of associates, colleagues, etc., colleagueship (rare): ita, quae nostra officia fuerunt, pro collegio et pro propinquitate et vivo et mortuo ei praestitimus, Serv. ad Cic. Fam. 4, 12, 3: Decium, expertum mihi concordi collegio virum, mecum consulem faciatis, Liv. 10, 13. 13; so id. 22, 3, and 24, 6: magister equitum ex collegio prioris anni, id. 4, 17, 9; so

collema.full: collēma, ătis, n., = κόλλημα, that which is glued or cemented together: fruticis Niloticae, Mart. Cap. 3, § 225.
collema.short: collēma, ătis, n., = κόλλημα, that which is glued or cemented together: fruticis Niloticae, Mart.

colleprosus.full: col-leprōsus (conl-), i, m., a fellow-leper, Sid. Ep. 6, 1.
colleprosus.short: col-leprōsus (conl-), i, m., a fellow-leper, Sid.

colleticus.full: collētĭcus, a, um, adj., = κολλητικός, suitable for gluing or sticking together: clysteria, Veg. 1, 46.
colleticus.short: collētĭcus, a, um, adj., = κολλητικός, suitable for gluing or sticking together: clysteria, Veg.

colletis.full: collētis, is, f., = κολλητίς, a plant, App. Herb. 3.
colletis.short: collētis, is, f., = κολλητίς, a plant, App.

collevo.full: col-lēvo (con-, -laevo), āre, v. a., to make entirely smooth, to smooth (post-class. and rare): plagam arboris falce, Plin. 17, 22, 35, § 192: asperitatem oculorum, Sen. Ep. 64, 7; cf.: interanea vesicae, Plin. 23, 1, 18, § 30.

colliberta.full: collīberta (conl-), ae, f., a fellowfreedwoman, Inscr. Orell. 575; 3927.
colliberta.short: collīberta (conl-), ae, f., a fellowfreedwoman, Inscr.

collibertus.full: col-lībertus (conl-), i, m., a fellowfreedman, Plaut. Poen. 4, 2, 88; Cic. Verr. 2, 5, 59, § 154 dub.; Dig. 36, 3, 18 al.
collibertus.short: col-lībertus (conl-), i, m., a fellowfreedman, Plaut.

collibet.full: col-lĭbet (conl-) or collŭbet (conl-), buit or bītum est, 2, v. impers., it pleases, it is agreeable (very rare, and only in the pret. tenses); in act.: si collibuisset, * Hor. S. 1, 3, 6; Col. 11, 1, 2: quae victoribus conlubuissent, * Sall. C. 51, 9; in pass.: utcumque animo conlubitum est meo, Plaut. Am. 1, 1, 187; 2, 2, 228; id. Cist. 1, 2, 6; id. Most. 1, 3, 137; id. Merc. 2, 1, 34: si quid conlubitum'st, Ter. Eun. 5, 8, 26 Fleck.; Cic. N. D. 1, 38, 108; id. Fam. 15, 16, 2; cf. Charis. 2, 1
collibet.short: col-lĭbet (conl-) or collŭbet (conl-), buit or bītum est, 2, v.

collibro.full: col-lībro (conl-), āre, v. a., to measure off. Cato, R. R. 19, 2 bis.

collicellus.full: collĭcellus, i, m. dim. collis, a very little hill, Agrim. p. 245; 272 Goes.

colliciae.full: col-lĭciae or collĭquĭae (conl-), ārum, f. con-liquor, a flowing together; hence, channels, drains, or gutters for conducting water in the fields, upon the roofs of buildings, etc., Col. 2, 8, 3; Plin. 18, 19, 49, § 179; Vitr. 6, 3; cf. Paul. ex Fest. p. 114, 4 Müll.

colliciaris.full: col-lĭcĭāris (conl-), e, adj. colliciae, pertaining to water-channels: tegula, a roof-tile, Cato, R. R. 14, 4.

colliculus.full: collĭcŭlus, i, m. dim. collis, a little hill (late Lat.), App. Flor. 1, 1, p. 340.

collido.full: col-līdo (conl-), līsi, līsum, 3, v. a. laedo, to clash, strike, dash, beat, or press together, etc. (rare; mostly post-Aug.; most freq. in Quint.). Prop.: umor ita mollis est, ut facile premi collidique possit, Cic. N. D. 3, 12, 31; Lucr. 1, 532: collidere manus, to clap, Quint. 2, 12, 10: dentes colliduntur, chatter, Sen. Ep. 11, 2: anulus ut fiat, primo colliditur aurum, Ov. A. A. 3, 221: mare inter se navigia collidit, Curt. 4, 3, 17; 9, 9, 16: amnis uterque colliditur, id. 8, 9, 8: silvam s

colliga.full: collĭga, ae, f. 1. colligo, a place for gathering nitrum, Plin. 31, 10, 46, § 113 Jan. (Sillig, colycas).

colligatio.full: collĭgātĭo (conl-), ōnis, f. 2. colligo, a binding together, connection (rare). Prop.: ex his colligationibus, Cic. Univ. 7, 21: tota operis colligatio, Val. Max. 8, 14, 6; cf.: inter quattuor (elementa), Macr. Somn. Scip. 1, 6, 28.— In mechanics, a ligature, band, fastening, Vitr. 10, 1.— Trop. (only in Cic.): causarum omnium, Cic. Div. 1, 56, 127: colligatione naturali omnia fiunt, id. Fat. 14, 31: artior societatis propinquorum, id. Off. 1, 17, 53.

colligo1.full: col-lĭgo (conl-), lēgi, lectum, 3, v. a. [2. lego, ĕre], to gather or collect together into a whole or to a point, to assemble, draw or bring together, collect (class. and very freq.), Prop. In gen. Of things: omnia praesegmina, Plaut. Aul. 2, 4, 34: stipulam, Ter. Ad. 5, 3, 62; cf.: omnia furtim, Lucil. ap. Non. p. 273, 28: radices palmarum, Cic. Verr. 2, 5, 33, § 87: apes in vas, Varr. R. R. 2, 16, 37: ossa, Tib. 3, 2, 19; cf. reliquias, Suet. Tib. 54 fin.; id. Calig. 3: materiem nostram Post

colligo2.full: col-lĭgo (conl-), āvi, ātum, 1, v. a., to bind, tie, or fasten together, to connect, bind, tie up (in good prose). Prop.: omne colligatum solvi potest, Cic. Univ. 11, 35: corpora colligata vinculis naturalibus, id. ib.; cf. id. ib. 5, 13: vasa (of warlike implements; cf. the preced. art., I. A. 1. fin.), Plaut. Ps. 4, 3, 16: manus, id. Ep. 5, 2, 23; cf. id. ib. 5, 2, 25, and the common expression in the formula: i, lictor, colliga manus, tie the prisoner's hands, Cic. Rab. Perd. 4, 13; Liv. 1, 2

collimitaneus.full: col-līmĭtānĕus (conl-), a, um, adj., bordering upon; with dat.: Phrygia Galatiae, Sol. 40, 9.
collimitaneus.short: col-līmĭtānĕus (conl-), a, um, adj., bordering upon;

collimitium.full: col-līmĭtĭum (conl-), ii, n. limes, the boundary between two countries, Sol. 49, 6: collimitia Romana, Amm. 15, 4, 1.

collimito.full: col-līmĭto (conl-), āre, and collī-mĭtor, āri, to border upon (post-class. and very rare); with dat., Amm. 31, 2, 14; Sol. 25.
collimito.short: col-līmĭto (conl-), āre, and collī-mĭtor, āri, to border upon (post-class.

collimo.full: collimo, āre, false read. for collineo, āre.

collina1.full: collīna, ae, f. collinus, hilly land, Innoc. de Cas. Litt. p. 224 Goes.

collina2.full: Collīna, ae, f. id., goddess of hills, Aug. Civ. Dei, 4, 8 (others read Collatina).

collineo.full: col-līnĕo (conl-), āvi, ātum, āre, v. a., to direct something in a straight line, to aim (rare, and except in Cic. only postclass.). Prop.: hastam aut sagittam aliquo, Cic. Fin. 3, 6, 22: manum et oculos, Julian. ap. Gell. 9, 1, 6: oculos ad umbram, App. M. 9, p. 237; id. Flor. 23.—* To take a right aim, Cic. Div. 2, 59, 121; cf. Madv. Fin. p. 382.—Hence, collīnĕātē, adv., in a direct line; trop., skilfully, artistically; in sup., Jul. Val. Alex. M. 3, 48; so id. ib. 3, 58.

collino.full: col-lĭno (conl-), lēvi, lĭtum, 3, v. a., to besmear, to cover over, defile, pollute: aliquid, aliquā re (rare; not in class. prose). Prop.: ora venenis, Ov. R. Am. 351: tabulas cerā, Gell. 17, 9, 17: crines adulteros pulvere, * Hor. C. 1, 15, 20 (cf. Verg. A. 12, 99: foedare in pulvere crines): caeno collitus, Plaut. Poen. 4, 2, 4.— Trop.: pulchrum ornatum turpes mores pejus caeno collinunt, Plaut. Most. 1, 3, 133; id. Poen. 1, 2, 96.

collinus.full: collīnus, a, um, adj. collis, of or pertaining to a hill, found or growing on a hill, hilly, hill- (class.). In gen.: genus agrorum (opp. to campestre and montanum), Varr. R. R. 1, 6, 2: vineae, id. ib. 1, 6, 5; Col. 12, 21, 1: loca, id. 3, 2, 6: aqua, id. 1, 5, 3: vina, id. 12, 21, 4: frumentum, Cels. 2, 18.— Esp.: Collīnus, a, um, adj., pertaining to the hills in the northeastern part of Rome (the Quirinal and Viminal), Colline: regio urbis Collina, Varr. L. L. 5, § 45: tribus, id. ib. 5, § 56

colliquefactus.full: col-lĭquĕfactus (conl-), a, um, Part. [liquefio], made fluid, liquefied, dissolved, melted (very rare): glacies, Varr. R. R. 2, 4, 6: venenum in potione, * Cic. Clu. 62, 173.

colliquesco.full: col-lĭquesco (conl-), lĭqui, ĕre, v. inch. n., to become fluid, to liquefy, melt, dissolve (rare). Prop.: cum aurum colliquisset, Varr. ap. Non. p. 334, 27 sq.: cum aes colliquisset, id. ib. (but Neue, Formenl. 2, 486, would read collicuisset in both these passages): in pice colliquescere, Col. 12, 22, 2: igni, App. Mag. p. 306, 10.— Trop.: lacrimis, to melt into tears, Fronto, Nep. Am. 2.

collis.full: collis, is (abl. reg. colle, e. g. Ov. M. 1, 698; 14, 90; 14, 333; 14, 822; 14, 836; Caes. B. G. 1, 24; 2, 18; Sall. J. 52, 3: Aventino, Liv. 1, 3, 9 et saep.; colli, Lucr. 2, 317 and 322; Auct. Aetn. 466; gen. plur. collium, Tac. Agr. 37; Lact. Opif. Dei, 10), m. cel-, root of ex-cello, celsus; cf. calamus, high ground, a hill (opp. mons and campus), Lucr. 5, 1373; Cic. Verr. 2, 3, 18, § 47; Caes. B. G. 2, 8; 7, 19: altus, Ov. M. 15, 306: aperti, Verg. G. 2, 112: aprici, id. E. 9, 49: celsus, i

collisio.full: collīsĭo (conl-), ōnis, f. collido, a dashing or striking together, a concussion, shock: partūs abjecti, Just. 11, 12, 6.— Transf., of letters in a word: πνεῖν, χεἰν, ῥεῖν, non sunt integra, sed ex collisione contracta. Macr. Diff. 19, § 17.

collisus1.full: collīsus (conl-), a, um, Part., from collido.
collisus1.short: collīsus (conl-), a, um, Part., from collido.

collisus2.full: collīsus (conl-), ūs, m. collido, a striking together, collision (very rare): margaritarum, Plin. 9, 35, 56, § 114: dentium, Cael. Aur. Acut. 2, 12.

collitus.full: collĭtus (conl-), a, um, Part., from collino.
collitus.short: collĭtus (conl-), a, um, Part., from collino.

collocatio.full: collŏcātĭo (conl-), ōnis, f. colloco, a putting together, arrangement, a setting up, erecting, placing, collocation (except in rhet. use, very rare). In gen.: siderum, Cic. Univ. 9, 26: moenium, Vitr. 5, 3. — Esp. in speech: verborum, Cic. de Or. 3, 43, 171; 2, 13, 54; id. Or. 25, 83; 70, 232; Quint. 1, 10, 22; cf. id. 8, prooem. § 6; 8, 3, 41; 9, 4, 58; 9, 4, 89: argumentorum, Cic. de Or. 2, 42, 181: rerum, Quint. 3, 3, 8. — Esp.: filiae, an endowing, giving in marriage (v. colloco, I. B.), Cic

colloco.full: col-lŏco (conl-), āvi, ātum, 1, v. a., to place together, to arrange, to station, lay, put, place, set, set up, erect, etc., a thing (or person) somewhere (class. in prose and poetry; cf.: statuo, pono, sisto). Lit. In gen.; constr. usu. with in and abl. (cf. Ramsh. Gr. p. 467 sq.; Zumpt, Gr. § 489); more rarely with in and acc.; also with other prepositions, or absol. With in and abl.: istam conloca cruminam in collo plane, Plaut. As. 3, 3, 67: in rostris collocati, Cic. Sest. 38, 83: aliquem i

collocupleto.full: col-lŏcŭplēto (conl-), āvi, 1, v. a., to make very rich, to enrich (prob. only in the foll. exs.). Prop.: se, Ter. Heaut. 2, 3, 17.— Trop., to embellish, enrich, adorn: rei honestandae et collocupletandae causā, Auct. Her. 2, 18, 28.

collocutio.full: collŏcūtĭo (conl-), ōnis, f. colloquor, a (familiar or private) conversation, conference (very rare): hominum, Cic. Tusc. 1, 13, 30; id. Att. 12, 1, 2: venire cum aliquo in collocutionem, Auct. Her. 1, 15, 25.—In plur.: familiarissimae cum aliquo, Cic. Phil. 11, 2, 5: in sermonibus collocutionibusque aliquid videre, id. Fam. 1, 9, 4.

collocutor.full: collŏcūtor (conl-), ōris, m. id., he who talks with another (eccl. Lat.), Tert. adv. Prax. 5; Aug. Conf. 9, 6.

colloquium.full: collŏquĭum (conl-), ii, n. id., a conversation, conference, discourse (class. in prose and poetry; not in Hor.): colloquium cum conveniunt in unum locum loquendi causā, Varr. L. L. 6, § 57 Müll.; Titin. ap. Non. p. 256, 16: eo ad colloquium venerunt, Caes. B. G. 1, 43: in colloquium venire, id. ib. 1, 35: in Antonii congressum colloquiumque veniendum est, Cic. Phil. 12, 11, 26: pervenire ad conloquium alicujus, id. ib. 9, 1, 2: denos ut ad colloquium adducerent, Caes. B. G. 1, 43: de aliquā re i

colloquor.full: col-lŏquor (conl-), cūtus, 3, v. dep., to talk together, converse, to hold a conversation, a parley, or a conference (in good prose); constr. commonly cum aliquo, inter se, or absol.; in Plaut. several times as verb act. with acc. With cum aliquo, Ter. Hec. 1, 2, 56; Cic. Brut. 60, 218; id. Tusc. 1, 41, 98; id. Div. 1, 30, 64; id. Att. 16, 8, 1; id. Fam. 1, 9, 10; Nep. Paus. 2, 4: cum aliquo per aliquem, Caes. B. G. 1, 19; Nep. Alcib. 5, 3: cum aliquo per litteras, Cic. Fam. 1, 7, 1; id. Att. 6,

colluceo.full: col-lūcĕo (conl-), ēre, v. n., to give light on every side, to shine brightly, to be wholly illuminated, to be bright or brilliant (class. in prose and poetry; not in Hor.). Prop. Absol.: sol, qui tam longe lateque colluceat, Cic. N. D. 2, 15, 40: caelum conlucet omnibus, id. Univ. 9 med.: taeda per undas, * Lucr. 6, 883: collucent ignes, Verg. A. 9, 166; so, faces, id. ib. 4, 567; Curt. 3, 8, 22: per campum, Tac. A. 3, 4: lampades undique, Ov. H. 14, 25: pocula, Cat. 64, 45: plumae ignium modo,

collucesco.full: col-lūcesco, colluxi, 3, v. inch. n., to lighten up (late Lat.): colluxit flamma, Albin. ad Liv. 1, 287.— Transf., to become clear, intelligible, Boëth. Syllog. Hypoth. 1, p. 623.

colluco.full: col-lūco (conl-), āre, v. a. lux, to make light, to clear or thin a forest, etc.: collucare est succisis arboribus locum luce implere, Fest. s. v. sublucare, p. 348, 18 Müll. (explained in a different manner by Paul. ex Fest. p. 37, 12 ib.): lucum, Cato, R. R. 139: arborem, Col. 2, 21, 3.

colluctatio.full: colluctātĭo (conl-), ōnis, f. colluctor, a wrestling, struggling, contending with something (post-Aug. prose). Prop.: in colluctatione vel pancratio, Dig. 9, 2, 7; so of the fighting of oxen, Col. 6, 2, 4.— Trop., the death struggle, Sen. Q. N. 3, 18, 1. —Of an embracing in love, App. M. 9, p. 219, 12; Lact. 1, 17.—Of a difficult utterance: est aliis concursus oris et cum verbis suis colluctatio, Quint. 11, 3, 56.

colluctator.full: colluctātor (conl-), ōris, m. id., prop. a wrestler; hence, in gen., an anlagonist, adversary, Lact. Opif. Dei, 1, 7.

colluctor.full: col-luctor (conl-), āri, v. n., to struggle, contend, wrestle with (post-Aug. and rare); constr. with cum aliquo, alicui, or absol.: praedonibus, Prud. Ham. 523.—Absol., Just. 13, 8, 8; App. M. 2, p. 129.—Trop.: cum agro, Col. 1, 3, 9; cf.: cum solo, Plin. 27, 2, 2, § 5: cum petulantiā morbi, Gell. 12, 5, 9.

colludium.full: collūdĭum (conl-), ii, n. colludo (post-class.). A sporting, playing together: delphinorum, Sol. 12; so Symm. Ep. 3, 5.— A secret, deceptive understanding, collusion, esp. in justice, Amm. 18, 5, 1; Cod. Th. 9, 42, 20; 11, 42, 7; Symm. Ep. 4, 20.

colludo.full: col-lūdo (conl-), si, sum, 3, v. n., to play or sport together, play with (very rare). Prop., with dat.: (puer) gestit paribus colludere, * Hor. A. P. 159.—Poet.: aut summā nantes in aquā colludere plumas, * Verg. G. 1, 369: DIGITIS COLLVDENTIBVS TRADERE PECORA, Inscr. Orell. 3166.— Jurid. t. t., to keep up false appearances with one to the injury of a third person, to have a secret understanding with one, to act collusively, * Cic. Verr. 2, 2, 24, § 58; Dig. 3, 4, 7, § 9; 41, 5, 7; Sen. Contr.

collugeo.full: col-lūgĕo (conl-), ēre, v. n., to lament, grieve together, Cael. Aur. Tard. 2, 5, 88.

collum.full: collum, i, n. (ante-class. access. form collus, i, m., Naev., Cato, Lucil., Att., Caecil., Varr. ap. Non. p. 200, 14 sq.; Plaut. Capt. 2, 2, 107; 4, 3, 2; and, acc. to Non. l. l., also id. Am. 1, 1, 289: nec collos mihi Calvus persuaserit, Quint. 1, 6, 42; Front. Ep. ad M. Caes. 2, 16) [cf. Germ. Hals]. Prop., the neck, of men and animals: accipite si vultis hoc onus in vostros collos, Cato, l.l.: anseris, Lucil. l.l.: pavonis, Varr. l. l.: columbarum, Lucr. 2, 802; cf. Cic. Ac. 2, 7, 19; id. N.

collumino.full: col-lūmĭno (conl-), āre, v. a., to illuminate on all sides (post-class. and very rare): aliquem, App. de Deo Socr. p. 45, 39; Prud. adv. Symm. 2, 830.

colluo.full: col-lŭo (conl-), lŭi, lūtum, 3, v. a., to wash thoroughly, wash out, rinse (mostly post-Aug.; not in Cic.); constr. aliquid, or aliquid aliquā re; rarely aliquid de aliquā re: metretam amurcā, Cato, R. R. 100; Pers. 1, 18: os de oleo, Plin. 23, 4, 38, § 77: decocto, id. 23, 6, 56, § 105: dentes aquā, id. 20, 6, 23, § 53: gemma melle colluta, id. 37, 10, 56, § 155.—Poet.: ora, to moisten, wet, i. e. to quench thirst, * Ov. M. 5, 447 (cf.: abluere sitim, Lucr. 4, 877).—* Absol., to wash up (earth)

collurchinatio.full: col-lurchĭnātĭo (conl-, and -lurcĭn-), ōnis, f. lurcor, gross gluttony, gormandizing (post-class. and rare), App. Mag. p. 322, 33; Claud. Mam. Stat. An. 2, 9 fin.

collusio.full: collūsĭo (conl-), ōnis, f. colludo, II., a secret, deceptive understanding, collusion, * Cic. Verr. 2, 3, 13, § 33: inter raptae patrem et raptorem, Sen. Contr. 2, 11, 22: per collusionem, id. ib. 5, 31 fin.: illa inter virum et uxorem nota collusio, App. Mag. p. 322, 13; Dig. 40, 16: de collusione detegendā, ib. 40, 4; 8, 5, 19; 17, 1, 8; 12, 2, 30, § 3.

collusor.full: collūsor (conl-), ōris, m. colludo. A companion in play, playmate (in good prose), Cic. Phil. 2, 23, 56; 2, 39, 101; 5, 5, 13; * Suet. Calig. 41; Plin. Ep. 9, 33, 8; Dig. 11, 5, 1, § 1.—* (Acc. to colludo, II.) He who has a secret understanding with one to the injury of a third, in law, Cod. Th. 7, 20, 2.

collusorie.full: collūsōrĭē (conl-), adv. collusor, II., in a concerted manner, collusively: litigare de hereditate, Dig. 30, 1, 50, § 2.

collustrium.full: collustrĭum, ĭi, n. collustro, a corporation that procured the lustration of the fields of a district, Inscr. Orell. 1773.

collustro.full: col-lustro (conl-), āvi, ātum, 1, v. a., to lighten on all sides, to illumine, brighten (rare but class.; most freq. in Cic.). Prop.: sol omnia clarissimā luce collustrans, Cic. N. D. 2, 36, 92; id. Div. 2, 43, 91; id. Rep. 6, 17, 17 (al. lustret).—* Transf.: collustrata in picturis, the brilliantly colored, bright (opp. opaca), Cic. Or. 11, 36.— Trop., to consider a thing on all sides, to inspect, survey: omnia oculis, Cic. Tusc. 5, 23, 65: omnia, Verg. A. 3, 651: cuncta, Tac. A. 2, 45.

collutio.full: collūtĭo (conl-), ōnis, f. colluo, a rinsing, washing, Scrib. Comp. 53; Cael. Aur. Tard. 4, 3, 39.

collutito.full: col-lŭtĭto (conl-), āre, v. freq. a. colluo; cf. Ritschl, prol. ad Plaut. p. 74, to soil, defile much; trop., Plaut. Trin. 3, 2, 67 Ritschl N. cr.; cf. Non. p. 84, 25 (al. collutulo).

colluviaris.full: collŭvĭāris porcus dicitur, qui cibo permixto et colluvie nutritur, Paul. ex Fest. p. 57, 8 Müll.
colluviaris.short: collŭvĭāris porcus dicitur, qui cibo permixto et colluvie nutritur, Paul.

colluvio.full: collŭvĭo (conl-), ōnis, and collŭvĭ-es, em, ē (the latter form not freq. before the Aug. per.; but exclusively used by Col., Pliny the elder, and Tac.; a third collat. form collŭvĭum, acc. to Isid. Diff. Verb. 40), f. colluo, a conflux or collection of filth, washings, sweepings, draff, swill. Prop. Colluvies, Dig. 43, 22, 1, §§ 2 and 4: cohortis et aedificii, Col. 2, 15, 8; cf. id. 1, 6, 24; 1, 5, 6: turbida nigro limo, Luc. 4, 311; Plin. 24, 19, 116, § 176.— Colluvio: colluvionibus sentinarum,
colluvio.short: collŭvĭo (conl-), ōnis, and collŭvĭ-es, em, ē (the latter form not freq.

collybista.full: collўbista, ae, m., = κολλυβιστής, a money-changer, banker, Hier. in Matt. 21, 12.
collybista.short: collўbista, ae, m., = κολλυβιστής, a money-changer, banker, Hier.

collybus.full: collўbus (collŭbus), i, m., = κόλλυβος [prob. of Phoenicio-Semitic origin, kindr. with the Heb. , to change], the exchange of coins of different kinds, or of different countries, agio. Prop., Cic. Att. 12, 6, 1; Cassiod. Parm. ap. Suet. Aug. 4.— Meton., the rate or premium of exchange, Cic. Verr. 2, 3, 78, § 181.

collyra.full: collȳra, ae, f., = κολλύρα, a kind of pastry of a round, elongated form, maccaroni, vermicelli, shred into broth, Plaut. Pers. 1, 3, 12.—Hence, collȳrĭcus, a, um, of vermicelli, vermicelli soup, Plaut. Pers. 1, 3, 15 and 17.
collyra.short: collȳra, ae, f., = κολλύρα, a kind of pastry of a round, elongated form, maccaroni, vermicelli, shred into broth, Plaut.

collyriolum.full: collȳrĭŏlum, i, n. dim. collyrium, a small collyrium, tent, pessary, etc., Macer. 4, 12.

collyris.full: collȳris, ĭdis (collȳrĭda, ae, Vulg. 2 Reg. 6, 19; id. Lev. 8, 26; cf.: cassida, chlamyda, etc.), f., = κολλυρίς. Lit., a roll or cake, Aug. in Gen. 8, 5 fin.; Vulg. Lev. 7, 12 (transl. of the Heb. ).— Meton. A head-dress of women, Tert. Cult. Fem. 2, 7.— A plant, also called malva erratica, App. Herb. 40.

collyrium.full: collȳrĭum, ii, n., = κολλύριον (a mass similar to the collyra-dough; hence, in medic. lang.), A tent, pessary, suppository, etc., Cels. 5, 28, 12; Col. 6, 6, 5; 6, 30, 8; Plin. 26, 12, 78, § 126; 28, 9, 37, § 139; Scrib. Comp. 142.— Esp., a liquid eyesalve, Cels. 7, 7, 4; * Hor. S. 1, 5, 30; Veg. 3, 16, 2; 3, 16, 8; 3, 18, 2.— Meton., a shaft, pillar, Sid. Ep. 2, 2.
collyrium.short: collȳrĭum, ii, n., = κολλύριον (a mass similar to the collyra-dough;

colminiana.full: Colminiana (Cato, R. R. 6, 1), Col-minia (Varr. R. R. 1, 24, 1), Culminia (Col. 5, 8, 8; 12, 51, 3; 12, 54, 1), Cominia (Plin. 15, 3, 4, § 13; Pall. Febr. 18, 4): olea, an unknown kind of olive-tree (concerning the varying readings, v. Schneid. N. cr.).

colo1.full: cŏlo, colŭi, cultum, 3, v. a. from the stem ΚΟΛ, whence βουκόλος, βουκολέω; cf.: colonus, in-cola, agri-cola (orig. pertaining to agriculture), to cultivate, till, tend, take care of a field, garden, etc. (freq. in all per. and species of composition). Prop. With acc.: fundum, Varr. R. R. 1, 1, 2: agrum, id. ib. 1, 2, 14; Cato, R. R. 61; Col. 1 pr.: agri non omnes frugiferi sunt qui coluntur, Cic. Tusc. 2, 5, 13; id. Agr. 2, 25, 67: arva et vineta et oleas et arbustum, Quint. 1, 12, 7: praedia,

colo2.full: cōlo, āvi, ātum, āre, v. a. colum, to filter, strain, to clarify, purify (post-Aug.): ceram, Col. 9, 16, 1: mel, id. 12, 11, 1: vinum sportā palmeā, Pall. Febr. 27: sucum linteo, Plin. 25, 13, 103, § 164: thymum cribro, Col. 7, 8, 7: aliquid per linteum, Scrib. Comp. 271: ad colum, Veg. 2, 28, 19: per colum, Apic. 4, 2: aurum, App. Flor. p. 343, 20: terra colans, Plin. 31, 3, 23, § 38: faex colata, id. 31, 8, 44, § 95.—Poet.: amnes inductis retibus, i. e. to spread out a fish-net, Manil. 5, 193.

colobathrarius.full: cōlŏbathrārius, ii, m. κωλόβαθρον, one who walks on stilts, Non. p. 115, 20.

colobicus.full: cŏlŏbĭcus, a, um, adj., = κολοβικός, mutilated, Firm. Math. 3, 14, 8.
colobicus.short: cŏlŏbĭcus, a, um, adj., = κολοβικός, mutilated, Firm.

colobium.full: cŏlŏbĭum, ii (cŏlŏbum, i, Cod. Th. 14, 10, 1), n., = κολόβιον, an undergarment with short sleeves, Serv. ad Verg. A. 9, 616.

colobos.full: cŏlŏbŏs, on, adj., = κολοβός, mutilated, curtailed, only in metre: versus, in which one syllable is wanting, = catalectus, Mall. Theod. Metr. 7: metrum, id. ib. 5; Marc. Vict. p. 2504 P.
colobos.short: cŏlŏbŏs, on, adj., = κολοβός, mutilated, curtailed, only in metre: versus, in which one syllable is wanting, = catalectus, Mall.

colocasia.full: cŏlŏcāsĭa, ae, f. (plur.: cŏlŏcāsĭa, ōrum, n., * Verg. E. 4, 20; Mart. 8, 33, 13), = κολοκασία or κολοκάσιον, an Egyptian bean; a magnificent plant of the lily kind, growing in the lakes and marshes of Egypt, whose beans, roots, and even the stalks and stems, were considered as luxuries, and from its large leaves drinking-cups (ciboria) were made, Plin. 21, 15, 51, § 87; Col. 8, 15, 4; Pall. Febr. 24, 14; id. Apr. 3, 5; cf. Voss ad Verg. l. l. (The colocasia of Virgil is supposed to be the Arum

colocasitis.full: Cŏlŏcāsītis, ĭdis, f., = Κολοκασῖτις, an island near the coast of Africa, Plin. 6, 29, 34, § 172.
colocasitis.short: Cŏlŏcāsītis, ĭdis, f., = Κολοκασῖτις, an island near the coast of Africa, Plin.

colocynthis.full: cŏlŏcynthis, ĭdis, f., = κολοκυνθίς, the colocynth or coloquintida, used as a purgative: Cucumis colocynthis, Linn.; Plin. 20, 3, 8, § 14; Pall. 1, 35, 9.
colocynthis.short: cŏlŏcynthis, ĭdis, f., = κολοκυνθίς, the colocynth or coloquintida, used as a purgative: Cucumis colocynthis, Linn.;

colon.full: cōlon or cōlum, i, n. (cōlus, i, m., Ser. Samm. 31, 1), = κῶλον (a member). The colon or great gut (the largest of the intestines), Plin. 11, 37, 79, § 202.—Esp., as the part affected by the colic: coli tormentum, Plin. 22, 22, 37, § 79: coli dolor, Scrib. Comp. 122.—Hence, A disease of the colon, the colic, Plin. 20, 15, 57, § 162; 31, 9, 45, § 102; Scrib. Comp. l. l.; Ser. Samm. l. l.— Transf., a member of a verse (pure Lat. membrum), * Quint. 9, 4, 78; of a poem, Aug. ap. Don. Vit. Verg. c. 1

colona.full: cŏlōna, ae, f. colonus, a countrywoman, Ov. F. 4, 692; 2, 646; Dig. 19, 2, 54 fin.; Inscr. Orell. 4644.

colonae.full: Cŏlōnae, ārum, f., = Κολωναί. a town in Troas, now prob. Chemali, Nep. Paus. 3, 3; the same called Cŏlōnē, ēs, Plin. 5, 30, 32, § 123.

colonarius.full: cŏlōnārĭus, a, um, adj. colonia, of or pertaining to the colonus, rustic (late Lat.): persona, Sid. Ep. 5, 19: condicio, Cod. Just. 1, 4, 24.

colonatus.full: cŏlōnātus, ūs, m. colonus, the condition of a rustic (post-class.), Cod. Th. 12, 1, 33; 14, 18, 1.

coloneus.full: Cŏlōnēus, a, um, adj., = Κολώνειος, of or pertaining to the Attic demos Colonos (Κολωνός): Oedipus (Οἰδίπους ἐπὶ Κολωνῷ), Cic. Sen. 7, 22; cf. absol.: Coloneus, the tragedy of Sophocles, App. Mag. p. 298, 6: locus, Cic. Fin. 5, 1, 3.
coloneus.short: Cŏlōnēus, a, um, adj., = Κολώνειος, of or pertaining to the Attic demos Colonos (Κολωνός): Oedipus (Οἰδίπους ἐπὶ Κολωνῷ), Cic.

colonia1.full: cŏlōnĭa, ae, f. colonus. (Acc. to colonus, I.) A possession in land, a landed estate, a farm, Col. 11, 1, 23; Dig. 19, 2, 24, § 4; 33, 7, 20.— An abode, dwelling in gen. (cf. 1. colo, I. B.), Plaut. Aul. 3, 6, 40; and humorously: molarum, for a mill, id. Ps. 4, 6, 38.—Far more freq., (Acc. to colonus, II.) A colony, colonial town, settlement: colonia dicta est a colendo: est autem pars civium aut sociorum, missa ubi rem publicam habeant ex consensu suae civitatis aut publico ejus populi unde pro

colonia2.full: Cŏlōnĭa, ae, f., a name given to several colonial or provincial cities, but always, in the class. lang., with a more definite appellation; as Colonia Agrippina or Agrippinensis, the present Cologne.
colonia2.short: Cŏlōnĭa, ae, f., a name given to several colonial or provincial cities, but always, in the class.

coloniarius.full: cŏlōnĭārĭus, ii, m., and -a, ae, f. colonia, II., native of a colony, Gai Inst. 3, § 56; 1, § 28; Ulp. Sent. 19, 4.
coloniarius.short: cŏlōnĭārĭus, ii, m., and -a, ae, f.

colonicus.full: cŏlōnĭcus, a, um, adj. colonus, I.. Of or pertaining to agriculture or husbandry: leges, Varr. R. R. 1, 2, 17: genus ovium, found upon any farm, common, Plin. 8, 47, 72, § 189; 26, 10, 62, § 96.— Subst.: cŏ-lōnĭca, ae, f., a farm-house, a rustic's hut, Aus. Ep. 4, 7.— Pertaining to a colony: cohortes, levied from colonies, Caes. B. C. 2, 19: decuriones, Suet. Aug. 46.

colonus.full: cŏlōnus, i, m. colo. A husbandman, tiller of the soil (opp. pastor), Cato, R. R. prooem. § 2; Varr. R. R. 2, prooem. § 5; id. L. L. 5, § 21 Müll.; Cic. de Or. 2, 71, 287; Hor. C. 1, 35, 6; 2, 14, 12; id. S. 2, 1, 35; 2, 2, 115; Verg. E. 9, 4; id. G. 1, 125; Ov. M. 1, 272; Sen. Ep. 114, 25.— Esp., a farmer, one who cultivates another's land, Caes. B. C. 1, 34; Cic. Caecin. 32, 94; Col. 1, 7, 1; Plin. Ep. 10, 8 (24), 5; Dig. 19, 2, 15 al. — A colonist, inhabitant of a colonial town, ἄποικος, Cic.

colophon1.full: Cŏlŏphon, ōnis (acc. -nem, Cic. Imp. Pomp. 12, 33; -na, Vell. 1, 4, 3; Tac. A. 2, 54), m., = Κολοφών, one of the twelve Ionian towns in Lydia, situated near the sea, and renowned for its cavalry, now perh. Zille or Altobosco, Mel. 1, 17, 2; Cic. Imp. Pomp. 12, 33; Liv. 37, 26, 5 sq.; Hor. Ep. 1, 11, 3. — Hence, Cŏlŏphōnĭus, a, um, adj., Colophonian: resina, Plin. 14, 20, 25, § 123 (also absol.: Colophonia, Scrib. Comp. 137 sq.): Idmon, Ov. M. 6, 8.—In plur.: Cŏlŏphōnii, ōrum, m., the Colophonian

colophon2.full: cŏlŏphōn, ōnos, m.: colophon dixerunt, cum aliquid finitum significaretur, Paul. ex Fest. p. 37, 14 Müll. [ = κολοφών, the summit, the top; cf. in Gr. κολοφῶνα ἐπιθεῖναι, v. Lidd. and Scott, s. v. κολοφών].
colophon2.short: cŏlŏphōn, ōnos, m.: colophon dixerunt, cum aliquid finitum significaretur, Paul.

color.full: cŏlor (old form cŏlos, like arbos, clamos, honos, etc., Plaut. Mil. 4, 4, 43; Lucr. 6, 208; 6, 1073; Sall. C. 15, 5, acc. to Prob. II. pp. 1456 and 1467 P.; Plin. 13, 15, 30, § 98; 35, 11, 42, § 150), ōris, m. root cal-, to cover; cf.: caligo, occulere, calyx, color, hue, tint. Lit. In gen.: varii rerum, Lucr. 2, 786: nequeunt sine luce Esse, id. 2, 795: aureus ignis, id. 6, 205: albus, id. 2, 823; cf.: color albus praecipue decorus deo est, Cic. Leg. 2, 18, 45: purpureus conchyli, Lucr. 6, 1073
color.short: cŏlor (old form cŏlos, like arbos, clamos, honos, etc., Plaut.

colorabilis.full: cŏlōrābĭlis, e, adj., = chromaticus, q. v., Mart. Cap. 9, § 942.

colorate.full: cŏlōrātē, adv., v. coloro, P. a. fin.

colorator.full: cŏlōrātor, ōris, m., a polisher, στιλβωτής et ινδικοπλάστης, Gloss. Lat.; Inscr. Murat. 887, 3.—Name of a comedy of Laberius, Gell. 6 ($3), 9, 4.
colorator.short: cŏlōrātor, ōris, m., a polisher, στιλβωτής et ινδικοπλάστης, Gloss.

coloratus.full: cŏlōrātus, a, um, v. coloro, P.a.

coloreus.full: cŏlōrĕus or -ĭus, a, um, adj. color, colored, variegated (rare, mostly class.): gausapes coloriae, August. ap. Charis. p. 80 P.; so, vestis, Dig. 34, 2, 33 fin.: tunicae coloreae, Vop. Aur. 46.

coloro.full: cŏlōro, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. id.. To give a color to, to color, tinge (class.): corpora, Cic. N. D. 1, 39, 110: lignum sinopide, Plin. 35, 6, 13, § 31: lineas testa trita, id. 35, 3, 5, § 16: medicamentum rubricā vel atramento, Scrib. Comp. 228: coloratum Tithoni conjuge caelum, Ov. Am. 2, 5, 35.— In partic., to color reddish or brownish, to tinge: cum in sole ambulem, natura fit ut colorer, Cic. de Or. 2, 14, 60; Quint. 5, 10, 81; Sen. Ep. 108, 4: pira sole, Plin. 15, 15, 16, § 54; Prop. 3 (4),

colossae.full: Cŏlossae, ārum, f., = Κολοσσαί, a city of Phrygia on the Lycus, now Khonas; to the church in this place Paul's Epistle to the Colossians was addressed, Plin. 5, 32, 41, § 145; Vulg. Col. 1, 2.—Hence, Cŏlos-senses, ium, m., the Colossians, the inhabitants of Colossœ, Ambros. Spir. Sanct. 2, 20.— Cŏlossīnus, a, um, adj., = Κολοσσῖνος, of or belonging to Colossœ: flos, Plin. 21, 9, 27, § 51.
colossae.short: Cŏlossae, ārum, f., = Κολοσσαί, a city of Phrygia on the Lycus, now Khonas;

colosseros.full: Cŏlossĕrōs, ōtis, m. Κολοσσόσ?̓́Ερως, the Colossal-love, an appellation of a large and beautiful man, Suet. Calig. 35.

colosseus.full: cŏlossēus (-ossiaeus, Plin. 36, 5, 4, § 26), a, um, adj., = κολοσσιαῖος, colossal, huge, gigantic (post-Aug. prose): statuae, Plin. 34, 7, 18, § 39; cf. id. 36, 5, 4, § 26; Suet. Vesp. 23: colosseum se pingi Nero jussit, Plin. 35, 7, 33, § 51.

colossicus.full: cŏlossĭcus, a, um, adj., = κολοσσικός, colossal, gigantic: Apollo, Vitr. 10, 6: signum colossicon, Plin. 34, 8, 19, § 54.— Comp. Gr. colossicoteros, -a, acc. -an, Vitr. 3, 5, 9, p. 98 Bip., and id. 10, 2, 4, p. 292 id. (prob. to be written with Greek letters).
colossicus.short: cŏlossĭcus, a, um, adj., = κολοσσικός, colossal, gigantic: Apollo, Vitr.

colossus.full: cŏlossus, i, m., = κολοσσός, a gigantic statue, a colossus, Plin. 35, 11, 40, § 128; Suet. Ner. 31; Stat. S. 1, 3, 51.—In partic., the celebrated Colossus at Rhodes; it was dedicated to the sun, and was 70 ells high, Plin. 34, 7, 18, § 41; Suet. Vesp. 18; Paul. ex Fest. p. 58, 2 Müll.
colossus.short: cŏlossus, i, m., = κολοσσός, a gigantic statue, a colossus, Plin.

colostra.full: cŏlostra (cŏlustra), ae, f. (cŏlo-stra, ōrum, n., Mart. 13, 38, 2; in sing.: cŏlostrum, Mart. l. l.; Serv. ad Verg. E. 2, 22), the first milk after delivery, the biestings, Plin. 28, 9, 33, § 123; 11, 41, 96, § 236; Col. 7, 3, 17; Pall. Nov. 13, 1.—As a dainty dish, Mart. l. l.—As a term of endearment, Plaut. Poen. 1, 2, 154; 1, 2, 177; Laber. ap. Non. p. 84, 13.

colostratio.full: cŏlostrātĭo, ōnis, f. colostrum, a disease of the young caused by the first milk of the mother, Plin. 11, 41, 96, § 236.—* cŏlostrāti, ōrum, m., those afflicted with colostratio, Plin. 28, 9, 33, § 123.

colotes1.full: cōlōtes, ae, m., = κωλώτης, a kind of lizard, called also stellio, ascalabotes, and galeotes, Plin. 9, 29, 46, § 87; 29, 4, 28, § 90.
colotes1.short: cōlōtes, ae, m., = κωλώτης, a kind of lizard, called also stellio, ascalabotes, and galeotes, Plin.

colotes2.full: Cōlōtes, ae, m., = Κωλωτής. An Epicurean philosopher of Lampsacus, Cic. Rep. 6, 7, 7; Macr. Somn. Scip. 1, 2.— A painter of Teos, Quint. 2, 13, 13.— A sculptor, Plin. 34, 8, 19, § 87; 35, 8, 34, § 54.

coluber.full: cŏlŭber, bri, m. akin to celer, a serpent, snake (poet.), Verg. G. 2, 320; 3, 418; id. A. 2, 471 (an imitation of Hom. Il. 22, 93: ὡς δὲ δράκων, κ. τ. λ.); Ov. M. 4, 620; 11, 775; Col. 10, 231.— Esp., as an attributive of the hair of Medusa, the Furies, the Hydra, etc., Lucr. 5, 27; Ov. M. 9, 73; 10, 21; Luc. 6, 664; Val. Fl. 6, 175.

colubra.full: cŏlū^bra, ae, f. coluber, a female serpent; and in gen., a serpent, snake, Lucil., Turp., and Varr. ap. Non. p. 201, 22 sq.; Hor. C. 1, 17, 8; id. S. 1, 8, 42; Ov. M. 6, 559; Juv. 5, 103; Cels. 5, 27, 3; Col. 10, 230; Plin. 32, 5, 19, § 53.—As an attributive of the hair of the Furies, Medusa, etc. (v. coluber), Ov. M. 4, 474; 4, 491; 4, 783; Luc. 9, 634.— Hence, prov.: quas tu edes colubras? i. e. art thou frantic? Plaut. Stich. 2, 1, 50 Ritschl N. cr.; and: colubra restem non parit, i.e. like p

colubrifer.full: cŏlubrĭfer, fĕra, fĕrum, adj. coluberfero, serpent-bearing, an epithet of Medusa (cf. coluber and colubra): monstrum, Ov. M. 5, 241: collum, Luc. 9, 677.

colubrimodus.full: cŏlubrĭmŏdus, a, um, adj. coluber-modus, serpent-like: capilli, Coripp. Fragm. 4.

colubrinus.full: cŏlubrīnus, a, um, adj. coluber, like a serpent; trop., cunning, wily (ante- and post-class.): ingenio esse, Plaut. Truc. 4, 3, 6: vis gestūs, Tert. Spect. 18.— Subst.: cŏlubrīna, ae, f., a plant, also called bryonia and dracontea, App. Herb. 14.

colubrosus.full: cŏlubrōsus, a, um, adj. id., serpentine, winding: actus (viae), Tert. adv. Val. 4.

colum1.full: cōlum, i, n. A vessel for straining, a strainer, colander, Cato, R. R. 11, 2; Verg. G. 2, 242; Col. 11, 2, 70; 12, 19, 4; 12, 38, 7; Plin. 36, 23, 52, § 173; App. M. 3, p. 130, 20; Scrib. Comp. 156 al.: colum nivarium, for cooling wine, Mart. 14, 103 inscr.; cf. id. 14, 104; Dig. 34, 2, 2.—* Poet., a bow-net, a net of wicker-work for catching fish, a wear, Aus. Ep. 4, 57; cf. 2. colo.

columba.full: cŏlumba, ae, f. columbus, a dove, pigeon, Cic. Ac. 2, 25, 79; id. Fin. 3, 5, 18; Plaut. As. 3, 3, 103; Varr. R. R. 3, 7; Col. 8, 8; Plin. 10, 34, 52, § 104; Pall. 1, 24; Ov. M. 1, 506; 5, 605; id. Am. 2, 6, 56; Hor. C. 1, 37, 18; 4, 4, 32; id. Epod. 16, 32; as sacred to Venus: Cythereiades, Ov. M. 15, 386; cf. Hyg. Fab. 197.—As a term of endearment, my dove, Plaut. Cas. 1, 1, 50 al.; cf. Vulg. Cant. 2, 10.

columbar.full: cŏlumbar, āris, n. columba, a kind of collar (so called from its similarity to the hole in a dove-cot), Plaut. Rud. 3, 6, 50.

columbarius.full: cŏlumbārĭus, a, um, adj. columba, pertaining to doves; only subst., cŏ-lumbārĭus, ii, m., a dove-keeper, Varr. R. R. 2, 7, 7; 3, 7, 5.— cŏlumbārĭum, ii, n. A dove-cot, pigeon-house, Varr. R. R. 3, 7, 4 sq.; Col. 8, 8, 3; 8, 8, 6; 8, 11, 3; Pall. 1, 24; Plin. 19, 9, 6, § 51; Dig. 10, 2, 8, § 1.— Transf. In archit., the gain or mortise in which rafters or joists lie, Vitr. 4, 2, 4.— A hole near the axle of a water-wheel, Vitr. 10, 9, 2.— An opening in the side of a vessel for the oars to pass thro

columbatim.full: cŏlumbātim, adv. id., after the manner of doves, like doves: da basia, Poët. ap. Anth. Lat. 1, 3, 219.

columbinaceus.full: cŏlumbīnācĕus, a, um, adj. columbinus, pertaining to a dove: pullus, a young dove, Cael. Aur. Acut. 2, 18, 111.

columbinus.full: cŏlumbīnus, a, um columba, pertaining to a dove or pigeon, dove-: pulli, Varr. R. R. 3, 7, 9; * Cic. Fam. 9, 18, 3; so also absol.: cŏlumbīni, ōrum, m., little doves, Mart. 13, 66: ovum, * Hor. S. 2, 4, 56: fimus, Plin. 17, 27, 47, § 259: stercora, id. 35, 6, 27, § 46. — Dove-colored: terra, Plin. 17, 7, 4, § 43: cicer, id. 18, 12, 32, § 124: vitis, id. 14, 3, 4, § 40: saxum, Pall. 1, 10, 3.
columbinus.short: cŏlumbīnus, a, um columba, pertaining to a dove or pigeon, dove-: pulli, Varr.

columbor.full: cŏlumbor, āri, v. dep. id., to bill or kiss like doves, Maecenas ap. Sen. Ep. 114, 5.

columbulatim.full: cŏlumbŭlātim, adv. columbulus, in the manner of little doves, like little doves: labra conserens labris, Matius ap. Gell. 20, 9, 2; cf. columbatim.

columbulus.full: cŏlumbŭlus, i, m., or -a, ae, f. dim. columbus, a little dove, Plin. Ep. 9, 25, 3.
columbulus.short: cŏlumbŭlus, i, m., or -a, ae, f.

columbus.full: cŏlumbus, i, m. κόλυμβος; cf.: calvus, color, a male dove or cock - pigeon (and transf., of male persons), Varr. L. L. 9, § 56; Plaut. Rud. 3, 6, 49; Cat. 29, 9; 68, 125; Hor. Ep. 1, 10, 5, A dove in gen. (very rare), Col. 8, 8, 1; Plin. 10, 9, 11, § 25.

columella1.full: cŏlŭmella (in MSS. often cŏlum-nella), ae, f. dim. columna, columen, a small column, a pillar, Cato, R. R. 20, 1; 22, 2; Cic. Leg. 2, 26, 66; id. Tusc. 5, 23, 65; Caes. B. C. 2, 10.— The foot or pedestal of a catapult, Vitr. 10, 15.— Trop., a pillar, support, prop (cf. columen), Lucil. ap. Don. Ter. Phorm. 2, 1, 57.

columella2.full: Cŏlŭmella, ae, m., a Roman cognomen in the gens Junia; so, M. Junius Moderatus Columella, of Hispania Bœtica, uncle of the following.— L. Junius Moderatus Columella, a well-known writer on husbandry, in the first century of the Christian era. He was of Gades, and a companion of Seneca and Celsus; his writings, De Re Rustica and De Arboribus, are yet extant; v. Schneid. Scriptt. Rei Rust. II. 2 praef.; Col. 7, 2, 4; 7, 10, 185; Plin. 8, 41, 63, § 153; 17, 9, 6, §§ 51 and 52; Pall. 1, 19, 3.
columella2.short: Cŏlŭmella, ae, m., a Roman cognomen in the gens Junia;

columellaris.full: cŏlŭmellāris, e, adj [columella], pillar-formed (rare): dentes, the grinders of horses, Varr. R. R. 2, 7, 2; Plin. 11, 37, 64, § 168; in vulg. Lat. colomelli, acc. to Isid. Orig. 11, 1, 48.
columellaris.short: cŏlŭmellāris, e, adj [columella], pillar-formed (rare): dentes, the grinders of horses, Varr.

columen.full: cŏlŭmen, ĭnis, n., and contr. cul-men, mis, n. root cel- of excello; cf.: celsus, culmus, calamus, collis, lit., that which rises in height, is prominent, projects; hence the point, top, summit, ridge. Form columen, inis, n. (only this form is used by Plautus, v. Ritschl, prol. ad Plaut. p. 65). An elevated object, a pillar, column: ego vitam agam sub altis Phrygiae columinibus, the lofty buildings, or perh. the mountain-heights, Cat. 63, 71 Ellis ad loc.; and of a pillar of fire: Phoebi fax, tr

columis.full: cŏlŭmis, e, adj., unhurt, safe; Gloss. Isid.: colume sanum, and columes salvos. (But, Plaut. Trin. 3, 3, 15, the true reading is incolumem; v. prol. ad Trin. p. 68 Ritschl.)

columna.full: cŏlumna, ae, f. root cel- of excello; v. columen, of which it is orig. a collat. form. A projecting object, a column, pillar, post (very freq.), Vitr. 4, 1, 1 sq.; 3, 3; Varr. R. R. 3, 5, 11: columnae et templa et porticus sustinent, tamen habent non plus utilitatis quam dignitatis, Cic. de Or. 3, 46, 180; Cic. Verr. 2, 1, 51, §§ 133 and 134; Quint. 5, 13, 40: columnae Doricae, Ionicae, Tuscanicae, Corinthiae, Atticae, Plin. 36, 22, 56, § 178 sq.; Vitr. 4, 1, 1 sqq.: Rostrata, a column ornamente

columnar.full: cŏlumnar, āris, n. for columnarium, a stone-quarry, marble-quarry, Inscr. Orell. 4034.

columnaris.full: cŏlumnāris, e, adj. columna, rising in the form of a pillar: lux, a pillar of fire, Prud. Ham. 476 (in imitation of the Heb. , Exod. 13, 21); cf. columnifer.

columnarius.full: cŏlumnārĭus, a, um, adj. columna, of or pertaining to a column; only subst., * cŏlumnārĭus, ii, m., one who was condemned at the Columna Maenia (v. columna, A.); therefore a criminal or debtor, Cael. ap. Cic. Fam. 8, 9, 4.— cŏlum-nārĭum, ii, n., a tribute for the pillars of a house, a pillar-tax, Cic. Att. 13, 6, 1; Caes. B. C. 3, 32; cf. columnar.

columnatio.full: cŏlumnātĭo, ōnis, f. id., a supporting by pillars: scaenae, App. Flor. 18, p. 359, 3.

columnatus.full: cŏlumnātus, a, um, adj. id., supported by posts or pillars (perh. only in the foll. exs.): tholus, Varr. R. R. 3, 5, 12: diversoria, Ambros. de Cain et Abel, 1, 5, 19: pons, Ampel. Lib. Mem. 8, 3.—Humorously: os, i. e. supported upon the hand, Plaut. Mil. 2, 2, 57; cf. id. ib. 2, 2, 54.

columnifer.full: cŏlumnĭfer, fĕra, fĕrum, adj. columna-fero, column-bearing: radius, a pillar of fire, Prud. Cath. 9, 51; cf. columnaris.

colurnus.full: cŏlurnus, a, um, adj. transp. for corulnus, from corulus = corylus, made of the hazel-bush: verna, Verg. G. 2, 396 Serv.; cf. Prisc. p. 595 P.: hastilia, Paul. ex Fest. p. 37, 7 Müll.

colurus.full: cŏlūrus, a, um, adj., = κόλουρος, mutilated; hence, In astron.: coluri circuli, = κόλουροι, the colures, two circles passing through the equinoctial and solstitial points, and cutting each other at right angles at the poles, Macr. Somn. Scip. 1, 15. — In metre: metrum, a syllable too short, Plotius, Metr. p. 2649 P.
colurus.short: cŏlūrus, a, um, adj., = κόλουρος, mutilated;

colus.full: cŏlus (i and), ūs (cf. Prisc. pp. 654 and 719 P.; Rudd. 1, p. 166, n. 100), f. (m., Cat. 64, 311; Prop. 4, 1, 72; 4, 9, 48) [root prob. kar-, to be bent or round; cf.: corona, curvus, collum], a distaff; sing. nom. colus, Tib. 2, 1, 63; Ov. M. 4, 229; Plin. 8, 48, 74, § 194; Claud. IV. Cons. Hon. 594; gen. colus, Val. Fl. 2, 148; acc. colum, * Cat. 64, 312; Ov. H. 9, 116; abl. colo, Tib. 1, 3, 86; Prop. 4 (5), 1, 72; Verg. A. 8, 409 (quoted by Prisc. p. 719 P.); Ov. Am. 2, 6, 46; id. A. A. 1, 70

colutea.full: cŏlūtĕa, ōrum, n., = κολουτέα, ἡ, a pod-like kind of fruit, Plaut. Pers. 1, 3, 7 dub. (Ritschl, colyphia).
colutea.short: cŏlūtĕa, ōrum, n., = κολουτέα, ἡ, a pod-like kind of fruit, Plaut.

coluthia.full: colūthĭa, ōrum, n., a kind of snail of a dark color, Plin. 37, 7, 27, § 84; 32, 11, 53, § 147.
coluthia.short: colūthĭa, ōrum, n., a kind of snail of a dark color, Plin.

colymbas.full: cŏlymbăs, ădis, f., = κολυμβάς (swimming; hence): olivae, prepared or put in brine, Col. 12, 47, 8; Plin. 15, 3, 4, § 16; 23, 3, 36, § 73; Pall. Nov. 22, 1.

colymbus.full: cŏlymbus, i, m., = κόλυμβος, a swimming-bath, Lampr. Elag. 23; Prud. στέφ. 12, 36.
colymbus.short: cŏlymbus, i, m., = κόλυμβος, a swimming-bath, Lampr.

colyphia.full: cōlȳphĭa (-līphĭa), ōrum, n., = τὰ κωλύφια, choice bits of meat, loin-pieces: collyrae facite ut madeant et Colyphia, Plaut. Pers. 1, 3, 13 Ritschl: comedunt colyphia paucae, Juv. 2, 53 Jan.—Form coliphia, Mart. 7, 67, 12; cf. Schneid. ad Veg. 6, 12, p. 105.
colyphia.short: cōlȳphĭa (-līphĭa), ōrum, n., = τὰ κωλύφια, choice bits of meat, loin-pieces: collyrae facite ut madeant et Colyphia, Plaut.

colyx.full: cŏlyx, ўcos, f., a cavern where natron is distilling, Plin. 31, 10, 46, § 113.
colyx.short: cŏlyx, ўcos, f., a cavern where natron is distilling, Plin.

coma.full: cŏma, ae, f., = κόμη, the hair of the head (hence barba comaeque, Ov. M. 7, 288), considered as an ornament for the head: comae dicuntur capilli cum aliquā curā compositi, Paul. ex Fest. p. 63, 13 Müll. (class., esp. in poetry and post-Aug. prose; very rare in Cic.).—With adj.: unguentis effluens calamistrata coma, Cic. Sest. 8, 18: madens, id. post Red. in Sen. 6, 13: fulva, ξανθή, Prop. 2, 2, 5: flava, Hor. C. 1, 5, 4; Tib. 1, 5, 44: myrtea, id. 3, 4, 28: longa, Hor. Epod. 11, 28: nitidae, Pro
coma.short: cŏma, ae, f., = κόμη, the hair of the head (hence barba comaeque, Ov.

comacum.full: comacum (cama-), i, n., a kind of cinnamon found in Syria, Plin. 12, 28, 63, § 135; 13, 2, 2, § 18; 1, ind. lib. 12, 63.
comacum.short: comacum (cama-), i, n., a kind of cinnamon found in Syria, Plin.

comana.full: Cŏmāna, ōrum, n., = Κόμανα. A town in Cappadocia, on the Sarus, now El Bostan, Plin. 6, 3, 3, § 8; Auct. B. Alex. 66; Just. Nov 31, 2.—Hence, Cŏmānenses, its inhabitants, Cod. Just. 11, 47, 10.— A town in Pontus, on the Iris, now Gumenek, near Tokat, Plin. 6, 3, 4, § 10; Auct. B. Alex. 34; 35; Just. Nov. 31, 1.

comarchus.full: cōmarchus, i, m., = κώμαρχος, a chief or governor of a village, a burgomaster, Plaut. Curc. 2, 3, 7.
comarchus.short: cōmarchus, i, m., = κώμαρχος, a chief or governor of a village, a burgomaster, Plaut.

comaron.full: cŏmăron, i, n., = κόμαρον. The fruit of the arbute-tree, Plin. 15, 24, 28, § 99. — A plant, also called fragum, App. Herb. 37.

comatorius.full: cŏmātōrĭus, a, um, adj. coma, of or pertaining to the hair; acus, a hair-pin, Petr. 21, 1.

comatulus.full: cŏmātŭlus, a, um, adj. dim. [comatus], having hair neatly or luxuriously curled (post-Aug.): pueri, Hier. Ep. 66, n. 8; so id. ib. 54, n. 13.

combe.full: Combē, ēs, f., the mother of the Curetes, Ov. M. 7, 383.
combe.short: Combē, ēs, f., the mother of the Curetes, Ov.

combibo1.full: com-bĭbo (conb-), bĭbi, 3, v. n. and a. Neutr., to drink with any one as a companion (very rare): aeque combibendi et convivandi peritissimus, Sen. Ep. 123, 15.— Act., to drink completely up, to absorb, to imbibe (the most common signif., rare before the Aug. per., in Cic. only once trop.). Prop.: combibunt guttura sucos, Ov. M. 13, 944; 7, 287: atrum venenum corpo re, * Hor. C. 1, 37, 28: ore lacrimas alicujus, Ov. A. A. 2, 326: lacrimas meas, to repress, conceal, id. H. 11, 54, Sen. Ep. 49, 1.

combibo2.full: combĭbo (conb-), ōnis, m. 1. combibo, a pot-companion, perh. only Lucil. ap. Non. p. 38, 13, and Cic. Fam. 9, 25, 2.

combinatio.full: combīnātĭo, ōnis, f. combino, a joining two by two, ζεῦξις κατὰ δύο, Gloss. Gr. Lat.

combino.full: com-bīno (conb-), no perf., ātum, 1, v. a. bini, to unite, combine (late Lat.): combinat ζευγνὐει, συνάπτει, Gloss. Lat.; ζευγίζω combino, Gloss. Gr. Lat.; part. perf. combinatus, Aug. Conf. 8, 6; Sid. Ep. 9, 8.

combretum.full: combrētum, i, n., a kind of rush, perh. Juncus maximus, Linn.; Plin. 21, 6, 16, § 30; 21, 19, 77, § 133.
combretum.short: combrētum, i, n., a kind of rush, perh.

combullio.full: com-bullĭo (conb-), īre, v. a., to boil fully, Apic. 8, 8, § 397.

comburo.full: com-būro (conb-), ussi, ustum, ĕre, v. a. root bur-, pur-; cf. burrus, Gr. πυρρός, pruna, Gr. πίμπρημι, and Lat. bustum, to burn up, consume (class.). Prop.: quae potuere Nec cum capta capi, nec cum combusta cremari, Enn. ap. Macr. S. 6, 1 (Ann. v. 360 Vahl.): fumo comburi nihil potest, Plaut. Curc. 1, 1, 54: flamma comburens impete magno, Lucr. 6, 153: is ejus (solis) tactus est, ut saepe comburat, Cic. N. D. 2, 15, 40: aedis, Plaut. Aul. 2, 6, 12: frumentum omne, Caes. B. G. 1, 5: naves, id. B

combustio.full: combustĭo, ōnis, f. comburo, a burning, consuming, Firm. Math. 4, 12.

combustum.full: combustum, i, n., v comburo, I. B.
combustum.short: combustum, i, n., v comburo, I.

combustura.full: combustūra, ae, f [comburo], a burning (post-class.), Apic. 4, 4, § 179; Vulg. Lev. 13, 28; Macer de Rosa, 21.
combustura.short: combustūra, ae, f [comburo], a burning (post-class.), Apic.

combustus.full: combustus, a, um, Part., from comburo.
combustus.short: combustus, a, um, Part., from comburo.

come1.full: cŏmē, ēs, f., = κόμη, a plant, also called tragopogon, prob Tragopogon crocifolius, Linn., crocus leaved goat's- beard, Plin. 27, 13, 117, § 142.
come1.short: cŏmē, ēs, f., = κόμη, a plant, also called tragopogon, prob Tragopogon crocifolius, Linn., crocus leaved goat's- beard, Plin.

come2.full: Cōmē, ēs, f., = Κώμη (a village). Come Hiera, a town in Caria, with a temple and an oracle of Apollo, Liv. 38, 12, 9. — Xylina Come, a small town in Pisidia, Liv 38, 15, 7.— Acoridos Come, a small town in Phrygia, Liv 38, 15, 12 Weissenb. ad loc.

comedo1.full: cŏm-ĕdo, ēdi, ēsum (comessum, Prol. ad Plaut. p 102 Ritschl), or estum, 3, v. a. (comesus, the more usual form, Cato, R. R. 58; Varr R. R. 1, 2, 11; Plaut. Trin. 2, 4, 5, Juv 1, 34; Valgius ap. Diom. p. 382 P—Hence, comessurus, Plaut. Ps. 4, 7, 25: comestus, Cato, R. R 50; Cic. Clu. 62, 173, acc. to Prisc. p. 893; and Val. Max. 9, 12, ext. 6, and Didius ap. Diom. l. l.—Contr forms: comes, Plaut. Most. 1, 1, 11: comest, id. ib. 3, 1, 26; id. Trin. 2, 1, 20, id. Truc. 2, 7, 36; Lucil, Titin., Afra

comedo2.full: cŏmĕdo, ōnis (cŏmĕdus, i, Paul. ex Fest. p. 58, 6 Müll.; cf. Lachm. ad Lucr. p. 139), m. 1. comedo, a glutton, gormandizer, Lucil. ap. Non. p. 11, 9; Varr. ib. p. 93, 21; cf. Paul. l. l.

comes.full: cŏm-ĕs, ĭtis, comm. con and 1. eo (lit. one who goes with another), a companion, an associate, comrade, partaker, sharer, partner, etc. (whether male or female; class. and freq.). In gen. Masc.: age, age, argentum numera, ne comites morer, Plaut. Ep. 5, 1, 25: confugere domum sine comite, Ter. Hec. 5, 3, 25: comes meus fuit, et omnium itinerum meorum socius, Cic. Fam. 13, 71: erat comes ejus Rubrius, Cic. Verr. 2, 1, 25, § 64: cui tu me comitem putas esse, id. Att. 8, 7, 1: ibimus, o socii comit

comesor.full: cŏmēsor (cŏmestor, Gloss. Philox.), ōris, m. 1. comedo, an eater, a gourmand, Tert. adv. Marc. 1, 1; Dig. 21, 1, 18.

comestibilis.full: cŏmestĭbĭlis, e, adj. id., eatable, Isid. Orig. 17, 7, 9.

comestio.full: cŏmestĭo, ōnis, f. id., a consuming, Isid. Orig. 20, 2, 2; Anthol. Lat. 3, 90, 7.

comestus.full: cŏmestus, a, um, v. comedo init.

comesus1.full: cŏmēsus, a, um, v. comedo init.

comesus2.full: cŏmēsus, ūs, m. 1. comedo, an eating, consuming, Isid. Orig. 20, 1, 1.

cometes1.full: cŏmētes, ae, m. (Lat. access. form nom. cometa, Prud. Cath. 12, 21; acc. cometam, Sen. Oct. 232; cometem, Serv. ad Verg. A. 10, 272; Schol. Juv. 6, 407; abl. cometā, Manil. 1, 824), = κομήτης, a comet, Plin. 2, 25, 22, § 89 sq.; Sen. Q. N. 7, 1, 5 et lib. 7 passim; Serv. ad Verg. A. 10, 272; Cic. N. D. 2, 5, 14; id. Div. 1, 11, 18; Verg. G. 1, 488; id. A. 10, 272; Sil. 8, 638; Luc. 1, 529 al.—In apposition with sidus, Tac. A. 14, 22; 15, 47; with stella, Just. 37, 2, 2.

cometes2.full: Cŏmētes, ae, m., a Greek proper name. One of the Lapithœ, Ov. M. 12, 284.— Father of Asterion, Val. Fl. 1, 356.
cometes2.short: Cŏmētes, ae, m., a Greek proper name.

comicus.full: cōmĭcus, a, um, adj., = κωμικός, of or pertaining to comedy, comic: poëta, Cic. Or. 20, 67: artificium, id. Rosc. Com. 10, 18: levitates, id. N. D. 3, 29, 72: res, the material of comedy, Hor. A. P. 89: scaenae, Vitr. 5, 8: gestus, Quint. 11, 3, 125: senarius, id. 9, 4, 140: ad morem, id. 1, 8, 3: virtus (Terentii), C. Caes. ap. Suet. Vit. Ter. 5: persona, Quint. 11, 3, 79; Plin. 25, 11, 88, § 137: auctores, Quint. 2, 10, 13.— Esp., represented in comedy: ut comici servi solent, Plaut. Capt. 4,
comicus.short: cōmĭcus, a, um, adj., = κωμικός, of or pertaining to comedy, comic: poëta, Cic.

cominium.full: Cōmĭnĭum, ĭi, n., a town of Samnium, Liv. 10, 39, 5 sq., and id. 10, 43, 1 sq.
cominium.short: Cōmĭnĭum, ĭi, n., a town of Samnium, Liv.

cominius1.full: Cominius, ii, m., a Roman proper name, Cic. Clu. 36, 99; id. Brut 78, 271; Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 10, § 24.
cominius1.short: Cominius, ii, m., a Roman proper name, Cic.

comis.full: cōmis, e, adj. etym. dub.; cf. concinnus, courteous, affable, kind, obliging, friendly, loving (class. in prose and poetry; on account of similarity of meaning, in MSS. very freq. interchanged with communis; hence the readings vary in the best edd.; cf. Liv. 25, 12, 9 Drak.; Suet. 2, p. 241 Wolf; Cic. Fin. 2, 25, 80 Madv.). Of persons: comes, benigni, faciles, suaves homines esse dicuntur qui erranti comiter monstrant viam (Enn.; cf. under adv.), Cic. Balb. 16, 36: illum negat et bonum virum et

comissabundus.full: cōmissābundus (cōmess-), a, um, adj. comissor, holding a riotous procession, revelling, banqueting, carousing: comissabundus temulento agmine per Indiam incessit (Alexander Magnus; in regard to his imitation of the procession in honor of Bacchus through Asia; v.
