Comp. 19.— Trop., confusion, disquiet, perturbation of mind (rare): conturbatio metus excutiens cogitata, a fear that drives away all thought, Cic. Tusc. 4, 8, 19; id. Top. 12, 52: mentis, id. Tusc. 4, 13, 30.

conturbator.full: conturbātor, ōris, m. id., that brings disorder or ruin (cf. conturbo, II.), poet. for ruinous, expensive, or costly (very rare): aper, Mart. 7, 27, 10: macellus, id. 10, 96, 9.

conturbatus.full: conturbātus, a, um, Part. and P. a., from conturbo.

conturbo.full: con-turbo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a., to throw into disorder or confusion, to confuse, derange, disorder, confound (rare, but class. in prose and poetry; most freq. in Lucr. and Cic.; not in Verg., Hor., or Quint.). In gen. Lit.: posituras principiorum corporis atque animi, Lucr. 4, 943; cf. id. 4, 958; 3, 483 al.: ordines Romanorum (militum), Sall. J. 50, 4; cf. id. ib. 98, 4: equites tormentis, Curt. 7, 2, 4: rempublicam, Sall. C. 37, 10; 48, 8; cf. rem, id. J. 79, 7: annus neglegentiā conturbatus a

conturmalis.full: con-turmālis, is, m., one of the same squadron (turma) (late Lat.), Amm. 16, 12, 45 al.— Transf.: omnis operae, a companion, Amm. 17, 1, 2.
conturmalis.short: con-turmālis, is, m., one of the same squadron (turma) (late Lat.), Amm.

conturmo.full: con-turmo, āre, v. a., to arrange in squadrons (turmae). se, Amm. 16, 12, 37.

contus.full: contus, i, m., = κοντός, a pole, pike (perh. not ante-Aug.), as an implement of a boat or ship, Verg. A. 5, 208; 6, 302; Tac. A. 14, 5; Suet. Calig. 32; as a weapon, Verg. A. 9, 510; Tac. A. 6, 35; id. H. 1, 44.—Prov.: non contis et remulco ferri, ut aiunt, sed velificatione plenā, Amm. 18, 5, 6: pedalis, i. q. membrum virile, Auct. Priap. 10, 3.
contus.short: contus, i, m., = κοντός, a pole, pike (perh.

contusio.full: contūsĭo, ōnis, f. contundo, a crushing, breaking, battering, bruising (rare). In gen.: olivae, Col. 12, 47, 3: falcis hebetioris, Plin. 17, 24, 37, § 227.— In medic. language, a bruise, contusion, Scrib. Comp. 101; 165 et saep.

contusum.full: contūsum, i, n., v. contundo, I. B.

contusus.full: contūsus, a, um, Part., from contundo.
contusus.short: contūsus, a, um, Part., from contundo.

contutor1.full: con-tūtor, ōris, m., a joint-guardian (jurid. Lat.), Dig. 27, 3, 9; 3, 5, 29.

contutor2.full: con-tūtor, ātus sum, 1, v. dep., to place in safety (late Lat.), Vulg. 2 Macc. 1, 19.

conubialis.full: cōnūbĭālis (less correctly connū-bĭālis; in the poets gen. to be read as four syll.; cf. conubium; only in Claud. Ep. 2, 18, cōnŭbiālis), e, adj. conubium, pertaining to wedlock, connubial, conjugal (poet.; perh. first used by Ov.): jura, Ov. H. 6, 41: vincla, Stat. Th. 5, 112: carmen, Claud. IV. Cons. Hon. 651: vectigal, id. Epist. 2, 18: foedus, Salv. Gub. 7, p. 244.—* Adv.: cō-nūbĭālĭter, in a conjugal manner, connubially: procum allegaret, Mart. Cap. 6, § 576.

conubium.full: cōnūbĭum (less correctly connū-bĭum; cf. Rib. prol. Verg. p. 393), ii (m the poets often trisyl., thus: conubio, Verg. A. 1, 73; 4, 126; 7, 253; Ov. M. 6, 428: conubia, Lucr. 3, 777: conubiis, Verg. A. 3, 136; 4, 168; v. Wagn. and Forbig. ad Verg. A. 1, 73; and cf. conubialis), n. nubo, marriage, wedlock (considered as a civil institution; while conjugium had regard to the physical union, cf. Dict. of. Antiq.). Prop. (very freq. in prose and poetry), Cic. de Or. 1, 9, 37; id. Off. 1, 17, 54; Sal

conula.full: cōnŭla, ae, f., a plant, = polion, App. Herb. 57.
conula.short: cōnŭla, ae, f., a plant, = polion, App.

conus.full: cōnus, i, m., = κῶνος, a cone. In gen., Lucr. 4, 430 and 432; Cic. N. D. 1, 10, 24; 2, 18, 47 al.— Esp., of conical bodies, The apex of a helmet, Verg. A. 3, 468; Ov. M. 3, 108; Plin. 10, 1, 1, § 2; cf. Isid. Orig. 18, 14, 2.— The cone of the cypress, Col. 6, 7, 2.— A kind of sundial, Vitr. 9, 8, 1.
conus.short: cōnus, i, m., = κῶνος, a cone.

convador.full: con-vādor, ātus, 1, v. dep., to bind one to appear in court by giving surely; facete: ubi tu es, qui me convadatus Veneriis vadimoniis, cited me to the court of Venus, i. e. made an appointment with me, Plaut. Curc. 1, 3, 5.

convalescens.full: convălescens, ntis, P. a. and subst., v. convalesco, I. fin.

convalescentia.full: convălescentĭa, ae, f. convalesco, convalescence, a regaining of health, Symm. Ep. 3, 11 fin.

convalesco.full: con-vălesco, lŭi, 3, v. inch. n., to recover from a disease, to regain health, to grow strong, gain strength, etc. (very freq., and class.). Lit., with ex, de, ab, or absol.: ex morbo, Cic. Fat. 12, 28 sq.; so id. Fam. 13, 29, 4; Suet. Aug. 59; cf.: de vulnere, Ov. H. 21, 211: nec omnes, qui curari se passi sunt, continuo etiam convalescant, Cic. Tusc. 3, 3, 5: eum sustulere (defatigatum vulneribus), isque convaluit, Cat. ap. Gell. 3, 7, 19: ne aegri quidem quia non omnes convalescunt, idcirco a

convallatio.full: convallātĭo, ōnis, f. convallo, an intrenchment, Tert. adv. Jud. 8.

convallis.full: con-vallis, is (abl. regularly convalle, e. g. Caes. B. G. 3, 20 fin.; Liv. 1, 12, 10; Verg. G. 2, 186; id. A. 6, 679 al.: convalli, Varr. R. R. 1, 12, 3; gen. plur. convallium, Plin. 36, 15, 23, § 100). f. (plur. post-class. access. form convallia, ium, n., sc. loca, Prud. στεφ. 10, 331 al.), a valley enclosed on all sides; cf. Paul. ex Fest. p. 42, 6 Müll.; Varr. L. L. 5, § 20 ib. (freq. and class. in prose and poetry); Lucr. 5, 1374; Cic. Agr. 2, 35, 96; Caes. B. G. 5, 32; Liv. 1, 38, 6; Verg

convallo.full: con-vallo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a.; lit., to surround with an intrenchment; hence, in gen., to surround, encircle (late Lat.): terras omnes Oceani ambitu, Gell. 12, 13, 20. —Trop., Tert. Carm. de Judicio Dom. 6.

convario.full: con-vărĭo, āre, v. a. and n. (post-class.). Act., to variegate: cutim maculationibus, App. Mag. p. 306, 14.— Neutr., to be different, to vary, Cael. Aur. Tard. 1, 1, 7.

convaso.full: con-vāso, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. vasa, to pack vessels or implements together, to pack up (the figure taken from milit. lang.; anteand post-class. and very rare). Lit.: aliquid convasassem, * Ter. Phorm. 1, 4, 13; so Sid. Ep. 7, 2.— Trop.: acclamationes, to pile up, Sid. Ep. 1, 9 fin.

convectio.full: convectĭo, ōnis, f. conveho, a carrying or bringing together: annonae, Amm. 14, 10, 4.

convecto.full: convecto, āre, v. freq. a. id., to bear, carry, or bring together in abundance (very rare): recentes praedas, Verg. A. 7, 749; cf. praedam, id. ib. 4, 405: ligones, dolabras, etc., e proximis agris, Tac. H. 3, 27: paleas, ligna, Cod. Th. 7, 4, 9; 13, 5, 10.

convector1.full: convector, ōris, m. conveho, one who carries or brings together; hence, Convector, the deity who presided over the gathering in of grain, Fab. Pict. ap. Serv. ad Verg. G. 1, 21.

convector2.full: con-vector, ōris, m., he who goes with one (on board ship, etc.), a fellow-passenger (very rare), * Cic. Att. 10, 17, 1; App. M. 1, p. 109.
convector2.short: con-vector, ōris, m., he who goes with one (on board ship, etc.), a fellow-passenger (very rare), * Cic.

conveho.full: con-vĕho, vexi, vectum, 3, v. a., to carry, bear, or bring together (in good prose). In gen.: frumentum ex finitimis regionibus in urbem, Caes. B. C. 1, 34 fin.; cf. Liv. 25, 13, 2; 24, 39, 11 al.: lintribus in eam insulam materiem, calcem, caementa, arma, * Cic. Mil. 27, 74; cf. Liv. 4, 60, 6: tus collectum Sabota camelis, Plin. 12, 14, 32, § 63: flores (apes), id. 11, 17, 18, § 58: cibos, id. 11, 18, 20, § 64.—Absol.: undique convehunt apes, Plin. 11, 30, 36, § 109: frumentum habere convectum,

convello.full: con-vello, velli (convulsi, Sen. Q. N. 2, 6, 4), vulsum (volsum), 3, v. a. To draw violently hither and thither something that is firm or quiet (esp. a tree, house, and the like); hence, to tear up, wrest from its position, to tear loose or away, to separate from, pull or pluck up (freq. and class.). Lit. In gen. Without designation of place from which, etc.: cum praecides caveto ne librum convellas, Cato, R. R. 40, 2: saxa turris hostium, quibus fundamenta continebantur, Caes. B. C. 2, 11; cf.

convelo.full: con-vēlo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a., to veil, to cover over (very rare). Lit.: caput, Gell. 19, 9, 10.— Trop.: ἐπαγωγήν multis argumentis, Gell. 7, 3, 44.

convena.full: convĕna, ae, adj. comm. [convenio], coming together, meeting: ego, qui amantis unā inter se facerem convenas, Plaut. Mil. 2, 1, 61: aquae, Amm. 23, 3, 8; 23, 6, 57; Sol. 37: serpentes, id. 47: convenā undique multitudine, Amm. 15, 5, 25.—Hence, subst. plur.: convĕnae, ārum, comm., a multitude collected together, assembled strangers, refugees, tramps, etc.: eodem convenae complures ex agro accessitavere, Cato ap. Gell. 18, 12, 7: Romulus pastores et convenas congregasse videtur, Cic. de Or. 1, 9,

conveniens.full: convĕnĭens, entis, Part. and P. a., from convenio.

convenienter.full: convĕnĭenter, adv., v. convenio, P. a. fin.

convenientia.full: convĕnĭentĭa, ae, f. convenio, II. A. 2., a meeting together, agreement, accord, harmony, symmetry, conformity, suitableness, fitness (a Ciceronian philosoph. word). With gen.: convenientia naturae cum extis, Cic. Div. 2, 15, 34; cf.: convenientia et conjunctio naturae, quam vocant συμπάθειαν, id. ib. 2, 60, 124; and: convenientia conservatioque naturae, id. Off. 1, 28, 100: partium (with pulchritudo, venustas), id. ib. 1, 4, 14: temporum (in cursibus stellarum, with constantia), id. N. D. 2, 21

convenio.full: con-vĕnĭo, vēni, ventum, 4 (fut. convenibo, Plaut. Cas. 3, 2, 18), v. n. and a. To come together, meet together, assemble (class. and freq.). In gen.: milites, qui ex provinciā convenerant, Caes. B. G. 1, 8: omnes ... eo convenerant, id. ib. 3, 16: totius fere Galliae legati ad Caesarem gratulatum convenerunt, id. ib. 1, 30: quanto multitudo hominum ad hoc judicium, Cic. Rosc. Am. 5, 11: amici privatique hospites ad eum defendendum convenerunt, Nep. Timoth. 4, 2: ad clamorem hominum, Caes. B. G.

conventicius.full: conventīcĭus or -tītĭus, a, um, adj. convenio, pertaining to coming together, or intercourse. * Adj.: patres conventicii, coming from various quarters, Plaut. Cist. 1, 1, 42.—* Subst.: conventī-cĭum, ii, n. (sc. aes), = τὸ ἐκκλησιαστικόν, money paid to the poorer Greek citizens for attendance in the assemblies of the people, Cic. Rep. 3, 35, 48.

conventiculum.full: conventĭcŭlum, i, n. dim. conventus (rare). An assembly, meeting, association: conventicula hominum, quae postea civitates nominatae sunt, Cic. Sest. 42, 91: plebei urbanae, id. Dom. 28, 74.— A place of assembly, Tac. A. 14, 15: ritus Christiani, Amm. 15, 5, 31; 27, 3, 13; Arn. 4, 152; Lact. 5, 11, 10.

conventio.full: conventĭo, ōnis, f. convenio, a meeting, assembling. In gen. (very rare), Cod. Th. 8, 8, 3; 16, 2, 14 al.— Esp. = contio, an assembly, meeting (very rare), Varr. L. L. 6, § 87 sq. Müll.; cf. Paul. ex Fest. p. 113, 10: in conventione = in contione.— Agreement, covenant, convention, compact, Dig. 2, 14, 1 sq.; Liv. 27, 30, 12; Sen. Ira, 3, 26, 4; Plin. Ep. 5, 1, 2; Tac. H. 3, 70 al.— In manum conventio, of a woman, the coming into the hands (manus) of her husband by marriage, Gai Inst. 3, 24; Ulp.

conventionalis.full: conventĭōnālis, e, adj. conventio, II. B., of or pertaining to an agreement or compact, conventional: stipulationes, Dig. 45, 1, 5, § 52.

conventiuncula.full: conventĭuncŭla, ae, f. dim. conventio, I., a small assembly, Aug. Ep. 56 fin.

convento.full: convento, āvi, 1, v. freq. n. [convenio], to meet often, Sol. 27, § 7.

conventum.full: conventum, i, n., v. convenio, P. a., 2.

conventus1.full: conventus, a, um, Part. of convenio.

conventus2.full: conventus, ūs (CONVENTVVS, C. I. L. II. p. 2416), m. convenio. (Acc. to convenio, I.) A meeting; in concr., an assembly (syn: coetus, contio, corona). Of persons. In gen. (for social intercourse, counsel, religious celebration, discussion, instruction. etc.; very freq., and class. in sing. and plur.): comitum, Ter. Hec. prol. alt. 27: celeberrimo virorum mulierumque conventu, Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 48, § 107; 2, 1, 52, § 137: nocturnus, id. Cai. 2, 6, 13: complures minime digni elegantis conventus aur

convenusto.full: con-vĕnusto, āre, v. a., to ornament, adorn (late Lat.): ecclesiam cultu, Sid. Ep. 7, 12: aliquid oratione, id. ib. 8, 6: Aurora primo convenustans habitu fenestras, Mart. Cap. poët. 2, § 219 al.

converbero.full: con-verbĕro, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a., to strike severely, to beat, bruise (post-Aug.). Lit.: faciem, Plin. 13, 22, 43, § 126: os, Curt. 7, 2, 5.— Trop.: vitia, to chastise, Sen. Ep. 121, 4; cf. id. Ira, 3, 20, 1.

convergo.full: con-vergo, ĕre, 3, v. n., to incline together (late Lat.): punctus quo cuncta convergunt, Isid. Orig. 3, 12, 1.

converritor.full: converrĭtor, ōris, m. converro, one who sweeps together, Cat. ap. App. Mag. p. 277, 13.

converro.full: con-verro (or -vorro), verri, versum, 3, v. a., to sweep or brush together, to sweep, clear away (mostly ante- and post-class.). Lit., Cato, R. R. 143, 2: hoc egomet, tu hoc convorre, Plaut. Stich. 2, 2, 27: capiam scopas atque hoc convorram, id. ib. 2, 2, 51; 2, 2, 64; Publ. Syr. ap. Prisc. p. 900 P.: stabulum, Col. 7, 6, 6: locum, id. 8, 6, 6: limina templorum osculis, Arn. 1, p. 36 al.— Meton.: hereditates omnium, to scrape together, * Cic. Off. 3, 19, 78 (al. convertere). —Humorously: alique

conversatio.full: conversātĭo, ōnis, f. converso (not ante-Aug.). * Frequent use, Sen. Ben. 3, 2, 2; cf. Cod. Th. 11, 21, 1 al.— Frequent abode in a place, Plin. 10, 33, 51, § 100; Dig. 11, 7, 12, § 1.— Intercourse, conversation (so most freq.): licentiosior cum viris, Sen. Exc. Contr. 6, 8: hominum, Vell. 2, 102, 3: multorum, Sen. Ep. 7, 1; Quint. 6, 3, 17; Tac. A. 12, 49; id. Or. 9: inter servos, Quint. 1, 2, 4.

conversator.full: conversātor, a companion, ὁμοδίαιτος, Gloss. Gr. Lat.

conversim.full: conversim, adv. converto, conversely (late Lat.), Mart. Cap. 5, § 491; Firm. Math. 2, 32.

conversio.full: conversĭo, ōnis, f. id., a turning round, revolving, revolution (class.). Lit. In gen.: caeli, Cic. Div. 2, 42, 89; id. Univ. 6 med.; id. Rep. 6, 18, 18: astrorum omnesque motus, id. Tusc. 1, 25, 62; cf. id. N. D. 2, 19, 49: caelestes, id. Leg. 1, 8, 24.—Hence, The periodical return of the seasons, caused by the revolution of the heavenly bodies: mensium annorumque, Cic. Univ. 14 fin.— Esp., in medic. lang., A turning round, inverting: vesicae, Plin. 8, 42, 67, § 166.—In plur.: vulvae, Plin. 24,

conversiuncula.full: conversĭuncŭla, ae, f. conversio, a slight change or alteration (eccl. Lat.), Salv. Ep. 4, p. 320.

converso.full: con-verso, āvi, ātum, 1, v. freq. * Act., to turn round: animus se ipse conversans, * Cic. Univ. 8 med.—More freq., In medial form conversor, ātus, 1 (post-Aug.; a favorite word of Seneca; not in Quint.), To abide, live, or dwell somewhere: in montibus (aquila), Plin. 10, 3, 3, § 6.— To live with, have intercourse with, keep company with: nobiscum, Sen. Ep. 41, 5; 55, 9 sqq.; 99, 21: inter humano sanguine delibutos, Sen. Contr. 1, 2.—Absol., Sen. Ira, 3, 8, 1; id. Ep. 108, 4.—Of animals, Col. 9,

conversus1.full: conversus, a, um, Part. of converro.

conversus2.full: conversus, a, um, Part. of converto.

conversus3.full: conversus, ūs, m. converto, a turning or twisting round, Macr. S. 7, 9, § 4.

convertibilis.full: convertĭbĭlis (convers-), e, adj. id., changeable (post-class.): propositiones, App. Dogm. Plat. 3, p. 33, 1 and 2 (al. conversibilis): deus convertibilis et demutabilis, Prud. Apoth. 344.—Hence, con-vertĭbĭlĭter, adv., changeably (late Lat.), Aug. Music. 5, 13.

converto.full: con-verto (-vorto), ti, sum, 3, v. a. and n. Act., to turn or whirl round, to wheel about, to cause to turn, to turn back, reverse; and with the designation of the terminus in quem, to turn or direct somewhere, to direct to or towards, to move or turn to, etc. (very freq. in all perr. and species of composition). Lit. In gen. With a simple acc.: caelos omnes, Lucr. 2, 1097; cf.: in infimo orbe luna convertitur, Cic. Rep. 6, 17, 17; id. Ac. 2, 39, 123; cf.: minore sonitu quam putaram, orbis hic i

convertor.full: con-vertor or -vortor, ti, acc. to Non. p. 480, dep. collat. form of converto; only in the line: sed fugam in se tamen nemo convortitur, Plaut. Am. 1, 1, 83; but the explanation is not satisfactory, and Fleck. reads: in fugam set tamen nemo convortitur, acc. to converto, I. A.; cf. Neue, Formenl. II. p. 330, and Ussing ad Plaut. 1. 1.

convescor.full: con-vescor, vesci, v. dep., to eat with one (eccl. Lat.), Aug. Ep. 18 al.

convestio.full: con-vestĭo, īvi, ītum, 4 (arch. inf. pass. convestirier, Poët. ap. Cic. Tusc. 1, 28, 69), v. a., to clothe, cover with clothing (rare, and mostly in ante-class. poetry). * Lit.: cruenta corpora, Enn. ap. Macr. S. 6, 2.— Transf.: prata herbis, Poët. ap. Cic. Tusc. l. l.; cf.: Topiarium laudavi: ita omnia convestivit hederā, Cic. Q. Fr. 3, 1, 2, § 5: domum lucis, to surround, id. Dom. 38, 101: omnia suā luce sol, * Lucr. 2, 147.

conveteranus.full: con-vĕtĕrānus, i, m., a fellow-veteran, Cod. Just. 5, 65, 2; Inscr. Orell. 3580.
conveteranus.short: con-vĕtĕrānus, i, m., a fellow-veteran, Cod.

convexio.full: convexĭo, ōnis, f. convexus, a vaulting, convexity, also concavity (post-class.; cf. convexitas): mundi, Gell. 14, 1, 8: rotunditatis solidae, Arn. 4, 129.

convexitas.full: convexĭtas, ātis, f. id., a vaulting, convex roundness, convexity, concavity (postAug.; perh. only in Plin. the elder): circuli, Plin. 18, 25, 57, § 217: mundi, id. 18, 25, 57, § 210: cava in caelo, id. 2, 64, 64, § 160: terrae, id. 18, 29, 69, § 283: insulae, id. 6, 32, 37, § 202.

convexo.full: con-vexo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a., to press or squeeze together (post-class., and perh. only in the foll. exs.): (multitudo) me male miseram convexavit, Soror Appii Caeci in Gell. 10, 6, 2: animal, Veg. Art. Vet. 3, 18, 6: membra, id. ib. 4, 25, 1: ilia cursu nimio, id. ib. 3, 65, 3.

convexus1.full: convexus, a, um, adj. conveho, vaulted, arched, rounded, convex, concave. Prop.: convexum id est ex omni parte declinatum, qualis est natura caeli, quod ex omni parte ad terram versus declinatum est, Paul. ex Fest. p. 58, 18 Müll. (poet., and in post-Aug. prose; not in Lucr., Quint., and Hor.): caelum, Ov. M. 1, 26; cf.: nutans convexo pondere mundus, Verg. E. 4, 50; and, mundus, Plin. 2, 2, 2, § 5; Cic. Arat. ap. N. D. 2, 44, 112 Creuz. N. cr.: foramina terrae, Ov. M. 6, 697: vallis, Plin. 5, 5

convexus2.full: convexus, ūs, m., = περιφέρεια, Gloss. Vet.

convibro.full: con-vī^bro, āvi, 1, v. n. and a. * Neutr., to move one's self rapidly: pedibus, Poët. ap. Fest. p. 206, 11.— Act., to move a thing quickly, set in rapid motion (late Lat.): linguam, App. Flor. 2, n. 12, p. 348, 40; Amm. 17, 7, 15.

convicanus.full: con-vīcānus (convīcānĕus, Cassiod. Hist. Eccl. 1, 11), i, m., one who is of the same village, a fellow-villager, Inscr. Fratr. Arv. p. 436 Marin.; Cod. Th. 11, 24, 6, § 1.

conviciator.full: convīcĭātor (convīt-), ōris, m. convicior, a railer, reviler (very rare), * Cic. Mur. 6, 13; Sen. Ira, 3, 24, 1; Suet. Tib. 11 al.

conviciolum.full: convīcĭŏlum, i, n. dim. convicium, a slight reproach, a taunt, Lampr. Alex. Sev. 28.

convicior.full: convīcĭor (convīt-), ātus, 1, v. dep. id.. to revile, reproach, taunt, rail at (rare; most freq. in Quint.; not in Cic.; cf., however, conviciator). Absol.: cum alius eum salutasset, alius conviciatus esset, * Varr. R. R. 2, 5, 1: ut accusare potius vere quam conviciari videantur, Liv. 42, 41, 3; Quint. 11, 1, 65; 6, 3, 78; * Suet. Tib. 53 al. — With dat.: contra dentientibus inhumane, Quint. 3, 8, 69; 5, 13, 40; Dig. 49, 1, 8; Paul. Sent. 5, 35, 3; Vulg. Ecclus. 8, 22.

convicium.full: con-vīcĭum (less correctly, acc. to Brambach, convītĭum, but preferred by B. and K., and by recent editors of Plaut. and Ter.), ii, n. most prob. kindr. with vox; cf. Dig. 47, 10, 15, § 4; Paul. ex Fest. p. 41, 20, a loud noise, a cry, clamor, outcry (class.). In gen.: ne clamorem hic facias neu convitium, Plaut. Bacch. 4, 8, 33; cf.: erant autem convivia non illo silentio ... sed cum maximo clamore atque convitio, Cic. Verr. 2, 5, 11, § 28: facere, Ter. Ad. 2, 1, 26 Ruhnk.: cantorum, Cic. Sest.

convictio1.full: convictĭo, ōnis, f. convinco, demonstration, proof (eccl. Lat.): rerum, Aug. Trin. 13, 1.

convictio2.full: convictĭo, ōnis, f. convivo, companionship, intercourse, intimacy with one ( = 2. convictus): jucundissima, Cic. Fil. ap. Cic. Fam. 16, 21, 4.— Transf., = convictor: convictiones domesticae, Cic. ad Q. Fr. 1, 1, 4, § 12.

convictor.full: convictor, ōris, m. id., he who lives with one, a table companion, messmate, familiar friend, Cic. Fil. ap. Cic. Fam. 16, 21, 5; Hor. S. 1, 4, 96; 1, 6, 47; Plin. Ep. 2, 6, 4; Sen. Ep. 7, 5; id. Ira, 3, 8, 2; id. Lud. Mort. Claud. 14, 2; Suet. Vit. Hor.

convictus1.full: convictus, a, um, Part., from convinco.
convictus1.short: convictus, a, um, Part., from convinco.

convictus2.full: convictus, ūs, m. convivo, a living together, intimacy, social intercourse. In gen. (syn.: societas, consuetudo): convictus humanus et societas, Cic. Off. 3, 5, 21; Lucceius ap. Cic. Fam. 5, 14, 3; Col. 1, 8, 5; Sen. Helv. 15, 2; id. Ep. 6, 5; Ov. Tr. 1, 8, 29; id. P. 2, 10, 9 al.— In partic., a banquet, feast, entertainment (not anteAug.), Vell. 2, 33, 4; Quint. 6, 3, 27; Plin. 14, 14, 16, § 95; Tac. A. 2, 28; 6, 9; 13, 15; 14, 4; Sen. Tranq. 17, 8; Juv. 11, 4 al.

convinco.full: con-vinco, vīci, victum, 3, v. a., to overcome, conquer; always beyond the circle of milit. lang. With personal objects, to convict of crime or error, refute (very freq. and class.). With simple acc.: quem ego jam hic convincam palam, Plaut. Am. 2, 2, 147: hujus si causa non manifestissimis rebus teneretur, tamen eum mores ipsius ac vita convincerent, Cic. Sull. 25, 71: verum enim invenire volumus, non tamquam adversarium aliquem convincere, id. Fin. 1, 5, 13: Aristonis jam fracta et convicta se

convinctio.full: con-vinctĭo, ōnis, f. vincio, gram. t. t., a connective particle, conjunction: veteres verba modo et nomina et convinctiones tradiderunt ... in convinctionibus complexus eorum esse judicaverunt; quas conjunctiones a plerisque dici scio, sed haec videtur ex συνδέσμῳ magis propria translatio, Quint. 1, 4, 18.

conviolo.full: con-vĭŏlo, āvi, 1, v. a., to violate, desecrate (eccl. Lat.), Prud. Psych. 398 al.

conviresco.full: con-vĭresco, ĕre, v. inch., to grow green, become verdant (late Lat.): litus insertis arboribus, Jul. Val. Rer. Gest. Alex. M. 3, 58.

conviscero.full: con-viscĕro, āre, v. a., to incorporate, unite, Tert. Carn. Chr. 20.

conviso.full: con-vīso, ĕre, v. a. (rare and mostly ante-class.), to consider attentively, look at, examine thoroughly: omnia loca oculis, Lucr. 2, 357: penitus res occultas, id. 1, 146: omnes saucios, Att. ap. Non. p. 398, 4 (Trag. Rel. v. 598 Rib.).—Poet.: omnia loca candida luce (sol et luna), Lucr. 5, 779; so Cic. Arat. 352.

convitio.full: con-vĭtĭo, no perf., ātum, 1, v. a., to attack or injure at the same time (late Lat.): si sternutamento fuerint convitiati (of epileptics), Cael. Aur. Tard. 1, 4, 22.

conviva.full: con-vīva, ae, comm. vivo (lit., one who lives with another; hence), one who feasts with another, a table companion, guest (freq. and class.). Masc., Plaut. Mil. 3, 1, 50; Ter. Eun. 3, 1, 17; id. Heaut. 1, 1, 120; Afran. ap. Non. p. 235, 25; Cic. Tusc. 1, 2, 3; id. Brut. 19, 75; Cat. 44, 10; Prop. 3 (4), 7, 45; Hor. S. 1, 1, 119 et saep.: deorum (Tantalus), id. C. 1, 28, 7.— Fem.: postquam conveni omnes convivas meas, Pompon. ap. Charis. p. 37 P. (Com. Rel. v. 16 Rib.).

convivalis.full: convīvālis (access. form convīvĭā-lis, Curt. 6, 2, 6 Zumpt N. cr.; as var. lect. in Liv. 39, 6, 8, and Macr. S. 2, 1), e, adj. convivium, of or pertaining to a feast, festal, convivial (rare; not ante-Aug.): oblectamenta ludionum, Liv. 39, 6, 8: fabulae, Tac. A. 6, 5: ludi, Curt. 5, 1, 37; 8, 4, 29; 8, 6, 14: sermones, Macr. S. 1, 1: carmen, Prud. Hamart. 317: vestis, Sen. Contr. 4, 25 al.—No comp. or sup.

convivator.full: convīvātor, ōris, m. convivor, he who gives an entertainment, the master of a feast (rare), * Hor. S. 2, 8, 73; Liv. 35, 49, 6; Sen. Ira, 3, 37, 3.

convivifico.full: convīvĭfĭco, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a., to quicken together, Vulg. Eph. 2, 5; id. Col. 2, 13.

convivium.full: con-vīvĭum, ii, n. vivo; lit., a living together; hence, a meal in company, a social feast, entertainment, banquet (freq. and class.): bene majores nostri accubitionem epularem amicorum, quia vitae conjunctionem haberet, convivium nominarunt, melius quam Graeci, qui hoc idem tum compotationem tum concenationem vocant, Cic. Sen. 13, 45: domi agitare, Plaut. Mil. 2, 2, 10: strategum te facio huic convivio, id. Stich. 5, 4, 20: sublatum'st convivium, id. Men. 3, 1, 19: Rhodium tangere in convivio,

convivo1.full: con-vīvo, vixi, 3, v. n. (post-Aug.). To live with: avaro, Sen. Ep. 104, 20: gladiatoribus, Lampr. Comm. 2: MECVM, Inscr. Marm. Pisaur. p. 42, n. 94; cf. Inscr. Marini Atti, p. 38.— For convivor, to eat, feast, or banquet together, Quint. 1, 6, 44: cum aliquo, id. 5, 9, 14; 7, 3, 31 al.

convivor.full: convīvor, ātus, 1, v. dep. (act. access. form convivas, Titin. ap. Non. p. 314, 17 (Com. Rel. v. 89 Rib.): convivat, Enn. ib. p. 474, 23: convivant, Pompon. ib. p. 21 (Com. Rel. v. 85 Rib.): convivare, Petr. 57, 2) [convivium], to feast or banquet with others, to carouse together (rare but class.), Ter. Heaut. 1, 2, 32; * Cic. Verr. 2, 3, 44, § 105: convivatum assidue duobus tricliniis, Suet. Caes. 48; id. Aug. 74; id. Claud. 32.— With acc., to consume, eat: accepta, Cael. Aur. Tard. 1, 1, 8 al.

convocatio.full: convŏcātĭo, ōnis, f. convoco, a convoking, calling, or assembling together: populi Romani, Cic. Red. in Sen. 15, 38.

convocium.full: convōcĭum, a supposed form to explain the etym. of convicium, Dig. 47, 10, 15, § 4, and Paul. ex Fest. p. 41, 26.
convocium.short: convōcĭum, a supposed form to explain the etym.

convoco.full: con-vŏco, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a., to call together, to convoke, assemble; to call (esp. for consultation, to arms, etc.; class.; freq. in Cic. and the histt.). Lit.: qui dissipatos homines congregavit et ad societatem vitae convocavit, Cic. Tusc. 1, 25, 62; cf.: dissipatos homines in societatem vitae, id. ib. 5, 2, 5; id. Leg. 1, 20, 53: piscatores ad se, id. Off. 3, 14, 58; cf.: principes Trevirorum ad se, Caes. B. G. 5, 4 al.: Athenis philosophos in locum unum, Cic. Leg. 1, 20, 53: auditores, id.

convolo.full: con-vŏlo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. n., to fly or flock together; hence, to come hastily together, to run together. Lit. (rare but class.): populus convolat, * Ter. Hec. prol. alt. 32: statim, Cic. Tusc. 3, 21, 50: causa, in quā furiae concitate tamquam ad funus rei publicae convolant, id. Sest. 51, 109: qui cunctā ex Italiā ad me revocandum convolaverunt, id. Dom. 22, 57: ad sellas consulum, Liv. 2, 28, 9: ad scholam, Cod. Th. 6, 27, 18.— Trop. (late Lat.): ad secundum legatarium, Dig. 30, 33: ad secund

convoluto.full: convŏlūto, no perf., ātum, 1, v. freq. a. convolvo, to whirl or roll round rapidly (very rare): cum omni exoletorum turbā, Sen. Ep. 114, 24 (id. Q. N. 7, 9, 2, the true read. is conluctatus, Haase, Fickert).

convolutus.full: convŏlūtus, a, um, Part., from convolvo.
convolutus.short: convŏlūtus, a, um, Part., from convolvo.

convolvo.full: con-volvo, volvi, vŏlūtum, 3, v. a., to roll together, roll up, roll round (first freq. in the post-Aug. per., esp. in Pliny the elder). Lit.: ignis semina convolvunt venti, Lucr. 6, 200 sq.: se sol, Cic. Div. 1, 23, 46: lubrica terga coluber, Verg. A. 2, 474 (in acc. with Hom. Il. 22, 95: δράκων ἑλισσόμενος): rapta turbines, Sen. Ep. 94, 67: se venae arborum, Plin. 16, 39, 76, § 198 al.—So in part. perf.: convoluti in semet dracones, Plin. 10, 72, 92, § 197: aër ignavo globo torpet, id. 2, 8, 6

convolvulus.full: convolvŭlus, i, m. convolvo. A caterpillar that wraps itself up in a leaf, Gr. ἴψ, Cato, R. R. 95, 1; Plin. 17, 28, 47, § 264.— A plant, bind-weed, Plin. 21, 5, 11, § 24.

convomo.full: con-vŏmo, ĕre, v. a., to bespew, vomit upon (perh. only in the foll. exs.): mensas hospitum, * Cic. Phil. 2, 30, 76: maritum, * Juv. 6, 101.

convoro.full: con-vŏro, āre, v. a., to eat up, devour: cadavera, Tert. adv. Marc. 1, 1.

convoveo.full: con-vŏvĕo, vōvi, vōtum, 2, v. a., to devour together: NEVE COMVOVISE, S. C. Bacch. 13 (v. Wordsworth, Fragm. and Spec. p. 172).—Here belongs also: convoti iisdem votis obligati, Paul. ex Fest. p. 42, 8.

convulnero.full: con-vulnĕro (-voln-), āvi, ātum, 1, v. a., to wound severety (post-Aug.). Lit.: eo magis convolneraberis et confodieris, quia nescis praebere jugulum, Sen. Tranq. 11, 5; Plin. Pan. 35, 3: jumenta, Curt. 5, 13, 17: os (apes), Plin. 8, 36, 54, § 129: gemmam vitis falce, Col. 4, 24, 18; Just. 2, 6 fin.: fistulas, to perforate, Front. Aquaed. 27 and 115.— Trop.: maledicta mores et vitam convulnerantia, Sen. Const. 17, 1: convulneratus libidinibus, id. Contr. 2, 9, 6.

convulsio.full: con-vulsĭo (-vols-), ōnis, f. convello, in medic. lang., cramp, convulsion, Scrib. Comp. 165; Plin. 20, 15, 60, § 168; 29, 3, 13, § 55.

convulsus.full: convulsus (-vols-), a, um, Part., from convello.
convulsus.short: convulsus (-vols-), a, um, Part., from convello.

conyza.full: cŏnȳza, ae, f., = κόνυζα, a plant, of two kinds: the male, the viscous elecampane: Inula viscosa, Linn.; called also cunila bubula, Plin. 19, 8, 50, § 165; the female, fleabane: Inula pulicaria, Linn.; Plin. 21, 10, 32, § 58; Pall. 1, 19, 3.
conyza.short: cŏnȳza, ae, f., = κόνυζα, a plant, of two kinds: the male, the viscous elecampane: Inula viscosa, Linn.;

coodibilis.full: cŏ-ŏdĭbĭlis, e, adj., exceedingly hateful, detestable (eccl. Lat.): haeretici, Tert. adv. Marc. 4, 9; 4, 36.
coodibilis.short: cŏ-ŏdĭbĭlis, e, adj., exceedingly hateful, detestable (eccl.

cooperatio.full: cŏ-ŏpĕrātĭo, ōnis, f., co-operation, Quint. Decl. 16 fin.; Cassiod. Complex. Tit. 1.

cooperator.full: cŏ-ŏpĕrātor, ōris, m., a joint-laborer, co-operator (eccl. Lat.), Hier. Ep. 143, 1; Aug. Civ. Dei, 16, 5 fin.; Vulg. Phil. 2, 25; id. 3 Joan. 8.
cooperator.short: cŏ-ŏpĕrātor, ōris, m., a joint-laborer, co-operator (eccl.

cooperculum.full: cŏ-ŏpercūlum, i, n., a cover, lid (very rare), Plin. 23, 6, 58, § 109; App. M. 6, p. 181, 39; Pall. Jun. 7, 9.
cooperculum.short: cŏ-ŏpercūlum, i, n., a cover, lid (very rare), Plin.

cooperimentum.full: cŏ-ŏpĕrĭmentum, i, n., a covering: personae, Bassus ap. Gell. 5, 7, 2.
cooperimentum.short: cŏ-ŏpĕrĭmentum, i, n., a covering: personae, Bassus ap.

cooperio.full: cŏ-ŏpĕrĭo, rŭi, rtum, 4 (contr. form coperiunt, Lucr. 6, 491; cf. Lachm. ap. Lucr. 2, p. 134 sq.), v. a., to cover wholly, to cover, cover over, overwhelm (class.; most freq. in part. perf.). Lit. Verb finit.: Cyrsilum quendam lapidibus cooperuerunt, Cic. Off. 3, 11, 48; so Liv. 4, 50, 5: tempestas atque tenebrae maria ac terras, Lucr. 6, 491; 5, 342: radices, Plin. 17, 26, 39, § 246: se multā fronde (vitis), Col. 5, 6, 36.— Part. perf.: coöperta membra pannis, Lucr. 6, 1269; so Cic. Fragm. ap.

cooperor.full: cŏ-ŏpĕror, ātus sum, 1, v. dep., to work with or together, combine, unite (late Lat.): praedicaverunt ubique, Domino coöperante, Vulg. Marc. 16, 20; Cassiod. Hist. Eccl. 9, 19.— Transf., of things: quoniam fides coöperabatur operibus ejus, Vulg. Jac. 2, 22: diligentibus Deum omnia cooperantur in bonum, id. Rom. 8, 28.

coopertorium.full: cŏŏpertōrĭum, ii, n., a cover, Dig. 34, 2, 38; Veg. Art. Vet. 3, 77, 5.
coopertorium.short: cŏŏpertōrĭum, ii, n., a cover, Dig.

cooptatio.full: cŏoptātĭo, ōnis, f. co-opto, an election, choice: collegiorum, Cic. Lael. 25, 96: censoria, id. Leg. 3, 12, 27: in Patres, i. e. a confirmation by the Senate of Senators nominated by the king, Liv. 4, 4, 7 Weissenb. ad loc.; Flor. 4, 4.

coopto.full: cŏ-opto, āvi, ātum, 1 (perf. subj. coop tassint, old formula in Liv. 3, 64, 10; contr. form copto, Cic. Fam. 3, 10, 9; cf. Lachm. ad Lucr. 2, p. 135), v. a.; publicists' t. t., to choose or elect to something, to admit or re ceive into some body by election, to elect to an office: senatores, Cic. Verr. 2, 2, 49, § 120: senatum, id. ib. 2, 2, 49, § 122; Liv. 23, 3, 5: tribunos plebis, id. 5, 10, 3 and 11; cf. id. 4, 16, 3: collegas, id. 3, 64, 9; cf.: collegam sibi, Suet. Aug. 27: magistrum equit

coorior.full: cŏ-ŏrĭor, ortus, 4, v. dep., to come forth, stand up, arise, appear, rise, break forth (class. in prose and poetry; most freq. in Lucr. and the hist., esp. Liv.; in Cic. rare, perh. only once). In gen.: ubi materiaï Ex infinito sunt corpora plura coorta, Lucr. 5, 408; cf. id. 5, 367; 5, 414; 5, 838 al.: ignes pluribus simul locis, Liv. 26, 27, 5 et saep.: bellum, Caes. B. G. 3, 7: de integro coörtum est bellum, Liv. 21, 8, 2; cf.: foedum certamen, id. 1, 6, 4: seditio intestina coörta, id. 5, 12

coortus1.full: cŏortus, a, um, Part., from coorior.
coortus1.short: cŏortus, a, um, Part., from coorior.

coortus2.full: cŏortus, ūs, m. coorior, a rising, originating: maris et terrae solisque, Lucr. 2, 1106: graviore coortu, id. 6, 672.

copa.full: cōpa (cūpa), ae, f. copo = caupo, a female tavern-keeper and castanet-dancer, who exhibited her arts in her ale-house (cf. crotalum), Verg. Cop. 1 Heyne and Wagner: matronae copas imitantes, Suet. Ner. 27.

copae.full: Cōpae, ārum, f., = Κῶπαι, an ancient town in Bœotia, now Topolia, Plin. 4, 7, 12, § 26; on the Copais palus, the large Copais lake, which was named after it, Liv. 33, 29, 6.
copae.short: Cōpae, ārum, f., = Κῶπαι, an ancient town in Bœotia, now Topolia, Plin.

cophes.full: Cŏphes, ētis, or Cŏphen, ēnis (acc. Copheta or Cophen), m., a river, a tributary of the Indus. Form Cophes, Plin. 6, 17, 21, § 62; 6, 20, 23, § 78.— Form Cophen, Mel. 3, 7, 1.

cophinus.full: cŏphĭnus, i, m., = κόφινος, a basket, Col. 11, 3, 51; Juv. 3, 14; 6, 542 al.; cf. Isid Orig. 20, 9, 9.
cophinus.short: cŏphĭnus, i, m., = κόφινος, a basket, Col.

copia1.full: cōpĭa, ae, f. co-ops, abundant power, wealth, riches, abundance (very freq. in all periods and species of composition). Of material objects. Of possessions, resources, wealth, supplies, riches, prosperity (syn.: divitiae, opes; opp. inopia): pro re nitorem et gloriam pro copiā, Plaut. Aul. 3, 6, 5: divitiarum fructus in copiā est; copiam autem declarat satietas rerum et abundantia, Cic. Par. 6, 2, 47; Plaut. Cist. 1, 1, 32: copiis rei familiaris locupletes et pecuniosi, Cic. Rosc. Com. 15, 44: u

copia2.full: Cōpĭa, ac, f. The goddess of abundance, Plaut. Ps. 2, 4, 46: bona, Ov. M. 9, 88: opulenta, Hor. C. 1, 17, 16; id. C. S. 60 al.— An appellation of the town Lugdunum (Lyons), in Gaul, Inscr. Orell. 194; 2325.— Hence, COPIENSIS, Inscr. Murat. 753, 3.

copiarius.full: cōpĭārĭus, ii, m. 1. copia, a purveyor, = parochus (late Lat.), Schol. ad Hor. S. 1, 5, 46.

copiata.full: cŏpĭāta or cŏpĭātes, ae, m., = κοπιάτης, a grave-digger, sexton (eccl. Lat.), Cod. Th. 7, 20, 12, § 2; 13, 1, 1; 16, 2, 15, § 1.
copiata.short: cŏpĭāta or cŏpĭātes, ae, m., = κοπιάτης, a grave-digger, sexton (eccl.

copiolae.full: cōpĭŏlae, ārum, f. dim. 1. copia, I. B. 2., a small number of troops, Brut. ap. Cic. Fam. 11, 13, 2.

copior.full: cōpĭor, āri, v. dep. 1. copia; milit. t. t. (cf. Gell. 17, 2, 9), to furnish or provide one's self abundantly with something: Romani multis armis et magno commeatu praedāque ingenti copiantur, Quadrig. ap. Gell. l. l., and Cael. ap. Non. p. 87, 8.

copiosus.full: cōpĭōsus, a, um, adj. 1. copia. Furnished abundantly with a thing, well supplied, having abundance, rich, copious, plentiful, abounding (in wealth, means of living, etc.) (very freq. and class., esp. in prose). In gen.; constr. with abl., ab, or absol.; rarely with gen. With simple abl. or ab and abl.: tu agris, tu aedificiis, tu argento, tu familiā, tu rebus omnibus ornatus et copiosus sis, Cic. Cat. 2, 8, 18: Arion grandi pecuniā et re bonā multā coplosus, Gell. 16, 19, 7: oppidum re cibariā,

copis1.full: cōpis (acc. to Varr. L. L. 5, § 92 Müll. N. cr., more prob. than cops, assumed by Prisc. p. 752 P. The nominative in neither form is found in use), is, adj. contr. from coops; cf. inops (ante-class. for the class. copiosus), abundantly supplied with something, abounding in, rich: ut amantem erilem copem facerem filium, Plaut. Bacch. 2, 3, 117: aliquem copem causarum facere, Turp. ap. Non. p. 84, 22 (Com. Rel. v. 61 Rib.); Pac. ib. (Trag. Rel. v. 307 id.): copi pectore, Plaut. Ps. 2, 3, 8.

copis2.full: cŏpis, ĭdis, f., = κοπίς, a short sword, Curt. 8, 14, 29; App. M. 11, p. 260, 33 dub. (MSS. crepides).
copis2.short: cŏpis, ĭdis, f., = κοπίς, a short sword, Curt.

copla.full: cōpla and cōplātus, v. copula and copulatus.

coponius.full: Cōpōnĭus, a, the name of a plebeian family at Rome, e. g. the two brothers, T. and C. Coponii, Cic. Cael. 10, 24; id. Balb. 23, 53.—Hence, Cōpōnĭānus, a, um, adj., of or pertaining to Coponius, Cic. Att. 12, 31, 2.
coponius.short: Cōpōnĭus, a, the name of a plebeian family at Rome, e.

coprea.full: coprĕa, ae, m., = κοπρίας, a low buffoon, a filthy jester (post-Aug.), Suet. Tib. 61; id. Claud. 8; cf. Dio Cass. 50, 28.
coprea.short: coprĕa, ae, m., = κοπρίας, a low buffoon, a filthy jester (post-Aug.), Suet.

copta.full: copta, ae, f., = κόπτη, a kind of cake made of pounded materials, Mart. 14, 68.— The same, or a similar kind, called cop-tŏplăcenta, Petr. 40, 4; Vesp. Judic. 46 (ap. Wernsd. Poët. Lat. Min. II. p. 234).
copta.short: copta, ae, f., = κόπτη, a kind of cake made of pounded materials, Mart.

coptos.full: Coptŏs, i, f., = Κοπτός, Κοπτώ, a trading town in the Thebaid, on the eastern side of the Nile, afterwards Justinianopolis, now Coft, Plin. 5, 9, 11, § 60; Juv. 15, 28; Amm. 22, 16, 2; Itin. Ant. p. 165, 6 al.—Hence, Coptis, tĭdis, adj. f., = Κοπτίς, of Coptos, Plin. 36, 6, 9, § 52.— Coptītēs, ae, adj. m., = Κοπτίτης, of Coptos: nomos, that of which Coptos was the capital, Plin. 5, 9, 9, § 49.— Coptītĭcus, a, um, adj., of Coptos, i. e. Egyptian: adyta, App. M. 2, p. 127, 11.
coptos.short: Coptŏs, i, f., = Κοπτός, Κοπτώ, a trading town in the Thebaid, on the eastern side of the Nile, afterwards Justinianopolis, now Coft, Plin.

copula.full: cōpŭla, ae (contr. form cōpla, in Wernsd. Poët. Lat. Min. IV. p. 535), f. coapio, that which binds together or binds fast, a band, rope, thong, tie (rare; not in Cic.). Lit.: tortae, ship's rigging, Att. ap. Non. p. 200, 33 (Trag. Rel. v. 577 Rib.); Plaut. Ep. 5, 1, 11: copulā vinctum ante se Thynem agere, Nep. Dat. 3, 2; cf.: copula dura canem tenet, a leash, Ov. Tr. 5, 9, 28; id. M. 7, 769; App. M. 7, p. 769: pectora copulae sparteae triturā continuā exulcerati (muli), id. ib. 9, p. 224 fin.—O

copulabilis.full: cōpŭlābĭlis, e, adj. copulo, that can be connected (eccl. Lat.): pedes, Aug. Music. 4, 16 med.

copulate.full: cōpŭlātē, adv., v. copulo, P. a. fin.

copulatim.full: cōpŭlātim, adv. copulo, in union, Diom. p. 402 P.

copulatio.full: cōpŭlātĭo, ōnis, f. id., a coupling, joining, connecting, uniting (several times in Cic. and Quint.). Prop.: atomorum inter se (with complexiones and adhaesiones), Cic. Fin. 1, 6, 19; cf.: copulatio rerum et coagmentatio naturae, id. N. D. 2, 46, 119. — Trop., of social union: primi congressus copulationesque, Cic. Fin. 1, 20, 69; cf. of marriage, Cod. Th. 9, 42, 2.—Of words: ordo rerum, et copulatio, Quint. 7, 10, 8; cf. id. 11, 2, 37: inoffensa vocum, id. 1, 10, 23 al.: syllabarum, verborum in

copulativus.full: cōpŭlātīvus, a, um, adj. copulo, of or pertaining to connecting, copulative (late Lat.): modus, Cod. Just. 6, 38, 4: conjunctiones, Mart. Cap. 3, § 286, and other gramm. —* Adv.: cōpŭlātīvē, connectedly: dicere (diequinti), Macr. S. 1, 4 med.

copulator.full: cōpŭlātor, ōris, m. id., a connecter, binder (late Lat.), Jul. Val. Rer. Gest. Alex. M. 1, 7.

copulatrix.full: cōpŭlātrix, īcis, f. copulator, she who couples, connects (late Lat.): amorum, Auct. Perv. Ven. 5; Aug. Trin. 11, 9 fin.

copulatus1.full: cōpŭlātus, a, um, Part. and P. a., from copulo.

copulatus2.full: cōpŭlātus, ūs, m. copulo (only in abl. sing.), a connecting or joining together: rationum consequentium, Arn. 1, p. 2.

copulo.full: cōpŭlo, āvi, ātum, 1 (part. perf., contr. cōplata, Lucr. 6, 1088; dep. collat. form cō-pŭlor, āri, v. I. A. b. infra), v. a. copula, to couple, bind, or tie together, to join, connect, unite (class.; most freq. in Cic.). Lit. In gen. With cum: hominem cum beluā, Cic. Ac. 2, 45, 139 fin.: caput et corpus cum aliquo, Plaut. Poen. 1, 2, 130. — With inter se: inter se quaedam possint coplata teneri, Lucr. 6, 1088.— With dat.: aurum auro, Lucr. 6, 1078: utrimque Armeniae majori Sophene copulatur, Pli

copulor.full: cōpŭlor, āri, v. dep., v. copulo, I. A. b.

coqua.full: cŏqua, ae, f. coquus, a female cook, Plaut. Poen. 1, 2, 38.

coquibilis.full: cŏquĭbĭlis (cŏcĭ-), e, adj. coquo, that can be easily cooked: caro, Plin. 16, 6, 8, § 25.

coquinarius.full: cŏquīnārĭus, a, um, adj. coquina, of or pertaining to the kitchen, culinary (rare): vasa, Plin. 33, 11, 49, § 140.—As the title of a work of Apicius, De arte coquinaria.— Access. form cŏquīnāris, e, adj.: culter, a kitchen-knife, Varr. ap. Non. p. 195, 17.

coquinatorius.full: cŏquīnātōrĭus (cŏcī-), a, um, adj. id., of or pertaining to the kitchen (late Lat.): instrumentum, Dig. 34, 2, 19, § 12: vasa, ib. 33, 9, 6.—Hence, subst.: COCINATORIVM, a kitchen, Inscr. Orell. 1359.

coquino.full: cŏquīno, āre, v. a. coquinus, to perform the office of a cook, perh. only Plaut. Ps. 3, 2, 64; 3, 2; 85 Lorenz with MSS. (Fleck. in both passages coquitare, ex conj.; cf. coquito); id. Aul. 3, 1, 3 Wagn., Ussing; cf. Non. p. 85, 31.

coquinus.full: cŏquīnus, a, um, adj. coquo, of or pertaining to cooking (rare): forum, Plaut. Ps. 3, 2, 1 and 2.— Subst.: cŏquīna, ae, f. A kitchen, Pall. 1, 37, 4; Arn. 4, p. 130; Non. p. 55, 18.— The art of cooking, cookery, App. Dogm. Plat. 2, p. 17, 4 (al. coquinaria).

coquitare.full: cŏquĭtāre, used by Plaut. acc to Paul. ex Fest. p. 61, 18 Müll.: pro coctitare id est frequenter coquere: an tu coquitatum te ire quoquam postulas? Plaut. Ps. 3, 2, 64 Fleck.; 3, 2, 85; v. coquino.

coquitatio.full: cŏquĭtātĭo, ōnis, f. coquito, a continuous cooking: diutina, App. M. 4, p. 152.

coquo.full: cŏquo, xi, ctum, 3, v. a. kindr. with Sanscr. pak; Gr. πεπ in πέπτω or πέσσω; Germ. backen; Engl. bake, to cook, to prepare by cooking, to bake, boil, roast, parch, steep, melt, heat (very freq. and class.). Lit.: cenam, Plaut. Aul. 3, 2, 17; id. Ps. 3, 2, 7: cottidie sic cena ei coquebatur, ut, etc., Nep. Cim. 4, 3: cibum, Lucr. 5, 1102; cf. cibaria, Liv. 3, 27, 3; 29, 25, 6; 44, 32, 11; 44, 35, 13 al.: qui illa coxerat, Cic. Tusc. 5, 34, 98: quae coxerat aere cavo, Ov. M. 4, 505: dulce dedit,

coquula.full: cŏquŭla, ae, and cŏquŭlum, i, v. cocu-.
coquula.short: cŏquŭla, ae, and cŏquŭlum, i, v.

coquus.full: cŏquus (ante-class. cŏquŏs; in many MSS. and inscrr. also cŏcus), i, m., a cook (very freq., esp. in Plaut., in whose comedies the cook takes a conspicuous place), Plaut. Ps. 3, 2, 11; Ter. Eun. 2, 2, 26; Varr. R. R. 3, 14, 3; Cic. Rosc. Am. 46, 134; Liv. 39, 6, 9; Mart. 14, 220, 1 sq.; Dig. 40, 4, 24 et saep.—In ancient times the cook baked also the bread; cf. Naev. ap. Paul. ex Fest. p. 58, 14 Müll.—From the ancient writing, quoquus for cocus, originates the pun upon the voc. coque and quoque,

cor.full: cor (ŏ, e. g. Ov. Tr. 5, 8, 28; id. P. 1, 3, 32), cordis (gen. plur. cordium, Vulg. Jer. 4, 4, and 1 Cor. 4, 5; acc. to Fragm. Bob. Nom. et Pron. p. 132, also cordum, but without example), n. kindr. with Sanscr. hrid; Gr. καρδία; Germ. Herz; Engl. heart, the heart (very freq. in all periods and species of composition). Lit., the heart, as the chief source of the circulation of the blood, and so of life, Cels. 4, 1; cf. Plin. 11, 37, 69. §§ 181 and 182: cor tineosum, opinor, habeo, Plaut. Cas. 2,

cora1.full: cŏra, ae, f., = κόρη (v. Lidd. and Scott in h. v. III.), the pupil of the eye, Aus. Ep. 16, 59.

cora2.full: Cŏra, ae, f., = Κόρη, a name of Proserpine, Inscr. Orell. 2361; cf. Serv. ad Verg. A. 3, 117.
cora2.short: Cŏra, ae, f., = Κόρη, a name of Proserpine, Inscr.

cora3.full: Cŏra, ae, f., = Κόρα, an ancient town of Latium, in the territory of the Volsci, now the village Cori, in the Campagna di Roma, Liv. 2, 16, 8; 2, 22, 2; Verg. A. 6, 775; Luc. 7, 392.—Cŏrāni, its inhabitants, Plin. 3, 5, 9, § 63.—Hence, Cŏrānus, a, um, adj., of Cora: ager, Liv. 8, 19, 5: lapis, Isid. Orig. 16, 4, 31.—Hence, Cŏrăcēsĭ-um, i, n., a town on the borders of Cilicia and Pamphylia, Liv. 33, 20, 4 and 5; Plin. 5, 27, 22, § 93; in the neighborhood of it is Mons Coracesius, Plin. 5, 27, 27,
cora3.short: Cŏra, ae, f., = Κόρα, an ancient town of Latium, in the territory of the Volsci, now the village Cori, in the Campagna di Roma, Liv.

coracesia.full: cŏrăcēsĭa, ae, f. κόραξ, a magical herb said to make water freeze, Plin. 24, 17, 99, § 156.

coracicus.full: cŏrăcĭcus, a, um, adj. κόραξ, of or belonging to the raven; only as subst.: cŏ-răcĭca, ōrum, n. (sc. sacra), the mysteries of Mithras, Inscr. Orell. 2343.

coracino.full: cŏrăcĭno, āre, v. n. id., to caw, croak, κρίιζειν, Isid. Orig. 12, 7, 43.

coracinus1.full: cŏrăcĭnus, a. um, adj., = κοράκῖνος, raven-black: color, Vitr. 8, 3, 14; so absol., coracinum, Dig. 32, 1, 78, § 5 (al. croconum).

coracinus2.full: cŏrăcīnus, i, m., = κορακῖνος, a species of river fish, esp. in the Nile, Plin. 9, 16, 24, § 57; 9, 18, 32, § 68; Mart. 13, 85 al.
coracinus2.short: cŏrăcīnus, i, m., = κορακῖνος, a species of river fish, esp.

coralium.full: cō^rā^lĭum or cū^rā^lĭum (cŏral-lum, Sid. Carm. 11, 110), ii, n., = κοράλλιον; Ion. κουράλιον, coral, esp. red coral, Plin. 32, 2, 11, § 21 sq.: curalium, id. 32, 2, 11, §§ 21 and 22: coralium, Ov. M. 4, 750; 15, 416; plur.: coralia, Claud. Nupt. Hon. et Mar. 169.—In the form corallius, i, f., Plin. 37, 10, 56, § 153; masc., Isid. Orig. 16, 8, 1.

coralli.full: Cŏralli, ōrum, m., a people of Lower Mœsia, on the Danube, on the coast of the Black Sea, Ov. P. 4, 2, 37; 4, 8, 83.—Hence, Cŏrallĭcus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to the Coralli: pelagus, Cassiod. Var. 6.
coralli.short: Cŏralli, ōrum, m., a people of Lower Mœsia, on the Danube, on the coast of the Black Sea, Ov.

corallinus.full: cŏrallĭnus, a, um, adj. κοράλλιον, coral-red: labra, Poëta in Anth. Lat. 1, p. 651 Burm.

corallis.full: cŏrallis, ĭdis, f., = κοραλλίς, a precious stone, unknown to us, Plin. 37, 10, 56, § 154.
corallis.short: cŏrallis, ĭdis, f., = κοραλλίς, a precious stone, unknown to us, Plin.

coralliticus.full: cō^rallītĭcus, a, um, adj.: lapis, a kind of white marble found in Asia Minor, Plin. 36, 8, 13, § 62; Isid. Orig. 16, 5, 9.
coralliticus.short: cō^rallītĭcus, a, um, adj.: lapis, a kind of white marble found in Asia Minor, Plin.

coralloachates.full: cŏrallŏăchātes, ae, m., = κοραλλοαχάτης, coral-agate, Plin. 37, 10, 54, § 139.
coralloachates.short: cŏrallŏăchātes, ae, m., = κοραλλοαχάτης, coral-agate, Plin.

coram.full: cōram, adv. and prep. prob. kindred with ōs, ōris. Object., in the presence of, before the eyes of, in the face of, before (freq. and class.). Adv.: vereor coram in os te laudare amplius, Ter. Ad. 2, 4, 5: omnia quae tute dudum coram me incusaveras, id. Phorm. 5, 8, 21: coram potius me praesente dixissent, Cic. Agr. 3, 1, 1: Manlius quoque ad restituendam aciem se ipse coram offert, i. e. before the soldiers, Liv. 2, 47, 4: ut veni coram, singultim pauca locutus, Hor. S. 1, 6, 56 et saep.: lenis

coramble.full: cŏramblē, ēs, f., = κοράμβλη, a kind of cabbage injurious to the eyes, Col. 10, 178.
coramble.short: cŏramblē, ēs, f., = κοράμβλη, a kind of cabbage injurious to the eyes, Col.

coranus.full: Cŏrānus, a, um, v. 3. Cora, II.

corax1.full: cŏrax, ăcis, m., = κόραξ, a raven, Sol. 40; lsid. Orig. 12, 7, 43.— Meton., in milit. lang., a hooked engine of war, a battering-ram (called in pure Latin corvus), Vitr. 10, 13, 7.
corax1.short: cŏrax, ăcis, m., = κόραξ, a raven, Sol.

corax2.full: Cŏrax, ăcis (acc. -acem, Cic. de Or. 3, 21, 81; -aca, Quint. 2, 17, 7), m., the most ancient Greek rhetorician in Sicily, a contemporary, perhaps also teacher, of Lysias, Cic. de Or. 1, 20, 91; id. Brut. 12, 46; Quint. 2, 17, 7; 3, 1, 8.—In a play upon words: quare Coracem istum vestrum patiamur nos quidem pullos suos excludere, etc., Cic. de Or. 3, 21, 81.

corax3.full: Cŏrax, ăcis, m., a mountain in Ætolia, Liv. 36, 30, 4; 37, 4, 7.
corax3.short: Cŏrax, ăcis, m., a mountain in Ætolia, Liv.

corbicula.full: corbĭcŭla, ae, f. dim. corbis, a little basket, Pall. Febr. 10, 6.

corbio.full: Corbĭo, ōnis, Masc., a Roman surname: Hortensius Corbio, Val. Max. 3, 5, 4. — Fem., a town of the Æqui, in Italy, Liv. 2, 39, 4; 3, 28, 10.— A town of Spain, in the territory of the Suessetani, near the modern Berga, Liv. 39, 42, 1.
corbio.short: Corbĭo, ōnis, Masc., a Roman surname: Hortensius Corbio, Val.

corbis.full: corbis, is (abl. regularly corbe: corbi, Cato, R. R. 136 twice), comm. corbes dicti quod curvatis virgis contexuntur, Isid. l. l.; but more prob. kindr. with κόλπος, a basket (esp. for use in gathering fruits, etc.). Masc., Auct. B. Hisp. 5, 1; Col. 11, 2, 99; Suet. Ner. 19; Prud. Dittoch. 147; cf. Col. 6, 3, 5 dub.— Fem., Serv. ad Verg. A. 1, 165; cf. Caper de Verb. Dub. p. 2248; Cic. Sest. 38, 82 (abl. corbe).— Of dub. gender, Varr. L. L. 5, § 139 Müll.; Cato, R. R. 136; Varr. R. R. 1, 50, 1 s

corbitus.full: corbītus, a, um, adj. corbis, with a scuttle, bower: navis, Lucil. ap. Non. p. 533, 18.—Hence, subst.: corbīta, ae, f., a slowsailing ship of burden: corbitae dicuntur naves onerariae, quod in malo earum summo pro signo corbes solerent suspendi, Paul. ex Fest. p. 37, 7 Müll.: corbita est genus navigii tardum et grande, Non. p. 533, 10; so * Cic. Att. 16, 6, 1; opp. celox, Plaut. Poen. 3, 1, 40; on account of its slow motion: homines spissigradissimos, Tardiores quam corbitae sunt in tranquillo m

corbona.full: corbōna, ae, f. Syrian, a treasurechamber, Hier. Ep. 27, 14; Vulg. Matt. 27, 6.

corbula.full: corbŭla, ae, f. dim. corbis, a little basket, Cato, R. R. 11, 5; Varr. R. R. 1, 15; id. L. L. 5, § 139; Col. 12, 50, 8; Plaut. Aul. 2, 7, 4; Caecil. ap. Non. p. 197, 29; Suet. Ner. 19 al.

corcholopis.full: corcholopis, a kind of ape having a tuft of hair at the end of its tail, Fest. p. 54 (where Lindem. reads cercolips, contr. to all MSS.; Müll. cercolopis).
corcholopis.short: corcholopis, a kind of ape having a tuft of hair at the end of its tail, Fest.

corchoros.full: corchŏros or -rus, i, m., = κόρχορος, a poor kind of pulse, growing wild: Corchorus olitorius, Linn.; Plin. 21, 32, 106, § 183; 25, 13, 92, § 144.
corchoros.short: corchŏros or -rus, i, m., = κόρχορος, a poor kind of pulse, growing wild: Corchorus olitorius, Linn.;

corcillum.full: corcillum, i, n. dim. corculum, a little heart: corcillum est quod homines facit, cetera quisquilia omnia, Petr. 75.

corculum.full: Corcŭlum, i, n. dim. cor, a little heart, Plaut. Most. 4, 2, 70; as a term of endearment, id. Cas. 4, 4, 14.—As a surname of Scipio Nasica, on account of his sagacity, Cic. Tusc. 1, 9, 18; id. Brut. 20, 70; Aur. Vict. Vir. Ill. 44, 6; and as masc. in plur.: Corculi cognominati, Plin. 7, 31, 31, § 118; cf. Paul. ex Fest. p. 61, 5 Müll.

corcus.full: corcus, i. m., a disease of the chest, Marc. Emp. 21 dub.

corcyra.full: Corcȳra (ў, Avien. Perieg. 663), ae, f., = Κέρκυρα. An island in the Ionian Sea, opposite Epirus; in fable, Scheria, the abode of Alcinous, now Corfu, Mel. 2, 7, 10; 4, 12, 19; Plin. 4, 12, 19, § 52 sq.; Cic. Fam. 16, 7 init. and fin.; 16, 9, 1; Caes. B. C. 3, 3; Nep. Them. 8, 3 al.—Hence, Corcȳ-raeus, a, um, adj., of Corcyra, Corcyræan: bellum, Nep. Them. 2, 1: epistula, written in Corcyra, Cic. Att. 6, 2, 10: horti, i. e. of Alcinous, Mart. 13, 37.—Subst.: Corcȳraei, ōrum, m., the inhabitants

cordatus.full: cordātus, a, um, adj. cor, II. B., wise, prudent, judicious, sagacious (mostly anteand post-class.): egregie cordatus homo, Enn. ap. Cic. Tusc. 1, 9, 18 (Ann. v. 335 Vahl.); cf. Cic. Rep. 1, 18, 30; Sen. Lud. Mort. Claud. 12, 2, v. 7; Vulg. Job, 34, 10.—Comp.: cordatior, Lact. 3, 20, 2.—Adv.: cordātē, with prudence, wisely (with docte and cate), Plaut. Mil. 4, 2, 97; id. Poen. 1, 1, 3.

cordax.full: cordax, ăcis, m., = κόρδαξ, the extravagant dance of Grecian comedy, distinguished by lively movement and wanton gesture, and by the rope which was kept passing through the hands of the dancers; the imitation of this dance was regarded as a mark of drunkenness or licentiousness: ducere, to dance it (κόρδακα ἕλκειν), Petr. 52, 9 (cf. Ter. Ad. 4, 7, 34).—Adject.: cordaces sententiae, i. e. tinnulae, staggering (together with modulatae), Fronto de Or. 2, p. 240 Mai.— Transf. of the trochaic rhythm,
cordax.short: cordax, ăcis, m., = κόρδαξ, the extravagant dance of Grecian comedy, distinguished by lively movement and wanton gesture, and by the rope which was kept passing through the hands of the dancers;

cordicitus.full: cordĭcĭtus, adv. cor, from the heart, deep in the heart, Sid. Ep. 4, 6.

cordolium.full: cor-dŏlĭum, ii, n. dolor, sorrow at heart, grief (ante- and post-class.), Plaut. Cist. 1, 1, 67; id. Poen. 1, 2, 86; App. M. 9, p. 226, 28.

corduba.full: Cordŭba, ae, f., = Κορδύβη, a town in Hispania Baetica, on the river Bætis, now Caes. B. C. 2, 19 al.—Cordŭbensis, e, adj., of Corduba, Plin. 3, 1, 3, § 7; 34, 2, 2, § 4; Auct. B. Alex. 57.—Hence. Cordŭ-benses, ium, m., the inhabitants of Corduba, Auct. B. Alex. 59.
corduba.short: Cordŭba, ae, f., = Κορδύβη, a town in Hispania Baetica, on the river Bætis, now Caes.

corduena.full: Cordŭēna, ae, f., = Γορδυηνή, a district of Greater Armenia, now Kurdistan, Amm. 16, 8, 20 al.—Hence, Cordŭēni, ōrum, m., the inhabitants of Corduena, now the Kurds, Sall. H. 4, 60 Dietsch; Plin. 6, 15, 17, § 44; Sext. Ruf. Brev. 20.—Called also Gordўaei, ōrum, m., Curt. 5, 1, 14; cf. id. 4, 10, 8; Plin. 6, 11, 12, § 30.
corduena.short: Cordŭēna, ae, f., = Γορδυηνή, a district of Greater Armenia, now Kurdistan, Amm.

cordyla.full: cordȳla, ae, f., = κορδύλη, the fry of the tunny-fish, Plin. 9, 15, 18, § 47; Mart. 3, 2, 4.
cordyla.short: cordȳla, ae, f., = κορδύλη, the fry of the tunny-fish, Plin.

corfidius.full: Corfīdĭus, ii, m., a Roman proper name, Cic. Lig. 11, 33.
corfidius.short: Corfīdĭus, ii, m., a Roman proper name, Cic.

corfinium.full: Corfīnĭum, ii, n., = Κορφίνιον, a very strongly fortified town of the Peligni, north of Sulmo, now Pelino, Cic. Att. 8, 3, 7; Caes. B. C. 1, 15 sq.; Luc. 2, 478 al.— Hence, Corfīnĭensis, e, adj., of or pertaining to Corfinium: clementia, i. e. exercised by Cæsar at this city, Cic. Att. 9, 16, 1; cf. exspectatio, i. e. of occurrences there, id. ib. 8, 5, 2.—In plur.: Corfīnĭenses, ium, m., the inhabitants of Corfinium, Plin. 3, 12, 17, § 106.— Corfīnĭus, a, um, adj., of Corfinium: ager, Front. Co
corfinium.short: Corfīnĭum, ii, n., = Κορφίνιον, a very strongly fortified town of the Peligni, north of Sulmo, now Pelino, Cic.

corgo.full: corgo apud antiquos pro adverbio, quod est profecto, ponebatur, Paul. ex Fest. p. 37 Müll.
corgo.short: corgo apud antiquos pro adverbio, quod est profecto, ponebatur, Paul.

coria.full: Cŏrĭa, ae, f., = Κορία, a name of the fourth Minerva, among the Arcadians, Cic. N. D. 3, 23, 59.
coria.short: Cŏrĭa, ae, f., = Κορία, a name of the fourth Minerva, among the Arcadians, Cic.

coriaceus.full: cŏrĭăcĕus, a, um, adj. corium, of leather: naves, made of leather, Amm. 24, 3, 11.

coriaginosus.full: cŏrĭāgĭnōsus, a, um, adj. coriago, afflicted with the coriago (late Lat.; perh. only in Veg.): equi, Veg. Art. Vet. 2, 10, 2; 2, 16, 1.

coriago.full: cŏrĭāgo, ĭnis, f. corium, a disease of the skin of animals, Col. 6, 13, 2; Veg. Art. Vet. 4, 12, 1; 5, 3, 1.

coriandratum.full: cŏrĭandrātum, i, n. coriandrum, coriander-water, Apic. 9, 1, § 410.

coriandrum.full: cŏrĭandrum or -dron, i, n.; also -drus, i, f. κορίαννον, coriander: Coriandrum sativum, Linn.; Cato, R. R. 157, 6 sq.; Col. 6, 33, 2; 11, 3, 29; Plin. 19, 7, 35, § 117 sq.; Varr. L. L. 5, § 103 Müll.; Plaut. Ps. 3, 2, 25; Apic. 4, 3, § 174 sq.

coriarius.full: cŏrĭārĭus, a, um, adj. corium, of or pertaining to leather frutex, i. e. useful for tanning leather, Plin. 24, 11, 54, § 91.— Hence, Subst.: cŏrĭārĭus, ii, m., a tanner, currier, Plin. 17, 9, 6, § 51; Inscr. Orell. 4074 al.

corinna.full: Cŏrinna, ae, f., = Κόπιννα. A celebrated Greek poetess of Tanagra, contemporary with Pindar, Prop. 2, 3, 21; Stat. S. 5, 3, 158.— A feigned name of the object of the poet Ovid's love, Ov. Am. 2, 17, 29; 3, 1, 49; id. Tr. 4, 10, 60; Mart. 8, 73, 10.

corinthia.full: Cŏrinthĭa, Cŏrinthĭārĭus, Cŏ-rinthĭenses, etc., v. Corinthus, II.

corinthus.full: Cŏrinthus, i (nom. Gr. Corinthos, Ov. M. 6, 416; acc. Gr. Corinthon, id. F. 4, 501; Mart. 9, 60; 10, 68), f. (masc., Inscr. Fratr. Arval. p. 30 Marin.: CORINTO DELETO), = Κόρινθος, Corinth, a celebrated commercial city in the Peloponnesus, pillaged and destroyed by Mummius, now the village Corinto or Gereme; it was situated on the Isthmus (hence, bimaris, Hor. C. 1, 7, 2; Ov. M. 5, 407; id. F. 4, 501; and: bimaris terra, Sen. Oedip. 282), Mel. 2, 3, 7; Plin. 4, 4, 5, § 11; Flor. 2, 16; Plaut. Me

corioli.full: Cŏrĭŏli, ōrum, m., = Κορίολα, a town in Latium, destroyed by Caius Marcius, who, on account of this, received the surname Cŏrĭŏlānus, Liv. 2, 33, 5 sq.—In plur.: Cŏrĭŏlāni, ōrum, m., the inhabitants of Corioli, Plin. 3, 5, 9, § 69.
corioli.short: Cŏrĭŏli, ōrum, m., = Κορίολα, a town in Latium, destroyed by Caius Marcius, who, on account of this, received the surname Cŏrĭŏlānus, Liv.

corion.full: cŏrĭon, ii, n., = κόριον, a plant, also called chamaepitys or hypericon, Plin. 26, 8, 53, § 85 (corissum, Sillig).
corion.short: cŏrĭon, ii, n., = κόριον, a plant, also called chamaepitys or hypericon, Plin.

corippus.full: Cŏrippus, i, m.; Flavius Cresconius, a Latin grammarian and poet, about the middle of the sixth century.

coris.full: cŏris, is or ĭdos, f., = κορίς, a plant, a species of hypericon, Plin. 26, 8, 51, § 86.— Also the seed of it, Plin. 26, 8, 73, § 119.
coris.short: cŏris, is or ĭdos, f., = κορίς, a plant, a species of hypericon, Plin.

corissum.full: cŏrissum, i, n., another name of the plant chamaepitys, Plin. 26, 8, 53, § 85.
corissum.short: cŏrissum, i, n., another name of the plant chamaepitys, Plin.

corium.full: cŏrĭum, ii, n. (ante-class. cŏrĭus, ii, m., Plaut. Poen. 1, 1, 11; id. Fragm. ap. Paul. ex Fest. p. 60, 7; Sillig reads caros in both places; Varr. ap. Non. p. 199, 16) [for scorium, kindr. with scortum; Sanscr. kar; old Germ. sceran; Gr. χόριον], skin, hide, leather. In gen. Prop., of animals, Cato, R. R. 135, 3; Varr. L. L. 7, § 84 Müll.; Lucr. 4, 935; Cic. N. D. 2, 47, 121; Caes. B. G. 7, 22; Plin. 13, 9, 19, § 63 et saep.: corium formā publicā percussum, of the leather money of the Lacedæmon

cormasa.full: Cormasa, ōrum, n., = Κύρμασα, a town in Pisidia, Liv. 38, 15, 7.
cormasa.short: Cormasa, ōrum, n., = Κύρμασα, a town in Pisidia, Liv.

cornelius.full: Cornēlĭus, a, subst., a designation of a Roman gens celebrated as embracing the most distinguished Roman men and women (the patrician Scipios, Sulla, the Gracchi and their mother, etc.; the plebeian Balbi, Mammulae, Merulae, etc.).—Also adj.; hence the numerous laws made by the different Cornelii, but esp. by L. Cornelius Sulla, were called Leges Corneliae; cf. Ernest. and Orell. Clav. Cicer. in Ind. Legum, p. 13 sq.; Dict. of Antiq.—Fŏrum Cor-nēlĭum, a town of the Lingones in Gallia Cisalpina,
cornelius.short: Cornēlĭus, a, subst., a designation of a Roman gens celebrated as embracing the most distinguished Roman men and women (the patrician Scipios, Sulla, the Gracchi and their mother, etc.;

corneolus.full: cornĕŏlus, a, um, adj. dim. [1. corneus]. Horny, of horn (very rare): introitus (auris), * Cic. N. D. 2, 57, 146.—* Transf., hard, firm, Petr. 43, 7.

cornesco.full: cornesco, ĕre, v. inch. n. [cornu], to become like horn, grow horny, turn to horn, Plin. 11, 49, 109, § 261.

cornetum.full: cornētum, i, n. 1. cornus, a grove of cornel-trees, Varr. L. L. 5, § 152 Müll.; cf. id. ib. § 146.

corneus1.full: cornĕus, a, um, adj. cornu. Of horn, horny, horn- (rare but class.): corneo proceroque rostro (ibes), * Cic. N. D. 1, 36, 101: ora, Ov. M. 8, 545: arcus, id. ib. 1, 697: pyxis, Plin. 29, 6, 39, § 142: laterna, Mart. 14, 61: crater, id. 12, 32, 12: ungula (equi), Luc. 6, 83; cf. solum, Varr. R. R. 2, 9, 4: porta Somni, Verg. A. 6, 894; cf. Stat. S. 5, 3, 288.— Hard as horn, horny (very rare): corpora piscatorum, Plin. 31, 9, 45, § 102; 7, 19, 18, § 80.— Trop.: fibra, hard-heartedness, insensibili

corneus2.full: cornĕus, a, um, adj. 1. cornus, of or belonging to the cornel-tree or cornelwood: virgulta, Verg. A. 3, 22: clavi, Cato, R. R. 18, 9: hastilia, Verg. A. 5, 557: venabula, Ov. H. 4, 83.

cornicen1.full: cornĭcen, cĭnis, m. cornu-cano; cf.: tibicen, tubicen, etc., a horn-blower, corneter, Liv. 2, 64, 10; Cic. Rep. 2, 22, 40; Juv. 2, 118; 3, 34 al.

cornicen2.full: Cornĭcen, ĭnis, m., a surname of several persons in the gens Oppia, Liv. 3, 35, 11 al.; also in the access. form Cornĭ-cĭnus, Cic. Att. 4, 2, 4.
cornicen2.short: Cornĭcen, ĭnis, m., a surname of several persons in the gens Oppia, Liv.

cornicor.full: cornīcor, āri, v. dep. cornix, to caw like a crow (very rare): quid grave secum inepte, Pers. 5, 12; cf. Prisc. p. 828 P.; Hier. Ep. 125, n. 16.

cornicula.full: cornīcŭla, ae, f. dim. id., a little crow, Hor. Ep. 1, 3, 19.

corniculans.full: cornĭcŭlans, antis, adj. 1. corniculum, horn-shaped, horned (late Lat.): luna, i. e. the new moon, Sol. 32, 17; Amm. 20, 3, 1; cf. corniculatus.

corniculanus.full: Cornĭcŭlānus, a, um, v. 2. Corniculum, B.

cornicularia.full: Cornĭcŭlārĭa, ae, f., a lost play of Plautus, Varr. L. L. 5, § 153 al.
cornicularia.short: Cornĭcŭlārĭa, ae, f., a lost play of Plautus, Varr.

cornicularius.full: cornĭcŭlārĭus, ii, m. 1. corniculum. In milit. lang. (prop. one who had been presented with a corniculum, and thereby promoted), an adjutant of a centurion, tribune, proprætor, etc. (post-Aug.), Val. Max. 6, 1, 11; Front. Strat. 3, 14, 1; Suet. Dom. 17; Inscr. Orell. 3465; Ascon. ad Cic. Verr. 2, 1, 28, § 71 al.— Transf. to civil offices, an assistant, aid, secretary, Cod. Th. 1, 15, 11; 7, 4, 32; 8, 4, 10; Firm. Math. 3, 6.

corniculatus.full: cornĭcŭlātus, a, um, adj. id., in the form of a horn, horned: luna, i. e. the new moon, App. de Deo Socr. p. 42, 1; cf. corniculans.

corniculum1.full: cornĭcŭlum, i, n. dim. cornu, a little horn. Prop., Plin. 9, 42, 67, § 143; 11, 28, 34, § 100.— Meton. A small tunnel of horn, Col. 7, 5, 15 and 20.— A horn-shaped ornament upon the helmet, as a reward for bravery, Liv. 10, 44, 5; Aur. Vict. 723; Suet. Gram. 9; cf. Plin. 10, 43, 60, § 124.

corniculum2.full: Cornĭcŭlum, i, n., an ancient town in Latium, Plin. 3, 5, 9, § 68; Liv. 1, 38, 4; Flor. 1, 11, 6.—Hence, Cornĭcŭlā-nus, a, um, adj., of Corniculum; so the father of Servius Tullius, Aur. Vict. Vir. Ill. 7; and his mother, Ov. F. 6, 628.
corniculum2.short: Cornĭcŭlum, i, n., an ancient town in Latium, Plin.

corniculus.full: cornĭcŭlus, i, m. 1. corniculum, the civil office of a cornicularius, Cod. Th. 1, 15, 11; 8, 7, 8.

cornifer.full: cornĭfer, fĕra, fĕrum, adj., having or bearing horns, horned (for the usu. corniger): cervi, Poët. ap. Mai, Auct. Class. 5, p. 456.
cornifer.short: cornĭfer, fĕra, fĕrum, adj., having or bearing horns, horned (for the usu.

cornificius.full: Cornĭfĭcĭus, a, the name of a Roman plebeian gens; so, Q. Cornificius, friend of Cicero and author of rhet. and gram. works, Cic. Fam. 12, 17, 2; Quint. 3, 1, 21 al.; Cic. Att. 1, 13, 3 al.— A Latin poet, Cat. 38, 1; Ov. Tr. 2, 436; Macr. S. 6, 5; cf. Don. Vit. Verg. 67.
cornificius.short: Cornĭfĭcĭus, a, the name of a Roman plebeian gens;

cornifrons.full: cornĭ-frons, ontis, adj. cornu, with horns on the forehead: armentae, Liv. And. ap. Non. p. 190, 21.

corniger.full: cornĭger, gĕra, gĕrum, adj. cornugero, having or bearing horns, horned (poet.): cervi, Lucr. 3, 751; Ov. M. 7, 701: matres haedi, Lucr. 2, 368: Taurus, Cic. poët. N. D. 2, 43, 110; Ov. M. 15, 511: juvencae, id. ib. 13, 926: Ammon, id. ib. 5, 17; 15, 309; cf. Stat. Th. 8, 201: fluvius Hesperidum, Verg. A. 8, 77; cf. Numicius, Ov. M. 14, 602: Lyaeus, id. Am. 3, 15, 17; v. Bacchus, I.—Subst.: cornĭgĕra, ōrum, n. (sc. animalia), horned animals, horned cattle, Plin. 11, 37, 85, § 212; 11, 45, 105, §

cornipes.full: cornĭ-pēs, pĕdis, adj. cornu, hornfooted, hoofed (poet.): capella, Cat. 19, 16: equi, Verg. A. 6, 591: Faunus, Ov. F. 2, 361: planta (Panis), Sil. 13, 338.—Also subst.: cornĭpēs, pĕdis, m. (so most freq. in Claud.), a horn-footed animal; of the horse, Sil. 3, 361; 7, 684; Claud. Fesc. 11, 11 al.; of the centaur Chiron, Claud. in Rufin. 2, 180 et saep.

corniscarum.full: Corniscārum divarum locus erat trans Tiberim cornicibus dicatus, quod in Junonis tutelā esse putabantur, Paul. ex Fest. p. 64, 7 Müll.; cf. Inscr. Grut. 88, 14.
corniscarum.short: Corniscārum divarum locus erat trans Tiberim cornicibus dicatus, quod in Junonis tutelā esse putabantur, Paul.

cornix.full: cornix, īcis, f. kindred with corvus and κορώνη, a crow, Lucr. 5, 1083: rauca, id. 6, 753: garrula, Ov. M. 2, 548: loquax, id. F. 2, 89; Plin. 10, 12, 14, § 30 al.; renowned as being long lived, Lucr. 5, 1083; Cic. Tusc. 3, 28, 69; Hor. C. 3, 17, 13; Ov. M. 7, 274; Plin. 7, 48, 49, § 153 et saep.; its appearance on the left side was considered as a favorable omen, Plaut. As. 2, 1, 12; Cic. Div. 1, 39, 85; Verg. E. 9, 15; Phaedr. 3, 18, 12; cf. Suet. Dom. 23; and its cries as a sign of rain, Verg

cornu.full: cornū, ūs (so Caes. B. C. 3, 68 Dint.; Luc. 7, 217; Plin. 28, 11, 46, § 163 et saep.; Curt. 4, 12, 11 al.; ū in the connection cornu bubuli and cornu cervini; also Cael. Aur. Tard. 3, 5, 76; Veg. Art. Vet. 1, 20, 1 al.; cf. esp. Neue, Formenl. 1, p. 355), n. (access. form cornum, i, n., Varr. R. R. 3, 9, 14; Ter. Eun. 4, 7, 5 Fleck.; Lucr. 2, 388; Ov. M. 2, 874; Scrib. Comp. 141; Gell. 14, 6, 2 al.; gen. plur. cornorum, Scrib. Comp. 60. —An access. form cornus, ūs, has been assumed on account of

cornualis.full: cornŭālis, e, adj. cornu, of or pertaining to horns: concertatio, with the horns, Cassiod. Var. 1, 37.

cornuarius.full: cornŭārĭus, ii, m. id., a maker of horns or trumpets, Dig. 50, 6, 6.

cornuatus.full: cornŭātus, a, um, adj. id., horn-like, horn-shaped: umbra, Poët. ap. Varr. L. L. 7, § 25.

cornucopiae.full: Cornūcōpĭae, v. cornu, I. A. fin.

cornulum.full: cornŭlum, i, n. dim. cornu, a little horn, = corniculum (late Lat.), Apic. 8, 1.

cornum1.full: cornum, i, n. 1. cornus, the cornelcherry, Verg. G. 2, 34; id. A. 3, 649; Hor. Ep. 1, 16, 9; Ov. M. 1, 105; 8, 665; 13, 816; Col. 12, 10, 3.—* = 1. cornus, II., Ov. M. 8, 408.

cornupeta.full: cornupĕta, ae, adj. comm., pushing or goring with the horns, Vulg. Exod. 21, 29; 21, 36.

cornus1.full: cornus, i, f. (cornus, ūs, f., Sil. 4, 552; Stat. Th. 7, 647), a cornel cherry-tree: Cornus mascula, Linn.; Plin. 16, 25, 42, § 103 sq.; Verg. G. 2, 448; Col. 5, 7, 1 al.— Meton., a javelin made of cornelwood, Verg. A. 9, 698; Sil. 10, 122; Stat. l. l. al.; cf. 1. cornum, II.

cornus3.full: Cornus, i, f., a city on the western coast of Sardinia, Liv. 23, 40, 5 sq.
cornus3.short: Cornus, i, f., a city on the western coast of Sardinia, Liv.

cornutus1.full: cornūtus, a, um, adj. cornu, horned: animalia, Varr. R. R. 2, 7, 2: aries, Col. 7, 3, 4.— Meton. (cf. cornu, I. B.): quadrupedes (i. e. elephanti), Varr. L. L. 7, § 39 Müll.: luna, Amm. 14, 2, 2.— Subst.: cornūti, ōrum, m. (= tauri), bullocks, Att. ap. Non. p. 395, 24 (Trag. Rel. v. 494 Rib.).— cornūtae, ārum, f., a kind of sea-fish. Plin. 32, 11, 53, § 145; Apic. 10, 3, § 454.— Trop.: syllogismus, a horned syllogism, a sophistical conclusion, sophism, = ceratina, Hier. Ep. 69, n. 2; cf.: cornut

cornutus2.full: Cornūtus, i, m., a Roman cognomen. Annaeus Cornutus, a grammarian, Gell. 2, 6.— M. Cornutus, a prætor during the consulate of Hirtius and Pansa, Cic. Phil. 14, 14, 37.
cornutus2.short: Cornūtus, i, m., a Roman cognomen.

coroebus.full: Cŏroebus, i, m., = Κόροιβος, son of Mygdon of Phrygia, who freed Cassandra. and fought for Priam against the Greeks before Troy, Verg. A. 2, 341; 2, 424.
coroebus.short: Cŏroebus, i, m., = Κόροιβος, son of Mygdon of Phrygia, who freed Cassandra.

corolla.full: cŏrolla, ae, f. dim. corona, a little crown or garland (mostly poet.), Plaut. Bacch. 1, 1, 37; Cat. 63, 66; Prop. 1, 16, 7; Plin. 8, 5, 5, § 13; Paul. ex Fest. p. 63, 14 Müll.

corollaria.full: cŏrollārĭa, ae, f. corolla, a female merchant of flower-garlands, Inscr. Orell. 4173.—As a title of a drama of Nævius, Varr. L. L. 7, § 60 Müll.

corollarium.full: cŏrollārĭum, ii, n. id.. Money paid for a garland of flowers; cf. Varr. L. L. 5, § 178; Plin. 21, 2, 3, § 5.—Hence, In gen., a gift, present, douceur, gratuity: hic tamquam festivum acroama, ne sine corollario de convivio discederet, ibidem emblemata evellenda curavit, Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 22, § 49; 2, 3, 50, § 118; 2, 3, 79, § 184; Phaedr. 5, 7, 34; Sen. Ben. 6, 17, 1; Plin. 9, 35, 58, § 120.— Transf., in later philos. writings, a corollary, deduction, Boeth. Consol. 3, pros. 10; 4, 3.

corona.full: cŏrō^na (in the ante-Aug. per. sometimes written chorona, acc. to Quint. 1, 5, 20; cf. the letter C), ae, f., = κορώνη, a garland, chaplet, wreath. Lit., of natural or artificial flowers, etc. (very freq. used for personal adornment at festivals, when sacrificing, or as a gift for friends, etc., for ornamenting the images of the gods, edifices, victims, the dead, etc.), Lucr. 5, 1399; Lex XII. Tab. ap. Plin. 21, 3, 5, § 7; Plaut. Men. 3, 1, 16; Cic. Fl. 31, 75; id. Leg. 2, 24, 60; Liv. 23, 11, 5

coronae.full: Cŏrōnae, ārum, f., name of the two daughters of the Theban Orion, Ov. M. 13, 698.
coronae.short: Cŏrōnae, ārum, f., name of the two daughters of the Theban Orion, Ov.

coronalis.full: cŏrōnālis, e, adj. corona, of or pertaining to a crown: flamma, issuing from a crown, App. M. 1, p. 106, 29.

coronamen.full: cŏrōnāmen, ĭnis, n. corono, a wreathing, crowning: vernum, App. M. 11, p. 261, 10.

coronamentum.full: cŏrōnāmentum, i, n. id., flowers for crowns or garlands, Cato, R. R. 8, 2; Plin. 21, 1, 1, § 1; 21, 9, 28, § 52 sq.; 22, 21, 26, § 53.— The garland or crown itself, Tert. Cor. Mil. 1; 7.

coronarius.full: cŏrōnārĭus, a, um, adj. corona, of or belonging to a wreath: anemonae, suitable for garlands, Plin. 21, 23, 94, § 164: aes, id. 33, 9, 46, § 131: lusus naturae, i. e. presenting a garland-like growth, id. 14, 3, 4, § 42: opus, stucco-work, Vitr. 7, 4 and 6; but also, the making of a golden crown, id. 9, praef. 10.—Esp. freq.: coronarium aurum, a present of gold collected in the provinces for a victorious general (orig. expended for a golden crown; cf. Liv. 38, 37, 4, and 39, 7, 1; but, afterward

coronator.full: cŏrōnātor, ōris, m. corono, a crowner, Aug. Serm. 318.

corone.full: Cŏrōnē, ēs, f., = Κορώνη, a city on the west coast of the Messenian bay, Liv. 39, 49, 1; Plin. 4, 5, 7, § 15.—Hence, adj.: Cŏrō-naeus, a, um, = Κορωναῖος, Coronean: sinus, now the Golfo de Coron, Plin. 4, 5, 7, § 15.
corone.short: Cŏrōnē, ēs, f., = Κορώνη, a city on the west coast of the Messenian bay, Liv.

coronea.full: Cŏrōnēa, ae, f., = Κορώνεια, a town in Bœotia, west of Lake Copais, Nep. Ages. 4, 5; Liv. 33, 29, 6 and 9 al.— Hence the adjj., Cŏrōnaeus or -ēus, a, um, of or belonging to Coronea: ager, Liv. 36, 20, 2.— Cŏrōnensis, e, the same: ager, Liv. 36, 20, 3.
coronea.short: Cŏrōnēa, ae, f., = Κορώνεια, a town in Bœotia, west of Lake Copais, Nep.

coroneola.full: cŏrōnĕŏla, ae, f [corona], an autumnal rose, Plin. 21, 4, 10, § 19 (coronioia, Sillig).
coroneola.short: cŏrōnĕŏla, ae, f [corona], an autumnal rose, Plin.

coroneus.full: Cŏrōneus (trisyl.), ei, m., = Κορωνεύς, a king in Phocis, father of Corone, who was changed to a crow (Κορώνη), Ov. M. 2, 569.
coroneus.short: Cŏrōneus (trisyl.), ei, m., = Κορωνεύς, a king in Phocis, father of Corone, who was changed to a crow (Κορώνη), Ov.

coronides.full: Cŏrōnīdes, ae, m., v. 2. Coronis, II.

coroniola.full: cŏrōnĭŏla, ae, f. dim. corona, a kind of autumnal rose, Plin. 21, 4, 10, § 19 bis.

coronis1.full: cŏrōnis, ĭdis, f., = κορωνίς, a curved line or flourish formed with a pen, which writers or transcribers were accustomed to make at the end of a book or chapter; hence, as in Gr. (cf. Lidd. and Scott, under κορωνίς), for the end: serā coronide longus, * Mart. 10, 1, 1.
coronis1.short: cŏrōnis, ĭdis, f., = κορωνίς, a curved line or flourish formed with a pen, which writers or transcribers were accustomed to make at the end of a book or chapter;

coronis2.full: Cŏrōnis, ĭdis, f., = Κορωνίς, daughter of the Thessalian Phlegyas, mother of Æsculapius by Apollo, Ov. M. 2, 542; Hyg. Fab. 161 and 202; Serv. ad Verg. A. 6, 618; acc. Gr. Coronida, Ov. M. 2, 599.—Hence, Cŏrōnīdes, ae, m., = Κορωνείδης, the son of Coronis, i. e. Æsculapius, Ov. M. 15, 624.
coronis2.short: Cŏrōnis, ĭdis, f., = Κορωνίς, daughter of the Thessalian Phlegyas, mother of Æsculapius by Apollo, Ov.

corono.full: cŏrōno, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. corona, to furnish with a garland or crown, to crown, wreathe (class., esp. freq. in the poets). Lit., aliquid or aliquem: templa, Ov. M. 8, 264; cf.: postes lauro, Quint. 8, 6, 32: aras, Prop. 3 (4), 10, 19. deos fragili myrto, Hor. C. 3, 23, 15: puppim, Ov. F. 4, 335: cratera, Verg. G. 2, 528 (cf.: magnum cratera coronā Induit, id. A. 3, 525); so, crateras magnos statuunt et vina coronant, id. A. 1, 724; 7, 147 Forbig. ad loc. (cf. Nitsch. ad Hom. Od. 1, 419; Buttma

coronopus.full: cŏrōnŏpūs, i, = κορωνόπους, crowfoot; acc. to Sprengel, Plantago coronopus, buckshorn-plantain, Plin. 21, 16, 59, § 99; 22, 19, 22, § 48.

coronula.full: cŏrōnŭla, ae, f. dim. corona, II. D.. The ornament on a mitre, Vulg. Exod. 39, 26.— The rim or border of the base of a laver, Vulg. 3, Reg. 7, 29.— A little crown above the horse's hoof, Veg. Art. Vet. 3, 55, 2.

corporalis.full: corpŏrālis, e, adj. corpus, corporeal, pertaining to the body (post-Aug.; most freq. in the jurists): voluptates, Sen. Ep. 78, 22: sapientiam Stoici corporalem dicunt, id. ib. 117, 2: pignora, Dig. 1, 1, 15: possessio, ib. 13, 7, 40: dicimus quaedam corporalia esse, quaedam incorporalia, Sen. Ep. 58, 11.—Adv.: corpŏrālĭter, corporally, bodily, Petr. 61, 7; Dig. 41, 2, 1; Arn. 5, p. 168.

corporalitas.full: corpŏrālĭtas, ātis, f. corporalis, corporality (late Lat.), Tert. adv. Herm. 36.

corporasco.full: corpŏrasco, ĕre, v. inch. n. [corpus], to assume a body, become incarnate (eccl. Lat.): Deus, Claud. Mam. Stat. Anim. 1, 14.

corporatio.full: corpŏrātĭo, ōnis, f. corporo, an assuming of a body, incarnation (late Lat.), Tert. Carn. Chr. 4; Mart. Cap. 7, § 732.

corporativus.full: corpŏrātīvus, a, um, adj. corporatus, of or pertaining to the forming of a body (late Lat.): adjutoria, Cael. Aur. Tard. 1, 6, 183.

corporatura.full: corpŏrātūra, ae, f. id., the corporeal nature or structure (very rare): pecoris, Col. 6, 2, 15.—In plur.: ampliores, Vitr. 6, 1, 3.

corporatus.full: corpŏrātus, i, m., v. corporo fin.

corporeus.full: corpŏrĕus, a, um, adj. corpus, corporeal. In gen. (rare but class.; most freq. in Lucr.): corporeum et aspectabile itemque tractabile, Cic. Univ. 4: res, id. Fin. 3, 14, 45; Lucr. 2, 186: ignis, Cic. N. D. 2, 15, 41: natura, Lucr. 1, 303; 1, 330: e principiis, id. 4, 536: tela, id. 3, 177: vox, id. 4, 527; 4, 542; opp. incorporeus, Mart. Cap. 6, § 607.— In partic. Composed of flesh, fleshly (several times in Ov. and Plin. the elder): umerus (Pelopis, opp. eburneus), Ov. M. 6, 407: dapes, id. ib.

corporicida.full: corpŏrĭcīda, ae, m. corpus-caedo, a butcher, μακελλιτης, Gloss. Gr. Lat.

corporo.full: corpŏro, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. corpus, to make or fashion into a body, to furnish with a body. Prop.: semen tempore ipso animatur corporaturque, Plin. 7, 15, 13, § 66; cf. id. 10, 53, 74, § 148.—In part. perf.: corporatus Christus et veste carnis indutus, Lact. 4, 26; Tert. Pall. 2: undique mundus, * Cic. Univ. 2 B. and K.— Transf. Of a picture: quae (pictura) prius quam coloribus corporatur, umbra tingitur, Non. p. 37, 13.— To make a body or corpse, i. e. to kill: corporare est interficere et qua

corporosus.full: corpŏrōsus, a, um, adj. corpus, corpulent, gross, Cael. Aur. Acut. 3, 17.

corpulentia.full: corpŭlentĭa, ae, f. corpulentus, corpulence, grossness or fleshiness of body (very rare), Plin. 11, 53, 118, § 283; Sol. 40.— Corporeity (late Lat.), Tert. Carn. Chr. 3 al.

corpulentus.full: corpŭlentus, a, um, adj. corpus, corpulent, fleshy, fat (rare, and only anteclass. and post-Aug.): corpulentior atque habitior, Plaut. Ep. 1, 1, 8: litigator, Quint. 6, 1, 47: homo corpulentus et pinguis, Gell. 7, 22, 1: pecus, Col. 6, 3, 5.— Great: corpulentis Ennius pro magnis dixit, nos corpulentum dicimus corporis obesi hominem, Paul. ex Fest. p. 62, 12 Müll.— Physical, corporeal (late Lat.), Tert. adv. Herm. 19.

corpus.full: corpus, ŏris, n. cf. Sanscr. kar-, to make; Lat. creo, any object composed of materials perceptible by the senses, body, substance (opp. anima and animus; cf. the definition in Dig. 41, 3, 30 pr.). Lit. (very frequent in every period and species of composition). In gen., a body, whether living or lifeless: tangere aut tangi nisi corpus nulla potest res, Lucr. 1, 305: animi voluptates et dolores nasci fatemur e corporis voluptatibus et doloribus, etc., Cic. Fin. 1, 17, 55; cf. id. Tusc. 4, 10, 23

corpusculum.full: corpuscŭlum, i, n. dim. corpus, a little body, most freq. of atoms, Lucr. 2, 152; 2, 530; 4, 199; Cic. N. D. 1, 24, 66 sq.: quantula hominum, Juv. 10, 173.— Esp.: florum, i.e. a collection, Just. praef. — As a term of endearment: melliculum, Plaut. Cas. 4, 4, 23.

corrado.full: cor-rādo (conr-), si, sum, 3, v. a., to scrape or rake together (rare; mostly anteand post-class.). Lit.: corpora, Lucr. 6, 304; cf. id. 6, 444.—Esp., of money, Plaut. Poen. 5, 6, 26; Ter. Ad. 2, 2, 34; Dig. 26, 7, 4 al.; and of the collecting together of one's effects for sale, Ter. Heaut. 1, 1, 89. —* Trop., to procure with difficulty: fidem dictis nostris, Lucr. 1, 402.

corrasus.full: corrāsus (conr-), a, um, Part., from corrado.
corrasus.short: corrāsus (conr-), a, um, Part., from corrado.

corrationalitas.full: cor-rătĭōnālĭtas (conr-), ātis, f., analogy ( = analogia), Aug. Music. 6, 17.
corrationalitas.short: cor-rătĭōnālĭtas (conr-), ātis, f., analogy ( = analogia), Aug.

correctio.full: correctĭo (conr-), ōnis, f. corrigo, an amendment, improvement, correction. In gen. (rare, but in good prose): correctio et emendatio philosophiae veteris, Cic. Fin. 4, 9, 21; cf.: veteris Academiae, id. Ac. 1, 12, 43: quādam adhibita, id. Off. 3, 2, 7: morum, Suet. Tib. 42; id. Dom. 8: delicto dolere, correctione gaudere, Cic. Lael. 24, 90.— Esp., as a rhet. figure, the recalling of a word in order to use a stronger or more significant one in its place, Gr. ἐπανόρθωσις, Cic. de Or. 3, 53, 204:

corrector.full: corrector (conr-), ōris, m. id., a corrector, improver. In gen. (rare but class.): corrector atque emendator nostrae civitatis, Cic. Balb. 8, 20: asperitatis et invidiae et irae, Hor. Ep. 2, 1, 129: unus legum usus, Liv. 45, 32, 7: peccantium, Sen. Ira, 2, 10, 7 al.—Absol., Ter. Ad. 4, 7, 24: corrector Bestius, i. e. a preacher of morals, Hor. Ep. 1, 15, 37: pessimus quisque correctorem asperrime patitur, Sen. Ira, 3, 36, 4. — In the time of the emperors, the title of a kind of land-bailiff, a g

correctura.full: correctūra (conr-), ae, f. corrector, II., the office of a corrector, Aur. Vict. Caes. 35; 39; Aus. Parent. 24, 11.

correctus.full: correctus (conr-), a, um, Part. and P. a., from corrigo.

correcumbens.full: cor-rĕcumbens (conr-), entis, Part. [recumbo], lying down with any one, Tert. Test. An. 4.
