corregionales.full: corrĕgĭōnāles, ĭum, m. con-regio, the adjoining people (late Lat.), Aug. Civ. Dei, 2, 17.

corregno.full: cor-regno (conr-), āre, v. n., to reign together with one (late Lat.), Tert. adv. Jud. 8; Paul. Nol. Carm. 25, 227.

correpo.full: cor-rēpo (conr-), psi, 3, v. n., to creep or slink to a place, to creep (rare but class.): intra murum, Varr. R. R. 2, praef. § 3; Col. 1, praef. § 15: in aliquam onerariam, Cic. Att. 10, 12, 2: correpunt membra pavore, creep, * Lucr. 5, 1218.—Fig.: in dumeta, Cic. N. D. 1, 24, 68 (v. Schoemann ad h. l.).

correpte.full: correptē (conr-), adv. corripio, shortly: dicere aliquid, Gell. 6, 9.—Comp., Ov. P. 4, 12, 13.

correptio.full: correptĭo (conr-), ōnis, f. id. (not ante-Aug., and rare). A laying hold of, seizing: manus, Gell. 20, 10, 8: (morbi), Scrib. Comp. 171.— Trop., reproof, reproach, Tert. Pudic. 14.— A shortening, decreasing: dierum (opp. crescentia), Vitr. 9, 9: syllabae (opp. productio), Quint. 7, 9, 13; cf. vocum, id. 9, 3, 69.

correpto.full: correpto, āre, 1, v. n. freq. [correpo], to creep (late Lat.): rursum matris in alvum, Juvenc. 2, 192.

correptor.full: correptor (conr-), ōris, m. corripio, a reprover, censurer (cf. correptio, I. B.); the reading of some editions of Sen. Ira, 2, 10, 7, and 3, 36, 4, for which Haase has corrector, q. v.

correptus.full: correptus (conr-), a, um, Part., from corripio.
correptus.short: correptus (conr-), a, um, Part., from corripio.

corresupinatus.full: cor-rĕsŭpīnātus (conr-), a, um, Part. [resupino], bent backwards at the same time, Tert. Anim. 48.

corresuscito.full: cor-rĕsuscĭto (conr-), āvi, ātum, 1, v. a., to raise from the dead together (eccl. Lat.), Tert. Res Carn. 23; Hier. adv. Jov. 1, 38 al.

correus.full: cor-rĕus (conr-), i, m., a partaker in guilt, a joint criminal, Dig. 34, 3, 3, § 3.
correus.short: cor-rĕus (conr-), i, m., a partaker in guilt, a joint criminal, Dig.

corrhagon.full: Corrhăgon or -gum, i, n., a fortress in Macedonia, Liv. 31, 27, 2.
corrhagon.short: Corrhăgon or -gum, i, n., a fortress in Macedonia, Liv.

corrideo.full: cor-rīdĕo (conr-), ēre, v. n., to laugh together or aloud (ante- and post-class.). Lit., Aug. Conf. 4, 8: alicui, Vulg. Gen. 21, 6.— Trop.: perfusa lepore Omnia corrident, Lucr. 4, 81.

corrigia.full: corrī^gĭa (conr-), ae, f. corrigo. A shoe-tie, shoe-latchet, Varr. ap. Non. p. 448, 26; Cic. Div. 2, 40, 84; Plin. 30, 4, 12, § 35. — A rein for a horse, Edict. Diocl. p. 26.

corrigo.full: cor-rĭgo (conr-), rexi, rectum, 3, v. a. rego, to make straight, set right, bring into order. Lit. (rare): catenas, Cato, R. R. 18 fin.: alicui digitum, Plin. 7, 20, 19, § 83: verbaque correctis incidere talia ceris, smoothed out, erased, Ov. M. 9, 529: corpus informe gibbo, Aug. ap. Macr. S. 2, 4: vulvas conversas, Plin. 24, 5, 13, § 22; cf.: malas labentes, Suet. Aug. 99: cursum (navis), Liv. 29, 27, 14; cf.: se flexus (fluminum), Plin. 3, 1, 3, § 16.— Prov.: curva, to attempt to make crooked

corripio.full: cor-rĭpĭo (conr-), rĭpŭi, reptum, 3, v. a. rapio, to seize or snatch up, to collect, to seize upon, take hold of (very freq., and class. in prose and poetry). Lit. In gen.: hominem conripi ac suspendi jussit in oleastro, Cic. Verr. 2, 3, 23, § 57; Caes. B. C. 3, 109; cf. Ov. M. 9, 217 al.: arcumque manu celeresque sagittas, Verg. A. 1, 188; cf.: lora manu, Ov. M. 2, 145: fasces, Sall. C. 18, 5: arma, Vell. 2, 110 et saep.: corpus, to rise up quickly, start up: ex somno, Lucr. 3, 164; Verg. A. 4,

corrivalis.full: cor-rīvālis (conr-), is, m., a joint rival, Quint. Decl. 14, 12.
corrivalis.short: cor-rīvālis (conr-), is, m., a joint rival, Quint.

corrivatio.full: corrīvātĭo (conr-), ōnis, f. corrivo, a drawing together of streams of water (Pliny): aquae pluviae, Plin. 31, 3, 27, § 44; 33, 4, 21, § 74; 36, 15, 24, § 124.

corrivium.full: corrīvĭum (conr-), ii, n. cum-rivis, the confluence of brooks: conriviis Idaeis, Auct. Itin. Alex. Magn. 19 Mai.

corrivo.full: cor-rīvo (conr-), āvi, ātum, 1, v. a., to conduct streams of water together, to draw together into one stream (post-Aug.): venas aquarum, Sen. Q. N. 3, 19, 4; cf. aquam, Dig. 39, 3, 3; Plin. 31, 4, 30, § 53: liquorem salis, id. 6, 14, 17, § 43: Tiberim piscinis, id. 3, 5, 9, § 53; with in aliquid, id. 6, 16, 18, § 47.

corroboramentum.full: corrōbŏrāmentum (conr-), i, n. corroboro, a means of strengthening; trop.: exercitia et corroboramenta virtutis, Lact. 3, 12, 35.

corroboro.full: cor-rōbŏro (conr-), āvi, ātum, 1, v. a., to strengthen or invigorate, to make strong, to corroborate (in good prose; most freq. in Cic.). Lit.: (puerilis tua vox) se corroboravit, Cic. Sest. 4, 10: cum is jam se corroboravisset ac vir inter viros esset, i. e. had become stronger, greater, was grown up, id. Cael. 5, 11; cf. id. ib. 17, 41; Suet. Tib. 11: cerebrum, Plin. 11, 37, 49, § 134: stomachum, id. 20, 23, 99, § 263: torpentis membrorum partis, id. 24, 4, 7, § 13: militem opere assiduo, Suet

corroco.full: corrŏco, ōnis, m., a kind of fish, now unknown, Aus. Ep. 4, 60.
corroco.short: corrŏco, ōnis, m., a kind of fish, now unknown, Aus.

corrodo.full: cor-rōdo (conr-), si, sum, 3, v. a., to gnaw, gnaw to pieces (very rare): Platonis Politiam (mures), Cic. Div. 2, 27, 59 ter: ossa, * Juv. 15, 80.

corrogatio.full: corrŏgātĭo (conr-), ōnis, f. corrogo, a bringing together, Vulg. Ecclus. 32, 3.

corrogo.full: cor-rŏgo (conr-), āvi, ātum, 1, v. a., to bring together by entreaty, to bring together, collect (rare, but in good prose): suos necessarios ab atriis, Cic. Quint. 6, 25; so of personal objects, id. Phil. 3, 8, 20; Quint. 10, 1, 18; Plin. Ep. 2, 14, 9: auxilia ab sociis, Liv. 43, 9, 7: pecuniam ad necessarios sumptus, Caes. B. C. 3, 102: nummulos de nepotum donis, Cic. Verr. 2, 3, 79, § 184: vela cum antennis ex navibus, Liv. 33, 48, 5 al.

corrosus.full: corrōsus (conr-), a, um, Part., from corrodo.
corrosus.short: corrōsus (conr-), a, um, Part., from corrodo.

corrotundo.full: cor-rŏtundo (conr-), āvi, ātum, 1, v. a., to make round, to round off (postAug.). Prop.: cometarum corpus, Sen. Q. N. 7, 26, 2; 4, 3, 5; Petr. 39, 15.— Trop.: enthymemata sua gestu velut corrotundant, Quint. 11, 3, 102.—* Transf., of money (cf. rotundo, and our phrase, a round sum), to make up a sum of money: centies sestertium, Petr. 76, 8.

corruda.full: corrūda (conr-), ae, f., wild asparagus, Cato, R. R. 6, 3; Varr. R. R. 1, 24, 4; Col. 11, 3, 43; Plin. 19, 8, 42, § 145.
corruda.short: corrūda (conr-), ae, f., wild asparagus, Cato, R.

corrugis.full: cor-rūgis (conr-), e, adj. ruga, having wrinkles or folds, corrugate: sinus (chlamydis), Nemes. Cyn. 92.

corrugo.full: cor-rūgo (conr-), no perf., ātum, 1, v. a., to make full of wrinkles, to wrinkle, corrugate (very rare): olivam, Col. 12, 50, 19; cf. acina, id. 12, 39, 3.—Poet.: ne sordida mappa Corruget nares, i. e. produce loathing, cause disgust, Hor. Ep. 1, 5, 23 (cf. Quint. 11, 3, 80).

corrugus.full: corrūgus (conr-), i, m. of the same stem with arrugia; in the lang. of mining, a canal, water-conduit, Plin. 33, 4, 21, § 74.

corrumpo.full: cor-rumpo (conr-), rūpi, ruptum (rumptum), 3, v. a. (orig., to break to pieces; hence), To destroy, ruin, waste, bring to naught (class., but less freq. than in the signif. II.]. Lit.: reliquum frumentum flumine atque incendio corruperunt, Caes. B. G. 7, 55: domum et semet igni conrumpunt, Sall. J. 76, 6; cf.: plura igni, id. ib. 92, 3; 92, 8: res familiares, id. ib. 64, 5: ungues dentibus, i. e. to bite, Prop. 2, 4, 3 (13).— Trop.: diem, Plaut. Men. 4, 2, 31: animo malest: corrupta sum atque ab

corruo.full: cor-rŭo (conr-), ŭi, 3, v. n. and a. Neutr. To fall together, fall or tumble down, fall, sink to the ground, etc. (class. in prose and poetry). Lit.: tabernae mihi duae corruerunt, Cic. Att. 14, 9, 1; cf.: aedes corruerunt, id. Top. 3, 15: triclinium supra convivas, Quint. 11, 2, 13: quicquid superstruxeris corruet, id. 1, 4, 5: quid labefactum viribus ignis, Ov. M. 2, 403; cf.: arbor labefacta Ictibus innumeris, id. ib. 8, 777; so, arbor, Suet. Dom. 15: statuae equestres, id. Vit. 9 et saep.: p

corrupte.full: corruptē (conr-), adv., v. corrumpo, P. a. fin.

corruptela.full: corruptēla (conr-), ante-class. also corrumptēla, ae, f. corrumpo, that which corrupts, a corrupting, corruption, seduction, bribery, etc. Prop. (freq. and class. in sing. and plur.): mores hac (sc. cantūs) dulcedine corruptelaque depravati, Cic. Leg. 2, 15, 38: collapsus est hic in corruptelam suam, Plaut. Truc. 3, 2, 3: quem (adulescentulum) corruptelarum illecebris irretisses, Cic. Cat. 1, 6, 13: stupra dico et corruptelas et adulteria, id. Tusc. 4, 35, 75; cf. Suet. Claud. 16: via una corrup

corruptibilis.full: corruptĭbĭlis (conr-), e, adj. id., liable to decay, corruptible, perishable (eccl. Lat.), Lact. 6, 25; Arn. 2, 68 al.—Comp., Aug. de Vera Relig. 41.

corruptibilitas.full: corruptĭbĭlĭtas (conr-), ātis, f. corruptibilis, corruptibility, perishableness (eccl. Lat.), Tert. adv. Marc. 2, 16.

corruptio.full: corruptĭo (conr-), ōnis, f [corrumpo]. Act., a corrupting, spoiling, seducing: militum, bribery, Tac. A. 11, 2: judicii, Ascon. ad Cic. Verr. 1, 6, 15, p. 131 Bait. —Absol.: eo usque corruptionis provectus est, ut, etc., Tac. A. 2, 55.— Pass., a corrupt condition, corruption (very rare): totius corporis, Cic. Tusc. 4, 13, 29.— Trop.: opinionum, Cic. Tusc. 4, 13, 29.

corruptivus.full: corruptīvus (conr-), a, um, adj. id., corruptible, perishable (eccl. Lat.), Tert. Res Carn. 50.—corruptīvē, adv., Boëth Arist. Top. 7, 2, p. 721.

corruptor.full: corruptor (conr-; corrumptor, Plaut. Trin. 2, 1, 14 Ritschl), ōris, m. id., a corrupter, misleader, seducer, briber: latebricolarum hominum (amor), Plaut. Trin. 2, 1, 14: civium, id. Poen. 3, 6, 21: juventutis, Cic. Cat. 2, 4, 7: estne in corruptorem marito justior potestas? Hor. S. 2, 7, 63; cf.: virginum Vestalium, Suet. Dom. 8: nostri, Cic. Rab. Post. 3, 6; cf.: tribus venditor et corruptor, id. Planc. 16, 38.

corruptorius.full: corruptōrĭus (conr-), a um, adj. corrumpo, destructible, corruptible, perishable (eccl. Lat.), Tert. adv. Marc. 2, 16: sensus in homine, id. ib.

corruptrix.full: corruptrix (conr-), īcis, f. corruptor, she that corrupts or seduces; or adj., corrupting (very rare): tam depravatis moribus, tam corruptrice provinciā, Cic. Q. Fr. 1, 1, 6, § 19: licentia, rerum corruptrix et morum, Amm. 25, 3, 18.

corruptus.full: corruptus (conr-), a, um, Part. and P. a., from corrumpo.

corruspor.full: cor-ruspor (conr-), āri, v. dep., to search carefully after, = conquiro, Plaut. Fragm. ap. Paul. ex Fest. p. 62 Müll.

corsae.full: corsae, ārum, f., = κόρσαι; in arch., the outer strip in the moulding about a door, a girder, Vitr. 4, 6, 3 sq.

corsica.full: Corsĭca, ae (Corsis, ĭdis, Prisc. Perieg. 470), f. (among the Greeks, Κύρνος, Κορσίς), the island Corsica, in the Mediterranean Sea, renowned in ancient times for the honey and wax of wild bees; the place of banishment of Seneca the philosopher, Liv. Epit. 17; Sen. Cons. Helv. 6, 2; Tac. H. 2, 16; Mel. 2, 7, 19; Plin. 3, 6, 12, § 80; Monum. Scip. ap. Inscr. Orell. 552; Cic. N. D. 3, 20, 52 al.— Hence adjj. Cor-sus, a, um, Corsican, Ov. F. 6, 194.—In plur.: Corsi, ōrum, m., the Corsicans, Liv. 42

corsoides.full: corsŏīdes, is, m., = κορσοειδής (hairlike), an unknown precious stone, Plin. 37, 10, 56, § 153.
corsoides.short: corsŏīdes, is, m., = κορσοειδής (hairlike), an unknown precious stone, Plin.

corsus.full: Corsus, a, um, v. Corsica, II. A.

cortex.full: cortex, ĭcis, m. and rar. f. (cf. Quint. 1, 5, 35) [Sanscr. kart, to cut, split; Gr. κείρω; cf. culter], the bark, rind, shell, hull. Prop., of plants: obducuntur libro aut cortice trunci, Cic. N. D. 2, 47, 120. In gen. Masc., Varr. ap. Non. p. 199, 26; Verg. G. 2, 74; id. A. 7, 742; Ov. M. 1, 554; id. F. 2, 649; Plin. 2, 103, 106, § 226 al.; cf. infra.— Fem., Lucr. 4, 48; Verg. E. 6, 63; Ov. M. 10, 512; 14, 630; Mart. 14, 209; Scrib. Comp. 60.— In partic., the bark of the cork-tree, cork, used

corticatus.full: cortĭcātus, a, um, adj. cortex, covered with a bark (very rare): pars (sarmenti), Pall. Mart. 1, 2: pix, resin taken from a tree with a portion of the bark, Col. 12, 23, 1.

corticeus.full: cortĭcĕus, a, um, adj. id., of bark or cork, Varr. R. R. 1, 40; 3, 16; Plin. 11, 21, 24, § 71 (cortice, Sillig); Aus. Mos. 246 al.

corticosus.full: cortĭcōsus, a, um, adj. id., abounding in bark: radix, Plin. 20, 19, 78, § 205: tus, id. 12, 14, 32, § 59.

corticulus.full: cortĭcŭlus, i, m. dim. id., a small or thin rind, bark, or shell, Col. 12, 47, 10; 12, 50, 10.

cortina.full: cortīna, ae, f., a round vessel, a kettle, caldron (for cooking, liquids, etc.), Cato, R. R. 66, 1; Plin. 15, 6, 6, § 22 al.; 36, 26, 65, § 191; Plaut. Poen. 5, 5, 12.— In partic., the tripod of Apollo, in the form of a caldron, Verg. A. 3, 92; 6, 347; Ov. M. 15, 635.—Hence, also, a tripod as a sacred offering, Suet. Aug. 52.— Meton., of any thing caldron-shaped, an arch, a circle (very rare); the cault of heaven, Enn. ap. Varr. L. L. 7, § 48 Müll. N. cr. (Ann. v. 9 Vahl.); the circle of a theat
cortina.short: cortīna, ae, f., a round vessel, a kettle, caldron (for cooking, liquids, etc.), Cato, R.

cortinale.full: cortīnāle, is, n. cortina, the caldron-room, the place where new wine was boiled down in the cortina, Col. 1, 6, 19.

cortinipotens.full: Cortīnĭ-pŏtens, entis, adj. id., powerful on the tripod, an epithet of Apollo, Lucil. ap. Non. p. 258, 33.

cortinula.full: cortīnŭla, ae, f. dim. id., a small kettle, Amm. 29, 1, 31 dub. (v. Wagner ad h. l.).

cortona.full: Cortōna, ae, f., a very ancient town in Etruria, northwest of Lake Trasimenus, Liv. 9, 37, 12; 22, 4, 1.—Hence, Cortōnen-sis, e, adj., of Cortona: montes, Liv. 22, 4, 2.—Cortōnenses, its inhabitants, Plin. 3, 5, 8, § 52.
cortona.short: Cortōna, ae, f., a very ancient town in Etruria, northwest of Lake Trasimenus, Liv.

cortumio.full: cortumio, an old word of the augurial lang., perh. equiv. to contumio, from contueor, Varr. L. L. 7, § 9 Müll.
cortumio.short: cortumio, an old word of the augurial lang., perh.

cortuosa.full: Cortuosa, ae, f., a town of Etruria, Liv. 6, 4, 9.
cortuosa.short: Cortuosa, ae, f., a town of Etruria, Liv.

cortynia.full: Cortȳnia (Gort-), ae, f., a town of Crete, Varr. R. R. 1, 7, 6; cf. Gortyna.
cortynia.short: Cortȳnia (Gort-), ae, f., a town of Crete, Varr.

coruncanius.full: Cŏruncānĭus, a, name of a Roman plebeian gens, Cic. Planc. 8, 20; id. Brut. 14, 55; Liv. 1, 38; Tac. A. 11, 24; Sen. Vit. Beat. 21, 3; id. Ep. 114, 13.
coruncanius.short: Cŏruncānĭus, a, name of a Roman plebeian gens, Cic.

coruscamen.full: cŏruscāmen, ĭnis, n. corusco, a glittering, a flash (post-class.), App. de Deo Socr. p. 226 Bip.

coruscatio.full: cŏruscātĭo, ōnis, f. id., a glittering, a flash, coruscation (post-class.): (margaritarum), Sol. 53 fin.: immanis, Vop. Car. 8.

coruscifer.full: cŏruscĭfer, fĕra, fĕrum, adj. coruscusfero, lightning-bearing (post-class.): caelum, Mart. Cap. 8, § 808.

corusco.full: cŏrusco, āre, v. a. and n. (the access. form conisco is found in some copies of Lucr. 2, 320, and Cic. Fragm. ap. Quint. 8, 3, 21) [root scar-, to leap; Gr. σκαίρω; cf. also κορύσσω; v. Lidd. and Scott, s. v.]. To thrust or push with the horns (very rare): agni ludunt blandeque coruscant, Lucr. 2, 320: frontem, Juv. 12, 6: caput opponis cum eo coruscans, Cic. Fragm. ap. Quint. 8, 3, 21.— Transf., to move quickly, to vibrate, shake, brandish, wave, tremble, etc. (poet.). Act.: duo Gaesa manu, Ver

coruscus.full: cŏruscus, a, um, adj. corusco, II. (poet.). In waving motion, waving, vibrating, tremulous: silvae, Verg. A. 1, 164: ilices, id. ib. 12, 701.—Humorously: omnia corusca prae tremore fabulor, i. e. trembling, Plaut. Rud. 2, 6, 42.— Flashing, gleaming, glittering: fulgura, Lucr. 5, 296.—So of lightning: ignis, Lucr. 6, 203; Hor. C. 1, 34, 6: lumina, Lucr. 6, 283.—Also: vis fulminis, Poët. ap. Cic. Tusc. 2, 9, 21: sol, Verg. G. 1, 234; cf.: radii (solis), Ov. M. 1, 768: lampades, id. ib. 12, 247: vi

corvinus.full: corvīnus, a, um, adj. corvus, of or pertaining to the raven, raven-: ovum, Plin. 10, 12, 15, § 32: nigredo, App. M. 2, p. 118, 31.— Corvīnus, i, m., a surname in the gens Valeria; cf. Gell. 9, 11; Flor. 1, 13, 20 Duker.

corvus.full: corvus, i, m. root kar-, kal-, to sound; cf.: καλέω, κόραξ, etc., a raven, Plin. 10, 43, 60, § 121 sq.; acc. to the fable, orig. white, changed to a black bird in punishment for treachery, Ov. M. 2, 541 sq.; on account of its gift of prophecy (oscen, Hor. C. 3, 27, 11), consecrated to Apollo, Ov. M. 5, 329 (hence, Phoebeïus ales, id. ib. 2, 545: Delphicus ales, Petr. 122; cf. also Stat. Th. 3, 506); its flight to the right indicated good fortune, Plaut. As. 2, 1, 12; Cic. Div. 1, 39, 85.— Prov.:

corybas.full: Cŏrўbas, antis, m., = Κορύβας. Plur.: Cŏrўbantes, ium, m. (sing. Corybas, Claud. IV. Cons. Hon. 148 al.), = Κορύβαντες, the priests of Cybele, whose religious service consisted in noisy music and wild armed dances, later interchanged with Curetes (q. v.), Hor. C. 1, 16, 8; Ov. F. 4, 210; Sen. Herc. Oet. 1877; Lact. 1, 13, 5; cf. Serv. ad Verg. A. 3, 111; Diom. p. 474 P.—Sing., Juv. 5, 25; Mart. 1, 70, 10; Claud. IV. Cons. Hon. 150; id. Rapt. Pros. 1, 208.—Hence, Cŏrўbantĭus, a, um, adj., of the

coryceum.full: cōrўcēum, i, n., = κωρυκεῖον, the place in the palæstra where the athletae exercised themselves by striking a suspended sack filled with fig-grains, flour, sand, etc. (v. Lidd. and Scott, s. v. κώρυκος, II.), Vitr. 5, 11, 2; cf. 1. corycus.
coryceum.short: cōrўcēum, i, n., = κωρυκεῖον, the place in the palæstra where the athletae exercised themselves by striking a suspended sack filled with fig-grains, flour, sand, etc.

corycius.full: Cōrўcĭus, a, um, adj., = Κωρύκιος, Corycian. Of or belonging to the Corycian mountain cave (Κωρύκιον ἄντρον) on Parnassus, famous in ancient fable: Co rycium nemus, i. e. Parnassian, Stat. Th. 7, 347: umbra, id. S. 5, 3, 5.—Hence, Cōrўcĭdes Nymphae, the daughters of Plistus, Ov. M. 1, 320.— Of or pertaining to the promontory Corycus; v. 2. Corycus, II.
corycius.short: Cōrўcĭus, a, um, adj., = Κωρύκιος, Corycian.

corycomachia.full: cōrўcŏmăchĭa, ae, f., = κωρυκομαχία, the exercise of the athletae with the corycus (v. 1. corycus), Cael. Aur. Tard. 5, 11, 134.
corycomachia.short: cōrўcŏmăchĭa, ae, f., = κωρυκομαχία, the exercise of the athletae with the corycus (v.

corycus1.full: cōrўcus (cōrĭ-), i, m., = κώρυκος, a leathern sack filled with sand, flour, etc., by means of which the athletae exercised in the palæstra; only fig.: corycus laterum et vocis meae Bestia, Cic. Phil. 13, 12, 26 B. and K., Halm; cf. Klotz and Orell. ad loc.
corycus1.short: cōrўcus (cōrĭ-), i, m., = κώρυκος, a leathern sack filled with sand, flour, etc., by means of which the athletae exercised in the palæstra;

corycus2.full: Cōrўcus or -ŏs, i, m., = Κώρυκος, a promontory in Cilicia, with a town and harbor of the same name, and a cave, very celebrated in ancient times; also famous for its production of saffron; now Khorgos, Mel 1, 13, 2; Plin. 5, 27, 22, § 92; Cic. Fam. 12, 13, 2; Liv. 33, 20, 4 al.: Corycus mons, Sen. Q. N. 3, 11, 2.—Hence, Cōrў-cĭus, a, um, adj., Corycian: specus, Mel. 1, 13, 3: antra, Plin. 31, 2, 20, § 30: crocus, Hor. S. 2, 4, 68; cf. Plin. 21, 6, 17, § 31; in the same sense, nimbus, Mart. 9, 39
corycus2.short: Cōrўcus or -ŏs, i, m., = Κώρυκος, a promontory in Cilicia, with a town and harbor of the same name, and a cave, very celebrated in ancient times;

corydalus.full: cŏrўdălus, i, m., = κορυδαλός, the crested lark, Serv. ad Verg. E. 2, 1.
corydalus.short: cŏrўdălus, i, m., = κορυδαλός, the crested lark, Serv.

corydon.full: Cŏrўdon, ōnis, m., = Κορυδών, Greek proper name; of a shepherd, Verg. E. 2, 1 sq.; Prop. 2 (3), 34, 73.al.
corydon.short: Cŏrўdon, ōnis, m., = Κορυδών, Greek proper name;

corylenus.full: Cŏrўlēnus, i, f., = Κορυληνός, a city of Æolis, Liv. 37, 21, 5.
corylenus.short: Cŏrўlēnus, i, f., = Κορυληνός, a city of Æolis, Liv.

coryletum.full: cŏrўlētum or cŏrŭlētum, i, n. corylus, a hazel-thicket, a copse of hazeltrees, Ov. F. 2, 587.

corylus.full: cŏrўlus or cŏrŭlus, i, f., = κόρυλος, a hazel or filbert shrub, Cato, R. R. 18, 9; Verg. E. 1, 14; id. G. 2, 65; Ov. M. 10, 93 al.
corylus.short: cŏrўlus or cŏrŭlus, i, f., = κόρυλος, a hazel or filbert shrub, Cato, R.

corymbia.full: cŏrўmbĭa, ae, f., = κορυμβία, a species of the plant ferula, Plin. 19, 9, 56, § 175.
corymbia.short: cŏrўmbĭa, ae, f., = κορυμβία, a species of the plant ferula, Plin.

corymbiatus.full: cŏrymbĭātus, a, um, adj. corymbus, set round with clusters of ivy-berries, corymbiated: discus, Gall. ap. Treb. Claud. 17, § 5.

corymbifer.full: Cŏrymbĭfer, feri, adj. m. [corymbusfero], bearing clusters of ivy-berries, an epithet of Bacchus, Ov. F. 1, 393.

corymbion.full: cŏrymbĭon, ii, n., = κορύμβιον, hair curled in the form of clusters of ivy-berries, Petr. 110, 1 and 5.
corymbion.short: cŏrymbĭon, ii, n., = κορύμβιον, hair curled in the form of clusters of ivy-berries, Petr.

corymbites.full: cŏrymbītes, ae, m., = κορυμβίτης, a species of the plant tithymalus, Plin. 26, 8, 44, § 70.
corymbites.short: cŏrymbītes, ae, m., = κορυμβίτης, a species of the plant tithymalus, Plin.

corymbus.full: cŏrymbus, i, m., = κόρυμβος, a cluster of fruit, a cluster of flowers of different plants; so esp. freq. of a cluster of ivyberries, Verg. E. 3, 39; Ov. M. 3, 665; Juv. 6, 52; for the crowning of Bacchus, Prop. 2, 30 (3, 28), 39; 3 (4), 17, 29; of Osiris, Tib. 1, 7, 45: ferulae, Plin. 19, 9, 56, § 175: elaphobosci, id. 22, 22, 37, § 79 al.— Meton. Of carved clusters for the ornamenting of ships, Val. Fl. 1, 273; 4, 691.— The nipple, Ser. Samm. 20, 356.— An elevation of earth, Auct. Aetn. 106.
corymbus.short: cŏrymbus, i, m., = κόρυμβος, a cluster of fruit, a cluster of flowers of different plants;

corynaeus.full: Cŏrўnaeus, i, m., name of two Trojans, companions of Æneas, Verg. A. 6, 228; 9, 571; 12, 298.
corynaeus.short: Cŏrўnaeus, i, m., name of two Trojans, companions of Æneas, Verg.

coryphaeus.full: cŏrўphaeus, i, m., = κορυφαῖος, a leader, chief, head: Epicureorum Zeno, Cic. N. D. 1, 21, 59.
coryphaeus.short: cŏrўphaeus, i, m., = κορυφαῖος, a leader, chief, head: Epicureorum Zeno, Cic.

coryphasia.full: Cŏrўphāsĭa, ae, f., = κορυφασία (v. Anthol. Gr. 1, p. 226), a title of Minerva (from her worship at Cŏrўphāsĭum, a promontory on the south coast of Messenia, Plin. 4, 5, 9, § 18), Arn. 4, p. 137.

coryphe.full: Cŏrўphē, ēs, or Cŏrўpha, ae, f., daughter of Oceanus, mother of the fourth Minerva, Cic. N. D. 3, 23, 59; Arn. 4, p. 137.
coryphe.short: Cŏrўphē, ēs, or Cŏrўpha, ae, f., daughter of Oceanus, mother of the fourth Minerva, Cic.

coryphia.full: coryphĭa, ōrum, n., a kind of murex or snail, yielding a purple dye, Plin. 32, 7, 27, § 84; 32, 11, 53, § 147.
coryphia.short: coryphĭa, ōrum, n., a kind of murex or snail, yielding a purple dye, Plin.

corysidia.full: corysidia, ae, f., another name of the plant Minyas, Plin. 24, 17, 100, § 157 (corinthia, Sillig).
corysidia.short: corysidia, ae, f., another name of the plant Minyas, Plin.

corythus.full: Cŏrўthus, i, m., = Κόρυθος. An ancient town in Etruria, so named from its mythical founder, later called Cortona, Verg. A. 7, 209; 10, 719.—Poet., in gen., for Etruria, Verg. A. 9, 10; and for Italia, id. ib. 3, 170 Forbig. ad loc.— A companion of Perseus, Ov. M. 5, 125.— Son of Paris and Œnone, Ov. M. 7, 361.— One of the Lapithæ, Ov. M. 12, 290.

corytos.full: cōrȳtŏs or -tus (˘˘ Sid. Carm. 11, 56), i, m., = κωρυτός, a quiver, Verg. A. 10, 169 Serv.; Ov. Tr. 5, 7, 15; Sil. 7, 443; Stat. Th. 4, 269.—Poet.: velox corytus et arcus, Stat. Th. 7, 660.

coryza.full: cŏrȳza, ae, f., = κόρυζα, a catarrh, Cael. Aur. Acut. 2, 17, 101.
coryza.short: cŏrȳza, ae, f., = κόρυζα, a catarrh, Cael.

cos1.full: cōs, cōtis, f. Sanscr. ça, to whet, sharpen; cf. cautes, any hard stone, flintstone, Cic. Div. 1, 17, 33; Liv. 1, 36, 4 and 5; Curt. 4, 6, 8; 5, 3, 8; 8, 11, 23; Verg. E. 8, 43. — In partic., a whetstone, hone, grindstone, Plin. 36, 22, 47, § 164; Hor. C. 2, 8, 16; Quint. 2, 12, 8.— Trop.: ipsam iracundiam fortitudinis quasi cotem esse dicebant, Cic. Ac. 2, 44, 135; cf. id. Tusc. 4, 19, 43; Hor. A. P. 304.

cos2.full: Cōs or Cŏus (Cō^ŏs), i, f., = Κῶς or Κόως, one of the Sporadic Islands in the Myrtoan Sea, on the coast of Caria, celebrated for the cultivation of the vine and for weaving; the birthplace of Hippocrates, Apelles, and Philetas, now Stanco.; nom. Cos, Varr. Fragm. p. 363 Bip.; Mel. 2, 7, 4; Plin. 5, 31, 36, § 135 al.: Cous, Liv. 37, 16, 2. —Acc. Coum, Curt. 3, 1, 19 Zumpt N. cr.; Plin. 2, 108, 112, § 245; Tac. A. 2, 75.—Abl. Coo, Cic. Att. 9, 9, 2; Plin. 13, 1, 2, § 5; Stat. S. 1, 2, 252: Co, Pli
cos2.short: Cōs or Cŏus (Cō^ŏs), i, f., = Κῶς or Κόως, one of the Sporadic Islands in the Myrtoan Sea, on the coast of Caria, celebrated for the cultivation of the vine and for weaving;

cosa.full: Cŏsa, ae (on coins also Cossa; access. form Cŏsae, ārum, Verg. A. 10, 168), f., = Κόσσα and Κόσσαι. An ancient town in Etruria, not far from the coast, now Ansedonia, above Orbitello, Mel. 2, 4, 9; Liv. Ep. 14; id. 22, 11, 6; Plin. 3, 5, 8, § 51; Vell. 1, 14, 6; Tac. A. 2, 39 al.—Hence, Cŏ-sānus (Coss-), a, um, adj., of Cosa: litus, Plin. 3, 6, 12, § 81: portus, Liv. 22, 11, 6: praedia, Suet. Vesp. 2.—Subst., Cŏsā-num, i, n. The territory around Cosa, Caes. B. C. 1, 34.— A country seat near Cosa

coscinomantia.full: coscĭnŏmantīa, ae, f., = κοσκινομαντεία, a divination by the sieve, Aug. 5, p. 426.
coscinomantia.short: coscĭnŏmantīa, ae, f., = κοσκινομαντεία, a divination by the sieve, Aug.

cosconius.full: Coscōnĭus, a, name of a Roman plebeian gens; esp., C. Cosconius, prætor during Cicero's consulate, also known as a writer on antiquities, Varr. L. L. 6, § 39, and § 89 Müll.; Cic. Sull. 14, 42; id. Brut. 69, 242.— C. Cosconius Calidianus, an inferior orator, Cic. Brut. 69, 242.— A writer of epigrams, Mart. 2, 77, 1; 3, 69, 7.
cosconius.short: Coscōnĭus, a, name of a Roman plebeian gens;

cosmeta.full: cosmēta, ae, m., = κοσμήτης, he who ornaments one, an adorner; a designation of a slave who had charge of the wardrobe and decoration of his mistress, Juv. 6, 477.
cosmeta.short: cosmēta, ae, m., = κοσμήτης, he who ornaments one, an adorner;

cosmicos.full: cosmĭcŏs, a, um, adj., = κοσμικός (syn. mundanus), of or belonging to the world; as subst. cosmĭcŏs, i, m., a citizen of the world, a cosmopolite, Mart. 7, 41, 1.— cosmĭca, ōrum, n., worldly things, Mart. 7, 41, 2.

cosmittere.full: cosmittere, old form for committere, acc. to Paul. ex Fest. p. 67, 8 Müll.
cosmittere.short: cosmittere, old form for committere, acc.

cosmoe.full: Cosmoe, ōrum, m., = Κόσμοι, a high council of the Cretans, answering to the Lacedaemonian Ephori, Cic. Rep. 2, 33, 58 fin. Moser N. cr.
cosmoe.short: Cosmoe, ōrum, m., = Κόσμοι, a high council of the Cretans, answering to the Lacedaemonian Ephori, Cic.

cosmographia.full: cosmō^grăphĭa, ae, f., = κοσμογραφία, a description of the universe, Cassiod. Inst. Div. Litt. 25.
cosmographia.short: cosmō^grăphĭa, ae, f., = κοσμογραφία, a description of the universe, Cassiod.

cosmographus.full: cosmŏgrăphus, i, m., = κοσμογράφος, one who describes the world, a cosmographer, Auct. Progen. Aug. 2; Mythogr. Lat. 3, 6, 35.
cosmographus.short: cosmŏgrăphus, i, m., = κοσμογράφος, one who describes the world, a cosmographer, Auct.

cosmus.full: Cosmus, i, m., a celebrated maker of, and dealer in unguents at Rome, Juv. 8, 86; Mart. 11, 8, 9; 1, 89, 2; 14, 110, 1.—Hence, Cosmĭānus, a, um, adj., named or derived from Cosmus: ampullae, Mart. 3, 82, 26; and subst.: Cosmĭānum, i, n. (sc. unguentum), an unguent made by him, Mart. 12, 55, 7; 11, 15, 6.
cosmus.short: Cosmus, i, m., a celebrated maker of, and dealer in unguents at Rome, Juv.

cossigerare.full: cossĭgĕrāre (perh. corrupted), word of unknown meaning, Att. ap. Non. p. 61, 24.

cossinius.full: Cossinius, a, a Roman gentile name, Cic. Balb. 23, 53 al.
cossinius.short: Cossinius, a, a Roman gentile name, Cic.

cossus1.full: cossus, i, m., a kind of larva under the bark of trees, Plin. 11, 33, 38, § 113; 17, 24, 37, § 220; 30, 13, 39, § 115.
cossus1.short: cossus, i, m., a kind of larva under the bark of trees, Plin.

cossus2.full: Cossus, i, m., a surname in the gens Cornelia (cf. Paul. ex Fest. p. 41, 9 Müll.); so esp. the military tribune in the war with the Veientes, A. Cornelius Cossus, Liv. 4, 19, 1 sq.; and id. 4, 30, 4 sqq.; Verg. A. 6, 841; Juv. 8, 21 al.
cossus2.short: Cossus, i, m., a surname in the gens Cornelia (cf.

cossutianae.full: Cossŭtĭānae Tabernae, a place near Cæsena in Gallia Cispadana, Q. Cic. ap. Cic. Fam. 16, 27, 2.
cossutianae.short: Cossŭtĭānae Tabernae, a place near Cæsena in Gallia Cispadana, Q.

cossutianus.full: Cossŭtĭānus, i, m., a Roman proper name; esp. Cossutianus Capito, Tac. A. 11, 6; 16, 33.
cossutianus.short: Cossŭtĭānus, i, m., a Roman proper name;

cossutius.full: Cossŭtĭus, a, name of a Roman gens, Suet. Caes. 1; Vitr. 7, pr. 15 al.
cossutius.short: Cossŭtĭus, a, name of a Roman gens, Suet.

costa.full: costa, ae, f., a rib, Cels. 8, 1; Plin. 11, 37, 82, § 207; Plaut. Ps. 1, 2, 4; Lucr. 5, 1297; Verg. G. 1, 273; id. A. 1, 211; Ov. H. 9, 111; Stat. Th. 2, 9; Mart. 9, 48, 10.— Transf., a side, a wall: aheni, Verg. A. 7, 463: ratis, Pers. 6, 31; cf. navium, Plin. 13, 9, 19, § 63: corbium, id. 16, 18, 30, § 75.— Absol., Verg. A. 2, 16 al.
costa.short: costa, ae, f., a rib, Cels.

costabilis.full: costābĭlis, e, adj. costa, riblike (late Lat.), Cassiod. Var. 3, 48.

costamomum.full: costămōmum, i, n. costum - amomum, an aromatic plant, similar to the costum and amomum, Dig. 39, 4, 16, § 7.

costatus.full: costātus, a, um, adj. costa, having ribs, ribbed: bene costati boves, Varr. R. R. 2, 5, 8.

costum.full: costum, i, n. (access. form, like the Greek, costŏs, i, f., Luc. 9, 917), = κόστος, an Oriental aromatic plant: Costus Arabicus, Linn.; Plin. 12, 12, 25, § 41; Ov. M. 10, 308; Hor. C. 3, 1, 44 al.; freq. used in the preparation of costly unguents, Plin. 13, 1, 2, § 15 sq.; 13, 1, 2, § 18; in offerings, Prop. 4 (5), 6, 5. for the preservation of fruits, Col. 12, 20, 5 al.

cosyra.full: Cŏsȳra (Coss-) or Cossūra, ae, f., a small island between Sicily and Africa, now Pantellaria, Ov. F. 3, 567; Plin. 3, 8, 14, § 92; Sil. 14, 272; Mel. 2, 7, 18.
cosyra.short: Cŏsȳra (Coss-) or Cossūra, ae, f., a small island between Sicily and Africa, now Pantellaria, Ov.

cothon.full: Cōthōn, ōnis, m. orig. a Semitic word, but identified by the Greeks with κώθων. In gen., a name given to any artificial harbor, Paul. ex Fest. p. 37, 9 Müll.— Esp. The artificial inner harbor of Carthage, Serv. ad Verg. A. 1, 427.— A similar harbor at Adrumetum, Auct. B. Afr. 62 sq.— The name of several islands, Plin. 4, 12, 19, § 56; Mel. 2, 7, 11.

cothurnatio.full: cŏthurnātĭo, ōnis, f. cothurnatus, a tragic representation, Tert. adv. Val. 13.

cothurnatus.full: cŏthurnātus, a, um, adj. cothurnus, of or pertaining to the cothurnus, lit. buskined; hence, elevated, lofty, tragic (opp. excalceatus, comic, Sen. Ep. 8, 8; 76, 31; not ante-Aug.): Maronis grande opus, Mart. 5, 5, 8: Lycophron, Ov. lb. 529: vates, id. Am. 2, 18, 18: deae, id. F. 5, 348: sermo, Macr. S. 7, 5 fin.: scelera, Lact. 6, 20.—* adv.: cŏ-thurnātē, loftily, tragically; only comp. (late Lat.): cothurnatius, Amm. 28, 1, 4.

cothurnus.full: cŏthurnus, i, m., = κόθορνος, a high Grecian shoe. In gen., Cic. Fin. 3, 14, 46; id. Phil. 3, 6, 16; Vell. 2, 82, 4 al.— Esp. A high Grecian hunting-boot, laced up in front, and covering the whole foot, Verg. E. 7, 32; id. A. 1, 337; Juv. 6, 506.— The high shoe or buskin worn by tragic actors (while soccus was the shoe of the comic actor), Hor. A. P. 80; 280; id. S. 1, 5, 64 al.—Hence, Meton. Tragedy, Hor. A. P. 80.— A subject of tragedy Juv. 15, 29.— An elevated style, in poetry, Verg. E. 8, 10
cothurnus.short: cŏthurnus, i, m., = κόθορνος, a high Grecian shoe.

coticula.full: cōtĭcŭla, ae, f. dim. cos. A small touchstone, a test, βάσανος, Plin. 33, 8, 43, § 126.— A small stone mortar for medical use, Plin. 31, 9, 45, § 100; cf. Isid. Orig. 4, 11, 7.

cotinus.full: cŏtĭnus, i, m., a shrub that furnishes a purple color: Rhus cotinus, Linn.; Plin. 16, 18, 30, § 73.
cotinus.short: cŏtĭnus, i, m., a shrub that furnishes a purple color: Rhus cotinus, Linn.;

cotiso.full: Cŏtĭso, ōnis, m., a king of the Getæ, Suet. Aug. 63; called also king of the Dacians, Hor. C. 3, 8, 18.
cotiso.short: Cŏtĭso, ōnis, m., a king of the Getæ, Suet.

cotonea.full: cŏtōnĕa, ae, f., a plant, wallwort, comfrey, black briony, Plin. 26, 7, 26, § 42.
cotonea.short: cŏtōnĕa, ae, f., a plant, wallwort, comfrey, black briony, Plin.

cotoriae.full: cōtōrĭae, ārum, f. cos, a whetstonequarry, Dig. 39, 4, 15 (al. cotariae).

cottabus.full: cottăbus, i, m., = κότταβος (a social sport consisting in dashing a liquid upon a brazen vessel; v. Lidd. and Scott under κότταβος; hence humorously transf.), a clap, stroke: ne bubuli in te cottabi crebri crepent, Plaut. Trin. 4, 3, 4.
cottabus.short: cottăbus, i, m., = κότταβος (a social sport consisting in dashing a liquid upon a brazen vessel;

cottana.full: cottăna (also cotona, coctona, and coctăna), ōrum, n. Syrian; Gr. κόττανα, a kind of small Syrian fig, Plin. 13, 5, 10, § 51; Mart. 7, 52; Juv. 3, 83; Stat. S. 4, 9, 28 al.
cottana.short: cottăna (also cotona, coctona, and coctăna), ōrum, n.

cottidianus.full: cottīdĭānus and cō^tīd- (less correctly quŏtīd-), a, um (cŏtīd-, Mart. 11, 1, 2; but cōtĭd-, Cat. 68, 139), adj. cottidie. Prop. In gen., of every day, daily: febris, Ter. Hec. 3, 2, 22: labor, Caes. B. G. 3, 17: consuetudo, id. B. C. 3, 85: usus, id. B. G. 4, 33: agger, id. ib. 7, 22: sermo, Cic. Fam. 1, 1. 2: victus, id. de Or. 1, 54, 232: vita, id. Pis. 26, 64: sumptus, Nep. Dion; 7, 2: cubiculum, Cels. 1, 3: cotidianis diebus = cottidie, Cael. Aur. Tard. 2, 1.— Esp., abl. adverb.: cottīdĭāno
cottidianus.short: cottīdĭānus and cō^tīd- (less correctly quŏtīd-), a, um (cŏtīd-, Mart.

cottidie.full: cottī-dĭē or cŏtīdĭē (v. Osann ad Cic. Rep. p. 475; less correctly quŏtīdĭē, v. Neue, Formenl. I. p. 676 sq.), adv. quotdies, daily (class.; cf. in dies): ibatne ad Bacchidem? Pa. Cotidie, Ter. Hec. 1, 2, 82: minari, Cic. Phil. 1, 2, 5: cotidie vel potius in dies singulos breviores litteras ad te mitto: cotidie enim magis suspicor te in Epirum profectum, id. Att. 5, 7 init.: cotidie augere, id. Mil. 13, 34; Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 8, § 18; id. Or. 34, 120: te cotidie pluris facio, id. Fam. 3, 4, 2: hae

cottidio.full: cottīdĭō (cotīd-), adv., for cottidie, daily, Q. Caepio ap. Charis. p. 174 P.
cottidio.short: cottīdĭō (cotīd-), adv., for cottidie, daily, Q.

cottius.full: Cottĭus, ii, m., the name of two kings of northern Italy, the father, who was a contemporary and friend of Augustus, Amm. 15, 10, 2 and 7, and the son (cf. Dio Cass. 60, 14), after whose death Nero made the country a Roman province, Suet. Ner. 18; id. Tib. 37; Aur. Vict. Caes. 5, 2.—Hence, Adjj. Cottĭus, a, um, Cottian: Alpes Cottiae, the Cottian Alps, west of Augusta Taurinorum, whose highest point is Alpis Cottia, now Mont Genèvre, Tac. H. 1, 87; Amm. 15, 10, 2.— Cottĭānus, a, um, the same: ci
cottius.short: Cottĭus, ii, m., the name of two kings of northern Italy, the father, who was a contemporary and friend of Augustus, Amm.

cotton.full: Cotton, ōnis, f., a town of Æolis, in Asia Minor, Liv. 37, 21, 5.
cotton.short: Cotton, ōnis, f., a town of Æolis, in Asia Minor, Liv.

cottus.full: Cottus or Cŏtus, i, m., v. Cotys.
cottus.short: Cottus or Cŏtus, i, m., v.

cotula.full: cŏtŭla (cŏtўla), ae, f., = κοτύλη, a small vessel, as a measure, equal to a hemina or half a sextarius, Fann. Pond. 12; Mart. 8, 71, 8; Veg. Art. Vet. 3, 6, 8 al.
cotula.short: cŏtŭla (cŏtўla), ae, f., = κοτύλη, a small vessel, as a measure, equal to a hemina or half a sextarius, Fann.

coturnium.full: coturnium, i. q. cuturnium, q. v.

coturnix.full: cō^turnix (ō, * Lucr. 4, 641; ŏ, Ov. Am. 2, 6, 27; Juv. 12, 97), īcis, f. a sono vocis, Paul. ex Fest. p. 37, 4 Müll., a quail, Plin. 10, 23, 33, § 64 sq.; Plaut. Capt. 5, 4, 6; Varr. R. R. 3, 5, 7 al.—As a term of endearment, Plaut. As. 3, 3, 76.

cotyla2.full: Cŏtўla, ae, m., a Roman surname, Cic. Phil. 5, 2, 5; 8, 10, 28.
cotyla2.short: Cŏtўla, ae, m., a Roman surname, Cic.

cotyledon.full: cŏtўlēdon, ŏnis, f., = κοτυληδών, a plant, navelwort: Cotyledon umbilicus, Linn.; Plin. 25, 13, 101, § 159.
cotyledon.short: cŏtўlēdon, ŏnis, f., = κοτυληδών, a plant, navelwort: Cotyledon umbilicus, Linn.;

cotys.full: Cŏtўs, tyis (acc. -tȳn, rarely -tym; abl. -tye), and Cŏtus, i, m., = Κότυς, the name of several Thracian princes. A ruler of the coast of Thrace B. C. 382-356, son-in-law of Iphicrates, Nep. Iphicr. 3, 4; id. Timoth. 1, 2; Val. Max. 3, 7, ext. 7.— Cotys II., king of the Odrysæ, an ally of Perseus in his war against Rome, Liv. 42, 29, 12; 42, 51, 10; 42, 67, 4; Eutr. 4, 6.— Cotys III., king of the Odrysæ, Cic. Pis. 34, 84; Caes. B. C. 3, 4; 3, 36; Luc. 5, 54.— Cotys V., grandson of III., Tac. A.

cotytto.full: Cŏtytto, ūs, f., = Κοτυττώ, the goddess of lewdness, who was originally worshipped in Thrace, later in Athens also, Juv. 2, 92. —Cŏtyttia, ōrum, n., = Κοτύττια, her festival, Hor. Epod. 17, 56; Verg. Cat. 5, 19.
cotytto.short: Cŏtytto, ūs, f., = Κοτυττώ, the goddess of lewdness, who was originally worshipped in Thrace, later in Athens also, Juv.

cous.full: Cŏus, i, and Cōus, a, um, v. 2. Cos.
cous.short: Cŏus, i, and Cōus, a, um, v.

coutor.full: cŏ-ūtor, ūti, v. n.: aliquo, to associate with, have dealings with, = συγχρῆσθαι, Vulg. Joan. 4, 9.

covinarius.full: cŏvīnārĭus (cŏvinn-), ii, m. covinus, a soldier who fought from a chariot, Tac. Agr. 35 and 36.

covinus.full: cŏvīnus (cŏvinn-), i, m. Celtic, a war-chariot of the Britons and Belgæ, Mel. 3, 6, 5; Luc. 1, 426; Sil. 17, 422.—Also a travelling chariot, a kind of tilbury, Mart. 12, 24, 1.

coxa.full: coxa, ae, f., the hip. Prop, Cels. 4, 22, 1; 8, 1 fin.; 8, 10, 5; Cael. Aur. Tard. 4, 3, 38; cf. also coxendix.—Hence, The hip-bone, Plin. Ep. 2, 1, 5.— Transf., in the Agrimensores: agrorum, a bend inwards (with angulus), Sic. Fl. p. 6 Goes.

coxendix.full: coxendix, ĭcis (ī, Plaut. Bacch. 5, 2, 40; Lucil. ap. Non. p. 94, 6; I, Ser. Samm. 702; 968), f. kindr. with coxa, the hip. Prop., Varr. R. R. 1, 20; Lucil. ap. Non. p. 94, 6; Plaut. Bacch. 5, 2, 40; Suet. Aug. 8.— The hip-bone, Plin. 10, 61, 81, § 168; 28, 11, 49, § 179.

coxim.full: coxim, adv. coxa; cf.: cessim, cossim, on the hips (late Lat.): insidens, App. M. 3, p. 129, 19.

coxo.full: coxo, ŏnis, m. coxa, hobbling, Non. p. 25, 18.

crabra.full: Crabra (ae) aqua, an aqueduct or water conduit that extended from Tusculum to the Tiber, Cic. Agr. 3, 2, 9; id. Fam. 16, 18, 3; Front. Aquaed. 9.
crabra.short: Crabra (ae) aqua, an aqueduct or water conduit that extended from Tusculum to the Tiber, Cic.

crabro.full: crābro, ōnis, m., a hornet: Vespa crabro, Linn.; Plin. 11, 21, 24, § 71 sq.; Ov. M. 11, 335; Verg. G. 4, 245 al.—Prov.: irritare crabrones, to stir up a hornet's nest, Plaut. Am. 2, 2, 84.
crabro.short: crābro, ōnis, m., a hornet: Vespa crabro, Linn.;

cracca.full: cracca, ae, f., a kind of pulse, perh. wild vetch, Plin. 18, 16, 41, § 142.
cracca.short: cracca, ae, f., a kind of pulse, perh.

cracens.full: crăcens, entis kindr. with gracilis; v. the letter C, slender, neat, graceful: cracentes = graciles, Enn. ap. Paul. ex Fest. p. 53, 7 Müll. (Ann. v. 497 Vahl.).

cragos.full: Crăgŏs or -us, i, m., = Κράγος, a promontory and chain of mountains in Lycia, the abode of the Chimæra, Mel. 1, 15, 3; Plin. 5, 27, 27, § 98; 5, 27, 28, § 101; Hor. C. 1, 21, 8; Ov. M. 9, 646.
cragos.short: Crăgŏs or -us, i, m., = Κράγος, a promontory and chain of mountains in Lycia, the abode of the Chimæra, Mel.

crambe.full: crambē, ēs, f., = κράμβη, a kind of cabbage, Plin. 20, 9, 33, § 79.—Prov.: crambe repetita, warmed over, for something repeated, an old story, Juv. 7, 154.
crambe.short: crambē, ēs, f., = κράμβη, a kind of cabbage, Plin.

cranii.full: Cranĭi, ōrum, m., = Κράνιοι, the inhabitants of a town on the island of Cephallenia, now Granea, Liv. 38, 28, 6.
cranii.short: Cranĭi, ōrum, m., = Κράνιοι, the inhabitants of a town on the island of Cephallenia, now Granea, Liv.

cranon.full: Crānon (Crann-), ōnis, f., = Κράνων, a town of Thessaly, in the Vale of Tempe, Cic. de Or. 2, 86, 352; Liv. 36, 10, 1; 42, 64, 7; Val. Max. 1, 8, ext. 7.—Hence, Crānōnĭ-us, a, um, adj., of Cranon: ager, Liv. 42, 64, 7.
cranon.short: Crānon (Crann-), ōnis, f., = Κράνων, a town of Thessaly, in the Vale of Tempe, Cic.

crantor.full: Crantor, ŏris, m., = Κράντωρ. In fable, the armor-bearer of Peleus, slain by the centaur Demoleon, Ov. M. 12, 367.— A distinguished Grecian philosopher of the old Academic school, Cic. Ac. 1, 9, 34; 2, 44, 135; id. Fin. 5, 3, 7; id. Tusc. 1, 48, 115; Hor. Ep. 1, 2, 4 al.

crapula.full: crāpŭla, ae, f., = κραιπάλη, excessive wine-drinking, intoxication, inebriation, Plaut. Most. 5, 2, 1; id. Ps. 5, 1, 46; Cic. Verr. 2, 3, 11, § 28; id. Phil. 2, 12, 30; Liv. 9, 30, 9; Plin. 21, 20, 83, § 142 et saep.— Meton., a resin producing intoxication, which was sometimes mingled with wine, Plin. 14, 20, 25, § 124 sq.; 23, 1, 24, § 46.
crapula.short: crāpŭla, ae, f., = κραιπάλη, excessive wine-drinking, intoxication, inebriation, Plaut.

crapularius.full: crāpŭlārĭus, a, um, adj. crapula, pertaining to intoxication: unctio, preventive of inebriation, Plaut. Stich. 2, 1, 74.

crapulatio.full: crāpŭlātĭo, ōnis, f. id., an intoxicating (late Lat.), Cassiod. An. 11.

crapulatus.full: crāpŭlātus, a, um, adj. id., drunken with wine, inebriated, Vulg. Psa. 77, 65.

crapulentus.full: crāpŭlentus, a, um, adj. id., very much intoxicated, Amm. 29, 5, 54.

crapulosus.full: crāpŭlōsus, a, um, adj. id., inclined to drunkenness (late Lat.): libidines, Firm. Math. 8, 20.

cras.full: crās, adv. root ka-, ku-, to lighten, burn; Gr. καίω; cf. Sanscr. cvas, the same, to-morrow, αὔριον (freq. and class.). With tempp. fut.: rus cras cum filio Cum primo luci ibo hinc, Ter. Ad. 5, 3, 54: scies fortasse cras, summum perendie, Cic. Att. 12, 44, 3: cras donaberis haedo, Hor. C. 3, 13, 3: Qui non est hodie, cras minus aptus erit, Ov. R. Am. 94 et saep.—With ellipsis of verb: negat Eros hodie: cras mane putat (sc. venturum esse), early to-morrow morning, Cic. Att. 10, 30, 2.— With temp.

crassamen.full: crassāmen, ĭnis, n. crasso, the thick sediment of a liquid, the dregs (cf. crassamentum, II.), Col. 12, 25, 2; 12, 42, 2.

crassamentum.full: crassāmentum, i, n. id. (post-Aug.), the thickness of an object. In gen.: portarum, Plin. 16, 40, 77, § 210: surculi, Gell. 17, 9, 7.— Esp., the thick sediment of a liquid, the dregs, grounds, Col. 12, 12, 1.

crassedo.full: crassēdo, ĭnis, f. crassus, thickness, fig.: ingenii, stupidity, Fulg. cont. Verg.

crassesco.full: crassesco, ĕre, v. inch., to grow thick, to thicken, grow dense or hard, grow large or fat (post-Aug.; most freq. in Pliny the elder): turtures milio, etc., Col. 8, 9, 2: sues, Plin. 13, 18, 32, § 110: ceparum capita, id. 19, 6, 32, § 103: pili quadrupedibus senectute, id. 11, 39, 94, § 231: mel (opp. dilutum), id. 11, 13, 13, § 32; cf.: vinum vetustate, id. 23, 1, 22, § 40: aër in nubes, id. 2, 43, 44, § 114: crassescente limo, id. 33, 5, 26, § 86.

crassicius.full: Crassĭcĭus (-tĭus), ĭi, m., a grammarian of Rome, Cic. Phil. 13, 2, 3; Suet. Gram. 18.
crassicius.short: Crassĭcĭus (-tĭus), ĭi, m., a grammarian of Rome, Cic.

crassificatio.full: crassĭfĭcātĭo, ōnis, f. crassifico, a making thick or fat; hence, thickness: viscosa, Cael. Aur. Tard. 5, 3, 56; id. Acut. 1, 14, 115.

crassifico.full: crassĭfĭco, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. crassusfacio, to make thick, thicken, make fat, fatten, Cael. Aur. Tard. 2, 14, 208; 5, 2, 39 al.— Pass., to thicken, become dense, Cael. Aur. Tard. 2, 13, 180.

crassipes.full: Crassĭpēs, pĕdis crassus-pes, thickfoot, a surname of the gens Furia, Liv. 38, 42, 4; the most celebrated is Furius Crassipes, Cicero's son-in-law, Cic. Fam. 1, 7, 11 al.
crassipes.short: Crassĭpēs, pĕdis crassus-pes, thickfoot, a surname of the gens Furia, Liv.

crassitas.full: crassĭtas, ātis, f. crassus, thickness, density, App. de Mundo, p. 65, 15.

crassities.full: crassĭtĭes, ēi, f. id., thickness, density, App. M. 7, p. 189, 38.

crassitudo.full: crassĭtūdo, ĭnis, f. crassus, thickness, density. Abstr. (in good prose): postes ...Quantā firmitate facti et quantā crassitudine, Plaut. Most. 3, 2, 135: parietum, Caes. B. C. 2, 8: libramentum, in quo nulla omnino crassitudo sit, Cic. Ac. 2, 36, 116: columnarum, Vitr. 4, 4, 2: fornicum, Liv. 44, 11, 5 al.: stipites feminis crassitudine, Caes. B. G. 7, 73; cf. id. ib. 3, 13: aëris, Cic. Div. 1, 42, 93: cerae, Plin. 27, 9, 47, § 71: mellis, id. 28, 12, 50, § 187: (ostrea) crassitudine potius spe

crassivenius.full: crassĭvēnĭus, a, um, adj. crassusvena, having thick veins: acer, Plin. 16, 15, 26, § 66.

crasso.full: crasso, no perf., ātum, 1, v. a. crassus, to make thick, thicken, condense (postclass.): pili crassantur in setas, App. M. 3, p. 139, 39: crassatus aër, Amm. 19, 4, 6; 19, 4, 8; 20, 3, 5.

crassundia.full: crassundĭa, ōrum, n. id., the thick intestines, Varr. L. L. 5, § 111 Müll. N. cr.

crassus1.full: crassus, a, um, adj. Sanscr. kart-, to spin; cf.: crates, cartilago, etc.; as opp. to flowing, thin, lean, delicate, etc., solid, thick, dense, fat, gross, etc. (freq. and class. in prose and poetry). Lit.: semina (opp. liquida), Lucr. 4, 1259; cf.: crassius semen, id. 4, 1244: corpus, id. 6, 857: unguentum, Hor. A. P. 375: paludes, Verg. G. 2, 110: cruor, id. A. 5, 469: aquae, greatly swollen, Ov. Am. 3, 6, 8: ager, Varr. R. R. 1, 24, 1; Cic. Fl. 29, 71; cf.: terga (agri), Verg. G. 2, 236: homo

crassus2.full: Crassus, i, m., a family name in the gens Licinia. The most distinguished were, L. Licinius Crassus, a celebrated orator, a contemporary of Cicero, Cic. Brut. 38, 143; id. Off. 1, 30, 108 et saep.; cf. id. Brut. prol. pp. 68-77 Ellendt.— M. Licinius Crassus, the triumvir.—Hence, Crassĭānus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to the triumvir Crassus: exercitūs clades (in the war with the Parthians), Vell. 2, 82, 2; cf.: Crassiana clades, Plin. 6, 16, 18, § 47; Flor. 4, 9, 7.
crassus2.short: Crassus, i, m., a family name in the gens Licinia.

crastinus1.full: crastĭnus, a, um, adj. cras. Of to-morrow; to-morrow's (freq. and class. in prose and poetry): dies, Plaut. Stich. 4, 2, 55; Cic. Att. 15, 8, 2; Prop. 2 (3), 15, 54.al.: Titan, Verg. A. 4, 118: Cynthius, Ov. F. 3, 345: Aurora, Verg. A. 12, 76: lux, id. ib. 10, 244; cf.: stella diurna, Plaut. Men. 1, 2, 62: hora. Verg. G. 1, 425: tempora, * Hor. C. 4, 7, 17: dapes, Mart. 3, 58, 42: egestas, id. 3, 10, 3: quies, Luc. 7, 26 al.—In Gr. constr., of the person: crastinus aspicis Triobrem ( = cras), Si

crastinus2.full: Crastĭnus, i, m., a Roman surname, Caes. B. C. 3, 91; 3, 99; Luc. 7, 471; Flor. 4, 2, 46 al.
crastinus2.short: Crastĭnus, i, m., a Roman surname, Caes.

crataegis.full: crătaegis, is, f., another name of the plant satyrion, Plin. 26, 10, 63, § 99.
crataegis.short: crătaegis, is, f., another name of the plant satyrion, Plin.

crataegon.full: crătaegon, ŏnis, or crătaegŏs, i, m., = κραταιγών or κράταιγος, a plant, called in pure Lat. aquifolia, Plin. 27, 8, 40, § 63.
crataegon.short: crătaegon, ŏnis, or crătaegŏs, i, m., = κραταιγών or κράταιγος, a plant, called in pure Lat.

crataegum.full: crătaegum, i, n., = κραταιγόν, the kernel of the fruit of the box-tree, Plin. 16, 30, 52, § 120.
crataegum.short: crătaegum, i, n., = κραταιγόν, the kernel of the fruit of the box-tree, Plin.

crataeis.full: Crătaeis, ĭdis, f., = Κραταιίς, the mother of Scylla, Ov. M. 13, 749; Verg. Cir. 65; cf. Plin. 3, 5, 10, § 73.
crataeis.short: Crătaeis, ĭdis, f., = Κραταιίς, the mother of Scylla, Ov.

crataeogonon.full: crătaeŏgŏnon, i, n., and crătaeŏgŏnŏs,, i, f., = κραταιόγονον, the common fleawort, Plin. 27, 8, 40, § 62 sq.
crataeogonon.short: crătaeŏgŏnon, i, n., and crătaeŏgŏnŏs,, i, f., = κραταιόγονον, the common fleawort, Plin.

cratera.full: crātēra (acc. to Paul. ex Fest. p. 53, 10, and Non. p. 547, 25 sq., sometimes crē-terra; cf. Naev. Trag. Rel. v. 45 Rib.), ae, f., and (mostly poet.) crātēr, ēris, m., = κρατήρ, Ion. κρητήρ, a vessel in which wine was mingled with water, a mixing-vessel or bowl (mostly poet.). Prop. Cratera, ae, Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 59, § 131 Zumpt N. cr.; id. Fam. 7, 1, 2 Orell. N. cr.; id. Arat. 387; Liv. 5, 25, 10; 5, 28, 2; Curt. 4, 8, 16; Hor. C. 3, 18, 7; id. S. 2, 4, 80; Pers. 2, 52; Hyg. Astr. 2, 30; Inscr.

craterites.full: crătĕrītes, ae, m. κρατερός, a very hard unknown precious stone, Plin. 37, 10, 56, § 154.

craterus.full: Crătĕrus (-ros), i, m., = Κρατερός, A general of Alexander the Great, Nep. Eum. 2, 2; 3, 3; 4, 1; Curt. 4, 3, 1 al.— A famous physician at Rome in the time of Cicero, Cic. Att. 12, 13, 1; 12, 14, 4; Hor. S. 2, 3, 161; Pers. 3, 65.
craterus.short: Crătĕrus (-ros), i, m., = Κρατερός, A general of Alexander the Great, Nep.

crates1.full: Crătes, is, m., = Κράτης, a Greek proper name. A Theban philosopher, App. Mag. p. 26 Bip.; id. Flor. p. 126 sq.— Crates Mallotes, a grammarian, Suet. Gram. 2; Varr. L. L. 8, § 64.— Crates, an Academic philosopher of Athens, Cic. Ac. 1, 9, 34.
crates1.short: Crătes, is, m., = Κράτης, a Greek proper name.

crates2.full: crătes, is, f., falsely assumed as nom. instead of cratis, q. v.
crates2.short: crătes, is, f., falsely assumed as nom.

crathis.full: Crāthis, ĭdis, m., = Κρᾶθις, a river in Magna Graecia, whose water was said to redden the hair, now Crati or Gratti, Plin. 3, 11, 15, § 97; 31, 2, 9, § 13; 31, 2, 10, § 14; Ov. M. 15, 315; id. F. 3, 581.
crathis.short: Crāthis, ĭdis, m., = Κρᾶθις, a river in Magna Graecia, whose water was said to redden the hair, now Crati or Gratti, Plin.

craticius.full: crātĭcĭus or -tĭus, a, um, adj. cratis, composed of wicker-work, wattled: parietes, lattice-work, Vitr. 2, 8 fin.; Dig. 17, 2, 15; Pall. 1, 19, 2.

craticula.full: crātĭcŭla, ae, f. dim. id., prop., fine hurdle - work; hence, a small gridiron, Mart. 14, 221, 1; Cato, R. R. 13, 1; Petr. 31, 11; 70, 7.

craticulum.full: craticulum a Graeco κρατεῦται deducitur, Paul. ex Fest. p. 53, 11 Müll. [more prob. immediately from crates].
craticulum.short: craticulum a Graeco κρατεῦται deducitur, Paul.

craticulus.full: crātĭcŭlus, a, um, adj. dim. [cratis], composed of lattice-work, wattled: lucernae, Cato, R. R. 13, 1: aliter alii.

cratinus.full: Crătīnus, i, m., = Κρατῖνος a celebrated Grecian comic poet of the old comedy, a contemporary of Eupolis and Aristophanes, Hor. Ep. 1, 19, 1; id. S. 1, 4, 1; Pers. 1, 123; Quint. 10, 1, 65.
cratinus.short: Crătīnus, i, m., = Κρατῖνος a celebrated Grecian comic poet of the old comedy, a contemporary of Eupolis and Aristophanes, Hor.

cratio.full: crātĭo, īre, v. a. cratis, to harrow (rare): herbam, Plin. 18, 28, 67, § 258.

cratippus.full: Crătippus, i, m., = Κράτιππος, a distinguished peripatetic philosopher at Athens, a teacher of Cicero's son, Cic. Off. 1, 1, 1; 2, 2, 8; id. Div. 1, 3, 5; Cic. Fil. ap. Cic. Fam. 16, 21, 3.
cratippus.short: Crătippus, i, m., = Κράτιππος, a distinguished peripatetic philosopher at Athens, a teacher of Cicero's son, Cic.

cratis.full: crātis, is (nom. sing. only Veg. Art. Vet. 1, 56, 5; acc. sing. cratim, Plaut. Poen. 5, 2, 65), f. Sanscr. kart, to spin; cf. crassus, wicker-work, a hurdle. Lit. In gen. Sing. (rare): flexilis, Plin. 16, 40, 77, § 209; 10, 44, 61, § 126: juncea, id. 21, 14, 49, § 84; Juv. 11, 82.— Plur. (so most freq.; and by the ancient gram. sometimes regarded as plur. tantum; v. Neue, Formenl. I. p. 455), Cato, R. R. 10, 2; 11, 4; Verg. A. 11, 64; Hor. Epod. 2, 45; Col. 12, 15, 1 al.— Esp. A harrow; sing., P

creabilis.full: crĕābĭlis, e, adj. creo, that can be made or created (post-class. and rare): materia, App. Trism. 85, 12; Aug. Conf. 12, 19 al.

creagra.full: crĕāgra, ae, f., = κρεάγρα, a fleshhook (late Lat.), Mart. Cap. 9, § 997; Vulg. 2 Par. 4, 11 al.
creagra.short: crĕāgra, ae, f., = κρεάγρα, a fleshhook (late Lat.), Mart.

creamen.full: crĕāmen, ĭnis, n. creo, the elements of which created things consist (late Lat.), Prud. Ham. 505.

creatio.full: crĕātĭo, ōnis, f. id. (very rare). A creating, producing, begetting: liberorum, Dig. 1, 7, 15, § 2.—Absol.: non hujus creationis, i. e. not of man's building, Vulg. Heb. 9, 11.— An electing to an office, a choice: magistratuum, Cic. Leg. 3, 3, 10: tutoris, Dig. 26, 7, 39, § 6.

creator.full: crĕātor, ōris, m. id.. A creator, author, begetter, founder. In gen. (very rare): ipse deūm, Cic. poët. Div. 2, 30, 64; cf. thus of a father, Ov. M. 8, 309: creator atque opifex rerum, Luc. 10, 266: hujus urbis, Romulus, Cic. Balb. 13, 31.— The creator of the world, etc., God (eccl. Lat.), opp. creatura, Vulg. Rom. 1, 25; id. 1 Pet. 4, 19.—With gen.: mundi, Vulg. 2, Macc. 7, 23: omnium, id. Eccli. 24, 12 al.— One who elects or appoints to an office, Cod. Just. 10, 31, 59; Dig. 50, 8, 2, § 7 al.

creatrix.full: crĕātrix, īcis, f. creator, she who brings forth or produces, a mother (poet.): natura rerum, Lucr. 1, 630 al.: mea, patria (with genetrix), Cat. 63, 50: diva (of a mother), Verg. A. 8, 534; cf.: Alexandri Magni, Olympias, Aur. Vict. Epit. 40: dira bellorum (tellus), Sil. 15, 184; Ambros. Fid. 4, 30, 3.

creatura.full: crĕātūra, ae, f. creo, only concr., a creature, thing created (late Lat.), Tert. Apol. 30; Prud. Ham. 508: omnes creaturae tuae, Vulg. Tob. 8, 7.— The creation: Deus caelorum et Dominus totius creaturae, Vulg. Jud. 9, 17: Dei, id. Apoc. 3, 14 al.

creber.full: crēber, bra, brum (sup. creberrimus; but crebrissimus, Gell. 2, 30, 2; cf. Rudd. I. p. 170; and CEREBERRIMVS, Inscr. Orell. 68), adj. from cre-, root of cresco, Corn. Beitr. p. 356, that exists or takes place in a continuous multitude, following closely together or one after another (hence with continuus, Quint. 12, 10, 46; opp. rarus). Thick, close, pressed together, frequent, numerous, repeated (very freq., and class.). Of material subjects: lucus avius, Crebro salicto oppletus, Plaut. Aul. 4,

crebratus.full: crēbrātus, a, um, adj. creber, thick, close: telae pexitas, Plin. 11, 24, 28, § 81.

crebresco.full: crēbresco (in MSS. and edd. sometimes euphon. crēbesco, bŭi, like rubesco, from ruber), brŭi, 3, v. inch. [creber], to become frequent, to increase, grow strong; of a rumor, report, to spread abroad (perh. not ante-Aug.; most freq. in Tac.): crebrescunt optatae aurae, Verg. A. 3, 530: gestus cum ipsā orationis celeritate, Quint. 11, 3, 111: horror, Verg. A. 12, 407: bellum, Tac. H. 2, 67: tum crebescere fragor, Plin. Ep. 7, 27, 8: seditio, Tac. H. 1, 39: licentia et impunitas, id. A. 3, 60: invi

crebrisuro.full: crēbrĭsūro, apud Ennium significat vallum crebris suris id est palis munitum, Paul. ex Fest. p. 59, 3.
crebrisuro.short: crēbrĭsūro, apud Ennium significat vallum crebris suris id est palis munitum, Paul.

crebritas.full: crēbrĭtas, ātis, f. creber, thickness, closeness, frequency: spissae venarum, Vitr. 2, 10, 2: caeli, id. 9, 8, 3: fluctuum, Sall. H. Fragm. ap. Serv. ad Verg. A. 1, 116 (3, 42 Dietsch): litterarum, Cic. Att. 13, 18 init.: crebritas et magnitudo officiorum, id. Fam. 3, 1, 1: sententiarum (with concinnitas), id. Brut. 95, 327.

crebritudo.full: crēbrĭtūdo, ĭnis, f. creber, for crebritas, Sisenn. ap. Non. p. 91, 30 dub.

credibilis.full: crēdĭbĭlis, e, adj. credo, worthy of belief, credible: credibile est quod sine ullo teste auditoris opinione firmatur, Cic. Inv. 1, 30, 48 (class. in prose and poetry): tametsi verissimum esse intellegebam, tamen credibile fore non arbitrabar, Cic. Verr. 2, 5, 61, § 158: narrationes, id. Or. 36, 124; cf. Quint. 4, 2, 52: imago rerum, id. 4, 2, 123: ratio, id. 5, 12, 13: suspicio, id. 9, 2, 90 et saep.: magnum narras, vix credibile, * Hor. S. 1, 9, 52; cf.: vix credibile dictu, Curt. 5, 13, 22: c

credito.full: crēdĭto, āre, v. freq. a. credo, to believe firmly, Fulg. Myth. 1, p. 6.

creditor.full: crēdĭtor, ōris, m. credo, I., a creditor. Prop., Dig. 50, 16, 10 sq.; Cic. Phil. 6, 4, 11; id. Quint. 23, 74; Liv. 6, 14, 5; Sen. Ep. 87, 6; 119, 1; Quint. 3, 6, 84; * Hor. S. 2, 3, 65 et saep.— Trop., of the belly, Plin. 26, 8, 28, § 43.

creditrix.full: crēdĭtrix, īcis, f. creditor, a female creditor, Dig. 20, 5, 16; 42, 6, 38 al.

creditum.full: crēdĭtum, i, n., v. credo, I. B.

credo.full: crēdo, dĭdi, dĭtum, 3 (pres. subj. creduam, Plaut. Poen. 3, 5, 2: creduas, id. Bacch. 3, 3, 72; id. Trin. 3, 1, 5: creduat, id. Bacch. 3, 4, 5; 4, 7, 6: creduis, id. Am. 2, 2, 49; id. Capt. 3, 4, 73: creduit, id. Truc. 2, 2, 52; inf. credier, id. Poen. 2, 43; crevi for credidi, id. Cist. 1, 1, 1), v. a. Sanscr. crat, crad, trust, and dha-; v. 2. do. Orig. belonging to the lang. of business, to give as a loan, to loan, lend, make or loan to any one: (vilicus) injussu domini credat nemini; quod do

credulitas.full: crēdŭlĭtas, ātis, f. credulus, easiness of belief, credulity (first freq. after the Aug. per.; never in Cic.): credulitas error est magis quam culpa, Plancus ap. Cic. Fam. 10, 23, 1; Quint. 5, 3, 7; Tac. A. 2, 40; Curt. 7, 7, 8; Ov. M. 15, 498; id. P. 1, 1, 44.—Of fishes trusting themselves to the hook, Ov. M. 13, 934; 15, 101; cf. credulus.—As a person, together with Error, Ov. M. 12, 59.

credulus.full: crēdŭlus, a, um, adj. credo, II. C. 2., that easily believes a thing, credulous, easy of belief, confiding. Prop. (freq. and class.). Absol.: in fabulis stultissima persona est improvidorum et credulorum senum, Cic. Lael. 26, 100: stultus auditor et credulus, id. Font. 6, 13; Quint. 11, 1, 71; Tac. H. 1, 12 fin.; Hor. C. 1, 5, 9; Ov. M. 3, 432 et saep.—Of fishes trusting to the hook, Ov. M. 8, 858; cf. credulitas; and of animals anticipating no danger, Hor. Epod. 16, 33.— With dat.: non ego cred

crematio.full: crĕmātĭo, ōnis, f. cremo, a burning, consuming by fire, cremation (post-Aug. and rare), Plin. 23, 2, 31, § 64; Prud. στεφ. 6, 88.

cremator.full: crĕmātor, ōris, m. id., a burner, consumer by fire (eccl. Lat.): Deus, Tert. adv. Marc. 5, 16.

crementum.full: crēmentum, i, n. cresco. Growth, increase (very rare): corporum, Varr. ap. Non. p. 169, 14: lunae, Plin. 11, 37, 55, § 149 (incrementum, Sillig).— Crementum est semen masculi, Isid. Orig. 9, 5, 5; 11, 1, 15.

cremera.full: Crĕmĕra, ae, f., a small river in Etruria, near Veii, made famous by the heroic death of the Fabii, now La Varca or Valca, Liv. 2, 49 fin.; Ov. F. 2, 205; Gell. 17, 21, 13.—Poet.: Cremerae legio, i. e. the Fabii, Juv. 2, 155.—Hence, Crĕmĕrensis, e, adj., of Cremera: dies, the day of the disastrous conflict at Cremera (with Alliensis), Tac. H. 2, 91.
cremera.short: Crĕmĕra, ae, f., a small river in Etruria, near Veii, made famous by the heroic death of the Fabii, now La Varca or Valca, Liv.

cremia.full: crĕmĭa, ōrum (sing. cremium, i, Vulg. Psa. 101, 4), n. cremo, dry fire-wood, brushwood, Col. 12, 19, 3; Dig. 32, 55, § 4.

cremo.full: crĕmo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. Sanscr. çar, çri, to boil, roast; cf. carbo, to burn, consume by fire (freq. and class.; cf. comburo). In gen.: ignis silvas cremarat, Lucr. 5, 1242; cf.: poëtam igni, Suet. Calig. 27 fin.: omnes collegas suos vivos, Val. Max. 6, 3, 2; Curt. 4, 8, 9: damnatum poenam sequi oportebat, ut igni cremaretur, Caes. B. G. 1, 4; Curt. 8, 9, 32; 5, 6, 7: urbem incendiis, Plin. 17, 1, 1, § 5: cremare et diruere urbem, Liv. 28, 19, 12: Ilium, Hor. C. 4, 4, 53: lectum, Suet. Caes.

cremona.full: Crĕmōna, ae, f., = Κρεμώνη, the town Cremona in Gallia Cisalpina, on the Po, Liv. 21, 25, 2; 31, 10, 3; Verg. E. 9, 28; Tac. H. 2, 17; 2, 22 sq.; Suet. Vesp. 7 et saep.— Hence, Crĕmōnensis, e, adj., of Cremona: ager, Tac. H. 3, 15: coloni, Liv. 33, 23, 6: proelium, Tac. H. 3, 48.—In plur. subst.: Crĕmōnenses, ium, m., the inhabitants of Cremona, Tac. H. 2, 70; 3, 19 al.
cremona.short: Crĕmōna, ae, f., = Κρεμώνη, the town Cremona in Gallia Cisalpina, on the Po, Liv.

cremonis jugum.full: Cremōnis jŭgum, a part of the Pennine Alps, now Grimsel, Liv. 21, 38, 7.
cremonis jugum.short: Cremōnis jŭgum, a part of the Pennine Alps, now Grimsel, Liv.

cremor.full: crĕmor, ōris, m. kindr. with cremo, the thick juice obtained from animal or vegetable substances, thick broth, pap, etc., Cato, R. R. 86; Plaut. Pers. 1, 3, 15; Cels. 3, 7, 2; 6, 6, 26; Ov. M. Fac. 95.

cremum.full: crĕmum, i, n., = cremor, Ven. Fort. 11, 14, 1.

cremutius.full: Crĕmūtĭus, ĭi, m., a Roman proper name: A. Cremutius Cordus, a Roman historian under Tiberius, distinguished by his frankness, Tac. A. 4, 34; Sen. Suas. 7, p. 44; Quint. 10, 1, 104; Sen. Cons. Marc. 1, 2.
cremutius.short: Crĕmūtĭus, ĭi, m., a Roman proper name: A.

crena.full: crena, ae, f., corrupted word, Plin. 11, 37, 68, § 180; Sillig ad h. 1.; Jan. taeniis.
crena.short: crena, ae, f., corrupted word, Plin.

crenaeus.full: Crēnaeus, i, m., a centaur, Ov. M. 12, 313.
crenaeus.short: Crēnaeus, i, m., a centaur, Ov.

crene.full: Crēnē, ēs, f., a town of Æolis, Liv. 37, 21, 5.
crene.short: Crēnē, ēs, f., a town of Æolis, Liv.

creo1.full: crĕo (old form cerĕo, in Varr. L. L. 6, § 81 Müll.), āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. kindred with Sanscr. kar, kri, to make, to bring forth, produce, make, create, beget (very freq. in every period and species of composition). Lit. In gen.: rerum primordia pandam, Unde omnes natura creet res auctet alatque, Lucr. 1, 51: animalia, id. 2, 1152: genus humanum, id. 5, 820: mortalia saecla, id. 5, 789: fruges, id. 2, 170: ignem, id. 1, 799; cf.: ignes e lignis, id. 1, 910 et saep.: (Silvius) Aenean Silvium creat

creo2.full: Crĕo, or, anal. to the Gr., Crĕon, ontis, m., = Κρέων. A king of Corinth, who betrothed his daughter Creusa to Jason, Hyg. Fab. 25; Sen. Med. 526; Hor. Epod. 5, 64.— A brother of Jocaste, at Thebes, Hyg. Fab. 72; Stat. Th. 12, 477; 12, 678.

crepae.full: crepae, i. q. caprae, she-goats, acc. to Paul. ex Fest. p. 48, 16 Müll.

crepatura.full: crĕpātūra, ae, f. crepo, a fissure, crack (late Lat.): parietum, Schol. Juv. 3, 196.

crepax.full: crĕpax, ācis, adj. id., sounding, creaking: mola, Maecen. ap. Sen. Ep. 114, 6.

creper.full: crĕper, ĕra, ĕrum, adj. Sabine; kindr. with Sanscr. kshapā, night, and Gr. κνέφας, dusky, dark; hence, trop., uncertain, obscure, doubtful, wavering (ante- and post-class.), Varr. L. L. 6, § 5; 7, § 77; cf. Non. p. 13, 15 sq.; Paul. ex Fest. p. 52, 18 Müll. * Lit., only subst.: crĕpĕrum, i, n., darkness: noctis, Symm. Ep. 1, 7.— Trop.: res, Pac. ap. Non. p. 13, 29; Att. ib. p. 21 sq.; Varr. 1. 1.: belli certamina, Lucr. 5, 1295: oracla, Varr. ap. Non. p. 14, 4.

crepida.full: crĕpĭda, ae, f., = κρηπίς, the sole which served the Greeks, and the Romans who adopted Grecian habits, as a shoe, a sandal (pure Lat. solea; cf. Gell. 13, 21, 5 sq.), Cic. Rab. Post. 10, 27; Liv. 29, 19, 12; Suet. Tib. 13; id. Calig. 52; Hor. S. 1, 3, 127; Pers. 1, 127 al.—Prov.: ne sutor supra crepidam (judicaret), let the cobbler stick to his last, Plin. 35, 10, 36, § 85; Val. Max. 8, 12, ext. 3.
crepida.short: crĕpĭda, ae, f., = κρηπίς, the sole which served the Greeks, and the Romans who adopted Grecian habits, as a shoe, a sandal (pure Lat.

crepidarius.full: crĕpĭdārĭus, a, um, adj. crepida, of or pertaining to the sole or sandal: sutor, a sandal-maker, shoemaker, Sempr. Asell. ap. Gell. 13, 21, 8: culter, Gell. ib.

crepidatus.full: crĕpĭdātus, a, um, adj. id., wearing sandals, Cic. Pis. 38, 92 and 93; Suet. Dom. 4: fabula, a kind of Græco-Roman tragedy, Don. Ter. Ad. prol. 7; cf. Neukirch. Fab. Tog. pp. 15 and 57.

crepido.full: crĕpīdo, ĭnis, f. κρηπίς. Prop., a ground, basis, foundation, a socle, pedestal, base, Plin. 36, 9, 14, § 66; Stat. S. 1, 1, 58: altaris, Vulg. Lev. 1, 15.— Transf., an elevated enclosure, a high projection, an edge, brim, brink, border, dam, dike, pier, shore, bank, etc., Cic. Verr. 2, 5, 37, § 97; Varr. R. R. 3, 11, 2; Verg. A. 10, 653; Liv. 27, 18, 6; Curt. 5, 1, 28; Sen. Contr. 3, 17; Vitr. 4, 6, 3 et saep.— Trop.: omnia tamquam crepidine quādam comprehensione longiore sustinentur, Cic. Or.

crepidula.full: crĕpĭdŭla, ae, f. dim. crepida, a small sandal, Plaut. Pers. 4, 2, 3; cf. Gell. 13, 21, 5.

crepidulum.full: crĕpĭdŭlum, i, n., v. crepitulum fin.

crepis.full: crēpis, ĭdis, f., = κρηπίς, an unknown plant, Plin. 21, 16, 59, § 99.
crepis.short: crēpis, ĭdis, f., = κρηπίς, an unknown plant, Plin.

crepitacillum.full: crĕpĭtācillum, i, n. dim. crepitaculum, a small rattle, Lucr. 5, 229; Tert. adv. Marc. 3, 8.

crepitaculum.full: crĕpĭtācŭlum, i, n. crepito, a rattle, Quint. 9, 4, 66; Mart. 14, 54; Mart. Cap. 1, § 7; 9, §§ 909, 927.

crepito.full: crĕpĭto, āre, v. freq. n. [crepo], to rattle much, to creak, crackle, clatter, rustle, rumble, chatter, murmur, etc. (poet. or in post-Aug. prose): dentibus, Plaut. Rud. 2, 6, 52; Lucr. 5, 746: tenui rostro, Ov. M. 11, 735; cf. id. ib. 6, 97: lapillis unda, id. ib. 11, 604: multā grandine nimbi, Verg. A. 5, 459; cf. id. G. 1, 449: leni vento brattea, id. A. 6, 209: duris incudibus enses, to ring, id. G. 2, 540; cf. arma, Tib. 2, 5, 73; Ov. M. 1, 143; 15, 783: fulvo auro rami, id. ib. 10, 648: fl

crepitulum.full: crĕpĭtŭlum (crĕpic-; i, n.) ornamentum capitis, idem enim in capitis motu crepitum facit, Paul. ex Fest. p. 52, 19 Müll. —Form crĕpĭdŭlum, Tert. Pall. 4.

crepitus.full: crĕpĭtus, ūs, m. crepo, a rattling, creaking, clattering, clashing, rustling, a noise, etc. (in good prose). In gen.: cardinum, Plaut. Curc. 1, 3, 1; cf. claustrorum (with sonitus), id. ib. 1, 3, 47: carbasi, Lucr. 6, 110: e motu frenorum, Varr. R. R. 2, 7, 12: dentium, a chattering, Cic. Tusc. 4, 8, 19: pedum, id. Top. 12, 52: armorum, Liv. 25, 6, 21; 38, 17, 5: alarum (anserum). id. 5, 47, 4: plagarum, Cic. Verr. 2, 5, 62, § 162: inlisae manus umeris, Sen. Ep. 56, 1: tibiarum et scabellorum, S

crepo.full: crĕpo, ŭi, ĭtum, 1, v. n. and a. [Sanscr. krap, to lament; cf. crabro] (mostly poet. or in post-Aug. prose; in class. prose, concrepo). Neutr., to rattle, crack, creak, rustle, clatter, tinkle, jingle, chink, etc. In gen.: foris, Plaut. Am. 1, 2, 34; Ter. Ad. 2, 3, 11: fores, id. Eun. 5, 7, 5; id. Heaut. 1, 1, 121; 3, 3, 52: intestina (with crepitant), Plaut. Men. 5, 5, 26: herba Sabina ad focos, Prop. 4 (5), 3, 58. cf. Ov. F. 4, 742: sonabile sistrum, id. M. 9, 784 (cf. crepitanti sistro, Prop.

crepulus.full: crĕpŭlus, a, um, adj. crepo, rattling, resounding, crashing (late Lat.): buccae, Sid. Ep. 9, 13, 2: fragor, id. ib. 4, 15.

crepundia.full: crĕpundĭa, ōrum, n. id., a rattle; and specif., Most freq., a child's rattle (cf. Ruhnk. ad Ter. Eun. 4, 6, 15), Plaut. Mil. 5, 6; id. Rud. 4, 4, 37; 5, 3, 7; id. Cist. 3, 5; 3, 4; 1, 4; Cic. Brut. 91, 313 Jahn ad loc.; Plin. 11, 51, 112, § 270.—Hence, † A CREPVNDIIS, from childhood, Inscr. Orell. 1183.— An amulet, App. Mag. p. 310, 19.— Rattling musical instruments, Just. 30, 1, 9.

crepusci.full: crĕpusci, qui eodem tempore erant nati, Varr. L. L. 6, § 5 [creper].
crepusci.short: crĕpusci, qui eodem tempore erant nati, Varr.

crepusculascens.full: crĕpuscŭlascens, entis, Part. [crepusculum], growing dusk, dusky: hora, Sid. Ep. 8, 3.

crepusculum.full: crĕpuscŭlum, i, n. creper, twilight, dusk (cf. Varr. L. L. 6, § 5 Müll.); and in partic., evening twilight, the dusk of the evening (opp. diluculum, the morning twilight, dawn; poet. or in post-Aug. prose). Prop., Plaut. Cas. prol. 40; Ov. M. 1, 219; 15, 681; id. F. 4, 735; Plin. 18, 25, 58, § 219; Suet. Ner. 26 al.— In gen., darkness: iter per opaca crepuscula, Ov. M. 14, 122; cf. id. ib. 11, 596.

cres.full: Cres, ētis, v. Creta, II. A.

crescentia.full: crescentĭa, ae, f. cresco, an increase, augmentation: dierum (opp. brevitates), Vitr. 9, 9, 7.

cresco.full: cresco, crēvi, crētum, 3 (inf. perf. sync. cresse, Lucr. 3, 683), v. inch. n. [1. creo]. Orig., of things not previously in existence, to come forth, grow, to arise, spring, be born, become visible, appear (so mostly poet.) Lit.: cetera, quae sursum crescunt sursumque creantur, Lucr. 6, 527: quaecumque e terrā corpora crescunt (for which, subsequently, exoriuntur), id. 1, 868: corpore de patrio ac materno sanguine crescunt, id. 4, 1210: hic et acanthus Et rosa crescit, Verg. Cul. 397.—So esp. fr

cresius.full: Crēsĭus, a, um, v. 1, Creta, II. B.

creta1.full: Crēta, ae (nom. Crētē, Mel. 2, 7, 12; Ov. M. 8, 118; 9, 668; 9, 735; acc. Creten, id. ib. 8, 99; Hor. C. 3, 27, 34 al.; on the contrary, Cretam, Verg. A. 3, 129 al.), f., = Κρήτη, Crete, an island in the Mediterranean Sea, distinguished in ancient times by its fruitfulness and very early cultivation, now Candia, Mel. l. l.; Plin. 4, 12, 20, § 58; Verg. A. 3, 104; Hor. Epod. 9, 29; Cic. Fl. 13, 30; id. Phil. 2, 38, 97; Vell. 2, 34, 1; Varr. R. R. 1, 7, 6; Plin. 15, 11, 10, § 37.— Hence, Crēs, Crē

creta2.full: crēta, ae, f. orig. adj., from 1. Creta, Cretan earth, i. e. chalk, white earth or clay. Prop., Plin. 35, 17, 57, § 195 sq.; Cato, R. R. 39, 2; Varr. R. R. 1, 7, 8 al.; esp. used for cleansing garments, Plaut. Aul. 4, 9, 6.—Hence, trop.: creta est profecto horum hominum oratio, i. e. removes all trouble from the mind, Plaut. Poen. 5, 2, 10 sq.— Also used as a cosmetic, Hor. Epod. 12, 10; Mart. 6, 93, 9; 8, 33, 17 al.; for seals, Cic. Fl. 16, 37; cf. cretula, for marking the goal in a race-course

cretaceus.full: crētācĕus, a, um, adj. 2. creta, chalk-like, cretaceous: siligo, Plin. 18, 9, 20, § 86.

cretaeus.full: Crētaeus, a, um, v. 1. Creta, II. C.

cretanus.full: Crētānus, i, v. 1. Creta, II. D.

cretarius.full: crētārĭus, a, um, adj. 2. creta, of or pertaining to chalk: ARS, Inscr. Grut. 641, 3.— Subst.: crētārĭa, ae, f. (sc. taberna), a shop for Cretan earth, Varr. L. L. 8, § 55 Müll.

cretatus.full: crētātus, a, um, adj. id., marked with chalk. Prop.: fasciae, Cic. Att. 2, 3, 1: pedes, Plin. 35, 18, 58, § 201: bos (decorated as an offering), Juv. 10, 66: Fabulla, whitened, Mart. 2, 41, 11.— Transf.: ambitio, i. e. of the candidates for office, clothed in white (candidatorum), Pers. 5, 177.

cretensis.full: Crētensis, e, v. 1, Creta, II. E.

creteus.full: crētĕus, a, um, adj. 2. creta, made of chalk or clay: persona, Lucr. 4, 298.

crethmos.full: crēthmŏs, i, f., = κρῆθμος, sea-fennel: Crithmum maritimum, Linn.; Plin. 25, 13, 96, § 155; 26, 8, 50, § 82.
crethmos.short: crēthmŏs, i, f., = κρῆθμος, sea-fennel: Crithmum maritimum, Linn.;

cretica.full: crētĭca, ae, and crētĭcē, ēs, v. 1. Creta, II. F. 2. b.
cretica.short: crētĭca, ae, and crētĭcē, ēs, v.

creticus.full: Crētĭcus, a, um, v. 1. Creta, II. F.

cretifodina.full: crētĭ-fŏdīna, ae, f. 2. creta, a chalk- or clay-pit, Dig. 7, 1, 13, § 5 al.

cretio.full: crētĭo, ōnis, f. cerno, II.; jurid. t. t., the format declaration by the heir of his intention to enter upon his inheritance. Prop., Gai Inst. 2, § 7; 2, 164 sqq.; 2, 171 sqq.; Ulp. Fragm. 22, 25 sqq.; Varr. L. L. 6, § 81 Müll.: simplex, fruitless, i. e. where there is no property, Cic. Att. 11, 12, 4: libera, without restrictions by the testator, id. ib. 13, 46, 3; id. de Or. 1, 22, 101 al.— Meton., an inheritance, Plin. 2, 26, 24, § 95 fin.

cretis.full: Crētis, ĭdis, v. 1. Creta, II. G.

cretosus.full: crētōsus, a, um, adj. 2. creta, abounding in chalk or clay: locus, Cato, R. R. 8, 1; Plin. 15, 18, 19, § 72: terra, Varr. R. R. 1, 9, 3; Plin. 18, 19, 49, § 175: rura Cimoli, Ov. M. 7, 463.

cretula.full: crētŭla, ae, f. dim. id., white clay, used for sealing, = terra sigillata, Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 26, § 58; Plin. 35, 7, 31, § 49.

cretura.full: crētūra, ae, f. cerno; concr., the siftings of corn, bran, chaff (late Lat.), Pall. 1, 24, 3.

cretus1.full: crētus, a, um, Part., from cerno.
cretus1.short: crētus, a, um, Part., from cerno.

cretus2.full: crētus, a, um, Part., from cresco. q. v. I. A. fin.
cretus2.short: crētus, a, um, Part., from cresco.

creusa.full: Crĕūsa, ae, f., = Κρέουσα. A daughter of king Creon, of Corinth, married to Jason, and on that account put to death by Medea by means of a charmed offering (a garment, acc. to Hor. Epod. 5, 65; a garment and a golden chain, acc. to Sen. Med. 571 sq.; a crown, acc. to Ov. Ib. 601; Plin. 2, 105, 109, § 235), Hyg. Fab. 25; Sen. Med. 496; 509 al.— A daughter of Priam, and wife of Æneas, Verg. A. 2, 738.— A town, with a harbor, in Bœotia, Liv. 36, 21, 5; 42, 56, 5.—Also called Creūsis, acc. to the Gr

cribello.full: crībello, no perf., ātum, 1, v. a. cribellum, to pass through a sieve, to sift (late Lat.), Pall. 1, 41, 3; Theod. Prisc. 1, 17 al.

cribellum.full: crībellum, i, n. dim. cribrum, a small sieve (late Lat.), Pall. Febr. 24; id. Jun. 11.

cribrarius.full: crībrārĭus, a, um, adj. id., pertaining to a sieve: cribrarius alica, sifted, Plin. 18, 11, 29, §115.—Subst.: † crībrārĭus, a sieve-maker, κοσκινοποιός, Gloss. Gr. Lat.

cribro.full: crībro, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. id., to pass through a sieve, to sift (perh. not anteAug.), Col. 12, 51, 1; Plin. 17, 11, 15, § 76 al.

cribrum.full: crībrum, i, n. from root cer, whence cerno, a sieve, searce, riddle, Cato, R. R. 25, 76, 3; Plaut. Rud. 1, 2, 14; Cic. Div. 2, 27, 59; Col. 8, 5, 16; Plin. 18, 11, 28, § 108 sq.; Ov. M. 12, 437; Pers. 3, 112 et saep.— Facete, of a slave whose back was pierced by goads: carnificum cribrum, Plant. Most. 1, 1, 52.—Prov.: imbrem in cribrum gerere, i. e. to labor in vain, Plaut. Ps. 1, 1, 100.

crimen.full: crīmen, ĭnis, n. contr. for cernimen, from cerno, II. C.; lit., a judicial decision, verdict, judgment; hence, transf., like the Gr. κρῖμα, of the subject of such a decision, and with partieular reference either to the accuser or to the accused. Subject., or with reference to the accuser, a charge, accusation, reproach; esp. when unfounded, a calumny, slander (very freq. in every period and species of composition): criminin' me habuisse fidem? Plaut. Bacch. 4, 3, 15; cf. Ter. Hec. 5, 2, 13: hae

criminalis.full: crīmĭnālis, e, adj. crimen, of or pertaining to crime, criminal (jurid. Lat.): causa, Cod. Just. 9, 41, 15: accusatio, ib. 3, 35, 3.—Adv.: crīmĭnālĭter, criminally: agi furti, Dig. 47, 2 fin.

criminatio.full: crīmĭnātĭo, ōnis, f. criminor, an accusation, complaint, calumny (in good prose): criminatione in me absentem uti, Cic. Agr. 3, 1, 3: criminatio tua quae est? Roscium cum Flavio pro societate decidisse, id. Rosc. Com. 13, 37; id. de Or. 2, 79, 321; Liv. 1, 54, 8 al.—In plur., Cic. Lael. 18, 65; Liv. 7, 5, 1; 9, 26, 19; Tac. A. 6, 25; Suet. Caes. 55; Just. 12, 14, 3 al.

criminator.full: crīmĭnātor, ōris, m. id., an accuser, a calumniator (very rare): meus, Plaut. Bacch. 4, 7, 28: in alios (opp. sui obtegens), Tac. A. 4, 1.—Of the devil, Lact. 2, 8, 6; 6, 4, 2.

criminatrix.full: crīmĭnātrix, īcis, f. criminator, a female accuser, calumniator, Vulg. Paul. ad Tit. 2, 3.

crimino.full: crīmĭno, āre, 1, v. a.; collat. form of criminor, to accuse, make an accusation: aliquem apud aliquem, Plaut. Ps. 1, 5, 78.— Absol.: apud aliquem, Enn. ap. Non. p. 470, 16 (Sat. v. 9 Vahl.).— Pass.: Sullanas res defendere criminor, Cic. Agr. 3, 4, 13 dub. Orell. N. cr.: criminatum esse ab aliquo, Hyg. Astr. 2, 18.

criminor.full: crīmĭnor, ātus, 1, v. dep. crimen, I.. With a personal object, to accuse one of crime, to complain of, impeach, calumniate (rare but class.): hanc metui ne me criminaretur tibi, Ter. Eun. 5, 2, 16; so, aliquem alicui, Tac. Or. 42; Suet. Calig. 56; cf. under β: Q. Metellum apud populum Romanum criminatus est, bellum illum ducere, etc., Cic. Off. 3, 20, 79; cf. Liv. 1, 54, 8: Patres, id. 31, 6, 4: auctores, Quint. 1, 5, 11: inopinantem, Suet. Tib. 64 al.— With things as objects, to complain of, to

criminosus.full: crīmĭnōsus, a, um, adj. crimen, I., full of reproaches, reproachful, accusalory, calumniating, slanderous (class.): ne cum me nimium gratum illi esse dicant, id mihi criminosum esse possit, Cic. Planc. 2, 4; Cic. Verr. 2, 2, 67, § 162; cf.: in hunc, id. Sull. 13, 36: nomen, id. Planc. 19, 46: orationes, Liv. 8, 12, 14: iambi, Hor. C. 1, 16, 2: criminosissimus liber, Suet. Caes. 75; cf. Quint. 9, 2, 23: ille acerbus, criminosus, popularis homo ac turbulentus, Cic. Clu. 34, 94.—Hence, subst.: crīm

crimisus.full: Crīmīsus (in MSS. and edd. also Crī-messus, Crīmissus, Crīnīsus, and Crīnissus), i, m., = Κριμῖσός (Κριμισσός), a river on the south-west coast of Sicily, Nep. Timol. 2, 4; Verg. A. 5, 38; Claud. Rapt. Pros. 2, 57; Hyg. Fab. 273.

crinalis.full: crīnālis, e, adj. crinis, of or pertaining to the hair, hair- (poet., or in post-Aug. prose): vitta, Verg. A. 7, 403; Ov. M. 4, 6; 5, 617: aurum, Verg. A. 11, 576; Stat. Achill. 2, 97: acus, a hair-pin, App. M. 8, p. 207, 4; for which subst.: crīnāle, is, n., Ov. M. 5, 53: dentes, i. e. of a hair-comb, Claud. B. Gild. 137: corpore polypus, i. e. furnished with hair-like feelers, Ov. Hal. 30; cf. Plin. 9, 29, 46, § 86 (s. v. crinis, II. B.).

criniger.full: crīnĭger, gĕri, m. adj. crinis-gero, having long hair, Luc. 1, 458 dub. (al. cirrigeros, with long curls).

crininus.full: crĭnĭnus, a, um, adj., = κρίνινος, made of lilies, lily-: unguentum, Dig. 34, 2, 21; cf. crinon.
crininus.short: crĭnĭnus, a, um, adj., = κρίνινος, made of lilies, lily-: unguentum, Dig.

crinio.full: crīnĭo, no perf., ītum, 4, v. a. crinis, to provide or cover with hair; as verb. finit. rare, and only transf. of leaves of plants: frondibus crinitur arbos, Stat. S. 4, 5, 10; id. Th. 4, 217.—But freq., In part. perf.: crīnītus, a, um, covered with hair, hairy; esp., having long hair or locks, long-haired. Lit.: Apollo, Enn. ap. Cic. Ac. 2, 28, 89: lopas, Verg. A. 1, 740: male puella, Ov. A. A. 3, 243: turbae (sc. puerorum), Mart. 12, 49: colla equorum, Stat. Th. 6, 418 al.— Transf.: galea trip

crinis.full: crīnis, is, m. (fem., Atta ap. Non. p. 202, 29; acc. to the latter also Plaut. Most. 1, 3, 69; and so in Ritschl) [kindr. with crista; cf. κόρυς, κορυφή], the hair. Prop. (class.; esp. freq. in the poets), Cic. Verr. 2, 3, 33, § 76; Caes. B. G. 1, 51; id. B. C. 3, 9; Liv. 1, 13, 1; 3, 7, 8 et saep.; Verg. A. 1, 480; Cat. 64, 391; Hor. C. 2, 5, 24; 2, 19, 20 et saep.: capere crines, i. e. to marry (since the matrons distinguished themselves from maidens by their hair-dress), Plaut. Most. 1, 3, 69

crinitus.full: crīnītus, a, um, v. crinio, II.

crinon.full: crĭnon or crĭnum, i, n., = κρίνον, a lily, Plin. 21, 5, 11, § 24.— An unguent, Dig. 34, 2, 21 (where others read crinina; v. crininus).† † crīŏbŏlĭum, ii, n., = κριοβόλιον, a ram as an offering, Inscr. Orell. 1899 sq.
crinon.short: crĭnon or crĭnum, i, n., = κρίνον, a lily, Plin.

crisa.full: Crīsa, ae, f., = Κρῖσα, an ancient town of Phocis, on the sea, now Crisso, Plin. 4, 3, 4, § 8.—Hence, adj.: Crīsaeus, a, um, of Crisa: sinus = κόλπος Κρισαῖος, Plin. 4, 3, 4, § 7.
crisa.short: Crīsa, ae, f., = Κρῖσα, an ancient town of Phocis, on the sea, now Crisso, Plin.

crisimus.full: crĭsĭmus, a, um, adj., = κρίσιμος, decisive, critical: dies, the day of a crisis, in disease, Cael. Aur. Acut. 1, 14, 108; Censor. 14, 9.
crisimus.short: crĭsĭmus, a, um, adj., = κρίσιμος, decisive, critical: dies, the day of a crisis, in disease, Cael.

crisis.full: crĭsis, is, f., = κρίσις, medic. t. t., a decision, crisis, Sen. Ep. 83, 4.

criso.full: crīso or crisso, āvi, 1, v. n., to move the haunches (in mal. part.; of a female, as ceveo of a male), Lucil. ap. Non. p. 19, 26; Juv. 6, 322; Mart. 14, 203; Auct. Priap. 19, 4 Büch.; cf. Charis. p. 260 P.; Diom. p. 293 ib.; v. Lachm. ad Lucr. vol. 2, p. 276 sq.

crispans.full: crispans, ntis, Part. of crispo, q. v.

crispicans.full: crispĭcans, antis, Part., from the unused v. a. crispico, āre [crispus], curling, ruffling: mare ventus, Gell. 18, 11, 3.
crispicans.short: crispĭcans, antis, Part., from the unused v.
