crispicapillus.full: crispĭcăpillus, οὐλόθριξ having curled hair, Gloss. Lat. Gr.
crispicapillus.short: crispĭcăpillus, οὐλόθριξ having curled hair, Gloss.

crispinus.full: Crispīnus, a, a Roman surname, Cic. Font. 1, 1; Liv. 24, 39, 12; Hor. S. 1, 1, 120 al.; Capitol. M. Antonin. 27.
crispinus.short: Crispīnus, a, a Roman surname, Cic.

crispisulcans.full: crispĭsulcans, antis, Part. [crispussulco], undulating, serpentine: igneum fulmen, Poët. ap. Cic. Top. 16, 61.

crispitudo.full: crispĭtūdo, ĭnis, f. crispus, a tremulous or vibratory motion, Arn. 2, p. 73.

crispo.full: crispo, no perf., ātum, 1, v. a. and n. id.. Act., to curl, crisp, crimp (poet. or in post-Aug. prose). Prop.: capillum, Plin. 29, 4, 26, § 82: feminae cincinnos, Maec. ap. Sen. Ep. 114, 5.— Transf. To make variegated, rough, uneven; to cover or plant with something, to strew over: tellurem apio viridi, to border, Col. 10, 166: mixtum aurum cono, Stat. Th. 8, 568: alma novo crispans pelagus Tithonia Phoebo, Val. Fl. 1, 311; cf. Zumpt ad Rutil. 2, 13: quādam rugatione crispari corpora, Cael. Aur.

crispulus.full: crispŭlus, a, um, adj. dim. [id.], curled, having curled hair, crisped, crimped (post-Aug.). Prop.: comatus et crispulus, Sen. Ep. 66, 25; cf. id. ib. 95, 24; Mart. 5, 61, 1.—* Trop., of discourse, elaborate, artificial, Fronto, Or. Ep. 3, p. 248.

crispus1.full: crispus, a, um, adj. kindred with crinis, crista; cf. cresco. Originally of the hair, curled, crisped, crimped: cincinni, Plaut. Truc. 2, 2, 32; cf. coma, Sil. 16, 120; and: leo crispioribus jubis, Plin. 8, 16, 18, § 46.—Of persons, having curled hair, curlyheaded, Plaut. Capt. 3, 4, 115; id. Rud. 1, 2, 37; Ter. Hec. 3, 4, 26.—* Trop., of discourse, artistic, elaborate: crispum agmen orationis, Gell. 1, 4, 4; cf. crispulus, II.— Transf. Curled, uneven, waving, wrinkled: parietes abiete crispā, E

crispus2.full: Crispus, i, m., a Roman surname; so esp. of the well-known Roman historian C. Sallustius.
crispus2.short: Crispus, i, m., a Roman surname;

crista1.full: crista, ae, f. cf. cer- in cerebrum, pro-ceres, = cel- in excello. Prop., a tuft on the head of animals; most freq. of the comb of a cock, Varr. R. R. 3, 9, 4 and 5; Plin. 10, 56, 77, § 156; Juv. 13, 233 al.; of a lapwing, Ov. M. 6, 672; Plin. 10, 29, 44, § 86; of a serpent, Ov. M. 7, 150; 15, 669; Plin. 11, 37, 44, § 122.—Prov.: illi surgunt cristae, his crest rises, he carries his head high, i. e. he is conceited, Juv. 4, 70.— Transf. A tuft of leaves on plants: foliorum, Plin. 22, 22, 43, § 8

crista2.full: Crista, ae, m., a Roman surname, Liv. 24, 40, 8.
crista2.short: Crista, ae, m., a Roman surname, Liv.

cristatus.full: cristātus, a, um, adj. crista, that has a tuft or crest, tufted, crested. Lit.: ales, Ov. F. 1, 455; cf.: cristati oris ales, id. M. 11, 597: aves, i. e. galli, Mart. 14, 223: draco, Ov. M. 4, 599; Plin. 8, 13, 13, § 35.— Transf., crested, plumed: cassis pennis, Ov. M. 8, 25: galeae, Liv. 9, 40, 3: jubar, Stat. Th. 3, 223: Achilles, Verg. A. 1, 468.

cristula.full: cristŭla, ae, f. dim. id., a small crest or tuft, Col. 8, 2, 8 (al. cristis).

critae.full: crĭtae, ārum, m., = κριταί, the judges among the Hebrews , Tert. adv. Gnost. 3.
critae.short: crĭtae, ārum, m., = κριταί, the judges among the Hebrews , Tert.

crithologia.full: crīthŏlŏgĭa, ae, f., = κριθολογία, a gathering of barley, Cod. Just. 11, 27, 1; Cod. Th. 14, 26, 1.
crithologia.short: crīthŏlŏgĭa, ae, f., = κριθολογία, a gathering of barley, Cod.

crithote.full: Crīthōtē, ēs, f., = Κριθωτή, a town in Chersonesus Thracia, Nep. Timoth. 1, 3; Plin. 4, 11, 18, § 48.
crithote.short: Crīthōtē, ēs, f., = Κριθωτή, a town in Chersonesus Thracia, Nep.

critias.full: Crĭtĭas, ae, m., = Κριτίας, one of the thirty tyrants at Athens, Cic. Tusc. 1, 40, 96; id. de Or. 2, 22, 93; Nep. Thras. 2, 7.
critias.short: Crĭtĭas, ae, m., = Κριτίας, one of the thirty tyrants at Athens, Cic.

criticus.full: crĭtĭcus, a, um, adj., = κριτικός, fit or suitable for deciding, capable of judging. Adj., only as a medic. t. t. (cf. crisimus), decisive, critical: accessio morbi, Aug. Conf. 6, 1 fin.—More frequent, Subst.: crĭtĭ-cus, i, m., a critic, Cic. Fam. 9, 10, 1 (also ap. Suet. Gram. 14); Quint. 2, 1, 4; Hor. Ep. 2, 1, 51.
criticus.short: crĭtĭcus, a, um, adj., = κριτικός, fit or suitable for deciding, capable of judging.

crito.full: Crīto, ōnis, m., = Κρίτων, a rich citizen of Athens, a disciple and friend of Socrates, Cic. Tusc. 1, 43, 103 al.— A Grecian physician of Trajan's time, Mart. 11, 60, 6.
crito.short: Crīto, ōnis, m., = Κρίτων, a rich citizen of Athens, a disciple and friend of Socrates, Cic.

critobulus.full: Crĭtŏbūlus, i, m., a Greek proper name. A disciple of Socrates, Cic. Sen. 17, 59.— A Grecian physician, Curt. 9, 5, 25; Plin. 7, 57, 37, § 124.
critobulus.short: Crĭtŏbūlus, i, m., a Greek proper name.

critognatus.full: Critognatus, i, m., a chief of the Arverni, Caes. B. G. 7, 77.
critognatus.short: Critognatus, i, m., a chief of the Arverni, Caes.

critolaus.full: Crĭtŏlāus, i, m. A peripatetic philosopher, who was sent with Carneades and the Stoic Diogenes as an ambassador to Rome, Cic. de Or. 1, 11, 45; 2, 37, 155; id. Tusc. 5, 17, 51; id. Fin. 5, 5, 14; Gell. 6 ($3), 14, 9; 17, 21, 48; Tert. Anim. 5.— A leader of the Achaians, in a war with the Romans, Cic. N. D. 3, 38, 91; Flor. 2, 16, 2.— A Sicilian at Henna, Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 26, § 59.

criumetopon.full: Crīūmĕtōpon, i, n., = Κριοῦ μέτωπον (Ramsbrow), a promontory at the southern extremity of the Tauric Chersonesus, Plin. 4, 12, 26, § 86; 10, 23, 30, § 60; written as Greek, Mel. 2, 1, 3.— A promontory at the southwestern point of Crete, now Cape Crio, Plin. 4, 12, 20, § 59; written as Greek, Mel. 2, 7, 12.
criumetopon.short: Crīūmĕtōpon, i, n., = Κριοῦ μέτωπον (Ramsbrow), a promontory at the southern extremity of the Tauric Chersonesus, Plin.

crobylos.full: crōbўlŏs, i, m., = κρώβυλος, a roll of hair knotted on the crown of the head, Tert. Virg. Vel. 10; cf. Serv. ad Verg. A. 4, 138.
crobylos.short: crōbўlŏs, i, m., = κρώβυλος, a roll of hair knotted on the crown of the head, Tert.

crocale.full: Crŏcălē, ēs, f., a companion of Diana, Ov. M. 3, 169.
crocale.short: Crŏcălē, ēs, f., a companion of Diana, Ov.

crocallis.full: crocallis, ĭdis, f., an unknown, cherryshaped precious stone, Plin. 37, 10, 56, § 154.
crocallis.short: crocallis, ĭdis, f., an unknown, cherryshaped precious stone, Plin.

crocatio.full: crocātĭo, ōnis, f. crocio, the croaking of ravens, Paul. ex Fest. p. 53, 3.

crocatus.full: crŏcātus, a, um, adj. crocus, saffronyellow: semen, Plin. 16, 34, 62, § 147: vestis, Fronto, Ep. ad M. Caes. 2, 1.

croceus.full: crŏcĕus, a, um, adj. id., of or pertaining to saffron, saffron-. Prop.: odores, Verg. G. 1, 56: flores, id. ib. 4, 109: tinctus, saffron-sauce, Plin. 10, 48, 68, § 134: color, id. 27, 10, 59, § 83.— Transf., saffron-colored, yellow, golden: lutum, Verg. E. 4, 44: cubile, id. G. 1, 447: acanthus, id. A. 1, 649: chlamys, id. ib. 11, 775 al.: comae, Ov. A. A. 1, 530: honor, a saffron-tint, Sil. 8, 444.

crocias.full: crŏcĭas, ae, m., = κροκίας, an unknown, saffron-colored precious stone, Plin. 37, 11, 73, § 191.
crocias.short: crŏcĭas, ae, m., = κροκίας, an unknown, saffron-colored precious stone, Plin.

crocidismus.full: crŏcĭdismus, i, m., = κροκιδισμός; of the sick, a picking off of flocks (of wool, etc.), Cael. Aur. Acut. 1, 3, 34; 1, 6, 48; cf. carphologia.

crocino.full: crŏcĭno, āre, v. a. crocum, to anoint with saffron-ointment: jumenta, Gargil. Mart. de Cura Boum, p. 457 Bip.

crocinus.full: crŏcĭnus, a, um, adj., = κρόκινος, of or pertaining to saffron, saffron-. Adj.: semen, Plin. 21, 19, 73, 124: unguentum, Cels. 3, 18: color, Scrib. Comp. 173: tunica, saffron-colored, Cat. 68, 134.— Subst.: crŏcĭnum, i, n. (sc. oleum), saffron-oil, Prop. 3 (4), 10, 22.— The color of saffron, saffron-yellow, Dig. 32, 1, 78, § 5.— Transf., as a term of endearment, Plaut. Curc. 1, 2, 7.
crocinus.short: crŏcĭnus, a, um, adj., = κρόκινος, of or pertaining to saffron, saffron-.

crocio.full: crōcĭo, īre, v. n., = κρώζω, to cry or croak as a raven [cf. glocio, clango], Plaut. Aul. 4, 3, 2; App. Flor. 23, p. 366, 19.

crocis.full: crŏcis, ĭdis, f., = κροκίς, an unknown plant, Plin. 24, 17, 102, § 167.
crocis.short: crŏcis, ĭdis, f., = κροκίς, an unknown plant, Plin.

crocito.full: crŏcĭto, āre, v. freq. n. [crocio, with change of quantity], to croak loudly: corvus, Auct. Philom. 28; Anthol. Lat. 5, 123, 24.

crocitus.full: crōcītus, ūs, m. crocio, the croaking of the raven, Non. p. 45, 18.

croco.full: crŏco, āre, v. a., to dye saffron-yellow, Isid. Orig. 6, 11, 4; cf. crocatus.

crocodes.full: crŏcōdes, is, n., = κροκῶδες, a (saffron-like) eye-salve, Inscr. Orell. 4233 sq.
crocodes.short: crŏcōdes, is, n., = κροκῶδες, a (saffron-like) eye-salve, Inscr.

crocodilea.full: crŏcŏdīlĕa, ae, f., = κροκοδειλέα, the excrement of the crocodile, as a medicament, Plin. 28, 8, 28, § 108 (cf. Hor. Epod. 12, 11).
crocodilea.short: crŏcŏdīlĕa, ae, f., = κροκοδειλέα, the excrement of the crocodile, as a medicament, Plin.

crocodilina.full: crŏcŏdīlĭna, ae, f., = κροκοδειλίνη (cf. Lidd. and Scott, under κροκόδειλος, II.; v. also ceratina), a sophism called crocodile, a crocodile-conclusion, Quint. 1, 10, 5.

crocodilion.full: crŏcŏdīlĭon (-lĕon), ii, n., = κροκοδείλιον, a plant, so called from the rough skin of its stalk, Plin. 27, 8, 41, § 64.
crocodilion.short: crŏcŏdīlĭon (-lĕon), ii, n., = κροκοδείλιον, a plant, so called from the rough skin of its stalk, Plin.

crocodilus.full: crŏcŏdīlus, i, m., = κροκόδειλος, a crocodile, Plin. 8, 25, 37, § 89 sq.; 28, 8, 28, § 107 sq.; Cic. N. D. 2, 48, 124; 2, 52, 129; 1, 29, 82; Sen. Q. N. 4, 2, 13.—In the metathesis corcŏdīlus, Phaedr. 1, 25, 4 and 6; Mart. 3, 93, 7 Schneid.; cf. Ritschl in Rhein. Mus. vol. 9, p. 478 sq.
crocodilus.short: crŏcŏdīlus, i, m., = κροκόδειλος, a crocodile, Plin.

crocofantia.full: crŏcŏfantĭa (crŏcŭ-, -phantĭa), ae, f. [κρόκος, ὑφαίνειν], = crocota, q. v., Dig. 34, 2, 25, § 10.

crocomagma.full: crŏcŏmagma, ătis, n., = κροκόμαγμα, the residuum of saffron, after the extraction of the oil, Plin. 21, 20, 82, § 139; Cels. 5, 18, 9 al.
crocomagma.short: crŏcŏmagma, ătis, n., = κροκόμαγμα, the residuum of saffron, after the extraction of the oil, Plin.

crocota.full: crŏcōta, ae, f. (sc. vestis), ὁ κροκωτός (sc. χιτών), a saffron-colored court-dress (for women), Naev. and Nov. ap. Non. p. 548, 26 sq.; Plaut. ib. 538, 13; App. M. 11, p. 261, 2; Auct. Har. Resp. 21, 44; cf. crocotula.

crocotarius.full: crŏcōtārĭus, a, um, adj. crocota, of or belonging to the preparation of saffron-colored garments: infectores, Plaut. Aul. 3, 5, 47.

crocotillum.full: crocotillum, valde exile, Plaut. ap. Paul. ex Fest. p. 52, 20; cf. Fest. p. 301, 26 sq. Müll. N. cr. (certainly corrupt).

crocotinum.full: crocotinum genus operis pistorii, Paul. ex Fest. p. 53, 5 Müll.

crocotta.full: crŏcotta (cŏrŏc-) or crŏcūta, ae, m., an unknown witd animal in Ethiopia, perh. the hyena, Plin. 8, 21, 30, § 72; 8, 30, 45, § 107; Capitol. Anton. 10.
crocotta.short: crŏcotta (cŏrŏc-) or crŏcūta, ae, m., an unknown witd animal in Ethiopia, perh.

crocotula.full: crŏcōtŭla, ae, f. dim. crocota, a saffron-colored court-robe (for women), Plaut. Ep. 2, 2, 47; Verg. Cat. 5, 21.

crocum.full: crŏcum, i, n., and crŏcus, i, m. (fem., App. M. 10, p. 255, 30), = κρόκος, saffron: Crocus sativus, Linn.; masc. usu. of the plant, neutr. of the essence, etc., but the distinction is not closely observed. Crocus, Verg. G. 4, 182; id. Cul. 399; plur. nom. croci, Ov. M. 4, 393; acc. crocos, Prop. 4 (5), 1, 16; Ov. F. 4, 442; Juv. 7, 208.— Crocum, Sall. H. 1, 80 Dietsch; Cels. 5, 11; Plin. 21, 6, 17, § 31 sq.— Gen. incert., Lucr. 2, 416; Ov. F. 1, 342; 5, 318; Sall. H. 2, 23, 2 Dietsch; Col. 9, 4,
crocum.short: crŏcum, i, n., and crŏcus, i, m.

crodunum.full: Crodunum, i, n., a place in Gallia Narbonensis, now Gourdan, Cic. Font. 5, 9.
crodunum.short: Crodunum, i, n., a place in Gallia Narbonensis, now Gourdan, Cic.

croesus.full: Croesus, i, m., = Κροῖσος, a king of Lydia, celebrated for his riches, Cic. Div. 1, 19, 37; id. Fin. 2, 27, 87; Hor. Ep. 1, 11, 2; Just. 1, 7, 2 sqq.; Prop. 2 (3), 26, 23.al.— Appel. for a rich man, in contrast with Irus, Ov. Tr. 3, 7, 42; and in plur., Mart. 11, 6, 4.—Hence, Croesĭus, a, um, adj., of Crœsus: opes, Mart. Cap. 6, § 578.
croesus.short: Croesus, i, m., = Κροῖσος, a king of Lydia, celebrated for his riches, Cic.

crommyuacris.full: Crŏmmўū-ācris (Crŏmў-), ĭdis, f., = Κρομύου ἄκρις, the most northern point of Cyprus, Cass. ap. Cic. Fam. 12, 13, 4 fin.
crommyuacris.short: Crŏmmўū-ācris (Crŏmў-), ĭdis, f., = Κρομύου ἄκρις, the most northern point of Cyprus, Cass.

cromyon.full: Crŏmўon (Cremmўon, Plin. 4, 7, 11, § 23), ōnis, m., = Κρομύων, a village in Megaris, afterwards belonging to Corinth, laid waste by a wild sow, which was slain at last by Theseus, Ov. M. 7, 435.

cronia.full: Crŏnĭa, ōrum, n., = τὰ Κρόνια, a festival of Saturn, celebrated in Greece, and especially at Athens, Att. ap. Macr. S. 1, 7, 37.
cronia.short: Crŏnĭa, ōrum, n., = τὰ Κρόνια, a festival of Saturn, celebrated in Greece, and especially at Athens, Att.

cronos.full: Crŏnŏs (-us), i, m., = Κρόνος, the god of time, = Saturnus, Sid. Carm. 15, 61 al.
cronos.short: Crŏnŏs (-us), i, m., = Κρόνος, the god of time, = Saturnus, Sid.

crosmis.full: crosmis, is, f., a kind of sage, App. Herb. 101.
crosmis.short: crosmis, is, f., a kind of sage, App.

crotalia.full: crŏtălĭa, ōrum, n., = κροτάλια, a rattling ear-pendant, composed of several pearls, Petr. 67; Plin. 9, 35, 56, § 114.
crotalia.short: crŏtălĭa, ōrum, n., = κροτάλια, a rattling ear-pendant, composed of several pearls, Petr.

crotalisso.full: crŏtălisso, āre, 1, v. n., = κροταλίζω, to rattle or sound with the castanet, Macr. Diff. 21, 8.

crotalistria.full: crŏtălistrĭa, ae, f. κροταλίζω, a (female) castanet dancer, Prop. 4 (5), 8, 39. — Poet., transf., a (rattling) stork, P. Syrus ap. Petr. 55 (cf. Ov. M. 6, 97).

crotalum.full: crŏtălum, i, n., = κρόταλον, a rattle, a bell, castanet, used to accompany wanton dances, P. Scip. ap. Macr. S. 2, 10; Cic. Pis. 9, 20 al.
crotalum.short: crŏtălum, i, n., = κρόταλον, a rattle, a bell, castanet, used to accompany wanton dances, P.

crotaphos.full: crŏtăphŏs, i, m., = κρόταφος, a pain in the temples, Cael. Aur. Tard. 11, 4.
crotaphos.short: crŏtăphŏs, i, m., = κρόταφος, a pain in the temples, Cael.

croto.full: Crŏto (Crŏton, Sil. 11, 18, 5; Cic. Att. 9, 19, 3), ōnis, comm. (and Crŏtōna, ae, f., Just. 20, 4; also Cortōna, like corcodilus for crocodilus; cf. Ritschl in Rhein. Mus. vol. 8, p. 475, and vol. 9, p. 480), = Κρότων, a town founded by the Achaians, on the east coast of Bruttium, now Crotone, Mel. 2, 4, 8; Plin. 3, 11, 15, § 97; Liv. 24, 3, 1 sq.; Cic. Att. 9, 19, 3; Ov. M. 15, 15 al.—Hence, Crŏtōnĭātes, ae, m., = Κροτωνιάτης, an inhabitant of Crotona: Alcmaeo, Cic. N. D. 1, 11, 27.—In plur.: C

crotopiades.full: Crŏtōpĭădes, ae, m., = Κροτωπιάδης, a Crotopiade, i. e. Linus (whose mother, Psamathe, was the daughter of the Grecian king Crotopus), Ov. Ib. 478.
crotopiades.short: Crŏtōpĭădes, ae, m., = Κροτωπιάδης, a Crotopiade, i.

crotos.full: Crŏtŏs, i, m., = Κρότος, a constellation, the Archer; pure Lat. Sagittarius, Col. 10, 57; access. form Crŏtōn, Hyg. Fab. 224 dub.
crotos.short: Crŏtŏs, i, m., = Κρότος, a constellation, the Archer;

cruciabilis.full: crŭcĭābĭlis, e, adj. crucio, tormenting, torturing, painful, excruciating, miserable (rare; not in Cic.): cruciabilem me accipito, Plaut. Ps. 4, 1, 40 Ritschl: exitu periit, Gell. 3, 9, 7; cf. mors, Arn. adv. Gent. 2: silentio fatigatus, App. M. 10, p. 239, 20. — Susceptible of torture: animae, Lact. 7, 20, 9.—Adv.: crŭcĭābĭlĭter, with torture, Plaut. Ps. 4, 1, 40 Fleck., Lorenz: interfecti, Auct. B. Afr. 46.

cruciabilitas.full: crŭcĭābĭlĭtas, ātis, f. cruciabilis, torment, torture: cruciabilitates animi, Plaut. Cist. 2, 1, 3.

cruciabundus.full: crŭcĭābundus, a, um, adj. crucio, torturing, tormenting, Cypr. Ep. 55.

cruciamen.full: crŭcĭāmen, ĭnis, n. id., torture, torment, pain: leti, Prud. Cath. 10, 90.

cruciamentum.full: crŭcĭāmentum, i, n. id., torture, torment, pain (very rare): vidi ego multa saepe picta quae Acherunti fierent Cruciamenta, Plaut. Capt. 5, 4, 2; id. As. 2, 2, 52: carnificum (with tormenta morborum), Cic. Phil. 11, 4, 8: ut orbitatis cruciamenta sentiret, Arn. 7, p. 43.

cruciarius.full: crŭcĭārĭus, a, um, adj. crux, of or pertaining to the cross, or, in gen., to torture. Adj.: exitus, full of torture, Tert. Praescr. Haeret. 2 dub. (al. cruciatorios): poenae, Sid. Ep. 8, 6.— Subst., one who is crucified, Petr. 112; Sen. Contr. 3, 21.—Hence, As a term of reproach, one fit for the gallows, a gallows-bird, App. M. 10, p. 242: longum est quae cruciarius ille conflavit, Amm. 29, 2, 9.

cruciatio.full: crŭcĭātĭo, ōnis, f. crucio, a torturing, Vulg. Sap. 6, 9.

cruciator.full: crŭcĭātor, ōris, m. crucio, a tormenter, torturer, Arn. 1, p. 23; Firm. Math. 3, 13, 6.

cruciatus.full: crŭcĭātus, ūs, m., torture, torment, a torturing, execution, etc. (often syn. with supplicium; freq. and class. in sing. and plur.). Lit., of the body: dedisti hodie in cruciatum Chrusalum, Plaut. Bacch. 4, 4, 36; id. Ep. 5, 1, 5; id. Ps. 3, 1, 12; Ter. And. 4, 4, 47; id. Hec. 5, 2, 7; Caes. B. G. 1, 31, 12; Cic. Verr. 2, 1, 4, § 9; 2, 5, 63, § 163; id. Rosc. Am. 41, 119; Sall. C. 51, 15; id. J. 24, 10; Liv. 29, 18, 14 Drak. N. cr.; Quint. 5, 4, 2; Ov. M. 9, 179 et saep.: cruciatu malo dignus, P
cruciatus.short: crŭcĭātus, ūs, m., torture, torment, a torturing, execution, etc.

crucifer.full: crŭcĭfer, fĕri, m. crux-fero, the crossbearer, i. e. Christ, Prud. Cath. 3, 1.

crucifigo.full: crŭcĭfīgo, ēre, better separated, cruci figo; v. crux.
crucifigo.short: crŭcĭfīgo, ēre, better separated, cruci figo;

crucifixor.full: crŭcĭfixor, ōris, m. crux-figo, a crucifier (eccl. Lat.), Paul. Nol. Ep. 18, 7.

crucio.full: crŭcĭo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. crux. Orig., to put to death on the cross, to crucify (only in eccl. Lat.), Lact. Mort. Pers. 2, 1.— In gen., to put to the rack, to torture, torment (freq. and class., esp. in the signif. B.). Physically: cum vigiliis et fame cruciaretur, Cic. Fin. 2, 20, 65: tribunos militum verberatos servilibusque omnibus suppliciis cruciatos trucidando occidit, Liv. 29, 18, 14 Drak. N. cr.: cum cruciabere dirae Sanguine serpentis, Ov. M. 2, 651: cruciataque diris Corpora tormenti

crucisalus.full: Crŭcĭsălus, i, m. crux-salio, a name facetiously formed in imitation of Chrysalus, i. e. a cross-dancer: facere aliquem Crucisalum ex Chrysalo, Plaut. Bacch. 2, 3, 128.

crucium.full: crŭcĭum, quod cruciat. Unde Lucilius vinum insuave crucium dixit, Paul. ex Fest. p. 53, 4 Müll.

crudaria.full: crūdārĭa vēna argenti, a vein of silver that lies directly on the surface in a mine, Plin. 33, 6, 31, § 97.
crudaria.short: crūdārĭa vēna argenti, a vein of silver that lies directly on the surface in a mine, Plin.

crudelis.full: crūdēlis, e, adj. cf. Gr. κρύος; Lat. crudus, cruor, caro, morally rude or unfeeling, with exclusive reference to conduct towards persons or things, hard, unmerciful, hard-hearted, cruel, severe, fierce (freq. and class. in prose and poetry). Of living subjects. With in and abl.: crudeles gaudent in tristi funere fratris, Lucr. 3, 72; cf.: crudelis in calamitate hominis consularis, Cic. de Or. 2, 48, 198: cui nimis videtur senatus in conservandā patriā fuisse crudelis, id. Pis. 8, 17.— With in a

crudelitas.full: crūdēlĭtas, ātis, f. crudelis, harshness, severity, cruelty, barbarity (in good prose and very freq.): crudelitas est atrocitas animi in exigendis poenis, Sen. Clem. 2, 4, 1: crudelitas est inclinatio ad asperiora, id. ib. 2, 4, 3: ista in nostros homines crudelitas, Cic. Verr. 2, 5, 88, § 150; id. Off. 2, 8, 27; 3, 11, 46; id. Sest. 65, 135; id. Phil. 11, 3, 8; id. Rep. 1, 3, 5; Caes. B. G. 7, 77; Sall. C. 51, 14; Nep. Alcib. 4, 4; Liv. 3, 53, 7; 42, 8, 5 et saep.; Prud. Perieg. 2291 al.: in me

crudeliter.full: crūdēlĭter, adv., v. crudelis fin. b.

crudesco.full: crūdesco, dŭi, 3, v. inch. n. [crudus], to grow harsh or violent, to increase, grow worse (poet. and in post-Aug. prose; perh. not before Virg.): coepit crudescere morbus, Verg. G. 3, 504; so, pugnae, id. A. 7, 788: ferrum magicā linguā, Sil. 1, 431: irae, Stat. Th. 2, 680; cf.: crudescente irā, Just. 8, 4, 4: seditio, Tac. H. 3, 10: noxa, Symm. Ep. 8, 57.

cruditas.full: crūdĭtas, ātis, f. id. (lit. indigestion; hence, meton.), (Effectus pro causa.) An overloading, repletion of the stomach, Cic. Sen. 13, 44; id. Fam. 9, 18, 4; id. Fat. 15, 34; Quint. 2, 21, 19; 5, 9, 11; Col. prooem. § 16; 6, 6, 1 al.— Transf., of plants: arbores laborant et fame et cruditate, superabundance of nutritious juices, Plin. 17, 24, 37, § 219.— (Abstr. pro concr.) Undigested food: cruditates digerunt daucum, plantago, etc., Plin. 26, 7, 25, § 41; cf.: cruditas fructuum, i. e. bitterne

cruditatio.full: crūdĭtātĭo, ōnis, f. crudito, i. q. cruditas, an overloading of the stomach, indigestion, Cael. Aur. Tard. 5, 2, 29.

crudito.full: crūdĭto, āre, v. a. crudus, to suffer from indigestion, Tert. Jejun. 16; id. Apol. 9.

crudus.full: crūdus, a, um, adj. root kru-, of Gr. κρύος; cf. cruor, crudelis, bloody, bleeding, trickling with blood, etc. Prop. (so rare): vulnus, Plin. Ep. 5, 16, 11: vulnera, Ov. Tr. 3, 11, 19; id. P. 1, 3, 16.— Transf. Of food, raw, not cooked: quid tu curas, utrum crudum an coctum edim? Plaut. Aul. 3, 2, 15: exta, Liv. 29, 27, 5: carnem mandere, Suet. Ner. 37.—So also of undigested food: pavo, Juv. 1, 143; cf. trop.: lectio non cruda sed multā iteratione mollita et velut confecta, Quint. 10, 1, 19; and

cruentatio.full: crŭentātĭo, ōnis, f. cruento, a staining with blood: altaris, Tert. adv. Marc. 4, 39.

cruente.full: crŭentē, adv., v. cruentus fin. a.

cruenter.full: crŭenter, adv., v. cruentus fin. b.

cruentifer.full: crŭentĭfer, fĕra, fĕrum, adj. cruentus-fero, bloody: signa, Tert. Jud. Dom. 10.

cruento.full: crŭento, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. cruentus, to make bloody, to spot with blood (class.). Lit.: vigiles, Enn. ap. Macr. S. 1, 4: manus suorum sanguine, Nep. Epam. 10, 3; cf. Liv. 23, 9, 4, and Tac. H. 1, 58 fin.: cornipedem ferratā calce, Sil. 17, 541: gladium, Cic. Inv. 2, 4, 14; cf. tela, Ov. M. 8, 424: ōs, id. ib. 4, 104: dextras, id. ib. 11, 23: cruentati redeunt, id. ib. 3, 572: ut sequenti die Luna se in Aquario cruentaret, would appear to be stained with blood, Suet. Dom. 16.— Trop.: haec te la

cruentus.full: crŭentus, a, um, adj. cruor, spotted, covered, or stained with blood, bloody. Prop. (freq. and class.): cruentus sanguine civium Romanorum, Cic. Phil. 4, 2, 4; cf.: sanguine fraterno, Hor. S. 2, 5, 15: caede filii, Just. 38, 8, 4: cadaver Clodii, Cic. Mil. 13, 33: vehiculum, Liv. 1, 48, 8: gladius, Quint. 4, 2, 13; 6, 1, 30: praetexta C. Caesaris, id. ib. § 31: vestis, id. 5, 9, 1: busta, Prop. 2, 13 (3, 5), 38: sputa, id. 4 (5), 5, 68 et saep.: victoria, Sall. C. 58, 21: pax, Tac. A. 1, 10: ite

crumena.full: crŭmēna (crŭmīna), ae, f. for scrumena; root scru-, of scrutor, scrotum, a small money-purse or bag (usually hanging from the neck). Prop., Plaut. Truc. 3, 1, 7 sq.; id. As. 3, 3, 63; 3, 3, 71; id. Ps. 1, 2, 37.— Transf., like our purse, for money: non deficiente crumenā, Hor. Ep. 1, 4, 11; Juv. 11, 38.

crumilla.full: crŭmilla, ae, f. dim. crumena, a little purse, Plaut. Pers. 4, 6, 5.

crumino.full: crŭmīno, āre, v. a. id., to fill like a purse, Ven. Vit. S. Mart. 2, 350.

cruor.full: crŭor, ōris, m. cf. κρέας, κρύος, caro, crudus. Blood (which flows from a wound), a stream of blood (more restricted in meaning than sanguis, which designates both that circulating in bodies and that shed by wounding): e nostro cum corpore sanguis Emicat exsultans alte spargitque cruorem, Lucr. 2, 194; Tac. A. 12, 47; and: cruor inimici recentissimus, Cic. Rosc. Am. 7, 19 (cf.: sanguis per venas in omne corpus diffunditur, id. N. D. 2, 55, 138 al.; v. sanguis; cf., however, under II.; class.; mo

cruppellarii.full: cruppellarii, ōrum, m. Celtic, harnessed combatants among the Gauls, Tac. A. 3, 43.

cruralis.full: crūrālis, e, adj. crus, of or belonging to the legs, crural: fasciae, Petr. 40, 5; Dig. 34, 2, 25.

cruricrepida.full: Crūrĭcrĕpĭda, ae, m. crus-crepo, Rattle-shin, the feigned name of a slave, about whose legs blows or chains rattle, Plaut. Trin. 4, 3, 14.

crurifragius.full: crūrĭfrāgĭus, i, m. crus-frango], one whose legs or shins are broken, Plaut. Poen. 4, 2, 64 (cf. crus).

crus.full: crūs, ūris, n. etym. dub.; prob. kindr. with curro, currus; cf. celer, and -cello in recello, etc., the leg, shank, shin. Prop., Cels. 8, 1 fin.: perque fabam repunt (grues) et mollia crura reponunt, Enn. ap. Serv. ad Verg. G. 3, 76 (Ann. v. 545 Vahl.); imitated by Verg. G. 3, 76, and Sil. 16, 444; so Lucr. 3, 478; 3, 652; Cic. N. D. 1, 36, 101; Caes. B. G. 6, 27; Plin. 10, 46, 63, § 129; Quint. 11, 3, 139; Ov. M. 1, 306; 4, 580 et saep. The legs of criminals were frequently broken, as a punishm

crusculum.full: cruscŭlum, i, n. dim. crus, a small leg or shank, Plaut. Fragm. ap. Paul. ex Fest. p. 52, 20 Müll.; cf. Paul. ib. p. 53, 1 ib.

crusma.full: crusma, ătis, n., = κροῦσμα, a musical piece or tune played upon a stringed instrument, Mart. 6, 71, 1; Censor. Fragm. 11.
crusma.short: crusma, ătis, n., = κροῦσμα, a musical piece or tune played upon a stringed instrument, Mart.

crusmaticus.full: crusmătĭcus, a, um, adj., = κρουσματικός, suitable for playing on a musical instrument: pars musicae, Censor. Fragm. 11.
crusmaticus.short: crusmătĭcus, a, um, adj., = κρουσματικός, suitable for playing on a musical instrument: pars musicae, Censor.

crusta.full: crusta, ae, f. cf. crudus, the hard surface of a body, the rind, shell, crust, bark, etc. In gen.: luti, Lucr. 6, 626; cf. soli, Dig. 39, 2, 9: panis, Plin. 19, 8, 53, § 168: glandis, id. 15, 28, 34, § 112: piscium, id. 9, 28, 44, § 83: locustarum, id. 9, 30, 50, § 95: ulcerum, the scab, Cels. 5, 9; cf. id. 5, 10: fluminis, a covering or crust of ice, Verg. G. 3, 360 et saep.— In partic., t. t. of plastic art, inlaid, chased, or embossed work on walls or vessels, plasterwork, stucco-work, mosaic

crustarius.full: crustārĭus, a, um, adj. crusta, II., pertaining to embossed work. Adj.: tabernae, Paul. ex Fest. p. 53, 6.— Subst.: crustārĭus, ii, m., one who makes embossed or chased figures, on plate, etc., Plin. 33, 12, 55, § 157.

crusto.full: crusto, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. crusta, to cover with a rind, shell, incrustation, plaster-work, embossed figures, etc. (post-Aug.): mala gypso, Plin. 15, 17, 18, § 64: domum marmoribus, to incrust, Luc. 10, 114; cf. Isid. Orig. 19, 3: portam crasso ferro, Amm. 24, 2, 14: vasa potoria crustata, Paul. ex Fest. p. 53, 6 Müll.: crustata crassities pectoris et ventris, incased with fat, App. M. 7, p. 189, 18.—Subst.: crustāta, ōrum, n. (sc. animalia), crustaceous animals, shellfish, Plin. 11, 37, 62, §

crustosus.full: crustōsus, a, um, adj. id., covered with a hard rind, crusted: bdellium crustosius, Plin. 12, 9, 19, § 36.

crustula.full: crustŭla, ae, f. dim. id., a little rind, shell, or crust, Arn. 2, p. 84.

crustularius.full: crustŭlārĭus, ii, m. crustulum, one who makes pastry, a confectioner, Sen. Ep. 56, 3.

crustulum.full: crustŭlum, i, n. dim. crustum, small pastry, confectionery, Varr. L. L. 5, § 107 Müll.; Hor. S. 1, 1, 25; 2, 4, 47; Juv. 9, 5; Sen. Ep. 99, 27; Inscr. Grut. 100, 5 al.

crustum.full: crustum, i, n. access. form to crusta, pastry, any thing baked, Hor. Ep. 1, 1, 78; Verg. A. 7, 115; Inscr. Grut. 173, 4; 373, 8.

crustumeria.full: Crustŭmĕrĭa, ae, f. (Liv. 2, 19, 2; 3, 42, 3); Crustŭmĕrĭum, ii, n. (Plin. 3, 5, 9, § 68); Crustŭmĕri, ōrum, m. (Verg. A. 7, 631); and Crustŭmĭum, ii, n. (Sil. 8, 367), an ancient town in the country of the Sabines, north-east of Fidenæ later belonging to the Tuscans, now Monte Rotondo; cf. O. Müll. Etrusk. 1, p. 113.— Hence, * Crustŭmĕrīnus, a, um, adj., of Crustumeria: secessio, Varr. L. L. 5, § 81 Müll.— Crustŭmīnus, a, um, adj., the same: ager, Varr. R. R. 1, 14, 3; Plin. 3, 5, 8, § 52; 3, 5

crux.full: crux, ŭcis, f. (m., Enn. ap. Non. p. 195, 13; Gracch. ap. Fest. s. v. masculino, p. 150, 24, and 151, 12 Müll.) [perh. kindred with circus]. Lit. In gen., a tree, frame, or other wooden instruments of execution, on which criminals were impaled or hanged, Sen. Prov. 3, 10; Cic. Rab. Perd. 3, 10 sqq.— In partic., a cross, Ter. And. 3, 5, 15; Cic. Verr. 2, 1, 3, § 7; 2, 1, 4, § 9; id. Pis. 18, 42; id. Fin. 5, 30, 92; Quint. 4, 2, 17; Tac. A. 15, 44; Hor. S. 1, 3, 82; 2, 7, 47; id. Ep. 1, 16, 48 et

cryphiolathronia.full: Crўphĭŏlăthrŏnĭa, ae, f. κρύφιοσλάθρα, the name of an imaginary country, Plaut. Mil. 1, 1, 43 Ritschl (ex conj.; Brix, Scytholatronia).

crypta.full: crypta, ae, f., = κρύπτη, a concealed, subterrunean passage, a vault, cavern, cave, grotto, pit, Varr. ap. Non. p. 169, 11; Suet. Calig. 58; Juv. 5, 106 al.—As a place of deposit, Vitr. 6, 8.— Esp.: crypta Neapolitana, a dark grotto in the neighborhood of Naples, through which was a shorter passage to Puteoli, now Grotta di Napoli, Sen. Ep. 57, 1.
crypta.short: crypta, ae, f., = κρύπτη, a concealed, subterrunean passage, a vault, cavern, cave, grotto, pit, Varr.

cryptarius.full: cryptārĭus, ii, m. crypta, a superintendent of vaults, Inscr. Orell. 2566.

crypticus.full: cryptĭcus, a, um, adj., = κρυπτικός, covered, concealed: arcus, Sid. Ep. 1, 5.
crypticus.short: cryptĭcus, a, um, adj., = κρυπτικός, covered, concealed: arcus, Sid.

cryptoporticus.full: cryptŏportĭcus, ūs, f. vox hibrida, from κρυπτός and porticus, a covered gallery or passage, a vault, a hall, Plin. Ep. 2, 17, 16 sq.; 5, 6, 27 sq. al.

crystallinus.full: crystallĭnus, a, um, adj., = κρυστάλλινος, made of crystal, crystalline, crystal. Adj.: calices, Capitol. Ver. 5: pila, Plin. 37, 2, 10, § 28: centra in sapphiris, id. 37, 9, 39, § 120.— Subst.: crystallĭ-num, i, n. (sc. vas), Sen. Ira, 3, 40, 2.— Mostly plur, Juv. 6, 155; Mart. 1, 53, 6; 9, 59, 13; Plin. 37, 2, 11, § 30: PRAEPOSITVS A CRYSTALLINIS, Inscr. Orell. 2953.
crystallinus.short: crystallĭnus, a, um, adj., = κρυστάλλινος, made of crystal, crystalline, crystal.

crystallion.full: crystallĭon, ii, n., = κρυστάλλιον, a plant, also called psyllion, Plin. 25, 11, 90, § 140 (Jan. crysallion).
crystallion.short: crystallĭon, ii, n., = κρυστάλλιον, a plant, also called psyllion, Plin.

crystalloides.full: crystallŏīdes, is, adj., = κρυσταλλοειδής, crystal-like, Theod. Prisc. p. 4, 2 med.
crystalloides.short: crystallŏīdes, is, adj., = κρυσταλλοειδής, crystal-like, Theod.

crystallum.full: crystallum, i, n. (analog. to the Gr. crystallus, i, m., Sol. 15 fin.), = κρύσταλλος. Ice, Auct. Priap. 63, 6.— A crystal, mountain- or rock-crystal, Plin. 37, 2, 9, § 23; Sen. Q. N. 3, 25, 12; Plin. 36, 26, 66, § 192; Curt. 3, 3, 8; Stat. S. 1, 2, 126.— Meton. Any thing made of crystal, a crystal vase for drinking, Mart. 9, 22, 7; 10, 66, 5.— That which is similar to crystal. —So of the glittering precious stone of a ring: aquosa, Prop. 4 (5), 3, 52.

ctesias.full: Ctēsĭās, ae, m., = Κτησίας, a famous physician of Cnidus in Caria, author of a history of the East, Plin. 2, 106, 110, § 238; Aug. Civ. Dei, 18, 2.
ctesias.short: Ctēsĭās, ae, m., = Κτησίας, a famous physician of Cnidus in Caria, author of a history of the East, Plin.

ctesibius.full: Ctēsĭbĭus, i, m., a mechanic of Alexandria, distinguished for his inventions in hydraulics, Vitr. 9, 6 (al. 9), p. 280 Bip.—Hence, Ctēsĭbĭcus, a, um, adj., of Ctesibius: machina, Vitr. 10, 12.
ctesibius.short: Ctēsĭbĭus, i, m., a mechanic of Alexandria, distinguished for his inventions in hydraulics, Vitr.

ctesiphon1.full: Ctēsĭphōn, ontis, m., = Κτησιφῶν, an Athenian defended by Demosthenes, Cic. de Or. 3, 56, 213 al.
ctesiphon1.short: Ctēsĭphōn, ontis, m., = Κτησιφῶν, an Athenian defended by Demosthenes, Cic.

ctesiphon2.full: Ctēsĭphōn, ontis, f., = Κτεσιφῶν, a town in Assyria, residence of the Parthian kings, Plin. 6, 26, 30, § 122; Tac. A. 6, 42; Amm. 23, 6, 23; Eutr. 8, 3; Spart. Sev. 16, 1.
ctesiphon2.short: Ctēsĭphōn, ontis, f., = Κτεσιφῶν, a town in Assyria, residence of the Parthian kings, Plin.

cuba.full: Cŭba, ae, f. cubo, the goddess who protects the lying down of children, Varr. ap. Don. Ter. Phorm. 1, 1, 15.

cuballa.full: Cuballa, ae, f., a town in Gallograecia, Liv. 38, 18, 5.
cuballa.short: Cuballa, ae, f., a town in Gallograecia, Liv.

cubatio.full: cŭbātĭo, ōnis, f. cubo, a lying down, Varr. L. L. 8, § 54 Müll.

cubator.full: cŭbātor, ōris, m. cubo, he who lies down, Paul. Nol. Ep. 21, 4.

cubicularius.full: cŭbĭcŭlārĭus, a, um (cŭbĭcŭlāris, e; gen., Cic. Div. 2, 65, 134; dat., id. Tusc. 5, 20, 59; but ap. Suet. Aug. 7, the better read. is cubiculi Lares; v. cubiculum, I.), adj. cubiculum, of or pertaining to a sleepingchamber. Adj.: lucerna, Mart. 14, 39 in lemm.: gausapina, id. 14, 147 in lemm.: stragula, Plin. 8, 58, 83, § 226.— Subst.: cŭ-bĭcŭlārĭus, ii, m., a chamber-servant, valet-de-chambre: hunc vestri janitores, hunc cubicularii diligunt, Cic. Verr. 2, 3, 4, § 8; id. Att. 6, 2, 5: manere ..

cubiculatus.full: cŭbĭcŭlātus, a, um, adj. id., furnished with bedchambers or state-rooms: naves, Sen. Ben. 7, 20, 3.

cubiculum.full: cŭbĭcŭlum (cŭbīclum, per sync., Mart. 10, 30, 17 dub.), i, n. cubo, an apartment for reclining or (more freq.) for sleeping (cf. cubo), a resting- or sleepingchamber, a bedchamber. Prop., Plaut. Most. 3, 2, 7; Serv. Galba ap. Cic. de Or. 2, 65, 263; Cic. Verr. 2, 3, 23, § 56; Plin. Ep. 1, 3, 1; Quint. 10, 3, 25; Tac. A. 14, 44; Suet. Caes. 49: Lares cubiculi, Suet. Dom. 17; id. Aug. 7 Roth ex conj. Lips.; v. cubicularius init.— Transf. The elevated seat of the emperor in the theatre, Suet. Ner.

cubicus.full: cŭbĭcus (cўb-), a, um, adj., = κυβικός, cubic, cubical: rationes, Vitr. 5, praef. 3: soliditas, Mart. Cap. 2, § 102.
cubicus.short: cŭbĭcus (cўb-), a, um, adj., = κυβικός, cubic, cubical: rationes, Vitr.

cubile.full: cŭbīle, is, n. cubo, a place of rest, a couch, bed. Lit. Of men, Lucr. 5, 814; 5, 985; Cic. Tusc. 5, 32, 90; 2, 17, 39; Liv. 30, 5, 10; Hor. S. 1, 3, 100; Curt. 5, 2, 15: salutatorium, an audience - chamber, Plin. 15, 11, 10, § 38.— In partic., a marriage-bed, Poët. ap. Cic. Fam. 9, 22, 1; Cat. 61, 183; Verg. A. 3, 324; Ov. M. 2, 592; 10, 635 et saep.— Of animals, the nest, lair, hole, kennel, etc.; of the mouse: mus pusillus ... aetatem uni cubili numquam committit suam, Plaut. Truc. 4, 4, 16.—

cubital.full: cŭbĭtal, ālis, n. id., a cushion for leaning on, an elbow-cushion, Hor. S. 2, 3, 255 (quoted in Fronto Ep. ad M. Caes. 1, 1).

cubitalis.full: cŭbĭtālis, e, adj. cubitum, pertaining to the elbow; hence, as a measure, a cubit long, Liv. 24, 34, 9; Plin. 12, 12, 26, § 45; Pall. Febr. 18, 6 al.: simulacrum cubitali majus, Suet. Galb. 4.

cubitio.full: cŭbĭtĭo, ōnis, f. 1. cubitus, a lying down, Aug. Ep. 151.

cubitissim.full: cŭbĭtissim, a corrupt word in Plaut. Cas. 5, 2, 42; acc. to some, adv., lying down.
cubitissim.short: cŭbĭtissim, a corrupt word in Plaut.

cubito.full: cŭbĭto, āvi, 1, v. freq. n. [cubo], to lie down often, to be accustomed to lie down (rare): anus hic solet cubitare, Plaut. Curc. 1, 1, 76; Cic. Cael. 15, 36: humi (pavones), Col. 8, 11 fin.: super pedes cubitantis reclinis, Tac. A. 14, 5.—Of sexual intercourse: cum aliquā (aliquo), Plaut. Curc. 1, 1, 57; id. Stich. 4, 1, 41; Quint. 8, 3, 22.

cubitor.full: cŭbĭtor, ōris, m. id., he who lies down: bos, that often lies down in ploughing, Col. 6, 2, 11.

cubitorius.full: cŭbĭtōrĭus, a, um, adj. id., of or belonging to a reclining posture: vestimenta, clothing worn at table, Petr. 30, 11.

cubitum.full: cŭbĭtum, i, n. (cŭbĭtus, i, m., Cels. 8, 1; 8, 16; Non. p. 201, 16) [id.], the elbow (serving for leaning upon). Prop., Cels. 1. 1.; Plin. 11, 45, 102, § 249; Plaut. Stich. 2, 1, 13; Verg. A. 4, 690; Ov. M. 7, 343; Hor. C. 1, 27, 8; id. S. 2, 4, 39; Quint. 11, 3, 93 al.— Meton. The bending, curvature of a shore: orae, Plin. 3, 13, 18, § 111. — As a measure of length, the distance from the elbow to the end of the middle finger, an ell, a cubit, Lucil. ap. Non. p. 201, 18; Plaut. Poen. 4, 2, 15; C

cubitura.full: cŭbĭtūra, ae, f. cubo, a lying down, Plaut. ap. Non. p. 198, 25.

cubitus1.full: cŭbĭtus, ūs, m. id., a lying down (very rare). Prop.: supini, proni, in latera, Plin. 28, 4, 14, § 54.— Esp., of coitus (for concubitus), in plur., Plaut. Am. 5, 1, 70.— Meton. (abstr. pro concr.), a bed, couch: foliis cubitus sibi sternunt, Plin. 24, 9, 38, § 59.

cubo.full: cŭbo, ŭi, ìtúm, 1 (perf. subj. cubaris, Prop. 2 (3), 15, 17; perf. inf. cubasse, Quint. 8, 2, 20; cf. also Neue, Formenl. II. p. 478), v. n. cf. κύπτω, to lie down. Of persons. In gen., to be in a recumbent posture, to recline: in lecticā cubans. Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 23, § 51: ut etiam legationes audiret cubans, Suet. Vesp. 24; id. Aug. 33; 43: cubans auspicatur qui in lecto quaerit augurium, Paul. ex Fest. p. 66, 5 Müll.: pisces cubantes = jacentes, flat, Col. 8, 17, 9.—Far more freq. and class., W

cubus.full: cŭbus, i, m., = κύβος, a die, cube, Vitr. 5, praef. 4.— As a measure, Rhem. Fann. 61.— A cubic number, Gell. 1, 20, 6.
cubus.short: cŭbus, i, m., = κύβος, a die, cube, Vitr.

cuccuru.full: cuccuru (cŭcurru), a word of unknown signif.: Afranius in Cinerario: id me celabat cuccuru. An nomen est ut veru, genu? Charis. p. 214 P. (Afran. Com. Rel. v. 22 Rib.); cf. cucurio.
cuccuru.short: cuccuru (cŭcurru), a word of unknown signif.: Afranius in Cinerario: id me celabat cuccuru.

cuci.full: cūci, n. indecl. Pers.; Gr. κοῦκι, a tree similar to the palm; acc. to Sprengel, Hyphaene coriacea, Plin. 13, 9, 18, § 62.

cucubalus.full: cucubălus, i, f., the plant called also strychnos and strumus, Plin. 27, 8, 44, § 68; Marc. Emp. p. 250.
cucubalus.short: cucubălus, i, f., the plant called also strychnos and strumus, Plin.

cucubo.full: cūcŭbo, āre, v. n. cf. κωκύω, of the screech-owl, to hoot, Auct. Carm. Philom. 14 dub.

cucullatus.full: cŭcullātus, a, um, adj. cucullus, hooded, having a hood (late Lat.): vestis, Isid. Orig. 19, 24, 17.

cucullio.full: cŭcullĭo (cŭculĭo, Cato, R. R. 2, 3), ōnis, m. id., a covering for the head, a cap, Cato, 1. 1.; Lampr. Elag. 32; Capitol. Ver. 4.

cucullus.full: cŭcullus, i, m. (cŭculla, ae, f., in eccl. Lat., Paul. Nol. 21, 389; Hier. Vit. Hil. 46; Ennod. Ep. 9, 14) [root kal-, of cella, clam, καλύπτω; cf. culleus], a covering. Of the head, a cap, hood, fastened to a garment, Col. 1, 8, 9; Mart. 11, 98, 10; Juv. 3, 170; as a disguise, id. 8, 145 al.— Of the feet, Capitol. Pert. 8 dub.— Of merchandise, a conical wrapper or case, Mart. 3, 2, 5.

cuculo.full: cŭcŭlo, āre, v. n. cuculus, onomatop. of the cuckoo, to cry cuckoo, Auct. Carm. Philom. 35.

cuculus.full: cŭcūlus (cŭcŭlus, Auct. Carm. Philom. 35), i, m. Sanscr. ku-, to cry; cf. κωκύω, a cuckoo, Plin. 18, 26, 66, § 249; as a term of reproach, Plaut. As. 5, 2, 73; id. Ps. 1, 1, 94; esp. of foolish men, id. Trin. 2, 1, 18; and of dilatory husbandmen, who are not through with their pruning until the cuckoo is heard (after the vernal equinox), Plin. 1. 1.; Hor. S. 1, 7, 31; cf. Plin. 18, 26, 66, § 249; Voss ad Verg. G. 2, 403.

cucuma.full: cŭcŭma, ae, f. coquo. A cookingvessel, a kettle, Petr. 135, 4; Dig. 48, 8, 1.— Perh., a small private bath (opp. thermae), Mart. 10, 79, 4.

cucumella.full: cŭcŭmella, ae, f. dim. cucuma, a little kettle, Dig. 8, 5, 17.

cucumeraceus.full: cŭcŭmĕrācĕus, a, um, adj., cucumber-like, of cucumber, Theod. Prisc. p. 2, 3.
cucumeraceus.short: cŭcŭmĕrācĕus, a, um, adj., cucumber-like, of cucumber, Theod.

cucumerarium.full: cŭcŭmĕrārĭum, ii, n. cucumis, a cucumber-field (eccl. Lat., transl. of the Heb. , Isa. 1, 8), Tert. adv. Jud. 3; Hier. in Isa. 1, 1, 8.

cucumis.full: cŭcŭmis, ĕris (is, sometimes in the Nat. Hist. of Pliny; e. g. acc. cucumim, Plin. 9, 2, 1, § 3; 20, 1, 2, § 3; abl. cucumi, id. 20, 9, 40, § 103 al.; together with cucumeris, id. 19, 5, 23, § 68; 19, 12, 61, § 186: cucumeres, id. 19, 5, 24, § 69 (cucumis, Sillig): cucumerum, id. 19, 5, 23, § 68 al.), m. A cucumber, Col. 11, 3, 48; Plin. 19, 5, 23, § 64 sq.; Pall. Mart. 9, 7; Varr. R. R. 1, 2, 25; Verg. G. 4, 122 al.— A sea-plant, similar in color and odor to the cucumber, Plin. 9, 2, 1, § 3.
cucumis.short: cŭcŭmis, ĕris (is, sometimes in the Nat.

cucurbita.full: cŭcurbĭta, ae, f., a gourd. Prop., Col. 11, 3, 48 sq.; Plin. 19, 5, 24, § 69 sq.; Pall. Mart. 9, 16.— Transf., in medic. lang., a cup, cupping-glass (of similar form), Scrib. Comp. 46; 67; Juv. 14, 58: cucurbitae medicinales, Plin. 32, 10, 42, § 123 al.— Trop., a blockhead, Petr. 39.

cucurbitarius.full: cŭcurbĭtārĭus, ii, m. cucurbita, a gourd planter, Hier. Ep. 112, n. 22.

cucurbitatio.full: cŭcurbĭtātĭo, ōnis, f. cucurbita, II., a cupping, Cael. Aur. Tard. 2, 1, 32.

cucurbitinus.full: cŭcurbĭtīnus, a, um, adj. cucurbita, like or similar to a gourd: pira, the gourdpear, Cato, R. R. 7, 4; Plin. 15, 15, 16, § 56: ficus, Cloatius ap. Macr. S. 2, 16, 1; 2, 15, 6.

cucurbitula.full: cŭcurbĭtŭla, ae, f. dim. id.. Silvestris, the bitter gourd, Scrib. Comp. 106. — A cupping-glass, Cels. 2, 11; 3, 18.

cucurbitularis.full: cŭcurbĭtŭlāris, is, f. cucurbitula, the field cypress, = chamaepitys, Isid. Orig. 17, 9, 86.

cucurio.full: cūcūrĭo, īre, v. n. root kar-, to sound; cf. Gr. κρέκω, κραυγή, to crow, Auct. Carm. Philom. 25.

cucus.full: cucus, i, m., a daw: interea Cucus, si in ludum iret, potuisset fieri ut probe litteras sciret, Plaut. Pers. 2, 1, 6.
cucus.short: cucus, i, m., a daw: interea Cucus, si in ludum iret, potuisset fieri ut probe litteras sciret, Plaut.

cucutium.full: cucutĭum, ii, n. cf. cucullus, a kind of hood, Treb. Poll. Claud. 17, 6.

cudo1.full: cūdo, ĕre, v. a., to strike, beat, pound, knock (rare and only ante-class., and in postAug. prose). Prop.: aurum pilis, Plin. 33, 4, 21, § 69 (v. Sillig N. cr.): semina, to beat out, thresh, Col. 2, 10, 14; Lucr. 1, 1044; 4, 187.—Prov.: istaec in me cudetur faba, i. e. I must smart for that, Ter. Eun. 2, 3, 90 Don.— Transf. (of metals), to prepare by beating or hammering, to forge; of money, to stamp, coin: plumbeos nummos, Plaut. Most. 4, 2, 11: argentum, Ter. Heaut. 4, 4, 18: anulum, to make,

cudo2.full: cūdo, ōnis, m., a helmet made of raw skin; abl. cudone, Sil. 8, 495; 16, 59; cf.: cudon, περικεφαλαίας εἶδος, Gloss. Philox.
cudo2.short: cūdo, ōnis, m., a helmet made of raw skin;

cuferion.full: cuferion, ii, n., the nose-bleed, a disease of horses, Veg. Art. Vet. 3, 37.
cuferion.short: cuferion, ii, n., the nose-bleed, a disease of horses, Veg.

cuicuimodi.full: cuicuimŏdi (ante-class. quoiquoi mŏdi) [quisquis-modus], euphon. form for cujuscujusmodi (very rare in MSS., but vouched for by the ancient grammarians; v. Kuhner, Gram. I. p. 398; 405 sq.), of what sort, kind, or nature soever: sisne necne ut esse oportet, malus, bonus quoiquoi modi, Plaut. Bacch. 3, 2, 16: velim omnia quam diligentissime, cuicuimodi sunt, scribas, Cic. Att. 3, 22, 4; Cic. Verr. 2, 5, 41, § 107 Zumpt and Halm ad loc.; cf. Madv. ad id. Fin. 3, 9, 30: cuicuimodi fuerit illa (lex)

cuimodi.full: cuimŏdi quis-modus for cujusmodi = qualis, of what kind or nature soever: cuimodi esset, Gell. 9, 13, 4; 12, 2, 2; 12, 15, 1; 13, 29, 1 al.
cuimodi.short: cuimŏdi quis-modus for cujusmodi = qualis, of what kind or nature soever: cuimodi esset, Gell.

cujas.full: cūjas (archaic quōjas), ātis, or (anteand post-class.) uncontr. cūjātis, is, pron. interrog. [pronom. stem quo-; cf.: quis, qui], whence originating? of what country, family, or town? whence? from what place? = ποδαπός; nom. cujatis (quoj-), Enn. ap. Cic. Balb. 22, 51; Att. ap. Non. p. 426, 24; Plaut. Curc. 3, 37; id. Men. 2, 2, 66; id. Poen. prol. 109; 5, 2, 33; App. M. 1, p. 104, 16; 8, p. 212, 31: quem cum percunctaretur Scipio, quis et cujas et cur id aetatis in castris fuisset? etc., Liv. 2
cujas.short: cūjas (archaic quōjas), ātis, or (anteand post-class.) uncontr.

cujus1.full: cūjus (archaic quōjus), a, um, pron. interrog. [pronom. stem quo-], pertaining to whom? of whom? whose? (most freq. in Plaut. and Ter.): quoja vox sonat procul? Plaut. Curc. 1, 2, 18; id. Ps. 2, 4, 11; id. Rud. 2, 3, 2; id. Trin. 1, 2, 7: illa mulier, id. Merc. 4, 3, 20; cf. id. ib. 1, 2, 87: fidicina, id. Ep. 2, 2, 109: virgo, Ter. Eun. 2, 3, 29: puer, id. ib. 4, 4, 24: navis, Plaut. Stich. 2, 2, 46: cujum pecus? an Meliboei? Verg. E. 3, 1; 5, 87.—Absol.: quojam esse te vis maxime, ad eum duco

cujus2.full: cūjus (archaic quōjus), a, um, pron. rel. [from cujus, gen. of qui], pertaining to whom, of whom, whose (rare): cujum id censebis esse reddes, ancient form of an oath in Gell. 16, 4, 2; cf.: argentum ego pro istisce ambabus, quojae erant, domino dedi, Plaut. Rud. 3, 4, 40: is denique, cuja ea uxor fuerat, Plin. Secundus, Fragm. ap. Gell. 9, 16, 5: ea caedes si potissimum crimini datur, detur ei cuja interfuit, non ei cuja nihil interfuit, Cic. Fragm. ap. Prisc. p. 950 P.: ut optimā condicione si

cujuscemodi.full: cūjuscĕmŏdi (quōj-) or cūjuscĕ mŏdi quisce-modus, of what kind or nature soever (late Lat.): voces, App. M. 8, p. 209, 9.
cujuscemodi.short: cūjuscĕmŏdi (quōj-) or cūjuscĕ mŏdi quisce-modus, of what kind or nature soever (late Lat.): voces, App.

cujuscumquemodi.full: cūjuscumquĕmŏdi, a false read. for cujusque modi, Sall. C. 39, 6.

cujusdammodi.full: cūjusdammŏdi, better cūjusdam mŏdi, of some sort, Cic. Fin. 5, 12, 36; id. Div. 2, 14, 34.
cujusdammodi.short: cūjusdammŏdi, better cūjusdam mŏdi, of some sort, Cic.

cujusmodi.full: cūjusmŏdi (quōj-), also cūjus mŏdi quis-modus = qualis, of what kind: cupio cognoscere iter tuum cujusmodi sit, Cic. Fam. 15, 20, 3; Auct. B. Afr. 31; Plaut. Most. 3, 2, 132.— Of whatever kind, Cic. Fam. 4, 7, 4 (al. leg. cuicuimodi); id. Tusc. 5, 41, 121 (al. cuicuimodi); Plaut. Bacch. 3, 2, 16.
cujusmodi.short: cūjusmŏdi (quōj-), also cūjus mŏdi quis-modus = qualis, of what kind: cupio cognoscere iter tuum cujusmodi sit, Cic.

cujusmodicumque.full: cūjusmŏdicumquē, adv. quicumque-modus, of whatever kind: cujusmodicumque mater sit, Cic. Clu. 6, 17 Ramsey (where B. and K. read cujuscumque modi).

cujusnam.full: cūjusnam, cūjanam, cūjumnam, v. 1. cujus, β.

cujusquemodi.full: cūjusquĕmŏdi (quōj-) or cūjus-quĕ mŏdi quisque modus, of whatever kind, Cic. Fin. 2, 1, 3; 2, 7, 22; Lucr. 4, 135.
cujusquemodi.short: cūjusquĕmŏdi (quōj-) or cūjus-quĕ mŏdi quisque modus, of whatever kind, Cic.

cujusvis.full: cūjusvis, cujavis, cujumvis from cujus-vis, gen. of quivis, to whomever pertaining, whosesoever, of any one: cujavis oratio insimulari potest, si, etc., App. Mag. p. 326, 13.
cujusvis.short: cūjusvis, cujavis, cujumvis from cujus-vis, gen.

cularo.full: Culăro, ōnis, m., a town in Gallia Narbonensis, afterwards Gratianopolis, now Grenoble, Cic. Fam. 10, 23, 7.
cularo.short: Culăro, ōnis, m., a town in Gallia Narbonensis, afterwards Gratianopolis, now Grenoble, Cic.

culcita.full: culcĭta (in MSS. also culcĭtra), ae, f. etym. dub.; acc. to Varr. L. L. 5, § 167 Müll.; Paul. ex Fest. p. 50, 8, from calco, a sack filled with feathers, wool, hair, etc., for lying upon, warming, etc.; a bed, cushion, mattress, pillow, Cato, R. R. 10 fin.; 11 fin.; Varr. ap. Non. p. 86, 5 sq.; Cic. Tusc. 3, 19, 46; Sen. Ep. 87, 2; 108, 23; Suet. Tib. 54 al. —Of a little cushion or patch for the eye, Plaut. Mil. 4, 4, 42.—Of a resting-place in a conservatory of birds, Varr. R. R. 3, 5, 14.— In t

culcitarius.full: culcĭtārĭus, ii, m. culcita, a cushion-maker, acc. to Diom. p. 313 P.

culcitella.full: culcĭtella, ae, f. dim. id., a little cushion or mattress, transf. in mal. part., Plaut. Most. 4, 2, 14; cf.: sponda interior regiae lecticae, Suet. Caes. 49.

culcitula.full: culcĭtŭla, ae, f. dim. id., a small cushion or mattress, Lucil. ap. Non. p. 35, 20; cf. Diom. p. 326, 20 K.

culex1.full: cŭlex, ĭcis, m. (f., Plaut. Cas. 2, 3, 22), a gnat, midge (comprising very many species), Plin. 11, 2, 1, § 2 sq.; 11, 35, 41, § 118; 17, 27, 44, § 255; Plaut. Curc. 4, 2, 14; Lucr. 3, 391; Hor. S. 1, 5, 14; Col. 11, 3, 60; Mart. 3, 93, 9 al.—Also the title of a writing of Verg.; cf. Heyn. Verg. tom. iv. prooem.—As a term of reproach for a wanton lover, Plaut. Cas. 2, 3, 22.

culicellus.full: cŭlĭcellus, i, m. dim. 1. culex, a little gnat: amasio Tullae, i. e. buzzing round her, Ser. ap. Diom. p. 513 P.

culiculare.full: cŭlĭcŭlārĕ, is, n. id., a fly-net (late Lat.; cf. conopeum), Schol. Juv. 6, 80.

culiculus.full: cŭlĭcŭlus, dim. id., a little gnat, κωυώπιον, Gloss. Cyrill.

culigna.full: cŭligna, ae, f., = κυλίχνη, a small drinking-vessel, a cup, Cato, R. R. 132, 1; Fragm. ap. Paul. ex Fest. p. 55, 2 Müll.
culigna.short: cŭligna, ae, f., = κυλίχνη, a small drinking-vessel, a cup, Cato, R.

culina.full: cŭlīna (old orthogr. cŏlīna, acc. to Non. p. 55, 18 sq.), ae, f. Sanscr. çar, çri, to cook, mix, a kitchen. Prop., Plaut. Most. 1, 1, 1; id. Truc. 2, 7, 53; Varr. R. R. 1, 13, 2; Cic. Fam. 15, 18, 1; Sen. Ep. 114, 26; Petr. 2; Hor. S. 1, 5, 73; 2, 5, 80; cf. of a portable kitchen, Sen. Ep. 78, 23; Juv. 3, 250.— Transf. Culina vocatur locus, in quo epulae in funere comburuntur, Paul. ex Fest. p. 65, 12.— Meton., food, fare, victuals: Murenā praebente domum, Capitone culinam, Hor. S. 1, 5, 38; so

culinarius.full: cŭlīnārĭus, a, um, adj. culina, pertaining to the kitchen, culinary, kitchen-. Adj.: operae, Fronto, B. Parth. p. 201.— Subst.: cŭlīnārĭus, ii, m., a kitchen servant, Scrib. Comp. 230.

culiola.full: cūlĭŏla (cull-) cortices nucum viridium, dicta a similitudine culeorum, quibus vinum sive oleum continetur, Paul. ex Fest. p. 50, 12 Müll.
culiola.short: cūlĭŏla (cull-) cortices nucum viridium, dicta a similitudine culeorum, quibus vinum sive oleum continetur, Paul.

culix.full: culix, ĭcis, m., an unknown plant, Plin. 19, 5, 23, § 68.—Also culex, Pall. Mart. 9, 8.
culix.short: culix, ĭcis, m., an unknown plant, Plin.

cullearis.full: cullĕāris (cūl-), e, adj. culleus, II. A., of the measure of a culleus: labrum, Cato, R. R. 154: dolia, Vitr. 6, 9.

culleus.full: cullĕus (cūl-, and in the signif. II. B., cōl-), i (nom. plur. cullea, neutr., Cato ap. Varr. R. R. 1, 2, 7; Non. p. 197; gen. plur. culleūm, Cato, R. R. 11, 1), m., = κολεός, Ion. κουλεός (a sheath; hence), a leather bag, a sack for holding liquids. Prop.: Te ipsam culleo ego cras faciam ut deportere in pergulam, Plaut. Ps. 1, 2, 78; Nep. Eum. 8, 7; Plin. 7, 20, 19, § 82.—Parricides were sewed up in bags and drowned, Cic. Rosc. Am. 25, 70; id. Inv. 2, 50, 149; Sen. Clem. 1, 15; Dig. 48, 9, 9; C

culmen.full: culmen, ĭnis, contr. form of columen, q. v.

culmeus.full: culmĕus, a, um, adj. culmus, of siraw: tecti culmina, Paul. Nol. Carm. 13, 387.

culmosus.full: culmōsus, a, um, adj. culmus, stalklike, poet.: fratres, sprung from the dragonteeth, Sid. Carm. 6, 72.

culmus.full: culmus, i, m. kindr. with culmen, a stalk, stem, esp. of grain, straw, Varr. R. R. 1, 48, 3 (Cod. Vindob. culmen); Cic. Sen. 15, 51; Verg. G. 1, 111; 1, 317 al.—Of other plants: milii, panici, Plin. 18, 7, 10, § 52: holci, id. 27, 10, 63, § 90: lilii, Stat. S. 3, 3, 128.

culpa.full: culpa, ae, f. kindr. in root with scelus; cf. Sanscr. skhal-, errare, crime, fault, blame, failure, defect (as a state worthy of punishment; on the contr. delictum, peccatum, etc., as punishable acts; diff. from scelus, which implies an intentional injury of others; but culpa includes in it an error in judgment). Prop. In gen. (very freq. in every period and species of composition): delictum suum Suamque ut culpam expetere in mortalem sinat, Plaut. Am. 1, 2, 33; cf.: non C. Rabirium culpa delict

culpabilis.full: culpābĭlis, e, adj. culpa, worthy of blame, culpable, criminal (post-class.): aliquid (opp. laudabile), App. Mag. p. 223: opinio de diis (opp. digna), Arn. 7, p. 222. —Comp.: tanto culpabilius est, non observare quod possis, Tert. ad Uxor. 2, 1.—Adv.: culpābĭlĭter, culpably, Symm. Ep. 9, 40. —Comp., Paul. Nol. Ep. 39, 4; Cael. Aur. Acut. 3, 17, 172.

culpatio.full: culpātĭo, ōnis, f. culpo, a reproach, blame, Gell. 10, 22, 2.

culpatus.full: culpātus, a, um, Part. and P. a., from culpo.

culpito.full: culpĭto, āre, v. freq. a. culpo, to blame or reproach severely or harshly: jusjurandum, Plaut. Cist. 2, 1, 28.

culpo.full: culpo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. culpa. To reproach or blame a person or thing as wrong or faulty, to censure, reprove, disapprove, condemn (syn.: reprehendo, vitupero; opp. laudo, probo, etc.; rare; mostly post-Aug.; never in the Cic. per.). With personal objects: quos modo culpavi, Ov. M. 10, 581: illum, Quint. 8, 4, 23: alium, id. 4, 2, 26: Neronem, Suet. Vit. Pers. —Pass.: laudatur (prodigus) ab his, culpatur ab illis, Hor. S. 1, 2, 11; 1, 4, 25; id. C. 4, 5, 20; Quint. 3, 6, 60: cum ob id culpare

culte.full: cultē, adv., v. colo, P. a. fin.

cultello.full: cultello, no perf., ātum, 1, v. a. cultellus. To make in the shape of a knife: spinam dorsi, Plin. 8, 25, 38, § 91; 32, 2, 5, § 13 Sillig N. cr.— To level land by the coulter, Front. Limit. p. 43 Goes.

cultellulus.full: cultellŭlus, i, m. dim. id., a little knife, Sol. 38.

cultellus.full: cultellus, i, m. dim. culter, a small knife. Prop., Varr. R. R. 1, 69, 2; id. Fragm. ap. Non. p. 195, 18; Hor. Ep. 1, 7, 51; Plin. 12, 25, 54, § 115 al.— Lignei, wooden pegs or pins, Vitr. 7, 3.

culter.full: culter, tri, m. kindr. with Sanscr. kar, to wound, kill; cf. per-cello, clades. Orig. a plough-coulter, ploughshare, Plin. 18, 18, 48, § 171 sq.— In gen., a knife; so a vintner's knife, Col. 4, 25, 2; 12, 45, 4; a butcher's knife, Plaut. Rud. 1, 2, 46; Liv. 3, 48, 5: qui ad cultrum bovem emunt, i. e. for slaughter, Varr. R. R. 2, 5, 11; Suet. Tib. 25; Scrib. Comp. 13; a razor: cultros metuens tonsorios, Cic. Off. 2, 7, 25: cultrum tonsorium super jugulum meum posui, Petr. 108, 11; Plin. 7, 59, 5

culticula.full: cultĭcŭla fusticulus quidam ligneus in sacris dicebatur, Paul. ex Fest. p. 50, 9 Müll., where Lind. reads culcitula.
culticula.short: cultĭcŭla fusticulus quidam ligneus in sacris dicebatur, Paul.

cultio.full: cultĭo, ōnis, f. 1. colo. Agri, a cultivation, preparation of ground, agriculture, Cic. Sen. 16, 57; Cic. Verr. 2, 3, 97, § 226 (others, less correctly, agricultio in one word; v. agricultio): cultionis labor, Ambros. Fug. Saec. 8, 49.— (In acc. with colo, II. B.) Veneration, reverence, Arn. 4, p. 146; 5, p. 178.

cultor.full: cultor, ōris, m. id.. Prop., one who bestows care or labor upon a thing, an elaborator, cultivator, etc.: agrorum, Liv. 2, 34, 11; 4, 25, 4: agri, id. 40, 29, 3; cf. agricultor: virentis agelli, Hor. A. P. 117: terrae, Cic. N. D. 2, 39, 99: vitis, a vine-dresser, id. Fin. 5, 14, 40: alveorum, a bee-master, apiarist, Col. 9, 3, 1.—Poet., of a bullock: pauperis agri, Ov. F. 5, 515.— Absol., a cultivator or tiller of land, a husbandman, planter, Sall. J. 46, 5; Liv. 21, 34, 1; 28, 11, 9; Quint. 2,

cultrarius.full: cultrārĭus, ii, m. culter, a slayer of the victim (for sacrifice), Suet. Calig. 32; Inscr. Orell. 4175.

cultratus.full: cultrātus, a, um, adj. id., knifeshaped: folia, Plin. 13, 4, 7, § 30.

cultrix.full: cultrix, īcis, f. cultor. Prop., she who labors at or cares for a thing: earum rerum quas terra gignit ... augendarum et alendarum quandam cultricem esse, quae sit scientia atque ars agricolarum, Cic. Fin. 5, 14, 39.— A female inhabitant: nemorum Latonia virgo, Verg. A. 11, 557; cf.: montibus Idri (Diana), Cat. 64, 300 Sillig N. cr.: collis (Janiculi) haec aetas, Ov. F. 1, 245.— Poet., transf., of things as subjects: foci secura patella, Pers. 3, 26.— Trop., a female worshipper: deorum montium,

cultura.full: cultūra, ae, f. 1. colo. A cultivating, care, cultivation: agri, Varr. R. R. 2, praef. § 4; Cic. Sen. 15, 54; Suet. Aug. 42 al.: agelli, Lucr. 5, 1366; cf. Cic. Agr. 2, 30, 83; 2, 35, 94; id. Fl. 29, 71, and agricultura: vitis, id. Fin. 5, 14, 39.—In plur.: agri culturas docuit usus, Lucr. 5, 1447.— Absol., agriculture, tillage, husbandry, in the broadest sense (cf. agricola), Varr. R. R. 1, 18; 1, 7; Quint. 10, 2, 2; Hor. C. 3, 24, 14.—In plur., of the several parts of husbandry, Col. 11, 1, 30

cultus1.full: cultus, a, um, Part. and P. a., from 1. colo.

cultus2.full: cultus, ūs, m. 1. colo. Prop., a laboring at, labor, care, cultivation, culture (rare): quod est tam asperum saxetum, in quo agricolarum cultus non elaboret? Cic. Agr. 2, 25, 66: agricolae, id. Leg. 1, 1, 1: agrorum, Liv. 4, 12, 7; Quint. prooem. § 26; cf. id. 8, 3, 75: (oves) neque sustentari neque ullum fructum edere ex se sine cultu hominum et curatione possent, Cic. N. D. 2, 63, 158; cf.: cultus et curatio corporis, id. ib. 1, 34, 94: omnis cultus fructusque Cereris in iis locis interisse, C

culullus.full: cŭlullus, i, m. (acc. to Acro upon Hor. C. 1, 31, 11, orig. a sacrificial vessel for liquids; later, in gen.), a drinking-vessel, beaker, goblet, cup, bowl, Hor. l. l.; id. A. P. 434.

culus.full: cūlus, i, m. perh. kindr. with κοῖλος, of a curving form; cf. 1. anus, the posteriors, fundament, Cat. 23, 19; 33, 4; 97, 2; Mart. 3, 98, 1.

cum1.full: cum (archaic form COM, found in an inscr., COM PREIVATVD; in MSS. sometimes quom or quum), prep. with abl. [for skom, Sanscr. root sak, together; cf. sequor, and Gr. κοινός, σὐν], designates in gen. accompaniment, community, connection of one object with another (opp. sine, separatim, etc.), with, together, together with, in connection or company with, along with; sometimes also to be translated and. In gen., Plaut. Am. prol. 95: qui cum Amphitruone abiit hinc in exercitum, id. ib. prol. 125: cu
cum1.short: cum (archaic form COM, found in an inscr., COM PREIVATVD;

cum2.full: Cum (ante-class. quom; freq. in MSS. of Cicero; the post-class. form quum is incorrectly given in many MSS. and edd.), conj. [pronom. stem ka- or kva- with acc. case ending]. Of time, when, as, while, sometimes = after, since. In adverbial clauses dependent on non-preterite predicates. The time designated by cum being indefinite, when, if, whenever, always with indic., except in the instances A. 2. Cum with pres. indic., often equivalent to si. With principal predicate in pres.: nam omnes id fac

cumae.full: Cūmae, ārum (Cȳmē, Stat. S. 4, 3, 65; gen. Cymes, Sil. 13, 494), f., = Κύμη, an ancient colony of the Chalcidians, in Campania, on the sea-coast, renowned on account of its Sibyl, Mel. 2, 4, 9; Plin. 3, 5, 9, § 61; Lucr. 6, 748; Cic. Div. 1, 43, 98; id. Tusc. 3, 12, 27; Verg. A. 6, 2; Hor. Ep. 1, 15, 11; Ov. M. 14, 104; Vell. 1, 4, 1; Cael. ap. Cic. Fam. 8, 1, 2; Juv. 3, 2 et saep.— Hence, Cūmānus, a, um, adj., of Cumæ, Cumæan. Adj.: ager, Cic. Agr. 2, 25, 66: litora, Tac. A. 15, 46: linum, Plin

cumalter.full: cumalter significat cum altero, dictum ab antiquis ita brevitatis causā, ut sodes pro si audes, scilicet pro scias licet, sis pro si vis, Paul. ex Fest. p. 50, 10.
cumalter.short: cumalter significat cum altero, dictum ab antiquis ita brevitatis causā, ut sodes pro si audes, scilicet pro scias licet, sis pro si vis, Paul.

cumanus.full: Cūmānus, a, um, v. Cumae, II.

cumatilis.full: cūmātĭlis (cȳm-), e, adj. from κῦμα, with the Lat. ending ilis. Adj., of the waves: deus, i. e. Neptune, Commod. 10, 1.— Esp., sea-colored, water-colored, blue: colos, Titin. ap. Non. p. 548, 11 (Com. Rel. v. 114 Rib.).— Subst.: cūmātĭle, is, n., a bluish garment, Plaut. Ep. 2, 2, 49.

cumera.full: cŭmĕra, ae, f. (cŭmĕrum, i, n., Varr. L. L. 7, § 34 Müll.; Paul. ex Fest. p. 50, 7 ib.) [cf. Gr. καμάρα, Lat. camera], a chest, box, or basket, to keep grain in, Hor. S. 1, 1, 53 Acro; id. Ep. 1, 7, 30; for the utensils of a bride, Paul. ex Fest. p. 63, 12; Varr. l. l.

cuminatus.full: cŭmīnātus (cўm-), a, um, adj. cuminum, seasoned or mixed with cumin, Pall. Nov. 22, 5.— Subst.: cŭmīnātum, i, n., cumin-spice, Apic. 1, 29.

cumininus.full: cŭmīnīnus (cўm-), a, um, adj. id., of cumin: oleum, App. Herb. 74.

cuminum.full: cŭmīnum (cўm-), i, n., = κύμῖνον, cumin, a plant: Cuminum (Cyminum), Linn.; said to produce paleness, Plin. 20, 14, 57, § 159 sq.; Pall. Mart. 9, 17: exsangue, Hor. Ep. 1, 19, 18: pallens, Pers. 5, 55.
cuminum.short: cŭmīnum (cўm-), i, n., = κύμῖνον, cumin, a plant: Cuminum (Cyminum), Linn.;

cummis.full: cummis, is, and cummi, indecl., v. gummi.
cummis.short: cummis, is, and cummi, indecl., v.

cumprime.full: cumprīmē, adv., especially, particularly, Quadrig. ap. Gell. 17, 2, 14: adprime crebrius est, cumprime rarius, traductumque ex eo est, quod cumprimis dicebant pro eo, quod est imprimis, Gell. ib.

cumque.full: cumquĕ (quomquĕ or cunquĕ), adv. cum-que, serves for the generalizing of any action, event, time, etc., however, whenever, howsoever, whensoever, -ever, -soever. Usu. with pronn. and pronom. advv.: quicumque, qualiscumque, etc., ubicumque, quotienscumque, etc.— Very rarely standing alone: quae demant cumque dolorem, which remove pain in general, any pain, Lucr. 2, 21: cum solis lumina cumque Inserti fundunt radii per opaca domorum, in whatever manner, id. 2, 114: mihi cumque salve Rite vocanti,

cumulare.full: cŭmŭlāre, is, n., = commissura renum, Veg. Art. Vet. 6, 1, 2; 6, 2, 2 Schneid. N. cr.
cumulare.short: cŭmŭlāre, is, n., = commissura renum, Veg.

cumulate.full: cŭmŭlātē, adv., v. cumulo, P. a. fin.

cumulatim.full: cŭmŭlātim, adv. cumulatus, abundantly, in heaps, in abundance (ante- and post-class., and very rare): positum in doliis, Varr. R. R. 3, 15, 2; Prud. Apoth. 717; 739.

cumulatus.full: cŭmŭlātus, a, um, Part. and P. a., from cumulo.

cumulo.full: cŭmŭlo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a., to form into a heap, to accumulate, heap, or pile up (class.). In gen. Prop. (mostly post-Aug.; esp. in Curt. and Tac.): materiem, Lucr. 1, 989: nubila, id. 6, 191; 6, 518: stipites, Curt. 6, 6: harenas, id. 5, 1, 30: nivem, id. 5, 4, 88: arma in ingentem acervum, Liv. 45, 33, 1: pyram truncis nemorumque ruinā, Stat. Th. 6, 85.— Trop.: benefacta, Plaut. Capt. 2, 3, 64: omnia principatūs vocabula, Tac. H. 2, 80: honores in eam, id. A. 13, 2: tantum honorum atque opum

cumulus.full: cŭmŭlus, i, m. Sanscr. çva, to swell; Gr. κυέω, κύω; cf. κῦμα, a heap, as coming to a point, a pile, a mass piled up (class.; esp. freq. in the signif. II.): in hoc immenso aliarum super alias acervatarum legum cumulo, Liv. 3, 34, 6; cf.: hostium coacervatorum, id. 22, 7, 5; 5, 48, 3: corpus obrutum superstratis Gallorum cumulis, id. 9, 29, 19; and: armorum cumulos coacervare id. 5, 39, 1: caesorum corporum, id. 22, 59, 3: saxei, Plin. 31, 10, 46, § 111: eminens (aquae in poculis), id. 2, 65, 65

cunabula.full: cūnābŭla, ōrum, n. cunae, a cradle. Prop., Cic. Div. 1, 36, 79.—Of the resting-place of young animals, Verg. G. 4, 66; Plin. 10, 33, 51, § 99.— Meton. The cradle, i. e. the earliest abode, dwellingplace: Jovis parvi, Prop. 3 (4), 1, 27. gentis nostrae, Verg. A. 3, 105.— Like our cradle, for birth, origin: a primis cunabulis, from earliest childhood, Col. 1, 3, 5: qui non in cunabulis sed in campo sunt consules facti, i. e. not by their descent, Cic. Agr. 2, 36, 100: a primis cunabulis hujus urbi

cunae.full: cūnae, ārum (cūna, ae, Prud. Dipt. 112), f., a cradle. Prop.: tune etiam cubitare solitu's in cunis puer? Plaut. Ps. 4, 7, 81: opus est cunis, incunabulis, id. Truc. 5, 13; Cic. Sen. 23, 83; id. Tusc. 1, 39, 93; Quint. 1, 1, 21; Ov. F. 6, 167; id. M. 10, 392; Pers. 2, 31; Juv. 6, 89; Mart. 11, 39, 1; Suet. Aug. 94 et saep.—Of the nests of young birds, Ov. Tr. 3, 12, 10.— Meton., like our cradle, for birth or earliest childhood, Ov. M. 3, 313; 9, 67; cf. cunabula, II. B.

cunctabundus.full: cunctābundus (cont-), a, um, adj. cunctor, lingering, loitering, delaying (very rare): (milites) cunctabundosque et resistentes egressos castris esse, Liv. 6, 7, 2: nusquam cunctabundus nisi cum in senatu loqueretur, Tac. A. 1, 7: verba, Mamert. in Jul. 18, 6: amnis, Eum. Pan. Const. 18, 3.

cunctalis.full: cunctālis, e, adj. cunctus, general, Mart. Cap. 1, § 34.

cunctamen.full: cunctāmen (cont-), ĭnis, n. cunctor, a delaying, hesitating, Paul. Nol. 24, 416.

cunctans.full: cunctans (cont-), antis, v. cunctor, P. a. 1.

cunctanter.full: cunctanter (cont-), adv., v. cunctor, P. a., 2. fin.

cunctatio.full: cunctātĭo (cont-), ōnis, f. cunctor, a delaying, lingering, in a good or (more freq.) in a bad sense, a tarrying, delay, hesitation, doubt (subject., while mora is object.; freq. and in good prose): danda brevis cogitationi mora ... in hac cunctatione, etc., Quint. 11, 3, 157: studium semper adsit, cunctatio absit, Cic. Lael. 13, 44: boni nescio quo modo tardiores sunt ... ita ut non numquam cunctatione ac tarditate ... otium atque dignitatem amittant, id. Sest. 47, 100: Sabini, Caes. B. G. 3, 1

cunctator1.full: cunctātor (cont-), ōris, m. id., one who acts with hesitation or tardiness, a delayer, loiterer, lingerer (not in Cic.); in a bad sense, Cael. ap. Cic. Fam. 8, 10, 3: cunctato ex acerrimo bellatore factus, Liv. 6, 23, 5.—In a good sense, a considerate or cautious person (magister equitum Fabium) pro cunctatore segnem, pro cauto timidum compellabat, Liv. 22, 12, 12; so with cautus, Tac. H. 2, 25: non cunctator iniqui Labdacus, Stat. Th. 3, 79; cf.: Atheniensium populum celerem et supra vires auda

cunctator2.full: Cunctātor, ōris, m., a surname of the dictator Q. Fabius Maximus (prob. retained as a title of honor, from the reproach of his master of horse; v. 1. cunctator); cf. Liv. 30, 26, 9; 28, 40, 6; Quint. 8, 2, 11, and cunctor.
cunctator2.short: Cunctātor, ōris, m., a surname of the dictator Q.

cunctatrix.full: cunctātrix, icis, f. cunctator, one who hesitates, acts deliberately (late Lat.): lenta virtus omnis et diuturna cunctatrix, Ambros. Ep. 67, 5.

cunctatus.full: cunctātus, a, um, formerly assumed as P. a. of cunctor; in comp., Plin. Ep. 2, 16, 4; Suet. Caes. 60; Tac. A. 1, 71; but in all these passages recent edd. read cunctantior, cunctantius; v. cunctor, P. a. and adv.
cunctatus.short: cunctātus, a, um, formerly assumed as P.

cuncticinus.full: cunctĭcĭnus, a, um, adj. cunctuscano, prop. sounding all together; hence, concordant, harmonious (opp.simplex), Mart. Cap. 9, § 905.

cunctim.full: cunctim, adv. cunctus, all together, in a body, collectively, for conjunctim (very rare, perh. only in App.): cunctim et coacervatim (opp.: singulatim ac discretim), App. Flor. 9, p. 347, 6; id. de Deo Socr. 4, p. 43, 39 Hildebr. (al. cuncti).

cunctiparens.full: cunctĭ-părens, entis, m. id., parent of all, Prud. στεφ. 14, 128.

cunctipotens.full: cunctĭ-pŏtens, entis, m. adj. id., all-powerful, omnipotent: Jesus (i. e. omnipotens), Prud. στεφ. 7, 56.

cuncto.full: cuncto, āre, 1, v. n. (ante-class. collat. form of cunctor), to delay, hesitate, Enn. ap. Non. p. 469, 27 (Com. Rel. v. 3 Vahl.): cunctas? intus alii festinant, Plaut. Cas. 4, 2, 13: cunctant subferre laborem, Att. ap. Non. p. 469, 24 (Trag. Rel. v. 72 Rib.).

cunctor.full: cunctor (in many MSS. and edd. also contor), ātus, 1 (archaic inf. cunctarier, Lucr. 3, 67), v. dep. cf. Sanscr. çank, to be anxious; Gr. ὄκνος, to delay action (from deliberation or indolence), to linger, loiter, hesitate, doubt (freq. and class.); constr. absol., with the inf. or a subj.-clause. Of personal subjects. Absol., so the verse of Ennius upon the dictator Q. Fab. Maximus Cunctator: unus homo nobis cunctando restituit rem, Enn. ap. Cic. Off. 1, 24, 84 (Ann. v. 313 Vahl.; also cited Ci

cunctus.full: cunctus, a, um, and more freq. in plur. cuncti, ae, a, adj. contr. from conjunctus, all in a body, all together, the whole, all, entire (cf. Paul. ex Fest. p. 50, 15 Müll.: cuncti significat quidem omnes, sed conjuncti et congregati; very freq. and class.). Sing. Masc.: senatus, Cic. Fam. 4, 4, 3: senatus populusque, Liv. 9, 6, 7: terrarum orbis, Verg. A. 1, 233: pelagi fragor, id. ib. 1, 154: in ordinem, Cic. Leg. 3, 14, 32: a populo, id. Fam. 3, 11, 2.— Fem.: Aegyptus, Cic. Agr. 2, 16, 41: Gal
cunctus.short: cunctus, a, um, and more freq.

cuneatim.full: cŭnĕātim, adv. cuneo, in the form of a wedge, wedge-shaped (rare): constiterunt hostes, Caes. B. G. 7, 28; App. M. 8, p. 165 Bip.

cuneatio.full: cŭnĕātĭo, ōnis, f. id., a wedgeshaped point: narium, Scrib. Comp. 47.

cuneatus.full: cŭnĕātus, a, um, Part. and P. a., from cuneo.

cuneo.full: cŭnĕo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. cuneus (rare, and not ante-Aug.; cf. cuneatim). To fasten with wedges, to wedge up: si quid cuneandum sit in ligno clavisve figendum, Plin. 16, 40, 76, § 206: unus lapis facit fornacem, ille, qui latera inclinata cuneavit et interventu suo vinxit, the key-stone, Sen. Ep. 118, 16.—* Trop., of discourse, to press in, force in: si oratio cohaeret et sequitur, non, si per vim cuneatur, Quint. 4, 3, 4.— To make wedge-shaped; of places: (Britannia) iterum se in diversos angu

cuneolus.full: cŭnĕŏlus, i, m. dim. id., a little wedge, a small gore, Cic. Univ. 13; Col. 4, 29, 10; Pall. Febr. 17, 3.

cuneus1.full: cŭnĕus, i, m. cf. Sanscr. çā, çān, to sharpen; Lat. cos, cautes, a wedge. Prop., Cato, R. R. 10, 3; 11, 4; Att. ap. Cic. Tusc. 2, 10, 23; Verg. G. 1, 144; Hor. C. 1, 35, 18: jamque labant cunei, i. e. the plugs or wedges by which the ship's hull was made tight, Ov. M. 11, 514: Britannia in cuneum tenuatur, is shaped like a wedge, Tac. Agr. 10; cf. cuneo, II.—* Trop.: hoc cuneo veritatis omnis extruditur haeresis, Tert. adv. Marc. 1, 21 fin.— Meton. Troops drawn up for battle in the form of a wed

cuneus2.full: Cŭnĕus, i, m., a promontory in Lusitania, now Cabo St. Maria, the extreme southern point of Portugal, Mel. 3, 1, 6; Plin. 4, 21, 35, § 116.
cuneus2.short: Cŭnĕus, i, m., a promontory in Lusitania, now Cabo St.

cunicularis.full: cŭnīcŭlāris, e, adj. cuniculus, of or pertaining to the rabbit, rabbit-: herba, Marc. Emp. 14 fin.

cunicularius.full: cŭnīcŭlārĭus, ii, m. cuniculus, II. B.; in milit. lang., a miner, Veg. Mil. 2, 11; Amm. 24, 4, 22.

cuniculatim.full: cŭnīcŭlātim, adv. cuniculus, II. A., in channels, Plin. 9, 33, 52, § 103; v. cuniculatus fin.

cuniculator.full: cŭnīcŭlātor, ōris, m. ( = cunicularius), a miner, Lact. ad Stat. Th. 2, 418.

cuniculatus.full: cŭnīcŭlātus, a, um, adj. cuniculus, in the form of a channel or tube (post-Aug. and rare): rostrum, Plin. 9, 36, 61, § 130 Sillig and Jan. (al. cuniculatim).

cuniculosus.full: cŭnīcŭlōsus, a, um, adj. cuniculus, II., abounding in caves: Celtiberia, Cat. 37, 18.

cuniculus.full: cŭnīcŭlus, i, m. Spanish, a rabbit, cony, Gr. κόνικλος or κύνικλος. Prop., Varr. R. R. 3, 12, 6; Plin. 8, 55, 81, § 217; Mart. 13, 60.— Transf. (from their habit of burrowing in the ground; cf. Varr. l. l.; collat. form, cŭnīcŭlum, i, n., acc. to Paul. ex Fest. p. 50, 4, but perh. an acc.; v. Müll. ad loc.), a passage under ground, a hole, pit, cavity, canal, etc. In gen., Cic. Off. 3, 23, 90; Col. 8, 17, 4; Plin. 2, 80, 82, § 193; 6, 27, 31, §§ 128 and 135.— In partic., milit. t. t., a mine, Ca

cunila.full: cŭnīla (cŏnīla), ae, f., a plant, a species of origanum; form cunila, Plaut. Trin. 4, 2, 93; Col. 6, 13, 1; Plin. 19, 8, 50, § 165; 20, 16, 61, § 169; form conila, Arn. 6, 17 fin.; App. Herb. 122.
cunila.short: cŭnīla (cŏnīla), ae, f., a plant, a species of origanum;

cunilago.full: cŭnīlāgo, ĭnis, f., a species of cunila, Plin. 19, 8, 50, § 165; 20, 16, 63, § 171 al.
cunilago.short: cŭnīlāgo, ĭnis, f., a species of cunila, Plin.

cunina.full: Cūnīna, ae, f. cunae, the goddess who protects children in the cradle, Varr. ap. Non. p. 167, 32; Lact. 1, 20, 36; Aug. Civ. Dei, 4, 11; Inscr. Grut. 96, 9.

cunire.full: cunīre est stercus facere, Paul. ex Fest. p. 50, 16 Müll. [cf. inquino, and Sanscr. knuj, to stink].

cunnilingus.full: cunnĭ-lingus, i, m., i. q. cunnum lingens, Mart. 12, 59, 10; Auct. Priap. 78, 2 al.

cunnus.full: cunnus, i, m. cf. Sanscr. çushi, ditch; Gr. κυσός, the female pudenda. Prop., Mart. 1, 90, 7; 3, 72, 6; 3, 81, 4; Auct. Priap. 28, 5.—Also of animals: mulae, Cat. 96, 6. — Transf., of the person, an unchaste female, Hor. S. 1, 2, 36; 1, 3, 107; Auct. Priap. 69, 1 al.—As an obscene word, avoided acc. to Cic. Or. 45, 154; id. Fam. 9, 22, 3.

cunulae.full: cūnŭlae, ārum, f. dim. cunae, a little cradle, Prud. Cath. 7, 164; 11, 98.

cupa1.full: cūpa, ae, f. cf. κύπτω, a tub, cask, tun, vat, etc., for holding liquids, esp. wine, Varr. ap. Non. p. 83, 24 sq.; Pall. 1, 18, 2; 1, 38, 1; Cic. Pis. 27, 67 (but acc. to Ernesti, a female vintner; cf. copa); Caes. B. C: 2, 11; Luc. 4, 420; also for grain, Dig. 19, 2, 31; and for the ashes of the dead, a niche, Inscr. Orell. 2697; 4550.

cupa2.full: cūpa, ae, f., = κώπη (v. Lidd. and Scott in h. v.), the handle of an oil-mill, a crooked handle, Cato, R. R. 12, 21.

cuparius.full: cūpārĭus, ĭi, m. 1. cupa, a cooper, Inscr. Orell. 4176 sq.

cupavo.full: Cŭpāvo, ōnis, m., a Ligurian, Verg. A. 10, 186.
cupavo.short: Cŭpāvo, ōnis, m., a Ligurian, Verg.

cupedia.full: cūpēdĭa, cūpēdĭnārĭus, cūpēdĭ-um, cūpēdo, v. cupp-.

cupella.full: cūpella, ae, f. dim. 1. cupa, a small vat or cask, Pall. Febr. 25, 12; Apic. 1, 2.

cupencus.full: Cŭpencus, i, m., a priest of the Sabines, Verg. A. 12, 539; Sil. 4, 537; cf.: sane sciendum, cupencum Sabinorum linguā sacerdotem vocari, Serv. ad Verg. l. l.; esp., a priest of Hercules, Gloss. ap. Serv. l. l.
cupencus.short: Cŭpencus, i, m., a priest of the Sabines, Verg.

cupidineus.full: Cŭpīdĭnĕus, adj., v. cupido, II. A. 2. β.

cupiditas.full: cŭpĭdĭtas, ātis (gen. plur. rarely -tatium, Cic. Sest. 66, 138; Sen. Ep. 5, 7), f. cupidus, a desire, wish, longing, in a good and (more freq.) in a bad sense. In a good sense, a longing, desire. With gen.: insatiabilis quaedam veri videndi, Cic. Tusc. 1, 19, 44: cognoscendi, id. ib.: imitandi, id. Brut. 92, 317: mirabilis pugnandi, Nep. Milt. 5, 1 al.: justi et magni triumphi, Cic. Pis. 25, 59: gloriae, id. ib.: mira studiorum, Tac. Or. 2: cibi, appetite, Cels. 2, 3 al.— With ad: tanta cupidita

cupido.full: cŭpīdo (cūpēdo or cuppēdo, Lucr. 1, 1082; 4, 1090; 5, 45), ĭnis, f. (m., Plant. Am. 2, 2, 210; Hor. C. 2, 16, 15; 3, 16, 39; 3, 24, 51; id. S. 1, 1, 61; id. Ep. 1, 1, 33; Ov. M. 8, 74; 9, 734; Sil. 4, 99; and personified in all authors; v. the foll.) [cupidus], access. form of cupiditas, desire, wish, longing, eagerness, in a good and (more usu.) in a bad sense (very freq. in the poets and histt., esp. in Sall.; twice in Quint., but in Cic. only as personified). In gen. In a good sense: cupido c

cupidus.full: cŭpĭdus, a, um, adj. cupio, longing, desiring, desirous, eager, in a good and bad sense, wishing, loving, fond, etc. (very freq. and class.); constr. with gen., abl., inf., in, or absol. In a good sense. Of persons. With gen.: ejus videndi cupidus, Ter. Hec. 3, 3, 12; so, huc redeundi, abeundi a milite, Vosque hic videndi, id. ib. 1, 2, 16: redeundi domum, id. ib. 3, 1, 3: bellandi, Caes. B. G. 1, 2: te audiendi, Cic. de Or. 2, 4, 16: valde spectandi, id. ib. 1, 35, 162: satis faciendi rei publi

cupiennius.full: Cŭpĭennĭus, ii, m., a Roman proper name, Cic. Att. 16, 16, 14.
cupiennius.short: Cŭpĭennĭus, ii, m., a Roman proper name, Cic.

cupiens.full: cŭpĭens, entis, Part. and P. a., from cupio.

cupienter.full: cŭpĭenter, adv., v. cupio, P. a. fin.

cupio.full: cŭpĭo, īvi or ĭi, ītum, 3 (imperf. subj. cŭpīret, Lucr. 1, 72; quoted ap. Non. p. 506 fin., and ap. Prisc. p. 879 P.), v. a. Sanscr kup, to be in active motion, to be angry; cf. recupero, to long for a thing, to desire, wish (designating a natural, involuntary inclination, or an unbridled or passionate desire, while volo indicates an energetic will, and opto a deliberate wish or choice, Cic. Mil. 12, 32; Sen. Ep. 116, 2; cf. Klotz in Jahn's Neues Jahrb. 1834, II. p. 119 sq.; freq. in every per.

cupisco.full: cŭpisco, ĕre, 3, v. inch. [cupio], to wish, desire (late Lat.): Deum videre, Aug. de Music. 4, 4; cf. Prisc. p. 824 P.

cupitor.full: cŭpītor, ōris, m. id., one who desires or wishes (very rare; perh. only in the foll. exs.): incredibilium, Tac. A. 15, 42: matrimonii, id. ib. 12, 7: amicitiae, App. Flor. 3, p. 807.

cupitus.full: cŭpītus, a, um, v. cupio, I. A. α.

cupla1.full: cūpla, ae, f., = copula, q. v., Isid. Orig. 19, 19, 6.

cuppedia.full: cuppēdĭa (cūp-), ae, f. cuppes. * Fondness for dainties, daintiness, lickerishness, Cic. Tusc. 4, 11, 26; cf. Non. p. 85.— Plur., dainty dishes, delicacies (late Lat.): conjectabamus ad cenulam non cuppedias ciborum, sed argutias quaestionum, Gell. 7 (6), 13, 2; 7 (6), 16, 6; Amm. 25, 2, 2; 26, 7, 1; 30, 1, 20; cf. cuppedium.

cuppedinarius.full: cuppēdĭnārĭus (cūp-), a, um, adj., of or pertaining to dainty dishes or delicacies. Adj.: Forum, a place in Rome, Symm. Ep. 8, 19; cf. 2. cuppedo, and cuppes, II.— Subst.: cuppēdĭnārĭus, ii, m., he who prepares delicacies or tidbits, a confectioner, Ter. Eun. 2, 2, 25; Lampr. Heliog. 30.
cuppedinarius.short: cuppēdĭnārĭus (cūp-), a, um, adj., of or pertaining to dainty dishes or delicacies.

cuppedium.full: cuppēdĭum (cūp-), ii, n. cuppes, a tidbit, Varr. L. L. 5, § 146 Müll.; mostly plur.: cuppēdĭa, ōrum, n. (a later form coppādĭa, ōrum, n., Apic. 5, 1; 7, 6; 8, 6), dainty dishes, tidbits, delicacies (anteand post-class.): nil moror cuppedia, Plaut. Stich. 5, 4, 32; cf. Paul. ex Fest. p. 48, 15 Müll.; cf. cuppes, II.

cuppedo2.full: cuppēdo (cūp-), ĭnis, f. orig. a collat. form of cupido, q. v; hence, in partic., a desire for delicacies, a tidbit, delicacy: Forum cupedinis, a place in Rome where delicacies were sold, Varr. L. L. 5, § 146 Müll.; id. ap. Don. ad Ter. Eun. 2, 2, 25; Paul. ex Fest. p. 48, 15 Müll.; App. M. 1, p. 113, 14 (Hildebr.: forum cupidinis); cf. cuppedinarius, and cuppes, II.

cuppes.full: cuppes (cūp-), ĕdis, m. adj., fond of delicacies, dainty: blandiloquentulus, harpago, mendax, cuppes, etc., Plaut. Trin. 2, 1, 13.— Cuppes et cuppedia antiqui lautiores cibos nominabant; inde et macellum forum cupedinis appellabant, etc., Paul. ex Fest. p. 48, 15 Müll.; cf. 2. cuppedo.

cupra.full: Cūpra, ae, f., the name of two cities in Picenum, Mel. 2, 4, 6; Plin. 3, 13, 18, § 111; Sil. 8, 434.—Hence, Cūprenses, ium, m., their inhabitants, Plin. l. l.
cupra.short: Cūpra, ae, f., the name of two cities in Picenum, Mel.

cupressetum.full: cū^pressētum, i, n. cupressus, a grove or plantation of cypress - trees, a cypress wood, Cato, R. R. 151, 1; Cic. Leg. 1, 5, 15.

cupresseus.full: cū^pressĕus, a, um, adj. id., of cypress, cypress.: signa Junonis, Liv. 27, 37, 12: foliatura, Vitr. 2, 9.

cupressifer.full: cū^pressĭfer, fĕra, fĕrum, adj. cupressus-fero, cypress - bearing: Erymanthus, Ov. H. 9, 87: Cyllenes jugum, id. F. 5, 87.

cupressinus.full: cū^pressĭnus (cȳ^press-, Vulg. Cant. 1, 16), a, um, adj., = κυπαρίσσινος, of cypress, cypress-: frondes, Col. 2, 2, 11: coni, id. 6, 7, 2: oleum, Plin. 23, 4, 45, § 88.

cupressus.full: cū^pressus, i, and less freq. ūs, f. (m. acc. plur. rectosque cupressos, Enn. ap. Gell. 13, 20, 13, and ap. Non. p. 195; rare collat. form cўpărissus, i, f., Verg. A. 3, 680; cf. infra B.; and in late Lat. cȳ^pres-sus, i, f., Vulg. Ecclus. 24, 17; Isid. Orig. 17, 7, 34), = κυπάρισσος, the cypress, an evergreen tree sacred to Pluto and used at funerals: Cupressus sempervirens, Linn.— Sing. nom., Hor. C. 4, 6, 10; Plin. 16, 33, 60, § 142; 16, 40, 78, § 212; Ov. M. 10, 106.—Gen. cupressi, Cato, R.

cupreus.full: cū^prĕus (cȳ^pr-), a, um, adj. cuprum, of copper, copper-: bidentes, Pall. Jul. 5: acus, Treb. Claud. 14 (for Plin. 23, 3, 37, § 74, v. Cyprius, s. v. Cyprus).

cuprinus.full: cū^prĭnus (cȳ^pr-), a, um, adj. cuprum, of copper, copper-: clavus, Pall. Jan. 15, 18: cauterium, Veg. Art. Vet. 1, 14, 3 al.

cuprum.full: cū^prum, i, n., v. Cyprus, II. A.

cupula1.full: cūpŭla, ae, f. dim. 1. cupa, a little tub or cask, Dig. 33, 6, 3.— A small burying-vault: Renier, Inscr. Afric. 3373; 3584 al.—Sync. form CVPLA, Inscr. Afric. 3172.
