cupula2.full: cūpŭla, ae, f. dim. 2. cupa, a small, crooked handle, Cato, R. R. 21, 3.

cur.full: cūr (old orthog. quor; cf. Vel. Long. p. 2236 P.; and in MSS. sometimes cor, v. Lachm. ad Lucr. II. p. 171 sq.), adv. contr. from quare; cf. Vel. Long. p. 2231 P. and the letter C; acc. to Voss, Etym. s. h. v.; Analog. 4, 21, and Hand, Turs. II. p. 175, from cui rei; cf.: quoi rei, Plaut. Poen. 2, 33, = quam ob rem, for what reason, wherefore, why, to what purpose, from what motive. Rel.: duae causae sunt, cur tu frequentior in isto officio esse debeas quam nos, Cic. Fam. 15, 20, 2; so, causae,

cura.full: cūra, ae, f. caveo; cf. curo init., care, solicitude, carefulness, thought, concern. Trouble (physical or mental), bestowed on something; solicitude, care, attention, pains (syn.: diligentia, opera, studium, labor, etc.; opp. neglegentia, etc.; v. the foll.; very freq. in every per. and species of composition). Lit. In gen. Ab. sol.: curantes magnā cum curā, Enn. ap. Cic. Div. 1, 48, 107: magnā cum curā ego illum curari volo, Plaut. Men. 5, 4, 7; cf. id. ib. 5, 4, 9: in aliquā re curam ponere (j

curabilis.full: cūrābĭlis, e, adj. curo, that is to be apprehended or feared: vindicta, Juv. 16, 21 dub.— Curable (cf.: sanabilis, medicabilis), Cael. Aur. Tard. 4, 7, 93.

curagendarius.full: cūrăgendārĭus, ii, m. cura, I. A. 2. b., -ago, a manager, overseer, Cod. Th. 6, 29, 1.

curandus.full: cūrandus, i, m., v. curo, II. B. β.

curans.full: cūrans, ntis, P. a., v. curo, II. B. β.

curate.full: cūrātē, adv., v. curo, P. a. fin.

curatio.full: cūrātĭo, ōnis, f. curo, a taking care of something, administration, oversight, care, management, charge (rare but class.). In gen.: me sinas curare ancillas, quae mea est curatio, Plaut. Cas. 2, 3, 45; cf. id. Poen. 1, 2, 144: cultus et curatio corporis, Cic. N. D. 1, 34, 94; cf. id. ib. 2, 63, 158: curatio et administratio rerum, id. ib. 1, 1, 2: corporum, Liv. 25, 38: frumenti, Cic. Att. 15, 11, 1: vini, Col. 12, 25, 4: quid tibi hanc curatiost rem? (for hujus rei; cf. aditio) why does this tr

curator.full: cūrātor (old orthog. COERATOR, v. the foll.), ōris, m. id., he who cares for or takes charge of a thing, a manager, overseer, superintendent, keeper. In gen.: ludorum, Plaut. Poen. prol. 36: suntoque aediles coeratores urbis annonae ludorumque solemnium, Cic. Leg. 3, 3, 6: viae Flaminiae, id. Att. 1, 1, 2: aviarii, a bird-keeper, Varr. R. R. 3, 5, 5; cf. apum, Col. 9, 9, 1: pavonini gregis, id. 8, 11, 2; and gallinarius, Varr. R. R. 3, 9, 7: fidus negotiorum, Sall. J. 71, 3: munerum ac venationu

curatoria.full: cūrātōrĭa, ae, f. curatorius, guardianship, = ἐπιτροπή, several times in Dig. 27, 1, 1 and 2, always written as Greek, κουρατορία, etc.

curatoricius.full: cūrātōrīcĭus or -tĭus, a, um, adj. curator, I., of or belonging to an overseer: equi, the horses of a provincial commissary, Cod. Th. 11, 1, 29.

curatorius.full: cūrātōrĭus, a, um, adj. curator, II., pertaining to guardianship: STIPENDIA VETERANORVM, Inscr. Orell. 4968.— Of or pertaining to a guardian: nomen, Gai Inst. 4, 82.

curatrix.full: cūrātrix, ĭcis, f. curator, II., a female guardian, Non. p. 150, 29.

curatura.full: cūrātūra, ae, f. curo, management, care, attendance, Ter. Eun. 2, 3, 25 Ruhnk.

curatus.full: cūrātus, a, um, Part. and P. a., of curo.

curculio.full: curcŭlĭo (gurgŭlĭo, Plaut. Trin. 4, 3, 9 Ritschl, Fleck.; Pall. 1, 19, 2; id. Jun. 3; also in some MSS. of the authors cited infra), ōnis, m. kindr. with circulus, circus, a corn-worm, weevil, Cato, R. R. 92; Varr. R. R. 1, 57, 63; Col. 1, 6, 15 sq.; Plin. 18, 11, 73, § 302; Serv. ad Verg. G. 1, 186. — Form gurgulio = membrum virile, Pers. 4, 38.— Curcŭlĭo, the name of a comedy of Plautus.

curculiunculus.full: curcŭlĭuncŭlus, i, m. dim. curculio, a little weevil, in comic lang. for something trifling, worthless, Plaut. Rud. 5, 2, 38 (v. the passage in connection).

cures.full: Cŭres, ium, m. (parvi, Ov. F. 2, 135) and f. (Tatiae, Prop. 5, 9, 74), = Κύρεις or Κύρις [curis, Sabine word, = hasta, Ov. F. 2, 477], the ancient chief town of the Sabines, Varr. L. L. 5, § 51 Müll.; Cic. Fam. 15, 20, 1; Verg. A. 6, 811; 8, 638; Ov. M. 14, 778 al.; Liv. 1, 13, 5; 1, 18, 1; Flor. 1, 2, 1; cf. Quirites.— Meton., the inhabitants of Cures, Ov. F. 3, 201; 6, 216.— Hence, Cŭren-sis, e, adj., of Cures: turba, Ov. F. 3, 94. — Subst.: Cŭrenses, ium, m., the inhabitants of Cures, Varr. L

curetes.full: Cūrētes, um, m., = Κουρῆτες, the most ancient inhabitants of the island of Crete, who paid their worship to Jupiter (as the Corybantes, who, at a later date, were identified with them, celebrated the worship of Cybele) with noisy music and armed dances, Hyg. Fab. 139; Lucr. 2, 629; Verg. A. 3, 131 Heyne; id. G. 4, 151; Ov. M. 4, 282; id. F. 4, 210; Sen. Herc. Oet. 1877; Val. Max. 2, 4, 4; Lact. 1, 11, 46 al.— Hence, Cūrētis, ĭdis, f. adj., lit. pertaining to the Curetes; hence, poet. for Cretan:
curetes.short: Cūrētes, um, m., = Κουρῆτες, the most ancient inhabitants of the island of Crete, who paid their worship to Jupiter (as the Corybantes, who, at a later date, were identified with them, celebrated the worship of Cybele) with noisy music and armed danc

curetis2.full: Cūrētis, ĭdis, v. Curetes, II. A.

curia.full: cūrĭa, ae, f. kindr. with Quiris, Quirites; cf. the letter C, a curia or court, one of the thirty parts into which Romulus divided the Roman people, ten for each of the three tribes; each curia contained ten gentes, Varr. ap. Dion. Hal. 2, 83; Liv. 1, 13, 6; Aur. Vict. Vir. Ill. 2, 12; Dig. 1, 2, 2; Paul. ex Fest. p. 49, 1 Müll.— Meton. A structure built for the religious services of a curia (sometimes also serving for other purposes), Varr. L. L. 5, § 155 Müll.; Fest. p. 174, 6 ib.: veteres, on

curiales.full: curiāles mensae, in quibus immolabatur Junoni, quae curis appellata est, Paul. ex Fest. p. 64, 11.
curiales.short: curiāles mensae, in quibus immolabatur Junoni, quae curis appellata est, Paul.

curialis.full: cūrĭālis, e, adj. curia, of or pertaining to a curia, i. e. Belonging to the same curia, district, or division of the people; subst.: cūrĭālis, is, m., a member of the same curia, = δημότης: neque quisquam curialium Venit, Plaut. Aul. 2, 2, 2: Cimonem etiam in suos curialis hospitalem fuisse, Cic. Off. 2, 18, 64; cf. Paul. ex Fest. p. 49, 13 Müll.: curiales ejusdem curiae ut tribules et municipes.— Pertaining to the religious services of the curiœ: curiales flamines curiarum sacerdotes, Paul. ex

curianus.full: Cŭrĭānus, a, um, v. Curius, II.

curiatii.full: Cūrĭātĭi (Cŭrĭi, Prop. 3, 3, 7, or 4, 2, 7 Müll.), ōrum, m., an Albanian gens, subsequently transplanted to Rome, from which were descended the three Curiatii who fell in the contest with the Roman Horatii, Liv. 1, 24, 1 sq.; Cic. Inv. 2, 26, 78 al.: cecini Curios fratres, Prop. l. l.

curiatim.full: cūrĭātim, adv. curia, by curiæ (very rare): populum consuluit, *Cic. Rep. 2, 17, 31 (but in Gell. 15, 27, 2, the better read. is curiatum).

curiatius.full: Curiatius, ĭi, m., a Roman proper name: Curiatius Maternus, v. Maternus.
curiatius.short: Curiatius, ĭi, m., a Roman proper name: Curiatius Maternus, v.

curiatus.full: cūrĭātus, a, um, adj. curia, of or pertaining to the curiæ: comitia, in which the people voted according to curiæ (orig. the only ruling assembly; later limited by the comitia centuriata to cases of arrogation (adoption), the choice of priests, the conferring of the chief command; cf. comitium, II.; Dict. of Antiq.), Lael. Felix ap. Gell. 15, 27, 2; Cic. Agr. 2, 11, 26 sq.; Liv. 5, 52, 15 al.: lex, passed in such comitia, Cic. Agr. 2, 10, 26; 2, 11, 28 sq.; Liv. 9, 38, 15; 5, 46, 11; Gell. 5, 19

curidius.full: Curidius, ii, m., a Roman proper name, Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 20, § 44.
curidius.short: Curidius, ii, m., a Roman proper name, Cic.

curietae.full: Cūrietae, ārum, m., the inhabitants of Curieta, an island on the coast of Illyria, now Veglia, Plin. 3, 21, 25, § 139.—Hence, Cūrietĭcus, a, um, adj., of Curieta: litus, Flor. 4, 2, 31.
curietae.short: Cūrietae, ārum, m., the inhabitants of Curieta, an island on the coast of Illyria, now Veglia, Plin.

curii.full: Cŭrĭi, ōrum, m., v. Curiatii init.

curio1.full: cūrĭo, ōnis, m. curia. The priest of a curia, Varr. L. L. 5, § 83; 6, § 46 Müll.: maximus, he who presided over all the curiæ, Liv. 27, 8, 1; cf. Paul. ex Fest. p. 126, 17 Müll.— Post-Aug., a crier, herald, = praeco, Mart. lib. 2 praef.; Treb. Gall. 12.

curio2.full: Cūrĭo, ōnis, m., a surname in the gens Scribonia; v. Scribonius; hence, Cū-rĭōnĭānus, a, um, adj., of or pertaining to Curio, Auct. B. Afr. 52 fin.
curio2.short: Cūrĭo, ōnis, m., a surname in the gens Scribonia;

curio3.full: cūrĭo, ōnis, m. adj. cura (a humorously-formed word, corresp. with curiosus), wasted by sorrow, lean, emaciated: agnus, Plaut. Aul. 3, 6, 27 sq. (v. the passage in connection); cf. Paul. ex Fest. p. 60, 3 Müll.

curionatus.full: cūrĭōnātus, ūs, m. 1. curio, I., the office of priest of a curia, Paul. ex Fest. p. 49, 9 Müll. (cf. curionius).

curionius.full: cūrĭōnĭus, a, um, adj. 1. curio, I., of or pertaining to the priest of a curia: curionium aes dicebatur quod dabatur curioni ob sacerdotium curionatus, Paul. ex Fest. p. 49, 19 Müll.: curionia sacra, quae in curiis fiebant, id. ib. p. 62, 11.

curiositas.full: cūrĭōsĭtas, ātis, f. curiosus, desire of knowledge, curiosity, inquisitiveness (very rare), Cic. Att. 2, 12, 2; Macr. S. 1, 11, 45; Tert. adv. Haeret. 17; id. Apol. 25.

curiosolites.full: Cūrĭŏsŏlītes, um, m., a Gallic tribe in Armorica (Gall. Lugdun.), near the mod. Corseult, south of St. Malo, Caes. B. G. 7, 75; acc. Curiosolitas, id. ib. 2, 34; 3, 7; 3, 11 al. —The same called Cārĭosvĕlītes, Plin. 4, 18, 32, § 107.
curiosolites.short: Cūrĭŏsŏlītes, um, m., a Gallic tribe in Armorica (Gall.

curiosulus.full: cūrĭōsŭlus, a, um, adj. dim. [curiosus], somewhat curious, a little inquisitive; transf.: ventus, App. M. 10, p. 254, 8.

curiosus.full: cūrĭōsus, a, um, adj. cura. (Acc. to cura, I.) Bestowing care or pains upon a thing, applying one's self assiduously, careful, diligent, thoughtful, devoted (class.; esp. freq. in Cic.). In gen. With in or ad: in omni historiā curiosus, Cic. Tusc. 1, 45, 108: si me nihilo minus nosti curiosum in re publicā quam te, id. Att. 5, 14, 3: ad investigandum curiosior, id. Fam. 4, 13, 5.— With gen. (post-Aug.): medicinae, Plin. 25, 2, 3, § 7: memoriae, Aur. Vict. Caes. 20 fin.: curiosissimus famae suae,

curis.full: cŭris or quĭris, ītis, f. Sabine, a spear, Ov. F. 2, 477; cf. Macr. S. 1, 9, 16; Paul. ex Fest. p. 49, 10 Müll.; v. Quirites.—Hence, Cŭrītis (Quĭrītis), is, f., a surname of Juno as protector of spearmen, Mart. Cap. 2, § 149; Inscr. Orell. 1303 sq.; 8659.

curito.full: cūrĭto, āre, v. freq. a. curo, to take care of, to cherish, App. M. 7, p. 194, 2.

curius1.full: cūrĭus, a, um, adj. cura, II., full of sorrow, grievous: infortunio, Plaut. Ps. 4, 7, 44 dub. (Ritschl, curvo).

curius2.full: Cŭrĭus, a, the name of a Roman gens; thus M'. Curius Dentatus, the conqueror of the Samnites, Sabines, Lucanians, and of Pyrrhus; celebrated for his moderation, Cic. Sen. 16, 55 sq.; Aur. Vict. Vir. Ill. 33; Hor. C. 1, 12, 41; Juv. 11, 78; Flor. 1, 15; 1, 18; Cic. Sull. 7, 23; Val. Max. 4, 3, 5 sq. et saep.— Appel. for a bold and moderate man; in plur.: (Nenia) et maribus Curiis et decantata Camillis, Hor. Ep. 1, 1, 64; Juv. 2, 3.—Hence, Cŭrĭānus, a, um, adj., of or pertaining to a Curius, Curia
curius2.short: Cŭrĭus, a, the name of a Roman gens;

curo.full: cūro (old orthog. COERO and COIRO, Inscr. Orell. 31; 560; 570: coeret, coerari, coerandi, Cic. Leg. 3, 4, 10), āvi, ātum, 1 (perf. subj. curassis, Plaut. Most. 2, 2, 93; id. Ps. 1, 3, 3; id. Poen. 3, 1, 50; inf. pass. curarier, id. Capt. 3, 5, 79), v. a. cura, to care for, take or have care of, to be solicitous for, to look or attend to, trouble one's self about, etc. (very freq. in every period and species of composition); constr. with the acc., the acc. with the gerundive, the inf. with ut, ne

curotrophoe.full: cūrŏtrŏphoe = κουροτρόφοι, nourishing children: nymphae ab alimoniā infantum, Serv. ad Verg. E. 10, 62.
curotrophoe.short: cūrŏtrŏphoe = κουροτρόφοι, nourishing children: nymphae ab alimoniā infantum, Serv.

currax.full: currax, ācis, adj. curro, running fast, quick, swift (post-class. and rare): servus, Dig. 21, 1, 18.—Poet.: laquei, which are bound on the feet of running animals, Grat. Cyn. 89.

curriculum.full: currĭcŭlum, i, n. id., a running, course, race. Lit. In gen. (mostly ante-class.): conicere se in curriculum, Plaut. Merc. 5, 2, 91; cf.: pedes in curriculum conferre, Varr. ap. Non. p. 263, 6: facere unum curriculum, Plaut. Trin. 4, 4, 11; cf.: ita celeri curriculo fui propere a portu, id. Stich. 2, 2, 13.— Abl. curriculo adverb., in a quick course, at full speed, swiftly, hastily, Plaut. Ep. 1, 1, 12; id. Most. 2, 1, 15; 3, 3, 26; id. Mil. 2, 6, 43; Ter. Heaut. 4, 4, 11 al.— In partic., a runn

currilis.full: currīlis, e, adj. currus, of or for a chariot (late Lat.): praesepia equorum currilium, Vulg. 3 Reg. 4, 26: certamina, chariot-races, Ambros. Cant. Cantic. 7, 12: currilis equus, σὺν ἅρματι ἀγωνιζόμενος ἵππος, Gloss. Labb.; cf. also curulis.

curro.full: curro, cŭcurri (old form cĕcurri, acc. to Gell. 7, 9, 14: curri, Varr. Imp. ap. Front. Ep. 2 Mai; Tert. Fug. in Pers. 12; Arn. 4, 4), cursum, 3, v. n. kindr. with celer, coruscus, to run, to move quickly (on foot, on a horse, ship, etc.), to hasten, fly (very freq. in every period and species of composition). Lit. Of living beings: si ingrederis curre, si curris advola, Cic. Att. 2, 23, 3: propere, Ter. Ad. 3, 2, 56: per vias, Plaut. Poen. 3, 1, 24: per totum conclave pavidi, Hor. S. 2, 6, 113:

currulis.full: currūlis, e, adj. currus, of or belonging to a chariot, or a chariot-race: rabies equorum (post-class. and rare), App. M. 9, p. 221: strepitus (opp. equester fremitus), Fronto Ep. 3 Mai; cf. curulis.

currus.full: currus, ūs, m. curro, a chariot, car, wain. Lit. In gen., Poët. ap. Varr. L. L. 5, § 153 Müll.; Cic. Att. 13, 21, 3; Lucr. 3, 642; Cic. Div. 2, 70, 144; Verg. A. 5, 819; id. G. 3, 359; Sen. Ira, 3, 21, 2 et saep.— In partic. A triumphal car, Cic. Cael. 14, 34; Suet. Caes. 49; Flor. 1, 5, 6; Hor. Epod. 9, 22; Ov. M. 13, 252 al. — Meton., a triumph, Cic. Fam. 15, 6, 1; Plin. 5, 5, 5, § 36; Flor. 4, 2, 89; Prop. 3 (4), 9, 53; Luc. 1, 316 et saep.; cf. Sil. 6, 345 Drak.— A war-chariot ( = esseda), C

cursatio.full: cursātĭo, ōnis, f. curso, a running, Don. ad Ter. Hec. 3, 1, 35.

cursilitas.full: cursĭlĭtas, ātis, f. curro, a running about, Fulg. Myth. 3, 3; cf. Auct. Class. 3, p. 81 Mai.

cursim.full: cursim, adv. id., quickly, swiftly, hastily, speedily (class.): currere, Plaut. Ps. 1, 3, 124; Afran. ap. Charis. p. 186 P.: hoc cito et cursim est agendum, Plaut. Poen. 3, 1, 64: rapi ad carnuficem, id. ib. 1, 2, 156: agmine acto, Liv. 27, 16, 9: dicere aliena (opp. sensim dicere quod causae prodesset), Cic. Phil. 2, 17, 42: arripere aliquid, id. de Or. 2, 89, 364: pergere ad aliquid, id. Tusc. 5, 5, 13 et saep.

cursio.full: cursĭo, ōnis, f. id., a running, Varr. L. L. 5, § 11 Müll.

cursitatio.full: cursĭtātĭo, ōnis, f. cursito, a running about hither and thither, Sol. 42, 2.

cursito.full: cursito, āre, v. freq. n. [curso], to run about, run hither and thither (rare). In gen.: sursum deorsum, * Ter. Eun. 2, 2, 47; cf.: huc et illuc, Hor. C. 4, 11, 10; id. S. 2, 6, 107: modo ad Celsum modo ad Nepotem, Plin. Ep. 6, 5, 5; Suet. Tib. 38: excalciatos, id. Vesp. 10.— In partic. To race, run races: quomodo Ladas aut Boius cum Sicyoniis cursitarint, Auct. Her. 4, 3, 4.— Of the motion of atoms: huc et illuc casu et temere, Cic. N. D. 2, 44, 115.

curso.full: curso, āre, v. freq. n. [curro], to run hither and thither, to and fro (rare but class.): ultro et citro, Cic. Rosc. Am. 22, 60: huc illuc, id. Att. 9, 9, 2; Tac. A. 15, 50; id. H. 5, 20: ad aliquem, Ter. Eun. 2, 2, 56 Bentl. N. cr.: per foros, Cic. Sen. 6, 17: per urbem, Tac. A. 2, 82: in omnes vias, Val. Fl. 4, 108.—Impers.: cursari rursum prorsum, Ter. Hec. 3, 1, 35.— Act. (late Lat.), to run over, traverse: nunc jam compactis cursanda syllaba est formis, Mart. Cap. poët. 3, § 262. (In Tac. A

cursor1.full: cursor, ōris, m. id., a runner, and partic., A runner in a race, racer, Lucr. 2, 78; Cic. Tusc. 2, 23, 56; id. Div. 2, 70, 144; also a competitor in a chariot-race: ut cupidi cursor frena retentat equi, Ov. P. 3, 9, 26.— A courier, post (mostly postAug.), Nep. Milt. 4, 3 (transl. of the Gr. ἡμεροδρόμος); Plin. 2, 71, 73, § 181; Plin. Ep. 7, 12 fin.; Suet. Ner. 49; Mart. 3, 100, 1 al.— A slave who ran before the chariot of a grandee, a forerunner (post-Aug.), Sen. Ep. 87, 9; 123, 7; Suet. Ner. 30

cursor2.full: Cursor, ōris, m. id., a surname of L. Papirius, Liv. 9, 16, 11; Ampel. 18; Aur. Vict. Vir. Ill. 31; Eutr. 2, 8.

cursorius.full: cursōrĭus, a, um, adj. id., of or pertaining to running or to a race-course (late Lat.). Adj.: terminus, Front. Colon. p. 141 Goes.— Subst. cursōrĭa, ae, f. (sc. navis), a yacht, cutter, Sid. Ep. 1, 5.— cursōrĭum, ĭi, n., = cursus publicus, a public post, mail, Auct. Lim. p. 261 Goes.

cursualis.full: cursŭālis, e, adj. cursus, of or pertaining to a course, running (late Lat.): equi, post-horses, Cod. Just. 12, 51, 19: raeda, a stage-coach, Cod. Th. 12, 12, 9: sollicitudo, i. e. speed in running, ib. 6, 29, 7.— Hasty, speedy: ministerium, Cassiod. Var. 5, 5.

cursura.full: cursūra, ae, f. curro, a running (ante-class.), Plaut. Bacch. 1, 1, 34; id. Merc. 1, 2, 10; id. As. 2, 2, 61; id. Most. 4, 1, 5; id. Trin. 4, 2, 164; Varr. R. R. 2, 7, 15 al.

cursus.full: cursus, ūs, m. id., a running (on foot, on a horse, chariot, ship, etc.), a course, way, march, passage, voyage, journey, etc. (very freq.). Lit. Of living beings: ingressus, cursus, accubitio, etc., Cic. N. D. 1, 34, 94: ibi cursu, luctando ... sese exercebant, Plaut. Bacch. 3, 3, 24; cf. id. Most. 1, 2, 73, and Hor. A. P. 412: quique pedum cursu valet, etc., Verg. A. 5, 67: cursu superare canem, Hor. Ep. 1, 18, 51: milites cursu exanimati, Caes. B. G. 2, 23: huc magno cursu intenderunt, at ful

curtilius.full: Curtĭlĭus, ĭi, m., a Roman proper name, Cic. Att. 14, 6, 1; 14, 10, 2 al.
curtilius.short: Curtĭlĭus, ĭi, m., a Roman proper name, Cic.

curtius.full: Curtĭus, a, the name of a Roman gens. C. Curtius Postumus, a partisan of Cæsar, Cic. Att. 9, 2, a, 3; id. Fam. 2, 16, 7; id. Q. Fr. 2, 5, 3.— Q. Curtius Rufus, the historiographer of Alexander the Great, etc., Plin. Ep. 7, 27, 2; Tac. A. 11, 21.— Curtius Nicia, of Cos, freedman of a Curtius, a friend of Pompey, Cic. Fam. 9, 10, 1 sq.; Suet. Gram. 14.—Hence, Adj. Lacus Curtius, a place in Rome named after a certain Curtius, Varr. L. L. 5, § 148 Müll.; Liv. 7, 6, 5; Ov F. 6, 403; also called Lacus
curtius.short: Curtĭus, a, the name of a Roman gens.

curto.full: curto, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. curtus, to shorten, diminish (not ante-Aug., and very rare): aliquid, Cels. 7, 9: radices, Pall. Feb. 10, 3.— Trop., to diminish: rem, Pers. 6, 34; cf.: Quantulum enim summae curtabit quisque dierum, Hor. S. 2, 3, 124.

curtus.full: curtus, a, um, adj. root in Sanscr. kart, to cut; cf. Germ. kurz, shortened, mutilated, broken, short (class.; most freq. in the poets). Lit.: dolia, pots (chamber vessels), Lucr. 4, 1026; cf. vasa, Juv. 3, 271: pergula, Prop. 4 (5), 5, 70. testa, Mart. 3, 82, 3; cf. testu, Ov. F. 2, 645 al.. calix, Mart. 1 92, 6, : curtum temone jugum, Juv. 10, 135: latus, Mart. 12, 32, 13: Judaei, i. e. circumcised, Hor. S. 1, 9, 70; cf. equus, castrated, Prop. 4 (5), 1, 20. but curto mulo, with shortened tail

curulis.full: cŭrūlis (curr-), e, adj. currus, of or pertaining to a chariot. In gen.: equi, the four horses provided at the public cost for the games of the circus, Liv. 24, 18, 10; cf. Paul. ex Fest. p. 49, 14 Müll.; Cod. Th. 15, 5, 3; 15, 10, 1: ludi, Min. Fel. Oct. 37 fin.: triumphus, i. e. upon a chariot (in opp. to an ovatio, on horseback or on foot), Suet. Aug. 22: Juno curulis, in an ancient form of prayer in Serv. ad Verg. A. 1, 17.— Esp.: sella curulis, the curule chair, official chair, adopted from

curvabilis.full: curvābĭlis, e, adj. curvo, that may be bent, flexible: ulmus et fraxinus, Pall. Nov. 15, 2.

curvamen.full: curvāmen, ĭnis, n. id., a bending, bend, vaulting (not ante-Aug.; perh. first used by Ov.): patriae curvamina ripae, Ov. M. 9, 450; 2, 130; 3, 672: haec (villa) unum sinum molli curvamine amplectitur, Plin. Ep. 9, 7, 4: caeli, of the climate, Gell. 14, 1, 10.

curvatio.full: curvātĭo, ōnis, f. id., a bending (very rare), Col. 4, 12, 2.

curvatura.full: curvātūra, ae, f. id., a bending, rounding, bend (not ante-Aug.). Abstr., Vitr. 2, 8, 11; Plin. 2, 17, 14, § 72; 10, 19, 21, § 42 al.— Concr., a vault: camerae, an arched ceiling, Vitr. 7, 3: rotae, i. e. the rim, Ov. M. 2, 108.

curvesco.full: curvesco, ĕre, v. n., to be crooked, curved, to make a curve (late Lat.): mare curvescens, Amm. 22, 8, 5; Ambros. in Luc. 9, 9; id. de Isaac et An. 7, 60; id. in Psa. 118, 26.

curvitas.full: curvĭtas, ātis, f. curvus, crookedness, Macr. Somn. Scip. 1, 15, 7.

curvo.full: curvo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. id., to crook, bend, bow, curve (not ante-Aug.; v. Orell. ad Cic. N. D. 1, 24, 66). Lit.: curvari manus et aduncos crescere in ungues, Ov. M. 2, 479: bimā cornua fronte (vitulus), Verg. G. 4, 299: trabes, Ov. M. 7, 441; Prop. 3 (4), 22, 38. flexile cornu, Ov. M. 5, 383; 11, 324; cf.: ingentem arcum manu, Stat. Achill. 1, 487: rotundas Curvat aper lances, i. e. by its weight, Hor. S. 2, 4, 41: Calabros sinus (Hadria), id. C. 1, 33, 16: portus curvatus in arcum, Verg. A.

curvor.full: curvor, ōris, m. curvus, crookedness, perh. only in Varr. L. L. 5, § 104, and 7, § 25 Müll.

curvus.full: curvus (-vŏs), a, um, adj. root kar-, whence κορώνη; cf.: circus, varus, crooked, curved, bent (opp. rectus; mostly poet.). Prop.: aratrum, Lucr. 5, 933; 6, 1253; Verg. G. 1, 170: rastri, Cat. 64, 39: culter, Sen. Hippol. 53: falces, Verg. G. 1, 508: calamus, Cat. 63, 22: arbor, Ov. M. 5, 536: arcus, id. ib. 9, 114: dens, id. Am. 3, 10, 14: ungues, Varr. R. R. 2, 9, 4; Hor. Epod. 5, 93: lyra, id. C. 1, 10, 6; 3, 28, 11: crinale, Ov. M. 5, 53: (equi) alvus, Verg. A. 2, 51: carinae, id. G. 1, 360:

cuscolium.full: cuscŏlĭum (-cŭlĭum), ii, n., the scarlet berry of the holm oak, Plin. 16, 8, 12, § 32.
cuscolium.short: cuscŏlĭum (-cŭlĭum), ii, n., the scarlet berry of the holm oak, Plin.

cusinius.full: Cusinius, ii, m., a Roman proper name, Cic. Att. 12, 38, 4; 12, 41, 3.
cusinius.short: Cusinius, ii, m., a Roman proper name, Cic.

cusio.full: cūsĭo, ōnis, f. cudo, a stamping of money, Cod. Th. 11, 16, 18.

cuso.full: cūso, āre, v. freq. [id.], acc. to Prisc. p. 890 P.

cusor.full: cūsor, ōris, m. id., a coiner of money, Cod. Just. 10, 64, 1.

cuspidatim.full: cuspĭdātim, adv. cuspido, to a point, with a point: decisus calamus, Plin. 17, 14, 24, § 102.

cuspido.full: cuspĭdo, no perf., ātum, 1, v. a. cuspis, to make pointed, to point (only in the foll. pass.): hastilia, Plin. 11, 37, 45, § 126; cf. id. 18, 19, 49, § 179.

cuspis.full: cuspis, ĭdis, f. etym. dub., a point, the pointed end of any thing (freq., esp. in the poets). Prop.: asserum, * Caes. B. C. 2, 2: vomeris, Plin. 18, 18, 48, § 172. acuta contorum, Verg. A. 5, 208: acuta teli, Ov. M. 1, 470: hastae, id. ib. 5, 9; 6, 78: jaculi, id. ib. 7, 673: medicata, Sil. 13, 197: aquilae, the pointed end of the standard; Gr. στύραξ, Suet. Caes. 62 et saep.— Meton. (pars pro toto). A spear, javelin, lance, Verg. A. 11, 41; 12, 386; Hor. C. 4, 6, 8; id. S. 2, 1, 14; Ov. M. 6,

cuspius.full: Cuspĭus, ĭi, m., a Roman proper name, Cic. Fam. 13, 6, 1 al.
cuspius.short: Cuspĭus, ĭi, m., a Roman proper name, Cic.

cussiliris.full: cussĭlīris, is, e, adj. root sku-, to cover, hide; cf.: obscurus, scutum, cowardly (an ancient word for ignavus, acc. to Paul. ex Fest. p. 50, 13 Müll.).

custodela.full: custōdēla, ae, f. custos (ante-class. form for custodia; in later Lat. preserved only in the vulgar lang.; cf. Paul. ex Fest. p. 51, 5 Müll.), a watch, guard, care, etc.: qui more antiquo in custodelam suom conmiserunt caput, Plaut. Rud. 3, 2, 10: in custodelam nos tuam ut recipias et tutere, id. ib. 3, 3, 34: (capram) in custodelam simiae concredere, id. Merc. 2, 1, 9: familiam pecuniamque tuam endo mandatelā tutelā custodelāque meā (esse aio), an ancient judicial formula in Gai Inst. 2, § 104

custodia.full: custōdĭa, ae, f. id., a watching, watch, guard, care, protection (freq. and class.). In gen. Lit.: in tuam custodiam meque et meas spes trado, Plaut. Most. 2, 1, 59: agitare custodiam, to keep guard, id. Rud. 3, 6, 20: iis impedimentis custodiae ac praesidio VI. milia hominum unā reliquerunt, Caes. B. G. 2, 29: sub hospitum privatorum custodiā esse, Liv. 42, 19, 5: tam fida canum, Cic. N. D. 2, 63, 158: pastoris, Col. 8, 4, 3: paedagogorum, Quint. 1, 2, 25: dura matrum, care, oversight, Hor. Ep.

custodiarium.full: custōdĭārĭum, ii, n. custos, a watchhouse (late Lat.), Tert. ad Martyr. 2; Inscr. Orell. 1391.

custodiarius.full: custōdĭārĭus, ĭi, m. id., a jailer, Inscr. Orell. 1541.

custodio.full: custōdĭo, īvi, or ĭi, ītum, 4 (fut. pass. custodibitur, Plaut. Capt. 3, 5, 71), v. a. id., to watch, protect, keep, defend, guard (freq. and class.). In gen. With material objects: Q. Caepio Brutus pro consule provinciam Macedoniam, tueatur, defendat, custodiat incolumemque conservet, Cic. Phil. 10, 11, 26: tuum corpus domumque, id. Mil. 25, 67: quod me receperit, juverit, custodierit, id. Planc. 10, 26; cf.: in meā salute custodiendā, id. ib. 1, 1: me non solum amicorum fidelitas, sed etiam uni

custoditio.full: custōdītĭo, ōnis, f. custodio. In gen., guardianship, care: custoditio est opera ad custodiendum quid sumpta, Paul. ex Fest. p. 61, 15.— Transf., a keeping, observance: legum, Vulg. Sap. 6, 19.

custos.full: custos, ōdis, comm. root sku-, to cover, hide, etc.; cf. scutum, κεύθω, Germ. Haut, Haus, Corss. Ausspr. I. p. 353, a guard, watch, preserver, keeper, overseer, protector, defender, attendant, etc., protectress, etc., in a friendly or hostile sense (freq. and class.). In gen. Of living beings. In gen.: antiqua erilis fida custos corporis, Enn. Med. ap. Non. p. 39, 2 (Trag. Rel. v. 289 Vahl.); cf. in masc.: corporis, a body-guard, Liv. 24, 7, 4; so plur., Nep. Dat. 9, 3; Suet. Calig. 55 al.: Comm

cusus.full: Cusus, i, m., a small river in Germania, now prob. the Waag, Tac. A. 2, 63 fin.
cusus.short: Cusus, i, m., a small river in Germania, now prob.

cuticula.full: cŭtīcŭla, ae, f. dim. cutis, the skin, Juv. 11, 203; Pers. 4, 18; on the long ī, v. Prisc. p. 612 P.

cutilia.full: Cŭtĭlĭa, ae, f., an ancient city in the Sabine land, on a lake called Lacus Cutiliae, now Lago di Contigliano, Varr. ap. Plin. 3, 12, 17, § 109; Paul. ex Fest. 51, 8.—Also in plur.: Cŭtĭlĭae, ārum, Liv. 26, 11, 10; Suet. Vesp. 24; Cels. 5, 6; Sen. Q. N. 3, 25, 6; Paul. ex Fest. p. 51, 8 Müll.—Hence, Cŭtĭlĭensis, e, adj.: Lacus, Varr. L. L. 5, § 71 Müll.; Macr. S. 1, 7, 28 sq.; and Cŭtĭlĭus, a, um, adj., of Cutilia: Cutiliae aquae, Plin. 2, 95, 96, § 209; 31, 2, 6, § 10; Cael. Aur. Tard. 3, 2, 45
cutilia.short: Cŭtĭlĭa, ae, f., an ancient city in the Sabine land, on a lake called Lacus Cutiliae, now Lago di Contigliano, Varr.

cutina.full: Cutina, ae, f., a city of the Vestini, Liv. 8, 29, 13.
cutina.short: Cutina, ae, f., a city of the Vestini, Liv.

cutio.full: cŭtĭo, ōnis, m., a small insect, milleped, Marc. Emp. 8.
cutio.short: cŭtĭo, ōnis, m., a small insect, milleped, Marc.

cutis.full: cŭtis, is (acc. cutem, App. Mag. p. 306, 14), f. kindr. with κύτος; Sanscr. gudh; Germ. Haut, the skin. Prop., Planc. ap. Cic. Fam. 10, 18, 3; Cels. 2, 8; Plin. 28, 12, 50, § 183 sq.; Quint. 11, 3, 78; Hor. C. 1, 28, 13; id. A. P. 476; Sen. Ep. 95, 16; 123, 7 al.—In plur., Plin. 6, 31, 36, § 200; 11, 37, 45, § 128.— Prov.: curare cutem, to take care of one's skin, i. e. to make much of one's self, Hor. Ep. 1, 2, 29; 1, 4, 15 (for which pelliculam curare, id. S. 2, 5, 38): cogere aliquem intra su

cuturnium.full: cuturnĭum vas, quo in sacrificiis vinum fundebatur, Paul. ex Fest. p. 51, 1 Müll.
cuturnium.short: cuturnĭum vas, quo in sacrificiis vinum fundebatur, Paul.

cyamias.full: cўămĭas, ae, f. cyamos, the beanstone, a precious stone, Plin. 37, 11, 73, § 188.

cyamos.full: cўămŏs or -us, i, m., = κύαμος, a plant, called also colocasia, Egyptian bean, Plin. 21, 15, 51, § 87.
cyamos.short: cўămŏs or -us, i, m., = κύαμος, a plant, called also colocasia, Egyptian bean, Plin.

cyane.full: Cўănē, ēs, f., = Κυάνη, a fountain near Syracuse, Plin. 3, 8, 14, § 89; Ov. F. 4, 469; id. P. 2, 10, 26.—In fable, a nymph changed into this fountain for her grief at the loss of Proserpine, Ov. M. 5, 409 sq.; Sil. 14, 515; Claud. Rapt. Pros. 3, 245.
cyane.short: Cўănē, ēs, f., = Κυάνη, a fountain near Syracuse, Plin.

cyaneae.full: Cȳănĕae, ārum, f., v. cyaneus, II.

cyanee.full: Cȳănĕē, ēs, f., = Κυανέη, a nymph, daughter of Mæander, mother of Caunus and of Byblis, Ov. M. 9, 452.
cyanee.short: Cȳănĕē, ēs, f., = Κυανέη, a nymph, daughter of Mæander, mother of Caunus and of Byblis, Ov.

cyaneus.full: cȳănĕus, a, um, adj., = κυάνεος. Dark-blue, sea-blue: cyaneo colore avis, Plin. 10, 32, 47, § 89: stagna, Prud. Psych. 858.— Cȳănĕae, ārum, f., = Κυάνεαι, the two small rocky islands at the entrance of the Pontus Euxinus, called also Symplegades, q. v., Ov. Tr. 1, 10, 34; Mel. 2, 7, 3: errantes, Val. Fl. 4, 561.—Hence, Cȳă-nĕus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to the Cyaneæ: cautes, Luc. 2, 716: montes, Val. Fl. 2, 381: rupes, id. 4, 637: ruinae, Mart. 7, 19, 3: insulae, Mel. 2, 7, 3; Plin. 4, 13,

cyanos.full: cўănŏs or -us, i, m., = κύανος. The blue corn-flower, blue-bottle: Centaurea cyanus, Linn.; Plin. 21, 8, 24, § 48; 21, 11, 39, § 68.— A precious stone, a species of lapis lazuli, Plin. 37, 9, 38, § 119.

cyathisso.full: cўăthisso, āre, v. n., = κυαθίζω, to fill a cyathus, Plaut. Men. 2, 2, 29; Macr. de Diff. 41, 8; Auct. de Verb. 8, § 14 Jan.

cyathus.full: cўăthus, i, m., = κύαθος, a small ladle for transferring the wine from the mixing-bowl (crater) to the drinking-cup (cf. Becker, Gall. 3, p. 221). Prop., Varr. L. L. 5, § 124 Müll.; Plaut. Stich. 5, 4, 24; id. Ps. 4, 2, 2; Hor. S. 1, 6, 117; Juv. 9, 47; Suet. Caes. 49 al.— As a measure, both dry and liquid (particularly for wine), the twelfth part of a sextarius, Hor. C. 3, 8, 13; 3, 19, 12; Plin. 14, 9, 11, § 85; or ten Greek drachmæ, Plin. 21, 34, 109, § 185; cf. Rhemn. Fann. Pond. 80.
cyathus.short: cўăthus, i, m., = κύαθος, a small ladle for transferring the wine from the mixing-bowl (crater) to the drinking-cup (cf.

cybaeus.full: cўbaeus, a, um, adj. κύπη, κυβή, cupa, pertaining to a kind of merchantship: navis maxima, Cic. Verr. 2, 5, 17, § 44.—Absol.: cўbaea, ae, f., a transport or merchant-ship, Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 8, § 17.

cybele.full: Cўbĕlē or Cўbēbē, ēs, and Cўbĕ-lă, ae, f., = Κυβέλη and Κυβήβη. A goddess, originally Phrygian, later worshipped in Rome also as Ops or Mater Magna, whose priests were called Galli. Form Cybele, Cat. 63, 8; Verg. A. 11, 768; Mart. 1, 71, 10.— Form Cybela, Tert. adv. Nat. 1, 10.— Form Cybebe, Verg. A. 10, 220; Prop. 3, 17 (4, 16), 35; Phaedr. 3, 17, 3; Sil. 8, 365; 17, 3; Cat. 63, 9; Phaedr. 3, 17, 4; 4, 1, 4; Luc. 1, 600.— Hence, Cўbĕ-lēĭus, a, um, adj., pertaining to Cybele: Attis, Ov. M. 10, 1
cybele.short: Cўbĕlē or Cўbēbē, ēs, and Cўbĕ-lă, ae, f., = Κυβέλη and Κυβήβη.

cybiarius.full: cўbĭārĭus, ii, m. cybium, a dealer in salt fish, Arn. 2, p. 70 dub.

cybindis.full: cўbindis (cўmin-), ĭdis, m., = κύβινδις, the night hawk: nocturnus accipiter cybindis vocatur, Plin. 10, 8, 10, § 24.
cybindis.short: cўbindis (cўmin-), ĭdis, m., = κύβινδις, the night hawk: nocturnus accipiter cybindis vocatur, Plin.

cybiosactes.full: Cўbĭŏsactes, ae, m., = Κυβιοσάκτης, a dealer in salt fish; nickname of the thirteenth Ptolemy, and later of the emperor Vespasian, Suét. Vesp. 19.
cybiosactes.short: Cўbĭŏsactes, ae, m., = Κυβιοσάκτης, a dealer in salt fish;

cybistra.full: Cybistra, ōrum, n., a town of Cappadocia, Cic. Fam. 15, 2, 2 and 4; id. Att. 5, 18, 1 al.
cybistra.short: Cybistra, ōrum, n., a town of Cappadocia, Cic.

cybium.full: cўbĭum or -ĭon, ii, n., = κύβιον. A tunny-fish, Varr. L. L. 5, § 77 Müll.; Mart. 11, 27, 3; cf. Paul. ex Fest. p. 52, 15 Müll.— Meton., a dish made of pieces of the tunny-fish salted and chopped, Plin. 9, 15, 18, § 48; 32, 11, 53, § 151; Mart. 5, 79, 3.

cyceon.full: cўcĕōn, ōnis, m., = κυκεών, a drink made of barley-grits, grated goats'-cheese, and wine, Arn. 5, p. 174 sq.
cyceon.short: cўcĕōn, ōnis, m., = κυκεών, a drink made of barley-grits, grated goats'-cheese, and wine, Arn.

cychramus.full: cychrămus, i, m., = κύχραμος, a bird migrating with quails, perh. the ortolan, Plin. 10, 23, 33, §§ 66 and 68.
cychramus.short: cychrămus, i, m., = κύχραμος, a bird migrating with quails, perh.

cycladatus.full: cyclădātus, i, m., adj. cyclas, clothed with a cyclas, Suet. Calig. 52.

cyclaminos.full: cyclămīnŏs, i, f. (-on, i, n., Plin. 21, 9, 27, § 51; 21, 11, 38, § 64), = κυκλάμῖνος and κυκλάμι^νον, the plant sowbread: Cyclamen Europaeum, Linn.; of several kinds, Plin. 25, 9, 67, § 114 sq.

cyclas.full: cȳclas, ădis, f., = κυκλάς (circular; hence as in Greek; cf. Liddell and Scott in h. v. l.), a state-robe of women, with a border running round it, Prop. 4 (5), 7, 40. Juv. 6, 259; Vop. Sat. 9; Lampr. Alex. Sev. 41, 1; Serv. ad Verg. A. 1, 649 al.— Cȳclădes, um, f., = Κυκλάδες, the Cyclades, islands lying in a circle round Delos, in the Ægean Sea, off the coast of the Peloponnesus, Mel. 2, 7, 11; Plin. 4, 12, 22, § 65 sq.; Caes. B. C. 3, 3; Nep. Milt. 2, 5; Liv. 34, 26, 11; Verg. A. 3, 127; Ov.

cyclicus.full: cўclĭcus, a, um, adj., = κυκλικός, prop. circular; hence, Cyclicus scriptor, a cyclic poet, one of the epic poets who treated in regular order the cycle of myths from the beginning of the world to the time of Telemachus, Hor. A. P. 136: cyclica carmina, cyclic poems, Isid. Orig. 6, 17, 4; cf. Liddell and Scott, s. v. κυκλικός, II.— Forming a complete cycle, encyclopædic: disciplinae, Mart. Cap. 9, § 998.
cyclicus.short: cўclĭcus, a, um, adj., = κυκλικός, prop.

cyclophoreticus.full: cȳ^clŏphŏrētĭcus, a, um, adj., = κυκλοφορητικός, moved in a circle, circular: cyma, Mart. Cap. 8, p. 275 (written as Greek by Kopp, § 814).
cyclophoreticus.short: cȳ^clŏphŏrētĭcus, a, um, adj., = κυκλοφορητικός, moved in a circle, circular: cyma, Mart.

cyclops.full: Cȳ^clops, ōpis (acc. -ōpem or -ōpa), m., = Κύκλωψ (a round eye), a Cyclops; in plur.: Cyclopes, um, the Cyclopes, a fabulous race of giants on the coast of Sicily; said to have each but one eye, and that in the middle of the forehead; to them were ascribed the walls called Cyclopean; plur., Cic. Div. 2, 19, 43; Plin. 7, 56, 57, §§ 195-198; Verg. A. 6, 630; 8, 424; Hor. C. 1, 4, 7; Ov. M. 3, 305 et saep.; sing. κατʼ ἐξοχήν, the Cyclops Polyphemus, Verg. A. 3, 617; Hor. A. P. 145; Ov. M. 13, 744 s

cyclus.full: cȳ^clus, i, m., = κύκλος, a circle. Lit.: cycli axium, Isid. Orig. 3, 36.— Transf. Astron. t. t., a cycle, recurring period: paschalis, the Easter cycle of ninety-five years, Isid. Orig. 6, 17, 1: lunae, the lunar cycle of nineteen years, id. ib. 6, 17, 5.— Med. t. t., a periodic change, a recurrence: resumptionis, Cael. Aur. Tard. 1, 1, 21: metasyncriticus, id. ib. 1, 1, 24; cf.: cyclo curare, Veg. Art. Vet. 5, 5, 3; 3, 6, 1.— An instrument for branding, Veg. Vet. 2, 5, 3; 2, 6, 11.
cyclus.short: cȳ^clus, i, m., = κύκλος, a circle.

cycnarium.full: cȳ^cnārĭum, ĭi, n. κύκνος, a kind of eye-salve, Inscr. Orell. 4234.

cycneius.full: Cȳcnēïus (Cȳgn-), a, um, adj., of or pertaining to the Boeotian Cycnus, the son of Hyrie: Tempe, in Bœotia, Ov. M. 7, 371.
cycneius.short: Cȳcnēïus (Cȳgn-), a, um, adj., of or pertaining to the Boeotian Cycnus, the son of Hyrie: Tempe, in Bœotia, Ov.

cycneus.full: cȳcnēus (cȳgn-), a, um, adj., = κύκνειος. Of or belonging to a swan, swan's-: tamquam cycnea vox et oratio, i. e. the last speech, Cic. de Or. 3, 2, 6: plumae, Ov. Tr. 4, 8, 1.— Cȳcnēa (al. Cygnaea) Specula, a hill near Brixia, now still Cigneo, Cat. 67, 32.

cycnus1.full: cȳ^cnus (in MSS. and edd. freq. also cȳ^gnus; y, Hor. C. 4, 3, 20; Aus. Ep. 20, 8), i, m., = κύκνος, the swan; celebrated for its singing, esp. for its dying song; consecrated to Apollo, Cic. Tusc. 1, 30, 73; Plin. 10, 23, 32, § 63; Lucr. 4, 181; 4, 910; Verg. E. 7, 38; id. A. 1, 393; Ov. M. 5, 387; Hor. C. 4, 3, 20 et saep.; attached to the chariot of Venus, Ov. M. 10, 708; id. A. A. 3, 809.— Prov.: quid contendat hirundo cycnis? Lucr. 3, 7; so also: certent cycnis ululae, Verg. E. 8, 55.— Meto

cycnus2.full: Cȳ^cnus (Cȳ^g-), i, m. A king of the Ligurians, son of Sthenelus, related to Phæton, who was changed to a swan and placed among the stars, Ov. M. 2, 367; Verg. A. 10, 189; cf. Hyg. Fab. 154; id. Astr. 3, 7. — A son of Neptune and Calyce; he was father of Tenes, and was changed into a swan, Ov. M. 12, 72 sq., cf. Hyg. Fab. 157.† † cўdărum, i, n., = κύδαρος, a sort of ship, acc. to Gell. 10, 25, 5.

cydippe.full: Cȳdippē, ēs, f., = Κυδίππη. The mistress of Acontius, Ov. H. 20; 21; id. A. A. 1, 457.— A Nereid, Verg. G. 4, 339; Hyg. Fab. praef.

cydnos.full: Cydnŏs or Cydnus, i, m., = Κύδνος, a river in Cilicia, famed for its cold and tonic waters, now Kara - Su or Tersustschai, Mel. 1, 13, 1; Plin. 5, 27, 22, § 92; Cic. Phil. 2, 11, 26; Vitr. 8, 3, 6; Curt. 3, 4, 7 sq.; 3, 5, 1 sqq.; Tib. 1, 7, 13 al.
cydnos.short: Cydnŏs or Cydnus, i, m., = Κύδνος, a river in Cilicia, famed for its cold and tonic waters, now Kara - Su or Tersustschai, Mel.

cydonia.full: Cўdōnĭa or Cўdōnēa, ae, f., = Κυδωνία, an ancient and celebrated town on the north coast of Crete, now Canea, Mel. 2, 7, 12; Plin. 4, 12, 20, § 59 Sillig N. cr.; Flor. 3, 7, 4.— Hence, Cўdon, ōnis, m. A Cydonian, Verg. A. 12, 858.— A son of Phorcus, Verg. A. 10, 325.—In plur., Luc. 7, 229.— Cўdō-nĭus, a, um, adj., Cydonian: spicula, poet. for Cretan, Verg. E. 10, 59; cf. arcus, Hor. C. 4, 9, 17.—So esp. freq. Cydonia (and Latinized cotonia, cotonea) mala; also absol.: cўdōnĭa (cŏtōnĭa, cŏtōnĕa),
cydonia.short: Cўdōnĭa or Cўdōnēa, ae, f., = Κυδωνία, an ancient and celebrated town on the north coast of Crete, now Canea, Mel.

cygneius.full: Cȳgnēïus, Cȳgnēus, and Cȳ^gnus, v. Cycn-.

cylindratus.full: cўlindrātus, a, um, adj. cylindrus, in the form of a cylinder, cylindrical: siliquae, Plin. 18, 12, 33, § 125.

cylindrus.full: cўlindrus, dri, m., = κύλινδρος, a cylinder. Prop., Cic. N. D. 1, 10, 24; id. Fat. 19, 41.— Meton. A cylindrical stone for levelling the ground, a roller, etc., Cato, R. R. 129; Verg. G. 1, 178; Plin. 19, 8, 46, § 158; Vitr. 10, 6 al.— A precious stone ground off in the form of a cylinder, Plin. 37, 5, 20, § 78; 37, 8, 34, § 113; Juv. 2, 61 al.
cylindrus.short: cўlindrus, dri, m., = κύλινδρος, a cylinder.

cyllaros.full: Cyllărŏs or -us, i, m., = Κύλλαρος. A Centaur, Ov. M. 12, 393 and 408.— The horse of Pollux, given to him by Juno, Verg. G. 3, 90; Stat. Th. 6, 327; Val. Fl. 1, 426; cf. Mart. 8, 21, 5; 8, 28, 8.

cyllene.full: Cyllēnē, ēs and ae, f., = Κυλλήνη. A high mountain in the north-eastern part of Arcadia, on which, acc. to the myth, Mercury was born and brought up; hence, consecrated to him, now Zyria, Plin. 10, 30, 45, § 87; Ov. F. 2, 276; 5, 87; Verg. A. 8, 139. — Hence, Cyllēnĭus, a, um, adj., Cyllenian: mons, Mel. 2, 3, 5: proles, i. e. Mercury, Verg. A. 4, 258; in this sense also subst.: Cyllēnĭus, ĭi, m., Verg. A. 4, 252; 4, 276; Ov. M. 1, 713; 2, 720 et saep.— Of or pertaining to Mercury: proles, i. e.
cyllene.short: Cyllēnē, ēs and ae, f., = Κυλλήνη.

cylonius.full: Cўlōnīus or -ēus, a, um, adj., = Κυλώνειος, pertaining to Cylon, the well-known Athenian: scelus = ἄγος Κυλώνειον, the crime committed by the murder of Cylon's partisans at the altar of Athene, where they had sought asylum, Cic. Leg. 2, 11, 28.
cylonius.short: Cўlōnīus or -ēus, a, um, adj., = Κυλώνειος, pertaining to Cylon, the well-known Athenian: scelus = ἄγος Κυλώνειον, the crime committed by the murder of Cylon's partisans at the altar of Athene, where they had sought asylum, Cic.

cyma.full: cȳma (cūma), ătis, n., and ae, f., = κῦμα, a young sprout of a cabbage; neutr., Lucil. ap. Non. p. 195, 5; Col. 10, 129; fem., id. 11, 3, 24; 12, 54, 3; Plin. 19, 8, 41, § 137 sq.; 20, 9, 35, § 90 al.— A hollow sphere, spherical layer, stratum: quarum (naturarum) circa ... centron, aquae primum, aërisque sequens, tertium ignis cyma commemorant, Mart. Cap. 8, § 814 Kopp ad loc.; cf. the context.
cyma.short: cȳma (cūma), ătis, n., and ae, f., = κῦμα, a young sprout of a cabbage;

cymaeus.full: Cȳmaeus, a, um, v. 1. Cyme, II.

cymatium.full: cȳmătĭum (cūm-) or -on, ii, n., = κυμάτιον (a small wave); in architecture, The volute of an Ionic column, Vitr. 3, 5, 7; 4, 1, 7.— A channel, a waved moulding, an ogee, Vitr. 3, 5, 10; 4, 3, 6; 4, 3, 8; 4, 6, 2; Tert. Idol. 8.
cymatium.short: cȳmătĭum (cūm-) or -on, ii, n., = κυμάτιον (a small wave);

cymba.full: cymba (cumba), ae, f., = κύμβη, a boat, skiff, first used by the Phœnicians, Plin. 7, 55, 57, § 208; Afran. in Non. p. 535, 31; Cic. Off. 3, 14, 59; Ov. M. 1, 293; id. F. 6, 777 al.—In partic., the boat of Charon which transported the dead, Verg. A. 6, 303; Hor. C. 2, 3, 28; Prop. 3 (4), 18, 24; Stat. S. 2, 1, 186.— Trop.: non est ingenii cymba gravanda tui, i. e. meddle not with themes above your powers, Prop. 3, 3 (4, 2), 22; cf. Ov. A. A. 3, 26; Quint. 12, 10, 37.
cymba.short: cymba (cumba), ae, f., = κύμβη, a boat, skiff, first used by the Phœnicians, Plin.

cymbalaris.full: cymbălāris, is, f., a plant, also called cotyledon, App. Herb. 43.
cymbalaris.short: cymbălāris, is, f., a plant, also called cotyledon, App.

cymbalicus.full: cymbălĭcus, a, um, adj., = κυμβαλικός, pertaining to a cymbal: voces, Ven. Carm. 2, 10 fin.
cymbalicus.short: cymbălĭcus, a, um, adj., = κυμβαλικός, pertaining to a cymbal: voces, Ven.

cymbalisso.full: cymbălisso, āre, v. n., = κυμβαλίζω, to strike the cymbals, Cass. Hem. ap. Non. p. 90, 25.

cymbalista.full: cymbălista, ae, m., = κυμβαλιστἠς, a cymbal-player, App. de Deo Socr. p. 49, 18.
cymbalista.short: cymbălista, ae, m., = κυμβαλιστἠς, a cymbal-player, App.

cymbalistria.full: cymbălistrĭa, ae, f., = κυμβαλίστρια, a female cymbal-player, Petr. 22 fin.; Inscr. Orell. 2449 sq.
cymbalistria.short: cymbălistrĭa, ae, f., = κυμβαλίστρια, a female cymbal-player, Petr.

cymbalitis.full: cymbălītis, is, f., = κυμβαλῖτις, sc. herba, = cymbalaris, Marc. Emp. 14.

cymbalum.full: cymbălum, i, n. (gen. plur. cymbalum, Cat. 63, 21), = κύμβαλον, a cymbal. Prop., an instrument consisting of two hollow plates of brass, which emit a ringing sound when struck together. They were used in the festivals of Cybele and Bacchus, and on other festive occasions; also to hinder the flight of bees, etc. (usu. in plur.), Lucr. 2, 619; Cat. 63, 21; 63, 29; Ov. F. 4, 213; Verg. G. 4, 64; Liv. 39, 8; Cic. Pis. 9, 20 sq.; Plin. 5, 1, 1, § 7; Quint. 11, 3, 59; Plin. Ep. 2, 14, 13.— Transf., in

cymbium.full: cymbĭum, ii, n., = κυμβίον, a small drinking-vessel, a cup, bowl, Varr. ap. Non. p. 545, 28; Verg. A. 3, 66; 5, 267; Mart. 8, 6, 2; cf. Macr. S. 5, 21; Paul. ex Fest. p. 51, 10 Müll.— A lamp in the same form, App. M. 11, p. 261. 40.
cymbium.short: cymbĭum, ii, n., = κυμβίον, a small drinking-vessel, a cup, bowl, Varr.

cymbula.full: cymbŭla, ae, f. dim. cymba, a small boat, Plin. Ep. 8, 20, 7.

cyme1.full: Cȳmē, ēs, f., = Κύμη, a town of Æolis, near the mod. Sanderli or Sandarlio, Mel. 1, 18, 1; Plin. 5, 30, 32, § 121; Nep. Alcib. 7, 1; Liv. 37, 11, 15; Vell. 1, 4, 4; Tac. A. 2, 47.— Hence, Cȳmaeus, a, um, adj., of Cyme: Athenagoras, Cic. Fl. 7, 17: fundus, id. ib. 20, 46: Antigonus, Varr. R. R. 1, 1, 8; Col. 1, 1, 9.—In plur.: Cȳmaei, ōrum, m., inhabitants of Cyme, Liv. 38, 39, 8.
cyme1.short: Cȳmē, ēs, f., = Κύμη, a town of Æolis, near the mod.

cymine.full: Cymīnē, ēs, f., a town in Thessaly, Liv. 32, 13, 10.
cymine.short: Cymīnē, ēs, f., a town in Thessaly, Liv.

cymodoce.full: Cȳmŏdŏcē, ēs, or Cȳmŏdŏcēa, ae, f., a Nereid, Verg. A. 5, 826; 10, 225; Hyg. Fab. praef.
cymodoce.short: Cȳmŏdŏcē, ēs, or Cȳmŏdŏcēa, ae, f., a Nereid, Verg.

cymosus.full: cȳmōsus, a, um, adj. cyma, full of shoots: stirps, Col. 10, 138.

cymothoe.full: Cȳmŏthŏē, ēs, f., = Κυμοθόη. A Nereid, Verg. A. 1, 144; Prop. 2 (3), 26, 16; Sil. 3, 58 al.— A fountain in Achaia, Plin. 4, 5, 6, § 13.

cymula.full: cўmŭla, ae, f. dim. cyma, a tender sprout: coriandri, Plin. Val. 1, 44.

cyna.full: cyna, ae, f., a tree in Arabia that produced cotton: Bombax ceiba, Linn.; Plin. 12, 11, 22, § 39.
cyna.short: cyna, ae, f., a tree in Arabia that produced cotton: Bombax ceiba, Linn.;

cynacantha.full: cўnăcantha, ae, f., = κυνάκανθα, dog-thorn, dog-rose; perh. Rosa canina, Linn.; Plin. 11, 35, 41, § 118.
cynacantha.short: cўnăcantha, ae, f., = κυνάκανθα, dog-thorn, dog-rose;

cynaegirus.full: Cўnaegīrus, i, m., = Κυναίγειρος, an Athenian, famous for his valor in the battle of Marathon, Just. 2, 9, 16; Suet. Caes. 68.
cynaegirus.short: Cўnaegīrus, i, m., = Κυναίγειρος, an Athenian, famous for his valor in the battle of Marathon, Just.

cynamolgi.full: Cўnămolgi, ōrum, m., = Κυναμολγοί (dog-milkers), a wild tribe of Ethiopia, Plin. 6, 30, 35, § 195.
cynamolgi.short: Cўnămolgi, ōrum, m., = Κυναμολγοί (dog-milkers), a wild tribe of Ethiopia, Plin.

cynanche.full: cўnanchē, ēs, f., = κυνάγχη, an inflammation of the throat, which caused the tongue to be thrust out, Cael. Aur. Acut. 3, 1, 3.
cynanche.short: cўnanchē, ēs, f., = κυνάγχη, an inflammation of the throat, which caused the tongue to be thrust out, Cael.

cynapes.full: Cўnāpes, ae, m., a river which empties into the Euxine, Ov. P. 4, 10, 49.
cynapes.short: Cўnāpes, ae, m., a river which empties into the Euxine, Ov.

cynegetica.full: Cўnēgĕtĭca, ōrum, n. ( = τὰ κυνηγετικά, from κυνηγετικός, venaticus, pertaining to the chase), Cynegetics, the name given to poems on hunting by Gratius Faliscus and Nemesianus in Latin, and by Oppianus in Greek.

cyneus.full: Cўnēus, a, um, adj., = Κύνειος (of Dogs): mare, the Hellespont, Hyg. Fab. 111; 243.
cyneus.short: Cўnēus, a, um, adj., = Κύνειος (of Dogs): mare, the Hellespont, Hyg.

cynice2.full: Cўnĭcē, ēs, f., = Κυνική, the Cynic sect, Aus. Epigr. 27.
cynice2.short: Cўnĭcē, ēs, f., = Κυνική, the Cynic sect, Aus.

cynicus.full: Cўnĭcus, i, m., = κυνικός (doglike). Subst., a Cynic philosopher, a Cynic, Cic. de Or. 3, 17, 62; id. Fin. 3, 20, 68; Hor. Ep. 1, 17, 18; Juv. 13, 121: nudi dolia, i. e. of Diogenes, id. 14, 309.—Hence, adj.: Cўnĭcus, a, um, Cynic: institutio, Tac. A. 16, 34: cena, Petr. 14; and in * adv.: Cўnĭcē, after the manner of the Cynics, Plaut. Stich. 5, 4, 22.— Suffering by σπασμὸς κυνικός, spasmodic distortion, Plin. 25, 5, 24, § 60; cf. Cels. 4, 2, 2.

cyniola.full: cўnĭŏla, ae, f., a kind of lettuce, Veg. Art. Vet. 3, 4, 29.
cyniola.short: cўnĭŏla, ae, f., a kind of lettuce, Veg.

cynismus.full: cўnismus, i, m., = κυνισμός, Cynical philosophy or conduct, Cassiod. Hist. Eccl. 7, 2.
cynismus.short: cўnismus, i, m., = κυνισμός, Cynical philosophy or conduct, Cassiod.

cynocardamon.full: cўnŏcardămon, i, n., = κυνοκάρδαμον, a kind of nasturtium, App. Herb. 20.
cynocardamon.short: cўnŏcardămon, i, n., = κυνοκάρδαμον, a kind of nasturtium, App.

cynocauma.full: cўnŏcauma, ătis, n., = κυνόκαυμα, the heat of the dog-days, Plin. Val. 3, 14.
cynocauma.short: cўnŏcauma, ătis, n., = κυνόκαυμα, the heat of the dog-days, Plin.

cynocephalea.full: cўnŏcĕphălēa (-līa), ae, f. (cўnŏ-cĕphălĭon, ii, n., App. Herb. 87), = κυνοκεφάλαιον, dog's-head, a magical plant, called also osiritis, Plin. 30, 2, 6, § 18.

cynocephalus.full: cўnŏcĕphălus, i, m., = κυνοκέφαλος. An ape with a dog's head (in Africa): Simia inuus, Linn.; Plin. 6, 30, 35, § 190; 8, 54, 80, § 216; 37, 9, 40, § 124; Cic. Att. 6, 1, 25.— The dog-headed Anubis, Tert. Apol. 6.— A kind of wild man, Isid. Orig. 11, 3, 15; 12, 2, 32.

cynodon.full: cўnŏdon, ontis, adj., having pairs of projecting teeth, Isid. Orig. 11, 3, 7 al.
cynodon.short: cўnŏdon, ontis, adj., having pairs of projecting teeth, Isid.

cynoglossos.full: cўnŏglōssŏs, i, f., = κυνόγλωσσον, hound's-tongue, a plant. Cynoglossum officinale, Linn.; Plin. 25, 8, 41, § 81.— Another kind producing small burs, Plin. 25, 8, 41, § 81 fin.
cynoglossos.short: cўnŏglōssŏs, i, f., = κυνόγλωσσον, hound's-tongue, a plant.

cynoides.full: cўnŏīdes, is, n., = κυνοειδές (doglike), another name of the plant psyllion, Plin. 25, 11, 90, § 140.
cynoides.short: cўnŏīdes, is, n., = κυνοειδές (doglike), another name of the plant psyllion, Plin.

cynomazon.full: cўnŏmāzon, i, n., dog - bread, a plant, App. Herb. 109.
cynomazon.short: cўnŏmāzon, i, n., dog - bread, a plant, App.

cynomorion.full: cўnŏmŏrĭon, ii, n., = κυνομόριον, a plant, broom-rape, also called orobanche, Plin. 22, 25, 80, § 162.
cynomorion.short: cўnŏmŏrĭon, ii, n., = κυνομόριον, a plant, broom-rape, also called orobanche, Plin.

cynomyia.full: cўnŏmyia, ae, f., = κυνόμυια, the herb fleabane, Plin. 25, 11, 90, § 140.
cynomyia.short: cўnŏmyia, ae, f., = κυνόμυια, the herb fleabane, Plin.

cynophanes.full: cўnŏphănes, um, m., = κυνοφανεῖς = cynocephali, men with dogs' heads, Tert. Apol. 8.
cynophanes.short: cўnŏphănes, um, m., = κυνοφανεῖς = cynocephali, men with dogs' heads, Tert.

cynops.full: cўnops, ōpis, f., = κύνωψ, a plant, dog's-eye, Plin. 21, 17, 61, § 101.
cynops.short: cўnops, ōpis, f., = κύνωψ, a plant, dog's-eye, Plin.

cynorrodon.full: cўnorrŏdon (-rhŏd-), i, n., and -da, ae, f., = κυνόρροδον. The dog-rose: Rosa canina, Linn. Form -oda, Plin. 8, 41, 63, § 152; 24, 13, 74, § 121.—Form -odon, Plin. 29, 4, 30, § 94; 25, 2, 6, §§ 17 and 18 al. — The blossom of the red lily: cynorrodon, Plin. 21, 5, 11, § 24.
cynorrodon.short: cўnorrŏdon (-rhŏd-), i, n., and -da, ae, f., = κυνόρροδον.

cynos1.full: Cȳnŏs (-nŭs), i, f., = Κῦνος, a harbor of Locris, at the northern end of the Opuntian bay, Liv. 28, 6, 12; Mel. 2, 3, 4.
cynos1.short: Cȳnŏs (-nŭs), i, f., = Κῦνος, a harbor of Locris, at the northern end of the Opuntian bay, Liv.

cynosarges.full: Cўnŏsarges, is, n., a gymnasium near Athens sacred to Hercules, Liv. 31, 24, 18.
cynosarges.short: Cўnŏsarges, is, n., a gymnasium near Athens sacred to Hercules, Liv.

cynosbatos.full: cўnosbătŏs, i, f., = κυνόσβατος. The dog-rose or wild-brier, Plin. 16, 37, 71, § 179; Col. 11, 3, 4; App. Herb. 87.— Cynosbatos, also called cynapanxis or neurospastos, the black currant: Ribes nigrum, Linn.; Plin. 24, 14, 74, § 121; also called cўnospastos (κυνόσπαστος), id. ib.— The caper - bush: Capparis spinosa, Linn.; Plin. 13, 23, 44, § 127.

cynoscephalae.full: Cўnoscĕphălae, ārum, f., = Κυνὸς κεφαλαί (dog's-heads), name of two hills near Scotussa in Thessaly, Liv. 33, 7, 3; 33, 16, 1; 36, 8, 3.
cynoscephalae.short: Cўnoscĕphălae, ārum, f., = Κυνὸς κεφαλαί (dog's-heads), name of two hills near Scotussa in Thessaly, Liv.

cynos2.full: cўnos dexia, ae, f., = κυνὸς δεξιά, a sea-polypus, Plin. 32, 11, 53, § 147.
cynos2.short: cўnos dexia, ae, f., = κυνὸς δεξιά, a sea-polypus, Plin.

cynosorchis.full: cўnŏsorchis, is, f., = κυνόσορχις, hound's-cod, a plant, Plin. 27, 8, 42, § 65.
cynosorchis.short: cўnŏsorchis, is, f., = κυνόσορχις, hound's-cod, a plant, Plin.

cynossema.full: Cўnossēma, ātis, n., = κυνὸς σῆμα, a promontory of the Thracian Chersonese where Hecuba was buried, Plin. 4, 11, 18, § 49; Mel. 2, 2, 7; Sol. 10, 22; Mart. Cap. 6, § 658; cf. Ov. M. 13, 570.
cynossema.short: Cўnossēma, ātis, n., = κυνὸς σῆμα, a promontory of the Thracian Chersonese where Hecuba was buried, Plin.

cynosura1.full: Cўnŏsūra, ae, f., = Κυνόσουρα (hound's-tail). The constellation at the north pole, the Cynosura, or Lesser Bear, Cic. Ac. 2, 20, 66; id. poët. N. D. 2, 41, 105 and 106; Caes. Germ. Arat. 187; Ov. F. 3, 107 al.—Hence, Cўnŏsūris, ĭdis, f. adj., of or pertaining to the Cynosura: Ursa, the Lesser Bear, Ov. Tr. 5, 3, 7: cauda, Caes. Germ. Arat. 189.— A town in Arcadia, Stat. Th. 4, 295.

cynosura2.full: cўnŏsūra ōva = κυνόσουρα ὠά, addle-eggs, Plin. 10, 60, 80, § 167 (id. 10, 58, 79, § 160, called also hypenemia or zephyria ova, wind-eggs, in pure Lat. urina ova).
cynosura2.short: cўnŏsūra ōva = κυνόσουρα ὠά, addle-eggs, Plin.

cynosurae.full: Cўnŏsūrae, ārum, f., = Κυνόσουρα, a promontory in Attica, west of Marathon, now Schoinia, or Cap Cabala, Cic. N. D. 3, 22, 57; Lact. 1, 10, 12.
cynosurae.short: Cўnŏsūrae, ārum, f., = Κυνόσουρα, a promontory in Attica, west of Marathon, now Schoinia, or Cap Cabala, Cic.

cynozolon.full: cўnozŏlon, i, n., = κυνόζολον, a plant, called also chamaeleon and ulophonon, prob. Chamaeleon niger, Linn.; Plin. 22, 18, 21, § 47.
cynozolon.short: cўnozŏlon, i, n., = κυνόζολον, a plant, called also chamaeleon and ulophonon, prob.

cynthus.full: Cynthus, i, m., = Κύνθος, a mountain of Delos, celebrated as the birthplace of Apollo and Diana, now Montecintio, Plin. 4, 12, 22, § 66; Ov. M. 2, 221; 6, 204 al.— Hence, Cynthĭus, a, um, adj., of or pertaining to Cynthus, Cynthian: mons, Plin. 4, 12, 22, § 66 Sillig.—As subst., Cynthĭus, ii, m., the Cynthian god, i. e. Apollo, Prop. 2 (3), 34, 80; Hor. C. 1, 21, 2; Ov. F. 3, 346 al.— Cynthĭa, ae, f., the Cynthian goddess, i. e. Diana, Hor. C. 3, 28, 12; Ov. M. 2, 465; 7, 755; id. F. 2, 91 al.—
cynthus.short: Cynthus, i, m., = Κύνθος, a mountain of Delos, celebrated as the birthplace of Apollo and Diana, now Montecintio, Plin.

cyparissa.full: Cўpărissa (-ia), ae, f., a town in Messenia, now Arkadhia, Plin. 4, 5, 7, § 15; Liv. 32, 21; called also Cўpărissae, ārum, Mel. 2, 3, 9.—Hence, Cўpărissĭus, a, um, adj., of or pertaining to Cyparissa: sinus, Gulf of Arkadhia, Plin. l. l.; Mel. l. l.
cyparissa.short: Cўpărissa (-ia), ae, f., a town in Messenia, now Arkadhia, Plin.

cyparissiae.full: cўpărissĭae, ārum, f., a kind of fiery meteors, Sen. Q. N. 1, 15, 4; Paul. ex Fest. p. 51, 13 Müll. (Cyparissae, id. ib. p. 64, 2).
cyparissiae.short: cўpărissĭae, ārum, f., a kind of fiery meteors, Sen.

cyparissias.full: cўpărissĭas, ae, m., a species of tithymalus, Plin. 26, 8, 43, § 70.
cyparissias.short: cўpărissĭas, ae, m., a species of tithymalus, Plin.

cyparissifer.full: cўpărissĭfer, fĕri, m. adj. cyparissus-fero, cypress-bearing: Lycaeus, Sid. Carm. 23, 417.

cyparissius.full: Cўpărissĭus, a, um, v. Cyparissa, II.

cyparissos.full: cўpărissŏs, i, f., a plant, App. Herb. 3.
cyparissos.short: cўpărissŏs, i, f., a plant, App.

cyparissus.full: cўpărissus and Cўpărissus, i, v. cupressus.

cypassis.full: Cўpassis, ĭdis, f., the mistress of the poet Ovid, Ov. Am. 2, 7, 17 sq.
cypassis.short: Cўpassis, ĭdis, f., the mistress of the poet Ovid, Ov.

cyperis.full: cўpēris, ĭdos, f., = κυπειρίς, the root of the plant cyperos, Plin. 21, 18, 70, § 117.
cyperis.short: cўpēris, ĭdos, f., = κυπειρίς, the root of the plant cyperos, Plin.

cyperos.full: cўpērŏs, i, m. (cўpērum, i, n., Varr. R. R. 3, 16, 13), = κύπειρος, a kind of rush, Plin. 21, 18, 70, §§ 117 and 118.

cyphi.full: cȳphi, is, n., = κῦφι, an Egyptian perfuming powder, Scrib. Comp. 70; Hier. in Jovin. 2, 8.
cyphi.short: cȳphi, is, n., = κῦφι, an Egyptian perfuming powder, Scrib.

cypirus.full: cўpīrus, i, m., = κύπειρος, a plant, pure Lat. gladiolus, Plin. 21, 17, 67, § 107; 21, 18, 69, § 115.—A kindr. species is called cўpīra, ae, f., Plin. 21, 18, 70, § 117.
cypirus.short: cўpīrus, i, m., = κύπειρος, a plant, pure Lat.

cypriacus.full: Cȳ^prĭăcus, a, um, v. Cyprus, II. C.

cyprianus.full: Cyprĭānus, i, m., Cyprian, a celebrated Church father of the third century, bishop at Carthage, Lact. 5, 1, 24; Hier. Ep. 58, n. 10; Sulp. Sev. Dial. 1, 3.
cyprianus.short: Cyprĭānus, i, m., Cyprian, a celebrated Church father of the third century, bishop at Carthage, Lact.

cypriarches.full: Cȳ^prĭarches, ae, m., a prefect of Cyprus, Vulg. Macc. 2, 12, 2.
cypriarches.short: Cȳ^prĭarches, ae, m., a prefect of Cyprus, Vulg.

cypricus.full: Cȳ^prĭcus, a, um, v. Cyprus, II. B.

cyprinum.full: cyprĭnum, i, n., = κύπρινον, a fragrant oil, made from the blossoms of the cyprus (κύπρος), cyprus-oil, cyprus-ointment, Plin. 15, 7, 7, § 28; 13, 1, 2, § 5 sq.; 28, 8, 28, § 109; Cels. 2, 33; 4, 20 al.
cyprinum.short: cyprĭnum, i, n., = κύπρινον, a fragrant oil, made from the blossoms of the cyprus (κύπρος), cyprus-oil, cyprus-ointment, Plin.

cyprinus.full: cyprīnus, i, m., = κυπρῖνος, a species of carp, Plin. 9, 51, 74, § 162; 9, 16, 25, § 58.
cyprinus.short: cyprīnus, i, m., = κυπρῖνος, a species of carp, Plin.

cypris.full: Cȳ^pris, ĭdis, v. Cyprus, II. D.

cyprius vicus.full: Cyprius Vīcus, a street in Rome: a cypro, quod ibi Sabini cives additi consederunt, qui a bono omine id appellarunt; nam cyprum Sabine bonum, Varr. L. L. 5, § 159 Müll.; cf. Liv. 1, 48, 6.
cyprius vicus.short: Cyprius Vīcus, a street in Rome: a cypro, quod ibi Sabini cives additi consederunt, qui a bono omine id appellarunt;

cyprius.full: Cȳ^prĭus, a, um, v. Cyprus, II. A.

cyprus1.full: Cȳ^prus (-ŏs), i, f., = Κύπρος, an island in the Mediterranean Sea, on the coast of Asia Minor, renowned for its fruitfulness, its rich mines, especially of copper, and for the worship of Venus, Mel. 2, 7, 5; Plin. 5, 31, 35, § 129; Cic. Att. 9, 9, 2; id. Fam. 15, 4, 15; Hor. C. 1, 3, 1; 1, 19, 10; Ov. M. 10, 270 et saep. — Hence, Cȳ^prĭus, a, um, adj., Cyprian: merces, Hor. C. 3, 29, 60: trabs, id. ib. 1, 1, 13: tellus, i. e. Cyprus, Ov. M. 10, 645: laurus, Plin. 15, 30, 39, § 127 et saep.— But
cyprus1.short: Cȳ^prus (-ŏs), i, f., = Κύπρος, an island in the Mediterranean Sea, on the coast of Asia Minor, renowned for its fruitfulness, its rich mines, especially of copper, and for the worship of Venus, Mel.

cyprus2.full: cȳ^prus or cȳ^prŏs, i, f., = κύπρος, a tree growing in Cyprus and Egypt; the flower of which yielded the cyprinum: Lawsonia alba, Linn.; Plin. 12, 24, 51, § 109; 23, 4, 46, § 90.
cyprus2.short: cȳ^prus or cȳ^prŏs, i, f., = κύπρος, a tree growing in Cyprus and Egypt;

cyprus3.full: cȳ^prus, a Sabine word, = bonus, v. 1. Cyprius.
cyprus3.short: cȳ^prus, a Sabine word, = bonus, v.

cypsela.full: Cypsĕla, ōrum, n., = Κύψελα, a town in Thrace, on the Hebrus, now Ipsala, Plin. 4, 11, 18, § 43; Liv. 31, 16; 38, 40.—Also Cypsĕla, ae, f., Mel. 2, 2, 6.
cypsela.short: Cypsĕla, ōrum, n., = Κύψελα, a town in Thrace, on the Hebrus, now Ipsala, Plin.

cypselus1.full: cypsĕlus (-ellus), i, m., = κύψελος, a kind of swallow, Plin. 10, 39, 55, § 114.
cypselus1.short: cypsĕlus (-ellus), i, m., = κύψελος, a kind of swallow, Plin.

cypselus2.full: Cypsĕlus, i, m., = Κύψελος, a tyrant at Corinth, Cic. Tusc. 5, 37, 109.—Hence, Cypsĕlĭdes, ae, m., = Κυψελίδης, the descendant of Cypselus, i. e. Periander, Verg. Cir. 463.
cypselus2.short: Cypsĕlus, i, m., = Κύψελος, a tyrant at Corinth, Cic.

cyra.full: Cȳra or Cyrrha, ae, f., = Cyrenae, Ov. lb. 537.
cyra.short: Cȳra or Cyrrha, ae, f., = Cyrenae, Ov.

cyras.full: Cȳras, ae, m., a mountain in Africa, Just. 13, 7.
cyras.short: Cȳras, ae, m., a mountain in Africa, Just.

cyrene1.full: Cȳrēnē, ēs, and Cȳrēnae, ārum, f., the chief town of a province of the same name in Libya, now Kuren, celebrated for its trade, and as the birthplace of Callimachus, Eratosthenes, and Aristippus, Mel. 1, 8, 2; Plin. 5, 5, 5, § 31; Sall. J. 19, 3; Plaut. Rud. prol. 41; Cic. Planc. 5, 13; Nep. Ages. 8, 6; Sil. 8, 57; Cat. 7, 4; Sol. 27, 44.— Hence, Cȳrēnăĭcus, a, um, adj., Cyrenaic: provincia, or absol.: Cȳrē-năĭca, ae, f., the province Cyrenaica, in Libya, Mel. 1, 8, 1; Plin. 5, 5, 5, § 31 sq.; a
cyrene1.short: Cȳrēnē, ēs, and Cȳrēnae, ārum, f., the chief town of a province of the same name in Libya, now Kuren, celebrated for its trade, and as the birthplace of Callimachus, Eratosthenes, and Aristippus, Mel.

cyrene2.full: Cȳrēnē, ēs, f., = Κυρήνη. A nymph, mother of Aristæus, Verg. G. 4, 376; 4, 354; Just. 13, 7.— A nymph, mother of Idmon, Hyg. Fab. 14.— A fountain in Thessaly, Serv. ad Verg. G. 4, 354.

cyretiae.full: Cyretĭae, ārum, f., a town of Thessaly, Liv. 31, 41, 5; 36, 10, 5.
cyretiae.short: Cyretĭae, ārum, f., a town of Thessaly, Liv.

cyrnos.full: Cyrnŏs (Cyrnus, Sen. Epigr. 1, 2), i, f., = Κύρνος, the island Corsica, Plin. 3, 6, 12, § 80.—Hence, Cyrnēus, a, um, adj., Cyrneian or Corsican: taxi, Verg. E. 9, 30: tellus, Sen. l. l.

cyropolis.full: Cȳrŏpŏlis, is, f., = Κυρόπολις, a town in Sogdiana, Curt. 7, 6, 16.
cyropolis.short: Cȳrŏpŏlis, is, f., = Κυρόπολις, a town in Sogdiana, Curt.

cyrrhestica.full: Cyrrhestĭca (Cyrres-), ae, or -cē, ēs, f., a province of Syria, called after its town Cyrrhus, Plin. 5, 23, 19, § 81; Cic. Att. 5, 18, 1; 5, 21, 2.
cyrrhestica.short: Cyrrhestĭca (Cyrres-), ae, or -cē, ēs, f., a province of Syria, called after its town Cyrrhus, Plin.

cyrrhus.full: Cyrrhus (Cyrrus), i, f., = Κύρρος, a town in Syria, Plin. 5, 23, 19, § 81; Tac. A. 2, 57.
cyrrhus.short: Cyrrhus (Cyrrus), i, f., = Κύρρος, a town in Syria, Plin.

cyrsilus.full: Cyrsĭlus, i, m., = Κυρσίλος, an Athenian, Cic. Off. 3, 11, 48.
cyrsilus.short: Cyrsĭlus, i, m., = Κυρσίλος, an Athenian, Cic.

cyrtaei.full: Cyrtaei or Cyrtii, ōrum, m., = Κύρτιοι, a Median tribe, celebrated as slingers, Liv. 37, 40, 9; 42, 58, 13.
cyrtaei.short: Cyrtaei or Cyrtii, ōrum, m., = Κύρτιοι, a Median tribe, celebrated as slingers, Liv.

cyrus.full: Cȳrus, i, m., = Κῦρος. The founder of the Persian monarchy, Cic. Leg. 2, 22, 56; id. Brut. 29, 112; id. Div. 1, 23, 46; Hor. C. 2, 2, 17; 3, 29, 27; called Cyrus Major, Lact. 4, 5, 7.— Cyrus Minor, a brother of Artaxerxes Mnemon, killed in the battle at Cunaxa, Cic. Div. 1, 25, 52; id. Sen. 17, 59; Nep. Alcib. 9, 5.— An architect of the time of Cicero, Cic. Q. Fr. 2, 2, 2; id. Att. 2, 3, 2; id. Mil. 17, 46.—Hence, Cȳrēa, ōrum, n., the structures raised by him, Cic. Att. 4, 10, 2.— The name of a

cyssus.full: Cyssūs, untis, f., = Κυσσοῦς, a town and harbor in Ionia, Liv. 36, 43, 10 and 13.
cyssus.short: Cyssūs, untis, f., = Κυσσοῦς, a town and harbor in Ionia, Liv.

cysthos.full: cysthŏs, i, m., = κύσθος, the female pudenda, Aus. Epigr. 123, 5.
cysthos.short: cysthŏs, i, m., = κύσθος, the female pudenda, Aus.

cytae.full: Cўtae, ārum, f., = Κυ^ταία, a town in Colchis, the birthplace of Medea, Plin. 4, 12, 26, § 86.— Hence, Cўtaeaeus, a, um, adj., Cytæan; poet. for Medean, i. e. magical: carmina, Prop. 1, 1, 24.— Cў-taeus, a, um, adj., Cytæan; poet. for Colchian: terrae, i. e. Colchis, Val. Fl. 6, 693: proceres, the Colchians, id. 6, 595; and absol.: Cўtaei, ōrum, m., the same, Val. Fl. 6, 428.— Cўtaeis, ĭdis, f., the Cytæan woman, i. e. Medea: nocturna, Prop. 2, 4, 7 (17).
cytae.short: Cўtae, ārum, f., = Κυ^ταία, a town in Colchis, the birthplace of Medea, Plin.

cythera.full: Cўthēra, ōrum, n., = Κύθηρα, an island in the Ægean Sea, south-west of the promontory Malea, celebrated for the worship of Venus, now Cerigo, Mel. 2, 7, 10; Plin. 4, 12, 19, § 56; Verg. A. 1, 680; Ov. F. 4, 286; id. Am. 2, 17, 4 et saep.— Hence, Cў-thĕrēus, a, um, adj., of Cythera, Cytherean: Venus, Hor. C. 1, 4, 5; and far more freq. as subst., Cўthĕrēa, ae, f., Venus, Prop. 2 (3), 14, 25; Hor. C. 3, 12, 4; Ov. M. 10, 717; id. F. 4, 673; Verg. A. 1, 257.— Poet. collat. form: Cўthērē, ēs, f., Ve
cythera.short: Cўthēra, ōrum, n., = Κύθηρα, an island in the Ægean Sea, south-west of the promontory Malea, celebrated for the worship of Venus, now Cerigo, Mel.

cythere.full: Cўthērē, ēs, f., v. Cythera, II. A. 2.

cytheris.full: Cўthēris, ĭdis, f., a mistress of Antonius (Cic. Fam. 9, 26, 2; id. Att. 10, 10, 5 al.), who is sarcastically called Cўthērĭus, Cic. Att. 15, 22 fin.; Plin. 8, 16, 21, § 55.
cytheris.short: Cўthēris, ĭdis, f., a mistress of Antonius (Cic.

cythnos.full: Cythnŏs or -us, i, f., = Κύθνος, one of the Cyclades, now Thermia, Mel. 2, 7, 11; Plin. 4, 12, 22, § 66; Liv. 31, 15, 8; Ov. M. 5, 252; Tac. A. 3, 69; id. H. 2, 8.—Hence, Cythnius, a, um, adj., of Cythnos, Cythnian: Timanthes Cythnos, Quint. 2, 13, 13.
cythnos.short: Cythnŏs or -us, i, f., = Κύθνος, one of the Cyclades, now Thermia, Mel.

cytinus.full: cўtĭnus, i, m., = κύτινος, the calyx of the pomegranate blossom, Plin. 23, 6, 59, § 110.
cytinus.short: cўtĭnus, i, m., = κύτινος, the calyx of the pomegranate blossom, Plin.

cytis1.full: Cўtis, is, f., an island at the entrance of the Arabian Gulf, producing chrysolite; now Perim, Plin. 6, 29, 34, § 170.
cytis1.short: Cўtis, is, f., an island at the entrance of the Arabian Gulf, producing chrysolite;

cytis2.full: cўtis, is, f., = κύτις, an unknown precious stone, Plin. 37, 10, 56, § 154.
cytis2.short: cўtis, is, f., = κύτις, an unknown precious stone, Plin.

cytisorus.full: Cўtĭsōrus, i, m., = Κυτίσσωρος, son of Phrixus, and founder of Cytorus, Mel. 1, 19, 8; Val. Fl. 5, 463.
cytisorus.short: Cўtĭsōrus, i, m., = Κυτίσσωρος, son of Phrixus, and founder of Cytorus, Mel.

cytisus.full: cўtĭsus, i, comm. (cўtĭsum, i, n., Varr. R. R. 2, 1, 17; 2, 2, 19), = κύτισος, a shrubby kind of clover much valued by the ancients, perh. the shrubby snail-clover: Medicago arborea, Linn.; Varr. R. R. 2, 1, 17; Col. 5, 12: Plin. 13, 24, 47, § 130; Verg. E. 1, 79; 2, 64 al.

cytorus.full: Cўtōrus (-ŏs), i, m., = Κύτωρος, a mountain abounding in boxwood, and a town upon it, in Paphlagonia, now Kidros, Mel. 1, 19, 8; Plin. 6, 2, 2, § 5; Cat. 4, 13; Verg. G. 2, 437; Val. Fl. 5, 106 al.—Hence, Cўtōrĭăcus, a, um, adj., of Cytorus, Cytorian: de monte, Ov. M. 6, 132: pecten, i. e. made of boxwood, id. ib. 4, 311.— Cўtōrĭus, a, um, adj., of Cytorus: in jugo, Cat. 4, 11: montes, Plin. 16, 16, 28, § 71.
cytorus.short: Cўtōrus (-ŏs), i, m., = Κύτωρος, a mountain abounding in boxwood, and a town upon it, in Paphlagonia, now Kidros, Mel.

cyzicos1.full: Cȳzĭcŏs or Cȳzĭcus, i, m., a king of the Dolones, after whom the town of Cyzicum was named, Val. Fl. 3, 9 sqq.; Mel. 1, 19, 2; Hyg. Fab. 16.
cyzicos1.short: Cȳzĭcŏs or Cȳzĭcus, i, m., a king of the Dolones, after whom the town of Cyzicum was named, Val.

cyzicos2.full: Cȳzĭcos, i, f., v. Cyzicum init.

cyzicum.full: Cȳzĭcum, i, n. (access. form analog. to the Gr. Cȳzĭcus, i, f., Prop. 3 or 4, 22, 1; and Cȳzĭcŏs, Ov. Tr. 1, 10, 29; Auct. Priap. 76, 13), = Κύζικος, a town celebrated in ancient times, in Mysia, on an island or peninsula of the same name in the Propontis, now Chizico, Atraki, or Balkiz, Mel. 1, 19, 2; Plin. 5, 32, 40, § 142; Flor. 3, 5, 15; Sall. H. 3, 16 sqq.; and 4, 61, 14 Dietsch.—Hence, Cȳzĭcēnus, a, um (cf. upon the formation of the word Varr. L. L. 8, § 81 Müll.), adj., of or belonging to

d.full: D, d (n. indecl., sometimes f. sc. littera), the flat dental mute, corresponding in character and sound to the English d and the Greek Δ, was the fourth letter of the Latin alphabet, and was called de: Ter. Maur. p. 2385 P., Auson. Idyll. 12, de Litt. Monos. 14. But at the end of a syllable, or after another consonant, its sound was sharpened, so that the grammarians often discuss the question whether d or t should be written, especially in conjunctions and prepositions. Illa quoque servata est

dabanegoris regio.full: Dabanegoris Rĕgio, a part of Arabia, Plin. 6, 28, 32, § 150.
dabanegoris regio.short: Dabanegoris Rĕgio, a part of Arabia, Plin.

dabar.full: Dabar, ăris, m., a Numidian, a relative of Masinissa and an intimate friend of Bocchus, Sall. J. 108 and 109.
dabar.short: Dabar, ăris, m., a Numidian, a relative of Masinissa and an intimate friend of Bocchus, Sall.

dabla.full: dabla, ae, f. Arab. word, a kind of Arabian palm, which bears a delicious fruit, Plin. 13, 4, 7, § 34.

daci.full: Dāci, ōrum, m., Δακοί, the Dacians, a famous warlike people, akin to the Thracians. They occupied what is now Upper Hungary, Transylvania, Moldavia, Wallachia, Bessarabia. Subdued by Trajan, they received Roman civilization, and thence retain in part the name Rumanians, Plin. 4, 12, 25; Caes. B. G. 6, 25; Tac. G. 1; id. H. 1, 79; 3, 46; Suet. Caes. 44; id. Aug. 8; Flor. 4, 12, 3; Hor. S. 2, 6, 53 et saep. In sing., Dācus, i, m., a Dacian (usually collect.), Verg. G. 2, 497; cf. Voss. ad loc.; Ho
daci.short: Dāci, ōrum, m., Δακοί, the Dacians, a famous warlike people, akin to the Thracians.

dactyli.full: Dactўli, ōrum, m., v. dactylus, no. VII.

dactylicus.full: dactўlĭcus, a, um, adj., = δακτυλικός, dactylic: numerus, Cic. Or. 57: pes, Prud. στεφ. 3, 209: metra, Serv. Centim. p. 1820 P.; versus, Diom. p. 494 P. al.
dactylicus.short: dactўlĭcus, a, um, adj., = δακτυλικός, dactylic: numerus, Cic.

dactyliotheca.full: dactўlĭŏthēca, ae, f., = δακτυλιοθήκη. A casket to keep rings in, Mart. 11, 59, 4; 14, 123, title.— Transf., a collection of seal-rings and jewels, Plin. 37, 1, 5, § 11; Caesaris, Murat. Inscr. 907, 3.

dactylis.full: dactўlis, ĭdis, f., a kind of grape; cf. the following, no. II.
dactylis.short: dactўlis, ĭdis, f., a kind of grape;

dactylus.full: dactўlus, i, m., = δάκτυλος (a finger, hence meton.). A sort of muscle: "ab humanorum unguium similitudine appellati," Plin. 9, 61, 87, § 184.— A kind of grape, Col. 3, 2, 1; called also dacty-lis, Plin. 14, 3, 4, § 40.— A sort of grass, Plin. 24, 19, 119, § 182.— A precious stone, Plin. 37, 10, 61, § 170.— The date, Pall. Oct. 12, 1; Apic. 1, 1 al.— In metre, a dactyl, ¯ ˘ ˘ (in allusion to the three joints of the finger), Cic. Or. 64, 217; id. de Or. 3, 47, 182; Quint. 9, 4, 81 et saep.— Dactў
dactylus.short: dactўlus, i, m., = δάκτυλος (a finger, hence meton.).

dacus.full: Dācus, a, um, v. Daci, no. II. B.

dadastana.full: Dădastăna, ae, f., a city of Bithynia, near the borders of Galatia; here the Emperor Jovian died, Amm. Marc. 25, 10; 26, 23.—Plur. form, Dadastă-nae, arum, Jornand. Regn. Succ. p. 53.
dadastana.short: Dădastăna, ae, f., a city of Bithynia, near the borders of Galatia;

daduchus.full: dādūchus, i, m., Gr. δᾳδοῦχος, the torch - bearer.—Plur.: dādūchi, the priests of Ceres (Demeter) at Eleusis, who guided the initiated with torches to the temple on the fifth day of the Mysteries, Front. Ep. ad Verr. 1; Fabrett. Inscr. 676, no. 29.

daedala.full: Daedăla, ōrum, n., Δαίδαλα. A fortified place in Caria, Plin. 5, 27, 29, § 103; Liv. 37, 22, 3.—Hence, insulae Daedaleae, two small islands off the coast of Caria, Plin. 5, 31, 35, § 131.— The name of a region in India, Curt. 8, 10, 19; cf. Daedali montes, Justin. 12, 7.

daedale.full: daedăle, adv., artistically, skilfully, v. 1, daedalus, fin.

daedalion.full: Daedălĭōn, ōnis, m., Δαιδαλίων, a king of Trachis, son of Lucifer, and brother of Ceyx, who was changed into a hawk, Ov. M. 11, 295 sq. † daedălus, a, um, adj., = δαίδαλος, artificial, skilful (poet. and in postclass. prose). Act.: Minerva, Enn. ap. Paul. ex Fest. p. 68, 6 Müll. (Fr. Inc. Lib. xxi. Vahl.): daedalam a varietate rerum artificiorumque dictam esse apud Lucretium terram, apud Ennium Minervam, apud Vergilium Circen, facile est intellegere, cum Graece δαιδάλλειν significet variare, Pau
daedalion.short: Daedălĭōn, ōnis, m., Δαιδαλίων, a king of Trachis, son of Lucifer, and brother of Ceyx, who was changed into a hawk, Ov.

daedalus.full: Daedălus, i, m. (acc. Gr. Daedalon, Ov. M. 8, 261; Mart. 4, 49), Δαίδαλος. The mythical Athenian architect of the times of Theseus and Minos, father of Icarus, and builder of the Cretan labyrinth, Ov. M. 8, 159; 183; id. Tr. 3, 4, 21; Verg. A. 6, 14 Serv.; Mel. 2, 7, 12: Plin. 7, 56, 57; Hyg. Fab. 39; Cic. Brut. 18, 71; Hor. Od. 1, 3, 34; Mart. 4, 49, 5; Sil. 12, 89 sq., et saep.— Hence, Daedălē^us, a, um, adj., Daedalian, relating to Daedalus: Daedălēo Icaro, Hor. Od. 2, 20, 13: Ope Daedălēa, i

daemon1.full: daemon, ŏnis, m., = δαίμων, a spirit, genius, lar (post-class.). In gen.: App. de Deo Socr. p. 49, 5: bonus = ἀγαθοδαίμων, in astrology, the last but one of the twelve celestial signs, Firm. Math. 2, 19: melior, Jul. Val. Res gest. A. M. 1, 27.— In eccl. writers: κατʼ ἐξοχήν, an evil spirit, demon, Lact. 2, 14; Vulg. Levit. 17, 7; id. Jacob. 2, 19; Tert. Apol. 22 init., et saep.
daemon1.short: daemon, ŏnis, m., = δαίμων, a spirit, genius, lar (post-class.).

daemon2.full: Daemon, ŏnis, m., the name of a Greek sculptor, Plin. 34, 8, 19, § 87.
daemon2.short: Daemon, ŏnis, m., the name of a Greek sculptor, Plin.

daemones.full: Daemŏnes, is, m., the name of an old man, a character in the Rudens, Plaut. Rud. Prol. 33; ib. 4, 7, 20.
daemones.short: Daemŏnes, is, m., the name of an old man, a character in the Rudens, Plaut.

daemoniacus.full: daemŏnĭăcus, a, um, adj., = δαιμονιακός, pertaining to an evil spirit, demoniac, devilish (eccl. Lat.). Adj.: ratio, Tert. Anim. 46: potentia, Lact. 4, 15. — Subst.: daemoniacus, i, m., a demoniac, one possessed by an evil spirit, Firm. Math. 3, 6; Sulpic. Sever. Vit. S. Mart. 18.
daemoniacus.short: daemŏnĭăcus, a, um, adj., = δαιμονιακός, pertaining to an evil spirit, demoniac, devilish (eccl.

daemonicola.full: daemŏnĭcŏla, ae, m. daemon-colo, a worshipper of devils, a heathen, Aug. Conf. 8, 2.

daemonicus.full: daemŏnĭcus, a, um, adj., = δαιμονικός, belonging to an evil spirit, demoniac, devilish (eccl. Lat.): impetus, Tert. Res. Carn. 58: aras coli, Prud. στεφ. 36: fraudes, Lact. 4, 13, 16.
daemonicus.short: daemŏnĭcus, a, um, adj., = δαιμονικός, belonging to an evil spirit, demoniac, devilish (eccl.

daemonium.full: daemŏnĭum, ii, n., = δαιμόνιον. A lesser divinity, a little spirit, Manil. 2, 938; Tert. Apol. 32.— An evil spirit, demon, App. Mag. p. 315, 10; Vulg. Deut. p. 32, 17; Psa. 95, 5 et saep.; Tert. Apol. 21 al.

daesitiatae.full: Daesĭtĭātae, ārum, m., a people in the south of Pannonia Superior, Pl. 3, 22, 26, § 143; Vell. Pat. 2, 115.
daesitiatae.short: Daesĭtĭātae, ārum, m., a people in the south of Pannonia Superior, Pl.

dagnades.full: dagnades, um, f., a kind of birds in Egypt, Paul. ex Fest. p. 68, 15 Müll.
dagnades.short: dagnades, um, f., a kind of birds in Egypt, Paul.

dahae.full: Dăhae (less correctly written Daae, v. Bramb. s. v.), ārum, m., Δάαι, a Scythian tribe beyond the Caspian Sea, Mel. 1, 2, 5; Plin. 6, 17, 19, § 50; Liv. 35, 48; id. 37, 38; Tac. A. 2, 3; 11, 8; 10; Curt. 8, 3, 1; 16 al.; Verg. A. 8, 728; Luc. 2, 296; 7, 429; Sil. 13, 764; cf. Δάοι, Herod. 1, 125; Strab. p. 304; Ritter, Erdk. 7, 627 sq.; 668 sq.—In sing.: Dăhă, Prud. contr. Symm. 2, 807.

dahippus.full: Dăhippus, i, m., Δάϊππος, a sculptor, son and pupil of Lysippus, Plin. 34, 8, 19, § 87.
dahippus.short: Dăhippus, i, m., Δάϊππος, a sculptor, son and pupil of Lysippus, Plin.

daiphron.full: Daïphron, ŏnis, m., Δαίφρων, a Grecian sculptor, Plin. 34, 8, 19, § 87.
daiphron.short: Daïphron, ŏnis, m., Δαίφρων, a Grecian sculptor, Plin.

dalion.full: Dalion, ōnis, m. A physician, Plin. 20, 17, 73, § 191.— An historian, id. 6, 30, 35, § 194.

dalivus.full: dalivus, a word of unknown signif.; acc. to some, = supinus; acc. to others, = stultus or insanus, Paul. ex Fest. 68, 1 Müll.
dalivus.short: dalivus, a word of unknown signif.;

dalmatae.full: Dalmătae or Delmătae (so very often in the best MSS. and inscrr., and on coins; cf. Vel. Long. p. 2233; Cassiod. p. 2287, and Orell. ad Hor. Od. 2, 1, 16), ārum, m., Δαλμάται, the Dalmatians, on the eastern coast of the Adriatic, Cic. Fam. 5, 11, 3; Tac. H. 3, 12; 50; Suet. Tib. 9; Flor. 4, 12, 3; 10; Inscr. Orell. no. 1833; 3037 al.—Adj.: montes Dalmatae, Stat. S. 4, 7, 14.— Hence, Dalmătĭa (Delm-), ae, f., Δαλματία, the country on the eastern coast of the Adriatic Sea, Dalmatia, Plin. 3, 22, 2
dalmatae.short: Dalmătae or Delmătae (so very often in the best MSS.

dama2.full: Dāma, ae, m., name of a slave, Hor. S. 1, 6, 38; 2, 5, 18; 101; 2, 7, 54.
dama2.short: Dāma, ae, m., name of a slave, Hor.

damalio.full: dămălĭo, ōnis, m. δάμαλος, a calf, Lampr. Alex. Sever. 22, 8.

damalis.full: Dămălis is (is or ĭdis, acc. to Probus, p. 124 Lindem.), f., the name of a woman, Hor. Od. 1, 36, 13 sq.

damascus.full: Dămascus (-os, Luc 3, 215; cf. Prob. II. p. 1462 fin. P., p. 121 Lindem.), i, f., Δαμασκός, Heb. Dammesek or Darmesek, the very ancient capital of Coelesyria, on the Chrysorrhoas, celebrated for its terebinths, and, since the time of the Emperor Diocletian, for its fabrics in steel, now Dameshk, Curt. 3, 12 sq.; Plin. 5, 18, 16, § 74; 13, 6, 12, § 54; Flor. 3, 5, 29; Stat. S. 1, 6, 14; Vulg. Gen. 14, 12.—Hence, Damascus, a, um, adj., of Damascus (eccl. Lat.), Vulg. Gen. 15, 2.— Dăma-scēnus, a, u

damasichthon.full: Dămăsichthōn, ŏnis, m., Δαμασίχθων, son of Amphion and Niobe, slain by Apollo, Ov. M. 6, 254 al.
damasichthon.short: Dămăsichthōn, ŏnis, m., Δαμασίχθων, son of Amphion and Niobe, slain by Apollo, Ov.

damasippus.full: Dămăsippus, i, m., Δαμάσιππος (tamer of horses), Prætor 672 A. U. C., a follower of Marius, who acted with great cruelty towards the adherents of Sylla; afterwards put to death by order of Sylla, Sall. C. 51, 32; Vell. 2, 26, 2; Cic. Fam. 9, 21, 3.— A surname in the gens Licinia, Caes. B. C. 2, 44; Cic. Fam. 7, 23, 2 sq.; id. Att. 12, 29 fin.; 33, 1 al.— Name of a bankrupt merchant and ridiculous Stoic philosopher, Hor. S. 2, 3, 16 sqq.— Name of an actor, Juv. 8, 147.
damasippus.short: Dămăsippus, i, m., Δαμάσιππος (tamer of horses), Prætor 672 A.

damasonion.full: damasōnĭon, ii, n, = δαμασώνιον, a plant = alisma, Plin. 25, 10, 77, § 124.
damasonion.short: damasōnĭon, ii, n, = δαμασώνιον, a plant = alisma, Plin.

damium.full: dāmium, ii, n.: sacrificium, quod fie bat in operto in honorem Bonae Deae. Dea quoque ipsa DAMIA et sacerdos ejus DAMIATRIX appellabatur, Paul. ex Fest. p. 68, 8 Müll [δᾶμος = δῆμος]; cf. "damium, θυσίαι ὑπαίθριοι γινόμεναι," Gloss. Lab.
damium.short: dāmium, ii, n.: sacrificium, quod fie bat in operto in honorem Bonae Deae.

damma.full: damma (dama), ae, f. (m., Verg. Ec. 8, 28; Georg. 3, 539; A. 8, 641; Stat. Ach. 2, 408; cf. Quint. 9, 3, 6) [R. dam-, v. domo], a general name for beasts of the deer kind; a fallow deer, buck, doe, antelope, chamois, Plin. 8, 53, 79, § 214; 11, 37, 45, § 124; Verg. G. 1, 308; 3, 410; Hor. Od. 1, 2, 12; Ov. M. 1, 442; 10, 539; 13, 832; id. F. 3, 646; Juv. 11, 121; Sen. Hippol. 62; Sid. Ep. 8, 6.— Transf., venison: nil damma sapit, Juv. 11, 121; Ov. M. 13, 832.

dammula.full: dammŭla, ae, f. dim., v. damula.

damnabilis.full: damnābĭlis, e, adj. damno, worthy of condemnation, damnable (late Lat. for damnandus, or dignus qui damnetur): invidia, Treb. XXX. Tyrann. 17: res (with turpes), Salv. 6: ad mea ipsa verba, i. e. by my own rule, Sid. Ep. 6, 1 fin. Comp.: facinus, Salv. 4.—Adv.: damnābĭlĭter, culpably, Aug. Ep. 23.

damnas.full: damnas, indecl. do, v. damnum, bound to make a gift or contribution, hence an old legal t. t., condemned, sentenced to do any thing (esp. to pay a fine). With sing.: TANTVM AES DARE DOMINO DAMNAS ESTO, Lex Aquilia in Dig. 9, 2, 2; so, damnas esto dare illi omnia, Auct. ap. Quint. 7, 9, 12; id. ib. 9; Inscr. Orell. no. 4425 and 4428; Tab. Heracl. ap. Harbold. Mon. Leg. p. 104: S. C. ap. Front. Aquaed. 129 al.— With plur.: decem dare damnas sunto, Dig. 30, 122; ib. 32, 34, 1.

damnaticius.full: damnāticĭus (or -tius), a, um, adj. damno, condemned, sentenced: "Κατάκριτον damnaticium," Gloss. Gr. Lat. (late Lat.): etsi nihil de damnaticiis participarent, Tert. Praescr. Haeret. 34 fin.

damnatio.full: damnātĭo, ōnis, f. id., condemnation (good prose). Prop. In gen.: (video) omnes damnatos, omnes ignominia affectos, omnes damnatione ignominiaque dignos illuc facere, etc., Cic. Att. 7, 3, 5; Cic. Verr. 2, 2, 41: quid est illa damnatione judicatum, nisi, etc.? id. Clu. 20: si damnatio ingruit, Tac. A, 4, 35: certi damnationis, Suet. Tib. 61 al.—In eccl. Lat. esp. of the displeasure of God: quorum damnatio justa est, Vulg. Rom. 3, 8; 8, 1.—In plur.: reorum acerbissimae damnationes (opp. libidinos
