In this sense also subst., dēversōrĭum (old form dēvors-), ii, n. (for syn. cf.: caupona, hospitium, taberna, popina, ganea), Cic. de Sen. 23, 84; id. Fam. 6, 19; id. Att. 4, 12; Liv. 1, 51; 21, 63; Suet. Vit. 7 al.: studiorum, non libidinum, Cic

deversus.full: dēversus, i. e. deorsum versus, Paul. ex Fest. p. 71, 1 Müll.

deverticulum.full: dēvertĭcŭlum (many MSS. and some edd. dīvert-, old form dēvort-), i, n. deverto. A by-road, by-path, side-way. Prop.: quae deverticula flexionesque quaesivisti? Cic. Pis. 22, 53; Ter. Eun. 4, 2, 7; Curt. 3, 13, 9; Suet. Ner. 48; Plin. 31, 3, 25, § 42; Front. Aquaed. 5: fluminis, a branch, Dig. 41, 3, 45; 44, 3, 7.— Trop., a deviation, digression: legentibus velut deverticula amoena quaerere, Liv. 9, 17; cf. Quint. 10, 1, 29; 9, 2, 79: aquarum calidarum, i. e. a mode of cure (deviating from the s

deverto.full: dē-verto or dēvorto, ti, sum (in MSS. often confounded with diverto), 3, v. a. and n. Act. To turn away, turn aside any thing: comites suo hortatu, Luc. 6, 317: acies, id. 2, 470: ventura fata suo cursu, id. 6, 591; cf. Aur. Vict. Caes. 38.— Far more freq., Pass. with mid. force, to turn one's self aside; and with esp. reference to the term. ad quem, to turn or betake one's self to any place; to turn in, put up at (in the latter sense esp. freq. in Plaut., whereas Cicero commonly uses the act. f
deverto.short: dē-verto or dēvorto, ti, sum (in MSS.

devescor.full: dē-vescor, vesci, v. dep. a., to eat up, devour, poet.: animas, Stat. Th. 1, 604.

devestio.full: dē-vestĭo, īre, v. a., to undress (a word used by Ap.): se, Ap. M. 3, p. 138, 24 al.

devestivus.full: dēvestīvus, a, um, adj., undressed: genitura, Tert. adv. Val. 14.
devestivus.short: dēvestīvus, a, um, adj., undressed: genitura, Tert.

devexitas.full: dēvexĭtas, ātis, f. devexus, a declivity, a sloping: loci, Plin. Ep. 8, 8, 3: litoris, id. 2, 65, 65, § 165.

devexus.full: dēvexus, a, um, adj. deveho, of places, inclining downwards, sloping, shelving, steep (class.—for syn. v. declivis). Lit.: lucus Vestae, qui a Palatii radice in novam viam devexus est, Cic. Div. 1, 45; cf. Liv. 44, 35: mundus in Austros, Verg. G. 1, 241; and: devexus in planum, Plin. Pan. 7, 1, 1: ut de locis superioribus haec declivia et devexa cernebantur, * Caes. B. G. 7, 88: arva, Ov. M. 8, 330: margo (lacus), id. ib. 9, 334 (with acclivus): Orion, i. e. towards his setting, Hor. Od. 1, 28,

deviator.full: dēvĭātor, ōris, m. devio, one who leaves the way, a forsaker: puritatis (Pseud.), August. ad Frat. Erem. 29.

devictio.full: dēvictĭo, ōnis, f. devinco, a conquering: mortis, Tert. adv. Marc. 1, 108.

devigesco.full: dē-vĭgesco, ĕre, v. inch. n., to lose one's vigor, Tert. Anim, 27.

devincio.full: dē-vincĭo, nxi, nctum, 4 (perf. sync. devinxti, Plaut. As. 5, 1, 21), v. a., to bind fast, tie up (class.; esp. freq. in trop. signif.). Lit.: servum, Plaut. Men. 5, 2, 92; cf. leonem, Plin. 8, 16, 21, § 54: Dircam ad taurum, Plaut. Ps. 1, 2, 65: aliquem fasciis, Cic. Brut. 60, 217; cf.: opercula plumbo, Liv. 40, 29.—In Greek constr.: devinctus tempora lauro, encircled, crowned, Tib. 2, 5, 5 et saep.— Trop., to bind together, to unite closely; to engage, to oblige, lay under obligation: totam It

devinco.full: dē-vinco, vīci, victum, 3, v. a., to conquer completely, overcome, subdue. Prop. (class.; for syn. cf.: vinco, supero, fundo, fugo, profligo, subigo, subicio, domo): Galliam Germaniamque, Caes. B. C. 3, 87; id. B. G. 7, 34; Hirt. ib. 8, 46: devincere et capere Capuam, Cic. Agr. 2, 33, 90: Poenos classe, id. de Sen. 13, 44; cf.: Crotoniatas maximo proelio, id. N. D. 2, 2: Sabaeae reges, Hor. Od. 1, 29, 3: serpentem, Ov. H. 6, 37: flumina, Stat. S. 5, 5, 63 et saep.—With ut and subj.: Catonis sent

devinctio.full: dēvinctĭo, ōnis, f. devincio, a binding, ensnaring: magicae, enchantments, Tert. Spect. 2.

devinctus.full: dēvinctus, a, um, Part. and P. a., from devincio.

devio.full: dē-vĭo, āvi, 1, v. n., to turn from the straight road, to go aside, to deviate (late Lat.; for de via declinare or devertere). Prop., Macr. Somn. Scip. 1, 22; Aug. Doctr. Christ. 3, 36 fin.— Trop., Macr. S. 5, 15; Symm. Ep. 9, 121: a vero, Vulg. Exod. 23, 2.

devirginatio.full: dēvirgĭnātĭo, ōnis, f. devirgino, a deflouring, Scrib. Comp. 18.

devirginator.full: dēvirgĭnātor, διαπαρθενευτής, a deflourer, Gloss. Vet.

devirgino.full: dē-virgĭno, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a., to deprive of virginity, to deflour. Prop., Petr. 25, 1; Dig. 1, 18, 21: juvenculam, Vulg. Sirach, 20, 2.— Transf. in the pass., of young persons, to quit the period of youth, Varr. ap. Non. 458, 26.

devitatio.full: dēvītātĭo, ōnis, f. devito, an avoiding: legionum, Cic. Att. 16, 2, 4.

devito.full: dē-vīto, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a., to avoid, go out of the way of, shun (rare but class.): illos fluctus, Plaut. Rud. 1, 2, 79; cf.: procellam temporis, Cic. Verr. 1, 3, 8: malum, Ter. And. 3, 5, 5: letum, Lucr. 3, 1092: dolorem, Cic. Tusc. 2, 26: exiguum censum turpemque repulsam, Hor. Ep. 1, 1, 44: suspicionem, Suet. Tib. 11: δυσφημίαν nominis, id. Aug. 92: stultitiam, Vulg. Eccl. 2, 3.

devius.full: dē-vĭus, a, um, adj. via, lying off the high-road; out of the way, devious (class.; for syn. cf.: avius, invius). Lit.: iter, a by-way, Cic. Att. 4, 3, 4; 14, 10, 1 (cf. avius); Suet. Galb. 20: oppidum, Cic. Pis. 36 fin.: saltus, Liv. 41, 19: calles, id. 22, 14: rura, Ov. M. 1, 676.—Subst.: dēvia, ōrum, n., lonely, unfrequented places: per aspera ac devia, Suet. Tib. 60: in devia terrarum, Luc. 4, 161.— Transf., of living beings dwelling in out-of-the-way places, retired, sequestered: Anagnini,

devoco.full: dē-vŏco, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a., to call off, call away; also to call down.—With abl. of the place whence after de, ab, ex, rarely without a prep.; and with reference to the term. ad quem (cf. de, no. II. B.), to call, to fetch by calling to any place, with ad or in (rare but class.). Lit.: aliquem de provincia ... ad gloriam, ad triumphum, etc., Cic. Prov. Cons. 12, 29: suos ab tumulo, Liv. 4, 39; cf.: ex praesidiis, id. 33, 18: refixa sidera caelo, Hor. Epod. 17, 5; cf.: Jovem caelo sacrificio, P

devolo.full: dē-vŏlo, āre, v. n., to fly down or away (very rare). Lit. To fly down: devolant angues jubati deorsum in impluvium, Plaut. Am. 5, 1, 56: Iris per caelum, Verg. A. 4, 702: sibi de caelo devolaturam in sinum victoriam, Liv. 7, 12, 13.— To fly away: turdus devolet illuc, ubi, etc., Hor. S. 2, 5, 11: phoenicem devolavisse in Aegyptum, Plin. 10, 2, 2, § 5.— Transf., to hasten down, to fly or hasten away: de tribunali, Liv. 2, 29: in terram, Lucr. 6, 205: praecipites in forum, Liv. 3, 15; cf.: raptim

devolvo.full: dē-volvo, volvi, vŏlūtum, 3, v. a., to roll or tumble down (class.). Lit.: saxa in musculum, Caes. B. C. 2, 11, 1, and 2; cf. saxa (amnis), Quint. 12, 10, 61: auratas trabes, Verg. A. 2, 449: tonitrua, i. e. to imitate it (by rolling down balls behind the scenes), Phaedr. 5, 7, 23: clipeos e muris, Curt. 4, 3 fin.: panem ex igne, Cat. 59, 4: corpora in humum, Ov. M. 7, 574: se toris, Val. Fl. 1, 235 et saep.—Poet.: fusis mollia pensa, i. e. to spin off, Verg. G. 4, 349.— Pass. in mid. force, to

devomo.full: dē-vŏmo, ĕre, v. a., to vomit forth, Caecil. ap. Gell. 2, 23, 13.

devorabilis.full: dēvŏrābĭlis, e, adj. devoro, that can be devoured: tegmen, Alcim. Ep. 77.

devoratio.full: dēvŏrātĭo, ōnis, f. id., a devouring: carnis, Tert. Res. carn. 54.—With gen. subject.: piscis, Vulg. Tobiae, 12, 3; id. Ezech. 34, 5.

devorator.full: dēvŏrātor, ōris, m. id., a devourer (late Lat.), Tert. Res. carn. 32; Vulg. Sap. 12, 5; id. Luc. 7, 35.

devoratorius.full: dēvŏrātōrĭus, a, um, adj. id., devouring: crimina devoratoria salutis, destructive to, Tert. Idol. 1.—As subst.: dē-vŏrātōrĭum, i, n., the devouring maw: mortis, Ambros. Ep. 4, 5 fin.

devoratrix.full: dēvŏrātrix, īcis, f. devorator, she that devours: puerorum, Porphyr. ad Hor. Ep. 1, 13, 10: hominum, Vulg. Ezech. 36, 13.

devoro.full: dē-vŏro, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a., to swallow, swallow down, gulp down, devour (class.; esp. freq. in transf. signif.—for syn. cf.: edo, comedo, vescor, pascor, mando). Lit., of the physical act: id quod devoratur, Cic. N. D. 2, 54, 135: ovum gallinaceum integrum, Cato R. R. 71: laseris paululum, Cels. 4, 4, 4: salivam suam, id. 2, 6, 98; lapides, Plin. 8, 10, 10, § 29: succum, id. 20, 23, 98, § 260: fumum, id. 26, 6, 16, § 30 et saep.— Transf. Of inanimate subjects, to swallow up, ingulf, absorb: de

devortium.full: dēvortĭum, ii, n. deverto, a by-way, by-road: itinerum, Tac. Agr. 19, 5 Halm (Ritter, divortia).

devotamentum.full: dēvōtāmentum, i, n. devoveo, a cursing, anathema, Tert. adv. Gnost. 2.

devotatio.full: dēvōtātio, ōnis, f. id., a making of vows, consecration, Vulg. 3 Reg. 8, 38; August. 4 Quaest. in Hept. 40.

devote.full: dēvōtē, adv., devotedly, faithfully, v. devoveo, P. a. fin.

devotio.full: dēvōtĭo, ōnis, f. devoveo. A devoting, consecrating. Prop.: Deciorum devotiones, the devoting of themselves, Cic. N. D. 3, 6, 15; cf. vitae, id. Rab. Post. 1 fin.; capitis, id. Dom. 57; a vow, Vulg. Act. 23, 1. — Transf., fealty, allegiance, devotedness (late Lat.): alicujus erga rempublicam, Treb. Poll. Gall. 14: Aquileiensium pro Romanis, Capitol. Maxim. et Balb. 11: quis fortes animat devotio mentes, Nemes. Cyneg. 83 al.—Hence, (Cf. devotus, P. a. no. B.) In Christian authors, piety, devotion

devoto.full: dē-vōto, āvi, ātum, 1, v. intens. a. [id.]. To dedicate, devote (rare): et me dicabo atque animam devotabo hostibus, Att. ap. Non. 98, 13 (but Cic. Par. 1, 2, 12, read devota vita); and, To bewitch, enchant: sortes, Plaut. Cas. 2, 6, 36: devotatus defixusque, Ap. Herb. 7.— To invoke with vows: numina, Ap. M. 9, p. 227, 4: asinos cum Iside, Minuc. Fel. Oct. 28, 5. — To curse: se, August. 4 Quaest. in Hept. 40.

devotor.full: dēvōtor et dēvōtrix dicitur qui imprecatur, Serv. Verg. A. 4, 607 [id.].
devotor.short: dēvōtor et dēvōtrix dicitur qui imprecatur, Serv.

devotus.full: dēvōtus, a, um, Part. and P. a., from devoveo.

devoveo.full: dē-vŏvĕo, vōvi, vōtum, 2, v. a. To vow, devote (usually to a deity). Prop. (class.): Marti ea, quae bello ceperint, Caes. B. G. 6, 17, 3; so, Dianae pulcherrimum, Cic. Off. 3, 25, 95: gnatam pro muta agna, Hor. S. 2, 3, 219 et saep.; esp. freq.: se diis, or simply se, to devote one's self to death, to sacrifice one's self, Cic. N. D. 2, 3 fin.; id. Fin. 2, 19, 61: se pro aere alieno, in jesting allusion to the death of the Decii, id. Phil. 11, 6, 13: se pro patria Quiritibusque Romanis, Liv. 5,

devulsus.full: dēvulsus, a, um, Part., from devello.
devulsus.short: dēvulsus, a, um, Part., from devello.

dexamenus.full: Dexămĕnus, i, m., the name of a centaur; i. q. Eurytion, Ov. Ib. 406.
dexamenus.short: Dexămĕnus, i, m., the name of a centaur;

dexippus.full: Dexippus, i, m. Δέξιππος, a Greek proper name, Cic. Fam. 14, 3, 3.

dexius.full: Dexĭus, ĭi, m., a Roman proper name, Cic. Fam. 7, 23, 4.
dexius.short: Dexĭus, ĭi, m., a Roman proper name, Cic.

dexo.full: Dexo, ōnis, f., Δεξων, a Greek proper name, Cic. Verr. 2, 5, 42 al.
dexo.short: Dexo, ōnis, f., Δεξων, a Greek proper name, Cic.

dextans.full: dextans, antis, m. contr. from de and sextans: as dempto sextante, Varr. L. L. 5, § 172 Müll., ten twelfths of any thing (mostly post-Aug.; Cic. writes instead: pars dimidia et tertia, Fam. 13, 29, 4; cf.: remissis senio et trientibus, id. Sest. 25, 55), Varr. l. l.: jugeri, Col. 5, 1, 12: horae, Plin. 18, 32, 75, § 324: gradus neque crassiores dextante, neque tenuiores dodrante, Vitr. 3, 3: pro semisse dextans, Suet. Ner. 32.

dextella.full: dextella, ae, f. dim. dextra, a little right hand: Quintus filius illius, ut scribis, est dextella, Cic. Att. 14, 20, 5.

dexter.full: dexter, tĕra, tĕrum, and more freq. tra, trum (dat. plur. fem.: dextrabus manibus, Liv. Andron. ap. Non. 493, 20.—Comp. dextĕrĭor; sup. dextĭmus), adj. dex-ter, root dek-, Gr. δέκομαι, whence δάκτυλος, digitus; cf. Germ. Finger, from fangen; cf. also Sanscr. dakshinas, on the right hand, and Gr. δεξ-ιός, to the right, on the right side, right (opp. laevus, sinister). Prop.: ut ante oculos fuerit qui dexter hic idem nunc sit laevus, Lucr. 4, 302: manus, Plaut. Mil. 2, 2, 49; 50; id. Capt. 2, 3, 8
dexter.short: dexter, tĕra, tĕrum, and more freq.

dextera.full: dextĕra or dextra, ae, f. (as in most langg.; cf. Gr. δεξιά, Germ. die Rechte, etc.; sc. manus), the right hand (freq. a sign of greeting, of fidelity; a symbol of strength, courage, etc.). Prop.: cedo sis dexteram, Plaut. Poen. 1, 2, 102; Ter. Heaut. 3, 1, 84: quod ego te per hanc dextram oro, id. And. 1, 5, 54; cf.: per dexteram te istam oro, quam, etc., Cic. Deiot. 3; cf. also Sall. J. 10, 3; Hor. Ep. 1, 7, 94 al.; and: dexterae, quae fidei testes esse solebant, Cic. Phil. 11, 2, 5: fidem mor

dextra.full: dextrā, praep. [orig. dextrā, abl. of preceding], on the right of (post-Aug.); with acc.: dextra sinistraque januam, Gell. 16, 5, 3: dextra viam stratam, Liv. 8, 15, 8: dextra ac sinistra aquilonem, Vitr. 1, 6, 10; id. 6, 11, 3; Paul. ex Fest. p. 206, 18 al.

dextere.full: dextĕre and dextrē, adv., dexterously, skilfully: dextre obeundo officia, Liv. 1, 34 fin.—Comp.: nemo dexterius fortunā est usus, Hor. S. 1, 9, 45.
dextere.short: dextĕre and dextrē, adv., dexterously, skilfully: dextre obeundo officia, Liv.

dexteritas.full: dextĕrĭtas, ātis, f. dexter, II.. Dexterity, aptness, readiness in doing good offices (rare and not ante-Aug.): tanta inerat comitas Scipioni atque ad omnia naturalis ingenii dexteritas, Liv. 28, 18, 6; 37, 7, 15; Gell. 13, 16, 1 al.—* Prosperity, felicity, Arn. 7, p. 225.

dextimus.full: dextĭmus, a, um, v. dexter, no. I.

dextrale.full: dextrāle, is, n. id., a bracelet (late Lat.), Cypr. Habit. Verg. med.; Vulg. Exod. 35, 22 al.

dextraliolum.full: dextrālĭŏlum, i, n. dim. dextrale, a little bracelet, Vulg. Judith, 10, 3.

dextralis.full: dextrālis, is, f. dextra, a hatchet, Isid. 19, 19, 11.

dextratio.full: dextrātĭo, ōnis, f. dexter, a movement towards the right side (a religious ceremonial), Sol. 45, 15.

dextratus.full: dextrātus, a, um, adj. id., lying to the right (late Lat.): ager, pars, Auct. de Limit. p. 298 Goes.

dextrocherium.full: dextrŏchĕrĭum, ii, n. vox hibrida, from dexter and χείρ, a bracelet (late Lat.), Capitol. Max. 6, 8; 27, 8: gemmatum, Schol. Juv. 9, 50.

dextrorsum.full: dextrorsum or dextrorsus, or uncontracted dextrovorsum (or -ver-sum), adv. dexter-versus, towards the right side, to the right, Att. ap. Cic. Div. 1, 22, 44: ille sinistrorsum hic dextrorsum abit, Hor. S. 2, 3, 50: dextrorsus pergere, Liv. 6, 31, 5: dextrovorsum, Plaut. Curc. 1, 1, 70; id. Rud. 1, 2, 87; 2, 3, 38: dextroversum separari, Lact. 6, 7 fin.
dextrorsum.short: dextrorsum or dextrorsus, or uncontracted dextrovorsum (or -ver-sum), adv.

dia.full: Dīa, ae, f., Δῖα. The old name of the island of Naxos, Ov. M. 3, 690; 8, 174. — A city in the Chersonesus Taurica, Plin. 4, 12, 26, § 86.— An island near Crete, now Standia, id. 4, 12, 20, § 61.— A woman's name. The mother of Mercury, Cic. N. D. 3, 22, 56.— The wife of Ixion, and mother of Pirithous, Hyg. F. 155.

diaartymaton.full: dĭăartўmătōn, i, n., = διὰ ἀρτυμάτων, a kind of salve, Cael. Aur. Tard. 3, 8, 116.
diaartymaton.short: dĭăartўmătōn, i, n., = διὰ ἀρτυμάτων, a kind of salve, Cael.

diabathrarius.full: dĭăbā^thrārĭus, ii, m. diabathrum, the maker of a sort of slipper, a shoemaker, Plaut. Aul. 3, 5, 39.

diabathrum.full: dĭăbā^thrum, i, n., = διάβαθρον, a sort of slipper, Naev. ap. Varr. L. L. 7, § 53 Müll. (v. 60 Rib.); cf. Paul. ex Fest. p. 74, 9 Müll.
diabathrum.short: dĭăbā^thrum, i, n., = διάβαθρον, a sort of slipper, Naev.

diabetes.full: dĭăbētes, ae, m., = διαβήτης, a siphon; called also sipho, Col. 3, 10, 2.
diabetes.short: dĭăbētes, ae, m., = διαβήτης, a siphon;

diablintes.full: Dĭā^blintes, um, m., a people in Gallia Lugdunensis, near the present Mayenne, in the Department de la Sarthe, Caes. B. G. 3, 9 fin.; called also Diablinti, Plin. 4, 18, 32, § 107.
diablintes.short: Dĭā^blintes, um, m., a people in Gallia Lugdunensis, near the present Mayenne, in the Department de la Sarthe, Caes.

diabole.full: dĭăbŏle, ēs, f., = διαβολή, a rhet. t. t., false accusation, slander (pure Lat. criminatio), Jul. Rufin. de Fig. p. 209 Ruhnk.
diabole.short: dĭăbŏle, ēs, f., = διαβολή, a rhet.

diabolicus.full: dĭăbŏlĭcus, a, um, adj., = διαβολικός, devilish, diabolical, Paul. Nol. 29, 11: viri, Vulg. 3 Reg. 21, 13.
diabolicus.short: dĭăbŏlĭcus, a, um, adj., = διαβολικός, devilish, diabolical, Paul.

diabolus.full: dĭăbŏlus, i, m., = διάβολος, a devil, Tert. Anim. 35; Vulg. 3 Reg. 21, 13.—Esp., the devil, Tert. adv. Marc. 2, 10; Vulg. 1 Johan. 3, 8 al. et saep. With long a, in Paul. Nol. 26, 528.
diabolus.short: dĭăbŏlus, i, m., = διάβολος, a devil, Tert.

diacatochia.full: dĭăcătŏchĭa, ae, f., = διακατοχή, possession, Cod. Just. 11, 58, 7.
diacatochia.short: dĭăcătŏchĭa, ae, f., = διακατοχή, possession, Cod.

diacatochus.full: dĭăcătŏchus, i, m., = διακάτοχος, a possessor, Cod. Th. 10, 16, 1.
diacatochus.short: dĭăcătŏchus, i, m., = διακάτοχος, a possessor, Cod.

diacecaumene.full: dĭăcĕcaumĕne, es, f., = διακεκαυμένη, sc. γῆ, the torrid zone, Sol. 32, 37; cf. Hygin. Astr. 1, 8.

diacheton.full: dĭăchĕton, i, n., a small plant in Rhodes; called also crysisceptrum, Plin. 24, 13, 69, § 112 (Jan. diaxylon).
diacheton.short: dĭăchĕton, i, n., a small plant in Rhodes;

diachylon.full: dĭăchȳlōn = διὰ χυλῶν, a sort of medicine, Cael. Aur. Acut. 2, 18; 2, 29 al.
diachylon.short: dĭăchȳlōn = διὰ χυλῶν, a sort of medicine, Cael.

diachyton.full: dĭăchўton, i, n. (sc. vinum), = διαχυτόν, a sort of sweet wine, Plin. 14, 9, 11, § 84.

diacisson.full: dĭăcissōn = διακισσῶν, an ointment, Theod. Prisc. 4, 1.

diacodion.full: dĭăcōdīōn, i, n., = διὰ κωδειῶν, a sort of medicine prepared from poppy-juice, Plin. 20, 18, 76, § 200; 20, 19, 79, § 207 sq.; Isid. Or. 4, 9, 9 al.
diacodion.short: dĭăcōdīōn, i, n., = διὰ κωδειῶν, a sort of medicine prepared from poppy-juice, Plin.

diaconatus.full: dĭācŏnātus, ūs, m. (and dĭācŏnī-um, i, n., Sever. Sulp. vita Mart. 5 al.) [diaconus], the office of deacon, deaconship, Hier. Ep. 22, 12 al.

diaconicus.full: dĭācŏnĭcus, a, um, adj. diaconus, belonging to a deaconship: loca, Cod. Th. 16, 5, 30.—Subst.: dĭācŏnĭcum, i, n., a place for storing the vessets of the altar, Cod. Theod. 16, 5, 10.

diaconus.full: dĭācŏnus, i (collat. form in plur.: diacones, Vulg. Tim. 3, 8; 12: diaconibus, id. Phil. 1, 1), m., = διάκονος, in eccl. Lat., a servant or minister of the church, a deacon, Tert. Praescr. 3; Cod. Just. 1, 3, 6 et saep. —dĭācŏnissa, ae, f., a deaconess, Cod. Just. 1, 3, 9; Orell. Inscr. 4872 al.

diacope.full: dĭăcŏpe, es, f., = διακοπή, gram. t. t., a tmesis, Charis. p. 246 P.

diacopus.full: dĭăcŏpus, i, m., = διάκοπος, an opening or sluice in a dam for leading off the water, Dig. 47, 11, 10.
diacopus.short: dĭăcŏpus, i, m., = διάκοπος, an opening or sluice in a dam for leading off the water, Dig.

diadema.full: dĭădēma, ătis, n. (diadēma, ae, f., Pompon. ap. Prisc. p. 679 P. [Com. v. 163 Rib.]; Ap. M. 10, p. 253, 10), = διάδημα, a royal head-dress, a diadem (for syn. cf.: infula, vitta, redimiculum), Cic. Phil. 2, 34, 85; 3, 5, 12; Quint. 9, 3, 61; Suet. Caes. 79; Hor. C. 2, 2, 21; Juv. 8, 259; Vulg. Apoc. 12, 3 al.

diademalis.full: dĭădēmālis, e, adj. diadema, pertaining to or wearing a diadem: frons, Diacont. 2, 31.

diadematus1.full: dĭădēmātus, a, um, adj. id., adorned with a diadem: Apollo, Plin. 34, 8, 19, § 79. —Hence,

diadematus2.full: Dĭădēmātus, i, m., a Roman surname, Cic. Post. Red. ad Quir. 3, 6.
diadematus2.short: Dĭădēmātus, i, m., a Roman surname, Cic.

diadochos.full: dĭădŏchos, i, m., = διάδοχος, a jewel resembling the beryl, Plin. 37, 10, 57, § 157.
diadochos.short: dĭădŏchos, i, m., = διάδοχος, a jewel resembling the beryl, Plin.

diadota.full: dĭădŏta, ae, m., = διαδότης a distributor (pure Lat.: divisor, diribitor), Cod. Th. 7, 4, 28.
diadota.short: dĭădŏta, ae, m., = διαδότης a distributor (pure Lat.: divisor, diribitor), Cod.

diadumenus.full: dĭădūmĕnus, a, um, adj., = διαδούμενος, wearing a diadem: juvenis, Plin. 34, 8, 19, § 55: statua, Sen. Ep. 65, 5.— Antoninus Diadumenus, a Roman emperor, son and successor of Macrinus; cf. Lampr. Anton. Diadum. 4.
diadumenus.short: dĭădūmĕnus, a, um, adj., = διαδούμενος, wearing a diadem: juvenis, Plin.

diaeresis.full: dĭaerĕsis, is, f., = διαίρεσις. In gram., the dividing of one syllable into two, as aquaï for aquae, Serv. ad Verg. A. 7, 464.— In rhet., a figure, pure Lat. distributio, distribution, Jul. Rufin. 21, p. 242.

diaeta.full: dĭaeta (zaeta or zēta, Lampr. Heliog. 29 fin.; 30; and in many MSS. in the foll. passages; cf. the letter D), ae, f., = δίαιτα. A mode of living prescribed by a physician, diet: sola diaeta curari, Cael. Aur. Tard. 2, 12, 146.—Trop.: sed ego diaeta curari incipio, chirurgiae taedet, Cic. Att. 4, 3, 3.— A dwelling - place, dwelling room, summer-house, etc. (post-Aug.), Plin. Ep. 2, 17, 15; Suet. Claud. 10; Stat. S. 2, 2, 83; Dig. 7, 1, 13; 32, 55, § 3; Orell. Inscr. 4373 et saep.

diaetarchus.full: dĭaetarchus, i, m., = διαίταρχος, one who has the care of apartments, a valetde-chambre, Inscr. Orell. 2912.—Called also † dĭaetarcha, ae, m., ib. 2913. And v. the foll. art.
diaetarchus.short: dĭaetarchus, i, m., = διαίταρχος, one who has the care of apartments, a valetde-chambre, Inscr.

diaetarius.full: dĭaetārĭus, ii, m. diaeta, no. II., a valet-de-chambre, Dig. 33, 7, 12, § 42, ib. 4, 9, 1.

diaeteta.full: dĭaetēta, ae, m., = διαιτητής, an umpire (pure Lat. arbiter), Cod. 2, 13, 27 al.
diaeteta.short: dĭaetēta, ae, m., = διαιτητής, an umpire (pure Lat.

diaetetice.full: dĭaetētĭcē, ēs, f., = διαιτητική, dietetics, Scrib. Comp. 200 al.
diaetetice.short: dĭaetētĭcē, ēs, f., = διαιτητική, dietetics, Scrib.

diaeteticus.full: dĭaetētĭcus, a, um, adj., = διαιτητικός, belonging to diet: libri, curatio, Cael. Aur. Tard. 2, 12, 145.—Subst., diaetetici, ōrum, m., physicians who cure by diet (opp. chirurgi), Scrib. Comp. 200 (cf. Cic. Att. 4, 3, 3).
diaeteticus.short: dĭaetētĭcus, a, um, adj., = διαιτητικός, belonging to diet: libri, curatio, Cael.

diaglaucium.full: dĭaglaucĭum or -on, ii, n., a salve made from the herb glaucium, Plin. 27, 10, 59, § 83; Scrib. Comp. 22.
diaglaucium.short: dĭaglaucĭum or -on, ii, n., a salve made from the herb glaucium, Plin.

diagonalis.full: dĭăgōnālis, e, adj. [from διαγώνιος and the Lat. ending alis), diagonal: linea, Vitr. 9, 1; 6, 5.—And subst., dĭăgōnĭum, ii, n.: diagonii linea, id. 6, 4.

diagondas.full: Dĭăgondas, ae, m., = Διαγόνδας, a Theban lawgiver, Cic. Leg. 2, 15, 37.
diagondas.short: Dĭăgondas, ae, m., = Διαγόνδας, a Theban lawgiver, Cic.

diagonios.full: dĭăgōnĭŏs, on, = διαγώνιος, adj., diagonal: linea, Vitr. 6, 3, 3: structura, id. 6, 8, 7 al.
diagonios.short: dĭăgōnĭŏs, on, = διαγώνιος, adj., diagonal: linea, Vitr.

diagoras.full: Dĭăgŏras, ae, m., Διαγόρας. An atheistic philosopher and poet of Melos, a contemporary of Pindar, Cic. N. D. 1, 1; 1, 23; 42; 3, 37; Val. Max. 1, 2.— One of the most famous athletes in the Olympic games, a native of Rhodes, Cic. Tusc. 1, 46, 111; Gell. 3, 15, 3.

diagramma.full: dĭagramma, ătis, n., = διάγραμμα, in music, the scale, gamut, Vitr. 5, 4.
diagramma.short: dĭagramma, ătis, n., = διάγραμμα, in music, the scale, gamut, Vitr.

diagrydium.full: dĭagrydĭum, ĭi, n., = διαγρύδιον, the juice of the plant scammonea, Cael. Aur. Acut. 2, 12 al.
diagrydium.short: dĭagrydĭum, ĭi, n., = διαγρύδιον, the juice of the plant scammonea, Cael.

diaiteon.full: dĭăĭtĕon = διὰ ἰτεῶν, a salve made of the juice of the willow, Cael. Aur. Tard. 2, 13.
diaiteon.short: dĭăĭtĕon = διὰ ἰτεῶν, a salve made of the juice of the willow, Cael.

dialectica.full: dĭălectĭca, ae, f., and orum, n., and dĭălectĭce, ēs, v. dialecticus, no. II.
dialectica.short: dĭălectĭca, ae, f., and orum, n., and dĭălectĭce, ēs, v.

dialectice.full: dĭălectĭcē, adv., dialectically, v. the foll. no. I.

dialecticus.full: dĭălectĭcus, a, um, adj., = διαλεκτικός, belonging to disputation, dialectical. Adj.: captiones, Cic. Fin. 2, 6, 17: disputationes, Quint. 5, 14, 27: pars, id. 12, 2, 13 et saep.: sapientiae professor, Plin. 7, 53, 54, § 180.—Adv., dialecticē, dialectically: disputare, Cic. Fin. 2, 6, 17: dicta multa, id. Ac. 1, 2, 8: probare, Quint. 1, 10, 37.— Subst. dĭălectĭcus, i, m., a dialectician, logician, Cic. Or. 32, 113; id. Fin. 2, 6, 15; Quint. 2, 4, 41; 7, 3, 41 al.— dĭă-lectĭca, ae, f. (sc. ars),
dialecticus.short: dĭălectĭcus, a, um, adj., = διαλεκτικός, belonging to disputation, dialectical.

dialectos.full: dĭălectos or -us, i, f., = διάλεκτος, a dialect, Suet. Tib. 56.
dialectos.short: dĭălectos or -us, i, f., = διάλεκτος, a dialect, Suet.

dialepidos.full: dĭălĕpĭdos = διὰ λεπίδος, an unguent made with the scales that fly from metal in hammering, Marc. Emp. 9; Inscr. Orell. 4233 al.
dialepidos.short: dĭălĕpĭdos = διὰ λεπίδος, an unguent made with the scales that fly from metal in hammering, Marc.

dialeucos.full: dĭăleucos, on, adj., = διάλευκος, intermixed with white, whitish: crocum, Plin. 21, 6, 17, § 33.
dialeucos.short: dĭăleucos, on, adj., = διάλευκος, intermixed with white, whitish: crocum, Plin.

dialibanum.full: dĭălĭbănum, i, n., = διὰ λιβάνων or λιβάνου, a salve made with frankincense, Marc. Emp. 9.
dialibanum.short: dĭălĭbănum, i, n., = διὰ λιβάνων or λιβάνου, a salve made with frankincense, Marc.

dialion.full: dĭālĭon, ĭi, n., = διάλιον or διήλιον, the plant heliotropium, Ap. Herb. 49.
dialion.short: dĭālĭon, ĭi, n., = διάλιον or διήλιον, the plant heliotropium, Ap.

dialis.full: Dĭālis, e, adj. from Dis, in Diespiter = Juppiter. Of or belonging to Jupiter: flamen, the priest of Jove (instituted by Numa, and the most distinguished of the flamines), Varr. L. L. 5, § 84; 6, § 16 Müll.; Fabius Pictor and Massurius Sabinus ap. Gell. 10, 15; Liv. 5, 52 fin.; Tac. A. 3, 58; Vell. 2, 43; Suet. Caes. 1; Ov. F. 2, 282 et saep.; called also: Dialis sacerdos, Suet. Dom. 4.—Subst.: Dialis, Fab. Pict. l. l.; Tac. A. l. l.; Ov. F. 3, 397: conjux sancta Dialis, his wife (who sometimes

dialogismos.full: dĭălŏgismos, i, m., = διαλογισμός, rhet. t. t., a consideration, Jul. Rufin. de Fig. 20, p. 211 sq.

dialogista.full: dĭălŏgista, ae, m., = διαλογιστής, an able disputant, Vulc. Gallic. Avid. Cass. 3.
dialogista.short: dĭălŏgista, ae, m., = διαλογιστής, an able disputant, Vulc.

dialogus.full: dĭălŏgus, i, m., = διάλογος, a (philosophical) conversation, a dialogue (for syn. cf.: colloquium, contio, contentio, oratio), Cic. Or. 44 fin.; id. Brut. 60 fin.; Quint. 5, 14, 27; 6, 3, 44 al. (written as Greek, Cic. Att. 5, 5; 15, 13; Quint. 9, 2, 31; in the last passage transl. by sermocinatio).
dialogus.short: dĭălŏgus, i, m., = διάλογος, a (philosophical) conversation, a dialogue (for syn.

dialutense.full: dĭălutense genus purpurae, a sort of purple mussel found half in the mud [lutum; acc. to others, = διάλυτος, dissolutus], Plin. 9, 37, 6, § 131 Sillig.
dialutense.short: dĭălutense genus purpurae, a sort of purple mussel found half in the mud [lutum;

dialysis.full: dĭălўsis, is, f., = διάλυσις, rhet. t. t., a separation, Rutil. Lup. 1, 15, p. 52.

dialyton.full: dĭălўton, i, n., = διάλυτον, rhet. t. t., i. q. dialysis, Jul. Rufin. de Fig. 18, p. 240.

diamastigosis.full: dĭămastīgōsis, is, f., = διαμαστίγωσις, a severe scourging, Tert. ad Mart. 4.
diamastigosis.short: dĭămastīgōsis, is, f., = διαμαστίγωσις, a severe scourging, Tert.

diameliloton.full: dĭămĕlĭlōtōn = διὰ μελιλώτων, a salve made of meliloton, Cael. Aur. Tard. 1, 3 al.
diameliloton.short: dĭămĕlĭlōtōn = διὰ μελιλώτων, a salve made of meliloton, Cael.

diameliton.full: dĭămĕlĭtōn = διὰ μελίτων, a salve made of honey, Theod. Prisc. 4, 1.
diameliton.short: dĭămĕlĭtōn = διὰ μελίτων, a salve made of honey, Theod.

diametros.full: dĭămē^tros, i, f., = διάμετρος, a diameter, Col. 5, 2, 7; Vitr. 10, 14; Macr. Somn. Scip. 1, 20 sq. al.— Adj., central: radiatio, Firm. Math. 4, 1 med.
diametros.short: dĭămē^tros, i, f., = διάμετρος, a diameter, Col.

diametrum.full: dĭămetrum, i, n. (that is wanting to the measure), the wantage, loss, Cod. Theod. 13, 5, 38.

diamisyos.full: dĭămĭsўos = διὰ μίσυος, a salve made of misy (vitriolic earth), Marc. Emp. 9.
diamisyos.short: dĭămĭsўos = διὰ μίσυος, a salve made of misy (vitriolic earth), Marc.

diamoron.full: dĭămŏrōn, i, n., = διὰ μόρων, a medicament composed of the juice of black mulberries and honey, Pall. Sept. 16; Cael. Aur. Acut. 3, 3, 18.
diamoron.short: dĭămŏrōn, i, n., = διὰ μόρων, a medicament composed of the juice of black mulberries and honey, Pall.

diana.full: Dĭāna (in inscrr. also, DEANA, Orell. 1453; 1462; 1546. Also written Jana, Varr. R. R. 1, 37, 3; cf. Nigid. ap. Macr. S. 1, 9. The i measured long, Cinna ap. Suet. Gramm. 11; Verg. A. 1, 499; Hor. C. 1, 21, 1; cf. Diom. p. 436 P.; hence also, Deiana, Enn. ap. Ap. de Deo Socr.), ae, f. for Divana, Gr. Διώνη for Διϝωνη; root DI-, DIV-; cf. Gr. Ζεύς, also Jovis (Diovis), Deus, dies, divus, etc., orig. an Italian divinity, afterwards regarded as identical with the Gr. Ἄρτεμις, the daughter of Jupite

dianoea.full: dĭănœa, ae, f., = διάνοια, rhet. t. t., by which a fact is exhibited instead of a conception, Jul. Rufin. de Fig. 18, p. 210.

dianome.full: dĭănŏme, ēs, f., = διανομή, distribution of money (in canvassing for office), Plin. Ep. 10, 117 fin.; ib. 118.
dianome.short: dĭănŏme, ēs, f., = διανομή, distribution of money (in canvassing for office), Plin.

diapanton.full: dĭăpantōn = διὰ πάντων, universally: CORONATO, Inscr. Orell. 2627 sq.
diapanton.short: dĭăpantōn = διὰ πάντων, universally: CORONATO, Inscr.

diapasma.full: dĭăpasma, ătis, n., = διάπασμα, a scented powder for sprinkling on any thing, Plin. 13, 2, 3, § 19; 21, 19, 73, § 125; Mart. 1, 88, 5.
diapasma.short: dĭăpasma, ătis, n., = διάπασμα, a scented powder for sprinkling on any thing, Plin.

diapason.full: dĭăpāsōn = διὰ πασῶν (sc. χορδῶν), in music, the whole octave, Vitr. 5, 4, 8; Plaut. 2, 22, 20; Mart. Cap. 9, § 944; so too, dĭăpente = διὰ πέντε, a fifth, Mart. Cap. 9, § 934 al.; dĭătessărōn = διατεσσάρων, a fourth, id. 2, § 107; Vitr. 5, 4, 8; disdĭăpāsōn = δὶς διὰ πασῶν, a double octave, Plin. 2, 22, 20, § 84; Mart. Cap. 2, § 199 al. (All these words should perhaps be written here, as in Macr. Somn. Scip. 2, 1, in Greek letters.)

diapente.full: dĭăpentĕ = διὰ πέντε, n. indecl. V. diapason.— A medicine made of five ingredients, Veg. 2, 36, 1.

diaphonia.full: dĭăphōnĭa, ae, f., = διαφωνία, disharmony, discord, Isid. Or. 3, 19, 3.
diaphonia.short: dĭăphōnĭa, ae, f., = διαφωνία, disharmony, discord, Isid.

diaphora.full: dĭăphŏra, ae, f., = διαφορά, rhet. t. t., distinction (repetition of the same word in different meanings), Rutil. Lup. 12, p. 43.

diaphoresis.full: dĭăphŏrēsis, is, f., = διαφόρησις, in the later medic. lang., A sweat, Theod. Prisc. de Diaeta, 14.— Meton., an exhaustion, Cael. Aur. Acut. 1, 15.
diaphoresis.short: dĭăphŏrēsis, is, f., = διαφόρησις, in the later medic.

diaphoreticus.full: dĭăphŏrētĭcus, a, um, adj., = διαφορητικός, promoting perspiration, sudorific, diaphoretic: solutio, Cael. Aur. Acut. 1, 17.
diaphoreticus.short: dĭăphŏrētĭcus, a, um, adj., = διαφορητικός, promoting perspiration, sudorific, diaphoretic: solutio, Cael.

diaphragma.full: dĭaphragma, ătis, n., = διάφραγμα, the diaphragm, midriff, Cael. Aur. Tard. 2, 12 (in Cels. 2, 7, written as Greek).
diaphragma.short: dĭaphragma, ătis, n., = διάφραγμα, the diaphragm, midriff, Cael.

diapontius.full: Dĭăpontĭus, ĭi, m., = διαπόντιος, beyond seas, a feigned name in Plautus.
diapontius.short: Dĭăpontĭus, ĭi, m., = διαπόντιος, beyond seas, a feigned name in Plautus.

diaporesis.full: dĭăpŏrēsis, is, f., = διαπόρησις, rhet. t. t., a doubting, perplexity, Aquil. Rom. 10, p. 151: est addubitatio, Mart. Cap. 5, § 523.

diapsalma.full: dĭapsalma, ătis, n., = διάψαλμα, a pause in music, Hier. Ep. 28.
diapsalma.short: dĭapsalma, ătis, n., = διάψαλμα, a pause in music, Hier.

diapsoricum.full: dĭapsōrĭcum, i, n., = διὰ ψωρικῶν, an eye-salve, Marc. Emp. 9.
diapsoricum.short: dĭapsōrĭcum, i, n., = διὰ ψωρικῶν, an eye-salve, Marc.

diarium.full: dĭārĭum, ii, n. dies. A daily allowance of food or pay (so only in the plur.), Cic. Att. 8, 14; Hor. Ep. 1, 14, 40; Sen. Contr. 4, 27 fin.; cf. Charis. p. 21 P.— * A diary, journal: diarium, quam Graeci ἐφημερίδα vocant, Asel. ap. Gell. 5, 18, 8; cf. Isid. Or. 1, 43, 1.

diarrhoea.full: dĭarrhoea, ae, f., = διάῤῥοια, diarrhœa, Cael. Aur. Acut. 3, 19.
diarrhoea.short: dĭarrhoea, ae, f., = διάῤῥοια, diarrhœa, Cael.

diasostes.full: dĭăsostes, ae, m., = διασώστης, a sort of policemen, Julian. Epit. nov. 123, § 532 and 537.
diasostes.short: dĭăsostes, ae, m., = διασώστης, a sort of policemen, Julian.

diaspermaton.full: dĭaspermatōn, i, n., = διὰ σπερμάτων, a drug made from seeds, Isid. Or. 4, 9, 9; Cael. Aur. Tard. 3, 8, 116.
diaspermaton.short: dĭaspermatōn, i, n., = διὰ σπερμάτων, a drug made from seeds, Isid.

diastema.full: dĭastēma (short ĕ, Sid. Carm. 15, 64), ătis, n., = διάστημα, space between, distance, interval (late Lat.). In gen., Sid. Ep. 8, 11 med.— Esp., in music, an interval, Mart. Cap. 9, § 948; Censor. 13.

diastematicus.full: dĭastēmătĭcus, a, um, adj., = διαστηματικός, having pauses, intervals: vox (opp. continua), Mart. Cap. 9, § 937.
diastematicus.short: dĭastēmătĭcus, a, um, adj., = διαστηματικός, having pauses, intervals: vox (opp.

diastole.full: dĭastŏle, ēs, f., = διαστολή, in gram., The diastole, Diom. p. 470 P. al.— The comma, Donat. p. 1742 P.
diastole.short: dĭastŏle, ēs, f., = διαστολή, in gram., The diastole, Diom.

diastoleus.full: dĭastŏleus, ei, m., = διαστολεύς, an auditor of accounts, Cod. 4, 69, 4.
diastoleus.short: dĭastŏleus, ei, m., = διαστολεύς, an auditor of accounts, Cod.

diastylos.full: dĭastȳlos, on, adj., = διάστυλος, having columns far apart, diastyle: species aedium, Vitr. 3, 3, 1 sq.
diastylos.short: dĭastȳlos, on, adj., = διάστυλος, having columns far apart, diastyle: species aedium, Vitr.

diasyrmos.full: dĭăsyrmos, i, m., = διασυρμός, mockery, reviling, Mart. Cap. 5, § 524.
diasyrmos.short: dĭăsyrmos, i, m., = διασυρμός, mockery, reviling, Mart.

diasyrticus.full: dĭăsyrtĭcus, a, um, adj., = διασυρτικός, mocking, reviling: Spart. Carac. 10: praedicatio, Hier. adv. Ruf. 1, no. 1.—Adv.: dĭăsyrtĭcē, mockingly, Serv. Verg. A. 2, 193.
diasyrticus.short: dĭăsyrtĭcus, a, um, adj., = διασυρτικός, mocking, reviling: Spart.

diatessaron.full: dĭătessărōn = διὰ τεσσάρων, n. indecl. v. diapason.— A medicine made of four ingredients, Cael. Aur. Acut. 2, 18, 112; Plin. Val. 3, 22.

diathyra.full: dĭăthўra, ōrum, n., = διάθυρα, an enclosure before the door of a Greek house (called, in Roman houses, prothyra), Vitr. 6, 10.
diathyra.short: dĭăthўra, ōrum, n., = διάθυρα, an enclosure before the door of a Greek house (called, in Roman houses, prothyra), Vitr.

diatoichon.full: dĭătoichon, i, n., = διάτοιχον, a sort of brick-work, Plin. 36, 22, 51, § 172 ex conj., v. Sillig. ad h. 1.
diatoichon.short: dĭătoichon, i, n., = διάτοιχον, a sort of brick-work, Plin.

diatonicus.full: dĭătŏnĭcus, a, um, adj., = διατονικός, diatonic, in music: modulatio, Mart. Cap. 9, § 959; § 963.— Neutr. as subst.: diatonicon, i, a kind of masonry filled in with rubble, Plin. 36, 22, 51, § 172.
diatonicus.short: dĭătŏnĭcus, a, um, adj., = διατονικός, diatonic, in music: modulatio, Mart.

diatonus.full: dĭătŏnus, a, um, adj., = διάτονος (extended). In architecture: lateres, band-stones, which run through the thickness of a wall and bind it together, Vitr. 2, 8, 7.— In music: diatonum, i, the natural or diatonic series of notes without breaks or intervals, the diatonic scale, Vitr. 5, 4, 3 sq.; Macr. Somn. Scip. 2, 4.

diatretarius.full: dĭā^trētārĭus, ii, m. diatretus, one who does perforated or filigree work, a turner, carver, Cod. Theod. 13, 4, 2 al.

diatretus.full: dĭā^trētus, a, um, adj., = διάτρητος, pierced with holes, filigree, carved, embossed: calix, Dig. 9, 2, 27, § 29.—Subst.: dĭătrēta, ōrum, n., pierced work, filigree-work, Mart. 12, 70, 9.
diatretus.short: dĭā^trētus, a, um, adj., = διάτρητος, pierced with holes, filigree, carved, embossed: calix, Dig.

diatriba.full: dĭā^trĭba, ae, f., = διατριβή, a learned discussion.—Transf., a school, Gell. 1, 26; 17, 20, 4 al.
diatriba.short: dĭā^trĭba, ae, f., = διατριβή, a learned discussion.—Transf., a school, Gell.

diatritaeus.full: dĭā^trĭtaeus, a, um, adj., = διατριταῖος, of the space of three days: tempus, Cael. Aur. Acut. 1, 3, 35; cf. the foll.
diatritaeus.short: dĭā^trĭtaeus, a, um, adj., = διατριταῖος, of the space of three days: tempus, Cael.

diatritus.full: dĭā^trĭtus, i, f., = διάτριτος, the return of a fever on the third day, Cael. Aur. Tard. 1, 1 (twice); 1, 3, 57 al.
diatritus.short: dĭā^trĭtus, i, f., = διάτριτος, the return of a fever on the third day, Cael.

diatyposis.full: dĭătўpōsis, is, f., = διατύπωσις, rhet. t. t., a description, representation, Mart. Cap. 5, § 524 al.

diaula.full: dĭaula, ae, f., a plant, Ap. Herb. 93.
diaula.short: dĭaula, ae, f., a plant, Ap.

diaulos.full: dĭaulos, i, m., = δίαυλος, a double course (in which the runner, after reaching the goal, ran the same distance back), Vitr. 5, 11; Hyg. Fab. 173.
diaulos.short: dĭaulos, i, m., = δίαυλος, a double course (in which the runner, after reaching the goal, ran the same distance back), Vitr.

diazeugmenon.full: dĭăzeugmĕnon, i, n., = διαζεύγμενον, in rhet., a separation, disjunction, Mart. Cap. 5, § 536.
diazeugmenon.short: dĭăzeugmĕnon, i, n., = διαζεύγμενον, in rhet., a separation, disjunction, Mart.

diazeuxis.full: dĭăzeuxis, is, f., = διάζευξις, rhet. t. t., = diaeresis, a separation, Prob. p. 1438 P.

diazoma.full: dĭăzōma, ătis, n., = διάζωμα, a space between the seats in a theatre, Vitr. 5, 6, 7; cf. balteus, no. 2. d.
diazoma.short: dĭăzōma, ătis, n., = διάζωμα, a space between the seats in a theatre, Vitr.

dibalo.full: dī-bālo, āre, v. a., to bleat abroad, i. e. to make common or contemptible by clamor; to injure, Caecil. ap. Varr. L. L. 7, § 103 Müll. (Rib. Com. v. 249).

dibaphus.full: dĭbăphus, a, um, or us, um, adj., = δίβαφος, double dyed (once with scarlet and then with purple): purpura, Plin. 9, 39, 63, § 137; 21, 8, 22, § 45.—Because the Roman magistrates wore garments striped with purple, Trop.: dibaphus, i, f. ( = ἡ δίβαφος, sc. ἐσθής), the purple staterobe of a high magistrate: Curtius noster dibaphum cogitat, sed eum infector moratur, Cic. Fam. 2, 16 fin. (id. Att. 2, 9, 2, written as Greek).
dibaphus.short: dĭbăphus, a, um, or us, um, adj., = δίβαφος, double dyed (once with scarlet and then with purple): purpura, Plin.

dibrachys.full: dībrăchys = δίβραχυς, a metrical foot consisting of two short syllables, a dibrach, Diom. p. 471 P.; Mar. Victor. p. 2486 ib. (pure Lat. bibrevis).
dibrachys.short: dībrăchys = δίβραχυς, a metrical foot consisting of two short syllables, a dibrach, Diom.

dibucino.full: dī-būcĭno, āre, v. a., to trumpet forth, acc. to Vel. Long. p. 2227 P.; Cassiod. p. 2294 ib.

dica.full: dĭca, ae, f., = δίκη, law t. t., a lawsuit, judicial process, action. Usually in the phrase dicam scribere (alicui) = δίκην γράφειν τινί, to bring an action against any one, Plaut. Aul. 4, 10, 30; Ter. Ph. 1, 2, 77; 2, 2, 15; Cic. Verr. 2, 2, 14, § 37; 2, 2, 17, § 42: subscribere, Plaut. Poen. 3, 6, 5; and stronger, impingere, to bring a heavy action against one, Ter. Ph. 2, 3, 92: e lege Rupilia sortiri dicas oportere, to select the jury by lot, Cic. Verr. 2, 2, 17.
dica.short: dĭca, ae, f., = δίκη, law t.

dicabula.full: dĭcābŭla and dĭcĭbŭla, ōrum, n. dicax, chatter, idle talk (late Lat.), Mart. Cap. 8, § 809; Tert. adv. Val. 20.

dicacitas.full: dĭcācĭtas, ātis, f. id., biting wit, raillery, banter (for syn. cf.: sal, facetiae, cavillatio, lepos, urbanitas): dicacitas sine dubio a dicendo, quod est omni generi commune, ducta est; proprie tamen significat sermonem cum risu aliquos incessentem, Quint. 6, 3, 21; cf. Cic. de Or. 2, 54, 218; 2, 60, 244; id. Or. 26; Quint. 6, 3, 29 al.

dicaculus.full: dĭcācŭlus, a, um, adj. id.. * Talkative, loquacious: amatrix, Plaut. As. 3, 1, 8.— Facetious, witty (perh. only in Appul.): puella (with lepida), Ap. M. 2, p. 118, 2: sermo, id. ib. 3, 135, 9.—Adv.: dĭcācŭlē, keenly, satirically, facetiously: dixerat probrum, Ap. M. 1, p. 106, 20: tractabat lurconem, id. ib. 8, p. 213, 6.

dicaearchia.full: Dĭcaearchī^a, ae, f., the old name of Puteoli, now Puzzuolo, Plin. 3, 5, 9, § 61; cf. Paul. ex Fest. p. 72, 4 Müll.—Also called Dĭcarchis, ĭdos, f., Petr. 120, 68; and: Dicarchi moenia, Stat. Silv. 2, 2, 96.— Derivv. Dĭcaearchi, the inhabitants of that city.—Gen. plur. in Greek form, Dicaearcheum, Lucil. ap. Paul. ex Fest. p. 122, 14 Müll. (cf. Lachm. ad Lucr. vol. 2, p. 193 and 281).— Dĭcarchē-us, a, um, adj., of Dicaearchia or Puteoli: sinus, Stat. Silv. 2, 2, 110: urbs, Sil. 13, 385: proles,
dicaearchia.short: Dĭcaearchī^a, ae, f., the old name of Puteoli, now Puzzuolo, Plin.

dicaearchus.full: Dĭcaearchus, i, m., Δικαίαρχος. The founder of Dicaearchia, Stat. Silv. 2, 2, 96.— A pupil of Aristotle, a famous philosopher and geographer, Cic. Tusc. 1, 10; 31 fin.; id. Off. 2, 5; Varr. R. R. 1, 2, 16 al.

dicaeologia.full: dĭcaeŏlŏgia, ae, f., = δικαιολογία, a rhet. t. t., a plea, defence, Rutil. Lup. 3, p. 81.
dicaeologia.short: dĭcaeŏlŏgia, ae, f., = δικαιολογία, a rhet.

dicarcheus.full: Dĭcarchēus, a, um, v. Dicaearchia, no. II. B.

dicatio.full: dĭcātĭo, ōnis, f. 1. dico, no. II. B. 1.. A formal declaration of intention to become a citizen, Cic. Balb. 11 (v. the passage in its connection).— = praedicatio, a praising. Prop., Cod. Theod. 9, 3, 2. — As a title: tua dicatio, your Reverence, Cod. Theod. 11, 30, 1; Lact. Mort. pers. 48 al.

dicatus.full: dĭcātus, a, um, P. a., v. 1. dico.

dicax.full: dĭcax, ācis, adj. 1. dico, talking sharply, satirical, sarcastic, acute, witty (class.): Demosthenes non tam dicax fuit quam facetus. Est autem illud acrioris ingenii, hoc majoris artis, Cic. Or. 26, 90; cf. Quint. 6, 3, 21; so with facetus, Cic. de Or. 2, 54, 221; id. Cael. 28, 67; with venustus and urbanus, *Catull. 22, 2; with lascivus, Caelius in Quint. 6, 3, 41; with cavillator, Plaut. Truc. 3, 2, 15 et saep.: Satyri, Hor. A. P. 225: dicax in aliquem, Cic. Phil. 2, 31 fin.: argutia, Gell. 1

dice.full: dīcĕ and dīcēbo, v. 2. dico init.

dichalcum.full: dĭchalcum, i, n., = δίχαλκον, a small coin, the fourth (acc. to others, the fifth) part of an obolus, Vitr. 3, 1; cf. Plin. 21, 34, 109, § 185.
dichalcum.short: dĭchalcum, i, n., = δίχαλκον, a small coin, the fourth (acc.

dichomenion.full: dĭchŏmēnĭon, ĭi, n., = διχομήνιον, a plant, App. Herb. 64.
dichomenion.short: dĭchŏmēnĭon, ĭi, n., = διχομήνιον, a plant, App.

dichoneutus.full: dĭchōneutus, a, um, adj., = δισ-χώνευτος, recast, adulterated: aes, Cod. Theod. 11, 21, 1.
dichoneutus.short: dĭchōneutus, a, um, adj., = δισ-χώνευτος, recast, adulterated: aes, Cod.

dichoreus.full: dĭchŏrēus, i, m., = διχορεῖος, a double trochee, Cic. Or. 63, 212 sq.
dichoreus.short: dĭchŏrēus, i, m., = διχορεῖος, a double trochee, Cic.

dichotomos.full: dĭchŏtŏmos, on, adj., = διχότομος, cut in two, halved (pure Lat. dimidiatus), Macr. Somn. Scip. 1, 6; Firm. Math. 4 praef.
dichotomos.short: dĭchŏtŏmos, on, adj., = διχότομος, cut in two, halved (pure Lat.

dichronus.full: dī^chrŏnus, a, um, adj., = δίχρονος, of two quantities, common (pure Lat. anceps): vocales, Victor. p. 1966 P. al.; Mart. Cap. 9, § 982.
dichronus.short: dī^chrŏnus, a, um, adj., = δίχρονος, of two quantities, common (pure Lat.

dicimonium.full: dīcĭmōnĭum, i, n. 2. dīco, speaking, oratory, an antiquated word acc. to Varr. L. L. 6, § 61 ex conj. Müll.

dicio.full: dĭcĭo, ōnis (less correctly, ditio; occurs only in the gen., dat., acc., and abl. sing., and in plur. once, Prud. Psych. 221; so Hemsterhuis, Orat. p. 7.—Georges rejects the dat. sing., but v. infra; cf. Neue, Formenl. 1, 514 sq.), f. root dic-; Sanscr. dicami, point out; Gr. δείκνυμι; Lat. dico; cf.: condicio, judex, a t. t., milit. and polit., dominion, sovereignty, authority, rule, sway, power. Prop.: Commagenem, dicionis regiae usque ad id tempus, etc., Suet. Vesp. 8: Poenum quod inter Alpes

dicis.full: dicis, gen. [v. 2. dico], in the phrase dicis causa or gratia, orig. a jurid. t. t., meaning for the sake of judicial form; hence, in gen., for form's sake, for the sake of appearance, λόγου χάριν: ut illis aliquid nummulorum dicis causa daret, Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 24; id. Att. 1, 18, 5 Orell. N. cr.; Nep. Att. 8; Dig. 29, 5, 1, § 34: dicis gratia, ib. 13, 6, 4; Inst. 1, 103 sq.; 2, 252.— Transf.: si Pontifici accidat dicis causa epulanti, Plin. 28, 2, 5, § 27; Arn. 3, 16 Orell. N. cr.: dicis ergo =

dico1.full: dĭco, āvi, ātum, 1 (dixe for dixisse, Val. Ant. ap. Arn. 5, 1; DICASSIT dixerit, Paul. ex Fest. p. 75, 15; rather = dicaverit), v. a. orig. the same word with 2. dīco; cf. the meaning of abdĭco and abdīco, of indĭco and indīco, dedĭco, no. II. A. al., Corss. Ausspr. 1, 380. To proclaim, make known. So perh. only in the foll. passage: pugnam, Lucil. ap. Non. 287, 30.—Far more freq., Relig. t. t., to dedicate, consecrate, devote any thing to a deity or to a deified person (for syn. cf.: dedico, co
dico1.short: dĭco, āvi, ātum, 1 (dixe for dixisse, Val.

dico2.full: dīco, xi, ctum, 3 (praes. DEICO, Inscr. Orell. 4848; imp. usu. dic; cf. duc, fac, fer, from duco, etc., DEICVNTO, and perf. DEIXSERINT, P. C. de Therm. ib. 3673; imp. dice, Naev. ap. Fest. p. 298, 29 Müll.; Plaut. Capt. 2, 2, 109; id. Bac. 4, 4, 65; id. Merc. 1, 2, 47 al.; cf. Quint. 1, 6, 21; fut. dicem = dicam, Cato ap. Quint. 1, 7, 23; cf. Paul. ex Fest. p. 72, 6 Müll.—Another form of the future is dicebo, Novius ap. Non. 507 (Com. v. 8 Rib.). —Perf. sync.: dixti, Plaut. As. 4, 2, 14; id. Tri

dicrotum.full: dicrŏtum, i, n. (sc. navigium), = δίκροτος (two-oared), a galley with two banks of oars, Cic. Att. 5, 11, 4; 16, 4 fin.—Also called dicrŏta, ae, f. (sc. navis), Auct. B. Alex. 47, 2.

dictabolarium.full: dictābŏlārĭum, ii, n. dicto, i. q. dicterium, a satirical saying, plur., Laber. ap. Fronto de Or. 1.

dictaeus.full: Dictaeus, a, um, v. Dicte, no. II. A.

dictamen.full: dictāmen, inis, n. dicto, late Lat. for dictum, praescriptum, praeceptum.

dictamnum.full: dictamnum, or -us, i, v. Dicte, no. II. B.

dictata.full: dictāta, ōrum, n., lessons, exercises, etc., v. dicto fin.
dictata.short: dictāta, ōrum, n., lessons, exercises, etc., v.

dictatio.full: dictātĭo, ōnis, f. dicto, a dictating, dictation (late Lat.), Dig. 29, 1, 4 al.

dictatiuncula.full: dictātĭuncŭla, ae, f. dim. dictatio, a short dictation, Hier. adv. Vigil. 3.

dictator.full: dictātor, ōris, m. dicto, qs. a commander. A dictator, the chief magistrate in several Italian states, elected by the Romans in seasons of emergency for six months, and armed with absolute authority; formerly called Magister populi, and also Praetor Maximus, Cic. Leg. 3, 3, 9; id. Rep. 1, 40; Liv. 7, 3; Cic. Rep. 2, 32; Liv. 2, 18; Lydus de Magistr. 1, 36-38 et saep.; cf. Mommsen, Hist. Book I. ch. 2; 1, p. 330 N. Y. ed. Anthon's Smith's Antiq. p. 360; Kreuz. Excurs. XII. to Cic. Leg. p. 509.—Th

dictatorius.full: dictātōrĭus, a, um, adj. dictator, of or belonging to a dictator; dictatorial: gladius, Cic. Clu. 44, 123: majestas, Liv. 4, 14; 8, 30: fulmen, id. 6, 39: invidia, id. 22, 26; cf. animadversio, Vell. 2, 68 fin.: juvenis, i. e. the son of the dictator, Liv. 7, 4.

dictatrix.full: dictātrix, īcis, f. id., a dictatress, comic., Plaut. Pers. 5, 1, 18.

dictatura.full: dictātūra, ae, f. id.. The office of a dictator, dictatorship, Cic. Phil. 1, 1 fin.; id. Off. 3, 31, 112; * Caes. B. C. 3, 2; Liv. 6, 39; 7, 3 fin.; Quint. 3, 8, 53; Suet. Caes. 76; id. Aug. 52 et saep.—* The work of dictating to pupils; only in a play upon the double meaning in the sentence: Sullam nescisse litteras, qui dictaturam deposuerit, Caes. ap. Suet. Caes. 77.

dicte.full: Dictē, ēs, f., Δίκτη, a mountain in the eastern part of Crete (now Sethia), in a cave of which Jupiter, acc. to fable, was concealed from Saturn, Plin. 24, 17, 102, § 164.— Derivv., Dictaeus, a, um, adj., Dictaean, among poets for Cretan: arva, Verg. A. 3, 171: saltus, id. ib. 4, 73: rura, Ov. M. 3, 2: greges, id. F. 5, 118: antrum, Verg. G. 4, 152: Nymphae, id. E. 6, 57: rex, i. e. Jupiter, id. G. 2, 536; also, Minos, Ov. M. 8, 43: Telestes, id. 9, 717: Dictaeae astra coronae, i. e. of Ariadne,
dicte.short: Dictē, ēs, f., Δίκτη, a mountain in the eastern part of Crete (now Sethia), in a cave of which Jupiter, acc.

dicterium.full: dictērĭum, ii, n., = δεικτήριον, a witty saying, a bon-mot (pure Lat. dictum). —Plur., Pompcn. ap. Macr. S. 2, 1, 14; Varr. ap. Non. 101, 3: dicteria dicere in omnes, Mart. 6, 44, 3.
dicterium.short: dictērĭum, ii, n., = δεικτήριον, a witty saying, a bon-mot (pure Lat.

dicticos.full: dictĭcŏs, on, adj., = δεικτικός. Gen., pointing: digitus quem Graeci dicticon vocant, Cael. Aur. Tard. 5, 1, 21.— Esp., rhet. t. t., demonstrative: enthymema, Jul. Vict. Art. Rhet. 11.

dictio.full: dictĭo, ōnis, f. 2. dico, a saying, speaking, uttering, delivery. In gen. (Good prose, for the most part only in jurid. and rhetor. lang.) Sententiae, Cic. Inv. 2, 4: testimonii, i. e. the right of giving testimony, *Ter. Ph. 2, 1, 63: causae, a defending, pleading, Cic. Quint. 10, 35; id. Sest. 17 fin.; * Caes. B. G. 1, 4, 2; Liv. 7, 5 al.: multae ovium et boum, Cic. Rep. 2, 9 fin.— Kinds of delivery, style, diction: seposuisse a ceteris dictionibus eam partem dicendi, quae, etc., id. de Or. 1,

dictiosus.full: dictĭōsus, a, um, adj. dictum, perhaps facetious, satirical, Varr. L. L. 6, § 61 Müll.

dictito.full: dictĭto, āvi, ātum, 1, v. intens. a. [dicto], to say often or emphatically; to declare, maintain, assert repeatedly (good prose). In gen.: non, obsecro, es, quem semper te esse dictitasti, Ter. Ph. 5, 1, 16.; cf. Liv. 3, 20; 9, 18: qui ita dictitat, iis esse metuendum, etc., Cic. Verr. 1, 2, 4; 1, 3, 8; 1, 10, 28; 2, 1, 8: ut Lacedaemonii suos omnes agros esse dictitarint, quos spiculo possent attingere, id. Rep. 3, 9: Caelius profectus, ut dictitabat, ad Caesarem pervenit, as he alleged, or pre

dicto.full: dicto, āvi, ātum, 1, v. freq. a. 2. dico, to say often; to pronounce, declare, or assert repeatedly. In gen. (very rare): rogarem te, ut diceres pro me tu idem, qui illis orationem dictavisses, Cic. Fin. 4, 22 fin.: mercemur servum qui dictet nomina, Hor. Ep. 1, 6, 50; cf. Gell. 4, 1, 2.—Far more freq. and class., In partic. To dictate to one for writing: quod non modo Tironi dictare, sed ne ipse quidem audere scribere, Cic. Att. 13, 9; 7, 13 b. fin.; 2, 23; Quint. 2, 4, 12; 10, 3, 18; Plin. Ep.

dictor.full: dictor, ōris, m. 2. dico, one who says something, a speaker (late Lat.), Aug. Doctr. Chr. 4, 19 al.

dictum.full: dictum, i, n., v. 2. dico, II.

dicturio.full: dictŭrĭo, īre, v. desid. a., to long to say or tell (late Lat.): fortiter a se facta semper dicturiunt, Macr. S. 7, 2, 7; 2, 3, 16.

dictus1.full: dictus, a, um, Part., from 2. dico.

dictus2.full: dictus, ūs, m. 2. dico, a saying, speech, Aur. Vict. epit. 14.

dictynna.full: Dictynna, ae, f., Δίκτυννα. The nymph Britomartis, so called because, when pursued by Minos, she sprang into a net (δίκτυον; cf. Callim. Hymn. Dian. 189 sq.), Verg. Cir. 304.— An appellation of Diana, Ov. M. 2, 441; 5, 619; id. F. 6, 755; Tib. 1, 4, 25; Stat. Th. 9, 632.—Hence, Dictynnaeum (-nēum), i, n., a place sacred to the goddess Dictynna, near Sparta, Liv. 34, 38, 5.— Dictynnaeus mons (τὸ Δικτύνναιον), a promontory on the N. W. coast of Crete, where a temple of Diana stood, now Cape Sparta

dictys.full: Dictys, ўos, m., Δίκτυς. A mariner changed by Bacchus into a dolphin, Ov. M. 3, 615.— A centaur, slain at the wedding of Pirithoüs, Ov. M. 12, 334 sq.— A fisherman on the island of Seriphos, who saved Perseus from drowning, Stat. S. 2, 1, 95.— Dictys Cretensis, the traditional author of a mythical history of the Trojan war, in Greek; preserved to us in the Latin translation of L. Septimius, v. Teuffel, Roem. Lit. § 416, 1-4.

didascalicus.full: dĭdascălĭcus, a, um, adj., = διδασκαλικός, pertaining to instruction, didactic (ante- and post-class.): opusculum, Aus. Ep. 17.—Subst.: Dĭdascălica, ōn or ōrum, n., the title of a work by Attius, in Gell. 3, 11, 4 al.; cf. Madvig Opuscc. Acadd. prior. pp. 87-110.
didascalicus.short: dĭdascălĭcus, a, um, adj., = διδασκαλικός, pertaining to instruction, didactic (ante- and post-class.): opusculum, Aus.

diditus.full: dīdĭtus, a, um, Part., from 1. dido.

didius.full: Dīdĭus, a, um, the name of a Roman plebeian gens; so T. Didius, consul in the year 656 a. u. c., Cic. Planc. 25, 61; Ov. F. 6, 568 al.; Didius Julianus, emperor of Rome in the year 193 A. D., whose life is written by Spartianus.— Adj.: Lex Didia sumptuaria, of the year 610 a. u. c., Macr. S. 2, 13, 6. Another law: Lex Caecilia Didia, of the year 656, Cic. Sest. 64, 135; id. Att. 2, 9, 1 al.
didius.short: Dīdĭus, a, um, the name of a Roman plebeian gens;

dido1.full: dī-do (also written disdo; v. the foll.), didĭdi, didĭtum, 3, v. a., to give out, spread abroad, disseminate, distribute (anteclass. and poet.; esp. in Lucr.; once in Tac.). Lit.: numquam ego argentum ... disdidi, Cato ap. Fronto Ep. ad Anton. 1, 2, p. 150: in venas cibum, Lucr. 2, 1136; 4, 956; 6, 947; cf. id. 3, 703; 4, 633: omne per caules palati, id. 4, 623; cf. id. 3, 246; 5, 269; 6, 1166.—Absol.: dide, disice, Caecil. ap. Cic. Cael. 16, 37 (Com. Frag. v. 239 Rib.).— Trop.: dum munia didit

dido2.full: Dīdō, ūs and ōnis, f., Διδώ, the celebrated foundress of Carthage, daughter of the Tyrian king Belus, wife of Sichaeus, and sister of Pygmalion; called also Elisa or Elissa.—Nom. Dido, Verg. A. 1, 299; 340; 360 et saep.; Ov. Am. 2, 18, 25; id. F. 3, 545; 640.—Gen. Dīdōnis, Just. 11, 10, 13; Aug. Conf. 1, 13; Macr. Sat. 4, 3, 6 al.: Dīdūs, Cornutus ap. Charis. p. 102 P.—Dat. Dīdō, Macr. Sat. 5, 2, 14 (dub. al. Didoni): Dīdōni, Tert. Anim. 33.—Acc. Dīdō, Verg. A. 4, 383; Ov. H. 7, 7; 133 (in both
dido2.short: Dīdō, ūs and ōnis, f., Διδώ, the celebrated foundress of Carthage, daughter of the Tyrian king Belus, wife of Sichaeus, and sister of Pygmalion;

didrachmon.full: dī^drāchmon, i, and dī^drāchma, ătis, n., = διδραχμον, a double drachma, Tert. Praescr. 11; Vulg. Matt. 17, 23 al.
didrachmon.short: dī^drāchmon, i, and dī^drāchma, ătis, n., = διδραχμον, a double drachma, Tert.

diduco.full: dī-dūco, xi, ctum, 3, v. a., to draw apart; to part, split, separate, sever, sunder, divide (class.). Lit. In gen.: ventus eas (sc. nubes) leviter diducit, Lucr. 6, 215: cum compresserat digitos pugnumque fecerat ... cum autem diduxerat et manum dilataverat, etc., Cic. Or. 32, 113; of the graceful movements of the arms in dancing: molli diducit candida gestu brachia, Prop. 3, 15, 5 (Müll. al. deducit): candida seu molli diducit brachia motu, Stat. S. 3, 5, 66; cf. oculum, Cels. 7, 7, 4: supercil

diductio.full: dīductĭo, ōnis, f. diduco, an expanding, separating (very rare; perh. only in Seneca): ostendit intentionem spiritus velocitas ejus et diductio, Sen. Q. N. 2, 8, 2: in diductione rerum, in dividing, separating the elements, id. ib. 3, 13, 2.

diductus.full: dīductus, a, um, Part., from diduco.
diductus.short: dīductus, a, um, Part., from diduco.

didymae.full: Dĭdўmae, ārum, f. A group of islands on the coast of Troas, Plin. 5, 31, 38, § 138.— Islands on the coast of Lycia, Plin. 5, 31, 35, § 131. (In Ov. M. 7, 469, the better reading is Didyme.)

didymaeus.full: Dĭdўmaeus, a, um, adj. of Didyma, a city of Ionia: oraculum Didymaei Apollinis, Plin. 5, 29, 31, § 112; cf. ib. 6, 16, 18, § 49; Macr. Sat. 1, 17, 64, and v. Didyme, no. III.

didymaon.full: Dĭdўmāon, ŏnis, m., the name of a skilful artificer, Verg. A. 5, 359.
didymaon.short: Dĭdўmāon, ŏnis, m., the name of a skilful artificer, Verg.

didyme.full: Dĭdўmē, ēs, f. An island near Sicily, Plin. 3, 9, 14, § 94; Mel. 2, 7, 18; Ov. F. 4, 475.— An island in the Aegaean Sea, Ov. M. 7, 469.— A city in Ionia (also called Dĭdўma, Δίδυμα), in the Milesian territory, now Jeronda or Joran, with a temple and oracle of Apollo, called Dĭdў-mēon, i, n., Διδυμεῖον, Curt. 7, 5, 28; cf. Mütz. and Zumpt, ad h. l.—Hence also, Dĭdўmeus (trisyl.), ei, m., = Διδυμεύς, the Didymean, i. e. Apollo, Mel. 1, 17, 1.

diechidnon.full: dĭĕchī^dnōn δἰ ἐχιδνῶν, a medicine, Cael. Aur. Tard. 3, 2 sub fin.
diechidnon.short: dĭĕchī^dnōn δἰ ἐχιδνῶν, a medicine, Cael.

diecula.full: dĭēcŭla, ae, f. dim. dies, the short space of a day, one little day, a little while, Plaut. Ps. 1, 5, 88; Ter. And. 4, 2, 27; Cic. Att. 5, 21, 13; and repeatedly in Ap.; so Met. 1, p. 106; ib. 6, 179.

dierectus.full: di-ērectus (in Plaut. always trisyllabic), a um, P. a. erigo, qs. stretched out and raised on high, i. e. crucified (only in Plautus and Varro; not in Terence), an abusive expression, like the English Go and be hanged! gallowsbird, etc. (cf. furcifer, and v. Brix ad Plaut. Trin. 457; Lorence ad Plaut. Most. 837): i hinc dierectus, Plaut. Merc. 1, 72: abin dierectus, id. ib. 4, 4, 16; id. Cas. 1, 15; id. Poen. 1, 1, 32: recede hinc dierecte, id. Bacch. 4, 1, 7: abi dierecte, id. Most. 1, 1, 8; id

dies.full: dĭes (dīes, Liv. Andron. Fragm. Odys. 7), ēi (ēī, Verg. A. 4, 156; Hor. S. 1, 8, 35 et saep.; dissyl.: di-ei, Ter. Eun. 4, 7, 31; also gen. dies, die, and dii—dies, as in acies, facies, pernicies, etc., Enn. ap. Gell. 9, 14; Ann. v. 401 Vahl.; Cic. Sest. 12, 28 ap. Gell. l. l.: die, Prisc. p. 780 P.; even in Verg. G. 1, 208, where Gellius reads dies, v. Wagner ad loc., nearly all MSS. have die; cf. Rib. and Forbig. ad loc.; so, die, Plaut. Ps. 4, 7, 59; id. Capt. 4, 2, 20; Caes. B. G. 7, 11, 5;

diesis.full: dĭĕsis, is, f., = δίεσις. In ancient music, A quarter-tone, Vitr. 5, 4; Macr. Somn. Scip. 2, 1 fin.— The first audible tone of an instrument, Vitr. 5, 3.

diespiter.full: Dĭespĭter, tris, m. Dies, Sanscr. Divas, L. divus; cf. ho-dier-nus, and πατήρ, pater; cf. Corss. Ausspr. 1, 233; 2, 458, another name for Juppiter, Varr. L. L. 5, § 66 and 9, § 75 and 77 Müll.; Plaut. Capt. 4, 4, 1; id. Poen. 3, 4, 29; 4, 2, 47; Hor. Od. 1, 34, 5; 3, 2, 29; Gell. 5, 12, 5; Macr. S. 1, 15; Arn. 2, p. 93; of Pluto, Lact. 1, 14, 5.

dieteris.full: dĭĕtēris, ĭdis, f., = διετηρίς, a period of two years, Censor. 18, 2.
dieteris.short: dĭĕtēris, ĭdis, f., = διετηρίς, a period of two years, Censor.

diezeugmenon.full: dĭezeugmĕnon, i, n., = διεζευγμένον, rhet. t. t. (pure Lat. disjunctum), a separation of equal circumstances, Aquil. Rom. de Fig. 43, p. 187.— Plur., musical t. t., = τετράχορδα διεζευγμένα, two tetrachords, forming a scale, Vitr. 5, 4, 5.

diffamatio.full: diffāmātĭo, ōnis, f. diffamo, a publishing, promulgation (late Lat.), Aug. Civ. D. 3, 31.

diffamia.full: diffāmĭa, ae, f. dis-fama, defamation (late Lat.), Aug. Civ. D. 3, 31 al.

diffamo.full: dif-fāmo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. fama, to spread abroad by an ill report; to publish, divulge. Prop. (rare and not anteAug.): vulgat adulterium diffamatumque parenti Indicat, Ov. M. 4, 236; cf. prava, Tac. A. 14, 22: nomen pessimum super virginem, Vulg. Deut. 22, 19.— To decry, defame, malign: viros feminasque procacibus scriptis, Tac. A. 1, 72; cf.: aliquem probroso carmine, id. ib. 15, 49: aliquem probris, Ap. M. 1, p. 107; Vulg. Matt. 9, 31.— With acc. and inf.: diffamat, incendio repentino domu

diffarreatio.full: diffarrĕātĭo, ōnis, f., an ancient form of Roman divorce (cf.: remancipatio, divortium, repudium): genus sacrificii, quo inter virum et mulierem fiebat dissolutio. Dicta diffarreatio, quia fiebat farreo libo adhibito, Paul. ex Fest. p. 74, 13 Müll. (opp. confarreatio); Inscr. Orell. 2648; v. confarreatio.
diffarreatio.short: diffarrĕātĭo, ōnis, f., an ancient form of Roman divorce (cf.: remancipatio, divortium, repudium): genus sacrificii, quo inter virum et mulierem fiebat dissolutio.

diffensus.full: diffensus, a, um, Part. [dis- FENDO = ferio, trudo], deferred, protracted: dilatus, XII. Tab. ap. Fest. p. 273, 26 Müll. (for which others read diffisus; cf. Dig. 2, 11, 2, § 3, and v. diffindo, II. B.).

differens.full: diffĕrens and diffĕrenter, v. differo, P. a.

differentia.full: diffĕrentĭa, ae, f. differo, a difference, diversity (cf.: discrepantia, distantia, discrimen, diversitas, variatio—good prose, esp. freq. in Quint.). With gen.: honesti et decori, Cic. Off. 1, 27, 94: naturarum, id. ib. 1, 31, 112: morum, Petr. 84, 1: personarum, locorum temporumque, Quint. 12, 10, 70: nostri Graecique sermonis, id. 9, 4, 146 et saep.—In plur.: Graeci sermonis, Quint. 11, 2, 50.— With in: quanta differentia est in principiis naturalibus, Cic. Fin. 5, 7, 19; Quint. 3, 7, 25; 3,

differitas.full: diffĕrĭtas, ātis, f. id. (ante- and postclass.; v. the preceding art.), a difference, Lucr. 4, 636; Arn. 2, p. 54; 7, p. 233.

differo.full: dif-fĕro, distŭli, dīlātum, differre (inf. differrier, Lucr. 1, 1088. In tmesi: disque tulissent, Plaut. Trin. 4, 1, 14), v. a. and n. Act., to carry different ways; to spread abroad, scatter, disperse, separate (cf.: reicere, proferre, procrastinare, producere, ampliare, prorogare—class.). Lit.: scintillas agere ac late differre favillam, Lucr. 2, 675; cf.: favillam longe (ventus), id. 6, 692: nubila (vis venti), id. 1, 273; Verg. G. 3, 197: ignem (ventus), Caes. B. C. 2, 14, 2: casae venti mag

differtus.full: dif-fertus, a, um, Part. [farcio, kept asunder, stretched out by stuffing, i. e.], stuffed full, filled, crowded (cf.: plenus, refertus, confertus—rare but class.; not in Cicero): plena lictorum provincia, differta exactoribus, * Caes. B. C. 3, 32, 4: corpus odoribus, Tac. A. 16, 6: Forum Appi nautis, Hor. S. 1, 5, 4: differtum forum populumque = forum differtum populo, id. Ep. 1, 6, 59.

diffibulo.full: dif-fībŭlo, āre, v. a., to unclasp, unbuckle: chlamydem, Stat. Th. 6, 570: vincula, Sid. Ep. 3, 3.

difficile.full: diffĭcĭlē, adv., with difficulty; v. foll. art. fin., no. α.

difficilis.full: dif-fĭcĭlis, e (old form difficul, like facul, famul, simul, etc., Varr. ap. Non. 111, 25), adj. facilis; hence, far from easy to do, to accomplish, to bear, etc.; v. facilis, hard, difficult, troublesome (very freq. and class.). In gen.: nulla est tam facilis res, quin difficilis siet, quom invitus facias, Ter. Heaut. 4, 6, 1; cf. Plaut. Trin. 3, 2, 20; and: sacrorum diligentiam difficilem, apparatum perfacilem esse voluit, Cic. Rep. 2, 14 Mos.: quae facilia ex difficillimis animi magnitudo red
difficilis.short: dif-fĭcĭlis, e (old form difficul, like facul, famul, simul, etc., Varr.

difficiliter.full: diffĭcĭlĭter, adv., with difficulty; v. difficilis fin., no. γ.

difficultas.full: diffĭcultas, ātis (gen. plur. difficultatium, Liv. 9, 31, 14; Gell. 14, 2, 3), f. difficilis, difficulty, trouble, distress, poverty, want. In gen. (freq. in good prose in sing. and plur. With gen.: ineundi consilii, Cic. Rep. 1, 34: discendi (with labor), id. Div. 1, 47, 105: dicendi, id. de Or. 1, 26, 120: navigandi, id. ib. 1, 18, 82; Caes. B. G. 3, 12 fin.: belli gerendi, id. ib. 3, 10: faciundi pontis, id. ib. 4, 17, 2 et saep.: viarum, id. ib. 7, 56, 2; id. B. C. 1, 70; cf. loci, Sall. J.

difficulter.full: diffĭculter, adv., with difficulty; v. difficilis fin., no. β.

diffidens.full: diffīdens and diffīdenter, v. diffido, P. a.

diffidentia.full: diffīdentĭa, ae, f. diffido, want of confidence, mistrust, distrust, diffidence (class.).—Without gen.: fidentiae contrarium est diffidentia, Cic. Inv. 2, 54, 165; cf. id. Tusc. 4, 37, 80; so Quint. 5, 7, 1; 8 prooem. § 27; 9, 2, 72; Ov. R. Am. 543 al.— With gen.: diffidentiam rei simulare, Sall. J. 60, 5: memoriae, Quint. 11, 3, 142: causae, Plin. Ep. 5, 1, 7: praesentium, Tac. H. 1, 72: copiarum, Suet. Oth. 9 al.—With a dependent clause (cf. diffido, no. β: non tam diffidentiā, futurum quae im

diffido.full: dif-fīdo, fīsus (post-class. perf. diffidi), 3, v. n., to distrust; to be diffident or distrustful, to despair (freq. and class.). With dat. (so most freq.): eum potius (corrupisse), qui sibi aliqua ratione diffideret, quam eum, qui omni ratione confideret, Cic. Clu. 23, 63: sibi, Plaut. Rud. prol. 82; Cic. Prov. Cons. 16, 38: memoriae alicujus, id. Part. Or. 17, 59: sibi patriaeque, Sall. C. 31, 3: suis rebus, Caes. B. G. 5, 41, 5: veteri exercitui, Sall. J. 52, 6; 32, 5; 46, 1; 75, 1: suae atq

diffindo.full: dif-findo, fĭdi, fissum (also diffīsum), 3, v. a., to cleave asunder, to divide (rare but class.). Lit.: vitem mediam per medullam, Cato R. R. 41, 2: malos, Enn. ap. Non. 114, 7 (Ann. v. 389 ed. Vahl., where the read. is, as in Non., defindunt): ramum, Varr. R. R. 1, 40 fin.: terram, Lucr. 6, 584: saxum, Cic. Div. 1, 13 fin.: semen compressu suo (terra), id. de Sen. 15, 51: natem, Hor. S. 1, 8, 47: tempora plumbo, Verg. A. 9, 589; Suet. Gram. 11 et saep.— Poet.: urbium portas muneribus, i. e. to

diffingo.full: dif-fingo, ĕre, v. a., to form differently, to remodel, to make anew (very rare; perh. only in the foll. passages). Prop.: ferrum incude, Hor. C. 1, 35, 39.— Trop.: neque diffinget infectumque reddet, Quod fugiens semel hora vexit, to alter, Hor. C. 3, 29, 47 (but in id. S. 2, 1, 79 read diffindere).

diffissio.full: diffissĭo, ōnis, f. diffindo, no. II. B., the putting off or deferring of business to the following day: in dierum diffissionibus comperendinationibusque, Gell. 14, 2, 1.

diffissus.full: diffissus, a, um, Part., from diffindo.
diffissus.short: diffissus, a, um, Part., from diffindo.

diffisus.full: diffīsus, a, um, Part., from diffido and diffindo.
diffisus.short: diffīsus, a, um, Part., from diffido and diffindo.

diffiteor.full: dif-fĭtĕor, ēri, v. dep. a. [fateor], to disavow, to deny (very rare; perh. only in the foll. passages—for syn. v. denego init.): numquam diffitebor multa me simulasse invitum, Planc. in Cic. Fam. 10, 8, 4; so with acc. and inf., Quint. 2, 17, 5: obscenum opus, Ov. Am. 3, 14, 28; Aus. Caes. 14.

difflatus.full: difflātus, ūs, m. difflo, a blowing in an opposite direction: ventorum, Amm. 15, 11, 18.

diffletus.full: dif-flētus, a, um, Part. [fleo], wept out, drained with weeping (post-class. and very rare): oculi, App. M. 1, p. 104; cf.: cognita clade uxor totos efflevit oculos, Pseudo uint. Decl. 6, 4.

difflo.full: dif-flo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a., to blow apart, disperse by blowing: flatu disturbare, Non. 97, 10 (ante- and post-class.): pars difflatur vento, Lucil. ap. Non. 97, 12: legiones spiritu, Plaut. Mil. 1, 1, 17: nubila (nimbi), Aus. Ephem. fin.: pulverem (ventus), Prud. Hamart. 388.—Fig., of political strife: difflantibus procellis rempublicam, Amm. 25, 9, 7.

diffluo.full: dif-flŭo, ĕre, v. n., to flow in different directions, to flow away (class.; repeatedly in Lucr.—cf.: laxo, rescindo, solvo). Lit.: diffluere humorem cernis, Lucr. 3, 436; cf.: ut nos quasi extra ripas diffluentes coerceret, Cic. Brut. 91 fin.; cf.: in plures partes (Rhenus), divides itself, Caes. B. G. 4, 10, 4: ut ab summo tibi diffluat altus acervus, Lucr. 3, 198.—Poet., of that from which any thing flows: duo juvenes, Sudore multo diffluentes, dripping with perspiration, Phaedr. 4, 25, 23; s

diffluus.full: difflŭus, a, um, adj. diffluo, flowing asunder, overflowing, Matius ap. Macr. S. 2, 16, 5.

diffluvio.full: dif-flŭvĭo, āre, v. a. fluvius; cf. quadrifluvium (qs. to part into two streams, i. e.), to divide, to split: vitem, Col. Arb. 7, 5; cf. Schneid. ad Pall. 12, 15, 3, p. 207 sq.

diffluxio.full: diffluxĭo, ōnis, f. diffluo, a flowing off, discharge, Cael. Aur. Acut. 2, 18.

diffors.full: diffors, -rtis, adj. dis-fors: oratio, a kind of defence, by which the act charged is admitted, but justified, Jul. Victor, Art. Rhet. 3, 3; 5.

diffractus.full: diffractus, a, um, Part., from diffringo.
diffractus.short: diffractus, a, um, Part., from diffringo.

diffringo.full: dif-fringo (dīfr-), no perf., fractum, 3, v. a., to break in pieces, to shatter (very rare): crura, Plaut. As. 2, 4, 68: axem, Suet. Caes. 37: gubernaculum, id. Aug. 17: basin Colossici Apollinis, Vitr. 10, 6.

diffugio.full: dif-fŭgĭo, fūgi, 3, v. n., to fly asunder, flee in different directions, to disperse, scatter (class.): diffugiebat enim varium genus omne ferarum, Lucr. 5, 1337 sq.; 3, 256; cf. id. 1, 762 sq.: vox una diffugit in multas aures, id. 4, 564: metu perterriti repente diffugimus, Cic. Phil. 2, 42, 108; id. Fam. 15, 1, 5; id. Off. 3, 32, 114; Suet. Caes. 82; Hor. C. 1, 35, 26; Verg. A. 2, 212; 4, 123; Ov. F. 2, 211; id. M. 7, 257 et saep.: diffugiunt stellae, id. ib. 2, 114; cf.: diffugere nives, to

diffugium.full: diffŭgĭum, ii, n. diffugio, a fleeing in different directions, a dispersion: proximorum diffugia, Tac. H. 1, 39 fin.

diffugo.full: dif-fŭgo, āvi, 1, v. a., to put to flight, scatter: nebulis diffugatis, August. in Psa. 41, 10: episcopos, Marcel. Com. Chron. An. 484.

diffulguro.full: dif-fulgŭro, āre, v. a., to scatter lightning around, Sid. Carm. 11, 20.

diffulmino.full: dif-fulmĭno, āre, v. a., to scatter a multitude, qs. by lightning, Sil. 5, 276.

diffumigo.full: dif-fūmĭgo, āre, v. a., to fumigate, Theod. Prisc. 4, 1.

diffundito.full: diffundĭto, āre, v. freq. a. diffundo, to pour out, scatter, spread (very rare; perh. only post-class.): pretium per domos, Amm. 18, 5, 6: aliquid ex sese, id. 21, 1, 11: ubique sese diffunditans, id. 16, 12: amoris vi diffunditari ac didier, to be consumed, wasted, Plaut. Merc. prol. 54.

diffundo.full: dif-fundo, fūdi, fūsum, 3, v. a., to spread by pouring, to pour out, pour forth (very freq. and class.). Lit.: (glacies) liquefacta se diffunderet, Cic. N. D. 2, 10: sanguis per venas in omne corpus diffunditur, id. ib. 2, 55, 138: (unda) diffunditur Hellesponto, Cat. 64, 359; cf.: tum freta diffundi jussit, to pour themselves forth, Ov. M. 1, 36: vinum de doliis, to draw off, bottle off; to fill, Col. 12, 28, 3; so of racking off wine, id. 3, 2, 26; Hor. Ep. 1, 5, 4 Krüg. ad loc.; Ov. F. 5, 517

diffusilis.full: diffūsĭlis, e, adj. diffundo, diffusive: aether, Lucr. 5, 467.

diffusio.full: diffūsĭo, ōnis, f. diffundo. The spreading out, extending: maris, Mart. Cap. 6, § 661.— Cheerfulness: animi, Sen. Vit. Beat. 5, 1.

diffusor.full: diffūsor, ōris, m. id. no. I. 1., a drawer-off of liquids: OLEARIVS, Inscr. Orell. 4077.

diffusus.full: diffūsus, a, um, Part. and P. a., from diffundo.

diffututus.full: dif-fŭtūtus, a, um, adj. futuo, exhausted by indulgence: mentula, Cat. 29, 14.

digamia.full: dĭgămĭa, ae, f., = διγαμία, a marrying twice, Tert. Monog. 6 al.
digamia.short: dĭgămĭa, ae, f., = διγαμία, a marrying twice, Tert.

digammon.full: dĭgammon, i, or dĭgamma, ătis, n., also dĭgammos, i, f. (sc. littera), = δίγαμμον (sc. στοιχεῖον) or δίγαμμα, the Aeolic double gamma or digamma (ϝ), represented in Latin sometimes by V, sometimes by F, which, written upside down, thus, F, the Emperor Claudius wished to substitute for both F and V, Quint. 1, 7, 27; cf. Tac. A. 11, 14; Suet. Claud. 41 (v. the letters F and V). Digammon, Quint. 1, 4, 7 Zumpt and Meyer N. cr.; Prob. Verg. G. 1, 70; Don. p. 1736 P. Lind. N. cr.; Cassiod. p. 2292 P.—
digammon.short: dĭgammon, i, or dĭgamma, ătis, n., also dĭgammos, i, f.

digamus.full: dĭgămus, a, adj., = δίγαμος, that has been married twice, Tert. Exh. ad Cast. 7; Hier. Ep. 2 fin. al.
digamus.short: dĭgămus, a, adj., = δίγαμος, that has been married twice, Tert.

digentia.full: Dĭgentĭa, ae, f., a small, clear stream that flowed by Horace's villa, and fell into the Anio about nine miles above Tibur, near the village of Mandela, now Licenza, Hor. Ep. 1, 18, 104.
digentia.short: Dĭgentĭa, ae, f., a small, clear stream that flowed by Horace's villa, and fell into the Anio about nine miles above Tibur, near the village of Mandela, now Licenza, Hor.

digeries.full: dīgĕrĭes, ēi, f. digero, an orderly distribution, a disposition, arrangement (late Lat.), Macr. S. 1; praef. § 7; 1, 16, § 38. Digestion, Cod. Theod. 14, 4, 4, § 2; 14, 20, 21, § 2.

digero.full: dī-gĕro, gessi, gestum, 3, v. a., to force apart, separate, divide, distribute (cf.: dispono, distribuo, divido, dispenso, ordino, compono). Lit. Ingen. (so mostly post-Aug.): (insulae) interdum discordantibus ventis digeruntur (opp. junctae copulataeque), Plin. Ep. 8, 20, 6; cf. nubes (opp. congregare), Sen. Q. N. 7, 22: nimbos, Plin. 31, 4, 30, § 53; Plin. Ep. 2, 17, 9: digesti colores, Ov. F. 5, 213: stercoris pars in prata digerenda, Col. 11, 2, 18: radix digesta, Plin. 24, 17, 102, § 161: i

digestibilis.full: dīgestĭbĭlis, e, adj. digero, I. B. 1., pertaining to digestion (late Lat.): cibus, i. e. digestible, easy of digestion, Cael. Aur. Tard. 1, 5, 159: oxygarum, i. e. promoting digestion, Apic. 1, 34.

digestilis.full: dīgestĭlis, e, adj. id., promoting digestion (late Lat.): meatus, Cassiod. Hist. Eccl. 6, 3.

digestim.full: dīgestim, adv. digero, in order: aliquid scribere, Prud. στεφ. 3, 129.

digestio.full: dīgestĭo, ōnis, f. id.. A dividing of food, dissolving, digestion (post-Aug.): sive concoctio sit illa, sive tantum digestio, Cels. 1 praef. § 63; 2, 14, § 7: facilis ciborum, Quint. 11, 3, 19; Capitol. Ver. 4; Sol. 27, 13; in plur., Macr. S. 7, 4.— An orderly distribution, division, arrangement. In gen.: annorum, Vell. 2, 53 fin.: (Italiae) in literas, i. e. an orderly description (shortly before, descriptio), Plin. 3, 5, 6, § 46.— Esp., as rhet. t. t., enumeration = μερισμός, Cic. de Or. 3, 53

digestivus.full: dīgestīvus, a, um, adj. id. I. B. 1., pertaining to digestion, digestive: vis, Macer, Carm. 1, 18.

digestorius.full: dīgestōrĭus, a, um, adj. id., promoting digestion (late Lat.): medicamentum, Plin. Val. 2, 8: embamma, Marc. Empir. 20.

digestus1.full: dīgestus, a, um, Part. and P. a., from digero.

digestus2.full: dīgestus, ūs, m. digero, a distributing: sanctarum opum, i. e. management of the imperial treasury, Stat. S. 3, 3, 86.

digitabulum.full: dĭgĭtābŭlum, i, n. digitus, a glove worn in gathering olives: melior ea quae digitis nudis legitur quam illa quae cum digitabulis, Varr. R. R. 1, 55, 1 (al. digitalibus); cf. δακτυλήθρα, digitabulum, Gloss. Philox. p. 73, 17.

digitalis.full: dĭgĭtālis, e, adj. id., of or belonging to the finger: gracilitas, Plin. 14, 3, 4, § 40: crassitudo, id. 22, 20, 23, § 48; cf. Varr. R. R. 1, 55, 1 Schneid. and Gesn. (al. digitabulis).

digitatus.full: dĭgĭtātus, a, um, adj. id., having fingers or toes: aves, Plin. 11, 47, 107, § 256.

digitillum.full: dĭgĭtillum (-tellum), i, n. dim. id., the plant house-leek, Col. 12, 7, 1; Plin. 18, 17, 45, § 159; 25, 13, 102, § 160; 26, 15, 92, § 163 al.

digitulus.full: dĭgĭtŭlus, i, m. dim. id., a little finger, Plaut. Rud. 3, 4, 15; id. Bacch. 4, 4, 24; Ter. Eun. 2, 2, 53; Varr. ap. Non. 135, 24: aniculae collum digitulis duobus oblidere, Cic. Scaur. Fragm. § 10 al.— Transf., of the parrot's foot, a toe, App. Flor. 2, p. 349; of the claw of a crab, Varr. Sat. Men. 9, 1 Oehler (Riese, digitis).

digitus1.full: dĭgĭtus, i, m. Gr. δάκτυλος; cf. Germ. Zehe, Eng. toe; from root δεκ(δέχομαι), to grasp, receive; cf. Germ. Finger, from fangen, Georg Curtius Gr. Etym. 133. Corssen, however, still refers digitus to root dik-, dico, δείκνυμι, as the pointer, indicator, Ausspr. 1, 380; cf. dico, a finger. Prop.: tot (cyathos bibimus), quot digiti sunt tibi in manu, Plaut. Stich. 5, 4, 24; id. Most. 5, 1, 69; id. Mil. 2, 2, 47; 4, 2, 57 et saep.—The special designations: pollex, the thumb; index or salutaris, the

digitus2.full: Dĭgĭtus, i, m., a proper name; in plur.: Digiti Idaei = Δάκτυλοι Ἰδαῖοι, the priests of Cybele, Cic. N. D. 3, 16, 42; cf. Arn. 3, 41 and 43, and v. Dactylus.
digitus2.short: Dĭgĭtus, i, m., a proper name;

digladiabilis.full: dīglădĭābĭlis, e, adj. digladior, full of contention, fierce: dissidium, Prud. Cath. 3, 147.

digladior.full: dī-glădĭor, āri, v. dep. n. [gladius], to fight for life and death, to contend fiercely (a Ciceron. word). Prop.: cives inter se sicis, Cic. Leg. 3, 9, 20.— Transf., to contend warmly, dispute, sc. with words: de quibus inter se digladiari solent (philosophi), Cic. Off. 1, 9, 28: cum aliquo tot voluminibus, id. Ac. Fragm. ap. Non. 65, 14; cf. coupled with depugnare, id. ib. 15: digladientur illi, per me licet, id. Tusc. 4, 21.

diglossos.full: dī^glōssos, i, f., δίγλωσσος = bilinguis, name of a plant: sedum alum, App. Herb. 58.
diglossos.short: dī^glōssos, i, f., δίγλωσσος = bilinguis, name of a plant: sedum alum, App.

digma.full: dīgma, ătis, n., = δεῖγμα, a specimen, Cod. Th. 14, 4, 9.
digma.short: dīgma, ătis, n., = δεῖγμα, a specimen, Cod.

dignabilis.full: dignābĭlis, e, adj. dignor, worthy, Alcim. Ep. 10 al.

dignanter.full: dignanter, adv., courteously, etc., v. dignor fin.

dignatio.full: dignātĭo, ōnis, f. dignor, a considering worthy (mostly post-Aug.; esp. in Tac. and Suet.). Lit., a deeming worthy, respect, esteem, regard (very rarely): dignatione aliquem diligere, Suet. Calig. 24: diu in summa dignatione regis vixit, Just. 28, 4, 10.—Far more freq., Transf., with respect to the person who enjoys such esteem, dignity, honor, reputation, for dignitas: de dignatione laborat, Cic. Att. 10, 9, 2 (al. dignitate): reddere honorem sacerdotiis dignatione sua, Liv. 10, 7, 12; 2, 16, 5

digne.full: dignē, adv., worthily, fitly, becomingly, v. dignus fin.
digne.short: dignē, adv., worthily, fitly, becomingly, v.

dignitas.full: dignĭtas, ātis (gen. plur. dignitatum, Sen. Ben. 2, 17, 1; Plaut. Ep. 9, 5, 3; Vop. Florian. 6, 2: -tatium, Sen. Polyb. 17, 2), f. dignus. Lit., a being worthy, worth, worthiness, merit, desert (so, rarely, and perh. only in Cic.): Lamia petit praeturam: omnesque intelligunt nec dignitatem ei deesse nec gratiam, Cic. Fam. 11, 17; id. Agr. 2, 2, 3: dignitas consularis, a being worthy of the office of consul, id. Mur. 13: pro dignitate laudare, id. Rosc. Am. 12, 33. Meton. (the cause for the effec

dignitosus.full: dignĭtōsus, a, um, adj. dignitas, dignified, respectable, ἀξιωματικός, Gloss. Philox.: homo, Petr. 57, 10.

digno.full: digno, āre, 1, v. a. dignus, to deem worthy: quis caelestes dignet decorare hostiis, Pac. ap. Non. 98, 15; so with inf., id. ib. 470, 20; ap. Serv. Verg. A. 11, 169; and in Diomed. p. 395 P.; Att. ap. Non. 470, 19: hunc tanto munere digna, Calvus ap. Serv. l. l.; so with abl., Cic. Arat. 34.— Dignor, āri, pass.: egone Pelopis digner domo, Att. ap. Non. 281, 7; so with abl., Cic. de Or. 3, 7; id. Inv. 2, 39, 114; id. Ac. 1, 10, 36; id. Oecon. Fragm. ap. Prisc. p. 793 P.; Verg A. 3, 475; and with

dignor.full: dignor, ātus, 1, v. dep. a. [dignus], to deem worthy or deserving (mostly poet. and in post-Aug. prose). Aliquem aliqua re: haud equidem tali me dignor honore, Verg. A. 1, 335; so, aliquem honore, Ov. M. 1, 194; 3, 521; Suet. Vesp. 2 fin. al.: te alio funere, Verg. A. 11, 169: hunc mensa, cubili (dea), id. E. 4, 63: aliquem non sermone, non visu, Tac. A. 4, 74 fin.: libellum veniā, Ov. Tr. 3, 14, 51; id. Pont. 1, 8, 9 al.— With inf. as object, like the Gr. ἀξιῶ and ἀξιοῦμαι, to regard as fit, be

dignorant.full: dīgnōrant, signa imponunt, ut fieri solet in pecoribus, Paul. ex Fest. p. 72, 16 Müll.
dignorant.short: dīgnōrant, signa imponunt, ut fieri solet in pecoribus, Paul.

dignoscentia.full: dīgnoscentĭa, ae, f. dignosco, the power of distinguishing, knowledge (eccl. Lat.): mali et boni, August. de Gen. 2, 9 fin.

dignus.full: dignus, a, um, adj. i. e. DIC-nus; root in Sanscr. daç-as, fame; Gr. δοκέω, δόξα; Lat.: decet, decus, worthy, deserving (in a good or ill sense), of things, suitable, fitting, becoming, proper (very freq. in all periods and kinds of writing).—Constr., in the most finished models of composition, with the abl. pretii, a relative sentence, or absol.; in the Aug. poets also freq. with the inf.; otherwise with ut, the gen., or the acc. of a neutr. pron. or adj.
