With abl. (so most freq.): dignus domin

digredior.full: dī-grĕdĭor, gressus, 3, v. dep. n. [gradior], to go apart or asunder, to separate, part; to go away, depart, = discedere (class.). Lit.: luna tum congrediens cum sole, tum digrediens, Cic. N. D. 2, 40, 103; cf.: digredimur paulum rursumque ad bella coimus, Ov. M. 9, 42: ita utrique digrediuntur, Sall. J. 22 fin.; cf.: digredimur flentes, Ov. H. 18, 117: ubi digressi, Verg. A. 4, 80.—With term. a quo: numquam est a me digressus, Cic. Sull. 12: ab aliquo, id. Fam. 4, 12; 12, 18; id. Att. 3, 9; Cae

digressio.full: dīgressĭo, ōnis, f. digredior, a parting, separating; a going away, departing, departure. * Lit. (in this signif. more freq. digressus): congressio, tum vero digressio nostra, Cic. Q. Fr. 1, 3, 4.—More freq., Trop., a going aside, deviation; esp. in lang., digression: qualis ad adjuvandum (sc. amicum) digressio (sc. a recto, referring to Cic. Lael. 17), Gell. 1, 3, 14: a proposita oratione, Cic. Brut. 85; so of speech, id. Inv. 1, 51; id. de Or. 2, 77, 312; 3, 53 fin.; Quint. 4, 2, 19; 9, 1, 28;

digressivus.full: dīgressīvus, a, um, adj. id., pertaining to digression, digressive: relatio, Cassiod. Inst. Div. litt. 4.

digressus1.full: dīgressus, a, um, Part., from digredior.
digressus1.short: dīgressus, a, um, Part., from digredior.

digressus2.full: dīgressus, ūs, m. digredior, a parting, separating; a going away, departure. Lit. (good prose): congressus nostri lamentationem pertimui, digressum vero non tulissem, Cic. Q. Fr. 1, 3, 4; opp. accessus, id. N. D. 2, 19, 50; c. c. discessus, id. de Sen. 23, 85; cf. also id. Pis. 26, 63; id. Att. 1, 5, 4; Plin. 11, 29, 35, § 107 al. — Trop. only in Quint., a deviating in speech, digression, Quint. 10, 5, 17; 4, 3, 14; in plur., id. 10, 1, 49.

digrunnio.full: dī-grunnĭo, īre, v. n., to grunt hard, Phaedr. 5, 5, 27 (unless we should rather read degrunnit).

dii.full: dii. Nom. plur., from deus, q. v.— Arch. gen., from dies, q. v.

diiambus.full: dĭĭambus, i, m., = διΐαμβος, a double iambus: ˘¯˘¯, Don. p. 1739 P.; Diom. p. 477 ib. et saep. (in Ter. Maur. p. 2415 P., written as Greek).
diiambus.short: dĭĭambus, i, m., = διΐαμβος, a double iambus: ˘¯˘¯, Don.

dijudicatio.full: dījūdĭcātĭo, ōnis, f. dijudico, a judging, deciding, determining, Cic. Leg. 1, 21, 56.

dijudicatrix.full: dījūdĭcātrix, īcis, f. id., she that judges or decides: virtus omnium rerum, App. Dogm. Plat. 2, p. 15, 23; p. 179 Bip.

dijudico.full: dī-jūdĭco, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. With the idea of the verb predominating, to judge by discerning or distinguishing; to decide, determine (class.). Prop.: ego dicam, quod mihi in mentem venit: tu dijudica, Ter. Heaut. 5, 2, 33; so absol., Quint. 12, 7, 8 al.: aliena melius quam sua, Ter. Heaut. 3, 1, 98: callide verbis controversias, non aequitate, Cic. Caecin. 17, 49; so, controversiam, id. Fin. 3, 2, 6: causam, Liv. 40, 16: litem, Hor. C. 3, 5, 54 et saep.—With acc. and inf.: quam (sc. uxorem) om

dijugatio.full: dījŭgātĭo, ōnis, f. dijugo, a separation, Arn. 2, p. 53.

dijugo.full: dī-jŭgo (disj-), no perf., ātum, 1, v. a., to separate: aliquem ab aliquo (with dijunxit), Arn. 5, p. 162.

dijunctim.full: dījunctim, dījunctio, dījunctus, and dījungo, v. disj.
dijunctim.short: dījunctim, dījunctio, dījunctus, and dījungo, v.

dilabidus.full: dīlābĭdus, a, um, adj. dilabor, that soon goes to pieces: vestes, Plin. 8, 55, 81, § 219.

dilabor.full: dī-lābor, lapsus, 3, v. dep. n., to fall asunder, go to pieces, melt away, dissolve (class.). Lit. In gen.: glacies liquefacta et dilapsa, Cic. N. D. 2, 10, 26; cf. nix, Liv. 21, 36, 6: nebula, id. 41, 2, 4: calor, Verg. A. 4, 705: Vulcanus (i. e. ignis), Hor. S. 1, 5, 73: aestus, Tac. A. 14, 32 et saep.—Of a river, to flow apart, flow away, hoc quasi rostro finditur Fibrenus, et divisus aequaliter ... rapideque dilapsus cito in unum confluit, Cic. Leg. 2, 3, 6: amnis presso in solum alveo dilab

dilaceratio.full: dīlăcĕrātĭo, ōnis, f. dilacero, a tearing apart, tearing to pieces, Arn. 2, p. 74; Vulg. Nahum, 3, 1.

dilacero.full: dī-lăcĕro, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a., to tear to pieces, to tear apart (mostly poet. and in post-Aug. prose). Lit.: dilaceranda feris dabor, * Cat. 64, 152; cf. Ov. H. 12, 116: dominum (canes), id. M. 3, 250: natum, id. H. 11, 112: muliebre corpus tormentis, Tac. A. 15, 57: aliquid (spiculā), to lacerate, wound, Cels. 7, 5, 2: leonem, Vulg. Judic. 14, 6.— Trop.: annum integrum ad dilacerandam rem publicam quaerere, Cic. Mil. 9, 24: res publica dilacerata, Sall. J. 41, 5 Kritz. (prob. an imitation of T

dilamino.full: dī-lāmĭno, āre, v. a. lamina, to split in two: nuces, Ov. Nux, 73.

dilancinatus.full: dī-lancĭnātus, a, um, Part. [lancino], torn to pieces, torn apart (late Lat.): membra, Prud. στεφ. 5, 155: vitalia, Amm. 22, 15, 19.

dilanio.full: dī-lănĭo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a., to tear to pieces, to dilacerate (rare but class.): (Clodii cadaver) canibus dilaniandum reliquisti, Cic. Mil. 13; cf. id. poët. Tusc. 2, 10, 24; Ov. M. 6, 645; 10, 387; Tac. A. 11, 22; 36; Vulg. Luc. 2, 39 al.—Trop.: animam (c. c. dispergere), Lucr. 3, 538.—In a Gr. construction: dilaniata comas, Ov. Am. 3, 9, 52.

dilapidatio.full: dīlăpĭdātĭo, ōnis, f. dilapido, a squandering, wasting: bonorum, Cod. Th. 4, 20, 1.

dilapido.full: dī-lăpĭdo, āre, v. a., lit., to scatter like stones; hence, to throw away, squander, to consume (very rare): nostras triginta minas, Ter. Ph. 5, 7, 4; cf. facultates, Firm. Math. 6, 10: grandine hominumque boumque labores, to destroy, Col. 10, 330.

dilapsio.full: dīlapsĭo, ōnis, f. dilabor, decay, destruction, Aug. Civ. D. 22, 12.

dilapsus.full: dīlapsus, a, um, Part., from dilabor.
dilapsus.short: dīlapsus, a, um, Part., from dilabor.

dilargior.full: dī-largĭor, ītus, 4, v. dep. a., to give away or bestow liberally; to lavish (very rare): aliquid alicui, * Cic. Agr. 2, 29 fin.; cf. Suet. Caes. 20: pecuniam Magis, Tac. A. 16, 30: foedera sociis, Latium (i. e. jus Latii) externis, id. H. 3, 55.!*? In pass. signif.: aerarium dilargitur populo Romano, C. Gracchus ap. Prisc. p. 793 P.: dilargitis proscriptorum bonis, Sall. ap. Gell. 15, 13, 8 (Hist. 1, 31 Dietsch): dilargitis quae amant, Lact. 7, 1, 13.

dilatatio.full: dīlātātĭo, ōnis, f. dilato, an extending, enlarging (late Lat.): laminae, Tert. Anim. 37 fin.: superiorum, id. Praescr. 47: cordis, Vulg. Prov. 21, 4.

dilatator.full: dīlātātor, ōris, m. id., he who propagates, a propagator: Latinae linguae, Cassiod. Inst. Div. Litt. 21.

dilatio.full: dīlātĭo, ōnis, f. differo, B. 3., a putting off, delaying, deferring (good prose). With gen.: temporis, Cic. Phil. 3, 1, 2: comitiorum, id. de Imp. Pomp. 1, 2: belli, Liv. 9, 43; 45: foederis, id. 9, 5: exitii, Tac. A. 6, 4 fin. al.— Absol.: alter (consul) nullam dilationem patiebatur, Liv. 21, 52; 7, 14; 40, 57; Sen. de Ira, 3, 12: solatium dilationis et morae, Suet. Ner. 15; Vulg. Act. 25, 17 al.; in plur., Liv. 5, 5; Vell. 2, 79, al.—Esp. law t. t., the adjournment of a legal hearing or judgm

dilato.full: dīlāto, āvi, ātum, 1, v. freq. a. and n. differo. Act., to spread out, dilate; to enlarge, amplify, extend (class.; esp. freq. in Cic.). Lit.: (stomachi) partes eae, quae sunt infra, dilatantur, quae autem supra, contrahuntur, Cic. N. D. 2, 54, 135: manum (opp. comprimere digitos), id. Or. 32, 113: globum farinae, Varr. L. L. 5, § 107 Müll.: fundum, Cic. Fin. 3, 15, 48: castra, Liv. 27, 46 (opp. coartatio plurium): aciem, id. 31, 21: cicatricem, Plin. 17, 27, 42, § 251: patulos rictus, Ov. M. 6,

dilator.full: dīlātor, ōris, m. differo, B. 3., a delayer, a dilatory person, Hor. A. P. 172; Isid. 10, 77.

dilatorius.full: dīlātōrĭus, a, um, adj. id., delaying, dilatory: exceptiones (opp. peremptoriae), Dig. 44, 1, 3.

dilatura.full: dīlātūra, ae, f. id., a postponement, delay (post-Aug.): si unius diei dilaturam fecissent, Sen. Apoc. 14, 3.

dilatus.full: dīlātus, a, um, Part., from differo.
dilatus.short: dīlātus, a, um, Part., from differo.

dilaudo.full: dī-laudo, 1, v. a., to praise in all respects, to praise very much: libros, Cic. Att. 6, 2, 9 (v. Orell. ad h. l.); id. ib. 6, 3, 3.

dilaxo.full: dī-laxo, āre, v. n., to stretch apart: cruribu' crura dilaxat, Lucil. ap. Porph. ad Hor. S. 1, 2, 125.

dilectio.full: dīlectĭo, ōnis, f. diligo, love (late Lat.): dei, Tert. adv. Marc. 4, 27: mea, Vulg. Psa. 108, 4 et saep.

dilector.full: dīlector, ōris, m. id., a lover (postclass.), App. Flor. no. 9, p. 347; Tert. adv. Marc. 4, 23.

dilectus1.full: dīlectus, a, um, Part. and P. a., from diligo.

dilemma.full: dĭlemma, ătis, n. (δίλημμα), a double proposition, a dilemma; in logic, an argument in which an adversary is pinned between two difficulties, Serv. Verg. A. 2, 675, and 10, 449.

diligens.full: dīlĭgens, entis, Part. and P. a., diligent, careful, etc., v. diligo fin.

diligenter.full: dīlĭgenter, adv., attentively, carefully, diligently, earnestly; v. diligo, P. a. fin.
diligenter.short: dīlĭgenter, adv., attentively, carefully, diligently, earnestly;

diligentia.full: dīlĭgentĭa, ae, f. diligens, carefulness, attentiveness, earnestness, diligence (freq. and class.; cf.: labor, aerumna, opera, industria, assiduitas, sedulitas, studium, cura). In gen.: reliqua sunt in cura, attentione animi, cogitatione, vigilantia, assiduitate, labore; complectar uno verbo, quo saepe jam usi sumus, diligentia, qua una virtute omnes virtutes reliquae continentur, Cic. de Or. 2, 35, 150 (v. the whole chapter in connection). With praepp.: pro mea summa in re publica diligentia, C

diligibilis.full: dīlĭgĭbĭlis, e, adj. diligo, estimable, amiable, Hier. Phil. 5, 1.

diligo.full: dī-lĭgo, lexi, lectum, 3, v. a. 2. lego. Prop., to distinguish one by selecting him from others; hence, in gen., to value or esteem highly, to love (v. amo init., and cf. faveo, studeo, foveo, cupio; very freq. and class.). Prop.: nihil est enim virtute amabilius, nihil quod magis alliciat ad diligendum: quippe cum propter virtutem et probitatem etiam eos, quos numquam vidimus, quodam modo diligamus, Cic. Lael. 8, 28; cf. id. ib. 9, 29 sq.; 14, 50; id. Rep. 1, 10 fin.; 1, 12 et saep. (cf. also t

dilogia.full: dĭlŏgĭa, ae, f. (διλογία), ambiguity, as a rhetorical figure, Pseud. Ascon. Cic. Verr. 1, 9, 26.

dilophos.full: dĭlŏphos, a, on, adj., = δίλοφος, with two crests, two-crested: ales, Mart. Cap. 2, § 177.
dilophos.short: dĭlŏphos, a, on, adj., = δίλοφος, with two crests, two-crested: ales, Mart.

dilorico.full: dī-lōrīco, no perf., ātum, 1, v. a., to tear apart, tear open one's dress (very rare): tunicam, * Cic. de Or. 2, 28, 124; so, vestem, App. M. 6, p. 177; 7, p. 191.

diloris.full: dĭlōris, e, adj. vox hibrida, from δίς and lorum, double-thonged, i. e., doublestriped: vestis, Vop. Aur. 46, 6: interula, id. Bonos. 15, 8.

diluceo.full: dī-lūcĕo, ēre, v. n., lit., to be light enough to distinguish objects apart; hence, trop., to be clear, evident (rare): dilucere brevi fraus coepit, Liv. 8, 27 fin.; cf. id. 3, 16; 25, 29 fin.: emolumentum ejus in animo tuo dilucebit, Gell. 16, 8, 16.—With a subject-clause: satis dilucet, hanc capionem posse dici, Gell. 7, 10, 3.

dilucesco.full: dīlūcesco, luxi, 3, v. inch. n. [diluceo], to grow light, to begin to shine, to dawn; in the perf., to shine (rare but class.). Impers.: cum jam dilucesceret, Cic. Cat. 3, 3: jam dilucescebat, cum signum consul dedit, Liv. 36, 24; and so transf.: discussa est illa caligo ... diluxit, patet, videmus omnia, Cic. Phil. 12, 2, 5.— Pers.: omnem crede diem tibi diluxisse supremum, etc., * Hor. Ep. 1, 4, 13; cf. Gell. 3, 2.— Trop.: donec diluxit rerum genetalis origo, Lucr. 5, 176: ista dilucescant all

dilucidatio.full: dīlūcĭdātĭo, ōnis, f. dilucido, an illustrating, explaining; clearness, distinctness (late Lat.), Cassiod. Complex. 1 Cor. 6.

dilucide.full: dīlūcĭdē, adv., clearly, brightly; plainly, evidently, distinctly; v. dilucidus fin.

dilucidus.full: dīlūcĭdus, a, um, adj. diluceo, clear, bright (syn.: clarus, illustris, perspicuus, conspicuus). Lit. (rare): zmaragdi, Plin. 37, 5, 18, § 70.— Trop., of speech, clear, plain, distinct, evident (in Cic. and Quint.): oratio, Cic. Fin. 3, 1, 3: verbis uti, id. Inv. 1, 20 fin.; cf. verba, Quint. 8 prooem. § 26: sermo, id. 5, 14, 33; 11, 1, 53: enuntiatio, id. 7, 3, 2 al.—Comp.: omnia dilucidiora non ampliora facientes, Cic. Or. 5 fin.—Sup. does not occur.—Adv.: dīlūcĭdē. (Acc. to no. I.) Clearly, b

diluculat.full: dīlūcŭlat, ābat, 1, v. impers. [diluculum], it grows light, it dawns; perh. only Gell. 2, 29, 7; 7, 1, 6.

diluculum.full: dīlūcŭlum, i, n. diluceo, daybreak, dawn (cf. crepusculum), Plaut. Am. 2, 2, 105; Cic. Rosc. Am. 7, 19; id. Att. 16, 13, a; cf. Macr. S. 1, 3 fin.; Censor. 24; Vulg. Luc. 24, 1 et saep.—In plur., Fronto, Ep. ad Anton. 1, 5.

diludium.full: dī-lūdĭum, ii, n. ludus, a restingtime, intermission between plays, Hor. Ep. 1, 19, 47.

diluo.full: dī-lŭo, ŭi, ūtum, 3, v. a., to wash to pieces, wash away; to dissolve, dilute, cause to melt away; to wash, drench (freq. and class.). Lit. Ingen.: ne aqua lateres diluere posset, * Caes. B. C. 2, 10, 6: sata laeta boumque labores, Verg. G. 1, 326; cf.: sanguine diluitur tellus, is soaked, Furius Antias ap. Gell. 18, 11, 4: unguenta lacrimis, Ov. P. 1, 9, 53: alvum helleboro, Gell. 17, 15, 4: vulnus cruris aceto, Petr. 136, 7; cf.: ulcus ovi albore, Scrib. Comp. 24: colorem, i. e. to wash out, w

dilutus.full: dīlūtus, a, um, P. a., diluted, thin, weak, soft (perh. only post-Aug.). Lit.: potio (opp. meraca), Cels. 1, 3; cf.: vinum dilutius pueris, sonibus meracius, id.; and: potio quam dilutissima, id.: solum dilutius, Plaut. 17, 20, 33, § 144; hence also subst., dīlūtum, i, n., a liquid in which something has been dissolved, a solution, Plin. 27, 7, 28, § 46: rubor, id. 22, 22, 46, § 92: amethystus dilutior, paler, id. 37, 9, 40, § 122; colos, id. 37, 5, 18, § 67: urina, Cels. 2, 6: odor, slight, fai

diluvialis.full: dīlŭvĭālis, e, adj. diluvium, of a deluge or flood: irruptio, i. e. diluvium, Sol. 9, 8.

diluvies.full: dīlŭvĭes, ēi, f., also dīlŭvĭum, ii, n., and dīlŭvĭo, ōnis, f. diluo, lit., a washing away of the earth; hence, Transf., an inundation, flood, deluge (in all three forms only poet. and in post-Aug. prose; yet in Seneca, Quaestt. Natt., diluvium stands for the general deluge; v. infra, β). Diluvies, Lucr. 5, 255; 6, 292; Hor. C. 3, 29, 40; 4, 14, 28; Plin. 9, 4, 3, § 8.— Diluvium, Verg. A. 12, 205; Ov. M. 1, 434; Sen. Q. N. 3, 27; 29; Plin. Ep. 8, 17; Flor. 4, 2, 3; cf. Vulg. Matt. 24, 38 al.— Di
diluvies.short: dīlŭvĭes, ēi, f., also dīlŭvĭum, ii, n., and dīlŭvĭo, ōnis, f.

diluvio1.full: dīlŭvĭo, āre, v. a. diluvies, to inundate. to deluge, Lucr. 5, 387.

diluvium.full: dīlŭvĭum, ii, n., v. diluvies, β.

dimachae.full: dĭmăchae, ārum, m., = διμάχαι, soldiers who fought both on foot and on horseback, Anglice dragoons; a sort of troops among the Macedonians, Curt. 5, 13, 8.
dimachae.short: dĭmăchae, ārum, m., = διμάχαι, soldiers who fought both on foot and on horseback, Anglice dragoons;

dimachaerus.full: dĭmăchaerus, a, um, adj., = διμάχαιρος, fighting with two swords: gladiator, Inscr. Orell. 2584.
dimachaerus.short: dĭmăchaerus, a, um, adj., = διμάχαιρος, fighting with two swords: gladiator, Inscr.

dimadesco.full: dī-mădesco, dui, 3, v. inch., to melt away: nives, Luc. 6, 479.

dimano.full: dī-māno (dem-), āre, v. n., to flow different ways, to spread abroad (very rare): meus hic forensis labor dimanavit ad existimationem hominum paulo latius, Cic. Cael. 3, 6.

dimensio.full: dīmensĭo, ōnis, f. dimetior, a measuring. Prop.: quadrati, Cic. Tusc. 1, 24, 57.— Transf., the axis of the earth, Hygin. Astr. 1, 3.— Extent, dimensions, in gen., Macr. Somn. Scip. 1, 6, 36; 2, 2, 3 al.—So plur. Amm. 23, 6, 11.— Trop.: vocum, Quint. 9, 4, 45: versuum, id. 48; cf. id. 52 and 85.

dimensus.full: dīmensus, a, um, Part., from dimetior.
dimensus.short: dīmensus, a, um, Part., from dimetior.

dimeter.full: dĭmĕter (-trus), a, um, adj., = δίμετρος, of two measures or metres (late Lat.): versus, a dimeter, Diom. p. 506 P.; and simply dimetrus (sc. versus), Ter. Maur. p. 2437 ib.
dimeter.short: dĭmĕter (-trus), a, um, adj., = δίμετρος, of two measures or metres (late Lat.): versus, a dimeter, Diom.

dimetior.full: dī-mētĭor, mensus, 4, v. dep. a., to measure any thing, to measure out (v. demetior init.—rare but class.): studium dimetiendi caeli atque terrae, Cic. de Sen. 14, 49: dimetiri et dinumerare syllabas, id. Or. 43, 147: campum ad certamen, Verg. A. 12, 117: mundum, Quint. 12, 11, 10; cf. id. 9, 4, 112.—Hence, part. as subst.: dīmētĭens, entis, f., the diameter (διάμετρος), Plin. 2, 23, 21, § 86 sq.!*? In pass. signif.: columnae altitudo dimetiatur in partes duodecim, Vitr. 3, 3; 5, 9; Quint. 8 pro

dimeto.full: dī-mēto, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a., and dī-mētor, āri, 1, v. dep., to measure out, mark out, to fix the limits of (rare; perh. only in the foll. passages): locum castris, Liv. 8, 38; cf.: dimetata signa, Cic. N. D. 2, 43, 110 (Baiter, demetata).—Depon. form: eorum enim cursus dimetati cognovimus, etc., id. ib. 2, 62, 155.

dimetria.full: dĭmē^trĭa, ae, f., = διμετρία, a poem consisting of iambic dimeters, Aus. Ep. 16, 104.
dimetria.short: dĭmē^trĭa, ae, f., = διμετρία, a poem consisting of iambic dimeters, Aus.

dimicatio.full: dīmĭcātĭo, ōnis, f. dimico, a fight, combat, furious encounter (cf.: pugna, proelium, certamen, contentio, acies; freq. and good prose). Lit., Caes. B. C. 3, 111, 2; Hirt. B. G. 8, 11; Liv. 25, 6 fin.; 31, 35 fin.; Suet. Aug. 10; 17; Plin. 8, 7, 7, § 18; Front. Strat. 2, 1, 11 et saep.—In plur., Caes. B. G. 7, 86, 3; Front. Strat. 1, 11, 12.— With gen.: proelii, Cic. Q. Fr. 1, 1, § 5: universae rei, a pitched battle, general engagement, Liv. 1, 38; for which, universa, id. 22, 32. — Transf. beyo

dimico.full: dī-mĭco, āvi (e. g. dimicavere, Vell. 2, 85, 1; dimicaverant, Caes. B. C. 2, 4, 3; dimicassent, Vell. 2, 85, 5 al.; dimicuisse, Ov. Am. 2, 7, 2; 2, 13, 28), ātum, 1, v. n., lit., to brandish one's weapons against the enemy, i. e. to fight, struggle, contend (freq. and class.). Lit.: manum conserere atque armis dimicare, Caes. B. C. 1, 20, 4: armis cum aliquo, Nep. Milt. 1, 2: ferro pro patria, Liv. 1, 24: acie cum aliquo, id. 2, 49 fin.; for which: in acie, Caes. B. G. 7, 64, 2: proelio, id. ib.

dimidiatio.full: dīmĭdĭātĭo, ōnis, f. dimidio, a halving, dividing into halves: salutis, Tert. adv. Marc. 1, 24.

dimidiatus.full: dīmĭdĭātus, P. and P. a., from dimidio.

dimidietas.full: dīmĭdĭĕtas, ātis, f., a half, Pompei. Gr. 4, n. 8, p. 63.
dimidietas.short: dīmĭdĭĕtas, ātis, f., a half, Pompei.

dimidio.full: dīmĭdĭo, no perf., ātum, 1, v. a. dimidius, to divide into two equal parts, to halve (as a finite verb, very rare): quid dimidias Christum? Tert. de Carn. Chr. 5.— Trop.: viri dolosi non dimidiabunt dies suos, i. e. shall not live half the life of men, Vulg. Psa. 54, 23; cf. also, id. Job, 21, 21; but freq. and class. in the perf. part. dīmĭ-dĭātus, halved, half (acc. to Varr. ap. Gell. 3, 14, 19, applied to a whole, which is divided into halves; whereas dimidius is applied to a half; or, as Gel

dimidium.full: dīmĭdĭum, ii, n., the half, v. the foll. II.
dimidium.short: dīmĭdĭum, ii, n., the half, v.

dimidius.full: dī-mĭdĭus, a, um, adj. medius, half (for the diff. between it and dimidiatus, v. dimidio). As an adj., until the Aug. per. only in connection with pars, e. g.: dimidiam partem nationum subegit, Plaut. Curc. 3, 77; id. Aul. 4, 10, 37; id. Rud. 4, 4, 79; Lucr. 1, 618 sq.; 5, 720; Cic. N. D. 2, 40, 103; id. Rosc. Com. 11, 32; id. Fam. 13, 29, 4; Caes. B. G. 6, 31, 5; id. B. C. 1, 27; 3, 101 (twice); Sall. J. 64, 5; Suet. Caes. 42; Front. Strat. 2, 3, 21; Ov. F. 5, 122; id. Tr. 1, 2, 44 et saep.— Si

diminuo.full: dī-mĭnŭo (or dimmĭnuo), ĕre, v. a., to break into small pieces, to dash to pieces, to break (v. deminuo—rare; perh. only ante-class.): qui ego illi speculo dimminuam caput, Plaut. Most. 1, 3, 109; cf.: caput homini, id. Men. 2, 2, 30: caput tuum, Ter. Eun. 4, 7, 33: cerebrum tibi, id. Ad. 4, 2, 32; Lucr. 1, 614.— To violate, outrage, destroy by outrage: veritates, Vulg. Psa. 11, 1: de verbis libri, id. Apoc. 22, 19 (perh. deminuerit is a better reading).

diminutio.full: dīmĭnūtĭo, ōnis, f., another reading for deminutio, Hyg. F. 30 in Maj. Auct. Class. v. 3, p. 13, and Vulg. Rom. 11, 12 al.
diminutio.short: dīmĭnūtĭo, ōnis, f., another reading for deminutio, Hyg.

dimissio.full: dīmissĭo, ōnis, f. dimitto. A sending in different directions, a sending out, sending forth (very rare): dimissiones libertorum ad faenerandas provincias, Cic. Par. 6, 2, 46: sanguinis, i. e. blood-letting, Gell. 10, 8 in lemm.—* A dismissing, discharging: propugnatorum atque remigum, Cic. Verr. 2, 5, 33, § 86.— The remission (of pain, fever, etc.; opp. accessio), Cael. Aur. Acut. 2, 3, 13; 2, 18, 108 al.

dimissor.full: dīmissor, ōris, m. id., a forgiver, pardoner (eccl. Lat.): peccatorum, Tert. adv. Marc. 4, 10 al.

dimissoriaelitterae.full: dīmissōriaelitterae dicuntur, quae vulgo apostoli dicuntur (notice sent to a higher judge): dimissoriae autem dictae, quod causa ad eum, qui appellatus est, dimittitur, Dig. 50, 16, 106; cf. ib. 49, 6, 1.
dimissoriaelitterae.short: dīmissōriaelitterae dicuntur, quae vulgo apostoli dicuntur (notice sent to a higher judge): dimissoriae autem dictae, quod causa ad eum, qui appellatus est, dimittitur, Dig.

dimissus.full: dīmissus, a, um, Part., from dimitto.
dimissus.short: dīmissus, a, um, Part., from dimitto.

dimitto.full: dī-mitto, mīsi, missum, 3, v. a. With particular reference to the prep., to send different ways, to send apart, i. e., To send out or forth in different directions, to send about (class.). With acc.: Naevius pueros circum amicos dimittit, Cic. Quint. 6, 2: consules designatos circum provincias, Suet. Aug. 64: litteras circum municipia, Caes. B. C. 3, 22, 1; cf.: litteras circa praefectos, Liv. 42, 51: litteras per omnes provincias, Caes. B. C. 3, 79, 4; with which cf.: nuntios per agros, id. B.

dimotus.full: dīmōtus, a, um, Part., from dimoveo.
dimotus.short: dīmōtus, a, um, Part., from dimoveo.

dimoveo.full: dī-mŏvĕo, ōvi, ōtum (DISMOTUM, v. infra), 2, v. a. (in MSS. and edd. often confounded with demoveo, q. v.; not freq. before the Aug. per.; not in Caes. and Quint.; perh. not in Cic., where demovere appears everywhere to be the better reading). To move asunder, to part, put asunder, separate, divide: terram aratro, Verg. G. 2, 513; cf.: glebas aratro, Ov. M. 5, 341: aera (c. c. dispellere umbras), Verg. A. 5, 839; cf. auras, id. ib. 9, 645: cinerem foco, Ov. M. 8, 642: undas, Lucr. 6, 891; Ov. M.

dinaea.full: Dinaea or Dinea, ae, f., a Roman female name, Cic. Clu. 7, 21; 12, 33 al.
dinaea.short: Dinaea or Dinea, ae, f., a Roman female name, Cic.

dinarchus.full: Dīnarchus, i, m., = Δείναρχος, an Attic orator, an imitator of Demosthenes, Cic. de Or. 2, 23, 94; id. Brut. 9, 36.
dinarchus.short: Dīnarchus, i, m., = Δείναρχος, an Attic orator, an imitator of Demosthenes, Cic.

dindymus.full: Dindўmus (-os), i, m., and Dindў-mon, i, n., = Δίνδυμον, a mountain in Mysia near Pessinus, sacred to Cybele, Plin. 5, 32, 40, § 142; Prop. 3 (4), 22, 3; Cat. 63, 91; Ov. F. 4, 249.—Also, Dindўma, ōrum, n., = Δίνδυμα, τά, Verg. A. 9, 618; 10, 252; Ov. M. 2, 223; id. F. 4, 234.— Hence, Dindўmēnē, ēs, f., = Δινδυμηνή, the goddess Cybele, who was worshipped there, Hor. C. 1, 16, 5.—Gen.: Dindymenae, Cat. 63, 13.— Dindў-mārĭus, ĭi, m., a priest of Cybele, Commod. 17, 6.
dindymus.short: Dindўmus (-os), i, m., and Dindў-mon, i, n., = Δίνδυμον, a mountain in Mysia near Pessinus, sacred to Cybele, Plin.

dine.full: dīnē, es, f., = δίνη, a whirlwind: vertex ille est, vel uti dicitur dine, etc., Ap. de Mundo, 12, p. 62, 32 (dub. Hild. Helicias).
dine.short: dīnē, es, f., = δίνη, a whirlwind: vertex ille est, vel uti dicitur dine, etc., Ap.

dino.full: Dīno or Dīnōn, ōnis, m., = Δείνων, a Greek historian of the time of Philip of Macedonia, Cic. Div. 1, 23, 46; Nep. Con. 5; Plin. 10, 49, 70, § 136.
dino.short: Dīno or Dīnōn, ōnis, m., = Δείνων, a Greek historian of the time of Philip of Macedonia, Cic.

dinocrates.full: Dīnō^crătes, is, m., = Δεινοκράτης, a Grecian architect in the time of Alexander the Great, Vitr. 2, praef. 1 sq.; Val. Max. 1, 4 extr. 1.
dinocrates.short: Dīnō^crătes, is, m., = Δεινοκράτης, a Grecian architect in the time of Alexander the Great, Vitr.

dinomache.full: Dīnŏmăchē, ēs, f., = Δεινομάχη, the mother of Alcibiades; hence, poet.: Dinomaches ego sum—as much as to say, I am a person of quality, Pers. 4, 20.
dinomache.short: Dīnŏmăchē, ēs, f., = Δεινομάχη, the mother of Alcibiades;

dinomachus.full: Dīnŏmăchus, i, m., = Δεινόμαχος, a Greek philosopher, Cic. Fin. 5, 8, 21; id. Off. 3, 33, 119.
dinomachus.short: Dīnŏmăchus, i, m., = Δεινόμαχος, a Greek philosopher, Cic.

dinosco.full: dī-nosco (old form, dīgnosco—no perf. nor sup.), ĕre, 3, v. a. dis, 2.; nosco, to know apart, to distinguish, discern one thing from another (perh. not ante-Aug.). With ab: vix ut dinosci possit a mastiche verā, Plin. 12, 17, 36, § 72. — With abl.: civem dinoscere hoste, Hor. Ep. 1, 15, 29: ut possem curvo dinoscere rectum, id. ib. 2, 2, 44: aera tinnitu, Quint. 11, 3, 31: vocem auribus, speciem oculis, id. ib. 18: aliquid sapore, Col. 2, 2, 20.— With accus.: suos et alienos, Col. 8, 5, 7: vera

dinumerabilis.full: dīnŭmĕrābĭlis, e, adj. dinumero, that may be numbered, calculable, Cassiod. in Psa. 150 fin.

dinumeratio.full: dīnŭmĕrātĭo, ōnis, f. id., a counting over, reckoning up, enumeration. In gen. (very rare): noctium ac dierum, Cic. Rep. 3, 2 fin.; cf. (dierum), Paul. Sent. 5, 33: (personarum), Dig. 38, 10, 10, § 16; Vulg. 2 Par. 2, 17.— Esp., as a figure of speech, i. q. Gr. ἀπαρίθμησις, Cic. de Or. 3, 54, 207; quoted ap. Quint. 9, 1, 35 (who, however, does not regard it as a figure); 9, 3, 91 Spald.

dinumerator.full: dīnŭmĕrātor, ōris, m. id., a reckoner, calculator: syllabarum, Aug. in Psa. 55, 10.

dinumero.full: dī-nŭmĕro, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a., to count over, reckon up, enumerate. In gen. (class.): stellas, Cic. Off. 1, 43, 154: annos, id. Rep. 2, 15; cf. horas, Plin. 2, 73, 75, § 185: tempora, * Verg. A. 6, 691: noctes, Ov. M. 11, 574 al.: syllabas (c. c. dimetiri), Cic. Or. 43, 147: spoliata templa, Quint. 6, 1, 3: exercitum, Plin. 4, 11, 18, § 43: generis gradus, Ov. F. 2, 622.—Absol.: centuriat Capuae, dinumerat, Cic. Att. 16, 9 fin.— In Plaut. and Ter. in partic., mercantile t. t., to count out, pay

dinummium.full: dĭ-nummĭum, ii, n. vox hibr., from δίς and nummus, a tax of two nummi, Cod. Theod. 14, 27, 2.

dinuptila.full: dĭnuptĭla, ae, f., a plant = bryonia, App. Herb. 66.
dinuptila.short: dĭnuptĭla, ae, f., a plant = bryonia, App.

dio.full: dĭo or -ōn, ōnis, m., = Δίων. A brother-in-law of the elder Dionysius, of Syracuse, the pupil and friend of Plato. His life was written by Nepos and Plutarch; cf. also Cic Tusc. 5, 35; id. de Or. 3, 34; Jornand. 2, 92.— An Academic philosopher, Cic. Ac. 2, 4, 12.— A Stoic philosopher, Cic. Leg. 3, 5 fin. dub. (al. Diogenes).— Dio Halaesinus, Cic. Verr. 2, 1, 10 al.

diobolaris.full: dĭōbŏlāris, e, adj. vox hibr., διώβολον, with ending -aris, that costs or is worth two oboli: scorta, Plaut. Poen. 1, 2, 58; cf. id. Fragm. ap. Varr. L. L. 7, § 64; Paul. ex Fest. p. 74, 6 Müll.: anus, Plaut. Ps. 2, 2, 64.—Hence, dĭōbŏlārĭa, ae, f., the title of a comedy otherwise unknown, Fulg. 566, 7.

diochares.full: Dĭŏchăres, is, m., a freedman of Caesar, Cic. Att. 11, 6, 7.—Hence, Dĭŏchă-rīnus, a, um, adj., of Diochares: litterae, id. ib. 13, 45, 1.
diochares.short: Dĭŏchăres, is, m., a freedman of Caesar, Cic.

diocletianus.full: Dĭoclētĭānus, i, m., C. Aurelius Valerius, a Roman emperor from 284-305 A. D., Aurel. Vict. Caes. 38; id. Epit. 39; Eutrop. 9, 13 sq.; before his accession to the throne named Diocles, Aur. Vict. Ep. 39.

diodorus.full: Dĭŏdōrus, i, m., = Διόδωρος. A Peripatetic philosopher, a pupil of Critolaüs, Cic. Fin. 5, 5; id. Ac. 2, 24; id. Tusc. 5, 30 sq.— A famous dialectician, Cic. Fat. 6; Plin. 7, 53, 54, § 180.— Siculus, a well-known historian of the time of Augustus. His work, entitled Βιβλιοθήκη, of which a portion is still extant, is mentioned by Plin. H. N. praef. § 25; Lact. 1, 13, 8.

diodotus.full: Dĭŏdŏtus, i, m., = Διόδοτος, a Stoic, and teacher of Cicero, Cic. Brut. 90; id. Fam. 9, 4; id. Att. 2, 20; id. Ac. 2, 36; id. Tusc. 5, 39 et saep.; Tac. Or. 30.
diodotus.short: Dĭŏdŏtus, i, m., = Διόδοτος, a Stoic, and teacher of Cicero, Cic.

dioecesis.full: dĭœcēsis, is, f., = διοίκησις. A governor's jurisdiction, a district, Cic. Fam. 3, 8, 4 (ib. 13, 53 and 67, written as Greek); Cod. Theod. 7, 6, 3; Amm. 17, 7, 6.— In eccl. Lat., a bishop's jurisdiction, a diocese, Sid. Ep. 7, 6 med.; sometimes also a parish, id. ib. 9, 16.

dioecetes.full: dĭœcētes, ae, m., = διοικητής, an overseer of the revenue, royal treasurer, Cic. Rab. Post. 8, 22; 10, 28.
dioecetes.short: dĭœcētes, ae, m., = διοικητής, an overseer of the revenue, royal treasurer, Cic.

diogenes.full: Dĭŏgĕnes, is, m., = Διογένης. Apolloniates, a celebrated Ionian philosopher, pupil of Anaximenes, Cic. N. D. 1, 12, 29.— The well-known Cynic philosopher of Sinope, Cic. Tusc. 1, 43, 104; id. N. D. 3, 34; id. Mur. 36 et saep.— A Stoic, teacher of Carneades and Laelius, Cic. Div. 1, 3, 6; id. Fin. 2, 8; id. Tusc. 4, 3; id. de Sen. 7 et saep.— A friend of M. Caelius Rufus, Cic. Fam. 2, 12, 2; id. Cael. ib. 8, 8, 10.

diogmitae.full: dĭōgmītae, ārum, m., = ΔΙΩΓΜΙΤΑΙ [from διωγμός, pursuit], a sort of lightarmed frontier troops kept for the pursuit of robbers, Amm. 27, 9; Capitol. Anton. Philos. 21.
diogmitae.short: dĭōgmītae, ārum, m., = ΔΙΩΓΜΙΤΑΙ [from διωγμός, pursuit], a sort of lightarmed frontier troops kept for the pursuit of robbers, Amm.

diomedes.full: Dĭŏmēdes, is, m., = Διομήδης. A son of Tydeus, king of Aetolia, and Deipyle, the successor of Adrastus in Argos; a famous hero at the siege of Troy, after which he went to Apulia, where he founded Argyripa (Arpi), Ov. M. 13, 100 sq.; 14, 457; Verg. A. 1, 752; 8, 9; Hor. S. 1, 5, 92; id. A. P. 146 et saep.—As grandson of Oeneus called Oenides, Ov. M. 14, 512: Diomedis Campus, the region about Cannae in Apulia, on the Aufidus, Liv. 25, 10; cf. Paul. ex Fest. p. 75 Müll.—Deriv., Dĭŏmēdēus (-īus), a

dione.full: Dĭōnē, ēs (-a, ae, Cic. N. D. 3, 23, 59), f., = Διώνη. The mother of Venus, Cic. l. l.; Hyg. praef.; Claud. Rapt. Pros. 3, 433.—Hence, Dĭōnæus, a, um, adj., of Dione: vestis, the garment worked by Dione for her daughter, Claud. Epith. Pall. et Cel. 102.—Far more freq. as in Greek, Venus, Ov. F. 2, 461; 5, 309; id. Am. 1, 14, 33 al.—Hence, Dĭōnæus, a, um, adj., of Dione (Venus): mater, Venus herself (with reference to Aeneas), Verg. A. 3, 19; hence, Dionaeus Caesar, as the descendant of Iulus, Ae

dionymus.full: dĭōnўmus, a, um, adj., = διώνυμος, with a double name, Prisc. 580 P.
dionymus.short: dĭōnўmus, a, um, adj., = διώνυμος, with a double name, Prisc.

dionysia1.full: Dĭŏnȳsia, ae, f., a noted dancer, Cic. Rosc. Com. 8; Gell. 1, 5.
dionysia1.short: Dĭŏnȳsia, ae, f., a noted dancer, Cic.

dionysiacus.full: Dĭŏnȳsĭăcus, a, um, v. Dionysus, II. C.

dionysias.full: Dĭŏnȳsĭas, ădis, v. Dionysus, no. II. B.

dionysius.full: Dĭŏnȳsĭus, ii, m., = Διονύσιος, the name of several celebrated Greeks; esp., The elder Dionysius, tyrant of Syracuse, Nep. Dio, 1; id. Reg. 2; Cic. Tusc. 5, 20 sq.; id. N. D. 3, 33 sq. al.— His son, likewise tyrant of Syracuse, Nep. Dio, 3 sq.; Just. 21, 1 sq.; Cic. Tusc. 3, 12; id. Fam. 9, 18; Val. Max. 6, 9, 6 extr.— Heracleotes, a pupil of Zeno of Citium, at first a Stoic, afterwards a Cyrenaic, Cic. Fin. 5, 31; id. Tusc. 2, 25; 3, 9; id. Ac. 2, 22 fin.— A Stoic, contemporary with Cicero, Cic
dionysius.short: Dĭŏnȳsĭus, ii, m., = Διονύσιος, the name of several celebrated Greeks;

dionysonymphas.full: dĭŏnȳsŏnymphas, ădis, f., = διονυσονυμφάς, a plant, i. q. casignete, q. v., Plin. 24, 17, 102, § 165.
dionysonymphas.short: dĭŏnȳsŏnymphas, ădis, f., = διονυσονυμφάς, a plant, i.

dionysopolitae.full: Dĭŏnȳsŏpŏlītae, ārum, m., the inhabitants of Dionysopolis, a city of Magna Phrygia, Cic. Q. Fr. 1, 2, 2, § 4; Plin. 5, 29, 29, § 106; id. 4, 10, 17, § 44.
dionysopolitae.short: Dĭŏnȳsŏpŏlītae, ārum, m., the inhabitants of Dionysopolis, a city of Magna Phrygia, Cic.

dionysus.full: Dĭŏnȳsus or -os, i, m., = Διόνυσος, the Greek name of Bacchus (not in the Aug. poets), Cic. N. D. 3, 21; 23; Att. ap. Macr. S. 6, 5; Plaut. Stich. 5, 2, 13; Aus. Epigr. 30.— Derivv., Dĭŏnȳsĭus, a, um, adj., of or pertaining to Bacchus; Dĭŏ-nȳsia, ōrum, n., = Διονύσια, τά (sc. ἱερά), the festival of Bacchus, in Greece celebrated every three years (Lat. Bacchanalia), Plaut. Curc. 5, 2, 45; id. Cist. 1, 1, 91; 1, 3, 8; id. Ps. 1, 1, 57; Ter. Heaut. 1, 1, 110 Don.; id. ib. 4, 4, 11.— Dĭŏnȳsĭas, ădis
dionysus.short: Dĭŏnȳsus or -os, i, m., = Διόνυσος, the Greek name of Bacchus (not in the Aug.

diopetes.full: dĭŏpĕtes, is, m., = διοπετής (falling from heaven): rana, a sort of frog, rainfrog, called also, calamites, Plin. 32, 7, 24, § 70; 32, 10, 50, § 139.
diopetes.short: dĭŏpĕtes, is, m., = διοπετής (falling from heaven): rana, a sort of frog, rainfrog, called also, calamites, Plin.

diophanes.full: Dĭŏphănes, is, m., = Διοφάνης. Of Mitylenae, teacher of Tib. Gracchus, Cic. Brut. 27, 104.— Of Nicaea, a Latin author on husbandry, Varr. R. R. 1, 1, 8 al.

dioptra.full: dĭoptra, ae, f., = δίοπτρα, an optical instrument to measure the height of places, Vitr. 8, 6; for measuring the sun's shadow, Plin. 2, 69, 69, § 176.
dioptra.short: dĭoptra, ae, f., = δίοπτρα, an optical instrument to measure the height of places, Vitr.

dioryctos.full: Dĭōryctos, i, m., = διωρυκτός [διῶρυξ], a trench or canal, in Acarnania, between Leucadia and the continent, Plin. 4, 1, 2, § 5.
dioryctos.short: Dĭōryctos, i, m., = διωρυκτός [διῶρυξ], a trench or canal, in Acarnania, between Leucadia and the continent, Plin.

dioryx.full: dĭōryx, ўgis, f., = διῶρυξ, a canal: manu factus amnis, ex Nili alveo dioryge adductus, Mel. 3, 8 fin.
dioryx.short: dĭōryx, ўgis, f., = διῶρυξ, a canal: manu factus amnis, ex Nili alveo dioryge adductus, Mel.

dios1.full: Dĭos bălănus, i, m., = Διὸς βάλανος, a kind of chestnut, perh. the large sweet chestnut, Plin. 15, 23, 25, § 93.
dios1.short: Dĭos bălănus, i, m., = Διὸς βάλανος, a kind of chestnut, perh.

dios2.full: Dĭos pneuma, ătis, n., = Διὸς πνεῦμα, a species of rosemary, App. Herb. 79.
dios2.short: Dĭos pneuma, ătis, n., = Διὸς πνεῦμα, a species of rosemary, App.

diospyros.full: Dĭospўros, i, m., = Διόσπυρος, a plant, otherwise called lithospermon, stonecrop, Plin. 27, 11, 74, § 98.
diospyros.short: Dĭospўros, i, m., = Διόσπυρος, a plant, otherwise called lithospermon, stonecrop, Plin.

diota.full: dĭōta, ae, f., = διώτη, a two-handled vessel, a wine-jar, Hor. C. 1, 9, 8.
diota.short: dĭōta, ae, f., = διώτη, a two-handled vessel, a wine-jar, Hor.

diovis.full: Dĭŏvis or Dĭjŏvis, is, m. collat. form of Jovis, old nom. for later Juppiter, q. v.; cf. Diespiter, the old Italian name for Juppiter, acc. to Varr. L. L. 5, § 66 Müll.; Gell. 5, 12, 1 and 6; Inscr. in Bullet. del Inst. 1846.

diox.full: diox, genus piscis frequens in Ponto, Paul. ex Fest. 75, 3 Müll.
diox.short: diox, genus piscis frequens in Ponto, Paul.

diphilus.full: Dīphĭlus, i, m., = Δίφιλος. A celebrated Greek comic writer of Sinope, imitated by Plautus, Plaut. Cas. prol. 32; id. Rud. prol. 32; Ter. Ad. prol. 6; Vell. 1, 16, 3. — An architect employed by Quintus Cicero, Cic. Q. Fr. 3, 1, 1.— Secretary of Crassus, Cic. de Or. 1, 30, 136.

diphryges.full: diphrўges, is, f., = διφρυγές, τό, a kind of slag formed in furnaces when copper is melted, Plin. 34, 13, 37, § 135; Cels. 5, 7, 22; Scrib. Comp. 227 and 247.
diphryges.short: diphrўges, is, f., = διφρυγές, τό, a kind of slag formed in furnaces when copper is melted, Plin.

diphthongus.full: diphthongus, i, f., = δίφθογγος, a diphthong, Mart. Cap. 3, § 277; Prisc. p. 561 P. al.
diphthongus.short: diphthongus, i, f., = δίφθογγος, a diphthong, Mart.

diphyes.full: dĭphўes, is, f., = διφυής, a precious stone, otherwise unknown, Plin. 37, 10, 57, § 157.
diphyes.short: dĭphўes, is, f., = διφυής, a precious stone, otherwise unknown, Plin.

diplangium.full: dī^plangīum, īi, n., = διπλαγγεῖον, a double vessel (pure Lat. duplex vas), Theod. Prisc. 1, 19 (cf. Scrib. Comp. 73).
diplangium.short: dī^plangīum, īi, n., = διπλαγγεῖον, a double vessel (pure Lat.

diplasius.full: dī^plăsĭus, a, um, adj., = διπλάσιος, twofold, duplicate: ex ratione diplasia, hoc est duplici, Mart. Cap. 9, § 934.
diplasius.short: dī^plăsĭus, a, um, adj., = διπλάσιος, twofold, duplicate: ex ratione diplasia, hoc est duplici, Mart.

diplinthius.full: diplinthĭus, a, um, adj., = διπλίνθιος, two bricks thick: parietes, Vitr. 2, 8, 17.
diplinthius.short: diplinthĭus, a, um, adj., = διπλίνθιος, two bricks thick: parietes, Vitr.

diplois.full: dī^plŏïs, ĭdis, f., = διπλοΐς, a double robe to be wrapped around the body, a cloak, mantle, Sulpic. Sever. Hist. Sacr. 1, 35, 7; Vulg. Psa. 108, 28; id. Baruch, 5, 2; Acro on Hor. Ep. 1, 17, 25; Nov. ap. Non. 316, 5.
diplois.short: dī^plŏïs, ĭdis, f., = διπλοΐς, a double robe to be wrapped around the body, a cloak, mantle, Sulpic.

diploma.full: dī^plōma, ătis (dat. and abl. plur. regul. diplomatibus, Tac. H. 2, 65; Plin. Ep. 10, 122; Suet. Aug. 50; Murat. Inscr. 885, 4), n., = δίπλωμα, a letter folded double, viz., A state letter of recommendation given to persons travelling to the provinces, Cic. Fam. 6, 12, 3; id. Att. 10, 17, 4; id. Pis. 37; Tac. H. 2, 54; Plin. Ep. 10, 14 al.— In gen., a document drawn up by a magistrate, assuring to the holder some favor or privilege, a diploma, Suet. Aug. 50; id. Calig. 38; Sen. Clem. 1, 10 fin.;

diplomarius.full: diplōmārĭus, ii, m. diploma, one who carried out the imperial letters of recommendation, Inscr. Orell. 2917.

dipondium.full: dĭpondĭum = dupondium, q. v., Vulg. Luc. 12, 6.

dipsacos.full: dipsăcos, i, f., = δίψακος, the plant teasel, Dipsacus fullonum, Linn.; Plin. 27, 9, 47, § 71.
dipsacos.short: dipsăcos, i, f., = δίψακος, the plant teasel, Dipsacus fullonum, Linn.;

dipsas1.full: dipsas, ădis, f., = διψάς, a kind of serpent whose bite causes violent thirst, the Coluber Vipera, Linn.; Plin. 23, 8, 80, § 152; Mart. 3, 44, 7; Luc. 9, 610; 718; Sil. 3, 313; Vulg. Deut. 8, 15.
dipsas1.short: dipsas, ădis, f., = διψάς, a kind of serpent whose bite causes violent thirst, the Coluber Vipera, Linn.;

dipsas2.full: Dipsas, ădis, f., a name given to an old bawd, Ov. Am. 1, 8, 2.
dipsas2.short: Dipsas, ădis, f., a name given to an old bawd, Ov.

dipteros.full: diptĕros, on, adj., = δίπτερος, with two wings: aedes, Vitr. 3, 1, 7 praef.
dipteros.short: diptĕros, on, adj., = δίπτερος, with two wings: aedes, Vitr.

diptota.full: diptōta, ōrum, n., = δίπτωτα. In the later gramm., nouns that have only two cases, diptotes, Diomed. p. 288 P. et saep.; cf.: diptotos forma, Ars Consent. p. 2033 fin. ib.

diptycha.full: diptўcha, ōrum, n., = δίπτυχα. A writing-tablet of two leaves (late Lat.), Cod. Theod. 15, 9, 1; Symm. Ep. 2, 80 al.— The double shell of the oyster, Ambros. Hexaem. 5, 8.

dipylon.full: Dĭpўlon, i, n., = Δίπυλον, a gate at Athens that closed the Ceramicus, and through which one passed in going to the Academy, Cic. Fin. 5, 1, 1; Liv. 31, 24, 8.
dipylon.short: Dĭpўlon, i, n., = Δίπυλον, a gate at Athens that closed the Ceramicus, and through which one passed in going to the Academy, Cic.

dipyros.full: dĭpўros, on, adj., = δίπυρος, twice burned, Phaëthon, Mart. 4, 47, 2.
dipyros.short: dĭpўros, on, adj., = δίπυρος, twice burned, Phaëthon, Mart.

dirado.full: dī-rādo, rāsi, 3, v. a., to scratch slightly: tergum piscis, Cassiod. Varr. 11, 40.

dirae.full: Dīrae, ārum, f., the Furies, v. dirus, I. B. 2.
dirae.short: Dīrae, ārum, f., the Furies, v.

dirce.full: Dircē, ēs (acc. Dircam, Plaut. Ps. 1, 2, 65), f., = Δίρκη. A fountain N. W. of Thebes, in Boeotia, Plin. 4, 7, 12, § 25; Ov. M. 2, 239; Stat. Th. 1, 38.— Meton., poet., the region lying around this fountain, Stat. Th. 2, 322.—Hence, Dircæus, a, um, adj., Dircean; hence (pars pro toto), Boeotian: Thebae, Prop. 3, 17, 33 (4, 16, 33 M.); cf. ager, Stat. Ach. 1, 12: arva, Claud. Laud. Stil. 1, 320: Amphion, Verg. E. 2, 24: cygnus, i. e. Pindar, Hor. C. 4, 2, 25: heros, i. e. Polynices, Stat. Th. 2,

dircenna.full: Dircenna, ae, f., a fountain in Spain, near Bilbilis, Mart. 1, 50, 17.
dircenna.short: Dircenna, ae, f., a fountain in Spain, near Bilbilis, Mart.

dircion.full: dircĭon, ii, n., a plant also known as Apollinaris herba, a kind of solanum, Ap. Herb. 23.
dircion.short: dircĭon, ii, n., a plant also known as Apollinaris herba, a kind of solanum, Ap.

directa.full: dīrectā (sc. viā), perpendicularly, see dirigo, P. a. fin. c.

directarius.full: dīrectārĭus, ii, m. dirigo, one who secretly enters a house in order to steal, a sneak-thief, burglar (very rare), Dig. 47, 11, 7; Paul. Sent. 5, 4.

directe.full: dīrectē, adv., directly, straight, etc., v. dirigo, P. a. fin. a.
directe.short: dīrectē, adv., directly, straight, etc., v.

directiangulus.full: dīrectĭangŭlus, a, um, adj. directus-angulus, right-angled, rectangular, Mart. Cap. 6, § 712.

directilineus.full: dīrectĭlīnĕus, a, um, adj. directus-linea, rectilinear, Mart. Cap. 6, § 711.

directim.full: dīrectim, adv., directly, straightway, etc., v. dirigo, P. a. fin. d.
directim.short: dīrectim, adv., directly, straightway, etc., v.

directio.full: dīrectĭo, ōnis, f. dirigo (a very rare word). A making straight or even, a levelling: plana coagmentorum, Vitr. 7, 3, 5 sq.— Concr., a straight line, App. de Mundo, p. 57.— Trop. A directing, aiming, towards any thing: quaedam rationis ad veritatem, Quint. 3, 6, 30.— Righteousness, uprightness, Vulg. Psa. 44, 6; 118, 7.

directitude.full: dīrectĭtūde, ĭnis, f. directus, rightness, correctness: aeterna, Cassiod. in Psa. 101, 30.

directo.full: dīrecto, adv., directly, in a straight line, v. dirigo, P. a. fin. b.
directo.short: dīrecto, adv., directly, in a straight line, v.

directorius.full: dīrectōrĭus, a, um, adj. dirigo, that directs or sends in any direction, directory: litterae, Cod. Theod. 14, 15, 3, § 1.

directura.full: dīrectūra, ae, f. id., a making straight, even, a levelling, Vitr. 7, 3, 5.

directus.full: dīrectus, a, um, Part. and P. a., from dirigo.

diremptio.full: dĭremptĭo, ōnis, f. dirimo, a separation: aequitatis, Val. Max. 4, 7, 1.

diremptus1.full: dĭremptus, a, um, Part., from dirimo.
diremptus1.short: dĭremptus, a, um, Part., from dirimo.

diremptus2.full: dĭremptus, ūs, m. dirimo, a separation, Cic. Tusc. 1, 29, 71.

direptio.full: dīreptĭo, ōnis, f. diripio, a plundering, pillaging (rare, but good prose): urbs relicta direptioni et incendiis, Cic. Fam. 4, 1, 2; cf. urbis, Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 52; * Caes. B. C. 2, 12: oppidi (with expugnatio), Suet. Claud. 21: profanorum sacrorumque, Quint. 8, 3, 69: sociorum (with vexatio), Cic. Cat. 1, 7, 18.—In plur., Cic. Fam. 4, 13, 2; Liv. 44, 1 fin.— The stealing, rape: aurei velleris, Amm. 22, 8, 15.

direptor.full: dīreptor, ōris, m. id., a plunderer (very rare; cf.: fur, praedo, raptor), Cic. Phil. 3, 11, 27; id. Cat. 2, 9 fin.; Tac. H. 3, 33.

direptus1.full: dīreptus, a, um, Part., from diripio.
direptus1.short: dīreptus, a, um, Part., from diripio.

direptus2.full: dīreptus, ūs, m. diripio, a plundering, Spart. Sever. 19.

diribeo.full: dĭrĭbĕo, no perf., ĭtum, 2, v. a. dishabeo, like dirimo, from dis-emo, to keep apart, hence, pub. law t. t., to lay apart, separate, divide, sort, the tablets or ballots taken out of the ballot-box, in order to determine who has the majority: dum de te quinque et septuaginta tabellae diribeantur, Cic. Pis. 40, 96 Halm: tabellas, id. Q. Fr. 3, 4, 1; id. Planc. 20, 49 Kayser, cf. Wund. ad loc.: suffragia, Varr. R. R. 3, 2, 1: sententias, Val. Max. 9, 12, 7; also absol., Varr. R. R. 3, 5, 18 (al. d

diribitio.full: dĭrĭbĭtĭo, ōnis, f. diribeo, a separating or sorting of the tablets taken from the ballot-box, Cic. Planc. 6, 14; Symm. Laud. in Patr. 3, p. 40 ed. Mai.

diribitor.full: dĭrĭbĭtor, ōris, m. id., the separater or sorter of the ballots used in voting, Cic. Pis. 15, 36; id. post Red. in Sen. 11, 28; Aus. Grat. Act. 5.— Transf., in gen., a distributor, App. M. 2, 32, p. 137 ed. Oud.; Amm. 18, 5, 6.

diribitorium.full: dĭrĭbĭtōrĭum, ii, n. (sc. aedificium; in Dio Cass. 55, 8: τὸ δειριβιτώριον) [id.], the building in which the ballots were sorted (v. diribeo), Suet. Claud. 18; Plin. 6, 40, 76, § 201; 36, 15, 24, § 102 Sillig. N. cr.

dirigo.full: dī-rĭgo or dērĭgo (the latter form preferred by Roby, L. G. 2, p. 387; cf. Rib. Proleg. ad Verg. p. 401 sq.; so Liv. 21, 19, 1; 21, 47, 8; 22, 28 Weissenb.; id. 22, 47, 2 Drak.; Lach. ad Lucr. 4, 609; Tac. A. 6, 40 Ritter; acc. to Brambach, s. v., the two forms are different words, de-rigo meaning to give a particular direction to; di-rigo, to arrange in distinct lines, set or move different ways; cf. describo and discribo. But the distinction is not observed in the MSS. and edd. generally), rex
dirigo.short: dī-rĭgo or dērĭgo (the latter form preferred by Roby, L.

dirimo.full: dĭrĭmo, ēmi, emptum (perf. dirempsi, cited as error, Charis. 220 P.), 3, v. a. disĕmo, like diribeo, from dis-habeo, to take apart; to part, separate, divide (class.; esp. freq. in the trop. sense—cf.: findo, scindo, divello, separo, sejungo, segrego, secerno). Lit.: dirimi corpus distrahive, Cic. N. D. 3, 12; cf. Lucr. 6, 1075: Tiberis Veientem agrum a Crustumino dirimens, Plin. 3, 5, 9, § 53; cf.: castris Ilerdam, Luc. 4, 33: sontes justis (Minos), Claud. ap. Rufin. 2, 477: oppida nostra unius

diripio.full: dī-rĭpĭo, ŭi, eptum, 3, v. a. rapio, to tear asunder, tear in pieces (class.). In gen. (rarely): Pentheum diripuisse aiunt Bacchas, Plaut. Merc. 2, 4, 1: Hippolytum (equi), Ov. A. A. 1, 338; id. F. 5, 310: nec opinantes (leae), Lucr. 5, 1319: membra manibus nefandis, Ov. M. 3, 731 et saep.: venti diripiunt fretum, Stat. Th. 5, 367. — In partic. Milit. t. t., to lay waste, ravage, spoil, plunder an enemy's territory or possessions (so most freq.): bona alicujus, Caes. B. G. 7, 3, 1; 7, 42, 3; 7,

diritas.full: dīrĭtas, ātis, f. dirus (rare but class.), lit. fearfulness, viz., Of fate, fatal mischief, misfortune: si qua invecta diritas casu foret, Cic. Poët. Tusc. 3, 14: totius diei, Suet. Ner. 8; cf. ominis, Gell. 4, 9, 10.— Of character, fierceness, cruelty: omni diritate atque immanitate teterrimus, Cic. Vatin. 3 fin.: quanta in altero diritas, in altero comitas! id. de Sen. 18 fin.: morum (Tiberii), Suet. Tib. 21.

dirumpo.full: dī-rumpo or disr-, rūpi, ruptum, 3, v. a., to break or dash to pieces; to break, burst asunder (rare but class.). Lit.: tabulā caput, Plaut. Bacch. 3, 3, 37: ne medius disrumpar miser, id. Curc. 2, 1, 7: cum se in nubem induerint (venti) ejusque tenuissimam quamque partem coeperint dividere atque disrumpere, Cic. Div. 2, 19, 44: imagines, Tac. H. 1, 55: homo diruptus, i. e. that has a rupture (c. c. dirutus), Cic. Phil. 13, 12.—In an obscene sense, Plaut. Cas. 4, 3, 11 al.— Trop. To break off, s
dirumpo.short: dī-rumpo or disr-, rūpi, ruptum, 3, v.

diruo.full: dī-rŭo, rŭi, rŭtum, 3, v. a., to tear asunder, overthrow, demolish, destroy (class. —cf.: deleo, diluo, exstinguo, everto, demolior). Prop.: maceriam, Ter. Ad. 5, 7, 10: urbem, Cic. Inv. 1, 40, 73; id. Q. Fr. 1, 1, 8, § 25; Suet. Caes. 54; Ov. M. 12, 551 et saep.: muros, Nep. Con. 4 fin.: templa, Suet. Calig. 60: arcum circi, id. Ner. 25: monumentum, id. Dom. 8; Hor. C. 3, 30, 4: fores ira, Prop. 4 (5), 9, 14. arbusta, Verg. A. 10, 363: regna Priami, Prop. 2, 28, 54 (3, 26, 8 M.); cf. id. 4 (5),

diruptio.full: dīruptĭo, ōnis, f. dirumpo, a tearing asunder, tearing to pieces: magnorum corporum, Sen. Q. N. 2, 15.

diruptus.full: dīruptus, a, um, Part., from dirumpo.
diruptus.short: dīruptus, a, um, Part., from dirumpo.

dirus.full: dīrus, a, um, adj. Sanscr. root dī, to flee; Gr. δέος, δείδω, δεινός, fearful, awful (for syn. cf.: saevus, atrox, ferox, crudelis, trux, furens, furiosus, immitis). Orig. belonging to the lang. of augurs; of fate, ill-omened, ominous, boding, portentous: QVAE AVGVR INIVSTA, NEFASTA VITIOSA DIRA DEFIXERIT, IRRITA INFECTAQVE SVNTO, Cic. Leg. 2, 8 fin.; cf. id. Div. 1, 16: tristissima exta sine capite fuerunt, quibus nihil videtur esse dirius, id. ib. 2, 15 fin.; cf.: bubo, dirum mortalibus omen,

dirutio.full: dīrŭtĭo, ōnis, f. diruo, a destruction, Inscr. Grut. 3, 9.

dirutus.full: dīrŭtus, a, um, Part., from diruo.
dirutus.short: dīrŭtus, a, um, Part., from diruo.

dis1.full: dīs, dītis, adj., rich, v. dives.

dis2.full: Dīs, ītis (nom. Dītis, Petr. Poët. 120, 76; Quint. 1, 6, 34; cf. Serv. Verg. A. 6, 273; the nom. Dis very rare in the poets; Aus. Idyl. 12: de deis, 3), m. cf.: dīus, divus, deus, orig. denoting godhead, deity, in general, and of Jupiter in partic.; cf.: Diespiter and Diovis = Juppiter; afterwards exclusively as the designation of the god of the infernal regions, the Greek Pluto, connected with pater, Varr. L. L. 5, § 66 Müll.; identified by Caesar with the Celtic god of night, cf. Caes. B. G. 6

dis3.full: dĭs, an inseparable particle Sanscr. dva, two: dvis, twice; Gr. δίς (δϝις); cf.: bis, bini, dubius, duo; also Sanscr. vi- (for dvi-) = dis-, occurs before vowels only in dishiasco; it stands unchanged before c, p, q, t, s, and di; loses its s before b, d, g, l, m, n, r, and v; and becomes dif-before f. So, discedo, dispar, disquiro, distraho, dissolvo; dibalo, dido, digero, dilabor, dimetior, dinumero, dirigo, divello, etc. Before j (i) we have sometimes dī-, as in dijudico, dijungo, and sometim

discalceatus.full: dis-calcĕātus, a, um, adj., unshod, barefooted, Suet. Ner. 51; Vulg. Deut. 25, 10 al.
discalceatus.short: dis-calcĕātus, a, um, adj., unshod, barefooted, Suet.

discapedino.full: dis-căpēdĭno, āvi, 1, v. a. capedo, manus, to hold the hands apart, App. Flor. 3, p. 141.

discaveo.full: dis-căvĕo, ēre, v. n., to be on one's guard against, keep away from, beware of: malo, Plaut. Men. 2, 1, 24.

discedo.full: dis-cēdo, cessi, cessum, 3 (perf. sync. discesti, Plaut. As. 2, 1, 3), v. n. (With the notion of dis predominating.) To part asunder, divide, separate (rare but class.; cf.: linquo, relinquo, desero, desum, destituo, deficio). Lit.: cum terra discessisset magnis quibusdam imbribus, Cic. Off. 3, 9: caelum, opens, id. Div. 1, 43, 97; 1, 44, 99, i. e. clears off, Verg. A. 9, 20 (this last is quoted in Sen. Q. N. 7, 20): sulcus vomere, Luc. 6, 382: VT SODALITATES DECVRIATIQVE DISCEDERENT, SC. ap. Ci

discentia.full: discentĭa, ae, f. disco, a learning (late Lat.), Tert. Anim. 23 and 24.

disceptatio.full: disceptātĭo, ōnis, f. discepto, a dispute, disputation, debate, discussion, disquisition. In gen. (good prose in sing. and plur.; cf. for syn.: controversia, concertatio, altercatio, contentio, jurgium, rixa, disputatio): cum quibus omnis fere nobis disceptatio contentioque est, Cic. Div. 2, 72, 150: non disceptatio modo, sed etiam altercatio, Liv. 38, 32; so absol., Cic. Off. 1, 11, 34; id. Deiot. 2, 5: rationum et firmamentorum contentio adducit in angustum disceptationem, id. Part. Or. 30, 10

disceptator.full: disceptātor, ōris, m. discepto, an umpire, arbitrator, judge: disceptator id est rei sententiaeque moderator, Cic. Part. Or. 3, 10: IVRIS DISCEPTATOR, QVI PRIVATA IVDICET IVDICARIVE IVBEAT, PRAETOR ESTO, id. Leg. 3, 3, 8: nec vero quisquam privatus erat disceptator aut arbiter litis, id. Rep. 5, 2; cf. id. Cael. 15; Plaut. Most. 5, 2, 16; Cic. Fl. 38, 97; id. Agr. 1, 7 fin.; id. Fam. 13, 26, 2; * Caes. B. G. 7, 37, 5; Liv. 1, 50; 8, 23; Asin. Pollio ap. Quint. 9, 4, 132 al.

disceptatrix.full: disceptātrix, īcis, f. disceptator, a female umpire, arbitrator, judge (very rare): dialectica veri et falsi quasi disceptatrix et judex, * Cic. Ac. 2, 28, 91; Lampr. Commod. 5.

discepto.full: discepto, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. dis and capio. Jurid. t. t. (lit., to seize hold of and separate; hence, to stop the dispute), to decide, determine, judge a controversy, = dijudicare (cf.: dissero, disputo; good prose, but rare): res juste sapienterque, Cic. Mil. 9: hanc causam si in foro dicerem eodem audiente et disceptante te, id. Deiot. 2, 6; cf.: ipso exercitu disceptante, Liv. 5, 4: jus dicebat disceptabatque controversias, id. 41, 20; cf.: controversias inter se jure ac judicio, aut ... bel

discernenter.full: discernenter, adv., with a distinction, etc.; v. discerno, P. a. fin.
discernenter.short: discernenter, adv., with a distinction, etc.;

discernibilis.full: discernĭbĭlis, e, adj. discerno, that may be distinguished, discernible: similitudo, Aug. Enchir. 90.

discerniculum.full: discernĭcŭlum, i, n. id.. * The bodkin in a woman's head-dress, which parted the hair, a hair-bodkin, Lucil. ap. Non. 35, 31; cf. Varr. L. L. 5, § 129.—* Trop., a difference: coloris, Gell. 17, 15, 4; Ambros. Apol. Dav. Alt. 4, 26.

discerno.full: dis-cerno, crēvi, crētum, 3, v. a., to separate, set apart. Lit., to separate, part, divide (freq. since the Aug. per.): equas, ne inter se pugnare possint, Varr. R. R. 2, 7, 10: ordines (preceded by senatus a populo secretus), Liv. 34, 54: lignum a carnibus, Plin. 13, 4, 7, § 33: Lusitaniam a Baetica, id. 4, 21, 35, § 116: neque mons erat, qui fines eorum discerneret, i. e. to mark out, determine, Sall. J. 79, 3; cf. poet.: (saxum) telas auro, to interweave with gold, Verg. A. 4, 264; 11, 75: h

discerpo.full: dis-cerpo, psi, ptum, 3, v. a. carpo, to pluck or tear in pieces, to rend, to mangle (class.). Lit.: animus nec secerni nec dividi nec discerpi nec distrahi potest, Cic. Tusc. 1, 29, 71; cf. id. N. D. 1, 11, 27: inter orgia Bacchi discerptum iuvenem sparsere per agros, Verg. G. 4, 522: aliquem, Liv. 1, 16; Suet. Caes. 17: semiustum cadaver (canes), id. Dom. 15: membra gruis, Hor. S. 2, 8, 86 et saep.: in parvas partīs aurum, Lucr. 2, 829; Vulg. Judic. 4, 6 al.— Transf., to scatter, disperse, des

discerptio.full: discerptĭo, ōnis, f. discerpo, a tearing in pieces, rending: discerptiones eorum, Vulg. 4 Esdr. 12, 32: juris humani, Liv. 41, 24, 10 Madvig. (al. dissertio).

discessio.full: discessĭo, ōnis, f. discedo. (Very rarely), a separation of married persons, Ter. And. 3, 3, 36; of the people into parties (with seditio), Gell. 2, 12: stellarum et discessiones et coetus, separations and conjunctions, id. 14, 1, 8; cf.: plebei a patribus, et aliae dissensiones, Sall. H. Fragm. 1, 9 Dietsch.— A going away, departure, removal. In gen. (very rarely; cf. discessus): Nonanus desolatus aliorum discessione, Tac. A. 1, 30 fin.: necessaria, Macr. S. 1, 5, 3.—Far more freq., In partic.

discessus1.full: discessus, a, um, Part., from discedo.
discessus1.short: discessus, a, um, Part., from discedo.

discessus2.full: discessus, ūs, m. discedo. A going asunder, separation, opening (very rare): caeli, i. e. lightning, Cic. Div. 2, 28, 60: est interitus quasi discessus et secretio ac diremptus earum partium, quae ante interitum junctione aliqua tenebantur, id. Tusc. 1, 29, 71.— A going away, departure, removal. In gen. (class.): ut me levarat tuus adventus, sic discessus afflixit, Cic. Att. 12, 50: subitus (with praeceps profectio), Att. ap. Cic. Att. 9, 10, 6: ab urbe, Cic. ib. 8, 3, 3: praeclarus e vita, id.

disceus.full: discĕus, i, m., = δίσκος (a quoit), a sort of comet shaped like a quoit, Plin. 2, 25, 22, § 89.
disceus.short: discĕus, i, m., = δίσκος (a quoit), a sort of comet shaped like a quoit, Plin.

discidium.full: discĭdĭum, ii, n. discindo. A tearing asunder, dividing, parting (freq. in Lucr., elsewh. rare): partibus ejus (sc. corporis) discidium parere et nexus exsolvere, Lucr. 1, 220; cf. id. 249; 452; 2, 120; 3, 839 al.: nubis, id. 6, 293: humi, Sol. 1 med.: terrarum, Amm. 27, 4 al.— A separation of persons or things, a disagreement, discord; also divorce (freq. and class.; see Madvig. ad Cic. Fin. 1, 13, 44, and the Excurs. ib. p. 812 sq.): neque per vinum umquam ex me exoritur discidium in convivio,

discido.full: dis-cīdo, ĕre, v. a. caedo, to cut in pieces (very rare; perh. only in the foll. passages): aliquod in multas partīs ferro, Lucr. 3, 659; id. 669.

discinctus.full: discinctus, a, um, Part., from discingo.
discinctus.short: discinctus, a, um, Part., from discingo.

discindo.full: dī-scindo, cĭdi, cissum, 3, v. a., to tear or cleave asunder, to cut asunder, divide, rend, tear (class.—for syn. cf.: findo, scindo, dirimo, divello, separo, secerno). Lit.: salicem Graecam discindito, Cato R. R. 40, 2: vestem, Ter. Ad. 1, 2, 4 (quoted Cic. Cael. 16, 38); Suet. Caes. 84; id. Ner. 42 al.; cf. tunicam, Cic. de Or. 2, 47, 195: purpureos amictus manu, Verg. A. 12, 602: labrum, Ter. Ad. 4, 2, 20; cf.: maxillam ictu, Suet. Calig. 58: artus, Verg. G. 3, 514: nubem (vis venti), Lucr. 6

discingo.full: dis-cingo, nxi, nctum, 3, v. a., to ungird, deprive of the girdle. Lit.: discinctā tunicā fugiendum est, Hor. S. 1, 2, 132; Vell. 2, 41 fin.; cf.: tunicati et discincti, Suet. Aug. 100: jam discingitur armis, Sil. 8, 34.—As a milit. punishment: destrictis gladiis discinctos destituit, Liv. 27, 13; Suet. Aug. 24 and 100: cum tenues nuper Marius discinxerit Afros, had disarmed, i. e. conquered, Juv. 8, 120; cf.: peltatam Amazona Scythico nodo, Mart. 9, 101, 5.— Trop. In verb finit.: mihi crede, in

disciplina.full: discī^plīna (also uncontr. DISCIPVLINA, Num. Hadr. ap. Eckh. D. N. V. 6, p. 503; the Cod. palimps. Cic. Rep. 2, 19, prima manu has likewise DISCIPVLINA: so, discipulina, Plaut. Most. 1, 2, 75 Lorenz; id. As. 1, 3, 49 Fleck.; cf. Ussing ad loc.), ae. f. discipulus, instruction, tuition, teaching in the widest sense of the word (for syn. cf.: ars, litterae, doctrina, scientia, cognitio, humanitas—very freq. and good prose). Lit.: ad aliquem disciplinae causa concurrere (for which, shortly after: i

disciplinabilis.full: discī^plīnābĭlis, e, adj. disciplina, to be learned by teaching, Cassiod. Var. 4, 33; Isid. 2, 24, 9.—Hence, adv.: discī^plīnā-bĭlĭter, in an instructive manner, Cassiod. in Psalt. praef. 4; id. in Psa. 150, 4.

disciplinatus.full: discī^plīnātus, a, um, adj. id., instructed, disciplined (late Lat.), Vulg. Jacob. 3, 13 al.; Alcim. Avit. 4, 46: disciplinatior, Tert. Fug. in persec. 1, fin.

disciplinosus.full: discī^plīnōsus, a, um, adj. id., docile: gladiator, Cato ap. Non. 463, 5; cf. Gell. 4, 9, 12.

discipulatus.full: discĭpŭlātus, ūs, m. discipulus, the condition of a disciple, discipleship, Tert. Praescr. Haeret. 22; Cassiod. Var. 5, 40.

discipulus.full: discĭpŭlus, i, m. disco, and root of puer, pupilla; cf. Sanscr., putras, son; Gr. πῶλος; Engl., foal, a learner, scholar, pupil, disciple. In gen., Plaut. Bacch. 1, 2, 44 sq.; Cic. Div. 1, 3, 6; 1, 23, 46; id. N. D. 3, 7 et saep.—Trop. Prov.: discipulus est prioris posterior dies, Pub. Syr. 120 (Rib).—In the fem.: discĭpŭla, ae, a female scholar or disciple: ego te dedam discipulam cruci, Plaut. Aul. 1, 1, 20; Plin. 35, 11, 40, § 147; Hor. S. 1, 10, 91; Vulg. Act. 9, 36 al.—Cf. transf., of the n

discissio.full: discissĭo, ōnis, f. discindo, a separation, division (late Lat., v. the class. discidium), Aug. Ep. 261 al.

discissura.full: discissūra, ae, f. id., a rending asunder, a rent (late Lat.): corporis, Ambros. Serm. 13.

discissus.full: discissus, a, um, Part., from discindo.
discissus.short: discissus, a, um, Part., from discindo.

discludo.full: dis-clūdo, si, sum, 3, v. a. claudo (rare but classical; already obsolete in the time of Macrobius, v. Macr. S. 6, 4). To shut up separately, to keep separate; orig. belonging to household lang.: dispares disclusos habere pisces, Varr. R. R. 3, 17, 4.— With the notion of dis predominant, to keep apart, to separate, divide: pares cum paribus jungi res, et discludere mundum, Lucr. 5, 438; so of the act of creation, imitated by Vergil: discludere Nerea ponto, to separate, cut off, Verg. E. 6, 35: p

disclusio.full: disclūsĭo, ōnis, f. discludo, a separation: loci, App. de Deo Socr. init.

disclusus.full: disclūsus, a, um, Part., from discludo.
disclusus.short: disclūsus, a, um, Part., from discludo.

disco.full: disco, dĭdĭci, 3 (part. fut.: sic disciturum, etc., App. ap. Prisc. p. 887 P.), v. a. from the root da-, Gr. δεδαώς, δαῆναι; dak-, cf. doceo, doctus, Gr. διδάσκω, to learn, to learn to know, to become acquainted with, etc. (for syn. cf.: capio, percipio, concipio, comprehendo, intellego, cognosco, nosco, agnosco, animadverto, calleo, scio—very freq. in all periods and sorts of writing). With acc.: litteras Graecas senex didici, Cic. de Sen. 8, 26; id. Tusc. 1, 13, 29: so, litteras, Plaut. Truc.

discobino.full: discŏbīno, āvi, 1, v. a. dis-scobina, to file away, to scratch, destroy by scratching: simulacra, Arn. 6, 14.

discobolus.full: discŏbŏlus, i, m., = δισκοβόλος, the thrower of the discus or quoit, a famous piece of sculpture by Myron, Quint. 2, 13, 10; Plin. 34, 8, 19, § 57; also by Naucydes, Plin. ib. § 80; and a painting by Tauriscus, id. 35, 11, 40, § 144.
discobolus.short: discŏbŏlus, i, m., = δισκοβόλος, the thrower of the discus or quoit, a famous piece of sculpture by Myron, Quint.

discoctus.full: discoctus, a, um, Part., from discoquo.
discoctus.short: discoctus, a, um, Part., from discoquo.

discoides.full: discŏï_des, is, adj., = δισκοειδής, quoit-shaped: figura, Theod. Prisc. 4, 2.
discoides.short: discŏï_des, is, adj., = δισκοειδής, quoit-shaped: figura, Theod.

discolius.full: discŏlĭus pes = δισκολιός, a verse consisting of an iambus, pyrrhichius, and trochaeus, Atil. Fortun. p. 2687 P.
discolius.short: discŏlĭus pes = δισκολιός, a verse consisting of an iambus, pyrrhichius, and trochaeus, Atil.

discolor.full: dis-cŏlor, ōris (abl. -ori, Flor. 1, 16, 7; Curt. 3, 3, 26—post-class. form of the fem. discolora, in the signif. of II. A.: lana, Prud. στεφ. 10, 302: serta, Symm. Laud. in Val. 2, 1 ed. Mai.: venustas, Mart. Cap. 4 init.; and once discoloria vestis, Petr. 97, 3), adj., of another color, not of the same color (opp. concolor). Lit. With dat.: neutra pars esse debet discolor lanae (shortly before: si palatum atque lingua concolor lanae est), Col. 7, 3, 2: (vestis) sumatur fatis discolor alba meis

discolorius.full: discŏlōrĭus and discŏlōrus, a, um, v. the preced. art. init.
discolorius.short: discŏlōrĭus and discŏlōrus, a, um, v.

disconcinnus.full: dis-concinnus, a, um, adj., unsuitable, ill-matched: oculos (opp. concinnos), Fronto de Or. 2.
disconcinnus.short: dis-concinnus, a, um, adj., unsuitable, ill-matched: oculos (opp.

disconduco.full: dis-condūco, ĕre, v. n., not to be profitable or conducive, to be injurious, prejudicial: nil disconducit huic rei, Plaut. Trin. 4, 2, 85.

disconvenientia.full: dis-convĕnĭentĭa, ae, f. disconvenio, want of agreement, inconsistency (opp. convenientia), Tert. Test. An. 6.

disconvenio.full: dis-convĕnĭo, īre, v. n., to disagree; to be inharmonious, inconsistent (very rare): aestuat et vitae disconvenit ordine toto, Hor. Ep. 1, 1, 99.—Impers.: eo disconvenit inter Meque et te, Hor. Ep. 1, 14, 19: disconveniens deo, Lact. de Ira D. 3, 1.

discooperio.full: dis-cŏŏpĕrĭo, pĕrui, pertum, 4, v. a., to uncover, disclose, lay bare, expose (eccl. Lat.): caput, Vulg. Lev. 21, 10: turpitudinem, id. ib. 18, 7: verecundiora patris, id. Ezech. 22, 10.— Transf., to put off, take off, remove a covering: pallium, id. Ruth, 3, 4.— Trop., to expose, disclose: peccata, id. Thren. 4, 22.

discophorus.full: discŏphŏrus, i, m., = δισκοφόρος, one who carries a dish (discus, II.), a dishbearer, Hier. in Daniel, praef.
discophorus.short: discŏphŏrus, i, m., = δισκοφόρος, one who carries a dish (discus, II.), a dishbearer, Hier.

discoquo.full: dis-cŏquo, xi, ctum, 3, v. a., to boil to pieces, to boil thoroughly (post-Aug.), Cels. 6, 9; Plin. 22, 25, 70, § 142; 32, 7, 26, § 81; 23, 6, 60, § 113; Vulg. Ezech. 24, 5 al.

discordabilis.full: discordābĭlis, e, adj. discordo, disagreeing, discordant: ingenio haud discordabili, Plaut. Capt. 2, 3, 42.

discordia.full: discordĭa, ae, f. discors, disunion, disagreement, dissension, variance, discord (class.), Plaut. Truc. 2, 4, 66; Ter. Hec. 4, 4, 71; Cic. Tusc. 4, 9, 21; id. Lael. 7, 24; id. Off. 1, 25, 85; id. Mur. 39, 83; Sall. C. 5, 2; Liv. 2, 24 et saep.; Verg. E. 1, 72; id. A. 7, 545; Hor. Epod. 4, 2; id. S. 1, 4, 60 et saep. —In plur., Cic. Lael. 7, 23; id. Off. 1, 25, 86; id. Fin. 1, 13, 44; id. Mur. 23, 47; Suet. Calig. 26; id. Claud. 25; Vulg. Prov. 6, 19 et saep.— Transf. The subject of strife: Idae

discordialis.full: discordĭālis, false reading in Plin. 37, 10, 54, § 142, instead of discordiam, v. Sillig, ad h. l.

discordiosus.full: discordĭōsus, a, um, adj. discordia, full of discord, prone to discord (very rare; cf. discors and v. Krebs, Antibarb. p. 369): volgus seditiosum atque discordiosum, * Sall. J. 66, 2: domus, Sid. Ep. 6, 2.— Hence, adv.: discordĭōsē, in a spirit of discord, Aug. Bapt. 3, 15, 20.

discorditas.full: discordĭtas, ātis, f. discors, disunion, discord, Pac. ap. Non. 97, 1.

discordium.full: discordĭum, i, n. discors, discord, dissension.—Plur.: publica discordia, Calp. Ecl. 1, 57.

discordo.full: discordo, āre, v. n. id., to be at variance, to differ, to quarrel (rare but class.). Lit.: discordare inter se, Ter. And. 3, 3, 43: cupiditates in animis dissident atque discordant, Cic. Fin. 1, 13, 44: animus a se ipse dissidens secumque discordans, id. ib. 1, 18, 58: cum Cheruscis, Tac. A. 12, 28: adversus ventrem (membra), Quint. 5, 11, 19.— Transf., to be unlike, out of harmony with; to disagree, be inconsistent with, opposed to: ab oratione (vox), id. 11, 3, 45; cf. id. 8, 3, 18: a se fort

discoriatio.full: discŏrĭātĭo, ōnis, f. dis-corium, a flaying, removal of the skin, Soran. qu. Med. 245 (cf. discorio, ἀποδέρω, Gloss.).

discors.full: dis-cors, cordis (nom. f. discordis, Pompon. ap. Prisc. p. 726 Com., v. 164 Rib.), adj. cor, discordant, disagreeing, inharmonious, at variance; opp. concors (class.). Prop. Of persons: homines non contentione, non ambitione discordes, * Cic. Agr. 2, 33, 91: ad alia discordes, Liv. 4, 26: in civitate discordi, Tac. H. 2, 10: vexillarii discordium legionum, id. A. 1, 38.—Poet.: Tanais discors, Hor. C. 3, 29, 28 et saep.; of Minotaurus: fetus, Ov. M. 8, 133: civitas secum ipsa discors, Liv. 2, 23:

discrebilis.full: discrēbĭlis, e, adj. discerno, that can be discerned, discernible: vox, Jul. Val. Res Gest. Alex. M. 3, 42 Mai.

discredo.full: dis-crēdo, dĭdi, dĭtum, 3, v. a., to be incredulous towards, not to believe (late Lat.), Jul. Val. Res Gest. Alex. M. 3, 58 Mai.; Commod. praef. 3, al.

discrepabilis.full: discrĕpābĭlis, e, adj. discrepo, irreconcilable, discrepant, Cassiod. in Psa. 100, 1.

discrepans.full: discrĕpans, antis, Part. and P. a., from discrepo.

discrepantia.full: discrĕpantĭa, ae, f. discrepo, discordance, dissimilarity, discrepancy (a Ciceron. word): rerum et verborum, Cic. Fin. 3, 12 fin.: scripti et voluntatis, id. Top. 25 fin.: nulla, id. Off. 1, 31, 111.

discrepatio.full: discrĕpātĭo, ōnis, f. id., a discrepancy, dispute: inter consules fuit, Liv. 10, 18, 7; cf. Drak. ad Liv. 21, 31, 8.

discrepito.full: discrĕpĭto, āre, v. freq. n. [id.], to disagree wholly, to be altogether different (a Lucretian word): res longe, Lucr. 6, 1105; id. 2, 1018: inter se (with disjunctum), id. 3, 803.

discrepo.full: dis-crĕpo, ŭi, 1, v. n., to differ in sound, to sound differently, discordantly, not to harmonize (for syn. cf.: differo, disto, intersum). Lit. (rare; perh. only in Cic.): ut in fidibus aut tibiis, quamvis paulum discrepent, tamen id a sciente animadverti solet: sic videndum est in vita, ne forte quid discrepet, etc., Cic. Off. 1, 40 fin.; id. Rep. 2, 42, 69; id. de Or. 3, 50, 196.—Far more freq., Trop., to disagree, be different, to vary, differ: peccata, quia discrepant, aeque discrepant, Cic

discresco.full: dis-cresco, crēvi, 3, v. n., to grow broad, grow out, Lact. de Mort. Pers. 33, 10.

discretim.full: discrētim, adv., separately, v. discerno fin.

discretio.full: discrētĭo, ōnis, f. discerno (postclass.). A separation: cum vis aliqua utrumque (corpus et animam) discreverit, quae discretio mors vocetur, Macr. Somn. Scip. 1, 6, 17; Lact. 7, 12, 4.— A difference, distinction: sine discretione, Pall. Jul. 4, 5; Amm. 17, 1 al.— Discernment, discrimination, capacity for distinguishing (late Lat.): ne, propter discretionem difficilem, jus incertum sit, Vulg. 1 Cor. 12, 10: boni ac mali, id. Hebr. 5, 14.

discretivus.full: discrētīvus, a, um, adj. id., serving to distinguish, Prisc. p. 1021; 1061 al. P.— Adv.: discrētīvē, by way of distinction, Donat. ad Ter. Eun. 1, 2, 43.

discretor.full: discrētor, ōris, m. id., he who discerns or judges, a discerner: cogitationum deus, Vulg. Hebr. 4, 12 al.

discretus.full: discrētus, a, um, Part., from discerno.
discretus.short: discrētus, a, um, Part., from discerno.

discretorium.full: discrētōrĭum, ii, n., = διάφραγμα, the diaphragm, Cael. Aur. Tard. 2, 12, 143.
discretorium.short: discrētōrĭum, ii, n., = διάφραγμα, the diaphragm, Cael.

discribo.full: dī-scrībo, scripsi, scriptum, 3, v. a., to distribute, divide among several persons, apportion, assign: (class.) quodne (argentum) ego discripsi porro illis quibus debui? Ter. Phorm. 5, 8, 30: quorum ipsorum bona, quantacumque erant, statim suis comitibus compotoribusque discripsit, Cic. Phil. 5, 8, 22: urbis partīs ad incendia, Cic. Cat. 1, 4, 9: duodena jugera in singulos homines, id. Agr. 2, 31, 85: populum in tribus tres, curiasque triginta, etc., id. Rep. 2, 8: civitatibus jura, id. ib. 1,

discrimen.full: discrīmen, ĭnis, n. contr. from discerimen à discerno; cf. crimen from cerno, lit., that which separates or divides two things from each other (for syn. cf.: differentia, discrepantia, diversitas, distantia); hence, Lit., an intervening space, interval, distance, division, separation: cum (duo maria) pertenui discrimine separarentur, Cic. Agr. 2, 32, 87: minimum quos inter et hostem Discrimen murus clausaque porta facit, Ov. Pont. 1, 8, 62: aequo discrimine, Lucr. 5, 690; Verg. A. 5, 154: parvum

discriminalis.full: discrīmĭnālis, e, adj. discrimino, that serves to divide or part (late Lat.): acus, a pin or bodkin that parts the hair, a hair-pin, Hier. Ruf. 3, 42.—Also, subst.: discrīmĭnāle, is, n., a head-dress, Vulg. lsa. 3, 20.

discriminatim.full: discrīmĭnātim, adv. id., with a difference or distinction (very rare), Varr. R. R. 1, 7, 7.

discriminatio.full: discrīmĭnātĭo, ōnis, f. id., rhet. t. t., = παραδιαστολή, the contrasting of opposite thoughts, Rufin. Schem. lex. § 20.

discriminator.full: discrīmĭnātor, ōris, m. id., one who distinguishes or discriminates (late Lat) = distinctor, Aug. ap. Joann. 20, 12.

discriminatrix.full: discrīmĭnātrix, īcis, f. discriminator, she who distinguishes (late Lat.): fandi ac nefandi, Nazar. Pan. ad Const. 7.

discrimino.full: discrīmĭno, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. discrimen, to divide, part, separate (very rare; cf. divido, dispertio): aliquid, Varr. R. R. 1, 23, 4: Etruriam discriminat Cassia, * Cic. Phil. 12, 9: late agros, Verg. A. 11, 144: crinem, Vulg. Jud. 10, 3.— Trop., to distinguish: notae, quibus inter se similia discriminentur, Sen. Ep. 95 fin. et saep.: verba, Varr. L. L. 9, § 104 Müll.— To divide, apportion: vigiliarum somnique tempora, Liv. 21, 4, 6.

discriminosius.full: discrīmĭnōsĭus, adv. comp. [id.], more decisively, Jul. Val. Res Gest. Alex. 2, 24.

discriptio.full: dīscriptio, ōnis, f. discribo, a division, distribution, apportionment: civitatis, Cic. Sest. 65, 137: populi, id. Planc. 18, 45: privatarum possessionum, id. Off. 1, 7, 21; id. Tusc. 4, 1, 1; 5, 24, 68; id. Rep. 1, 46, 70; id. N. D. 1, 33, 92 al. (In these passages, formerly descriptio, q. v.)

discruciatus1.full: discrŭcĭātus, a, um, Part., from discrucio.
discruciatus1.short: discrŭcĭātus, a, um, Part., from discrucio.

discruciatus2.full: discrŭcĭātus, ūs, m., violent torture, torment, Prud. Ham. 836. From
discruciatus2.short: discrŭcĭātus, ūs, m., violent torture, torment, Prud.

discrucio.full: dis-crŭcĭo, no perf., ātum, 1, v. a., to torture violently, to torment (repeatedly in Plaut. and Cic.; elsewh. rare). Physically: aliquem discruciatum necare, Cic. Phil. 13, 18, 37; Amm. 27, 12, 3.—More freq., Mentally, with se or in the mid. form, to torment one's self; to be troubled, vexed, chagrined: quid te discrucias? Plaut. Fragm. ap. Non. 143, 3: ego discrucior miser amore, Plaut. Cas. 2, 3, 58; id. Poen. 1, 2, 155.—With acc. and inf., Plaut. Bacch. 3, 3, 31; Cic. Att. 14, 6; Cat. 66, 76

discubitio.full: discŭbĭtĭo, ōnis, f. discumbo, a place for lying down, a couch, Inscr. Orell. 2106.

discubitus.full: discŭbĭtus, ūs, m. id., a reclining at table, Val. Max. 2, 1, 9.— Transf., a place at table: amare primos discubitus, Vulg. Luc. 20, 46 al.

disculcio.full: dis-culcĭo, āre, 1, v. a. calceo, to unshoe, remove the shoe from, Diom. 374 P.

discumbo.full: dis-cumbo, cŭbŭi, cŭbĭtum, 3, v. n., to lie down. More freq., to recline at table for the purpose of eating (cf. accumbo—so esp. freq. since the Aug. per.): discubuimus omnes praeter illam, Cic. Att. 5, 1, 4; Lucr. 3, 912; Quint. 11, 2, 13; Suet. Caes. 48; Tib. 2, 5, 95; Verg. A. 1, 708; Ov. M. 8, 566; Vulg. Johan. 12, 2 al.—Sometimes of a single person (yet always with the accessory idea of a number reclining at the same time): in convivio Germanici cum super eum Piso discumberet, Tac. A. 3, 14

discuneatus.full: dis-cŭnĕātus, a, um, adj., wedged apart, kept asunder as by a wedge: conchae, Plin. 9, 30, 48, § 90.
discuneatus.short: dis-cŭnĕātus, a, um, adj., wedged apart, kept asunder as by a wedge: conchae, Plin.

discupio.full: dis-cŭpĭo, ĕre, v. n. (in famil. lang. for vehementer cupio), to desire greatly, to long for: discupio dicere, Plaut. Trin. 4, 2, 87: te videre, Cael. ap. Cic. Fam. 8, 15, 2: se vendere, Cat. 106, 2.

discurro.full: dis-curro, curri and cucurri (perf. discucurri, Liv. 25, 25, 9; Sen. Contr. 4, 2; Suet. Calig. 32: discurrisse, Curt. 4, 15, 5; oftener curri, Liv. 34, 37; 3, 7, 32; Sen. Ep. 90, 36; Curt. 4, 15, 10 al.), cursum, 3, v. n. To run different ways, to run to and fro, run about (not freq. till after the Aug. per.; in Cic not at all): in muris armata civitas, * Caes. B. C. 3, 105, 3: deus in montibus altis, Ov. F. 2, 285: plebs pileata tota Urbe, Suet. Ner. 57: circa deum delubra, Liv. 26, 9; cf.: cir

discursatio.full: discursātĭo, ōnis, f. discurso, a running hither and thither, a running about (post-Aug. and rare): officiosa per urbem, Sen. Brev. Vit. 3: magna, Front. Strat. 1, 5 fin.: animalium, Lact. Opif. D. 3.

discursator.full: discursātor, ōris, m. id., one who runs hither and thither, one who runs about (late Lat.): pedites et leves, Amm. 16, 12, 21; cf. hostis, id. 29, 5, 7; 14, 2, 6.

discursim.full: discursim, adv. discurro, by running or going about, Macr. S. 7, 1, 1 (dub.); Jul. Val. Res Gest. Alex. 1, 51.

discursio.full: discursĭo, ōnis, f. id., a running different ways, scattering (late Lat.): discursiones predatoriae, scattered raids for plunder, foragings, Amm. 15, 4, 11.— A hasty passing through: discursione rapidā maturabant, Amm. 31, 9, 2.

discurso.full: discurso, āre, v. freq. a. and n. id.. Neutr., to run about, hasten up and down (post - Aug. and rare): multum in agendo discursantem, salientem, etc.... non agere dixit (Domitius Afer) sed satagere, Quint. 6, 3, 54; cf. id. 11, 3, 126; Flor. 3, 18, 10.— Act., to traverse (late Lat.): Gallias, Amm. 15, 5, 4.

discursor.full: discursor, ōris, m. id., one who runs about, (Pseud.) Augustin. ad Frat. Erem. Serm. 5.

discursus1.full: discursus, a, um, Part., from discurro.
discursus1.short: discursus, a, um, Part., from discurro.

discursus2.full: discursus, ūs, m. discurro. A running to and fro, a running about (mostly post-class.): magno clamore discursuque passim fugae se mandant, Hirt. B. G. 8, 29, 2; Liv. 25, 25; Quint. 1, 12, 10; Plin. Ep. 1, 9, 7; Ov. F. 2, 223; Juv. 1, 86; Val. Fl. 5, 428 al.— Transf. A pace, gait: acri discursu, Amm. 14, 7, 16. — Of inanimate things: radicum, Plin. 17, 20, 33, § 144: venarum, id. 34, 12, 29, § 118: macularum, id. 16, 15, 26, § 66: telorum, Val. Max. 3, 1, 1.— In late Lat. (acc. to discurro, III.)

discus1.full: discus, i, m., = δίσκος. A quoit, an implement for exercise in ancient gymnastics, Stat. Th. 6, 646 sq.; Prop. 3, 14, 10 (4, 13, 10 M.); Hor. C. 1, 8, 11; id. S. 2, 2, 13; id. A. P. 380; Ov. M. 10, 177 al.— Prov.: qui discum audire quam philosophum malunt, i. e. who prefer trifles to serious things, Cic. de Or. 2, 5, 21.— A dish, so called because shaped like a quoit, App. M. 2, p. 125; Vulg. Matt. 14, 8.— The disc of a dial, a sundial, Vitr. 9, 9, 1.

discus2.full: Discus, i, m., the name of a freedman, Ter. Eun. 3, 5, 60.
discus2.short: Discus, i, m., the name of a freedman, Ter.

discusse.full: discussē, adv., minutely, accurately, etc., v. discutio fin.
discusse.short: discussē, adv., minutely, accurately, etc., v.

discussio.full: discussĭo, ōnis, f. discutio (very rare). A shaking, Sen. Q. N. 6, 19, 2.— An examination, discussion. In gen. (late Lat. for disputatio, quaestio): sequitur illa discussio, quid sit, etc., Macr. Somn. Scip. 1, 16, 8; Tert. Pudic. 11.— In partic., in the later period of the empire, a revision of the public accounts in the provinces, Cod. Just. 10, 30, 1; Symm. Ep. 5, 74.

discussor.full: discussor, ōris, m. id., an examiner (late Lat.). In gen., Macr. Somn. Scip. 1, 21, 8.— In partic., in the later period of the empire, one who revised the accounts of the public revenue in the provinces, an auditor, Gr. λογοθέτης, Cod. Just. 10, tit. 30; Symm. Ep. 5, 76 al.

discussorius.full: discussōrĭus, a, um, adj. id., discutient, dissolving: vis, Plin. 30, 8, 22, § 75.

discussus1.full: discussus, a, um, Part., from discutio.
discussus1.short: discussus, a, um, Part., from discutio.

discussus2.full: discussus, ūs, m. discutio, a dashing, agitating: (lupus) si haesit in hamo, tumultuoso discussu laxat volnera, Plin. 32, 2, 5, § 13.

discutio.full: dis-cŭtĭo, cussi, cussum, 3, v. a. quatio, to strike asunder, dash to pieces, shatter, etc. In gen.: dentes, Lucil. ap. Non. 455, 18: deum delubra, Lucr. 6, 418; cf.: columna rostrata tota ad imum fulmine discussa est, Liv. 42, 20: ne saxa ex catapultis lateritium discuterent, Caes. B. C. 2, 9, 3; cf.: aliquantum muri tribus arietibus, Liv. 21, 12: rostro (navis) discusso, shattered, Auct. B. Alex. 46, 2; cf.: tempora cava ictu, Ov. M. 2, 625: ora saxo, id. ib. 4, 519: percussam aquam, Plin. 28,

disdiapason.full: disdĭăpāsōn, indecl., = δὶς διὰ πασῶν, a double octave in music, Mart. Cap. 9, § 950; Vitr. 5, 4, 9 al.; cf. diapason.
disdiapason.short: disdĭăpāsōn, indecl., = δὶς διὰ πασῶν, a double octave in music, Mart.

disemus.full: dĭsēmus, a, um, adj., = δίσημος, dissyllabic, Mart. Cap. 9, § 978; § 981.
disemus.short: dĭsēmus, a, um, adj., = δίσημος, dissyllabic, Mart.

diserte.full: dĭsertē, adv., clearly, etc., v. dissero, P. a. fin. .

disertim.full: dĭsertim, adv., clearly, expressly, etc., v. dissero, P. a. fin. .
disertim.short: dĭsertim, adv., clearly, expressly, etc., v.

disertiones.full: dĭsertĭōnes divisiones patrimoniorum inter consortes, Paul. ex Fest. p. 72, 8; cf. Müll. ad h. l.
disertiones.short: dĭsertĭōnes divisiones patrimoniorum inter consortes, Paul.

disertitudo.full: dĭsertĭtūdo, ĭnis, f. disertus, eloquence (late Lat.), Hier. Ep. 50, no. 5; Vulg. Isa. 33, 19.

disertus.full: dĭsertus, a, um, v. dissero, P. a.

disglutino.full: dis-glūtĭno, āre, v. a., to disjoin, disunite (late Lat.): conjuncta (with dissuere), Hier. Ep. 66, no. 12.

disgrego.full: dis-grĕgo, āre, v. a., to separate, divide (opp. congrego; late Lat.), Mart. Cap. 3, § 289; 9, § 913.

disgregus.full: disgrĕgus, a, um, adj. disgrego, different, unlike (with dispar), Mart. Cap. 9, § 892.
