dochmius.full: dochmĭus, ii, m., = δόχμιος (sc. πούς), the dochmiac foot in poetry, whose fundamental scheme is ˘ ̄́ ̄́ ˘ ̄́, of which, however, about thirty modifications are described, Cic. Or. 64 fin.; Quint. 9, 4, 79 al.

docibilis.full: dŏcĭbĭlis, e, adj. doceo, that learns easily, teachable, apt (late Lat.), Tert. Mon. 12 al.; Ambros. in Psa. 47, 21 fin.; Vulg. 2 Tim. 2, 24: docibiles Dei, disciples of God, taught by God, id. Johan. 6, 45.

docibilitas.full: dŏcĭbĭlĭtas, ātis, f., aptness in learning, docility, acc. to Isid. Sent. 5, 14.
docibilitas.short: dŏcĭbĭlĭtas, ātis, f., aptness in learning, docility, acc.

docilis.full: dŏcĭlis, e, adj. doceo, easily taught, docile. Prop. (freq. and class.).—Absol.: belua docilis et humanis moribus assueta, Cic. Rep. 2, 40; id. de Or. 2, 19, 80; Liv. 23, 29; Quint. 2, 9, 3; Hor. C. 3, 11, 1; id. Carm. Sec. 45 et saep.; cf. in the comp., Quint. 1, 12, 9; 4, 2, 24.—With ad: ad agriculturam, Varr. R. R. 1, 17, 3; Cic. Fam. 7, 20, 3; id. Tusc. 2, 6; Curt. 8, 31, 16; in the comp., Plaut. Bacch. 1, 2, 56.—With abl.: habebant luscinias Graeco atque Latino sermone docilis, Plin. 10, 42

docilitas.full: dŏcĭlĭtas, ātis, f. docilis, aptness for being taught, docility. Prop., Cic. Sest. 42, 91; id. Fin. 5, 13, 36; Nep. Att. 1, 3; Plin. 8, 1, 1, § 3; 8, 42, 64, § 157: ad omnes fere artes, Suet. Tit. 3.—* Transf., in a moral sense, gentleness, Eutr. 10, 4.

docis.full: dŏcis, ĭdis, f., = δοκίς, a fiery meteor, App. de Mundo, p. 58, 23.
docis.short: dŏcis, ĭdis, f., = δοκίς, a fiery meteor, App.

docte.full: docte, adv., v. doceo, P. a. fin.

docticanus.full: doctĭcănus, a, um, adj. doctus-cano, singing skilfully: sensus, Mart. Cap. 2, § 122.

doctificus.full: doctĭfĭcus, a, um, adj. doctus-facio, making learned: Ardor (i. e. Pallas), Mart. Cap. 1 init.; id. 6, § 567.

doctiloquus.full: doctĭlŏquus, a, um, adj. doctus-loquor, speaking learnedly (ante- and postclass.): oratores, Enn. ap. Varr. L. L. 7, § 41 Müll. (Ann. v. 568, ed. Vahl.): juvenis, Mart. Cap. 9, § 903.

doctisonus.full: doctĭ-sŏnus, a, um, adj. doctus, skilfully sounding: artes, Sid. Carm. 15, 180.

doctor.full: doctor, ōris, m. doceo, a teacher, instructor, Cic. de Or. 1, 6, 23; 3, 15, 57; id. Div. 1, 3, 6; id. Or. 33, 117; Quint. 2, 2, 2; Hor. C. 4, 6, 25; id. S. 1, 1, 26; Vulg. Matt. 22, 35 et saep.

doctrina.full: doctrīna, ae, f. doctor, teaching, instruction (class.; cf.: litterae, artes, disciplina, praecepta, scientia, humanitas). Prop.: non aliqua mihi doctrina tradita, sed in rerum usu causisque tractata, Cic. de Or. 1, 48, 208; 1, 3, 11; id. Off. 44, 155: puerilis, id. de Or. 3, 31, 125; id. Mur. 30, 63; id. Sest. 56; Quint. 2, 8, 3; 6, 3, 12; 12, 2, 1 (in these passages of Quint. opp. natura; cf. also Hor. Ep. 1, 18, 100); id. 2, 12, 8; Hor. C. 4, 4, 33 et saep.— Transf. Object., the knowledge imp

doctrinalis.full: doctrīnālis, e, adj. doctrina, theoretical: scientia, Isid. Orig. 2, 24, 14; Cassiod. Inst. Lib. Litt. praef.

doctrix.full: doctrix, īcis, f. doctor, she who instructs, an instructress, teacher: (sapientia) doctrix est disciplinae Dei, Vulg. Sap. 8, 4; August. de Mor. Eccl. Cath. 16; Serv. Verg. A. 12, 159; Prisc. 1122 P.

doctus.full: doctus, a, um, Part. and P. a., from doceo.

documen.full: dŏcŭmen (dŏcĭmen), ĭnis, n., v. documentum init.

documentatio.full: dŏcŭmentātĭo, νουθεσία, a reminding, Gloss. Lat. Gr.

documentum.full: dŏcŭmentum, i (dŏcŭmen, Lucr. 6, 392; and dŏcĭmen, Ter. Maur. p. 2425 P.), n. doceo: documenta quae exempla docendi causa dicuntur, Varr. L. L. 6, § 62 Müll., a lesson, example (either for instruction or warning); a pattern, warning; a proof, instance, specimen, etc. (class.). With gen.: P. Rutilius documentum fuit hominibus nostris virtutis, antiquitatis, prudentiae, Cic. Rab. Post. 10, 27; cf. Suet. Aug. 51: humanorum casuum, Liv. 45, 40, 6: periculi, id. 1, 52, 4: fidei dare, id. 22, 39: eloq

dodecaeteris.full: dōdĕcăĕtēris, ĭdis, f., = δωδεκαετηρίς, a period of twelve years, Censor. 18, 6.
dodecaeteris.short: dōdĕcăĕtēris, ĭdis, f., = δωδεκαετηρίς, a period of twelve years, Censor.

dodecatemorion.full: dōdĕcătēmŏrĭon, ii, n., = δωδεκατημόριον, in astronomy, the twelfth part of a constellation, Manil. 2, 694; 699 al.
dodecatemorion.short: dōdĕcătēmŏrĭon, ii, n., = δωδεκατημόριον, in astronomy, the twelfth part of a constellation, Manil.

dodecatheon.full: dōdĕcăthĕon, i, n., = δωδεκάθεον, an herb, so called after the twelve greater gods; perh. Primula vulg., Linn.; Plin. 25, 4, 9, § 28; cf. Marc. Emp. 27.
dodecatheon.short: dōdĕcăthĕon, i, n., = δωδεκάθεον, an herb, so called after the twelve greater gods;

dodona.full: dōdōna, ae (-ē, es, Plin. 2, 103, 106, § 228; Claud. III. Cons. Hon. 117), f., = Δωδώνη, a city in Epirus, famed on account of its very ancient oracle of Jupiter, situated in an oak-grove, Cic. Div. 1, 43, 95; Plin. l. l.; Prop. 2, 21, 3 (3, 14, 3 M.); Ov. Tr. 4, 8, 43; Luc. 6, 426 al.— Meton. The sacred oak-grove of Dodona, Verg. G. 1, 149 Serv.— The Dodonean priests, Nep. Lys. 3, 2.— Derivv. Dōdō-naeus, a, um, adj., of Dodona, Dodonean: quercus, Cic. Att. 2, 4; cf. Ov. M. 7, 623: oraculum, Cic

dodra.full: dōdra, ae, f. dodrans, a drink composed of nine ingredients, Aus. Epigr. 86 and 87; called also: * dodralis potio, id. ib. 86 in lemm.

dodrans.full: dōdrans, antis, m., nine twelfths or three fourths of any thing (v. as, I.). In gen.: alicujus aedificii reliquum dodrantem emere, Cic. Att. 1, 14 fin.; cf.: solvere dodrantem, Mart. 8, 9: heres ex dodrante, Nep. Att. 5, 2; Suet. Caes. 83: jugeri, Col. 5, 1, 11; Liv. 8, 11: operae, Col. 2, 4, 8: dodrantes semuncias horarum, Plin. 2, 14, 11, § 58: pondo dodrans, Scrib. Comp. 45 et saep.— Esp. As a measure of length, nine inches, Plin. 36, 9, 14, § 71; Suet. Aug. 79; Front. Aquaed. 65.— As a measu
dodrans.short: dōdrans, antis, m., nine twelfths or three fourths of any thing (v.

dodrantalis.full: dōdrantālis, e, adj. dodrans, of nine inches: stirps, Col. 5, 6, 12: rami, Plin. 15, 30, 39, § 131: altitudo, Col. 11, 3, 44.

dodrantarius.full: dōdrantārĭus, a, um, adj. id., of or belonging to a dodrans: tabulae, the debtbooks introduced in consequence of the lex Valeria feneratoria, Cic. Font. Fragm. 2 Niebuhr.

doga.full: dŏga, ae, f., = δοχή, a sort of vessel (perhaps a measure), Vop. Aur. 48; cf. doga βούττης, Gloss. Philox.
doga.short: dŏga, ae, f., = δοχή, a sort of vessel (perhaps a measure), Vop.

dogma.full: dogma, ătis, n. (also fem.: Pythagoream dogmam doctus, Laber. ap. Prisc. p. 679 fin. P.), = δόγμα, a philosophic tenet, doctrine, dogma, Cic. Ac. 2, 43, 133; id. Fin. 2, 32, 105; Mart. 1, 9; Juv. 13, 121; Vulg. Job, 13, 4 al. (in Cic. Ac. 2, 9, 27, written as Greek). — A decree, order (eccl. Lat.): crudele regis, Vulg. Esth. 4, 3; cf. id. Act. 16, 4.

dogmaticus.full: dogmătĭcus, a, um, adj., = δογματικός, pertaining to a philosophic doctrine, dogmatic: lites, Aus. Idyll. 17, 16.
dogmaticus.short: dogmătĭcus, a, um, adj., = δογματικός, pertaining to a philosophic doctrine, dogmatic: lites, Aus.

dogmatistes.full: dogmătistes, ae, m., = δογματιστής, one who maintains dogmata, a dogmatist, Rufin. 2 Invect. in Hier. no. 25.
dogmatistes.short: dogmătistes, ae, m., = δογματιστής, one who maintains dogmata, a dogmatist, Rufin.

dogmatizo.full: dogmătīzo, āre, v. n., = δογματίζω, to propound a dogma, Aug. Ep. 57, 8 fin.

dolabella1.full: dŏlābella, ae, f. dim. dolabra, a small pick-axe, hatchet, Col. 2, 24, 4 sq.

dolabella2.full: Dŏlābella, ae, m. nom. pr., the name of a Roman family in the gens Cornelia, of which the best-known individual is P. Cornelius Dolabella, Cicero's son-in-law, Cic. Fam. 2, 16, 5 al.—Hence, Dŏlābel-lĭānus, a, um, adj.: pira, named after a Dolabella otherwise unknown, Col. 5, 10, 18; 12, 10, 4; Plin. 15, 15, 16, § 54.

dolabra.full: dŏlābra, ae, f. dolo, a mattock, pickaxe, as a milit. implement, Liv. 9, 37; 21, 11; Tac. H. 3, 20; 27; Curt. 8, 4; 9, 5; Juv. 8, 248; an agricultural implement, Col. Arb. 10, 2; Pall. Jan. 3, 3; id. Febr. 21, 2; a butcher's implement, Dig. 33, 7, 18; cf. Fest. s. v. SCENA, p. 318, 18 Müll.

dolabrarius.full: dŏlābrārĭus, ii, m. dolabra, a pickaxe-maker, Inscr. Orell. 4071; 4081.

dolabratus.full: dŏlābrātus, a, um, adj. id., mattockshaped: securis, Pall. 1, 43, 3 (in Caes. B. G. 7, 73, 2, read delibratis).

dolamen.full: dŏlāmen, ĭnis, n. dolo, a hewing: trunci, App. Flor. 1.

dolatilis.full: dŏlātĭlis, e, adj. id., easily hewn: lapides, Auct. de Lim. ap. Goes. p. 270.

dolatorium.full: dŏlātōrĭum, ii, n. id., an implement for hewing stones; as a transl. of λαξευτήριον, Hier. Ep. 106 fin.

dolatus.full: dŏlātus, ūs, m. id., a hewing: gemmae, Prud. Psych. 836.

dolens.full: dŏlens, Part. and P. a., from doleo.

dolenter.full: dŏlenter, adv., v. doleo, P. a.

dolentia.full: dŏlentĭa, ae, f. doleo, pain, Laev. ap. Gell. 19, 7, 9.

dolentulus.full: dŏlentŭlus, a, um, dim. adj. [dolens]: maritus, Ren. Inscr. Afric. 3844.

doleo.full: dŏlĕo, ŭi, ĭtum (doliturus, Liv. 39, 43 fin.; Prop. 1, 15, 27; Verg. A. 11, 732; Hor. Epod. 15, 11; id. S. 1, 2, 112; 1, 10, 89; Ov. M. 9, 257 al.; cf. also under !*?), 2, v. n. and a. [perh. root in Sansc. dar-, dal-, to tear apart; cf. Gr. δέρω, to flay; Ger. zehren, to consume; Eng. tear]. Corporeally, to feel pain, suffer pain, be in pain, to ache: nequeo caput Tollere, ita dolui, itaque ego nunc doleo, etc., Plaut. Truc. 2, 6, 45; id. Aul. 3, 1, 5: doleo ab animo, doleo ab oculis, doleo ab

doliaris.full: dōlĭāris, e, adj. dolium, of a cask: vinum, in cask, i. e. new, not yet drawn off, Dig. 18, 6, 1, § 4: anus, like a barrel, Plaut. Ps. 2, 2, 64.

doliarius.full: dōlĭārĭus, a, um, adj. id., of a cask or casks. Adj.: DOLEARIA OFFICINA, Inscr. Orell. 4888.— Subst.: dōlĭārĭ-um, ii, n., the place where wine-casks are kept; corresp. to our wine-cellar, Dig. 18, 1, 35, § 7.

dolicha.full: Dŏlĭcha, ae, or -e, ēs, f., a city of Thessalia, Liv. 42, 53, 6; 44, 2, 8.
dolicha.short: Dŏlĭcha, ae, or -e, ēs, f., a city of Thessalia, Liv.

dolichenus.full: Dŏlĭchēnus and Dŏlŏcēnus, an epithet of Jupiter, v. Marini Att. de' Frat. Arv. p. 538 sq.
dolichenus.short: Dŏlĭchēnus and Dŏlŏcēnus, an epithet of Jupiter, v.

dolichodromos.full: dŏlĭchō^drŏmos, i, m., = δολιχοδρόμος, the long course in racing, of twenty stadia, Hyg. Fab. 273.
dolichodromos.short: dŏlĭchō^drŏmos, i, m., = δολιχοδρόμος, the long course in racing, of twenty stadia, Hyg.

dolichos1.full: Dŏlĭchos, i, m., The name of a gladiator, Hor. Ep. 1, 18, 19.
dolichos1.short: Dŏlĭchos, i, m., The name of a gladiator, Hor.

dolichos2.full: dŏlĭchos, i, m., = δόλιχος, a plant, perhaps the kidney-bean, Plin. 16, 44, 92, § 244.
dolichos2.short: dŏlĭchos, i, m., = δόλιχος, a plant, perhaps the kidney-bean, Plin.

dolidus.full: dŏlĭdus, a, um, adj. dolor, painful (late Lat.): motus, Cael. Aur. Acut. 3, 3, 11.

doliolum.full: dōlĭŏlum, i, n. dim. dolium, a small cask. Prop., Col. 12, 44, 3; Liv. 5, 40. — Nom. propr.: Dōliŏla, ōrum, n., a place in Rome, acc. to Varr. L. L. 5, § 157 Müll.; Paul. ex Fest. p. 69, 8 Müll.— Doliola florum, the calyx, Plin. 11, 13, 13, § 32; cf. Schneid. on Varr. R. R. p. 579.

dolito.full: dŏlĭto, āre, v. freq. n. [doleo], to pain greatly, to ache, Cato R. R. 157, 7.

dolium.full: dōlĭum, ii, (plur. written DOLEA, Calend. ap. Orell. Inscr. II. p. 381), n. cf. Gr. δαίδαλος, δαιδάλεος, skilfully wrought; Lat. dolo, a very large jar of globular form, with a wide mouth (cf.: vas, arpa, seria, cadus, lagena, culeus, amphora, urna, congius, cyathus, urceus, testa, etc.): dolium aut seria, Varr. ap. Serv. Verg. A. 6, 31; Cato R. R. 69, 1; Juv. 14, 308; Varr. R. R. 3, 15, 2; Col. 11, 2, 70; Plaut. Cist. 2, 2, 7; Ter. Heaut. 3, 1, 51; Hor. C. 3, 11, 27; id. Epod. 2, 47 et saep.: d

dolo1.full: dŏlo, āvi, ātum, 1 (access. form of the part. pass. dolītus, Varr. ap. Non. 99, 17, and 436, 15), v. a. cf. Sanscr. dar-, dal-, to tear apart; whence doleo; Lat. dolium, to chip with an axe, to hew. Lit.: materiem, Cato R. R. 31 fin.: taleas, Cat. 45: robur, Cic. Div. 2, 41, 86: scyphum caelo, Varr. ap. Non. 99, 18: perticas in quadrum, Col. 8, 3, 7: stipes falce dolatus, Prop. 4 (5), 2, 59. dolato confisus ligno, Juv. 12, 57; cf.: non est e robore dolatus, Cic. Ac. 2, 31, 100: de lapidibus dola

dolo2.full: Dŏlo, ōnis, m. nom. propr., = Δόλων. A spy of the Trojans in the Trojan war, Ov. M. 13, 98, Verg. A. 12, 347 Serv, Macr S. 5, 16 al.— A son of Priam, Hyg. Fab 90.

dolopes.full: Dŏlŏpes, um (sing. acc. Dolopem, Liv. 42, 58), m., = Δόλοπες, the Dolopes or Dolopians, a people in Thessaly, renowned in fable, Plin. 4, 2, 3, § 6 (who reckons them among the Aetolians); Cic. Rep. 2, 4, 8; Verg. A. 2, 7; Ov. M. 12, 364; Nep. Cim. 2, 5.— Derivv. Dŏlŏpēĭus, a, um, adj., of the Dolopes, Dolopian: busta, Val. Fl. 2, 10.— Dŏlŏpēis, ĭdis, f., adj., Dolopian: urbs, i. e. Ctimene, Hyg. Fab. 14.— Dŏlŏpĭa, ae, f., the part of Thessaly formerly inhabited by the Dolopes, Liv. 32, 13 al.

dolor.full: dŏlor, ōris, m. doleo, pain, smart, ache (freq. and class.; for syn. cf.: aegrimonia, maeror, maestitia, luctus, plangor, tristitia, angor, anxietas, cura, sollicitudo). Corporeal: dolor est motus asper in corpore, alienus a sensibus, Cic. Tusc. 2, 15: dolores atque carnificinas facere, Cato ap. Gell. 10, 3, 17: corporis, Lucr. 4, 1075: capitis, id. 6, 785: dentium, oculorum, id. 6, 660: pedum, Cic. Brut. 34, 130: articulorum, id. Att. 1, 5 fin.: laterum, Hor. S. 1, 9, 32 et saep.—Of the pangs o

dolorosus.full: dŏlōrōsus, a, um, adj. dolor, painful, full of sorrow (late Lat.): loci, Veg. Vet. 4, 22: exstantia, Cael. Aur. Tard. 4, 5.

dolositas.full: dŏlōsĭtas, ātis, f. dolosus, deceit, Vulg. Sir. 37, 3.

dolosus.full: dŏlōsus, a, um, adj. dolus, crafty, cunning, deceitful (rare, and mostly poet.; for syn. cf.: subdolus, fraudulentus, fallax; callidus, astutus, vafer, veterator, etc.): conservus, Plaut. Mil. 2, 2, 43: fidicina, id. Epid. 3, 2, 36: mulier, Hor. S. 2, 5, 70: gens, Ov. M. 14, 92: vulpes, Phaedr. 1, 13, 11 et saep.: consilia, Poët. ap. Cic. Rab. Post. 2, 4: artes, Ov. M. 15, 473; August. in Ev. Joan. Tract. 116, 5: statera, false, Vulg. Prov. 20, 23; cf. pondera, id. Mich. 6, 11.— With inf.: amici

dolus.full: dŏlus, i, m. Sanscr. dal-bhas, deceit; Gr. δόλος, cunning, δέλεαρ, bait. Orig., a device, artifice; hence, evil intent, wrongdoing with a view to the consequences (opp. culpa, negligence; cf. also: fallacia, fraus, astutia, calliditas).—In the older, and esp. the jurid. lang.: dolus malus, a standing expression for guile, fraud, deceit: doli vocabulum nunc tantum in malis utimur, apud antiquos etiam in bonis rebus utebatur. Unde adhuc dicimus Sine dolo malo, nimirum quia solebat dici et bonus, P

doma.full: dōma, ătis, n., = δῶμα, a roof, house, dwelling (eccl. Lat.), Hier. Ep. 106, no. 63, Vulg. 2 Reg. 5, 8 al.
doma.short: dōma, ătis, n., = δῶμα, a roof, house, dwelling (eccl.

domabilis.full: dŏmābĭlis, e, adj. domo, that may be tamed, tamable (a poet. word): Cantaber, Hor. C. 4, 14, 41; Ov. M. 9, 253.

domefactus.full: dŏmĕfactus, a, um, adj. domo-facio, tamed, subdued.—Transf.: tellus aratro, Petr. 99, 3.

domesticatim.full: dŏmestĭcātim, adv. domesticus, in the house, at home: apparare aliquid (opp. oblocare macellariis), Suet. Caes. 26.

domesticatus.full: dŏmestĭcātus, ūs, m. id., the office and dignity of the princeps domesticorum (also called primiceriatus), Cassiod. Var. 10, 11 and 12.

domestice.full: dŏmestĭce, adv., v. the foll. art. fin.

domesticus.full: dŏmestĭcus, a, um, adj. domus, of or belonging to the house. Lit. (very rare): dico intra domesticos parietes, Cic. Deiot. 2, 5: vestis, a garment to wear in the house, id. Fin. 2, 24; Suet. Aug. 73 al.: domesticus otior, i. e. at home, Hor. S. 1, 6, 128.—Far more freq. and class., Transf., of or belonging to one's family; domestic, familiar, household. In gen. Adj.: in luctu domestico. Cic. Vatin. 13; cf. Ov. M. 13, 578: maeror, Suet. Calig. 5: domesticis praeceptis ernditus. Cic. Rep. 1, 22 fi

domicenium.full: dŏmĭcēnĭum, ii, n. domus-cena, a meal at home, household fare: triste, Mart. 5, 78, 1: trinoctiale, id. 12, 77, 5.

domicilium.full: dŏmĭcĭlĭum, ii, n. domus and cel-, root of celare, to conceal; cf.: cella, occulere, a habitation, dwelling, domicile, abode (freq. and class.; for syn. cf.: aedes, domus, tectum, casa, tugurium, habitatio, mansio, sedes, etc.). Prop., Plaut. Mil. 2, 5, 41; Cic. Arch. 4, 9; id. N. D. 2, 60; id. Rep. 1, 13; id. Brut. 73 fin.; Caes. B. G. 1, 30, 3; id. B. C. 1, 86, 3; Vulg. Marc. 5, 3 et saep.— Trop. (esp. freq. in Cic.): nulla alia in civitate, nisi in qua populi potestas summa est, ullum domicil

domicurius.full: dŏmĭcūrius, ii, m. domus-cura, a steward, Ren. Insc. Afr. 260.

domiducus.full: Dŏmĭdūcus, i, m., and Dŏmĭdūca, ae, f. domus-duco, the god that conducts home, epithet of Jupiter and Juno, as deities of marriage, who bring the bride to her husband's home, Aug. Civ. D. 6, 9; 7, 3; Mart. Cap. 2, § 149.
domiducus.short: Dŏmĭdūcus, i, m., and Dŏmĭdūca, ae, f.

domina.full: dŏmĭna, ae (dat. and abl. plur. only dominis, Curt. 3, 12, 8; Inscr. Orell. 1629), f. dominus. Prop., mistress, she who rules or commands, esp. in a household, = hera, materfamilias, Plaut. Cist. 4, 2, 107; id. Stich. 2, 1, 24; Ter. Heaut. 2, 3, 57; Quint. 5, 11, 34 sq.; Ov. M. 4, 5; Juv. 6, 376; 377 al. — In gen., like the Gr. δέσποινα, a mistress, lady: sit sane Fors domina campi, Cic. Pis. 2; cf.: haec una virtus omnium est domina et regina virtutum, id. Off. 3, 6, 28: voluptates blandissimae

dominans.full: dŏmĭnans, antis, v. dominor, P. a.

dominanter.full: dŏmĭnanter, adv., v. dominor, P. a.

dominatio.full: dŏmĭnātĭo, ōnis, f. dominor, rule, dominion. Prop., among the republican Romans, mostly with an odious secondary meaning, unrestricted power, absolute dominion, lordship, tyranny, despotism (good prose; for syn. cf.: regnum, dicio, imperium, potestas, magistratus), Cic. Rep. 1, 32 (opp. libertas, id. ib. 1, 43; Asin. Pollio ap. Cic. Fam. 10, 31, 3; Sall. J. 31, 16; Liv. 3, 39; 4, 5; 6, 18; Tac. A. 6, 42 al.); Cic. Rep. 2, 9; 19; id. Phil. 3, 14, 34; id. Agr. 1, 6 fin.; id. Att. 8, 3, 6; Sall. C.

dominator.full: dŏmĭnātor, ōris, m. id., ruler, lord: rerum Deus, Cic. N. D. 2, 2, 4; Lact. 2, 14, 2; Vulg. Exod. 34, 6 al.

dominatrix.full: dŏmĭnātrix, īcis, f. dominator, a female ruler, mistress (very rare): caeca ac temeraria dominatrix animi cupiditas, * Cic. Inv. 1, 2, 2: freti (Creta), Sen. Hippol. 85; Vulg. Jerem. 13, 18.

dominatus.full: dŏmĭnātus, ūs (dat. dominatu, Caes. ap. Gell. 4, 16, 8), m. dominor, rule, command; esp. absolute rule, sovereignty, mastery, tyranny (good prose; most frequent in Cicero; for syn. v. dominatio). Prop., Cic. Rep. 1, 27 (opp. libertas; cf. opp. servitus, id. Deiot. 11, 30); id. Tusc. 5, 20; id. Phil. 11, 14, 36; id. de Or. 2, 55, 225; id. Div. 1, 25, 53; id. Off. 2, 1, 2; Caes. B. C. 1, 4 fin.—In plur., Cic. Rep. 1, 39; Prud. Ham. 517.— Transf.: animi, Cic. Rep. 1, 38; cf. consilii, id. ib.: cupi

dominicus.full: dŏmĭnĭcus (contr. DOMNICUS, Inscr. Orell. 3201), a, um, adj. dominus, of or belonging to a lord or master (rare; not in Cic.). Prop.: gannire ad aurem numquam didici dominicam, Afran. ap. Isid. Differ. 86 (v. 282 Rib.): rationes pecuariae, Varr. R. R. 2, 10, 10: habitationes, Col. 9 praef. § 1: palatum, Sen. Ep. 47: vinum, Petr. 31, 2: jussus, id. 28, 7: GENIUS, Inscr. Orell. 1721: APOTHECA, ib. 2591 al.— Transf. Since the formation of the empire, imperial: res, Cod. Just. 7, 38: coloni, ib. 3,

dominium.full: dŏmĭnĭum, ii, n. id.. (Acc. to dominus, II. B. 1.) A feast, banquet (very rare): dominia convivia, Lucil. ap. Non. 281, 25 (with sodalitia); * Cic. Verr. 2, 3, 4 Zumpt N. cr.; S. C. ap. Gell. 2, 24, 2.— Jurid. t. t., property, right of ownership (absolute ownership, opp. possessio, cf. Sandars, Just. Inst. Introd. p. 47); esp. paramount ownership, eminent domain: in eo solo dominium Populi Romani est vel Caesaris: nos autem possessionem tantum habere videmur, Gai. Inst. 2, 7: dominium et jus eor

dominor.full: dŏmĭnor, ātus (ante-class. inf domina rier, Verg. A. 7, 70), 1, v. dep. n. [dominus], to be lord and master, to have dominion, bear rule domineer (freq. and class.; for syn. cf.: regno, impero, jubeo, praesum). Prop., absol.: imperare quam plurimis, pollere, regnare, dominari, Cic. Rep. 3, 12; so, absol., id. 1, 33; id. Rab. Post. 14, 39; Sall. C. 2, 2; Liv. 33, 46; Tac. A. 4, 7; id. H. 1, 21; Verg. A. 2, 363 et saep.—With in and abl.: in capite fortunisque hominum, Cic. Quint. 30, 94; so, in al

dominulus.full: dŏmĭnŭlus, i, m. dim. id., a little lord, lordling, Dig. 32, 1, 41, § 4.

dominus.full: dŏmĭnus (in inscrr. sometimes written by syncop. DOMNVS), i, m. Sanscr. damanas, he who subdues, root dam-; Gr. δαμάω, δάμνημι, v. domo Prop., one who has subdued or conquered; hence, a master, possessor, ruler, lord, proprietor, owner (cf. herus). Prop.: quam dispari Dominare domino! Poëta ap. Cic. Off. 1, 39, 139: nec domo dominus, sed domino domus honestanda est, etc., Cic. ib. 39, 139; cf. id. Fin. 1, 18, 58: (vilicus) consideret, quae dominus imperaverit, fiant, etc., Cato R. R. 5, 3 sq.; s

domiporta.full: dŏmĭporta, ae, f. domus-porto, she that carries her house on her back, a poet. epithet of the snail, Poëta ap. Cic. Div. 2, 64, 133.

domiseda.full: dŏmĭsĕda, ae, f. domus-sedeo, she who stays at home, domestic (cf. sedentarius), an epithet of a woman, Inscr. Orell. 4639.

domitianus.full: Dŏmĭtĭānus, i, m., T. Flavius, a Roman emperor, son of Vespasian, and brother of Titus, who reigned 81-96 A.D., Suet. Dom. passim; Tac. H. 3, 86.—Hence, Dŏ-mĭtĭānus, a, um, adj.: via, a road constructed by him, a branch of the Via Appia, running from Sinuessa to Puteoli, Stat. S. 4 praef.; id. ib. 4, 3: mensis, i. e. October, in which the Emperor Domitian was born, Suet. Dom. 13.

domitius1.full: dŏmĭtĭus, a, um, adj. domus, pertaining to the house: deus, who protects those married in the house, August. Civ. D. 6, 9.

domitius2.full: Dŏmĭtĭus, a, um, adj., the appellation of a Roman gens. So Cn. Domitius Calvinus, tribune A. U. C. 695; consul 701, Cic. Sest, 53, 113; id. Vatin. 7, 16 al.—Cn. Domitius, censor 638 A. U. C., who conquered the Allobroges, Cic. Verr. 2, 1, 55; id. Clu. 42, 119; id. Font. 12; Val. Max. 2, 9, 6; and after whom, perhaps, was named the Domitia Via, in Gaul, id. ib. 4.—Cn. Domitius Aënobarbus, from whom is named the Lex Domitia de sacerdotiis, 649 A. U. C., Cic. Agr. 2, 7, 18; Gell. 15, 11, 2; Tac. Di
domitius2.short: Dŏmĭtĭus, a, um, adj., the appellation of a Roman gens.

domito.full: dŏmĭto, āre, v. freq. a. domo, to tame, break in (very rare; perh. first used by Verg.): boves, Verg. G. 1, 285: quadrupedum omne genus, Manil. 4, 234: elephantos, Plin. 8, 8, 8, § 25.—Poet.: currus (i. e. a team), Verg. A. 7, 163.

domitor.full: dŏmĭtor (also post-class. dŏmātor, Amm. 21, 5; but Tib. 4, 1, 116, the true reading is domante), ōris, m. id., a tamer, breaker (rare but class.). Prop.: equorum, Cic. Off. 1, 26, 90; Verg. A. 7, 189; 651 al.; Inscr. Orell. 4179.— Transf., a subduer, vanquisher, conqueror: vexator furoris, domitor armorum, Cic. Mil. 13 fin.; cf.: belli externi, Tac. H. 2, 76 fin.: Persarum (with victor), Cic. Rep. 1, 3; cf.: Hispaniae Galliaeque, Liv. 21, 43: Trojae, Hor. Ep. 1, 2, 19: maris (Neptunus), Verg. A.

domitrix.full: dŏmĭtrix, īcis, f. domitor, she who tames or subdues (very rare). Prop.: equorum Epidaurus, Verg. G. 3, 44; cf.: FERARVM DOMITRICEM DIANAM, Inscr. Orell. 1447; and poet.: ferarum clava (Herculis), Ov. H. 9, 117.— Transf.: rerum omnium (ferrum), Plin. 36, 16, 25, § 127.

domitura.full: dŏmĭtūra, ae, f. domo, a taming, breaking (very rare): boum, Col. 6, 2, 1; Plin. 8, 45, 70, § 179.

domitus1.full: dŏmĭtus, a, um, Part., from domo.
domitus1.short: dŏmĭtus, a, um, Part., from domo.

domitus2.full: dŏmĭtus, ūs, m. domo, a taming: quadrupedum, Cic. N. D. 2, 60, 151.

domnaedius.full: domnaedĭus, ii, m. dominus-aedes, a landlord, Inscr. Orell. 4787; cf.: Marini Atti, 2, p. 644.

domnifunda.full: domnĭfunda, ae, f. domina-fundus, a landlady, Inscr, Orell. 4584.

domnipraedia.full: domnipraedĭa, ae, f. domina-praedium, a landlady, Inscr. Orell. 104.

domo.full: dŏmo, ui, ĭtum (also dŏmāvi, Poëta ap. Charis. p. 252 P.; cf. Flor. 3, 22, 6: domata, Petr. 74, 14), 1, v. a. Sanscr. root dam-, dām - yāmi, to be tame; Gr. δαμνηι, δάμαρ, δαμάλης, δμώς; Germ. zähmen; Eng. tame, to tame, to break (class.; for syn. cf.: vinco, supero, devinco, fundo, fugo, profligo, subigo, subicio). Lit.: boves, Varr. R. R. 1, 20, 2; Plaut. Pers. 2, 3, 7; 13; cf. poet.: vim taurorum, Enn. ap. Charis. p. 252 P. (Trag. v. 315 ed. Vahl.): et condocefacere feras beluas, Cic. N. D. 2
domo.short: dŏmo, ui, ĭtum (also dŏmāvi, Poëta ap.

domucula.full: dŏmŭcŭla, ae, f. dim. domus, a little house, a porch, Vulg. 3 Reg. 7, 8.

domuitio.full: dŏmŭĭtĭo, ōnis, f. for domum itio; cf.: reditum ac domum itionem dari, Cic. Div. 1, 32, 68, a returning home (ante- and postclass.), Pac. and Lucil. ap. Non. 96, 2 sq.; Att. ib. 357, 9; Poëta (Enn.) ap. Auct. Her. 3, 21, 34 (cf. Enn. Trag. v. 270 ed. Vahl.); App. M. 2 fin.

domuncula.full: dŏmuncŭla, ae, f. dim. domus, a small house (not ante- Aug.), Vitr. 6, 10; App. M. 4, p. 146, 31; Val. Max. 4, 4, 8; Dig. 47, 12, 3 fin. (perh. also App. M. 4, p. 154, inst. of domuscula).

domus.full: dŏmus, ūs and i, 2d and 4th decl., f. Sanscr. damas, house; Gr. root δέμ-ω, to build, whence δόμος, δεσ-πότης for δεμσπότης; cf. Germ. Zimmer; Eng. timber, etc., a house, home (for syn. cf. aedes, casa, domicilium, habitatio; mansio, sedes, tectum, tugurium; aedificium, moles). —Forms of the cases. Sing. Nom.: domus, Plaut. Am. 1, 1, 206; id. Bacch. 3, 1, 6 al.; Ter. And. 5, 3, 20; id. Eun. 5, 9, 8 al.; Cic. Lael. 27, 103; id. Rep. 1, 43; 3, 9 et saep.— Gen., in the comic poets only the ante-cla
domus.short: dŏmus, ūs and i, 2d and 4th decl., f.

donabilis.full: dōnābĭlis, e, adj. dono. That deserves to be presented with.—Trop., infortunio hominem praedicas donabilem, Plaut. Rud. 3, 2, 40.— That deserves to be presented, Ambros. Serm. 59.

donarium.full: dōnārĭum, ii, n. donum, the place in a temple where the votive offerings were kept, a temple treasure-chamber (perh. not ante-Aug.), Luc. 9, 516; App. M. 1, p. 221. — Meton. A temple, sanctuary, altar, Verg. G. 3, 533 Serv.; Ov. F. 3, 335; id. Am. 2, 13, 13.— A votive offering, Liv. 42, 28; Gell. 2, 10, 3; Aur. Vict. Caes. 35; Vulg. Exod. 36, 3 al.

donaticus.full: dōnātĭcus, a, um, adj. dono, given as a present, presented: hastae, Cato ap. Fest. s. v. OPTIONATUS, p. 201, 28 Müll.: DONATICAE coronae dictae, quod his victores in ludis donabantur, etc., Paul. ex Fest. p. 69, 5 sq. Müll.

donatio.full: dōnātĭo, ōnis, f. id., a presenting, a donation; in abstr. and concr. (for syn. cf.: donum, largitio, munus, donativum), Cic. Phil. 4, 4, 9; Cic. Verr. 2, 3, 80; id. Opt. Gen. 7, 19; id. Rosc. Am. 9; Just. Inst. 2, 7, de donationibus; the same title appears in Dig. 39, 5, and 6; Cod. Just. 5, 3; Vulg. Rom. 5, 17 al.; cf. Rein's Privatr. p. 202 sq., and 340.

donativum.full: dōnātīvum, i, n. id., a largess, donative given by the emperor to each soldier of the army, at his accession or majority, or other extraordinary occasion (v. congiarium, II.), Suet. Calig. 46; id. Galb. 16; Tac. H. 1, 18; 37 fin. al.; opp. congiarium, Plin. Pan. 25, 2; Tac. A. 12, 41; Suet. Ner. 7 al.—Adj., Inscr. Grut. 421, 1.

donator.full: dōnātor, ōris, m. id., a giver, donor (post-Aug.; in the jurists very freq.), Dig. 42, 1, 49; Just. Inst. 2, 7, § 2; Cod. Just. 8, 54, 1 et saep.; Sen. Hippol. 1217.

donatrix.full: dōnātrix, īcis, f. donator, she who gives, a female donor, Cod. Just. 8, 54, 20; Prud. στεφ. 11, 191.

donatus.full: Dōnātus, i, m. Aelius D., a celebrated Roman grammarian of the fourth century of our era, teacher of Jerome, and commentator on Terence; cf. Baehr's Lit. Gesch. p. 533 sq., and 68.— Tiberius Claudius D., a commentator on Vergil, who lived about A.D. 400; cf. Baehr's Lit. Gesch. p. 91; Teuffel, Röm. Lit. § 423.

donax.full: dŏnax, ăcis, m., = δόναξ. A sort of reed or cane, Cyprus-reed, Plin. 16, 36, 66, § 165; 24, 11, 50, § 86; 32, 10, 52, § 141.— A sea-fish = solen, Plin. 32, 11, 53, § 151.— The male scallop or pecten, Plin. 32, 9, 32, § 103.— Dŏnax, a Greek proper name, Ter. Eun. 4, 7, 2, and 4.

donec.full: dōnĕc, conj. [shortened from ante- and post-class. form dōnĭcum, from old dative doni (dioni; for root, etc., v. dies) and conj. cum; prop. at the time of day when; form donicum, Liv. And., Cato and Plaut. ap. Charis. p. 178 P.; Cato, R. R. 146, 2; 149, 2; 161, 3; Plaut. Aul. 1, 1, 19; id. Capt. 2, 2, 89; id. Most. 1. 2, 34; id. Ps. 4, 7, 72; id. Truc. 1, 1, 18; Fragm. ap. Prisc. p. 692 P.; Nep. Ham. 1, 4.—In the Inscr. of Orell. 4370 DONIQVIES is i. q. DONIQUE IS, and donique = donicum; so, don

donifico.full: dōnĭfĭco, āre, v. n. donum-facio, to make presents, Hyg. Fab. 112.

dono.full: dōno, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. donum. To give one something as a present; to present, bestow; to grant, vouchsafe, confer (freq. and class.). In gen. Prop.: donavi ei, quae voluit, quae postulavit: te quoque ei dono dedi, Plaut. Mil. 4, 5, 5; cf. id. Poen. 2, 23: non pauca suis adjutoribus large effuseque donabat, Cic. Rosc. Am. 8 fin.: munera ista civibus tuis, id. Tusc. 5, 32, 90: praedam militibus, Caes. B. G. 7, 11 fin.: catenam ex voto Laribus, Hor. S. 1, 5, 65 et saep.: alicui non unius diei gr

donum.full: dōnum, i, n. do, a gift, present. In gen., Plaut. Am. prol. 138 sq.; id. Most. 1, 3, 27 sq.; id. Mil. 4, 2, 26; Cic. Clu. 9 fin.; id. Tusc. 5, 7, 20; id. Lael. 15, 55 et saep.: dona mittunt et munera, Plaut. Mil. 3, 1, 121; so with munus (usu. dona muneraque, = bribery), id. Cist. 1, 1, 95; Cic. Clu. 24, 66; id. Arch. 8, 18; id. de Or. 2, 71; id. de Sen. 12, 40; Dig. 38, 1, 7 al.— In partic. A present brought to a deity, a votive offering, sacrifice, Plaut. Rud. prol. 23; Lucr. 4, 1237; 6, 752;

donusa.full: Dŏnūsa, ae, f., a small island in the Aegean Sea, east of Naxos, now Denusa, a place of banishment under the emperors, Mel. 2, 7, 11; Plin. 4, 12, 23, § 69; Verg. A. 3, 125; Tac. A. 4, 30.
donusa.short: Dŏnūsa, ae, f., a small island in the Aegean Sea, east of Naxos, now Denusa, a place of banishment under the emperors, Mel.

dorcadion.full: dorcădĭon, ii, n., name of a plant, App. Herb. 14 and 62.
dorcadion.short: dorcădĭon, ii, n., name of a plant, App.

dorcas.full: dorcas, ădis (also dorx = δόρξ; acc. pl. dorcas, m., Grat. Cyn. 200, and dorcus, i, m., = δόρκος, Edict. Diocl. 4, no. 45), f., = δορκάς, a gazelle, antelope: Antilope dorcas, Linn.; Lucr. 4, 1161; Mart. 10, 65, 13; 13, 98, 1.

dorceus.full: Dorceus, ei, m., Δορκεύς (qs. gazellecatcher), the name of one of Actaeon's hounds, Ov. M. 3, 210; Hyg. Fab. 181.

dorcium.full: Dorcĭum, i, f. (Gr. Δόρκιον), the name of a female slave, Ter. Phorm. 1, 2, 102.

dores.full: Dōres, um, m. (Gr. gen. pl. Dorieon, Vitr. 4, 1, 5), Δωριεῖς, the Dorians, Cic. Rep. 2, 4, 8; id. Fl. 27, 64; their progenitor, Dōrus, i, m., son of Hellen, Vitr. 4, 1; or of Neptune, acc. to Serv. Verg. A. 2, 27— Derivv. Dōrĭcus, a, um, adj., Doric: gens, Plin. 6, 2, 2, § 7: genus (architecturae), Vitr. 4, 6: aedes, id. ib.: symmetria, id. ib.: castra, Prop. 4 (5), 6, 34. dicta, i. e. in the Doric dialect, Quint. 8, 3, 59 (al. adv. Dōrĭce dicta; so Suet. Tib. 56: Dorice Rhodii loquuntur); hence

dorias.full: Dōrĭas, ae, m. (Gr. Δωριάς), a character in the Eunuchus of Terence, Ter. Eun. 3, 6, 32 al.

dorice.full: Dōrĭce, adv., in the Doric manner, v. Dores, II. A.
dorice.short: Dōrĭce, adv., in the Doric manner, v.

dorio.full: Dōrĭō, ōnis, m. (Gr. Δωρίων), Dorio, a character in the Phormio of Terence, Ter. Phorm. 3, 2, 1.

dorippa.full: Dōrippa, ae, f., the name of a woman, Plaut. Merc. 4, 1, 17.
dorippa.short: Dōrippa, ae, f., the name of a woman, Plaut.

dormio.full: dormĭo, īvi or ii, ītum, 4 (futur. dormibo, Plaut. Trin. 3, 2, 100: dormibit, Cato R. R. 5, 5), v. n. Sanscr. R. drā-, drayami, I sleep; Gr. δαρθάνω, to sleep (cf.: dormito, sopio, sterto). Lit., sup.: Quin tu is dormitum? Ph. Dormio, ne occlamites, Plaut. Curc. 1, 3, 27; cf.: ire dormitum, id. Most. 3, 2, 4; 16; id. Ps. 2, 2, 70; Hor. S. 1, 5, 48; 1, 6, 119 et saep.; cf. also: dormitum dimittitur, Hor. Ep. 1, 7, 73.—Pass. impers.: minimum dormitur in illo (lecto), Juv. 6, 269.—Prov.: non omnibu

dormisco.full: dormisco, ĕre, 3, v. inch. [dormio], to fall asleep, Prisc. 824 P.

dormitatio.full: dormītātĭo, ōnis, f. dormito, sleep (eccl. Lat.), Vulg. Psa. 131, 4; id. Prov. 23, 21; Hil. in Psa. 118, 4, 7; Hier. in Naum, 3, 18 sq.

dormitator.full: dormītātor, ōris, m. id., a sleeper, sluggard, commonly understood of a thief, who sleeps by day and steals by night; but better, in gen., as a dreamer, stupid fellow, only Plaut. Trin. 4, 2, 20, and 142 Brix ad loc.

dormitio.full: dormītĭo, ōnis, f. dormio, a sleeping (only ante- and post-class.), Varr. ap. Non. 100, 1 and 2; Vulg. Johan. 11, 13.—In eccl. Lat., death, Tert. Patient. 9; Vulg. 2, Macc. 12, 45 al.; cf. also Inscr. Orell. 4461.

dormito.full: dormīto, āvi, 1, v. freq. n. [id.], to be sleepy, drowsy, to begin to sleep, fall asleep. Lit., Plaut. Am. 2, 2, 175; id. Trin. 1, 2, 133; Cic. Att. 2, 16; id. Div. 1, 28, 59; Hor. A. P. 105.— Poet. transf.: jam dormitante lucerna, i. e. going out, Ov. H. 19, 195.— Trop., to be dreaming, sluggish, stupid, slow, to linger: ad hoc diei tempus dormitasti in otio. Quin tu abs te socordiam omnem reice, etc., Plaut. As. 2, 1, 5; id. Bacch. 2, 3, 6; id. Trin. 4, 2, 139 Brix; Hor. A. P. 359; Quint. 10,

dormitor.full: dormītor, ōris, m. id., a sleeper, Mart. 10, 4.

dormitorius.full: dormītōrĭus, a, um, adj. id., of or for sleeping (post-Aug.): cubiculum, Plin. Ep. 5, 6, 21: so, membrum, id. ib. 2, 17, 9; and subst., dormitorium, ii, n., a sleeping-room, dormitory, Plin. 30, 6, 17, § 51.

doron.full: dōron, i, n., = δῶρον, a gift, Lat. munus, Plin. 35, 14, 49, § 171.
doron.short: dōron, i, n., = δῶρον, a gift, Lat.

dorso.full: Dorso, ōnis, m., a Roman surname, Liv. 5, 46; 7, 28 al.
dorso.short: Dorso, ōnis, m., a Roman surname, Liv.

dorsualis.full: dorsŭālis, e, adj. dorsum, of or on the back, dorsal (post-class): notae equi, App. M. 11, p. 266, 32; cf.: crustae ferarum, Amm. 22, 15; and, pinnae, Sol. 12.—Subst.: dorsualia, ium, n., a cover for the back of beasts, Trebell. Gallien. 8.

dorsum.full: dorsum, i, n. (masc. dorsus, Plaut. Mil. 2, 4, 44; quoted ap. Non. 203, 6) [cf. Gr. δειρή, δέρη, neck], the back (in class. prose, only of beasts of burden; poet. and later also of men; cf.: tergum, tergus). Prop., Plaut. l. l.; id. Ep. 1, 1, 85; id. Trin. 3, 2, 93; Plin. 11, 37, 86, § 214; Verg. G. 3, 116; Hor. S. 1, 9, 21.—Prov.: dorsus prurit, i. e. I begin to take, Plaut. Mil. 2, 4, 44.— Transf., of things analogous in form or position: jugi, i. e. the ridge, summit of a hill, * Caes. B. G.

dorus.full: Dōrus, i, m. (Gr. Δῶρος). The legendary ancestor of the Dorians, v. Dores init — The name of a philosopher, Sen. Ben. 7, 6.— A character in the Eunuchus of Terence, Ter. Eun. 3, 2, 19.

doryclus.full: Dŏrȳ^clus, i, m., from Mount Tmarus in Epirus, husband of Beroë, Verg. A. 5, 620, and 647.
doryclus.short: Dŏrȳ^clus, i, m., from Mount Tmarus in Epirus, husband of Beroë, Verg.

dorycnion.full: dŏrycnion, ii, n., = δορύκνιον, a poisonous plant, Plin. 21, 31, 105, § 179; 28, 7, 21, § 74 al.; Scrib. Comp. 191.
dorycnion.short: dŏrycnion, ii, n., = δορύκνιον, a poisonous plant, Plin.

dorylaeum.full: Dŏrўlaeum, i, n., a city of Phrygia, Cic. Fl. 17, 39; Plin. 5, 29, 31, § 119.—Its inhabitants are called Dŏrўlenses, ium, m., id. ib.; and Dŏrўlaei, ōrum, Plin. 5, 29, 29, § 105.
dorylaeum.short: Dŏrўlaeum, i, n., a city of Phrygia, Cic.

dorylas.full: Dŏrўlas, ae, m. (Δορύλας), a Greek proper name, Ov. M. 5, 129; 132; 12, 380.

doryphorus.full: Dŏrўphŏrus (-os), i, m., = δορυφόρος, the Lance-bearer, a statue by Polycletus, famous in ancient times, Cic. Brut. 86, 296; id. Or. 2; Quint. 5, 12, 21 Spald.; Plin. 34, 8, 19, § 55.
doryphorus.short: Dŏrўphŏrus (-os), i, m., = δορυφόρος, the Lance-bearer, a statue by Polycletus, famous in ancient times, Cic.

dos.full: dōs, ōtis (gen. plur. dotium, Dig. 23, 3, 9, § 1 al.; dotum, Val. Max. 4, 4, 11; Tert. Cult. Fem. 2, 9), f. 1. do, like the Sicilian δωτίνη, from διδόναι, Varr. L. L. 5, § 175 Müll., a marriage portion, dowry (for syn. cf.: donum, largitio, munus, donatio, etc.). Prop., Plaut. Am. 2, 2, 209; id. Ep. 2, 1, 11 et saep.; Ter. And. 5, 4, 47; id. Heaut. 5, 1, 64 sq. al.; Cic. Caecin. 25 fin.; id. Fl. 35; id. Att. 14, 13, 5; Caes. B. G. 6, 19, 1; Hor. S. 1, 2, 131; id. Ep. 1, 6, 36 et saep.—Cf. on the

dossennus1.full: dossennus or dossēnus (also dors-), i, m. dorsum, prop., hunchback, hence, the standing character of a deceitful soothsayer in the Atellanic comedies (like maccus, bucco, pappus), Pompon. ap. Non. 513, 9; 514, 23; 516, 22; Sen. Ep. 89, 6; Fest. s. v. TEMETVM, p. 364 Müll.; cf. Munk, De Fabulis Atellanis, p. 35 sq. and p. 121; Ritschl, Parerga praef. p. 13.— Transf., = scurra, a fool, clown, jester, ironically said of Plautus, as representing the characters of the parasites, Hor. Ep. 2, 1, 173.
dossennus1.short: dossennus or dossēnus (also dors-), i, m.

dossennus2.full: Dossennus or Dossēnus (also Dors-), a Roman proper name, Plin. 14, 13, 15, § 92; id. ap. Indic. libr. 14 and 15.
dossennus2.short: Dossennus or Dossēnus (also Dors-), a Roman proper name, Plin.

dossuarius.full: dossŭārĭus, a, um, adj. dorsum, that carries on its back, that bears burdens (very rare): aselli, Varr. R. R. 2, 6 fin.: jumenta, beasts of burden, id. ib. 2, 10, 5.

dotalis.full: dōtālis, e, adj. dos, of or belonging to a dowry or portion (of the wife, and sometimes of the husband), dotal: aedes, Plaut. Mil. 4, 4, 30; 4, 6, 63; cf. praedia, Cic. Att. 15, 20, 4: regia, Verg. A. 9, 737; 11, 369; cf. regnum, Ov. M. 4, 705; id. F. 6, 593: patria, id. M. 8, 67: tellus, id. H. 4, 163: agri, Hor. Ep. 1, 6, 21: arma, Sil. 17, 75 et saep.: servus, Plaut. As. 1, 1, 72; cf. Dig. 24, 1, 28; Sen. Contr. 3, 21: Tyrii, Verg. A. 4, 104.

doto1.full: dōto, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. id., to endow, to portion (esp. richly); in the verb. finit. rare (and perh. not ante-Aug.): filiam splendidissime maritavit, dotavitque, Suet. Vesp. 14: sanguine Trojano et Rutulo dotabere, virgo, Verg. A. 7, 318; Claud. Nupt. Hon. et Mar. 290; cf. id. IV. Cons. Hon. 648.—And transf.: in Arabia et olea dotatur lacrima, is furnished with an exudation, Plin. 12, 17, 38, § 77; Pall. poet. Insit. 63; Vulg. Gen. 30, 20.—Far more freq. and class.: dōtātus, a, um, P. a., well

doto2.full: Dōto, ūs, f., = Δωτώ, a sea-nymph, Verg. A. 9, 102; Val. Fl. 1, 134 al.
doto2.short: Dōto, ūs, f., = Δωτώ, a sea-nymph, Verg.

dracaena.full: drăcaena, ae, f., = δράκαινα, a shedragon, acc. to Don. p. 1747 P.; Prisc. p. 643 and 684 ib.; Cledon. p. 1896 ib.
dracaena.short: drăcaena, ae, f., = δράκαινα, a shedragon, acc.

drachma.full: drachma (old form, drachŭma, like Alcumena, Aesculapius, Plaut. Trin. 2, 4, 23; Ter. Heaut. 3, 3, 40), ae (gen plur. drachmūm, Varr. L. L. 9, § 85 Müll.; usually drachmarum, Ter. Heaut. 3, 3, 40; Cic. Fl. 19, 43), f., = δραχμή. A small Greek coin, a drachma or drachm, of about the same value as the Roman denarius, Enn. ap. Cic. Div. 1, 52; Plaut. Ps. 1, 1, 84 sq.; Ter. And. 2, 6, 20; Cic. Fam. 2, 17; id. Fl. 15, 34; Hor. S. 2, 7, 43 et saep.— As a weight, the eighth part of an uncia, the half of
drachma.short: drachma (old form, drachŭma, like Alcumena, Aesculapius, Plaut.

draco1.full: drăco, ōnis (gen. dracontis, Att. ap. Non. 426, 2; acc. dracontem, id. ap. Charis. p. 101 P.), m., = δράκων, a sort of serpent, a dragon (cf.: serpens, anguis, coluber, hydrus, vipera, aspis). Prop. (those of the tame sort, esp. the Epidaurian, being kept as pets by luxurious Romans), Cic. Div. 2, 30; 66; Plin. 8, 17, 22, § 61; 29, 4, 20, § 67; Suet. Aug. 94; Sen. de Ira, 2, 31 al. —As the guardian of treasures, Cic. Phil. 13, 5, 12; Phaedr. 4, 20; Fest. s. h. v. p. 67, 12 sq. Müll.— Meton. Name

draco2.full: Drăco, ōnis, m., a proper name. The Athenian lawgiver, Cic. Rep. 2, 1; id. de Or. 1, 44, 197; Gell. 11, 18.— One of Actaeon's hounds, Hyg. Fab. 181.
draco2.short: Drăco, ōnis, m., a proper name.

draconarius.full: drăcōnārĭus, ii, m. draco, II. B., a standard-bearer, Veg. Mil. 2, 7; 13; Amm. 20, 4.

draconigena.full: drăcōnĭgĕna, ae, comm. dracogigno, dragon-born (poet.): urbs, i. e. Thebes, Ov. F. 3, 865: hostis, i. e. Alexander the Great (whom Olympias was said to have conceived by a serpent, acc. to Just. 11, 11, 3; 12, 16, 2), Sid. Carm. 2, 80.

dracontarium.full: drăcontārĭum, ii, n. draco, a garland or wreath twisted like a serpent, Tert. Cor. Mil. 15; Inscr. Don. cl. 1, no. 91.

draconteus.full: dracontĕus, a, um, adj. id., of a serpent, serpent's: pedes, Mythogr. Lat. 1, 128; Serv. Verg. G. 3, 113.

dracontia.full: drăcontĭa, ae, f., drăcontĭas, ae, m., = δρακοντίας, or drăcōnītis, ĭdis, f., a precious stone, Plin. 37, 10, 57, § 108; Sol. 43.
dracontia.short: drăcontĭa, ae, f., drăcontĭas, ae, m., = δρακοντίας, or drăcōnītis, ĭdis, f., a precious stone, Plin.

dracontion.full: drăcontĭon, ĭi, n., = δρακόντιον, a kind of wheat, Plin. 18, 7, 12, § 64 al.
dracontion.short: drăcontĭon, ĭi, n., = δρακόντιον, a kind of wheat, Plin.

dracontios.full: drăcontĭos vītis, an excellent kind of vine, Col. 3, 2, 28.
dracontios.short: drăcontĭos vītis, an excellent kind of vine, Col.

dracontium.full: drăcontĭum, ii, n., = δρακόντιον, dragon-wort, Arum dracunculus, Linn.; Plin. 24, 16, 91, § 142; called also dracontia radix, Veg. 5, 66, 1.
dracontium.short: drăcontĭum, ii, n., = δρακόντιον, dragon-wort, Arum dracunculus, Linn.;

dracunculus.full: drăcuncŭlus, i, m. dim. draco. A small serpent, dragonet, Lampr. Alex. Sev. 14; Jul. Val. Rer. Gest. Alex. 1, 5.— A thread twisted like a serpent, Inscr. Orell. 1572.— A sort of fish, dragonet, Plin. 32, 11, 53, § 148.— The plant tarragon, Artemisia dracunculus, Linn.; Plin. 24, 16, 91, § 142.

drama.full: drāma, ătis, n., = δρᾶμα, a drama, play, Aus. Ep. 18, 15.—Hence, drāmătĭ-cum poëma, dramatic, Diom. p. 480 P.
drama.short: drāma, ătis, n., = δρᾶμα, a drama, play, Aus.

drancae.full: Drancae or Drangae, ārum, m., a Persian or Bactrian tribe, Plin. 6, 23, 25, § 94; Curt. 6, 6, 18; 8, 3, 9.—Hence, Dran-caeus or Drangaeus, a, um, adj., of the Drancae, Val. Fl. 6, 106; 507.
drancae.short: Drancae or Drangae, ārum, m., a Persian or Bactrian tribe, Plin.

drapeta.full: drāpĕta, ae, m., = δραπέτης, a fugitive slave, runaway, Plaut. Curc. 2, 3, 11.
drapeta.short: drāpĕta, ae, m., = δραπέτης, a fugitive slave, runaway, Plaut.

draucus.full: draucus, i, m., a sodomite, Mart. 9, 27, 10; id. 1, 96, 12; cf.: draucus, καταπύγων, Gloss. Philox.
draucus.short: draucus, i, m., a sodomite, Mart.

draus.full: Draus or Dravus, i, m., the river Drave in Hungary, Plin. 3, 25, 28, § 147; Flor. 4, 12, 8.
draus.short: Draus or Dravus, i, m., the river Drave in Hungary, Plin.

drenso.full: drenso, āre, v. n., expresses the note of the swan, Auct. Philom. 23.

drepana.full: Drĕpăna, ōrum, n., = Δρέπανα, a town on the western coast of Sicily, now Trapani, Cato acc. to Serv. Verg. A. 3, 707, Plin. 3, 8, 14, § 90; Liv. 28, 41; Flor. 2, 2, 12.—Called also Drĕpănum, Verg. A. 3, 707, and Drĕpăne (es), f., Sil. 14, 269. The promontory in its neighborhood is called Promontorium Drepanum, Plin. 3, 8, 14, § 88.—Drĕpănĭtānus, a, um, of Drepanum: pupilus, Cic. Verr. 2, 2, 57, § 140.—Plur. as subst.: Drĕpănĭtāni, the inhabitants of the promontory of Drepanum, Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 1
drepana.short: Drĕpăna, ōrum, n., = Δρέπανα, a town on the western coast of Sicily, now Trapani, Cato acc.

drepanis.full: drĕpănis, is, f., = δρεπανίς, the martin, Hirundo apus, Linn.; Plin. 11, 47, 101, § 257.
drepanis.short: drĕpănis, is, f., = δρεπανίς, the martin, Hirundo apus, Linn.;

drimyphagia.full: drīmўphăgĭa, ae, f., = δριμυφαγία, the eating of acrid food, Cael. Aur. Tard. 2, 1, 26; 2, 6, 93.
drimyphagia.short: drīmўphăgĭa, ae, f., = δριμυφαγία, the eating of acrid food, Cael.

drindio.full: drindĭo, īre, v. n., expresses the cry of the weasel, Auct. Philom. 61.

dromas.full: drŏmas, ădis, m., = δρομάς. A dromedary, Liv. 37, 40; Curt. 5, 2, 5; Vop. Aur. 28.—Called also drŏmĕdārĭus, ii, m., Hier. Vit. Malchi, 10; Vulg. Isa. 60, 6.— Drŏmas, ădis, m., the name of one of Actaeon's hounds, Ov. M. 3, 217.

dromo1.full: drŏmo, ōnis, m., = δρόμων (the runner). A sort of shell-fish, Plin. 32, 11, 53, § 148.— A kind of vessel rapidly propelled by many oars, a cutter, Cod. Just. 1, 27, 2; cf. Isid. Orig. 19, 1, 14.

dromo2.full: Drŏmō, ōnis, m., Gr. Δρόμων, the name of a slave, Ter. Ad. 3, 3, 22; cf. id. Heaut. 2, 3, 34.

dromos.full: drŏmos, i, m., = δρόμος. A place for running; a race-course, Grut. Inscr. 339, 2.— Esp., as nom. prop., Drŏmŏs, i, m., the plain near Sparta, on which the Lacedaemonian youth exercised, Liv. 34, 27, 5.— Dromos Achilleos, a peninsula west of the Crimea, on which Achilles was said to have run a race, Plin. 4, 12, 26, § 83.

dropacator.full: drōpăcātor, ōris, and drōpăci-sta, ae, m., one who depilates, Gloss.
dropacator.short: drōpăcātor, ōris, and drōpăci-sta, ae, m., one who depilates, Gloss.

dropacismus.full: drōpăcismus, i, m., = δρωπακισμός, the removal of hair by plasters of pitch, Cael. Aur. Tard. 2, 6, 93.
dropacismus.short: drōpăcismus, i, m., = δρωπακισμός, the removal of hair by plasters of pitch, Cael.

dropaco.full: drōpăco, āre, v. a., to depilate, Theod. Prisc. 4, 1.

dropax.full: drōpax, ăcis, m., = δρώπαξ, a pitchointment, depilatory, Mart. 3, 74; 10, 65, 8; Cael. Aur. Tard. 1, 1, 36 sq.
dropax.short: drōpax, ăcis, m., = δρώπαξ, a pitchointment, depilatory, Mart.

drosolithus.full: drŏsŏlĭthus, i, m., δροσόλιθος, dewstone, a precious stone now unknown, Plin. 37, 11, 73, § 190.
drosolithus.short: drŏsŏlĭthus, i, m., δροσόλιθος, dewstone, a precious stone now unknown, Plin.

druentia.full: Drŭentĭa, ae, f., a tributary river of the Rhodanus, now Durance, Liv. 21, 31, 9; Sil. 3, 468; Aus. Mos. 479.
druentia.short: Drŭentĭa, ae, f., a tributary river of the Rhodanus, now Durance, Liv.

druides.full: Drŭĭdes, um (Drŭĭdae, ārum, Cic. Div. 1, 41; Tac. A. 14, 30; id. H. 4, 54; Suet. Claud. 25; Luc. 1, 451.—Dub. form acc. Druidas, Mel. 3, 2, 3; Plin. 30, 1, 4, § 13), m., the Druids, the priests and wise men of the Gauls, Caes. B. G. 6, 13 sq.; Luc. 1. 1.; Plin. 16, 44, 95, § 249.—Hence, Drŭïas, ădis, f., a Gallic priestess and prophetess, a Druidess, Lampr. Alex. Sev. 60.—Called also Drŭis, ĭdis, Inscr. Orell. 2200; Vop. Aur. 44; Numer. 15.

drungus.full: drungus, i, m., a body of soldiers, a troop (late Lat.), Veg. Mil. 3, 16; Vop. Prob. 19.
drungus.short: drungus, i, m., a body of soldiers, a troop (late Lat.), Veg.

druppa.full: druppa or drūpa (sc.) oliva = δρύππα (v. Lidd. and Scott under δρυπεπής), an over-ripe, wrinkled olive, Plin. 15, 1, 2, § 6; and absol. drupa, ae, f., id. 15, 7 7, § 26; 17, 24, 37, § 230; 19, 5, 26, § 78.

drusus.full: Drūsus, i, m., a well-known Roman surname in the Livian family, first assumed by the Livius who slew the Gallic general Drausus, Suet. Tib. 3.—Esp. M. Livius Drusus, uncle of Cato Uticensis, murdered by Q. Varius, Cic. Arch. 3, 6; Vell. 2, 13.— Claudius Drusus Nero, son of Tib. Claudius Nero and Livia Drusilla, father of Germanicus, the theme of Hor. C. 4, 4; Suet. Claud. 1; Tac. A. 1, 33.— Hence, Drūsĭānus, a, um, adj.: fossa, Tac. A. 2, 8, or Drūsīnus, a, um, adj.: fossae, a canal on the Lower
drusus.short: Drūsus, i, m., a well-known Roman surname in the Livian family, first assumed by the Livius who slew the Gallic general Drausus, Suet.

dryades.full: Drўădes, um (dat. Graec. dryasin, Prop. 1, 20, 12; dub. al. adryasin; cf. ib. 32 and 34), f., = Δρυάδες, wood-nymphs, dryads, Prop. 1, 20, 45; Verg. E. 5, 59; id. G. 1, 11; Ov. M. 3, 507; 6, 453 al.—In the sing., Dryas, Mart. 9, 62.

dryas1.full: Drўas, antis, m., = Δρύας. The father of Lycurgus king of Thrace, Hyg. Fab. 132; Serv. Verg. A. 3, 14.—Hence, Drўantīdes, ae, m., i. e. Lycurgus, Ov. Ib. 347; cf. Hyg. and Serv. 1. 1.— One of the Lapithae, Ov. M. 12, 290 sq.— A sharer in the Calydonican hunt, Ov. M. 8, 307.

dryitis.full: drўītis, ĭdis, f., = δρυῖτις, an unknown precious stone, Plin. 37, 11, 73, § 188.
dryitis.short: drўītis, ĭdis, f., = δρυῖτις, an unknown precious stone, Plin.

drymo.full: Drȳmo, ūs, f., = Δρυμώ, a sea-nymph, Verg. G. 4, 336; Hyg. Fab. praef.
drymo.short: Drȳmo, ūs, f., = Δρυμώ, a sea-nymph, Verg.

dryope.full: Drўŏpe, ēs, f., = Δρυόπη. The mother of Amphissus by Apollo, Ov. M. 9, 331; 364 sq.— The mother of Tarquitus by Faunus, Verg. A. 10, 551.

dryophonon.full: drўŏphŏnon, i, n., = δρυόφονον, a sort of fern, Plin. 27, 9, 49, § 73.
dryophonon.short: drўŏphŏnon, i, n., = δρυόφονον, a sort of fern, Plin.

dryops.full: Drўops, ŏpis, m. One of the Dryopes, a people of Epirus, Ov. Ib. 490; usu. plur.: Drўŏpes, um, the Dryopians, Plin. 4 praef.; Verg. A. 4, 146.— The name of a warrior, Verg. A. 10, 346.

dryopteris.full: drўoptĕris, ĭdis, f., = δρυοπτερίς, a plant similar to the preceding, Plin. 27, 9, 48, § 72.
dryopteris.short: drўoptĕris, ĭdis, f., = δρυοπτερίς, a plant similar to the preceding, Plin.

drysidae.full: Drўsĭdae, ārum, m., the Druids, Amm. 15, 9, 4; 8.
drysidae.short: Drўsĭdae, ārum, m., the Druids, Amm.

dualis.full: dŭālis, e, adj. duo, that contains two: numerus (nasi), i. e. the dual number, duality, Lact. Opif. D. 10, 9.—In gram. lang.: numerus, the dual, Quint. 1, 5, 42 al.

dualitas.full: dŭālĭtas, ātis, f., the number two, Cassiod. Var. 11, 2.
dualitas.short: dŭālĭtas, ātis, f., the number two, Cassiod.

dubenus.full: dubenus apud antiquos dicebatur qui nunc dominus, Paul. ex Fest. p. 67, 7 Müll.
dubenus.short: dubenus apud antiquos dicebatur qui nunc dominus, Paul.

dubie.full: dŭbĭe, adv., doubtfully, v. dubius fin.

dubietas.full: dŭbĭĕtas, ātis, f. dubius, doubt, uncertainty (post-class.), Amm. 20, 4; Eutr. 6, 19.

dubiosus.full: dŭbĭōsus, a, um, adj. id., doubtful, dubious (post-class.): fabulae, Gell. 3, 3, 3: hoc (with inexplicabile), id. 5, 10, 15.

dubis.full: Dūbis, is, m., = Δοῦβις, a river in Gallia Belgica, now Doubs, Caes. B. G. 1, 38, 4.
dubis.short: Dūbis, is, m., = Δοῦβις, a river in Gallia Belgica, now Doubs, Caes.

dubitabilis.full: dŭbĭtābĭlis, e, adj. dubito, doubtful (very rare). Pass., to be doubted: verum, Ov. M. 1, 223: virtus, id. ib. 13, 21. — Act., feeling doubt: pectus, Prud. Apoth. 649.

dubitanter.full: dŭbĭtanter, adv., doubtingly, v. dubito fin. A.

dubitatim.full: dŭbĭtātim, adv., hesitatingly, v. dubito fin. B.

dubitatio.full: dŭbĭtātĭo, ōnis, f. dubito. A wavering in opinion or judgment; a being uncertain, a doubting; uncertainty, doubt. Prop. In gen. (freq. and good prose). Absol.: nec tibi sollicitudinem ex dubitatione mea, nec spem ex affirmatione, afferre volui, Cic. Fam. 9, 17 fin.: cum res non conjecturā, sed oculis ac manibus teneretur, neque in causa ulla dubitatio posset esse, id. Cluent. 7, 20: in ea obscuritate ac dubitatione omnium, id. ib. 27: quod quamquam dubitationem non habet, tamen rationes afferend

dubitativus.full: dŭbĭtātīvus, a, um, adj. dubito, doubtful (late Lat.): sensus, Tert. adv. Marc. 2, 25 fin.—Adv.: dŭbĭtātīve, doubtfully: pronuntiare, Tert. Car. Chr. 23 fin.

dubitator.full: dŭbĭtātor, ōris, m. id., a doubter (late Lat.); with gen., Tert. adv. Haeret. 33.

dubito.full: dŭbĭto, āvi, ātum, 1, v. freq. n. and a. [for duhibitare, freq. from duhibeo, i. e. duohabeo (cf. habitare from habeo), to have or hold, as two, v. dubius; cf. also Gr. δοιάζω from δοιοί; Germ. zweifeln from zwei], to vibrate from one side to the other, to and fro, in one's opinions or in coming to a conclusion (freq. in all periods and sorts of composition; in class. prose usually with negations or in a negative interrogation, as: non dubito, haud dubito, quis dubitat? etc. To waver in opinion

dubius.full: dŭbĭus, a, um, adj. for duhibius, duohabeo, held as two or double, i. e. doubtful; cf. dubito, Corss. Ausspr. 2, 1027. Moving in two directions alternately, vibrating to and fro, fluctuating (cf. ambiguus, anceps, incertus, perplexus, duplex). Lit. (very rare): ut vas non quit constare, nisi humor Destitit in dubio fluctu jactarier intus, Lucr. 6, 556; cf.: fluctibus dubiis volvi coeptum est mare, Liv. 37, 16, 4.—Far more freq. and class., Trop., vacillating in mind, uncertain. Act. Wavering in

ducalis.full: dŭcālis, e, adj. dux, of or belonging to a leader or commander (post-class.): tunicae, Valer. Imp. ap. Vop. Aurel. 13.—Adv.: dŭcālĭter, like a leader or general: antecedere, Sid. Ep. 5, 13.—Comp., Sid. Ep. 8, 6.

ducator.full: dŭcātor, ōris, m. id., a general, prince, chief (post-class.): civitatis, Tert. adv. Jud. 13.

ducatrix.full: dŭcātrix, īcis, f. ducator, a female leader: vitiorum iracundia, App. Dogm. Plat. 2, p. 14.

ducatus.full: dŭcātus, ūs, m. dux, military leadership, command = ἡγεμονία (post-Aug.), Suet. Tib. 19; Flor. 3, 21, 2; Just. 2, 15, 14; Vulg. Sirach, 7, 4: calculis omnibus ducatum latrones ei deferunt, App. M. 7, p. 191 med.— In gen., guidance (eccl. Lat.): caecus autem si caeco ducatum praestet, Vulg. Matt. 15, 14.— Transf., authority: quaerere a domino ducatum, Vulg. Sir. 7, 4 al.

ducena.full: dŭcēna, ae, f. duceni, the office of a ducenarius, Cod. Th. 12, 1, 5.

ducenarius.full: dŭcēnārĭus, a, um, adj. id., containing two hundred, of or relating to two hundred (post-Aug.): pondera, Plin. 7, 20, 19, § 83: procuratores, i. e. who received a salary of 200 sestertia, Suet. Claud. 24 (cf. Dio Cass. 53, 15): praefectus, Inscr. Orell. 3444; cf. ib. 946; 2648.—Plur. as subst.: ducenarii, Cod. Just. 10, 19, 1: judices, petty judges (chosen from persons possessed of 200 sestertia), Suet. Aug. 32.—Subst.: dŭ-cēnārius, ii, m., in milit. lang., the commander of 200 men, Veg. Mil. 2,

duceni.full: dŭcēni, ae, a (gen. ducenūm, Sen. N. Q. 3, 7, 3; Liv. 7, 25; Plin. 9, 3, 2, § 4), num. distr., two hundred each, two hundred, Plaut. Ps. 3, 2, 40; Hirt. B. G. 8, 4; Liv. 9, 19; 40, 18; Plin. 7, 2, 2, § 28 et saep.

ducentesima.full: dŭcentēsĭma, ae, f. (sc. pars) [ducenti], the two hundredth part, as a tax; one half per cent., Tac. A. 2, 42; Suet. Calig. 16.

ducenti.full: dŭcenti, ae, a (sing. ducentum, Lucil. ap. Non. 493 fin.; Col. 5, 3, 7; gen. ducentūm, Liv. 32, 37 al.; Varr. R. R. 3, 2, 15: ducentarum, Nep. Them. 2, 5: -torum, Front. Aq. 7), num. [duo-centum], two hundred. Lit., Plaut. Bacch. 4, 4, 55; 58; 4, 8, 27 et saep.— Transf., for a large number (indefinite), Plaut. As. 2, 2, 10; Cat. 37, 7 sq.; Hor. S. 1, 3, 11; 1, 10, 60; 1, 4, 9; 1, 6, 42 al.

ducenties.full: dŭcentĭes or -ĭens, adv. num. ducenti, two hundred times. Lit., Cic. Phil. 2, 16, 40; Cels. 2, 14 fin.— Transf., for many times indefinitely, Cat. 29, 15.

ducianus.full: dŭcĭānus, a, um, adj. dux, of or belonging to a leader or commander (late Lat.): officium, Cod. Th. 15, 11, 2: apparitores, ib. 11, 25, 1: judicium, Cod. Just. 7, 62, 38.—Subst.: ducianus, i, m., a commander's servant, Cod. Th. 7, 16, 3; Cod. Just. 1, 27, 2, § 8.

duco.full: dūco, xi, ctum, 3 (imp. duc; but duce, Plaut. Ep. 3, 3, 18; id. Most. 1, 4, 11; id. Poen. 5, 4, 59; id. Rud. 2, 3, 55; id. Trin. 2, 2, 103; id. Truc. 2, 5, 26.—Perf. sync.: duxti, Varr. ap. Non. 283, 32; Cat. 91, 9; Prop. 1, 3, 27), v. a. cf. Goth. tiuh-an; O. H. Germ. zieh-an, to draw; Germ. -zog, in Herzog, commander, duke, to lead, conduct, draw, bring forward, in all senses; very freq. passing over into the signif. of the compounds abducere, deducere, adducere, producere, etc., and of the sy

ductabilitas.full: ductābĭlĭtas, ātis, f. ducto, aptness to be duped, Att. ap. Non. 150, 13.

ductarius.full: ductārĭus, a, um, adj. id., of or for drawing: funis, perh. only Vitr. 10, 2; 3 and 5.

ductilis.full: ductĭlis, e, adj. duco, that may be led, guided, or conducted (post-Aug. and rare): scena, movable, Serv. Verg. G. 3, 24: flumen aquae riguae, i. e. a canal, Mart. 12, 31, 2: aes, i. e. that may be hammered out thin, Plin. 34, 8, 20, § 94 sq.; cf. aurum, Vulg. Num. 8, 4.

ductim.full: ductim, adv. id., by drawing (very rare): major pars operis in vinea ductim, potius quam caesim faciendaest (for which, shortly after: ductu falcis, non ictu), Col. 4, 25, 2: invergere in me liquores, in good draughts, Plaut. Curc. 1, 2, 13 (cf.: pocula duces Lesbii, Hor. C. 1, 17, 21).

ductio.full: ductĭo, ōnis, f. id., a leading, a leading off or away (very rare; perh. not anteAug.): aquarum, Vitr. 1, 1; 10, 19: alvi, Cels. 2, 12; 4, 24 fin.: ut ducere quis posset eos in quos habet jus ductionis, Dig. 43, 30, 3, § 1.

ductito.full: ductĭto, āvi, v. freq. a. id., to lead, to lead with one (a Plautin. word). Prop. In gen., Plaut. Rud. 2, 7, 26.— In partic., to lead home a wife, to marry, Plaut. Poen. 1, 2, 60.— Trop., to deceive: ego follitim ductitabo, Plaut. Epid. 3, 2, 15.

ducto.full: ducto, āvi, ātum, 1, v. freq. a. id., to lead or draw, conduct (very freq. in Plaut.; elsewh. perh. only in Ter., Sall., and once in Tac.; not in Cic., Caes., or the Aug. authors). Lit. In gen.: aliquem, Plaut. Most. 3, 2, 158: restim ductans, Ter. Ad. 4, 7, 34 Ruhnk.: exercitum per saltuosa loca, Sall. J. 38, 1; so, exercitum, id. C. 11, 5; 17, 7; id. J. 70, 2; * Tac. H. 2, 100; cf.: equites in exercitu, Sall. C. 19, 3; Amm. 14, 10, 11 (acc. to Quint. 8, 3, 44, this phraseology was regarded by

ductor.full: ductor, ōris, m. id., a leader, commander, chief, general (class.; a favorite word of Vergil, used by him more than 20 times; cf.: dux, imperator, princeps, praetor, praefectus, etc.): exercitus, * Cic. Tusc. 1, 37; Liv. 1, 28: itineris, a guide, id. 7, 41; 10, 21 fin.; Verg. A. 2, 14; 8, 6; 129 et saep.; cf. apum (in their battles), id. G. 4, 88; of the leaders in warlike games, id. A. 5, 133; 249; Suet. Tib. 6: classis, a pilot, Verg. A. 6, 334; Ov. M. 12, 574: aquarum Tibris, the king of rive

ductrix.full: ductrix, īcis, f. ductor, a female chief, a general: Penthesilea, Dar. Phryg. 36.

ductus1.full: ductus, a, um, Part., from duco.
ductus1.short: ductus, a, um, Part., from duco.

ductus2.full: ductus, ūs, m. duco, a leading, conducting (class.). Lit. In gen.: aquarum, Cic. Off. 2, 4, 14; id. Leg. 2, 1, 2; cf. the work of Frontinus: De aquaeductibus; in this sense also simply ductus, id. ib. 5 sq.: aequali ductu porticus, a line, row, Lucr. 4, 426: muri, Cic. Rep. 2, 6, 11: litterarum, form, shape, Quint. 1, 1, 25; 10, 2, 2; Plin. 8, 3, 3, § 6: oris (with vultus), lineaments, Cic. Fin. 5, 17, 47: liniarum, Plin. 37, 12, 74, § 195.— In partic., military lead, conduct, generalship, comma

dudum.full: dūdum, adv. temp. [diu-dum, it is some time since; cf. Don. Ter. And. 3, 4, 3; Prisc. p. 1018 P. Hence]. A short time ago, a little while ago (in Plaut. and Ter. freq., and repeatedly in Cicero's philos. writings and letters, and in Vergil; elsewh., except in the compound jamdudum, very rare; not in Caes.; cf. also diu, pridem): quid ille revortitur, qui dudum properare se aibat, Plaut. Am. 2, 2, 29; 1, 1, 231; 2, 1, 73; 3, 2, 35; id. Trin. 2, 4, 29 et saep.; Ter And. 3, 4, 12; id. Heaut. 3, 3,

duella.full: dŭella, ae, f. duo, a Roman weight = two sextulae, or the third part of an uncia, Rhemn. Fann. de Pond. 23; Isid. Or. 16, 25.

duellis.full: dŭellis, is, m. duellum = bellum, a warrior, Arn. 1, p. 10.

duellius.full: Dŭellĭus (in MSS. and inscrr. also written Dŭīlius and Duillius), a, um duellum = bellum; cf. Cic. Or. 45, 153; Quint. 1, 4, 15, a Roman gens; esp., C., the famous conqueror of the Carthaginians, in honor of whom the Columna rostrata was erected, 493 A. U. C., Cic. Rep. 1, 1; id. de Sen. 13, 44; id. N. D. 2, 66; id. Planc. 25; Plin. 16, 39, 74, § 192; Sil. 6, 665; cf. Inscr. Orell. 549.— M., a tribune of the people, A. U. C. 283, Liv. 2, 55 al.

duicensus.full: dŭĭcensus dicebatur cum altero, id est, cum filio census, Paul. ex. Fest. p. 66, 14 Müll. [duis = bis and censeo].
duicensus.short: dŭĭcensus dicebatur cum altero, id est, cum filio census, Paul.

duis.full: dŭis, verb., v. do init.— Num., v. bis init.

duitae.full: dŭītae, ārum, m. duo, heretics who believed in two gods, Prud. Hamart. praef. 37.

duitas.full: dŭĭtas, ātis, f. id., the state of being two, duality, Dig. 50, 16, 242, § 3; δυάς, duitas, Gloss.

dulcacidus.full: dulcăcĭdus, a, um, adj. dulcis-acidus, of a sourish-sweet flavor (late Lat.): liquor, Seren. Sammon. 11, 151; 32, 607.

dulcator.full: dulcātor, ōris, m. dulco, a sweetener: fontis amari, Paul. Nol. Carm. 23, 237.

dulce.full: dulce, adv., sweetly, pleasantly, v. dulcis, fin. .

dulcedo.full: dulcēdo, ĭnis, f. dulcis, sweetness. Lit., a sweet taste (rare): radix amara cum quadam dulcedine, Plin. 25, 6, 30, § 66; Vulg. Exod. 15, 25.—Far more freq. and class., Trop., pleasantness, agreeableness, delightfulness, charm: nimia aquarum, Lucr. 6, 1266; cf.: frugum et vini, Liv. 5, 33: vini, Plin. 14, 22, 28, § 137: aut aliquem fructum capiant dulcedinis almae (shortly before opp. dolor), Lucr. 2, 971; cf. Cic. Fin. 2, 13; 2, 34, 114; id. Leg. 1, 17 fin.; Verg. G. 1, 412; 4, 55: honoris et p

dulcesco.full: dulcesco, dulcui, 3, v. inch. n. [id.], to become sweet, Cic. de Sen. 15, 53; Plin. 3, 18, 22, § 127; 31, 7, 41, § 70; Paul. Nol. Carm. 17, 23.

dulcia.full: dulcĭa, ōrum, v. dulcis, I. B.

dulciarius.full: dulcĭārĭus, a, um, adj. dulcia, of confections, making sweetmeats: vascula, to hold confections, Inscr. Orell. 114.— Esp. of persons: pistor, a confectioner, pastry-cook, Mart. 14, 222 in lemm.; App. M. 10, p. 244, 30.—Hence, subst., dulciari-us, ii, m., a pastry-cook, Lampr. Heliog. 27; Treb. Claud. 14; Veg. Mil. 1, 7.

dulciculus.full: dulcĭcŭlus, a, um, adj. dim. [dulcis], sweetish (very rare): potio, * Cic. Tusc. 3, 19, 46; caseus, as a term of endearment, * Plaut. Poen. 1, 2, 179.

dulcifer.full: dulcĭfer, ĕra, ērum, adj. dulcis-fero, containing sweetness, sweet (very rare): ficus, Enn. ap. Charis. p. 103 P. (v. 71 Vahl.): cantharus, * Plaut. Ps. 5, 1, 17.

dulcifico.full: dulcĭfĭco, āvi, 1, v. a. dulcis-facio, to sweeten: oratio jejunium dulcificat, Petr. Chrysol. Serm. Dub. 6.

dulciloquus.full: dulcĭlŏquus, a, um, adj. dulcis-loquor, sweetly speaking (late Lat. and rare): calami, Aus. Idyll. 20, 4: ars Orphei, Sid. Ep. 8, 11.

dulcimodus.full: dulcĭ-mŏdus, a, um, adj. dulcis, sweetly modulated (late Lat.): psalmi, Prud. Psych. 664.

dulcinervis.full: dulcĭnervis, e, adj. dulcis-nervus, sweetly-stringed (late Lat.): arcus, Mart. Capt. 9, § 917.

dulciola.full: dulcĭŏla, ōrum, n. dim. dulcis, little sugar-cakes: mellita, App. M. 4, p. 115, 12.

dulciorelocus.full: dulcĭōrĕlŏcus, a, um, adj. dulcisos-loquor, speaking with a sweet mouth, an epithet of Nestor, Laev. ap. Gell. 19, 7, 13.

dulcis.full: dulcis, e, adj. from gulcis, by dissimilation; cf. ten-ebrae from root tam-; root in Sanscr. gul-jam, sweetness; Gr. γλυκύς, γλυκερός, sweet, sweet (very freq.; cf.: suavis, venustus, jucundus, gratus, acceptus, amoenus, etc.). Lit., opp. amarus: (animal) sentit et dulcia et amara, Cic. N. D. 3, 13; cf. Plaut. Cist. 1, 1, 72: mel, id. Asin. 3, 3, 24; id. Truc. 2, 4, 20; cf.: liquor mellis, Lucr. 1, 938; 4, 13: aqua, id. 6, 890: poma, id. 5, 1377; Hor. S. 2, 5, 12: vinum, id. C. 3, 12, 1; cf. mer

dulcisonorus.full: dulcĭsŏnōrus, a, am, adj. dulcissonorus, sweetly sounding: res Serv. Centim. p. 24 Santen. (p. 467, 17 Keil).

dulcisonus.full: dulcĭsŏnus, a, um, adj. dulcis-sonus, sweetly sounding: murmur, Sid. Carm. 6, 5; Cassiod. in Psalt. praef.

dulcitas.full: dulcĭtas, ātis, f. dulcis, sweetness, pleasantness (ante- and post-classical). Lit.: fici, App. de Mundo, 74, 34.— Trop.: conspirantis animae, Att. ap. Non. 96, 27 (Trag. v. 640 Rib.): tanta, Caecil. ap. Non. ib. (Com. v. 218 Rib.).

dulcitudo.full: dulcĭtūdo, ĭnis, f. dulcis, sweetness (very rare). Lit.: gustatus, qui dulcitudine praeter ceteros sensus commovetur, Cic. de Or. 3, 25, 99.— Trop., pleasantness, agreeableness, charm: usurarum, Dig. 42, 8, 10, § 10: CVM QVA VIXIT ANNIS XIII. CVM MAGNA DVLCITVDINE, in great tenderness (acc. to dulcis, II. B.), Inscr. Grut. 752, 3; so Inscr. Fabr. 250, 4.

dulco.full: dulco, ātus, āre, 1, v. a. id., to sweeten (late Lat.), Sid. Ep. 5, 4; id. Carm. 2, 105.

dulcor.full: dulcor, ōris, m. id., sweetness (cf. the opp. amaror; late Lat.), Tert. adv. Marc. 1. 6; 3, 5; Vulg. Sirach, 11, 3 al.

dulcoro.full: dulcōro, āre, 1, v. a. dulcor, to sweeten (late Lat.): amaritudinem, Hier. Ep. 22, 9; id. ib. 69, 9: animam, Vulg. Prov. 27, 9: mare mortuum et amaras aquas, Hier. ap. Psa. 76.—Hence, P. a.: dulcōrātus, a, um, sweetened, Plin. Val. 1, 2 al.

dulgibini.full: Dulgĭbīni, ōrum, m. (Δουλγούμνιοι), Ptol., a Germanic tribe on the banks of the Weser, in the present Lippe - Detmold, Paderborn, and Pyrmont, Tac. G. 34.

dulice.full: dūlĭce, adv., = δουλικῶς, in the manner of a slave, servilely, Plaut. Mil. 2, 2, 58.
dulice.short: dūlĭce, adv., = δουλικῶς, in the manner of a slave, servilely, Plaut.

dulichium.full: Dūlĭchĭum, ii, n. (Δουλίχιον Hom., Δολίχαι Strab.), an island of the Ionian Sea, southeast of Ithaca, belonging to the kingdom of Ulysses, perhaps one of the Echinades, but its situation is uncertain, Mel. 2, 7, 10; Plin. 4, 12, 19, § 54; Verg. A. 3, 271; Ov. Tr. 1, 5, 67; called also Dūlĭ-chĭa, ae, f. (sc. insula), Prop. 2, 14, 4 (3, 6, 4 M.).—Hence, Dūlĭchĭus, a, um, adj., of Dulichium, or poet., of Ulysses.— So, dux, i. e. Ulysses, Ov. M. 14, 226; id. R. Am. 272; cf. juvenis, Prop. 2, 21, 13

dulorestes.full: Dūlŏrestes, is (Dolorestes), m., the title of a tragedy of Pacuvius, Prisc. 668 P. v. Rib. Trag. Rel. p. 91 sq. and 364.
dulorestes.short: Dūlŏrestes, is (Dolorestes), m., the title of a tragedy of Pacuvius, Prisc.

dum.full: dum, conj. [for dium, acc. from dius; cf. diu, Corss. Ausspr. 2, 856], denotes the temporal relation of two actions to cach other, As contemporaneous, or, As in immediate succession, so that with the commencement of one action the other ceases. As contemporaneous. Without respect to the limits of the two actions, while, whilst, during the time in which. In gen., construed with the indicative, except in oratio obliqua, where the subjunctive was sometimes used. In Aug. poets and late prose the sub

dumalis.full: dūmālis, e, adj. dumus, bushy, bristly: coma, Mart. Cap. 4, § 329.

dumesco.full: dūmesco, ĕre dumus, to be overgrown with bushes, acc. to Diom. p. 335 P.
dumesco.short: dūmesco, ĕre dumus, to be overgrown with bushes, acc.

dumetum.full: dūmētum or dummetum (another form: DUMECTA antiqui quasi DUMICETA appellabant, quae nos dumeta, Paul. ex Fest. p. 67, 10 Müll.), i, n. id., thorn-bushes, thorn-hedge, thicket. Lit., Cic. Tusc. 5, 23; Verg. G. 1, 15; Hor. C. 3, 4, 63; 3, 29, 23 al.— Trop.: cur orationem tantas in angustias et Stoicorum dumeta compellimus? Cic. Ac. 2, 35: quod cum efficere voltis (i. e. deum significare) in dumeta conrepitis, id. N. D. 1, 24 fin.
dumetum.short: dūmētum or dummetum (another form: DUMECTA antiqui quasi DUMICETA appellabant, quae nos dumeta, Paul.

dumicola.full: dūmĭcŏla, ae, m. [dumus-colo], that dwells in thickets, Avien. Perieg. 895.

dummodo.full: dummŏdo, v. dum, I. B. 2. a. .

dumnorix.full: Dumnŏrix, ĭgis, m., an Aeduan, brother of Divitiacus, Caes. B. G. 1, 3 al.
dumnorix.short: Dumnŏrix, ĭgis, m., an Aeduan, brother of Divitiacus, Caes.

dumosus.full: dūmōsus (also dummosus; old form dusmōsus, like Casmena, Casmili, etc., Liv. Andron. ap. Paul. ex Fest. p. 67, 5 Müll.), a, um, adj. dumus, full of thornbushes, bushy (rare): rupes, Verg. E. 1, 77; cf. saxa, Ov. M. 10, 535: montes, Col. 4, 33, 5; colles, id. Poët. 10, 150: arva, Verg. G. 2, 180.

dumtaxat.full: dumtaxat (less correctly, duntax-at; in ante-Aug. monuments perh. always written separately; often in inscriptions separated by some words: dum ... taxat; cf. also Lex ap. Fest. p. 246, 12 Müll.), adv. dum-taxo; hence, lit., as far as it holds good, extends. To this extent, so far, in so far, as far as this matter is concerned: sin autem jejunitatem et siccitatem ... dummodo sit polito ... in Attico genere ponit, hoc recte dumtaxat, Cic. Brut. 82, 285: nos animo dumtaxat vigemus, id. Att. 4, 3 f

dumus.full: dūmus (old form dusmus, v. dumosus), i, m. dusmus for densimus, from densus, a thorn-bush, bramble, Cic. Tusc. 5, 23, 65; Verg. G. 3, 315; 338; 4, 130; id. A. 4, 526 et saep.

duo.full: dŭŏ, ae, ŏ (acc. masc. duo as freq. as duos; cf. ambo. Passages with duo, Att. ap. Charis. p. 101 P.; Plaut. Ep. 2, 2, 4; 3, 2, 37; id. Most. 3, 2, 89; 147; 148; id. Ps. 1, 3, 99; 4, 2, 43; Varr. R. R. 1, 18, 5; 3, 1, 9; Cic. Rep. 1, 10; 1, 13; 2, 14; 2, 19; Cic. Verr. 2, 2, 9; id. Tull. § 19 Beier N. cr.; id. Fam. 3, 4, 2; 7, 25, 2; id. Att. 9, 11, A, 2; Caes. B. G. 7, 69, 2; Liv. 6, 42 fin.; 35, 21; Suet. Calig. 41; id. Oth. 1, 5; Verg. A. 11, 285; Hor. S. 1, 7, 15 al.—Gen. duūm, Naev. ap. Cha

duodecajugum.full: dŭŏdĕcăjŭgum, i, n. vox hybr., δυόδεκα + jugum, a team of twelve animals, Ambros. in Psa. 118, Serm. 4.

duodecas.full: dŭōdĕcas, ădis, f., = δυωδεκάς, the number twelve, Tert. Praescr. 49.
duodecas.short: dŭōdĕcas, ădis, f., = δυωδεκάς, the number twelve, Tert.

duodecennis.full: dŭŏdĕcennis, e, adj. duodecim-annus, twelve years old, Sulpic. Sever. Dial. 1, 10; 3, 2.

duodecennium.full: dŭŏdĕcennĭum, ii, n. duodecennis, a period of twelve years, Cod. Th. 2, 27, 1, § 6.

duodecies.full: dŭŏdĕcĭes (or -ĭens, quadrisyl., Auct. Carm. de Phoenice, 28), adv. num. duodecim, twelve times, Cic. Verr. 2, 2, 75; Liv. 38, 28.

duodecim.full: dŭŏdĕcim, card. num. [duo-decem], twelve, Plaut. Ep. 5, 2, 10; Cic. Rep. 2, 17; Caes. B. G. 1, 5, 2 et saep.—So, duodecim (and more freq. XII.) Tabulae, the laws of the Twelve Tables, Cic. Off. 1, 12; Quint. 5, 14, 18; Varr. L. L. 5, § 22 Müll. et saep.; called also absol.: duodecim (or XII.), Cic. Leg. 2, 23 (repeatedly); id. Off. 3, 16 al. (v. Wordsworth, Fragm. and Spec. pp. 253-265).

duodecimus.full: dŭŏ-dĕcĭmus, a, um, ord. num., the twelfth (a common word in Caes.): legio, Caes. B. G. 2, 23, 4; 2, 25, 1; 3, 1, 1; 7, 62, 4; id. B. C. 3, 34, 3.—Adv.: dŭŏdĕcĭmo, for the twelfth time: consul, Capitol. Anton. Pius, 1, § 8.

duodecimvir.full: dŭŏdĕcim-vir, vĭri, m., one of the twelve commissioners, Inscr. Orell. 3969.
duodecimvir.short: dŭŏdĕcim-vir, vĭri, m., one of the twelve commissioners, Inscr.

duodenarius.full: dŭŏdēnārĭus, a, um, adj. duodeni, containing twelve: numerus, Varr. L. L. 5, § 34 Müll.

duodeni.full: dŭŏ-dēni, ae, a, distr. num., twelve each; twelve: uxores habent deni duodenique inter se communes, Caes. B. G. 5, 14, 4: duodena describit in singulos homines jugera, Cic. Agr. 2, 31, 85; Liv. 5, 33; cf.: fossa duplex duodenūm pedum, Caes. B. G. 7, 36, 7: milia, id. ib. 7, 75, 3: astra, Verg. G. 1, 232; cf. signa, Ov. M. 13, 618: nec inveniuntur qui velint debere rei publicae, praesertim duodenis assibus, at twelve per cent., Plin. et Traj. Epist. 54, 1.

duodennium.full: dŭŏdennium, ii, n., the space of twelve years, Mythogr. Vat. 3, p. 163 med. (al. duodecennium).
duodennium.short: dŭŏdennium, ii, n., the space of twelve years, Mythogr.

duodenonaginta.full: dŭŏ-dē-nōnāginta (written LXXXVIII.), card. num., eighty-eight, Plin. 3, 16, 20, § 118.

duodequadrageni.full: dŭŏ-dē-quā^drāgēni, ae, a, distr. num., thirty-eight each: pedum columnae, Plin. 36, 2, 2, § 6; and 36, 15, 24, § 114.

duodequadragesimus.full: dŭŏ-dē-quādrāgēsĭmus, a, um, ordin. num., the thirty-eight: anno, Liv. 1, 40.

duodequadraginta.full: dŭŏ-dē-quā^drāginta, card. num., thirty-eight, Cic. Tusc. 5, 20; Liv. 35, 40.

duodequinquageni.full: dŭŏ-dē-quinquāgēni, ae, a, distr. num., forty-eight each; forty-eight: diebus, Plin. 2, 8, 6, § 38.

duodequinquagesimus.full: dŭŏ-dē-quinquāgēsĭmus, a, um, ordin. num., the forty-eighth: anno, Cic. Brut. 44: die, Col. 9, 14, 4.

duodequinquaginta.full: dŭŏ-dē-quinquāginta, card. num., forty-eight, Col. 9, 14, 1; 12, 5, 1 (written IIL., Lex. Acil. Repet. 32 al.).

duodesexagesimus.full: dŭŏ-dē-sexāgēsĭmus, a, um, ordin. num., the fifty-eighth: annus, Vell. 2, 53, 13.

duodetricesimus.full: dŭŏ-dē-trīcēsĭmus, a, um, ordin. num., the twenty - eighth: dies, Varr. ap. Gell. 3, 10, 6.

duodetriciens.full: dŭŏ-dē-trīcĭens, adv. num., twentyeight times, Cic. Verr. 2, 3, 70 Zumpt N. cr.

duodetriginta.full: dŭŏ-dē-trīginta, card. num., twentyeight, Liv. 33, 36 fin.; Suet. Tib. 1 al.

duodeviceni.full: dŭŏ-dē-vīcēni, ae, a, distr. num., eighteen each: denarii, Liv. 21, 41.

duodevicesimus.full: dŭŏ-dē-vīcēsĭmus (or viges-), a, um, ordin. num., the eighteenth, Cato and Varr. ap. Non. 100, 11 sq.: pars tauri, Plin. 2, 73, 75, § 184; Plin. Ep. 6, 20, 5; and, per tmesin: duo enim devicesima Olympiade, Plin. 35, 8, 34, § 55.

duodeviginti.full: dŭŏ-dē-vīginti, card. num., eighteen, Plaut. Poen. 4, 2, 74 sq.; Cic. Ac. 2, 41, 128; id. Rep. 2, 22; Caes. B. G. 2, 5 fin.; id. B. C. 3, 71 al.; cf. also: annis mille centum et duobus de viginti fere, etc., Eutr. 10, 9.

duoetvicesimani.full: dŭŏ-et-vīcēsĭmāni, ōrum, m. duoet-vicesimus, soldiers of the twenty-second legion, Tac. H. 4, 37; 5, 1.

duoetvicesimus.full: dŭŏ-et-vīcēsĭmus, a, um, ordin. num., the twenty-second: anno, Fab. Pict. ap. Gell. 5, 4: legio, Tac. H. 1, 18; 1, 55; 4, 24; 4, 37; cf. the preced. art.

duovir.full: dŭŏvir, vĭri, and usu. plur. dŭŏvĭri (less correctly dŭumvĭri, Zumpt, Gram. § 124; Krebs, Antibarb. p. 391; in MSS. and Inscr. usu. II. vir, II. viri; but, DVOVIRES, Inscr. Orell. 3808: DVOVIRI, ib. 3886, v. infra), ōrum, m. du + vir, a Roman board or court consisting of two persons. Perduellionis, an extraordinary criminal court, the duumviri, anciently selected by the kings or the people for each case as it arose; so in the trial of Horatius, Liv. 1, 26; of M. Manlius, id. 6, 20; of C. Rabiriu

duplaris.full: dŭplāris, e, adj. duplus, containing double (late Lat.): numerus, Macr. Somn. Scip. 1, 6; 2, 1: miles, one who receives double pay as a reward, Veg. Mil. 2, 7; also in the form DUPLARIUS, Inscr. Orell. 2003; 3476 al., v. duplicarius.

duplatio.full: dū^plātĭo, ōnis, f. duplo, a doubling, Dig. 9, 4, 31.

duplex.full: dū^plex, ĭcis (abl. commonly duplici; duplice, Hor. S. 2, 2, 122), adj. duo-plico, twofold, double. Lit.: et duplices hominum facies et corpora bina, Lucr. 4, 452; cf. aër (with geminus), id. 4, 274: cursus (with duae viae), Cic. Tusc. 1, 30: pars (opp. simplex), Quint. 8, 5, 4; cf. id. 4, 4, 5: modus (opp. par and sesquiplex), Cic. Or. 57, 193 et saep.: duplici de semine, Lucr. 4, 1229: quem locum duplici altissimo muro munierant, Caes. B. G. 2, 29, 3: fossa duodenūm pedum, id. ib. 7, 36 fin.:

duplicarius.full: dū^plĭcārĭus, ii, m. duplex, a soldier who receives double pay as a reward, Varr. L. L. 5, § 90 Müll.; Liv. 2, 59 fin.; Inscr. Orell. 3533; 4994 (cf. Caes. B. C. 3, 53 fin.; Liv. 7, 37; and 24, 47); also written DUPLICIARIUS, Inscr. Orell. 3534; see also duplaris.

duplicatio.full: dū^plĭcātĭo, ōnis, f. duplico, a doubling (post-Aug.): radiorum, i. e. reflection, Sen. Q. N. 4, 8; Dig. 9, 4, 31: temporis, ib. 48, 19, 8.— Esp., As arithm. t. t., a doubling, multiplication by two, Mart. Cap. 7, § 750.— As jurid. t. t., the answering of one objection by another, turning an objection upon an adversary, Gai. 4, 127.— As rhet. fig., = ἀναδίπλωσις, the repetition of a word in beginning a clause, Ruf. Schem. Lex. § 8.

duplicato.full: dū^plĭcāto, adv., twice as much, v. duplico fin.
duplicato.short: dū^plĭcāto, adv., twice as much, v.

duplicator.full: dū^plĭcātor, ōris, m. duplico, a doubler, magnifier, Sid. Ep. 3, 13.

duplicitas.full: dū^plĭcĭtas, ātis, f. duplex, a being double, doubleness (late Lat.): aurium, Lact. Opif. Dei 8: narium, id. ib. 10.

dupliciter.full: dū^plĭcĭter, adv., doubly, on two accounts, v. duplex fin.
dupliciter.short: dū^plĭcĭter, adv., doubly, on two accounts, v.

duplico.full: dū^plĭco, āvi, ātum, 1 (u long, Verg. E. 2, 67), v. a. duplex, to double (class.) Lit.: numerum dierum, Cic. N. D. 1, 22; so, numerum, id. Rep. 2, 20 (twice); Caes. B. G. 4, 36, 2; Tac. H. 2, 30: modum hastae, Nep. Iphicr. 1 fin.: exercitum, Cic. Att. 5, 18, 2; cf. copias, Liv. 7, 7: fructum, Varr. R. R. 1, 69, 1; cf.: reditum pretio, Col. 12, 52, 2: rem, Pers. 6, 78: stipendium legionibus in perpetuum, Suet. Caes. 26: tributa, id. Vesp. 16: verba, i. e. to repeat, Cic. Or. 39, 135 (with iterare

duplio.full: dū^plĭo, ōnis, m. duplus, the double of any thing (very rare), XII. Tab. ap. Fest. S. V. VINDICIAE, p. 376, 30 Müll.; Plin. 18, 3, 3, § 12; cf. Paul. ex Fest. p. 66, 13 Müll.— Esp., the double of the perfect number, six, i. e. twelve, = διπλασίων; cf. Vitr. 3, 1, 6.

duplo1.full: dū^plo, āre, v. a. id., to double (only in jurid. Lat., for the class. duplico), Dig. 40, 12, 20; Gai. ib. 38, 10, 3; cf.: duplabis duplicabis, Paul. ex Fest. p. 76, 2 Müll.

duplo2.full: dū^plo, adv., doubly, v. duplus fin.

duplus.full: dū^plus, a, um, adj. duplex, double, twice as large, twice as much. Adj.: dupla et tripla intervalla, Cic. Univ. 7: pars, id. ib.: scrobes, Plaut. Fragm. ap. Prisc. p. 751 P.: pecunia, Liv. 29, 19: donativum, Suet. Dom. 2.— Subst. dū^plum, i, n., the double of any thing: a terra ad lunam centum viginti sex milia stadiorum esse, ab ea usque ad solem duplum, Plin. 2, 21, 19, § 83; Plaut. Poen. 1, 1, 56: furem dupli condemnari, feneratorem quadrupli, Cato R. R. praef.; Cic. Off. 3, 16, 65: decrevit

dupondiarius.full: dū^pondĭārĭus, a, um, adj. dupondius, containing two asses. Prop.: orbiculus, Col. 4, 30, 4.—Subst.: dŭpondĭ-ārĭus, ii, m. (sc. nummus), a two-as piece, Plin. 34, 2, 2, § 4.— Transf., like diobolaris, worth two coppers, i. e. worthless, bad: dominus, Petr. 58, 5: homo, id. 74, 15.

dupondius.full: dū^pondĭus, ii, m., or dŭpondĭum, ii (cf. Varr. L. L. 9, 49, § 81; also, dĭpon-dĭum, Gromat. Vet. p. 28, 14; p. 167, 11), n. duo-pondus, the sum of two asses. As a coin, Varr. L. L. 5, § 169; 9, § 81 Müll.; Plin. 33, 3, 13, § 42; Cic. Quint. 16, 53; Petr. 14, 3 al.— Transf., need, want, Petr. 58, 13.— As a measure, two feet, Col. 3, 13, 5; 3, 15, 2 et saep.
dupondius.short: dū^pondĭus, ii, m., or dŭpondĭum, ii (cf.

durabilis.full: dūrābĭlis, e, adj. duro, lasting, durable (rare; not ante-Aug.): quod caret alterna requie durabile non est, Ov. H. 4, 89; Col. 12, 38, 7; 12, 55, 1: vox, Quint. 11, 3, 23 al.—Comp.: durabilior materies, App. Mag. p. 314, 13.—Sup. does not occur.—Adv.: dūrābĭlĭter, in a lasting manner, Cassiod. Hist. Eccl. 1, 9.

durabilitas.full: dūrābĭlĭtas, ātis, f. durabilis, lastingness, durability (late Lat.): frumentorum, Pall. 1, 36, 2.

duracinus.full: dūrăcĭnus, a, um, adj. durus-acinus, orig. of the grape, hard-berried, hard (only fit for eating): uva, Cato R. R. 7, 2; Plin. 14, 1, 3, § 14; Suet. Aug. 76; Mart. 13, 22; cf. vites, Col. 3, 2, 1.—Transf., of other fruits: persica, Plin. 15, 12, 11, § 39; id. 15, 28, 34, § 113; Pall. Febr. 25, 32: cerasa, Plin. 15, 25, 30, § 103.

duramen.full: dūrāmen, ĭnis, n. duro, hardness, concr. (very rare): aquarum, i. e. ice, Lucr. 6, 530.—Of a hardened or ligneous vinebranch, see the foll., I.

duramentum.full: dūrāmentum, i, n. id., a hardening in concreto. Lit., a hardened, i. e. ligneous vine-branch, Col. 4, 21, 1; Plin. 17, 23, 35, § 208; Pall. Febr. 12, 1.—Called also duramen, Col. 4, 22, 1.— Transf., a means of hardening, stimulus: humanae imbecillitatis efficacissimum duramentum est necessitas, Val. Max. 2, 7, 10.— Trop., firmness (with robur), Sen. Tranq. An. 1.

duranius.full: Dŭrănĭus, ii, m., a river in Gallia, now Dordogne, Auson. Idyll. 9, 464; Sidon. Carm. 22, 103.
duranius.short: Dŭrănĭus, ii, m., a river in Gallia, now Dordogne, Auson.
