durateus.full: dūrătĕus, a, um, adj., = δονράτεος, wooden, only of the Trojan horse: equus, Lucr. 1, 477 (the Homeric ἵππος δονράτεος, Od. 8, 493; 512); cf. durius.
durateus.short: dūrătĕus, a, um, adj., = δονράτεος, wooden, only of the Trojan horse: equus, Lucr.

durator.full: dūrātor, ōris, m. duro, one who hardens, a hardener, Pac. Pan. Theod. 33.

duratrix.full: dūrātrix, īcis, adj. f. [durator], that renders durable, Plin. 14, 1, 3, § 17.

dure.full: dūre, adv., hardly, v. durus fin.

dureo.full: dūrĕo, ēre, 2, v. n. durus, to be hard, Serv. Verg. E. 1, 91; Prisc. 800 P.

duresco.full: dūresco, rui, 3, v. inch. n., to grow hard, to harden. Prop.: durescit humor, * Cic. N. D. 2, 10, 26; so in the praes.: limus, Verg. E. 8, 80: campus, id. G. 1, 72: corpus, Ov. M. 8, 607: curalium, id. ib. 15, 417: oraque duruerant, id. ib. 2, 831: durescente materia, Tac. G. 45.— Trop.: in alicujus lectione, qs. to become ossified, Quint. 2, 5, 21; 10, 5, 16.

dureta.full: durēta, ae, f. a Span. word, a wooden bathing-tub, Suet. Aug. 82 fin.

duricordia.full: dūrĭcordĭa, ae, f. durus-cor, hardheartedness (eccl. Lat.), Tert. adv. Marc. 5, 4; 13.

duricorius.full: dūrĭcŏrĭus, a, um, adj. durus-corium, hard-skinned: ficus, Cloatius ap. Macr. S. 2, 16.

duris.full: Duris, is, m., a Greek author, of Samos, Cic. Att. 6, 1, 18; Plin. 7, 2, 2, § 30 al.
duris.short: Duris, is, m., a Greek author, of Samos, Cic.

duritas.full: dūrĭtas, ātis, f. durus, hardness, harshness: orationis (with severitas), Cic. Or. 16 fin.

duriter.full: dūrĭter, adv., hardly, etc., v. durus fin.

duritia.full: dūrĭtĭa, ae (also rarely dūrĭtĭes, Cels. 3, 24; 6, 18, 6 al.; acc.: duritiem, * Lucr. 4. 268; Cat. 66, 50; Ov. M. 1, 401; 4, 751; id. H. 4, 85 Jahn. N. cr.; abl.: duritie, Plin. Pan. 82, 6; Suet. Ner. 34), f. durus, hardness. Lit. In gen.: saxi, Lucr. 4, 269; cf. Ov. M. 1, 401; and 4, 751: ferri, Cat. 66, 50: adamantina, Plin. 37, 11, 73, § 189: lactis coacti, id. 23, 7, 64, § 126: pellis, Ov. M. 3, 64 sq. et saep.— Esp., in medic. lang., induration: praecordiorum, Cels. 3, 24: alvi, Suet. Ner.

duritudo.full: dūrĭtūdo, ĭnis, f. durus, II. B., harshness, cruelty, Cato ap. Gell. 17, 2, 20; id. ap. Non. 100, 23.

durius1.full: dūrĭus or dūrēus, a, um, adj., = δούριος or δούρειος, equus, the Trojan horse, Aur. Vict. Orig. 1; Paul. ex Fest. p. 82, 12. —Poet. transf.: duria nox, i. e. the night in which the Greeks descended from the interior of the horse, Val. Fl. 2, 573; cf. durateus.
durius1.short: dūrĭus or dūrēus, a, um, adj., = δούριος or δούρειος, equus, the Trojan horse, Aur.

durius2.full: Dŭrĭus, ii, m. (Dūrĭa, ae, m., Claud. in Laud. Ser. Reg. 72), one of the principal rivers of Spain, now the Douro, Mel. 3, 1, 7 sq.; Plin. 4, 20, 34, § 112 sq.; Sil. 1, 234 al.

duriusculus.full: dūrĭuscŭlus, a, um, adj. dim. [durus, II. A.], somewhat hard, rough, or harsh (perh. only in the foll. passages).—Of expression: Catullus, Plin. H. N. praef. § 2; cf. versus, Plin. Ep. 1, 16, 5.

duro.full: dūro, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. and n. durus, to make hard, to harden (mostly ante-class. and post-Aug.; not in Cic.). Lit. Act.: quae nobis durata ac spissa videntur, Haec, etc., Lucr. 2, 444; so in the part. perf.: coria (with condurare ferrum), id. 6, 970; cf. cutis, Ov. M. 4, 577: caementa calce (opp. interlita luto), Liv. 21, 11: ova in aqua, Plin. 29, 3, 11, § 45: pontus frigore, Ov. P. 4, 9, 85: nives solo, Hor. C. 3, 24, 39: aqua salibus, i. e. strongly saturated, Col. 7, 4 fin., v. durus, I.:

durocortorum.full: Dūrŏcortŏrum, i, n., Δουρικόρτορα, the capital of the Remi in Gallia Belgica, now Rheims, Caes. B. G. 6, 44, 1.
durocortorum.short: Dūrŏcortŏrum, i, n., Δουρικόρτορα, the capital of the Remi in Gallia Belgica, now Rheims, Caes.

duronius.full: Duronius, ii, m., a Roman proper name, Cic. de Or. 2, 68, 274 al.
duronius.short: Duronius, ii, m., a Roman proper name, Cic.

durus.full: dūrus, a, um, adj. etym. dub.; cf. Sanscr. root dhar, to fix, confirm, hard. Lit. Orig. as affecting the sense of feeling: et validi silices ac duri robora ferri, Lucr. 2, 449; so, silex, Verg. A. 6, 471: ferrum, Hor. C. 3, 11, 31: cautes, Verg. A. 4, 366; Ov. M. 4, 672: bipennes, Hor. C. 4, 4, 57: ligones, id. Epod. 5, 30: aratrum, id. S. 1, 1, 28: compes, id. Epod. 4, 4: pellis, Lucr. 6, 1195; Verg. G. 3, 502: arva, id. ib. 2, 341; cf. cutis, Ov. M. 8, 805: alvus, Cels. 6, 18, 9; Hor. S. 2, 4,

dusaritis.full: Dūsaritis myrrha, a kind of myrrh, Plin. 12, 16, 35, § 69.
dusaritis.short: Dūsaritis myrrha, a kind of myrrh, Plin.

duumvira.full: dŭumvĭra, ae, f. duumvir, the wife of a duumvir, Renier, Inscr. Afr. 3914.

duumviralicius.full: dŭumvĭrālicius, ii, m. duumviralis, one who has been a duumvir, Inscr. Orell. 3721 (Momms. 635; 189).

duumviralis.full: dŭumvĭrālis, e, adj. duumviri, of or belonging to a duumvir, duumviral. Adj.: POTESTATE, Inscr. Fabr. p. 29, 129.— More freq., Subst.: duumviralis, is, m., one who has been a auumvir, Dig. 50, 3, 1; Inscr. Orell. 3727; 3816.

duumviralitas.full: dŭumvĭrālĭtas, ātis, f. duumviralis, the office and dignity of a duumvir, duumvirate, Cod. Just. 5, 27, 1.

duumviratus.full: dŭumvĭrātus (also DVOMVIR., Inscr. Momms. 2378), ūs, m. duumviri, the office of a duumvir, duumvirate, Plin. Ep. 4, 22, 1; Dig. 50, 3, 1; Inscr. Orell. 3817 (Momms. 2096; 4059).

dux.full: dux, dŭcis, com. duco, a leader, conductor, guide (for syn. cf.: imperator, ductor, tyrannus, rex, princeps, praetor, auctor). In gen.: illis non ducem locorum, non exploratorem fuisse, Liv. 9, 5, 7; cf. itineris, Curt. 5, 4: itinerum, Caes. B. G. 6, 17, 1: regendae civitatis (with auctor publici consilii), Cic. de Or. 3, 17, 63: dux isti quondam et magister ad despoliandum Dianae templum fuit, Cic. Verr. 2, 3, 21: nil desperandum Teucro duce et auspice Teucro, Hor. C. 1, 7, 27: tu dux et comes

dyas.full: dўas, ădis, f., = δυάς, the number two, Macr. Somn. Scip. 1, 6, 18; 1, 12, 5; Aug. Conf. 4, 15.
dyas.short: dўas, ădis, f., = δυάς, the number two, Macr.

dymas.full: Dўmas, antis, m., = Δύμας, the father of Hecuba, Ov. M. 11, 761; Serv. Verg. A. 7, 320; Hyg. Fab. 91; 111.—Hence, Dў-mantis, ĭdis, adj., of Dymas: proles, i. e. Hecuba; and, as subst.: Dўman-tis, ĭdis, f., the daughter of Dymas, i. e. Hecuba, Ov. M. 13, 620.
dymas.short: Dўmas, antis, m., = Δύμας, the father of Hecuba, Ov.

dyme.full: Dȳme, ēs, f., = Δύμη, an old sea-coast town in Achaia, west of Olenos, now perhaps Kaminitza, Plin. 4, 5, 6, § 13.—Also called Dȳmae, ārum, f., Liv. 27, 31; 32, 21; 38, 29.—Hence, Dȳmaeus, a, um, adj., of Dymae, Dymaean: ager, Liv. 27, 31 fin.—In plur. subst.: Dȳmaei, ōrum, m., the Dymaeans, Cic. Att. 16, 1.
dyme.short: Dȳme, ēs, f., = Δύμη, an old sea-coast town in Achaia, west of Olenos, now perhaps Kaminitza, Plin.

dynamice.full: dўnămĭcē, es, f., = δυναμική, the science of forces, dynamics, Fulg. Myth. 3. 10.
dynamice.short: dўnămĭcē, es, f., = δυναμική, the science of forces, dynamics, Fulg.

dynamis.full: dўnămis, is, f., = δύναμις. * A store, plenty (cf. the Lat. vis), Plaut. Ps. 1, 2, 77.— A square number (cf. potestas, Mart. Cap. 2, § 106), Arn. 2, p. 60.

dynastes.full: dўnastes, ae, m., = δυνάστης, a ruler, prince (partic. of a small country), Cic. Phil. 11, 12 fin.; Caes. B. C. 3, 3, 2; Nep. Dat. 2; id. Ages. 7.— Of the triumvirs at Rome: si erit nebulo iste cum his dynastis in gratia, Cic. Att. 2, 9, 1.
dynastes.short: dўnastes, ae, m., = δυνάστης, a ruler, prince (partic.

dyodecas.full: dўōdĕcas, ădis, f., = δυωδεκάς, a tweive, a dozen, Tert. Praescr. 49.
dyodecas.short: dўōdĕcas, ădis, f., = δυωδεκάς, a tweive, a dozen, Tert.

dyonymus.full: dўōnўmus, a, um, adj., = δυώνυμος, having two names, Prisc. p. 580.
dyonymus.short: dўōnўmus, a, um, adj., = δυώνυμος, having two names, Prisc.

dyraspes.full: Dўraspes, is, m., a river in Scythia, Ov. Pont. 4, 10, 53.
dyraspes.short: Dўraspes, is, m., a river in Scythia, Ov.

dyrrachium.full: Dyrrăchĭum (Dyrrh-), ii, n., = Δυρράχιον, a famous sea-coast town of Grecian Illyria, the landing-place of those coming from Italy, formerly called Epidamnus, now Durazzo, Mel. 2, 3, 12; Plin. 3, 23, 26, § 145; Cic. Pis. 38; id. Att. 3, 22 fin.; id. Fam. 14, 1, 6 sq.; Liv. 29, 12 et saep.—Its inhabitants are called Dyrră-chīni, ōrum, m., = Δυρραχηνοί, Cic. Att. 3, 22 fin.; id. Prov. Cons. 3.—Also Dyr-răchēni, Dig. 50, 15, 8.
dyrrachium.short: Dyrrăchĭum (Dyrrh-), ii, n., = Δυρράχιον, a famous sea-coast town of Grecian Illyria, the landing-place of those coming from Italy, formerly called Epidamnus, now Durazzo, Mel.

dyscolus.full: dyscŏlus, a, um, adj., = δύσκολος, of a bad temper, peevish, irritable, Vulg. 1 Pet. 2, 18.
dyscolus.short: dyscŏlus, a, um, adj., = δύσκολος, of a bad temper, peevish, irritable, Vulg.

dysenteria.full: dўsentĕrĭa, ae, f., = δυσεντερία, a flux, dysentery, Plin. 26, 8, 28, § 45; 28, 9, 33, § 128; Cael. Aur. Tard. 4, 6, 84 sq.; Vulg. Act. 28, 8 (in Cels. 4, 15; and Cic. Fam. 7, 26, written as Greek).
dysenteria.short: dўsentĕrĭa, ae, f., = δυσεντερία, a flux, dysentery, Plin.

dysentericus.full: dўsentĕrĭcus, a, um, adj., = δυσεντερικός, pertaining to dysentery, dysenteric: passio, Pall. Febr. 31 fin. (= δυσεντερικὰ πάθη Cic. Fam. 7, 26, 1).—Subst.: dysen-tericus, i, m., one who has the dysentery, Plin. 22, 24, 55, § 116 sqq.; 26, 8, 28, § 44 sq.; Scrib. Comp. 85; Firm. Math. 8.
dysentericus.short: dўsentĕrĭcus, a, um, adj., = δυσεντερικός, pertaining to dysentery, dysenteric: passio, Pall.

dyseros.full: dўsĕrōs, ōtis, adj., = δύσερως, loving unfortunately, Aus. Epigr. 92, 1.
dyseros.short: dўsĕrōs, ōtis, adj., = δύσερως, loving unfortunately, Aus.

dyspepsia.full: dyspepsĭa, ae, f., = δυσπεψία, indigestion, dyspepsia, Cato R. R. 127, 1.
dyspepsia.short: dyspepsĭa, ae, f., = δυσπεψία, indigestion, dyspepsia, Cato R.

dysphoricus.full: dysphŏrĭcus, a, um, adj., = δυσφορικός, unfortunate, Firm. Math. 8, 12.
dysphoricus.short: dysphŏrĭcus, a, um, adj., = δυσφορικός, unfortunate, Firm.

dyspnoea.full: dyspnoea, ae, f., = δύσπνοια, a difficulty of breathing, Plin. 23, 4, 47, § 92; 26, 7, 19, § 33 (in Cels. 4, 4, written as Greek). —Hence,
dyspnoea.short: dyspnoea, ae, f., = δύσπνοια, a difficulty of breathing, Plin.

dyspnoicus.full: dyspnŏĭcus, i, m., = δυσπνοϊκός, one who labors under difficulty of breathing.— Plur., Plin. 24, 6, 14, § 23; Cael. Aur. Acut. 2, 28, 147.
dyspnoicus.short: dyspnŏĭcus, i, m., = δυσπνοϊκός, one who labors under difficulty of breathing.— Plur., Plin.

dysprophoron.full: dysprŏphŏron, i, n., = δυσπρόφορον, a mispronunciation, Mart. Cap. 5, § 514.
dysprophoron.short: dysprŏphŏron, i, n., = δυσπρόφορον, a mispronunciation, Mart.

dysuria.full: dўsūrĭa, ae, f., = δυσουρία, retention of urine, dysury, Cael. Aur. Tard. 5, 4, 64 (in Cic. Att. 10, 10, 3, written as Greek).— Hence,
dysuria.short: dўsūrĭa, ae, f., = δυσουρία, retention of urine, dysury, Cael.

dysuriacus.full: dўsūrĭăcus, i, m., = δυσουριακός, one who suffers from suppression of urine, Firm, Math. 8.
dysuriacus.short: dўsūrĭăcus, i, m., = δυσουριακός, one who suffers from suppression of urine, Firm, Math.

e.full: E, e, indecl. n. or (sc. littera) fem., a vowel corresponding to both the ε and the η of the Greeks, Ter. Maur. p. 2386 P.; Aus. Idyll. de Litter. Monos. 3 and 4; Mart. Cap. 3, § 235. Its sound varied; short e being sounded sometimes like Engl. e in men (so in pater, inter, etc.), sometimes more nearly like short i, as in Engl. pin (so in famelia, mereto, Menerva, etc.); whence, in the literary language, it passed, in a large class of words, into ĭ (familia, merito, etc.), though retained in the

eadem.full: eādem, adv. abl. f., from idem, sc. viā, operā, or parte. By the same way (rare): ut ventum est in trivium, eadem qua ceteri fugere noluit, Cic. Div. 1, 54, 123: eadem revertens, Liv. 5, 46, 3: eadem et Romanos sequentes impetus rapit, id. 4, 33, 12.— Transf. (Sc. operā, sometimes expressed, Plaut. Capt. 2, 3, 90; id. Bacch. 1, 1, 26; prop., by the same piece of work, i. e.) At the same time, likewise (ante-class.), Plaut. Trin. 2, 4, 180 (cf. Brix. ad loc.) eādem ego ex hoc quae volo exquaesive

eale.full: ĕălē, ēs, f., a large animal found in Ethiopia; acc. to Cuvier, the two-horned rhinoceros, Plin 8, 21, 30, § 73.
eale.short: ĕălē, ēs, f., a large animal found in Ethiopia;

eapropter.full: ĕā-propter (= propter ea), adv., on that account, therefore, Ter. And. 5, 5, 3 Fleck. Pomp. Bon. Com. p. 238 Rib.
eapropter.short: ĕā-propter (= propter ea), adv., on that account, therefore, Ter.

eapse.full: ĕapse, v. ipse init. † ĕărĭnus, a, um, adj., = ἐαρινός, of the color of spring, i. e. green: oves purpureas et earinas, Tert. Hab. mul. 8.

earinus.full: Eărĭnus (-nos), i, = Ἑαρινός, the name of a slave, cited as an example of poet. license, and scanned ēăr-, Mart. 9, 2, 13.
earinus.short: Eărĭnus (-nos), i, = Ἑαρινός, the name of a slave, cited as an example of poet.

eatenus.full: ĕā-tĕnus, adv. is, designates the limit to which an action or condition extends, so far (rare; perh. not before Cic., for in Plaut. Most. 1, 2, 50, the right reading is protenus); followed by quatenus, Cels. 2, 10; Dig. 47, 2, 92: caules lactucae ab imo depurgatos eatenus, qua tenera folia videbuntur, etc., Col. 12, 9, 1; followed by qua, id. 4, 7, 2; id. Arb. 8, 2; Quint. 1, 11, 1.— With quoad: hoc civile, quod vocant, eatenus exercuerunt, quoad populum praestare voluerunt, Cic. Leg. 1, 4, 14;

ebeneus.full: ĕbĕnĕus (hĕb-), a, um, adj. hebenus, q. v., of ebony, ebon (ante-class.), Mart. Capt. 1, § 80.

ebibo.full: ē-bĭbo, bi, bĭtum, 3, v. a., to drink up, drain (not in Cic. or Caes.). Lit.: quid comedent? quid ebibent? Ter. Heaut. 2, 3, 14; so with comedere, Plaut. Trin. 2, 1, 20; id. Ps. 5, 2, 11; hirneam vini, id. Am. 1, 1, 276: poculum, id. Curc. 2, 3, 80: ubera lactantia, Ov. M. 6, 342 et saep.: elephantos dracones, i. e. to suck their blood, Plin. 8, 12, 12, § 34; cf. sanguinem, Plaut. Curc. 1, 2, 65: cum vino simitu imperium, to drink up, forget through drinking, Plaut. Am. 2, 1, 84 (cf. in the simp

ebiscum.full: ĕbiscum, i, n., = hibiscum, q. v. Scribon. 80 and 82.

ebito.full: ēbīto, ĕre, false reading in Plaut. Stich. 4, 2, 28, for bitat, v. Ritschl ad h. l.
ebito.short: ēbīto, ĕre, false reading in Plaut.

eblandior.full: ē-blandĭor, ītus, 4, v. dep. a., to obtain by flattery or coaxing (rare but class.): enitere, elabora vel potius eblandire, effice, ut, etc., Cic. Att. 16, 16 C, § 12; cf. Plin. 9, 8, 8, § 28; Liv. 27, 31: unum consulatus diem, Tac. H. 3, 37: solitudinem ruris, Col. 8, 11, 1.— Of inanimate subjects, to foster, mature by mildness: caelo fecunditatem omnem eblandito, Plin. 16, 27, 51, § 118; cf. Vitr. 7, 5, 5; and somewhat diferently: ut eblandiatur lac igneam saevitiam, i. e. mitigate and drive i

ebora.full: Ebŏra, ae, f. A castle in Spain, perh. the present Ixar, Mel. 3, 1, 8; Cic. Att. 16, 4, 2: ex conjec. Turneb. (Bait. Baream).— A municipium in Lusitania, also called Libertas Julia, now Ebora, Mel. 3, 1, 4; Plin. 4, 22, 35, § 117.

eboracum.full: Eborācum, i, n., the capital of the Brigantes in Britain, now York, Eutr. 8, 19; Inscr. Orell. 190 al.
eboracum.short: Eborācum, i, n., the capital of the Brigantes in Britain, now York, Eutr.

eborarius.full: ĕbŏrārĭus (ebŭr-), ii, m. ebur, a worker in ivory, Cod. Just. 10, 64, 1; Inscr. Orell, 4180; 4302.

eboreus.full: ĕbŏrĕus, a, am, adj. id., made of ivory, ivory: Juppiter, Plin. 36, 5, 4, § 40: mensae, Dig. 33, 7, 12, § 43: oppida, Quint. 6, 3, 61 Spald.

ebriacus.full: ēbrĭācus, a, um, adj. ebrius; cf. merācus, from merus, drunken: homo, Laber. ap. Non. 108, 7 (Rib. Com. v. 10) dub.

ebriamen.full: ēbrĭāmen, ĭnis, n. ebrio, intoxicating liquor, strong drink, Tert. de Jejun. 9.

ebrietas.full: ēbrĭĕtas, ātis, f. ebrius, drunkenness, ebriety (cf.: ebriositas, crapula), * Cic. Tusc. 4, 12; Sen. Ep. 83, 16 sq.; Quint. 1, 11, 2: Plin. 14, 22, 28, § 142: in proelia trudit inermem, * Hor. Ep. 1, 5, 16; Ov. A. A. 1, 597: tumultuosa, Vulg. Prov. 20, 1 al.—Plur., carouses, Sen. Ep. 24, 16; Col. 1 praef. § 16. — Transf., of things: nimio liquore abundat rumpitque se pomi ipsius ebrietas, i. e. excess of juice, Plin. 13, 4, 9, § 45.

ebrio.full: ēbrĭo, āre, 1, v. a. id., to make drunk, to intoxicate (late Lat.). Lit.: mulieres, Macr. S. 7, 6, § 16.— Trop.: animas, Macr. Somn. Scip. 1, 12, 10.

ebriolatus.full: ēbrĭŏlātus, a, um, adj. ebriolus, a little intoxicated, rather tipsy, Laber. ap. Non. 108, 6.

ebriolus.full: ēbrĭŏlus, a, um, adj. dim. [ebrius], a little intoxicated, rather tipsy, perh. only in Plaut. Curc. 2, 3, 15; 1, 3, 36.

ebriositas.full: ēbrĭōsĭtas, ātis, f. ebriosus, addiction to drink, sottishness, Cic. Tusc. 4, 12, 27.

ebriosus.full: ēbrĭōsus, a, um, adj. ebrius, given to drinking, addicted to drunkenness. Prop.: hunc scribunt ebriosum esse, Cic. Fat. 5, 10: plurimum interesse inter ebrium et ebriosum, Sen. Ep. 83, 11.—As subst.: ēbrĭōsus, i, m., a drunkard, sot: exempla ebriosorum, Cic. Ac. 2, 17, 53; Plin. 30, 15, 51, § 145 al.—Comp., Cat. 27, 4.— Transf.: acina, i. e. full of juice, juicy, Cat. 27, 4.

ebrius.full: ēbrĭus, a, um, adj. etym. dub.; perh. root φρήν; cf. sobrius, who has drunk enough, had his fill, corresp. with satur. Prop. (very rare): cum tu satura atque ebria eris, puer ut satur sit facito, Ter. Hec. 5, 2, 3 Ruhnk.; cf. saturitate, Plaut. Capt. 1, 1, 35.—Far more freq. and class., full of drink, drunk, intoxicated (cf. also: potus, ebriosus, temulentus, vinolentus): homo hic ebrius est ... Tu istic, ubi bibisti? Plaut. Am. 2, 1, 25; 1, 1, 116; id. Aul. 4, 10, 19, sq. al.; Cic. Mil. 24, 65;

ebromagus.full: Ebromagus, i, f., a city in the province of Gaul, now Bram, Cic. Font. 5, 9 Halm (Kayser, Cobiamachus, § 19).
ebromagus.short: Ebromagus, i, f., a city in the province of Gaul, now Bram, Cic.

ebulinus.full: ĕbŭlīnus, a, um, adj. ebulum, of elder-wood, Plin. Val. 1, 64.

ebullio.full: ē-bullĭo, īre, 4 (and post-class. ēbullo, āre, 1), v. n. and a. Neutr., to boil up, bubble up (post-class.). Lit.: fontium venae ebullant, Tert. de Pall. 2.— Trop., to come forth bubbling, to appear boisterously: dum risus ebullit App. M. 2, p. 128.—Poet.: o si Ebullit patrui praeclarum funus! i. e. utinam patruus moriatur, Pers. 2, 10 Dübner: priusquam hujus monstri idoli artifices ebullissent, Tert. Idol. 3: de Perside, to hurry confusedly away, Vulg. 2 Mac. 1, 12.— Act. (class., but rare). Li

ebullitio.full: ēbullītĭo, ōnis, f. ebullio, a bubbling up or out: scintillantis olei, Mythogr. Lat. 1, 231 fin.—Plur., Serv. Verg. G. 1, 110.

ebulum.full: ĕbŭlum, i, n., and ĕbŭlus, i, m., Dane-wort, dwarf-elder: Sambucus ebulus, Linn.; Cato R. R. 37, 2; Plin. 26, 11, 73, § 119 sq.; Verg. E. 10, 27; Col. poët. 10, 10 al.
ebulum.short: ĕbŭlum, i, n., and ĕbŭlus, i, m., Dane-wort, dwarf-elder: Sambucus ebulus, Linn.;

ebur.full: ĕbur, ŏris (cf. Quint. 1, 6, 22 sq.), n. Copt. ebu; cf. Sanscr. ibhas, elephant; whence Gr. ἐλέφας, Semit. article el being prefixed, ivory. Prop., Cic. Leg. 2, 18; id. Brut. 73 fin.; id. Par. 1, 3; Quint. 2, 21, 9; Verg. G. 1, 57; id. A. 10, 137; 12, 68; Hor. C. 1, 31, 6; id. Ep. 2, 1, 96 et saep.—Prov.: ebur atramento candefacere, v. atramentum.— Meton. Things made of ivory. So of statues, Verg. G. 1, 480; Ov. M. 15, 792; of the tibia, Verg. G. 2, 193; of a scabbard, Ov. M. 4, 148; of the sell

eburatus.full: ĕbŭrātus, a, um, adj. ebur, adorned or inlaid with ivory: lecti, Plaut. Stich. 2, 2, 53: vehicula, id. Aul. 2, 1, 46: sella, Lampr. Heliog. 4 fin.

eburini.full: Eburīni, ōrum, m., a people of Lucania, Plin. 3, 11, 15, § 98.—Hence, Eburī-nus, a, um, adj.: juga, Sall. H. 3, 67 Dietsch; p. 222 ed. Gerl. min.
eburini.short: Eburīni, ōrum, m., a people of Lucania, Plin.

eburneolus.full: ĕburnĕŏlus, a, um, adj. dim. [eburneus], of ivory: fistula, Cic. de Or. 3, 60, 225 (for which, in Gell. 1, 11, 16, eburnea).

eburneus.full: ĕburnĕus, and (mostly poet.) ĕbur-nus, a, um, adj. ebur, of ivory. eburneus: signum, Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 1; Ov. M. 4, 354: lectus, Suet. Caes. 84: praesepe, id. Calig. 55: quadrigae, id. Ner. 22: tabulae, id. ib. 31 al.; so, tulit eburneos dentes mille, etc., ivory tusks, i. e. elephants' tusks, Liv. 37, 59, 3.— ebur-nus: humerus, Verg. G. 3, 7: pecten, id. A. 6, 647: vagina, id. ib. 9, 305: porta, id. ib. 6, 699; Hor. C. 3, 27, 41: lyra, id. ib. 2, 11, 22: lecti, id. S. 2, 6, 103: currus, Ov. H. 1
eburneus.short: ĕburnĕus, and (mostly poet.) ĕbur-nus, a, um, adj.

eburobrittium.full: Ebŭrŏbrittĭum (-britĭum), i, n., a town of Lusitania, Plin. 4, 21, 35, § 113.
eburobrittium.short: Ebŭrŏbrittĭum (-britĭum), i, n., a town of Lusitania, Plin.

eburones.full: Eburōnes, um, m., a nation of Gallia Belgica, extending from Liege to Aix-laChapelle, Caes. B. G. 2, 4; 4, 6; 5, 24 sq.; 6, 31 sq.; Oros. 6, 7.
eburones.short: Eburōnes, um, m., a nation of Gallia Belgica, extending from Liege to Aix-laChapelle, Caes.

ebusus.full: Ebŭsus or Ebŭsos, i, f., an island of the Mediterranean, on the coast of Spain, now Iviza or Yvica, Liv. 22, 20, 7; Sil. 3, 363; Mela, 2, 7, 21; Plin. 3, 5, 11, § 28; 15, 19, 21, § 82; Manil. 4, 368.—Scanned Ebūsus, Avien. Perieg. 621.—Also called Ebōsīa, ae, f., Stat. S. 1, 6, 15.—Hence, Ebusitā-nus, a, um, adj., of Ebusus, Plin. 3, 5, 11, § 76: humus, Mela, 2, 7, 22.
ebusus.short: Ebŭsus or Ebŭsos, i, f., an island of the Mediterranean, on the coast of Spain, now Iviza or Yvica, Liv.

ecaudis.full: ēcaudis, e, adj. e-cauda, without a tail, only trop.: versus = μείουροι or σκάζοντες, Diom. p. 499 P.

ecbasis.full: ecbăsis, is, f., = ἔκβασις, pure Lat. digressio, a digression, Serv. Verg. G. 1, 209
ecbasis.short: ecbăsis, is, f., = ἔκβασις, pure Lat.

ecbatana.full: Ecbătăna, ōrum, n., = τὰ Ἐκβάτανα (Ecbătăna, ae. f., Lucil. ap. Non. 533, 30; Ecbătănae, ārum, f., App. de Mundo, p. 69, 18), the principal city of Media, now Hamadan, Curt. 4, 5, 8; 5, 8, 1; Plin. 6, 13, 16, § 42; Tac. A. 15, 31 al.
ecbatana.short: Ecbătăna, ōrum, n., = τὰ Ἐκβάτανα (Ecbătăna, ae.

ecbolas.full: ecbŏlas, ădis, f., = ἐκβολάς, a sort of Egyptian grape (so called from its promoting abortion), Plin. 14, 18, 22, § 118.
ecbolas.short: ecbŏlas, ădis, f., = ἐκβολάς, a sort of Egyptian grape (so called from its promoting abortion), Plin.

ecca.full: ecca, eccam, v. ecce, II. D.

ecce.full: ecce, adv. demonstr. [perh. from locat. form of pronom. stem i, with demonstr. ending -ce; hence, in comedy often scanned ĕce, Corss. Aussp. 2, 636, 1026 sq. —Ribbeck explains ecce as indef. form ec, as in ecquis, ecquando, etc., strengthened by demonstr. ce, Lat. Part. p. 42 sq.; and Curt. refers it to root oc- of oculus; cf. eccere, Gr. Etym. p. 457], points out an object with emphasis, lo! see! behold! (constr. class. with nom. or clause, and ante-class. also with acc.). In gen.: quem quaero,

eccentros.full: eccentros, i, adj., = ἔκκεντρος, out of the centre, eccentric: terra, Mart. Cap. 8, § 849 al.
eccentros.short: eccentros, i, adj., = ἔκκεντρος, out of the centre, eccentric: terra, Mart.

eccere.full: eccĕre or ĕcĕre, interj. ecce and abl. of res, see there in fact! lo in truth! Corss. Aussp. 2, 858, 1028; cf. Ribbeck, Partik., p. 43 sq.; not from Ceres, but cf. Ussing ad Plaut. Am. 550, an exclamation of surprise, like Engl. there! (emphatic, only in the foll. passages): Plaut. Am. 2, 1, 4; id. Casin. 2, 6, 34; id. Men. 2, 3, 50; id. Trin. 2, 2, 105; id. Pers. 2, 4, 29; Ter. Ph. 2, 2, 5 (but in Plaut. Mil. 2, 2, 52: ecce autem, Fleck. Lorenz).

eccheuma.full: eccheuma, ătis, n., = ἔκχευμα, a pouring out, Plaut. Poen. 3, 3, 88.
eccheuma.short: eccheuma, ătis, n., = ἔκχευμα, a pouring out, Plaut.

eccillam.full: eccillam, eccillum, eccistam, v. ecce, II. D.

ecclesia.full: ecclēsĭa (ēcclĕsĭa, Sedul. 5, 358; Venant. Carm. 3, 6, 24; and ĕclĕsĭa, Paul. Nol. Carm. 15, 117; 28, 32), ae, f., = ἐκκλησία, an assembly of the (Greek) people. Prop.: et ecclesia consentiente, senate and people, in the free cities of Greece: bule et ecclesia, Plin. et Traj. Ep. 111, 1. — Transf. In eccl. Lat. A religious assembly of Christians, a Christian congregation, a church (eccl. Lat.; very freq.): die ecclesiae, etc., Vulg. Matt. 18, 17; id. Philem. 2; Aug. Ep. 190, 5, 19.— The Church,

ecclesiastes.full: Ecclēsĭastes, ae, m., = ἐκκλησιαστής, the Preacher. Lit.: filius David, i. e. Solomon, Vulg. Eccl. 1, 1.— Transf.: Ecclesiastes, a book of the Old Testament, Tert. Monog. 3; Isid. Orig. 6, 2, 19.
ecclesiastes.short: Ecclēsĭastes, ae, m., = ἐκκλησιαστής, the Preacher.

ecclesiasticus.full: ecclēsĭastĭcus, a, um, adj., = ἐκκλησιαστικός, of or belonging to the Church, ecclesiastical. Adj.: pax, Tert. Pudic. 22. — Subst.: ecclesiasticus, i, m. A church officer, Cod. Th. 1, 3, 22.— The name of the Book of Sirach, Isid. Orig. 6, 2, 31.
ecclesiasticus.short: ecclēsĭastĭcus, a, um, adj., = ἐκκλησιαστικός, of or belonging to the Church, ecclesiastical.

ecclesiecdicus.full: ecclēsĭecdĭcus, i, m., = ἐκκλησιεκδικός, a church proctor, Cod. Th. 1, 5, 34, 5.
ecclesiecdicus.short: ecclēsĭecdĭcus, i, m., = ἐκκλησιεκδικός, a church proctor, Cod.

ecclesiola.full: ecclēsĭŏla, ae, f. dim. ecclesia, a small church, Alcim. Ep. 39, 71 al.

eccum.full: eccum, eccos, v. ecce, II. D.

ecdicus.full: ecdĭcus, i, m., = ἐκδικός, i. q. cognitor or defensor civitatis, a syndic, solicitor of a community (esp. in Asia Minor), Cic. Fam. 13, 56, 1 and 3; Plin. Ep. 10, 111, 1.

ecetra.full: Ecĕtra, ae, f., = Ἐχέτρα, a city of the Volsci, Liv. 4, 61, 4; 6, 31. Its inhabitants are Ecĕtrāni, ōrum, m., = Ἐχέτρανοι, Liv. 2, 25; 3, 4, 2 sq.
ecetra.short: Ecĕtra, ae, f., = Ἐχέτρα, a city of the Volsci, Liv.

echea.full: ēchēa, ōrum, n., = ἠχεῖα, vessels to increase the sound of the actors' voices in a theatre, sounding-vessels, Vitr. 5, 5, 2 (1, 1, 9 written as Greek).
echea.short: ēchēa, ōrum, n., = ἠχεῖα, vessels to increase the sound of the actors' voices in a theatre, sounding-vessels, Vitr.

echecrates.full: Echecrătes, ae, m., = Ἐχεκράτης, a Pythagorean philosopher, a contemporary of Plato, Cic. Fin. 5, 29, 87.
echecrates.short: Echecrătes, ae, m., = Ἐχεκράτης, a Pythagorean philosopher, a contemporary of Plato, Cic.

echeneis.full: ĕchĕnēis, ĭdis, f., = ἐχενηΐς, the sucking-fish, remora, Echeneis remora, Linn.; Plin. 9, 25, 41, § 79; 35, 1, 1, § 2 sq.; Luc. 6, 675; Ov. Hal. 99; Isid. 12, 6, 34.
echeneis.short: ĕchĕnēis, ĭdis, f., = ἐχενηΐς, the sucking-fish, remora, Echeneis remora, Linn.;

echidna.full: ĕchidna, ae, f., = ἔχιδνα, an adder, viper. The Furies were said to have them twined in their hair; hence: stipite te Stygio tumidisque adflavit Echidnis E tribus una soror, Ov. M. 10, 313.— Nom. prop. Lernaea, the Lernaean hydra, killed by Hercules, Ov. M. 9, 69; 158; id. F. 5, 405.— A monster, half woman and half serpent, the mother of Cerberus, Ov. M. 4, 501.—Hence, Echidnēus, a, um, adj., of Echidna: canis, i. e. Cerberus, Ov. M. 7, 408.
echidna.short: ĕchidna, ae, f., = ἔχιδνα, an adder, viper.

echinades.full: Ĕchīnădes, um, f., = Ἐχινάδες, a small group of islands in the Ionian Sea, at the mouth of the Acheloüs, Mel. 2, 7, 10; Plin. 2, 85, 87, § 201; 4, 12, 19, § 53; Ov. M. 8, 589.
echinades.short: Ĕchīnădes, um, f., = Ἐχινάδες, a small group of islands in the Ionian Sea, at the mouth of the Acheloüs, Mel.

echinatus.full: ĕchīnātus, a, um, adj. echinus, a hedge-hog, set with prickles, prickly: calyx, Plin. 15, 23, 25, § 92: capitula echinata spinis, id. 27, 9, 47, § 71: folia, id. 22, 9, 11, § 24.

echinometrae.full: ĕchīnŏmētrae, ārum, m., = ἐχινομῆτραι, a sort of sea-urchin, Plin. 9, 31, 51, § 100.
echinometrae.short: ĕchīnŏmētrae, ārum, m., = ἐχινομῆτραι, a sort of sea-urchin, Plin.

echinophora.full: ĕchīnŏphŏra, ae, f., = ἐχινοφόρα, a sort of concha, Plin. 32, 11, 53, § 147 (Sillig, actinophoroe).
echinophora.short: ĕchīnŏphŏra, ae, f., = ἐχινοφόρα, a sort of concha, Plin.

echinopus.full: ĕchīnŏpūs, ŏdis, m., = ἐχινόπους, a kind of thorn, otherwise unknown, Plin. 11, 8, 8, § 18.
echinopus.short: ĕchīnŏpūs, ŏdis, m., = ἐχινόπους, a kind of thorn, otherwise unknown, Plin.

echinus1.full: ĕchīnus, i, m., = ἐχῖνος, a hedgehog, urchin. Prop., usually the (edible) sea-urchin, Echinus esculentus, Linn.; Varr. L. L. 5, § 77 Müll.; Afran. ap. Non. 216, 11; Plin. 9, 31, 51, § 100 sq.; Hor. Epod. 5, 28; id. S. 2, 4, 33; 2, 8, 52; id. Ep. 1, 15, 23; Petr. 69, 7.—The land-urchin (otherwise called erinaceus), Claud. Idyll. 2, 17; cf. Isid. Orig. 12, 6, 57.— Transf., of things having a similar shape. A copper vessel for the table, perh. to wash out the cups in, a rinsing-bowl, Hor. S. 1, 6,
echinus1.short: ĕchīnus, i, m., = ἐχῖνος, a hedgehog, urchin.

echinus2.full: Ĕchīnus or -os, i, f., = Ἐχῖνος. A city of Phthiotis, in Thessaly, Mel. 2, 3, 6; Plin. 4, 7, 14, § 28; Liv. 32, 33 al.— A city of Acarnania, Plin. 4, 1, 2, § 5.

echion1.full: ĕchĭon, i, n., = ἔχιον, a medicament prepared from the ashes of adders, Plin. 29, 6, 38, § 119.
echion1.short: ĕchĭon, i, n., = ἔχιον, a medicament prepared from the ashes of adders, Plin.

echion2.full: Ĕchīon, ŏnis, m. One of the heroes who sprang up from the dragon's teeth sown by Cadmus; the husband of Agave and father of Pentheus, Ov. M. 3, 126; 10, 686; Stat. Th. 4, 569; Hyg. Fab. 178.—Hence: Echione natus, for Pentheus, Ov. M. 3, 526.— Derivv. Echīŏnĭdes, ae, m., the son of Echion, i. e. Pentheus, Ov. M. 3, 513 and 701.— Echīŏnĭus, a, um, adj., meton. for Cadmean or Theban: hydrus, i. e. killed by Cadmus, Val. Fl. 8, 343: dens, id. 7, 554: aula, id. 7, 301; cf. arces, Ov. Tr. 5, 5, 53: no

echios.full: ĕchĭos, i, f., = ἔχιος, viper's bugloss, a plant which was taken as a remedy for the viper's bite, Plin. 25, 9, 58, § 104.
echios.short: ĕchĭos, i, f., = ἔχιος, viper's bugloss, a plant which was taken as a remedy for the viper's bite, Plin.

echis.full: ĕchis, is, m., a plant, called also pseudoanchusa, and doris, Plin. 22, 20, 24, § 50.
echis.short: ĕchis, is, m., a plant, called also pseudoanchusa, and doris, Plin.

echite.full: echīte, ēs, f., = ἐχίτη, a plant, a kind of clematis, Plin. 24, 15, 89, § 139.
echite.short: echīte, ēs, f., = ἐχίτη, a plant, a kind of clematis, Plin.

echitis.full: ĕchītis, is, m., = ἐχίτης, adder-stone, Plin. 37, 11, 72, § 187.
echitis.short: ĕchītis, is, m., = ἐχίτης, adder-stone, Plin.

echo.full: ēcho, ūs, f., = ἠχώ, repercussion of sound, echo (pure Lat. imago), Plin. 36, 15, 24, § 100; Pers. 1, 102; Aus. Mos. 297; id. Ep. 10, 23; 25, 68; Vulg. Sap. 17, 18.—Personified as a nymph, Ov. M. 3, 358 sq.; Aus. Epigr. 11, 7; 99, 1.
echo.short: ēcho, ūs, f., = ἠχώ, repercussion of sound, echo (pure Lat.

echoicus.full: ēchōĭcus, a, um, adj., = ἠχωϊκός, echoing: elegi, Sid. Ep. 8, 11: metrum, in which one or more final syllables echo or rhyme to a preceding part of the verse, Serv. Centim. p. 1826 P. (cf. Burm. Anthol. Lat. 1, p. 558).
echoicus.short: ēchōĭcus, a, um, adj., = ἠχωϊκός, echoing: elegi, Sid.

ecligma.full: eclīgma, ătis, n., = ἔκλειγμα, a medicine to be taken by letting it melt in the mouth, an electuary, Plin. 21, 21, 89, § 154; 24, 7, 23, § 38; 26, 8, 35, § 110.—Hence, ecligmătĭum, ii, dim. n., Theod. Prisc. 2, 17.
ecligma.short: eclīgma, ătis, n., = ἔκλειγμα, a medicine to be taken by letting it melt in the mouth, an electuary, Plin.

eclipsis.full: eclīpsis, is, f., = ἔκλειψις (a forsaking, being absent): solis, an eclipse of the sun, Auct. Her. 3, 22, 36: lunae, Hyg. Astr. 4, 14; and without gen., Plin. 2, 12, 9, § 53 (pure Lat. defectio and defectus).
eclipsis.short: eclīpsis, is, f., = ἔκλειψις (a forsaking, being absent): solis, an eclipse of the sun, Auct.

eclipticus.full: ecliptĭcus, a, um, adj., = ἐκλειπτικός, belonging to an eclipse: signa, Manil. 4, 816; 846 (cf. Plin. 2, 16, 13, § 68): linea, the ecliptic, Serv. Verg. A. 10, 216.
eclipticus.short: ecliptĭcus, a, um, adj., = ἐκλειπτικός, belonging to an eclipse: signa, Manil.

ecloga.full: eclŏga, ae, f., = ἐκλογή, a selection, consisting of the finest passages, from a written composition. In gen.: eclogas ex Annali descriptas, Varr. ap. Charis. p. 97 P.— In partic., a short poem of any kind, like the poems in the Sylvae of Statius; cf. Stat. S. 3 praef.; 4 praef.; the Idyls of Ausonius; cf. Aus. Idyll. 10 praef.; the Odes of Horace, id. ib. 11 praef., and in many MSS. of Horace; and in the grammarians the Bucolica of Vergil are also called Eclogae, Eclogues; cf. Heyne de Carm. Bu
ecloga.short: eclŏga, ae, f., = ἐκλογή, a selection, consisting of the finest passages, from a written composition.

eclogarius.full: eclŏgārĭus, a, um, adj. ecloga, of or belonging to a selection; only as subst. eclŏgārĭum, i, n., a collection of selected poems, the title of a book of Ausonius, Weber, Corp. Poet. Lat. pp. 1254 sqq.— eclŏgārii, ōrum, m., sc. libri, = eclogae, select passages from a work, Cic. Att. 16, 2 fin. Orell. N. cr.

ecnephias.full: ecnĕphĭas, ae, m., = ἐκνεφίας, a hurricane supposed to be produced by blasts from two opposite clouds, Plin. 2, 48, 49, § 131 (in Sen. Q. N. 5, 12, written as Greek).
ecnephias.short: ecnĕphĭas, ae, m., = ἐκνεφίας, a hurricane supposed to be produced by blasts from two opposite clouds, Plin.

econtra.full: ēcontra = contra, q. v. I. E. 4.

ecphora.full: ecphŏra, ae, f., = ἐκφορά, a projection in buildings (pure Lat. projectura), Vitr. 3, 3, 16; 6, 2, 2.
ecphora.short: ecphŏra, ae, f., = ἐκφορά, a projection in buildings (pure Lat.

ecpyrosis.full: ecpȳrōsis, eos, f., = ἐκπύρωσις, a burning utterly, Nigid. ap. Serv. Verg. Ecl. 4, 10; cf. ib. 6, 41; Censor. 18, 11.
ecpyrosis.short: ecpȳrōsis, eos, f., = ἐκπύρωσις, a burning utterly, Nigid.

ecquando.full: ecquando, adv. interrog. [ec, cf. ecce, and quando], ever, at any time; in a passionate (esp. indignant) interrogation (rare but class.): ecquando te rationem factorum tuorum redditurum putasti? ecquando his de rebus tales viros audituros existimasti? Cic. Verr. 2, 2, 17; 2, 5, 26; Cael. ap. Cic. Fam. 8, 15; Liv. 3, 67; Sen. de Ira, 3, 28; Val. Fl. 2, 395.—With nisi (= num unquam ... nisi), Cic. Fin. 5, 22, 63; id. Agr. 2, 7, 17.— With interrog particle ne suffixed (pleonastic): ecquandone tibi

ecqui1.full: ecqui, ecquae, or ecqua (cf. Zumpt ad Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 11, § 25, and v. aliqui), ecquod (gen. is not in use), pron. interr. adj. [ec, cf. ecce, and qui], Is there any one who? Any? in impassioned interrogation, i. q. num qui, quae (qua) quod. Prop. (with a subst.; class.): ecqui pudor est? ecquae religio, Verres? ecqui metus? Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 8; cf. id. Sest. 52.—In the fem.: ecquae, Plaut. Bacch. 2, 3, 1; id. Stich. 2, 2, 42; Cic. Ac. 2, 26 fin.; id. Att. 8, 12, 4; Ov. H. 16, 341; but: ecqua, P

ecqui2.full: ecqui, adv.; see the foll. art. II. B.

ecquis.full: ecquis, ecquid (abl. ecqui, v. infra, II. B.), pron. interrog. subst., Is there any one who? Any, any one, any body, any thing? in impassioned interrogation, i. q. num quis, quid (class.). Prop.: aperite hoc: heus, ecquis hic est? ecquis hoc aperit ostium? Plaut. Am. 4, 1, 12; so, ecquis, id. Bacch. 4, 1, 9 sq.; id. Most. 4, 2, 19 sq.; id. Capt. 2, 3, 99 et saep.; Ter. Eun. 3, 3, 16 sq.; Liv. 3, 68; Verg. A. 9, 51; Hor. S. 2, 7, 34 al.: ecquid, Plaut. As. 3, 3, 58; id. Curc. 1, 2, 39; Ter. Heaut

ecquo.full: ecquo, adv., v. ecquis, II. C.

ecragino.full: ecrāgīno, āre, 1, v. n., = ἐκραγῆναι, to break forth, Petr. 61, 9.

ecstasis.full: ecstăsis, is, f., = ἔκστασις, a being beside one's self, ecstasy, trance, rapture (eccl. Lat.), Tert. Anim. 45 al.
ecstasis.short: ecstăsis, is, f., = ἔκστασις, a being beside one's self, ecstasy, trance, rapture (eccl.

ectasis.full: ectăsis, is (acc. -in), f., = ἔκτασις, the lengthening of a vowel short by nature: si brevis est per naturam, sed hoc loco ectasin fecit, Serv. Verg. A. 1, 343.

ecthlipsis.full: ecthlipsis, is, f., = ἔκθλιψις, gram. t. t., ecthlipsis, the elision of a final m with its vowel before an initial vowel, Diom. 2, p. 436; Charis. 4, p. 249.

ectomon.full: ectŏmon, i, n., = ἔκτομον, black hellebore, Plin. 25, 5, 21, § 51.
ectomon.short: ectŏmon, i, n., = ἔκτομον, black hellebore, Plin.

ectroma.full: ectrōma, ătis, n., = ἔκτρωμα, an abortion, Tert. adv. Haer. 7.
ectroma.short: ectrōma, ătis, n., = ἔκτρωμα, an abortion, Tert.

ectropa.full: ectrŏpa, ae, f., = ἐκτροπή, i. q. deversorium, an inn, Varr. ap. Non. 393, 1.

ectypus.full: ectўpus, a, um, adj., = ἔκτυπος, engraved in relief, embossed, Plin. 35, 12, 43, § 152; 37, 10, 63, § 173; cf.: imago eminente gemma, Sen. Ben. 3, 26.
ectypus.short: ectўpus, a, um, adj., = ἔκτυπος, engraved in relief, embossed, Plin.

edacitas.full: ĕdācĭtas, ātis, f. edax, voracity, gluttony, Plaut. Pers. 1, 2, 7; Cic. Q. Fr. 3, 9, 9; id. Fam. 7, 26, 1; Ambros. Luc. 7, § 142.

edax.full: ĕdax, ācis, adj. 1. edo; cf. Sanscr. adakas, voracious, gluttonous. Prop., Plaut. Pers. 3, 3, 16; Ter. Eun. prol. 38; id. Heaut. prol. 38; Cic. Fl. 17, 41; id. Fam. 9, 20, 2 (abl. edaci, as in Ov. M. 15, 354; Val. Fl. 6, 420 et saep.); Hor. S. 2, 2, 92; id. Ep. 2, 1, 173; Ov. Tr. 1, 6, 11: vultur, rapacious, id. Am. 2, 6, 33 et saep.—Sup.: edacissima animalia, Sen. Ep. 60, 2.— Poet. transf., of inanimate and abstr. things, devouring, destroying: ignis, Verg. A. 2, 758; Ov. M. 9, 202; id. F. 4, 7

edeatroe.full: edeatroe, qui praesunt regiis epulis, dicti ἀπὸ τῶν ἐδεσμάτων, Paul. ex Fest. p. 82, 20 Müll. [ἐδέατροι, seneschals of the table, carvers, v. Lidd. and Scott s. v.].
edeatroe.short: edeatroe, qui praesunt regiis epulis, dicti ἀπὸ τῶν ἐδεσμάτων, Paul.

edecimo.full: ē-dĕcĭmo (-decumo), no perf., ātum, 1, v. a. (to select the tithes; hence, in gen.), to pick out, select (late Lat.), Symm. Ep. 5, 81; 9, 21; Macr. S. 1, 5; 2, 1; cf.: edecimata (ex-) electa, Paul. ex Fest. p. 80, 6 Müll.

edento.full: ē-dento, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. dens, to render toothless, knock out the teeth (perh. only in the foll. passages): malas alicui, Plaut. Rud. 3, 2, 48: edentatae beluae morsus, Macr. S. 7, 3.

edentulus.full: ē-dentŭlus, a, um, adj. id., toothless. Prop. (ante- and post-class.): vetulae, Plaut. Most. 1, 3, 118; cf. id. Cas. 3, 2, 20; id. Men. 5, 2, 111; Prud. στεφ. 10, 305: bestia muraena, Tert. Pall. 5.—* Transf., of wine ripened by age, Plaut. Poen. 3, 3, 87.

edera.full: ĕdĕra, ae, and its derivatives, v. hed-.
edera.short: ĕdĕra, ae, and its derivatives, v.

edessa.full: Ĕdessa, ae, f., = Ἔδεσσα. A city of Macedonia, the burial-place of the kings, Liv. 45, 29; Just. 7, 1, 7.—Hence, Edes-saeus, a, um, adj., of Edessa: Antiphilus (dux), Liv. 42, 51.— A city of Mesopotamia, in the province of Osrhoëne, now Rhoa or Orfa, Plin. 5, 24, 21, § 86; Tac. A. 12, 12; Amm. 20, 11, 4; 21, 7, 7; and where Caracalla died, Aur. Vict. Epit. 21; Eutr. 8, 11. —Hence, Edessēnus, a, um, adj., of Edessa: sepulcra, Amm. 18, 7.

edibilis.full: ĕdĭbĭlis, e, adj. 1. edo, eatable, that may be taken as food: potio, Cassiod. Var. 12, 4.

edico.full: ē-dīco, xi, ctum, 3 (old form, subj.: EXDEICATIS; gerund.: EXDEICENDUM, S. C. de Bacchan.; imperat.: edice, Verg. A. 11, 463; Stat. Th. 12, 598), v. a. A t. t. of magistrates, to declare, publish, make known a decree, ordinance, etc.; hence, to establish, decree, ordain by proclamation (cf.: praecipio, mando, jubeo). In gen., with ut or ne: consulem edicere, ut senatus senatusconsulto ne obtemperet ... edicere est ausus, ut senatus ad vestitum rediret, Cic. Pis. 8; so id. Vatin. 14; id. Q. Fr. 1
edico.short: ē-dīco, xi, ctum, 3 (old form, subj.: EXDEICATIS;

edictalis.full: ēdictālis, e, adj. edictum, by edict, according to edict (late Lat.): possessio bonorum, Dig. 38, 6, 1, § 4: programma, i. e. the imperial edict, Cassiod. Var. 1, 31; 2, 24.

edictio.full: ēdictĭo, ōnis, f. edico, an order, edict, for the usual edictum; only Plaut. Capt. 4, 2, 31; 43; id. Ps. 1, 2, 10; 39.

edicto.full: ēdicto, āvi, 1, v. freq. a. id., to speak out, proclaim, publish (only in Plaut.): tute edictas facta tua, Plaut. Am. 2, 2, 184: aliquid alicui, id. Ep. 1, 2, 2; id. Men. 4, 2, 79.

edictum.full: ēdictum, i, n. id.. A proclamation, ordinance, edict, manifesto of the Roman magistrates (cf.: senatus consultum, scitum, jussum; decretum, epistola, rescriptum), e. g. of the ediles, Cic. Phil. 9, 7 fin.; id. Off. 3, 17, 71; Gell. 4, 2; Dig. 21, 1; of a tribune of the people, Cic. de Imp. Pomp. 19 fin.; of a dictator, Liv. 8, 34; of the consuls, id. 8, 7; 24, 8; of the proconsuls, id. 26, 12; of Caesar in the civil war, Caes. B. C. 2, 19; of the emperor, Just. Inst. 1, 2, 6; Vulg. Luc. 2, 1 (cf

edisco.full: ē-disco, dĭdĭci, 3, v. a., to learn by heart, commit to memory (class.). Prop.: ut non legantur modo (poetae) sed etiam ediscantur, Cic. Tusc. 2, 11, 27; cf.: haec discenda, imo ediscenda sunt, Sen. Ep. 123 fin.: Demosthenem in primis legendum vel ediscendum potius putem, Quint. 10, 1, 105: ad verbum ediscendus libellus, Cic. Ac. 2, 44, 135; id. de Or. 1, 34, 157: ad verbum, Quint. 11, 2, 44: Lepta ediscat Hesiodum et habeat in ore Τῆς δʼ ἀρετῆς ἱδρῶτα, Cic. Fam. 6, 18 fin.: magnum numerum versu

edissero.full: ē-dissĕro, rŭi, rtum, 3, v. a., to analyze in words, to set forth, unfold, explain, relate, tell (rare but class.): jam animum advorte ac mihi quae dicam edissere, Plaut. Capt. 5, 2, 14; cf.: neque necesse est edisseri a nobis quae finis funestae familiae, Cic. Leg. 2, 22; and: cum agi, non quemadmodum agantur, edisseri oportet, Liv. 44, 41: Laelius eadem edisseruit (for which, shortly before, exposuit), id. 27, 7: res gestas, id. 34, 52: cunctandi utilitates, Tac. H. 3, 52: viam gerendi belli,

edissertator.full: ēdissertātor, ōris, m. edisserto, an explainer: harum rerum, Aus. Sapient. prol. fin.

edissertio.full: ēdissertĭo, ōnis, f. edissero, an analysis, exposition: Scripturarum, Hier. in Matt. 21.

edisserto.full: ē-disserto, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a., to analyze, set forth, explain, relate (rare, and mostly ante- and post-class.; not in Cic. or Caes.): ordine omne uti quidque actum'st, Edissertavit, Plaut. Am. 2, 1, 53; id. Cas. 5, 2, 36; id. Stich. 2, 1, 30; Arn. 1, p. 34; Tert. Res Carn. 33: neque aggrediar narrare, quae edissertando minora vero fecero, * Liv. 22, 54, 8.

editicius.full: ēdĭtīcĭus or -tĭus, a, um, adj. 2. edo, II. C. 2., set forth, announced, proposed; only in the connection, judices, the judges in the causa sodaliciorum chosen by the plaintiff, Cic. Planc. 15, 36; 17, 41; id. Mur. 23, 47.

editio.full: ēdĭtĭo, ōnis, f. 2. edo, II.. Prop. A bringing forth, a birth (late Lat.), Dig. 50, 2, 2, § 6; Tert. adv. Jud. 1.— A putting forth, publishing of a work (postAug.), Sen. Ben. 4, 28; Quint. Ep. ad Tryph. § 2; prooem. § 7; Plin. Ep. 1, 2, 5; 2, 10, 6; 3, 15, 1 et saep.— Concr., like our edition = ἔκδοσις, qui versus in omni editione invenitur, Quint. 5, 11, 40; 12, 10, 55. — Trop. A statement, representation. In gen.: in tam discrepante editione, Liv. 4, 23.— Jurid. t. t., a declaration, designati

editor.full: ēdĭtor, ōris, m. id.. * That which brings forth or produces: nocturnae aurae (Volturnus), Luc. 2, 423.— (Acc. to 2. edo, II. D.), an exhibitor (late Lat.): ludorum, Vop. Carin. 21; Capitol. Anton. Phil. 23; Inscr. Orell. 3762.

editum.full: ēdĭtum, i, n., v. 2. edo fin.

editus1.full: ēdĭtus, a, um, Part. and P. a., from 2. edo.

editus2.full: ēdĭtus, ūs, m. 2. edo, a voiding, excrement: boum, Dig. 32, 1, 55, § 6.

edo1.full: ĕdo, ēdi, ēsum, 3 (sup.: esum, Plaut. Curc. 2, 1, 13; id. Men. 3, 1, 11; id. Stich. 1, 3, 28: esu, id. Ps. 3, 2, 35.—The contr. forms es, est, estis, etc., are very freq. in prose and poetry: est, Verg. A. 4, 66; 5, 683; Hor. S. 2, 2, 57: esset, id. ib. 2, 6, 89; Verg. G. 1, 151: esse, Quint. 11, 3, 136; Juv. 15, 102: esto, Cato R. R. 156, 1.—Hence, also in the pass.: estur, Plaut. Most. 1, 3, 78; id. Poen. 4, 2, 13; Cels. 27, 3; Ov. Pont. 1, 1, 69; and: essetur, Varr. L. L. 5, § 106 Müll.—Archa

edo2.full: ē-do, dĭdi, dĭtum, 3, v. a., to give out, put forth, bring forth (freq. and class.). In gen.: foras per os est editus aër, Lucr. 3, 122; cf.: sputa per fauces tussi, id. 6, 1189: urinam, Plin. 28, 4, 7, § 38; cf. stercus, Col. 2, 14: animam, to breathe out, i. e. to die, expire, Cic. Sest. 38, 83; Ov. H. 9, 62; cf.: extremum vitae spiritum, Cic. Phil. 12, 9: vitam, id. Fin. 5, 2, 4; id. Planc. 37, 90: clamorem, to send forth, utter, id. Div. 2, 23; cf.: miros risus, id. Q. Fr. 2, 10, 2: fremitum

edo3.full: ĕdo, ōnis, m. 1. edo, a glutton, Varr. ap. Non. 48, 19.

edoceo.full: ē-dŏcĕo, cŭi, ctum, 2, v. a., to teach thoroughly; to instruct, inform, apprise one of any thing (class.; for syn. cf.: doceo, perdoceo, erudio, praecipio, instituo). —With acc. pers. and rei: eadem haec intus edocebo, quae ego scio, Stratippoclem, Plaut. Ep. 5, 1, 56; so id. Trin. 2, 2, 91; Sall. C. 16, 1; Liv. 1, 20; Plin. Pan. 26 al.; cf. in the pass.: Cicero per legatos cuncta edoctus, Sall. C. 45, 1; Liv. 25, 40; Tac. A. 13, 47; Luc. 1, 587; and with acc. pers. and inf.: Etruscam Edocuit ge

edolo.full: ē-dŏlo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a., to cut or hew out, to prepare by hewing. * Lit.: lingulas, Col. 8, 11, 4.— Trop., to work out, prepare, finish (rare): libellum, Varr. ap. Non. 448, 17: quod jusseras edolavi, Enn. ap. Cic. Att. 13, 47, 1 (cf. Rib. Trag. Fragm. p. 237): puerum, Varr. ap. Non. 392, 30.

edom.full: Edom, indecl. m. Esau, elder son of the patriarch Isaac: Esau, ipse est Edom, Vulg. Gen. 36, 1 al.; Isid. Orig. 7, 6, 33.— A nation descended from Esau, Vulg. Num. 20, 14; id. 4 Reg. 3, 26 et saep. — Transf., the country of the Edomites, Vulg. Num. 21, 4 et saep.

edomino.full: Ē-dŏmĭno, āvi, 1, v. a., to control absolutely; pass., Arn. 5, no. 11 init.

edomito.full: ē-dŏmĭto, āre, v. freq. a., to tame completely, thoroughly, Ven. Carm. 9, 1, 143.

edomo.full: ē-dŏmo, ŭi, ĭtum, 1, v. a., to tame completely, conquer, overcome, vanquish, subdue (rare; mostly poet. and in postAug. prose). Prop.: (Roma) edomito sustulit orbe caput, Ov. F. 4, 256; cf. id. A. A. 3, 114.— Transf.: pastinaca edomita, opp. agrestis, Col. 9, 4, 5: aes igni, to melt, Plin. 33, 3, 20, § 65: ramum oleae curvando, id. 17, 19, 30, § 137: vitiosam naturam ab eo sic edomitam et compressam esse doctrina, ut, etc., * Cic. Fat. 5, 10 (al. domitam): feritatem, Col. 11, 3, 37; Lact. 4, 25,

edoni.full: Ēdōni, ōrum, m., = Ἠδωνοί, a people of Thrace, east of the Strymon, Plin. 4, 11, 18, § 40; celebrated as worshippers of Bacchus, Hor. C. 2, 7, 27, v. Bacchus.—Derivv., ēdōnus, a, um, adj., Edonic. Edoni populi = Edoni, Sol. 9, § 1.— Esp., poet. for Thracian: Boreae, Verg. A. 12, 365; cf. venti, Val. Fl. 6, 340: hiemes, Stat. Th. 5, 78: juga, Ov. Tr. 4, 1, 42: currus, Stat. Th. 12, 733: Bacchus, Ov. R. Am. 593.— As subst.: ēdōnus, i, m., = Ἠδωνός, a spur of the Pangaeus range, in southeastern Thr
edoni.short: Ēdōni, ōrum, m., = Ἠδωνοί, a people of Thrace, east of the Strymon, Plin.

edor.full: edor = ador, Paul. ex Fest. p. 10 Müll., v. ador.

edormio.full: ē-dormĭo, īvi or ii, 4, v. n. and a., to sleep out, sleep away; to sleep off (rare, but class.; usually of persons who are intoxicated). Neutr. absol.: cumque (vinolenti) edormiverunt, etc., Cic. Ac. 2, 17, 52. — Act., with acc.: edormi crapulam et exhala, Cic. Phil. 2, 12 fin.: nocturnum vinum, Gell. 6, 10 fin.—Poet.: Fufius ebrius olim Cum Ilionam edormit, i. e. sleeps through the part of the sleeping Iliona, * Hor. S. 2, 3, 61: dimidium ex hoc (tempore) edormitur, is slept away, Sen. Ep. 99.

edormisco.full: ēdormisco, ĕre, v. inch. a. [edormio], to sleep out, to sleep off a debauch (perh. only in the foll. passages): crapulam, Plaut. Rud. 2, 7, 28: hoc villi, Ter. Ad. 5, 2, 11: unum somnum, Plaut. Am. 2, 2, 65.

educatio.full: ēdŭcātĭo, ōnis, f. 2. edŭco, a breeding, rearing, training, bringing up, education (good prose). Of men, Cic. de Or. 3, 31, 124; id. Leg. 3, 13; Quint. 1, 1, 21; 1, 2, 6; Tac. A. 3, 52; id. G. 20 et saep.— Transf. Of animals, Cic. Fin. 3, 19; id. Rosc. Am. 22 fin.; Col. 7, 12, 11; 8, 11, 1.— Of plants, Plin. 16, 25, 39, § 94; Macr. S. 1, 7.

educator.full: ēdŭcātor, ōris, m. id., a rearer, bringer - up (rare, but good prose). Prop., of a foster-father, Cic. Planc. 33, 81; Quint. 7, 1, 14; cf. Cic. N. D. 2, 34.— Transf., of tutors, pedagogues, Tac. A. 11, 1; 12, 41; 14, 3; Dig. 40, 2, 13 et saep.

educatrix.full: ēdŭcātrix, īcis, f. educator. She who brings up, a nurse, Col. 8, 11, 14; Inscr. Don. 14, no. 39.— Transf.: earum (rerum) parens est educatrixque sapientia, Cic. Leg. 1, 24, 62.

educatus.full: ēdŭcātus, ūs, m. 2. edŭco, bringing up, Tert. Res Carn. 60.

educo1.full: ē-dūco, xi, ctum, 3 (imper., educe, Plaut. Pers. 4, 1, 11; id. Stich. 5, 6, 1: educ, Cic. Cat. 1, 5, 10; Alcim. 5, 248 al.—Inf. pass. parag., educier, Plaut. Truc. 5, 16), v. a., to lead forth, draw out, bring away (very freq. and class.). In gen.: novam nuptam foras, Plaut. Cas. 4, 3, 1; so with personal objects, fidicinam, id. Ep. 3, 4, 36 (opp. introducere): eram, id. Mil. 4, 6, 53: virginem, id. Pers. 4, 1, 11; Cic. Q. Fr. 3, 3 fin. al.; cf. also: populum e comitio, Varr. R. R. 1, 2, 9: muli

educo2.full: ēdŭco, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. 1. educo, II. A. 4. b., to bring up a child physically or mentally, to rear, to educate (very freq. and class.): educit obstetrix, educat nutrix, instituit paedagogus, docet magister, Varr. ap. Non. 447, 33 (but this distinction is not strictly observed; see the foll. and 1. educo, II. A. 4. b.). Prop.: hera educavit (puellam) magna industria, Plaut. Cas. prol. 44 sq.: Athenis natus altusque educatusque Atticis, id. Rud. 3, 4, 36: bene pudiceque educatu'st usque ad ado

eductio.full: ēductĭo, ōnis, f. 1. educo, a moving out, removal, emigration (ante- and postclass.): e castris, Cato ap. Fest. s. v. PROPERAM, p. 253, 33 Müll.: in qua eductione, Lact. 4, 10, 6.— A stretching forth, formation: si unius uberis eductione pendebunt (sc. apum agmina), Pall. 7, 7, 6.

eductor.full: ēductor, ōris, m. 1. educo, II. A. 4. b., a bringer-up, tutor (for the usual educator), Fronto Ep. ad Amic. 15.

edulco.full: ē-dulco, āre, v. a., to sweeten: vitam, Matius ap. Gell. 15, 25, 2, and ap. Non. 106, 25.

edulia.full: Ĕdūlĭa and Ĕdūlĭca, ae, v. Edusa.

edulis.full: ĕdūlis, e, adj. 1. edo, eatable (rare). Adj.: capreae, Hor. S. 2, 4, 43.— Subst., in the plur., edulia, ium, n., eatables, food (for syn. cf.: alimenta, cibus, cibaria, esca, penus, victus, opsonium, pulmentum, etc.), Afran. ap. Non. 28, 30; Varr. ap. Non. 108, 22; Suet. Calig. 40 Oud. N. cr.; Dig. 1, 16, 6 fin.; Gell. 7, 16, 4; 17, 11 fin.; cf. Varr. L. L. 6, § 84 Müll.—In the postclass. per., heterocl., gen. eduliorum, App. M. 5, p. 160; dat. eduliis, Gell. 19, 9, 3; nom. sing. edulium, Fulg.

edulium.full: ĕdūlĭum, ii, n., v. the preced. fin.

eduresco.full: ē-dūresco, ĕre, v. inch. n., to grow hard, Cael. Aur. Acut. 2, 34, 182.

eduro.full: ē-dūro, āre, 1, v. n. and a. Neut., to last out, continue, endure (post-Aug. and very rare): solis fulgor in ortus edurat, Tac. G. 45: ulla effigies litterarum, Gell. 14, 1, 18.— Act., to harden, Col. 11, 1, 7.

edurus.full: ē-dūrus, a, um, adj., exceedingly hard, very hard (very rare): pirus, Verg. G. 4, 145. —Trop., harsh, cruel: eduro ore negare, Ov. A. A. 3, 476.
edurus.short: ē-dūrus, a, um, adj., exceedingly hard, very hard (very rare): pirus, Verg.

edusa.full: Ĕdūsa, ae, f. 1. edo, the goddess that presides over children's food, Varr. ap. Non. 108, 22; August. Civ. D. 4, 34; called also ĕdūlĭa, ae, f., Don. Ter. Ph. 1, 1, 15; ĕdūlĭca, ae, f., August. Civ. D. 4, 11; and ĕdūla, ae, f., Tert. ad Nat. 2, 11.

eetion.full: Ēĕtĭon, ōnis, m., = Ἠετίων, the father of Andromache, and king of Thebe, in Cilicia, Ov. Tr. 5, 5, 44; id. F. 4, 280.—Hence, ēĕtĭōnēus, a, um, pertaining to Eëtion: Thebae, Ov. M. 12, 110.
eetion.short: Ēĕtĭon, ōnis, m., = Ἠετίων, the father of Andromache, and king of Thebe, in Cilicia, Ov.

effabilis.full: effābĭlis, e, adj. effor, that may be uttered, utterable (post-class.): nemini effabilis, App. Mag. p. 315, 41.

effaecatus.full: ef-faecātus, a, um, adj. ex-faex, purified from the dregs, refined; trop.: voluptas animi (with purgata), App. Dogm. Plat. 2, pp. 22, 37.

effafilatum.full: effafilatum, exertum, quod scilicet omnes exerto brachio sint exfilati, id est extra vestimentum filo contextum, Paul. ex Fest. p. 83, 6, v. Müll. ad h. l.
effafilatum.short: effafilatum, exertum, quod scilicet omnes exerto brachio sint exfilati, id est extra vestimentum filo contextum, Paul.

effamen.full: effāmen, ĭnis, n. effor, an enunciation, proposition, Mart. Cap. 4, § 327.

effarcio.full: ef-farcĭo and -fercio (ec-f-), no perf., fertus, 4, v. a., to stuff, cram, fill out (very rare): intervalla grandibus saxis, * Caes. B. G. 7, 23, 2: bibite, este, ecfercite vos, Plaut. Most. 1, 1, 62.—Hence, effer-tus, a, um, P. a., filled out, full, ample: fame effertus, Plaut. Capt. 3, 1, 6: hereditas effertissima, id. ib. 4, 1, 8; cf. id. As. 2, 2, 16.
effarcio.short: ef-farcĭo and -fercio (ec-f-), no perf., fertus, 4, v.

effascinatio.full: effascĭnātĭo, ōnis, f. effascino, a bewitching, charming; in the plur., Plin. 19, 4, 19, § 50; 37, 10, 54, § 145.

effascino.full: ef-fascĭno, āre, v. a., to bewitch, charm, fascinate, Plin. 7, 2, 2, § 16; Gell. 9, 4, 7.

effatio.full: effātĭo, ōnis, f. effor, a speaking, acc. to Serv. Verg. A. 3, 463.

effatum.full: effātum, i, n., v. effor fin.

effatus.full: effātus, ūs, m. effor, a speaking (postclass.), Tert. Anim. 6.

effecte.full: effecte, adv., in fact, really; effectually, v. efficio, P. a., 2. fin.

effectio.full: effectĭo, ōnis, f. efficio (only in the philos. lang. of Cicero). A doing, performing, effecting, practising: artis, Cic. Fin. 3, 7, 24: recta (a transl. of κατόρθωσις), id. ib. 3, 14, 45.—* I. q. causa efficiens, the producing or efficient cause, Cic. Ac. 1, 2, 6.

effectivus.full: effectīvus, a, um, adj. id., effective, productive: causa, velut pater filii, Boëth. in Porphyr. 2, p. 58 al.—Esp. as, subst.: effectīva, ae, f. (sc. ars), practical art, productive art: sed effectivae quoque aliquid simile scriptis orationibus consequetur, Quint. 2, 18, 5.

effector.full: effector, ōris, m. id., an effecter, producer, author (a Ciceronian word), Cic. Univ. 5 fin.; id. Div. 2, 26; id. de Or. 1, 33, 150 (quoted in Quint. 10, 3, 1; for which, perfector, Cic. de Or. 1, 60 fin.).

effectorius.full: effectōrĭus, a, um, adj. effector, effectual, resistless: vis, August. Immort. Anim. 14; 15; id. Gen. ad Lit. Op. Imp. 4, 16.

effectrix.full: effectrix, īcis, f. id., she who effects, produces, causes; perh. only Cic. Fin. 2, 17, 55; id. Univ. 10, 32.

effectus1.full: effectus, a, um, Part. and P. a., from efficio.

effectus2.full: effectus, ūs, m. efficio, a doing, effecting. In gen., execution, accomplishment, performance: ad effectum consiliorum pervenire, Planc. ap. Cic. Fam. 10, 8, 4: operis, Liv. 21, 7: ad effectum aliquid adducere, id. 33, 33, 8; cf. spei, id. 21, 57; Prop. 3, 9, 27 (4, 8, 27 M.): ut peccatum est, patriam prodere, etc., quae sunt in effectu: sic timere, etc., peccatum est, etiam sine effectu, Cic. Fin. 3, 9, 32: effectum consilii morata tempestas est, Curt. 8, 13, 22; cf.: cum opera (sc. oppugnation

effecundo.full: ef-fēcundo (effoec-), āre, 1, v. a., to make fruitful, to fertilize, Vop. Prob. 21.

effeminate.full: effēmĭnāte, adv., v. effemino, P. a. fin.

effeminatio.full: effēmĭnātĭo, ōnis, f. effemino, effeminacy (late Lat.): corporis, Firm. Math. 7, 16: animi, Hier. in Isa. 14, 52, 2.

effeminatus.full: effēmĭnātus, a, um, Part. and P. a., from effemino.

effemino.full: ef-fēmĭno, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. femina, to make feminine. * Lit.: effeminarunt eum (sc. aërem) Junonique tribuerunt, Cic. N. D. 2, 26, 66.— Trop., to make womanish, effeminate, to enervate: fortitudinis praecepta sunt, quae effeminari virum vetant in dolore, Cic. Fin. 2, 29, 94: corpus animumque virilem, * Sall. C. 11, 3: animos, Caes. B. G. 1, 1, 3: homines (with remollescere), id. ib. 4, 2 fin.; cf.: cogitationibus mollissimis effeminamur, Cic. Tusc. 1, 40: vultus, id. Or. in Clod. Fragm. 5, p.

efferasco.full: effĕrasco, ĕre, v. inch. n. [2. effero], to become savage, fierce, Amm. 18, 7, 5.

efferate.full: effĕrāte, adv., v. 2. effero, P. a. fin.

efferatio.full: effĕrātĭo, ōnis, f. effero, a making savage, Hier. Ep. 107, 2.

efferatus.full: effĕrātus, a, um, Part. and P. a., from 2. effero.

efferitas.full: effĕrĭtas (ecf-), ātis, f. efferus, an excessively wild state, wildness, degeneracy (opp. mansuetudo), Cic. Sest. 42, 91: quas (terras) peragrans undique omnem ecferitatem expuli, id. Tusc. Poet. 2, 8, 20 fin. (al. feritatem); Lact. Mort. Pers. 9, 2.

effero1.full: ef-fĕro or ecfĕro (cf. Neue, Formenl. 2, 766), extŭli, ēlatum, efferre or ecferre, v. a., to bring or carry out, to bring forth (very freq. and class.). Lit. In gen.: ex navi, Plaut. Am. 2, 1, 82; cf. tela, etc., ex aedibus Cethegi, Cic. Cat. 3, 3 fin.: argentum jubeo jam intus efferri foras, Plaut. Bacch. 1, 1, 62; cf. id. ib. 4, 9, 127; id. Most. 2, 1, 58; id. Mil. 4, 8, 4: argentum ad aliquem, id. Epid. 5, 1, 27; id. Truc. 3, 1, 16: machaeram huc, id. Mil. 2, 5, 53; cf. id. Stich. 2, 2, 28: p

effero2.full: ef-fĕro, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. ex-ferus, to make wild, savage, fierce (class.; most freq. since the Aug. per.). Physically: terram immanitate beluarum efferari, Cic. N. D. 2, 39, 99: speciem oris, Liv. 2, 23; cf. vultum, Suet. Calig. 50: efferantia sese ulcera, becoming aggravated, malignant, Plin. 26, 14, 87, § 146.—Poet.: Mars efferat aurum, i. e. works up into weapons, Stat. Achill. 1, 425; cf.: homo qui magnae artis subtilitate tantum efferavit argentum, i. e. wrought into the figures of beast

effertus.full: effertus, a, um, Part. and P. a., from effarcio.

efferus.full: ef-fĕrus, a, um, adj., very wild, fierce, savage (poet. and post-class.; freq. in Verg.): proles, Lucr. 2, 604; cf. juventus, Verg. A. 8, 6: Dido, id. ib. 4, 642: Chimaera, id. ib. 7, 787: mens Caci, id. ib. 8, 205; cf.: vis animi, id. ib. 10, 898: corda, Val. Fl. 1, 798: ira, id. 5, 517: virtus Bebrycis, id. 2, 648: facta tyranni, Verg. A. 8, 484: facinus, Sen. Phoen. 264; Flor. 4, 12, 12; 4, 12, 48; Sen. Element. 1, 13, 4.
efferus.short: ef-fĕrus, a, um, adj., very wild, fierce, savage (poet.

effervens.full: effervens, entis, Part. and P. a., from effervo.

effervesco.full: ef-fervesco, ferbui (so Cic. Cael. 31, 77 al.; ante- and post-class. fervi, Cato R. R. 115, 1; Tac. A. 1, 74), 3, v. inch. n. To boil up or over, to foam up, to effervesce, ferment, to grow violent, rage (class.). Lit.: dictum fretum a similitudine ferventis aquae, quod in fretum saepe concurrat aestus atque effervescat, Varr. L. L. 7, § 22 Müll.; cf.: aquae, quae effervescunt subditis ignibus, Cic. N. D. 2, 10, 27: ubi satis efferverit (vinum mustum), Cato R. R. 115, 1; cf. Col. 12, 25, 4: effe

effervo.full: ef-fervo, ĕre (praes. effervent, Vitr. 2, 6, 5), v. n., to boil up or over (poet. and in post-Aug. prose): in agros Aetna, Verg. G. 1, 471: quatenus in pullos animales vortier ova Cernimus alituum vermesque effervere, qs. to come boiling forth, i. e. to swarm forth, Lucr. 2, 928; cf. Verg. G. 4, 556; id. Dir. 15; Stat. Th. 4, 664.—Hence, effer-vens, entis, P. a., boiling with passion, i. e. fervent, ardent: siquidem laetitia dicitur exsultatio quaedam animi gaudio efferventior eventu rerum expet

effeto.full: effēto (effecto), āre, to put out of use, to abolish, Cassiod. Var. 9, 15 ante med.
effeto.short: effēto (effecto), āre, to put out of use, to abolish, Cassiod.

effetus.full: ef-fētus (not effoetus), a, um, adj., that has brought forth young, that has laid eggs (mostly poet. and in post-Aug. prose). Lit. (mostly in Col.): cum effetae loca genitalia tumebunt, Col. 7, 7, 4; 7, 12, 11; 9, 1, 7.—Poet.: simul effetas linquunt examina ceras, Luc. 9, 285.— Meton. (causa pro effectu). Exhausted, worn out by bearing: aliquae (gallinae) in tantum, ut effetae moriantur, Plin. 10, 53, 74, § 146; cf. Sall. C. 53, 5.— Transf., in gen., exhausted, worn out: tellus, * Lucr. 2, 1150;
effetus.short: ef-fētus (not effoetus), a, um, adj., that has brought forth young, that has laid eggs (mostly poet.

efficacia.full: effĭcācĭa, ae, f. efficax, efficacy, efficiency, virtue (post-Aug.), Plin. 11, 5, 4, § 12; Amm. 14, 8, 5; 16, 12, 25; Vulg. Sirach, 9, 4; Lact. de Ira D. 10, 37.

efficacitas.full: effĭcācĭtas, ātis, f. id., efficacy, efficiency, power; perh. only Cic. Tusc. 4, 13, 31; Q. Cic. Petit. Cons. 3, 10.

efficaciter.full: effĭcācĭter, adv., efficaciously, effectually, v. efficax fin.

efficax.full: effĭcax, ācis, adj. efficio, efficacious, effectual, powerful, efficient (mostly postAug.; not in Cic. and Caes; but cf. efficacitas): nosti Marcellum, quam tardus et parum efficax sit, Cael. ap. Cic. Fam. 8, 10, 3; cf.: ultor contemptae religionis, Val. Max. 1, 1, 19: Hercules, Hor. Epod. 3, 17: scientia (magica), id. ib. 17, 1: preces, Liv. 9, 20: studium promerendi amoris, Suet. Calig. 3 init.: breve et efficax iter est per exempla, Sen. Ep. 6, 5: admonitiones, id. ib. 8, 2 al.: herba in dolo

efficiens.full: effĭcĭens, entis, Part. and P. a., from efficio.

efficienter.full: effĭcĭenter, adv., efficiently, v. efficio, P. a. 1.

efficientia.full: effĭcĭentĭa, ae, f. efficio, efficient power, efficiency, influence (rare; mostly in philos. lang.), Cic. N. D. 2, 37, 95; id. Fat. 9, 19: spiritalis, Hil. in Psa. 131, 24: inenarrabilis, id. Trin. 3, 18; Lact. Opif. D. 19, 7.

efficio.full: ef-fĭcĭo (ecfacio), fēci, fectum, 3 (perf. subj. effexis, Plaut. As. 3, 5, 63; id. Poen. 1, 3, 19; inf. pass. ecfiĕri, id. Pers. 5, 1, 9; Lucr. 6, 761), v. a., to make out, work out; hence, to bring to pass, to effect, execute, complete, accomplish, make, form (very freq. in all periods and sorts of writing). In gen. With acc.: male quod mulier facere incepit, nisi id ecficere perpetrat, Plaut. Truc. 2, 5, 12 sq.; cf. id. Pers. 5, 1, 9; Caes. B. C. 1, 36 fin.; 1, 61, 2: magna facinora, Plaut. Ps

effictio.full: effictĭo, ōnis, f. effingo, rhet. t. t., a representing, portraying of corporeal peculiarities, Auct. Her. 4, 49, 63.

effictus.full: effictus, a, um, Part., from effingo.
effictus.short: effictus, a, um, Part., from effingo.

effigia.full: effĭgĭa, ae, f., v. effigies init.

effigiatus.full: effĭgĭātus, ūs, m. effigio, a representing, portraying, App. Flor. 15, p. 350, 36.

effigientia.full: effĭgĭentĭa, ae, f. effingo, the creating, fashioning.—Transf. = the Creator, Mart. Cap. 9, § 922.

effigies.full: effĭgĭes, ēi (ante-class. form nom.: effĭgĭa, Plaut. Rud. 2, 4, 7; Afran. ap. Non. 493, 2; Inscr. Orell. 7416 λ.—Nom. plur.: effigiae, Lucr. 4, 105.—Acc. plur.: effigias, id. 4, 42 and 85), f. effingo, I., an (artistic) copy, imitation of an object (in concreto— for syn. cf.: imago, pictura, simulacrum, signum, statua, tabula). (Class.) With the accessory idea of resemblance obtained by imitation, a likeness, portrait, image, effigy. Lit.: formarum, Lucr. 4, 105; cf. id. ib. 42 and 85: Veneris,

effigio.full: effĭgĭo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. effigies, to form, fashion, portray (late Lat.): hominem (Deus), Prud. Cath. 10, 4: aliquem imaginibus, Sid. Ep. 6, 12; Amm. 14, 6, 9.

effiguratio.full: effĭgūrātĭo, ōnis, f., rhet. t. t., = προσωποποιΐα, a representation, Rufin. de Schem. p. 275.

effindo.full: ef-findo, ĕre, v. a., to divide, cleave: fluctus rectos, Manil. 4, 283.

effingo.full: ef-fingo, finxi, fictum, 3, v. a., orig., to work out by pressing = fingendo exprimere, ἐκμάσσειν (v. fingo).—Hence, To form, fashion (artistically—class.; most freq. in the trop. sense; cf.: formo, informo, conformo, fingo, reddo, instituo, etc.). Lit.: oris lineamenta in tabula: Veneris Coae pulchritudinem aspersione fortuita, Cic. Div. 1, 13, 23: sui dissimilia, id. N. D. 3, 9, 23: deum imagines in species hominum, Tac. H. 5, 5 et saep.—Poet.: (Daedalus) casus alicujus in auro, Verg. A. 6, 32

effirmo.full: ef-firmo, āre, v. a., to strengthen, encourage, Att. ap. Non. 256, 18.

efflagitatio.full: efflāgĭtātĭo, ōnis, f. efflagito, an urgent demand, pressing request (very rare), * Cic. Fam. 5, 19, 2; Plancus, ib. 10, 24, 6.

efflagitatus.full: efflāgĭtātus, ūs, m. id., an earnest or urgent request: coactu atque efflagitatu meo, Cic. Verr. 2, 5, 29.

efflagito.full: ef-flāgĭto, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a., to demand or ask urgently, to request earnestly (class.; for syn. cf.: posco, flagito, exigo, obsecro, etc.): epistolam, Cic. Q. Fr. 2, 11: libros, Quint. Ep. ad Tryph. § 3: judicio rum desiderio tribunicia potestas efflagitata est, Cic. Div. in Caecil. 3, 8: collationes, Suet. Ner. 38: notum ensem, Verg. A. 12, 759; Suet. Tib. 12 fin.: signum pugnae, Liv. 3, 60: misericordiam alicujus (with requirere), Cic. Mil. 34 et saep.—With ut: cum iste a Cn. Dolabella effl

efflammans.full: ef-flammans, antis, adj. flammo, emitting flames, flaming, blazing: stellae, Mart. Cap. 2, § 207.

effleo.full: ef-flĕo, ēvi, 2, v. a., to weep out, exhaust by weeping: oculos, Quint. decl. 6, 4.

efflicte.full: efflicte and efflictim, advv., v. effligo.

efflicto.full: efflicto, āre, v. freq. a. effligo, to strike dead, Plaut. Stich. 4, 2, 26.

effligo.full: ef-flīgo, xi, ctum, 3, v. a., to strike dead, to kill, destroy (very rare): qui filium misit ad effligendum Pompeium, Cic. Att. 9, 19, 2: nisi pedatu tertio omnis efflixero (with obtruncavero and occidero), Plaut. Cist. 2, 1, 50; cf.: rabidos canes (with caedere), Sen. Ira, 1, 15: viperas et natrices, id. ib. 2, 31 fin.; Plaut. As. 4, 2, 9.—Hence, efflictim, adv., to death, desperately. —With amare, deperire, etc., i. e. amare usque donicum effligatur, Prob. ap. Charis. p. 178 (ante-class.); Nae

efflo.full: ef-flo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. and n., to blow or breathe out (mostly poet. and post-Aug. prose). Act. In gen.: (Sol) suos efflavit ignes, Lucr. 5, 652; cf.: ignes Aetnaeos faucibus, Verg. A. 7, 786: ignes ore et naribus, Ov. M. 2, 85: lucem elatis naribus (equi solis), Verg. A. 12, 115: mare patulis naribus, Ov. M. 3, 686; cf.: nimbos in sublime (balaenae), Plin. 9, 6, 6, § 16: pulverem, id. 29, 6, 39, § 138: vina somno, Stat. Th. 5, 209: omnem colorem, i. e. to lose, Lucr. 2, 833 et saep.: bestio

effloreo.full: ef-flōrĕo, ēre, v. n., to bloom or blossom forth, Tert. Jud. Dom. 209; Vulg. Psa. 102, 14 al.

effloresco.full: ef-flōresco, rui, 3, v. inch. n., to bloom or blossom. Lit. (eccl. Lat.), Vulg. Sirach, 51, 19; id. Isa. 18, 5.— Trop. (repeatedly in Cic.), to bloom, spring up, flourish (in youth, beauty, etc.): ex rerum cognitione efflorescat et redundet oportet oratio, Cic. de Or. 1, 6, 20; cf.: utilitas ex amicitia, id. Lael. 27; so id. Rep. 1, 29: amor, id. Fin. 1, 20, 69: si quidem efflorescit ingenii laudibus, Cic. Cael. 31, 76.

effluesco.full: efflŭesco, ĕre, 3, v. inch. [effluo], to revel, riot: sumptuosis conviviis, Ambros. de Off. M. 2, 21, 109.

effluo.full: ef-flŭo, xi, 3, v. n. (and very rarely a.), to flow or run out, to flow forth (class.; esp. freq. in the trop. sense). Lit.: facit effluere imbres, Lucr. 6, 512: una cum sanguine vita, Cic. Tusc. 2, 24 fin.: umor e cavis populi nigrae, Plin. 24, 8, 32, § 47: sucina petris, id. 37, 2, 11, § 35: amnis in oceanum, id. ib.: ne qua levis effluat aura, escape, Ov. M. 6, 233.—Poet.: ambrosiae et nectari' linctus, Lucr. 6, 971, v. Lachm. ad h. l.— Act.: ne (amphorae) effluant vinum, Petr. 71, 11; cf. Cl

effluus.full: efflŭus, a, um, adj. effluo, flowing out (late Lat.): ignis, Avien. Progn. Arat. 1717: amnis in pontum cadit, id. Perieg. 1162.

effluvium.full: efflŭvĭum, ii, n. id., a flowing out, an outlet (post-Aug. and very rare): umoris e corpore, Plin. 7, 51, 52, § 171: lacus, Tac. A. 12, 57: cerebri effluvio exspirare, Vell. 2, 120 fin., v. Kritz. ad h. l.

effoco.full: ef-fōco, āre, v. a. faux, to suffocate, smother.—Trop.: bonis suis effocantur, Sen. Brev. Vit. 2, 3 dub. (al. offoco).

effodio.full: ef-fŏdĭo, also exf- and ecf- (cf. Neue, Formenl. 2, 767, 769), fōdi, fossum, 3 (inf. pass.: ecfodiri, Plaut. Mil. 2, 3, 44; 2, 4, 21), v. a., to dig out, dig up (class.): nec ferrum, aes, argentum, aurum effoderetur, Cic. Off. 2, 3 fin.: carbones e sepulcris, Plin. 35, 6, 25, § 41: lapides puteis, id. 36, 22, 45, § 161: aulam auri plenam, Plaut. Aul. 4, 8, 9; cf. thensaurum, id. Trin. 3, 3, 53; 4, 4, 8: opes, Ov. M. 1, 140; and facetiously: ex hoc sepulcro vetere (i. e. ex sene avaro) viginti mi

effor.full: ef-for, ātus, 1, v. dep. a. (defect. In use only: effor, Cav. ap. Diom. p. 375 P.: effaris, App. M. 7, 25, p. 199, 6: effatur, Verg. A. 10, 523 al.: effamini, Arn. 7, 41: effantur, App. Mund. prooem. p. 56, 22: effabor, Lucr. 5, 104: effabere, Luc. 8, 346: effabimur, Cic. Ac. 2, 30, 97: effantes, App. Mund. p. 65, 5; imp.: effare, Verg. A. 6, 560; inf.: effari, id. ib. 4, 76; as pass., poët. ap. Cic. Tusc. 2, 17, 39; part.: effatus, Verg. A. 3, 463 al.; as pass. v. infra: effando, Liv. 5, 15, 10

efforo.full: ef-fŏro, āre, v. a., to bore through, perforate: truncum, Col. 9, 1, 3.

effossio.full: effossĭo, ōnis, f. effodio, a digging out; in the plur.: laboriosae, Cod. Just. 11, 6, 3.

effoveo.full: ef-fŏvĕo, ēre, v. a., to refresh: carnem, Veg. 4, 28, 2 dub.

effractarius.full: effractārĭus, ii, m. effractor, a house-breaker, burglar, Sen. Ep. 68, 4.

effractor.full: effractor, ōris, m. effringo, a housebreaker, burglar (jurid. Lat.), Dig. 1, 15, 3; 47, 17, 1; Sid. Ep. 9, 7.

effractura.full: effractūra, ae, f. id., house-breaking, burglary (jurid. Lat.): effracturae fiunt plerumque in insulis in horreisque, Dig. 1, 15, 3, § 2; 38, 2, 48.

effrenate.full: effrēnāte, adv., unrestrainedly, violently, v. effreno, P. a. fin.

effrenatio.full: effrēnātĭo, ōnis, f. effreno, unbridled impetuosity: impotentis animi, Cic. Phil. 5, 8, 22.

effrenatus.full: effrēnātus, a, um, Part. and P. a., from effreno.

effrenis.full: effrēnis, e, adj., v. effrenus init.

effreno.full: ef-frēno or ecfr-, no perf., ātum, 1, v. a., to unbridle, let loose (very rare).— Poet. transf.: Vulturnum Effrenat, Sil. 9, 496.—Far more freq., effrēnātus, a, um, P. a. Unbridled, without a rein: equi, Liv. 40, 40, 5: equi velut effrenati passim incerto cursu feruntur, id. 37, 41, 10.— Transf., ungoverned, unrestrained, unruly (a favorite word of Cicero): homines secundis rebus effrenatos tamquam in gyrum rationis duci oportere, Cic. Off. 1, 26, 90: populi soluti effrenatique, id. Rep. 1, 34;
effreno.short: ef-frēno or ecfr-, no perf., ātum, 1, v.

effrenus.full: ef-frēnus, a, um (also effrenis mula, Plin. 8, 44, 69, § 171; Sen. de Ira, 3, 15, 2), adj. ex-frenum, free from the bridle, unbridled (not ante Aug., and mostly poet. for effrenatus; cf. also: infrenus, infrenatus). Lit.: equus, Liv. 4, 33, 7.— Trop., unbridled, unrestrained: gens, Verg. G. 3, 382: amor, Ov. M. 6, 465: juventa, Stat. Achill. 1, 277: profatu, id. Silv. 5, 3, 103.
effrenus.short: ef-frēnus, a, um (also effrenis mula, Plin.

effrico.full: ef-frĭco, xi (Tert. adv. Marc. 4, 12), ātum, 1, v. a., to rub off or out (post-Aug. and very rare). Lit.: sordium enormem illuviem operose, App. M. 1, p. 105, 9: calices, id. ib. 4, p. 145, 31: spicas decerptas, Tert. l. l.— Trop.: rubigo animorum effricanda est, Sen. Ep. 95, 37.

effringo.full: ef-fringo, frēgi, fractum, 3, v. a. and n. Act., to break off, to break open: effringere quam aperire putant robustius, Quint. 2, 12, 1 (class.): cardines foribus, Plaut. Am. 4, 2, 6; id. As. 2, 3, 8; more freq.: fores, id. Stich. 2, 2, 3; id. Bacch. 4, 2, 4; id. Mil. 4, 6, 35; Ter. Ad. 1, 2, 8; 23; 40; Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 23; cf. valvas, id. ib. 43: januam, id. Mur. 15, 33: tabernas, Suet. Ner. 26: carcerem, Tac. A. 1, 21: cistam, * Hor. Ep. 1, 17, 54; poet.: urbem, to storm, Stat. Th. 9, 556; cf.

effrondesco.full: ef-frondesco, dui, 3, v. inch. n., to put forth leaves, be covered with foliage, Vop. Prob. 19, 3.

effrons.full: ef-frons, ntis, adj. (putting forth the forehead, i. e. trop.), barefaced, shameless: consilium, Vop. Num. 13.

effrutico.full: ef-frŭtĭco, āre, v. a. and n. (late Lat.). * Act., to put forth, produce, transf., Tert. Anim. 27 fin.—* Neutr., to shoot or grow forth, Tert. ad Nat. 1, 5.

effugatio.full: effŭgātĭo, ōnis, f. effugo, a putting to flight: dolorum, [Hilar.] Anon. in Job, 3, p. 238.

effugia.full: effŭgĭa vocari veteri more solet hostia, quae ad aras adducta est immolanda, si casu effugeret, Serv. Verg. A. 2, 140.
effugia.short: effŭgĭa vocari veteri more solet hostia, quae ad aras adducta est immolanda, si casu effugeret, Serv.

effugio.full: ef-fŭgĭo, fūgi (inf. pass. effugiri, Pseud. Syr. Sent. 815 Rib.), 3, v. n. and a. (class. and freq., esp. in the active sense). Neutr., to flee away; or, with reference to the result, to escape: effugias ex urbe inanis, Plaut. Trin. 3, 2, 75; so, ex urbe, id. ib. 2, 4, 196: e proelio, Cic. Phil. 2, 29: e manibus, id. de Imp. Pomp. 9 al.; cf. transf.: ex sitella (sors), Plaut. Cas. 2, 6, 44: a vita marituma, id. Bacch. 2, 3, 108: a quibus, Cic. Sest. 54 fin.: patriă, Plaut. Merc. 3, 4, 75: foras,

effugium.full: effŭgĭum, ii, n. effugio, a flecing away, flight (rarely, but class.; cf.: perfugium, refugium, asylum): effugiumque fugae prolatet copia semper, Lucr. 1, 983: effugium praecludere eunti, id. 3, 523; cf. id. 1, 974: dare effugium alicui, Liv. 23, 1, 8; Tac. H. 1, 43: patēre in publicum, Liv. 24, 26: nullam ne ad effugium quidem navem habentibus, id. 21, 43 et saep.: mortis, Cic. Verr. 2, 5, 64 fin.—In the piur.: ob nostra effugia, Verg. A. 2, 140; Tac. A. 12, 56; 15, 63.— Concr., a means or way

effugius.full: effŭgĭus, a, um, adj. effugio, escaping: hostia, Serv. Verg. A. 2, 140.

effugo.full: ef-fŭgo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a., to put to flight (late Lat.), Hier. Ep. 18, no. 19; Vulg. Sirach, 30, 20; id. 1 Macc. 1, 56.

effulgeo.full: ĕf-fulgĕo, si, 2 (inf. effulgĕre, Verg. A. 8, 677; Claud. VI. Cons. Hon. 546), v. n., to shine or gleam forth, to glitter (not anteAug.). Lit.: nova lux oculis effulsit, Verg. A. 9, 731; cf. Liv. 22, 1; 28, 15; 41, 21: auro Ductores longe effulgent, Verg. A. 5, 133; cf.: auro (fluctus), id. ib. 8, 677: nimbo (Pallas), id. ib. 2, 616 (Forbig. ad loc.; Rib. and Lad. limbo): veste nivea (sacerdos), Sil. 3, 695: ornatu, Tac. A. 13, 13: sol, Vulg. Sirach, 50, 7.— Trop.: omnis Graeciae fabulositas ex

effultus.full: ef-fultus, a, um, Part. [fulcio], propped up, supported (poet. and in post-class. prose): effultus stratis velleribus, Verg. A. 7, 94; cf. id. ib. 8, 368; Stat. S. 3, 1, 5; App. M. 2, p. 123.

effumigatus.full: ef-fūmĭgātus, a, um, Part. [fumigo], smoked out, driven out by smoke: coluber, Tert. ad Mart. 1.

effumo.full: ef-fūmo, āre, v. n., to emit smoke, to smoke: moles, Auct. Aetn. 497.

effundo.full: ef-fundo (or ecf-), fūdi, fūsum, 3, v. a., to pour out, pour forth, shed, spread abroad (class.; esp. freq. in the transf. and trop. signif.). Lit.: vinum in barathrum (i. e. ventrem), Plaut. Curc. 1, 2, 28; cf. Cic. Pis. 10: aquam oblatam in galea, Front. Strat. 1, 7, 7: humorem, Cels. 7, 15: lacrimas, Lucr. 1, 126; Cic. Planc. 42, 101: imbrem (procella), Curt. 8, 13: se in oceanum (Ganges), Plin. 2, 108, 112, § 243: Sangarius flumen in Propontidem se effundit, Liv. 38, 18, 18; cf. pass. in mid

effusio.full: effūsĭo, ōnis, f. effundo, a pouring out, pouring forth, shedding (a Ciceron. word). Lit.: atramenti, Cic. N. D. 2, 49, 127: aquae liquor et effusio, i. e. its property of pouring forth, fluidity, id. ib. 2, 10, 26: sanguinis, Vulg. Judic. 9, 24; cf. alvi, Capitol. Gord. Tert. 28, 6.— Transf. A pouring or rushing out of people: effusiones hominum ex oppidis, Cic. Pis. 22, 51.— Profusion, prodigality, Cic. Part. 23, 81; id. Att. 7, 3, 3; Liv. 44, 9; Vop. Flor. 1.—In the plur.: pecuniarum effusion

effusor.full: effūsor, ōris, m. id., a prodigal, waster, Aug. Serm. de Divers. 27 fin.

effusorie.full: effūsōrĭe, adv. effusus, effundo, i. q. effuse, 1., far and wide, dispersedly, Amm. 31, 16 fin.

effusus.full: effūsus, a, um, Part. and P. a., from effundo.

effuticius.full: effūtīcĭus or -tĭus, a, um, adj. effutio, prattling, unmeaning, inarticulate: euax verbum nihil significat, sed effuticium naturaliter est, a mere natural utterance or sound, Varr. L. L. 7, § 92 Müll.

effutio.full: ef-fūtĭo, no perf., ītum, 4, v. a. FVTIO, acc. to Prisc. p. 631 P., to blab out, babble forth, to prate, chatter, utter (class.): multa ore, Lucr. 5, 910; so, aliquid, Cic. N. D. 1, 30, 84; * Hor. A. P. 231; Gell. 5, 1; cf.: effutita temere (vaticinia), Cic. Div. 2, 55, 113: de mundo, id. N. D. 2, 37, 94.— Absol. To blab, tell secrets: eo perperam olim dixi, ne vos foris effutiretis; and absol., Ter. Ph. 5, 1, 19.— To talk idly: ex tempore, Cic. Tusc. 5, 31, 88.

effutuo.full: ef-fŭtŭo (ec-f-), ŭi, 3, v. a., to waste in debauchery: ecfututa latera, Cat. 6, 13: aurum, Poëta ap. Suet. Caes. 51 fin.

egelido.full: ē-gĕlĭdo, āre, v. a. gelidus, to thaw away, Sid. Ep. 4, 1.

egelidus.full: ē-gĕlĭdus, a, um, adj. (Ex priv. as in effrenare.) Not cold; lukewarm, tepid (poet. and in post-Aug. prose): potio et frigidae propior, Cels. 4, 18 fin.; cf. aqua (opp. frigida), id. 6, 18; cf. Suet. Aug. 82: tepores, Cat. 46, 1; cf. ver (with mollissimus annus), Col. poët. 10, 282: hiemes, Aus. Ep. 24, 97: Notus (opp. gelidus Boreas), Ov. Am. 2, 11, 10: Mosella, Aus. Ep. 2, 4.—* (Ex intensive, as in edurus, efferus, etc.) Chilly, chill, cold: flumen, Verg. A. 8, 610; Forbig. ad loc. (Rib. ecgel

egelo.full: ē-gĕlo, no perf., ātus, 1, v. a., to take off the chill, make lukewarm: leviter egelatum, Cael. Aur. Acut. 3, 5, 58; id. Tard. 4, 3.

egens.full: ĕgens, entis, Part. and P. a., from egeo.

egenulus.full: ĕgēnŭlus, a, um, adj. dim. [egenus], needy, Paul. Nol. 29, 12.

egenus.full: ĕgēnus, a, um, adj. egeo, in want of, in need of, destitute or void of any thing (rare, and mostly poet. for egens). With gen.: (nos) omnium, Verg. A. 1, 599; Liv. 9, 6: omnis spei, Tac. A. 1, 53: aquarum (regio), id. ib. 15, 3 fin.; cf. id. ib. 4, 30: decoris, Sil. 6, 304.— With abl.: commeatu, Tac. A. 12, 46; 15, 12.— Absol.: res, i. e. indigent, needy, necessitous, Plaut. Capt. 2, 3, 46; id. Poen. 1, 1, 2; Verg. A. 6, 91; 8, 365; 10, 367: frater, Vulg. Deut. 15, 11.— Poor, worthless, beggarly

egeo.full: ĕgĕo, ŭi, 2 (part. fut. egitura, Tert. adv. Marc. 4, 24), v. n. cf. Gr. ἀχήν, poor; root αχ-, αγχ, in ἄχος, ἄγχω, etc.; Lat. angustus, angina, to be needy (for syn. cf.: indigeo, careo, vaco). Prop. Absol. (so usually in Plaut. and Ter.), to be needy, to be in want, to be poor: me in divitiis esse agrumque habere, egere illam autem, Plaut. Trin. 3, 2, 57; cf. id. Most. 1, 3, 73; id. Truc. 2, 1, 12; 4, 2, 32; id. Trin. 2, 2, 49; id. Capt. 3, 4, 49; Ter. Heaut. 5, 2, 11; Cic. Rosc. Com. 8 (opp. lo

egeria.full: Ēgĕrĭa (Aeg-), ae, f., = Ἠγερία, a nymph or Camoena celebrated in Roman mythology, the wife and instructress of Numa, with two sacred groves and fountains, the one near Rome, opposite the Porta Capena, the other in the neighborhood of Aricia, Liv. 1, 19; 21; Val. Max. 1, 2, 1; Ov. F. 3, 154; 261 sq.; 4, 669; id. M. 15, 482 sq.; Verg. A. 7, 763; 775; Juv. 3, 12 sq.
egeria.short: Ēgĕrĭa (Aeg-), ae, f., = Ἠγερία, a nymph or Camoena celebrated in Roman mythology, the wife and instructress of Numa, with two sacred groves and fountains, the one near Rome, opposite the Porta Capena, the other in the neighborhood of Aricia, Liv.

egeries.full: ēgĕrĭes, em, e, f. egero, excrement, dung (late Lat.), Sol. 40, 11; Paul. Nol. Carm. 32, 281.

egermino.full: ē-germĭno, āvi, 1, v. n., to put forth, shoot, sprout, Col. 4, 17, 4; 27, 4; 32, 5.

egero.full: ē-gĕro, gessi, gestum, 3, v. a., to carry, bear or bring out, to lead or draw out, to discharge (not ante-Aug.). Lit.: praedam ex hostium tectis, Liv. 6, 3 Drak.; cf. id. 9, 31; 25, 25: pecuniam ex aerario, id. 30, 39 fin.: fluctus (e navi), Ov. M. 11, 488: stercus e columbariis, Col. 2, 14, 1: humanas opes a Veiis, Liv. 5, 22: humum scrobibus, Col. 2, 2, 19; Ov. M. 7, 243: tantum nivis, Liv. 21, 37: silices umeris, Plin. 33, 4, 21, § 71: aquam vomitu, to discharge, void, vomit, Curt. 7, 5; cf.
