egersimon.full: ĕgersĭmon, i, n., = ἐγέρσιμον, a means of excitement, Mart. Cap. 9, § 911.
egersimon.short: ĕgersĭmon, i, n., = ἐγέρσιμον, a means of excitement, Mart.

egesta.full: Egesta, ae, f., the Greek name of Segesta (sc. Ἔγεστα), Fest. p. 340, 5 Müll.
egesta.short: Egesta, ae, f., the Greek name of Segesta (sc.

egestas.full: ĕgestas, ātis, f. egeo, indigence, extreme poverty, necessity, want (very freq. and class.; for syn. cf.: indigentia, inopia, penuria, paupertas, mendicitas): ista paupertas, vel potius egestas ac mendicitas, Cic. Parad. 6, 1, 45; Plaut. Ps. 2, 4, 2; id. Trin. 2, 2, 57; 77; 4, 2, 5 al.; Cic. Rosc. Am. 49 fin.; id. Cat. 2, 11 fin.; id. Inv. 1, 47, 88; * Caes. B. G. 6, 24, 4; Verg. G. 1, 146; 3, 319; id. A. 6, 276 et saep.; cf. in plur.: egestates tot egentissimorum hominum, Cic. Att. 9, 7, 5.—Of

egestio.full: ēgestĭo, ōnis, f. egero, a carrying out or off, an emptying, voiding (post-Aug. and rare): cadaverum et ruderum, Suet. Ner. 38: ventris et urinae, Cael. Aur. Tard. 5, 10; for which simply egestio, Suet. Claud. 44 fin.; Veg. Vet. 5, 14, 6: publicarum opum, a wasting, squandering, Plin. Ep. 8, 6, 7.

egestivus.full: ēgestīvus, a, um, adj. id..—In medic. lang., purgative: vis, Macer de Anetho, 14.

egestosus.full: ĕgestōsus, a, um, adj. egestas, very poor, indigent, Aur. Vict. Epit. 12 al.

egestus1.full: ēgestus, a, um, Part., from egero.
egestus1.short: ēgestus, a, um, Part., from egero.

egestus2.full: ēgestus, ūs, m. egero, a carrying out, emptying, voiding (post-Aug. and very rare): alto egestu penitus cavare terras, Stat. S. 4, 3, 42: ventris, Sen. Q. N. 3, 30, 4.

egigno.full: ē-gigno, ĕre, to procreate, produce, bring forth: et altos interdum ramos egigni corpore vivo, Lucr. 2, 703 Lachm. N. cr.
egigno.short: ē-gigno, ĕre, to procreate, produce, bring forth: et altos interdum ramos egigni corpore vivo, Lucr.

eglecopala.full: eglecopala, ae, f., a Gallic name for blue marl, Plin. 17, 8, 4, § 46.
eglecopala.short: eglecopala, ae, f., a Gallic name for blue marl, Plin.

egnatia.full: Egnātĭa, ae, f. A city and harbor on the coast of Appulia, now Torre d' Agnazzo or Monopoli, Plin. 2, 107, 111, § 240; the same called Gnatia, Hor. S. 1, 5, 97 sq.; Mel. 2, 4, 7; Inscr. in Avellino Bull. Arch. Ottobre, 1845.— The name of a female, v. Egnatius fin.

egnatius.full: Egnātĭus, i, m., a Roman proper name. L. Egn. Rufus, friend of Cicero, Cic. Fam. 13, 43 sq.; id. Att. 7, 18, 4 al.— M. Egn. Rufus, the name of an edile, 733 A. U. C., who set on foot a conspiracy against Augustus, Suet. Aug. 19; Vell. 2, 91 sq.; Sen. Clem. 1, 9; id. Brev. Vit. 5; Tac. A. 1, 10.—Hence, Egnātĭānus, a, um, adj., of Egnatius: scelus, Vell. 2, 93. — Egnatia Maximilla, Tac. A. 15, 71.
egnatius.short: Egnātĭus, i, m., a Roman proper name.

egnatuleius.full: Egnātŭlēĭus, i, m., L., a quaestor who deserted with the legio Martia from Antony to Octavius, Cic. Phil. 3, 3, 7.
egnatuleius.short: Egnātŭlēĭus, i, m., L., a quaestor who deserted with the legio Martia from Antony to Octavius, Cic.

ego.full: ĕgō^ (ŏ always in poets of the best age, as Cat., Verg., Hor., etc.; ō ante-class. and post-Aug., as Juv. 17, 357; Aus. Epigr. 54, 6, v. Corss. Ausspr. 2, 483; gen. mei; dat. mihi; acc. and abl. me; plur., nom., and acc. nos; gen., mostly poet., nostrum; gen. obj. nostri, rarely nostrum; for the gen. possess. the adj. noster was used, q. v.; cf. Roby, Gram. 1, § 388; dat. and abl. nobis; mi in dat. for mihi, part., Varr. R. R. 2, 5; Lucr. 3, 106; Verg. A. 6, 104; in prose, Cic. Fam. 7, 24, 2; id
ego.short: ĕgō^ (ŏ always in poets of the best age, as Cat., Verg., Hor., etc.;

egomet.full: ĕgŏmet, v. the preced. art. and met.

egranatus.full: ē-grānātus, a, um, adj. granum, shelled, emptied: carinae, Plin. Val. 3, 14.

egredior.full: ē-grĕdĭor, gressus, 3 (inf. egredier, Plaut. Poen. 3, 4, 32), v. dep. n. and a. Neutr., to go or come out, come forth (class.). Lit. In gen., with e or ex: foras e fano, Plaut. Rud. 2, 3, 4; cf.: e fano huc, id. ib. 3, 2, 49: e cubiculo, Cic. Rep. 1, 12: ex oppido, Caes. B. G. 2, 13, 2; 7, 11, 7: ex suis finibus, id. ib. 6, 31, 4: ex castris, id. ib. 6, 36, 2: e curia, Liv. 2, 48; 7, 31 et saep.—With a or ab: ab sese, Plaut. Truc. 4, 3, 78; id. Epid. 3, 2, 44; Ter. And. 1, 3, 21; id. Ph. 5, 1, 5

egregiatus.full: ēgrĕgĭātus, ūs, m. egregius, II., the rank and title of an Egregius in the later per. of the empire, similar to Your Excellency, Cod. Th. 8, 4, 3; 10, 7, 1 al.

egregius.full: ē-grĕgĭus, a, um (sup.: mulier egregiissimă formă, Pac. ap. Prisc. 3, p. 600 fin. P.; Rib. Fragm. Trag. p. 105: egregiissime grammatice, Gell. 14, 5, 3.—Vocat.: egregi or egregie, Gell. 14, 5, 1 sq.), adj. ex-grex, Corss. Ausspr. 1, 504; hence, chosen from the herd, i. e., distinguished, surpassing, excellent, eminent (for syn. cf.: praeclarus, eximius, divinus, magnificus). In gen. (class.): in procuratione civitatis, egregius, Cic. de Or. 1, 49, 215; cf.: in bellica laude, id. Brut. 21, 84: in
egregius.short: ē-grĕgĭus, a, um (sup.: mulier egregiissimă formă, Pac.

egressio.full: ēgressĭo, ōnis, f. egredior, a going out or forth (post-Aug.). Lit.: nocturna (ex castello), App. M. 8, p. 208, 7; Hier. Ep. 78, 1: eorum ex Aegypto, Vulg. Num. 1, 1; and so in gen. of the Exodus: filiorum Israel, id. ib. 33, 38; 1 Reg. 18, 30.— Trop., in rhet. lang., a digression in speaking, like παρέκβασις, Quint. 4, 3, 12; 15; 3, 9, 4; cf. ib. 4, 3: de egressione.—In plur., id. 11, 3, 164; 12, 10, 60.

egressus1.full: ēgressus, a, um, Part., from egredior.
egressus1.short: ēgressus, a, um, Part., from egredior.

egressus2.full: ēgressus, ūs, m. egredior, a going out or away (class.). Lit. In gen., egress, departure. In abstr.: frequentia sua vestrum egressum (sc. in provinciam) ornando, * Cic. Pis. 13 fin.: Caesar rarus egressu, Tac. A. 15, 53.—In plur., Sall. J. 35, 5 Kritz; Tac. A. 3, 33; 11, 12; id. Or. 6; Ov. F. 1, 138.—Of birds, a flying out, flight, Ov. M. 11, 748; Col. 8, 8, 1.— In concreto: per tenebrosum et sordidum egressum extraho Gitona, Petr. 91, 3.—In plur., Tac. A. 16, 10; and poet. of the mouths of the

egula.full: ĕgŭla, ae, f. perh. kindr. with ἀχλύς, a kind of sulphur, Plin. 35, 15, 50, § 175.

egurgito.full: ē-gurgĭto, āre, v. a. gurges, to pour out, cast out (with the access. notion of extravagance), to lavish: argentum domo, Plaut. Ep. 4, 2, 12.

ehem.full: ĕhem, interj., an exclamation of joyful surprise, ha! what! ehem, optume! quam dudum tu advenisti? Plaut. As. 2, 4, 43; id. Most. 3, 2, 38; id. Mil. 4, 9, 5; id. Rud. 3, 5, 25; Ter. And. 2, 5, 6: ehem, pater me, tu hic eras? id. Eun. 1, 2, 6; 3, 2, 9; id. Ad. 1, 2, 1; App. M. 2, p. 124, 29.
ehem.short: ĕhem, interj., an exclamation of joyful surprise, ha! what! ehem, optume! quam dudum tu advenisti? Plaut.

eheu.full: ēheu, interj., an interjection of pain or grief, ah! alas! Plaut. Capt. 1, 2, 49; 5, 3, 18; id. Trin. 2, 4, 102; id. Mil. 4, 8, 32 al.; Ter. Heaut. 1, 1, 31; id. Hec. 1, 1, 17; id. Phorm. 1, 4, 10.—Often followed by quam: eheu, quam ego nunc totus displiceo mihi, Ter. Heaut. 5, 4, 20; Hor. S. 1, 3, 66. (The epic and lyric poets have everywhere ēheu; and hence many moderns, partly in accordance with better MSS., read everywhere heu heu; cf. Burmann, Voss, Wagner, and Ribbeck, Verg. E. 2, 58; also
eheu.short: ēheu, interj., an interjection of pain or grief, ah! alas! Plaut.

eho.full: ĕhŏ, interj.; in the comic poets, used in asking, commanding, or scolding, ha? ho! holla! soho! In vehement questions, Plaut. Ep. 3, 4, 69; 5, 2, 22; id. Bacch. 4, 7, 5: eho tu, id. Merc. 1, 2, 77; Ter. And. 5, 4, 5; id. Eun. 4, 4, 24; id. Phorm. 2, 3, 35.— In impetuous commands, Plaut. Most. 3, 2, 157; id. Men. 2, 3, 78; id. Ps. 1, 3, 114; Ter. Ad. 5, 9, 13: eho puer, id. Hec. 4, 4, 97.— In angry remonstrance or invective, Plaut. Bacch. 3, 3, 40; id. Mil. 3, 2, 12; id. Pers. 3, 3, 2; Ter. And.

ei1.full: ĕī, dat. of is, q. v.

ei2.full: ei, interj., oh! etc., Plaut. Cas. 3, 6, 7; Ter. And. 1, 1, 46, v. hei.

eia.full: ēiă (in MSS. also hēiă), interj. εἴα. An expression of joy or of pleased surprise. In admiring an object, ah! ah ha! indeed! Plaut. Rud. 2, 4, 8; id. Men. 2, 3, 30; Ter. Heaut. 5, 5, 19; 3, 2, 10.— In gentle remonstrance or persuasion, ah! come! heia, mea Juno, non decet te, etc., Plaut. Cas. 2, 3, 14; id. Truc. 4, 2, 8; id. Bacch. 4, 3, 16; 3, 3, 4; Ter. Eun. 5, 8, 35: heia quam ferocula est! Turp. ap. Non. p. 75, 30 (Rib. Fragm. Com. p. 98).— In strong affirmation, Plaut. Ps. 1, 3, 40; id. Bac

eicio.full: ē-ĭcĭo (or ejicio), jēci, jectum, 3 (eicit, dissyl., Lucr. 3, 877; 4, 1272), v. a. jacio, to cast, thrust, or drive out; to eject, expel (class.). Lit. In gen.: aliquem e senatu, Cic. de Sen. 12 fin.; Liv. 43, 15; cf.: ex oppido, Caes. B. C. 1, 30, 3: de senatu, Liv. 40, 51; 41, 26: de collegio, Cic. Q. Fr. 2, 5: a suis diis penatibus, id. Quint. 26, 83: finibus, Sall. J. 14, 8: domo, Plaut. As. 1, 3, 9; Caes. B. G. 4, 7, 3; cf.: aedibus foras, Plaut. As. 1, 2, 1: omnes amasios foras, id. Truc.
eicio.short: ē-ĭcĭo (or ejicio), jēci, jectum, 3 (eicit, dissyl., Lucr.

eidem.full: ĕīdem, dat. of idem, q. v.

eii.full: eii and eiius, v. is init.

ejaculo.full: ējăcŭlo, āre, v. the foll. init.

ejaculor.full: ē-jăcŭlor, ātus, 1, v. dep. a. (and in the act. form: se in salum ejaculaverat, Gell. 16, 19, 21), to shoot out, to hurl or throw out (rare, and not ante-Aug.): aquas, Ov. M. 4, 124; id. F. 1, 270: se in altum (sanguis), id. M. 6, 259: umbram in forum, Plin. 4, 12, 23, § 73.!*? ejaculari, pass., Scrib. Comp. 84.

ejectamentum.full: ējectāmentum, i, n. ejecto, that which is cast out, refuse (very rare): cetera maris, Tac. G. 45; App. Mag. 35, p. 297.

ejecticius.full: ējectīcĭus or -tĭus, a, um, adj. eicio, that casts out, ejects: vulva, i. e. that has miscarried, Plin. 11, 37, 84, § 210.

ejectio.full: ējectĭo, ōnis, f. id., a casting or throwing out (very rare): sanguinis, a spitting of blood, Vitr. 1, 6, 3: mortem et ejectionem timemus, i. e. banishment, exile, * Cic. Att. 2, 18, 1; Vulg. Thren. 2, 14: articuli, i. e. dislocation, Cael. Aur. Tard. 2, 1, 28.

ejecto.full: ējecto, āvi, ātum, 1, v. freq. a. id., to cast out, to throw up (a poet. word of the Aug. per.): arenas, Ov. M. 5, 353: favillam, id. ib. 2, 231: undas in campos, Sil. 10, 320: quicquid ab auriferis fossis, Stat. S. 3, 3, 89: cruentas dapes ore, i. e. to vomit, Ov. M. 14, 211; cf.: saniem per ora, Luc. 3, 658.

ejectus1.full: ējectus, a, um, Part., from eicio.
ejectus1.short: ējectus, a, um, Part., from eicio.

ejectus2.full: ējectus, ūs, m. eicio, a casting out, emission: largior animai foras, i. e. a breathing out, Lucr. 4, 961.

ejulabilis.full: ējŭlābĭlis, e, adj. ejulo, wailing loudly: plangor, App. M. 4, p. 143, 31.

ejulabundus.full: ējŭlābundus, a, um, adj. id., abandoned to wailing, Jul. Val. Rer. Gest. Alex. M. 2, 16.

ejulatio.full: ējŭlātĭo, ōnis, f. ejulo, a wailing, lamenting, * Plaut. Capt. 2, 1, 7; * Cic. Leg. 2, 23 fin.

ejulatus.full: ējŭlātus, ūs, m. id., a wailing, lamenting, Cic. Tusc. 2, 23, 55; Auct. Or. de Har. Resp. 18, 39; Gell. 1, 26, 7; Vulg. Gen. 27, 38.

ejulito.full: ējŭlĭto, āvi, 1, v. freq. a. id., to lament greatly, Lucil. ap. Varr. L. L. 7, § 103 Müll., and ap. Non. 21, 20.

ejulo.full: ējŭlo, āre (also dep. hejulor, āri, Prisc. 797), v. n. and a. [from the exclamation hei, heu; cf. Doëd. Syn. 3, p. 156]. Neutr., to wail, lament, Plaut. Aul. 2, 4, 39; 4, 9, 17; 4, 10, 66; id. Merc. 4, 1, 16; * Cic. Tusc. 2, 7, 19; Gell. 12, 5, 9; Vulg. Job, 35, 9 al.— Act., to bewail, lament over a person or thing (post - class.): fortunas meas, App. M. 3, p. 129: sese altius, id. ib. 4, p. 153, 24.

ejuncesco.full: ē-juncesco, ĕre, v. inch. n. [juncus], to grow or shoot up like a rush: vitis, Plin: 17, 22, 35, § 182.

ejuncidus.full: ē-juncĭdus, a, um, adj. id., grown or shot up like a rush, lean, meagre, slender: ejuncidum ἐκλεπτωθέν, Gloss. Philox.: sarmentum, Varr. R. R. 1, 31, 3: mulieres, id. ib. 2, 10, 8: vitis, Plin. 17, 22, 35, § 173.

ejuno.full: Ējūno, inlerj., by Juno; v. Juno.

ejuratio.full: ējūrātĭo (ējĕrātio, Tert. Spect. 4; cf. ejuro), ōnis, f. ejuro, II., an abjuring, i. e. a resigning, abdication, laying down of an office (post-Aug.). Prop.: ignominiosa consulum, Val. Max. 2, 7, 7 fin.— Transf., a resigning: bonae spei, Sen. Vit. Beat. 26, 5.

ejuro.full: ē-jūro (mostly post-Aug., Cic. Fam., v. infra, and ējĕro, like pejero, class., Scip. ap. Cic. de Or. 2, 70, 285 twice; Cic. Phil. 12, 7, 18; Cic. Verr. 2, 3, 60, § 137; Tert. Spect. 24; id. Idol. 18), āvi, ātum, 1, v. a., to refuse or reject by oath, to abjure, a t. t. of jurid., polit., and mercant. lang. In jurid. lang.: forum or judicem iniquum sibi, to reject, refuse on oath a court or a judge, as unjust, Scip. l. l.; Cic. Verr. l. l.; id. Phil. 12, 7, 18 Manut. and Wernsd.— In polit. law la

ejus.full: ējus, gen. of is, ea, id. q. v.

ejusdemmodi.full: ējusdemmŏdi idem - modus, of the same kind, such (usually written as two words), Varr. L. L. 9, § 84 and § 110 Müll.; Cic. Q. Fr. 1, 1, 4, § 14; al. Gell. 16, 8, 10.
ejusdemmodi.short: ējusdemmŏdi idem - modus, of the same kind, such (usually written as two words), Varr.

ejusmodi.full: ējusmŏdi is-modus, usually written ejus modi (sometimes trisyl.), of that kind, of such a kind, such: qui cum ingeniis conflictatur ejusmodi, Ter. And. 1, 1, 66 al.: genus belli est ejus modi, Cic. de Imp. 2, 6 al. — So, in such a manner, = ita: quam viam tensarum atque pompae ejus modi exegisti, ut, etc., Cic. Verr. 2, 1, 59, § 154.— —ējuscemŏdi, i. q. ejusmodi, Gell. 16, 8 med. al.
ejusmodi.short: ējusmŏdi is-modus, usually written ejus modi (sometimes trisyl.), of that kind, of such a kind, such: qui cum ingeniis conflictatur ejusmodi, Ter.

elabor.full: ē-lābor, elapsus (elabsus), 3, v. dep. n. and a. Neutr., to slip or glide away, to fall out, get off, escape (class.). Lit.: anguilla est, elabitur, Plaut. Ps. 2, 4, 57; so of a snake, Liv. 1, 56; 26, 19; Verg. G. 1, 244; Ov. M. 9, 63: cum se convolvens sol elaberetur et abiret, Cic. Div. 1, 23, 46: (animal) ex utero elapsum, id. N. D. 2, 51, 128; cf. id. Cat. 1, 6 fin.: elapsae manibus tabellae, Ov. M. 9, 571; cf.: gladius ei e manu, Just. 33, 2, 3: jumentum e manibus curantium elapsum, Liv. 44

elaboratio.full: ēlăbōrātĭo, ōnis, f. elaboro, persevering labor, careful diligence, Auct. Her. 4, 22, 32.

elaboratus.full: ēlăbōrātus, ūs, m. id., persevering labor, only in abl., App. Flor. p. 346.

elaboro.full: ē-lăbōro, āvi, ātum, 1, v. n. and a. Neutr., to labor, endeavor, exert one's self, take pains either successfully or perseveringly = eniti (class.; most freq. in Cic.).— Constr. with ut, in aliqua re, in aliquid, with acc. and inf. as object, or absol. With ut: enitere, elabora, vel potius eblandire, effice, ut, etc., Cic. Att. 16, 16 C, § 12; id. Q. Fr. 1, 1, 14 fin.; id. de Or. 2, 72 fin.; Q. Cic. Petit. Cons. 5, 18 (twice); and pass. impers.: aperte elaboratur, ut verba verbis respondeant, Ci

elacatenes.full: ēlăcătēnes, um, m., = ἠλακατῆνες, a large sea-fish, a tunny, so called from its resemblance in shape to a spindle, ἠλακάτη, Plin. 32, 11, 53, § 149 (dub.; Jan. and Sillig ictinus, iulis).—Also called ēlăcătae, Col. 8, 17, 12. Here belongs elacatena genus salsamenti, quod appellatur vulgo melandrea, Paul. ex Fest. p. 76, 15 Müll.
elacatenes.short: ēlăcătēnes, um, m., = ἠλακατῆνες, a large sea-fish, a tunny, so called from its resemblance in shape to a spindle, ἠλακάτη, Plin.

elaea.full: Ĕlaea, ae, f., = Ἐλαία, a city of Aeolis, Mel. 1, 8, 1; Plin. 5, 30, 32, § 121; Liv. 36, 43 al.
elaea.short: Ĕlaea, ae, f., = Ἐλαία, a city of Aeolis, Mel.

elaeemporia.full: ĕlaeempŏrĭa, ae, f., = ἐλαιεμπορία, traffic in oil, the oil-trade, Dig. 50, 4, 18, § 19.
elaeemporia.short: ĕlaeempŏrĭa, ae, f., = ἐλαιεμπορία, traffic in oil, the oil-trade, Dig.

elaeogarum.full: ĕlaeŏgărum, i, n., a fish-sauce with oil, Apic. 7, 3.
elaeogarum.short: ĕlaeŏgărum, i, n., a fish-sauce with oil, Apic.

elaeomeli.full: ĕlaeŏmĕli, n. indecl., = ἐλαιόμελι, a sort of manna which exudes from the branches of the olive-tree, Plin. 15, 7, 7, § 32; 23, 4, 50, § 96.

elaeon.full: ĕlaeōn, ōnis, m., = ἐλαιών, a plantation of olives, Tert. adv. Marc. 4, 39 fin.
elaeon.short: ĕlaeōn, ōnis, m., = ἐλαιών, a plantation of olives, Tert.

elaeothesium.full: ĕlaeŏthĕsĭum, ii, n., = ἐλαιοθέσιον, the anointing-room in a bath, Vitr. 5, 11, 2.
elaeothesium.short: ĕlaeŏthĕsĭum, ii, n., = ἐλαιοθέσιον, the anointing-room in a bath, Vitr.

elaeus.full: Ĕlaeūs, ūntis, f., = Ἐλαιοῦς, a city on the Hellespont in the Thracian Chersonesus, Liv. 31, 16, 5 Drak. N. cr.; Plin. 4, 11, 18, § 49.—Elēüs, Mel. 2, 2, 7.
elaeus.short: Ĕlaeūs, ūntis, f., = Ἐλαιοῦς, a city on the Hellespont in the Thracian Chersonesus, Liv.

elambo.full: ē-lambo, ĕre, 3, v. a., to lick away, remove by licking: mox ut elambente matris lingua detersa sint (animalia), Mar. Vict. Art. Metr. 4, 2, 5.

elamentabilis.full: ē-lāmentābĭlis, e, adj., very lamentable: gemitus, Cic. Tusc. 2, 24, 57 Mos. N. cr.
elamentabilis.short: ē-lāmentābĭlis, e, adj., very lamentable: gemitus, Cic.

elanguesco.full: ē-languesco, gui, 3, v. inch. n., to grow faint, feeble, to slacken, relax (not ante-Aug.): ut elanguescendum aliena ignavia esset, Liv. 1, 46, 7; so in the praes., id. 35, 45; Vell. 2, 111 fin.; Plin. 9, 30, 48, § 91; Sil. 4, 140 al.—In the perf.: elanguimus, patres conscripti, nec jam ille senatus sumus qui, etc., Tac. H. 4, 42 fin.; Suet. Galb. 1: differendo deinde elanguit res, Liv. 5, 26, 3; cf.: neque tamen elanguit cura hominum eā morā, id. 23, 23, 8; so Gell. 16, 3, 2; Val. Fl. 4, 572.

elanguidus.full: ēlanguĭdus, a, um, adj. ex + languidus, utterly weary, Fortun. Vit. Martin. 1, 296.

elaphoboscon.full: ĕlăphŏboscon, i, n., = ἐλαφοβόσκον (deer-food), wild parsnips, Plin. 22, 22, 37, § 79.
elaphoboscon.short: ĕlăphŏboscon, i, n., = ἐλαφοβόσκον (deer-food), wild parsnips, Plin.

elapidatus.full: ē-lăpĭdātus, a, um, Part. [lapido], cleared from stones: solum, Plin. 17, 4, 3, § 30; 17, 10, 14, § 69; 18, 16, 43, § 145.

elapsus.full: ēlapsus, a, um, Part., from elabor.
elapsus.short: ēlapsus, a, um, Part., from elabor.

elaqueo.full: ē-lăquĕo, no perf., ātum, 1, v. a., to extricate from snares or fetters; to disentangle, unfetter (post-class.). Lit.: aliquem, Amm. 30, 1, 11.— Trop.: aliquem a vinculo angoris, Sid. Ep. 8, 9: constantiam animi, Prud. adv. Symm. 2, 147.

elargior.full: ē-largĭor, īri, v. dep. a., to give out, distribute, bestow: patriae carisque propinquis quantum elargiri deceat, Pers. 3, 71; Jul. Firm. Math. 3, 10.

elassesco.full: ē-lassesco, ĕre, v. inch. n., to become exhausted, faint, weary.—Trop.: nimia germinatio, Plin. 16, 25, 41, § 98.

elate1.full: ēlāte, adv., loftily, proudly; v. 1. effero, P. a. fin.

elate2.full: ĕlăte, ēs, f., = ἐλάτη, a sort of firtree, Lat. abies, Plin. 12, 28, 62, § 134; 23, 5, 53, § 99.— The envelope or leaf of the palm-bud, Vulg. Cant. 5, 11.
elate2.short: ĕlăte, ēs, f., = ἐλάτη, a sort of firtree, Lat.

elatea.full: Ĕlătēa or -īa, ae, f., = Ἐλάτεια. A city of Phocis, Plin. 4, 7, 12, § 27; Liv. 28, 7; Plaut. Bacch. 4, 2, 9 al.— A city of Thessaly, Liv. 42, 54.

elateius.full: Ĕlătēïus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Elatus, a prince of the Lapithae: Caeneus, i. e. his son, Ov. M. 12, 497: proles, the same, id. ib. 12, 189; v. Caeneus.
elateius.short: Ĕlătēïus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Elatus, a prince of the Lapithae: Caeneus, i.

elaterium.full: ĕlătērĭum, ii, n., = ἐλατήριον, a medicine prepared from the juice of the wild cucumber, Cels. 5, 12; 6, 5; Scribon. Comp. 70, 224; Plin. 20, 1, 3, § 5 al.
elaterium.short: ĕlătērĭum, ii, n., = ἐλατήριον, a medicine prepared from the juice of the wild cucumber, Cels.

elatine.full: ĕlătīne, ēs, f., = ἐλατίνη, a plant of the genus Antirrhinum, Plin. 27, 9, 50, § 74.
elatine.short: ĕlătīne, ēs, f., = ἐλατίνη, a plant of the genus Antirrhinum, Plin.

elatio.full: ēlātĭo, ōnis, f. 1. effero, a carrying out. Lit. (post-class.): FERRI, Inscr. Fratr. Arval. ap. Marin. 43 and 402.— In partic. A carrying to the grave, a burial: mortui, Dig. 11, 7, 14, § 3.— A lifting or raising up: onerum, Vitr. 8, 10: maris, i. e. high waves, Vulg. Psa. 92, 6. — Trop. (class.). A being carried away or hurried along; transport, passion: laetitia quasi gestientis animi elatio voluptaria, Cic. Fin. 3, 10 fin. (cf.: efferri laetitiā, under effero, II. B.).— Exaltation, elevation:

elatites.full: ĕlătītes, ae, m., = ἐλατίτης, a kind of blood-stone, Plin. 36, 20, 38, § 147 (dub. Jan. miltiten).
elatites.short: ĕlătītes, ae, m., = ἐλατίτης, a kind of blood-stone, Plin.

elatro.full: ē-lātro, āre, v. a., to bark out, cry aloud: aliquid acriter, Hor. Ep. 1, 18, 18.

elatus.full: ēlātus, a, um, Part. and P. a., from effero, exalted, elevated, lofty, high.

elaudare.full: ēlaudāre plus quam nominare, Paul. ex Fest. p. 76, 4 Müll.

elautus.full: ēlautus, a, um, Part., from elavo.
elautus.short: ēlautus, a, um, Part., from elavo.

elaver.full: Ĕlăver, ĕris, n., a river in Gaul emptying into the Liger, now Allier, Caes. B. G. 7, 34; 35; 53 fin.
elaver.short: Ĕlăver, ĕris, n., a river in Gaul emptying into the Liger, now Allier, Caes.

elavo.full: ē-lăvo, lāvi, lautum, lōtum, 1, v. a., to wash out or away, to wash clean (very rare; not in the Cic. per.). Lit.: elota cerussa, Cels. 6, 6, no. 3: elota oliva, Col. 12, 52, 21.— Transf.: elautae ambae sumus opera Neptunia, washed in the sea, wrecked, Plaut. Rud. 3, 3, 37; so, in mari elavare, to wash or bathe in the sea, i. e. to be shipwrecked, ruined, id. ib. 2, 7, 21; 5, 2, 20.— Hence, trop.: nos mare acerrumum: nam in mari repperi, hic elavi bonis, have lost, been stripped of property, id.

elea.full: Ĕlĕa, ae, f., = Ἐλέα, a city of Lucania, the birth-place of Parmenides and Zeno, the founders of the Eleatic philosophy, in Lat. also called Velia, Cic. N. D. 3, 33, 82.— Hence, Zeno Elĕātes, of Elea, Cic. Tusc. 2, 22, 52; and: Elĕātĭci philosophi, Eleatic, id. Ac. 2, 42, 129.
elea.short: Ĕlĕa, ae, f., = Ἐλέα, a city of Lucania, the birth-place of Parmenides and Zeno, the founders of the Eleatic philosophy, in Lat.

elecebra.full: ēlĕcĕbra (also exlec-), ae, f. elicio, a female allurer, wheedler, sponger (a Plautin. word), Plaut. Men. 2, 3, 26; id. Bacch. 4, 9, 20; cf. Paul. ex Fest. p. 76, 5 Müll.

electarium.full: ēlectārĭum (also ēlectuārium), ii, n. ecligma, a medicament that melts in the mouth, an electuary, Cael. Aur. Tard. 2, 13; 169, 176 al.; cf. Isid. Orig. 4, 9, 10.

electe.full: ēlecte, adv., choicely, v. eligo, P. a.

electilis.full: ēlectĭlĭs, e, adj. eligo, choice, dainty (with probus): piscatus, Plaut. Most. 3, 2, 41: partes, App. M. 10, p. 245, 35.

electio.full: ēlectĭo, ōnis, f. id., a choice, selection, * Cic. Or. 20, 68; Quint. 1, 12, 4; Prooem. § 2; 3, 4, 8; Vell. 2, 72 fin.; Tac. A. 6, 22; id. Or. 23 al.: vitiatarum electiones, i. e. the option given to a violated maiden, whether her ravisher shall be put to death or shall marry her, Tac. Or. 35.—Esp. of the election of believers to the divine favor (eccl. Lat.), Vulg. Rom. 9, 11; id. 1 Thess. 1, 4.

electo1.full: ēlecto, āre, v. freq. a. elicio, to get out artfully, worm out a secret (a Plautin. word), Plaut. As. 2, 2, 29; id. Merc. 1, 2, 111; cf.: electabo, eliciam, Paul. ex Fest. p. 76, 6.

electo2.full: ēlecto, āre, v. freq. a. eligo, to choose, select: legionem, Plaut. Truc. 2, 6, 27.

elector1.full: ēlector, ōris, m. id., a chooser, selecter, Auct. Her. 4, 4, 7.

elector2.full: ēlector, ŏris, m., = ἠλέκτωρ, the shining sun, Plin. 37, 2, 11, § 31; Isid. Orig. 16, 24, 1.
elector2.short: ēlector, ŏris, m., = ἠλέκτωρ, the shining sun, Plin.

electra.full: Ēlectra, ae (nom. with long a, Prop. 2, 14, 5 (3, 6, 5 M.); Ov. F. 4, 177; Cic. Arat. 36; acc.: Electrān, Ov. Tr. 2, 395; id. F. 4, 32; 174), f., = Ἠλέκτρα. Daughter of Atlas and Pleione, one of the seven Pleiades, and mother of Dardanus by Jupiter, Ov. F. 4, 31 sq.; 174; Verg. A. 8, 135; Serv. ib. 7, 207; 10, 272; Hyg. Fab. 155 and 192. —Hence, ēlectrĭus, a, um, adj.: tellus, i. e. Samothrace, Val. Fl. 2, 431.— Daughter of Agamemnon and Clytemnestra, and sister of Orestes, Prop. 2, 14, 5 (3, 6,

electreus.full: ēlectrĕus, a, um, adj. electrum, made of amber: nummi, Lampr. Alex. Sev. 25.

electrifer.full: ēlectrĭfer, ĕra, ĕrum, adj. electrumfero, producing amber, abounding in amber: alni, Claud. Fescenn. 12, 14.

electrinus.full: ēlectrīnus, a, um, adj. electrum, of amber, made of amber (post-class.): patera, Treb. Poll. XXX. Tyr. 13: vasa, Dig. 34, 2, 32, § 5: anuli, Marc. Empir. 8.

electrius.full: Ēlectrĭus, a, um, v. Electra, I.

electrix.full: ēlectrix, īcis, f. elector, she that selects or chooses, Vulg. Sap. 8, 4.

electrum.full: ēlectrum, i, n., = ἤλεκτρον. Amber (pure Lat. succinum), Plin. 37, 2, 11, § 31; Ov. M. 15, 316.—Plur., Verg. E. 8, 54. — Meton., an amber ball, carried by Roman ladies in their hands to keep them cool.—Plur., Ov. M. 2, 365; cf. Böttig. Sabina, II. p. 210.— A mixed metal (natural or artificial) resembling amber in color, Plin. 33, 4, 23, § 81 al.; Isid. Orig. 16, 24, 2; Verg. A. 8, 402; 624; Sil. 1, 229.— Meton., an article made of amber, Mart. 8, 51; Juv. 14, 307.

electrus1.full: ēlectrus, a, um, adj. electrum, of amber: nummi, Lampr. Alex. Sev. 25, 9.

electrus2.full: Ēlectrus, i, m., son of Perseus and father of Alcmena, Plaut. Am. prol. 99; called also Electryon, Hyg. Fab. 244.
electrus2.short: Ēlectrus, i, m., son of Perseus and father of Alcmena, Plaut.

electus1.full: ēlectus, a, um, Part. and P. a., choice, excellent; v. eligo.

electus2.full: ēlectus, ūs, m. eligo, a choice: necis, Ov. H. 2, 144 Loers. N. cr.

eleemosyna.full: ĕlĕēmŏsўna, ae, f., = ἐλεημοσύνη, alms (eccl. Lat.), Tert. Patient. 7; Aug. Civ. D. 21, 27; Vulg. Matt. 6, 2 al.

elegans.full: ēlĕgans (in some MSS. eligans; cf. Beier Cic. Orr. Fragmm. p. 105), antis, adj. prob. collat. form of eligens, from eligo, Cic. N. D. 2, 28, 72. In the ante-class. period in a bad sense, luxurious, effeminate, fastidious, nice: elegans homo non dicebatur cum laude; sed id fere verbum ad aetatem M. Catonis vitii, non laudis fuit ... ex quibus verbis (Catonis) apparet, elegantem dictum antiquitus non ab ingenii elegantia, sed qui nimis lecto amoenoque cultu victuque esset, etc., Gell. 11, 2, 1; cf

elegantia.full: ēlĕgantia, ae, f. elegans. * A being nice or particular; exquisiteness, fastidiousness (ante-class. and very rare): ejus elegantia meam extemplo speciem spernat, Plaut. Mil. 4, 6, 20.—Far more freq., Taste, propriety, refinement, grace, elegance (cf.: gustus, sapor, judicium). With gen.: tu eloquentiam ab elegantia doctrinae segregandam putes, Cic. de Or. 1, 2, 5: vitae, Tac. A. 14, 19: morum, id. ib. 5, 8: capilli (with venustas oris), Plin. 35, 10, 36, § 67: ac subtilitas operum, id. 16, 15, 2

elegatus.full: ĕlĕgātus, i, m., an unknown kind of fish, Aus. Epigr. 4, 59.
elegatus.short: ĕlĕgātus, i, m., an unknown kind of fish, Aus.

elegi.full: ĕlĕgi, ōrum, m., = ἔλεγοι, elegiac verses, an elegy, Tib. 2, 4, 13; Prop. 4 (5), 1, 135; Hor. C. 1, 33, 3; id. Ep. 2, 2, 91; id. A. P. 77; Ov. F. 2, 3; Juv. 1, 4; Tac. Or. 10 al.
elegi.short: ĕlĕgi, ōrum, m., = ἔλεγοι, elegiac verses, an elegy, Tib.

elegia.full: ĕlĕgīa (ĕlĕgēa, in Ov. ĕlĕgēĭă), ae, f., = ἐλεγεία. An elegy: form elegia, Quint. 10, 1, 58; 93; Stat. S. 1, 2, 7; Mart. 5, 30, 4; Aus. Parent. 7, 1; form elegea, Quint. 1, 8, 6; form elegeia, Ov. Am. 3, 1, 7; 3, 9, 3; id. R. Am. 379.— A kind of reed: est et obliqua harundo, non in excelsitatem nascens, sed juxta terram fruticis modo se spargens, suavissima in teneritate animalibus: vocatur a quibusdam elegia, Plin. 16, 36, 66, § 167.

elegiacus.full: ĕlĕgī^ăcus, a, um, adj., = ἐλεγιακός, elegiac: carmen, Diom. p. 507 P.; Serv. p. 1824 ib.; Mart. Cap. 5, 168.
elegiacus.short: ĕlĕgī^ăcus, a, um, adj., = ἐλεγιακός, elegiac: carmen, Diom.

elegidarion.full: ĕlĕgīdārĭon, ii, n. elegidion, a short elegy, Petr. 109, 8.

elegidion.full: ĕlĕgīdĭon, ii, n., = ἐλεγείδιον, a short elegy, Pers. 1, 51.
elegidion.short: ĕlĕgīdĭon, ii, n., = ἐλεγείδιον, a short elegy, Pers.

elegion.full: ĕlĕgīon (also ĕlĕgēon), ii, n., = ἐλεγεῖον, an elegiac poem, an elegy, Aus. Epigr. 94, 2.—In plur., id. Parent. 29, 2.
elegion.short: ĕlĕgīon (also ĕlĕgēon), ii, n., = ἐλεγεῖον, an elegiac poem, an elegy, Aus.

elego.full: ē-lēgo, āvi, 1, v. a., to convey away (from the family) by bequest, to bequeath away, Petr. 43, 5; Gai. Inst. 2, 215.

elegus1.full: ĕlĕgus, a, um, adj., = ἔλεγος, elegiac: metrum, Diom. p. 502 P.
elegus1.short: ĕlĕgus, a, um, adj., = ἔλεγος, elegiac: metrum, Diom.

eleis.full: Ēlēïs, ĭdis, f., adj., v. Elis, II. C.

eleleus.full: Ĕlĕleus, ei, m., = Ἐλελεύς [from ἐλελεῦ, the cry of the Bacchantes], a surname of Bacchus, Ov. M. 4, 15.—Hence, ĕlĕlēĭdes = Bacchae, Ov. H. 4, 47.
eleleus.short: Ĕlĕleus, ei, m., = Ἐλελεύς [from ἐλελεῦ, the cry of the Bacchantes], a surname of Bacchus, Ov.

elelisphacos.full: ĕlĕlisphăcos, i, m., = ἐλελίσφακος, a kind of sage, Plin. 22, 25, 71, § 146; 25, 10, 73, § 120; 26, 15, 89, § 150.
elelisphacos.short: ĕlĕlisphăcos, i, m., = ἐλελίσφακος, a kind of sage, Plin.

elementarius.full: ĕlĕmentārĭus, a, um, adj. elementum, II., belonging to the elements or rudiments, elementary (post-Aug. and very rare): senex, an old schoolmaster, Sen. Ep. 36: litterae, elementary knowledge, Capitol. Pert. 1.

elementicius.full: ĕlĕmentīcĭus or -tĭus, a, um, adj. id., elementary, elemental: substantiae, Tert. de Anima, 32.

elementum.full: ĕlĕmentum, i, n. root al-, to nourish; Gr. ἄν-αλ-τος, ἄλσος; Lat. alo, alimentum, etc.; cf. Sanscr. al-akā, a girl, a first principle, element (cf.: initium, principium, exordium, primordium); Gr. στοιχεῖον. Lit., in plur.: nec de elementis video dubitari quatuor esse ea, Plin. 2, 5, 4, § 10; Lucr. 1, 827; 913; 2, 393 et saep.; Cic. Ac. 1, 7, 26; Sen. Q. N. 3, 12 sq.; Quint. 2, 17, 38; 3, 8, 31; Ov. M. 15, 237; 1, 29; Vulg. 2 Pet. 3, 10.—In sing., Plin. 10, 69, 88, § 191; 11, 36, 42, § 119; 31,

elenchus.full: ĕlenchus, i, m., = ἔλεγχος. A costly trinket, ear-pendant, Plin. 9, 35, 56, § 113; Juv. 6, 459; Dig. 34, 2, 32, § 8; cf. Boettig. Sabina II. p. 56.— Plur., part of the title of a work of M. Pompilius Andronicus: adeo inops ut coactus est praecipuum illud opusculum suum, annalium Ennii elenchorum XVI. milibus nummum vendere, etc., prob. a review, refutation, Suet. Gram. 8.

elentesco.full: ē-lentesco, ĕre, v. inch. n. [lenteo], to become clammy or soft: panis, Cael. Aur. Acut. 2, 18.

elephantiasis.full: ĕlĕphantĭăsis (-tĭōsis, Veg. A. V. 4, 3, 4; August. de Gen. ad Lit. 9, 10), is, f., = ἐλεφαντίασις, a very virulent kind of leprosy, elephantiasis, Plin. 26, 1, 5, § 7 sq.; 20, 10, 42, § 109; 20, 14, 52, § 144; Veg. A. V. 1, 9; 1, 16; 4, 3, 4 (in Cels. 3, 25, written as Greek). Also called ĕlĕphas, q. v., and ĕlĕphantĭa, ae, Scrib. Comp. 250; and ĕlĕphantĭcus morbus, Isid. Orig. 4, 8, 12. One who labors under it is called ĕlĕphantĭăcus, Firm. Math. 8, 19 fin.; Hier. in Ezech. 6, 18, 6; and ĕlĕph

elephanticus.full: elephanticus, i, v. preced. art. fin.

elephantine.full: Ĕlĕphantīne, ēs, f., = Ἐλεφαντίνη, a small but very fertile island of the Nile, in the Thebaid, with a city of the same name, now Jezyret-Assuan, Mel. 1, 9, 2; 9; Varr. R. R. 1, 7, 6; Tac. A. 2, 61; Plin. 24, 17, 102, § 163.—Also called Elĕphantis, ĭdis, f., Plin. 5, 9, 10, § 59; Vitr. 8, 2, 6.
elephantine.short: Ĕlĕphantīne, ēs, f., = Ἐλεφαντίνη, a small but very fertile island of the Nile, in the Thebaid, with a city of the same name, now Jezyret-Assuan, Mel.

elephantinus.full: ĕlĕphantĭnus, a, um, adj. elephas. Belonging to the elephant: tergum, Mel. 1, 5, 2.— = ἐλεφάντινος, pure Lat. eburnĕus, of ivory: liber, consisting of ivory tablets, Vop. Tacit. 8: atramentum, ivoryblack, Plin. 35, 6, 25, § 42: compositio (emplastri), Cels. 5, 19, 24 Daremb.

elephantis.full: Ĕlĕphantis, ĭdis (Gr. gen. ĭdos, Mart. 12, 43, 4), f., = Ἐλεφαντίς. An island of the Nile, v. Elephantine.— The name of a licentious Greek poetess, Suet. Tib. 43; Mart. 12, 43, 4; Plin. 28, 7, 24, § 81.

elephantus.full: ĕlĕphantus, i, and ĕlĕphās, antis (rarely ĕlĕphans, antis, Plin. 8, 1, 1, § 1; Hor. Ep. 2, 1, 196; of the second form the nom. sing., and of the first the oblique cases are most freq.), m. (fem., Plaut. Stich. 1, 3, 14), = ἐλέφας, an elephant.—Form elephantus, Plaut. Mil. 1, 1, 25; 30; id. Stich. 1, 3, 14; Ter. Eun. 3, 1, 23; Cic. N. D. 1, 35; 2, 47 fin.; id. de Sen. 9, 27; Liv. 44, 41; Plin. 6, 19, 22, § 66 et saep. Its tough hide suggests the expression: elephanti corio circumtentus, i. e. thi
elephantus.short: ĕlĕphantus, i, and ĕlĕphās, antis (rarely ĕlĕphans, antis, Plin.

eleus1.full: Ēlēus, a, um, v. Elis, II. A.

eleusin.full: Ĕleusin, īnis (acc. Eleusin, Front. Strat. 4, 7, 44; Lat. form Eleusina, ae, Front. Ep. ad Ver. 1, p. 178; Cl. Mam. Grat. Act. Jul. 9, 3; Oros. 1, 7; and acc. to MSS. Eleusinam in Cic. N. D. 1, 42, 119; Liv. 31, 25, 2; cf. Salaminam from Salamis, q. v.), f., = Ἐλευσίν, a very ancient city of Attica, famous for its mysteries of Ceres, now Lepsina, Plin. 4, 7, 11, § 23; Cic. Att. 6, 6, 2; id. N. D. 1, 42, 119; Liv. 31, 26; Tac. H. 4, 83; Ov. F. 4, 507; id. M. 7, 439; Stat. Th. 2, 382 al.— Hence, ĕ

eleusium.full: Eleusĭum, ii, f., a female name, Plaut. Aul. 2, 5, 7.
eleusium.short: Eleusĭum, ii, f., a female name, Plaut.

eleutheria.full: ĕleuthĕrĭa, ae, f., = ἐλευθερία, liberty, Plaut. Stich. 3, 1, 21.
eleutheria.short: ĕleuthĕrĭa, ae, f., = ἐλευθερία, liberty, Plaut.

eleutherius.full: Ĕleuthĕrĭus, i, m., = Ἐλευθέριος (Liberator), the surname of a god: Liber, Arn. 6, p. 207.—Hence, ĕleuthĕrĭa, ōrum, n., the festival of Jupiter Eleutherius, feast of liberty, celebrated in honor of the victory at Plataea, Plaut. Pers. 1, 1, 29.
eleutherius.short: Ĕleuthĕrĭus, i, m., = Ἐλευθέριος (Liberator), the surname of a god: Liber, Arn.

eleutherocilices.full: Ĕleuthĕrŏcĭlĭces, um, m. (free Cilicians), a people (probably the aborigines) in the mountains of Cilicia, Cic. Att. 5, 20, 5; id. Fam. 15, 4, 10.

elevatio.full: ēlĕvātĭo, ōnis, f. elevo. A lifting up, raising (late Lat.): manuum, Vulg. Psa. 140, 2 al.— Trop. Gram. t. t., the elevation: vocis (= ἄρσις, opp. depositio), Mart. Cap. 9, § 974; Isid. 1, 16, 21.— Rhet. t. t., a lessening, disparaging; a species of irony, Quint. 9, 2, 50; Mart. Cap. 5, § 525.

elevator.full: ēlĕvātor, ōris, m. id., one who raises up, a deliverer (eccl. Lat.): meus (deus), Vulg. 2 Reg. 22, 3.

elevo.full: ē-lĕvo, no perf., ātum, 1, v. a. Lit., to lift up, raise (very rare): contabulationem, Caes. B. C. 2, 9, 5 and 7: lumbos in altum, App. M. 4, p. 143: arcam, Vulg. Gen. 7, 17.—Poet.: elevat hunc pluma, i. e. turns into a bird, Claud. Eutr. 1, 295: aura preces, i. e. carry away, disperse, = auferat, dissipet, Prop. 1, 8, 12: fructum, to gather in, Col. 3, 21, 5: statura elevata, i. e. tall, Capit. Ant. Phil. 13.—More freq., Trop. To lighten, alleviate: aegritudinem (with obtundere), Cic. Tusc. 3,

elias1.full: Ēlĭas, ădis, v. Elis, II. D.

elias2.full: Ēlīās (Helias), ae, and Elia, ae, m., Elijah, a prophet of the Jews: form Elias, Lact. 4, 11, 6; form Elia, Prud. Cath. 7, 27.
elias2.short: Ēlīās (Helias), ae, and Elia, ae, m., Elijah, a prophet of the Jews: form Elias, Lact.

elices.full: ēlĭces, um, m. e-liquor; cf. colliciae, a trench for drawing off water, a drain, Col. 2, 8, 3; 11, 2, 82; cf. Paul. ex Fest. p. 76, 2 Müll.; Serv. Verg. G. 1, 109; v. also elix.

elicio.full: ē-lĭcĭo, lĭcŭi and lexi (elicuit, Caes. B. C. 3, 100, 2: elexisse, Arn. 5, p. 154), lĭcìtum (part. elicitus, Stat. Th. 4, 414; Luc. 9, 932; Vell. 2, 104, 4), 3, v. a. lacio, to draw out, entice out, to lure forth, to bring out, to elicit (class.). Lit. In gen.: aliquem hinc foras, Plaut. Bacch. 3, 1, 17; cf. id. Men. 5, 6, 3: hostem ex paludibus silvisque, Caes. B. G. 7, 32, 2: omnes citra flumen, id. ib. 6, 8, 2: hostes in suum locum, id. ib. 5, 50, 3: aliquem ad pugnam. id. B. C. 3, 38. 1; 3,

elicitus.full: ēlĭcĭtus, a, um, Part., v. elicio.

elicius.full: Ēlĭcĭus, ii, m. elicio, I. B., a surname of Jupiter, because from him celestial signs or omens were obtained (or, acc. to others, because he was called down by incantations), Liv. 1, 20 fin.; Ov. F. 3, 328; Varr. L. L. 6, § 94 Müll.; Liv. 1, 31, 8; Plin. 2, 53, 54, § 140.

elido.full: ē-līdo, si, sum, 3, v. a. laedo. To knock, strike, or dash out, to tear out, to force out, squeeze out. Lit.: aurigam e curru, Cic. Rep. 2, 41: oculos, Plaut. Rud. 3, 2, 45; Verg. A. 8, 261: ignem velut e silice, Plin. 11, 37, 86, § 214; cf.: flammas ex sese, id. 18, 35, 84, § 358: ignes nubibus, Ov. M. 6, 696: aërem lituis, Luc. 7, 476: partum, i. e. to produce abortion, Cels. 1, 7; Plin. 25, 3, 7, § 25: litteras, to strike out by syncope, to elide, Gell. 5, 12, 5: vina praelis, i. e. to press

eligo.full: ē-lĭgo, lēgi, lectum, 3, v. a. lĕgo, to pick out, choose, elect (class.; esp. in the trop. sense; cf.: coöpto, designo, deligo, seligo): pedes e capite et e collo pullorum, Varr. R. R. 3, 9, 14: uvam ad edendum (with legere), id. ib. 1, 54, 2: herbas, to pluck up, to weed out, id. ib. 1, 47; Col. 4, 5; cf. trop., Cic. Tusc. 3, 34, 83 and 84: ex malis minima, Cic. Off. 3, 1, 3: ut de tribus Antoniis eligas quem velis, id. Phil. 10, 2, 5: a multis commodissimum quodque, id. Inv. 2, 2, 5: ut in com

elimatio.full: ēlīmātĭo, ōnis, f. elimo. Prop., a filing away: ligni, Marc. Emp. 4, 12.— Transf., an elucidation, explanation, Justin. praef. 3 de Emend. Cod. § 3.— A reducing, lessening: carnis, Cael. Aur. Tard. 5, 11, 138.

elimator.full: ēlīmātor, ōris, m. id., a cleanser, purifier (eccl. Lat.); of Christ, Tert. adv. Marc. 4, 35.

elimea.full: Ĕlĭmēa or -īa, ae, f., = Ἐλίμεια, a district to the southwest of Macedonia, Liv. 31, 40; 42, 53 al.; also called Elimiōtis, ĭdis, f., Liv. 45, 30, 6.
elimea.short: Ĕlĭmēa or -īa, ae, f., = Ἐλίμεια, a district to the southwest of Macedonia, Liv.

elimes.full: ēlīmes ex-limes, ἄποικος, παρόριος, Gloss. Philox.

elimino.full: ē-līmĭno, no perf., ātum, 1, v. a. limen, to turn out of doors (a poet. word, mostly ante- and post-class.). Lit.: aliquem, Pac., Att., and Pompon. ap. Non. 38, 31 sq.; cf.: aliquem soli patrii finibus, to banish, Sid. Ep. 4, 10: se, to go out, Enn. ap. Non. 39, 4; Varr. ib. 292, 23: gradus, to move out, an old poet ap. Quint. 8, 3, 31.— * Trop.: dicta foras, to blab, Hor. Ep. 1, 5, 25.

elimo.full: ē-līmo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a., to file up, viz., Prop.: elimata scobis, filings, Plin. 34, 18, 50, § 170.— Transf., to polish. Lit., Ov. M. 4, 176; Macr. Somn. Scip. 1, 12 fin.: dentes, to clean, Tert. Poen. 11.— To elaborate, cultivate; to finish, perfect: σχόλιον aliquod, Att. ap. Cic. Att. 16, 7, 3; cf. Quint. 2, 7, 5: animum, Aug. contra Acad. 2, 7: elimati, i. q. eruditi, Gell. praef. § 19: Aeneida, id. 17, 10, 7.— To lessen, diminish: vires, Cael. Aur. Tard. 2, 14, 217.—Hence, ēlī-mātus, a,

elimpido.full: ē-limpĭdo (elym-), āvi, 1, v. a., to cleanse out, make quite clean (late Lat.): vulnera, Veg. Vet. 2, 27, 4; 4, 28, 2; 1, 26, 2.

elinguis.full: ē-linguis, e, adj. lingua. Lit., deprived of a tongue, Aus. Ep. 23, 14; Cassiod. Hist. Eccl. 6, 15.— Transf. In gen., speechless, Cic. Fl. 10, 22; Liv. 10, 19 (with mutus); id. post Red. 3, 7 (with mutus and tacitus); Gell. 5, 1, 9.— Pregn., without eloquence, Cic. Brut. 26, 100; Cels. praef. med.; Tac. Or. 36 fin. (opp. disertus).

elinguo.full: ē-linguo, āre, v. a. id., to deprive of the tongue, Plaut. Aul. 2, 2, 72; cf.: ELINGVATVS linguam amisit, Fronto de Diff. Voc. p. 2200 fin. P.

elino.full: ē-lĭno, lēvi, 3, v. a., to bedaub, defile: vestimenta luto, Lucil. ap. Non. 103, 30 (maculavit, Non.; but perh. more correctly, to cleanse completely).

eliquamen.full: ēlĭquāmen, false read. in Col. 8, 14, 3, for liquamina.

eliquatio.full: ēlĭquātĭo, ōnis, f. eliquo, a liquefying, dissolving: materiae, Cael. Aur. Acut. 2, 32, 166.

eliquatus.full: ēlĭquātus, a, um, adj. id., clear.— Comp.: sensa doctrinae, Mar. Mercat. in Verb. Jul. 9, 4.

eliquesco.full: ē-lĭquesco, ĕre, v. inch. n. [liqueo], to become liquid by being pressed out: olea, Varr. R. R. 1, 55, 4.

eliquium.full: ēlĭquĭum, ii, n. eliquo (post-class.). An outlet; in plur., Sol. 18, 1.— A decrease, diminution; in plur.: lunae (opp. adauctus), Sol. 23, § 22.

eliquo.full: ē-lĭquo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. To clarify, strain (post-Aug.). Lit.: vinum a faecibus, Col. 12, 27; cf. id. 12, 19, 4; Sen. Q. N. 3, 26.— Trop.: aliquid plorabile, to recite slowly or without energy, * Pers. 1, 35: canticum ore tereti semihiantibus labellis, App. Flor. 2, 15, p. 351, 11.— (With the notion of the simplex predominating.) To cause to flow clearly, to pour forth: fluviales aquas (mons), App. M. 10, p. 253.—Fig.: in unum necesse est summitas magnitudinis aliquetur, Tert. adv. Marc. 1,

elis.full: Ēlis, ĭdis (acc. Elin, Ov. M. 2, 679; 5, 608; 12, 550; Stat. S. 2, 6, 47; Plin. 2, 71, 73, § 181; 7, 20, 20, § 84: Elidem, Nep. Alcib. 4, 4; abl. usually Elide; but Eli, Cic. N. D. 3, 23, 59; id. Fam. 13, 26, 2), f., = Ἦλις; also ālis, Alidis = Dor. Ἀλις (Plaut. Capt. prol. 9, 26, 31; cf. Aleus, id. ib. 27), the most westerly district of the Peloponnesus, with a capital of the same name, in the vicinity of which Olympia was situated, Mel. 2, 3, 4; Plin. 4, 6, 10, § 22; Cic. Div. 1, 41; Verg. A

elisio.full: ēlīsĭo, ōnis, f. elido. A striking out, forcing out: lacrimae, pressing out, Sen. Ep. 99, 18.— In the later grammarians, the striking out of a letter, elision.

elissa.full: Ĕlissa or Ĕlīsa, ae, f., = Ἔλισσα, another name (occurring only in poetry) for Dido, Verg. A. 4, 335; 610; 5, 3; Ov. Am. 2, 18, 31; id. F. 3, 553 al.—Hence, ĕlis-saeus (Elīsaeus), a, um, adj., poet. for Carthaginian: patres, Sil. 6, 346: tyrannus, i. e. Hannibal, id. 2, 239: lacerti, id. 15, 524.
elissa.short: Ĕlissa or Ĕlīsa, ae, f., = Ἔλισσα, another name (occurring only in poetry) for Dido, Verg.

elisus.full: ēlīsus, a, um, Part., from elido.
elisus.short: ēlīsus, a, um, Part., from elido.

elius.full: Elius, i, v. Elis, II. B.

elix.full: ēlix, ĭcis, m. elicio, a channel for diverting a stream: elix, ἀναπνοὴ ὀχετοῦ, Gloss.; usually in plur., v. elices.

elixatura.full: ēlixātūra, ae, f. elixo, a thorough boiling; concr., any thing boiled, Apic. 9, 1 al.

elixo.full: ēlixo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. elixus, to boil thoroughly, seethe (late Lat.), Apic. 2, 1; 3, 6 al.

elixus.full: ē-lixus, a, um, adj., lix, thoroughly boiled, boiled, seethed. Lit., Varr. ap. Non. 62, 14; Plin. 20, 6, 23, § 54; Hor. S. 2, 2, 74; Juv. 3, 294; 13, 85; cf. the punning use of the word, Plaut. Poen. 1, 2, 67; id. Most. 5, 1, 66.— Transf., qs. sodden, i. e., soaked, wet through: calcei, Varr. ap. Non. 48, 27: balneator, Mart. 3, 7: nates, i. e. quite flabby after the bath, Pers. 4, 40.
elixus.short: ē-lixus, a, um, adj., lix, thoroughly boiled, boiled, seethed.

elleborine.full: ellĕbŏrīne (hell-), es, f., = ἑλλεβορίνη, a kind of hellebore, Plin. 13, 20, 35, § 114; id. 27, 9, 52, § 76.
elleborine.short: ellĕbŏrīne (hell-), es, f., = ἑλλεβορίνη, a kind of hellebore, Plin.

elleborismus.full: ellĕbŏrismus, i, m., = ἑλλεβορισμός, a purgative made from hellebore: destillandus etiam elleborismus, Cael. Aur. Tard. 1, 4, 108.
elleborismus.short: ellĕbŏrismus, i, m., = ἑλλεβορισμός, a purgative made from hellebore: destillandus etiam elleborismus, Cael.

elleborites.full: ellebŏrītes (hell-), ae, m., = ἑλλεβορίτης, hellebore wine, Plin. 14, 16, 19, § 110.
elleborites.short: ellebŏrītes (hell-), ae, m., = ἑλλεβορίτης, hellebore wine, Plin.

elleboro.full: ellĕbŏro (hell-) (no perf. nor sup.), are, v. a. elleborus, to purify with hellebore, Cael. Aur. Tard. 4, 3, 77.

elleborosus.full: ellĕbŏrōsus (hell-), a, um, adj. id., in need of hellebore (i. e.), out of his senses: Gr. Quaeso, sanun es? Tr. Sum elleborosus. Gr. Ut ego cerritus, Plaut. Rud. 4, 3, 67.

elleborus.full: ellĕbŏrus (hell-), i, m., and ellĕ-bŏrum (hell-), i, n., hellebore, in pure Lat. veratrum, a plant much used by the ancients as a remedy for mental diseases, epilepsy, etc.; the best grew on the island of Anticyra, in the Aegean Sea, Pl. 25, 5, 21; id. 25, 13, 94; Gell. 17, 15; Plaut. Ps. 4, 7, 89; Verg. G. 3, 451; Hor. Ep. 2, 2, 137; Cels. 2, 13; Sen. Ep. 83, 25.
elleborus.short: ellĕbŏrus (hell-), i, m., and ellĕ-bŏrum (hell-), i, n., hellebore, in pure Lat.

ellipsis.full: ellipsis (en-l-), is, f., = ἔλλειψις, in rhet. lang., an ellipsis (pure Lat. detractio), Quint. 8, 6, 21; cf. id. 1, 5, 40; Schol. Juv. 1, 89.
ellipsis.short: ellipsis (en-l-), is, f., = ἔλλειψις, in rhet.

ellychnium.full: ellychnĭum, ii, n., = ἐλλύχνιον, a lamp-wick, Plin. 23, 4, 41, § 84; 28, 11, 47, § 168; Vitr. 8, 1; Stat. S. 4, 9, 29.
ellychnium.short: ellychnĭum, ii, n., = ἐλλύχνιον, a lamp-wick, Plin.

eloco.full: ē-lŏco, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a., to let or hire out, to let out to farm: fundum, Cic. Verr. 2, 3, 22; cf. bovem, Col. 1, 7, 6: funus, Plin. 21, 3, 7, § 10; cf.: sese curandum, id. 26, 1, 3, § 4.—Transf.: gentem Judaeorum, i. q. ejus vectigalia, Cic. Fl. 28 fin.

elocutilis.full: ēlŏcūtĭlis, e, adj. eloquor, oratorical: facundia, App. M. 11, p. 258, 12.

elocutio.full: ēlŏcūtĭo, ōnis, f. id.. Prop., a speaking out, utterance, expression: pluralis, Dig. 22, 5, 12.— Transf., in rhet. lang., oratorical delivery, elocution; the Gr. φράσις (cf.: locutio, dictio, stilus, etc.), Cic. Inv. 1, 7, 9; Quint. prooem. § 22; 8 prooem. § 13; 8, 1, 1 et saep.

elocutorius.full: ēlŏcūtōrĭus, a, um, adj. id., pertaining to oratorical expression: elocu-toria, ae, and elocutrix, īcis, f., as a translation of ῥητορική, rhetoric, Quint. 2, 14, 2.

elocutus.full: ēlŏcūtus, a, um, Part., from eloquor.
elocutus.short: ēlŏcūtus, a, um, Part., from eloquor.

elogio.full: ēlŏgĭo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. elogium, to describe briefly, to state (late Lat.), Cael. Aur. Tard. 2, 1, 16; 5, 4, 66.

elogium.full: ē-lŏgĭum, ii, n. logus; cf. Rost. Opusc. Plaut. I. p. 93 sq., an utterance, short saying, sentence.—In partic. A short maxim, saying: Solonis, Cic. de Sen. 20, 73.— An inscription on a tombstone (so most freq.), Cato ap. Gell. 3, 7, 19; Cic. de Sen. 17, 61; id. Fin. 2, 35; id. Tusc. 1, 14, 31; id. Pis. 29 fin.; Suet. Claud. 1 al. (Vide old examples of such Elogia in Orell. Inscr. 534 sq.) Also on doors, Plaut. Merc. 2, 3, 74; on the images of ancestors, Suet. Galb. 3; on votive tablets, id. Cali

elonginquo.full: ē-longinquo, āvi, 1, v. a. and n. e-longinquus, to remove, Ambros. Enarr. in Psa. 43, § 45.

elongo.full: ēlongo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. and n. e-longe. Act., to remove, keep aloof (late Lat.): auxilium tuum a me, Vulg. Psa. 21, 20: judicium a nobis, id. Isa. 59, 9 al.— To prolong, protract: diem ejus, Vulg. Isa. 14, 1; cf. elongo, μακρύνω, ἀφίστημι, Gloss. Philox.— Neutr., to withdraw, depart: ecce elongavi fugiens, Vulg. Psa. 54, 7; id. Sir. 35, 22; id. Jer. 2, 5; Ambros. in Luc. 3, § 32.

eloquens.full: ēlŏquens, entis, Part. and P. a., from eloquor.

eloquenter.full: ēlŏquenter, adv., eloquently, v. eloquor, P. a. fin.

eloquentia.full: ēlŏquentĭa, ae, f. eloquor, a being eloquent, eloquence, Cic. Part. 23, 79; id. de Or. 1, 5, 19; 1, 32, 146; Quint. 9, 17, 2; 2, 16, 7; Tac. Or. 8, 30 et saep.

eloquium.full: ēlŏquĭum, ii, n. id.. In Aug. poets, and their imitators among prose writers, for eloquentia, eloquence, * Hor. A. P. 217; * Verg. A. 11, 383; Ov. Tr. 1, 9, 46; id. M. 13, 63; 322 al.; Vell. 2, 68, 1; Plin. 11, 17, 18, § 55.— In late Lat., declaration, communication in gen., Diom. p. 413 P.; Mamert. Pan. Maxim. 9: eloquia pulchritudinis, fine words, Vulg. Gen. 49, 21; id. Prov. 4, 20 al.

eloquor.full: ē-lŏquor, ēlŏcūtus (or ēloquūtus), 3, v. dep. a., to speak out, speak plainly, to utter; to pronounce, declare, state, express: eloqui hoc est, omnia quae mente conceperis promere atque ad audientes perferre, Quint. 8 prooem. § 15 (class.). In gen. (so most freq. in Plautus). With acc.: id quod sentit eloqui non posse, Cic. Tusc. 1, 3, 6; so, praeclare cogitata mentis, id. Brut. 72 fin.: audita, Plaut. Am. 1, 1, 45: nomen meum, id. ib. prol. 18: argumentum hujus tragoediae, id. ib. 51; 96: rem,

elotus.full: ēlōtus, a, um, Part., from elavo.
elotus.short: ēlōtus, a, um, Part., from elavo.

elpenor.full: Elpēnor, ŏris, m., = Ἐλπήνωρ, one of the companions of Ulysses, whom Circe changed into swine, Juv. 15, 22; being afterwards disenchanted, he fell from a roof while drunk, and broke his neck, Ov. Tr. 3, 4, 19; id. M. 14, 252; id. Ib. 483.
elpenor.short: Elpēnor, ŏris, m., = Ἐλπήνωρ, one of the companions of Ulysses, whom Circe changed into swine, Juv.

elpinice.full: Elpĭnīce, ēs, f., sister of Cimon, Nep. Cim. 1, 2.
elpinice.short: Elpĭnīce, ēs, f., sister of Cimon, Nep.

eluacrus.full: ēlŭācrus, a, um, adj. eluo, for washing out or rinsing: labrum, a wash-tub, Cato R. R. 10, 4, and 11, 3 dub. (al. vinarium).

eluceo.full: ē-lūcĕo, xi, 2, v. n., to shine out, shine forth (class.; esp. freq. in the trop. sense and in Cic.). Lit.: inter flammas circulus elucens, Cic. Rep. 6, 16, 16.—Poet., of the golden glittering of bees, Verg. G. 4, 98: illa flamma, quae ex L. Marcii capite eluxit, Val. Max. 1, 6, 2.— Trop., to shine out, show itself; to be apparent, manifest (cf.: appareo, exsisto, effero): scintilla ingenii jam tum elucebat in puero, Cic. Rep. 2, 21; cf. id. Cael. 19, 45; id. Off. 1, 29, 103; 1, 28, 98; id. de O

elucesco.full: ēlūcesco, ĕre, 3, v. inch. n. [eluceo], to shine forth, begin to shine (late Lat.), August. Retr. 1, 13: elucesco, παρεκφαινειν, Gloss.—Esp., to dawn: donec dies elucescat, Vulg. 2 Pet. 1, 19.—Impers.: cum jam elucesceret, Vulg. 1 Reg. 9, 26.

elucido.full: ē-lūcĭdo, āre, v. a. lucidus, to light, enlighten (late Lat.): aliquem, Vulg. Sir. 24, 31.

elucifico.full: ē-lūcĭfĭco, āre, v. a. lucificus, to deprive of light, to blind, Laber. ap. Non. 106, 21; id. ap. Gell. 10, 17 fin., al. lucificare.

eluctabilis.full: ēluctābĭlis, e, adj. eluctor, from which one may extricate one's self: aquae, Sen. Q. N. 6, 8, 4.

eluctatio.full: ēluctātĭo, ōnis, f. id., a struggling, struggle.—Trop.: adversus mala, Lact. 3, 11.

eluctor.full: ē-luctor, ātus, 1, v. dep. n. and a. (perh. not ante-Aug.). Neutr., to struggle out, force one's way out: aqua omnis, Verg. G. 2, 244; so of streams, Sen. Q. N. 4, 2; Luc. 2, 219.—Trop.: ipse, compositus alias, et velut eluctantium verborum, promptius eloquebatur, i. e. hesitating in speech, unready, Tac. A. 4, 31.— Act., to struggle out of any thing; also, to surmount a difficulty, to obtain by striving: tot ac tam validas manus, Liv. 24, 26 fin.: nives, Tac. H. 3, 59; cf.: locorum difficultate

elucubro.full: ē-lūcubro, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. (elucu-bror, deponent: epistolam, quam eram elucubratus, Cic. Att. 7, 19), to compose by lamplight, i. e. at night, with great labor, Cic. Brut. 90 fin.; Tac. Or. 9; Col. 10 praef. fin.

elucus.full: ē-lūcus, i, m. lux.—Prop., one who has been awake all night; hence, a drowsy or dreaming person, Gell. 4, 19, 1; cf. id. 16, 12, 3; Tert. Cor. Mil. 7; cf. Paul. ex Fest. p. 75, 17 Müll.

eludo.full: ē-lūdo, si, sum, 3, v. n. and a. * Neutr., to finish play, i. e. cease to sport or roll: ipsum autem mare sic terram appetens litoribus eludit, ut, etc., Cic. N. D. 2, 39, 100 (Bait. cludit): solebat Aquilius litus ita definire, qua fluctus eluderet, id. Top. 7, 31 (al. alluderet); cf. Quint. 5, 14, 34: eludere proprie gladiatorum est cum vicerint, et eludere est finem ludo imponere, Don. ad Ter. Eun. 1, 1, 10.— Act. To win from one at play (very rare).—Constr. aliquem or aliquem aliquid: anulus

elugeo.full: ē-lūgĕo, xi, 2, v. a., to mourn for any one, to be in mourning for (rare): virum (mulier), Dig. 3, 2, 10; ib. 11: patriam, Cic. Fam. 9, 20 fin.—With cognate acc.: luctum, Gell. 7, 5, 4.—Absol.: quid, cum eluxerunt, sumunt? have completed their time of mourning, Liv. 34, 7, 10.

elumbis.full: ē-lumbis, e, adj. lumbus, hip-shot, having the hip dislocated. Lit.: evulso lumbo, Paul. ex Fest. p. 76, 13 Müll. (dub.). — Trop., of style: Ciceronem male audisse a Bruto, ut ipsius verbis utar, tamquam fractum atque elumbem, i. e. enervated, Tac. Or. 18.—* Transf.: virus, i. e. that weakens, enervates, Prud. στεφ. 2, 216.

eluminatio.full: ēlūmĭnātĭo, an enlightening, φωτισμός, Gloss. Philox.

eluminatus.full: ē-lūmĭnātus, a, um, adj. lumen, deprived of light, blinded, Sid. Ep. 8, 11 fin.

eluo.full: ē-lŭo, ŭi, ūtum, 3, v. a., to wash out, rinse out; to wash off, wash clean (class.). Lit.: vascula, Plaut. Aul. 2, 3, 3: patinas, id. Capt. 4, 2, 66: argentum (the silver vessels, the plate), id. Ps. 1, 2, 29: bacas immundas, Col. 12, 52, 21; 6, 3, 4: os, Cels. 3, 4: maculas vestium, Plin. 20, 8, 28, § 72; cf. Plaut. Poen. 1, 1, 71; Cic. Verr. 2, 5, 46; id. Sest. 29, 63: purpureum colorem omnibus undis, Lucr. 6, 1077; so, colorem, Quint. 1, 1, 5; cf. atramentum, Plin. 35, 6, 25, § 43: aliquid ex

elusa.full: Ĕlŭsa, ae, f., a city in Gallia Aquitania, now Eauze, Claud. in Rufin. 1, 137; Amm. 15, 11, 14.—Hence,
elusa.short: Ĕlŭsa, ae, f., a city in Gallia Aquitania, now Eauze, Claud.

elusates.full: Elusātes, ium, m., a Gallic tribe in Aquitania, Caes. B. G. 3, 27; Plin. 4, 19, 33, § 108.
elusates.short: Elusātes, ium, m., a Gallic tribe in Aquitania, Caes.

elusco.full: ē-lusco, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. luscus, to make one-eyed, to deprive of an eye (late Lat.), Dig. 9, 2, 5, § 3; 10, 4, 17; 13, 3, 3 al.

elusus.full: ēlūsus, a, um, Part., from eludo.
elusus.short: ēlūsus, a, um, Part., from eludo.

elutio.full: ēlūtĭo, ōnis, f. eluo, a washing: panis, Cael. Aur. Tard. 1, 1, 12.

elutrio.full: ēlūtrĭo, no perf., ātum, 1, v. a. id., to wash out. Lit.: lintea, Laber. ap. Gell. 16, 7, 5: vellus, Plin. 9, 38, 62, § 133.—* Transf., to decant, rack off, Plin. 14, 17, 21, § 114.

elutus.full: ēlūtus, a, um, Part. and P. a., from eluo and elavo.

eluvies.full: ēlŭvĭes, em, e, f. eluo, a washing away of impurities, a flowing off, discharge. Lit., Plin. 2, 82, 84, § 197; Pall. 1, 40, 4; Juv. 3, 32: ventris, Lucil. ap. Non. 103, 33; Aur. Vict. Epit. 9 fin.— In gen., an overflowing, an inundation of a river, etc.: eluvie mons est deductus in aequor, Ov. M. 15, 267; Tac. A. 13, 57.— Meton., a chasm, abyss, ravine produced by the violent rushing of water, Curt. 5, 4 fin. (shortly before: vorago concursu cavata torrentium); 6, 4 fin.—In plur. (with voragines

eluvio.full: ēlŭvĭo, ōnis, f. id., older form of eluvies, a washing away, overflowing, inundation: aquarum eluviones, Cic. Div. 1, 49, 111: eluviones et exustiones terrarum, Cic. Rep. 6, 21, 23; id. Off. 2, 5, 16.

eluxurior.full: ē-luxŭrĭor, āri, v. dep. n., to put forth luxuriantly: vites pampinis, Col. Arb. 3, 2.

elymais.full: Ĕlymāis, ĭdis, f., = Ἐλυμαΐς, a district of Persia, in the west of the modern province of Iran, Plin. 6, 25, 28, § 111 al.— Hence, ĕlymaeus, a, um, adj., = Ἐλυμαῖος, Elymaean, Liv. 37, 40.—Plur. subst.: ĕlymaei, ōrum, m., the inhabitants of Elymaïs, Liv. 35, 48 al.
elymais.short: Ĕlymāis, ĭdis, f., = Ἐλυμαΐς, a district of Persia, in the west of the modern province of Iran, Plin.

elysii.full: Elysii, ōrum, m. A people of Eastern Germany, between the Oder and the Vistula, Tac. G. 43.— The Elysian Fields, v. the foll. II.

elysium.full: Ēlўsĭum, ii, n., = Ἠλύσιον, the abode of the blest, Elysium, Verg. A. 5, 735 Serv.; 6, 542; 744 al.; cf. Heyne Verg. A. 6, 675 sq.; and ejusd. libri Exc. VIII. p. 1019 Wagn.—Hence, ēlўsĭus, a, um, adj., Elysian: campi, Verg. G. 1, 38; Tib. 1, 3, 58; Ov. Ib. 175; cf. ager, Mart. 10, 101: plagae, id. 6, 58: domus, Ov. M. 14, 111; cf. sedes, Luc. 3, 12: Chaos, Stat. Th. 4, 520: rosae, Prop. 4 (5), 7, 60. puella, i. e. Proserpine, Mart. 10, 24.— Subst.: Elysii, ōrum, m. (sc. campi), the Elysian Fiel
elysium.short: Ēlўsĭum, ii, n., = Ἠλύσιον, the abode of the blest, Elysium, Verg.

em1.full: em, i. q. eum, v. is init.

em2.full: em, interj., = hem, Ter. Ad. 5, 3, 4; Varr. R. R. 1, 2, 5; 1, 56.

em3.full: em, interj., = en (freq. in Plaut. and Ter. in best MSS.), Plaut. Merc. 2, 2, 42; id. Bacch. 4, 8, 29; id. Trin. prol. 3 (v. Brix ad loc.); id. ib. 1, 2, 148; id. Most. 5, 2, 58; id. Men. 2, 1, 26; id. Am. 2, 2, 146 Ussing ad loc.; Ter. Eun. 3, 2, 6 al., v. en.

emaceratus.full: ē-măcĕrātus, a, um, Part. [macero], emaciated, Sen. Cons. ad Marc. 10 fin.

emacesco.full: ē-măcesco, cŭi, 3, v. inch. n., to become emaciated (very rare), Cels. 2, 2.

emacio.full: ē-măcĭo, no perf., ātum, 1, v. a., to waste away, make lean, emaciate (belonging to econom. lang.), Col. 2, 10, 25; 2, 10, 1; 4, 6, 3; Plin. 18, 10, 25, § 101 Sillig N. cr.

emacitas.full: ĕmācĭtas, ātis, f. emax, a propensity to buy, a desire to be always buying, Col. 4, 3, 1; Plin. Ep. 3, 7, 8.

emacresco.full: ē-macresco, crŭi, 3, v. inch. n., to grow lean, to become emaciated (very rare), Cels. 2, 4 and 5.

emaculo.full: ē-măcŭlo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a., to clear from spots, to purify (post-Aug.). Lit., Plin. 21, 19, 75, § 129; Gell. 6, 5, 9; App. Mag. p. 278; Macr. S. 7, 13.— Transf.: domum odoribus Arabicis, Amm. 29, 1.

emanatio.full: ēmānātĭo, onis, f. emano, an emanation (late Lat.), Vulg. Sap. 7, 25; Hilar. Synod. 20.

emancipatio.full: ēmancĭpātĭo (emancup-), ōnis, f. emancipo.—Jurid. t. t. In the strict sense of the term, the releasing of a son (by means of a thrice-repeated mancipatio and manumissio) from the patria potestas, so as to render him independent, emancipation (v. emancipo), Gai. Inst. 1, 132; Ulp. Fragm. 10, 1; Just. Inst. 1, 12, § 6; Quint. 11, 1, 65.— Transf. in gen. The formal surrender of any thing, the delivery of authority over a thing: fundorum, conveyance, Plin. Ep. 10, 3, 3.— Familiae, a fictitious alien

emancipator.full: ēmancĭpātor, ōris, m. id., an emancipator (post-class.), Prud. Cath. 7, 184.

emancipo.full: ē-mancĭpo (ēmancŭpo), āvi, ātum, 1, v. a.—Jurid. t. t. In the strict sense, to put out of the hand and power of the paterfamilias; to declare free and independent, to emancipate a son from the patria potestas by the thrice-repeated act of mancipatio and manumissio, Dig. 1, 132 sq.; Ulp. Fragm. 10, 1; Just. Inst. 1, 12, § 6; Liv. 7, 16; Plin. Ep. 4, 2, 2 et saep.; cf. Sandars, Just. Inst. introd. p. 37 sq.— In a wider sense, to give from under one's own power or authority into that of another. Pr

emanco.full: ē-manco, āvi, 1, v. a. mancus, to maim, Labien. ap. Sen. Contr. 5, 33 fin.

emaneo.full: ē-mănĕo, nsi, 2, v. n. * To stay without, remain beyond, Stat. Th. 7, 650.— Milit. t. t., to stay away beyond one's leave of absence, to exceed one's furlough, Dig. 49, 16, 3, § 4.

emano.full: ē-māno, āvi, ātum, 1, v. n., to flow out (class.; esp. freq. in the trop. signif. and in Cic.). Lit., Lucr. 3, 583; Cic. poët. Div. 2, 30; Col. 6, 32, 1; Gell. 19, 5, 6 al.— Trop. To spring out of, to arise, proceed, emanate from: alii quoque allo ex fonte praeceptores dicendi emanaverunt, Cic. Inv. 2, 2, 7; cf. id. Cael. 8, 19: ex quo (loco) vis omnis oportet emanet ratiocinationis, id. Inv. 1, 37, 67; cf. id. de Or. 1, 42, 189: hinc haec recentior Academia emanavit, id. ib. 3, 18 fin.: istinc

emansio.full: ēmansĭo, ōnis, f. emaneo, II., a remaining absent beyond one's furlough, Dig. 49, 16, 4, § 15.

emansor.full: ēmansor, ōris, m. id., one who exceeds his furlough, Dig. 49, 16, 3, § 2; ib. § 5 al.

emarcesco.full: ē-marcesco, -marcui, 3, v. inch. n., to wither away (very rare).—Trop., to dwindle away, disappear: auctoritas, Plin. 15, 29, 36, § 121: refugium, Hier. Ies. 5, 17, 4: cor meum, fainted, Vulg. Isa. 21, 4 al.† † emarcus, i a Gallic word, a kind of vine, producing a wine of middling quality, Col. 3, 2, 25 (called also marcus, Plin. 14, 2, 4, § 32).

emargino.full: ē-margĭno, āre, v. a., to deprive of its edge: ulcera, Plin. 28, 9, 41, § 147.

emasculator.full: ēmascŭlātor, ōris, m. emasculo, a pederast, App. Mag. p. 321, 40.

emasculo.full: ē-mascŭlo, āre, v. a. masculus, to castrate, emasculate (post-class.): asinum, App. M. 7, p. 198: sacerdotes herbis quibusdam, i. e. to render impotent, Serv. Verg. A. 6, 661.

emathia.full: Ēmăthĭa, ae, f., = Ἠμαθία, a district of Macedonia, Plin. 4, 10, 17, § 33; Liv. 44, 44, 5; Justin. 7, 1, 1.— In poet. meton. Macedonia, Verg. G. 4, 390.— Thessaly, and esp. for Pharsalia, Verg. G. 1, 492 Serv. and Heyne; v. the foll.— Derivv. ēmăthĭus, a, um, adj., Emathian, i. e. in poet. meton., Macedonian: Perses, Corn. Sever. ap. Sen. Suas. 7: campi, Ov. M. 5, 313: dux, i. e. Alexander, id. Tr. 3, 5, 39; of the same: manes, Stat. S. 3, 2, 117; cf. tecta, i. e. of Alexandria, Luc. 10, 58.— Th
emathia.short: Ēmăthĭa, ae, f., = Ἠμαθία, a district of Macedonia, Plin.

ematuresco.full: ē-mātūresco, rŭi, 3, v. inch. n., to grow quite ripe, to come to maturity (very rare). In gen.: semen, Plin. 25, 4, 17, § 36: segetes, Gell. 2, 29, 7.—* Trop., to grow softer, be mitigated: ira Caesaris, Ov. Tr. 2, 124.

ematuro.full: ē-mātūro, āre, v. a., to ripen completely, to bring to maturity: fruges (calor), Eumen. Grat. Act. ad Const. 10.

emax.full: ĕmax, ācis, adj. emo; cf.: edax, bibax, etc., eager to buy, fond of buying, Cato R. R. 2 fin.; * Cic. Par. 6, 3, 51; Nep. Att. 13, 1: domina, Ov. A. A. 1, 421.— Poet.: non tu prece poscis emaci, i. e. that vows a price for its fulfilment, Pers. 2, 3.

embaenetica.full: embaenĕtĭca, ae, f., = ἐμβαινετική, an artificial appetite, Cael. ap. Cic. Fam. 8, 1, 4 Bait. (al. emetica, q. v.).
embaenetica.short: embaenĕtĭca, ae, f., = ἐμβαινετική, an artificial appetite, Cael.

embamma.full: embamma, ătis, n., = ἔμβαμμα, a sauce, Col. 12, 57 fin.; Plin. 20, 14, 53, § 147; 22, 22, 44, § 88 al.
embamma.short: embamma, ătis, n., = ἔμβαμμα, a sauce, Col.

embasicoetas.full: embăsĭcoetas, ae, m., = ἐμβασικοίτας, i. q. cinaedus, and likewise the name of an obscenely shaped drinking - vessel; hence, in a double sense, Petr. 24, 1 and 2.

embasis.full: embăsis, is, f., = ἔμβασις, a bathing in any thing, Cael. Aur. Acut. 3, 8, 18; 3, 17, 151 al.
embasis.short: embăsis, is, f., = ἔμβασις, a bathing in any thing, Cael.

embates.full: embătes, is, m., = ἐμβάτης, archit. t. t., a model, Lat. modulus, Vitr. 1, 2, 4.

emblema.full: emblēma, ătis (abl. plur. emblematis, Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 22; * Quint. 2, 4, 27), n., = ἔμβλημα, inlaid work. Raised ornaments on vessels, Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 17; 22 sq.; Dig. 34, 2, 32 et saep.— Tessellated work, mosaic, Lucil. ap. Cic. Or. 44; id. de Or. 3, 43, 171; id. Brut. 79, 274; Varr. R. R. 3, 2, 4.

embola.full: embŏla, ae, f., = ἐμβολή, a putting on board, shipment (late Lat.), Cod. Th. 1, 2, 10; Novell. 163, 2.
embola.short: embŏla, ae, f., = ἐμβολή, a putting on board, shipment (late Lat.), Cod.

emboliaria.full: embŏlĭārĭa, ae, f. embolium, an actress who performed in the interludes, Plin. 7, 48, 49, § 158; Inscr. Murat. 660, 4.

embolimaeus.full: embŏlĭmaeus, a, um, adj., = ἐμβολιμαῖος, inserted, intercalary (pure Lat. intercalaris): dies, Aus. Eclog. de Rat. Dier. 13. Called also embŏlĭmus = ἐμβόλιμος, Sol. 1.
embolimaeus.short: embŏlĭmaeus, a, um, adj., = ἐμβολιμαῖος, inserted, intercalary (pure Lat.

emboline.full: embŏlīnē, es, f., a plant, now unknown, Plin. 13, 20, 35, § 114.
emboline.short: embŏlīnē, es, f., a plant, now unknown, Plin.

embolismus.full: embŏlismus, a, um, adj., = ἐμβολισμός, intercalary: dies, Sol. 1, § 42: annus, leap-year, Isid. Orig. 6, 17, 21 sq.—As subst.: embolismus, i, m., the interposition, intercalation, Isid. 6, 17, 23.
embolismus.short: embŏlismus, a, um, adj., = ἐμβολισμός, intercalary: dies, Sol.

embolium.full: embŏlĭum, ii, n., = ἐμβόλιον, something thrown in; in scenic lang., an interlude, ballet, Cic. Sest. 54, 116 (embolia pertinent ad gestus saltatorios, Schol.).
embolium.short: embŏlĭum, ii, n., = ἐμβόλιον, something thrown in;

embolum.full: embŏlum, i, n., = ἔμβολον, the beak of a ship: aēneum, Petr. 30, 1.
embolum.short: embŏlum, i, n., = ἔμβολον, the beak of a ship: aēneum, Petr.

embolus.full: embŏlus, i, m., = ἔμβολος, in mechanics, the piston of a pump, Vitr. 10, 12.
embolus.short: embŏlus, i, m., = ἔμβολος, in mechanics, the piston of a pump, Vitr.

embrocha.full: embrŏcha, ae, f., = ἐμβροχή, a wet poultice, Theod. Prisc. 1, 33.
embrocha.short: embrŏcha, ae, f., = ἐμβροχή, a wet poultice, Theod.

emeditatus.full: ē-mĕdĭtātus, a, um, Part. [meditor], studied out, studied, artfully devised: fletus, App. M. 2, p. 126.

emedullatus.full: ē-mĕdullātus, a, um, Part. [medullo], deprived of the marrow. * Lit.: radix, Plin. 22, 22, 43, § 87.—* Trop.: virtutes, enervated, feeble, Sid. Ep. 8, 6.

emendabilis.full: ēmendābĭlis, e, adj. emendo, that may be amended, capable of correction: error, Liv. 44, 10, 3: aetas, Sen. Clem. 2, 7.

emendate.full: ēmendātē, adv., faultlessly, perfectly, purely, v. emendo, P. a. fin.
emendate.short: ēmendātē, adv., faultlessly, perfectly, purely, v.

emendatio.full: ēmendātĭo, ōnis, f. emendo, a correction, amendment, emendation, Cic. Fin. 4, 9 (with correctio); Quint. 1, 5, 34; 2, 4, 10; 13; Plin. 8, 51, 78, § 210; Dig. 48, 19, 16, § 2 et saep.

emendator.full: ēmendātor, ōris, m. id., a corrector, amender, Cic. Balb. 8, 20; id. Phil. 2, 17 fin.; id. Brut. 74, 259; Plin. Pan. 6, 2; id. Ep. 6, 5, 4; Vulg. Sap. 7, 15.

emendatorius.full: ēmendātōrĭus, a, um, adj. id., corrective (late Lat.): ignis, i. e. purifying, Aug. in Psa. 27 init.

emendatrix.full: ēmendātrix, īcis, f. emendator, she who corrects or amends: vitiorum emendatricem legem esse oportet, Cic. Leg. 1, 22, 58; id. Tusc. 4, 32, 69.

emendatus.full: ēmendātus, a, um, Part. and P. a., from emendo.

emendico.full: ē-mendīco, no perf., ātum, 1, v. a., to obtain by begging (post-Aug.): stipem a populo, Suet. Aug. 91 fin.: pecunias, id. Caes. 54; Cod. Th. 9, 2, 14 al.

emendo.full: ē-mendo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. mendum, to free from faults, to correct, improve, amend (cf. corrigo—class.; not in Caes.): tota civitas emendari et corrigi solet continentia principum, Cic. Leg. 3, 13, 30; cf. Quint. 2, 2, 7; 2, 4, 14; 9, 3, 89: leviter tuum consilium (with conformare), Cic. Mur. 29: consuetudinem vitiosam, id. Brut. 75: vitia adolescentiae multis virtutibus, Nep. Them. 1: facta priora novis, Ov. F. 4, 596: res Italas legibus, Hor. Ep. 2, 1, 3: legem severius, Suet. Aug. 34: sucos

emensio.full: ēmensĭo, ōnis, f. emetior, the completion of a course: lunaris, Isid. 6, 17, 29.

emensus.full: ēmensus, a, um, Part., from emetior.
emensus.short: ēmensus, a, um, Part., from emetior.

ementior.full: ē-mentĭor, ītus, 4, v. dep. a., to put forth or utter falsely, to feign, fabricate, pretend (class.): quae dixisti modo, Omnia ementitus, Plaut. Am. 1, 1, 255: aliquid, Cic. Balb. 2, 5; id. Phil. 2, 33, 83; id. Opt. Gen. 7, 21; Sall. C. 49, 4; Liv. 9, 18; 21, 63, 5 al.—And with acc. and inf. as object, Cic. Planc. 30, 73; Liv. 1, 8; Suet. Calig. 51; Tac. A. 2, 66; 13, 47; id. H. 2, 42 al.; also: aliquem, to feign being any one, Plaut. Trin. 4, 2, 143; Petr. 82, 3.—Absol.: ego haec omnia Chrysogo

emeo.full: ē-mĕo, no perf., ātum, 1, v. a., to pass through, traverse: emeato mari, Amm. 29, 5, 5.

emercor.full: ē-mercor, ātus, 1, v. dep. a., to buy up, purchase, bribe (post-Aug.): adulterium ingentibus donis, Tac. A. 13, 44: aditum principis, id. ib. 16, 1: avaritiam praefecti, id. ib. 12, 45; cf. id. ib. 12, 14.!*? emercor, part. perf. in pass. signif., Amm. 21, 6, 8; 26, 2, 4.

emere.full: emere antiqui dicebant pro accipere, Paul. ex Fest. p. 4, 18, and 76, 1 Müll.; cf. adimo and demo.
emere.short: emere antiqui dicebant pro accipere, Paul.

emereo.full: ē-mĕrĕo, ŭi, ĭtum, 2, v. a., and (perh. not ante-Aug.) ē-mĕrĕor, ĭtus, 2, v. dep. a. To obtain by service, to gain, earn, merit, deserve. In gen. (rare; not in Cic.): quid ego emerui mali? Plaut. Aul. 4, 10, 5: honores, Prop. 4 (5), 11, 61. mihi altior sollicitudo, quale judicium hominum, emererer, accessit, Quint. 4, prooem. § 1; cf.: emerendi favoris gratia canunt, id. 4, 1, 2: pecuniam ex eo quaestu uberem, Gell, 6, 7, 5.—Poet., with inf. clause as object: Ennius emeruit Contiguus poni, Scipi

emergo.full: ē-mergo, si, sum, 3, v. a. and n. Act., to bring forth, bring to light, raise up (very rare; mostly with se, or pass. in mid. sense), to come forth, come out, to rise up, emerge (not in Plaut., Caes., Verg., or Hor.). Lit.: emersere e gurgite vultus Nereides, Cat. 64, 14: ex undis Cancri pars sese emergit in astra, Manil. 5, 198; se torrens imo hiatu, Auct. Aetn. 118: se lux pelago, Avien. Perieg. 126: tibi (somnianti) subito sum visus emersus e flumine, Cic. Div. 2, 68; so, emersus e palude, Li

emerita.full: Ēmĕrĭta, ae, f., a city of Lusitania, now Merida, Mela, 2, 6, 4; Plin. 9, 41, 65, § 141.—Hence, ēmĕrĭtānus, a, um, adj., of Emerita, Murat. Inscr. 1550, 1.— ēmĕrĭtensis, e, adj., of Emerita: conventus, Plin. 4, 22, 35, § 117.—Emeri-tenses, ium, m., the inhabitants of Emerita, Tac. H. 1, 78.
emerita.short: Ēmĕrĭta, ae, f., a city of Lusitania, now Merida, Mela, 2, 6, 4;

emeritus.full: ēmĕrĭtus, a, um, Part. and subst., from emereo, q. v.

emersus1.full: ēmersus, a, um, Part., from emergo.
emersus1.short: ēmersus, a, um, Part., from emergo.

emersus2.full: ēmersus, ūs, m. emergo, a coming out, coming forth, an appearing, emerging (not ante-Aug.): serpentium, Plin. 22, 22, 46, § 95: fluminis, id. 9, 22, 38, § 75: stellae, id. 18, 25, 58, § 218; Col. 7, 3, 24: hostium, Vitr. 10, 22.

emeticus.full: ēmĕtĭcus, a, um, adj., = ἐμετικός, emetic, turning the stomach: bolbus, App. Herb. 55.—Hence, subst.: † ĕmĕtĭca, ae, f., = ἐμετική, an incitement to vomit, an emetic (employed by the Roman gourmands as the means of renewed gluttony), Cael. ap. Cic. Fam. 8, 1, 4 (cf. bibit et vomit, Juv. 6, 432; dub.; Bait. embaeneticam; al. pineticam, or peneticam).
emeticus.short: ēmĕtĭcus, a, um, adj., = ἐμετικός, emetic, turning the stomach: bolbus, App.

emetior.full: ē-mētĭor, mensus, 4, v. dep. a., to measure out (not freq. till after the Aug. per.). Lit.: spatium oculis, Verg. A. 10, 772: longitudines et altitudines vocis, Gell. 16, 18, 4.— Transf. To pass through, pass over, traverse a certain space: cum freta, cum terras omnis, tot inhospita saxa Sideraque emensae ferimur, Verg. A. 5, 628; 11, 244; Tib. 3, 4, 17; Liv. 27, 43; 31, 24; 38, 17 fin.; Plin. 7, 20, 20, § 84; Tac. A. 11, 32; 15, 16 al.; cf. poet.: pelagi terraeque laborem, Sil. 4, 53; and in Ta

emeto.full: ē-mĕto, ĕre, v. a., to mow away, mow down: plus frumenti agris, Hor. Ep. 1, 6, 21: fruges, Manil. 5, 245.

emicatim.full: ēmĭcātim, adv. emico, springing forth: prosiliens, Sid. Ep. 2, 13 fin.

emicatio.full: ēmĭcātĭo, ōnis, f. id., a springing forth: emicationes silvarum, App. de Mundo, p. 71, 29.

emico.full: ē-mĭco, cŭi (cf. Quint. 1, 6, 17), cātum, 1, v. n., to spring out, spring forth, to break forth, appear quickly (not freq. till after the Aug. per.; in Cic. and Caes. not at all). Lit.: emicat ex oculis, spirat quoque pectore flamma, Ov. M. 8, 356: flamma ex monte, Plin. 2, 88, 89, § 203: multi calami ex una radice, id. 27, 8, 40, § 62: dracones de extis, id. 11, 37, 77, § 197: fulgura ab omni parte caeli, Curt. 8, 4: corpore sanguis (so Lachm.; Munro, e corpore), Lucr. 2, 195: uterque pronus ca

emigratio.full: ēmī^grātĭo, ōnis, f. emigro, a removal from a place, emigration (late Lat. for migratio): inquilinorum, Dig. 39, 2, 28.

emigro.full: ē-mī^gro, āvi, ātum, 1, v. n. and a. Neutr., to remove, depart from a place, to emigrate (rare but classical): Se. Quid tu ais? num hinc emigrasti? Me. Quem in locum? etc., Plaut. Men. 5, 2, 70 sq.; cf. id. Most. 2, 2, 72; Dig. 19, 2, 27: ex illa domo, Cic. Verr. 2, 5, 12: domo, id. ib. 2, 2, 36; Caes. B. G. 1, 31, 14.—Trop.: e vita, Cic. Leg. 2, 19, 48.—Absol.: in hasce aedis pedem nemo intro tetulit, semel ut emigravimus, Plaut. Most. 2, 2, 40; Just. 5, 10, 9: qui post hunc casum emigraverunt,

eminatio.full: eminatio, false read. in Plaut. Capt. 4, 2, 19: conminatio, Brix: minatio, Fleck., Ritschl.

eminens.full: ēmĭnens, entis, Part. and P. a., from emineo.

eminenter.full: ēmĭnenter, adv., highly, eminently, v. emineo, P. a. fin.

eminentia.full: ēmĭnentĭa, ae, f. eminens, a standing out, projecting; concr., a prominence, protuberance. Lit., Cic. N. D. 1, 38, § 174 (with soliditas); App. Flor. no. 18, p. 359; and in plur., Plin. 37, 10, 63, § 174. —Hence, in painting, the prominent, i. e. light parts, Cic. Ac. 2, 7, 20 (opp. umbrae). — Trop., excellence: quaedam formarum, Gell. 5, 11, 9: senectutis suae, Vulg. 2 Macc. 6, 19.—Hence, per eminentiam, i. q. κατʼ ἐξοχήν, preëminently, par excellence, Ulp. Fragm. 11, 3: reperiet, eminentiam cu

emineo.full: ē-mĭnĕo, ŭi, 2, v. n., to stand out, project (freq. and class.). Lit. In gen. (syn.: exstare, excedere): cum ex terra nihil emineret, quod contemplationi caeli officere posset, Cic. Div. 1, 42: globus terrae e mari, id. Tusc. 1, 28: stipites ex terra, Caes. B. G. 7, 73, 6; cf.: stipites ab ramis, id. ib. § 3: belua ponto, Ov. M. 4, 690: rupes aequore, Luc. 2, 667: moles aquā, Curt. 4, 2, 21: oculi extra terram, Plin. 17, 21, 35, § 154: balaena dorso multum super aquas, id. 9, 6, 5, § 14: super c

eminiscor.full: ē-mĭniscor, mentus, 3, v. dep. a. [v. comminiscor], to devise, contrive: EMINISCITVR, COMMINISCITVR, REMINISCITVR, SVBMINISCITVR, Not. Tir.: EMENTVM, excogitatio, Gloss. Isid.: ingeniosior ad eminiscendum, Auct. Her. 2, 7, 10; 2, 8, 12. Acc. to conjecture, also in Nep. Alcib. 2, 1 Heusing N. cr. (others read: comminisci and reminisci); and Varr. L. L. 6, § 44 Müll. N. cr. (al. reminisci).

eminor.full: eminor, āri, false read. in Plaut. Capt. 4, 2, 11: minor, Fleck.

eminulus.full: ēmĭnŭlus, a, um, adj. dim. [emineo], projecting a little (perh. only in Varro): genua (boum), Varr. R. R. 2, 5, 8: dentes, id. ib. 2, 9, 3: spina, id. ib. § 4.

eminus.full: ē-mĭnus, adv. manus; cf. the opp. comminus; lit., hands apart, i. e. not hand to hand, aloof, at fighting distance with missiles, a spear's-throw off (cf.: longe, procul). Prop., a milit. t. t., used of fighting with missiles, spears, etc. (class.), mostly opp. comminus: eminus fundis, sagittis reliquisque telis pugnabatur, Caes. B. C. 1, 26. 1; cf. Sall. J. 50, 4; 101, 4; Nep. Alcib. 10, 6; Tac. H. 3, 27; Verg. A. 10, 346; 645; 776; Liv. 38, 21, 13 saep.; of throwing fire, etc.: alii faces de m

emiror.full: ē-mīror, āri, v. dep. a. (qs. ex intimo animo demiror), to wonder greatly at (very rare): aequora, Hor. C. 1, 5, 8 Orell. N. cr.; so App. M. 4, p. 274 Oud. N. cr. (al. miratus); Placid. p. 251 Munck.

emisceo.full: ē-miscĕo, ēre, v. a., to mingle by pouring out, to mix: vina, Manil. 5, 244.

emissarium.full: ēmissārĭum, ii, n. emitto, an outlet: lacūs, a drain, Cic. Fam. 16, 18; Plin. 33, 4, 21, § 75; Suet. Claud. 20, 32: vomicae, Scrib. Comp. 229; cf. collectionis, id. ib. 206.

emissarius.full: ēmissārĭus, ii, m. id.; sent out, put forth; hence, An emissary, scout, spy, Cic. Verr. 2, 2, 8 Ascon.; 2, 3, 40; id. Fam. 7, 2, 3; Vell. 2, 18 fin.; Suet. Galb. 15; id. Dom. 11.— Transf., in eccl. Lat. An attendant, one of the guard, Vulg. 1 Reg. 22, 17.— Caper emissarius, the scapegoat, sent to bear the sins of the people to the wilderness, Vulg. Levit. 16, 8 al.— In botany, a young branch, a shoot, Plin. 17, 23, 35, § 208.

emissicius.full: ēmissīcĭus or -tĭus, a, um, adj. id., sent out, put forth; transf.: oculi, i. e. prying about, spying, Plaut. Aul. 1, 1, 2: ocelli, Tert. Pall. 3.

emissio.full: ēmissĭo, ōnis, f. id., a sending out, darting forth (rare). Prop., a letting go: radiorum ex oculis, a darting forth, Gell. 5, 16, 2: mortui sunt in emissione, in exile, Vulg. Baruch. 2, 25.—* Meton., power of projecting or hurling; in plur.: graviores telorum, Cic. Tusc. 2, 24, 57; a letting go, releasing: anguis, id. Div. 2, 29, 62 (thrice).

emissor.full: ēmissŏr, ōris, m. id., he who sends out, throws out: Liber et Libera seminum commotores et emissores, August. Civ. D. 7, 3.

emissus1.full: ēmissus, a, um, Part., from emitto.
emissus1.short: ēmissus, a, um, Part., from emitto.

emissus2.full: ēmissus, ūs, m. emitto, a sending forth, emission, Lucr. 4, 205.

emitesco.full: ē-mītesco, ĕre, v. inch. n., to become mild or mellow: mel, Col. 9, 14, 10 Schneid. N. cr.

emitto.full: ē-mitto, mīsi, missum, 3, v. a., to send out, send forth, to let out, let go (freq. and class.). Lit. In gen.: quibuscum tamquam e carceribus emissus sis, Cic. Lael. 27, 101; cf.: aperiam carceres et equos emittere incipiam, Varr. R. R. 2, 7, 1: ex porta ludis cum emissu'st lepus, Plaut. Pers. 3, 3, 31: aliquem e carcere, Cic. Planc. 12 fin.: aliquem ex vinculis, Plaut. Capt. 2, 3, 48; Cic. Tusc. 1, 31: aliquem e custodia, id. ib. 1, 49, 118 (cf. Nep. Cim. 1).—As milit. t. t., to send out agains

emmanes.full: emmănes, is, m., = ἐμμανής, the plant hyoscyamus, App. Herb. 4.
emmanes.short: emmănes, is, m., = ἐμμανής, the plant hyoscyamus, App.

emmoton.full: emmŏton, i, n., = ἔμμοτον, a salve spread on lint, Theod. Prisc. 1, 28.
emmoton.short: emmŏton, i, n., = ἔμμοτον, a salve spread on lint, Theod.

emo.full: ĕmo, ēmi, emptum, 3 (perf. subj. emissim, Plaut. Cas. 2, 5, 39), v. a. the same word with EMERE=accipere, Paul. ex Fest. pp. 4, 18, and 76, 1 Müll.; cf. adimo and demo; prop., to take; root yam; Sanscr. yamati, hold fast, Fick, Vergl. Wört. p. 158 sq.; cf. Georg Curtius Gr. Etym. p. 598 note, to buy, purchase (very freq. in all periods and kinds of composition). Lit.: is postquam hunc emit, dedit eum, etc., Plaut. Capt. prol. 19: qui puellam ab eo emerat, id. Rud. prol. 59: emit hosce de praeda,

emoderor.full: ē-mŏdĕror, āri, v. dep. a., to moderate: dolorem verbis, i. e. to vent, Ov. R. Am. 130.

emodulor.full: ē-mŏdŭlor, āri, v. dep. a., to sing, celebrate: Musam, Ov. Am. 1, 1, 30.

emolior.full: ē-mōlĭor, ītus (inf. pass. parag. emolirier, Plaut. Bacch. 4, 5, 2), 4, v. dep. a., to move out, bring out by effort (very rare): fretum (venti), to stir up, agitate, Sen. Agam. 476: nauseam pituitae per nares, Col. 8, 5, 21; cf. Cels. 4, 6: negotium, to effect, accomplish, Plaut. Bacch. 4, 5, 2.

emollio.full: ē-mollĭo, ii, ītum, 4, v. a., to make soft, to soften (perh. not ante-Aug.). Lit.: humor arcus fundasque et jaculorum amenta emollierat, Liv. 37, 41; Cels. 8, 4: ova macerata, Plin. 10, 60, 80, § 167; 18, 7, 17, § 77; 20, 2, 6, § 11 al.— Transf.: colores, to soften, make more delicate, Plin. 35, 17, 57, § 198.— Trop. In a good sense, to make mild or gentle, to mollify: mores, Ov. P. 2, 9, 48: severa praecepta, Aur. Vict. Epit. 48.— In a bad sense, to enervate, render effeminate: exercitum (Capua

emolo.full: ē-mŏlo, no perf., ĭtum, 3, v. a., to grind up. Lit.: hordeum, Veg. Vet. 5, 23, 7; Ambros. Ep. 64, 3; id. de Tob. 21, 83.— Transf., to grind out, consume by grinding: granaria, Pers. 6, 26.

emolumenticius.full: ēmŏlŭmentĭcĭus, a, um, adj. emolumentum, relating to gain, terror, dread of losing profits, Cassiod. Var. 9, 6.

emolumentum.full: ēmŏlŭmentum or ēmŏlĭmentum (cf. monumentum), i, n. emolior; lit., a working out; hence, A striving for success, i. e. effort, exertion, labor (cf. elaboro; rarely): neque enim magnum emolumentum esse potest, can present no great difficulty, Varr. R. R. 3, 14, 1 (but in Caes. B. G. 1, 34, the true reading is molimento). —* Concr., a work, a building, etc.: vetera, Cod. Th. 15, 1, 19.—Far more freq., The attainment of success, i. e. gain, profit, advantage, benefit (syn.: lucrum, quaestus, compend

emoneo.full: ē-mŏnĕo, ēre, v. a., to admonish: te ut, etc., Cic. Fam. 1, 7, 9 Bait. (dub.;al. moneo).

emorior.full: ē-mŏrĭor, mortuus, 3 (old form of the inf. emoriri, Ter. Eun. 3, 1, 42; but Plaut. Ps. 4, 7, 124, moriri, Ritschl), v. dep. n., to die off, to die, depart, decease, v. Doed. Syn. 3, p. 183 sq. (freq. and class.). Lit.: emori me malim, Plaut. Asin. 4, 2, 1; so id. Aul. 4, 5, 1; Ter. Phorm. 5, 7, 63; Cic. Pis. 7, 15; id. Off. 3, 32, 114; id. Tusc. 1, 40, 96; id.
