Par. 3, 2, 24; Sall. C. 20, 9; id. J. 14 fin.; Ov. M. 3, 391; Plaut. Cas. 2, 5, 26 sq.; Ter. Eun. 5, 2, 49; Cic. de Or. 1, 57, 243; id. d
emorior.short: ē-mŏrĭor, mortuus, 3 (old form of the inf.

emortualis.full: ēmortŭālis, e, adj. emorior, of or belonging to death: dies (opp. natalis), the day of one's death, Plaut. Ps. 4, 7, 139.

emortuus.full: ēmortuus, a, um, Part., dead, from emorior.
emortuus.short: ēmortuus, a, um, Part., dead, from emorior.

emotus.full: ēmōtus, a, um, Part., from emoveo.
emotus.short: ēmōtus, a, um, Part., from emoveo.

emoveo.full: ē-mŏvĕo (exmov-, Plaut. Truc. 1, 1, 59), mōvi, mōtum, 2 (perf. sync. emostis, Liv. 37, 53 fin.), v. a., to move out, move away, remove (mostly post-Aug.; esp. in Livy; not in Cic. and Caes.). Lit.: multitudinem e foro, Liv. 25, 1: plebem de medio, id. 6, 38: legatos curiā, id. 30, 23; cf.: milites aedificiis, 27, 3: aliquos senatu, id. 45, 15; and: postes cardine, Verg. A. 2, 493: Antiochum ultra juga Tauri, Liv. 37, 53 fin.; 38, 12; 42, 42; 50; cf.: aliquos cis Vulturnum, id. 26, 34: labias pri

empanda.full: Empanda paganorum dea, Paul. ex Fest. p. 76, 11 Müll.

empedocles.full: Empĕdŏcles, is (gen. -cli, Gell. 4, 11, 9; acc. -clem, Cic. Ac. 1, 12, 44; -clen, id. ib. 2, 5, 14 al.), m., = Ἐμπεδοκλῆς, a famous natural philosopher of Agrigentum, about 460 B. C., Lucr. 1, 716 sq.; Cic. N. D. 1, 12; id. de Or. 1, 50, 217; id. Tusc. 1, 9, 19; Quint. 1, 4, 4; 3, 1, 8; Plin. 29, 1, 4, § 5; Gell. 17, 21, 14; Hor. Ep. 1, 12, 20; id. A. P. 465.—Hence, Empĕdoclēus, a, um, adj., Empedoclean: sanguis (acc. to his doctrine, the soul), Cic. Tusc. 1, 17 fin.— Subst.: Empĕdoclēa, ōrum, n

empetros.full: empĕtros, i, m., = ἔμπετρος, a plant called in pure Lat. calcifraga, Plin. 27, 9, 51, § 75.
empetros.short: empĕtros, i, m., = ἔμπετρος, a plant called in pure Lat.

emphanisticum.full: emphănistĭcum, i, n., = ἐμφανιστικόν, a duty paid by a priest for the ordination, Julian. Ep. Nov. c. 50, § 191.
emphanisticum.short: emphănistĭcum, i, n., = ἐμφανιστικόν, a duty paid by a priest for the ordination, Julian.

emphasis.full: emphăsis, is, f., = ἔμφασις, a figure of rhet., emphasis, rhetorical stress (cf.: pondus, significatio), Quint. 9, 2, 64; 8, 2, 11; 8, 3, 86 al.
emphasis.short: emphăsis, is, f., = ἔμφασις, a figure of rhet., emphasis, rhetorical stress (cf.: pondus, significatio), Quint.

emphragma.full: emphragma, ătis, n., = ἔμφραγμα, a stoppage, obstruction, Veg. Vet. 2, 12 and 19 (1, 40; 47 Bip.).
emphragma.short: emphragma, ătis, n., = ἔμφραγμα, a stoppage, obstruction, Veg.

emphyteusis.full: emphўteusis, ĕos, f., = ἐμφύτευσις (lit., an implanting), in jurid. lang., a permanent tenure of land upon condition of cultivating it properly, and paying a stipulated rent, a sort of fee-farm or copyhold, Cod. Just. 4, 66, 1; Just. Inst. 3, 25, 3; cf. Rein's Privatr. p. 168 sq.; Dict. of Antiquities, s. v. emphyteusis.
emphyteusis.short: emphўteusis, ĕos, f., = ἐμφύτευσις (lit., an implanting), in jurid.

emphyteuta.full: emphўteuta, ae, m., = ἐμφυτεύτης, the lessee in the tenure of emphyteusis, Cod. Just. 4, 66, 1 sq.; called also emphўteu-tĭcārĭus, ib. 11, 62, 1; the latter also adj., of or belonging to emphyteusis: praedium, contractus, ib. 4, 66, 2 sq.
emphyteuta.short: emphўteuta, ae, m., = ἐμφυτεύτης, the lessee in the tenure of emphyteusis, Cod.

emphyteuticus.full: emphўteutĭcus, a, um, adj., = ἐμφυτευτικός, of or pertaining to emphyteusis: jus, contractus, etc., Cod. Just. 4, 66, 1 sq.; cf. the preced. art.
emphyteuticus.short: emphўteutĭcus, a, um, adj., = ἐμφυτευτικός, of or pertaining to emphyteusis: jus, contractus, etc., Cod.

empirice.full: empīrĭce, ēs (-ca, ae, Marc. de Med. 6), f., = ἐμπειρική, empiricism in medicine, i. e. a system founded wholly on practice, Plin. 29, 1, 4, § 5.—Hence, empīrĭcus, i, m., an empiric, a physician whose knowledge of medicine is derived from experience only, Cic. Ac. 2, 39, 122 (in Cels. praef. and 5 init., written as Greek); their writings were called empīrĭca, ōrum, n., Plin. 20, 12, 48, § 120.

emplastratio.full: emplastrātĭo, ōnis, f. emplastro, in horticult. lang., the insertion of a small piece of the bark in inoculating a tree, etc., scutcheon-grafting, budding, Col. 5, 11, 1; id. Arb. 26, 1; 11, 2, 59; Plin. 17, 16, 26, § 118 sq.; Pall. Jun. 5, 2.

emplastro.full: emplastro, no perf., ātum, 1, v. a., in horticult. lang., to inoculate by inserting a bit of the bark with the eye, to scutcheongraft, to bud, Col. 5, 11, 10; 11, 2, 37; Pall. Mai. 6; id. Nov. 7, 7.

emplastrum.full: emplastrum, i, n. (or emplastra, ae, f., Gell. 16, 7 fin.), = ἔμπλαστρον. In medic. lang., a plaster. Prop., Cels. 5, 17; 19; Cato, R. R. 39, 2; Plin. 21, 4, 10, § 15; 34, 10, 22, § 103 et saep.—* Trop.: quid est jusjurandum? Emplastrum aeris alieni, Laber. ap. Gell. 16, 7 fin. — In horticult. lang., the band of bark which surrounds the eye in ingrafting, the scutcheon, Col. 5, 11, 10; id. Arb. 26, 9 sq.; Plin. 17, 16, 26, § 121; Pall. Febr. 17, 1 al.

emplecton.full: emplecton, i, n., = ἔμπλεκτον (lit., interwoven), rubble-work, a sort of masonry in which the space between two walls is filled with broken stones and mortar, Plin. 36, 22, 51, § 171 (Vitr. 2, 8, 7, as Greek).
emplecton.short: emplecton, i, n., = ἔμπλεκτον (lit., interwoven), rubble-work, a sort of masonry in which the space between two walls is filled with broken stones and mortar, Plin.

emponema.full: empŏnēma, ătis, n., = ἐμπόνημα, the value added to land by culture: melioratio, vel ea quae emponemata dicuntur, Cod. 4, 66, 2; Julian. Epit. Nov. 7, 34.
emponema.short: empŏnēma, ătis, n., = ἐμπόνημα, the value added to land by culture: melioratio, vel ea quae emponemata dicuntur, Cod.

emporeticus.full: empŏrētĭcus, a, um, adj., = ἐμπορητικός, of or pertaining to trade: charta, i. e. packing-paper, Plin. 13, 12, 23, § 76, 78; Isid. Orig. 6, 10, 5.
emporeticus.short: empŏrētĭcus, a, um, adj., = ἐμπορητικός, of or pertaining to trade: charta, i.

emporia.full: Empŏrĭa, ōrum, n., = Ἐμπόρια, a district on the shore of the Lesser Syrtis, Liv. 29, 25 sq.
emporia.short: Empŏrĭa, ōrum, n., = Ἐμπόρια, a district on the shore of the Lesser Syrtis, Liv.

emporiae.full: Empŏrĭae, ārum, f., = Ἐμπορίαι, a city of Hispania Tarraconensis, near the Pyrenees, Mel. 2, 6, 5; Plin. 3, 3, 4, § 22; Liv. 21, 60; Sil. 3, 369.—Its inhabitants were called Empŏritāni, Liv. 34, 16, 4.
emporiae.short: Empŏrĭae, ārum, f., = Ἐμπορίαι, a city of Hispania Tarraconensis, near the Pyrenees, Mel.

emporium.full: empŏrĭum, ii, n., = ἐμπόριον, a place of trade, a market-town, market, emporium, mart, Plaut. Am. 4, 1, 4; Varr. R. R. 2, 9, 6; Cic. Att. 5, 2, 2; Liv. 21, 57; 35, 10 fin.; 41, 1; 27; Vitr. 2, 8; Plin. 6, 20, 23, § 72 al.
emporium.short: empŏrĭum, ii, n., = ἐμπόριον, a place of trade, a market-town, market, emporium, mart, Plaut.

emporus.full: empŏrus, i, m., = ἔμπορος, a trader, merchant, Aus. Epist. 22, 28.—Emporos, title of a play of Philemon (the Mercator of Plautus), Plaut. Merc. 1, 1, 5.
emporus.short: empŏrus, i, m., = ἔμπορος, a trader, merchant, Aus.

emprosthotonia.full: emprosthŏtŏnĭa, ae, f., = ἐμπροσθοτονία, a disease in which the limbs are drawn forward and stiffen, Cael. Aur. Acut. 3, 6, 61.—The same called empro-sthŏtŏnos (=ἐμπροσθότονος) morbus, id. ib. 3, 6, 65.—Hence, emprosthŏtŏ-nĭcus, a, um, adj., = ἐμπροσθοτονικός, suffering from this disease, id. ib. § 69.
emprosthotonia.short: emprosthŏtŏnĭa, ae, f., = ἐμπροσθοτονία, a disease in which the limbs are drawn forward and stiffen, Cael.

empticius.full: emptīcĭus (emt-) or -tĭus, a, um, adj. emo, bought, purchased: glans, Varr. R. R. 3, 2, 12: salsamenta, id. ib. 3, 17, 7.— Of slaves, Sen. Contr. 7, 21, 24: Spendon et Hermes empticii, Inscr. Orell. 2812: empticius an domi natus? Petr. 47, 12; Vulg. Exod. 12, 44 al.

emptio.full: emptĭo (emt-), ōnis, f. id., a buying, purchase (cf.: sectio, mercatura, etc.). Prop., Varr. R. R. 2, 2, 5; 2, 3, 5; Cic. Caecin. 6, 17; id. Att. 12, 3; Plin. 33, 3, 13, § 43; Tac. H. 3, 34 et saep.; cf., on its legal relations, Gai. Inst. 3, 139; the title: De emptione et venditione, Just. Inst. 3, 23; Dig. 18, 1; and Rein's Privatr. p. 329 sq.: equina, i. e. of horses (with boum and asinorum), Varr. R. R. 2, 7, 6.— Transf. A purchase, i. e. an article purchased: ex illis emptionibus nullam des

emptito.full: emptĭto (emt-), āvi, ātum, 1, v. freq. a. id., to be in the habit of purchasing, to purchase often (very rare; perh. not anteAug.), Col. 8, 10, 6; Plin. Ep. 6, 19, 15; Tac. A. 14, 41.

emptivom militem.full: emptivom militem, mercenarium, Paul. ex Fest. p. 77, 5 Müll. [id.].

emptor.full: emptor (emt-), ōris, m. id., a buyer, purchaser (cf.: negotiator, mercator, caupo, institor), Plaut. Poen. 1, 2, 128 sq.; id. Pers. 4, 4, 31; Cic. Off. 3, 12, 51; id. Phil. 2, 38; id. Caecin. 7, 19; Hor. S. 1, 2, 88; id. Ep. 2, 2, 167 et saep.; cf., on the laws affecting him, the authorities cited under emptio: pretiosus dedecorum, i. e. who buys them dearly (=magno pretio emens), Hor. C. 3, 6, 32: familiae, the imaginary purchaser of an inheritance per aes et libram, Suet. Ner. 4 Bremi; cf. Rei

emptrix.full: emptrix (emtr-), īcis, f. emptor, she who buys, Dig. 21, 2, 63; Cod. Just. 4, 54, 1.

empturiens.full: emptŭrĭens (emt-), entis, adj. emo, desiring to buy, Varr. R. R. 2 prooem. § 6.

emptus.full: emptus (emt-), a, um, Part., from emo.
emptus.short: emptus (emt-), a, um, Part., from emo.

empyicus.full: empȳĭcus, i, m., = ἐμπῦϊκός, suffering from abscesses or expectoration of blood, Marc. Emp. 7; Theod. Prisc. 2, 10.
empyicus.short: empȳĭcus, i, m., = ἐμπῦϊκός, suffering from abscesses or expectoration of blood, Marc.

empylus.full: Empylus, i, m., =Ἔμπυλος, a rhetorician of Rhodes, Cic. ap. Quint. 10, 6, 4.
empylus.short: Empylus, i, m., =Ἔμπυλος, a rhetorician of Rhodes, Cic.

empyrius.full: empўrĭus (-rĕus), a, um, adj., = ἐμπύριος, fiery: mundi sublimitates, August. Civ. D. 10, 27.
empyrius.short: empўrĭus (-rĕus), a, um, adj., = ἐμπύριος, fiery: mundi sublimitates, August.

emugio.full: ē-mūgĭo, īre, v. a., to bellow out, cry aloud (very rare), Quint. 2, 12, 9; Auct. Aetn. 294.

emulgeo.full: ē-mulgĕo, no perf., lsum, 2, v. a., to milk out. Prop.: exiguum lactis, Col. 7, 3, 17.— Poet., in gen., to drain out, exhaust: paludem, Cat. 68, 110: serum, id. 80, 8.

emulsus.full: ēmulsus, a, um, Part., from emulgeo.
emulsus.short: ēmulsus, a, um, Part., from emulgeo.

emunctio.full: ēmunctĭo, ōnis, f. emungo, a wiping or blowing of the nose, Quint. 11, 3, 80.

emunctorium.full: ēmunctōrĭum, ii, n. id., a pair of snuffers, Vulg. Exod. 25, 38; 37, 23.

emunctus.full: ēmunctus, a, um, Part., from emungo.
emunctus.short: ēmunctus, a, um, Part., from emungo.

emundatio.full: ēmundātĭo, ōnis, f. emundo, a cleansing (late Lat.), Tert. Marc. 4, 9; id. Bapt. 5; Vulg. Levit. 15, 13 al.

emundo.full: ē-mundo, no perf., ātum, 1, v. a., to clean out, make quite clean (a favorite word of Columella; not in Juv. 14, 67, where the right reading is emendat): bubilia, Col. 2, 15, 7; cf. id. 9, 14, 7; 11, 2, 71: humum, id. 6, 30, 2: pennas gallinae, id. 8, 4, 4: vinum, to purify, id. 12, 23, 2; cf. segetes, id. 11, 2, 7 al.— Trop., to cleanse, purify from sin (eccl. Lat.): conscientiam nostram, Vulg. Hebr. 9, 14 et saep.

emungo.full: ē-mungo, nxi, nctum, 3 (perf. sync. emunxti, Plaut. Most. 5, 1, 60, followed by emunxisti), v. a., to wipe or blow the nose. Lit.: se, Auct. Her. 4, 54; Auct. ap. Suet. Vit. Hor.—Also mid.: ut neque spuerent neque emungerentur, Varr. ap. Non. 481, 18: emungeris, Juv. 6, 147.— Transf. In gen.: tu ut oculos emungare ex capite per nasum tuos, i. e. that your eyes may be knocked out, Plaut. Cas. 2, 6, 39: Aesopus naris emunctae senex, clean-nosed, i. e. of nice discernment, keen, acute, Phaedr. 3, 3

emunio.full: ē-mūnĭo, īvi or ii, ītum, 4, v. a., to fortify, secure, provide with a wall (not ante-Aug.). Lit.: locum arcis in modum, Liv. 24, 21 fin.: non opus est arduos colles emunire, Sen. Clem. 1, 19, 6.— Transf. To strengthen, make secure: obice postes, Verg. A. 8, 227: murum opere, Liv. 26, 46, 2: caveam retibus, Col. 8, 8, 4: sola et latera horreorum, id. 1, 6, 16.— To protect, defend: vites caveis ab injuria pecoris, Col. 5, 6, 21.— To build up, elevate for defence: murus, ut in suspecto loco, supra
emunio.short: ē-mūnĭo, īvi or ii, ītum, 4, v.

emusco.full: ē-musco, āre, v. a. muscus, to clear from moss: oleas, Col. 11, 2, 41.

emutatio.full: ēmūtātĭo, ōnis, f. emuto, a change, alteration (with novitas), Quint. 8, 6, 51.

emuto.full: ē-mūto, no perf., ātum, 1, v. a., to change, alter (perh. only in the foll. passages; cf.: muto, immuto, commuto), Manil. 5, 149: emutatis in perversum dicendi figuras, Quint. 8, 2, 19.

emys.full: ĕmys, ўdis, f., = ἐμύς, a kind of freshwater tortoise, Plin. 32, 4, 14, § 32.
emys.short: ĕmys, ўdis, f., = ἐμύς, a kind of freshwater tortoise, Plin.

en.full: ēn, interj. etym. dub.; cf. Gr. ἤν, ἠνί; acc. to Rib. Lat. Part. p. 34 sq. compounded of obsolete interjection e and enclitic ne, as in quin, etc., lo! behold! see! see there! (class.; most freq. in Verg.; in Plaut. and Ter. often em, q. v.). In presenting in a lively (or indignant) manner something important or unexpected (en habet vim indignationis, Donat. ad Ter. Phorm. 2, 3, 1).—With nom. (so usually, v. Krebs, Antibarb. p. 407): ubi rorarii estis? en sunt. Ubi sunt accensi? Ecce, Plaut. Fra

enallage.full: ĕnallăge, es, f., = ἐναλλαγή, a change of words (as, vos, O Calliope, precor, Verg. A. 9, 525), Gramm.
enallage.short: ĕnallăge, es, f., = ἐναλλαγή, a change of words (as, vos, O Calliope, precor, Verg.

enargia.full: ĕnargīa, ae, f., = ἐνάργεια, rhet. t. t., a vivid description, Rufin. de Schem. p. 275; Isid. Orig. 2, 20, 4; 2, 21, 33.

enaris.full: ēnāris, e, adj. e-naris, without a nose, = ἄῤῥιν, Serv. Verg. A. 9, 716.

enarmonius.full: ĕnarmŏnius (ĕnhar-, also -monĭ-cus), a, um, adj., = ἐναρμόνιος, enharmonic; as subst. (sc. melodiae genus), = ἐναρμόνιον μέλος, the technical name in Greek music of a kind of melody, in which quarter-tones predominated, Mart. Cap. 9, § 930: modulatio, id. 9, § 942 al.; Macr. Somn. Scip. 2, 4, 13.
enarmonius.short: ĕnarmŏnius (ĕnhar-, also -monĭ-cus), a, um, adj., = ἐναρμόνιος, enharmonic;

enarrabilis.full: ēnarrābĭlis, e, adj. enarro, that may be related, represented, or explained (very rare; not ante-Aug.): textus clipei, Verg. A. 8, 625: motus, Quint. 6, 3, 6: foeditas, id. 12, 10, 76: aliquid, Sen. Ep. 121 med.

enarratio.full: ēnarrātĭo, ōnis, f. enarro, a detailed exposition, interpretation: ineffabilis sanctusque sermo, cujus enarratio modum hominis excedat, Lact. 4, 9, 3; Quint. 1, 4, 2 sq.; 1, 8, 18 al.— Esp., the reckoning in metre, scanning: syllabarum, Sen. Ep. 88, 3.— Conversation, Vulg. Sirach, 9, 23; 38, 26.

enarrativus.full: ēnarrātīvus, a, um, adj. id., pertaining to a detailed exposition: genus poëmatis, Diom. p. 479 P.

enarrator.full: ēnarrātor, ōris, m. id., an explainer, expounder, interpreter (post-class.), Gell. 13, 30, 1: Sallustii, id. 18, 4, 2; 18, 6, 8.

enarro.full: ē-narro, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a., to explain in detail, to expound, interpret (rare but class.): omnem rem modo seni, Quo pacto haberet, enarramus ordine, Ter. Ad. 3, 3, 11; Plaut. Am. 1, 3, 27; id. Mil. 2, 1, 1; Ter. Heaut. 2, 3, 32; Cic. Inv. 1, 20; id. Div. 1, 26; Liv. 27, 50; Quint. 10, 1, 101 Spald.: poëmata, id. 1, 2, 14 Spald.; Plin. 36, 13, 19, § 87; Gell. 13, 10, 2; 18, 9, 4.—Hence, ēnarrātĭus, adv. comp., more explicitly: scribere, Gell. 10, 1, 7 (opp. breviter et subobscure); 13, 12, 5.

enascor.full: ē-nascor, -nātus, 3, v. dep. n., to issue forth, to sprout or spring up, to arise, to be born (not freq. till after the Aug. per.; in Plaut., Ter., and Cic. not at all): quod enasci colicoli vix queunt, Varr. R. R. 1, 41, 4; so of plants, Col. 5, 4, 2; 11, 3, 48; Liv. 32, 1 fin.; 43, 13; Quint. 6, 3, 77; Suet. Aug. 94 al.; also: rami enati, shot out, * Caes. B. G. 2, 17, 4; v. G. Long ad h. l.: dentes ex mento, Varr. R. R. 2, 9, 3; cf.: cornua (cervorum) cutibus, Plin. 11, 37, 45, § 128: aliquid

enater.full: ēnătēr, ĕris, m., = ἐινάτηρ, the husband of a deceased man's sister, Inscr. Orell. 4943.
enater.short: ēnătēr, ĕris, m., = ἐινάτηρ, the husband of a deceased man's sister, Inscr.

enato.full: ē-năto, āvi, 1, v. n., to swim out or away, to escape by swimming (very rare). Lit., Vitr. 6 praef.; Hor. A. P. 20; Phaedr. 4, 21, 14; App. M. p. 121, 3 al.— Trop., to extricate one's self, to get off: reliqui habere se angustius videntur; enatant tamen, Cic. Tusc. 5, 30, 87; Petr. 57, 10.

enatus.full: ēnātus, a, um, Part., from enascor.
enatus.short: ēnātus, a, um, Part., from enascor.

enavatae.full: ēnāvātae, false reading for navatae, Tac. H. 3, 74.
enavatae.short: ēnāvātae, false reading for navatae, Tac.

enavigo.full: ē-nāvĭgo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. n. and a. Neutr., to sail out, sail away. Lit.: de ea civitate, Dig. 45, 1, 122: Rhodum, Suet. Tib. 11.—Absol., Curt. 9, 9, 13.—* Trop.: tamquam e scrupulosis cotibus enavigavit oratio, has escaped from, Cic. Tusc. 4, 14, 33.— Act., to traverse by sailing, to sail over: undam, Hor. C. 2, 14, 11: sinum, Plin. 9, 3, 2, § 6: (Indum), id. 6, 17, 21, § 60.

encaenia.full: encaenĭa, ōrum, n., = ἐγκαίνια, τά, a consecration or dedication festival, Aug. in Joann. 84 (cf. Spald. ad Quint. 7, 2, 33); Petr. S. 35, 7.—Hence,
encaenia.short: encaenĭa, ōrum, n., = ἐγκαίνια, τά, a consecration or dedication festival, Aug.

encaenio.full: encaenĭo, āre, to consecrate: novam tunicam, Aug. in Joann. 84.
encaenio.short: encaenĭo, āre, to consecrate: novam tunicam, Aug.

encanthis.full: encanthis, ĭdis, f., = ἐγκανθίς, a swelling of the eyelid, Cels. 7, 7, 5.
encanthis.short: encanthis, ĭdis, f., = ἐγκανθίς, a swelling of the eyelid, Cels.

encardia.full: encardĭa, ae, f., = ἐγκαρδία, an unknown precious stone, with the figure of a heart on it, Plin. 37, 10, 58, § 159.
encardia.short: encardĭa, ae, f., = ἐγκαρδία, an unknown precious stone, with the figure of a heart on it, Plin.

encarpa.full: encarpa, ōrum, n., = ἔγκαρπα, an architect. ornament, festoons of fruit, Vitr. 4, 1, 7.
encarpa.short: encarpa, ōrum, n., = ἔγκαρπα, an architect.

encathisma.full: encăthisma, ătis, n., = ἐγκάθισμα, a sitting bath, Cael. Aur. Acut. 3, 18; id. Tard. 5, 4, 69; Sext. Plac. 9, 17.— A fomentation, Cael. Aur. Tard. 2, 1, 23.
encathisma.short: encăthisma, ătis, n., = ἐγκάθισμα, a sitting bath, Cael.

encausticus.full: encaustĭcus, a, um, adj., = ἐγκαυστικός, encaustic, done in the encaustic manner. Adj.: picturae, Plin. 35, 11, 39, § 122.— Subst.: encaustica, ae, f. (sc. ars), = ἐγκαυστική, encaustic painting, encaustic, Plin. 35, 11, 39, § 122.
encausticus.short: encaustĭcus, a, um, adj., = ἐγκαυστικός, encaustic, done in the encaustic manner.

encaustus.full: encaustus (encaut-), a, um, adj., = ἔγκαυστος, burned in, encaustic. Adj.: genus pingendi, the encaustic mode of painting, Plin. 35, 11, 41, § 149; cf., respecting it, O. Müller, Archäol. § 320: Phaëthon, Mart. 4, 47, 1.— Subst.: en-caustum (encaut-), i., n., = ἔγκαυστον, the purple-red ink of the later Roman emperors, Cod. Th. 7, 20, 1; August. contra Faust. 3, 18; Cod. Just. 1, 23, 6 al.
encaustus.short: encaustus (encaut-), a, um, adj., = ἔγκαυστος, burned in, encaustic.

encautarium.full: encautārĭum, ii, n., the public archives, Cod. Th. 13, 10, 8.
encautarium.short: encautārĭum, ii, n., the public archives, Cod.

enceladus.full: Encĕlădus, i, m., = Ἐγκέλαδος, one of the giants upon whom Jupiter hurled Ætna, Verg. A. 3, 578; 4, 179; Prop. 2, 1, 39; Ov. Am. 3, 12, 27; id. Pont. 2, 2, 11; Stat. Th. 3, 595; Hyg. Fab. praef.
enceladus.short: Encĕlădus, i, m., = Ἐγκέλαδος, one of the giants upon whom Jupiter hurled Ætna, Verg.

encheliae.full: Encheliae (Encheleae), ārum, m., a people of Illyria, Mela, 2, 3, 11; Plin. 3, 21, 25, § 139; Luc. 3, 189.
encheliae.short: Encheliae (Encheleae), ārum, m., a people of Illyria, Mela, 2, 3, 11;

enchiridion.full: enchīrĭdĭon, ii, n., = ἐγχειρίδιον, a manual, Dig. 1, 2, 2.
enchiridion.short: enchīrĭdĭon, ii, n., = ἐγχειρίδιον, a manual, Dig.

enchorius.full: enchōrĭus, a, um, adj., = ἐγχώριος, in or of the country, native, Philorg. ad Verg. G. 4, 298: aves, Isid. Orig. 12, 7, 1: avium genera, Ambros. Hexaem. 5, 14.
enchorius.short: enchōrĭus, a, um, adj., = ἐγχώριος, in or of the country, native, Philorg.

enchrysa.full: enchrȳsa, ae, another name of the plant anchusa, Plin. 22, 21, 25, § 51.
enchrysa.short: enchrȳsa, ae, another name of the plant anchusa, Plin.

enclima.full: enclĭma, ătis, n., = ἔγκλιμα, the inclination of the equator to the horizon, the elevation of the pole, Vitr. 9, 9.
enclima.short: enclĭma, ătis, n., = ἔγκλιμα, the inclination of the equator to the horizon, the elevation of the pole, Vitr.

encliticus.full: enclĭtĭcus, a, um, adj., = ἐγκλιτικός; in gram., which leans upon or throws back its accent, enclitic, Prisc. p. 977 P. al.; cf. Mart. Cap. 3, § 272.

encolpiae.full: encolpĭae, ārum, m., = ἐγκολπίαι ἄνεμοι, winds that arise in a bay, App. de Mundo, p. 61, 40 (in Sen. Q. N. 5, 8 written as Greek).
encolpiae.short: encolpĭae, ārum, m., = ἐγκολπίαι ἄνεμοι, winds that arise in a bay, App.

encomboma.full: encombōma, ătis, n., = ἐγκόμβωμα, a white garment worn by girls, Varr. ap. Non. 543, 1.
encomboma.short: encombōma, ătis, n., = ἐγκόμβωμα, a white garment worn by girls, Varr.

encomiographus.full: encōmĭogrăphus, i, m., = ἐγκωμιόγραφος, the composer of a eulogy, a eulogist, panegyrist, M. Aur. in Fronto Ep. ad M. Caes. 2, 9.
encomiographus.short: encōmĭogrăphus, i, m., = ἐγκωμιόγραφος, the composer of a eulogy, a eulogist, panegyrist, M.

encomium.full: encōmĭum, i, n., = ἐγκώμιον, praise, eulogy, Quint. 7, 2, 33 (ex conject. Gesn. Halm, encenia).
encomium.short: encōmĭum, i, n., = ἐγκώμιον, praise, eulogy, Quint.

encratitae.full: Encrătītae, ārum, m., = Ἐγκρατῖται ("the Continent"), a sect of Gnostics, Cod. Th. 16, 19, 1; Hier. adv. Jovin. 1, 13.
encratitae.short: Encrătītae, ārum, m., = Ἐγκρατῖται ("the Continent"), a sect of Gnostics, Cod.

encrinomenos.full: Encrīnŏmĕnos, i, m., = Ἐγκρινόμενος ("the Admitted" among the Athletae), a statue by Alcamenes, Plin. 34, 8, 19, § 72.
encrinomenos.short: Encrīnŏmĕnos, i, m., = Ἐγκρινόμενος ("the Admitted" among the Athletae), a statue by Alcamenes, Plin.

encyclios.full: encȳclĭos, on, adj., = ἐγκύκλιος, of or belonging to a circle: disciplina = ἐγκύκλιος παιδεία, the circle of arts and sciences, the course of study which every Grecian youth went through before entering upon professional studies, Vitr. 1, 1; 6 praef.; cf. Quint. 1, 10, 1.
encyclios.short: encȳclĭos, on, adj., = ἐγκύκλιος, of or belonging to a circle: disciplina = ἐγκύκλιος παιδεία, the circle of arts and sciences, the course of study which every Grecian youth went through before entering upon professional studies, Vitr.

encymos.full: encȳmŏs, on, adj., = ἔγκυμος, juicy, Plin. 25, 5, 21, § 51 Jan.
encymos.short: encȳmŏs, on, adj., = ἔγκυμος, juicy, Plin.

encytus.full: encўtus (enchўt-), i, m., = ἔγχυτος, a kind of pastry, a cake, Cato R. R. 80.
encytus.short: encўtus (enchўt-), i, m., = ἔγχυτος, a kind of pastry, a cake, Cato R.

endo.full: endo, praep., v. in init.; also the words compounded with endo (indu), as, endogredior, endoperator, etc., v. under in(im-), ingredior, imperator, etc.

endromidatus.full: endrŏmĭdātus, a, um, adj., wearing an endromis, Sid. Ep. 2, 2.
endromidatus.short: endrŏmĭdātus, a, um, adj., wearing an endromis, Sid.

endromis.full: endrŏmis, ĭdis, f., = ἐνδρομίς, a coarse woollen cloak in which the heated athletae wrapped themselves after their exercises, Mart. 4, 19; 14, 126; Juv. 3, 102. But afterwards a fine sort worn as an article of luxury: Tyriae, id. 6, 246 Rup.
endromis.short: endrŏmis, ĭdis, f., = ἐνδρομίς, a coarse woollen cloak in which the heated athletae wrapped themselves after their exercises, Mart.

endymion.full: Endўmĭon, ōnis, m., = Ἐνδυμίων, a beautiful youth of Mount Latmos, in Caria, who, on account of his love for Juno, was condemned by Jupiter to perpetual sleep. While in this state Luna fell violently in love with him, Cic. Tusc. 1, 38, 92: Endymionis somnus, i. e. perpetual sleep, id. Fin. 5, 20, 55; Prop. 2, 15, 15 (3, 7, 15 M.); Ov. A. A. 3, 83 al.— Transf., a beautiful, beloved youth in gen., Juv. 10, 318; App. M. 1, p. 107.— Hence, Endў-mĭōnēus, a, um, adj., of Endymion: sopores, Aus. Idyll.
endymion.short: Endўmĭon, ōnis, m., = Ἐνδυμίων, a beautiful youth of Mount Latmos, in Caria, who, on account of his love for Juno, was condemned by Jupiter to perpetual sleep.

enecatrix.full: ēnĕcātrix, īcis, f. eneco, a murderess, Tert. adv. Marc. 1, 29 fin.

eneco.full: ē-nĕco or ēnĭco, cŭi (enicavit, Plaut. As. 5, 2, 71), ctum (less freq. enecatum; in the part. enecatus, Plin. 18, 13, 34, § 127; 30, 12, 34, § 108; and, enectus, id. 7, 9, 7, § 47; 26, 15, 90, § 159), 1 (old form of the fut. perf. enicasso, Plaut. Most. 1, 3, 55 and 66), v. a., to kill off, kill completely, to kill, stay (freq. and class., esp. in the transf. signif.; syn.: neco, interficio, interimo, conficio, caedo, occido, concido, trucido, jugulo, obtrunco, etc.). Lit.: puer ambo anguis enic

enectus.full: ēnectus, a, um, Part., from eneco.
enectus.short: ēnectus, a, um, Part., from eneco.

enema.full: ĕnĕma, ătis, n., = ἔνεμα, a clyster, enema, Theod. Prisc. 2, 1.
enema.short: ĕnĕma, ătis, n., = ἔνεμα, a clyster, enema, Theod.

energema.full: ĕnergēma, ătis, n., = ἐνέργημα, effect, efficacy (late Lat.), Tert. Praesc. 30; Carn. Christ. 34. In Prudentius written and scanned ĕnergĭma, Apoth. 468.
energema.short: ĕnergēma, ătis, n., = ἐνέργημα, effect, efficacy (late Lat.), Tert.

energia.full: ĕnergīa, ae, f., = ἐνέργεια, energy, efficiency, Hier. Ep. 50.
energia.short: ĕnergīa, ae, f., = ἐνέργεια, energy, efficiency, Hier.

energumenos.full: ĕnergūmĕnos, i, m., = ἐνεργούμενος, possessed of the devil (pure Lat.: a daemone correptus), Sulp. Sev. Dial. 1, 20, 9; 3, 6, 2.
energumenos.short: ĕnergūmĕnos, i, m., = ἐνεργούμενος, possessed of the devil (pure Lat.: a daemone correptus), Sulp.

enervatio.full: ēnervātĭo, ōnis, f. enervo, a state of weakness, enervation: voluptatis, Arn. 3, p. 105.

enervis.full: ē-nervis, e, adj. nervus, nerveless, enervated, weak, effeminate (rare and postAug., for enervatus; cf. enervo): corpus, Petr. poët. 119, 25: homo, Sen. Thyest. 176: compositio (with effeminata), Quint. 9, 4, 142; cf. orator (with solutus), Tac. Or. 18 fin.: et fluxum spectaculum, Plin. Pan. 33, 1; Val. Max. 6, 4, 2; 8, 8 init. al.—Adv.: enervĭter, weakly: blandus, August. cont. Faust. 22, 50.

enervo.full: ē-nervo, āvi, ātum, 1 (scanned ĕnervans and ĕnervātum in Prud. Cath. 8, 64; contra Symm. 2, 143), v. a. enervis, to take out the nerves or sinews. Prop. (rare and post-class.): poplites securi, App. M. 8, p. 215: cerebella, Apic. 4, 2; 7, 7: enervatus Melampus, i. e. unmanned, Claud. in Eutr. 1, 315.— Transf., in gen., to enervate, weaken, render effeminate (class.; esp. freq. in the part. perf.): non plane me enervavit senectus, Cic. de Sen. 10, 32: corpora animosque, Liv. 23, 18: artus undis,
enervo.short: ē-nervo, āvi, ātum, 1 (scanned ĕnervans and ĕnervātum in Prud.

enervus.full: ēnervus, a, um, adj., = enervis, enervated, weak: enerva et exossa saltatio, App. M. 2, p. 104, 3.
enervus.short: ēnervus, a, um, adj., = enervis, enervated, weak: enerva et exossa saltatio, App.

engibata.full: engībăta, um, n., a glass manikin made to move up and down in a vessel of water, the Cartesian imp, Vitr. 10, 12.
engibata.short: engībăta, um, n., a glass manikin made to move up and down in a vessel of water, the Cartesian imp, Vitr.

engonasi.full: Engŏnăsi or Engŏnăsin = Ἐν γόνασι(ν) (upon the knees), the Kneeler, the constellation Hercules; in pure Lat. Nixus and Ingeniculus, Cic. poët. N. D. 2, 42, 108; Manil. 5, 646; Hyg. Astr. 2, 6; 3, 5.—Collat. form, engonasis, Mart. Cap. 8, § 827.
engonasi.short: Engŏnăsi or Engŏnăsin = Ἐν γόνασι(ν) (upon the knees), the Kneeler, the constellation Hercules;

engonaton.full: engŏnăton, i, n., a sort of sun-dial, Vitr. 9, 9.
engonaton.short: engŏnăton, i, n., a sort of sun-dial, Vitr.

enguion.full: Engŭĭon (also written Engўon), i, n., = Ἐγγύιον, a city in the interior of Sicily, now Gangi Vetere, Sil. 14, 249.— Deriv.: Engŭīnus, a, um, adj., of Enguion: civitas, Cic. Verr. 2, 3, 43, § 193; and Enguīni, ōrum, m., its inhabitants, Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 44; 2, 5, 72; Plin. 3, 8, 14, § 91.
enguion.short: Engŭĭon (also written Engўon), i, n., = Ἐγγύιον, a city in the interior of Sicily, now Gangi Vetere, Sil.

enhaemon.full: ĕnhaemon, i, n., = ἔναιμον (sc. φάρμακον), a styptic medicine, Plin. 12, 17, 38, § 77.

enhydris.full: ĕnhȳ^dris, ĭdis, f., = ἐνυδρίς, a water-snake, Plin. 30, 3, 8, § 21; 32, 7, 26, § 82.
enhydris.short: ĕnhȳ^dris, ĭdis, f., = ἐνυδρίς, a water-snake, Plin.

enhydros.full: ĕnhȳ^dros (us), i, m., = ἔνυδρος, an unknown gem, Plin. 37, 11, 73, § 190; Sol. 37; 67; Isid. 16, 13, 9.
enhydros.short: ĕnhȳ^dros (us), i, m., = ἔνυδρος, an unknown gem, Plin.

enim.full: ĕnim, conj. [comp. of ĕ for pronom. stem i, and nam], a demonstrative corroborative particle. (Its position is regularly after the first word, or the first two or more closely connected words in the sentence; only in the comic writers sometimes at the beginning. Put after est in the fourth place: in eo est enim illud, Cic. Off. 1, 20, 67: ab omnibus est enim, etc., id. Deiot. 13, 37; al., see below. Put after quoque: id quoque enim traditur, Liv. 2, 18; 3, 50; 23, 12; 27, 22; 30, 1; 33, 30; 36,

enipeus.full: Ĕnīpeus (trisyl.), i, m., = Ἐνῖπεύς. A river in Thessaly that flows into the Penēus, Verg. G. 4, 368; Luc. 7, 116; as a river-god, the lover of Tyro, daughter of Salmoneus, and by her the father of Pelias and Neleus, Prop. 1, 13, 21; 3, 19, 13 (4, 18, 13 M.); Ov. M. 6, 116; Hyg. Fab. 157: voc. Enīpeu, Ov. M. 7, 229.— A river in Pieria, Liv. 44, 8, 2; 44, 20, 3.— A Roman youth, Hor. C. 3, 7, 23.

enispe.full: Ĕnispē, ae, f., a city of Arcadia, Sen. Troad. 844; Stat. Th. 4, 286.
enispe.short: Ĕnispē, ae, f., a city of Arcadia, Sen.

enisus.full: ēnīsus, a, um, Part. and P. a., from enitor.

eniteo.full: ē-nĭtĕo, tŭi, 2, v. n., to shine forth, shine out, gleam, brighten (class.). Lit.: fruges enitent, Att. ap. Cic. Tusc. 2, 5; cf.: myrtus floridis ramulis, Cat. 61, 21: campus, Verg. G. 2, 211: caelum, i. e. to become fine again, clear up, Gell. 19, 1, 7: tantum egregio decus enitet ore, Verg. A. 4, 150.— Trop., to shine forth, to be eminent, distinguished (a favorite expression of Cicero): quod in eis orationibus, quae Philippicae nominantur, enituerat Demosthenes, Cic. Att. 2, 1, 3; cf. id. Inv

enitesco.full: ē-nĭtesco, -nitŭi, 3, v. inch. n., to shine forth, shine out, become bright (freq. in the post-Aug. per.). Lit.: ut (oculi) in hilaritate enitescant, Quint. 11, 3, 75.—Poet.: enitescis pulchrior multo (Barine), Hor. C. 2, 8, 6.— Trop., to shine forth, become distinguished: sibi novum bellum exoptabat, ubi virtus enitescere posset, Sall. C. 54, 4: gloria, Auct. Her. 4, 44, 57; cf. Gell. 17, 21, 33: facundia, Quint. 10, 5, 14; cf. Tac. Or. 20: utque studiis honestis et eloquentiae gloria enitescer

enitor.full: ē-nītor, -nīsus or -nixus (enixus, of bodily exertion, esp. of childbirth: enisus, of labor for an end, esp. of mental effort, etc., v. infra), 3, v. dep. n. and act. Neutr. To force or work one's way out; or (more freq.) to force one's way up, to mount up, climb, ascend. Lit.: per angustias aditus et ingruentem multitudinem, Tac. A. 16, 5; cf. Liv. 30, 24; 21, 36: dum cohortes in aequum eniterentur, Tac. A. 2, 80 fin.: adeo erat impedita vallis, ut in ascensu, nisi sublevati a suis, primi non f
enitor.short: ē-nītor, -nīsus or -nixus (enixus, of bodily exertion, esp.

enixe.full: ēnixē and ēnixim, advv., v. preced. fin.

enixus1.full: ēnixus, a, um, Part. and P. a., from enitor.

enixus2.full: ēnixus, ūs, m. enitor, a bringing forth, birth, Plin. 7, 6, 5, § 42; 10, 63, 83, § 180; 10, 64, 84, § 183.

enna.full: Enna, Ennaeus, and Ennensis v. Henn-.

ennaeteris.full: Ennăĕtēris, ĭdis, f., = ἐνναετηρίς, a period of nine years, Censor. 18, 4.
ennaeteris.short: Ennăĕtēris, ĭdis, f., = ἐνναετηρίς, a period of nine years, Censor.

ennam.full: ennam, etiamne, Paul. ex Fest. p. 76, 2.

enneadecaeteris.full: ennĕădĕcăĕtēris, rĭdis, f., = ἐννεακαιδεκαετηρίς, the space of nineteen years, Censor. 18, 3; Ambros. Ep. 10, 84.
enneadecaeteris.short: ennĕădĕcăĕtēris, rĭdis, f., = ἐννεακαιδεκαετηρίς, the space of nineteen years, Censor.

enneadicus.full: ennĕădĭcus, a, um, adj., = ἐννεαδικός, of the number nine (pure Lat. nonarius): anni, Firm. Math. 5, 3.
enneadicus.short: ennĕădĭcus, a, um, adj., = ἐννεαδικός, of the number nine (pure Lat.

enneaphthongos.full: ennĕaphthongos, on, adj., = ἐννεάφθογγος, nine-toned, producing nine tones or sounds: chelys, Mart. Cap. 1, § 66.
enneaphthongos.short: ennĕaphthongos, on, adj., = ἐννεάφθογγος, nine-toned, producing nine tones or sounds: chelys, Mart.

enneaphyllon.full: ennĕăphyllon, i, n., = ἐννεάφυλλον, a caustic plant with nine leaves; acc. to Sprengel, Dentaria enneaphylla, Linn.; Plin. 27, 9, 54, § 77.
enneaphyllon.short: ennĕăphyllon, i, n., = ἐννεάφυλλον, a caustic plant with nine leaves;

enneas.full: ennĕas, ădis, f., = ἐννεάς, the number nine, Censor. 14, 14; Mart. Cap. 7, § 741.
enneas.short: ennĕas, ădis, f., = ἐννεάς, the number nine, Censor.

ennius.full: Ennĭus, i, m. Q. Ennius, the most celebrated Roman poet of the ante-class. period, the father of Roman epic poetry, born at Rudiae, in Calabria, 515, died 585 A. U. C.; Ter. And. prol. 18; Cic. Brut. 18, 73 sq.; Hor. Ep. 2, 1, 50.—Cf. respecting him, Teuffel's Gesch. der Röm. Lit. p. 157 sq., Bernhardy's Grundriss der Röm. Lit. pp. 188 sq., 360 sq., and the authorities cited by both.— Derivv. Ennĭā-nus, a, um, adj., Ennian: versus, Sen. Ep. 108; cf. Gell. 12, 2, 7: distichon, Mart. Cap. 1, § 42:

ennoea.full: ennoea, ae, f., = ἔννοια, an idea, notion, one of the aeons of Valentinus, Tert. adv. Val. 7.
ennoea.short: ennoea, ae, f., = ἔννοια, an idea, notion, one of the aeons of Valentinus, Tert.

ennoematicus.full: ennŏēmătĭcus, a, um, adj., = ἐννοηματικός, intellectual, notional; hence, gram. t. t., indirect: definitio, Cassiod. in Ps. 5, 6.
ennoematicus.short: ennŏēmătĭcus, a, um, adj., = ἐννοηματικός, intellectual, notional;

ennosigaeus.full: Ennŏsĭgaeus, i, m., = Ἐννοσίγαιος, the earth-shaker, a surname of Neptune, Juv. 10, 182; Amm. 17, 7 fin.
ennosigaeus.short: Ennŏsĭgaeus, i, m., = Ἐννοσίγαιος, the earth-shaker, a surname of Neptune, Juv.

eno.full: ē-no, āvi, 1, v. n. and a. Neutr., to swim out, swim away, escape by swimming. Prop. (rare but class.): facile, * Plaut. Rud. 1, 2, 81: e concha, * Cic. Fin. 3, 19, 63: in Erythraeam, Liv. 44, 28; cf.: in terram, id. 33, 41.— Poet. transf., of flying, * Lucr. 3, 591; * Verg. A. 6, 16; Sil. 12, 95. — Act., to traverse by swimming, i. e. to sail through a place (in post-Aug. poets): orbem fretis, Val. Fl. 5, 316: has valles, Sil. 3, 662.

enoch.full: Ēnōch, m. indecl., a Hebrew patriarch, son of Seth, Aus. Ephem. 4, 42; Isid. Orig. 7, 6, 11; Alcim. Avit. 4, 180.

enodabilis.full: ēnōdābĭlis, e, adj. enodo, explicable, Ambros. in Luc. 10, § 147.

enodatio.full: ēnōdātĭo, ōnis, f. enodo, a denouement, development, explanation, Cic. Top. 7, 31; id. N. D. 3, 24, 62.

enodator.full: ēnōdātor, ōris, m. id., an explainer: vocis, Tert. Pall. 6.

enodis.full: ēnōdis, e, adj. nodus, free from knots, without knots (poet. and in post-Aug. prose). Prop.: trunci, Verg. G. 2, 78; cf. cedri, Claud. Rapt. Pros. 3, 360: nitor arborum, Plin. 5, 1, 1, § 14: harundo, Mart. Cap. 9, § 906.— Transf., smooth, supple: artus (al. arcus) laterum, Claud. ap. Eutr. 2, 361.— Trop., of speech, clear, plain, intelligible: elegi, Plin. Ep. 5, 17, 2; Ambros. Ep. 1, 12; id. in Luc. 7, § 136 init.

enodo.full: ē-nōdo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a., to free from knots. Lit.: vitem, Cato, R. R. 33, 1; 44; Col. 5, 6, 14.— Transf.: arcum, i. e. to deprive of the string, to unstring, App. M. 5, p. 172.— Trop., of speech, to free from obscurity, i. e. to make plain, to explain, elucidate, unfold, declare (mostly ante-class.; syn.: expedio, extrico, enucleo, expono, interpretor, explano, explico): quod quaero abs te enoda, et qui sis explica, Att. ap. Non. 15, 7; cf. Enn. Pac., Turp., and Varr. ib. 11 sq.: nomina, Cic

enorchis.full: ĕnorchis, is, f., = ἔνορχις, an unknown precious stone, Plin. 37, 10, 58, § 159.
enorchis.short: ĕnorchis, is, f., = ἔνορχις, an unknown precious stone, Plin.

enormis.full: ē-normis, e, adj. norma, out of rule (post-Aug.). Irregular, unusual: toga, Quint. 11, 3, 139: vici (with huc et illuc flexi), Tac. A. 15, 38.—Far more freq., Immoderate, immense, enormous (cf.: immensus, immodicus, summus, maximus, effusus): enormes sunt (umbrae) cerasis, Plin. 17, 12, 17, § 88: spatium (with immensum), Tac. Agr. 10; cf. hastae (with immensa scuta), id. A. 2, 14: gladii (opp. parva scuta), id. Agr. 36: Colossi, Stat. S. 1, 3, 51; cf. corpus, Suet. Calig. 50: proceritas, id. Vit

enormitas.full: ēnormĭtas, ātis, f. enormis (postAug.). Irregularity, Quint. 9, 4, 27.— Hugeness, vastness, enormous size, Sen. Const. Sap. 18: onerum, Veg. Vet. 2, 54; 59 Bip.; Spart. Carac. 2; Capitol. Gord. 29 al.

enotesco.full: ē-nŏtesco, ēnŏtŭi, 3, v. inch. n., to become known abroad, to become known (postAug. and rare): ut eloquentia per gentes enotesceret, Sen. Ben. 3, 32.—In the perf., Plin. Ep. 2, 10, 3; Tac. H. 3, 34 fin.; Suet. Oth. 3 (with divulgare).

enoto.full: ē-nŏto, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a., to mark out, note down (not ante-Aug. and rare): meditabar aliquid enotabamque, Plin. Ep. 1, 6, 1: figuras, id. ib. 6, 16, 10: verbum cui tribus litteris, Quint. 1, 7, 27: signa nostra, App. M. 9, p. 237.—Poet.: pictis anas enotata pennis, Petr. poët. Sat. 93, 2, 4.

enrythmos.full: enrythmos, on, adj., = ἔνρυθμος, rhythmical, in harmony: tempora, Mart. Cap. 9, § 972; cf. § 970.
enrythmos.short: enrythmos, on, adj., = ἔνρυθμος, rhythmical, in harmony: tempora, Mart.

ens.full: ens, entis, n. sum, a thing; formed, like essentia, after the Gr. οὐσία, by Flavius (or Fabianus), acc. to Quint. 8, 3, 33 Spald. N. cr., but first used by Caesar, acc. to Prisc. 18, 8, 75: entia (= τὰὄντα), Quint. 2, 14, 2.

ensiculus.full: ensĭcŭlus, i, m. (also ensĭcŭla, ae, f., acc. to Probus ap. Prisc. p. 618 fin.), dim. ensis, a little sword, rapier, Plaut. Rud. 4, 4, 112 sq.

ensifer.full: ensĭfer, fĕra, fĕrum, adj. ensis-fero, sword-bearing: Orion (like the Gr. ξιφήρης), Luc. 1, 665: Celeneus, Val. Fl. 3, 406: catervae, Stat. Th. 4, 321.

ensiger.full: ensĭger, gera, gerum, adj. ensis-gero, sword-bearing: Orion, Ov. A. A. 2, 56; id. F. 4, 388.

ensipotens.full: ensĭ-pŏtens, entis, adj., mighty in using the sword; cf. Narsus, Coripp. 4, 366.
ensipotens.short: ensĭ-pŏtens, entis, adj., mighty in using the sword;

ensis.full: ensis, is, m. Sanscr. root as-, asyati, hurl; asi, sword, a sword, brand. Prop. (almost exclusively in the poets; synon. with gladius, acc. to Quint. 10, 1, 11; cf. also spatha, acinaces, sica, mucro, pugio), Lucr. 5, 1293; Cic. poët. ap. Gell. 15, 6, 3; and id. N. D. 2, 63 fin.; Tib. 1, 3, 47; 1, 10, 1: ensem haesurum jugulo puto, Ov. Tr. 1, 1, 484; Verg. A. 2, 393; 553 et saep.; Liv. 7, 10, 9.— Meton. War, Sil. 7, 167; Stat. S. 4, 7, 45; cf.: lateque vagatur ensis, i. e. slaughter, Luc. 2, 102

entaticus.full: entătĭcus, a, um, adj., = ἐντατικός, stretching, stimulating. Adj.: emplastron, Fulg. Myth. 3, 7.— Subst.: enta-tĭcus, i, m., a plant = satyrion, App. Herb. 15.
entaticus.short: entătĭcus, a, um, adj., = ἐντατικός, stretching, stimulating.

entelechia.full: entĕlĕchīa, ae, f., = ἐντελέχεια, in the lang. of the Aristotelian philosophy, actuality, Tert. Anim. 32; Macr. Somn. Scip. 1, 14; cf. Cic. Tusc. 1, 10, 22 (v. Lidd. and Scott, s. v. ἐντελέχεια).
entelechia.short: entĕlĕchīa, ae, f., = ἐντελέχεια, in the lang.

entella.full: Entella, ae, f., = Ἔντελλα, a city in the interior of Sicily, now Rocca d' Entella, Sil. 14, 204.—Hence, Entellīni, ōrum, m., the inhabitants of Entella, Plin. 3, 8, 14, § 91.—In sing., Entellinus, Cic. Verr. 2, 3, 87.—And adj.: Entellinus senatus, id. ib.
entella.short: Entella, ae, f., = Ἔντελλα, a city in the interior of Sicily, now Rocca d' Entella, Sil.

entellus.full: Entellus, i, m., a Sicilian hero, famous as a pugilist, Verg. A. 5, 387 sq.
entellus.short: Entellus, i, m., a Sicilian hero, famous as a pugilist, Verg.

enterocele.full: entĕrŏcēle, ēs, f., = ἐντεροκήλη, a rupture, hernia, Plin. 26, 13, 83, § 134; Mart. 10, 56; 11, 84.—Hence, entĕrŏcēlĭcus, i, m., one suffering from hernia, Plin. 26, 8, 49, § 79 al.; Mart. 12, 70.
enterocele.short: entĕrŏcēle, ēs, f., = ἐντεροκήλη, a rupture, hernia, Plin.

entheatus.full: enthĕātus, a, um, adj. enthĕus, divinely inspired, Mart. 12, 57.

entheca.full: enthēca, ae, f., = ἐνθήκη. A store, Cod. Th. 14, 3, 7; Dig. 32, 67, § 2 al.— A magazine, Cod. Th. 15, 1, 12.— A hoard, August. Serm. 355, 4.

entheus.full: enthĕus, a, um, adj., = ἔνθεος. Pass., divinely inspired (a poet. word of the post-Aug. per.), Mart. 11, 84; Stat. S. 1, 2, 227; 3, 5, 97; Sen. Med. 382 al.—* Act., inspiring: mater, i. e. Cybele, Mart. 5, 41, 3.

enthusiastae.full: enthūsĭastae, ārum, m., a sect of heretics, Cod. Th. 16, 5, 65, § 5.
enthusiastae.short: enthūsĭastae, ārum, m., a sect of heretics, Cod.

enthymema.full: enthȳmēma, ătis, n., = ἐνθύμημα, rhetor. and dialect. t. t. A reflection, meditation, an argument (pure Lat. commentatio), Quint. 5, 10, 1; 5, 14, 1; 24; 8, 5, 4 et saep.; Cic. Top. 14; Juv. 6, 450.— A conclusion drawn from the contrary, Cic. Top. 13, 55; Quint. 8, 5, 9.

enthymesis.full: enthȳmēsis, is, f., = ἐνθύμησις, animation (late Lat.), Tert. adv. Val. 9 fin. al.
enthymesis.short: enthȳmēsis, is, f., = ἐνθύμησις, animation (late Lat.), Tert.

enubilo.full: ē-nūbĭlo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a., to free from clouds, to make clear (eccl. Lat.). Lit., Tert. Apol. 35.— Trop.: veritatem, Paul. Carm. 21, 667 al.

enubo.full: ē-nūbo, psi, 3, v. n. (a Livian word). To marry out of one's rank: e patribus, Liv. 4, 4, 7; 10, 23, 4.— In gen., to marry and leave the paternal house, Liv. 26, 34, 3, v. Weissenb. ad Liv. 39, 19, 5.

enubro.full: enubro inhibenti, Paul. ex Fest. p. 76, 16 Müll.

enucleate.full: ēnūclĕāte, adv., plainly, without ornament, v. enucleo, P. a. fin.
enucleate.short: ēnūclĕāte, adv., plainly, without ornament, v.

enucleatus.full: ēnūclĕātus, a, um, Part. and P. a., from enucleo.

enucleo.full: ē-nūclĕo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a., to take out the kernels, to clear from the husk. Lit.: bacas, Scribon. Comp. 233; Marc. Emp. 20; Apic. 4, 5: uva passa enucleata, id. 10, 1.— Trop., to lay open, make clear, explain (cf.: enodo, extrico, expedio, etc.): haec nunc enucleare non ita necesse est, Cic. Tusc. 5, 8, 23; id. Part. 17; Gell. 19, 8, 14; Cod. Just. 1, 17 in lemm. —Hence, ēnūclĕātus, a, um, P. a. Clear, pure, unadulterated: suffragia (opp. eblandita), i. e. given from pure conviction, free fr

enudatio.full: ēnūdātĭo, ōnis, f. enudo, a laying bare: animae, mentis, Ambros. Noë. 29, 112.

enudo.full: ē-nūdo, āre, v. a., to lay bare, to deprive of, trop. (late Lat.): Romam suis civibus, Cassiod. Var. 10, 13 al.—(In Cic. Leg. 1, 9, 26, false reading for enodo).

enumeratio.full: ē-nŭmĕrātĭo, ōnis, f. enumero, a counting up, enumerating. In gen.: malorum, Cic. Leg. 3, 10: bonorum et malorum, id. Part. Or. 17, 58: singulorum argumentorum, id. Clu. 24: oratorum, id. Brut. 36 fin.— In rhetor. lang., a recapitulation (Gr. ἀνακεφαλαίωσις), Cic. Inv. 1, 29, 45; 1, 52; Quint. 5, 14, 11; 6, 1, 1 al.

enumero.full: ē-nŭmĕro, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a., to reckon up, count over, count out (class.). In gen.: jamne enumerasti id, quod ad te rediturum putes? Ter. Ad. 2, 2, 28: dies, * Caes. B. C. 3, 105, 2: peculium, i. e. to rate, estimate, Plaut. As. 2, 4, 91: pretium, to count out, to pay, Cic. Rosc. Am. 46, 133. — In partic., to enumerate in speaking, to recount, relate (so most freq.): enumerare possum, quae sit in figuris animantium descriptio partium, Cic. N. D. 2, 47, 121; cf. Sall. C. 51, 9: stipendia, Liv.

enundino.full: ē-nundĭno, āre, v. a., to buy, purchase (eccl. Lat.); trop.: Spiritum Sanctum, Tert. Idol. 9.

enuntiatio.full: ēnuntĭātĭo (enunciat-), ōnis, f. enuntio, in rhetor. and dialect. lang., a declaration, enunciation, proposition, Cic. Fat. 1; 10; 12; Quint. 7, 3, 2; 9, 1, 23.

enuntiativus.full: ēnuntĭātīvus (enunciat-), a, um, adj. id., declarative, enunciative, Sen. Ep. 117, 12 sq.—As gram. t. t. = ἀπαγγελτικός, demonstrative, picturesque: genus poëmatis, Diom. 479 P.

enuntiator.full: ēnuntĭātor, ōris, m. id., a revealer, declarer: verborum Dei, August. Qu. in Heptat. 2, 17.

enuntiatrix.full: ēnuntĭātrix (enunciat-), īcis, f [id.], she who enounces or declares: ars (rhetorice), Quint. 2, 15, 21: sensuum (lingua), Prud. στεφ. 10, 771.
enuntiatrix.short: ēnuntĭātrix (enunciat-), īcis, f [id.], she who enounces or declares: ars (rhetorice), Quint.

enuntiatum.full: ēnuntĭātum (enunciat-), i, n., a proposition; v. enuntio, II.

enuntio.full: ē-nuntĭo (enuncio), āvi, ātum, 1, v. a., to say out (esp. something that should be kept secret), to divulge, disclose, to report, tell. Prop. (good prose): ut, quod meae concreditumst taciturnitati clam, ne enuntiarem, quoiquam, Plaut. Trin. 1, 2, 106: sociorum consilia adversariis, Cic. Rosc. Am. 40, 117; cf. Caes. B. G. 1, 17, 5: rem Helvetiis per indicium, id. ib. 1, 4, 1; cf.: dolum Ciceroni per Fulviam, Sall. C. 28, 2: mysteria, Cic. Mur. 11, 25; id. de Or. 1, 47, 206; cf. Liv. 10, 38; 23,

enuptio.full: ēnuptĭo, ōnis, f. enubo, a marrying out of one family into another: gentis, Liv. 39, 19, 5 Weissenb. ad loc.

enutrio.full: ē-nūtrĭo, īvi or ii, ītum, 4, v. a., to bring up, to nourish, feed, support (rare and not ante-Aug.). Lit.: puerum sub antris, Ov. M. 4, 289: purpurae lutense genus, Plin. 9, 37, 61, § 131: platanum, id. 12, 1, 4, § 8.— Trop., to promote, nourish: unde origines aedificiorum sint institutae, et quibus rationibus enutritae et progressae sint gradatim ad hanc finitionem, Vitr. 2, 1 fin.: ingenia, Quint. 8 prooem. 2: verbis fidei, Vulg. 1 Tim. 4, 6.
enutrio.short: ē-nūtrĭo, īvi or ii, ītum, 4, v.

enutritio.full: ēnūtrītĭo, ōnis, f. enutrio, nourishment, i. e. instruction: magistrorum, Hier. in Matt. 4 ad 24, 19.

enyo.full: Enȳō, ūs, f., = Ἐνυώ, the goddess of war, pure Lat. Bellona (only in post-Aug. poets). Prop., Sil. 10, 203; Stat. Th. 8, 657.— Meton., war, battle: navalis, Mart. Spect. 24, 3.
enyo.short: Enȳō, ūs, f., = Ἐνυώ, the goddess of war, pure Lat.

eo1.full: ĕo, īvi or ii (īt, Verg. A. 9, 418 al.; cf. Lachm. ad Lucr. vol. 2, p. 206 sq.: isse, issem, etc., for ivisse, etc., Ter. Hec. 2, 1, 25; Cic. Rosc. Am. 23, 64; id. Phil. 14, 1, 1; Ov. M. 7, 350 et saep.: isti, Turp. ap. Non. 4, 242: istis, Luc. 7, 834, etc., v. Neue Formenl. 2, 515), īre (inf. pass. irier, Plaut. Rud. 4, 7, 16), ĭtum, v. n. root i-, Sanscr. ēmi, go; Gr. εἶμι; causat. ἵημι = jacio, Georg Curtius Gr. Etym. p. 403, to go (of every kind of motion of animate or inanimate things), to

eo2.full: ĕō, adv. old dat. and abl. form of pron. stem i; cf. is. In locat. and abl. uses, Of place=in eo loco, there, in that place (rare): quid (facturus est) cum tu eo quinque legiones haberes? Cic. Ep. ad Brut. 1, 2, 1: quo loco ... ibi ... eoque, Cels. 8, 9, 1: eo loci, Tac. A. 15, 74; Plin. 11, 37, 50, § 136; so trop.: eo loci, in that condition: res erat eo jam loci, ut, etc., Cic. Sest. 13, 68; Tac. A. 14, 61; Dig. 5, 1, 52, § 3.— Of cause=eā re. Referring to a cause or reason before given, there

eoad.full: ĕōăd, adv. inverted from adeo; cf. quoad, until: nuptias eludit, eoad dum puerorum avus fato concessit, App. Mag. 68, p. 318, 13 (cf. adeo, I. A. 2.).

eodem.full: ĕōdem, adv. old dat. and abl. of idem, of place. Of the place in which, with gen. loci, in the same place (rare): res eodem est loci quo reliquisti, Cic. Att. 1, 13, 5: additi eodem (i. e. in Aventino) novi cives, Liv. 1, 33, 2: arduum est eodem loci potentiam et concordiam esse, Tac. A. 4, 4; Suet. Aug. 65; id. Calig. 53.— Of the place to which. To the same place, to the same point: Orgetorix omnes clientes obaeratosque suos eodem conduxit, Caes. B. G. 1, 4, 2; 4, 28; 5, 11: ego pol te redigam

eon.full: eon, ōnis, f., an unknown tree, Plin. 13, 22, 39, § 119.
eon.short: eon, ōnis, f., an unknown tree, Plin.

eos.full: Ēōs (only in nom.), f., = Ἠώς, the dawn (pure Lat. Aurora), Ov. F. 3, 877; 4, 389; Sen. Herc. Oet. 615.— Meton., the East, the Orient, Luc. 9, 544.— Derivv. ē^ōus, a, um. Adj. Belonging to the morning, morning-: Atlantides absconduntur, i. e. disappear, set in the morning, Verg. G. 1, 221.—More freq., Belonging to the east, eastern, orient (a favorite word of the Aug. poets): domus Aurorae, Prop. 2, 14, 10 (3, 10, 8 M.): equus, id. 4 (5), 3, 10: Arabes, Tib. 3, 2, 24; cf.: domus Arabum, Verg. G.
eos.short: Ēōs (only in nom.), f., = Ἠώς, the dawn (pure Lat.

epactae.full: ĕpactae, ārum, f., = ἐπακταί (sc. ἡμέραι), intercalary days, Isid. Or. 6, 17, 29 and 31.

epagoge.full: ĕpăgōge, ēs, f., = ἐπαγωγή, rhet. t. t. = inductio, induction, Rufin. de Fig. O. 26, p. 215 Ruhnk.

epalimma.full: epalimma genus vilissimi unguenti, Paul. ex Fest. p. 82, 15 Müll.

epaminondas.full: Ĕpămīnōndas, ae, m., = Ἐπαμεινώνδας, the famous general of the Thebans, victor at Leuctra and Mantinea, Nep. Epam.; Just. 6, 7 sq.; Cic. de Or. 3, 34, 139; id. Tusc 1, 2, 4; 1, 15, 33 al.
epaminondas.short: Ĕpămīnōndas, ae, m., = Ἐπαμεινώνδας, the famous general of the Thebans, victor at Leuctra and Mantinea, Nep.

epanadiplosis.full: ĕpănădiplōsis, is, f., = ἐπαναδίπλωσις, rhet. t. t., a repetition of the same word, Rufin. de Schem. § 9, p. 233 Ruhnk.

epanaphora.full: ĕpănăphŏra, ae, f., = ἐπαναφορά, rhet. t. t., a repetition of the same word at the beginning of several successive clauses, Rufin. de Schem. Lex. 6, p. 231 al.

epanodus.full: ĕpănŏdus, i, f., = ἐπάνοδος, rhet. t. t., a return to the same word, Rufin. de Schem. Lex. 19, p. 241 al.

epanorthosis.full: ĕpănorthōsis, is, f., = ἐπανόρθωσις, rhet. t. t., a correction of one's self in speaking, Rufin. de Schem. 15, p. 238 al.

epaphaeresis.full: ĕpăphaerĕsis, is, f., = ἐπαφαίρεσις, a repeated removal: barbae, Mart. 8, 52; Veg. Vet. 5, 24, 5.
epaphaeresis.short: ĕpăphaerĕsis, is, f., = ἐπαφαίρεσις, a repeated removal: barbae, Mart.

epaphroditus.full: Ĕpaphrŏdītus, i, m., a freedman of the Emperor Nero, Suet. Ner. 49; Tac. A. 15, 55.—Hence, ĕpaphrŏdītĭānus, a um, adj., of Epaphroditus: horti, Front. Aquaed. 68.— An eminent Christian of Philippi, Vulg. Phil. 2, 25; 4, 18.
epaphroditus.short: Ĕpaphrŏdītus, i, m., a freedman of the Emperor Nero, Suet.

epaphus.full: Ĕpăphus, i, m., =Ἔπαφος, the son of Jupiter Ammon and Io, and builder of Memphis in Egypt, Ov. M. 1, 748; Hyg. Fab. 140.
epaphus.short: Ĕpăphus, i, m., =Ἔπαφος, the son of Jupiter Ammon and Io, and builder of Memphis in Egypt, Ov.

epastus.full: ē-pastus, a, um, Part. [pasco], eaten up: escae, Ov. Hal. 119.

ependytes.full: ĕpendўtes, ae, m., = ἐπενδύτης, an outer garment, Hier. Vit. Hil. 4.
ependytes.short: ĕpendўtes, ae, m., = ἐπενδύτης, an outer garment, Hier.

epenthesis.full: ĕpenthĕsis, is, f., = ἐπένθεσις, the insertion of a letter, Serv. ad Verg. G. 1, 164.
epenthesis.short: ĕpenthĕsis, is, f., = ἐπένθεσις, the insertion of a letter, Serv.

epeus.full: Ĕpēus (Ĕpīus, Plaut. Bacch. 4, 9, 13), i, m., = Ἐπειός, son of Panopeus, the contriver of the Trojan horse, Verg. A. 2, 264; Ov. F. 3, 825; Hyg. Fab. 108; Plaut. l. l. and Fragm. in Varr. L. L. 7, § 38 Müll.; Paul. ex Fest. p. 82, 12 Müll.

ephalmator.full: ĕphalmātor, ōris, m. vox hibr., ἐφάλλομαι and Lat. ending ator, a tumbler, dancer, Firm. Math. 8, 15.

ephebeum.full: ĕphēbēum or -īum, i, n., = ἐφηβεῖον, a hall set apart for the youth in the palaestra, Vitr. 5, 11, 2.
ephebeum.short: ĕphēbēum or -īum, i, n., = ἐφηβεῖον, a hall set apart for the youth in the palaestra, Vitr.

ephebia.full: ĕphēbī^a, ae, f., = ἐφηβεία or ἐφηβία. Puberty, Don. ad Ter. And. 1, 1, 24.— Transf., the evidences of puberty, Cael. Aur. Acut. 3, 17, 40.— = ephebeum, Vulg. 2 Macc. 4, 9.
ephebia.short: ĕphēbī^a, ae, f., = ἐφηβεία or ἐφηβία.

ephebicus.full: ĕphēbĭcus, a, um, adj., = ἐφηβικός, of or belonging to a youth: chlamyda, App. M. 10, p. 253, 32.
ephebicus.short: ĕphēbĭcus, a, um, adj., = ἐφηβικός, of or belonging to a youth: chlamyda, App.

ephebitus.full: ĕphēbītus, i, m. ephebus, one who has reached the age of adolescence, Varr. ap. Non. 140, 18 dub.

ephebus.full: ĕphēbus, i (gen. plur. contr. ephebūm, Stat. Th. 4, 232), m., = ἔφηβος, a male Greek youth from 18 to 20 years of age (cf.: puer, adolescens, juvenis, adultus, pubes), Ter. Eun. 5, 1, 8; Cic. Fl. 21, 51; id. N. D. 1, 28, 79; Suet. Aug. 98; id. Ner. 12; Hor. Ep. 2, 1, 171; Ov. A. A. 1, 147 al.: is postquam excessit ex ephebis (after the Gr. ἐξελθεῖν ἐξ ἐφήβων), i. e. after he had come to the age of manhood, Ter. And. 1, 1, 24 Ruhnk. (also cited in Cic. de Or. 2, 80, 327).

ephedra.full: ĕphĕdra, ae, f., = ἐφέδρα, the plant horse-tail, Plin. 26, 7, 20, § 36.—Called, also, ĕphĕdros, Plin. 26, 13, 83, § 133.
ephedra.short: ĕphĕdra, ae, f., = ἐφέδρα, the plant horse-tail, Plin.

ephelis.full: ĕphēlis, ĭdis, f., = ἐφηλίς, freckles, Cels. 6, 5.
ephelis.short: ĕphēlis, ĭdis, f., = ἐφηλίς, freckles, Cels.

ephemeris.full: ĕphēmĕris, ĭdis, f., = ἐφημερίς, a day-book, diary, ephemeris (cf.: commentarius, tabulae, scriptio, acta, etc.), Cic. Quint. 18, 57; Nep. Att. 13, 6; Sen. Ep. 123; Plin. 29, 1, 5, § 9; Prop. 3 (4), 23, 20; Ov. Am. 1, 12, 25 al.: ephemeridas ejus vitae composuit, Treb. Poll. Gallien. 18, 6.
ephemeris.short: ĕphēmĕris, ĭdis, f., = ἐφημερίς, a day-book, diary, ephemeris (cf.: commentarius, tabulae, scriptio, acta, etc.), Cic.

ephemeron.full: ĕphēmĕron, i, n., = ἐφήμερον, an unknown plant, Plin. 25, 13, 107, § 170.
ephemeron.short: ĕphēmĕron, i, n., = ἐφήμερον, an unknown plant, Plin.

ephesius.full: Ĕphĕsius, a, um, adj., see the foll. art.
ephesius.short: Ĕphĕsius, a, um, adj., see the foll.

ephesus.full: Ĕphĕsus, i, f., = Ἔφεσος, an old and celebrated commercial city of Ionia, with a temple to Diana, now ruins near the village of Ayasaluk, Mel. 1, 17, 2; Plin. 5, 29, 31, § 131 sqq.; Plaut. Bacch. 2, 1, 2; 2, 3, 75; 102; 4, 9, 124 et saep.—Derivv., ĕphĕsĭus, a, um, adj., Ephesian: Diana, Plaut. Bacch. 2, 3, 73; id. Mil. 2, 5, 1; Cic. Div. 1, 23 fin.: mater, born at Ephesus, id. Phil. 3, 6, 15: pecunia, deposited in the temple there, Caes. B. C. 3, 33 fin.; 3, 105, 1. —Subst.: Ephesii, ōrum, m., t
ephesus.short: Ĕphĕsus, i, f., = Ἔφεσος, an old and celebrated commercial city of Ionia, with a temple to Diana, now ruins near the village of Ayasaluk, Mel.

ephi.full: ephi, n. indecl., a Hebrew measure, used for grain, oil, etc.; an ephah, Vulg. Exod. 16, 36 et saep.

ephialtes.full: Ĕphĭāltes (ĕphĭālta, ae, Sid. praef. Carm. 7, 25), ae, m., = Ἐφιάλτης. The son of Aloeus and brother of Otus, one of the stormers of heaven, killed by Apollo, Hyg. Fab. 28; Claud. B. Get. 75; Verg. Cul. 234.— The betrayer of the Spartans at Thermopyiae, Front. Strat. 2, 2, 13.

ephippiatus.full: ĕphippĭātus, a, um, adj., furnished with an ephippium: equites, Caes. B. G. 4, 2, 5.
ephippiatus.short: ĕphippĭātus, a, um, adj., furnished with an ephippium: equites, Caes.

ephippium.full: ĕphippĭum, ii, n., = ἐφίππιον, a horse-cloth, caparison, housing (cf. clitellae): tegimen equi ad mollem vecturam paratum, Non. p. 108, 30 (pure Lat. stragulum); Varr. R. R. 2, 7, 15; id. ap. Non. l. l.; Caes. B. G. 4, 2, 4; Cic. Fin. 3, 4, 15; Gell. 5, 5, 3 al.—Prov.: optat ephippia bos piger, optat arare caballus, i. e. each envies the other's condition, Hor. Ep. 1, 14, 43.
ephippium.short: ĕphippĭum, ii, n., = ἐφίππιον, a horse-cloth, caparison, housing (cf.

ephod.full: ephod, n. indecl., part of the clothing of the Hebrew priest, Vulg. Exod. 25, 7 al.

ephorus1.full: ĕphŏrus, i (nom. plur. ephoroe = ἔφοροι, Val. Max. 1, 41, ext. 8), m., = ἔφορος, a member of a well-known body of Spartan magistrates, the Ephori, Cic. Leg. 3, 7, 16; id. Tusc. 1, 42, 100; id. Off. 2, 23; Nep. Them. 7, 2; id. Ages. 4.

ephorus2.full: Ĕphŏrus, i, m., = Ἔφορος, a celebrated Greek historian of Cumae, a disciple of Isocrates, Cic. de Or. 2, 13 fin.; 23; id. Brut. 56, 204; id. Or. 51, 172; Quint. 9, 4, 87 al.
ephorus2.short: Ĕphŏrus, i, m., = Ἔφορος, a celebrated Greek historian of Cumae, a disciple of Isocrates, Cic.

ephyra.full: Ĕphўra, ae, and (poet.) Ĕphўre, ēs, f., = Ἐφύρα, Ion. Ἐφύρη, another name for Corinth, Plin. 4, 4, 5, § 11; Ov. M. 2, 240; 7, 391; Stat. S. 2, 2, 34; so named, according to the myth, after a sea-nymph, Ephyre, Verg. G. 4, 343; Hyg. Fab. 275.— Derivv. ĕphўrēïus, a, um, adj., Ephyrean, Corinthian: aera, Verg. G. 2, 464; cf. Corinthus, II. A. 6.— ĕphўraeus or ĕphўrēus, a, um, adj., the same: litus, Stat. Th. 6, 253: moenia, i. e. of Syracuse (a colony of Corinth), Sil. 14, 180; cf. ib. 52; also Dyr
ephyra.short: Ĕphўra, ae, and (poet.) Ĕphўre, ēs, f., = Ἐφύρα, Ion.

epibata.full: ĕpĭbăta, ae, m., = ἐπιβάτης (one who mounts). A rider of a camel, Hyg. Grom. p. 10 b.— A soldier on board a ship (pure Lat. classiarius miles), Auct. B. Alex. 11, 4; Auct. B. Afr. 20, 1; 62, 1; 63, 4; Vitr. 2, 8.
epibata.short: ĕpĭbăta, ae, m., = ἐπιβάτης (one who mounts).

epibole.full: ĕpĭbŏle, ēs, f., = ἐπιβολή, rhet. t. t., an addition, accumulation of similar words, Rutil. Lup. de Fig. 7, p. 24.

epicedion.full: ĕpĭcēdīon or -īum, ii, n., = ἐπικήδειον, a funeral song, dirge, Stat. S. 2 praef.; 5, 3 and 5 in lemm.
epicedion.short: ĕpĭcēdīon or -īum, ii, n., = ἐπικήδειον, a funeral song, dirge, Stat.

epicertomesis.full: ĕpĭcertŏmēsis, is, f., = ἐπικερτόμησις, rhet. t. t., a sneer, sarcasm, Rufin. de Fig. 1, p. 196.

epicharmus.full: Ĕpĭcharmus, i, m., = Ἐπίχαρμος. A famous Pythagorean philosopher and comic poet of Cos, who resided, after his early youth, in Syracuse (whence his surname of Siculus), Cic. Tusc. 1, 8; Hor. Ep. 2, 1, 58; Plin. 20, 9, 34, § 89 al.—Hence, Epicharmīum illud, a saying of Epicharmus, Gell. 1, 15, 15.— The name of a poem by Ennius, Cic. Ac. 2, 16 fin. al.; v. Vahlen, Ennianae Poesis Reliquiae, p. 167 sq.

epichirema.full: ĕpĭchīrēma, ătis, n., = ἐπιχείρημα, rhet. t. t., a kind of argument or syllogism, Quint. 5, 10, 2 sq.; 5, 14, 5 al.

epichysis.full: ĕpĭchўsis, is, f., = ἐπίχυσις, a vessel for pouring out, Varr. L. L. 5, § 124 Müll.; Plaut. Rud. 5, 2, 32.
epichysis.short: ĕpĭchўsis, is, f., = ἐπίχυσις, a vessel for pouring out, Varr.

epicitharisma.full: ĕpĭcĭthărisma, ătis, n., = ἐπικιθάρισμα, the music after the play, the finale, Tert. adv. Val. 33.
epicitharisma.short: ĕpĭcĭthărisma, ătis, n., = ἐπικιθάρισμα, the music after the play, the finale, Tert.

epiclerus.full: Ĕpiclērus, i, f., = Ἐπίκληρος, An Only Daughter and Heiress, title of a comedy of Menander, Cic. Lael. 26, 99; Quint. 10, 1, 70.
epiclerus.short: Ĕpiclērus, i, f., = Ἐπίκληρος, An Only Daughter and Heiress, title of a comedy of Menander, Cic.

epiclintae.full: ĕpiclintae, ārum, m., = ἐπικλίνται, earthquakes that move with a horizontal motion, App. de Mundo, 65, 23.
epiclintae.short: ĕpiclintae, ārum, m., = ἐπικλίνται, earthquakes that move with a horizontal motion, App.

epicoenus.full: ĕpĭcœnus, a, um, adj., = ἐπίκοινος, in gram., of both genders, epicene (pure Lat. promiscuus): genus, Don. p. 1746 fin.; cf. Quint. 1, 4, 24.
epicoenus.short: ĕpĭcœnus, a, um, adj., = ἐπίκοινος, in gram., of both genders, epicene (pure Lat.

epicopus.full: ĕpĭcōpus, a, um, adj., = ἐπίκωπος, furnished with oars: phaselus, Cic. Att. 14, 16 init.
epicopus.short: ĕpĭcōpus, a, um, adj., = ἐπίκωπος, furnished with oars: phaselus, Cic.

epicrates.full: Ĕpīcrătes, ae, m., = Ἐπικρατής. The victorious, supreme; so Cicero names Pompey, Att. 2, 3.— A philosopher or rhetorician of Athens, Cic. Fil. Fam. 16, 21. — A native of Agyrium, Cic. Verr. 2, 2, 9.

epicrocum.full: ĕpī^crŏcum, i, n., = ἐπίκροκον (v. Lid. and Scott sub h. v.), a fine, transparent garment worn by women, Naev. ap. Varr. L. L. 7, § 53 Müll.; Varr. ap. Non. 318, 25; cf. Paul. ex Fest. p. 82, 13 Müll.— Transf., adj., transparent, fine, thin, Plaut. Pers. 1, 3, 16.

epictetus.full: Ĕpictētus, i, m., = Ἐπίκτητος, a famous Stoic philosopher of Hierapolis in Phrygia, Gell. 1, 2, 6 sq.
epictetus.short: Ĕpictētus, i, m., = Ἐπίκτητος, a famous Stoic philosopher of Hierapolis in Phrygia, Gell.

epicurus.full: Ĕpĭcūrus, i, m., = Ἐπίκουρος, the famous Greek philosopher of Gargettus, in Attica, the author of the Epicurean philosophy, so called after him, which assumed pleasure to be the highest good, Cic. Fin. 1, 9, 29; 2, 2 sq.; id. Ac. 2, 42; id. Tusc. 1, 34; 2, 3, 8 et saep.—Deriv., ĕpĭcūrēus, a, um, adj., of Epicurus, Epicurean: medicamenta doloris, i. e. pleasure, Cic. Fin. 2, 7 fin.: secta, Suet. Gram. 8.—More freq. subst.: ĕpĭcūrēi, ōrum, m., the adherents of the Epicurean philosophy, Epicureans,
epicurus.short: Ĕpĭcūrus, i, m., = Ἐπίκουρος, the famous Greek philosopher of Gargettus, in Attica, the author of the Epicurean philosophy, so called after him, which assumed pleasure to be the highest good, Cic.

epicus.full: ĕpĭcus, a, um, adj., = ἐπικός, epic: poëta (Ennius), Cic. Opt. Gen. 1, 2: poëma, id. ib. 1, 1; cf. carmen, Quint. 10, 1, 62; Fulg. Myth. 1, 2.—Plur. as subst.: ĕpĭci, ōrum, m., the epic poets, Quint. 10, 1, 51.
epicus.short: ĕpĭcus, a, um, adj., = ἐπικός, epic: poëta (Ennius), Cic.

epicyclus.full: ĕpĭcȳ^clus, i, m., = ἐπίκυκλος, a small circle having its centre on the circumference of a greater circle, an epicycle, Mart. Cap. 8, § 879.
epicyclus.short: ĕpĭcȳ^clus, i, m., = ἐπίκυκλος, a small circle having its centre on the circumference of a greater circle, an epicycle, Mart.

epidamnus.full: Ĕpĭdamnus (-os), i, f., = Επίδαμνος, an older name of Dyrrachium, Mel. 2, 3, 13; Plin. 3, 23, 26, § 145; Plaut. Men. 2, 1, 38; id. ib. prol. 33, 49; 51; 72 al.— Derivv. ĕpĭdamnĭus, a, um, adj., Epidamnian: natio, Plaut. Men. 2, 1, 33.— ĕpĭdamnĭensis, e, the same: cives, id. ib. 5, 7, 11; cf. id. ib. prol. 32; 57.
epidamnus.short: Ĕpĭdamnus (-os), i, f., = Επίδαμνος, an older name of Dyrrachium, Mel.

epidaphna.full: Ĕpĭdaphna, ae, f. (nom. Ĕpĭdaph-nes, Plin. 5, 21, 18, § 79), = Ἐπιδάφνη or Ἐπὶ Δάφνης (i. e. near the village of Daphne), another name for Antioch on the Orontes, Tac. A. 2, 83.

epidaurum.full: Ĕpĭdaurum, i, n., a colonial city of Dalmatia, Plin. 3, 22, 26, § 143; cf. Auct. B. Alex. 44 fin.
epidaurum.short: Ĕpĭdaurum, i, n., a colonial city of Dalmatia, Plin.

epidaurus.full: Ĕpĭdaurus, i, f., = Ἐπίδαυρος. A city in Argolis, on the Saronic Gulf, with a famous temple of Aesculapius, now Pidhavro, Mel. 2, 3, 8; Plin. 4, 5, 9, § 17; Liv. 45, 28; Cic. N. D. 3, 34, 83; Verg. G. 3, 44 al.— Derivv. ĕpĭdaurĭus, a, um, adj., of Epidaurus, Epidaurian: litora, Ov. M. 15, 643: tellus, id. ib. 7, 436; cf. rura, Stat. Th. 4, 123: serpens, Hor. S. 1, 3, 27: nutrix Semeles, Beroe, Ov. M. 2, 278: deus, Prop. 2, 1, 61; called also simply Epidaurius, Ov. M. 15, 723; id. P. 1, 3, 21. —S

epidemetica.full: ĕpĭdēmētĭca, ōrum, n., = ἐπιδημητικά, a payment in commutation for the liability to the quartering of troops, Cod. Th. 12, 41.
epidemetica.short: ĕpĭdēmētĭca, ōrum, n., = ἐπιδημητικά, a payment in commutation for the liability to the quartering of troops, Cod.

epidemus.full: ĕpĭdēmus, a, um, adj., = ἐπίδημος, epidemic: species luis, Amm. 19, 4, 7.
epidemus.short: ĕpĭdēmus, a, um, adj., = ἐπίδημος, epidemic: species luis, Amm.

epidermis.full: ĕpĭdermis, ĭdis, f., = ἐπιδερμίς, the surface-skin, cuticle, Veg. Vet. 2, 61, 1.
epidermis.short: ĕpĭdermis, ĭdis, f., = ἐπιδερμίς, the surface-skin, cuticle, Veg.

epidicazomenos.full: Ĕpĭdĭcāzŏmĕnos, i, m. (or Epidicazomene, ēs, f.), the title of a Greek comedy of Apollodorus, imitated by Terence in his Phormio, Ter. Phorm. prol. 26.

epidicticalis.full: ĕpĭdīctĭcālis, e, adj., = ἐπιδεικτικός, pertaining to a norm, normal: terminus, Auct. de Limit. p. 250 sq. Goes.
epidicticalis.short: ĕpĭdīctĭcālis, e, adj., = ἐπιδεικτικός, pertaining to a norm, normal: terminus, Auct.

epidicticus.full: ĕpĭdīctĭcus, a, um, adj., = ἐπιδεικτικός, for display, declamatory: in illo epidictico genere, quod diximus proprium sophistarum, Cic. Or. 13, 42 (written as Greek, id. ib. 11, 37; 61, 207).
epidicticus.short: ĕpĭdīctĭcus, a, um, adj., = ἐπιδεικτικός, for display, declamatory: in illo epidictico genere, quod diximus proprium sophistarum, Cic.

epidicus.full: Ĕpĭdĭcus, i, m., the name of a comedy of Plautus, taken from that of a slave, who is one of the characters.
epidicus.short: Ĕpĭdĭcus, i, m., the name of a comedy of Plautus, taken from that of a slave, who is one of the characters.

epidipnis.full: ĕpĭdīpnis, ĭdis, f., = ἐπιδειπνίς, a dessert, Petr. 69, 6; Mart. 11, 31.
epidipnis.short: ĕpĭdīpnis, ĭdis, f., = ἐπιδειπνίς, a dessert, Petr.

epidius.full: Ĕpĭdĭus, ii, m. A Roman rhetorician, teacher of M. Antony and Augustus, Plin. 17, 25, 38, § 243; Suet. Rhet. 4.— Marullus, a tribune of the people in the time of Caesar, Suet. Caes. 79 sq.† † ĕpĭdixis, is, f., = ἐπίδειζις, a specimen of acting, Inscr. Orell. 2620.

epidromus.full: ĕpī^drŏmus, i, m., = ἐπίδρομος. A cord running up and down for opening and closing a net, Cato, R. R. 13, 1 Schneid.; Plin. 19, 1, 2, § 11.— The sail in the after-part of a ship, acc. to Isid. Orig. 19, 3, 3.

epigenes.full: Ĕpĭgĕnes, is, m., a Greek author, Varr. R. R. 1, 1, 8; cf. Sen. Q. N. 3 al.
epigenes.short: Ĕpĭgĕnes, is, m., a Greek author, Varr.

epignomus.full: Ĕpignōmus, i, m., the name of a character in Plaut. Stich. 2, 2, 47.
epignomus.short: Ĕpignōmus, i, m., the name of a character in Plaut.

epigoni.full: Ĕpĭgŏni, ōrum, m., = Ἐπίγονοι, the After-born. The sons of the seven heroes who went together against Thebes, Hyg. Fab. 71; as the name of a tragedy of Aeschylus, translated into Latin by Attius, Cic. Opt. Gen. 6, 18; id. Tusc. 2, 25, 60; id. Off. 1, 31, 114.— The children of the soldiers of Alexander the Great by Asiatic women, Just. 12, 4 fin.
epigoni.short: Ĕpĭgŏni, ōrum, m., = Ἐπίγονοι, the After-born.

epigramma.full: ĕpĭgramma, ătis, n. (dat. plur. epigrammatis, Cic. Att. 1, 16, 15.—Gen. plur.: epigrammatōn, Mart. 1 praef.; 1, 2; -matum, Suet. Aug. 85), = ἐπίγραμμα. An inscription; on the base of a statue, Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 57; on an offering, Nep. Paus. 1, 3; on tombstones, Petr. 115 fin.; as a brand, id. ib. 103, 4.— An epigram, Cic. Tusc. 1, 34, 84; id. Arch. 10, 25; Quint. 1, 5, 20; Suet. Caes. 73 et saep.; so the Epigrammata of the poet Martial.

epigrammatarius.full: ĕpĭgrammătārĭus, ii, m. epigramma, an epigrammatist (late Lat.), Vop. Florian. 3; id. Saturn. 7.

epigrammaticus.full: ĕpĭgrammătĭcus, a, um, adj., = ἐπιγραμματικός, epigrammatic: poëta Martialis, Spart. Ael. Ver. 5.
epigrammaticus.short: ĕpĭgrammătĭcus, a, um, adj., = ἐπιγραμματικός, epigrammatic: poëta Martialis, Spart.

epigrammation.full: ĕpĭgrammătĭon, ii, n., = ἐπιγραμμάτιον, a short epigram, Varr. L. L. 7, § 28 Müll. (written by Müller as Greek).
epigrammation.short: ĕpĭgrammătĭon, ii, n., = ἐπιγραμμάτιον, a short epigram, Varr.

epigrammatista.full: ĕpĭgrammătista, ae, m., = ἐπιγραμματιστής, an epigrammatist, Sid. Ep. 4, 1.
epigrammatista.short: ĕpĭgrammătista, ae, m., = ἐπιγραμματιστής, an epigrammatist, Sid.

epigri.full: ĕpī^gri, ōrum, m., wooden pins, pegs, Sen. Ben. 2, 12 fin.; Isid. Orig. 19, 69, 7.
epigri.short: ĕpī^gri, ōrum, m., wooden pins, pegs, Sen.

epilepsia.full: ĕpĭlēpsia, ae, f., = ἐπιληψία, the falling sickness, epilepsy, Lat. morbus comitialis, Lampr. Heliog. 20: boum, Veg. Vet. 5, 32; Cael. Aur. Tard. 1, 4, 60 sq.
epilepsia.short: ĕpĭlēpsia, ae, f., = ἐπιληψία, the falling sickness, epilepsy, Lat.

epilepticus.full: ĕpĭlēptĭcus, i, m., adj., = ἐπιληπτικός, epileptic, Auct. Fragm. Jur. Antejust. p. 38 ed. Mai.: passio = morbus comitialis, epilepsy, Cael. Aur. Tard. 2, 30, 162.
epilepticus.short: ĕpĭlēptĭcus, i, m., adj., = ἐπιληπτικός, epileptic, Auct.

epileus.full: ĕpĭlēus, i, m., a sort of hawk, Plin. 10, 8, 9, § 21.
epileus.short: ĕpĭlēus, i, m., a sort of hawk, Plin.

epilogus.full: ĕpĭlŏgus, i, m., = ἐπίλογος, a winding up of a speech, peroration, epilogue (= peroratio or conclusio), Cic. Brut. 33 fin.; Quint. 6, 1, 55; 4, 1, 28; Cic. de Or. 2, 69; id. Tusc. 1, 47; id. Planc. 34; id. Att. 4, 15, 4; Quint. 6, 1, 37; 50 et saep.
epilogus.short: ĕpĭlŏgus, i, m., = ἐπίλογος, a winding up of a speech, peroration, epilogue (= peroratio or conclusio), Cic.

epimedion.full: ĕpĭmēdĭon, ii, n. An unknown plant, Plin. 27, 9, 53, § 76.— A stairrail, balustrade, Inscr. Orell. 3301.

epimelas.full: ĕpĭmĕlās, antis, m., = ἐπιμέλας, a gem superficially black, otherwise unknown, Plin. 37, 10, 58, § 161.
epimelas.short: ĕpĭmĕlās, antis, m., = ἐπιμέλας, a gem superficially black, otherwise unknown, Plin.

epimenia.full: ĕpĭmēnĭa, ōrum, n., = ἐπιμήνια, provisions for a month, a month's rations (Lat. menstrua), Juv. 7, 120.
epimenia.short: ĕpĭmēnĭa, ōrum, n., = ἐπιμήνια, provisions for a month, a month's rations (Lat.

epimenides.full: Ĕpĭmĕnĭdes, is, m., = Ἐπιμενίδης, a famous Greek poet and prophet of Crete, Cic. Leg. 2, 11, 28; id. Div. 1, 18; Varr. L. L. 7, § 3 Müll.; Plin. 7, 48, 49, § 154; 7, 52, 53, § 175.—Perh. named after him: genus (bulborum) Epimenidu (i. e. Ἐπιμενίδου), Plin. 19, 5, 30, § 93 Sillig N. cr.
epimenides.short: Ĕpĭmĕnĭdes, is, m., = Ἐπιμενίδης, a famous Greek poet and prophet of Crete, Cic.

epimerismos.full: ĕpĭmĕrismos, i, m., = ἐπιμερισμός, rhet. t. t., the summing up of the heads of an argument, Mart. Cap. 5, § 564.

epimetheus.full: Ĕpĭmētheus, ei, m., = Ἐπιμηθεύς, in the Greek mythology, a son of Iapetus and Clymene, the husband of Pandora, Hyg. Fab. praef. 142.—Whence his daughter Pyrrha is called ĕpĭmēthis, ĭdis, f., = Ἐπιμηθίς, Ov. M. 1, 390.
epimetheus.short: Ĕpĭmētheus, ei, m., = Ἐπιμηθεύς, in the Greek mythology, a son of Iapetus and Clymene, the husband of Pandora, Hyg.

epimetrum.full: ĕpĭmē^trum, i, n., = ἐπίμετρον, what is given over the measure, over-measure, Cod. Th. 12, 6, 15.
epimetrum.short: ĕpĭmē^trum, i, n., = ἐπίμετρον, what is given over the measure, over-measure, Cod.

epinicium.full: ĕpĭnīcĭum, ii, n., = ἐπινίκιον, a song of victory: canere, Vulg. 1 Par. 15, 21.— Plur.: cantare, Suet. Ner. 43 fin.— Transf., in plur., a festival for victory: agere Hierosolymis, Vulg. 2 Macc. 8, 33.
epinicium.short: ĕpĭnīcĭum, ii, n., = ἐπινίκιον, a song of victory: canere, Vulg.

epinyctis.full: ĕpĭnyctis, ĭdis, f., = ἐπινυκτίς. Night-blains, pustules that arise in the night, Plin. 20, 2, 6, § 12 (in Cels. 5, 28, 15, written as Greek).— A kind of sore in the eyelid; also called syce, Plin. 20, 6, 21, § 44.

epionicus.full: ĕpĭōnĭcus versus = versus Ionicus a majore, Prisc. de Metr. Ter. p. 1319 P.
epionicus.short: ĕpĭōnĭcus versus = versus Ionicus a majore, Prisc.

epipactis.full: ĕpĭpactis, ĭdis, f., = ἐπιπακτίς, an herb; also called helleborine, Plin. 13, 20, 35, § 114; 27, 9, 52, § 76 (dub.; Jan. epicactis).
epipactis.short: ĕpĭpactis, ĭdis, f., = ἐπιπακτίς, an herb;

epipedos.full: ĕpĭpĕdos, ŏn, adj. ἐπι+πέδον, plain, level, Censor. Fr. 6, 2.

epipetron.full: ĕpĭpĕtron, i, n., = ἐπίπετρον, a plant that grows on rocks, Plin. 21, 15, 52, § 89.
epipetron.short: ĕpĭpĕtron, i, n., = ἐπίπετρον, a plant that grows on rocks, Plin.

epiphanes.full: Ĕpĭphănes, is, m., = Ἐπιφανής, the son of Antiochus, king of Commagene, Tac. H. 2, 25 fin.
epiphanes.short: Ĕpĭphănes, is, m., = Ἐπιφανής, the son of Antiochus, king of Commagene, Tac.

epiphania1.full: Ĕpĭphănĭa or -ēa, ae, f., = Ἐπιφάνεια, a city of Cilicia, Plin. 5, 27, 22, § 93; Cic. Fam. 15, 4, 7 sq.
epiphania1.short: Ĕpĭphănĭa or -ēa, ae, f., = Ἐπιφάνεια, a city of Cilicia, Plin.

epiphania2.full: Ĕpĭphănĭa, ōrum, n., = Ἐπιφάνια, the festival of the Epiphany, Cod. Th. 15, 5, 5.
epiphania2.short: Ĕpĭphănĭa, ōrum, n., = Ἐπιφάνια, the festival of the Epiphany, Cod.

epiphonema.full: ĕpĭphōnēma, ătis, n., = ἐπιφώνημα. —In rhet., an exclamation, Quint. 8, 5, 11; 11, 1, 52; Sen. Contr. 1, praef. 23.

epiphora.full: ĕpĭphŏra, ae, f., = ἐπιφορά. An afflux; as a disease, a defluxion of humors, Col. 6, 17, 8; Plin. 20, 9, 40, § 103; 29, 6, 38, § 118 al. (in Cic. Fam. 16, 23, written as Greek).— As a rhet. fig., a repetition, Rufin. de Fig. 1, 8, p. 30.

epiplexis.full: ĕpī^plexis, is, f., = ἐπίπληξις, rhet. t. t., a reproof, Rufin. de Fig. 21, p. 212.

epiploce.full: ĕpī^plŏcē, ēs, f., = ἐπιπλοκή, rhet. t. t., a connection, Rufin. de Fig. 13, p. 44.

epiredium.full: ĕpĭrēdĭum, ii, n. ἐπί-reda; perh. derived immediately from the Greeks, who adopted the Gallic reda into their language, a thong by which a horse was attached to a cart, Juv. 8, 66; Quint. 1, 5, 68.

epirensis.full: Ēpīrensis, e, v. Epirus, II. C.

epirus.full: Ēpīrus or -os, i, f., = Ἤπειρος, the province of Epirus, in the north of Greece, now part of Albania, Mel. 2, 3, 4 sq.; 2, 7, 10; Plin. 4, 1, 1, § 1 sqq.; Cic. Att. 2, 4, 5; id. Pis. 40, 96; Varr. R. R. 2, praef. 7; Verg. G. 1, 59; id. A. 3, 292; Ov. M. 8, 283; Stat. Achil. 1, 428 et saep.— Derivv. ēpīrōtēs, ae, m., = Ἠπειρώτης, an inhabitant of Epirus, an Epirote, Plin. 3, 11, 15, § 98; Aur. Vict. Vir. Ill. 33; scanned ēpĭrōtēs, Aus. Profess. 15, 13.—Adj., of Epirus: Epirotae equi, Veg. Vet. 6,
epirus.short: Ēpīrus or -os, i, f., = Ἤπειρος, the province of Epirus, in the north of Greece, now part of Albania, Mel.

episcenium.full: ĕpiscēnĭum, ii, n., = ἐπισκήνιον, a portion of a theatre, the story over the stage, Vitr. 7, 5, 5; called, also, ĕpiscēnos = ἐπίσκηνος, id. 5, 7, 3; cf. Müller's Archäol. d. K. § 289.
episcenium.short: ĕpiscēnĭum, ii, n., = ἐπισκήνιον, a portion of a theatre, the story over the stage, Vitr.

episcopalis.full: ĕpīscŏpālis, e, adj. episcopus, episcopal: solium, Prud. στεφ. 33.—Adv.: ĕpīscŏpālĭter, episcopally, Aug. Conf. 5, 13.

episcopatus.full: ĕpīscŏpātus, ūs, m. id., the office and dignity of a bishop, episcopate, Tert. Bapt. 17; Amm. 27, 3, 12; Vulg. Psa. 108, 7 al.

episcopus.full: ĕpīscŏpus, i, m., = ἐπίσκοπος, an overseer, superintendent. In gen., Dig. 50, 4, 18, § 7; Inscr. Orell. 4024 (in Cic. Att. 7, 11 fin., written as Greek).— In partic., a bishop (eccl. Lat.), Amm. 15, 7, 7; Vulg. Phil. 1, 1 al.
episcopus.short: ĕpīscŏpus, i, m., = ἐπίσκοπος, an overseer, superintendent.

episcynium.full: ĕpiscўnĭum, ii, n., = ἐπισκύνιον, the eyebrows.—Trop., sternness, severity, Tert. Pall. 4.
episcynium.short: ĕpiscўnĭum, ii, n., = ἐπισκύνιον, the eyebrows.—Trop., sternness, severity, Tert.

epistalma.full: ĕpistalma, ătis, n., = ἐπίσταλμα, a commission of the emperor, Cod. Just. 7, 37, 3.
epistalma.short: ĕpistalma, ătis, n., = ἐπίσταλμα, a commission of the emperor, Cod.

epistates.full: ĕpistătes, ae, m., = ἐπιστάτης, an overseer, superintendent, Cato, R. R. 56; Tert. Mart. 3.
epistates.short: ĕpistătes, ae, m., = ἐπιστάτης, an overseer, superintendent, Cato, R.

epistolicus.full: ĕpīstŏlĭcus, a, um, adj., = ἐπιστολικός, pertaining to or consisting of letters, epistolic: Epistolicae Quaestiones, the title of a work of Cato, Gell. praef. § 9; 7, 10, 2; and of Varro, id. 14, 7, 4; 14, 8, 2.
epistolicus.short: ĕpīstŏlĭcus, a, um, adj., = ἐπιστολικός, pertaining to or consisting of letters, epistolic: Epistolicae Quaestiones, the title of a work of Cato, Gell.

epistolium.full: ĕpīstŏlĭum, ii, n., = ἐπιστόλιον, a short letter, note, Cat. 68, 2.
epistolium.short: ĕpīstŏlĭum, ii, n., = ἐπιστόλιον, a short letter, note, Cat.

epistrategia.full: ĕpistrătēgīa, ae, f., = ἐπιστρατηγεία, the office of the second in command, Inscr. Orell. 516.
epistrategia.short: ĕpistrătēgīa, ae, f., = ἐπιστρατηγεία, the office of the second in command, Inscr.

epistrategus.full: ĕpistrătēgus, i, m., = ἐπιστράτηγος, the second in command, second prefect, Inscr. Orell. 3881.
epistrategus.short: ĕpistrătēgus, i, m., = ἐπιστράτηγος, the second in command, second prefect, Inscr.

epistrophe.full: ĕpistrŏphē, ēs, f., = ἐπιστροφή, rhet. t. t., a returning (pure Lat. reversio), Rufin. de Schem. 16, p. 238.

epistula.full: ĕpistŭla (also in Cic. and ante- and post-class., ĕpistŏla, Corss. Ausspr. 2, 141; but cf. Brambach, Hülfsb. p. 35 sq. Ritschl, Opusc. 2, 493 note), ae, f., = ἐπιστολή. In gen., a written communication, a letter, epistle (cf.: litterae, codicilli): venio nunc ad tuas litteras, quas pluribus epistolis accepi, Cic. Q. Fr. 3, 1, 3, § 8; Plaut. Bacch. 3, 6, 32; 4, 9, 83; id. Mil. 4, 6, 10 et saep.; Cic. Phil. 2, 31; Cic. Verr. 2, 3, 69 fin.; id. Fam. 2, 4 et saep.; Hor. Ep. 2, 2, 22; Ov. H. 15, 219;

epistularis.full: ĕpistŭlāris (epistol-, v. epistula init.), e, adj. epistula, of or belonging to a letter, epistolary. Adj.: chartae, letter-paper, Mart. 14, 11 in lemm.; Dig. 33, 9, 3, § 10: colloquium, epistolary, Aug. Ep. ad Marcell. 5.— Subst.: epistŭlāris, is, f., a messenger of the Eagle of Jupiter: epistularis tua, Mart. Cap. 9, § 896.—Plur.: epistulāres, ium, m., state secretaries, Cod. Th. 6, 30, 7.

epistularius.full: ĕpistŭlārĭus, a, um, adj., = epistularis, of or belonging to a letter. Adj.: scriptio, Ennod. 1, ep. 22.— Subst.: epīstŭlarĭi, ōrum, m., state secretaries, Salv. Gub. D. 5, 7.
epistularius.short: ĕpistŭlārĭus, a, um, adj., = epistularis, of or belonging to a letter.

epistylium.full: ĕpistȳlĭum, ii, n., = ἐπιστύλιον, in arch., the cross-beam that rests on the columns, the architrave, Vitr. 3, 1 sq.; 4, 3; 5, 1; Varr. R. R. 3, 5, 11; Plin. 36, 14, 21, § 96; cf. Paul. ex Fest. p. 82, 11 Müll. Isid. Orig. 15, 8, 15; 19, 10, 24; Vulg. 3 Reg. 7, 6 al.
epistylium.short: ĕpistȳlĭum, ii, n., = ἐπιστύλιον, in arch., the cross-beam that rests on the columns, the architrave, Vitr.

episynaloephe.full: ĕpĭsўnăloephē, ēs, f., = ἐπισυναλοιφή, gram. t. t., a coalescing of two syllables into one, Diom. p. 437 P. al.

epitaphista.full: ĕpĭtăphista, ae, m., = ἐπιταφιστής, a composer of funeral orations, Sid. Ep. 11, 9 fin.
epitaphista.short: ĕpĭtăphista, ae, m., = ἐπιταφιστής, a composer of funeral orations, Sid.

epitaphium.full: ĕpĭtăphĭum, ii, n., = ἐπιτάφιον, or epitaphius, m., = ἐπιτάφιος λόγος, a funeral oration, eulogy. In gen., Inscr. Drell. 1022; 4518.— Esp., of the famous oration of Pericles over the fallen Athenians, in Plato's Menexenus, Cic. Tusc. 5, 12, 36.
epitaphium.short: ĕpĭtăphĭum, ii, n., = ἐπιτάφιον, or epitaphius, m., = ἐπιτάφιος λόγος, a funeral oration, eulogy.

epithalamium.full: ĕpĭthălămĭum, ii, n., = ἐπιθαλάμιον, a nuptial song, epithalamium, Treb. Poll. Gallien. 11. Quintilian calls the wellknown Carmen nuptiale of Catullus (62) Epithalamium, Quint. 9, 3, 16.
epithalamium.short: ĕpĭthălămĭum, ii, n., = ἐπιθαλάμιον, a nuptial song, epithalamium, Treb.

epitheca.full: ĕpĭthēca, ae, f., = ἐπιθήκη, an addition, increase, Plaut. Trin. 4, 3, 18.
epitheca.short: ĕpĭthēca, ae, f., = ἐπιθήκη, an addition, increase, Plaut.

epithema.full: ĕpĭthĕma, ătis, n., = ἐπίθεμα, in medic. lang., a poultice or lotion, epithem, Scrib. Comp. 160; Marc. Empir. 20; Mart. Cap. 3, § 225.
epithema.short: ĕpĭthĕma, ătis, n., = ἐπίθεμα, in medic.

epithematium.full: ĕpĭthĕmătĭum, ii, n., = ἐπιθεμάτιον, in medic. lang., a small epithem, Marc. Empir. 20, 27.
epithematium.short: ĕpĭthĕmătĭum, ii, n., = ἐπιθεμάτιον, in medic.

epitherapeusis.full: ĕpĭthĕrăpeusis, is, f., = ἐπιθεράπευσις (a second remedy), rhet. t. t., Pseudo Ascon. ad Cic. Verr. 2, 1, 9, § 27.
epitherapeusis.short: ĕpĭthĕrăpeusis, is, f., = ἐπιθεράπευσις (a second remedy), rhet.

epitheton.full: ĕpĭthĕton, i, n., = ἐπίθετον, in gram., an epithet, adjective, Quint. 8, 2, 10; 8, 3, 20; Macr. S. 6, 5 al.
epitheton.short: ĕpĭthĕton, i, n., = ἐπίθετον, in gram., an epithet, adjective, Quint.
