epithymon.full: ĕpĭthўmon, i, n., = ἐπίθυμον, the flower of thyme, Plin. 26, 8, 35, § 55; id. 11, 66, § 106; 12, 81, § 130.
epithymon.short: ĕpĭthўmon, i, n., = ἐπίθυμον, the flower of thyme, Plin.

epitimesis.full: ĕpĭtīmēsis, is, f., = ἐπιτίμησις, rhet. t. t., a reproof, Rufin. de Fig. 21, p. 212.

epitogium.full: ĕpĭtŏgĭum, ii, n. vox hibr. from ἐπί and toga, a garment drawn over the toga, an upper garment, acc. to Quint. 1, 5, 68.

epitome.full: ĕpĭtŏmē (nom. ĕpĭtŏma, Cic. Att. 12, 5, 3), ēs, f., = ἐπιτομή, an abridgment, epitome, Cic. Att. 12, 5, 3; 13, 8.—In plur., Col. 1, 1, 10: librum in epitomen cogere, Aus. Ep. 19 al.

epitomo.full: ĕpĭtŏmo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. epitome, to abridge, epitomize (post-class.; cf.: excerpo, abbrevio): historiam, Treb. Poll. XXX. Tyr. 30 fin.: aliquid, Veg. M. 1, 8 fin.

epitonium.full: ĕpĭtŏnĭum, ii, n., = ἐπιτόνιον (also written ĕpistŏmion = ἐπιστόμιον), a bung, stopple, the cock in a water-pipe, Varr. R. R. 3, 5, 16; Vitr. 9, 8, 11 al.; Sen. Ep. 86, 6; Dig. 19, 1, 17, § 8.
epitonium.short: ĕpĭtŏnĭum, ii, n., = ἐπιτόνιον (also written ĕpistŏmion = ἐπιστόμιον), a bung, stopple, the cock in a water-pipe, Varr.

epitoxis.full: ĕpĭtoxis, ĭdis, f., = ἐπιτοξῖτις, the notch in a catapult, in which the cord lay, Vitr. 10, 15.
epitoxis.short: ĕpĭtoxis, ĭdis, f., = ἐπιτοξῖτις, the notch in a catapult, in which the cord lay, Vitr.

epitrapezios.full: Ĕpitrăpēzios, i, m., = ἐπιτραπέζιος, at table: Hercules, i. e. the statue of Hercules at the dessert-table, Stat. S. 4, 6 in lemm.; cf. Mart. 9, 44.
epitrapezios.short: Ĕpitrăpēzios, i, m., = ἐπιτραπέζιος, at table: Hercules, i.

epitrepontes.full: Ĕpitrĕpontĕs, um, m., = Ἐπιτρέποντες, title of a play of Menander, Quint. 10, 1, 70; Sid. Ep. 4, 12.
epitrepontes.short: Ĕpitrĕpontĕs, um, m., = Ἐπιτρέποντες, title of a play of Menander, Quint.

epitritos.full: ĕpī^trĭtos, a, um, adj., = ἐπίτριτος, containing four thirds. In gen. (pure Lat. sesquitertius), in the relation of four to three, Gell. 18, 14, 5; Macr. Somn. Scip. 2, 1, § 15 al.; cf. as fin.— Pes, a metrical foot, consisting of three long syllables and one short (a spondee with an iambus or trochee): ˘¯¯¯, ¯˘¯¯, ¯¯ ˘¯, ¯¯¯˘, Diom. p. 477 P. et saep.
epitritos.short: ĕpī^trĭtos, a, um, adj., = ἐπίτριτος, containing four thirds.

epitrochasmos.full: ĕpī^trŏchasmos, i, m., = ἐπιτροχασμός, rhet. t. t., a hurried accumulation of several points, Aquila Rom. de Fig. 6, p. 148.

epitrope.full: ĕpī^trŏpē, ēs, f., = ἐπιτροπή, rhet. t. t., a surrendering, Rutil. 2, 17, p. 130 al.

epitropus.full: ĕpī^trŏpus or -os, i, m., = ἐπίτροπος, a factor, steward, Aus. Ep. 22, 2.
epitropus.short: ĕpī^trŏpus or -os, i, m., = ἐπίτροπος, a factor, steward, Aus.

epityrum.full: ĕpĭtȳrum, i, n., = ἐπίτυρον, a dish made of preserved olives, Cato R. R. 119; Col. 12, 49, 9; Plaut. Mil. 1, 1, 24; cf. Varr. L. L. 7, § 86 Müll.
epityrum.short: ĕpĭtȳrum, i, n., = ἐπίτυρον, a dish made of preserved olives, Cato R.

epiurus.full: ĕpĭūrus, i, m., = ἐπίουρος, a wooden pin, a peg, Pall. Nov. 7, 14.
epiurus.short: ĕpĭūrus, i, m., = ἐπίουρος, a wooden pin, a peg, Pall.

epizeuxis.full: ĕpīzeuxis, is, f., = ἐπίζευξις, gram. t. t., an energetic repetition of a word, Charis. p. 250 P. al.

epizygis.full: ĕpīzўgis, ĭdis, f., = ἐπιζυγίς, a pin at the hole of the balista, to keep the cord, when drawn through, in its place, Vitr. 10, 17.
epizygis.short: ĕpīzўgis, ĭdis, f., = ἐπιζυγίς, a pin at the hole of the balista, to keep the cord, when drawn through, in its place, Vitr.

epodes.full: ĕpŏdĕs, um, m., a kind of sea-fish, Ov. Hal. 126; Plin. 32, 11, 54, § 152.
epodes.short: ĕpŏdĕs, um, m., a kind of sea-fish, Ov.

epodos.full: ĕpōdos, i, m., = ἐπωδός (singing to), a form of lyric metre invented by Archilochus, in which a longer verse is followed by a shorter one, not including the elegiac distich. So in Roman literature, the Epodi of Horace, Ter. Maur. p. 2422 P.; Diom. p. 482 ib.; Quint. 10, 1, 96; Aus. Ep. 10, 37; 16, 2.
epodos.short: ĕpōdos, i, m., = ἐπωδός (singing to), a form of lyric metre invented by Archilochus, in which a longer verse is followed by a shorter one, not including the elegiac distich.

epogdoos.full: ĕpogdŏŏs, -ŏus, acc. ŏŏn or ŏum, adj., = ἐπόγδοος, containing a whole and an eighth: numerus, the proportion of nine to eight, Macr. Somn. Scip. 2, 1, 14; Mart. Cap. 2, § 109; Fulg. Myth. 3, 9.

epomphalion.full: ĕpomphălĭon, ĭi, n., = ἐπομφάλιον, a plaster for the uterus, Fulg. Myth. 2, 5 fin.
epomphalion.short: ĕpomphălĭon, ĭi, n., = ἐπομφάλιον, a plaster for the uterus, Fulg.

epona.full: Ĕpŏna, ae, f. from equus; cf. Gr. ἵππος; but referred to root ap- of apo by Fick, Wörterb. p. 425, the protecting goddess of horses, asses, etc., Tert. ad Nat. 1, 11; id. Apol. 16; Juv. 8, 157; Prud. Apoth. 197; App. M. 3, p. 141; Inscr. Orell. 402; 1792 sq.

epops.full: ĕpops, ŏpis, m., = ἔποψ, the hoopoe, Ov. M. 6, 674; Verg. Cul. 251; cf. upupa.
epops.short: ĕpops, ŏpis, m., = ἔποψ, the hoopoe, Ov.

epoptae.full: ĕpoptae, ārum, m., = ἐπόπται, beholders; persons fully initiated into the Eleusinian mysteries, who attained the third and highest grade, that of intuition, Tert. adv. Val. 1.

eporedia.full: Ĕpŏrĕdĭa, ae, f., = Ἐπορεδία, a Roman colony in Gallia Cisalpina, in the district of the Salassi, on the Duria, now Ivrea, Plin. 3, 17, 21, § 123; Brut. ap. Cic. Fam. 11, 20 fin.; Vell. 1, 15, 5; Tac. H. 1, 70.
eporedia.short: Ĕpŏrĕdĭa, ae, f., = Ἐπορεδία, a Roman colony in Gallia Cisalpina, in the district of the Salassi, on the Duria, now Ivrea, Plin.

eporedias.full: eporedias Galli bonos equorum domitores vocant, Plin. 3, 17, 21, § 123; cf. Epona init.
eporedias.short: eporedias Galli bonos equorum domitores vocant, Plin.

eporedorix.full: Ĕpŏrĕdŏrix, ĭgis, m., = Ἐπορέδοριξ, Paraphr. A noble Aeduan, who served in Caesar's army, Caes. B. G. 7, 38 sq.; 7, 54 sq.; 7, 76.— Another Aeduan of the same name, Caes. B. G. 7, 67 fin.

epos.full: ĕpos (occurring only in the nom. and acc.), n., = ἔπος, a heroic poem, an epic; nom., Hor. S. 1, 10, 43; acc., Mart. 12, 95; Aus. Prof. 5, 10.

epoto.full: ē-pōto (ex-poto, Plaut. Trin. 2, 4, 5, v. infra), āvi, pōtum (in late Lat. potatum, v. fin.), 1, v. a., to drink out, off, or up, to drain, quaff, swallow (in the verb. finit. rare, and only post-Aug.; in the part. perf. class.): epotum venenum, Cic. Clu. 62, 173: medicamentum, Liv. 8, 18: potionem, Quint. 7, 2, 17; 25; Ov. M. 5, 453 al.: epoto poculo, Cic. Clu. 60, 168: poculum, Liv. 40, 24: amphoram, Suet. Tib. 42; Phaedr. 3, 1, 1; Vulg. Ezech. 23, 34: remedia, Amm. 16, 5, 8: argentum expotum,

epotus.full: ēpōtus, a, um, Part., v. epoto init.

epularis.full: ĕpŭlāris, e, adj. epulum, of or belonging to a banquet. Adj.: epularis accubitio amicorum, at a banquet, Cic. de Sen. 13 fin.: sacrificium ludorum, id. de Or. 3, 19 fin.; cf. 1. epulo, II.: sermo, App. M. 2, p. 123.— Subst.: EPULARES appellabantur, qui in quibusdam ludis nocte epulabantur, Paul. ex Fest. p. 82, 10 Müll.

epulatio.full: ĕpŭlātĭo, ōnis, f. epulor, feasting, eating (very rare), Lucil. ap. Non. 204, 18; Col. 12, 3, 2; Petr. 141, 10; Suet. Calig. 18; Val. Max. 2, 5, 4 extr.; Vulg. Sap. 19, 11.

epulator.full: ĕpŭlātor, ōris, m. id., a feaster, carouser, Ambros. Cant. Cantic. 5, 5 init. al.

epulatorium.full: ĕpŭlātōrĭum, ii, n. id., a feast, banquet, carouse, Ambros. Fragm. Saec. 8, 45.

epulo1.full: ĕpŭlo, ōnis (also EPOLONUS, i, acc. to Paul. ex Fest. p. 78, 11 Müll.), m. epulum, a guest at a feast or banquet, a feaster, carouser. In gen. (mostly post-class.), Cic. Att. 2, 7, 3; App. M. 2, p. 123; 9, p. 235; Firm. Math. 5, 4 fin.—Far more freq., In partic.: Tresviri or Septemviri Epulones (in inscrr. also SEPTEMVIR and SEPTEMVIRI [VII. VIR.] EPVLONVM), a t. t. of relig. lang., a college of priests, composed at first of three and afterwards of seven persons, who superintended the sacrificia

epulo2.full: Ĕpŭlo, ōnis, m., a proper name, Verg. A. 12, 459.
epulo2.short: Ĕpŭlo, ōnis, m., a proper name, Verg.

epulor.full: ĕpŭlor, ātus, 1, v. dep. n. and a. [epulum], to hold an entertainment, to feast, banquet. Neutr. (class.): ut in voluptate sit, qui epuletur, Cic. Fin. 2, 5, 16; id. de Sen. 13, 45; id. Tusc. 1, 47, 113; id. Att. 5, 9; Liv. 42, 56; 44, 31; Tac. H. 3, 38.—With abl., to feast upon, Verg. A. 3, 224; id. G. 2, 537; Vulg. Deut. 12, 12 al.— Act., to eat, feast upon (not ante-Aug.): aliquem epulandum ponere mensis, Verg. A. 4, 602; cf. Ov. M. 15, 111; Sen. Troad. 1108; so, pullos, Plin. 8, 43, 68, § 17

epulum.full: ĕpŭlum, i, n., and in the plur. heterocl. ĕpŭlae, ārum (EPULAM antiqui etiam singulariter posuere, Paul. ex Fest. p. 82, 14 Müll.), f. etym. dub.; perh. contr. from edipulum, from edo, sumptuous food or dishes (cf.: daps, commissatio, convivium, cena, etc.). Prop. (only in the plur.): si illi congestae sint epulae, Plaut. Trin. 2, 4, 70: mensae conquisitissimis epulis exstruebantur, Cic. Tusc. 5, 21, 62: vino et epulis onerati, Sall. J. 76 fin.; so opp. vinum, Liv. 8, 16; 9, 18 Drak.; 23, 18; Ne
epulum.short: ĕpŭlum, i, n., and in the plur.

epytus.full: Ēpўtus, i, m., a distinguished Trojan, Verg. A. 2, 340.—Hence, ēpўtĭdes, ae, m., son of Epytus, and attendant of Iulus, id. ib. 5, 547.
epytus.short: Ēpўtus, i, m., a distinguished Trojan, Verg.

equa.full: ĕqua, ae, f. equus, a mare, Varr. R. R. 2, 7, 4; Cic. Verr. 2, 1, 10; Verg. G. 1, 59; 3, 266; Hor. C. 2, 16, 35 et saep.—Dat. and abl. plur. equis, Varr. R. R. 2, 1, 19; Col. 6, 37, 8; Plin. 11, 41, 96, § 237; 8, 42, 64, § 156; Dig. 50, 13, 2; also, equabus, Pall. Mart. 13, 1 and 5; Serv. Verg. G. 3, 268; Cod. Just. 11, 75, 1.

equarius.full: ĕquārĭus, a, um, adj. id., of or belonging to horses (very rare). Adj.: medicus, a farrier, Val. Max. 9, 15, 2.— Subst. ĕquārius, ii, m., a stableboy, groom, Sol. 45, § 8.— ĕquāria, ae, f. (sc. res), a stud of horses: grandes, Varr. R. R. 2, prooem. § 6.

eques.full: ĕquĕs, ĭtis, m. id., a horseman, rider. In gen.: it eques et plausu cava concutit ungula terram, Enn. ap. Macr. S. 6, 1 (Ann. v. 419 ed. Vahlen); Liv. 26, 2; 28, 9; Dig. 9, 2, 57; Ov. F. 5, 700 (of Castor; cf. Hor. C. 1, 12, 26; id. S. 2, 1, 26); Hor. C. 4, 11, 27 (of Bellerophon; cf. id. ib. 3, 12, 8); id. Ep. 1, 2, 65; 1, 10, 38 al.—Poet. transf., of horse and rider: quadrupes, Enn. ap. Non. 106, 31; Gell. 18, 5; and Macr. S. 6, 9 (who, like the other ancient grammarians, consider eques = equu

equester.full: ĕquester, tris, tre (m. equestris, Liv. 27, 1, 11; Verg. A. 5, 667 al.; v. Zumpt, Gram. § 100, A. 1.; like acris, celebris, celeris, etc.), adj. eques, belonging to a horseman, equestrian. In gen. (very rare): equestres statuae inauratae, Cic. Verr. 2, 2, 61; id. Phil. 6, 5; 9, 6; Suet. Tit. 2: equi, riding - horses, Vulg. 3 Reg. 4, 26.—Far more freq., In partic. Of or belonging to cavalry: proelium, Caes. B. G. 1, 18 fin.; 1, 48, 4; 2, 8, 2 et saep. (cf.: equestris pugna, Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 55):

equidem.full: ĕquĭdem, adv. comp. of the interj. ĕ and quidem enclit.; cf. edepol, a demonstrative corroborative particle, verily, truly, indeed, at all events, = certe, revera, etc. (freq. and class.). In gen. Without other particles. With 1. pers. in affirming a fact concerning one's self, or confirming a previous remark; equidem Sosia Amphitruonis sum, Plaut. Am. 1, 1, 255; 2, 1, 26; 32: i in malam rem. Mi. Ibi sum equidem, id. Poen. 1, 2, 82: nihil inquit, equidem novi, Cic. Div. 1, 6, 11: equidem et ante

equiferus.full: ĕquĭ-fĕrus, i, m. equus, a wild horse, Plin. 28, 10, 45, § 159; 28, 13, 55, § 197.

equile.full: ĕquīle, is, n. id.; cf.: bubile, caprile, ovile, etc., a stable for horses, Cato, R. R. 14, 2; Varr. R. R. 2, 7, 15; Suet. Calig. 55.

equimentum.full: ĕquīmentum, i, n. id., a fee for covering, Varr. ap. Non. 69, 27.

equimulga.full: ĕquĭ-mulga, ae, m. [equus-mulgeo), a mare-milker, Sid. Ep. 4, 1, 43 (al. equimulgos).

equinus.full: ĕquīnus, a, um, adj. equus, of or belonging to horses: pecus, Varr. R. R. 2, 7, 7; cf. genus, Col. 6, 27, 1: lac, Varr. R. R. 2, 11, 1: stercus, id. ib. 1, 38, 3 al.: cervix, Hor. A. P. 1: cauda, id. Ep. 2, 1, 45: ubera, id. Epod. 8, 8: pedes, Plin. 4, 13, 27, § 95: seta, * Cic. Tusc. 5, 21, 62: emptio (i. e. equorum), Varr. R. R. 2, 7, 6: pullus, Vulg. Sir. 23, 30.

equio.full: ĕquĭo, īre, v. n. id., of mares, to be in heat, Plin. 10, 63, 83, § 181; perh. also Col. 6, 38, 1.

equiria.full: ĕquīrĭa, ōrum, n. id., the annual horse-races, held on the 27th of February and the 14th of March in the Campus Martius, in honor of Mars, Varr. L. L. 6, § 13 Müll.; Ov. F. 2, 859; 3, 519; Paul. ex Fest. p. 81, 12, and 131, 13 Müll., s. v. MARTIALIS CAMPVS, p. 96.

equirine.full: equĭrīne, jusjurandum per Quirinum, Paul. ex Fest. p. 81, 13 Müll.; cf.: ecastor, ejuno.

equisaetum.full: ĕquĭsaetum, i, n. equus-seta, the plant horse-tail, equisetum arvense, Linn., Plin. 26, 13, 83, § 132; also called ĕquĭsae-tis, is, f., id. 18, 28, 67, § 259; and ĕquĭ-sēta, ae, f., App. Herb. 40, no. 1 al.

equiso.full: ĕquīso, ōnis, m. equus, a groom, stableboy (ante- and post-class.), Varr. ap. Non. 105, 14; 32 sq.; Val. Max. 7, 3 ext. 2; App. M. 7, p. 194: equisones nautici, who draw vessels along by ropes, Varr. ap. Non. 106, 1; id. 451, 4.

equitabilis.full: ĕquĭtābĭlis, e, adj. equito, that may be ridden over, smooth: planities, Curt. 4, 9, 10: campi, Amm. 22, 15.

equitatio.full: ĕquĭtātĭo, ōnis, f. id., a riding, Plin. 28, 4, 14, § 54.

equitatus1.full: ĕquĭtātus, ūs, m. id.. * In abstr., = equitatio, a riding: atteri equitatu, Plin. 28, 15, 61, § 218.— In concr. Cavalry (very freq.), Caes. B. G. 1, 15, 1; 2; 1, 18, 5; 1, 24, 1 et saep.: ferreus, harnessed cavalry, Amm. 19, 1.— Dat. equitatu, Caes. B. G. 1, 18 fin.; 1, 39, 5; 1, 52 fin.; also, equitatui, id. ib. 1, 42, 5; 7, 4, 9; id. B. C. 3, 89, 3.—In plur., Caes. B. C. 1, 61, 3; 3, 8, 1; Cic. Font. 2; Sall. J. 46, 7; Flor. 3, 11, 8.— The equestrian order (very rare), Plin. 33, 2, 9, § 35; cf

equitatus2.full: ĕquĭtātus, ūs, m. equio, a being in heat, of mares (with hinnitus), Lucil. ap. Varr. L. L. 7, § 103 Müll.

equitiarius.full: ĕquĭtĭārĭus, ii, m. equitium, the inspector of a stud, Firm. Math. 8, 13.

equitium.full: ĕquĭtĭum, ii, n. equus, a stud of horses, Col. 6, 27, 1; Dig. 6, 1, 1; 7, 8, 12, § 4 al.; cf. Varr. R. R. 2, 1, 10.

equito.full: ĕquĭto, āvi, ātum, 1, v. n. and a. [eques], to ride. Neutr. In gen. (class.): cum in illo nostro exercitu equitaret, Cic. Deiot. 10; Sall. J. 6, 1; Suet. Caes. 57; Hor. C. 2, 9, 24 al.: in equo, Dig. 9, 2, 57; cf.: in equuleis, Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 20; v. Equuleus, II. A.; and: in arundine longa, Hor. S. 2, 3, 248.— In partic. (acc. to eques, II. A.): EQVITARE antiqui dicebant equum publicum merere, Paul. ex Fest. 81, 15 Müll.— Transf. To skirmish, manœuvre: illa (certatio) qua tu contra Alfenum equ

equula.full: ĕquŭla, ae, f. dim. equa. A little mare, a filly, Varr. ap. Non. 106, 12.— Transf., of a voluptuous woman, Plaut. Fragm. ap. Prisc. p. 617 P.

equuleus.full: ĕquŭlĕus or ĕcŭlĕus, i, m. dim. equus, a young horse, a colt, foal. Lit., Varr., Pompon., and Cic. ap. Non. 105, 11 sq.; Liv. 31, 12.— Transf. Eculeos argenteos nobilis aufert, horses wrought in silver, works of art, Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 20, § 42; cf. the sarcastic pun: jactabit se et in his equitabit equuleis, Emi, pecuniam solvi, on these hobbies, id. ib. § 43.— As an instrument of torture, a wooden rack in the shape of a horse, Cic. Mil. 21 fin.; id. Poët. Tusc. 3, 28, 67; Curt. 6, 10, 10; Sen. E

equulus.full: ĕquŭlus, i, m. dim. id., a small young horse, a foal, Varr. R. R. 2, 7, 13; 2, 8 fin.; * Cic. N. D. 2, 14, 38.

equus.full: ĕquus, i (gen. plur. equūm, Verg. G. 2, 542; Stat. Th. 4, 409 al.), m. Sanscr. acvas; Gr. ἵππος (ἴκκος); cf. Epŏna; root, ak-, to be sharp or swift; cf. Gr. ἄκρος, ὠκύς; Lat. acus, ocior, a horse, steed, charger. Prop. In gen. (cf.: caballus, canterius, mannus), Varr. R. R. 2, 7; Col. 6, 27 sq.; Plin. 8, 42, 64, § 154 sq.; Pall. Mart. 13; Enn. ap. Cic. de Sen. 5, 14 (Ann. v. 441 ed. Vahlen); Plaut. Bacch. 1, 1, 39; id. Men. 5, 2, 109; Cic. Rep. 1, 43; 1, 7, 9 et saep.: equus = equa, Varr. R. R.

equus tuticus.full: Equus Tūtĭcus, i, m., a town in Samnium, now S. Eleuterio, Cic. Att. 6, 1, 1; cf. the interpreters of Hor. S. 1, 5, 87; and Mommsen in Bullett. d. Inst. 1847, p. 170, and 1848, p. 7 sq.
equus tuticus.short: Equus Tūtĭcus, i, m., a town in Samnium, now S.

er1.full: ēr, ēris, m. χήρ, a hedgehog, Nemes. Cyneg. 57.

er2.full: Er (Her), Eris, m., a Pamphylian, who, according to legend (cited in Plato Polit. 10, 12, p. 626), rose from the dead, Cic. Rep. 6, 3; 6 sq.
er2.short: Er (Her), Eris, m., a Pamphylian, who, according to legend (cited in Plato Polit.

era.full: ĕra (less correctly, hera; v. erus), ae (archaic gen. sing. ĕrāï, Aus. Idyll. 7, 5), f. erus. Prop., the mistress of a house, with respect to the servants; the mistress, lady: nunquam era errans (i. e. Medea), etc., Enn. ap. Auct. Her. 2, 22, 34 (Trag. v. 287 Vahl.): servus Dat (puellam) erae suae, Plaut. Cas. prol. 44 sq.; so id. ib. 2, 5, 3; 2, 8, 70; id. Am. 1, 1, 105; Ter. And. 4, 2, 4; id. Eun. 4, 3, 12; 5, 3, 8. So, era major and era minor, the old and young mistress, the lady of the house

eradicatio.full: ērādīcātĭo, ōnis, f. eradico, a rooting out, Tert. Res. Carn. 27 fin.; Vulg. Isa. 37, 26; cf.: eradicationem posuisti me, i. e. an example of utter destruction, id. Thren. 3, 45.

eradico.full: ē-rādīco (exr-), āvi, ātum, 1 (archaic inf. eradicarier, Plaut. Aul. 2, 4, 21), v. a., to pluck up by the roots, to root out, eradicate (an ante-class. word). Lit.: ex terra enata, Varr. R. R. 1, 27, 2: plantationem, Vulg. Matt. 15, 13; 13, 29 al.— Transf.: aliquem, to root out, utterly destroy, Plaut. Pers. 5, 2, 38; id. Truc. 3, 1, 15; id. Merc. 4, 4, 35; id. Bacch. 5, 1, 6; Ter. And. 4, 4, 22; id. Heaut. 3, 3, 28; Vulg. Jer. 18, 7.—* Trop.: pugnis memorandis suis hominum aures, i. e. to wear

erado.full: ē-rādo, si, sum, 3, v. a., to scratch out, scrape off (ante-class. and since the Aug. per.). Lit.: eradere atque eruere terram, Varr. L. L. 5, § 136 Müll.: muscum, Col. 4, 24, 6: medullam, id. Arb. 9 fin.; Plin. 17, 21, 35, § 162: aliquem (albo), to strike out, erase, Plin. Pan. 25, 3; Tac. A. 4, 42 fin.; cf.: inscriptos titulos monumento, Paul. Sent. 1, 21, 8; Amm. 15, 6, 2: corticem, Vulg. Sap. 13, 11.—Poet. transf.: genas, i. e. to shave off the beard (for which, shortly before, vellere), Pro

erana.full: Ĕrăna, ae, f., a town in Cilicia, near Mount Amanus, Cic. Fam. 15, 4, 8.
erana.short: Ĕrăna, ae, f., a town in Cilicia, near Mount Amanus, Cic.

eranthemis.full: ēranthĕmis, idis, f., = ἠρανθεμίς, another name for the plant anthemis, the chamomile, Plin. 22, 21, 26, § 53.
eranthemis.short: ēranthĕmis, idis, f., = ἠρανθεμίς, another name for the plant anthemis, the chamomile, Plin.

eranus.full: ĕrănus, i, m., = ἔραϝος, a fund contributed for mutual protection against want: concessum est eranum habere ... si tali conlatione non ad turbas et ad inlicitos coetus, sed ad sustinendam tenuiorum inopiam utuntur, Plin. Ep. 10, 93; cf. ib. 92; Tert. Apol. 39.
eranus.short: ĕrănus, i, m., = ἔραϝος, a fund contributed for mutual protection against want: concessum est eranum habere ...

erasinus.full: Ĕrăsīnus, i, m., = Ἐρασῖνος, a river of Argolis, now Kephalari, Mel. 2, 3, 9; Plin. 2, 103, 106, § 225; Ov. M. 15, 276; cf. Sen. N. Q. 3, 26, 3. † ĕrăsīnus, i, m., = Ἐρασῖϝος, a favorite boy, Aus. Idyll. 7 praef.
erasinus.short: Ĕrăsīnus, i, m., = Ἐρασῖνος, a river of Argolis, now Kephalari, Mel.

erasistratus.full: Ĕrăsistrătus, i, m., = Ἐρασίστρατος, a famous physician of Alexandria in the time of Ptolemy Lagus, the founder of a medical school, Plin. 29, 1, 3, § 5; Val. Max. 5, 7 ext. 1; Cels. praef. 3, 4; 4, 4 et saep.
erasistratus.short: Ĕrăsistrătus, i, m., = Ἐρασίστρατος, a famous physician of Alexandria in the time of Ptolemy Lagus, the founder of a medical school, Plin.

erastes.full: ĕrastes, ae, m., = ἐραστής, a lover, M. Aurel. ap. Fronto Ep. ad M. Caes. 1, 10.
erastes.short: ĕrastes, ae, m., = ἐραστής, a lover, M.

erasus.full: ērāsus, a, um, Part., from erado.
erasus.short: ērāsus, a, um, Part., from erado.

eratine.full: Ĕrătīnē, es, f., = Ἐρατειϝή, a nymph, a daughter of Venus, Mart. Cap. 9, § 905.
eratine.short: Ĕrătīnē, es, f., = Ἐρατειϝή, a nymph, a daughter of Venus, Mart.

erato.full: Ĕrătō (occurring only in the nom.), f., = Ἐρατώ. The muse of lyric and amorous poetry, Ov. F. 4, 195; 349; id. A. A. 2, 16; 425; Aus. Idyll. 20, 6.— Meton., a Muse in gen., Verg. A. 7, 37 Serv.; Claud. Mall. Theod. 282.— A queen of Armenia, Tac. A. 2, 4.
erato.short: Ĕrătō (occurring only in the nom.), f., = Ἐρατώ.

eratosthenes.full: Ĕrătosthĕnes, is, m., = Ἐρατοσθέϝης, a celebrated geographer, poet, and philosopher of Alexandria, under Ptolemy Euergetes, Varr. R. R. 1, 2, 3; Cic. Att. 2, 6; Caes. B. G. 6, 24, 2; Plin. Elench. 2; 5; 2, 108, 112; Quint. 1, 1, 16; 11, 2, 14 al.
eratosthenes.short: Ĕrătosthĕnes, is, m., = Ἐρατοσθέϝης, a celebrated geographer, poet, and philosopher of Alexandria, under Ptolemy Euergetes, Varr.

erebus.full: Ĕrĕbus, i, m., = Ἔρεβος. The god of darkness, son of Chaos, and brother of Nox, Cic. N. D. 3, 17 fin.; Hyg. Myth. praef.; Verg. A. 4, 510; Ov. M. 14, 404.— The Lower World, Verg. G. 4, 471 Serv.; id. A. 6, 247; 7, 140; Ov. M. 5, 543; 10, 76, al.—Hence, ĕrĕbēus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to the Lower World: colubrae, Ov. lb. 229.

erechtheus.full: Ĕrechtheus (trisyl.), ei, m., = Ἐρεχθεύς, a fabled king of Athens, father of Procris, Orithyia, Chthonia, and Creüsa, who devoted themselves to death for their country, Cic. Tusc. 1, 48, 116; id. Fin. 5, 22, 62; id. N. D. 3, 19; id. Sest. 21, 48; Ov. M. 6, 667 sq.; 7, 697; Just. 2, 6, 12.— Derivv. ĕrechthēus, a, um, adj., Erechthean, and poet. for Athenian: domus, Ov. F. 5, 204: arces, id. M. 8, 548; cf. litus, Val. Max. 6, 1, 1 ext.— ĕrecthī-dae, ārum, m., poet., the Athenians, Ov. M. 7, 430.—
erechtheus.short: Ĕrechtheus (trisyl.), ei, m., = Ἐρεχθεύς, a fabled king of Athens, father of Procris, Orithyia, Chthonia, and Creüsa, who devoted themselves to death for their country, Cic.

erecte.full: ērecte, adv., boldly, v. erigo, P. a. fin.

erectio.full: ērectĭo, ōnis, f. erigo, a setting up, erecting: tignorum, Vitr. 10, 5 fin.; 8 praef.; Vulg. Num. 10, 21.— Trop., pride, insolence, Vulg. Job, 22, 20.

erectus.full: ērectus, a, um, Part. and P. a., from erigo.

erembi.full: Ĕrembi, ōrum or um, m., = Ἐρεμβοί, the Troglodytes in Africa, Avien. Descr. Orb. 271; Prisc. Perieg. 170 al.
erembi.short: Ĕrembi, ōrum or um, m., = Ἐρεμβοί, the Troglodytes in Africa, Avien.

eremigo.full: ē-rēmĭgo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a., to row or sail through or over, to navigate (post-Aug. and very rare): undas, Sil. 14, 190: septentrionem, Plin. 2, 67, 67, § 168.

eremita.full: ĕrēmīta, ae., m., = ἐρημίτης, an eremite, hermit, Sulpic. Sever. Dial. 17.
eremita.short: ĕrēmīta, ae., m., = ἐρημίτης, an eremite, hermit, Sulpic.

eremitis.full: ĕrēmītis, ĭdis, adj. f., = ἐρημιτίς, solitary, recluse, Sid. Ep. 9, 3.

eremodicium.full: ĕrēmŏdĭcĭum, ii, n., = ἐρημοδικίοϝ, a default of appearance before a court at the appointed time, Dig. 4, 4, 7 fin.; 46, 7, 13; Cod. Just. 3, 1, 13, § 3; Tert. adv. Matyr. 3.
eremodicium.short: ĕrēmŏdĭcĭum, ii, n., = ἐρημοδικίοϝ, a default of appearance before a court at the appointed time, Dig.

eremus.full: ĕrēmus (ĕrĕmus, Prud. Cathem. 5, 89; id. Psych. 371), a, um, adj., = ἔρημος, waste, desert (late Lat.). Adj.: loca, Cod. Just. 11, 57, 4.— Subst.: ĕrēmus, i, m. (sc. locus), or f. (sc. regio), a wilderness, desert, Tert. Idol. 5; Sulpic. Sever. Dial. 1, 15; Vulg. Deut. 1, 19 al.

erepo.full: ē-rēpo, psi, 3 (pluperf. subj. sync. erepsemus, Hor. S. 1, 5, 79), v. n. and a. (anteclass. and since the Aug. period.). Neutr., to creep out, crawl forth. In gen., Plaut. Aul. 4, 4, 1; Varr. R. R. 3, 15; Sil. 15, 617; Stat. Th. 11, 581.— Esp., in an upward direction, to creep or clamber up, Suet. Tib. 60.—Poet. transf. of a building, to rise, Stat. S. 2, 2, 30.— Trop.: pecunia quoque circa paupertatem plurimum morae habet, dum ex illa erepat, Sen. Ep. 101, 2.— Act. * To creep through: totum agr

erepticius.full: ēreptīcĭus or -tius, a, um, adj. eripio, that is taken away from one for punishment, Ulp. Fragm. 19, 17.

ereptio.full: ēreptĭo, ōnis, f. id., a forcible taking away, seizure of a possession, Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 5: animae, Tert. Spect. 2.

ereptor.full: ēreptor, ōris, m. id., a robber, plunderer: bonorum, Cic. Quint. 8: libertatis, id. Sest. 51.—Plur.: terrarum, Tac. A. 13, 55 fin.

ereptus.full: ēreptus, a, um, Part., from eripio.
ereptus.short: ēreptus, a, um, Part., from eripio.

eretria.full: Ĕrĕtrĭa, ae, f., = Ἐρετρία. The principal city on the island of Euboea, the birthplace of the philosopher Menedemus, now Palaeo Castro, Plaut. Merc. 3, 4, 59; Mel. 2, 7, 9; Plin. 4, 12, 21, § 64; Cic. Ac. 2, 42; Liv. 32, 16; 35, 38 al.— Derivv., ĕrĕtrĭus, a, um, adj., Eretrian: creta, Plin. 33, 13, 57, § 163; so, terra, Cels. 5, 15; 6, 3.—Subst.: Eretria, ae, f., Plin. 35, 6, 21, § 38; Vitr. 7, 14.— ĕrĕtrĭ-ensis, e, adj., of Eretria: Gongylus, Nep. Paus. 2.—Subst., ĕrĕtrienses, ium, m., the inha

eretum.full: Ērētum, i, n., = Ἤρητοϝ, an ancient city of the Sabines, now Grotta Marozza (acc. to G. Long, Rimane), Verg. A. 7, 711; Liv. 3, 26; 29 al.—Hence, ērētīnus, a, um, adj., of Eretum, Tib. 4, 8, 4.
eretum.short: Ērētum, i, n., = Ἤρητοϝ, an ancient city of the Sabines, now Grotta Marozza (acc.

erga.full: ergā, praep. [syncop. for e-regā, from ex and root rag-, to reach upward, be upright; cf. ergo, v. Corss. Ausspr. 1, 448 sqq.], over against, opposite to (cf.: adversus, versus, contra, e regione, e contrario). Lit., of locality (ante- and post-classical and rare): quae med erga aedes habet, i. e. opposite me, Plaut. Truc. 2, 4, 55 (al. modo erga): erga regiam, App. Dogm. Plat. p. 9, 21.— Trop.: aliquem, more rarely aliquid, of feelings and conduct towards a person. Of friendly feelings, etc. (s

ergasterium.full: ergastērĭum, ii, n., = ἐργαστήριοϝ, a workshop, Cod. Just. 1, 3, 2; 12, 41, 2.
ergasterium.short: ergastērĭum, ii, n., = ἐργαστήριοϝ, a workshop, Cod.

ergasticus.full: ergastĭcus, a, um, adj., = ἐργαστικός, to be done: schemata; as geom. t. t., problems (opp. apodictica, theorems), Mart. Cap. 6, § 715.
ergasticus.short: ergastĭcus, a, um, adj., = ἐργαστικός, to be done: schemata;

ergastularis.full: ergastŭlāris, e, adj., v. the foll.

ergastularius.full: ergastŭlārĭus, a, um, adj. ergastulum, of or belonging to a workhouse or house of correction (late Lat.). Adj.: servus, Amm. 14, 11 fin.—Also: in tenebris ergastularibus, Sid. Ep. 7, 9.— Subst.: ergastularii, ōrum, m. (sc. servi), overseers of a penitentiary, Col. 1, 8, 17.

ergastulum.full: ergastŭlum, i, n. ἐργάζομαι, a workhouse for offenders (slaves, debtors, etc.), a house of correction, penitentiary. Prop., Col. 1, 6, 3; 1, 8, 16; Cic. Clu. 7, 21; id. Rab. Perd. 7, 20; Liv. 2, 23; 7, 4; Suet. Aug. 32; id. Tib. 8 al.; Vulg. Exod. 6, 6 al.— Transf., in plur., ergastula, ōrum, n. (like stabula, servitia, mancipia, etc.), the inmates of a workhouse, penitentiary convicts, * Caes. B. C. 3, 22, 2; Brutus ap. Cic. Fam. 11, 13, 2; Plin. 18, 6, 7, § 36; Flor. 4, 8, 1; Juv. 14, 24 al.—I

ergata.full: ergăta, ae, m., = ἐργάτης, a sort of capstan or windlass, Vitr. 1, 1; 10, 4.
ergata.short: ergăta, ae, m., = ἐργάτης, a sort of capstan or windlass, Vitr.

ergetum.full: Ergētum, i, n., a city of Sicily, now La Citadella, Sil. 14, 250.—Ergētīni, ōrum, m., its inhabitants, Plin. 3, 8, 14, § 91.
ergetum.short: Ergētum, i, n., a city of Sicily, now La Citadella, Sil.

ergo.full: ergō (rarely with short o in Ov. and the post-Aug. poets, Ov. H. 5, 59 Lennep.; id. Tr. 1, 1, 87; Luc. 9, 256; Val. Fl. 2, 407; Claud. Ep. 4, 17), adv. for e-regō, from ex and root rag-, to extend upward; cf. Gr. ὀρέγω, L. rego, Germ. ragen; v. erga, and Corss. Ausspr. 1, 448 sqq., proceeding from or out of. With gen. (placed after it, like causa and gratia), in consequence of, on account of, because of (ante-class, but not in Plaut. or Ter.): quojus rei ergo, Cato R. R. 141, 2: hujus rei ergo,
ergo.short: ergō (rarely with short o in Ov.

ergolabus.full: ergŏlăbus, i, m., = ἐργολάβος, a contractor for work (pure Lat. redemptor), Cod. Just. 4, 59, 1.
ergolabus.short: ergŏlăbus, i, m., = ἐργολάβος, a contractor for work (pure Lat.

erice.full: ĕrīce, ēs, f., = ἐρείκη, heath, broom, ling, Plin. 24, 9, 39, § 64; 11, 16, 15, § 41 sq. —Hence, ĕrīcaeus, a, um, adj., of the heath-flower, i. e. collected from it: mel (= mel sylvestre), Plin. 11, 16, 15, § 41.
erice.short: ĕrīce, ēs, f., = ἐρείκη, heath, broom, ling, Plin.

erichtho.full: Ĕrichthō, ūs, f., = Ἐριχθώ, a Thessalian witch consulted by Pompey, Luc. 6, 508; hence transf., of another witch, Ov. H. 15, 139.
erichtho.short: Ĕrichthō, ūs, f., = Ἐριχθώ, a Thessalian witch consulted by Pompey, Luc.

erichthonius.full: Ĕrichthŏnĭus, ii, m., = Ἐριχθόϝιος. A son of Vulcan, king of Athens, and the first who yoked four horses together to a chariot, Verg. G. 3, 113 Serv.; Plin. 7, 56, 57, § 202; Ov. M. 2, 553; 9, 424; Hyg. Fab. 166.—Hence, ĕrichthŏnĭus, a, um, adj.: populus, i. e. Athenian, Prop. 2, 6, 4: arces, Verg. Cul. 30 Forbig. ad loc.— A son of Dardanus, the father of Tros and king of Troy, Ov. F. 4, 33; cf. Serv. Verg. A. 8, 130.—Hence, ĕrichthŏnĭus, a, um, adj., Trojan: arces, Verg. Cul. 333 Forbig.; 342.

ericinium.full: Ericinium, ii, n., a city of Thessaly, in Perrhaebia, Liv. 36, 13; 39, 25 fin.
ericinium.short: Ericinium, ii, n., a city of Thessaly, in Perrhaebia, Liv.

ericinus.full: ērĭcīnus, a, um, adj. ericius, of the hedgehog: caro, August. cont. Faust. 30, 1; cf. Plin. Val. 5, 33.

ericius.full: ērĭcĭus, ii, m. er, a hedgehog, urchin. Prop., Varr. ap. Non. 49, 10, and 106, 18; cf. Isid. Orig. 12, 3, 7; Vulg. Isa. 14, 23; 34, 11 (as translation of Heb. kipōd, which was probably a bird—perh. the bittern. But the LXX. and Gesenius, Thes. Heb. s. v., sustain the Vulgate).— Transf., in milit. lang., a beam armed with sharp spikes to keep off assailants, Caes. B. C. 3, 67, 5 and 6; Sall. Fragm. ap. Non. 555, 2.

eridanus.full: Ērĭdănus, i, m., = Ἠριδανός. The mythical and poetical name of the river Po, Plin. 3, 16, 20, § § 117, 120; Verg. G. 4, 372; id. A. 6, 659; Prop. 1, 12, 4; 4 (5), 10, 39; Ov. M. 2, 324; 372; Mart. Cap. 6, § 640.— The constellation Eridanus, Cic. Arat. 389; Hyg. Astr. 2, 32; Mart. Cap. 8, § 838 al.

erifuga.full: ĕrĭ-fŭga (less correctly, heri-), ae, m. (erus-fugio), a runaway, a slave who absconds from his master: erifugae Famuli, Cat. 63, 51.

erigeron.full: ērĭgĕron, ontis, m., = ἠριγέρωϝ, the plant groundsel, Senecio vulg., Linn.; Plin. 25, 13, 106, § 167 sq.; 22, 25, 64, § 133.
erigeron.short: ērĭgĕron, ontis, m., = ἠριγέρωϝ, the plant groundsel, Senecio vulg., Linn.;

erigo.full: ē-rĭgo, rexi, rectum, 3, v. a. rego, to raise or set up, to erect (very freq. and class.). Lit. In gen.: rubrum jubar, Lucr. 4, 404: caput, id. 5, 1208: ar borem (with extollere), Cic. Fin. 5, 14, 39: hominem, to form erect, id. Leg. 1, 9, 26: os, id. ib. 3, 85; jacentem, Curt. 7, 3, 17: hastas, Liv. 1, 27, 8; 33, 10: digitum, Quint. 11, 3, 120: manus ad tectum, id. 11, 3, 118; cf.: scalas ad moenia, Liv. 32, 14: agmen in adversum clivum, to lead up, id. 9, 31 fin.: cf. id. 3, 18; 9, 43; 10, 26;

erigone.full: Ērĭgŏne, ēs, f., = Ἠριγόϝη. The daughter of Icarius, who hung herself through grief for her father's death, and was rewarded for it by being translated to the sky as the constellation Virgo, Hyg. Fab. 130; 254; Verg. G. 1, 33 Serv.; Ov. M. 6, 125.—Hence, ērĭgŏnēĭus, a, um, adj.: Canis, i. e. Maera, the hound of Icarius, who was placed along with her in the sky, Ov. F. 5, 723; for which: Canis Erigones, Col. 10, 400.— Daughter of Aegisthus and Clytemnestra, Hyg. Fab. 122; Dict. Cret. 6, 2, 4.— As

erigonus.full: Ĕrĭgōnus, i, m., = Ἐριγώϝ or Ἐρίγωϝ, a river of Macedonia, now Tzerna, Liv. 31, 39, 6; 39, 53 fin.
erigonus.short: Ĕrĭgōnus, i, m., = Ἐριγώϝ or Ἐρίγωϝ, a river of Macedonia, now Tzerna, Liv.

erilis.full: ĕrī^lis (less correctly hĕrīlis, v. erus), e, adj. erus, of the master or mistress of a family, the master's, the mistress's (poet.; esp. in Plaut.): erum fefelli, in nuptias conjeci erilem filium, Ter. And. 3, 4, 23; cf. id. Ad. 3, 2, 3; so, filius, Plaut. Bacch. 2, 3, 117; id. Most. 1, 1, 20; 79; Ter. Eun. 2, 2, 58; id. ib. 5, 5, 20; id. Phorm. 1, 1, 5: filia, Plaut. Aul. 1, 1, 35; id. ib. 2, 3, 8; id. Cist. 2, 3, 8: amica, id. Mil. 2, 1, 37; 44; id. ib. 2, 3, 3; cf. concubina, id. ib. 2, 3, 6

erillus.full: Ērillus (Hērillus), i, m., a Stoic philosopher of Carthage, who flourished about B. C. 260, Cic. Fin. 2, 13, 43; id. Tusc. 5, 30, 85; Lact. 3, 7, 8.,—Hence, ērillĭi (Her-), ōrum, m., the disciples of Erillus, Cic. de Or. 3, 17, 62.
erillus.short: Ērillus (Hērillus), i, m., a Stoic philosopher of Carthage, who flourished about B.

erinaceus.full: ērĭnācĕus (herin-), i, m. er; cf. ericius, a hedgehog, Plin. 8, 37, 56, § 133; 10, 63, 83, § 174 al. (Sillig; dub.—Jan. irenaceus).

erindes.full: Erindes, is, m., a river between Media and Hyrcanea, Tac. A. 11, 10.
erindes.short: Erindes, is, m., a river between Media and Hyrcanea, Tac.

erineos.full: ĕrīnĕos, i, f., = ἐριϝεός, a plant, perh. the Campanula Rapunculus, Linn., Plin. 23, 7, 65, § 131.
erineos.short: ĕrīnĕos, i, f., = ἐριϝεός, a plant, perh.

erinna.full: Ērinna, ae, f., = Ἤριϝϝα, a famous Lesbian poetess, contemporary with Sappho, Plin. 34, 8, 19, § 57.—Gen. Erinnēs, Prop. 2, 3, 22.
erinna.short: Ērinna, ae, f., = Ἤριϝϝα, a famous Lesbian poetess, contemporary with Sappho, Plin.

erinys.full: Ĕrīnys (or, less correctly, Erinnys; cf. Wagner ad Verg. A. 2, 337), ўos, f., = Ἐριννύς (Ἐρινύς), one of the Furies, Verg. A. 7, 447; 570; Ov. M. 1, 241; 4, 490; 11, 14 et saep.—Acc. Erinyn, Ov. M. 1, 725.—In plur.: Erinyes, the Furies, Prop. 2, 20, 29 (3, 13, 29 M.); Ov. H. 11, 103.—Acc. Erinyas, Stat. Th. 11, 345.— Transf. Of Helen: Trojae patriae communis Erinys, the scourge, curse, Verg. A. 2, 573.— Appellatively, fury, frenzy, madness = furor, Verg. A. 2, 337: civilis, i. e. civil war, Luc.

eriophoros.full: ĕrĭŏphŏros, i, m., = ἐριοφόρος (woolbearer), a kind of bulbous plant, Plin. 19, 2, 10, § 32.
eriophoros.short: ĕrĭŏphŏros, i, m., = ἐριοφόρος (woolbearer), a kind of bulbous plant, Plin.

erioxylon.full: ĕrĭoxўlon, i, n., = ἐριόξυλοϝ, cotton, Dig. 32, 1, 70, § 9.
erioxylon.short: ĕrĭoxўlon, i, n., = ἐριόξυλοϝ, cotton, Dig.

eriphia.full: ĕrĭphīa, ae, f., = ἐριφεία, a plant, Plin. 24, 18, 103, § 168.
eriphia.short: ĕrĭphīa, ae, f., = ἐριφεία, a plant, Plin.

eriphyla.full: Ĕrĭphȳla, ae, or -ē, ēs, f., = Ἐριφύλη, daughter of Talaüs, and wife of Amphiaraüs, whom she betrayed to Polynices for a golden necklace, for which she was slain by her son Alcmaeon.—Form -a, Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 18, § 39; id. Inv. 1, 50, 94; Prop. 2, 16, 29 (3, 8, 29 M.); 3, 13, 57 (4, 12, 57 M.).— Form -e, Ov. A. A. 3, 13; Verg. A. 6, 445.— Plur.: multae Eriphylae, Juv. 6, 655, v. Amphiaraus.—Hence, ĕrĭphȳlaeus, a, um, adj., of Eriphyla: penates, Stat. Th. 4, 211.
eriphyla.short: Ĕrĭphȳla, ae, or -ē, ēs, f., = Ἐριφύλη, daughter of Talaüs, and wife of Amphiaraüs, whom she betrayed to Polynices for a golden necklace, for which she was slain by her son Alcmaeon.—Form -a, Cic.

eripio.full: ē-rĭpĭo, ĭpŭi, eptum, 3, v. a. rapio, to snatch, tear, or pull out; to snatch away, take away (freq. and class.; cf.: capio, prehendo, sumo, demo, adimo, rapio, furor). Lit. In gen.: tibias ex ore, Plaut. Stich. 5, 4, 36; cf.: bolum e faucibus, Ter. Heaut. 4, 2, 6: hirundines ex nido, Plaut. Rud. 3, 4, 67; 3, 1, 8: ex manibus alicujus, Cass. ap. Cic. Fam. 12, 13, 1; Cic. Verr. 2, 1, 4, § 9: torrem ab igne, Ov. M. 8, 457: ensem vaginā, Verg. A. 4, 579 et saep.: aliena bona, Plaut. Pers. 1, 2, 11;

eris.full: Ĕris, ĭdos, f., = Ἔρις, the goddess of strife, Hyg. F. 92.
eris.short: Ĕris, ĭdos, f., = Ἔρις, the goddess of strife, Hyg.

erisma.full: ĕrisma, ae, f., and ĕrisma, ătis, n., = ἔρεισμα, a buttress, Front. Aquaed. 18; Vitr. 6, 11, 6 (heterocl. gen. plur.: eris matorum, id. 10, 1, 2).
erisma.short: ĕrisma, ae, f., and ĕrisma, ătis, n., = ἔρεισμα, a buttress, Front.

eristalis.full: ĕristălis, is, f., an unknown precious stone, Plin. 37, 10, 58, § 160 (dub.—Jan. erythallis).
eristalis.short: ĕristălis, is, f., an unknown precious stone, Plin.

erithace.full: ĕrĭthăce, ēs, f., = ἐριθάκη, bee-bread, sandarach, called also sandaraca and cerinthus, Plin. 11, 7, 7, § 17 (in Varr. R. R. 316, 8 and 23, written as Greek).
erithace.short: ĕrĭthăce, ēs, f., = ἐριθάκη, bee-bread, sandarach, called also sandaraca and cerinthus, Plin.

erithacus.full: ĕrĭthăcus, i, m., = ἐρίθακος, an unknown bird, Plin. 10, 29, 44, § 86.
erithacus.short: ĕrĭthăcus, i, m., = ἐρίθακος, an unknown bird, Plin.

erithales.full: ĕrĭthăles, is, n., = ἐριθαλές, little houseleek, Plin. 25, 13, 102, § 160.
erithales.short: ĕrĭthăles, is, n., = ἐριθαλές, little houseleek, Plin.

eritudo.full: eritūdo (her-): servitudo, Paul. ex Fest. p. 83, 1 Müll.; cf.: eritudo dominatio, Placid. Gloss. p. 460; and: eritudo δεσποτεία, Gloss. Labb. [erus = herus].

erivo.full: ē-rīvo, āre, v. a., to draw out, draw off: pluvias aquas, Plin. 17, 26, 40, § 249.

eriza.full: Ĕriza, ae, f., = Ἔριζα, a town of Magna Phrygia, Liv. 38, 14, 1.—Hence, ĕrizēnus, a, um, adj., of Eriza: regio, Plin. 10, 43, 60, § 124.
eriza.short: Ĕriza, ae, f., = Ἔριζα, a town of Magna Phrygia, Liv.

erneum.full: ernĕum, i, n., a cake baked in an earthen pot, Cato R. R. 81.
erneum.short: ernĕum, i, n., a cake baked in an earthen pot, Cato R.

erodo.full: ē-rōdo, no perf., rōsum, 3, v. a., to gnaw off or away, to consume. Prop.: vites (animalia), Plin. 30, 15, 52, § 146; cf. frondes, Col. poet. 10, 323.— Transf. In gen., to eat away, corrode: aes, ferrum (aqua), Plin. 31, 2, 19, § 28: arbores sale, id. 12, 9, 20, § 37.— Esp. in medic. lang., of erosive remedies, Cels. 5, 28; Plin. 24, 11, 52, § 89; 34, 15, 46, § 176.

erogatio.full: ērŏgātĭo, ōnis, f. erogo. A giving out, paying out, a division, distribution: pecuniae, * Cic. Att. 15, 2 fin.; so Dig. 25, 1, 3; 50, 4, 14; Cod. Just. 12, 38, 16 al.: aquarum, Front. Aquaed. 77; so in the plur., id. ib. 3; cf. Plin. Ep. 10, 35; id. Pan. 41, 1; Tac. A. 13, 50 al.—* A repeal, abrogation: legis, Tert. Idol. 5.

erogator.full: ērŏgātor, ōris, m. id., one who pays out or gives away (late Lat.): alicujus praestationis, Cod. Just. 12, 38, 16: virginis, i. e. who gives her away in marriage, Tert. Pud. 16.

erogatorius.full: ērŏgātōrĭus, a, um, adj. id., of or for distributing (water): modulus, Front. Aquaed. 34.

erogito.full: ē-rŏgĭto, āre, v. freq. a. id., to find out by asking, to inquire: ex aliquo, quid, etc., Plaut. Capt. 5, 1, 32; Sil. 10, 476: qui neque cujatis esset, unquam potuimus multa erogitantes sciscere, Att. Tr. 625 (Rib. Fragm. Trag. p. 217).

erogo.full: ē-rŏgo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. Orig., a pub. law t. t., to expend, pay out money from the public treasury, after asking the consent of the people: pecunias ex aerario, Cic. Vat. 12; cf. Cic. Verr. 2, 3, 71; 2, 5, 19; id. Q. Fr. 1, 2, 4, § 14; Liv. 22, 23; 33, 47 al.; cf.: pecuniam in classem, Cic. Fl. 13: in aes alienum, id. Att. 6, 1, 21: unde in eos sumptus, pecunia erogaretur, Liv. 1, 20; Vulg. Marc. 5, 26.— Transf. beyond the pub. law sphere, to pay, pay out, disburse, expend (cf.: pendo, expen

eros.full: Ĕros, ōtis, m., = Ἔρως. Love as a person; Lat. Amor, Cupido, Nemes. Ecl. 4 lem.— In gen., a common name of Roman slaves or freedmen, Cic. Fam. 12, 26; id. Att. 10, 15; 15, 15; 20; Dig. 6, 1, 5 fin. et saep.— The name of an actor in the time of Cicero, Cic. Rosc. Com. 11.

erosio.full: ērōsĭo, ōnis, f. erodo, an eating away, erosion, in plur.: genarum, Plin. 23, 3, 34, § 70.

erosus.full: ērōsus, a, um, Part., from erodo.
erosus.short: ērōsus, a, um, Part., from erodo.

erotema.full: ĕrōtēma, ătis, n., = ἐρώτημα, an inquiry, a question, Mart. Cap. 5, § 524.
erotema.short: ĕrōtēma, ătis, n., = ἐρώτημα, an inquiry, a question, Mart.

erotopaegnion.full: Ĕrōtŏpaegnĭon, i, n., = ἐρωτοπαίγνιον, a love song, Aus. Edyll. 13 fin.—Esp. plur.: ĕrōtopaegnia, ōn, the title of a book of poems by Laevius, Gell. 2, 24, 9.
erotopaegnion.short: Ĕrōtŏpaegnĭon, i, n., = ἐρωτοπαίγνιον, a love song, Aus.

erotundatus.full: ē-rŏtundātus, a, um, Part. [rotundo], rounded off, polished.—Trop.: structura verborum (with levis), Sid. Ep. 9, 7.

erotylus.full: ĕrōtўlus, i, m., = ἐρωτύλος, an unknown precious stone, Plin. 37, 10, 58, § 160.
erotylus.short: ĕrōtўlus, i, m., = ἐρωτύλος, an unknown precious stone, Plin.

errabundus.full: errābundus, a, um, adj. erro, wandering to and fro, wandering about (rare; not in Cic. or Caes.): odor, floating about, Lucr. 4, 692: nunc errabundi domos suos pervagarentur, Liv. 1, 29; cf. Suet. Caes. 31: naves (with dispersae), Auct. B. Afr. 2, 4: naves vagabantur, ib. 21, 3: trieris, ib. 44, 2: agmen, Curt. 8, 4, 6.—Poet. transf.: vestigia bovis, Verg. E. 6, 58.

errantia.full: errantia, ae, f. id., a wandering: animi, Att. ap. Non. 204, 13 (Rib. Fragm. Trag. p. 196).

erraticus.full: errātĭcus, a, um, adj. id., wandering to and fro, wandering about, roving, erratic (mostly ante-class. and post-Aug.). In gen.: stellae, planets, Auct. ap. Gell. 3, 10, 2; 14, 1, 11; 18; Sen. Q. N. 7, 23: Delos, Ov. M. 6, 333: homo, Gell. 9, 2, 6: sanguis, i. e. herpetic, Plin. 26, 13, 84, § 136; cf. transf.: vitis serpens multiplici lapsu et erratico, * Cic. de Sen. 15, 52.— Esp. in botany, of plants that spring up here and there wild, i. q. silvestris, wild: brassica, Cato R. R. 157, 12; Plin.

erratilis.full: errātĭlis, e, adj. id., wandering: ferae, Cassiod. Var. 1, 21.

erratio.full: errātĭo, ōnis, f. id., a wandering, roving about. Lit.: hac multo propius ibis et minor est erratio, Ter. Ad. 4, 2, 41; Plaut. Rud. 1, 2, 90; Cic. N. D. 2, 21, 56; id. Univ. 6.— Trop.: in factis dictisque, Lact. 5, 17, 29; Hyg. Astr. 2, 2.

errativus.full: errātīvus (al. ERRATICIVS) animus est, qui solet errare et desinit, Fronto de Differ. Voc. p. 2200 P.

errator.full: errātor, ōris, m. id., a wanderer, Fest. p. 344, 34.—Transf., of the river Maeander: terris totiens crrator in isdem, Ov. H. 9, 55.

erratum.full: errātum, i, n., v. 1. erro, I. B. 2. b.

erratus.full: errātus, ūs, m. erro, a wandering, roving about (poet. and in post-Aug. prose): longis erratibus actus, Ov. M. 4, 567.

erro1.full: erro, āvi, ātum, 1, v. n. and a. [root er-, to go; desiderative forms, ἔρχομαι (ἐρσκ-); and Lat. (ers-o) erro, to seek to reach; hence, to wander; cf. Germ. irren; Engl. err, etc., v. Georg Curtius Gr. Etym. p. 546 sq.]. Neutr. In gen. Prop., to wander, to wander or stray about, to wander up and down, to rove (freq. and class.; cf. vagor, palor): propter te errans patria careo, Ter. Heaut. 2, 3, 16; cf.: cum vagus et exsul erraret, Cic. Clu. 62, 175: ignari hominumque locorumque Erramus vento hu

erro2.full: erro, ōnis, m. 1. erro, a wanderer, vagabond, vagrant, Tib. 2, 6, 6; Ov. H. 15, 53.—Used esp. of slaves: ut errones aliquem cujus dicantur invenient, Plin. Ep. 2, 10, 5; Edict. Aedil. ap. Gell. 4, 2, 1; Dig. 21, 1, 17, § 14; 49, 16, 4 fin.; Hor. S. 2, 7, 113.—Of the queen-bee: dux, Col. 9, 10 fin. —Of the planets, Nigid. ap. Gell. 3, 10, 2; 14, 1, 11.—Of vagabond soldiers: nec nostros servire sinant errorribus agros, Verg. Dir. 70 Rib.

erroneus.full: errōnĕus, a, um, adj. id., wandering about, straying: vagus atque erroneus, Sen. Ben. 6, 11, 2: canes, Col. 7, 12, 5: erroneus, ἀλήτης, πλάνος, Gloss. Labb.

error.full: error, ōris, m. id., a wandering. In gen., a wandering, straying or strolling about (rare and mostly poet.). Lit.: ad quos Ceres in illo errore venisse dicitur, Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 49, § 108: error ac dissipatio civium (sc. mercatorum), id. Rep. 2, 4, 7 Mos. (cf. erratio, I.): navium pars ex errore eodem conferebatur, Auct. B. Afr. 11; cf. Ov. H. 16, 29; id. M. 14, 484; id. Tr. 4, 10, 100; Verg. A. 1, 755; 6, 532 et saep.—Transf., of the motion of atoms, Lucr. 2, 132; of the meanderings of rivers,

erubescentia.full: ērŭbescentĭa, ae, f. erubesco, a blushing for shame, shamefacedness (postclass.), Tert. ad Nat. 1, 16; id. Poen. 10.

erubescibilis.full: ērŭbescĭbĭlis, e, adj. id., of which one should be ashamed, Cassiod. Amic. 21, 5.

erubesco.full: ē-rŭbesco, bŭi, 3, v. inch. n. and a. Neutr., to grow red, to redden. In gen.: vidi te totis erubuisse genis, Ov. Am. 2, 8, 16; id. M. 4, 330; id. Pont. 2, 1, 36. — In partic., to redden or blush with shame, to feel ashamed. Absol., with praepp. or abl.: erubui mecastor misera propter clamorem tuum, etc., Plaut. Truc. 2, 2, 36; Ter. Ad. 4, 5, 9: quas (voluptates) non erubescens persequitur nominatim, Cic. N. D. 1, 40, 111 fin.; id. Rosc. Com. 3, 8; id. Vatin. 16, 39; id. Fin. 2, 9, 28; id. Fam.

eruca.full: ērūca, ae, f. A caterpillar, cankerworm, Col. 11, 3, 63, p. 464 Bip.; Pall. 1, 35 saep.; Col. 10, 333; Plin. 17, 24, 37, § 229, but here Sillig reads uruca, q. v.— A sort of cole-wort, Brassica eruca, Linn.; Col. 11, 3, 29; 10, 109; 372; Plin. 19, 8, 44, § 154; Hor. S. 2, 8, 51; Mart. 3, 75; Vulg. Amos, 4, 9.

erucius.full: Erucius, ii, m., a Roman proper name, Cic. Rosc. Am. 13 al.
erucius.short: Erucius, ii, m., a Roman proper name, Cic.

eructatio.full: ēructātĭo, ōnis, f. eructo, a casting or throwing upward (post-class. and rare): altera (exhalatio) arida est atque animae similis, quae terrenis eructationibus surgit, App. de Mundo, p. 60, 40.— Transf., an utterance: judiciorum Dei per voces prophetarum, Hilar. in Psa. 41, 12.

eructo.full: ē-ructo, āre, v. a. To belch or vomit forth, to throw up (rare but class.). Prop.: unde tu nos turpissime eructando ejecisti, Cic. Pis. 6, 13: saniem eructans, Verg. A. 3, 632; cf. Col. 8, 8, 10.— Trop.: caedem sermonibus suis, i. e. to talk of murder when drunk, Cic. Cat. 2, 5, 10.— Ingen., to cast forth, emit, exhale: Tartarus horriferos eructans faucibus aestus, Lucr. 3, 1012: aquam, Varr. R. R. 3, 14, 2: odorem, id. ib. 1, 4, 4: noxium virus, Col. 1, 5, 6: harenam, Verg. A. 6, 297: flammas,

eructus.full: ēructus, a, um, P. a., v. † 2. erugo.

erudero.full: ē-rūdĕro, no perf., ātum, 1, v. a., to clear from rubbish (very rare). Lit.: solum, Varr. R. R. 2, 2, 7.— Trop.: volumen de supervacuis sententiis, Sid. Ep. 5, 15; 5, 7; Ambros. Ep. 22, 2.

erudio.full: ē-rŭdĭo, īvi or ii, ītum, 4, v. a., qs. to free from roughness, i. e. to polish, educate, instruct, teach (freq. and class.; cf.: doceo, edoceo, praecipio, instituo). Prop.: studiosos discendi erudiunt atque docent, Cic. Off. 1, 44, 156: aliquem, id. Div. 2, 2 (with docere); id. de Or. 3, 9, 35 (with instituere); id. ib. 2, 1, 12; Quint. prooem. § 1; 6 et saep.: filios ad majorum instituta (with instituere), Cic. Verr. 2, 3, 69; cf. id. Tusc. 1, 26: aliquem artibus, id. Fam. 1, 7 fin.; cf. id. R
erudio.short: ē-rŭdĭo, īvi or ii, ītum, 4, v.

eruditio.full: ērŭdītĭo, ōnis, f. erudio, an instructing, instruction (cf.: doctrina, disciplina, scientia, intellegentia, cognitio). Prop.: de ejus eruditione quod labores, nihil est, quoniam ingenium ejus nosti, Cic. Q. Fr. 3, 1, 4 fin.; cf. Quint. 2, 3, 10; Gell. 11, 7, 3.— Far more freq., Transf., learning, knowledge, erudition, obtained by instruction: qui praeclara eruditione atque doctrina aut utraque re ornati, Cic. Off. 1, 33; id. de Or. 2, 1; id. Fin. 1, 21, 71; id. Tusc. 1, 2, 4; id. Div. 2, 63 fin.

eruditor.full: ērŭdītor, ōris, m. id., an instructor, teacher (post-class.), Tert. Pall. 4; Hier. Vit. Hil.; Vulg. Rom. 2, 20 al.

eruditrix.full: ērŭdītrix, īcis, f. eruditor, an instructress, Flor. 2, 6, 38.

eruditulus.full: ērŭdītŭlus, i, m. dim. 1. eruditus, somewhat skilled or experienced (in love), said jocosely, Cat. 57, 7.

eruditus1.full: ērŭdītus, a, um, Part. and P. a., from erudio.

eruditus2.full: ērŭdītus, ūs, m. erudio, instruction; in abl. sing., Tert, adv. Val. 29.

erugatio.full: ērūgātĭo, ōnis, f. 1. erugo, a clearing from wrinkles: cutis, Plin. 28, 12, 50, § 184.

erugo1.full: ē-rūgo, āre, v. a., to clear from wrinkles, to smooth, Plin. 13, 12, 26, § 82; 21, 19, 74, § 127; 28, 12, 50, § 183.

erugo2.full: ē-rūgo, ĕre, semel factum significat, quod eructare saepius, Paul. ex Fest. p. 83, 1 Müll.—Hence, * ēructus, a, um, P. a., belched out; transf., impure, bad: vinum (with fetidum), Gell. 11, 7, 3.
erugo2.short: ē-rūgo, ĕre, semel factum significat, quod eructare saepius, Paul.

erumpo.full: ē-rumpo, rūpi, ruptum, 3, v. a. and n. Act., to cause to break or burst forth; to burst, sunder (rare; mostly ante-class.). Lit.: (brassica) tumida concoquit, eadem erumpit, Cato, R. R. 157, 3: ignes, Lucr. 1, 725; cf. id. 6, 583; Cic. Arat. 111: Achates et Aeneas erumpere nubem ardebant, Verg. A. 1, 580: cum sanguis eruptus est, Scrib. Comp. 84: se erumpere, in the neuter signif., to break or burst forth, Lucr. 4, 1111; cf.: portis se foras erumpunt, Caes. B. C. 2, 14, 1: et caput, unde altus p

erunco.full: ē-runco, āre, v. a., to weed out: herbas, Col. 2, 10, 28: areas, id. 11, 3, 14.

eruo.full: ē-rŭo, ŭi, ŭtum, 3, v. a., to cast forth, throw out; to dig, tear, or pluck out (freq. and class.). Lit. In gen.: qui sciet, ubi quidque positum sit, quaque eo veniat, is, etiam si quid obrutum erit, poterit eruere, Cic. Fin. 4, 4 fin.; so, aurum terrā, Ov. Am. 3, 8, 53; cf.: caprificos sepulcris, Hor. Epod. 5, 17: gemmam vadis, Mart. 8, 28; Tac. A. 2, 69: segetem ab radicibus imis, Verg. G. 1, 320; cf.: pinum radicibus, id. A. 5, 449 Heyne N. cr.; and: herbam radicitus, Plin. 21, 11, 36, § 62:

eruptio.full: ēruptĭo, ōnis, f. erumpo, II., a breaking out, bursting forth. Lit. In gen.: (elephanti) universi eruptionem tentavere, Plin. 8, 7, 7, § 21; 16, 10, 19, § 45; 18, 17, 44, § 150 al.—In plur., Plin. 24, 15, 86, § 136.— In partic. In milit. lang., a sally: ex oppido eruptionem fecerunt, Caes. B. G. 2, 33, 2; 3, 3, 3; 3, 5, 2; 3, 6, 1 et saep.— In medic. lang., concr., a breaking out, eruption of morbid matter, Plin. 23 prooem. 5, § 8; 24, 9, 38, § 63; 20, 7, 26, § 67; 20, 8, 27, § 71; 26, 11, 73, §

eruptor.full: ēruptor, ōris, m. erumpo, one who makes a sally, Amm. 24, 5, 9.

eruptus.full: ēruptus, a, um, Part., from erumpo.
eruptus.short: ēruptus, a, um, Part., from erumpo.

erus.full: ĕrus (less correctly, hĕrus, v. infra), i, m. Sanscr. root, har-; har-āmi, I seize; har-anam, hand; Gr. χείρ, χέρης; Lat. heres, hirudo; but the form erus is that of the best MSS.; cf. Ritschl, Opusc. 2, 409; Brix ad Plaut. Trin. 1, 2, 24. Lit., the master of a house or family, in respect to servants: erum atque servom saluere, Plaut. Trin. 2, 4, 34: iis, qui vi oppressos imperio coercent, sit sane adhibenda saevitia, ut eris in famulos, si aliter teneri non possunt, Cic. Off. 2, 7, 24; cf.: non

erutor.full: ērŭtor, ōris, m. eruo, a rescuer: erutor meus es tu, Domine, Vers. Lat. Psa. 69, 6, ap. August. in Psa. 69 (cf.: implicatus sum, erue, August. ib.).

erutus.full: ērŭtus, a, um, Part., from eruo.
erutus.short: ērŭtus, a, um, Part., from eruo.

ervilia.full: ervĭlĭa, ae, f. ervum, a kind of pulse, the bitter vetch, Varr. R. R. 1, 32, 2; Col. 2, 13, 1; Ser. Samon. 585; cf. Paul. ex Fest. p. 82, 21 Müll.

ervum.full: ervum (her-), i, n. Gr. ἐρέβινθος, ὄροβος; root, ar- for al-; cf. alo, a kind of pulse, the bitter vetch, ervum ervilia, Linn.; Verg. E. 3, 100 Voss.; Col. 2, 10, 34; 11, 2, 10; Pall. Jan. 8; Ov. Med. fac. 55; Hor. S. 2, 6, 117.

erycinus.full: Ĕrўcīnus, a, um, v. Eryx, II.

erymanthus.full: Ĕrўmanthus, i, m., = Ἐρύμανθος. A chain of mountains in Arcadia, on the borders of Elis, where Hercules slew the boar named after the place, Ov. H. 9, 87; id. M. 5, 608; Mart. 11, 69.— Derivv. ĕrўmanthĭus, a, um, adj., Erymanthian: belua, Cic. Tusc. 2, 9, 22: aper, id. ib. 4, 22, 55; and sarcastically, with Verres immanissimus, Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 43 fin.: mater, i. e. Atalanta, from Tegea, in Arcadia, Stat. Th. 12, 805.— ĕrўmanthēus, a, um, adj., Erymanthian: monstrum, Val. Fl. 1, 374.— ĕrўmanthĭa

erynge.full: ērynge, ēs, f., and ēryngĭon, ii, n., = ἠρύγγη and ἠρύγγιον, a sort of thistle; acc. to some, the eringo, Eryngium campestre, Linn.; acc. to others, the spotted yellow thistle, Scolymus maculatus, Linn.; Plin. 22, 7, 8, § 18 sq.; Col. 6, 5, 2; Scrib. Comp. 153; 165; Veg. Vet. 1, 17, 14; 4, 3, 7.
erynge.short: ērynge, ēs, f., and ēryngĭon, ii, n., = ἠρύγγη and ἠρύγγιον, a sort of thistle;

erysichthon.full: Ĕrўsichthōn (Eris-), ŏnis, m., = Ἐρυσίχθων, son of the Thessalian king Triopas; he cut down the grove of Ceres, for which he was punished with a raging hunger, that caused him to devour his own flesh, Ov. M. 8, 471 sq.; cf. Hyg. Astr. 2, 14.
erysichthon.short: Ĕrўsichthōn (Eris-), ŏnis, m., = Ἐρυσίχθων, son of the Thessalian king Triopas;

erysimum.full: ĕrўsĭmum, i, n., = ἐρύσιμον, a sort of grain, called also irio, Plin. 18, 10, 22, § 96.
erysimum.short: ĕrўsĭmum, i, n., = ἐρύσιμον, a sort of grain, called also irio, Plin.

erysipelas.full: ĕrўsĭpĕlas, ătis, n., = ἐρυσίπελας, a reddish eruption on the skin, St. Anthony's fire, erysipelas, Cels. 5, 28, 11 (id. 5, 26, 31 and 33, written as Gr.).
erysipelas.short: ĕrўsĭpĕlas, ătis, n., = ἐρυσίπελας, a reddish eruption on the skin, St.

erysisceptrum.full: ĕrўsiscēptrum, i, n., = ἐρυσίσκηπτρον, a low thorny shrub, also called adipsatheon, Plin. 24, 13, 69, § 112 al.; App. Herb. 109.
erysisceptrum.short: ĕrўsiscēptrum, i, n., = ἐρυσίσκηπτρον, a low thorny shrub, also called adipsatheon, Plin.

erysithales.full: ĕrўsĭthăles, is, n., = ἐρυσίθαλες, a plant with a yellow flower, Plin. 26, 13, 85, § 137; cf. id. 25, 13, 102, § 160.
erysithales.short: ĕrўsĭthăles, is, n., = ἐρυσίθαλες, a plant with a yellow flower, Plin.

erythallis.full: ĕrythallis, is, f., a gem now unknown, Plin. 37, 10, 58, § 160.
erythallis.short: ĕrythallis, is, f., a gem now unknown, Plin.

erythea.full: Ĕrўthēa or -_ia, ae, f., = Ἐρύθεια, a small island in the Bay of Cadiz, where the giant Geryon dwelt, Mel. 3, 6, 2; Plin. 4, 21, 36, § 120; Prop. 5, 9, 2.— Derivv. ĕrўthīus, a, um, adj., Erythean: ad litora Gades, Sil. 16, 195.— ĕrўthēïs, ĭdis, f., Erythean: boves, Ov. F. 1, 543: praeda, id. ib. 5, 649.
erythea.short: Ĕrўthēa or -_ia, ae, f., = Ἐρύθεια, a small island in the Bay of Cadiz, where the giant Geryon dwelt, Mel.

erythinus.full: ĕrўthīnus, i, m., = ἐρυθῖνος, a red kind of sea-mullet, Plin. 9, 16, 23, § 166; Ov. Hal. 104.
erythinus.short: ĕrўthīnus, i, m., = ἐρυθῖνος, a red kind of sea-mullet, Plin.

erythrae.full: Ĕrȳ^thrae, ārum, f., = Ἐρυθραί. A city of Boeotia, near Mount Cithaeron, Plin. 4, 7, 12, § 26; Stat. Th. 7, 265.—By it was founded, One of the twelve chief cities of Ionia, Plin. 31, 2, 10, § 14; Cic. Verr. 2, 1, 19, § 49; Liv. 44, 28.—Hence, ĕrȳ^thraeus, a, um, adj., Erythraean: Sibylla, Cic. Div. 1, 18; Varr. ap. Serv. Verg. A. 6, 36: terra, Liv. 36, 45: triremes, id. 37, 11.—Subst.: Erythraea, ae, f., the district of Erythrae, Liv. 37, 12; 44, 28.— Erythraei, ōrum, m., the inhabitants of Eryt

erythraeus.full: ĕrythraeus, a, um, adj., = ἐρυθραῖος, reddish: aries, Col. 7, 2 fin.; 7, 3, 2; cf. Plin. 8, 48, 73, § 191.— As an adj. prop., v. Erythrae, II. B., and Erythras, II.
erythraeus.short: ĕrythraeus, a, um, adj., = ἐρυθραῖος, reddish: aries, Col.

erythraicon.full: ĕrythrăĭcon, i, n., = ἐρυθραϊκόν, a species of the plant satyrion, Plin. 26, 10, 63, § 97.
erythraicon.short: ĕrythrăĭcon, i, n., = ἐρυθραϊκόν, a species of the plant satyrion, Plin.

erythranos.full: ĕrȳ^thrănos, on, = ἐρυθρανός, red: cissus erythranos similis hederae, Plin. 24, 10, 49, § 82.—Hence, † ĕrythrănon, i, n., = ἐρυθρανόν, a kind of ivy with reddish berries, Plin. 16, 34, 62, § 147.
erythranos.short: ĕrȳ^thrănos, on, = ἐρυθρανός, red: cissus erythranos similis hederae, Plin.

erythras.full: Ĕrȳ^thras, ae, m., = Ἐρύθρας, a fabulous king of southern Asia (Arabia or Persia), after whom the Red Sea, or the Arabian and Persian Gulfs, were named, Mel. 3, 8, 1; Plin. 6, 23, 28, § 107; Curt. 8, 9. —Deriv., ĕrȳ^thraeus, a, um, adj., Erythraean: mare, the Red Sea (pure Lat. Mare rubrum), Mel., Plin., and Curt. l. l.: alga, i. e. in the Persian Gulf, Mart. 10, 16: lapilli, pearls, fished up in the Persian Gulf, id. 5, 37; cf. Stat. S. 4, 6, 18.—Poet., in a wider sense, Indian: orae, Stat. Th.
erythras.short: Ĕrȳ^thras, ae, m., = Ἐρύθρας, a fabulous king of southern Asia (Arabia or Persia), after whom the Red Sea, or the Arabian and Persian Gulfs, were named, Mel.

erythrocomos.full: ĕrythrŏcŏmos, on, adj., = ἐρυθρόκομος, red-haired: genus, a kind of pomegranate-tree, Plin. 13, 19, 34, § 113.
erythrocomos.short: ĕrythrŏcŏmos, on, adj., = ἐρυθρόκομος, red-haired: genus, a kind of pomegranate-tree, Plin.

erythrodanus.full: ĕrythrŏdănus, i, m., = ἐρυθρόδανον, madder, Rubia tinctorum, Linn. (pure Lat. rubia); Plin. 24, 11, 56, § 94.
erythrodanus.short: ĕrythrŏdănus, i, m., = ἐρυθρόδανον, madder, Rubia tinctorum, Linn.

erythros.full: ĕrȳthros, on, adj., = ἐρυθρός, red: rhus, Plin. 24, 11, 55, § 93: venenum, id. 21. 31, 105, § 179.
erythros.short: ĕrȳthros, on, adj., = ἐρυθρός, red: rhus, Plin.

eryx.full: Ĕryx, ȳcis, m., = Ἔρυξ, the name of a high mountain in the northwestern angle of Sicily, and of a city near it famous for its temple of Venus. According to fable, it was named from the Sicilian king Eryx, son of Butes and Venus, and brother of Aeneas; the mountain is now called S. Giuliano, Mel. 2, 7, 17; Plin. 3, 8, 14, § 90; Ov. A. A. 2, 420; id. F. 4, 874; id. M. 2, 221; Verg. A. 1, 570; 5, 24; 419; 630; 772; Hyg. Fab. 260. The mountain is also called ĕrўcus, i (mons), m., Cic. Verr. 2, 2, 8;
eryx.short: Ĕryx, ȳcis, m., = Ἔρυξ, the name of a high mountain in the northwestern angle of Sicily, and of a city near it famous for its temple of Venus.

esaias.full: Ē^sāĭās, ae, m. Heb., the Jewish prophet Isaian, Lact. 4, 11, 10; Prud. στεφ. 5, 524.—Hence, ēsāĭānus, a, um, adj., of Isaiah, Sulp. Sev. Ep. 2, 10.

esca.full: esca, ae (gen. sing. escas, Liv. Andron. ap. Prisc. p. 679 P.), f. for edca, v. esco, and edo; cf. Varr. L. L. 6, § 84 Müll., food, both of men and beasts (class.; cf.: victus, cibus, cibaria, alimenta, edulia, opsonium, pulmentum; epulae, daps, etc.). In gen. Lit.: dii nec escis aut potionibus vescuntur, Cic. N. D. 2, 28; id. Div. 1, 51; id. Fin. 2, 28; Plaut. Men. 1, 1, 12; id. Most. 3, 2, 2; id. Mil. 2, 6, 98; Verg. G. 4, 17; Hor. S. 2, 2, 72 et saep.—In plur., Plaut. Cas. 2, 8, 56; id. Men.

escalis.full: escālis, e, adj. esca. Pertaining to food: argentum (with potorium), eatingvessels, Dig. 33, 10, 8.—* Belonging to bait: vulnus, Poët. Anthol. Lat. 2, p. 453 Burm.

escarius.full: escārĭus, a, um, adj. id.. Pertaining to food, eating: mensa, Varr. L. L. 5, § 120 Müll.; cf. Paul. ex Fest. p. 77, 11 Müll.: vasa, Plin. 36, 26, 67, § 198; cf. argentum, Dig. 34, 2, 19, § 12; 34, 2, 32, § 2; and absol.: escāria, ōrum, n., Juv. 12, 46: uvae, fit for eating, Plin. 14, 3, 4, § 42. —* Of or belonging to bait: vincla, Plaut. Men. 1, 1, 18.

escatilis.full: escātĭlis, e, adj. id., edible (postclass.), Tert. Poen. 5; id. adv. Marc. 1, 1.

escendo.full: ē-scendo (exs-), di, sum, 3, v. n. and a. [scando]. Neutr., to climb up, mount up, ascend from a place (cf. ascendo init.; also: scando, peto, incedo, ingredior; rare but class.). In gen. Lit.: ex alto puteo ad summum, Plaut. Mil. 4, 4, 14: in currum, id. Merc. 5, 2, 90: in caelum, id. Trin. 4, 2, 100; Cic. Tusc. 1, 29, 71: in rotam, id. ib. 5, 9, 24 Klotz N. cr.: in rostra, id. Off. 3, 20, 80; cf.: in contionem, id. Q. Fr. 1, 2, 5; Liv. 8, 33: in malum (navis), id. 30, 25 fin.: in equum, id. 23

escensio.full: ēscensĭo, ōnis, f. escendo, an ascension, a mounting, climbing, going up: adversus regem escensionem a Paesto facientem pugnare, Liv. 8, 17, 9: in agrum Uticensem, id. 27, 5, 8: ad urbem, id. 27, 29, 7; 28, 8, 8; 37, 17, 3.—Plur.: in agros, Liv. 29, 28, 5.— Esp., a disembarkation, landing: ab navibus in terram, Liv. 22, 20, 4: classis escensionem ad populandum fecit, id. 44, 10, 11.

escensus.full: ēscensus, ūs, m. id., a mounting, ascending, only in abl. sing., Tac. A. 13, 39 Nipperd. (al. ascensu).

eschara.full: eschăra, ae, f., = ἐσχάρα. The base or pedestal of a military engine, Vitr. 10, 17, 20.— In medic. lang., a scar, scab, Cael. Aur. Tard. 5, 1 fin.

escharosis.full: eschărōsis, ĕos, f., = ἐσχάρωσις, the formation of a scab, Cael. Aur. Tard. 1, 4, 118.
escharosis.short: eschărōsis, ĕos, f., = ἐσχάρωσις, the formation of a scab, Cael.

escharoticus.full: eschărōtĭcus, a, um, adj. eschara, = ἐσχαρωτικός, producing a scar, escharotic, Cael. Aur. Tard. 1, 1 fin.

escifer.full: escĭfer, ĕra, ĕrum, adj. esca-fero, food-bringing: volucres, Paul. Nol. Carm. 19, 223.

escit.full: escit, for erit, v. sum init.

esco.full: esco, āre, v. a. for edsco, from edo, Corss. Ausspr. 2, 257, to eat: escandi gratia, Sol. 40 fin.

esculentus.full: escŭlentus, a, um, adj. id., fit for eating, good to eat, eatable, edible, esculent; cf. poculentus: frusta, Cic. Phil. 2, 25 fin.; cf. id. N. D. 2, 49; 56 fin.; Scaev. ap. Gell. 4, 1, 17; Dig. 33, 9, 3. § 3: animalia (with innocua), Plin. 8, 55, 81, § 219: merces, Col. 11, 3, 50: ōs, i. e. filled with food. Plin. 8, 25, 37, § 90.—Comp.: a vino et esculentioribus cibis abstinere, i. e. more delicate, Hier. Ep. 22, 11.

esculetum.full: escŭlētum, escŭlĕus, escŭlīnus, and escŭlus, v. aesc-.
esculetum.short: escŭlētum, escŭlĕus, escŭlīnus, and escŭlus, v.

escunt.full: escunt, for erunt, v. sum init.

esito.full: ēsĭto, āvi, ātum, 1, v. freq. a. 1. edo, to be wont to eat, to eat (ante- and post-class.): brassicam, Cato R. R. 157, 10 (cited in Plin. 20, 9, 33, § 83; Plaut. Capt. 1, 2, 85; id. Ps. 3, 2, 41; Gell. 4, 11, 1 and 9.

esor.full: ēsor, ōris, m. id., an eater: prandiorum optimorum, Front. de Fer. Alsiens. 3.

esox.full: ĕsox, ŏcis, m., = ἴσοξ, a fish of the Rhine, a kind of pike, Plin. 9, 15, 17, § 44 (dub. Jan. isox).
esox.short: ĕsox, ŏcis, m., = ἴσοξ, a fish of the Rhine, a kind of pike, Plin.

esquiliae.full: Esquĭlĭae (less correctly, Exqui-liae, Aesquiliae), ārum, f. perh. from aesculus, a kind of oak, the largest of the seven hills of Rome, with several separate heights (whence the plur. form); added to the city by Servius Tullius; now the heights of Santa Maria Maggiore, Varr. L. L. 5, § 49 Müll.; Liv. 1, 44; Ov. F. 3, 246; 6, 601; Prop. 3 (4), 23, 24; Hor. S. 1, 8, 14; Tac. A. 15, 40; Suet. Tib. 15; Juv. 11, 51 et saep. In earlier times low people were buried there; hence: atrae, Hor. S. 2, 6, 3
esquiliae.short: Esquĭlĭae (less correctly, Exqui-liae, Aesquiliae), ārum, f.

essedarius.full: essĕdārĭus, a, um, adj. essedum, of or belonging to a war-chariot: mulier, Petr. 45, 7.—Hence, as subst.: essedari-us, i, m. A fighter in a (Gallic or British) war-chariot, Caes. B. G. 4, 24, 1; 5, 15, 1; 5, 19, 1; Cic. Fam. 7, 6 fin.— In the Roman circus, a gladiator, Petr. 36, 6; Suet. Calig. 35; id. Claud. 21; Inscr. Orell. 2566; v. essedum.

essedones.full: Essēdŏnes, um, m., = Ἐσσηδόνες, a Scythian people on the river Tanais, Mel. 2, 1, 2; Plin. 4, 12, 26, § 88 al.† † essĕdum, i, n. (in the poets, on account of the metre, as plur. only: esseda, ōrum, v. the foll.—essĕda, ae, f.: essedas transcurrentes, Sen. Ep. 56; cf.: bigae, quadrigae) [a Celtic word], a two-wheeled war-chariot of the Gauls and Britons (cf.: raeda, cisium, currus, vehiculum), Caes. B. G. 4, 32 sq.; 5, 9, 3; 5, 16, 2; 5, 19, 1; Verg. G. 3, 204; afterwards also among the Romans fo
essedones.short: Essēdŏnes, um, m., = Ἐσσηδόνες, a Scythian people on the river Tanais, Mel.

essentia.full: essentĭa, ae, f. sum, the being or essence of a thing; transl. of the Gr. οὐσία: haec interpretatio (rhetorices) non minus dura est, quam illa Flavii essentia atque entia, Quint. 2, 14, 2; 3, 6, 23; 8, 3, 33: cupio, propitiis auribus tuis, essentiam dicere. Ciceronem auctorem hujus verbi habeo, Sen. Ep. 58, 6.

essentialiter.full: essentĭālĭter, adv. essentia, essentially (late Lat.), Aug. de Trin. 7, 2.

essui.full: Essŭi, ōrum, m., a Gallic tribe, perhaps identical with the Esubii and Sesuvii, west of the Sequana, acc. to G. Long, in the modern diocese of Séez, Caes. B. G. 5, 24, 2.
essui.short: Essŭi, ōrum, m., a Gallic tribe, perhaps identical with the Esubii and Sesuvii, west of the Sequana, acc.

estrix.full: estrix, īcis, f. esor, a female glutton or gormandizer, Plaut. Cas. 4, 1, 20.

estur.full: ēstur, for editur, v. 1. ĕdo init.

esubii.full: Esubĭi, ōrum, m. a Gallic tribe west of the Sequana, Caes. B. G. 3, 7 fin.; prob. the same as Essui, q. v.

esurialis.full: ēsŭrĭālis, e, adj. esuries, of or belonging to hunger, comic.: venter gutturque resident esuriales ferias, are keeping hunger-holidays, i. e. have nothing to eal, Plaut. Capt. 3, 1, 8; quoted, Front. de Fer. Aliens. 3.

esurienter.full: ēsŭrĭenter, adv., hungrily, v. I. esurio fin.

esuries.full: ēsŭrĭes, ēi, f. 1. esurio, hunger (postclass.). Lit., Hier. Ep. 125, 33; Alcim. 2, 18; Vulg. Deut. 28, 20.— Trop.: avida ignorantiae, Sid. Ep. 6, 6.

esurigo.full: ēsŭrīgo, ĭnis, f. id., hunger, Var. ap. Non. 106, 15.

esurio1.full: ēsŭrĭo (ess-), no perf., ītum, īre (fut. esuribo, Pompon. and Nov. ap. Non. 479 sq.; Pompon. v. 64; Nov. v. 22 Rib.), v. desid. n. and a. [1. edo], to desire to eat, to suffer hunger, be hungry, to hunger. Lit. (class.), Plaut. Capt. 4, 2, 86; 4, 4, 4; id. Cas. 3, 6, 6 et saep.; Cic. Tusc. 5, 34; Cic. Verr. 2, 5, 34; Cael. ap. Cic. Fam. 8, 17 fin.; Hor. S. 1, 2, 115; 1, 3, 93 et saep.: esuriendi semper inexplebilis aviditas, canine hunger, Plin. 11, 54, 118, § 283.—In the part. fut. act.: (spes

esurio2.full: ēsŭrĭo (ess-), ōnis, m. 1. esurio, a hungry person, Petr. 44, 2.—In a punning jest, with saturio, Plaut. Pers. 1, 3, 23.

esuritio.full: ēsŭrītĭo, ōnis, f. id., a hungering, hunger (rare; not in Cic.), Cat. 23, 14; Gell. 16, 3, 3 sq.; Mart. 1, 100.—In plur, Cat. 21, 1.

esuritor.full: ēsŭrītor, ōris, m. id., a hungry person, Mart. 3, 14, 1.

esus1.full: ēsus, a, um, Part., v. 1. edo.

esus2.full: ēsus, ūs, m. 1. edo, an eating (anteclass. and post-Aug.): esui condi, Varr. R. R. 1, 60; cf.: esui dare alicui, Plin. 20, 17, 69, § 178: agni, Vulg. Exod. 12, 4: esui esse, Gell. 4, 1, 20: esum et potum eximere, Tert. Anim. 43.— Concr., food, Alcim. 5, 258.

esus3.full: Ēsus (Hēsus), i, m., a Gallic deity, to whom human blood was offered, Inscr. Orell. 1993; Luc. 1, 445; Lact. 1, 21, 3.
esus3.short: Ēsus (Hēsus), i, m., a Gallic deity, to whom human blood was offered, Inscr.

et.full: ĕt, conj. [Sanscr. ati, beyond; Gr. ἔτι, besides, yet; Lat. et-iam, at-avus], serves to connect, in the most general manner, single words or entire sentences, and. In gen.: qui illius impudentiam norat et duritudinem, Cato ap. Gell. 17, 2, 20: te sale nata precor, Venus et genetrix patris nostri, Enn. ap. Non. 378, 16 (Ann. v. 53 ed. Vahlen): blande et docte percontat, Naev. ap. Non. 474, 7: ut, quoad possem et liceret, a senis latere numquam discederem, Cic. Lael. 1, 1: de quo praeclare et mult

eta.full: ēta, n., indecl., the seventh letter of the Greek alphabet, Ter. Maur. Litt. 43; Aus. Idyll. 12, 12, 3.
eta.short: ēta, n., indecl., the seventh letter of the Greek alphabet, Ter.

etenim.full: ĕt-ĕnim, conj., subjoins a corroborative clause, or one which contains the reason of a preceding statement, for, truly, and indeed, because that, since (not freq. till class. times, esp. in Cic.): verum profecto hoc petere me precario a vobis jussit ... Etenim ille, etc., Plaut. Am. prol. 26; Ter. And. 2, 6, 9; id. Eun. 5, 9, 44: praeclare quidem dicis; etenim video jam, quo pergat oratio, Cic. Rep. 3, 32; id. de Sen. 5 fin. et saep.: quippe etenim, Lucr. 1, 104; 2, 547; 3, 800; 5, 1062 al.: tut
etenim.short: ĕt-ĕnim, conj., subjoins a corroborative clause, or one which contains the reason of a preceding statement, for, truly, and indeed, because that, since (not freq.

eteocles.full: Ĕtĕōclēs, is and ĕos, m., = Ἐτεοκλῆς, son of Oedipus and Jocasta, brother of Polynices; he was the cause of the Theban war, described by the Roman poet Statius in the Thebais, Cic. Off. 3, 21, 82; Hyg. Fab. 76; gen. Eteoclis, Stat. Th. 3, 214: Eteocleos, id. ib. 12, 421; acc. Eteoclea, id. ib. 7, 688.— Hence, ĕtĕōclēus, a, um, adj., of Eteocles: contentiones, App. M. 10, p. 245, 30.
eteocles.short: Ĕtĕōclēs, is and ĕos, m., = Ἐτεοκλῆς, son of Oedipus and Jocasta, brother of Polynices;

etereius.full: Eterëĭus, i, m., a freedman of the Roman knight Corellius, Plin. 17, 17, 26, § 122. —Hence, Eterëĭānus, a, um, adj., of Etereius: nux, Plin. 15, 23, 25, § 94; 17, 17, 26, § 122.
etereius.short: Eterëĭus, i, m., a freedman of the Roman knight Corellius, Plin.

etesiacus.full: ĕtēsĭăcus, a, um, adj., = ἐτησιακός, of the trade-winds: vitis, Plin. 14, 3, 4, § 36.
etesiacus.short: ĕtēsĭăcus, a, um, adj., = ἐτησιακός, of the trade-winds: vitis, Plin.

etesiae.full: ĕtēsĭae, ārum, m., = ἐτησίαι (sc. ἄνεμοι), the winds that blow annually during the dog-days for forty days, Etesian winds, trade-winds, Sen. Q. N. 5, 10 sq.; Col. 11, 2, 56; 58; Lucr. 6, 716; Cic. N. D. 2, 53; id. Fam. 2, 15 fin.; id. poët. Or. 45; Caes. B. C. 3, 107; Liv. 37, 23 et saep.—In sing.: ete-sias, ae, m., = ὁ ἐτησίας, Plin. 18, 34, 77, § 335.

etesius.full: ĕtēsius, a, um, adj., = ἐτήσιος, yearly. Prop.: flabra aquilonum = etesiae, Lucr. 5, 742; 6, 730 Munro ad loc.; cf. id. 6, 715 sqq.— Transf.: lapis, a kind of stone, Plin. 36, 22, 43, § 157.
etesius.short: ĕtēsius, a, um, adj., = ἐτήσιος, yearly.

ethecae.full: ethĕcae, ārum, f., = ἐκθέται, a gallery or portico, Vulg. Ezech. 41, 15.
ethecae.short: ethĕcae, ārum, f., = ἐκθέται, a gallery or portico, Vulg.

ethice.full: ēthĭcē, ēs, f., = ἠθική, moral philosophy, ethics, Quint. 2, 21, 3; 12, 2, 15; also ēthĭca, ae, f., Lact. 3, 13.
ethice.short: ēthĭcē, ēs, f., = ἠθική, moral philosophy, ethics, Quint.

ethicus.full: ēthĭcus, a, um, (scanned ĕthĭcīs, Prud. Hamart. 583), adj., = ἠθικός, moral, ethic (post-class.): res, ethics, Gell. 1, 2, 4: dictio, which shows the character, Sid. Ep. 8, 11.— Hence adv.: ēthĭcos = ἠθικῶς, morally: dicere, Sen. Contr. 2, 12, 8.

ethnicalis.full: ethnĭcālis, e, adj., heathenish, pagan: litterae, Tert. Spect. 5.
ethnicalis.short: ethnĭcālis, e, adj., heathenish, pagan: litterae, Tert.

ethnice.full: ethnĭcē, adv., v. the foll. fin.

ethnicus.full: ethnĭcus, a, um, adj., = ἐθνικός, heathenish, pagan; and subst.: ethni-cus, i, m., a heathen, Tert. Pud. 9; Vulg. Matt. 5, 47; 18, 17.—Adv.: ethnĭce, heathenishly: vivere, Tert. Pud. 9.
ethnicus.short: ethnĭcus, a, um, adj., = ἐθνικός, heathenish, pagan;

ethologia.full: ēthŏlŏgĭa, ae, f., = ἠθολογία, the art of depicting or imitating character, Quint. 1, 9, 3; Sen. Ep. 95, 66; Suet. Gramm. 4.
ethologia.short: ēthŏlŏgĭa, ae, f., = ἠθολογία, the art of depicting or imitating character, Quint.

ethologus.full: ēthŏlŏgus, i, m., = ἠθολόγος, one who jestingly imitates the manners, actions, gestures, etc., of others, a mimic: mimus, Cic. de Or. 2, 59, 242; 2, 60, 244.
ethologus.short: ēthŏlŏgus, i, m., = ἠθολόγος, one who jestingly imitates the manners, actions, gestures, etc., of others, a mimic: mimus, Cic.

ethopoeia.full: ēthŏpoeĭa, ae, f., = ἠθοποιΐα, rhet. t. t., an expression of character, Rutil. Lup. de Fig. 1, 21, p. 66 al.; cf. the foll. art., II.

ethos.full: ēthos, ĕos, n., = ἦθος. * Manners, morals, Sid. Carm. 15, 101.—* A depicting of character.—In acc. plur.: ethē, Plin. 35, 10, 36, § 98; in abl. plur.: in ethesin Terentius poscit palmam, Varr. ap. Non. 374, 9.

etiam.full: ĕtĭam, conj. [cf. Gr. ἔτι; with ending -am, as in quoniam, nunciam, etc.; cf. Brix ad Plaut. Trin. prol. 3], annexes a fact or thought to that which has already been said, and also, and furthermore, also, likewise, besides (syn. quoque). In gen.: hoc etiam ad malum accersebatur malum, Plaut. Bacch. 3, 3, 22; cf. Ter. And. 1, 3, 10; Cic. de Sen. 6, 16; id. N. D. 2, 52, 130: tute istic (dixisti) etiam astante hoc Sosia, Plaut. Am. 2, 2, 115: sed etiam est, paucis vos quod monitos voluerim, id. Cap

etiamdum.full: ĕtĭamdum (also written separately), hitherto, even till now, still, yet (rare; usually after a negative; cf.: etiamtum, etiamnum): dissimulabo, hos quasi non videam neque esse hic etiamdum sciam, Plaut. Mil. 4, 2, 2: nihil etiamdum harpagavit, id. Ps. 4, 2, 2; id. Truc. 1, 2, 72; id. Rud. 5, 3, 25: neque etiamdum scit pater, Ter. Heaut. 2, 1, 17: cum poteris igitur (veni), quoniam etiamdum abes, Cic. Att. 13, 31, 1 (cf. Hand Turs. II. p. 322 sq.; Krebs, Antibarb. p. 425 sq.).
etiamdum.short: ĕtĭamdum (also written separately), hitherto, even till now, still, yet (rare;

etiamnum.full: ĕtĭam-num and (more freq., always in Cic. and Caes.) ĕtĭam-nunc (also written separately, etiam num ... nunc), conj., yet, till now, still, even now, even to this time, even at this time. In gen. (in all periods): Ev. Etiamnunc mulier intu'st? Sy. Etiam, Plaut. Merc. 4, 5, 14; Varr. R. R. 3, 2, 3; Plaut. Stich. 5, 4, 16; Varr. ap. Non. 11, 15; Sen. Contr. 4, 26: de materia loquor orationis etiamnunc, non ipso de genere dicendi, Cic. Or. 34, 119: ut mihi permirum videatur quemquam exstare, qui et
etiamnum.short: ĕtĭam-num and (more freq., always in Cic.

etiamsi.full: ĕtĭam-si (also written separately), a concessive conditional particle, = καὶ εἰ, more emphatic than etsi, even if, although, albeit. With indic.: etiamsi alterum tantum perdundum est, Plaut. Ep. 3, 4, 81: etiamsi dudum fuerat ambiguum hoc mihi: Nunc non est, Ter. Hec. 4, 4, 26: ista veritas etiamsi jucunda non est, mihi tamen grata est, Cic. Att. 3, 24 fin.; so opp. tamen, id. Brut. 84, 290; Quint. 5, 10, 13; opp. certe, Cic. de Or. 1, 17 fin.; id. Opt. Gen. 2, 6; Liv. 40, 15, 15: eundem igitur
etiamsi.short: ĕtĭam-si (also written separately), a concessive conditional particle, = καὶ εἰ, more emphatic than etsi, even if, although, albeit.

etiamtum.full: ĕtĭam-tum and (more rarely) ĕtĭam-tunc, conj., even then, till that time, till then, still. With imperf. tense (so usually): omnes etiamtum retinebant illum Pericli sucum; sed erant paulo uberiore filo, Cic. de Or. 2, 22 fin.: etiamtum vita hominum sine cupiditate agitabatur, Sall. C. 2, 1; id. J. 63, 6: manebant etiamtum vestigia monentis libertatis, Tac. A. 1, 74: nam etiamtum Agricola Britanniam obtinebat, id. Agr. 39; Suet. Tib. 42; so with cum, while ... still: cum isti etiamtum de Sthenio
etiamtum.short: ĕtĭam-tum and (more rarely) ĕtĭam-tunc, conj., even then, till that time, till then, still.

etruria.full: Ē^trūrĭa (Het-), ae, f., a country of central Italy, Mel. 2, 4, 2; Plin. 3, 5, 8, § 50; Cic. Div. 1, 41, 92; id. Cat. 2, 3 fin.; Varr. L. L. 5, § 32 Müll.; Liv. 1, 35, 9; Verg. A. 8, 494; 12, 232 et saep.—Deriv., ē^truscus, a, um, adj., of Etruria, Etruscan: litus, Mel. 2, 7, 19; Hor. C. 1, 2, 14; id. C. Sec. 38; id. Epod. 16, 40: mare, id. C. 3, 29, 35: juga, Verg. A. 8, 480: duces, id. ib. 11, 598: manus Porsenae, Hor. Epod. 16, 4: disciplina, the Etruscan religion, Cic. Fam. 6, 6, 3; Plin. 2,
etruria.short: Ē^trūrĭa (Het-), ae, f., a country of central Italy, Mel.

etsi.full: et-si, conj. [et, II. H.], like etiamsi, a concessive conditional particle, though, although, albeit. Prop. With indic.: gaudeo, etsi nihil scio, quod gaudeam, Plaut. Capt. 4, 2, 62: etsi scio ego, Philumena, meum jus esse ... ego tamen, etc., Ter. Hec. 2, 2, 1: etsi abest maturitas aetatis, jam tamen personare aures ejus, etc., Cic. Fam. 6, 18, 3: ergo, etsi conferre manum pudor iraque monstrat, Obiciunt portas tamen, Verg. A. 9, 44 et saep.: vapulo hercle ego invitus tamen, Etsi malum merui, P

etymologia.full: ĕtўmŏlŏgĭa, ae, f., = ἐτυμολογία, etymology, Cic. Ac. 1, 8, 32; Quint. 1, 6, 1; 28; 7, 3, 25 et saep. (Cic. Top. 8, 35, written as Greek, and transl. by veriloquium).
etymologia.short: ĕtўmŏlŏgĭa, ae, f., = ἐτυμολογία, etymology, Cic.

etymologice.full: ĕtўmŏlŏgĭce, ēs, f., = ἐτυμολογική, etymology, Varr. L. L. 7, § 4 Müll. (ib. 7, § 109, written as Greek).
etymologice.short: ĕtўmŏlŏgĭce, ēs, f., = ἐτυμολογική, etymology, Varr.

etymologicus.full: ĕtўmŏlŏgĭcus, a, um, adj., = ἐτυμολογικός, etymological: ratio, Gell. 1, 18, 1.
etymologicus.short: ĕtўmŏlŏgĭcus, a, um, adj., = ἐτυμολογικός, etymological: ratio, Gell.

etymologos.full: ĕtўmŏlŏgos, i, m., = ἐτυμολόγος, an etymologist, Varr. L. L. 6, § 39 Müll.
etymologos.short: ĕtўmŏlŏgos, i, m., = ἐτυμολόγος, an etymologist, Varr.

etymon.full: ĕtўmon, i, n., = ἔτυμον, the origin of a word: etymon habere, to be derived, Varr. R. R. 1, 48, 2: etyma (with origines), Gell. 18, 4, 11 al.
etymon.short: ĕtўmon, i, n., = ἔτυμον, the origin of a word: etymon habere, to be derived, Varr.

eu.full: eu, interj., = εὖ, well! well done! bravo! an exclamation of joy or approbation, Plaut. Most. 1, 4, 26; Ter. Phorm. 3, 1, 14; Plaut. Mil. 4, 4, 10; Ter. Eun. 1, 2, 74; Hor. A. P. 328.—Esp.: Eu Hercle! Plaut. Men. 5, 1, 31; id. Rud. 3, 5, 41; id. Most. 3, 1, 58 al. Cf. Hand, Turs. II. p. 609 sq.; and see euge.
eu.short: eu, interj., = εὖ, well! well done! bravo! an exclamation of joy or approbation, Plaut.

euadne.full: Euadne (Euhadne, Evadne), ēs, f., = Εὐάδνη, wife of Capaneus, one of the "Seven before Thebes;" when her husband's body was burned, she threw herself on the pile, Prop. 3, 13, 24 (4, 12, 24 M.); 1, 15, 21; Verg. A. 6, 447; Ov. Tr. 4, 3, 64; Mart. 4, 75; Hyg. Fab. 243.— A nymph, daughter of Asopus, Ov. Am. 2, 21, 52.
euadne.short: Euadne (Euhadne, Evadne), ēs, f., = Εὐάδνη, wife of Capaneus, one of the "Seven before Thebes;" when her husband's body was burned, she threw herself on the pile, Prop.

euander.full: Euander (Gr. nom. -drus, Verg. A. 8, 100, 185 al.; voc. -dre, id. ib. 11, 55. Less correctly, Evander), dri, m., = Εὔανδρος. Son of Carmenta (v. Carmentis), born at Pallantium, in Arcadia; he emigrated to Italy sixty years before the Trojan war, and there founded the city Pallanteum, Liv. 1, 5; Ov. F. 1, 471; 497, 583; 2, 279; 4, 65; 5, 91; Verg. A. 8, 52; 119; 9, 9; 10, 515; Hor. S. 1, 3, 91.—Hence, Euandrĭ-us, a, um, adj., Evandrian: ensis, i. e. of Pallas, the son of Evander, Verg. A. 10, 394

euax.full: euax, interj. only Plautine, expressive of delight at some tidings or event, hail! joy! good! Plaut. Bacch. 2, 3, 13; 4, 4, 72; Cassiod. 4, 4, 13.

euboea.full: Euboea, ae, f., = Εὔβοια, an island in the Aegean Sea, separated from Boeotia by Euripus, now Negroponte, Mel. 2, 7, 9; Plin. 4, 12, 21, § 63; Ov. M. 13, 660 al.— Derivv. Eubŏĭcus, a, um, adj., Euboean: litus, Prop. 2, 26, 38 (3, 22, 18 M.); cf. cautes, i. e. the promontory Caphareus, Verg. A. 11, 260: sinus, Prop. 4 (5), 1, 114. undae, Ov. M. 9, 218: Anthedon, in Boeotia, opposite Euboea, id. 7, 232; 13, 905; cf.: cultor aquarum, i. e. Glaucus, from Anthedon, id. ib. 14, 4: urbs, i. e. Cumae, a
euboea.short: Euboea, ae, f., = Εὔβοια, an island in the Aegean Sea, separated from Boeotia by Euripus, now Negroponte, Mel.

eubolion.full: eubŏlĭon, ii, n., i. q. dictamnus, the plant dittany, App. Herb. 62.

eubuleus.full: Eubūleus, ei, m., one of the Anaces or Dioscuri, Cic. N. D. 3, 21, 53.
eubuleus.short: Eubūleus, ei, m., one of the Anaces or Dioscuri, Cic.

eubulidas.full: Eubūlĭdas, ae, m., a Greek proper name, Cic. Verr. 2, 3, 23 al.
eubulidas.short: Eubūlĭdas, ae, m., a Greek proper name, Cic.

euchadia.full: Euchadia, ae, f., a Greek proper name, Cic. Pis. 36, 89.
euchadia.short: Euchadia, ae, f., a Greek proper name, Cic.

eucharis.full: euchăris, is, adj., = εὔχαρις, agreeable, grateful, Vulg. Sir. 6, 5.
eucharis.short: euchăris, is, adj., = εὔχαρις, agreeable, grateful, Vulg.

eucharistia.full: euchăristĭa, ae, f., = εὐχαριστία. A thanksgiving, Tert. adv. Haer. 47.— The Lord's supper in the Christian Church, the eucharist, Cypr. Ep. 10.
