eucharisticon.full: euchăristĭcon, i, n., = εὐχαριστικόν, thanksgiving, Tert. Praescr. Haeret. 47; the name of a poem of thanks addressed by Statius to the Emperor Domitian, Stat. S. 4, 2.
eucharisticon.short: euchăristĭcon, i, n., = εὐχαριστικόν, thanksgiving, Tert.

euclides.full: Euclīdes, is, m., = Εὐκλείδης, a Greek proper name, Euclid. A philosopher of Megara, a disciple of Socrates and founder of the Megaric sect, Cic. Ac. 2, 42, 129; Gell. 6, 10, 10; Sid. Carm. 2, 176.— A mathematician in Alexandria under Ptolemy Philadelphus, Cic. de Or. 3, 33, 132.
euclides.short: Euclīdes, is, m., = Εὐκλείδης, a Greek proper name, Euclid.

eucnemos.full: eucnēmos, on, = εὔκνημος, with beautiful legs, Plin. 34, 8, 19, § 82.
eucnemos.short: eucnēmos, on, = εὔκνημος, with beautiful legs, Plin.

eudaemon.full: Eudaemon, ŏnis, com., = Εὐδαίμων (fortunate), the Greek appellation of the southern part of Arabia (Arabia Felix), Mel. 3, 8, 6; Plin. 6, 27, 31, § 138; Sol. 33, 4; and of its inhabitants, Vop. Aurel. 33; Capitol. Macr. 12.
eudaemon.short: Eudaemon, ŏnis, com., = Εὐδαίμων (fortunate), the Greek appellation of the southern part of Arabia (Arabia Felix), Mel.

eudemus.full: Eudēmus, i, m., = Εὔδημος, a Greek proper name, Cic. Div. 1, 25, 53.—Also a Greek physician, Tac. A. 4, 3 al.
eudemus.short: Eudēmus, i, m., = Εὔδημος, a Greek proper name, Cic.

eudiaeon.full: eudiaeon lineum filum, quod medici extremo in clysterio relinquunt, per quod κλυσμός emittitur, Paul. ex Fest. p. 78, 13 Müll.
eudiaeon.short: eudiaeon lineum filum, quod medici extremo in clysterio relinquunt, per quod κλυσμός emittitur, Paul.

eudoses.full: Eudoses, um, a tribe of Germany, mentioned only by Tac. G. 40.
eudoses.short: Eudoses, um, a tribe of Germany, mentioned only by Tac.

eudoxus.full: Eudoxus, i, m., = Εὔδοξος, a Greek astrologer, a disciple of Plato, Cic. Div. 2, 42, 87; id. Rep. 1, 14 al.
eudoxus.short: Eudoxus, i, m., = Εὔδοξος, a Greek astrologer, a disciple of Plato, Cic.

euenus.full: Euēnus (-nos, also Ēvēnus), i, m., = Εὔηνος, a king of Etolia, father of Marpessa; in despair at the loss of whom he threw himself into the river Lycormas, Hyg. Fab. 242; Prop. 1, 2, 18.— The river formerly called Lycormas, now the Fidari, Ov. H. 9, 141; id. M. 9, 104; Mel. 2, 3, 10; Plin. 4, 4, 5, § 11.—Deriv.. Euēnīnus, a, um, adj., of the river Evenus, Ov. M. 8, 528.
euenus.short: Euēnus (-nos, also Ēvēnus), i, m., = Εὔηνος, a king of Etolia, father of Marpessa;

euerganeus.full: euergănĕus, a, um, adj. εὐεργός, well-wrought, well-joined: trabes, Vitr. 5, 1, 9.

euethes.full: euēthes, is, adj., = εὐἡθης (good-natured, hence), simple, silly (pure Lat. stultus), Amm. 22, 8, 33.
euethes.short: euēthes, is, adj., = εὐἡθης (good-natured, hence), simple, silly (pure Lat.

eugalacton.full: eugălacton, i, n., = εὐγάλακτον, another name of the plant glaux, Plin. 27, 9, 58, § 82.
eugalacton.short: eugălacton, i, n., = εὐγάλακτον, another name of the plant glaux, Plin.

euganei.full: Eugănĕi, ōrum, m., a people of northern Italy, Plin. 3, 19, 23, § 130 sq.; Liv. 1, 1. —Hence, Eugăneus, a, um, adj., of the Euganei, Euganean: gentes, Plin. 3, 20, 24, § 133: lacus, Mart. 4, 25, 4: agna, Juv. 8, 15.
euganei.short: Eugănĕi, ōrum, m., a people of northern Italy, Plin.

euge.full: eugĕ (eugē or eugae, Ter. And. 2, 2, 8), interj., = εὖγε, an exclamation of joy, applause, admiration, etc., well done! good! bravo! (cf. eu; freq. in Plaut. and Ter., and in the Vulg.). In gen.: euge, euge, perbene, Ab saxo avortit fluctus ad litus scapham, Plaut. Rud. 1, 2, 75; id. Aul. 4, 6, 11; id. Ep. 3, 2, 21; id. Stich. 5, 6, 5; id. Mil. 4, 1, 20 et saep.; Ter. And. 2, 2, 8; id. Heaut. 4, 2, 10; Pers. 5, 167; 1, 75; as an indecl. subst., n.: euge tuum, id. 1, 50; Mart. 2, 27, 3: euge, wel

eugeneus.full: eugĕnēus or -īus, a, um, adj., = εὐγενής, well-born, i. e. noble, generous; applied to wine of good quality: (vinum), Cato R. R. 6, 4; Varr. R. R. 1, 25: (uvae), Col. 3, 2, 16.
eugeneus.short: eugĕnēus or -īus, a, um, adj., = εὐγενής, well-born, i.

euhan.full: Euhan (cf. Lach. ad Lucr. 5, 743; also, Euan, Prisc. 1, 29; not Evan, as in many edd.), m., = Εὐάν, a surname of Bacchus, Lucr. 5, 742; Ov. M. 4, 15; Mart. Cap. 8, § 804.—Hence, euhans, antis (cf. Gr. εὐάζων), adj., crying Euhan! an epithet of the Bacchantes, Cat. 64, 391; Sil. 1, 101; Prop. 2, 3, 18.—Poet. with acc.: euhantes orgia, celebrating the rites of Bacchus with the cry Euhan! Verg. A. 6, 517.

euhemerus.full: Euhēmĕrus, i, m., = Εὐήμερος, a Greek poet and philosopher, Cic. N. D. 1, 41, 119; Varr. R. R. 1, 48, 2; Lact. 1, 11, 33 al.
euhemerus.short: Euhēmĕrus, i, m., = Εὐήμερος, a Greek poet and philosopher, Cic.

euhius.full: Euhius (cf. Lach. ad Lucr. 5, 743; also, Euius; less correctly, as in some edd., Evius), ii, m., a surname of Bacchus, Lucr. 5, 742; Cic. Fl. 25, 60; Hor. C. 1, 18, 9; 2, 11, 17; Col. poët. 10, 424.—Acc. Euhion, Pers. 1, 102; Ov. A. A. 1, 563; voc. Euhie, Stat. Th. 2, 72; Col. poët. 10, 224.—Hence, Euhius (Evius), a, um, adj., of or belonging to Bacchus, Bacchic: terga, i. e. tympana, Stat. Ach. 2, 15.— Euhĭas, ădis, f., a Bacchante, Hor. C. 3, 25, 9.

euhoe.full: euhoe (dissyl.; also, euoe; less correctly, ēvoe; cf. Lach. ad Lucr. 5, 743), interj., = εὐοῖ, a shout of joy at the festivals of Bacchus: euhoe Bacche, Plaut. Men. 5, 2, 82; Ov. A. A. 1, 563; Cat. 64, 255; Verg. A. 7, 389; Hor. C. 2, 19, 5 and 7; cf.: euhan euhoe euhoe euhius, Enn. Tr. 150.

euhydrium.full: Euhȳdrĭum, ĭi, n., a city of Thessaly, Liv. 32, 13, 9.
euhydrium.short: Euhȳdrĭum, ĭi, n., a city of Thessaly, Liv.

eumaeus.full: Eumaeus, i, m., = Εὔμαιος, the swineherd of Ulysses in Homer, Varr. R. R. 2, 4, 1; Hyg. Fab. 126.
eumaeus.short: Eumaeus, i, m., = Εὔμαιος, the swineherd of Ulysses in Homer, Varr.

eumeces.full: eumēces, is, n., = εὐμῆκες (very long). A kind of balsam-tree, Plin. 12, 25, 54, § 114.— An unknown gem, Plin. 37, 10, 58, § 160.

eumedes.full: Eumēdes, is, m., = Εὐμήδης, a Trojan herald, father of Dolon, Ov. Tr. 3, 4, 27; Verg. A. 12, 346.
eumedes.short: Eumēdes, is, m., = Εὐμήδης, a Trojan herald, father of Dolon, Ov.

eumelus.full: Eumēlus, i, m., = Εὔμηλος. A king of Patrae, Ov. M. 7, 390.— A companion of Aeneas, Verg. A. 5, 665.

eumenes.full: Eumĕnes, is, m., = Εὐμένης, a famous general under Alexander the Great, and after his death governor of Cappadocia, Nep. Eum.; Just. 13, 4 sq.; Curt. 10, 4, 3.
eumenes.short: Eumĕnes, is, m., = Εὐμένης, a famous general under Alexander the Great, and after his death governor of Cappadocia, Nep.

eumenides.full: Eumĕnĭdes, um, f., = Εὐμενίδες (the benevolent, the gracious ones), a euphemistic name for the Furies, Cic. N. D. 3, 18, 46; Hor. C. 2, 13, 36; Verg. G. 1, 278; 4, 483; id. A. 4, 469 al.—In the sing.: Eumenis, a Fury, Sil. 2, 559; Stat. Th. 12, 423.
eumenides.short: Eumĕnĭdes, um, f., = Εὐμενίδες (the benevolent, the gracious ones), a euphemistic name for the Furies, Cic.

eumetria.full: eumē^trĭa, ae, f., = εὐμετρία, symmetry, Veg. Vet. 4, 2, 21.
eumetria.short: eumē^trĭa, ae, f., = εὐμετρία, symmetry, Veg.

eumitres.full: eumitres, ae, m., an unknown precious stone, Plin. 37, 10, 58, § 160.
eumitres.short: eumitres, ae, m., an unknown precious stone, Plin.

eumolpus.full: Eumolpus, i, m., = Εὔμολπος, a fabulous Thracian singer and priest of Ceres, who brought the Eleusinian mysteries and the culture of the vine to Attica, Plin. 7, 56, 57, § 199.—His descendant of the same name, the son of Musaeus, Ov. M. 11, 93.—A sacerdotal family in Athens also bore, after him, the name Eumolpĭdae, ārum, m., Εὐμολπίδαι, Cic. Leg. 2, 14, 35; Nep. Alc. 4 al.
eumolpus.short: Eumolpus, i, m., = Εὔμολπος, a fabulous Thracian singer and priest of Ceres, who brought the Eleusinian mysteries and the culture of the vine to Attica, Plin.

euneos.full: eunĕos, false reading for eureos, q. v.).
euneos.short: eunĕos, false reading for eureos, q.

eunuchinus.full: eunūchīnus, a, um, adj. eunuchus, of or belonging to a eunuch: facies, Hier. Ep. 22, 27.

eunuchion.full: eunūchĭon, ii, n., = εὐνούχιον, a kind of lettuce that subdues amatory desires, Plin. 19, 8, 38, § 127.
eunuchion.short: eunūchĭon, ii, n., = εὐνούχιον, a kind of lettuce that subdues amatory desires, Plin.

eunuchismus.full: eunūchismus, i, m., = εὐνουχισμός, an unmanning, Cael. Aur. Tard. 1, 4, 118.
eunuchismus.short: eunūchismus, i, m., = εὐνουχισμός, an unmanning, Cael.

eunuchizatus.full: eunūchīzātus, a, um, Part. [εὐνουχιζω], made a eunuch, mutilated, Hier. contr. Jov. 1, 7.

eunucho.full: eunūcho, āre, v. a. eunuchus, to make a eunuch of, to unman: se, Varr. ap. Non. 106, 8.

eunuchus.full: eunūchus, i, m., = εὐνοῦχος, a eunuch. Prop., Cic. Or. 70, 232; Mart. 3, 82; Juv. 6, 366; 378; 12, 35; Vulg. Gen. 37, 36 et saep.— (Sc. fabula.) Fem., the name of one of Terence's comedies.
eunuchus.short: eunūchus, i, m., = εὐνοῦχος, a eunuch.

euoe.full: euoe or euhoe, interj., v. euhoe.

euonymos.full: euōnўmos, i, f., = εὔωνυμος (of good, prosperous name), name of a tree (spindle-tree) in Lesbos, Plin. 13, 22, 38, § 118.
euonymos.short: euōnўmos, i, f., = εὔωνυμος (of good, prosperous name), name of a tree (spindle-tree) in Lesbos, Plin.

eupalium.full: Eupălium, ii, n., = Εὐπάλιον, a city of western Locris, Liv. 28, 8.—The same called Eupalia, Plin. 4, 3, 4, § 7.
eupalium.short: Eupălium, ii, n., = Εὐπάλιον, a city of western Locris, Liv.

eupator.full: Eupător, ŏris, m., = Εὐπάτωρ, a surname of Mithridates, king of Pontus, Plin. 33, 12, 54, § 151.
eupator.short: Eupător, ŏris, m., = Εὐπάτωρ, a surname of Mithridates, king of Pontus, Plin.

eupatoria.full: eupătŏrĭa, ae, f., = εὐπατορία, a plant, called also agrimonia, agrimony, Plin. 25, 6, 29, § 56.
eupatoria.short: eupătŏrĭa, ae, f., = εὐπατορία, a plant, called also agrimonia, agrimony, Plin.

eupelios.full: eupĕlĭos, i, f., = εὐπέλιος, a plant, called also daphnoides, App. Herb. 58; see the foll. art.
eupelios.short: eupĕlĭos, i, f., = εὐπέλιος, a plant, called also daphnoides, App.

eupetalos.full: eupĕtălos, i, f., = εὐπέταλος, an unknown precious stone, perh. the opal, Plin. 37, 10, 56, § 161.
eupetalos.short: eupĕtălos, i, f., = εὐπέταλος, an unknown precious stone, perh.

euphonia.full: euphōnia, ae, f., = εὐφωνία, euphony, Donat. p. 1751 P.
euphonia.short: euphōnia, ae, f., = εὐφωνία, euphony, Donat.

euphorbea.short: euphorbĕa, ae, f., an African plant, Plin.

euphorbus.full: Euphorbus, i, m., = Εὔφορβος. Son of Panthus, a brave Trojan, whose soul Pythagoras asserted had descended to himself, through the process of transmigration, Ov. M. 15, 161; Gell. 4, 11 fin.— A celebrated Greek physician, after whom was named the plant euphorbea; cf. Plin. 5, 1, 1, § 16.

euphorio.full: Euphŏrĭo and -on, ōnis, m., = Εὐφορίων, a grammarian and poet, born at Chalcis, in Euboea, who flourished in the time of Ptolemy Euergetes, Varr. R. R. 41, 9; Cic. Div. 2, 64, 132; id. Tusc. 3, 19, 45; Quint. 10, 1, 56; Suet. Tib. 70 al.
euphorio.short: Euphŏrĭo and -on, ōnis, m., = Εὐφορίων, a grammarian and poet, born at Chalcis, in Euboea, who flourished in the time of Ptolemy Euergetes, Varr.

euphranor.full: Euphrānor, ŏris, m., = Εὐφράνωρ. A celebrated painter and sculptor, a contemporary of Praxiteles, Quint. 12, 10, 6; 12; Plin. 34, 8, 19, § 50; 35, 11, 40, § 128; Juv. 3, 217.— An architect, Vitr. 7, 14.

euphrates.full: Euphrātes (in Inscr. also EVFRATES), is, m., = Εὐφράτης, A wellknown river in Syria, which rises in Armenia, and, after its junction with the Tigris, empties into the Persian Gulf, now Frat, Mel. 1, 11, 2; 3, 8, 5; Plin. 5, 24, 20, § 83 sqq.; Prud. Ham. 562; Cic. N. D. 2, 52, 130; Plin. Pan. 14; abl. Euphratē, Luc. 8, 358.— Meton., the dwellers on its banks, Verg. G. 1, 509.—Hence, Euphrā-taeus, a, um, = Εὐφραταῖος, of the Euphrates, i. e. Armenian: diademata, Stat. S. 2, 2, 122.— Euphrātis, ĭdi

euphrone.full: euphrŏne, es, f., = εὐφρόνη (the propitious), euphemism for night: ut euethen Graeci dicimus stultum, et noctem euphronen, et furias Eumenidas, Amm. 22, 8, 33; cf. Lidd. and Scott, s. v. εὐφρόνη.
euphrone.short: euphrŏne, es, f., = εὐφρόνη (the propitious), euphemism for night: ut euethen Graeci dicimus stultum, et noctem euphronen, et furias Eumenidas, Amm.

euphrosyne.full: Euphrŏsўne, es, f., = Εὐφροσύνη, one of the graces, Sen. Ben. 1, 3, 6.
euphrosyne.short: Euphrŏsўne, es, f., = Εὐφροσύνη, one of the graces, Sen.

euphrosynum.full: euphrŏsўnum or -on, i, n., = εὐφρόσυνον, a plant, called also buglossos, Plin. 25, 8, 40, § 81.
euphrosynum.short: euphrŏsўnum or -on, i, n., = εὐφρόσυνον, a plant, called also buglossos, Plin.

euplia.full: euplia, ae, f., an unknown plant, Plin. 25, 10, 81, § 130.
euplia.short: euplia, ae, f., an unknown plant, Plin.

euplocamus.full: euplŏcămus, i, m., = εὐπλόκαμος, having beautiful locks, Lucil. ap. Non. 35, 31.
euplocamus.short: euplŏcămus, i, m., = εὐπλόκαμος, having beautiful locks, Lucil.

eupolemus.full: Eupŏlĕmus, i, m., = Εὐπόλεμος, a Greek proper name, Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 22.
eupolemus.short: Eupŏlĕmus, i, m., = Εὐπόλεμος, a Greek proper name, Cic.

eupolis.full: Eupŏlis, ĭdis, m., = Εὔπολις, a celebrated comic poet in Athens, contemporary with Aristophanes, Hor. S. 1, 4, 1; Vell. 1, 16; Quint. 1, 10, 18; 10, 1, 66; 12, 10, 65 al.; acc. Eupolin, Hor. S. 2, 3, 12: Eupolidem, Pers. 1, 124; Cic. Brut. 9, 15.
eupolis.short: Eupŏlis, ĭdis, m., = Εὔπολις, a celebrated comic poet in Athens, contemporary with Aristophanes, Hor.

eupteron.full: euptĕron, i, n., = εὔπτερον, a plant, called also polytrichon, App. Herb. 51.
eupteron.short: euptĕron, i, n., = εὔπτερον, a plant, called also polytrichon, App.

eureos.full: eurĕos, i, m., an unknown precious stone, Plin. 37, 10, 58, § 161.
eureos.short: eurĕos, i, m., an unknown precious stone, Plin.

eurinus.full: eurĭnus, i, m., = εὔρινος: ventus, an east wind, Col. 11, 2, 14.
eurinus.short: eurĭnus, i, m., = εὔρινος: ventus, an east wind, Col.

euripice.full: eurĭpĭce, ēs, f., = εὐριπική, a kind of rush, Plin. 21, 18, 71, § 119.
euripice.short: eurĭpĭce, ēs, f., = εὐριπική, a kind of rush, Plin.

euripides.full: Eurīpĭdes, is, m., = Εὐριπίδης, a celebrated Athenian tragic poet, Quint. 10, 1, 67 sq.; Gell. 15, 20; dat. Euripidae, id. 7, 3 med.; Cic. Tusc. 1, 26 fin.; 1, 48; 3, 14 et saep.—Hence, Eurīpĭdēus, a, um, adj., of Euripides: carmen, Cic. Tusc. 3, 25.
euripides.short: Eurīpĭdes, is, m., = Εὐριπίδης, a celebrated Athenian tragic poet, Quint.

euripus.full: eurīpus (-os), i, m., = εὔριπος, a narrow channel, strait. Prop. In gen., Cic. Mur. 17; Plin. 6, 23, 26, § 99; 2, 97, 100, § 219.— In partic.: Eurīpus, i, m., = Εὔριπος, the channel between Boeotia and Euboea, now Egripo, Mel. 2, 7, 9; Plin. 4, 12, 21, § 63; Cic. N. D. 3, 10, 24; Liv. 28, 6; 31, 24; Luc. 5, 235 al.— Transf., a canal, conduit, aqueduct. In gen.: ductus aquarum, quos isti nilos et euripos vocant, Cic. Leg. 2, 1, 2; Vitr. 7, 5; Front. Aquaed. 84; Sen. Ep. 83; Plin. 5, 10, 11, § 63;
euripus.short: eurīpus (-os), i, m., = εὔριπος, a narrow channel, strait.

euroaquilo.full: eurŏ-ăquĭlo, ōnis, m., the northeast wind, Vulg. Act. Apost. 27, 14; cf. the foll. two articles.
euroaquilo.short: eurŏ-ăquĭlo, ōnis, m., the northeast wind, Vulg.

euroauster.full: eurŏ-auster dictus, quod ex una parte habeat Eurum, ab altera Austrum, Isid. Orig. 13, 11, 6.
euroauster.short: eurŏ-auster dictus, quod ex una parte habeat Eurum, ab altera Austrum, Isid.

euronotus.full: eurŏ-nŏtus, i, m., = εὐρόνοτος, the south-southeast wind, that which is between eurus and notus, Col. 11, 2, 42; Plin. 2, 47, 46, § 120; Vitr. 1, 6.
euronotus.short: eurŏ-nŏtus, i, m., = εὐρόνοτος, the south-southeast wind, that which is between eurus and notus, Col.

europa.full: Eurōpa, ae, and Eurōpe, ēs, f., = Εὐρώπη. Daughter of the Phoenician king Agenor, sister of Cadmus, and mother of Sarpedon and Minos by Jupiter, who, under the form of a bull, carried her off to Crete, Ov. M. 2, 836 sq.; Hyg. Fab. 155; 178; nom. Europe, Hor. C. 3, 27, 25; 57; Prop. 2, 28, 52; gen. Europae, Mel. 2, 7, 12; acc. Europen, Ov. A. A. 1, 323; Juv. 8, 34: Europam, Varr. R. R. 2, 5, 5; Ov. H. 4, 55.— Poet. transf., the portico in the Field of Mars, which was adorned with a painting repre
europa.short: Eurōpa, ae, and Eurōpe, ēs, f., = Εὐρώπη.

eurotas.full: Eurōtas, ae, m., = Εὐρώτας, the principal river of Laconia, on the banks of which Sparta stood, now Basilipotamo, Mel. 2, 3, 9; Plin. 4, 5, 8, § 16; Cic. Inv. 2, 21, 96; id. Tusc. 5, 34, 98; Ov. M. 2, 247; id. Am. 2, 17, 32 et saep.; nom. Eurōta, Cic. poët. Tusc. 2, 15 fin.; acc. Eurotan, Ov. M. 10, 169.
eurotas.short: Eurōtas, ae, m., = Εὐρώτας, the principal river of Laconia, on the banks of which Sparta stood, now Basilipotamo, Mel.

eurotias.full: eurōtĭas, ae, m., = εὐρωτίας, an unknown precious stone, Plin. 37, 10, 58, § 161.
eurotias.short: eurōtĭas, ae, m., = εὐρωτίας, an unknown precious stone, Plin.

eurous.full: eurōus, a, um, adj. eurus; cf.: arctous, Lesbous, eastern, orient: fluctus, Verg. A. 3, 533.

eurus.full: eurus, i, m., = εὖρος, the southeast wind (pure Lat. Vulturnus), Col. 11, 2, 65; 5, 5, 15; Sen. Q. N. 5, 16; Plin. 2, 47, 46, § 119; Gell. 2, 22, 7 sq.; Vitr. 1, 6; Hor. C 1, 28, 25; 2, 16, 24 al.—In plur., Verg. G. 2, 339; 441; Ov. H. 11, 9 al.— Transf. The east wind, Ov. Tr. 1, 2, 27 (opp. Zephyrus); id. M. 1, 61; Manil. 4, 589.— Hence, Poet., the east, Val. Fl. 1, 539; Claud. Laud. Stil. 2, 417.— Wind, in gen., Verg. G. 3, 382.
eurus.short: eurus, i, m., = εὖρος, the southeast wind (pure Lat.

euryalus1.full: Eurўālus, i, m., = Εὐρύηλος, a hill near Syracuse, Liv. 25, 25.
euryalus1.short: Eurўālus, i, m., = Εὐρύηλος, a hill near Syracuse, Liv.

euryalus2.full: Eurўălus, i, m., = Εὐρύαλος. A friend of Nisus, Verg. A. 5, 294; 9, 179 sq.; Ov. Tr. 1, 5, 23.— A king of Thessaly, Ov. Ib. 289.

eurydamas.full: Eurўdămas, antis, m., = εὐρυδάμας (the wide-ruling), a surname of Hector, Ov. H. 329.
eurydamas.short: Eurўdămas, antis, m., = εὐρυδάμας (the wide-ruling), a surname of Hector, Ov.

eurydica.full: Eurўdĭca, ae, f., = Εὐρυδίκη, the name of a slave of Rhea Sylvia; Euridica, Enn. ap. Cic. Div. 1, 20.
eurydica.short: Eurўdĭca, ae, f., = Εὐρυδίκη, the name of a slave of Rhea Sylvia;

eurydice.full: Eurўdĭce, ēs, f., = Εὐρυδίκη. The wife of Orpheus, who died of the bite of a serpent. Orpheus obtained from Pluto permission to bring her back from the Lower World, under promise that he would not look back at her on the way. But, as he did not keep this promise, she returned to the Lower World, Ov. M. 10, 31 sq.; Verg. G. 4, 486 sqq.; Hyg. Fab. 164.— Daughter of Danaüs, Hyg. Fab. 170.

eurylochus.full: Eurўlŏchus, i, m., = Εὐρύλοχος, the only one of the companions of Ulysses who withstood Circe's magic cup, Ov. M. 14, 252; 287.
eurylochus.short: Eurўlŏchus, i, m., = Εὐρύλοχος, the only one of the companions of Ulysses who withstood Circe's magic cup, Ov.

eurymedon.full: Eurўmĕdon, ontis, m., = Εὐρυμέδων. A river of Pamphylia, Liv. 33, 41; 37, 23; Mel. 1, 14, 1; Avien. Descr. Orb. 1015.— An Athenian general in the Peloponnesian war, Just. 4, 4, 11; 4, 5, 7.— A son of Faunus, Stat. Th. 11, 32.

eurymenae.full: Eurўmĕnae, ārum, f., = Εὐρυμεναί, a city of Thessaly, Liv. 39, 25 al.; Val. Fl. 2, 14.
eurymenae.short: Eurўmĕnae, ārum, f., = Εὐρυμεναί, a city of Thessaly, Liv.

eurymus.full: Eurўmus, i, m., = Εὔρυμος, a seer, father of the seer Telemus, Hyg. Fab. 125 and 128.—Whence, Eurўmĭdes, ae, m., the surname of Telemus, Ov. M. 13, 771.
eurymus.short: Eurўmus, i, m., = Εὔρυμος, a seer, father of the seer Telemus, Hyg.

eurynome.full: Eurўnŏme, ēs, f., = Εὐρυνόμη, daughter of Oceanus and Tethys, mother of Leucothoë, Ov. M. 4, 210 sq.
eurynome.short: Eurўnŏme, ēs, f., = Εὐρυνόμη, daughter of Oceanus and Tethys, mother of Leucothoë, Ov.

eurypylus.full: Eurўpўlus, i, m., = Εὐρύπυλος. Son of Hercules and king of the island of Cos, Ov. M. 7, 363.—Hence, Eurўpў-lis, ĭdis, f., adj., Eurypylan, poet. i. q. Coan: textura, Prop. 4 (5), 5, 23.— Son of Euaemon of Thessaly, and leader of a body of troops before Troy, Ov. M. 13, 357; Verg. A. 2, 114; Hyg. Fab. 97; Cic. Tusc. 2, 16, 38.

eurysthenes.full: Eurysthĕnes, is, m., = Εὐρυσθένης, son of Aristodemus, king of Sparta, brother of Procles, Nep. Ages. 1, 2; Cic. Div. 2, 43, 191.
eurysthenes.short: Eurysthĕnes, is, m., = Εὐρυσθένης, son of Aristodemus, king of Sparta, brother of Procles, Nep.

eurystheus.full: Eurystheus (trisyl.), ei, m., = Εὐρυσθεύς, son of Sthenelus and grandson of Perseus, a king of Mycenae, who, at the command of Juno, imposed upon Hercules his famous twelve labors, Cic. Tusc. 2, 8, 20; Ov. H. 9, 7; 45; id. M. 9, 203; 274; Hyg. Fab. 30; acc. Eurysthea, Verg. G. 3, 4.— Hence, Eurysthēus, a, um, adj., Eurysthean, Stat. Th. 4, 304.
eurystheus.short: Eurystheus (trisyl.), ei, m., = Εὐρυσθεύς, son of Sthenelus and grandson of Perseus, a king of Mycenae, who, at the command of Juno, imposed upon Hercules his famous twelve labors, Cic.

eurythmia.full: eurythmĭa, ae, f., = εὐρυθμία, in architect., beautiful arrangement, proportion, harmony of the parts, Vitr. 1, 2; 6, 2.
eurythmia.short: eurythmĭa, ae, f., = εὐρυθμία, in architect., beautiful arrangement, proportion, harmony of the parts, Vitr.

eurytus.full: Eurўtus, i, m., = Εὔρυτος. King of Oechalia and father of Iole, Ov. M. 9, 356.—Whence Iole is called Eurўtis, ĭdis, f., Ov. M. 9, 395; id. H. 9, 133.— A centaur, Ov. M. 12, 220.—Also called Eurўtĭon, ōnis, m., Ov. A. A. 1, 593 (cf. Hom. Od. 21, 285).— An Argonaut, Val. Fl. 1, 439 al.

euscheme.full: euschēmē, adv., = εὐσχήμως, becomingly, gracefully, handsomely, Plaut. Mil. 2, 2, 58; id. Trin. 3, 1, 24.
euscheme.short: euschēmē, adv., = εὐσχήμως, becomingly, gracefully, handsomely, Plaut.

eusebes1.full: eusĕbes, is, n., = εὐσεβές, an unknown precious stone, Plin. 37, 10, 58, § 161.
eusebes1.short: eusĕbes, is, n., = εὐσεβές, an unknown precious stone, Plin.

eusebes2.full: Eusĕbes, is, m., = Εὐσεβής, a surname of Ariobarzanes, Cic. Fam. 15, 2.
eusebes2.short: Eusĕbes, is, m., = Εὐσεβής, a surname of Ariobarzanes, Cic.

eusebius.full: Eusĕbĭus, ii, m., a Latin rhetorician, Rufin. p. 191 Bait.
eusebius.short: Eusĕbĭus, ii, m., a Latin rhetorician, Rufin.

eustomachus.full: eustŏmăchus, a, um, adj., = εὐστόμαχος, good for digesting, Gargil. 1, 3; Theod. Prisc. 7.
eustomachus.short: eustŏmăchus, a, um, adj., = εὐστόμαχος, good for digesting, Gargil.

eustylos.full: eustȳlos, on, adj., = εὔστυλος, with pillars evenly arranged, Vitr. 3, 2.
eustylos.short: eustȳlos, on, adj., = εὔστυλος, with pillars evenly arranged, Vitr.

euterpe.full: Euterpe, ēs, f., = Εὐτέρπη, the muse of music, Hor. C. 1, 1, 33; Aus. Idyll. 20, 4.
euterpe.short: Euterpe, ēs, f., = Εὐτέρπη, the muse of music, Hor.

euthalos.full: euthalos, i, f., a kind of laurel, also called daphnoides, Plin. 15, 30, 39, § 132 (al. eupetalos).
euthalos.short: euthalos, i, f., a kind of laurel, also called daphnoides, Plin.

eutheriston.full: euthĕriston, i, n., = εὐθέριστον, a balsam-tree, Plin. 12, 25, 54, § 114.
eutheriston.short: euthĕriston, i, n., = εὐθέριστον, a balsam-tree, Plin.

euthia.full: euthīa, ae, f., = εὐθεῖα, a straight line, Mart. Cap. 9, § 958.
euthia.short: euthīa, ae, f., = εὐθεῖα, a straight line, Mart.

euthygrammum.full: euthygrammum, i, n., = εὐθύγραμμον, an architect's rule, Vitr. 1, 1.
euthygrammum.short: euthygrammum, i, n., = εὐθύγραμμον, an architect's rule, Vitr.

eutrapelus.full: Eutrăpĕlus, i, m., = Εὐτράπελος (witty), a surname given to P. Volumnius, a friend of Marc Antony, Cic. Att. 15, 8, 1; Hor. Ep. 1, 18, 31 al.
eutrapelus.short: Eutrăpĕlus, i, m., = Εὐτράπελος (witty), a surname given to P.

eutropius.full: Eutrŏpĭus, ii, m., Flavius, a Roman historian in the middle of the fourth century of the Christian era, contemporary with the Emperor Julian, and author of a Breviarium Historiae Romanae, Amm. 29, 1, 36; Greg. Naz. Ep. 137 sq.; Symm. Ep. 3, 46 sqq.; cf. Teuffel, Roem. Liter. 936.
eutropius.short: Eutrŏpĭus, ii, m., Flavius, a Roman historian in the middle of the fourth century of the Christian era, contemporary with the Emperor Julian, and author of a Breviarium Historiae Romanae, Amm.

euxinus.full: Euxīnus, a, um, adj., = Εὔξεινος (hospitable), an epithet of the Black Sea. Usually connected with Pontus. In Ovid also freq.: Euxinum mare, Ov. Tr. 4, 8, 42; 4, 10, 97; 5, 10, 2; id. Pont. 4, 6, 46; cf. aequor, id. Tr. 5, 2, 63: aquae, id. Pont. 2, 6, 2: fretum, id. ib. 2, 2, 2: undae, id. ib. 4, 8, 1: vada, id. ib. 4, 9, 2: litus, id. Tr. 5, 10, 13; id. Pont. 4, 3, 51.—And absol.: Euxīnus, i, m. (sc. Pontus), Ov. Tr. 2, 197; 4, 1, 60.
euxinus.short: Euxīnus, a, um, adj., = Εὔξεινος (hospitable), an epithet of the Black Sea.

euzomon.full: euzōmon, i, n., = εὔζωμον, a sort of cabbage (pure Lat. eruca), Plin. 20, 13, 49, § 126.
euzomon.short: euzōmon, i, n., = εὔζωμον, a sort of cabbage (pure Lat.

eva.full: Ēva (Hēva, Vulg. Gen. 4, 1; id. 2 Cor. 11, 3 al.), ae, f., Eve, the first woman, Tert. Virg. vel. 5; Prud. Hamort. 741.

evacuatio.full: ēvăcŭātĭo, ōnis, f. evacuo, an evacuating; trop., a weakening: fidei, Tert. adv. Marc. 4, 24.

evacuo.full: ē-văcŭo, no perf., ātum, 1, v. a., to empty out, evacuate (post-Aug.). Lit.: alvum, Plin. 20, 6, 23, § 52; 32, 9, 33, § 104. — Trop. To rid one's self of, lay aside: quae pueruli erant, Vulg. 1 Cor. 13, 11.— To make void, cancel: obligationem, Cod. Just. 8, 43, 4; Vulg. 1 Cor. 1, 17.

evado.full: ē-vādo, si, sum, 3 (perf. sync. evasti, Hor. S. 2, 7, 68; Sil. 15, 796; perf. evadi. Treb. Poll. Trig. Tyr. 5, 6), v. n. and a. Neutr., to go or come out, go forth (freq. and class.). Lit. In gen.: si (apes) ex alvo minus frequentes evadunt, Varr. R. R. 3, 16, 36: ex aqua, Plaut. Rud. 1, 2, 86: ex balineis, Cic. Cael. 27, 65: oppido, Sall. J. 56, 5: undis, Verg. A. 9, 99: puteo, Phaedr. 4, 9, 11: abiit, excessit, evasit, erupit, Cic. Cat. 2, 1: per praeruptum saxum in Capitolium, Liv. 5, 46: in

evagatio.full: ēvăgātĭo, ōnis, f. evagor, a wandering, straying: stellarum, Plin. 2, 17, 14, § 72; Sen. Ep. 65, 17.

evaginatio.full: ē-vāgīnātĭo, ōnis, f. evagino, a spreading out, extending, Arn. 1, 50 Orell.

evagino.full: ē-vāgīno, no perf., ātum, 1, v. a. vagina, to draw out of the scabbard, to unsheath (post-class.): gladio sua sponte evaginato, Just. 1, 9, 8; Hyg. Fab. 164; Vulg. Exod. 15, 10: pugionem, id. Judith, 13, 9.

evago.full: ē-văgo, 1, v. n. collat. form of depon. evagor, q. v.: Famae nam nobilitas late ex stirpe praeclara evagat, Att. ap. Non. 467, 28 (Rib. Fragm. Trag. p. 219).

evagor.full: ē-văgor, ātus, 1, v. dep. n. and a. Neutr., to wander forth, to roam about; to scatter or spread about, to extend (class.). Lit.: ne longius evagatae (incubantes gallinae) refrigerent ova, Col. 8, 5, 14: cappari evagatur per agros, Plin. 19, 8, 48, § 163: Nilus, id. 10, 33, 49, § 94: ignis ulterius, Dig. 9, 2, 30, § 3.— In milit. lang., to march to and fro, make evolutions, manœuvre: nullo ad evagandum relicto spatio, Liv. 22, 47, 3; 23, 47, 5.— Trop., to spread, extend, digress: qui appetitus l

evalesco.full: ē-vălesco, lŭi, 3, v. inch. n., to become strong, increase in strength, to increase, grow (cf.: vix illa, quae παραγόμενα vocant, nobis permittimus, sed hoc feliciter, evaluit, Quint. 8, 6, 32; not ante-Aug.). Lit.: cum evaluissent flagella pedes binos, Plin. 17, 15, 25, § 116; cf. rami, id. 16, 30, 54, § 125.— Trop. In gen.: adjuta cura natura magis evalescit, Quint. 2, 8, 5; Tac. A. 14, 58 fin.: affectatio quietis in tumultum evaluit, strengthened into, etc., id. H. 1, 80: indoles naturalis, a

evallo1.full: ē-vallo, āvi, 1, v. a. vallum, to cast out (only in the foll. passages): nos foras, Varr. ap. Non. 102, 6: aliquem, Titin. ib. 5 (Rib. Com. Fragm. p. 144).

evallo2.full: ē-vallo, ĕre, v. a. 2. vallus, to winnow out, to cleanse from the husks, to husk, to hull, Plin. 18, 10, 23, §§ 97 and 99.

evanesco.full: ē-vānesco, nŭi, 3 (part. fut. evaniturus, Lact. 5, 4 fin.), v. inch. n., to vanish or pass away, to die away, to disappear (class.). Lit. In gen.: Bacchi cum flos evanuit (with diffugere in auras), Lucr. 3, 222: evanescere paulatim et decrescere pondus, id. 5, 536: evanescere stinguique colorem, id. 2, 828: pruna, Varr. R. R. 2, 4, 6: aquae, to evaporate, Sen. Q. N. 3, 24; cf.: vinum et salsamentum vetustate, i. e. to lose its strength, become vapid, Cic. Div. 2, 57: cornuaque extremae velut eva

evangelicus.full: ēvangĕlĭcus (eua-), a, um, adj., = εὐαγγελικός, evangelical: scriptura, Tert. adv. Marc. 39: vox, Prud. Apoth. 495 et saep.
evangelicus.short: ēvangĕlĭcus (eua-), a, um, adj., = εὐαγγελικός, evangelical: scriptura, Tert.

evangelista.full: ēvangĕlista (eua-), ae, m., = εὐαγγελιστής, an evangelist, Prud. Cathem. 6, 77 et saep.; Vulg. Act. 21, 8.
evangelista.short: ēvangĕlista (eua-), ae, m., = εὐαγγελιστής, an evangelist, Prud.

evangelium.full: ēvangĕlĭum (eua-), ii, n., = εὐαγγέλιον. Good news, Cic. Att. 2, 3, 1, written as Greek, εὐαγγέλια.— The Gospel (eccl. Lat.), Vulg. Matt. 4, 23 et saep.

evangelizator.full: ēvangĕlīzātor (eua-), ōris, m. evangelium, a preacher of the Gospel, Tert. Cor. Mil. 9; id. Praescr. 4.

evangelizo.full: ēvangĕlīzo (eua-), āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. and n., = εὐαγγελίζω (eccl. Lat.). Act., to preach, declare, proclaim, always with the accessory notion of bringing good tidings, proclaiming the Gospel: vobis gaudium magnum, Vulg. Luc. 2, 10: Christum Iesum, id. Act. 5, 42.—Pass., Vulg. Luc. 16, 16; id. Gal. 1, 11.— To evangelize, to win to the Gospel by preaching, to preach to: Sion, Vulg. Isa. 40, 9.—Pass.: pauperes evangelizantur, Vulg. Matt. 11, 5 al.— Neutr., to preach, proclaim the Gospel, Vulg. Psa

evanidus.full: ēvānĭdus, a, um, adj. evanesco, vanishing, passing away (not ante-Aug., and very rare). Lit.: pectora, Ov. M. 5, 435: oleae, i. e. frail, without strength, Col. Arb. 17, 3; cf. arbores, Vitr. 2, 10: materia vetustate, id. 2, 8: evanida et siticulosa calx, id. 7, 2; and, viriditas, Plin. 37, 5, 18, § 70.— Trop.: amor, Ov. R. Am. 653: gaudium (with leve), Sen. Ep. 35.

evanno.full: ē-vanno, ĕre, v. a. vannus, to cast out the chaff of grain from the fan, to winnow. * Lit.: acus, Varr. R. R. 1, 52 fin.—* Transf., to cast out: aliquem, Pompon. ap. Non. 19, 23 (Rib. Com. Fragm. p. 239).

evaporatio.full: ēvăpōrātĭo, ōnis, f. evaporo, an evaporating, evaporation: terrae, Sen. Q. N. 1, 1, 6; 6, 13, 1: nivis, Gell. 19, 5, 6.

evaporativus.full: ēvăpōrātīvus, a, um, adj. id., evaporating, apt to evaporate: virtus, Cael. Aur. Acut. 3, 8, 83.

evaporo.full: ē-văpōro, āre, v. a., to disperse in vapor, to evaporate (post-class.), Gell. 19, 5, 7 and 8; Tert. Pall. 6 fin.

evasio.full: ēvāsĭo, ōnis, f. evado, a going out, Vulg. Judith, 12, 20.

evasto.full: ē-vasto, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a., to lay utterly waste, to devastate (a favorite word of Livy; elsewh. very rare): omnia, Liv. 10, 15; 5, 5; 8, 37; 28, 44; 32, 33, 14 Drak. et saep.; Vop. Aurel. 15; Sil. 15, 185.

evectio.full: ēvectĭo, ōnis, f. eveho. * A going upwards, flying up, flight: sublimis, App. M. 5, p. 169.— In jurid. lang., a permit to travel by the public post, a post-warrant, Cod. Just. 12, 51, 3 sq.; Symm. Ep. 4, 6; Aug. Ep. 55.

evectus1.full: ēvectus, a, um, Part., v. eveho.

evectus2.full: ēvectus, ūs, m. eveho, a carrying out, exporting of goods from a place, Varr. R. R. 1, 16, 2 Schneid. N. cr.; Plin. 18, 5, 6, § 28.

eveho.full: ē-vĕho, xi, ctum, 3, v. a., to carry out or forth, to convey out, lead forth (rare but class.). Lit.: omnia (signa) ex fanis, ex locis publicis palam plaustris evecta exportataque esse, Cic. Verr. 2, 1, 20: aquas ex planis locis, Liv. 1, 38 fin.; cf. Plin. 2, 103, 106, § 224: stercus (with exportare), Cato R. R. 5, 8: merces (opp. inveho), Varr. R. R. 1, 16, 6; Dig. 10, 4, 5 et saep.: incaute se evehentes Masinissa excipiebat, throwing themselves out, rushing out, Liv. 29, 34: naves in altum, id

evelatum.full: ēvēlātum eventilatum, unde velabra, quibus frumenta ventilantur, Paul. ex Fest. p. 77, 15 Müll.
evelatum.short: ēvēlātum eventilatum, unde velabra, quibus frumenta ventilantur, Paul.

evello.full: ē-vello, velli (Cic. Sest. 28; id. de Or. 1, 53 fin.), post-class., vulsi (Flor. 4, 12, 38; Sen. ad Marc. Consol. 16, 7 al.), vulsum, 3, v. a., to tear, pull, or pluck out (class.). Lit.: linguam se evellisse M. Catoni, Cic. Sest. 28: ferrum, * Caes. B. G. 1, 25, 3: arborem, Liv. 33, 5: dentes, Plin. 30, 3, 8, § 25 et saep.: spinas agro, Hor. Ep. 1, 14, 5; cf.: ebulum, cicutam e segete, Plin. 17, 9, 6 § 55: clavos sepulcris, id. 34, 15, 44, § 151: statuam de monumento, Dig. 47, 12, 2.— Poet.: od

evenio.full: ē-vĕnĭo, vēni, ventum, 4 (praes. subj. evenat, Enn. ap. Non. 507, 20; Plaut. Trin. 1, 2, 3; id. Mil. 4, 1, 19: evenant, id. Ep. 3, 1, 2), v. n., to come out, come forth. Lit. (very rare): merses profundo: pulchrior evenit, Hor. C. 4, 4, 65: tota arundo serius praedicto tempore evenit, comes up, grows up, Col. 4, 32, 2: sine modo rus eveniat, Plaut. Cas. 2, 8, 1: Capuam, id. Rud. 3, 2, 17; cf.: evenit sermo Samuelis Israeli, Vulg. 1 Reg. 3, 21.—Far more freq. and class., Trop. In gen., to fall ou

eventilo.full: ē-ventĭlo, no perf., ātum, 1, v. a., to set in motion (the air), to fan (post-Aug.). Lit.: (aërem graviorem) emendant assiduo linteorum jactatu eventilando, Plin. 31, 3, 28, § 49; cf. Just. 44, 1 fin.: frumenta, to winnow, i. e. to purify by winnowing, Col. 1, 6, 23.—* Trop.: opes eventilatae, i. e. scattered, dissipated, Sid. Ep. 1, 9.

eventum.full: ēventum, i, n., v. evenio fin.

eventus.full: ēventus, ūs, m. evenio, II.. An occurrence, accident, event; fortune, fate, lot (rare but class.): mihi a peritis in Asia praedictum est, fore eos eventus rerum qui acciderunt, Cic. Div. 1, 28: in incerto reliqui temporis eventu, id. Quint. 26, 83; Tac. Agr. 22; id. A. 2, 26: maerere hoc ejus (sc. Scipionis) eventu, vereor ne invidi magis quam amici sit, Cic. Lael. 4, 14: militum, Liv. 7, 26; cf. id. 7, 8; 8, 7 al.: navium suarum, Caes. B. G. 4, 31: patriae, Liv. 33, 48 et saep.: quid reliquis a

everbero.full: ē-verbĕro, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a., to strike violently, to beat (rare and not ante-Aug.). Lit.: os oculosque hostis, Quint. 2, 4, 18; cf. pectus suis armis, Val. Fl. 6, 737: clipeum alis, Verg. A. 12, 866; cf.: cineres alis, Ov. M. 14, 578: mare, fluctus remis, Curt. 4, 3, 18; 9, 4, 13: spiritum cursu parum libero, Sen. Q. N. 5, 12.— Trop.: cum haec taliaque sollicitas ejus aures everberarent, kept striking, besieged, Amm. 14, 11, 4: animum alicujus ad inquirendum, i. e. to stimulate, excite, Gell.

evergo.full: ē-vergo, ĕre, v. a., to send out, send forth: montes nullos apertos evergunt rivos, send forth, pour forth, Liv. 44, 33, 2.

everriator.full: ēverrĭātor vocatur, qui jure accepta hereditate justa facere defuncto debet, quae si non fecerit, seu quid in ea re turbaverit, suo capite luat. Id nomen ductum a verrendo. Nam exverrae sunt purgatio quaedam domus, ex qua mortuus ad sepulturam ferendus est, quae fit per everriatorem certo genere scoparum adhibito, ab extra verrendo dictarum, Paul. ex Fest. p. 77, 18 sq. Müll.
everriator.short: ēverrĭātor vocatur, qui jure accepta hereditate justa facere defuncto debet, quae si non fecerit, seu quid in ea re turbaverit, suo capite luat.

everriculum.full: ēverrĭcŭlum, i, n. everro, a sweepnet, drag-net. Prop., for taking a large number of fishes, Varr. R. R. 3, 17, 7; App. Mag. p. 294; cf. Non. p. 34; and: everriculum, quod Graece σαγήνη dicitur, Dig. 47, 10, 13, § 7.— Trop.: everriculum malitiarum omnium, the drag-net, i. e. the sweeperaway of all basenesses, Cic. N. D. 3, 30, 74: quod umquam hujuscemodi everriculum ulla in provincia fuit? i. e. a plunderer, sarcastically applied to Verres, Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 24, 53; cf. everro, II.

everro.full: ē-verro, verri, versum, 3, v. a., to sweep out (class.). Lit.: stercus ex aede Vestae, Varr. L. L. 6, § 32 Müll.; cf.: purgamenta salsamentorum officinis, Col. 8, 17, 12: aedes, Titin. ap. Non. 192, 11: solum stabuli, Varr. R. R. 2, 2, 7: everrere et purgare stabula, Col. 7, 4, 5: domum, Vulg. Luc. 15, 8.—Poet.: aequor retibus, Manil. 4, 285, v. verro.— Transf., of cleansing a wound: egestis vel eversis omnibus, quae tumorem moverant, Veg. Vet. 3, 30 fin.— Trop., to clean out, plunder completely

eversio.full: ēversĭo, ōnis, f. everto, I. B.. Lit. An overthrowing. In gen.: columnae, Cic. Phil. 1, 2, 5.—In plur.: eversiones vehiculorum, Plin. 22, 17, 20, § 43.— Esp., a destructive overthrow, subversion, destruction: templorum, Quint. 5, 10, 97: urbis, Flor. 1, 12, 7; cf. Quint. 8, 3, 69. —In plur.: eversiones urbium, Flor. 2, 16, 1.— A turning out, expulsion from one's possession: possidentium, Flor. 3, 13, 9.— A turning out, expulsion: matricis, Cael. Aur. Tard. 2, 1, 28.— Trop. (acc. to I. A. 2.), su

eversor.full: ēversor, ōris, m. everto, a subverter, destroyer. Prop.: Carthaginis et Numantiae, Quint. 8, 6, 30; cf.: regnorum Priami (Achilles), Verg. A. 12, 545: regnorum cometes, i. e. presaging their destruction, Sil. 8, 639.— Trop.: civitatis, Cic. Part. 30 fin.: hujus imperii, id. Sest. 7, 17; juris humani, Plin. 28, 1, 2, § 6: pecuniae (with interceptor), i. e. who squanders it, Cod. Th. 12, 6, 1.

eversus.full: ēversus, a, um. Swept out, v. everro.— Overthrown, v. everto.

everto.full: ē-verto or -vorto, ti, sum, 3, v. a., to overturn, turn upside down (syn. demolior, destruo, extinguo, diruo, deleo, etc.). Lit. In gen. (very rare): aequora ventis, to upturn, agitate, Verg. A. 1, 43; cf. aquas, Ov. H. 7, 42: mare, Sen. Ep. 4: campum, i. e. to plough, Val. Fl. 7, 75: cervices, to twist, Ter. Heaut. 2, 3, 131 Ruhnk.—More freq. and class. (not in Caes.), In partic. To overturn any thing from its position, to overthrow, upset, throw down: naviculam, Cic. de Or. 1, 38, 174; id. Par

evestigatus.full: ē-vestīgātus, a, um, Part. [vestigo], traced out, found out, discovered, investigated (very rare), Ov. M. 15, 146; Sen. Contr. 9.

evexus.full: ēvexus, a, um, adj. eveho, rounded off at the top, rounding upwards: mundus, Mart. Cap. 8, § 816.

evibro.full: ē-vībro, āre, v. a. Lit., to swing forwards, to hurl, throw: scorpiones rotundos lapides, Amm. 24, 4, 16.— Trop., to set in motion, to move, excite: animos, Gell. 1, 11, 1: eum ad rabiem, Amm. 14, 1, 10.

evictio.full: ēvictĭo, ōnis, f. evinco, II. A. 2., jurid. t. t., a recovering of one's property by a judicial decision, a recovery, eviction, Dig. 21, tit. 2; Cod. Just. 8, 45, De evictionibus.

evictus.full: ēvictus, a, um, Part., from evinco.
evictus.short: ēvictus, a, um, Part., from evinco.

evidens.full: ē-vĭdens, entis, adj. video, of things (like perspicuus), apparent, visible, evident, manifest, plain, clear (good prose; most freq. since the Aug. per.; syn. perspicuus, manifestus, apertus, dilucidus): flos (lappae) non evidens, sed intus occultus, Plin. 21, 17, 64, § 104: si quid est evidens, de quo inter omnes conveniat, etc., Cic. N. D. 3, 4; cf. id. Ac. 2, 6, 18: perspicuae et evidentes res, id. ib. 2, 15; cf. res (opp. dubia), Liv. 39, 34: causae (opp. obscurae), Cels. praef. fin.: exposi

evidentia.full: ēvĭdentĭa, ae, f. evidens, clearness, distinctness.—In rhet. lang., clearness, perspicuity; used by Cicero along with perspicuitas, as a transl. of ἐνάργεια. Cic. Ac. 2, 6, 17; cf. Quint. 6, 2, 32; 4, 2, 63; 9, 2, 40.— A proof: magna suae ostensionis, of his own manifestation, Vulg. 2 Macc. 3, 24.

evideor.full: ē-vĭdĕor, ēri, 2, v. pass. [ex+video], to appear completely or plainly, with nom. and inf., Arn. 2, 54.

evigesco.full: ē-vĭgesco, ĕre, 3, v. inch. n., to lose liveliness or vigor, Tert. Anim. 38.

evigilatio.full: ēvĭgĭlātĭo, ōnis, f. evigilo, a waking up, awakening, Aug. Solil. 1, 1; id. Civ. D. 17, 18, 1.

evigilo.full: ē-vĭgĭlo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. n. and a. Neutr. To wake up, awak, Plin. Ep. 1, 5, 8; 9, 36, 1; Quint. 9, 4, 12; Suet. Aug. 78; Stat. S. 5, 3, 128; Vulg. Gen. 28, 16.— To be wakeful, vigilant.—Trop.: in quo evigilaverunt curae et cogitationes meae, si? etc., Cic. Par. 2, 17; Vulg. 1 Cor. 15, 34.— Act., to watch through, pass without sleeping: nox evigilanda, Tib. 1, 8, 64.— Transf., to elaborate carefully, to compose, prepare (cf. elucubro). Lit.: libros, Ov. Tr. 1, 1, 108; cf. Gell. 1, 7, 4.— * Trop

evigoratus.full: ē-vĭgōrātus, a, um, Part. [vigoro], deprived of vigor or liveliness (post-class.), Tert. Pall. 4; id. Apol. 17.

evilesco.full: ē-vīlesco, lŭi, 3, v. inch. n., to become vile, worthless, despicable (post - Aug. and very rare): nullis sordibus pretium carae pietatis evilescit, Val. Max. 5, 4, 7: pericula, Tac. H. 3, 53: propter quae usque eo eviluit, ut passim ac propalam contemptui esset, Suet. Claud. 15.

evincio.full: ē-vincĭo, nxi, nctum, 4, v. a., to bind up, to bind or wind round with something (not ante-Aug., and mostly poet.): simul diademate caput Tiridatis evinxit, Tac. A. 15, 2; cf. id. ib. 6, 43.—More freq. in the part. perf.: viridi Mnestheus evinctus oliva, Verg. A. 5, 494; cf. palmae, i. e. wound round with the cestus, id. ib. 5, 364: comae (sc. vittā), Ov. Am. 3, 6, 56: evincta pudicā Fronde manus, crowned with laurel, Stat. Th. 1, 554.—With acc. respectiv.: puniceo stabis suras evincta cothurno,

evinco.full: ē-vinco, vici, victum, 3, v. a. (not anteAug.). To overcome completely, to conquer, vanquish: evicit omnia assuetus praedae miles, Liv. 10, 17 fin.: imbelles, Aeduos, Tac. A. 3, 46.— Transf. beyond the milit. sphere (freq.): lacrimis evicta, overcome, Verg. A. 4, 548: dolore, to induce, id. ib. 4, 474: precibus, Ov. F. 3, 688; Tac. A. 4, 57 fin.: blandimentis vitae, id. ib. 15, 64: donis, i. e. to bribe, id. ib. 12, 49 et saep.: in gaudium evicta domus, moved, Tac. H. 2, 64 fin.; cf.: ad miserat

evinctus.full: ēvinctus, a, um, Part., from evincio.
evinctus.short: ēvinctus, a, um, Part., from evincio.

eviolo.full: ēvĭŏlo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a., to violate, Prop. 1, 7, 16 (dub.; v. evolvo, B. 2.).

eviratio.full: ēvĭrātĭo, ōnis, f. eviro, a depriving of manhood: pilorum, i. e. a removing, Plin. 29, 1, 8, § 26.

eviratus.full: ēvĭrātus, a, um, Part. and P. a., from eviro.

eviresco.full: ē-vĭresco, ĕre, v. inch. n., to fade, become pale, Varr. ap. Non. 101, 32.

eviro.full: ē-vĭro, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. vir, to deprive of virility, to emasculate, unman, (rare): omnes pueros, Varr. ap. Non. 46, 12: corpus, Cat. 63, 57; Arn. 5, p. 187.— Transf., to weaken, make faint, deprive of strength: corpore evirato animae substantia turbatur, Cael. Aur. Tard. 1, 5, 178: emissus (sanguis) rationabiliter relevat, enormiter ablatus evirat vel turbat, Veg. 1, 36, 2; 1, 38, 12.—Hence, ēvĭrātus, a, um, P. a., unmanly, effeminate: eviratior spadone, Mart. 5, 41, 1 (with mollior).

eviscero.full: ē-viscĕro, no perf., ātum, 1, v. a. (poet. and in post-class. prose). To deprive of the entrails, to disembowel. Lit., Enn. ap. Cic. Tusc. 1, 44, 107 (Trag. v. 413 ed. Vahl.); Pac. ap. Cic. Div. 2, 64 fin.— Hence, In gen., to tear to pieces, lacerate: columbam (accipiter), Verg. A. 11, 723.— Trop.: opes, i. e. to dissipate, squander, exhaust, Cod. Just. 3, 29, 7: fidem, Ambros. Luc. 4, § 26; cf.: cum ceteri amnes abluant terras et eviscerent, Sen. Q. N. 4, 2, 10.—* To take out of the bowels or i

evitabilis.full: ēvītābĭlis, e, adj. 1. evito, avoidable. Prop.: telum, Ov. M. 6, 234.— Trop.: mala (opp. inevitabilia), Sen. Q. N. 2, 50, 2.

evitatio.full: ēvītātĭo, ōnis, f. id., an avoiding (post - Aug.): malorum, Quint. 5, 10, 33: periculi, Sen. Q. N. 2, 39: fastidii, Vop. Aur. 22.

evito1.full: ē-vīto, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a., to shun, avoid (class.; most freq. since the Aug. per.): tela amictu, Cat. 116, 7: metaque fervidis Evitata rotis, Hor. C. 1, 1, 5: fraxinum, Ov. M. 12, 123: bidental, Pers. 2, 27 et saep.—Of abstract objects: causas suspicionum offensionumque, Cic. Lael. 24: dolorem, id. Fin. 5, 7 fin.: continuatos pedes, id. Or. 57, 194; cf. asperitatem, Quint. 1, 5, 42: ejusmodi verba, id. 9, 4, 145: expositionem, id. 4, 2, 75; 4, 1, 71 et saep.

evito2.full: ē-vīto, āre, āvi, v. a. vita, to deprive of life, to kill (ante- and post-class.): vidi, Priamo vi vitam evitari, Enn. ap. Cic. Tusc. 1, 35, 85 (Trag. v. 129 ed. Vahl.): evitat vitam regi, Att. ap. Non. 449, 32 (Rib. Trag. Fragm. p. 181): tres juvenes, App. M. 3, p. 133 (al. enecasse); cf. Ἐναρίζω, evito, Gloss. Gr. Lat.

evocati.full: ēvŏcāti, ōrum, m., v. evoco, B. 2. fin.

evocatio.full: ēvŏcātĭo, ōnis, f. evoco, a calling out, calling forth (very rare). In gen.: inferorum, an evoking, Plin. 30, 1, 2, § 6: deorum ex urbibus obsessis, Macr. S. 3, 9. — In partic. A summoning of a debtor, Hirt. B. Alex. 56 fin.— A calling out, summoning of soldiers on an occasion of sudden danger, Auct. Her. 3, 2, 3: militiae, Jul. Val. Rer. Gest. Alex. 2, 7; cf. Don. Ter. Eun. 4, 7, 2; Serv. Verg. A. 7, 614.

evocativus.full: ēvŏcātīvus, a, um, adj. id., pertaining to summoning: stipendia, Inscr. Orell. 3460; 4968.

evocator.full: ēvŏcātor, ōris, m. id., one who calls to arms: servorum et civium perditorum, Cic. Cat. 1, 11, 27.

evocatorius.full: ēvŏcātōrĭus, a, um, adj. id., citing, summoning (late Lat.): epistola, Sid. Ep. 8, 12.

evoco.full: ē-vŏco, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a., to call out, call forth; to bring out, draw forth (class. —syn. invito, cito, etc.). Lit. In gen.: (Tullia) evocavit virum e curia, Liv. 1, 48: gubernatorem a navi huc, Plaut. Am. 3, 3, 12: aliquem huc foras, id. Cas. 2, 3, 54; id. Bacch. 5, 1, 29; id. Poen. 1, 2, 46: hinc foras, id. Rud. 2, 5, 22: intus foras, id. Men. 1, 3, 35; id. Ps. 2, 2, 10: aliquem ante ostium, id. Men. 4, 2, 111: mercatores undique ad se, to call together, summon, Caes. B. G. 4, 20, 4; cf.: a

evolatio.full: ēvŏlātĭo, ōnis, f. evolo, an escaping, rising out of: mortis, Hier. in Psa. 54.

evolito.full: ē-vŏlĭto, āre, v. freq. n., to fly out frequently, Col. 8, 8, 1.

evolo.full: ē-vŏlo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. n., to fly out or forth, to fly away, to fly up (class.). Lit.: ex quercu (aquila), Cic. Leg. 1, 1, 2: extra septa, Varr. R. R. 3, 9, 15.—Absol.: evolandi potestas, Col. 8, 15, 1: longius, Dig. 41, 1, 5, § 6: aut saepe ex humili sede sublima evolat, Att. ap. Non. 489, 5 (Rib. Trag. Fragm. p. 211): evolare ubi nec Pelopidarum facta neque famam audiam, Poet. ap. Cic. Att. 15, 11, 3; id. Fam. 7, 30, 1; cf. id. ib. 7, 28; id. Att. 14, 12, 2; and Rib. Trag. Fragm. p. 252: evo

evolutio.full: ēvŏlūtĭo, ōnis, f. evolvo, I. B. 1., an unrolling or opening of a book; hence, a reading: quid poëtarum evolutio voluptatis affert? Cic. Fin. 1, 7, 25.

evolutus.full: ēvŏlūtus, a, um, Part., from evolvo.
evolutus.short: ēvŏlūtus, a, um, Part., from evolvo.

evolvo.full: ē-volvo, volvi, vŏlūtum, 3 (per diaeresin ēvŏlŭam, Cat. 66, 74: ēvŏlŭisse, Ov. H. 12, 4), v. a., to roll out, roll forth; to unroll, unfold (class.). Lit.: (vis venti) Arbusta evolvens radicibus haurit ab imis, Lucr. 6, 141; cf. silvas, Ov. M. 12, 519: cadavera turribus, Luc. 6, 171: montes corpore, Ov. M. 5, 355: saxa nudis lacertis, Luc. 3, 481: intestina, Cels. 7, 16 et saep.: vestes, to open, unfold, Ov. M. 6, 581: volumen epistolarum, to open, Cic. Att. 9, 10, 4: panicum furfure, i. e. to c
evolvo.short: ē-volvo, volvi, vŏlūtum, 3 (per diaeresin ēvŏlŭam, Cat.

evomo.full: ē-vŏmo, ŭi, ĭtum, 3, v. a., to spew out, vomit forth (class.). Lit.: (haec avis scribitur) conchas cum concoxerit, evomere, Cic. N. D. 2, 49; Suet. Claud. 44; id. Ner. 2; Tac. A. 12, 67; Vulg. Jonah, 2, 11 al.— Transf.: quod (urbs) tantam pestem evomuerit forasque ejecerit, Cic. Cat. 2, 1 fin.: herbas, to put forth, Col. 8, 15, 3: ignes (Vesbius), Sil. 17, 594: pecuniam devoratam, to disgorge, give up, Cic. Pis. 37: Nilus in Aegyptium mare se evomit, discharges itself, empties, Plin. 5, 9, 10, §

evulgo.full: ē-vulgo (evolgo), āvi, ātum, 1, v. a., to bring out among the people, to publish, divulge (not ante-Aug., and very rare): civile jus repositum in penetralibus pontificum evulgavit, Liv. 9, 46: arcanum, Tac. H. 1, 4: injurias, id. A. 13, 19: pudorem, id. ib. 14, 14.—With an object-sentence in direct discourse: sic evulgari jussit, Tac. A. 13, 9.

evulsio.full: ēvulsĭo, ōnis, f. evello, a pulling out: dentis, Cic. N. D. 3, 22, 57.— Eradication, utter destruction, Vulg. Jerem. 12, 17.

evulsus.full: ēvulsus, a, um, Part., from evello.
evulsus.short: ēvulsus, a, um, Part., from evello.

ex.full: ex or ē (ex always before vowels, and elsewh. more freq. than e; e. g. in Cic. Rep. e occurs 19 times, but ex 61 times, before consonants—but no rule can be given for the usage; cf., e. g., ex and e together: qui ex corporum vinculis tamquam e carcere evolaverunt, Cic. Rep. 6, 14. But certain expressions have almost constantly the same form, as ex parte, ex sententia, ex senatus consulto, ex lege, ex tempore, etc.; but e regione, e re nata, e vestigio, e medio, and e republica used adverbially;
ex.short: ex or ē (ex always before vowels, and elsewh.

exabundo.full: ex-ăbundo, āre, to abound exceedingly (late Lat.): immensarum divitiarum copiis, Salv. adv. Avar. 4, 6.
exabundo.short: ex-ăbundo, āre, to abound exceedingly (late Lat.): immensarum divitiarum copiis, Salv.

exabusus.full: ex-ăbūsus, a, um, Part. [abutor], abusing greatly, Amm. 25, 7, 8.

exacerbatio.full: exăcerbātĭo, ōnis, f. exacerbo, an exasperation, Rufin. de Schem. 11, p. 274: peccatorum, i. e. because of, Salv. Gub. Dei, 4, 7.— Esp., of the stirring of divine anger by the Jews in the wilderness, the provocation, Vulg. Hebr. 3, 8; 15.

exacerbatrix.full: exăcerbātrix, īcis, f. id., she who exasperates, Salv. Gub. Dei, 3, 9.

exacerbesco.full: ex-ăcerbesco, ĕre, v. inch. n., to become exasperated, irritated, angry: quis est tam mitis quin exacerbescat, App. Mag. p. 327, 28.

exacerbo.full: ex-ăcerbo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. (not anteAug.). To exasperate, irritate, provoke, make angry; to grieve, afflict: ut recenti aliqua ira exacerbarentur animi, Liv. 2, 35 fin.; 46; 6, 18; 8, 33; Suet. Tib. 62; 75; Plin. Ep. 8, 5, 2; Vulg. Psa. 9, 24 al.— In jurid. Lat., to aggravate, increase a punishment: supplicia, Dig. 48, 19, 16 fin.; cf.: crimen verbis impiis, Paul. Sent. 5, 29, 1; pass. impers.: crimine majestatis facto maxime exacerbatur in milites, ib. 48, 4, 7, § 4.

exacervans.full: ex-ăcervans, antis, Part. [acervo], heaping up exceedingly: tela, Amm. 23, 5, 3.

exacesco.full: ex-ăcesco, ăcŭi, 3, v. inch. n., to become sour (rare): ficus, Col. 12, 17, 1.

exacon.full: exăcon (-cum), i, n., the Gallic name of the herb centaureum (centaury), Plin. 25, 6, 31, § 68.
exacon.short: exăcon (-cum), i, n., the Gallic name of the herb centaureum (centaury), Plin.

exacte.full: exacte, adv., exactly, precisely, accurately, v. exigo, P. a. fin.
exacte.short: exacte, adv., exactly, precisely, accurately, v.

exactio.full: exactĭo, ōnis, f. exigo. * A driving out, expelling: (regum), Cic. de Or. 1, 9, 37 (perh. only on account of the preceding exactis regibus).— A demanding, exacting, requisition. In gen.: in exhibendis operariis, Lact. Mort. Pers. 7, 8: quotidiana, operis, Col. 11, 1, 26.—Hence, the supervision, conduct of a public work; cf. exactor, II. A.: operum publicorum, Cic. Dom. 20, 51.—Far more freq., In partic., a calling in, collecting of debts, Cic. Att. 5, 1; id. Leg. 2, 20, 51; Liv. 38, 38; Dig. 42,

exactor.full: exactor, ōris, m. id.; cf. also exactio. * A driver-out, expeller: regum (Junii Valeriique), Liv. 9, 17, 11.— A demander, exactor (cf.: redemptor, manceps, magister; also: publicanus, portitor). In gen.: operis, i. e. an overseer, superintendent, enforcer of any kind of labor, Col. 3, 13, 10; cf. Liv. 45, 37; so, assiduus studiorum, Quint. 1, 3, 14; cf.: asper recte loquendi, id. 1, 7, 34: molestissimus sermonis Latini, Suet. Gramm. 22: supplicii, an executioner, Liv. 2, 5; cf. Tac. A. 11, 37, a

exactrix.full: exactrix, īcis, f. exactor, she who demands: rescriptorum, Aug. Ep. 135.

exactus1.full: exactus, a, um, Part. and P. a., from exigo.

exactus2.full: exactus, ūs, m. exigo, a sending off or away: mercis, i. e. disposal, sale, Quint. Decl. 12, 19.

exacuo.full: ex-ăcŭo, ŭi, ūtum, 3, v. a., to make very sharp, to sharpen, make pointed (class.). Lit.: ferramenta cote, Plin. 28, 4, 12, § 47; 34, 14, 41, § 146: ridicas, Col. 11, 2, 12: vallos furcasque bicornes, Verg. G. 1, 264: spicula, id. ib. 4, 74: dentes, id. ib. 3, 255: metas in angustissimas vertices, Col. 2, 18, 2: cornua in leve fastigium, Plin. 11, 37, 45, § 124 et saep.— Transf., of taste: aceto exacuendo, for making pungent, Plin. 19, 5, 30, § 93; of the sight: aciem oculorum, id. 24, 11, 59, §

exacutio.full: exăcūtĭo, ōnis, f. exacuo, a sharpening, pointing: calami, Plin. 17, 14, 24, § 106.

exadversum.full: ex-adversum (-vors-) and ex-adversus (-vors-), adv. and praep. Lit. from opposite; hence, over against, opposite, vis-a\-vis. Adv.: apud ipsum lacum est pistrilla, et exadversum fabrica, Ter. Ad. 4, 2, 44: video exadvorsum Pistoclerum, Plaut. Bacch. 4, 7, 37: ea sita erat exadvorsum, Ter. Phorm. 1, 2, 47: inque earum locum bina castra exadversum constituta erant, Suet. Caes. 40 Roth; App. Flor. p. 353; Amm. 23, 6, 72.—With dat.: exadvorsum ei loco Tonstrina erat quaedam, Ter. Phorm. 1, 2, 38: Sa

exadvocatus.full: ex-advŏcātus, i, m., one who has been an advocate, an ex-advocate, Aug. Civ. D. 22, 8.
exadvocatus.short: ex-advŏcātus, i, m., one who has been an advocate, an ex-advocate, Aug.

exaedificatio.full: ex-aedĭfĭcātĭo, ōnis, f. exaedifico, a building, erecting, completion of an edifice; trop. of an oration: ipsa autem exaedificatio posita est in rebus et verbis, Cic. de Or. 2, 15, 63; Ambros. in Psa. 118, Serm. 4, § 15.

exaedifico.full: ex-aedĭfĭco, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. To finish building, to build up, erect, construct (rare but class.). Lit.: oppidum, * Caes. B. C. 1, 15, 2; cf. Liv. 30, 1 fin.: Capitolium (with efficere), Cic. Verr. 2, 5, 19: domos et villas, Sall. C. 12, 3: templa deum, Liv. 1, 56: hibernacula, id. ib. 30, 3; navem, Cic. Verr. 2, 5, 18: hunc mundum, id. Ac. 2, 40 fin.— Trop., to finish, complete: ne graveris exaedificare id opus, quod instituisti, Cic. de Or. 1, 35, 164; cf.: suam incohatam ignaviam, Plaut. T

exaequatio.full: exaequātĭo, ōnis, f. exaequo, an equalling. * Lit., a levelling: agrorum, Serv. Verg. G. 1, 95; concr., a level, a plane, Vitr. 5, 12, 4.— Trop., a levelling, an equality: hanc ipsam exaequationem non fero (cf., shortly before: aequato omnium cultu), Liv. 34, 4, 14.

exaequo.full: ex-aequo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. To make even or level with any thing. Lit. (very rarely): inferior pars (ex transtillis) sub aqua exaequanda, etc., Vitr. 5, 12, 3: tumulos tumulis exaequabant, Auct. B. Hisp. 5 fin.— Transf.: aurum auro expendetur, argentum argento exaequabitur, shall be balanced, compensated, Plaut. Rud. 4, 4, 43.—Freq. and class., Trop., to place on a level, regard as equal, to equal: ii, qui sunt in amicitiae conjunctionisque necessitudine superiores, exaequare se cum inferiorib

exaeresimus.full: exaerĕsĭmus, a, um, adj., = ἐξαιρέσιμος, that may be omitted, taken out: quod suos dies mensisque congruere volunt ... non numquam eximant unum aliquem diem ex mense: quos illi exairesimos dies nominant, Cic. Verr. 2, 2, 52. § 129.
exaeresimus.short: exaerĕsĭmus, a, um, adj., = ἐξαιρέσιμος, that may be omitted, taken out: quod suos dies mensisque congruere volunt ...

exaestuatio.full: exaestŭātĭo, ōnis, f. exaestuo, a boiling up, a fermentation (post-class.). Lit., Sol. 5, 17.— Trop.: animi, Non. 464, 10.

exaestuo.full: ex-aestŭo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. n. and a., to boil up, foam up, ferment (not freq. till after the Aug. period; in Cic. and Caes. not at all). Neut. Lit. In gen.: exaestuat mare, Liv. 26, 42 fin.; Curt. 6, 4: fretum, id. 4, 2: unda ima verticibus, Verg. G. 3, 240: Aetna fundo imo, id. A. 3, 577: bitumen e terra, Just. 1, 2, 7: Nilus in fossas, Suet. Aug, 18.— In partic., to effervesce, to glow with heat: Aegyptus torrenti calore solis exaestuat, Just. 2, 1, 16.— Absol.: ut exaestuarat, had overheated

exaggeranter.full: exaggĕranter, adv., copiously, v. exaggero fin. * 1.

exaggeratio.full: exaggĕrātĭo, ōnis, f. exaggero, a heaping or raising up. * Lit. concr., in plur., Just. 2, 1 fin. (al. aggerationes).— Trop., elevation, exaltation (very seldom); amplitudinem et quasi quandam exaggerationem quam altissimam animi, * Cic. Tusc. 2, 26, 64: aliqua speciosa orationis, cumulation, exaggeration, Gell. 13, 24, 9; cf. ib. § 16.

exaggerator.full: exaggĕrātor, ōris, m. id., one who increases, an enlarger: famae, Hier. Ep. 22, 8; id. ad Eustoch. 28.

exaggero.full: ex-aggĕro, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a., to raise a mound, dam, or dike; to heap up (class.; cf.: acervo, coacervo, cumulo, aggero). Lit.: aggesta humo planitiem, Curt. 6, 5: terram, Plin. 19, 8, 41, § 139: clivum super capita columnarum, id. 36, 14, 21, § 96: locum operibus, to surround with ramparts, Vitr. 10, 22: pluribus stramentis exaggerandum est aviarium, to be abundantly filled, supplied, Col. 8, 11, 9.— Transf., to enlarge, increase by heaping up: rem familiarem, Cic. Off. 1, 26, 92; so, magnas

exagitatio.full: exăgĭtātĭo, ōnis, f. exagito, a disturbance (late Lat.): mentis, Acr. ad Hor. S. 2, 3, 208.

exagitator.full: exăgĭtātor, ōris, m. exagito, II. B. 1., one who severely blames, a censurer: omnium rhetorum, Cic. Or. 13, 42.

exagito.full: ex-ăgĭto, āvi, ātum, 1, v. freq. a., to drive out of its position or place; to stir up, rouse up, disturb. Lit. (very seldom): ut quicquid faecis subsederit exagitet, et in summum reducat, Col. 12, 19, 4: vis (venti) exagitata foras erumpitur, Lucr. 6, 583. —Poet.: lustra ferarum Venatu, to disturb, Sil. 16, 553: lepus hic aliis exagitandus erit, to rouse, start, Ov. A. A. 3, 662; cf. Petr. 131, 7.— Trop., to rouse up (qs. like a wild beast), to disquiet, harass, persecute, disturb, torment. In

exagium.full: exăgĭum, ii, n. ex-ago; cf. examen, II., a weighing, weight; a balance (late Lat.), Theod. et Val. Nov. 25; Inscr. Orell. 3166; cf. Ἐξάγιοϝ pensatio; ἐξαγιάζω examino, Gloss. Philox.

exagoga.full: exăgōgă, ae, f., = ἐξαγωγή (pure Lat. evectio), an exportation of goods, export, Plaut. Rud. 3, 2, 17; id. Truc. 4, 2, 6: bonorum exagogae, id. ib. 2, 7, 2; cf.: Exagogen evectionem, Paul. ex Fest. p. 80, 15 Müll.

exalapo.full: ex-ălăpo, āvi, 1, v. a., to box on the ears: exalapandus et flagellandus, August. in Psa. 49, 6.

exalbesco.full: ex-albesco, bŭi, 3, v. inch. n., to become white. Lit. (very rarely), Gell. 12, 1, 12.—More freq., Trop., to grow white, turn pale from fright, etc., Enn. ap. Cic. de Or. 3, 58, 218; and in Fin. 5, 11, 31; Cic. Ac. 2, 15, 48; id. de Or. 1, 26, 121.

exalbidus.full: ex-albĭdus, a, um, adj., whitish, white (repeatedly in Pliny): rami (arboris), Plin. 12, 17, 39, § 78: folia urticae, id. 24, 19, 112, § 172: vina, id. 23, 1, 22, § 40.
exalbidus.short: ex-albĭdus, a, um, adj., whitish, white (repeatedly in Pliny): rami (arboris), Plin.

exalbo.full: ex-albo, no perf., ātum, 1, v. a. albus, to make white, Tert. adv. Marc. 4, 10; 4, 8.

exalburnatus.full: ex-alburnātus, a, um, adj. alburnum, deprived of the alburnum: robur, Plin. 16, 40, 76, § 204.

exaltatio.full: exaltātĭo, ōnis, f. exalto. Exaltation, elevation (eccl. Lat.): ab exaltatione tua dispersae sunt gentes, Vulg. Isa. 33, 3. — Trop., pride, haughtiness: non congruit professoribus humilitatis, Tert. Cult. Fem. 3; cf. oculorum, Vulg. Prov. 21, 4: stultorum, id. ib. 3, 35.

exaltative.full: exaltātīve, adv. id., in an exalted state, under inspiration: propheta se convertit, Cassiod. in Psa. 9, 33.

exalto.full: ex-alto, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. altus (postAug.; mostly eccl. Lat.). To raise, elevate, exalt: deus alia exaltat, alia submittit, Sen. Q. N. 3 prooem.: TERMINOS VETVSTATE COLLAPSOS, Inscr. Fabr. p. 748, no. 555: solium, Vulg. Isa. 14, 13.— Trop.: exaltare, Deus, be praised, Vulg. Psa. 56, 5: vocem, id. Isa. 13, 2 et saep.— To deepen: fodiunt (sulcos) et exaltant in tres pedes, Col. 3, 13, 4: sulcum, id. 3, 13, 9: orbem ablaqueationis, id. 4, 4, 2.

exaluminatus.full: ex-ălūmĭnātus, a, um, adj. alumen, of the color of alum: uniones, Plin. 9, 35, 56, § 113.

examarico.full: ex-ămārĭco, āvi, 1, v. a., to imbitter exceedingly: doloribus [Hilar.] Anon. in Job, 2, p. 137.

exambio.full: ex-ambĭo, ii, ītum, 4, v. n. and a. (late Lat.). Neut., to go round asking, soliciting: ad Martyras, Cypr. Ep. 20.— Act., to ask, solicit a person: viros, mulierculas, Mamert. Grat. Act. ad Julian. 19: suffragium tui favoris, Symm. Ep. 7, 49: exambita regia, Amm. 26, 7.

examen.full: ex-āmen, ĭnis, n. for ex-agmen, from ex and ago; cf. contamino and contagies, flamen and flagrare. A multitude issuing forth or flying out, a swarm. Primarily and class. of a swarm of bees: res rusticae laetae sunt tum pecudum pastu, apium examinibus, florum omnium varietate, Cic. de Sen. 15 fin.; so, apium, id. Off. 1, 44, 157; id. Div. 1, 33 fin.; Liv. 4, 33 et saep.; cf. Varr. R. R. 3, 16, 29; Col. 9, 3 fin.; 9, 4 fin. et saep.; Plin. 11, 10, 10, § 23; Verg. G. 2, 452; 4, 21; 103 et saep.— Tr

examinate.full: exāmĭnātē, adv., carefully, considerately, v. examino, P. a. fin.

examinatio.full: exāmĭnātĭo, ōnis, f. examino. Lit., i. q. libratio, an equipoise, equilibrium, Vitr. 10, 8.— Trop., a weighing, examination (post-class.), Dig. 3, 5, 8; 47, 14, 1 fin.

examinator.full: exāmĭnātor, ōris, m. id.. * Lit., a weigher, Cassiod. Var. 6, 18 fin.— Trop., an examiner (late Lat.), Tert. Apol. 9; Aug. contr. Cresc. 3, 73.

examinatorius.full: exāmĭnātōrĭus, a, um, adj. id., belonging to an examination: martyria fidei, Tert. adv. Gnost. 7.

examinatrix.full: exāmĭnātrix, īcis, f. id., she that tests or tries: tentatio, August. Sanct. Virg. 46.

examinatus.full: exāmĭnātus, a, um, Part. and P. a., from examino.

examino.full: exāmĭno, āvi, ātum, 1, v. n. and a. [examen]. * (acc. to examen, I.).— Neut., to form swarms, to swarm: examinant alvi, Col. 9, 14, 5.— (acc. to examen, II.). Lit. Act., to weigh (class.): (aër) tamquam paribus examinatus ponderibus, Cic. Tusc. 1, 19, 43; cf.: ad certum pondus, * Caes. B. G. 5, 12, 4.—* Neut.: alicui, to be in equilibrium with a thing, to counterbalance, counterpoise, Vitr. 10, 8.— Trop., act., to weigh, ponder, consider, examine, try, test (class.): non aurificis statera, sed q

examplexor.full: ex-amplexor, āri, v. dep. a., to clasp, embrace, Auct. Her. 4, 52 fin.

examurco.full: ex-ămurco, āre, v. a. amurca.Prop., to cleanse from dregs.—Transf., to deprive of moisture, to dry, App. M. 4, p. 149, 14.

examussim.full: ex-ămussim, adv. amussis, by the rule, i. e., exactly, precisely, perfectly (= ad amussim, Varr. R. R. 2, 1, 26; Gell. 1, 4, 1; 20, 1, 34); cf. Sisenn. ap. Charis. p. 178; Non. 9, 6 sq.; p. 80, 19 Müll. (ante- and post-class.): aedes Factae probe, examussim, Plaut. Most. 1, 2, 19: rem examussim disputare, id. Men. prol. 50; App. M. 2, p. 128, 13: nae ista edepol ... examussim est optuma, Plaut. Am. 2, 2, 213; App. M. 4, p. 150, 33; id. ib. 11, p. 271; cf. Hand, Turs. II. p. 664.

exancillatus.full: ex-ancillātus, a, um, Part. [ancillor], serving like a slave: anima falsis dis, Tert. Apol. 17 fin.

exanclo.full: ex-anclo (less accurately -antlo), āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. (an archaic word; mostly ante-class.; cf. Quint. 1, 6, 40), to draw or bring out as a servant. Lit. In gen.: clavum, Pac. ap. Non. 29, 2, 7.— In partic., to draw out a liquid = exhaurio: vinum poculo pauxillulo saepe, Plaut. Stich, 1, 3, 116.—Poet.: nisi patrem materno sanguine exanclando ulciscerer, i. e. spilling, shedding = effundendo, Enn. ap. Non. 292, 16 (Rib. Trag. Fragm. p. 32), exanclare, effundere, Non. ib.— Trop., to go through, s

exanimabiliter.full: ex-ănĭmābĭlĭter, adv. exanimo, half dead with fear or horror, Nov. ap. Non. 376, 12.

exanimalis.full: ex-ănĭmālis, e, adj. pass. (perh. only in Plaut.), lifeless, dead: ni illum exanimalem faxo, Plaut. Bacch. 4, 8, 7.—Act., deadly: curae exanimales, id. Rud. 1, 4, 2.

exanimatio.full: exănĭmātĭo, ōnis, f. exanimo. A depriving of breath, suffocating: volvarum, i. e. hysterical passion, Plin. 32, 3, 13, § 28 (for which suffocatio, id. 20, 5, 15, § 30, and strangulatus, id. 26, 15, 90, § 153).— Trop., terror, fright: exanimatio metus subsequens et quasi comes pavoris, Cic. Tusc. 4, 8, 19; cf. id. ib. 4, 6, 13: si cavebimus, ne in perturbationes atque exanimationes incidamus, id. Off. 1, 36, 131.

exanimis.full: ex-ănĭmis, e, and ex-ănĭmus, a, um (cf. Wagner ad Verg. A. 4, 8; the latter form common in the plur., of which the former has only exanimes, nom. and acc.), adj. anima, lifeless, dead (mostly postAug.; not in Cic. and Caes.; cf.: inanimis, exanimatus, mortuus). Lit. Form exanimis: (columba) Decidit exanimis, Verg. A. 5, 517; cf. id. ib. 5, 481: ut exanimem labentem ex equo Scipionem vidit, Liv. 25, 34 fin.: aliquamdiu jacuit, Suet. Caes. 82 et saep.: corpus, Ov. M. 14, 728; 10, 721; 13, 438; Pli
exanimis.short: ex-ănĭmis, e, and ex-ănĭmus, a, um (cf.

exanimo.full: ex-ănĭmo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. To deprive of air or wind. Lit.: folles, i. e. to press together, so as to force out the air, Auct. Aetnae, 560.— Transf. (in pass.), to be out of breath, weakened, exhausted: simul fore ut duplicato cursu Caesaris milites exanimarentur et lassitudine conficerentur, Caes. B. C. 3, 92, 2: milites cursu ac lassitudine exanimati, id. B. G. 2, 23, 1; 3, 19, 1; Plaut. As. 2, 1, 17; id. Cas. 3, 5, 8; 3, 3, 10.— Of impers. or abstr. things, to be weakened: (vini faex) cele

exanthema.full: exanthēma, ătis, n., = ἐξάνθημα, an eruption on the skin, exanthema, Marc. Emp. 19 (in Cels. 5, 28, 15, written as Greek).
exanthema.short: exanthēma, ătis, n., = ἐξάνθημα, an eruption on the skin, exanthema, Marc.

exaperio.full: ex-ăpĕrĭo, īre, v. a., to open wide, throw open (very rare): exapertae repente delubri fores, et audita major humana vox, Tac. H. 5, 13: implicatissimam nodositatem, to undo, unloose, Aug. Conf. 10.

exaporior.full: ex-ăpŏrĭor, āri, v. dep., to be in utter perplexity: nec aporiati exaporiantur, Ruf. Aquil. Orig. in Cant. p. 305.

exapto.full: ex-apto, āre, v. a., to fit, adjust: Deo coronas, App. M. 11, p. 271, 19.

exaptus.full: ex-aptus, a, um, adj., fastened (very rare): exaptum pendere onus ingens, Lucil. ap. Non. 235, 7; cf.: ex quo orbe pendeant exapta catenis tintinabula, Varr. ap. Plin. 36, 13, 19, § 92; so Fronto Fer. Als. p. 213 Mai.
exaptus.short: ex-aptus, a, um, adj., fastened (very rare): exaptum pendere onus ingens, Lucil.

exaquesco.full: ex-ăquesco, escĕre, v. n., to turn to water: mundus tum exignescere, tum exaquescere videtur, Censor. 18, 11.

exaratio.full: exărātĭo, ōnis, f. exaro (late Lat.). * A ploughing up, Mart. Cap. 6, § 637.— * Transf., a writing, composition, Sid. Carm. 9, 335.

exarchus.full: exarchus, i, m., = ἔξαρχος, a superintendent, overseer: monasteriorum, Just. Nov. 133, 4.
exarchus.short: exarchus, i, m., = ἔξαρχος, a superintendent, overseer: monasteriorum, Just.

exardeo.full: ex-ardĕo, ēre, 2, v. a. (eccl. Lat.). Prop., to burn: ignis, Vulg. Sir. 16, 7; cf. ib. 28, 14; 27.— Trop., of the feelings, to be inflamed, blaze out: in brevi ira, Vulg. Psa. 2, 13: in desideriis suis, id. Rom. 1, 27.

exardesco.full: ex-ardesco, arsi, arsum, 3, v. inch. n., qs. to blaze out, i. e. to kindle, take fire (class.; esp. freq. in the trop. sense and in Cic.; cf.: ardeo, ferveo, caleo, flagro, candeo, uro, etc., incendor, inflammor, etc.). Lit.: nulla materies tam facilis ad exardescendum est, quae, etc., Cic. de Or. 2, 45 fin.: sulphur exardescens, Plin. 35, 15, 50, § 175.— Transf., of the sun's heat: exarsit dies, Mart. 3, 67, 6.—And of a fiery color: fulgor carbunculi exardescens, Plin. 37, 7, 25, § 94.— Trop.,

exarefio.full: ex-ārĕfīo, ĕri, v. pass. [arefacio], to dry up, become completely dry: fucus marinus, Plin. 26, 10, 66, § 103.

exaresco.full: ex-āresco, rŭi, 3, v. inch. n., to dry up, become completely dry (rare, but class.). Lit.: vestimenta uvida, Plaut. Rud. 2, 7, 20: frumentum, Varr. R. R. 1, 32: silva omnis radicitus, Suet. Galb. 1: amnes, Cic. Pis. 33, 82; id. Div. 1, 19 fin.; cf. fontes, * Caes. B. C. 3, 49, 5: lacus et stagna, Dig. 41, 1, 12: lacrimae, to dry up, Cic. Att. 10, 14.— Trop.: neque dum exarui ex amoenis rebus et voluptariis, Plaut. Mil. 3, 1, 46: sic omnis fetus repressus, exustusque flos siti veteris ubertatis e

exaridus.full: ex-ārĭdus, a, um, adj., dried up, quite dry.—Trop.: status Judaeorum (with emortuus), Tert. Res. Carn. 30.
exaridus.short: ex-ārĭdus, a, um, adj., dried up, quite dry.—Trop.: status Judaeorum (with emortuus), Tert.

exarmatio.full: ex-armātĭo, ōnis, f. exarmo, a weakening, lessening: fluxurarum, Cypr. Sing. Cler. 39.

exarmo.full: ex-armo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a., to deprive of arms, to disarm (post-Aug.). Lit.: cohortes, Tac. H. 2, 76 fin.: dextras, Luc. 5, 356: Medos, id. 8, 387; Col. 7, 3, 5; cf. Lampr. Hel. 21.— Transf. Navem, i. e. to unrig, dismantle, Sen. Cons. ad Helv. 17, 6; id. Contr. 3, 15, 9.—Absol., to lose the rigging of a ship: et si exarmavit, tamen reliquias navigii aptat ad cursum, Sen. Ep. 30, 3; cf. Dig. 14, 2, 2.— (Causa pro effectu.) To deprive of strength, to weaken: serpentem diro veneno, i. e. to rend

exaro.full: ex-ăro, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a., to plough or dig up (class.). Lit.: radices, Cato. R. R. 61; id. ap. Plin. 17, 18, 30, § 127; Plin. 18, 6, 8, § 46: sepulcra, Cic. Leg. 2, 23, 58: terminos (with deicere), Dig. 10, 1, 4, § 4: deum, puerum, Cic. Div. 2, 23, 51; 2, 38, 80. — Transf. To raise, produce by tillage: tantum frumenti, ut, etc., Cic. Verr. 2, 5, 38; cf. Zumpt, ib. 2, 3, 47.— In gen., to plough, till, cultivate, Varr. R. R. 1, 10, 1; Plin. 18, 3, 3, § 9: locum de integro, Col. 2, 18, 3: agrum,

exarticulatus.full: ex-artĭcŭlātus, a, um, adj., inarticulate, irregular: sonus tinnitusque, Tert. ad Nat. 1, 8.
exarticulatus.short: ex-artĭcŭlātus, a, um, adj., inarticulate, irregular: sonus tinnitusque, Tert.

exasciatus.full: ex-ascĭātus, a, um, Part. [ascio], hewn out; hence, in gen., properly prepared: opus, Plaut. As. 2, 2, 93.

exasperatio.full: exaspĕrātĭo, ōnis, f. exaspero, a roughness, Scrib. Comp. 222; Veg. Vet. 5, 61, 1.— Bitterness, exasperation, Tert. adv. Marc. 2, 16; Macr. S. 7, 12, 38.

exasperatrix.full: exaspĕrātrix, īcis, f. id., she who irritates or exasperates, Vulg. Ezech. 2, 8.

exaspero.full: ex-aspĕro, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a., to make rough, to roughen (not ante-Aug.). Lit.: fauces, Cels. 1, 3; cf.: summam cutem, id. 3, 27: arterias, Plin. 22, 23, 48, § 100: corpus, id. 31, 6, 34, § 67: tussim, id. 23, 4, 51, § 97: faucium vitio exasperatur vox, Quint. 11, 3, 20: undas, to roughen, stir up, Ov. Am. 2, 11, 27: mare fluctibus, Liv. 37, 12 fin. (cf. aspero).—Poet.: aegida innumeris signis, i. e. to adorn with raised sculptures, Claud. III. Cons. Honor. 193: ensem saxo, to sharpen, whet, Si

exauctoritas.full: exauctōrĭtas, ātis, f. exauctoro, a discharge from military service, Cod. Th. 8, 5, 35.

exauctoro.full: ex-auctōro, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. Milit. t. t., to discharge from service (after sixteen years of service, before the end of the usual term of twenty years, i. e. before the regular missio; see missio. This discharge was either an honorable one or a punishment. The honorably discharged soldiers remained four years in the army as a separate corps under a vexillum, with peculiar privileges; cf. mitto, dimitto). Prop. Of an honorable discharge (not ante-Aug.): omnes milites exauctorati domum dimitter

exaudibilis.full: exaudībĭlis, e, adj. exaudio, that may be heard or listened to, Aug. Sol. 1, 1.— Giving ear to requests, listening, Schol. Juv. 13, 248.

exaudio.full: ex-audĭo, īvi or ii, ītum, 4, v. a. To hear or perceive clearly (class.): Nec satis exaudiebam, nec sermonis fallebar tamen, Quae loquerentur, Plaut. Epid. 2, 2, 55; cf. id. Merc. 4, 3, 8; id. Men. 3, 2, 13; id. Trin. 3, 3, 25: cum aliquantulum progressus esset, subito exaudivit hinnitum, Cic. Div. 1, 33 fin.; cf. id. Att. 13, 48; Caes. B. G. 6, 39, 1; 7, 61, 3; id. B. C. 1, 66, 1; 3, 105, 3; Liv. 1, 29; 2, 27; 5, 52; 8, 33 et saep.: maxima voce, ut omnes exaudire possint, dico semperque dicam,
exaudio.short: ex-audĭo, īvi or ii, ītum, 4, v.

exauditio.full: exaudītĭo, ōnis, f. exaudio, II. B., a hearkening to, granting: oratio exauditione dei dignior, Aug. Civ. D. 21, 24; Vulg. 2 Chron. 33, 19.

exauditor.full: exaudītor, ōris, m. id., one who hearkens to, grants, Vulg. Sirach, 35, 19.

exaugeo.full: ex-augĕo, ēre, v. a., to increase exceedingly (rare): amplius, Enn. ap. Fest. p. 193 Müll. (Ann. v. 270 ed. Vahlen): benefacta majorum tuorum exauge, Plaut. Stich. 2, 1, 9; ib. 32: opinionem, Ter. Heaut. 2, 2, 3.

exauguratio.full: exaugŭrātĭo, ōnis, f. exauguro, a desecrating, profaning: omnium sacellorum exaugurationes, Liv. 1, 55, 3.

exauguro.full: ex-augŭro, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a., to apply to profane uses a thing which has been consecrated, to desecrate, profane (very rare): fana, Cato ap. Fest. s. v. NEQVITVM, p. 162, 32 Müll.; cf. Liv. 1, 55: vestalem, Gell. 6, 7, 14: sacerdotes, Capitol. M. Aurel. 4.

exauspico.full: ex-auspĭco, āvi, 1, v. n., to take an augury from any thing: ex vinculis, Plaut. Capt. 3, 5, 108.

exballisto.full: ex-ballisto, āre, v. a. ballista, a comically formed word, to put an end to, to finish or conquer with the ballista: Ballionem exballistabo lepide, Plaut. Ps. 2, 1, 10.

exbibo.full: exbĭbo, ĕre, = ebibo, to drink out, drink up: neque illic calidum exbibit in prandium, Plaut. Mil. 3, 2, 19 (Ritschl, bibit).
exbibo.short: exbĭbo, ĕre, = ebibo, to drink out, drink up: neque illic calidum exbibit in prandium, Plaut.

exbola.full: exbŏla, ae, f., = ἐκβολή, a kind of missile, weapon, Naev. ap. Varr. L. L. 7, § 108 (Com. Rel. p. 24 Rib.).
exbola.short: exbŏla, ae, f., = ἐκβολή, a kind of missile, weapon, Naev.

exbures.full: exbures exinteratas, sive exburae, quae exbiberunt, quasi epotae, Paul. ex Fest. p. 79, 11 Müll.
exbures.short: exbures exinteratas, sive exburae, quae exbiberunt, quasi epotae, Paul.

excaecator.full: excaecātor, ōris, m. excaeco, one who blinds, Aug. Serm. 43 ex Homil. 50.

excaeco.full: ex-caeco, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a., to blind, make blind (rare). Lit.: num ergo is excaecat nos aut orbat sensibus? etc., * Cic. Ac. 2, 23, 74; Plin. 20, 18, 76, § 200; Flor. 2, 20, 5.— Transf. To deprive a plant of the eyes or buds, Col. 11, 3, 45; Plin. 17, 22, 35, § 175.— To stop up a river, a channel, etc., Ov. M. 15, 272; id. Pont. 4, 2, 17; Cels. 7, 7 fin.—* To darken or dull a bright color: fulgor (argenti) excaecatus, Plin. 33, 9, 46, § 131.— Trop.: oculos animosque (fama), Petr. 141, 5: form

excalceo.full: ex-calcĕo (-calcĭo), āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. (the deponent form, v. below), to take off the shoes. In gen.: petiit, ut sibi pedes praeberet excalciandos, Suet. Vit. 2.—More freq. with a personal object and in the part. perf.: excalciatus cursitare, unshod, barefoot, Suet. Vesp. 8; Mart. 12, 88; cf. mid. in the verb. finit.: neque umquam aut nocte aut die excalcearetur aut discingeretur, Vell. 2, 41 fin.; and as a verb. dep.: ut nemo se excalceatur, Varr. ap. Non. 478, 16.— In partic., of tragedians,

excaldatio.full: excaldātĭo, ōnis, f. excaldo, a washing or bathing in warm water (late Lat.), Capitol. Albin. 5 al.

excaldo.full: ex-caldo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. caldus, to wash or bathe in warm water (late Lat.), Marc. Empir. 26; Apic. 4, 2 al.

excalesco.full: ex-călesco, ĕre, v. inch. n., to become warm, Theod. Prisc. 4, 1 med.

excalfacio.full: ex-calfăcĭo, no perf., factum, 3, v. a., to warm, to heat (post-Aug.; esp. freq. in Pliny the Elder): excalfacit, Plin. 21, 20, 82, § 139; 21, 21, 89, § 155: excalfieri, id. 24, 7, 28, § 42; Scrib. Comp. 158: lacus sole excalfactus, Plin. 37, 2, 11, § 37; 37, 10, 54, § 148: ad excalfaciendos nervos, id. 21, 22, 93, § 163.

excalfactio.full: excalfactĭo, ōnis, f. excalfacio, a warming, heating, Plin. 31, 9, 45, § 105.

excalfactorius.full: excalfactōrĭus, a, um, adj. id., warming, heating (a Plinian word), Plin. 21, 18, 72, § 120; 24, 11, 64, § 105; 25, 13, 95, § 152.

excalfio.full: excalfīo, pass. of excalfacio, q. v.

excandefacio.full: ex-candĕfăcĭo, fēci, 3, v. a., to heat, inflame (perh. only in the foll. passages), trop.: excande me fecerunt cupiditate (tmesis), Varr. R. R. 3, 4, 1: annonam macelli, i. e. to enhance, raise, id. ib. 3, 2, 16; cf. exardesco and incendo.

excandeo.full: ex-candĕo, ēre, 2, v. a. and n. Act., to make bright, whiten: cutem, Schol. Juv. 2, 107.— Neut., to gleam, glisten, be bright: lapides, Jul. Val. Rer. Gest. Alex. 3, 22.

excandescentia.full: excandescentĭa, ae, f. excandesco, nascent anger, passionateness, irascibility, Cic. Tusc. 4, 9, 21; cf. App. Dogm. Plat. 1 fin.

excandesco.full: excandesco, dŭi, 3, v. inch. n., to grow hot, to take fire, kindle, to glow (class.). Lit.: cum bitumen et sulphur additum est, excandescet, Cato R. R. 95; Col. 7, 5, 16. — Trop., to glow, to burn, esp. with anger: haec nullam habent vim, nisi irā excanduit fortitudo, * Cic. Tusc. 4, 19, 43: id postquam resciit, excanduit, Cael. ap. Cic. Fam. 8, 12, 2; cf. Petr. 53, 8; 57, 1; Suet. Claud. 40; id. Ner. 40: in aliquem, id. Vesp. 14; cf.: in exteros, Col. 7, 12, 5: in ultionem, Flor. 2, 18, 8: exca

excantator.full: excantātor, ōris, m. excanto, a charmer, one who removes by enchantment: venatorum morsuum, Hier. in Joel Prol.

excanto.full: ex-canto, āvi, ātum (excantassit = excantaverit, Tab. XII. ap. Sen. Q. N. 4, 7, 2), 1, v. a., to charm out or forth, to bring out by enchantment (not in Cic. or Caes.), Varr. ap. Non. 102, 11; Lucil. and Plaut. ib.; * Prop. 3, 3, 49 (4, 2, 49 M.); * Hor. Epod. 5, 45; Luc. 6, 686; 9, 931: QVI FRVGES EXCANTASSIT, i. e. had removed them by enchantment into another field, Tab. XII. ap. Plin. 28, 2, 4, § 17; cf. Sen. Q. N. 4, 7, 2; Serv. Verg. E. 8, 99; Aug. C. D. 8, 19.

excarnifico.full: ex-carnĭfĭco, no perf., ātum, 1, v. a., to cut or tear any one to pieces (a rare word). Lit.: aliquem, Cic. N. D. 3, 33 fin.; Suet. Vit. 17; Sen. Ep. 24.— Trop., to torment, torture: aliquem, Ter. Heaut. 4, 6, 9: excarnificatus animus, Sen. de Ira, 3, 4: comitem, Amm. 14, 5, 1; 14, 9, 6.

excastratus.full: ex-castrātus, a, um, Part. [castro], emasculated. Lit., Gell. 9, 9, 10.— Transf., shelled, husked: sinapi, Scrib. Comp. 9.

excaudico.full: ex-caudĭco (-cōdico), āre, v. a. [caudex), to weed out, root up = exstirpare. Prop., Lex ap. Front. Aquaed. 129.— Transf., to dig round, i. q. ablaqueare: ablaqueandae sunt vites, quod Itali excodicare appellant, Pall. Jan. 1.— Trop., to extirpate, root out: silvam libidinum eradicare et excaudicare, Tert. Pudic. 16.

excavatio.full: excăvātĭo, ōnis, f. excavo, a hollowing out: lapidis, Sen. Q. N. 4, 3, 3.

excavo.full: ex-căvo, no perf., ātum, 1, v. a., to hollow out. Lit.: trullam, Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 27 fin.: cavernam sibi rostro, Plin. 9, 27, 43, § 82: ripas, id. 10, 33, 49, § 95: terram, id. 33 prooem.: lapides excavant aquae, Vulg. Job, 14, 19.— Transf., in mal. part., Auct. Priap. 51, 4.

excedo.full: ex-cēdo, cessi, cessum, 3 (subj. perf. sync. excessis, Ter. And. 4, 4, 21), v. n. and a. Neut., to go out, go forth or away, to depart, retire, withdraw (freq. and class.; cf.: discedo, deficio, destituo, desero, linquo, relinquo). Lit. In gen., with ex and abl., with abl. alone, or absol.: ex istoc loco, Plaut. Aul. 1, 1, 18: e medio, Ter. Hec. 4, 3, 14: ex civitate, Caes. B. G. 6, 8, 8: ex Italia, Cic. Phil. 12, 6, 14: e templo, Liv. 29, 19; for which, templo, id. 39, 5: ex finibus, Caes. B. G

excellens.full: excellens, Part. and P. a., from excello.

excellenter.full: excellenter, adv., excellently; v. excello, P. a. 1. fin.

excellentia.full: excellentia, ae, f. excello, P. a. 1., superiority, excellence, perfection (abstr. and rel.): magna cum excellentia praestantiaque animantium reliquarum, Cic.
