Calig. 18; 26 et saep.: consessus, spectators assembled at gladiatorial shows, Cic. Sest. 58, 124; cf. locus, a place for witnessing the same, id. Mur. 35, 73: gladiatoria corporis firmitas, id. Phil. 2, 2

gladiatura.full: glădĭātūra, ae, f. gladius, gladiator, a fighting of gladiators, or their profession (post-Aug. and very rare): adduntur e servitiis gladiaturae destinati, Tac. A. 3, 43: ut requiem gladiaturae haberet, Schol. Juv. 6, 105; Firm. 5, 27.

gladiolus.full: glădĭŏlus, i, m. dim. gladius. A small sword: lingulam veteres dixere gladiolum oblongum, in speciem linguae factum, Gell. 10, 25, 3: gladiolo solito cinctus, App. M. 2, p. 122; 3, p. 131.—In plur. heterocl. glădĭŏla: nec gladiola (quisquam ferat), atqui Messala dixit, Quint. 1, 6, 42 (cf. gladius init.).— Glădĭŏlus, i, title of a comedy by Livius Andronicus, Fest. s. v. pedibus, p. 210 b. Müll.— The sword-lily, Plin. 21, 11, 38, § 65; 21, 17, 67, § 107 sq.; al. Pall. 1, 37.

gladium.full: glădĭum, ii, n., v. gladius init.

gladius.full: glădĭus, ĭi, m. (also archaic glă-dĭum, ii, n., Lucil. ap. Non. 208, 13; cf. Varr. L. L. 9, § 81 Müll.; Quint. 1, 5, 16; v. gladiola under gladiolus, I.) [perh. akin to clades, cardo; cf. κλαδάσαι, to brandish], a sword (syn. the poet. ensis, acc. to Quint. 10, 1, 11; cf. also: spatha, acinaces, sica, pugio). Lit.: arripuit gladium, Plaut. Capt. 4, 4, 7; id. Cas. 2, 4, 28: eripite isti gladium, quae sui est impos animi, id. Cas. 3, 5, 9: succincti gladiis media regione cracentes, Enn. ap. Paul.

glaeba.full: glaeba (less correctly glēba), ae, f. cf. globus. Prop., a small piece or lump of earth, a clod (cf. gramen, herba, faenum, caespes): ingens, Lucr. 6, 553: glaebis terrarum saepe friatis, id. 1, 887: fecundae, id. 1, 212; so Verg. G. 1, 94; Hor. C. 3, 6, 39: si glaebis aut saxis aut fustibus aliquem de fundo praecipitem egeris ... non esse arma cespites neque glaebas, etc., Cic. Caecin. 21, 60: omnes, qui ullam agri glaebam possiderent, Cic. Verr. 2, 3, 11, § 28; so, nec ulli glaeba ulla agri as

glaebalis.full: glaebālis (glēb-), e, adj. glaeba. Of or relating to clods (post-class.): agger, consisting of clods, Amm. 23, 5, 15.— In law Lat. (acc. to glaeba, II. A.), of or relating to lands: collatio, a tax paid from lands, land-tax, Cod. Th. 6, 2, 3; 4, 8, 11 et saep.

glaebarius.full: glaebārĭus (glēb-), a, um, adj. glaeba, of or relating to clods: e quis (bubus) ut dicti valentes glaebarii, qui facile proscindunt glebas, clod-breakers, Varr. L. L. 7, 4, 95, § 74.

glaebatim.full: glaebātim (glēb-), adv. id., by clods (post-class.): agros glaebatim metiri, Lact. Mort. Pers. 23, 2.

glaebatio.full: glaebātĭo (glēb-), ōnis, f. id., a tax levied on land, land-tax, Cod. Th. 6, 2, 12.

glaebosus.full: glaebōsus (glēb-), a, um, adj. id., full of clods, cloddy (post-Aug.), App. M. 1, 2: terra glaebosior, Plin. 35, 16, 53, § 191.

glaebula.full: glaebŭla (glēb-), ae, f. dim. id.. Prop., a small clod or lump of earth (postAug.): frumenta lapillisque carent et glaebulis, quas per trituram fere terrena remittit area, Col. 1, 6, 23; Val. Max. 5, 3, 3 ext.— Meton. A little farm, small piece of land: saturabat glaebula talis patrem ipsum turbamque casae, Juv. 14, 166; App. M. 9, p. 233.— Of other things, a small piece, little lump: myrrhae, Vitr. 8, 3: nivis, Scrib. Comp. 199: ex metallo, Plin. Ep. 10, 16, 3.

glaebulentus.full: glaebŭlentus (glēb-), a, um, adj. id., cloddy, consisting of earth: animalia, App. de Deo Socr. p. 46.

glaesaria.full: Glaesārĭa (Glēs-), ae (sc. insula), f. glaesum, an amber island in the North Sea, also called Burcana, Plin. 4, 13, 27, § 97; 37, 3, 11, § 42.

glaesum.full: glaesum (glēsum, glessum), i, n. cf. Germ. Glas; gleissen = glänzen, to glimmer; Engl. glass, amber, Tac. G. 45; Plin. 37, 3, 11, § 42.—Hence, glaesārĭus, a, um, adj., of amber, amber-: insula, which produces amber, Plin. 4, 13, 27, § 97; 37, 3, 11, § 42.

glandarius.full: glandārĭus, a, um, adj. glans, of or belonging to acorns or mast: silva, producing acorns, Cato, R. R. 1, 7; Varr. R. R. 1, 7, 9.

glandifer.full: glandĭfer, ĕra, ĕrum, adj. glans-fero, acorn-bearing, glandiferous (very rare): quercus, Lucr. 5, 939; Cic. Leg. 1, 1, 2.

glandionida.full: glandĭŏnĭda, ae, f. glandium, i. q. glandium, a savory kernel or glandule in pork: suilla, Plaut. Men. 1, 3, 27 Ritschl (al. glandionicam).

glandium.full: glandĭum, ii, n. glans, a delicate kernel or glandule in meat, esp. in pork, Plaut. Curc. 2, 3, 44; id. Capt. 4, 4, 7; id. Stich. 2, 2, 36; Plin. 8, 51, 77, § 209; 16, 38, 73, § 185.

glando.full: glando, ĭnis, f. id., in late Latin for glans, an acorn, Avien. Perieg. 285; 1189.

glandulae.full: glandŭlae, ārum, f. dim. id.; lit., a little acorn; hence, transf.. The glands of the throat, called also tonsillae: in ipsis cervicibus glandulae positae sunt, quae interdum cum dolore intumescunt, Cels. 4, 1. — Swollen glands in the neck, enlarged tonsils, Cels. 2, 1 fin.; 8, 4.— I. q. glandium, the neck-piece, delicate bits, esp. of pork, Mart. 3, 82, 21; 7, 20, 4; Apic. 4, 1, § 117.

glandulosus.full: glandŭlōsus, a, um, adj. glandulae, II., full of kernels, glandulous: cervix suis, Col. 7, 9, 1.

glanis.full: glanis, is and ĭdis, and glanus, i, m., = γλάνις and γλάνος, a kind of shad, Plin. 9, 43, 67, § 145; 32, 10, 45, § 128; 32, 11, 53, § 148.
glanis.short: glanis, is and ĭdis, and glanus, i, m., = γλάνις and γλάνος, a kind of shad, Plin.

glans.full: glans, glandis, f. kindr. with βάλανος, an acorn, and, in gen., any acorn-shaped fruit, beechnut, chestnut, etc. Lit.: bubus glandem prandio depromere, Plaut. Truc. 3, 1, 2; Cato, R. R. 54; 60; Col. 6, 3; Plin. 16, 5, 6, § 15 sq.; Lucr. 5, 1416; Cic. Or. 9, 31; Verg. G. 1, 148; Ov. M. 1, 106 et saep.: glandis appellatione omnis fructus continetur, ut Javolenus ait, Dig. 50, 16, 236.— Transf. An acorn-shaped ball of lead or clay which was hurled at the enemy, Lucr. 6, 179; 307; Caes. B. G. 5, 43,

glarea.full: glārĕa, ae, f., gravel (cf. arena, sabulum, suburra, rudus): eo loco pulvis, non glarea injecta est, Cic. Q. Fr. 3, 2, 2, § 4; Varr. R. R. 1, 9, 2: vias glareà substruendas locaverunt, Liv. 41, 27, 5; Col. 4, 22, 8; Tib. 1, 7, 59; Verg. G. 2, 212; Vitr. 2, 4, 2; Vulg. Job, 30, 6.

glareosus.full: glārĕōsus, a, um, adj. glarea, full of gravel, gravelly: terra, Varr. R. R. 1, 9, 3: sabulosaque arva, Col. 2, 10, 23: loca, id. Arb. 21, 1: rivi, Plin. 26, 8, 56, § 88: flumen saxa glareosa volvens, Liv. 21, 31, 11 dub. (al. globosa).

glastum.full: glastum, i, n., the herb woad, used in dyeing blue, usually called Isatis tinctoria, Linn.; Plin. 22, 1, 2, § 2.
glastum.short: glastum, i, n., the herb woad, used in dyeing blue, usually called Isatis tinctoria, Linn.;

glauce.full: Glauce, ēs, f., = Γλαύκη. The mother of the third Diana, Cic. N. D. 3, 23, 58.— Another name of Creüsa, wife of Jason, Hyg. F. 25.— An Amazon, Hyg. F. 163.

glauceum.full: glaucēum, i, n., = γλαύκειον, a bluish-colored plant, celandine, usually called glaucion, Col. poët. 10, 104.
glauceum.short: glaucēum, i, n., = γλαύκειον, a bluish-colored plant, celandine, usually called glaucion, Col.

glauceus.full: glaucĕus, a, um, adj. glaucion, of celandine: sucus, Scrib. Comp. 22.

glaucia.full: Glaucĭa, ae, m. 1. glaucus, a Roman surname in the gens Servilia and Mallia, Cic. de Or. 2, 61; 65; id. Rosc. Am. 7, 19; 34, 96.

glaucicomans.full: glaucĭcŏmans, antis, adj. 1. glaucus-, 2. como, with bluish - gray foliage, bluish-gray: oliva, Juvenc. 3, 622.

glaucina.full: glaucĭna, ōrum, n., = γλαύκινα, ointment of celandine, glaucium ointment, Mart. 9, 26, 2; Dig. 34, 2, 21.
glaucina.short: glaucĭna, ōrum, n., = γλαύκινα, ointment of celandine, glaucium ointment, Mart.

glaucion.full: glaucĭon, ii, n., = γλαύκιον, the (bluish) plant celandine: Chelidonium glaucium, Linn.; Plin. 27, 10, 59, § 83.—In plur., Mart. 9, 27, 2.
glaucion.short: glaucĭon, ii, n., = γλαύκιον, the (bluish) plant celandine: Chelidonium glaucium, Linn.;

glauciscus.full: glauciscus, i, m., = γλαυκίσκος, a bluish-colored fish, otherwise unknown, Plin. 32, 10, 46, § 129; 32, 11, 53, § 148.
glauciscus.short: glauciscus, i, m., = γλαυκίσκος, a bluish-colored fish, otherwise unknown, Plin.

glaucito.full: glaucĭto, āre, v. n., the natural note of puppies, to yelp: glaucitat et catulus, Auct. Carm. Philom. 60.

glaucoma.full: glaucōma, ătis, n. (also glaucū-ma, ae, f., Plaut. Mil. 2, 1, 70 Ritschl, N. cr.), = γλαύκωμα, an obscuration of the crystalline lens, a cataract, Plin. 29, 6, 38, § 117 al.; Prud. Ham. 90.—Comically: alicui glaucumam ob oculos obicere, qs. to throw dust in his eyes, Plaut. Mil. 2, 1, 70.

glaucopis.full: glaucōpis, ĭdis, f., = γλαυκῶπις (gray-eyed, an epithet of Minerva), the owl: si meus aurita gaudet glaucopide Flaccus, Mart. 7, 87 dub. (ex conject. Scalig., al. lagopode; v. lagopus). † glaucus, a, um, adj., = γλαυκός, bright, sparkling, gleaming, grayish (poet. and in post-Aug. prose; cf.: caeruleus, caesius): undae, Lucr. 1, 719; so of water: amictus (Nymphae), Verg. A. 12, 885; cf.: amictus (dei Tiberini), id. ib. 8, 33: sorores, i. e. the Nereides, Stat. Th. 9, 351: ulva, Verg. A. 6, 416:
glaucopis.short: glaucōpis, ĭdis, f., = γλαυκῶπις (gray-eyed, an epithet of Minerva), the owl: si meus aurita gaudet glaucopide Flaccus, Mart.

glaucus.full: Glaucus, i, m., = Γλαῦκος, a Greek proper name. A son of Sisyphus, devoured by his own horses, Verg. G. 3, 267.— The commander of the Lycians in the Trojan war, a friend of Diomede, Hor. S. 1, 7, 17.— A fisherman of Anthedon, in Eubœa, who was changed into a sea-god, Ov. M. 13, 906 sq.; 14, 9; 38; 68; 7, 233: Glauci chorus, the Nereids, Verg. A. 5, 823; Stat. Th. 7, 335.
glaucus.short: Glaucus, i, m., = Γλαῦκος, a Greek proper name.

glaux.full: glaux, cis, f., = γλαύξ, a plant, called also eugalacton, Plin. 27, 9, 58, § 82.
glaux.short: glaux, cis, f., = γλαύξ, a plant, called also eugalacton, Plin.

gleba.full: glēba, and its derivv., v. glaeba, etc.

glechon.full: glēchon, ōnis, m., = γλήχων, pennyroyal: pulegium, App. Herb. 92.
glechon.short: glēchon, ōnis, m., = γλήχων, pennyroyal: pulegium, App.

glechonites.full: glēchōnītes, is, m., = γληχωνίτης, wine flavored with pennyroyal, pennyroyal wine, Col. 12, 35.
glechonites.short: glēchōnītes, is, m., = γληχωνίτης, wine flavored with pennyroyal, pennyroyal wine, Col.

gleucinus.full: gleucĭnus, a, um, adj., = γλεύκινος, of must, made from must: oleum, Col. 12, 53; Plin. 15, 7, 7, § 29.
gleucinus.short: gleucĭnus, a, um, adj., = γλεύκινος, of must, made from must: oleum, Col.

glinon.full: glīnon, i, n., = γλῖνος, a kind of maple-tree, Plin. 16, 15, 26, § 67.
glinon.short: glīnon, i, n., = γλῖνος, a kind of maple-tree, Plin.

glirarium.full: glīrārĭum, ii, n. glis, a place for keeping dormice, Varr. R. R. 3, 15, 1.

glis.full: glis, glīris, m. perh. kindred with γαλέη, a dormouse: Sciurus glis, Linn.; Glis esculentus, Blumenb.; a delicacy with the Romans, Varr. R. R. 3, 15; Plin. 8, 57, 82, § 223 sq.; Mart. 13, 59; Apic. 8, 9; Petr. 31; Amm. 28, 4: in silva mea est glis nullus, Varr. ap. Charis. p. 69 and 106 P.: glirium examina, Plaut. Fragm. ap. Non. 119, 26.

gliscerae.full: gliscĕrae mensae gliscentes, id est crescentes, per instructionem epularum scilicet, Paul. ex Fest. p. 98 Müll.
gliscerae.short: gliscĕrae mensae gliscentes, id est crescentes, per instructionem epularum scilicet, Paul.

glisco.full: glisco, ĕre, v. n. perh. kindred with cresco, Paul. ex Fest. s. h. v. p. 98 Müll.; cf. Doed. Syn. 1, p. 21, to grow up, swell up, spread, blaze up, burst out (mostly poet. and in post-Aug. prose; cf. crebresco). Lit.: ignis Alexandri Phrygio sub pectore gliscens, kindling, Lucr. 1, 474; so of fire, Sil. 14, 308; cf. Serv. Verg. A. 12, 9: gliscit, ut ignis oleo, Cic. Hortens. Fragm. ap. Non. 22, 21 (Cic. 10, p. 63 Kays.): suffusa veneno Tenditur, ac sanie gliscit cutis, swells, Stat. Th. 1, 107:

glisomarga.full: glīsomarga (glisso-, or glysso-), ae, f., a kind of marl, Plin. 17, 8, 4, § 46.
glisomarga.short: glīsomarga (glisso-, or glysso-), ae, f., a kind of marl, Plin.

globatim.full: glŏbātim, adv. globus, in clusters, bands, troops (late Lat.): per vicina digressi praedones, Amm. 27, 9.

globo.full: glŏbo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. id., to make into a ball, to make round or spherical (postAug. and perh. only pass. and mid.). Lit.: dependentes ubique guttae parvis globantur orbibus, Plin. 2, 65, 65, § 163; 18, 13, 34, § 130: formam mundi in speciem orbis absoluti globatam esse, id. 2, 2, 2, § 5.— Transf., to form into a body or crowd, to crowd together: si ante exortum solis nubes globabuntur, hiemem asperam denuntiabunt, Plin. 18, 35, 78, § 344; 11, 17, 17, § 53; cf.: coturnices globatae vehement

globositas.full: glŏbōsĭtas, ātis, f. globosus, rotundity, sphericalness, globosity (post-class.): terrae, Macr. Somn. Scip. 1, § 16, 23, 16.

globosus.full: glŏbōsus, a, um, adj. globus, round as a ball, spherical, globose (class.): (mundum) globosum est fabricatus, quod σφαιροειδὲς Graeci vocant, Cic. Univ. 6; cf.: stellae globosae et rotundae, id. Rep. 6, 15: mundus, id. N. D. 2, 45, 116; cf.: forma (mundi), id. ib. 2, 19, 49: terra, id. ib. 2, 39, 98: saxum, Pac. ap. Auct. Her. 2, 23, 36; Liv. 38, 29, 4.

globulus.full: glŏbŭlus, i, m. dim. id., a little ball, a globule (post-Aug. and very rare). Lit.: (chrysocollae) globulis sudore resolutis, Plin. 33, 5, 27, § 89.— Esp. a lump of food, dumpling, Cato, R. R. 79; Varr. L. L. 5, § 107 Müll.— Med. t. t., a pill, Scrib. 13 al.— Trop., of speech, a rounding: melliti verborum, Petr. 1.

globus.full: glŏbus, i, m. kindr. with glomus, a round body, a ball, sphere, globe. Lit. In gen.: cum duae formae praestantes sint, ex solidis globus (sic enim σφαῖραν interpretari placet), ex planis autem circulus aut orbis, qui κύκλος Graece dicitur, Cic. N. D. 2, 18, 47: ille globus, quae terra dicitur, id. Rep. 6, 15: terrae, id. Tusc. 1, 28, 68; cf. stellarum, id. Rep. 6, 16; 6, 17: solis et lunae, Lucr. 5, 472; cf. lunae, id. 5, 69: cum caelum discessisse visum est atque in eo animadversi globi, fire-b

glocidare.full: glōcidāre et † gluttīre gallinarum proprium est, cum ovis incubiturae sunt, Paul. ex Fest p. 99 Müll. N. cr.; cf. the foll. art.
glocidare.short: glōcidāre et † gluttīre gallinarum proprium est, cum ovis incubiturae sunt, Paul.

glocio.full: glōcĭo, īre, v. n., to cluck as a hen, Col. 8, 5, 4; cf. the preced. art.

gloctoro.full: gloctŏro, āre, v. n., to cry as a stork, Auct. Carm. Philom. 29.

glomerabilis.full: glŏmĕrābĭlis, e, adj. glomero, rounded, round (very rare): sidus Pleiadum, Manil. 4, 520: orbis lunae, id. 1, 221.

glomeramen.full: glŏmĕrāmen, ĭnis, n. id., a rounding; concr., a round body, ball (poet. and perh. ante- and post-class.): dissimiles formae glomeramen in unum conveniunt, Lucr. 2, 686: lunae, id. 5, 726.—In plur.: nec retinentur enim inter se glomeramina quaeque, i. e. the round atoms, Lucr. 2, 454: dilue praeterea glomeramina, i. e. pills, Ser. Samm. 55, 999.

glomerarius.full: glŏmĕrārĭus, ii, m. id., one eager to collect men for war (glomerare manum bello, Verg. A. 2, 315), Sen. Contr. 1, 8, 13.

glomeratim.full: glŏmĕrātim, adv. glomero, in heaps or crowds, = turmatim (post-class.): glomeratim ingredi in sedilia, Macr. S. 6, 4, 3.

glomeratio.full: glŏmĕrātĭo, ōnis, f. id. I., of horses, a bringing of the legs together into a ball, a trotting (or, as others say, a prancing or an ambling): Asturcones, quibus non vulgaris in cursu gradus, sed mollis alterno crurum explicatu glomeratio, Plin. 8, 42, 67, § 166; cf. Verg. G. 3, 117.

glomero.full: glŏmĕro, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. glomus, to wind or form into a ball, gather into a round heap, to conglobate, glomerate (poet. and in post-Aug. prose). Lit.: lanam in orbes, Ov. M. 6, 19: sic terram deus, ne non aequalis ab omni Parte foret, magni speciem glomeravit in orbis, id. ib. 1, 35; 9, 222: Eae (offae) maxime glomerantur ex ficis et farre mixto, Varr. R. R. 3, 5, 4: ubi venae inter se implicatae glomerantur, Cels. 7, 22; so, glomerata viscera, Ov. M. 8, 401: atra favilla volat glomerataque

glomerosus.full: glŏmĕrōsus, a, um, adj. glomus, like a ball, round, glomerous (post-Aug. and very rare), Col. 9, 3, 1.

glomus.full: glŏmus (glōm-, Lucr. 1, 360; v. Lachm.), ĕris, n. for glob-mus, kindr. with globus, a ball or clue of yarn, thread, etc. (very rare). In gen.: lanae, Lucr. 1, 360 (v. Lachm. ad h. l.); Hor. Ep. 1, 13, 14: lini, Plin. 36, 13, 19, § 91: staminis albi, Scrib. Comp. 142.— In partic.: glomus in sacris crustulum cymbi figura ex oleo coctum appellatur, Paul. ex Fest. p. 98 Müll. (in Cato and Varro globus).

gloria.full: glōrĭa, ae, f. Sanscr. cru, to hear; crav-as, fame; Gr. κλύω, κλέος; Lat. cluo, clueo, inclutus, from the root clŭo; lit., rumor, fame; hence also, like κλέος, pregn., glory, fame, renown, praise, honor (syn.: laus, laudatio, gloriatio, elogium, etc.). Lit. In gen.: te inmortali adficere gloria, Plaut. Am. 5, 2, 10: viri (Q. Fabii) gloria claret, Enn. ap. Macr. S. 6, 1 (Ann. v. 315 Vahl.): ut summae gloriae sint a virtute proficiscentia, dedecoris vero praecipui existimentur, quae voluptas suade

gloriabundus.full: glōrĭābundus, a, um, adj. glorior, glorying, exulting (post-class. and very rare): aliqua re, Gell. 5, 5, 4; Lact. 5, 13, 15.

gloriatio.full: glōrĭātĭo, ōnis, f. id., a glorying, boasting, vaunting, exulting (a word formed by Cic.): ex quo efficitur, gloriatione, ut ita dicam, dignam esse beatam vitam, Cic. Fin. 3, 8, 28; 4, 18, 50: ubi est ergo gloriatio tua, Vulg. Rom. 3, 27.

gloriator.full: glōrĭātor, ōris, m. id., a boaster, braggart, App. Flor. p. 357.

glorificatio.full: glōrĭfĭcātĭo, ōnis, f. glorifico, glorification (eccl. Lat.), Aug. Tract. 105, 3 fin.

glorifico.full: glōrĭfĭco, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. glorificus, to glorify (eccl. Lat.): deum, Tert. Idol. 22; Prud. Hamart. fin.; Vulg. Exod. 15, 2 et saep.—Pass., Vulg. Exod. 14, 4 al.

glorificus.full: glōrĭfĭcus, a, um, adj. gloria-facio, full of glory, glorious (post-class.), Cod. Just. 2, 8, 7, § 2.

gloriola.full: glōrĭŏla, ae, f. dim. gloria, a small glory, a little glory (a word formed by Cic.): nosmet ipsi vivi gloriola nostra perfruamur, Cic. Fam. 5, 12, 9; 7, 5, 3.

glorior.full: glōrĭor, ātus, 1, v. dep. a. and n. id., to glory, boast, vaunt, to brag of any thing, pride one's self on any thing (class.); constr. with acc., or an object- or relative-clause, with abl., de, in aliqua re, or absol. With acc. of pron. (cognate acc.): vellem equidem idem posse gloriari quod Cyrus, Cic. de Sen. 10, 32: ut de me ipso aliquid more senum glorier, id. ib. 23, 82: in eum haec gloriantem impetum facit, Liv. 1, 12, 9.—With direct object (post-class. and rare; cf. Weissenb. ad Liv. 27,

gloriosus.full: glōrĭōsus, a, um, adj. gloria. (Acc. to gloria, I.) Full of glory, glorious, famous, renowned (syn.: illustris, praeclarus, magnificus): de clarorum hominum factis illustribus et gloriosis satis hoc loco dictum, Cic. Fin. 1, 11, 37: quae si in privatis gloriosa sunt, id. Deiot. 14, 40: magnificum illud Romanisque hominibus gloriosum, ut Graecis de philosophia libris non egeant, id. Div. 2, 2, 5: in illa fuga, nobis gloriosa, id. ib. 1, 28, 59: mors, id. ib. 1, 24, 51: consilia, id. Att. 8, 12, 5

glos.full: glos, glōris, f. Gr. γάλοως, Att. γάλως, a husband's sister, sister-in-law. Lit., Dig. 38, 10, 4, § 6; Paul. ex Fest. p. 98 Müll.; Charis. p. 27; Aus. Idyll. monos. de hist. 13.— Acc. to Non. 557, 6, also for fratria, but without an example.

glossa.full: glossa, ae, f., = γλῶσσα, an obsolete or foreign word that requires explanation; for the usual glossema, Aus. Ep. 127 (in Quint. 1, 1, 35, written as Greek).—Hence, glossae, a term applied to collections of such words with explanations: tesca aiunt sancta esse, Qui glossas scripserunt, Varr. L. L. 7, § 10 Müll; cf. glossema.
glossa.short: glossa, ae, f., = γλῶσσα, an obsolete or foreign word that requires explanation;

glossarium.full: glossārĭum, ii, n. glossa, a vocabulary or glossary of antiquated or foreign words that need explanation: vos philosophi meri estis, ut M. Cato ait, mortuaria glossaria; namque colligitis lexidia, res tetras et inanes, etc., Gell. 18, 7, 3.

glossema.full: glossēma, ătis, n., = γλώσσημα, an antiquated or foreign word needing explanation: circa glossemata etiam, id est voces minus usitatas, non ultima ejus professionis diligentia, Quint. 1, 8, 15: camillam (apud Ennium), qui glossemata interpretati, dixerunt administram, Varr. L. L. 7, § 34 Müll.: glossemata nobis praecipit, Asin. ap. Suet. Gramm. 22.—Hence, Glos-sēmăta, ōrum, n., a name given to collections of such words with explanations: naucum ait Aelius Stilo omnium rerum putamen: Glossematoru
glossema.short: glossēma, ătis, n., = γλώσσημα, an antiquated or foreign word needing explanation: circa glossemata etiam, id est voces minus usitatas, non ultima ejus professionis diligentia, Quint.

glossematicus.full: glossēmătĭcus, a, um, adj., = γλωσσηματικός, of or belonging to obsolete or foreign words: genus locutionum, Diom. p. 434 P.
glossematicus.short: glossēmătĭcus, a, um, adj., = γλωσσηματικός, of or belonging to obsolete or foreign words: genus locutionum, Diom.

glossopetra.full: glossŏpĕtra, ae, f., = γλωσσοπέτρα, a precious stone resembling the human tongue, Plin. 37, 10, 59, § 164; Sol. 37 med.
glossopetra.short: glossŏpĕtra, ae, f., = γλωσσοπέτρα, a precious stone resembling the human tongue, Plin.

glottis.full: glottis, ĭdis, f., = γλωττίς, a little bird, Plin. 10, 23, 33, § 66.
glottis.short: glottis, ĭdis, f., = γλωττίς, a little bird, Plin.

glubo.full: glūbo, ĕre, v. a. and n. Gr. γλύφω; cf. sculpo (ante-class.). Act., to deprive of its bark, to bark, peel: salictum glubito arteque alligato, Cato, R. R. 33, 5: ramos, Varr. R. R. 1, 55, 2.—In mal. part.: (Lesbia) Glubit magnanimos Remi nepotes (v. deglubo), Cat. 58, 5.— Neutr., to cast off its shell or bark: materies, Cato, R. R. 31, 2; 17, 1.

glucidatum.full: glucidatum suave et jucundum. Graeci enim γλυκὺν dulcem dicunt, Paul. ex Fest. p. 98 Müll.

gluma.full: glūma, ae, f. glubo, a hull or husk, esp. of corn (cf.: stramentum, palea, acus): arista et granum omnibus fere notum; gluma paucis. Itaque id apud Ennium solum scriptum scio esse, Varr. R. R. 1, 48, 1 sq. (cf. Enn. p. 174 Vahl.); Paul. ex Fest. s. h. v. p. 98 Müll.

gluo.full: gluo συστύφω (to draw together), Gloss. Philox. (hence glutus, gluten, glus).

glus.full: glus, ūtis, f. Gr. γλοιός, sticky oil; γλία, slime, gluten, glue; for the usual gluten, Aus. Idyll. monos. per interr. 12, 10; Veg. Vet. 3, 66.

glut glut.full: glut glut, an onomatop. word imitating the sound of water falling through a narrow aperture, Poët. ap. Anthol. Lat. 2, 405 Burm.

gluten.full: glūten, ĭnis, n. (masc. acc. to Mart. Cap. 3, § 296), and glūtĭnum, i, n. v. glus; cf. λισός, λισσός, smooth; γλίσχρος, sticky, glue. Lit., form gluten: collectumque haec ipsa ad munera gluten, Verg. G. 4, 40; Lucr. 6, 1069; Verg. G. 4, 160; Cels. 8, 7; Plin. 16, 40, 79, § 215 al.; form glutinum. glutinum ferunt Daedalum invenisse, Varr. ap. Charis. p. 67 and 106; Sall. Fragm. ib.; Cels. 5, 5; Plin. 11, 39, 94, § 231; 13, 12, 26, § 82; 28, 17, 71, § 236; Vitr. 7, 10; Aus. Idyll. 12, 10 al.— Tran

glutinamentum.full: glūtĭnāmentum, i, n. glutino, that which is glued together, a glued or pasted place in paper, Plin. 13, 12, 25, § 81.

glutinarius.full: glūtĭnārĭus, ii, m. gluten, a glueboiler, Inscr. Orell. 4198.

glutinatio.full: glūtĭnātĭo, ōnis, f. glutino, a gluing together; transf., in medic., a drawing together, closing of wounds: vulneris, i. e. a closing up, Cels. 7, 27, § 28.

glutinativus.full: glūtĭnātīvus, a, um, adj. id., in medic., that glues or draws together (postclass.): virtus, App. Herb. 72; 77.

glutinator.full: glūtĭnātor, ōris, m. id., a gluer together of books, a bookbinder, Cic. Att. 4, 4, b, 1; Inscr. Orell. 2925 (cf. ib. 4198).

glutinatorius.full: glūtĭnātōrĭus, a, um, adj. id., in medic., that glues or draws together: virtus, Theod. Prisc. de Diaet. 10.

glutineus.full: glūtĭnĕus, a, um, adj. gluten, gluey, glutinous, Rutil. Itin. 1, 610.

glutino.full: glūtĭno, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. gluten, to glue, glue together. Lit.: chartas, Plin. 22, 25, 60, § 127: fragmenta vitri, id. 29, 3, 11, § 51.— Transf., in medic., to close up, join an opening, esp. a wound: glutinantia medicamenta, Cels. 7, 4: cicatricibus glutinandis, Plin. 33, 6, 35, § 105: praecisos nervos, id. 25, 5, 19, § 43; Cels. 7, 28; cf.: si orae vulneris se glutinarunt, id. 7, 27 fin.

glutinosus.full: glūtĭnōsus, a, um, adj. id., full of glue, gluey, glutinous, viscous, tenacious: terra, Col. 1 praef. § 24: caro, Cels. 2, 22.— Comp.: pus et sanguine et sanie, Cels. 5, 26, 20.—Sup.: terra, Col. 3, 11, 10: resina, Cels. 6, 7, 5.

glutio.full: glūtĭo or gluttio, īvi or ĭi, ītum, 4, v. a. kindr. with Sanscr. glri, to swallow down; hence also gula and the redupl. gurgulio, to swallow or gulp down: gluttit, ἐγκάπτει, Gloss. (mostly post-Aug.). Lit.: nimio sunt crudae (collyrae), nisi quas madidas gluttias, Plaut. Pers. 1, 3, 15: epulas, Juv. 4, 29: micularum minimum cum vino destillatum gluttivi, Fronto Ep. 5, 40 Mai.; Vulg. Job, 7, 19.— Transf., of sound, to utter interruptedly, as if swallowing: cum glutiunt vocem velut strangulati, Pl
glutio.short: glūtĭo or gluttio, īvi or ĭi, ītum, 4, v.

gluto.full: glūto or glutto, ōnis, m. 1. glutio, a glutton, gormandizer, Pers. 5, 112; Poët. ap. Anth. Lat. 2, 405; cf. Paul. ex Fest. s. v. ingluvies, p. 112 Müll.; Schol. Jus. 4, 17; 29; Isid. Orig. 10, 114.

glutus.full: glūtus or gluttus, a, um, adj. lit., part. of † gluo, drawn together; hence opp. to crumbling, friable, tenacious, well-tempered, soft: locus bipalio subactus siet beneque terra tenera siet beneque glutus siet, Cato, R. R. 45, 1; also ap. Plin. 17, 18, 29, § 125.—Here too belongs glittis subactis, levibus, teneris, Paul. ex Fest. p. 98 Müll. N. cr.
glutus.short: glūtus or gluttus, a, um, adj.

glycera.full: Glўcĕra, ae, f., = Γλυκερά, a Greek female name. A celebrated courtesan at Athens, the mistress of the poet Menander, Mart. 14, 187.— A mistress of Horace, Hor. C. 1, 19, 5; 1, 30, 3.— A mistress of Tibullus, Hor. C. 1, 33, 2.
glycera.short: Glўcĕra, ae, f., = Γλυκερά, a Greek female name.

glycerium.full: Glўcĕrĭum, ii, f., = Γλυκέριον, the name of a female character in the Andria of Terence, Ter. And. 1, 1, 108.
glycerium.short: Glўcĕrĭum, ii, f., = Γλυκέριον, the name of a female character in the Andria of Terence, Ter.

glycon.full: Glўcon or Glўco, ōnis, m., = Γλύκων, a Greek proper name. A wrestler, Hor. Ep. 1, 1, 30.— A physician, Suet. Aug. 11.
glycon.short: Glўcon or Glўco, ōnis, m., = Γλύκων, a Greek proper name.

glyconius.full: Glўcōnīus, a, um, adj., = Γλυκώνειος, Glyconic: metrum, so called from its inventor, Glycon, Sid. Ep. 9, 13.
glyconius.short: Glўcōnīus, a, um, adj., = Γλυκώνειος, Glyconic: metrum, so called from its inventor, Glycon, Sid.

glycymeris.full: glўcўmĕris, ĭdis, f., = γλυκυμερίς, a kind of shell-fish, Plin. 32, 11, 53, § 147; Macr. S. 2, 9 med.
glycymeris.short: glўcўmĕris, ĭdis, f., = γλυκυμερίς, a kind of shell-fish, Plin.

glycyrrhiza.full: glўcyrrhīza, ae, f., = γλυκύῤῥιζα, licorice-root, Plin. 22, 9, 11, § 24.—Also called glўcyrrhīzon, i, n., = γλυκύῤῥιζον, Plin. 11, 54, 119, § 284 (called by Cels. 5, 23, dulcis radix).
glycyrrhiza.short: glўcyrrhīza, ae, f., = γλυκύῤῥιζα, licorice-root, Plin.

glycyside.full: glўcўsīde, ēs, f., = γλυκυσίδη, a peony, Plin. 25, 4, 10, § 29; 27, 10, 60, § 84 sq.; collat. form glўcўsis, ĭdis, f., App. Herb. 64.
glycyside.short: glўcўsīde, ēs, f., = γλυκυσίδη, a peony, Plin.

gnaphalion.full: gnaphălĭon, ii, n., = γναφάλιον, the herb cudweed, cotton-grass, Plin. 27, 10, 61, § 88.
gnaphalion.short: gnaphălĭon, ii, n., = γναφάλιον, the herb cudweed, cotton-grass, Plin.

gnarigavit.full: gnarigavit significat apud Livium (Andron.) narravit, Paul. ex Fest. p. 95 Müll. N. cr. [gnarus].
gnarigavit.short: gnarigavit significat apud Livium (Andron.) narravit, Paul.

gnaritas.full: gnārĭtas, ātis, f. gnarus, knowledge (very rare): locorum, Sall. Fragm. ap. Non. 116, 22; Amm. 16, 2, 10.

gnarivisse.full: gnarivisse narrasse, Paul. ex Fest. p. 95 Müll. N. cr.; cf.: † gnaritur γνωρίζεται, Gloss. Philox.

gnarus.full: gnārus, a, um (also ante- and postclass. form gnārŭris, e, Plaut. Most. 1, 2, 17; id. Poen. prol. 47; Aus. Ep. 22, 19; Arn. 3, 113; and cf.: gnaruris γνώριμος, Gloss. Philox.—Another form is † nārus, like navus, notus, acc. to Cic. Or. 47, 158), adj. Sanscr. gna-, ganāmi, know; Gr. γιγνώσκω; Lat. gnosco, nosco, narrare, etc., knowing or acquainted with a thing; skilful, practised, expert (syn. doctus, eruditus, peritus). Lit. (rare but class.); constr. with gen., or with a rel. or object-clause;
gnarus.short: gnārus, a, um (also ante- and postclass.

gnatho.full: Gnătho, ōnis, m., = Γνάθων, a parasite in the Eunuchus of Terence; hence used to denote a parasite in gen., Cic. Lael. 25, 93 sq.; id. Phil. 2, 6, 15; Sid. Ep. 3, 13.— Deriv.: Gnăthōnĭci, ōrum, m., qs. disciples of Gnatho, Gnathonites, i. e. parasites, Ter. Eun. 2, 2, 33.
gnatho.short: Gnătho, ōnis, m., = Γνάθων, a parasite in the Eunuchus of Terence;

gnatia.full: Gnātia, ae, i. q. Egnatia, Hor. S. 1, 5, 97, v. Egnatia.

gnatus.full: gnātus, a, um, v. natus under nascor.

gnave.full: gnāve, gnāvĭtas, gnāvĭter, gnāvus, v. under nav-.

gneus.full: Gnēus (also Gnaeus or Cnaeus), i, m., a Roman praenomen, cf. Quint. 1, 7, 28.
gneus.short: Gnēus (also Gnaeus or Cnaeus), i, m., a Roman praenomen, cf.

gnidus.full: Gnĭdus or Gnĭdos (also Cnĭd-), i, f., = Κνίδος, a Doric city in Caria, celebrated for its statue of Venus, the workmanship of Praxiteles; now Cnido, Mel. 1, 16, 2; Plin. 5, 28, 29, § 104; Hor. C. 1, 30, 1; 3, 28, 13; Ov. M. 10, 531; Cic. de Imp. Pomp. 12, 33; Liv. 37, 16.— Deriv. Gnĭdĭus (Cn-), a um, adj., of or belonging to Gnidus, Gnidian: Venus, Plin. 36, 5, 4, § 23: Gyges, Hor. C. 2, 5, 20: granum, i. e. the seed of the mezereon, Plin. 13, 21, 35, § 114: arundo, i. e. Gnidian writingreed, Au
gnidus.short: Gnĭdus or Gnĭdos (also Cnĭd-), i, f., = Κνίδος, a Doric city in Caria, celebrated for its statue of Venus, the workmanship of Praxiteles;

gnipho.full: Gnīpho, ōnis, m., a Roman surname: M. Antonius Gnipho, a rhetorician at Rome in the time of Cicero, Quint. 1, 6, 23 al.
gnipho.short: Gnīpho, ōnis, m., a Roman surname: M.

gnitus.full: gnitus et gnixus a genibus prisci dixerunt, Paul. ex Fest. p. 96 Müll. N. cr.; v. 1. nitor.
gnitus.short: gnitus et gnixus a genibus prisci dixerunt, Paul.

gnome.full: gnōme, ēs, f., = γνώμη, a sentence, maxim; pure Lat., sententia, Fronto Ep. 3, 11 Mai.
gnome.short: gnōme, ēs, f., = γνώμη, a sentence, maxim;

gnomon.full: gnōmon, ŏnis, m., = γνώμων, the pin or style of a sundial, the gnomon, Plin. 2, 72, 74, § 182; Vitr. 1, 6; 9, 8; Mart. Cap. 6, 194.
gnomon.short: gnōmon, ŏnis, m., = γνώμων, the pin or style of a sundial, the gnomon, Plin.

gnomonicus.full: gnōmŏnĭcus, a, um, adj., = γνωμονικός, of or belonging to a gnomon, and, in gen., of or belonging to a sundial, gnomonic. Adj.: rationes, Vitr. 9, 3 fin.: res, id. 1, 1 fin.— Subst. gnōmŏ-nĭca, ae, and gnōmŏnĭce, es, f., = γνωμονική, the art of making or judging of sundials, the art of dialling, gnomonics, Gell. 1, 9, 6; Vitr. 1, 3; Plin. 2, 76, 78, § 187. — gnōmŏnĭci, ōrum, m., = γνωμονικοί, persons skilled in gnomonics, diallists, Sol. 37, 3.
gnomonicus.short: gnōmŏnĭcus, a, um, adj., = γνωμονικός, of or belonging to a gnomon, and, in gen., of or belonging to a sundial, gnomonic.

gnostice.full: gnostĭcē, es, f., = γνωστική, insight, the power of perceiving, Fulg. Myth. 3, 10.
gnostice.short: gnostĭcē, es, f., = γνωστική, insight, the power of perceiving, Fulg.

gnostici.full: Gnostĭci, ōrum, m., = Γνωστικοί, the Gnostics, a religious sect in the first centuries of the Christian era, Aug. de Haeres. 6. So a work of Tertullian is entitled: adversus Gnosticos.
gnostici.short: Gnostĭci, ōrum, m., = Γνωστικοί, the Gnostics, a religious sect in the first centuries of the Christian era, Aug.

gnosus.full: Gnōsus or Gnōsos (also Gnoss- and Cnoss-), i, f., = Κνωσός (Κνωσσός), the ancient capital of Crete, the residence of Minos; now Cnosson, Mel. 2, 7, 12; Plin. 4, 12, 20, § 59; Luc. 3, 185 Cort. N. cr.; Lact. 1, 11, 46.— Derivv. Gnōsĭus (Gnoss-, Cnōs-, or Cnoss-), a, um, adj., of or belonging to Gnosus, or poet., in gen., to Crete, Gnosian, Cretan: Ctesiphon, of Gnosus, Plin. 7, 37, 38, § 125: Epimenides, id. 7, 48, 49, § 154: calami spicula, Hor. C. 1, 15, 17: castra, of Minos, Ov. M. 8, 40: regn
gnosus.short: Gnōsus or Gnōsos (also Gnoss- and Cnoss-), i, f., = Κνωσός (Κνωσσός), the ancient capital of Crete, the residence of Minos;

gnotus.full: gnōtus, a, um, v. nosco init.

gobius.full: gōbĭus (also cōb-), ii, and gōbio, ōnis, m., = κωβιός, a fish of small value, the gudgeon, Ov. Hal. 128; Plin. 9, 57, 83, § 175; Mart. 13, 88; Juv. 11, 37; Aus. Idyll. 10, 131; form cobio, Plin. 32, 11, 53, § 146.
gobius.short: gōbĭus (also cōb-), ii, and gōbio, ōnis, m., = κωβιός, a fish of small value, the gudgeon, Ov.

golgoe.full: Golgoe or Golgi, ōrum, m., = Γολγοί, a town of Cyprus, famous for the worship of Aphrodite (Venus), Plin. 5, 31, 35, § 130; Cat. 36, 14; 64, 96.
golgoe.short: Golgoe or Golgi, ōrum, m., = Γολγοί, a town of Cyprus, famous for the worship of Aphrodite (Venus), Plin.

gomorra.full: Gŏmorra or Gŏmorrha, ae, f., = Γόμοῤῥα, the city of Gomorrha, in Palestine, Vulg. Gen. 10, 19; 14, 2; 19, 28 et saep.; called also Gŏmorrhum, Tert. Apol. 40; Sol. 35.— Deriv.: Gŏmorrhaeus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Gomorrha: ruinae, Prud. Ham. 844.
gomorra.short: Gŏmorra or Gŏmorrha, ae, f., = Γόμοῤῥα, the city of Gomorrha, in Palestine, Vulg.

gomphi.full: Gomphi, ōrum, m., = Γόμφοι, a town of Thessaly on the Penēus, now Kalabaki, Plin. 4, 8, 15, § 29 sq.; Caes. B. C. 3, 80, 1: Liv. 31, 41; 32, 14; 36, 13 al.— Deriv. Gomphenses, ium, m., the inhabitants of Gomphi, Gomphians, Caes. B. C. 3, 81.
gomphi.short: Gomphi, ōrum, m., = Γόμφοι, a town of Thessaly on the Penēus, now Kalabaki, Plin.

gomphus.full: gomphus, i, m., = γόμφος, a nail, peg, Tert. Mag. 12; Stat. S. 4, 3, 48.
gomphus.short: gomphus, i, m., = γόμφος, a nail, peg, Tert.

gongylis.full: gongўlis, ĭdis, f., = γογγυλίς, a rape, turnip, Col. poët. 10, 421.
gongylis.short: gongўlis, ĭdis, f., = γογγυλίς, a rape, turnip, Col.

goniaea.full: goniaea, ae, f., a precious stone, otherwise unknown, Plin. 37, 10, 59, § 164.
goniaea.short: goniaea, ae, f., a precious stone, otherwise unknown, Plin.

gonni.full: Gonni, ōrum, m., a town of Thessaly near the Vale of Tempe, now Lycóstomo, Liv. 33, 10; 36, 10.—Also in the sing.: Gonnus, i, m., Liv. 42, 54; 67; 44, 6.
gonni.short: Gonni, ōrum, m., a town of Thessaly near the Vale of Tempe, now Lycóstomo, Liv.

gonnocondylum.full: Gonnocondўlum, i, n., a town of Thessaly, Liv. 39, 25 fin.
gonnocondylum.short: Gonnocondўlum, i, n., a town of Thessaly, Liv.

gonorrhoea.full: gŏnorrhoea, ae, f., = γονόρροια, a seminal flux, gonorrhœa, Firm. Math. 3, 7, 8.
gonorrhoea.short: gŏnorrhoea, ae, f., = γονόρροια, a seminal flux, gonorrhœa, Firm.

gordianus.full: Gordĭānus, i, m., a Roman proper name; in partic., the name of three Roman emperors, Capitol. Gord.— Deriv. Gordĭānus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to the emperor Gordian, Gordian: LEGIO, Inscr. Grut. 53, 10; Inscr. Don. cl. 3, no. 48.
gordianus.short: Gordĭānus, i, m., a Roman proper name;

gordium.full: Gordĭum, ii, n., = Γόρδιον, a city of Phrygia Major on the Sangarius, famous for the Gordian knot (v. Gordius), Plin. 5, 32, 42, § 146; Liv. 38, 18, 10 sqq.; Curt. 3, 1, 12 sqq.—Hence, Gordĭensis, e, adj., of Gordium, Scrib. 172.
gordium.short: Gordĭum, ii, n., = Γόρδιον, a city of Phrygia Major on the Sangarius, famous for the Gordian knot (v.

gordius.full: Gordĭus, ii, m., = Γόρδιος, a king of Gordium, in Phrygia Major, famous for the inextricable knot on his chariot, which Alexander the Great cut with his sword, Curt. 3, 1, 15 sqq.; Just. 11, 7, 13 sqq.—Hence, Gordĭus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Gordius: nodus, i. e. an insoluble problem, Amm. 14, 11, 1.
gordius.short: Gordĭus, ii, m., = Γόρδιος, a king of Gordium, in Phrygia Major, famous for the inextricable knot on his chariot, which Alexander the Great cut with his sword, Curt.

gordiutichos.full: Gordiūtīchos, n., a town of Phrygia Major, Liv. 38, 13.
gordiutichos.short: Gordiūtīchos, n., a town of Phrygia Major, Liv.

gordueni.full: Gordŭēni (Cord-) or Gordyaei (Cord-) or Gordaei, ōrum, m., a people of Armenia, the modern Kurds, Plin. 6, 15, 17, § 118; Curt. 5, 1, 7: Gordyaeorum montes, Plin. 6, 27, 31, § 129.
gordueni.short: Gordŭēni (Cord-) or Gordyaei (Cord-) or Gordaei, ōrum, m., a people of Armenia, the modern Kurds, Plin.

gorge.full: Gorge, ēs, f., a daughter of Œneus, and sister of Meleager and Dejanira, who was changed into a bird, Ov. M. 8, 543; Hyg. Fab. 174; the same, Gorgis, ĭdis, ib. 97.
gorge.short: Gorge, ēs, f., a daughter of Œneus, and sister of Meleager and Dejanira, who was changed into a bird, Ov.

gorgias.full: Gorgĭas, ae, m., = Γοργίας. A famous Greek sophist of Leontini, a contemporary of Socrates, Cic. Inv. 1, 5, 7; id. Fin. 2, 1, 1; id. de Or. 1, 22, 103; id. Brut. 8, 30; id. Or. 12, 39 et saep.— A rhetorician in Athens, instructor of Cicero's son, and author of the rhetorical work from which excerpts have been made by Rutilius Lupus, Cic. Fam. 16, 21, 6.— A sculptor of Sparta, Plin. 34, 8, 19, § 49.

gorgo.full: Gorgo, ŏnis, or -gūs (also Gorgŏ-na, ae, Prud. στεφ. 10, 278), f., = Γοργώ, a daughter of Phorcus, called Medusa, whose hair consisted of snakes, and who turned all she looked upon to stone; she was killed by Perseus. Her head was fixed on the shield of Pallas, and from her blood sprang the winged horse Pegasus, Ov. M. 4, 699; 5, 180; 202; Verg. A. 2, 616; 8, 438; Val. Fl. 3, 54; Mart. 9, 26, 5; Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 56, § 124.—In apposition: ora Medusae Gorgonis anguineis cincta fuisse comis, Ov. Tr
gorgo.short: Gorgo, ŏnis, or -gūs (also Gorgŏ-na, ae, Prud.

gorgobina.full: Gorgobĭna, ae, f., a city on the borders of Aquitania, settled by the Boii, perhaps the modern Charlieu, on the Loire, Caes. B. G. 7, 9, 6.
gorgobina.short: Gorgobĭna, ae, f., a city on the borders of Aquitania, settled by the Boii, perhaps the modern Charlieu, on the Loire, Caes.

gorgonidonii.full: Gorgŏnĭdōnĭi campi, a name comically formed, qs. Gorgon-fields, Plaut. Mil. 1, 1, 13; v. Ritschl ad h. l.
gorgonidonii.short: Gorgŏnĭdōnĭi campi, a name comically formed, qs.

gorgonifer.full: gorgŏnĭfer, ĕri, m. Gorgo-fero, the Gorgon-bearer, a poet. epithet of Perseus: PERSEO INVICTO, Inscr. ap. Gud. 56, 8.

gortyn.full: Gortyn, ȳnos, v. the foll. art.

gortyna.full: Gortȳna, ae, and Gortȳne, ēs (also Cortȳnia, ae, Varr. R. R. 1, 7, 6; and Gortyn, nos, acc. to the Gr. Γόρτυν, Val. Fl. 1, 709), f., = Γορτύνη, an important and very ancient city of Crete, Mel. 2, 7, 12; Plin. 4, 12, 20, § 59; 12, 1, 5, § 11; Luc. 3, 186; Sen. Troad. 821.— Derivv. Gortȳnĭus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to the city of Gortyna, Gortynian; and poet., in gen., for Cretan (cf. Gnosius, under Gnosus, II. A.): judex, of Gortyna, Cic. Phil. 5, 5, 13: canis, Varius ap. Macr. S. 6, 2: st
gortyna.short: Gortȳna, ae, and Gortȳne, ēs (also Cortȳnia, ae, Varr.

gorytos.full: gōrȳtos (-us) or cōrȳtos (˘˘, Sid. Carm. 11, 56), i, m., = γωρυτός. A quiver, Verg. A. 10, 169; Ov. Tr. 5, 7, 15; Stat. Th. 4, 269 al.— An arrow: velox, Stat. Th. 7, 660.

gossympinus.full: gossympĭnus, i, f., the cotton-tree, Gossypium arboreum, Linn.; Plin. 12, 10, 21, § 39.—Also called gossypion or gos-sipion, ii, n., Plin. 19, 1, 2, § 14.
gossympinus.short: gossympĭnus, i, f., the cotton-tree, Gossypium arboreum, Linn.;

gothi.full: Gŏthi, ōrum, m., = Γόθοι, the Goths, the great tribe of Northern Germany: huc possem victos inde referre Gŏthos, Aus. Epigr. 3 fin.; Inscr. Orell. 1135; 1159; and scanned Gōthi, id. ib. 1162 (of the year A. D. 565). Usually regarded as the same tribe, called, at an earlier period, Gŏthō-nes or Gŏtōnes, Tac. A. 2, 62; and, Gŭtōnes, Plin. 4, 14, 28, § 99; 37, 2, 11, § 35; but these were more probably the Getae, i. e. the Prussians and Lithuanians; cf. Holzmann ad Tac. G. p. 260 sq.— Derivv.: Gŏthĭ
gothi.short: Gŏthi, ōrum, m., = Γόθοι, the Goths, the great tribe of Northern Germany: huc possem victos inde referre Gŏthos, Aus.

gothini.full: Gothīni, ōrum, m., a Celtic tribe that inhabited the region about the modern Cracow, Tac. G. 43.
gothini.short: Gothīni, ōrum, m., a Celtic tribe that inhabited the region about the modern Cracow, Tac.

gothones.full: Gothones and Gotones, um, v. Gothi.

grabatulus.full: grăbātŭlus, i, m. dim. grabatus, a little couch, a pallet (post-class.), App. M. 1, p. 107 sq.; 2, p. 121.

grabatus.full: grăbātus, i, m. Macedonian, = κράβατος, a small or low couch, a pallet, campbed (syn.: lectus, cubile, stratum, torus), Cic. Div. 2, 63, 129; Lucil. ap. Non. 181, 29; Petr. 97; Sen. Ep. 18; 20; Verg. M. 5; Mart. 6, 39, 4; 12, 32, 11; Cat. 10, 22: argento inaurato tectus, Scaev. Dig. 33, 7, 20 fin.; Vulg. Marc. 2, 4; id. Act. 5, 15; collat. form grăbātum, i, n., Cael. Aur. Acut. 2, 37.

gracchus.full: Gracchus, i, m., a Roman family name in the gens Sempronia; the most celebrated are the two brothers Ti. and C. Sempronius Gracchus, sons of Ti. Sempronius and Cornelia, daughter of Scipio Africanus the elder, Cic. Brut. 86, 296; id. Phil. 7, 6, 17: Cornelia, mater Gracchorum, id. Brut. 58, 210; Juv. 6, 168: Gracchi de seditione querentes, id. 2, 24.— Deriv. Gracchā-nus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to a Gracchus, Gracchan: judices, i. e. the knights who were made judges by a law of C. Gracchus,
gracchus.short: Gracchus, i, m., a Roman family name in the gens Sempronia;

gracilens.full: grăcĭlens, entis, adj. gracilis, slender, thin, for the usual gracilis, Naev. ap. Non. 116, 8; cf. gracilentus.

gracilentus.full: grăcĭlentus, a, um, adj. id., slender, thin (ante- and post-class. for the usual gracilis): filum, Enn. ap. Non. 116, 8 (Ann. v. 259 Vahl.): equus, Gell. 4, 12, 2.

gracilesco.full: grăcĭlesco, ĕre, v. inch. n. [gracilis], to become slender, small (post-class.): obeliscus gracilescens, Amm. 17, 4: pyramidum magnitudo gracilescit paulatim, id. 22, 15.

gracilipes.full: grăcĭlĭpes, pĕdis, adj. gracilis-pes, slender-footed: ciconia, Publ. Syr. ap. Petr. 55.

gracilis.full: grăcĭlis, e (also ante-class. grăcĭlus, a, um, Lucil. ap. Non. 489, 21; plur.: gracilae virgines, Ter. Eun. 2, 3, 22), adj. Sanscr. karc, to be lean; old Lat. cracentes, slender (Enn. Ann. 497 Vahl.); cf. Gr. κολοκάνος, thin, slight, slender, slim; meagre, lean (poet. and in Aug. prose; not in Cic.; but cf. gracilitas; syn.: exilis, tenuis, macer). Physically: in gracili macies crimen habere potest, Ov. R. Am. 328: gracili sic tamque pusillo, Hor. S. 1, 5, 69: quis multa gracilis te puer in rosa

gracilitas.full: grăcĭlĭtas, ātis, f. gracilis, slenderness, thinness, leanness, meagreness. Lit. (class.; syn.: macies, subtilitas): erat eo tempore in nobis summa gracilitas et infirmitas corporis, Cic. Brut. 91, 313: cervicis et crurum, Suet. Calig. 50: crurum, id. ib. 3; id. Dom. 18: digitalis (vitis), Plin. 14, 3, 4, § 40; cf.: papyrum in gracilitatem fastigatum, id. 13, 11, 22, § 71.—Plur.: habet certos sui studiosos (Lysias), qui non tam habitus corporis opimos, quam gracilitates consectentur, Cic. Brut.

gracilitudo.full: grăcĭlĭtūdo, ĭnis, f. gracilis, slenderness, for the class. gracilitas, Att. ap. Non. 116, 6 (Fragm. Trag. v. 88 Rib.).

gracillo.full: gracillo, āre, v. n., to cackle or cluck as a hen: cucurrire solet gallus, gallina gracillat, Auct. Carm. Philom. 25.

gracilus.full: grăcĭlus, a, um, v. gracilis init.

graculus.full: grācŭlus (gracc-), i, m. from its note gra gra, Quint. 1, 6, 37; Isid. Orig. 12, 7, 45, a jackdaw, Corvus monedula, Linn.; Plin. 11, 37, 79, § 201; 11, 47, 107, § 256; 8, 27, 41, § 101; Phaedr. 1, 3, 4; Mart. 1, 116, 6. — Prov. Vetus adagium est: Nihil cum fidibus graculo, i. e. ignorant persons have nothing to do with poetry, Gell. N. A. praef. § 19.— Graculus Aesopi, i. e. one who decks himself out in borrowed plumes, makes a fine show with other people's property, Tert. adv. Val. 12 (cf. Phae

gradalis.full: grădālis, e, adj. gradus, step by step (post-class.): pugna, Diom. p. 473 P.

gradarius.full: grădārĭus, a, um, adj. id., of or belonging to steps, going or proceeding step by step (very rare; not in Cic.). Lit.: equus gradarius, a pacer, ambler, Lucil. ap. Non. 17, 25: pugna, Diom. p. 473 P.— Trop., of a deliberate speaker: Cicero quoque noster gradarius fuit, Sen. Ep. 40, 11.

gradatim.full: grădātim, adv. id., step by step, by degrees, little by little, gradually (class.; syn.: sensim, paulatim, pedetentim): nihil ita pedetentim et gradatim tum accessus a te ad causam facti, tum recessus, ut, etc., Cic. Fam. 9, 14, 7: gradatim ascendere, id. de Or. 3, 61, 227; cf. id. Part. 15, 54: quid opus erat te gradatim istuc pervenire? Sumpsisses tuo jure. Quid autem est istuc gradatim? id. N. D. 1, 32, 89; cf.: gradatim respondens, id. Tusc. 1, 24, 57: ad pauciores deducere, id. ib. 2, 65, 1

gradatio.full: grădātĭo, ōnis, f. id.. * Lit., the making of a staircase or series of steps, as in a theatre: lapideis et marmoreis copiis gradationes (theatri) ab substructione fieri debent, the seats ascending by gradations, Vitr. 5, 3.— Trop., rhet. t. t., a gradation or climax in speaking, Gr. κλῖμαξ: gradatio est, in qua non ante ad consequens verbum descenditur, quam ad superius conscensum est, hoc modo: Nam quae reliqua spes manet libertatis, si illis et quod libet, licet; et quod licet, possunt; et quo

gradatus.full: grădātus, a, um, adj. id., furnished with steps (post-Aug.): densis gradatisque corticum pollicibus ut orbibus, Plin. 13, 4, 7, § 29; Plin. Ep. 5, 6, 17.

gradilis.full: grădĭlis, e, adj. id., of or belonging to steps (post-class.): templum Genii, having steps, Amm. 23, 1: panis, from the steps, i. e. distributed to the poor from an elevated place, Cod. Th. 14, 17, 3 sq. (for which: quem panis alit gradibus dispensus ab altis, Prud. adv. Symm. 1, 584; 2, 948); Schol. Juv. 7, 174.

gradior.full: grădĭor, gressus, 3, v. dep. n. [Sanscr. kra-, kram, to go; Goth. skrei-tan; Germ. schreiten, Schritt], to take steps, to step, walk, go (rare but class.; cf.: eo, grassor, incedo, vado, pergo, etc.): jam vero alia animalia gradiendo, alia serpendo ad pastum accedunt, alia volando, alia nando, etc., Cic. N. D. 2, 47, 122; cf.: quasdam (bestias) esse gradientes, id. Tusc. 5, 13, 38: si graderere tantum, quantum loquere, jam esses ad forum, Plaut. Ps. 4, 7, 138: si maledicetis, vostro gradiar limi

gradivicola.full: Grādīvĭcŏla, ae, m. Gradivus, a worshipper of Mars, Sil. 4, 222.

gradivus.full: Grādīvus (once Grădīvus, Ov. M. 6, 427), i, m. perh. from gradior, he who steps forth, marches out, a surname of Mars: (Numa) Salios item duodecim Marti Gradivo legit, Liv. 1, 20, 4: rex Gradive, Verg. A. 10, 542: Nymphas venerabar agrestes Gradivumque patrem, id. ib. 3, 35: Homericus, Juv. 13, 113: jure venis, Gradive, Ov. F. 2, 861; Juv. 2, 128; so absol.: Gradivus, id. ib. 3, 677; 5, 556; id. M. 14, 820; 15, 863.

gradus.full: grădus, ūs (archaic gen. sing. graduis, Varr. ap. Non. 494, 17; dat. gradu, Lucil. ap. Fest. s. v. remeligines, p. 276 Müll.), m. kindr. with Sanscr. kram, to go; v. gradior, a step, pace (cf.: gressus, passus, incessus). Lit.: ad hanc conversionem, quae pedibus et gradu non egeret, ingrediendi membra non dedit, Cic. Univ. 6: quaenam vox ex te resonans meo gradu remoram facit? Lucil. l. l.: gradum proferre pedum, Enn. ap. Fest. S. V. PEDUM, p. 249, a Müll. (Trag. v. 248 Vahl.): quo nunc incerta

graea.full: Graea, ae, f., = Γραῖα, an ancient town in Bœotia, near Oropus (mentioned by Hom. Il. 2, 498), Stat. Th. 7, 332.
graea.short: Graea, ae, f., = Γραῖα, an ancient town in Bœotia, near Oropus (mentioned by Hom.

graeae.full: Graeae, ārum, f., = Γραῖαι (old women), daughters of Phorcus (hence Phorcydes) and Ceto, sisters and guardians of the Gorgons, gray-haired from their birth, having but one eye and one tooth among them, Hyg. praef. p. 7 Munck.
graeae.short: Graeae, ārum, f., = Γραῖαι (old women), daughters of Phorcus (hence Phorcydes) and Ceto, sisters and guardians of the Gorgons, gray-haired from their birth, having but one eye and one tooth among them, Hyg.

graecalis.full: Graecālis, e, v. Graeci, II. F.

graecanice.full: Graecānĭce, adv., v. Graecanicus, under Graeci, II. C. fin.

graecanicus.full: Graecānĭcus, a, um, v. Graeci, II. C.

graecatus.full: Graecātus, a, um, Part. and P. a., from Graecor.

graece.full: Graece, adv., v. Graeci, II. A. fin. 1.

graeci.full: Graeci, ōrum, m., = Γραικοί, the Grecians, Greeks: contendunt Graecos, Graios memorare solent sos, Enn. ap. Fest. p. 301 Müll. (Ann. v. 358 Vahl.): eos septem, quos Graeci sapientes nominaverunt, Cic. Rep. 1, 7: apud Graecos, id. ib. 1, 3, 5; id. Fl. 27, 64: quia Graecorum sunt antiquissima quaeque Scripta vel optima, etc., Hor. Ep. 2, 1, 28.—Sing.: Graecus, i, m., a Greek: processit ille, et Graecus apud Graecos non de culpa sua dixit, etc., Cic. Fl. 7, 17: ignobilis, Liv. 39, 8, 3: Graecus Gra
graeci.short: Graeci, ōrum, m., = Γραικοί, the Grecians, Greeks: contendunt Graecos, Graios memorare solent sos, Enn.

graecia.full: Graecia, ae, v. Graeci, II. B.

graecigena.full: Graecĭgĕna, ae, m. Graecus-gigno; cf. Grajugena, a Greek by birth (late Lat.), Aug. Civ. D. 18, 18 fin.

graecisso.full: graecisso (-izo), āre, v. n., = Γραικίζω, to imitate the Greeks, to adopt a Grecian manner or tone: atque adeo hoc argumentum graecissat; tamen Non atticissat; verum sicelissat, Plaut. Men. prol. 7; v. Ritschl ad h. l.: graecizat, Consent. 1063 P.

graecitas.full: Graecĭtas, ātis, f. Graecus, Greek, the Greek language (post-class.): facundia Graecitatis, Cod. Th. 14, 9, 3.

graecor.full: graecor, ātus, 1, v. dep. n. [Graeci], to imitate the Greeks, live in the Greek manner: si Romana fatigat Militia assuetum Graecari, Hor. S. 2, 2, 11; cf.: congraecor, pergraecor.—Hence, * graecātus, a, um, P. a., made or composed in the Greek manner: graecatior epistola, App. Mag. p.329.—Plur. as subst.: graecāti, ōrum, m., imitators of the Grecian mode of life, Tert. Pall. 4.

graecostadium.full: Graecostădĭum, ii, n., perh. i. q. Graecostasis: restitutum post incendium, Capitol. Anton. 8.

graecostasis.full: Graecostăsis, is, f., = Γραικόστασις (Greek station or place), a building in Rome, near the Curia and Comitium, where at first Grecian and afterwards other foreign ambassadors took up their abode, Varr. L. L. 5, § 155 Müll.; Cic. Q. Fr. 2, 1, 3; Plin. 7, 60, 60, § 212; 33, 1, 6, § 19 al.; cf. Becker's Antiq. I. p. 284.
graecostasis.short: Graecostăsis, is, f., = Γραικόστασις (Greek station or place), a building in Rome, near the Curia and Comitium, where at first Grecian and afterwards other foreign ambassadors took up their abode, Varr.

graeculio.full: Graecŭlĭo, v. Graeculus, under Graeci, II. D.

graeculus.full: Graecŭlus, a, um, v. Graeci, II. D.

graecus1.full: Graecus, a, um, v. Graeci, II. A.

graii.full: Grāii or Grāi, ōrum (gen. plur. Graium, Enn. ap. Prob. ad Verg. E. 6, 31; Lucr. 2, 600; 5, 405; 6, 754 et saep.), m., a less freq. and mostly poet. form for Graeci, the Grecians, Greeks: Musas quas Grai memorant, Enn. ap. Varr. L. L. 7, § 26 Müll. (Ann. v. 2 Vahl.): cujus ob os Grai ora obvertebant sua, Poët. (perh. Enn.) ap. Cic. Tusc. 3, 18, 39: Pergama circum Hac fugerent Grai, Verg. A. 1, 467: est locus, Hesperiam Grai cognomine dicunt, id. ib. 1, 530; cf. Lucr. 3, 100: Graiorum obscura repe

graioceli.full: Grāiocĕli, ōrum, m., a Gallic tribe in the valleys of Mont Cenis, Caes. B. G. 1, 10, 4 (others read Garoceli).
graioceli.short: Grāiocĕli, ōrum, m., a Gallic tribe in the valleys of Mont Cenis, Caes.

grajugena.full: Grājŭgĕna, ae, m. Graius-gigno; cf. Graecigena, a Grecian by birth, a Greek (poet.): Grajugena, Pac. ap. Cic. N. D. 2, 36, 91: equus Grajugenarum, Lucr. 1, 477: Grajugenūmque domos suspectaque linquimus arva, Verg. A. 3, 550.—Adj.: Grajugenae reges, Stat. Th. 6, 215.

graius.full: Grāius, a, um, v. Graii, II.

grallae.full: grallae, ārum, f. contr. from an obsolete dim., gradula, from gradus; cf. rallum, from rado, stilts, Varr. ap. Non. 115, 21 sq.; cf. the foll. art.

grallator.full: grallātor, ōris, m. grallae, one who goes or runs on stilts, Plaut. Poen. 3, 1, 27; Arn. 2, 88; cf. Varr. L. L. 7, § 69 Müll.; id. ap. Non. 115, 21; Paul. ex Fest. p. 97 Müll.

gramen.full: grāmen, ĭnis, n. Sanscr. root gar-, to swallow; Gr. βορ- in βιβρώσκω, βορά; Lat. -vorus, in carnivorus, vorare, etc.; hence, fuller root gras-; Gr. γράστις; Lat. grāmen for gras-men; cf. Germ. Gras; Engl. grass, grass (cf.: herba, faenum, cespes, glaeba). Sing.: prostrati in gramine molli, Lucr. 2, 29; 5, 1392; Hor. Epod. 2, 24: cervus graminis immemor, id. C. 1, 15, 30: aprici campi, id. A. P. 162: graminis herba, a blade of grass, Verg. E. 5, 26; Liv. 1, 24, 5: floreum, flowery turf, Mart. 9,

gramiae.full: grāmĭae, ārum, f. from γλάμη, a viscous humor, rheum, that collects in the corners of the eyes, Plin. 25, 13, 96, § 155; cf.: gramiae oculorum sunt vitia, quas alii glamas vocant, Paul. ex Fest. p. 96 Müll. N. cr.; cf. Non. 119, 18, and v. gramiosus.

gramineus.full: grāmĭnĕus, a, um, adj. gramen, of grass, covered with grass, grassy. In gen.: campus, Verg. A. 5, 287: palaestrae, id. ib. 6, 642: sedile, id. ib. 8, 176: arae, id. ib. 12, 119: corona obsidionalis, a grass crown presented by those who were delivered from a siege to their deliverer, among the Romans the highest mark of military honor, Liv. 7, 37, 2; cf. Plin. 22, 3, 4, § 6; Gell. 5, 6, 8; cf. Dict. of Antiq. p. 309.— In partic., of Indian reed, bamboo: hasta (Minervae), Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 56, § 12

graminosus.full: grāmĭnōsus, a, um, adj. id., full of grass, grassy: ager, Col. 1 praef. § 25; 7, 9, 8: solum, id. 6 praef. § 1.

gramiosus.full: grāmĭōsus, a, um, adj. gramiae, full of matter or pus: gramiae pituitae oculorum. Caecilius: Gramiosis oculis ipsa, Non. 119, 19 (Com. Fragm. v. 268 Rib.); v. gramiae.

gramma1.full: gramma, ae, f., = γραμμή, a line in writing, a stroke of the pen (post-class.), Macr. Somn. Scip. 1, 5; App. Herb. 108.
gramma1.short: gramma, ae, f., = γραμμή, a line in writing, a stroke of the pen (post-class.), Macr.

gramma2.full: gramma, ătis, n., = γράμμα, a weight of two oboli, Fann. de Pond. 8; 25.
gramma2.short: gramma, ătis, n., = γράμμα, a weight of two oboli, Fann.

grammateus.full: grammăteus, ĕos, m., = γραμματεύς, a scribe, secretary (post-class.): unus, quem cuncti grammatea dicebant, App. M. p. 265, 14.
grammateus.short: grammăteus, ĕos, m., = γραμματεύς, a scribe, secretary (post-class.): unus, quem cuncti grammatea dicebant, App.

grammatias.full: grammătĭas, ae, m., = γραμματίας, jasper striped with white lines, Plin. 37, 9, 37, § 118 (dub.; Jan. monogrammos).
grammatias.short: grammătĭas, ae, m., = γραμματίας, jasper striped with white lines, Plin.

grammatica.full: grammătĭca, ae, v. 1. grammaticus, II. B.

grammaticalis.full: grammătĭcālis, e, adj. grammatica, of or perlaining to grammar, grammatical: figurae, Sid. Ep. 7, 9: palaestra, id. Carm. 23, 212.—Adv.: grammătĭ-cālĭter, grammatically: declinare, Treb. XXX. Tyr. 10, § 5.

grammatice1.full: grammătĭce, ës, v. 1. grammaticus, II. B.

grammaticomastix.full: grammătĭcŏmastix, īgis, m., = γραμματικομάστιξ, a scourge (i. e. reviler, persecutor) of grammarians, Aus. Idyll. 12 in lemm.
grammaticomastix.short: grammătĭcŏmastix, īgis, m., = γραμματικομάστιξ, a scourge (i.

grammaticus1.full: grammătĭcus, a, um, adj., = γραμματικός, of or belonging to grammar, grammatical: ars, Auct. Her. 4, 12, 17; Quint. 1, 5, 54: possis illud grammaticum, hoc rhetoricum magis dicere, id. 9, 3, 2: grammaticas ambire tribus et pulpita, the tribes of the grammarians, Hor. Ep. 1, 19, 40: cum eundem (Tuditanum) de rebus grammaticis scripsisse constet, Varr. L. L. 6, § 36 Müll.— Subst. grammătĭcus, i, m., a grammarian in the more extended sense of the word, a philologist: appellatio grammaticorum Graeca
grammaticus1.short: grammătĭcus, a, um, adj., = γραμματικός, of or belonging to grammar, grammatical: ars, Auct.

grammaticus2.full: grammătĭcus, i, v. 1. grammaticus, II. A.

grammatista.full: grammătista, ae, m., = γραμματιστής, a teacher of grammar or of languages: sunt qui litteratum a litteratore distinguant, ut Graeci grammaticum a grammatista: et illum quidem absolute, hunc mediocriter doctum existiment, Suet. Gramm. 4; id. ib. 24; Mart. Cap. 3, § 229.
grammatista.short: grammătista, ae, m., = γραμματιστής, a teacher of grammar or of languages: sunt qui litteratum a litteratore distinguant, ut Graeci grammaticum a grammatista: et illum quidem absolute, hunc mediocriter doctum existiment, Suet.

grammatodidascalus.full: grammătŏdĭdascălus, i, m., = γραμματοδιδάσκαλος, i. q. grammatista, a teacher of language, Mart. Cap. 3, § 229 (as Greek, Kopp).

grammatophylacium.full: grammătŏphўlăcĭum, ii, n., = γραμματοφυλάκιον, a place for keeping state papers, archives, Dig. 48, 19, 9, § 6.
grammatophylacium.short: grammătŏphўlăcĭum, ii, n., = γραμματοφυλάκιον, a place for keeping state papers, archives, Dig.

grammicus.full: grammĭcus, a, um, adj., = γραμμικός, of or belonging to (geometrical) lines, geometrical: rationes, Vitr. 9, 1: deformationes, draughts, sketches, id. 3 praef. fin.
grammicus.short: grammĭcus, a, um, adj., = γραμμικός, of or belonging to (geometrical) lines, geometrical: rationes, Vitr.

granarium.full: grānārĭum, i, n. granum, a place where corn is kept, a granary, Varr. L. L. 5, § 105 Müll.; but usually in plur.: grā-nārĭa, ōrum, n., in the same sense (syn.: herreum, sirus, cumera): triticum condi oportet in granaria sublimia, quae perflentur vento, etc., Varr. R. R. 1, 57, 1 sq.; Col. 1, 6, 10; Plin. 18, 30, 73, § 302; Pall. 1, 19; Plaut. Truc. 2, 6, 42; Vitr. 6, 9; Cic. Fin. 2, 26, 84; Hor. S. 1, 1, 53; Pers. 5, 110 al.

granatim.full: grānātim, adv. granum, grain by grain, by single grains (post-class.): digerere acervum, App. M. 6, p. 177, 27.

granatus.full: grānātus, a, um, adj. granum, having many grains or seeds: mala, quae Punica vocantur, i. e. a pomegranate, Col. 12, 42, 1.—Hence, subst.: grānātum, i, n., a pomegranate: granata, Col. 12, 46, 2; Plin. 15, 28, 34, § 115; 20, 14, 53, § 149.

grandaevitas.full: grandaevĭtas, ātis, f. grandaevus, great age, longevity (ante-class.), Pac. and Att. ap. Non. 116, 12 sq. (Pac. Fragm. Trag. v. 162; Att. Fragm. Trag. v. 68, 245 Rib.).

grandaevus.full: grandaevus, a, um, adj. grandisaevum, in years, old, aged (poet. and in post-Aug. prose): Nereus, Verg. G. 4, 392: Alethes, id. A. 1, 121: Emathion, Ov. M. 5, 99: pater, id. ib. 8, 519: patres, id. ib. 7, 160: senes, Tac. H. 3, 33: manus, i. e. the Senate, Sil. 16, 653: alios (deos) esse grandaevos semperque canos, alios juvenes atque pueros, Plin. 2, 7, 5, § 17: apes, Verg. G. 4, 178: consilia, of an aged man, Val. Fl. 7, 348.

grande.full: grandē, adv., v. grandis, fin. B.

grandesco.full: grandesco, ĕre, v. inch. n. [grandis], to become great, to grow (poet. and in postAug. prose): quicque sua de materia grandescere alique (preceded by crescere), Lucr. 1, 191; cf. id. 2, 1122; 1160: lentiscus triplici solita grandescere fetu, Cic. poët. Div. 1, 9, 15: grandescunt frumenta, Col. 2, 20, 2: hordeum, Pall. Jun. 2: lignum intus, Plin. 15, 3, 3, § 10.

grandiculus.full: grandĭcŭlus, a, um, adj. dim. [id.], rather large, of moderate size: globi, Plaut. Poen. 2, 35: virgo, Ter. And. 4, 5, 19.

grandifer.full: grandĭfer, ĕra, ĕrum, adj. grandisfero, bearing or producing great things, productive: hae arationes, Cic. Phil. 2, 39, 101; cf. Mart. Cap. 5, § 511: loci facies palmis arboribus grandifera, Auct. Itin. Alex. 20, 51: facta, Nazar. Paneg. Const. 3.

grandificus.full: grandĭfĭcus, a, um, adj. grandis-facio, acting greatly, nobly (late Lat.): mens, Amm. 18, 6, 22.

grandiloquus.full: grandĭlŏquus, i, m. grandis-loquor, speaking grandly or loftily: et grandiloqui, ut ita dicam, fuerunt cum ampla et sententiarum gravitate et majestate verborum, Cic. Or. 5, 20; cf. Quint. 10, 1, 66: stilus, Serv. Verg. Vit.—In a bad sense, grandiloquent: isti grandiloqui (i. e. Stoici), boasters, Cic. Tusc. 5, 31, 89.

grandineus.full: grandĭnĕus, a, um, adj. grando, full of hail (late Lat.): nimbi, Alcim. 3, 329: frigus, id. 5, 190; cf. the foll. art.

grandino.full: grandĭno, āre, 1, v. impers. [id.], to hail. Lit.: quare hieme ningat, non grandinet, Sen. Q. N. 4, 4, 1; Aur. Vict. Vir. Ill. 73, 7.— Transf.: sagittis, plumbo et saxis grandinat, nivit, Pac. ap. Non. 507, 28.— To hail upon: vinea grandinata est, August. ap. Psa. 49.

grandinosus.full: grandĭnōsus, a, um, adj. id., full of hail (post-Aug.): qualitas caeli, Col. 3, 1, 6.

grandio.full: grandĭo, īre, v. a. and n. grandis (ante-class.). Act., to make great, increase, enlarge: grandire est grandem facere, Varr. Rer. Divin. Lib. I.: cum aut humus semina concipere non possit, aut recepta non reddat, aut edita grandire nequeat, Plaut. Aul. (1, 1, 10): Testudineum istum tibi ego grandibo gradum, Non. 115, 1 sq.—Mid.: nec grandiri frugum fetum posse, nec mitescere, to become great, to grow (cf. grandesco), Pac. ap. Non. 115, 11 (Fragm. Trag. v. 142 Rib.).— Neutr., to become great, to

grandis.full: grandis, e, adj. cf. gradus; also Germ. gross; Engl. great, full-grown, large, great, full, abundant (class.; most freq. of things; for syn. cf.: magnus, ingens, amplus, procerus, vastus, enormis). Lit. In gen.: ita, quicquid (olerum) erat, grande erat, Plaut. Cas. 5, 2, 35; cf.: ager novatus et iteratus, quo meliores fetus possit et grandiores edere, Cic. de Or. 2, 30, 131: quae seges grandissima atque optima fuerit, Varr. R. R. 1, 52; 1: farra, old poet. ap. Macr. S. 5, 20 fin.: frumenta, Verg

grandiscapius.full: grandiscāpĭus, a, um, adj. grandis-scapus, having a large stem or trunk: arbores, ut ita dicam, grandiscapiae (shortly before: magnarum arborum truncos cum scapo suo transferri), Sen. Ep. 86, 19.

grandisonus.full: grandĭsŏnus, a, um, adj. grandissonus, high-sounding (late Lat.): modi, Sedul. 1, 2.

granditas.full: grandĭtas, ātis, f. grandis, greatness. * Lit., of age (acc. to grandis, I. B.): aetatis granditas, Sisenn. ap. Non. 115, 13. — Trop., of style (v. grandis, II. B.), grandeur, sublimity (very rare): idque apparet ex genere et granditate verborum, * Cic. Brut. 31, 121: non illi vis, non granditas, non sublimitas defuit, Plin. Ep. 6, 21, 5.

granditer.full: grandĭter, adv., v. grandis fin. A.

grandiusculus.full: grandĭuscūlus, a, um, adj. dim. [grandis, I. B.]. pretty well grown up: virgo, Ter. And. 4, 5, 19 (dub.; Fleck. grandicula).

grando.full: grando, ĭnis, f. (masc., Varr. ap. Non. 208, 11) [Sanscr. hrād-uni, storm; Gr. χάλαζα for χαλαδ-ια], hail, a hail-storm. Lit., Plaut. Most. 1, 2, 58; id. Merc. 5, 2, 19; Cic. N. D. 3, 35, 86; Liv. 28, 37, 7; Verg. G. 1, 449; Hor. C. 1, 2, 2; 3, 1, 29 et saep.: nimbus cum saxea grandine subito est exortus ingens, hailstones, Auct. B. Afr. 47, 1.—In plur.: terrere animos, nimbis, nivibus, grandinibus, etc., Cic. N. D. 2, 5, 14: grandines ruunt, Plin. 2, 38, 38, § 103.— Transf., poet., a shower, i.

graneus.full: grānĕus, a, um, adj. granum, of corn, only as subst.: grānĕa, ae, f. (sc. puls), a sort of frumenty or pap made of pounded corn, Cato, R. R. 86; Hier. Paralip. 1, 23.

granicus.full: Grānīcus, i, m., = Γράνικος, a small river in Mysia, which has its source in Mount Ida, and is famous for the victory of Alexander the Great over the Persians which took place on its banks, Mel. 1, 19, 2; Plin. 5, 32, 40, § 141; Ov. M. 11, 763; Curt. 3, 1, 9.
granicus.short: Grānīcus, i, m., = Γράνικος, a small river in Mysia, which has its source in Mount Ida, and is famous for the victory of Alexander the Great over the Persians which took place on its banks, Mel.

granifer.full: grānĭfer, ĕra, ĕrum, adj. granumfero, grain-bearing, a poet. epithet of ants: agmen, Ov. M. 7, 638.

granius.full: Grānĭus, a, name of a Roman gens: Q. Granius, a praeco, famous for his puns, Lucil. ap. Cic. Brut. 43, 160; 46, 172; Cic. Planc. 14, 33 al.
granius.short: Grānĭus, a, name of a Roman gens: Q.

grannus.full: Grannus, i, m. Ers. and Trel. grian, the sun, a surname of Apollo in several Germanic, Dacian, and Scottish inscriptions, Inscr. Orell. 1997 sq. (cf. Grynēus).

granosus.full: grānōsus, a, um, adj. granum, full of grains: folliculi, Plin. 21, 31, 105, § 177: cortex, id. 21, 4, 10, § 14.

granulum.full: grānŭlum, i, n. dim. id., a small grain (late Lat.), Claud. Mam. Stat. An. 1, 21.

granum.full: grānum, i, n. root gar-; Sanscr. ǵaramí, wear away; whence Gr. γέρων, γραῦς; cf. γῦρις, fine flour, a grain, seed, small kernel: tritici, Plaut. Stich. 4, 1, 52; Cic. Div. 1, 36, 78; cf. Varr. R. R. 1, 48, 2; Col. 2, 9, 13: uvae, Ov. Tr. 4, 6, 10; Val. Max. 9, 12, 8 ext.: turis, Plaut. Poen. 2, 3; cf. turea, Ov. F. 4, 410: fici, Cic. de Sen. 15, 52; Plin. 24, 5, 10, § 16: piperis, a pepper-corn, id. 12, 7, 15, § 30; 23, 8, 78, § 150: papaveris, Ov. Tr. 5, 2, 24 et saep.: salis, Plin. 23, 8, 77,

graphiarius.full: grăphĭārĭus, a, um, adj. graphium, of or belonging to writing-styles: theca, a style-case, Suet. Claud. 35.—Also subst.: grăphĭārĭum, ii, n., Mart. 14, 21.

graphicus.full: grăphĭcus, a, um, adj., = γραφικός, of or belonging to painting or drawing, graphic. Lit., only subst.: grăphĭce, ēs, f. (sc. ars), like ἡ γραφική, the art of drawing, Plin. 35, 10, 36, § 77.— Transf. Picturesque, fine (very rare): eminentes expressiones graphicoteram efficient in aspectu delectationem (Gr. compar. γραφικωτεραν), Vitr. 4, 4.— Of persons, exquisite, elegant, masterly, notable, skilful: graphicum mortalem Antiphonem! Plaut. Stich. 4, 1, 64; cf. id. Ps. 1, 5, 104; 2, 4, 9: nugator,
graphicus.short: grăphĭcus, a, um, adj., = γραφικός, of or belonging to painting or drawing, graphic.

graphiolum.full: grăphĭŏlum, i, n. dim. graphium, a small scion = surculus, Ven. Carm. 5, 15 in lemm.

graphis.full: grăphis, ĭdis and ĭdos, f., = γραφίς. A drawing-pencil, sketching-pen: pingere collibitum est: graphidem date, Ser. ap. Diom. p. 516 P.— Transf., drawing; a draught, design: architectum oportet graphidos scientiam habere, Vitr. 1, 1, 4: alias multa graphidis vestigia exstant in tabulis ac membranis ejus, Plin. 35, 10, 36, § 68.
graphis.short: grăphis, ĭdis and ĭdos, f., = γραφίς.

graphium.full: grăphĭum, ĭi, n., = γραφίον (pure Lat. scriptorium, Isid. 6, 9, 2), a writingstyle, Ov. Am. 1, 11, 23; Sen. Clem. 1, 14; Plin. 16, 38, 73, § 184; Suet. Caes. 82; id. Calig. 28; id. Claud. 15.

grasos.full: grāsŏs, i, m., = γρᾶσος, a kind of seaweed, Plin. 13, 25, 48, § 135.
grasos.short: grāsŏs, i, m., = γρᾶσος, a kind of seaweed, Plin.

grassatio.full: grassātĭo, ōnis, f. grassor, a rioting (post-Aug. and very rare): nocturnae, Plin. 13, 22, 43, § 126; cf. the foll. art. and grassatura.

grassator.full: grassātor, ōris, m. id.. A vagabond, idler: poëticae artis honos non erat. Si qui in ea re studebat, aut sese ad convivia applicabat, grassator vocabatur, Cato ap. Gell. 11, 2, 5.— A disorderly person, one who goes rioting about (esp. at night, whether for fun and enjoyment or for robbery), a rioter, a waylayer, street-robber, footpad: hoc modo viator quoque bene vestitus causa grassatori fuisse dicetur, cur ab eo spoliaretur, Cic. Fat. 15, 34: grassatorum plurimi palam se ferebant succincti fer

grassatura.full: grassātūra, ae, f. id., a rioting, waylaying: in primis tuendae pacis a grassaturis et latrociniis seditionumque licentia curam habuit, Suet. Tib. 37; Dig. 48, 19, 16, § 6.

grassor.full: grassor, ātus, 1 (inf. pres. grassarier, Prud. Ham. 651; act. collat. form grassabamus, App. M. 7, 7), v. dep. n. and a. [gradior], to go, go about (not in Cic. and Cæs.; cf.: gradior, incedo, vado, pergo). Lit. In gen. (mostly ante-class.): hoc grassari gradu, Plaut. Poen. 3, 1, 11: siccine hic cum uvida veste grassabimur? id. Rud. 1, 4, 31; id. Bacch. 5, 2, 19: sine eam pedibus grassari, Titin. ap. Non. 316, 3: recte grassatur via, Nov. ib. 5; Ov. Tr. 2, 477: certum'st moriri, quam hunc pati g

gratatorius.full: grātātōrĭus, a, um, adj. grator, gratulatory (post-class.): apices, Sid. Ep. 5, 16.

grates.full: grātes (usually only in the nom. and acc. plur.; in the abl. gratibus, Tac. A. 12, 37), f. gratus, thanks rendered (esp. to the gods: gratias agere being the usual form to human beings), thanksgiving: ut Ephesiae Dianae lauta laudes Gratesque agam, Plaut. Mil. 2, 5, 2: diis laudes gratesque agunt, Liv. 7, 36, 7; 26, 48, 3; cf. in the following the passages, Tac. A. 1, 69 and 12, 37: vobis (dis) grates ago atque habeo, Plaut. Pers. 5, 1, 4: grates deis immortalibus agere habereque, Liv. 23, 11, 1

gratia.full: grātĭa, ae, f. gratus; lit., favor, both that in which one stands with others and that which one shows to others. (Acc. to gratus, I.) Favor which one finds with others, esteem, regard, liking, love, friendship (syn. favor): pluris pauciorum gratiam faciunt pars hominum quam id quod prosint pluribus, Plaut. Trin. 1, 1, 12: perspicio nihili meam vos facere gratiam, id. Curc. 1, 2, 68: ut majores ejus (Plancii) summum in praefectura florentissima gradum tenuerint et dignitatis et gratiae, Cic. Pla

gratiae.full: Grātiae, ārum, v. gratia, I. B. 2.

gratianopolis.full: Grātĭānŏpŏlis, is, f., a city in Gallia Narbonensis, now Grenoble in Dauphiné, Aug. Civ. Dei, 21, 7, 2; Sid. Ep. 3, 14.
gratianopolis.short: Grātĭānŏpŏlis, is, f., a city in Gallia Narbonensis, now Grenoble in Dauphiné, Aug.

gratianus.full: Grātĭānus, a, um, and Grātiānus, i, v. Gratius, II.
gratianus.short: Grātĭānus, a, um, and Grātiānus, i, v.

gratidius.full: Grātĭdĭus, a, name of a Roman gens, Cic. Leg. 3, 16, 36 al.— Deriv. Grā-tĭdĭānus, a, um, adj., of or pertaining to a Gratidius, Cic. Brut. 45, 168 al.
gratidius.short: Grātĭdĭus, a, name of a Roman gens, Cic.

gratificatio.full: grātĭfĭcātĭo, ōnis, f. gratificor, a showing kindness, doing favors, obligingness, complaisance (rare but class.): conjungitur impudens gratificatio cum acerba injuria, Cic. Agr. 3, 2, 6; id. Mur. 20, 42; id. N. D. 1, 44, 122; Plin. 21, 3, 9, § 12.

gratificor.full: grātĭfĭcor, ātus (act. collat. form gratificat, Cassiod. Var. 7, 6 init.: gratificavit, Vulg. Eph. 1, 6), 1, v. dep. n. and a. [gratus+ facio], to do a favor to a person, to oblige, gratify; also to do a thing as a favor, to make a present of, surrender, sacrifice a thing (class.; cf.: condono, largior): gratificatur mihi gestu accusator: inscientem Cn. Pompeium fecisse significat, Cic. Balb. 6, 14; cf.: quod Pompeio se gratificari putant, id. Fam. 1, 1, 4; Tac. A. 4, 19: ut sit ipsa libertas, i

gratificus.full: grātĭfĭcus, a, um, adj. gratus + facio, kind, obliging (late Lat.): pectus, Paul. Petr. Vit. S. Mart. 2, 716: dominus, Porphyr. Paneg. ad Constant. 1, 6.

gratilla.full: grātilla, ae, f., a kind of cake, otherwise unknown, Arn. 7, 230.
gratilla.short: grātilla, ae, f., a kind of cake, otherwise unknown, Arn.

gratiositas.full: grātĭōsĭtas, ātis, f. gratiosus, agreeableness (post-class.): novitatis gratiositas, Tert. adv. Marc. 1, 9.

gratiosus.full: grātĭōsus, a, um, adj. gratia, full of favor. Enjoying favor, in favor, popular, regarded, beloved, agreeable, etc. (class.; a favorite expression with Cicero, and used mostly of persons): ego Plancium et ipsum gratiosum esse dico et habuisse in petitione multos cupidos sui gratiosos, etc., Cic. Planc. 19, 46: homini honesto, sed non gratiosiori quam Cn. Calidius est, Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 20, § 44: cum adversario gratiosissimo contendat, id. Quint. 1, 2: homines potentes, gratiosi, diserti, id. Cael

gratis.full: grātīs, adv., v. gratia, B. fin.

gratius.full: Grātĭus, a, name of a Roman gens. Gratius, ii, m., the opponent of the poet Archias, Cic. Arch. 4, 8; 6, 12.— Gratius Faliscus, a contemporary of Ovid, author of a poem on hunting, Cynegeticon, Ov. P. 4, 16, 34.— Deriv.: Grātĭānus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to a Gratius, Gratian: vasa ex argento, Plin. 33, 11, 49, § 139.—Subst.: Grātiānus, i, m., son and co-regent of the emperor Valentinian I., from 367 to 383 A. D.
gratius.short: Grātĭus, a, name of a Roman gens.

grator.full: grātor, ātus, 1, v. dep. n. and a. [gratus], to manifest joy, to wish one joy, to congratulate, to rejoice with, rejoice (mostly poet. or in post-Aug. prose; not in Cic.; class. gratulor, congratulor): nec tibi me in hac re gratari decet, Att. ap. Serv. Verg. A. 5, 40: inveni, germana, viam: gratare sorori, Verg. A. 4, 478; Ov. M. 6, 434: invicem inter se gratantes, Liv. 9, 43, 17: nescia, gratentur consolenturne parentem (by zeugma), Ov. M. 1, 578: Jovis templum gratantes ovantesque adire, Liv.

gratuitus.full: grātŭītus (grātŭĭtum, Stat. S. 1, 6, 16), a, um, adj. gratia, that is done with, out pay, reward, or profit; free, spontaneous, voluntary, gratuitous (class.): ea (examina apium) vel aere parta vel gratuita contingunt, Col. 9, 8, 1: quid? liberalitas gratuitane est an mercenaria? si sine praemio benigna est, gratuita: si cum mercede, conducta, Cic. Leg. 1, 18, 48; cf.: probitas gratuita, id. Fin. 2, 31, 99: hominum caritas et amicitia gratuita est, id. N. D. 1, 44, 122: ne gratuita quidem suffra

gratulabundus.full: grātŭlābundus, a, um, adj. gratulor, congratulating: Quo se omnis multitudo gratulabunda effudit, Liv. 7, 33, 18; Suet. Galb. 19.—With dat.: velut gratulabundus patriae exspiravit, Just. 6, 8, 13.

gratulatio.full: grātŭlātĭo, ōnis, f. id., a manifestation of joy; a wishing joy, congratulation; a rejoicing, joy (class.). In gen., constr. usu. with gen. or absol.: nuntiatur mihi, tantam isti gratulationem esse factam, ut, etc., Cic. Verr. 1, 8, 21: gratulationes habere, id. Mil. 35, 98: unius diei, id. Pis. 3, 7: laudis nostrae gratulatio tua, id. Att. 1, 17, 6: quam (imaginem parentis sui) paucis ante diebus laureatam in sua gratulatione conspexit, during the congratulations made to him (on account of obta

gratulator.full: grātŭlātor, a congratulator, Mart. 10, 74, 1 (also in a spurious passage in Cic. Fin. 2, 33, 108; v. Madv. ad h. l.).

gratulatorius.full: grātŭlātōrĭus, a, um, adj. gratulor, congratulatory (post-class.): epistola, Capitol. Max. et Balb. 17: cena, Jul. Val. Rer. Gest. Alex. 3, 34 al.—Adv.: grātŭ-lātōrĭē, in a congratulatory manner: mirari, Aug. Conf. 8, 6.

gratulor.full: grātŭlor, ātus, 1, v. dep. n. and a. [gratus]. To manifest one's joy, i. e. to wish a person joy, to congratulate; or to rejoice (freq. and class.; cf. grator).—Constr., alicui, (alicui) de aliqua re or aliquid, quod, rarely in, pro aliqua re, aliqua re, alicui rei, an object-clause, or absol.: unum illud nescio, gratulerne tibi, an timeam, etc., Cic. Fam. 2, 5, 2; cf. id. ib. 2, 9, 1: gratulor tibi, mi Balbe, vereque gratulor, id. ib. 6, 12, 1: ipse mihi gratulatus sum, id. ib. 3, 11, 2: sibi,

gratus.full: grātus, a, um, adj. Sanscr. har-jami, love, desire; Gr. χαίρω, χάρμα, χάρις. Pass., beloved, dear, acceptable, pleasing, agreeable (syn.: acceptus, jucundus, optatus, dulcis, blandus, suavis; in this signif. in ante-Aug. prose, viz. in Cic. and Cæs., only of things; gratiosus, mostly of persons). Of things: non ille (amor tuus) quidem mihi ignotus, sed tamen gratus et optatus: dicerem jucundus, nisi id verbum in omne tempus perdidissem, Cic. Fam. 5, 15, 1; cf.: illud tamen dicam, mihi id, quod f

graupius.full: Graupĭus (Gramp-) mons, a mountain in the north of Britain, Tac. Agr. 29.
graupius.short: Graupĭus (Gramp-) mons, a mountain in the north of Britain, Tac.

gravabilis.full: grăvābĭlis, e, adj. gravo, oppressive, troublesome (post-class.): cibi, Cael. Aur. Tard. 3, 17: vomitus capiti, id. ib. 4, 3: odor, id. Acut. 1, 15, 136.

gravamen.full: grăvāmen, ĭnis, n. id., trouble, physical inconvenience (late Lat.), Cassiod. Varr. 9, 2; Cod. Just. 5, 30, 5.

gravastellus.full: grāvastellus, i, m. dim. † gravaster, from † gravus, kindr. to γραῦς and the Ger. grau; Engl. gray; the ground-form of ravus, a gray-headed fellow: quis est haec muliercula et illic gravastellus qui venit? Plaut. Ep. 5, 1, 14; cf.: gravastellus senior, Paul. ex Fest. p. 96 Müll. (where it is erroneously derived from gravis; moreover, he reads s. v. Ravi coloris, p. 272, in Plautus, ravistellus).

gravatim.full: grăvātim, adv. gravo, with difficulty, unwillingly (very rare for the usual gravate): cadere, Lucr. 3, 387: haud gravatim socia arma Rutulis junxit, Liv. 1, 2, 3.

gravatio.full: grăvātĭo, ōnis, f. id., heaviness, oppression (post-class.): post cibum, Cael. Aur. Acut. 2, 32, 171; id. Tard. 5, 10, 96; 4, 3, 33.

gravedinosus.full: grăvēdĭnōsus, a, um, adj. gravedo, subject to colds or catarrhs, that easily takes cold. Lit.: sunt alii ad alios morbos procliviores: itaque dicimus gravedinosos quosdam, quosdam torminosos, non quia jam sint, sed quia saepe sint, *Cic. Tusc. 4, 12, 27.— Transf., that produces colds: ervum, Plin. 18, 15, 38, § 139.

gravedo.full: grăvēdo, ĭnis, f. gravis. Heaviness of the limbs, cold in the head, catarrh: quasi gravedo profluat, Plaut. As. 4, 1, 51; Cels. 4, 2, 4; Cic. Att. 10, 16, 6; 16, 14, 4; Cat. 44, 13; Plin. 23, 1, 6, § 10; 25, 13, 94, § 150; 30, 4, 11, § 31.—In plur., Cels. 1, 2; of heaviness in the head produced by intoxication: ad crapulae gravedines, Plin. 20, 13, 51, § 136.— Pregnancy, Nemes. Cyneg. 132.

graveolens.full: grăvĕŏlens (also separately: grave olens), entis, adj. gravis-, 1. oleo. * Strong - smelling: graveolentia centaurea, Verg. G. 4, 270.— In a bad sense. illsmelling, noisome, rank: fauces graveolentis Averni, Verg. A. 6, 201; App. de Mundo, p. 74.
graveolens.short: grăvĕŏlens (also separately: grave olens), entis, adj.

graveolentia.full: grăvĕŏlentĭa, ae, f. graveolens, II., an offensive or rank smell, fetidness (Plin. ian): alarum, Plin. 22, 22, 43, § 87: oris, id. ib.: narium, id. 20, 9, 36, § 92.

gravesco.full: grăvesco, ĕre, v. inch. n. [gravis], to become burdened or heavy (poet. and in postAug. prose). Lit. In gen.: fetu nemus omne gravescit, i. e. becomes loaded, filled, Verg. G. 2, 429.— In partic., to become pregnant: cameli lac habent, donec iterum gravescant, Plin. 11, 41, 96, § 236.— Trop., to become grievous or bad, to grow worse: aerumna gravescit, Lucr. 4, 1069: impetus, id. 6, 337: haec in morte, id. 3, 1022: valetudo Augusti, Tac. A. 1, 5: publica mala in dies, id. ib. 14, 51.— To be cumb

graviditas.full: grăvĭdĭtas, ātis, f. gravidus, pregnancy (very rare; perh. ἅπαξ εἰρημ.); ab eo (Sole) Luna illuminata graviditates et partus afferat maturitatesque gignendi, *Cic. N. D. 2, 46, 119.

gravido.full: grăvĭdo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. id., to burden, load. In gen.: gravidavit = implevit. Caecilius: Per mysteria hic inhoneste gravidavit probro, Non. 118, 12 sq. (Caecil. Com. Fragm. v. 223 Rib.).— In partic., to impregnate: gravidari ex aliquo, Aur. Vict. Epit. 14.—Transf.: quae (terra) gravidata seminibus omnia pariat et fundat ex sese, *Cic. N. D. 2, 33, 83.

gravidus.full: grăvĭdus, a, um, adj. gravis, burdened, loaded; hence in partic., pregnant, with child, with young (class.; syn. praegnans, fetus). Lit. Adj.: mater, Enn. ap. Cic. Ac. 2, 17, 52 (Trag. v. 57 Vahl.): puero gravida, Plaut. Am. 2, 2, 87: gravida esse ex aliquo viro, id. ib. prol. 111; Ter. Hec. 3, 3, 32; for which also simply aliquo, Plaut. Am. 3, 1, 18 and 19: de semine Jovis, Ov. M. 3, 260: virgo ex eo compressu, Ter. Ad. 3, 4, 28: prius gravida facta est, Plaut. Cist. 2, 3, 73: facere gravidam a

gravis.full: grăvis, e, adj. Sanscr. gurus (root gar-); Gr. βαρύς, heavy; gravis, for gar-uis; cf. also Brutus.
