With respect to weight, heavy, weighty, ponderous, burdensome; or pass., loaded, laden, burdened (opp. levis, light; in most of its significations corresp. to the Gr. βαρύς; cf. onerosus, onerarius). Lit. Absol. or with abl. In gen.: imber et ignis, spiritus et gravis terra, Enn. ap. Varr. L. L. 7, § 37 Müll.; so, tellus, Ov. M. 7, 355: corpora, Lucr. 2, 225 sq.; cf. id. 5, 450 sq.: limus, id. 5, 4

graviscae.full: Grăviscae, ārum (also Grăvisca, ae, Vell. 1, 15, 2), f., a small town of Etruria, belonging to the territory of Tarquinii, near the modern Le Saline or S. Clementino, on the river Marta, Mel. 2, 4, 9; Plin. 3, 5, 8, § 51; Liv. 40, 29; 41, 16; Verg. A. 10, 184; Sil. 8, 475.— Deriv. Grăviscā-nus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Graviscœ, Graviscan: vina, Plin. 14, 6, 8, § 67.— In plur. subst.: Grăviscāni, ōrum, m., the inhabitants of Graviscœ, Graviscans, Dig. 31, 1, 30; Inscr. Grut. 407, 1.

gravisonus.full: grăvĭsŏnus, a, um, adj. gravis-sonus, having a deep or heavy sound, as defin. of sonorus, Serv. Verg. A. 1, 53.

gravitas.full: grăvĭtas, ātis, f. gravis, weight, heaviness. Lit., in gen.: omnibus ejus (terrae) partibus in medium vergentibus nihil interrumpat, quo labefactari possit tanta contentio gravitatis et ponderum, Cic. N. D. 2, 45, 116; cf.: per inane moveri gravitate et pondere, id. Fat. 11, 24; Lucr. 3, 1054; cf. also: cuncta necesse est Aut gravitate sua ferri primordia rerum, Aut, etc., id. 2, 84: nostros propter gravitatem armorum, quod, etc., Caes. B. G. 5, 16, 1: tum etiam gravitate et tarditate navium imp

gravitudo.full: grăvĭtūdo, ĭnis, f. gravis, a cold in the head, catarrh (very rare): sine ructu et gravitudine, Apic. 3, 6, 76: arterica, Vitr. 1, 6, 3.

graviusculus.full: grăvĭuscŭlus, a, um, adj. dim. [gravis, I. B. 1.], of tones, rather deep: sonus, Gell. 1, 11, 13.

gravo.full: grăvo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. gravis. To charge with a load, to load, burden, weigh down, oppress (mostly poet. and in postAug. prose). Lit.: praefectum castrorum sarcinis gravant, Tac. A. 1, 20; cf.: ferus Actora magno Ense gravat Capaneus, Stat. Th. 10, 257: non est ingenii cymba gravanda tui, Prop. 3, 3 (4, 2), 22: aegraque furtivum membra gravabat onus, Ov. H. 11, 38: gravantur arbores fetu, Lucr. 1, 253; cf.: sunt poma gravantia ramos, Ov. M. 13, 812: ne, si demissior ibis, Unda gravet pennas,

gregalis.full: grĕgālis, e, adj. grex, of or belonging to the herd or flock. Lit.: equi, Varr. R. R. 2, 7, 6: equae, Plin. 10, 63, 83, § 181: pecua, App. M. 6, p. 182.— Transf., in gen., belonging to the same host or multitude. In a good sense, subst.: grĕ-gāles, ĭum, m., comrades, companions: nos nihil sumus, gregalibus illis, quibus te plaudente vigebamus, amissis, Cic. Fam. 7, 33, 1; id. de Or. 2, 62, 253.— In a bad sense, of the common sort, common (mostly post-Aug.): gregali sagulo amictus, i. e. a common

gregarius.full: grĕgārĭus, a, um, adj. id., of or belonging to a flock or herd. Lit.: gregariorum pastorum disciplinam repudiasse, Col. 6 praef. § 1.— Transf., in gen., of the common sort, common (most freq. in milit. lang.): milites, common soldiers, privates, in opp. to the officers: id etiam gregarii milites faciunt inviti, ut, etc., Cic. Planc. 30, 72; Sall. C. 38, 6; Curt. 7, 2; and in sing.: miles, Liv. 42, 34, 5; Tac. H. 5, 1: eques, id. ib. 3, 51: gregariam militiam sortitus, Just. 22, 1.—Rarely beyond

gregatim.full: grĕgātim, adv. id., in flocks, herds, or swarms. Lit., of animals: haec facienda, si gregatim pecora laborant: illa deinceps, si singula, Col. 6, 5 fin.: apes rempublicam habent, consilia privatim ac duces gregatim, Plin. 11, 5, 4, § 11: elephanti gregatim semper ingrediuntur, id. 8, 5, 5, § 11; 9, 15, 18, § 47.— Transf., in troops or crowds: videtis cives Romanos gregatim conjectos in lautumias, Cic. Verr. 2, 5, 57, § 148; Just. 13, 8; Plin. 4, 12, 26, § 89: accidit, ut nova contra genera morbo

grego.full: grĕgo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. id., to collect into a flock or herd, to gather into a host, to collect, assemble (poet. and only postAug.): Levitas ad se gregavit, Sulp. Sev. Chron. 1, 19, 6: Idaliae volucres caeloque domoque gregatae, Stat. Achill. 1, 373: oves, Paul. Nol. Carm. 17, 200: solus qui caedibus hausi Quinquaginta animas: totidem totidemque gregati Ferte manus, all together, Stat. Th. 8, 668 (al. gregatim).

gremialis.full: grĕmĭālis, e, adj. gremium, growing in a cluster from the stump, pollard: si arbores caeduae fuerunt vel gremiales, Dig. 24, 3, 7, § 12.

gremium.full: grĕmĭum, ii, n. Sanscr. garbh-as, child; cf. germen, the lap, bosom (freq. and class.; cf. sinus). Lit.: in gremium imbrem aureum (mittere), Ter. Eun. 3, 5, 37: (Juppiter) puer lactens Fortunae in gremio sedens, mammam appetens, Cic. Div. 2, 41, 86; id. Brut. 58, 211; id. Leg. 2, 25, 63; Cat. 45, 2; Verg. A. 11, 744 al.—Poet.: quiipse sui gnati minxerit in gremium, i. e. has dishonored his son's wife, Cat. 67, 30.— Transf.: terra gremio mollito et subacto semen sparsum excipit, Cic. de Sen. 15,

gressio.full: gressĭo, ōnis, f. gradior, a stepping, step, pace, Pac. ap. Macr. S. 6, 5.

gressus1.full: gressus, a, um, Part., from gradior.
gressus1.short: gressus, a, um, Part., from gradior.

gressus2.full: gressus, ūs, m. gradior, a stepping, going, step, course, way. Lit. (poet. and post-class.; cf.: gradus, passus, incessus, ingressus): tendere gressum ad moenia, Verg. A. 1, 410; so in sing., id. ib. 6, 389; 11, 29.—In plur.: gressus glomerare superbos, Verg. G. 3, 117; 4, 360; Val. Fl. 1, 183; Plin. 8, 12, 12, § 33; Gell. 1, 11, 6; 11, 13, 10.— Transf. Poet., of the course of a vessel: huc dirige gressum, Verg. A. 5, 162.— A pace, as a measure of length, Gromat. Vet. p. 373, 9.

grex.full: grex, grĕgis, m. (fem., Lucil. ap. Charis. p. 72 P.; Lucr. 2, 662; Inscr. ap. Maff. Mus. Veron. 127, 4) [Sanscr. root jar-, come together; Gr. ἀγείρω, ἀγορά], a flock, herd, drove, swarm (cf.: armentum, jumentum, pecus). Lit., of animals: pecudes dispulsae sui generis sequuntur greges, Cic. Att. 7, 7, 7; cf.: greges armentorum reliquique pecoris, id. Phil. 3, 12, 31: nobilissimarum equarum, Cic. Verr. 2, 2, 7, § 20: asinorum, Varr. R. R. 2, 6, 2: lanigeri, Verg. G. 3, 287: vir gregis ipse caper,

grias.full: grĭas, ădis, f., a plant, App. Herb. 50.
grias.short: grĭas, ădis, f., a plant, App.

gricenea.full: gricenea funis crassus, acc. to Paul. ex Fest. p. 99, 4 Müll.

grinnes.full: Grinnes, ium, f., a place in Gallia Belgica, near the modern Druten or Warich and Bochstein, Tac. H. 5, 20.
grinnes.short: Grinnes, ium, f., a place in Gallia Belgica, near the modern Druten or Warich and Bochstein, Tac.

griphus.full: grīphus, i, m., = γρῖφος (a net; hence transf.), an intricate or puzzling question, a riddle, enigma (post-class. and very rare): griphos dissolvere, Gell. 1, 4, 4; v. App. Flor. 9; Aus. Idyll. 11.

groco.full: groco, āre, 1, v. n., to croak as a raven, Apul. de Deo Soc. prol. p. 366, 19 (Hild. crocare).

groma.full: grōma or grūma, ae, f. A surveyor's pole or measuring-rod, acc. to Paul. ex Fest. s. v. p. 72 Müll. and Non. 63, 6.— Hence, Transf., the centre of a camp, where the measuring-rod was planted, so as to divide the camp into four quarters by streets meeting at that point, Hyg. de Limit. p. 164 Goes.

gromaticus.full: grōmātĭcus (grūm-), a, um, adj. groma, of or belonging to field-surveying or castrametation. Adj.: disciplina, Cassiod. Varr. 3, 52.— Subst.: grōmā-tĭca (grūm-), ae, f., the art of field-surveying or castrametation, Cassiod. Varr. 3, 52.— grōmātĭci, ōrum, m., writers on field-surveying, Hyg. de Mun. Castr. § 12.

gromphaena.full: gromphaena, ae, f., a kind of amaranth: Amaranthus tricolor, Linn.; Plin. 26, 7, 23, § 40.
gromphaena.short: gromphaena, ae, f., a kind of amaranth: Amaranthus tricolor, Linn.;

gromphena.full: gromphēna, ae, f., a Sardinian bird of the crane species, Plin. 30, 15, 52, § 146.
gromphena.short: gromphēna, ae, f., a Sardinian bird of the crane species, Plin.

grosa.full: grosa, ae, f., a tool of a silversmith, Arn. 6, 14.
grosa.short: grosa, ae, f., a tool of a silversmith, Arn.

grosphus1.full: grosphus, i, m., = γρόσφος, the point of a javelin, Arn. 6, 200.
grosphus1.short: grosphus, i, m., = γρόσφος, the point of a javelin, Arn.

grosphus2.full: Grosphus, a Roman surname, Hor. C. 2, 16 lemm.

grossitudo.full: grossĭtūdo, ĭnis, f. 2. grossus, thickness=crassitudo (late Lat.), Vulg. Jer. 52, 21; 3, Reg. 7, 26; Sol. 43.

grossulus.full: grossŭlus, i, m. dim. 1. grossus, a small unripe fig, Col. 5, 10, 10; Auct. ap. Macr. S. 2, 16, 5.

grossus1.full: grossus, i, m. and f., an unripe fig, Cato, R. R. 94; Cels. 5, 12; Plin. 23, 7, 63, § 125; 17, 27, 43, § 254.

grossus2.full: grossus, a, um, adj. kindred with crassus, thick (late Lat.): virga, Cassiod. Hist. Eccl. 10, 33.—Comp.: vestis grossior, Sulp. Sev. Dal. 1, 21; Vulg. Ezech. 41, 25; 1 Reg. 12, 10; 2 Chron. 10, 10.—Sup., Cassiod. in Psa. 29, 12; cf.: grossus παχύς, Gloss. Philox.—Hence, adv. only comp.: gros-sĭus, more roughly: definire, Aug. de Duab. Anim. 11, 15.

grudii.full: Grudĭi, ōrum, m., a people of Gallia Belgica, now Groede or Gronde, Caes. B. G. 5, 39.
grudii.short: Grudĭi, ōrum, m., a people of Gallia Belgica, now Groede or Gronde, Caes.

grumentum.full: Grumentum, i, n., a town of Lucania, near the modern Saponara, Liv. 23, 37, 10; 27, 41, 1 sq.; Plin. 14, 6, 8, § 69.— Hence, Grumentīni, ōrum, m., the inhabitants of Grumentum, Plin. 3, 11, 15, § 98.
grumentum.short: Grumentum, i, n., a town of Lucania, near the modern Saponara, Liv.

grumulus.full: grūmŭlus, i, m. dim. grumus, a little hill, hillock (post-Aug.), Plin. 19, 6, 34, § 112; App. M. 6; Ambros. de Elia, 6, 18.

grumus.full: grūmus, i, m., a little heap, hillock of earth: grumus terrae collectio minor tumulo, Paul. ex Fest. p. 96 Müll.; Att. ap. Non. 15, 24; Col. 2, 17, 4; Vitr. 2, 1; 8, 3; Auct. B. Hisp. 24.
grumus.short: grūmus, i, m., a little heap, hillock of earth: grumus terrae collectio minor tumulo, Paul.

grunda.full: grunda στέγη καὶ τὸ ὑπὲρ τὸν πυλεῶνα ἐξέχον, ὑπόστεγον, Gloss. Philox.
grunda.short: grunda στέγη καὶ τὸ ὑπὲρ τὸν πυλεῶνα ἐξέχον, ὑπόστεγον, Gloss.

grundiles.full: Grundīles or Grundūles, ium, m., an appellation of the Lares, Cass. Hem. ap. Diom. p. 379 P.; Non. 114, 31; Arn. 1, 15.
grundiles.short: Grundīles or Grundūles, ium, m., an appellation of the Lares, Cass.

grunnio.full: grunnĭo (also ante-class. grundio), īvi or ĭi, ītum, 4, v. n., to grunt. Lit., said of swine: grunnit tepido lacte satur, Varr. ap. Non. 114, 27: grunnientem aspexi scrofam, Laber. ib. 30: Apion maximum piscium esse tradit porcum: grunnire eum, cum capiatur, Plin. 32, 2, 9, § 19; Juv. 15, 22: grundibat graviter pecus suillum, Quadrig. ap. Diom. p. 379 P.— Transf., of other creatures: agni grundibant, Quadrig. ap. Non. 465, 1: cruento ita ore grundibat miser, Caecil. ib. (Com. Fragm. v. 103 Rib.)

grunnitus.full: grunnītus, ūs, m. grunnio, a grunting of swine: aut grunnitum (audiunt), cum jugulatur, suis, Cic. Tusc. 5, 40, 116.

gruo.full: grŭo, ĕre, v. n. grus, the note of the crane, to crunk, crunkle: gruere dicuntur grues, ut sues grunnire, Paul. ex Fest. p. 97: grus gruit, Auct. Carm. de Philom. 23.

grus.full: grus, grŭis (also in the nom. sing. gruis, Phaedr. 1, 8, 7), f. (m., Hor. S. 2, 8, 87) [Gr. γέρανος, akin to γέρων], a crane, Plin. 10, 23, 30, § 60; Cic. N. D. 2, 49, 125; Mart. 13, 75; Cels. 2, 18; Lucr. 4, 181; regarded by the Romans as a delicacy, Hor. S. 2, 8, 87; Gell. 7, 16, 5; Stat. S. 4, 6, 8.— Transf. (with reference to the form of a crane's bill), a besieging machine, battering-ram, called also corvus, Vitr. 10, 19.

gry.full: gry, n. indecl., = γρῦ, the least trifle: ne gry quidem ferre hinc potes, Plaut. Most. 3, 1, 67 Weise (recent edd. write γρῦ).

gryllo.full: gryllo, āre, v. n. gryllus, the note of the cricket, to chirp: et gryllus gryllat, Auct. Carm. de Philom. 62.

gryllus1.full: gryllus (also grillus), i, m., = γρύλλος. A cricket or grasshopper, Plin. 29, 6, 39, § 138.— Transf., in painting, a kind of comic figures, Plin. 35, 10, 37, § 114.

gryllus2.full: Gryllus, i, m., =Γρύλλος, a Greek proper name. A son of Xenophon, who fell in the battle at Mantinea, and was celebrated by Aristotle in a monogram entitled Γρύλλος, Quint. 2, 17, 14.— A Roman proper name, Mart. 1, 60, 3; 2, 14, 13.
gryllus2.short: Gryllus, i, m., =Γρύλλος, a Greek proper name.

grynia.full: Grȳnīa, ae, f., and Grȳnĭum (also Grūnium in some editt. of Nep.), ii, n., = Γρύνεια and Γρύνιον, a small town in Æolis, with a temple of Apollo, Plin. 5, 30, 32, § 121; 32, 6, 21, § 59; Nep. Alc. 9, 3.— Deriv. Grȳnēus, a, um, adj., = Γρύνειος, of or belonging to Grynia, Grynian: Apollo, Verg. A. 4, 345: nemus, id. E. 6, 72.
grynia.short: Grȳnīa, ae, f., and Grȳnĭum (also Grūnium in some editt.

gryps.full: gryps, grўphis (grȳphus, i, Mel. 2, 1, 1; 3, 7, 2), m., = γρύψ, a fabulous fourfooted bird, a griffin: Pegasos equino capite volucres et gryphas auritos aduncitate rostri fabulosos reor, illos in Scythia, hos in Aethiopia, Plin. 10, 49, 70, § 136; Mel. 2, 1, 1; Claud. VI. Cons. Hon. 30; Sid. Carm. 22, 66 and 67.—Prov.: Jungentur jam grypes equis, i. e. the impossible shall happen, Verg. E. 8, 27.

grypus.full: grȳpus, i, m., = γρυπός, hook-nosed, as a surname: alter, cui propter nasi magnitudinem cognomen Grypo fuit, Just. 39, 1, § 9.
grypus.short: grȳpus, i, m., = γρυπός, hook-nosed, as a surname: alter, cui propter nasi magnitudinem cognomen Grypo fuit, Just.

gubernabilis.full: gŭbernābĭlis, e, adj. guberno, susceptible of being governed, controllable: sive anima est mundus sive corpus natura gubernabile, Sen. Q. N. 3, 29, 2.

gubernaculum.full: gŭbernācŭlum (poet. contr. gŭ-bernāclum, Lucr. 4, 904; Verg. A. 5, 176; 859; 6, 349 al.), i, n. guberno, a helm, rudder (cf. clavus). Lit.: hominis, non sapientis inventa sunt navigia, additis a tergo gubernaculis, quae huc atque illuc cursum navigii torqueant: exemplum a piscibus tractum, qui cauda reguntur, etc., Sen. Ep. 90; cf.: piscium meatus gubernaculi modo regunt (caudae), Plin. 11, 50, 111, § 264: ut cruribus velut gubernaculis demissis cursum dirigeret, Front. 3, 13, 6: hic ille naufra

gubernatio.full: gŭbernātĭo, ōnis, f. guberno, a steering, piloting of a ship (Ciceron.). Lit.: si in ipsa gubernatione negligentia est navis eversa, Cic. Fin. 4, 27, 76; cf. id. ib. 3, 7, 24. — Transf., in gen., direction, management, government: summi imperii gubernatione districtus, Cic. de Or. 3, 32, 131: civitatis, id. Rep. 1, 2: tantarum rerum, id. Cat. 3, 8, 18: consilii, id. Inv. 2, 54, 164: summi consilii, id. Vat. 15, 36.

gubernator.full: gŭbernātor, ōris, m. id., a steersman, pilot (cf.: magister, navarchus, nauclerus, navicularius). Lit.: si tu proreta isti navi's, ego gubernator ero, Plaut. Rud. 4, 3, 75; id. Am. 3, 2, 69: gubernator clavum tenens sedet in puppi quietus, Cic. de Sen. 6, 17; id. Phil. 7, 9, 27; id. Ac. 2, 31, 100; id. de Inv. 1, 34, 58; id. Rep. 1, 40; 5, 3; Quint. 2, 17, 24; 34; 4, 1, 61; Verg. A. 3, 269; 5, 12; 6, 337 et saep.—Prov.: tranquillo quilibet gubernator est, Sen. Ep. 85 med.— Transf., a director, r

gubernatrix.full: gŭbernātrix, īcis, f. gubernator, II., a conductress, directress: an fortunam collaudem, quae gubernatrix fuit? Ter. Eun. 5, 9, 16: ista praeclara gubernatrice civitatum eloquentia rem publicam dissipaverunt, Cic. de Or. 1, 9, 38.

gubernio.full: gŭbernĭo, ōnis, m., v. gubernius fin.

gubernius.full: gŭbernĭus, ii, m. guberno, a steersman, pilot, for the usual gubernator, Laber. ap. Gell. 16, 7, 10.—Another form: † gŭ-bernĭo, ōnis, m., acc. to Isid. Orig. 19, 1, 4.

guberno.full: gŭberno, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a., = κυβερνῶ, to steer or pilot a ship (class.). Lit.: dum clavum rectum teneant navemque gubernent, Enn. ap. Isid. Orig. 19, 2 (Ann. v. 472 Vahl.): ut si nautae certarent, quis eorum potissimum gubernaret, Cic. Off. 1, 25, 87: tranquillo mari gubernare, id. Rep. 1, 6.—Prov.: gubernare e terra, i. e. to guide those who are in peril while keeping in safety one's self, Liv. 44, 22, 14: quilibet nautarum tranquillo mari gubernare potest, id. 24, 8, 12; cf. gubernator, I.

gubernum.full: gŭbernum, i, n. guberno, a helm, rudder (ante-class. for the class. gubernaculum): proras despoliate et detondete guberna, Lucil. ap. Non. 490, 32; Lucr. 2, 553; 4, 439.

gugerni.full: Gugerni (Cug-, ap. Plin. Sillig.; Gub-, Jan.), ōrum, m., a people of Germany, in the modern Cleves, Plin. 4, 17, 31, § 106; Tac. H. 4, 26; 5, 16; 18.

gula.full: gŭla, ae, f. root gar, to swallow; Sanscr. gir-āmi; Gr. βορ- in βορά, βιβρώσκω; cf.: voro, gurges, glutio, v. Georg Curtius Gr. Etym. p. 470, the gullet, weasand, throat (cf.: faux, guttur, jugulum). Lit.: gula nervo et carne constat, Plin. 11, 37, 66, § 176; 11, 37, 79, § 201; 24, 15, 80, § 130: cum it dormitum, follem sibi obstringit ob gulam, ne quid animae forte amittat dormiens, Plaut. Aul. 2, 4, 23: illi jam interstringam gulam, id. ib. 4, 4, 32: quem obtorta gula de convivio in vincula ab

gulliocae.full: gulliocae nucum juglandium summa et viridia putamina, Paul. ex Fest. p. 98 Müll.; Lucil. Fragm. inc. v. 164.
gulliocae.short: gulliocae nucum juglandium summa et viridia putamina, Paul.

gulo.full: gŭlo, ōnis, m. gula, II.; cf. Paul. ex Fest. s. v. ingluvies, p. 112, a gormandizer, epicure, glutton (post-class.), App. Mag. p. 295; Macr. S. 7, 12, 9.

gulositas.full: gŭlōsĭtas, ātis, f. gulosus, gluttony (late Lat.), Ps.-Aug. ad Frat. Erem. Serm. 31.

gulosus.full: gŭlōsus, a, um, adj. gula, II., gluttonous, luxurious, dainty (post-Aug.; cf.: edax, vorax): oculis quoque gulosi sunt, Sen. Q. N. 3, 18 fin.: nil est miserius nec gulosius Santra, Mart. 7, 20, 1: gulosum Fictile, i. e. containing dainty food, Juv. 11, 19: abstinentia, i. e. an abstinence that enhances enjoyment, Hier. Ep. 107, 10.—Transf.: nimium lector gulosus, i. e. a too voracious reader (acc. to others, an over-fastidious reader), Mart. 10, 59, 5.—Adv.: gŭlōse, gluttonously: gulosius condir

gulussa.full: Gulussa or Gulūsa, ae, m., a son of Masinissa, king of Numidia, Sall. J. 5; cf. Plin. 8, 10, 10 fin.
gulussa.short: Gulussa or Gulūsa, ae, m., a son of Masinissa, king of Numidia, Sall.

gumen.full: gūmen, ĭnis, n., gum, post-class. for gummi, Pall. 12, 7, 15; Isid. 17, 7, 70.

gumia.full: gŭmĭa, ae, com., a glutton, gourmand: Lucil. ap. Cic. Fin. 2, 8, 24; id. ap. Non. 118, 2; App. Mag. p. 311; Paul. ex Fest. s. v. ingluvies, p. 112 Müll.
gumia.short: gŭmĭa, ae, com., a glutton, gourmand: Lucil.

gummatus.full: gummātus, a, um, adj. gummi, containing gum, gummy (post-class.): in cerasis et in omnibus gummatis, Pall. 11, 12, 6; cf. the foll. art.

gummeus.full: gummĕus, a, um, adj. id., containing gum, gummy: succina, Aus. Idyll. 6, 79.

gummi.full: gummi or cummi, indecl. n., com-mis and cummis, or gummis, is, f. (gen. Graec. gummeos, Mart. Cap. 3, § 225), = κόμμι, gum, Plin. 16, 26, 45, § 108; 24, 1, 1, § 3 al.; 13, 12, 26, § 66; Col. 12, 52, 16 et saep. (in Plin. cummi or cummis is the reading in the best MSS.).

gummino.full: gummĭno, āre, v. n., to distil gum: gumminet, Pall. 2, 16 fin. (al. germinet).

gummitio.full: gummītĭo, ōnis, f. gummi, a besmearing with gum, Col. 12, 52, 17.

gummosus.full: gummōsus, a, um, adj. id., full of gum, gummy: folia, Plin. 22, 9, 11, § 24; 16, 38, 72, § 181 al. (in these passages the better reading is cumminosus).

gummus.full: gummus, i, m., = gummi, Gargil. Mart. de Pom. 16.

gurdonicus.full: gurdōnĭcus, a, um, adj. gurdus, doltish, stupid: homo, Sulp. Sev. Dial. 1, 26.

gurdus.full: gurdus, i, m. Spanish, a dolt, jolterhead, numskull: gurdos, quos pro stolidis accipit vulgus, ex Hispania duxisse originem audivi, Quint. 1, 5, 57; cf.: gurdus lentus, inutilis, Gloss. Isid.; Laber. ap. Gell. 16, 7, 8 (Com. Fragm. v. 13 Rib.).

gurges1.full: gurges, ĭtis, m. v. gula; and cf. βάραθρον, vorago, a raging abyss, whirlpool, gulf (syn.: vorago, barathrum). Lit. (class.): non Rheni fossam gurgitibus illis redundantem, Cic. Pis. 33, 81: turbidus hic coeno vastaque voragine gurges Aestuat, Verg. A. 6, 296: multamque trahens sub gurgite arenam Volturnus, Ov. M. 15, 714: alterno procurrens gurgite pontus, Verg. A. 11, 624: per medios gurgites (opp. vada), Liv. 21, 5, 14: deficientibus animis hauriebantur gurgitibus, id. 22, 6, 7: caenosus, the

gurges2.full: Gurges, ĭtis, m., a surname. Q. Fabius, Q. F. M. N. Gurges, Macr. S. 2, 9.— Fabius Gurges, Juv. 6, 266.— C. Volcatius Gurges, Plin. 7, 53, 54, § 181.

gurgito.full: gurgĭto, āre, 1, v. a. gurges, to engulf, flood: vino nimis gurgitati mentis oppressione torpescunt, Cassiod. in Psa. 35, 8.

gurgulio1.full: gurgŭlĭo, ōnis, m. kindred with glutio; v. gurges, gula, the gullet, weasand, windpipe: hircus cervice et collo brevi, gurgatione longiore, Varr. R. R. 2, 3, 2; Cic. Fragm. Or. pro Tullio, 10; Lact. Op. D. 11; Arn. 3, 107: huic gurgulio est exercitor, Plaut. Trin. 4, 3, 9

gurgulio2.full: gurgŭlĭo, ōnis, collat. form of curculio, q. v.

gurgustidonii.full: Gurgustĭdōnĭi, vulg. lect. in Plaut. Mil. 1, 1, 13, inst. of Gorgonidonii, q. v.

gurgustiolum.full: gurgustĭŏlum, i, n. dim. gurgusti. um, a small, mean dwelling, a hut, shanty, App. M. 1, p. 112 and 147.

gurgustium.full: gurgustĭum, ii, n. kindred with gurgulio, perh. with reference to its straitness, a small, mean dwelling, a hovel, hut: nescio quo e gurgustio te prodire, Cic. Pis. 6, 13: in gurgustio habitare, id. N. D. 1, 9, 22: modicum, Suet. Gramm. 11; Ambros. de Bono Mort. 1, 5 al.

gustabilis.full: gustābĭlis, e, adj. gusto, appetizing, Ambros. de Noe, 15, 52.

gustatio.full: gustātĭo, ōnis, f. id.; a first tasting of food; hence, the first light dish of a Roman meal, an antepast, whet: jussi discubuimus, et gustatione mirifica initiati vino etiam Falerno inundamur, Petr. 21, 6; 31, 8.

gustator.full: gustātor, oris, m. id., the taster: digitus, i. e. the forefinger, used in tasting (= δάκτυλος λιχανός), Hier. in. Isa. 11, 40, 12.

gustatorium.full: gustātōrĭum, ii, n. id., the vessels containing an antepast, an antepast, collation, whet (v. gustatio), Plin. Ep. 5, 6, 37; Petr. 34; Mart. 14, 88 in lemm.

gustatus.full: gustātus, ūs id.; a tasting of food; hence. The taste, as one of the five senses: gustatus, qui sentire eorum, quibus vescimur, genera debet, Cic. N. D. 2, 56, 141; id. de Or. 3, 25, 99: existimaverim omnibus (animalibus) sensum et gustatus esse, Plin. 10, 71, 91, § 196.— The taste, flavor of any thing. Lit.: varietas pomorum eorumque jucundus non gustatus solum, sed odoratus etiam et aspectus, Cic. N. D. 2, 63, 158: (uva) primo est peracerba gustatu, id. de Sen. 15, 53.— Trop.: libidinosi verae

gusto.full: gusto, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. gustus, to taste, to take a little of any thing (freq. and class.; cf.: libo, manduco, edo, etc.). Lit. In gen.: cum biduum ita jejunus fuissem, ut ne aquam quidem gustarem, Cic. Fam. 7, 26, 1: leporem et gallinam et anserem gustare fas non putant, Caes. B. G. 5, 11: gustatus sanguis, Plin. 8, 16, 19, § 52: celerius panis mandendus quam vinum gustandum, Cels. 4, 3: gustare de potione, Suet. Tit. 2: herba subsalsa gustanti, Plin. 21, 29, 103, § 175: alypon acre gustatu

gustulum.full: gustŭlum, i, n. dim. gustus. A small dish of food, a whet, relish, App. M. 9, p. 232.— Transf., a kiss: dulcem et amarum gustulum carpis, App. M. 2, p. 119.

gustum.full: gustum, i, n., v. gustus, I. 2. a.

gustus.full: gustus, ūs, m. kindred with Sanscr. ǵush, to be fond of; Gr. γεύω, γεύομαι, γεῦσις, taste, a tasting of food, a partaking slightly or eating a little of any thing (mostly post-Aug.; not in Cic.; cf.: gustatus, sapor). Lit. In gen.: minister inferre epulas et explorare gustu solitus, Tac. A. 12, 66: explorare aliquid gustu, Col. 1, 8, 18; 2, 2, 20; cf. Plin. 31, 10, 46, § 114: gustu libata potio, Tac. A. 13, 16: cum ille ad primum gustum concidisset, Suet. Ner. 33: sine crebro salis gustu, Plin.

gutta1.full: gutta, ae (archaic gen. sing. guttaiï, Lucr. 6, 614), f. etym. dub., a drop of a fluid (cf.: stilla, stiria). Lit.: numerus quem in cadentibus guttis, quod intervallis distinguitur, notare possumus, Cic. de Or. 3, 48, 186: guttae imbrium quasi cruentae, id. N. D. 2, 5, 14: gutta cavat lapidem, consumitur annulus usu, Ov. P. 4, 10, 5: si ego in os meum hodie vini guttam indidi, Plaut. Cas. 2, 3, 30: guttam haud habeo sanguinis (prae metu), id. Most. 2, 2, 76; cf. Verg. A. 3, 28: gutta per attonit

gutta2.full: Gutta, ae, m., a Roman surname, Cic. Clu. 26, 71; 36, 98.
gutta2.short: Gutta, ae, m., a Roman surname, Cic.

guttatim.full: guttātim, adv. gutta, by drops, drop by drop (ante- and post-class.): lacrimae guttatim cadunt, Enn. ap. Non. 116, 1 (Trag. v. 238 Vahl.): pluvia guttatim labitur, Arn. 2, 84; App. M. 3, p. 130: cor guttatim contabescit, Plaut. Merc. 1, 2, 92.

guttatus.full: guttātus, a, um, adj. id. I. B. 1., spotted, speckled: gallinae, Mart. 3, 58, 15: equus, dappled, piebald, Pall. 4, 13, 4.

guttula.full: guttŭla, ae, f. dim. gutta, a little drop (ante- and post-class.): ah, guttula pectus mihi ardens aspersisti, Plaut. Ep. 4, 1, 27: favorum guttulae, Paul. Nol. Carm. 21, 427.

guttur.full: guttur, ŭris, n. (ante-class.; also m. in acc. sing. gutturem, Plaut. Mil. 3, 2, 22; id. Aul. 2, 4, 25; Nov. Com. Fragm. v. 118 Rib.), the gullet, throat (cf.: faux, gula, jugulum): da meo gutturi gaudium, Plaut. Curc. 1, 2, 10; 49: venter gutturque resident ferias, id. Capt. 3, 1, 8: guttur homini tantum et suibus intumescit, Plin. 11, 37, 68, § 179: quis tumidum guttur miratur in Alpibus? Juv. 13, 162: (tamquam si in Alpibus gutturosos homines admireris, ubi tales sunt plurimi scilicet: nam la

gutturnium.full: gutturnium vas, ex quo aqua in manus datur: ab eo, quod propter oris angustias guttatim fluat, Paul. ex Fest. p. 98 Müll.
gutturnium.short: gutturnium vas, ex quo aqua in manus datur: ab eo, quod propter oris angustias guttatim fluat, Paul.

gutturosus.full: guttŭrōsus, a, um, adj. guttur, that has a tumor in the throat, goitred (postclass.): si quis naturā gutturosus sit, Dig. 21, 1, 12, § 2; Paul. ex Fest. 112, 2; Schol. Juv. 13, 162; cf. guttur.

gutus.full: gutus (less correctly guttus), i, m. gutta, a narrow-necked vessel, flask, cruet, from which liquids (wine, oil, ointments, etc.) are poured by drops: qui vinum dabant, ut minutatim funderent, a guttis gutum appellarunt, Varr. L. L. 5, § 124 Müll.: faginus, Plin. 16, 38, 73, § 185; Gell. 17, 8, 5; Juv. 3, 263; 11, 158; Mart. 14, 52 in lemm.: cum paterā gutus, Hor. S. 1, 6, 118.

gyaros.full: Gўăros, i, and Gўăra, ae, f., and Gўăra, ōrum, n., = Γύαρος, Γύαρα, a small barren island in the Ægean Sea, one of the Cyclades, used by the Romans under the empire as a place of exile for criminals, now Chiura, Cic. Att. 5, 12, 1 sq.; Varr. ap. Plin. 8, 29, 43, § 104; Verg. A. 3, 76; Tac. A. 3, 68 sq.; 4, 30; Juv. 10, 170; 1, 73; Plin. 4, 12, 23, § 69; 8, 57, 82, § 222.
gyaros.short: Gўăros, i, and Gўăra, ae, f., and Gўăra, ōrum, n., = Γύαρος, Γύαρα, a small barren island in the Ægean Sea, one of the Cyclades, used by the Romans under the empire as a place of exile for criminals, now Chiura, Cic.

gyas.full: Gўas or Gўes, ae, m., = Γύης. A giant with a hundred arms, Hor. C. 2, 17, 14; Ov. Tr. 4, 7, 18; id. F. 593 (this the better read. inst. of Gyges).— A companion of Æneas, Verg. A. 1, 222; 5, 118; 12, 460. — A Latin, slain by Æneas, Verg. A. 10, 318.
gyas.short: Gўas or Gўes, ae, m., = Γύης.

gygaeus.full: Gȳ^gaeus, a, um, v. the foll. art.

gyges.full: Gȳges, is or ae, m., = Γύγης. A king of Lydia, famous for the possession of a ring with which he could render himself invisible, Cic. Off. 3, 19, 78; Just. 1, 7, 17 sq. — Deriv. Gȳgaeus, a, um, adj., in poet. transf., of or belonging to Lydia, Lydian: Lydia Gygaeo tincta puella lacu, a lake near Sardes (the Homer. λίμνη Γυγαίη), Prop. 3, 11 (4, 10), 18; cf. Plin. 5, 29, 30, § 110.— A Trojan, slain by Turnus, Verg. A. 9, 762.— A beautiful youth, Hor. C. 2, 5, 20; 3, 7, 5 (but as a name of the gia
gyges.short: Gȳges, is or ae, m., = Γύγης.

gylippus.full: Gўlippus, i, m., = Γύλιππος. An Arcadian, who came to Italia with Evander, Verg. A. 12, 272.— A famous Spartan general in the Peloponnesian war, Just. 4, 4; Tib. 4, 1, 199.

gymnas.full: gymnas, ădis, f., = γυμνάς, wrestling, the exercise of wrestling (in post-Aug. poetry): Herculeā turpatus gymnade, Stat. Th. 4, 106; id. S. 4, 2, 47; Prud. Cont. Sym. 2, 517.—Plur.: exercere protervas Gymnadas, Stat. Ach. 1, 358.
gymnas.short: gymnas, ădis, f., = γυμνάς, wrestling, the exercise of wrestling (in post-Aug.

gymnasiarchus.full: gymnăsĭarchus, i, m., = γυμνασίαρχος, the master of a gymnasium, a gymnasiarch, Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 42, § 92; Sid. Ep. 2, 2; Val. Max. 9, 10, 2 ext.—Also, gym-năsĭarcha, ae, m., = γυμνασιάρχης, Val. Max. 9, 12, 7 ext.; Inscr. Grut. 465, 2.
gymnasiarchus.short: gymnăsĭarchus, i, m., = γυμνασίαρχος, the master of a gymnasium, a gymnasiarch, Cic.

gymnasium1.full: gymnăsĭum, ii, n., =γυμνάσιον, a public school among the Greeks for gymnastic exercises, a gymnasium. Lit., Plaut. Am. 4, 1, 3; id. Bacch. 3, 3, 21; id. Ep. 2, 2, 13; Cic. Tusc. 2, 15, 151; id. Rep. 3, 32; 4, 4: virgineum (in Sparta), Prop. 3, 14, 2; Ov. H. 16, 151; Cels. 5, 11; 15; Plin. Ep. 10, 40, 2; Quint. 2, 8, 3 al.—Comically: gymnasium flagri, qs. school for the scourge, whipping-post, a term of reproach applied to one who is often flogged, Plaut. As. 2, 2, 31; cf.: totus doleo, ita me is
gymnasium1.short: gymnăsĭum, ii, n., =γυμνάσιον, a public school among the Greeks for gymnastic exercises, a gymnasium.

gymnasium2.full: Gymnăsium, ii, f. (Γυμνάσιον, dim. of Γυμνάς), name of a Greek maiden: Gymnasium mea, Plaut. Cist. 1, 1, 109.

gymnasticus.full: gymnastĭcus, a, um, adj., = γυμναστικός, of or belonging to bodily exercise, gymnastic (Plautinian, for which Cic. uses gymnicus): pro exercitu gymnastico et palaestrico hoc habemus, Plaut. Rud. 2, 1, 7: arte gymnastica, disco, hasta, pila, id. Most. 1, 2, 72 (a spurious line).
gymnasticus.short: gymnastĭcus, a, um, adj., = γυμναστικός, of or belonging to bodily exercise, gymnastic (Plautinian, for which Cic.

gymnicus.full: gymnĭcus, a, um, adj., = γυμνικός, of or for bodily exercise, gymnastic: ludi qui gymnici nominantur, Cic. Tusc. 2, 26, 62: ludi, Plin. 7, 56, 57, § 205: certamina, Suet. Ner. 53.
gymnicus.short: gymnĭcus, a, um, adj., = γυμνικός, of or for bodily exercise, gymnastic: ludi qui gymnici nominantur, Cic.

gymnosophistae.full: gymnŏsŏphistae, ārum, m., = γυμνοσοφισταί (naked philosophers), Indian ascetics, gymnosophists, a sect of hermits who disregarded the decencies of life, Plin. 7, 2, 2, § 22; App. Flor. p. 351; Prud. Ham. 404 al.; cf. Cic. Tusc. 5, 27, 77; Val. Max. 3, 3 ext. 6.
gymnosophistae.short: gymnŏsŏphistae, ārum, m., = γυμνοσοφισταί (naked philosophers), Indian ascetics, gymnosophists, a sect of hermits who disregarded the decencies of life, Plin.

gynaeceum.full: gўnaecēum or gўnaecīum (gun-), i, n., = γυναικεῖον. Among the Greeks, the inner part of the house where the women dwelt, the women's apartments, Plaut. Most. 3, 2, 68; 72; Ter. Phorm. 5, 6, 26; Cic. Phil. 2, 37, 95.— Among the Romans, the emperor's seraglio, where also women spun and wove the imperial garments: matresfamilias ingenuae ac nobiles in gynaeceum rapiebantur, Lact. de Mort. Pers. 21; Veg. Mil. 1, 7; Cod. Just. 9, 27, 5; 11, 7, 5.
gynaeceum.short: gўnaecēum or gўnaecīum (gun-), i, n., = γυναικεῖον.

gynaeciarius.full: gўnaecĭārĭus, ii, m. gynaeceum, II., the overseer of a seraglio, Cod. Just. 11, 7, 3.—Also called gўnaecĭus, ii, m., Cod. Th. 10, 20, 2.

gynaeconitis.full: gўnaecōnītis, ĭdis, f., = γυναικωνῖτις, i. q. gynaeceum, I., the women's apartments in a Grecian house, Nep. Vit. praef. § 7; Vitr. 6, 10.

gyndes.full: Gyndes (also Gindes), is, m., = Γύνδης, a tributary of the Tigris, in Assyria, now Diala or Kerkah, Tib. 4, 1, 141; Sen. de Ira, 3, 21, 1 (but in Tac. A. 11, 10, the better read. is Gindes).
gyndes.short: Gyndes (also Gindes), is, m., = Γύνδης, a tributary of the Tigris, in Assyria, now Diala or Kerkah, Tib.

gypseus.full: gypsĕus, a, um, adj. gypsum. Of gypsum (post-class.), Spart. Sever. 22, § 3. — Covered or plastered with gypsum, = gypsatus: facies (mulierum), Hier. Ep. 38, 3.

gypso.full: gypso, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. id., to cover or coat with gypsum, to plaster: opercula, Col. 12, 39, 2: vas, id. ib. 43.—Poet.: gypsati pedes, the feet of a prisoner marked with gypsum, to show that he was to be sold for a slave, Tib. 2, 3, 60; Ov. Am. 1, 8, 64.— Hence, gypsātus, a, um, P. a., covered or coated with gypsum: quibus illa (Medea) manibus gypsatissimis persuasit, ne sibi illae vitio verterent, quod abesset a patria, with hands thickly coated with gypsum (of actors who played women's par

gypsoplastes.full: gypsoplastes, ae, m., = γυψοπλάστης, a worker in gypsum or stucco, Cassiod. Varr. 7, 5.
gypsoplastes.short: gypsoplastes, ae, m., = γυψοπλάστης, a worker in gypsum or stucco, Cassiod.

gypsum.full: gypsum, i, n., = γύψος, white lime plaster, gypsum. Lit., Plin. 36, 24, 59, § 182; 14, 19, 24, § 120; 20, 9, 39, § 98; Col. 12, 20, 8; Cato, R. R. 39, 1 al.— Transf., figures in gypsum, plaster images: plena omnia gypso Chrysippi, Juv. 2, 4.
gypsum.short: gypsum, i, n., = γύψος, white lime plaster, gypsum.

gyrinus.full: gўrīnus, i, m., = γυρῖνος, a young frog not yet fully developed, a tadpole: ranae pariunt minimas carnes nigras, quas gyrinos vocant, Plin. 9, 51, 74, § 159.
gyrinus.short: gўrīnus, i, m., = γυρῖνος, a young frog not yet fully developed, a tadpole: ranae pariunt minimas carnes nigras, quas gyrinos vocant, Plin.

gyro.full: gȳro, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. and n. gyrus. Act., to turn round in a circle, wheel round (post-Aug. and very rare).— Lit.: animal difficile se gyrabit, Veg. Vet. 3, 5. — To go around a thing: omnes greges, Vulg. Gen. 30, 32; id. Judith, 13, 12.— Neutr., to turn around: post tergum eorum, Vulg. 2 Reg. 5, 23: per viam, id. Eccl. 1, 6: per meridiem, id. 1 Macc. 13, 20: Ambros. in Psa. 118; Serm. 12, § 20.— Transf.: gȳrātus, made in a circular form, rounded: chlamys orbe gyrato laciniosa, Plin. 5, 10, 1

gyrton.full: Gyrton, ōnis, or Gyrtōnē, ēs, f., a town of Thessaly, between Pharsalia and Larissa, now the village Tatári, Liv. 36, 10; 42, 54; Plin. 4, 9, 16, § 32; form Gyrtone, Sen. Troad. 831.
gyrton.short: Gyrton, ōnis, or Gyrtōnē, ēs, f., a town of Thessaly, between Pharsalia and Larissa, now the village Tatári, Liv.

gyrus.full: gȳrus, i, m., = γῦρος, a circle, esp. that which is described by a horse in its movements (mostly poet.; cf.: circus, circulus, orbis, orbita). Lit.: nec equi variare gyros in morem nostrum docentur, Tac. G. 6; so of a circular course, ring, for horses, Verg. G. 3, 115: carpere gyrum, id. ib. 3, 191: curvo brevius compellere gyro, Tib. 4, 1, 93; Manil. 5, 74; Ov. A. A. 3, 384; Luc. 1, 425 et saep.: adytis cum lubricus anguis ab imis Septem ingens gyros, septena volumina traxit, Verg. A. 5, 85: d
gyrus.short: gȳrus, i, m., = γῦρος, a circle, esp.

gytheum.full: Gythēum or Gythī^um, i, n., = Γύθειον or Γύθιον, a seaport in Laconia, on the Eurotas, now Paleopoli, Plin. 6, 34, 39, § 214; Cic. Off. 3, 11, 49; Liv. 34, 38; 25, 27. — Deriv.: Gythĕātes, ae, m., adj., = Γυθεάτης, of or belonging to Gythēum, Gytheatic: pontus, Mela, 2, 3, 9: sinus, Plin. 4, 5, 8, § 16.
gytheum.short: Gythēum or Gythī^um, i, n., = Γύθειον or Γύθιον, a seaport in Laconia, on the Eurotas, now Paleopoli, Plin.

h.full: H, h, the eighth letter of the Latin alphabet and the weakest guttural. The sign is borrowed from the Greek, in which H was the old form of the spiritus asper, corresp. to the Latin H-sound (HEKATON, ἑκατόν, ΗΟΣ, ὅς, etc.). Even some of the ancients doubted whether the Latin H was properly a letter: si H littera est, non nota, Quint. 1, 5, 19; cf.: H litteram, sive illam spiritum magis quam litteram dici oportet, etc., Gell. 2, 3, 1. Before the fall of the republic, the sound of H before vowels
h.short: H, h, the eighth letter of the Latin alphabet and the weakest guttural.

ha!.full: ha! interj. Ha hae or hahae, an exclamation of joy, thank heavens! hahae, nunc demum mi animus in tuto locost, Plaut. Ps. 4, 5, 1.— Ha ha he, or in one word, hahahe, an exclamation of laughter or derision, ha! ha! ha! Chr. Ha, ha, he! Me. Quid risisti? Ter. Heaut. 5, 1, 13; Plaut. Ps. 4, 1, 36; Ter. And. 4, 4, 15; id. Eun. 3, 1, 36; 3, 2, 44; id. Hec. 5, 4, 22; id. Phorm. 2, 3, 64: hahahe, jam teneo, quid sit, Plaut. Poen. 3, 5, 23.

habena.full: hăbēna, ae, f. habeo; lit., that by which a thing is held; hence, in partic., a thong, strap. Lit.: ille (turbo) actus habenā, Verg. A. 7, 380: cum jaculum parvā Libys amentavit habenā, Luc. 6, 221: Balearis tortor habenae, id. 3, 710: in scalis latuit metuens pendentis habenae, i. e. of the whip-lash, whip, Hor. Ep. 2, 2, 15: molles galeae habenae, Val. Fl. 6, 365: plantarum calces tantum infimae teguntur: cetera prope nuda et teretibus habenis vincta sunt, shoestrings, Gell. 13, 21, 5.— Esp.,

habentia.full: hăbentĭa, ae, f. habeo, II. A., possessions, property, substance (ante-class.): animos eorum habentia inflarat, Quadrig. ap. Non. 119, 32; Plaut. Truc. prol. 21. (dub.; dum habent, Spengel).

habenula.full: hăbēnŭla, ae, f. dim. habena, II. A., a small strip of diseased flesh which is cut out from the body: tum ab ora vel vulsella vel hamo apprehensam tamquam habenulam excidere, Cels. 7, 28; id. 7, 7, 8 fin.; 20 fin.

habeo.full: hăbĕo, ŭi, ĭtum, 2 (archaic perf. subj. habessit, Cic. Leg. 2, 8, 19; inf. haberier, Plaut. Mil. 2, 6, 111), v. a. and n. etym. dub.; cf. Gr. κώπη, handle; Lat. capio; Germ. haben, Haft; Engl. have, to have, in the widest sense of the word, to hold, keep, possess, cherish, entertain, occupy, enclose, contain (cf.: teneo, possideo, etc.). In gen. Of personal subjects. With persons or things as objects: SI INTESTATO MORITVR, CVI SVVS HERES NEC SIT, AGNATVS PROXIMVS FAMILIAM HABETO, Fragm. XII. Tab

habilis.full: hăbĭlis, e, adj. habeo, II. B. 2., that may be easily handled or managed, manageable, suitable, fit, proper, apt, expert, light, nimble, swift (class.). Lit.: (calcei) habiles et apti ad pedem, Cic. de Or. 1, 54, 231; cf.: (natura homini) figuram corporis habilem et aptam ingenio humano dedit, id. Leg. 1, 9, 26; res aptae, habiles et ad naturam accommodatae, id. Fin. 4, 20, 56: brevitate habiles gladii, Liv. 22, 46, 5: ensis, Verg. A. 9, 305: arcus, id. ib. 1, 318: pharetra ad tela, Val. Fl. 3,

habilitas.full: hăbĭlĭtas, ātis, f. habilis, aptitude, ability: omitto opportunitates habilitatesque reliqui corporis, Cic. Leg. 1, 9, 27.

habitabilis.full: hăbĭtābĭlis, e, adj. habito, habitable. Lit. (class.): regiones, Cic. Tusc. 1, 20, 45: cinguli (terrae), id. Rep. 6, 20: media plaga (terrae), Ov. M. 1, 49: orae, Hor. C. 4, 14, 5: caelum, Ov. F. 4, 611: non habitabile frigus, id. Tr. 3, 4, 51.— Poet. transf., inhabited: Tarpeiae rupes Superisque habitabile saxum, Sil. 1, 541.

habitaculum.full: hăbĭtācŭlum, i, n. id., a dwellingplace, habitation (post-class.). Lit.: leonis, Gell. 5, 14, 21: avium, Pall. 1, 23.— Transf., of the body, as the dwellingplace of the soul, Prud. Cath. 10, 39.

habitatio.full: hăbĭtātĭo, ōnis, f. id., a dwelling, inhabiting: ad habitationem praebere mansionem, Pall. 1, 9, 1: aquarum, Firm. Math. 2, 10 init. Transf., a dwelling, habitation.— Lit. (class.; cf.: domus, domicilium, sedes, mansio, tectum): scelestae haec aedes, impiast habitatio, Plaut. Most. 2, 2, 73; cf. id. ib. 67: ut nobis haec habitatio Bona, fausta ... eveniat, id. Trin. 1, 2, 2: peto a te, ut ei de habitatione accommodes, Cic. Fam. 13, 2: sumptus habitationis, id. Cael. 7, 17; Cato, R. R. 128; Col.

habitatiuncula.full: hăbĭtātĭuncŭla, ae, f. dim. habitatio, a little dwelling (late Lat.): in specubus habitatiunculas habere, Hier. in Obad. med.

habitator.full: hăbĭtātor, ōris, m. habito, a dweller in a house, tenant, occupant: tuam (domum) in Carinis mundi habitatores Lamiae conduxerunt, Cic. Q. Fr. 2, 3, 7: inesse aliquem habitatorem in hac caelesti ac divina domo, id. ib. 2, 35, 90: tumultu habitatorum, Liv. 21, 62, 3 al.: testa in illa vidit habitatorem magnum, Juv. 14, 311; Sen. Ep. 45, 10; Plin. Pan. 50, 3.— Transf., an inhabitant of a country, etc.: incolae atque habitatores, Cic. N. D. 2, 56, 140: civitas habitatoribus vacua, Amm. 24, 2, 3: hab

habitatrix.full: hăbĭtātrix, īcis, f. habitator, she that inhabits, Aus. Idyll. 10, 82.

habitio.full: hăbĭtĭo, ōnis, f. habeo, a having: debitio gratiae, non habitio, cum pecunia confertur, Gell. 1, 4, 7.

habito.full: hăbĭto, āvi, ātum, 1 (gen. plur. of the part. pres. habitantum, Ov. M. 14, 90), v. freq. a. and n. habeo. In gen., to have frequently, to be wont to have (anteclass. and very rare): epicrocum, Varr. ap. Non. 318, 25: comas, id. ib. 27.— In partic., to have possession of, to inhabit a place; and more freq. neut., to dwell, abide, reside, live anywhere (the class. signif. of the word; cf.: colo, incolo, commoror). Lit. Act.: centum urbes habitant magnas, Verg. A. 3, 106: silvas, id. E. 6, 2: hoc n

habitudo.full: hăbĭtūdo, ĭnis, f. habitus, P. a., from habeo, condition, plight, habit, appearance, figure of the body (mostly ante- and postclass., for the class. habitus): qui color, nitor, vestitus, quae habitudo est corporis! *Ter. Eun. 2, 2, 11; cf.: bona corporis, Auct. Her. 4, 10, 15: habitus atque habitudo, dress and figure, App. M. 9, p. 235: ancillae, id. ib. 2, p. 118.—Plur.: tam varias habitudines corporis participat, App. Mag. p. 282, 29.

habituo.full: hăbĭtŭo, āre, v. a. id., to bring into a condition or habit of body; in pass., to be constituted or conditioned in any manner, to be in any condition or habit of body (post-class.): si nutrix malo suco atque corpore habituari videatur, Cael. Aur. Tard. 1, 4, 79; id. ib. 4, 8, 109.

habiturio.full: hăbĭtūrĭo, īre, v. desid. a. [habeo], to desire to have, to long for any thing: si arationes Habituris, Plaut. Truc. 1, 2, 47.

habitus1.full: hăbĭtus, a, um, Part. and P. a., from habeo, q. v. fin.

habitus2.full: hăbĭtus, ūs, m. 1. habitus, P. a., from habeo, the condition or state of a thing (class.). Lit. In gen., condition, plight, habit, deportment, appearance of the body (in sing. and plur.): cum ille vir (Q. Metellus) integerrima aetate, optimo habitu, maximis viribus eriperetur bonis omnibus, Cic. Cael. 24, 59: qui habitus et quae figura non procul abesse putatur a vitae periculo, id. Brut. 91, 313; cf.: qui non tam habitus corporis opimos quam gracilitates consectentur, id. ib. 16, 64: mediocris,

habrodiaetus.full: Habrŏdĭaetus, i, m., = Ἁβροδίαιτος (living delicately), an epithet of the painter Parrhasius, Plin. 35, 10, 36, § 71.
habrodiaetus.short: Habrŏdĭaetus, i, m., = Ἁβροδίαιτος (living delicately), an epithet of the painter Parrhasius, Plin.

hac.full: hāc, adv., v. hic fin. III. 1.

hactenus.full: hac-tĕnus (a strengthened archaic form, hacĕtĕnus, acc. to Mar. Victor. p. 2457 P.—Separated per tmesin, Verg. A. 5, 603; 6, 62; Ov. M. 5, 642), adv. hic- tenus; lit., as far as to this side; hence, to indicate a limit, so far, thus far (cf. hucusque). In space. Lit. (very rare), to this place, thus far: hactenus summus inaurato crater erat asper acantho, Ov. M. 13, 700: hactenus dominum est illa secuta suum, id. Tr. 1, 10, 22; id. Am. 2, 11, 16; cf.: hactenus in occidentem Germaniam novimus, Ta
hactenus.short: hac-tĕnus (a strengthened archaic form, hacĕtĕnus, acc.

hadranum.full: Hādrānum (also Adr-), i, n., = Ἅδρᾶνον, a town of Sicily, near Mount Ætna, Sil. 14, 250.—Hādrānĭtāni, its inhabitants, Plin. 3, 8, 14, § 91.
hadranum.short: Hādrānum (also Adr-), i, n., = Ἅδρᾶνον, a town of Sicily, near Mount Ætna, Sil.

hadria.full: Hā^drĭa (Adria), ae. F., the name of two Italian cities. In Picenum, the birthplace of the emperor Hadrian, now Atri, Liv. 24, 10, 10; Mel. 2, 4, 6; Plin. 3, 13, 18, § 110; Spart. Hadr. 1.— Derivv. Hadrĭānus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Hadria, Hadrian: ager, Liv. 22, 9, 5; Plin. 3, 13, 18, § 110: gallinae, id. 10, 53, 74, § 146.— Subst.: Hadriānus, i, m., the emperor Hadrian, Ael. Spart. Hadr. 1 sq.; Eutr. 8, 5 sqq.—Hence, Hădrĭānā-lis, e, adj., of or belonging to the emperor Hadrian: SODAL

hadrobolon.full: hadrŏbōlon, i, n., = ἁδρόβωλον (in big lumps), a kind of black gum, Plin. 12, 9, 19, § 35.
hadrobolon.short: hadrŏbōlon, i, n., = ἁδρόβωλον (in big lumps), a kind of black gum, Plin.

hadrosphaerum.full: hadrosphaerum, i, n., = ἁδρόσφαιρον, a kind of spikenard with large leaves, Plin. 12, 12, 26, § 44.
hadrosphaerum.short: hadrosphaerum, i, n., = ἁδρόσφαιρον, a kind of spikenard with large leaves, Plin.

hadrumetum.full: Hadrūmētum (Adrūm-), i, n. (also Hadrumetus, i, f., Mart. Cap. 6, § 670), = Ἁδρούμητος, a city of Africa propria, the capital of the province Byzacene, Mel. 1, 7, 2; Plin. 5, 4, 3, § 25; Caes. B. C. 2, 23; Liv. 30, 29.— Deriv. Hadrūmētīnus (Adr-), a, um, adj., of or belonging to Hadrumetum, Hadrumetine: Clodius Albinus, of Hadrumetum, Capitol. Albin. 1: navis, Vulg. Act. 27, 2.—Subst.: Hadrūmētī-ni, ōrum, m. plur., the inhabitants of Hadrumetum, Hadrumetines, Auct. B. Afr. 97, 2.

haedilia.full: Haedĭlĭa, ae, f., prob. a mountain near the Sabine villa of Horace, Hor. C. 1, 17, 9 (so the Codd.; Bentley conjectured haeduleae, from haedulea, a little kid; but see Orell. and Dillenb. ad h. 1.).

haedillus.full: haedillus (hoed-), i, m. dim. haedus, a little kid, kidling; as a term of endearment, Plaut. As. 3, 3, 77.

haedinus.full: haedĭnus (hoed-), a, um (* acc. to others, -īnus), adj. id., of a kid, kid-: coagulum, Varr. R. R. 2, 11, 4: pelliculae, Cic. Mur. 36, 75.—As subst.: haedina, ae, kid's flesh, Cael. Aur. Acut. 1, 11, 95.

haedulus.full: haedŭlus (hoed-), i, m. dim. haedus, a little kid: pinguissimus, Juv. 11, 66.

haedus.full: haedus (less correctly hoedus, and archaic aedus or ēdus; cf. Quint. 1, 5, 19, and see the letter H; Sabine, fedus, like fircus for hircus, cf. Varr. L.L. 5, § 97 Müll., and see the letter F), i, m. Sanscr. huda, ram; O. H. Germ. Geiz; cf. Gr. χίμαρος, a young goat, a kid (cf.: hircus, caper). Lit., Varr. R. R. 2, 3, 4; 8; Cic. de Sen. 16, 56; Verg. G. 4, 10; Hor. C. 3, 18, 5; id. Epod. 2, 60; Mart. 10, 87, 17.—As a fig. for wantonness: tenero lascivior haedo, Ov. M. 13, 791; as a fig. of weakne
haedus.short: haedus (less correctly hoedus, and archaic aedus or ēdus;

haemachates.full: haemăchātes, ae, m., = αἱμαχάτης, blood-colored agate, a precious stone, Plin. 37, 10, 54, § 139.
haemachates.short: haemăchātes, ae, m., = αἱμαχάτης, blood-colored agate, a precious stone, Plin.

haematicon.full: haemătĭcon, i, n., = αἱματικόν (bloody), a sort of shrub, App. Herb. 77.
haematicon.short: haemătĭcon, i, n., = αἱματικόν (bloody), a sort of shrub, App.

haematinus.full: haemătĭnus, a, um, adj., = ἁιμάτινος, blood-red, blood-colored: vitrum, Plin. 36, 26, 67, § 197.
haematinus.short: haemătĭnus, a, um, adj., = ἁιμάτινος, blood-red, blood-colored: vitrum, Plin.

haematites.full: haemătītes, ae, m., = αἱματίτης. blood-stone, a kind of red iron-ore, hematite, Plin. 36, 16, 25, §§ 129, 130; 36, 20, 37, § 144.—In apposition: lapis haematites purgat, Cels. 5, 3.— A red-colored precious stone, Plin. 37, 10, 60, § 169.

haematopus.full: haemătŏpūs, pŏdis, m., = αἱματόπους (blood-foot), in Plin. 10, 47, 64, § 130, v. l. for himantopus, q. v.
haematopus.short: haemătŏpūs, pŏdis, m., = αἱματόπους (blood-foot), in Plin.

haemesis.full: haemēsis, is, f., an inflammatory disease of the eye, Theod. Prisc. 1, 10.
haemesis.short: haemēsis, is, f., an inflammatory disease of the eye, Theod.

haemimontus.full: Haemĭmontus (Aemi-), i, m., a province of Thrace, adjoining Mount Hœmus, Vop. Aur. 17, 2; Treb. Poll. Claud. 11, 3; Sext. Ruf. 9; Notit. Dign. Imp. Occid. 1. —Hence, Haemĭmontāni (Aemi-), ōrum, m., the inhabitants of Hœmimontus, Amm. 27, 4, 11.
haemimontus.short: Haemĭmontus (Aemi-), i, m., a province of Thrace, adjoining Mount Hœmus, Vop.

haemon.full: Haemon, ŏnis, m., = Αἵμων, a son of Creon, king of Thebes, the lover of Antigone, Prop. 2, 8, 21; Ov. Tr. 2, 402; id. Ib. 563; Hyg. Fab. 72.
haemon.short: Haemon, ŏnis, m., = Αἵμων, a son of Creon, king of Thebes, the lover of Antigone, Prop.

haemonia.full: Haemŏnĭa (Aemŏnia), ae, f., a poetical name of Thessaly, Ov. M. 1, 568; 2, 543; 8, 815; id. R. Am. 249; id. F. 5, 381: nivalis, Hor. C. 1, 37, 20.— Derivv. Haemŏnĭus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Hœmonia (Thessaly), Hœmonian (Thessalian): gens, Ov. Tr. 1, 10, 30: urbs, i. e. Trachin, id. M. 11, 652: Acastus, id. ib. 11, 410: juvenis, i. e. Jason, id. ib. 7, 132: puer, i. e. Achilles, id. F. 5, 400: equi, i. e. of Achilles, id. Tr. 3, 11, 28: lyra, the same, id. ib. 4, 1, 16: arcus, i. e. the
haemonia.short: Haemŏnĭa (Aemŏnia), ae, f., a poetical name of Thessaly, Ov.

haemophthisicus.full: haemophthĭsĭcus, i, m., = αἱμοφθισικός, a person with corrupted blood, Aem. Mac. de Beton.
haemophthisicus.short: haemophthĭsĭcus, i, m., = αἱμοφθισικός, a person with corrupted blood, Aem.

haemoptyicus.full: haemoptўĭcus (not -toĭcus), i, m., = αἱμοπτυικός, one who spits blood, Marc. Emp. 16 med.; Cael. Aur. Tard. 3, 2, 35.
haemoptyicus.short: haemoptўĭcus (not -toĭcus), i, m., = αἱμοπτυικός, one who spits blood, Marc.

haemorrhagia.full: haemorrhăgĭa, ae, f., = αἱμορραγία, a violent bleeding, hemorrhage, bleeding at the nose, Plin. 23, 7, 67, § 132.
haemorrhagia.short: haemorrhăgĭa, ae, f., = αἱμορραγία, a violent bleeding, hemorrhage, bleeding at the nose, Plin.

haemorrhoicus.full: haemorrhŏĭcus, i, m., = αἱμορροϊκός, that has the hemorrhoids or piles, Firm. Math. 3, 3, 7; 3, 15, 2.
haemorrhoicus.short: haemorrhŏĭcus, i, m., = αἱμορροϊκός, that has the hemorrhoids or piles, Firm.

haemorrhoida.full: haemorrhŏĭda, ae, f. (discharging blood; written as Greek, αἱμορροΐς, Cels. 6, 18, 9). In medic., the piles, hemorrhoids, Plin. 23, 7, 71, § 137; Cael. Aur. Tard. 5, 1, 2; Amm. 30, 6, 5.

haemorrhois.full: haemorrhŏis, ĭdis, f., = αἱμορροΐς, a kind of poisonous serpent, Plin. 23, 1, 23, § 43; 20, 20, 81, § 210; Luc. 9, 806.
haemorrhois.short: haemorrhŏis, ĭdis, f., = αἱμορροΐς, a kind of poisonous serpent, Plin.

haemorrhousa.full: haemorrhousa, ae, f., = αἱμορροῦσα, she that has a hemorrhage, eccl. (cf. Vulg. Matt. 9, 20).
haemorrhousa.short: haemorrhousa, ae, f., = αἱμορροῦσα, she that has a hemorrhage, eccl.

haemostasis.full: haemostăsis, is, f., = αἱμόστασις, a plant that stops the flow of blood, App. Herb. 59.
haemostasis.short: haemostăsis, is, f., = αἱμόστασις, a plant that stops the flow of blood, App.

haemus.full: Haemus (Aemus) or Haemos, i, m., = Αἷμος. A high range of mountains in Thrace, now called the Great Balkan, Mel. 2, 2, 2; Plin. 4, 11, 18, § 41; Liv. 4, 21 sq.; Ov. M. 6, 87; 2, 219; 10, 77; id. F. 1, 390; Hor. C. 1, 12, 6 et saep.— A celebrated actor, Juv. 3, 99; 6, 198.
haemus.short: Haemus (Aemus) or Haemos, i, m., = Αἷμος.

haereo.full: haerĕo, haesi, haesum, 2, v. n. etym. dub., to hang or hold fast, to hang, stick, cleave, cling, adhere, be fixed, sit fast, remain close to any thing or in any manner (class. and very freq., esp. in the trop. sense; cf. pendeo); usually constr. with in, the simple abl. or absol., less freq. with dat., with ad, sub, ex, etc. Lit.: ut videamus, terra penitusne defixa sit, et quasi radicibus suis haereat, an media pendeat? Cic. Ac. 2, 39, 122; so, terra ima sede semper haeret, id. Rep. 6, 18: ling

haeresco.full: haeresco, ĕre, v. inch. n. [haereo], to stick, adhere (Lucretian): primordia in terris, Lucr. 2, 477; 4, 742.

haeresiarcha.full: haerĕsĭarcha, ae, m., = αἱρεσιάρχης, a leader of a sect, heresiarch (eccl. Lat.), Sid. Ep. 7, 6; Aug. Ep. 253.
haeresiarcha.short: haerĕsĭarcha, ae, m., = αἱρεσιάρχης, a leader of a sect, heresiarch (eccl.

haeresis.full: haerĕsis (scanned hĕrĕsis in Prud. Psych. 725; Ham. 64), is and ĕos, f., = αἵρεσις. A (philosophical or religious) sect, a school of thought (=secta): Cato in ea est haeresi, quae nullum sequitur florem orationis, Cic. Par. prooem. § 2; as Greek, id. Fam. 15, 16, 3: Pythagorae haeresim sequi, Vitr. 5 praef.— Heretical religious doctrine, heresy, Tert. adv. Haer. 1 sq. et saep.: Ariana, the Arian heresy, Sid. Ep. 7, 6: plurimae sectae et haereses, Lact. 4, 30, 2.— Hĕrĕsis, personif., Prud. Psych.

haeretice.full: haerĕtĭce, adv., v. the foll. art. I. fin.

haereticus.full: haerĕtĭcus, a, um, adj., = αἱρετικός, of or belonging to heretical religious doctrines, heretical (eccl. Lat.). Adj.: commissatio, Tert. adv. Haer. 41: nigredo, Arat. Act. Apost. 1, 611.—Adv.: haerĕtĭce, heretically, Cassiod. Hist. Eccl. 5, 36.— Subst.: haerĕtĭcus, i, m., a heretic, Tert. adv. Hermog. 27; id. de Bapt. 115; so the title of Tertullian's work: de Praescriptione adversus haereticos.
haereticus.short: haerĕtĭcus, a, um, adj., = αἱρετικός, of or belonging to heretical religious doctrines, heretical (eccl.

haesitabundus.full: haesĭtābundus, a, um, adj. haesito, II., stammering, faltering, hesitating: expalluit notabiliter et haesitabundus inquit: Interrogavi, etc., Plin. Ep. 1, 5, 13.

haesitantia.full: haesĭtantĭa, ae, f. id., a stammering: linguae, Cic. Phil. 3, 6, 16.

haesitatio.full: haesĭtātĭo, ōnis, f. id., a hesitating (rare but good prose). Of speech, a stammering: qui timor! quae dubitatio! quanta haesitatio tractusque verborum! Cic. de Or. 2, 50, 202: deformis, Quint. 11, 2, 48.— Mental uncertainty, irresolution, perplexity, embarrassment, hesitation (rare but class.): si facile inveneris quid dicas, noli ignoscere haesitationi meae, Cic. Fam. 3, 12, 2: non mediocris haesitatio est, hinc justitiae proposita imagine, inde pietatis, Quint. 12, 1, 40; 11, 2, 48: haesitati

haesitator.full: haesĭtātor, ōris, m. id., one who hesitates, is undecided: sum et ipse in edendo (libros) haesitator, Plin. Ep. 5, 11, 2.

haesito.full: haesĭto, āvi, ātum, 1, v. freq. n. [haereo], to stick fast, remain fixed in a place. Lit. (rare; not in Cic.): ut, si eam paludem Romani perrumpere conarentur, haesitantes premerent ex loco superiore, Caes. B. G. 7, 19, 2: ita in vadis haesitantis frumenti acervos sedisse illitos limo, Liv. 2, 5, 3; Lucr. 6, 334; 5, 697.— Prov.: haesitare in eodem luto, i. e. to be exposed to the same danger, Ter. Phorm. 5, 2, 15.— Trop. (opp. firmness), to be uncertain, hesitating. * In speech: linguā haesitant

hageter.full: hāgētēr, ēris, m., = ἁγητήρ, the leader, guide: Hercules, Plin. 34, 8, 19, § 56.
hageter.short: hāgētēr, ēris, m., = ἁγητήρ, the leader, guide: Hercules, Plin.

hagiographa.full: Hăgĭŏgrăpha, ōrum, n., = Αγιόγραφα, the last of the three principal divisions of the Old Testament Scriptures, Hier. in. Reg. praef.; id. Ep. 106, 110.
hagiographa.short: Hăgĭŏgrăpha, ōrum, n., = Αγιόγραφα, the last of the three principal divisions of the Old Testament Scriptures, Hier.

hagiographus.full: hăgĭogrăphus, i, m., = ἁγιόγραφος, a sacred writer, Hier. Ep. 1, 12.
hagiographus.short: hăgĭogrăphus, i, m., = ἁγιόγραφος, a sacred writer, Hier.

halaesa.full: Halaesa, Halaesinus, and Ha-laesus, v. Halesa, etc.

halagora.full: hălăgŏra, as, f. ἅλσ-ἀγορά, the saltmarket, Plaut. Poen. 5, 5, 34 dub.

halapanta.full: halapanta significat omnia mentientem, Paul. ex Fest. p. 101, 18 Müll. (perh. the same word as halophanta, q. v.).

halatio.full: hālātĭo, ōnis, f. halo, a breathing, breath, Cassiod. in Psa. 37, 12.

halatus.full: hālātus, ūs, m. id., a breath of perfume, odor, fragrance (post-class.): florum, Mart. Cap. 1, § 7: Arabici, id. 2, § 215.

hales.full: Hales, ētis, m., a small river in Lucania near Velia, now Halente, Cic. Fam. 7, 20, 1; id. Att. 16, 7, 5.
hales.short: Hales, ētis, m., a small river in Lucania near Velia, now Halente, Cic.

halesa.full: Hălēsa (Halaesa and Alēsa), ae, f., = Ἅλαισα, a town on the northern coast of Sicily, on the river Halesus, now ruins near the village Iusa, Sil. 14, 218; Cic. Verr. 2, 2, 7, § 19; 2, 2, 75, § 185.— Deriv. Hălēsīnus (Halaes- and Alēs-), a, um, adj., of or belonging to Halesa: civitas, Cic. Fam. 13, 32, 1: Dio, of Halesa, Cic. Verr. 2, 2, 7, § 19; 2, 3, 73.—Subst.: Hă-lēsīni, ōrum, m. plur., the inhabitants of Halesa, Halesines, Plin. 3, 8, 14, § 91.
halesa.short: Hălēsa (Halaesa and Alēsa), ae, f., = Ἅλαισα, a town on the northern coast of Sicily, on the river Halesus, now ruins near the village Iusa, Sil.

halesus.full: Hălēsus (Halaesus and Alēsus), i, m., = Ἅλαισος. Son of Agamemnon and Clytemnestra or Brisēis, the founder of Falisci, Verg. A. 7, 724; 10, 352; 411; Ov. F. 4, 73; id. Am. 3, 13, 31.— One of the Lapithœ, Ov. M. 12, 462.— A small river on the northern coast of Sicily, on which the town Halesa was situated, Col. poët. 10, 268; Sol. 5, 20.
halesus.short: Hălēsus (Halaesus and Alēsus), i, m., = Ἅλαισος.

haliacmon.full: Hălĭacmon (Aliacmon), ŏnis, m., a stream forming the boundary between Macedonia and Thessaly, now Vistritza, Plin. 4, 10, 17, § 34; Caes. B. C. 3, 37; Liv. 42, 53, 5; Claud. B. G. 179.
haliacmon.short: Hălĭacmon (Aliacmon), ŏnis, m., a stream forming the boundary between Macedonia and Thessaly, now Vistritza, Plin.

haliaeetos.full: hălĭœĕtos (haly-), i, m., = ἁλιαίετος, the osprey or sea-eagle: Falco haliaetus, Linn.; Plin. 10, 3, 3, § 10; Nisus, the father of Scylla, was changed into one, Ov. M. 8, 146; Verg. Cir. 535.
haliaeetos.short: hălĭœĕtos (haly-), i, m., = ἁλιαίετος, the osprey or sea-eagle: Falco haliaetus, Linn.;

haliartus.full: Hălĭartus, i, f., = Ἁλίαρτος, a city of Bœotia near the modern village of Mazi, Plin. 4, 7, 12, § 26; Nep. Lys. 3; Liv. 42, 46; 56; 63.—Hence, Hălĭartii, ōrum, m., its inhabitants, Liv. 42, 46.
haliartus.short: Hălĭartus, i, f., = Ἁλίαρτος, a city of Bœotia near the modern village of Mazi, Plin.

halicacabus.full: hălĭcācăbus, i, f. (sc. herba) = ἁλικάκαβος, a plant called in pure Latin vesicaria, Plin. 21, 31, 105, § 180; Cels. 5, 20, 3.

halicarnassus.full: Hălĭcarnassus (-sos) or Hali-carnāsus, i, f., = Ἁλικαρνασσός, a city of great antiquity in Caria, the birthplace of the historians Herodotus and Dionysius, also celebrated for the mausolēum erected there, now Bodrun or Boudroum, Mel. 1, 16, 2 and 3; Plin. 5, 29, 29, § 107; Cic. Tusc. 3, 31, 75; id. Q. Fr. 1, 1, 8, § 25; Liv. 37, 10, 11. — Derivv. Hălĭcarnasseus, ĕi and ĕos, m. adj., = Ἁλικαρνασσεύς, of Halicarnassus: Scylax, Cic. Div. 2, 42, 88: Dionysius, Quint. 3, 1, 16: Cleon, Nep. Lys. 5.— H
halicarnassus.short: Hălĭcarnassus (-sos) or Hali-carnāsus, i, f., = Ἁλικαρνασσός, a city of great antiquity in Caria, the birthplace of the historians Herodotus and Dionysius, also celebrated for the mausolēum erected there, now Bodrun or Boudroum, Mel.

halicyensis.full: Hălĭcўensis, e, adj., of or belonging to the city Halicyœ (Ἁλικύαι) in Sicily (now Salemi), Halicyœan: civitas, Cic. Verr. 2, 3, 6, § 13: Sopater quidam, of Halicyœ, id. ib. 2, 2, 28, § 68.—Plur. subst.: Halicy-enses, ium, m., the inhabitants of Halicyœ, Halicyœans, Cic. Verr. 2, 3, 40, § 91; Plin. 3, 8, 14, § 91.
halicyensis.short: Hălĭcўensis, e, adj., of or belonging to the city Halicyœ (Ἁλικύαι) in Sicily (now Salemi), Halicyœan: civitas, Cic.

halieuticus.full: hălĭeutĭcus, a, um, adj., = ἁλιευτικός, of or belonging to fishing: boletar, Gall. ap. Treb. Claud. 17.—Subst.: Halieutica, ōrum, n., a title of a poem on fishing. by Ovid; cf. Plin. 32, 2, 5, § 11.
halieuticus.short: hălĭeutĭcus, a, um, adj., = ἁλιευτικός, of or belonging to fishing: boletar, Gall.

halimon.full: hălĭmŏn, i, n., = ἅλιμον, a plant, the orach (Atriplex halimus of Linn.), Plin. 17, 24, 37, § 239; cf. id. 22, 22, 33, § 73.
halimon.short: hălĭmŏn, i, n., = ἅλιμον, a plant, the orach (Atriplex halimus of Linn.), Plin.

haliphloeos.full: hăliphloeos, i, f., = ἁλίφλοιος (seabark), a species of oak, Plin. 16, 6, 8, § 24.
haliphloeos.short: hăliphloeos, i, f., = ἁλίφλοιος (seabark), a species of oak, Plin.

halipleumon.full: hălipleumon, ŏnis, m., = ἁλιπλεύμων (sea-lungs), a kind of fish, otherwise unknown, Plin. 32, 11, 53, § 149.
halipleumon.short: hălipleumon, ŏnis, m., = ἁλιπλεύμων (sea-lungs), a kind of fish, otherwise unknown, Plin.

halito.full: hālĭto, āre, v. freq. a. halo, to breathe out: flammam halitantes, Enn. ap. Diom. p. 336 P. (Trag. v. 217 Vahl.).—So perh. also: Scio spiritum ejus majorem esse multo quam folles taurini halitant, Plaut. Fragm. Bacch.; cf. Ritschl in Rhein. Mus. 1846, p. 580.

halitus.full: hālĭtus (alitus), ūs, m. id., breath, exhalation, steam, vapor. Lit. (poet. and in post-Aug. prose): Nemeaeus leo Frendens efflavit graviter extremum halitum, his last breath, * Cic. poët. Tusc. 2, 9, 22: aegris faucibus exsuperat gravis halitus, Pers. 3, 88: quae (i. e. nebulae aestusque) velut halitus sursum feruntur, Lucr. 6, 478: a pulmone halitus graveolentia, i. e. stinking breath, Plin. 28, 12, 53, § 194; so, oris, id. 21, 20, 83, § 142; 28, 4, 14, § 56; cf.: artificis halitus oris, Juv.

hallelujah.full: hallĕlūjah (āllĕlūia), interj. Hebr. halal, to praise; Jah = Jehovah, praised be God! praise the Lord! Form hall-, August. Ep. 86, 178; Sid. Ep. 2, 10; Prud. Nol. Carm. 37, 56. Form all-, Vulg. Job, 13, 22; Psa. 104, 1; Apoc. 19, 1, 3, 4 al.—Deriv. hallĕlūjătĭcus, a, um: psalmi, devoted to praise, containing hallelujahs, August. Psa. 105.

hallucinor.full: hallūcĭnor, āri, and its derivatives, v. aluc-.
hallucinor.short: hallūcĭnor, āri, and its derivatives, v.

halmyridion.full: halmyrĭdĭon, ii, n., = ἁλμυρίδιον (saltish), a kind of cabbage, Plin. 19, 8, 41, § 142.
halmyridion.short: halmyrĭdĭon, ii, n., = ἁλμυρίδιον (saltish), a kind of cabbage, Plin.

halmyrrhax.full: halmyrrhax, ăgis, m., = ἁλμύρραξ, a kind of saltpetre, Plin. 31, 10, 46, § 106.
halmyrrhax.short: halmyrrhax, ăgis, m., = ἁλμύρραξ, a kind of saltpetre, Plin.

halo.full: hālo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. n. and a., to breathe (poet.; cf.: feo, spiro). Neutr., to breathe, to emit vapor or fragrance, be fragrant: invitent croceis halantes floribus horti, Verg. G. 4, 109: ture calent arae sertisque recentibus halant, id. A. 1, 417.— Act., to breathe out, exhale: et nardi florem, nectar qui naribus halat, Lucr. 2, 848; 6, 221; 391; Mart. 10, 48.

halonem.full: halonem, id est hesterno vino languentem, Paul. ex Fest. s. v. ELUCUM, p. 75 Müll.
halonem.short: halonem, id est hesterno vino languentem, Paul.

halophanta.full: hălŏphanta, ae, m, = ἁλοφάντης (a word comically formed after the analogy of sycophanta, συκοφάντης), a salt-informer, i. q. a rascal, scoundrel, Plaut. Curc. 4, 1, 2; cf. Non. 126, 7, and see halapanta.
halophanta.short: hălŏphanta, ae, m, = ἁλοφάντης (a word comically formed after the analogy of sycophanta, συκοφάντης), a salt-informer, i.

halos.full: hălōs, ō, f., = ἅλως (a round threshing-floor), a circle round the sun or moon, a halo, pure Lat. corona: circa solem visum coloris varii circulum, qualis esse in arcu solet. Hunc Graeci halo vocant: nos dicere coronam aptissime possumus, etc., Sen. Q. N. 1, 2, 1.—Called also hălўsis (prob. corrupted from ἅλως), App. de Mundo, p. 64, 16.
halos.short: hălōs, ō, f., = ἅλως (a round threshing-floor), a circle round the sun or moon, a halo, pure Lat.

halosis.full: hălōsis, is, f., = ἅλωσις, a taking by storm, capture, Petr. 89, 1 (in Suet. Ner. 38, written as Greek).
halosis.short: hălōsis, is, f., = ἅλωσις, a taking by storm, capture, Petr.

halter.full: halter, ēris, m., = ἁλτήρ, in gymnastics, leaden weights held in the hands in leaping exercises, to add to the impetus of the body, the dumb-bells of modern gymnastics, Mart. 14, 49, 1; 7, 67, 6 (pure Lat. manipuli, Cael. Aur. Tard. 5, 2, 38).
halter.short: halter, ēris, m., = ἁλτήρ, in gymnastics, leaden weights held in the hands in leaping exercises, to add to the impetus of the body, the dumb-bells of modern gymnastics, Mart.

halus.full: Halus, i, f., a small place in Assyria, near Artemita, only mentioned by Tac. A. 6, 41.
halus.short: Halus, i, f., a small place in Assyria, near Artemita, only mentioned by Tac.

halys.full: Hălys, yos, m., = Ἅλυς. A river in Asia Minor, flowing between Paphlagonia and Cappadocia, now Kisil-Irmak: secundum Halyn, Mel. 1, 19, 9; Plin. 6, 2, 2, § 6; 6, 3, 3, § 8: circa Halyn, Liv. 38, 16, 13: Croesus Halym penetrans magnam pervertet opum vim, Cic. Div. 2, 56, 115; cf.: Croeso fatalis Halys, Luc. 3, 272.—Acc.: Halym, also Curt. 4, 11, 3.— A man's name, Stat. Th. 2, 574.—As a surname, Inscr. Grut. 877, 9.

hama.full: hăma (ama), ae, f., = ἄμη, a waterbucket, esp. for extinguishing fires, a firebucket, Plin Ep. 10, 42, 2; Juv. 14, 305; Dig. 1, 15, 3; 33, 7, 12, §§ 18, 21 (in Plaut. Mil. 3, 2, 42, false reading for aula, Lorenz ad loc.).
hama.short: hăma (ama), ae, f., = ἄμη, a waterbucket, esp.

hamadryas.full: Hămādrўas, ădis, f., = Ἁμαδρυάς, a wood-nymph, hamadryad; in sing., Stat. S. 1, 3, 63; in plur., Verg. E. 10, 62; Prop. 2, 32 (3, 30), 37; Ov. M. 1, 690; 14, 624; id. F. 2, 155; dat. Grœc.: Hamadryasin, Prop. 1, 20, 32 (like ib. 12 Dryasin, and ib. 34 Thyniasin).
hamadryas.short: Hămādrўas, ădis, f., = Ἁμαδρυάς, a wood-nymph, hamadryad;

hamae.full: Hamae, ārum, f., a place in Campania, near Cumœ, mentioned only by Liv. 23, 35, 3.
hamae.short: Hamae, ārum, f., a place in Campania, near Cumœ, mentioned only by Liv.

hamarthritis.full: hămarthrītis, is, f. ἅμα-ἀρθρῖτις, the general gout, Cael. Aur. Tard. 5, 2, 28.

hamartigenia.full: Hămartĭgĕnīa, ae, f., = Ἁμαρτιγένεια, The Origin of Sin, the title of a poem by Prudentius.
hamartigenia.short: Hămartĭgĕnīa, ae, f., = Ἁμαρτιγένεια, The Origin of Sin, the title of a poem by Prudentius.

hamatilis.full: hāmātĭlis, e, adj. hamatus, with hooks, i. e. performed by or furnished with hooks (ante- and post-class.): piscatus, Plaut. Rud. 2, 1, 10: spiculum scorpii, Tert. adv. Gnost. 1.

hamatus.full: hāmātus, a, um, adj. hamus, furnished with a hook, hooked. Lit.: ungues, Ov. M. 12, 563: harundo, id. ib. 5, 384: sentes, id. ib. 2, 799.— Transf., shaped like a hook, hooked, crooked: hamatis uncinatisque corporibus concreta haec esse dicat, * Cic. Ac. 2, 38, 121: ensis, i. q. harpe, Ov. M. 5, 80 (cf.: ferrum curvo tenus abdidit hamo, id. ib. 4, 720).— Trop.: hos ego viscatis hamatisque muneribus non sua promere puto, sed aliena corripere, i. e. catching, alluring, Plin. Ep. 9, 30, 2 (cf. with

hamaxa.full: hămaxa, ae, f., = ἅμαξα, a wagon, Capitol. Max. duob. 6 (in Gell. 2, 21, 9, in the signification of septentriones, written as Greek).
hamaxa.short: hămaxa, ae, f., = ἅμαξα, a wagon, Capitol.

hamaxagoga.full: hămaxăgōga, ae, m., = ἁμαξαγωγός, one who carries off any thing in a wagon, in comic transf.: bonorum, Plaut. Truc. 2, 7, 2.
hamaxagoga.short: hămaxăgōga, ae, m., = ἁμαξαγωγός, one who carries off any thing in a wagon, in comic transf.: bonorum, Plaut.

hamaxitis.full: hămaxītis, ĭdis, f., a plant, i. q. agrostis, App. Herb. 77.
hamaxitis.short: hămaxītis, ĭdis, f., a plant, i.

hamaxo.full: hămaxo, āre, v. a. ἅμαξα, a wagon, to yoke to a wagon, Plaut. Truc. 2, 2, 22.

hamaxobii.full: Hămaxŏbĭi or -bĭoe, ōrum, m., = Ἁμαξόβιοι (living, going about in wagons), a Scythian people, Mel. 2, 1, 2; Plin. 4, 12, 25 (cf. Hor. C. 3, 24, 9; Just. 2, 2).—In sing.: Hamaxobio instabilior, Tert. adv. Marc. 1, 1.
hamaxobii.short: Hămaxŏbĭi or -bĭoe, ōrum, m., = Ἁμαξόβιοι (living, going about in wagons), a Scythian people, Mel.

hamilcar.full: Hămilcar (Amilcar), ăris, m. A general, son of Gisgo, slain in besieging Syracuse, Cic. Div. 1, 24, 50; Val. Max. 1, 7, ext. 8.— Hamilcar Barca, the father of Hannibal, Cic. Off. 3, 26, 99; Nep. Ham.; Liv. 21, 2 sq.; Val. Max. 6, 6, 2; Sil. 1, 72 al.

hamillus.full: Hămillus, i, m., the name of a teacher, Juv. 10, 224.
hamillus.short: Hămillus, i, m., the name of a teacher, Juv.

hamiota.full: hāmĭōta, ae, m. hamus, an angler (ante-class.): conchitae atque hamiotae, Plaut. Rud. 2, 2, 5: hamiotae aucupesque, Varr. ap. Non. 25, 10.

hammitis.full: hammītis, ĭdis, f., = ἁμμῖτις, a precious stone, otherwise unknown, Plin. 37, 10, 60, § 167.
hammitis.short: hammītis, ĭdis, f., = ἁμμῖτις, a precious stone, otherwise unknown, Plin.

hammochrysos.full: hammŏchrȳsos (amm-), i, m., = ἀμμόχρυσος (gold sand), a precious stone unknown to us, perh. golden mica, Plin. 37, 11, 73, § 188; Isid. 16, 15, 5.
hammochrysos.short: hammŏchrȳsos (amm-), i, m., = ἀμμόχρυσος (gold sand), a precious stone unknown to us, perh.

hammodytes.full: hammŏdўtes (amm-), ae, m., = ἁμμοδύτης (sand-crawler), an African serpent, Sol. 27, 33; Isid. 12, 4, 39; Luc. 9, 716 al.
hammodytes.short: hammŏdўtes (amm-), ae, m., = ἁμμοδύτης (sand-crawler), an African serpent, Sol.

hammon.full: Hammōn (Amm-), ōnis, m., = Ἄμμων, an Egyptian and Libyan deity, worshipped (in the present oasis Siwah) in the form of a ram, and identified by the Greeks and Romans with Ζεύς and Jupiter; hence, Juppiter Hammon. Connected with his temple was an oracle often consulted by the ancients, Cic. N. D. 29 fin.; id. Div. 1, 43, 95; 1, 1, 3; Curt. 4, 7, 3 sq.; Luc. 9, 514 al. (cf. Cat. 7, 5).—Hence, Hammonis cornu, a gold-colored precious stone of the shape of a ram's horn, Ammonite, Plin. 37, 10, 60, §
hammon.short: Hammōn (Amm-), ōnis, m., = Ἄμμων, an Egyptian and Libyan deity, worshipped (in the present oasis Siwah) in the form of a ram, and identified by the Greeks and Romans with Ζεύς and Jupiter;

hamotrahones.full: hāmotrăhōnes alii piscatores, alii, qui unco cadavera trahunt, Paul. ex Fest. p. 102 Müll.
hamotrahones.short: hāmotrăhōnes alii piscatores, alii, qui unco cadavera trahunt, Paul.

hamula.full: hāmŭla, ae, f. dim. hama, a small water-bucket: habilem lymphis hamulam, Col. poët. 10, 387.

hamulus.full: hāmŭlus, i, m. dim. hamus, a small hook: piscarius, a small angle, Plaut. Stich. 2, 1, 17.—As a surgical instrument, Cels. 7, 7, 4 and 7.

hamus.full: hāmus, i, m. kindr. with ἁπ-, ἅπτω, a hook. Lit. In gen.: taleae pedem longae, ferreis hamis infixis, totae in terram infodiebantur, Caes. B. G. 7, 73 fin.: hamis ferreis pectitur stupa, heckles, Plin. 19, 1, 3, § 17: loricam consertam hamis, little hooks, Verg. A. 3, 467.— In partic. A fish-hook; hence, in gen., an angle (so most freq.): hisce hami atque haec harundines sunt nobis quaestu, Plaut. Rud. 2, 1, 5: divine Plato escam malorum appellat voluptatem, quod ea videlicet homines capiantur,

hannibal.full: Hannĭbal (Annibal), ălis (ālis, Enn. Sat. 14 Vahl.), = Ἀννίβας [Phoen.], a Punic surname. The most celebrated of the name is Hannibal, son of Hamilcar, the leader of the Carthaginians in the second Punic war, Nep. Han. 1 al.; Liv. 21, 1 al.; Hor. C. 4, 8, 16; Cic. de Or. 1, 48, 210 al.: et Romani suum Hannibalem habent, Liv. 27, 16, 10. —Prov.: Hannibal ad portas, of imminent and great danger, Cic. Fin. 4, 9, 22: Mithridates, odio in Romanos Hannibal, a Hannibal, Vell. 2, 18, 1.

hanno.full: Hanno (Anno), ōnis, m., = Ἄννων, a Punic name. The most celebrated of the name is Hanno, general of the Carthaginians, who, about the year 500 B.C., navigated the western coast of Africa, Plin. 5, 1, 1, § 8; Cic. Tusc. 5, 32, 90.
hanno.short: Hanno (Anno), ōnis, m., = Ἄννων, a Punic name.

hanula.full: hanŭla parva delubra, quasi fanula, Paul. ex Fest. p. 103, 8 Müll.
hanula.short: hanŭla parva delubra, quasi fanula, Paul.

hapalopsis.full: hăpălopsis, ĭdis, f., a spice, Plaut. Ps. 3, 2, 47 Ritschl N. cr.
hapalopsis.short: hăpălopsis, ĭdis, f., a spice, Plaut.

hapaluria.full: hăpălūrĭa, ae, f. hapalus, a vessel for soft eggs, Aus. Ep. 20 dub.

hapalus.full: hăpălus, a, um, adj., = ἁπαλός, soft; only with ova, Apic. 7, 17; Scrib. Comp. 104; Marc. Emp. 20.
hapalus.short: hăpălus, a, um, adj., = ἁπαλός, soft;

haphe.full: hăphē (aphē), ēs, f., = ἁφή (a touching, handling; hence), the yellow sand with which wrestlers, after being anointed, were sprinkled. Lit.: flavescit haphe, Mart. 7, 67, 5.— Transf., the dust of a road, Sen. Ep. 57, 1.
haphe.short: hăphē (aphē), ēs, f., = ἁφή (a touching, handling;

hapsus.full: hapsus, i, m., = ἅψος (a binding together; hence), a lock of wool used in bandaging: lanae, Cels. 4, 6, 9; 7, 26, 5.
hapsus.short: hapsus, i, m., = ἅψος (a binding together;

hara.full: hăra, ae, f., a pen or coop for animals: anserum, a goose-pen, Varr. R. R. 3, 10, 3 sq.; Col. 8, 14, 5; Plaut. As. 2, 4, 24 al.; a hog-stye, Varr. R. R. 2, 4, 14; Col. 7, 9, 9; Ov. H. 1, 104; cf.: confer nunc, Epicure noster, ex hara producte, non ex schola, confer, etc., Cic. Pis. 16, 37: hara suis, as a term of reproach, Plaut. Most. 1, 1, 39.
hara.short: hăra, ae, f., a pen or coop for animals: anserum, a goose-pen, Varr.

harena.full: hărēna (better than ărēna, Bramb. s. v. Rib. Prol. Verg. p. 422, and v. infra), ae, f. Sabin. fas-ena; from Sanscr. root bhas-, to shine, gleam, Corss. Ausspr. 1, 102. Prop., sand (syn.: sabulum, glarea, suburra): harenae tria genera, Plin. 36, 23, 54, § 175: magnus congestus harenae, Lucr. 6, 724; 726: litoris incurvi bibulam pavit aequor harenam, the thirsty sand of the curved shore, id. 2, 376; so, bibula harena, Verg. G. 1, 114 (Rib. and Forbig., but Conington arena): sicca, id. ib. 1, 389:

harenaceus.full: hărēnācĕus (aren-), a, um, adj., sandy, = harenosus (only in Plin.): terra, Plin. 17, 7, 4, § 43 al.
harenaceus.short: hărēnācĕus (aren-), a, um, adj., sandy, = harenosus (only in Plin.): terra, Plin.

harenarius.full: hărēnārĭus (aren-), a, um, adj. harena. Prop., of or pertaining to sand: lapis, sandstone (= lapis bibulus of Verg.), Serv. Verg. G. 2, 348.— Transf., of or pertaining to the amphitheatre: fera, destined for the arena, Arn. 29, 1.— Hence, subst., hărēnārĭus, i, m. A combatant in the amphitheatre, a gladiator, Dig. 22, 5, 21; 36, 1, 5; Cod. Just. 3, 27, 11; Petr. 126, 6; Inscr. Orell. 4063 (but cf. Orell. ad loc.).— A teacher of the elements of arithmetic (the figures being drawn in sand), Tert.

harenatio.full: hărēnātĭo (aren-), ōnis, f. id. Prop., a sanding, plastering with sand.— Transf., a plastering, cementing, Vitr. 7, 3, 9.

harenatus.full: hărēnātus (aren-), a, um, adj. id., sanded, covered or mixed with sand (very rare): calx, Cato, R. R. 18, 7; Inscr. Grut. 207.—As subst.: hărēnātum, i (sc. opus), n., sand-mortar, Vitr. 7, 4; Plin. 36, 23, 55, § 176 sq.

harenifodina.full: hărēnĭfŏdīna (aren-), ae, f. harena - fodio, a sand-pit (late Lat. for harenaria; s. v. harenarius, III. B.), Dig. 7, 1, 13, § 5; 24, 3, 7; Varr. L. L. 5, § 7 Müll.

harenivagus.full: hărēnĭvăgus (aren-), a, um, adj. harena - vagus, wandering over sands: Cato, Luc. 9, 941.

harenosus.full: hărēnōsus (aren-), a, um, adj. harena, full of sand, sandy: Ladon, Ov. M. 1, 702: terra, id. ib. 14, 82; Plin. 17, 7, 4, § 44: litus Libyae, Verg. A. 4, 257: urina, Plin. 23, 3, 36, § 73: lapis harenosior, id. 33, 6, 33, § 101: quod sit harenosissimum subsidat, id. 27, 4, 5, § 20.—As subst.: hărē-nōsum, i, n., a sandy place: quae humi arido atque harenoso gignuntur, Sall. J. 48, 3.—Plur.: hărēnōsa, ōrum, opp. lutosa, Plin. 32, 6, 21, § 60.

harenula.full: hărēnŭla (aren-), ae, f. dim. id., fine sand, a grain of sand, Plin. 30, 3, 8, § 24.

hariolatio.full: hărĭŏlātĭo (ar-), ōnis, f. hariolor, a soothsaying, prophesying, Enn. ap. Cic. Div. 1, 31, 66 (Fragm. Trag. 42 Rib.).

hariolor.full: hărĭŏlor (ar-), āri, v. dep. n. [hariolus], to foretell, prophesy, divine. Lit.: Προθεσπίζω igitur, non hariolans, ut illa (Cassandra) cui nemo credidit, sed conjectura prospiciens, Cic. Att. 8, 11, 3: quaestus causa hariolari, id. Div. 1, 58, 132.—Comically: mirabar, quod dudum scapulae gestibant mihi, Hariolari quae occeperunt sibi esse in mundo malum, Plaut. As. 2, 2, 50.— Transf., in a bad sense (like vaticinor), to speak foolishly, to talk silly stuff, nonsense (ante-class.), Plaut. Cist. 4

hariolus.full: hărĭŏlus (ar-), i, m., and harĭŏla, ae, f. Sanscr. hira, entrails; Gr. χορδή, χολάδες; cf. haruspex, a soothsayer, prophet, prophetess (= augur, auspex, haruspex, extispex). Masc.: hariolos, haruspices Mitte omnes: quae futura et quae facta, eloquar, Plaut. Am. 5, 2, 2; cf.: ut haruspices, augures, harioli, vates et conjectores nobis essent colendi, Cic. N. D. 1, 20, 55; Plaut. Cas. 2, 6, 4; id. Men. prol. 76; id. Poen. 3, 5, 46; Ter. Phorm. 4, 4, 27; Cic. Div. 1, 2, 4; Phaedr. 3, 3, 6 et saep.—
hariolus.short: hărĭŏlus (ar-), i, m., and harĭŏla, ae, f.

harmodius.full: Harmŏdĭus, ĭi, m., = Ἁρμόδιος, a famous Athenian, murderer of Hipparchus, Cic. Tusc. 1, 49, 116; Plin. 7, 23, 23, § 87; Gell. 9, 2.
harmodius.short: Harmŏdĭus, ĭi, m., = Ἁρμόδιος, a famous Athenian, murderer of Hipparchus, Cic.

harmoge.full: harmŏgē, ēs, f., = ἁρμογή, a proper combination or mingling of colors, Plin. 35, 5, 11, § 29.— Transf., harmony of sound, Varr. Sat. Men. 63, 18.
harmoge.short: harmŏgē, ēs, f., = ἁρμογή, a proper combination or mingling of colors, Plin.

harmonia1.full: harmŏnĭa, ae (archaic gen. sing. harmoniaï, Lucr. 3, 131), f., = ἁρμονία, an agreement of sounds, consonance, concord, harmony; pure Lat. concentus. Lit.: velut in cantu et fidibus, quae harmonia dicitur, Cic. Tusc. 1, 10, 20; cf.: harmoniam ex intervallis sonorum nosse possumus: quorum varia compositio etiam harmonias efficit plures, id. ib. 1, 18, 41: ad harmoniam canere mundum, id. N. D. 3, 11, 27: numeros et geometriam et harmoniam conjungere, id. Rep. 1, 10; Vitr. 5, 4, 6.— Transf. Concord,

harmonia2.full: Harmŏnĭa, ae, f., daughter of Mars and Venus, the wife of Cadmus, and mother of Semele, Ino, Agave, and Polydorus, Hyg. Fab. 6; 148; 159.—Acc.: Harmonien, Ov. A. A. 3, 86.
harmonia2.short: Harmŏnĭa, ae, f., daughter of Mars and Venus, the wife of Cadmus, and mother of Semele, Ino, Agave, and Polydorus, Hyg.

harmonice.full: harmŏnĭcē, ēs, f., = ἁρμονική, the science of sounds, harmonics, Vitr. 5, 3, 8.— Called harmŏnĭca, ae, f., Vitr. 5, 4, 1.
harmonice.short: harmŏnĭcē, ēs, f., = ἁρμονική, the science of sounds, harmonics, Vitr.

harmonicus.full: harmŏnĭcus, a, um, adj., = ἁρμονικός, of or belonging to agreement or harmony, harmonious, harmonic (very rare): res, Varr. L. L. 10, § 64 Müll.: harmonica ratio, quae cogit rerum naturam sibi ipsam congruere, Plin. 2, 109, 113, § 248: tinnitus, Mart. Cap. 1, § 27.
harmonicus.short: harmŏnĭcus, a, um, adj., = ἁρμονικός, of or belonging to agreement or harmony, harmonious, harmonic (very rare): res, Varr.

harpa.full: harpa, ae, f., = ἅρπη (a sickle, transf.), a harp (late Lat.), Ven. Carm. 7, 8, 63.
harpa.short: harpa, ae, f., = ἅρπη (a sickle, transf.), a harp (late Lat.), Ven.

harpacticon.full: harpactĭcon, false read. in Plin. 35, 15, 50, § 176; v. 1. harpax.

harpaga.full: harpăga, ae, f., = ἁρπάγη, a hook, for the usual harpago, Sisenn. ap. Non. 556, 20.
harpaga.short: harpăga, ae, f., = ἁρπάγη, a hook, for the usual harpago, Sisenn.

harpaginetulus.full: harpăgĭnētŭlus, i, m. dim. harpago, a small hook, Vitr. 7, 5, 3 dub.

harpago1.full: harpăgo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. ἁρπάζω, to rob, plunder (Plautin.): aurum mihi intus harpagatum est, Plaut. Aul. 2, 2, 24; id. Bacch. 4, 4, 11; id. Ps. 1, 2, 6; 4, 2, 2.

harpago2.full: harpăgo ōnis, m. ἁρπάγη, a hook for drawing things to one's self, for tearing down any thing, etc., a grappling-hook, grapple, drag (pure Lat. manica, manus ferrea). Lit., Caes. B. G. 7, 81, 1; id. B. C. 1, 57, 2; Liv. 30, 10; Curt. 4, 2; Plin. 7, 56, 57, § 209; Dig. 33, 7, 12, § 21.—* Transf., a rapacious person: blandiloquentulus harpago, mendax, cuppes, etc., Plaut. Trin. 2, 1, 13.

harpagus.full: Harpăgus i, m., a Median nobleman, to whom Astyages committed his grandson Cyrus to be destroyed, but by whom he was preserved alive, Just. 1, 4 sq.; Sen. de Ira, 3, 15, 1.
harpagus.short: Harpăgus i, m., a Median nobleman, to whom Astyages committed his grandson Cyrus to be destroyed, but by whom he was preserved alive, Just.

harpalus.full: Harpălus, i, m., one of Cicero's slaves, Cic. Fam. 16, 24, 1.
harpalus.short: Harpălus, i, m., one of Cicero's slaves, Cic.
