harpalyce.full: Harpălўcē, ēs, f., = Ἁρπαλύκη, the daughter of the Thracian king Harpalycus, brought up as a warrior, Verg. A. 1, 317 Serv.; Hyg. Fab. 193; 252; 254.
harpalyce.short: Harpălўcē, ēs, f., = Ἁρπαλύκη, the daughter of the Thracian king Harpalycus, brought up as a warrior, Verg.

harpastum.full: harpastum, i, n., = ἁρπαστόν, a hand-ball: sive harpasta manu pulverulenta rapis, Mart. 4, 19, 6; 7, 67, 4.
harpastum.short: harpastum, i, n., = ἁρπαστόν, a hand-ball: sive harpasta manu pulverulenta rapis, Mart.

harpax1.full: harpax, ăgis, adj., = ἅρπαξ, drawing to itself, rapacious.—Lit., of amber and brimstone: in Syria feminas verticillos inde (i. e. ex electro) facere et vocari harpaga, quia folia paleasque et vestium fimbrias rapiat, Plin. 37, 2, 11, § 37; so of sulphur, id. 35, 15, 50, § 176 (the correct reading, see Sillig ad h. l.).
harpax1.short: harpax, ăgis, adj., = ἅρπαξ, drawing to itself, rapacious.—Lit., of amber and brimstone: in Syria feminas verticillos inde (i.

harpax2.full: Harpax, ăgis, m. ἅρπαξ, the name of a slave, Plaut. Ps. 2, 2, 58 sq.; 4, 2, 53 sq. —Also in voc.: Harpage, Plaut. Ps. 2, 2, 70.

harpe.full: harpē, ēs, f., = ἅρπη. A sickleshaped sword, a falchion, cimeter, Ov. M. 5, 69; 176; Luc. 9, 663; Val. Fl. 4, 388.— A species of falcon, tassel gentle: Falco gentilis, Linn.; Plin. 10, 74, 95, § 204.

harpocrates.full: Harpŏcrătēs, is, m., = Ἁρποκράτης, The Egyptian god of silence, represented with his finger on his mouth; acc. to others, a Greek philosopher, who enjoined silence respecting the nature of the gods, Varr. L. L. 5, § 57 Müll. N. cr. (cf. Ov. M. 9, 692).—* Transf., a silent person, Cat. 74, 4.
harpocrates.short: Harpŏcrătēs, is, m., = Ἁρποκράτης, The Egyptian god of silence, represented with his finger on his mouth;

harpyiae.full: Harpȳiae (trisyl.; scanned as a quadrisyl. Hārpўĭās, Rutil. Itin. 1, 608), ārum, f., = Ἅρπυιαι (qs. the spoilers). Mythical rapacious monsters, half bird and half woman, the Harpies, Verg. A. 3, 212 sq.; 6, 289; Hor. S. 2, 2, 40; Val. Fl. 4, 428; Hyg. Fab. 14.—In sing.: Harpyia Celaeno, Verg. A. 3, 365.— Transf., in sing., a rapacious person, a harpy, Sid. Ep. 5, 7.— Also in sing., the name of one of Actœon's hounds, Ov. M. 3, 215.

harudes.full: Harūdes, um, m., a Germanic tribe in the army of Ariovistus, perh. the same as the Charudes in the Chersonesus Cimbrica (in the Northern Jütland), Caes. B. G. 1, 31, 10; 1, 37, 2; 1, 51, 2 Monum. Ancyr.
harudes.short: Harūdes, um, m., a Germanic tribe in the army of Ariovistus, perh.

harundifer.full: hărundĭfer (ar-), ĕra, ĕrum, adj. harundo - fero, reed-bearing, crowned with reeds: caput, Ov. F. 5, 637.

harundinaceus.full: hărundĭnācĕus (ar-), a, um, adj. harundo, like a reed, Plin. 18, 7, 10, § 58.

harundinarius.full: hărundĭnārĭus (ar-), ii, m. id. II. B., a dealer in limed twigs, Inscr. Orell. 4199.

harundinatio.full: hărundĭnātĭo (ar-), ōnis, f. id. II. L., the poling of vines, the propping with reeds, Varr. 1, 8, 3 (ex conj. Schneid. The vulg. reading is: Canusini in harundulatione in ficis).

harundinetum.full: hărundĭnētum (ar-), i, n. harundo, II., a thicket or jungle of reeds, Cato, R. R. 6, 3; Varr. R. R. 1, 24, 4; Col. 4, 32, 3; Plin. 10, 8, 10, § 28; Vulg. Josue, 16, 8; 17, 9.

harundineus.full: hărundĭnĕus (ar-), a, um, adj. id.. Of reeds, reedy: silva, Verg. A. 10, 710: paniculae, Plin. 8, 32, 50, § 117: cuneoli, Col. 4, 29, 10: ripae, Stat. Th. 6, 174.—Poet.: carmen, a shepherd's song, Ov. Tr. 4, 1, 12. — Like a reed: radix, Plin. 24, 16, 93, § 150: mensura aurea, Vulg. Apoc. 21, 15.

harundinosus.full: hărundĭnōsus (ar-), a, um, adj. id., abounding in reeds: Cnidus, Cat. 36, 13.

harundo.full: hărundo (better than ărundo, Bramb. s. v.; Wagn. Orthog. Verg. p. 441; Rib. Prol. Verg. p. 422, though the latter is freq. in MSS. and edd.; v. infra), ĭnis, f. etym. dub.; perh. from root ar-, to set in motion; Sanscr. aras, swift; aranjas, a wood, as that which grows; cf.: ulmus, ulva, alnus, Corss. Ausspr. 1, 530 sq.. Prop., the reed, cane (taller than canna; cf. also: culmus, calamus, stipula), Cato, R. R. 6, 3; Plin. 16, 36, 64, § 156 sqq.: intus medullam sabuci (habent) ... inanitatem haru

haruspex.full: hăruspex (ar-), ĭcis, m. Sanscr. hirā, entrails; Gr. χολάδες, χορδή; cf. hariolus, Georg Curtius Gr. Etym. p. 202 sq., a soothsayer, diviner among the Etruscans, who foretold future events from the inspection of the entrails of victims; from this people they were introduced among the Romans (syn.: hariolus, augur, auspex, extispex). Lit.: haruspices mitte omnis, Plaut. Am. 5, 2, 2: quid enim habet haruspex, cur pulmo incisus etiam in bonis extis dirimat tempus et proferat diem? Cic. Div. 1, 39,

haruspica.full: hăruspĭca (ar-), ae, f. haruspex, a female haruspex or soothsayer, Plaut. Mil. 3, 1, 99.— = haruspicium, Plin. 7, 56, 57, § 203.

haruspicalis.full: hăruspĭcālis, e, adj. id., of a soothsayer: ars, Serv. Verg. A. 4, 56.

haruspicinus.full: hăruspĭcīnus (ar-), a, um, adj. id., of or relating to the inspection of victims. Adj.: quod Etruscorum declarant et haruspicini et fulgurales et tonitruales libri, Cic. Div. 1, 33, 72.— Subst.: hăruspĭ-cīna, ae, f. (sc. ars), the art of divining, divination: oratio, quae haruspicinae disciplina continetur, Cic. Div. 2, 23, 50; id. Fam. 6, 18, 1.

haruspicium.full: hăruspĭcĭum (ar-), ii, n. id., inspection of victims, divination, Cat. 90, 2.

hasdrubal.full: Hasdrŭbal (Asdr-), ălis, m., a Punic name. The most celebrated are, Son of Mago, the founder of the power of Carthage, Just. 19, 1.— Son of Hanno, who fought in Sicilia during the first Punic war, Cic. Verr. 2, 3, 54, § 125.— The son-inlaw of Hamilcar Barcas, Nep. Hann. 3, 2; Liv. 21, 1 sq.— The son of Hamilcar Barcas, brother of Hannibal, defeated B. C. 207 at the Metaurus, Liv. 27, 18 sq.; 49 sq.; Nep. Hann. 3, 3; Cat. 1, 2; Hor. C. 4, 4, 38; 72; Ov. F. 6, 770.— Son of Gisco, third Carthaginia
hasdrubal.short: Hasdrŭbal (Asdr-), ălis, m., a Punic name.

hasta.full: hasta (asta), ae, f. Sanscr. hastas, hand; cf. Gr. root χαδ- in χανδάνω, pre-hendo, a spear (syn.: hastile, dolo, gaesum, sarisa, sparus, lancea, pilum, spiculum, telum, etc.). Lit. Most freq. as a military weapon, a lance, pike, javelin (cf. Becker's Antiq. III. 2, p. 242 sq.): nec eminus hastis aut comminus gladiis uteretur, Cic. de Sen. 6, 19: dum transit, striderat hasta, Enn. ap. Prisc. p. 817 P. (Ann. v. 365 Vahl.): Hastati spargunt hastas, id. ap. Macr. S. 6, 1 (Ann. v. 287 ib.): evelli j

hastarium.full: hastārĭum, ii, n. hasta, I. B., an auction-catalogue, Tert. Ap. 13; id. ad Nat. 1, 10.

hastarius.full: hastārĭus, a, um, adj. id., of or belonging to the spear: censio, Paul. ex Fest. 54, 12.— Of or belonging to auctions, auction-: PRAETOR, Inscr. Grut. 379, 7.

hastatus.full: hastātus, a, um, adj. hasta, I. A., armed with a spear. In gen. (very rare): Bellona, Stat. Th. 2, 718: prima utcumque acies hastata: ceteris praeusta aut brevia tela, Tac. A. 2, 14: currum decem milia hastatorum sequebantur, Curt. 3, 3, 10; 4, 15, 7.— In partic., milit. t. t.: hastāti, ōrum, m., the first line of a Roman army drawn up in order of battle (behind them were the Principes and Triarii): hastati dicti qui primi hastis pugnabant, Varr. L. L. 5, § 89 Müll.: hastati spargunt hastas, Enn

hastile.full: hastīle (also astīle), is, n. hasta, the shaft of a spear or javelin. Lit.: ferrum, quod ex hastili in corpore remanserat, Nep. Epam. 9: hastili nixus, Cic. Rab. Perd. 7, 21: missile telum hastili abiegno, Liv. 21, 8, 10.— Transf. (Pars pro toto.) A spear, javelin, in gen. (poet.): torquere hastilia lenta, Ov. M. 8, 28; Verg. A. 1, 313; 5, 557; 12, 489; Sen. Hippol. 397: curvatum, Juv. 7, 127.— In gen., a piece of wood in the form of a shaft (poet. and in post-Aug. prose). So of branches, Verg.

hastula.full: hastŭla, ae, f. dim. id.. A little spear, Fronto de Or. 1 med.— Transf. A little branch, Sen. Q. N. 2, 31, 2.— Hastula regia, a plant, called also asphodelus, asphodel, Plin. 21, 17, 68, § 109; App. Herb. 32.

haterianus.full: Hatĕrĭānus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Haterius (a jurist), Cic. Fam. 9, 18, 3.
haterianus.short: Hatĕrĭānus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Haterius (a jurist), Cic.

hau1.full: hau (also au), interj., an exclamation of pain or grief, Oh! ah! au, nullan tibi lingua'st? Plaut. Stich. 1, 3, 104; id. Cist. 3, 15; Ter. And. 4, 4, 12; 42; id. Eun. 4, 3, 14; id. Heaut. 5, 3, 13; id. Ad. 3, 2, 38; id. Phorm. 5, 1, 27 et saep.
hau1.short: hau (also au), interj., an exclamation of pain or grief, Oh! ah! au, nullan tibi lingua'st? Plaut.

haud.full: haud or haut (in the form hau, before consonants, several times in Plautus acc. to the Cod. Ambros., and in Inscr. Orell. 4848: HEIC. EST. SEPVLCRVM. HAV. PVLCRVM. PVLCRAI. FEMINAE; also Tac. A. 2, 36; 6, 43 (49), Nipperdey, Ritter; hence, also hauscio = haud scio; cf. Ritschl, prol. ad Plaut. Trin. p. 99 sq. and p. 325), adv. perh. orig. hau = οὐ, v. Ritschl l. l. But cf. Hand, Turs. III. 15.—Acc. to Corss. Ausspr. 1, 205, haud = pronom. stem ho + au (Sanscr. ava, away) + de, as in unde, etc.,
haud.short: haud or haut (in the form hau, before consonants, several times in Plautus acc.

hauddum.full: hauddum and haudquāquam, v. haud, II. A. and B.

haurio.full: haurĭo, hausi, haustum, 4 (archaic imperf. hauribant, Lucr. 5, 1324; perf. subj. haurierint, Varr. ap. Prisc. p. 905 P.; part. perf. haurītus, App. M. 3, p. 139; 6, p. 178; supin. hauritu, id. ib. 2, p. 121; part. fut. hauritura, Juv. in Joh. 2, 253: hausurus, Verg. A. 4, 383; Sil. 7, 584; 16, 11: hausturus, Sen. Q. N. 4, 2, 1; dep. perf. foramen fama est lucem hausum, Sol. 5, 15), v. a. perh. for haus-io; cf. hio, hisco; prop. to empty, to draw up or out, to draw (class., esp. freq. in the tran

hauritorium.full: haurītōrĭŭm, ii. n., = ἀντλητήριον (a bucket), Gloss. Philox.

hauritus.full: haurītus, a, um, v. haurio init.

haustor.full: haustor (aus-), ōris, m. haurio, a drawer (post-Aug. and very rare): aquarum, water-drawer, Firm. Math. 8, 29.— Poet.: ultimus aquae, drinker, Luc. 9, 591.—Esp., he who fills casks with wine, Inscr. Orell. 5089.

haustrum.full: haustrum (also austrum), i, n. id., a machine for drawing water, Lucr. 5, 516; cf. Non. 13, 5.

haustus1.full: haustus, a, um, Part., from haurio.
haustus1.short: haustus, a, um, Part., from haurio.

haustus2.full: haustus, ūs, m. haurio, a drawing. Lit.: aqua, quae non sit haustus profundi, Col. 1, 5, 1: puteus in tenues plantas facili diffunditur haustu, Juv. 3, 227; Mel. 2, 4, 4: aquae ductus, haustus, iter, actus, etc.... a jure civili sumitur, the right of drawing, * Cic. Caecin. 26, 74; Dig. 8, 3, 1: haustus ex fonte privato, ib. 8, 3, 3, § 3. — Transf., a drinking, swallowing, drawing in; and concr., a drink, draught (poet. and in post-Aug. prose; for the most part only in the plur.): largos haustus

heautontimorumenos.full: Hĕautontīmōrūmĕnos, i, m., = Ἑαυτὸν τιμωρούμενος, The Self-tormentor, the title of a comedy of Terence, Ter. Heaut. prol. 5 (= Ipse se puniens, Cic. Tusc. 3, 27, 65).
heautontimorumenos.short: Hĕautontīmōrūmĕnos, i, m., = Ἑαυτὸν τιμωρούμενος, The Self-tormentor, the title of a comedy of Terence, Ter.

hebdomada.full: hebdŏmăda, ae, f. hebdomas, the number seven: annorum, librorum, Gell. 3, 10, 17.—Esp., = hebdomas, seven days, Gell. 3, 10, 14; Isid. de Nat. R. 3; Vulg. Gen. 29, 27 sq.; id. Exod. 34, 22 al.

hebdomadalis.full: hebdŏmădālis, e, adj. id., of or belonging to a week, weekly: festa, Sid. Ep. 9, 3 med.

hebdomas.full: hebdŏmas, ădis, f., = ἑβδομάς, the number seven, seven days: libri, qui inscribuntur Hebdomades, Gell. 3, 10, 1: septima fere hebdomade, id est, nono et quadragesimo die, Varr. ib. § 7: hebdomadibus lunae, on every seventh day of the moon, Gell. 15, 2, 3.—Of the critical seventh day in diseases: symphoniam Lysonis vellem vitasses, ne in quartam hebdomada incideres, Cic. Fam. 16, 9, 3 (cf. collat. form hebdomada, s. v.).
hebdomas.short: hebdŏmas, ădis, f., = ἑβδομάς, the number seven, seven days: libri, qui inscribuntur Hebdomades, Gell.

hebdomaticus.full: hebdŏmătĭcus (-mădĭcus), a, um, adj., = ἑβδοματικός, relating to the number seven: septeni et noveni anni, qui hebdomatici a Graecis atque enneatici appellantur, i. e. critical, decisive of one's fate, Firm. Math. 4, 14 med.
hebdomaticus.short: hebdŏmătĭcus (-mădĭcus), a, um, adj., = ἑβδοματικός, relating to the number seven: septeni et noveni anni, qui hebdomatici a Graecis atque enneatici appellantur, i.

hebe.full: Hēbē, ēs, f. =Ἥβη (youth), the goddess of youth (pure Lat. Juventas), the daughter of Juno, cup-bearer to the gods, and, after the deification of Hercules, his wife, Ov. M. 9, 400; Prop. 1, 13, 23; Cat. 68, 116; Serv. Verg. A. 1, 28; 5, 134 al.

hebeninus.full: hĕbĕnĭnus, or ĕbĕnĭnus, a, um, adj., ἐβένινος, of ebony: tigna, Hier. Ezech. 27, 16: dentes, id. ib.
hebeninus.short: hĕbĕnĭnus, or ĕbĕnĭnus, a, um, adj., ἐβένινος, of ebony: tigna, Hier.

hebenus.full: hĕbĕnus (less correctly ĕbĕnus, Rib. Prol. Verg. p. 421), i. f., Gr. ἕβενος, ἔβενος, the ebon-tree, ebony: Diospyros ebenum, Linn.; Plin. 16, 40, 76, § 204; 6, 30, 35, § 197; Verg. G. 2, 117; Ov. M. 11, 610; Pers. 5, 135; cf. Isid. Orig. 17, 7, 36.

hebeo.full: hĕbĕo, ēre, v. n., to be blunt or dull (perh. not ante-Aug.). Lit.: ferrum nunc hebet? Liv. 23, 45, 9.— Trop., to be dull, sluggish, inactive, not lively: gelidus tardante senecta Sanguis hebet, Verg. A. 5, 396: corpus hebet somno, Val. Fl. 4, 41: stella hebet, id. 5, 371: et jam Plias hebet, Luc. 2, 722: ipsi hebent mira diversitate naturae, cum iidem homines sic ament inertiam et oderint quietem, lounge about, Tac. G. 15: quid stolidi ad speciem notae novitatis hebetis? are amazed, Aus. Epigr.

hebes.full: hĕbes, ĕtis (acc. sing. hebem, Enn. and Caecil. ap. Charis. p. 107 P.; abl. hebeti; but hebete, Cels. 7, 3), adj. hebeo, blunt, dull, in opp. to pointed or sharp (class.; esp. freq. in the trop. sense). Lit.: cujus (lunae) et nascentis et insenescentis alias hebetiora alias acutiora videntur cornua, Cic. Fragm. ap. Non. 122, 1: tela leviora atque hebetiora, id. Har. Resp. 1, 2: quo latiora (ossa) quaque parte sunt, hoc hebetiora, Cels. 8, 1, 66: ponite jam gladios hebetes, pugnetur acutis, Ov. A

hebesco.full: hĕbesco, ĕre, v. inch. n. [hebeo], to grow blunt, dull, dim, or faint (rare but class.). Lit.: acumina (gladiorum) densis ictibus hebescebant, Amm. 16, 12, 54: hebescunt sensus, membra torpent, Plin. 7, 50, 51, § 168: hebescebant (oculi), Suet. Tib. 68: berylli hebescunt, Plin. 37, 5, 20, § 76: hebescere sidera, Tac. A. 1, 30: hebescere dextras, Sil. 8, 19.— Trop.: sic mentis acies se ipsam intuens nonnumquam hebescit, Cic. Tusc. 1, 30, 73; cf.: nos vicesimum jam diem patimur hebescere aciem hor

hebetatio.full: hĕbĕtātĭo, ōnis, f. hebeto, dulness, dimness: oculorum, Plin. 28, 6, 16, § 58: nascitur ex assiduitate laborum animorum hebetatio quaedam ac languor, Sen. Tranq. An. 15, 12.

hebetatrix.full: hĕbĕtātrix, īcis, f. adj. id., that makes dull or dim: umbra, i. e. darkening (shortly before: umbra terrae lunam hebetari), Plin. 2, 13, 10, § 57.

hebetesco.full: hĕbĕtesco, ĕre, v. inch. n. [hebes], to grow dull, dim, or faint (post-Aug. and very rare): aciem in cultris tonsorum, Plin. 28, 7, 23, § 79: acies oculi hebetescit ac paene caligat, Cels. 6, 6, 37: dolor hebetescit, Scrib. Comp. 56.

hebeto.full: hĕbĕto, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. id., to make blunt or dull, to blunt, dull, dim, deaden, weaken (perh. not ante-Aug.; not in Cic.). Lit.: hastas, Liv. 8, 10, 3: vulneribus suis ferrum hostium, id. 30, 35, 8: tela, Sil. 16, 105: aciem oculorum, Plin. 20, 6, 21, § 47: oculos, Lact. 6, 2: visus alicui, Verg. A. 2, 605: dies hebetarat sidera, had dimmed, Ov. M. 5, 444: umbra terrae lunam hebetari, Plin. 2, 13, 10, § 57; cf.: smaragdos in sole hebetari, id. 37, 5, 18, § 69; 28, 7, 23, § 79: auster aures

hebetudo.full: hĕbĕtūdo, ĭnis, f. id., bluntness, dulness (post-class.; cf. hebetatio): sensuum, Macr. Somn. Scip. 1, 14: superba istorum, Aug. Civ. D. 7, 21.

hebraei.full: Hĕbraei, ōrum, m., = Ἑβραῖοι, the Hebrews: Hebraei, qui nunc Judaei: igitur et litterae Hebraeae, Tert. Apol. 18; cf.: postea vero cum in deserto consedissent, amiserunt vetus nomen Hebraei, et Judaei sunt appellati, Lact. 4, 10; 2, 13, 8. — Derivv. Hĕbræus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to the Hebrews, Hebrew: terrae, Tac. H. 5, 2: liquores, i. e. balsam, Stat. S. 5, 1, 213 (cf. Plin. 12, 25, 54, § 111): lingua, litterae, Aug. Civ. D. 18, 39; 42: codices, id. ib. 43.— Hē^brā^ĭcus, a, um, adj., t
hebraei.short: Hĕbraei, ōrum, m., = Ἑβραῖοι, the Hebrews: Hebraei, qui nunc Judaei: igitur et litterae Hebraeae, Tert.

hebria.full: hebria, ae, f., a wine-vessel, Charis. p. 63 P.
hebria.short: hebria, ae, f., a wine-vessel, Charis.

hebrus.full: Hĕbrus, i, m., = Ἕβρος. The principal river in Thrace, which rises in Mount Hœmus, and flows into the Ægean Sea, now the Maritza, Mel. 2, 2, 2; 8; Verg. E. 10, 65; id. G. 4, 463; and esp. ib. v. 523 sqq.; id. A. 1, 317; Hor. Ep. 1, 3, 3; id. C. 3, 25, 10; Ov. F. 3, 737; id. M. 2, 257; 11, 50 et saep.: sacer, on account of the festivals of Bacchus celebrated on its banks, id. H. 2, 114.— A Trojan, slain by Mezentius, Verg. A. 10, 696.— The name of a beautiful youth, Hor. C. 3, 12, 6.

hecaerge.full: Hĕcăergē, ēs, f.,=Ἑκαέργη. The name of Diana, Serv. ad Verg. A. 11, 532.— One of the daughters of Boreas, Claud. Laud. Stil. 3, 253 and 308.

hecale.full: Hĕcălē, ēs, f., = Ἑκάλη, a poor old woman who kindly received Theseus, celebrated by Callimachus, Plin. 22, 22, 44, § 88; App. M. 1, p. 112; Plaut. Cist. 1, 1, 50; Ov. R. Am. 747; cf. Petr. 135, 8, 16.
hecale.short: Hĕcălē, ēs, f., = Ἑκάλη, a poor old woman who kindly received Theseus, celebrated by Callimachus, Plin.

hecataeus.full: Hĕcătaeus, i. m., =Ἑκαταῖος, a famous historian and geographer of Miletus, son of Hegesander, Plin. 6, 17, 20, § 55; Solin. 19, 2; 40, 6: Milesius, Avien. Or. Mar. 42.

hecate.full: Hĕcătē, ēs, f., = Ἑκάτη, daughter of Perses, or Persœus, and Asteria, sister of Latona, the presider over enchantments, conjurations, etc.; she is often identified with Diana, Luna, and Proserpina, and is therefore represented with three heads, Cic. N. D. 3, 18, 46; Verg. A. 4, 511 Serv.; Ov. M. 7, 74; 94; 194; 14, 405; id. F. 1, 141; Hor. S. 1, 8, 33; Sen. Phaedr. 420 et saep. — Derivv. Hĕcătēĭus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Hecate, Hecateian: carmina, i. e. magical incantations, Ov. M. 14,
hecate.short: Hĕcătē, ēs, f., = Ἑκάτη, daughter of Perses, or Persœus, and Asteria, sister of Latona, the presider over enchantments, conjurations, etc.;

hecato.full: Hĕcăto, ōnis, m., = Ἑκάτων, a philosopher of Rhodes, pupil of Panœtius, Cic. Off. 3, 15, 63; 3, 23, 89.
hecato.short: Hĕcăto, ōnis, m., = Ἑκάτων, a philosopher of Rhodes, pupil of Panœtius, Cic.

hecatombe.full: hĕcătombē, ēs, f., = ἑκατόμβη, a great sacrifice of a hundred oxen, a hecatomb (ante- and post-class.): facere hecatomben, Varr. ap. Non. 131, 19; Juv. 12, 101 al.—In plur.: celebratis hecatombis, Treb. Gall. 9.—Dim. hĕcătombĭon, ii, n., Sid. Carm. 9, 205.
hecatombe.short: hĕcătombē, ēs, f., = ἑκατόμβη, a great sacrifice of a hundred oxen, a hecatomb (ante- and post-class.): facere hecatomben, Varr.

hecatompolis.full: hĕcătompŏlis, acc. in, f., = ἑκατόμπολις, having a hundred cities: Creta, Isid. 14, 6, 15.

hecatompylos.full: hĕcătompўlos, on (-os, com.; -on, neut.), adj., = ἑκατόμπυλος, of a hundred gates: hecatompylos Thebas nemo non novit, Amm. 22, 16, 2; cf. Hyg. Fab. 275.

hecatontas.full: hĕcătontas, ădis, f., = ἑκατοντάς, the number one hundred, Mart. Cap. 7, § 734, 746.
hecatontas.short: hĕcătontas, ădis, f., = ἑκατοντάς, the number one hundred, Mart.

hector.full: Hector, ŏris (Hectōris, Enn. ap. Cic. Tusc. 2, 17, 39 = Trag. v. 25 Vahl.; id. ap. Varr. L. L. 10, § 70 Müll. = Trag. v. 130 Vahl.; acc. Hectorem, id. ap. Cic. Tusc. 1, 44, 105 = Trag. v. 129 Vahl.; cf. Varr. L. L. l. l.), m., = Ἕκτωρ, son of Priam and Hecuba, husband of Andromache, the bravest of the Trojans, slain and dragged three times around Troy by Achilles, Enn. ap. Macr. S. 6, 2; Verg. A. 1, 483; 2, 270; 282; 522; 6, 166; Hor. C. 2, 4, 10; 4, 9, 22; id. Epod. 17, 12; id. S. 1, 7, 12.— De

hecuba.full: Hĕcŭba, ae, and Hĕcŭbē, ēs, f., = Ἑκάβη, the daughter of Dymas, wife of Priam; after the destruction of Troy the slave of Penelope, changed through rage into a dog, Verg. A. 2, 501; 515; Ov. M. 13, 423; 549 sq.; 577; Cic. Tusc. 3, 26, 63; id. Fat. 15, 34.—Transf., an ugly old woman (opp. to Andromache), Mart. 3, 76, 4.
hecuba.short: Hĕcŭba, ae, and Hĕcŭbē, ēs, f., = Ἑκάβη, the daughter of Dymas, wife of Priam;

hecyra.full: Hĕcўra, ae, f., = Ἑκυρά, The Stepmother, the title of a comedy of Terence.
hecyra.short: Hĕcўra, ae, f., = Ἑκυρά, The Stepmother, the title of a comedy of Terence.

hedera.full: hĕdĕra (ĕdĕra), ae, f., ivy, Hedera helix, Linn.; sacred to Bacchus, and hence wound around the thyrsus; also made into garlands with which poets were crowned, Plin. 16, 34, 62, § 144; Ov. F. 3, 767; id. M. 5, 338; Varr. ap. Serv. Verg. E. 7, 25; Verg. ib. 7, 38; 8, 13; id. G. 2, 258; Hor. C. 1, 1, 29; 1, 25, 17; id. Ep. 1, 3, 25; Juv. 7, 29 al. —In plur., Verg. E. 4, 19; id. G. 4, 124 al.
hedera.short: hĕdĕra (ĕdĕra), ae, f., ivy, Hedera helix, Linn.;

hederaceus.full: hĕdĕrācĕus (ĕd-) or -ĭus, a, um, adj. hedera, of ivy, ivy-. Lit.: materia, Cato, R. R. 111: folia, Plin. 16, 24, 38, § 92.— Transf., ivy-colored, ivygreen: calcei, Vop. Aurel. 49: patina argentea, Gallien. ap. Treb. Poll. Claud. 17, 5 Peter.

hederatus.full: hĕdĕrātus (ĕd-), a, um, adj. id., adorned or crowned with ivy: patina argentea, Gall. ap. Treb. Claud. 17 dub. (Peter, hederaceam): frons, Nemes. Ecl. 3, 18: pompae, Bacchic, Paul. Nol. Carm. 26, 278: Liber, Tert. Cor. Mil. 7.

hederiger.full: hĕdĕrĭger (ĕd-), ĕra, ĕrum, adj. id., ivy-bearing: Maenades, Cat. 63, 23.

hederosus.full: hĕdĕrōsus (ĕd-), a, um, adj. id., full of ivy: antrum, Prop. 4 (5), 4, 3.

hedone.full: Hēdŏnē, ēs, f., = Ἡδονή (delight), one of the œons of Valentinian, Tert. adv. Val. 8.
hedone.short: Hēdŏnē, ēs, f., = Ἡδονή (delight), one of the œons of Valentinian, Tert.

heduphagetica.full: Hēdŭphăgētĭca, ōrum, n., = Ἡδυφαγητικά (i. e. belonging to sweet eating), the title of a poem of Ennius; cf. Vahl. Ennius, p. xci. and 166 sq.

hedychrum.full: hēdȳ^chrum, i, n., = ἡδύχρουν, a sweet-smelling ointment used for beautifying the skin; a cosmetic balsam: psaltriam adducamus, hedychri incendamus scutellam, Cic. Tusc. 3, 19, 46.
hedychrum.short: hēdȳ^chrum, i, n., = ἡδύχρουν, a sweet-smelling ointment used for beautifying the skin;

hedymeles.full: Hēdўmĕles, ae, m. ἡδύ + μέλος, name of a musician, Juv. 6, 383.

hedyosmos.full: hēdўosmos, i, m., = ἡδύοσμος, the herb wild mint, Plin. 35, 15, 51, § 181.
hedyosmos.short: hēdўosmos, i, m., = ἡδύοσμος, the herb wild mint, Plin.

hedypnois.full: hēdypnŏis, ĭdis, f., = ἡδυπνοΐς, a species of succory, Plin. 20, 8, 31, § 75.
hedypnois.short: hēdypnŏis, ĭdis, f., = ἡδυπνοΐς, a species of succory, Plin.

hedysma.full: hēdysma, ătis, n., = ἥδυσμα (perfume), a sweet-smelling ingredient in ointments, a perfume, balsam (opp. stymma), Plin. 13, 1, 2, § 7.
hedysma.short: hēdysma, ătis, n., = ἥδυσμα (perfume), a sweet-smelling ingredient in ointments, a perfume, balsam (opp.

hegesaretos.full: Hēgēsārētos, i, m., a Thessalian, Caes. B. C. 3, 35.
hegesaretos.short: Hēgēsārētos, i, m., a Thessalian, Caes.

hegesias.full: Hēgēsĭas, ae, m. A Cyrenaic philosopher, Cic. Tusc. 1, 34, 83 sq.; Val. Max. 8, 9, 3.— A rhetorician and historian, Cic. Brut. 83, 286; id. Or. 67, 226 al.

hegesinus.full: Hēgēsīnus, i, m., an Academic philosopher, Cic. Ac. 2, 6, 16.
hegesinus.short: Hēgēsīnus, i, m., an Academic philosopher, Cic.

hehae.full: hĕhae, interj.; an exclamation, he! he! Enn. ap. Varr. L. L. 7, § 93 Müll. (Trag. v. 207 Vahl.).

hei.full: hei (also ei), interj., an exclamation of grief or fear, ah! woe! freq. joined with mihi, ah me! woe is me! hei, perii miser! Plaut. Am. 2, 2, 36: hei, occidi! id. Aul. 2, 1, 28: hei, non placet convivium! id. Amph. 2, 2, 173: hei, vereor, ne quid Andria apportet mali, Ter. And. 1, 1, 46: hei, metuo lenonem ne, etc., id. Phorm. 3, 2, 6: hei, video uxorem, id. ib. 5, 3, 14 ei mihi, qualis erat! Enn. ap. Serv. ad Verg. A. 2, 274; imitated by Verg. A. 2, 274: hei mihi, perii hercle! Plaut. Aul. 2,
hei.short: hei (also ei), interj., an exclamation of grief or fear, ah! woe! freq.

heic.full: heic, adv., v. hic, III. 2 init.

heius.full: Hēïus, i, m. (Ἥϊος), a Greek proper name, Cic. Verr. 2, 5, 18, 47 al.

helciarius.full: helcĭārĭus, ii, m. helcium, one who draws small vessels up the stream, Mart. 4, 64, 22; Sid. poët. Ep. 2, 10.

helcium.full: helcium, ii, n., = ἕλκιον, that with which a load is drawn, a yoke, horse-collar, App. M. 8, p. 222 and 227.
helcium.short: helcium, ii, n., = ἕλκιον, that with which a load is drawn, a yoke, horse-collar, App.

helcysma.full: helcysma, ătis, n., = ἕλκυσμα, the dross of molten silver, silver-dross, Plin. 33, 6, 35, § 105.
helcysma.short: helcysma, ătis, n., = ἕλκυσμα, the dross of molten silver, silver-dross, Plin.

helena.full: Hĕlĕna, ae, or Hĕlĕnē, ēs, f., = Ἑλένη. Daughter of Jupiler and Leda, sister of Castor and Pollux and of Clytemnestra, and wife of Menelaüs, who, on account of her beauty, was carried off by Paris to Troy, and thus became the cause of the Trojan war, Cic. Phil. 2, 22, 55; Verg. A. 7, 364; Ov. M. 13, 200; 14, 669; Prop. 3, 8 (4, 7), 32; 3, 14 (4, 13), 19; Hor. C. 1, 3, 2; 4, 9, 16; id. S. 1, 3, 107; Hyg. Fab. 81 and 118: Penelope venit, abit Helene, a Helen, Mart. 1, 62, 6.— Transf., in naut. lan
helena.short: Hĕlĕna, ae, or Hĕlĕnē, ēs, f., = Ἑλένη.

helenium.full: hĕlĕnĭum, ii, n., = ἑλένιον, a plant, perh. the elecampane, Plin. 21, 10, 33, § 59; 21, 21, 91, § 159.
helenium.short: hĕlĕnĭum, ii, n., = ἑλένιον, a plant, perh.

helenius.full: Hĕlĕnius, ii, m., a Latin proper name, Cic. Att. 5, 12, 2.
helenius.short: Hĕlĕnius, ii, m., a Latin proper name, Cic.

helenus.full: Hĕlĕnus, i, m., = Ἕλενος, son of Priam and Hecuba, a celebrated soothsayer, Cic. Div. 1, 40, 89; Verg. A. 3, 295; 329 sq.; Ov. M. 13, 99; Just. 17, 3.
helenus.short: Hĕlĕnus, i, m., = Ἕλενος, son of Priam and Hecuba, a celebrated soothsayer, Cic.

heleoselinon.full: hĕlēŏsĕlīnon or hĕlīŏsĕlīnum, i, n., = ἑλειοσέλινον, smallage, celery, Apium graveolens, Linn.; Plin. 19, 8, 37, § 124; 20, 11, 46, § 117; Pall. Apr. 3.
heleoselinon.short: hĕlēŏsĕlīnon or hĕlīŏsĕlīnum, i, n., = ἑλειοσέλινον, smallage, celery, Apium graveolens, Linn.;

helepolis.full: hĕlĕpŏlis, is, f., = ἑλέπολις (citytaking), a besieging engine, invented by Demetrius Poliorcetes, Vitr. 10, 22; Amm. 23, 4.
helepolis.short: hĕlĕpŏlis, is, f., = ἑλέπολις (citytaking), a besieging engine, invented by Demetrius Poliorcetes, Vitr.

helernus.full: Hĕlernus, i, m., a grove by the Tiber, the birthplace of Carna, Ov. F. 6, 105.
helernus.short: Hĕlernus, i, m., a grove by the Tiber, the birthplace of Carna, Ov.

heliacus.full: Hēlĭăcus, a, um, adj., = Ἡλιακός, relating to Helios (the sun): Heliaca tradere, to offer sacrifices to Helios, Inscr. Orell. 2343.
heliacus.short: Hēlĭăcus, a, um, adj., = Ἡλιακός, relating to Helios (the sun): Heliaca tradere, to offer sacrifices to Helios, Inscr.

heliades.full: Hēlĭădĕs, um, f., = Ἡλιάδες, daughters of Helios and sisters of Phaëthon, who were changed into poplars (acc. to others, into alders) and their tears into amber, Hyg. Fab. 154; Ov. M. 2, 340 (cf. Verg. A. 10, 190, with id. E. 6, 62): nemus Heliadum, i. e. poplar- or alder-grove, Ov. M. 10, 91: Heliadum lacrimae, i. e. amber, id. ib. 10, 263; called also: Heliadum gemma, Mart. 9, 14, 6; hence: capaces Heliadum crustae, i. e. of amber, Juv. 5, 38.
heliades.short: Hēlĭădĕs, um, f., = Ἡλιάδες, daughters of Helios and sisters of Phaëthon, who were changed into poplars (acc.

helianthes.full: hēlĭanthes, is, n., = ἡλιανθές, the sunflower, Plin. 24, 17, 102, § 165.
helianthes.short: hēlĭanthes, is, n., = ἡλιανθές, the sunflower, Plin.

helicaon.full: Hĕlĭcāon, ŏnis, m., = Ἑλικάων, son of Antenor and founder of Patavium (Padua): Helicaonis orae, i. e. Patavian, Mart. 10, 93, 1.—Hence, Hĕlĭcāŏnĭus, a, um, adj.: regio, the same, id. 14, 152, 2.
helicaon.short: Hĕlĭcāon, ŏnis, m., = Ἑλικάων, son of Antenor and founder of Patavium (Padua): Helicaonis orae, i.

helice.full: hĕlĭcē, ēs, f., = ἑλίκη (a winding). A kind of slender, flexible willow, Plin. 16, 37, 69, § 177.— As nom. propr.: Hĕlĭcē. The constellation of the Great Bear, Cic. Ac. 2, 20, 66; Ov. F. 3, 108; Val. Fl. 1, 17.— Transf., the North, Grat. Cyneg. 55; Sen. Herc. Oet. 1539.— A maritime town of Achaia, swallowed up by the sea, Ov. M. 15, 293; Plin. 2, 92, 94, § 206; Sen. Q. N. 6, 23, 4.

helichrysos.full: hĕlĭchrȳ^sos, i, m., and -um, i, n., = ἑλίχρυσος, the herb marigold, Gnaphalium stoechas, Linn.; acc. to others, Tanacetum annuum, Linn.; Plin. 21, 11, 38, § 65 sq.; 21, 25, 96, § 168.
helichrysos.short: hĕlĭchrȳ^sos, i, m., and -um, i, n., = ἑλίχρυσος, the herb marigold, Gnaphalium stoechas, Linn.;

helicon.full: Hĕlĭcon, ōnis, m., = Ἑλικών, a mountain in Bœotia, sacred to Apollo and the Muses, now Zagará, Plin. 4, 3, 4, § 8; 4, 7, 12, § 25; Ov. M. 2, 219; 5, 254; 663; id. F. 4, 193; Verg. A. 7, 641; 10, 163 al.— Derivv. Hĕlĭcōnĭus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Helicon, Heliconian: collis, i. e. Helicon, Cat. 61, 1: Tempe, a beautiful valley on Mount Helicon, Ov. Am. 1, 1, 15: mella, Claud. Laud. Ser. 10: Naïs, id. Epigr. 5.— Hĕlĭcōnĭădes, um, f., the Heliconians, a poet. designation of the Muses, Luc
helicon.short: Hĕlĭcon, ōnis, m., = Ἑλικών, a mountain in Bœotia, sacred to Apollo and the Muses, now Zagará, Plin.

heliocallis.full: hēlĭŏcallis, ĭdis, f., = ἡλιοκαλλίς, the sunflower, also called helianthes, Plin. 24, 17, 102, § 165.
heliocallis.short: hēlĭŏcallis, ĭdis, f., = ἡλιοκαλλίς, the sunflower, also called helianthes, Plin.

heliocaminus.full: hēlĭŏcămīnus, i, m., = ἡλιοκάμινος, an apartment exposed to the sun, used as a winter abode, Plin. Ep. 2, 17, 20; Dig. 8, 2, 18 pr.
heliocaminus.short: hēlĭŏcămīnus, i, m., = ἡλιοκάμινος, an apartment exposed to the sun, used as a winter abode, Plin.

heliodorus.full: Hēlĭŏdōrus, i, m. A celebrated surgeon, Juv. 6, 372.— A celebrated rhetorician, Hor. S. 1, 5, 2.

heliogabalus.full: Hēlĭŏgăbălus (Elagab-), i, m., a Roman emperor, Aur. Vict. Caes. 23; Spart. Car. 11 al.
heliogabalus.short: Hēlĭŏgăbălus (Elagab-), i, m., a Roman emperor, Aur.

heliopolis.full: Hēlĭŏpŏlis, is, f., = Ἡλιόπολις. A city of Lower Egypt, Cic. N. D. 3, 21, 54; Macr. S. 1, 23, 10.— Derivv. Hē-lĭŏpŏlītes, ae, adj., of or belonging to Heliopolis, Heliopolite: nomos, Plin. 5, 9, 9, § 49: Zeus, an Assyrian designation of Sol, acc. to Macr. S. 1, 23; cf. in the foll.—Subst.: Hēlĭŏpŏlītae, ārum, m. plur., the inhabitants of Heliopolis, Heliopolites, Plin. 36, 26, 67, § 197.— Hēlĭŏpŏlītānus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Heliopolis, Heliopolitan: civitas, Amm. 17, 4: JVPPITER, Ins

helioscopion.full: hēlĭoscŏpĭon, ii, n., = ἡλιοσκόπιον, a species of heliotropium, Plin. 22, 21, 29, § 57; called also: helioscopum, App. Herb. 108.
helioscopion.short: hēlĭoscŏpĭon, ii, n., = ἡλιοσκόπιον, a species of heliotropium, Plin.

helioscopios.full: hēlĭoscŏpĭos, ii, m., = ἡλιοσκόπιος, a kind of tithymalus or spurge, Plin. 26, 8, 42, § 69.
helioscopios.short: hēlĭoscŏpĭos, ii, m., = ἡλιοσκόπιος, a kind of tithymalus or spurge, Plin.

heliotropium.full: hēlĭŏtrŏpĭum, ii, n., = ἡλιοτρόπιον. The plant turnsole, heliotrope, Varr. R. R. 1, 46; Plin. 2, 41, 41, § 109; 22, 21, 29, § 57. — A precious stone with green and brown streaks, striped jasper, Plin. 37, 10, 60, § 165.—Called also: hēlĭŏtrŏpĭos (gemma), Mart. Cap. 1, § 75: heliotropius lapis, Prisc. Perieg. 254.

helix.full: hĕlix, ĭcis, f., = ἕλιξ (wound, twisted). A kind of ivy, Cic. Univ. 9, 27; Plin. 16, 34, 62, § 145 sqq.— A kind of willow, Plin. 16, 37, 69, § 177.— In archit., a whorl, a small ornament on the capital of Corinthian columns, Vitr. 4, 1, 12.

helladicus.full: Hellădĭcus, a, um, adj., = Ἑλλαδικός, of or from Greece, Grecian, Greek: genus picturae, Plin. 35, 10, 36, § 75.
helladicus.short: Hellădĭcus, a, um, adj., = Ἑλλαδικός, of or from Greece, Grecian, Greek: genus picturae, Plin.

hellanicus.full: Hellānīcus, i, m., a Greek historian of Lesbos, an older contemporary of Herodotus, Cic. de Or. 2, 12, 53; Gell. 15, 23.
hellanicus.short: Hellānīcus, i, m., a Greek historian of Lesbos, an older contemporary of Herodotus, Cic.

hellas.full: Hellas, ădis, f., = Ἑλλάς. Hellas, the main-land of Greece, Mel. 2, 3, 3 sq.; Plin. 4, 7, 11, § 23.— A female proper name, Hor. S. 2, 3, 277.

helle.full: Hellē, ēs (gen. Hellis, Sid. Carm. 9, 41), f., = Ἕλλη, daughter of Athamas and Nephele, sister of Phrixus; she fled with the latter from her step-mother Ino on a ram with a golden fleece to Colchis, but was drowned in the strait called, after her, Hellespontus (the sea of Helle), Ov. M. 11, 195; id. F. 3, 857 sq.; Prop. 2, 26, 5 (3, 21, 5 M.); 3 (4), 22, 5; Col. poët. 10, 155; Hyg. Fab. 2 and 3: Mater Helles, Ov. H. 19, 123.

hellen.full: Hellēn, ēnis, m., = Ἕλλην, a son of Deucalion, and king of Thessaly, from whom the Greeks were called Hellenes, Plin. 4, 7, 14, § 28.
hellen.short: Hellēn, ēnis, m., = Ἕλλην, a son of Deucalion, and king of Thessaly, from whom the Greeks were called Hellenes, Plin.

hellespontus.full: Hellespontus, i, m., = Ἑλλήσποντος, the Sea of Helle, the Hellespont, so named after Helle, who was drowned in it, the modern Dardanelles, Mel. 1, 1, 5; 1, 3, 1; Plin. 4, 11, 18, § 49; 4, 12, 24, § 75; 4, 13, 27, § 92; Enn. ap. Varr. L. L. 7, § 21 Müll. (Ann. v. 371 Vahl.); Cic. Fin. 2, 34, 112; Ov. M. 13, 407 et saep.—Separate: qua ponto ab Helles, Poët. ap. Cic. Or. 49, 163; cf. pure Lat.: mare in Helles, Ov. Tr. 1, 10, 15.— Transf., the shores of the Hellespont, the land around the Propontis,
hellespontus.short: Hellespontus, i, m., = Ἑλλήσποντος, the Sea of Helle, the Hellespont, so named after Helle, who was drowned in it, the modern Dardanelles, Mel.

helluatio.full: hellŭātĭo (hēl-), ōnis, f. helluor, a gormandizing, gluttony, Pseudo-Cic. Or. Post Red. ap. Sen. 6, 13; Treb. Poll. Gall. 4.

helluo.full: hellŭo (hēluo), ōnis, m., a gormandizer, glutton, squanderer: fraus, helluo, Ganeo! Ter. Heaut. 5, 4, 10: ille gurges atque helluo, natus abdomini suo, Cic. Pis. 17, 41: impurus, id. Agr. 1, 1, 2: me ipsum ut contempsit helluo patriae! id. Sest. 11, 26.
helluo.short: hellŭo (hēluo), ōnis, m., a gormandizer, glutton, squanderer: fraus, helluo, Ganeo! Ter.

helluor.full: hellŭor (hēluor), ātus, 1, v. dep. n. and a. [helluo], to gormandize, devour (Ciceron.; cf.: decoquo, abligurio): cum Graecis jam in exostra helluabatur, Cic. Prov. Cons. 6, 14; id. Sest. 52, 111: quasi helluari libris, si hoc verbo in tam clara re utendum est, id. Fin. 3, 2, 7: ille gurges helluatus tecum simul rei publicae sanguine, id. Dom. 47, 124.!*? Helluatus as pass., Verg. Cat. 5, 11.

hellusii.full: Hellusii, ōrum, m., a German tribe, mentioned only by Tac. G. 46.
hellusii.short: Hellusii, ōrum, m., a German tribe, mentioned only by Tac.

helops.full: hĕlops (also ĕlops and ellops), ŏpis, m., = ἔλλοψ, a very savory sea-fish, perh. the sword-fish; acc. to others, the sturgeon, Enn. Hed. 6 (p. 166 Vahl.); Ov. Hal. 96; Varr. R. R. 2, 6, 2; Col. 8, 16, 9; Plin. 9, 17, 27, § 61; 32, 11, 54, § 153; Quint. 5, 10, 21; Gell. 7, 16, 5.
helops.short: hĕlops (also ĕlops and ellops), ŏpis, m., = ἔλλοψ, a very savory sea-fish, perh.

helorus.full: Hĕlōrus (or Elōrus), i, m., = Ἔλωρος or Hĕlōrum, i, n., = Ἔλωρον, a river on the eastern coast of Sicily, now Atellaro, al. Abisso, Verg. A. 3, 698; Cic. Verr. 2, 5, 34, § 90: clamosus, Sil. 14, 269: flumen Elorum, Plin. 3, 8, 14, § 89.—At its mouth was situated the city Hĕlōrus (El-), i, f., Liv. 24, 35 init.; Plin. 32, 2, 7, § 16; the vale of which was called Hĕlōrĭa Tempē, Ov. F. 4, 477; and the inhabitants, Hĕlōrīni (El-), Cic. Verr. 2, 3, 43, § 103.
helorus.short: Hĕlōrus (or Elōrus), i, m., = Ἔλωρος or Hĕlōrum, i, n., = Ἔλωρον, a river on the eastern coast of Sicily, now Atellaro, al.

heluatio.full: hēluātio, hēluo, etc., v. helluatio, etc.

helvacea.full: helvacea genus ornamenti Lydii, dictum a colore boum, qui est inter rufum et album appellaturque helvus, Paul. ex Fest. p. 99 Müll. N. cr.
helvacea.short: helvacea genus ornamenti Lydii, dictum a colore boum, qui est inter rufum et album appellaturque helvus, Paul.

helvecones.full: Helvecōnes, um, m., a northern Germanic tribe, between the Rugii and Burgundiones, on the west of the Vistula, Tac. G. 43.
helvecones.short: Helvecōnes, um, m., a northern Germanic tribe, between the Rugii and Burgundiones, on the west of the Vistula, Tac.

helvella.full: helvella (helvēla, Paul. ex Fest. p. 103 Müll.), ae, f. dim. † helus, i. q. olus, a small potherb: fungos, helvellas, herbas omnes ita condiunt, ut nihil possit esse suavius, Cic. Fam. 7, 26, 2; cf.: helvela olera minuta, Paul. ex Fest. p. 103: helvola λαχανάρια, Gloss. Philox.

helvenacus.full: helvĕnācus, a, um, adj. helvus, pale yellow, yellowish: vitis, a particular kind of wine, Plin. 14, 2, 4, § 32: genus palmitum, Col. 5, 5, 16: vinum, Plin. 23, 1, 24, § 47.—Also: helvĕnācĭus, a, um, adj.: vites, Col. 3, 2, 55.

helveolus.full: helvĕŏlus, a, um, adj. id., pale yellow, yellowish: vinum, a particular kind of wine (cf. helvenacus and helvolus), Cato, R. R. 6, 4; 24, 2 (quoted, Plin. 14, 4, 5, § 46, in the form helvinum vinum). Also in the form helvolus, a, um: uvae, Col. 3, 2, 23; Plin. 14, 2, 4, § 29.

helvetii.full: Helvētĭi, ōrum, m., the Helvetians, a people of Gallia Lugdunensis, in modern Switzerland, Caes. B. G. 1, 1; 4 sq.; Tac. G. 28; id. H. 1, 67; Plin. 4, 17, 31, § 106; Cic. Prov. Cons. 13, 33; id. Balb. 14, 32 et saep. — Derivv. Helvētĭus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to the Helvetians, Helvetian: ager, Caes. B. G. 1, 2: civitas, id. ib. 1, 12.— Helvētĭcus, a, um, adj., the same: proelium, Caes. B. G. 7, 9, 6.
helvetii.short: Helvētĭi, ōrum, m., the Helvetians, a people of Gallia Lugdunensis, in modern Switzerland, Caes.

helvidius.full: Helvĭdius, a, the name of a Roman gens, Cic. Clu. 70, 198; Juv. 5, 36 al.
helvidius.short: Helvĭdius, a, the name of a Roman gens, Cic.

helvii.full: Helvĭi (Helvi), ōrum, m., a people of Gallia Narbonensis, whose capital, called Alba Helvorum and Alba Helvia, was celebrated for its wine, now Alps, in Viviers, Départ. Ardèche, Caes. B. G. 7, 7; 75; id. B. C. 1, 35; Plin. 3, 4, 5, § 36; 14, 3, 4, § 43. — Deriv.: Helvĭcus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to the Helvii, Helvian: vinum, Plin. 14, 1, 3, § 18.
helvii.short: Helvĭi (Helvi), ōrum, m., a people of Gallia Narbonensis, whose capital, called Alba Helvorum and Alba Helvia, was celebrated for its wine, now Alps, in Viviers, Départ.

helvina.full: Helvīna (Elv-), ae, f., a surname of Ceres, Juv. 3, 320 [perh. from the Gallic people Helvii].
helvina.short: Helvīna (Elv-), ae, f., a surname of Ceres, Juv.

helvius.full: Helvĭus, a, the name of a Roman gens, Cic. de Or. 2, 66, 266; Suet. Caes. 52; 85 al.
helvius.short: Helvĭus, a, the name of a Roman gens, Cic.

helvus.full: helvus, a, um, adj. perh. a weakened form of gilvus, yellow, light bay: color vaccarum, Varr. R. R. 2, 5, 9; cf.: color boum, qui est inter rufum et album, appellatur helvus, Paul. ex Fest. s. v. † helvacea, p. 99 Müll.

helxine.full: helxīnē, ēs, f., = ἑλξίνη. A prickly plant, otherwise unknown, Plin. 21, 16, 56, § 94.— A plant, otherwise called perdicium: Parietaria officinalis, Linn.; Plin. 22, 17, 19, § 41.

hem.full: hem (also em, and often confounded in MSS. and edd. with em and en, q. v.), interj., an expression of surprise, in a good or bad sense; of admiration, joy, of grief, indignation, etc. (like the intensive ehem, an expression of joyful surprise), oho! indeed! well! well to be sure! hah! alas! alack! Ag. Ego sum ipsus, quem tu quaeris. Ha. Hem! quid ego audio? Plaut. Poen. 5, 2, 86; cf. Ter. And. 3, 1, 4: hem, Pamphile, optime te mihi offers, id. ib. 4, 2, 3: Er. Itane Chrysis? hem! My. Nos quidem
hem.short: hem (also em, and often confounded in MSS.

hemeresios.full: hēmĕrēsĭos, on, adj., = ἡμερἠσιος, of a day: (Pamphilus) absolvit uno die tabellam, quae vocata est Hemeresios, puero picto, Plin. 35, 11, 40, § 124.
hemeresios.short: hēmĕrēsĭos, on, adj., = ἡμερἠσιος, of a day: (Pamphilus) absolvit uno die tabellam, quae vocata est Hemeresios, puero picto, Plin.

hemeris.full: hēmĕris, ĭdis, f., = ἡμερίς, a species of oak, Plin. 16, 6, 8, § 22; 16, 6, 9, § 26.
hemeris.short: hēmĕris, ĭdis, f., = ἡμερίς, a species of oak, Plin.

hemerobion.full: hēmĕrŏbĭon, ĭi, n., = ἡμερόβιον, an insect that lives but a day, an ephemeron: erumpit volucre quadrupes, nec ultra unum diem vivit, unde hemerobion vocatur, Plin. 11, 36, 43, § 120.
hemerobion.short: hēmĕrŏbĭon, ĭi, n., = ἡμερόβιον, an insect that lives but a day, an ephemeron: erumpit volucre quadrupes, nec ultra unum diem vivit, unde hemerobion vocatur, Plin.

hemerocalles.full: hēmĕrŏcalles, is, n., = ἡμεροκαλλές (one day beautiful), a sort of lily, the daylily, Plin. 21, 10, 33, § 59; 21, 21, 90, § 158.
hemerocalles.short: hēmĕrŏcalles, is, n., = ἡμεροκαλλές (one day beautiful), a sort of lily, the daylily, Plin.

hemerodromus.full: hēmĕrŏdrŏmus, i, m., = ἡμεροδρόμος (who runs the day through), a courier (pure Lat. cursor, Plin. 2, 71, 73, § 181): nisi speculator (hemerodromos vocant Graeci) ingens die uno cursu emetiens spatium, etc., Liv. 31, 24, 4.—In plur.: hemerodromœ, Nep. Milt. 4, 3.
hemerodromus.short: hēmĕrŏdrŏmus, i, m., = ἡμεροδρόμος (who runs the day through), a courier (pure Lat.

hemicadium.full: hēmĭcădĭum, i, n., = ἡμικάδιον, the half of a cadus, Isid. 20, 7, 1.
hemicadium.short: hēmĭcădĭum, i, n., = ἡμικάδιον, the half of a cadus, Isid.

hemicillus.full: hēmĭcillus, i, m., = ἡμίκιλλος, a mule, as a term of reproach, Cic. Att. 13, 51, 1 (dub.; al. Micyllus).
hemicillus.short: hēmĭcillus, i, m., = ἡμίκιλλος, a mule, as a term of reproach, Cic.

hemicranium.full: hēmĭcrānĭum, ii, n., and hēmĭ-crānia, ae, f., = ἡμικράνιον, a pain on one side of the head, headache, Cael. Aur. Tard. 1, 1, 4; Marc. Emp. 2; Ser. Samm. 2 in lemm.; Plin. Val. 1. 8.—Deriv. hēmĭ-crānĭci, ōrum, m., sufferers from headache, Theod. Prisc. 2, 1.
hemicranium.short: hēmĭcrānĭum, ii, n., and hēmĭ-crānia, ae, f., = ἡμικράνιον, a pain on one side of the head, headache, Cael.

hemicyclium.full: hēmĭcyclium, ĭi, n., = ἡμικύκλιον, a half-circle, semicircle, Vitr. 9, 8, 5; Plin. Ep. 5, 6, 33.— In partic. A semicircular recess, with seats, Cic. Lael. 1, 2; Sid. Ep. 2, 2.— A semicircular public place furnished with rows of seats for learned discussions, Suet. Gramm. 17.— A semicircular kind of sundial, Vitr. 9, 8, 1.
hemicyclium.short: hēmĭcyclium, ĭi, n., = ἡμικύκλιον, a half-circle, semicircle, Vitr.

hemicyclus.full: hēmĭcyclus, i, m., = ἡμίκυκλος, a half-circle, semicircle, Ambros. in Psa. 118, Serm. 12, 20.
hemicyclus.short: hēmĭcyclus, i, m., = ἡμίκυκλος, a half-circle, semicircle, Ambros.

hemicylindrus.full: hēmĭcўlindrus, i, m., = ἡμικύλινδρος, a half-cylinder, Vitr. 9, 3.
hemicylindrus.short: hēmĭcўlindrus, i, m., = ἡμικύλινδρος, a half-cylinder, Vitr.

hemina1.full: hēmīna (ēmīna), ae, f., = ἡμίνα, a measure, the half of a sextarius, Rhem. Fan. de Pond. 67; for liquids, Cato, R. R. 57, 1; Plaut. Mil. 3, 2, 18; Sen. de Ira, 2, 33; for salt, Cels. 4, 15 fin.; for corn, id. 4, 10 fin.; as a measure, in gen., Pers. 1, 129.
hemina1.short: hēmīna (ēmīna), ae, f., = ἡμίνα, a measure, the half of a sextarius, Rhem.

hemina2.full: Hēmīna, ae, m., surname of the historian L. Cassius.
hemina2.short: Hēmīna, ae, m., surname of the historian L.

heminaria.full: hēmīnārĭa, ōrum, n. hemina, presents of the measure of a hemina: Fabius Maximus incusans Augusti congiariorum, quae amicis dabantur, exiguitatem heminaria esse dixit, Quint. 6, 3, 52.

hemiolios.full: hēmĭŏlĭos, on, adj., = ἡμιόλιος, one and a half (pure Lat. sesquialter), Gell. 18, 14, 4; Vitr. 3, 1, 6; Macr. Somn. Scip. 2, 1; Mart. Cap. 9, § 978 et saep.
hemiolios.short: hēmĭŏlĭos, on, adj., = ἡμιόλιος, one and a half (pure Lat.

hemionion.full: hēmĭŏnĭon, ĭi, n., = ἡμιόνιον, a plant, called also asplenum, Asplenium hemionitis, Linn.; Plin. 27, 5, 17, § 34; App. Herb. 56.
hemionion.short: hēmĭŏnĭon, ĭi, n., = ἡμιόνιον, a plant, called also asplenum, Asplenium hemionitis, Linn.;

hemisphaerium.full: hēmisphaerĭum, ĭi, n., = ἡμισφαίριον, a half-globe, hemisphere. In gen., Varr. R. R. 3, 5, 17; id. L. L. 7, § 7 Müll.; Hyg. Astr. 4, 13; Macr. Somn. Scip. 1, 15; 20; of the earth, Mela, 1, 1, 2; Mart. Cap. 6, § 602; 8, § 873 al.— In partic., a cupola, dome, Vitr. 5, 10, 5.
hemisphaerium.short: hēmisphaerĭum, ĭi, n., = ἡμισφαίριον, a half-globe, hemisphere.

hemistichium.full: hēmistĭchĭum, ĭi, n., = ἡμιστίχιον, a half-verse, hemistich: Enniano hemistichio usus est, Pseudo Ascon. Cic. Verr. 2, 1, 18.
hemistichium.short: hēmistĭchĭum, ĭi, n., = ἡμιστίχιον, a half-verse, hemistich: Enniano hemistichio usus est, Pseudo Ascon.

hemistrigium.full: hēmistrĭgĭum, ĭi, n., a measure, half a striga, Hyg. Grom. p. 1, 1 al.
hemistrigium.short: hēmistrĭgĭum, ĭi, n., a measure, half a striga, Hyg.

hemitheus.full: hēmĭthĕus, i, m., = ἡμίθεος, a demigod, Mart. Cap. 2, § 156; 160; Auct. ap. Serv. Verg. E. 9, 47.
hemitheus.short: hēmĭthĕus, i, m., = ἡμίθεος, a demigod, Mart.

hemitonium.full: hēmĭtŏnĭum, ĭi, n., = ἡμιτόνιον, a half-tone, semitone: intervalla tonorum et hemitoniorum, Vitr. 5, 4, 3; Mart. Cap. 9, § 930; 963; Hyg. Astr. 4, 14; Macr. S. 2, 1, 22.
hemitonium.short: hēmĭtŏnĭum, ĭi, n., = ἡμιτόνιον, a half-tone, semitone: intervalla tonorum et hemitoniorum, Vitr.

hemitriglyphus.full: hēmĭtrīglўphus, i, m., = ἡμιτρίγλυφος; in archit., a half-triglyph, Vitr. 4, 3.

hemitritaeus.full: hēmĭtrĭtaeus, i, m., = ἡμιτριταῖος. A semi-tertian ague, Mart. 12, 91, 2; 2, 40, 1; Cael. Aur. Acut. 2, 22, 133; Ser. Samm. 52 (in Cels. 3, 3, written as Greek).— One who has the semi-tertian ague, Mart. 4, 81, 3.

hemitritaicus.full: hēmĭtrĭtăĭcus, a, um, adj., = ἡμιτριταικός, of or belonging to the semi-tertian ague: febres, Marc. Emp. 30; Cael. Aur. Acut. 2, 10; id. Tard. 1, 4.
hemitritaicus.short: hēmĭtrĭtăĭcus, a, um, adj., = ἡμιτριταικός, of or belonging to the semi-tertian ague: febres, Marc.

hendecasyllabi.full: hendĕcăsyllăbi, ōrum, m., = ἑνδεκασύλλαβοι, verses of eleven syllables, Cat. 12, 10; Plin. Ep. 4, 14, 8; 7, 4, 1; cf. Diom. p. 509 P.
hendecasyllabi.short: hendĕcăsyllăbi, ōrum, m., = ἑνδεκασύλλαβοι, verses of eleven syllables, Cat.

heniochi.full: Hēnĭŏchi, ōrum, m., = Ἡνίοχοι, a people of Asiatic Sarmatia, Plin. 6, 4, 4, § 12; Val. Fl. 6, 42; Sen. Thyest. 1048.— Derivv. Hēnĭŏchus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to the Heniochi, Heniochian: rates, Ov. P. 4, 10, 26.— Hē-nĭŏchĭus, a, um, adj., the same: montes, Plin. 6, 9, 10, § 26.
heniochi.short: Hēnĭŏchi, ōrum, m., = Ἡνίοχοι, a people of Asiatic Sarmatia, Plin.

heniochus1.full: Hēnĭŏchus, a, um, v. Heniochi, II. A.

heniochus2.full: Hēnĭŏchus, i, m., = Ἡνίοχος (rein-holder), the constellation of the Wagoner, pure Lat. Auriga, Plin. 18, 31, 74, § 312; Manil. 1, 361; Hyg. Astr. 3, 12.
heniochus2.short: Hēnĭŏchus, i, m., = Ἡνίοχος (rein-holder), the constellation of the Wagoner, pure Lat.

henna.full: Henna, less correctly Enna, ae, f., = Ἕννα, a city of great antiquity in the centre of Sicily, with a famous temple of Ceres: it was from here that Pluto carried off Proserpine; now Castro Giovanni, Mel. 2, 7, 16; Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 48, § 107 sq.; Ov. F. 4, 422; 455; 462; Hyg. F. 146.— Derivv. Hennensis (Enn-), e, adj., of or belonging to Henna: Ceres, Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 49, § 107 sq.—Subst.: Hen-nenses (Enn-), ium, m. plur., the inhabitants of Henna, Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 48, § 106; Liv. 24, 39; Plin. 3
henna.short: Henna, less correctly Enna, ae, f., = Ἕννα, a city of great antiquity in the centre of Sicily, with a famous temple of Ceres: it was from here that Pluto carried off Proserpine;

henosis.full: hĕnōsis, is, f., = ἕνωσις (union), one of the œons of Valentinian, Tert. adv. Val. 37.
henosis.short: hĕnōsis, is, f., = ἕνωσις (union), one of the œons of Valentinian, Tert.

henotes.full: hĕnŏtes, ētis, f., = ἑνότης (unity), one of the œons of Valentinian, Tert. adv. Val. 37.
henotes.short: hĕnŏtes, ētis, f., = ἑνότης (unity), one of the œons of Valentinian, Tert.

hepar.full: hēpar (ēpar), ătis. n., = ἧπαρ, the liver (pure Lat. jecur), Marc. Emp. 14 fin.— m., = ἥπατος, a kind of fish, hepatus, Plin. 32, 11, 53, § 149.

hepatarius.full: hēpătārĭus, a, um, adj. hepar, I., of or belonging to the liver: morbus, the liver-complaint (comically for love), Plaut. Curc. 2, 1, 24.

hepatia.full: hēpătĭa, ōrum, n., = ἡπάτια (little) liver, Lucil. ap. Non. 119, 22; Petr. 66; App. Mag. p. 300.
hepatia.short: hēpătĭa, ōrum, n., = ἡπάτια (little) liver, Lucil.

hepaticus.full: hēpătĭcus, i, m., = ἡπατικός, belonging to the liver: morbus, Isid. 4, 7, 21.— Plur. as subst.: hēpătĭci, ōrum, they who have the liver-complaint, Plin. 27, 12, 105, § 130 (in Cels. 4, 8, written as Greek).— Liver-colored: aloë, Pall. 11, 14, 8.
hepaticus.short: hēpătĭcus, i, m., = ἡπατικός, belonging to the liver: morbus, Isid.

hepatites.full: hēpătītes, ae, m., = ἡπατίτης, the liver-stone, Plin. 36, 20, 38, § 147.
hepatites.short: hēpătītes, ae, m., = ἡπατίτης, the liver-stone, Plin.

hepatitis.full: hēpătītis, ĭdis, adj., = ἡπατῖτις, like the liver, liver-colored: aloë, Marc. Emp. 8, 1.—Subst.: hēpătītis, idis, f., a precious stone, otherwise unknown, Plin. 37, 11, 71, § 186.
hepatitis.short: hēpătītis, ĭdis, adj., = ἡπατῖτις, like the liver, liver-colored: aloë, Marc.

hepatizon.full: hēpătīzon, ontis, n., = ἡπατίζον, like liver, liver-colored: aes Corinthium, Plin. 34, 2, 3, § 8.
hepatizon.short: hēpătīzon, ontis, n., = ἡπατίζον, like liver, liver-colored: aes Corinthium, Plin.

hephaestia.full: Hēphaestĭa, ae, f., a city of Lemnos, Plin. 4, 12, 23, § 73; Liv. 33, 35, 2.
hephaestia.short: Hēphaestĭa, ae, f., a city of Lemnos, Plin.

hephaestio.full: Hēphaestĭo, ōnis, m., = Ἡφαιστίων, a favorite of Alexander the Great, and one of his generals, Curt. 3, 12, 9; 4, 16, 16; Nep. Eum. 2.
hephaestio.short: Hēphaestĭo, ōnis, m., = Ἡφαιστίων, a favorite of Alexander the Great, and one of his generals, Curt.

hephaestitis.full: hēphaestītis, ĭdis, f., = ἡφαιστῖτις, a precious stone, otherwise unknown, Plin. 37, 10, 60, § 166.
hephaestitis.short: hēphaestītis, ĭdis, f., = ἡφαιστῖτις, a precious stone, otherwise unknown, Plin.

hephthemimeres.full: hephthēmĭmĕres, is, f., = ἑφθημιμερής (sc. τομή), in hexameter or Iambic verse, the cœsura which occurs after the first half of the fourth foot, Lat. semiseptenaria (insectio), Diom. 497, 9 and 23; Serv. de Cent. Metr. 1817 P.

hepsema.full: hepsēma, ătis, n., = ἕψημα, must boiled down to a thick consistence, pure Lat. sapa, Plin. 14, 9, 11, § 80.
hepsema.short: hepsēma, ătis, n., = ἕψημα, must boiled down to a thick consistence, pure Lat.

heptagoniae.full: Heptăgōnĭae, ārum, f., a small place near Sparta, Liv. 34, 38, 5.
heptagoniae.short: Heptăgōnĭae, ārum, f., a small place near Sparta, Liv.

heptagonos.full: heptăgōnos, on, adj., = ἑπτάγωνος, seven-cornered, having seven angles, Boëth. Arithm. 2, 6, p. 1021.
heptagonos.short: heptăgōnos, on, adj., = ἑπτάγωνος, seven-cornered, having seven angles, Boëth.

heptaneuros.full: heptăneuros, i, f., a plant, App. Herb. 61.
heptaneuros.short: heptăneuros, i, f., a plant, App.

heptaphonos.full: heptăphōnos, on, adj., = ἑπτάφωνος, seven times sounding, that gives a sevenfold echo: porticus (Olympiae), Plin. 36, 15, 23, § 100.
heptaphonos.short: heptăphōnos, on, adj., = ἑπτάφωνος, seven times sounding, that gives a sevenfold echo: porticus (Olympiae), Plin.

heptaphyllon.full: heptăphyllon, i, n., = ἑπτάφυλλον (seven-leaf), a plant, otherwise unknown, App. Herb. 116.
heptaphyllon.short: heptăphyllon, i, n., = ἑπτάφυλλον (seven-leaf), a plant, otherwise unknown, App.

heptapleuros.full: heptăpleuros, i, f., = ἑπτάπλευρος (seven-sided), the larger kind of the plant plantago, the greater plantain, Plin. 25, 8, 39, § 80.
heptapleuros.short: heptăpleuros, i, f., = ἑπτάπλευρος (seven-sided), the larger kind of the plant plantago, the greater plantain, Plin.

heptapylos.full: Heptăpўlos, on (-os, c., -on, n.), adj., = ἑπτάπυλος, seven-gated, an epithet of the city of Thebes: Thebas Heptapylos accessimus, App. M. 4, p. 146.—Also in Latinized form: Cadmus Thebas Heptapylas condidit, Hyg. F. 275.
heptapylos.short: Heptăpўlos, on (-os, c., -on, n.), adj., = ἑπτάπυλος, seven-gated, an epithet of the city of Thebes: Thebas Heptapylos accessimus, App.

heptas.full: heptas, ădis, f., = ἑπτάς, the number seven, Mart. Cap. 2, § 108; 7, § 738 (in Macr. Somn. Scip. 1, 6, written as Greek).
heptas.short: heptas, ădis, f., = ἑπτάς, the number seven, Mart.

heptasemos.full: heptăsēmos, on, adj., = ἑπτάσημος; in prosody, of seven times, containing seven units of time (pure Lat. septenarius): basis, Diom. p. 505 P.; Mart. Cap. 9, § 978.

heptastadium.full: Heptastădĭum, ĭi, n., = Ἑπταστάδιον, a mole of seven stadia in length, connecting the isle of Pharos with the mainland, Amm. 22, 16, 10.
heptastadium.short: Heptastădĭum, ĭi, n., = Ἑπταστάδιον, a mole of seven stadia in length, connecting the isle of Pharos with the mainland, Amm.

heptasyllabus.full: heptăsyllăbus, a, um, adj., = ἑπτασύλλαβος, seven - syllabled, Mar. Victor. p. 2613.
heptasyllabus.short: heptăsyllăbus, a, um, adj., = ἑπτασύλλαβος, seven - syllabled, Mar.

heptateuchos.full: Heptăteuchos, i, m., = Ἑπτάτευχος, the first seven books of the Old Testament, Sid. Ep. 5, 15.
heptateuchos.short: Heptăteuchos, i, m., = Ἑπτάτευχος, the first seven books of the Old Testament, Sid.

hepteris.full: heptēris, is, f., = ἑπτήρης (ναῦς), a galley with seven banks of oars, Liv. 37, 23, 5; ib. 24, 3 and 30, 2.
hepteris.short: heptēris, is, f., = ἑπτήρης (ναῦς), a galley with seven banks of oars, Liv.

hera2.full: Hēra, ae, f., = Ἥρα, the Grecian goddess Hera, corresp. to the Juno of the Romans, Sol. 2, 10; Inscr. Orell. 2225 (although here, perh., HERA is i. q. FORTVNA). — Deriv.: Hēraea, ōrum, n., = Ἡραῖα, τά, the festival of Hera, Liv. 27, 30, 9 sq.
hera2.short: Hēra, ae, f., = Ἥρα, the Grecian goddess Hera, corresp.

hera3.full: Hēra, ae, f., = Ἥρα, another name of Hybla Minor in Sicily, Cic. Att. 2, 1, 5.
hera3.short: Hēra, ae, f., = Ἥρα, another name of Hybla Minor in Sicily, Cic.

heraclea.full: Hēraclēa or Hēraclīa, ae, f., = Ἡράκλεια (city of Heracles or Hercules), the name of several cities.—In partic. A seaport of Lucania, on the river Siris, a colony of Tarentum, and the birthplace of the painter Zeuxis, now Policoro, Mel. 2, 4, 8; Plin. 3, 11, 15, § 97; Cic. Arch. 4, 6; Liv. 1, 18; 8, 24.— Deriv.: Hēraclēen-ses or Hēraclīenses, ĭum, m., the inhabitants of Heraclea, Heracleans, Cic. Arch. 4, 6 sq.; id. Balb. 8, 21.— A very ancient city of Sicily, a colony from Crete, called in earl
heraclea.short: Hēraclēa or Hēraclīa, ae, f., = Ἡράκλεια (city of Heracles or Hercules), the name of several cities.—In partic.

heracleopolis.full: Hērāclĕŏpŏlis, is, f., = Ἡρακλέους πόλις, a city of Egypt upon an ancient island of the Nile, which has become part of its western bank, now Ahnas, Mart. Cap. 6, § 676.—Hence, Hērāclĕŏpŏlītes, ae, adj., of Heracleopolis: nomos, Plin. 36, 13, 19, § 84.—Plur. subst.: Hērāclĕŏpŏlī-tae, ārum, m., the inhabitants of Heracleopolis, Plin. 36, 13, 19, § 86.
heracleopolis.short: Hērāclĕŏpŏlis, is, f., = Ἡρακλέους πόλις, a city of Egypt upon an ancient island of the Nile, which has become part of its western bank, now Ahnas, Mart.

heracleotes.full: Hēraclēōtes, ae, m., = Ἡρακλειώτης, of or belonging to Heraclea, Heracleote, born in Heraclea: tractus, in Æolis, Plin. 5, 30, 32, § 122: Dionysius ille, a disciple of Zeno, perh. of Heraclea in Lucania, Cic. Ac. 2, 22, 71: Zeuxis, perh. from the same place, id. Inv. 2, 1, 1; Plin. 35, 9, 36, § 61.— Subst.: Hēraclēōtae, ārum, m. plur., the inhabitants of Heraclea, Heracleotes: in Caria, Cic. Fam. 13, 56, 2.
heracleotes.short: Hēraclēōtes, ae, m., = Ἡρακλειώτης, of or belonging to Heraclea, Heracleote, born in Heraclea: tractus, in Æolis, Plin.

heracleoticus.full: Hēraclēōtĭcus, a, um, adj., = Ἡρακλειωτικός, of or belonging to Heraclea, Heracleotic: origanum, Plin. 20, 16, 62, § 170: nux, Opp. ap. Macr. S. 2, 14.
heracleoticus.short: Hēraclēōtĭcus, a, um, adj., = Ἡρακλειωτικός, of or belonging to Heraclea, Heracleotic: origanum, Plin.

heracleum.full: Hērāclēum, i, n., = Ἡράκλειον, a city in Macedonia, on the border of Thessaly, Liv. 44, 2 sqq.
heracleum.short: Hērāclēum, i, n., = Ἡράκλειον, a city in Macedonia, on the border of Thessaly, Liv.

heracleus1.full: Hēraclēus or -clĭus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Heraclea (in Lydia), Heraclean: lapis, also called Lydius, Plin. 33, 8, 43, § 126; of the magnet, id. 36, 16, 25, § 127.
heracleus1.short: Hēraclēus or -clĭus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Heraclea (in Lydia), Heraclean: lapis, also called Lydius, Plin.

heracleus2.full: Hĕrāclēus or -clĭus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Hercules; v. Hercules, II. D.
heracleus2.short: Hĕrāclēus or -clĭus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Hercules;

heraclides1.full: Hēraclīdes, ae, m., a proper name. A physician, Cels. 3, 6.— Called Ponticus, a Greek philosopher of Heraclea in Pontus, a pupil of Plato and Speusippus, and afterwards of Aristotle, Cic. Leg. 3, 6; id. Tusc. 5, 3, 8 al.— Heraclides Ponticus the younger, a grammarian, Gell. ap. Prisc. 705 P.— A painter, Plin. 35, 11, 40, § 135.
heraclides1.short: Hēraclīdes, ae, m., a proper name.

heraclides2.full: Hēraclīdes, ae, v. Hercules, II. E.

heracliensis.full: Hēraclīensis, e, v. Heraclea, I. B. and II. B.

heraclitus.full: Hērāclītus, i, m., = Ἡράκλειτος. A celebrated Greek philosopher of Ephesus, who wrote in an obscure style (hence called ὁ σκοτεινός, the Obscure), Cic. Div. 2, 64, 133; id. Fin. 2, 5, 15; id. N. D. 3, 14, 35; id. Tusc. 5, 36, 105; Lucr. 1, 639: nec consulto dicis occulte tamquam Heraclitus, Cic. N. D. 1, 26, 74.— Deriv.: Hēraclītĕi, ōrum, m., the disciples of Heraclitus, App. Doctr. Plat. 1, p. 2, 41.— A pupil of Clitomachus and Philo, Cic. Ac. 2, 4, 12.— An ambassador sent by king Philip to Han

heraclius.full: Hēraclius, a, um, v. 1. Heraclëus and Hercules, II. D.

heraea.full: Hēraea, ae, f. Hera, a fortified city in Arcadia, on the Alphēus, Liv. 28, 7 sq.

heraeus.full: Hēraeus, a, um, v. 2. Hera, II.

herba.full: herba, ae, f. old Lat. forb-ea; Gr. φορβή; Sanscr. root bhar-, to nourish, springing vegetation, grass, green stalks or blades, green crops, herbage, an herb (cf.: gramen, faenum, caespes, glaeba): herba cubile Praebebat, multa et molli lanugine abundans, Lucr. 5, 816: in molli consedimus herba, Verg. E. 3, 55: cum ceteris in campo exercentibus in herba ipse recubuisset, Cic. de Or. 2, 71, 287: abicere se in herba, id. ib. 1, 7, 28: fusus per herbam (agricola), Verg. G. 2, 527 al.: invitant (Pec

herbaceus.full: herbācĕus, a, um, adj. herba, grassy, grass-colored, grass-green, Plin. 19, 6, 33, § 110; cf.: folia herbacei coloris, id. 20, 13, 51, § 134: flos, id. 21, 19, 75, § 128 (opp. albus), id. 26, 8, 35, § 55: oleum, id. 23, 4, 49, § 95: chrysocolla, id. 33, 5, 27, § 90.

herbans.full: herbans, antis, adj. herba, producing grass or herbage, full of grass: prata, App. M. 7, p. 194 Oud. N. cr. (al. herbentia).

herbaria.full: herbārĭa, ae, f. (sc. ars) [herba], the knowledge of plants, botany: herbariam et medicamentariam a Chirone volunt repertam, Plin. 7, 56, 57, § 196.

herbarium.full: herbārium, ii, n. herbarius, a collection of dried plants, an herbarium, Cassiod. Inst. Div. Litt. 31.

herbarius.full: herbārĭus, ĭi, m. herba, one skilled in plants, a botanist, Plin. 20, 17, 73, § 191; 25, 13, 109, § 174.

herbaticus.full: herbātĭcus, a, um, adj. id., living on grass or herbs, grass-eating (post-class.): animalia, Vop. Prob. 19, 4.

herbesco.full: herbesco, ĕre, v. inch. n. [id.], to grow into green stalks or blades: elicere herbescentem viriditatem, Cic. de Sen. 15, 51: campi semper herbescunt, Amm. 31, 2, 19.

herbessus.full: Herbessus (Herbēsus), i, f., a town of Sicily, Liv. 24, 30 al.
herbessus.short: Herbessus (Herbēsus), i, f., a town of Sicily, Liv.

herbeus.full: herbĕus, a, um, adj. herba, grasscolored, grass-green: oculi, Plaut. Curc. 2, 1, 16.

herbido.full: herbĭdo, āre, 1, v. a. herbidus, to give a grassy appearance to: terras, Mart. Cap. 1, § 75.

herbidus.full: herbĭdus, a, um, adj. herba. Full of grass or herbs, grassy: campi, Varr. R. R. 2, 1, 16; Liv. 9, 2, 7: Epiros, Ov. M. 8, 282: segetes, full of weeds, Col. 1, 6, 22: potus, obtained from herbs, Plin. 24, 6, 19, § 28: insulae herbidae omnes harundine et junco, Plin. Ep. 8, 20, 5: ripae, Amm. 14, 3, 4.— Like grass, grassy, grass-colored: folium herbidi coloris, Plin. 12, 14, 31, § 56: lux, Prud. Psych. 863.

herbifer.full: herbĭfer, ĕra, ĕrum, adj. herba-fero, producing grass or herbs, grassy, herbiferous (poet. and in post-Aug. prose): colles, Ov. M. 14, 9: Acis, id. F. 4, 468: Pelius mons, Plin. 25, 8, 53, § 94.

herbigradus.full: herbĭgrădus, a, um, adj. herbagradior, going in the grass, a poet. epithet of the snail, Poët. ap. Cic. Div. 2, 64, 133.

herbilis.full: herbĭlis, e, adj. herba, fed with grass: anser, Lucil. ap. Serv. Verg. G. 1, 129; cf. Paul. ex Fest. p. 100 Müll.

herbipotens.full: herbĭpŏtens, entis, adj. herba-potens, skilled in herbs (poet.): manus (Circes), Boëth. Cons. 4, 3, 9.

herbita.full: Herbĭta, ae, f., = Ἑρβίτα, a town in Sicily, Cic. Verr. 2, 3, 32, § 75.— Deriv. Herbĭtensis, e, adj., of or belonging to Herbita, Herbitan: ager, Cic. Verr. 2, 3, 18, § 47.—Subst.: Herbĭtenses, ĭum, m. plur., the inhabitants of Herbita, Herbitans, Cic. Verr. 2, 2, 65, § 156.
herbita.short: Herbĭta, ae, f., = Ἑρβίτα, a town in Sicily, Cic.

herbosus.full: herbōsus, a, um, adj. id.. Full of grass or herbs, grassy: campus, Hor. C. 3, 18, 9: Palatia, Tib. 2, 5, 25: Apidanus, Prop. 1, 3, 6: flumen, Verg. G. 2, 199: pascua, Ov. M. 2, 689: moretum, id. F. 4, 367: herbosissima stramenta, Cato, R. R. 54, 2.— Grass-colored, grass - green (post-class.): marmor, Sid. Carm. 5, 38: calcei smaragdineae fluctu viriditatis, Mart. Cap. 1, § 66.

herbula.full: herbŭla, ae, f. dim. id., a little herb: cervae perpurgant se quadam herbula, quae seselis dicitur, Cic. N. D. 2, 50, 127; Sen. Vit. Beat. 9; Quint. 1, 3, 5.

herbuscula.full: herbuscŭla, ae, f. dim. id., a little herb or plant: quaedam, Mart. Cap. 2, § 100.

herceus.full: Hercēus, i, m., = Ἑρκεῖος (of or belonging to the court-yard), an epithet of Jupiter, as the protector of the house and its enclosure (pure Lat. Penetralis): Herceus Juppiter intra conseptum domus cujusque colebatur, quem etiam deum penetralem appellabant, Paul. ex Fest. p. 101 Müll. N. cr.; Hyg. F. 91; Sen. Agam. 469; cf. Serv. Verg. A. 2, 469: ara Hercei Jovis, Ov. Ib. 286 (al. Rhoetei).—Hence, also: Herceae arae, Luc. 9, 979 (dub.).
herceus.short: Hercēus, i, m., = Ἑρκεῖος (of or belonging to the court-yard), an epithet of Jupiter, as the protector of the house and its enclosure (pure Lat.

hercisco.full: hercisco or ercisco, ĕre, v. a. contr. from herctum or erctum and cisco, as a v. inch. from cieo; cf. herctum, in the old jurid. lang., to proceed to the division of an inheritance, to divide an inheritance. Lit.: idcirco qui, quibus verbum herctum cieri oporteat, nesciat, idem herciscundae familiae causam agere non possit, Cic. de Or. 1, 56, 237: arbitrum familiae herciscundae postulavit, id. Caecin. 7, 19; Dig. 10, 2; cf. App. M. 9, p. 229.— Transf.: nos viae herciscundae contendentes, i. e. d

herctum.full: herctum or erctum, i, n. HORCTUM et FORCTUM pro bono dicebant, Paul. ex Fest. p. 102 Müll.; perh. kindr. with heres. In the old jurid. lang., an inheritance, estate, patrimony; only in the connection herctum (erct-) ciere (whence is derived herciscere), to divide an inheritance: qui, quibus verbum herctum cieri oporteat, nesciat, Cic. de Or. 1, 56, 237: herctum non citum, an undivided inheritance, Gell. 1, 9, 12; cf. Don. ap. Serv. Verg. A. 8, 642: herctum citum fit inter consortes, Paul. ex Fes

herculaneum.full: Hercŭlānĕum (Hercŭlānĭum, Plin. 3, 5, 9, § 62; but the modern form Herculanum is not Lat.; in Cic. Att. 7, 3, 1, read Aeculanum; v. Orell. ad loc.), ĕi, n., = Ἡράκλειον, a town of Campania, situated on the sea-coast, between Naples and Pompeii, and buried along with the latter city by an eruption of Vesuvius, A. D. 79, Mel. 2, 4, 9; Plin. 3, 5, 9, § 62; Sisenn. ap. Non. 207, 9; Liv. 10, 45; Vell. 2, 16, 2; Sen. Q. N. 6, 26 fin.; Flor. 1, 16.— Derivv. Her-cŭlānĕus (-lanus), a, um, adj., of or bel

herculaneus.full: Hercŭlānĕus, a, um, v. Herculaneum, II. A., and Hercules, II. B.

herculanus.full: Hercŭlānus, a, um, v. Hercules, II. C.

hercularia.full: hercŭlārĭa, ae, f., a plant, i. q. sideritis, App. Herb. 72.
hercularia.short: hercŭlārĭa, ae, f., a plant, i.

hercule.full: hercŭle and hercŭles, v. Hercules, I. B.

hercules.full: Hercŭles, is and i (the latter in Cic. Ac. 2, 34, 108 Goer.; cf. Plin. ap. Charis. p. 107 P.: Herculei, Cat. 55, 13), m., = Ἡρακλῆς, Etrusc. HERCLE (whence, by the insertion of a connecting vowel, the Latin form arose; cf. Alcumena for Ἀλκμήνη; v. also under B. the voc. hercle), son of Jupiter and Alcmena, husband of Dejanira, and, after his deification, of Hebe, the god of strength, and the guardian of riches, to whom, therefore, tithes were offered; he was also the guide of the Muses (Musagete
hercules.short: Hercŭles, is and i (the latter in Cic.

herculeus.full: Hercŭlĕus, a, um, v. Hercules, II. A.

hercynia.full: Hercўnĭa silva, = Ἑρκύνιος δρυμός, the Hercynian Forest, in ancient Germany, sixty days' journey in length and nine in width, extending from the Schwarzwald, or Black Forest, on the north-east, to the Harz, Caes. B. G. 6, 24 sq.; Mel. 3, 3, 3; Tac. G. 28.—Called also: Hercynius saltus, Plin. 4, 12, 25, § 80; 10, 47, 67, § 132; Tac. G. 30; Liv. 5, 34, 4; and: Hercynium jugum, Plin. 4, 14, 28, § 100.—Also absol.: Hercynia, ae, f., Tac. A. 2, 45 fin.
hercynia.short: Hercўnĭa silva, = Ἑρκύνιος δρυμός, the Hercynian Forest, in ancient Germany, sixty days' journey in length and nine in width, extending from the Schwarzwald, or Black Forest, on the north-east, to the Harz, Caes.

hercynna.full: Hercynna or Hercȳna, ae, f., a female companion of Proserpina, to whom a temple was dedicated at Lebadia, Liv. 45, 27, 8.
hercynna.short: Hercynna or Hercȳna, ae, f., a female companion of Proserpina, to whom a temple was dedicated at Lebadia, Liv.

herdonea.full: Herdōnea or -ia, ae, f., a city of the interior of Apulia, now Ordona, Liv. 25, 21, 1; 27, 1, 3; Sil. 8, 569 (perh. also in Liv. 24, 20, 8, inst. of Ardoneas).—Herdōni-enses, ĭum, m., the inhabitants of Herdonia, Plin. 3, 11, 16, § 105.
herdonea.short: Herdōnea or -ia, ae, f., a city of the interior of Apulia, now Ordona, Liv.

herdonius.full: Herdonĭus, ĭi, m., a proper name: Turnus H., of Aricia, Liv. 1, 50 sq.: Appius H., a Sabine, id. 3, 15 sq.
herdonius.short: Herdonĭus, ĭi, m., a proper name: Turnus H., of Aricia, Liv.

here2.full: Hērē, ēs, f., the goddess of inheritance, Enn. ap. Paul. ex Fest. p. 100 Müll. (Ann. v. 108 Vahl.).
here2.short: Hērē, ēs, f., the goddess of inheritance, Enn.

herediolum.full: hērēdĭŏlum, i, n. dim. heredium, a small inheritance, small patrimony, Col. 1, praef. § 13; Gell. 19, 7, 1: herediolum, majorum regna meorum, Aus. Idyll. 3, 1: ex iguum, App. Mag. p. 338, 6: num ipsum heredioli pretium invidiosum est? id. ib. p. 338, 17.

heredipeta.full: hērēdĭpĕta, ae, m. heredium-peto, one that strives after an inheritance, a legacy-hunter, Petr. S. 124, 2; Schol. Juv. 3, 129.

hereditarie.full: hērēdĭtārĭē, adv., v. the foll. art.

hereditarius.full: hērēdĭtārĭus, a, um, adj. hereditas, of or relating to an inheritance, inherited, hereditary (class.): auctio, Cic. Caecin. 5, 13; cf.: lites, Quint. 3, 10, 2: agri, Plin. Ep. 7, 11, 1: cognomen quod habes hereditarium, Cic. Rep. 6, 11: imperium, Curt. 10, 7 fin.: jus, Flor. 3, 13 fin.: bellum, id. 3, 17: paupertas (with vetus), Val. Max. 4, 3, 8: res, an inheritance, Gai. Inst. 2, 9: aes alienum, id. ib. 3, 84 al.—Adv.: hērēdĭtārĭē, by inheritance (late Lat.), Vulg. Ezech. 46, 16.

hereditas.full: hērēdĭtas, ātis (gen. plur. hereditatium, Cic. Dom. 15, 35; Inscr. Orell. 107 al.; but usu. hereditatum, Cic. Verr. 2, 3, 7, § 16; id. Agr. 1, 3, 8), f. heres, heirship, inheritance. Abstr.: hereditas est successio in universum jus, quod defunctus habebat tempore mortis, Dig. 50, 16, 24: si istiusmodi mi fundus hereditate obvenerit, Varr. R. R. 1, 12, 2; Plin. 17, 1, 1, § 4; cf.: quoniam habes istum equum, aut emeris oportet aut hereditate possideas aut, etc. ... sed neque emisti, neque heredita

heredito.full: hērēdĭto, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. id., to inherit (late Lat.): bona sua, Salv. adv. Av. 3, 10 med.: terram, Vulg. Psa. 24, 13 al.

heredium.full: hērēdĭum, ĭi, n. id., an hereditary estate: bina jugera quod a Romulo primum divisa viritim, quae heredem sequerentur, heredium appellarunt, Varr. R. R. 1, 10, 2; cf.: heredium, praedium parvulum, Paul. ex Fest. p. 99 Müll.; Nep. Cat. 1, 1: in XII. Tabulis legum nostrarum nusquam nominatur villa, semper in significatione ea hortus, in horti vero heredium, Plin. 19, 4, 19, § 50.

herem marteam.full: herem marteam antiqui accepta hereditate colebant, quae a nomine appellabatur heredum, et esse una ex Martis comitibus putabatur, Paul. ex Fest. p. 100 Müll. N. cr.; cf. heres init.
herem marteam.short: herem marteam antiqui accepta hereditate colebant, quae a nomine appellabatur heredum, et esse una ex Martis comitibus putabatur, Paul.

herennius.full: Hērennĭus, a, the name of a Roman gens, e. g. C. Herennius, to whom the Rhetorica of Cornificius is dedicated: M. Herennius, an orator, Cic. Brut. 45, 166; id. Mur. 17, 36: Herennius Gallus, Tac. H. 4, 13; 19; 26 sq.: Herennius Senecio, a historian under Domitian, id. Agr. 2; 45; a Samnite Herennius, Liv. 9, 1; Flor. 1, 16, 10.— Deriv.: Hērennĭānus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to a Herennius, Herennian: coheredes, Cic. Att. 13, 6, 2.
herennius.short: Hērennĭus, a, the name of a Roman gens, e.

heres.full: hēres (ēres, Inscr. Orell. 188 al.), ēdis (archaic acc. sing. herem, Naev. ap. Non. 486, 33; Inscr. Orell. 4379; cf. the art. † herem), comm. Sanscr. har-āmi, seize; har-anam, hand; Gr. χείρ, χέρης; cf. erus, an heir, heiress. Lit.: testamento facto mulier moritur: facit heredem ex deunce et semuncia Caecinam, ex duabus sextulis M. Fulcinium, Cic. Caecin. 6, 17; cf.: me nemo nisi amicus fecit heredem, etc. ... aliquem palam heredem factitare, id. Phil. 2, 16, 41: mulier testamento fecit heredem

heri.full: hĕri or hĕre (in here neque e plane neque i auditur, Quint. 1, 4, 7: here nunc e littera terminamus: at veterum comicorum adhuc libris invenio: Heri ad me venit, quod idem in epistulis Augusti, quas sua manu scripsit aut emendavit, deprehenditur, id. 1, 7, 22; cf. Charis. p. 180 P.; Prisc. p. 1011 ib.; v. esp. Neue, Formenl. 2, p. 685), adv. for hesi; cf. hes in hesternus; v. the letter R; kindred with Sanscr. hyas; Goth. gis-tra; Germ. gestern; Engl. yesterday; Gr. χθές, orig. χες, yesterday. L
heri.short: hĕri or hĕre (in here neque e plane neque i auditur, Quint.

herie.full: Hērĭē, ēs, f., a female companion of Juno: Herie Junonis, in formula (of prayer), ap. Gell. 13, 22, 1.
herie.short: Hērĭē, ēs, f., a female companion of Juno: Herie Junonis, in formula (of prayer), ap.

herilus.full: Hērĭlus, i, m., a king of Prœneste, son of the goddess Feronia, Verg. A. 8, 563.
herilus.short: Hērĭlus, i, m., a king of Prœneste, son of the goddess Feronia, Verg.

hermacreon.full: Hermācreon, ontis, m., a Greek proper name, Cic. Inv. 1, 30, 47.
hermacreon.short: Hermācreon, ontis, m., a Greek proper name, Cic.

hermagoras.full: Hermăgŏras and Hermăgŏra (the latter is the Ciceron. form acc. to Quint. 1, 5, 61), ae, m., = Ἑρμαγόρας. A celebrated Greek rhetorician of Rhodes, Cic. Brut. 78, 271; id. Inv. 1, 6, 8; 1, 9, 12; 1, 11, 16; Quint. 3, 1, 16; 3, 5, 14 et saep.— Hermăgŏrēi, ōrum, m., his disciples, Quint. 3, 1, 16; 3, 5, 4; 7, 4, 4.— Another rhetorician of Temnos in Æolis, in the time of Augustus, Quint. 3, 1, 19; Tac. Or. 19.
hermagoras.short: Hermăgŏras and Hermăgŏra (the latter is the Ciceron.

hermandica.full: Hermandĭca, ae, f., a city of Hispania, perh. the modern Salamanca, Liv. 21, 5, 7.
hermandica.short: Hermandĭca, ae, f., a city of Hispania, perh.

hermaphroditus.full: hermăphrŏdītus, i, m., = ἑρμαφρόδιτος, a hermaphrodite, acc. to the myth, so called after the son of Hermes and Aphrodite, who, when bathing, grew together with Salmacis into one person: gignuntur et utriusque sexus, quos hermaphroditos vocamus, olim androgynos vocatos et in prodigiis habitos, nunc vero in deliciis, Plin. 7, 3, 3, § 34; cf. Ov. M. 4, 285 sq.; 383; Hyg. Fab. 271; Mart. 10, 4, 6.— Transf., adj.: hermaphroditae equae. Plin. 11, 49, 109, § 262.
hermaphroditus.short: hermăphrŏdītus, i, m., = ἑρμαφρόδιτος, a hermaphrodite, acc.

hermarchus.full: Hermarchus, i, m. Of Mitylene, a disciple of Epicurus, Cic. Fin. 2, 30, 96; id. N. D. 1, 33, 93; id. Ac. 2, 30, 97.— Of Chios, Auct. Harusp. Resp. 16, 34.

hermathena.full: Hermăthēna, ae, f., =Ἑρμῆσ-Ἀθηνᾶ, a double bust of Mercury and Minerva, Cic. Att. 1, 1, 5; 1, 4, 3.
hermathena.short: Hermăthēna, ae, f., =Ἑρμῆσ-Ἀθηνᾶ, a double bust of Mercury and Minerva, Cic.

hermeneuma.full: hermēneuma, ătis, n., = ἑρμήνευμα, explanation, exposition, interpretation, Sen. Excerpt. Contr. 9, 3, 4 (id. Contr. 26, written as Greek).
hermeneuma.short: hermēneuma, ătis, n., = ἑρμήνευμα, explanation, exposition, interpretation, Sen.

hermeracles.full: Hermēracles, is, m., = Ἑρμῆσ-Ἡρακλῆς, a double bust of Mercury and Hercules, Cic. Att. 1, 10, 3.
hermeracles.short: Hermēracles, is, m., = Ἑρμῆσ-Ἡρακλῆς, a double bust of Mercury and Hercules, Cic.

hermeros.full: Hermĕros, ōtis, m., = Ἑρμῆσ-Ἔρως, a double bust of Mercury and Amor, Plin. 36, 5, 4, § 33.
hermeros.short: Hermĕros, ōtis, m., = Ἑρμῆσ-Ἔρως, a double bust of Mercury and Amor, Plin.

hermes.full: Hermes or Herma, ae, m., = Ἑρμῆς (Hermes, Mercury; hence transf., cf. Liddell and Scott under Ἑρμῆς), a Hermes pillar, Hermes, a head carved on the top of a square pedestal or post; such pillars of Hermes stood, esp. in Athens, in several public places and before private houses, Macr. S. 1, 19; Serv. Verg. A. 8. 138; Nep. Alcib. 3; Cic. Leg. 2, 26, 65; id. Att. 1, 8, 2; Juv. 8, 53.— Deriv.: Hermae-um, i, n., a temple of Hercules, Hermœum. The name of a summer-house: in diaetam, cui nomen est Her
hermes.short: Hermes or Herma, ae, m., = Ἑρμῆς (Hermes, Mercury;

hermes trimaximus.full: Hermes Trĭmaxĭmus (= τρις μέγιστος, a surname of the Egyptian Hermes), a philosophical writer of the second century after Christ, Amm. 21, 14, 5.
hermes trimaximus.short: Hermes Trĭmaxĭmus (= τρις μέγιστος, a surname of the Egyptian Hermes), a philosophical writer of the second century after Christ, Amm.

hermesias.full: hermēsĭas, ădis, f., a kind of medical composition for children, Plin. 24, 17, 102, § 166.
hermesias.short: hermēsĭas, ădis, f., a kind of medical composition for children, Plin.

herminius.full: Hermĭnĭus, a. Name of an ancient Roman family of Etruscan origin, Liv. 2, 10; 3, 65; Sil. 5, 580.— A Trojan, Verg. A. 11, 642.— Herminius mons, a mountain range of Lusitania, Hirt. B. Alex. 48; Suet. Caes. 54.

hermione.full: Hermĭŏnē, ēs, and Hermĭŏna, ae, f., = Ἑρμιόνη. Daughter of Menelāus and Helen, Ov. P. 2, 11, 15; Hyg. Fab. 122; Prop. 1, 4, 6; Verg. A. 3, 328 al.— A maritime city of Argolis, now Kastri, Mel. 2, 3, 8; Liv. 31, 41, 5; Plin. 4, 5, 9, § 18.— Derivv. Hermĭŏnēus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Hermione: statio, Verg. Cir. 471.— Hermĭŏnĭus, a, um, adj., the same: ager, Plin. 4, 12, 19, § 56.— Hermĭŏnĭcus, a, um, adj., the same: ager, Liv. 31, 44, 1.
hermione.short: Hermĭŏnē, ēs, and Hermĭŏna, ae, f., = Ἑρμιόνη.

hermiones.full: Hermĭōnes, um, m., a name applied to the people of Central Germany, from whom are descended the Suevi, Hermunduri, Chatti, and Cherusci, Mel. 3, 3 fin.; Plin. 4, 14, 28, § 100; Tac. G. 2, 7.
hermiones.short: Hermĭōnes, um, m., a name applied to the people of Central Germany, from whom are descended the Suevi, Hermunduri, Chatti, and Cherusci, Mel.

hermippus.full: Hermippus, i, m., = Ἕρμιππος, a Greek proper name, Cic. Fl. 19 sq.; id. Q. Fr. 1, 2, 2, § 4 al.
hermippus.short: Hermippus, i, m., = Ἕρμιππος, a Greek proper name, Cic.

hermodorus.full: Hermŏdōrus, i, m. An Ephesian prince, Cic. Tusc. 5, 36, 105; Plin. 34, 5, 11, § 21.— A famous architect of Salamis, Cic. de Or. 1, 14, 62; cf. Vitr. 3, 2.

hermogenes.full: Hermŏgĕnes, is, m., a proper name, e. g. Cic. Att. 12, 25; 13, 24; Suet. Dom. 10 al.; Tigellius Herm., v. Tigellius.— Deriv.: Hermŏgĕnĭānus, a, um, adj., belonging to one Hermogenes: equi, Cod. Theod. 10 6, 1.
hermogenes.short: Hermŏgĕnes, is, m., a proper name, e.

hermu aelig;doelig;on.full: Hermu Ædœŏn = Ἑρμοῦ αἰδοῖον, a precious stone, now unknown, Plin. 37, 10, 60, § 166.
hermu aelig;doelig;on.short: Hermu Ædœŏn = Ἑρμοῦ αἰδοῖον, a precious stone, now unknown, Plin.

hermubotane.full: hermūbŏtănē, ēs, f., = Ἑρμοῦ βοτάνη, the herb Mercury, also called hermubasilion, App. Herb. 82; cf. hermupoa.
hermubotane.short: hermūbŏtănē, ēs, f., = Ἑρμοῦ βοτάνη, the herb Mercury, also called hermubasilion, App.

hermula.full: hermŭla, ae, f. dim., a small Hermes pillar, Cassiod. Var. 3, 51; Balb. de Limit. p. 142 Goes.

hermunduri.full: Hermundŭri, ōrum, m. (= Ἑρμόνδοροι, Strab.), a Germanic people on the Elbe, neighbors of the Chatti, Plin. 4, 14, 28, § 100; Tac. G. 41; id. A. 2, 63; 12, 29 sq.; 13, 57.

hermupoa.full: hermūpŏa, ae, f., = Ἑρμοῦ πόα, the herb Mercury, Plin. 25, 5, 18, § 38.
hermupoa.short: hermūpŏa, ae, f., = Ἑρμοῦ πόα, the herb Mercury, Plin.

hermus.full: Hermus, i, m., = Ἕρμος, an auriferous river in Æolis, now Sarabat, Mel. 1, 17, 3; Plin. 5, 29, 31, § 119; Verg. G. 2, 137; id. A. 7, 721.
hermus.short: Hermus, i, m., = Ἕρμος, an auriferous river in Æolis, now Sarabat, Mel.

hernia.full: hernĭa, ae, f. perhaps from ἔρνος, sprout, like ramex from ramus, a rupture, hernia, Cels. 7, 18; 13; Mart. 3, 24, 10.

hernici.full: Hernĭci, ōrum, m. herna = saxum in the Sabine and Marscar lang., an Italian people in Latium, between the Æqui and Volsci, Liv. 2, 22; 40 sq.; cf.: Hernici dicti a saxis, quae Marsi herna dicunt, Paul. ex Fest. p. 100 Müll.— Deriv.: Hernĭ-cus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to the Hernici, Hernician: ager, Plin. 3, 5, 9, § 63: terra, Ov. F. 3, 90: saxa, Verg. A. 7, 684; Sil. 4, 226; 8, 393; cf. Stat. S. 4, 5, 56. Subst.: Hernĭcus, i, m., the Hernician, collect., Juv. 14, 180.

herniosus.full: hernĭōsus, a, um, adj. hernia, ruptured, having a rupture: patruus, Verg. Cat. 5, 39.—Plur. subst.: hernĭōsi, ōrum, m., ruptured persons, Lampr. Heliog. 25, 6.

hero.full: Hēro, ūs, f., = Ἡρώ. A priestess of Aphrodite, in Sestos, beloved by Leander of Abydos, who repeatedly swam to her across the Hellespont, but at length was drowned, Ov. H. 18 and 19; id. Am. 2, 16, 31.— Deriv.: Hērōus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Hero: turres, Luc. 9, 955.— One of the Danaïdes, Hyg. Fab. 170.— A daughter of Priam, Hyg. Fab. 90.

herodes.full: Hērōdes, is, m., = Ἡρώδης. A king of Judea, Hor. Ep. 2, 2, 184; Macr. S. 2, 4: Herodis dies, the Sabbath, Pers. 5, 180. —Hence, adj.: Hērōdĭānus, a, um, of Herod.—Only as subst. plur.: Hērōdĭā-ni, ōrum, m., the followers of Herod, Herodians, Vulg.
