Marc. 3, 6 al.— Surnamed Atticus, a celebrated Greek sophist under the Antonines, Gell. 1, 2; 9, 2; 19, 12.— A freedman of Atticus, Cic. Att. 6, 1, 25.

herodius.full: hĕrōdĭus, ĭi, and hĕrōdio, ōnis, m., an unknown bird, perhaps the stork, Vulg. Deut. 14, 16 (transl. of the Hebr. , in the Engl. transl. the little owl), id. Lev. 11, 17.
herodius.short: hĕrōdĭus, ĭi, and hĕrōdio, ōnis, m., an unknown bird, perhaps the stork, Vulg.

herodotus.full: Hērŏdŏtus, i, m., = Ἡρόδοτος, celebrated as the earliest Greek historian, born at Halicarnassus, 484 B. C.: quamquam et apud Herodotum, patrem historiae et apud Theopompum sunt innumerabiles fabulae, Cic. Leg. 1, 1, 5; id. de Or. 2, 13, 55; cf. Quint. 10, 1, 73; 101; 9, 4, 16; 18.
herodotus.short: Hērŏdŏtus, i, m., = Ἡρόδοτος, celebrated as the earliest Greek historian, born at Halicarnassus, 484 B.

heroicus.full: hērōĭcus, a, um, adj., = ἡρωϊκός, of or relating to (mythical) heroes, heroic: vetus opinio est, jam usque ab heroicis ducta temporibus, Cic. Div. 1, 1, 1: tempora, id. N. D. 3, 21, 54; Quint. 1, 11, 17: aetates, Cic. Tusc. 5, 3, 7: Medea et Atreus, heroicae personae, id. N. D. 3, 29, 71: sublimitas heroici carminis, of the heroic poem, of the epic, Quint. 1, 8, 5; cf.: heroici carminis sonus, Tac. Or. 10: carmen, Serv. Verg. A. 1 init.: versus, usually herous versus (v. herous), Prisc. p. 1256
heroicus.short: hērōĭcus, a, um, adj., = ἡρωϊκός, of or relating to (mythical) heroes, heroic: vetus opinio est, jam usque ab heroicis ducta temporibus, Cic.

heroina.full: hērōīna (hērōīnē), ae, f., = ἡρωΐνη, a demi-goddess, heroine, Prop. 1, 13, 31; 2, 2, 9; cf.: formosae heroinae, i. e. Cassandra, Andromache, Helena, etc., id. 1, 19, 13; cf. herois.
heroina.short: hērōīna (hērōīnē), ae, f., = ἡρωΐνη, a demi-goddess, heroine, Prop.

heroion.full: hērōīon, ii, n., = ἡρώειον, v. l. for heroum; v. 2. herous fin.

herois.full: hērōis, ĭdis, f., = ἡρωΐς, a demi-goddess, heroine: heroidum ac dearum personis effictis, Suet. Ner. 21: veteres heroidas aequare, Ov. Am. 2, 4, 33.—In Gr., dat. plur. heroisin, Ov. Tr. 5, 5, 43.— Hērōĭdes, the title of the Epistles of Ovid, acc. to Prisc. p. 908 P.
herois.short: hērōis, ĭdis, f., = ἡρωΐς, a demi-goddess, heroine: heroidum ac dearum personis effictis, Suet.

herophile.full: Hērŏphĭlē, ēs, f., = Ἡροφίλη, a priestess of Apollo, Tib. 2, 5, 68.
herophile.short: Hērŏphĭlē, ēs, f., = Ἡροφίλη, a priestess of Apollo, Tib.

heros.full: hēros, ōis, m., = ἥρως, a demi-god, hero. Lit.: heroum veteres casus imitari, Cic. de Or. 2, 47, 194: ille deum vitam accipiet divisque videbit Permixtos heroas, Verg. E. 4, 16: magnanimi heroes, id. A. 6, 649: incipit Aeneas heros, id. ib. 6, 103; called also: Troius heros, id. ib. 451: Laertius heros, i. e. Ulysses, Ov. Tr. 5, 5, 3: quem virum aut heroa lyra vel acri Tibia sumis celebrare, Clio? Hor. C. 1, 12, 1: Ajax heros, id. S. 2, 3, 193: intererit multum, divusne loquatur an heros, id. A.
heros.short: hēros, ōis, m., = ἥρως, a demi-god, hero.

herostratus.full: Hērostrătus, i, m., = Ἡρόστρατος, the notorious Ephesian who, in order to make himself famous, set fire to the temple of Diana at Ephesus, Sol. 40, 3.
herostratus.short: Hērostrătus, i, m., = Ἡρόστρατος, the notorious Ephesian who, in order to make himself famous, set fire to the temple of Diana at Ephesus, Sol.

herous1.full: Hērōus, a, um, adj., of Hero; v. Hero, I. B.
herous1.short: Hērōus, a, um, adj., of Hero;

herous2.full: hērōus, a, um, adj., = ἡρῳος, of or relating to a hero, heroic. Adj.: labores, Stat. S. 4, 7, 2: chelys, id. ib. 1, 3, 102; cf.: carmen, Quint. 1, 8, 5; Prop. 3, 3 (4, 2), 16: versus, heroic or epic verse, Cic. Leg. 2, 27, 68; Quint. 1, 5, 28: pes, an heroic or epic foot, Cic. de Or. 3, 47, 182.— As subst. hērōus, i, m., an epic verse: apte Jungitur herous cum breviore modo, Ov. Am. 2, 17, 22; Mart. 3, 20, 6: in herois, Quint. 10, 1, 88 Zumpt N. cr.; also: herous, qui est idem dactylus, Quint. 9
herous2.short: hērōus, a, um, adj., = ἡρῳος, of or relating to a hero, heroic.

herpes.full: herpes, ētis, m., = ἕρπης. A cutaneous eruption that creeps and spreads, Plin. 26, 14, 87, § 145; and perh. Lucil. ap. Non. 117, 22, where others read herpestica (in Cels. 5, 28, 3, written as Greek).— Herpes quoque animal a Graecis vocatur, quo praecipue sanantur quaecumque serpunt, Plin. 30, 13, 39, § 116.

herpesticus.full: herpestĭcus, a, um, adj., = ἑρπηστικός, spreading, eating: gangraena, Lucil. ap. Non. 117, 22 (al. herpes ita; v. herpes, I.).
herpesticus.short: herpestĭcus, a, um, adj., = ἑρπηστικός, spreading, eating: gangraena, Lucil.

herpyllum.full: herpyllum, i, n., = ἕρπυλλον, a climbing evergreen plant, also called sisymbrium, creeping thyme, App. Herb. 105; also called herpyllus, id. ib. 99.
herpyllum.short: herpyllum, i, n., = ἕρπυλλον, a climbing evergreen plant, also called sisymbrium, creeping thyme, App.

herse.full: Hersē, ēs, f., = Ἕρση, a daughter of Cecrops, beloved by Mercury, Ov. M. 2, 559; 724 sq.
herse.short: Hersē, ēs, f., = Ἕρση, a daughter of Cecrops, beloved by Mercury, Ov.

hersilia.full: Hersĭlĭa, ae, f., the wife of Romulus, Ov. M. 14, 830 sq.; Liv. 1, 11, 2; Macr. S. 1, 6.
hersilia.short: Hersĭlĭa, ae, f., the wife of Romulus, Ov.

heruli.full: Hĕrŭli (ĕrŭli), ōrum, m., the Herulians, the people of Northern Germany who penetrated into Italy and dissolved the western Roman Empire, Amm. 23, 1, 3; Paul. Diac. Longob. 1, 1; Claud. Mamert. Pan. ad Maxim. 5; Genethl. 7.—In sing. collect.: cursu Herulus, Sid. Carm. 7, 236.
heruli.short: Hĕrŭli (ĕrŭli), ōrum, m., the Herulians, the people of Northern Germany who penetrated into Italy and dissolved the western Roman Empire, Amm.

hesiodus.full: Hēsĭŏdus, i, m., = Ἡσίοδος, the Greek poet Hesiod, Gell. 3, 11; 17, 21, 3; Vell. 1, 7, 1; Quint. 10, 1, 52; 5, 11, 19; Cic. N. D. 1, 14, 36; id. Off. 1, 15, 98.— Derivv. Hēsĭŏdēus or -īus, a, um, adj., = Ἡσιόδειος, of or relating to Hesiod, Hesiodic: illud Hesiodium laudatur a doctis, Cic. Brut. 4, 15: carmina, Sid. Carm. 9, 213.— Hēsĭŏdĭcus, a, um, adj., the same: carmen, Serv. Verg. G. 2, 176.
hesiodus.short: Hēsĭŏdus, i, m., = Ἡσίοδος, the Greek poet Hesiod, Gell.

hesione.full: Hēsĭŏnē, ēs, and Hēsĭŏna, ae, f., = Ἡσιόνη. A daughter of Laomedon, king of Troy, whom Hercules rescued from a seamonster and gave in marriage to Telamon, to whom she bore Teucer, Ov. M. 11, 211 sq.; Verg. A. 8, 157; Hyg. Fab. 31; 89; 97.— The title of a tragedy of Nœvius, Varr. L. L. 7, § 107 Müll.; Gell. 10, 25, 3.
hesione.short: Hēsĭŏnē, ēs, and Hēsĭŏna, ae, f., = Ἡσιόνη.

hesperia.full: Hespĕria, ae, f., v. Hesperus, II. A. 2.

hesperides.full: Hespĕrĭdes, um, f., v. Hesperus, II. B. 2. b.

hesperie.full: Hespĕrĭē, ēs, f., = Ἑσπερίη, a daughter of the river Cebren, who was killed by the bite of a snake, Ov. M. 11, 769.
hesperie.short: Hespĕrĭē, ēs, f., = Ἑσπερίη, a daughter of the river Cebren, who was killed by the bite of a snake, Ov.

hesperis.full: Hespĕris, ĭdis, v. Hesperus, II. B.

hesperius.full: Hespĕrĭus, a, um, v. Hesperus, II. A.

hesperugo.full: hespĕrūgo, ĭnis, f. Hesperus, the evening star, Sen. Med. 877.

hesperus.full: Hespĕrus or -os, i, m., = Ἕσπερος (the evening; pure Lat., with the digamma, vesper; hence transf.), the evening star, Hesperus; acc. to the myth, the son of Cephalus and Aurora; cf. Hyg. Astr. 2, 42; or, acc. to another myth, the son of Iapetus and Asia, and brother of Atlas; cf. Serv. Verg. A. 1, 530, and 4, 484: infima est quinque errantium terraeque proxima stella Veneris, quae φωσφόρος Graece, Latine dicitur Lucifer, cum antegreditur solem, cum subsequitur autem Hesperos, Cic. N. D. 2, 20,
hesperus.short: Hespĕrus or -os, i, m., = Ἕσπερος (the evening;

hesternus.full: hesternus, a, um, adj. hes, whence heri, analog. with hodiernus, of yesterday, yesterday's: disputatio hesterni et hodierni diei, Cic. de Or. 3, 21, 81; cf.: hesterno die, id. N. D. 2, 29, 73: hesterno sermone, id. Rep. 3, 12 fin.: die, id. Cat. 2, 3, 6: nocte Ov. H. 19, 72: sermone, Cic. Ac. 2, 6, 18: disputatione, id. Tusc. 2, 4, 10: panis, Cels. 1, 3: reliquiae, of yesterday, Plaut. Pers. 1, 2, 25: jus, Ter. Eun. 5, 4, 17: cena, Plin. Pan. 6, 3, 3; Juv. 9, 44: minutal, id. 14, 129: fercula, H

hestiaeotis.full: Hestĭaeōtis, ĭdis, f., = Ἑστιαιῶτις, a district in Thessaly between Olympus and Ossa, Plin. 31, 2, 9, § 13.
hestiaeotis.short: Hestĭaeōtis, ĭdis, f., = Ἑστιαιῶτις, a district in Thessaly between Olympus and Ossa, Plin.

hetaeria.full: hĕtaerĭa, ae, f., = ἑταιρία, a (religious) brotherhood, fraternity, Traj. ap. Plin. Ep. 10, 43, 1; id. ib. 10, 97, 7.
hetaeria.short: hĕtaerĭa, ae, f., = ἑταιρία, a (religious) brotherhood, fraternity, Traj.

hetaerice.full: hĕtaerĭcē, ēs, f., = ἑταιρική, a body of horse-guards in the Macedonian army, Nep. Eum. 1, 6.
hetaerice.short: hĕtaerĭcē, ēs, f., = ἑταιρική, a body of horse-guards in the Macedonian army, Nep.

heteroclitus.full: hĕtĕrō^clĭtus, a, um, adj., = ἑτερόκλιτος, in gram. lang., varying in declension, heteroclite, Charis. p. 23 P.; Prisc. p. 1065 ib.
heteroclitus.short: hĕtĕrō^clĭtus, a, um, adj., = ἑτερόκλιτος, in gram.

heterocranea.full: hĕtĕrocrānĕa or -ĭa, ae, f., = ἑτεροκρανία, headache on one side of the head, also called hemicrania, Plin. 31, 9, 45, § 99; Marc. Emp. 2.
heterocranea.short: hĕtĕrocrānĕa or -ĭa, ae, f., = ἑτεροκρανία, headache on one side of the head, also called hemicrania, Plin.

hetriculum.full: Hetricŭlum, i, n., a city of the Bruttii, Liv. 30, 19, 10.
hetriculum.short: Hetricŭlum, i, n., a city of the Bruttii, Liv.

hetruria.full: Hetrūria, ae, f., and Hetruscus, a, um, v. Etruria.
hetruria.short: Hetrūria, ae, f., and Hetruscus, a, um, v.

hetta.full: hetta res minimi pretii, quasi hieta, id est hiatus hominis atque oscitatio. Alii pusulam dixerunt esse, quae in coquendo pane solet assurgere, a qua accipi rem nullius pretii, cum dicimus: Non hettae te facio, Paul. ex Fest. p. 99 Müll. N. cr. [perhaps kindred with the Gr. ἥττων, ἥσσων, less, meaner; cf. the foll. art.].
hetta.short: hetta res minimi pretii, quasi hieta, id est hiatus hominis atque oscitatio.

hettematicus.full: hettēmătĭcus, a, um, adj., = ἡττηματικός, poor of its kind, Firm. Math. 3, 9.
hettematicus.short: hettēmătĭcus, a, um, adj., = ἡττηματικός, poor of its kind, Firm.

heu!.full: heu! interj. (constr. absol. or with acc., rarely with nom. or voc.; cf. Huschke ad Tib. 2, 6, 28; Forbig. and Wagn. ad Verg. A. 2, 274. The passages cited for heu mihi, etc., Hand, Turs. III. 68 sq., are mostly corrected in recent edd.) An exclamation of grief or pain, oh! ah! alas! heu heu, quam ego malis perdidi modis, quod tibi detuli et quod dedi! Plaut. Ps. 1, 3, 26: quatenus, heu nefas! Virtutem incolumem odimus, Hor. C. 3, 24, 30; cf.: palam captis gravis, heu nefas heu, id. ib. 4, 6, 17

heureta.full: heurĕta, ae, m., = εὑρετής, an inventor, inventive person, Plaut. Ps. 2, 4, 9.
heureta.short: heurĕta, ae, m., = εὑρετής, an inventor, inventive person, Plaut.

heus!.full: heus! interj. Used in calling attention, ho! ho there! hark! holloa! heus, reclude: heus, Tranio, etiamne aperis? ... heus vos, pueri, quid istic agitis? Plaut. Most. 4, 2, 28 sq.; cf.: Syre, Syre inquam, heus, heus Syre, Ter. Heaut. 2, 3, 107; so, heus, heus, id. Eun. 2, 3, 45; 3, 3, 24; id. Ad. 4, 4, 17: heus, Phaedrome, exi, exi, exi, inquam ocius, Plaut. Curc. 2, 2, 26; cf.: heus, Staphyla, prodi, id. Aul. 2, 6, 1: heus, Strobile, sequere propere me, id. ib. 2, 2, 86: heus, ecquis hic est? h

hexachordos.full: hexăchordos, on, adj., = ἑξάχορδος, having six musical strings or stops: machina, a water - organ with six stops, Vitr. 10, 13.
hexachordos.short: hexăchordos, on, adj., = ἑξάχορδος, having six musical strings or stops: machina, a water - organ with six stops, Vitr.

hexaclinon.full: hexaclīnon, i, n., = ἑξάκλινον, a couch to hold six persons, Mart. 9, 60, 9.
hexaclinon.short: hexaclīnon, i, n., = ἑξάκλινον, a couch to hold six persons, Mart.

hexaemeron.full: Hexăēmĕron, i, n., = Ἑξαήμερον (of or in six days), the six days of the creation, Ambros. Ep. 6, 42; also the title of a work on the creation of the world, by Ambrosius; cf. Ambros. Ep. 6, 42.
hexaemeron.short: Hexăēmĕron, i, n., = Ἑξαήμερον (of or in six days), the six days of the creation, Ambros.

hexagonum.full: hexăgōnum, i, n., = ἑξάγωνον, a six-sided figure, hexagon, Col. 5, 2, 10 (in Varr. R. R. 3, 16, 5 written as Greek); also called hexăgōnium, Ambros. Hexaēm. 5, 21, 69.
hexagonum.short: hexăgōnum, i, n., = ἑξάγωνον, a six-sided figure, hexagon, Col.

hexameter.full: hexămĕter (hexămetrus, Ter. Maur. p. 2430 P.), tri, m., = ἑξάμετρος (of six measures), with or without versus, a verse consisting of six feet, a hexameter: versus, Lucil. ap. Porphyr. Hor. S. 1, 5, 87; so, metrum, Isid. 1, 38, 6: Antipater ille Sidonius solitus est versus hexametros aliosque variis modis atque numeris fundere ex tempore, Cic. de Or. 3, 50, 194: hexametrorum instar versuum, id. Or. 66, 222: liber scriptus ab eo hexametris versibus, Suet. Aug. 85: in longis versibus qui hexametri

hexaphoros.full: hexăphŏros, on, adj., = ἑξαφόρος, one of six who carry a load together: phalangarii, Vitr. 10, 8 med.— Borne by six together; subst.: hexăphŏrum, i, n., = ἑξάφορον, a litter borne by six men, Mart. 2, 81, 1: non debes ferri mortuus hexaphoro, id. 6, 77, 10.
hexaphoros.short: hexăphŏros, on, adj., = ἑξαφόρος, one of six who carry a load together: phalangarii, Vitr.

hexaptota.full: hexaptōta, ōrum, n. (sc. nomina), = ἑξάπτωτα, in gram., nouns that have six cases, Prisc. p. 673 P.; Isid. 1, 6, 43.

hexapylon.full: Hexăpўlon, i, n., = Ἑξάπυλον, a gate in Syracuse with six entrances, Liv. 24, 21; 32; 39.
hexapylon.short: Hexăpўlon, i, n., = Ἑξάπυλον, a gate in Syracuse with six entrances, Liv.

hexas.full: hexas, ădis, f., = ἑξάς, the number six, Mart. Cap. 2, § 108 al.
hexas.short: hexas, ădis, f., = ἑξάς, the number six, Mart.

hexastichus.full: hexastĭchus, a, um, adj., = ἑξάστιχος, of six lines or rows: hordeum, perh. our long-eared barley, Hordeum caeleste, Linn.; Col. 2, 9, 4: myrtus, Plin. 15, 29, 37, § 122.
hexastichus.short: hexastĭchus, a, um, adj., = ἑξάστιχος, of six lines or rows: hordeum, perh.

hexastylos.full: hexastўlos, on, adj., = ἑξάστυλος, having six columns, Vitr. 3, 2, 7.
hexastylos.short: hexastўlos, on, adj., = ἑξάστυλος, having six columns, Vitr.

hexecontalithos.full: hexēcontălĭthos, i, m., = ἑξηκοντάλιθος (sixty-colored stone), a precious stone, otherwise unknown, Plin. 37, 10, 60, § 167; Solin. 31.
hexecontalithos.short: hexēcontălĭthos, i, m., = ἑξηκοντάλιθος (sixty-colored stone), a precious stone, otherwise unknown, Plin.

hexeris.full: hexēris, is, f., = ἑξήρης (ναῦς), a vessel with six banks of oars, Liv. 37, 23, 5; 29, 9, 8.—Abl. hexere, Val. Max. 1, 8, ext. 11.
hexeris.short: hexēris, is, f., = ἑξήρης (ναῦς), a vessel with six banks of oars, Liv.

hiantia.full: hĭantĭa, ae, f. hio, an opening: oris, Tert. Anim. 10.

hiasco.full: hĭasco, ĕre, v. inch. n. [id.], to open, break open (ante- and post-class.): ubi primum nuces pineae incipiunt hiascere, Cato, R. R. 17, 2; Gargil. de Re Hort. 2, 1.

hiatus.full: hĭātus, ūs, m. id., an opening, aperture, cleft (class. in sing. and plur.; cf. rima, rictus). Lit.: animalia cibum partim oris hiatu et dentibus ipsis capessunt, partim unguium tenacitate arripiunt, Cic. N. D. 2, 47, 122: oris, Suet. Claud. 27; Verg. A. 11, 680.—Without oris: ne immodicus hiatus rictum distendat, Quint. 1, 11, 9: extremus exspirantis, id. 6, 2, 31: Nemeaeus magnus hiatus Ille leonis, Lucr. 5, 24; cf.: quinquaginta atris immanis hiatibus Hydra, i. e. open mouths, Verg. A. 6, 576

hiberes.full: Hĭbēres (less correctly, Ibēres), um, m., = Ἴβηρες. Iberians, the Greek name for Spaniards, Cat. 9, 6.—In sing. collect.: me peritus Discet Hiber Rhodanique potor, Hor. C. 2, 20, 20: durus Iber, Luc. 6, 258.—Hence, Hĭbērus (Ib-), a, um, adj., of or belonging to the Iberians or Spaniards, Iberian, Spanish: gurges, i. e. the Western Ocean, Verg. A. 11, 913; Ov. M. 7, 324: minium, Prop. 2, 3, 11: piscis, i. e. scomber, Hor. S. 2, 8, 46: pastor, i. e. Geryon, Ov. M. 9, 184; cf. vaccae, i. e. Geryon'
hiberes.short: Hĭbēres (less correctly, Ibēres), um, m., = Ἴβηρες.

hiberna.full: hīberna, ōrum, n., v. hibernus, II. B.

hibernaculum.full: hībernācŭlum, i, n. hiberno, a winter residence, winter apartment. In gen., Vitr. 1, 2, 4; 7, 4, 4; Plin. Ep. 2, 17, 7.— In partic., in milit. lang., hī-bernācŭla, ōrum, n., tents for winterquarters, an encampment for winter, winter tents (opp. hiberna, winter-quarters in gen.): hibernacula Carthaginiensium lignea ferme tota erant, Liv. 30, 3, 8: hibernacula etiam, res nova militi Romano, aedificari coepta, id. 5, 2, 1 Weissenb. ad loc.; 22, 32, 1; Tac. A. 2, 23; 14, 38; Nep. Eum. 8, 4.

hibernalis.full: hībernālis, e, adj. hibernus, wintry, winter-: glacies, Vulg. Sap. 16, 29.

hibernia.full: Hĭbernĭa, ae, f. (= Ἰουερνία Ptol.), the island now called Ireland, Caes. B. G. 5, 13, 2; Plin. 4, 16, 30, § 103; Tac. Agr. 24.— Also called Iverna, ae, Mel. 3, 6, 6: Ju-verna, ae, Juv. 2, 160; and (acc. to the Gr. form Ἰέρνη Strab.) Ierna, ae, App. de Mundo, p. 60; and Iernē, ēs, Claud. Laud. Stil. 2, 251; IV. Cons. Hon. 33.

hiberno.full: hīberno, āvi, ātum, 1, v. n. hibernus, to pass the winter, to winter. In gen.: furcillas reducit hibernatum in tecta, Varr. R. R. 1, 8, 6: (thynni) ubicumque deprehensi usque ad aequinoctium, ibi hibernant, Plin. 9, 15, 20, § 51: exercitum in agrum Vescinum hibernatum duxit, Liv. 10, 46, 9: novas (naves) Panormi subducit, ut in sicco hibernarent, id. 29, 1, 14.— In partic., in milit. lang., to keep in winter-quarters: jam vero quemadmodum milites hibernent, quotidie sermones ac litterae perferun

hibernus.full: hībernus, a, um, adj. root Sanscr. himas, Gr. χιών, snow, v. hiems; for hiemernus (hīm-), cf. χειμερινός, of or belonging to winter, wintry, winter-. Adj.: hiberno tempore, Lucr. 5, 699: tempus, id. 5, 940; cf.: in aprico maxime pratuli loco, quod erat hibernum tempus anni, considerent, Cic. Rep. 1, 12: temporibus hibernis, Cic. Verr. 2, 5, 10, § 26: menses, id. ib.: annus, i. e. winter-time, Hor. Epod. 2, 29: exortus solis, Plin. 6, 17, 21. § 57: occasus, id. 5, 5, 5, § 34: navigatio, Cic. Att.

hibiscum.full: hĭbiscum (also ĕbiscum, Scrib. 80; 82; and hĭbiscus, i, f., Serv. Verg. E. 2, 30), i, n., = ὶβίσκος, the marsh-mallow, Althaea officinalis, Linn.; Plin. 20, 4, 14, § 29; 19, 5, 27, § 89; Verg. E. 10, 71: haedorumque gregem viridi compellere hibisco, i. e. with a marsh-mallow twig, id. ib. 2, 30.

hibrida.full: hibrĭda or hybrĭda (ibr-), ae, comm. most prob. kindred with ὑβρίζω, ὕβρις, qs. unbridled, lawless, unnatural; hence, of animals produced from two different species, a mongrel, hybrid. Lit.: in nullo genere aeque facilis mixtura cum fero (quam in suibus), qualiter natos antiqui hybridas vocabant ceu semiferos, Plin. 8, 53, 79, § 213.— Transf., of persons, one born of a Roman father and a foreign mother, or of a freeman and a slave: ibique postea ex hybridis, libertinis servisque conscripserat, A

hic.full: hīc, haec, hōc (gen. hujus, monosyl., Plaut. Am. prol. 51; 96; 1, 1, 115; dat. huïc, Sidon. Carm. 7, 145; Avien. Descr. Orb. 22; dat. sing. fem. hae rei, Cato, R. R. 14, 3; acc. HONC for hunc, C. I. L. 1, 32; nom. plur. hic, Enn. ap. Philarg. ad Verg. G. 4, 230 = Ann. v. 414 Vahl.; Varr. L. L. 6, § 73 Müll.; fem. haec, v. infra, B. init.; dat. and abl. hibus, Plaut. Curc. 4, 2, 20; cf. Varr. L. L. 8, § 78 Müll.; v. Neue, Formenl. 2, p. 203 sqq.), pron. demonstr. [from the pronom. root i (whence

hice.full: hice, haece, hoce, v. hic, I. B.

hicetaon.full: Hĭcĕtāon, ŏnis, m., = Ἱκετάων, son of Laomedon king of Troy, App. de Deo Socr. p. 152, 9.—Hence, Hĭcĕtāŏnĭus, a um, of Hicetāon: Thymoetes, i. e. his son, Verg. A. 10, 123.
hicetaon.short: Hĭcĕtāon, ŏnis, m., = Ἱκετάων, son of Laomedon king of Troy, App.

hicetas.full: Hĭcĕtas, ae, m., = Ἱκέτας. A tyrant of Leontini, Nep. Tim. 2, 3.— A philosopher of Syracuse, Cic. Ac. 2, 39, 123 dub. (al. Nicetas).

hicine1.full: hicine, haecine, hocine, v. hic, I. B.

hicine2.full: hicine, adv., v. hic, III. 2 init.

hicne.full: hicne, haecne, etc., v. hic, B. fin.

hiemalis.full: hĭĕmālis, e, adj. hiems, of or belonging to winter, wintry, winter-. Adj. (class.): arbores ut hiemali tempore tempestive caedi putentur, Cic. Div. 2, 14, 33: dies, Col. 11, 1, 21: circulus, i. e. the tropic of Capricorn, Hyg. Astr. 3, 26: hiemalem vim perferre, Cic. Tusc. 5, 27, 77: circum murum planities limosa hiemalibus aquis paludem fecerat, by the rains of winter, Sall. J. 37, 4: nimbi, Ov. M. 9, 105 (for which: hibernae aquae Albulae, id. F. 2, 390): faba, winter bean, Plin. 18, 23, 52, §

hiematio.full: hĭĕmātĭo, ōnis, f. hiemo, a passing the winter, wintering: reliquum (mellis) hiemationi relinquatur, Varr. R. R. 3, 16, 34.

hiemo.full: hĭĕmo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. n. and a. [hiems]. Neutr. Of persons, to pass the winter, to winter; of soldiers, to keep in winter-quarters: ubi piratae quotannis hiemare soleant, Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 47, § 104: naviget ac mediis hiemet mercator in undis, Hor. Ep. 1, 16, 71: assidue in Urbe, Suet. Aug. 72: tres (legiones), quae circum Aquileiam hiemabant, ex hibernis educit, Caes. B. G. 1, 10, 3: legionem hiemandi causa collocaret, id. ib. 3, 1: cupio scire quid agas et ubi sis hiematurus, Cic. Fam. 7, 9,

hiempsal.full: Hĭempsal, ălis, m. Son of Micipsa and king of Numidia, Sall. J. 5, 7; 11, 3; Flor. 3, 8, 4; Suet. Caes. 71.— Another king of Numidia, perh. son of the former, Sall. J. 17.— A king of Mauritania, Cic. Vatin. 5, 12 al.

hiems.full: hĭems or hiemps, ĕmis, f. Gr. χιών, χεῖμα; Sanscr. himas, snow, the winter, winter time, rainy season (cf.: bruma, solstitium). Lit.: aestatem autumnus sequitur, post acer hiemps fit, Enn. ap. Prisc. p. 647 P. (Ann. v. 406 Vahl.): solvitur acris hiems grata vice veris et Favoni, Hor. C. 1, 4, 1: crudelis, Enn. ap. Prisc. p. 891 P. (Ann. v. 482 Vahl.); opp. to aestas, Dig. 43, 20, 1, §§ 31 and 32: dies primus est veris in Aquario, aestatis in Tauro, autumni in Leone, hiemis in Scorpione, Varr. R.

hiera1.full: hĭĕra, ae, f. (sc. antidotus), = ἱερά (sacred; Lat. sacra), a sort of antidote against poison, Scrib. Comp. 99; 156.— Perh. = corona, a garland: hieran fecimus, Sen. Ep. 83, 4.

hiera2.full: Hĭĕra, ae, f. The name of several islands, Mel. 2, 7, 18; Plin. 2, 106, 110, § 238; 4, 12, 23, § 70 al.— Hĭĕra Cōme, a place in Caria, Liv. 38, 12, 10; cf. 38, 15, 7; 37, 19, 7.

hierabotane.full: hĭĕrābŏtănē (also separately hie-ra botane), ēs, f., = ἱερὰ βοτάνη (sacred plant), a plant, also called verbenaca, vervain, Verbena officinalis, Linn.; Plin. 25, 9, 59, § 105; Scrib. Comp. 163.
hierabotane.short: hĭĕrābŏtănē (also separately hie-ra botane), ēs, f., = ἱερὰ βοτάνη (sacred plant), a plant, also called verbenaca, vervain, Verbena officinalis, Linn.;

hieracia.full: hĭĕrācĭa, ae, f., = ἱερακία, hawkweed, Plin. 20, 7, 26, § 60.
hieracia.short: hĭĕrācĭa, ae, f., = ἱερακία, hawkweed, Plin.

hieracitis.full: hĭĕrācītis, ĭdis, f., = ἱερακῖτις (hawk-stone), a precious stone, otherwise unknown, Plin. 37, 10, 60, § 167; 37, 11, 72, § 187.
hieracitis.short: hĭĕrācītis, ĭdis, f., = ἱερακῖτις (hawk-stone), a precious stone, otherwise unknown, Plin.

hieracium.full: hĭĕrācĭum, ĭi, n., = ἱεράκιον, a sort of eye-salve, Plin. 34, 11, 27, § 114.
hieracium.short: hĭĕrācĭum, ĭi, n., = ἱεράκιον, a sort of eye-salve, Plin.

hierapolis.full: Hĭĕrāpŏlis, is, f., = Ἱεράπολις. A city of Great Phrygia, now Pambouk Kaleh, Vitr. 8, 3, 10; Plin. 2, 93, 95, § 208; Vulg. Col. 4, 13.—Hence, Hĭĕrāpŏ-lītae, ārum, m., the inhabitants of Hierapolis, Plin. 5, 29, 29, § 105.— Hĭĕrā-pŏlītāni, ōrum, m., the same, Macr. S. 1, 7; Dig. 43, 20, 1.

hieraticus.full: hĭĕrātĭcus, a, um, adj., = ἱερατικός, belonging to sacred uses, hieratic: charta hieratica appellatur antiquitus religiosis tantum voluminibus dicata, quae ablutione Augusti nomen accepit, sicut secunda Liviae, a conjuge ejus. Ita descendit hieratica in tertium nomen, Plin. 13, 12, 23, § 74.
hieraticus.short: hĭĕrātĭcus, a, um, adj., = ἱερατικός, belonging to sacred uses, hieratic: charta hieratica appellatur antiquitus religiosis tantum voluminibus dicata, quae ablutione Augusti nomen accepit, sicut secunda Liviae, a conjuge ejus.

hieremias.full: Hĭĕrĕmīas, ae, m., the prophet Jeremiah, Prud. Ham. 450.
hieremias.short: Hĭĕrĕmīas, ae, m., the prophet Jeremiah, Prud.

hiericus.full: Hĭĕrĭcūs, untis, f., = Ἱερικοῦς, the city of Jericho, in Palestine, Plin. 5, 14, 15, § 70; 13, 4, 9, § 44.—Also called Jĕrĭcho, = Ἱεριχώ, Prud. Psych. 536; acc. Jerichon, Prud. Ham. 480 Dressel.
hiericus.short: Hĭĕrĭcūs, untis, f., = Ἱερικοῦς, the city of Jericho, in Palestine, Plin.

hiero.full: Hĭĕro, ōnis, m., = Ἱέρων. Ruler of Syracuse, a friend of the poet Simonides, Cic. N. D. 1, 22, 60; 3, 34, 83.— A son of Hierocles, and ruler of Syracuse in the latter half of the third century B.C., a friend of the Romans, Plaut. Men. 2, 3, 59; Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 12, § 49; Liv. 21, 49; 22, 37; 24, 4; 26, 40; Just. 23, 4, 1; Sil. 14, 80.—Deriv. Hĭĕrōnĭcus, a, um, adj., of or pertaining to Hiero: lex frumontaria, Cic. Verr. 2, 2, 13, § 32 sq.; 2, 2, 60, § 147; 2, 3, 6, § 14 sq.

hierocaesaria.full: Hĭĕrŏcaesărīa or -ēa, ae, f., = Ἱεροκαισάρεια, a city of Lydia, Tac. A. 2, 47. —Hence, Hĭĕrŏcaesărĭenses, ium, m., its inhabitants, Tac. A. 3, 62.
hierocaesaria.short: Hĭĕrŏcaesărīa or -ēa, ae, f., = Ἱεροκαισάρεια, a city of Lydia, Tac.

hierocles.full: Hĭĕrō^cles, is, m., = Ἱεροκλῆς, a celebrated orator of Alabanda, an older contemporary of Cicero, Cic. Brut. 95, 325; id. de Or. 2, 23, 95; id. Or. 69, 231.
hierocles.short: Hĭĕrō^cles, is, m., = Ἱεροκλῆς, a celebrated orator of Alabanda, an older contemporary of Cicero, Cic.

hierodulus.full: hĭĕrŏdūlus, i, m., = ἱερόδουλος, a temple servant, Firm. Math. 8, 21.
hierodulus.short: hĭĕrŏdūlus, i, m., = ἱερόδουλος, a temple servant, Firm.

hieroglyphicus.full: hĭĕroglўphĭcus, a, um, adj., = ἱερογλυφικός, hieroglyphic: litterae, Macr. S. 1, 21, 12: notae, Amm. 17, 4, 8.
hieroglyphicus.short: hĭĕroglўphĭcus, a, um, adj., = ἱερογλυφικός, hieroglyphic: litterae, Macr.

hierographicus.full: hĭĕrŏgrăphĭcus, a, um, adj., = ἱερογραφικός, i. q. hieroglyphicus, hierographic: litterae, Amm. 22, 15, 30 dub. (al. hieroglyphicas).
hierographicus.short: hĭĕrŏgrăphĭcus, a, um, adj., = ἱερογραφικός, i.

hieromnemon.full: hĭĕrŏmnēmon, ŏnis, m., = ἱερομνήμων, a precious stone, also called erotylos, Plin. 37, 10, 58, § 160.
hieromnemon.short: hĭĕrŏmnēmon, ŏnis, m., = ἱερομνήμων, a precious stone, also called erotylos, Plin.

hieronica.full: hĭĕrŏnīca, ae, m., = ἱερονίκης, a conqueror in the sacred games: Neapolin albis equis introiit, disjecta parte muri, ut mos hieronicarum est, Suet. Ner. 25; Inscr. Orell. 2160; 2628 sq. al.
hieronica.short: hĭĕrŏnīca, ae, m., = ἱερονίκης, a conqueror in the sacred games: Neapolin albis equis introiit, disjecta parte muri, ut mos hieronicarum est, Suet.

hieronicus.full: Hĭĕrōnĭcus, a, um, v. Hiero, II. fin.

hieronymus.full: Hĭĕrōnўmus, i, m., = Ἱερώνυμος. a ruler of Syracuse, the grandson and successor of the younger Hiero, Liv. 24, 4 sq. — A Greek peripatetic philosopher of Rhodes, Cic. Fin. 2, 3, 8; 5, 5, 14; id. Tusc. 2, 6, 15; 5, 30, 84; 5, 31, 87 sq.; 5, 41, 118.— Jerome, a celebrated father of the Church in the fifth century of the Christian era, Sulp. Sev. Dial. 1, 8.

hierophanta.full: hĭĕrŏphanta or -tēs, ae, m., = ἱεροφάντης, a teacher of religious rites and ceremonies, a high-priest, hierophant, Arn. 5, 174; Hier. adv. Jovin. 1, 49 fin.: agrorum, in the country, Cod. Th. 16, 4, 10; Inscr. Orell. 2305; 2351 sq. (in Nep. Pelop. 3, 2, the word is spurious).
hierophanta.short: hĭĕrŏphanta or -tēs, ae, m., = ἱεροφάντης, a teacher of religious rites and ceremonies, a high-priest, hierophant, Arn.

hierophantria.full: hĭĕrŏphantrĭa, ae, f., = ἱεροφάντρια, a priestess, Inscr. Orell. 2361.
hierophantria.short: hĭĕrŏphantrĭa, ae, f., = ἱεροφάντρια, a priestess, Inscr.

hierophylax.full: hĭĕrŏphўlax, ăcis, m., = ἱεροφύλαξ, the keeper of a temple (pure Lat. aedituus), Dig. 33, 1, 20, § 1.
hierophylax.short: hĭĕrŏphўlax, ăcis, m., = ἱεροφύλαξ, the keeper of a temple (pure Lat.

hierosolyma.full: Hĭĕrŏsŏlўma, ōrum, n. (secondary forms; v. infra), = Ἱεροσόλυμα, the city of Jerusalem, in Palestine, Plin. 5, 14, 15, § 70; Cic. Fl. 28, 67 sq.; Tac. H. 2, 4; 5, 1; 8; 9; Suet. Ner. 40; id. Tit. 5; Flor. 3, 5, 30.— Also, fem. acc.: Hĭĕrŏsŏlўmam, Flor. 3, 5, 30; cf. Vulg. Matt. 16, 21; Marc. 10, 32 sq.; Lact. Epit. 46, 7.—In neutr.: Hiĕrū^-sălem, Prud. Psych. 811; Lact. de Pass. Chr. 25; and in many other eccl. fathers. —Also abbrev.: Sŏlўma, ōrum, n., Mart. 11, 65, 5, acc. to Tac.; so called fr

hieto.full: hĭĕto, āre, v. freq. n. and a. [for hiato, from hio; cf. Diom. p. 336 P.], to open the mouth wide, to gape, yawn (ante-class.): ego dum hieto, Plaut. Men. 3, 1, 4; cf. id. Fragm. ap. Diom. p. 336 P.: praei hercle tu, qui mihi oscitans hietansque restas, Caecil. ib.; Cn. Mat. ib.—*Transf., in gen., to open wide, throw open: hietantur fores, Laber. ap. Diom. p. 336 P. (Com. Rel. v. 89 Rib.).

hilaira.full: Hilaīra, ae, f., = Ἱλάειρα, daughter of Leucippus and bride of Ida, Prop. 1, 2, 16.
hilaira.short: Hilaīra, ae, f., = Ἱλάειρα, daughter of Leucippus and bride of Ida, Prop.

hilaresco.full: hĭlăresco, ĕre, v. inch. n. [hilaris], to grow cheerful or merry: cum amicorum domus fumat, hilaresco, Varr. ap. Non. 121, 12.

hilaria1.full: hĭlărĭa, ae, f. hilaris, gayety, merriment: ebriulati mentem hilaria arripuit, Laber. ap. Non. 108, 4 (Com. Rel. v. 52 Rib.).

hilaria2.full: hĭlărĭa, ōrum, n., v. hilaris, II.

hilaris.full: hĭlăris, e, and hĭlărus, a, um, adj., = ἱλαρός [cf. Sanscr. hlād, rejoice; Gr. χλαρός; Engl. glad], cheerful, of good cheer, lively, gay, blithe, merry, jocund, jovial.—Adj. (class.; syn. laetus). Form hilaris: oderunt hilarem tristes tristemque jocosi, Hor. Ep. 1, 18, 89; cf.: hoc (vultu) tristes, hoc hilares sumus, Quint. 11, 3, 72: si tristia dicamus hilares, id. ib. 67: esse vultu hilari atque laeto, Cic. Tusc. 1, 42, 100: hilari animo esse, id. Q. Fr. 2, 13, 1; cf.: aliquem hilari ingenio e
hilaris.short: hĭlăris, e, and hĭlărus, a, um, adj., = ἱλαρός [cf.

hilaritas.full: hĭlărĭtas, ātis, f. hilaris, cheerfulness, gayety, good-humor, joyousness, merriment, hilarity (class.): hilaritatem illam, qua hanc tristitiam temporum condiebamus, in perpetuum amisi, Cic. Att. 12, 40, 3; cf.: tristitia deductis, hilaritas remissis (superciliis) ostenditur, Quint. 11, 3, 79: hilaritate et lascivia, Cic. Fin. 2, 20, 65: itaque hilaritatis plenum judicium ac laetitiae fuit, id. de Or. 1, 57, 243: hilaritas illa nostra et suavitas, id. Fam. 9, 11, 1: erat in M. Druso adulescente

hilaritudo.full: hĭlărĭtūdo, ĭnis, f. hilaris, cheerfulness, merriment (ante-class. for the class. hilaritas): numquam ego te tristiorem Vidi esse: quid cedo tam abhorret hilaritudo? Plaut. Cist. 1, 1, 56: onera te hilaritudine, id. Mil. 3, 1, 83: ut in ocellis hilaritudo est! id. Rud. 2, 4, 8.

hilaro.full: hĭlăro, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. hilaris, to make cheerful, to cheer, gladden, exhilarate (rare but class.): omnes jucundum motum, quo sensus hilaretur, Graece ἡδονήν, Latine voluptatem vocant, Cic. Fin. 2, 3, 8: Periclis suavitate maxime hilaratae sunt Athenae, id. Brut. 11, 44; Ov. Pont. 4, 4, 37: picas mirum in modum hilarari, si interim audierint id verbum, rejoice, Plin. 10, 42, 59, § 118: ut cum caelo hilarata videatur (terra), Cic. N. D. 2, 40, 102: hilaratus vultus, Plin. 36, 5, 4, § 13: Fest

hilarodos.full: hilarodos lascivi et delicati carminis cantator, Paul. ex Fest. p. 101, 10 Müll.
hilarodos.short: hilarodos lascivi et delicati carminis cantator, Paul.

hilarulus.full: hĭlărŭlus, a, um, adj. dim. [hilaris], cheerful, contented: Atticae, quoniam, quod optimum in pueris est, hilarula est, meis verbis suavium des, Cic. Att. 16, 11 fin.

hilarus1.full: hĭlărus, a, um, adj., v. hilaris.

hilarus2.full: Hĭlărus, i, m., name of a Roman freedman, Cic. Att. 1, 12, 2 et saep.
hilarus2.short: Hĭlărus, i, m., name of a Roman freedman, Cic.

hillae.full: hillae, ārum, f. dim. hira, the smaller and anterior intestines of animals (other than men and sheep). Lit.: ab hoc ventriculo lactes in homine et ove, per quas labitur cibus, in ceteris hillae, a quibus capaciora intestina ad alvum, Plin. 11, 37, 79, § 200.— Transf. In gen., intestines, entrails: hillas intestina veteres esse dixerunt, Non. 122, 7; Laber. ap. Non. 122, 10.—In mal. part., Laber. ap. Non. 12. —* A kind of sausage, smoked sausage, Hor. S. 2, 4, 60.

hilotae.full: Hīlōtae, ārum, m., = Εἵλωτες, the original inhabitants of the city Helos (Ἕλος), in Laconia, afterwards the bondsmen of the Spartans, the Helots, Nep. Paus. 3, 6.— Called also Ilotae, ārum, Liv. 34, 27, 9.
hilotae.short: Hīlōtae, ārum, m., = Εἵλωτες, the original inhabitants of the city Helos (Ἕλος), in Laconia, afterwards the bondsmen of the Spartans, the Helots, Nep.

hilum.full: hīlum, i, n. the primitive of nihilum, i. e. ne-hilum and nihil; etym. unknown; acc to Festus: hilum putant esse, quod grano fabae adhaeret, ex quo nihil et nihilum, Paul. ex Fest. p. 101 Müll.; cf.: hilum breve quoddam, Non. 121, 3; acc. to Varr. L. L. 5, § 111 Müll., perh. kindr. with hillae, a little thing, a trifle; usually with a negative, not in the least, not a whit, nothing at all (ante-class.): (Ennius) Quae dedit ipsa capit, neque dispendi facit hilum; quod valet: nec dispendi facit qu

himantopus.full: hĭmantŏpūs, pŏdis, m., = ἱμαντόπους, ποδος, Lat. loripes, thongfoot, a kind of long-legged water-fowl, Plin. 10, 47, 64, § 130.— Plur.: Hĭmantŏpŏdes, um, m., a people of Æthiopia, Plin. 5, 8, 8, § 46; Mel. 3, 10, 3; Sol. 31, 6; Jul. Val. Res. Gest. Alex. 3, 19.
himantopus.short: hĭmantŏpūs, pŏdis, m., = ἱμαντόπους, ποδος, Lat.

himella.full: Hĭmella, ae, m., a small river in the Sabine territory, now Aia, Verg. A. 7, 714.
himella.short: Hĭmella, ae, m., a small river in the Sabine territory, now Aia, Verg.

himera.full: Hīmĕra, ae, = Ἱμέρα. M. and f., a river of Sicily, which divides into two branches, of which the northern one is now called Fiume Grande, and the southern Fiume Salso, Mel. 2, 7, 17; Plin. 3, 8, 14, § 90; Liv. 24, 6; Sil. 14, 233.— F., the city of Himera, situated on the northern branch of the river of the same name, between Lilybœum and Pelorus, Mel. 2, 7, 16; Cic. Verr. 2, 2, 35, § 86; 2, 4, 33, § 73.—Also Hīmĕra, ōrum, n., Ov. F. 4, 475.— Deriv.: Hīmĕraeus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to the

hinc.full: hinc, adv. for hince, locative form from hic, from this place. hence. In space: Imus huc: illuc hinc: cum illuc ventum est, ire illinc lubet, Enn. ap. Gell. 19, 10, 12 (Trag. v. 258 Vahl.): abiit hinc in exercitum, Plaut. Am. prol. 125: In ea via, quae est hinc in Indiam, Cic. Fin. 3, 14, 45: qui hinc Roma veneramus, id. Agr. 2, 34, 94; cf.: hinc a nobis profecti, id. Tusc. 1, 13, 29: Ex Sicilia testes erant ii, qui, etc. ... et hinc homines maxime illustres, etc., Cic. Verr. 2, 1, 6, § 17: hinc

hinnibilis.full: hinnībĭlis, e, adj. hinnio, that neighs, neighing (post-class.): quod hinnibile est, equus est, App. Dogm. Plat. 3, p. 30: exscreatus, Cael. Aur. Tard. 5, 10, 119.

hinnibundus.full: hinnĭbundus, a, um, adj. id., constantly neighing: equi, Quadrig. ap. Non. 122, 14 (Lachm. ad Lucr. 2, p. 236 ex conj.; MSS. hinnibunde).

hinnio.full: hinnĭo, īre (perf. hinnisset, Val. Max. 7, 3, ext. 2), v. n., to neigh, whinny: ut si finias equum, genus est animal, species mortale, differentia irrationale (nam et homo mortale erat), proprium hinniens, Quint. 7, 3, 3; Lucr. 5, 1077; Quint. 1, 5 fin.: hinnientium dulcedines, i. e. of horses, Laev. ap. App. Mag. p. 294.—Poet., of the centaur Chiron, Sid. Carm. 14, 29.—Hence, * hinnĭenter, adv., with neighing: hinnibunde pro hinnienter, Non. 122, 13.

hinnitat.full: hinnītat χρεμετιζει, Gloss. Philox. [freq. v. hinnio].

hinnitus.full: hinnītus, ūs, m. hinnio, a neighing: subito exaudivit hinnitum, Cic. Div. 1, 33, 73; Lucr. 5, 1073; Verg. G. 3, 94; Hor. C. 2, 16, 34.—In plur., Ov. M. 2, 154; 669; Suet. Ner. 46.

hinnulea.full: hinnŭlĕa (-ŭla), ae, f. hinnuleus, a young hind, Arn. 5, 185.

hinnuleus.full: hinnŭlĕus, i, m. hinnus, a young stag or roebuck, Prop. 3, 13, 35; Hor. C. 1, 23, 1; Plin. 28, 9, 42, § 150.—As adj.: cervus, Scrib. 13.— A young mule, Varr. L. L. 9, § 28 Müll.

hinnulus.full: hinnŭlus, i, m. dim. id., a young mule: tu tuum sodalem Hinnulo videas strigosiorem, Maecen. ap. Suet. Vit. Hor. (al. hinno me v. str-); cf. Plin. 8, 44, 69, § 172 Sill. N. cr.; and: hinnulus ὁ ἐξ ἵππου καὶ ὄνου, Gloss. Philox.; Vulg. Prov. 5, 19; Cantic. 2, 17; Isid. 12, 1, 22.

hinnus.full: hinnus, i, m., = ἵννος, a mule (from a stallion and a she-ass; opp. mulus, from a he-ass and a mare): ex equa et asino fit mulus: contra ex equo et asina hinnus ... Hinnus est ex equo et asina, minor quam mulus corpore, etc., Varr. R. R. 2, 8, 1; 6; cf.: hinnos et hinnas sub quo sensu accipere debeamus Varro designat: ait enim ex equis et hinnulis (leg. asinabus) qui nascantur, hinnos vocari, Non. 122, 4 sq.; Col. 6, 37, 5.— Transf., in the form ginnus, i, m., = γίννος, a little stunted mule: no
hinnus.short: hinnus, i, m., = ἵννος, a mule (from a stallion and a she-ass;

hio.full: hĭo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. n. and a. [weakened from ΧΑΩ, χαίνω, χάσκω; cf. Germ. gähnen]. Neutr., to open, stand or be open, to gape. Lit. In gen. (mostly poet. and in post-Aug. prose): hiavit humus multa, Sall. Fragm. ap. Non. 318, 29; cf.: (calor) venas astringit hiantes, Verg. G. 1, 91: vasti specus hiant defractis membris (colossi Rhodii), Plin. 34, 7, 18, § 41; Hor. Epod. 8, 5: nec flos ullus hiat pratis, Prop. 4 (5), 2, 45. cf.: hiantia lilia, Ov. A. A. 2, 115: quercum patulis rimis hiantem, Ge

hippacare.full: hippacāre est celeriter animam ducere ab equi halitu, qui est supra modum acutus, Paul. ex Fest. p. 101 Müll.; cf.: † hippicare = oscitare, badare, Gloss. Isid.
hippacare.short: hippacāre est celeriter animam ducere ab equi halitu, qui est supra modum acutus, Paul.

hippace.full: hippăcē, ēs, f., = ἱππάκη. Cheese made of mare's milk, Plin. 28, 9, 34, § 131; 28, 14, 58, § 204.— A plant, now unknown, Plin. 25, 8, 44, § 83.

hippagines.full: hippāgĭnes naves, quibus equi vehuntur, quas Graeci ἱππαγωγούς dicunt, Paul. ex Fest. p. 101 Müll.; so Gell. 10, 25, 5; cf. hippagogi and hippegus.
hippagines.short: hippāgĭnes naves, quibus equi vehuntur, quas Graeci ἱππαγωγούς dicunt, Paul.

hippagogi.full: hippăgōgi, ōrum (Gr. acc.-gūs, v. infra), f., = ἱππαγωγοί, vessels for transporting horses, cavalry-transports: quinque et triginta naves, quas hippagogus vocant, ab Elea profectae, cum equitibus Gallis equisque, Liv. 44, 28, 7; cf. hippagines and hippegus.

hippalus.full: Hippălus, i, m., another name of the wind Favonius, in the Indian Ocean, Plin. 6, 23, 26, § 104.
hippalus.short: Hippălus, i, m., another name of the wind Favonius, in the Indian Ocean, Plin.

hipparchus.full: Hipparchus, i, m., = Ἵππαρχος. A son of Pisistratus tyrant of Athens, and brother of Hippias, killed by Harmodius and Aristogiton, Gell. 17, 21, 7.— A celebrated astronomer of Nicœa, Cic. Att. 2, 6, 1; Plin. 2, 26, 24, § 95; 2, 12, 9, § 53; 2, 77, 79, § 188; Mel. 3, 7, 7 al.

hipparinus.full: Hippărīnus, i, m., = Ἱππαρῖνος, the name of the father of Dion, Nep. Dion. 1, 1.
hipparinus.short: Hippărīnus, i, m., = Ἱππαρῖνος, the name of the father of Dion, Nep.

hipparis.full: Hippăris, is, m., a small river of Sicily, flowing by the city of Camarina, whence it is now called Fiume di Camarana, Sil. 12, 230.
hipparis.short: Hippăris, is, m., a small river of Sicily, flowing by the city of Camarina, whence it is now called Fiume di Camarana, Sil.

hippasus.full: Hippăsus, i, m. Son of Eurytus, Ov. M. 8, 313.— A centaur, Ov. M. 12, 352.

hippegus.full: hippēgus, i, f., = ἱππηγός (sc. navis), a transport for cavalry, Plin. 7, 56, 57, § 209; cf. hippagogi.

hippeus.full: hippeus (dissyl.), ĕï, m., = ἱππεύς (horseman), a kind of comet: hippeus equinas jubas (habet), Plin. 2, 25, 22, § 90.
hippeus.short: hippeus (dissyl.), ĕï, m., = ἱππεύς (horseman), a kind of comet: hippeus equinas jubas (habet), Plin.

hippias.full: Hippias, ae, m., = Ἱππίας. A son of Pisistratus tyrant of Athens, and brother of Hipparchus, after whose assassination he fled to the Persians; he fell in the battle of Marathon, Cic. Att. 9, 10, 3; Gell. 9, 2, 10.— A famous sophist of Elis in the time of Socrates, Cic. Brut. 8, 30; 85, 292; id. de Or. 3, 32, 127 al.— A famous painter, Plin. 35, 11, 40, § 141.

hippius.full: Hippius, ii, m., a Roman proper name, Cic. Fam. 13, 76. † Hippius, id est equester, Neptunus dictus est, etc., Paul. ex Fest. p. 101 Müll. [= Ἵππειος or Ἵππιος].
hippius.short: Hippius, ii, m., a Roman proper name, Cic.

hippo.full: Hippo, ōnis, m., = Ἱππών, the name of several cities. A city of Numidia, also with the surname of regius, Gr. Ἱππὼν βασιλικός, afterwards a bishop's see, now Bonah, Mel. 1, 7, 1; Liv. 29, 3, 7; Sil. 3, 259.— Hippo Diarrhytus, Ἱππὼν διάρρυτος, a city of Zeugitana, west of Utica, now Ben Zert, Plin. 5, 4, 3, § 23; 9, 8, 8, § 26; Sol. 27 med. — Deriv.: Hippōnensis, e, adj., of or belonging to Hippo: sinus, Mel. 1, 7, 2; Plin. 5, 4, 3, § 23: colonia, Plin. Ep. 9, 33, 2. —Subst.: Hippōnenses, ium, m.
hippo.short: Hippo, ōnis, m., = Ἱππών, the name of several cities.

hippocamelus.full: hippŏcămēlus, i, m., = ἱπποκάμηλος, a fabulous animal, half horse and half camel, Aus. Epigr. 70.
hippocamelus.short: hippŏcămēlus, i, m., = ἱπποκάμηλος, a fabulous animal, half horse and half camel, Aus.

hippocampus.full: hippŏcampus or -os, i, m., = ἱππόκαμπος, a sea-horse: Syngnathus hippocampus, Linn.; Plin. 32, 11, 53, § 149; 32, 7, 23, § 67; 32, 9, 30, § 93; 36, 5, 4, § 26; Naev. and Lucil. ap. Non. 120, 17 and 19.
hippocampus.short: hippŏcampus or -os, i, m., = ἱππόκαμπος, a sea-horse: Syngnathus hippocampus, Linn.;

hippocentaurus.full: hippŏcentaurus, i, m., = ἱπποκέϝταυπος, a fabulous creature, half horse and half man, hippocentaur, Cic. N. D. 2, 2, 5; id. Tusc. 1, 37, 90; Plin. 7, 3, 3, § 35: si quis rem quae in rerum natura non est aut esse non potest, velut hippocentaurum stipuletur, Gai. Inst. 3, 97 a.
hippocentaurus.short: hippŏcentaurus, i, m., = ἱπποκέϝταυπος, a fabulous creature, half horse and half man, hippocentaur, Cic.

hippocomus.full: hippŏcŏmus, i, m., = ἱπποκόμος, a groom, Cod. Th. 8, 5, 37.
hippocomus.short: hippŏcŏmus, i, m., = ἱπποκόμος, a groom, Cod.

hippocoon.full: Hippŏcŏon, ontis, m. Of Amyclœ, father of Enœsimus, who took part in the Calydonian hunt, Ov. M. 8, 314 and 363; Hyg. Fab. 173.— A companion of Æneas, an archer, Verg. A. 5, 492; Hyg. Fab. 273.

hippocoum.full: hippocoum vinum ex insula Coo dictum ab agro generoso, cui nomen est Hippo, Paul. ex Fest. p. 101 Müll.
hippocoum.short: hippocoum vinum ex insula Coo dictum ab agro generoso, cui nomen est Hippo, Paul.

hippocrates.full: Hippocrătes, is, m., = Ἱπποκράτης, the celebrated Greek physician of Cos, founder of the art of medicine, Cels. praef.; Cic. de Or. 3, 33, 132; Quint. 3, 6, 64.— Deriv.: Hippocrătĭcus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Hippocrates, Hippocratic: laniena, Prud. στεφ. 10, 497.— A Syracusan, brother of Epicydes, Liv. 24, 35; 36 al.
hippocrates.short: Hippocrătes, is, m., = Ἱπποκράτης, the celebrated Greek physician of Cos, founder of the art of medicine, Cels.

hippocrene.full: Hippocrēnē, ēs, f., = Ἱπποκρήνη, a fountain near Mount Helicon, sacred to the Muses, and which is fabled to have been produced by a stroke of Pegasus's hoof, Ov. F. 5, 7; Sol. 7 med. (in Hor. Ep. 1, 3, 10: fons Pindaricus, and in Pers. prol. 1: fons caballinus).— Derivv. Hippocrē-naeus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Hippocrene: fontes, Auct. de Laud. Herc. 5.— Hippocrēnĭdes, um, f., the Muses so named from the Hippocrene, Serv. Verg. E. 7, 21.
hippocrene.short: Hippocrēnē, ēs, f., = Ἱπποκρήνη, a fountain near Mount Helicon, sacred to the Muses, and which is fabled to have been produced by a stroke of Pegasus's hoof, Ov.

hippodamantium.full: hippŏdămantĭum vīnum, a sort of wine, otherwise unknown, Plin. 14, 7, 9, § 75.
hippodamantium.short: hippŏdămantĭum vīnum, a sort of wine, otherwise unknown, Plin.

hippodamas.full: Hippŏdămas, antis, m., = Ἱπποδάμας, the father of Perimele, Ov. M. 8, 592.
hippodamas.short: Hippŏdămas, antis, m., = Ἱπποδάμας, the father of Perimele, Ov.

hippodame.full: Hippŏdămē, ēs, and Hippŏdămīa or -mēa, ae, f., = Ἱπποδάμη or Ἱπποδάμεια. Daughter of Œnomaüs, king of Elis; she became the wife of Pelops, who won her in a race with her father, Enn. ap. Cic. Tusc. 3, 12, 26 (Trag. v. 398 Vahl.); Prop. 1, 2, 20; 1, 8, 35; Ov. H. 8, 70; Verg. G. 3, 7 Serv.; Hyg. Fab. 243; 84.— Daughter of Adrastus, and wife of Pirithoüs, at whose wedding took place the battle of the Centaurs and Lapithœ, Ov. M. 12, 210; 224; id. H. 17, 248; Hyg. Fab. 33.
hippodame.short: Hippŏdămē, ēs, and Hippŏdămīa or -mēa, ae, f., = Ἱπποδάμη or Ἱπποδάμεια.

hippodamus.full: Hippŏdămus, i, m., = Ἱππόδαμος, the horse-tamer, a poet. epithet of Castor, Mart. 7, 57, 2.
hippodamus.short: Hippŏdămus, i, m., = Ἱππόδαμος, the horse-tamer, a poet.

hippodromos.full: hippodrŏmos, i, m., = ἱππόδρομος, a race-course for horses, hippodrome, Plaut. Bacch. 3, 3, 27; Plin. Ep. 5, 6, 19; Mart. 12, 50, 5; Sid. Ap. 2, 2.
hippodromos.short: hippodrŏmos, i, m., = ἱππόδρομος, a race-course for horses, hippodrome, Plaut.

hippolapathon.full: hippŏlăpăthon, i, n., = ἱππολάπαθον, horse-sorrel, a plant, Plin. 20, 21, 85, § 232.
hippolapathon.short: hippŏlăpăthon, i, n., = ἱππολάπαθον, horse-sorrel, a plant, Plin.

hippolyte.full: Hippŏlўtē, ēs, and Hippŏlўta, ae, f., = Ἱππολύτη. An Amazon, daughter of Mars, taken captive in the war of the Amazons by Theseus, to whom she bore Hippolytus, Hyg. Fab. 30; Just. 2, 4, 23; Plaut. Men. 1, 3, 17.— The wife of Acastus, king of Magnesia, who conceived a passion for Peleus, and, because she met with no return of affection from him, accused him to her husband of an attempt upon her virtue, Hyg. Fab. 14 med.; Hor. C. 3, 7, 18.
hippolyte.short: Hippŏlўtē, ēs, and Hippŏlўta, ae, f., = Ἱππολύτη.

hippolytus.full: Hippŏlўtus, i, m., = Ἱππόλυτος, son of Theseus and Hippolyte; his step-mother Phœdra fell in love with him, but, on her advances being repelled, she accused him to her husband of attempts upon her chastity; the king in his rage cursed him and devoted him to destruction; whereupon he was torn to pieces by his horses; he was, however, restored to life by Æsculapius, and taken by Diana, under the name of Virbius, to the grove near Aricia, where he afterwards received divine honors, Ov. M. 15, 497 s
hippolytus.short: Hippŏlўtus, i, m., = Ἱππόλυτος, son of Theseus and Hippolyte;

hippomanes.full: hippŏmănes, is, n., = ἱππομανές (horse-heat, horse-rage). A slimy humor that flows from a mare when in heat, and which was used to excite desire, Verg. G. 3, 280 sq.; Tib. 2, 4, 8; Prop. 4, 5, 18 (cf. Verg. A. 4, 516).— A plant that was supposed to put mares in heat, Serv. Verg. G. 3, 281.— A small black membrane on the forehead of a new-born foal, used in making love-potions, Plin. 8, 42, 66, § 165; 28, 11, 49, § 180; Juv. 6, 132.

hippomarathum.full: hĭppŏmărăthum or -on, i, n., = ἱππομάραθον, horse-fennel, wild fennel, Plin. 20, 23, 96, § 258.
hippomarathum.short: hĭppŏmărăthum or -on, i, n., = ἱππομάραθον, horse-fennel, wild fennel, Plin.

hippomeneis.full: Hippŏmĕnēis, ĭdis, f., = Ἱππομενηΐς, Limone, a daughter of Hippomenes of Athens, who, as a punishment for unchastity, was thrown by her father to a horse to be devoured, Ov. Ib. 337; cf. id. ib. 461 (al. Hippomeneia).
hippomeneis.short: Hippŏmĕnēis, ĭdis, f., = Ἱππομενηΐς, Limone, a daughter of Hippomenes of Athens, who, as a punishment for unchastity, was thrown by her father to a horse to be devoured, Ov.

hippomenes.full: Hippŏmĕnes, ae, m., = Ἱππομένης, son of Megareus, who conquered Atalanta, the daughter of Schœneus, in a race, and thus obtained her as his wife, Ov. M. 10, 575 sq.; 632; Hyg. Fab. 185; Serv. Verg. A. 3, 113.
hippomenes.short: Hippŏmĕnes, ae, m., = Ἱππομένης, son of Megareus, who conquered Atalanta, the daughter of Schœneus, in a race, and thus obtained her as his wife, Ov.

hipponax.full: Hippōnax, actis, m., = Ἱππώναξ, a Greek poet of Ephesus, who wrote in iambics, celebrated for the bitterness of his satires, Cic. N. D. 3, 38, 91; Plin. 36, 5, 4, § 12. — Deriv.: Hippōnactēus, a, um, adj., of Hipponax, in the style of Hipponax, Hipponactean: praeconium, i. e. a bitter, biting poem (of Licinius Calvus), Cic. Fam. 7, 24, 1.—Subst.: Hippōnacteus, i, m. (sc. versus), the sort of iambic verse invented by Hipponax: senarios et Hipponacteos effugere vix possumus, Cic. Or. 56, 189.
hipponax.short: Hippōnax, actis, m., = Ἱππώναξ, a Greek poet of Ephesus, who wrote in iambics, celebrated for the bitterness of his satires, Cic.

hipponensis.full: Hippōnensis, e, v. Hippo, II. B.

hipponicus.full: Hippŏnīcus, i, m., = Ἱππόνικος, an Athenian, father-in-law of Alcibiades, Nep. Alcib. 2.
hipponicus.short: Hippŏnīcus, i, m., = Ἱππόνικος, an Athenian, father-in-law of Alcibiades, Nep.

hippoperae.full: hippŏpērae, ārum, f., = ἱπποπῆραι, saddle-bags, Sen. Ep. 87, 7.
hippoperae.short: hippŏpērae, ārum, f., = ἱπποπῆραι, saddle-bags, Sen.

hippophaes.full: hippŏphăes, is, n., = ἱπποφαές, a plant (perh. the Euphorbia spinosa, Linn.), Plin. 21, 15, 54, § 91; 22, 12, 14, § 29.
hippophaes.short: hippŏphăes, is, n., = ἱπποφαές, a plant (perh.

hippophaeston.full: hippŏphaeston, i, n., = ἱππόφαιστον, a prickly plant (perh. Centaurea calcitrapa, Linn.), Plin. 27, 10, 66, § 92.
hippophaeston.short: hippŏphaeston, i, n., = ἱππόφαιστον, a prickly plant (perh.

hippopheon.full: hippophĕon, i, n., a plant, Plin. 26, 8, 35, § 55.
hippopheon.short: hippophĕon, i, n., a plant, Plin.

hippophlomon.full: hippophlŏmon, i, n., = ἱππόφλομον, white mandrake, Plin. 25, 13, 94, § 148.
hippophlomon.short: hippophlŏmon, i, n., = ἱππόφλομον, white mandrake, Plin.

hippophobas.full: hippŏphŏbas, ădis, f., = ἱπποφοβάς, a plant, Plin. 24, 17, 102, § 161.
hippophobas.short: hippŏphŏbas, ădis, f., = ἱπποφοβάς, a plant, Plin.

hippopodes.full: Hippŏpŏdes, um, m., = Ἱππόποδες, a fabulous race of men, with horses' feet, Plin. 4, 13, 27, § 95; Mel. 3, 6, 8.
hippopodes.short: Hippŏpŏdes, um, m., = Ἱππόποδες, a fabulous race of men, with horses' feet, Plin.

hippopotamus.full: hippŏpŏtămus, i, m., = ἱπποπόταμος, a river - horse, hippopotamus, Plin. 8, 25, 39, § 95; Mel. 1, 9, 3; Amm. 22, 15.
hippopotamus.short: hippŏpŏtămus, i, m., = ἱπποπόταμος, a river - horse, hippopotamus, Plin.

hipposelinum.full: hippŏsĕlīnum, i, n., = ἱπποσέλινον, a sort of wild parsley; lit., horse-parsley, Plin. 19, 8, 37, § 124; Pall. Apr. 3 (Col. 11, 3, 36, written as Greek, and translated by olus atrum).
hipposelinum.short: hippŏsĕlīnum, i, n., = ἱπποσέλινον, a sort of wild parsley;

hippotades.full: Hippŏtădes, ae, m., = Ἱπποτάδης, the descendant of Hippotes, i. e. Æŏlus (as the son of Segesta, a daughter of the Trojan Hippotes), Ov. M. 4, 663; 11, 431; 14, 224: Hippotadae regnum, i. e. the Æolic (Liparic) Isles, id. ib. 14, 86; cf. ib. 15, 707.
hippotades.short: Hippŏtădes, ae, m., = Ἱπποτάδης, the descendant of Hippotes, i.

hippothous.full: Hippŏthŏus, i, m., son of Cercyon, who took part in the Calydonian hunt, Ov. M. 8, 306.
hippothous.short: Hippŏthŏus, i, m., son of Cercyon, who took part in the Calydonian hunt, Ov.

hippotoxotae.full: hippŏtoxŏtae, ārum, m., = ἱπποτοξόται, mounted archers, Caes. B. C. 3, 4, 5; Auct. B. Afr. 19, 6 (pure Lat., equites sagittarii, Tac. A. 2, 16; Curt. 5, 4).
hippotoxotae.short: hippŏtoxŏtae, ārum, m., = ἱπποτοξόται, mounted archers, Caes.

hippuris.full: hippūris, ĭdis, f., = ἵππουρις, horsetail, a water-plant; pure Lat., equisetum, Plin. 26, 13, 83, § 132; App. Herb. 39.
hippuris.short: hippūris, ĭdis, f., = ἵππουρις, horsetail, a water-plant;

hippurus.full: hippūrus, i, m., = ἵππουρος, a fish (perh. golden carp, gold fish, Coryphaena hippurus, Linn.), Ov. Hal. 95; Plin. 9, 16, 24, § 57; 32, 11, 53, § 149.
hippurus.short: hippūrus, i, m., = ἵππουρος, a fish (perh.

hippus.full: hippus, i, m., = ἵππος, a sea-fish, otherwise unknown, Plin. 32, 11, 53, § 149.
hippus.short: hippus, i, m., = ἵππος, a sea-fish, otherwise unknown, Plin.

hir.full: hir or ir, indecl. n. from χείρ, like heres from χῆρος, and hiems from χεῖμα, χειμών, a hand: quibu' vinum Defusum e pleno siet, ir siphove, cui nil Dempsit, i. e. the palm of the hand, used in tasting wine, Lucil. ap. Cic. Fin. 2, 8, 23; cf. Charis. p. 12 P.; Prisc. p. 648 ib.; 698 ib.

hira.full: hīra, ae, f., the empty gut; called also intestinum jejunum, Gr. νῆστις, Macr. Somn. Scip. 1, 6 fin.; Plaut. Curc. 2, 1, 23; Arn. 7, 24.
hira.short: hīra, ae, f., the empty gut;

hircinus.full: hircīnus (hirquīnus), a, um, adj. hircus, of a goat, goat's: barba, Plaut. Ps. 4, 2, 12: sanguis, Plin. 20 prooem. § 2; 37, 4, 15, § 59: pelles, id. 12, 17, 40, § 81: folles, Hor. S. 1, 4, 19: sidus, i. e. the constellation Capricorn, Prud. Apoth. 621.—Comically: alae, that have a goatish smell, Plaut. Poen. 4, 2, 51.

hircipes.full: Hircĭpes, pĕdis, m. hircus - pes, goat-footed, an appellation of Pan, Mart. Cap. 9, § 906.

hirco.full: hirco, āre, v. n., to howl, of the sound of the lynx, Auct. Carm. de Philom. 51.

hircosus.full: hircōsus, a, um, adj. hircus, that smells like a goat, goatish: senex, Plaut. Merc. 3, 3, 14: gens centurionum, Pers. 3, 77: subulcus, Mart. 10, 98, 10; cf.: licet scripti sint inter hircosos, possint tamen inter unguentatos placere, Sen. Fragm. ap. Gell. 12, 2, 11; Mart. 12, 59, 5.

hirculus.full: hircŭlus, i, m. dim. id.. A little goat, Auct. Priap. 86, 16 (Ps.-Catull. 19, 16). — A plant, otherwise unknown, Plin. 12, 12, 26, § 46.

hircuosus.full: hircŭōsus, a, um, adj. id., goatish: Pan, App. M. 5, p. 169 fin.

hircus.full: hircus (also hircŭus and ircus; cf. Quint. 1, 5, 20; and the Sabine form, FIRCUS, Varr. L. L. 5, § 97 Müll.; cf. haedus init.), i, m., a he-goat, buck (cf. haedus, caper). Lit., Verg. E. 3, 8; 91; id. G. 3, 312; Hor. Epod. 16, 34; id. A. P. 220 (Plin. 37, 4, 15, § 60: foedissimum animalium).— Transf. Like caper, a goatish smell, the rank smell of the armpits: hircum ab alis (sapere), Plaut. Ps. 2, 4, 48: alarum, Cat. 71, 1: an gravis hirsutis cubet hircus in alis, Hor. Epod. 12, 5: pastillos Ruf

hirnea.full: hirnĕa (also irnea), ae, f., a jug for holding liquids, Cato, R. R. 81; Plaut. Am. 1, 1, 273; 276.
hirnea.short: hirnĕa (also irnea), ae, f., a jug for holding liquids, Cato, R.

hirnula.full: hirnŭla, ae, f. dim. hirnea, a small jug or pitcher for liquids; in an unaspirated form: irnela vasis genus in sacris, Paul. ex Fest. p. 105 Müll. N. cr. (but urnulas is the true reading in Cic. Par. 1, 2, 11).

hirpi.full: Hirpi, ōrum, m., a very ancient Sabine family near Rome, in the territory of the Falisci, Plin. 7, 2, 2, § 19; Sol. 2, § 26.
hirpi.short: Hirpi, ōrum, m., a very ancient Sabine family near Rome, in the territory of the Falisci, Plin.

hirpini.full: Hirpīni (Irpīni), ōrum, m., a people of Lower Italy, between Campania, Lucania, and Apulia, Plin. 3, 11, 16, § 99; Liv. 22, 61, 11; 23, 37; 27, 15: in Hirpinis, in the territory of the Hirpini, Cic. Div. 1, 36, 79; Plin. 2, 93, 95, § 208; so, ex Hirpinis, Liv. 22, 13 init.: in Hirpinis, id. 23, 1.— Deriv. Hirpīnus (Irp-), a, um, adj., of or belonging to the Hirpini: ager, fundus, Cic. Agr. 3, 2, 8: pubes, Sil. 8, 571.
hirpini.short: Hirpīni (Irpīni), ōrum, m., a people of Lower Italy, between Campania, Lucania, and Apulia, Plin.

hirpus.full: hirpus or irpus, in the Sabine lang., the wolf, Paul. ex Fest. p. 106, 1 Müll.; Serv. ad Verg. A. 11, 785.
hirpus.short: hirpus or irpus, in the Sabine lang., the wolf, Paul.

hirquitallio.full: hirquitallĭo, īre, v. n. hircus, of new - born children, to acquire a strong voice: in secunda hebdomade vel incipiente tertia vocem crassiorem et inaequabilem fieri: quod Aristoteles appellat τραγίζειν, antiqui nostri † hirquitallire: et inde ipsos putant † hirquitallos appellari, quod tum corpus hircum olere incipiat, Censor. de Die Nat. 14, 7; cf.: † hirquitalli pueri primum ad virilitatem accedentes, a libidine scilicet hircorum dicti, Paul. ex Fest. p. 101 Müll. N. cr.; and without the aspi

hirquitallus.full: hirquitallus, i, v. the preced. art.

hirrio.full: hirrĭo (irrio), īre, v. n., of dogs, to snarl: hirrire = garrire, quod genus vocis est canis rabiosae, Paul. ex Fest. p. 101 Müll. N. cr.; cf.: hirrit ὅταν κύων ἀπειλῇ ὑλακτῶν, Gloss. Philox.: veluti est canibus innatum, ut, etsi non latrant, tamen hirriant, Sid. Ep. 7, 3; Diom. 367 P.

hirritus.full: hirrītus (irr-), ūs, m. hirrio, a snarling of dogs, Sid. Ep. 9, 16 in carm.

hirsutia.full: hirsūtĭa, ae, f. hirsutus, roughness, shagginess: nullae setarum, Sol. 25, § 10.

hirsutus.full: hirsūtus, a, um, adj. primary form HIRSUS, a variation of hirtus, rough, shaggy, bristly, prickly, hirsute = δασύς. Lit. (class.; syn. hirtus, pilosus, villosus): quarum (animantium) aliae villis vestitae, aliae spinis hirsutae, Cic. N. D. 2, 47, 121; Col. 7, 2, 6: pectus Herculis, Prop. 4 (5), 9, 49. crura genaeque, Mart. 10, 65, 9: supercilium, Verg. E. 8, 34: et glacialis Hiems canos hirsuta capillos, Ov. M. 2, 30: barba, id. ib. 13, 766: capilli, id. H. 9, 63: juba (galeae), Prop. 4 (5), 10,

hirtipili.full: hirtipili durorum pilorum homines, Paul. ex Fest. p. 101 Müll. N. cr.

hirtius.full: Hirtĭus, a, name of a Roman gens.; in partic., A. Hirtius, consul A. U. C. 711, and author of the eighth book of Cœsar's Commentaries on the Gallic war: he fell before Mutina, Cic. Att. 7, 4, 2; Q. Cic. ap. Cic. Fam. 16, 27, 1.—Hirtīnus, a, um, of Hirtius: proelium, the battle in which Hirtius met his death, Asin. Pollio ap. Cic. Fam. 10, 33, 4.
hirtius.short: Hirtĭus, a, name of a Roman gens.;

hirtuosus.full: hirtŭōsus, a, um, false read. in App. M. 5, p. 169, inst. of hircuosus.

hirtus.full: hirtus, a, um, adj., rough, hairy, shaggy, = δασύς (mostly post-Aug.; cf. hirsutus, hispidus, pilosus, villosus, setosus). Lit.: oves, Varr. R. R. 2, 2, 19: hirto corde quosdam homines nasci proditur, Plin. 11, 37, 70, § 185: ora (Scythis), Curt. 4, 13: frons, Sil. 16, 121: toga, Luc. 2, 386; Quint. 12, 10, 47; cf. tunica, Nep. Dat. 3, 2: setae in corpore, Ov. M. 13, 850; cf. comae, Curt. 5, 6 fin.: saxa dumis, Stat. S. 3, 1, 13; cf. saepes, Col. poët. 10, 27; and: ager spinigeris stirpibus, Pru
hirtus.short: hirtus, a, um, adj., rough, hairy, shaggy, = δασύς (mostly post-Aug.;

hirudo.full: hĭrūdo, ĭnis, f. (also called sanguisūga), a leech, blood-sucker, Plin. 32, 10, 42, § 122: ego me convortam in hirudinem atque exsugebo sanguinem, Plaut. Ep. 2, 2, 4.—Fig., of any thing that exhausts, etc.: aerarii, Cic. Att. 1, 16, 11: non missura cutem, nisi plena cruoris, hirudo, Hor. A. P. 476.

hirundineus.full: hĭrundĭnĕus, a, um, adj. hirundo, of or belonging to swallows (post-class.): adventus, of the swallows, Sid. Ep. 2, 14; cf. the foll. art.

hirundininus.full: hĭrundĭnīnus, a, um, adj. id., of or belonging to swallows, swallows' (class.): sanguis, fel, Plin. 30, 14, 46, § 133: nidus, Plaut. Rud. 3, 1, 6; Mart. 11, 18, 20.

hirundo.full: hĭrundo, ĭnis, f. (weakened from χελιδών), a swallow. Lit., Plin. 10, 33, 49, § 92; 10, 24, 34, § 70; Plaut. Rud. 3, 1, 12; Verg. G. 1, 377; id. A. 12, 474; Ov. F. 2, 853; Hor. Ep. 1, 7, 13.—As a term of endearment: dic me anaticulam, columbam vel catellum, Hirundinem, monedulam, etc., Plaut. As. 3, 3, 104.—Prov.: quid contendat hirundo cycnis? Lucr. 3, 6 (for which: certent cycnis ululae, Verg. E. 8, 55).— Transf., a flying sea - fish, sea - swallow, Exocoetus volitans s. evolans, Linn.; Plin.

hisco.full: hisco, ĕre, v. inch. n. and a. [hio; whence also hiasco]. Neutr., to open, gape, yawn. In gen.: tellus, ait, hisce, Ov. M. 1, 546; cf.: magnae nunc hiscite terrae, Poët. ap. Quint. 9, 2, 26: rima hiscit, Plin. 17, 14, 24, § 108: st, tace, aedes hiscunt, Plaut. Ps. 4, 1, 42.— In partic., to open the mouth, to mutter (so most freq. and class.): respondebisne ad haec? aut omnino hiscere audebis? * Cic. Phil. 2, 43, 111: adversus dictatoriam vim, Liv. 6, 16, 3: adversus praepotentis viros, id. 45, 2

hispalis.full: Hispălis, is, f., a city of Hispania Baetica, now Sevilla, Plin. 2, 97, 100, § 219; Caes. B. C. 2, 18; 20; Asin. Pollio ap. Cic. Fam. 10, 32, 3.—In the neut. form: Hispal, ălis, Mel. 2, 6, 4; Plin. 3, 1, 3, § 11; Sil. 3, 392.— Deriv.: Hispălensis or Hispălĭensis, e, adj., of or belonging to the city Hispalis: Hispalensis conventus, Plin. 3, 1, 3, §§ 7, 11.—Subst.: Hispă-lienses, ium, m. plur., the inhabitants of Hispalis, Tac. H. 1, 78.
hispalis.short: Hispălis, is, f., a city of Hispania Baetica, now Sevilla, Plin.

hispane.full: Hispānē, adv., after the manner of Spain, v. Hispani, II. A. fin.
hispane.short: Hispānē, adv., after the manner of Spain, v.

hispani.full: Hispāni, ōrum, m., the Spaniards, Liv. 21, 27; Tac. A. 1, 78; Suet. Caes. 76 al. — Derivv. Hispānus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to the Spaniards, Spanish: mare, Plin. 3, 5, 10, § 74: aurum, Mart. 7, 88, 7: Tarraco, id. 10, 104, 4: populi, Liv. 21, 19: equites, Caes. B. G. 5, 26: cohortes, id. B. C. 3, 88: legio, Tac. H. 1, 6: acies, Luc. 3, 454: gladio cingi, Liv. 7, 10, 5.—* Adv.: Hispānē: Hispane non Romane memoretis loqui me, Enn. ap. Charis. p. 180 P. (Ann. v. 495 Vahl.).— Hispā-nĭa, ae, f
hispani.short: Hispāni, ōrum, m., the Spaniards, Liv.

hispellum.full: Hispellum, i, n., a city of Umbria, at the foot of the Apennines, now Spello, Plin. 3, 14, 19, § 113; Sil. 8, 458; Inscr. Orell. 3885. —Hispellātes, ium, m., the inhabitants of Hispellum, Plin. Ep. 8, 8, 6.
hispellum.short: Hispellum, i, n., a city of Umbria, at the foot of the Apennines, now Spello, Plin.

hispido.full: hispĭdo, āre, v. a. hispidus, to make bristly, prickly: spinosis fastigiis hispidatur, Sol. 26 dub. (al. hispida turgescit).

hispidus.full: hispĭdus, a, um, adj., rough, shaggy, hairy, bristly, prickly. Lit. (poet. and in post-Aug. prose; syn. v. hirtus): facies, Hor. C. 4, 10, 5; cf. frons, Verg. A. 10, 210: membra, Juv. 2, 11: corpus Nereïdum squamis, Plin. 9, 5, 4, § 9: mater (of a shegoat with young), Mart. 3, 58, 37: herba, Plin. 22, 6, 7, § 17: agri, i. e. dirty, foul with rain, = squalidi, Hor. C. 2, 9, 2: Eurus procellis, Val. Fl. 1, 612.—Poet., per hypallagen: sic hispida turpes Proelia villosis ineunt complexibus ursi, Sta
hispidus.short: hispĭdus, a, um, adj., rough, shaggy, hairy, bristly, prickly.

hispo.full: Hispo, ōnis, m., a Roman surname, Cic. Fam. 13, 65; 14, 1; Juv. 2, 50.
hispo.short: Hispo, ōnis, m., a Roman surname, Cic.

hispulla.full: Hispulla, ae, f., the name of a woman, Juv. 6, 74; 12, 11; Plin. Ep. 4, 19 tit.
hispulla.short: Hispulla, ae, f., the name of a woman, Juv.

hister1.full: Hister, tri (less correctly Ister), m., = Ἴστρος, the lower part of the Danube (the upper part, Danubius). Prop. In gen.: Ponticum simul et Hadriaticum mare et Histrum amnem et Alpes conspici posse, Liv. 40, 21: turbidus et torquens flaventes Hister arenas, Verg. G. 3, 350: stat vetus urbs, ripae vicina binominis Histri, Ov. P. 1, 8, 11.— Esp.: Histro fallacior, an epithet applied by Tertullian to Marcion; because the river, on account of its strong eddies and many mouths, was dangerous to the n
hister1.short: Hister, tri (less correctly Ister), m., = Ἴστρος, the lower part of the Danube (the upper part, Danubius).

histon.full: histon, ōnis, m., = ἱστών, the place where a loom stands, a weaving-room: habere institutos histonas, Varr. R. R. 1, 2, 21.
histon.short: histon, ōnis, m., = ἱστών, the place where a loom stands, a weaving-room: habere institutos histonas, Varr.

historia.full: histŏrĭa, ae, f., = ἱστορία, a narrative of past events, history (syn.: annales, fasti). Lit.: historia testis temporum, lux veritatis, vita memoriae, magistra vitae, nuntia vetustatis, qua voce alia nisi oratoris immortalitati commendatur? Cic. de Or. 2, 9, 36: erat enim historia (initio) nihil aliud nisi annalium confectio, etc., id. ib. 2, 12, 51 sq.; cf. id. Leg. 1, 2, 5 sq.; Gell. 5, 18; Plin. Ep. 5, 8; v. the art. annalis: videtisne, quantum munds sit oratoris historia? ... Nam quis nescit
historia.short: histŏrĭa, ae, f., = ἱστορία, a narrative of past events, history (syn.: annales, fasti).

historialis.full: histŏrĭālis, e, adj. historia, of or belonging to history, historical (late Lat.): venerabilis patriarchae Joseph historialis diligentia, i. e. related in sacred history, Sid. Ep. 6, 12.

historice2.full: histŏrĭcē, ēs, f., = ἱστορική, explanation, interpretation of an author: finitae quidem sunt partes duae, quas haec professio pollicetur, id est ratio loquendi et enarratio auctorum: quarum illam methodicen, hanc historicen vocant, Quint. 1, 9, 1.
historice2.short: histŏrĭcē, ēs, f., = ἱστορική, explanation, interpretation of an author: finitae quidem sunt partes duae, quas haec professio pollicetur, id est ratio loquendi et enarratio auctorum: quarum illam methodicen, hanc historicen vocant, Quint.

historicus.full: histŏrĭcus, a, um, adj., = ἱστορικός, of or belonging to history, historical. Adj.: earum rerum historiam non tam historico quam oratorio genere perscripsit, Cic. Brut. 83, 286; cf. Plin. Ep. 7, 9, 8: sermo, Cic. Or. 36, 124: fides, Ov. Am. 3, 12, 42: nitor, Quint. 10, 1, 33: prosopopœïae, id. 3, 8, 53: lingua, Sen. Q. N. 1, 13 fin.: homines litterati et historici, versed in history, Cic. Mur. 7, 16: fides, credibility, Aug. Civ. Dei, 15, 9; id. Ep. 143, 12; Vop. Aur. 35.— Subst.: histŏrĭcus, i,
historicus.short: histŏrĭcus, a, um, adj., = ἱστορικός, of or belonging to history, historical.

historiographus.full: histŏrĭŏgrăphus, i, m., = ἱστοριογράφος, a writer of history, historiographer (post-class.), Capitol. Gord. 11, 21; Ambros. Ep. 42, 2; Cassiod. Eccl. Hist. 1, 1; Hier. Galat. 2, 14.
historiographus.short: histŏrĭŏgrăphus, i, m., = ἱστοριογράφος, a writer of history, historiographer (post-class.), Capitol.

histri.full: Histri (less correctly Istri), ōrum, m., the people of Istria, Istrians, a barbarous Illyrian tribe subdued by the Romans B. C. 177: principes Histrorum, Liv. 41, 11; Plin. 3, 19, 23, § 129: Histrorum gentem originem a Colchis ducere, Just. 32, 3, 13: per Histros Hister emittitur, Mel. 2, 3 fin. —Hence, Histria (Istria), ae, f., a country on the eastern shore of the Adriatic Sea, extending from Trieste to the Sinus Flanaticus: Histria ut peninsula excurrit, Plin. 3, 19, 23, § 129; Liv. 39, 55.—D
histri.short: Histri (less correctly Istri), ōrum, m., the people of Istria, Istrians, a barbarous Illyrian tribe subdued by the Romans B.

histriculus.full: histrĭcŭlus λογοποιός, Gloss. Philox. [dim. from histrio; cf. the foll. art.].

histricus.full: histrĭcus, a, um, adj. hister, histrio, of or belonging to stage-players: imperator histricus, the manager, Plaut. Poen. prol. 4; cf. imperium, the management, id. ib. 44.

histrio.full: histrio, ōnis, m. Etrusc. prim. form HISTER, Liv. 7, 2, 6; Val. Max. 2, 4, 4; whence histricus and histriculus, a stage-player, actor, either tragic or comic (syn.: actor, mimus, tragoedus, comoedus). Lit.: quod verbum in cavea dixit histrio, Plaut. Truc. 5, 39; Liv. 7, 2; Val. Max. 2, 4, 4; Cic. Fin. 3, 7, 24; id. Par. 3, 2, 26; id. de Or. 1, 5, 18; 1, 61, 258; id. de Sen. 19, 70; Plaut. Am. prol. 69; 77 sq.; id. Capt. prol. 13 et saep.: ex pessimo histrione bonum comoedum fieri, Cic. Rosc. Com

histrionalis.full: histrĭōnālis, e, adj. histrio, of or belonging to a stage-player, like an actor (a word of Tac.): studium, Tac. A. 1, 16: modi, id. Or. 26: favor, id. ib. 29.

histrionia.full: histrĭōnĭa, ae, f. (sc. ars) [id.], the art of stage-playing, dramatic art: facere histrioniam, to assume the character of an actor, Plaut. Am. prol. 90; Macr. S. 2, 10, 12: exercere, Petr. Fr. 10.

histrionicus.full: histrĭōnĭcus, a, um, adj. id., of or belonging to a player, histrionic (post-class.): operae, Dig. 32, 1, 73: gestus, Amm. 14, 6, 18.—Subst.: histrĭōnĭca, ae, f., the player's art, Lampr. Heliog. 12, 1.

hiulco.full: hĭulco, no perf., ātum, 1, v. a. hiulcus, to cause to gape or split open, to break into chinks: cum gravis exustos aestus hiulcat agros, Cat. 68, 62: per hiulcatos agros, Fortun. Carm. 6, 12, 6.

hiulcus.full: hĭulcus, a, um, adj. hio, gaping, split, cleft, opened, open. Lit. (only poet.): ubi hiulca siti findit Canis aestifer arva, Verg. G. 2, 353: Aegyptus, Stat. Th. 4, 708: venae fluminis, id. ib. 9, 450: juga montis Tauri, Sol. 38 fin.: nubes, Claud. Cons. Prob. et Olybr. 206: nimbi, id. Rapt. Pros. 2, 230: vulnus, Sid. Ep. 6, 7: ova, Claud. III. Cons. Hon. 4 praef.: mucro, i. e. ungues ferrei, Prud. στεφ. 10, 452: ictus, id. ib. 5, 113.— * Poet. transf., act., cleaving, destroying: fulmen, Stat.

ho!.full: ho! interj., an expression of astonishment, oh! ho! tune is eras? Ter. Phorm. 5, 7, 52 dub. (al. oh!).
ho!.short: ho! interj., an expression of astonishment, oh! ho! tune is eras? Ter.

hoc1.full: hoc, abl. and neutr. of hic, q. v.

hodie.full: hŏdĭē, adv. contr. from hoc die, on this day, to-day. Lit.: quem quidem negat Eros hodie: cras mane putat, Cic. Att. 13, 30, 2; so opp. cras, Ov. R. Am. 94; Hor. Ep. 1, 16, 33: hodie mane, this morning, Cic. Att. 13, 9, 1: hodie cum diluculo, Plaut. Am. 2, 2, 111: hodie numquam ad vesperum vivam! id. As. 3, 3, 40: pridie Vinalia, qui dies hodie est, Cic. Phil. 14, 5, 14: Nonae sunt hodie Sextiles, Cic. Verr. 1, 10, 31: hodie tricesima sabbata, Hor. S. 1, 9, 69: equidem te, nisi nunc, hodie nusqu

hodiernus.full: hŏdĭernus, a, um, adj. hodie, of this day, to-day's. Lit.: quod ex hodierno ejus edicto perspicere potestis, Cic. Phil. 4, 3, 7: disputatio hesterni et hodierni diei, id. de Or. 3, 21, 81: hodierno die, mane, today, id. Cat. 3, 9, 21: ante hodiernum diem, id. ib. 3, 8, 20: quis scit an adiciant hodiernae crastina summae Tempora di superi? Hor. C. 4, 7, 17: (Servio Tullio regnante) multo diutius Athenae jam erant quam est Roma ad hodiernum diem, Cic. Brut. 10, 39. —Poet. for hodie: sic venias, ho

hodoedocos.full: hŏdoedŏcos latro atque obsessor viarum, Paul. ex Fest. p. 103 Müll. [= όδοιδόκος].
hodoedocos.short: hŏdoedŏcos latro atque obsessor viarum, Paul.

hodoeporicon.full: hŏdoepŏrĭcon, i, n., = όδοιπορικόν, an itinerary, Hier. Ep. 108, 8.
hodoeporicon.short: hŏdoepŏrĭcon, i, n., = όδοιπορικόν, an itinerary, Hier.

hoedus.full: hoedus, i, and its derivv., v. haed.
hoedus.short: hoedus, i, and its derivv., v.

holce.full: holcē, ēs, f., = ὁλκή, a drachma: holceque a drachma non re sed nomine differt, Fann. de Pond. 19.
holce.short: holcē, ēs, f., = ὁλκή, a drachma: holceque a drachma non re sed nomine differt, Fann.

holcus.full: holcus, i, m., = όλκός, a sort of grain, mouse - barley, Hordeum murinum, Linn.; Plin. 27, 10, 63, § 90.
holcus.short: holcus, i, m., = όλκός, a sort of grain, mouse - barley, Hordeum murinum, Linn.;

holeraceus.full: hŏlĕrācĕus (ŏlĕr-), a, um, adj. holus, resembling herbs, vegetable: frutex, Plin. 26, 8, 53, § 85.

holerarium.full: hŏlĕrārĭum (ŏlĕr-), i, n. id., a vegetable-garden, kitchen-garden: olerarium, λαχανάριον, Gloss.

holerator.full: hŏlĕrātor (ŏlĕr-), ōris, m. holero, one who cultivates vegetables, a market-gardener: holerator, λαχανοπώλης, Gloss. Philox.

holero.full: hŏlĕro (ŏlĕro), āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. holus, to plant with vegetables: hortulos, Matt. ap. Prisc. p. 722 P.: holeratus, holeribus consitus, Not. Tir. p. 168.

holocaustum.full: hŏlŏcaustum, i, n., = ὁλόκαυστον, a whole burnt - offering, holocaust, Prud. Apoth. 537; id. Psych. 784; Vulg. Exod. 40, 6; id. Lev. 4, 7 al.; cf. the foll. art.
holocaustum.short: hŏlŏcaustum, i, n., = ὁλόκαυστον, a whole burnt - offering, holocaust, Prud.

holocautoma.full: hŏlŏcautōma, ătis, n., = ὁλοκαύτωμα, a whole burnt-offering, holocaust, Tert. adv. Jud. 5; id. adv. Marc. 5, 5 fin.; Vulg. Jer. 6, 20; id. Ev. Marc. 12, 33 al. (in some edd. falsely holocaustoma).
holocautoma.short: hŏlŏcautōma, ătis, n., = ὁλοκαύτωμα, a whole burnt-offering, holocaust, Tert.

holochrysus.full: hŏlŏchrȳsus, i, f., = ὁλόχρυσος, a plant, otherwise unknown, Plin. 21, 8, 24, § 48; 21, 20, 85, § 148; App. Herb. 128.
holochrysus.short: hŏlŏchrȳsus, i, f., = ὁλόχρυσος, a plant, otherwise unknown, Plin.

holocyron.full: hŏlŏcўron, i, n., = ὁλόκυρον, a plant, called also chamaepitys, ground-pine, App. Herb. 26.
holocyron.short: hŏlŏcўron, i, n., = ὁλόκυρον, a plant, called also chamaepitys, ground-pine, App.

holographus.full: hŏlŏgrăphus, a, um, adj., = ὁλόγραφος, entirely autograph (late Lat.): epistula, entirely written by one's own hand, autograph, Hier. adv. Ruf. 3, 5: membrana, Sid. Ep. 9, 11 med.: testamentum, Isid. Orig. 5, 24.
holographus.short: hŏlŏgrăphus, a, um, adj., = ὁλόγραφος, entirely autograph (late Lat.): epistula, entirely written by one's own hand, autograph, Hier.

holoporphyrus.full: hŏlŏporphўrus, a, um, adj., = ὁλοπόρφυρος, entirely purple: stola, Varr. ap. Non. 537, 30: vestis, Isid. Orig. 19, 22, 14.
holoporphyrus.short: hŏlŏporphўrus, a, um, adj., = ὁλοπόρφυρος, entirely purple: stola, Varr.

holoschoenos.full: hŏloschoenos, i, m., = ὁλόσχοινος, a sort of rush, Plin. 21, 18, 69, § 113.
holoschoenos.short: hŏloschoenos, i, m., = ὁλόσχοινος, a sort of rush, Plin.

holosericus.full: hŏlŏsērĭcus, a, um, adj., = ὁλοσηρικός, all of silk: vestis, Lampr. Heliog. 20; Vop. Aur. 45; id. Tac. 10; Cod. Th. 15, 9, 1. —Collat. form, hŏlŏsērĭcātus, a, um, Aug. in Psa. 85, 3.
holosericus.short: hŏlŏsērĭcus, a, um, adj., = ὁλοσηρικός, all of silk: vestis, Lampr.

holosiderus.full: hŏlŏsĭdērus, a, um, adj., = ὁλοσίδηρος, all iron: spatula, Theod. Prisc. 1, 28.
holosiderus.short: hŏlŏsĭdērus, a, um, adj., = ὁλοσίδηρος, all iron: spatula, Theod.

holosphyratus.full: hŏlosphȳrātus, a, um, adj., = ὁλοσφύρᾶτος (Doric for ὁλοσφύρητος, all hammered), beaten, solid: aes, Plin. 33, 4, 24, § 82.
holosphyratus.short: hŏlosphȳrātus, a, um, adj., = ὁλοσφύρᾶτος (Doric for ὁλοσφύρητος, all hammered), beaten, solid: aes, Plin.

holosteon.full: hŏlostĕon, i, n., = ὁλόστεον, a whitish plantain, Plantago albicans, Linn.; Plin. 27, 10, 65, § 91.
holosteon.short: hŏlostĕon, i, n., = ὁλόστεον, a whitish plantain, Plantago albicans, Linn.;

holothuria.full: hŏlŏthūrĭa, ōrum, n., = ὁλοθούρια, τά, a sort of water-polype, Holothuria priapus, Linn.; Plin. 9, 47, 71, § 154.
holothuria.short: hŏlŏthūrĭa, ōrum, n., = ὁλοθούρια, τά, a sort of water-polype, Holothuria priapus, Linn.;

holoverus.full: hŏlŏvērus, a, um, adj. vox hybr. from ὅλος-verus, quite real; entirely of purple: vestimenta, Cod. Th. 10, 21, 3.

holus.full: hŏlus (better than ŏlus; archaic he-lus; cf.: helus et helusa antiqui dicebant, quod nunc holus et holera, Paul. ex Fest. p. 100 Müll. A form, holu, anciently helu, can be inferred from helvola, helvella, and olvatum; v. Müll. Paul. ex Fest. p. 203, b), ĕris (gen. plur. holerorum for holerum, Lucil. ap. Non. 490, 25; dat. plur. holeris for holeribus, Cato, R. R.), n. Sanscr. haris, green; Gr. χλόη; cf.: helvus. helvola, Helvius; O. H. Germ. grucni; Germ. grün; Engl. green, etc.. Kitchen or garde

holusculum.full: hŏluscŭlum, i, n. dim. holus, a small herb or vegetable, a little cabbage (class.), Cic. Att. 6, 1, 13; Hor. S. 2, 6, 64; Juv. 11, 79; Gell. 19, 7, 1.

homeltium.full: homeltium pilei genus, Paul. ex Fest. p. 103 Müll.

homeriacus.full: Hŏmērĭăcus, Hŏmērĭcus, and Hŏmērius, a, um, and Hŏmērista, ae, v. Homerus.
homeriacus.short: Hŏmērĭăcus, Hŏmērĭcus, and Hŏmērius, a, um, and Hŏmērista, ae, v.

homerocento.full: Hŏmērŏcento, ōnis, m. Homeruscento, a poem made up of verses from Homer, Tert. de Praescr. 39; Hier. Ep. 103, 7.

homeromastix.full: Hŏmērŏmastix, īgis, m., = Ὁμηρομάστιξ (Homer's scourge), the censurer of Homer. Lit., an epithet given to the critic Zoilus, Vitr. 7 praef.— Transf., in gen., a censorious person: ut obiter caveam istos Homeromastigas, etc., Plin. H. N. praef. § 28.
homeromastix.short: Hŏmērŏmastix, īgis, m., = Ὁμηρομάστιξ (Homer's scourge), the censurer of Homer.

homeronides.full: Hŏmērŏnĭdes, ae, m., v. the foll. art. II. E.

homerus.full: Hŏmērus, i, m., = Ὅμηρος, the Greek poet Homer, Cic. Tusc. 1, 1, 3; 1, 32, 79; id. Rep. 2, 10; id. Brut. 10, 40; id. Arch. 8, 19; id. de Or. 3, 34, 137; Vell. 1, 5, 2; Quint. 10, 1, 47 sq.; Hor. A. P. 359 al.— Derivv. Hŏmērĭcus, a, um, adj., = Ὁμηρικός, of or belonging to Homer, Homeric: versus, Cic. Div. 1, 25, 52; cf. dispositio, Quint. 5, 12, 14: facultas eloquendi, id. 10, 1, 81: more, id. 7, 10, 11: Ajax, Cic. Div. 2, 39, 82; cf. Agamemno, id. Tusc. 3, 26, 62: senex, i. e. Nestor, Plin. Ep.
homerus.short: Hŏmērus, i, m., = Ὅμηρος, the Greek poet Homer, Cic.

homicida.full: hŏmĭcīda, ae, comm. homo-caedo, a man-slayer, homicide, a murderer, murderess (syn.: interfector, sicarius, percussor). Lit.: statuendum tibi esse, utrum illi, qui istam rem gesserunt, homicidaene sint, an vindices libertatis ... Confiteor eos plus quam sicarios, plus quam homicidas, plus etiam quam parricidas esse, Cic. Phil. 2, 12, 30 sq.; Juv. 2, 26; Quint. 7, 3, 34: an, qui se interficit, homicida sit, id. 7, 3, 7: mandatores caedis perinde ut homicidae puniuntur, Paul. Sent. 5, 23, 11: qui,

homicidalis.full: hŏmĭcīdālis, e, adj. homicida, homicidal, murderous (late Lat.), Pseudo-Hilar. in Job, 1, p. 101.

homicidarius.full: hŏmĭcīdārĭus or hŏmŏcīdĭā-rĭus, a, um, adj. homicida and homicidium, of or relating to man-slaying, homicidal: sanguis, Auct. Pan. ad Const. 4.
homicidarius.short: hŏmĭcīdārĭus or hŏmŏcīdĭā-rĭus, a, um, adj.

homicidium.full: hŏmĭcīdĭum, ĭi, n. homicida, manslaughter, homicide, murder (post-class.): si quis homicidii accusetur, Quint. 3, 10, 1; 4, 2, 52; 11, 3, 59; Petr. 137; Plin. 18, 3, 3, § 12; Tac. G. 21.

homo.full: hŏmo, ĭnis (archaic form hemonem hominem dicebant, Paul. ex Fest. p. 100 Müll.; cf. humanus init., and nēmo, from nĕ-hĕmo: homōnem, Enn. ap. Prisc. p. 683 P. = Ann. v. 141 Vahl.: hŏmōnes, Naev. 1, 1), comm. root in humus, Gr. χαμαί; cf. Germ. -gam in Bräutigam; O. H. Germ. gomo; Goth. guma; Old Engl. goom; Engl. groom; cf. also Gr. ἐπιχθόνιοι; Hebr. Adam, a human being, man. Lit. In gen.: animal hoc providum, sagax, multiplex, acutum, memor, plenum rationis et consilii quem vocamus hominem, prae
homo.short: hŏmo, ĭnis (archaic form hemonem hominem dicebant, Paul.

homocidalis.full: hŏmŏcīdālis, e, adj. homo-caedo, murderous: animus suus, Anon. (Hilar.) in Job, 1, p. 101.

homoeomeria.full: hŏmoeŏmĕrīa, ae, f., = ὁμοιομέρεια; in the philosophy of Anaxagoras, the homogeneousness of the elements or first principles, Lucr. 1, 830; Serv. Verg. A. 4, 625.

homoeopropheron.full: hŏmoeŏprŏphĕron, i, n., = ὁμοιοπρόφερον, alliteration, as in the verse of Ennius (ap. Prisc. p. 947 P. = Ann. v. 113 Vahl.): o Tite tute Tati tibi tanta tyranne tulisti, Mart. Cap. 5, § 514.
homoeopropheron.short: hŏmoeŏprŏphĕron, i, n., = ὁμοιοπρόφερον, alliteration, as in the verse of Ennius (ap.

homoeoptoton.full: hŏmoeoptōton, i, n., = ὁμοιόπτωτον, similar case-endings, Mart. Cap. 5, § 532; Charis. 251 P.; cf. Quint. 9, 3, 78 sqq.
homoeoptoton.short: hŏmoeoptōton, i, n., = ὁμοιόπτωτον, similar case-endings, Mart.

homoeoteleuton.full: hŏmoeŏtĕleuton, i, n., = ὁμοιοτέλευτον, like ending, rhyme, Mart. Cap. 5, § 532; Charis. 251 P.
homoeoteleuton.short: hŏmoeŏtĕleuton, i, n., = ὁμοιοτέλευτον, like ending, rhyme, Mart.

homole.full: Hŏmŏlē, ēs, f., = Ὁμόλη, a high mountain in Thessaly, near Tempe, Verg. A. 7, 675.—At the foot of it was the city Hŏmŏlĭum, Plin. 4, 9, 16, § 32; Liv. 42, 38, 10.— Deriv. Hŏmŏlōĭ-des, um, f. (sc. portae), = Ὁμολωίδες πύλαι, the Homoloian gate in Thebes (so named from the Cadmeans, who came from Mount Homole), Stat. Th. 7, 252.
