homole.short: Hŏmŏlē, ēs, f., = Ὁμόλη, a high mountain in Thessaly, near Tempe, Verg.

homologus.full: hŏmŏlŏgus, i, m., = ὁμόλογος, a later colonist, Cod. Theod. 11, 24, 6, § 3.
homologus.short: hŏmŏlŏgus, i, m., = ὁμόλογος, a later colonist, Cod.

homonymia.full: hŏmōnўmĭa, ae, f., = ὁμωνυμία, homonymy, Fronto, Diff. Verb. p. 353.
homonymia.short: hŏmōnўmĭa, ae, f., = ὁμωνυμία, homonymy, Fronto, Diff.

homonymus.full: hŏmōnўmus, a, um, adj., = ὁμώνυμος, of the same name, homonymous: sicut in his, quae homonyma vocantur: ut, Taurus animal sit, an mons, an signum in caelo, an nomen hominis, an radix arboris, nisi distinctum non intelligitur, Quint. 8, 2, 13.
homonymus.short: hŏmōnўmus, a, um, adj., = ὁμώνυμος, of the same name, homonymous: sicut in his, quae homonyma vocantur: ut, Taurus animal sit, an mons, an signum in caelo, an nomen hominis, an radix arboris, nisi distinctum non intelligitur, Quint.

homotonus.full: hŏmŏtŏnus, a, um, adj., = ὁμότονος, stretched alike or in unison: nervi, funes, etc., Vitr. 1, 1 med.
homotonus.short: hŏmŏtŏnus, a, um, adj., = ὁμότονος, stretched alike or in unison: nervi, funes, etc., Vitr.

homousius.full: hŏmŏūsius, a, um, adj., = ὁμοούσιος, of like substance, consubstantial (Lat. consubstantialis): Trinitas, Hier. Ep. 77, 2.
homousius.short: hŏmŏūsius, a, um, adj., = ὁμοούσιος, of like substance, consubstantial (Lat.

homullulus.full: hŏmullŭlus, i, m. dim. homullus, a manikin, Prisc. p. 614 P.

homullus.full: hŏmullus, i, m. dim. homo, a little man, manikin: brevis hic est fructus homullis, Lucr. 3, 914: quid cessat hic homullus, ex argilla et luto fictus Epicurus, etc., Cic. Pis. 25, 59.

homuncio.full: hŏmuncĭo, ōnis, m. dim. id., a little man, manikin: ego homuncio hoc non facerem? Ter. Eun. 3, 5, 42: homuncio hic, qui multa putat praeter virtutem homini cara esse (opp. deus), Cic. Ac. 2, 43, 134: (Augustus Horatium) inter alios jocos homuncionem lepidissimum appellat, Suet. Vit. Hor.; Sen. Ep. 116, 6: quadringenta tibi si quis deus aut similis dis homuncio, Juv. 5, 133.

homuncionitae.full: hŏmuncĭōnītae, ārum, m. homuncio, a Christian sect who considered Jesus as man only, Prud. Apoth. 552 in lemm.

homunculus.full: hŏmuncŭlus, i, m. dim. homo, a little or weakly man, a manikin: hui, Homunculi quanti estis! Plaut. Rud. 1, 2, 66; id. Capt. prol. 51; cf. id. Trin. 2, 4, 90: hem! nos homunculi indignamur, si quis, etc., Sulpic. ap. Cic. Fam. 4, 5, 4: neque tam desipiens fuisset, ut homunculis similem deum fingeret, Cic. N. D. 1, 44, 123: ut homunculus unus e multis, etc., id. Tusc. 1, 9, 17; cf.: humilis homunculus, id. ib. 5, 23, 64; App. M. 9, p. 222.

honestamentum.full: hŏnestāmentum, i, n. honesto, an ornament, grace (rare; not in Cic.): nullo honestamento eget virtus, Sen. Ep. 66, 2.— In plur.: omnia honestamenta pacis, Sall. Or. ad Caes. 2: morum, App. Mag. p. 276: orationis, Gell. 10, 26, 4; Cod. Theod. 12, 1, 4.

honestas.full: hŏnestas, ātis, f. honestus, honorableness. (Acc. to honestus, I.) Honorable consideration which a man enjoys, honor, reputation, character, respectability, credit, opp. to turpitudo (class.; cf.: existimatio, dignitas). Lit.: quid est honestas nisi honor perpetuus ad aliquem secundo populi rumore delatus. Lact. 3, 8, fin.: unde pudor, continentia, fuga turpitudinis, appetentia laudis et honestatis? Cic. Rep. 1, 2; cf.: fugiendae turpitudinis adipiscendaeque honestatis causa, id. Tusc. 2, 27, 66

honestitudo.full: hŏnestĭtūdo, ĭnis, f. honestus, honorableness, virtue (ante-class. for honestas, II.): tua honestitudo Danaos decipit diu, Att. ap. Non. 121, 1 (Trag. Fr. v. 501 Rib.): horrida Europae, id. ib. 120, 31 (Fragm. Tr. v. 16 Rib.).

honesto.full: hŏnesto, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. id., to clothe or adorn with honor; to honor, dignify; to adorn, grace, embellish (class.; cf. honoro), with personal or inanimate objects. With personal objects quom me tanto honore honestas, Plaut. Capt. 2, 2, 106; 2, 1, 50; cf.: quod non dignos homines honore honestatos videbam, Sall. C. 35, 3 Kritz.: tantam laudem, quantā vos me vestris decretis honestatis, nemo est assecutus, Cic Cat 4, 10, 20: Saturnini imagine mortem ejus honestare, id. Rab. Perd. 9, 24; id. S

honestus.full: hŏnestus, a um, adj. honos, honor, qs. furnished or clothed with honor, full of honor, honorable. Regarded with honor, enjoying respect or consideration, honored, distinguished, honorable, respectable, noble, = honoratus: qui me honore honestiorem fecit, Plaut. Capt. 2, 3, 32: cum honos sit praemium virtutis judicio studioque civium delatum ad aliquem; qui eum sententiis, qui suffragiis adeptus est, is mihi et honestus et honoratus videtur, etc., Cic. Brut. 81, 281: satis honestam honoratamque i

honor.full: hŏnor or hŏnos (the latter form almost exclusively in Cic., who has honor only Phil. 9, 6 fin., and Fragm. pro Tull. 21; also in Caes., Liv., Sall., Prop., Verg., Nep., and Curt.; but honor in Sen., Vell., Ov.; and Hor. and Tac. use both forms. Honos was antiquated in Quintilian's day, v. Quint. 1, 4, 13; Neue, Formenl. 1, 168 sq.), ōris (archaic gen. honorus, like venerus, Lex Puteol. ap. Haubold, n. 7), m. perh. Sanscr. hu-, call, honor, repute, esteem in which a person or thing is held. Lit.
honor.short: hŏnor or hŏnos (the latter form almost exclusively in Cic., who has honor only Phil.

honorabilis.full: hŏnōrābĭlis, e, adj. honoro, that procures honor or esteem, honorable (very rare): haec ipsa sunt honorabilia quae videntur levia atque communia, salutari, appeti, decedi, assurgi, etc., * Cic. de Sen. 18, 62: personae, Amm. 30, 4, 16: honorabilior omnium, Vulg. Dan. 13, 4.—Adv.: hŏnōrābĭlĭter, honorably: colebatur, Amm. 29, 2; so, sepelire, Capitol. Macr. 5.

honorarium.full: hŏnōrārĭum, ĭi, n., v. honorarius, I. B.

honorarius.full: hŏnōrārĭus, a, um, adj. honor, of or relating to honor, done for the sake of conferring honor, honorary. In gen. Adj. (class.): cum essem in provincia legatus, quamplures ad praetores et consules vinum honorarium dabant: numquam accepi, ne privatus quidem, Cato ap. Isid. Orig. 20, 3: frumentum, Cic. Pis. 35, 86: tumulus, i. e. a cenotaph, Suet. Claud. 1: arbiter, i. e. one chosen out of respect by the parties themselves (opp. to one chosen by the judge), Cic. Tusc. 5, 41, 120; id. Fat. 17, 39; c

honorate.full: hŏnōrātē, adv., v. honoro, P. a. fin.

honoratio.full: hŏnōrātĭo, ōnis, f. honoro, a mark of respect, honor (post-class.), Arn. 7, 221; Mart. Cap. 1, § 7; Paul. ex Fest. s. v. gradivus, p. 97 Müll.

honoratus.full: hŏnōrātus, a, um, Part. and P. a., from honoro.

honoriades.full: Hŏnōrĭădes, ae; -ĭānus, a, um; -ĭas, adis, v. Honorius.

honorificentia.full: hŏnōrĭfĭcentĭa, ae, f. honorificus, a doing of honor, honor (post-class.): imperialis, Symm. Ep. 6, 36; Vop. Aur. 25, 6; Ambros. de Abr. 2, 10, 69; id. de Jacob, 2, 2, 7.

honorifico.full: hŏnōrĭfĭco, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. id., to do honor to, to honor (eccl. Lat.): regem magnum, Lact. 7, 24 fin.: Deum, id. Ira D. 23: Salvatorem, Aug. Ep. 119.

honorificus.full: hŏnōrĭfĭcus, a, um, adj. honor + facio, that does honor, honorable (class.): numquam ab eo mentio de me nisi honorifica, Cic. Phil. 2, 15, 39: cum tu a me rebus amplissimis atque honorificentissimis ornatus esses, id. Fam. 5, 2, 1: orationem meam in te honorificam fuisse, id. ib. § 3: honorificentissima verba, id. Phil. 14, 11, 29: seria partitur (Domitius Marsus) in tria genera, honorificum, contumeliosum, medium, Quint. 6, 3, 108; cf. id. ib. § 6: si quid honorificum pagina blanda sonat, Mart.

honoriger.full: hŏnōrĭger, ĕra, ĕrum, adj. honorgero, that brings honor, honorable (late Lat.): nota virginitatis, Tert. Verg. Vell. 10.

honorinus.full: Hŏnōrīnus, i, m., i. q. Honor, the god of honor, Aug. Civ. Dei, 4, 21 dub. (al. Honor).

honoripeta.full: hŏnōrĭpĕta, ae. m. honor-peto, striving for honors, ambitious, App. Dogm. Plat. 2, p. 20.

honorius.full: Hŏnōrĭus, ĭi, m., son of the emperor Theodosius I., and brother of Arcadius, the first emperor of the western Roman empire, Claud. Nupt. Hon. 118; Aur. Vict. Epit. 48 fin.— Derivv. Hŏnōrĭānus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to the emperor Honorius, Honorian: thermae, Cod. Theod. 15, 1, 50.— Hŏnōrĭădes, ae, m., a male descendant, son of the emperor Honorius, Claud. Nupt. Hon. et Mar. 341.— Hŏnōrĭas, ădis, f., a female descendant, daughter of the emperor Honorius, Claud. Laud. Seren. 130.
honorius.short: Hŏnōrĭus, ĭi, m., son of the emperor Theodosius I., and brother of Arcadius, the first emperor of the western Roman empire, Claud.

honoro.full: hŏnōro, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. (depon.: Dionysius Platonem in litore occurrens honoratus est, Sol. 1, § 123; 2, § 26; Ampel. 2, 5) [honor], to clothe or adorn with honor; to honor, respect; to adorn, ornament, embellish, decorate (class.; cf. honeste): mortem ejus (Ser. Sulpicii) non monumento sed luctu publico esse honorandam putarem, Cic. Phil. 9, 3, 5: ornandi honorandique potestas, id. ib. 5, 17, 45 Orell. N. cr.: honorandus sum, quia tyrannum occidi (opp. puniendus), Quint. 3, 6, 74; cf. id. 7

honorus.full: hŏnōrus, a, um, adj. honor, analog. with decorus from decor (poet. and in postAug. prose). * Worthy of honor, honorable, Stat. Th. 5, 40.— That confers honor, honorable: carmen, glorifying, Val. Fl. 4, 342: fama, Stat. Th. 2, 629: mors, id. ib. 4, 230: oratio, Tac. A. 1, 10 fin.: quae in Drusum patrem Germanici honora et magnifica Augustus fecisset, id. ib. 3, 5: honora de Germanico disserebat, id. ib. 4, 68.

honus.full: hŏnus and hŏnustus, v. onus init.

hoplites.full: hoplītes, ae, m., = ὁπλίτης, a heavyarmed man, Plin. 35, 10, 36, § 71, v. Sillig. ad h. l.
hoplites.short: hoplītes, ae, m., = ὁπλίτης, a heavyarmed man, Plin.

hoplomachus.full: hoplŏmăchus, i, m., = ὁπλομάχος, a heavy-armed combatant, a sort of gladiator, Suet. Calig. 35; Mart. 8, 74, 1; Firm. Math. 8, 21; Inscr. Orell. 2566.
hoplomachus.short: hoplŏmăchus, i, m., = ὁπλομάχος, a heavy-armed combatant, a sort of gladiator, Suet.

hora1.full: hōra, ae (archaic gen. sing. horāï, Lucr. 1, 1016.—In abl. plur. HORABVS, Inscr. Orell. 4601), f. kindred with ὥρα; Zend yare, year; ayara, day; orig. for ϝοsara, from ϝέαρ, ver, (lit., a definite space of time, fixed by natural laws; hence, as in Greek). An hour. Lit. (among the Romans, of varying length, according to the time of year, from sunrise to sunset being reckoned as twelve hours; cf.: aetas, aevum, tempus, dies): aestiva, Mart. 12, 1, 4; cf.: viginti milia passuum horis quinque duntax

hora2.full: Hō^ra, ae, f. perh. an old form for hĕra, lady, the wife of Quirinus (Romulus), who was worshipped as a goddess (called, before her death, Hersilia, Ov. M. 14, 830): Quirine pater, veneror, Horamque Quirini, Enn. ap. Non. 120, 2 (Ann. v. 121 Vahl.): Hora Quirini, Gell. 13, 22, 2; cf.: pariter cum corpore nomen Mutat Horamque vocat, Ov. M. 14, 851.

horaeus.full: hōraeus, a, um, adj., = ὡραῖος (sc. τάριχος), salted in season: scomber, pickled mackerel, Plaut. Capt. 4, 2, 71.

horalis.full: hōrālis, e, adj. hora, of or belonging to an hour (late Lat.): spatium, i. e., of an hour, Venant. Vit. S. Mart. 4, 364.

horarium.full: hōrārĭum, ĭi, n. id., a dial, clock (late Lat.), Censorin. de Die Nat. 23 med.

horatius1.full: Hŏrātĭus, a, name of a Roman gens. Horatii, the three brothers, in the time of Tullus Hostilius, who fought against the Alban Curiatii, Liv. 1, 24 sq.— Horatius Cocles, who, in the war with Porsenna, defended a bridge single-handed, Liv. 2, 10.— Q. Horatius Flaccus, the famous Augustan poet, Juv. 7, 62.—In fem.: Hŏ-rātĭa, ae, the sister of the Horatii, Liv. 1, 26 fin.— Derivv. Hŏrātĭus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to a Horatius, Horatian: gens, Liv. 1, 26: virtus, Verg. Cul. 359: lex, Liv. 3, 5
horatius1.short: Hŏrātĭus, a, name of a Roman gens.

horatius2.full: Hŏrātĭus, a, um, adj., v. 1. Horatius, II. A.

horconia.full: horconia, ae, f., a sort of wine in Campania, Plin. 14, 2, 4, § 35.
horconia.short: horconia, ae, f., a sort of wine in Campania, Plin.

horctum.full: horctum et forctum pro bono dicebant, Paul. ex Fest. p. 102 Müll.: cf. fortis init.
horctum.short: horctum et forctum pro bono dicebant, Paul.

horda.full: horda, ae, f., archaic i. q. forda, a cow that is with calf: quae sterilis est vacca, taura appellata; quae praegnans, horda: ab eo in fastis dies hordicalia nominantur, quod tunc hordae boves immolantur, Varr. R. R. 2, 5, 6; v. fordus.

hordeaceus.full: hordĕācĕus (or ord-), a, um, adj. hordeum, of or relating to barley, barley-: farina, Cato, R. R. 157, 5; Plin. 20, 13, 51, § 135: panis, id. 18, 11, 26, § 103: farrago, Col. 11, 2, 99: messis, Plin. 18, 29, 71, § 295: pira, barley-pears, i. e., ripe at the barleyharvest, Col. 5, 10, 18.

hordearius.full: hordĕārĭus (also ordearius and hordĭarius), a, um, adj. id., of or relat. ing to barley, barley-: pira, barley-pears, i. e. pears that are ripe at barley-harvest, Plin. 15, 15, 16, § 55 (also called hordeacea pira, Col. 5, 10, 18); so, pruna, Plin. 15, 13, 12, § 41: hordiarium aes, quod pro hordeo equiti Romano dabatur, Paul. ex Fest. p. 102 Müll.; cf. Liv. 1, 43, 9 (Weissenb. ad loc.): Gai. Inst. 4, 27: antiquissimum in cibis hordeum, sicut Atheniensium ritu apparet et gladiatorum cognomine, qu
hordearius.short: hordĕārĭus (also ordearius and hordĭarius), a, um, adj.

hordeius.full: hordēĭus, a, um, adj. id., of or relating to barley, barley-: lolligiunculae, Plaut. Casin. 2, 8, 58.

hordeolus.full: hordeŏlus, i, m. dim. id., a sty in the eye, Marc. Empir. 8; Isid. 4, 8, 16.

hordeum.full: hordĕum (also ordeum, and arch. fordeum acc. to Quint. 1, 4, 14), i. n. Sanscr. root ghars-, to rub, grind; O. H. Germ. Gers-ta, barley, Plin. 18, 7, 10, § 58; Cato, R. R. 35, 2; Varr. R. R. 2, 4, 6; Col. 2, 9, 3 sq.; Liv. 27, 13, 9; Suet. Aug. 24: frugibus legatis hordeum continetur, Paul. Sent. 3, 6, 78.—In plur., Verg. E. 5, 36; id. G. 1, 317; on account of this plur. he was abused by the poet Bavius; v. Bavius; cf. also: hordea et mulsa non alio vitiosa sunt, quam quod singularia pluraliter

horesti.full: Horesti, ōrum, m., a tribe in North Britain, in the modern Stirling, or the north part of Lanark, Tac. Agr. 38 (al. Boresti).
horesti.short: Horesti, ōrum, m., a tribe in North Britain, in the modern Stirling, or the north part of Lanark, Tac.

horia.full: hŏrĭa (oria), ae, f., a small vessel, a fishing-smack (cf.: celox, catascopium, prosumia, lembus, etc.): horia navicula piscatoria, Non. 533, 20; Plaut. Rud. 4, 2, 5; 4, 3, 81; Gell. 10, 25, 5.
horia.short: hŏrĭa (oria), ae, f., a small vessel, a fishing-smack (cf.: celox, catascopium, prosumia, lembus, etc.): horia navicula piscatoria, Non.

horiola.full: hŏrĭŏla, ae, f. dim. horia, a skiff, fishing-boat, Plaut. Trin. 4, 2, 100; Gell. 10, 25, 5.

horior.full: hŏrĭor, hori, and hŏrĭtor, āri, v. dep. prim. forms of hortor, from the root ΟΡΩ, whence ὄρνυμι, ὁρμή, ὁρμάω, etc., to urge, incite, encourage: hortatur quod vulgo dicimus, veteres nonnulli horitur dixerunt, ut Ennius libro XVI. (29): prandere jubet horiturque. Idem in X. (28): horitatur induperator, Diom. p. 378 P. (Ann. v. 409 and 350 Vahl.).
horior.short: hŏrĭor, hori, and hŏrĭtor, āri, v.

horistice.full: hŏristĭcē, ēs, f., = ὁριστική, the defining or theoretical part of grammar, Diom. p. 421 P.
horistice.short: hŏristĭcē, ēs, f., = ὁριστική, the defining or theoretical part of grammar, Diom.

horizon.full: hŏrīzon, ontis, m., = ὁρίζων (sc. κύκλος or ἀήρ). The horizon (pure Lat. finiens and finitor), Macr. Somn. Scip. 1, 15 fin.; id. S. 7, 14 fin.; Hyg. Astr. 1, 4.— A line drawn through the centre of a sundial, Vitr. 9, 8.

hormenos.full: hormĕnos, i, m., = ὅρμενος, the Greek name of wild asparagus, Plin. 19, 8, 42, § 151 (as Greek, Jan.).
hormenos.short: hormĕnos, i, m., = ὅρμενος, the Greek name of wild asparagus, Plin.

horminum.full: hormīnum, i, n., = ὅρμινον, the herb clary, a kind of sage, Salvia horminum, Linn.; Plin. 22, 25, 76, § 159; 18, 10, 22, § 96.
horminum.short: hormīnum, i, n., = ὅρμινον, the herb clary, a kind of sage, Salvia horminum, Linn.;

hormiscion.full: hormiscĭon, ĭi, n., = ὁρμίσκος, a precious stone, otherwise unknown, Plin. 37, 10, 60, § 168.
hormiscion.short: hormiscĭon, ĭi, n., = ὁρμίσκος, a precious stone, otherwise unknown, Plin.

hornotinus.full: hornōtĭnus, a, um, adj. hornus, of this year, this year's: nuces, Cato, R. R. 17, 2: frumentum, Cic. Verr. 2, 3, 18, § 45: virgae, Col. 5, 6 fin.

hornus.full: hornus, a, um, adj. contr. for hōrinus = ὥρινος from ὥρα, of this year, this year's (not in Cic.; but cf. hornotinus): agni, Prop. 4, (5), 3, 61: fruge, Hor. C. 3, 23, 3: vina, id. Epod. 2, 47: palea, id. S. 2, 6, 88. —Adv.: horno, this year: utrum anno an horno te abstuleris a viro? Lucil. ap. Non. 121, 8: horno messis magna fuit, Plaut. Most. 1, 3, 3; Varr. ap. Non. 121, 10.

horologiaris.full: hōrŏlŏgĭāris, e, adj. horologium, of or belonging to a horologe or clock: TEMPLVM, i. e. provided with a clock, Inscr. Orell. 1276; cf. abbrev., HOROLOGIAR. TEMPLVM, id. 925.

horologicus.full: hōrŏlŏgĭcus, a, um, adj., = ὡρολογικός, of or belonging to a clock: vasa, Mart. Cap. 6, 194.
horologicus.short: hōrŏlŏgĭcus, a, um, adj., = ὡρολογικός, of or belonging to a clock: vasa, Mart.

horologium.full: hōrŏlŏgĭum, ĭi, n., = ὡρολόγιον, a clock, horologe, either a sundial or a waterclock, Plin. 2, 76, 78, § 187; 7, 60, 60, § 213; Varr. R. R. 3, 5, 17; Cic. Fam. 16, 18, 2; Vitr. 9, 8 sq.; Inscr. Orell. 2032; 3298 sq.
horologium.short: hōrŏlŏgĭum, ĭi, n., = ὡρολόγιον, a clock, horologe, either a sundial or a waterclock, Plin.

horoscopicus.full: hōroscŏpĭcus, a, um, adj. horoscopus, indicating the hour: vasa, Plin. 2, 72, 74, § 182.— Relating to nativities: libri, Fulg. Myth. 1, 12 al.—As subst.: hōroscŏ-pĭca, ae, f., the casting of nativities, Mythogr. Lat. 3, 13.

horoscopium.full: hōroscŏpīum or -pĭum, ii, n., = ὡροσκοπεῖον or -σκόπιον, an instrument used in the casting of nativities, Sid. Ep. 4, 3.
horoscopium.short: hōroscŏpīum or -pĭum, ii, n., = ὡροσκοπεῖον or -σκόπιον, an instrument used in the casting of nativities, Sid.

horoscopo.full: hōroscŏpo, āre, v. n., = ὡροσκοπέω, to take the time of one's nativity, to draw a horoscope, Manil. 3, 296; Firm. Math. 5, 1.

horoscopus.full: hōroscŏpus, a, um, adj., = ὡροσκόπος, that shows the hour. Adj.: vasa, Plin. 2, 72, 74, § 182; Mart. Cap. 6, § 595.— Subst.: horoscopus, i. m., a nativity, horoscope, Pers. 6, 18; Manil. 3, 190; 200 sq.; Aug. Civ. Dei, 5, 2 sq.
horoscopus.short: hōroscŏpus, a, um, adj., = ὡροσκόπος, that shows the hour.

horrearius.full: horrĕārĭus, ĭi, m. horreum, the superintendent of a storehouse or magazine, Dig. 19, 2, 60, § 9; 9, 3, 5, § 3; 10, 4, 5; Inscr. Orell. 3214 al.

horreaticus.full: horrĕātĭcus, a, um, adj. id., of or belonging to a storehouse: species, i. e. the corn stored up in a magazine Cod. Theod. 11, 14, 3.

horrende.full: horrendē, adv., v. horreo, P. a. fin.

horrentia.full: horrentĭa, ae, f. horreo, a shuddering, horror (post-class. for horror), Tert. adv. Marc. 4, 24.

horreo.full: horrĕo, ui, ēre, v. n. and a. [for horseo, kindred to Sanscr. hrish, to stand erect, to bristle], to stand on end, stand erect, to bristle. Lit. (for the most part only poet.; not in Ciceron. prose): in corpore pili, ut arista in spica hordei, horrent, Varr. L. L. 6, § 49 Müll.; cf.: et setae densis similes hastilibus horrent, Ov. M. 8, 285: saepe horrere sacros doluit Latona capillos, Tib. 2, 3, 23: horrentibus per totum corpus villis, Plin. 8, 40, 61, § 150: horrentes barbae, Petr. 99: horrent

horreolum.full: horrĕŏlum, i, n. dim. horreum, a small barn or granary, Val. Max. 7, 1 fin.

horresco.full: horresco, horrŭi, 3, v. inch. n. and a. [horreo], to rise on end, stand erect, to bristle up, grow rough. Lit. (mostly poet.; cf. horreo): rettulit ille gradus horrueruntque comae, Ov. F. 2, 502: tum segetes altae campique natantes Lenibus horrescunt flabris, Verg. G. 3, 199: bracchia coeperunt nigris horrescere villis, Ov. M. 2, 478; cf.: setis horrescere coepi, id. ib. 14, 279: horrescit telis exercitus asper utrimque, Enn. ap. Macr. S. 6, 4 (Ann. v. 385 Vahl.); cf.: arma rigent, horrescunt te

horreum1.full: horrĕum, i, n. cf.: farreum, farina, a storehouse; esp. for preserving grain, a barn, granary, magazine (syn.: sirus, granarium, cumera): illi Capuam cellam atque horreum Campani agri esse voluerunt, Cic. Agr. 2, 33, 89: si proprio condidit horreo, Quicquid de Libycis verritur areis, Hor. C. 1, 1, 9; Cic. Verr. 2, 3, 8, § 20; Caes. B. C. 3, 42, 4: illius immensae ruperunt horrea messes, Verg. G. 1, 49; cf. Tib. 2, 5, 84: si, quicquid arat impiger Appulus, Occultare meis dicerer horreis, Hor. C.

horreum2.full: Horrĕum, i, n., a city of Molossis in Epirus, of uncertain site, Liv. 45, 26, 10.
horreum2.short: Horrĕum, i, n., a city of Molossis in Epirus, of uncertain site, Liv.

horribilis.full: horrĭbĭlis, e, adj. horreo, terrible, fearful, dreadful, horrible (freq. and class.). Lit.: quod hanc tam tetram, tam horribilem tamque infestam rei publicae pestem toties jam effugimus, Cic. Cat. 1, 5, 11: homini accidere nihil posse, quod sit horribile aut pertimescendum, id. Fam. 5, 21 fin.: species, * Caes. B. G. 7, 36, 2: spectaculum, Sall. J. 101, 11: sonitus, id. ib. 99, 2: di magni, horribilem et sacrum libellum! Cat. 14, 12: tempestas, Cic. Rep. 2, 6: formidines, id. Fin. 1, 19, 63: hor

horricomis.full: horrĭcŏmis, e, adj. horreo-coma, with hair on end, bristly, shaggy (Appuleian): canes, App. M. 4, p. 151: hircus, id. ib. 7, p. 192.

horridulus.full: horrĭdŭlus, a, um, adj. dim. [horridus], standing up, projecting forth, protuberant; rough, rugged, rude. Lit.: papillae, Plaut. Ps. 1, 1, 66: caput ungunt horridulum, Lucil. ap. Non. 423, 1: puer, Mart. 10, 98, 9: comes, shabby, poor, Pers. 1, 54. — Trop., of discourse or style, rude, rough, unpolished, simple, unadorned: tua illa horridula mihi atque incomta visa sunt, Cic. Att. 2, 1, 1: orationes Catonis, id. Or. 45, 152: horridula ejus verba et rudia flosculos Tullianos appellans, Amm. 29, 1

horridus.full: horrĭdus, a, um, adj. horreo, standing on end, sticking out, rough, shaggy, bristly, prickly: non hac barbula, qua ista delectatur, sed illa horrida, quam in statuis antiquis et imaginibus videmus, Cic. Cael. 14, 33: caesaries, Ov. M. 10, 139: pluma, id. Am. 2, 6, 5: apes horridi pili, Col. 9, 3, 1; cf.: apes horridae aspectu, Plin. 11, 18, 19, § 59: sus, Verg. G. 4, 407; cf.: videar tibi amarior herbis, Horridior rusco, id. E. 7, 42: densis hastilibus horrida myrtus, id. A. 3, 23; cf.: arbor sp

horrifer.full: horrĭfer, ĕra, ĕrum (archaic gen. plur. horriferum, Pac. ap. Cic. Or. 46, 155), adj. horror-fero, that brings trembling or terror, terrible, dreadful, horrible, horrific (poet.): unde horrifer Aquiloni' stridor gelidas molitur nives, Att. ap. Cic. Tusc. 1, 28, 68: Boreas, Ov. M. 1, 65; 15, 471: axis, Val. Fl. 5, 518: nix, id. 5, 307: prodigium horriferum, Pac. ap. Cic. Or. 46, 155: aestus (Tartari), Lucr. 3, 1012: Aegis (= δεινή, Hom.), Verg. A. 8, 435: Erinys, Ov. M. 1, 725: voces, Lucr. 5, 996

horrificabilis.full: horrĭfĭcābĭlis, e, adj. horrificus, causing terror, horrific: luctus, Att. ap. Non. 226, 4 (Trag. Rel. v. 617 Rib.).

horrifico.full: horrĭfĭco, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. horrificus, to make rough or terrible, to cause terror (poet. and in post-Aug. prose): flatu placidum mare matutino Horrificans Zephyrus, ruffling, = crispans, Cat. 64, 271: ore ferarum Et rictu horrificant galeas, Sil. 3, 389: carcer, catenae, fuga, exsilium horrificaverant dignitatem, had made terrible, Flor. 3, 21, 10 Duk.: mentes, Claud. Bell. Get. 250.—Absol.: multaque praeterea vatum praedicta piorum Terribili monitu horrificant, cause horror, Verg. A. 4, 465

horrificus.full: horrĭfĭcus, a, um, adj. horror-facio, that causes tremor or terror, terrible, dreadful, frightful, horrific (poet. and in postAug. prose): bustum, Lucr. 3, 906: letum, Verg. A. 12, 851: ruinae (Aetnae), id. ib. 3, 571: lapsu (Harpyiarum), id. ib. 3, 225: fulmen, Val. Fl. 2, 97: acta, id. 3, 423: caesaries, Luc. 2, 372: poena, Gell. 20, 1 fin.— Adv.: horrĭfĭcē, in a manner to cause dread, with affright: horrifice fertur divinae Matris imago, Lucr. 2, 609; 4, 36.

horripilatio.full: horrĭpĭlātĭo, ōnis, f. horripilo, a bristling of the hair, Vulg. Eccl. 27, 15.

horripilo.full: horrĭpĭlo, āre, v. n. horreo-pilus, to bristle with hairs, be shaggy (post-class.): aures immodicis horripilant auctibus, App. M. 3, p. 140: horripilo ὀρθοτριχάω, horripilatur ὀρθοτριχεῖ, Gloss. Philox.

horrisonus.full: horrĭsŏnus, a, um, adj. horreo-sonus, sounding dreadfully, that makes a horrid sound (poet.): fretum, Cic. poët. Tusc. 2, 10, 23; cf. flatus, Luc. 2, 455: fragor, Lucr. 5, 109: fremitus, Verg. A. 9, 55: cardo, id. ib. 6, 573: buxus, Val. Fl. 2, 584: flagellum, id. 7, 149.

horror.full: horror, ōris, m. horreo, a standing on end, standing erect, bristling. Lit. (only poet. and very rare): comarum, Luc. 5, 154; Val. Fl. 1, 229: pontus non horrore tremit, i. e. was not ruffled, agitated, Luc. 5, 446; cf.: montes horrore nivali semper obducti, Amm. 15, 10, 1.—* Trop., roughness, rudeness of speech: veterem illum horrorem malim quam istam novam licentiam, Quint. 8, 5, 34.— Transf. (cf. horreo, II.). A shaking, trembling. In gen. (poet. and in post-Aug. prose): tremulo ramos horrore

horsum.full: horsum, adv. contr. from hoc = huc and vorsum, hitherwards, hither, this way (ante-class.): pergunt, Ter. Hec. 3, 4, 36: horsum se capessit, Plaut. Rud. 1, 2, 83; id. Mil. 2, 3, 33: te adiget horsum insomnia Ter. Eun. 2, 1, 13.

hortalus.full: Hortălus, i, m., surname of the orator Q. Hortensius and his descendants, Cic. Att. 2, 25, 1; 4, 15, 4; Suet. Tib. 47; Tac. A. 2, 37.
hortalus.short: Hortălus, i, m., surname of the orator Q.

hortamen.full: hortāmen, ĭnis, n. hortor, an incitement, encouragement, exhortation (not anteAug.): non est hortamine longo Nunc, ait, utendum, Ov. M. 1, 277: Decii eventus, ingens hortamen ad omnia pro re publica audenda, Liv. 10, 29, 5: clamoris et verberis, Pall. Mart. 11, 3.—In plur.: hortamina, laudes, Val. Fl. 6, 93: cibos et hortamina pugnantibus gestant, Tac. G. 7 fin.

hortamentum.full: hortāmentum, i, n. id., an incitement, encouragement (not in Cic. or Cæs.) ea cuncta Romanis hortamento erant, Sall J. 98, 7: celeritatis, Gell. 13, 24, 21: virtutis Just. 3, 5, 9.—In plur.: in conspectu parentum conjugumque ac liberorum, quae magna etiam absentibus hortamenta animi, etc., Liv. 7, 11, 6: victoriae, Tac. H. 4, 18; Lact. 5, 19, 9; 4, 1, 8.

hortanum.full: Hortānum, i, n., a city of Etruria (probably called after the Etruscan goddess Horta, Paul. ex Fest. 4, 8; cf. Müll. Etrusk. II. p. 62), now Orte, Plin. 3, 5, 8, § 52.—Hence, Hortīnus, a, um, of Hortanum: classes, Verg. A. 7, 716.
hortanum.short: Hortānum, i, n., a city of Etruria (probably called after the Etruscan goddess Horta, Paul.

hortatio.full: hortātĭo, ōnis, f. hortor, an encouragement, exhortation (class.): jam hoc loco non hortatione neque praeceptis, sed precibus tecum fraternis ago, Cic. Q. Fr. 1, 1, 14, § 41: hortatio non est necessaria, id. Fam. 9, 14, 7: mihi grata tua est hortatio, id. Fin. 5, 2, 6: ille in castigationem, hic in hortationem amorum compositus, Quint. 3, 8, 54 Spald.: clamor (oppidanorum) permixtus hortatione, etc., Sall. J. 60, 2: remigum, Liv. 40, 4, 12: Hortationes ad philosophiam, the title of a treatise by

hortativus.full: hortātīvus, a, um, adj. hortor, that serves for encouragement or exhortation, hortative: genus (dicendi), Quint. 5, 10, 83: adverbia, i. e. eia, age, etc., Prisc. p. 1021 P.

hortator1.full: hortātor, ōris, m. id., an inciter, encourager, exhorter (class.; cf.: monitor, impulsor, admonitor): cum ejus studii tibi et hortator et magister esset domi, Cic. de Or. 1, 55, 234: studiorum, Quint. 10, 3, 23: scelerum, Verg. A. 6, 529; Ov. M. 13, 45: isto hortatore, auctore, intercessore, Cic. Rosc. Am. 38, 110: hortatore non egetis, id. Phil. 11, 2, 3: hortatore bono, Enn. ap. Fest. p. 363 Müll. (Ann. v. 471 Vahl.): quasi in mari Solet hortator remiges hortarier, Plaut. Merc. 4, 2, 5; cf.: r

hortator2.full: Hortātor, ōris, m. id., a Roman surname, Liv. 8, 15.

hortatorius.full: hortātōrĭus, a, um, adj. hortator, encouraging, cheering (late Lat.): irrisio, Aug. Conf. 8, 11 fin.: mandata, Ambros. Cant. Cantic. 3, 3: locus hortatorius ad fidem, Ambros. in Luc. 8, 30.

hortatrix.full: hortātrix, īcis, f. id., she that incites, encourages, or exhorts: blanda hortatrix voluptas, Pac. Trag. Fragm. v. 195 Rib.: gloria hortatrix animosi leti, Stat. Th. 9, 717: illa velut hortatrix manus, Quint. 11, 3, 103.

hortatus.full: hortātus, ūs, m. id., incitement, encouragement, exhortation (in class. prose only in abl. sing.): haec vox hujus hortatu praeceptisque conformata, nonnullis aliquando saluti fuit, Cic. Arch. 1, 1: aliorum consilio, hortatu, auctoritate, id. Fam. 13, 29, 7: suorum omnium hortatu, Caes. B. C. 3, 86, 1: hortatu suo, Ov. Tr. 5, 14, 46; Luc. 6, 317.—Dat.: hortatui, Macr. S. 7, 5.— With obj. gen.: hortatus laudum, Sil. 12, 67.—In plur., Ov. M. 3, 242; 7, 339; Val. Fl. 3, 550; 4, 81 al.

hortensianus.full: Hortensĭānus, a, um, adj., v. 2. Hortensius, II. B.

hortensis.full: hortensis, e, adj. hortus, of or belonging to a garden, garden-: lira, Col. 9, 4, 4: DII, Inscr. Orell. 1626: IOVIS, Inscr. ap. Marin. Fratr. Arv. p. 390.

hortensius1.full: hortensĭus, a, um, adj. id., of or belonging to a garden, garden-. Adj.: bulbi, Plin. 20, 9, 40, § 105: batis, id. 26, 8, 50, § 82.— Subst., in plur.: horten-sia, ōrum, n., garden-herbs, Plin. 19, 6, 31, § 98; 19, 8, 39, § 131; 26, 4, 10, § 22.

hortensius2.full: Hortensĭus (HORTÉSIVS, Inscr. Fabr. p. 235, n. 619), the name of a Roman gens; so, in partic.: Q. Hortensius Hortalus, a celebrated orator in the time of Cicero, Cic. Brut. 88, 301 sq.; Quint. 11, 3, 8; 12, 11, 27; Gell. 1, 5, 2; Tac. A. 2, 37. After him is named the treatise of Cicero entitled Hortensius, of which fragments remain (Bait. XI. 55 sqq.).—Hortensĭa, ae, f., his daughter, also celebrated for her skill in oratory, Val. Max. 8, 3, 3; cf. Quint. 1, 1, 6.— Derivv. Hortensĭus, a, um, adj

hortinus.full: Hortīnus, a, um, adj., v. Hortanum.

hortor.full: hortor, ātus, 1 (archaic inf. pres. hortarier, Plaut. Merc. 4, 2, 5), v. dep. for horitor, v. horior, to urge one strongly to do a thing, to incite, instigate, encourage, cheer, exhort (freq. and class.; cf.: moneo, admoneo, suadeo). In gen., constr. aliquem, aliquem ad or in aliquid, ut, ne, with the simple subj., de aliqua re, aliquid, with the inf. or absol. With acc. pers.: coquos, Plaut. Merc. 4, 2, 5 sq.: hacc, quae supra scripta sunt, eo spectant, ut te horter et suadeam, Cic. Fam. 13, 4,

hortualis.full: hortŭālis, e, adj. hortus, of or belonging to a garden, garden- (post-class. for hortensis): species strychni, App. Herb. 74: pastinaca, id. ib. 8: herpillos, id. ib. 99.

hortulanus.full: hortŭlānus, a, um, adj. hortulus, of or belonging to a garden, garden- (postclass. for hortensis). Adj.: maritimusque secessus, Tert. Poen. 11: porcellus, i. e. stuffed with garden-herbs, Apic. 8, 7, § 384. — Subst.: hortulanus, i, m., a gardener, Macr. S. 7, 3 med.; App. M. 4, p. 143; 9, p. 235 sq.; Inscr. Orell. 4200.

hortulus.full: hortŭlus, i, m. dim. hortus, a little garden. Lit., Cat. 61, 92; Juv. 3, 226; Plin. 35, 10, 36, § 105; as part of a vineyard, Col. 4, 18, 2.—In plur.: hortuli, garden-grounds, Cic. Off. 3, 14, 58; id. Fin. 5, 1, 2; id. Clu. 13, 37; Col. 4, 18, 2.— Transf.: Cupidinis, i. e. pudenda muliebria, App. Ἀνεχ. 17.— Trop.: cujus (Democriti) fontibus Epicurus hortulos suos irrigavit, Cic. N. D. 1, 43, 120.

hortus.full: hortus, i, m. cf.: heres, co-hors; χόρτος, an enclosure for plants; hence, a garden, a pleasure - garden, fruit - garden, kitchen - garden, vineyard (syn.: pomarium, viretum, viridarium). Lit.: sed is clam patrem etiam hac nocte illa per hortum transiit ad nos, Plaut. Truc. 2, 1, 37: abii ad hortum nostrum, id. Most. 5, 1, 4; Col. 10, 11, 3; Plin. 19, 4, 19, § 50; Cic. de Sen. 16, 56; id. Off. 3, 14, 58; id. Phil. 2, 6, 15; Lact. 2, 7; 7, 25; Plin. Ep. 2, 17, 15 et saep.: horti Epicuri, in which

horus.full: Hōrus, i, m., Ὧρος, name of the sun among the Egyptians, Macr. S. 1, 21, 13.
horus.short: Hōrus, i, m., Ὧρος, name of the sun among the Egyptians, Macr.

hospes.full: hospĕs, ĭtis (gen. plur. hospitium, Liv. 4, 35, 4), m.; hospĭta, ae, f. (cf. antistita from antistes, sospita from sospes, sacerdota from sacerdos, etc., but hospes, f., Att. ap. Non. 279, 11; Trag. Fragm. v. 51 Rib.: hospes amica, Ov. F. 6, 510: Aurora, Stat. Th. 6, 272; Sen. Agam. 318 al.) [= hostipets, hostis, a stranger; pa-, root of pasco, pater, to feed, hence], He who entertains a stranger, a host (one who entertains gratuitously, as a friend: caupo, one who entertains for pay); form hosp

hospitaculum.full: hospĭtācŭlum,, i, n. hospita, a lodging-house, inn, Dig. 9, 3, 5, § 1.

hospitalis.full: hospĭtālis, e, adj. hospes, of or relating to a guest or host, hospitable, ξένιος, ξενικός. Lit. Adj. (class.): illam ipsam sedem hospitalem, in quam erit deductus, publicam populi Romani esse dicet, Cic. Agr. 2, 17, 46: deversorium, Liv. 21, 63 fin.: cubiculum, guest-chamber, id. 1, 58: beneficia, id. 2, 14 fin.: aves, set before a guest, Varr. R. R. 3, 2, 3; cf.: cena Augusti, Plin. 33, 4, 24, § 83: umbra, Hor. C. 2, 3, 10: tessera, which guests gave to the host, Plaut. Poen. 5, 2, 87 sq.; cf.

hospitalitas.full: hospĭtālĭtas, ātis, f. hospitalis. Hospitality: recte etiam a Theophrasto est laudata hospitalitas, Cic. Off. 2, 18, 64; Mart. 4, 64, 28.—* A being a guest, i. e. a living in a foreign country, a sojourning: lege temporalis hospitalitatis, Macr. Somn. Scip. 1, 21, § 34.

hospitator.full: hospĭtātor, ōris, m. hospitor, a lodger, guest: mei hospitatores, App. M. 4, p. 145, 28.

hospitiolum.full: hospĭtĭŏlum, i, n. dim. hospitium, a little inn (late Lat.), Hier. Ep. 47, 11; 108, 44.

hospitium.full: hospĭtĭum, ĭi, n. hospes. Hospitality (class.): quos ego universos adhiberi liberaliter, optimum quemque hospitio amicitiaque conjungi dico oportere, Cic. Q. Fr. 1, 1, 5, § 16; cf.: quocum mihi amicitiam res publica conciliavit, hospitium voluntas utriusque conjunxit, etc., id. Deiot. 14, 39: gratia atque hospitiis florens hominum nobilissimorum ... cum Metellis, erat ei hospitium, id. Rosc. Am. 6, 15: pro hospitio quod sibi cum eo esset, Cic. Verr. 2, 2, 8, § 23: vetus hospitium renovare, id. D

hospitivus.full: hospĭtīvus, a, um, adj. hospes, of or belonging to a host: viridaria, his host's, Spart. Hadr. 12, 5.

hospitor.full: hospĭtor, ātus, 1, v. dep. n. [id.], to be a guest, to put up, lodge, sojourn as a guest (post-Aug.). Lit.: mensores postibus hospitaturi nomen ascribunt, Cod. Th. 7, 8, 4; Petr. 77, 4.— Transf. (cf. hospitalis, II.): Gangem in quodam lacu hospitari; inde lenem fluere, Plin. 6, 18, 22, § 65: castanea translata nescit hospitari pavetque novitatem, id. 17, 20, 34, § 149.— Trop.: quid aliud voces animum quam deum in humano corpore hospitantem, Sen. Ep. 31; id. Vit. Beat. 23.

hospitus.full: hospĭtus, a, um, occurring only in the fem. sing. and neutr. plur. hospita; v. hospes.
hospitus.short: hospĭtus, a, um, occurring only in the fem.

hostia.full: hostĭa (also fostia), ae, f. 2. hostio, acc. to Paul. ex Fest. p. 102 Müll., an animal sacrificed, a victim, sacrifice (cf.: victima). Lit.: cum Trebatius doceat, hostiarum genera esse duo, unum in quo voluntas dei per exta disquiritur, alterum, in quo sola anima deo sacratur, unde etiam haruspices animales has hostias vocant, Macr. S. 3, 5, 1: illud ex institutis pontificum et haruspicum non mutandum est, quibus hostiis immolandum cuique deo, Cic. Leg. 2, 12, 29: ea prodigia partim majoribus ho

hostiatus.full: hostĭātus, a, um, adj. hostia, provided with victims: candidatas venire hostiatasque, Plaut. Rud. 1, 5, 12.

hosticapas.full: hosticapas, hostium captor, Paul. ex Fest. p. 102 Müll. [hostis-capio; the final s is archaic, as in PARICIDAS for parricida].

hosticus.full: hostĭcus, a, um, adj. hostis. Of or belonging to an enemy, hostile (mostly poet. and in post-Aug. prose; not in Cic. or Cæs.): ager, Liv. 44, 13: tellus, Ov. P. 1, 3, 65: moenia, Hor. C. 3, 2, 6: vindemia, Ov. F. 4, 893: manus, Plaut. Capt. 2, 1, 49; 2, 2, 61: ensis, Hor. S. 1, 9, 31: incursiones, Col. praef. § 19: tumultus, Flor. 3, 10, 17.—In neutr. as subst.: hostĭcum, i, the enemy's territory: castra in hostico incuriose posita, Liv. 8, 38, 2: raptae ex hostico messes, Plin. Pan. 29, 3: tran

hostifer.full: hostĭfer, ĕra, ĕrum, adj. hostis-fero, hostile: quisquam, Manil. 1, 420 dub.

hostificus.full: hostĭfĭcus, a, um, adj. hostis-facio, that deals in a hostile manner, hostile (anteclass.): o dirum hostificumque diem! Att. ap. Non. 485, 24 (Fragm. Trag. v. 80 Rib.): bellum, Cic. Dom. 23, 60.—* Adv.: hostĭ-fĭcē, in a hostile manner, Att. ap. Non. 224, 11 (Fragm. Trag. v. 82 Rib.).

hostilina.full: Hostĭlīna, ae, f. hostio = aequo, a goddess that promotes the growth of corn in equal ears, Aug. Civ. Dei, 3, 8.

hostilis.full: hostīlis, e, adj. hostis. Of or belonging to an enemy, hostile. In gen. (class.): amator simili'st oppidi hostilis, Plaut. Truc. 1, 2, 68: terra, Cic. Inv. 1, 55, 108: manus, id. Tusc. 1, 35, 85: naves, Hor. Epod. 9, 19: domus, id. ib. 5, 53: aratrum, id. C. 1, 16, 21: manus, Plaut. Capt. 2, 2, 61: cadavera, Sall. C. 61, 8: vis, Plaut. Capt. 2, 2, 52: condictiones pactionesque (with bellicae), Cic. Off. 3, 29, 108: minae, Tac. A. 13, 57: metus, of the enemy, Sall. J. 41, 2: spolia, Liv. 29, 35,

hostilitas.full: hostīlĭtas, ātis, f. hostilis, enmity, hostility, Cassiod. Var. 4, 50.

hostilius.full: Hostīlĭus, a, name of a Roman gens. Hostus Hostilius, who fought victoriously against the Sabines, Liv. 1, 12.— His grandson, Tullus Hostilius, the third king of Rome, Liv. 1, 22 sqq.; Cic. N. D. 2, 3, 9.— L. Hostilius Tubulus, prœtor in A. U. C. 611, a rude person, Lucil. ap. Cic. N. D. 1, 23, 63. — Deriv. Hostīlĭus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to a Hostilius, Hostilian: Curia, built by king Tullus Hostilius, Liv. 1, 22; 30; Varr. L. L. 5, § 155 Müll.: Hostiliis Laribus immolabant, quod ab his
hostilius.short: Hostīlĭus, a, name of a Roman gens.

hostimentum.full: hostīmentum, i, n. 1. hostio, a recompense, requital: hostimentum beneficii pensatio, Paul. ex Fest. p. 102 Müll.; cf.: hostimentum est aequamentum, Non. 3, 26 (ante-class.): audi atque auditis hostimentum adjungito, Enn. ap. Fest. p. 270 Müll. (Trag. v. 154 Vahl.): par pari datum hostimentum'st, opera pro pecunia, Plaut. As. 1, 3, 20: beneficiis hostimentum peperisti grave, Att. ap. Non. 315, 19; Serv. Verg. A. 2, 156.

hostio1.full: hostio, īre, v. a., to make even, return like for like, to recompense, requite: hostire (ab antiquis) ponebatur pro aequare. Fest. s. v. status dies, p. 314 Müll.; ib. s. v. redhostire, p. 270 (ante-class.): nisi coërceo Protervitatem atque hostio ferociam, Pac. ap. Fest. s. v. redhostire, p. 270; and ap. Non. 121, 16 (Trag. Rel. v. 346 Rib.): quin promitto hostire contra, ut merueris, Plaut. As. 2, 2, 110.

hostio2.full: hostio, īre, v. a., to strike: hostia dicta est ab eo, quod est hostire ferire, Paul. ex Fest. p. 102 Müll. (ante-class.): quae mea comminus machaera atque hasta hostibit e manu, Enn. ap. Fest. s. v. redhostire, p. 270 Müll. (Trag. v. 212 Vahl.).

hostis.full: hostis (also fos-), is, comm. Sanscr. root ghas-, to eat, consume, destroy; Germ. Gast; cf. also hasta, a stranger, foreigner; afterwards transf., an enemy (cf.: adversarius, inimicus, perduellis): equidem etiam illud animadverto, quod qui proprio nomine perduellis esset, is hostis vocaretur, lenitate verbi rei tristitiam mitigatam. Hostis enim apud majores nostros is dicebatur, quem nunc peregrinum dicimus ... quamquam id nomen durius effecit jam vetustas: a peregrino enim recessit et proprie i

hostius.full: Hostĭus, a, name of a Roman gens, Sall. H. 4, p. 228 Gerl. Min. (Dietsch, 4, 27; Hostilius); Sen. Q. N. 1, 16 al.
hostius.short: Hostĭus, a, name of a Roman gens, Sall.

hostorium.full: hostōrĭum, ĭi, n. 1. hostio, an instrument used in levelling a measure of corn, etc., a strickle, Prisc. p. 688 P.

hostus1.full: hostus, i, m. perh. a rustic term for haustus, the yield of an olive-tree, Cato, R. R. 6, 2; Varr. R. R. 1, 24, 2.

hostus2.full: Hostus, i, m., a Roman prœnomen, as Hostus Hostilius, Liv. 1, 12; Macr. S. 1, 6: Hostus Lucretius Tricipitinus, Liv. 4, 30 al.
hostus2.short: Hostus, i, m., a Roman prœnomen, as Hostus Hostilius, Liv.

huc.full: huc (old form hoc, like illoc, istoc, Plaut. Capt. 3, 1, 19; id. Truc. 2, 2, 27 et saep.; Ter. Eun. 3, 2, 48; Planc. ap. Cic. Fam. 10, 21, 5; Cic. Brut. 11, 10, 3; Nep. Phoc. 3, 3; Verg. A. 8, 423; Petr. 39; Inscr. Orell. 4394; 4471; 4814; cf. Serv. ad Verg. A. l. l.), adv., to this place, hither, = δεῦρο. Lit.: imus huc, illuc hinc: cum illuc ventum est, ire illinc lubet, etc., Enn. ap. Gell. 19, 10, 12 (Trag. v. 258 Vahl.): huc illinc venire, Ter. Ad. 4, 5, 39: jam huc adveniet miles, Plaut. B
huc.short: huc (old form hoc, like illoc, istoc, Plaut.

hucine.full: hucĭnē, adv., v. huc, II. E.

hucusque.full: hucusque, adv., v. huc, I. D. and II. D.

hui.full: hui, interj., an exclamation of astonishment or admiration, hah! ho! oh! hui, homunculi quanti estis, Plaut. Rud. 1, 2, 65: hui, dixti pulchre! Ter. Phorm. 2, 1, 72: triginta? hui, percara est! id. ib. 3, 3, 25: hui, tam cito? ridiculum, id. And. 3, 1, 16: Ch. Prorsum nihil intelligo. Sy. Hui, tardus est! id. Heaut. 4, 5, 28: hui, quantam fenestram ad nequitiam patefeceris! id. ib. 3, 1, 71: videbam sermones: Hui! fratrem reliquit? Cic. Att. 6, 6, 3; 5, 11, 1: hui quam diu de nugis! id. ib. 13,
hui.short: hui, interj., an exclamation of astonishment or admiration, hah! ho! oh! hui, homunculi quanti estis, Plaut.

hujuscemodi.full: hūjuscĕmŏdi and hūjusmŏdi, v. under modus.

humanitas.full: hūmānĭtas, ātis, f. humanus, human nature, humanity, in a good sense; the qualities, feelings, and inclinations of mankind. In gen. (for the most part only in Cic.): magna est vis humanitatis, multum valet communio sanguinis, Cic. Rosc. Am. 22, 63: naturas hominum vimque omnem humanitatis penitus perspicere, id. de Or. 1, 12, 53: humanitatis societas, id. Rep. 2, 26: communis humanitatis jus, id. Fl. 11, 24; cf.: communis humanitatis causa, id. Quint. 16, 51: peterem errato veniam ex humanitate

humanitus.full: hūmānĭtus, adv. humanus, like divinitus from divinus, humanly, after the manner of men. In gen. (very rare but class.): ferre humana humanitus, Afran. ap. Non. 514, 20 (Com. Fragm. v. 290 Rib.); so, quicquam facere, Turp. ib. (Com. Fragm. v. 165 Rib.): si quid me (i. e. mihi) fuerit humanitus, Enn. ap. Fest. p. 161 Müll. (Ann. v. 128 Vahl.): si quid mihi humanitus accidisset, i. e. should I die, Cic. Phil. 1, 4, 10; and: si quid ei humanitus attigisset, App. Mag. 337: ursi coëunt humanitus strat

humano.full: hūmāno, āvi, ātum, 1 humanus, to make human; only used in the pass. of the incarnation of Christ: promittentes Deum propter salutem credentium visualiter humanandum, Cassiod. in Psa. praef.; so, verbum humanatum, id. Hist. Eccles. 6, 22.
humano.short: hūmāno, āvi, ātum, 1 humanus, to make human;

humanus.full: hūmānus (old form: HEMONA humana et HEMONEM hominem dicebant, Paul. ex Fest. p. 100 Müll.; cf. homo init.), a, um, adj. homo, of or belonging to man, human. In gen.: esse aliquem humana specie et figura, qui tantum immanitate bestias vicerit, ut, etc., Cic. Rosc. Am. 22, 63: simulacra, id. Rep. 3, 9: caput, a human head, Hor. A. P. 1; Flor. 1, 7, 8: succidiae, Cato ap. Gell. 13, 24, 12: Cyclopis venter ... Carnibus humanis distentus, human flesh, Enn. ap. Prisc. p. 870 P. (Ann. v. 327 Vahl,): hu
humanus.short: hūmānus (old form: HEMONA humana et HEMONEM hominem dicebant, Paul.

humatio.full: hŭmātĭo, ōnis, f. humo, a burying (very rare; cf.: sepultura, funus, exsequiae): de humatione et sepultura dicendum, Cic. Tusc. 1, 43, 102: locus qui recipiat humationem, Dig. 43, 24, 22, § 4.

humator.full: hŭmātor, ōris, m. id., he who buries or inters: consulis, Luc. 7, 799.

humerale.full: hŭmĕrāle, hŭmĕrus, etc., v. umerale, umerus, etc.

humesco.full: hūmesco, hūmĭdus, etc., v. umesco, umidus, etc.

humiliatio.full: hŭmĭlĭātĭo, ōnis, f. humilio, an humbling, humiliation (post-class.), Tert. Verg. Vel. 13; id. adv. Herm. 7; id. Patient. 13; Vulg. Mic. 6, 14.

humilifico.full: hŭmĭlĭfĭco, āre, v. a. humilis - facio, to make humble, to humble (post - class.), Tert. Poen. 9.

humilio.full: hŭmĭlĭo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. humilis, to abase, humble (late Lat.): corpus, quod humiliatur in passionibus, Tert. adv. Marc. 5, 20 fin.: frustra nos hic humiliamus, ut ibi possimus esse majores, Hier. adv. Jovin. 1, 18: publicanus vultu humiliatus atque dejectus, Tert. Or. 13; Sid. Ep. 5, 14 fin.: ad humiliandum celsitudinem potestatis, Amm. 30, 4, 2.

humilis.full: hŭmĭlis, e, adj. humus; like χαμαλός from χαμαί, on the ground, i. e., low, lowly, small, slight (class.; esp. freq. in the trop. signif.). Lit.: arbores et vites et ea quae sunt humiliora neque se tollere a terra altius possunt, Cic. Tusc. 5, 13, 37; cf.: turrim humilem parvamque fecerant, Caes. B. C. 2, 8, 1 sq.: humilior munitio, id. ib. 3, 63, 2: (naves) humiliores quam quibus in nostro mari uti consuevimus, id. B. G. 5, 1, 2: humiles habitare casas, Verg. E. 2, 29: domus, Hor. C. 3, 1, 22:

humilitas.full: hŭmĭlĭtas, ātis, f. humilis, lowness (acc. to humilis, I.). Lit.: naves omnes actuarias imperat fieri, quam ad rem humilitas multum adjuvat (shortly before: naves paulo facit humiliores), Caes. B. G. 5, 1, 3: arborum, Sall. J. 49, 5: aliorum animalium ea est humilitas, ut cibum terrestrem rostris facile contingant, low stature, Cic. N. D. 2 47, 122: sidera multum inter se aut altitudine aut humilitate distantia, id. Tusc. 5, 24, 69: quanta humilitate luna feratur, terram paene contingens, id. Di

humilito.full: hŭmĭlĭto, āre, 1, v. a. humilis, to humiliate, disgrace: maternum genus, Schol. Bob. ad Cic. Sull. 8, 25 (p. 364 Bait.).

humo.full: hŭmo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. humus, to cover with earth, to inter, bury. Lit. (rare but class.; cf.: sepelio, tumulo): in terram cadentibus corporibus iisque humo tectis, e quo dictum est humari, Cic. Tusc. 1, 16, 36: cum ignotum quendam projectum mortuum vidisset eumque humavisset, id. Div. 1, 27, 56: corpora, id. Tusc. 1, 45, 108: caesorum reliquias uno tumulo humaturus, Suet. Calig. 3: humatus et conditus est, id. Vit. Hor.; Plin. 30, 7, 20, § 64; Prop. 3, 16 (4, 15), 29: sepulcrum ubi mortuus s

humus.full: hŭmus, i (archaic form of the abl. sing. humu, Varr. ap. Non. 488, 6 and 48, 26), f. (archaic masc. humum humidum pedibus fodit, Laev. ap. Prisc. p. 719 P.: humidum humum, Gracch. ib.) [from the prim. form ΧΑΜ, whence χα^μαί, χα^μόθεν, χα^μα^λός, Lat. humilis; kindr. with Sanscr. Xám, earth; Gr. χθών], the earth, the ground, the soil. Lit. (class.; cf.: terra, solum, tellus): humus erat immunda, lutulenta vino, coronis languidulis et spinis coöperta piscium, Cic. Fragm. Or. pro Gall. ap. Quint.
humus.short: hŭmus, i (archaic form of the abl.

hunni.full: Hunni (Chunni and Chūni), ōrum, m., the Huns, Amm. 31, 2; Claud. ap. Rufin. 1, 321; 2, 270; Veg. Vet. 3 praef. 1. Form Chuni, Aus. Epigr. 1, 8.—Sing.: Chū-nus, Claud. in Eutr. 2, 238.— Deriv. Hunniscus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to the Huns, Hunnish: equus, Claud. in Eutr. 4, 4; 7.
hunni.short: Hunni (Chunni and Chūni), ōrum, m., the Huns, Amm.

hyacinthaeus.full: hўăcinthaeus, a, um, adj., = ὑακίνθαιος, of or belonging to the hyacinth, hyacinthine (post-class. for hyacinthinus): ordo, a row of hyacinths, Ven. Carm. 8, 8, 20; 6, 270.
hyacinthaeus.short: hўăcinthaeus, a, um, adj., = ὑακίνθαιος, of or belonging to the hyacinth, hyacinthine (post-class.

hyacinthinus.full: hўăcinthĭnus, a, um, adj., = ὑακίνθινος, of or belonging to the hyacinth, hyacinthine: flos, the hyacinth, Cat. 61, 93: laena, i. e. hyacinth-colored, Pers. 1, 32.
hyacinthinus.short: hўăcinthĭnus, a, um, adj., = ὑακίνθινος, of or belonging to the hyacinth, hyacinthine: flos, the hyacinth, Cat.

hyacinthizontes.full: hўăcinthīzontes, um, m., = ὑακινθιζοντες, hyacinth-colored: berylli, Plin. 37, 5, 20, § 77; Sol. 55 fin.
hyacinthizontes.short: hўăcinthīzontes, um, m., = ὑακινθιζοντες, hyacinth-colored: berylli, Plin.

hyacinthus.full: Hўăcinthus or -os, i, m., = Ὑάκινθος, a beautiful Spartan youth, son of Œbalus, beloved by Apollo, and accidentally killed by a blow of his quoit; from his blood sprang the flower of the same name, marked with the exclamation AI, Ov. M. 10, 162 sq.; Hyg. Fab. 272; Plin. 21, 11, 38, § 66; Serv. Verg. E. 3, 63.—Plur.: sed gladiator erat; facit hoc illos Hyacinthos, i. e. as beautiful as Hyacinthus, Juv. 6, 110.— Hўăcinthĭa, ōrum, n., the festival in honor of Hyacinthus, in Sparta, Ov. M. 10, 219.—
hyacinthus.short: Hўăcinthus or -os, i, m., = Ὑάκινθος, a beautiful Spartan youth, son of Œbalus, beloved by Apollo, and accidentally killed by a blow of his quoit;

hyades.full: Hўădes, um, f., = Ὑάδες (the rainers), the Hyades, a group of seven stars in the head of Taurus (called in pure Lat. suculae; v. 3. sucula), Cic. N. D. 2, 43, 111; Plin. 18, 26, 66, § 247; 37, 7, 28, § 100; cf. id. 2, 39, 39, § 106. They were fabled as daughters of Atlas and sisters of Hyas and of the Pleiades, Ov. F. 5, 165 sq.; id. M. 3, 595; 13, 293; Verg. A. 3, 516; Hor. C. 1, 3, 14.— In sing.: Hyas, ădis, the Hyad, collect., Stat. S. 1, 6, 22.
hyades.short: Hўădes, um, f., = Ὑάδες (the rainers), the Hyades, a group of seven stars in the head of Taurus (called in pure Lat.

hyaena.full: hўaena, ae, f., = ὕαινα, a hyena, Plin. 8, 30, 44, § 105; Ov. M. 15, 410.— A seafish, a kind of sole, Plin. 32, 11, 54, § 154.
hyaena.short: hўaena, ae, f., = ὕαινα, a hyena, Plin.

hyaenius.full: hўaenĭus, a, um, adj. hyaena, of or named from the hyena: gemma, a precious stone, otherwise unknown, Plin. 37, 10, 60, § 168; Isid. Orig. 16, 14.

hyale.full: Hўălē, ēs, f., = Ὑάλη, a nymph, companion of Diana, Ov. M. 3, 171.
hyale.short: Hўălē, ēs, f., = Ὑάλη, a nymph, companion of Diana, Ov.

hyalinus.full: hўălĭnus, a, um, adj., = ὑάλινος. Of glass, glass-: sphaera, Fulg. Myth. praef.: pulvis, Mart. Cap. 6, § 575.— Glass-green, green: pennae, Mart. Cap. 1, § 66 sq. al.

hyaloides.full: hўălŏīdes, is, adj., = ὑαλοειδής, grassgreen: umor, Theod. Prisc. 4, 2 fin.
hyaloides.short: hўălŏīdes, is, adj., = ὑαλοειδής, grassgreen: umor, Theod.

hyalus.full: hўălus, i, m., = ὕαλος, glass. Lit.: Milesia vellera Carpebant hyali saturo fucata colore, i. e. with glass - green color, Verg. G. 4, 335.— Transf., glassgreen color, Prud. στεφ. 12, 53; Aus. Idyll. 10, 418.

hyampolis.full: Hўampŏlis, is, f., = Ὑάμπολις, a town of Phocis, on the borders of Bœotia, its ruins near the village of Vogdhani, Plin. 4, 7, 12, § 27; Liv. 32, 18, 6; Stat. Th. 7, 345.
hyampolis.short: Hўampŏlis, is, f., = Ὑάμπολις, a town of Phocis, on the borders of Bœotia, its ruins near the village of Vogdhani, Plin.

hyantes.full: Hўantes, um, m., = Ὕαντες, the Hyantes, an old name of the Bœotians, Plin. 4, 7, 12, § 26.— Derivv. Hўan-tēus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to the Hyantes (Bœotians), Hyantean, Bœotian: Iolāus, Ov. M. 8, 310: Aganippe, id. ib. 5, 312: aqua, i. e. Castalian, Mart. 12, 3, 12.— Hўantĭus, a, um, adj., the same: sorores, i. e. the Muses, Stat. S. 2, 7, 8; cf. Camenae, Sid. Ep. 8, 9 in carm.: juvenis, i. e. Actœon, as grandson of Cadmus, Ov. M. 3, 147.
hyantes.short: Hўantes, um, m., = Ὕαντες, the Hyantes, an old name of the Bœotians, Plin.

hyarotis.full: Hўărōtis, ĭdis, f., = Ὑαρῶτις (or Ὑδραώτης), a river in India, a tributary of the Indus, now Ravi, Curt. 9, 1, 7.
hyarotis.short: Hўărōtis, ĭdis, f., = Ὑαρῶτις (or Ὑδραώτης), a river in India, a tributary of the Indus, now Ravi, Curt.

hyas1.full: Hўas, antis (acc. Hўān, Ov. F. 5, 179), m., = Ὕας, a son of Atlas, and father or brother of the Hyades, Hyg. Fab. 192; Ov. F. 5, 170.—Hence, Sidus Hyantis, the Hyades, id. ib. 5, 734.

hybla.full: Hybla, ae, and Hyblē, ēs, f., =Ὕβλη, a mountain of Sicily abounding in flowers and bees, with a city of the same name, Plin. 11, 13, 13, § 32; Verg. E. 7, 37; Ov. Tr. 5, 13, 22; Sil. 14, 200; Mart. 7, 88, 8; 10, 12, 3; Mel. 2, 7, 16.— Derivv. Hy-blaeus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Mount Hybla, Hyblean: apes, Verg. E. 1, 55: mella, Mart. 11, 42: avena, i. e. of the Sicilian Theocritus, Calp. Ecl. 4, 6, 3.— Hyblenses, ĭum, m., the inhabitants of the city of Hybla, Hybleans, Plin. 3, 8, 14, § 9
hybla.short: Hybla, ae, and Hyblē, ēs, f., =Ὕβλη, a mountain of Sicily abounding in flowers and bees, with a city of the same name, Plin.

hydaspes.full: Hўdaspes, is, m., = Ὑδάσπης. A river of India, a tributary of the Indus, now Jeloum, Mel. 3, 7, 6; Plin. 6, 20, 23, § 71; Curt. 4, 5, 3; 8, 12, 8; Verg. G. 4, 211; Hor. C. 1, 22, 8; Luc. 8, 227 al.—To denote the East: repressor Hydaspis, Petr. 123 fin.— Deriv.: Hўdaspēus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to the Hydaspes, Hydaspean; poet. also for Indian: gemmae, Claud. III. Cons. Hon. 4: Erythrae, Sid. Carm. 2, 447.— A companion of Æneas, Verg. A. 10, 747.— An Indian or Ethiopian slave, Hor. S. 2, 8

hydatis.full: hўdătis, ĭdis, f., = ὑδατίς, a watercolored gem, otherwise unknown, Mart. Cap. 1, § 75.
hydatis.short: hўdătis, ĭdis, f., = ὑδατίς, a watercolored gem, otherwise unknown, Mart.

hyderos.full: hўdĕros, i, m., = ὕδερος (i. q. ὕδρωψ), the dropsy, Cael. Aur. Tard. 3, 8, 97 sq.

hydra.full: Hȳdra, ae, f., = Ὕδρα [kindred with Sanscr. udri; Ang.-Sax. oter, otor; Engl. and Germ. Otter; cf. also the Gr. ἔνυδρις], the water-serpent killed by Hercules near the Lernean Lake, the Hydra, with seven heads; as fast as one of them was cut off two sprang up in its stead; it is also called Echidna: Lernaea pestis, Hydra, Lucr. 5, 27; Ov. M. 9, 192; Hor. C. 4, 4, 61; id. Ep. 2, 1, 10; Hyg. Fab. 30; 34; 151. As identified with Echidna, the mother of Cerberus, Cic. poët. Tusc. 2, 9, 22.—Prov.: vid
hydra.short: Hȳdra, ae, f., = Ὕδρα [kindred with Sanscr.

hydragogia.full: hydrăgōgĭa, ae, f., = ὑδραγωγία, an aqueduct, canal: venae (sunt) hydragogiae, Varr. ap. Non. 209, 20.
hydragogia.short: hydrăgōgĭa, ae, f., = ὑδραγωγία, an aqueduct, canal: venae (sunt) hydragogiae, Varr.

hydragogus.full: hydrăgōgus, a, um, adj., = ὑδραγωγός, that carries off water. Adj.: utendum aquiducis medicamentis, quae Graeci hydragoga vocaverunt, Cael. Aur. Tard. 3, 8, 119.— Subst.: hydrage-gos, i, f., a plant, called also chamaedaphne and daphnites, App. Herb. 27.
hydragogus.short: hydrăgōgus, a, um, adj., = ὑδραγωγός, that carries off water.

hydragonus.full: hydrăgŏnus, i, f., a water - plant, App. Herb. 67.
hydragonus.short: hydrăgŏnus, i, f., a water - plant, App.

hydraletes.full: hydrălĕtes, ae, m., = ὑδραλέτης, a water-mill, Vitr. 10, 10 Schneid. N. cr. (al. hydraulae).
hydraletes.short: hydrălĕtes, ae, m., = ὑδραλέτης, a water-mill, Vitr.

hydrargyrus.full: hydrargўrus, i, m., = ὑδράργυρος, quicksilver artificially prepared, Plin. 33, 8, 41, § 123; 33, 3, 20, § 64.
hydrargyrus.short: hydrargўrus, i, m., = ὑδράργυρος, quicksilver artificially prepared, Plin.

hydraula.full: hydraula, ae, or hydraules, ae, m., = ὑδραύλης, one who plays on the waterorgan, Suet. Ner. 54; Petr. 36; acc. -am, Mart. Cap. 9, § 924.
hydraula.short: hydraula, ae, or hydraules, ae, m., = ὑδραύλης, one who plays on the waterorgan, Suet.

hydraulicus.full: hydraulĭcus, a, um, adj., = ὑδραυλικός, of or belonging to the water-organ, hydraulic: machinae, water-organs, Vitr. 9, 9; 10, 13; called also organa, Plin. 7, 37, 38, § 125; Suet. Ner. 41.
hydraulicus.short: hydraulĭcus, a, um, adj., = ὑδραυλικός, of or belonging to the water-organ, hydraulic: machinae, water-organs, Vitr.

hydraulus.full: hydraulus, i, m., = ὕδραυλος, a water-organ, Cic. Tusc. 3, 18, 43; Plin. 9, 8, 8, § 24.
hydraulus.short: hydraulus, i, m., = ὕδραυλος, a water-organ, Cic.

hydrela.full: Hydrēla, ae, f., a city of Caria, Liv. 37, 56, 3.— Deriv. Hydrēlā-tānus, a, um, adj., of Hydrela: ager, Liv. 37, 56, 3.— Hydrēlītae, ārum, m., the inhabitants of Hydrela, Plin. 5, 29, 29, § 105.
hydrela.short: Hydrēla, ae, f., a city of Caria, Liv.

hydreum.full: hydrēum, i, n., v. the foll. art.

hydreuma.full: hydreuma, ătis, n., = ὕδρευμα, a resting-place for caravans, where they get water, a watering - place, Plin. 6, 23, 26, § 103 (al. hydreum).
hydreuma.short: hydreuma, ătis, n., = ὕδρευμα, a resting-place for caravans, where they get water, a watering - place, Plin.

hydreus.full: hydrĕus, a, um, adj. hydrus, of or belonging to the water - serpent: germen, Mart. Cap. 7, § 729.

hydria.full: hydrĭa, ae, f., = ὑδρία (a water-pot; hence, in gen.), a jug, ewer, urn: argenteae, Cic. Verr. 2, 2, 19, § 47: in hydriam sortes conicere, id. ib. 2, 2, 51, § 127: farris, Sulp. Sever. Hist. Sacr. 1, 43. Of the cinerary urns in tombs, Inscr. Orell. 4546 sq.— Hydria, a comedy of Menander, Quint. 11, 3, 91.

hydrinus.full: hydrīnus, a, um, adj. hydrus, of or from a water-snake: vulnera, Prud. στεφ. 10, 884.

hydrius.full: hydrĭus, a, um, adj. ὕδωρ, of or be longing to water, water-: puer (for Aquarius), the constellation of the Waterman, Prud. Apoth. 622.

hydrocele.full: hydrŏcēlē, ēs, f., = ὑδροκήλη, a watery rupture, hydrocele, Mart. 12, 84, 3.
hydrocele.short: hydrŏcēlē, ēs, f., = ὑδροκήλη, a watery rupture, hydrocele, Mart.

hydrocelicus.full: hydrŏcēlĭcus, i, m., = ὑδροκηλικός, afflicted with a hydrocele, Plin. 30, 8, 22, § 74.
hydrocelicus.short: hydrŏcēlĭcus, i, m., = ὑδροκηλικός, afflicted with a hydrocele, Plin.

hydrochous.full: Hydrŏchŏus, i, m., = Ὑδροχόος (water-pourer), the constellation Aquarius, Cat. 66, 94.
hydrochous.short: Hydrŏchŏus, i, m., = Ὑδροχόος (water-pourer), the constellation Aquarius, Cat.

hydrogaratus.full: hydrŏgărātus, a, um, adj. hydrogarum, seasoned with hydrogarum: isicia, Apic. 2, 2, 45.

hydrogarum.full: hydrŏgărum, i, n., = ὑδρόγαμον, garum mixed with water, Lampr. Heliog. 29, 5.
hydrogarum.short: hydrŏgărum, i, n., = ὑδρόγαμον, garum mixed with water, Lampr.

hydrogeron.full: hydrŏgĕron, ontis, m., = ὑδρογέρων, a plant, called in pure Lat. senecio, groundsel, App. Herb. 75.
hydrogeron.short: hydrŏgĕron, ontis, m., = ὑδρογέρων, a plant, called in pure Lat.

hydrolapathum.full: hydrŏlăpăthum, i, n., = ὑδρολάπαθον, water-dock, Rumex aquaticus, Linn.; Plin. 20, 21, 85, § 232.
hydrolapathum.short: hydrŏlăpăthum, i, n., = ὑδρολάπαθον, water-dock, Rumex aquaticus, Linn.;

hydromantia.full: hydrŏmantīa, ae, f., = ὑδρομαντεία, divination by water, hydromancy, Aug. Civ. Dei, 7, 35; Plin. 37, 11, 73, § 192; Isid. 8, 9, 13.
hydromantia.short: hydrŏmantīa, ae, f., = ὑδρομαντεία, divination by water, hydromancy, Aug.

hydromeli.full: hydrŏmĕli (-mel), ĭtis, n., = ὑδρόμελι, a beverage made of honey and water, honey-water, mead, hydromel, Plin. 14, 17, 20, § 113; 22, 13, 15, § 34; 27, 5, 20, § 37; Pall. Jul. 7; Isid. Or. 20, 3 (al. hydromelum). form hydromel, -llis, n., Theod. Prisc. 2, 2; 2, 17; Plin. Val. 1, 32.
hydromeli.short: hydrŏmĕli (-mel), ĭtis, n., = ὑδρόμελι, a beverage made of honey and water, honey-water, mead, hydromel, Plin.

hydrophobia.full: hydrŏphŏbĭa, ae, f., = ὑδροφοβία, dread of water, hydrophobia, Cael. Aur. Acut. 3, 9, 98 sq. (in Cels. 5, 27, 2, written as Greek; and in Ov. P. 1, 3, 23, designated by formidatae aquae).
hydrophobia.short: hydrŏphŏbĭa, ae, f., = ὑδροφοβία, dread of water, hydrophobia, Cael.

hydrophobicus.full: hydrŏphŏbĭcus, a, um, adj., = ὑδροφοβικός, of or belonging to hydrophobia, hydrophobic: passio, i. e. hydrophobia, Cael. Aur. Acut. 3, 9, 99; 3, 16, 137.
hydrophobicus.short: hydrŏphŏbĭcus, a, um, adj., = ὑδροφοβικός, of or belonging to hydrophobia, hydrophobic: passio, i.

hydrophobus.full: hydrŏphŏbus, a, um, = ὑδροφόβος, affected with hydrophobia. Adj.: homines, Cael. Aur. Acut. 3, 9, 99: jumenta, Veg. Vet. 3, 31.— Subst.: hydrŏphŏbus, i, m., Plin. 29, 5, 32, § 99.
hydrophobus.short: hydrŏphŏbus, a, um, = ὑδροφόβος, affected with hydrophobia.

hydrophylax.full: hydrŏphўlax, ăcis, m., = ὑδροφύλαξ, one who has the care of the water, a water-inspector, Cod. Just. 11, 42, 10.
hydrophylax.short: hydrŏphўlax, ăcis, m., = ὑδροφύλαξ, one who has the care of the water, a water-inspector, Cod.

hydropicus.full: hydrōpĭcus, a, um, adj., = ὑδρωπικός, dropsical: si nolis sanus, curres hydropicus, Hor. Ep. 1, 2, 34.—Plur. subst.: hydropici, ōrum, m., dropsical persons, Plin. 20, 1, 3, § 8 (o short in Aemil. Mac. de Allio.).
hydropicus.short: hydrōpĭcus, a, um, adj., = ὑδρωπικός, dropsical: si nolis sanus, curres hydropicus, Hor.

hydropisis.full: hydrōpĭsis, is, f., = ὑδρώπισις, the dropsy, Plin. 20, 1, 3, § 8; cf. the two foll. artt.
hydropisis.short: hydrōpĭsis, is, f., = ὑδρώπισις, the dropsy, Plin.

hydropismus.full: hydrōpismus, i, m., = ὑδρωπισμός, the dropsy, Cael. Aur. Acut. 1, 14, § 108; cf. the preced. and foll. artt.
hydropismus.short: hydrōpismus, i, m., = ὑδρωπισμός, the dropsy, Cael.

hydrops.full: hydrops, ōpis, m., = ὕδρωψ, the dropsy, Cels. 3, 21; Hor. C. 2, 2, 13; Cael. Aur. Tard. 3, 8, 96 sqq.—Plur.: hydrōpes, um, the several kinds of dropsy, Cael. Aur. Tard. 3, 8, 98.
hydrops.short: hydrops, ōpis, m., = ὕδρωψ, the dropsy, Cels.

hydroselinum.full: hydrŏsĕlīnum, i, n., = ὑδροσέλινον, marsh selinum, App. Herb. 79.
hydroselinum.short: hydrŏsĕlīnum, i, n., = ὑδροσέλινον, marsh selinum, App.

hydrus1.full: hydrus or -os, i, m., = ὕδρος, a water-serpent, serpent (cf.: chelydrus, chersydrus, anguis, serpens). Lit., Plin. 29, 4, 22, § 72; Verg. G. 4, 458; id. A. 7, 753; Ov. M. 13, 804: marini, Plin. 6, 23, 26, § 98. In the hair of the Furies, of Medusa, etc., Verg. A. 7, 447; Val. Fl. 2, 195; Ov. M. 4, 800; hence poet. transf.: nam si Vergilio puer et tolerabile desit Hospitium, caderent omnes a crinibus hydri, i. e. all his poetic fire would have come to naught (referring to his description of the F
hydrus1.short: hydrus or -os, i, m., = ὕδρος, a water-serpent, serpent (cf.: chelydrus, chersydrus, anguis, serpens).

hydrus2.full: Hydrūs, untis, f., = Ὑδροῦς, a city of Calabria, under a mountain of the same name, now Otranto, Plin. 3, 11, 16, § 101; Cic. Fam. 16, 9, 2; id. Att. 15, 21, 3; 16, 5, 3; Mel. 2, 4, 7.—In masc., avius Hydrus, of the city and mountain, Luc. 5, 375.—The city is also called Hydruntum, i, n., Liv. 36, 21, 5; Plin. 3, 11, 16, § 100.
hydrus2.short: Hydrūs, untis, f., = Ὑδροῦς, a city of Calabria, under a mountain of the same name, now Otranto, Plin.

hyemalis.full: hўĕmālis and hyems, v. hiemalis, etc.

hyes.full: Hyes, ae, m., = Ὕης, one of the first three Dioscuri, Cic. N. D. 3, 21, 53 (acc. to Lobeck's conject.).
hyes.short: Hyes, ae, m., = Ὕης, one of the first three Dioscuri, Cic.

hyettus.full: Hyettus, i, f., = Ὑηττός, a city of Bœotia, north of lake Copais, near the modern Strobiki, Plin. 36, 16, 25, § 128.
hyettus.short: Hyettus, i, f., = Ὑηττός, a city of Bœotia, north of lake Copais, near the modern Strobiki, Plin.

hygea.full: Hўgēa or Hўgīa (Hygĭeia), ae, f., = Ὑγεία, daughter of Æsculapius, and goddess of health, Plin. 34, 8, 19, § 80; 35, 11, 40, § 137; Mart. 11, 60, 6; Inscr. Orell. 440; 1576 sq.
hygea.short: Hўgēa or Hўgīa (Hygĭeia), ae, f., = Ὑγεία, daughter of Æsculapius, and goddess of health, Plin.

hyginus.full: Hygīnus (Higinus, Gell. 1, 14, 1; 1, 21, 2; 5, 8, 1 et saep.), i, m., surname of two Roman authors. C. Julius Hyginus, author of a collection of fables and of a treatise on astronomy, Suet. Gramm. 20; Gell. 1, 14.— The author of a treatise De limitibus constituendis.

hygra.full: hygra, ae, f., = ὑγρά (liquid), a kind of eye-salve, Scrib. Comp. 37.
hygra.short: hygra, ae, f., = ὑγρά (liquid), a kind of eye-salve, Scrib.

hygremplastrum.full: hygremplastrum, i, n., = ὑγρέμπλαστρον, a wet plaster, Plin. 34, 15, 46, § 155.
hygremplastrum.short: hygremplastrum, i, n., = ὑγρέμπλαστρον, a wet plaster, Plin.

hygrophobia.full: hygrŏphŏbĭa, ae, f., = ὑγροφοβία, a dread of liquids, as water, wine, etc., Cael. Aur. Acut. 3, 9, 98.
hygrophobia.short: hygrŏphŏbĭa, ae, f., = ὑγροφοβία, a dread of liquids, as water, wine, etc., Cael.

hylactor.full: Hўlactor, ŏris, m., name of a hound of Actœon, Ov. M. 3, 224; Hyg. Fab. 181.
hylactor.short: Hўlactor, ŏris, m., name of a hound of Actœon, Ov.

hylaeus.full: Hȳlaeus, i, m., = Ὑλαῖος (v. Chandler, Gr. Accent. § 239). A centaur who offered violence to Atalanta, Ov. A. A. 2, 191; Verg. A. 8, 294.—Hence, Hylaeus, a, um, adj., of Hylœus: ramus, Prop. 1, 1, 13: gens, Val. Fl. 6, 74: ille etiam (i. e. Milanion) Hylaei percussus vulnere rami, Prop. 1, 1, 13.— One of Actœon's hounds, Ov. M. 3, 213; Hyg. Fab. 181.

hylas.full: Hўlas, ae, m., = Ὕλας, a beautiful youth of Œchalia (or Argos), companion of Hercules in the Argonautic expedition, who was carried off by the nymphs, and long sought for by Hercules in vain, Prop. 1, 20, 6; Ov. A. A. 2, 110; Juv. 1, 164; Val. Fl. 3, 596; Hyg. Fab. 14; Verg. E. 6, 44 (where, by poet. license, the voc. is scanned Hўlā, Hȳl', like the Gr. Ἆρες, Ἄρες, Mart. 9, 11, 15).
hylas.short: Hўlas, ae, m., = Ὕλας, a beautiful youth of Œchalia (or Argos), companion of Hercules in the Argonautic expedition, who was carried off by the nymphs, and long sought for by Hercules in vain, Prop.

hylax.full: Hўlax, ăcis, Barker, the name of a dog, Verg. E. 8, 107.
hylax.short: Hўlax, ăcis, Barker, the name of a dog, Verg.

hyle.full: hȳlē, ēs, f., = ὕλη (wood; hence), stuff, materials, matter, Attei. ap. Suet. Gramm. 10; Macr. S. 1, 17 fin.

hyles.full: Hȳles, ae, m., a centaur, Ov. M. 12, 378.
hyles.short: Hȳles, ae, m., a centaur, Ov.

hyleus.full: Hўleus (dissyl.), ei, m., one who took part in the Calydonian hunt, Ov. M. 8, 312.
hyleus.short: Hўleus (dissyl.), ei, m., one who took part in the Calydonian hunt, Ov.

hyllus.full: Hyllus (Hȳlus), i, m., = Ὕλλος or Ὕλος, a son of Hercules by Dejanira, and husband of Iole, Ov. H. 9, 44; id. M. 9, 279; Stat. Th. 8, 508.
hyllus.short: Hyllus (Hȳlus), i, m., = Ὕλλος or Ὕλος, a son of Hercules by Dejanira, and husband of Iole, Ov.

hylonome.full: Hȳlŏnŏmē, ēs, f., = Ὑλονόμη, the beautiful wife of the centaur Cyllarus, Ov. M. 12, 405 sq.
hylonome.short: Hȳlŏnŏmē, ēs, f., = Ὑλονόμη, the beautiful wife of the centaur Cyllarus, Ov.

hymen.full: Hȳ^men, ĕnis, and Hўmĕnaeus or -os, i, m., = Ὑμήν, Ὑμέναιος, the god of marriage, of weddings, Hymen. Lit.: dum illam educunt huc novam nuptam foras, suavi cantu concelebra omnem hanc plateam Hymenaeo! Io Hymen Hymenaee! Io Hymen! Plaut. Cas. 4, 3, 1 sqq.; 15 sq.: jam veniet virgo, jam dicetur Hymenaeus. Hymen o Hymenaee, Hymen ades o Hymenaee, Cat. 62, 5 (acc. to the Gr. Ὑμὴν ὦ Ὑμέναιε); 62, 10 sq.; for which: io Hymen Hymenaee io, Io Hymen Hymenaee, id. 61, 124; 144 sq.: vulgus Hymen Hymenaee
hymen.short: Hȳ^men, ĕnis, and Hўmĕnaeus or -os, i, m., = Ὑμήν, Ὑμέναιος, the god of marriage, of weddings, Hymen.

hymenaeus.full: Hymenaeus (-os) and Hymeneï-us, a, um, see the preced. art.
hymenaeus.short: Hymenaeus (-os) and Hymeneï-us, a, um, see the preced.

hymettus.full: Hўmettus or -os, i, m., = Ὑμηττός, a mountain near Athens, famed for its honey and its marble, Plin. 4, 7, 11, § 24; Cic. Fin. 2, 34, 112; Hor. C. 2, 6, 14; Ov. M. 7, 702; Mart. 7, 88; Val. Fl. 1, 396 et saep.— In fem.: Attica (perh. of the region about Hymettus), App. M. 1 init.— Deriv.: Hўmettĭus, a, um, adj., of or from Hymettus, Hymettian: mel, Cic. Fragm. ap. Non. 240, 33; Hor. S. 2, 2, 15: cera, Ov. M. 10, 284: columnae, Plin. 36, 3, 3, § 7: trabes, Hor. C. 2, 18, 3.
hymettus.short: Hўmettus or -os, i, m., = Ὑμηττός, a mountain near Athens, famed for its honey and its marble, Plin.

hymnidicus.full: hymnĭdĭcus, a, um, adj. hymnus + dico, singing hymns (late Lat.), Avien. Carm. 178.

hymnio.full: hymnio, īre, v. a. hymnus, to sing hymns (post-class.): hymnite matres pro receptis parvulis, Prud. στεφ. 1, 118.

hymnis.full: Hymnis, ĭdis, f., a comedy of Cœcilius Statius, Cic. Fin. 2, 7, 22.
hymnis.short: Hymnis, ĭdis, f., a comedy of Cœcilius Statius, Cic.

hymnisonus.full: hymnĭsŏnus, a, um, adj. hymnussonus, singing hymns, singing praises (post-class.): chori, Paul. Nol. Carm. 28, 230; 22, 200; cf. the foll. word.

hymnizo.full: hymnīzo, āre, 1, v. n., = ὑμνίζω, ὑμνέω, to sing hymns, worship by song: nonne illi in ignibus hymnizabant, Aug. in Psa. 33, 22.

hymnodicus.full: hymnōdĭcus, a, um, adj., = ὑμνῳδικός, singing hymns, singing praises, Firm. Math. 8, 25; cf. the preced. and foll. artt.
hymnodicus.short: hymnōdĭcus, a, um, adj., = ὑμνῳδικός, singing hymns, singing praises, Firm.

hymnologus.full: hymnŏlŏgus, i, m., = ὑμνολόγος, a singer of hymns or praises, Firm. Math. 3, 6; 12; Inscr. Orell. 2617.
hymnologus.short: hymnŏlŏgus, i, m., = ὑμνολόγος, a singer of hymns or praises, Firm.

hymnus.full: hymnus, i, m., = ὕμνος, a song of praise, a hymn: hymnus cantus est cum laude Dei, Aug. Enarr. in Psa. 148, 17; Ambros. Expos. Psa. 118, prol. § 3; Lucil. ap. Non. 330, 9; Prud. Cath. 37 praef.; 4, 75: divinorum scriptor hymnorum, Lact. 4, 8, 14; Vulg. Psa. 60 tit.; id. Matt. 26, 30.
hymnus.short: hymnus, i, m., = ὕμνος, a song of praise, a hymn: hymnus cantus est cum laude Dei, Aug.

hyophthalmos.full: hўophthalmos, i, m., = ὑόφθαλμος (swine's eye), a plant, called also Aster Atticus, App. Herb. 60.
hyophthalmos.short: hўophthalmos, i, m., = ὑόφθαλμος (swine's eye), a plant, called also Aster Atticus, App.

hyoscyaminus.full: hўoscўămĭnus, a, um, adj., =ὑοσκυάμινος, made of henbane, henbane-: oleum, Plin. 23, 4, 49, § 94.
hyoscyaminus.short: hўoscўămĭnus, a, um, adj., =ὑοσκυάμινος, made of henbane, henbane-: oleum, Plin.

hyoscyamus.full: hўoscўămus, i, m., = ὑοσκύαμος, the herb henbane, called also Apollinaris and altercum, Plin. 25, 4, 17, § 35; Cels. 5, 27, 14; Col. 6, 38, 3.—In a corrupted form: jusquiamus, i, m., Pall. 1, 35, 5; Veg. Vet. 2, 12, 5.
hyoscyamus.short: hўoscўămus, i, m., = ὑοσκύαμος, the herb henbane, called also Apollinaris and altercum, Plin.

hyosiris.full: hўŏsĭris, is, f., = ὑοσερίς, a plant resembling endive; acc. to Sprengel, Centaurea nigra, Linn.; Plin. 27, 10, 64, § 90.
hyosiris.short: hўŏsĭris, is, f., = ὑοσερίς, a plant resembling endive;

hypaepa.full: Hўpaepa, ōrum, n., = Ὕπαιπα, a small town in Lydia, now Beréki, Ov. M. 6, 13; 11, 152; Petr. 133.—Hence, Hў-paepēni, ōrum, m., its inhabitants, Plin. 5, 29, 31, § 120; Tac. A. 4, 55.
hypaepa.short: Hўpaepa, ōrum, n., = Ὕπαιπα, a small town in Lydia, now Beréki, Ov.

hypaethrus.full: hypaethrus or -os, a, um, adj., = ὕπαιθρος, that is in the open air, uncovered. Adj.: ambulationes, Vitr. 5, 9 med.: loca (with aperta), id. ib.— Subst. hy-paethros, i, m., a temple open or without roof, Vitr. 3, 2, 1.— hypaethrum, i, n., an open building, Dig. 33, 7, 12, § 20; id. 50, 16, 242, § 2.— hypaethra, ōrum, n., uncovered, open walks, Vitr. 1, 2.
hypaethrus.short: hypaethrus or -os, a, um, adj., = ὕπαιθρος, that is in the open air, uncovered.

hypallage.full: hўpallăgē, ēs, f., = ὑπαλλαγή, a rhetorical figure, by which the relations of things seem to be mutually interchanged (as: dare classibus austros instead of classes austris), Serv. ad Verg. A. 3, 61.
hypallage.short: hўpallăgē, ēs, f., = ὑπαλλαγή, a rhetorical figure, by which the relations of things seem to be mutually interchanged (as: dare classibus austros instead of classes austris), Serv.

hypanis.full: Hўpănis, is, m., = Ὕπανις. A river of European Sarmatia, now the Boug, Mel. 2, 1, 6; Plin. 4, 12, 26, § 83; 11, 36, 43, § 120; Cic. Tusc. 1, 39, 94; Verg. G. 4, 370; Ov. M. 15, 285.— A Trojan, Verg. A. 2, 340.

hypasis.full: Hўpăsis or Hўphăsis, is, m., = Ὕφασις, a river in India, a tributary of the Indus, now Sutledge, Plin. 2, 73, 75, § 183; 6, 17, 21, § 62; Curt. 9, 1, 35.
hypasis.short: Hўpăsis or Hўphăsis, is, m., = Ὕφασις, a river in India, a tributary of the Indus, now Sutledge, Plin.

hypata.full: Hўpăta, ae, f., = Ὑπάτη, a small town of Thessaly, near the Penēus, now Neópatra, Liv. 36, 16, 4.—Hence, Hўpătaei, ōrum, m., its inhabitants, Liv. 36, 14; cf. exsules, id. 41, 25, 3.
hypata.short: Hўpăta, ae, f., = Ὑπάτη, a small town of Thessaly, near the Penēus, now Neópatra, Liv.

hypate.full: hўpătē, ēs, f., = ὑπάτη, the lowest, deepest string of a musical instrument, Vitr. 5, 4, 6; 6, 1 med. (as Greek, Mart. Cap. 9, § 931).
hypate.short: hўpătē, ēs, f., = ὑπάτη, the lowest, deepest string of a musical instrument, Vitr.

hypatius.full: hўpătĭus or Hypasius, a false reading for Lasus, Mart. Cap. 9, § 936; v. Kopp ad loc.
hypatius.short: hўpătĭus or Hypasius, a false reading for Lasus, Mart.

hypatoides.full: hўpătŏīdes, is, n., = ὑπατοειδής, a kind of musical modulation, Mart. Cap. 9, § 965 sq.
hypatoides.short: hўpătŏīdes, is, n., = ὑπατοειδής, a kind of musical modulation, Mart.

hypecoon.full: hўpēcŏon, i, n., = ὑπήκοον, a plant, called Hypecoum procumbens, Linn.; Plin. 27, 11, 67, § 93.
hypecoon.short: hўpēcŏon, i, n., = ὑπήκοον, a plant, called Hypecoum procumbens, Linn.;

hypelate.full: hўpĕlătē, ēs, f., = ὑπελάτη, a plant, called also hypoglottion, danaë, and carpophyllon, broad-leaved holly, Plin. 15, 30, 39, § 131.
hypelate.short: hўpĕlătē, ēs, f., = ὑπελάτη, a plant, called also hypoglottion, danaë, and carpophyllon, broad-leaved holly, Plin.

hypenemius.full: hўpēnĕmĭus, a, um, adj., = ὑπηνέμιος, containing wind, windy: ova, windeggs, Plin. 10, 58, 79, § 160; id. 10, 60, 80, § 166 (in Varr. R. R. 2, 1, 19, written as Greek).
hypenemius.short: hўpēnĕmĭus, a, um, adj., = ὑπηνέμιος, containing wind, windy: ova, windeggs, Plin.

hyperbaton.full: hўperbăton, i, n., = ὑπέρβατον, a rhet. fig., transposition of words (pure Lat. transgressio), Quint. 9, 3, 91; cf. id. 8, 6, 62 sq.; 9, 1, 6 al.
hyperbaton.short: hўperbăton, i, n., = ὑπέρβατον, a rhet.

hyperbolaeus.full: hўperbŏlaeus, a, um, adj., = ὑπερβόλαιος, extreme: soni, Vitr. 5, 4, 7 sq.
hyperbolaeus.short: hўperbŏlaeus, a, um, adj., = ὑπερβόλαιος, extreme: soni, Vitr.

hyperbole.full: hўperbŏlē, ēs, f., = ὑπερβολή, a rhet. fig., exaggeration, hyperbole (pure Lat. superlatio and superjectio), Quint. 8, 6, 67 sq.; 8, 4, 29; Sen. Ben. 7, 23 (in Cic. Top. 10, 45, and Fam. 7, 32, 2, written as Greek).
hyperbole.short: hўperbŏlē, ēs, f., = ὑπερβολή, a rhet.

hyperbolicus.full: hўperbŏlĭcus, a, um, adj., = ὑπερβολικός, excessive, overstrained, hyperbolical: instrumenta, Sid. Ep. 7, 2 med. (Cujac. reads hypobola = ὑπόβολα, pledged). —Adv.. hўperbŏlĭcē, hyperbolically: dictum, Hier. ap. Jes. 2, 6, 25; id. ap. Galat. 4, 15; 16.
hyperbolicus.short: hўperbŏlĭcus, a, um, adj., = ὑπερβολικός, excessive, overstrained, hyperbolical: instrumenta, Sid.

hyperbolus.full: Hўperbŏlus, i, m., an Athenian orator, Cic. Brut. 62, 224; id. Rep. 4, 10; Quint. 1, 10, 18 al.
hyperbolus.short: Hўperbŏlus, i, m., an Athenian orator, Cic.

hyperborei.full: Hўperbŏrĕi, ōrum, m., = Ὑπερβόρεοι (-ειοι), a fabulous people living at the extreme north, the Hyperboreans, Mel. 1, 2, 4 sq.; 3, 5, 1; Plin. 4, 12, 26, § 89; Cic. N. D. 3, 23, 57.— Derivv. Hўper-bŏrĕus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to the Hyperboreans, Hyperborean, poet., also i. q. northern: campi, Hor. C. 2, 20, 16: orae, Verg. G. 3, 196: glacies, id. ib. 4, 517; cf. pruinae, Val. Fl. 8, 210: ursa, Luc. 5, 23: septentrio, Verg. G. 3, 381: Pallene, Ov. M. 15, 356: triumphus (gained over the Ca
hyperborei.short: Hўperbŏrĕi, ōrum, m., = Ὑπερβόρεοι (-ειοι), a fabulous people living at the extreme north, the Hyperboreans, Mel.

hypercatalectus.full: hўpercătălectus or hўpercă-tălectĭcus, versus = ὑπερκατάληκτος or ὑπερκαταληκτικός, in prosody, a verse that has at the end a syllable or a foot too much, hypercatalectic, Serv. p. 1817 P.; Prisc. p. 1216 ib.
hypercatalectus.short: hўpercătălectus or hўpercă-tălectĭcus, versus = ὑπερκατάληκτος or ὑπερκαταληκτικός, in prosody, a verse that has at the end a syllable or a foot too much, hypercatalectic, Serv.

hyperia.full: Hўpĕrīa or -ēa, ae, f., a fountain at Pherœ, in Thessaly, Plin. 4, 8, 15, § 29; Val. Fl. 4, 375.
hyperia.short: Hўpĕrīa or -ēa, ae, f., a fountain at Pherœ, in Thessaly, Plin.

hypericon.full: hўpĕrīcon (-īcum), i, n., = ὑπέρεικον, a plant, called also chamaepitys and corion, ground-pine, Plin. 26, 8, 53, § 85.
hypericon.short: hўpĕrīcon (-īcum), i, n., = ὑπέρεικον, a plant, called also chamaepitys and corion, ground-pine, Plin.

hyperides.full: Hўpĕrīdes, is, m., = Ὑπερίδης, a celebrated orator in Athens, Quint. 10, 1, 77; Cic. de Or. 1, 13, 58; 3, 7, 28; id. Or. 26, 90; 31, 110; id. Ac. 1, 3, 10 al.
hyperides.short: Hўpĕrīdes, is, m., = Ὑπερίδης, a celebrated orator in Athens, Quint.

hyperion.full: Hўpĕrīon, ŏnis, m., = Ὑπερίων. Son of a Titan and the Earth, father of the Sun, Hyg. Fab. praef.; Cic. N. D. 3, 21, 54; Ov. M. 4, 192; 241.— Deriv.: Hўpĕ-rīŏnĭus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Hyperion, Sol. Avien. Arat. 396.— The Sun: interea fugit albu' jubar Hyperionis cursum, Enn. ap. Prisc. p. 658 P. (Ann. v. 547 Vahl.); so Laber. ap. Gell. 10, 17, 4; Ov. M. 8, 565; id. F. 1, 385; Stat. S. 4, 4, 27.— Hyperionis urbs, i. q. Heliopolis, a city of Lower Egypt, with a temple of the Sun, Ov. M

hypermnestra.full: Hўpermnestra, ae, and Hў-permnestrē, ēs (and mutilated Hy-permestra, Hyg. Fab. 168; Serv. ad Verg. A. 10, 497; Prop. 5, 7, 63 Müll.; like Clytemestra for Clytaemnestra), f., = Ὑπερμνήστρη, the youngest of the daughters of Danăus, the only one who preserved her husband's life, Ov. H. 14, 1 sq.; Prop. 4 (5), 7, 63.
hypermnestra.short: Hўpermnestra, ae, and Hў-permnestrē, ēs (and mutilated Hy-permestra, Hyg.

hyperocha.full: hўpĕrŏcha, ae, f., = ὑπεροχή, excess, superabundance, Dig. 20, 4, 20.
hyperocha.short: hўpĕrŏcha, ae, f., = ὑπεροχή, excess, superabundance, Dig.

hyperthyrum.full: hўperthўrum, i, n., = ὑπέρθυρον, the lintel of a door-way, Vitr. 4, 6 dub. (al. hypothyrum).
hyperthyrum.short: hўperthўrum, i, n., = ὑπέρθυρον, the lintel of a door-way, Vitr.

hyphear.full: hўphĕar, ăris, n., = ὕφεαρ, the mistletoe, Plin. 16, 44, 93, § 245 sq.; 16, 30, 52, § 120.
hyphear.short: hўphĕar, ăris, n., = ὕφεαρ, the mistletoe, Plin.

hyphen.full: hўphen, indecl. n., = ὑφʼ ἕν, a rhetorical figure, by which two words are united as one, Diom. p. 429 P.; Serv. ad Verg. A. 1, 192.

hypnale.full: hypnălē, ēs, f., = ὑπναλή, a kind of adder, Sol. 27, 31.
hypnale.short: hypnălē, ēs, f., = ὑπναλή, a kind of adder, Sol.

hypnotice.full: hypnōtĭcē, ēs, f., = ὑπνωτική, a soporific plant, App. Herb. 74.
hypnotice.short: hypnōtĭcē, ēs, f., = ὑπνωτική, a soporific plant, App.

hypnoticus.full: hypnōtĭcus, a, um, adj., = ὑπνωτικός, putting to sleep, soporific, Theod. Prisc. 2, 31.† † hўpŏbăsis, is, f., = ὑπόβασις, the pedestal, base of a monument: MARMOREA, Inscr. Orell. 1541; 1670.
hypnoticus.short: hypnōtĭcus, a, um, adj., = ὑπνωτικός, putting to sleep, soporific, Theod.

hypobolimaeus.full: Hўpŏbŏlĭmaeus, i, m., = Ὑποβολιμαῖος, The Counterfeit, the title of a comedy by Menander and Caecilius, Quint. 1, 10, 18; Gell. 15, 14, 5; Fest. s. v. noxia, p. 174 Müll.
hypobolimaeus.short: Hўpŏbŏlĭmaeus, i, m., = Ὑποβολιμαῖος, The Counterfeit, the title of a comedy by Menander and Caecilius, Quint.

hypobrychium.full: hўpobrўchĭum, ĭi, n., = ὑποβρύχιον, a drowning whirlpool: irrespirabile, Tert. Idol. 24.
hypobrychium.short: hўpobrўchĭum, ĭi, n., = ὑποβρύχιον, a drowning whirlpool: irrespirabile, Tert.

hypocausis.full: hўpŏcausis, is, f., = ὑπόκαυσις, a furnace that heats from below, Vitr. 5, 10, 1 sqq.
hypocausis.short: hўpŏcausis, is, f., = ὑπόκαυσις, a furnace that heats from below, Vitr.

hypocaustum.full: hўpŏcaustum or -on, i, n., = ὑπόκαυστον, a bathing-room heated from below, a sweating-chamber (pure Lat. vaporarium), Vitr. 5, 10; Plin. Ep. 2, 17, 23; 11; Stat. S. 1, 5, 59; Dig. 17, 1, 16 al.— Adj.: diaetae hypocaustae, sweating-rooms, Dig. 32, 9, 55, § 3.
