hypocaustum.short: hўpŏcaustum or -on, i, n., = ὑπόκαυστον, a bathing-room heated from below, a sweating-chamber (pure Lat.

hypochoeris.full: hўpŏchoeris, ĭdis, f., = ὑποχοιρίς, a plant, otherwise unknown, Plin. 21, 15, 52, § 89.
hypochoeris.short: hўpŏchoeris, ĭdis, f., = ὑποχοιρίς, a plant, otherwise unknown, Plin.

hypochondria.full: hўpŏchondrĭa, ōrum, n., = ὑποχόνδρια, τά, the soft part of the body from the ribs to the groin, the abdomen, Theod. Prisc. de Diaet. 10.
hypochondria.short: hўpŏchondrĭa, ōrum, n., = ὑποχόνδρια, τά, the soft part of the body from the ribs to the groin, the abdomen, Theod.

hypochyma.full: hўpŏchўma, ătis, n., = ὑπόχυμα, a cataract in the eye, Marc. Emp. 8 med.
hypochyma.short: hўpŏchўma, ătis, n., = ὑπόχυμα, a cataract in the eye, Marc.

hypochysis.full: hўpŏchўsis, is, f., = ὑπόχυσις, a cataract in the eye (pure Lat. suffusio), Plin. 25, 12, 91, § 143 (in Cels. 6, 6, 35, written as Greek).
hypochysis.short: hўpŏchўsis, is, f., = ὑπόχυσις, a cataract in the eye (pure Lat.

hypocisthis.full: hўpŏcisthis, ĭdis, f., = ὑποκισθίς, a parasitic plant that grows on the cisthus: Asarum hўpocistis, Linn.; Plin. 24, 10, 31, § 81; 26, 8, 48, § 81; 28, 16, 92, § 177 al.
hypocisthis.short: hўpŏcisthis, ĭdis, f., = ὑποκισθίς, a parasitic plant that grows on the cisthus: Asarum hўpocistis, Linn.;

hypocoriasis.full: hўpŏcŏrĭăsis, is, f., = ὑποκορίασις, a disease under the pupil of the eye in cattle, Veg. Vet. 2, 16, 1.
hypocoriasis.short: hўpŏcŏrĭăsis, is, f., = ὑποκορίασις, a disease under the pupil of the eye in cattle, Veg.

hypocorisma.full: hўpŏcŏrisma, ătis, n., = ὑποκόρισμα, in gramm., a diminutive, Charis. p. 24 P.
hypocorisma.short: hўpŏcŏrisma, ătis, n., = ὑποκόρισμα, in gramm., a diminutive, Charis.

hypocrisis.full: hўpocrĭsis, is, f., = ὑπόκρισις, an imitation of a person's speech and gestures, mimicry, Don. Vit. Verg. 11.— Transf., hypocrisy, pretended sanctity (eccl. Lat.), = pietatis simulatio, Vulg. Matt. 23, 28; id. Luc. 12, 1.
hypocrisis.short: hўpocrĭsis, is, f., = ὑπόκρισις, an imitation of a person's speech and gestures, mimicry, Don.

hypocrita.full: hўpocrĭta or -es, ae, m., = ὑποκριτής. A mime who accompanied the delivery of an actor by gestures, Suet. Ner. 24; Quint. 2, 17, 12; 11, 3, 7.— In eccl. Lat., a hypocrite, Vulg. Job, 8, 13; id. Matt. 6, 2; id. Luc. 12, 56 al.

hypodiaconus.full: hўpŏdĭācŏnus, i, m., = ὑποδιάκονος, a sub-deacon, Cod. Theod. 16, 2, 7; Hier. Ep. 51, 2.
hypodiaconus.short: hўpŏdĭācŏnus, i, m., = ὑποδιάκονος, a sub-deacon, Cod.

hypodidascalus.full: hўpŏdĭdascălus, i, m., = ὑποδιδάσκαλος, an under-teacher, Cic. Fam. 9, 18, 4.
hypodidascalus.short: hўpŏdĭdascălus, i, m., = ὑποδιδάσκαλος, an under-teacher, Cic.

hypogeson.full: hўpŏgēson, i, n., = ὑπόγεισον, a kind of houseleek that grows in the gutters of roofs, Plin. 25, 13, 102, § 160.
hypogeson.short: hўpŏgēson, i, n., = ὑπόγεισον, a kind of houseleek that grows in the gutters of roofs, Plin.

hypogeus.full: hўpŏgēus, a, um, adj., = ὑπόγαιος, underground: loca, Cael. Aur. Tard. 2, 37, 191.—Hence, subst.: hўpŏgēum or hў-pŏgaeum, i, n., = ὑπόγειον (ὑπόγαιον), a vault or cellar under ground, Vitr. 6, 11; a burying-vault, sepulchre, Petr. 111, 2; Inscr. Grut. 1114, 3.
hypogeus.short: hўpŏgēus, a, um, adj., = ὑπόγαιος, underground: loca, Cael.

hypoglossa.full: hўpoglossa, ae, f., = ὑπόγλωσσον, a kind of butcher's broom or ruscus: Ruscus hypoglossum, Linn.; Plin. 27, 11, 67, § 93.
hypoglossa.short: hўpoglossa, ae, f., = ὑπόγλωσσον, a kind of butcher's broom or ruscus: Ruscus hypoglossum, Linn.;

hypoglottion.full: hўpoglottĭon, ĭi, n., = ὑπογλώττιον, a plant, called also daphne and hypelate, broad-leaved ruscus: Ruscus hypophyllum, Linn.; Plin. 15, 30, 39, § 131.
hypoglottion.short: hўpoglottĭon, ĭi, n., = ὑπογλώττιον, a plant, called also daphne and hypelate, broad-leaved ruscus: Ruscus hypophyllum, Linn.;

hypographum.full: hўpogrăphum, i, n., = ὑπόγραφον, a rough draught, sketch: prima carminis hypographa, Aug. ap. Don. Vit. Verg. 12.
hypographum.short: hўpogrăphum, i, n., = ὑπόγραφον, a rough draught, sketch: prima carminis hypographa, Aug.

hypolysos.full: hўpŏlўsos, i, f., = ὑπόλυσος, a plant, also called Artemisia, App. Herb. 10.
hypolysos.short: hўpŏlўsos, i, f., = ὑπόλυσος, a plant, also called Artemisia, App.

hypomelis.full: hўpŏmēlis, ĭdis, f., = ὑπομηλίς, a kind of sourish fruit, Pall. Dec. 4, 1 (dub.).
hypomelis.short: hўpŏmēlis, ĭdis, f., = ὑπομηλίς, a kind of sourish fruit, Pall.

hypomnema.full: hўpomnēma, ătis, n., = ὑπόμνημα, a written remark, memorandum, note: in exscribendis hypomnematis, Cic. Fil. ap. Cic. Fam. 16, 21, 8 (in Cic. Att. 2, 1, 2; 15, 23; 16, 14, 4, written as Greek).
hypomnema.short: hўpomnēma, ătis, n., = ὑπόμνημα, a written remark, memorandum, note: in exscribendis hypomnematis, Cic.

hypomnematographus.full: hўpomnēmătŏgrăphus, i, m., = ὑπομνηματογράφος (late Lat. for commentariensis), a registrar, Cod. Theod. 12, 1, 192; Cod. Just. 10, 31, 59.

hypomochlion.full: hўpŏmochlĭon, ĭi, n., = ὑπομόχλιον, the support of a lever, a fulcrum, Vitr. 10, 8.
hypomochlion.short: hўpŏmochlĭon, ĭi, n., = ὑπομόχλιον, the support of a lever, a fulcrum, Vitr.

hypomone.full: hўpŏmŏnē, ēs, f., = ὑπομονή, rhet. t. t., a holding back of the principal thought for a surprise (pure Lat. sustentatio, inopinatum), Rufin. Fig. Sent. 34; cf. Quint. 9, 2, 22.

hypophora.full: hўpŏphŏra, ae, f., = ὑποφορά, a rhet. fig., an objection made by an opponent, Mart. Cap. 5, § 563.
hypophora.short: hўpŏphŏra, ae, f., = ὑποφορά, a rhet.

hypopodium.full: hўpŏpŏdĭum, ĭi, n., = ὑποπόδιον, a footstool, Paul. Sent. 3, 6, 65.
hypopodium.short: hўpŏpŏdĭum, ĭi, n., = ὑποπόδιον, a footstool, Paul.

hypostasis.full: hўpostăsis, is, f., = ὑπόστασις, a substance, personality, hypostasy, Cod. Just. 1, 1, 6; Hier. Ep. ad Damas, 15.
hypostasis.short: hўpostăsis, is, f., = ὑπόστασις, a substance, personality, hypostasy, Cod.

hypotaurium.full: hўpŏtaurĭum, ĭi, n., = ὑποταύριον, the part of the body between the scrotum and fundament, Veg. Vet. 1, 46.
hypotaurium.short: hўpŏtaurĭum, ĭi, n., = ὑποταύριον, the part of the body between the scrotum and fundament, Veg.

hypotenusa.full: hўpŏtēnūsa, ae, f., = ὑποτείνουσα, the hypothenuse, Hyg. de Limit. p. 176 Goes. Boëth. Art. Geom. p. 408, 20.—Hence, hў-pŏtēnūsālis, e, adj., of or belonging to the hypothenuse, Boëth. Art. Geom. p. 412, 5 al.
hypotenusa.short: hўpŏtēnūsa, ae, f., = ὑποτείνουσα, the hypothenuse, Hyg.

hypotheca.full: hўpŏthēca, ae, f., = ὑποθήκη, a pledge, security (esp. of immovable things; whereas pignus is used of movable things; cf. also: arra, arrabo), a mortgage, Just. Inst. 4, 6, § 7; Dig. 13, 7, 9; 20, 1, 2 et saep. (in Cic. Fam. 13, 56, 2, written as Greek).—Hence, hўpŏthēcārĭus, a, um, adj. hypotheca, of or relating to a mortgage: actio, Dig. 20, 4, 1 fin.: creditor, id. 42, 7, 1.
hypotheca.short: hўpŏthēca, ae, f., = ὑποθήκη, a pledge, security (esp.

hypotheticus.full: hўpŏthĕtĭcus, i, m., = ὑποθετικός, a mathematician who proceeds hypothetically, App. Dogm. Plat. 3 fin. p. 40.
hypotheticus.short: hўpŏthĕtĭcus, i, m., = ὑποθετικός, a mathematician who proceeds hypothetically, App.

hypotrachelium.full: hўpŏtrăchēlĭum, ĭi, n., = ὑποτραχήλιον, in archit., the neck of a column below the capital, Vitr. 3, 2 sq.; 4, 3; 7.
hypotrachelium.short: hўpŏtrăchēlĭum, ĭi, n., = ὑποτραχήλιον, in archit., the neck of a column below the capital, Vitr.

hypotrimma.full: hўpotrimma, ătis, n., = ὑπότριμμα, a sauce made of all sorts of condiments, Apic. 1, 33, § 34.
hypotrimma.short: hўpotrimma, ătis, n., = ὑπότριμμα, a sauce made of all sorts of condiments, Apic.

hypsa.full: Hypsa, ae, f., a river in Sicily, now Belici, Plin. 3, 8, 14, § 90; Sil. 14, 228.
hypsa.short: Hypsa, ae, f., a river in Sicily, now Belici, Plin.

hypsaeus.full: Hypsaeus, i, m., a surname of P. Plautius, Cic. Att. 3, 8, 3.
hypsaeus.short: Hypsaeus, i, m., a surname of P.

hypseus.full: Hypseus (dissyll.), ei, m., one who was present at the nuptials of Perseus, Ov. M. 5, 98.
hypseus.short: Hypseus (dissyll.), ei, m., one who was present at the nuptials of Perseus, Ov.

hypsicrates.full: Hypsicrătes, is, m., a grammarian, Gell. 16, 12.
hypsicrates.short: Hypsicrătes, is, m., a grammarian, Gell.

hypsipyle.full: Hypsĭpўlē, ēs, f., = Ὑψιπύλη, daughter of Thoas, queen of Lemnos in the time of the Argonauts; she saved her father when the women killed all the men; she also entertained Jason, Stat. Th. 4, 739 sq.; Ov. H. 6, 1 sq.; Val. Fl. 2, 90 sq.; Prop. 1, 15, 18: Hypsipyles patria, i. e. Lemnos, Ov. M. 13, 399.—Hence, Hypsĭpўlēus, a, um, adj.: tellus, i. e. Lemnos, Ov. F. 3, 82.
hypsipyle.short: Hypsĭpўlē, ēs, f., = Ὑψιπύλη, daughter of Thoas, queen of Lemnos in the time of the Argonauts;

hypsoma.full: hypsōma, ătis, n., = ὕψωμα, height, Tert. ad Scap. 3.
hypsoma.short: hypsōma, ătis, n., = ὕψωμα, height, Tert.

hyrcani.full: Hyrcāni, ōrum, m., = Ὕρκανοι, the Hyrcanians on the Caspian Sea, Mel. 1, 2, 5; 3, 5, 4; Plin. 6, 13, 15, § 36; Tac. A. 6, 36; 43; 11, 8; Cat. 11, 5; Sil. 13, 474 al. Macedones Hyrcani, the Hyrcanians intermixed with Macedonians in Lydia, Plin. 5, 29, 31, § 120; Tac. A. 2, 47.— Derivv. Hyrcānus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to the Hyrcanians, Hyrcanian: mare, i. e. the Caspian Sea, Prop. 2, 30 (3, 28), 20: sinus, Mel. 3, 5, 3 sq.: montes, Plin. 31, 3, 26, § 43: luci, Val. Fl. 6, 114: canis, Lucr.
hyrcani.short: Hyrcāni, ōrum, m., = Ὕρκανοι, the Hyrcanians on the Caspian Sea, Mel.

hyrgaletici.full: Hyrgălētĭci campi, the Hyrgaletic plains, on the borders of Phrygia and Caria, Plin. 5, 29, 31, § 113.
hyrgaletici.short: Hyrgălētĭci campi, the Hyrgaletic plains, on the borders of Phrygia and Caria, Plin.

hyrie.full: Hўrĭē, ēs, f., = Ὑρίη, a lake, and town situated by it, in Bœotia, Ov. M. 7, 271; 380; Plin. 4, 7, 12, § 26.
hyrie.short: Hўrĭē, ēs, f., = Ὑρίη, a lake, and town situated by it, in Bœotia, Ov.

hyrieus.full: Hўrĭeus (trisyl.), ei, m., = Ὑριεύς, a poor Bœotian, father of Orion, Ov. F. 5, 499; 535.—Hence, Hўrĭēŭs (quadrisyl.), a, um, adj.: Hўrĭēa proles, i. e. Orion, Ov. F. 6, 719.
hyrieus.short: Hўrĭeus (trisyl.), ei, m., = Ὑριεύς, a poor Bœotian, father of Orion, Ov.

hyrtacus.full: Hyrtăcus, i, m., father of Nisus, Verg. A. 9, 406.—Hence, Deriv.: Hyrtă-cĭdes, i. e. Nisus, Verg. A. 9, 176 sq.; Ov. Ib. 631.
hyrtacus.short: Hyrtăcus, i, m., father of Nisus, Verg.

hysginum.full: hysgĭnum, i, n., = ὕσγινον, the darkred color obtained from the plant ὕσγη, Plin. 9, 41, 65, § 140; 21, 26, 97, § 170; Vitr. 7, 14; Dig. 32, 1, 78, § 5.
hysginum.short: hysgĭnum, i, n., = ὕσγινον, the darkred color obtained from the plant ὕσγη, Plin.

hysopites.full: hȳsōpītes (hysso-), ae, m., = ὑσσωπίτης (οἶνος), hyssop-wine, Plin. 14, 16, 19, § 109; Col. 12, 35.
hysopites.short: hȳsōpītes (hysso-), ae, m., = ὑσσωπίτης (οἶνος), hyssop-wine, Plin.

hysopum.full: hȳsōpum (hysso-), i, n., = ὕσσωπος, hyssop: Hyssopus officinalis, Linn.; Plin. 25, 11, 87, § 136; 26, 11, 70, § 114; 26, 12, 76, § 124: asperges me hyssopo, et mundabor, Vulg. Psa. 50, 8 al.—And in a form corresp. to the Gr., hyssōpus, i, f., Cels. 4, 8; Col. 7, 5 fin.—Also scanned hȳsŏpum, Aemil. Mac. de Hyssopo.
hysopum.short: hȳsōpum (hysso-), i, n., = ὕσσωπος, hyssop: Hyssopus officinalis, Linn.;

hystaspes.full: Hystaspes, is or i, m., = Ὑστάσπης, father of the Persian king Darius I., Plin. 6, 27, 31, § 133; Just. 1, 10, 6; Nep. Milt. 3; Reg. 1.
hystaspes.short: Hystaspes, is or i, m., = Ὑστάσπης, father of the Persian king Darius I., Plin.

hystericus.full: hystĕrĭcus, a, um, adj., = ὑστερικός, hysterical, Mart. 11, 71, 1; 11, 7, 11.
hystericus.short: hystĕrĭcus, a, um, adj., = ὑστερικός, hysterical, Mart.

hysterologia.full: hystĕrŏlŏgĭa, ae, f., = ὑστερολογία, a rhet. fig., the hysteron proteron, Serv. ad Verg. A. 9, 816.
hysterologia.short: hystĕrŏlŏgĭa, ae, f., = ὑστερολογία, a rhet.

hystricosus.full: hystrĭcōsus, a, um, adj. hystrix, prickly, thorny (late Lat.), trop.: hystricosae et lividae mentis homo, Hier. in. Ruf. 1, 7.

hystriculus.full: hystrĭcŭlus, a, um, adj. id., prickly, hairy, bearded (post-class.): hystriculus, δασύπρωκτος, Gloss. Philox.: pusio, Arn. 5, 174: puer, Tert. Pall. 4 dub. (al. striculus, ustriculus).

hystrix.full: hystrix (histrix), ĭcis, f., = ὕστριξ, a porcupine, Plin. 8, 35, 53, § 125; Calp. Ecl. 6, 14; Claud. Idyll. 4.
hystrix.short: hystrix (histrix), ĭcis, f., = ὕστριξ, a porcupine, Plin.

i.full: I, i, the ninth letter of the Latin alphabet, a vowel; for even the old grammarians distinguished it from the consonant written with the same character; see the letter J. The short i is, next to ë, the least emphatic of the Latin vowels, and serves, corresp. to the Gr. o, as a connecting sound in forming compounds: aerĭfodina, aerĭpes, altitudo, altĭsonus, arcitenens, homĭcida, etc. It is often inserted in Latin words derived from Greek: mina, techina, cucinus, lucinus (for mna, techna, cycnus,
i.short: I, i, the ninth letter of the Latin alphabet, a vowel;

iacchus.full: Ĭacchus, i, m., = Ἴακχος. A poetic and mystical appellation of Bacchus, Verg. E. 7, 61; id. G. 1, 166; Cic. Leg. 2, 14, 34; Cat. 64, 251; Ov. M. 4, 15.— Poet. transf., like Bacchus, wine: (Silenum) Inflatum hesterno venas, ut semper, Iaccho, Verg. E. 6, 15: multo madefactus, Col. poët. 10, 309.

iadera.full: Ĭādĕra, ae, f., a city of Illyria, now Zara, Mel. 2, 3, 13; also called ĭāder, Plin. 3, 26, 30, § 152; 3, 21, 25, § 140 al.; Luc. 4, 405.—Hence, ĭādertīni, ōrum, m., the inhabitants of ladera, Auct. B. Alex. 42.
iadera.short: Ĭādĕra, ae, f., a city of Illyria, now Zara, Mel.

iaera.full: Ĭaera, ae, f., = Ἴαιρα, the name of a sea-nymph or Nereid, Hom. Il. 18, 42; but Lat. only as the name of an Oread or woodnymph: sylvestris, Verg. A. 9, 673; Hyg. Fab. praef.
iaera.short: Ĭaera, ae, f., = Ἴαιρα, the name of a sea-nymph or Nereid, Hom.

ialysus.full: ĭālўsus-ĭālўsus or os-os, i, m., = Ἰάλυσος. A son of the fourth Sol, acc. to Cic. N. D. 3, 21, 54; a famous picture of him by Protogenes, at Rhodes, afterwards in Rome, Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 60, § 135; id. Or. 2, 5; Plin. 35, 10, 36, § 102; Gell. 15, 31, 3.— f., an ancient city of Rhodes, now the village of Ialiso, Mel. 2, 7, 4; Plin. 5, 31, 35, § 132.— Hence, Deriv. ĭālўsĭus, a, um, adj., of lalysus: Telchines, Ov. M. 7, 365.
ialysus.short: ĭālўsus-ĭālўsus or os-os, i, m., = Ἰάλυσος.

iambelegus.full: ĭambĕlĕgus, a, um, adj., = ἰαμβέλεγος, consisting of an iambic measure (diiambus) hypercatalectic and a dactylic penthemimeris: metrum, Serv. de Cent. Met. 9, § 17.
iambelegus.short: ĭambĕlĕgus, a, um, adj., = ἰαμβέλεγος, consisting of an iambic measure (diiambus) hypercatalectic and a dactylic penthemimeris: metrum, Serv.

iambeus.full: ĭambēus, a, um, adj., = ἰαμβεῖος, iambic: trimetri, Hor. A. P. 253.
iambeus.short: ĭambēus, a, um, adj., = ἰαμβεῖος, iambic: trimetri, Hor.

iambicinus.full: ĭambĭcĭnus, a, um, adj. iambus, iambic: numerus, Mart. Cap. 9, § 977 al.

iambicus.full: ĭambĭcus, a, um, adj., = ἰαμβικός, iambic: pes, Diom. p. 473 P.: versus, id. p. 516 sq.; ib. et saep.
iambicus.short: ĭambĭcus, a, um, adj., = ἰαμβικός, iambic: pes, Diom.

iamblichus.full: Ĭamblĭchus, i, m., = Ἰάμβλιχος, an Arabian emir, Cic. Fam. 15, 1, 2.
iamblichus.short: Ĭamblĭchus, i, m., = Ἰάμβλιχος, an Arabian emir, Cic.

iambus.full: ĭambus, i, m., = ἴαμβος, an iambic foot, an iambus. Lit., Hor. A. P. 251; Cic. de Or. 3, 47, 182; id. Or. 57, 192; Quint. 9, 4, 47; 48; 80; Diom. p. 473 P. et saep.— Transf., an iambic poem, iambic poetry: quem Hipponactis iambus laeserat aut qui erat Archilochi versu vulneratus, Cic. N. D. 3, 38, 91; so in sing., Hor. A. P. 79; Quint. 10, 1, 96.—In plur., Hor. C. 1, 16, 3; 24; id. Ep. 1, 19, 23; 2, 2, 59; Quint. 10, 1, 9; 59.
iambus.short: ĭambus, i, m., = ἴαμβος, an iambic foot, an iambus.

iamidae.full: Ĭămĭdae, ārum, m., the descendants of Iamus, son of Apollo, Cic. div. 1, 41, 91.
iamidae.short: Ĭămĭdae, ārum, m., the descendants of Iamus, son of Apollo, Cic.

iamphoryna.full: Ĭamphŏrȳna (-īna, -ynna), ae, f., the capital of the Mœdi in Macedonia, now Vrania or Ivorina, in the upper valley of the Moráva, Liv. 26, 25, 8.
iamphoryna.short: Ĭamphŏrȳna (-īna, -ynna), ae, f., the capital of the Mœdi in Macedonia, now Vrania or Ivorina, in the upper valley of the Moráva, Liv.

ianthe.full: Ĭanthē, ēs, f., daughter of Telestes, in Creta, Ov. M. 9, 715 sq.
ianthe.short: Ĭanthē, ēs, f., daughter of Telestes, in Creta, Ov.

ianthinus.full: ĭanthĭnus, a, um, adj., = ἰάνθινος, violet-blue, violet-: color, Plin. 21, 8, 22, § 45: vestis, id. 21, 6, 14, § 27.—Subst.: ĭan-thĭnum, i, n., violet, the color, Dig. 32, 70, § 13.—Plur.: ĭanthĭna, ōrum, violet-colored garments, Mart. 2, 39, 1.
ianthinus.short: ĭanthĭnus, a, um, adj., = ἰάνθινος, violet-blue, violet-: color, Plin.

ianthis.full: ĭanthis, ĭdis, f., = ἰανθίς, a violetcolored flower, Marc. Emp. 17.
ianthis.short: ĭanthis, ĭdis, f., = ἰανθίς, a violetcolored flower, Marc.

iapetides.full: Ĭāpĕtĭdes, ae, m., a player on the cithara, Ov. M. 5, 111.
iapetides.short: Ĭāpĕtĭdes, ae, m., a player on the cithara, Ov.

iapetus.full: Īăpĕtus, i, m., = Ἰαπετός, a Titan, son of Uranos and Gœa, the father of Atlas, Prometheus, and Epimetheus, Hyg. F. praef.; 54; 142; 144; Verg. G. 1, 279; Lact. 2, 10, 7 sq.: satus Iapeto, i. e. Prometheus, Ov. M. 1, 82; called also Iapeti genus, Hor. C. 1, 3, 27.— Deriv. īăpĕtīŏnĭdes, ae, m., a male descendant of Iapetus: Atlas, Ov. M. 4, 632: fratres gemini, i. e. Prometheus and Epimetneus, Claud. Eutr. 2, 49.
iapetus.short: Īăpĕtus, i, m., = Ἰαπετός, a Titan, son of Uranos and Gœa, the father of Atlas, Prometheus, and Epimetheus, Hyg.

iapis.full: Ĭāpis, ĭdis, m., the physician of Æneas, Verg. A. 12, 391; Aus. Epigr. 19.
iapis.short: Ĭāpis, ĭdis, m., the physician of Æneas, Verg.

iapydes.full: Ĭāpўdes, um, m., = Ἰάπυδες, a people of Illyria, in the present military frontier of Croatia, Plin. 3, 18, 22, § 127; Liv. 43, 5; Cic. Balb. 14, 32.— Hence, ĭāpys, ўdis, adj., of or belonging to the Iapydes: Iapydis arva Timavi, Verg. G. 3, 475.— ĭāpўdĭa, the country of the Iapydes, Plin. 3, 21, 25, § 140; Tib. 4, 1, 108; called Iāpŭ-dia, Sall. H. Fragm. 1, 11 Dietsch.
iapydes.short: Ĭāpўdes, um, m., = Ἰάπυδες, a people of Illyria, in the present military frontier of Croatia, Plin.

iapys.full: Iāpys, ўdis, v. Iapydes, II. B.

iapyx.full: Ĭāpyx, ўgis, m., = Ἰάπυξ, a son of Dœdalus, who ruled in Southern Italy (Apulia or Calabria), Plin. 3, 11, 16, § 102; Ov. M. 15, 52.— Transf. A river in the south of Italy, Plin. 3, 11, 16, § 102.— A wind that blows in the south of Italy, the west-northwest of the Greeks, Hor. C. 1, 3, 4; Verg. A. 8, 710.— Deriv. ĭāpўgĭa, ae, f., that part of Southern Italy (Apulia or Calabria) over which Iapyx ruled, Iapygia, Plin. 3, 11, 16, § 102; Ov. M. 15, 703; Serv. Verg. G. 3, 475.— Derivv. ĭāpўgĭus, a, u
iapyx.short: Ĭāpyx, ўgis, m., = Ἰάπυξ, a son of Dœdalus, who ruled in Southern Italy (Apulia or Calabria), Plin.

iarba.full: Ĭarba, Iarbas, or Hĭarbas, ae, m., a king of Mauritania, Ov. F. 3, 552 sq.; Verg. A. 4, 36; Juv. 5, 45.—Hence, ĭarbī-ta, ae, m., a Mauritanian, Hor. Ep. 1, 19, 15; cf. respecting him, Weichert: De Iarbita Timagenis aemulatore, Grimm. 1821.
iarba.short: Ĭarba, Iarbas, or Hĭarbas, ae, m., a king of Mauritania, Ov.

iardanis.full: Ĭardănis, ĭdis, f., the daughter of Iardanus, i. e. Omphale, Ov. H. 9, 103.
iardanis.short: Ĭardănis, ĭdis, f., the daughter of Iardanus, i.

iasides.full: Īăsĭdes, ae, v. 1. Iasius, II. B. b.

iasione.full: īăsĭōnē, ēs, f., = ἰασιώνη, a plant bearing a white flower, perhaps bind-weed: Convolvulus sepium, Linn.; Plin. 21, 17, 65, § 105; 22, 22, 39, § 82.
iasione.short: īăsĭōnē, ēs, f., = ἰασιώνη, a plant bearing a white flower, perhaps bind-weed: Convolvulus sepium, Linn.;

iasis.full: Īăsis, ĭdis, f., v. 1. Iasius, II. B. c.

iasius1.full: Īăsĭus, ĭi, m., = Ἰάσιος. Son of Jupiter and Electra, beloved of Ceres, Verg. A. 3, 168; Ov. Am. 3, 10, 25.—Called also īăsĭon, Ov. M. 9, 423; id. Tr. 2, 300; Hyg. F. 270; id. Astr. 2, 22.— King of Argos and father of Atalanta, Hyg. F. 70.— Derivv. īăsĭus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Iasius, Iasian, poet. for Argive: virgo, i. e. Io, daughter of the Argive king Inachus, Val. Fl. 4, 353.— īăsĭdes, ae, m., a male descendant of Iasius: Palinurus, Verg. A. 5, 843; applied to Adrastus, Stat. Th.

iasius2.full: Īăsĭus, a, um. Of or belonging to Iasius; v. 1. Iasius, II. B. a.— Of or belonging to the city of Iassus; v. Iassus, II. A.

iason.full: Ĭāson or Ĭāso (e. g. Mel. 1, 19, 5), ŏnis, m., = Ἰάσων. Jason, a famous Grecian hero, son of Æson, king of Thessaly, the leader of the Argonauts, a sharer in the Calydonian boar-hunt, the husband of Medea, and afterwards of Crĕūsa, Cic. Tusc. 4, 32, 69; Ov. M. 7, 5 sq.; 8, 301; 348; Val. Fl. et saep.; Hyg. F. 12, 14; 16: quo jam mercator Iason clausus et armatis obstat casa candida nautis, i. e. when the fresco in the portico of Agrippa, representing Jason and his sailors, is hidden by the white

iaspachates.full: ĭaspăchātes, ae, m., = ἰασπαχάτης, a sort of agate, jasper-agate, Plin. 37, 10, 54, § 139.
iaspachates.short: ĭaspăchātes, ae, m., = ἰασπαχάτης, a sort of agate, jasper-agate, Plin.

iaspideus.full: ĭaspĭdēŭs, a, um, adj. iaspis, of the jasper kind, jasper - like: gemmae, Plin. 37, 10, 56, § 156.

iaspis.full: ĭaspis, ĭdis, f., = ἴασπις, a green - colored precious stone, jasper, Plin. 37, 8, 37, § 115; Mart. 5, 11, 1; 9, 60, 20: fulva, Verg. A. 4, 261.—As a term of endearment: vale (Maecenas), mel gentium, Cilniorum smaragde, iaspi figulorum, berylle Porsenae, Aug. ap. Macr. S. 2, 4, 12.—Hence,
iaspis.short: ĭaspis, ĭdis, f., = ἴασπις, a green - colored precious stone, jasper, Plin.

iaspius.full: ĭaspĭus, a, um, adj. iaspis, of jasper: lapilli, Anth. Lat. 1, p. 413 Burm.

iasponyx.full: ĭaspŏnyx, ўchis, f., = ἰασπόνυξ, a sort of jasper, jasper-onyx, Plin. 37, 9, 37, § 118.
iasponyx.short: ĭaspŏnyx, ўchis, f., = ἰασπόνυξ, a sort of jasper, jasper-onyx, Plin.

iassus.full: Ĭassus or Ĭāsus, i, f., = Ἰασσός or Ἰᾶσός, an ancient and wealthy town on the coast of Caria, now Askem or Asyn Kalessi, Plin. 5, 29, 29, § 107; 9, 8, 8, § 27; Liv. 32, 33; 33, 30; 37, 17.— Derivv. ĭassĭus or ĭāsĭus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Iassus, Iassian: sinus. Mel. 1, 16 fin.; Plin. 5, 29, 29, § 107.— ĭas-senses, ĭum, m., the inhabitants of Iassus, Iassians, Liv. 37, 17.
iassus.short: Ĭassus or Ĭāsus, i, f., = Ἰασσός or Ἰᾶσός, an ancient and wealthy town on the coast of Caria, now Askem or Asyn Kalessi, Plin.

iatralipta.full: ĭātrălipta or -es, ae, m., = ἰατραλείπτης, a physician who cures by anointing, an ointment-doctor, Cels. 1, 1; Plin. Ep. 10, 4, 1; Petr. 28, 3.
iatralipta.short: ĭātrălipta or -es, ae, m., = ἰατραλείπτης, a physician who cures by anointing, an ointment-doctor, Cels.

iatraliptice.full: ĭātrăliptĭcē or ĭātrăleptĭcē, ēs, f., = ἰατραλειπτική, the art of healing with ointments, the ointment-cure, Plin. 29, 1, 2, § 4; cf. the preced. art.† † ĭātrŏmēa, ae, f., = ἰατρόμαια, a female physician, midwife, Inscr. Orell. 4232.
iatraliptice.short: ĭātrăliptĭcē or ĭātrăleptĭcē, ēs, f., = ἰατραλειπτική, the art of healing with ointments, the ointment-cure, Plin.

iatronices.full: ĭātrŏnīces, ae, m., = ἰατρονίκης, the conqueror of physicians, Plin. 29, 1, 5, § 9.
iatronices.short: ĭātrŏnīces, ae, m., = ἰατρονίκης, the conqueror of physicians, Plin.

iarartes.full: Ĭarartes, is, m., = Ἰαξάρτης, a river of Central Asia, now Syr-Daria (i. e. Yellow River), Mel. 3, 5, 6; Plin. 6, 13, 15, § 36 al.
iarartes.short: Ĭarartes, is, m., = Ἰαξάρτης, a river of Central Asia, now Syr-Daria (i.

iazyges.full: Ĭāzўges or Jāzўges (trisyl.), um, m., = Ἰάζυγες, a sarmatian people on the Danube, Plin. 4, 12, 25, § 80; Tac. A. 12, 29; Ov. Tr. 2, 191; id. P. 4, 7, 9.
iazyges.short: Ĭāzўges or Jāzўges (trisyl.), um, m., = Ἰάζυγες, a sarmatian people on the Danube, Plin.

iberis.full: ĭbēris, idis, f., = ἰβηρίς, a kind of cress, Plin. 25, 8, 49, § 87; App. Herb. 20.
iberis.short: ĭbēris, idis, f., = ἰβηρίς, a kind of cress, Plin.

iberus.full: Ibērus (Hib-), a, um, and i, v. Hiberes, I. A. l. and ll.
iberus.short: Ibērus (Hib-), a, um, and i, v.

ibex.full: ībex, ĭcis, m., a kind of goat, the chamois, Plin. 8, 53, 79, § 214; Isid. Orig. 12, 1; Hier. Job, 31, 1.
ibex.short: ībex, ĭcis, m., a kind of goat, the chamois, Plin.

ibi.full: ĭbĭ_, adv. from the pronom. root I, is, with dat. ending as in tibi, sibi, in loc. sense as in ubi; cf. Sanscr. suffix bhjam; Corss. Ausspr. 1, 169, in that place, there, = ἐνταῦθα (cf. istic). Lit., in space: ibi cenavi atque ibi quievi in navi noctem perpetem, Plaut. Am. 2, 2, 100; tandem abii ad praetorem. Ibi vix requievi, id. Capt. 2, 2, 6: nempe in foro? De. Ibi, id. As. 1, 1, 104: in Asiam hinc abii, atque ibi, etc., Ter. Heaut. 1, 1, 59: Demaratus fugit Tarquinios Corintho et ibi suas fo

ibidem.full: ĭbīdem (always ĭbĭdem in Plaut.; v. infra; so Juvenc. 3, 80; Paul. Nol. Carm. 19, 48), adv. ibi, with demonstr. suff. dem, as in idem, tandem, tantundem, etc., in the same place, in that very place, just there. Lit., in space: sarmenta concidito minute et ibidem inarato, Cato, R. R. 37, 3: cenati discubuerunt ibidem, Cic. Inv. 2, 4, 14: ille, cujus merces erant, in gladium ibidem incumberet, id. ib. 2, 51, 154: quod ibidem recte custodire poterunt, id ibidem custodiant, id. Quint. 27, 84: ne hīc

ibis.full: ībis, is and ĭdis (nom. plur. ibes, Cic. N. D. 1, 36, 101; 2, 50, 126; gen. ibium, Plin. 30, 15, 49, § 142; gen. sing. ibidis, Ov. H. 57; acc. plur. ibidas, Mel. 3, 8 fin.; acc. sing. ibim, Cic. N. D. 1, 29, 82; id. Tusc. 5, 27, 78; Plin. 10, 48, 68, § 134: ibin, Juv. 15, 3; Ov. H. 98), f., = ἶβις, a bird held sacred by the Egyptians, and which lived on water-animals, the ibis: Numenius ibis, Cuv.; Cic. N. D. 1, 36, 101; 2, 50, 126; id. Tusc. 5, 27, 78; Plin. 8, 27, 41, § 97; Mel. 3, 8, 9.— Tran

ibycus.full: Ībўcus, i, m., = Ἴβυκος. A Greek lyric poet of Rhegium, celebrated on account of the cranes which he called upon as witnesses of his murder, Cic. Tusc. 4, 33, 71; Stat. S. 5, 3, 152; Aus. Idyll. de Hist. 12, 12. — A poor man, otherwise unknown, Hor. C. 3, 15, 1.

icadius.full: Īcădĭus, ĭi, m., = Ἰκάδιος, a notorious robber, Cic. Fat. 3, 5.—Called also īcă-dĭon: Rhonches Icadionque cum dixit Lucilius cognomina piratarum posuit, Fest. s. v. rhondes, p. 270 Müll. N. cr.; cf.: Icadion nomen saevissimi piratae, Paul. ex Fest. p. 106 ib.— A son of Apollo, Serv. ad Verg. A. 3, 332.
icadius.short: Īcădĭus, ĭi, m., = Ἰκάδιος, a notorious robber, Cic.

icaria.full: Īcărĭa, ae, f., an island in the Icarian sea, now Nicaria, Mel. 2, 7, 11.—Called īcăros in Plin. 4, 12, 23, § 68.
icaria.short: Īcărĭa, ae, f., an island in the Icarian sea, now Nicaria, Mel.

icariotis.full: Īcărĭōtis, idis, v. Icarus, II. B. 3.

icaris.full: Īcăris, idis, v. Icarus, II. B. 2.

icarus.full: Īcărus, i, m., = Ἴκαρος. A son of Dœdalus, who, on his flight from Crete, fell into the Ægean Sea, Ov. M. 8, 195 sq.; Hor. C. 2, 20, 13; Hyg. F. 40.— Derivv. īcărĭus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Icarus, Icarian: aquae, the part of the Ægean Sea named after Icarus, Ov. Tr. 1, 1, 90.—Also absol.: īcărĭum (sc. mare), Ov. F. 4, 283; 566: fluctus, Hor. C. 1, 1, 15: litus, Ov. H. 18, 50.— Icăros, i, f., one of the Sporades, Plin. 4, 12, 23, § 68.— =Ἰκάριος, son of Œbalus, king of Sparta, the fathe

icas.full: īcas, ădis, f., = εἰκάς (the number twenty), the twentieth day of the month, kept as a festival in honor of Epicurus (because Epicurus was born on the 20th of the month Gamelion), Plin. 35, 2, 2, § 5 (for which: omnibus mensibus vicesimo die lunae dent ad eorum epulas, etc., Cic. Fin. 2, 31, 101).
icas.short: īcas, ădis, f., = εἰκάς (the number twenty), the twentieth day of the month, kept as a festival in honor of Epicurus (because Epicurus was born on the 20th of the month Gamelion), Plin.

iccius.full: Iccĭus, ĭi, m., a Roman proper name, Cic. Phil. 3, 10. 26; Hor. C. 1, 29, 1.
iccius.short: Iccĭus, ĭi, m., a Roman proper name, Cic.

icelos.full: Ĭcĕlos, i, m., = Ἴκελος (like), a son of Somnus (so called as producing dreams), Ov. M. 11, 640.
icelos.short: Ĭcĕlos, i, m., = Ἴκελος (like), a son of Somnus (so called as producing dreams), Ov.

iceni.full: Icēni, ōrum, m., a people in the southeastern part of Great Britain, the modern Kent, Tac. A. 12, 31 sq.
iceni.short: Icēni, ōrum, m., a people in the southeastern part of Great Britain, the modern Kent, Tac.

ichneumon.full: ichneumon, ŏnis, m., = ἰχνεύμων. An animal which tracks the crocodile and destroys its eggs; the Egyptian rat or ichneumon, Plin. 8, 24, 35, § 88; 8, 25, 37, § 90 sq.; Cic. N. D. 1, 36, 101; Mart. 7, 87, 5; Nemes. Cyneg. 54.— An insect, the ichneumon-fly, Sphex sabulosus, Linn.; Plin. 10, 74, 95, § 204; 11, 21, 24, § 72.

ichnobates.full: Ichnŏbătes, ae, m., = Ἰχνοβάτης (that follows the trail), one of Actœon's hounds, Ov. M. 3, 207; Hyg. Fab. 181.
ichnobates.short: Ichnŏbătes, ae, m., = Ἰχνοβάτης (that follows the trail), one of Actœon's hounds, Ov.

ichnographia.full: ichnogrăphĭa, ae, f., = ἰχνογραφία. a ground-plot, plan, Vitr. 1, 2, 2.

ichnusa.full: Ichnūsa, ae, f., = Ἰχνοῦσα, a very ancient name of the island of Sardinia, Plin. 3, 7, 13, § 85; Sil. 12, 358.
ichnusa.short: Ichnūsa, ae, f., = Ἰχνοῦσα, a very ancient name of the island of Sardinia, Plin.

ichthyocolla.full: ichthўŏcolla, ae, f., = ἰχθυόκολλα. A kind of sturgeon, the huso, Acipenser huso, Linn.; Plin. 32, 7, 24, § 72.— The glue made from it, isinglass, sturgeon-bladder, Cels. 5, 2; Plin. 7, 56, 57, § 198.

ichthyophagi.full: Ichthўŏphăgi, ōrum, m. (ἰχθυοφάγοι, fish-eaters), the name of several nations living upon fish, Plin. 6, 23, 25, § 95; Greek gen. plur. Ichthyophagōn, id. 6, 28, 32, § 51.

icilius.full: Icilius, a, the name of a Roman gens: Sp. Icilius, Liv. 2, 58: L. Icilius, id. 3, 44; hence: lex Icilia, id. 3, 32.
icilius.short: Icilius, a, the name of a Roman gens: Sp.

icio.full: ī^cĭo and ī^co), īci, ictum (forms in use, only pres. icit, iciunt, icere; perf. icit, icisse; pluperf. iceram, iceras; fut. perf. icero; pass. pres. icitur, icimur; perf. ictus est; and part. ictus, a, um; pres. ĭco, Prisc. 886 P.; but īcit, Lucr. 3, 160; Plaut. Mil. 2, 2, 50; pres. icio, Gell. 4, 17, 8; Prisc. 877 P.), 3, v. a. Gr. ἰπ-, ἴπτομαι, to injure; ἴψ, a worm; ἴκρια, scaffolding; cf. Ἴκαρος, ἐν-ιπή, to strike, hit, smite, stab, sting (cf.: ferio, percutio, verbero, pulso). Lit. (rare b
icio.short: ī^cĭo and ī^co), īci, ictum (forms in use, only pres.

icon.full: īcon, ŏnis, f., = εἰκών, an image, figure: fictae ceră icones, Plin. 8, 54, 80, § 215.
icon.short: īcon, ŏnis, f., = εἰκών, an image, figure: fictae ceră icones, Plin.

iconicus.full: īcŏnĭcus, a, um, adj., = εἰκονικός, of or belonging to an image, imitating a figure, copied from life: duces, of the size of life, Plin. 35, 8, 34, § 57: simulacrum aureum, Suet. Calig. 22.
iconicus.short: īcŏnĭcus, a, um, adj., = εἰκονικός, of or belonging to an image, imitating a figure, copied from life: duces, of the size of life, Plin.

iconismus.full: īcŏnismus, i, m., = εἰκονισμός, an imaging, representation by an image, Sen. Ep. 97, 67.
iconismus.short: īcŏnismus, i, m., = εἰκονισμός, an imaging, representation by an image, Sen.

iconium.full: Īcŏnĭum, ĭi, n., = Ἰκόνιον, a city of Lycaonia, now Koniyeh, Plin. 5, 27, 25, § 95; Cic. Fam. 3, 7, 4.
iconium.short: Īcŏnĭum, ĭi, n., = Ἰκόνιον, a city of Lycaonia, now Koniyeh, Plin.

icosaproti.full: īcŏsăprōti, ōrum, m., = εἰκοσάπρωτοι, the twenty chief councilmen in the municipia and colonies, Dig. 50, 4, 18, § 26; cf. decaproti and decemprimi.
icosaproti.short: īcŏsăprōti, ōrum, m., = εἰκοσάπρωτοι, the twenty chief councilmen in the municipia and colonies, Dig.

icosaprotia.full: īcŏsăprōtia, ae, f., = εἰκοσαπρωτία, the dignity of the icosaproti, Dig. 50, 4, 18, § 26.
icosaprotia.short: īcŏsăprōtia, ae, f., = εἰκοσαπρωτία, the dignity of the icosaproti, Dig.

icterias.full: ictĕrĭas, ădis, f. (sc. gemma), = ἰκτερίας, a precious stone, otherwise unknown, Plin. 37, 10, 61, § 170.

ictericus.full: ictĕrĭcus, i, m., = ἰκτερικός, ill of the jaundice, jaundiced, Juv. 6, 565.—Plur. subst.: ictĕrĭci, ōrum, m., persons suffering with jaundice, Plin. 20, 9, 34, § 87; Ambros. in Psa. 118, Serm. 10, 23.
ictericus.short: ictĕrĭcus, i, m., = ἰκτερικός, ill of the jaundice, jaundiced, Juv.

icterus.full: ictĕrus, i, m., = ἴκτερος, a yellow bird, otherwise unknown, the sight of which was said to cure the jaundice (ἴκτερος), Plin. 30, 11, 29, § 94.
icterus.short: ictĕrus, i, m., = ἴκτερος, a yellow bird, otherwise unknown, the sight of which was said to cure the jaundice (ἴκτερος), Plin.

ictis.full: ictis, ĭdis, f., = ἴκτις, a kind of weasel, Plin. 29, 4, 16, § 50: nunc ictim tenes, Plaut. Capt. 1, 2, 81.
ictis.short: ictis, ĭdis, f., = ἴκτις, a kind of weasel, Plin.

ictus1.full: ictus, a, um, Part., from ico.
ictus1.short: ictus, a, um, Part., from ico.

ictus2.full: ictus, ūs (gen. sing. icti, Quadrig. ap. Gell. 9, 13, 17), m. ico, a blow, stroke, stab, thrust, bite, sting (freq. and class.). Lit. In gen.: a bestiis ictus, morsus, impetus, Cic. Off. 2, 6, 19: pro ictu gladiatoris, id. Mil. 24, 65: neque ictu comminus neque conjectione telorum, id. Caecin. 15, 43: scutis uno ictu pilorum transfixis et colligatis, Caes. B. G. 1, 25: non caecis ictibus procul ex improviso vulnerabantur, Liv. 34, 14, 11: ictu scorpionis exanimato altero, Caes. B. G. 7, 25, 3: p

icuncula.full: īcuncŭla, ae, f. dim. icon, a small image or figure: puellaris, Suet. Ner. 56.

ida.full: Īda, ae, or Īdē, ēs, f., = Ἴδα or Ἴδη. A high mountain in Crete, where the infant Jupiter was hid, watched over by the Curetes, and fed by Amalthea; now Psiloriti, Verg. A. 12, 412; Ov. M. 4, 293; id. Am. 3, 10, 25; id. F. 4, 207; 5, 115 al.; in Prop. 3, 1, 27, this mountain and no. II. are confounded.— Deriv.: īdaeus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Ida, Idean: mons, i. e. Ida, Verg. A. 3, 105; Mel. 2, 7, 12: antra, Ov. M. 4, 289: Juppiter, Verg. A. 7, 139: Dactyli, Plin. 37, 10, 61, § 170; the
ida.short: Īda, ae, or Īdē, ēs, f., = Ἴδα or Ἴδη.

idaeus1.full: Īdaeus, a, um, adj., v. the preced. art. I. B. and II. B.

idaeus2.full: Īdaeus, i, m. A herald and charioteer of Priam, Verg. A. 6, 485.— Another Trojan, Verg. A. 9, 500.

idalium.full: Īdălĭum, ĭi, n., = Ἰδάλιον, a mountaincity in Cyprus, sacred to Venus; now Dalin, Plin. 5, 31, 35, § 135; Verg. A. 1, 681.—Called also īdălĭa, ae, f., Verg. A. 1, 693; 10, 52 (where domus is nom. sing., not plur.; v. Wagn. ad loc.).— Deriv. īdălĭus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Idalium, Idalian; poet. also for Cyprian: vertex, the Idalian mountain, Prop. 2, 13, 54 (3, 5, 38 M.): Venus, id. ib. 5, 760: astrum, i. e. Venus, Prop. 4 (5), 6, 59. acus, of Venus, Claud. Rapt. Pros. 2, 16: sagitta,
idalium.short: Īdălĭum, ĭi, n., = Ἰδάλιον, a mountaincity in Cyprus, sacred to Venus;

idas.full: Īdas, ae, m., = Ἴδας. Son of Aphareus, king of Messene, who took part in the Calydonian boar-hunt, Prop. 1, 2, 17; Ov. M. 8, 305; id. F. 5, 701.— A companion of Diomedes, Ov. M. 14, 504.— One slain in the wedding of Perseus, Ov. M. 5, 90.— A Trojan, slain by Turnus, Verg. A. 9, 575.— A Thracian, Verg. A. 10, 351.

idcirco.full: idcirco or iccirco, adv. id-circa, on that account, for that reason, therefore (freq. and class.; cf.: itaque, igitur, ergo; ideo, propterea; quare, quam ob rem, etc.). Absol. (rare): idcirco moneo vos ego hoc, Plaut. Rud. prol. 28: ille Cliniae servos tardiusculus est: Idcirco huic nostro tradita'st provincia, Ter. Heaut. 3, 2, 5: quod id quod factum sit, aliud alii videatur esse, et idcirco alius alio nomine id appellet, Cic. Inv. 1, 8, 11; Caes. B. C. 1, 42, 3: data Romanis venia est indigna

idea.full: ĭdĕa, ae, f., = ιδέα, a (Platonic) idea, archetype, Sen. Ep. 58 med. (in Cic. Or. 3, 10; id. Ac. 1, 8, 30; id. Tusc. 1, 24, 58, as Greek).
idea.short: ĭdĕa, ae, f., = ιδέα, a (Platonic) idea, archetype, Sen.

idealis.full: ĭdĕālis, e, adj. idea, existing in idea, ideal (late Lat.): forma, Mart. Cap. 7, § 731: quaedam prudentia, id. 8, § 816 al.

idem.full: īdem, ĕădem, ĭdem (masc. eidem, freq. in MSS. and inscrr.; v. Lachm. ad Lucr. 1, 120; rarely isdem or eisdem; plur. nom. eidem; dat. and abl. eisdem; usu. contr. idem, isdem; not iidem, iisdem; v. Neue, Formenl. 2, 198 sqq.), pron. [from the pronom. root I, whence is, and the demonstr. suff. dem; root of dies, day, time; hence, just, exactly, Corss. Aussp. 2, 855], the same. In gen.: deinde quod nos eadem Asia atque idem iste Mithridates initio belli Asiatici docuit, Cic. de Imp. Pomp. 7, 19: qu

identidem.full: ĭdentĭdem (not idem-), adv. idem + ti (= ἔτι) + dem (root dies), v. Corss. Ausspr. 2, p. 456; 855, repeatedly, several times, often, now and then, at intervals, ever and anon; continually, constantly, habitually (class.; cf.: subinde, interdum): ne te uxor sequatur, respectas identidem, Plant. Men. 1, 2, 51; so, haec ego admirans, referebam tamen oculos ad terram identidem, Cic. Rep. 6, 18 fin.: scindens dolore identidem intonsam comam, Att. ap. Cic. Tusc. 3, 26, 62: cogitato identidem, tibi qua

ideo.full: ĭdĕo, adv. id-eo, i. e. this for this, for that reason, on that account, therefore (class.; esp. freq. in Quint.; cf.: eo, idcirco; ergo, igitur, itaque). Relatively. With causal particles, quod, quia, quoniam. With quod: ideo quod plerique deducuntur ad molas, Varr. R. R. 2, 6, 5: re quidem ipsa ideo mihi non satis facio, quod nullam partem tuorum meritorum consequi possum, Cic. Tusc. 1, 8, 6; so, ideo quod, id. Rosc. Am. 30, 85; id. Att. 3, 14, 2; cf. id. Q. Fr. 3, 1, 7, § 23: ne me foliis ide

idiographus.full: ĭdĭŏgrăphus, a, um, adj., =ἰδιόγραφος, written with one's own hand: liber Vergilii, autograph, Gell. 9, 14, 7.
idiographus.short: ĭdĭŏgrăphus, a, um, adj., =ἰδιόγραφος, written with one's own hand: liber Vergilii, autograph, Gell.

idioma.full: ĭdĭōma, ātis, n., = ἰδίωμα, a peculiarity in language, idiom, Charis. p. 255 P.
idioma.short: ĭdĭōma, ātis, n., = ἰδίωμα, a peculiarity in language, idiom, Charis.

idiota.full: ĭdĭōta, ae, m., = ἰδιώτης, an uneducated, ignorant, inexperienced, common person (cf. rudis): quidni et tu idem illitteratum me atque idiotam diceres? Lucil. ap. Non. 38, 24: quae non modo istum hominem ingeniosum atque intelligentem, verum etiam quemvis nostrum, quos iste idiotas appellat, delectare possent, Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 2, § 4; cf. id. Pis. 26, 62: ludos nobis idiotis relinquet, id. ib. 27, 65: posteaquam rem paternam ab idiotarum divitiis ad philosophorum regulam perduxit, id. Sest. 51, 1
idiota.short: ĭdĭōta, ae, m., = ἰδιώτης, an uneducated, ignorant, inexperienced, common person (cf.

idioticus.full: ĭdĭōtĭcus, a, um, adj., = ἰδιωτικός, uneducated, ignorant, unskilful (post-class.): rudem, impolitam et idioticam compellare, Tert. Testim. An. 1.
idioticus.short: ĭdĭōtĭcus, a, um, adj., = ἰδιωτικός, uneducated, ignorant, unskilful (post-class.): rudem, impolitam et idioticam compellare, Tert.

idiotismus.full: ĭdĭōtismus, i, m., = ἰδιωτισμός, the common or vulgar manner of speaking, Sen. Contr. 3 praef. § 5; 2, 11 fin.
idiotismus.short: ĭdĭōtismus, i, m., = ἰδιωτισμός, the common or vulgar manner of speaking, Sen.

idistaviso.full: Idistaviso or Idisiaviso the latter form ex conj. Grimm; Germ. from Idisi, maiden, and Viso, meadow; cf. Grimm, Deutsche Mythol. p. 372 ed. II., qs. the maiden's meadow; is approved by Nipperd. ad loc., and has been adopted in the text by Halm; the MS. form, explained as splendid meadow, from ancient Germ. id = nitens, the sup. of which is idista, Grimm, Gram. Einl. p. xlii, is retained by Ritter, a plain bordering on the Visurgis, (the modern Weser); perh. near the modern Minden, Tac. A. 2, 16.
idistaviso.short: Idistaviso or Idisiaviso the latter form ex conj.

idmon.full: Idmon, ŏnis, m., = Ἴδμων. The father of Arachne, a native of Colophon, Ov. M. 6, 8.— Deriv.: Idmŏnĭus, a, um, adj., of or related to Idmon, Idmonian: Arachne, Ov. M. 6, 133.— A prophet in Argos, the son of Apollo and Cyrene, one of the Argonauts, Ov. Ib. 506; Hyg. Fab. 14.— A Rutulian, messenger of Rutulus, Verg. A. 12, 75.— The physician of Adrastus, of Epidaurus, Stat. Th. 3, 398.

idoleum.full: īdōlēum or -īum, ii, n., = εἰδωλεῖον, an idol-temple, Tert. Cor. Mil. 10 med.; Hier. Ep. 22, 29: scanned īdŏlĭum, Prud. Apoth. 186; στεφ. 11, 52; Symm. 1, 612.
idoleum.short: īdōlēum or -īum, ii, n., = εἰδωλεῖον, an idol-temple, Tert.

idolicus.full: īdōlĭcus, a, um, adj., = εἰδωλικός, of or belonging to idols, idolatrous, idol-: res, Tert. Idol. 13: templum, Paul. Nol. Carm. 22, 61 (here scanned with o short).
idolicus.short: īdōlĭcus, a, um, adj., = εἰδωλικός, of or belonging to idols, idolatrous, idol-: res, Tert.

idololatres.full: īdōlŏlatres, ae, m., = εἰδωλολάτρης, an idol-worshipper, idolater, Tert. Idol. 1 sq.; 14; id. Apol. 24 al.
idololatres.short: īdōlŏlatres, ae, m., = εἰδωλολάτρης, an idol-worshipper, idolater, Tert.

idololatria.full: īdōlŏlatrīa, ae, f., = εἰδωλολατρεία, idol-worship, idolatry, Tert. Idol. 1 sq.; Hier. in Jesai. 57.
idololatria.short: īdōlŏlatrīa, ae, f., = εἰδωλολατρεία, idol-worship, idolatry, Tert.

idololatris.full: īdōlŏlā^tris, ĭdis, f., = εἰδωλολατρίς, she who worships idols, an idolatress, Prud. Ham. 403 (MSS. idololatrix).
idololatris.short: īdōlŏlā^tris, ĭdis, f., = εἰδωλολατρίς, she who worships idols, an idolatress, Prud.

idolothytus.full: īdōlŏthўtus, a, um, adj., = εἰδωλόθυτος, of or belonging to sacrifices to idols: sollemnia, Tert. Idol. 13: voluptates, id. Spect. 13.
idolothytus.short: īdōlŏthўtus, a, um, adj., = εἰδωλόθυτος, of or belonging to sacrifices to idols: sollemnia, Tert.

idolum.full: īdōlum or -on, i, n., = εἴδωλον. an image, form, esp. a spectre, apparition, ghost: idola atque atomos vincere Epicuri volam, Lucil. ap. Non. 478, 29: mox apparebat idolon, senex macie et squalore confectus, etc., Plin. Ep. 7, 27, 5 (in Cic. Fin. 1, 6, 21; Fam. 15, 16, 1 and 2, written as Greek).— In the Church fathers, an idol: idolorum cultor, Aug. in. Psa. 78, 3; id. Serm. 123, 3: venerator idolorum, id. Conf. 8, 2: deficere a cultu idolorum, Lact. Mort. Pers. 2, 6; Tert. Idol. 1 sq.; id. Spe

idomeneus.full: Īdŏmĕneus (quadrisyl.), ĕi, m., = Ἰδομενευς, a king of Crete, the leader of the Cretans against Troy, Verg. A. 3, 401; Ov. M. 12, 358; Hyg. Fab. 81; 270.
idomeneus.short: Īdŏmĕneus (quadrisyl.), ĕi, m., = Ἰδομενευς, a king of Crete, the leader of the Cretans against Troy, Verg.

idomenius.full: Idŏmĕnius, a, um, adj., pertaining to the Macedonian city Idomene, Idomenian: Idomeniosne (to be scanned as a quinquesyl.) petam montes? Cat. 64, 178.
idomenius.short: Idŏmĕnius, a, um, adj., pertaining to the Macedonian city Idomene, Idomenian: Idomeniosne (to be scanned as a quinquesyl.) petam montes? Cat.

idoneitas.full: ĭdōnĕĭtas, ātis, f. idoneus, fitness, meetness, usefulness (late Lat.): servi, Aug. Serm. de Div. 106, 3.

idoneus.full: ĭdōnĕus, a, um, adj. Sanscr. root indh-, idh-, to kindle; prop. bright, conspicuous; cf. Idus, fit for something (esp. for an action), meet, proper, becoming, suitable, apt, capable, convenient, sufficient (of persons and things; class. and very freq. in prose and poetry; syn.: aptus, opportunus); constr. most commonly with ad, qui, the dat., or absol.; less freq. with in aliquid, the abl., or the inf. With ad: tot quidem non potuisti adducere homines magis ad hanc rem idoneos, etc., Plaut. Poen

idos.full: īdos, n., = εἶδος, Lat. species, a form, shape, Sen. Ep. 58, 17 sqq. (written sometimes as Greek).

idulis.full: īdūlis, e, adj. Idus, belonging to the Ides: idulis ovis dicebatur, quae omnibus idibus Jovi mactabatur, Paul. ex Fest. p. 104 Müll.; cf. Fest. S. V. SACRAM VIAM, p. 290 b fin.; Macr. S. 1, 15; cf. Ov. F. 1, 56.

idumaea.full: Ĭdūmaea, ae, f., = Ἰδουμαία, a region of Palestine, Plin. 5, 14, 15, § 70.—Called also poet. ĭdūmē, es, f., Val. Fl. 1, 12; Luc. 3, 216.— Deriv.: ĭdūmaeus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Idumea, Idumean; poet. also for Palestinian, Jewish: palmae, Verg. G. 3, 12: triumphi, over Judea, Mart. 2, 2, 5: porta, Juv. 8, 160.
idumaea.short: Ĭdūmaea, ae, f., = Ἰδουμαία, a region of Palestine, Plin.

iduo.full: īdŭo, āre, acc. to Macr. S. 1, 15, § 17, an Etrusc. word, i. q. dividere, from the root vid; whence viduus and divido.

idus.full: Īdus (often eidus, v. Inscr. Orell. 42), ŭum, f. acc. to Macr. S. 1, 15, from the Etrusc. † iduo, to divide; hence, qs. the divided or half month; but prob. Sanscr. root, indh-, idh-, to kindle, lighten; indu, moon; prop. the days of light, of the moon, one of the three days in each month from which the other days were reckoned in the Roman calendar, the Ides; it fell upon the fifteenth day of March, May, July, and October; upon the thirteenth day in the remaining months (cf.: Kalendae, Nonae):

idyia.full: Ĭdyia (trisyl.), ae, f., = Ἰδυῖα, the wife of Æētes and mother of Medea, Cic. N. D. 3, 19, 48; Hyg. Fab. 25.
idyia.short: Ĭdyia (trisyl.), ae, f., = Ἰδυῖα, the wife of Æētes and mother of Medea, Cic.

idyllium.full: Īdyllĭum or ēdyllĭum, ii, n., = Εἰδύλλιον, an Idyl, pastoral poem, Plin. Ep. 4, 14, 9.—Plur., the title of a collection of little poems by Ausonius.
idyllium.short: Īdyllĭum or ēdyllĭum, ii, n., = Εἰδύλλιον, an Idyl, pastoral poem, Plin.

iesus.full: Ĭēsus (in late Lat. also dissyl.), u, m., = Ἰησοῦς, Jesus Christ, Juvenc. 2, 106; Prud. Apoth. 770 al.

igilium.full: Igilĭum, ĭi, n., a small island in the Tyrrhene Sea, now Giglio, Mel. 2, 7, 19; Caes. B. C. 1, 34, 2; Rutil. 1, 305.
igilium.short: Igilĭum, ĭi, n., a small island in the Tyrrhene Sea, now Giglio, Mel.

igitur.full: ĭgĭtur, conj. [pronom. stem i- of is; suffix -ha (-dha); Gr. -θα; Sanscr. -iha, here; -tur, = -tus (Sanscr. -tas), as in penitus, antiquitus, etc., from thence], introduces an inference or deduction, then, therefore, thereupon, accordingly, in these circumstances (in class. prose usu. placed after the first word of the clause; cf. below, III.; syn.: itaque, ergo; cf.: eo, ideo, idcirco, propterea; quamobrem, quare, etc.). In gen. (rare): SI. IN. IVS. VOCAT. NI. IT. ANTESTATOR. IGITVR EM. CAPITO,

ignarus.full: ignārus, a, um (also, † ignarures ἀγνοοῦντες, Gloss. Philox.; v. gnarus init.), adj. in-gnarus, like ignavus, ignotus, from the negative in and gnavus, gnotus, ignorant of a thing, not knowing, unacquainted with, inexperienced, unaware (syn.: inscius, nescius, insciens). Lit. (freq. and class.); constr. usu. with the gen.; less frequently with a rel.-clause, with acc. and inf., with inf. alone, or absol. With gen.: ait se peregrinum esse, hujus ignarum oppidi, Plaut. Poen. 3, 3, 43: imprudens ha
ignarus.short: ignārus, a, um (also, † ignarures ἀγνοοῦντες, Gloss.

ignavesco.full: ignāvesco, ĕre, v. inch. n. [ignavus], to grow inactive or slothful: anima nec quiescit nec ignavescit, Tert. Anim. 43 fin.

ignavia.full: ignāvĭa, ae, f. id., inactivity, laziness, idleness, sloth, listlessness, cowardice, worthlessness (syn.: socordia, desidia, inertia, pigritia, segnities; opp.: fortitudo, alacritas). Lit. (class.): dare argentum adulescenti, qui exaedificaret suam incohatam ignaviam, Plaut. Trin. 1, 2, 95: venit mihi ignavia; ea mihi tempestas fuit; mi adventu suo grandinem imbremque attulit, id. Most. 1, 2, 57 Lorenz ad loc.: contraria fortitudini ignavia, Cic. Inv. 2, 54, 165; so opp. fortitudo, id. Cat. 2, 1

ignavio.full: ignāvĭo, īre, v. a. id., to render inactive, slothful, or dispirited, Att. ap. Non. 123, 13; id. ib. 126, 15 (Trag. Rel. p. 282 Rib.).

ignavus.full: ignāvus, a, um, adj. in-gnavus, navus, inactive, lazy, slothful, idle, sluggish, listless, without spirit, cowardly, dastardly (syn.: iners, socors; opp.: strenuus, alacer, fortis). Lit., of living beings (freq. and class.): homines, Plaut. Rud. 3, 5, 49: si non fecero Ei male aliquo pacto, me esse dicito ignavissimum, id. Bacch. 3, 6, 27: quid ergo ille ignavissumus mi latitabat? id. Trin. 4, 2, 82; 1, 2, 128; id. Poen. 4, 2, 24: homo inertior, ignavior, magis vir inter mulieres proferri non po

ignefacio.full: ignĕfăcĭo, ĕre, 3, v. a. ignis + facio, to make fiery; only in part. perf. ignefactus, Theod. Prisc. 2, 2, 15.

igneolus.full: ignĕŏlus, a, um, adj. dim. [igneus], fiery (post-class.): vigor, Prud. Cath. 3, 186.

ignesco.full: ignesco, ĕre, v. inch. n. (in pass. ignescitur, Laber. ap. Non. 481, 7; Fragm. Com. v. 26 Rib.) [ignis], to take fire, to become inflamed, to burn, kindle (syn.: inardesco, exardesco). Lit.: ex quo eventurum nostri putant, ut ad extremum omnis mundus ignesceret, * Cic. N. D. 2, 46, 118: lumen capere atque ignescere, Ov. M. 15, 847.— Transf., of color: purpura et candor et tertium ex utroque ignescens, kindling, breaking into a flame, Plin. 37, 2, 8, § 21. — Trop., to burn with passion, to glow (

igneus.full: ignĕus, a, um, adj. id., of fire, fiery, on fire, burning, burning-hot (cf.: fervidus, calidus). Lit.: sidera tota esse ignea, Cic. N. D. 2, 15, 40; cf. sol, Verg. G. 4, 426: arces (i. e. caelum), Hor. C. 3, 3, 10: ignea vis caeli, ether, Ov. M. 1, 26: ignea vis, fire, as one of the primary elements, acc. to Heraclitus, Cic. N. D. 3, 14, 35: Aetne, Ov. M. 15, 341: Chimaera, Hor. C. 2, 17, 13: aestas, id. ib. 1, 17, 2: ardor, of fire, Auct. Her. 4, 33, 44: celeritas, motus, Cic. N. D. 2, 9, 24.—

ignia.full: ignia vitium vasorum fictilium, Paul. ex. Fest. p. 105 Müll. [perh. = ἴκνυον, i. e. κόνιον, σμῆμα, Hesych.].

igniarius.full: ignĭārĭus, a, um, adj. ignis, of or belonging to fire. Adj.: lapis, flint, Marc. Emp. 33 med.— Subst.: ignĭārĭum, ĭi, n., an implement for producing fire, Plin. 16, 40, 76, § 207.

ignicans.full: ignĭcans, antis, adj. id., flaming, fiery-colored: grana, Jul. Val. Rer. Gest. Alex. 3, 21.

ignicolor.full: ignĭcŏlor or -ōrus, a, um, adj. ignis-color, fire-colored, flame-colored: nubes, Juvenc. in Matt. 4, 26, 557.

ignicomans.full: ignĭcŏmans, antis, adj. igniscoma, having fiery hair, fiery-haired; poet.: stellae, Avien. Arat. 8.

ignicomus.full: ignĭcŏmus, a, um, adj. id., fieryhaired: sol, Aus. Ep. 7, 9: leo, Nemes. Cyneg. 214; cf. preced. art.

igniculus.full: ignĭcŭlus, i, m. dim. ignis, a small fire, a little flame, a spark. Lit.: quaedam exigua animalia igniculi videntur in tenebris, Quint. 12, 10, 76; Plin. 35, 15, 52, § 184; Juv. 3, 102.— Transf., of color, a glittering, sparkling: onyx Indica igniculos habet, Plin. 37, 6, 24, § 90; 37, 7, 25, § 93.— Trop., fire, sparks, vehemence, etc. (freq. in Cic.): quo tolerabilius feramus igniculum desiderii tui, i. e. vehemence, Cic. Fam. 15, 20, 2: (natura) parvulos nobis dedit igniculos, quos celeriter m

ignifer.full: ignĭfer, ĕra, ĕrum, adj. ignis-fero, fire-bearing, fiery (poet.). Lit.: aether, Lucr. 5, 459; 490: fulmen, id. 6, 379: lampades, id. 2, 25: axis, Ov. M. 2, 59: sidus, Prud. ap. Symm. 2, 1027: tauri, Val. Fl. 8, 342.—* Trop.: ignifero mentes furiabat in iram Hortatu, Sil. 17, 294.

ignifluus.full: ignĭflŭus, a, um, adj. ignis-fluo, flowing with fire, emitting fire: cavernae, Claud. III. Cons. Hon. 196.

ignigena.full: Ignĭgĕna, ae, m. ignis-gigno, the fire-born, a poetical epithet of Bacchus, whose mother, Semele, was killed by lightning, Ov. M. 4, 12; cf. ib. 3, 305 sq.

ignigenus.full: ignĭgĕnus, a, um, adj. id., producing fire: asinus, whose pack was on fire, App. M. 7, p. 197.

igninus.full: ignīnus, a, um, adj. ignis, standing in the fire; as subst.: ignīnus, i, m., a fireman, App. M. 7, p. 197, 2 Hild.

ignio.full: ignĭo, īvi or ĭi, ītum, 4, v. a. id., to ignite, set on fire, make red-hot (post-class.): ut igniverint, Prud. στεφ. 10, 1077.—Hence, ignītus, a, um, P. a., fiery, glowing. Lit.: liquor, Serv. Verg. A. 6, 33: aether, App. de Mundo, p. 57: tela, id. ib. p. 61.— Comp.: quod vinum natura esset ignitius, Gell. 17, 8, 10.—Sup.: draconis effigies ignitissima, Jul. Var. Rer. Gest. Alex. 3, 56.— Trop.: ingenium, Prud. Ham. 546; Sid. Ep. 1, 11.
ignio.short: ignĭo, īvi or ĭi, ītum, 4, v.

ignipes.full: ignĭpes, pĕdis, adj. ignis-pes, fieryfooted (poet.): equi, Ov. M. 2, 392; Stat. Th. 1, 27: tauri, Mart. Spect. 27.

ignipotens.full: Ignĭpŏtens, entis, adj. ignis-potens, potent in fire, ruler of fire, ignipotent, a poet. epithet of Vulcan (Vergilian): deus, Verg. A. 12, 90.—Also as subst.: Ignĭpŏ-tens = Vulcan, id. ib. 8, 414; 423; 628; 710; 10, 243.

ignis.full: ignis, is (abl. usu. igni; poet. and postAug. igne; so Plin. ap. Charis. p. 98 P.; Charis. p. 33 P.; Prisc. p. 766 P.; and always in Mart., e. g. 1, 21, 5; 4, 57, 6; cf. Neue, Formenl. 1, 223 sq.; scanned ignis, Verg. E. 3, 66; id. G. 3, 566; Ov. H. 16, 230; Lucr. 1, 663; 853; but ignīs, Hor. C. 1, 15, 36), m. Sanscr. agnis, fire; Lith. ugn-is; Slav. ogný; Gr. αἴγλη, ἀγλαός, fire (com mon in sing. and plur.; cf. flamma, incendium). Lit.: lapidum conflictu atque tritu elici ignem videmus, Cic. N.

ignispicium.full: ignispĭcĭum, ĭi, n. ignis-specio, a divining from fire, divination by fire, Plin. 7, 56, 57, § 203.

ignitabulum.full: ignītābŭlum, i, n. ignio, an implement for producing fire. Lit., Sol. 11, § 19; cf.: ignitabulum ignis receptaculum, Paul. ex Fest. p. 105 Müll.—* Trop.: ingenii virtutisque, Macr. S. 2, 8, 4.

ignitulus.full: ignītŭlus, a, um, adj. dim. [ignitus, from ignio], somewhat fiery (post-class.): Mercurius, Tert. ad. Nat. 1, 10 fin.

ignitus.full: ignītus, a, um, P. a., from ignio.

ignivagus.full: ignĭvăgus, a, um, adj. ignis-vagor, spreading like fire, like wild-fire (late Lat.): denuntiatio, Mart. Cap. 9, § 896.

ignivomus.full: ignĭvŏmus, a, um, adj. ignis-vomo, vomiting fire (late Lat.): sol, Lact. (Venant.) Serm. de Resurr. Dom. 3.

ignobilis.full: ignōbĭlis, e, adj. in-nobilis (gno-), unknown. Lit., in gen. (mostly anteclass.): ubi ego Sosia nolim esse, tu esto sane Sosia; nunc, quando ego sum, vapulabis, ni hinc abis, ignobilis, Plaut. Am. 1, 1, 284: quis hic est qui oculis meis ob viam ignobilis obicitur? id. Ps. 2, 1, 18: peregrina facies hominis atque ignobilis, id. ib. 4, 2, 9.— Esp. Unknown to fame, not renowned, undistinguished, obscure (class.): quod inglorius sit atque ignobilis ad supremum diem perventurus, Cic. Tusc. 3, 24, 57:

ignobilitas.full: ignōbĭlĭtas, ātis, f. ignobilis. Want of fame, obscurity (rare but class.): num igitur ignobilitas aut humilitas aut etiam popularis offensio sapientem beatum esse prohibebit? Cic. Tusc. 5, 36, 103: virorum, Ov. M. 6, 319: artificis, Plin. 34, 8, 19, § 69.— Low birth, mean origin. Lit. (rare but class.): multis viris fortibus ne ignobilitas generis obiceretur, Cic. Mur. 8, 17: hoc propter ignobilitatem paternam minus suspecto, Platorem occidit, Liv. 44, 30, 3.— Transf., of things, inferior quali

ignominia.full: ignōmĭnĭa, ae, f. in - nomen; qs. a deprivation of one's good name, of one's honor as a citizen, disgrace, dishonor, ignominy, esp. as the result of civil or military punishment (class.; in sing. and plur.; cf.: infamia, dedecus, probrum, opprobrium). A legal and military term: censoris judicium nihil fere damnato nisi ruborem affert. Itaque, ut omnis ea judicatio versatur tantummodo in nomine, animadversio illa ignominia dicta est, Cic. Fragm. ap. Non. 24, 9 sq. (Rep. 4, 6 Mos.); Cic. Clu. 47,

ignominiatus.full: ignōmĭnĭātus, a, um, adj. ignominia, disgraced, Gell. 8, 15 in lemm.

ignominiosus.full: ignōmĭnĭōsus, a, um, adj. ignominia, disgraceful, shameful, ignominious (not freq. till after the Aug. per.). Of persons: exsul eras, ignominiosus, branded with public ignominy, Quint. 7, 1, 8: filia, Dig. 48, 5, 24; cf.: quid eos qui huic ignominioso agmini fuere obvii, existimasse putatis, Liv. 2, 38, 4: quibusdam judiciis damnati ignominiosi fiunt, velut furti, vi bonorum raptorum, etc., Gai. Inst. 4, 182.— Hence, subst.: ignōmĭnĭōsus, i, m., a person branded with ignominy, one publicly disgr

ignorabilis.full: ignōrābĭlis, e, adj. ignoro, unknown (rare but class.): separare, quod levius, facilius, non ignorabile, non fortuitum, non necessarium fuerit, * Cic. Inv. 2, 32, 99: libri litteris ignorabilibus praenotati, App. M. 11, p. 268: alterum illud ignorabilius obscuriusque est, Gell. 9, 12, 4 (Plaut. Ps. 2, 1, 18, false reading for ignobilis).— * Adv.: ignōrābĭlĭter, in an unknown manner: laminae ignorabiliter litteratae, i. e. covered with unknown characters, App. M. 3, p. 137, 6.

ignorans.full: ignōrans, antis, Part. and P. a., from ignoro.

ignoranter.full: ignōranter, adv., v. ignoro, P. a. fin.

ignorantia.full: ignōrantĭa, ae, f. ignorans, from ignoro, want of knowledge or information, ignorance (mostly post-Aug.; only once in Cic., for Cic. Fl. 20, 46, is a gloss; cf. Klotz, Cic. Lael. 19, 70; syn. ignoratio). With gen. obj.: ignorantia loci, * Caes. B. C. 3, 68, 2: locorum, Suet. Galb. 20; cf.: imperii Romani, Tac. A. 1, 59: scripturae, Suet. Calig. 41: discriminis sui, Quint. 6, 1, 47: praeteritae culpae, Ov. H. 20, 189: veri, id. M. 7, 92: recti, Tac. Agr. 1: bonarum rerum, Nep. Ages. 8, 5.— Absol.

ignoratio.full: ignōrātĭo, ōnis, f. ignoro, want of knowledge or acquaintance, ignorance (freq. in Cic.; elsewh. rare). With gen. obj.: timentibus ceteris propter ignorationem locorum, Cic. Rep. 1, 17, 29; so, numquam antea visi regis, Curt. 3, 12, 17: stirpis et generis, Cic. Lael. 19, 70: dialecticae, id. Fin. 3, 12, 41: causarum, id. Div. 2, 22, 49: juris, id. Leg. 1, 6, 18: maximarum rerum (with summus error), id. N. D. 1, 1, 2 fin.: veritatis, id. ib. 1, 16, 43: sui, id. Clu. 39, 109: virtutis, id. Rep. 1,

ignoro.full: ignōro, āvi, ātum, 1 (old form of inf. pres. pass. ignorarier, Ter. Phorm. 5, 7, 38), v. a. and n. ignarus, not to know (a person or thing), to have no knowledge of, to be unacquainted with, to be ignorant of, to mistake, misunderstand (a person or thing—class.; cf. nescio).—Constr. with acc., with acc. and inf., or rel. clause, with de, quin, or absol. With acc.: siquidem istius regis (Anci) matrem habemus, ignoramus patrem, Cic. Rep. 2, 18: erras si id credis et me ignoras, Clinia, do not know
ignoro.short: ignōro, āvi, ātum, 1 (old form of inf.

ignoscens.full: ignoscens, entis, Part. and P. a., from ignosco.

ignoscentia.full: ignoscentĭa, ae, f. ignosco, pardon, forgiveness (post-class. and very rare).— Plur., Gell. 7, 3, 47.

ignoscibilis.full: ignoscĭbĭlis, e, adj. id., pardonable, excusable (post-class. and very rare): hic vester vestitus, Castrit. ap. Gell. 13, 21, 1.

ignosco.full: ignosco, nōvi, nōtum, 3 (plqpf. sync. ignosset, Sil. 8, 619; part. fut. ignosciturus, Piso Frugi ap. Prisc. p. 887; Ambros. de Noë, 13, 47; also ignoturus, Cic. ap. Prisc. p. 886), v. a. 2. in-gnosco, nosco; lit., not to wish to know, not to search into; hence, with esp. reference to a fault or crime, to pardon, forgive, excuse, overlook (class.; syn.: parco, indulgeo); constr. alicui (aliquid, quod, si, etc.), with simple aliquid or absol. Alicui (aliquid, quod, si, etc.): hoc ignoscant dii imm

ignotus1.full: ignōtus, a, um, Part., from ignosco.
ignotus1.short: ignōtus, a, um, Part., from ignosco.

ignotus2.full: ignōtus, a, um, adj. in-gnotus, notus. Pass., unknown. In gen.: quamquam ad ignotum arbitrum me appellis: si adhibebit fidem, Etsi est ignotus, notus: si non, notus ignotissimus est, Plaut. Rud. 4, 3, 104 sq.: dubitabitis, judices, quin ab hoc ignotissimo Phryge nobilissimum civem vindicetis? Cic. Fl. 17, 40: ignoti homines et repentini quaestores celeriter facti sunt, id. Brut. 64, 242: homo ignotus et novus, id. Rep. 1, 1: nos pluribus ignotissimi gentibus, id. ib. 1, 17: longinqua eoque ignot

iguvium.full: Īgŭvĭum, ĭi, n., a city of Umbria, now Gubbio, Cic. Att. 7, 13, b, 6; Caes. B. C. 1, 12; Liv. 45, 43; Sil. 8, 461.—Hence, īgŭ-vĭnātes, ium, m., its inhabitants, Cic. Balb. 20, 47; and īgŭvīni, ōrum, m., Caes. B. C. 1, 12; Plin. 15, 7, 7, § 31; and Iguini, id. 3, 14, 19, § 113.
iguvium.short: Īgŭvĭum, ĭi, n., a city of Umbria, now Gubbio, Cic.

ile.full: īle, is, and īlĕum, ei, and īlĭum, ii, n., usually plur. īlĭa, ĭum, n. (heterocl. dat. sing. ilio, in the pun with Ilio from Ilion, Poët. ap. Serv. Verg. A. 7, 499; dat. plur. iliis, Cels. 4, 1 fin.), that part of the abdomen which extends from the lowest ribs to the pubes, the groin, flank. Lit., Ov. M. 3, 216; 12, 486; Verg. G. 3, 507; id. A. 7, 499; Hor. Epod. 3, 4: ilium vitia, Plin. 20, 5, 15, § 31: ducere ilia, to draw the flanks together, become broken-winded, Hor. Ep. 1, 1, 9; so, traher
ile.short: īle, is, and īlĕum, ei, and īlĭum, ii, n., usually plur.

ileos.full: īlĕos, i, m., = εἰλεός, a severe kind of colic, the iliac pains, Plin. 30, 7, 20, § 59; 20, 6, 23, § 53; 32, 9, 31, § 101 al. (in Cels. 4, 13, written as Greek, called intestinorum tormentum, Cael. Aur. Acut. 3, 17, 138).
ileos.short: īlĕos, i, m., = εἰλεός, a severe kind of colic, the iliac pains, Plin.

ilerda.full: Ĭlerda, ae, f., a city in Hispania Tarraconensis, on the Sicoris, now Lerida, Caes. B. C. 1, 41 sq.; Hor. Ep. 1, 20, 13; Luc. 4, 144; 261.—Hence, ĭlerdenses, ium, m., its inhabitants, Plin. 3, 3, 4, § 24.
ilerda.short: Ĭlerda, ae, f., a city in Hispania Tarraconensis, on the Sicoris, now Lerida, Caes.

ilergavonenses.full: Ilergavonenses (Illurg-), ium, m., Liv. 22, 21, 6; Caes. B. C. 1, 60, 2.—Called also Ilergāŏnes, um, m., a people of Hispania Tarraconensis, on the sea-coast, near the mouth of the Ebro, Plin. 3, 3, 4, § 20.—Hence, Illurgavonensis, e, adj., of the Illurgavonenses: cohors, Caes. B. C. 1, 60, 4.

ilergetes.full: Ilergētes, um, m., a people of Hispania Tarraconensis, on the north of the Iberus, Plin. 3, 3, 4, § 21; Liv. 21, 23; 61; 22, 21; 26, 49 al.
ilergetes.short: Ilergētes, um, m., a people of Hispania Tarraconensis, on the north of the Iberus, Plin.

ilex.full: īlex, ĭcis, f., a kind of oak, the holmoak or great scarlet oak (cf. quercus, aesculus, robur), Quercus ilex, Linn.; Plin. 16, 6, 8, § 19; 16, 8, 12, § 32; 16, 18, 30, § 73; Enn. ap. Macr. S. 6, 2 (Ann. v. 194 Vahl.); Verg. E. 7, 1; id. A. 12, 702; Hor. C. 3, 13, 14; Ov. M. 1, 112; 8, 237: arbor felix, Macr. S. 3, 20, 2 et saep.—Poet.: porcus ilice pastus, i. e. with acorns, Mart. 14, 70, 2.
ilex.short: īlex, ĭcis, f., a kind of oak, the holmoak or great scarlet oak (cf.

ilia2.full: Īlĭa, ae, f., a poetical name of Rhea Silvia, daughter of Numitor and mother of Romulus and Remus, Enn. ap. Charis. p. 70 P. (Ann. v. 56 Vahl.); Verg. A. 1, 274; Ov. F. 2, 383; 598; Hor. C. 1, 2, 17; 3, 9, 8; 4, 8, 22.— Deriv.: īlĭădes, ae, m., son of Ilia. Adj.: Romulus Iliades Iliadesque Remus, Ov. Am. 3, 4, 40: pater, i. e. Romulus, id. F. 4, 23: fratres, i. e. Romulus and Remus, id. ib. 3, 62.— Subst., i. e. Romulus, Ov. M. 14, 781 and 824.
ilia2.short: Īlĭa, ae, f., a poetical name of Rhea Silvia, daughter of Numitor and mother of Romulus and Remus, Enn.

iliacus1.full: Īlĭăcus, a, um, v. Ilium, II. B.

iliacus2.full: īlĭăcus, a, um, adj. ileos, relating to the colic: passio, Cael. Aur. Acut. 2, 17, 171; 3, 21, 206: dolor, 3, 20, 195.—As subst. plur.: īlĭăci, ōrum, m., sufferers from colic, Cael. Aur. Acut. 3, 17, 173.

iliades.full: Īlĭădes, ae. A Trojan, v. Ilium, II. D.— Son of Ilia, v. Ilia, II.

ilias.full: Īlĭas, ădis, v. Ilium, II. E.

ilicet.full: īlĭcet, adv. i, root of īre, and licet; cf. scilicet and videlicet; lit., one may go; hence, In the oldest per. of the lang., a t. t. with which an assembly was dismissed when the business on hand was at an end, you may go; it is over: semper ilicet finem rei significat, ut actum est. Sic judices de concilio dimittebantur, suprema dicta cum praeco pronunciasset ilicet, quod significat ire licet, Don. Ter. Phorm. 1, 4, 31; cf. id. Ter. Heaut. 5, 2, 20; Serv. Verg. A. 2, 424; so, at the end of fun

ilicetum.full: īlĭcētum, i, n. ilex, a grove of holmoaks, forest of oaks, Mart. 12, 18, 20; Fest. s. v. tifata, p. 366 Müll.

iliceus.full: īlĭcĕus, a, um, adj. id., of holm-oak, oaken: trabes, Stat. Th. 6, 101; cf. iligneus and ilignus.

ilico.full: īlĭco (less correctly illĭco, Ritschl ad Plaut. Trin. 3, 1, 7), adv. in-loco, in that very place, on the spot, there. Lit. (anteclass.): his persuadent, ut ilico manerent: pars ilico manent, Cass. Hem. ap. Non. 325, 10: manete ilico, Caecil. ib. 12; Naev. ib. 7: ilico habitato, Att. ib.: otiose nunc jam ilico hic consiste, Ter. Ad. 2, 1, 2 Don.: sta ilico, id. Phorm. 1, 4, 18.— Transf. * Ilico illo, to that place, thither, Non. 325, 5; Turp. ap. Non. l. l. (Com. Fragm. v. 105 Rib.).— Of time, En
ilico.short: īlĭco (less correctly illĭco, Ritschl ad Plaut.

ilienses1.full: Īlĭenses, ium, v. Ilium, II. C.

ilienses2.full: Ilĭenses, ium, m., a people in Sardinia, regarded by Mela as the earliest inhabitants of the island, Liv. 40, 19, 6; Mel. 2, 7, 19.
ilienses2.short: Ilĭenses, ium, m., a people in Sardinia, regarded by Mela as the earliest inhabitants of the island, Liv.

iligneus.full: īlignĕus, a, um, adj. ilex, of holmoak, oaken: subscudes, Cato, R. R. 18, 9: frons, Col. 6, 3, 7: frutices, id. 7, 6, 1; cf. iliceus and ilignus.

ilignus.full: īlignus, a, um, adj. id., of holm-oak, oaken: pedibus, Ter. Ad. 4, 2, 46 (al. iligneis): canalibus, Verg. G. 3, 330.

iliona.full: Īlĭŏna, ae, and Īlĭŏnē, ēs, f., = Ἰλιόνη, the eldest daughter of Priam, the wife of Polymnestor, a king in Thrace, Verg. A. 1, 653 Serv.; Hyg. Fab. 109; 240; 243; Cic. Ac. 2, 27, 88.—The title of a tragedy by Pacuvius, Hor. S. 2, 3, 61; cf. Cic. Tusc. 1, 44, 106; and see the fragments, Trag. Rel. p. 100 sq. Rib.
iliona.short: Īlĭŏna, ae, and Īlĭŏnē, ēs, f., = Ἰλιόνη, the eldest daughter of Priam, the wife of Polymnestor, a king in Thrace, Verg.

ilioneus.full: Īlĭŏneus (quadrisyl.), ei, m., = Ἰλιονεύς. The youngest son of Niobe, Ov. M. 6, 261.— A Trojan, a follower of Æneas, Verg. A. 1, 521.

iliosus.full: īlĭōsus, i, m. 1. ilia, one who suffers with the colic, Plin. 20, 4, 13, § 26.

ilipa.full: Ilipa, ae, f., a city of Hispania Bœtica, upon the right bank of the Bœtis (Guadalquiver), its ruins near Peñaflor, Plin. 3, 1, 3, § 11; Liv. 35, 1, 11.
ilipa.short: Ilipa, ae, f., a city of Hispania Bœtica, upon the right bank of the Bœtis (Guadalquiver), its ruins near Peñaflor, Plin.

ilithyia.full: Īlīthyia (quadrisyl.), ae, f., = Εἰλείθυια (the daughter of Juno), the goddess of the Greeks who aided women in childbirth, Lat. Juno Lucina, Hor. Carm. Sec. 14; Ov. M. 9, 283; id. Am. 2, 13, 21.
ilithyia.short: Īlīthyia (quadrisyl.), ae, f., = Εἰλείθυια (the daughter of Juno), the goddess of the Greeks who aided women in childbirth, Lat.

ilium1.full: Īlĭum or Īlĭon, ĭi, n., = Ἴλιον, a poetical name for Troja, the city of Ilium, Troy, Verg. A. 1, 68; 5, 261; Hor. C. 1, 15, 33; Ov. M. 6, 95; 13, 408; Cic. Div. 1, 14, 24 et saep.—Called also īlĭos, i, f., acc. to the Gr. Ἴλιος, Hor. C. 4, 9, 18; id. Epod. 14, 14; Ov. A. A. 1, 363; id. M. 14, 467.—Also a later Ilium, built upon the coast, Liv. 35, 43, 3; 37, 9, 7.— Derivv. īlĭus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Ilium, Ilian, Trojan: tellus, Verg. A. 9, 285: res, id. ib. 1, 268: matres, Hor. Epod
ilium1.short: Īlĭum or Īlĭon, ĭi, n., = Ἴλιον, a poetical name for Troja, the city of Ilium, Troy, Verg.

ilius.full: Ilius, a, um, v. Ilium, II. A.

illabefactus.full: illăbĕfactus (inl-), a, um, adj. in-labefactus, unshaken, unbroken, unimpaired (poet.): vincula, Ov. P. 4, 8, 10: concordia, id. ib. 4, 12, 30.

illabor.full: illābor (inl-), psus, 3, v. dep. n. [inlabor], to fall, slip, slide, glide, or flow into; to fall down, sink down (rare but class.). Lit.: quo (i. e. in stomachum) primo illabuntur ea, quae accepta sunt ore, Cic. N. D. 2, 54, 135; Plin. 5, 29, 31, § 113: antennis illabitur ebria serpens, Claud. III. Cons. Stil. 367: notae jugis illabitur Aetnae, id. Rapt. Pros. 3, 330: si fractus illabatur orbis, should fall in, tumble to ruins, Hor. C. 3, 3, 7: tepet illabentibus astris Pontus, Stat. Ach. 1, 13

illaboratus.full: illăbōrātus (inl-), a, um, adj. in-laboratus, not labored, unwrought, uncultivated, acquired without labor, spontaneous (post-Aug.): terra, Sen. Ep. 90 fin.: fructus, Quint. 12, 10, 79: oratio (with simplex), id. 4, 1, 60: virtus (with obvia), id. 12, 2, 2: haec omnia fluunt illaborata, id. 10, 1, 111.

illaboro.full: illăbōro (inl-), āre, v. n. in-laboro, to work upon, labor at: illaborare domibus (i. e. aedificandis), to work at building houses, Tac. G. 46 fin.

illacerabilis.full: illăcĕrābĭlis (inl-), e, adj. in-lacerabilis, that cannot be torn: spolium, Sil. 5, 138.

illacessitus.full: illăcessītus (inl-), a, um, adj. inlacessitus, unprovoked, unattacked (postAug.): marcentem diu pacem illacessiti nutrierunt, Tac. G. 36; id. Agr. 20.

illacrimabilis.full: illăcrĭmābĭlis (inl-), e, adj. in-lacrimabilis. Unwept, unlamented, ἄκλαυστος: sed omnes illacrimabiles Urgentur ignotique longa Nocte, Hor. C. 4, 9, 26 (cf. indefletus, Ov. M. 7, 611).— That is not or cannot be moved by tears, pitiless, inexorable: Pluto, Hor. C. 2, 14, 6: urna, Aus. Epit. 36, 3.

illacrimo.full: illăcrĭmo (inl-), āvi, ātum, 1, v. n., and illăcrĭmor (inl-), ātus, 1, v. dep. in-lacrimo, to weep at or over a thing, to bewail, lament (not freq. till after the Aug. period). Lit. With dat.: quid dicam de Socrate? cujus morti illacrimari soleo Platonem legens? Cic. N. D. 3, 33, 82: perge, aude, nate; illacrima patris pestibus, id. poët. Tusc. 2, 9, 21: casu (i. e. casui), Nep. Alc. 6, 4: qui meo infelici errori unus illacrimasti, Liv. 40, 56, 6; Ov. Tr. 5, 8, 6; Suet. Vesp. 15.—* With acc.: ej

illaesibilis.full: illaesĭbĭlis (inl-), e, adj. in-laedo, that cannot be hurt, invulnerable (eccl. Lat.): deus, Lact. Ira D. 17 med.; Tert. adv. Val. 27.

illaesus.full: illaesus (inl-), a, um, adj. id., unhurt, unharmed, uninjured, unimpaired (perh. not ante-Aug.): illaeso corpore, Ov. H. 15, 168: corpus, Suet. Claud. 16: partes, Ov. M. 2, 826: artus, id. ib. 12, 489: illaesus et indemnis evasit, Sen. Ep. 9 fin.; Sil. 5, 125; 13, 536; Mart. 1, 7, 2: gallina, Plin. 15, 30, 40, § 136; 23, 1, 27, § 56: valetudo, Suet. Tib. 68.—* Adv.: illaesē, without hurt, Paul. Nol. Carm. 21, 157.

illaetabilis.full: illaetābĭlis (inl-), e, adj. in-laetabilis, cheerless, joyless, gloomy, sad (poet.): ora, Verg. A. 3, 707: murmur, id. ib. 12, 619: hymen (with funestus), Sen. Troad. 861: onus, i. e. a dead child, Stat. Th. 5, 633: munus (with grave), id. ib. 3, 706.

illamentatus.full: illāmentātus (inl-), a, um, adj. inlamentor, unmourned, unlamented (eccl. Lat.): illamentatus et insepultus, Vulg. 2 Macc. 5, 10.

illapsus1.full: illapsus (inl-), a, um, Part., from illabor.
illapsus1.short: illapsus (inl-), a, um, Part., from illabor.

illapsus2.full: illapsus (inl-), ūs, m. illabor, a falling, gliding, or flowing in: umoris illapsus atque exitus, Col. 2, 2, 11: serpentino illapsu, Ambros. Ep. 6, 42: gregis illapsu fremebundo territus, Sil. 3, 463.

illaqueatum.full: illăquĕātum (inl-), alii pro vincto utuntur, alii pro soluto, Paul. ex Fest. p. 113 Müll.; cf. the foll. art.
illaqueatum.short: illăquĕātum (inl-), alii pro vincto utuntur, alii pro soluto, Paul.

illaqueo.full: illăquĕo (inl-), āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. inlaqueo, to ensnare, take in a snare (cf.: irretio, illigo, implico). * Lit.: volucres, Prud. Cath. 3, 41.— Trop., to entrap, entangle (very rare): cur illaquetur hic? Pac. ap. Non. 470, 7 (Trag. Rel. p. 85 Rib.): munera navium Saevos illaqueant duces, Hor. C. 3, 16, 16: illaqueatus jam omnium legum periculis, irretitus odio bonorum omnium, Auct. Harusp. Resp. 4, 7; cf. the preced. art.

illargio.full: illargĭo (inl-), īre, v. a. in-largio, to give to, bestow upon: pecuniam illargibo tibi, Cato ap. Non. 470, 27.

illatabilis.full: illātābĭlis (inl-), e, adj. in-latus, without breadth, a word formed by Gellius to express the Gr. ἀπλατής, Gell. 1, 20, 9.

illatebro.full: illătē^bro (inl-), āre, v. a. in-latebro, to hide in a corner or lurking-place: inermi illatebrant sese, Quadrig. ap. Gell. 17, 2, 3; and ap. Non. 129, 24.

illatenus.full: illātĕnus or illactĕnus, adv. illetenus, so far (post-class. and very rare): navitas precum ejus (Arionis) commiseritum esse illactenus, ut, etc., Gell. 16, 19, 11: litteras illatenus, qua dixi, legendas praebebat, App. Mag. p. 326; cf. Fronto Ter. Als. 4.

illatio.full: illātĭo (inl-), ōnis, f. infero, a carrying or bringing in (post-class.). Lit. In gen.: mortui, i. e. burying, interment, Dig. 11, 7, 2, § 3 al.: FERRI, Inscr. ap. Marin. Fratr. Arv. 43.— In partic., an impost, duty: auctae, Cassiod. Var. 2, 16.— Trop. In gen.: stupri, i. e. a causing, committing, Paul. Sent. 5, 4, 1. — In partic., a logical inference, conclusion: vel illativum rogamentum. quod ex acceptionibus colligitur et infertur, App. Dogm. Plat. 3, pp. 34, 15.

illativus.full: illātīvus (inl-), a, um, adj. id., inferring, concluding, illative (cf. illatio, II. B.): particulae, Plin. ap. Diom. p. 410 P.— Subst.: illātīvum, an inference, conclusion: universale, particulare, Apul. Dogm. Plat. 3, p. 34, 24.

illatro.full: illātro (inl-), āre, v. n. in-latro, to bark at any thing (poet.): manibus, Luc. 6, 729: illatrat jejunis faucibus Orthrus, Sil. 13, 845.

illatus.full: illātus (inl-), a, um, Part., from infero.
illatus.short: illātus (inl-), a, um, Part., from infero.

illaudabilis.full: illaudābĭlis (inl-), e, adj. in-laudabilis, not worthy of praise (post-Aug.): carmen, Stat. S. 5, 5, 33: illaudatus est quasi illaudabilis, qui neque mentione aut memoria ulla dignus neque umquam nominandus est, Gell. 2, 6, 17; cf. Serv. Verg. G. 3, 5.

illaudandus.full: illaudandus (inl-), a, um, adj. inlaudo, not praiseworthy: facta plebis, Tert. Carm. adv. Marc. 3, 6.

illaudatus.full: illaudātus (inl-), a, um, adj. id., not praised, unpraised, without fame, obscure. Lit. (post-Aug.): gubernator illaudatus, inglorius subit portum, Plin. Ep. 9, 26, 4; Stat. Th. 11, 10; Sil. 14, 632; Claud. ap. Ruf. 2, 225.—* Poet. for illaudabilis, unworthy of praise, blamable, detestable, = abominandus: Busiris, Verg. G. 3, 5 Serv.; cf. Gell. 2, 6, 17.

ille.full: ille (old orthog., olle), a, ud (ollus, a, um, Enn. ap. Varr. L. L. 7, § 42 Müll.; Verg. A. 5, 197; in dramat. poets often ĭlle, v. Corss. Ausspr. II. p. 624), gen. illī^us (usu. illĭus in epic and lyric poets; Cic. de Or. 3, 47, 183; illīus in the time of Quint; cf. Ritschl, Opusc. 2, 683 sqq.; 696; gen. sing. m. illi, Cato ap. Prisc. p. 694; dat. sing. f. olli, Verg. A. 1, 254; Cato, R. R. 153 and 154; abl. plur. † ab oloes = ab illis, Paul. ex Fest. p. 19 Müll.); pron. demonstr. [Etym. dub.,
ille.short: ille (old orthog., olle), a, ud (ollus, a, um, Enn.

illecebra.full: illĕcĕbra (inl-), ae, f. illicio, an enticement, in a good or bad sense, an inducement, attraction, charm, allurement, bait, lure. Lit. (class.; in sing. and plur.; a favorite word of Cic.; cf.: invitatio, invitamentum). With gen. (subj. or obj.): quae tanta in ullo homine juventutis illecebra fuit, quanta in illo? Cic. Cat. 2, 4, 8: maxima est illecebra peccandi impunitatis spes, id. Mil. 16, 43: voluptas est illecebra turpitudinis, id. Leg. 1, 11, 31: fallax illecebra admirationum, Gell. 10, 1

illecebro.full: illĕcĕbro (inl-), āre, v. a. illecebra, to entice (late Lat.): oculos carnis, Aug. Serm. 113.

illecebrosus.full: illĕcĕbrōsus (inl-), a, um, adj. illecebra, full of allurement, very enticing, attractive, seductive (ante- and post-class.): istoc illecebrosius Fieri nihil potest, Plaut. Bacch. 1, 1, 54: sapor, Prud. adv. Symm. 2, 144: insidiae, Amm. 30, 1.—Adv.: illĕcĕ-brōsē, enticingly, attractively.—Comp.: agi, Amm. 30, 5, 7 (but not in Plaut. Mil. 3, 2, 36; v. Ritschl ad h. l.).

illectamentum.full: illectāmentum (inl-), i, n. illecto, means of allurement, an allurement, charm (post-class.): lenonia, App. Mag. p. 335, 32: magica, id. ib. 338, 41.

illectatio.full: illectātĭo (inl-), ōnis, f. id., an attraction, charm (post-class. and very rare, for the class. illecebra): jucundae sermonum, Gell. 18, 2, 1.

illectio.full: illectĭo (inl-), ōnis, f. illicio, allurement, charm: blandimentorum illectione seduco, Cassiod. in Psa. 120, 8.

illecto.full: illecto (inl-), āvi, ātum, 1, v. freq. a. id., to allure, attract, invite (eccl. Lat.): patres, Tert. Carm. adv. Marc. 2, 3.

illectus1.full: illectus (inl-), a, um, Part., from illicio.
illectus1.short: illectus (inl-), a, um, Part., from illicio.

illectus2.full: illectus (inl-), a, um, adj. in-lectus, from 2. lego. * Not collected, not gathered together: stipula illecta sunt spicae in messe dejectae necdum lectae, Dig. 50, 16, 30, § 1.— Not read, unread (very rare): si non accipiet scriptum illectumque remittet, Lecturam spera, Ov. A. A. 1, 469; App. Flor. 18.

illectus3.full: illectus (inl-), ūs, m. illicio, an allurement, enticement, with a play upon the word lectus: magis illectum tuum quam lectum metuo, Plaut. Bacch. 1, 1, 21.—Abl.: illectu, Jul. Val. Rer. Gest. Alex. 3, 17 al.

illegitimus.full: illēgĭtĭmus (inl-), a, um, unlawful, not permitted, Paul. Sent. 5, 4, 15.—Adv.: illēgĭtĭmē, unlawfully, illegitimately: qui concipiuntur, Gai. Inst. 1, § 89.
illegitimus.short: illēgĭtĭmus (inl-), a, um, unlawful, not permitted, Paul.

illepidus.full: illĕpĭdus (inl-), a, um, adj. in-lepidus, impolite, unmannerly, rude, unpleasant, disagreeable (rare but class.): inamabilis, inlepidus vivo, Malevolente ingenio natus, Plaut. Bacch. 4, 3, 3: parens avarus, illepidus, in liberos difficilis, Cic. N. D. 3, 29, 72: homines, Gell. 18, 4, 10: deliciae illepidae atque inelegantes, Cat. 6, 2: votum (with invenustum), id. 36, 17: verba durae et illepidae novitatis, Gell. 11, 7, 1.—Adv.: illĕpĭdē (inl-), impolitely, rudely, inelegantly: qui istoc pacto t

illevigatus.full: illēvĭgātus (illaev- or inl-), a, um, adj. in-laevigatus, not smooth, rough, harsh: sonus (with inconditus), Diom. p. 499 P.
illevigatus.short: illēvĭgātus (illaev- or inl-), a, um, adj.

illex1.full: illex (inl-), ēgis, adj. in-lex, without law, contrary to law, lawless (anteclass.); as a term of reproach: impure, inhoneste, injure, inlex, labes popli, Plaut. Pers. 3, 3, 4; Caecil. ap. Non. 10, 24 (Com. Fragm. v. 60 Rib.).

illex2.full: illex or illix (inl-), ĭcis, adj. illicio, alluring, enticing, seductive (ante- and post-class.). Adj.: oculi, App. Mag. p. 323: ars, Prud. adv. Symm. 2, 6: halitus, id. Psych. 328.—More freq., Subst. com. A decoy, lure: aedis nobis area'st, auceps sum ego, Esca'st meretrix, lectus illex est, amatores aves, Plaut. As. 1, 3, 67.— Transf., a seducer, a seductress: malae rei tantae fuimus illices, Plaut. Poen. 3, 4, 35: illex animi Venus, App. Mag. p. 295.

illibabilis.full: illībābĭlis (inl-), e, adj. in-libo, incapable of diminution: sapientia, Lact. 2, 7, 33.

illibatus.full: illībātus (inl-), a, um, adj. in-libo, undiminished, unimpaired, uninjured, unharmed (not freq. till after the Aug. per.): veteres illibataeque divitiae, * Cic. Sest. 43, 93: vires, Liv. 42, 30, 6: robur, Col. 12, 1, 1: imperium, Liv. 3, 61, 5: magnitudo, Vell. 2, 48: gloria, Tac. A. 2, 46: libertas, Just. 28, 4: quae (with integra), Plin. Pan. 25, 1: versus, complete, unabridged, Diom. p. 497 P.: potestas, Rescript. ap. Just. Inst. 1, 8, 2: foedera prisci tori, unviolated, Luc. 2, 342: virginit

illiberalis.full: illībĕrālis (inl-), e, adj. in-liberalis, unworthy of a freeman, ignoble, ungenerous, sordid, mean, disobliging (class.; mostly of things): illiberales et sordidi quaestus mercenariorum omnium, quorum operae, non quorum artes emuntur, Cic. Off. 1, 42, 150: labor, id. Fin. 1, 1, 3: facinus, Ter. Ad. 3, 4, 3: duplex omnino est jocandi genus, unum illiberale, petulans, flagitiosum, obscenum: alterum elegans, urbanum, ingeniosum, facetum, Cic. Off. 1, 29, 104: res ad cognoscendum non illiberalis, id

illiberalitas.full: illībĕrālĭtas (inl-), ātis, f. illiberalis, conduct unworthy of a freeman, ignoble or ungenerous behavior, meanness, stinginess (very rare): habenda est ratio rei familiaris, sed ita, ut illiberalitatis avaritiaeque absit suspicio, Cic. Off. 2, 18, 64; id. Att. 8, 6, 3.
