inarculum.full: inarcŭlum virgula erat ex malo Punico incurvata, quam regina sacrificans in capite gestabat, Paul. ex Fest. p. 113 Müll. N. cr. [in-arcus].
inarculum.short: inarcŭlum virgula erat ex malo Punico incurvata, quam regina sacrificans in capite gestabat, Paul.

inardesco.full: ĭn-ardesco, arsi, 3, v. inch.n., to kindle, take fire, burn, glow (poet. and in post-Aug. prose). Lit.: nubes Solis inardescit radiis, Verg. A. 8, 623: arbusculae in igne ut ferrum inardescentes, Plin. 13, 25, 51, § 140: nec munus (i. e. vestis) umeris Herculis Inarsit aestuosius, Hor. Epod. 3, 18: inardescunt genae, Sen. Herc. Oet. 251. — Trop.: affectus omnis languescat necesse est, nisi voce, vultu, totius prope habitu corporis inardescat, Quint. 11, 3, 2: cupidine vindictae inardescere, Tac.

inarefactus.full: ĭn-ārĕfactus, a, um, adj., dried: sanguis ranarum, Plin. 32, 10, 42, § 121 dub.
inarefactus.short: ĭn-ārĕfactus, a, um, adj., dried: sanguis ranarum, Plin.

inaresco.full: ĭn-āresco, ārui, 3, v. inch. n., to become dry in any place, to dry up, become quite dry (post-Aug.). Lit.: in sole, Plin. 26, 8.40, § 66; for which: caenum illitum sole, id. 31, 6, 32, § 61: opus, Vitr. 7, 3: medicamenta, Cels. 5, 17 fin.: fructus ante maturitatem, Col. 4, 24, 3: germina multa cum inaruere, Plin. 27, 11, 71, § 95: nihil facilius quam lacrimas inarescere, Quint. 6, 1, 27.— Trop., to dry up, become exhausted: ne (liberalitas) nimia profusione inarescat, Plin. Ep. 2, 4, 4.

inargento.full: ĭn-argento, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. in-argentum, to overlay with silver, to silver: aes, Paul. Sent. 5, 25, 5. — Mostly Part.: ĭnargentātus, a, um, overlaid with silver, silvered over (post-Aug.): lamina aerea, Plin. 21, 2, 3, § 5: lecti, Dig. 33, 10, 3 praef. § 3.

inargutus.full: ĭn-argūtus, a, um, adj., not acute, without acuteness (post - class.): sententia non inarguta, Dig. 7, 5, 5, § 1.—Adv.: in-argūtē, not acutely: non mehercule inargute nec incallide opposuisti hoc Tullianum, Gell. 12, 13, 19.
inargutus.short: ĭn-argūtus, a, um, adj., not acute, without acuteness (post - class.): sententia non inarguta, Dig.

inarime.full: Īnărĭmē, ēs, f., = εἰν Ἀρίμοις (Hom. Il. 2, 783), an island in the Tyrrhene Sea, on the coast of Campania, now Ischia, Plin. 3, 6, 12, § 82; Verg. A. 9, 716 Heyne; Ov. M. 14, 89; Val. Fl. 3, 208; Stat. S. 2, 2, 76; Sil. 12, 148; Luc. 5, 101: Inarime a Graecis dicta Pithecusa, Mart. Cap. 6, § 644.

inarmo.full: ĭn-armo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a., to arm (eccl. Lat.), Ven. Fort. Vit. Leob. 7.

inaro.full: ĭn-ăro, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a., to plough in, cover by ploughing. Lit.: sarmenta, Cato, R. R. 37, 3: fabalia pro stercore, Varr. R. R. 1, 23. 3; cf.: disjectum fimum, Col. 2, 5, 2: semina abjecta, Plin. 18, 18, 47, § 169: arbores, Col. 2, 2, 11. — Transf. To plough, till, cultivate: solum, Plin. 18, 14, 36, § 136: agrum, Dig. 43, 23, 9.— To enter or write in a list, Commod. 70, 15.— To mark: stigmatibus vultum, Ambros. Exhort. Virg. 12, § 83.

inarticulatus.full: ĭn-artĭcŭlātus, a, um, adj., indistinct, inarticulate (post-class.), Arn. 2, 59: vox, Prisc. 537 P.
inarticulatus.short: ĭn-artĭcŭlātus, a, um, adj., indistinct, inarticulate (post-class.), Arn.

inartificialis.full: ĭn-artĭfĭcĭālis, e, adj., inartificial, not according to the rules of art (post-Aug.): illas (probationes) ἀτέχνους, id est inartificiales; has ἐντέχνους, id est artificiales vocaverunt, Quint. 5, 1, 1: probationes, id. 5, 5, 2; cf. id. 5, 10, 11: argumenta, Mart. Cap. 5, § 474; § 557; § 560.—Adv.: ĭnartĭfĭ-cĭālĭter, inartificially: se gerere (opp. artificialiter), Quint. 2, 17, 42.
inartificialis.short: ĭn-artĭfĭcĭālis, e, adj., inartificial, not according to the rules of art (post-Aug.): illas (probationes) ἀτέχνους, id est inartificiales;

inascensus.full: ĭn-ascensus, a, um, adj., not mounted or ascended: locus (rostra), Plin. Pan. 65, 3.
inascensus.short: ĭn-ascensus, a, um, adj., not mounted or ascended: locus (rostra), Plin.

inaspectus.full: ĭn-aspectus, a, um, adj., unseen, Stat. Th. 1, 50.
inaspectus.short: ĭn-aspectus, a, um, adj., unseen, Stat.

inaspicuus.full: ĭn-aspĭcŭus, a, um, adj., invisible: notae, Aus. Ep. 23, 22.
inaspicuus.short: ĭn-aspĭcŭus, a, um, adj., invisible: notae, Aus.

inassatus.full: ĭnassātus, a, um, Part. [in-asso], roasted (post-Aug.): pulmo, Plin. 30, 8, 22, § 74; 30, 10, 27, § 88.

inassero.full: ĭnassĕro, āre, v. a. in-asser, to cover with beams, Inscr. Grut. 207, 2.

inassignatus.full: ĭn-assignātus, a, um, adj., unassigned (post class.): inodus agrorum, Aggen. p. 70 Goes.
inassignatus.short: ĭn-assignātus, a, um, adj., unassigned (post class.): inodus agrorum, Aggen.

inassuetus.full: ĭn-assŭētus, a, um, adj., unaccustomed (poet. and in post-Aug. prose): equi, Ov. F. 4, 450: manus, id. A. A. 1, 300: at vestigia nuda sinusque Cingere, inassuetum, i. e. unusual, Sil. 3, 236: opere inassueto Galliis, Fragm. Or. Claud. ap. Grut. 502, 2, 37.

inattaminatus.full: ĭnattāmĭnātus, a, um, adj. 2. inattamino, uninjured, unhurt, Tert. de Cor. Mil. c. ult.

inattenuatus.full: ĭn-attĕnŭātus, a, um, adj., undiminished, unweakened: fames, unappeased, Ov. M. 8, 846.
inattenuatus.short: ĭn-attĕnŭātus, a, um, adj., undiminished, unweakened: fames, unappeased, Ov.

inattritus.full: ĭn-attrītus, a, um, adj., not rubbed away, not worn: aurum, Paul. Nol. Carm. 10, 254.
inattritus.short: ĭn-attrītus, a, um, adj., not rubbed away, not worn: aurum, Paul.

inaudax.full: ĭn-audax, ācis, adj., not daring, timorous: raptor, Hor. C. 3, 20, 3.
inaudax.short: ĭn-audax, ācis, adj., not daring, timorous: raptor, Hor.

inaudibilis.full: ĭn-audībĭlis, e, adj., inaudible: melodia nobis, Censor. D. 13.
inaudibilis.short: ĭn-audībĭlis, e, adj., inaudible: melodia nobis, Censor.

inaudientia.full: ĭn-audĭentĭa, ae, f., disobedience, Cypr. Ep. 28.

inaudio.full: ĭn-audĭo (arch. ind-audio, cf. Ritschl Proleg. ad Plaut. p. 143), īvi or ĭi, ītum, 4, v. a., to hear, learn, esp. something secret (mostly ante-class. and in the tempp. perff.): quod ego inaudivi, accipite, Pac. ap. Non. 126, 23: unde hoc tam repente jucundum inaudivi melum? Nov. ib. 21: quorum erupit illa vox de qua ego ex te primum quiddam inaudieram, Cic. Fragm. ib. 20; cf.: numquid de quo inaudisti? id. Att. 6, 1, 20: metus ne de hac re quippiam indaudiverit, Plaut. Most. 3, 1, 11; id. Merc.

inauditiuncula.full: ĭn-audītĭuncŭla, ae, f. dim., a little lecture or lesson: disciplinae grammaticae, Gell. 5, 21, 4.

inauditus1.full: ĭnaudītus, a, um, Part., from inaudio.
inauditus1.short: ĭnaudītus, a, um, Part., from inaudio.

inauditus2.full: ĭn-audītus, a, um, adj., unheard. (On account of its novelty or strangeness.) Unheard-of, unusual, strange, new (freq. and class.; a favorite word of Cic.): nihil dicam reconditum, nihil aut inauditum vobis aut cuiquam novum, Cic. de Or. 1, 31, 137; cf. id. Rep. 2, 12: quod nobis inauditum est, Quint. 1, 6, 9: novum est, non dico inusitatum, verum omnino inauditum, Cic. Caecin. 13, 36; cf. id. Vatin. 14, 33: novum crimen et ante hunc diem inauditum, id. Leg. 1, 1: insignis quaedam, inaudita, nov

inauguratio.full: ĭnaugŭrātĭo, ōnis, f. inauguro, a consecration; hence, transf., a beginning (post-class.), Tert. adv. Valent. 11.

inauguro.full: ĭn-augŭro, āvi, ātum, 1, v. n. and a. Lit. To take omens from the flight of birds, to practise augury, to divine: per sacram viam augures ex arce profecti solent inaugurare, Varr. L. L. 5, § 47 Müll.: impetritum, inauguratum'st: quovis admittunt aves, Plaut. As. 2, 1, 11: Palatinum Romulus, Aventinum Remus ad inaugurandum templa capiunt, Liv. 1, 6, 4: agedum, divine tu, inaugura, fierine possit, quod nunc ego mente concipio, Liv. 1, 36, 4. —Hence, b. inaugŭrāto, adv. (lit. abl. absol.), after co

inaurator.full: ĭnaurātor, ōris, m. inauro, a gilder (post-class.), Firm. 4, 15; 8, 26; Inscr. Orell. 4201; Inscr. Grut. 1074, 12.

inauratura.full: ĭnaurātūra, ae, f. id., a gilding, Front.—Piur., Gromat. Vet. 97, 8.

inauratus1.full: ĭnaurātus, a, um, Part. and P. a., from inauro.

inauratus2.full: ĭn-aurātus, a, um, adj., not gilded, not ornamented with gold: inauratae atque illautae mulieris, Titin. ap. Charis. p. 181 P.
inauratus2.short: ĭn-aurātus, a, um, adj., not gilded, not ornamented with gold: inauratae atque illautae mulieris, Titin.

inaures.full: ĭnaures, ĭum, f. in-auris, ear-drops, ear-rings, ornaments for the ear, Plaut. Men. 3, 3, 17; Plin. 9, 55, 81, § 172; 32, 2, 7, § 16; cf. Isid. Orig. 19, 31.

inaurio.full: ĭnaurĭo, īre, v. a. id., to give hearing to, to cause to hear (post-class.): surdos (Christus), Lact. Epit. 45, 2.— To grant (in answer to prayer), Hilar. in Psa. 53, 54.

inauritus.full: ĭn-aurītus, a, um, adj., without ears: animalia, Gell. 7, 6, 1 dub.; v. 2. inauditus, III.
inauritus.short: ĭn-aurītus, a, um, adj., without ears: animalia, Gell.

inauro.full: ĭn-auro, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a., to cover or overlay with gold, to gild (class.; most freq. in the part. perf.). Lit.: tegulas aereas, Plin. 33, 3, 18, § 57; Vitr. 7, 8: maurata statua, Cic. Verr. 2, 2, 21, § 50: columna extrinsecus, id. Div. 1, 24, 48: Romulus (i. e. statua Romuli), id. Cat. 3, 8, 19: palla, Auct. Her. 4, 47, 60: vestis, i. e. inwrought with gold, Ov. M. Fac. 18.— Trop., to gild, i. e. to make rich: puto, te malle a Caesare consuli quam inaurari, Cic. Fam. 7, 13, 1: ut te Confesti

inauspicato.full: ĭnauspĭcātō, adv., v. the foll. art.

inauspicatus.full: ĭn-auspĭcātus, a, um, adj. At which no auspices were taken, without auspices: lex, Liv. 7, 6, 11.—Hence, in-auspĭcāto, adv. (lit. abl. absol.), without consulting the auspices: quod inauspicato pomoerium transgressus esset (Ti. Gracchus), Cic. Div. 1, 17, 33.— Of bad omen, unlucky, inauspicious (only post-Aug.): inauspicatarum animantium vice, Plin. 18, 1, 1, § 4: nomen, id. 3, 23, 26, § 145: exemplum, id. 7, 16, 15, § 136: garrulitas (cornicis), id. 10, 12, 14, § 68: bibente conviva mensam toll

inausus.full: ĭn-ausus, a, um, adj., not ventured, unattempted (poet. and in post-Aug. prose): ne quid inausum Aut intractatum scelerisve dolive fuisset, Verg. A. 8, 205: nefas, Val. Fl. 1, 807: quid enim per hosce dies inausum intemeratumve vobis? Tac. A. 1, 42: sciat animus nihil inausum esse fortunae, Sen. Ep. 91 med.—Plur. as subst.: ĭn-ausa, ōrum, n., unattempted things, deeds beyond daring: quae inausa audeat, Sen. Thyest. 20.
inausus.short: ĭn-ausus, a, um, adj., not ventured, unattempted (poet.

inauxiliatus.full: ĭnauxĭlĭātus, a, um 2. in - auxilior, not supported, Vulg. Sap. 12, 16.

inavarus.full: ĭnăvārus, a, um 2. in-avarus, not greedy, not avaricious, Cassiod. Var. 1, 3.

inaversibilis.full: ĭnāversĭbĭlis, e, adj. 2. in-aversus, that cannot be turned aside, unalterable: aeternitas (with immobilis and insolubilis), App. Trim. p. 100 med. (al. inaversabilis or inversibilis).

incaeduus.full: in-caedŭus (incīdŭus, Stat. Th. 6, 9?*!0), a, um, adj., not cut or felled, uncut, unhewn (poet. and in post-class. prose): lucus, Ov. F. 2, 435: silva, id. Am. 3, 1, 1; Stat. Th. 6, 90: intonsi montes, silvosi, incaedui, Serv. Verg. E. 5, 63.

incalanto.full: incălanto, invocanto, Paul. ex Fest. p. 114 Müll. [in-calo].

incalationes.full: incălātĭōnes, invocationes, Paul. ex Fest. p. 107 Müll.

incalative.full: incălātīve, vocative, Paul. ex Fest. p. 114 Müll.

incalcatus.full: in-calcātus, a, um, adj., untrodden: humus, Paul. Nol. Carm. 16, 110.
incalcatus.short: in-calcātus, a, um, adj., untrodden: humus, Paul.

incalesco.full: in-călesco, calŭi, 3, v. inch. n., to grow warm or hot, to glow (mostly poet.; not in Cic.). Lit.: incalescente sole, Liv. 22, 6, 9: anni tempore jam incalescente, Col. 2, 4, 1: cum videas ordinem rerum per constituta procedere ... aestas suo tempore incaluit, Sen. Q. N. 3, 16, 3 Haase (al. incanduit): incaluerant vino, Liv. 1, 57, 8; cf.: incaluit vis illa mali (i. e. veneni), Ov. M. 9, 161: quis nostro curvum te funere vidit? Atram quis lacrimis incaluisse togam? to glow with burning tears, Pr

incalfacio.full: in-calfăcĭo, ĕre, v. a., to warm, to heat (poet.): culmos Titan incalfacit, Ov. F. 4, 919: cultros (hostia), id. M. 15, 735.

incallidus.full: in-callĭdus, a, um, adj., unskilful, incapable, simple, stupid: servus non incallidus, i. e. shrewd, knowing, Cic. Clu. 16, 47: non incallidi homines, id. Inv. 1, 3, 4: incallidus alioqui et facilis juventa, Tac. A. 3, 8: judex formae, incompetent, Sabin. Her. 3, 55; cf.: fuit in jure non incallidus, Capit. Macrin. 13. — Adv.: incallĭdē, unskilfully: in his tribus generibus non incallide tergiversantur, Cic. Off. 3, 33, 118: opposuisse hoc Tullianum, Gell. 12, 13, 19: conquirere, id. 7. 3, 45.
incallidus.short: in-callĭdus, a, um, adj., unskilful, incapable, simple, stupid: servus non incallidus, i.

incallo.full: incallo, āre, v. a. in-callum, to render callous (late Lat.): carnem indurat et incallat, Veg. Vet. 2, 27.

incandesco.full: in-candesco, dŭi, 3, v. inch. n., to become warm or hot, to glow, to kindle (poet. and in post-Aug. prose): volat illud (plumbum) et incandescit eundo, Ov. M. 2, 728: vetus accensis incanduit ignibus ara, id. ib. 12, 12: spumis incanduit unda, Cat. 64, 13: tempestas totoque auctumni incanduit aestu, Verg. G. 3, 479: pars magna terrarum alto pulvere incanduit, Plin. Pan. 30, 3: aestas incanduit, Sen. Q. N. 3, 16, 3 (dub.; Haase, incaluit).—Trop.: studii mei ardor incanduit, was kindled, became st

incandido.full: in-candĭdo, āre, v. a., to make white, to cleanse (eccl. Lat.): maculas, Firm. de Err. Relig. 28.

incanesco.full: in-cānesco, canŭi, 3, v. inch. n., to become white, to turn gray or hoary (poet.): tortaque remigio spumis incanuit unda, Cat. 63, 13: ornusque incanuit albo Flore piri, Verg. G. 2, 71: gelu magnoque incanuit imbre Caucasus, Val. Fl. 6, 611: cum pigra incanuit aetas, Sil. 3, 328.

incantamentum.full: incantāmentum, i, n. incanto, a charm, incantation (post-Aug.): valeantne aliquid verba et incantamenta carminum, Plin. 28, 2, 3, § 10: anile, Amm. 16, 8, 2: anilia incantamenta, id. 29, 2, 3.

incantatio.full: incantātĭo, ōnis, f. id., an enchanting, enchantment (post-class.): magicae, Firm. Math. 5, 5: incantationum vires, Tert. Hab. Mul. 2.

incantator.full: incantātor, ōris, m. incanto, an enchanter, wizard (post-class.), Tert. Idol. 9; Isid. 8, 9, 15; Mos. et Rom. Leg. Coll. 15, 1, 2.

incanto.full: in-canto, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. and n. * To sing in, with dat.: passer incantans saepiculae (i. e. in saepicula), App. M. 8, p. 210, 26. — In partic. To say over, mutter, or chant a magic formula against some one: QVI MALVM CARMEN INCANTASSET, Fragm. XII. Tab. ap. Plin. 28, 2, 4, § 17.— Transf. To consecrate with charms or spells: incantata vincula, lovelcnots, Hor. S. 1, 8, 49.— To bewitch, enchant: quaesisti, quod mihi emolumentum fuerit incantandi (sc. illam)? App. Mag. p. 305: incantata mulier

incanus.full: in-cānus, a, um, adj., quite gray, hoary (poet. and in post-Aug. prose): homo crispus, incanus, Plaut. Rud. 1, 2, 37: mentum, Verg. G. 3, 311: barba, Col. 8, 2, 9: labra Famis, Ov. M. 8, 804: caput, Suet. Dom. 20. —Poet.: saecula, hoary centuries, Cat. 95, 6.
incanus.short: in-cānus, a, um, adj., quite gray, hoary (poet.

incapabilis.full: incăpābĭlis, e, adj. 2. in-capio, incomprehensible (late Lat.): deus, Arrian. ap. Aug. Ep. 174; cf.: incapabilis ἀχώρητος, Gloss. Philox.

incapabilitas.full: incăpābĭlĭtas, ātis, f. incapabilis, incomprehensibility (eccl. Lat.): ecce incapabilitatem habet Pater, quae non est tua, Aug. cont. Max. 1, 9, 2.

incapax.full: in-căpax, ācis, adj., incapable (postclass.): sacramenti, Prud. στεφ. 10, 588: aedes incapax solvi, indissoluble, indestructible, id. ib. 348.
incapax.short: in-căpax, ācis, adj., incapable (postclass.): sacramenti, Prud.

incapistro.full: in-căpistro, āvi, 1, v. a., to halter or muzzle; trop., to fetter, entangle: aliquem malis erroribus, App. M. 11, p. 266, 30.

incarno.full: incarno, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. in-caro, orig., to make flesh; hence, in pass.: in-carnārī, ātus, to be made flesh, become incarnate (eccl. Lat.), Claud. Mam. Stat. An. 1, 12; Salv. adv. Avar. 3, 2; Cassiod. Hist. Eccl. 2, 9 al.

incassus.full: in-cassus, a, um, adj., vain: non incassa futura temptamina, Sulp. Sev. Dial. 3, 10, 3.
incassus.short: in-cassus, a, um, adj., vain: non incassa futura temptamina, Sulp.

incastigatus.full: in-castīgātus, a, um, adj., unpunished, unreproved: nec me dimittes incastigatum, Hor. Ep. 1, 10, 45.
incastigatus.short: in-castīgātus, a, um, adj., unpunished, unreproved: nec me dimittes incastigatum, Hor.

incastratura.full: in-castrātūra, ae, f., a tenon, Vulg. Exod. 26, 17 sq.; 36, 22.
incastratura.short: in-castrātūra, ae, f., a tenon, Vulg.

incatholicus.full: in-căthŏlĭcus, a, um, adj., not catholic; perh. only as subst. plur.: incăthŏ-lĭci, ōrum, heretics: ab incatholicis catholica laceratur ecclesia, Cassiod. Anim. 12.
incatholicus.short: in-căthŏlĭcus, a, um, adj., not catholic;

incautela.full: incautēla, ae, f. incautus, want of foresight, incautiousness (late Lat.): per incautelam deperire, Salvian. Gub. D. 6 med.

incautus.full: in-cautus, a, um, adj. Act., incautious, heedless, improvident, inconsiderate (class.; syn. improvidus): ut in ipsum incautum atque etiam imparatum incideret, Caes. B. G. 6, 30, 2; Cic. Rosc. Am. 7, 20: Trebonius oppressus est ab hoste incautus, id. Phil. 11, 2, 5; id. Planc. 22, 53; id. N. D. 2, 1, 1: minime incautus patronus, id. Brut. 70, 246: ab secundis rebus incauti, Liv. 5, 44, 6: ad credendum pavor, id. 9, 12, 8. — Comp.: incautior fuissem, nisi, etc., Cic. Fam. 9, 24, 1: juventa, Liv. 3

incavillatio.full: incăvillātĭo per despectum irrisio, Paul. ex Fest. p. 107, 15 Müll.

incavillor.full: in-căvillor, āri, v. dep., to revile, mock at: joco regem, Gell. 5, 5 in lemm.

incavo.full: in-căvo, āre, v. a., to hollow out, make hollow: aliquid, Col. 4, 25, 2.

incedo.full: in-cēdo, cessi, cessum (sync. perf. incesti, Plaut. Cas. 3, 6, 11), 3, v. n. and a., to go, step, or march along at a measured pace (class.). Lit. In gen. Neutr.: tenero et molli ingressu suspendimus gradum: non ambulamus, sed incedimus, Sen. Q. N. 7, 31: per vias, Plaut. Merc. 2, 3, 71; cf.: socios per ipsos, Verg. A. 5, 188: viā, Plaut. Curc. 1, 1, 32: tota in urbe, Ov. F. 6, 653: quacumque incederet, Cic. Div. 1, 24, 49: quam taeter incedebat, quam truculentus, id. Sest. 8, 19: incessit deind

inceleber.full: in-cĕlĕber, bris, bre, adj., not celebrated, not known to fame (post - Aug.): vallis, Sil. 8, 379: advocatus, Gell. 1, 22, 6: libri, id. 5, 14, 2.
inceleber.short: in-cĕlĕber, bris, bre, adj., not celebrated, not known to fame (post - Aug.): vallis, Sil.

incelebratus.full: in-cĕlebrātus, a, um, adj., not made known, not spread abroad (post-Aug.): ab aliis incelebrata (opp. digna cognitu), Tac. A. 6, 7 fin.: multa per invidiam scriptorum incelebrata sunt, Sall. H. Fragm. 1, 57 Kritz (dub.; Dietsch reads celata).
incelebratus.short: in-cĕlebrātus, a, um, adj., not made known, not spread abroad (post-Aug.): ab aliis incelebrata (opp.

incenatus.full: in-cēnātus (in-coen-), a, um, adj. 2. in-cenatus, that has not dined or eaten, dinnerless, hungry, fasting (ante- and postclass.): bibat aquam mulsam, cubet incenatus, Cato, R. R. 156, 4: superi incenati sunt, et cenati inferi, Plaut. Aul. 2, 7, 6: senex, id. Cas. 4, 2, 9; cf.: incenis: pridie incenato dare medicamenta, Scrib. Comp. 140.

incendefacio.full: incendĕfăcĭo, fēci, 3, v. a. incendo-facio, to set on fire: carraginem, Treb. Claud. 8.

incendialis.full: incendĭālis, e, adj. incendium, of or belonging to fires, fire-: tunica, Tert. ad Nat. 1, 18.

incendiarius.full: incendĭārĭus, a, um, adj. id., causing a conflagration, setting on fire, fire-. Adj.: avis, fire-bird, Plin. 10, 13, 17, § 36: oleum, Veg. Mil. 4, 8; 18: tela, Amm. 20, 11. — Subst.: incendĭārĭus, ii, m., an incendiary, Tac. A. 15, 67; Suet. Vit. 17: incendiarii, qui consulto incendium inferunt, Paul. Sent. 5, 3, 6.

incendiosus.full: incendĭōsus, a, um, adj. id., burning, hot (post - class.): folia gustu, App. Herb. 58: solis fervor incendiosior, Fulg. Myth. 1, 15.

incendium.full: incendĭum, ĭi, n. incendo, a burning, fire, conflagration. Lit. (freq. and class.; equally common in sing. and plur.): incendium facere, to set fire to, Cic. Par. 4, 2, 31; Caes. B. G. 5, 19 fin.: excitare, restinguere, Cic. Mur. 25, 51 (v. under II.): in ipso urbis incendio, Caes. B. C. 1, 5, 3: frumentum flumine atque incendio corruperunt, id. B. G. 7, 55, 8: omnia incendiis vastare, Hirt. B. G. 8, 25, 1; cf.: nihil cogitant nisi caedes, nisi incendia, nisi rapinas, Cic. Cat. 2, 5, 10: si ince

incendo.full: incendo, di, sum, 3 (archaic form of the perf. subj. incensit = incenderit, sicut incepsit = inceperit, Paul. ex Fest. p. 107 Müll.), v. a. in-candeo; cf.: accendo and succendo, to set fire to, to kindle, burn (freq. and class.; syn. inflammare). Lit.: cupas taedā ac pice refertas incendunt, Caes. B. C. 2, 11, 2: tus et odores, Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 37, § 77; cf. odores, id. Tusc. 3, 18, 43: lychnos, Verg. A. 1, 727: oppida sua omnia, vicos, reliqua privata aedificia incendunt, Caes. B. G. 1, 5, 2: a
incendo.short: incendo, di, sum, 3 (archaic form of the perf.

incenis.full: in-cēnis (in-coen-), e, adj. in-cenatus, that has not dined, dinnerless: senex, Plaut. Cas. 4, 1, 18 (cf. incenatus, id. ib. 4, 2, 9).

inceno.full: in-cēno (in-coen-), āre, 1, v. n., to dine there, to dine in or at a place: incenante eo, Suet. Tib. 39 dub. (al. cenante eo).

incense.full: incensē, false read. in Gell. 10, 3, 13, instead of impense; v. impendo fin.

incensio.full: incensio, ōnis, f. incendo, a setting on fire, burning (rare but class.): Capitolii, Cic. Cat. 3, 4, 9: incensione urbem liberavi, id. Sull. 11, 33: turis, Arn. 7, 234.

incensitus.full: incensĭtus, a, um, adj. 2. in-censeo, not assessed, not enrolled in the census, Cod. Th. 10, 23, 1.

incensor.full: incensor, ōris, m. incendo, one who kindles or sets fire to (post-class.). Lit.: messium, Dig. 48, 19, 16, § 9; Paul. Sent. 5, 20; Mos. et Rom. Leg. Coll. 12, 3, 2: specularum, i. e. who kindles beacons, App. de Mundo, p. 69. — Trop., an inciter, instigator: turbarum, Amm. 31, 9, 4.

incensum.full: incensum, i, n. id.. A setting fire to, lighting (eccl. Lat.): hora incensi, Ambros. de Virg. 3.— Concr., incense: incenso imposito, Inscr. Fratr. Arv. ap. Marin. p. 639; Sulp. Sev. Chron. 1, 47, 4; cf. Isid. Orig. 4, 12: incensum θυμίαμα, Gloss. Phil. — In gen., sacrifice: incensum abominatio est mihi, Tert. adv. Jud. 5; Vulg. Sap. 18, 21; id. Ecclus. 45, 20.

incensus1.full: incensus, a, um, Part., from incendo.
incensus1.short: incensus, a, um, Part., from incendo.

incensus2.full: incensus, a, um, adj. 2. in-census, not estimated, not assessed, unregistered; said of one who has not given in an account of himself and his property to the censor: hominem incensum vendere, Cic. Caecin. 34, 99: populus, Liv. 4, 8, 3: lex de incensis lata, id. 1, 44, 1; Ulp. Fragm. 11, 11.

incentio.full: incentĭo, ōnis, f. incino. A blowing or playing upon an instrument (postclass.): incentiones tibiarum, Gell. 4, 13, 3. — A charm, enchantment; plur., Gell. 16, 11, 2.

incentivus.full: incentīvus, a, um, adj. id., that strikes up, sets the tune (ante- and post-class.). Lit.: tibia, the treble flute (opp. succentive, that plays the accompaniment), Varr. R. R. 1, 2, 15.— Transf., superior: vita pastorum (opp. succentiva vita agricolarum), Varr. R. R. 1, 2, 16.— Trop., that provokes or incites: lues, Prud. Hamart. 250. —Hence, Subst.: incentīvum, i, n., an incentive: peccaminis, Prud. Apoth. 929: vitiorum, Hier. Ep. 52, 3.— Adv.: incen-tīvē, Ven. Fort. Vit. Leob. 10.

incentor.full: incentor, ōris, m. id., one who sets the tune or begins to sing, a precentor, singer (post-class.). Lit.: carminis, Paul. Nol. Carm. 15, 32: incentore canam Phoebo Musisque magistris, Avien. Perieg. 895; Isid. 6, 9, 13.— Trop., an inciter, exciter: igneus turbarum, Amm. 15, 1, 2: civilis belli, Oros. 5, 19: rebellionis totius, id. 6, 11.

inceps.full: inceps, deinceps, Paul. ex Fest. p. 107 Müll.

inceptio.full: inceptĭo, ōnis, f. incipio, a beginning, undertaking (rare but class.): tam praeclari operis, Cic. Ac. 2, 38, 119: patrociniorum, App. Mag. p. 317, 5.—Absol. (opp. depositio), Quint. 11, 3, 46.— Transf., enterprise, undertaking: inceptio est amentium, non amantium, Ter. And. 1, 3, 13.

incepto.full: incepto, āre, v. freq. a. id., to begin, undertake, attempt (ante- and post-class.): inceptas facinus facere, Plaut. Curc. 1, 1, 23; so, with inf.: loqui, id. Trin. 4, 3, 23: canere, Gell. 1, 11, 3: quo iter inceptas? Plaut. Truc. 1, 2, 28: quid inceptas? Ter. Eun. 5, 8, 1.— Esp., to begin business, cum aliquo, i. e. to quarrel: si cum illo inceptas homine, Ter. Phorm. 4, 3, 24.

inceptor.full: inceptor, ōris, m. id., a beginner (anteand post - class.): o mearum voluptatum omnium inventor, inceptor, perfector! Ter. Eun. 5, 8, 4: carminis, Avien. Arat. init.

inceptum.full: inceptum, i, n., v. incipio fin.

inceptus1.full: inceptus, a, um, Part., from incipio.
inceptus1.short: inceptus, a, um, Part., from incipio.

inceptus2.full: inceptus, ūs, m. incipio, a beginning, undertaking (rare): foedum inceptu, foedum exitu, Liv. praef. 10: magno in omnia inceptu veneram, Sen. Ep. 108, 15: eriles, Val. Fl. 6, 124.

incerniculum.full: incernĭcŭlum, i, n. incerno, a sieve, searce, Cato, R. R. 13, 1; Lucil. ap. Non. 88, 26.— As a lit. transl. of the Gr. τηλία, a square stand on which the Greek flourdealers set out flour, etc., for sale, Plin. 8, 44, 69, § 175.

incerno.full: in-cerno, ĕre, v. a., to sift upon a thing, to cover or bestrew with sifting; to sift, scatter with a sieve: terram cribro, Cato, R. R. 48, 2; Col. 5, 6, 6: super fricaturam incernatur marmor, Vitr. 7, 1: incretum ( = per incerniculum sive cribrum inspersum), sifted in, Hor. S. 2, 4, 75 Orell. (but in Plin. 37, 6, 23, § 87, the correct read. is redimitum; v. Sillig. ad h. l.).

incero.full: in-cēro, no perf., ātum, 1, v. a. incero, to smear or cover over with wax: canaliculum, Cels. 8, 8, § 1. — Poet.: genua deorum, i. e. to smear the knees of the gods by constant embraces and kisses; to be persistent in prayers, Juv. 10, 55 (cf. Prud. cont. Symm. 1, 203; others explain, to attach waxen tablets, containing written prayers, to the knees of the statues of gods; cf.: tacitas preces in templo deis allegasti, App. Mag. 54, p. 309); so, genua Dianae, Prud. Apoth. 457: lapides (religio),

incerto2.full: incerto, āre, v. a. incertus, to render doubtful or uncertain (ante- and postclass.): longa dies meum incertat animum, Plaut. Ep. 4, 1, 18: prospectum (cursus), App. M. 11, p. 265: singultu lacrimoso sermonem incertans, making indistinct, inaudible, id. ib. 5, p. 164: me incertat dictio, Pac. ap. Non. 123, 30 (Trag. Rel. p. 79 Rib.).

incertum.full: incertum, i, n., v. incertus, II. 2.

incertus.full: incertus, a, um (archaic gen. plur. incertūm, Pac. ap. Non. 495, 27), adj. 2. incertus; hence, acc. to certus. Object., of things whose (external or internal) qualities are not firmly established, uncertain, unsettled, doubtful, untrustworthy, not fast, not firm (class.): amicus certus in re incerta cernitur, Enn. ap. Cic. Lael. 17, 64 (Trag. v. 428 Vahl.); cf. id. ap. Non. 166, 22 (Trag. v. 12 Vahl.): incerti socii an hostes essent, Liv. 30, 35, 9: incertus (infans) masculus an femina esset, id

incessabilis.full: incessābĭlis, e, adj. 2. in-cesso, unceasing, incessant (post-class.): labor, Mart. Cap. 1, 14; Cael. Aur. Tard. 4, 6.—Adv.: in-cessābĭlĭter, incessantly, Mart. Cap. 9, 303; Hier. Ep. 64.

incessans.full: incessans, antis, adj. 2. in-cessans, incessant (post-class.): virtus, Cassiod. Complex. Act. Apost. 11.— Adv.: incessan-ter, incessantly: inhaerere, Cod. Just. 11, 42, 10 fin.: legebat auctores antiquos, Sid. Ep. 8, 11 med.

incesso.full: incesso, cessīvi (less freq. cessi. Tac H. 2, 23; 3, 77; Luc. 5, 680), 3, v. a. incedo, to fall upon, assault, assail, attack (perh. not ante-Aug.). Lit.: quae (pars corporis) cum jaculis saxisque incesseretur, Liv. 8, 24, 15: vagos suos pro hostibus lapidibus incessebant, id. 26, 10, 7; cf.: infestis digitis ora et oculos, Suet. Calig. 25; id. Claud. 8: feras argenteis vasis incessivere tum primum noxii, Plin. 33, 3, 16, § 53: telorum lapidumque jactu, Ov. M. 13, 566: a pueris ii more quodam ge

incessus.full: incessus, ūs, m. incedo, a going, walking, pace, gait. Lit. In gen. (class.): status, incessus, sessio, accubitio, vultus, oculi, manuum motus teneant illud decorum, Cic. Off. 1, 35, 128; cf. id. Or. 18, 59: citus modo, modo tardus, Sall. C. 15, 8: fractus, effeminate, unmanly, Quint. 5, 9, 14; cf.: in incessu mollior, Ov. A. A. 3, 306: incessus Seplasia dignus, Cic. Pis. 11, 24: erectus, Tac. H. 1, 53: omnibus animalibus certus et uniusmodi incessus est, Plin. 10, 38, 54, § 111: vera incessu pa

incestificus.full: incestĭfĭcus, a, um, adj. incestusfacio, that defiles himself, that commits a bad action: nefandus, incestificus, exsecrabilis, Sen. Phoen. 223.

incesto.full: incesto, āvi, 1, v. a. incestus, to pollute, defile (poet. and in post-Aug. prose). In gen.: totamque incestat funere classem, Verg. A. 6, 150: aras, Stat. S. 5, 5, 4: diem (Furiae), id. Th. 11, 120; Claud. Cons. Mall. Theod. 267.— In partic., to dishonor, defile with lust: puellam, Plaut. Poen. 5, 2, 136: filiam, Tac. A. 6, 19: se, Suet. Tib. 43: thalamos novercae, Verg. A. 10, 389.

incestum.full: incestum, i, v. 1. incestus, II. B.

incestuosus.full: incestŭōsus, a, um, adj. 2. incestus, incestuous, lewd, Hilar. in Psa. 130, 3.

incestus1.full: incestus, a, um, adj. 2. in-castus, unclean (in a moral and religious sense), impure, polluted, defiled, sinful, criminal (as an adj. mostly poet. and in post-Aug. prose). In gen.: cum verborum contumeliis optimum virum incesto ore lacerasset, Cic. Phil. 11, 2, 5: saepe Diespiter Neglectus incesto addidit integrum, punished the good with the bad, Hor. C. 3, 2, 30: catervae Incestarum avium, that feed on corpses, Stat. Th. 9, 27: profana illic omnia, quae apud nos sacra: rursum concessa apud illo

incestus2.full: incestus, ūs, m. 1. incestus, II., unchastity, incest (mostly Ciceron.): quaestio de incestu, Cic. Mil. 22, 59; id. Brut. 32, 122; 124; id. N. D. 3, 30, 74 Klotz; Liv. 4, 44 Weissenb.; Val. Max. 6, 3, 7.

incharaxo.full: in-chăraxo, āre, v. a., to scratch into, to open by scratching (late Lat.): avem, Apic. 6, 5, § 228.

incibo.full: in-cĭbo, āre, v. a., to provide with food, to feed (late Lat.), Schol. Juv. 10, 231.

incicur.full: incĭcur, ŏris, adj. 2. in-cicur, not tame, wild: incicorem immansuetum et ferum. Pacuvius: reprime incicorem iracundiam, Paul. ex Fest. s. h. v. p. 108 Müll.

incido1.full: incĭdo, cĭdi, cāsum, 3 (fut. part. act. incasurus, Plin. 2, 27, 27, § 97; perf. scanned incĭdĕrunt, Lucr. 6, 1174), v. n. in-cado, to fall into or upon a thing, to fall, light upon (freq. and class.). Lit. In gen., constr. with in and acc.; less freq. with other prepp., with the dat., or absol. With in and acc.: in foveam, Cic. Phil. 4, 5, 12: ex spelunca saxum in crura ejus incidit, id. Fat. 3, 6: e nubi in nubem vis incidit ardens fulminis, Lucr. 6, 145; cf. id. 296: in segetem flamma, falls,

incido2.full: incīdo, cīdi, cīsum, 3, v. a. in-caedo, to cut into, cut through, cut open, cut up (class.). Lit.: teneris arboribus incisis atque inflexis, Caes. B. G. 2, 17, 4: arbores, Plin. 12, 14, 30, § 54; 32, § 58: inciditur vitro, lapide, osseisve cultellis, id. 12, 25, 54, § 115; cf.: palmes inciditur in medullam, id. 14, 9, 11, § 84: venam, to open, id. 29, 6, 58, § 126; Cels. 2, 8; Tac. A. 16, 19; cf.: incisi nervi, Plin. 11, 37, 88, § 218: circa vulnus scalpello, Cels. 5, 27, 3: pinnas, to clip, Cic

inciens.full: incĭens, entis, adj. kindr. with ἔγκυος, ἐγκύμων, pregnant, with young: oves, Varr. R. R. 2, 2, 8: pavones, Col. 8, 11, 8: sues, Plin. 11, 37, 84, § 211: partus incientis pecoris, Col. 7, 3, 16.

incilis.full: incīlis, e, adj. contr. from incīdilis, from incido, cut in: fossae, i. e. ditches, trenches for carrying off water, Cato, R. R. 155, 1.— Far more freq., Substt. incīle, is, n., a ditch, trench: incilia aperire, Cato, R. R. 155, 1: ducere incile, Dig. 43, 13, 1; App. M. 9, p. 221: in incili omnia adhaeserunt, Cael. ap. Cic. Fam. 8, 5, 3.— incīlis, is, m., transl.: inciles διώρυγες (i. e. διώρυχες), Gloss. Philox.

incilo.full: incīlo, āre, v. a., to rebuke, blame (anteclass.): jure increpet inciletque, Lucr. 3, 963: me oratione, Pac. ap. Non. 125, 5 (Trag. Fragm. v. 136 Rib.); Lucil. ib. 7: spernere, incilare probris, Att. ib. 1: factum alicujus, id. ib. 3 (Trag. Fragm. v. 41, 430, 458 Rib.).

incinctus.full: incinctus, a, um, Part., from incingo.
incinctus.short: incinctus, a, um, Part., from incingo.

incinefactus.full: incĭnĕfactus, a, um, adj., = in cineres redactus, made ashes, Commod. Instr. 41, 12.
incinefactus.short: incĭnĕfactus, a, um, adj., = in cineres redactus, made ashes, Commod.

incinerarium.full: incĭnĕrārĭum muliebre ministerium (hair - dressing), Charis. p. 78 P. (cf. cinifio).

incingo.full: incingo, xi, ctum, 3, v. a. in-cingo, to enclose with a girdle; hence, to gird, gird about, surround (mostly poet. and in postAug. prose; not used by Cic. in prose; esp. freq. in the part. perf.): (aras) verbenis silvaque incinxit agresti, Ov. M. 7, 242: urbes turritis moenibus, id. Am. 3, 8, 47: incingi zonā, id. H. 9, 66: Arcadiam Peloponnesiacae gentes undique incingunt, Mel. 2, 3: pars sese tortis serpentibus incingebant, Cat. 64, 259.— Mid.: (Tisiphone) Induitur pallam tortoque incingitur a

incingulum.full: incingŭlum, i, n. incingo, a girdle: cingulum a cingendo, quod incingulum plerumque dicitur, Non. 47, 25.

incino.full: incĭno, ĕre, v. a. and n. in-cano, to blow or sound, to sing (very rare; not in Cic.). Act.: varios incinit ore modos, Prop. 2, 22 (3, 15), 6: frequentamenta quaedam varia, Gell. 1, 11, 12.— Neutr.: si modulislenibus tibicen incinat, Gell. 4, 13, 1.

incipio.full: incĭpĭo, cēpi, ceptum, 3 (archaic incepsit inceperit, Paul. ex Fest. p. 107 Müll.), v. a. and n. [in-capio; lit., to seize upon, lay hold of; opp. to desinere; hence, with the accessory idea of action), to begin to do something, to take in hand (syn. incoho; in class. prose, viz. in Cic., only in the tempp. press., while coepi is used in the tempp. perff.); constr. usually with the inf., less freq. absol., with the acc., ab, or adv. of place or time. Act. With inf.: ut homines mortem vel optare
incipio.short: incĭpĭo, cēpi, ceptum, 3 (archaic incepsit inceperit, Paul.

incipisso.full: incĭpisso (also incĭpesso), ĕre, v. a. incipio, to begin (Plautin.): quid hic homo tantum incipissit facere cum tantis minis? Plaut. Capt. 4, 2, 22: nugas ineptiasque maxumas, id. ib. 3, 3, 17: magnam rem, id. Mil. 2, 2, 73: sic rationem, ib. 82: brevem orationem, id. Capt. 2, 1, 19; id. Trin. 4, 2, 42.

incircum.full: in-circum, prep., round about: quod incircum cum locum aquae frigidae et caldae multae, Varr. L. L. 5, § 25 Müll.; cf. Hand, Turs. ad h. v.
incircum.short: in-circum, prep., round about: quod incircum cum locum aquae frigidae et caldae multae, Varr.

incircumcisus.full: in-circumcīsus, a, um, adj., uncircumcised (eccl. Lat.), Tert. adv. Jud. 2; Prud. Psych. 389.

incircumscriptus.full: in-circumscriptus, a, um, adj., unlimited, infinite (eccl. Lat.): dominus, Prud. Apoth. 863.
incircumscriptus.short: in-circumscriptus, a, um, adj., unlimited, infinite (eccl.

incise.full: incīsē, adv., v. incīdo fin. C. 2.

incisim.full: incīsim, adv. incisus, from 2. incīdo, in short clauses (very rare): haec quidem duo binis pedibus incisim; deinde membratim, etc. (shortly before: incise membratimve), Cic. Or. 63, 213: incisim et membratim tractata oratio, id. ib. 67, 225.

incisio.full: incīsĭo, ōnis, f. 2. incīdo. A cutting into, cut, incision: ne incisio vulnus exasperet, Ambros. in Psa. 37, § 42. — Transf. Rhet. t. t, an incision, i. e. a division, member, clause of a sentence, Gr. κόμμα: de eorum (circuituum) particulis et tamquam incisionibus disserendum est, Cic. Or. 61, 206: in incisionibus et in membris, id. ib. 64, 216; cf. incisum under 2. incido fin. C.— Gramm. t. t., a cæsura, Diom. p. 496 P.— A griping, colic: interiorum, Veg. Vet. 1, 39.

incisum.full: incīsum, i, v. 2. incīdo fin. C.

incisura.full: incīsūra, ae, f. 2. incīdo, a cutting into, incision, incisure (post-Aug.). In gen., Col. 12, 54, 1; Plin. 11, 39, 94, § 231. —Plur., Vulg. Lev. 21, 5.— In partic. A natural incision, indentation; as in the palm of the hand, the bodies of insects, in leaves, etc., Plin. 11, 52, 114, § 274; 11, 1, 1, § 1; 15, 11, 11, § 37; 26, 8, 29, § 46.— In painting, a division between the light and shade, Plin. 33, 13, 57, § 163.

incisus1.full: incīsus, a, um, Part., from 2. incīdo.

incisus2.full: incīsus, ūs, m. 2. incīdo, an incision: proximo anno ab incisu, Plin. 16, 12, 23, § 60.

incitabulum.full: incĭtābŭlum, i, n. incito, an incentive, stimulus: ingenii virtutisque, Gell. 15, 2, 3.

incitamentum.full: incĭtāmentum, i, n. id., an incitement, inducement, incentive. In abstr. with gen. or ad: et periculorum et laborum, * Cic. Arch. 10, 23: educandi, Plin. Pan. 27, 1: turbarum, Amm. 21, 12 al.: ad honeste moriendum, Curt. 9, 5, 4; so, ad incessendum, id. 3, 11, 5.— With quo and comp.: inclinatio senatus incitamentum Tiberio fuit quo promptius adversaretur, Tac. A. 2, 38.— In plur.: incitamenta irarum, Tac. A. 1, 55: victoriae, id. Agr. 32: spei, Curt. 4, 14, 1 al.— In concr., of persons (in Tac.)

incitate.full: incĭtātē, adv., v. incito, P. a. fin.

incitatio.full: incĭtātĭo, ōnis, f. incito, an inciting, incitement in an act. and pass. sense (Ciceron.). Act., an inciting, rousing, instigating: languentis populi, Cic. de Or. 2, 9, 35: acris et vehemens, id. ib. 2, 43, 183.— Pass., violent motion, rapidity, vehemence, ardor, energy. Lit.: qui (sol) tanta incitatione fertur, ut, celeritas ejus quanta sit, ne cogitari quidem possit, Cic. Ac. 2, 26, 82: ejaculari incitatione, Scrib. Comp. 84.— Trop.: est quaedam animi incitatio atque alacritas naturaliter inna

incitator.full: incĭtātor, ōris, m. id., an inciter, instigator (post-class.): Fauni vaticinantium incitatores, Front. Eloqu. med.; Prud. στεφ. 10, 67: male sanus, Amm. 28, 1.

incitatrix.full: incĭtātrix, īcis, f. incitator, she that incites or instigates (eccl. Lat.): ad vitia, Arn. 2, 64: libidinum (opulentia), Lact. Ira D. 23: licentiae, Nazar. Pan. ad Const. 34.

incitatus1.full: incĭtātus, a, um, Part. and P. a., from incito.

incitatus2.full: incĭtātus, ūs, m. incito, rapid motion; v. l. for incitu, Plin. 2, 45, 45, § 116.

incitega.full: incĭtēga machinula, in qua constituebatur in convivio vini amphora, de qua subinde deferrentur vina, Paul. ex Fest. p. 107 Müll. [mutilated from ἐγγυθήκη or ἀγγοθήκη; v. Müll. N. cr.].
incitega.short: incĭtēga machinula, in qua constituebatur in convivio vini amphora, de qua subinde deferrentur vina, Paul.

incito.full: in-cĭto, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a., to set in rapid motion, to hasten, urge forwards; and with se, to put one's self in rapid motion, to hasten, rush (freq. and class.). Lit. In gen.: vehementius equos incitare, Caes. B. C. 2, 41, 4: saxa per pronum, Sall. H. 3, 22 Dietsch: hastas, Val. Fl. 1, 409: stellarum motus tum incitantur, tum retardantur, Cic. N. D. 2, 40, 103: naves longas remis, Caes. B. G. 4, 25, 1; cf.: lintres magno sonitu remorum incitatae, id. ib. 7, 60, 4: navigio remis incitato, id. i

incitus1.full: in-cĭtus, a, um, adj., set in rapid motion, rapid, swift, violent (poet.): venti vis, Lucr. 1, 271: inciti atque alacres Delphini, Cic. poët. N. D. 2, 35, 89: hasta, Verg. A. 12, 492: silex, Sil. 1, 491: longis Porticibus conjux fugit, Val. Fl. 1, 728.
incitus1.short: in-cĭtus, a, um, adj., set in rapid motion, rapid, swift, violent (poet.): venti vis, Lucr.

incitus2.full: incĭtus, a, um, adj. 2. in-citus, unmoved; hence, of a chessman that cannot be moved, immovable: (calculi) qui moveri omnino non possunt, incitos dicunt. Unde et egentes homines inciti vocantur, quibus spes ultra procedendi nulla restat, Isid. Orig. 18, 67.—As substt. incĭtae, ārum (sc. calces), f., and incĭta, ōrum, n. Used only in the ante- and post-class. authors in the transf. phrase, ad incita or ad incitas aliquem redigere, deducere, redire, etc., to bring to a stand-still, reduce to extre

incitus3.full: incĭtus, ūs, m. in-cieo, quick motion: adsiduo mundi incitu, Plin. 2, 45, 45, § 116.

incivilis.full: in-cīvīlis, e, adj., unmannerly, impolite, uncivil; hence, also, unreasonable, unjust (post-class.): homo ferus et incivilis ingenii, Eutr. 9, 27: saevi atque inciviles animi, Aur. Vict. Caes. 22: verba, tam improba ac tam incivilia, Gell. 10, 6, 3: poenae, Dig. 48, 19, 9: factum, ib. 50, 13, 3; cf. ib. 23, 2, 67. — Neutr. plur. as subst.: in-cīvīlĭa, ĭum, n., impolite acts, rudeness: multis incivilibus gestis, Eutr. 10, 13. — Adv.: incīvīlĭter, without civility, uncourteously: aliquem tractare,
incivilis.short: in-cīvīlis, e, adj., unmannerly, impolite, uncivil;

incivilitas.full: incīvīlĭtas, ātis, f. incivilis, uncourteousness, incivility (post - class. and very rare): per incivilitatem militis, Amm. 18, 2, 7; 29, 5.

inclamatio.full: inclāmātĭo, ōnis, f. inclamo, a calling out, exclaiming against one (postclass.): imprecationis et comminationis, Tert. adv. Marc. 4, 41.

inclamito.full: inclāmĭto, āre, v. freq. a. id., to call out or exclaim against one; hence, to abuse, scold: inclamitor quasi servus, Plaut. Ep. 5, 2, 46.

inclamo.full: in-clāmo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. and n. To cry out to, to call upon, in a good or bad sense. In a good sense (class.), to call upon for assistance, to invoke. With acc.: comitem suum inclamavit, Cic. Inv. 2, 4, 14: Fulvium Taurea nomine inclamavit, Liv. 26, 15, 11: delphinus inclamatus a puero, Plin. 9, 8, 8, § 25: nomen alicujus, Cael. ap. Quint. 4, 2, 124.— Absol.: ita te para, ut, si inclamaro, advoles, call out, Cic. Att. 2, 18 fin.; cf. id. ib. 2, 20, 5: nemo inclamavit patronorum, id. de Or.

inclango.full: inclango, ĕre, 3, v. n. (late Lat.), Jul. ap. Aug. cont. Sec. VI. 28.

inclaresco.full: in-clāresco, rŭi, 3, v. inch. n. Lit., to become clear or light (late Lat.): ubi primum dies inclaruit, Amm. 25, 1, 1. — Trop., to become famous or celebrated (postAug.): docendi genere maxime inclaruit, Suet. Gramm. 17; cf. ib. 18: neque mea fortuna neque tua gloria inclaruisset, Tac. A. 12, 37; Plin. 35, 11, 40, § 130: in auro caelando, id. 33, 12, 55, § 154: quae artes pluribus inclaruere exemplis, id. 7, 37, 38, § 125.

inclarus.full: in-clārus, a, um, adj., obscure (late Lat. and very rare): fides, Symm. Ep. 3, 4.
inclarus.short: in-clārus, a, um, adj., obscure (late Lat.

inclemens.full: in-clēmens, entis, adj., unmerciful, rigorous, harsh, rough, severe (as an adj. perh. not ante-Aug. and very rare; not in Cicero): increpabant inclementem dictatorem, Liv. 8, 32, 13: signifer, Sil. 8, 440: verbo inclementiori appellari, Liv. 9, 34, 23: inclementissimus, Macr. Somn. Scip. 1, 10.— Adv.: inclēmenter, rigorously, harshly, roughly, severely: in aliquem dicere, Plaut. Am. 2, 2, 110; id. Ps. 1, 1, 25: loqui alicui, id. Poen. 5, 5, 44: increpantes, Liv. 32, 22, 1: nihil dictum, id. 22,
inclemens.short: in-clēmens, entis, adj., unmerciful, rigorous, harsh, rough, severe (as an adj.

inclementia.full: inclēmentĭa, ae, f. inclemens, unmercifulness, rigor, harshness, roughness, severity (poet. and in post-class. prose): divum inclementia, divum, Has evertit opes, Verg. A. 2, 602: durae mortis, id. G. 3, 68: gravis fati, Stat. S. 1, 4, 50: maris, Claud. B. G. 210: caeli, Just. 9, 2: dirae formae (Plutonis), Claud. Rapt. Pros. 1, 82.

inclinabilis.full: inclīnābĭlis, e, adj. inclino, that readily leans to any thing, prone.—Trop.: in pravum inclinabiles animi, Sen. Ep. 94, 40.— Not to be moved or bent (lat. Lat.): atque immobilis permansit, (Hilar.) Anon. in Job, 1, p. 104.

inclinamentum.full: inclīnāmentum, ī, n. id., in gram., the formative termination of a word: inclinamentum hujuscemodi verborum, ut vinosus, mulierosus, numosus, signat copiam quandam immodicam rei, Nigid. ap. Gell. 4, 9, 2.

inclinatio.full: inclīnātĭo, ōnis, f. id., a leaning, bending, inclining to one side (class., esp. in the trop. signif.). Lit. In gen.: (corporis) ingressus, cursus, accubitio, inclinatio, sessio, etc., Cic. N. D. 1, 34, 94: corporis, Quint. 1, 11, 16: fortis ac virilis laterum, id. ib. 18: incumbentis in mulierculam, id. 11, 3, 90: alternā egerunt scobem, Plin. 16, 43, 83, § 227: merso navigio inclinatione lateris unius, id. 8, 51, 77, § 208.— In plur.: variis trepidantium inclinationibus, Tac. H. 2, 35; Plin.

inclinativus.full: inclīnātīvus, a, um, adj. id., in gram., the Greek ἐγκλιτικός, enclitic: conjunctiones, Prisc. p. 1225 P.: pronomina, id. 1062 P.

inclinatus1.full: inclīnātus, a, um, Part. and P. a., from inclino.

inclinatus2.full: inclīnātus, ūs, m. inclino, in gram., the formation or derivation of a word: simili inclinatu, Gell. 3, 12, 3.

inclinis1.full: inclīnis, e, adj. in-clino, bending, bowing (post-Aug. and very rare): cervix, Val. Fl. 4, 307: inclinis atque humilis, Min. Fel. Oct. 3 fin.

inclinis2.full: inclīnis, e, adj. 2. in-clino, unbending, unalterable, Manil. 1, 596.

inclino.full: in-clīno, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. and n. clino, clinatus. Act., to cause to lean, bend, incline, turn a thing in any direction; to bend down, bow a thing. Lit. In gen. (mostly poet. and in post-Aug. prose): vela contrahit malosque inclinat, Liv. 36, 44, 2: genua arenis, Ov. M. 11, 356: (rector maris) omnes Inclinavit aquas ad avarae litora Trojae, id. ib. 11, 209: inclinato in dextrum capite, Quint. 11, 3, 119; id. ib. 69: inclinata utrolibet cervix, id. 1, 11, 9: pollice intus inclinato, id. 11, 3,

inclitus.full: inclĭtus, a, um, v. inclutus init.

includo.full: in-clūdo, si, sum, 3, v. a. claudo, to shut up, shut in, confine, enclose, imprison, keep in (class.).—Constr. with in and abl., in and acc., rarely with the simple abl., dat., or absol. Lit. With in and abl.: habemus senatusconsultum inclusum in tabulis, tamquam in vagina reconditum, Cic. Cat. 1, 2, 4: armatos in cella Concordiae, id. Phil. 3, 12, 31: in uno cubiculo, Cic. Verr. 2, 2, 53, § 133: in curia, id. Att. 6, 1, 6; 6, 2, 8: omne animal in mundo intus, id. Univ. 10: dum sumus inclusi in

inclusio.full: inclūsĭo, ōnis, f. includo, a shutting up, confinement. * Lit.: Bibulum, cujus inclusione contentus non eras, interficere volueras, Cic. Vatin. 10, 24. — * Trop., rhet. t. t., the Gr. ἐπαναδίπλωσις, Rufin. p. 234.

inclusor.full: inclūsor, ōris, m. id., one who encloses, enchases (late Lat.): auri atque gemmarum, setter, Hier. in Jer. 5, 24.

inclusus.full: inclūsus, a, um, Part., from includo.
inclusus.short: inclūsus, a, um, Part., from includo.

inclutus.full: inclŭtus and inclĭtus (not inclytus; the first syll. accented acc. to Cic. Or. 48, 159), a, um, adj. in-clueo; cf. the Gr. κλυτός, from κλύω, much heard of, talked of, praised; hence, celebrated, renowned, famous, illustrious, glorious (syn.: nobilis, clarus; anteclass. and mostly poet.; not in Cæs. nor used by Cic.). Of persons: hic occasus datu'st: at Horatius inclutu' saltu ..., Enn. ap. Fest. p. 178 Müll. (Ann. v. 164 Vahl.): Jovi opulento, incluto, supremo, etc., Plaut. Pers. 2, 3, 1: inclu

incoactus.full: in-cŏactus, a, um, adj., not compelled, voluntary (post-Aug. and rare): omne honestum injussum incoactumque est, Sen. Ep. 66 med. (false read. for incohata, Val. Max. 4, 7).
incoactus.short: in-cŏactus, a, um, adj., not compelled, voluntary (post-Aug.

incoctilis.full: incoctĭlis, e, adj. incoquo. * Cooked in any thing: incoctile ἐνεψημένον, Gloss. Philox.—* Transf., subst.: in-coctĭlĭa, ium, n. (sc. vasa), vessels overlaid or washed with metal, tinned vessels, Plin. 34, 17, 48, § 162.

incoctio.full: incoctĭo, ōnis, f. id., a boiling in any thing, an incoction (late Lat.), Cael. Aur. Tard. 4, 3, 62.

incoctus1.full: incoctus, a, um, Part., from incoquo.
incoctus1.short: incoctus, a, um, Part., from incoquo.

incoctus2.full: incoctus, a, um, adj. 2. in-coquo, uncooked, raw (ante-class. and rare): incoctum non expromet, bene coctum dabit, Plaut. Mil. 2, 2, 53: collyrae facite ut madeant et colyphia: incocta ne mihi detis, id. Pers. 1, 3, 13: caro, Fab. Pict. ap. Gell. 10, 15, 12.—Hence, fig.: incocto pure, the bad humor not worked off, Hier. cont. Luc. 19.

incoenatus.full: incoenatus, incoenis, etc., v. incenatus, incenis, etc.

incoeptum.full: incoeptum and incoepto, v. inceptum and incepto.

incoercitus.full: incoercitus, adj. 2. in-coërceo, unrestrained: incoercitos affectus, Jul. ap. Aug. C. Saec. Jul. 4, 41.

incogitabilis.full: in-cōgĭtābĭlis, e, adj. Act., thoughtless, inconsiderate (ante- and post - class.): nunc demum scio, me fuisse excordem, caecum, incogitabilem, Plaut. Mil. 2, 6, 63; Lact. 1, 8.— Pass., inconceivable, incomprehensible (post-class.): immensitas efficientiae, Mart. Cap. 9, § 922: dementia, Amm. 15, 3: incogitabile est, eandem esse causam, etc., Fragm. Jur. Civ. p. 23 Mai.

incogitans.full: incōgĭtans, antis, adj. 2. in-cogito, thoughtless, inconsiderate (ante- and postclass.): ni fuissem incogitans, Ter. Phorm. 1, 3, 3: adeon' te esse incogitantem atque impudentem, ut? etc., id. ib. 3, 2, 14; Aus. Sap. Periandr. 15.

incogitantia.full: incōgĭtantĭa, ae, f. incogitans, thoughtlessness, inconsiderateness, Plaut. Merc. 1, 1, 27.

incogitatus.full: incōgĭtātus, a, um, adj. 2. in-cogito. Pass., unconsidered, unstudied (postAug.): opus, Sen. Ben. 6, 23 med.: alacritas, id. Ep. 57: incogitata dicere, App. Flor. p. 364 (de Deo. Soc. p. 102 Hild.).— Act., thoughtless, inconsiderate (ante- and postclass.): animus, Plaut. Bacch. 4, 3, 1: ne incogitati dicere cogerentur, Lampr. Alex. Sev. 16.

incogito.full: in-cōgĭto, āre, v. a., to think of, contrive, design ( = intendere, moliri; perh. formed after the Gr. ἐννοεῖν): fraudem socio, Hor. Ep. 2, 1, 122.

incognitus.full: in-cognĭtus, a, um, adj. Not examined, untried: vestra solum legitis, vestra amatis, ceteros causā incognitā condemnatis, Cic. N. D. 2, 29, 73: res, id. Caec. 10, 29.— Not known, unknown (class.; esp. freq. in Cic.): ne incognita pro cognitis habeamus, Cic. Off. 1, 6, 18: insperatum omnibus consilium, incognitum certe, id. Phil. 4, 1, 3: falsa aut incognita res, id. Ac. 1, 12, 45: effata fatidicorum, id. Leg. 2, 8, 20: quae omnia fere Gallis erant incognita, Caes, B. G. 4, 20, 3; so with dat., i

incognoscibilis.full: in-cognoscĭbĭlis, e, adj., incomprehensible, not to be known or discerned: Deus, Hilar. in Psa. 143, 8.
incognoscibilis.short: in-cognoscĭbĭlis, e, adj., incomprehensible, not to be known or discerned: Deus, Hilar.

incognosco.full: in-cognosco, ĕre, 3, v. inch. n., to learn, find out a thing: ut incognosceret, quisnam esset, App. Flor. p. 362, 22 (dub. al. ut inde cognosceret).

incohamenta.full: incŏhāmenta (incho-), ōrum, n. incoho, first principles, rudiments, elements (post-class.), Mart. Cap. 6, § 576: incohamentorum primordia, id. 5, § 437 al.

incohatio.full: incŏhātĭo (incho-), ōnis, f. id., a beginning (late Lat.), Aug. Ep. 120 al.

incohativus.full: incŏhātīvus (incho-), a, um, adj. id., beginning, denoting a beginning, inchoative; in gram.: verba, Charis. p. 223 P.; Diom. p. 333 P.; Prisc. p. 824 P. et saep.

incohator.full: incŏhātor (incho-), ōris, m. id., a beginner (post-class.): mortis (Cain), Prud. Ham. 27 praef.

incohibeo.full: incŏhĭbeo, ēre, false read. in Lncr. 3, 444, inst. of is cohibessit; v. Lachm. ad h. l.

incohibilis.full: incŏhĭbĭlis, e, adj. in-cohibeo, that cannot be held or kept together (post-class.): illo genere oneris tam impedito ac tam incohibili, Gell. 5, 3, 4.— That cannot be restrained: cursus, Amm. 24, 1, 5: ardor, id. 14, 2.

incoho.full: incoho (better than inchŏo, Plaut. Trin. 1, 2, 95; cf. Corss. Ausspr. 1, 109; Cic. Rep. 1, 35 Mai.; 3, 2; Front. p. 154 Rom.; Marin. Fratr. Arv. p. 363; Bramb. p. 291 sq.), āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. and n. for in-coco; from in and Sanscr. root kuk-, to take, grasp. Act., to lay the foundation of a thing, to begin, commence (syn. incipere; opp. absolvere, perficere; class.). In gen. With acc.: ut Phidias potest a primo instituere signum idque perficere, potest ab alio incohatum accipere et absolvere, C

incoinquinabiliter.full: incoinquĭnābĭlĭter, adv. in-coinquinabilis (eccl. Lat.), Aug. de Nat. Boni, 44.

incoinquinatus.full: in-cŏinquĭnātus, a, um, adj., unde filed, unpolluted (late Lat.): corpus, Vulg. Sap. 8, 20: mulier, id. ib. 3, 13; Ambros. Apol. David, 11, 56.
incoinquinatus.short: in-cŏinquĭnātus, a, um, adj., unde filed, unpolluted (late Lat.): corpus, Vulg.

incola.full: incŏla, ae, comm. (f. Phaedr. 1, 6, 6; Prud. Ham. 642) [in-colo], an inhabitant of a place, a resident. Lit.: optati cives, populares, incolae, accolae, advenae omnes, Plaut. Aul. 3, 1, 1: incola est, qui in aliquam regionem domicilium suum contulit, quem Graeci πάροικον appellant, Dig. 50, 16, 239: opp. civis; peregrini autem atque incolae officium est, etc., a foreign resident ( = Gr. μέτοικος), Cic. Off. 1, 34, 125; cf.: Tarquinium, non Romanae modo sed ne Italicae quidem gentis, . . incolam

incolatus.full: incŏlātus, ūs, m. 2. incolo, a resid?*!ing, a dwelling in a place (post-class.), Dig. 50, 1, 34; Cod. Th. 12, 1, 5; 12 al.; Inscr. Orell. 3725.— Transf.: per incolatum Spiritus Sancti, Tert. Res. Carn. 26.

incolo1.full: in-cŏlo, lŭi, 3 (post-class. collat. form incŏlo, āre: paradisum incolare et custodire, Tert. Res. Carn. 26 fin.; whence incolatus), v. a. and n. Lit. (for the simple colere), to cultivate (late Lat.): in his terris, quas incolunt (rusticani), Cod. Th. 13, 1, 3. — Transf., to dwell or abide in a place, to inhabit (class.). Act. (only so in Cic.): jam qui incolunt eas (sc. maritimas) urbes, etc., Cic. Rep. 2, 4: illam urbem, Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 10, § 21; id. Ac. 2, 45, 137: Delum, Cic. Verr. 2, 1, 1

incolorate.full: incŏlōrātē, adv. 2. in-coloratus: without coloring or palliation, i. e., without alleging a cause, Dig. 4, 4, 18.

incolumis.full: in-cŏlŭmis, e (abl. sing. regularly incolumi; incolume, Pomp. and Cic. ap. Charis. p. 108 P.), adj., unimpaired, uninjured, in good condition, still alive, safe, sound, entire, whole (class. and freq.; syn.: salvus, intactus, integer): urbem et cives integros incolumesque servavi, Cic. Cat. 3, 10 fin.: salvum atque incolumem exercitum transducere, Caes. B. C. 2, 32, 12; cf. id. ib. 1, 72, 3; Cic. Fin. 4, 8, 19: ut haec retinere per populum Romanum incolumia ac salva possimus, id. Div. ap. Caccil

incolumitas.full: incŏlŭmĭtas, ātis, f. incolumis, good condition, soundness, safety (class.): incolumitas est salutis tuta atque integra conservatio, Cic. Inv. 2, 56, 169: in incolumitate, id. Post Red. ad Quir. 1, 3: concordi populo et omnia referenti ad incolumitatem et ad libertatem suam, id. Rep. 1, 32; cf.: incolumitatem ac libertatem retinere, id. Inv. 2, 56, 168: deditis pollicebatur, Caes. B. C. 3, 28, 2: mundi, Cic. N. D. 2, 46 fin.— In plur., Cic. Deiot. 14, 40; Arn. 2, 52.

incomis.full: in-cōmis, e, adj., unpleasant: vita, Macr. S. 1, 7 med.—Adv.: incōmĭter, ungracefully, without pleasantry: haud incomiter, Flor. 4, 8, 4.
incomis.short: in-cōmis, e, adj., unpleasant: vita, Macr.

incomitatus.full: in-cŏmĭtātus, a, um, adj., unaccompanied, unattended (rare and mostly poet.; not in Cic., for in de Or. 1, 55, 234, the correct read. is incompta): virginibus in Illyrico incomitatis vagari licet, Varr. R. R. 2, 10, 9: funera, Lucr. 6, 1225: externis virtus incomitata bonis, Ov. P. 2, 3, 35: vestigia ferre, to go without company, alone, Sil. 9, 101.
incomitatus.short: in-cŏmĭtātus, a, um, adj., unaccompanied, unattended (rare and mostly poet.;

incomitem.full: incŏmĭtem sine comite, Paul. ex Fest. p. 107 Müll.; cf. incomitatus.

incomitio.full: in-cŏmĭtĭo, āre, v. a., prob. to insult or reproach in public: incomitiare significat tale convicium facere, pro quo necesse sit in comitium, hoc est in conventum venire. Plautus (Curc. 3, 40): quaeso ne me incomities, Paul. ex Fest. p. 107 Müll.: licetne inforare, si incomitiare hau licet? Plaut. Curc. 3, 1, 31; cf. sqq.

incomium.full: incomĭum, ii, n., one of the ingredients of an ointment, otherwise unknown, Veg. Vet. 6, 28, 18.
incomium.short: incomĭum, ii, n., one of the ingredients of an ointment, otherwise unknown, Veg.

incomma.full: incomma or encomma, ătis, n. ἔγκομμα, an incision, mark; hence, the standard height of soldiers, Veg. Mil. 1, 5; Hier. in. Jovin. 2, 34; cf.: incomma mensura militum, Gloss. Isid.

incommeabilis.full: in-commĕābĭlis, e, adj., not traversable, impassable: via, Amm. 16, 11, 8 (al. difficiles).
incommeabilis.short: in-commĕābĭlis, e, adj., not traversable, impassable: via, Amm.

incommendatus.full: in-commendātus, a, um, adj., unrecommended; poet., given up, abandoned: tellus, sc. ventis, Ov. M. 11, 435.

incomminatus.full: incommĭnātus, a, um, false read. in App. Mag. 10, p. 241, for in comminata.

incomminutus.full: incommĭnūtus, a, um, adj. 2. incomminuo, not broken, entire: ut fundamentum immobilis, tamquam adamas incomminutus, (Hilar.) Anon. in Job, 2, p. 137.

incommiscibilis.full: in-commiscĭbĭlis, e, adj., that cannot be mixed (post-class.): animus, Tert. Anim. 12.
incommiscibilis.short: in-commiscĭbĭlis, e, adj., that cannot be mixed (post-class.): animus, Tert.

incommobilitas.full: in-commōbĭlĭtas, ātis, f., immovableness, insensibility; a transl. of the Gr. ἀοργησία, App. Dogm. Plat. 2, 14, 28.

incommodesticus.full: incommŏdestĭcus, a, um, adj., a comically formed word for incommodus, Plaut. Capt. 1, 1, 19.
incommodesticus.short: incommŏdestĭcus, a, um, adj., a comically formed word for incommodus, Plaut.

incommoditas.full: incommŏdĭtas, ātis, f. incommodus, inconvenience, incommodiousness, unsuitableness; disadvantage, damage, loss, injury (mostly ante- and post-class.; syn.: incommodum, molestia, difficultas): incommoditas denique huc omnis redit (opp. commoditates), Ter. And. 3, 3, 35: in ista incommoditate alienati illius animi et offensi illud inest tamen commodi, quod, etc., * Cic. Att. 1, 17, 7: temporis, unseasonableness, Liv. 10, 11, 3: incommoditate abstinere me apud convivas commodo commemini, impropriet

incommodo.full: incommŏdo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. n. and a. [id.]. Neutr., to occasion inconvenience or trouble to any one, to be inconvenient, troublesome, annoying (rare): alicui, Ter. And. 1, 1, 135: alicui nihil, Cic. Quint. 16, 51; id. Q. Fr. 1, 2, 3, § 10: ipsa scientia, etiam si incommodatura sit, gaudeant, id. Fin. 5, 19, 50; App. Mag. 8, p. 202, 10.— Pass. impers.: obnoxium eum dici, cui quid ab eo, cui esse obnoxius dicitur, incommodari et noceri potest, Gell. 7, 17, 3.— Act., to render inconvenient or trou

incommodus.full: in-commŏdus, a, um, adj., inconvenient, unsuitable, unfit, unseasonable, troublesome, disagreeable. Adj. Of things (class. and freq.): iter, Ter. Hec. 3, 4, 1: res, id. ib. 4, 2, 27: valetudo, Cic. Brut. 34, 130: colloquium pro re nata non incommodum, id. Att. 14, 6, 1: ne voce quidem incommodā, Liv. 3, 14, 6: severitas morum, id. 27, 31, 7: conflictatio turbae, Quint. 3, 8, 29; 1, 7, 16: eorum controversiam non incommodum videtur cum utrorumque ratione exponere, Cic. Inv. 1, 34, 57: naves propu
incommodus.short: in-commŏdus, a, um, adj., inconvenient, unsuitable, unfit, unseasonable, troublesome, disagreeable.

incommote.full: incommōtē, adv. 2. in-commotus, immovably, unchangeably, firmly: permanere, Cod. Just. 1, 1, 7.

incommunicabilis.full: in-commūnĭcābĭlis, e, adj., incommunicable (late Lat.): nomen, Vulg. Sap. 14, 21.
incommunicabilis.short: in-commūnĭcābĭlis, e, adj., incommunicable (late Lat.): nomen, Vulg.

incommunicatus.full: incommūnĭcātus, a, um, adj. incommunico, shared with: alteri, Jul. Val. Rer. Gest. Alex. 1, 13.

incommunis.full: in-commūnis, e, adj., not common (post-class.): incommunes ceteris, Tert. Pall. 3 fin.; Gell. 12, 9, 1.
incommunis.short: in-commūnis, e, adj., not common (post-class.): incommunes ceteris, Tert.

incommutabilis.full: in-commūtābĭlis, e, adj., unchangeable, immutable (rare but class.): omnia verbi principia incommutabilia viderentur (opp. commutabilia), Varr. L. L. 9, § 99 Müll.: status rei publicae, * Cic. Rep. 2, 33, 57: bonum, Aug. Retract. 1, 9.— Adv.: in-commūtābĭlĭter, unchangeably, immutably, Aug. Ep. 3, 3; id. Trin. 7, 1.
incommutabilis.short: in-commūtābĭlis, e, adj., unchangeable, immutable (rare but class.): omnia verbi principia incommutabilia viderentur (opp.

incommutabilitas.full: incommūtābĭlĭtas, ātis, f. incommutabilis, unchangeableness, immutability (late Lat.); with aeternitas, Aug. Conf. 12, 12.

incommutatus.full: incommūtātus, a, um, adj. 2. incommuto, unchangeable (late Lat.), August. de Manich. 11.

incomparabilis.full: in-compărābĭlis, e, adj., that cannot be equalled, incomparable (post-Aug.): sublimitas, Plin. 7, 25, 26, § 94: magister, Quint. 1, 2, 11; freq. in epitaphs: MARITO, CONIVGI, etc., Inscr. Grut. 486, 7; 432, 8.—Comp.: divinitatis gloria, Ambros. de Isaac et An. 8, 78; cf. in sup.: ALVMNO KARISSIMO ET INCOMPARABILISSIMO, Inscr. ap. Fabr. p. 147 no. 183.—Adv.: incompărābĭlĭter, incomparably, Aug. Civ. Dei, 21, 9; id. ap. Hier. Ep. 67, 7.
incomparabilis.short: in-compărābĭlis, e, adj., that cannot be equalled, incomparable (post-Aug.): sublimitas, Plin.

incomparatus.full: incompărātus, a, um, adj. 2. in-, 1. comparo, unequalled, incomparable, for incomparabilis, as an epithet of one deceased: CONIVGI INCOMPARATISSIMO, Inscr. ap. Fabr. p. 421, no. 386.

incompassibilis.full: in-compassĭbĭlis, e, adj., that cannot suffer with another, share another's sufferings (eccl. Lat.): Pater, Tert. ap. Prax. 29.
incompassibilis.short: in-compassĭbĭlis, e, adj., that cannot suffer with another, share another's sufferings (eccl.

incompellabilis.full: incompellābĭlis, e 2. in-, 2. compello, that cannot be named, not to be addressed by name (eccl. Lat.), Rufin. Invect. ap. Hier. 2, 29 fin.

incompertus.full: in-compertus, a, um, adj., of which one has no information, unknown (not anteAug.): inter cetera vetustate incomperta hoc quoque in incerto positum, Liv. 4, 23, 3: ne quid incompertum deferret, id. 10, 40, 10; 9, 26, 15: origo atque natura ejus incomperta est mihi, Plin. 34, 13, 38, § 137: qualis sit ea incompertum habeo, I do not know, id. 12, 8, 16, § 32.
incompertus.short: in-compertus, a, um, adj., of which one has no information, unknown (not anteAug.): inter cetera vetustate incomperta hoc quoque in incerto positum, Liv.

incompetens.full: in-compĕtens, entis, adj., insufficient (late Lat.), Theod. Prisc. 2, 17.—Adv.: in-compĕtenter, insufficiently, Cod. Just. 1, 3, 19; Cassiod. Var. 5, 14.
incompetens.short: in-compĕtens, entis, adj., insufficient (late Lat.), Theod.

incompletus.full: in-complētus, a, um, adj., uncompleted, incomplete (late Lat.): consilia, Firm. Math. 5, 2.
incompletus.short: in-complētus, a, um, adj., uncompleted, incomplete (late Lat.): consilia, Firm.

incompos.full: incompos, ŏtis, adj. 2. in-compos, not having control over (late Lat.): incompotem mentis hominem, [App.] Polem. Physiog. p. 125.

incompositus.full: in-compŏsĭtus, a, um, adj. Not compounded, simple, Ambros. Hexaëm. 1, 7, 25; Boëth. Inst. Arith. 1, 17: trinitas incompositae naturae corrumpi non potest, Ambros. Ep. 81, 8.— Not well put together, not properly arranged, out of order, disordered, disarranged, discomposed (perh. not ante-Aug.). Lit.: agmen, Liv. 5, 28, 7: hostes (opp. compositi), id. 44, 38 fin.: det motus incompositos, Verg. G. 1, 350.— Transf., of style: incomposito dixi pede currere versus Lucili, disordered, irregular, Hor. S

incomprehensibilis.full: incomprĕhensĭbĭlis, e, adj. 2. incomprehendo, that cannot be seized or held, that cannot be grasped (post-Aug.). Lit.: parvitas arenae, Col. 10 praef. § 4: alces incomprehensibili fuga pollet, that cannot be overtaken, Sol. 20.— Neutr. as subst.: constare ex comprehensibili et incomprehensibili, Tert. Ap. 48. — Trop. (The fig. is of a wrestler.) In disputando incomprehensibilis et lubricus, Plin. Ep. 1, 20, 6 Döring.— Of the mind, incomprehensible, inconceivable: vitiosae consuetudinis immensum

incomprehensus.full: in-comprĕhensus, a, um, adj., not comprehended, incomprehensible (post-class.): manet virtus, Prud. Ap. 821. (In Cic. Ac. 2, 29, 95, the correct reading is non comprehensa.)
incomprehensus.short: in-comprĕhensus, a, um, adj., not comprehended, incomprehensible (post-class.): manet virtus, Prud.

incomptus.full: in-comptus (incomt-), a, um, adj., unadorned, inelegant, artless, rude (rare but class.). Lit.: incomptis Curium capillis, Hor. C. 1, 12, 41; so Ov. M. 9, 789; cf. caput, Hor. Epod. 5, 16; and: nuda, nudis incompta capillis, Ov. M. 4, 261.— In Comp.: incomptiore capillo, Suet. Aug. 69: ungues, unpared, untrimmed, Cic. Ac. Fragm. ap. Aug. contr. Acad. 3, 7, IV. 2, p. 471 Orell.: apparatus, Tac. G. 14.— Trop., of speech: ut mulieres esse dicuntur nonnallae inornatae, quas id ipsum deceat: sic haec
incomptus.short: in-comptus (incomt-), a, um, adj., unadorned, inelegant, artless, rude (rare but class.).

inconcessibilis.full: inconcessĭbĭlis, e, adj. 2. in-concedo, inadmissible (post-class.): delicta, Tert. Pud. 9 fin.

inconcessus.full: in-concessus, a, um, adj., not allowed, impossible (not ante-Aug. and rare): hymenaei, unlawful, forbidden, Verg. A. 1, 651; cf. ignes, Ov. M. 10, 153: spes, id. ib. 9, 638: cum totum exprimere paene sit homini inconcessum, Quint. 10, 2, 26.
inconcessus.short: in-concessus, a, um, adj., not allowed, impossible (not ante-Aug.

inconcilio.full: in-concĭlĭo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a., to win over to one's side, to gain over artfully (anteand post-class.). In gen.: inconciliasti, comparasti, commendasti, vel ut antiqui, per dolum decepisti, Paul. ex Fest. p. 107 Müll.: inconciliastin' eum, qui mandatu'st tibi? Plaut. Trin. 1, 2, 99; id. Most. 3, 1, 85: ille quod in se fuit accuratum habuit, quod posset mali faceret in me, inconciliaret copias omnis meas, has done his best to injure me, to win over by trickery all my resources, id. Bacch. 3, 6,

inconcinnitas.full: inconcinnĭtas, ātis, f. inconcinnus, inelegance, awkwardness, impropriety (postAug.): vitatis sententiarum ineptiis atque inconcinnitate, Suet. Aug. 86; App. Dogm. Plat. 2, pp. 14, 21.

inconcinnus.full: in-concinnus, a, um, adj., inelegant, awkward, absurd (rare but class.): qui in aliquo genere inconcinnus aut multus est, is ineptus dicitur, * Cic. de Or. 2, 4, 17: personamque feret non inconcinnus utramque, Hor. Ep. 1, 17, 29: asperitas agrestis et inconcinna gravisque, id. ib. 1, 18, 6.— Adv. in two forms (in both post-class.), awkwardly, absurdly. inconcinnē: causificare, App. M. 10, p. 242, 39.— incon-cinnĭter: vertere in aliquam rem, Gell. 10, 17, 2.
inconcinnus.short: in-concinnus, a, um, adj., inelegant, awkward, absurd (rare but class.): qui in aliquo genere inconcinnus aut multus est, is ineptus dicitur, * Cic.

inconcretus.full: in-concrētus, a, um, adj., bodiless, incorporeal (eccl. Lat.): substantia, Nazar. Pan. Const. 14.
inconcretus.short: in-concrētus, a, um, adj., bodiless, incorporeal (eccl.

inconculcabilis.full: inconculcābĭlis, e, adj. 2 in-conculco, not capable of being trodden under foot (eccl. Lat.), Fulg. Rusp. Incarn. Filii, 50.

inconcussus.full: in-concussus, a, um, adj., unshaken, undisturbed, firm, constant, unchanged (post-Aug.). Lit.: caelestia sidera, Luc. 2, 268; so, vestigia, id. 2, 248.— Trop.: inconcussus ipse et immotus, Plin. Pan. 82, 2; cf.: inconcussus injuriā, Sen. de Ira, 3, 25: certaminibus, Tac. A. 2, 43 fin.: florebant hilares inconcussique Penates, Stat. S. 5, 1, 142: otium, Sen. Ep. 67 fin.: pax, Tac. H. 2, 6: gaudium, Sen. Vit. Beat. 3.—Adv.: inconcussē, firmly, resolutely, Cod. Th. 11, 61, 6; Aug. Retract. 1, 11.
inconcussus.short: in-concussus, a, um, adj., unshaken, undisturbed, firm, constant, unchanged (post-Aug.).

incondemnatus.full: in-condemnātus, a, um, adj., uncondemned, Cato ap. Gell. 13, 24, 12.
incondemnatus.short: in-condemnātus, a, um, adj., uncondemned, Cato ap.

incondite.full: incondĭtē, adv., see the foll. art. fin.

inconditus.full: incondĭtus, a, um, adj. (Acc. to condo, I.) Not made, uncreated (post-class.): ne quid innatum et inconditum praeter solum deum crederemus, Tert. adv. Hermog. 18.— (Acc. to condo, II.) Not stored up: fructus, Col. 1, 5, 6; 3, 2, 1.— Without order, irregular, disordered, confused, unformed, uncouth, rude (the class. signif. of the word): inconditum non ordinate compositum, Paul. ex Fest. p. 107 Müll.: acies, with inordinata, Liv. 44, 39, 1; so, agmen, Tac. A. 2, 12: ordo ramorum, Plin. 16, 30, 53

inconexio.full: in-cōnexĭo (-conn-), ōnis, f., rhet. t. t., = ἀσύνδετον, the omission of a copulative particle, asyndeton, Jul. Ruf. de Schem. Lex. 20.

inconexus.full: in-cōnexus (inconn-), a, um, adj., not joined together, disconnected (late Lat.): res, Aus. Edyll. ad Paul. 12.— Transf., gram. t. t., = ἀσυνάρτητος, of metrical construction, loose, disjointed, said of verses in which various forms of rhythm succeed one another, Mar. Vict. de Metr. p. 2534 P.; p. 2550 P.
inconexus.short: in-cōnexus (inconn-), a, um, adj., not joined together, disconnected (late Lat.): res, Aus.

inconfectus.full: in-confectus, a, um, adj., not wrought out, undigested (late Lat.), Hier. Ep. 119, no. 1; Cels. 4, 16 (dub.).
inconfectus.short: in-confectus, a, um, adj., not wrought out, undigested (late Lat.), Hier.

inconfusibilis.full: inconfūsĭbĭlis, e, adj. 2. in-confusus, that cannot be embarrassed or confused (late Lat.): operarius, Vulg. 2 Tim. 2, 15.— Adv.: inconfūsĭbĭlĭter, without confusion: misceri, Claud. Mam. Stat. An. 1, 15.

inconfusus.full: inconfūsus, a, um, adj. id., unconfused (post-Aug.). Lit.: ut inconfusus eat (mundus), Sen. Q. N. 2, 45: recursus, Claud. VI. Cons. Hon. 622.— Trop., unembarrassed, not disconcerted: animus intrepidus inconfususque, Sen. Q. N. 3 praef. fin.; id. de Ira, 1, 12, 3.

incongelabilis.full: incongĕlābĭlis, e, adj. 2. in-congelo, that cannot be frozen: mare omne, Gell. 17, 8, 16.

incongressibilis.full: incongressĭbĭlis, e, adj. 2. incongredior, unapproachable, inaccessible: Deus, Tert. adv. Marc. 2, 27.

incongruens.full: in-congrŭens, tis, adj., inconsistent, incongruous, unsuitable (post-Aug.): sententia, Plin. Ep. 4, 9, 19: quod est incongruens et absurdum, ut, etc., Lact. 3, 8, 35. —With dat.: Stoica disciplina pleraque est et sibi et nobis incongruens, Gell. 12, 5, 5.— With subject.-clause: incongruens est in labris habere bonitatem, Lact. 3, 16, 4; 12, 17, 6.— Sup., Aug. Don. Persev. 61.— * Adv.: incongrŭenter, unsuitably, Tert. de Baptism. 19.
incongruens.short: in-congrŭens, tis, adj., inconsistent, incongruous, unsuitable (post-Aug.): sententia, Plin.

incongruentia.full: in-congrŭentĭa, ae, f., unsuitableness, incongruity (late Lat.): definitionis, Tert. Anim. 6; id. adv. Marc. 2, 25.
incongruentia.short: in-congrŭentĭa, ae, f., unsuitableness, incongruity (late Lat.): definitionis, Tert.

incongruus.full: in-congrŭus, a, um, adj., inconsistent, incongruous, unsuitable = incongruens, inconveniens (post-class.): quam incongruo ambitu amplectar, Val. Max. 4, 1, 12: inter se propositiones, App. Dogm. Plat. 3; Veg. Mil. 2, 19; Symm. ep. 4, 8.—Adv.: incon-grŭē, unsuitably, Macr. S. 5, 13; Aug. ad Hier. ep. 17.
incongruus.short: in-congrŭus, a, um, adj., inconsistent, incongruous, unsuitable = incongruens, inconveniens (post-class.): quam incongruo ambitu amplectar, Val.

inconivens.full: in-cōnīvens (also inconnīvens), entis, adj. 2. in-conniveo, that does not close the eyes (late Lat.). Lit.: stare solitus Socrates dicitur, Gell. 2, 1, 2.— Trop., of the eye, that does not close, unclosing: justitiae oculus, Amm. 29, 2, 20.

inconjugus.full: in-conjŭgus, a, um, adj.: verba (epithets, etc.), not applicable to ordinary names (e. g. fulminat and tonat can be said of Jupiter only), Prisc. p. 1065 P.
inconjugus.short: in-conjŭgus, a, um, adj.: verba (epithets, etc.), not applicable to ordinary names (e.

inconnivus.full: inconnīvus (better incōnīvus), a, um, adj. 2. in-coniveo, that does not close the eyes, sleepless (Appuleian; cf. inconivens): vigiliae, App. M. 6, p. 179, 5. — Of the eyes, not closing: oculi, App. M. 2, p. 124, 19.

inconscius.full: in-conscĭus, a, um, adj., unaware, unconscious (late Lat.), Cassiod. Var. 10, 4 (but in Liv. 21, 12, 4, the correct reading is insciis).
inconscius.short: in-conscĭus, a, um, adj., unaware, unconscious (late Lat.), Cassiod.

inconscriptus.full: in-conscriptus, a, um, adj., not arranged (late Lat.): incondita, id est inconscripta, Serv. ad Verg. E. 2, 4.
inconscriptus.short: in-conscriptus, a, um, adj., not arranged (late Lat.): incondita, id est inconscripta, Serv.

inconsentaneus.full: in-consentānĕus, a, um, adj., unsuitable, unfit (late Lat.), Mart. Cap. 3, § 228 al.
inconsentaneus.short: in-consentānĕus, a, um, adj., unsuitable, unfit (late Lat.), Mart.

inconsequens.full: in-consĕquens, tis, adj., not logically consequent, inconsequent (post-class.): locutio, Ascon. ad Cic. Verr. 2, 9: per inconsequens, Gell. 14, 1, 10.—Adv.: inconsĕ-quenter, inconsequentially, illogically, Cael. Aur. Acut. 3, 4, 36; 3, 17, 172.
inconsequens.short: in-consĕquens, tis, adj., not logically consequent, inconsequent (post-class.): locutio, Ascon.

inconsequentia.full: inconsĕquentĭa, ae, f. inconsequens, want of logical connection, inconsequence (post-Aug.): rerum foedissima, Quint. 8, 6, 50.

inconsiderans.full: in-consīdĕrans, tis, adj., inconsiderate (late Lat.): inconsiderantissime Marcion, Tert. adv. Marc. 2, 29 fin.—Adv.: in-consīdĕranter, inconsiderately: tutor, qui inconsideranter pupillum abstinuit hereditate, Dig. 26, 10, 3, § 17; Hier. p. 108, n. 20.
inconsiderans.short: in-consīdĕrans, tis, adj., inconsiderate (late Lat.): inconsiderantissime Marcion, Tert.

inconsiderantia.full: inconsīdĕrantĭa, ae, f. inconsiderans, want of reflection, inconsiderateness (= temeritas, incuria): alicujus inconsiderantiam sustinere (where some read considerantiam), Cic. Q. Fr. 3, 9, 2: mirari inconsiderantiam (al. inconsiderationem), Suet. Claud. 39; Salv. Gub. Dei, 1, 11.

inconsideratio.full: inconsīdĕrātĭo, ōnis, f., inconsiderateness (late Lat.): mentis, Salv. de Gub. Dei, 1 extr.; cf. inconsiderantia. — From in-consīdĕrātus, a, um, adj. (class.). Act., thoughtless, heedless, inconsiderate (cf. inconsultus): nos ita leves atque inconsiderati sumus, Cic. Div. 2, 27, 59: quam natura muliebris facit inconsideratam, Auct. Her. 4, 16, 23: inconsideratior in secunda, quam in adversa fortuna, Nep. Con. 5; so in comp., Quint. 2, 15, 28.— Pass., unconsidered, unadvised, inconsiderate: cupid
inconsideratio.short: inconsīdĕrātĭo, ōnis, f., inconsiderateness (late Lat.): mentis, Salv.

inconsilium.full: in-consĭlĭum, ĭi, n., ill-advisedness, thoughtlessness, = ἀβουλία, Gloss. Gr. Lat.
inconsilium.short: in-consĭlĭum, ĭi, n., ill-advisedness, thoughtlessness, = ἀβουλία, Gloss.

inconsitus.full: inconsĭtus, a, um, adj. 2. in-consero, unsown, untilled ( = incultus): ager, Varr. L. L. 5, § 36 Müll.

inconsolabilis.full: inconsōlābĭlis, e, adj. 2. in-consolor, inconsolable, trop. incurable: vulnus, Ov. M. 5, 426: malum, Amm. 29, 2, 14: maeror, Ambros. de Elia. et Jejun. 16, § 60.

inconsonans.full: in-consŏnans, antis, adj., ill-sounding, unsuitable; with incongruum, Pompei. ap. Donat. de Barb. 6. — Adv.: in-consŏnanter, unsuitably; with inconsequenter, Vet. Interpr. Iren. 5, 17.

inconspectus.full: in-conspectus, a, um, adj., indiscreet, imprudent (post-class.): inconspectum aliquid temere dicere, Gell. 17, 21, 1.
inconspectus.short: in-conspectus, a, um, adj., indiscreet, imprudent (post-class.): inconspectum aliquid temere dicere, Gell.

inconspicuus.full: in-conspĭcŭus, a, um, adj., not conspicuous, not remarkable ( = inglorius, ignobilis; post-Aug.): mors, Flor. 4, 2, 67.— Invisible: stella, Mart. Cap. 8, § 838; id. 6, § 593.
inconspicuus.short: in-conspĭcŭus, a, um, adj., not conspicuous, not remarkable ( = inglorius, ignobilis;

inconspretus.full: inconsprētus, a, um, adj. 2. inconsperno, not despised or slighted: non improbatus, Paul. ex Fest. p. 107 Müll.

inconstabilitio.full: inconstābĭlītĭo, ōnis, f., not standing firmly, Vulg. 4 Esdr. 15, 16.
inconstabilitio.short: inconstābĭlītĭo, ōnis, f., not standing firmly, Vulg.

inconstans.full: in-constans, antis, adj., inconstant, changeable, fickle, capricious, inconsistent (class.). Of persons: mihi ridicule es visus esse inconstans, qui eundem et laederes, et laudares, Cic. Rosc. Com. 6, 19: populus in omnibus inconstantissimus, Sen. Ep. 99.— Of inanim. and abstr. things: inconstans est, quod ab eodem de eadem re diverse dicitur, Cic. Inv. 1, 50, 93: litterae, id. Fam. 10, 16: venti, Plin. 18, 35, 80, § 352: medendi arte nulla inconstantior, id. 29, 1, 1, § 2: quid inconstantius De
inconstans.short: in-constans, antis, adj., inconstant, changeable, fickle, capricious, inconsistent (class.).

inconstantia.full: inconstantĭa, ae, f. inconstans, inconstancy, changeableness, fickleness (class.). Of persons: quid est inconstantia, mobilitate, levitate, cum singulis hominibus, tum vero universo senatui turpius? Cic. Phil. 7, 3, 9: levitate implicata, id. Vatin. 1, 3: fama inconstantiae, id. Fam. 1, 9: inconstantiae notam habere, Plin. ap. Trogas, 11, 52, 114, § 276: nemo doctus umquam mutationem consilii inconstantiam dixit esse, Cic. Att. 16, 7, 3; id. N. D. 3, 14.— Of inanim. and abstr. things: fulgoris,

inconstruo.full: inconstrŭo, 3, v. a. in-construo, to build up with (late Lat.), Fulg. Serm. 11.

inconsuetus.full: in-consŭētus, a, um, adj. Unusual (post-Aug.): sermo, Vitr. praef. 5: salsitudo, id. 1, 4.— Unused, unaccustomed; with gen.: opimae mensae, Sil. 11, 282.

inconsulte.full: inconsultē and inconsultō, advv., v. 1. inconsultus fin.

inconsultus1.full: in-consultus, a, um, adj. Not consulted, unasked (so perh. not in Cic.): inconsulto senatu, Liv. 36, 36, 2; so, inconsulto se, Suet. Tib. 52: me inconsulto, Amm. 17, 5, 12; 27, 2 fin.; Ambros. Ep. 6, 43; Plin. Ep. 10, 107, 2; Symm. Ep. 4, 8; 5, 18 al.— Transf., not regarded, not respected: inconsulta potestate superiore, Amm. 27, 2, 9: inconsulta pietate, Cod. Th. 15, 1, 37: inconsulta clementia, ib. 15, 15, 1. — Act. Without advice, not advised (poet.): inconsulti abeunt, sedemque odere Sibylla

inconsultus2.full: inconsultus, ūs, m. 2. in-consulo, the not advising with another (anteclass.; only in the abl. sing.): inconsultu meo, without consulting me, Plaut. Trin. 1, 2, 130.

inconsummatio.full: inconsummātĭo, ōnis, f. 2. in-consummo, incompleteness, imperfection: generationis, Tert. adv. Val. 10.

inconsummatus.full: in-consummātus, a, um, adj., unfinished, incomplete, imperfect (post-class.); with rudis, Amm. 31, 14; with subagrestis, id. 21, 10, 8.— Trop., of persons, uncultivated, not well educated, Ambros. de Fide, 2, 15, § 129.
inconsummatus.short: in-consummātus, a, um, adj., unfinished, incomplete, imperfect (post-class.);

inconsumptibilis.full: inconsumptĭbĭlis, e, adj. in-consumo, not to be consumed, indestructible: perennitas, Cassiod. in Psa. 127, 2.

inconsumptus.full: in-consumptus, a, um, adj., unconsumed, undiminished (Ovidian): pars turis, Ov. M. 7, 592: jecur, id. P. 1, 2, 41: juventa, id. M. 4, 17.
inconsumptus.short: in-consumptus, a, um, adj., unconsumed, undiminished (Ovidian): pars turis, Ov.

inconsutilis.full: inconsūtĭlis, e, adj. 2. in-consuo, not sewed together, without seam: tunica, Vulg. Joh. 19, 23.

inconsutus.full: in-consūtus, a, um, adj., not sewed together, without seam (eccl. Lat.): tunica, Hier. Ep. 22, 19.
inconsutus.short: in-consūtus, a, um, adj., not sewed together, without seam (eccl.
