Lit.: locus tactu indolescit, Cels. 8, 9: oculi indolescunt, Plin. 31, 3, 27, § 45.— With acc., to feel pain at: tactum hominum, Just. 12, 13, 9.— Trop., to feel pain or grief, to be grieved, troubled at any thing.—Constr. with acc. and inf., quod, or absol.; poet. also with abl. and acc. With inf.: quis (fuit), qui non indoluerit, tam sero se ... cognoscere? Cic. Phil. 2, 25: aequari adulescentes senect

indoloria1.full: in-dŏlōrĭa, ae, f. 2. in-dolor, i. q. indolentia (late Lat.; cf. Madv. ad Cic. Fin. 2, 4, 11), absence of pain, Sid. Ep. 14.

indoloris.full: in-dŏlōris, e, adj. 2. in-dolor, free from pain, Gloss. Philox: indoloria medicamenta, i. q. anodyna, Cael. Aur. Tard. 2, 4, 79.

indolorius.full: indŏlōrĭus, a, um, adj. id., painless, Hier. in Eph. 4, 17-19.—Hence, n. plur. as subst.: indŏlōrĭa, = anodyna, anæsthetics, Cael. Aur. Tard. 2, 4, 79; cf. indoloria, ἀνάλγητα, Gloss.

indomabilis.full: in-dŏmābĭlis, e, adj. 2. in-domo, that cannot be broken in or tamed, untamable, Plaut. Cas. 4, 3, 12: tauri, Mythogr. Lat. 2, 136: cervix, Cassiod. Var. 10, 29.

indominabilis.full: in-dŏmĭnābĭlis, e, adj. 2. in-dominus, that cannot be mastered, Gloss. Philox.

indomitabilis.full: indŏmĭtābĭlis, e, adj. indomitus, not to be subdued (eccl. Lat.), Victor Tunon. Poenit. 30.

indomitus.full: in-dŏmĭtus, a, um, adj., untamed, unsubdued, ungoverned, unrestrained; untamable, ungovernable, fierce, wild (class.). Lit.: boves indomitos emere, unbroken, Varr. R. R. 2, 5, 11: equus, Auct. Her. 4, 46, 59; Hor. S. 2, 2, 10; cf.: indomitā cervice feri, id. Ep. 1, 3, 34.— Trop.: pastores indomiti, spe libertatis excitati, Caes. B. C. 1, 57: indomitae et praeferoces nationes, Tac. A. 15, 27: acer et indomitus libertatisque magister, Juv. 2, 77.— Of things concr. and abstr.: oculi, Plaut. Bacch.
indomitus.short: in-dŏmĭtus, a, um, adj., untamed, unsubdued, ungoverned, unrestrained;

indonatus.full: in-dōnātus, a, um, adj., without a present (late Lat.), Lampr. Heliog. 28, 6.
indonatus.short: in-dōnātus, a, um, adj., without a present (late Lat.), Lampr.

indormio.full: in-dormĭo, īvi, ītum, 4, v. n., to sleep or fall asleep at, on, or over a thing; constr. with dat., with in, or with abl. (class. only in the trop. signif.). Lit.: congestis undique saccis Indormis, Hor. S. 1, 1, 71: unctis cubilibus, id. Epod. 5, 69: alienis amplexibus, Petr. 79.— Transf., to be asleep, i. e. to be numb, torpid, of a limb, Veg. Vet. 3, 23, 15; 5, 46, 2. — Trop., to go to sleep over a thing, i. e. to do it negligently, be careless about. With in: in isto homine colendo tam indor

indormis.full: indormis, e, adj. 2. in-dormio, i. q. insomnis, sleepless, Gloss. Philox.

indotatus.full: in-dōtātus, a, um, adj., unportioned, portionless (class. only in the trop. signif.). Lit.: virgo, Ter. Ad. 4, 7, 11; id. Phorm. 1, 2, 70; 5, 7, 45: soror, Hor. Ep. 1, 17, 46.— Transf. (poet.): corpora, that have not received the usual honors paid to the dead, Ov. M. 7, 609.— Trop., unadorned, poor: cujus artem cum indotatam esse et incomptam videres, verborum eam dote locupletasti et ornasti, Cic. de Or. 1, 55, 234.
indotatus.short: in-dōtātus, a, um, adj., unportioned, portionless (class.

indubitabilis.full: in-dŭbĭtābĭlis, e, adj. 2. in-dubito, that cannot be doubted, indubitable (postAug. and post-class.), Quint. 4, 1, 55; 4, 5, 13; Dig. 28, 5, 9, § 8,—Hence, adv.: in-dŭ-bĭtābĭlĭter, indubitably, without doubt, doubtless, Arn. 5, 183.

indubitandus.full: in-dŭbĭtandus, a, um, adj. id., not to be doubted, indubitable (late Lat.): veritas, Aug. Ep. 19, 2.

indubitanter.full: in-dŭbĭtanter, adv. id., indubitably, without doubt (post-class.): probatur, Dig. 37, 11, 2: invictus, Aug. de Vera Relig. 46.

indubitate.full: indŭbĭtātē and indŭbĭtātō, advv., v. indubitatus fin.

indubitatus.full: in-dŭbĭtātus, a, um, adj., undoubted, without doubt, certain, sure (post-Aug.): in iis ero, quae indubitata sunt, brevior, Quint. 9, 4, 2: litterarum inter se conjunctio, id. 1, 1, 31: spes, Plin. 31, 3, 27, § 45: indubitatum est, id. 23, 1, 21, § 36: juris est, Dig. 42, 1, 49.— Comp.: illius aestatis fluxus indubitatior est, Dig. 43, 13, 1, § 8.—Advv.: in-dŭbĭtātē and indŭbĭtātō, undoubtedly. Form indubitate (class.); sup., Oros. 3, 23 fin. (a false read. ap. Liv. 33, 40, 5; Vell. 2, 60, 4).—*
indubitatus.short: in-dŭbĭtātus, a, um, adj., undoubted, without doubt, certain, sure (post-Aug.): in iis ero, quae indubitata sunt, brevior, Quint.

indubito.full: in-dŭbĭto, āvi, ātum, 1, v. n., to doubt of (poet.); with dat.: viribus tuis, Verg. A. 8, 404: tuis moribus, Stat. S. 3, 5, 110.

indubius.full: in-dŭbĭus, a, um, adj., not doubtful, certain (post-Aug.): innocentia plurimorum, Tac. A. 14, 45: exempla, Quint. 5, 13, 24.— Hence, adv.: indŭbĭē, doubtlessly, Cassiod. Fragm. in Auct. Class. Tom. 3, 355 Mai.
indubius.short: in-dŭbĭus, a, um, adj., not doubtful, certain (post-Aug.): innocentia plurimorum, Tac.

induco.full: in-dūco, xi, ctum, 3 (imp. induce for induc, Varr. R. R. 3, 2, 18; induxti for induxisti, Ter. And. 5, 3, 12; induxis for induxeris, Plaut. Capt. 1, 2, 46), v. a. in-duco, to lead, bring, or conduct into a place; to lead or bring in (class.); constr. with in and acc., dat., acc. only, or absol. Lit. With in and acc.: oves et armenta in rura, Varr. R. R. 1, 2, 12: aliquem in viam, id. ib. 3, 2, 18: exercitum in Macedoniam, Liv. 31, 28, 2: cohortem praetoriam in medios hostes, Sall. C. 60, 5: prin

inductibilis.full: inductĭbĭlis, e, adj. induco, that may be drawn or smeared over a thing (late Lat.), Cael. Aur. Acut. 2, 37, 201; 203.

inducticius.full: inductīcĭus or -tĭus, a, um, adj. id., introduced, Gloss. Philox.; Aug. de Duab. Anim. 12, 18.

inductio.full: in-ductĭo, ōnis, f. id., a leading or bringing into, introducing, admission (class.). Lit.: nos aquarum inductionibus terris fecunditatem damus, Cic. N. D. 2, 60, 152: horum (juvenum in circum), introduction, exhibition, Liv. 44, 9, 5; so on the stage: ficta personarum, Cic. de Or. 3, 53, 205: prima trullis frequentetur inductio, a plastering, Pall. 1, 15.—Of a striking out, erasing of writing (cf. induco, 1. C. 3.): lituras, inductiones, superductiones ipse feci, Dig. 28, 4, 1.— Transf., concr.

inductivus.full: inductīvus, a, um, adj. induco, relating to an assumption, Prisc. 1144 P.— Hence, inductīvē, adv., by yielding: indulgere (late Lat.), Cael. Aur. Tard. 1, 5, 157.

inductor.full: inductor, ōris, m. id., one who stirs up or rouses one, a chastiser, scourger: acerrimi, Plaut. As. 3, 2, 6.

inductorium.full: inductōrĭum, i, n. id., a covering: facere inductorium, Plin. Val. 1, 3.

inductorius.full: inductōrĭus, a, um, adj. id., misleading, August. contr. Acad. 1, 4.

inductrix.full: inductrix, īcis, f. id., she that misleads or deceives, App. Flor. 23 fin. al.

inductura.full: inductūra, ae, f. id., a covering, coating (late Lat.), Cael. Aur. Acut. 3, 17, 148.

inductus1.full: inductus, a, um, Part. and P. a., from induco.

inductus2.full: inductus, ūs, m. (only in abl. sing.) [induco], an inducement, persuasion (rare but class.): hujus persuasu et inductu, Cic. Fragm. ap. Quint. 5, 10, 69: inductu alieno facere aliquid, at another's persuasion, Auct. Her. 2, 17, 26.

inducula.full: indūcŭla, ae, f. induo, a kind of under-garment worn by females, Plaut. Ep. 2, 2, 39.

indugredior.full: indu-gredior, v. ingredior and in init.

indulceo.full: in-dulceo, ēre, v. n. in-dulcis, to become very sweet, Gloss. Philox.

indulcitas.full: in-dulcĭtas, false read. for dulcitas, Caecil. ap. Non. 96, 29; v. Com. Rel. p. 60 Rib.

indulco.full: in-dulco, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a., to make sweet, to sweeten (late Lat.). Lit.: aquam amaram, Tert. adv. Jud. 13; Vulg. Sirach, 38, 5.— Trop., to speak sweetly, Vulg. Sirach, 12, 15.

indulcoro.full: in-dulcōro, 1, v. a., to make very sweet, Gloss. Philox.

indulgens.full: indulgens tis, Part. and P. a., from indulgeo.

indulgentia.full: indulgentĭa, ae, f. indulgens, indulgence, gentleness, complaisance, tenderness, fondness (class.). Of persons: quid est dignius, in quo omnis nostra diligentia indulgentiaque consumatur? Cic. Verr. 2, 1, 44, § 112: in hujus (matris) sinu indulgentiaque educatus, Tac. Agr. 4: a corporis obsequio indulgentiaque discedere, Cic. Leg. 1, 23, 60; with benevolentia, id. ib. 13, 35: materiam sibi ducis indulgentia quaerit, Juv. 7, 21.—With in and acc.: Caesaris in se, Caes. B. G. 7, 63, 8: ejus nimia i

indulgeo.full: indulgĕo, si, tum, 2, v. n. and a. [etym. dub.; cf. dulcis], to be courteous or complaisant; to be kind, tender, indulgent to; to be pleased with or inclined to, to give one's self up to, yield to, indulge in a thing (as joy or grief); to concede, grant, allow. V. n. (class.); constr. with the dat. In gen.: Aeduorum civitati Caesar praecipue indulserat, Caes. B. G. 1, 10; 7, 40: sic sibi indulsit, ut, etc., indulged himself so, took such liberties, Nep. Lys. 1, 3: indulgebat sibi liberalius, qua

indulgitas.full: indulgĭtas, ātis, f. indulgeo, indulgence, for indulgentia (ante-class.): indulgitate victus, Sisenn. ap. Non. 126, 9: indulgitate liberum, Cael. ap. Serv. ad Verg. G. 2, 345.

indultor.full: indultor, ōris, m. id., a favorer (late Lat.): legis, Tert. adv. Marc. 4, 9.

indultum.full: indultum, i, n. id., indulgence, permission, grace, favor (post-class.): legis, Cod. Th. 4, 15, 1: principis, id. ib. 3, 10, 1.

indultus1.full: indultus, a, um, Part., from indulgeo.
indultus1.short: indultus, a, um, Part., from indulgeo.

indultus2.full: indultus, ūs, m. indulgeo, leave, permission (late Lat.): indultu clementiae tuae scribere, Sid. Ep. 1, 11.

indumentum.full: indūmentum, i, n. induo, a garment (post-class.). Lit.: indumenta induere, Gell. 16, 19, 12: oris, a mask, Bass. ap. Gell. 5, 7.— Transf., a covering, clothing: carnis indumenta, i. e. bodies, Prud. Cath. 9. 99.— Trop.: indumento justitiae velare, Lact. 6, 13, 12.

induo.full: indŭo, ŭi, ūtum, ĕre, v. a. cf. Gr. ἐνδύω, to put on an article of dress or ornament (class.). Lit.: Herculi tunicam, Cic. Tusc. 2, 8, 20: sibi torquem, id. Fin. 2, 22, 73: galeam, Caes. B. G. 2, 21: zmaragdos et sardonychas, Plin. 37, 6, 23, § 85: anulum, Cic. Off. 3, 9, 38: alicui insignia Bacchi, Ov. M. 6, 598.— Pass., with a Gr. acc.: Androgei galeam clipeique insigne decorum Induitur, Verg. A. 2, 392: et eamst (sc. vestem) indutus? Ter. Eun. 4, 4, 40: scalas, to place a ladder on one's shou

indupedio.full: indŭpĕdĭo and indŭpĕdītus, a, um; v. impedio, etc., and in init.

induperans.full: indŭpĕrans, antis, Part.; v. imperans and in init.

indupero.full: indŭpĕro, indŭpĕrātor, etc.; v. impero, etc., and in init.

induratus.full: indūrātus, a, um, Part. and P. a., from induro.

induresco.full: in-dūresco, rŭi, 3, v. inch. n., to become hard, to harden (cf. percallesco; postAug.). Lit.: si vetus condyloma jam induruit, Cels. 6, 18, 8: grana, Col. 2, 20, 2. — Trop.: miles induruerat pro Vitellio, had become unalterably firm in his attachment to Vitellius, Tac. H. 3, 61: in pravum, to become hardened in, Quint. 1, 3, 12.

induro.full: in-dūro, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. and n., to make hard, to harden (poet. and post-Aug.). Act. Lit.: nivem Indurat Boreas, Ov. Tr. 3, 9, 14: sues indurantes attritu arborum costas, Plin. 8, 52, 78, § 212.— Trop., to harden, steel: indurandus est animus, Sen. Ep. 51: adversus omnia, quae accidere possunt, id. ib. 4: frontem, to render shameless, id. Ben. 7, 28.— Neutr., to become hard, harden: quae (creta) si induraverit, Veg. 3, 82, 2.— Hence, indūrā-tus, a, um, P. a., hardened. Lit.: robora indurata

indus1.full: Indus, a, um, adj., = Ἰνδός, of or belonging to India, Indian (as an adj. almost exclusively poet.): ebur, Verg. A. 12, 67: dens, ivory, Cat. 64, 48: belua, i. e. elephas, Ov. Tr. 4, 6, 7: conchae, pearls, Prop. 1, 8, 39 (1, 8 b. 13 M.).—Plur.: Indi, ōrum, the inhabitants of India, Indians, Cic. Div. 2, 46, 96: extremi, Cat. 11, 2; Mela, 1, 2, 3 sq.; 3, 7?*!, 3.—In sing.: Indus, i, m. Trop. An Indian, collect., Verg. G. 2, 172; Ov. A. A. 3, 130.— An elephant's driver, mahout, Liv. 38, 14, 2.— Tr
indus1.short: Indus, a, um, adj., = Ἰνδός, of or belonging to India, Indian (as an adj.

indus2.full: Indus, i, m., = Ἰνδός, the name of two rivers. The Indus, that empties into the Indian Ocean, now Sind, Cic. N. D. 2, 52, 130; Mel. 3, 7; Plin. 6, 20, 23, § 71; Ov. Tr. 5, 3, 24 al.— A river in Caria, Plin. 5, 28, 29, § 103; Liv. 38, 14, 2.
indus2.short: Indus, i, m., = Ἰνδός, the name of two rivers.

indusiarius.full: indūsĭārĭus, ĭi, m. indusium, a maker of women's under-garments, Plaut. Aul. 3, 5, 35; cf.: indusiarii vestiarii, Gloss. Isid.

indusiatus.full: indūsĭātus (in Varr. L. L. 5, § 131, written intusiatus; cf. indusium), a, um, adj. id., that has on an under-garment (ante- and post-class.), Plaut. Ep. 2, 2, 47: pueri, App. M. 2, p. 123; 10, p. 253.

indusio.full: indūsĭo, āre, v. a. id., to clothe (postclass.): aliqua re, Mart. Cap. 1, § 65; 2, § 114.

indusium.full: indūsĭum (in Varr. L. L. 5, § 131, written intusium), ĭi, n. induo, a woman's under - garment, Varr. l. l.: indusium est vestimentum, quod corpori intra plurimas vestes adhaeret, quasi intusium, Non. 539, 32; cf. indusium χιτωνίσκος, Gloss. Philox.

industria1.full: industrĭa, ae, f. industrius, diligence, activity, assiduity, industry: ingenium industriā alitur, Cic. Cael. 19, 45: in agendo, id. de Imp. Pomp. 11, 29: qui in scribendo tantum industriae ponam, spend so much pains on writing, id. Fam. 3, 9, 3: magnā industriā bellum apparavit, Nep. Ages. 3, 2: itineris, assiduity on the journey, Suet. Aug. 8: illi numquam super industriam fortuna fuit, did not surpass his assiduity, Sall. J. 95, 4 al.: qui ipsus se contemnit, in eo est indoles industriae, Pla

industria2.full: Industrĭa, ae, f., a city in Liguria, on the right bank of the Padus, now Monteù di Po, near Chivasso, Plin. 3, 5, 7, § 49; 3, 16, 20, § 122.—Hence, Industrĭ-ensis, e, adj., Tab. Aenea ap. Maff. Mus. Ver. p. 230.
industria2.short: Industrĭa, ae, f., a city in Liguria, on the right bank of the Padus, now Monteù di Po, near Chivasso, Plin.

industriosus.full: industrĭōsus, a, um, adj. industria, very active, diligent, or industrious (postAug.), Cassiod. Var. 8, 33; Sen. Prov. 2 dub.; Val. Max. 3, 4, 2 dub.—Hence, adv.: industrĭōsē, very industriously, Cassiod. Var. 5, 1; Suet. Vit. Juv.— Comp., Fronto ad M. Caes. 4, 3 med.— Sup., Cato ap. Charis. p. 181 P.

industrius.full: industrĭus, a, um, adj. perh. indo for in, and struo; lit. building within, i. e. active within; hence, active, diligent, assiduous, industrious (class.): homo gnavus et industrius, Cic. Verr. 2, 3, 21, § 53: homines vigilantes, sobrii, industrii, id. Cael. 31, 74; id. Att. 8, 11, 13, § 1: vir acer et industrius in rebus gerendis, id. Tusc. 5, 20, 57: industrios ac ignavos pax in aequo tenet, Tac. A. 12, 12: petit aquilas armis industrius, Juv. 8, 52.—Comp.: industrior or industriior (ante-class

indutiae.full: indūtĭae (less correctly -cĭae), ārum, f. for indu-itiae, from indu for in and ire, a going into rest or retirement; cf. Aur. ap. Gell. 1, 25, 17; hence, a cessation of hostilities, a truce, armistice (class.). Lit.: indutiae sunt belli feriae, Varr. ap. Gell. 1, 25, 2; cf. the context: cum triginta dierum essent cum hoste pactae indutiae, Cic. Off. 1, 10, 33: biennii, Liv. 10, 5, 12: indutias facere, Cic. Phil. 8, 7, 20: inire aequis condicionibus, Plin. Pan. 11, 5: petere, Nep. Ages. 2: conser

indutilis.full: indūtĭlis e, adj. induo, that can be inserted or joined in: vomis, Cato, R. R. 135, 2 dub.

indutiomarus.full: Indŭtĭomărus (Induciom-), i, m., a chief of the Treviri, Caes. B. G. 5, 3.
indutiomarus.short: Indŭtĭomărus (Induciom-), i, m., a chief of the Treviri, Caes.

indutor.full: indūtor, tōris, m. induo, a wearer (late Lat.): fabularum sartor aut indutor, Aug. c. Faust. 8.

indutorius.full: indūtōrĭus, a, um, adj. id., that can be put on: pellis, Paul. Sent. 3, 6, § 79.

indutus1.full: indūtus, a, um, Part., from induo.
indutus1.short: indūtus, a, um, Part., from induo.

indutus2.full: indūtus, ūs, m. induo, a putting on (very rare; only indutui and indutibus in use): prius dein quae indutui, tum amictui quae sunt tangam, Varr. L. L. 5, § 131 Müll.; Symm. Ep. 3, 10; Varr. L. L. 10, § 27 Müll.: vestis, quam indutui gerebat, Tac. A. 16, 4: habebat indutui ad corpus tunicam interulam, App. Flor. n. 9, p. 346; id. Mag. p. 310, 23.—Concr., apparel, raiment: indutibus imperatoriae majestatis ornatus, Amm. 30, 7, 4; 24, 2, 5.

induviae.full: indŭvĭae, ārum, f. id., clothes, garments (ante- and post-class.): tuae, Plaut. Men. 1, 3, 9: nudata induviis, Prud. Psych. 578.

induvium.full: indŭvĭum, false reading for inductis, Plin. 13, 4, 7, § 35; v. Sillig ad h. l.
induvium.short: indŭvĭum, false reading for inductis, Plin.

inebrae.full: inebrae, aves, quae in auguriis aliquid fieri prohibent; et prorsus omnia inebra appellantur, quae tardant vel morantur agentem, Paul. ex Fest. p. 109 Müll.
inebrae.short: inebrae, aves, quae in auguriis aliquid fieri prohibent;

inebriatio.full: ĭnēbrĭātĭo, ōnis, f. inebrio, inebriation (late Lat.), Aug. de Civ. Dei, 16, 1.

inebriator.full: ĭnēbrĭātor, ōris, m. inebrio, one who makes drunk (late Lat.), Tert. adv. Marc. 5, 18.

inebrio.full: ĭn-ēbrĭo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a., to make drunk, inebriate (poet. and post-Aug.). Lit.: palma vescentes inebriat, Plin. 12, 22, 47, § 103; id. 14, 1, 3, § 17; Sen. Ep. 83, 27. — Transf., of colors, to saturate' amethystum inebriatur Tyrio, Plin. 9, 41, 65, § 139.— Of plants: inebriatae radices, i. q. nimis irrigatae, Plin. 17, 26, 40, § 247.— Trop.: aurem, to fill full of talk, Juv. 9, 113.

inedax.full: ĭn-ĕdax, ācis, adj., not voracious, that eats little, Gloss. Philox.
inedax.short: ĭn-ĕdax, ācis, adj., not voracious, that eats little, Gloss.

inedia.full: ĭnĕdĭa, ae, f. 2. in-edo, an abstaining from food, fasting (class.): tenebrae oboriuntur, genua inediā succidunt, Plaut. Curc. 2, 3, 30: vigiliis et inedia necatus, Cic. Fin. 5, 27, 82: inediam sustinere, Cels. 1, 3: inediā vitam finire, i. e. to starve one's self to death, Plin. Ep. 3, 7, 1; cf.: inediā mori, Gell. 3, 10, 15.— In plur.: inedias durare, Plin. 11, 54, 118, § 283.

ineditus.full: ĭn-ēdĭtus, a, um, adj., not made known, unknown: cura, Ov. P. 4, 16, 39.
ineditus.short: ĭn-ēdĭtus, a, um, adj., not made known, unknown: cura, Ov.

ineffabilis.full: ĭn-effābĭlis, e, adj., unutterable, unpronounceable (Plinian): nomina, Plin. 5 praef. § 1: verba, id. 28, 2, 4, § 20.— Adv.: ĭneffābĭlĭter, unutterably, ineffably (late Lat.): Deus ineffabiliter artifex, Aug. Enchir. 89.
ineffabilis.short: ĭn-effābĭlis, e, adj., unutterable, unpronounceable (Plinian): nomina, Plin.

ineffabilitas.full: ĭn-effābĭlĭtas, ātis, f. id., unutterableness, ineffableness (late Lat.): visionis, Aug. Ep. 147.

ineffectus.full: ĭneffectus, a, um, adj. 2. in-efficio, not carried out, incomplete, Hier. in Didym. de Spir. Sanc. 5, 8 init.

inefficacia.full: ĭn-effĭcācĭa, ae, f. inefficax, inefficacy (late Lat.): libertatis, Auct. Itin. Alex. M. 94.

inefficax.full: ĭn-effĭcax, ācis, adj., ineffectual, inefficient (post-Aug.). With gen.: vox inefficax verborum, unproductive of, unable to produce, Sen. Ira, 1, 3.— Absol.: ratio, Sen. Ira, 1, 10: dii, id. Ben. 4, 4.— Comp., Plin. 34, 11, 25, § 109: parentes inefficacissimi, i. e. very weak, Inscr. ap. Grut. 415, 10.—Adv.: ĭneffĭcācĭter, ineffectually, in vain, Dig. 49, 8, 2; Cod. Just. 6, 35, 2; Symm. Ep. 6, 53.

ineffigiabilis.full: ĭn-effĭgĭābĭlis, e, adj. 2. in-effigio, that cannot be portrayed or delineated (late Lat.): anima, Tert. Anim. 24.

ineffigiatus.full: ĭn-effĭgĭātus, a, um, adj. id., without form, shapeless (post-class.): fetus (with informis), Gell. 17, 10, 3: anima, Tert. Anim. 9.

ineffrenatus.full: ĭn-effrēnātus, a, um, adj., unbridled, trop. (late Lat.): cupiditates, Mos. et Rom. Leg. Coll. 6, 4.
ineffrenatus.short: ĭn-effrēnātus, a, um, adj., unbridled, trop.

ineffugibilis.full: ĭn-effŭgĭbĭlis, e, adj. 2. in-effugio, unavoidable, inevitable (post-class.): necessitas ultionis, App. de Mundo, p. 75 fin.

ineffusus.full: ĭn-effūsus, false reading for in effusum, App. M. 2, p. 122.
ineffusus.short: ĭn-effūsus, false reading for in effusum, App.

inelaboratus.full: ĭn-ēlăbōrātus, a, um, adj., unlabored, unstudied, trop. (post-Aug.): oratio, Sen. Tranq. 1, 9: deliciae, Cassiod. Var. 8, 31.— Obtained without labor: pabulum, Ambros. ap. Luc. 7, § 124.
inelaboratus.short: ĭn-ēlăbōrātus, a, um, adj., unlabored, unstudied, trop.

inelegans.full: ĭn-ēlĕgans, antis, adj., not choice or elegant; tasteless, inelegant (class.): orationis non inelegans copia, Cic. Brut. 81, 282: deliciae (with illepidae), Cat. 6, 2: odor non inelegans, a not unpleasant odor, Plin. 21, 25, 98, § 169.— Transf., unreasonable, inconsistent (late Lat.): nam inelegans esse visum est ex heredis persona incipere obligationem, Gai. Inst. 3, 100.— Adv.: ĭnēlĕganter, not choicely, tastelessly, inelegantly: scribere, Cic. Brut. 26, 101; Gell. 17, 2, 26: dividere, without
inelegans.short: ĭn-ēlĕgans, antis, adj., not choice or elegant;

inelegantia.full: ĭn-ēlĕgantĭa, ae, f., tastelessness, inelegance; only as law t. t., want of harmony, inconsistency (with the general system of law; cf. Austin, Jurisprud. Lect. XXX. p. 552): inelegantia juris motus, Gai. Inst. 1, 84; 85.

ineloquax.full: ĭn-ēlŏquax, ācis, adj. 2. in-eloquor, unutterable (late Lat.): gemitibus ineloquacibus, Novat. de Trin. 29.

ineloquens.full: ĭn-ēlŏquens, entis, adj. id., ineloquent (eccl. Lat.): indocti et ineloquentes, Lact. Opif. D. 20, 5.

ineloquibilis.full: ĭn-ēlŏquĭbĭlis, e, adj. id., unutterable, ineffable, for ineffabilis (eccl. Lat.): fructus, Lact. 7, 11: praemium, id. 7, 5, 9.

ineluctabilis.full: ĭn-ēluctābĭlis, e, adj., from which one cannot extricate one's self, unavoidable, inevitable (poet. and post-Aug.). Lit.: caenum, Stat. Th. 9, 502.— Trop.: tempus, Verg. A. 2, 324: fatum, id. ib. 8, 334; Vell. 2, 57 fin.
ineluctabilis.short: ĭn-ēluctābĭlis, e, adj., from which one cannot extricate one's self, unavoidable, inevitable (poet.

ineluibilis.full: ĭn-ēlŭĭbĭlis, e, adj. 2. in-eluo, that cannot be washed out, indelible (eccl. Lat.): fucus, Lact. 7, 20, 9: maculae, id. Ira D. 23, § 24.

inemendabilis.full: ĭn-ēmendābĭlis, e, adj., that cannot be amended, incorrigible (post-Aug.): pravitas, Quint. 1, 1, 37: incommoda oris, id. 11, 3, 12: affectus, Sen. Ira, 3, 41.
inemendabilis.short: ĭn-ēmendābĭlis, e, adj., that cannot be amended, incorrigible (post-Aug.): pravitas, Quint.

inemendatus.full: ĭn-ēmendātus, a, um, adj., unamended, incorrect (late Lat.): dum de inemendatis scribuntur inemendatiora, Hier. in Ezech. 40, 5; Serv. Verg. A. 1, 565.
inemendatus.short: ĭn-ēmendātus, a, um, adj., unamended, incorrect (late Lat.): dum de inemendatis scribuntur inemendatiora, Hier.

inemensus.full: ĭn-ēmensus, a, um, adj., unmeasured, Not. Tir. p. 18.
inemensus.short: ĭn-ēmensus, a, um, adj., unmeasured, Not.

inemeribilis.full: ĭnēmĕrĭbĭlis, e, adj. 2. in-emereor, that cannot be merited, cannot be earned (late Lat.), Tert. Res Carn. 18.

inemigrabilis.full: inēmigrābĭlis, e, adj. 2. in-emigro (eccl. Lat.): immobilis et inemigrabilis Deus, not capable of removing, (Hilar.) Anon. in Job, 2, p. 128.

inemorior.full: in-ēmŏrĭor, tuus, 3, v. dep., to die in or at any thing (for the more usual immorior); with dat.: spectaculo, Hor. Epod. 5, 34.

inemptus.full: ĭn-emptus (inemtus), a, um, adj., unbought, unpurchased (poet. and postAug.): dapes, Verg. G. 4, 133; Hor. Epod. 2, 48: consulatus, Tac. H. 2, 60.
inemptus.short: ĭn-emptus (inemtus), a, um, adj., unbought, unpurchased (poet.

inenarrabilis.full: ĭn-ēnarrābĭlis, e, adj., that cannot be related or described, indescribable (mostly post-Aug.): mira quadam et incredibili atque inenarrabili pietate, Vell. 2, 99, 2: labor, Liv. 44, 5, 1: tabes (jecoris), id. 41, 15, 2: natura fluminum, Sen. Q. N. 3, 22: ratio, Quint. 11, 3, 177: habitus, Plin. 8, 7, 7, § 21.
inenarrabilis.short: ĭn-ēnarrābĭlis, e, adj., that cannot be related or described, indescribable (mostly post-Aug.): mira quadam et incredibili atque inenarrabili pietate, Vell.

inenarrativus.full: ĭn-ēnarrātīvus, a, um, adj. 2. inenarro, not adapted for relation, Tert. adv. Val. 27.

inenarratus.full: ĭn-ēnarrātus, a, um, adj., unexplained (late Lat.): quod reliquimus inenarratum, Gell. 12, 6, 1: verba, id. 19, 14, 5.
inenarratus.short: ĭn-ēnarrātus, a, um, adj., unexplained (late Lat.): quod reliquimus inenarratum, Gell.

inenatabilis.full: ĭnēnătābĭlis, e, adj. 2. in-enato, from which one cannot swim out (post-class.): profundum, Tert. Idol. 24.

inenodabilis.full: ĭnēnōdābĭlis, e, adj. 2. in-enodo, that cannot be freed from knots, cannot be unravelled (only in the trop. signif. class.). Lit.: capillus, App. Mag. p. 276, 15.— Trop., that cannot be explained, inexplicable, Att. ap. Non. 15, 10 (Fragm. Trag. v. 75 Rib.): res, Cic. Fat. 9, 18.

inenormis.full: ĭn-ēnormis, e, adj., not irregular, not immoderate (post-class.): proceritas, App. M. 2, p. 115, 22.
inenormis.short: ĭn-ēnormis, e, adj., not irregular, not immoderate (post-class.): proceritas, App.

inenuntiabilis.full: ĭnēnuntĭābĭlis, e, adj. 2. in-enuntio, unspeakable (post-class.): quiddam, Censor. de Die Nat. 19.

ineo.full: ĭn-ĕo, īvi and ĭi, ĭtum, īre (iniri only ap. Vop. Procul. 12, 7; fut. iniet, Sen. Ben. 21, 2), v. a. and n. To go into, to enter a place (class.). Lit. In gen., constr. with acc., or with in and acc. With acc.: illius domum, Cic. Deiot. 3, 8: urbem, Liv. 3, 24, 8: Argolicas acies non ignarus ini (i. e. inii), Stat. Th. 8, 107: convivia, Cic. Rosc. Am. 18, 52: viam, iter, to enter on a journey, id. Mur. 12, 26.—Pass.: nemus nullis illud initur equis, Ov. F. 3, 266: (Hispania) prima Romanis inita
ineo.short: ĭn-ĕo, īvi and ĭi, ĭtum, īre (iniri only ap.

in eopte.full: in eopte eo ipso, Paul. ex Fest. p. 110 Müll.

ineptia.full: ĭneptĭa, ae, f. ineptus, silliness, folly, absurdity (in sing. ante- and post-class.): tua, Ter. Ad. 4, 7, 31; Plaut. Merc. prol. 26. — Plur.: ĭneptĭae, ārum, sillinesses, fooleries, trifles, absurdities (class.): omnium ineptiarum haud scio an ulla sit major, quam, etc., Cic. de Or. 2, 4, 18; id. ib. 124, 111; id. Rosc. Am. 16, 47: paene aniles, id. Tusc. 1, 39, 93: sententiarum, Suet. Aug. 86: hujusmodi ineptiis se immiscere, Mos. et Rom. Leg. Coll. 15, 2, 3.

ineptio.full: ĭneptĭo, īre, v. n. id., to talk or act absurdly, to trifle, play the fool (poet.): ineptis, Ter. Ad. 5, 8, 11; id. Phorm. 2, 3, 73: desinas ineptire, Cat. 8, 1.

ineptiola.full: ĭneptĭŏla, ae, f. dim. ineptiae, an absurdity, folly, Aus. Idyll. 11.

ineptitudo.full: ĭneptĭtūdo, ĭnis, f. ineptus, for ineptia, absurdity: homo ineptitudinis cumulatus, Caecil. ap. Non. 128, 15 (Com. Fragm. v. 61 Rib.).

ineptus.full: ĭneptus, a, um, adj. 2. in-aptus, unsuitable, impertinent, improper, tasteless, senseless, silly, pedantic, absurd, inept, without tact (class.): quem enim nos ineptum vocamus, is mihi videtur ab hoc nomen habere ductum, quod non sit aptus. Idque in sermonis nostri consuetudine perlate patet. Nam qui aut tempus quid postulet, non videt, aut plura loquitur, aut se ostentat, aut eorum quibuscum est, vel dignitatis, vel commodi rationem non habet, aut denique in aliquo genere aut inconcinnus aut mu

inequitabilis.full: ĭn-ĕquĭtābĭlis, e, adj., that cannot be ridden upon, unfit for riding: campi, Curt. 8, 14, 3.
inequitabilis.short: ĭn-ĕquĭtābĭlis, e, adj., that cannot be ridden upon, unfit for riding: campi, Curt.

inequito.full: ĭn-ĕquĭto, āre, v. n. and a., to ride upon or over any thing (post-class.). Lit., with dat.: Sarmatae patentibus campis inequitant, Flor. 4, 12, 20: horrenti fascino, Arn. 4, 7.— Transf., with acc.: Aurora caelum inequitabat, traversed the sky, i. e. the day broke, App. M. 3, p. 129; id. ib. 6, p. 177 fin.—And in mal. part.: vestras matronas, Arn. 4, 131.— Trop.: medicina audet inequitare philosophiae, i. e. to insult, Macr. S. 7, 15, 15: frustra inequitas nobis, Arn. 7, p. 235.

inermat.full: ĭnermat armis spoliat, Paul. ex Fest. p. 110.

inermis.full: ĭn-ermis, e, and in-ermus, a, um (v. Neue, Formenl. 2, p. 88), adj. 2. in-arma, unarmed, without weapons, defenceless. Form inermis. Lit.: si spoliatum, inermem recepisset Antonium, Cic. Fam. 12, 10, 3: inermibus vim facere (opp. arma. tis), id. Caecin. 22, 63; cf. ib. 12; 61, 60 sq.: milites, Caes. B. G. 3, 29: manus peditum inermium, Brut. ap. Cic. Fam. 11, 10, 3: praedas ex agro inermi ac nudo praesidiis agens, Liv. 29, 4, 7; cf. Plin. 5, 9, 10, § 51: frater tendebat inermes infelix palmas, V
inermis.short: ĭn-ermis, e, and in-ermus, a, um (v.

inerrabilis.full: ĭn-errābĭlis, e, adj. 2. in-erro, unerring (post-class.): meatus, App. Dogm. Plat. 1, p. 7, 27: orbis, id. de Mundo, p. 58, 6: computatio, August. Civ. Dei, 21, 8.

inerrans.full: ĭn-errans, tis, adj., not wandering, immovable, fixed; of the fixed stars: stellae eae, quae inerrantes vocantur, Cic. N. D. 2, 21, 54; 3, 20, 51; Lact. 2, 5, 18.
inerrans.short: ĭn-errans, tis, adj., not wandering, immovable, fixed;

inerro.full: ĭn-erro, 1, v. n., to wander or ramble about in a place (poet. and post-Aug.). Lit.: Diana montibus, Plin. Ep. 1, 6, 3; cf.: ignis aedibus, Stat. S. 1, 5, 58.— Trop.: memoria imaginis oculis inerrabat, swam before the eyes, Plin. Ep. 7, 27, 6: quod tibi si versus noster totusve, minusve, vel bene sit notus, summo vel inerret in ore, Tib. 4, 1, 202 (dub.; Müll. inhaereat).— Of those engaged in dancing: decoros ambitus, App. M. 10, p. 253, 19.

iners.full: ĭners, ertis (abl. inerti, Plin. 16, 43, 83, § 227: inerte, Ov. P. 1, 5, 8; 1, 10, 14), adj. 2. in-ars, unskilled in any art or trade, without skill, unskilful (class.): ut perhibetur iners, ars in quo non erit ulla, Lucil. ap. Serv. ad Verg. A. 4, 158: artes, quibus qui carebant, inertes a majoribus nominabantur, Cic. Fin. 2, 34, 115: versus, artless ( = sine arte et gravitate facti), Hor. A. P. 445.—In partic., = iners dicendi, arte dicendi carens: homo non inertissimus, Cic. Div. in Caecil. 2

inersitudo.full: ĭnersĭtūdo, ĭnis, f. iners, for inertia, inactivity, idleness, Gloss. Philox.

inertia.full: ĭnertĭa, ae, f. id., want of art or skill, unskilfulness, ignorance. Lit. (rare but class.): animi (spectantur), quemadmodum affecti sint, virtutibus, vitiis; artibus, inertiis, Cic. Part. 10, 35; Petr. 135, 6. — Transf., in gen., inactivity, idleness, laziness (very freq.): inertia atque torpedo, Cato ap. Gell. 11, 2, 6: id largiamur inertiae nostrae, Cic. de Or. 1, 15, 68: castigare segnitiem hominum atque inertiam, id. ib. 1, 41, 185: laboris, aversion to labor, id. Rosc. Com. 8, 24: operis,

inerticulus.full: ĭnertĭcŭlus, a, um, adj. dim. [id.], inactive, that produces no effect; a term applied to a sort of grape that yields a good but not intoxicating wine, Col. 3, 2, 24; Plin. 14, 2, 4, § 31.

ineruditio.full: ĭn-ērŭdītĭo, ōnis, f., want of learning, Vulg. Eccl. 4, 30; cf.: ineruditio ἀπαιδευσία, Gloss. Philox.
ineruditio.short: ĭn-ērŭdītĭo, ōnis, f., want of learning, Vulg.

ineruditus.full: ĭn-ērŭdītus, a, um, adj., uninstructed, unlearned, illiterate, ignorant, awkward (class.): non ergo Epicurus ineruditus, sed ii indocti, qui, etc., Cic. Fin. 1, 21, 72: ne quis illud tam ineruditum absurdumque respondeat, id. Ac. 2, 43, 132: judex, Quint. 10, 1, 32; cf id. 8 prooem. § 26.— Of abstr. things: voluptates, unrefined, coarse, Quint. 1, 12, 18.—Adv.: ĭnērŭdītē, unlearnedly, ignorantly, awkwardly (post-Aug.): non inerudite ad declamandum ficta materia, Quint. 1, 10, 33.
ineruditus.short: ĭn-ērŭdītus, a, um, adj., uninstructed, unlearned, illiterate, ignorant, awkward (class.): non ergo Epicurus ineruditus, sed ii indocti, qui, etc., Cic.

inerumpibilis.full: ĭnērumpĭbĭlis, e, adj. 2. in-erumpo, not to be torn (late Lat.): tunica Christi, Cassiod. Hist. Eccl. 1, 14.

inescatio.full: ĭnescātĭo, ōnis, f. inesco, an alluring, a satiating, Aug.

inesco.full: ĭn-esco, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. To allure with bait, to entice (syn.: prolecto, illicio; mostly post- Aug.). Lit.: sicut muta animalia cibo inescantur, Petr. 140; cf.: velut inescatam temeritatem ferocioris consulis, Liv. 22, 41, 5.— Trop., to entice, deceive: homines, Ter. Ad. 2, 2, 12: specie parvi beneficii inescamur, Liv. 41, 23, 8: inescandae multitudinis causa, Vell. 2, 13.— To fill with food, to satiate (only in part. perf. and in App.): gravi odore sulphuris inescatus, App. M. 9, p. 228, 22

inesus.full: ĭn-ēsus, a, um, adj., uneaten, Gloss. Philox.
inesus.short: ĭn-ēsus, a, um, adj., uneaten, Gloss.

ineuscheme.full: in-euschēmē, false reading in Plaut. Trin. 3, 1, 24 (ei euscheme, Fleck., Ritschl, Wagner: sane euscheme, Brix).

inevectus.full: ĭn-ēvectus, a, um, adj. in-evehi, borne or mounted upon (poet.): ne quisquam ... Iret inevectus caelum super, Verg. Cul. 339: tendit inevectus radios Hyperionis ardor, id. ib. 100.

inevitabilis.full: ĭn-ēvītābĭlis, e, adj., unavoidable, inevitable (post-Aug.): fulmen, Ov. M. 3, 301: mala, Sen. Q. N. 2, 50: fatum, Curt. 4, 6, 11; cf.: sors fati, id. 10, 1, 14: crimen, Tac. A. 1, 74.—Plur. subst.: ĭnēvītābĭlĭa, Sen. Ep. 30, 6.—Adv.: ĭn-ēvītābĭlĭter, unavoidably, inevitably: nos compellit, Aug. Enchir. 13.
inevitabilis.short: ĭn-ēvītābĭlis, e, adj., unavoidable, inevitable (post-Aug.): fulmen, Ov.

inevolutus.full: ĭn-ēvŏlūtus, a, um, adj., not rolled out, unopened, of book-rolls: liber, Mart. 11, 1, 4.
inevolutus.short: ĭn-ēvŏlūtus, a, um, adj., not rolled out, unopened, of book-rolls: liber, Mart.

inevulsibilis.full: ĭn-ēvulsĭbĭlis, e, adj. 2. in-evulsus, that cannot be torn away, inseparable (eccl. Lat.): membrum Ecclesiae, Aug. contra Don. 3, 10.

in8.full: ĭn-exāmĭnātus, a, um, adj., unexamined (post-class.): mulieres, Mart. Cap. 9, § 895; Firm. 1, 2.
in8.short: ĭn-exāmĭnātus, a, um, adj., unexamined (post-class.): mulieres, Mart.

inexcitabilis.full: ĭn-excĭtābĭlis, e, adj., from which one cannot be aroused: somnus, Sen. Ep. 83, 13.
inexcitabilis.short: ĭn-excĭtābĭlis, e, adj., from which one cannot be aroused: somnus, Sen.

in9.full: ĭn-excītus, a, um, adj., unmoved, quiet, calm: Ausonia atque immobilis ante, Verg. A. 7, 623.
in9.short: ĭn-excītus, a, um, adj., unmoved, quiet, calm: Ausonia atque immobilis ante, Verg.

inexcoctus.full: ĭn-excoctus, a, um, adj., unexhausted (late Lat.): glaeba, Sid. Carm. 7, 380.
inexcoctus.short: ĭn-excoctus, a, um, adj., unexhausted (late Lat.): glaeba, Sid.

inexcogitabilis.full: ĭn-excōgĭtābĭlis, e, adj. 2. in-excogito, inconceivable, incomprehensible (eccl. Lat.), Lact. Inst. 1, 8; Tert. adv. Val. 37.

in10.full: ĭn-excōgĭtātus, a, um, adj., not thought of, not found out, not invented (postAug.): remedium, Plin. 36, 15, 24, § 107 (but not in Suet. Dom. 14, where the correct read. is excogitatus).
in10.short: ĭn-excōgĭtātus, a, um, adj., not thought of, not found out, not invented (postAug.): remedium, Plin.

inexcultus.full: ĭn-excultus, a, um, adj., unadorned; with rudes villae, Gell. 13, 23, 1.

inexcusabilis.full: ĭn-excūsābĭlis, e, adj., that cannot be excused, inexcusable (poet. and post-class.): ne te retrahas, et inexcusabilis absis, Hor. Ep. 1, 18, 58: tempus, Ov. M. 7, 511: onera, that cannot be refused, Dig. 5, 1, 50: necessitas, Cod. Th. 11, 16, 7 al.—Comp., Ambros. de Vocat. Gent. 2, 4.
inexcusabilis.short: ĭn-excūsābĭlis, e, adj., that cannot be excused, inexcusable (poet.

inexcusatus.full: ĭn-excūsātus, a, um, adj., not excused, Ambros. de Jac. et Vit. Beat. 2, 2, 1 init.
inexcusatus.short: ĭn-excūsātus, a, um, adj., not excused, Ambros.

inexcussus.full: ĭnexcussus, a, um, adj. 2. in-excutio, unshaken, not terrified, Verg. Cul. 302.

inexercitatus.full: ĭn-exercĭtātus, a, um, adj. Untrained, unexercised, unpractised, unskilful (class.): rudis et inexercitatus miles, Cic. Tusc. 2, 16, 38; so, miles, Front. Strat. 2, 1, 9: homo non hebes, neque inexercitatus, Cic. de Or. 2, 17, 72: promptus et non inexercitatus ad dicendum, id. Brut. 36, 136: histriones, id. de Sen. 18, 64: copiae, Nep. Eum. 3, 3: eloquentia, Tac. Or. 5.— Unemployed, not busy (rare): homo, Cels. praef. fin.

inexercitus.full: ĭn-exercĭtus, a, um, adj., unemployed, for inexercitatus (post-class.), Macr. S. 7, 8, 1.
inexercitus.short: ĭn-exercĭtus, a, um, adj., unemployed, for inexercitatus (post-class.), Macr.

inexesus.full: ĭn-exēsus, a, um, adj., unconsumed, Min. Fel. Octav. 35, 3.
inexesus.short: ĭn-exēsus, a, um, adj., unconsumed, Min.

inexhaustus.full: ĭn-exhaustus, a, um, adj., unexhausted (poet. and post-Aug.): metalla, Verg. A. 10, 174: urbes, not plundered, Sil. 14, 686: pubertas, not enfeebled, Tac. G. 20; id. H. 5, 7 (but not in Cic. Fin. 3, 2, 7; v. Madv. ad h. l.).

inexoptabilis.full: ĭn-exoptābĭlis, e, adj., not desirable, Not. Tir. p. 106.
inexoptabilis.short: ĭn-exoptābĭlis, e, adj., not desirable, Not.

inexorabilis.full: ĭn-exōrābĭlis, e, adj. That cannot be moved by entreaty, inexorable (class.). Of persons, constr. with in, adversus, contra, or dat. With in and acc.: qui inexorabilis in ceteros esse visus sum, Cic. Sull. 31, 87.— With adversus: adversus te et rem tuam, Liv. 34, 4, 18.— With contra: contra improbos nocentesque, Gell. 14, 4, 3.— With dat.: delictis, Tac. A. 11, 18.— (ε) Absol.: ni me inexorabilem faxis, Pac. ap. Non. 184, 4: judices, Cic. Tusc. 1, 5, 10: Achilles, Hor. A. P. 121.— Of inanim. and

inexorabilitas.full: ĭnexōrābĭlĭtas, ātis, f. inexorabilis, inexorability, Serv. Verg. A. 12, 199.

inexoratus.full: ĭn-exōrātus, a, um, adj., not entreated, not prayed for, unasked (post-class.): beneficia praebere, Arn. 3, 114.
inexoratus.short: ĭn-exōrātus, a, um, adj., not entreated, not prayed for, unasked (post-class.): beneficia praebere, Arn.

inexortus.full: ĭn-exortus, a, um, adj., that has not originated, without a beginning, = ἄναρκτον, Gloss.
inexortus.short: ĭn-exortus, a, um, adj., that has not originated, without a beginning, = ἄναρκτον, Gloss.

inexpedibilis.full: ĭn-expĕdĭbĭlis, e, adj. 2. in-expedio, unavoidable, inevitable (late Lat.): morae, Amm. 31, 13, 15.

inexpeditus.full: ĭn-expĕdītus, a, um, adj., not free. Entangled, confused: sicut pugna inexpeditior in angustiis, ita caedes atrocior fuit, Liv. 24, 16, 3 (al. impeditior).— Not ready, not quick at any thing (postclass.). Of persons: in rebus obeundis, Arn. 7, 247.— Of things, not easy, difficult: inexpeditissimum est traducere, Arn. 5, 182.
inexpeditus.short: ĭn-expĕdītus, a, um, adj., not free.

inexperientia.full: ĭn-expĕrĭentĭa, ae, f., inexperience (late Lat.), Tert. Anim. 20.
inexperientia.short: ĭn-expĕrĭentĭa, ae, f., inexperience (late Lat.), Tert.

inexperrectus.full: ĭn-experrectus, a, um, adj., unawakened: sopitus vinis et inexperrectus, Ov. M. 12, 317.
inexperrectus.short: ĭn-experrectus, a, um, adj., unawakened: sopitus vinis et inexperrectus, Ov.

inexpers.full: ĭn-expers, pertis, adj., unacquainted with, having no share in; with gen.: Bacchi, Avien. Descr. Orb. 920: famae, id. ib. 1391.
inexpers.short: ĭn-expers, pertis, adj., unacquainted with, having no share in;

inexpertus.full: ĭn-expertus, a, um, adj., untried (not in Cic. or Cæs.). Act., that has not made trial of, unacquainted with, inexperienced in, unaccustomed to a thing: qui lascivia inexperti advenerant, Tac. A. 16, 5: exercitus bonis inexpertus atque insuetus, Liv. 23, 18, 10: animus ad contumeliam inexpertus, id. 6, 18, 4: dulcis inexpertis cultura potentis amici: expertus metuit, Hor. Ep. 1, 18, 86.— Pass., that has not been tried, untried, unproved: legiones civili bello inexpertae, Tac. H. 2, 75; 1, 8: fid
inexpertus.short: ĭn-expertus, a, um, adj., untried (not in Cic.

inexpiabilis.full: ĭn-expĭābĭlis, e, adj. 2. in-expio, that cannot be atoned for, inexpiable (class.): religio, Cic. Tusc. 1, 12, 27: scelus, Auct. Har. Resp. 27.— Transf., implacable, irreconcilable, obstinate: bellum, Liv. 4, 35, 8; 41, 24, 7; Quint. 2, 16, 2: odium Romanorum in Hannibalem, Liv. 39, 51, 4 Drak. N. cr.; 2, 17, 2: invidia, Suet. Caes. 78.— Adv.: ĭn-expĭābĭlĭter, inexpiably, irremediably: corruptus, Aug. de Gen. ad Litt. 11, 13.

inexpiatus.full: ĭn-expĭātus, a, um, adj., not atoned for, unexpiated (late Lat.): dedecus, Aug. Ep. ad Dioscor. 56.
inexpiatus.short: ĭn-expĭātus, a, um, adj., not atoned for, unexpiated (late Lat.): dedecus, Aug.

inexplacabilis.full: ĭn-explācābĭlis, e, adj., implacable, irreconcilable: explacabilis, inexplacabilis, Not. Tir. p. 106.
inexplacabilis.short: ĭn-explācābĭlis, e, adj., implacable, irreconcilable: explacabilis, inexplacabilis, Not.

inexplanabilis.full: ĭn-explānābĭlis, e, adj., inexplicable (late Lat.), Mart. Cap. 4, § 329.
inexplanabilis.short: ĭn-explānābĭlis, e, adj., inexplicable (late Lat.), Mart.

inexplanatus.full: ĭn-explānātus, a, um, adj., indistinct, inarticulate (post-Aug.): linguae esse, to speak indistinctly, Plin. 11, 37, 65, § 174.
inexplanatus.short: ĭn-explānātus, a, um, adj., indistinct, inarticulate (post-Aug.): linguae esse, to speak indistinctly, Plin.

inexplebilis.full: ĭn-explēbĭlis, e, adj. 2. in-expleo, that cannot be filled, insatiable (class.). Lit.: inexplebilis potu, Plin. 11, 25, 30, § 88. stomachus, Sen. Ep. 89 fin.; cf.: populi fauces, Cic. Rep. 1, 43, 66.— Trop.: cupiditas, Cic. Tusc. 5, 6, 16: vir inexplebilis virtutis veraeque laudis, Liv. 28, 17, 2: honorum fames, Flor. 3, 21, 6: colloquiorum, Sen. Cons. ad Helv. 15, 1.

in11.full: ĭn-explētus, a, um, adj., not filled, unsatisfied, unsated (poet.). Lit.: alvus, Stat. Th. 2, 518.— Transf.: lumen, Ov. M. 3, 439.— Trop.: questus, Stat. S. 3, 3, 8: amor, id. Th. 6, 703: caedes, id. ib. 667; Hier. in Isai. 13, 47, 2: inexpletus lacrimans (= inexpletum), incessantly, Verg. A. 8, 559.
in11.short: ĭn-explētus, a, um, adj., not filled, unsatisfied, unsated (poet.).

in12.full: ĭn-explĭcābĭlis, e, adj., that cannot be unfolded or loosened, inextricable, intricate (class. only in the trop. signif.). Lit.: vinculum, Curt. 3, 1, 13: error viarum, Plin. 36, 13, 19, § 87: laquei, Quint. 5, 10, 101.— Transf.: viae continuis imbribus, impassable, Liv. 40, 33, 2. — Trop., inexplicable: o rem, inquis, difficilem et inexplicabilem! atqui explicanda est, Cic. Att. 8, 3, 6; 10, 2, 2; 15, 9, 2; id. Ac. 2, 29, 95; 2, 30, 97: facilitas, Liv. 37, 52, 9: ambiguitas, Gell. 14, 2, 3: mul
in12.short: ĭn-explĭcābĭlis, e, adj., that cannot be unfolded or loosened, inextricable, intricate (class.

in13.full: ĭn-explĭcātus, a, um, adj., unexplained (post-class.): partes, Arn. 7, 219.
in13.short: ĭn-explĭcātus, a, um, adj., unexplained (post-class.): partes, Arn.

inexplicitus.full: ĭn-explĭcĭtus, a, um, adj. Not to be unfolded or traced: (anguis) tractus, Prud. Cath. 3, 153.— Unexplained, inexplicit, obscure (poet.): dicta, Stat. Th. 2, 510: Platones, Mart. 9, 48, 1.

inexplorate.full: ĭnexplōrātē and ĭnexplōrātō, advv., v. inexploratus fin.

in14.full: ĭn-explōrātus, a, um, adj., unexplored, not examined, unknown (not in Cic. or Cæs.): vada, Liv. 26, 48, 4; 39, 51, 6; 43, 4, 6: inventio mihi, Plin. 35, 6, 25, § 43.— Advv. ĭn-explōrātē, without examining beforehand: non temere, nec inexplorate, Gell. 5, 19, 5.— ĭn-explō-rātō, without previous examination (a favorite word of Livy): ibi inexplorato profectus, in insidias praecipitatus, Liv. 21, 25, 9; 6, 30, 4; 22, 4, 4; 27, 26, 6.
in14.short: ĭn-explōrātus, a, um, adj., unexplored, not examined, unknown (not in Cic.

inexpugnabilis.full: ĭn-expugnābĭlis, e, adj., that cannot be taken by assault, impregnable, inexpugnable (class.) Lit.: arx, Liv. 2, 7, 6: urbes, id. 5, 6, 9; Vell. 2, 115, 3.— Trop., unconquerable, in assured safety: homo, Cic. Tusc. 5, 14, 41: terra, impenetrable, Plin. 33, 4, 21, § 72: gramen, that cannot be rooted out, Ov. M. 5, 486: pectus Amori, id. ib. 11, 767: finitio verborum, Quint. 7, 3, 18: necessitas dormiendi, Cels. 3, 20.
inexpugnabilis.short: ĭn-expugnābĭlis, e, adj., that cannot be taken by assault, impregnable, inexpugnable (class.) Lit.: arx, Liv.

inexpugnatus.full: ĭn-expugnātus, a, um, adj., unconquered (late Lat.), in a trop. sense: voluntas, Paul. Nol. Ep. ad Vitric. 18, 5.
inexpugnatus.short: ĭn-expugnātus, a, um, adj., unconquered (late Lat.), in a trop.

in15.full: ĭn-expŭtābĭlis, e, adj. 2. in-exputo, incalculable, incomputable: numerus, Col. 9, 4, 6.

inexsaturabilis.full: ĭn-exsătŭrābĭlis (ĭnexătŭr-), e, adj., insatiable (late Lat.): appetitus, Arn. 2, 71.
inexsaturabilis.short: ĭn-exsătŭrābĭlis (ĭnexătŭr-), e, adj., insatiable (late Lat.): appetitus, Arn.

inexsecrabilis.full: ĭn-exsecrābĭlis, e, adj., not execrable, not accursed, Not. Tir. p. 152.
inexsecrabilis.short: ĭn-exsecrābĭlis, e, adj., not execrable, not accursed, Not.

inexsecutio.full: ĭn-exsĕcūtĭo, ōnis, f., pursuit, prosecution: inefficax, Jul. Val. Res Gest. Alex. M. 2, 34.
inexsecutio.short: ĭn-exsĕcūtĭo, ōnis, f., pursuit, prosecution: inefficax, Jul.

inexsolubilis.full: ĭn-exsŏlūbĭlis, e, adj. in-exsolvo, indestructible, Ambros. Ep. 9, 70 al.

inexspectatus.full: ĭn-exspectātus (inexp-), a, um, adj., unexpected (class.). Of persons: in armis Hostis adest, Ov. M. 12, 65.— Of inanim. and abstr. things: quanta vis! quam inexspectata! Cic. Or. 2, 55, 225: nihil insolitum, nihil inexspectatum est, Sen. Ep. 107: aliquid, Quint. 9, 2, 22; id. 8, 3, 74: accidisse, id. 9, 2, 24.

inexquisitus.full: ĭn-exquīsītus, a, um, adj., not to be inquired into, unsearchable (eccl. Lat.): judicia Dei, Hilar. in Psa. 118, 12, 14.
inexquisitus.short: ĭn-exquīsītus, a, um, adj., not to be inquired into, unsearchable (eccl.

in16.full: ĭn-exstinctus (in- ext-), a, um, adj., unextinguished, unextinguishable (Ovidian). Lit.: ignis, Ov. F. 6, 297.— Trop.: fames, unappeasable, Ov. Ib. 6, 428: nomen, imperishable, id. Tr. 5, 14, 36: libido, insatiable, id. F. 1, 413.
in16.short: ĭn-exstinctus (in- ext-), a, um, adj., unextinguished, unextinguishable (Ovidian).

inexstinguibilis.full: ĭn-exstinguĭbĭlis (inext-), e, adj., unextinguishable (ante- and post-class.). Lit.: flamma, Lact. 7, 19: ignis, Vulg. Matt. 3, 12; ib. Marc. 9, 42.— Trop.: mala consuetudo, indelible, Varr. ap. Non. 131, 6.
inexstinguibilis.short: ĭn-exstinguĭbĭlis (inext-), e, adj., unextinguishable (ante- and post-class.).

inexstirpabilis.full: ĭn-exstirpābĭlis (inext-), e, adj. 2. in-exstirpo, that cannot be rooted out: radices, Plin. 15, 20, 22, § 84.

inexsuperabilis.full: ĭn-exsŭpĕrābĭlis (inexup-), e, adj., that cannot be crossed or passed over, insurmountable (a favorite word with Livy). Lit.: Alpes, Liv. 5, 34, 6: ripa, id. 44, 35, 8: serrae, id. 21, 30, 7: manu, Vell. 2, 32, 4; cf. id. 2, 120, 2.—Comp.: inexsuperabilior saltus fuit, Liv. 36, 17, 3.— Trop.: vis fati, unconquerable, invincible, Liv. 8, 7, 8: bonum, unsurpassable, Sen. Ep. 85.—Plur. as subst.: inexsuperabilibus vim afferre, to overcome impossibilities, Liv. 38, 20, 8.
inexsuperabilis.short: ĭn-exsŭpĕrābĭlis (inexup-), e, adj., that cannot be crossed or passed over, insurmountable (a favorite word with Livy).

inexterminabilis.full: ĭn-extermĭnābĭlis, e, adj. 2. in-extermino, that cannot be exterminated, immortal (post-class.): homo, Claud. Mam. Stat. Anim. 2, 10.

inextricabilis.full: ĭn-extrīcābĭlis, e, adj. 2. in-extrico, that cannot be disengaged or disentangled, inextricable (poet. and post-Aug.). Lit.: error (of the mazes of the labyrinth, from which one could not find his way out), Verg. A. 6, 27: cortex, that cannot be disengaged or separated. Plin. 16, 39, 74, § 188: litus, where one cannot disembark, Sil. 4, 584.— Trop.: errores, Lact. 3, 17, 17: Stomachi inextricabilia vitia, incurable, Plin. 20, 21, 86, § 232: perfectio, inexplicable, indescribable, id. 11, 2, 1, §

inextricatus.full: ĭn-extrīcātus, a, um, adj., undeveloped, Gloss. Philox.
inextricatus.short: ĭn-extrīcātus, a, um, adj., undeveloped, Gloss.

infabre.full: in-fā^brē, adv., in an unworkmanlike manner, unskilfully, rudely (opp. affabre; not in Cic. or Cæs.): pestem novā figurā factam, commissam infabre, Pac. ap. Non. 40, 31, and 248, 22 (Trag. Rel. p. 93 Rib.): vasa, non infabre facta, Liv. 36, 40, 12: sculptum, Hor. S. 2, 3, 22.
infabre.short: in-fā^brē, adv., in an unworkmanlike manner, unskilfully, rudely (opp.

infabricatus.full: in-făbrĭcātus, a, um, adj., unwrought, unfashioned (poet. and in late Lat. prose): robora, * Verg. A. 4, 400.— Trop., unfinished, rude: verba, Ennod. Ep. 2, 6: confabulatio, id. ib. 8, 59.
infabricatus.short: in-făbrĭcātus, a, um, adj., unwrought, unfashioned (poet.

infacetiae.full: infăcētĭae (or infĭc-), ārum, f. plur. [infacetus], rude jests, coarse jokes or puns: pleni ruris et infacetiarum Annales Volusi, Cat. 36, 19.

infacetus.full: in-făcētus (infĭc-), a, um, adj., coarse, blunt, rude, unmannerly, not witty, stupid (class.). Of persons: inficetus (homo), Plaut. Truc. 2, 4, 4: Canius nec infacetus, et satis litteratus, Cic. Off. 3, 14, 58: saeclum (with insipiens), Cat. 43, 8.— Of things: non inficetum mendacium, Cic. Cael. 29, 69: dictum, Suet. Gramm. 23; Mart. 5, 78, 30.— Adv.: infăcētē (infĭc-), coarsely, rudely, unwittily, stupidly (not in Cic. or Cæs.): quem haud infacete Pompeius Xerxem togatum vocare assueverat, Vell
infacetus.short: in-făcētus (infĭc-), a, um, adj., coarse, blunt, rude, unmannerly, not witty, stupid (class.).

infactus.full: infactus, for infectus, acc. to the reading of some, in Tert. Apol. 11.

infacundia.full: infācundĭa, ae, f. infacundus, want of eloquence, Gell. 11, 16, 9.

infacundus.full: in-fācundus, a, um, adj., ineloquent (not in Cic. or Cæs.): vir acer, nec infacundus, Liv. 4, 49, 12; Suet. Claud. 40; Gell. 18, 3, 6.— Comp.: infacundior, Liv. 7, 4, 4.
infacundus.short: in-fācundus, a, um, adj., ineloquent (not in Cic.

infaeco.full: in-faeco, āre, v. a. in-faex, to pollute: animam concretione carnis (late Lat.), Tert. Anim. 53 fin.

infallibiliter.full: in-fallĭbĭlĭter, adv. 2. in-fallo, infallibly (late Lat.), Aug. Praedest. Sanct. 15, 2.

infalsatus.full: in-falsātus, a, um, adj., falsified (late Lat.): codices, Aug. contra Faust. 13, 4 fin.
infalsatus.short: in-falsātus, a, um, adj., falsified (late Lat.): codices, Aug.

infamatio.full: infāmātĭo, ōnis, f. infamo, a calumny, defamation (post-class.), Non. p. 263, 8.

infamia.full: infāmĭa, ae, f. (infamis], ill fame, ill report of a person or thing; bad repute, dishonor, disgrace, infamy (class.; cf.: ignominia, opprobrium): hominum immortalis est infamia, Plaut. Pers. 3, 1, 27: in infamiam populo ponere, id. Trin. 3, 3, 11: atque indignitas rei, Caes. B. G. 7, 56: haec res est mihi infamiae, Ter. And. 2, 6, 13: illa indicia senatoria operta dedecore et infamia, Cic. Clu. 22, 61: ignominiam et infamiam ferre, id. Tusc. 4, 20, 45: in summa infamia esse, Ter. Heaut. 2, 3, 1

infamis.full: in-fāmis, e, adj. 2. in-fama, of ill report, ill spoken of, disreputable, notorious, infamous (class.): homines ceteris vitiis atque omni dedecore infames, Cic. Clu. 47, 130: Metellus, infamis auctor deserendae Italiae, Liv. 27, 11, 12: captarum pecuniarum suspicione, id. 42, 45, 8: Valens ob lucra et quaestus infamis, Tac. H. 2, 56: filius, Quint. 9, 2, 79: ut inops infamis ne sim, Plaut. Trin. 3, 2, 63.— Of things: domus infamis et pestilens, Plin. Ep. 7, 27, 5: digitus, the middle finger, bec

infamo.full: in-fāmo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. infamis, to bring into ill repute, to brand with infamy, to disgrace, dishonor, defame (rare but class.). Lit.: ut tua moderatio et gravitas aliorum infamet injuriam, Cic. Fam. 9, 12: Juppiter infamat seque suamque domum, Prop. 3, 11, 28 (4, 10, 28 M.): hunc infamatum, branded, Nep. Alc. 11: infamata dea, ill-famed, ill-renowned, Ov. M. 14, 446: Acheloön, Stat. Th. 7, 416: suspecti testes, quos vitae humilitas infamaverit, Paul. Sent. 5, 15, 1.— Transf., to blame, ac

infandus.full: in-fandus, a, um, adj., unspeakable, unutterable, unheard of, unnatural, shocking, abominable (class.): res crudelis, infanda, Cic. de Or. 2, 79, 322: impurum atque infandum corpus, id. Sest. 55, 117: epulae, i. e. of human flesh, Liv. 23, 5 fin.: dolor, Verg. A. 2, 3: amor, id. ib. 4, 85: labores, id. ib. 1, 597: bellum, id. ib. 7, 583: mors, id. ib. 10, 673: dies, id. ib. 2, 132: Cyclopes, id. ib. 3, 644: stuprum, Liv. 1, 59, 8: caedes, id. 4, 32, 12; 29, 8, 8; Plin. 28, 7, 23, § 77.— In the n
infandus.short: in-fandus, a, um, adj., unspeakable, unutterable, unheard of, unnatural, shocking, abominable (class.): res crudelis, infanda, Cic.

infans.full: in-fans (infas, Momms. Inscr. R. N. 66; 5376; Inscr. Grut. 688, 2), fantis (gen. plur. infantium, but infantum, Plin. Ep. 9, 20, 14), adj. in-for, that cannot speak, without speech, mute, speechless (class.): seu rubra Canicula findet Infantes statuas, Hor. S. 2, 5, 40: filius Croesi, Gell. 5, 9, 1: scribit Herodotus, Croesi filium, cum infans esset, locutum, Cic. Div. 1, 53, 121.— Transf., not capable of speech, not eloquent: infantes et insipientes homines, Cic. Inv. 1, 3, 4.— Comp.: infantior

infantarius.full: infantārĭus, a, um, adj. infans, that has to do with infants (poet. and post-class.). — Only substt. infantārĭa, ae, f., a woman fond of infants, Mart. 4, 88, 3.— infantārĭi, ōrum, m. plur., sacrificers of infants, an epithet applied to the Christians, who were accused of offering up children, Tert. ad Nat. 1, 2.

infantia.full: infantĭa, ae, f. id., inability to speak. Lit.: linguae, Lucr. 5, 1031.— In partic., want of eloquence: infantia ejus, qui rem norit, sed eam explicare dicendo non queat, Cic. de Or. 3, 35, 142: incredibilis accusatorum, id. Att. 4, 16, 8: infantiae in dicendo, Quint. 5, 13, 38. — Transf., infancy, early childhood: quantum in infantia praesumptum est temporis, adulescentiae acquiritur, Quint. 1, 1, 19: prima ab infantia, from earliest infancy, Tac. A. 1, 4: nostra infantia caelum hausit Aventini

infanticida.full: infantĭcīda, ae, m. and f. infans-caedo, a child-murderer, an infanticide (late Lat.), Tert. Apol. 4; id. ad Nat. 1, 15.

infanticidium.full: infantĭcīdĭum, ĭi, n. infanticida, child-murder, infanticide (late Lat.), Tert. Apol. 2.

infantilis.full: infantĭlis, e, adj. infans, of or belonging to infants or little children (post-class.): vestis, Dig. 34, 2, 25: blandimenta, Just. 17, 3, 20: uterus, little, young, App. M. 5, p. 164, 12.— Hence, adv.: infantĭlĭter, like a child, Hier. Orig. in Jer. Hom. 1, p. 750.

infanto.full: infanto, āre, v. a. id., to nourish or feed as an infant (late Lat.), Tert. adv. Marc. 1, 14.

infantula.full: infantŭla, ae, f. dim. id., a little girl (post-class.), App. M. 10, p. 252, 15; Sid. Ep. 7, 2 al.

infantulus.full: infantŭlus, i, m. dim. id., a little infant (post-class.), App. M. 8, p. 207, 39; Nazar. Paneg. Const. 16, 6; Hier.in Isai. 3, 7, 16.

infarcio.full: in-farcĭo (infercio), si, sum and tum, 4, v. a. To stuff into any thing. Lit.: in eas partes largum salem infarcito, Col. 12, 53, 2: crumenis turpe lucrum, Prud. Psych. 459.— Pass.: parietes quos appellant formaceos, inferciuntur verius quam struuntur, Plin. 35, 14, 48, § 169. — Trop.: inferciens verba, Cic. Or. 69, 231; Tert. Anim. 6.— Aliquid aliqua re, to stuff with something: bracteas leviore materiā, Plin. 33, 1, 6, § 25: se cibo, Lact. Most. Pers. 49, 3: crinibus, Tert. Pall. 4: stercoribu
infarcio.short: in-farcĭo (infercio), si, sum and tum, 4, v.

infarsus.full: infarsus and infersus, a, um, Part., from infarcio.
infarsus.short: infarsus and infersus, a, um, Part., from infarcio.

infascinabilis.full: in-fascĭnābĭlis, e, adj. 2. in-fascino, that cannot be bewitched, Gloss. Philox.

infascinate.full: in-fascĭnātē, adv. id., without being bewitched, Gloss. Philox.

infastidibilis.full: in-fastīdĭbĭlis, e, adj., not to be loathed, not repulsive: sedulitas, Cassiod. Inst. Div. Litt. 16.
infastidibilis.short: in-fastīdĭbĭlis, e, adj., not to be loathed, not repulsive: sedulitas, Cassiod.

infastiditus.full: in-fastīdītus, a, um, adj., not loathed, not loathsome (late Lat.): cadaver, Sid. Carm. 16, 124: suggestio, Cassiod. Var. 5, 41.
infastiditus.short: in-fastīdītus, a, um, adj., not loathed, not loathsome (late Lat.): cadaver, Sid.

infatigabilis.full: in-fătīgābĭlis, e, adj., indefatigable (post-Aug.): cursus, Plin. 28, 19, 78, § 257: quiddam est virtus, Sen. Vit. Beat. 7: animus, id. Ep. 66 med.; Lact. 7, 27 fin.; Macr. S. 1, 21, 17.— Adv.: in-fătīgābĭlĭter, indefatigably: gaudere, Aug. Ep. 32 ad Paul.
infatigabilis.short: in-fătīgābĭlis, e, adj., indefatigable (post-Aug.): cursus, Plin.

infatigatus.full: in-fătīgātus, a, um, adj., unwearied (late Lat.): viatrix, Mart. Cap. 6, § 582.
infatigatus.short: in-fătīgātus, a, um, adj., unwearied (late Lat.): viatrix, Mart.

infatigo.full: in-fătīgo, āre, v. a., not to weary, Not. Tir. p. 118.

infatuatio.full: infătŭātĭo, ōnis, f. infatuo, infatuation (late Lat.), Hilar. in Job, 3, p. 219.

infatuo.full: infătŭo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. in-fatuor, to make a fool of, to infatuate (class.): aliquem, Cic. Phil. 3, 9, 22; id. Fl. 20, 47; Sen. Suas. 2 fin.: verbis, Auct. B. Afr. 16, 1: quemque adulatio infatuat, Sen. Ep. 59 med.: hominem, Amm. 15, 8, 2. — Transf., to deprive of taste, make flat: infatuatum sal, Hier. Ep. 2, 6.

infaustus.full: in-faustus, a, um, adj., unfortunate, unpropitious (poet. and post-Aug.): infaustas exurite puppes, Verg. A. 5, 635: nomen, id. ib. 7, 717: auspicium, id. ib. 11, 347: gradus, Ov. M. 3, 36: dies, Tac. H. 2, 91: castra, id. A. 1, 30.—Neutr. subst.: in-faustum, i, n., a misfortune: infausto Atheniensium, Plin. 16, 36, 66, § 169.—Adv.: infaustē, unfortunately (late Lat.), Cassiod. An. 12.
infaustus.short: in-faustus, a, um, adj., unfortunate, unpropitious (poet.

infavorabilis.full: in-făvōrābĭlis, e, adj., unfavorable (post-class.): sententia, Dig. 37, 6, 6.—Adv.: in-făvōrābĭlĭter, unfavorably: respondere, Dig. 50, 2, 2, § 6.
infavorabilis.short: in-făvōrābĭlis, e, adj., unfavorable (post-class.): sententia, Dig.

infectio1.full: infectĭo, ōnis, f. 2. in-factus, a non-performance of a thing, a doing nothing (late Lat.): fortunae (al. effectione), Eum. Pan. ad Const. Caes. 18, 6.

infectio2.full: infectĭo, ōnis, f. inficio, a dyeing (late Lat.): capillorum, Theod. Prisc. 1, 1: purpurae, Ambros. Apol. David, 8, § 45.

infectivus.full: infectīvus, a, um, adj. id., pertaining to dyeing.—Only subst. plur.: infectī-va, ōrum, n., dye-stuffs, dyes, Vitr. 7, 14, 2.

infector.full: infector, ōris, m. id., a dyer (class.): eum infector moratur, Cic. Fam. 2, 16, 7: lanarum, Plin. 20, 7, 25, § 59.— Adj., dyeing: infector ille sucus, Plin. 11, 3, 2, § 8.

infectorius.full: infectōrĭus, a, um, adj. id., that serves for dyeing (late Lat.): alumen, Marc. Emp. 4.—Subst.: infectōrĭum, ĭi, n., a dye-house, Gr. βαφεῖον, Gloss. Philox.

infectrix.full: infectrix, f. id., one that infects (eccl. Lat.), Jul. ap. Aug. c. Sec. Resp. Jul. II. 105.

infectus1.full: infectus, a, um, adj. 2. in-factus. Not made or done, unwrought, unmade, undone, unperformed, unfinished (class.): ubi cognovit, opera quae facta infectaque sient, Cato, R. R. 2, 1: ea, quae sunt facta, infecta refert, Plaut. Am. 3, 2, 3: et id, quod indicatum non sit, pro infecto haberi oportere, Cic. Inv. 2, 27, 80: omnia pro infecto sint, let all be regarded as undone, Liv. 9, 11, 3: infecta pace, without having effected a peace, Ter. Eun. 1, 1, 8; Liv. 37, 1, 6; 32, 37, 5: damnum infectum, a

infectus2.full: infectus, a, um, Part., from inficio.
infectus2.short: infectus, a, um, Part., from inficio.

infectus3.full: infectus, ūs, m. inficio, a dyeing (post-Aug.).—In abl.: lanarum, Plin. 8, 48, 73, § 193.

infecunditas.full: in-fēcundĭtas, ātis, f. infecundus, unfruitfulness (post-Aug.): agrorum, Col. prooem. 1, 1: terrarum, Tac. A. 4, 6: apum, Plin. 11, 16, 16, § 50: bienni, Sall. H. Fragm. 3, 1 Dietsch.

infecundus.full: in-fēcundus, a, um, adj., unfruitful (rare): ager frugum fertilis, arbore infecundus, Sall. J. 17, 5; Verg. G. 2, 48; Ov. Tr. 3, 14, 34.— Comp.: infecundior materia, Col. 2, 4, 7.— * Adv.: infēcundē, unfruitfully, i. e. meagrely, sparingly: infecunde atque jejune laudare, Gell. 19, 3, 2.
infecundus.short: in-fēcundus, a, um, adj., unfruitful (rare): ager frugum fertilis, arbore infecundus, Sall.

infelicitas.full: in-fēlīcĭtas, ātis, f. infelix, ill-luck, misfortune (rare but class.): quid hoc infelicitatis? Ter. Ad. 4, 5, 5: haruspicum, Cic. Div. 2, 29 fin.: gravior, Liv. 40, 55 fin. al.— Plur.: miseriae et infelicitates, calamities, App. Dogm. Plat. 2, p. 17, 37.

infelicito.full: infēlīcĭto (or infēlīco, v. infra), āre, 1, v. a. infelix, to render unhappy, make wretched, plague (ante-class.): di me et te infelicitent, Plaut. Cas. 2, 3, 30 (Ritschl et MSS.; al. infelicent): Hercle illum infelicitent di, id. Merc. 2, 3, 99 (Ritschl; al. infelicent): ut te di omnes infelicitent, Caecil. ap. Non. 126, 26 (but Com. Fragm. v. 114 Rib., infelicent).— Form infelico: di illum infelicent omnes, Plaut. Poen. 2, 1, 1.

infelix.full: in-fēlix, īcis, adj., unfruitful, not fertile: vulgus infelicem arborem eam appellat, quoniam nihil ferat, nec seratur unquam, Plin. 24, 9, 41, § 68; cf. id. 16, 26, 45, § 108; hence, of the gallows, Cic. Rab. Perd. 4, 13; cf. Liv. 1, 26, 6: tellus frugibus, Verg. G. 2, 239; cf. ib. 2, 314: lolium, id. E. 5, 37.— Transf. Unfortunate, unhappy, miserable (class.): crux infelici et aerumnoso comparabatur, Cic. Verr. 2, 5, 62, § 162: homo miserrimus atque infelicissimus, id. Rosc. Am. 41, 119: patri
infelix.short: in-fēlix, īcis, adj., unfruitful, not fertile: vulgus infelicem arborem eam appellat, quoniam nihil ferat, nec seratur unquam, Plin.

infenso.full: infenso, āre, v. a. and n. infensus, to treat in a hostile manner, to ravage, destroy (Tacitean). V. a.: bello Armeniam, Tac. A. 13, 37: pabula, id. ib. 6, 34.— V. n., to act like an enemy, to be hostilely disposed: quasi infensantibus Dis, Tac. A. 13, 41.

infensus.full: infensus, a, um, adj. 2. in-fendo, hostile, inimical, enraged (class.; cf. infestus): infenso atque inimico animo venire, Cic. Verr. 2, 2, 61, § 149.— With dat.: Drances infensus Turno, Verg. A. 11, 122: opes principibus infensae, dangerous, Tac. A. 11, 1. — With in and acc.: infensioribus in se quam in illum judicibus, Liv. 39, 6, 5: infensius servitium, hard, oppressive, Tac. A. 1, 81: valetudo, illness, sickness, id. ib. 14, 56; 4, 48; Suet. Vit. 14; Vop. Aur. 36. — Sup.: infensissima virtus,

infer.full: infer, a, um, v. inferus init.

inferax.full: in-fĕrax, ācis, adj., unfruitful (late Lat.): silvae, Hier. Homil. ex Orig. 2.
inferax.short: in-fĕrax, ācis, adj., unfruitful (late Lat.): silvae, Hier.

inferi.full: infĕri, ōrum, v. inferus, I. B.

inferiae.full: infĕrĭae, ārum, f. plur. [inferi], sacrifices in honor of the dead (class.); nom., Ov. M. 13, 613; abl., id. Ib. 454: alicui inferias afferre, Cic. N. D. 3, 16, 42; cf.: absenti ferat inferias, Verg. A. 9, 215; so, referre, Hor. C. 2, 1, 28: alicui dare, Ov. F. 5, 422: mittere, id. M. 11, 381: accipere, id. ib. 8, 488: inferias alicui facere, Tac. H. 2, 95: inferias his annua religione instituit, Suet. Calig. 15; id. Claud. 11; id. Vit. 11 al.

inferialis.full: infĕrĭālis, e, adj. inferiae, of or belonging to a funeral: officia, App. M. 8, p. 204. — Hence, infĕrĭālĭa, ōrum, n. plur., = inferiae, sacrifices to the dead, Gloss. Philox.

inferius2.full: infĕrĭus, a, um, adj. infero, that is offered or sacrificed (ante- and post-class.): vinum, sacrificial wine, Cato, R. R. 132, 2; 134, 3; Arn. 4, 138.

infermentatus.full: in-fermentātus, a, um, adj., unleavened (late Lat.): panes, Paul. Nol. Carm. 23, 47.
infermentatus.short: in-fermentātus, a, um, adj., unleavened (late Lat.): panes, Paul.

infermentum.full: in-fermentum, i, n., unleavened bread, Gloss. Philox.
infermentum.short: in-fermentum, i, n., unleavened bread, Gloss.

infernalis.full: infernālis, e, adj. infernus, nether, lower, belonging to the lower regions, infernal (post-class.): nox, Alcim. Avit. 2, 290: Juppiter, i. e. Pluto, Prud. adv. Symm. 1, 389.

infernas.full: infernas, ātis, adj. infernus, of or from the lower country, lowland (rare): abies, Plin. 16, 39, 76, § 197; Vitr. 2, 10: navicularii, Inscr. Orell. 1084: terra, Mart. Cap. 6, § 603.

inferne.full: infernĕ, adv., v. infernus, a, um, fin.

infernus.full: infernus, a, um, adj. infer, lower, that which lies beneath (mostly poet. and postAug.). In gen.: hic sese infernis de partibus erigit Hydra, from beneath, Cic. poët. N. D. 2, 44, 114: superi infernique Di, Liv. 24, 38, 8: stagna, id. 8, 24, 3: auster, Plin. 2, 47, 48, § 128: mare, the Tuscan Sea, Luc. 2, 400.— In partic., underground, belonging to the Lower Regions, infernal: rex, Pluto, Verg. A. 6, 106: Juno, Proserpine, id. ib. 6, 138: sedes, id. ib. 8, 244: tenebrae, id. ib. 7, 325: infernas

infero.full: in-fĕro, intŭli, illātum, inferre, v. a., to carry, bring, put, or throw into or to a place (class.); constr. with in and acc., ad, or the dat. Lit. With in and acc.: in equum, to bring or set upon a horse, Caes. B. G. 6, 29: coronam in curiam, Liv. 44, 14, 3: Scipio lecticula in aciem inlatus, id. 24, 42, 5: in portum quinqueremes, id. 28, 17, 5; cf. id. 26, 21, 6; 10, 2, 13: arma in Italiam, Nep. Ham. 4, 2: bello in provinciam illato, Cic. Fam. 15, 2, 1; id. Sest. 27, 58; Liv. 9, 25, 2.— With

infertilis.full: in-fertĭlis, e, adj., unfruitful, ἄγονος, Gloss. Philox.
infertilis.short: in-fertĭlis, e, adj., unfruitful, ἄγονος, Gloss.

infertilitas.full: in-fertĭlĭtas, ātis, f., unfruitfulness, ἀγονία, Gloss. Philox.
infertilitas.short: in-fertĭlĭtas, ātis, f., unfruitfulness, ἀγονία, Gloss.

infertor.full: infertor, ōris, m. (infero), one who serves up dishes, a waiter, steward, παραθέτης, Gloss. Philox.; Schol. Juv. 5, 83; 9, 109.

infertus.full: infertus, a, um, Part., from infercio.
infertus.short: infertus, a, um, Part., from infercio.

inferus.full: infĕrus, a, um (ante-class. collat. form of the nom. sing. infer: ubi super inferque vicinus permittet, Cato, R. R. 149), adj. cf. Sanscr. adh-aras, adh-amas, the lower, lowest; and Lat. infra, that is below, underneath, lower; opp. superus. Posit. In gen.: inferus an superus tibi fert Deus funera, Liv. Andr. ap. Prisc. p. 606 P.; cf.: Di Deaeque superi atque inferi, Plaut. Cist. 2, 1, 36; Ter. Phorm. 4, 4, 6; cf. also: ut ex tam alto dignitatis gradu ad superos videantur deos potius quam ad inf

infervefacio.full: in-fervĕfăcĭo, fēci, factum, 3, v. a. (pass. fīo, factus, fĭēri), to cause to boil in any thing; or simply to cause to boil, to boil: infervefacito paulisper, Cato, R. R. 156, 7: liquatum acetum, Col. 12, 17, 2: cum infervefiunt, Scrib. Comp. 271: omnia infervefacta, Col. 9, 13, 5.

inferveo.full: in-fervĕo, ēre, v. n., to boil in any thing; to boil, seethe: facito bis aut ter inferveat, Cato, R. R. 108; Cels. 5, 25, 4: mel Atticum ter infervere facito, Col. 12, 38, 5.

infervesco.full: in-fervesco, ferbŭi, 3, v. inch. n., to boil down, to boil, to grow hot, be heated: fabae tertia pars ut infervescat, Cato, R. R. 90: mulsum quod inferbuit, Cels. 2, 30: hoc ubi inferbuit, Hor. S. 2, 4, 67: ne infervescat aqua sole, be heated, Plin. 19, 12, 60, § 183.— Poet.: solem infervescere fronti arcet, to burn on the forehead, Sil. 13, 341.

infestatio.full: infestātĭo, ōnis, f. infesto, a disturbing, troubling (post-class.), Tert. Apol. 1.

infestator.full: infestātor, ōris, m. id., a disturber, troubler (post-Aug. and very rare), Plin. 6, 28, 32, § 143.

infestivus.full: in-festīvus, a, um, adj., not agreeable, not pleasant, inelegant (post-class.): subagresti ingenio et infestivo, Gell. 1, 5, 3.— Adv.: infestīvĭter, inelegantly: cetera vertit non infestiviter, i. e. quite elegantly, Gell. 9, 9, 9.
infestivus.short: in-festīvus, a, um, adj., not agreeable, not pleasant, inelegant (post-class.): subagresti ingenio et infestivo, Gell.

infesto.full: infesto, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. infestus, to attack, trouble, molest, disturb, infest (mostly post-Aug.). Lit.: Scylla latus dextrum, laevum Charybdis infestant, Ov. M. 13, 730: eas insulas infestari beluis, Plin. 6, 32, 37, § 205: morbis, id. 17, 24, 37, § 216: mari infestato latrociniis, Vell. 2, 73: vulnera et nimius calor et nimium frigus infestant, Cels. 5, 26, 6 fin.: hostem, Front. Strat. 2, 3, 16: sagittis infestari, id. ib. 2, 13, 7; Sen. Ep. 71, 18; Lact. Epit. 59, 7.— Transf., in gen., t

infestus.full: in-festus, a, um, adj. 2. in-festus for fenstus, from fendo; whence defendo, infensus, made unsafe, disturbed, molested, infested; unquiet, unsafe (class.; cf. infensus). Lit.: via excursionibus barbarorum infesta, Cic. Prov. Cons. 2, 4: iter, id. Phil. 12, 10: civitas, Liv. 3, 24: omnia infesta serpentibus, Sall. J. 89: sua tuta omnia, infesta hostium (omnia), Liv. 2, 49: vita, Cic. Rosc. Am. 11: infestum agrum reddere, to make unsafe, Liv. 2, 11: mare infestum habere, to disturb, render insecu

infibulo.full: in-fībŭlo (-fiblo), āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. in-fibula, to clasp, buckle, or button together, to close with a clasp or pin (rare): infibulati sacrificabant flamines propter usum aeris antiquissimum aereis fibulis, Paul. ex Fest. p. 113 Müll.; Serv. Verg. A. 4, 262.— Esp. Med. t. t.: adulescentulos interdum vocis, interdum valetudinis causa, to infibulate, Cels. 7, 25, 3.— In cookery, to fasten together that which is larded or stuffed, Apic. 8, 7, § 372.

inficiens2.full: infĭcĭens, entis, adj. 2. in-facio, that does nothing, inactive (ante-class.): homo, Varr. L. L. 6, § 78 Müll.: apes (with inertes), id. R. R. 3, 16, 8.

inficio.full: in-fĭcĭo, fēci, fectum, 3, v. a. in-facio, to put or dip into any thing; hence, Lit., to stain, dye, color, tinge with: quia tibi suaso infecisti pallulam, Plaut. Truc. 2, 2, 16: omnes se Britanni vitro inficiunt, Caes. B. G. 5, 14: lana infecta conchylio, Plin. 32, 7, 25, § 77: arma infecta sanguine, Verg. A. 5, 413; cf.: locum sanguine, Tac. H. 2, 55: diem, to discolor, darken, Ov. M. 13, 601: populi sole infecti, nondum exusti, Plin. 6, 19, 22, § 70: palpebrae mulieribus infectae quotidiano,

infidelis.full: in-fĭdēlis, e, adj., that cannot be relied upon, unfaithful, faithless. In gen. (rare but class.): si hoc sibi sument, nullam esse fidem, quae infideli data sit, Cic. Off. 3, 29, 106: Bellovaci, qui ante erant per se infideles, Caes. B. G. 7, 59: non infideles arbitrae Nox et Diana, Hor. Epod. 5, 50: obsecro, infidelior mihi ne fuas, quam ego sum tibi, Plaut. Capt. 2, 3, 83: ut ex infidelissimis (sociis) firmissimos redderem, Cic. Fam. 15, 4, 14: silex ad structuram infidelis, Plin. 36, 22, 49,
infidelis.short: in-fĭdēlis, e, adj., that cannot be relied upon, unfaithful, faithless.

infidelitas.full: infĭdēlĭtas, ātis, f. infidelis, unfaithfulness, faithlessness, infidelity: amicitiarum, Cic. Tusc. 5, 22: infidelitatis suspicionem sustinere, * Caes. B. C. 2, 33. — In plur.: quantae infidelitates in amicitiis, Cic. Mil. 26, 69.

infidigraphus.full: infīdigrăphus, a, um, adj. vox hybr., infidus- γράφω, writing faithlessly (eccl. Lat.): infidelis Deo nec infidigraphus nec ingratus, (Hilar.) Anon. in Job, 1, 124.

infidus.full: in-fīdus, a, um, adj., not to be trusted, unsafe, faithless, treacherous, false (class.): quos fidos amicos habuisset, quos infidos, Cic. Lael. 15, 53: nihil stabile quod infidum est, id. ib. 18, 65: gentes, id. Prov. Cons. 13, 33; cf.: civitas Rhodiorum, Sall. C. 51, 5: genus Numidarum, id. J. 46, 3: scurra, Hor. Ep. 1, 18, 4: societas regni, Liv. 1, 14: pax, id. 9, 45: promissa, Val. Fl. 2, 578: mare, Lucr. 2, 557; cf. Verg. G. 1, 254. — With dat.: istis infidus, Sall. H. Fragm. 1, 48, 15 Diet
infidus.short: in-fīdus, a, um, adj., not to be trusted, unsafe, faithless, treacherous, false (class.): quos fidos amicos habuisset, quos infidos, Cic.

infigo.full: in-fīgo, xi, xum, 3, v. a., to fix, thrust, drive, or fasten in. Lit.: gladium hosti in pectus, Cic. Tusc. 4, 22, 50: ferreis hamis infixis, Caes. B. G. 7, 73 fin.: hastam portae, Verg. A. 9, 746: signum, Cic. Div. 2, 31: (sagitta) infigitur arbore, remains fixed, sticks fast, Verg. A. 5, 504: vulnus infixum, made by a thrust, id. ib. 4, 689: infixa corpori extrahere, things stuck in the body, Plin. 26, 12, 79, § 128; cf.: infixum moenibus hostem deicere, standing firmly on, Sil. 11, 173: infixu

infigurabilis.full: infĭgūrābĭlis, e, adj. 2. in-figura, shapeless, ill-shaped, deformed: fornix, Amm. 24, 4, 15.

infimatis.full: infĭmātis (infŭm-), is, adj. infimus, one of the lowest (in condition, rank, etc.), opp. summas: ego infumatis infumus, Plaut. Stich. 3, 2, 37; cf. Prisc. 943 P.: infimates ὑστερεύοντες, Gloss.

infimitas.full: infĭmĭtas, ātis, f. id., lowness, humility (late Lat.): sortis, Amm. 29, 11: obsequiorum, id. 17, 13, 12; Aug. 1 Music. 9, 15.

infimo.full: infĭmo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. id., to make low, to lower (post-class.): deos, App. M. 1, p. 106, 2: ingenia ad miserias infimata (opp. ad beatitudinem sublimata), id. de Deo Socr. p. 44, 8.

infimus.full: infĭmus, a, um, v. inferus, III. A.

infindo.full: in-findo, fĭdi, fissum, 3, v. a., to cut into, to cleave (poet.): telluri sulcos, Verg. E. 4, 33; so poet., sulcos, for to plough up, make by sailing, id. A. 5, 142: silvam, Dig. 50, 66: volat cava pinus infinditque salum, cuts through, sails through, Val. Fl. 1, 687.

infinibilis.full: infīnībĭlis, e, adj. 2. in-finio, endless (post-class.): materia, App. Dogm. Plat. 1, p. 4, 1; Mart. Cap. 2, § 203.

infinitas.full: infīnĭtas, ātis, f. 2. in-finis, boundlessness, endlessness, infinity: locorum, boundlessness, endless extent, Cic. N. D. 1, 26, 73: rerum atque naturae, id. Tusc. 5, 36 fin.: naturae, id. Ac. 2, 37; Plin. 2, 2, 1, § 3: mundorum, Amm. 15, 1, 4: populi, Hilar. in Matt. 14, 11; Aug. Ver. Relig. 43.—Absol.: in infinitatem omnem peregrinari (sc. animo), Cic. Tusc. 5, 39, 114; id. N. D. 1, 19, 50.

infinitio.full: infīnītĭo, ōnis, f. infinitus, boundlessness, infinity: infinitio ipsa, quam ἀπειρίαν vocant, Cic. Fin. 1, 6, 21.

infinitivus.full: infīnītīvus, a, um, adj. id., unlimited, indefinite: modus, or absol.: infī-nītīvus, i, m.; in gram., the infinitive, Mart. Cap. 3, § 310 sqq.; Isid. Orig. 1, 8; Diom. p. 331 P. al.

infinitus.full: in-fīnītus, a, um, adj., not enclosed within boundaries, boundless, unlimited. Lit.: quod finitum est habet extremum ... nihil igitur cum habeat extremum, infinitum sit necesse est, Cic. Div. 2, 50, 103: aër, materia, id. Ac. 2, 37, 118: imperium, Cic. Verr. 2, 3, 91: potestas, id: Agr. 2, 13, 33; Liv. 3, 9: magnitudines infinitissimae, Boëth. Inst. Arithm. 1, 4. — Subst.: infī-nītum, i, n., boundless space, the infinite: ex infinito coorta, Lucr. 5, 367.— Transf. Without end, endless, infinite:
infinitus.short: in-fīnītus, a, um, adj., not enclosed within boundaries, boundless, unlimited.

infirmatio.full: infirmātĭo, ōnis. f. 1. infirmo, a weakening, invalidating. Rerum judicatarum, Cic. Agr. 2, 3, 8; 2, 4, 10.— Transf., a refuting, disproving: judicatio est, quae ex infirmatione et confirmatione rationis nascitur controversia, Cic. Inv. 1, 13, 18; 2, 21, 62.

infirmis.full: infirmis, e, adj., v. infirmus init.

infirmitas.full: infirmĭtas, ātis, f. infirmus, want of strength; weakness, feebleness. Lit.: puerorum, Cic. de Sen. 10, 33: summa gracilitas et infirmitas corporis, id. Fam. 7, 1: oculorum, Plin. Ep. 7, 21: propter sexus infirmitatem, Ulp. Fragm. 11, 1: aetatis, Paul. Sent. 1, 7, 2. — In partic. (sc. corporis, valetudinis), infirmity, indisposition, sickness: suspicionem infirmitatis dare, Suet. Tib. 72: infirmitate correptus, Just. 28, 3; Plin. Ep. 10, 6, 1: infirmitate impeditus, Dig. 4, 6, 38.— Transf. Of th

infirmo1.full: infirmo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. and n. infirmus. Act., to deprive of strength, to weaken, enfeeble. Lit.: legiones, Tac. A. 15, 10: munimenta madore, Sall. Fragm. ap. Non. 138, 6: hominem, Cels. 2, 12.— Trop. To invalidate, disprove, refute: res tam leves infirmare ac diluere, Cic. Rosc. Am. 15, 42; with tollere, id. N. D. 2, 59, 147; with frangere, id. de Or. 131: fidem testis, id. Rosc. Com. 15, 45: fidem alicui, id. Att. 15, 26. — To annul, make void: legem, Liv. 34, 3; Quint. 7, 1, 49: contract

infirmo2.full: in-firmo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a., to establish in, fix, or confirm in (late Lat.), Cael. Aur. Acut. 3, 4, 36.

infirmus.full: in-firmus, a, um (post-class. infir-mis, e, Amm. 20, 6), adj., not strong, weak, feeble. Lit.: viribus infirmis, Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 43, § 95: valetudo, id. Brut. 48, 180: classis inops et infirma, Cic. Verr. 2, 5, 33, § 86: valetudo infirmissima, id. de Or. 1, 45. —Hence, infirm, indisposed, sick: sum admodum infirmus, Cic. Ac. 1, 4, 14; Plin. Ep. 7, 26: pecus, i. e. sheep, Ov. Ib. 44: lumen solis, weak, feeble, Luc. 5, 545: infirmior est panis ex polline, less nourishing, Cels. 2, 18: infirmissim

infit.full: in-fit, v. def. (infĭunt, Mart. Cap. 2, § 220: infe ἄρξαι, Gloss.: infĭo, Varr. ap. Prisc. 8 fin.), he (she, it), begins: infit me percontarier, Plaut. As. 2, 2, 76: laudare formam virginis, id. Rud. prol. 51. postulare plorans ejulans, ut, etc., id. Aul. 2, 4, 39: commutare animum (with adoritur), Lucr. 3, 515: erigere caput, id. 5, 1208: ita farier, Verg. A. 11, 242. — In partic. He begins to speak: his vocibus infit, Verg. A. 5, 708; cf.: talibus, id. ib. 10, 860: tum ita Tullus infit: Romani

infitens.full: infĭtens, entis, Part., from infiteor, that does not confess, Gloss. Philox.; cf. the foll. art.
infitens.short: infĭtens, entis, Part., from infiteor, that does not confess, Gloss.

infiteri.full: infĭtēri non fateri, Paul. ex Fest. p. 112 Müll.

infitiae.full: infĭtĭae (infĭcĭae), ārum, f. 2. infateor, denial; only in the acc. in connection with ire, and very rarely without a negative, except in ante-class. Lat.: infitias ire, to deny (not in Cic. or Cæs.); constr. with acc. and inf., aliquid or absol.: quī lubet ire infitias mihi facta quae sunt? Plaut. Men. 2, 3, 45: ille infitias ibit, Ter. Ad. 3, 2, 41: omnia infitias ire, Plaut. Cist. 4, 1, 9; so without a negative: infitias eunt mercedem se belli Romanis inferendi pactos, Liv. 10, 10, 8. — With

infitialis.full: infĭtĭālis (infĭc-), e, adj. infitiae, negative, consisting in denial: quaestio, Cic. Top. 24, 92: status, Quint. 3, 6, 15; 32.

infitiatio.full: infĭtĭātĭo (infĭc-), ōnis,f. infitior, a denial. In gen.: causam infitiatione defendere, Cic. de Or. 2, 25, 105: ipsam negationem infitiationemque, id. Part. 29, 102. — In partic., a denying or disowning of a debt, Sen. de Ira, 2, 9, 1: circumscriptiones, furta, fraudes, infitiationes, Dig. 47, 2, 69.

infitiator.full: infĭtĭātor (infĭc-), ōris, m. id., a denier, esp. one who denies a debt or refuses to restore a deposit: ille infitiator, Cic. de Or. 1, 37, 168; with fraudulentus, Sen. Ben. 3, 27: lentus, a bad debtor, Cic. Cat. 2, 10.

infitiatrix.full: infĭtĭātrix (infĭc-), īcis, f. id., she that denies or disowns, Prud. Psych. 680.

infitior.full: infĭtĭor (infĭc-), ātus, 1, v. dep. a. [infitiae], not to confess, to contradict, deny, disown. In gen.: omnia infitiatur ea, quae dudum confessa est mihi, Plaut. Cist. 4, 1, 9: cum id posset infitiari, repente confessus est, Cic. Cat. 3, 5, 11: verum, id. Part. Or. 14: neque infitiandi ratio, neque defendendi facultas, Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 47: resistere aut infitiando aut definiendo, id. Part. Or. 29, 102: notitiam alicujus, Ov. P. 4, 6, 42: fama factis infitianda tuis, to be refuted by thy deeds,

infixus.full: infixus, a, um, Part., from infigo.
infixus.short: infixus, a, um, Part., from infigo.

inflabellatus.full: inflābellātus, a, um, Part. [from the obs. inflabello], breathed into (late Lat.): corporibus ignis, Tert. adv. Val. 23.

inflabilis.full: inflābĭlis, e, adj. inflo, that may be inflated (late Lat.): viscus, Lact. Opif. D. 11, 4.— Puffing up, causing wind: cibi, Cael. Aur. Acut. 2, 40, 233.

inflacceo.full: in-flaccĕo, ēre, v. n., to become flaccid or weak; hence, trop., to become useless: inflaccebunt condiciones, Enn. ap. Non. 110, 14 dub. (Vahl. Enn. p. 142 reads: sin flaccebunt).
