lactes.full: lactes, ium (in sing. lactis, is, only, acc. to Prisc. p. 686, erroneously on account of lactis agninas), f. root lag-; Gr. λαγαρός; cf. Lat. languidus, laxus, the intestines; esp. the smaller intestines, chitterlings (anteclass. and post - Aug.): ab hoc ventriculo lactes in homine et ove, per quas labitur cibus: in ceteris hillae, Plin. 11, 37, 79, § 200: ita cibi vocivitate venio lassis lactibus, i. e. empty, famished, Plaut. Curc. 2, 3, 40: pulmone et lactibus unctis, Pers. 2, 30. —Prov.: adl

lactesco.full: lactesco, ĕre, v. inch. n. [lacteo]. * To turn to milk: omnis fere cibus matrum lactescere incipit, Cic. N. D. 2, 51, 128; Plin. 20, 21, 84, § 230 al.— To have milk for suckling, to become capable of giving suck: asinae praegnantes continuo lactescunt, Plin. 11, 41, 96, § 237: pectore, Aug. Ep. 150: segetes facit lactescere, to become milky, Serv. Verg. G. 1, 315; v. 2. Lactans.

lacteus.full: lactĕus, a, um, adj. lac. Of milk, milky; full of milk (mostly poet.). Lit.: umor, Ov. M. 15, 79: ubera, Verg. G. 2, 525.— In partic., milk-drinking, sucking: vernae, Mart. 3, 58, 22: porcus, id. 3, 47, 12.— Transf., milk-white, milkcolored, milky: colla, Verg. A. 8, 660: cervix, id. ib. 10, 137: gemma, Mart. 8, 45, 2: circulus, the Gr. γαλαξίας κύκλος, the Milky Way, Cic. Rep. 6, 16, 16; also, via, Ov. M. 1, 168.— Illa Livi lactea ubertas, pure, Quint. 10, 1, 32.

lacticinium.full: lactĭcīnĭum, i, n. id., milk-food, food prepared with milk, Apic. 7, 11.—Also, † lactĭcīnĭa (ōrum) ὠόγαλα (a dish prepared with milk and eggs), Gloss. Philox.

lacticolor.full: lactĭcŏlor, ōris, adj. lac-color, milkcolored, Aus. Ep. 7, 54.

lacticularius.full: lactĭculārĭus, † lactĭculōsus, λιπογάλακτος, deprived of milk (also absol.), Gloss. Philox.
lacticularius.short: lactĭculārĭus, † lactĭculōsus, λιπογάλακτος, deprived of milk (also absol.), Gloss.

lactidiacus.full: lactĭdĭăcus, λελακτισμένος (that kicks, or that has been wounded by kicking), Gloss. Philox.
lactidiacus.short: lactĭdĭăcus, λελακτισμένος (that kicks, or that has been wounded by kicking), Gloss.

lactifer.full: lactĭfer, fĕra, fĕrum, adj. lac-fero, milk-bringing, producing milk: Silvanus, Inscr. ap. Mur. 70, 6.

lactilago.full: lactĭlāgo, ĭnis, f. lac, a plant, called also chamaedaphne, App. Herb. 27.

lactineus.full: lactĭnĕus, a, um, adj. id., milk-colored, white, Ven. Carm. 8, 1, 27.

lactito.full: lactĭto, 1, v. freq. a. 1. lacto, to give suck, to suckle (poet.), Ps.-Mart. 7, 102, 3.

lacto1.full: lacto, āvi, ātum (used almost exclusively in the part. pres.), 1, v. a. and n. lac. To contain milk, to have milk, to give suck: ubera lactantia, Ov. M. 6, 342; 7, 321; Lucr. 5, 885: ubera quae non lactaverunt, Vulg. Luc. 23, 29: quaecunque (femina) id temporis lactans est, Gell. 12, 1, 17.— To suck milk, to take the breast, to suck: puer lactans, Liv. Andron. ap. Non. 153, 26 (Trag. Rel. v. 38 Rib.); cf.: infans lactavit, Aus. Epit. 32: anni lactantes, the suckling years (of a child), id. Idyll
lacto1.short: lacto, āvi, ātum (used almost exclusively in the part.

lacto2.full: lacto, āvi, ātum, 1, v. freq. a. lacio, to allure, wheedle, flatter, deceive with fair words, to dupe, cajole (mostly ante-class.): dictis lenibus lactare aliquem, Att. ap. Non. 16, 17: frustrando lactans, id. ib.: ita me amor lapsum animi ludificat...retinet, lactat largitur, Plaut. Cist. 2, 1, 9: animos, Ter. And. 5, 4, 9; 4, 1, 24: si te lactaverint peccatores, Vulg. Prov. 1, 10: nec lactes quemquam labiis tuis, id. ib. 24, 28.

lactoris.full: lactŏris, f. lac, a kind of milky plant, Plin. 24, 18, 104, § 168.

lactosus.full: lactōsus, = γαλακτώδης, milk-like, milky, Gloss. Philox.

lactuca.full: lactūca, ae, f. lac. Lettuce, Plin. 19, 8, 38, § 125 sqq.; Col. 10, 179; 11, 3, 25 sq.; Verg. M. 76; Cels. 2, 32; Mart. 13, 14, 1; several species are described by Plin. H. N. 20, 7, 24, § 58 sqq.— Lactuca marina, the plant wolf's-milk, Cels. 5, 7; Col. 6, 15, 2.

lactucarius.full: lactūcārĭus, ĭi, m. id., a dealer in lettuce, acc. to Diom. p. 313 P.

lactucinus.full: Lactūcīnus, i, m. lactuca, a Roman surname in the familia Valeria, Plin. 19, 4, 19, § 59.

lactucosus.full: lactūcōsus, a, um, adj. id., full of lettuce, Diom. p. 316 P.

lactucula.full: lactūcŭla, ae, f. dim. id., a small, young lettuce, Col. 10, 111; Suet. Aug. 77; Pall. 1, 30.

lacturcia.full: Lacturcĭa, ae, f. lac, a goddess who presided over the corn swelling with milk, Aug. Civ. Dei, 4, 8 (al. deum Lacturnum); cf. 2. Lactans.

lacturnus.full: Lacturnus, l, v. the preced. art.

laculatus.full: lăcŭlātus, a, um, adj. lacus, four-cornered, checkered: vestis, woven in square compartments or checks, with inwoven or embroidered pictures (v. lacus, V.), Isid. Orig. 19, 22, 11.

lacuna.full: lăcūna (collateral form lŭcūna; cf. Lachm. ad Lucr. vol. 2, p. 205; lăcūnā-tūra, App. Flor. 15, p. 351, 2 Hildebrand; v. infra), ae, f. lacus, a ditch, pit, hole; esp. a place where water collects, a pool, pond. Lit. (mostly poet.): lacuna, id est aquae collectio, a lacu derivatur, quam alii lamam, alii lustrum dicunt, Paul. ex Fest. p. 117 Müll.: vastae, Lucr. 6, 552: vastae Orci, id. 1, 116; 6, 538: cavae, Verg. G. 1, 117; 3, 365.—Poet.: salsae, i. e. the sea, Lucr. 5, 794; 3, 1044; also, Nept

lacunar.full: lăcūnar, āris (nom. lacūnārĭum, Isid. Orig. 15, 8, 6; gen. plur. lacunariorum for lacunarium, Vitr. 4, 3, 1 al.; dat. plur. lacunariis, id. 5, 2), n. lacuna, a wainscoted and gilded ceiling of an unvaulted chamber, a panel-ceiling, a ceiling (so called from its sunken spaces; class.), Vitr. 7, 2: non ebur neque aureum Mea renidet in domo lacunar, Hor. C. 2, 18, 2: gladium e lacunari seta equina aptum demitti jussit, Cic. Tusc. 5, 21, 62: primus lacunaria pingere instituit (Polygnotus), Plin. 35,

lacunarius.full: lăcūnārĭus, ii, m. lacuna, a gravedigger (late Lat.), Firm. Math. 8, 21; cf.: lacunarius, λακκοπολός, Gloss. Philox.

lacunatura.full: lăcūnātūra, ae, f., v. lacuna, I. B. fin.

lacuno.full: lăcūno, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. lacuna. * To hollow out, to fret or pit: lacunati tori, Plin. 15, 10, 9, § 35.— To panel like a lacunar: summa lacunabant alterno murice conchae, Ov. M. 8, 564.

lacunosus.full: lăcūnōsus, a, um, adj. id.. Full of holes, ponds, or sloughs: convallis, App. M. 1, p. 105, 21; cf.: (via) lacunosis incilibus voraginosa, id. ib. 9, p. 221, 1.— In gen., full of hollows, gaps, or cavities: nihil eminens, nihil lacunosum, Cic. N. D. 2, 18, 47: vena, Plin. 16, 43, 83, § 226.

lacus.full: lăcus, ūs (gen. laci, Vulg. Dan. 6, 17; 24; id. Jer. 37, 15; Cassiod. Var. 11, 14; dat. and abl. plur. lacis, Anthol. Lat. 5, 71, 10: lacibus, Plin. 23, 1, 20, § 33; usually lacubus, Ov. M. 12, 278 al.), m. root lak, to tear; Gr. λάκος, λακερός, λάκκος; Lat. lacer, lacinia, lacuna, lāma; cf. lacerna; originally any thing hollow, hence. A large vessel for liquids, a basin, tank, tub; esp. a vat into which the wine flowed from the press, Cato, R. R. 25; 67, 2; Col. 12, 18, 3: tu quoque devotos, Ba

lacusculus.full: lăcuscŭlus, i, m. dim. lacus. A little lake (only in Columella), Col. 4, 8, 2; id. Arb. 10, 4.— A receptacle or bin for keeping olives, Col. 12, 50, 3 sq.

lacuturris.full: lăcŭturris, is (sc. caulis), m. lacusturris, a kind of cabbage, Plin. 19, 8, 41, § 141.

lacydes.full: Lăcўdes, is, m., = Λακύδης, an Academician of Cyrene, a pupil of Arcesilas, Cic. Ac. 2, 6, 16; id. Tusc. 5, 37, 107.
lacydes.short: Lăcўdes, is, m., = Λακύδης, an Academician of Cyrene, a pupil of Arcesilas, Cic.

lacydon.full: Lăcўdon, ŏnis, m., the name of the port of Marseilles: Massiliensium portus, Mel. 2, 5.
lacydon.short: Lăcўdon, ŏnis, m., the name of the port of Marseilles: Massiliensium portus, Mel.

lada.full: lāda or lēda, ae, f., and lēdon, i, n., = λῆδον. a shrub in Cyprus from which a resin was obtained, the Cistus Creticus, Linn.; form lada, Plin. 12, 19, 43, § 97; form leda, id. 12, 17, 37, § 75; form ledon, id. 26, 8, 30, § 47.
lada.short: lāda or lēda, ae, f., and lēdon, i, n., = λῆδον.

ladanum.full: lādănum or lēdănum, i, n. λήδανον, the resinous juice obtained from the shrub lada, ladanum, Plin. 26, 8, 30, § 47 al.

ladas.full: Lādas, ae, m., = Λάδας, a runner of Alexander the Great, whose name became a proverb for swiftness, Sol. 1, § 96; Mart. 10, 100, 5; 2, 86, 8; Cat. 55, 25; Auct. Her. 4, 3, 4; Sen. Ep. 85, 4: pauper locupletem optare podagram Ne dubitet Ladas, Juv. 13, 97.
ladas.short: Lādas, ae, m., = Λάδας, a runner of Alexander the Great, whose name became a proverb for swiftness, Sol.

ladon.full: Lādon, ōnis, m., = Λάδων. A river of Arcadia which flows into the Alphēus; the fabled father of Daphne: harenosus, Ov. M. 1, 702; Mel. 2, 3, 5; Sen. Q. N. 6, 25, 2; cf. Serv. Verg. E. 3, 63; id. ad Aen. 3, 91.— The name of one of Actæon's hounds, Ov. M. 3, 216.

laeana.full: Laeāna, ae, f., a town of Arabia, Plin. 6, 28, 32, § 156.—Hence, Laeānīta, ae, m., an inhabitant thereof, Plin. 6, 28, 32, § 156.—Laeānītĭcus, a, um, adj., Plin. 6, 28, 32, § 156.
laeana.short: Laeāna, ae, f., a town of Arabia, Plin.

laeca.full: Laeca, ae, m., a Roman surname; e. g. M. Porcius Laeca, one of Catiline's fellowconspirators, Sall. C. 17: fuisti apud Laecam illa nocte, Catilina, Cic. Cat. 1, 4, 9.
laeca.short: Laeca, ae, m., a Roman surname;

laecasin.full: laecasin, an imprecation ( = Gr. λαικίζειν), go to: dico frigori, Petr. S. 42, 2.

laedo.full: laedo, si, sum, 3, v. a. perh. for lavido, root lu-; cf.: luo, solvo, and Germ. los-, to hurt by striking, wound, injure, damage (syn.: saucio, vulnero). Lit.: lora laedunt bracchia, Plaut. Truc. 4, 3, 9: lembus ille mihi laedit latus, id. Bacch. 2, 3, 47: tua laesuro subtrahe colla, Ov. R. Am. 90: frondes laedit hiems, id. F. 6, 150: teneros laedunt prima juga juvencos, id. H. 4, 21; cf.: thymum laeditur imbribus, Plin. 21, 10, 31, § 56: aliquem vulnere, Ov. M. 4, 601: quid me dente captas laed

laelaps.full: Laelaps, ăpis, m. λαίλαψ, hurricane, name of a dog, Ov. M. 3, 211; 7, 771.

laelius.full: Laelĭus, a, name of a Roman gens.— So esp., C. Lælius, a friend of Scipio Africanus: in quo Laeliu' clamores, σοφὸς ille, solebat Edere, Lucil. ap. Cic. de Fin. 2, 8, 24; cf.: nec dubitare illum (C. Laelium) in omni sermone appellare sapientem, Cic. Lael. 1, 1; id. Brut. 21, 82; cf. Hor. S. 2, 1, 65; 72. Cicero's treatise on Friendship is named after him.— D. Lælius, a writer of moderate abilities, Lucil. ap. Cic. de Or. 2, 6, 25.— Another D. Lælius, perh. a son of the preceding, an adherent of
laelius.short: Laelĭus, a, name of a Roman gens.— So esp., C.

laena.full: laena, ae, f., = χλαίνη, a lined upper garment, a cloak, mantle: laena vestimenti genus habitu duplicis. Quidam appellatam existimant Tusce, quidam Graece, quam χλανίδα dicunt, Paul. ex Fest. p. 117 Müll. Usually worn by the flamens over the toga, Cic. Brut. 14, 56; Serv. Verg. A. 4, 262. Also by persons of distinction,-Verg. l. l.; Sil. 15, 424; Pers. 1, 31; Juv. 5, 131; 3, 283; v. Dict. of Antiq.
laena.short: laena, ae, f., = χλαίνη, a lined upper garment, a cloak, mantle: laena vestimenti genus habitu duplicis.

laenas.full: Laenas, ātis, a surname in the gens Popilia, v. Popilius.
laenas.short: Laenas, ātis, a surname in the gens Popilia, v.

laeotomus.full: laeŏtŏmus, i, f., = λαιότομος, the chord of a segment of a circle, Vitr. 9, 8, 6 Schneid. N. cr. (al. lacotomus).
laeotomus.short: laeŏtŏmus, i, f., = λαιότομος, the chord of a segment of a circle, Vitr.

laertes.full: Lāërtes, ae (nom. Laërta, Sen. Troad. 699; gen. Laërtis, acc. to Prisc. p. 705 P.), m., = Λαέρτης, the father of Ulysses, Att. ap. Non. 314, 20 (Trag. Rel. v. 131 Rib.); Cic. de Sen. 15, 54; Ov. H. 1, 113.— Hence, Lāërtĭus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Laertes, Laertian: regna, i. e. Ithaca, Verg. A. 3, 272: heros, i. e. Ulysses, Ov. M. 13, 124; id. Tr. 5, 5, 3: proles, Verg. Cul. 326.— Lāërtĭădes, ae, m., = Λαερτιάδης, a male descendant of Laertes: his son Ulysses, Att. ap. App. de Deo Socr.

laertius.full: Lāërtius, a, um. Adj., from Laërtes, q. v. II. A.— An inhabitant of Laertes, a seaport town in Cilicia, e. g. Diogenes Laërtius, a Greek historian in the third century of the Christian era.

laesio.full: laesĭo, ōnis, f. laedo, a hurting, injuring. Lit. (only in late Lat.): si quod, absente socio, ad laesionem fecit, Dig. 10, 3, 28: quae non ad publicam laesionem respiciunt, ib. 2, 14, 7, § 14: irritat laesio dolorem, Lact. Ira D. 17 med.: regis, Vulg. 1 Esdr. 4, 14: nulla laesio est in eo quia credidit Deo, id. Dan. 6, 23.—* Rhet. t. t., a personal attack by an orator on his opponent: purgatio, conciliatio, laesio, optatio atque exsecratio, Cic. de Or. 3, 53, 205.

laestrygon.full: Laestrȳgon (Lestr-), ŏnis, m., more freq. in plur.: Laestrȳgŏnes, um, m., = Λαιστρυγόνες, an ancient people of Italy, originally in Campania, in the region around Formiæ, and afterwards in Sicily, who are fabled to have been savages and cannibals, Plin. 3, 5, 9, § 59; 7, 1, 2, § 9; Gell. 15, 21; Juv. 15, 18; Mart. Cap. 6, § 641. —In sing., Ov. M. 14, 233.—Of Laestrygonians in Sicily, Sil. 14, 125.—Hence, Laestrȳgŏnĭus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to the Læstrygonians, Læstrygonian. In Formiae:

laesura.full: laesūra, ae, f. laedo, a hurting, injuring (post-class.): divitiarum, loss, Tert. Patient. 7: ANIMI, Inscr. Grut. 828, 10.

laesus.full: laesus, a, um, Part., from laedo.
laesus.short: laesus, a, um, Part., from laedo.

laetabilis.full: laetābĭlis, e, adj. laetor, joyful, glad, gladsome (class.): quid habet ista res aut laetabile, aut gloriosum? Cic. Tusc. 1, 21, 49: nihil laetabile, id. ib. 4, 17, 37: factum, Ov. M. 9, 255: sidus alicui, Val. Fl. 6, 606.— Comp., Mamert. Genethl. 18.

laetabundus.full: laetābundus, a, um, adj. id., greatly rejoicing, full of joy, joyful (post-class.): laetabundus is dicitur, qui abunde laetus est, Gell. 11, 15, 8: his dictis, Mart. Cap. 1, § 23; Vulg. Isa. 35, 2.

laetamen.full: laetāmen, ĭnis, n. id., dung, manure (post-Aug.), Plin. 18, 16, 40, § 141: anserum, Pall. 1, 23.

laetans.full: laetans, antis, Part. and P. a., from laetor.

laetatio.full: laetātĭo, ōnis, f. laetor, rejoicing, exultation, joy (for the usual laetitia): diutina, Caes. B. G. 5, 52 fin.

laeticulosus.full: laetĭcŭlōsus, a, um, adj. laetor, too joyful, overjoyful: tu laeticulosus (al. lacticulosus), Petr. Fragm. Trag. 57 Burm.

laeticus.full: laetĭcus, a, um, adj., v. 2. laetus.

laetifico.full: laetĭfĭco, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. laetificus, to cheer, gladden, delight; constr. with abl. (rare but class.): non illum gloria pulsi Laetificat Magni, Luc. 3, 48: sol laetificat terram, Cic. N. D. 2, 40, 102; Vulg. Psa. 21, 7: corda, id. ib. 19, 9; 103, 15.— Mid., to rejoice, be glad respecting any thing: nunc eo alii laetificantur Meo malo et damno, Plaut. Aul. 4, 9, 15.— In partic., in agriculture, to render fruitful, to fertilize, enrich, manure the ground: Indus agros laetificat et mitigat, Ci

laetificus.full: laetĭfĭcus, a, um, adj. laetus-facio, making glad, gladdening, glad, joyful, joyous (poet.): fetus, Lucr. 1, 193; cf. vites, Enn. ap. Cic. Tusc. 1, 28, 69 (Trag. v. 193 Vahl.): gau (i. e. gaudium), id. ap. Aus. Technop. 144 (Ann. v. 451 Vahl.): tumultus, Stat. Th. 8, 261: plausus, id. ib. 12, 521. —In neutr. plur. as subst.: laetĭfĭca, ōrum, joyful news: laetifica referre alicui, Sen. Troad. 597.

laetisco.full: laetisco, 3, v. n. inch. [laetus], to rejoice, Sisenn. ap. Non. 133, 2.

laetitia.full: laetĭtĭa, ae, f. id., joy, esp. unrestrained joyfulness, gladness, pleasure, delight (cf.: gaudium, hilaritas). Lit.: laetitia opinio recens boni praesentis, in quo efferri rectum esse videatur, Cic. Tusc. 4, 7, 14: laetitia dicitur exsultatio quaedam animi gaudio efferventior eventu rerum expetitarum, Gell. 2, 27, 3: judicium plenum laetitiae, Cic. de Or. 1, 57, 243: percipere laetitiam ex re, id. ib. 1, 44, 197: prae laetitia lacrumae prosuliunt mihi, Plaut. Stich. 3, 2, 13: ut mea laetitia la

laetitudo.full: laetĭtūdo, ĭnis, f. id., ante-class. for laetitia, joy: me excitasti ex luctu in laetitudinem, Att. ap. Non. 132, 12: affecti laetitudine, id. ib. 13 (Trag. Fragm. v. 61, 259 Rib.).

laeto.full: laeto, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. id., to make joyful, to delight, cheer, gladden. Lit. (ante- and post-class.): oculos specie laetavisti optabili, Liv. Andron. ap. Non. 132, 32: te ut triplici laetarem bono, Att. ib.: frontem alicujus serena venustate, App. M. 3, p. 134, 16.— In partic., of the soil, to fertilize, render fertile, manure (postclass.): in laetandis arboribus, Pall. 1, 6, 18: loca sterilia, id. 1, 6, 13.

laetor.full: laetor, ātus, 1, v. dep. n. [lit. pass. of laeto], to rejoice, feel joy, be joyful or glad at any thing (syn. gaudeo); constr. with abl., with in, de, ex, or super and abl., with neutr. acc., with acc. and inf., poet. with gen. With abl.: ut quisquam amator nuptiis laetetur, Ter. Hec. 5, 3, 37: et laetari bonis rebus et dolere contrariis, Cic. Lael. 13, 47: sua re gesta, id. Rep. 1, 42, 65: laetor tum praesenti, tum sperata tua dignitate, id. Fam. 2, 9, 1: laetabitur cor meum quasi a vino, Vulg.

laetorius.full: Laetōrĭus, a, adj., the name of a Roman gens, Mart. 12, 26, 13 (but lex Plaetoria is the true reading, Cic. Off. 3, 15, 61: id. N. D. 3, 30, 74; Cod. Th. 8, 12, 2).
laetorius.short: Laetōrĭus, a, adj., the name of a Roman gens, Mart.

laetus1.full: laetus, a, um, adj. Sanscr. root prī-, to cheer; prētis, joy, love; cf. Gr. πραΰς, πρᾷος; Germ. Friede, Freude; cf. also Latin gentile name, Plaetorius, joyful, cheerful, glad, gay, joyous, rejoicing, pleased, delighted, full of joy. Lit., constr. absol., with de, the gen., the inf., or acc. and inf. Absol.: laeti atque erecti, Cic. Font. 11, 33: alacres laetique, id. Sest. 1, 1: vultus, id. Att. 8, 9, 2: dies laetissimi, id. Lael. 3, 12.—In neutr. plur. as subst.: litterae tuae partim laeta par

laetus2.full: laetus, i, m., in late Lat., a foreign bondman who received a piece of land to cultivate, for which he paid tribute to his master, a serf, Amm. 20, 8, 13; Eum. Pan. 21, 1.—Hence, laeta, ōrum, n., the land so cultivated, Cod. Th. 7, 20, 10.— laetĭcus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to a laetus: laeticae terrae, Cod. Th. 13, 11, 9.
laetus2.short: laetus, i, m., in late Lat., a foreign bondman who received a piece of land to cultivate, for which he paid tribute to his master, a serf, Amm.

laeva.full: laeva, ae, f., the left hand, v. laevus, I. B. 1.
laeva.short: laeva, ae, f., the left hand, v.

laevi.full: Laevi (Lēvi), ōrum, m., the Lævi, an ancient people of Liguria, between the Po and the Ticinus, Liv. 33, 37, 6; 5, 35, 2; Plin. 3, 17, 21, § 124.
laevi.short: Laevi (Lēvi), ōrum, m., the Lævi, an ancient people of Liguria, between the Po and the Ticinus, Liv.

laevianus.full: Laevĭānus, a, um, v. Laevius, II.

laevinus.full: Laevīnus, i, m. laeva, a Roman surname in the gens Valeria, Plin. 35, 2, 2, § 8. Esp. M. Valerius Laevinus, consul during the second Punic war, Liv. 26, 40.— C. Valerius Laevinus, prætor and consul about B. C. 180, Liv. 40, 44, 2; ib. § 7.— P. Valerius Laevinus, lampooned by Horace, Hor. S. 1, 6, 12; 19.

laevius.full: Laevĭus, ii, m., a Roman poet of the ante-clussical period, Gell. 2, 24, 8; 19, 9, 7; Aus. Edyll. 13.—Hence, Laevĭānus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to the poet Lævius, Lævian: carmen, Gell. 19, 7, 2: verba, id. 19, 7, 12.
laevius.short: Laevĭus, ii, m., a Roman poet of the ante-clussical period, Gell.

laevorsum.full: laevorsum and laevorsus, adv. laevus-versum, on the left hand, to or towards the left (post-class.): laevorsum vel dextrorsum, App. Flor. 1, p. 340, 41; cf. Paul. ex Fest. p. 117 Müll.; Amm. 14, 3, 2: laevorsus flexus itinere, id. 31, 10, 11 al.

laevus.full: laevus, a, um, adj. cf. Gr. λαιός, left, on the left side (mostly poet.; syn.: sinister, scaevus). Lit.: ut idem nunc sit laevus; et e laevo sit mutua dexter, Lucr. 4, 301 (325): manus, Cic. Ac. 2, 47, 145: ab laeva manu, Plaut. Aul. 4, 3, 1: habeo equidem hercle oculum. Py. At laevom dico, Plaut. Mil. 4, 7, 24: latus, Ov. M. 12, 415: auris id. ib. 12, 336: pes, id. ib. 12, 101: umerus, id. H. 9, 62: Pontus, lying to the left, id. P. 4, 9, 119: iter, Verg. A. 5, 170: habena, Hor. Ep. 1, 15, 12:

laganum.full: lăgănum, i, n., = λάγανον, a kind of cake made of flour and oil, Hor. S. 1, 6, 115; Cels. 8, 7, § 23 al.: lagana azyma, Vulg. Exod. 29, 2; id. Num. 6, 15.
laganum.short: lăgănum, i, n., = λάγανον, a kind of cake made of flour and oil, Hor.

lagarina.full: Lagarīna, orum, n. plur. (sc. vina), a kind of wine, Plin. 14, 6, 8, § 69.

lagena.full: lăgēna (also lăgaena, lăgoena, and lăgōna), ae, f., = λάγηνος, a large earthen vessel with a neck and handles, a flask, flagon, bottle: quasi tu lagenam dicas, ubi vinum solet Chium esse, Plaut. Curc. 1, 1, 78; Cic. Fam. 16, 26, 2; Quint. 6, 3, 10; Hor. S. 2, 8, 41; 81; id. Ep. 2, 2, 134; Juv. 12, 60; 14, 271 et saep.—Also made of other materials, Plin. 16, 31, 56, § 128: Syra nigri defruti, of glass, Mart. 4, 46, 9.
lagena.short: lăgēna (also lăgaena, lăgoena, and lăgōna), ae, f., = λάγηνος, a large earthen vessel with a neck and handles, a flask, flagon, bottle: quasi tu lagenam dicas, ubi vinum solet Chium esse, Plaut.

lageos.full: lăgēos, i, f., = λάγειος, a Greek species of vine: et passo Psithia utilior, tenuisque Lageos, Verg. G. 2, 93; Isid. Orig. 17, 5, 16.—lăgēos, a, um, adj.: vitis, Plin. 14, 3, 4, § 39: Macr. S. 2, 16, 7.
lageos.short: lăgēos, i, f., = λάγειος, a Greek species of vine: et passo Psithia utilior, tenuisque Lageos, Verg.

lageus.full: Lāgēus, a, um, v. Lagus, II.

lago.full: lago, inis, f., a plant, otherwise called schite; and scammonia tenuis, Plin. 24, 15, 89, § 139.
lago.short: lago, inis, f., a plant, otherwise called schite;

lagois.full: lăgōis, ĭdis, f., = λαγωΐς, a kind of bird, perh. heath-cock, grouse (or the same as lagopus, white grouse): peregrina, Hor. S. 2, 2, 22; Schol. Cruq. ad loc.
lagois.short: lăgōis, ĭdis, f., = λαγωΐς, a kind of bird, perh.

lagon.full: Lāgōn, ŏnis, m., name of a boy: nos facimus Bruti puerum, nos Lagona vivum, Mart. 9, 51, 5 (al. Langona).
lagon.short: Lāgōn, ŏnis, m., name of a boy: nos facimus Bruti puerum, nos Lagona vivum, Mart.

lagonoponos.full: lăgŏnŏpŏnos, false reading for adligato raphano, Plin. 20, 4, 13, § 24.
lagonoponos.short: lăgŏnŏpŏnos, false reading for adligato raphano, Plin.

lagophthalmos.full: lăgophthalmos, i, m., = λαγωφθαλμός (hare-eye), a person afflicted with a disease of the eye, in which the upper lid does not cover the eye, Cels. 7, 7, 9, § 93 sqq.
lagophthalmos.short: lăgophthalmos, i, m., = λαγωφθαλμός (hare-eye), a person afflicted with a disease of the eye, in which the upper lid does not cover the eye, Cels.

lagopus.full: lăgōpūs, ŏdis, f., = λαγώπους, hare'sfoot. An Alpine bird, perh. white grouse, Plin. 10, 48, 68, § 133 (see also glaucopis, Mart. 7, 87).— The herb hare's-foot, Plin. 26, 8, 34, § 53.

lagos.full: Lagos, i, f., a city in Great Phrygia, Liv. 38, 15, 2.
lagos.short: Lagos, i, f., a city in Great Phrygia, Liv.

laguncula.full: lăguncŭla, ae, f. dim. lagena, a small flask, small bottle, Col. 12, 38, 6; 8; Plin. Ep. 2, 6, 2; 1, 6, 3: novae, Vulg. Job, 32, 19; id. Jer. 13, 12; 48, 12.

laguncularis.full: lăguncŭlāris, e, adj. laguncula, of or belonging to a small bottle: pix, Marc. Emp. 36.

lagunculus.full: lăguncŭlus, i, m., a kind of pastry (al. lucunculus), Stat. S. 1, 6, 17.
lagunculus.short: lăguncŭlus, i, m., a kind of pastry (al.

lagus.full: Lāgus, i, m., the father of Ptolemy I. king of Egypt: regia Lagi, Luc. 10, 527: famosa moenia Lagi, Juv. 6, 83: flumina Lagi, i. e. Nilus, Sil. 17, 592.—Hence, Lāgēus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Lagus, Lagian, poet. for Egyptian: Nilus, Luc. 1, 684; cf. amnis, Sil. 1, 196: litora, Mart. 10, 26, 4: ratis, Sil. 10, 322.
lagus.short: Lāgus, i, m., the father of Ptolemy I.

laicus.full: lāĭcus, a, um, adj., = λαϊκός, of or belonging to the people or laity, not priestly, not consecrated: non habeo laicos panes, loaves not consecrated, Vulg. 1 Reg. 21, 4.— Subst.: lāĭcus, i, m., a layman, laic, one not belonging to the priesthood (eccl. Lat.), Tert. Exhort. ad Castit. 7; opp. clericus, Hier. adv. Lucif. 3 al.
laicus.short: lāĭcus, a, um, adj., = λαϊκός, of or belonging to the people or laity, not priestly, not consecrated: non habeo laicos panes, loaves not consecrated, Vulg.

lais.full: Lāïs, ĭdis and ĭdos, f., = Λαΐς, the name of two courtesans of Corinth celebrated for their beauty. Lais, who flourished during the Peloponnesian war: dicitur et multis Lais amata viris, Ov. Am. 1, 5, 12; Cic. Fam. 9, 26, 2 (acc. Laida); Prop. 2, 6, 1 (gen. Laidos).— Lais, a contemporary of Demosthenes, Gell. 1, 8, 3 sqq.; Plin. 28, 7, 23, § 81.—Acc. plur.: Laidas et Glyceras, lascivae nomina famae, Aus. Epigr. 18, 1.
lais.short: Lāïs, ĭdis and ĭdos, f., = Λαΐς, the name of two courtesans of Corinth celebrated for their beauty.

laius.full: Lāĭus or Lajus, i (voc. Lai, Stat. Th. 7, 355), m., = Λάιος, son of Labdacus, king of Thebes, and father of Œdipus, Cic. Tusc. 4, 33, 71; id. Fat. 13, 30; Stat. Th. 2, 7; 66. —Hence, Lāĭădes, ae, m., a male descendant of Laius, i. e. Œdipus, Ov. M. 7, 759.

lalage.full: Lălăgē, ēs, f., = Λαλαγή, the name of a girl, Hor. C. 1, 22, 10; 23; 2, 5, 16; of a woman: LIVIA LALAGE, Inscr. ap. Mur. 1367, 1.
lalage.short: Lălăgē, ēs, f., = Λαλαγή, the name of a girl, Hor.

laletania.full: Lălētānĭa, ae, f., a region in Hispania Tarraconensis, where the vine was cultivated, Ep. Pompei ad Senat. 5; Sall. Hist. Fragm. 2, 96, 5 Dietsch; Mart. 1, 50, 22.— Hence, Lălētānus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Laletania, Laletanian: vina, Plin. 14, 6, 8, § 71.—Plur.: Lălētāni, ōrum, m., inhabitants of Laletania, Laletanians, Plin. 3, 3, 4, § 21 (dub.; al. Lacetani).
laletania.short: Lălētānĭa, ae, f., a region in Hispania Tarraconensis, where the vine was cultivated, Ep.

lalisio.full: lālīsĭo, ōnis, m. (African), the foal of a wild ass, Plin. 8, 44, 69, § 174; Mart. 13, 97.

lallo.full: lallo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. n., to sing lalla or lullaby, to sing as a nurse to a child: iratus mammae, lallare recusas, will not let yourself be sung to sleep, Pers. 3, 17; Hier. Ep. 14, 3: lallare βαβάζειν, Gloss. Philox.

lallum.full: lallum, i, n., or lallus, i, m. lallo, a singing lalla or lullaby (post-class.), Aus. Ep. 16, 91.
lallum.short: lallum, i, n., or lallus, i, m.

lama.full: lāma, ae, f. (cf.: lacus, lacer). A slough, bog, fen: lacuna id est aquae collectio, quam alii lamam, alii lustrum, Paul. ex Fest. p. 117 Müll.: viribus uteris per clivos, flumina, lamas, Hor. Ep. 1, 13, 10.— A kind of mastic: Pistacia lentiscus, Linn.; Plin. 12, 17, 36, § 72 (al. lainam).

lambero.full: lambĕro, āre, v. a., to tear to pieces (ante-class.): lamberat scindit ac laniat, Paul. ex Fest. p. 118 Müll.—Prov.: lepide, Charine, meo me ludo lamberas, you beat me at my own game, pay me in my own coin, Plaut. Ps. 2, 4, 53.

lambito.full: lambĭto, āre, v. freq. a. lambo, to lick, lap up: Aegyptii canes e Nilo numquam nisi currentes lambitant, Sol. 15, 12.

lambitus.full: lambĭtus, ūs, m. id., a licking: lupam primo lambitu pueros detersisse, Aur. Vict. Orig. Gentis R. 20.

lambo.full: lambo, bi, bitum (perf. lambuerunt, Vulg. Jud. 7, 7 al.), 3, v. a. root lap-; Gr. λάπτω, λαφύσσω; Lat. labrum, labium; Germ. Löffel, spoon; Eng. lip, to lick, lap; to touch (class.; cf.: lingo, sugo, ligurio). Lit.: hi canes, quos tribunal meum vides lambere, Cic. Verr. 2, 3, 11, § 28: lagonae collum, Phaedr. 1, 25, 10: lambent cibos (pisces), Col. 8, 17, 11: manum, Mart. 4, 30, 4: sanguinem, Plin. Pan. 48, 3: crustula, Juv. 9, 5: jucundasque puer qui lamberat ore placentas, Lucil. ap. Prisc. 10

lambrica.full: Lambrīca, ae, f., a town in Hispania Tarraconensis, Mel. 3, 1.
lambrica.short: Lambrīca, ae, f., a town in Hispania Tarraconensis, Mel.

lambrus.full: Lambrus, i, m., a small river in northern Italy, a tributary of the Po, Plin. 3, 19, 23, § 131 al.
lambrus.short: Lambrus, i, m., a small river in northern Italy, a tributary of the Po, Plin.

lamella.full: lāmella, ae, f. dim. lamina, a small plate of metal, Vitr. 7, 3: paucae lamellae argenti, a few small silver coins, Sen. Vit. Beat. 21, 3; id. Brev. Vit. 12, 2: stella e lamella aerea, Paul. ex Fest. p. 351.

lamellula.full: lāmellŭla, ae, f. dim. lamella, a small plate of metal: glebulas emi, lamellulas paravi, Petr. 57, 6.

lamenta.full: lāmenta, ae, f. (collat. form of lamentum, q. v.): lamentas, fletus facere, Pac. ap. Non. 132, 28 (Trag. Fragm. v. 175 Rib.).

lamentabilis.full: lāmentābĭlis, e, adj. lamentor, mournful, lamentable (class.). Full of sorrow, expressing sorrow: afflictus et jacens, et lamentabili voce deplorans, Cic. Tusc. 2, 13, 32: carmen, Stat. S. 5, 3, 1.— Causing sorrow, deplorable: funera sumptuosa et lamentabilia, Cic. Leg. 2, 25, 64: regnum, Verg. A. 2, 4: tributum, Ov. M. 8, 263.

lamentarius.full: lāmentārĭus, a, um, adj. lamentum, mournful, causing tears: aedes, Plaut. Capt. 1, 1, 28.

lamentatio.full: lāmentātĭo, ōnis, f. lamentor, a wailing, moaning, weeping, lamenting, lamentation (class.; cf.: querela, questus, lamentum, plangor, planctus): lamentatio (est) aegritudo, cum ejulatu, Cic. Tusc. 4, 8, 18: aegritudo, lacrumae, lamentatio, Plaut. Merc. 5, 2, 29: lugubris fletusque maerens, Cic. Tusc. 1, 13, 30: plangore et lamentatione complerimus forum, id. Or. 38, 131; Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 21, § 47: cottidianae virginis, id. Font. 17, 47: (funeris), id. Leg. 2, 23, 59; Plin. 8, 7, 7, § 21: nox lam

lamentatrix.full: lāmentātrix, īcis, f. lamentator, she who bewails, Vulg. Jer. 9, 17.

lamento.full: lāmento, āvi, 1, v. n. (collat. form of lamentor), Vulg. Matt. 11, 17; id. Luc. 7, 32.

lamentor.full: lāmentor, ātus, 1, v. dep. n. and a. [lamentum], to wail, moan, weep, lament (class.). Neutr.: lamentari, cruciari, Plaut. Mil. 4, 2, 40: quod nunc lamentari, id. Pers. 1, 3, 94: praeter ceteras lamentari, Ter. And. 1, 1, 94: lapides flere ac lamentari cogere, Cic. de Or. 1, 57, 245: Hebiliter lamentari, id. Tusc. 2, 21, 49; id. Phil. 12, 1, 2: ac plangere, Suet. Ner. 49: quid ego hic animo lamentor, Enn. ap. Don. Ter. Phorm. 5, 4, 2 (Ann. v. 210 Vahl.): Thetis quoque lamentando pausam fecit fil

lamentum.full: lāmentum, i, n. perh. for clamentum, from clamo, a wailing, moaning, weeping, lamentation, lament (class., only in plur.): virum, Lucr. 6, 242 Lachm.: negat se velle mortem suam dolore amicorum et lamentis vacare, Cic. de Sen. 20, 73: se lamentis lacrimisque dedere, id. Tusc. 2, 21, 48: lamentis lacrimisque extinctos prosequi, Liv. 25, 38: lamenta ac lacrimas cito ponunt, Tac. G. 27: in sordibus, lamentis luctuque jacēre, Cis. Pis. 36, 88: lamentis gemituque et femineo ululatu Tecta fremunt, Ver

lamia1.full: lămĭa, ae, f., = λαμία. A witch who was said to suck children's blood, a sorceress, enchantress: neu pransae lamiae vivum puerum extrahat alvo, Hor. A. P. 340; App. M. 1, p. 110, 3; 5, p. 164, 6.—Transf.: lamiae turres, nursery tales, Tert. adv. Val. 3.— A sort of flatfish, Plin. 9, 24, 40, § 78.— A species of owl, Vulg. Isa. 34, 14.

lamia2.full: Lămĭa, ae, m., a surname in the gens Aelia, Cic. Sest. 12, 29; id. Fam. 12, 29, 3; id. Att. 11, 7, 2; Hor. C. 1, 26, 8; 3, 17, 2; Juv. 4, 154; 6, 385; Tac. A. 6, 27; Suet. Dom. 1.—Hence, Lămĭānus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to a Lamia, Lamian: horti, Cic. Att. 12, 21, 2; Suet. Calig. 59.
lamia2.short: Lămĭa, ae, m., a surname in the gens Aelia, Cic.

lamia3.full: Lămĭa, ae, f., = Λαμία, a city in Phthiotis, now Zeitun, Liv. 27, 30, 1; 32, 4, 3; Plin. 4, 7, 14, § 28.
lamia3.short: Lămĭa, ae, f., = Λαμία, a city in Phthiotis, now Zeitun, Liv.

lamina.full: lāmĭna or lammĭna, and sync. lamna (e. g. Hor. C. 2, 2, 2; id. Ep. 1, 15, 36; Val. Fl. 1, 123; Vitr. 7, 9; also, lamina, id. 5, 3), ae, f., a thin piece of metal, wood, marble, etc., a plate, leaf, layer, lamina [root la, = ἐλα- of ἐλαύνω; cf. ἐλατός]. Lit. (class.): cum lamina esset inventa, Cic. Leg. 2, 23, 58: tigna laminis clavisque religant, Caes. B. C. 2, 10, 3: cataphracta rum tegimen ferreis laminis consertum, Tac. H. 1, 79: plumbi, Plin. 34, 18, 50, § 166: ex argento laminas ducere, id.

lamnula.full: lamnŭla, ae, f. dim. lamina for lamella, a little plate of metal (eccl. Lat.): triumphi laurea lamnulis ornatur, Tert. Coron. Mil. 12 dub. (al. lamnis).

lampabilis.full: lampābĭlis, e, adj. lampo, shining (eccl. Lat.), Cassiod. in Psa. praef. 17.

lampadarius.full: lampădārĭus, ii, m. lampas, a lampbearer, torch-bearer (post-class.), Cod. Just. 12, 60, 10; Inscr. Orell. 2930; 2845 (called in Suet. Aug. 29, servus praelucens).

lampadias.full: lampădĭas, ae, m., = λαμπαδίας, a comet resembling a blazing torch, Plin. 2, 25, 22, § 90.
lampadias.short: lampădĭas, ae, m., = λαμπαδίας, a comet resembling a blazing torch, Plin.

lampadio.full: Lampadio, ōnis, m., the name of a slave, Plaut. Cist. 2, 3, 50.
lampadio.short: Lampadio, ōnis, m., the name of a slave, Plaut.

lampadiscus.full: Lampădiscus, i, m., the name of a slave, Plaut. Cist. 2, 3, 2.
lampadiscus.short: Lampădiscus, i, m., the name of a slave, Plaut.

lampado.full: lampădo, ōnis, m., i. q. bulbus, Theod. Prisc. de Diaeta, 9.

lampas.full: lampăs, ădis (late Lat. also lampă-da, ae, Jul. Val. Rer. G. Alex. 3, 28: lampadarum, Vulg. Ezech. 1, 13), f., = λαμπάς, a light, torch, flambeau (mostly poet.; cf.: lucerna, lychnus, laterna). Lit.: lampades ardentes, Plaut. Men. 5, 2, 86: illatae lampades, Att. ap. Cic. N. D. 3, 16, 41: lampadas igniferas, Lucr. 2, 25: vidi argenteum Cupidinem cum lampade, Cic. Verr. 2, 2, 47, § 115: pinguis, Ov. M. 4, 403: pingues lampades, Lucr. 4, 403: ardens, Verg. A. 9, 535: Salmoneus, dum flammas Jovis i

lampetie.full: Lampĕtĭē, ēs, f., = Λαμπετίη, a daughter of the sun-god and sister of Phaëthon, who was changed into a tree, Ov. M. 2, 349; Hyg. Fab. 154; Prop. 3, 12 (4, 11), 29.
lampetie.short: Lampĕtĭē, ēs, f., = Λαμπετίη, a daughter of the sun-god and sister of Phaëthon, who was changed into a tree, Ov.

lampetra.full: lampetra, μύραινα, the lamprey, Gloss. Philox.

lampia.full: Lampīa or Lampēa, ae, f., a town in Arcadia, Stat. Th. 4, 290.
lampia.short: Lampīa or Lampēa, ae, f., a town in Arcadia, Stat.

lampo.full: lampo, āvi, 1, v. n. lampas, to shine (eccl. Lat.); only trop. of eloquence, Cassiod. Inst. Div. Litt. 21.

lampon.full: Lampon, ōnis, m., = Λάμπων, the name of a horse, Sil. 16, 334.
lampon.short: Lampon, ōnis, m., = Λάμπων, the name of a horse, Sil.

lampridius.full: Lamprĭdĭus, ii, m. Aelius, a Roman historiographer, one of the Scriptores Historiae Augustae, Vopisc. Prob. 2 fin.; cf. Teuffel, Gesch. der Röm. Lit. § 397, 4.— A Latin orator of the fifth century, Sid. Ep. 8, 11; cf. Teuffel, Gesch. der Röm. Lit. § 459, 6.

lampsacum.full: Lampsăcum, i, n., and Lampsă-cus (-os), i, f., = Λάμψακος, a city of Mysia, on the Hellespont, now Lamsaki. —Form Lampsacum, Cic. Verr. 2, 1, 24, § 63; Mel. 1, 19.—Form Lampsacus, Val. Fl. 2, 624; Ov. Tr. 1, 10, 26.—Hence, Lampsăcēnus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Lampsacum, Lampsacene: urbs, Val. Max. 7, 3, 4: homines, i. e. inhabitants of Lampsacum, Lampsacenes, Cic. Verr. 2, 1, 24, § 63.—Subst.: Lampsăcēni, ōrum, m., the inhabitants of Lampsacum, the Lampsacenes, Cic. Verr. 2, 1, 32, § 81.
lampsacum.short: Lampsăcum, i, n., and Lampsă-cus (-os), i, f., = Λάμψακος, a city of Mysia, on the Hellespont, now Lamsaki.

lampus.full: Lampus, i, m. One of Actæon's hounds, Hyg. Fab. 181.— One of the four horses of the sun, Fulg. Myth. 1, 11.

lampyris.full: lampȳris, ĭdis, f., = λαμπυρίς, a glowworm, Plin. 11, 28, 34, § 98.
lampyris.short: lampȳris, ĭdis, f., = λαμπυρίς, a glowworm, Plin.

lamus.full: Lămus, i, m., = Λάμος. A mythic king of the Læstrygonians, a son of Neptune, and the founder of Formiæ, Hor. C. 3, 17, 1; Sil. 8, 530; hence, urbs Lami, i. e. Formiæ, Ov. M. 14, 233.— A son of Hercules and Omphale, Ov. H. 9, 54.— The name of a horse, Sil. 16, 474.

lamyrus.full: lămўrus, i, m., = λάμυρος, a seafish, Ov. Hal. 120; Plin. 32, 11, 53, § 149 (Jahn, larinus).
lamyrus.short: lămўrus, i, m., = λάμυρος, a seafish, Ov.

lana.full: lāna, ae, f. Gr. λάχνη, λάχνος, λῆνος, Dor. λᾶνος; cf. λάοιος, and v. Varr. L. L. 5, § 113 Müll., wool, Plaut. Men. 1, 2, 12; Varr. R. R. 2, 2, 18; Cic. de Or. 2, 68, 277; Col. 7, 2, 4: lanam cārĕre, to card wool, Plaut. Men. 5, 2, 46; so, lanam trahere, Juv. 2, 54: lanam deducere, id. 7, 224: lanas ducere, to spin wool, Ov. M. 4, 34: lanam expediendam conducere, for carding and spinning, Dig. 7, 8, 12: lanas tingere murice, to dye, Ov. M. 6, 9; cf.: lanam fucare veneno Assyrio, Verg. G. 2, 465:

lanaris.full: lānāris, e, adj. lana, woolly, woolbearing (ante-class.): pecus, Varr. R. R. 2, 9, 1.

lanarius1.full: lānārĭus, a, um, adj. id., of or belonging to wool, wool- (post-Aug.; cf.: lanifer, laniger, lamificus, lanatus). Adj.: herba, fuller's-weed, soapwort, Plin. 24, 18, 105, § 169; so, radix, Col. 11, 2, 35.— Substt. lānārĭus, ii, m., a worker in wool, Plaut. Aul. 3, 5, 34; cf. Arn. 2, 70; Firm. Math. 8, 19: † lanarius coactiliarius, a maker of fulled stuffs, a fuller, Inscr. Orell. 4206: † lanarius pectinarius, a woolcarder, ib. 4207.— † lānārĭa, ae, f., a wool-factory, wool-spinning establishment

lanarius2.full: Lānārĭus, ii, m., the surname of P. Calpurnius, Cic. Off. 3, 16, 66.
lanarius2.short: Lānārĭus, ii, m., the surname of P.

lanatus1.full: lānātus, a, um, adj. lana, furnished with wool, bearing wool, woolly (mostly poet. and post-Aug.). Lit.: lanatae oves, i. e. unshorn, Col. 7, 3, 2: pelles, id. 6, 2, 4: de lanata pelle, Veg. 3, 7, 1; 5, 42, 2: animalia, Juv. 15, 11.—Subst.: lānātae, ārum, f., wool-bearers, for sheep, Juv. 8, 155.— Transf.: vitis, downy, covered with down, Col. 3, 2: mala, Plin. 15, 14, 14, § 48: lupus, soft like wool, id. 9, 17, 28, § 61.—Comp.: folia lanatiore canitie, white like wool, Plin. 21, 20, 84, § 147.—

lanatus2.full: Lānātus, i, m., a surname in the gens Menenia, Liv. 4, 13.
lanatus2.short: Lānātus, i, m., a surname in the gens Menenia, Liv.

lancea.full: lancĕa, ae, f. λόγχη, acc. to Paul. ex Fest. p. 118 Müll.; acc. to Varr. ap. Gell. 15, 30 fin., of Spanish origin, a light spear, with a leather thong fastened to the middle of it, a lance, spear (cf.: telum, spiculum, hastile, pilum, jaculum, etc.): Suevi lanceis configunt, Sisenn. ap. Non. 556, 8: lancea infesta ... medium femur trajecit voluseni, Hirt. B. G. 8, 48: ceteri sparos aut lanceas portabant, Sall. C. 56, 3: Romanus miles missili pilo aut lanceis assultans, Tac. H. 1, 79; 3, 27: lata

lanceatus.full: lancĕātus, a, um, adj. lancea, made into a lance, lance-formed: armabitur ferro et ligno lanceato, Vulg. 2, Reg. 23, 7.

lanceo.full: lancĕo, āre, v. a. lancea, to wield or handle a lance (eccl. Lat.), Tert. adv. Jud. 9; id. adv. Marc. 13.

lanceola.full: lancĕŏla (lancĭŏla), ae, f. dim. id., a small lance, Capitol. Maxim. jun. 4; App. M. 8, p. 214, 7.

lanceolatus.full: lancĕŏlātus, a, um, adj. lanceola, armed with a little lance or point, lanceolated, lanceolate: plantago, Macer de Plantagine, 5.

lancia.full: Lancĭa, ae, f., a city of Hispania Tarraconensis, now Castro, Flor. 4, 12; cf. Mann. Hispan. p. 358.—Hence, Lancĭen-ses, ium, m., the inhabitants of Lancia, Plin. 3, 3, 4, § 28.— A city of the same name in Lusitania, whose inhabitants were called Lancĭenses, Plin. 4, 22, 35, § 118; cf. Mann. Hispan. p. 335.
lancia.short: Lancĭa, ae, f., a city of Hispania Tarraconensis, now Castro, Flor.

lanciarius.full: lancĭārĭus (lancĕār-), ĭi, m. lancea, a lancer (post-class.), Amm. 21, 13, 16; Cassiod. Hist. 6, 35; Vulg. Act. 23, 23.

lancicula.full: lancĭcŭla, ae, f. dim. lanx, a small dish or platter (post-class.), Arn. 2, 59.

lancinator.full: lancĭnātor, ōris, m. lancino, one that tears to pieces, a render, lacerater: gregum, Prud. στεφ. 10, 1057.

lancino.full: lancĭno, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. cf. lacer, to tear to pieces, to rend, mangle, lacerate (poet. and post-Aug.). Lit.: alium ira in cubili suo confodit ... alium intra leges celebrisque spectaculum fori lancinavit, Sen. de Ira, 1, 2, 2: morsu aliquem, Plin. 9, 6, 5, § 13: conjux membratim lancinatur, Arn. 1, 20: tot sinus Pelopennesi oram lancinant, indent, cut up, Plin. 4, 5, 9, § 19.— Trop., to destroy, consume, waste: Cat. 29, 18: vitam (al. lanciniare), to fritter away, waste, Sen. Ep. 32, 2: cre

lancula.full: lancŭla (langŭla, Varr. L. L. 5, 25, 34), ae, f. dim. lanx, a small balance, Vitr. 10, 8.

lanerum.full: lanerum, vestimenti genus ex lana sucida confectum, Paul. ex Fest. p. 118 Müll.
lanerum.short: lanerum, vestimenti genus ex lana sucida confectum, Paul.

lanestris.full: lānestris, e, adj. lana, woollen, of wool (post-class.): pallium, Vop. Aur. 29, 1.

laneus.full: lānĕus, a, um, adj. id., woollen, of wool. Lit.: pallium, Cic. N. D. 3, 34, 83: culcita ob oculos, Plaut. Mil. 4, 4, 42: infula, Verg. G. 3, 487: thorax subuculae, Suet. Aug. 82: coma flaminis, i. e. his woollen fillet, Stat. S. 5, 3, 183: effigies, little woollen figures which were distributed at the Compitalia, acc. to Paul. ex Fest. p. 121 Müll.— Prov.: dii irati laneos pedes habent, i. e. the vengeance of the gods comes unperceived, Macr. S. 1, 8, 5; Petr. 44, v. 789.— Transf. Covered with a

langa.full: langa, ae, f. Celtic, a kind of lizard, from whose urine the stone called langurium (lyncurium) was said to be produced, Plin. 37, 2, 11, § 34.

langobardi.full: Langŏbardi, ōrum, m., a people of northern Germany, west of the Elbe, Tac. G. 40; id. A. 2, 45; 11, 17: gens etiam Germana feritate ferocior, Vell. 2, 106, 2.
langobardi.short: Langŏbardi, ōrum, m., a people of northern Germany, west of the Elbe, Tac.

languefacio.full: languĕfăcĭo, fēci, factum, 3, v. a. langueo-facio, to make faint, weary, languid: incitare languentes et languefacere excitatos, Cic. Leg. 2, 15, 38.

languens.full: languens, Part. and P. a., v. langueo fin.

langueo.full: languĕo, ēre, 2, v. n. root lag-; Gr. λαγαρός, λάγνος, lewd; Lat. laxare, lactes; cf. Sanscr. lang-a, prostitute; Gr. λαγώς, hare, λαγόνες, the flanks, womb, to be faint, weary, languid (cf.: languesco, marceo, torpeo). Lit. In gen.: cum de via languerem, was fatigued with my journey, Cic. Phil. 1, 5, 12: per assiduos motus languere, to be wearied, Ov. H. 18, 161.—Poet.: flos languet, droops, Prop. 4 (5), 2, 46. Val. Fl. 7, 24 al.: languet aequor, the sea is calm, Mart. 10, 30, 12: lunae languet

languesco.full: languesco, gŭi, 3, v. inch. n. [langueo], to become faint, weak, languid (class.; syn.: torpesco, marcesco). Lit. In gen.: corpore languescit, Cic. Fin. 4, 24, 65: orator metuo ne languescat senectute, id. de Sen. 9, 28: corpora, Ov. Tr. 3, 3, 39; Plin. Pan. 18: vites languescunt, Plin. 18, 15, 37, § 138: cum flos, succisus aratro, languescit moriens, droops, withers, Verg. A. 9, 436: Bacchus in amphora Languescit, becomes mild or mellow, Hor. C. 3, 16, 34: luna languescit, becomes obscured, Tac

languidulus.full: languĭdŭlus, a, um, adj. dim. [languidus], withered, faded. * Lit.: coronae, Cic. Fragm. ap. Quint. 8, 3, 66.—* Transf.: somnus, proceeding from faintness, languid, Cat. 64, 332.

languidus.full: languĭdus, a, um, adj. langueo, faint, weak, dull, sluggish, languid (class.; cf.: lassus, fessus, fatigatus, defessus). Lit. In gen.: homines vino languidi, Cic. Cat. 2, 5, 10; cf.: vino vigiliisque languidus, Cic. Verr. 2, 3, 12, § 31: pecus, id. Fin. 2, 13, 39: boves Collo trahentes languido, Hor. Epod. 2, 64.—Transf., of things: (oculi) languidi et torpentes, dull, Quint. 11, 3, 76; cf.: vultus non languidus, id. 11, 3, 159: flumen, sluggish, Hor. C. 2, 14, 17; so, aqua, Liv. 1, 4: ventus, g

languificus.full: languĭfĭcus, a, um, adj. langueofacio, that makes faint or feeble: Leo, Aus. Ecl. in Versib. Q. Cic. 6.

languor.full: languor, ōris, m. langueo, faintness, feebleness, weariness, sluggishness, languor, lassitude. Lit. In gen. (class.; cf.: torpor, torpedo, veturnus): ubi saepe ad languorem tua duritia dederis octo validos lictores. Plaut. As. 3, 2, 28: haec deambulatio me ad languorem dedit, has fatigued me, Ter. Heaut. 4, 6, 3: (animus) cum languore corporis nec membris uti nec sensibus potest, on account of lassitude of the body, Cic. Div. 2, 62, 128: languore militum et vigiliis periculum augetur, Caes. B. G

languria.full: langūrĭa, ae, f., a kind of lizard, Plin. 37, 2, 11, § 34.
languria.short: langūrĭa, ae, f., a kind of lizard, Plin.

langurium.full: langūrĭum, ii, n., a kind of amber, also called lyncurium, Plin. 37, 2, 11, § 34; cf. langa.
langurium.short: langūrĭum, ii, n., a kind of amber, also called lyncurium, Plin.

laniamentum.full: lănĭāmentum, i, n. lanio, a tearing to pieces, August. Ep. 2, 26.

laniarius.full: lănĭārĭus, a, um, adj. lanius, pertaining to a butcher.—Only as subst. lă-nĭārĭum, i, n., a butcher's stall (anteclass.), Varr. R. R. 2, 4, 3.— lănĭā-rĭus, i, m., a butcher, Inscr. Grut. p. 1035, n. 4.

laniatio.full: lănĭātĭo, ōnis, f. 1. lanio, a tearing in pieces, a mangling, lacerating (postAug.): caedes hominum et laniationes, Sen. Clem. 2, 4, 2.

laniator.full: lănĭātor id., μακελλάριος, a butcher, i. q. lanius, Gloss. Philox.
laniator.short: lănĭātor id., μακελλάριος, a butcher, i.

laniatorium.full: lănĭātōrĭum, μακελλεῖον, κρεωπωλεῖον, a butcher's stall, i. q. laniena, Gloss. Philox.
laniatorium.short: lănĭātōrĭum, μακελλεῖον, κρεωπωλεῖον, a butcher's stall, i.

laniatus.full: lănĭātus, ūs, m. 1. lanio, a tearing in pieces, a mangling, lacerating. Lit. (rare but class.): ferarum, *Cic. Tusc. 1, 43, 104: avium, Amm. 24, 2, 8.—In plur.: avium ferarumque laniatibus objectus, Val. Max. 1, 6, 11: quid efferatius quam quod membra et artus debitoris brevissimo laniatu distrahantur, Gell. 20, 1, 19.— Trop., anguish, remorse: si recludantur tyrannorum mentes, posse adspici laniatus, Tac. A. 6, 6.

lanicia.full: lānĭcĭa, ae, and lānĭcĭes, ēi, v. lanicius.
lanicia.short: lānĭcĭa, ae, and lānĭcĭes, ēi, v.

lanicius.full: lānĭcĭus, a, um, adj. lana, of wool, woolly, fleecy: grex, Arn. 5, 174.—Hence, subst.: lānĭcĭum or -tĭum, ii, n. (anteclass. collat. form lānĭcĭa or -tĭa, ae, f., Laber. ap. Non. 212, 22; Com. Fragm. v. 67 Rib.; post-class. collat. form lānĭcĭes or -tĭes, ēi, f., Tert. adv. Marc. ap. Carm. 2, 24), wool. Lit. (poet. and in post-Aug. prose): si tibi lanicium curae, Verg. G. 3, 384: e lanicia Attica vestitus, Laber. ap. Non. 212, 22: Seres lanicio silvarum nobiles, Plin. 6, 17, 20, § 54; 8, 47, 72,

lanicutis.full: lānĭcŭtis, e, adj. lana-cutis, woollyskinned: aries, Laber. ap. Tert. Pall. 1.

lanienus.full: lānĭēnus, a, um, adj. lanius, of a butcher, butcher's: tabernae, Varr. ap. Non. 532, 20.—Hence, subst.: lānĭēna, ae, f. A butcher's stall: per myropolia et lanienas, Plaut. Ep. 2, 2, 15: lanienae et tabernae conjunctae, Liv. 44, 16 fin.— A mangling, dissecting, Prud. στεφ. 10, 497: omnique laniena excruciatus, torture, mutilation, Amm. 29, 1, 44.

lanifer.full: lānĭfer, fĕra, fĕrum, adj. lana-fero, wool-bearing, i. e. cotton-bearing: arbores, Plin. 13, 14, 28, § 90.

lanificium.full: lānĭfĭcĭum, ii, n. lanificus, the working of wool, i. e. spinning, weaving, etc. (ante-class. and post-Aug.): de lanificio neminem metuo, una aetate quae sit, Plaut. Merc. 3, 1, 22: lanificii curam suscipere, Col. 12 praef. § 9: usum lanificii docere, Just. 2, 6, 5; 2, 4, 8: filiam et neptes lanificio assuefacere, Suet. Aug. 64.

lanificus.full: lānĭfĭcus, a, um, adj. lana-facio, wool-working, that works in wool, i. e. spinning, weaving, etc. (poet.): manus, Tib. 2, 1, 10: ars, Ov. M. 6, 6; Claud. in Eutr. 2, 382: sorores, the spinning sisters, i. e. the Fates, Mart. 6, 58, 7; cf. Juv. 12, 66.— Subst.: lānĭfĭca, ae, f., a wool-spinner, Dig. 33, 7, 12, § 5 sq.

laniger.full: lānĭger, gĕra, gĕrum, adj. lana-gero, wool-bearing, fleecy (poet. and in post-Aug. prose): pecus, Att. ap. Cic. Div. 1, 22, 44: greges, Verg. G. 3, 287: arbores, i. e. cottontrees, Plin. 12, 10, 21, § 38: fertilitas, of insects. id. 11, 24, 28, § 80.— Subst. lānĭger, gĕri, m., a ram, Ov. M. 7, 312. —Of a lamb: timens, Phaedr. 1, 1, 6.—Of the constellation of the Ram, for Aries, Manil. 1, 672; 2, 200 al.— lānĭgĕra, ae, f., a lamb, sheep, Sil. 15, 703.

lanio1.full: lănĭo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. etym. dub.; cf. lacer, δάκνω, to tear or rend in pieces, to mangle, lacerate (class.; cf.: lacero, discerpo, dilanio). Lit.: hominem, Cic. Fam. 7, 1, 3: corpora a feris laniata, id. Tusc. 1, 45, 108: lanianda viscera praebere, Liv. 9, 1, 9: laniando dentibus hostem exspirare, id. 22, 51, 9: foede crura brachiaque, Tac. H. 1, 41: vestem, Ov. M. 5, 398: vestes, Quint. 11, 3, 174: Priamiden laniatum corpore toto vidit, Verg. A. 6, 494: digitis ora, Ov. A. A. 3, 678: carme

lanio2.full: lănĭo, ōnis, m. 1. lanio, a butcher (post-class.): lanionis instrumentum, Dig. 33, 7, 18; 1, 2, 2, § 24: quis tibi tunc, lanio, cernenti talia sensus, Sedul. Carm. 2, 127.

laniolum.full: lănĭŏlum, i, n. dim. lanius, a little butcher's stall, Fulg. Myth. 1 praef.

lanionius.full: lănĭōnĭus, a, um, adj. id., of or belonging to a butcher (post-Aug.): mensa, a butcher's stall, Suet. Claud. 15.

lanipendens.full: lānĭpendens, σταθμοῦχος, γυνὴ ἡ τὸν σταθμὸν παρέχουσα ταῖς ἄλλαις, one who weighs out wool for spinning, a spinning-mistress, Gloss. Philox.; cf. Inscr. Orell. 2820.
lanipendens.short: lānĭpendens, σταθμοῦχος, γυνὴ ἡ τὸν σταθμὸν παρέχουσα ταῖς ἄλλαις, one who weighs out wool for spinning, a spinning-mistress, Gloss.

lanipendium.full: lānĭpendĭum, i, m. lana-pendo, the distribution of wool (late Lat.), Caes. Aul. Reg. ad Verg. 30.

lanipendius.full: lānĭpendĭus (collat. form †lānĭ-pendus, Inscr. ap. Spon. Miscell. Antiq. p. 223; Inscr. Don. Cl. 8, 57), a, um, adj. id., that weighs out wool, portions it out for spinning (post-class.); only as subst. lānĭpendĭus, i, m., one who weighs out wool: lanipendius, σταθμοῦχος ἐριδίων, Gloss. Philox.— lānĭpendĭa, ae, f., Dig. 24, 1, 31 init.; Schol. Juv. 6, 476.

lanipes.full: lānĭpēs, pĕdis, m. lana-pes, with wool on the feet (i. e. wrapped round), woolfooted: senex, Cass. ap. Quint. 5, 11, 24.

lanista.full: lănista, ae, m., a trainer of gladiators, fencing-master (class.; cf.: gladiator, athleta, pugil). Lit.: num ille lanista omnino jam a gladiatore recessisse videtur, Cic. Rosc. Am. 40, 118: reus, tamquam clemens lanista, id. Att. 1, 16, 3: regia verba lanistae, Juv. 11, 8: circumforaneus, Suet. Vit. 12: lanistarum familias ex urbe expellere, id. Aug. 42; Juv. 6, 215.—So of fowls: rixosarum avium, Col. 8, 2, 5.— Transf., an inciter, instigator, agitator; one who stimulates to wrong or violence: h
lanista.short: lănista, ae, m., a trainer of gladiators, fencing-master (class.;

lanistatura.full: lănistātūra, ae, f. lanista, the profession of a lanista, Inscr. Tab. Aen. Heracl. ap. Mazoch. p. 424, 49.

lanisticius.full: lănistīcĭus, a, um, adj. id., of or belonging to a trainer of gladiators: familia, Petr. Fragm. Trag. 45, 4.

lanius.full: lănĭus, ĭi, m. 1. lanio, a butcher (cf. macellarius): lanii, qui concinnant liberis orbas ovīs, Plaut. Capt. 4, 2, 39; id. Ps. 1, 2, 63: cetarii, lanii, coqui, Ter. Eun. 2, 2, 26; Plaut. Trin. 2, 4, 6; cf. Cic. Off. 1, 42, 150: ab lanio cultro arrepto, Liv. 3, 48: cum de laniis aut vinariis ageretur, Suet. Claud. 40 init.; Varr. R. R. 2, 5, 11; Phaedr. 3, 4, 1.— Transf., an executioner (ante-class. and very rare): arcesse hostias, victimas, lanios, Plaut. Ps. 1, 3, 93 and 98.—Abusively, of a sur

lanivinus.full: Lānĭvīnus, a, um, and Lānĭvĭ-um, v. Lanuvium, II.
lanivinus.short: Lānĭvīnus, a, um, and Lānĭvĭ-um, v.

lannae.full: lannae, λοβοί, ear-flaps, Gloss. Philox. (sync. for laminae; v. lamina).

lano.full: lāno, ἐριοφορέω, Gloss. Philox., to bear or wear wool.

lanoculus.full: lānŏcŭlus, qui lana tegit oculi vitium, Paul. ex Fest. p. 118 Müll.
lanoculus.short: lānŏcŭlus, qui lana tegit oculi vitium, Paul.

lanositas.full: lānōsĭtas, ātis, f. lanosus, woolliness (post-class.), Tert. Pall. 3.

lanosus.full: lānōsus, a, um, adj. lana, full of wool, woolly (post-Aug.): uterus, Col. 7, 3, 7: vellus, App. M. 8, p. 214, 29.

lanterna.full: lanterna (ante-class. and later lā-terna), ae, f. Gr. λαμπτήρ, root in λάμπω; cf. Lat. limpidus, lepor, lepidus, lĕpus, a lantern, lamp, torch: a portu illic nunc cum laterna huc advenit, Plaut. Am. prol. 149: laterna Punica, id. Aul. 3, 6, 30: linea lanterna, Cic. Att. 4, 3, 5: hic caulis olebit lanternam, Juv. 5, 88; Plin. 11, 16, 16, § 49.

lanternarius.full: lanternārĭus, ii, m. lanterna, a lantern-bearer, guide: Catilinae, Cic. Pis. 9, 20.

lanugineus.full: lānūgĭnĕus, a, um, adj. lanugo, for lanuginosus, woolly, downy (post-class.): folia, App. Herb. 62.

lanugino.full: lānūgĭno, āvi, 1, v. n. lanugo, to be of wool (late Lat.): lanuginans trama, Aug. in Job, 38.

lanuginosus.full: lānūgĭnōsus, a, um, adj. lanugo, woolly, downy (Plinian): araneus, Plin. 29, 4, 27, § 85: vermiculus, id. 30, 15, 47, § 139: lanuginosa et aspera folia, id. 25, 8, 45, § 83. —Comp.: herba lanuginosior, Plin. 22, 20, 24, § 50.

lanugo.full: lānūgo, ĭnis, f. cf. Gr. λάχνη, Lat. lāna, woolly substance, down, of plants, of the cheeks, etc. (poet. and in post-Aug. prose). Lit.: flaventem primā ianugine malas Dum sequeris Clytium, Verg. A. 10, 324; so, primaque par sacrae lanugo senectae, Juv. 13, 59; cf.: comae graciles et lanuginis instar, Ov. Am. 1, 14, 23: signarat dubia teneras lanugine malas, id. M. 13, 754: a prima lanugine, Suet. Oth. 12: herba cubile praebebat, multa et molli lanugine abundans, Lucr. 5, 817: folia araneosa lanu

lanula.full: lānŭla, ae, f. dim. lana, a little wool, a small lock of wool (perh. only in Celsus), Cels. 6, 9 fin.; 7, 27, 1.

lanuvium.full: Lānŭvĭum (Länĭv-), ii, n., a town of Latium, on the Via Appia, now Cività Lavinia, Cic. Agr. 2, 35, 96; id. Mil. 10, 27; 17, 45; id. Div. 1, 44, 99; Liv. 3, 29; cf. Mann. Ital. 1, p. 635.—Hence, Lānŭvīnus (Lānĭv-), a, um, adj., of or belonging to Lanuvium, Lanuvian: ager, Cic. Div. 1, 36, 79; Hor. C. 3, 27, 3: colei, Cic. Fam. 9, 22, 4: magistratus, Liv. 41, 16.—Subst.: Lā-nŭvīnum, i, n., an estate at Lanuvium, Cic. Att. 9, 9, 4.—Plur.: Lānŭvīni, ōrum, m., inhabitants of Lanuvium, Lanuvians, Cic
lanuvium.short: Lānŭvĭum (Länĭv-), ii, n., a town of Latium, on the Via Appia, now Cività Lavinia, Cic.

lanx.full: lanx, lancis, f. cf. λέκος, λεκάνη, a plate, platter, charger, dish (class.; cf.: patina, patella, magis, scutula). In gen.: in lancibus, Plaut. Curc. 2, 3, 45: in filicatis lancibus, Cic. Att. 6, 1, 13: pomum de caelata sumere lance, Ov. P. 3, 5, 20: cumulantque oneratis lancibus aras, Verg. A. 8, 284: inter lances mensasque nitentes, Hor. S. 2, 2, 4: rotundae lances, id. ib. 2, 4, 41: qui furtum quaerere velit, nudus quaerat, linteo cinctus, lancem habens, etc., Gai. Inst. 3, 192 sqq.; cf. Pau

laocoon.full: Lāŏcŏon (Laucŏon), ontis, m., = Λαοκόων, a son of Priam and Hecaba, priest of the Thymbrean Apollo, who was killed, with his two sons, at the altar by two serpents, Verg. A. 2, 41; 201; Hyg. Fab. 135: sicut in Laocoonte, in the statue of Laocoon, Plin. 36, 5, 4, § 37.—Form Laucoön, Petr. 89.
laocoon.short: Lāŏcŏon (Laucŏon), ontis, m., = Λαοκόων, a son of Priam and Hecaba, priest of the Thymbrean Apollo, who was killed, with his two sons, at the altar by two serpents, Verg.

laodamia.full: Lāŏdămīa, ae, f., = Λαοδάμεια, a daughter of Acastus; she followed her husband Protesilāus, who had been slain by Hector, to the Lower World, Hyg. Fab. 243; Ov. P. 3, 1, 110; id. H. 13, 2; Cat. 68, 74.
laodamia.short: Lāŏdămīa, ae, f., = Λαοδάμεια, a daughter of Acastus;

laodice.full: Lāŏdĭcē, ēs, f., = Λαοδίκη. A daughter of Priam, who married Helicāon, son of the Thracian king, Antenor, Hyg. Fab. 80.— A woman, otherwise unknown, Ov. H. 19, 135.— The wife of Antiochus, Val. Max. 9, 14, 1 ext.

laodicea.full: Lāŏdĭcēa, ae, f., = Λαοδίκεια, the name of several cities. In Cœle-Syria, near Lebanon, now Jusy, Mel. 1, 12.— In Phrygia Major, also called Lāŏdĭcīa, and Laudĭcēa, now Eski Hissar, Cic. Fam. 2, 17, 4; 15, 4, 2; Plin. 5, 28, 29, § 105; Vulg. Apoc. 1, 11 al.— Hence, Lāŏdĭcensis, e, adj., of or belonging to Laodicea, Laodicean: civitas, Cic. Fam. 5. 20, 2; 13, 67, 1.— Lāŏdĭcēni (Lau-dĭcēni, Cass. ap. Cic. Fam. 12, 13, 4, v. h. l.), ōrum, m., inhabitants of Laodicea, Plin. 5, 23, 19, § 82.
laodicea.short: Lāŏdĭcēa, ae, f., = Λαοδίκεια, the name of several cities.

laomedon.full: Lāŏmĕdon, ontis, m., = Λαομέδων, the father of Priam and Ganymede, king of Troy, Cic. Tusc. 1, 26, 65; Prop. 2, 14 (3, 6), 2; Hor. C. 3, 3, 22; Ov. M. 6, 96; id. F. 6, 729; Hyg. Fab. 89.—Hence, Lāŏmĕdontēus, a, um, adj., = Λαομεδόντειος, of or belonging to Laomedon, poet., Trojan: gens, Verg. A. 4, 542: arva, Ov. M. 11, 196: flammae, i. e. the Vestal fire brought by Æneas to Rome, Sil. 1, 543.— Lāŏmĕdontĭus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Laomedon, poet., Trojan: heros, i. e. Æneas, Verg. A. 8,
laomedon.short: Lāŏmĕdon, ontis, m., = Λαομέδων, the father of Priam and Ganymede, king of Troy, Cic.

lapathum.full: lăpăthum, i, n., and lăpăthus, i, f. (m., Lucil.; v. infra. Ante-class. collat. form lăpăthĭum, ii, Varr. ap. Non. 550, 17; id. L. L. 5, § 103 Müll.), n., = λάπαθον or λάπαθος, sorrel.—Form lapathum, Plin. 20, 21, 85, § 231.—Form lapathus, Col. poët. 10, 373.—In masc., Lucil. ap. Cic. Fin. 2, 8, 24.—In a dub. form: lapathi brevis herba, Hor. S. 2, 4, 29; id. Epod. 2, 57.
lapathum.short: lăpăthum, i, n., and lăpăthus, i, f.

lapathus.full: Lăpăthüs, untis, f., a fort or castle in Thessaly, at Tempe, Liv. 44, 2; 6.
lapathus.short: Lăpăthüs, untis, f., a fort or castle in Thessaly, at Tempe, Liv.

lapicida.full: lăpĭcīda (lăpĭdĭcīda), ae, m. lapiscaedo, a quarryman, stone-cutter: qui lapides caedunt, lapicidas dici, Varr. L. L. 8, § 62 Müll.; Liv. 1, 59, 10: lapidicida, Sid. Ep. 3, 12.

lapicidinae.full: lăpĭcīdīnae († LAPICAEDINAE, Inscr. Orell. 1243.—Collat. form lapidicinae; v. infra), ārum, f. id., stone-quarries (class.): in lapicidinas facite deductus siet, Plaut. Capt. 3, 5, 78; 5, 1, 24: in Chiorum lapidicinis, Cic. Div. 1, 13, 23; Plin. 36, 7, 11, § 55: lapidicinae ubi exciduntur lapides, Paul. ex Fest. p. 118 Müll. N. cr.; Vulg. 2 Par. 34, 11.

lapicidinarius.full: lăpĭcīdīnārĭus, ii, m., a superintendent of stone-quarries, Inscr. Orell. 3246; cf.: †lapicidinarius, λαξευτής, Gloss. Philox. —Collat. form: †lapidicinarius, λιθοξόος, Gloss. Philox.
lapicidinarius.short: lăpĭcīdīnārĭus, ii, m., a superintendent of stone-quarries, Inscr.

lapicini.full: Lapicīni, ōrum, m., a people of Liguria, Liv. 41, 19.
lapicini.short: Lapicīni, ōrum, m., a people of Liguria, Liv.

lapidaris.full: lăpĭdāris, e, adj. lapis, of stone, stone-: TERMINI, Inscr. Orell. 4334.

lapidarius.full: lăpĭdārĭus, a, um, adj. id., of or belonging to stones, stone- (ante-class. and post-Aug.): latomiae, stone-quarries, Plaut. Capt. 3, 5, 65: navis, that carries stones, Petr. 117: lapidariae litterae, cut in stone, id. 58: †OPIFICES, stone-cutters, Inscr. Orell. 4208.—Subst.: lăpĭdārĭus, ii, m., a stonecutter, Dig. 13, 6, 5, § 7; Inscr. Orell. 4220; Vulg. Sirach, 45, 13.—* Full of stones, stony, for lapidosus: campi, Sol. 2, 6.

lapidatio.full: lăpĭdātĭo, ōnis, f. lapido, a throwing of stones, a stoning (class.). Lit.: fit magna lapidatio, Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 43, § 95: magna, id. de Or. 2, 47, 197; id. Dom. 6, 14; Aur. Vict. Vir. Ill. 73.—In plur.: lapidationes persaepe vidimus, Cic. Sest. 36, 77.— A shower of stones (post-class.): non diu lapidatione terruere Romanos, Flor. 3, 9, 6.—Transf., a hail-storm: grandinis lapidatio, Imp. Constant. Cod. 9, 18, 4.

lapidator.full: lăpĭdātor, ōris, m. id., a stoner, thrower of stones: percussor, lapidator, Cic. Dom. 5, 13.

lapidesco.full: lăpĭdesco, ĕre, v. inch. n. [lapis], to become stone, turn to stone, to petrify (Plinian): spongiae ipsae lapidescunt, Plin. 24, 13, 73, § 120: in balano lapidescit duritia, id. 16, 6, 8, § 21; 32, 2, 11, § 22.

lapideus.full: lăpĭdĕus, a, um, adj. id.. Of stone, consisting of stones, stone-. Lit. (class.): flumen marginibus lapideis, Varr. R. R. 3, 5, 9; Cic. Leg. 2, 18, 45: imber, a shower of stones, id. Div. 2, 28, 60; so, pluit lapideo imbri, Liv. 30, 38, 8: murus, id. 1, 38 fin.: in lapideo mortario terere, Plin. 34, 18, 50, § 169: duritia, id. 27, 11, 74, § 98: suggestus, Col. 9, 7, 1.— Trop. (ante-class.): lapideo sunt corde multi, quos non miseret neminis, Enn. ap. Fest. p. 162 Müll. (Trag. v. 174 Vahl.): lapi

lapidicaesor.full: lăpĭdĭcaesor, λατόμος, a stone-cutter, Gloss. Philox.

lapido.full: lăpĭdo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. and n. lapis, to throw stones at a person or thing, to stone ( = lapidibus obruo, percutio; not ante-Aug.). With personal object: exercitus imperatorem lapidavit, Flor. 1, 22; Petr. 93: eum lapidare coeperunt, Auct. B. Hisp. 23: Stephanum, Vulg. Act. 7, 58: Paulum, id. ib. 14, 18.— To cast stones upon, to bury: praeteriens aliquis nos lapidabit, Petr. 114, 11.— With an inanim. object: quo defunctus est die, lapidata sunt templa, Suet. Calig. 5.— Trop., to assail, assa

lapidositas.full: lăpĭdōsĭtas, ātis, f. lapidosus, a stony hardness (post-class.), Tert. Hab. Mul. 6.

lapidosus.full: lăpĭdōsus, a, um, adj. lapis, full of stones, stony. Lit.: lapidosa terra, Varr. R. R. 1, 9: montes, Ov. M. 1, 44: ager, id. ib. 8, 799: fluvius, id. ib. 15, 23.— Transf., hard as stone, stony: panis, Hor. S. 1, 5, 91: corna, Verg. G. 2, 34: genus pirorum, Pall. 3, 25, 1; 3, 25, 6: gemma, Plin. 37, 10, 54, § 145: chiragra, Pers. 5, 58.—Comp.: est lapidosius, Plin. 34, 12, 30, § 120.

lapillisco.full: lăpillisco (lăpillesco), ĕre, v. inch. n. [lapillus], to become stone, turn to stone; trop., to become hard, be distended (eccl. Lat.), Tert. ad Nat. 2, 12.

lapillulus.full: lăpillŭlus, i, m. dim. id., a very little stone, gravel-stone (late Lat.), Sol. 10, 12.

lapillus.full: lăpillus, i, m. dim. lapis, a little stone, a pebble (perh. not ante-Aug.). In gen.: invitat somnos crepitantibus unda lapillis, Ov. M. 11, 604; Plin. 10, 23, 30, § 59 sq. —Lucky days were marked with white, and unlucky ones with black stones (cf. calculus, 2. e.); hence: felix utraque lux diesque nobis Signandi melioribus lapillis, i. e. with white stones, Mart. 9, 53, 5; cf.: hunc Macrine, diem numera meliore lapillo, Pers. 2, 1; cf. also Plin. 7, 40, 41, § 131. —In trials at law, a white ston

lapio.full: lăpĭo, īre, v. a. lapis, to turn into stone, make hard like stone, to petrify, harden (ante-class.): lapit significat obdurefacit et lapidem facit. Pacuvius Periboea: lapit cor cura, Non. 23, 7 sq. (Pac. Fragm. Trag. v. 276 Rib.): lapit dolore afficit, Paul. ex Fest. p. 118 Müll.

lapis.full: lăpis, ĭdis (abl. lapi, Enn. ap. Prisc. 708 P.; gen. plur. lapiderum, C. Gell. ap. Charis. p. 40 P.), m. (f.: tanto sublatae sunt augmine tunc lapides, Enn. ap. Non. 211, 9) [etym. dub.; perh. from same root with rupes; cf. Corss. Ausspr. 1, 545; not connected with λᾶας, Georg Curtius Gr. Etym. p. 542], a stone (cf.: saxum, silex, cautes, cos, calculus). In gen.: stillicidi casus lapidem cavat, Lucr. 1, 313: undique lapides in murum jaci coepti sunt, Caes. B. G. 2, 6; cf. Cic. Mil. 15, 41: pars

lapitha.full: Lăpĭtha, ae, com., and Lăpĭthes, ae, m., a Lapitha; plur.: Lăpĭthae, ārum, m., = Λαπίθαι, the Lapithæ, a rude tribe of mountaineers in Thessaly, about Olympus, who fought with the Centaurs at the wedding of Pirithŏüs, king of the Lapithæ, Ov. M. 12, 261; 536; Hor. C. 1, 18, 8; 2, 12, 5; Cic. Pis. 10, 22.—Gen. plur.: Lapithūm, Verg. A. 7, 304.—Sing. gen.: Lapithae, Ov. M. 12, 250.—In fem. adjectively: Lapithae genus heroinae, Prop. 2, 2, 9 (Müll. heroine); cf.: Lapithes eques, Val. Fl. 5, 516.— H
lapitha.short: Lăpĭtha, ae, com., and Lăpĭthes, ae, m., a Lapitha;

lappa.full: lappa, ae, f., a bur, Verg. G. 1, 153; Ov. P. 2, 1, 14; Plin. 18, 17, 44, § 153; 21, 17, 64, § 104 al.— Lappa, ae, m., a Roman surname; e. g. Rubrenus Lappa, a tragedian, Juv. 7, 72.
lappa.short: lappa, ae, f., a bur, Verg.

lappaceus.full: lappācĕus, a, um, adj. lappa, burshaped, bur-like: capita, Plin. 22, 17, 19, § 41.

lappago.full: lappāgo, ĭnis, f. id., a plant resembling a bur, Plin. 26, 10, 65, § 102.

laprius.full: Laprĭus, ii, m., a surname of Jupiter, Enn. ap. Lact. 1, 22, 23 (Eutr. p. 173 Vahl.).
laprius.short: Laprĭus, ii, m., a surname of Jupiter, Enn.

lapsana.full: lapsăna (lampsăna), ae, f. (also lapsănium, ii, n., Hier. ap. Reg. S. Pachom. 52), = λαψάνη and λαμψάνη, an edible plant, charlock, Sinapis arvensis, Linn.; Plin. 20, 9, 37, § 96; Varr. R. R. 3, 16, 25; Cels. 2, 25.—Prov.: lapsanā vivere, to live on a meagre diet, Plin. 19, 8, 41, § 144.

lapsio.full: lapsĭo, ōnis, f. 1. labor, a sliding; trop., an inclination, tendency: haec in bonis rebus facilitas nominetur, in malis proclivitas, ut significet lapsionem, Cic. Tusc. 4, 12, 28.

lapso.full: lapso, āre, v. freq. n. [id.], to slip, slide, stumble, fall. Lit. (poet. and in postAug. prose): (Priamum) in multo lapsantem sanguine nati, Verg. A. 2, 551: sanguine suo et lubrico paludum lapsantes (equi), Tac. A. 1, 65: lapsantibus equis, id. H. 1, 79: lapsantem gressum firmare, Sil. 3, 632; Flor. 2, 10, 3: Gyan vidi lapsare cruentae Vulnere Myrmidonis, fall, Stat. Th. 5, 223: plantis lapsantibus, Amm. 14, 2, 6.— Trop. (post-class.): verba lapsantia, i. e. babbled forth, Gell. 1, 15, 1.

lapsus1.full: lapsus, a, um, Part., from 1. labor.

lapsus2.full: lapsus, ūs, m. 1. labor, a falling, fall; a slipping, sliding, gliding, running, flowing, flying, flight, etc. (class.). Lit.: ac celeri ferme percurrunt fulmina lapsu, Lucr. 6, 324: atque ea, quae lapsu tandem cecidere vetusto, Cic. poët. Div. 1, 11, 19: infrenis equi lapsu jacens, Verg. A. 10, 750: tum quassao nutant turres, lapsumque minantur, Luc. 6, 136: horrere lapsus tectorum assiduos, Juv. 3, 8.—Of a landslide: locus recenti lapsu terrae abruptus, Liv. 21, 36, 2: lapsu scalarum exanimatu

laquear.full: lăquĕar, āris (or lăquĕāre, Verg. Cul. 62; cf. Prisc. p. 691 P.; and: laqueare, συνίθωμα, Gloss. Philox.: lăquĕārĭum, ii, acc. to Isid. Orig. 19, 12), n. kindr. with laqueus and lacunar, a panelled or fretted ceiling (poet. and in post-Aug. prose; usu. in plur.): laquearia, quae nunc et in privatis domibus auro teguntur, Plin. 33, 3, 18, § 57: laetior quam laquearium auro, id. 12, 1, 5, § 9: dependent lychni laquearibus aureis, Verg. A. 1, 726: laquearia tecti, id. ib. 8, 25; Sil. 7, 142: caelat

laquearius.full: lăquĕārĭus, ii, m. laquear, one that makes panelled ceilings, a ceiling-maker (late Lat.): architecti, laquearii, Cod. Th. 13, 4, 2.— Perh. a kind of gladiator; v. the foll. art.

laqueator.full: lăquĕātor, ōris, m. laqueus, an ensnarer, a kind of gladiator who attempted to catch his adversary with a noose, acc. to Isid. Orig. 18, 56 (al. laquearius).

laqueatus1.full: lăquĕātus, a, um, Part., v. 1. laqueo.

laqueatus2.full: lăquĕātus, a, um, Part., v. 2. laqueo.

laqueo1.full: lăquĕo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. laqueus, to noose, ensnare, entangle (poet. and in post-Aug. prose). Lit.: extentis laqueare profundum Retibus, Manil. 5, 659: cassem Per senos circum usque sinus laqueabis, i. e. to plait, Grat. Cyn. 40: corpus laqueatum et distentum, Col. 6, 19, 3: laqueatis resistentium membris, Amm. 31, 2, 9: laqueatis cruribus (elephantorum), entangled, Sol. 20, 11.— Trop., to ensnare, etc.: si te forte oculi dextri laqueaverit error, Juvenc. 1, 537.

laqueo2.full: lăquĕo (or lăcŭo), āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. laquear, to adorn with a panelled or fretted ceiling (perh. only in the part.): tectis caelatis lacuatis, panelled, fretted, Enn. ap. Cic. Tusc. 1, 35, 85 (Trag. v. 121 Vahl.); Serv. Verg. A. 1, 726: tecta, Hor. C. 2, 16, 11: Jovis Capitolini templum, non laqueatum auro tantum, sed parietibus totis lammina inauratum, Liv. 41, 20, 9; cf.: considerat templum, videt undique tectum pulcherrime laqueatum, Cic. Verr. 2, 1, 51, § 133: laqueata tecta, id. Leg. 2, 1

laqueus.full: lăquĕus, i, m. cf. Gr. ἕλκω, draw, ὁλκός; Lat. lacio; perh. Germ. locken, a noose, snare (class.; cf. tendicula). Lit., Plaut. Truc. 2, 4, 41: saxa laqueis vinciebat, Sall. J. 94: laqueis falces avertebant, Caes. B. G. 7, 22: collum in laqueum inserere, Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 17, § 37: inicere laqueum, to throw over any one, Liv. 1, 26: inicere cervicibus laqueum, Suet. Vit. 17: laqueo gulam alicui frangere, to throttle, strangle, Sall. C. 55, 4: ad laqueum compellere aliquem, to the halter, Plin. 36,

lar1.full: Lār or Lars, Lartis, m., a prænomen of Etruscan origin (in Etruscan, usu: the prefix of the first-born, while a younger son was called Aruns. The name Lar, Lars, or Larth was an honorary appellation in Etruscan, = Engl. lord): Lars Tolumnius, rex Veientium, Cic. Phil. 9, 2; Liv. 4, 17, 1; 4, 58, 7: ad Lartem Porsenam, id. 2, 9 (nom. Lar, Charis. 110 P.).
lar1.short: Lār or Lars, Lartis, m., a prænomen of Etruscan origin (in Etruscan, usu: the prefix of the first-born, while a younger son was called Aruns.

lar2.full: Lār, Lăris, m., v. 1. Lares, ium.

lara.full: Lăra, ae, and Lărunda, ae, f., daughter of the river-god Almo, a nymph whose tongue was cut out by Jupiter on account of her talkativeness, and who was worshipped in Rome under the name of Tacita or Muta: Lara, Ov. F. 2, 599 sq.: Larunda, Varr. L. L. 5, § 74 Müll.; Lact. 1, 20, 35; Aus. Idyll. ap. Monos. de Deis, 9.
lara.short: Lăra, ae, and Lărunda, ae, f., daughter of the river-god Almo, a nymph whose tongue was cut out by Jupiter on account of her talkativeness, and who was worshipped in Rome under the name of Tacita or Muta: Lara, Ov.

laralia.full: Lărālĭa, ĭum, n. 1. Lares, a festival in honor of the Lares, celebrated on the first of May; the festival of the Lares, Paul. ex Fest. p. 253 Müll.

lararium.full: lărārĭum, ii, n. id., a part of the interior of a Roman house, in which the tutelar deities (Lares) were placed, the chapel of the Lares, Lampr. Alex. Sev. 29, 2; 31, 4 sq.

larbason.full: larbăson, i, n., antimony, Plin. 33, 6, 33, § 101 (Sillig, larbasim).

larcius.full: Larcĭus, i, m.: T. Larcius Flavus, a Roman dictator, Cic. Rep. 2, 32, 56; Liv. 2, 18, 5.

lardarius.full: lardārĭus, ii, m. lardum for laridum, a pork-butcher, pork-seller, Inscr. Grut. 647, 4.

larentia.full: Lārentĭa (Lārentīna, Lact. 1, 20 init.), ae, f. (also called Acca Larentia), acc. to the myth, the wife of Faustulus, and mother of the twelve Arval Brothers, who suckled and reared the twins Romulus and Remus, Ov. F. 3, 55; Liv. 1, 4, 7; Gell. 6, 7; Varr. L. L. 6, § 23 Müll.—Lārentā-lia, ium, n., the festival celebrated in honor of Larentia, on the 23d of December, Ov. F. 3, 57; Paul. ex Fest. p. 119 Müll.—Also in a lengthened form: †Lārentīnal, Varr. L. L. 6, 3, 58, § 23 Müll.

lares1.full: Lăres (old form † Lăses, Inscr. Fratr. Arval.; cf. Varr. L. L. 6, § 2 Müll.), um and ĭum (Larum, Varr. L. L. 5, § 49 Müll.; Cic. Rep. 5, 5, 7; id. N. D. 3, 25, 63; id. Leg. 2, 8, 19; Inscr. Orell. 961: Larium, Liv. 40, 52), m. old Lat. Lases; Etrusc. Laran, Lalan; root las-; cf. lascivus, tutelar deities, Lares, belonging orig. to the Etruscan religion, and worshipped especially as the presiders over and protectors of a particular locality (cf. Otfr. Müll. Etrusc. 2, p. 90 sq.): praestites, the

lares2.full: Lăres, ĭum, f., a city in Numidia, Sall. J. 90 Kritz N. cr.
lares2.short: Lăres, ĭum, f., a city in Numidia, Sall.

larga.full: Larga, ae, f., the name of a woman of bad repute, Juv. 14, 25.
larga.short: Larga, ae, f., the name of a woman of bad repute, Juv.

large.full: largē, adv., v. 1. largus fin. A.

largificus.full: largĭfĭcus, a, um, adj. largus-facio, bountiful, Lucr. 2, 627: grando mixta imbri largifico, Pac. ap. Cic. de Or. 3, 39, 157 (Trag. Fragm. v. 414 Rib.).

largifluus.full: largĭflŭus, a, um, adj. large-fluo, flowing copiously, copious (ante-class.): fons, Lucr. 5, 598.

largiloquus.full: largĭlŏquus, a, um, adj. large-loquor, talking copiously, talkative (Plautin.): largiloquae sumus: plus loquimur, quam sat est, Plaut. Cist. 1, 2, 2: lingua, id. Mil. 2, 3, 47.

largimentum.full: largīmentum, i, n. largior, for largitas, bounty, gift, Fulg. Myth. praef. 1.

largior.full: largĭor, ītus, 4 (ante-class. and poet.; collat. form of the imperf. largibar, Prop. 1, 3, 25; fut. largibere, Plaut. Bacch. 4, 7, 30; inf. largirier, id. As. 5, 2, 82.—Act. collat. form, v. fin.), v. dep. 1. largus, to give bountifully, to lavish, bestow, dispense, distribute, impart (class.; cf.: dono, suppedito). Lit. In gen.: amico homini mea ex crumena largiar, Plaut. Pers. 2, 3, 13: ex ea (dote) largiri te illi, id. Trin. 3, 3, 14: cenam esurientibus, id. Am. 1, 1, 155: qui eripiunt aliis,

largitas.full: largĭtas, ātis, f. 1. largus, abundance, bounty, liberality (rare but class.): largitas nimia, opp. parsimonia, Ter. Heaut. 3, 1, 32: quae istaec subita est largitas? id. Ad. 5, 9, 28: tui muneris, Cic. Brut. 4, 16: terra fruges cum maxima largitate fundit, id. N. D. 2, 62, 156.

largiter.full: largĭter, adv., v. 1. largus fin. B.

largitio.full: largītĭo, ōnis, f. largior, a giving freely, a granting, bestowing, dispensing, distributing, imparting. Lit. In gen. (class.): largitio, quae fit ex re familiari, fontem ipsum benignitatis exhaurit, Cic. Off. 2, 15, 52: largitione redemit militum voluntates, Caes. B. C. 1, 39 fin.: his pauca ad spem largitionis addidit, id. ib. 2, 28: maximas largitiones fecit, id. ib. 3, 31: largitio et communicatio civitatis, a granting, Cic. Balb. 13, 31: aequitatis, a distributing, dispensing, id. Mur. 20,

largitionalis.full: largītĭōnālis, e, adj. largitio, II., of or belonging to the imperial treasury: officiales, treasury-officers, masters of the treasury, Cod. Th. 12, 6, 13; also subst.: largī-tĭōnālis, is, m., a treasury-officer, Vop. Carin. 19.

largitor1.full: largītor, āri, false read. for largiri te, Plaut. Trin. 3, 3, 14; v. Ritschl ad h. l. and proleg. p. 68.

largitor2.full: largītor, ōris, m. largior, a liberal giver, a bestower, granter, dispenser, distributer, imparter. In gen. (rare; not in Cic.): multarum rerum ac maxume pecuniae largitor, Sall. J. 95: largitor voluntarius repente senatus factus, Liv. 6, 16: minime largitore duce, liberal, id. 6, 2; cf. praedae, id. 9, 42: Bacche, sacri largitor laticis, dispenser, Sil. 7, 164.— In partic., in a bad sense, a briber (class.): exsistunt in re publica plerumque largitores et factiosi, Cic. Off. 1, 19, 64: cujuscum

largitudo.full: largĭtūdo, ĭnis, f. 1. largus, liberality (for largitas): largitudo nusquam invenitur, nisi apud Nepotem, Charis. p. 78 P.

largitus1.full: largĭtus, adv., v. largus fin. C.

largitus2.full: largītus, a, um, Part., v. largior.

largiusculus.full: largĭuscŭlus, a, um, adj. dim. [1. largus], rather copious: haustus, Sol. 7, § 4.

largus1.full: largus, a, um, adj. perh. for lasgus; Sanscr. root lash, desire; Gr. λᾶ- in λιλαίομαι, λῆμα; cf. Lat. lascivus, abundant, copious, plentiful, large, much. In gen. (mostly poet. and in post-Aug. prose): pabula, abundant, Lucr. 5, 869: haustus, id. 1, 412: semen, id. 4, 1238: imbres, id. 1, 282; cf.: undae fluminis, id. 1, 1031: lux, id. 2, 806; cf.: (sol) cum terras larga luce compleverit, Cic. N. D. 2, 19, 49: odores, Ov. M. 4, 758: aër, Lucr. 4, 894—Comp.: largior ignis, Hor. S. 1, 8, 44: largi

largus2.full: Largus, i, m., a Roman surname, esp. in the gens Scribonia, Cic. Fam. 6, 8, 1; id. de Or. 2, 59, 240: P. Largus Caecina, Tac. A. 11, 33.—Hence, Largĭānus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to a Largus, Largian: senatusconsultum, Just. Inst. 3, 7 fin.
largus2.short: Largus, i, m., a Roman surname, esp.

laridum.full: lārĭdum, and sync. lardum (collat. form, lārĭda, ae, f., sc. caro, Cod. Th. 8, 4, 17), i, n. kindr. with λαρός, λαρινός, fattened, fat, the fat of bacon, lard.—Form laridum: quanta pernis pestis veniet! quanta labes larido! Plaut. Capt. 4, 3, 3; 4, 2, 67; id. Men. 1, 3, 27.—Form lardum: lardum ossa fracta solidat, Plin. 28, 16, 65, § 227; Hor. S. 2, 6, 64; 85; Mart. 5, 78; Juv. 11, 84.—In plur.: larda, Ov. F. 6, 169.

larifuga.full: lărĭfŭga, ae, m. 2. lar-fugio, a vagabond: larifuga nescio quis, Petr. 57, 3.

larignus.full: lărignus, a, um, adj. larix, of the larch-tree, larch-: materies, Vitr. 2, 9, 15.

larinum.full: Lārīnum, i, n., a town of Samnium, in the territory of the Frentani, near Teanum, now Larino, Cic. Att. 7, 13, 7; 7, 13, 6; id. Clu. 8, 27; Mel. 2, 4.—Hence, Lārī-nas, ātis, adj., of or belonging to the town of Larinum: Larinas socrus, Cic. Clu. 7: municipium, id. ib. 5.—In plur. subst.: Lā-rīnātes, ium, m., inhabitants of Larinum: in foro Larinatium, Cic. Clu. 13, 38.
larinum.short: Lārīnum, i, n., a town of Samnium, in the territory of the Frentani, near Teanum, now Larino, Cic.

larissa.full: Lārissa, ae, f., = Λάρισσα, the name of several cities. In Thessaly, on the Peneus, now Yeni-shehr or Larissa, Mel. 2, 3; Plin. 4, 8, 15, § 29; Caes. B. C. 3, 80; Hor. C. 1, 7, 11; Luc. 6, 355.— Hence, Lāris-saeus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to the town of Larissa, Larissean: Achilles, i. e. Thessalian, Verg. A. 2, 197; hence also, hasta, i. e. of Achilles, Ser. Samm. 46, 836: Coronis, Ov. M. 2, 542.—In plur. subst.: Lārissaei, ōrum, m., inhabitants of Larissa, Larisseans, Caes. B. C. 3, 81.—
larissa.short: Lārissa, ae, f., = Λάρισσα, the name of several cities.

larissus.full: Larissus (Larīsus), i, m., a river in Achaia, now Mana, Liv. 27, 31.
larissus.short: Larissus (Larīsus), i, m., a river in Achaia, now Mana, Liv.

larius.full: Lārĭus, ii, m., a lake in Gallia Cisalpina, on which Comum lay, now Lago di Como, Verg. G. 2, 159; Plin. Ep. 9, 7, 1; Plin. 3, 19, 23, § 131.—Hence, Lārĭus, a, um, adj., of Larius, Larian: Larium litus, Cat. 35, 4.
larius.short: Lārĭus, ii, m., a lake in Gallia Cisalpina, on which Comum lay, now Lago di Como, Verg.

larix.full: lărix, ĭcis f. (m. Vitruv., v. infra), = λάριξ, a larch, larch-tree, Plin. 16, 10, 19, § 43; Vitr. 2, 9, 14; Luc. 9, 920.

laronia.full: Lărōnĭa, ae, f., a female name, Juv. 2, 65; Mart. 2, 32, 5.
laronia.short: Lărōnĭa, ae, f., a female name, Juv.

lartidius.full: Lartidĭus, i, m., prop. name, an imitator of Ulysses, Cic. Att. 7, 1, 9.

larus.full: lărus (lăros), i, m., = λάρος, a ravenous sea-bird, perh. the mew, Vulg. Lev. 11, 16; id. Deut. 14, 15; cf.: larus, λάρος, Gloss. Philox.
larus.short: lărus (lăros), i, m., = λάρος, a ravenous sea-bird, perh.

larva.full: larva (ante-class. as trisyl. lārŭa), ae, f. 2. lar, a ghost, spectre: larvae stimulant virum, Plaut. Capt. 3, 4, 66: amator qui me et uxorem ludificatust larva, id. Cas. 3, 4, 2; id. Aul. 4, 4, 15: cum mortuis non nisi larvas luctari, Plin. praef. H. N. § 31.—As a term of reproach, hobgoblin, scarecrow: etiam loquere larŭa? Plaut. Merc. 5, 4, 20: nam haec quidem edepol larvarum plenast, possessed, id. Am. 2, 2, 145.— Transf. A mask (cf. persona): nil illi larva et tragicis opus esse cothurnis,

larvalis.full: larvālis (larŭālis), e, adj. larva, like a ghost, ghostly (post-Aug.): habitus, Sen. Ep. 25; so, si larvali habitu processeris, Lex ap. Paul. Sent. 3, 4, b, 2: macies larŭalis, Auct. Priap. 32, 13.

larvo.full: larvo, no perf., ātum (part. ante-class. larŭātus), 1, v. a. larva, to bewitch, enchant (ante- and post-class., and used almost exclusively in the part. perf.): artus larvari, Firm. Math. 3, 14.—P. a. as subst.: larvans, ntis, m., an enchanter, a dealer in magic: hunc denique qui larvam putat ipse est larvans, App. Mag. p. 315, 20 Hildeb. (al. larvatus).—Part. perf.: larŭātus, a, um, bewitched, enchanted: quid illi esse morbi dixeras? ... Num larvatust aut cerritus? Plaut. Men. 5, 4, 1: pro laru

larymna.full: Larymna, ae, f., the name of a small town in Bœotia, Mel. 2, 3; Plin. 4, 7, 12, § 26.
larymna.short: Larymna, ae, f., the name of a small town in Bœotia, Mel.

lasanum.full: lăsănum, i, n., = λάσανον, a utensil. Perh. a cooking-utensil, cooking-pot, Hor. S. 1, 6, 109.— A chamber utensil, closestool, Petr. 41, 9.
lasanum.short: lăsănum, i, n., = λάσανον, a utensil.
