Non. 210, 5.— Plur. lentes, Scrib. Comp. 114), f. (masc., Titin. ap. Non. 210, 5), a lentil: lens amat solum tenue, Plin. 18, 12, 31, § 123: Pelusiaca (Egyptian lentils were considered the best), Verg. G. 1, 228; cf. Mart. 13, 9, 1; Gell. 17, 8, 2.

lenteo.full: lentĕo, ēre, v. n. lentus, to proceed slowly: lentet opus, Lucil. ap. Prisc. p. 800 P.

lentesco.full: lentesco, ĕre, v. inch. n. [lentus], to become viscous or sticky; to become pliant, soft (perh. not ante-Aug.). Lit.: salix, si minus lenta est, in stercore obruenda, ut lentescat, Col. 11, 2, 92: sed picis in morem ad digitos lentescit habendo, becomes viscous, adheres, Verg. G. 2, 250: ut in picem resinamve lentescit, Tac. G. 45: gemma cerae modo lentescit, Plin. 37, 10, 70, § 185: metallum in virgulas lentescens, Hier. Ep. 24, n. 3.— Trop., to slacken, relax: lentescunt tempore curae, Ov. A.

lenticula.full: lentĭcŭla, ae, f. dim. 2. lens, a lentil. Lit.: faba vel lenticula, Cels. 2, 18: hoc mense lenticulam seres, Pall. 3, 4.— Transf. The shape of a lentil, lentilshape, Plin. 37, 12, 75, § 196.— A vessel shaped like a lentil: vasa fictilia (quas a similitudine lenticulas vocant), Cels. 2, 17, § 25; cf. Isid. Orig. 20, 7, 4; Vulg. 1 Reg. 10, 1.— A freckly eruption, freckles, Plin. 26, 1, 5, § 7: lenticulam tollunt galbanum et nitrum, Cels. 6, 5; cf. lentigo.

lenticularis.full: lentĭcŭlāris, e, adj. lenticula, like a lentil: ampulla lenticulari formā, lentilshaped, App. Flor. n. 9, p. 346, 26.

lentiginosus.full: lentīgĭnōsus, a, um, adj. lentigo, full of freckles, freckled: vir lentiginosi oris, Val. Max. 1, 7, 6 ext.

lentigo.full: lentīgo, ĭnis, f. 2. lens, a lentil-shaped spot. In gen.: stellio plenus lentigine, Plin. 29, 4, 28, § 90: chartae, id. 13, 12, 25, § 81.— In partic., a freckly eruption, freckles, lentigo: lentiginem habere, Plin. 30, 2, 6, § 16: faciem lentigine obducit, id. 29, 4, 22, § 73: lentiginem corrigere, id. 22, 25, 74, § 156: emendare, id. 23, 1, 16, § 23: sanare, id. 24, 9, 38, § 63: lentigines e facie tollere, id. 20, 2, 4, § 9.

lentinus.full: Lentīnus, i, m., the name of a man, Mart. 3, 43.
lentinus.short: Lentīnus, i, m., the name of a man, Mart.

lentipes.full: lentĭpēs, ĕdis, adj. lentus-pes, slowfooted, slow-paced: comes, Aus. Ep. 21, 40.

lentiscifer.full: lentiscĭfer, fĕra, fĕrum, adj. lentiscus-fero, bearing mastic-trees: Linternum, Ov. M. 15, 713.

lentiscinus.full: lentiscĭnus, a, um, adj. lentiscus, of or from the mastic-tree: oleum, Plin. 23, 2, 32, § 65: resina, id. 24, 6, 22, § 36; Cael. Aur. Acut. 2, 37, 197 al.

lentiscus.full: lentiscus, i, f., lentiscum, i, n., the mastic - tree, Pistacia lentiscus, Linn. Lit.: viridis semperque gravata Lentiscus, Cic. poët. Div. 1, 9, 15.— Transf. Mastic-oil, Cato, R. R. 7, 4; Varr. R. R. 1, 60; Plin. 15, 6, 6, § 21.— A toothpick of mastic-wood, Mart. 14, 22, 1; 3, 82, 9; 6, 74, 3.
lentiscus.short: lentiscus, i, f., lentiscum, i, n., the mastic - tree, Pistacia lentiscus, Linn.

lentitia.full: lentĭtĭa, ae (lentĭtĭes, ēi, Auct. Aetn. 540), f. lentus, pliancy, flexibility, toughness, viscosity, stickiness: virgas sequacis ad vincturas lentitiae, Plin. 16, 37, 68, § 174; 16, 40, 77, § 210: lactucae lentitiam pituitae digerunt, id. 20, 7, 26, § 64; cf. lentor.

lentitudo.full: lentĭtūdo, ĭnis, f. id., slowness, sluggishness, inactivity. Lit.: conjuratorum, Tac. A. 15, 51; Vell. 2, 11, 2.— Trop.: dulness, apathy, insensibility, Cic. Tusc. 4, 19, 43: omnino non irasci est non solum gravitatis, sed nonnumquam etiam lentitudinis, id. Q. Fr. 1, 1, 13, § 38.—Of speech: libros ejusdem lentitudinis ac teporis, dulness, heaviness, Tac. Or. 21, 6.

lento1.full: lento, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. id., to make flexible, to bend (poet. and in postclass. prose). Lit.: arcus lentare et fundere glandes, i. e. to draw a bow, Stat. Achill. 1, 436; so, arcus, id. Th. 1, 703: Gortynia cornua, id. ib. 3, 587.— Transf., to bend, i. e. ply the oar: Trinacriā lentandus remus in undā, Verg. A. 3, 384: remos, Sen. Agm. 437.— Trop. Of time, to draw out, prolong, lengthen, protract: lentare fervida bella, Sil. 8, 11: fata Romana lentata, Treb. Claud. 6.— To moderate: lentatus v

lento2.full: Lento, ōnis, m. lentus, sluggard, a Roman surname: Caesennius Lento, Cic. Phil. 11, 6, 3; 12, 9, 23.

lentor.full: lentor, ōris, m. lentus, pliancy, flexibility; toughness, stickiness, viscosity (Plinian; cf. lentitia): ad rotarum axes lentore fraxinus utilis, Plin. 16, 43, 84, § 229: lentor resinosus, id. 13, 6, 12, § 54: picis, id. 16, 11, 22, § 53: usque ad lentorem aliquid subigere, id. 17, 14, 24, § 111.

lentulus1.full: lentŭlus, a, um, adj. dim. [lentus], rather slow: lentulus aut restrictus, Cic. Att. 10, 11, 2.

lentulus2.full: Lentŭlus, i, m., a surname of a distinguished family in the gens Cornelia. Cn. Cornelius Lentulus Clodianus, consul 682 A. U. C., Cic. Balb. 8, 19; 14, 33; Cic. Verr. 2, 2, 39, § 95.— Cn. Cornelius Lentulus Marcellinus, consul 698 A. U. C., Cic. Q. Fr. 2, 1, 2; 2, 6, 5; id. Brut. 70, 247.— L. Cornelius Lentulus Crus, consul 705 A. U. C., Cic. Phil. 2, 21, 51; Hirt. B. G. 8, 50.— P. Cornelius Lentulus Sura, one of Catiline's fellow-conspirators, Cic. Cat. 3, 3 sq.; Sall. C. 46.— P. Cornelius Lent
lentulus2.short: Lentŭlus, i, m., a surname of a distinguished family in the gens Cornelia.

lentus.full: lentus, a, um, adj. cf. lenis, pliant, flexible, tough, tenacious, sticky, viscous (syn.: flexilis, tardus, serus). Lit.: viburna, Verg. E. 1, 26: vitis, id. ib. 3, 38: genistae, id. G. 2, 12: rami, id. ib. 4, 558: flagellum, Phaedr. 3, 6, 6: verbera, i. e. produced with the limber whip, Verg. G. 3, 208: argentum, id. A. 7, 634; Cat. 61, 106; Tib. 4, 1, 171: lentior salicis virgis, Ov. M. 13, 800: gluten visco et pice lentius, tougher, more tenacious, Verg. G. 4, 41: ita istaec nimis lenta vincl

lenullus.full: lēnullus, i, m. dim. 2. leno, a little pimp, Plaut. Poen. 2, 1, 25 (ap. Prisc. p. 614 P., lenulus).

lenuncularius.full: lēnuncŭlārĭus, ĭi, m. 2. lenunculus, for lembunculus, one who sails in a small vessel, Inscr. Orell. 3248; 4054; 4104.

lenunculus1.full: lēnuncŭlus, i, m. dim. 2. leno, a young go-between: aere militari tetigero lenunculum, Plaut. Poen. 5, 5, 7; cf. Prisc. p. 614 P.

lenunculus2.full: lēnuncŭlus, i, m. dim. for lembunculus, from lembus, a small sailingvessel, a bark, skiff: pauci lenunculi conveniebant, Caes. B. C. 2, 43: in lenunculo piscantes, Sall. Fragm. ap. Non. 534, 32: occursu lenunculorum, Tac. A. 14, 5: piscatorius, Amm. 14, 2, 10.

leo1.full: lĕo, lēre, v. a. The root of deleo; cf. Prisc. l. 9 fin.

leo2.full: lĕo, ōnis, m. Gr. λέων, λίς, a lion. Lit.: validus, Lucr. 5, 985: fulvus, Ov. H. 10, 85: ferus, id. M. 7, 373: magnanimus, id. Tr. 3, 5, 33: leoni praecipua generositas, Plin. 8, 16, 17, § 42: Gaetulus, Verg. A. 5, 351: Poenus, id. E. 5, 27: Phrygius, id. A. 10, 157: fulvus, id. ib. 4, 159: leonum animi index cauda, Plin. 8, 16, 17, § 42: leo alumnus, Juv. 14, 247: pardus, tigris, leo— si quid adhuc est quod fremat in terris violentius, id. 8, 36: leo femina, a she-lion, lioness (for leaena), Pl

leo3.full: Lĕo, ōnis, m.; only plur.: Lĕōnes, um, the priests of the Persian god Mithras: Leones Mithrae, Tert. adv. Marc. 1, 13.

leocorion.full: Lĕōcŏrĭon, i, n., = Λεωκόριον, a temple in Athens, reared in honor of the three daughters of Leos, who suffered themselves to be sacrificed in order to avert a famine: Leoidum est delubrum Athenis, quod Leocorion nominatur, Cic. N. D. 3, 19, 50.
leocorion.short: Lĕōcŏrĭon, i, n., = Λεωκόριον, a temple in Athens, reared in honor of the three daughters of Leos, who suffered themselves to be sacrificed in order to avert a famine: Leoidum est delubrum Athenis, quod Leocorion nominatur, Cic.

leoides.full: Lĕōĭdes, um, f., the daughters of Leos, Cic. N. D 3, 19, 50 Wyttenb. (Lambin., Leo natarum; B. and K., Leocorion, q. v.).
leoides.short: Lĕōĭdes, um, f., the daughters of Leos, Cic.

leon.full: Lĕon, ontis, m., = Λέων. The name of a town near Syracuse, now Magnisi; acc. Leonta, Liv. 24, 39, 13.— A ruler of Phlius, Cic. Tusc. 5, 3, 8.— A celebrated painter, Plin. 35, 11, 40, § 141.

leonidas.full: Lĕōnĭdas (nom. Lĕōnĭda, Just. 2, 11, 2), ae, m., = Λεωνίδας. A king of Sparta, who fell at Thermopylæ, Cic. Fin. 2, 30, 97; 2, 19, 62; id. Tusc. 1, 42, 101; 1, 49, 116; Nep. Them. 3.— The name of a slave, Plaut. As. 1, 1, 43 al.; v. also Leonides.

leonides.full: Lĕōnĭdes, ae, m. An instructor of Alexander the Great, Plin. 12, 14, 32, § 62; Quint. 1, 1, 9.— A teacher of the younger Cicero at Athens, Cic. Att. 14, 16, 3; 15, 16, A; id. Fam. 16, 21, 5.

leoninus1.full: lĕōnīnus, a, um, adj. 2. leo, of or belonging to a lion, a lion's. Lit.: concede audacter ab leonino cavo, Plaut. Men. 1, 2, 47: species, a lion-like appearance, Varr. R. R. 2, 9, 3: pellis, Plin. 37, 10, 54, § 142: jubae, id. ib.: adeps, id. 24, 17, 102, § 165.—* Trop.: leonina societas, a lion's partnership, i. e. in which one party gets all the profit and the other all the loss: Aristo refert: Cassium respondisse, societatem talem coiri non posse, ut alter lucrum tantum, alter damnum sentiret

leoninus2.full: Lĕōnīnus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to the emperor Leo, Leonine: lex, Cod. Just. 1, 3, 50.
leoninus2.short: Lĕōnīnus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to the emperor Leo, Leonine: lex, Cod.

leonnatus.full: Leonnātus, i, m., one of Alexander's generals, Nep. Eum. 2; Plin. 6, 23, 26, § 97.
leonnatus.short: Leonnātus, i, m., one of Alexander's generals, Nep.

leonteus.full: Lĕontĕus, ĕi, m., the name of a warrior, Stat. Th. 9, 133.
leonteus.short: Lĕontĕus, ĕi, m., the name of a warrior, Stat.

leontice.full: lĕontĭcē, ēs, f., = λεοντική, a plant, called also cacalia, Plin. 25, 11, 85, § 135; v. cacalia.† † lĕontĭcus, a, um, adj., = λεοντικός, of or belonging to a lion: SACRA, the offerings made to Mithras, who was represented under the form of a lion (cf. Arn. 6, 196; cf. also 3. Leo), Inscr. Orell. 2345; 2343.
leontice.short: lĕontĭcē, ēs, f., = λεοντική, a plant, called also cacalia, Plin.

leontini.full: Lĕontīni, ōrum, m., = Λεοντῖνοι, a very ancient town on the eastern side of Sicily, now Lentini, Mel. 2, 7, 16; Plin. 3, 8, 14, § 89; Cic. Verr. 2, 2, 66, § 160; Liv. 24, 7, 2.—Hence, Lĕontīnus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Leontini, Leontine: ager, Cic. Verr. 2, 3, 44, § 104; id. Phil. 2, 17, 43; id. Div. 1, 33, 73: campus, Cic. Verr. 2, 3, 18, § 47; id. Phil. 8, 8, 26; Sil. 14, 126.—Plur. subst.: Lĕontīni, ōrum, m., the inhabitants of Leontini, Leontines, Cic. Verr. 2, 3, 46, § 109.
leontini.short: Lĕontīni, ōrum, m., = Λεοντῖνοι, a very ancient town on the eastern side of Sicily, now Lentini, Mel.

leontios.full: lĕontĭos, ĭi, m., = λεόντιος, a precious stone of the color of a lion, otherwise unknown, Plin. 37, 11, 73, § 190.
leontios.short: lĕontĭos, ĭi, m., = λεόντιος, a precious stone of the color of a lion, otherwise unknown, Plin.

leontium.full: Lĕontĭum, i, f., = Λεόντιον, an Athenian hetæra, a friend of Epicurus, Cic. N. D. 1, 33, 93.
leontium.short: Lĕontĭum, i, f., = Λεόντιον, an Athenian hetæra, a friend of Epicurus, Cic.

leontocaron.full: lĕontŏcăron, i, n., = λεοντόκαρον, a plant, otherwise unknown, App. Herb. 57.
leontocaron.short: lĕontŏcăron, i, n., = λεοντόκαρον, a plant, otherwise unknown, App.

leontopetalon.full: lĕontŏpĕtălon, i, n., = λεοντοπέταλον, a plant, lion's-leaf: Leontice leontopetalum, Linn.; Plin. 27, 11, 72, § 96.
leontopetalon.short: lĕontŏpĕtălon, i, n., = λεοντοπέταλον, a plant, lion's-leaf: Leontice leontopetalum, Linn.;

leontophonos.full: lĕontŏphŏnos, i, m., = λεοντοφόνος (lion-killer), a small animal whose urine was said to be fatal to lions, Plin. 8, 38, 57, § 136.
leontophonos.short: lĕontŏphŏnos, i, m., = λεοντοφόνος (lion-killer), a small animal whose urine was said to be fatal to lions, Plin.

leontopodion.full: lĕontŏpŏdĭon, ĭi, n., = λεοντοπόδιον, i. q. leontopetalon, a plant, lion's-foot, Plin. 26, 8, 34, § 52; App. Herb. 7.

leopardinus.full: lĕŏpardīnus, a, um, adj. leopardus, of a leopard: adeps, Marc. Emp. 28.

leopardus.full: lĕŏpardus, i, m. λεόπαρδος, a leopard: leopardi Libyci, Vop. Prob. 19; Lampr. Heliog. 21.

leotychides.full: Lĕōtўchĭdes, ae, m., = Λεωτυχίδης, brother of Agesilāus, Nep. Ages. 1.
leotychides.short: Lĕōtўchĭdes, ae, m., = Λεωτυχίδης, brother of Agesilāus, Nep.

lepareses.full: Lĕpărēses, ium, v. Lipara, II. B.

lepas.full: lĕpas (lŏpas, Non. 551, 5), ădis, f., = λεπάς, a kind of shell-fish that adheres closely to rocks, a limpet: lopades genus conchae marinae, Non. l. l.: lepadas (lopadas, acc. to Non.), ostreas, captamus, Plaut. Rud. 2, 1, 8; id. Cas. 2, 8, 57.

lepidanus.full: Lĕpĭdānus, a, um, adj., v. 2. Lepidus.

lepidianus.full: Lĕpĭdĭānus, a, um, adj., v. 2. Lepidus.

lepidium.full: lĕpĭdĭum, i, n., = λεπίδιον, a plant, garden-cress, pepperwort: Lepidium sativum, Linn.; Plin. 19, 8, 51, § 166; Col. 11, 3, 16; 41; 12, 8, 3.
lepidium.short: lĕpĭdĭum, i, n., = λεπίδιον, a plant, garden-cress, pepperwort: Lepidium sativum, Linn.;

lepidotis.full: lĕpĭdōtis, is, f. λεπιδωτός, scaly, a precious stone, otherwise unknown, Plin. 37, 10, 62, § 171.

lepidulus.full: lĕpĭdŭlus, a, um, adj. dim. [1. lepidus], rather pleasant, rather witty (post-class.): infacetus et impar lepidulis, Mart. Cap. 7, § 726; 8, § 807.

lepidus1.full: lĕpĭdus, a, um, adj. lepos, pleasant, agreeable, charming, fine, elegant, neat (esp. freq. in Plaut. and Ter.; in Cic. very rare). In gen.: fui ego bellus, lepidus, Plaut. Capt. 5, 2, 3: nugator, id. Curc. 4, 1, 1: virgo, id. ib. 1, 3, 11: mortalis, id. Truc. 5, 1, 57: o lepidum patrem! Ter. And. 5, 4, 45: ego usa sum benigno et lepido et comi, id. Hec. 5, 3, 39: lepida es, id. ib. 5, 1, 26: forma lepida et liberalis, Plaut. Ep. 1, 1, 41: mores, id. Most. 2, 3, 12: fama, id. Trin. 2, 2, 98: faci

lepidus2.full: Lĕpĭdus, i, m., a surname in the gens Aemilia; e. g. M. Aemilius Lepidus, consul 675 A. U. C., an enemy of Sylla, Cic. Cat. 3, 10, 24; Cic. Verr. 2, 3, 91, § 212.—Another M. Aemilius Lepidus, triumvir with Antony and Octavius, Cic. Mil. 5, 13; id. Phil. 5, 14, 39; v. his letters to Cicero ap. Cic. Fam. 10, 34 sq.—Hence, Lĕpĭdā-nus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Lepidus, Lepidan: bellum, Sall. H. Fragm. 3, 63 Dietsch.— Lĕpĭdĭānus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Lepidus, Lepidian: tumultus, whi
lepidus2.short: Lĕpĭdus, i, m., a surname in the gens Aemilia;

lepis.full: lĕpis, ĭdis, f., = λεπίς, a scale (pure Lat. squama): similiter squamae aeris, quam vocant lepida, Plin. 34, 11, 24, § 107.
lepis.short: lĕpis, ĭdis, f., = λεπίς, a scale (pure Lat.

lepista.full: lĕpista (lĕpesta and lĕpasta), ae, f., = λεπαστή, a drinking - vessel, goblet: lepista genus vasis aquarii, Paul. ex Fest. p. 115 Müll.: lepistae aut fictiles aut aëneae, Varr. ap. Non. 547, 26: ferunt pulchras crateras aureasque lepistas, Naev. ap. Mar. Vict. p. 2587 P.—Form lepesta, Varr. ap. Prisc. p. 714 P.; Varr. L. L. 5, § 123 Müll.—Form lepasta, Varr. ap. Non. 547, 24; Serv. Verg. E. 7, 33.
lepista.short: lĕpista (lĕpesta and lĕpasta), ae, f., = λεπαστή, a drinking - vessel, goblet: lepista genus vasis aquarii, Paul.

lepontii.full: Lēpontĭi, ōrum, m., = Ληπόντιοι, a people of Cisalpine Gaul, on the Ticinus; their territory is the modern Val Leventina, Caes. B. G. 4, 10; Plin. 3, 20, 24, § 134; cf. Mann. Ital. 1, p. 181 sq.—Hence, * Lēpontĭcus, i, m., a Lepontian, Sil. 4, 235.
lepontii.short: Lēpontĭi, ōrum, m., = Ληπόντιοι, a people of Cisalpine Gaul, on the Ticinus;

lepor.full: lĕpor and lĕpos, ōris, m. perh. root lamp-; Gr. λάμπω, λαμπρός; cf. Lat. limpidus, lanterna, pleasantness, agreeableness, attractiveness, charm. In gen.: quasi salsa muriatica esse autumantur sine omni lepore et sine suavitate, Plaut. Poen. 1, 2, 32: aurea, pavonum ridenti imbuta lepore Saecla, Lucr. 2, 502; 4, 1133: omnis vitae lepos, Plin. 31, 7, 41, § 88.— In partic. Of behavior, pleasantness, grace, politeness, amiability: affluens omni lepore ac venustate, Cic. Verr. 2, 5, 54, § 142: in quo

leporarius.full: lĕpŏrārĭus, a, um, adj. lepus, of or belonging to a hare, hare-: lageos (vitis) est, quae Latine leporaria dicitur: nam λαγὼς lepus, Serv. Verg. G. 2, 93.—Subst.: lĕpŏ-rārĭum, ii, n., a place where hares and other wild animals are kept; a preserve, warren, cover, Varr. R. R. 3, 3; 3, 12; Gell. 2, 20, 4.

leporinus.full: lĕpŏrīnus, a, um, adj. lepus, of a hare, hare-: coagulum, Varr. R. R. 2, 11, 4; Cels. 5, 5: cinis, Plin. 28, 11, 46, § 166: lana, Dig. 32, 70, 9.

lepra.full: lē^pra, ae, f., = λέπρα, the leprosy. Sing. (late Lat.): plaga leprae, Vulg. Lev. 13, 9 al.; Scrib. Comp. 250; Juvenc. 1.— Plur.: leprae, ārum (class.): lepras sedare, Plin. 24, 8, 33, § 48: curare, id. 20, 21, 86, § 234: emendare, id. 22, 25, 74, § 156: sanare, id. 32, 9, 31, § 97: tollere, id. 20, 17, 70, § 181.
lepra.short: lē^pra, ae, f., = λέπρα, the leprosy.

lepreum.full: Leprĕum or Leprĕon (Leprĭon or Leprĭum), i, n., and Leprĕos (-us), i, f., = Λέπρεον, a sea-coast town in Elis, south of Pylos; its ruins are near the modern town Strobitza, Cic. Att. 6, 2, 3; Plin. 4, 5, 6, § 14; cf. Mann. Griechenland, p. 525 sq.
lepreum.short: Leprĕum or Leprĕon (Leprĭon or Leprĭum), i, n., and Leprĕos (-us), i, f., = Λέπρεον, a sea-coast town in Elis, south of Pylos;

leprosus.full: lĕprōsus, a, um, adj. lepra, leprous (late Lat.). Lit.: viri, Sedul. 4, 191.— Trop.: nil tam leprosum aut putridum, Prud. στεφ. 2, 285.

lepta.full: Lepta, ae, m. λεπτός, weak, a Roman surname: Q. Lepta, praefectus fabrūm, Cic. Fam. 3, 7, 4; cf. id. ib. 5, 20, 4. To him are addressed the letters, Cic. Fam. 6, 18 and 19.

leptis.full: Leptis, is (abl. Lepte, Cod. Just. 1, 27, 2, § 1), f., = Λέπτις, the name of two cities on the coast of Africa. Leptis Magna, situated on the Great Syrtis, now Lebdah, Mel. 1, 7, 5; Plin. 5, 4, 3, § 25; Sall. J. 19, 3; 77, 1; Dig. 50, 15, 8, § 11.—Hence, Lep-tĭmagnensis, e, adj., of Leptis Magna: civitas, Cod. Just. 1, 27, 2.— Leptis Minor, near Hadrumetum, the birthplace of the emperor Septimius Severus, near the modern Lamta, Mel. 1, 7, 2; Sall. J. 19, 1; Cic. Verr. 2, 5, 59, § 155; Liv. 30, 2

leptomeres.full: leptŏmĕres, is, n., = λεπτομερές, consisting of fine particles, Theod. Prisc. de Diaeta, 10.
leptomeres.short: leptŏmĕres, is, n., = λεπτομερές, consisting of fine particles, Theod.

leptomericus.full: leptŏmĕrĭcus, a, um, adj., = λεπτομερικός, consisting of fine particles: virtus, Theod. Prisc. de Diaeta, 10.
leptomericus.short: leptŏmĕrĭcus, a, um, adj., = λεπτομερικός, consisting of fine particles: virtus, Theod.

lepton centaurium.full: lepton centaurĭum (-ĭon), n., = λεπτὸν κενταύριον, the lesser centaury: centaureum minus, Plin. 25, 6, 31, § 68.
lepton centaurium.short: lepton centaurĭum (-ĭon), n., = λεπτὸν κενταύριον, the lesser centaury: centaureum minus, Plin.

leptophyllon.full: leptŏphyllon, i, n., = λεπτόφυλλον, a species of the herb tithymalus, Plin. 26, 8, 45, § 71.
leptophyllon.short: leptŏphyllon, i, n., = λεπτόφυλλον, a species of the herb tithymalus, Plin.

leptopsephos.full: leptopsēphos, i, m., = λεπτόψηφος, a kind of porphyry with white spots, Plin. 36, 7, 11, § 57.
leptopsephos.short: leptopsēphos, i, m., = λεπτόψηφος, a kind of porphyry with white spots, Plin.

leptorax.full: leptŏrax, ăgis, f., = λεπτόραξ, a kind of grape-vine with very small berries (like our Levant currants), Plin. 14, 1, 3, § 15.
leptorax.short: leptŏrax, ăgis, f., = λεπτόραξ, a kind of grape-vine with very small berries (like our Levant currants), Plin.

leptynticus.full: leptyntĭcus, a, um, adj., = λεπτυντικός, making thin or meagre: caeparum virtus leptyntica, Theod. Prisc. de Diaeta, 10.
leptynticus.short: leptyntĭcus, a, um, adj., = λεπτυντικός, making thin or meagre: caeparum virtus leptyntica, Theod.

lepus.full: lĕpus, ŏris, m. (com., Varr. R. R. 3, 12; Plin. 8, 55, 81, § 217; v. infra) [cf. Aeol. and Sicil. λέπορις, collat. form of λαγώς, Varr. L. L. 5, § 101 Müll.; id. R. R. 3, 12; but Curt. compares lepor, lepidus, root in Gr. λάμπω], a hare, Varr. R. R. 3, 12; Plin. 8, 55, 81, § 217: lepus multum somni affert, qui illum edit, Cato ap. Diomed. p. 358 P.; Plaut. Pers. 3, 3, 31: auritosque sequi lepores, Verg. G. 1, 308: pavidus, Hor. Epod. 2, 35; id. C. 1, 37, 18: dare semesum leporem, Juv. 5, 167.—Of

lepusculus.full: lĕpuscŭlus (contr. acc. plur. lepusclos, Poët. ap. Lampr. Alex. Sev. 38), m. dim. lepus, a young or little hare, leveret, a hare. Lit.: in qua (insula) lepusculos vulpeculasque saepe vidisses, Cic. N. D. 1, 31, 88; Col. 9, 9 fin.— Transf., Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 21, § 47.

leria.full: lerĭa, ornamenta tunicarum aurea, Paul. ex Fest. p. 115 Müll.

lerna.full: Lerna, ae, and Lernē, ēs, f., = Λέρνη, a forest and marsh near Argos, through which flowed a stream of the same name; the abode of the Lernæan Hydra, which Hercules slew with the help of Iolāus, and then drained the marsh: belua Lernae, Verg. A. 6, 287: anguifera, Stat. S. 2, 181: fecunda veneno, id. Theb. 9, 340: haec dextra Lernam Placavit, Cic. poët. Tusc. 2, 9, 22: et Lerne pulsa tridente palus, Prop. 2, 26, 48 (3, 22, 20), where Müll. Lernae: Lerne, also a town situated there, acc. to Mel.
lerna.short: Lerna, ae, and Lernē, ēs, f., = Λέρνη, a forest and marsh near Argos, through which flowed a stream of the same name;

lesbia.full: Lesbĭa, ae, f., the name of a woman, one of the dramatis personae in Ter. And.
lesbia.short: Lesbĭa, ae, f., the name of a woman, one of the dramatis personae in Ter.

lesbos.full: Lesbos (-us), i (acc. Lesbum, Tac. A. 2, 54), f., = Λέσβος, a celebrated island in the Ægean Sea, off the coast of Troy and Mysia, the birthplace of Pittacus, Alcæus, Arion, Sappho, and Theophrastus, and famous for its wine; now Mityleni: sed quam capiam civitatem cogito ... Lesbumne, Plaut. Merc. 3, 4, 62; Mel. 2, 7, 4; Plin. 5, 31, 39, § 139; Cic. Att. 9, 9, 2; Ov. M. 11, 55: nota, Hor. Ep. 1, 11, 1.—Hence, Lesbĭăcus, a, um, adj., Lesbian: Lesbiaci libri, a work of Dicæarchus on the immortalit

lessus.full: lessus, acc. um (only in acc. sing.), m., a wailing, cry, funeral lamentation: mulieres genas ne radunto, neve lessum funeris ergo habento, Cic. Leg. 2, 23, 59; but a false reading for pausam, Plaut. Truc. 4, 2, 18.

lesura.full: Lĕsūra (Lĕsōra, Sid. Carm. 24, 44), ae, m. A mountain in Gaul that produced excellent cheese, now La Lozère, Plin. 11, 42, 97, § 240.— Lĕsŭra, a small river in Belgium, that runs into the Moselle, Aus. Mosell. 365.

letabilis.full: lētābĭlis, e, adj. letum, deadly, fatal: lues, Amm. 19, 4, 7.

letalis.full: lētālis (lēthāl-), e, adj. id., deadly, fatal, mortal (mostly poet. and late Lat.): vulnus, Verg. A. 9, 580; Suet. Caes. 82: harundo, Verg. A. 4, 73; ensis, Ov. M. 13, 392: serpens, Stat. Th. 6, 40: dapes, Val. Fl. 2, 155: hiems, Ov. M. 2, 827: venenum, Plin. 11. 35, 41, § 118: lac gustasse letale est, id. 11, 41, 96, § 236; Aug. Serm. 351, 5: ferrum, Juv. 15, 165.—In neutr., adverbially, in a deadly manner: letale minari, Stat. S. 4, 4, 84: letale furens, id. Th. 12, 760.—Plur. subst.: lētālĭa,

lethaea.full: Lēthaea, ae, f., the wife of Olĕnus, who, on account of her pride, was turned into stone, Ov. M. 10, 70.
lethaea.short: Lēthaea, ae, f., the wife of Olĕnus, who, on account of her pride, was turned into stone, Ov.

lethaeus.full: Lēthaeus, a, um, v. Lethe, II.

lethargia.full: lēthargĭa, ae, f., = ληθαργία, drowsiness, lethargy, Cael. Aur. Acut. 1, 6, 49; 2, 9, 45.
lethargia.short: lēthargĭa, ae, f., = ληθαργία, drowsiness, lethargy, Cael.

lethargicus.full: lēthargĭcus, a, um, adj., = ληθαργικός, drowsy, lethargic: morbus, Plin. 23, 1, 6, § 10: somnus, Aug. Ep. 48 ad Vincent.; Cael. Aur. Acut. 1, 3, 38 al.— Subst.: lē-thargĭcus, i, m., one affected with lethargy, a lethargic person: ut lethargicus hic cum fit pugil et medicum urget, Hor. S. 2, 3, 30; Plin. 24, 6, 16, § 25: lethargicos excitare labor est, id. 26, 11, 72, § 118.
lethargicus.short: lēthargĭcus, a, um, adj., = ληθαργικός, drowsy, lethargic: morbus, Plin.

lethargus.full: lēthargus, a, um, adj., Gr. λήθαργος, drowsy, lethargic: morbus, Plin. 23, 1, 6, § 10; Schol. Juv. 6, 613.—Esp. as subst. lēthargus, i, m. (sc. morbus), drowsiness, lethargy (in Cels. 3, 20, written as Greek): lethargo grandi est oppressus, Hor. S. 2, 3, 145; cf.: gravi lethargo oppressus, Serv. Sulp. ap. Quint. 4, 2, 106: olfactoriis excitatur, Plin. 30, 11, 29, § 97: in lethargum vergere, id. 32, 10, 38, § 116.— Plur.: ocimum facit lethargos, Plin. 20, 12, 48, § 119; 28, 8, 29, § 116.— (Sc. ho

lethe.full: Lēthē, ēs, f., = Λήθη (forgetfulness), the river Lethe, in the infernal regions, from which the Shades drank and obtained forgetfulness of the past: pocula Lethes, Ov. P. 2, 4, 23: da mihi hebetantem pectora Lethen, id. ib. 4, 1, 17: soporifera, id. Tr. 4, 1, 47: immittere Lethen Stygiam alicui in viscera, i. e. forgetfulness, Luc. 5, 221: aqua Lethes, i. q. soporifera, Ov. M. 11, 603.— Hence, Lēthaeus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Lethe, Lethean. Lit.: ratis, Tib. 3, 5, 24: amnis, Verg. A. 6
lethe.short: Lēthē, ēs, f., = Λήθη (forgetfulness), the river Lethe, in the infernal regions, from which the Shades drank and obtained forgetfulness of the past: pocula Lethes, Ov.

lethusa.full: lēthūsa, ae, f., the white poppy, App. Herb. 35.
lethusa.short: lēthūsa, ae, f., the white poppy, App.

letifer.full: lētĭfer (lēth-), fĕra, fĕrum, adj. letum, death-bringing, death-dealing, deadly, fatal (poet.): arcus, Verg. A. 10, 169: ictus, Ov. M. 8, 362: dextra, id. ib. 12, 606: vestis, id. ib. 9, 166: anguis, Stat. Th. 5, 628: certamen, Cat. 64, 390: annus, Verg. A. 3, 139: autumnus, Juv. 4, 57.—In prose: rabies letifer morbus canibus, Col. 7, 12 fin.—Transf.: locus, a place in the body where a wound is fatal, a mortal part, Ov. M. 5, 133.

leto.full: lēto (lētho), āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. id., to kill, slay: Lycurgiden letavit, Ov. Ib. 505: Paris hunc letat, Verg. Cul. 323: letata corpora, Ov. M. 3, 55 (the conjectural reading letatus, Cic. Leg. 3, 8, 19, is very dub.; v. Orell. ad loc., where leto datus is proposed; B. and K., necatus).

letum.full: lētum (sometimes written lēthum, from a supposed connection with λήθη), i, n. acc. to Varr. L. L. 7, § 42 Müll., and Paul. ex Fest. p. 115 Müll., from λήθη; more prob. acc. to Prisc. p. 665 and 898 P., from leo, whence also deleo; root lī-; cf. Sanscr. vi-lī, to dissolve; Gr. λίμνη, λιμήν, λοιμός. death (ante-class., and in the class. period mostly poet.): ollus apparet in funeribus indictivis, cum dicitur: ollus leto datus est (qs. was given up to oblivion), Varr. L. L. 7, § 42 Müll.—The phrase
letum.short: lētum (sometimes written lēthum, from a supposed connection with λήθη), i, n.

letus.full: Letus, i, m., a mountain in Liguria, Liv. 41, 18; Val. Max. 1, 5. †† leuca (leuga), ae, f. a Celtic word, whence the Fr. lieue, a Gallic mile of 1500 Roman paces, a league: Λεύκη μέτρον τι Γαλακτικόν, Hesych.: leuca finitur passibus mille quingentis, Isid. Orig. 15, 16: cum et Latini mille passus vocent, et Galli leucas, et Persae parasangas, et rastas universa Germania, Hier. in Joel, 3, 18: exinde non millenis passibus sed leugis itinera metiuntur, Amm. 15, 11, 17: quarta leuga signabatur et d
letus.short: Letus, i, m., a mountain in Liguria, Liv.

leuca.full: Leuca, ae, f., a town in Calabria, near the Iapygian promontory, now S. Maria di Leuca: secretaque littora Leucae, Luc. 5, 376.
leuca.short: Leuca, ae, f., a town in Calabria, near the Iapygian promontory, now S.

leucacantha.full: leucăcantha, ae, f., and leucă-canthos, i, m., = λευκάκανθα. The white thorn, form leucacantha, Plin. 22, 16, 18, § 40; form leucacanthos, id. 21, 16, 56, § 94.— A plant, called also phalangites and leucanthemon, Plin. 27, 12, 98, § 124.
leucacantha.short: leucăcantha, ae, f., and leucă-canthos, i, m., = λευκάκανθα.

leucachates.full: leucăchātes, ae, m., = λευκαχάτης, the white agate, Plin. 37, 10, 54, § 139.
leucachates.short: leucăchātes, ae, m., = λευκαχάτης, the white agate, Plin.

leucadia.full: Leucădĭa, ae, and Leucas, ădis, f., = Λευκαδία, an island (previously a peninsula) in the Ionic Sea, opposite Acarnania, with a famous temple of Apollo, now S. Maura, Mel. 2, 7, 10; Plin. 4, 1, 2, § 5; Liv. 33, 17, 8; acc. Leucada, Ov. M. 15, 289; id. H. 15, 172.—Hence, Leucădĭus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to the island of Leucadia, Leucadian: aequor, Ov. H. 15, 166: litus, Plin. 4, 1, 2, § 5: vinum, id. 14, 7, 9, § 76; Plaut. Poen. 3, 3, 86: Dites damnosos maritos apud Leucadiam Oppiam, id.
leucadia.short: Leucădĭa, ae, and Leucas, ădis, f., = Λευκαδία, an island (previously a peninsula) in the Ionic Sea, opposite Acarnania, with a famous temple of Apollo, now S.

leucaethiopes.full: Leucaethĭŏpes, um, m., = Λευκαιθίοπες, the white Ethiopians of Libya, Plin. 5, 8, 8, § 43 (Jahn, Leucoe Aethiopes); called also Leucoaethiopes, Mel. 1, 4, 4.
leucaethiopes.short: Leucaethĭŏpes, um, m., = Λευκαιθίοπες, the white Ethiopians of Libya, Plin.

leucanthemis.full: leucanthĕmis, ĭdis, f., = λευκάνθεμις, the chamomile plant, Plin. 22, 21, 26, § 53.
leucanthemis.short: leucanthĕmis, ĭdis, f., = λευκάνθεμις, the chamomile plant, Plin.

leucanthemon.full: leucanthĕmon or -mum, i, n., = λευκάνθεμον, the name of three plants. The chamomile, called also anthemis, leucanthemis, etc., Plin. 22, 21, 26, § 53.— A plant, called also phalangites and leucacantha, Plin. 27, 12, 98, § 124.— A plant whose scent resembles that of southernwood (abrotonum), Plin. 21, 10, 34, § 60.
leucanthemon.short: leucanthĕmon or -mum, i, n., = λευκάνθεμον, the name of three plants.

leucanthes.full: leucanthes, is, n., = λευκανθές, the herb pellitory, Plin. 21, 30, 104, § 176.
leucanthes.short: leucanthes, is, n., = λευκανθές, the herb pellitory, Plin.

leucanthus.full: leucanthus, i, m., = λεύκανθος, a plant, otherwise unknown, App. Herb. 92.
leucanthus.short: leucanthus, i, m., = λεύκανθος, a plant, otherwise unknown, App.

leucargillos.full: leucargillos, i, f., = λευκάργιλλος, white clay, Plin. 17, 7, 4, § 42.
leucargillos.short: leucargillos, i, f., = λευκάργιλλος, white clay, Plin.

leucas.full: Leucas, ădis, f., = Λευκάς. For Leucadia, v. h. v.— The capital of the island Leucadia; v. Leucadia, B.— The promontory Leucata; v. Leucata. † leucaspis, ĭdis, adj., f., = λεύκασπις, armed with a white shield: phalanx, Liv. 44, 41.

leucaspis.full: Leucaspis, ĭdis, m., one of the companions of Æneas, Verg. A. 6, 334.
leucaspis.short: Leucaspis, ĭdis, m., one of the companions of Æneas, Verg.

leucata.full: Leucāta, ae, and Leucātē, ēs, f. (Leucāte, is, n., Serv. Verg. A. 3, 279.— Leucātes, ae, m., Claud. B. G. 185.— Leucas, ădis, f., Ov. H. 15, 172; Sen. Herc. Oet. 732), a promontory in the island of Leucadia, now Capo Ducato, Cic. Tusc. 4, 18, 41; Liv. 26, 26; 44, 1: Leucatae nimbosa cacumina montis, Verg. A. 3, 274; Liv. 36, 15; Plin. 4, 1, 2, § 5. † leucē, ēs, f., = λεύκη. The spotted dead-nettle: Lamium maculatum, Linn.; Plin. 27, 11, 77, § 102.— The white poplar, into which Leuce, the daughte
leucata.short: Leucāta, ae, and Leucātē, ēs, f.

leuce.full: Leucē, ēs, f., = Λευκή. The name of several islands. Near Crete, over against Cydonia, now Fort Suda, Plin. 4, 12, 20, § 61.— In the Euxine Sea, near the mouth of the Borysthenes, also called Achillea and Achillis insula, now Oulan Adassi, Fidonisi, or Serpents' Island, Mel. 2, 7, 2; Plin. 4, 13, 27, § 93.— A city in Laconia, Liv. 35, 27 init.

leuceoron.full: leucēŏron, i, n., = λευκήορον, a plant, called also leontopodion, Plin. 26, 8, 34, § 52; App. Herb. 7.
leuceoron.short: leucēŏron, i, n., = λευκήορον, a plant, called also leontopodion, Plin.

leuci.full: Leuci, ōrum, m., = Λεῦκοι, a people of Gallia Belgica, adjacent to the Lingones, whence, perh., the mod. Liège, Caes. B. G. 1, 40, 10; Plin. 4, 17, 31, § 106; Tac. H. 1, 64. —Collect., in sing.: Leucus, i, m., Luc. 1, 424.
leuci.short: Leuci, ōrum, m., = Λεῦκοι, a people of Gallia Belgica, adjacent to the Lingones, whence, perh., the mod.

leucippe.full: Leucippē, ēs, f., = Λευκίππη. The daughter of Thestor, Hyg. Fab. 190.— The wife of Ilus, and mother of Laomedon, Hyg. Fab. 250.— The wife of Thestius, Hyg. Fab. 14.— A Roman surname: AVRELIA LEVCIPPE, Inscr. ap. Grut. 761, 7.

leucippus.full: Leucippus, i, m., = Λεύκιππος. The father of Phœbe and Hilaira, who were carried off by Castor and Pollux, Ov. F. 5, 709.—Hence, Leucippis, ĭdis, f., a daughter of Leucippus, Prop. 1, 2, 15: te rapuit Theseus, geminas Leucippidas illi, Ov. H. 16, 327; Hyg. Fab. 80; Lact. 1, 10.— A son of Hercules, Hyg. Fab. 162.— A Grecian philosopher, a disciple of Zeno the Eleatic, Cic. Ac. 2, 37, 118; id. N. D. 1, 24, 66.

leucochrysos.full: leucochrȳsos, i, m., = λευκόχρυσος. A precious stone, a species of chrysolite, Plin. 37, 9, 44, § 128.— A white precious stone, clear as crystal, Plin. 37, 10, 62, § 172.

leucocomos.full: leucŏcŏmos or -us, a, um, adj., = λευκόκομος (white-haired; hence), having white leaves or blossoms: (mala) erythrocomis et leucocomis, Plin. 13, 19, 34, § 113.
leucocomos.short: leucŏcŏmos or -us, a, um, adj., = λευκόκομος (white-haired;

leucocoum.full: leucŏcōum, i, n., = λευκοκῶον, white Coan wine, Plin. 14, 8, 10, § 78.
leucocoum.short: leucŏcōum, i, n., = λευκοκῶον, white Coan wine, Plin.

leucogaea.full: leucŏgaea, ae, f., = λευκόγαια (of white earth), a precious stone almost unknown, Plin. 37, 10, 59, § 162.
leucogaea.short: leucŏgaea, ae, f., = λευκόγαια (of white earth), a precious stone almost unknown, Plin.

leucogaeus.full: leucŏgaeus, a, um, adj., = λευκόγαιος, of white earth: colles, a chain of hills in Campania, where chalk was dug, Plin. 18, 11, 29, § 114; 35, 15, 56, § 174.—Here were the leucogaei fontes, Plin. 31, 2, 8, § 12.
leucogaeus.short: leucŏgaeus, a, um, adj., = λευκόγαιος, of white earth: colles, a chain of hills in Campania, where chalk was dug, Plin.

leucographia.full: leucogrăphĭa, ae, f., = λευκογραφία, a precious stone, called also leucogaea, Plin. 37, 10, 59, § 162; al. leucographitin.
leucographia.short: leucogrăphĭa, ae, f., = λευκογραφία, a precious stone, called also leucogaea, Plin.

leucographis.full: leucogrăphis, ĭdis, f., = λευκογραφίς, a kind of St. Mary's thistle, Carduus leucographus, Linn., which was used as a remedy for spitting blood, Plin. 27, 11, 78, § 103.
leucographis.short: leucogrăphis, ĭdis, f., = λευκογραφίς, a kind of St.

leucoion.full: leucŏĭon (trisyl. leucoja, Col. poët. 10, 97), ĭi, n., = λευκόϊον, the white violet, Col. 9, 4, 4: candida leucoia, id. 10, 97.

leucon.full: Leucōn, ōnis, m. The name of one of Actæon's hounds, Ov. M. 3, 218.— A king of Pontus, Ov. Ib. 312.

leuconicus.full: Leucŏnĭcus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to the Leucŏnes (a people in Gaul), Leuconic: lanae, Mart. 11, 56, 9 dub.: sagae, id. 14, 159, 2, also dub.— Subst.: Leucŏ-nĭcum, i, n., Leuconic wool, Mart. 11, 21, 8.
leuconicus.short: Leucŏnĭcus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to the Leucŏnes (a people in Gaul), Leuconic: lanae, Mart.

leuconotus.full: leucŏnŏtus, i, m., = λευκόνοτος, the (white, i. e. clear, dry) south wind, more precisely, the south-southwest wind, Vitr. 1, 6, 10; Sen. Q. N. 5, 16, 6: leuconotus Libs, Aus. Technopaegn. de Deis, 12.
leuconotus.short: leucŏnŏtus, i, m., = λευκόνοτος, the (white, i.

leucopetra.full: Leucŏpĕtra, ae, f., = Λευκοπέτρα (white rock), a promontory in the territory of the Bruttii, near Rhegium, now Capo dell' Armi, Cic. Phil. 1, 3, 7; id. Att. 16, 6, 1; 16, 7, 1.
leucopetra.short: Leucŏpĕtra, ae, f., = Λευκοπέτρα (white rock), a promontory in the territory of the Bruttii, near Rhegium, now Capo dell' Armi, Cic.

leucophaeatus.full: leucŏphaeātus, a, um, adj. leucophaeus, clothed in dark gray or ash-colored garments, Mart. 1, 97, 5.

leucophaeus.full: leucŏphaeus, a, um, adj., = λευκόφαιος, ash - colored, dun - colored: pannus, Plin. 32, 10, 38, § 114: vellera, Vitr. 8, 3 med.
leucophaeus.short: leucŏphaeus, a, um, adj., = λευκόφαιος, ash - colored, dun - colored: pannus, Plin.

leucophoron.full: leucophŏron, i, n., = λευκοφόρον, gold-size, Plin. 35, 6, 17, § 36; 33, 3, 20, § 64.
leucophoron.short: leucophŏron, i, n., = λευκοφόρον, gold-size, Plin.

leucophryna.full: Leucŏphrўna, ae, f., = λευκοφρύνη (with white eyebrows), a surname of Diana in Magnesia, Tac. A. 3, 62; Arn. 6, 6.
leucophryna.short: Leucŏphrўna, ae, f., = λευκοφρύνη (with white eyebrows), a surname of Diana in Magnesia, Tac.

leucophthalmos.full: leucophthalmos, i, m., = λευκόφθαλμος (white eye), a precious stone, Plin. 37, 10, 62, § 171.
leucophthalmos.short: leucophthalmos, i, m., = λευκόφθαλμος (white eye), a precious stone, Plin.

leucopis.full: leucōpis, ĭdis, f., = λευκῶπις, a plant, called also artemisia, App. Herb. 10.
leucopis.short: leucōpis, ĭdis, f., = λευκῶπις, a plant, called also artemisia, App.

leucopoecilos.full: leucŏpoecĭlos, i, m., = λευκοποίκιλος (spotted with white), a precious stone, otherwise unknown, Plin. 37, 10, 62, § 171.
leucopoecilos.short: leucŏpoecĭlos, i, m., = λευκοποίκιλος (spotted with white), a precious stone, otherwise unknown, Plin.

leucos.full: leucos, on, adj., = λευκός, white, Plin. 10, 60, 79, § 164.
leucos.short: leucos, on, adj., = λευκός, white, Plin.

leucosia.full: Leucŏsĭa, ae, f., = Λευκοσία, a small island off the coast of Lucania, near Pæstum, now Licosa: Leucosiamque petit, tepidique rosaria Paesti, Ov. M. 15, 708; called also Leucothĕa, Mel. 2, 7, 18 (Jahn reads Leucasia, Plin. 3, 7, 13, § 85).
leucosia.short: Leucŏsĭa, ae, f., = Λευκοσία, a small island off the coast of Lucania, near Pæstum, now Licosa: Leucosiamque petit, tepidique rosaria Paesti, Ov.

leucosyri.full: Leucŏsўri, ōrum, m., = Λευκόσυροι, the white Syrians on the shores of the Euxine, afterwards called Cappadocians, Plin. 6, 3, 3, § 9; Curt. 6, 4, 17; Nep. Dat. 1, 1.
leucosyri.short: Leucŏsўri, ōrum, m., = Λευκόσυροι, the white Syrians on the shores of the Euxine, afterwards called Cappadocians, Plin.

leucothea.full: Leucŏthĕa, ae, and Leucŏthĕē, ēs, f., = Λευκοθέη. The name of Ino, daughter of Cadmus, after she was received among the sea-gods; afterwards confounded with the Italian goddess Matuta: Leucotheë Graiis Matuta vocabare nostris, Ov. F. 6, 545; so, Leucothee (others Leucothea), id. M. 4, 542: Ino Leucothea nominata a Graecis; Matuta habetur a nostris, Cic. Tusc. 1, 12, 28; id. N. D. 3, 15, 39; 3, 19, 48.—In Stat. Th. 9, 402, identical with Aurora.— Another name for Leucosia, v. h. v.— A fountain in
leucothea.short: Leucŏthĕa, ae, and Leucŏthĕē, ēs, f., = Λευκοθέη.

leucothoe.full: Leucŏthŏē, ēs, f., daughter of Orchamus, king of Babylon, and Eurynome, Ov. M. 4, 196; 204 sqq.
leucothoe.short: Leucŏthŏē, ēs, f., daughter of Orchamus, king of Babylon, and Eurynome, Ov.

leucozomus.full: leucŏzōmus, a, um, adj., = λευκόζωμος, with white sauce: pullus, Apic. 6, 9, § 254.
leucozomus.short: leucŏzōmus, a, um, adj., = λευκόζωμος, with white sauce: pullus, Apic.

leucrion.full: leucrĭon, ii, n., a plant, called also cynoglossa, hound's-tongue, App. Herb. 96.
leucrion.short: leucrĭon, ii, n., a plant, called also cynoglossa, hound's-tongue, App.

leucrocota.full: leucrŏcŏta (also lĕōcrŏcŏta and leucrŏcŭta), ae, f., a wild beast in India, otherwise unknown, Plin. 8, 21, 30, § 72; Sol. 52, 34.
leucrocota.short: leucrŏcŏta (also lĕōcrŏcŏta and leucrŏcŭta), ae, f., a wild beast in India, otherwise unknown, Plin.

leuctra.full: Leuctra, ōrum, n. (Leuctrae, ārum. f., Sol. 7), = Λεῦκτρα. A small town in Bæotia, where Epaminondas defeated the Spartans, now the village of Leuca, with the ruins of Eremo-Castro (cf. Mann. Griechenland, p. 238), Cic. Tusc. 1, 46, 110; id. Off. 1, 18, 61: Lacedaemoniorum mala pugna in Leuctris, id. Div. 2, 25, 54.—Hence, Leuctrĭcus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Leuctra, Leuctrian: pugna, Cic. Tusc. 1, 46, 110; v. supra: calamitas, id. Div. 1, 34, 74; id. Off. 2, 7 fin.—Cicero jestingly give

leudus.full: leudus, i, m. (Germ. Lied, Laut), a German song, Ven. Fort. 7, 8, 69.

leunculus.full: lĕuncŭlus, i, m. dim. leo, a small lion, Vulg. 3 Reg. 10, 20; id. 1 Par. 28, 17.

leus.full: lēus, a, um, adj., = λεῖος, smooth: brassica lea, Plin. 20, 9, 33, § 79.
leus.short: lēus, a, um, adj., = λεῖος, smooth: brassica lea, Plin.

leuson.full: leuson, i, n., = λοῦσσον, the inner part of the wood of the fir: (hoc lignum, proximum medullae) in abiete leuson Graeci vocant, Plin. 16, 39, 73, § 187.
leuson.short: leuson, i, n., = λοῦσσον, the inner part of the wood of the fir: (hoc lignum, proximum medullae) in abiete leuson Graeci vocant, Plin.

levabilis.full: lĕvābĭlis, e, adj. levo, that can be lightened: motus, Cael. Aur. Acut. 3, 7, 71.

levaci.full: Levāci, ōrum, m., a people of Gallia Belgica, allies of the Nervii, Caes. B. G. 5, 39; cf. Ukert, Gall. p. 374.
levaci.short: Levāci, ōrum, m., a people of Gallia Belgica, allies of the Nervii, Caes.

levamen.full: lĕvāmen, ĭnis, n. levo, an alleviation, mitigation, solace, consolation (mostly poet.): quod si esset aliquod levamen, id esset in te uno, * Cic. Att. 12, 16: dulce viatori lasso in sudore levamen, * Cat. 68, 61; * Prop. 4 (5), 11, 63. omnis curae casusque levamen, Amitto Anchisen, * Verg. A. 3, 709: ejus mali, Liv. 6, 35, 1.

levamentarius.full: lĕvāmentārĭus, a, um, adj. levamentum, of or for lightening (post-class.), Cod. Th. 13, 5, 1.

levamentum.full: lĕvāmentum, i, n. 1. levo, an alleviation, mitigation, consolation, comfort (class.): miseriarum, Cic. Fin. 5, 19, 53: doloris, Plin. Ep. 8, 19: sine levamento, Tac. A. 4, 66: tributi, id. H. 1, 8: nec aliud levamentum quam si certis sub legibus militia iniretur, id. A. 1, 17: praestare, Plin. 30, 3, 8, § 23: mihi illam rem fore levamento, Cic. Att. 12, 43, 1.

levana.full: Lĕvāna, ae, f. id., the goddess supposed to raise new-born infants from the ground, Aug. Civ. Dei, 4, 11.

levatio.full: lĕvātĭo, ōnis, f. id.. * A lifting up, raising, elevating: onerum levationes facere, Vitr. 10, 8; a metrical t. t. = ἄρσις, Aug. Mas. II. 18.— Trop. An alleviation, mitigation, relief (class.): alicui esse levationi, Cic. Fam. 6, 4, 5: ea, quae levationem habeant aegritudinum, may produce an alleviation, may alleviate, id. Tusc. 1, 49, 119: levationem invenire acerbissimis doloribus, id. ib. 5, 41, 121: doloris at officii debiti, id. Att. 12, 23, 3.— A diminishing (rare but class.): vitiorum, Ci

levator.full: lĕvātor, ōris, m. id., a lifter, a thief, Petr. 140 dub.

levatus1.full: lĕvātus, a, um, Part., from 1. lĕvo.

levatus2.full: lēvātus, a, um, Part., from 2. lēvo.

levenna.full: lĕvenna, ae, m., for 1. levis: (Laberius) hominem levennam pro levi dixit, Gell. 16, 7, 11.

leviculus.full: lĕvĭcŭlus, a, um, adj. dim. [1. levis]. * Very small, trivial, insignificant: quid significet prandium caninum, rem leviculam, diu et anxie quaesivimus, Gell. 13, 31, 15.— Somewhat light-minded, vain: leviculus sane noster Demosthenes, qui, etc., Cic. Tusc. 5, 36, 103.

levidensis.full: lĕvĭdensis, e, adj. 1. levis-densus, lightly wrought, thin. Lit.: levidensis vestis dicta, quod raro filo sit leviterque densata. Pavitensis contraria levidensi dicta, quod graviter pressa atque calcata sit; Isid. Orig. 19, 22, 19.—* Transf., slight, poor: munusculum, Cic. Fam. 9, 12, 2.

levifecit.full: lĕvĭfēcit, ἐξουθένησεν (he set at naught), Gloss. Philox.
levifecit.short: lĕvĭfēcit, ἐξουθένησεν (he set at naught), Gloss.

levifidus.full: lĕvĭ-fīdus, a, um, adj. 1. levis, of slight credit, untrustworthy: omnes sunt lenae levifidae, Plaut. Pers. 2, 2, 61.

levigatio.full: lēvĭgātĭo, ōnis, f. 1. levigo, a smoothing, Vitr. 7, 1, 4.

levigatus.full: lēvĭgātus, a, um, Part. and P. a., from 1. levigo.

levigo1.full: lēvĭgo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. 2. lēvis, to make smooth, to smooth (not in Cic.; syn. polio, dolo, limo). Lit.: omnes parietes tectorio levigantur, Varr. R. R. 3, 11, 3: aliquid opere tectorio, Col. 9, 7, 1; Plin. 17, 14, 24, § 101: ad levigandam cutem, id. 20, 3, 10, § 20: alvum, to make slippery, Gell. 4, 11, 4: scabritia levigatur dente conchāve, Plin. 13, 12, 25, § 81.— Transf., to make small, bruise small, pulverize, levigate: quae diligenter contrita levigantur, Col. 12, 41 fin.: semina, id.

levigo2.full: lĕvĭgo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. 1. levis, to make light, lighten: gravia, Cassiod. de Amic. prol. § 33: pondus sollicitudinis, Gregor. Ep. 7, 76: omni sarcinā, App. M. 4, p. 142, 23.

levio.full: lĕvio, āvi, v. a. id., to alleviate (late Lat.), Ven. Vit. Leob. 23.

levipes.full: lĕvĭpes, pēdis, adj. 1. levis-pes, lightfooted (rare), * Varr. R. R. 3, 12, 6: levipes Lepus, * Cic. Arat. 121.

levir.full: lēvir, ĭri, m. for dēvir, kindred with Sanscr. dēvar, whence juvān = juvenis; Gr. δαήρ, a husband's brother, brother-inlaw: viri frater levir est: apud Graecos δαὴρ appellatur, Dig. 38, 10, 4, § 6: levir dicitur frater mariti, quasi laevus vir, Non. 557, 8: levir est uxori meae frater meus (i. e. my brother is levir to my wife), Paul. ex Fest. p. 115 Müll. N. cr.

levis1.full: lĕvis, e, adj. for leg-vis; Sanscr. laghu-s, little; cf. O. H. Germ. ring-i; Germ. gering; Gr. ἐλαχύς, light in weight, not heavy (opp. gravis). Lit.: leviora corpora (opp. graviora), Lucr. 2, 227: aether, id. 5, 459: aura, id. 3, 196: levior quam pluma, Plaut. Men. 3, 2, 23: stipulae, Verg. G. 1, 289: armatura, light armor: levis armaturae Numidae, the light-armed Numidians, Caes. B. G. 2, 10; also, by metonymy, lightarmed troops; v. armatura, and cf.: sed haec fuerit nobis tamquam levis armatu

levis2.full: lēvis (erroneously laevis), e, adj. Gr. λεῖος, λευρός, smooth, smoothed, not rough, opp. asper (class.). Lit. In gen.: corpuscula quaedam levia, alia aspera, etc., Cic. N. D. 1, 24, 66: in locis (spectatur): leves an asperi, id. Part. Or. 10, 36: Deus levem eum (mundum) fecit et undique aequabilem, id. Univ. 6: pocula, smooth, shining, Verg. A. 5, 91: pharetrae, id. ib. 5, 558: brassica, Cato, R. R. 15, 7: levissima corpora, Lucr. 4, 659: coma pectine levis, Ov. M. 12, 409: nascunturque leves pe

levisomnus.full: lĕvĭsomnus, a, um, adj. 1. levissomnus, lightly sleeping: corda canum, Lucr. 5, 864.

levisticum.full: Lĕvistĭcum, i, n., i. q. Ligusticum (q. v.), Veg. 3, 52 Gesn.

levitas1.full: lĕvĭtas, ātis, f. 1. levis, lightness, as to weight. Lit. (rare): plumarum, Lucr. 3, 387; id. 4, 745: armorum, Caes. B. G. 5, 34: nulli fruticum levitas major, Plin. 13, 22, 42, § 123.—* Transf., poet., movableness, mobility: Termine, post illud levitas tibi libera non est: Qua positus fueris in statione, mane, Ov. F. 2, 673.— Trop. Light-mindedness, changeableness, fickleness, inconstancy, levity (freq. and class.): quid est inconstantiā, mobilitate, levitate turpius? Cic. Phil. 7, 3, 9: temere

levitas2.full: lēvĭtas (laev-), ātis, f. 2. lēvis, smoothness. Lit. (class.): speculorum, Cic. Univ. 14; id. de Or. 3, 25, 99; id. Univ. 6; Plin. 2, 3, 3, § 7: intestinorum, slipperiness, lubricity, Cels. 4, 16; 2, 8.— Trop., of speech, smoothness, fluency, facility: Demosthenes nihil levitate Aeschini et splendore verborum cedit, Cic. Or. 31, 110: verborum, Quint. 10, 1, 52: effeminata, id. 8, 3, 6.

levites.full: Lēvītes (Lēvīta, Prud. στεφ. 2, 39; 5, 30), ae, m., a Levite: Levita de tribu sacra, Prud. στεφ. 2, 39; 5, 30. Transf., a deacon, Sid. Ep. 9, 2.— Hence, Lē-vītĭcus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Levi or to the Levites, Levitical: genus Leviticum, Vulg. Deut. 17, 9: stirps, id. Ios. 3, 3.— Lēvītis, ĭdis, adj. f., of or belonging to the tribe of Levi: gentis Levitidis una Semper fida comes, of the Levites, Prud. Psych. 502.

levitonarium.full: lēvītōnārĭum, ii, n., an Egyptian monk's garment, Isid. Orig. 19, 22; Hier. praef. in Reg. S. Pachom. n. 4.
levitonarium.short: lēvītōnārĭum, ii, n., an Egyptian monk's garment, Isid.

levitudo.full: lēvĭtūdo (laev-), ĭnis, f. 2. levis, smoothness (post-class.): levitudo granorum (miliorum), Lact. Ira D. 10, 7.

levo1.full: lĕvo, āvi, ātum, 1 (old form of fut. perf. levasso, Enn. ap. Cic. de Sen. 1), v. a. 1. levis, to lift up, raise, elevate (syn.: extollo, erigo). Lit. (mostly poet. and in post-Aug. prose): ter sese attollens cubitoque annixa levavit, Verg. A. 4, 690: se de caespite, to rise, Ov. M. 2, 427: se saxo, id. F. 4, 528: cum se matura levarit progenies (avium), Juv. 14, 83: apis se confestim levat sublimius, Col. 9, 12, 1; Plin. 2, 16, 13, § 69; 36, 16, 24, § 122: per hiemem, quae altius levat Alpes, i.
levo1.short: lĕvo, āvi, ātum, 1 (old form of fut.

levo2.full: lēvo (laevo), āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. 2. levis, to make smooth, to smooth, polish. Lit.: levare ac radere tigna, Lucr. 5, 1267: corpus, * Cic. Fragm. Or. in Clod. et Cur. 5; Cels. 8, 3: magni levatique mensarum orbes, Sen. Helv. 11, 6: mensas, Stat. Th. 1, 519.— Trop., of speech, to smooth down, polish, soften: nimis aspera sano Levabit cultu, Hor. Ep. 2, 2, 123.—Hence, P. a.: lēvātus, a, um; comp.: quae levatiora levioraque sunt, more highly polished, Gell. 17, 8, 15.

levor.full: lēvor (laevor), ōris, m. id., smoothness: haud sine principali aliquo levore, Lucr. 2, 423: spectantur in chartis tenuitas, densitas, candor, levor, Plin. 13, 12, 24, § 78: levorem corpori afferre, id. 30, 14, 43, § 127; 37, 4, 15, § 56: vocis, Lucr. 4, 552.

lex.full: lex, lēgis, f. perh. Sanscr. root lag-, lig-, to fasten; Lat. ligo, to bind, oblige; cf. religio, a proposition or motion for a law made to the people by a magistrate, a bill (cf. institutum). Lit.: legem ferre: antiquare, Cic. Off. 2, 21, 73: rogare, id. Phil. 2, 29, 72: leges ac jura ferre, Juv. 2, 72: legem promulgavit pertulitque, ut, etc., Liv. 33, 46: Antonius fixit legem a dictatore comitiis latam, qua, etc., Cic. Att. 14, 12: legem sciscere de aliqua re, id. Planc. 14, 35: populus R. jus

lexanor.full: Lexānor, ŏris, m., name of a warrior, Val. Fl. 6, 686.
lexanor.short: Lexānor, ŏris, m., name of a warrior, Val.

lexidium.full: lexĭdĭum, i, n., = λεξίδιον, a little word: lexidia colligere, Gell. 18, 7, 3.
lexidium.short: lexĭdĭum, i, n., = λεξίδιον, a little word: lexidia colligere, Gell.

lexipyretos.full: lexĭpўrĕtos (-us), on and a, um, adj., = ληξιπύρετος, that allays fever, antifebrile, Plin. 20, 18, 76, § 201; Marc. Emp. 16.
lexipyretos.short: lexĭpўrĕtos (-us), on and a, um, adj., = ληξιπύρετος, that allays fever, antifebrile, Plin.

lexipyrexia.full: lexĭpўrexĭa, ae, f., = ληξιπυρεξία, a cessation of fever, Marc. Emp. 20.
lexipyrexia.short: lexĭpўrexĭa, ae, f., = ληξιπυρεξία, a cessation of fever, Marc.

lexis.full: lexis, ĕos (acc. plur. -eis), f., = λέξις, a word (ante-class. and post-Aug.): quam lepide lexeis compostae! Lucil. ap. Cic. de Or. 3, 43, 171; Charis. 249; 251 P.

lexobii.full: Lexobĭi (Lexovĭi), ōrum, m., a people in Gallia Lugdunensis, at the mouth of the Sequana, whence the name of the modern Lisieux, Départ. du Calvados, Caes. B. G. 3, 9 sq.; Plin. 4, 18, 32, § 107.
lexobii.short: Lexobĭi (Lexovĭi), ōrum, m., a people in Gallia Lugdunensis, at the mouth of the Sequana, whence the name of the modern Lisieux, Départ.

liaculum.full: liācŭlum, λειαντήρ (a polishing instrument), Gloss. Philox.

libacunculus.full: lībācuncŭlus, i, m. dim. libum, a little cake: de libacunculo, Tert. Spect. 27 (al. lucunculo).

libadion.full: lĭbădĭon, ĭi, n., = λιβάδιον, the herb centaury, Plin. 25, 6, 31, § 68.
libadion.short: lĭbădĭon, ĭi, n., = λιβάδιον, the herb centaury, Plin.

libamen.full: lībāmen, ĭnis, n. libo, that which is poured out in offerings to the gods, a drinkoffering, libation (poet. for libamentum), Ov. F. 3, 733: pingui cumulat libamine flammam, Val. Fl. 1, 204: setas Ignibus imponit, libamina prima, the hairs offered as a beginning of the sacrifice, Verg. A. 6, 246.—So (eccl. Lat.) of the Mosaic drinkofferings: vinum libaminum bibere, Vulg. Deut. 32, 38; id. 1 Par. 29, 21.— Transf., that which is thrown upon a funeral pile, an offering, Stat. Th. 6, 224.— Trop., the

libamentum.full: lībāmentum, i, n. id., that which is poured out in offerings to the gods, a drinkoffering, libation (class.). Lit.: ut sacrificiorum libamenta serventur, Cic. Leg. 2, 12, 29: libamenta Veneri solvere, Just. 12, 10, 4: haec ego nascentes laetus bacchatus ad aras libamenta tuli, offerings, Stat. S. 3, 1, 163: dona magnifica, quasi libamenta praedarum, first-fruits, Cic. Rep. 2, 24, 44: haec est lex sacrificii et libamentorum, Vulg. Lev. 6, 14 (cf. libamen, I. A.).— Trop. That which is tasted: vari

libanios.full: lĭbănĭos, ĭi, f., = λιβάνιος, a kind of vine, with the odor of frankincense, growing in the island of Thasos, Plin. 14, 18, 22, § 117.
libanios.short: lĭbănĭos, ĭi, f., = λιβάνιος, a kind of vine, with the odor of frankincense, growing in the island of Thasos, Plin.

libanitis.full: lĭbănītis, ĭdis, f., = λιβανῖτις, a plant, called also polion, App. Herb. 57.
libanitis.short: lĭbănītis, ĭdis, f., = λιβανῖτις, a plant, called also polion, App.

libanochrus.full: lĭbănŏchrūs, i, f., = λιβανόχρους (frankincense-colored), a precious stone, otherwise unknown, Plin. 37, 10, 62, § 171.
libanochrus.short: lĭbănŏchrūs, i, f., = λιβανόχρους (frankincense-colored), a precious stone, otherwise unknown, Plin.

libanotis.full: lĭbănōtis, ĭdis, f., = λιβανωτίς, rosemary, Plin. 19, 12, 62, § 187; 20, 16, 64, § 172.
libanotis.short: lĭbănōtis, ĭdis, f., = λιβανωτίς, rosemary, Plin.

libanus1.full: Lĭbănus (scanned Lībănus, Sedul. 4, 55), i, m., = Λίβανος (Hebr. Lĕbānōn), Mount Lebanon, in Syria, Plin. 5, 20, 17, § 77; Aus. Techn. Idyll. 12, 5; Vulg. 3 Reg. 4, 33.— Lībănus, a, um, adj., of Lebanon: Libana cedrus, Sedul. 4, 55.— Transf.: lĭbănus, i, c., frankincense (pure Lat. tus), Vulg. Sirach, 24, 21; 39, 18.

libanus2.full: Lĭbănus, i, m., the name of a slave, Plaut. As. 1, 1, 37.
libanus2.short: Lĭbănus, i, m., the name of a slave, Plaut.

libarius.full: lībārĭus, ii, m. libum, a pastry-cook, confectioner, Sen. Ep. 56, 3.

libatio.full: lībātĭo, ōnis, f. libo, a drink-offering, libation, Cic. Harusp. Resp. 10, 21: mensa, in qua epulae, libationesque reponuntur, Macr. S. 3, 11, 5.— A Mosaic drink-offering ( = libamentum), Vulg. Num. 28, 24 al.

libator.full: lībātor, ōris, m. id., one who makes a libation: cenarum libator, Front. de Fer. Als. ep. 3 Mai.

libatorium.full: lībātōrĭum, ĭi, n. id., the vessel in which a libation was offered, Vulg. 1 Macc. 1, 23; id. Esr. 2, 13.

libella.full: lībella, ae, f. dim. libra. An as, a small silver coin, the tenth part of a denarius: nummi denarii decuma libella, quod libram pondo aeris valebat, et erat ex argento parva, Varr. L. L. 5, § 174 Müll.: librales, unde etiam nunc libella dicitur et dupondius, appendebantur asses, Plin. 33, 3, 13, § 42; Cato, R. R. 15, 1: sunt enim in sestertio libellae decem, singulae viginti, teruncii quadraginta, Volus. Maec. 66.— In gen. Prov. for a very small sum of money, as with us a farthing, groat, cent:

libellaris.full: lĭbellāris, e, adj. libellus, of or belonging to books, book- (late Lat.): opus, a written work, writing, Sid. Ep. 9, 11.

libellatici.full: lĭbellātĭci, ōrum, m. id., a term applied to Christians who, during the persecutions, purchased false certificates of a magistrate that they had sacrificed in the heathen manner, Cypr. Ep. 55.

libellensis.full: lĭbellensis, is, m. id., an officer who presented petitions to the emperor and registered them, Cod. 7, 62, 32; 12, 19, 14; 3, 24, 3.

libellio.full: lĭbellĭo, ōnis, m. id.. * A notary, Varr. ap. Non. 133, 28.—* A poor bookseller: de capsa miseri libellionis, Stat. S. 4, 9, 21.

libellulus.full: lĭbellŭlus, i, m. dim. id., a very little book (post-class.), Mart. Cap. 3, § 289.

libellus.full: lĭbellus, i, m. dim. 3. liber. * The inner bark of a tree, used for writing-tablets: levis in aridulo malvae descripta libello (carmina), Cinna ap. Isid. Orig. 6, 12. — Transf., a little book, pamphlet, esp. a book written in pages, and not in long rolls: epistulae, quas primus videtur ad paginas et formam memorialis libelli convertisse (opp. transversa charta), Suet. Caes. 56. In gen.: scripsi etiam illud quodam in libello, Cic. de Or. 1, 21, 94: in quodam joculari libello, Quint. 8, 6, 73; 2,

libens.full: lĭbens (lŭb-), entis, P. a., v. libet.

libentia.full: lĭbentĭa (lŭb-), ae, f. libens, delight, pleasure, joy (ante- and post-class.): onustum pectus porto laetitia lubentiaque, Plaut. Stich. 2, 1, 3: postquam erili filio Largitu's dictis dapsilis lubentias, id. Ps. 1, 4, 3: libentiae gratiaeque conviviorum, Gell. 15, 2, 7.— Personified: Lĭbentĭa (Lŭb-), ae, f., the goddess of delight, Plaut. As. 2, 2, 2; cf. the foll. art.

libentina.full: Lĭbentīna (Lŭb-), ae, f. id., usually connected with Venus, the goddess of sensual pleasure, Venus: a lubendo libido, libidinosus ac Venus Libentina et Libitina, Varr. L. L. 6, § 47 Müll.; id. ap. Non. 64, 14; Cic. N. D. 2, 23, 61: lucus Veneris Lubentinae, Varr. ap. Non. 64, 14; Aug. Civ. Dei, 4, 8.

liber1.full: līber, ĕra, ĕrum (old form, loebesum et loebertatem antiqui dicebant liberum et libertatem. Ita Graeci λοιβὴν et λείβειν, Paul. ex Fest. p. 121 Müll.; cf. 2. Liber), adj. Gr. root λιφ-, λίπτω, to desire; cf. Sanscr. lub-dhas, desirous; Lat. libet, libido, that acts according to his own will and pleasure, is his own master; free, unrestricted, unrestrained, unimpeded, unshackled; independent, frank, open, bold (opp. servus, servilis). In gen.; constr. absol., with ab, the abl., and poet. also wit
liber1.short: līber, ĕra, ĕrum (old form, loebesum et loebertatem antiqui dicebant liberum et libertatem.

liber2.full: līber, ĕri (gen. plur. liberūm, Att. ap. Cic. Tusc. 3, 9; Turp. ap. Non. 495, 26; Cic. Verr. 2, 1, 15, § 40; 2, 1, 30, § 77; Tac. A. 2, 38; 3, 25 saep.; cf. Cic. Or. 46, 155; but also: liberorum, Cic. Verr. 2, 1, 30, § 76; 2, 5, 42, § 109), m. 1. liber, a child. Sing. (post-class. and rare): si quis maximam portionem libero relinquat, Cod. Just. 3, 28, 33; 5, 9, 8 fin.; Quint. Decl. 2, 8.— Plur., children (freq.; but in class. Lat. only of children with reference to their parents: pueri = childr

liber3.full: Līber, ĕri (Sabine collat. form, loebasius, acc. to Serv. Verg. G. 1, 7; cf. 1. liber, and libertas init.), m. Gr. λείβω, to pour; λοιβή, a drink - offering; Lat. libare, an old Italian deity, who presided over planting and fructification; afterwards identified with the Greek Bacchus: hunc dico Liberum Semelā natum, non eum, quem nostri majores auguste sancteque Liberum cum Cerere et Libera consecraverunt. Sed quod ex nobis natos liberos appellamus, idcirco Cerere nati nominati sunt Liber et Lib

liber4.full: lĭber, bri, m. Gr. λέπειν, to peel; λέπος, λεπίς; cf. λοβός, the inner bark or rind of a tree. Lit. In gen.: obducuntur libro aut cortice trunci, Cic. N. D. 2, 47, 120: colligatae libris (arundines), Varr. R. R. 1, 8, 4: udoque docent (germen) inolescere libro, Verg. G. 2, 77: natam libro et silvestri subere clausam, id. A. 11, 554; id. E. 10, 67: quam denso fascia libro, Juv. 6, 263.— Esp., because the ancients used the bark or rind of trees to write upon; usually the thin rind of the Egyptian

libera.full: Lībĕra, ae, f. 3. Liber. Proserpine, daughter of Ceres, and sister of Liber: hunc dico Liberum Semelā natum, non eum, quem nostri majores auguste sancteque Liberum cum Cerere et Libera consecraverunt, etc., Cic. N. D. 2, 24, 62; Cic. Verr. 2, 5, 14, § 36: Ceres et Libera, quarum sacra, etc., id. ib. 2, 5, 72, § 137: signa aënea Cereri, Libero Liberaeque posuerunt, Liv. 33, 25: supplicatio ad Cereris, Liberi Liberaeque fuit, id. 41, 28; for which in full: familia ad aedem Cereris, Liberi Liberaeq

liberalis1.full: lībĕrālis, e, adj. 1. liber, of or belonging to freedom, relating to the freeborn condition of a man. Lit.: liberalis causa or liberale judicium, a suit concerning a person's freedom, v. Dig. 40, 12, 1 sqq.; Paul. Sent. 5, 1, 1 sqq.: si quisquam hanc liberali caussa manu adsereret, Plaut. Curc. 4, 2, 4; cf. 5, 2, 68: manu eas adserat liberali causa, id. Poen. 4, 2, 84: nam ego liberali illam assero causa manu, I formally assert that she is freeborn, Ter. Ad. 2, 1, 40: judicium, Quint. 6, 3, 32:

liberalis2.full: Lībĕrālis, e, adj., of or belonging to Liber or Bacchus: ludi, a festival in honor of Bacchus, = Liberalia (v. infra), Naev. ap. Paul. ex Fest. p. 116 Müll.—Hence, subst.: Lībĕrālĭa, ĭum, n., a festival in honor of Liber, celebrated on the 17th of March, the day on which youths received the manly toga, Ov. F. 3, 713: Liberalium dies, a pontificibus agonium martiale appellatur, Macr. S. 1, 4, § 15: sacra, id. ib. 1, 18, § 22; Calend. Maff. ap. Inscr. Orell. II. p. 411: Liberalia tu accusas, Cic.
liberalis2.short: Lībĕrālis, e, adj., of or belonging to Liber or Bacchus: ludi, a festival in honor of Bacchus, = Liberalia (v.

liberalitas.full: lībĕrālĭtas, ātis, f. 1. liber, a way of thinking befitting a freeman; a noble, kind, or friendly disposition, noble spirit, kindness, affability. In gen. (rare): liberalitate liberos retinere satius est, quam metu, Ter. Ad. 1, 1, 32: qui ita vivunt, ut eorum probetur fides, liberalitas, kindness, Cic. Lael. 5, 19: (L. Cassius) homo, non liberalitate, ut alii, sed ipsa tristitia et severitate popularis, id. Brut. 25, 97.— In partic., generosity, liberality (the usual signif. of the word; syn.: b

liberatio.full: lībĕrātĭo, ōnis, f. libero, a freeing or becoming free, a delivering, releasing, release, liberation. In gen.: ipsa liberatione et vacuitate omnis molestiae gaudemus, Cic. Fin. 1, 11, 37: malorum, Quint. 5, 10, 33: culpae, Cic. Lig. 1, 1: rempublicam sub obtentu liberationis invadere, of setting it at liberty, Just. 5, 8, 12.— In partic. A discharge in a court of law, an acquittal: libidinosissimae liberationes, Cic. Pis. 36, 87.— In jurid. Lat., a discharge or release from debt, a payment: libe

liberator.full: lībĕrātor, ōris, m. id., a freer, deliverer, liberator: patriae liberatores, Cic. Phil. 1, 2, 6: urbis, Liv. 1, 60: nostri liberatores, Cic. Att. 14, 12, 2: liberator suus, Liv. 6, 14: scortorum, * Plaut. Pers. 3, 3, 14.— In apposition: liberator populus, Liv. 35, 18 fin.—So as an epithet of Jupiter (like Ζευς ἐλευθέριος): libare se liquorem illum Jovi liberatori, Tac. A. 15, 64; 16, 35.—So in eccl. Lat. freq. of God: refugium meum ac liberator meus, Vulg. Psa. 17, 3.— Transf.: liberator ille po

liberatrix.full: lībĕrātrix, īcis, f. liberator, she that releases, Eckhel. D. N. V. T. 6, p. 288.

libere.full: lībĕrē, adv., v. 1. liber fin. A.

libero.full: lībĕro, āvi, ātum, 1 (old form of the fut. perf. liberasso, Plaut. Most. 1, 3, 66), v. a. 1. liber, to make or set free, to free, liberate (syn. vindico). Lit., to release from slavery, to free, manumil: amicas emite, liberate, Plaut. Most. 1, 1, 22: liberem ego te? id. Men. 5, 7, 35: servos, Caes. B. C. 3, 9: sese, Cic. de Or. 1, 40, 182: aliquem vindictā liberare, Plin. Ep. 7, 16, 4.— Transf. In gen., to free, release, extricate, deliver (cf. levo) a person or thing from something (an obligati
libero.short: lībĕro, āvi, ātum, 1 (old form of the fut.

libertas.full: lībertas (old form, loebertas; v. 1. liber init.), ātis, f. 1. liber, the state or condition of a freeman, a being free, freedom, liberty, freedom from restraint or obligation, free will, etc. In gen.: quid est enim libertas? potestas vivendi, ut velis, Cic. Par. 5, 1, 34: ne majorem largiar ei, qui contra dicturus est, libertatem et licentiam, id. Ac. 2, 10, 30: praecidere sibi libertatem vivendi, Cic. Verr. 2, 3, 1, § 3: tabella dat populo eam libertatem, ut, quod velint, faciant, id. Planc. 6

libertina.full: lībertīna, ae, v. 1. libertinus, II. B.

libertinitas.full: lībertīnĭtas, ātis, f. libertinus, the condition of a freedman (jurid. Lat.), Dig. 22, 3, 14; 4, 8, 32; 49, 4, 2 med. al.

libertinium.full: lībertīnĭum, ii, n. libertinus, the property obtained by a freedman on the death of his patron: tenue, Calp. Decl. 14 fin. dub.

libertinus1.full: lībertīnus, a, um, adj. libertus, of or belonging to the condition of a freedman (opp. ingenuus, of the condition of a freeborn person; cf. in the foll. the passage Tac. A. 15, 57, and under II. A. the passage from Gai. Inst. 1, 10 and 11): homo liber, qui se vendidit, manumissus non ad suum statum revertitur, quo se abdicavit, sed efficitur libertinae condicionis, enters into the condition of a freedman, becomes a freedman, Dig. 1, 5, 21: in classem mille socii navales cives Romani libertini or

libertinus2.full: lībertīnus, i, v. 1. libertinus, II. A.

libertus.full: lībertus, a, um, adj. = liberatus, from libero, made free, set free, only as subst., one made free, a freedman, an emancipated person (so called in reference to the manumitter; cf. libertinus, II., and on the several classes of freedmen, v. Sanders ad Just. Inst. 1, 5, 3). Lit. līber-tus, i, m.: tibi servire mavelim Multo, quam alii libertus esse, Plaut. Mil. 4, 8, 47: nec mihi quidem libertus ullus est, id. Curc. 4, 3, 15: feci, e servo ut esses libertus mihi, Ter. And. 1, 1, 10: libertus Cossi

libet.full: lĭbet or lŭbet, libuit (lub-) and libitum (lub-) est (in Cic. perh. only in the latter form), 2, v. n. and impers. (libeo, es, etc., as a personal verb acc. to Caper ap. Prisc. p. 922 P.) [Sanscr. root lubh, cupere, desiderare; Gr. root λιφ- in λίπτω, λιψ; cf. Goth. liub-s; Germ. lieb, dear; Lat. līber], it pleases, is pleasing, is agreeable: mihi, I am disposed, I like, I please, I will.— Constr. with nom. of a demonstr. or rel. pronoun, with inf. or a subject-clause as subject, or impers. with
libet.short: lĭbet or lŭbet, libuit (lub-) and libitum (lub-) est (in Cic.

libethra.full: Lībēthra, ae, f. (or ōrum, n.; Lībē-thros or -us, i, m., Serv. Verg. E. 7, 21), = Λείβηθρα, a fountain near Magnesia, in Macedonia, sacred to the Muses, Mel. 2, 3, 2; Plin. 4, 9, 16, § 32.—Hence, Lībēthris, ĭdis, f., = Λειβηθρίς, Libethrian: fons, Mart. Cap. 6, § 654.—Plur. subst.: Lībēthrĭ-dĕs, the Muses: nymphae Libethrides, Verg. E. 7, 21.

libethrum.full: Lībēthrum, i, n., = Λείβηθρον, a city of Macedonia, near the fountain of Libethra, Liv. 44, 5, 12.
libethrum.short: Lībēthrum, i, n., = Λείβηθρον, a city of Macedonia, near the fountain of Libethra, Liv.

libici.full: Libĭci, ōrum, m., a people of Gallia Transpadana, Plin. 3, 17, 21, § 124; perh. identical with the Libui, v. Liv. 5, 35; 21, 38; 33, 37.
libici.short: Libĭci, ōrum, m., a people of Gallia Transpadana, Plin.

libidinitas.full: lĭbīdĭnĭtas (lŭbīd-), ātis, f. libido, desire, Laber. ap. Non. 491, 5.

libidinor.full: lĭbīdĭnor (lŭbīd-), āri, v. dep. id, to indulge or gratify lust (post-Aug.): cum libidinatur, Mart. 7, 67, 13: inceste libidinari, Suet. Ner. 28 fin.: abeunt libidinatum ad filias Moab, Tert. ad Gnost. 3; Petr. 138, 7.

libidinosus.full: lĭbīdĭnōsus (lŭbīd-), a, um, adj. libido, full of desire, passion, or lust, selfwilled, licentious, sensual, lustful, voluptuous, libidinous. Lit. (in a bad sense), Cic. Rep. Fragm. ap. Non. 491, 16 (Rep. 2, 41, 68 Mos.): homo libidinosissimus, Cic. Verr. 2, 2, 78, § 192: nihil (isto) luxuriosius, nihil libidinosius, id. Pis. 27, 66: libidinosior es quam ullus spado, Quint. 6, 3, 64: caper, lecherous, Hor. Epod. 10, 23.—Of inanim. and abstr. things: libidinosissimae liberationes, arbitrary, self

libido.full: lĭbīdo or lŭbīdo, ĭnis, f. libet, pleasure, desire, eagerness, longing, fancy, inclination (cf.: appetitio, optatio, cupiditas, cupido, studium). In gen.: ubilubido veniet nauseae, Cato, R. R. 156, 4; Plaut. Pers. 5, 2, 26; Lucr. 4, 779: ex bonis (perturbationibus) libidinem et laetitiam, ut sit laetitia praesentium bonorum, libido futurorum, Cic. Tusc. 4, 6, 11: ipsa iracundia libidinis est pars: sic enim definitur iracundia, ulciscendi libido, id. ib. 3, 5, 11; id. Fin. 3, 9, 32: non omnibus d

libita.full: lĭbĭta, ōrum, n., v. libet fin. 2.

libitina.full: Lĭbĭtīna, ae, f. libet, līber, the goddess of corpses, in whose temple everything pertaining to burials was sold or hired out, and where the registers of deaths were kept. Lit.: triginta funerum milia in rationem Libitinae venerunt, were registered, Suet. Ner. 39.— Transf. The requisites for burial, the apparatus of funerals: pestilentia tanta erat ut Libitina vix sufficeret, i. e. it was hardly possible to bury all the dead, Liv. 40, 19, 3: ne liberorum quidem funeribus Libitina sufficiebat, id

libitinarius.full: lĭbĭtīnārĭus, ii, m. Libitina, an undertaker (post-Aug.): designatores et libitinarii, Sen. Ben. 6, 38; cf.: si libitinarius, quos Graece νεκροθάπτας vocant, etc., Dig. 14, 3, 5, § 8.

libitinensis.full: Lĭbĭtīnensis, e, adj. id., of Libitina: porta, the gate at which the bodies of slain gladiators were carried out, Lampr. Commod. 16, 7.

libitus.full: lĭbĭtus, a, um, Part., from libet.
libitus.short: lĭbĭtus, a, um, Part., from libet.

libo1.full: lībo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. root λιβ-, λειβω, λοιβή; cf. Līber, delibutus, etc., to take a little from any thing. Lit. In gen.: libare gramina dentibus, to crop, Calp. Ecl. 5, 51.— In partic. To take a taste of a thing, to taste: jecur, Liv. 25, 16: pocula Bacchi, Verg. A. 3, 354: flumina libant Summa leves, to sip, id. G. 4, 54.— Poet., to touch a thing: cibos digitis, Ov. A. A. 1, 577: summam celeri pede libat harenam, id. M. 10, 653: cellulae limen, Petr. 136: oscula alicujus, to kiss, Verg. A.

libo2.full: Lĭbo, ōnis, m., a Roman surname in the gens Marcia and Scribonia, Cic. Att. 12, 5, 3; id. Brut. 23, 89; id. de Or. 2, 65, 263; id. Ac. 1, 1, 3; Hor. Ep. 1, 19, 8.
libo2.short: Lĭbo, ōnis, m., a Roman surname in the gens Marcia and Scribonia, Cic.

libonotus.full: lĭbŏnŏtus or -tos, i, m., = λιβόνοτος, a wind between south and south-west, pure Lat. austro-africus, Vitr. 1, 6, 10; Sen. Q. N. 5, 16, 6 Fick. (dub.; Haase, leuconotus); Plin. 2, 47, 46, § 120; Isid. 13, 11, 7.
libonotus.short: lĭbŏnŏtus or -tos, i, m., = λιβόνοτος, a wind between south and south-west, pure Lat.

libra.full: lībra, ae, f. cf. λίτρα; root cli-, clino, the Roman pound, of twelve ounces: as erat libra pondus, Varr. L. L. 5, § 169 Müll.: coronam auream libram pondo ex publica pecunia in Capitolio Iovi donum posuit, Liv. 4, 20: mulli binas libras ponderis raro exsuperant, Plin. 9, 17, 30, § 64: expende Hannibalem, quot libras in duce summo invenies? Juv. 10, 147: neque argenti in convivio plus pondo quam libras centum inlaturos, Gell. 2, 24, 2: dipondii pondo duas erant libras, Gai. Inst. 1, 122.— Transf

libralis.full: lībrālis, e, adj. libra, of or containing a pound, of a pound weight: pondus, Plin. 19, 2, 11, § 34: offae, Col. 6, 2, 7: veluti asses librales erant, Gai. Inst. 1, 122.

libramen.full: lībrāmen, ĭnis, n. libro, a balance, poise (late Lat.).—Trop.: judicii, Claud. Mam. Stat. Anim. 3, 13.

libramentum.full: lībrāmentum, i, n. id., that which gives to any thing a downward pressure; weight, gravity. Lit.: plumbi, Liv. 42, 63, 4.— A fall, descent of water: libramentum aquae, Plin. 31, 6, 31, § 57: quod libramentum cum exinanitum est, suscitat et elicit fontem, cum repletum, moratur et strangulat, of a spring that alternately rises and falls, Plin. Ep. 4, 30, 10: inferiore labro demisso ad libramentum modicae aquae receptae in fauces, palpitante ibi lingua ululatus elicitur, of the croaking of frogs, P

libraria.full: lĭbrārĭa, ae, f., v. 1. librarius, II., and 2. librarius, II. B.

librariolus.full: lĭbrārĭŏlus, i, m. dim. 2. librarius, a copyist, transcriber; a scribe, secretary, Cic. Att. 4, 4, 6; id. Balb. 6, 14: ex librariolis Latinis, id. Leg. 1, 2, 7.

librarius1.full: lībrārĭus, a, um, adj. libra. Of or containing a pound, of a pound weight (post-Aug.): frusta, Col. 12, 53, 4: as, Gell. 20, 1, 31.— Subst. lībrārĭus, ii, m., a weight, the sixteenth part of a modius, = sextarius: sextarius aequus aequo cum librario siet, sexdecimque librarii in modio sient, Plebisc. ap. Paul. ex Fest. p. 246 Müll.— lībrārĭa, ae, f., she that weighed out the wool to the female slaves, a forewoman, head-spinner, called also lanipendia, Juv. 6, 475 (by others referred to 2. librar

librarius2.full: lĭbrārĭus, a, um, adj. 3. liber, of or belonging to books: scriba librarius, a copyist, transcriber of books, Varr. R. R. 3, 2, 14; Cic. Agr. 2, 13, 32: libraria taberna, a bookseller's shop, Cic. Phil. 2, 9, 21: scriptor, a transcriber of books, Hor. A. P. 354: atramentum, ink for writing books, Plin. 27, 7, 28, § 52.—Hence, Subst. lĭ-brārĭus, i, m. A transcriber of books, a copyist, scribe, secretary, Cic. Agr. 2, 5, 13: librum ut tuis librariis daret, id. Att. 12, 40, 1: librarii mendum, Liv.

librate.full: lībrātē, adv., v. libro, P. a. fin.

libratio.full: lībrātĭo, ōnis, f. libro. A making level, levelling: fortasse qui Archimedis libros legit, dicet non posse fieri veram ex aqua librationem, Vitr. 8, 6, 3.— A horizontal position, level: circa terrae librationem, Vitr. 6, 1, 5.— A hurling off, hurling, slinging, Diom. p. 473 P.

librator.full: lībrātor, ōris, m. id.. A leveller, esp. by means of a water-level, a surveyor, Cato, R. R. 22, 1; Front. Aquaed. 105: superest ut tu libratorem vel architectum mittas, qui diligenter exploret, sitne lacus altior mari, Plin. Ep. 10, 50, 3.— One who throws or hurls weapons by hand (cf. funditor, a slinger): funditores libratoresque excutere tela et proturbare hostem jubet, Tac. A. 2, 20: libratoribus funditoribusque attributus locus, id. ib. 13, 39; Inscr. ap. Kellerm. Vigil. p. 55, n. 127.

libratura.full: lībrātūra, ae, f. libro, a making even: cutis, Veg. 2, 22, 3.

libratus.full: lībrātus, a, um, Part. and P. a., from libro.

libriger.full: lĭbrĭger, gĕri, m. 4. liber-gero, one who carries books, a book-carrier, colporteur, Paul. Nol. Ep. 28, 4.

librile.full: lībrīle, is, v. the foll. art.

librilis.full: lībrīlis, e, adj. libra. Of a pound, weighing a pound: tunica, Vop. Bonos. 15, 8: fundis librilibus sudibusque, Gallos proterrent, throwing stones of a pound each, Caes. B. G. 7, 81, 4.— Of or pertaining to weighing.—Hence, subst.: lībrīle, is, n. A balance, pair of scales: in librili perpendere, Gell. 20, 1, 34.— A scale-beam: librile scapus librae, Paul. ex Fest. p. 116 Müll.

librilla.full: librilla appellantur instrumenta bellica saxa scilicet ad bracchii crassitudinem in modum flagellorum loris revincta, Paul. ex Fest. p. 116 Müll. (Scalig. prefers to read † librilia; v. librilis, I.).
librilla.short: librilla appellantur instrumenta bellica saxa scilicet ad bracchii crassitudinem in modum flagellorum loris revincta, Paul.

libripens.full: lībrĭpens, pendis, m. libra-pendo. One who weighed or counted out the pay to soldiers, a paymaster, Plin. 33, 3, 13, § 43: impubes libripens esse non potest, Ael. ap. Prisc. 892 P.— One who held the balance, as if to weigh out money, at nominal sales: adhibitis non minus quam V. testibus civibus Romanis puberibus, item libripende, Gai. Inst. 1, § 113; Ulp. Fragm. 19, 3; cf. Plin. 33, 3, 13, § 43.

libro.full: lībro, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. libra. To balance, make even, level, to determine a level: aquam, to level water, i. e. to ascertain the fall of water by means of a level, Vitr. 8, 6, 3: collocationem libratam indicare, id 8, 6, 1.—Pass. impers.: libratur autem dioptris, Vitr. 8, 6, 1.— Transf., to make even or level: pavimenta, Cato, R. R. 18, 7.— To hold in equilibrium, to poise, balance: terra librata ponderibus, Cic. Tusc. 5, 24, 69: columnarum turbines ita librati perpenderunt, ut puero circumag

libs.full: Libs (Lips), ĭbis, adj., = Λίψ, Libyan; subst., a Libyan; of Antæus, Sid. Carm. 9, 94.— The west-south-west wind: ab occasu brumali Africus: Noton et Liba nominant, Plin. 2, 47, 46, § 119: velivolique maris constrator leuconotos libs, Aus. Technopaegn. de Deis, 12.—Form Lips: Africus furibundus apud Graecos Lips dicitur, Sen. Q. N. 5, 16, 5; cf. Suet. Fragm. § 151 (p. 231 Reiffersch.).

libui.full: Lĭbŭi, ōrum, m., a people of Gallia Transpadana, Liv. 5, 35; 21, 38; 33, 37; perh. identical with Libici, Plin. 3, 17, 21, § 124.
libui.short: Lĭbŭi, ōrum, m., a people of Gallia Transpadana, Liv.

libum.full: lībum (lībus, m., Nigid. ap. Non. 211, 31), i, n. libo; cf. Varr. L. L. 4, 22, a cake, pancake of meal, made with milk or oil, and spread with honey, Cato, R. R. 75: rustica liba, Ov. F. 3, 670: adorea liba per herbam Subiciunt epulis, Verg. A. 7, 109; Ov. F. 3, 761: plena domus libis venalibus, Juv. 3, 187.—Often used in offerings to the gods: liba absoluta esse et rem divinam paratam, Varr. R. R. 2, 8, 1: suum Baccho dicemus honorem, ... et liba feremus, Verg. G. 2, 394; Tib. 1, 7, 54; 1, 10,

liburni.full: Lĭburni, ōrum, m., the Liburnians, an Illyrian people, between Istria and Dalmatia, in the mod. Croatia, Mel. 2, 3, 12 and 13; Liv. 10, 2: regna Liburnorum, Verg. A. 1, 244.—In sing.: Lĭburnus, i, m., a Liburnian; esp., a Liburnian slave, such as were used in Rome as sedan-bearers, Juv. 3, 239; 4, 75.— Hence, Lĭburnus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to the Liburnians, Liburnian: terrae, Luc. 8, 38: rostra, Liburnian ships, Prop. 3, 9 (4, 10), 44.—Hence, Subst.: Lĭburna, ae, f., a light, fast-saili
liburni.short: Lĭburni, ōrum, m., the Liburnians, an Illyrian people, between Istria and Dalmatia, in the mod.

liburnus1.full: Lĭburnus, a, um, v. Liburni, I.

liburnus2.full: Lĭburnus, i, m. libet, the god of lustful enjoyment, Arn. 4, 9.

libya.full: Lĭbўa (Lĭbŭa, Plaut. Curc. 3, 76), ae, and Lĭbўē, ēs, f., = Λιβύη, Libya, Plin. 5, 6, 6, § 39; Cic. N. D. 1, 36, 101: Graecus Aristippus, qui servos proicere aurum In media jussit Libya, Hor. S. 2, 3, 100.— Transf., Africa.—Form Libya: mundus ... premitur Libyae devexus in Austros. Verg. G. 1, 240; Juv. 11, 25.—Form Libye: Libye torretur, Sil. 1, 194: tibi habe frumentum, O Libye, dum tubera mittas, Juv. 5, 119.— Hence, Lĭbўcus, a, um, adj., = Λιβυκός, of Libya, Libyan: fines, Verg. A. 1, 339: c

libyaegyptii.full: Lĭbў-aegyptĭi, ōrum, m., a people in the west of Libya interior, Mela, 1, 4, 3; Plin. 5, 8, 8, § 43 (al. Libyes Aegyptii).
libyaegyptii.short: Lĭbў-aegyptĭi, ōrum, m., a people in the west of Libya interior, Mela, 1, 4, 3;

libyphoenices.full: Lĭbў-phoenīces, um, m., = Λιβυφοίνικες, Libyphœnicians: a Libyan people in the territory of Byzacium, descended from Phœnicians, Liv. 21, 22, 3; 25, 40, 5; Plin. 5, 4, 3, § 24.
libyphoenices.short: Lĭbў-phoenīces, um, m., = Λιβυφοίνικες, Libyphœnicians: a Libyan people in the territory of Byzacium, descended from Phœnicians, Liv.

licens.full: lĭcens, entis, P. a., from licet.

licenter.full: lĭcenter, adv., v. licet, P. a. fin.

licentia.full: lĭcentĭa, ae, f. licet, freedom, liberty, leave to do as one pleases, license. In gen.: Dae. Licet ... licet ... licet. Tr. Hercules istum infelicet cum sua licentia, Plaut. Rud. 4, 6, 21: nobis nostra Academia magnam licentiam dat, ut, etc., Cic. Off. 3, 4, 20: pueris non omnem ludendi licentiam damus, id. ib. 1, 29, 103: tantum licentiae dabat gloria, id. de Sen. 13, 44: absolvendi, Tac. A. 14, 49: lasciviendi permittere militibus, Suet. Caes. 67.— In partic. Liberty which one assumes, boldnes

licentiatus.full: lĭcentĭātus, ūs, m. licentia, freedom, license: meo licentiatu, Laber. ap. Non. 212, 6 (Com. Fragm. v. 71 Rib.).

licentiosus.full: lĭcentĭōsus, a, um, adj. licentia, full of freedom or license, over-free, unbridled, unrestrained, wanton, licentious (post-Aug.): (ebor dicere) non minus est licentiosum, quam si sulfuri et gutturi subicerent in genitivo litteram o mediam, * Quint. 1, 6, 23: temeritas, App. M. 5, p. 165, 11.— Comp.: conversatio cum viris licentiosior, Sen. Excerpt. Contr. 6, 8, § 5.—Sup.: libidini licentiosissimum spatium praebere, Aug. adv. Pelag. 2, 7.—Adv.: lĭcentĭōsē (late Lat. and rare), Aug. Gen. ad Lit.

licentius.full: Lĭcentĭus, ii, m., the name of a Christian poet, Paul. Nol. Epist. 47, 51.
licentius.short: Lĭcentĭus, ii, m., the name of a Christian poet, Paul.

liceo1.full: lĭcĕo, cŭi, cĭtum, 2, v. n. Sanscr. root rik-, riktas, empty; Gr. λιπ-, λείπω, leave; Lat. lic-, linquo, licet, liceor; cf. Germ. leihen, verleihen, to be for sale; to have a price put upon it, to be valued, esteemed at so much. Lit. (rare but class.): omnia vaenibunt, quiqui licebunt, praesenti pecunia, Plaut.
