lupanaris.full: lŭpānāris, e, adj. lupanar, belonging to or characteristic of a lewd woman: infamia, App. M. 9, p. 229, 7.

lupanarium.full: lŭpānārĭum, ii, n. id., i. q. lupanar, Dig. 5, 3, 27 al.

lupanus.full: lŭpānus, a, um, adj. lupa, lewd: feminae, Commod. 59, 22.

lupariae.full: lŭpārĭae, ārum, f., brothels, Sext. Ruf. Reg. 2; Inscr. ap. Gud. 33, 1.

luparius.full: lŭpārĭus, ĭi, m. lupus, a wolf-hunter, Serv. Verg. G. 1, 139; cf.: luparius, λυκοθήρας, Gloss. Philox.

lupatus.full: lŭpātus, a, um, adj. id., furnished with wolf's teeth, i. e. iron prickles shaped like a wolf's teeth. Adj.: Gallia nec lupatis Temperet ora frenis, curbs studded with jagged points, Hor. C. 1, 8, 6. — Subst. (sc. freni or frena): lŭpāti, ōrum, m., and lŭpāta, ōrum, n., a curb armed with sharp teeth: equus adeo sprevit lupatos, ut, etc., Sol. 45: duris parere lupatis, Verg. G. 3, 208: asper equus duris contunditur ora lupatis, Ov. Am. 1, 2, 15: aurea lupata, Mart. 1, 105, 4.

luperca.full: Lŭperca, ae, f. v. Lupercus, a goddess of the old Romans, the wife of Lupercus, identified with the deified she-wolf that suckled Romulus, Arn. 4, 128; cf. Liv. 1, 4; Lact. 1, 20.

lupercal.full: Lŭpercal, ālis, n. Lupercalis, a grotto on the Palatine Hill, sacred to the Lycean Pan (Lupercus): gelidā monstrat sub rupe Lupercal, Verg. A. 8, 342; v. Serv. ad loc.: quamquam Velia non est vilior quam Lupercal, Cic. Fam. 7, 20, 1: forsitan et quaeras cur sit locus ille Lupercal, Ov. F. 2, 381.—Hence, Lŭpercālis, e, adj., of or belonging to the Lupercalia, Lupercal: sacrum, Suet. Aug. 31.— Hence, plur. as subst.: Lŭpercālĭa, ĭum and ōrum, n., the festival of the Lycean Pan (Lupercus), celebrat

lupercus.full: Lŭpercus, i, m. lupus, and perh. arceo. The Roman name of the Lycean Pan (so called because he protected the flocks from wolves), Just. 4, 3, 1.—Far more freq., A priest of the Lycean Pan: nudi Luperci, Verg. A. 8, 663; Ov. F. 2, 267: nec prodest agili palmas praebere Luperco, Juv. 2, 142. There were at first two classes of these priests, the Fabiani and the Quintiliani, to whom afterwards, in honor of Cæsar, were added the Juliani, Suet. Caes. 76. At first the priests were chosen only from the

lupia.full: Lupĭa (Luppia), ae, m., a river in the north-west of Germany, now the Lippe, Mela, 3, 3, 3; Vell. 2, 10, 5; Tac. A. 1, 60; 2, 7; id. H. 5, 22.
lupia.short: Lupĭa (Luppia), ae, m., a river in the north-west of Germany, now the Lippe, Mela, 3, 3, 3;

lupiae.full: Lū^pĭae, ārum, f. plur., a town of Calabria, Paul. Nol. 30, 85; cf. Mel. 2, 4.

lupicinus.full: Lŭpĭcīnus, i, m., the name of a man, Paul. Petr. Vit. S. Mart. 1, 369.
lupicinus.short: Lŭpĭcīnus, i, m., the name of a man, Paul.

lupillus.full: lŭpillus, i, m. dim. 2. lupinus, a small lupine, Plaut. Stich. 5, 4, 9.

lupinaceus.full: lŭpīnācĕus, a, um, adj. id., of or made of lupines: lomentum, App. Herb. 21.

lupinarius.full: lŭpīnārĭus, a, um, adj. id., of or for lupines: labrum, Cato, R. R. 10 and 11.— Subst.: lŭpīnārĭi, ōrum, m., dealers in lupines, Lampr. Alex. Sev. 33, 2.

lupinus1.full: lŭpīnus, a, um, adj. lupus, of or belonging to a wolf, wolf's: ubera, Cic. Cat. 3, 8, 19: juba, Prop. 4 (5), 10, 20. pellis, Plin. 28, 19, 78, § 257.— Transf., like a wolf: impetus, Enn. ap. Don. Ter. Phorm. 2, 2, 25 (Sat. v. 28 Vahl.): rictus, Prud. στεφ. 2, 98.

lupinus2.full: lŭpīnus, i, m., and lŭpīnum, i, n., a lupine: ibi lupinum bonum fiet, Cato, R. R. 34, 2; cf. Col. 12, 10, 1 sq.; Plin. 18, 14, 36, § 133; Pall. 1, 6, 14; 7, 3, 2: fetus viciae tristisque lupini, Verg. G. 1, 75: tunicam mihi malo lupini, Juv. 14, 153. —Esp., since, on the stage, lupines were used as mock-money, prov.: nec tamen ignorat quid distent aera lupinis, Hor. Ep. 1, 7, 23; cf.: Ag. Agite, inspicite. Co. Aurum est, profecto, spectatores, comicum, Plaut. Poen. 3, 2, 20; cf. also: si quis su
lupinus2.short: lŭpīnus, i, m., and lŭpīnum, i, n., a lupine: ibi lupinum bonum fiet, Cato, R.

lupodunum.full: Lūpŏdūnum, i, n., a German town near the sources of the Danube, now Ladenburg or Lupff, Aus. Mosell. 423.
lupodunum.short: Lūpŏdūnum, i, n., a German town near the sources of the Danube, now Ladenburg or Lupff, Aus.

lupor.full: lŭpor, āri, v. dep. n. [lupa, II.], to associate with lewd women: cum meretrice per vias lupantur, Atta ap. Non. 133, 11 (Com. Rel. v. 3 Rib.): impune lupari, Lucil. ib. 15.

lupula.full: lŭpŭla, ae, f. dim. id., a little she-wolf, transf., a witch, hag, App. M. 5, p. 164, 3.

lupus1.full: lŭpus, i, m. kindred with λύκος; Sanscr. vrika, and our wolf, a wolf. Lit.: torva leaena lupum sequitur, lupus ipse capellam, Verg. E. 2, 63; Plin. 10, 63, 88, § 173; 8, 22, 34, § 80: Martialis lupus, sacred to Mars, Hor. C. 1, 17, 9; so, Martius, Verg. A. 9, 566: lupus femina for lupa, a she-wolf, Enn. ap. Serv. Verg. A. 2, 355 (Ann. v. 70 Vahl.); id. ap. Non. 378, 18 (ib. v. 73): lupus masculinum (est), quamquam Varro ... lupum feminam dicit, Ennium Pictoremque Fabium secutus, Quint. 1, 6, 12.

lupus2.full: Lŭpus, a surname in the gens Rutilia, e. g. P. Lutilius Lupus, a rhetorician in the time of Augustus; v. Rutilius; cf. Cic. N. D. 1, 23, 63.
lupus2.short: Lŭpus, a surname in the gens Rutilia, e.

lura.full: lūra (lōra), ae, f. from same root as lorum, q. v., prop. a thong; hence, the mouth of a skin or leathern bag, which was closed by a thong: lura os cullei vel etiam utris: unde lurcones capacis gulae homines et bonorum suorum consumptores, Paul. ex Fest. p. 120.— Transf., a skin, leathern sack, Aus. Perioch. Odyss. 10 (In Lucil. ap. Cic. Tusc. 4, 21, 48, Fischer conjectures furi, v. h. l.).

lurchinabundus.full: lurchĭnābundus (lurcĭnābun-dus and lurchābundus), a, um, adj. 1. lurco, voracious, Cat. ap. Quint. 1, 6, 42; cf. Spald. ad loc.
lurchinabundus.short: lurchĭnābundus (lurcĭnābun-dus and lurchābundus), a, um, adj.

lurco1.full: lurco, āre, v. a., and lurcor, āri, v. dep. n. [perh. lura, to have a stomach of leather], to eat voraciously, to devour: lurcare est cum aviditate cibum sumere, Non. 10, 31: lardum, Pomp. ap. Non. 11, 6 (Com. Rel. v. 169 Rib.): ut lurcaretur lardum, Lucil. ib. 11, 2.

lurco2.full: lurco (lurcho, Serv. ad Verg. A. 6, 4; Prob. p. 1455 P.), ōnis, m., a gormandizer, glutton.—Lit.: lurco, edax, furax, fugax, Plaut. Pers. 3, 3, 16: vivite lurcones, comedones, vivite ventres, Lucil. ap. Non. 11, 9: lastaurum et lurconem et nebulonem popinonemque appellans, Suet. Gram. 15: lurcones capacis gulae homines et bonorum suorum consumptores, Paul. ex Fest. p. 120.

lurco3.full: Lurco, ōnis, m., a Roman surname. Esp., M. Aufidius, who was the first to fatten peacocks for the table, Varr. R. R. 3, 6, 1; Plin. 10, 20, 23, § 45.—So of M. Perpenna Lurco, Inscr. Grut. 237, 8.— Transf., a voluptuary, debauchee, App. M. 8, p. 213, 6.—Hence, Lurcōnĭānus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Lurco, Lurconian: Apiciana et Lurconiana condimenta, Tert. Anim. 33.
lurco3.short: Lurco, ōnis, m., a Roman surname.

luridatus.full: lūrĭdātus, a, um, adj [luridus], besmeared, defiled, Tert. adv. Marc. 4, 8.
luridatus.short: lūrĭdātus, a, um, adj [luridus], besmeared, defiled, Tert.

luridus.full: lūrĭdus, a, um, adj. luror, pale yellow, sallow, wan, ghastly, lurid. Lit.: luridi supra modum pallidi, Paul. ex Fest. p. 120; cf.: luridus, ὠχρός, πέλιος, ἰκτερικός, ὑπώπιος, Gloss. Philox.: luridus Orcus, Hor. C. 3, 4, 74: pallor, Ov. M. 4, 267: dentes, Hor. C. 4, 13, 10: bilis, Sen. Ep. 95; cf.: viden tu illi maculari corpus maculis luridis, *Plaut. Capt. 3, 4, 63: sol, Plin. Ep. 6, 20 fin.: luna, Sen. Med. 790.— Transf., that renders pale or ghastly: horror, Ov. M. 14, 198: aconita, id. ib.

luror.full: lūror, ōris, m. etym. dub.; cf.: pullus, lividus, a yellowish color, sallowness, paleness, Lucr. 4, 308: luror permanat in herbas, Claud. Rapt. Pros. 3, 238: lurore buxeo foedatus, App. M. 9, p. 222, 31.

luscinia.full: luscĭnĭa, ae, f. (luscĭnĭus, ĭi, m., Phaedr. 3, 18, 2 and 11; Sen. Ep. 76, 7; and, † luscĭnus, i, m., = ἀηδών, Gloss. Lat. Gr.) [for clus-cinia; Sanscr. root cru, to hear; Gr. κλύω; Lat. clueo, to be famous, akin to gloria and cano; hence, the melodious or glorious songstress], the nightingale, Plin. 10, 29, 43, § 81 sq.: luscinias soliti impenso prandere coëmptas, Hor. S. 2, 3, 245: vox luscinii, Sen. Ep. 76, 9.

lusciniola.full: luscĭnĭŏla, ae, f. dim. luscinia, a little nightingale: aves cantrices, ut lusciniolae ac merulae, Varr. R. R. 3, 5, 14; cf. id. L. L. 5, § 76 Müll.—Prov.: So. Pol magis metuo mihi in monendo ne defuerit optio. Ba. Pol ego metuo lusciniolae ne defuerit cantio, of one who possesses a thing in superabundance, Plaut. Bacch. 1, 1, 4 Fleck.

luscinius1.full: luscĭnĭus, ii, m., a nightingale; v. luscinia init.

luscinius2.full: luscĭnĭus, a, um, adj. luscinus, blinded, one-eyed, applied by Commodus to persons one of whose eyes he had destroyed, Lampr. Commod. 10, 6; cf. the foll. art.

luscinus1.full: luscĭnus, a, um, adj. luscus, oneeyed; plur. as subst.: luscĭni, ōrum, m., one-eyed persons: qui altero lumine orbi nascerentur, Coclites vocabantur, qui par vis utrisque Ocellae; Luscini injuriae cognomen habuere, Plin. 11, 37, 55, § 150.

luscinus2.full: Luscĭnus, i, m., a Roman surname: C. Fabricius Luscinus, Val. Max. 4, 3, 6; Liv. 33, 42 and 43; 37, 4.
luscinus2.short: Luscĭnus, i, m., a Roman surname: C.

luscinus3.full: luscĭnus, i, m., v. luscinia init.

luscitio.full: luscĭtĭo, ōnis, f. luscus, dimness of sight, Dig. 21, 1, 10, § 4: vitium oculorum, quod clarius vesperi quam meridie cernit, Paul. ex Fest. p. 120, 17 Müll.

luscitiosus.full: luscĭtĭōsus and luscĭōsus, a, um, adj. i. e. luscitionosus, from luscitio, that cannot see in the dusk or by lamp-light, dim-sighted, purblind: Pa. Quid jam? Sce. Quia luscitiosus. Pa. Verbero, edepol tu quidem caecus, non luscitiosus, Plaut. Mil. 2, 3, 51 sq. Lorenz ad loc.: vesperi non videre, quos appellant lusciosos, Varr. ap. Non. 135, 13: edepol idem caecus non lusciosus est, id. ib. 14; cf. also: luscitiosus qui vespere nihil videt, Isid. Orig. 10, 163: lusciosos nyctalopas a Graecis dict
luscitiosus.short: luscĭtĭōsus and luscĭōsus, a, um, adj.

luscus.full: luscus, a, um, adj. root luc of lux; with fundamental idea to glimmer; cf. Gr. λυγη, gloom, one-eyed: Le. Oculum ego ecfodiam tibi, si verbum addideris. Sc. Hercle qui dicam tamen: nam si sic non licebit, luscus dixero, Plaut. Trin. 2, 4, 64; id. Curc. 4, 2, 19: Appius cenabo, inquit, apud te, huic lusco, familiari meo C. Sestio: uni enim locum esse video, Cic. de Or. 2, 60, 246; Mart. 4, 65; Gai Inst. 3, 214: cum Gaetula ducem portaret belua luscum (of Hannibal), Juv. 10, 157: ambos perdidit il

lusio.full: lūsĭo, ōnis, f. ludo, a playing, play: in ludum discendi, non lusionis, Cic. Q. Fr. 3, 4, 6: pueri lusionibus vel laboriosis delectantur, id. Fin. 5, 20, 55: in ipsā lusione (pilae), in the act of playing, id. de Or. 1, 16, 73: pilaris lusio, Stat. S. 4 praef.

lusitania.full: Lūsĭtānĭa, ae, f., the western part of Spain, the mod. Portugal and a part of the Spanish provinces of Estremadura and Toledo, Caes. B. C. 1, 38, 2; Liv. 21, 43, 8; 27, 20; Mel. 2, 6, 3 sq.; 3, 1, 6; 3, 6, 2; Liv. Ep. 52; Plin. 4, 21, 35, § 113.—Hence, Lū-sĭtānus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Lusitania, Lusitanian: cerasa, Plin. 15, 25, 30, § 103: tela, Val. Max. 9, 1, n. 5.—In plur. subst.: Lūsĭtāni, ōrum, m., the Lusitanians, Cic. Brut. 23, 89; Liv. 35, 1; 37, 46 sq.; Plin. 4, 22, 35, § 116
lusitania.short: Lūsĭtānĭa, ae, f., the western part of Spain, the mod.

lusito.full: lūsĭto, āre, v. freq. n. [ludo], to play often or habitually (ante- and post-class.): aut coturnices dantur, quibuscum lusitent, Plaut. Capt. 5, 4, 6: alea festiva et honesta lusitabamus, Gell. 18, 13, 1: in labellis morsicatim, Naev. ap. Non. 139, 25.

lusius.full: Lusĭus, i, m., a river of Arcadia, Cic. N. D. 3, 22, 57.
lusius.short: Lusĭus, i, m., a river of Arcadia, Cic.

lusor.full: lūsor, ōris, m. ludo, one who plays at a game; a player. Lit.: sic ne perdiderit, non cessat perdere lusor, Ov. A. A. 1, 1, 451; Sen. Ben. 2, 17, 3: furtum factum domi et eo tempore quo alea ludebatur, licet lusor non fuerit qui quid eorum fecerit, impune fit, Dig. 11, 5, 1, § 2.—Poet. transf.: cum lusore catello, a playful little dog, Juv. 9, 611.— Trop. A humorous writer: tenerorum lusor amorum, Ov Tr. 4, 10, 1.— A banterer, mocker: te ut deludam contra, lusorem meum, Plaut. Am. 2, 2, 62.

lusorius.full: lūsōrĭus, a, um, adj. lusor, of or belonging to a player. Lit.: pila, a playing-ball, Plin. 7, 56, 57, § 205: alveus cum tesseris, id. 37, 2, 6, § 13.—Hence, Subst.: lūsōrĭum, ii, n., a place where shows of gladiators and wild beasts were given: statuit sibi triclinium in summo lusorio, Lampr. Heliog. 25; Lact. Mort. Persecut. 21.— Used for pleasure; hence, as subst.: lūsōrĭa, ae, f. (sc. navis), a vessel for pleasure, yacht, Sen. Ben. 7, 20, 3; and, transf., any kind of light vessel, cutter: lu

lustrabilis.full: lustrābĭlis, e, adj. lustro, conspicuous, περίβλεπτος (i. e. spectabilis), Gloss. Philox.

lustrago.full: lustrāgo, ĭnis, f. perh. from lustrum, a plant, also called verbenaca, App. Herb. 3.

lustralis.full: lustrālis, e, adj. 2. lustrum, relating to purification from guilt or the appeasing of the gods, lustral. Lit.: sacrificium, a sacrifice of purification, a propitiatory offering, Liv. 1, 28: aqua, lustral water, holy water, Ov. P. 3, 2, 73: exta, Verg. A. 8, 183: hostiae, App. Mag. p. 304 fin.: vota, Val. Fl. 3, 414: caput, atoning (of Iphigenia), Sen. Agam. 163.— [V. 2. lustrum.] Of or belonging to a period of five years, quinquennial: certamen, Tac. A. 6, 4: aurum, a tax levied every five year

lustramen.full: lustrāmen, ĭnis, n. lustro, a means of purification, Val. Fl. 3, 442; 409.

lustramentum1.full: lustrāmentum, i, n. id., a means of purification, Arn. in Psa. 118, Serm. 8.

lustramentum2.full: lustrāmentum, i, n. lustror, an incentive to lust: si quis lustramenti causā dederit cantharides, Dig. 48, 8, 3.

lustratio.full: lustrātĭo, ōnis, f. lustro, a purification by sacrifice, a lustration. Lit.: lustrationis sacro peracto, Liv. 40, 6; 40, 13, 2 sq.; Col. 2, 22, 5.— Transf. [v. lustro, II.], a going or wandering about: lustrationesque (ferarum), Cic. Tusc. 5, 27, 79: municipiorum, id. Phil. 2, 23, 57.

lustrator.full: lustrātor, ōris, m. id.. A purifier, cleanser: Gallus sacerdos ac lustrator, Schol. Juv. 6, 542.— A wanderer through a place, a traverser: Hercules lustrator orbis, App. Mag. p. 288, 25.

lustricus.full: lustrĭcus, a, um, adj. 2. lustrum, of or belonging to purification: dies, the eighth (or ninth) day after a child's birth, on which it was purified by a sacrifice and received a name, Suet. Ner. 6; Macr. S. 1, 16; Arn. 3, 102; cf.: lustrici dies infantium appellantur, puellarum octavus, puerorum nonus, qui his lustrantur atque eis nomina imponuntur, Paul. ex Fest. p. 120 Müll.

lustrificus.full: lustrĭfĭcus, a, um, adj. 2. lustrumfacio, purifying: cantus, Val. Fl. 3, 448.

lustro1.full: lustro, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. 2. lustrum, to purify by means of a propitiatory offering (syn.: procuro, expio). Lit.: agrum lustrare sic oportet. Impera suovetaurilia circumagi, etc., Cato, R. R. 141: in lustranda colonia ab eo, qui eam deduceret, Cic. Div. 1, 45, 102: ibi instructum exercitum omnem suovetaurilibus lustravit, Liv. 1, 44; 40, 6: tunc vitula innumeros lustrabat caesa juvencos, Tib. 1, 1, 25 (31 Müll.): aliquem taedis, id. 1, 2, 61: terque senem flammā, ter aquā, ter sulphure lustrat

lustro2.full: lustro, ōnis, m., i. q. vagus, wanderer, vagabond, Naev. in Lex. Vatic. tom. 8, p. 313; cf. Klussman, Naev. p. 232, and Com. Rel. v. 118 sq. Rib.

lustror.full: lustror, āri, v. dep. n. [1. lustrum], to frequent places of ill-repute: circum oppida, Lucil. Sat. 30, 68: lustrantur, comedunt quod habent, Plaut. Ps. 4, 7, 6: ubi fuisti, ubi lustratus, id. Cas. 2, 3, 29.

lustrum1.full: lustrum, i, n. 1. luo, lavo; cf.: monstrum, moneo, a slough, bog, morass, puddle. Lit.: prodigunt in lutosos limites ac lustra, ut volutentur in luto, Varr. R. R. 2, 4, 8.— Transf. A haunt or den of wild beasts: lustra ferarum, Verg. G. 2, 471; id. A. 3, 647: lustra horrida monstris, Val. Fl. 4, 370.— A wood, forest: postquam altos ventum in montes atque invia lustra, Verg. A. 4, 151: inter horrentia lustra, id. ib. 11, 570.— A house of ill-repute: ubi in lustra jacuisti? St. Egone in lustra? Pl

lustrum2.full: lustrum, i, n. 2. luo, a purificatory sacrifice, expiatory offering, lustration, made by the censors for the whole people once in five years, after completing the census, and in which a swine, a sheep, and a bull were offered (suovetaurilia): lustrum condere, to make the lustral sacrifice: lustrum condidit et taurum immolavit, Cic. de Or. 2, 66, 268: censu perfecto edixit, ut omnes cives Romani in campo primā luce adessent. Ibi exercitum omnem suovetaurilibus lustravit: idque conditum lustrum ap

lusus1.full: lūsus, a, um, Part., from ludo.
lusus1.short: lūsus, a, um, Part., from ludo.

lusus2.full: lūsus, ūs, m. ludo, a playing, play, game (not in Cic.). Lit.: virgineis exercent lusibus undas Naides, Ov. M. 14, 556: aleae, Suet. Calig. 41: calculorum, Plin. Ep. 7, 24: nec me offenderit lusus in pueris, Quint. 1, 3, 10; cf. id. 1, 1, 20: eburneas litterarum formas in lusum offerre, id. 1, 1, 26: ediscere inter lusum, id. 1, 1, 36: in lusu duodecim scriptorum, id. 11, 2, 38: regnum lusu sortiri, i. e. by throwing dice, Tac. A. 13, 15: solent quidam et cogere ad lusum, Dig. 11, 5, 2. — Transf

lutamentum.full: lŭtāmentum, i, n. 1. luto, that which is made of mud or clay, a mud or clay wall, Cato, R. R. 128.

lutarius.full: lŭtārĭus, a, um, adj. 2. lutum, of or be longing to mud. Living in mud: testudines, Plin. 32, 4, 14, § 32.— Living on mud: mullus, Plin. 9, 17, 30, § 65.

lutatius.full: Lŭtātĭus (Luctātĭus), a, the name of a Roman gens. So, Q. Lutatius Catulus, consul A. U. C. 652, Cic. Mur. 17, 36; id. Cael. 29, 70; a younger man of the same name, consul A. U. C. 676, id. Cat. 3, 10, 24; id. Balb. 15, 34.—Hence, Lŭtātĭānus (Luct-), a, um, adj., of or belonging to a Lutatius, Lutatian: praedia, Dig. 33, 1, 12.
lutatius.short: Lŭtātĭus (Luctātĭus), a, the name of a Roman gens.

lutea.full: lūtĕa, ae, f. 1. lutum, a false reading for uvam, Plin. 33, 5, 26, § 87.

lutensis.full: lŭtensis, e, adj. 2. lutum, found or living in mud: genus purpurarum, Plin. 9, 37, 61, § 131.

luteolus.full: lūtĕŏlus, a, um, adj. dim. [1. luteus], yellowish: mollia luteolā pingit vaccinia calthā, Verg. E. 2, 50: violae, Col. 9, 4, 4: olivae, id. 12, 47, 9.

luter.full: lūtēr, ēris, m., = λουτήρ, a hand-basin, laver, Hier. in Jov. 1, n. 20; Vulg. 3 Reg. 7, 26 al.
luter.short: lūtēr, ēris, m., = λουτήρ, a hand-basin, laver, Hier.

lutesco.full: lŭtesco, ĕre, v. inch. n. [2. lutum], to turn to mud, become muddy: litora, quae limo caenoque lutescunt, Col. 8, 17, 9: cava terra lutescit, Furius Antias ap. Gell. 18, 11; id. ap. Non. 133, 26.

lutetia.full: Lutetĭa, ae, f., a city in Gallia Lugdunensis, now Paris, Caes. B. G. 7, 57; Amm. 15, 11, 3 al.; called also Lutetia Parisiorum, Caes. B. G. 6, 3.
lutetia.short: Lutetĭa, ae, f., a city in Gallia Lugdunensis, now Paris, Caes.

luteus1.full: lūtĕus, a, um, adj. 1. lutum, prop. of or belonging to the yellow-weed; hence, in gen., of the color of lutum. Golden-yellow, saffron-yellow, orange-yellow. chrysocolla, Plin. 33, 5, 27, § 91; Varr. ap Non. 549, 22: pallor, Hor. Epod. 10, 16: pal la, Tib. 1, 7, 46.—Subst.: lūtĕum, i, n, yellow: color in luteum inclinatus, towards yellow, Plin. 24, 15, 86, § 136: color in luteum languescens, id. 27, 13, 109, § 133.— Esp., the yolk of an egg: lutea ex ovis quinque columbarum, Plin. 30, 15, 49, § 1

luteus2.full: lŭtĕus, a, um, adj. 2. lutum, of mud or clay. Lit.: defingit Rheni luteum caput, Hor. S. 1, 10, 37: opus, of a swallow's nest, Ov. F. 1, 157: aedificium, Plin. 7, 56, 57. § 194: toreuma, Mart. 4, 46, 16: homo, i. e. Adam, Prud. Cath. 3, 41.— Transf. Bemired, muddy: gallina si sit luteis pedibus, Plin. 30, 11, 28, § 93.— Besmeared, bedaubed: luteum ceromate corpus, Mart. 11, 47, 5: Vulcanus, Juv. 10, 132.— Trop., dirty, vile, worthless: blitea et lutea meretrix, Plaut. Truc. 4, 4, 1: homo, Cic. V

lutito.full: lūtĭto, āre, 1, v. freq. a. 1. luto, to bedaub; only trop., to bring into contempt, to asperse: nam hi mores majorum laudant, eosdem lutitant quos conlaudant, Plaut. Trin. 2, 2, 15 Brix ad loc.

luto1.full: lŭto, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. 2. lutum, to bedaub with mud or clay. Lit., Cato, R. R. 92: nidosque reversa lutabit hirundo, Calp. Ecl. 5, 17: lutati tituli statuarum, Lampr. Elag. 14.— Transf., to bedaub, besmear: ne lutet immundum nitidos ceroma capillos, Mart. 14, 50, 1: crassis lutatus amomis, Pers. 3, 104.

luto2.full: lūto, āvi, ātum, v. freq. a. for luito, from luo; cf. Paul. ex Fest. p. 116, 5 Müll.: litatum ... quasi luitatum, to pay: lutavi, Varr. ap. Non. 131, 21.

lutor.full: lūtor, ōris, m. luo, a washer, fuller: † lutor, πλύτης ἡλιαστής, Gloss. Philox.; Inscr. Gud. 17, 2.

lutosus.full: lŭtōsus, a, um, adj. 2. lutum, full of mud or loam, muddy, miry, dirty: terra, Cato ap. Plin. 18, 19, 49, § 176: ager, Col. 2, 45: rapa, id. 12, 54 (56), 1.

lutra.full: lūtra (lȳtra), ae, f. luo, an otter, Plin. 8, 30, 47, § 109; 32, 11, 53, § 144; form lytra, Varr. L. L. 5, § 79 Müll.

lutulentus.full: lŭtŭlentus, a, um, adj. 2. lutum, muddy. Lit.: sus, bedaubed with mud, Hor. Ep. 2, 2, 75: diluvio tellus lutulenta recenti, Ov. M. 1, 434: amnis, id. Am. 3, 6, 95: mula, Mart. 9, 23, 13.—* Transf., besmeared with ointment: et putri lutulenta de palaestra, Mart. 7, 67, 7.— Trop. Filthy, dirty, vile: lenone istoc non lutum est lutulentius, Plaut. Poen. 1, 1, 29: scio ego, multos jam lucrum lutulentos homines reddidit, id. Capt. 2, 2, 76: lutulente Caesonine, Cic. Pis. 12, 27: persona illa lutulent

lutulo.full: lŭtŭlo, āre, v. a. id., to bespatter with mud; trop., to asperse; old reading, Plaut. Trin. 2, 2, 15; for lutito, q. v., cf. Ritschl, Prol. ad Plaut. p. lxxiv.

lutum1.full: lūtum, i, n., a plant used in dyeing yellow, yellow-weed. dyer's-weed, weld: jam croceo mutabit vellera luto, Verg. E. 4, 44; Plin. 33, 5, 26, § 87; Vitr. 7, 14.— Transf., a yellow color, yellow, Verg. Cir. 316: nimius luto corpora tingit amor, Tib. 1, 9 (8), 52 Heyne ad loc.
lutum1.short: lūtum, i, n., a plant used in dyeing yellow, yellow-weed.

lutum2.full: lŭtum, i, n. (lŭtus, i, m., Quadrig. ap. Non. 212, 17) [luo], mud, mire. Lit.: volutari in luto, Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 24, § 53: cratesque luto integuntur, Caes. B. C. 2, 15; Quadrig. ap. Non. 212, 17: imbre lutoque Aspersus, Hor. Ep. 1, 11, 11: luto perfusa porticus, Juv. 14, 66: pinguia crura luto, id. 3, 247: luto opplere aliquem, Suet. Vesp. 5: in longa via et pulvis et lutum et pluvia, Sen. Ep. 96, 3: si quis aliquem luto obliniverit, Paul. Sent. 5, 4, 13: te pervolvam in luto, Ter. And. 4, 4, 3

lutus.full: lŭtus, i, m., v. 2. lutum init.

lux.full: lux, lūcis (adverb. abl. luce, luci, and lucu, and in these old forms also used as m.; v. infra; in Plaut. lux is usually m.; Brix ad Plaut. Capt. 5, 4, 11), f. luceo, light. Lit. In gen., the light of the sun and other heavenly bodies: cum id solis luce videatur clarius, Cic. Div. 1, 3, 6; id. Tusc. 1, 37, 90; id. Cat. 1, 3; id. Cael. 9: per umbras Stella facem ducens multā cum luce cucurrit, Verg. A. 2, 694: a lucifero donec lux occidat, till sunset, Juv, 13, 158. —The light, splendor, brightn

luxatio.full: luxātĭo, στρέμμα, i. q. luxatura, a dislocation, luxation, Gloss. Philox.

luxatura.full: luxātūra, ae, f. luxo, a dislocation, luxation, Marc. Emp. 36.

luxo.full: luxo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. Gr. λοξός, slanting, akin to obliquus, limus, licinus, to put out of joint, to dislocate. Lit.: luxatum si quod est, sanum faciet, Cato, R. R. 157: luxata in locum reponere, Sen. Ep. 104, 18: articulis luxatis, Plin. 30, 9, 23, § 79: luxata corpora, id. 31, 6, 37, § 71.— Transf., to put out of place, displace: luxare vitium radices, Plin. 17, 24, 37, § 227: luxatae machinae, fallen apart, id. 36, 15, 24, § 119: luxata cornua, id. 8, 45, 70, § 179.

luxor.full: luxor, āri, v. dep. luxus, to riot, revel, live luxuriously: luxantur a luxu dictum, id est luxuriantur, Paul. ex Fest. p. 120 Müll.; cf. Non. 55, 15: luxantur, lustrantur, Plaut. Ps. 4, 7, 5 Fleck.

luxuria.full: luxŭrĭa, ae, and luxŭrĭēs, ēi (v. Zumpt, Verr. 2, 2, 3, § 7, and 2, 5, 31, § 80; Roby, Gram. § 342; old gen. luxurii, Gracch. ap. Gell. 9, 14; the dat. of the fifth decl. is not in use, and the abl. is doubtful; v. Neue, Formenl. 1, 382 sqq.), f. luxus, rankness. Lit., rankness, luxuriance of trees and plants: luxuriem segetum tenerā depascit in herbā, Verg. G. 1, 112: si vitis luxuria se consumpserit, Plin. 17, 22, 35, § 181; 9, 2, 1, § 2.— Poet., transf., of animals: wantonness, friskiness, fr

luxurio.full: luxŭrĭo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. n., and luxŭ-rĭor, ātus, 1, v. dep. (cf. Quint. 9, 3, 7) [luxuria], to be rank, luxuriant, abound to excess (not in Cic. or Cæs.). Lit.: ager assiduā luxuriabat aquā, Ov. F. 4, 644: luxuriat Phrygio sanguine pinguis humus, id. H. 1, 53: cacumina virgarum ne luxurientur, Col. Arb. 11: ne (caules) in frondem luxurient, Plin. 19, 6, 34, § 113: in patulas comas, Ov. de Nuce, 20: ut seges in pingui luxuriabit humo, id. A. A. 1, 360.— Transf. To wanton, sport, skip, bound, fr

luxuriosus.full: luxŭrĭōsus, a, um, adj. luxuria, rank, luxuriant, exuberant. Lit.: frumenta, Cic. Or. 24, 81: seges, Ov. F. 1, 690: vitis valida et luxuriosa, Col. 5, 6, 36: vitis, id. 4, 21, 2.— Trop. Immoderate, excessive: luxurioso otio esse, Sall. J. 100: laetitia, Liv. 2, 21.— Immoderate, extravagant, wanton: luxuriosissimum dictum, Col. 8, 16: amor, Ov. R. Am. 746.— Excessive, profuse, luxurious, voluptuous: reprehendere luxuriosos, Cic. Fin. 2, 7, 21: multa et lauta supellex, non illa quidem luxuriosi ho

luxus1.full: luxus, a, um, adj. = Gr. λοξός; v. luxo, dislocated: luxum si quod est, Cato, R. R. 160: luxo pede, Sall. Fragm. ap. Prob. p. 1476 P. (Hist. 5, 2); cf.: luxa membra e suis locis mota et soluta, Paul. ex Fest. p. 119, 17 Müll.—Subst.: luxum, i, n., a dislocation: emplastrum utile ad luxa, vel fracta, Marc. Emp. 36.

luxus2.full: luxus, ūs, m. 1. luxus, a dislocation (ante- and post-class.): ad luxum aut fracturam alliga: sanum fiet, Cato, R. R. 160; App. Flor. p. 354 med.; Plin. Val. 2, 49.

luxus3.full: luxus, ūs (dat. luxu, Sall. J. 6; Tac. A. 3, 34; id. H. 2, 71) [root luc-; cf. pol-luceo, pol-lucte; v. Corss. Ausspr. 1, 368 sq.]. Excess, extravagance in eating and drinking, luxury, debauchery: adulescens luxu perditus, Ter. Ad. 4, 7, 42: in vino ac luxu, Cic. Verr. 2, 3, 25, § 62: aliquid luxu antecapere, Sall. C. 13: luxu atque desidiā corrupta civitas, id. ib. 57: luxu et saginae mancipatus, Tac. H. 2, 71; 4, 14: per luxum et ignaviam aetatem agere, i. e. luxuriously and slothfully, Sall.

lyaeus.full: Lўaeus, i, m., = Λυαῖος, Lyæus, the relaxer, unbender, deliverer from care. A surname of Bacchus: patri Lyaeo, Verg. A. 4, 58: corniger Lyaeus, Ov. Am. 3, 15, 17; id. M. 4, 11; 8, 274; 11, 68; Verg. G. 2, 229 al.— Transf., wine: uda Lyaeo Tempora, Hor. C. 1, 7, 22: Curam Dulci Lyaeo solvere, id. Epod. 9, 37: illic apposito narrabis multa Lyaeo, Ov. Am. 2, 11, 49.— Hence, Lўaeus, a, um, adj.: regales inter mensas laticemque Lyaeum, the Lyæan liquid, i. e. wine, Verg. A. 1, 686.
lyaeus.short: Lўaeus, i, m., = Λυαῖος, Lyæus, the relaxer, unbender, deliverer from care.

lycabas.full: Lўcăbas, ae, m., = Λυκάβας. A Tuscan who fled from his country on account of a murder, and who, for a slight shown to Bacchus, was changed into a dolphin, Ov. M. 3, 624.— An Assyrian, Ov. M. 5, 60.— A Centaur, Ov. M. 12, 302.

lycaeus.full: Lўcaeus, i, m., = Λυκαῖος, a mountain in Arcadia (now Dhiaforti), where Jupiter and Pan were worshipped, Plin. 4, 6, 10, § 21; Verg. G. 4, 539; Ov. M. 1, 217; Aug. Civ. Dei, 18, 17; Serv. Verg. A. 8, 343 and 344: saxa Lycaei, Verg. E. 10, 15.—Hence, Lўcaeus, a, um, adj., Lycean: Panos de more Lycaei, Verg. A. 8, 344: collis, Ov. M. 1, 698: nemus, id. ib. 8, 317: deus, i. e. Pan, Val. Fl. 6, 533.
lycaeus.short: Lўcaeus, i, m., = Λυκαῖος, a mountain in Arcadia (now Dhiaforti), where Jupiter and Pan were worshipped, Plin.

lycambes.full: Lўcambes, ae, m., = Λυκάμβης, a Theban who promised his daughter to Archilochus, and afterwards refused her; for which he was pursued by the poet with such bitter sarcasm that he hung both himself and his daughter: qualis Lycambae spretus infido gener, Hor. Epod. 6, 13; cf. id. Ep. 1, 19, 30. —Hence, Lўcambēus, a, um, adj., of Lycambes: sanguis, Ov. Ib. 54.
lycambes.short: Lўcambes, ae, m., = Λυκάμβης, a Theban who promised his daughter to Archilochus, and afterwards refused her;

lycaon1.full: Lўcāon, ŏnis, m., = Λυκάων, a king of Arcadia, father of Callisto, whom Jupiter, because he had defiled his altar with human sacrifices, turned into a wolf; acc. to Ovid, because he had tried to murder Jupiter himself, who was his guest, Ov. M. 1, 198; Hyg. Fab. 176 sq.; Cic. Fam. 3, 10, 10; acc. Lycaona, id. ib. 2, 526.— His grandson, also called Arcas, Ov. F. 6, 225.—Hence, Lўcāŏnĭus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Lycaon, Lycaonian: mensa, Ov. Ib. 433: parens, i. e. Callisto, id. M. 2, 496;
lycaon1.short: Lўcāon, ŏnis, m., = Λυκάων, a king of Arcadia, father of Callisto, whom Jupiter, because he had defiled his altar with human sacrifices, turned into a wolf;

lycaon2.full: lўcāon, ŏnis, m., = λυκάων, an animal of the wolf kind, Mela, 3, 9, 2; Plin. 8, 34, 52, § 123; Sol. 3.
lycaon2.short: lўcāon, ŏnis, m., = λυκάων, an animal of the wolf kind, Mela, 3, 9, 2;

lycaones.full: Lўcāŏnes, um, m., = Λυκάονες, the Lycaonians, a people of Asia Minor, between Cappadocia, Cilicia, and Pisidia, Mel. 1, 2, 5; Plin. 5, 29, 29, § 105.—Hence, Lўcāŏnĭus, a, um, adj., Lycaonian: Lycaoniumque Ericeten, Verg. A. 10, 749.— Subst.: Lўcāŏnia, ae, f., the country of the Lycaonians, Cic. Att. 5, 15, 3; Liv. 37, 54, 11; 38, 39; Vulg. Act. 14, 6.—Hence, adv.: Lўcāŏnĭcē, in the dialect of Lycaonia: dicentes, Vulg. Act. 14, 10.
lycaones.short: Lўcāŏnes, um, m., = Λυκάονες, the Lycaonians, a people of Asia Minor, between Cappadocia, Cilicia, and Pisidia, Mel.

lycaonis.full: Lўcāŏnis, idis, v. 1. Lycaon, II. B.

lycaonius.full: Lўcāŏnĭus, a, um, v. 1. Lycaon, II. A. and Lycaones.

lycapsos.full: lўcapsos, f., = λύκαψος, alkanet, Plin. 27, 11, 73, § 97 (al. lycopsis).

lycaunus.full: Lўcaūnŭs, i, m., the name of a warrior, Sil. 4, 203.
lycaunus.short: Lўcaūnŭs, i, m., the name of a warrior, Sil.

lyce.full: Lўcē, ēs, f., = Λύκη, the name of a woman, Hor. C. 4, 13, 1.
lyce.short: Lўcē, ēs, f., = Λύκη, the name of a woman, Hor.

lychnicus.full: lychnĭcus, a, um, adj., = λυχνικός, luminous, shining: lapis, a kind of white marble, also called lychnites, Hyg. Fab. 223.
lychnicus.short: lychnĭcus, a, um, adj., = λυχνικός, luminous, shining: lapis, a kind of white marble, also called lychnites, Hyg.

lychnidum.full: Lychnĭdum, i, n., and Lychnĭdus, i, f., = Λυχνιδός, a city of Illyria, near the Haliacmon, in the territory of the Dessaretes, Liv. 27, 32; 43, 9; 10; 21.
lychnidum.short: Lychnĭdum, i, n., and Lychnĭdus, i, f., = Λυχνιδός, a city of Illyria, near the Haliacmon, in the territory of the Dessaretes, Liv.

lychnion.full: lychnĭon, i, n., = λυχνίον, a lamp, light, Isid. 17, 9, 73.
lychnion.short: lychnĭon, i, n., = λυχνίον, a lamp, light, Isid.

lychnis.full: lychnis, ĭdis, adj. f., = λυχνίς, lightgiving, shining. Lit.: lychnides puellae, girls with lamps, Fulg. Myth. prooem. 1.— Subst.: lychnis, ĭdis, f. A kind of rose of a fiery red, Plin. 21, 4, 10, § 18.— Lychnis agria, another plant, Plin. 25, 10, 80, § 129.— A gem of a fiery color, Plin. 37, 7, 29, § 103.

lychnites.full: lychnītes, ae, m., = λυχνίτης, a kind of white marble, which was quarried in the Isle of Paros by lamp-light, Plin. 36, 5, 4, § 14.
lychnites.short: lychnītes, ae, m., = λυχνίτης, a kind of white marble, which was quarried in the Isle of Paros by lamp-light, Plin.

lychnitis.full: lychnītis, ītĭdis, f., = λυχνῖτις, a plant from which wicks were made, Plin. 25, 10, 74, § 121
lychnitis.short: lychnītis, ītĭdis, f., = λυχνῖτις, a plant from which wicks were made, Plin.

lychnobius.full: lychnŏbĭus, ii, m., = λυχνόβιος, one who lives by lamp-light, who turns night into day, Sen. Ep. 122, 17; v. lucifuga.
lychnobius.short: lychnŏbĭus, ii, m., = λυχνόβιος, one who lives by lamp-light, who turns night into day, Sen.

lychnuchus.full: lychnūchus, i, m., = λυχνοῦχος, a lamp-stand, candlestick, chandelier: ligneolus, Cic. Q. Fr. 3, 7, 2: pensiles, Plin. 34, 3, 8, § 14; Suet. Dom. 4; id. Caes. 37.
lychnuchus.short: lychnūchus, i, m., = λυχνοῦχος, a lamp-stand, candlestick, chandelier: ligneolus, Cic.

lychnus.full: lychnus (old Latinized form lucinus, Enn.; cf. Ritschl in Rhein. Mus. 10, p. 448 sq.), i, m., = λύχνος, a light, a lamp: pendentes lychni, Lucr. 5, 295: lux alia est solis et lychnorum, Cic. Cael. 28, 67; Verg. A. 1, 726; Stat. Th. 1, 520.

lycia.full: Lўcĭa (Lŭcĭa, Plaut. Curc. 3, 73 Fleck.), ae, f., = Λυκία, a country of Asia Minor, between Caria and Pamphylia, where was the volcano Chimæra, Mel. 1, 2, 6; 1, 15, 1; 2, 7, 4; Plin. 5, 27, 27, § 97: Chimaerifera Lycia, Ov. M. 6, 340; Stat. Th. 8, 200; Verg. A. 7, 721.—Hence, Lўcĭus, a, um, adj., Lycian: sagittae, Verg. A. 8, 166: pharetra, id. ib. 7, 816: cornu, id. ib. 11, 773: sortes, the oracle of Apollo at Patara, in Lycia, id. ib. 4, 346: deus, i. e. Apollo, Prop. 3 (4), 1, 38. cf. Macr. S

lycidas.full: Lўcĭdas, ae, m., = Λυκίδας, one of the Centaurs, who endeavored to carry off Hippodamia from Pirithoüs, Ov. M. 12, 310.— The name of a beautiful boy, Hor. C. 1, 4, 19.— The name of a shepherd, Verg. E. 7, 67; 9, 12.
lycidas.short: Lўcĭdas, ae, m., = Λυκίδας, one of the Centaurs, who endeavored to carry off Hippodamia from Pirithoüs, Ov.

lycimnia.full: Lўcīmnĭa (Lĭcȳm-), ae, f., the name of the wife of a king of Lydia, Verg. A. 9, 546 (al. Licymnia).
lycimnia.short: Lўcīmnĭa (Lĭcȳm-), ae, f., the name of the wife of a king of Lydia, Verg.

lycimnius.full: Lўcimnĭus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to the town of Lycimna (in Argolis), Lycimnian: stagna, Stat. Th. 4, 734.
lycimnius.short: Lўcimnĭus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to the town of Lycimna (in Argolis), Lycimnian: stagna, Stat.

lycinna.full: Lўcinna, ae, f., the name of a girl, Prop. 3, (4), 13, 6.
lycinna.short: Lўcinna, ae, f., the name of a girl, Prop.

lycisca.full: Lўcisca, ae, and Lўciscē, ēs, f. The name of a bitch, Verg. E. 3, 18; Ov. M. 3, 220.— A vile woman, Juv. 6, 122.
lycisca.short: Lўcisca, ae, and Lўciscē, ēs, f.

lyciscus.full: lўciscus, i, m., = λυκίσκος, a wolfdog: lycisci dicuntur canes nati ex lupis et canibus, cum inter se forte miscentur, Isid. Orig. 12, 2.— Lўciscus, the name of a beautiful boy, Hor. Epod. 11, 24.— A boy whose statue was made by Leochares, Plin. 34, 8, 19, § 79.
lyciscus.short: lўciscus, i, m., = λυκίσκος, a wolfdog: lycisci dicuntur canes nati ex lupis et canibus, cum inter se forte miscentur, Isid.

lycium1.full: Lўcĭum, and Lўcĭus, a, um, v. Lycia, II.
lycium1.short: Lўcĭum, and Lўcĭus, a, um, v.

lycium2.full: Lўcīum (less correctly Lўcēum, v. Ellendt ad Cic. de Or. 1, 21, 98), i, n., = Λύκειον, a gymnasium very near Athens, in which Aristotle taught, Cic. de Or. 1, 21, 98; id. Ac. 1, 4, 17; id. Div. 1, 13, 22; Liv. 31, 24, 18; Gell. 20, 5, 4.— Transf. The upper gymnasium of Cicero's Tusculan villa, with a library in it, Cic. Div. 1, 5, 8; 2, 3, 8.— A gymnasium of the emperor Hadrian at his Tiburtine villa, Spart. Hadr. 27.

lyco.full: Lyco, ōnis, m., a Peripatetic philosopher, a follower of Strato of Lampsacus, Cic. Tusc. 3, 32, 78.
lyco.short: Lyco, ōnis, m., a Peripatetic philosopher, a follower of Strato of Lampsacus, Cic.

lycomedes.full: Lўcŏmēdes, is, m., = Λυκομήδης, a king of the Isle of Scyros, with whom Achilles concealed himself disguised in female attire, and whose daughter Deidamia bore to the latter Pyrrhus or Neoptolemus, Cic. Lael. 20, 75 (where Neoptolemus is erroneously spoken of instead of Achilles); Stat. Achill. 1, 207.
lycomedes.short: Lўcŏmēdes, is, m., = Λυκομήδης, a king of the Isle of Scyros, with whom Achilles concealed himself disguised in female attire, and whose daughter Deidamia bore to the latter Pyrrhus or Neoptolemus, Cic.

lyconides.full: Lўcōnĭdēs, ae, m., the name of a man, Plaut. Aul. 4, 10, 49.
lyconides.short: Lўcōnĭdēs, ae, m., the name of a man, Plaut.

lycophon1.full: lўcŏphon, a plant, also called scelerata, App. Herb. 8.
lycophon1.short: lўcŏphon, a plant, also called scelerata, App.

lycophon2.full: Lўcŏphōn, ōntis, m., the name of a warrior, Stat. Th. 2, 610.
lycophon2.short: Lўcŏphōn, ōntis, m., the name of a warrior, Stat.

lycophos.full: lўcŏphōs, ōtis, n., = λυκόφως, the morning twilight, Macr. S. 1, 17, 37, p. 292 Bip.; Paul. ex Fest. p. 121 Müll.
lycophos.short: lўcŏphōs, ōtis, n., = λυκόφως, the morning twilight, Macr.

lycophron.full: Lўcŏphron, ŏnis, m., = Λυκόφρων, Lycophron of Chalcis, in Eubœa, the author of Cassandra, an Alexandrine grammarian and tragedian of the time of Ptolemy Philadelphus: utque cothurnatum periisse Lycophrona narrant, Ov. Ib. 531: latebrae Lycophronis atri, so called from his obscure style, Stat. S. 5, 3, 157.
lycophron.short: Lўcŏphron, ŏnis, m., = Λυκόφρων, Lycophron of Chalcis, in Eubœa, the author of Cassandra, an Alexandrine grammarian and tragedian of the time of Ptolemy Philadelphus: utque cothurnatum periisse Lycophrona narrant, Ov.

lycophthalmos.full: lўcophthalmos, i, m., = λυκόφθαλμος (wolf's-eye), a precious stone, Plin. 37, 11, 72, § 187; cf. Isid. 16, 15, 20.
lycophthalmos.short: lўcophthalmos, i, m., = λυκόφθαλμος (wolf's-eye), a precious stone, Plin.

lycopsis.full: lўcopsis (al. lўcapsos), is, f., = λυκοψίς, the wild bugloss, a plant resembling the alkanet, Plin. 27, 11, 73, § 97.

lycoreus.full: Lycōreus, ei and eos, m., a son of Apollo, Hyg. Fab. 161.
lycoreus.short: Lycōreus, ei and eos, m., a son of Apollo, Hyg.

lycorias.full: Lўcōrĭas, ădis, f., = Λυκωριάς, a seanymph, daughter of Nereus and Doris, Verg. G. 4, 339; Hyg. Fab. praef.
lycorias.short: Lўcōrĭas, ădis, f., = Λυκωριάς, a seanymph, daughter of Nereus and Doris, Verg.

lycoris.full: Lўcōris, ĭdis (acc. -orida, Ov. A. A. 3, 537; voc. Lycori, Verg. E. 10, 42; Mart. 1, 102, 1), f., also called Cythere, a freedwoman of the senator Volumnius Eutrapelus, the mistress of Cornelius Gallus, and afterwards of Marc Antony, Verg. E. 10, 22; 42; Ov. A. A. 3, 537; id. Am. 1, 15, 29 sq.; id. Tr. 2, 445; Prop. 2, 25 (3, 32), 91; Mart. 8, 73, 6.

lycormas.full: Lўcormas, ae, m., = Λυκόρμας, a river of Ætolia, Ov. M. 2, 245; afterwards called Chrysorrhoas, Hyg. Fab. 242.
lycormas.short: Lўcormas, ae, m., = Λυκόρμας, a river of Ætolia, Ov.

lycortas.full: Lўcortas, ae, m., = Λυκόρτας, a general (strategos, στρατηγός) of the Achæan League, Liv. 39, 35; 36.
lycortas.short: Lўcortas, ae, m., = Λυκόρτας, a general (strategos, στρατηγός) of the Achæan League, Liv.

lycos.full: lўcos, i, m., = λύκος, a kind of spider: araneus, et maxume qui lycos vocatur, Plin. 30, 6, 17, § 52; acc. lycon, id. 30, 11, 30, § 104.
lycos.short: lўcos, i, m., = λύκος, a kind of spider: araneus, et maxume qui lycos vocatur, Plin.

lycotas.full: Lўcōtas, ae, m., one of the Centaurs at the wedding of Pirithoüs, Ov. M. 12, 350.— A fictitious name of a man, probably meaning Postumius, Prop. 4 (5), 3, 1.
lycotas.short: Lўcōtas, ae, m., one of the Centaurs at the wedding of Pirithoüs, Ov.

lycotherses.full: Lўcŏtherses, is, m., a king of Illyria, whom his wife Agave, the daughter of Cadmus, murdered, in order to give the kingdom to her father, Hyg. Fab. 184; 340; 254.
lycotherses.short: Lўcŏtherses, is, m., a king of Illyria, whom his wife Agave, the daughter of Cadmus, murdered, in order to give the kingdom to her father, Hyg.

lyctus.full: Lyctus or -os, i, f., = Λύκτος, a city of Crete, east of Gnossus, a colony of the Lacedæmonians, Mel. 2, 7, 12; Plin. 4, 12, 20, § 59.—Hence, Lyctĭus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Lyctus, Lyctian, Cretan: Lyctius Idomeneus, Verg. A. 3, 401: classis, i. e. the Cretan, Ov. M. 7, 490.
lyctus.short: Lyctus or -os, i, f., = Λύκτος, a city of Crete, east of Gnossus, a colony of the Lacedæmonians, Mel.

lycurgus.full: Lўcurgus, i, m., = Λυκοῦργος. Son of Dryas, king of the Edones, who prohibited the worship of Bacchus to his subjects, and ordered all the vines to be destroyed, Ov. M. 4, 22; Prop. 4, 16, 23; Stat. Th. 4, 386; Hor. C. 2, 19, 16; Hyg. Fab. 132; 242.— Son of Pheres, a king of Nemea, Stat. Th. 5, 39. — Son of Aleus and Neæra, and father of Ancæus, a king of Arcadia; hence, Lў-curgīdes, ae, m., a male descendant of Lycurgus, i. e. Ancæus, Ov. Ib. 503; and: Lўcŏorgīdes, ae, m., the same, Prisc. 584

lycus.full: Lўcus or -os, i, m., = Λύκος. Son of Pandion, king of Lycia, Mela, 1, 15, 1.— A Theban, who, when Hercules descended into the Lower World, took possession of the sovereignty in Thebes, Hyg. Fab. 31 and 32. — One of the Centaurs at the wedding of Pirithoüs, Ov. M. 12, 332.— A companion of Diomedes, Ov. M. 14, 504.— One of the companions of Æneas, Verg. A. 1, 222.— An historian of Regium, the adoptive father of the tragic writer Lycophron; he wrote a history of Libya and Sicily, Plin. 31, 2, 19, §

lyde.full: Lȳdē, ēs, f., = Λύδη, the wife of the poet Antimachus of Claros, who attempted to console himself for her death by an elegiac poem which he named Lyde: Clario Lyde dilecta poëtae, Ov. Tr. 1, 6, 1.— The name of a female quack-doctor: turgida condīta pyxide Lyde, Juv. 2, 141.
lyde.short: Lȳdē, ēs, f., = Λύδη, the wife of the poet Antimachus of Claros, who attempted to console himself for her death by an elegiac poem which he named Lyde: Clario Lyde dilecta poëtae, Ov.

lydia.full: Lȳdĭa, ae, f., = Λυδία, a country in Asia Minor, the capital of which was Sardis, the fabled original land of the Etruscans, Plin. 5, 29, 30, § 110; Varr. R. R. 3, 17, 4; Cic. Fl. 27, 65; Liv. 38, 39, 16 et saep.—Hence, Lȳdĭus, a, um, adj. Lydian: regna, of Gyges, Tib. 4, 1, 199: aurifer amnis, i. e. Pactolus, id. 3, 3, 29: mitra, Prop. 3, 15 (4, 16), 30: pensa, which Omphale gave to Hercules, Mart. 9, 66, 11: nurus, i. e. Omphale, Sen. Oet. 371: sil. Plin. 33, 13, 56, § 160: lapis, a touchstone
lydia.short: Lȳdĭa, ae, f., = Λυδία, a country in Asia Minor, the capital of which was Sardis, the fabled original land of the Etruscans, Plin.

lygdamus.full: Lygdămus, i, m., a slave of Cynthia, the mistress of Propertius, Prop. 3, 4 (4, 5), 2; 4 (5), 7, 43.
lygdamus.short: Lygdămus, i, m., a slave of Cynthia, the mistress of Propertius, Prop.

lygdinus.full: lygdĭnus, a, um, adj., = λύγδινος, of white marble: horoscopus, Jul. Val. Rer. Gest. Alex. M. 1, 3.—Esp.: lygdinus lapis, a dazzling white marble found in the island of Paros, Plin. 36, 8, 13, § 62; Isid. Orig. 16, 5, 8 (the same as lygdos).
lygdinus.short: lygdĭnus, a, um, adj., = λύγδινος, of white marble: horoscopus, Jul.

lygdos.full: lygdos, i, f., = λύγδος, a white stone, = lygdinus lapis: candida, Mart. 6, 13, 3: vacua, id. 6, 42, 21.
lygdos.short: lygdos, i, f., = λύγδος, a white stone, = lygdinus lapis: candida, Mart.

lygmon.full: Lygmon, Müller's reading for Lucmo, Prop. 5, 1, 29.
lygmon.short: Lygmon, Müller's reading for Lucmo, Prop.

lygos1.full: lўgos, i, f., = λύγος, a plant, the chaste tree, agnus castus, Abraham's balm (in late Lat. vitex), Plin. 24, 9, 38, § 59.
lygos1.short: lўgos, i, f., = λύγος, a plant, the chaste tree, agnus castus, Abraham's balm (in late Lat.

lygos2.full: Lўgos, i, f., = Λύγος, an ancient name of Byzantium: oppidum Byzantium ... antea Lygos dictum, Plin. 4, 11, 18, § 46; Aus. de Clar. Urb. Carm. 1, 14.
lygos2.short: Lўgos, i, f., = Λύγος, an ancient name of Byzantium: oppidum Byzantium ...

lympha.full: lympha, ae, f. νύμφη, water; esp. clear river or spring water (poet.): lymphae puteales, Lucr. 6, 1178: fluviali spargere lympha, Verg. A. 4, 635; Ov. M. 2, 459: vulnera lymphis abluere, id. ib. 13, 531.— Also, the water in dropsical persons: lympha intercus, Ser. Samm. 27, 501.— Personified: Lympha. A rural deity, the goddess of water, Varr. R. R. 1, 1, 6.— Lymphae, i. q. Nymphae, Hor. S. 1, 5, 97; Inscr. Orell. 1639.

lymphaceus.full: lymphācĕus, a, um, adj. lympha, clear as water, clear as crystal, Mart. Cap. 6, § 569.

lymphaticus.full: lymphātĭcus, a, um, adj. lympha; cf. hydrophobia; hence, in gen., distracted, frantic, panic-struck: pavor, a panic, Liv. 10, 28, 10; 7, 17, 3: metus, Sen. Ep. 13, 9: somnia, Plin. 26, 8, 34, § 52: elleborum medetur melancholicis, insanientibus, lymphaticis, id. 25, 5, 24, § 60.— Transf. Comically: lymphatici nummi, that cannot keep quiet in one's purse, as if mad, Plaut. Poen. 1, 2, 135 Weise (al. lymphati).— lymphātĭcum, i, n., the disease of a lymphaticus, insanity: faxo actutum constiterit l

lymphatio.full: lymphātĭo, ōnis, f. lympho, distraction, frenzy, Plin. 37, 4, 15, § 61; 34, 15, 44, § 151.

lymphatus1.full: lymphātus, a, um, Part. and P. a., v. lympho.

lymphatus2.full: lymphātus, ūs, m. lympho, madness, Plin. 37, 10, 54, § 146.

lympho.full: lympho, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. and n. lympha. To water, dilute with water: admixto vino lymphato, id est, aqua temperato, Cael. Aur. Tard. 4, 3, 68.— To drive out of one's senses, to distract with fear, to make mad: urbem, Val. Fl. 3, 47: urbes incursibus, Stat. Th. 7, 113: hac herba pota lymphari homines, Plin. 24, 17, 102, § 164. —As neutr.: lymphantes animi, driven crazy, mad, Plin. 27, 12, 83, § 107.—Hence, lymphātus, a, um, P. a., distracted, crazy, beside one's self, mad: exercitum pavor inva

lymphor.full: lymphor, ōris, m. id., water: impermixtum lymphorem, Lucil. ap. Non. 212, 4.

lyncaeste.full: Lyncaestē, ēs, f., one of Actæon's hounds, Hyg. Fab. 181.
lyncaeste.short: Lyncaestē, ēs, f., one of Actæon's hounds, Hyg.

lyncestae.full: Lyncestae, ārum, m., = Λυγκησταί, a people in the south-western part of Macedonia, Liv. 45, 30, 6; Plin. 4, 10, 17, § 35.— Hence, Lyncestĭus, a, um, adj., Lyncestian: amnis, Ov. M. 15, 329; v. Sen. Q. N. 3, 20 fin.— Lyncestis, ĭdis, f. adj., Lyncestian: aqua, Plin. 2, 103, 106, § 230.— Lyncestus, a, um, adj., Lyncestian, Vitr. 8, 3, 17.
lyncestae.short: Lyncestae, ārum, m., = Λυγκησταί, a people in the south-western part of Macedonia, Liv.

lynceus.full: Lynceus (dissyl.), ĕi (gen. Lyncei, dissyl., Hor. S. 1, 2, 90 Orell. ad loc.; voc. Lynceu, Prop. 3, 32, 9), m., = Λυγκεύς, a Messenian, and one of the Argonauts, brother of Idas, and son of Aphareus, famed for the sharpness of his sight: non possis oculo quantum contendere Lynceus, Hor. Ep. 1, 1, 28: Lyncei oculi, id. S. 1, 2, 90; cf. Val. Fl. 1, 462; Hyg. Fab. 14; Val. Max. 1, 8, n. 14; Plin. 2, 17, 15, § 78; Ov. F. 5, 711; Prop. 2, 34 (3, 32), 9.—Hence, Lyncēus, a, um, adj., = Λύγκειος, of Lyn

lyncurion.full: lyncūrĭon or -ĭum, ii, n., = λυγκούριον, a hard, transparent gem, which, according to the opinion of the ancients, was formed of lynxes' urine; prob. the hyacinth or tourmaline, Plin. 8, 38, 57, § 137; 37, 2, 11, § 34; 37, 3, 13, § 52; cf. Ov. M. 15, 413; Sol. 2; Hier. Ep. 94, n. 16.—Called also lyncūrĭus, i, m., Isid. 12, 2, 20; 14, 4, 19; 16, 8, 8 (al. ligurius); and lĭgūrĭus, i, m., Hier. Ep. 64, 16; Vulg. Exod. 28, 19.
lyncurion.short: lyncūrĭon or -ĭum, ii, n., = λυγκούριον, a hard, transparent gem, which, according to the opinion of the ancients, was formed of lynxes' urine;

lyncus.full: Lyncus, i, = Λύγκος. Masc., a Scythian king, who attempted the life of his guest, Triptolemus, and was changed by Ceres into a lynx, Ov. M. 5, 650; Hyg. Fab. 259.— Fem., a city of Macedonia, the capital of the Lyncestae (q. v.), Liv. 26, 25, 4; 31, 33.

lynx.full: lynx, lyncis, com., = λύγξ, a lynx: lynces Bacchi variae (Bacchus was drawn by a team of lynxes), Verg. G. 3, 264: maculosae tegmine lyncis, id. A. 1, 323: lyncibus ad caelum vecta Ariadna tuis, Prop. 3, 15, 8 (4, 16, 18): colla lyncum, Ov. M. 4, 25: timidos agitare lyncas, Hor. C. 2, 13, 40: dejectus lyncis, a lynx-skin, Stat. Th. 4, 272.
lynx.short: lynx, lyncis, com., = λύγξ, a lynx: lynces Bacchi variae (Bacchus was drawn by a team of lynxes), Verg.

lyo.full: lўo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. λύω, to make liquid, to liquefy: ptisanam, Apic. 4, 4: pulpa lyata, id. 5, 1.

lyra.full: lўra, ae, f., = λύρα, a lute, lyre, a stringed instrument resembling the cithara, fabled to have been invented by Mercury and presented to Apollo, Hyg. Astr. 2, 7: curvae lyrae parens, Hor. C. 1, 10, 6: Threiciam digitis increpuisse lyram, Ov. H. 3, 118: mox cecinit laudes prosperiore lyrā, id. A. A. 3, 50; Val. Fl. 5, 100.— Transf. Lyric poetry, song: imbellis, Hor. C. 1, 6, 10: Aeoliae Lesbis amica lyrae, Ov. Am. 2, 18, 26; id. P. 3, 3, 45.— In gen., poetic genius: Inferior lyra, Stat. Th. 10,
lyra.short: lўra, ae, f., = λύρα, a lute, lyre, a stringed instrument resembling the cithara, fabled to have been invented by Mercury and presented to Apollo, Hyg.

lyrceius.full: Lyrcēĭus or Lyrcēus, a, um, adj., Lyrcean, of or near the Mount Lyrceum (Λύρκειον) between Arcadia and Argolis: tellus, Val. Fl. 4, 355: Lyrcea arva, Ov. M. 1, 598.
lyrceius.short: Lyrcēĭus or Lyrcēus, a, um, adj., Lyrcean, of or near the Mount Lyrceum (Λύρκειον) between Arcadia and Argolis: tellus, Val.

lyrcius.full: Lyrcīus or Lyrcēus (Lyrcaeus), i, m., a fountain in the Peloponnesus: aret Lyrcius (Lyrceus), Stat. Th. 4, 711.
lyrcius.short: Lyrcīus or Lyrcēus (Lyrcaeus), i, m., a fountain in the Peloponnesus: aret Lyrcius (Lyrceus), Stat.

lyricen.full: lўrĭcen, ĭnis, m. lyra-cano, a luteplayer, lyrist: fidicen, lyricen, cornicen, liticen, Aug. de Gramm. p. 1977 P.; cf.: lyricen, λυρῳδός, Gloss. Philox.

lyricus.full: lўrĭcus, a, um, adj. lyra, of or belonging to the lute or lyre, lyric: lyrici soni, Ov. F. 2, 94: vates, Hor. C. 1, 1, 35: senex, i. e. Anacreon, Ov. Tr. 2, 364: regnator lyricae cohortis, i. e. Pindar, Stat. S. 4, 7, 5.— Subst. lўrĭca, ōrum, n., lyric poems, Plin. Ep. 7, 17, 3; 3, 1, 7.— lўrĭcus, i, m., = λυρικός, a lyric poet, Sid. Ep. 4, 1: Bacchylides, Amm. 25, 4, 3.—Usually plur.: lўrĭci, ōrum, m., lyric poets, Quint. 9, 4, 53; 1, 8, 6; 8, 6, 71; 10, 1, 96; 61 (in Cic. Or. 55, written in Gr

lyristes.full: lўristes, ae, m., = λυριστής, a luteplayer, lyrist: audisses lectorem, vel lyristen, Plin. Ep. 1, 15, 2; 9, 17, 3; 9, 36, 4; Sid. Ep. 8, 11.
lyristes.short: lўristes, ae, m., = λυριστής, a luteplayer, lyrist: audisses lectorem, vel lyristen, Plin.

lyrnesus.full: Lyrnēsus (Lyrnessus), i, f., = Λυρνησός, a town in Troas, the birthplace of Briseis, Plin. 5, 30, 32, § 122: Lyrnessi domus alta, Verg. A. 12, 547.—Hence, Lyrnēsĭus (Lyrnessius), a, um, adj., Lyrnesian: moenia, Ov. M. 12, 108; 13, 176; id. H. 3, 45.— Lyrnēsis (Lyr-nessis), ĭdis, f. adj. (only used as subst.), the Lyrnesian (sc. maid or woman): abductā Lyrnesside tristis Achilles, i. e. Briseis, Ov. Tr. 4, 1, 15: audierat, Lyrnessi, tuos, abducta, dolores, id. A. A. 2, 403.
lyrnesus.short: Lyrnēsus (Lyrnessus), i, f., = Λυρνησός, a town in Troas, the birthplace of Briseis, Plin.

lyron.full: lyron, i, n., = λύρον, a plant, also called alisma, Plin. 25, 10, 77, § 124.
lyron.short: lyron, i, n., = λύρον, a plant, also called alisma, Plin.

lysander.full: Lўsander, dri, m., = Λύσανδρος. A celebrated Spartan general, conqueror of the Athenians, Cic. Off. 1, 22, 76; 1, 30, 109; Nep. Lys.— An ephor in Sparta, banished for injustice, Cic. Off. 2, 23, 80.

lysas.full: lysas, antis, f., a plant, also called artemisia, App. Herb. 10.
lysas.short: lysas, antis, f., a plant, also called artemisia, App.

lysiacus.full: Lўsĭăcus, a, um, v. Lysias, I. B.

lysiades.full: Lўsĭădes, ae, m., = Λυσιάδης, an Athenian, son of the philosopher Phædrus, Cic. Phil. 5, 5, 13.
lysiades.short: Lўsĭădes, ae, m., = Λυσιάδης, an Athenian, son of the philosopher Phædrus, Cic.

lysias.full: Lўsĭas, ae, m., = Λυσίας. Son of Cephalus, a famous orator of Athens: tum fuit Lysias, quem jam prope audeas oratorem perfectum dicere, Cic. Brut. 9, 35; cf. id. ib. 85, 293; id. de Or. 1, 54, 231; id. Or. 9, 29; Quint. 10, 1, 78; 12, 10, 24.—Hence, Lўsĭăcus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to the orator Lysias: gracilitas, Quint. 12, 10, 24.— A physician, Cels. 5, 18.— A celebrated sculptor, Plin. 36, 5, 4, § 2.

lysimachia1.full: lysĭmăchĭa, ae, f., = λυσιμαχία, a plant, Lysimachia vulgaris, Linn.; Plin. 26, 12, 82, § 131; 26, 14, 87, § 141.
lysimachia1.short: lysĭmăchĭa, ae, f., = λυσιμαχία, a plant, Lysimachia vulgaris, Linn.;

lysimachia2.full: Lȳsĭmăchīa, ae, f., or Lȳsĭmă-chēa, = Λυσιμάχεια, a city in Thrace, now Examili, Mela, 2, 2, 6; Plin. 4, 11, 18, § 48; Liv. 32, 34, 6 al.—Hence, Lȳsĭmăchĭ-enses, ĭum, m., the Lysimachians, Liv. 33, 38, 12.
lysimachia2.short: Lȳsĭmăchīa, ae, f., or Lȳsĭmă-chēa, = Λυσιμάχεια, a city in Thrace, now Examili, Mela, 2, 2, 6;

lysimachos.full: lȳsĭmăchos, i, m., = λυσίμαχος, a precious stone with golden veins, Plin. 37, 10, 62, § 62.
lysimachos.short: lȳsĭmăchos, i, m., = λυσίμαχος, a precious stone with golden veins, Plin.

lysimachus.full: Lȳsĭmăchus, i, m., = Λυσίμαχος, one of the generals of Alexander the Great, afterwards king of Thrace, and founder of Lysimachia, Cic. Tusc. 1, 43, 102; 5, 40, 117; Plin. 8, 16, 61, § 143; Just. 17, 1.— An Acarnanian, instructor of Alexander the Great, Just. 15, 3.— The discoverer of the herb lysimachia, Plin. 25, 7, 35, § 72.— The name of a man, Plaut. Merc. 2, 2, 41.
lysimachus.short: Lȳsĭmăchus, i, m., = Λυσίμαχος, one of the generals of Alexander the Great, afterwards king of Thrace, and founder of Lysimachia, Cic.

lysinoe.full: Lўsĭnŏē, ēs, f., = Λυσινόη, a city of Pisidia, Liv. 38, 15.
lysinoe.short: Lўsĭnŏē, ēs, f., = Λυσινόη, a city of Pisidia, Liv.

lysippus.full: Lȳsippus, i, m., = Λύσιππος, a celebrated brass-founder of Sicyon, to whom alone Alexander the Great gave permission to cast a statue of him, Cic. Fam. 5, 12, 7; id. Brut. 86, 296; Hor. Ep. 2, 1, 240; Plin. 7, 37, 38, § 125; 34, 7, 17, § 37; Quint. 12, 10, 9.
lysippus.short: Lȳsippus, i, m., = Λύσιππος, a celebrated brass-founder of Sicyon, to whom alone Alexander the Great gave permission to cast a statue of him, Cic.

lysis1.full: lўsis, is, f., = λύσις. A loosening, rupture: trabes frangunt suā lysi structuras, Vitr. 6, 11.— A talon, ogee, Vitr. 3, 4, 5; 5, 6, 6.

lysis2.full: Lȳsis, is, m., a small river in Asia Minor, Liv. 38, 15, 3.
lysis2.short: Lȳsis, is, m., a small river in Asia Minor, Liv.

lysis3.full: Lўsis, ĭdis, m., = Λύσις, a Pythagorean of Tarentum, instructor of Epaminondas, Cic. de Or. 3, 34, 139; id. Off. 1, 44, 155; Nep. Epam. 2.
lysis3.short: Lўsis, ĭdis, m., = Λύσις, a Pythagorean of Tarentum, instructor of Epaminondas, Cic.

lysistratus.full: Lȳsistrătus, i, m., the brother of Lysippus, who first made statues of gypsum, Plin. 34, 8, 19, § 91; 35, 12, 44, § 153.
lysistratus.short: Lȳsistrătus, i, m., the brother of Lysippus, who first made statues of gypsum, Plin.

lysiteles.full: Lȳsĭtĕlēs, is, m., the name of a man, Plaut. Trin. 5, 2, 28.
lysiteles.short: Lȳsĭtĕlēs, is, m., the name of a man, Plaut.

lyson.full: Lȳson, ōnis, m., = Λύσων, a celebrated sculptor, Plin. 34, 8, 19, § 34.
lyson.short: Lȳson, ōnis, m., = Λύσων, a celebrated sculptor, Plin.

lystra.full: Lystra, ae, f., or ōrum, n., a city in Lycaonia, north-west of Iconium, Vulg. Act. 14, 8; 14, 21.—Hence, Lystrēni, ōrum, m., the inhabitants of Lystra, Lystrenes, Plin. 5, 32, 42, § 147.
lystra.short: Lystra, ae, f., or ōrum, n., a city in Lycaonia, north-west of Iconium, Vulg.

lytrotes.full: lytrōtes, ae, m., = λυτρωτής, one of the Æons of Valentinus, Tert. adv. Val. 9.
lytrotes.short: lytrōtes, ae, m., = λυτρωτής, one of the Æons of Valentinus, Tert.

lytrum.full: lytrum, false read. for lustra; v. 2. lustrum, II. E.

lytta.full: lytta, ae, f., = λύττα, a worm under a dog's tongue, said to cause madness, Plin. 29, 5, 32, § 100.
lytta.short: lytta, ae, f., = λύττα, a worm under a dog's tongue, said to cause madness, Plin.

m.full: M, m, the twelfth letter of the Latin alphabet (J not being distinguished from I in the class. period), corresponds in form and sound to the Greek M; the Latin language, however, does not combine an initial m with n, as in the Greek μνᾶ, μνῆμα, μνίον, μνόος, etc.; hence, the Greek μνᾶ became Latin mĭna. The Latin language, unlike the Greek, tolerated a final m; but its sound was obscure, Prisc. p. 555 P. (cf. Quint. 12, 10, 31), and before an initial vowel, even in prose, was scarcely heard (hen
m.short: M, m, the twelfth letter of the Latin alphabet (J not being distinguished from I in the class.

macae1.full: Macae, ārum, m., a people in the north-eastern part of Arabia Felix, Prisc. Peri. 887.
macae1.short: Macae, ārum, m., a people in the north-eastern part of Arabia Felix, Prisc.

macae2.full: Macae, ārum, m., = οἱ Μάκαι (Herod. 4, 175), a people of Africa in the regio Syrtica, Mela, 3, 8, 6; Plin. 5, 5, 5, § 34; Sil. 3, 275; 15, 670.—Sing.: Maces, Sil. 9, 222. —Acc. Macen, Sil. 2, 60.

macaerinthe.full: macaerinthē, ēs, f. μάκαιρα, another name for rosmarinus: rosmarinum prophetae macaerinthen, Latini salutarem, App. Herb. 79.

macareus.full: Măcăreus (trisyl.), ĕi and ĕos, m., = Μακαρεύς. A son of Æolus, who lived in incest with his sister Canace, Ov. H. 11, 21; id. Ib. 564; Hyg. Fab. 242.—Hence, Măcărēïs, ĭdis, f., = Μακαρηΐς, daughter of Macareus, Isse; acc. Græc., Macarēïda, Ov. M. 6, 124.— A companion of Ulysses before Troy, and afterwards of Æneas in Italy, Ov. M. 14, 159; 441.—In voc. Græc., Macareu, Ov. M. 14, 318.— A Centaur, Ov. M. 12, 452.
macareus.short: Măcăreus (trisyl.), ĕi and ĕos, m., = Μακαρεύς.

macariotes.full: măcărĭŏtēs, ētis, f., = μακαριότης (happiness), one of the Æons of Valentinus, Tert. adv. Val. 8.
macariotes.short: măcărĭŏtēs, ētis, f., = μακαριότης (happiness), one of the Æons of Valentinus, Tert.

macatus.full: Macātus, i, m., a Roman surname: M. Livius Macatus, Liv. 27, 34.
macatus.short: Macātus, i, m., a Roman surname: M.

maccis.full: maccis, ĭdis, f., a fictitious spice, Plaut. Ps. 3, 2, 43 (al. macis).
maccis.short: maccis, ĭdis, f., a fictitious spice, Plaut.

maccius.full: Maccius, a, name of a Roman gens. —Hence, T. Maccius Plautus, the celebrated Roman comic poet; v. Plautus.
maccius.short: Maccius, a, name of a Roman gens.

maccus.full: maccus, i, m. cf. Sanscr. mūkas, dumb; Gr. μῶκος, mockery; also Μῶμος, a buffoon, punchinello, macaroni, in the Atellane plays: in Atellana Oscae personae inducuntur, ut maccus, Diom. p. 488 P.; cf. Inscr. Orell. 2621.— Transf., a simpleton, blockhead: macci et buccones, App. Mag. p. 325, 30.

macedo2.full: Măcĕdo, ŏnis, m., the name of a usurer, Dig. 14, 6, 1 init.—Hence, Măcĕ-dŏnĭānus, a, um, adj., relating to the usurer Macedo: senatusconsultum, a decree forbidding usurers to recover loans from heirs after they inherited their estates, Dig. 14, 6, 1.— Also the name of a phitosopher, a friend of Gellius, Gell. 13, 8, 4.
macedo2.short: Măcĕdo, ŏnis, m., the name of a usurer, Dig.

macedones.full: Măcĕdŏnes, um (Gr. acc. Macedonas, Auct. Her. 4, 32, 43; Liv. 26, 24, 5 et saep.; Sen. Ben. 5, 6, 1; Flor. 2, 8, 5; v. Neue, Formenl. 1, 328), m., = Μακεδόνες, the Macedonians, Mel. 2, 3, 1; Cic. Off. 2, 22, 76; Auct. Her. 4, 25, 34; 32; Liv. 7, 26; 30, 33 sq. et saep.—Hyrcani Macedones, v. Hyrcani.— In sing.: Măcĕdo (Macedon, Luc. 8, 694), ŏnis, m., a Macedonian: quid Macedo Alexander? i. e. Alexander the Great, Cic. Phil. 5, 17, 48; so Luc. 8, 694: diffidit urbium Portas vir Macedo, i. e. Phil

macedonianus.full: Măcĕdŏnĭānus, a, um, v. 2. Macedo, I.

macella.full: Macella, ae, f., = Μάκελλα, a town in Sicily, on the Crimisus, Liv. 26, 21.
macella.short: Macella, ae, f., = Μάκελλα, a town in Sicily, on the Crimisus, Liv.

macellarius.full: măcellārĭus, a, um, adj. macellum, of or belonging to the meat-market or provision-market: taberna, Val. Max. 3, 4, 4: negotiator artis macellariae, Inscr. Grut. 647, 5: ARS, Inscr. Orell. 4302.—Hence, Subst.: măcellārĭus, ĭi, m., a meat-seller, victualler: vendere apros macellario, Varr. R. R. 3, 2, 11; 3, 4, 2; Suet. Caes. 26: macellarios adjuvare, id. Vesp. 19.

macellinus.full: Măcellīnus, i, m. id., an epithet of the emperor M. Opilius Macrinus, who killed his slaves in his own house, Capit. Macr. 13.

macellum.full: măcellum, i (măcellus, i, m., Mart. 10, 96, 9), n. root μαχ-; cf. Gr. μάχομαι, to fight; cf. μάχαιρα, μάχη, and mactāre; prop. butcher's stall, shambles; hence, transf., meat-market, provision-market (where flesh, fish, and vegetables were sold). Lit.: venio ad macellum, rogito pisces, Plaut. Aul. 2, 8, 3: apud emporium atque in macello, id. Am. 4, 1, 4: nostin' porticum apud macellum hac deorsum? Ter. Ad. 4, 2, 34: excandefacere annonam macelli, Varr. R. R. 3, 2, 16; cf.: putarem annonam in mac

macellus1.full: măcellus, a, um, adj. dim. [1. macer; cf.: ut in his macer, macriculus, macellus; niger, nigriculus, nigellus, Varr. L. L. 8, § 79 Müll.; cf. Paul. ex Fest. s. v. altellus, p. 7 Müll.], rather meagre: homo, Lucil. ap. Non. 136, 32.

macellus2.full: măcellus, i, m., v. macellum init.

maceo.full: măcĕo, ēre, v. n. 1. macer, to be lean, meagre: quia ossa atque pellis totust: ita cura macet, Plaut. Aul. 3, 6, 28; cf. Non. 509, 11.

macer1.full: măcer, cra, crum, adj. Sanscr. root mak, to crush; Gr. μάσσω, knead; μαγεύς, baker; Germ. mager, lean, meagre. Lit., of living beings (most freq. of animals): taurus, opp. pinguis, Verg. E. 3, 100: boves, Varr. R. R. 2, 5, 12; Juv. 14, 146: turdi, Hor. S. 1, 5, 72: mustela, id. Ep. 1, 7, 33: ostreae inuberes et macrae, Gell. 20, 8; Quint. 6, 3, 58.—Of parts of the body: in macerrimis corporis partibus, Sen. Ep. 78, 8.—Humorously of a person: valeat res ludicra si me Palma negata macrum donata re

macer2.full: Măcer, cri, m., a Roman surname. C. Licinius Macer, an historian, Cic. Leg. 1, 2, 7; id. Brut. 67, 238; Liv. 4, 7, 12. — Aemilius Macer, a poet and a friend of Virgil and Ovid, Ov. Tr. 4, 10, 44; v. Aemilius.
macer2.short: Măcer, cri, m., a Roman surname.

maceratio.full: mācĕrātĭo, ōnis, f. macero, a steeping, soaking, maceration: diuturna, Vitr. 6, 2.— A making soft or tender, Arn. 4, 152.

maceresco.full: māceresco, ĕre, v. inch. n. [id.], to make soft or tender, Cato, R. R. 92.

maceria.full: mācĕrĭa, ae (post-class. form, mācĕ-rĭes, only nom. and acc., Afran. ap. Non. 138; Varr. R. R. 3, 5, 11; Prud. Hamart. 227; Inscr. Grut. 611, 13; Inscr. Orell. 4057), f. from macero, to soften; orig. a wall built of soft clay; cf. Gr. μάσσω, an enclosure, a wall (class.): maceriam sine calce ex caementis et silice altam pedes quinque facito, Cato, R. R. 15; cf. Varr. R. R. 1, 14, 4; 3, 5, 12: quid maceria illa ait in horto, quaest quae in noctes singulas latere fit minor? Plaut. Truc. 2, 2, 49:

maceriatus.full: mācĕrĭātus, a, um, adj. maceria, enclosed, walled in: SEPVLCRVM, Inscr Mur 1644, 14.

maceries1.full: măcĕrĭes, ēi, f [1. macer], distress, affliction (ante-class.), Afran. ap. Non. 138, 13.

maceriola.full: mācĕrĭŏla, ae, f. dim. maceria, a small enclosure, wall, Inscr. Mur. 492, 2.

macero.full: mācĕro, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. prob. from root μαγ-, μάσσω, to knead; through an adj. mācerus; v. Corss. Ausspr. 1, 395; cf. also măcer, to make soft or tender, to soften by steeping, to soak, steep, macerate (not in Cic. or Cæs.). Lit.: brassicam in aquam, Cato, R. R. 156, 5: salsamenta, Ter. Ad. 3, 3, 27: in piscina lupinum, Col. 1, 6, 21: semen lacte, id. 11, 3, 51: (ramos genistae) marinā aquā, Plin. 24, 9, 40, § 66: (siliginem) novem diebus maceratum ... subigunt, id. 18, 11, 27, § 106: grana

macerones.full: Măcĕrōnes, um, m., a people of Iberia, Plin. 6, 10, 11, § 29.
macerones.short: Măcĕrōnes, um, m., a people of Iberia, Plin.

macesco.full: măcesco, ĕre, v. inch. n. [maceo], to grow lean or thin, to become meagre (anteand post-Aug.): (apes) propter laborem asperantur et macescunt, Varr. R. R. 3, 16; 1, 55, 1: constat, arva segetibus ejus (hordei) macescere, become poor, Col. 2, 9, 14: feminis bubus demitur (cibus), quod macescentes melius concipere dicuntur, Varr. R. R. 2, 1, 17: tuo maerore maceror, Macesco, consenesco et tabesco miser, Plaut. Capt. 1, 2, 31.

macetae.full: Măcĕtae (Măcĕdae), ārum, m., = Μακέται. (As a less usual form for Μακεδόνες,) Macedonians: Macetae locupletissimo imperio aucti, Gell. 9, 3, 1.—Gen. plur. Măcĕtūm. Stat. S. 4, 6, 106; Sil. 14, 5; Luc. 2, 647; Claud. ap. Rufin. 2, 279; Aus. de Clar. Urb. 2, 9.— (Because Antiochus the Great was a descendant of Seleucus Nicator) = Syri, Sil. 13, 878.

machabaeus.full: Machabaeus, i, m., a surname of Judas, Vulg. 1 Macc. 1, 2 et saep.—Hence, Machabaei, ōrum, m., the Maccabees, Aug. Civ. Dei, 18, 36; Hier. Ep. 7, 6.
machabaeus.short: Machabaeus, i, m., a surname of Judas, Vulg.

machaera1.full: măchaera, ae, f., = μάχαιρα, a sword (ante-class. and post-Aug.): machaera atque hasta, Enn. ap Fest. s. v. redhostire, p. 270 Müll. (Trag. v. 212 Müll.): succincti corda machaeris, id. ap. Serv. ad Verg. A. 9, 678 (Ann. v. 392 ib.): eia machaeras, id. ib. 9, 38 (Ann. v. 585 ib.); Plaut. Curc. 3, 54: ni hebes machaera foret, id. Mil. 1, 1, 53; Sen. Ben. 5, 24 fin.; Suet. Claud. 15.—A weapon, in mal. part., Plaut. Ps. 4, 7, 85.
machaera1.short: măchaera, ae, f., = μάχαιρα, a sword (ante-class.

machaera2.full: Măchaera, ae, m., an auctioneer, Juv. 7, 9.
machaera2.short: Măchaera, ae, m., an auctioneer, Juv.

machaerium.full: măchaerĭum, ii, a false reading for machaeris, Plaut. Rud. 2, 2, 9.
machaerium.short: măchaerĭum, ii, a false reading for machaeris, Plaut.

machaerophorus.full: măchaerŏphŏrus, i, m., = μαχαιροφόρος, a sword-wearer, a satellite: machaerophoris centum sequentibus, i. e. soldiers armed in the Greek manner, Cic. Q. Fr. 2, 10, 2.
machaerophorus.short: măchaerŏphŏrus, i, m., = μαχαιροφόρος, a sword-wearer, a satellite: machaerophoris centum sequentibus, i.

machaerophyllon.full: măchaerŏphyllon, i, n., = μαχαιρόφυλλον (sword-leaf), a plant (al. macrophyllon). App. Herb. 78.
machaerophyllon.short: măchaerŏphyllon, i, n., = μαχαιρόφυλλον (sword-leaf), a plant (al.

machaon.full: Măchāon, ŏnis, m., = Μαχάων, son of Æsculapius, a famous surgeon of the Greeks before Troy, Cels. praef.; Prop. 2, 1, 61; Verg. A. 2, 263; Ov. P. 3, 4, 7 al.— Transf., in plur., surgeons, physicians: quid tibi cum medicis? dimitte Machaonas omnes, Mart. 2, 16, 5.—Hence, Ma-chāŏnĭcus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Machaon: ars, i. e. the art of surgery, Sid. Ep. 2, 12.— Măchāŏnĭus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Machaon, Machaonian, surgical: Machaoniā ope sanus, Ov. R. Am. 546: sucus, Stat. S
machaon.short: Măchāon, ŏnis, m., = Μαχάων, son of Æsculapius, a famous surgeon of the Greeks before Troy, Cels.

machetum.full: machetum, i, n., a kind of rose, Plin. 21, 4, 10, § 19.
machetum.short: machetum, i, n., a kind of rose, Plin.

machilla.full: māchilla, ae, f. dim. machina, a little machine: e machillā sustuli, Petr. 74, 13 dub. (al. e machina illam sustuli).

machimus.full: Machĭmus, i, m., = Μάχιμος, the name of one of Actæon's hounds, Hyg. Fab. 181.
machimus.short: Machĭmus, i, m., = Μάχιμος, the name of one of Actæon's hounds, Hyg.

machina.full: māchĭna, ae, f. = μηχανή, a machine, i. e. any artificial contrivance for performing work, an engine, fabric, frame, scaffolding, staging, easel, warlike engine, military machine, etc. Lit. In gen.: moles et machina mundi, Lucr. 5, 96: omnes illae columnae machinā appositā dejectae sunt, Cic. Verr. 2, 1, 55, § 145: torquet nunc lapidem, nunc ingens machina tignum, Hor. Ep. 2, 2, 73: trahuntque siccas machinae carinas, id. C. 1, 4, 2: frumentaria, Dig. 33, 7, 12.— Esp., A platform on which slaves

machinalis.full: māchĭnālis, e, adj. machina, of or belonging to machines (post-Aug.): scientia, Plin. 7, 37, 38, § 125: saxa machinali pondere, Aus. Ep. 21, 34.

machinamen.full: māchĭnāmen, ĭnis, n. machinor, a contrivance, device, Cassiod. Hist. Eccl. 9, 14.

machinamentum.full: māchĭnāmentum, i, n. id., a machine, engine; an instrument, organ (perh. not ante-Aug.; not in Cic. or Cæs.). Lit.: machinamenta alia quatiendis muris portabant, military engines, Liv. 24, 34: suspensum et nutans machinamentum, Tac. H. 4, 30: nihil tam ignarum barbaris, quam machinamenta et astus oppugnationum, id. A. 12, 45: tot genera machinamentorum ad extendendum femur, surgical instruments, Cels. 8, 20: singulis articulis singula machinamenta, quibus extorqueantur, aptata, Sen. Ep. 24, 14;

machinarius.full: māchĭnārĭus, a, um, adj. machina, of or belonging to machines, machine- (postclass.). Adj.: mola, which is worked by an animal by means of a machine, App. M. 7, p. 194, 20: asinus, Dig. 33, 7, 12: mensor, a surveyor, ib. 11, 6, 7: commentator, a machinist, machine-builder, Sol. 5.— Subst.: māchĭnārĭus, ii, m., one who works on a scaffold, Dig. 9, 2, 31.

machinatio.full: māchĭnātĭo, ōnis, f. machinor, artificial contrivance, mechanism, machinery (class.). Lit.: cum machinatione quadam moveri aliquid videmus, ut sphaeram, Cic. N. D. 2, 38, 97: data est quibusdam bestiis machinatio quaedam, et sollertia, power of contrivance, design, id. ib. 2, 48, 123.— Transf. (abstr. pro concreto), a machine, engine: tantae altitudinis machinationes, Caes. B. G. 2, 31: tanta, id. ib. 2, 30; 4, 17: navalis, id. B. C. 2, 10: tale machinationis genus, Liv. 37, 5.— Trop., a trick,

machinator.full: māchĭnātor, ōris, m. machinor, a maker of machines, a machinist, an engineer, architect (class.). Lit., of Archimedes: inventor ac machinator bellicorum tormentorum, Liv. 24, 34: machinatores, qui pegmata per se surgentia excogitant, Sen. Ep. 88, 19: magistri et machinatores quibus ingenium et audacia erat, Tac. A. 15, 42: deus rerum omnium machinator fecit hominem, maker, creator, Lact. 2, 11. — Trop., a contriver, inventor: harum omnium rerum machinatores, Cic. Agr. 1, 5, 16: omnium architectu

machinatrix.full: māchĭnātrix, īcis, f. machinator, an inventress: malorum facinorum, Sen. Med. 266.

machinatus.full: māchĭnātus, ūs, m. machinor, a contrivance, artifice, device (post-class.): suo machinatu, App. Mag. p. 321, 33; Sid. Ep. 5, 6.

machinor.full: māchĭnor, ātus, 1, v. dep. a. [machina], to contrive skilfully, to devise, design, frame, invent (class). In gen.: incredibile est, quantā operā machinata natura sit, Cic. N. D. 2, 59, 149: qui haec machinatus est, id. Univ. 3: haec duo musici machinati ad voluptatem sunt, versum atque cantum, id. de Or. 3, 44, 174: quod machiner inveniamque, Lucr. 3, 944; cf. Vitr. 1, 6 med.— In partic., to contrive artfully, to scheme, plot, = μηχανᾶσθαι: aliquam machinabor machinam, Unde aurum efficiam amanti

machinosus.full: māchĭnōsus, a, um, adj. id., skilfully constructed: navigium, Suet. Ner. 34.

machinula.full: māchĭnŭla, ae, f. dim. id., a little machine, Paul. Nol. Carm. 26, 458; Paul. ex Fest. p. 107, 3; p. 147, 2.

machio.full: māchĭo, ōnis, m. id., one who works on a scaffold, a mason: machiones dicti a machinis, quibus insistunt propter altitudinem parietum, Isid. Orig. 19, 8, 2 (hence, Fr. macon; Engl. mason).

machlyes.full: Machlўes, um, m., a fabled people of Africa: supra Nasamonas confinesque illis Machlyas androgynos esse utriusque naturae, Plin. 7, 2, 2, § 15.
machlyes.short: Machlўes, um, m., a fabled people of Africa: supra Nasamonas confinesque illis Machlyas androgynos esse utriusque naturae, Plin.

machorones.full: Măchŏrōnes, um, m., a people of Pontus, Plin. 6, 4, 4, § 11.
machorones.short: Măchŏrōnes, um, m., a people of Pontus, Plin.

macia.full: macĭa, ae, f., a plant, called by the Greeks ἀναγαλλίς, pimpernel, Marc. Emp. 1.
macia.short: macĭa, ae, f., a plant, called by the Greeks ἀναγαλλίς, pimpernel, Marc.

macies.full: măcĭes, ēi, f. maceo, leanness, thinness, meagreness (class.). Lit. Of living beings and the parts of their bodies: profectus est (ad bellum) Hirtius consul: at quā imbecillitate? quā macie? Cic. Phil. 7, 4, 12; id. Agr. 2, 34, 93: hoc maciem facit, Plin. 30, 7, 20, § 60: reducere ad maciem, id. 24, 8, 30, § 46: equi macie corrupti, * Caes. B. C. 3, 58: corpus macie extabuit, Cic. poët. Tusc. 3, 12, 26: turpis macies decentes Occupet malas, Hor. C. 3, 27, 53: tenet ora profanae Foeda situ macies

macilentus.full: măcĭlentus, a, um, adj. macies, lean, thin, meagre (ante- and post-class.): macilento ore, Plaut. Capt. 3, 4, 114: macilentis malis, id. As. 2, 3, 20: macilenti, macie tenuati, Paul. ex Fest. p. 125 Müll.: solum, poor, barren, Pall. Mart. 10, 1.—Comp.: macilentiores vultus, Vulg. Dan. 1, 10: macilentior equus, Pelagon. Vet. 13.

macio.full: măcĭo, āre, v. a. id., to make lean, thin, or meagre, to reduce (post-class.): Caspii maris fauces mirum in modum maciantur imbribus, crescunt aestibus, Sol. 15, 18; cf.: macio διακναίω, Gloss. Philox.

macir.full: macir, indecl., = μάκερ, a kind of red spicy bark brought from India, Plin. 12, 8, 16, § 32.
macir.short: macir, indecl., = μάκερ, a kind of red spicy bark brought from India, Plin.

maco.full: măco, ĕre, 3, v. a. cf. macellum, to maul, beat, hack: namque nullum Pejus macit homonem quamde mare saevum, Naev. ap. Paul. ex Fest. p. 397 Müll. ad loc.: ut nunc saepe boves lucae ferro male mactae Diffugiunt, Lucr. 5, 1339 Munro ad loc.

macor.full: măcor, ōris, m. maceo, leanness, meagreness (ante-class. for macies): corpus meum tali maerore, aegrore, macore senet, Pac. ap. Non. 137, 1 (Trag. Rel. v. 275 Rib.); cf. Prisc. 699 P.

macra.full: Mā^cra, ae, m. A river in Italy, between Liguria and Etruria, now Magra, Plin. 3, 5, 7, § 48; Liv. 39, 32, 2; 40, 41, 3.— Macra Cōmē, Gr. Μακρὰ κώμη, a town in Locris, on the border of Thessaly, Liv. 32, 13, 10.

macresco.full: mā^cresco, crŭi, 3, v. inch. n. [1. macer], to grow lean, meagre: algor eas et famis macrescere cogit, Varr. R. R. 2, 5, 15; 3, 5, 3: macrescit pecus, Col. 6, 3, 1: macrescunt animalia, Veg. Vet. 1, 7, 2: invidus alterius macrescit rebus opimis, grows thin at, pines away at, * Hor. Ep. 1, 2, 57: curionem agnum Plautus pro macro dixit, quasi cura macruisset, Paul. ex Fest. s. v. curionem, p. 60 Müll.

macri campi.full: Macri Campi (also Campi Ma-cri, Varr. R. R. 2 praef. § 6, and Liv. 41, 18), = Μακροὶ Κάμποι, a region in Gallia Cispadana, on the river Macra, in the vicinity of Parma and Modena, Varr. R. R. 2 praef. § 6; Col. 7, 2, 3; Liv. 41, 18, 5; 45, 12, 11.

macria.full: Macria, f., a small island near Eubœa, Plin. 2, 88, 90, § 204.
macria.short: Macria, f., a small island near Eubœa, Plin.

macriculus.full: macrĭcŭlus, a, um, adj. dim. [1. macer], lean, Varr. L. L. 8, 40, § 79 Müll.

macrinus.full: Mā^crīnus, i, m., the name of a man. A friend of the poet Persius, Pers. 2, 1.— A Roman emperor, Aus. Caes. 23.
macrinus.short: Mā^crīnus, i, m., the name of a man.

macris.full: Mā^cris, ĭdis, f., = Μακρις, the name of several islands. In the Ægean Sea, near Ionia, Liv. 27, 13; 28; 29.— An ancient name of the island of Eubœa, Plin. 4, 12, 21, § 64.— Of Chios, Plin. 5, 31, 38, § 136. — Of Icarus, Plin. 4, 12, 23, § 68.
macris.short: Mā^cris, ĭdis, f., = Μακρις, the name of several islands.

macritas.full: măcrĭtas, ātis, f. 1. macer, leanness, poorness, thinness (post-Aug. and rare for macies): arenae, Vitr. 2, 4: soli, Pall. Oct. 1, 2.

macritudo.full: mā^crĭtūdo, ĭnis, f. id., leanness, thinness, meagreness (for macies): ossa atque pellis sum, miser macritudine, Plaut. Capt. 1, 2, 26 Weise (1, 2, 32 Brix and Fleck., who read aegritudine; acc. to Non. 136, 2).

macrobii.full: Macrŏbĭi (Macrŏbĭoe, Schol. Juv. 10, 150), ōrum, m., = Μακρόβιοι (longlived). A people of Æthiopia, Mel. 3, 9, 1; Plin. 6, 30, 35, § 190; 7, 2, 2, § 28; Val. Max. 8, 13, 5 ext.— The inhabitants of Apollonia, in Macedonia, Plin. 4, 10, 17, § 37.

macrobius.full: Măcrŏbĭus, ii, m., = Μακρόβιος (living long): Aurelius Macrobius Ambrosius Theodosius, a Roman grammarian at the end of the fourth century, author of a commentary on Cicero's Somnium Scipionis, and of a treatise entitled Convivia Saturna lia, cf. Jan. Proleg. ad Macr. p. 1 sq.
macrobius.short: Măcrŏbĭus, ii, m., = Μακρόβιος (living long): Aurelius Macrobius Ambrosius Theodosius, a Roman grammarian at the end of the fourth century, author of a commentary on Cicero's Somnium Scipionis, and of a treatise entitled Convivia Saturna lia, cf.

macrocephali.full: Macrŏcĕphăli, ōrum, m., = Μακρο, κέφαλοι (i. e. people with great heads), a people of Pontus, Mela, 1, 19, 11; Plin. 6, 4, 4, § 11.

macrochera.full: macrŏchēra, ae, f., = μακρόχειρα, having long sleeves, long-sleeved: tunica, Lampr. Alex. Sev. 33, 4.
macrochera.short: macrŏchēra, ae, f., = μακρόχειρα, having long sleeves, long-sleeved: tunica, Lampr.

macrochir.full: Măcrŏchīr, m., = Μακρόχειρ, Longhand, = Lat. Longimanus, a surname of king Artaxerxes, Nep. Reg. 1, 3 sq.; Amm. 30, 8, 4.

macrocolum.full: măcrŏcōlum and măcrŏcol-lum, i, n., = μακρόκωλον, large-sized paper, royal paper, Cic. Att. 16, 3, 1; 13, 25, 3; Plin. 13, 12, 24, § 80.
macrocolum.short: măcrŏcōlum and măcrŏcol-lum, i, n., = μακρόκωλον, large-sized paper, royal paper, Cic.

macrocremnii montes.full: Macrocremnii montes, a chain of mountains near the Dniester, Plin. 4, 12, 26, § 82.
macrocremnii montes.short: Macrocremnii montes, a chain of mountains near the Dniester, Plin.

macrologia.full: macrŏlŏgĭa, ae, f., = μακρολογία, tediousness in speech (Lat. longiloquium), Pomp. Gram. Com. in Donat. de Barb. 3, 1, p. 293 Keil (as Greek, trans., longior quam oportet sermo, Quint. 8, 3, 53).
macrologia.short: macrŏlŏgĭa, ae, f., = μακρολογία, tediousness in speech (Lat.

macrones.full: Mā^crōnes, um, m., v. Macerones and Machorones.

mactabilis.full: mactābĭlis, e, adj. macto, deadly: plaga, Lucr. 6, 805.

mactatio.full: mactātĭo, ōnis, f. id., a slaying, killing (post-class.): innoxiorum animantium mactatio, Arn. 7, 213; Isid. Orig. 6, 19, 31.

mactator.full: mactātor, ōris, m. id., a slayer, murderer: mactator senum, Sen. Troad. 1002.

mactatus.full: mactātus, ūs, m. id., a slaying, killing: mactatu parentis, Lucr. 1, 99.

macto.full: macto, āvi, ātum, 1 (old form of perf. subj. mactassint, Enn., Afran., and Pompon. ap. Non. 342, 12 sq.), v. freq. a. macto, kindr. to Sanscr. makh, mah; intens. māmahyata, to slaughter, sacrifice; maha, victim; the ct in macto like vectum from veho; hence, Within the religious sphere, to offer, sacrifice, immolate any thing in honor of the gods: ferctum Jovi moveto et mactato sic, Cato, R. R. 134, 2; so id. ib. § 4: pultem dis mactat, Varr. ap. Non. 341, 28: nigras pecudes, Lucr. 3, 52: lectas
macto.short: macto, āvi, ātum, 1 (old form of perf.

mactus1.full: mactus, a, um, adj. root μακ, in μάκαρ, blessed; cf. μακρός. In relig. lang., of the gods, glorified, worshipped, honored, adored (only in the voc. macte, and rarely in the nom.): Juppiter te bonas preces precor, uti sies volens propitius mihi liberisque meis, mactus hoc fercto. Jove pater, macte vino inferio esto, Cato, R. R. 134, 2 and 3; cf. id. ib. 132, 2; for which: mactus hoc vino inferio esto, Arn. 7, 296: macte hoc porco piaculo immolando esto, Cato, R. R. 139 fin.: macte hisce suovitaur

mactus2.full: mactus, a, um, P. a. of maco, q. v., and cf. macto fin.

macula1.full: măcŭla, ae, f. for malocula, malcula, dim.; cf. Sanscr. mala, dirt, a spot, mark, stain (class.). Lit. In gen., Plin. 37, 10, 56, § 155: (bos) maculis insignis et albo, i. e. with white spots, Verg. G. 3, 56: maculis albis equus, id. A. 9, 49: maculis auro squalentibus ardens (rex apum), id. G. 4, 91: in ipsis quasi maculis (terra), ubi habitatur, in those spots, i. e. small places, Cic. Rep. 6, 19 fin.: parcit cognatis maculis similis fera, Juv. 15, 160; cf. 5, 104.— Transf., a mesh in a net, a

macula2.full: Măcŭla, ae, m., a Roman surname, e. g. of Q. Pompeius, Cic. Fam. 6, 19, 1.
macula2.short: Măcŭla, ae, m., a Roman surname, e.
