massaris.short: massăris, is, f., a grape from a wild vine, Plin.

massaticius.full: massātīcĭus or -tĭus, a, um, adj. massa, consisting of masses or lumps, Agrim. p. 265 Goes.

massicus.full: Massĭcus, i, m. (with or without mons), a mountain in Campania, celebrated for its excellent wine, now Monte Massico: per juga Massici montis, Liv. 22, 14: vertunt felicia Baccho Massica qui rastris (sc. juga, or arbusta), Verg. A. 7, 725: in Massici radices, Cic. Agr. 2, 25, 66.—Hence, Massĭcum vīnum, or simply Mas-sĭcum, i, n., wine of the Massicus, Massic wine: veteris pocula Massici, Hor. C. 1, 1, 19; 2, 7, 21: vina, id. S. 2, 4, 51: Bacchi umor, Verg. G. 2, 143; 3, 526.

massilia.full: Massĭlĭa, ae, f., = Μασσαλία, a celebrated seaport town in Gallia Narbonensis, a colony from Phocæa, and a seat of Greek civilization, now Marseilles, Plin. 3, 4, 5, § 35; cf. Caes. B. C. 2, 1; Cic. Off. 2, 8, 28; id. Fl. 26, 63; id. Font. 1, 3; Sil. 15, 169; Luc. 4, 257 et saep.—Hence, Massĭlĭānus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Massilia, Massilian: vinum, Mart. 13, 123 in lemm.— Mas-sĭlĭensis, e, adj., of or belonging to Massilia, Massilian: mores, i. e. Sybaritic, luxurious, Plaut. Cas. 5, 4
massilia.short: Massĭlĭa, ae, f., = Μασσαλία, a celebrated seaport town in Gallia Narbonensis, a colony from Phocæa, and a seat of Greek civilization, now Marseilles, Plin.

masso1.full: masso, 1, v. a., = μάσσω, to chew (late Lat.), Theod. Prisc. 1, 8; 2, 29.

massula.full: massŭla, ae, f. dim. 1. massa, a little lump or mass (post-Aug.), Col. 12, 38, 2: salis, id. 12, 48, 5.

massurius.full: Massŭrĭus (Măsŭrĭus) Sabinus, a celebrated jurist in the time of the emperor Tiberius, Dig. 1, 2, 2 fin.; Gell. 3, 16 fin.; 5, 19 al.: Masuri rubrica vetavit, Pers. 5, 90. —Hence, Masŭrĭānus, a, um, adj., of or pertaining to Massurius: deliramenta, M. Aurel. ap. Front. Ep. ad Caes. 2, 9 Mai.
massurius.short: Massŭrĭus (Măsŭrĭus) Sabinus, a celebrated jurist in the time of the emperor Tiberius, Dig.

massyli.full: Massȳli, ōrum, m., = Μασσύλιοι, a people in Africa, to the east of the Massaesyli, Plin. 5, 4, 4, § 30; Verg. A. 6, 60; Sil. 4, 512; 16, 171; Prud. στεφ. 4, 46; called Maesuli, Liv. 24, 48, 13.—Hence, Massȳ-lus and Massȳlĭus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to the Massyli, Massylian; poet. for African: Massyli equites, Verg. A. 4, 132: serpens, that guarded the orchards of the Hesperides, Mart. 10, 94, 1: Massylia signa, Sil. 16, 184.— Massȳlaeus or Mas-sylēus, a, um, adj., = Μασσυλαῖος or Μασσυλεῖ
massyli.short: Massȳli, ōrum, m., = Μασσύλιοι, a people in Africa, to the east of the Massaesyli, Plin.

mastarna.full: Mastarna, ae, m., an ancient (Tuscan) name of Mons Coelius, Oratio Claudii Aug. ap. Grut. 502.
mastarna.short: Mastarna, ae, m., an ancient (Tuscan) name of Mons Coelius, Oratio Claudii Aug.

mastaurenses.full: Mastaurenses, ĭum, m., the inhabitants of the city of Mastaura in Lydia, Plin. 5, 29, 31, § 120.
mastaurenses.short: Mastaurenses, ĭum, m., the inhabitants of the city of Mastaura in Lydia, Plin.

masticatio.full: mastĭcātĭo, ōnis, f. mastico, a chewing, mastication (post-class.): cibum masticatione exercere, Cael. Aur. Tard. 4, 3, 70.

mastichatus.full: mastĭchātus (mastĭcātus), a, um, adj. mastiche, furnished or seasoned with mastic (post-class.), Lampr. Heliog. 19, 4.

mastiche.full: mastĭchē (mastĭcē), ēs, f., = μαστίχη, mastic, an odoriferous gum from the mastic-tree, Plin. 12, 17, 36, § 72; 21, 16, 56, § 96; 14, 20, 25, § 122; Capitol. Gord. 19.— Post-class. collat. forms: mastĭcha, ae, f., Marc. Emp. 26; mastĭchum (ma-stĭcum), i, n., Pall. Oct. 14, 3 (al. mastichae), and mastix, mastĭchis, abl. mastichĕ, Ser. Samm. 156; 447; 423.
mastiche.short: mastĭchē (mastĭcē), ēs, f., = μαστίχη, mastic, an odoriferous gum from the mastic-tree, Plin.

mastichinus.full: mastĭchĭnus (mastĭcĭnus), a, um, adj., = μαστίχινος, of or belonging to mastic, mastic- (post-class.): oleum, Pall. Mart. 9, 3.
mastichinus.short: mastĭchĭnus (mastĭcĭnus), a, um, adj., = μαστίχινος, of or belonging to mastic, mastic- (post-class.): oleum, Pall.

mastico.full: mastĭco, 1, v. a., to chew (post-class.): aliquid, Pelag. Vet. 30; App. Herb. 79: portulaca mastucata, Theod. Prisc. de Diaeta, 10.

mastigia.full: mastīgĭa, ae, m., = μαστιγίας, a scoundrel, rascal, rogue. Lit. (anteclass.), Plaut. Curc. 4, 4, 11; id. Capt. 3, 4, 69; 3, 5, 1; id. Cas. 2, 6, 9; 2, 8, 10; id. Most. 1, 1, 1; 3, 1, 71; id. Poen. 1, 2, 108; 177; 178; id. Rud. 4, 83; id. Trin. 4, 3, 14: non manum abstines, mastigia? Ter. Ad. 5, 2, 6.— Transf., f., a whip, scourge (late Lat.), Sulp. Sev. Dial. 2, 3, 6.
mastigia.short: mastīgĭa, ae, m., = μαστιγίας, a scoundrel, rascal, rogue.

mastigo.full: mastīgo, 1, v. a., = μαστιγόω, to whip, scourge, Cypr. Serm. de Rat. Circumcis. p. 489.

mastigophorus.full: mastīgŏphŏrus, i, m., = μαστιγοφόρος, a whip-bearer, i. e. a beadle, policeman, an officer whose duty it was to maintain order at the public shows (post-class.), Prud. adv. Symm. 2, 516; Dig. 50, 4, 18, § 17; Arn. 2, 23.
mastigophorus.short: mastīgŏphŏrus, i, m., = μαστιγοφόρος, a whip-bearer, i.

mastos.full: mastos, i, m., = μαστός, a plant good for the breast, Plin. 26, 15, 92, § 163.
mastos.short: mastos, i, m., = μαστός, a plant good for the breast, Plin.

mastruca.full: mastrūca (mastrūga), ae, f. Sardinian; v. infra, a garment made of skins, a sheepskin, a skin: mastrucam, quod Sardum est, inridens Cicero ex industria dixit, Quint. 1, 5, 8: mastruca vestis Sardonica ex pelliculis ferarum, de qua Cicero pro Scauro: Quem purpura regalis non commovit, eum Sardorum mastruca mutavit? Isid. Orig. 19, 23, 5 (Orell. Cic. Fragm. Scaur. § 45, d, p. 268); so Prud. Symm. 2, 695.— As a term of abuse, a sheepskin, a ninny, Plaut. Poen. 5, 5, 34.

mastrucatus.full: mastrūcātus, a, um, adj. mastruca, clothed in a mastruca or in skins: latrunculi, Cic. Prov. Cons. 7, 15.

masturbator.full: masturbātor, ōris, m. masturbor, one who defiles himself (post-Aug.), Mart. 14, 203, 2.

masturbor.full: masturbor, 1, v. dep. perhaps from manus-stupro, to defile one's self (postAug.), Mart. 11, 104, 13; 9, 42, 7; cf. in the act. form masturbat, δέφει, δέφεται, Vet. Gloss.

masucium.full: masucĭum edacem a mandendo scilicet, Paul. ex Fest. p. 139 Müll.
masucium.short: masucĭum edacem a mandendo scilicet, Paul.

matella.full: mătella or mătēla, ae, f. dim. matula, a pot, a vessel for liquids. In gen.: matella aquae, Plaut. Fragm. ap. Non. 543, 17; Varr. ib. 19; Cato, R. R. 10; 11.—Prov.: mus in matella, of a person in difficulty, Petr. 58, 9.— In partic., a chamber-pot, Mart. 12, 32, 13; id. 6, 89, 1; 14, 119 in lemm.; Sen. Ben. 3, 26, 2.—Hence, prov.: matellam praestare alicui, i. e. to perform for one the most menial offices, Mart. 10, 11, 3.—Transf., of a prostitute, Petr. 45, 8.

matellio.full: mătellĭo, ōnis, m. dim. matula; cf. Varr. L. L. 5, § 119 Müll.; Paul. ex Fest. p. 126 ib., a pot, vessel (class.), Varr. ap. Non. 547, 7: Corinthius, Cic. Par. 5, 2, 38.

mateola.full: matĕŏla, ae, f., perh. a kind of mallet or beetle: si (talea) parum descendet, malleolo aut mateola adigito, Cato, R. R. 45, 2; 46, 2 (also ap. Plin. 17, 18, 29, § 126).

mater.full: māter, tris, f. root ma-; Sanscr. and Zend, to make, measure, like Gr. μήτηρ, the maker, akin with Dor. μάτηρ; Germ. Mutter; Engl. mother; cf.: materies, manus, a mother (dat. sing. matre, Corp. Inscr. Lat. 177; dat. plur. matris, Inscr. Grut. 90: matrabus, Inscr. Orell. 2089). Lit.: si quidem istius regis (sc. Anci Martii) matrem habemus, ignoramus patrem, Cic. Rep. 2, 18, 33: cur non sit heres matri suae? id. ib. 3, 10, 17: de pietate in matrem, id. Lael. 3, 11: Sassia mater hujus Aviti, id. C

matercula.full: mātercŭla, ae, f. dim. mater, a little mother (class.): tune igitur mea matercula? Plaut. Fragm. ap. Prisc. p. 601 P.: materculae suae festivus filius, * Cic. Fl. 36, 91; Hor. Ep. 1, 7, 7.

materfamilias.full: māterfămĭlĭas and māter fămĭ-lĭas, v. familia.

materia.full: mātĕrĭa, ae (gen. materiāi, Lucr. 1, 1051), and mātĕrĭes, ēi (only in nom. and acc. sing., and once gen. plur. materierum, Lact. 2, 12, 1; v. Neue, Formenl. 1, p. 383), f. from same root with mater, q. v., stuff, matter, materials of which any thing is composed; so the wood of a tree, vine, etc., timber for building (opp. lignum, wood for fuel); nutritive matter or substance for food (class.). Lit. In gen.: materia rerum, ex qua et in qua sunt omnia, Cic. N. D. 3, 39, 92; cf. id. Ac. 1, 6, 7: ma

materialis.full: mātĕrĭālis, e, adj. materia, of or belonging to matter, material (post-class.): influxio, Macr. Somn. Scip. 1, 12, 7; 10; Ambros. de Virg. 3, 1, 1.—Hence, adv.: mā-tĕrĭālĭter, according to the occasion (postclass.): in pectore viri iracundia materialiter regnans. Sid. Ep. 8, 11.

materiarius.full: mātĕrĭārĭus, a, um, adj. id., of or belonging to stuff, matter, wood, timber. In gen. (ante-class. and post-Aug.): fabrica, carpentry, Plin. 7, 56, 57, § 198: FABER, a carpenter, Inscr. Grut. 642, 6: NEGOCIATOR, a timber-merchant, Inscr. Orell. 4248. —Also subst.— mātĕrĭārĭus, ii, m. (sc. negotiator), a timber-merchant: si non hos materiarius remoratur, Plaut. Mil. 3, 3, 45: CLAVORVM, a maker of wooden nails, Inscr. Orell. 4164.— In partic.: haeretici materiarii, in eccl. Lat., those who believe

materiatio.full: mātĕrĭātĭo, ōnis, f. materia, woodwork, as beams, rafters, etc., Vitr. 4, 2, 1.

materiatura.full: mātĕrĭātūra, ae, f. id., a working in wood: materiatura fabrilis, carpenter's work, Vitr. 4, 2, 2.

materinus.full: mātĕrīnus, a, um, adj. materia, hard, solid: terra, Cato, R. R. 34, 2 dub.

materio.full: mātĕrĭo (no perf.), ātum, 1, v. a. id., to build of wood (rare but class.): eaque aedificia minime sunt materianda propter incendia, Vitr. 5, 12, 7: aedes male materiatae, of bad wood-work, Cic. Off. 3, 13, 54.

materiola.full: mātĕrĭŏla, ae, f. dim. id., a small matter (post-class.), Tert. Baptism. 17.

materior.full: mātĕrĭor, āri, v. dep. id., to fell or procure wood: erat eo tempore et materiari et frumentari necesse, Caes. B. G. 7, 73 init.

materiosus.full: mātĕrĭōsus, πολύϋλος (multam materiam habens), Gloss. Philox.

materis.full: matĕris or matăris (madăris), is, and matăra, ae, f. Celtic, a Celtic javelin, pike: nonnulli inter carros rotasque mataras ac tragulas subiciebant nostrosque vulnerabant, Caes. B. G. 1, 26, 3: humero matari trajecto, Liv. 7, 24, 3: materis Transalpina, Auct. Her. 4, 32, 43: Galli materibus configunt, Sisenn. ap. Non. 556, 8; id. ib. 9.
materis.short: matĕris or matăris (madăris), is, and matăra, ae, f.

maternus1.full: māternus, a, um, adj. mater, of or belonging to a mother, maternal (class.): sanguis, Enn. ap. Non. 292, 16 (Trag. v. 184 Vahl.): paternus maternusque sanguis, Cic. Rosc. Am. 24, 66: animus, Ter. Heaut. 4, 1, 24: nomen, Cic. Clu. 5, 12: menses, the months of pregnancy, Nemes. Cyn. 19: tempora, time of pregnancy, Ov. M. 3, 312: Caesar cingens maternā tempora myrto, i. e. of Venus, the mother of Æneas, from whom sprang the race of the Cæsars, Verg. G. 1, 28: arma (Aeneae), i. e. which his mother V

maternus2.full: Māternus, i, m., a Roman surname: Curiatius Maternus, Tac. Or. 2.
maternus2.short: Māternus, i, m., a Roman surname: Curiatius Maternus, Tac.

matertera.full: mātertĕra, ae, f. for materitera, mater and an obsol. fem. noun found in neutr. i-terum; cf. al-tera, a second mother, a mother's sister, an aunt by the mother's side: amita est patris soror: matertera est matris soror, Dig. 38, 10, 10, § 4; cf. ib. § 5: mea matertera (anulum gestitavit), Plaut. Curc. 5, 2, 4; Cic. Div. 1, 46, 104; id. de Or. 2, 1, 2; Ov. M. 3, 312: materteram uxorem ducere non licet, Gai. Inst. 1, 62; Mos. et Rom. Leg. Coll. 6, 2, 2.— Esp. Magna, i. e. aviae soror, Dig. 38, 10,

mathematice.full: măthēmătĭcē, ēs, f., v. mathematicus, II. B.

mathematicus.full: măthēmătĭcus, a, um, adj., = μαθηματικός, of or belonging to mathematics, mathematical (class.). Adj.: mathematica nota, Vitr. 1, 1: artes, Plin. 30, 1, 1, § 2: cogitatio, Macr. Somn. Scip. 2, 2: disciplinae, i. e. geometry, arithmetic, astronomy, music, geography, optics, Gell. 1, 9, 6.— Subst. Măthēmătĭcus, i, m. A mathematician, Cic. de Or 1, 3, 10; id. Ac. 2, 36, 116; id. Tusc. 1, 2, 5; Sen. Ep. 88, 26.— An astrologer (post-Aug.): mathematici, genus hominum potentibus infidum, sperantibus fa
mathematicus.short: măthēmătĭcus, a, um, adj., = μαθηματικός, of or belonging to mathematics, mathematical (class.).

mathesis.full: măthēsis, is (with the second syll. short: involvit măthĕsi, Prud. adv. Symm. 2, 893 al.; Sid. Carm. 5, 131), f., = μάθησις (lit., knowledge, science; hence, in partic.). The mathematics, mathesis (late Lat.): quadrifariae mathesis januae, Cassiod. Var. 1, 45; Fulg. Myth. 3, 10.— Astrology: mathesin scire, Spart. Hadr. 16; id. Ael. Vel. 3 fin.; Firm. Math. 1 praef. init.; Prud. adv. Symm. 2, 479.

matho.full: Mătho, ōnis, m., a rich speculator, afterwards a bankrupt, Juv. 1, 32; 7, 129.
matho.short: Mătho, ōnis, m., a rich speculator, afterwards a bankrupt, Juv.

matilica.full: Matilĭca, ae, f., a city in Umbria, the modern Matelica, Front. de Colon. p. 100 Goes.—Hence, Matilĭcātes, ĭum, m., the inhabitants of Matilica, Plin. 3, 14, 19, § 113.
matilica.short: Matilĭca, ae, f., a city in Umbria, the modern Matelica, Front.

matinus.full: Mătīnus, i, m., a mountain or promontory in Apulia, near the foot of Mount Garganus, now Matinata, Luc. 9, 185; Schol. Cruq. ad Hor. C. 1, 28, 3.—Hence, Mă-tīnus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Mount Matinus, Matinian: apis Matinae More, Hor. C. 4, 2, 27: litus, id. ib. 1, 28, 3: cacumina, id. Epod. 16, 28.— Mătīnus, i, m., a mountain in Apulia Daunia, Luc. 9, 185.
matinus.short: Mătīnus, i, m., a mountain or promontory in Apulia, near the foot of Mount Garganus, now Matinata, Luc.

matisco.full: Matisco, ōnis, m., a city of the Æduans, in Gallia Lugdunensis, on the Arar, the modern Maçon, Caes. B. G. 7, 90, 7.
matisco.short: Matisco, ōnis, m., a city of the Æduans, in Gallia Lugdunensis, on the Arar, the modern Maçon, Caes.

matius.full: Mătĭus, a, the name of a Roman gens. So, Cn. Matius, a poet and translator of the Iliad, Gell. 6, 6, 5; 9, 14, 14; Varr. L. L. 7, 5, § 96 Müll.; perh. the same with C. Matius, a friend of Cæsar and Cicero, Cic. Fam. 6, 12, 2; 7, 15; 11, 28; Plin. 12, 2, 6, § 13; Col. 12, 4, 2 al.—Hence, Mătĭā-nus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to a Matius, Matian: mala, a kind of apple, Col. 5, 10, 19; 12, 47, 5; Suet. Dom. 21: poma, Front. de Fer. Als. 3; Minutal, Apic. 4, 3.
matius.short: Mătĭus, a, the name of a Roman gens.

matrae.full: Matrae, ārum, f. (dat. plur. MATRABVS, for Matris, Inscr. Grut. 29, 1), or Matres, more freq. Matronae, the protecting goddesses of a country, city, or place: MATRIS AVGVSTIS D. D., Inscr. Grut. 90, 1; so ib. 2 sq.

matralis.full: mātrālis, e, adj. mater, pertaining to a mother: Matralia festa, Ov. F. 6, 533, or simply Matralia, the festival of Mater Matuta, i. e. Ino, celebrated annually on the 11th of June: Matralia Matris Matutae festa, Paul. ex Fest. p. 125 Müll.: Matralibus id faciunt matronae, Varr. L. L. 5, § 106 Müll.: ite, bonae matres, vestrum Matralia festum, Ov. F. 6, 475: festa Matralia, id. ib. 6, 533.

matresco.full: mātresco, ĕre, v. inch. n. [id.], to become a mother, to become like one's mother (ante-class.): utinam nunc matrescam ingenio, Pac. ap. Non. 137, 7 dub. (Trag. Rel. v. 139 Rib., maturescam): matrescere, μητράζειν, Onomast. Vet.

matricalis.full: mātrīcālis, e, adj. matrix, of or belonging to the womb or matrix (post-class.): herba, App. Herb. 65: vena, Veg. Vet. 1, 10, 7.

matricida.full: mātrĭcīda (scanned matrĭcĭda, Sid. Carm. 5, 291), ae, comm. mater-caedo, a mother's murderer, a matricide (rare but class.): quem scribis certissimum matricidam, Cic. Q. Fr. 1, 2, 2; Nep. Alc. 6, 2: cantavit Oresten matricidam, Suet. Ner. 21.—In tmesi: matrique cida Nero, Aus. de XII. Caes. 35 (al. matrīcīda Nero).

matricidium.full: mātrĭcīdĭum, ĭi, n. matricida, the murder of one's mother, matricide: accusari matricidii, Cic. Inv. 1, 13, 18.

matricula.full: mātrīcŭla, ae, f. dim. matrix, a public register, list, roll (post-class.), Veg. Mil. 1, 26; 2, 2; 5; Cod. Just. 12, 20, 3.

matriculus.full: matricŭlus, i, m., an unknown fish, App. Mag. p. 162.
matriculus.short: matricŭlus, i, m., an unknown fish, App.

matrimonialis.full: mātrĭmōnĭālis, e, adj. matrimonium, of or belonging to marriage, matrimonial (post-class.): tabulae, Firm. Math. 7, 17: lectulus, Quint. Decl. 1, 13.

matrimonium.full: mātrĭmōnĭum, ii, n. mater, wedlock, marriage, matrimony. Lit. (class.): ire in matrimonium, i. e. to be married, Plaut. Trin. 3, 3, 4: in matrimonium dare, opp. in concubinatum, id. ib. 3, 2, 65: alicujus tenere, to be one's spouse: te Q. Metelli matrimonium tenuisse sciebas, Cic. Cael. 14, 34: in matrimonium dare alicui filiam suam, to give in marriage, Caes. B. G. 1, 3: in matrimonium ducere alicujus filiam, to marry, Cic. Clu. 44, 125: in matrimonium petere sibi aliquam, to ask in marriage, S

matrimus.full: mātrimus (the quantity of the i is doubtful), a, um, (collat. form: matrimes ac patrimes dicuntur, quibus matres et patres adhuc vivunt, Paul. ex Fest. p. 126 Müll.), adj. id., that has a mother living: decem ingenui, decem virgines, patrimi omnes matrimique, Liv. 37, 3, 6; Auct. Har. Resp. 11; Tac. H. 4, 53; Macr. S. 1, 6, 13; Lampr. Heliog. 8; Vop. Aur. 19; Gell. 1, 12, 2; cf. patrimus.
matrimus.short: mātrimus (the quantity of the i is doubtful), a, um, (collat.

matrix.full: mātrix, īcis, f. id., a mother in respect to propagation (in lit. signif. not used of women). Lit., a breeding-animal: of breeding-cows, Varr. R. R. 2, 5, 12; of breeding-ewes, Col. 7, 3, 12; of laying-hens, id. 8, 2, 6; 8, 5, 11.— Transf. Of plants, the parent-stem, Suet. Aug. 94.— The womb, matrix (late Lat.): matricis dolor, Veg. Vet. 2, 17, 5; Sen. Contr. 2, 13, 6.— A public register, list, roll: in matricibus beneficiariorum, Tert. Fug. in Persec. 12.— Trop., a source, origin, cause (cf. ma

matrona1.full: mātrōna, ae, f. id., a married woman, wife, matron (whether she was in manu or not; consequently more general in its application than mater familias, which always denoted one who was in manu). In gen.: matronam dictam esse proprie, quae in matrimonium cum viro convenisset, quoad in eo matrimonio maneret, etiamsi liberi nondum nati forent: dictamque esse ita a matris nomine non adepto jam sed cum spe et omine mox adipiscendi: unde ipsum quoque matrimonium dicitur; matrem autem familias appellatam

matrona2.full: Matrŏna, ae, m. (f., Aus. Mos. 462; Sid. Pan. 812), a river in Gaul, now the Marne, Caes. B. G. 1, 1, 2; Amm. 15, 11, 3; Aus. Mos. 462; Sid. Carm. 5, 208.

matronalis.full: mātrōnālis, e, adj. 1. matrona, of or belonging to a married woman or matron, womanly, matronly (not in Cic.): oblitae decoris matronalis, of womanly honor, Liv. 26, 49 fin.: jam illi anilis prudentia, matronalis gravitas erat, Plin. Ep. 5, 16, 2: dignitas, Suet. Tib. 35: habitus, i. e. the stola, Dig. 47, 10, 15: genae, the matron's cheeks, Ov. F. 2, 828: labor, Col. 12 praef. § 7: sedulitas, id. ib. § 8.—Subst.: Mātrōnā-lĭa, ĭum, n., a festival celebrated by matrons in honor of Mars, on the 1s

matronatus.full: mātrōnātus, ūs, m. id., the dress of a matron or lady of rank, App. M. 4, p. 153, 9.

matroum.full: Matrōum, i, n., = Μητρῶον, a false read. for Matrem, Plin. 16, 27, 50, § 115.
matroum.short: Matrōum, i, n., = Μητρῶον, a false read.

matruelis.full: mātrŭēlis, is, m. mater, a mother's brother's son, a cousin-german, first-cousin on the mother's side (cf. patruelis, a father's brother's son; post class.), Dig. 48, 9, 1; Vict. de Orig. Gentis Rom. 13, 8.

matta.full: matta, ae, f., a mat made of rushes, Aug. contr. Faust. 5, 5; Schol. Juv. 5, 8; 6, 117 (also v. l. for lata, Ov. F. 6, 679).
matta.short: matta, ae, f., a mat made of rushes, Aug.

mattarius.full: Mattārĭus, ĭi, m. matta, one who sleeps on a mat (late Lat.), a name applied by the orthodox to a sect of Manichæans: quia in mattis dormiunt, Mattarii appellantur, Aug. contr. Faust. 5, 5; id. de Haeres. 46.

mattea.full: mattĕa (mattўa, mactĕa), ae, f., = ματτύα (v. Varr. L. L. 5, 22, § 112 Müll.), a dainty dish, dainty, delicacy, Suet. Calig. 38; Sen. Contr. 4, 27; Petr. 65: to mattea sola juvat (al. juvant, assuming a collat. form, mattĕum, i, n.), Mart. 10, 59, 4: inter quadrupedes mattea prima lepus, id. 13, 92, 2.

matteola.full: mattĕŏla (matĕŏla, mactĕŏla), ae, f. dim. mattea, a little delicacy, dainty (post class.), Arn. 7, 231.

matthaeus.full: Matthaeus, i, m., = Ματθαῖος, or Mattheus (eu diph.), St. Matthew the evangelist: publicanus, Vulg. Matt. 10, 3: Mattheus, as a dissyl., Prud. Apoth. 982.
matthaeus.short: Matthaeus, i, m., = Ματθαῖος, or Mattheus (eu diph.), St.

mattiacus.full: Mattĭăcus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Mattiacum (the mod. Wiesbaden): Mattiaci fontes, the warm mineral springs of Wiesbaden, Plin. 31, 2, 17, § 20: aquae, Amm. 29, 4, 3: pilae, soap-balls for coloring the hair, Mart. 14, 27: ager, Tac. A. 11, 20. —In plur. subst.: Mattĭăci, ōrum, m., the inhabitants of Mattiacum, Tac. G. 29; id. H. 4, 37.
mattiacus.short: Mattĭăcus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Mattiacum (the mod.

mattici.full: Mattici cognominantur homines malarum magnarum atque oribus late patentibus, Paul. ex Fest. p. 126 Müll. [ματύαι, i. q. γνάθοι, acc. to Hesych.].
mattici.short: Mattici cognominantur homines malarum magnarum atque oribus late patentibus, Paul.

mattiocopa.full: mattĭŏcŏpa, ae, m. ματτύα-κόπτω, prop. a cutter of dainties; hence, a skinflint (late Lat.), Amm. 15, 5, 4.

mattium.full: Mattĭum, ĭi, n., a city of Germany, the capital of the Chatti; acc. to some, Marburg; acc. to others, the town of Maden, near Fritzlar, Tac. A. 1, 56.
mattium.short: Mattĭum, ĭi, n., a city of Germany, the capital of the Chatti;

mattus.full: mattus or matus, a, um, adj. Sanscr. mad, to be drunk; cf. madidus, drunk, intoxicated, Petr. 41 fin.
mattus.short: mattus or matus, a, um, adj.

matula.full: mătŭla, ae, f., a vessel, pot for liquids (ante- and post-class.). In gen.: continentur mundo muliebri specula, matulae, unguenta, vasa unguentaria, Dig. 34, 2, 25, § 10. As a term of abuse, a simpleton, noodle (cf. Engl. colloq., a vessel): numquam ego te tam esse matulam credidi. Quid metuis? Plaut. Pers. 4, 3, 64.—Prov.: Est modus matulae, we should observe moderation, the title of a satire of Varro.— In partic., a chamber-pot, urinal: matula vas urinae, Paul. ex Fest. p. 125 Müll.; Plaut. Mo
matula.short: mătŭla, ae, f., a vessel, pot for liquids (ante- and post-class.).

matura.full: Mātūra, ae, f. maturus, a goddess that presides over the ripening of fruits, Aug. Civ. Dei, 14, 8 (al. Matuta).

maturatio.full: mātūrātĭo, ōnis, f. maturo, a hastening, accelerating, Auct. Her. 3, 2, 3.

maturator.full: mātūrātor, is, m. id., one who urges on, a hastener (late Lat.): itineris inchoati, Ven. Fort. Mauril. 15.

maturefacio.full: mātūrĕfăcĭo, fēci, factum, 3, v. a. maturus-facio, to make ripe, to ripen, mature (post-class.), Theod. Prisc. de Diaeta, 14.

maturesco.full: mātūresco, rŭi, 3, v. inch. n. [maturus], to become ripe, ripen, to come to maturity (class.). Lit., of fruits: cum maturescere frumenta inciperent, Caes. B. G. 6, 29, 4; id. B. C. 3, 49: fructus maturescens, Plin. 16, 26, 44, § 107.— Transf.: partus maturescunt ... novem lunae cursibus, * Cic. N. D. 2, 27, 69: nubilibus maturuit annis, ripened to marriageable years, i. e. a marriageable age, Ov. M. 14, 335: libros opinabar nondum satis maturuisse, Quint. Inst. Ep. ad Tryph. 1: si virtutes ejus

maturitas.full: mātūrĭtas, ātis, f. id.. Ripeness, maturity (class.). Lit.: frugum, Cic. Tusc. 1, 28, 68: neque multum a maturitate aberant (frumenta), Caes. B. C. 1, 48, 5; frumentorum, id. ib. 3, 49 fin.: celerius occidere festinatam maturitatem, an accelerated, precocious maturity, Quint. 6 praef. § 10.— Transf., the full or proper time for any thing, perfection, ripeness, maturity: maturitates gignendi, Cic. N. D. 2, 46, 119: ad maturitatem perducere, Plin. 19, 3, 15, § 44: pervenire, id. 13, 4, 7, § 33: ma

maturo.full: mātūro, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. and n. id.. Act., to make ripe, ripen, to bring to ma turity (class.). Lit., of fruits: uvas, Tib. 1, 4, 19: pomum, Plin. 16, 25, 41, § 102. —Pass.: maturari, to grow ripe, ripen, to come to maturity: frumenta maturantur, Plin. 18, 7, 10, § 60: omnia maturata, ripened, Cic. N. D. 1, 2, 4: uva maturata dulcescit, ripe, id. de Sen. 13, 53.— Transf., to make ripe, to ripen, mature, soften, bring to maturity: vitis alba suppurationes veteres maturat, Plin. 23, 1, 16, § 24

maturus.full: mātūrus, a, um (sup. usually maturissimus; less freq. maturrimus, Tac. A. 12, 65; cf. the adv.), adj. root, Sanscr. ma-, measure, time, whence mane, matutinus; cf.: manus, modus; hence, timely, ready in time, ripe, mature (class.). Lit., of fruits: poma matura et cocta (opp. cruda), Cic. Sen. 19, 71: uva, Verg. E. 10, 36: fruges, id. ib. 3, 80: maturissimae ficus, Col. 12, 17, 2.—With dat.: seges matura messi, ripe for harvesting, Liv. 2, 5.—Neutr. as subst.: quod maturi erat (opp. viride), Liv.

matuta.full: Mātūta, ae, f. root ma- of mane, maturus, q. v.. Matuta, the goddess of the morning or dawn, identical with Aurora, Lucr. 5, 656.— A name of Ino (Gr. Λευκοθέα), called by the Romans also Mater Matuta, Cic. Tusc. 1, 12, 28; id. N. D. 3, 19, 48; Ov. F. 6, 479; 6, 545 sq.: Ino, postquam se praecipitavit, Leucothea, materque Matuta (dicta est), Lact. 1, 21; who had a temple at Rome, Liv. 5, 19; 23; 6, 33; 7, 27; 25, 7; and at Satricum, id. 28, 11.

matutinalis.full: mātūtīnālis, e, adj. matutinus, of or belonging to the morning, early, morning- (post-class.): tempus, Auct. Carm. Phil. 15.

matutine.full: mātūtīnē and mātūtīnō, advv., v. matutinus fin.

matutinus.full: mātūtīnus, a, um, adj. Matuta; cf.: mane, manus, maturus, of or belonging to the morning, morning- (class.): tempora, the morning hours, Cic. Fam. 7, 1, 1: frigora, Hor. S. 2, 6, 45: dies, the morning, Col. 6, 2, 3: equi, i. e. Aurorae, Ov. F. 5, 160: radii, the morning sun, id. M. 1, 62: somni, Mart. 14, 125, 1: harena, i. e. the morning-hunt in the Circus, Ov. M. 11, 26: cliens, who comes early in the morning, Mart. 12, 68, 1: Juppiter, who is saluted early in the morning, id. 4, 8, 12: Aeneas

maurella.full: maurella, ae, f., a plant, otherwise unknown, Macer. Cam. 2, 34.
maurella.short: maurella, ae, f., a plant, otherwise unknown, Macer.

mauretania.full: Maurētānĭa (Maurīt-), ae, f., v. Mauri, C.

mauri.full: Mauri, ōrum, m. (Μαῦροι), the Moors, Mauritanians, the inhabitants of Mauritania: proxime Hispaniam Mauri sunt, Sall. J. 18, 10 sqq.; Plin. 5, 2, 1, § 17; 13, 15, 29, § 91; Liv. 21, 22, 3; Mel. 1, 4, 4.—In sing.: Maurus, i, m., a Moor, Juv. 11, 125; Luc. 4, 678.—Hence, Maurus, a, um, adj., = Μαῦρος, of or belonging to the Moors, Moorish, Mauritanian; also poet. for African: Maurae manus, i. e. Poenorum arma, Ov. F. 6, 213: angues, Hor. C. 3, 10, 18: jacula, id. ib. 1, 22, 2: Oceanus, Juv. 10, 14

mausoleum.full: Mausōlēum, i, v. Mausolus, II. A.

mausolus.full: Mausōlus, i, m., = Μαύσωλος, a king of Caria, husband of Artemisia, Cic. Tusc. 3, 31, 75; Gell. 10, 18, 1 sqq.; Mel. 1, 16, 3. —Hence, Mausōlēus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Mausolus, Mausolean. Lit.: sepulcrum, Prop. 3 (4), 1, 59. or absol.: Mausōlēum (Mēsōlum, Inscr. Orell. 4370), i, n., = Μαυσωλειον, the magnificent tomb erected for Mausolus by his wife Artemisia; it was one of the seven wonders of the world, Plin. 36, 5, 4, § 30; Mel. 1, 16, 3; Gell. 10, 18, 2; Prop. 3 (4), 1, 59. — Tran
mausolus.short: Mausōlus, i, m., = Μαύσωλος, a king of Caria, husband of Artemisia, Cic.

mavors.full: Māvors, vortis, m. from mah, magh, to cut; Gr. μάχη, μάχαιρα, and vor, root of vortere; i. e. the turner of the battle, old and poetic name for Mars (q. v.), the god of war, etc. Prop.: urbs Mavortis, i. e. Rome, Verg. A. 6, 872; 8, 630; 12, 179; Cic. N. D. 2, 26; 3, 24; Luc. 7, 569: Mavors pater, Val. Fl. 6, 178: genitor Mavors, Ov. F. 4, 828: Iliae Mavortisque puer, i. e. Romulus, Hor. C. 4, 8, 23.— Transf., war, battle: civili Mavorte, Aus Idyll. 4, 65.— Hence, Māvortius, a, um, adj., of or b

maxentius.full: Maxentĭus, i, m., a Roman emperor, Eutr. 10; Aur. Vict. Epit. 54.—Hence, Maxentĭānus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to the emperor Maxentius: milites, Lact. Mort. Pers. 44, 3.
maxentius.short: Maxentĭus, i, m., a Roman emperor, Eutr.

maxilla.full: maxilla, ae, f. dim. of a ground-form magsula (whence māla; root mag of μάσσω, to knead; μαγεύς. baker, etc.; cf. axilla, ala, from ago), the jawbone, jaw (postAug.). Lit.: quam litteram (X) etiam e maxillis et taxillis et vexillo ... consuetudo elegans Latini sermonis evellit, Cic. Or. 45, 153: maxillae superiores, Plin. 11, 37, 60, § 159; Suet. Calig. 58; Veg. Vet. 2, 40, 2: maxillam superiorem commovere solam, Amm. 22, 15, 15: cum in maxillis balanatum gausape pectas, you comb the anointed be

maxillaris.full: maxillāris, e, adj. maxilla, of or belonging to the jaw, maxillary (post-Aug.): dentes, the maxillary teeth, grinders, Cels. 6, 9; Plin. 11, 37, 63, § 166; 32, 7, 26, § 80; 32, 10, 50, § 139.

maximitas.full: maxĭmĭtas (maxŭmĭtas), ātis, f. maximus, greatness, magnitude (ante- and post-class.): immanis, Lucr. 2, 498: se in maximitatem producere, Arn. 6, 204.

maza.full: māza, ae, f., = μάζα, frumenty, for feeding dogs, Grat. Cyn. 307.
maza.short: māza, ae, f., = μάζα, frumenty, for feeding dogs, Grat.

mazaca.full: Māzăca, ae, f., = Μάζακα, the chief city of Cappadocia, now Kaisariyeh, Auct. B. Alex. 66, 4; Plin. 6, 3, 3, § 8; Eutr. 7, 6. —Also, Māzăca, ōrum, n., Vitr. 8, 3, 9; Plin. 2, 108, 112, § 244; and Māzăcum, i, n., Plin. 6, 3, 3, § 8.
mazaca.short: Māzăca, ae, f., = Μάζακα, the chief city of Cappadocia, now Kaisariyeh, Auct.

mazaces.full: Māzăces, um, m. A people of Numidia, afterwards called Mazacenses: Mazacum turba, Suet. Ner. 30.—In sing. collect.: Mazax, Luc. 4, 681; Claud. Laud. Stil. 1, 356.— A people near the Palus Mæotis, Plin. 6, 7, 6, § 21.

mazagae.full: Mazagae, ārum, f., a city in India, Curt. 8, 10, 22.
mazagae.short: Mazagae, ārum, f., a city in India, Curt.

mazices.full: Mazĭces, um, m., = Μάζικες, a people of Numidia, the same with Mazaces, q. v., Amm. 29, 25, 21 sqq.
mazices.short: Mazĭces, um, m., = Μάζικες, a people of Numidia, the same with Mazaces, q.

mazonomus.full: māzŏnŏmus, i, m. (acc. to others, māzŏnŏmon, i, n.; the m. form corresponds with the Greek word μαζονομος, sc. κύκλος), a dish, charger, Varr. R. R. 3, 4, 3: deinde secuti Mazonomo pueri magno discerpta ferentes Membra gruis, etc., Hor. S. 2, 8, 86 (cf. Schol. Aug. ad loc.); Nemes. de Aucup. 16.

me.full: me, for mihi, v. ego init.

meabilis.full: mĕābĭlis, e, adj. meo. * Pass., passable, that can be passed through: transitus vel bubus meabilis, Plin. 6, 1, 1, § 2.— * Act., passing through, penetrating: aër per cuncta rerum meabilis, Plin. 2, 5, 4, § 10.

meaculum.full: mĕācŭlum, i, n. id., a course, passage = meatus: vos, superi caelestesque, vestra recensebitis meacula, Mart. Cap. 8, § 813.

meamet.full: mĕāmet, for mea or mea ipsius: culpa, Plaut. Poen. 1, 3, 37.
meamet.short: mĕāmet, for mea or mea ipsius: culpa, Plaut.

meapte.full: meapte, for mea or mea ipsius: causa, Ter. Heaut. 4, 3, 8.
meapte.short: meapte, for mea or mea ipsius: causa, Ter.

meatim.full: mĕātim, adv. meus, in my manner, analog. to tuatim, after thy manner; acc. to Prisc. p. 949 P.; Donat. p. 1759 P.

meator.full: mĕātor, ōris, m. meo, a passenger, traveller, wanderer: DOLE MEATOR QVISQVIS HOC LEGIS CARMEN, Inscr. ap. Guarin. in Prosod. Lat. Fundam. p. 133: INTERPRES DIVVM COELI TERRAEQVE MEATOR, of Mercury, as the messenger of the gods, Inscr. Orell. 1417.

meatus.full: mĕātus, ūs, m. id., a going, passing, motion, course (poet. and post-Aug.). Lit.: solis lunaeque meatus, Lucr. 1, 128: caeli, Verg. A. 6, 850: aquilae, flight, Tac. H. 1, 62: spiritus, i. e. the breathing, respiration, Quint. 7, 10, 10: animae, Plin. Ep. 6 16, 13. — Transf., concr., a way, path, passage, Val. Fl. 3, 403: meatum vomiticnibus praeparare, Plin. 19, 5, 26, § 85: spirandi, id. 28, 13, 55, § 197: cur signa meatus Deseruere suos, left their paths, i. e. became darkened, eclipsed, Luc.

mechanema.full: mēchănēma, ătis, n., = μηχάνημα, a piece of mechanism, a trick (post-class.), Sid. Ep. 1, 9.
mechanema.short: mēchănēma, ătis, n., = μηχάνημα, a piece of mechanism, a trick (post-class.), Sid.

mechanicus.full: mēchănĭcus, a, um, adj., = μηχανικός, of or belonging to mechanics, mechanical (ante-class. and post-Aug.). Adj.: disciplina, Gell. 10, 12: opera, Lampr. Alex. Sev. 2, 2: ars, Firm. Math. 6, 31.— Subst. mēchănĭcus, i, m., a mechanic, Lucil. ap. Fest. s. v. petauristas, p. 206 Müll.: sipho, quem diabeten vocant mechanici, Col. 3, 10, 2; Suet. Vesp. 18.— mē-chănĭca, ae, f., mechanics: Cyriades mechanicae professor, Symm. Ep. 10, 38.— mēchănĭca, ōrum, n., works of mechanical art, App. Mag. 61, p. 3
mechanicus.short: mēchănĭcus, a, um, adj., = μηχανικός, of or belonging to mechanics, mechanical (ante-class.

mechanisma.full: mēchănisma, ătis, n., mechanical contrivance, mechanism, for mechanema (post-class.), Cassiod. Var. 1, 45.
mechanisma.short: mēchănisma, ătis, n., mechanical contrivance, mechanism, for mechanema (post-class.), Cassiod.

mechir.full: Mechir, iris, m., the name of an Egyptian month, answering nearly to the Roman January and a part of February, Plin. 6, 23, 26, § 106.
mechir.short: Mechir, iris, m., the name of an Egyptian month, answering nearly to the Roman January and a part of February, Plin.

mecon.full: mēcon, ōnis, f., = μήκων, a sort of poppy: tertium genus est tithymalon, mecona vocant, Plin. 20, 19, 80, § 209; App. Herb. 53; 91.
mecon.short: mēcon, ōnis, f., = μήκων, a sort of poppy: tertium genus est tithymalon, mecona vocant, Plin.

meconis.full: mēcōnis, ĭdis, f., = μηκωνἰς, a kind of lettuce with a milky juice of a soporiferous quality, like the poppy, Plin. 19, 8, 38, § 126; 20, 7, 26, § 67.
meconis.short: mēcōnis, ĭdis, f., = μηκωνἰς, a kind of lettuce with a milky juice of a soporiferous quality, like the poppy, Plin.

meconites.full: mēcōnītes, ae, m., = μηκωνίτης, a precious stone resembling a poppy, otherwise unknown, Plin. 37, 10, 63, § 173.
meconites.short: mēcōnītes, ae, m., = μηκωνίτης, a precious stone resembling a poppy, otherwise unknown, Plin.

meconium.full: mēcōnĭum, ii, n., = μηκώνιον. Poppy-juice, Plin. 20, 18, 76, § 202; 25, 12, 91, § 142.— A plant, called also peplis, Plin. 27, 12, 93, § 119.— The excrements of new-born children, Plin. 28, 4, 13, § 52.

mecum.full: mēcum, i. e. cum me, with me, like tecum, secum, etc., v. ego.

meddix.full: meddix (medix), icis, m. from the root med-, medeor; cf. Homeric μέδοντες, he who cares for, attends to, a curator, the title of a magistrate among the Oscans: meddix apud Oscos nomen magistratūs est. Ennius: summus ibi capitur meddix, occiditur alter, Paul. ex Fest. p. 123 Müll. (Enn. Ann. v. 296 Vahl.).—With the epithet tuticus (which prob. answers to the summus of Ennius, and is allied to totus), joined into one word, meddixtuticus or medixtuticus, Liv. 24, 19, 2; 26, 6, 13: is summus magistr

medea.full: Mēdēa, ae (arch. gen. Medeaï, Enn. ap. Cic. Tusc. 3, 26, 63; v. Enn. p. 127, v. 292 Vahl.; nom. Mēdē, acc. to id. p. 130, v. 311 Vahl.), and Mēdīa, f., = Μήδεια, a celebrated sorceress, daughter of Æetes, king of Colchis. She assisted her lover, Jason the Argonaut, in obtaining the golden fleece, accompanied him to Greece, and prevented her father, who was in pursuit, from overtaking them, by strewing the sea with her brother's limbs. When Jason afterwards repudiated her, in order to marry Creus

medela.full: mĕdēla (mĕdella, Lachm. ad Lucr. p. 204; Schol. Bob. ad Cic. Red. ad Quir. p. 251, 8 Bait.), ae, f. medeor, a healing, cure, a remedy (post-class.). Lit.: facere medelam, Gell. 12, 5, 3: facere medelarum miracula, id. 16, 11, 2: vulneribus medelas adhibere, App. M. 8, p. 210, 4.— Trop., a remedy, means of redress: legum, Gell. 20, 1, 22; Aus. Prof. 15: quibus rebus veluti medela adventus Alexandri fuit, Just. 11, 1, 7.

medeon.full: Medĕon, ōnis, m., = Μεδεών. A city in Dalmatia, Liv. 44, 23.— A city in Bœotia, Plin. 4, 7, 12, § 26.

medeor.full: mĕdĕor, 2, v. dep. n. [root madh, to be wise; Zend, madha, the healing art; cf. μάθος, also medicus, re-med-ium], to heal, cure, be good for or against a disease (syn.: medico, sano, curo); constr. with dat., rarely with contra, very rarely with acc. (class.). Lit. Of pers. subjects: medico non solum morbus ejus, cui mederi volet, cognoscendus est, Cic. de Or. 2, 44, 186.—Prov.: cum capiti mederi debeam, reduviam curo, i. e. to neglect matters of importance while attending to trifles, Cic. Rosc.

medi.full: Mēdi, ōrum, m., = Μῆδοι, the Medes; poet. also for the Assyrians, Persians, Parthians, Mel. 1, 2, 5; Cic. Off. 2, 12, 41; Hor. C. 1, 2, 51; 2, 16, 6; Luc. 8, 386; Pers. 3, 53.—In sing.: Medusque et Indus, Hor. C. 4, 14, 42: pervigil, Val. Fl. 5, 604.—Hence, Mēdus, a, um, adj., Median, Assyrian, etc.: Hydaspes, Verg. G. 4, 211: acinaces, Hor. C. 1, 27, 5: sagittae, Prop. 3, 10 (4, 11), 11: flumen, i. e. doubtless the Euphrates, the most famous river of the remote East; though some understand it t
medi.short: Mēdi, ōrum, m., = Μῆδοι, the Medes;

medialis1.full: mĕdĭālis, e, adj. medius, middle; subst.: mĕdĭāle, is, n., the middle (late Lat.), Sol. 20, 9 al.

medialis2.full: mĕdĭālis, e, adj.: medialem appellabant hostiam atram, quam meridie immolabant, Paul. ex Fest. p. 124 Müll.; cf. meridies init.
medialis2.short: mĕdĭālis, e, adj.: medialem appellabant hostiam atram, quam meridie immolabant, Paul.

mediamna.full: Mĕdĭamna, ae, f. medius-amnis, = Μεσοποταμία, Mesopotamia, Prisc. 1097 P.

medians.full: mĕdĭans, antis, P. a., v. medio.

medianus.full: mĕdĭānus, a, um, adj. medius, that is in the middle, middle (except Vitr., only post-class.): columnae, Vitr. 3, 2, 6: acroteria, id. 3, 5, 12: capita leonina, id. 3, 5, 15: digitus, Veg. Vet. 2, 40, 3: filius, Hier. Ep. 73, 3: porta, Inscr. Fabr. 463, 95.— Subst.: mĕdĭānum, i, n., the middle part, the middle: ex mediano coenaculi, Dig. 9, 3, 5, § 2.—Plur.: mediana malvarum, Apic. 4, 2, 133.

mediastinus.full: mĕdĭastīnus, i, m. id., a common servant, drudge, employed in all kinds of menial occupations (class.): tu illi mediastinus, Cato ap. Non. 143, 9: atque bubulcus, Lucil. ib. 7: exercitus collectus ex senibus desperatis, ex agresti luxuria, ex rusticis mediastinis, decoctoribus, Cic. Cat. 2, 3, 5 (dub.): tu mediastinus tacitā prece rura petebas, Hor. Ep. 1, 14, 14; Col. 2, 13, 7; 1, 9, 3: Prodicus instituens quam vocant iatralepticen, reunctoribus quoque medicorum, ac mediastinis vectigal invenit

mediatenus.full: mĕdĭātĕnus, adv. mediā tenus, like hactenus, as far as the middle, half way over, Mart. Cap. 6, § 683; 8, § 873 init.

mediator.full: mĕdĭātor, ōris, m. medius, a mediator (post-class., esp. in eccl. Lat.): tot mediatorum praesentia, App. M. 9, 36, p. 202: mediator unius non est, Vulg. Gal. 3, 20; cf. v. 19; id. Heb. 8, 6: mediator advenit, id est Deus in carne, Lact. 4, 25; Tert. Carn. 15; id. Resurr. 51 al.; Aug. Conf. 10, 42, 2 sq.

mediatrix.full: mĕdĭātrix, icis, f. mediator, a mediatrix (post-class.), Alcim. Avit. 5, 565.

medibile.full: mĕdĭbĭle, medicabile, Paul. ex Fest. p. 123, 21 Müll.

medica1.full: Mēdĭca, ae, f., = Μηδική [Media], an excellent kind of clover introduced from Media; Burgundy-clover, lucern (Medicago sativa), Verg. G. 1, 215; Plin. 18, 16, 43, § 144; Varr. R. R. 1, 42.
medica1.short: Mēdĭca, ae, f., = Μηδική [Media], an excellent kind of clover introduced from Media;

medica2.full: mĕdĭca, ae, a female physician; v 1. medicus, II. B.

medicabilis.full: mĕdĭcābĭlis, e, adj. medicor. Pass., that can be healed or cured, curable (poet. and not ante-Aug.): nullis amor est medicabilis herbis, Ov. M. 1, 523; id. H. 5, 149: vulnus, Sil. 10, 416.— Act., healing, curative, medicinal (post-Aug.): sucus, Col. 7, 10, 8: mel, Pall. Jan. 15, 19: carmen, soothing, Val. Fl. 4, 87.—Hence, adv.: mĕ-dĭcābĭlĭter, medicinally (post-class.), Pall. Febr. 31, 2.

medicabulum.full: mĕdĭcābŭlum, i, n. id., a healthy place (post-class.): aegris medicabula, App Flor. p. 353, 6.

medicamen.full: mĕdĭcāmen, ĭnis, n. id., a drug, medicament, in a good and a bad sense, meaning both a healing substance, remedy, medicine, and, as also medicamentum and the Gr. φάρμακον, a poisonous drug, poison (mostly poet. and in post-Aug. prose; only once in Cic.; cf., on the contrary, medicamentum). Lit., a remedy, antidote, medicine: violentis medicaminibus curari, * Cic. Pis. 6, 13: agrestia medicamina adhibent, Tac. A. 12, 51: facies medicaminibus interstincta, plasters, id. ib. 4, 57: medicamen habend

medicamentarius.full: mĕdĭcāmentārĭus, a, um, adj. medicamentum, of or belonging to drugs or to poisons; only subst. mĕdĭcāmen-tārĭus, ii, m. A druggist, apothecary, Plin. 19, 6, 33, § 110.— A preparer of poisons: homicida vel medicamentarius, Cod. Th. 3, 16, 1.— mĕdĭcāmentā-rĭa, ae, f., a female mixer of poisons: moecha vel medicamentaria, Cod. Th. 3, 16, 1.— The art of preparing drugs, pharmacy: medicamentaria a Chirone (reperta), Plin. 7, 56, 57, § 196.

medicamentosus.full: mĕdĭcāmentōsus, a, um, adj. id., that has a healing power, medicinal (perh. only ἅπαξ εἰρημ.; in Cato, R. R. 157, 2 dub.; al. medicamento): aqua, Vitr. 8, 3, 4.

medicamentum.full: mĕdĭcāmentum, i, n. medicor, a drug, remedy, physic, medicine, medicament. Lit.: medicamentum alicui dare ad aquam intercutem, Cic. Off. 3, 24, 92: haurire, Plin. 24, 19, 113, § 174: sumere, to take, Curt. 3, 6, 3: componere, to compound, Plin. 32, 9, 34, § 106: somnificum, id. 37, 10, 57, § 158: medicamenta salubria, Liv. 8, 18: salutaria, Cic. N. D. 2, 53, 132.—Also of remedies applied externally: medicamentis delibutus, Cic. Brut. 60, 217.— Transf., like the Gr. φάρμακον, a drug, a potion. A

medicatio.full: mĕdĭcātĭo, ōnis, f. id., lit., a healing, cure; hence, in agriculture, a besprinkling with vegetable juices, e. g., of lentils, to preserve them from the corn-worm, Col. 2, 10, 16.

medicator.full: mĕdĭcātor, ōris, m. id., a physician (post-class.): annunciari Christum medicatorem, Tert. adv. Marc. 3, 17; Avien. Arat. 216.

medicatus1.full: mĕdĭcātus, a, um, Part. and P. a., v. medico.

medicatus2.full: mĕdĭcātus, ūs, m. medicor, a charm (poet.), Ov. H. 12, 165.

medicinalis.full: mĕdĭcīnālis, e, adj. medicina, of or pertaining to medicine, medical, medicinal (not ante-Aug.): ars, Cels. praef.: cucurbitulae, cupping-glasses, Plin. 32, 10, 42, § 123: mortarium, id. 36, 22, 43, § 157: scalprum, Scrib. Compos. 53: digitus, the next to the little finger, Macr. S. 7, 13.

medicinus.full: mĕdĭcīnus, a, um, adj. 1. medicus, of or belonging to a physician or surgeon, medical (as adj. only ante- and post-class.; as subst. class.). Adj.: ars, the healing art, medicine, Varr. L. L. 5, § 93 Müll.; Hyg. Fab. 274; Aug. Conf. 4, 3.— Subst.: mĕdĭcīna, ae, f. (Sc. ars.) The healing or medical art, medicine, surgery: ut medicina (ars est) valetudinis, Cic. Fin. 5, 6, 16; id. Off. 1, 42, 151: medicina, quae ex observatione salubrium atque his contrariorum reperta est, Quint. 2, 17, 9: tertiam

medico.full: mĕdĭco, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. 1. medicus, to heal, cure (poet. and in post-Aug. prose for the class. medeor). Lit. With acc.: ego istum lepide medicabo metum, Plaut. Most. 2, 1, 40: (apes) odore galbani, Col. 9, 13, 7: vulneris aestus, Sil. 6, 98: furores, Nemes. Ecl. 2, 28.— With dat.: tremulis membris, Ser. Samm. 48, 902.— Transf. To impart the virtue of a remedy, give healing power to: hoc fusum labris splendentibus amnem Inficit, occulte medicans, Verg. A. 12, 418.— To besprinkle with the juic

medicor.full: mĕdĭcor, ātus, 1, v. dep. a. [id.], to heal, cure. Lit. (poet. and in post-Aug. prose). With dat.: senibus medicantur anhelis, Verg. G. 2, 135.— With acc.: cuspidis ictum, Verg. A. 7, 756.— Trop., to cure, relieve (ante-class.): cum ego possim in hac re medicari mihi, Ter. And. 5, 4, 41: alicui, id. ib. 5, 1, 12: ego istum lepide medicabor metum, Plaut. Most. 2, 1, 40 Weise (Lorenz, medicabo).

medicosus.full: mĕdĭcōsus, a, um, adj. id., healing (post-class.): fomentationes, Cael. Aur. Tard. 2, 1.

medicus1.full: mĕdĭcus, a, um medeor, of or pertaining to healing, healing, curative, medical (as adj., poet. and in post-Aug. prose). Adj.: medicas adhibere manus ad vulnera, Verg. G. 3, 455: ars, Ov. Tr. 5, 6, 12: potus, Nemes. Cyn. 222: vis, Plin. 36, 27, 69, § 202: salubritas, id. 5, 16, 15, § 72: usus, id. 22, 25, 81, § 163: digitus, the next to the little finger (cf. medicinalis), id. 30, 12, 34, § 108. —* Transf., magical: Marmaridae, medicum vulgus, ad quorum tactum mites jacuere cerastae, Sil. 3, 300.
medicus1.short: mĕdĭcus, a, um medeor, of or pertaining to healing, healing, curative, medical (as adj., poet.

medicus2.full: Mēdĭcus, a, um, v. Medi, II. B.

medietas.full: mĕdĭĕtas, ātis, f. medius, the middle, place in the middle, midst (in Cic. only as transl. of the Gr. μεσότης; elsewhere postclass.). Lit.: vix audeo dicere medietates, quas Graeci μεσότητας appellant, Cic. Univ. 7, 20: narium, Lact. 10, 19: totius loci, App. M. 2, p. 116, 6: sic feliciore loco medietatis est positus (sc. homo), App. Asclep. 6, p. 79: in mediatate distinctis aquis, Tert. de Bapt. 3.— Transf., a half, moiety (syn. dimidium): decoquere aliquid usque ad medietatem, Pall. Mart. 10,

medilunius.full: mĕdĭlūnĭus, a, um, adj. mediusluna, in the middle of the month, having half a disk, half-orbed (post-class): (luna) primo est corniculata, deinde medilunia, Mart. Cap. 7, § 738.

medimnum.full: mĕdimnum, i, n., and mĕdim-nus, i, m., = μέδιμνος, a Greek measure of corn, a Greek bushel (containing six modii): primus, secundus, tertius medimnus, Lucil. ap. Non. 213, 21; so in masc. form, Nep. Att. 2 fin.: medimnum tritici seritur, Cic. Verr. 2, 3, 47, § 112: ut quot jugera sunt sata, totidem medimna decumae debeantur, id. ib. 2, 3, 47, § 113; in gen. plur.: medimnūm, id. ib.; so id. ib. 2, 3, 37, § 84; 2, 3, 39, § 90; Varr. ap. Non. 495, 32 (cf. Neue, Formenl. 1, p. 107).
medimnum.short: mĕdimnum, i, n., and mĕdim-nus, i, m., = μέδιμνος, a Greek measure of corn, a Greek bushel (containing six modii): primus, secundus, tertius medimnus, Lucil.

medio.full: mĕdĭo, 1, v. a. medius, to halve, divide in the middle (post-class.), Apic. 3, 9. — Neutr., to be in the middle: melius Juno mediante, Pall. Mart. 10, 32.

mediocriculus.full: mĕdĭō^crĭcŭlus, a, um, adj. dim. [mediocris], rather middling: exercitus, Cato ap. Fest. p. 154, and Paul. ex Fest. p. 155 Müll.

mediocris.full: mĕdĭō^cris, e (ō usually; rarely ŏ), adj. medius, in a middle state between too much and too little, middling, moderate, tolerable, ordinary; sometimes also, not remarkable, indifferent, mediocre. In gen. (class.). Lit., of size, quantity, degree, etc., in material things: castellum, Sall. J. 92, 5: spatium, Caes. B. G. 5, 43: agmen, Hirt. B. G. 8, 9: intervallum, id. B. Alex. 30.— Of mind, character, ability, acts, achievements, etc.: C. L. Memmii fuerunt oratores mediocres, Cic. Brut. 36, 136:

mediocritas.full: mĕdĭō^crĭtas, ātis, f. mediocris. A middle state, a medium, mean; moderateness, moderation (class.): mediocritatem illam tenere, quae est inter nimium et parum, Cic. Off. 1, 25, 89; 1, 39, 140: in dicendo, mediocrity, id. de Or. 1, 25, 117: dicendi, id. Brut. 66, 235: vultus, i. e. a medium between excessive gayety and over-seriousness, Auct. Her. 3, 15, 26: auream quisquis mediocritatem Diligit, Hor. C. 2, 10, 5. —Of style: cum omnis virtus sit mediocritas, Cic. Brut. 40, 149: mediocritatis (ex

mediolanum.full: Mĕdĭōlānum or Mĕdĭōlānĭum, i, n. A city in Gallia Cisalpina, the capital of the Insubres, the mod. Milan. Form Mediolanum, Plin. 3, 17, 21, § 124; Just. 29, 5, 8; Tac. H. 1, 70; Aus. de Clar. Urb. 4, 1. Form Mediolanium, Liv. 5, 34, 9; 34, 46, 1; Suet. Aug. 20.—Hence, Mĕdĭōlā-nensis, e, adj., of or belonging to Milan, Milanese: (ager), Varr. R. R. 1, 8: praeco, Cic. Pis. 26, 62.—In plur.: Mĕdĭōlānen-ses, ĭum, m., the Milanese, Varr. R. R. 1, 8, 2. — The chief city of the Santoni in Gaul, on the

mediomatrici.full: Mĕdĭōmātrĭci, ōrum, m., a people of Gaul, on the Moselle, in the neighborhood of Metz, Caes. B. G. 4, 10.—Hence, Mĕdĭ-ōmātrĭcus, a, um, adj.—In sing., Inscr. Grut. 731, 12; and in fem., Inscr. Orell. 3523.
mediomatrici.short: Mĕdĭōmātrĭci, ōrum, m., a people of Gaul, on the Moselle, in the neighborhood of Metz, Caes.

medion1.full: mēdĭon, ii, n., = μήδιον, a medicinal plant, Plin. 27, 12, 79, § 104.
medion1.short: mēdĭon, ii, n., = μήδιον, a medicinal plant, Plin.

medion2.full: Mĕdĭon, ōnis, f., a city of Acarnania, Liv. 36, 11, 10; 36, 12, 1; 44, 23, 3.— Hence, Mĕdĭōnĭus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Medion.—Plur. subst.: Mĕ-dĭōnii, ōrum, m., the inhabitants of Medion, Liv. 36, 12, 3.
medion2.short: Mĕdĭon, ōnis, f., a city of Acarnania, Liv.

medioximus.full: mĕdĭoxĭmus (mĕdĭoxŭmus), a, um, adj. superlative of an obsolete mediox for medius. In the middle, middlemost: medio actum modo, Non. 141, 4: medioximus, μέσος, Gloss. Philox. (anteand post-class.): medioxumam quam duxit uxorem, Plaut. Cist. 2, 3, 67: ita me di deaeque superi atque inferi et medioxumi, i. e. holding a middle place between the supernal and infernal deities, id. ib. 2, 1, 35: tertium habent (deorum genus), quos medioximos Romani veteres appellant, quod et sui ratione et loco et pot

medipontus.full: medipontus, i, m., a kind of thick rope (ante-class.): medipontos privos loreos (al. melipontos), Cato, R. R. 3, 5; 12.
medipontus.short: medipontus, i, m., a kind of thick rope (ante-class.): medipontos privos loreos (al.

meditabundus.full: mĕdĭtābundus, a, um, adj. meditor, earnestly meditating, designing; with acc. (post-class.): Romanum meditabundus bellum, Just. 38, 3, 7.

meditamen.full: mĕdĭtāmen, ĭnis, n. id., a thinking of any thing, a preparation (poet.): meditamina belli, Sil. 8, 326: rerum, Prud. Psych. 234.

meditamentum.full: mĕdĭtāmentum, i, n. id., a thinking of any thing, a preparation. In gen.: belli, Tac. H. 4, 26; id. A. 15, 35: arietum meditamenta, thoughtfully prepared battering-rams, Amm. 23, 4, 10.— * In partic.; plur.: puerilia, rudiments taught to children at school, Gell. 8, 10 in lemm.

meditatio.full: mĕdĭtātĭo, ōnis, f. meditor, a thinking over any thing, contemplation, meditation (class.). Lit. (very rare): stultam esse meditationem futuri mali, aut fortasse ne futuri quidem, Cic. Tusc. 3, 15, 32. — Transf. Preparation for any thing (so most freq.): multa commentatio atque meditatio, Cic. de Or. 2, 27, 118; obeundi sui muneris, id. Phil. 9, 1, 2: meditatio atque exercitatio, id. Div. 2, 46, 96: nulla meditationis suspicio, id. Brut. 37, 139: mortis, Sen. Ep. 54, 2: campestris, Plin. Pan. 13

meditatiuncula.full: mĕdĭtātĭuncŭlā, ae, f. dim. of meditatio, a small or trifling preparation, Claud. Mam. de Stat. Anim. 1, 3.

meditativus.full: mĕdĭtātīvus, a, um, adj. meditor, meditative (post-class.): meditativa verba, which signify a desire to perform an action, also called desiderativa (as lecturio, etc.), Diom. p. 336 P.; Prisc. 825 ib.

meditator.full: mĕdĭtātor, ōris, m. id., one who thinks or plans, a meditator (post-class.): meditator (al. meditatus), Prud. στεφ. 5, 265.

meditatorium.full: mĕdĭtātōrĭum, ii, n. meditator. A preparation (eccl. Lat.): meditatorium Evangelii, Hier. Ep. 78.— A place of preparation, Hier. in Jovin. 2, 12.

meditatus1.full: mĕdĭtātus, a, um, Part. and P. a., from meditor, q. v.

meditatus2.full: mĕdĭtātus, ūs, m. meditor, a thinking, meditating upon any thing, a meditation, i. q. meditatio (post-class.), App. M. 3, p. 135, 31.

mediterraneus.full: mĕdĭ-terrānĕus, a, um, adj. mediusterra, midland, inland, remote from the sea, mediterranean (opp. to maritimus). Adj. (class.): nascitur ibi plumbum album in mediterraneis regionibus, in maritimis ferrum, Caes. B. G. 5, 12, 5: locus (opp. maritimus), Quint. 5, 10, 37: homines maxime mediterranei, Cic. Verr. 2, 5, 27, § 70: Enna mediterranea est maxime, id. ib. 2, 3, 83, § 191: commercium, Plin. 5, 10, 11, § 63: jurisdictiones, id. 5, 28, 29, § 105: copiae, Plin. Ep. 2, 17, 28.— Esp., in late La

mediterreus.full: mĕdĭterrĕus, a, um id., inland, remote from the sea, another form of the preceding word: mediterream melius quam mediterraneam Sisenna dici putat, Paul. ex Fest. p. 123, 22 Müll.
mediterreus.short: mĕdĭterrĕus, a, um id., inland, remote from the sea, another form of the preceding word: mediterream melius quam mediterraneam Sisenna dici putat, Paul.

meditor.full: mĕdĭtor, ātus, 1, v. dep. a. and n. Sanscr. madh-a, wisdom; Gr. μάθος, μανθάνω, μήδομαι; cf.: medeor, re-med-ium, etc.; act., to think or reflect upon, to muse over, consider, meditate upon; neutr., to think, reflect, muse, consider, meditate; to design, purpose, intend, etc.; constr. with acc., with ad, de, with dat., with inf., with a rel.-clause, or absol. (class.). Lit. With acc.: semulque cursuram meditabor ad ludos Olympios, Plaut. Stich. 2, 1, 34: ea para, meditare, cogita, quae, etc., Ci

meditrina.full: Mĕdĭtrīna, ae, f. medeor, with fem. suffix -tri-, as in nutrix, genetrix; v. Corss. Ausspr. 2, 522, the goddess of Healing; v. the foll. art.

meditrinalia.full: Mĕdĭtrīnālĭa, ĭum, n. Meditrina, a festival celebrated on the 11th of October in honor of Meditrina (on which occasion a libation of new wine was made for the first time): Octobri mense Meditrinalia dies dictus a medendo, quod Flaccus flamen Martialis dicebat, hoc die solitum vinum novum et vetus libari et degustari medicamenti causā: quod facere solent etiam nunc multi cum dicant: Novum vetus vinum libo: novo veteri vino morbo medeor, Varr. L. L. 6, § 21 Müll.: Meditrinalia dicta hac de causa.

meditullium.full: mĕdĭtullĭum, ii, n. medius and tollus, old form of tellus, q. v., the middle (ante- and post-class.): in finitimo, legitimo, aeditimo non plus inesse timum, quam in meditullio, tullium, Serv. ap. Cic. Top. 8, 36: in ipso meditullio scenae, App. M. 10, p. 254, 30: medio luci meditullio, id. ib. 5, p. 159: indifferentia ... nec bona nec mala sed velut in meditullio posita, Sen. ap. Hier. adv. Jovin. 1, p. 191 (Fragm. 45 Haas); Hier. Gal. 5, 19 sqq.; Jul. Val. Rer. Gest. Alex. 1, 32: virtutes in me

medius1.full: mĕdĭus, a, um, adj. Sanscr. madhya, the same; Gr. μέσος; Angl. - Sax. midd; Germ. Mitte; cf. dimidius, meridies (medi-), etc., that is in the middle or midst, mid, middle (class.). Adj. Lit.: terra complexa medium mundi locum, Cic. Rep. 6, 18, 18; cf. id. ib. 6, 17, 17: medium mundi locum petere, id. Tusc. 5, 24, 69: versus aeque prima, et media, et extrema pars attenditur, id. de Or. 3, 50, 192: ultimum, proximum, medium tempus, id. Prov. Cons. 18, 43: in foro medio, in the midst of the forum,

medius2.full: mĕdĭus fĭdĭus and mĕdĭusfĭdĭ-us, v. Fidius.

medobrega.full: Medobrēga (Medubrīga, Mun-dobrīga), ae, f., a city in Lusitania, now Portalegre, Auct. B. Alex. 48, 4.—Hence, Medubrīgenses, ĭum, m., the inhabitants of Medobrega, Auct. B. Alex. 48; Plin. 4, 22, 35, § 118; al. Medubricenses.—Also written † MEIDVBRIGENSES, Inscr. Orell. 162.
medobrega.short: Medobrēga (Medubrīga, Mun-dobrīga), ae, f., a city in Lusitania, now Portalegre, Auct.

medon.full: Mĕdon, ontis, m., = Μέδων. A Centaur, Ov. M. 12, 303.— Son of Codrus, king of Athens, the first archon; hence, Mĕdontĭdae, ārum, m., his descendants, Vell. 1, 2, 2.— One of Penelope's suitors; acc. Medonta, Sabin. Ep. 1, 47.

meduli.full: Mĕdŭli, ōrum, m., a people in Aquitanian Gaul, whose coast was famous for its oysters, in the mod. Medoc, Aus. Ep. 4, 2; 7, 1.—Hence, Mĕdŭlus or Mĕdŭ-lĭus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to the Meduli, Medulian, Plin. 32, 6, 21, § 62.— Mĕdŭlĭcus, a, um, adj., Medulian: supellex, i. e. oysters, Sid. Ep. 8, 12.
meduli.short: Mĕdŭli, ōrum, m., a people in Aquitanian Gaul, whose coast was famous for its oysters, in the mod.

medulla.full: mĕdulla, ae, f. medius, the marrow of bones; the pith of plants (class.). Lit., Hor. Epod. 5, 37: cumque albis ossa medullis, Ov. M. 14, 208: ossa regum vacuis exsucta medullis, Juv. 8, 90: per media foramina a cerebro medullā descendente, Plin. 11, 37, 67, § 178.— Transf., the pith, inside, kernel: vitis medullā, Col. 3, 18, 5; Plin. 16, 25, 42, § 103: frumenta, quae salsā aquā sparsa moluntur, candidiorem medullam reddunt, i. e. meal, flour, Plin. 18, 9, 20, § 87: medulla ventris, the inside,

medullaris.full: mĕdullāris, e, adj. medulla, situated in the marrow or inmost part (post-class.): dolor, App. M. 7, p. 193, 26.

medullatus.full: mĕdullātus, a, um, adj. id., possessed of marrow, marrowy; hence, rich, fat, abounding in richness (post-class.): convivium pinguium medullatorum, Vulg. Isa. 25, 6; cf. id. ib. 34, 6.

medulli.full: Mĕdulli, ōrum, m., an Alpine people in Sabaudia, Inscr. ap. Plin. 3, 20, 24, § 137; Vitr. 8, 3, 20.—Hence, Mĕdullīnus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to the Medulli, Medullian: Medullini te feret aura noti, i. e. Alpine wind, Aus. Ep. 5, 27.
medulli.short: Mĕdulli, ōrum, m., an Alpine people in Sabaudia, Inscr.

medullia.full: Medullĭa, ae, f., or Medullum, i, n., a little town in Latium, near the modern Monte Verde, Liv. 1, 33, 4; Plin. 3, 5, 9, § 68. —Hence, Medullīnus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Medullia, Medullian; as subst. Mĕdullīnus, i, m., a Roman surname; e. g. L. Furius Medullinus, Liv. 4, 25, 5.— Mĕdullīna, ae, f.: Livia Medullina, Suet. Claud. 26; Juv. 6, 322.—In plur. subst.: Medullīni, ōrum, m., inhabitants of Medullia, Inscr. Orell. 535.
medullia.short: Medullĭa, ae, f., or Medullum, i, n., a little town in Latium, near the modern Monte Verde, Liv.

medullinus.full: Medullīnus, a, um, adj. From Medulli.— From Medullia.

medullitus.full: mĕdullĭtus, adv. medulla, in the marrow, to the very marrow, in the inmost part (ante- and post-class.). Lit.: medullitus aquiloniam intus servat frigedinem, Varr. ap. Non. 139, 9.— Trop., inwardly, from the heart, thoroughly: qui mortalibus Versus propinas flammeos medullitus, Enn. ap. Non. 33, 7, and 139, 14 (Sat. v. 7 Vahl.): ut videas eam medullitus me amare, heartily, in one's inmost soul, Plaut. Most. 1, 3, 86: ostendit sese jam mihi medullitus, id. Truc. 2, 4, 85: gemens, Amm. 14, 1, 9: d

medullo.full: mĕdullo, 1, v. a. id., to fill with marrow (post-class.): cura nimia medullatos artus magni facit, App. Dogm. Plat. 2, 16, p. 21, 13: quando ossa incipiunt medullari, Aug. Anim. 4, 5; Ven. Carm. 3, 7 fin.

medullosus.full: mĕdullōsus, a, um, adj. id., full of marrow, marrowy (post-Aug.): umerus, Cels. 8, 1, 102 sq.

medullula.full: mĕdullŭla, ae, f. dim. id., marrow: anseris, Cat. 25, 2.

medullus.full: Medullus, i, m., a mountain in Hispania Tarraconensis, Flor. 4, 12, 50; Oros. 6, 21.
medullus.short: Medullus, i, m., a mountain in Hispania Tarraconensis, Flor.

medulus.full: Mĕdŭlus, a, um, adj., v. Meduli.

medus1.full: Mēdus, a, um, v. Medi, II. A.

medus2.full: Mēdus, i, m., son of Ægeus and Medea; the title of a tragedy of Pacuvius, Cic. Off. 1, 31, 114.
medus2.short: Mēdus, i, m., son of Ægeus and Medea;

medus3.full: Mēdus, i, m., = Μῆδος, a small river of Persia, a tributary of the Araxes, now the Polwar, Curt. 5, 4, 7; v. also Medi.
medus3.short: Mēdus, i, m., = Μῆδος, a small river of Persia, a tributary of the Araxes, now the Polwar, Curt.

medusa.full: Mĕdūsa, ae, f., = Μέδουσα, daughter of Phorcus; she captivated Neptune with her golden hair, and became by him the mother of Pegasus. Minerva, as a punishment, turned her hair into serpents, and gave to her eyes an enchanted power of converting everything they looked upon to stone. Perseus, provided with the shield of Pallas, slew her, and carried off her head, while from the blood that dropped from it serpents sprung, Ov. M. 4, 654; 793; Luc. 9, 626.—Hence, Mĕdūsaeus, a, um, adj., of or belongi
medusa.short: Mĕdūsa, ae, f., = Μέδουσα, daughter of Phorcus;

megabocchus.full: Mĕgăbocchus and -boccus, i, m. —Caius, a prætor in Sardinia, Cic. Scaur. § 40; id. Att. 2, 7, 3 Orell.

megabyzus.full: Mĕgăbyzus, i, m., = Μεγάβυζος. A priest of Diana at Ephesus, Plin. 35, 10, 36, § 93.— One of Darius's generals, Just. 7, 3, 7.— The name of a Persian eunuch, Quint. 5, 12, 21.

megaera.full: Mĕgaera, ae, f., = Μέγαιρα. One of the Furies, Verg. A. 12, 846; Claud. Rapt. Pros. 3, 387.— Transf., a fury: Megaera quaedam mortalis, Amm. 14, 1, 2.

megale.full: Mĕgălē, ēs, f., = Μεγάλη (the great, exalted), a surname of the Magna Mater, Calend. Verrii Fl. in Inscr. Orell. 2, p. 389; v. the foll.— Derivv. Mĕgă-lensis (Mĕgălēsis), e, adj. Of or belonging to the Magna Mater (only postAug.): ludorum Megalesium spectaculum, Tac. A. 3, 6 fin.: ludis Megalensibus, Gell. 2, 24, 1: Megalensibus sacris, Plin. 7, 37, 37, § 123.— Of or belonging to the Megalesia, Megalesian: Megalensis purpura, i. e. the festival dress of the prætor worn at the Megalesia, Mart. 10
megale.short: Mĕgălē, ēs, f., = Μεγάλη (the great, exalted), a surname of the Magna Mater, Calend.

megalensia.full: Mĕgălensĭa or Mĕgălēsĭa, ĭum, and Mĕgălensis, v. Megale, II. A.
megalensia.short: Mĕgălensĭa or Mĕgălēsĭa, ĭum, and Mĕgălensis, v.

megalesiacus.full: Mĕgălēsĭăcus, a, um, v. Megale, II. B.

megalia.full: Mĕgālĭa, ae, f., a small island of Campania, the modern Castel dell' Ovo, Stat. S. 2, 2, 80; called also Megaris, Plin. 3, 6, 12, § 82.
megalia.short: Mĕgālĭa, ae, f., a small island of Campania, the modern Castel dell' Ovo, Stat.

megalium.full: mĕgălīum (mĕgallīum), ii, n., = μεγάλειον, a kind of ointment: postea multo successit propter gloriam appellatum megalium, ex oleo balanino, balsamo, calamo, junco, xylobalsamo, casia, resina, Plin. 13, 1, 2, § 13.
megalium.short: mĕgălīum (mĕgallīum), ii, n., = μεγάλειον, a kind of ointment: postea multo successit propter gloriam appellatum megalium, ex oleo balanino, balsamo, calamo, junco, xylobalsamo, casia, resina, Plin.

megalographia.full: mĕgălŏgrăphĭa, ae, f., = μεγαλογραφία, the painting of large or grand subjects (opp. ῥυπαρογραφία, the painting of small subjects), Vitr. 7, 4, 4; 7, 5, 2.
megalographia.short: mĕgălŏgrăphĭa, ae, f., = μεγαλογραφία, the painting of large or grand subjects (opp.

megalobusus.full: Mĕgălŏbūsus (-byzus), i, m., = Μεγαλόβυζος, the father of Theotimus, Plaut. Bacch. 2, 3, 74.
megalobusus.short: Mĕgălŏbūsus (-byzus), i, m., = Μεγαλόβυζος, the father of Theotimus, Plaut.

megalopolis.full: Mĕgălŏpŏlis, is, f., or Mĕgălē pŏ-lis (acc. Mĕgălēn pŏlin), f., = Μεγαλόπολις or Μεγάλη πόλις, a city of Arcadia, the birthplace of Polybius.—Form Megalopolis, Liv. 36, 31, 6; 45, 28, 4.—Form Megale polis, Plin. 4, 6, 10, § 20; Liv. 32, 5, 5; 35, 36, 10.—Hence, Mĕgălŏpŏlītae, ārum, m., the inhabitants of Megalopolis, Liv. 28, 8.— Mĕgălŏpŏlītānus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Megalopolis, Megalopolitan, Liv. 36, 13.—Subst.: Mĕ-gălŏpŏlītāni, ōrum, m., the inhabitants of Megalopolis, Liv. 32, 22
megalopolis.short: Mĕgălŏpŏlis, is, f., or Mĕgălē pŏ-lis (acc.

megapenthes.full: Mĕgăpenthes, is, m., = Μεγαπένθης, a son of Prœtus, Hyg. Fab. 244.
megapenthes.short: Mĕgăpenthes, is, m., = Μεγαπένθης, a son of Prœtus, Hyg.

megara1.full: Mĕgăra, ae, m., a Numantine, Flor. 2, 18, 4.
megara1.short: Mĕgăra, ae, m., a Numantine, Flor.

megara2.full: Mĕgăra, ae, f., and Mĕgăra, ōrum, n. (abl. plur. Megaribus for Megaris, Plaut. Pers. 1, 3, 57), = τὰ Μέγαρα. A city in the country of Megaris, the birthplace of Euclid. Fem., Cic. Div. 1, 27, 57; Mart. 11, 43, 6.— Neutr., Plaut. Merc. 3, 4, 60; Liv. 28, 7, 16.— Mĕgă-ra, ae, f., a city of Sicily, Liv. 24, 30 sq.; Sil. 14, 273; Serv. ad Verg. E. 1, 55; v. Megaris, II.
megara2.short: Mĕgăra, ae, f., and Mĕgăra, ōrum, n.

megara3.full: Mĕgăra, ae, f., wife of Hercules, whom, in his madness, he destroyed, together with her children, Hyg. Fab. 31.
megara3.short: Mĕgăra, ae, f., wife of Hercules, whom, in his madness, he destroyed, together with her children, Hyg.

megareius1.full: Mĕgărēĭus, a, um, adj. 2. Megara, of or belonging to the city of Megara, Megareian (poet.): arva, Stat. Th. 12, 219.

megareius2.full: Mĕgărēĭus, a, um, adj., v. 2. Megareus.

megarensis.full: Mĕgărensis, e, adj. 2. Megara, of or belonging to the city of Megara: Nicias, of Megara, Plin. 7, 56, 57, § 196: homines Gell. 6, 10, 3.

megareus1.full: Mĕgărēus (quadrisyl.), a, um, adj. = Μεγαρεῖος, of or belonging to the city of Megara (in Megaris), Megarean (class.): Euclides Socratis discipulus, Megareus, Cic. Ac. 2, 42, 129.

megarea.full: Mĕgărēa, ōrum, n. plur., for Megara (a city of Sicily), or for Megarensia, sc. arva, Ov. F. 4, 471.

megareus2.full: Mĕgăreus (trisyl.), i, m., = Μεγαρεύς, a son of Neptune, and father of Hippomenes, Hyg. Fab. 157 and 185; Ov. M. 10, 605.—Hence, Mĕgărēĭus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Megareus, Megareian (poet.): heros, i. e. Hippomenes, Ov. M. 10, 659.
megareus2.short: Mĕgăreus (trisyl.), i, m., = Μεγαρεύς, a son of Neptune, and father of Hippomenes, Hyg.

megaricus.full: Mĕgărĭcus, a, um, adj., = Μεγαρικός, of or belonging to the city of Megara, Megaric: ager, Plin. 17, 7, 4, § 42: Megaricus sinus, a part of the Saronic Gulf, near Megara, id. 4, 12, 19, § 57: signa, i. e. of marble from Megara, Cic. Att. 1, 8, 2; 1, 9, 2.— Mĕgărĭci, ōrum, m., sc. philosophi, the followers of Euclid, Cic. Ac. 2, 42, 129.
megaricus.short: Mĕgărĭcus, a, um, adj., = Μεγαρικός, of or belonging to the city of Megara, Megaric: ager, Plin.

megaris.full: Mĕgăris, ĭdis, f., = Μεγαρίς. A country of Greece, between Attica and Phocis, Mel. 2, 3, 4; Plin. 4, 7, 11, § 23.— A city of Sicily, also called Megara, Cic. Verr. 2, 5, 25, § 63; Plin. 3, 8, 14, § 89.

megarus.full: Mĕgărus, a, um, adj. 2. Megara, of or belonging to the city of Megara, Megarean (poet.): sinus, Verg. A. 3, 689.

megas.full: Mĕgas, ae, m., = μέγας, a surname; e. g. Demetrius Megas, Cic. Fam. 13, 36, 1.
megas.short: Mĕgas, ae, m., = μέγας, a surname;

meges.full: Mĕges, ētis, m., = Μέγης, son of Phyleus, one of Helen's suitors, Hyg. Fab. 97.
meges.short: Mĕges, ētis, m., = Μέγης, son of Phyleus, one of Helen's suitors, Hyg.

megistanes.full: mĕgistānes, um, m., = μεγιστᾶνες the grandees of a kingdom, the magnates who were in the king's suite, Sen. Ep. 21, 4; Tac. A. 15, 27; Suet. Calig. 5.
megistanes.short: mĕgistānes, um, m., = μεγιστᾶνες the grandees of a kingdom, the magnates who were in the king's suite, Sen.

megiste.full: Mĕgistē, ēs, f., = Μεγίστη, a Roman name given to slaves, Inscr. Fabr. p. 189, n. 433.
megiste.short: Mĕgistē, ēs, f., = Μεγίστη, a Roman name given to slaves, Inscr.

megisto.full: Mĕgistō, ūs, or ōnis, f., = Μεγιστώ, daughter of Ceteus, Hyg. Astr. 2, 1.
megisto.short: Mĕgistō, ūs, or ōnis, f., = Μεγιστώ, daughter of Ceteus, Hyg.

mehe.full: mehe, for me, v. ego init.

mehercle.full: mehercle, mehercŭle, and me-hercŭles, v. Hercules.

meio.full: mēio, ĕre, v. n. for migio, kindred with Sanscr. mih, effundere; whence also mingo; cf. Gr. ὀμιχέω, ὀμίχλη, to make water: sacer est locus, extra Meiite, Pers. 1, 114: HOSPES AD HVNC TVMVLVM NE MEIAS, Inscr. Orell. 4781: mala meiens, Cat. 97, 8; cf. Juv. 1, 131. —Transf., of a vessel, Mart. 12, 32, 13.—In a double sense: ditior aut formae melioris meiat eodem, Hor. S. 2, 7, 52.—Prov.: caldum meiere et frigidum potare, i. e. to give more than one receives, Petr. 67, 10.

mel.full: mĕl, mellis (abl. sing. melli, Plaut. Truc. 2, 4, 20.—Gen. and dat. plur. obsol. acc. to Prisc. p. 744 P.), n. Gr. μέλι, honey; μέλισσα, bee; cf. mulsus, honey. Lit.: hoc est melli dulci dulcius, Plaut. Truc. 2, 4, 20 (Spengel, dulce): villa abundat lacte, caseo, melle, Cic. Sen. 16, 56; cf. Plin. 11, 14, 14, § 33: roscida mella, Verg. E. 4, 30: mellis vindemia, Col. 9, 15, 1.— Trop., honey for sweetness, pleasantness: poëtica mella, Hor. Ep. 1, 19, 44: hoc juvat et melli est, is pleasant, id. S

mela.full: Mĕla, ae, m. prob. from μέλας, a Roman proper name, Cic. Phil. 13, 2, 3: Pomponius Mela, a Roman geographer, a native of Spain, under the emperor Claudius; v. Teuffel, Röm. Litt. § 291.

melae.full: Melae, ārum, f., a town in the Samnite country, Liv. 24, 20; called also Meles, ĭum, Liv. 27, 1.
melae.short: Melae, ārum, f., a town in the Samnite country, Liv.

melambium.full: Melambĭum, i, n., a place in Thessaly, near Scotussa, Liv. 33, 6.
melambium.short: Melambĭum, i, n., a place in Thessaly, near Scotussa, Liv.

melamphyllon.full: mĕlamphyllon, i, n., = μελάμφυλλον, a plant, also called acanthus and paederos, Plin. 22, 22, 34, § 76.
melamphyllon.short: mĕlamphyllon, i, n., = μελάμφυλλον, a plant, also called acanthus and paederos, Plin.

melampodion.full: mĕlampŏdĭon, ii, n., = μελαμπόδιον, black hellebore, Plin. 25, 5, 21, § 47.
melampodion.short: mĕlampŏdĭon, ii, n., = μελαμπόδιον, black hellebore, Plin.

melampsythium.full: mĕlampsythĭum, ii, n., = μελαμψύθιον, black raisin-wine, Plin. 14, 9, 11, § 80.
melampsythium.short: mĕlampsythĭum, ii, n., = μελαμψύθιον, black raisin-wine, Plin.

melampus.full: Mĕlampūs, pŏdis, m., = Μελάμπους. Son of Amythāon, a celebrated physician and soothsayer, Cic. Leg. 2, 13, 33; Verg. G. 3, 550; Stat. Th. 3, 452.— Son of Atreus, Cic. N. D. 3, 21, 53.— Name of a dog, Ov. M. 3, 206.

melanaetos.full: mĕlănăĕtos, i, f., = μελανάετος, the black eagle; a small species of eagle, Plin. 10, 3, 3, § 6.
melanaetos.short: mĕlănăĕtos, i, f., = μελανάετος, the black eagle;

melanchaetes.full: Mĕlanchaetes, ae, m., = Μελαγχαίτης, black-hair, the name of a dog, Ov. M. 3, 232.
melanchaetes.short: Mĕlanchaetes, ae, m., = Μελαγχαίτης, black-hair, the name of a dog, Ov.

melancholia.full: mĕlanchŏlĭa, ae, f., = μελαγχολία, melancholy, Cael. Aur. Acut. 3, 12, 108.
melancholia.short: mĕlanchŏlĭa, ae, f., = μελαγχολία, melancholy, Cael.

melancholicus.full: mĕlanchŏlĭcus, a, um, adj., = μελαγχολικός, having black bile, atrabilious, melancholy: Aristoteles quidem ait, omnes ingeniosos melancholicos esse, Cic. Tusc. 1, 33, 80; cf. id. Div. 1, 37, 81: insania, Plin. 22, 25, 64, § 133: vertigines, id. 27, 12, 105, § 130.
melancholicus.short: mĕlanchŏlĭcus, a, um, adj., = μελαγχολικός, having black bile, atrabilious, melancholy: Aristoteles quidem ait, omnes ingeniosos melancholicos esse, Cic.

melancoryphos.full: mĕlancŏrўphos, i, m., = μελαγκόρυφος (having a black crown), the black cap, the name of a kind of snipe, Plin. 10, 29, 44, § 86: genus avium, quae Latine vocantur atricapillae, eo, quod summa eorum capita nigra sunt, Paul. ex Fest. p. 124, 15 Müll.; Plin. 10, 29, 44, § 86.
melancoryphos.short: mĕlancŏrўphos, i, m., = μελαγκόρυφος (having a black crown), the black cap, the name of a kind of snipe, Plin.

melancranis.full: mĕlancrānis, is, f., = μελάγκρανις (black-head), a kind of rush with black seeds, Plin. 21, 18, 69, § 112.
melancranis.short: mĕlancrānis, is, f., = μελάγκρανις (black-head), a kind of rush with black seeds, Plin.

melandryum.full: mĕlandrўum, i, n., = μελάνδρυον, a piece of salted tunny-fish: ceterā parte plenis pulpamentis sale asservantur melandrya vocantur, caesis quercus assulis simillima, i. e. like the black heart of oak, Plin. 9, 15, 18, § 48; Mart. 3, 77, 7; Varr. L. L. 5, 12, § 77 Müll.
melandryum.short: mĕlandrўum, i, n., = μελάνδρυον, a piece of salted tunny-fish: ceterā parte plenis pulpamentis sale asservantur melandrya vocantur, caesis quercus assulis simillima, i.

melaneus.full: Mĕlăneus (trisyl.), i, m., = Μελανεύς. Name of a Centaur, Ov. M. 12, 306.— Name of a dog, Ov. M. 3, 223.

melania.full: mĕlănĭa, ae, f., = μελανία (μέλας, Cels. 5, 28, 19), blackness, black spots, of the skin (post-Aug.), Plin. 24, 8, 29, § 44; 26, 14, 88, § 149 Sillig. (Jan. malandrias).

melanippe.full: Mĕlănippē, ēs, f., = Μελανίππη. Daughter of Desmon or Æolus, the mother by Neptune of Bœotus and Æolus, the founders of Bœotia and Æolia, Hyg. Fab. 186; Varr. R. R. 2, 5, 5.—Acc. plur.: Melanippas, Arn. 4, 26. She was the subject of two tragedies; by Attius, Varr. L. L. 7, 3, § 65 Müll.; Cic. Off. 1, 31, 114; and by Ennius, Gell. 5, 11, 12; cf. Juv. 8, 229.— A sister of Antiope, queen of the Amazons, taken captive by Hercules, Just. 2, 4, 23 sq.

melanius.full: Mĕlănĭus, ii, m., a Roman proper name, Inscr. Mur. 858, 5.
melanius.short: Mĕlănĭus, ii, m., a Roman proper name, Inscr.

melanteria.full: mĕlantērĭa, ae, f. (gen. sing. melanterias), = μελαντηρία, blacking, Scrib. Comp. 208.

melanthemum.full: mĕlanthĕmum, i, n., a reading in Plin. 22, 21, 26, § 53, for melanthion.
melanthemum.short: mĕlanthĕmum, i, n., a reading in Plin.

melanthium.full: mĕlanthĭum (-on), ii, n., = μελάνθιον, the plant gith, cultivated fennel-flower: gith e Graecis alii melanthion, alii melaspermon, vocant, Plin. 20, 17, 71, § 182; Col. poët. 10, 245; also chamomile, Plin. 22, 21, 26, § 53.—Called also mĕlanthum, Ser. Samm. 30.
melanthium.short: mĕlanthĭum (-on), ii, n., = μελάνθιον, the plant gith, cultivated fennel-flower: gith e Graecis alii melanthion, alii melaspermon, vocant, Plin.

melanthius.full: Mĕlanthĭus, ii, m., = Μελάνθιος. A goatherd of Ulysses, Ov. H. 1, 95.— A celebrated painter, Plin. 35, 7, 32, § 50; 35, 10, 36, § 76.

melantho.full: Mĕlanthō, ūs, f., = Μελανθώ, a seanymph, daughter of Neptune, Ov. M. 6, 120; cf. Serv. ad Verg. A. 5, 373.
melantho.short: Mĕlanthō, ūs, f., = Μελανθώ, a seanymph, daughter of Neptune, Ov.

melanthum.full: mĕlanthum, i, n., v. melanthium fin.

melanthus.full: Mĕlanthus, i, m., = Μέλανθος. A river in Sarmatia, Ov. P. 4, 10, 54.— One of the seamen whom Bacchus changed into dolphins, Ov. M. 3, 617.— The father of the Athenian king Codrus, Vell. 1, 2, 1.— Hence, Mĕlanthēus (quadrisyl.), a, um, adj., of or belonging to a Melanthus: caedes, Ov. Ib. 625.

melantias.full: Melantĭas, ădis, f., = Μελαντιάς, a town of Thrace, between the Propontis and the Pontus Euxinus, Amm. 30, 11, 1.
melantias.short: Melantĭas, ădis, f., = Μελαντιάς, a town of Thrace, between the Propontis and the Pontus Euxinus, Amm.

melanurus.full: mĕlănūrus, i, m., = μελάνουρος (black-tail), a kind of sea-fish, Enn. ap. App. Mag. p. 299 (Heduph. v. 7 Vahl.); Ov. Hal. 113; Col. 8, 16, 8; Plin. 32, 2, 8, § 17; 32, 11, 53, § 149.
melanurus.short: mĕlănūrus, i, m., = μελάνουρος (black-tail), a kind of sea-fish, Enn.

melapium.full: mēlăpĭum, ii, n., = μηλάπιον, an apple-pear, a kind of apple resembling a pear (al. melapia, melappia), Plin. 15, 14, 15, § 51.
melapium.short: mēlăpĭum, ii, n., = μηλάπιον, an apple-pear, a kind of apple resembling a pear (al.

melas1.full: Mĕlas, ănis and ae, m., = Μέλας (black). The name of several rivers. A river of Bœotia, now Mavropotami, Plin. 2, 103, 106, § 230; Sen. Q. N. 3, 25, 3; Stat. Th. 7, 273.— A river of Thrace, now Kavatch, Liv. 38, 40, 5; Mela, 2, 2, 8; Ov. M. 2, 274; Plin. 4, 11, 18, § 43.— A river of Sicily, now Nocito: sacrorumque Melan pascua laeta boum, Ov. F. 4, 476.— A river of Cappadocia, now Jochmah Su, Plin. 6, 4, 4, § 11.— A river of Cilicia, Plin. 5, 27, 22, § 93.— A son of Phryxus, Hyg. Fab. 3.— One of
melas1.short: Mĕlas, ănis and ae, m., = Μέλας (black).

melas2.full: mĕlas, ănos, = μέλας, a black spot on the skin, Cels. 5, 28, 18; cf. melania.
melas2.short: mĕlas, ănos, = μέλας, a black spot on the skin, Cels.

melaspermon.full: mĕlaspermon, i, n., = μελάνσπερμον, the plant gith, cultivated fennel-flower (v. melanthium), Plin. 20, 17, 71, § 182.
melaspermon.short: mĕlaspermon, i, n., = μελάνσπερμον, the plant gith, cultivated fennel-flower (v.

melculum.full: melcŭlum, i, n., and melcŭlus, i, m. dim. mel; v. melliculus, a term of endearment, = melliculum, Plaut. ap. Prisc. p. 610 P. (where some read melliculum); applied to a male person, in the voc. melcule: vale mel gentium, melcule, ebur ex Etruria, laser Aretinum, etc., Aug. ap. Macr. S. 2, 4 med.—Also, v. l. for melliculum, Plaut. Cas. 4, 4, 16 and 23.
melculum.short: melcŭlum, i, n., and melcŭlus, i, m.

meldi.full: Meldi, ōrum, m., a people of Gallia Celtica, between the Seine and Marne; their chief town answered to the modern Meaux, Caes. B. G. 5, 5; Plin. 4, 18, 32, § 107.
meldi.short: Meldi, ōrum, m., a people of Gallia Celtica, between the Seine and Marne;

mele.full: mĕlē, Gr. plur. of melos, v. 1. melos.

meleager.full: Mĕlĕăger and Mĕlĕăgros (-ag-rus), gri, m., = Μελέαγρος, son of the Calydonian king Œneus and Althæa, one of the combatants at the Calydonian boar-hunt. His life depended on the preservation of an extinguished brand; this his mother burned, out of revenge for the death of her brothers who had fallen by his hand, and he expired, Ov. M. 8, 299 sq.; id. H. 9, 151; Val. Fl. 1, 435; Hyg. Fab. 171 sq.; Serv. Verg. A. 7, 306.—Hence, Mĕlĕāgrēus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Meleager, Luc. 6, 365.— Mĕl
meleager.short: Mĕlĕăger and Mĕlĕăgros (-ag-rus), gri, m., = Μελέαγρος, son of the Calydonian king Œneus and Althæa, one of the combatants at the Calydonian boar-hunt.

meleagris.full: mĕlĕāgris, ĭdis, f., v. Meleager, B. 2.

meles1.full: mēles (maeles) and mēlis (mae-lis), is, f., a marten or badger, Varr. R. R. 3, 12, 3; Plin. 8, 38, 58, § 138; Grat. Cyneg. 340.
meles1.short: mēles (maeles) and mēlis (mae-lis), is, f., a marten or badger, Varr.

meles2.full: Mĕles, ētis, m., Μέλης, a river in Ionia, near Smyrna, on the banks of which, it is said, Homer was born, Plin. 5, 29, 31, § 118; Stat. S. 2, 7, 33; 3, 3, 60.—Hence, Mĕlētēus, a, um, adj., Meletean, poet. for Homeric: chartae, Tib. 4, 1, 200.— Mĕ-lētīnus, a, um, adj., Meletine: deae, dwelling at Meles, Ov. F. 4, 236.
meles2.short: Mĕles, ētis, m., Μέλης, a river in Ionia, near Smyrna, on the banks of which, it is said, Homer was born, Plin.

meles3.full: Mĕles, ium, f. plur., a village in the Samnite territory, Liv. 27, 1, 1.

melessi.full: Melessi, ōrum, m., a people in Hispania Baetica, Liv. 28, 3.
melessi.short: Melessi, ōrum, m., a people in Hispania Baetica, Liv.

melete.full: Mĕlĕtē, ēs, f., = Μελέτη. One of the Muses, Cic. N. D. 3, 21, 54.— A Roman surname: PORCIA MELETE, Inscr. Grut. 357, 7.— The name of a plant, called also chamaeleon, App. Herb. 25.

meletides.full: Meletīdes, ae, m., a foolish Athenian, App. Mag. p. 289, 26.
meletides.short: Meletīdes, ae, m., a foolish Athenian, App.

meliboea.full: Mĕlĭboea, ae, f., = Μελίβοια, a maritime town of Thessaly, at the foot of Mount Ossa, the birthplace of Philoctetes, now Kastri, Mel. 2, 3; Plin. 4, 7, 16, § 32; Liv. 36, 13, 6; 44, 13.—Hence, Derivv. Mĕlĭboeus, a, um, adj., Melibœan: purpura, Lucr. 2, 500; Verg. A. 5, 251.— Mĕlĭboeensis, e, adj., of or belonging to Melibœa, Serv. ad Verg. A. 5, 251.
meliboea.short: Mĕlĭboea, ae, f., = Μελίβοια, a maritime town of Thessaly, at the foot of Mount Ossa, the birthplace of Philoctetes, now Kastri, Mel.

meliboeus1.full: Mĕlĭboeus, i, m., = Μελίβοιος, name of a shepherd, Verg. E. 1, 6.
meliboeus1.short: Mĕlĭboeus, i, m., = Μελίβοιος, name of a shepherd, Verg.

meliboeus2.full: Mĕlĭboeus, a, um, v. Meliboea, II. A.

melica.full: mēlĭca, ae, f., perh. a kind of vessel (ante-class.), Varr. ap. Non. 545, 4; 12 and 23.

meliceris.full: mĕlĭcēris, ĭdis, f., = μελικηρίς, a kind of tumor, meliceris (the yellow matter of which looks like honey): melilotos contra meliceridas efficax, Plin. 21, 20, 87, § 151.—In sing., Veg. Vet. 2, 30 (in Cels. 5, 26, 20, called μελίκηρα).
meliceris.short: mĕlĭcēris, ĭdis, f., = μελικηρίς, a kind of tumor, meliceris (the yellow matter of which looks like honey): melilotos contra meliceridas efficax, Plin.

melicerta.full: Mĕlĭcerta and Mĕlĭcertes, ae, m., = Μελικέρτης, son of Ino and the Theban king Athamas. His mother, pursued by her husband in his madness, threw herself into the sea with Melicerta, who became a seagod, called by the Greeks Palaemon, and by the Romans Portunus, Ov. M. 4, 522; cf. Verg.
