G. 1, 437; Ov. F. 6, 485 sq.; Pers. 5, 103.
melicerta.short: Mĕlĭcerta and Mĕlĭcertes, ae, m., = Μελικέρτης, son of Ino and the Theban king Athamas.

melichloros.full: mĕlichlōros, i, m., = μελίχλωρος, a precious stone yellow as honey, Plin. 37, 11, 73, § 191.
melichloros.short: mĕlichlōros, i, m., = μελίχλωρος, a precious stone yellow as honey, Plin.

melichros.full: mĕlichros, ōtos, m., = μελίχρως, a precious stone of the color of honey, Plin. 37, 11, 73, § 191.
melichros.short: mĕlichros, ōtos, m., = μελίχρως, a precious stone of the color of honey, Plin.

melichrysos.full: mĕlĭchrȳsos, i, m., = μελίχρυσος, gold-colored chrysolite, Plin. 37, 9, 45, § 128.
melichrysos.short: mĕlĭchrȳsos, i, m., = μελίχρυσος, gold-colored chrysolite, Plin.

melicratum.full: mĕlicrātum, i, n., = μελίκρατον, water-mead, Veg. Vet. 3, 15, 22.
melicratum.short: mĕlicrātum, i, n., = μελίκρατον, water-mead, Veg.

melicus1.full: mĕlĭcus, a, um, adj., = μελικός, musical, tuneful, melodious: sonores, Lucr. 5, 334.— In partic., lyric, lyrical: poëma, Cic. Opt. Gen. Or. 1, 1.— Subst.: mĕlĭcus, i, m., a lyric poet: Simonides melicus, Plin. 7, 24, 24, § 89; 7, 56, 57, § 192.— mĕlĭca, ae, f., a lyric poem, ode, Petr. 64.
melicus1.short: mĕlĭcus, a, um, adj., = μελικός, musical, tuneful, melodious: sonores, Lucr.

melicus2.full: Mēlĭcus, a, um, adj., in vulg. lang. for Medicus, Median: gallinae, Varr. R. R. 3, 9, 19; Col. 8, 2, 4; Plin. 10, 21, 24, § 48.
melicus2.short: Mēlĭcus, a, um, adj., in vulg.

melie.full: Mĕlĭē, ēs, or Mĕlĭa, ae, f., = Μελία. A sea-nymph: Hestiaea, Melie, Ianthe, Hyg. Fab. praef.— A Bithynian nymph, beloved by the river-god Inachus, Ov. Am. 3, 6, 25.
melie.short: Mĕlĭē, ēs, or Mĕlĭa, ae, f., = Μελία.

melilotos.full: mĕlĭlōtos, i, f., = μελίλωτος, a kind of clover, melilot, also called sertula Campana: pars meliloton amant, Ov. F. 4, 440; cf. Plin. 21, 11, 37, § 63; 21, 7, 18, § 39.
melilotos.short: mĕlĭlōtos, i, f., = μελίλωτος, a kind of clover, melilot, also called sertula Campana: pars meliloton amant, Ov.

melimela.full: mĕlĭmēla, ōrum, n. plur., = μελίμηλα, honey-apples, previously called mustapples (mustea mala): quae antea mustea vocabant, nunc melimela appellant, Varr. R. R. 1, 59; cf.: mustea a celeritate mitescendi, quae nunc melimela dicuntur a sapore melleo, Plin. 15, 14, 15, § 51; Col. 5, 10 fin.; 12, 45; Hor. S. 2, 8, 31; Mart. 7, 25, 7. —In sing.: melimelum a dulcedine appellatum, quod fructus ejus mellis saporem habeat, vel quod in melle servetur, unde et quidam (Mart. 13, 24, 1) Si tibi Cecropio sat

melinus1.full: mēlīnus, a, um, adj. 1. meles, of or belonging to the marten; only subst. (sc. crumena): mēlīna, ae, f., a purse or wallet of marten-skin, Plaut. Ep. 1, 1, 20.

melinus2.full: mĕlĭnus, a, um, adj. mel, of or belonging to honey, honey-; only subst.: mĕlĭna, ae, f., mead: melinam promere, Plaut. Ps. 2, 4, 51 (al. mellinam); id. Ep. 1, 1, 21 (al. mellina).

melinus3.full: mēlĭnus, a, um, adj., = μήλινος, of or belonging to quinces, quince-; quinceyellow; only as subst.: mēlĭnum, i, n. (Sc. oleum.) Quince-oil, Plin. 13, 1, 2, § 11; 23, 6, 54, § 103.— (Sc. unguentum.) Quince-ointment, Plin. 13, 1, 2, § 5.— An eye-salve, Inscr. Tochōn, Cachets des Ocul. p. 61.— (Sc. vestimentum.) A quince-yellow garment, Plaut. Ep. 2, 2, 49.
melinus3.short: mēlĭnus, a, um, adj., = μήλινος, of or belonging to quinces, quince-;

melinus4.full: Mēlĭnus, a, um, adj. Melos, of or belonging to the island of Melos, Melian; subst.: Mēlĭnum, i, n., a kind of white color, Melian white: pigmentum, or simply Melinum, Plaut. Most. 1, 3, 106 Lorenz ad loc.; cf. Plin. 35, 6, 17, § 36; Vitr. 7, 7, 1: alumen, Plin. 35, 15, 52, § 188.

melior.full: mĕlĭor, melĭus cf. μᾶλλον, for μάλιον, v. bonus.

melioratio.full: mĕlĭōrātĭo, ōnis, f. melioro, a bettering, improvement, melioration (post-class.), Cod. Just. 4, 66, 2; 2, 19, 24.

melioresco.full: mĕlĭōresco, ĕre, v. inch. n., to begin to improve, grow better; βελτιοῦμαι, Gloss. Philox.

melioro.full: mĕlĭōro (no perf.), ātum, 1, v. a. melior, to make better, to better, improve (postclass.): meliorare proprietatem, Dig. 7, 1, 13: melioratum praedium, Cod. Just. 5, 71, 16; Cassiod. Var. 9, 3.

melisphyllum.full: mĕlisphyllum and mĕlisso-phyllon, i, n., = μελίφυλλον and μελισσόφυλλον (honey-leaf, bee-leaf), an herb of which bees are fond, balm-gentle, balm (also called apiastrum): trita melis phylla, et cerinthae ignobile gramen, Verg. G. 4, 63; Plin. 20, 11, 45, § 116; 21, 20, 86, § 149.
melisphyllum.short: mĕlisphyllum and mĕlisso-phyllon, i, n., = μελίφυλλον and μελισσόφυλλον (honey-leaf, bee-leaf), an herb of which bees are fond, balm-gentle, balm (also called apiastrum): trita melis phylla, et cerinthae ignobile gramen, Verg.

melissa.full: Mĕlissa, ae, f., = Μέλισσα. A nymph who is said to have invented the art of keeping bees, Col. 9, 2, 3.— Daughter of the Cretan king Melissus, who, together with her sister Amalthea, fed Jupiter with goats' milk, Lact. 1, 22, 19 sq

melissus.full: Mĕlissus, i, m., = Μέλισσος. (Also called Mĕlisseus, = Μελισσεύς.) A king of Crete, father of Melissa and Amalthea, Lact. 1, 22, 19; ib. § 28.— A grammarian and comic poet, librarian to Augustus, Ov. P. 4, 16, 30; cf. Suet. Gram. 21.— A philosopher of Samos, Cic. Ac. 2, 37, 118.

melita.full: Mĕlĭta, ae, or Mĕlĭtē, ēs, f., = Μελίτη. The isle of Malta, Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 46, § 103; Plin. 3, 8, 14, § 92.— An island off the coast of Dalmatia, now Meleda, Plin. 3, 26, 30, § 152; Ov. F. 3, 567.— A city of Ionia, Vitr. 4, 1.— A city of Cappadocia, Plin. 6, 3, 3, § 8.— A seanymph, Verg. A. 5, 825.
melita.short: Mĕlĭta, ae, or Mĕlĭtē, ēs, f., = Μελίτη.

melitaeus.full: Mĕlĭtaeus, a, um, adj., = Μελιταῖος, of or belonging to the Dalmatian island Melita, Melitæan: catuli, Plin. 30, 5, 14, § 43.
melitaeus.short: Mĕlĭtaeus, a, um, adj., = Μελιταῖος, of or belonging to the Dalmatian island Melita, Melitæan: catuli, Plin.

melitanus.full: Mĕlĭtānus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Melita, Melitan, Inscr. Grut. 751, 3.
melitanus.short: Mĕlĭtānus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Melita, Melitan, Inscr.

melitensis.full: Mĕlĭtensis, e, adj. Melita, of or belonging to the isle of Malta, Melitan, Maltese: vestis, Cic. Verr. 2, 2, 72, § 176: rosa, id. ib. 2, 5, 11, § 27.—In plur. subst.: Mĕ-lĭtensia, ĭum (sc. vestimenta), Melitan garments, Cic. Verr. 2, 2, 74, § 183 (but in Lucr. 4, 1130, the correct read. is alidensia).

melitesius.full: Mĕlĭtēsĭus, a, um, adj. id., Melitan, Maltese: Melitesia Coralia (al. Melitensia), Grat. Cyn. 404.

melitinus1.full: mĕlĭtĭnus, a, um, adj., = μελίτινος, of or belonging to honey, mixed with honey (post-class.): cera, Plin. Val. 3, 26.— Lapis, a kind of precious stone, Plin. 36, 19, 33, § 140.
melitinus1.short: mĕlĭtĭnus, a, um, adj., = μελίτινος, of or belonging to honey, mixed with honey (post-class.): cera, Plin.

melitinus2.full: Mĕlĭtīnus, i, a Roman proper name, Inscr. Visc. Opt. Varr. t. 1, p. 182; Inscr. Fabr. p. 45, n. 255.
melitinus2.short: Mĕlĭtīnus, i, a Roman proper name, Inscr.

melitis.full: † mēlītis, a false read. for chalcitis, Plin. 37, 11, 73, § 191.

melitites.full: mĕlĭtītes, ae, m., = μελιτίτης, a honey-drink made of honey and must, Plin. 14, 9, 11, § 85 (but a false read. for melitinus, Plin. 36, 19, 33, § 140).
melitites.short: mĕlĭtītes, ae, m., = μελιτίτης, a honey-drink made of honey and must, Plin.

meliton.full: melĭton, i, n., a kind of wine, Vitr. 8, 3.
meliton.short: melĭton, i, n., a kind of wine, Vitr.

melittaena.full: mĕlittaena (mĕlitaena), ae, f., = μελίτταινα. A plant, also called marrubium, App. Herb. 45.— A plant, also called melissophyllon, Plin. 21, 20, 86, § 149.

melitturgus.full: mĕlitturgus, i, m., = μελιττουργός, a bee-keeper, Varr. R. R. 3, 16, 3.
melitturgus.short: mĕlitturgus, i, m., = μελιττουργός, a bee-keeper, Varr.

melium.full: mēlĭum, ii, n., a dog's collar, v. mellum.
melium.short: mēlĭum, ii, n., a dog's collar, v.

melius1.full: mĕlĭus, comp. adj. and adv., v. bonus.

melius2.full: Mēlĭus, a, um, adj. 2. Melos, of or belonging to the isle of Melos, Melian: Diagoras Melius, dwelling in Melos, Cic. N. D. 1, 1, 2.

meliusculus.full: mĕlĭuscŭlus, a, um, adj. dim. [melius], somewhat better, rather better (anteclass. and post-Aug.).—Of a convalescent: qui meliusculus esse coepit, Cels. 3, 22; Ter. Hec. 3, 2, 19.—Of things: si eris verax, ex tuis rebus feceris meliusculas, Plaut. Capt. 5, 2, 15; cf. v. 6: apes coloris meliusculi, Col. 9, 3, 2: facies, Sen. Ben. 1, 3: spes, rather more, Varr. ap. Non. 394, 10.— In neutr. sing.: meliusculum est monere, Plaut. Curc. 4, 2, 3.—Adv.: mĕlĭuscŭlē. Rather better, pretty well (class.): c

melizomum.full: mĕlizōmum, i, n., = μελίζωμον, honey-sauce, Apic. 1, 2, 2.
melizomum.short: mĕlizōmum, i, n., = μελίζωμον, honey-sauce, Apic.

mella1.full: mella, ae, f. mel, perh. for mellea (sc. aqua), honey-water (post-Aug.), Col. 12, 11, 1; 12, 49, 3.

mella2.full: Mella or Mēla, ae, m., a river in Upper Italy, near Brescia, now Mella, Cat. 67, 33: curva legunt prope flumina Mellae, Verg. G. 4, 278.
mella2.short: Mella or Mēla, ae, m., a river in Upper Italy, near Brescia, now Mella, Cat.

mella3.full: Mella, ae, m., a Roman surname in the gens Annaea, e. g. M. Annaeus Mella, the father of Lucan.
mella3.short: Mella, ae, m., a Roman surname in the gens Annaea, e.

mellaceum.full: mellācĕum, i, n. mel, must (postclass. for sapa): sapa, quod nunc mellaceum dicimus, mustum ad mediam partem decoctum, Non. 551, 21.

mellaria.full: Mellāria, ae, f., a city in Hispania Baetica, Plin. 3, 1, 3, § 7—Hence, Mellā-rĭensis, e, adj., of or belonging to Mellaria; in plur. subst.: Mellārĭenses, ĭum, m., the inhabitants of Mellaria, Inscr. Grut. 321, 10.
mellaria.short: Mellāria, ae, f., a city in Hispania Baetica, Plin.

mellarius.full: mellārĭus, a, um, adj. mel, of or belonging to honey, honey- (post-Aug.): vasa mellaria, Plin. 21, 14, 49, § 82.—Hence, subst. mellārĭus, ii, m., a bee-keeper, beemaster (ante-class.), Varr. R. R. 3, 16, 17.— mellārium, ii, n., a beehive, apiary, Varr. R. R. 3, 16, 12.

mellatio.full: mellātĭo, ōnis, f. mello, a honeying, honey-gathering, taking of honey from the hive, Col. 11, 2, 50: aestiva, Plin. 11, 15, 15, § 41.

melleus.full: mellĕus, a, um, adj. mel, of or belonging to honey, honey- (post-Aug.). Lit.: sapor, Plin. 15, 14, 15, § 51: color, id. 11, 16, 16, § 48: sardonyches, id. 37, 6, 23, § 89: sucus, id. 36, 19, 33, § 140: crustum, Aus. Eph. Parecb. 12.— Transf., honeysweet, delightful, charming (post-class.): moduli, App. M. 6, p. 175, 31: adulatio, Aus. Ep. 18 fin.

melliculus.full: mellĭcŭlus, a, um, adj. dim. [id.], honey-sweet, honeyed: corpusculum melliculum! a coaxing epithet, Plaut. Cas. 4, 4, 23. —Subst.: mellĭcŭlum, i, n., honey-pet, honey-kin. Plaut. Cas. 4, 4, 14.—Collat. form melculum, q. v.

mellifer.full: mellĭfer, fĕra, fĕrum, adj. mel-fero, honey-bearing, honey-producing, melliferous (pcet.): apes, Ov. M. 15, 383: exercitus, Claud. Rapt. Pros. 2, 127.

mellifex.full: mellĭfex, fĭcis, m. mel-facio, i. q. mellarius, 1., a honey-maker, i. e. a keeper of bees: ubicunque saltus idonei sunt mellifici, Col. 9, 8, 8; better referred to mellificus, q. v.

mellificium.full: mellĭfĭcĭum, ii, n. id., the making of honey: ad mellificium aptissimum est thymum, Varr. R. R. 3, 16, 4; Col. 9, 13, 13.

mellifico.full: mellĭfĭco, 1, v. a. mellificus, to make honey (poet and in post-Aug. prose): sic vos non vobis mellificatis apes, Verg. ap Don. Vit. Verg. (but ap. Plin. 11, 18, 19, § 59, mella faciunt; v. Sillig).

mellificus.full: mellĭfĭcus, a, um, adj. mel-facio, honey-making, fit for making honey (postAug.): opus, Col. 9, 13, 14: saltus, id. 9, 8, 8; v. mellifex.

mellifluens.full: melliflŭens, tis, adj. mel-fluo, honey-dropping; trop., mellifluous, of a speaker: Nestor, Aus. Epist. 16, 14.

mellifluus.full: melliflŭus, a, um, adj. id., flowing with honey, honey-dropping (post-class.). Lit.: antra, Avien. Perieg. 468.— Trop., mellifluous: Homerus melliflui oris, Boëth. Metr. 5, 2, 2.

melligenus.full: mellĭgĕnus, a, um, adj., a false read. for melliginis, Plin. 16, 7, 10, § 28.
melligenus.short: mellĭgĕnus, a, um, adj., a false read.

melliger.full: mellĭger, gĕra, gĕrum, adj. mel-gero, honey-bearing (late Lat.), Aldh. Laud. Virgin. 4.

melligerus.full: Mellĭgĕrus, i, m., a Roman surname, Inscr. Mur. 1329, 1.
melligerus.short: Mellĭgĕrus, i, m., a Roman surname, Inscr.

melligo.full: mellīgo, ĭnis, f. mel. A honey-like juice, sucked by the bees from flowers, but not yet made into honey, bee-glue, bees'rosin, hive-dross (post-Aug.), Plin. 11, 6, 5, § 14; 16, 7, 10, § 28.— The juice of unripe grapes: uvae, Plin. 12, 27, 60, § 131.

mellilla.full: mellilla, ae, f. dim. 2. melinus, a term of endearment, little honey, little sweetheart: mea vita, mea mellilla, Plaut. Cas. 1, 1, 47 dub.

mellinia.full: mellĭnĭa, ae, f. mel, sweetness, deliciousness, delight: hoc nimio magnae melliniae mihist, Plaut. Truc. 4, 1, 6 Spengel (al. mellinae).

mellitulus.full: mellītŭlus, a, um, adj. dim. [mellitus], honey-sweet, darling (ante- and post-class.): corpusculum mellitulum! (al. melliculum), Plaut. Cas. 4, 4, 19: puella, Hier. Ep. 79, 6. —Subst.: mellītŭla, ae, f., little honey: mea mellitula, App. M. 3, 139, 3.

mellitus.full: mellītus, a, um, adj. mel, of honey, honey-. Lit.: melliti favi, Varr. R. R. 3, 16, 22: bellaria, id. ap. Gell. 13, 11: absorptio, Suet. Ner. 27.— Sweetened with honey, honey-sweet: placenta, Hor. Ep. 1, 10, 11.— Trop., honey-sweet, darling, lovely: mammillae, Plaut. Ps. 1, 2, 47: Cicero, * Cic. Att. 1, 18, 1: oculi, Cat. 47, 1: passer, id. 3, 6: verborum globuli, Petr. 1.—So in sup.: ubi ubi es mellitissime, Marc. Aur. ap. Front. Ep ad Caes. 4, 5 Mai.; cf.: mellitissimum savium, App. M. 2, 10,

mello.full: mello, 1, v. a. id., to make or collect honey, Pall. 7, 7, 1 dub.

mellona.full: Mellōna, ae, f. id., the goddess of bees and honey, Aug. Civ. Dei, 4, 24.—Called also Mellōnĭa, Arn. 4, 131.

melloproximus.full: Mellŏproxĭmus, i, m., vox hibr. [μέλλω-proximus], one who comes next in rank to the Proximus; v. h. v. under propior, Cod. Th. 6, 26, 16; Cod. Just. 12, 19, 5; 7; 14.

mellosus.full: mellōsus, a, um, adj. mel, of or from honey, honey-, honey-like (post-class. for melleus): mellosa dulcedo, Cael. Aur. Acut. 2, 29, 151.

mellum.full: mellum, i, n., a dog's collar, Varr. R. R. 2, 9, 15 Schneid. N. cr. (al. melium and maelium).—Also, millus, i: millus collare canum venaticorum, factum ex corio confixumque clavis ferreis eminentibus adversus impetum luporum, Paul. ex Fest. p. 151 Müll.—Also written melium, mil-lus, q. v.
mellum.short: mellum, i, n., a dog's collar, Varr.

melo1.full: Mēlo, ōnis, m., old Latin name for the Nile: Melo nomine alio Nilus vocatur, Paul. ex Fest. p. 124 Müll.; cf. id. p. 7 and p. 18; Serv. Verg. G. 4, 291: Melonis alba filia, i. e. the paper-reed growing in the Nile, Aus. Epist. 4, 75.
melo1.short: Mēlo, ōnis, m., old Latin name for the Nile: Melo nomine alio Nilus vocatur, Paul.

melo2.full: mēlo, ōnis, m., = μῆλον, an apple-shaped melon, for melopepo, Pall. 4, 9, 6; Vop. Carin. 17.
melo2.short: mēlo, ōnis, m., = μῆλον, an apple-shaped melon, for melopepo, Pall.

melocarpon.full: mēlōcarpon, i, n., a plant, also called aristolochia, App. Herb. 19.
melocarpon.short: mēlōcarpon, i, n., a plant, also called aristolochia, App.

melodes.full: mĕlōdes, is, m., = μελῴδης, a pleasing, charming singer (post-class.): Proculus melodes insonare pulsibus (al. melodis) Sid. Ep. 9, 15.—Also in fem.: Mĕlōdes, a Roman surname, Inscr. Grut. 1157, 3.
melodes.short: mĕlōdes, is, m., = μελῴδης, a pleasing, charming singer (post-class.): Proculus melodes insonare pulsibus (al.

melodia.full: mĕlōdĭa, ae. f., = μελῳδία, a pleasant song, melody, Mart. Cap. 9, § 905: melodiae compositor, Cassiod. Hist. Eccl. 1, 2.

melodicus.full: mĕlōdĭcus, a, um, adj., = μελωδικός, melodious: suavitas, Cassiod. Hist. Eccl. 8, 6.
melodicus.short: mĕlōdĭcus, a, um, adj., = μελωδικός, melodious: suavitas, Cassiod.

melodina.full: mĕlōdĭna, ōrum, n. melodia, a melody (ante-class.), Varr. ap. Non. 49, 33 dub.

melodunum.full: Melodūnum, i, n., a city of the Senones, the modern Melun, Caes. B. G. 7, 58, 2; 7, 60, 1.
melodunum.short: Melodūnum, i, n., a city of the Senones, the modern Melun, Caes.

melodus.full: mĕlōdus, a, um, adj., = μελῳδός, pleasantly singing, melodious (post-class.): virgines, Aus. Prof. 15, 8: carmen, Prud. Cath. 9, 2.—Hence, subst.: mĕlōda, ae, f., a melody: lyricae melodae, Ven. Carm. 9, 7, 13.
melodus.short: mĕlōdus, a, um, adj., = μελῳδός, pleasantly singing, melodious (post-class.): virgines, Aus.

melofolia.full: mēlŏfŏlĭa, ōrum, n., vox hibr. [μῆλον-folium], apples with a leaf on the side, Plin. 15, 14, 15, § 52.

melomeli.full: mēlŏmĕli (mēlĭmĕli), n., = μηλόμελι, the sirup of preserved quinces, Col. 12, 45, 3.
melomeli.short: mēlŏmĕli (mēlĭmĕli), n., = μηλόμελι, the sirup of preserved quinces, Col.

melopepo.full: mēlŏpĕpo, ōnis, m., = μηλοπέπων, an apple-shaped melon, cucumber-melon, not eaten till fully ripe, Plin. 19, 5, 23, § 67.
melopepo.short: mēlŏpĕpo, ōnis, m., = μηλοπέπων, an apple-shaped melon, cucumber-melon, not eaten till fully ripe, Plin.

melophyllon.full: mēlophyllon, i, n., a plant, also called millefolium, App. Herb. 88.
melophyllon.short: mēlophyllon, i, n., a plant, also called millefolium, App.

melopoeia.full: mĕlŏpoeĭa, ae, f., = μελοπολὶα, musical composition: melopoeia est habitus modulationis effectae, Mart. Cap. 9, § 965 al.
melopoeia.short: mĕlŏpoeĭa, ae, f., = μελοπολὶα, musical composition: melopoeia est habitus modulationis effectae, Mart.

melos1.full: mĕlos, i, n. (Greek plur. mele, Lucr. 2, 412.—In masc.: quosdam melos, Cato ap. Non. 213, 17; so Pac. and Varr. ib.), = μέλος, a tune, air, strain, song, lay (ante-class. and poet.): suave summum melos, Naev. ap. Non. 213, 11: quosdam melos, Cato ap. Non. 77, 7: Silvani melo Consimilis cantus, Att. ap. Cic. N. D. 2, 35, 89: longum, Hor. C. 3, 4, 2: Pegaseium, Pers. prol. —Greek plur.: cui brevia mela modifica recino, Aus. Parent. 27.

melos2.full: Mēlos, i, f., = Μῆλος, an island in the Ægean Sea, one of the Cyclades, now Milo, Mel. 2, 7, 11; Plin. 4, 12, 23, § 70; Paul. ex Fest. p. 124 Müll.—Hence, Mēlĭus, a, um, adj., of Melos: Diagoras Melius, Cic. N. D. 1, 1, 2.— Mēlĭnus, a, um, v. 4. Melinus.
melos2.short: Mēlos, i, f., = Μῆλος, an island in the Ægean Sea, one of the Cyclades, now Milo, Mel.

melosmos.full: melosmos, i, m., a plant, also called polion, App. Herb. 57.
melosmos.short: melosmos, i, m., a plant, also called polion, App.

melota.full: mēlōta, ae, or mēlōtē, ōs, f., = μηλωτή, a sheepskin (with the wool on): circumierunt in melotis, in pellibus caprinis, Vulg. Heb. 11, 37; Cael. Aur. Tard. 1, 4, 76. —Collat. form, mēlōtes, Isid. 19, 24, 19; and mēlōtis, idis, f., Ambros. Ep. 15, 9.
melota.short: mēlōta, ae, or mēlōtē, ōs, f., = μηλωτή, a sheepskin (with the wool on): circumierunt in melotis, in pellibus caprinis, Vulg.

melothron.full: mēlōthron (or mēlōtrum, Plin. 21, 9, 29, § 53), i, n., = μήλωθρον, a plant, the white bryony, called, in pure Lat., vitis alba, Plin. 23, 1, 16, § 21; 21, 9, 29, § 53.

melotis.full: Melōtis, ĭdis, f., a country of Thessaly, Liv. 32, 13.
melotis.short: Melōtis, ĭdis, f., a country of Thessaly, Liv.

melotris.full: mēlōtris, ĭdis, f., = μηλωτρίς, a probe or sound, mostly for the ears, Cael. Aur. Tard. 5, 4, 63.
melotris.short: mēlōtris, ĭdis, f., = μηλωτρίς, a probe or sound, mostly for the ears, Cael.

melpomene.full: Melpŏmĕnē, ēs, f., Μελπομένη (the songstress), the muse of tragic and lyric poetry: Melpomene, cui liquidam pater Vocem cum citharā dedit, Hor. C. 1, 24, 3; Mart. 4, 37, 1; Aus. Idyll. 20, 2.
melpomene.short: Melpŏmĕnē, ēs, f., Μελπομένη (the songstress), the muse of tragic and lyric poetry: Melpomene, cui liquidam pater Vocem cum citharā dedit, Hor.

memaceni.full: Memacēni, ōrum, m., a people of Asia, beyond the Caspian Sea, Curt. 7, 6.
memaceni.short: Memacēni, ōrum, m., a people of Asia, beyond the Caspian Sea, Curt.

membrana.full: membrāna, ae, f. membrum, the skin or membrane that covers parts of the body (class.). Lit.: natura oculos membranis tenuissimis vestivit, Cic. N. D. 2, 57, 142: cerebri, the membrane of the brain, meninges, Cels. 8, 4: membranis cicadae volant, Plin. 11, 28, 33, § 96: membranis volant fragilibus insecta, id. 11, 39, 94, § 228.— Esp., the skin or slough of snakes, Ov. M. 7, 272; Luc. 6, 679.— Transf. The thin skin of plants and other things, Plin. 15, 22, 24, § 88: corio et membrana Punica (tegu

membranaceus.full: membrānācĕus and -cĭus, a, um, adj. membrana, of skin or membrane, skinny, membranaceous (post-Aug.). Lit.: vespertilio, cui membranaceae pinnae uni, Plin. 10, 61, 81, § 168: PVGILLARES, of parchment, Inscr. Grut. 174, 7.— Like a skin or membrane: quibusdam cortex membranaceus, ut viti, arundini, Plin. 16, 31, 55, § 126.

membranarius.full: membrānārĭus, ii, m. id., a parchment-maker (post-class.), Edict. Dioclet. p. 20; cf. membranarius, διφθεροποιός, Gloss. Philox.

membraneus.full: membrānĕus, a, um, adj. id., of parchment (post-Aug.): pugillares membranei, Mart. 14, 7 in lemm.: codices, Dig. 32, 50, 1.

membranula.full: membrānŭla, ae, f. dim. id., a little skin or membrane. Lit.: membranula, quae sub cute calvariam cingit, Cels. 8, 4: oculi, membrane of the eye, id. 7, 7, 13. — Transf. A parchment: iisque imperes, ut sumant membranulam, Cic. Att. 4, 4, b, 1.— Plur., an instrument or document written on parchment: quae membranulis meā manu scriptis continebuntur, Dig. 32, 102 prooem.

membranulum.full: membrānŭlum, i, n. dim. id., for membranula, a little skin or membrane, App. M. 6, p. 184, 20.

membratim.full: membrātim, adv. membrum, by limbs or members, in the limbs, limb by limb, from member to member. Lit.: membratim vitalem deperdere sensum, Lucr. 3, 527: nunc peractis malis, quae membratim sentiuntur, dicemus de his, quae totis corporibus grassantur, in single limbs, Plin. 26, 11, 67, § 107: caedere, in pieces, id. 9, 15, 18, § 48.— Transf., piecemeal, singly, severally. In gen.: membratim enumerare, Varr. R. R. 1, 22; cf.: animalium naturae generatim membratimque ita se habent, Plin. 12 praef.

membratura.full: membrātūra, ae, f. membro, the formation of the limbs, constitution of the body, Vitr. 8, 5, 1.

membripotens.full: membrĭpŏtens, ntis, adj. membrum-potens, ruling in the members (eccl. Lat.), Jul. ap. Aug. c. Sec. Resp. Jul. 2, 11.

membro.full: membro, āre, v. a. membrum, to form limb by limb, to furnish with limbs: quinque et triginta diebus infans membratur, Censor. de Die Nat. 11; Dracont. Hex. 220.

membrosus.full: membrōsus, a, um, adj. id., large membered: hortorum custos membrosior aequo, i. e. majori mentula praeditus, Auct. Priap. prooem.

membrum.full: membrum, i, n. etym. dub.; perh. for mems-trum; cf. Sanscr. māmsa, flesh, a limb, member of the body (class.). Lit.: jam membrorum, id est partium corporis, alia videntur propter eorum usum a natura esse donata, ut manus, crura, pedes, etc. . . . alia quasi ad quendam ornatum, ut cauda pavoni, plumae versicolores columbis, viris mammae atque barba, Cic. Fin. 3, 5, 18; Plaut. Am. 5, 1, 66: defessa, Verg. G. 4, 438; Suet. Vesp. 20: hispida membra, Juv. 2, 11: membrum lacerum laesumve, Gell. 4, 2,

memecylon.full: mēmĕcўlon, i, n., = μημέκυλον, μιμαίκυλον, the edible fruit of the strawberrytree, Plin. 15, 24, 28, § 99.
memecylon.short: mēmĕcўlon, i, n., = μημέκυλον, μιμαίκυλον, the edible fruit of the strawberrytree, Plin.

memet.full: mēmet, acc. of ego with met, v. ego and met.

meminens.full: mĕmĭnens, P. a., v. memini fin.

memini.full: mĕmĭni, isse, v. n. Sanscr. man, think; upaman = Gr. ὑπομένειν, await; Gr. μεν- in μένω, Μέντωρ; μαν- in μαίνομαι, μάντις; μνᾶ- in μιμνήσκω, etc.; cf.: maneo, moneo, reminiscor, mens, Minerva, etc., to remember, recollect, to think of, be mindful of a thing; not to have forgotten a person or thing, to bear in mind (syn.: reminiscor, recordor); constr. with gen., with acc. of the person and of the thing, with de, with a rel.-clause, with ut, with cum; with the acc. and inf. (usually the inf. pres

memmius.full: Memmius, a, name of a Roman gens. mox Italus Mnestheus, genus, a quo nomine Memmi, Verg. A. 5, 117. So C. Memmius, a public man, who, being adjudged guilty of ambitus, went into exile to Athens, to him Cicero addressed several letters, and to him Lucretius dedicated his poem, De Rerum Natura; cf. Lucr. 1, 42.—Hence, Memmĭădes, ae, m., one of the Memmian gens, a Memmiade, a Memmius, Lucr. 1, 26.— Memmĭānus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to a Memmius: praedia, of C. Memmius, Cic. Att. 5, 1, 1.
memmius.short: Memmius, a, name of a Roman gens.

memnon.full: Memnon, ŏnis, m., = Μεμνων, son of Tithonus and Aurora, and king of the Ethiopians; he went to the aid of the Trojans, and was slain by Achilles: nigri Memnonis arma, Verg. A. 1, 489.—When burned on the funeral pile he is said to have been changed by Aurora into a bird, while from his ashes many other birds flew up, called Memnoniae or Memnonides, who every year flew from Ethiopia to Troy and fought over Memnon's tomb, Ov. M. 13, 600 sq.; id. ib. 13, 617; Plin. 10, 26, 37, § 74. The black marble
memnon.short: Memnon, ŏnis, m., = Μεμνων, son of Tithonus and Aurora, and king of the Ethiopians;

memor1.full: mĕmor, ŏris (anciently memoris, memore, acc. to Prisc. p. 772 P.; comp. memorior, id. p. 699 P.), adj. Sanscr. root smar-, in smarti, memory; smara, love; Gr. μάρτυς, witness; μέριμνα, care; cf.: memoria, mora, etc., not from memini, mindful of a thing, remembering; constr. with gen., with acc. and inf., with a rel,clause, and absol. In gen. With gen.: ut memor esses sui, Ter. And. 1, 5, 46: se eorum facti memorem fore, Caes. B. C. 1, 13: generis, Sall. C. 60, 7: pristinarum virtutum, Nep. Hann.

memor2.full: Mĕmor, ŏris, m., a Roman surname, lnscr. Mur. 1128, 5.
memor2.short: Mĕmor, ŏris, m., a Roman surname, lnscr.

memorabilis.full: mĕmŏrābĭlis, e, adj. memoro, memorable, remarkable, worthy of being remembered; heard of, conceivable; worthy to be mentioned, fit to be spoken of (class.): vir, Liv. 38, 53.—Comp.: memorabilior, Liv. 38, 53: auctores, Col. 1, 1: nomen, Verg. A. 2, 583: familiaritas, Cic. Lael. 1, 4: virtus, id. Phil. 13, 19, 44: hoccine credibile est. aut memorabile? Ter. And. 4, 1, 1: nec bellum est, nec memorabile, Plaut. Curc. 1, 1, 8: hoc memorabilest, ego tu sum, tu es ego, id. Stich 5, 4, 46: in qua pugna

memoraculum.full: mĕmŏrācŭlum, i, n. id., a monument (post-class.), App. Mag. p. 311, 3.

memoralis.full: mĕmŏrālis, e, false read. for memorialis, ap. Arn. 6, p. 196.

memoraliter.full: mĕmŏrālĭter, adv. memoria, serving to make mention, Ven. Fort. Carm. 4, 20.

memoralius.full: mĕmŏrālĭus, ii, m. memoro, a recorder, notary: ὑπομνηματογράφος, actuarius, memoralius, Gloss. Gr. Lat.

memorandus.full: mĕmŏrandus, a, um, P. a., v. memo ro fin. B.

memoratio.full: mĕmŏrātĭo, ōnis, f. memoro, a mentioning, Corn. Gall. 1, 291.

memorator.full: mĕmŏrātor, ōris, m. id., one who mentions or recounts, a relater (poet.): tui casūs memorator, Prop. 3 (4), 1, 33.

memoratrix.full: mĕmŏrātrix, īcis, f. memorator, she who mentions or relates (post-Aug.), Val. Fl. 6, 142.

memoratus1.full: mĕmŏrātus, a, um, Part. and P. a., v. memoro fin. A.

memoratus2.full: mĕmŏrātus, ūs, m. memoro, a mentioning, relating; a mention, relation (ante-class. and post-Aug.): istaec lepida sunt memoratui, Plaut. Bacch. 1, 1, 28: estne hoc miserum memoratu, id. Cist. 2, 1, 24: parva et levia memoratu, Tac. A. 4, 32; id. H. 2, 73; flumen memoratu dignum, Plin. 3, 10, 15, § 95.

memoria.full: mĕmŏrĭa, ae, f. memor. The faculty of remembering, memory, recollection (class.): ubi me fugiet memoria, Plaut. Bacch. 1, 1, 2: Edepol, memoria's optumad, id. Mil. 1, 1, 45: bona, Cic. Att. 8, 4, 2: segnis ac lenta, Sen. Ep. 74, 1: tenacissima, Quint. 1, 1, 19: Hortensius memoriā tantā fuit, ut, etc., Cic. Brut. 88, 301: hoc in memoria mea penitus insedit, id. de Or. 2, 28, 122: in memoriam redigere, to recall to mind, recollect, id. Fam. 1, 9, 9; so, in memoriam reducere, id. Inv 1, 52, 98 memo

memorialis.full: mĕmŏrĭālis, e, adj. memoria, of or belonging to memory or remembrance, memorial (post-Aug.): libellus. a memoran dum-book, Suet. Caes. 56.— Subst. Mĕmŏrĭālis, is, m., a historiographer Cod. Just. 12, 29, 1.— mĕmŏrĭāle, is, n. memorial, that which keeps in remembrance: Domine, tuum, Vulg. Psa. 135, 13; Arn. in Psa. 135.— mĕmŏrĭālia, ĭum, n. plur., memoirs, Dig. 50, 16, 44; Macr. S. 3. 6, 11.— The title of a book by Sabinus Masurius, Gell. 6 (7), 7, 8. Sabinus in septimo memoriall, id. 4, 20, 11

memoriola.full: mĕmŏrĭŏla, ae, f. dim. memoria. * Memory: memoriolā vacillare, Cic. Att. 12, 1, 2.— A monument, tomb, Inscr. Fabr. p. 85, 155; Inscr. Murat. 994, 7.

memoriosus.full: mĕmŏrĭōsus, a, um, adj. memoria, that has a good memory, Paul. ex Fest. p. 124 Müll.: memoriosus, et memoriose, Fronto de Differ. Voc. p. 2194 P.; cf.: memoriosus, μνημονικός, Gloss. Philox.— Hence, adj.: mĕmŏrĭōse, with a good memory, Fronto l. l.

memoritei.full: mĕmŏrĭtei adv., v. memor fin. B.

memoro.full: mĕmŏro, āvi, ātum (archaic inf. pass. memorarier, Plaut. Most. 1, 3, 99), 1, v. a. memor, to bring to remembrance, remind of, to mention, recount, relate, speak about or of, say, tell (class.). With acc.: memorare mores mulierum, Plaut. Aul. 3, 5, 50: nomen memora tuom mihi, id. Trin. 4, 2, 41: deos absentis testis memoras, callest on, id. Merc. 3, 4, 42: superbiam, Cic. Verr. 2, 1, 47, § 122: causas alicui, Verg. A. 1, 8: antequam arma inciperent, misere legatos amicitiam obsequiumque memoratur

memoror.full: mĕmŏror, ātus sum, v. dep. id., to remember, be mindful of (eccl. Lat.).— With gen., Vulg. Jer. 31, 14; Ambros. de Laps. Virg. 5, 19.—With acc., Vulg. Eccl. 7, 40 al.

memphis.full: Memphis, is and ĭdos, f., = Μεμφις, a city of Middle Egypt, celebrated as the residence of the Egyptian kings, now Metrahenny (fourteen miles south of Cairo), Mel. 1, 9, 9; Plin. 2, 85, 87, § 201; 5, 9, 9, § 50; Liv. 45, 11 sq.; Hor. C. 3, 26, 10; Tac. H. 4, 84; Prop. 3, 11, 34: quae colis, et Memphin, palmiferamque Pharon, Ov. Am. 2, 13, 7.— Hence, Memphītes, ae, m. adj., Memphite, of or from the city of Memphis, Egyptian: Memphiten plangere bovem, i. e. Apis, Tib. 1, 8 (7), 28 lapis, Plin. 36,
memphis.short: Memphis, is and ĭdos, f., = Μεμφις, a city of Middle Egypt, celebrated as the residence of the Egyptian kings, now Metrahenny (fourteen miles south of Cairo), Mel.

mena2.full: Mēna, ae, f. μήν, daughter of Jupiter, the goddess who presided over the physical condition of women, Aug. Civ. Dei, 4, 11; 7, 2.

mena3.full: Mena, ae, m., a Roman surname, Inscr. Grut. 241, col. 2.
mena3.short: Mena, ae, m., a Roman surname, Inscr.

menaechmi.full: Mĕnaechmi, ōrum, m., = Μέναιχμοι, a comedy of Plautus, so called from the two twin brothers of this name, the leading characters.
menaechmi.short: Mĕnaechmi, ōrum, m., = Μέναιχμοι, a comedy of Plautus, so called from the two twin brothers of this name, the leading characters.

menaenius.full: Mĕnaenĭus or Mĕnaenus, a, um, adj., of or from Menæ (Μέναι), a city of Sicily, now Mineo: Xenon Menaenus, Cic. Verr. 2, 3, 22, § 55.—In plur.: Mĕnaeni, ōrum, m., the inhabitants of Menæ, Cic. Verr. 2, 3, 43, § 102; also written Mĕ-nanīni, Plin. 3, 8, 14, § 91.
menaenius.short: Mĕnaenĭus or Mĕnaenus, a, um, adj., of or from Menæ (Μέναι), a city of Sicily, now Mineo: Xenon Menaenus, Cic.

menaeus1.full: Mĕnaeus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to the city of Menæ, in Sicily: comitata Menaeis (viris), Sil. 14, 266.
menaeus1.short: Mĕnaeus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to the city of Menæ, in Sicily: comitata Menaeis (viris), Sil.

menaeus2.full: mēnaeus, i, m., = μηναῖος, monthly; subst. (sc. circulus), a monthly circle (al. manacus), Vitr. 9, 8.

menalcas.full: Mĕnalcas, ae, m., the name of a shepherd, Verg. E. 5, 4; 2, 15.
menalcas.short: Mĕnalcas, ae, m., the name of a shepherd, Verg.

menalippe.full: Mĕnălippē (Mĕnălippa, Mĕlă-nippē), ēs, f., = Μεναλίππη, a sister of Antiope queen of the Amazons, taken prisoner by Hercules, Just. 2, 4, 23; Hyg. Fab. 186.— A tragedy of Attius, Cic. Off. 1, 31, 114; and of Ennius, Gell. 5, 11, 2; cf. Juv. 8, 229.
menalippe.short: Mĕnălippē (Mĕnălippa, Mĕlă-nippē), ēs, f., = Μεναλίππη, a sister of Antiope queen of the Amazons, taken prisoner by Hercules, Just.

menalippus.full: Mĕnălippus (orig. form Mĕlănip-pus), i, m., = Μελάνιππος, the slayer of Tydeus, who, while dying, bit the head of Menalippus, Stat. Th. 8, 719; 740.—The form Melanippus is found as the name of a tragedy of Attius, Cic. Tusc. 3, 9, 20.

menalius.full: Menalĭus, a false reading in Cic. N. D. 3, 22, 55; v. Creuz. ad loc.
menalius.short: Menalĭus, a false reading in Cic.

menander.full: Mĕnander or Mĕnandros (-us; Gr. gen. Menandru, acc. to Μενάνδρου, Ter. Eun., Heaut., and Ad.), i, m., = Μένανδρος, a celebrated Greek comic poet, whom Terence took as his model, Cic. Fin. 1, 2, 4; Ter. And. prol. 9; Prop. 3, 21, 28: nobilis comoediis, Phaedr. 5, 1, 9; Amm. 21, 4, 4.—Form Menandros, Ov. Am. 1, 15, 18: also Menandrus, Vell. 1, 16, 3.— A slave of Cicero, Cic. Fam. 16, 13.— A freedman of T. Ampius Balbus, Cic. Fam. 13, 70.—Hence, Mĕnandrēus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to the poet

menapii.full: Mĕnăpĭi, ōrum, m. plur. (Mĕnapis for Menapiis, Mart. 13, 54), a people of Belgic Gaul, between the Meuse and the Scheldt, Caes. B. G. 2, 4, 9; 4, 4, 2; Plin. 4, 17, 31, § 106; Tac. H. 4, 28; Inscr. Orell. 749.— Hence, Mĕnăpĭa, ae, f., the chief town of the Menapii, Aur. Vict. Caes. 39.— Mĕnăpĭcus, a, um, adj., of or pertaining to the Menapii, Edict. Diocl. p. 14.

menas.full: Mēnas, ae, m., = Μηνᾶς, a freedman of Sextus Pompeius, his lieutenant and commander of the pirate-fleet, which, with the hope of greater gain, he traitorously delivered up to Augustus, Vell. 2, 73; 77; Plin. 35, 18, 58, § 200.
menas.short: Mēnas, ae, m., = Μηνᾶς, a freedman of Sextus Pompeius, his lieutenant and commander of the pirate-fleet, which, with the hope of greater gain, he traitorously delivered up to Augustus, Vell.

menceps.full: menceps for menteceptos, from mens and capio, out of his senses, mad, acc. to Prisc. p. 668 P.
menceps.short: menceps for menteceptos, from mens and capio, out of his senses, mad, acc.

menda.full: menda, ae, f. v. mendum, a fault, defect, blemish of the body (poet. and postAug.). Lit.: in toto nusquam corpore menda fuit, Ov. Am. 1, 5, 18: nocte latent mendae, id. A. A. 1, 249.— Transf., a mistake, error, blunder, in writing, in books, a slip of the pen, Suet. Aug. 87: mendae istins indoles, Gell. 20, 6, 14; 1, 7, 3.

mendaciloquium.full: mendācĭlŏquĭum, ii, n. mendaciloquus, for mendacium, false-speaking, falsehood, mendacity: mendaciloquium, ψευδολογία, Gloss. Philox.

mendaciloquus.full: mendācĭlŏquus, a, um, adj. mendacium-loquor, false-speaking, lying, mendacious (ante- and post-class.): nihil est stolidius, Neque mendaciloquius, Plaut. Trin. 1, 2, 163.—As subst.: mendācĭlŏquus, i, m., a liar: mendaciloquorum doctrinae, Tert. adv. Psych. 2.

mendacitas.full: mendācĭtas, ātis, f. mendax, false hood, mendacity (eccl. Lat.), Tert. Praescr. 31.

mendacium.full: mendācĭum, ii, n. mendax, a lie, untruth, falsehood. Lit. (class.): dicere alicui mendacium de re aliquā, Plaut. Bacch. 4, 9, 33: mendacio fallere, Cic. Mur. 30, 62: vatum, Ov. F. 6, 253: famae, id. ib. 4, 311: immensa spirant mendacia, Juv. 7, 111: Titiae meae, cum quā sine mendacio vixi, i. e. honestly, without hypocrisy, Dig. 34, 2, 36: prophetāsti mendacium, Vulg. Jer. 20, 6; cf. id. ib. 27, 10: credere mendacio, to believe a lie, id. 2 Thess. 2, 11.— Esp., a fable, fiction (opp. historic tr

mendaciunculum.full: mendācĭuncŭlum, i, n. dim. mendacium, a little lie, trifling untruth, fib: quod tamen est mendaciunculis aspergendum (al. mendaciolis), Cic. de Or. 2, 59, 241 Orell. N. cr.

mendax.full: mendax, dācis, adj. mentior, given to lying, mendacious; subst., a liar. Lit.: mendacem esse adversus aliquem, Plaut. Poen. 1, 2, 188: cum mendaci homini, ne verum quidem dicenti, credere soleamus, Cic. Div. 2, 71, 146: Carthaginienses fraudulenti et mendaces, id. Agr. 2, 35, 95: aretalogus, Juv. 15, 16.—As subst.: mendax, dācis, m., a liar.—Prov.: mendacem memorem esse oportet, a liar should have a good memory, Quint. 4, 2, 91.— Comp.: Parthis mendacior, Hor. Ep 2, 1, 112.—Sup.: mendacissimus,

mendes.full: Mendēs, ētis, Mendēsīcus, and Mendēsĭus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to the Egyptian maritime town Mendes. Mendes: Asclepias, Suet. Aug. 94.— Mendesicus: ostium, Plin. 5, 10, 11, § 64.— Mendesius: nomos, Plin. 5, 9, 9, § 49: unguentum, id. 13, 1, 2, § 17.
mendes.short: Mendēs, ētis, Mendēsīcus, and Mendēsĭus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to the Egyptian maritime town Mendes.

mendicabulum.full: mendīcābŭlum, i, n. mendico, a beggar, mendicant (ante- and post-class.): hominum mendicabula, Plaut. Aul. 4, 8, 2: circumforaneum, App. M. 9, p. 218, 41.

mendicabundus.full: mendīcābundus, a, um, adj. id., begging, mendicant (eccl. Lat.): mendicabundā prece stipem rogare, Aug. Ep. 140.

mendicatio.full: mendīcātĭo, ōnis, f. id., a begging, obtaining by begging (post-Aug.): foeda vitae mendicatio, Sen. Ep. 101, 13.

mendicimonium.full: mendīcĭmōnĭum, ii, n. mendicus, beggary, indigence, Laber. ap. Gell. 16, 7, 2, and ap. Non. 140, 31.

mendicitas.full: mendīcĭtas, ātis, f. id., beggary, mendicity, pauperism, indigence (rare but class.): qui quidem ad mendicitatem properent se detrudere, Plaut. Men. 1, 3, 21; id. Rud. 2, 6, 30: in summā mendicitate esse, Cic. Rosc. Am. 31, 86: mendicitatem perpeti, id. Fin. 5, 11, 32: paupertatem novā mendicitate revocare, Petr. 125.

mendico.full: mendico, āvi, ātum, 1, v. n. and a., and mendīcor, ātus sum (archaio inf. mendicarier, Plaut. Capt. prol. 13), 1, v. dep. id., to beg, ask for alms, go a-begging; to beg for something, solicit, obtain by begging; constr. absol. and with acc. (poet. and post-class.): mendicantem vivere, to live by begging. Plaut. Capt 2, 2, 73: quando histrionem cogis mendicarier, id. ib. prol. 13; mendicum malim mendicando vincere, id. ib. 3, 4, 16.—Act.: a me mendicas malum, Plaut. Am. 4, 2, 12: aliquid mendica

mendiculus.full: mendīcŭlus, a, um, dim. adj. [mendicus], of a beggar, beggarly: inducula (opp. regilla), Plaut. Ep. 2, 2, 32.

mendicum.full: mendicum, velum quod in prora ponitur, Paul. ex Fest. p. 124 Müll.
mendicum.short: mendicum, velum quod in prora ponitur, Paul.

mendicus.full: mendīcus, a, um, adj., beggarly, needy, in want, indigent (class.). Lit.: paupertas si malum est, mendicus esse beatus nemo potest, Cic. Fin. 5, 28, 84; cf.: solos sapientes esse, si mendicissimi (sint), divites, id. Mur. 29, 61: mendicior, Tert. de Anim. 33: prandia, Mart. 14, 81.—As subst.: mendīcus, i, m., a beggar, mendicant: mendicum malim mendicando vincere, Quam, etc., Plaut. Bacch. 3, 4, 16: mendici, i. e. the priests of Cybele, Hor. S. 1, 2, 2.—As a term of abuse, a beggar, ragamuffin,
mendicus.short: mendīcus, a, um, adj., beggarly, needy, in want, indigent (class.).

mendositas.full: mendōsĭtas, ātis, f. mendosus, faultiness (eccl. Lat.): mendositatem corrigere, Aug. Ep. 71, 5; id. Civ. Dei, 15, 13.

mendosus.full: mendōsus, a, um, adj. mendum. Full of faults, fauity. Physically, full of faults or blemishes: equi facies, Ov. M. 12, 399.— In gen., erroneous, incorrect (class.): mendosum exemplar testamenti, Plin. Ep. 10, 75: mendosum est, etc., Cic. de Or. 2, 19, 83: mores, Ov. Am. 2, 4, 1.—Comp.: historia mendosior, Cic. Brut. 16, 62.— Transf. That commits faults, makes mistakes: cur servus societatis, qui tabulas conficeret, semper in Verrucii nomine certo ex loco mendosus esset, Cic. Verr. 2, 2, 77, § 18

mendum.full: mendum, i, n. Sanscr. manāk, a little; mindā, a defect; cf.: mancus, mendicus, a fault, error, blunder in writing (class.). Lit.: quod mendum ista litura correxit? Cic. Verr. 2, 2, 42, § 104: librariorum, id. Att. 13, 23, 2.— Trop.: Idus Martiae magnum mendum continent, mistake, error, Cic Att. 14, 22, 2.— A blemish, defect, in the face, etc.: rara tamen mendo facies caret, Ov. A. A. 3, 261.

menecles.full: Mĕnĕcles, is, m., = Μενεκλῆς, an Asiatic rhetorician from Alabanda, Cic. de Or. 2, 23, 95; id. Or. 69, 231.—Hence, Mĕ-nĕclĭus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Menecles the rhetorician: Meneclium studium, Cic. Brut. 95, 326.
menecles.short: Mĕnĕcles, is, m., = Μενεκλῆς, an Asiatic rhetorician from Alabanda, Cic.

menecrates.full: Mĕnecrătes, is, m., = Μενεκράτης. A poet of Ephesus, who wrote of husbandry, Varr. R. R. 1, 1, 9.— A freedman of Pompey, Plin. 35, 18, 58, § 200.

menedemus.full: Mĕnĕdēmus, i, m., = Μενέδημος. An Eretrian philosopher, a disciple of Plato, Cic. Ac. 2, 42, 129.— An Athenian rhetorician in the time of Crassus, Cic. de Or. 1, 19, 85.— A peripatetic philosopher from Rhodes, Gell. 13, 5, 3.— A Greek admitted to the privileges of citizenship, but afterwards executed, Cic. Att. 15, 19, 2.— A general of Alexander the Great, Curt. 7, 6, 13; 7, 7, 15.— The name of a man, one of the Dramatis Personae in Ter. Heaut.

menelaeus.full: Mĕnĕlāēus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Menelaüs: thalamus, Prop. 2, 12 (3, 7), 14.
menelaeus.short: Mĕnĕlāēus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Menelaüs: thalamus, Prop.

menelais.full: Menelāis, ĭdis and ĭdos, f., a city in Epirus, Liv. 39, 26.
menelais.short: Menelāis, ĭdis and ĭdos, f., a city in Epirus, Liv.

menelaius.full: Mĕnĕlaĭus, i, m., a mountain in Laconia, on the Eurotas, near Sparta, Liv. 34, 28.
menelaius.short: Mĕnĕlaĭus, i, m., a mountain in Laconia, on the Eurotas, near Sparta, Liv.

menelaus.full: Mĕnĕlāüs, i, m., = Μενέλαος. Son of Atreus, brother of Agamemnon, and husband of Helen, who eloped from him with Paris, Cic. Brut. 13, 50; id. Rep. 5, 9, 14; Auct. Her. 3, 21, 34; Ov. M. 13, 203; id. A. A. 2, 359.— Transf., a cuckold.— Jestingly of M. Lucullus, whose wife was seduced by C. Memmius, Cic. Att. 1, 18, 3.— Menelaus Marathenus, a Greek rhetorician, from the old Phoenician city of Marathus, Cic. Brut. 26, 100.— Menelai portus, a city with a port of the same name on the shore of the Me

menenianus.full: Mĕnēnĭānus, a, um, see the foll. art. II. B.
menenianus.short: Mĕnēnĭānus, a, um, see the foll.

menenius.full: Mĕnēnĭus, name of a Roman gens. Its most celebrated member was Menenius Agrippa, who told the people the fable of the belly and the limbs, Liv. 2, 16, 7; 2, 32, 8; 2, 33, 10.—Another Menenius in the time of Horace, noted as a foolish person, Hor. S. 2, 3, 287.— Hence, Mĕnēnĭus, a, um, adj., Menenian: tribus, a Roman tribe, Cic. Fam. 13, 9, 2.— Mĕnēnĭānus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Menenius, Menenian: judicium, i. e. of Menenius Agrippa, Liv. 2, 52, 8.
menenius.short: Mĕnēnĭus, name of a Roman gens.

menephron.full: Mĕnē^phron, ŏnis, m., = Μενεφρων, the name of an immoral person, Ov M. 7, 386; called also Mĕnō^phrus, Hyg. Fab. 253.
menephron.short: Mĕnē^phron, ŏnis, m., = Μενεφρων, the name of an immoral person, Ov M.

menestheus.full: Mĕnestheus (-steus), ei and eos, m., = Μενεσθευς, a man's name. A son of Iphicrates the Athenian, Nep. lphicr. 3.— A king of the Athenians, a leader in the Trojan war, Just. 2, 6.— A charioteer of Diomedes, Stat. Th. 6, 661; 712.— = Mnestheus, q. v.
menestheus.short: Mĕnestheus (-steus), ei and eos, m., = Μενεσθευς, a man's name.

meninga.full: mēninga, ae, f., = μῆνιγξ, the membrane which covers the brain, Theod. Prisc. 2, 2, 9.
meninga.short: mēninga, ae, f., = μῆνιγξ, the membrane which covers the brain, Theod.

meninx.full: Mēninx, ngis, f., = Μῆνιγξ, an island off the coast of Africa, near the Lesser Syrtis, the modern Jerbah, Plin. 5, 7, 7, § 41; Liv. 22, 31, 2 (Weissenb. Menige); Mel. 2, 7, 7; Sol. 27, 40; Sil. 3, 318.
meninx.short: Mēninx, ngis, f., = Μῆνιγξ, an island off the coast of Africa, near the Lesser Syrtis, the modern Jerbah, Plin.

menion.full: mēnĭon, ii, n., the name of a plant, also called menogenion, App. Herb. 64.
menion.short: mēnĭon, ii, n., the name of a plant, also called menogenion, App.

menippus.full: Mĕnippus, i, m., = Μένιππος. A Cynic philosopher famous for his bitter sarcasms, whence Varro gave to his satires the name of Menippeae, Cic. Ac. 1, 2, 8; Gell. 2, 18, 7; Macr. S. 1, 11, 42; 1, 7, 12; Arn. 6, 207. — A great Asiatic orator in the time of Cicero, from Stratonice, Cic. Brut. 91, 315.

menis.full: mēnis, ĭdis, f., = μηνίς, a little halfmoon, crescent, placed as an ornament at the beginning of books (post-class.): a primā menide libri, i. e. from the beginning, Aus. Prof. 25, 1.
menis.short: mēnis, ĭdis, f., = μηνίς, a little halfmoon, crescent, placed as an ornament at the beginning of books (post-class.): a primā menide libri, i.

menius.full: Mēnĭus, i, m., = Μήνιος, son of Lycaon, Ov. Ib. 472.
menius.short: Mēnĭus, i, m., = Μήνιος, son of Lycaon, Ov.

mennis.full: Mennis, is, f., a city of Assyria, in Adiabene, Curt. 5, 1, 15.
mennis.short: Mennis, is, f., a city of Assyria, in Adiabene, Curt.

mennonia.full: mennonĭa, ae, f., a reading for memnonia, Plin. 37, 10, 63, § 173.
mennonia.short: mennonĭa, ae, f., a reading for memnonia, Plin.

menoeceus.full: Mĕnoeceus, ĕi and ĕos, m., = Μενοικευς, son of the Theban king Creon, who sacrificed kimself for his country, Cic. Tusc. 1, 48, 116; Juv. 14, 240; Stat. Th. 10, 620; 651; 11, 709 al.; Hyg. Fab. 67.—Hence, Mĕnoecĕus, a um, adj., of or belonging to Menœceus, Menœcean, Stat. Th. 10, 756.
menoeceus.short: Mĕnoeceus, ĕi and ĕos, m., = Μενοικευς, son of the Theban king Creon, who sacrificed kimself for his country, Cic.

menoetes.full: Mĕnoetes, is, acc. en, m., = Μενοίτης. One of the companions of Æneas: compellat voce Menoetem, Verg. A. 5, 161.— An Arcadian slain by Turnus, Verg. A. 12, 517.

menoetius.full: Mĕnoetĭus, ii, m., = Μενοίτιος, the son of Actor and father of Patroclus, one of the Argonauts, Hyg. Fab. 14 and 97.—Hence, Mĕnoetĭădes, ae, m., = Μενοιτιάδης, the son of Menœtius, i. e. Patroclus, the friend of Achilles, Prop. 2, 1, 38.
menoetius.short: Mĕnoetĭus, ii, m., = Μενοίτιος, the son of Actor and father of Patroclus, one of the Argonauts, Hyg.

menogenes.full: Mēnŏgĕnes, is, m., a Roman sur name, i. e. of the consul M. Messala, Val. Max. 9, 14, 5; Plin. 7, 12, 10, § 54.— A famous sculptor, Plin. 34, 8, 19, § 88.
menogenes.short: Mēnŏgĕnes, is, m., a Roman sur name, i.

menogenion.full: mēnogĕnĭon, ii, n., = μήνη (moon) and γένειον (chin), a plant good for the cure of somnambulism, App. Herb. 64.
menogenion.short: mēnogĕnĭon, ii, n., = μήνη (moon) and γένειον (chin), a plant good for the cure of somnambulism, App.

menoides.full: mēnŏīdes = μηνοειδής, the moon during her first days, the new moon, Firm. Math. 4 praef. fin.
menoides.short: mēnŏīdes = μηνοειδής, the moon during her first days, the new moon, Firm.

menon.full: Mĕnōn, ōnis. m., = Μένων, the name of one of Plato's dialogues, Cic. Tusc. 1, 24, 57.

menotyrannus.full: Mēnŏtўrannus, i, m., = μηνοτύ ραννος, lord of the months, Inscr. Fabr. p. 666, 522; Inscr. Grut. 28, 6 al.
menotyrannus.short: Mēnŏtўrannus, i, m., = μηνοτύ ραννος, lord of the months, Inscr.

mens.full: mens, mentis (nom. sing. mentis: terra corpus est, at mentis ignis est, Enn. ap. Prisc. p. 764 P.; so too, istic est de sole sumptus; isque totus mentis est, Enn. ap. Varr. L. L. 5, § 59 Müll.; cf. Enn. p. 168, v. 6 and 7 Vahl.), f. from the root men, whence memini, q. v., and comminiscor, the mind, disposition; the heart, soul (class.). In gen.: fusi sine mente ac sine sensu ullo jaceant, Enn. ap. Non. 312, 26 (Ann. v. 134 Vahl.): nubilam mentem Animi habeo, Plaut. Cist. 2, 1, 6: mens animi, Ca

mensa.full: mensa, ae, f [Sanscr, ma, measure; Gr. μέτρον; cf. manus, mane, etc.], a table for any purpose, as a dining-table; a market-stand for meat, vegetables, etc.; a money-dealer's table or counter, a sacrificial table, etc. Lit. Of the table itself as a fabrid: non ferre mensam nisi crebris distinctam venis, Sen. Dial. 3, 35, 5: mensa inanis nunc si adponatur mihi, Plaut. Pers. 3, 1, 26: cibos in mensam alicui apponere, id. Men. 1, 3, 29: surgunt a mensā saturi, poti, id. Ps. 1, 3, 62: ad mensam cons

mensalis.full: mensālis, e, adj. mensa, of or belonging to the table, table- (post-class.): argentum mensale, silver table-service, Vop. Tac. 10: vinum, Auct. ap. Vop. Aurel. 9, 6: citharae species mensalis, Diom. 479, 12.

mensarius.full: mensārĭus, a, um, adj. id., of or belonging to the table or counter; only subst. mensārĭus, ii, m., a money-changer, banker In gen.: mensaril nummularii, Paul. ex Fest. p. 124, 17 Müll.: Cassius Parmens. ap. Suet. Aug. 4.— In partic., a public banker, who regulated the paying out of public moneys, Cic. Fl. 19, 44: quinqueviris creatis, quos mensarlos ab dispensatione pecuniae appellārunt, Liv. 7, 21: mensarii triumviri, id. 23, 21; 26, 36.— Mensārĭum, ii, n., table furniture, a table-cloth: coll

mensatim.full: mensātim, adv. mensa, by tables, from table to table (late Lat.), Juvenc. 3, 214.

mensio.full: mensĭo, ōnis, f. metior, a measuring, measure: vocum, metre, quantity, Cic. Or. 53, 177.

mensis.full: mensis, is (gen. plur. regularly mensium; freq. mensum, Plaut. Most. 1, 1, 78; Cic. Phil. 12, 9, 22; id. Verr 2, 74, 182 al.; Caes. B. G. 1, 5, 3; Ov. M. 8, 500; id. F. 5, 187; 424; Liv. 3, 24, 4; 3, 25, 4; Plin. 7, 11, 9, § 49 et saep.; v. Neue, Formenl. 1. p. 265 sq.), m. root ma-, measure; Sanscr mas; Gr. μην, the measure of time; cf. Goth. mena; Germ. Mond; Engl. moon, month, a month. Lit.: mensium nomina, Varr. L. L. 6, 4, § 33 Müll.; Censor 22: hunc mensem vortentem servare, the return of

mensor.full: mensor, ōris, m. metior, a measurer (post Aug.). In gen.: te maris, et terrae, numeroque carentis arenae Mensorem cohibent, Archyta, Hor. C. 1, 28, 1: frumentarius, a corn-measurer, Paul. Dig. 27, 1, 26.— In partic. A surveyor: non agricolae sed mensoris officium esse dicebam, Col. 6, 1: cautus humum longo signavit limite mensor, Ov. M. 1, 136.— An architect, Plin. Ep. 10, 27, 5; 10, 18, 3; Inscr. Orell. 3223.— Milit. t. t. An engineer, Amm. 19, 11, 8; Cassiod. Var. 3, 52.— One who measures out

mensorium.full: mensōrĭum, i, n. mensor, a basket (late Lat.): caput Johannis in mensorio accipere, Cassiod. H. E. 10, 15.

menstrualis.full: menstrŭālis, e, adj. menstruus, monthly, every month, for a month. In gen.: epulae, i. e. free entertainment for a month, Plaut. Capt. 3, 1, 23: sphaera, Prud. στεφ. 10, 538.— Of or belonging to the monthly courses of women, menstrual (post-Aug.): solum animal menstruale mulier est, Plin. 7, 15, 13, § 63: mulier men strualis, menstrual, id. 19, 10, 57, § 177: pannus, Marc. Emp. 35: tempus, Vulg. Lev 15, 25.

menstruo.full: menstrŭo, āre, v. n. and a. [id.]. Neutr., to have a monthly term, to be men struant (post-class.): mulier menstruans, Pall. 1, 35, 3.— Act., to pollute; trop.: pannus menstruatae justitiae nostrae, polluted, Vulg. Isa. 64, 6; cf. id. Ezech. 18, 6.

menstruus.full: menstrŭus, a, um, adj. mensis. Of or belonging to a month, that happens every month, monthly. In gen. (class.): ferias menstruas edicere, Varr. L. L. 6, § 13 Müll.: usura, Cic. Att. 6, 1, 3: ventorum ratio, Plin. 2, 47, 48, § 128.— Subst. menstrŭa, ōrum, n., the monthly sacri fices: ad menstrua solvenda montem ascendunt, Sall. Fragm. ap. Non. 492, 32. — menstrŭum, i, n.: menstruum meum Calend Septembr finitur, a monthly term of office, monthly service, Plin. Ep. 10, 24, 3.— In partic., of or bel

mensualis.full: mensŭālis, e, adj. mensis, of a month, monthly (post-class.): numerus, Gromat. Vet. p. 393, 12: speculatio, id. ib. p. 415, 13: stipendia, Fulg. Contin. Virg. p. 142, 3.

mensula.full: mensŭla, ae, f. dim. id., a little table (ante-class. and post-Aug.), Plaut. Most. 1, 3, 150; Petr. 136; App. M. 2, 11, p. 119.

mensularius.full: mensŭlārĭus, ii, m. mensula, a money-changer (post-Aug.), Sen. Contr. 4, 24, 2; Dig. 42, 5, 24, § 2; 2, 11, 47, § 1.

mensura.full: mensūra. ae, f. metior, a measuring, measure (class.). Lit.: mensuram facere alicujus, Ov A. A. 3, 265: agere, to measure, survey, Plin. Ep. 10, 28, 5: inire. Col 5, 3: res (quae) pondere numero mensura constant, Gai. Inst. 2, 196.— Transf., a measure, by which any thing is measured: majore mensurā reddere, Cic. Off. 1, 15, 48: qui modus mensurae medimnus appellatur, kind of measure, Nep. Att. 2, 6: mensuras et pondera invenit Phidon Argivus, aut Palamedes, Plin. 7, 56, 57, § 198: ex aquā, i. e.

mensurabilis.full: mensūrābĭlis, e, adj. mensura, that can be measured, measurable (post-class.): spatium, Prud. Apoth. 881.—Hence, men-sūrābĭlĭter, adv., measurably, Aug. Specul. 20.

mensuralis.full: mensūrālis, e, adj. id., of or belonging to measuring, measuring- (post-class.): mensuralis linea, Sicul. Fl. p. 19 Goes.— Plur. as subst.: mensūrālia, ium, n., the title of a work by Varro, Prisc. p. 817 P.— Hence, adv.: mensūrālĭter, by measure (post-class.), Hyg. de Limit. p. 167 Goes.

mensuratio.full: mensūrātĭo, ōnis, f. mensuro, a measuring, mensuration (post-class.): jugeri, Auct. de Limit. p. 264 Goes.: agrorum, Jul. Vict. Art. Rhet. 3, 5; p. 379, 12 Halm.

mensurator.full: mensūrātor, is, m. id., a measurer (late Lat.), Hier. in Psa. 44.

mensurnus.full: mensurnus, a, um, adj. mensis, monthly (for the more usual menstruus): spatium, * Cic. Inv. 1, 26, 39 (acc. to Prisc. p 595 P.; B. and K. menstrui spatii); so Novat. de Trinit.: divisiones. Cypr. Ep. 34.

mensuro.full: mensūro, 1, v. a. mensura, to measure (post-class.): fossa mensuratur, Veg. Mil. 1, 25; Gromat. Vet. p. 232, 9: fines, Hilar. in Psa. 15, 8: longitudinem, Vulg. Ezech. 45, 3; 48, 30 al.— Trop., to measure, estimate: suas opes viresque suorum, Coripp. Laud. Just. 3, 372.—Hence, mensūratē, adv., by measurement, Cassiod. in Psa. 69, 5.

mensus1.full: mensus, a, um, Part., from metior.
mensus1.short: mensus, a, um, Part., from metior.

mensus2.full: mensus. ūs (only in abl. sing.), m. [metior], a measuring, measure, v. l. ap. App. de Mundo, p. 253 dub.

menta.full: menta (mentha), ae, f., = μίντη, mint, acc. to the myth, so called from Menthe or Minthe, a nymph who was changed by Proserpine into this plant, Ov. M. 10, 729; 8, 663; Plin. 19, 8, 47, § 159: ructatrix, Mart. 10, 48, 10: serpens, Col. poët. 10, 119. —Prov.: decimatis mentham et rutam et omne olus, et praeteritis judicium, i. e. carefully attend to trifles and neglect weighty matters, Vulg. Luc. 11, 42; id. Matt. 23, 23.
menta.short: menta (mentha), ae, f., = μίντη, mint, acc.

mentagra.full: mentā^gra, ae, f. mentum - ἄγρα, formed after pod-agra; lit., chin-disease, an eruption, tetter on the chin (i. q. lichen, q. v.), Plin. 26, 1, 2, § 2.

mentalis.full: mentālis, e, adj. mens, mental (late Lat.): mentalibus oculis, Ps.-Aug. ad Frat. Erem. Serm. 19.

mentastrum.full: mentastrum, i, n. menta, wild mint, Plin. 19, 8, 47, § 159: silvestre, Col. 11, 3.

mentesanus.full: Mentēsānus, a, um, adj. Of or belonging to the city of Mentesa (Mentissa, Liv. 26, 17) in Hispania Baetica: ordo Mentesanus, Inscr. Grut. 384, 2.—In plur.: Mentesani Bastuli, Plin. 3, 3, 4, § 25.— Mentesani Oretani in Hispaniā Tarraconensi, Plin. 3, 3, 4, § 19; Liv. 26, 17.

mentiens.full: mentĭens, entis, Part., from mentior, q. v.
mentiens.short: mentĭens, entis, Part., from mentior, q.

mentigo.full: mentīgo, ĭnis, f. mentum, a kind of eruption, scab, on lambs (i. q. ostigo, q. v.), Col. 7, 5, 21.

mentio1.full: mentĭo, ōnis, f. from root man-, men-; v. memini, a calling to mind, a cursory speaking of, a making mention, mentioning, naming, mention: civitatis, Cic. Verr. 2, 5, 64, § 166: casu in eorum mentionem incidi, accidentally happened to mention them, id. Div. in Caecil. 15, 50: tui, mention of you, id. Att. 5, 9, 3: Graecorum, Juv. 3, 114.—With a foll. ut: mentionem fecit, ut reperirem, etc., Plaut. Cist. 1, 2, 15: mentione illatā a tribunis, ut liceret, Liv. 4, 1, 2; 4, 8, 4: mentionem facere ali

mentio2.full: mentĭo, ire, 4, v. n. (archaic collat. form of mentior, Prisc. 8, 6, 29, p. 799 P.): te mentire spirito sancto, v. l. for mentiri, Vulg. Act. 5, 3; for mentitus, pass. part., v. mentior fin., and cf. Neue, Formenl. 2, p. 297 sq.

mentior.full: mentĭor, ītus, 4 (fut. mentibitur, for mentietur, Plaut. Mil. 1, 1, 35; 2, 2, 99; v. Neue, Formenl. 2, p. 448), v. dep. n. and a. [prob. from root men-, whence mens, memini, q. v. Original meaning, to invent; hence], Neutr., to lie, cheat, deceive, etc.: mentiri palam, Plaut. Truc. 1, 2, 89: mentire, id. Poen. 3, 5, 18: adversus aliquem, id. Aul. 4, 7, 9: apud aliquem, id. Poen. 1, 1, 24: sibi, id. Am. 1, 2, 6: mihi, id. Capt. 3, 5, 46; Ter. Eun. 4, 4, 35: aperte, Cic. Ac. 2, 6, 18: in re aliquā

mentiosus.full: mentĭōsus, a, um, adj. menta, smelling strong of mint, Marc. Emp. 33.

mentitio.full: mentītĭo, ōnis, f. mentior, a lying, deception, Auct. Her. 3, 2, 3 dub.

mentitus.full: mentītus, a, um, Part., v. mentior fin. 2.

mento1.full: mento, ōnis, m. amplif. [mentum], one who has a long chin, long-chin, Arn. 3, 108.

mento2.full: Mento, ōnis, m. amplif. [id.], a Roman proper name. So C. Julius Mento, consul A. U. C. 323, Liv. 4, 26.

mentonomon.full: Mentonŏmon, i, n., a part of the shore of the German Ocean, Plin. 37, 2, 11, § 35 (better reading Metonomon, Jan.).
mentonomon.short: Mentonŏmon, i, n., a part of the shore of the German Ocean, Plin.

mentor.full: Mentor, ŏris, m., = Μέντωρ. The famous friend of Odysseus, Cic. Att. 9, 8, 2. — A celebrated artist in embossed work in metal, Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 18, § 38; Plin. 33, 12, 53, § 147.— Poet. transf., a Mentor-cup, a skilfully wrought drinking-vessel: rarae sine Mentore mensae, Juv. 8, 104: Mentora frangere, Mart. 11, 11, 5.— Hence, Mentŏrĕus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Mentor the artist, Mentorean: opus, Prop. 1, 14, 2: labores, Mart. 4, 39, 5.

mentula.full: mentŭla, ae, f., i. q. membrum virile, Cat. 20, 18, 21; 29, 14; 115, 8 et saep.; Mart. 6, 23, 2.

mentulatus.full: mentŭlātus, a, um, adj. mentula, having a mentula (rare).—Comp.: Priapo mentulatior, Auct. Priap. 37.

mentum1.full: mentum, i, n. root men-, min-, to project; cf.: minae, minari, etc., the chin of persons and animals; also, the chin with the hair that grows on it, the beard. Lit.: Herculis mentum paulo attritius, Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 43, § 94: attingere, Plin. 11, 45, 103, § 251: incana, Verg. A. 6, 809: caprarum, Plin. 8, 50, 76, § 204.— Transf., in archit., the projecting part of a cornice, which casts off the rain, the coping, Vitr. 4, 3, 6.

mentum2.full: mentum dicebant, quod nos commentum, Paul. ex Fest. p. 124 Müll.
mentum2.short: mentum dicebant, quod nos commentum, Paul.

menui.full: menui, the Indian name of a precious stone which the Greeks called xanthos, Plin. 37, 10, 60, § 169.
menui.short: menui, the Indian name of a precious stone which the Greeks called xanthos, Plin.

meo.full: mĕo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. n. kindr. with Sanscr. mī, to go, to go, to pass (poet. and in post-Aug. prose): quo simul meāris, Hor. C. 1, 4, 17: in orientem meavisse, Tac. A. 3, 34: meantes exercitus terrere, Quint. 8, 4, 3.— Trop., of inanim. and abstr. things: ita ut vix singula meent plaustra, Plin. 6, 14, 17, § 43: triremes, Tac. A. 4, 5: sidera, Ov. M. 15, 71: sol, Quint. 11, 2, 22: aura, id. 11, 3, 16: vapor per inane vacuum, Lucr. 2, 151: spiritus, Curt. 3, 5, 6: anima diversa in membra, Luc. 3

meopte.full: meopte, i. e. meo ipsius, v. meus.

mephiticus.full: mĕphītĭcus, a, um, adj. mephitis, mephitic, pestilential (post-class.): odor, Sid. Ep. 3, 13.

mephitis.full: mĕphītis, is, f., a noxious, pestilential exhalation from the ground, mephitis. Lit.: saevamque exhalat opaca mephitim, Verg. A. 7, 84: sulphureae, Pers. 3, 99.— Personified: Mĕphītis (Mĕfi-tis), is, f., a goddess who averts pestilential exhalations, Tac. H. 3, 34; Plin. 2, 93, 95, § 208; Inscr. Orell. 1795; cf. Serv. Verg. A. 7, 84: lucus Mephitis, Varr. L. L. 5, 7, § 49 Müll.: aedes, Paul. ex Fest. 351, 3.
mephitis.short: mĕphītis, is, f., a noxious, pestilential exhalation from the ground, mephitis.

mepte.full: mepte, i. e. me ipsum, Plaut. Men. 5, 8, 10.

meraculus.full: mĕrācŭlus (also sync., meraclus), a, um, adj. dim. [meracus], pretty pure, with very little mixture (post-Aug.): meraclo se percussit flore Libyco (al. meraco), Plaut. Cas. 3, 5, 15: vinum, Cels. 3, 19; Plin. 20, 19, 80, § 209.
meraculus.short: mĕrācŭlus (also sync., meraclus), a, um, adj.

meracus.full: mĕrācus, a, um, adj. merus, pure, unmixed, esp. of wine (class.). Lit.: vinum meracius, Cic. N. D. 3, 31, 78: uva, Prop. 2, 24 (3, 31), 27.— Transf., of other things: helleborum, Hor. Ep. 2, 2, 137; cf. Pers. 4, 16.— Trop.: libertas, Cic. Rep. 1, 43, 66: meracissimus scientiae fons, Sid. Ep. 3, 10.—Hence, adv.: mĕrācē, purely, without mixture (post-Aug.): minus, sed meracius bibere, Cels. 1, 3: rubere, Sol. 33, 18.—Transf.: purius, meracius amare, Sid. Ep. 4, 1.

meralis.full: mĕrālis, e, adj. id., pure, unmixed: calix, Marc. Emp. 27.

meratus.full: mĕrātus, a, um, adj., i. q. meracus, pure, Cael. Aur. Chron. 1, 1, 17 al.

mercabilis.full: mercābĭlis, e, adj. mercor, that can be bought, purchasable (poet.): meretrix, Ov. Am. 1, 10, 21.

mercalis.full: mercālis, e, adj. merx, for mercabilis, that can be bought, purchasable (postclass.): uxor, Cod. Just. 4, 7, 6.

mercans.full: mercans, antis, Part. and subst., v. mercor.

mercantia.full: mercantia, ae, f. mercor, trade (late Lat.), Ps.-Aug. ad Fratr. Erem. Serm. 3.

mercatilla.full: Mercātilla or Mercantilla, ae, f., a Roman proper name, Inscr. Marin. Iscriz. Alb. p. 73; Inscr. Mur. 1691, 6.
mercatilla.short: Mercātilla or Mercantilla, ae, f., a Roman proper name, Inscr.

mercatio.full: mercātĭo, ōnis, f. mercor, a dealing in wares, mercantile dealing (post-class.): pecunia in mercationibus perdita, in mercantile speculations, Gell. 3, 3, 14; Firm. Math. 3, 8 fin.

mercator.full: mercātor, ōris, m. id., a trader, merchant, esp. a wholesale dealer (opp. to caupo, a retailer; class.). Lit.: venalicii mercatoresque, Cic. Or. 70, 232: multi ad eos mercatores ventitant, Caes. B. G. 4, 3. — Transf. A dealer, speculator: non consules, sed mercatores provinciarum, Cic. post Red. in Sen. 4, 10.—Rarely of a petty dealer: vilis sacci mercator olentis, Juv. 14, 269.— A buyer, purchaser: signorum, Cic. Verr. 1, 20, 60: veneni, Juv. 13, 154.

mercatorius.full: mercātōrĭus, a, um, adj. mercator, mercantile (ante-class.): navis mercatoria, a merchant-vessel, Plaut. Bacch. 2, 3, 2.

mercatura.full: mercātūra, ae, f. mercor, trade, traffic, commerce (class.). Lit.: mercatura autem, si tenuis est, sordida putanda est; sin magna et copiosa, non est admodum vituperanda, Cic. Off. 1, 42, 151: mercaturas facere, to follow the pursuits of trade, Cic. Verr. 2, 5, 28, § 72.— Trop.: ad quos cum tanquam ad mercaturam bonarum artium sis profectus, to the purchase of, etc., Cic. Off. 3, 2, 6: utilitatum, id. N. D. 1, 44, 122.— Transf., goods, wares, merchandise (ante-Aug.), Plaut. Trin. 2, 2, 51.

mercatus.full: mercātus, ūs, m. id., trade, traffic, buying and selling (class.): apud aedem Veneris mercatus meretricius, Plaut. Poen. 1, 2, 129: turpissimus mercatus, Cic. Phil. 2, 3, 6: domesticus, id. ib. 3, 12, 30.— Transf., a place for trade, market-place. market, mart: postquam pater ad mercatum abiit, Plaut. Most. 4, 2, 55: frequens mercatus, Liv. 1, 30: mercatus conventusque Graeciae, Suet. Ner. 28: mercatu indicto, Cic. Verr. 2, 2, 53, § 133: Asiae Graeciaeque, Liv. 33, 32, 2; Tac. H. 3, 30: (Numa Po

mercedarius.full: mercēdārĭus, ii, m. merces, he who pays wages: ostende mercedarios tuos, Sen. Contr. 5, 33, 5 and 25; cf. Gloss. Isid. s. v., † 1. mercedonius.

mercedituum.full: mercēditŭum, mercenarium, quod mercede se tueatur, Paul. ex Fest. p. 124 Müll.
mercedituum.short: mercēditŭum, mercenarium, quod mercede se tueatur, Paul.

mercedonius1.full: mercēdŏnĭus, a, um, adj. 1. merces-do, of or belonging to the payment of wages: Mercedonios (dies) dixerunt a mercede solvendā, on which wages are paid, pay-days, Paul. ex Fest. p. 124 Müll.— Subst.: mercēdŏnĭus, ii, m., a payer of wages, paymaster: mercedonius, qui solvit mercedem; † mercedarius (an employer), qui dat mercedem pro labore sibi impenso, Gloss. Isid. 37.

mercedonius2.full: Mercēdŏnĭus or Mercēdī-nus, = Μερκηδόνιος, Μερκεδῖνος, mensis, an intercalary month of 22 or 23 days, inserted every two years in the calendar of Numa, Vet. Kalend. Rom. ap. Grut. 133; cf. so Laur. Lyd. de Mens. 4, 92.
mercedonius2.short: Mercēdŏnĭus or Mercēdī-nus, = Μερκηδόνιος, Μερκεδῖνος, mensis, an intercalary month of 22 or 23 days, inserted every two years in the calendar of Numa, Vet.

mercedula.full: mercēdŭla, ae, f. dim. 1. merces. Small wages, poor pay (class.): infimi homines mercedula adducti, Cic. de Or. 1, 45, 198: isto modo nec medico quicquam debere te nisi mercedulam dicis nec praeceptori, Sen. Ben. 6, 15, 1.— Hire, rent, income: constituere mercedulas praediorum, Cic. Att. 13, 11, 1.

mercenarius.full: mercēnārĭus (in old MSS. written mercennarius), a, um, adj. id., that does any thing for reward or pay; hired for money, wages, or pay; paid, hired, mercenary (opp. to gratuitus, without pay, gratuitous). Adj. Of persons: comes, Cic. Pis. 21, 49: miles, Liv. 24, 49: testes, hired, bribed, Cic. Fam. 3, 11, 3: praetor, Cic. Verr. 2, 5, 21, § 54.— Of inanim. and abstr. things: mercenaria arma, Liv. 30, 8: liberalitas gratuitane est, an mercenaria? Cic. Leg. 1, 18, 48: ancilla mercenariae stipis, Pl

merces1.full: merces, ēdis (irreg. acc. mercem, Claud. 6; Cons. Hon. 578), f. mereo, what is deserved or earned; hence, hire, pay, wages, salary, fee, reward, etc. (syn.: pretium, stipendium; class.). Lit.: manuum mercede inopiam tolerare, the wages of manual labor, Sall. C. 37, 7: ne ars tanta abduceretur ad mercedem atque quaestum, Cic. Div. 1, 41, 92: operae, Cic. Verr. 2, 1, 56, § 147: veterum officiorum, Juv. 5, 13: uti ab Arvernis Sequanisque Germani mercede arcesserentur, Caes. B. G. 1, 31: haec merces

merces2.full: merces, for merx, v. h. v.

mercimonium.full: mercĭmōnĭum, ii, n. merx, goods, wares, merchandise (ante-class. and postAug.): in vostris mercimoniis Emundis vendundisque, Plaut. Am. prol. 1; id. Most. 3, 3, 9; 12: quid agit meum mercimonium apud te? id. Curc. 4, 4, 8: videre cupio nostrum mercimonium, Turp. ap. Non. 213, 8: per tabernas, quibus id mercimonium inerat, quo flamma alitur, Tac. A. 15, 38.

mercor.full: mercor, ātus, 1 (archaic form, mercassitur for mercatus fuerit, Inscr. Grut. 512, 20.—Inf. mercarier for mercari, Hor. S. 2, 3, 24), v. dep. n. and a. [id.], to trade, traffic, deal in commodities (absol., Plaut. Merc. prol. 82), to buy, purchase something from a person (cf. nundinor). Lit., constr. with aliquid ab or de aliquo, with abl. or gen. of the price (class.): aliquid ab aliquo, Cic. Off. 1, 42, 150: fundum de pupillo, id. Fl. 20, 46: aliquid tanto pretio, id. Rosc. Am. 46, 133: hortos
mercor.short: mercor, ātus, 1 (archaic form, mercassitur for mercatus fuerit, Inscr.

mercurialis.full: Mercŭrĭālis, e, adj. Mercurius, of or belonging to the god Mercury: caduceum, App. M. 11, p. 262: unde frequentia Mercuriale Imposuere mihi cognomen compita, called me Mercury (as being a skilful man of business), Hor. S. 2, 3, 25.—Subst.: Mercŭrĭāles, ium, m., the name of a corporation of traders: Mercuriales M. Furium Flaccum de collegio ejecerunt, Cic. Q. Fr. 2, 5, 2.—With reference to Mercury as the god of scholars: Faunus, Mercurialium Custos virorum, Hor. C. 2, 17, 28.— Of or belonging to

mercuriolus.full: Mercŭrĭŏlus, i, m. dim. id., a little image of Mercury, App. Mag. p. 314, 16; 315, 4.

mercurius.full: Mercŭrĭus, ii, m., = Ἑρμῆς, Mercury, the son of Jupiter and Maia, the messenger of the gods; as a herald, the god of dexterity; in speaking, of eloquence; the bestower of prosperity; the god of traders and thieves; the presider over roads, and conductor of departed souls to the Lower World: Mercurius a mercibus est dictus. Hunc etenim negotiorum omnium aestimabant esse deum, Paul. ex Fest. p. 124 Müll.; Cic. N. D. 3, 22 sq.; Cic. Verr. 2, 5, 72, § 185; id. Arat. 277; Caes. B. G. 6, 17; Verg. A.
mercurius.short: Mercŭrĭus, ii, m., = Ἑρμῆς, Mercury, the son of Jupiter and Maia, the messenger of the gods;

merda.full: merda, ae, f. etym. dub.; cf. Gr. μορύσσειν, to defile, dung, ordure, excrement: corvorum, Hor. S. 1, 8, 37; Mart. 3, 17, 6; Veg. 2, 8, 4; Phaedr. 4, 17, 25.

merdaceus.full: merdācĕus, a, um, adj. merda, defiled with excrement (post-class.), Auct. Priap. 69, 8; Anthol. Lat. 3, 160, 6.

merdaleus.full: merdālĕus, a, um, adj. id., = merdaceus, q. v., Auct. Priap. 68, 8.

merenda1.full: mĕrenda, ae, f. mereo, q. v., an afternoon luncheon, taken between four and five o'clock (ante- and post-class.): merendam antiqui dicebant pro prandio, quod scilicet medio die caperetur, Paul. ex Fest. p. 123 Müll.: merenda dicitur cibus post meridiem qui datur, Non. 28, 32; Plaut. Most. 4, 2, 49; Afran. ap. Non. 28, 33: serae hora merendae, Calp. Ecl. 5, 60; cf. Isid. Orig. 20, 2, 12.—Also of feed or medicine for a beast: Cyprio bovi merendam, Ennius cum dixit, significat id, quod solet fieri

merenda2.full: Merenda, ae, m., a Roman surname: T. Antonius Merenda, a consul, A. U. C. 304, Liv. 3, 35.
merenda2.short: Merenda, ae, m., a Roman surname: T.

merendarius.full: mĕrendārĭus, ii, m. 1. merenda, one who takes an afternoon luncheon (postAug.), Sen. Contr. 5, 33 fin. dub. (al. mercenarios).

merendo.full: mĕrendo, 1, v. n. id., to take an afternoon luncheon (late Lat.): merenda est cibus, qui declinante die sumitur, quasi post meridiem edenda: Hinc merendare, quasi meridie edere, Isid. Orig. 20, 2, 12.

merens.full: mĕrens, entis, Part. and P. a. of mereo, q. v.

mereo.full: mĕrĕo, ŭi, ĭtum, 2, v. a., and mĕrĕor, ĭtus, 2, v. dep. cf. Gr. μέρος, μείρομαι, μόρος, etc.; hence, to receive one's share; cf. II. below, to deserve, merit, to be entitled to, be worthy of a thing; constr. with acc., with ut, with ne, with inf., and absol. In gen. With acc.: mereri praemia, Caes. B. G. 7, 34: laudem, id. ib. 1, 40, 5; Cic. Div. in Caecil. 18, 60: nec minimum decus, Hor. A. P. 286: amorem, Quint. 6 prooem.: favorem aut odium, id. 4, 1, 44: gratiam nullam, Liv. 45, 24, 7; Quint.

meretricabilis.full: mĕrĕtrīcābĭlis, e, and mĕrĕtrī-cārĭus, a, um, adj. meretrix, = meretricius, Cassiod. de Amic. 22, 46; id. ib. prol. § 55.
meretricabilis.short: mĕrĕtrīcābĭlis, e, and mĕrĕtrī-cārĭus, a, um, adj.

meretricius.full: mĕrē^trīcĭus, a, um, adj. meretrix, of or pertaining to harlots or prostitutes, meretricious. Adj. (class.): meretricia ornamenta, Plaut. Truc. 2, 2, 63: quaestus, Cic. Phil. 2, 18, 44: disciplina, Cic. Verr. 2, 3, 3, § 6: domus, a courtesan's house, Ter. Eun. 5, 5, 18: amores, Cic. Cael. 20, 48.— Subst.: mĕrē^trīcĭum, ii, n. The art of a courtesan: inmutari blandimentis, hortamentis, ceteris meretriciis, Plaut. Truc. 2, 2, 63.— The trade of a harlot: meretricium facere, Suet. Calig. 40.—Hence,

meretricor.full: mĕrĕtrīcor, ātus, 1, v. dep. id., to deal with harlots: meretricor ἑταιρεύω, Gloss. Philox.

meretricula.full: mĕrē^trīcŭla, ae, f. dim. id., a public prostitute, courtesan (class.): meretricula Leontium, Cic. N. D. 1, 33, 93; Hor. S. 2, 7, 46; Quint. 11, 3, 74.

meretrix.full: mĕrē^trix, īcis (gen. plur. meretricium, Plaut. Cas. 3, 3, 22: meretricum, id. Ep. 2, 2, 29; Ov. A. A. 1, 435), f. mereo; she who earns moncy; hence, a prostitute, harlot, courtesan: ita sunt hic meretrices omnes elecebrae argentariae, Plaut. Men. 2, 3, 26: meretricem indigne deperit, id. Bacch. 3, 3, 66: proterva meretrix procaxque, Cic Cael. 20, 49: meretrix inter multos se dividit, Sen. Ben. 1, 14, 4: stat meretrix certo cuivis mercabilis aere, Ov. Am. 1, 10, 21: Augusta, i. e. Messalina, Juv

mergae.full: mergae, ārum, f. root marg-, to clear away; cf.: ἀμέργω, ἀμέλγω, mulgo, amurca, a two-pronged pitchfork, with which corn, when cut, was made into heaps: mergae furculae, quibus acervi frugum fiunt, dictae a volucribus mergis, quia, ut illi se in aquam mergunt, dum pisces persequuntur, sic messores eas in fruges demergunt, ut elevare possint manipulos, Paul. ex Fest, p. 124 Müll.: mergas datus, ut hortum fodiat, Plaut. Poen. 5, 2, 58: multi mergis, alii pectinibus spicam ipsam legunt, Col. 2, 21,

merges.full: mergĕs, ĭtis, f. mergae. A sheaf: cerealis mergite culmi, Verg. G. 2, 517.— I. q. mergae, a two-pronged pitchfork, Plin. 18, 30, 72, § 296.

mergito.full: mergĭto, 1, v. a. freq. [mergo], to dip in, immerse: ter mergitamur, i. e. baptizamur (al. mersitamur), Tert. de Cor. Milit. 3.

mergo.full: mergo, si, sum, 3, v. a. cf. Sanscr. madsh-, majan, to dip; Zend, masga, marrow; Germ. Mark; Engl. marrow, to dip, dip in, immerse; absol. also to plunge into water, to sink. Lit. (class.): eos (pullos) mergi in aquam jussit, Cic. N. D. 2, 3, 7: aves, quae se in mari mergunt, id. ib. 2, 49, 124: putealibus undis, Ov. Ib. 391: Stygia undā, id. M. 10, 697: prodigia indomitis merge sub aequoribus, Tib. 2, 5, 80: ab hoc (the sword-fish) perfossas naves mergi, Plin. 32, 2, 6, § 15: mersa navis omnes

mergulus1.full: mergŭlus, i, m. mergo, the wick of a lamp: mergulus, ἐλλύχνιον, Gloss. Gr. and Lat.

mergulus2.full: mergŭlus, i, m. dim. mergus, a diver, a kind of bird, Vulg. Lev. 11, 17; id. Deut. 14, 17.

mergus.full: mergus, i, m. mergo. A diver, a kind of water-fowl, Varr. L. L. 5, § 78 Müll.: praesagiunt pluviam mergi, Plin. 18, 35, 87, § 362: mergi maria fugientes, id. ib.; Ov. M. 8, 625; cf.: aequor amat; nomenque tenet, quia mergitur illo, id. ib. 11, 795; Hor. Epod. 10, 22.—Jestingly: mergus agrarius, of one who is eager to possess lands, Capitol. Pertin. 9.— A vine-layer, Col. 4, 15, 1; Pall. 3, 16, 1.

meribibulus.full: mĕrĭbĭbŭlus, a, um, adj. merumbibulus, wine-bibbing (eccl. Lat.): puella, Aug. Conf. 9, 8.

merica.full: merica (moer-), sc. vitis or uva, an unknown kind of vine, v. l. ap. Col. 3, 2, 27; Plin. 14, 2. 4, § 35 (al. metica; Jan. mettica).

meridialis.full: mĕrīdĭālis, e, adj. meridies, of midday (post-class.): ventus (al. meridionalis), Gell. 2, 22, 14: temperatura, Tert. Anim. 25.

meridianus.full: mĕrīdĭānus, a, um, adj. id., of or belonging to mid-day, mid-day-. (Class.) Tempus, mid-day, noon, Cic. de Or. 3, 5, 17: sol, Plin. 12, 19, 42, § 86: somnus, id. Ep. 9, 40, 2; Lact. 2, 9, 9.—Hence, as subst.: mĕ-rīdĭāni, sc. gladiatores, mid-day combatants, gladiators who fought at mid-day, Suet. Claud. 34.—In abl. adv.: mĕrīdĭā-nō, sc. tempore, at mid-day, Plin. 2, 26, 25, § 96; 9, 8, 8, § 25.— Transf., of or belonging to the south or south side, southern, southerly, meridional: ager spectat ad

meridiatio.full: mĕrīdĭātĭo, ōnis, f. meridio, a midday nap, siesta (class.): et lucubrationes detraxi, et meridiationes addidi, Cic. Div. 2, 68, 142.

meridies.full: mĕrīdĭes, ēi, m. (f. ap. Amm. 26, 1, 9) [for medidies from medius-dies], mid-day, noon. Lit.: meridies ab eo, quod medius dies, Varr. L. L. 6, § 4 Müll.: ipsum meridiem cur non medidiem? credo, quod erat insuavius, Cic. Or. 47, 158; Quint. 1, 6, 30; Prisc. p. 551 P.: circiter meridiem, Plaut. Most. 3, 1, 52: ante meridiem, post meridiem, Cic. Tusc. 2, 3, 9: diem diffindere insiticio somno meridie, to take a nap at noon, Varr. R. R. 1, 2, 5: inclamare horam esse tertiam, itemque meridiem, Varr. L

meridio.full: mĕrīdĭo, 1, v. n., and mĕrīdĭor, 1, v. dep. meridies, to take a mid-day nap or siesta: jube, ad te veniam meridiatum, Cat. 32, 3: meridiari ante cibum, Cels. 1, 2: dum ea meridiaret, Suet. Calig. 38: inter acervos eorum meridiati sunt, i. e. have taken their ease, Vulg. Job, 24, 11.

meridionalis.full: mĕrīdĭōnālis, e, adj. id., southern, meridional (post-class.): plaga, Lact. 2, 9 (dub.; al. meridiana): signum, Firm. Math. 2, 12.

meridionarius.full: mĕrīdĭōnārĭus, a, um, adj. id., of or belonging to mid-day, meridional (postclass.): gloria quoius lemulcatus (lemniscatus) meridionaria, Tit. ap. App. de Orthogr. p. 130 Mai.

merinas.full: Merīnas, ātis, adj., of or belonging to the city of Merinum, in Apulia: Merinates ex Gargano, Plin. 3, 11, 16, § 105.
merinas.short: Merīnas, ātis, adj., of or belonging to the city of Merinum, in Apulia: Merinates ex Gargano, Plin.

meriones.full: Mērĭŏnes, ae, m., = Μηριόνης, a charioteer of Idomeneus, who piloted his ships from Crete to Troy, Ov. M. 13, 359; Hor. C. 1, 6, 15; 1, 15, 26.
meriones.short: Mērĭŏnes, ae, m., = Μηριόνης, a charioteer of Idomeneus, who piloted his ships from Crete to Troy, Ov.

merito2.full: mĕrĭto, āvi, ātum, 1, v. freq. a. mereo. * To earn, gain: vilicus, qui sestertia dena meritāsset, Cic. Verr. 2, 3, 50, § 119: Roscius histrio HS. D. annua meritāsse proditur, Plin. 7, 39, 40, § 129.— To serve for pay, to serve as a soldier, be a soldier: meritavere Cato ait pro meruere, Paul. ex Fest. p. 152 Müll.: Siculas meritare per oras, Sil. 10, 656.

meritorius.full: mĕrĭtōrĭus, a, um, adj. id., of or belonging to the earning of money, by which money is earned, for which money is paid, that brings in money (class.). In gen.: vehicula, Suet. Calig. 39: balinea, Plin. Ep. 2, 17: cenaculum, Suet. Vit. 7: artificia, Sen. Ep. 88, 1: salutatio, by which one hopes to obtain money, interested, id. Brev. Vit. 14, 3: in meritorio stabulo, Paul. Sent. 2, 31, 16.— Subst.: mĕrĭtōria, ōrum, n., places or rooms which are let out for a short time, Juv. 3, 234: facere, to le

meritum.full: mĕrĭtum, i, n., v. mereo fin. B. 1.

meritus.full: mĕrĭtus, a, um, Part. and P. a., from mereo, q. v. fin. B.

mermeros.full: Mermĕros, i, m., = Μέρμερος, one of the Centaurs present at the wedding of Pirithoüs, Ov. M. 12, 305.
mermeros.short: Mermĕros, i, m., = Μέρμερος, one of the Centaurs present at the wedding of Pirithoüs, Ov.

mermessius.full: Mermessĭus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to the city of Mermessus, in Phrygia, Mermessian: quicquid Mermessia dixit, i. e. the Hellespontine Sibyl, Tib. 2, 5, 67 (Müller, Marpesia).
mermessius.short: Mermessĭus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to the city of Mermessus, in Phrygia, Mermessian: quicquid Mermessia dixit, i.

mero.full: Mĕro, ōnis, m. merum, the wine-bibber, a nickname bestowed on the emperor Tiberius Claudius Nero, in allusion to his drinking propensities: propter nimiam vini aviditatem, pro Tiberio Biberius, pro Claudio Caldius, pro Nerone Mero vocabatur, Suet. Tib. 42.

merobibus.full: mĕrōbĭbus, a, um, adj. merum-bibo, that drinks wine unmixed (which among the ancients was the practice only of drunkards): anus multibiba atque merobiba, Plaut. Curc. 1, 1, 77.

meroe.full: Mĕrŏē, ēs, f., = Μερόη, a large and celebrated island of the Nile, in Ethiopia, now the province of Atbar, Mela, 1, 9, 2; Plin. 2, 73, 75, § 184; Ov. F. 4, 570; Luc. 10, 303; Juv. 6, 528.—Transf., in a lusus verbb. with merum, of a tippling woman (cf. merobibus), Aus. Epigr. 20.—Hence, Mĕ-rŏētĭcus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Meroë, Meroëtic: ebenus Meroëtica, Luc. 10, 117 Cort. (al. Mareotica).
meroe.short: Mĕrŏē, ēs, f., = Μερόη, a large and celebrated island of the Nile, in Ethiopia, now the province of Atbar, Mela, 1, 9, 2;

merois.full: mĕrŏis, ĭdis, f., = μεροΐς, a plant growing in Meroë, Plin. 24, 17, 102, § 163.
merois.short: mĕrŏis, ĭdis, f., = μεροΐς, a plant growing in Meroë, Plin.

merope.full: Mĕrŏpē, ēs, f., = Μερόπη, the mythic name of several persons. A daughter of Atlas and Pleione, one of the Pleiades, whose star is more obscure than the rest, because she wedded Sisyphus, a mortal, Ov. F. 4, 175. — A daughter of Sol and Clymene, and sister of Phaëthon, Hyg. Fab. 152.— The wife of Megareus, Hyg. Fab. 185.
merope.short: Mĕrŏpē, ēs, f., = Μερόπη, the mythic name of several persons.

merops1.full: Mĕrops, ŏpis, m., = Μέροψ. A king of Ethiopia, husband of Clymene, and reputed to be the father of Phaëthon, Ov. M. 1, 763; id.
