Tr. 3, 4, 30.— A king of the isle of Cos, from whose name its inhabitants in early times were called Meropes, Quint. 8, 6, 71.— A Roman proper name, Inscr. Mur. 887, 5.

merops2.full: mĕrops, ŏpis, m., = μέροψ, a bird that devours bees; hence also called apiastra, the bee-eater, Verg. G. 4, 14; cf. Plin. 10, 33, 51, § 99.
merops2.short: mĕrops, ŏpis, m., = μέροψ, a bird that devours bees;

merosus.full: mĕrōsus, a, um, adj. merus, pure, unmixed (post-class.): vinum, Agroet. de Orthogr. p. 2273 P.

mersio.full: mersĭo, ōnis, f. mergo, a dipping in, immersion: mersio, βύθισις, Gloss. Philox.

mersito.full: mersĭto, 1, v. freq. a. id., to dip in, immerse (post-class.): nares in bibendo, Sol. 45, 18.

merso.full: merso, āvi, ātum, 1, v. freq. a. id., to dip in, immerse (poet. and in post-Aug. prose). Lit.: balantumque gregem fluvio mersare salubri, Verg. G. 1, 272: balneo infertur, calida aqua mersatur, Tac. A. 15, 69.— Trop., to overwhelm: rerum copia mersat, drowns, destroys, Lucr. 5, 1008: mersor civilibus undis, plunge myself, Hor. Ep. 1, 1, 16.— Pass.: mersari, to set, of the stars, Mart. Cap. 8, § 844; cf. merto.

mersura.full: Mersūra, ae, f. merso (eccl. Lat.), Cassiod. in Psa. 54, 25.

mersus.full: mersus, a, um, Part., from mergo.
mersus.short: mersus, a, um, Part., from mergo.

merthryx.full: merthryx, ygis, f., a false reading for myrtis, Plin. 26, 11, 68, § 108.
merthryx.short: merthryx, ygis, f., a false reading for myrtis, Plin.

merto.full: merto, 1, v. freq. a. mergo, a collat. form of merso, to immerse, overwhelm (anteclass.): mertat pro mersat dicebant, Paul. ex Fest. p. 124 Müll.; cf. Quint. 1, 4, 14: quos hic non mertet metus, Att. ap. Non. 138, 33; 138, 2.

merula1.full: mĕrŭla, ae, f. (post-class. collat. form mĕrŭlus, i, m., Auct. Carm. Philom. 13), a blackbird, ousel, merle. Lit.: evolare merulas, Cic. Fin. 5, 15, 42: ut merula, quia sola volat, quasi mera volans nominaretur, Quint. 1, 6, 38; cf. Plin. 10, 29, 42, § 80; 10, 30, 45, § 87; 10, 53, 74, § 147.— Transf. A fish, the sea-carp: merulae virentes, Ov. Hal. 114; cf. Plin. 32, 11, 53, § 149.— A kind of hydraulic machine that produced a sound like the note of the blackbird, Vitr. 10, 12.

merula2.full: Mĕrŭla, ae, m., a Roman surname, e. g. Cn. Cornelius Merula, Liv. 33, 55.— L. Cornelius Merula, flamen Dialis, Vel. 2, 20; Val. Max. 9, 12, 5; Tac. A. 3, 58, 2.
merula2.short: Mĕrŭla, ae, m., a Roman surname, e.

merula3.full: Mĕrŭla, ae, m., a river of Liguria, now Arosia, Plin. 3, 5, 7, § 48.
merula3.short: Mĕrŭla, ae, m., a river of Liguria, now Arosia, Plin.

merulator.full: mĕrŭlātor, ōris, m. mero, a winedrinker, Inscr. Mur. 1442, 5.

merulentus.full: mĕrŭlentus, a, um, adj. merum, drunken, intoxicated (post-class.): Pierides, Fulg. Myth. praef.

merulinus.full: Mĕrŭlīnus, i, m., a Roman surname, Inscr. Raym. Guarin. Comm. 7, p. 41.
merulinus.short: Mĕrŭlīnus, i, m., a Roman surname, Inscr.

merus.full: mĕrus, a, um, adj. root mar-, to gleam; cf.: μάρμαρος, marmor, mare; hence, bright, pure, pure, unmixed, unadulterated, esp. of wine not mixed with water: merum antiqui dicebant solum: at nunc merum purum appellamus, Paul. ex Fest. p. 124 Müll. Lit.: vinum merum, Varr. ap. Non. 4, 295: vina, Ov. M. 15, 331.—Of other things: argentum merum, Plaut. As. 1, 3, 3: undae, Ov. M. 15, 323: lac, id. F. 4, 369: gustus, Col. 3, 21: claror, clear, unclouded, Plaut. Most. 3, 1, 111: mero meridie, Petr. 37.—H

merx.full: merx, cis (nom. sing. merces, Sall. Fragm. ap. Charis. p. 27 P.), f. mereo, goods, wares, commodities, merchandise (class.): invendibili merce oportet ultro emptorem adducere: Proba merx facile emptorem reperit, Plaut. Poen. 1, 2, 128: fallaces et fucosae, Cic. Rab. Post. 14, 40: peregrina et delicata, Plin. Ep. 4, 14, 1: femineae, for women, Ov. M. 13, 165: esculenta, eatables, victuals, Col. 11, 3: navem mercibus implere, Juv. 14, 288: sarmenta quoque in merce sunt, are an article of merchandi

mesa.full: mĕsa, ae, f., = μέση, middle, pure Lat. media (post-Aug.).—Of hemp: tria ejus (cannabis) genera: laudatissima est e medio, quae mesa vocatur, the middle sort, Plin. 19, 9, 56, § 174.† † mĕsancŭlon, i, n. (mĕsancŭla, ae, f.), = μεσάγκυλον, a javelin, with a thong (acc. to others, a poise or bent handle) attached to the middle, Gell. 10, 25; cf.: mesanculum, teli missilis genus, Paul. ex Fest. p. 125 Müll.
mesa.short: mĕsa, ae, f., = μέση, middle, pure Lat.

mesauloe.full: mesauloe (trisyl.), ōn, f., = μέσαυλοι.—In archit., narrow passages between two rooms or walls: inter duo autem peristylia itinera sunt, quae mesauloe dicuntur, Vitr. 6, 7 (10), 5; cf. andron.
mesauloe.short: mesauloe (trisyl.), ōn, f., = μέσαυλοι.—In archit., narrow passages between two rooms or walls: inter duo autem peristylia itinera sunt, quae mesauloe dicuntur, Vitr.

mese.full: mĕsē, ēs, f., = μέση, the middle note, the note A, Vitr. 5, 4, 5; 5, 5, 2.
mese.short: mĕsē, ēs, f., = μέση, the middle note, the note A, Vitr.

mesembria.full: Mĕsembrĭa, ae, f., = Μεσημβρία, a city in Thrace, on the Black Sea, now Missiori, Mel. 2, 2, 5; Plin. 4, 11, 18, § 45.— Hence, Mĕsembrĭăcus, a, um, adj., Mesembrian, Ov. Tr. 1, 10, 37.
mesembria.short: Mĕsembrĭa, ae, f., = Μεσημβρία, a city in Thrace, on the Black Sea, now Missiori, Mel.

mesene.full: Mĕsēnē, ēs, f., = Μεσήνη, the midland, a name of the district of Babylonia, Plin. 6, 27, 31, § 129; Amm. 24, 3, 12.
mesene.short: Mĕsēnē, ēs, f., = Μεσήνη, the midland, a name of the district of Babylonia, Plin.

meses.full: mĕses, ae, m., = μέσης, the northnortheast wind, between boreas and caecias, Plin. 2, 47, 46, § 120.
meses.short: mĕses, ae, m., = μέσης, the northnortheast wind, between boreas and caecias, Plin.

mesobrachys.full: mĕsŏbrăchys, m., = μεσόβραχυς (sc. pes), a poetical foot of five syllables, of which only the middle one is short (e. g. pulcherrĭmarum; opp. to mesomacros), Diom. p. 479 P.

mesochorus.full: mĕsŏchŏrus, i, m., = μεσόχορος, one who stands in the middle of a chorus (of dancers or singers) to lead it, a chorusleader (post-class.): cum mesochorus dedit signum, Plin. Ep. 2, 14, 7; Sid. Ep. 1, 2; Schol. Juv. 11, 172.
mesochorus.short: mĕsŏchŏrus, i, m., = μεσόχορος, one who stands in the middle of a chorus (of dancers or singers) to lead it, a chorusleader (post-class.): cum mesochorus dedit signum, Plin.

mesogites.full: Mĕsŏgītes, ae, m., a sort of wine from Mesogis (Messogis), a mountain of Lydia, Plin. 14, 7, 9, § 75.
mesogites.short: Mĕsŏgītes, ae, m., a sort of wine from Mesogis (Messogis), a mountain of Lydia, Plin.

mesoides.full: mĕsŏīdes, is, f., = μεσοειδής, a musical modulation (post-class.): mesoides, quae tonos aequales, mediosque custodit, Mart. Cap. 9, § 965 sq.
mesoides.short: mĕsŏīdes, is, f., = μεσοειδής, a musical modulation (post-class.): mesoides, quae tonos aequales, mediosque custodit, Mart.

mesolabium.full: mĕsŏlăbĭum, ii, n., = μεσολάβιον, a mathematical instrument for finding mean proportional lines, a mesolabe, Vitr. 9, 3, 14.
mesolabium.short: mĕsŏlăbĭum, ii, n., = μεσολάβιον, a mathematical instrument for finding mean proportional lines, a mesolabe, Vitr.

mesoleucos.full: mĕsŏleucos, i, m., = μεσόλευκος. A black precious stone with a white stripe, Plin. 37, 10, 63, § 174.— A plant, Plin. 27, 11, 77, § 102.

mesomacros.full: mĕsŏmăcros, i, m., = μεσόμακρος (sc. pes), a poetical foot of five syllables, of which only the middle one is long (e. g. avidissimus; opp. mesobrachys), Diom. p. 478 P.

mesomelas.full: mĕsŏmĕlas, ănos, f., = μεσομέλας, a white precious stone with a black stripe, Plin. 37, 10, 63, § 174.
mesomelas.short: mĕsŏmĕlas, ănos, f., = μεσομέλας, a white precious stone with a black stripe, Plin.

mesonauta.full: mĕsŏnauta, ae, m., = μεσοναύτης, a seaman who ranked between the pilot and the rowers, Pomp. ap. Ulp. Dig. 4, 9, 1, § 2.
mesonauta.short: mĕsŏnauta, ae, m., = μεσοναύτης, a seaman who ranked between the pilot and the rowers, Pomp.

mesonyctius.full: mĕsŏnyctĭus, a, um, adj., μεσονύκτιος, of midnight: afflatus, Isid. 5, 30, 4.— Hence, subst.: † mĕsŏnyctĭum, ii, n., = μεσονύκτιον, midnight (post-class.): CVIVS MESONYCTIVM FACTVM EST V. ID. DEC., i. e. midnight apparition, Inscr. Mur. 333.
mesonyctius.short: mĕsŏnyctĭus, a, um, adj., μεσονύκτιος, of midnight: afflatus, Isid.

mesopotamia.full: Mĕsŏpŏtămĭa, ae, f., = Μεσοποταμία, a country of Asia, between the Euphrates and Tigris, now called Al-Jezireh, Cic. N. D. 2, 52, 130; Isid. 13, 21, 10; Mel. 1, 11, 1; Plin. 5, 12, 13, § 66; Sall. H. 4, 51 Dietsch. —Hence, Mĕsŏpŏtămĭus, a, um, adj. (also written Mĕsŏpŏtămēnus), Mesopotamian (post-class.): milites, Val. ap. Vop. Aur. 11: Mesopotameni homines, Sall. H. 4, 53 Dietsch.—In plur. subst.: Mĕsŏpŏ-tămēsii, ōrum, m., the Mesopotamians, Spart. Hadr. 21, 12; Schol. Juv. 1, 104.† † mesŏpўlus
mesopotamia.short: Mĕsŏpŏtămĭa, ae, f., = Μεσοποταμία, a country of Asia, between the Euphrates and Tigris, now called Al-Jezireh, Cic.

mesosphaerum.full: mĕsosphaerum, i, n., = μεσόσφαιρον, a kind of nard with middle-sized leaves (v. hadrosphaerum and microsphaerum), Plin. 12, 12, 26, § 44.
mesosphaerum.short: mĕsosphaerum, i, n., = μεσόσφαιρον, a kind of nard with middle-sized leaves (v.

mespilum.full: mespĭlum, i, n., = μέσπιλον. A medlar, Plin. 15, 20, 22, § 84; Pall. Mart. 10, 19 and 22.— A medlar-tree, Pall. Insit. 69.

mespilus.full: mespĭlus, i, or mespĭla, ae, f., = μεσπίλη, a medlar-tree, Plin. 17, 10, 13, § 67; Pall. 3, 25, 32.— A medlar, Pall. de Insit. 69 and 105.
mespilus.short: mespĭlus, i, or mespĭla, ae, f., = μεσπίλη, a medlar-tree, Plin.

messalina.full: Messālīna or Messallīna, ae, f. The profligate wife of the emperor Claudius, daughter of M. Valerius Messalla Barbatus, Suet. Claud. 17; 26; Tac. A. 11, 1 sq.; Juv. 10, 333; cf. id. 6, 116 al.— The wife of the emperor Nero, Suet. Ner. 35; id. Oth. 10; Tac. A. 15, 68.

messalinus.full: Messālīnus (Messallīn-), i, m., a Roman surname, Tac. A. 2, 32; 4, 20; 5, 3; 3, 18; 34; id. Agr. 45; Plin. Ep. 4, 22, 5.
messalinus.short: Messālīnus (Messallīn-), i, m., a Roman surname, Tac.

messalla.full: Messalla (less correctly Messāla), ae, m., a Roman surname in the gens Valeria: Corvinus primus Messanam vicit, et pri mus ex familiā Valeriorum, urbis captae in se translato nomine, Messana appellatus est: paulatimque vulgo permutante litteras, Messalla dictus, Sen. Vit. Beat. 13. The most celebrated is the orator M. Valerius Messalla Corvinus, in the time of Cicero and Augustus, Cic. Att. 15, 17, 2; 16, 16, A, 5; Tib. 4, 1, 1; Hor. A. P. 371; Sen. Contr. 2, 12, 8.—In plur., Ov. P. 4, 16, 43.
messalla.short: Messalla (less correctly Messāla), ae, m., a Roman surname in the gens Valeria: Corvinus primus Messanam vicit, et pri mus ex familiā Valeriorum, urbis captae in se translato nomine, Messana appellatus est: paulatimque vulgo permutante litteras, Mess

messana.full: Messāna, ae, f., = Μεσσήνη. A Sicilian city, situated on the strait between Italy and Sicily, the mod. Messina, Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 8, § 17; Caes. B. C. 2, 3; Mel. 2, 7, 16: incumbens Messana freto, Sil. 14, 194.— Another name for Messene, in the Peloponnesus, Stat. Ach. 1, 422.—Hence, Messānĭus, a, um, adj., Messanic: moenia, Ov. M. 14, 17 Merkel.

messanius2.full: Messānĭus, a, um, v. Messana fin.

messapia.full: Messāpĭa (Mesāpĭa), ae, f., the old name of a part of Lower Italy (Apulia and Calabria): Messapia Apulia a Messapo rege appellata, Paul. ex Fest. p. 125 Müll.; cf. Plin. 3, 11, 16, § 99.—Hence, Messāpĭus (Mesāp-), a, um, adj., of or belonging to Messapia, Messapian, Apulian, Calabrian: arva, Ov. M. 14, 513.—In plur., as subst.: Messāpii (Mesāp-), ōrum, m., the Messapians, Liv. 8, 24.
messapia.short: Messāpĭa (Mesāpĭa), ae, f., the old name of a part of Lower Italy (Apulia and Calabria): Messapia Apulia a Messapo rege appellata, Paul.

messapus.full: Messāpus (Mesāp-), i, m., a mythic prince in Messapia, Verg. A. 7, 691; cf. Paul. ex Fest. s. v. Messapia, p. 125 Müll.
messapus.short: Messāpus (Mesāp-), i, m., a mythic prince in Messapia, Verg.

messeis.full: Messēis, ĭdis, f., = Μεσσηίς, a fountain in Thessaly, Plin. 4, 8, 15, § 30.—As adj., of or belonging to the fountain Messēis: Messeides undae, Val. Fl. 4, 374.
messeis.short: Messēis, ĭdis, f., = Μεσσηίς, a fountain in Thessaly, Plin.

messene.full: Messēnē, ēs, or Messēna (Messāna), ae, f., = Μεσσήνη, the capital of Messenia, in the Peloponnesus, on the river Pamisos, now Maura-Matia, Mel. 2, 3, 4; Plin. 4, 5, 7, § 15; Nep. Ep. 8; id. Pel. 4; Liv. 36, 31, 1; 32, 21, 23; Ov. M. 6, 417; cf. Messana, II.—Hence, Messēnĭus (Messā-nĭus), a, um, adj., = Μεσσήνιος, Messeni an: Messenia arva (al. Messania), Ov. M. 2, 679.— Subst. Messēnia, ae, f., the country around Messene, Plin. 4, 5, 7, § 15.— Messēnĭi, ōrum, m., the Messenians, Liv. 36, 31.
messene.short: Messēnē, ēs, or Messēna (Messāna), ae, f., = Μεσσήνη, the capital of Messenia, in the Peloponnesus, on the river Pamisos, now Maura-Matia, Mel.

messia1.full: Messĭa, ae, f. messio, the goddess of reaping, Tert. Spect. 8.

messia2.full: Messĭa Silva, ae, f., a wooded hill on the right bank of the Tiber, south-west of Veii, Liv. 1, 33, 9 Hertz (Weissenb. Maesia), Plin. 8, 58, 83, § 225 Jan. (al. Mesia).
messia2.short: Messĭa Silva, ae, f., a wooded hill on the right bank of the Tiber, south-west of Veii, Liv.

messias.full: Messīas, ae, m. Heb., the Anointed, Gr. Χριστός, the Messiah, Christ, Vulg. Johan. 4, 25; Lact. 4, 7, and in the eccl. fathers saepiss.

messio.full: messĭo, ōnis, f. 2. meto, a reaping: frumenti tria genera sunt messionis, Varr. R. R. 1, 50, 1; Vulg. Job, 29, 19; id. Jer. 51, 33; id. 2 Sam. 21, 9.

messis.full: messis, is (acc. sing. messim, Cato, R. R. 134; Plaut. Most. 1, 3, 5; id. Ep. 5, 2, 53; Varr. R. R. 3, 2, 6; v. Neue, Formenl. 1, p. 200), f. (masc.: non magno messe, Lucil. ap. Non. 213 fin.) [id.], a reaping and ingathering of the fruits of the earth, a harvest (class.). Lit.: messis proprio nomine dicitur in iis, quae metuntur, maxime in frumento, Varr. R. R. 1, 50, 1; Quint. 5, 9, 5; 8, 3, 8; Cic. de Or. 1, 58, 249; Verg. G. 1, 219 al.: seges matura messi, Liv. 2, 5: messem hordaceam facere,

messor.full: messor, ōris, m. id., a reaper (class.). Lit., Cic. de Or. 3, 12, 46: durus, Ov. M. 14, 643: feniseca, a mower, Col. 2, 18: dura messorum ilia, Hor. Epod. 3, 4: parce messoribus illis qui saturant urbem, Juv. 8, 117.— Personified: deus Messor, the god of the harvest, Serv. ad Verg. G. 1, 21.—* Trop., reaper of men: sator scelerum et messor maxume, Plaut. Capt. 3, 5, 3; cf. Vulg. Matt. 13, 30 and 39.

messorius.full: messōrĭus, a, um, adj. messor, of or belonging to a reaper (class.): messoria corbis, a reaper's basket, Cic. Sest. 38, 82: falces, Pall. 1, 43: opera, Col. 2, 13, 2.

messuarius.full: messŭārĭus, a, um, adj [messura], for messorius, of or belonging to reapers (post-class.): corbis, Serv. Verg. E. 8, 82.
messuarius.short: messŭārĭus, a, um, adj [messura], for messorius, of or belonging to reapers (post-class.): corbis, Serv.

messura.full: messūra, ae, f. 2. meto, a reaping (post-class.), Primas. ap. Gall. c. 6: messuram dicimus, non metitionem, Diom. p. 374 P. (dub.)

messus.full: messus, a, um, Part., v. 2. meto.

mestria.full: Mestria, ae, f., a Roman surname, Inscr. Fabr. p. 621, 181.
mestria.short: Mestria, ae, f., a Roman surname, Inscr.

mestrianus.full: Mestriānus, i, m., a Roman surname, Inscr. Malvas. Marm. Felsin. p. 253.
mestrianus.short: Mestriānus, i, m., a Roman surname, Inscr.

met.full: met, a pronominal suffix attached to substantive and (less freq.) adjective personal pronouns; Engl. self: egomet, mihimet, memet, nosmet, nobismet, tutemet, tibimet, vosmet, meamet; v. ego, tu, and meus.
met.short: met, a pronominal suffix attached to substantive and (less freq.) adjective personal pronouns;

meta.full: mēta, ae, f. root ma-, measure, whence Gr. μέτρον; Lat. manus, mane, etc. (q. v.), properly, that which marks a measured space, hence, any mark at a boundary or limit, esp., The conical columns set in the ground at each end of the Roman Circus, the goal, turning-post: metaque fervidis Evitata rotis, Hor. C. 1, 1, 5: aut prius infecto deposcit praemia cursu Septima quam metam triverit ante rota, Prop. 3, 20, 25; cf.: et modo lora dabo, modo verbere terga notabo, Nunc stringam metas interiore rotā

metabole.full: mĕtăbŏlē, ēs, f., = μεταβολή, the transition to another key or set of tones, Fulg. Myth. 3, 9, p. 128 Muncker: cf. written as Greek, Quint. 9, 4, 50.
metabole.short: mĕtăbŏlē, ēs, f., = μεταβολή, the transition to another key or set of tones, Fulg.

metabus.full: Mĕtăbus, i, m. A king of the Volsci, father of Camilla, Verg. A. 11, 540; Hyg. Fab. 252.— A son of Sisyphus, the founder of Metapontum, Serv. ad Verg. A. 11, 540.

metacismus.full: mĕtăcismus, i, m. for mytacismus, = μυτακισμός, from μῦ, a frequent repetition of the letter M, Mart. Cap. 5, § 514; also the pronunciation of M at the close of a word before a word beginning with a vowel, metacism, Diom. p. 448 P.

metagogeus.full: Mĕtăgōgeu͡s ĕi, m., = μεταγωγεύς, he who leads around; Lat. circumductor, one of the aeons of Valentinian, Tert. adv. Valent. 10.
metagogeus.short: Mĕtăgōgeu͡s ĕi, m., = μεταγωγεύς, he who leads around;

metagon.full: Mĕtăgon, ontis, m., = Μετάγων, the name of a dog, Grat. Cyn. 209.
metagon.short: Mĕtăgon, ontis, m., = Μετάγων, the name of a dog, Grat.

metalces.full: Metalces, ae, m., = Μεταλκής, one of the fifty sons of Ægyptus, slain by his wife Cleopatra, Hyg. Fab. 170.
metalces.short: Metalces, ae, m., = Μεταλκής, one of the fifty sons of Ægyptus, slain by his wife Cleopatra, Hyg.

metalepsis.full: metălepsis, is, f., = μετάληψις, in rhetoric, the use of one word for another which it suggests by association, as, the cause for the effect, or the reverse; especially when a second substitution is made, as when aristae is said for messis, and then for aestas or annus: est haec in metalepsi natura, ut inter id, quod transfertur, sit medius quidam gradus, nihil ipse significans, sed praebens transitum, Quint. 8, 6, 38: in metalepsin cadit, id. 6, 3, 52.
metalepsis.short: metălepsis, is, f., = μετάληψις, in rhetoric, the use of one word for another which it suggests by association, as, the cause for the effect, or the reverse;

metalis.full: mētālis, e, adj. meta, III. 3, conical (post-class.): forma, Paul. ex Fest. s. v. tutulum, p. 335 Müll.—Hence, adv.: mētālĭ-ter, conically (post-class.): majus corpus ejus quo umbra metaliter jacitur, quam umbra ipsa, Mart. Cap. 8, § 859; id. 8, § 870.

metallarius.full: mĕtallārĭus, ii, m., and mĕtallā-rĭa, ae, f. metallum, a man or a woman that works in a mine, a miner (post-class.), Cod. Just. 11, 6, 7.
metallarius.short: mĕtallārĭus, ii, m., and mĕtallā-rĭa, ae, f.

metallicus.full: mĕtallĭcus, a, um, adj. id., of or belonging to metal, metallic (post-Aug.). Adj.: molybdaena metallica, Plin. 34, 18, 53, § 173: natura, id. 27, 4, 5, § 15.— Subst.: mĕtallĭcus, i, m. A digger of metals, a mine-digger, miner: lavant eas arenas metallici, Plin. 34, 16, 47, § 157; Cod. Just. 11, 6, 7.— A person condemned to the mines, Dig. 48, 19, 10.— A worker in stone, Cassiod. Var. 7, 15.

metallifer.full: mĕtallĭfer, fĕra, fĕrum, adj. metallum-fero, yielding or abounding in metal, metalliferous (poet.): terra, Sil. 15, 500: Luna, Stat. S. 4, 4, 23.

metallinensis.full: Metallinensis, e, or Metellinen-sis, e, adj. Metallinum, of or belonging to the town of Metallinum (in Lusitania), Metallinian: colonia, Plin. 4, 21, 35, § 117.
metallinensis.short: Metallinensis, e, or Metellinen-sis, e, adj.

metallum.full: mĕtallum, i, n., = μέταλλον, a mine or quarry, of gold, silver, iron, or stone; voc. metalle, as if from metallus, Spart. Pesc. Nig. 126. Lit., the place where metals are dug, a mine: metalla vetera intermissa recoluit, et nova multis locis instituit, Liv. 39, 24: sandaracae, Vitr. 7, 7, 5: aurifera, gold-mines, Luc. 3, 209: silicum, stone-quarry, id. 4, 304: miniarium, Plin. 33, 7, 40, § 118: praeter annuum, quod ex metallis regiis capia, vectigal, Liv. 42, 12: herba tantae suavitatis, ut metal
metallum.short: mĕtallum, i, n., = μέταλλον, a mine or quarry, of gold, silver, iron, or stone;

metamelos.full: mĕtămĕlos, i, m., = μετάμελος, repentance (ante-class.): metamelos, filius inconstantiae, Varr. ap. Non. 79, 23 (Büch. § 239).
metamelos.short: mĕtămĕlos, i, m., = μετάμελος, repentance (ante-class.): metamelos, filius inconstantiae, Varr.

metamorphosis.full: mĕtămorphōsis, is, f., = μεταμόρφωσις, a transformation, metamorphosis; in plur.: Mĕtămorphōses, -ĕōn, the Metamorphoses, a well-known poem of Ovid; in Gr. acc. plur. Metamorphoseis, Tert. adv. Val. 12: censeo eam rem ad metamorphosis Ovidi adiciendam, Sen. Apocol. 9, 5; in Gr. dat. plur.: ut Ovidius lascivire in Metamorphosesi solet, Quint. 4, 1, 77.
metamorphosis.short: mĕtămorphōsis, is, f., = μεταμόρφωσις, a transformation, metamorphosis;

metanoea.full: mĕtănoea (quadrisyl.), ae, f., = μετάνοια, repentance (post-class.), Aus. Epigr. 12, 12.
metanoea.short: mĕtănoea (quadrisyl.), ae, f., = μετάνοια, repentance (post-class.), Aus.

metaphora.full: mĕtaphŏra, ae, f., = μεταφορά, a rhetorical figure, metaphor, a transferring of a word from its proper signification to another (called by Cic. de Or. 3, 38, 155, verbi translatio; post-Aug.), Quint. 8, 6, 18; (as Greek), id. 8, 6, 4 sqq.; Schol. Juv. 1, 169.
metaphora.short: mĕtaphŏra, ae, f., = μεταφορά, a rhetorical figure, metaphor, a transferring of a word from its proper signification to another (called by Cic.

metaphorice.full: mĕtaphŏrĭcē, adv. metaphora, metaphorically, figuratively (post-class.), Acron. ad Hor. Ep. 1, 20, 1.—Also mĕtaphŏrĭ-cōs, μεταφορικῶς, Acron. ad Hor. Ep. 1, 3, 29 sq.; Schol. Juv. 7, 103.

metaphrenum.full: mĕtăphrĕnum, i, n., = μετάφρενον, the upper part of the spine, Cael. Aur. Acut. 3, 16, 129 (as Greek, id. ib. 2, 29, 151; id. Tard. 3, 2, 31).
metaphrenum.short: mĕtăphrĕnum, i, n., = μετάφρενον, the upper part of the spine, Cael.

metapinus.full: Mĕtăpīnus, a, um etym. dub., Metapinic, an epithet of the second or middle of the three principal mouths of the Rhone: cujus ora appellata ... alterum Metapinum, Mart. Cap. 6, § 635; Plin. 3, 4, 5, § 32.

metaplasmus.full: mĕtaplasmus, i, m., = μεταπλασμός, a grammatical change, irregularity, metaplasm, e. g. in declension (post-Aug.): metaplasmus enim, et schematismos et schemata vocamus, Quint. 1, 8, 14; Mart. Cap. 3, § 326.
metaplasmus.short: mĕtaplasmus, i, m., = μεταπλασμός, a grammatical change, irregularity, metaplasm, e.

metaplasticos.full: mĕtaplastĭcōs, adv., = μεταπλαστικῶς, metaplastically, by the use of metaplasm: metaplasticos dicitur apud poëtas usurpari id quod propter necessitatem metri mutare consueverunt, Paul. ex Fest. p. 153 Müll.
metaplasticos.short: mĕtaplastĭcōs, adv., = μεταπλαστικῶς, metaplastically, by the use of metaplasm: metaplasticos dicitur apud poëtas usurpari id quod propter necessitatem metri mutare consueverunt, Paul.

metapontum.full: Mĕtăpontum, i, n., a town of Lucania, where Pythagoras lived and died, now Torre a Mare, Cic. Fin. 5, 2, 4; Liv. 1, 18, 8; Mela, 2, 4, 3; Plin. 3, 11, 15, § 97.—Hence, Mĕtăpontīnus, a, um, adj., Metapontine: ager, Liv. 24, 20.—In plur.: Mĕtă-pontīni, ōrum, m., the Metapontines, Liv. 22, 61.
metapontum.short: Mĕtăpontum, i, n., a town of Lucania, where Pythagoras lived and died, now Torre a Mare, Cic.

metarius.full: mētārĭus, a, um, adj. meta, of or belonging to limits or boundaries (post-class.): metaria circumscriptio, a limiting by boundaries, Arn. 2, 70.

metastasis.full: mĕtastăsis, is, f., = μετάστασις, a rhet. figure. A refusing, Agn. Roman. de Fig. 16, p. 155.— = metabasis, a passing over, transition, Julian. Rufin. de Schem. 23, p. 243.
metastasis.short: mĕtastăsis, is, f., = μετάστασις, a rhet.

metasyncriticus.full: mĕtăsyncrĭtĭcus, a, um, adj., = μετασυγκριτικός, belonging to the discharge of peccant humors: adjutoria, Cael. Aur. Acut. 3, 16, 134: cyclus, id. Tard. 1, 1, 24; 2, 1, 49.
metasyncriticus.short: mĕtăsyncrĭtĭcus, a, um, adj., = μετασυγκριτικός, belonging to the discharge of peccant humors: adjutoria, Cael.

metathesis.full: mĕtăthĕsis, is, f., = μετάθεσις, a transposition of the letters of a word, Diom. 2, p. 437 P.
metathesis.short: mĕtăthĕsis, is, f., = μετάθεσις, a transposition of the letters of a word, Diom.

metatio.full: mētātĭo, ōnis, f. metor, a measuring or meting out, a marking off a place (postAug.): vinearum, Col. 7, 15, 1.

metator.full: mētātor, ōris, m. id., one who metes out or marks off a place, a divider and fixer of boundaries (class.). Lit.: castrorum antea metator, nunc, ut sperat, urbis, Cic. Phil. 11, 5, 12; cf. id. ib. 14, 4, 10: templi, Lact. 4, 11.— Trop., a measurer: tempus arbiter et metator initii et finis, Tert. adv. Marc. 1, 8.

metatorius.full: mētātōrĭus, a, um, adj. metator, of or pertaining to measuring out, transf. (post-class.): pagina, a letter relative to the providing of quarters, Sid. Ep. 8, 11.

metatura.full: mētātūra, ae, f. metor, a measuring out, marking off a place (eccl. Lat.), Lact. 4, 11, 13.

metaurensis.full: Mĕtaurensis, e, adj. Metaurus, of or belonging to the river Metaurus, in Umbria: AGER, Inscr. Oliv. Marm. Pisaur. n. 30.—Subst.: Mĕtaurenses, ĭum, m., the inhabitants of that region, Metaurians, Plin. 3, 14, 19, § 114.

metaurus.full: Mĕtaurus, i, m., = Μέταυρος, the name of several rivers. A river in Umbria, celebrated for the defeat of Hasdrubal, the brother of Hannibal, now Meturo, Liv. 27, 43 sq.; Sil. 8, 486.—Hence, Mĕtau-rus, a, um, adj., of Metaurus: Metaurum flumen, Hor. C. 4, 4, 38.— A river in the Bruttian territory, now Marro, Plin. 3, 5, 10, § 73.
metaurus.short: Mĕtaurus, i, m., = Μέταυρος, the name of several rivers.

metaxa.full: mĕtaxa or mătaxa, ae, f., = μέταξα and μάταξα, raw silk, the web of silkworms. Lit., Dig. 39, 4, 16; Cod. Just. 11, 7, 10.— Transf., a rope: lini metaxa, Lucil. ap. Fest. s. v. rodus, p. 265 Müll.; Vitr. 7, 3.
metaxa.short: mĕtaxa or mătaxa, ae, f., = μέταξα and μάταξα, raw silk, the web of silkworms.

metaxarii.full: mĕtaxārĭi, ōrum, m. metaxa, silkdealers (post-class.), Cod. Just. 8, 14, 27.

metella.full: mĕtella, ae, f. (prob. adj., sc. machina), a basket filled with stones, which the besieged threw down on the heads of the besiegers (post-class.): ut de ligno crates facerent, quas metellas vocaverunt, lapidibusque complerent, etc. (al. metilas, medullas, metulas), Veg. Mil. 4, 6.

metellinus.full: Mĕtellīnus, a, um, adj. Metellus, of or belonging to a Metellus, Metelline: oratlo Metellina, i. e. against Metellus, Cic. Att. 1, 13 fin.

metellus.full: Mĕtellus, a etym. dub.; metellus = μισθιος, hired, i. e. a hired servant, Gloss. Philox.: metelli dicuntur in re militari quasi mercenarii, Attius in Annalibus: calones famulique metellique caculaeque; a quo genere hominum Caeciliae familiae cognomen putatur ductum, Paul. ex Fest. p. 146 and 147 Müll., the name of a Roman family in the gens Caecilia; its most famous members were: Q. Metellus Macedonicus, who made Macedonia a Roman province, and was renowned for his good-fortune, Vell. 1, 11, 1;

metempsychosis.full: mĕtempsȳchōsis, is, f., = μετεμψύχωσις, the transit of the soul, its transmigration from one body to another, a doctrine of the Pythagoreans, Porphyr. ad Hor. Ep. 2, 1, 52.
metempsychosis.short: mĕtempsȳchōsis, is, f., = μετεμψύχωσις, the transit of the soul, its transmigration from one body to another, a doctrine of the Pythagoreans, Porphyr.

metensomatosis.full: mĕtensōmătōsis, is, f., = μετενσωμάτωσις, a removing from one body into another, a change of body (eccl. Lat.), Tert. Anim. 31 and 32.
metensomatosis.short: mĕtensōmătōsis, is, f., = μετενσωμάτωσις, a removing from one body into another, a change of body (eccl.

meteoria.full: mĕtĕōrĭa, ae, f., = μετεωρία, forgetfulness, M. Aurel. ap. Front. ad M. Caes. 4, 7 (as Greek, Suet. Vit. Claud.).
meteoria.short: mĕtĕōrĭa, ae, f., = μετεωρία, forgetfulness, M.

meterea.full: Mĕtĕrēa turba, a people dwelling about the Danube and the Black Sea, Ov. Tr. 2, 191.
meterea.short: Mĕtĕrēa turba, a people dwelling about the Danube and the Black Sea, Ov.

methion.full: Mēthīon, ŏnis, m., the father of Phorbas, Ov. M. 5, 74.
methion.short: Mēthīon, ŏnis, m., the father of Phorbas, Ov.

methodice.full: mĕthŏdĭcē, ēs, f., = μεθοδική, the methodical part of grammar (post-Aug.): grammaticae partes duae, id est ratio loquendi, et enarratio auctorum: quarum illam methodicen, hanc historicen vocant, Quint. 1, 9, 1.
methodice.short: mĕthŏdĭcē, ēs, f., = μεθοδική, the methodical part of grammar (post-Aug.): grammaticae partes duae, id est ratio loquendi, et enarratio auctorum: quarum illam methodicen, hanc historicen vocant, Quint.

methodicus.full: mĕthŏdĭcus, a, um, adj., = μεθοδικός, methodical, belonging to a particular school (post-Aug.): medicina, Tert. Anim. 6: disciplina, Cael. Aur. Tard. 4, 1, 6: medici, Cels. praef. § 13.
methodicus.short: mĕthŏdĭcus, a, um, adj., = μεθοδικός, methodical, belonging to a particular school (post-Aug.): medicina, Tert.

methodium.full: mĕthŏdĭum, ii, n., = μεθόδιον, a witty conceit, a jest, joke (post-Aug.): Trimalchio ejusmodi methodio laetus, Carpe, inquit, etc. (al. metōdīum, i. e. μετωδεῖον, an inserted song), Petr. 36, 5.
methodium.short: mĕthŏdĭum, ii, n., = μεθόδιον, a witty conceit, a jest, joke (post-Aug.): Trimalchio ejusmodi methodio laetus, Carpe, inquit, etc.

methodus.full: mĕthŏdus and mĕthŏdos, i, f., = μέθοδος, a way of teaching, mode of proceeding, method (post-class.), Vitr. 1, 1, 4; Aus. Idyll. 11, 67; Cael. Aur. Tard. 2, 1, 49 (as Greek, Cels. praef. § 91); cf. methodicus.
methodus.short: mĕthŏdus and mĕthŏdos, i, f., = μέθοδος, a way of teaching, mode of proceeding, method (post-class.), Vitr.

methymna.full: Mēthymna, ae, f., = Μήθυμνα, a city in the island of Lesbos, famous as the birthplace of the poet Arion, and for its excellent wine, now Molivo, Mel. 2, 7, 4; Liv. 45, 31, 14: quot habet Methymna racemos, Ov. A. A. 1, 57.—Hence. Mēthymnaeus, a, um, adj., = Μηθυμναῖος, of or belonging to Methymna, Methymnean: Lesbos, Ov. M. 11, 55: Arion, of Methymna, Cic. Tusc. 2, 27, 67: merum, Prop. 4 (5), 8, 38. palmes, Verg. G. 2, 90.—In plur. subst.: Mēthymnaei, ōrum, m., the Methymneans, Curt. 4, 5, 19.— M
methymna.short: Mēthymna, ae, f., = Μήθυμνα, a city in the island of Lesbos, famous as the birthplace of the poet Arion, and for its excellent wine, now Molivo, Mel.

metia.full: Metĭa Porta, a false read. in Plaut.; cf. Ritschl ad Plaut. Ps. 1, 3, 97.

meticulosus.full: mĕtĭcŭlōsus, a, um, adj. metus, full of fear. Fearful, timid (ante- and postclass.): nullus est hoc meticulosus aeque, Plaut. Am. 1, 1, 137; Dig. 4, 2, 7: lepus, App. Flor. p. 341, 9.—* Frightful, terrible: res, Plaut. Most. 5, 1, 52.

metilius.full: Metilius, a, a Roman family name: M. Metilius, Liv. 5, 11.—Hence, Meti-lius, a, um, adj., of or belonging to a Metilius: Metilia lex, Plin. 35, 17, 57, § 197.
metilius.short: Metilius, a, a Roman family name: M.

metina.full: Metina, ae, f., an island near the coast of Gaul, opposite the mouth of the Rhone, Mart. Cap. 6, § 643.
metina.short: Metina, ae, f., an island near the coast of Gaul, opposite the mouth of the Rhone, Mart.

metior.full: mētĭor, mensus (post-class. metītus, Dig. 32, 1, 52), 4, v. dep. Sanscr. ma, to measure; cf. Gr. μέ-τρον, Lat. modus, to measure, mete (lands, corn); also, to measure or mete out, to deal out, distribute by measure (class.). Lit.: metiri agrum, Cic. Fam. 9, 17, 2: frumentum, Cic. Verr. 2, 3, 83, § 192: sol, quem metiri non possunt, id. Ac. 2, 41, 128: magnitudinem mundi, id. Off. 1, 43, 154: nummos, to measure one's money, i. e. to have a great abundance of it, Hor. S. 1, 1, 95: nummos modio, Pe

metiosedum.full: Mĕtĭōsēdum, i, n., a city in Gaul, now Meudon, Caes. B. G. 7, 61.
metiosedum.short: Mĕtĭōsēdum, i, n., a city in Gaul, now Meudon, Caes.

metiscus.full: Metiscus, i, m., a charioteer of Turnus, Verg. A. 12, 469.
metiscus.short: Metiscus, i, m., a charioteer of Turnus, Verg.

metitio.full: mētītĭo, ōnis, f. metior, = mensura, but not in use; v. Diom. 374 P.

metitor.full: mētītor, ōris, m. metior, a measurer (post-Aug.), Front. Aquaed. 79.

metitus.full: mētītus, a, um, v. metior init.

metius.full: Metĭus or Mettĭus (also Mettus), i, m., an Italian proper name. Metius (Mettius) Curtius, a Sabine chief, Liv. 1, 12 fin.; Varr. L. L. 5, § 149 Müll.— Metius Fufetius (acc. to others, Mettus Fufetius), an Alban general, who was put to death by the command of Tullus Hostilius, Liv. 1, 23 sq.; Verg. A. 8, 642; Flor. 1, 3, 8.—In gen. sing.: Mettoi Fubettoi, Enn. ap. Quint. 1, 5, 12 (Ann. v. 129 Vahl.; Halm, Mettoeo Fufettioeo).— M. Metius, a friend of Ariovistus, Caes. B. G. 1, 47; 1, 53 fin.
metius.short: Metĭus or Mettĭus (also Mettus), i, m., an Italian proper name.

meto1.full: mēto (no perf.), ātum, 1, v. a., to measure; v. metor fin.

meto2.full: mĕto, messŭi (Cato ap. Prisc. p. 903 P.; Mart. Cap. 3, § 319), messum, 3, v. a. and n. root ma-; Gr. ἀμάω, mow, reap; ἄμη, sickle; cf. messis, messor, to reap, mow, crop; of the vintage, to gather, gather in, collect; and poet. of the sucking of honey from flowers (class.). Lit.: cum est matura seges, metendum, Varr. R. R. 1, 50, 3: sunt autem metendi genera complura, Col. 2, 21, 2: in metendo occupatos, Caes. B. G. 4, 32: pabula falce, to cut, cut down, Ov. H. 6, 84: farra, id. F 2, 519: arva,

metoche.full: mĕtŏchē, ēs, f., = μετοχή, a participle (late Lat.), Aus. Epigr. 6, 7.
metoche.short: mĕtŏchē, ēs, f., = μετοχή, a participle (late Lat.), Aus.

metoecus.full: mĕtoecus, i, m., = μέτοικος, a stranger, sojourner, denizen, resident alien dwelling in a city without the rights of citizenship (post-class.), Eum. Pan. Flavens. Nom. Dict. 4 fin.: ager militi metoeco (al. modico) est assignatus, Front. de Colon. p. 134 Goes. (written mĕtycus, Gromat. Vet. 234, 19; 238, 7 Lachm.).
metoecus.short: mĕtoecus, i, m., = μέτοικος, a stranger, sojourner, denizen, resident alien dwelling in a city without the rights of citizenship (post-class.), Eum.

meton.full: Mĕton or Mĕto, ōnis, m., = Μέτων, a celebrated Athenian astronomer, who discovered the cycle of nineteen years, at the end of which the new and full moons again fall on the same days, Avien. Prognost. 48; Aus. Epis. 2, 12.—Hence Cicero says, jestingly, of a debtor named Meton, who promised to pay in a year's time: quando iste Metonis annus veniet? Cic. Att. 12, 3, 2; cf. id. ib. 12, 51, 3.
meton.short: Mĕton or Mĕto, ōnis, m., = Μέτων, a celebrated Athenian astronomer, who discovered the cycle of nineteen years, at the end of which the new and full moons again fall on the same days, Avien.

metonymia.full: mĕtōnўmĭa, ae, f., = μετωνυμία, a figure by which one name is changed for another, a change of names, metonymy (pure Lat. denominatio), Paul. ex Fest. p. 153 Müll.; Charis. p. 244 P. al.
metonymia.short: mĕtōnўmĭa, ae, f., = μετωνυμία, a figure by which one name is changed for another, a change of names, metonymy (pure Lat.

metonymicos.full: mĕtōnўmĭcōs, adv., = μετωνυμικῶς, metonymically, by metonymy, Porphyr. ad Hor. Epod. 13, 16; id. ad Hor. Ep. 1, 18, 9 sqq. al.
metonymicos.short: mĕtōnўmĭcōs, adv., = μετωνυμικῶς, metonymically, by metonymy, Porphyr.

metopa.full: mĕtŏpa, ae, f., = μετόπη, the space between two hollows; in architecture, the space between two dentils or two triglyphs, a metope (only in Vitr.): inter denticulos et inter triglyphos quae sunt intervalla, metopae nominantur, etc., Vitr. 4, 2, 4.
metopa.short: mĕtŏpa, ae, f., = μετόπη, the space between two hollows;

metopion.full: mĕtōpĭon or -um, ii, n. (also mĕ-tops, ōpis, Sol. 40), = μετώπιον. The gum of an African tree, also called ammoniacum, Plin. 12, 23, 49, § 107; Sol. 27, 47. — Oil of bitter almonds, almond-oil, Plin. 15, 7, 7, § 26 (Jahn, neopum).— An ointment made with galbanum, Plin. 13, 1, 2, § 8.

metoposcopus.full: mĕtōposcŏpus or -os, i, m., = μετωποσκόπος, a forehead inspector, one who tells fortunes by examining the forehead, a metoposcopist (post-Aug.), Suet. Tit. 2; cf. Plin. 35, 10, 36, § 88.
metoposcopus.short: mĕtōposcŏpus or -os, i, m., = μετωποσκόπος, a forehead inspector, one who tells fortunes by examining the forehead, a metoposcopist (post-Aug.), Suet.

metops.full: mĕtops, ŏpis, for metopion, v. h. v.

metor.full: mētor, ātus, 1, v. dep. meta, to measure, mete; to measure off, mark out (not in Cic.). In gen.: stadium Hercules pedibus suis metatus est, Gell. 1, 1, 2: caelum, Ov. F. 1, 309: Indiam, Plin. 6, 17, 21, § 57. —Poet., to traverse, pass through: nunc nemoris alti densa metatur loca, Sen. Hippol. 505: agros, Sil. 6, 58.— In partic. Act., to measure out, mark, or lay out: castra metati signa statuunt, Cael. ap. Non. 137, 18: castra, * Caes. B. C. 3, 13, 3: cum ortu solis castra metabatur, measured o

metreta.full: mĕtrēta, ae, f., = μετρητής, an Athenian measure for liquids, containing 12 congii (χόες) and 144 κοτύλαι (3/4 of the Attic medimnus, about 9 gallons English): picis liquidae metreta, Col. 12, 22, 1: se vendidisse navem, metretas quae trecentas tolleret, Plaut. Merc. prol. 75.— Transf., a tun, cask, jar: oleum si in metretam novam inditurus eris, Cato, R. R. 100: Hispanae, Mart. 5, 16, 7: olivariae, Col. 12, 47: hic tignum capiti incutit, ille metretam, Juv. 3, 246.
metreta.short: mĕtrēta, ae, f., = μετρητής, an Athenian measure for liquids, containing 12 congii (χόες) and 144 κοτύλαι (3/4 of the Attic medimnus, about 9 gallons English): picis liquidae metreta, Col.

metricus.full: mē^trĭcus, a, um, adj., = μετρικός, of or relating to measuring or measure (postAug.). In gen.: leges metricae, Plin. 11, 37, 88, § 219.— In partic., of or relating to metre, metrical: metrici pedes, Quint. 9, 4, 52; 48.— Subst.: mē^trĭcus, i, m., a prosodian (post-class.), Gell. 18, 15, 1.
metricus.short: mē^trĭcus, a, um, adj., = μετρικός, of or relating to measuring or measure (postAug.).

metrocomia.full: mētrŏcōmĭa, ae, f., = μητροκωμία, a village from which other villages have derived their inhabitants, a mother-village (post-class.), Cod. Th. 11, 24, 6; Cod. Just. 8, 10, 19.
metrocomia.short: mētrŏcōmĭa, ae, f., = μητροκωμία, a village from which other villages have derived their inhabitants, a mother-village (post-class.), Cod.

metrodorus.full: Mētrŏdōrus, i, m., = Μητρόδωρος. Metrodorus Lampsacenus or Atheniensis, an Epicurean, Cic. Tusc. 2, 3, 8; 2, 6, 17; 5, 9, 27.— M. Scepsius (from Scepsis, a city of Mysia), a rhetorical and Academic philosopher, famous for his memory, Cic. de Or. 2, 88, 360; 3, 20, 75; Plin. 34, 7, 16, § 34.— M. Stratonicēus (from Stratonice, a city of Caria), a pupil of Carneades, and an excellent orator, Cic. de Or. 1, 11, 45; id. Ac. 2, 6, 16.— Metrodorus Chius, a pupil of Democritus and teacher of Anaxarchus

metropolis1.full: mētrŏpŏlis, is, f., = μητρόπολις, a city from which other cities have been colonized, a mother-city; also, the chief city, metropolis of a province (post-class.). Lit., Cod. Just. 11, 21; Cod. Th. 13, 3, 11.— Trop.: metropolis et arx mentis, Hier. adv. Jovin. 2, 8.
metropolis1.short: mētrŏpŏlis, is, f., = μητρόπολις, a city from which other cities have been colonized, a mother-city;

metropolis2.full: Mētrŏpŏlis, is, f., = Μητρόπολις, the proper name of several cities, e. g. in Thessaly, between Pharsalus and Gomphi, Caes. B. C. 3, 80; Liv. 32, 13, 11.—Mētrŏ-pŏlītae, ārum, m., the inhabitants of Metropolis, Caes. B. C. 3, 81; cf. of others, Plin. 5, 29, 29, § 106; 5, 29, 31, § 120.
metropolis2.short: Mētrŏpŏlis, is, f., = Μητρόπολις, the proper name of several cities, e.

metropolita.full: mētrŏ-pŏlīta, ae, m., = μητροπολίτης, a bishop in a chief city, a metropolitan (post-class.): metropolita sacer, Ven. Carm. 3, 6, 20.
metropolita.short: mētrŏ-pŏlīta, ae, m., = μητροπολίτης, a bishop in a chief city, a metropolitan (post-class.): metropolita sacer, Ven.

metropolitanus1.full: mētrŏpŏlītānus, a, um, adj. 1. metropolis, of or belonging to a metropolis, metropolitan (post-class.): nomen, Cod. Just. 11, 21, 1.—Esp. subst.: Mētrŏ-pŏlītānus, i, m., a metropolitan, the bishop of a metropolitan church, Sid. Ep. 7, 9.

metropolitanus2.full: Mētrŏpŏlītānus, a, um, adj. 2. Metropolis, of or belonging to the city of Metropolis: campus, Liv. 38, 15.

metrum.full: mē^trum, i, n., = μέτρον, a measure; in partic., a poetical measure, metre; a verse (post-Aug.): rhythmi, id est numeri, spatio temporum constant: metra etiam ordine: ideoque alterum esse quantitatis videtur, alterum qualitatis, Quint. 9, 4, 46: metri necessitate cogi, id. 8, 6, 17; 1, 6, 2: metri causā, Gell. 4, 17, 9: Tibulli, i. e. elegiac metre, Mart. 4, 6, 4: exceptis metris Vergilii, i. e. verses, Col. 3, 10, 20 dub.
metrum.short: mē^trum, i, n., = μέτρον, a measure;

mettica.full: mettĭca vitis, an unknown species of vine, Col. 3, 2, 27; Plin. 14, 2, 4, § 35 (Sillig. Metica).
mettica.short: mettĭca vitis, an unknown species of vine, Col.

mettus.full: Mettus (Mettĭus), i, m., a Sabine prænomen, prob. the title of a magistracy among the Albans (cf. medix, meddix), e. g. Mettus Curtius, Liv. 1, 12; 1, 23 sqq.; v. Metius.
mettus.short: Mettus (Mettĭus), i, m., a Sabine prænomen, prob.

metuens.full: mĕtŭens, Part. and P. a., v. metuo fin.

metula.full: mētŭla, ae, f. dim. meta, a small pyramid, obelisk (post-Aug.), Plin. Ep. 5, 6, 35.

metuo.full: mĕtŭo, ŭi, ūtum (cf.: nimis ante metutum, Lucr. 5, 1140), 3, v. a. and n. metus, to fear, be afraid of a person or thing; to hesitate, not to venture, not to wish (syn.: vereor, formido, timeo); with inf., with ne, to fear lest; with ui or ne non, to fear that not; also of inanimate things, with acc., to fear, revere, reverence one; as a v. n., to fear, be afraid, be in fear, be apprehensive, esp. as the effect of the idea of threatening evil (whereas timere usually denotes the effect of some ex
metuo.short: mĕtŭo, ŭi, ūtum (cf.: nimis ante metutum, Lucr.

metus.full: mĕtus, ūs, m. (fem.: nulla in me est metus, Enn. ap. Paul. ex Fest. p. 123 Müll.: metus ulla, id. ap. Non. 214, 11; cf. Ann. v. 537, and Trag. v. 179 Vahl.; dat. metu, Tac. A. 11, 32; 15, 69), fear, dread, apprehension, anxiety; constr. with gen. object., with ne, with acc. and inf. Lit.: est metus futurae aegritudinis sollicita exspectatio, Cic. Tusc. 5, 18, 52; cf. id. ib. 4, 30, 64: metum excitari vel propriis vel communibus periculis, Mart. Cap. 5, § 505: in metu esse, to be in fear, be fear

metutus.full: mĕtūtus, a, um, Part., from metuo.
metutus.short: mĕtūtus, a, um, Part., from metuo.

meum.full: mēum, i, n., = μῆον, an umbelliferous plant, bear-wort, Plin. 20, 23, 94, § 253.
meum.short: mēum, i, n., = μῆον, an umbelliferous plant, bear-wort, Plin.

meus.full: mĕus, a, um (voc. meus for mi: proice tela manu, sanguis meus, Verg. A. 6, 835: Lolli meus, Sid. Ep. 1, 9; and: domine meus, id. ib. 4, 10; gen. plur meūm for meorum: pietas majorum meūm, Plaut. Cas. 2, 6, 66: meapte, Ter. Heaut. 4, 3, 8: meopte, Plaut. Most. 1, 2, 77: meāmet, id. Poen. 1, 3, 37; Sall. J. 85, 24; archaic form MIVS: MIEIS MORIBVS, Monum. Scip. in Inscr. Orell. 554; and mis = meis: ingens cura'st mis concordibus aequiperare, Enn. ap. Prisc. p. 955 P.; cf. Vahl. Enn. Ann. v. 131, p

mevania.full: Mēvānĭa, ae, f., a city in Umbria, now Bevagna, Liv. 9, 41, 13; Col. 3, 8, 3; Sil. 6, 647: nebulosa, Prop. 4 (5), 1, 123.— Hence, Mēvānas, ātis, comm., of or belonging to the city of Mevania Mevanas Varenus, Sil. 4, 546.—Subst.: Mēvānā-tes, ĭum, m., the inhabitants of Mevania, Mevanians, Plin. 3, 14, 19, § 113.— Mē-vānĭensis, e, adj., of or belonging to Mevania, Mevanian: boves, Philar. ad Verg. G. 2, 146.
mevania.short: Mēvānĭa, ae, f., a city in Umbria, now Bevagna, Liv.

mevia.full: Mēvĭa, ae, f., a woman fond of masculine sports, Juv. 1, 22.
mevia.short: Mēvĭa, ae, f., a woman fond of masculine sports, Juv.

mezentius.full: Mezentĭus (not Mezzent-, Mesdent-, Messent-, Mēdient-, or Mēdent-; cf. Rib. in Rhein. Mus. 1857, vol. 12, p. 418 sq.), i, m., a male proper name [of Oscan origin], a tyrant of Cære or Agylla, Liv. 1, 2; Paul. ex Fest. s. v. oscillum, p. 194 Müll.: contemptor divom Mezentius, Verg. A. 7, 648 sq.; cf. Macr. S. 3, 5; and Serv Verg. A. 1, 267; 7, 760; 9, 745.
mezentius.short: Mezentĭus (not Mezzent-, Mesdent-, Messent-, Mēdient-, or Mēdent-;

mi.full: mi. Dat. from ego.— Voc. from meus; v. h. vv.

mia.full: Mĭa Chărĭtōn = Χαρίτων μία, one of the Graces, Lucr. 4, 1162; v. Charites.
mia.short: Mĭa Chărĭtōn = Χαρίτων μία, one of the Graces, Lucr.

mica.full: mīca, ae, f. root smic-; Gr. σμικρός, μικρός; cf. micula; O. Germ. smahan, to belittle, a crumb, little bit, morsel, grain (poet. and in post-Aug. prose). Lit.: mica panis, Petr. 42: auri, Lucr. 1, 839: marmoris, Plin. 33, 4, 21, § 68: salis, a grain of salt, id. 22, 14, 16, § 37: amomi, id. 12, 18, 41, § 83: saliens (i. e. salis) mica, Hor. C. 3, 23, 12: tus in micas friatur, Plin. 12, 14, 32, § 65: de micis puerorum, Vulg. Marc. 7, 28.— Transf. A small diningroom, Mart. 2, 59, 1; Sen. Ep. 51,

micans.full: mĭcans, antis, Part. and P. a., from mico.

micarius.full: mīcārĭus, a, um, adj. mica, of or belonging to crumbs or little bits (post-Aug.): homo frugi, et micarius, a crumb-gatherer, i. e. frugal, economical, Petr. 73, 6.

micatio.full: mĭcātĭo, ōnis, f. mico, a quick motion: micatio λαχμός, Gloss. Philox.

micatus.full: mĭcātus, ūs, m. id., a quick motion (post-class.): linguarum micatibus, Mart. Cap. 4, § 331.

miccotrogus.full: Miccotrōgus, i, m., = Μικκότρωγος, the fictitious name of a parasite, Smallbiter, Plaut. Stich. 1, 3, 88.
miccotrogus.short: Miccotrōgus, i, m., = Μικκότρωγος, the fictitious name of a parasite, Smallbiter, Plaut.

miceo.full: micĕo, ēre, v. n., to bleat, of a hegoat (al. mutire), Auct. Phil. 58.

michael.full: Michāēl, ēlis, m., a Hebrew name, Vulg. Num. 13, 14 al.—Esp., Michael, the archangel, Vulg. Dan. 10, 13.
michael.short: Michāēl, ēlis, m., a Hebrew name, Vulg.

michaelium.full: Michăēlĭum, i, n., = Μιχᾳηλεῖον, the church of St. Michael, Cassiod. Hist. Eccl. 2, 19.
michaelium.short: Michăēlĭum, i, n., = Μιχᾳηλεῖον, the church of St.

micidus.full: mīcĭdus, a, um, adj. mica, thin, poor, Innocent. Agrar. p. 231 Goes.

micio.full: Micio, ōnis, m., name of a man, Ter. Ad. 5, 3, 7.
micio.short: Micio, ōnis, m., name of a man, Ter.

micipsa.full: Mĭcipsa, ae, m., son of Masinissa, and king of Numidia, Sall. J. 5 sq.; Flor. 3, 1. —In plur., poet. for Numidians, Africans, Juv. 5, 89.
micipsa.short: Mĭcipsa, ae, m., son of Masinissa, and king of Numidia, Sall.

mico.full: mĭco, ŭi (pf. subj. micaverit, Sol. 53), 1, v. n. Sanscr. mish-, to wink, to move quickly to and fro, to have a vibrating or tremulous motion, to quiver, shake, tremble, e. g. of the pulse; to beat, palpitate; to spring forth, of fountains; of the tremulous rays of the stars, to twinkle, sparkle, glitter, gleam, flash (class.). In gen.: venae et arteriae micare non desinunt, Cic. N. D. 2, 9, 24: linguis micat ore trisulcis, Verg. G. 3, 439: gladii, Liv. 6, 12, 9: corque timore micat, beats, palp

micon.full: Mĭcon, ōnis, m., = Μίκων, the name of a shepherd: cum me arbustum videre Miconis ... incidere falce, Verg. E. 3, 10: ramosa Micon vivacis cornua cervi, id. ib. 7, 30.—So, forte Micon senior, Canthusque Miconis alumnus, Calp. Ecl. 5, 1.
micon.short: Mĭcon, ōnis, m., = Μίκων, the name of a shepherd: cum me arbustum videre Miconis ...

microcosmus.full: micrŏcosmus, i, m., = μικρόκοσμος, a little world, world in miniature, microcosm, Isid. Orig. 3, 22, 2.
microcosmus.short: micrŏcosmus, i, m., = μικρόκοσμος, a little world, world in miniature, microcosm, Isid.

micropsychus.full: micropsȳchus, a, um, adj., = μικρόψυχος, little-minded, narrow-minded (postAug.), Plin. 22, 24, 51, § 110: Novius, Mart. 1, 87 lemm.
micropsychus.short: micropsȳchus, a, um, adj., = μικρόψυχος, little-minded, narrow-minded (postAug.), Plin.

microsphaerum.full: microsphaerum, i, n., = μικρόσφαιρον, small-leaved nard, Plin. 12, 12, 26, § 44.
microsphaerum.short: microsphaerum, i, n., = μικρόσφαιρον, small-leaved nard, Plin.

mictilis.full: mictĭlis, e, adj. mingo, that deserves to be defiled; hence, transf., despicable, worthless, bad (ante-class.): merx, Lucil. ap. Non. 137, 31.

mictorius.full: mictōrĭus, a, um, adj. mingo, that promotes urine, urinative, diuretic (postclass.): medicamenta, Cael. Aur. Acut. 3, 8, 86.

mictualis.full: mictŭālis, e, adj. id. (only post class). Relating to the passing of urine, wrinary: via, Cael. Aur. Tard. 5, 10, 91: viae, id. ib. 5, 10, 121.—Hence, subst.: mictŭālis, is, f., the urinary passage, Cael. Aur. Tard. 5, 4, 65.— That promotes urine, diuretic: virtus, App. Herb. 117.— Subst.: mictŭāle, is, n., a diuretic, Cael. Aur. Tard. 5, 10, 122 al.

micturio.full: mictŭrĭo, 4, v. desider. n. [mingo], to go to make water, to make water (only in Juvenal): micturiunt hic, Juv. 6, 309; 16, 46.

mictus.full: mictus, ūs, m. id., a making water, urinating (post-class.): sanguinis mictus, Cael. Aur. Tard. 5, 3, 59; 2, 1, 12.

micula.full: mīcŭla, ae, f. dim. mica, a little crumb, little grain, little bit (post-Aug.), Cels. 2, 5: exiguae, Arn. 2, 77.

midaium.full: Midaium, i, n., = Μιδάειον, a city of Phrygia, Plin. 5, 32, 41, § 145.—Hence, subst.: Midaeenses, ium, m., the inhabitants of Midaium, Cic. Fam. 3, 8, 3.—Also called Midaei, orum, m., Plin. 5, 29, 29, § 105.
midaium.short: Midaium, i, n., = Μιδάειον, a city of Phrygia, Plin.

midamus.full: Mīdāmus, i, m., one of the fifty sons of Ægyptus, who was slain by his wife, Hyg. Fab. 170.
midamus.short: Mīdāmus, i, m., one of the fifty sons of Ægyptus, who was slain by his wife, Hyg.

midas.full: Mĭdas or Mĭda, ae, m., = Μίδας, son of Gordius, and king of Phrygia. At his request he received from Bacchus, who wished to prove his gratitude for the hospitality Midas had accorded him, the boon that everything he touched should turn to gold. But as this extended also to food and drink, he implored the assistance of the god. The latter told him to bathe in the river Pactolus, the sands of which from that time became mixed with gold. Midas decided in favor of Pan a musical contest between him a
midas.short: Mĭdas or Mĭda, ae, m., = Μίδας, son of Gordius, and king of Phrygia.

mide.full: Mīdē, ēs, f., a city in Bœotia, Stat. Th. 7, 331.
mide.short: Mīdē, ēs, f., a city in Bœotia, Stat.

midea.full: Mīdea, ae, f., = Μίδεια, a city in Lycia, Stat. Th. 4, 45.
midea.short: Mīdea, ae, f., = Μίδεια, a city in Lycia, Stat.

midias.full: Mīdĭas, ae, m., = Μειδιας, the name of a Messenian, who invented the cuirass, Plin. 7, 56, 57, § 200.
midias.short: Mīdĭas, ae, m., = Μειδιας, the name of a Messenian, who invented the cuirass, Plin.

midinus.full: Mīdīnus, a, um, adj. Midas, of or belonging to Midas: Arcadicum ac Midinum sapis, i. e. after the manner of an ass, Mart. Cap. 6, § 577

migdilybs.full: Migdĭlybs, ўbis, m. μιγδην-λύψ, a mixed Libyan, i. e. of Libyan (African) and Tyrian descent, as the Carthaginians were, Plaut Poen. 5, 2, 73.

migma.full: migma, ătis, n., = μίγμα, a mixture, mixed provender, meslin: commistum mig ma, Vulg. Isa. 30, 24.
migma.short: migma, ătis, n., = μίγμα, a mixture, mixed provender, meslin: commistum mig ma, Vulg.

migratio.full: mī^grātĭo, ōnis, f. migro, a removal, a changing of one's habitation, migration (class.). Lit.: haec migratio nobis misera, Liv. 5, 53: migrationem esse mortem in eas oras, quas, qui vitā excesserunt, incolunt, Cic. Tusc. 1, 41, 98; cf. id. ib. 1, 12, 27; id. Cael. 8, 18.—* Trop.: cui verbo (fideliter) domicilium est proprium in officio, migrationes in alienum multae, transfers, metaphorical uses, Cic. Fam. 16, 17, 1.

migrator.full: mī^grātor, ōris, m. id., a wanderer: migrator μετανάστης, Gloss. Gr. Lat.

migro.full: mī^gro, āvi, ātum, 1 (migrassit for migraverit, Cic. Leg. 3, 4, 11), v. n. and a. [etym. dub.; cf. Sanscr. root mā, exchange; also meo]. Neutr., to remove from one place to another, to depart, flit, migrate (class.). Lit.: migrare e fano foras, Plaut. Curc. 2, 1, 1: ex urbe tu rus habitatum migres? Ter. Hec. 4, 2, 13: ad integra omnia, Liv. 5, 53: ad generum, Cic. Verr. 2, 2, 36, § 89: in tabernas, Hor. A. P. 229: Veios, Liv. 5, 53: Alexandriam vel Ilium, Suet. Caes. 79: finibus, Plin. 6, 17, 21
migro.short: mī^gro, āvi, ātum, 1 (migrassit for migraverit, Cic.

mihipte.full: mihipte, i. q. mihi ipsi, v. ego.

milanion.full: Mīlănĭon, ōnis, m., = Μειλανίων, the husband of Atalanta: flēsse Milaniona, Ov. A. A. 2, 188; id. Am. 3, 2, 29; Prop. 1, 1, 9.
milanion.short: Mīlănĭon, ōnis, m., = Μειλανίων, the husband of Atalanta: flēsse Milaniona, Ov.

mile.full: mile, mīlēsĭmus, etc., v. mille, millesimus, etc.

mileon.full: milĕon, i, n., the name of a plant, also called scelerata, App. Herb. 8.
mileon.short: milĕon, i, n., the name of a plant, also called scelerata, App.

miles.full: mīlĕs (MEILES, Inscr. Mur. 582; late form, milex, Gromat. Vet. p. 246, 19), ĭtis, comm. Sanscr root mil-, to unite, combine; cf.: mille, milites, quod trium millium primo legio fiebat, ac singulae tribus Titiensium, Ramnium, Lucerum milia singula militum mittebant, Varr. L. L. 5, § 89 Müll., a soldier. Lit. In gen.: miles, qui locum non tenuit, Cic. Clu. 46, 128: legere milites, to levy, raise, Pompei, ap. Cic. Att. 8, 12 a, 3: scribere, to enlist, enroll, Sall. J. 43, 3: deligere, Liv. 29, 1: o

milesium.full: mīlēsĭum, i, n., a kind of kingfisher, Plin. 32, 8, 27, § 87.
milesium.short: mīlēsĭum, i, n., a kind of kingfisher, Plin.

miletis.full: Mīlētis, ĭdis, f. Miletus. The daughter of Miletus, Byblis, Ov. M. 9, 634.— A Milesian woman, Caecil. ap. Diom. p. 378 P.

miletopolis.full: Mīlētŏpŏlis, is, f., = Μιλητόπολις, a city in European Sarmatia, founded by the Milesians, otherwise called Olbia Borysthenis or Olbiopolis, now Oczakow, Plin. 4, 12, 26, § 82.
miletopolis.short: Mīlētŏpŏlis, is, f., = Μιλητόπολις, a city in European Sarmatia, founded by the Milesians, otherwise called Olbia Borysthenis or Olbiopolis, now Oczakow, Plin.

miletus1.full: Mīlētus, i, m., = Μίλητος, the father of Caunus and Byblis, Ov. M. 9, 443.— Hence, Mīlētis, ĭdis, f., the daughter of Miletus: moesta, Ov. M. 9, 634.
miletus1.short: Mīlētus, i, m., = Μίλητος, the father of Caunus and Byblis, Ov.

miletus2.full: Mīlētus (-tos), i, f., = Μίλητος, the city of Miletus, in Caria, the birthplace of Thales, Mel. 1, 17, 1; Plin. 5, 29, 31, § 112; Cic. Att. 9, 9, 2.—Esp., as a proverb for luxury and wantonness: paupertas Romana perit, hinc fluxit ad istos et Sybaris colles, hinc et Rhodos et Miletos, Juv. 6, 296. —Hence, Mīlēsĭus, a, um, adj., = Μιλήσιος, of or belonging to the city of Miletus, Milesian: Milesia mulier, Cic. Clu. 11, 32: vellera, Verg. G. 3, 306: lana, Plin. 29, 2, 9, § 33: rosa, id. 21, 4, 10,
miletus2.short: Mīlētus (-tos), i, f., = Μίλητος, the city of Miletus, in Caria, the birthplace of Thales, Mel.

mileum.full: Mileum (Milevum), i, n., and Mi-levi, ōrum, m., a city in Numidia, Aug. adv. Don. 6, 20.—Hence, Milēvetānus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to the city of Mileum, Aug. Ep. 34.
mileum.short: Mileum (Milevum), i, n., and Mi-levi, ōrum, m., a city in Numidia, Aug.

miliaceus.full: mĭlĭăcĕus, a, um, adj. milium, of millet, millet puls, Paul. ex Fest. s. v. forma, p. 83, 12 Müll.

miliacus.full: mĭlĭăcus, a, um, adj. id., fed with mil let: ficedulas, sive quas miliacas vocant, millet-birds, perh. ortolans, Cael. Aur. Tard. 1, 1, 27

miliarensis.full: mīlĭārensis (millĭārensis), e, adj. mille, that contains a thousand (post-class.): porticus, either containing a thousand columns, or containing a thousand paces, Vop. Aur. 49: COHORS, Inscr. Marin. Frat. Arv. p. 630.

miliarius1.full: mīlīārīus or millĭārĭus, a, um, adj. id., containing or comprising a thousand. Adj.: decuriae, Varr. L. L. 9, § 87 Müll.: greges, id. R. R. 2, 10: clivus, of a thousand paces, id. ib. 3, 1: apri, weighing a thousand pounds, Sen. Ep. 110, 12: oleae, Plin. 17, 12, 19, § 93: ala, of a thousand men, Plin. Ep. 7, 31: COHORS, Inscr Grut. 482, 4: porticus, a thousand feet in length, Suet. Ner. 31: aevum, of a thousand years, Tert Anim 31.— Subst. mīlĭārĭum (mill-), ii, n. A mile-stone (which indicated
miliarius1.short: mīlīārīus or millĭārĭus, a, um, adj.

miliarius2.full: mĭlĭārĭus (mill-), a, um, adj. milium, of or belonging to millet, millet- (ante-class. and post-Aug.): miliariae (sc. aves) dictae a cibo, quod milio fiant pingues, Varr. L. L. 5, § 76 Müll.: aves, ortolans, id. R. R. 3, 5: herba, injurious to millet, Plin. 22, 25, 78, § 161.— Transf., subst.: mĭlĭārĭum (mill-), ii, n., a short and thick pillar which stood in the centre of the basin of an oil-mill to support the cupa, Cato, R. R. 20; 22.— In baths, a tall and narrow vessel for drawing and warmin

milichus.full: Mīlĭchus (Mīlicus), i, m., a king in Spain, Sil. 3, 104.
milichus.short: Mīlĭchus (Mīlicus), i, m., a king in Spain, Sil.

milifolium.full: mīlĭfŏlĭum and millefŏlĭum, ii, n. mille-folium, a plant, milfoil, yarrow; form milifolium: myriophyllus, quod nostri milifolium vocant, caulis est tener, similis feniculi, Plin. 24, 16, 95, § 152 Jan. (al. millefolium); used in medicine, id. 24, 19, 116, § 176 al.—Form millefolium, Plin. 25, 5, 19, § 42 Jan. (al. millefolia).

miliginus.full: mīlĭgĭnus, a, um, adj. milium, of millet (late Lat.), Dynam. 1, 14.

milio.full: mīlĭo, ōnis, m., for milvus, a kite, Marc. Emp. 33.
milio.short: mīlĭo, ōnis, m., for milvus, a kite, Marc.

milionia.full: Milionĭa, ae, f., a city of Italy, in the country of the Marsians, Liv. 10, 3; 34.
milionia.short: Milionĭa, ae, f., a city of Italy, in the country of the Marsians, Liv.

militaris.full: mīlitāris, e, adj. miles, of or belonging to a soldier, to war, or to military service, proper to or usual with soldiers, military, warlike, martial (class.): militares pueri, soldiers' children, officers' sons, Plaut. Truc. 5, 16: homo, id. Ep. 1, 1, 14: advena, id. Ps. 4, 1, 20: tribuni, Cic. Clu. 36, 99: vir, Tac. H. 2, 75: homines, Sall. C. 45, 2.— Also subst.: mīlĭtāris, is, m., a military man, soldier, warrior: cur neque militaris Inter aequales equitat? Hor. C. 1, 8, 5: praesidia militari

militarius.full: mīlĭtārĭus, a, um, adj. id., soldierlike, military (ante-class.): gradus, Plaut. Ps. 4, 4, 11.—Hence, adv.: mīlĭtārĭē, in a soldier-like or military manner (postclass.): militarie caesus, Treb. Trig. Tyrann. 22 dub.

militia.full: mīlĭtĭa, ae (-āi, Lucr. 1, 29), f. id., military service, warfare, war. Lit.: in militiae disciplinam profectus est, Cic. Imp. Pomp. 10, 28: militiam subterfugere, id. Off. 3, 26, 97: ferre, Hor. Ep. 1, 18, 55: tolerare, Verg. A. 8, 516: munus militiae sustinere, Caes. B. G. 6, 18: militiae vacatio, exemption from military service, id. ib. 6, 14: militiae magna scientia, Sall. J. 63, 2: militiam discere, id. C. 7, 4: praeclara, Vell. 2, 5, 1: Pompeii, id. 2, 40, 1: adversus Graecos, Just. 20, 1,

militiola.full: mīlĭtĭŏla, ae, f. dim. militia, a short, insignificant term of military service: semestribus militiolis tumens, Suet. Vit. Juv

milito.full: mīlĭto, āvi, ātum, 1, v. n. miles, to be a soldier, to perform military service, to serve as a soldier (syn.: stipendium mereo; class.). Lit.: in cujus exercitu Catonis filius tiro militabat, Cic. Off. 1, 11, 36: sub signis alicujus, Liv. 23, 42: adversus aliquem, Suet. Caes. 68: apud Persas, Curt. 6, 5, 7: vobiscum, id. 8, 8, 11: si inter vigiles Romae Sex annis militaverit, Ulp. Fragm. 3, 5.— Transf. To make war, wage war, war against; pass., with a homogeneous subject: libenter hoc et omne mi

mille.full: mille, in the plur. mīlia (or millia; archaic, MEILIA, Inscr. Orell. 3308; abl. sing. milli, Lucil. ap. Gell. 1, 16, and ap. Macr. S. 1, 5), num. adj. Sanscr. root mil-, combine, associate; Gr. ὅμιλος; cf. miles, a thousand, thousands. Lit. In gen., sometimes in sing. subst, with gen.; in plur, only subst. with gen.: equites mille viā breviore praemissi, Planc. ap. Cic. Fam. 10, 9, 3: mille et quingentis passibus abesse, Caes. B. G. 1, 22.—With gen.: mille drachumarum Olympicūm, Plaut. Trin. 2,

millefolia.full: millĕfŏlĭa, ae, f., false read. for milifolium, q. v., Plin. 25, 5, 19, § 42.

milleformis.full: millĕformis (millĭformis), e, adj. mille-forma, of a thousand forms (postclass.): pestis, Prud. Cath. 9, 55.

millenarius.full: millēnārĭus, a, um, adj. milleni, containing a thousand, millenary (postclass.): numerus, Aug. Civ. Dei, 20, 7: aevum, Tert. de Anim. 32: dux lanceariorum, commander of a thousand, Cassiod. Hist. Eccl. 6, 35.

milleni.full: millēni, ae, a, adj. num. distr. [mille], a thousand each, a thousand (post-class.; for mille numero is the true reading, Plaut. Bacch. 4, 9, 4), Gal. Inst. 2, 225; Dig. 31, 89, 1; Lampr. Heliog. 21, 7; 26, 7; Vulg. Num. 31, 5; id. 2 Reg. 18, 4; id. 1 Esdr. 8, 27.

millepeda.full: millĕpĕda, ae, f. mille-pes, thousandfeet, an insect, perh. the wood-louse, milleped, Plin. 20, 2, 6, § 12.— A hairy caterpillar, Plin. 29, 6, 39, § 136.

millesimus.full: millēsĭmus (-lensimus), a, um, adj. mille, the thousandth (class.): millesimam partem vix intellego, Cic. Att. 2, 4, 1; cf.: in millesimo corpore, Cels. 2, 6: inter mille rates tua sit millesima puppis, i. e. ultima, Ov H. 13, 97: usura, one for every thousand monthly, Sen. Ira, 3, 33: pagina, Juv. 7, 100. —In plur.: armillam, ex millesimis Mercurii factam, the thousandth part of gain vowed to Mercury, Petr. 67, 7.—Hence, adv.: millēsĭmum, for the thousandth time: Q pater quartum vel potius mill

millies.full: millĭes or mīlĭes (milliens or mi-liens), adv. id., a thousand times (class.): quinquies millies, Plin. 2, 23, 21, § 85: semel et tricies millies mille, Vitr. 1, 6.—Innumerable times: moreretur prius millies quam, Cic. Rab. Perd. 5, 15; id. Sest. 58, 123; id. Att. 7, 11, 1: genera juris millies mutata sunt, id. Rep. 3, 10, 17: millies melius, a thousand times better, id. Phil. 2, 44, 112: plus miliens audivi, more than a thousand times, Ter. Eun. 3, 1, 32.
millies.short: millĭes or mīlĭes (milliens or mi-liens), adv.

millimodus.full: millĭmŏdus, a, um, adj. mille-modus, thousand-fold, innumerable (postclass.): irae, Ven. Vit. S. Martin. 3, 303.

millio.full: millĭo, ōnis, m., a kind of hawk, Macr. Emp. 33.
millio.short: millĭo, ōnis, m., a kind of hawk, Macr.

milo1.full: Mĭlo and Mĭlon, ōnis, m., = Μίλων. A celebrated athlete of Crotona, Cic. Fat. 13, 30; id. Sen. 9, 27; 10, 33; Val. Max. 9, 12, 9 ext.; Vitr. 9 praef. § 2; Plin. 7, 20, 19, § 83.— A king of Pisa, in Elis, Ov. Ib. 327.
milo1.short: Mĭlo and Mĭlon, ōnis, m., = Μίλων.

milo2.full: Mĭlo, ōnis, m., a name assumed by T. Annius, as an admirer of Milo of Crotona, and the leader of a band of gladiators. He was the son of C. Papius Celsus and Annia, daughter of C. Annius, who adopted the grandson. He was tribune of the people with Clodius, B. C. 57, but afterwards killed the latter, and was defended by Cicero in an oration still extant (pro T. Annio Milone).—Hence, Mĭlōnĭānus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to T. Annius Milo, Milonian: tempora, i. e. the time when Milo was indicte
milo2.short: Mĭlo, ōnis, m., a name assumed by T.

milonius.full: Mīlōnĭus, i, m., the name of a parasite, Hor. S. 2, 1, 24.
milonius.short: Mīlōnĭus, i, m., the name of a parasite, Hor.

miltiades.full: Miltiădes, is, m., = Μιλτιάδης, the celebrated general of the Athenians, the victor in the battle of Marathon, Nep. Milt.; Cic. Tusc. 4, 19, 44; id. Rep. 1, 3, 5; id. Sest. 67, 141.
miltiades.short: Miltiădes, is, m., = Μιλτιάδης, the celebrated general of the Athenians, the victor in the battle of Marathon, Nep.

miltites lapis.full: miltītes lăpis = μιλτίτης λίθος, a kind of blood-stone, Plin. 36, 20, 38, § 147.
miltites lapis.short: miltītes lăpis = μιλτίτης λίθος, a kind of blood-stone, Plin.

miltos.full: miltos, i, f., = μιλτος, red-lead, minium, or native cinnabar, Plin. 33, 7, 38, § 115.
miltos.short: miltos, i, f., = μιλτος, red-lead, minium, or native cinnabar, Plin.

milua.full: milŭa (-va), ae, f. milvus, a she-kite, as a term of abuse, Petr. 75, 6.

miluago.full: milŭāgo (-vago), ĭnis, f. id., a kind of fish, = milvus, II. A., Isid. 12, 6, 36 (but a false read for lolligo, Plin. 32, 2, 6, § 15).

miluinus.full: milŭīnus (also milvīnus), a, um, adj. id., of or belonging to the kite (class.): plumae, Plin. 37, 10, 60, § 167.— Transf., resembling a kite, kite-like, i. e. rapacious: ungulae, i. e. a thief's clutches, Plaut. Ps. 3, 2, 63. pullus, Cic. Q. Fr. 1, 2, 2, § 6: miluinus pes, kite's foot, an herb so called from its resemblance to the foot of a kite, Col. 12, 7, § 1; cf. Plin. 27, 8, 35, § 57.— Subst.: miluīna (milvīna), ae, f. * (Sc. fames.) A kite's, i. e. a ravenous, appetite, voracity, Plaut. M

miluus.full: miluus (later also, milvus), i, m., a bird of prey, a kite, glede. Lit.: pulmentum ei deripuit miluos ... postulare ut sibi liceret miluom vadarier, Plaut. Aul. 2, 4, 37; 40; id. Rud. 4, 4, 80; Plin. 10, 10, 12, § 28: miluo est quoddam bellum quasi naturale cum corvo, Cic. N. D. 2, 49, 125: adulteretur et columba miluo, of something impossible, Hor. Epod. 16, 32.—Of rapacious men, a kite: male ego metuo miluos, Plaut. Poen. 5, 5, 13.—Prov.: dives arat Curibus, quantum non milvus oberret, so larg
miluus.short: miluus (later also, milvus), i, m., a bird of prey, a kite, glede.

milyadum.full: Milўădum Commūne, a district and city in Lycia, Cic. Verr. 2, 1, 38, § 95; called Milyas, ădis, f., Liv. 38, 39, 16.
milyadum.short: Milўădum Commūne, a district and city in Lycia, Cic.

mima.full: mīma, ae (in the dat. and abl. plur., mimabus, acc. to Cledonius, p. 1863 P.), f. mimus, a female mimic or mime, Cic. Phil. 2, 24, 58; 13, 11, 24; Hor. S. 1, 2, 56; Inscr. Orell. 2624.—In apposition: a mima uxore, Cic. Phil. 2, 8, 20.

mimallones.full: Mĭmallŏnes, um, f., = Μιμάλλονες, the Bacchantes (poet), Stat. Th. 4, 660; Sid. C. 1, 13.—Hence, Mĭmallŏnĕus, a, um, adj., Bacchantic, Bacchanalian (poet.), Pers. 1, 99.— Mĭmallŏnis, ĭdis, f., a Bacchante (poet.), Ov. A. A. 1, 541.
mimallones.short: Mĭmallŏnes, um, f., = Μιμάλλονες, the Bacchantes (poet), Stat.

mimarius.full: mīmārĭus, a, um, adj. mimus, for mimicus, of or belonging to a mime, mimic (post-class.): mimarii scurrae, Capitol Ver. 8, 1.— Subst.: mīmārĭus, ĭi, m., a mimic actor, Inscr. Orell. 2631.

mimas.full: Mĭmas, antis, m., = Μίμας. A mountain range in Ionia, opposite the Isle of Chios, a branch of Mount Tmolus, still called Mimas, Plin. 5, 29, 31, § 118; Ov M. 2, 222; Luc. 7, 451; Cic. Att. 16, 13, a, 2; id. Fragm. p. 580 Orell.; Amm. 31, 14, 8.— A giant: Typhoeus et validus Mimas, Hor. C. 3, 4, 53; Sil. 4, 278.— A Trojan: Mimanta, Verg. A. 10, 702.

mimiambi.full: mīmĭambi, ōrum, m., a mimic poem in iambics, mimic iambics (post-Aug.), Ter. de Metr. p. 2437 P.; Plin. Ep. 6, 21, 4.
mimiambi.short: mīmĭambi, ōrum, m., a mimic poem in iambics, mimic iambics (post-Aug.), Ter.

mimicus.full: mīmĭcus, a, um, adj., = μιμικός, of or belonging to mimes, mimic, farcical (class.). Lit.: ne aut scurrilis jocus sit, aut mimicus, farcical, extravagant, Cic. de Or. 2, 59, 239; Quint. 6, 1, 47 Spald.— Trop.: res mimicae et ineptae, Plin. Ep. 7, 29, 3: mors, mimic, feigned, Petr. 94 fin.—Hence, adv.: mīmĭcē, like a mime, farcically, Cat. 42, 8; Tert. Apol. 46; Sen. Contr. 2, 12, 5.
mimicus.short: mīmĭcus, a, um, adj., = μιμικός, of or belonging to mimes, mimic, farcical (class.).

mimmulus.full: mimmŭlus, i, m., the name of a plant, Plin. 18, 28, 67, § 259 dub. (Sillig, nummulus).
mimmulus.short: mimmŭlus, i, m., the name of a plant, Plin.

mimnermia.full: Mimnermĭa, ae, f., a surname of Venus: alii Venerem Mimnermiam vel Meminiam dicunt, quod meminerit omnium, Serv Aen. 1, 720.
mimnermia.short: Mimnermĭa, ae, f., a surname of Venus: alii Venerem Mimnermiam vel Meminiam dicunt, quod meminerit omnium, Serv Aen.

mimnermus.full: Mimnermus, i, m., = Μίμνερμος, a Greek elegiac poet of Colophon, the inventor of the pentameter, Hor. Ep. 1, 6, 65; 2, 2, 101: Mimnermi versus, i. e. elegiac poetry, Prop. 1, 9, 11.
mimnermus.short: Mimnermus, i, m., = Μίμνερμος, a Greek elegiac poet of Colophon, the inventor of the pentameter, Hor.

mimographus.full: mīmŏgrăphus, i, m., = μιμογράφος, a composer of mimes, a mimographer, Suet. Gram. 18; Inscr. Orell. 2622; Schol. Juv. 8, 186.
mimographus.short: mīmŏgrăphus, i, m., = μιμογράφος, a composer of mimes, a mimographer, Suet.

mimologus.full: mīmŏlŏgus, i, m., = μιμολόγος, an actor in mimic plays or farces, a mime, Firm. Math. 8, 8.
mimologus.short: mīmŏlŏgus, i, m., = μιμολόγος, an actor in mimic plays or farces, a mime, Firm.

mimula.full: mīmŭla, ae, f. dim. mima, a little mime, Cic. Phil. 2, 25, 61; id. Planc. 12, 30.

mimulus.full: mīmŭlus, i, m. dim. mimus, a little mime (post-class.), Arn. 2, 69 fin.

mimus.full: mīmus, i, m., = μῖμος. A mimic actor, mime, Cic. de Or. 2, 59, 242: oratori minime convenit distortus vultus gestusque: quae in mimis rideri solent, Quint. 6, 3, 29; Ov. A. A. 1, 501: nobilis, Juv. 8, 198. — A mimic play, mime, farce. Lit.: mimi exitus, Cic. Cael. 27, 65: tutor, mimus vetus, id. de Or. 2, 64, 259: mimos scribere, Ov. Tr. 2, 497: mimorum scriptor, Quint. 1, 10, 17: mimos commentari, Cic. Phil. 11, 6, 13: mimum agere, Suet. Caes. 39; Juv. 13, 110: mimus quis melior plorante gula?

min.full: min, for minium, v. h. v.

mina1.full: mĭna (mna, Plin. 35, 10, 36, § 107), ae, f., = μνᾶ. A Greek weight of a hundred Attic drachmas, a mina, Plin. 21, 34, 109, § 185; Rhem. Fann. de Ponder. 32 sq. — A Greek money of account. The silver mina; this was of 100 Attic drachmae or Roman denarii (about $18.05 of our currency): argenti, Plaut. As. 2, 3, 16; id. Poen. 2, 21; 5, 5, 8 al.—Also absol.: mina, Plaut. Trin. 2, 4, 2; id. Ps. 3, 2, 87; id. Poen. 5, 6, 22 al.; Cic. Tusc. 5, 32, 91; id. Leg. 2, 27, 68: minae bonae mala opera partae,

mina2.full: mĭna, ae, f. adj., smooth: mina ovis, smooth-bellied, with no wool on the belly: mina (id est ventre glabro), Varr R. R. 2, 2, 6: minae oves, a play on the double meaning of the word (v. 1. mina, II.), Plaut. Truc. 3, 1, 9.— Subst.: mĭna, ae, f.: minam Aelius vocitatam ait mammam alteram lacte deficientem, quasi minorem factam, Paul. ex Fest. p. 122 Müll.

minabiliter.full: mĭnābĭlĭter, adv. 1. minor, threateningly: minabiliter, ἀπειλητικῶς, Gloss. Philox.

minaciae.full: mĭnācĭae, arum, f. minae, menaces, threats, with a play upon the double meaning of minae; v. 1. mina: at ego oves et lanam et alia multa quae poscet dabo. Meliust te minis certare mecum quam minaciis, Plaut. Truc. 5, 55 sq. (but Plaut. Rud. 3, 5, 16; id. Capt. 4, 2, 22, the true reading is minae).

minae.full: mĭnae, ārum, f. root min-, only in Lat.; cf.: mentum, minari, and perh. mons, the projecting points or pinnacles of walls (only poet.). Lit.: minae murorum, Verg. A. 4, 88: moenium, Amm. 24, 2, 12; 24, 2, 19; 29, 6, 11; 20, 6, 2.— Trop., threats, menaces, of animate and inanimate things (class.). Of living beings: si quidem hercle Aeacidinis minis animisque expletus cedit, Plaut. As. 2, 3, 25: virtutem hominibus instituendo et persuadendo, non minis et vi ac metu tradi, Cic. de Or. 1, 58, 247: t

minaei.full: Minaei (Minnaei), ōrum, m., a people of Arabia, celebrated for their myrrh and frankincense, Plin. 6, 28, 32, § 155 sqq.; Prisc. Perieg. 888.—Hence, adj.: Mĭnae-us, a, um, of or belonging to the Minæi: tus, Plin. 12, 14, 30, § 53: murra, id. 12, 16, 35, § 69.
minaei.short: Minaei (Minnaei), ōrum, m., a people of Arabia, celebrated for their myrrh and frankincense, Plin.

minatio.full: mĭnātĭo, ōnis, f. 1. minor, a threatening, threat, menace, as an action (rare but class.): quae illaec est minatio? Plaut. Capt. 4, 2, 19: minationes, Cic. de Or. 2, 71, 288: imperiosis minationibus confutare, Tullius Tiro ap. Gell. 6 ($3), 3, 13 Hertz.

minator.full: mĭnātor, ōris, m. id., one who drives cattle with threats, a cattle-driver, a drover (post-class.), Tert. ad Nat. 2, 3 fin.

minatorius.full: mĭnātōrĭus, a, um, adj. minator, threatening (post-class.): sonitu minatoric (al. minaci), Amm 17, 7, 14.

minax.full: mĭnax, ācis, adj. 1. minor, lit., jutting out, projecting. Lit. (poet.): minaci Pendentem scopulo, overhanging, projecting, Verg. A. 8, 668: robur saxi, overlying, incumbent, Lucr. 1, 881.— Trop., threatening, menacing, full of threats or menaces (class.). Of living things: Indutiomarus iste minax atque arrogans, Cic. Font. 12, 36; Quint. 11, 3, 72: vituli nondum metuenda fronte minaces, Ov. Am. 3, 13, 15.— Sup.: adversus barbaros minacissimus, Suet. Calig. 51.— Of inanimate things: aequor saevu

minciades.full: Mincĭădes, ae, m. Mincius, the Minciade, i. e. Virgil, as born in Mantua, on the Mincius, Juvenc. 1, 10.

mincius.full: Mincĭus, ii, m., a river in Cisalpine Gaul, which runs by Mantua, a tributary of the Po, now Mincio, Verg. G. 3, 15: amnis, Liv. 24, 10, 7; Plin. 2, 103, 106, § 224.
mincius.short: Mincĭus, ii, m., a river in Cisalpine Gaul, which runs by Mantua, a tributary of the Po, now Mincio, Verg.

minctio.full: minctĭo, ōnis, f. mingo, a making water (post-class.), Veg. Vet. 1, 50.

minctura.full: minctūra, ae, f. id., a making water (post-class.), Veg. Vet. 1, 33 (al. mictura).

minctus.full: minctus, ūs, m. id. (late Lat.), Cael. Aur. signif 136.

mineo.full: mĭnĕo, ēre, false reading for meant, Lucr. 6, 563 and 1193; v. Lachm. ad h. l.
mineo.short: mĭnĕo, ēre, false reading for meant, Lucr.

minerrimus.full: minerrĭmus, pro minimo dixerunt, Paul. ex Fest. p. 122 Müll.

minerva.full: Mĭnerva (old orthogr. Menerva, like magester, leber, etc., acc. to Quint. 1, 4, 17), ae, f. from the root men, whence mens, memini, moneo, etc.; v. infra, a Roman goddess, identified with the Grecian Pallas Athene, the daughter of Zeus, and the goddess of wisdom, of sense and reflection, of the arts and sciences, of poetry, and of spinning and weaving: Minerva dicta, quod bene moneat. Hanc enim pagani pro sapientiā ponebant; Cornificius vero, quod fingatur pingaturque minitans armis, eandem dict

minerval.full: Mĭnerval, ālis, n. Minerva, a gift in return for instruction (ante- and postclass.), Varr R. R. 3, 2, 18; Tert. Idol. 10.

minervalicium.full: Mĭnervālĭcĭum, ii, n. Minerval, perh. for Minerval, a teacher's fee: Minervalicium, συστατικόν, Gloss. Philox.

minervalis.full: Mĭnervālis, e, adj. Minerva, of or belonging to Minerva (to learning, good sense, etc.), Minervan (post-class.): artes, Tert. Spect. 11 fin.: munus, Hier. Ep. ad Ephes. 6, 4: MAGISTER, Inscr. Orell. 2421.— In plur. subst.: Mĭnervālĭa, ĭum, n., festivities in honor of Minerva, Sergius, p. 1846 P

minervinus.full: Minervīnus, i, m. Minervius, the name of a Roman slave, Inscr. Mur. 479, 1.

minervius.full: Mĭnervĭus, a, um, adj. Minerva, of or belonging to Minerva, Minervian (postclass.): nomen, i. e. of Minerva, Arn. 4, 137; LEGIO, named after Minerva, Inscr. Orell. 922; 1767; 1894 et saep.: cives, i. e. Athenienses, because there was in Athens a temple of Minerva, Arn. 5, 175: versus, verses composed in honor of Minerva, Paul. ex Fest. s. v axamenta, p. 3 Müll.— Subst.: Mĭnervĭum, ii, n. A temple of Minerva, Varr. L. L. 5, § 47 Müll.; Arn. 6, 193.— A city and castle (hence also called Arx Minerv

mineus.full: mĭnĕus, a, um, adj. minium, of a cinnabar-red color: color rosarum, App. M. 4, 2, p. 143: circulus, id. Flor. 2, p. 348.

mingo.full: mingo, inxi, inctum and ictum, 3, v. a. root mig, whence also meio; cf. also the Greek ὀ μιχέω, to make water, to void urine: in me veniant mictum atque cacatum, Hor. S. 1, 8, 38: urina mingitur, Cels. 4, 20: ut quantum bibisset, tantum mingeret, Vop. ap. Bon. 14; Juv. 3, 107.—In mal. part., Cat. 67, 30.
mingo.short: mingo, inxi, inctum and ictum, 3, v.

miniaceus.full: mĭnĭācĕus, a, um, adj. minium, of cinnabar or minium, cinnabar-red, vermilion (only in Vitr.): expolitio, Vitr. 7, 9: cunei, id. 7, 4 med.; cf.: minatius (i. e. miniaceus), μιλτωδης, Gloss. Labb.

minianus.full: mĭnĭānus, a, um, adj. id., painted with red-lead or cinnabar: minianus Juppiter (i. e. statua Iovis), Cic. Fam. 9, 16, 8.

miniarius.full: mĭnĭārĭus, a, um, adj. id., of or belonging to minium or cinnabar (post-Aug.): miniarium metallum, a cinnabar mine, Plin. 33, 7, 40, § 118.— Subst.: mĭnĭā-rĭa, ae, f., or mĭnĭārĭum, ii, n., a cinnabar mine, Plin. 33, 7, 40, § 121.

miniatulus.full: mĭnĭātŭlus, a, um, adj. dim. [miniatus], colored with red-lead or cinnabar, colored red: cerula, Cic. Att. 16, 11, 1.

miniatus.full: mĭnĭātus, a, um, v. 1. minio, P. a.

minime.full: mĭnĭmē, adv., v. parvus fin., under minimus.

minimopere.full: mĭnĭmŏpĕre, i. e. minimo opere, not at all, Licin. ap. Prisc. 6.

minimus.full: mĭnĭmus, a, um, v. parvus fin.

mininus.full: mĭnīnus, a, um, adj. mina, costing a mina, of the worth of a mina: exta, Plaut. Ps. 1, 3, 95 Fleck.

minio1.full: mĭnĭo, no perf., ātum, 1, v. a. minium, to color with red-lead or cinnabar, to paint red: Jovem, Plin. 33, 7, 38, § 112; 35, 12, 45, § 157.—Hence, mĭnĭātus, a, um, P. a. Colored with red-lead or cinnabar, colored red, red: quae quidem, vereor, ne miniata cerula tua pluribus locis notandae sint, with your red-lead pencil, Cic. Att. 15, 14, 4; 16, 11, 1.— Of the color of cinnabar, cinnabar-red, of the parrot: avis torque miniato in cervicem distincta, Plin. 10, 42, 58, § 117.

minio2.full: Mĭnĭo, ōnis, m. A small river in Etruria, now Mignone: Minionis in arvis, Verg. A. 10, 183; Rutil. 1, 279.— A town on the river Minio, Mela, 2, 4, 9.

miniscitur.full: mĭniscĭtur, pro reminiscitur antiquitus dicebatur, Paul. ex Fest. p. 122 Müll.
miniscitur.short: mĭniscĭtur, pro reminiscitur antiquitus dicebatur, Paul.

minister.full: mĭnister, tra, trum, adj. (gen. plur. ministrūm, Stat. S. 3, 1, 86) [a double comp. in form, from minus and comp. ending -ter, Gr. τερ-ος; cf.: magister, sinister], that is at hand, that serves, ministers (as an adj. only poet. and later): lumina (i. e. oculi) propositi facta ministra tui, that further, promote; promotive, or in a subst. sense, Ov. H. 21, 114: minister Grex, Sil. 11, 274: ardor, Lucr. 5, 297: ministro baculo, with the aid of a staff, Ov. Ib. 261.— Subst. mĭnister, tri, m., an at

ministerialis.full: mĭnistĕrĭālis, e, adj. ministerium, ministering (late Lat.): spiritus, Rufin. Orig. Princip. 1, 5, 1.—Hence, mĭnistĕrĭāles, ĭum, m., imperial officers, Cod. Th. 8, 7, 5 al.

ministeriani.full: mĭnistĕrĭāni, ōrum, m., = ministeriales, imperial officers, Cod. Just. 12, 26 rubric.
ministeriani.short: mĭnistĕrĭāni, ōrum, m., = ministeriales, imperial officers, Cod.

ministeriarius.full: mĭnistĕrĭārĭus, a, um, adj. ministerium, of or belonging to service, serviceable: ministeriarius, ὑπηρετικός, Gloss. Phil.

ministerium.full: mĭnistĕrĭum, ii, n. minister, the office or functions of a minister, attendance, service, ministry, in a good or bad sense; an office, occupation, work, labor, employment, administration, etc. (not in Cic. or Cæs.; cf.: munus, officium). Lit.: sunt qui ita distinguant: quaedam beneficia esse, quaedam officia, quaedam ministeria: beneficium esse, quod alienus det: officium esse filii, uxoris, etc.: ministerium esse servi, quem conditio sua eo loco posuit, ut nihil eorum, quae praestat, imputet su

ministra.full: mĭnistra, ae, v. minister, II. B.

ministratio.full: mĭnistrātĭo, ōnis, f. ministro, service, assistance: commoda, Vitr. 6, 9, 2.

ministrator.full: mĭnistrātor, ōris, m. id., an attendant, waiter, servant (class.): (turbam) transeo ministratorum, per quos, signo dato, ad inferendam cenam discurritur, Sen. Ep. 95, 24: vinum dominicum ministratoris gratia est, cup-bearer, Petr. 31, 2; Dig. 50, 16, 203: MERCVRIVS, Inscr. Fabr. 114: accensos ministratores, Cato esse scribit, Varr. L. L. 7, § 18 Müll.: cum auriganti Caio ministratorem exhiberet, play the assistant, the instructor, Suet. Vit. 17: cum te ipsum, Sulpici, objurgabam, quod ministrato
