Th. 4, 160; Mart. 4, 64, 30.—Poet.: Alpheum linquens lucosque Molorchi, i. e. the Nemean Forest, Verg. G. 3, 19.—Hence, Mŏlor-chaeus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Molorchus (poet.), Tib. 4, 1, 13.
molorchus.short: Mŏlorchus, i, m., a poor vine-dresser near Nemea, who hospitably entertained Hercules when about to slay the lion of that place, Stat.

molorthus.full: mŏlorthus, i, m., a sounding-lead: gravis molorthus (al. molybdis), Stat. S. 3, 2, 30.
molorthus.short: mŏlorthus, i, m., a sounding-lead: gravis molorthus (al.

molossi.full: Mŏlossi, ōrum, m., = Μολοσσοί, the Molossians, a people in the eastern part of Epirus, Plin. 4 prooem.; Cic. Div. 1, 34, 76; Nep. Them. 8, 4.—They were so called from Molossus, the son of Pyrrhus, king of Epirus, and Andromache, acc. to Serv. Verg. A. 3, 297.—Hence,
molossi.short: Mŏlossi, ōrum, m., = Μολοσσοί, the Molossians, a people in the eastern part of Epirus, Plin.

molossia.full: Mŏlossĭa, ae, f., = Μολοσσία, Molossia, the country of the Molossi, in Epirus, Serv. Verg. A. 3, 297.
molossia.short: Mŏlossĭa, ae, f., = Μολοσσία, Molossia, the country of the Molossi, in Epirus, Serv.

molossiambos.full: mŏlossĭambos, i, m. molossus-iambus, a metrical foot consisting of three long syllables and an iambus (e. g. ādmīrābĭlēs), Diom. p. 478 P.

molossicus.full: Mŏlossĭcus, a, um, adj. Molossus, Molossian (ante- and post-class.): parasiti Molossici (v. Molossus, A.), i. e. as ravenous as Molossian hounds, Plaut. Capt. 1, 1, 18: carmen, consisting wholly of molossi (———; e. g.: Romani victores Germanis devictis), Diom. p. 513 P.

molossis.full: Mŏlossis, ĭdis, f., = Μολοσσίς, Molossis, the country of the Molossi, in the eastern part of Epirus, Liv. 8, 24.
molossis.short: Mŏlossis, ĭdis, f., = Μολοσσίς, Molossis, the country of the Molossi, in the eastern part of Epirus, Liv.

molossopyrrhichius.full: mŏlossŏ-pyrrhĭchĭus, ii, m. molossus-pyrrhichius, a metrical foot consisting of a molossus and a pyrrhichius (e. g. ādmīrābĭlĭs), Diom. p. 478 P.

molossospondeus.full: mŏlosso-spondēus, i, m. molossusspondeus, a metrical verse consisting of a molossus and a spondee (e. g. cōntūrbātōrēs), Diom. p. 479 P.

molossus1.full: Mŏlossus, a, um, adj., = Μολοσσός, of or belonging to the Molossi, Molossian: missi de gente Molossā, Ov. M. 1, 226: canes, famed for their strength, Hor. S. 2, 6, 114: rex, Juv. 12, 108: gladii, id. 14, 162.—Also, subst.: Mŏlossus, i, m. A Molossian (hound): Molossus acer, Verg. G. 3, 405: Molossūm for Molossorum, Lucr. 5, 1063.— In prosody: pes, a metrical foot consisting of three long syllables (e. g. Arpinas, evertunt), Quint. 9, 4, 82; Diom. p. 475 P.
molossus1.short: Mŏlossus, a, um, adj., = Μολοσσός, of or belonging to the Molossi, Molossian: missi de gente Molossā, Ov.

molossus2.full: Mŏlossus, i, m., son of Pyrrhus, king of Epirus, and Andromache, the progenitor of the Molossi, acc. to Serv. Verg. A. 3, 297.
molossus2.short: Mŏlossus, i, m., son of Pyrrhus, king of Epirus, and Andromache, the progenitor of the Molossi, acc.

molucrum.full: mŏlū^crum, i, n. mola. A millbroom, i. e. a broom for sweeping out a mill: molucrum, quo molae verruntur, quod Graeci μυλήκορον dicunt, Paul. ex Fest. p. 140 Müll.— A handle for turning a mill: molucrum, quo molae vertuntur, Paul. ex Fest. p. 142 Müll. dub.; al. teruntur; cf. A. supra.— A square log of wood at the place where sacrifices were offered, or where the mola salsa was sprinkled on the victim: Cloatius in libris sacrorum, molucrum esse, aiunt, ligneum (al. lignum) quoddam quadratum, ubi

molus2.full: Mŏlus or Mŏlos, i, m., = Μόλος, the father of Meriones, Hyg. Fab. 97.
molus2.short: Mŏlus or Mŏlos, i, m., = Μόλος, the father of Meriones, Hyg.

moly.full: mōly, ўos, n., = μῶλυ. A plant with a white flower and a black root, Plin. 25, 4, 8, § 26.— Another plant, a kind of nightshade, Plin. 21, 31, 105, § 180.

molybdaena.full: mŏlybdaena, ae, f., = μολύβδαινα. Sulphuret of lead, galena, Plin. 34, 18, 53, § 173.— The plant leadwort (pure Lat. plumbago), Plin. 25, 13, 97, § 155.

molybditis.full: mŏlybdītis, ĭdis, f., = μολυβδῖτις, the spume of lead, lead-ashes, Plin. 33, 6, 35, § 106.
molybditis.short: mŏlybdītis, ĭdis, f., = μολυβδῖτις, the spume of lead, lead-ashes, Plin.

molybdus.full: mŏlybdus, i, m., and mŏlybdis, ĭdis, f., = μόλυβδος and μολυβδις, lead (pure Lat. plumbum), Stat. S. 3, 2, 30; v. molorthus.
molybdus.short: mŏlybdus, i, m., and mŏlybdis, ĭdis, f., = μόλυβδος and μολυβδις, lead (pure Lat.

momar.full: momar, n., = μῶμαρ: Siculi stultum appellant, Paul. ex Fest. p. 140 Müll.
momar.short: momar, n., = μῶμαρ: Siculi stultum appellant, Paul.

momen.full: mōmen, ĭnis, n. for movimen, from moveo. Movement, motion: e salso consurgere momine ponti, i. e. from the salt billows, Lucr. 6, 474; so also id. 2, 632, and 4, 179; v. Lachm. (where others read numine); cf. id. 3, 144.— Weight, momentum; importance, moment (ante- and postclass.): momine parvo moveri, Lucr. 3, 188: nullius mominis esse, to be of no consequence, of no moment, Arn. 2, 77.—* A moment of time, Manil. 3, 675.

momentaliter.full: mōmentālĭter, adv. momentum, in a moment (post-class.), Fulg. Myth. 2, 3.

momentana.full: mōmentāna, ae, f. id., a delicate pair of scales for weighing gold and silver: momentana pro parva modicaque pecunia, Isid. Orig. 16, 25, 4.

momentaneus.full: mōmentānĕus, a, um, adj. id., short, of brief duration, momentary (eccl. Lat.): momentaneus ardor gentium, Tert. adv. Marc. 3, 17 dub.: vices rerum, Ambros. Ep. 2, 24 init.: felicitas, Fulg. Myth. 2, 17; Hier. Ep. 69 (83), 9; Vulg. 2 Cor. 4, 17.

momentarius.full: mōmentārĭus, a, um, adj. id., brief, of brief duration, momentary; quick (postclass.): maritus, i. e. who stays but a short time, App. M. 5, p. 164, 21: vita, id. ib. 2, p. 127, 24: cura, Dig. 34, 1, 8.— Transf., instantaneous: venenum, that operates quickly, App. M. 10, p. 281, 7.

momentosus.full: mōmentōsus, a, um, adj. id., rapid, momentary: rapina (apis), Ps.-Quint. Decl. 13, 12.

momentum.full: mōmentum, i, n. for movimentum, from moveo, a movement, motion (as an indwelling force; cf.: motio, motus; class.). Lit.: astra forma ipsa figuraque sua momenta sustentant, Cic. N. D. 2, 46, 117: pisces levi caudae in utrumque momento velocitatem suam flectunt, Sen. Ep. 90, 24: utque leves tactus momentaque parva sequantur, Ov. M. 4, 180.— Transf. An alteration, change, disturbance, movement, revolution: cetera populi Romani vectigalia, perlevi saepe momento fortunae, inclinatione temporis pende

mona.full: Mŏna, ae, f., = Μόνα, the name of two islands. The Isle of Man, near Britain, Caes. B. G. 5, 13.— The Isle of Anglesea, Tac. A. 14, 29; id. Agr. 14; 18; Plin. 2, 75, 77, § 187.
mona.short: Mŏna, ae, f., = Μόνα, the name of two islands.

monacha.full: mŏnăcha, ae, f., = μοναχή, a nun (eccl. Lat.), Hier. Ep. 39, 4.
monacha.short: mŏnăcha, ae, f., = μοναχή, a nun (eccl.

monachicus.full: mŏnăchĭcus, a, um, adj., = μοναχικός, monkish (post-class.): certamen, Just. Novell. Constit. 133, 5.
monachicus.short: mŏnăchĭcus, a, um, adj., = μοναχικός, monkish (post-class.): certamen, Just.

monachium.full: mŏnăchīum, ii, n., = μοναχεῖον, a monastery (post-class.), Impp. Valent. et Marc. Cod. Just. 1, 2, 13.
monachium.short: mŏnăchīum, ii, n., = μοναχεῖον, a monastery (post-class.), Impp.

monachus.full: mŏnăchus, i, m., = μοναχός (that lives alone), a monk (eccl. Lat.), Rutil. Nam. 1, 441; Sid. Ep. 5, 17; Hier. Ep. 22, 34.
monachus.short: mŏnăchus, i, m., = μοναχός (that lives alone), a monk (eccl.

monaeses.full: Mŏnaeses, is, m., a king of the Parthians: Monaeses et Pacori manus, Hor. C. 3, 6, 9 (Monaeses et Pacorus reges Persarum fuere, Schol. Acr.).
monaeses.short: Mŏnaeses, is, m., a king of the Parthians: Monaeses et Pacori manus, Hor.

monarcha.full: mŏnarcha, ae, m., = μονάρχης, an absolute ruler, a monarch (poet.): caeruli monarcha ponti, Vet. poët. ap. Mar. Victor. p. 2551 P.
monarcha.short: mŏnarcha, ae, m., = μονάρχης, an absolute ruler, a monarch (poet.): caeruli monarcha ponti, Vet.

monarchia.full: mŏnarchĭa, ae, f., = μοναρχία, absolute rule, monarchy (post-class. for unius dominatio, imperium singulare, regnum, regalis potestas), Capitol. Max. and Balb. 14; Tert. adv. Prax. 14; Lact. 1, 5, 23.
monarchia.short: mŏnarchĭa, ae, f., = μοναρχία, absolute rule, monarchy (post-class.

monarius.full: mŏnārĭus, a, um, adj. μόνος, having but one form in inflection: nomen, Gram. Vatic. de Nom. 68 (class., Auct. 5, p. 240 Mai.).

monas.full: mŏnas, ădis, f., = μονάς, unity; a unit, monad (post-class.), Macr. Somn. Scip. 1, 6, 7 sqq.; Tert. adv. Val. 37; id. Praescr. 49 fin. et saep.

monasterialis.full: mŏnastērĭālis, e, adj. monasterium, monastic, monasterial (eccl. Lat.): disciplina, Sid. Ep. 7, 9.

monasteriolum.full: mŏnastērĭŏlum, i, n. dim. id., a little monastery, Not. Tir. p. 192; Hier. Ep. 105, 4.

monasterium.full: mŏnastērĭum, ii, n., = μοναστήριον, a monastery (eccl. Lat.), Sid. Ep. 4, 25; 7, 17; Aug. ad Casul. Ep. 86.
monasterium.short: mŏnastērĭum, ii, n., = μοναστήριον, a monastery (eccl.

monastriae.full: mŏnastrĭae, ārum, f., = μονάστριαι, nuns (post-class.), Just. Novell. Constit. 123, 27; 44.
monastriae.short: mŏnastrĭae, ārum, f., = μονάστριαι, nuns (post-class.), Just.

monaules.full: mŏnaules, ae, m., = μοναύλης, a player on the single flute, Not. Tir. p. 173; cf. monaulos.
monaules.short: mŏnaules, ae, m., = μοναύλης, a player on the single flute, Not.

monauliter.full: mŏnaulĭter, adv., on a single flute (post-class.): sonare (al. monaliter alone), Mart. Cap. 9, § 906.
monauliter.short: mŏnaulĭter, adv., on a single flute (post-class.): sonare (al.

monaulos.full: mŏnaulos or mŏnaulus, i, m., = μόναυλος, a single flute, a flute with a single pipe (post-Aug.): fistulam et monaulum (invenit) Pan Mercurii, Plin. 7, 56, 57, § 204: saepe monaulon habet, Mart. 14, 64, 2; cf. monaules.
monaulos.short: mŏnaulos or mŏnaulus, i, m., = μόναυλος, a single flute, a flute with a single pipe (post-Aug.): fistulam et monaulum (invenit) Pan Mercurii, Plin.

monazontes.full: mŏnazontes, ĭum, m., = μονάζοντες (who live alone), monks (post-class.), Cod. Th. 12, 1, 63.
monazontes.short: mŏnazontes, ĭum, m., = μονάζοντες (who live alone), monks (post-class.), Cod.

monedula.full: mŏnēdŭla, ae, f., a jackdaw, daw, Corvus monedula, Linn.: examina graculorum monedularum, cui soli avi furacitas auri argentique praecipue mira est, Plin. 10, 29, 41, § 77; 17, 14, 22, § 99. Acc. to the myth, the nymph Arne was turned into a daw, for having betrayed her country for gold, Ov. M. 7, 465 sq.—Prov.: non plus aurum tibi quam monedulae committebant, Cic. Fl. 31, 76.—As a term of endearment, Plaut. As. 3, 3, 103; cf. id. Capt. 5, 4, 5.
monedula.short: mŏnēdŭla, ae, f., a jackdaw, daw, Corvus monedula, Linn.: examina graculorum monedularum, cui soli avi furacitas auri argentique praecipue mira est, Plin.

monela.full: mŏnēla, ae, f. moneo, a reminding, admonition (eccl. Lat.), Tert. Pat. 8; id. adv. Marc. 4, 34.

monemeron.full: mŏnēmĕron, i, n., = μονήμερον, a kind of eye-salve, Marc. Emp. 8.
monemeron.short: mŏnēmĕron, i, n., = μονήμερον, a kind of eye-salve, Marc.

moneo.full: mŏnĕo, ŭi, ĭtum, 2 (inf. pres. pass. monerier, Plaut. Capt. 2, 3, 36; perf. subj. moneris pro monueris, Pac. ap. Non. 507, 24 sq.; cf. Trag. Rel. p. 66 Rib.; likewise: di monerint meliora, Pac. ap. Non. l. l. p. 74 Rib.), v. a. causative from the root men; whence memini, q. v., mens, mentio; lit. to cause to think. Lit., to remind, put in mind of, bring to one's recollection; to admonish, advise, warn, instruct, teach (syn.: hortor, suadeo, doceo): bene mones; tute ipse cunctas, Enn. ap. Non. 46

moneris.full: mŏnēris, is, f., = μονήρης (sc. ναῦς), a vessel with a single bank of oars, a galley, Liv. 38, 38, 8 (cf. Tac. H. 5, 23).

moneta.full: Mŏnēta, ae (archaic gen. Monetas, Liv. Andron. ap. Prisc. p. 679 P.), f. moneo. The mother of the Muses, a transl. of the Gr. Μνημοσύνη: Μνημοσύνη Moneta, Gloss. Philox.; cf. Cic. N. D. 3, 18, 47; Hyg. Fab. praef.: filia Monetas, Liv. Andron. ap. Prisc. p. 679 P.— A surname of Juno, in whose temple at Rome money was coined: cum terrae motus factus esset, Ut sue plena procuratio fieret, vocem ab aede Junonis ex arce exstitisse; quocirca Junonem illam appellatam Monetam, Cic. Div. 1, 45, 101; cf.

monetalis.full: mŏnētālis, e, adj. moneta, of or belonging to the mint; minted, coined (class.): triumviri monetales, the directors of the mint, Dig. 1, 2, 2, § 30.—In jest of one who asks for money: monetali ascripsi, quod ille ad me pro consule, the money-man, Cic. Att. 10, 11, 5: aurum, coined, App. M. 7, p. 190, 21: pes monetalis, the Roman foot (because the standard was kept in the temple of Juno Moneta), Grom. Vet. p. 128, 2 sq.

monetarius.full: mŏnētārĭus, a, um, adj. id., of or belonging to the mint: FAMILIA, Inscr. Orell. 3226.—Hence, subst.: mŏnētārĭus, i, m., a master of the mint, Inscr. Mur. 968, 5: monetarii, minters, coiners (post-class.), Aur. Vict. Epit. Eutr. 35; Eutr. 9, 14; Vop. Aur. 38.

monile.full: mŏnīle, is, n. kindr. to Sanscr. mani; Lat. gemma, margarīta; Gr. μάννος, μόννος, a necklace, a collar (esp. of women, but also of boys and of animals), Paul. ex Fest. p. 138 Müll.; cf. Quint. 11, 1, 3: cum (Eriphyle) vidisset monile ex auro et gemmis, Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 18, § 39; Afran. ap. Non. 150, 28: colloque monile Baccatum, Verg. A. 1, 654; Plin. 37, 3, 11, § 44.—Plur.: monilia, jewels: toto posuere monilia collo, Juv. 2, 85: super gemmas et monilia calcare, App. M. 5, 1, p. 159: monilibus

monitio.full: mŏnĭtĭo, ōnis, f. moneo, a reminding, admonishing, advice, admonition, warning (rare but class.): objurgatio post turpe factum castigatio: monitio vero est ante commissum, Paul. ex Fest. p. 196 Müll.: monitio acerbitate, objurgatio contumeliā careat, * Cic. Lael. 24, 89; Suet. Tib. 18: volebat credi, monitione ejus futura praenoscere, id. Ner. 56: ut ne monitione quidem proficiant, Sen. Ep. 94, 39: officii, Col. 11, 1, 30.—In plur., Col. 11, 1, 6.

monito.full: mŏnĭto, āre, v. freq. a. id., to remind, admonish (post-class.), Venant. Vit. S. Mart. 2, 387; id. Carm. 5, 5, 23.

monitor.full: mŏnĭtor, ōris, m. id., one who reminds one of any thing, an admonisher, monitor (syn.: hortator, auctor). In gen.: nil opus fuit monitore, Ter. Heaut. 1, 1, 119: monitor et praemonstrator, id. ib. 5, 1, 2: est enim (hoc praeceptum) non tam acutum quam necessarium, magisque monitoris non fatui quam eruditi magistri, Cic. de Or. 2, 24, 99: stet ad latus monitor, Sen. Ep. 94, 72: officii, Sall. J. 85, 10: monitoris egere, Hor. Ep. 1, 18, 67.— In partic. The counsellor who furnishes an orator with h

monitorius.full: mŏnĭtōrĭus, a, um, adj. monitor, that serves to remind or admonish, monitory (post-Aug.): fulmen, Sen. Q. N. 2, 39, 2; id. ib. 2, 49, 1.

monitum.full: mŏnĭtum, i, n. moneo, admonition, advice, counsel (rare but class.): meis consiliis, monitis, etc., Cic. Fam. 5, 8, 2: tuis monitis praeceptisque, id. ib. 5, 13, 3: meas aures omnium praeceptis monitisque patuisse, id. Phil. 14, 7, 20; Vulg. Job, 1, 15; id. Deut. 21, 20.— A prophecy, prediction: deorum monita, Cic. Har. Resp. 25, 54: Carmentis Nymphae, Verg. A. 8, 336.

monitus1.full: mŏnĭtus, a, um, Part., from moneo.
monitus1.short: mŏnĭtus, a, um, Part., from moneo.

monitus2.full: mŏnĭtus, ūs, m. moneo, a reminding, warning, admonition. In gen. (only poet.): monitu nutricis, Ov. H. 18, 115: finierat monitus, id. M. 2, 103: laevo monitu pueros producit avaros, Juv. 14, 228: monitus acres tradere, Val. Fl. 1, 475. — In partic., admonition by the gods through omens, an omen, prognostic, prophecy, the will of the gods, a warning by oracles, lightning, etc. (class.): fortunae monitu, * Cic. Div. 2, 41, 86: revererique numinum monitus, Plin. Pan. 76: fulgarum, Plin. 2, 7, 5, §

monnula.full: monnŭla, ae, f., a darling, a late Lat. term of endearment, Inscr. Mur. 2083, 2.
monnula.short: monnŭla, ae, f., a darling, a late Lat.

monobelus.full: mŏnŏbĕlus, i, m., = μονόβελος (all shaft): i. q. magno pene praeditus, Heliog. ap. Lampr. Heliog. 8, 7.
monobelus.short: mŏnŏbĕlus, i, m., = μονόβελος (all shaft): i.

monobolon.full: mŏnŏbŏlon, i, n., = μόνοσ-βόλος, a single throw, i. e. leaping alone, a game in which various feats of bodily agility are performed without the aid of a leapingpole; diff. from the contomonobolon, where the performer is furnished with such a pole (post-class.), Cod. Just. 3, 43, 3.
monobolon.short: mŏnŏbŏlon, i, n., = μόνοσ-βόλος, a single throw, i.

monoceros.full: mŏnŏcĕros, ōtis, m., = μονόκερως, a unicorn: asperrimam autem feram monocerotem, reliquo corpore equo similem, capite cervo, pedibus elephanto, cauda apro, mugitu gravi, uno cornu nigro mediā fronte cubitorum duūm eminente, Plin. 8, 21, 31, § 76; Sol. 52, 39.
monoceros.short: mŏnŏcĕros, ōtis, m., = μονόκερως, a unicorn: asperrimam autem feram monocerotem, reliquo corpore equo similem, capite cervo, pedibus elephanto, cauda apro, mugitu gravi, uno cornu nigro mediā fronte cubitorum duūm eminente, Plin.

monochordos.full: mŏnŏchordos, on, adj., = μονόχορδος, of one string: cithara, Aeron. ad Hor. A. P. 216.—Subst.: mŏnŏchordon, i, n., μονόχορδον, the monochord, tonometer, Boëth. Instr. Mus. 1, 27 al.† † mŏnŏchŏrĭus, ii, m., = μόνοσ-χόρος, one who dances alone, who executes a pas seul, Not. Tir. p. 173.
monochordos.short: mŏnŏchordos, on, adj., = μονόχορδος, of one string: cithara, Aeron.

monochromata.full: mŏnochrōmăta, ōrum, n., = μονοχρώματα, paintings of but one color (postAug.), Plin. 33, 7, 39, § 117; 35, 8, 34, § 56.
monochromata.short: mŏnochrōmăta, ōrum, n., = μονοχρώματα, paintings of but one color (postAug.), Plin.

monochromateus.full: † mŏnochrōmătēus, a, um, adj., = μονοχρωμάτειος, a false reading for mox neogrammatea, Plin. 35, 5, 11, § 29.
monochromateus.short: † mŏnochrōmătēus, a, um, adj., = μονοχρωμάτειος, a false reading for mox neogrammatea, Plin.

monochromatos.full: mŏnochrōmătos, on, adj., = μονοχρώματος, one-colored, of a single color (post-Aug.): picturam singulis coloribus, et monochromaton dictam, Plin. 35, 3, 5, § 15; cf. monochromata.
monochromatos.short: mŏnochrōmătos, on, adj., = μονοχρώματος, one-colored, of a single color (post-Aug.): picturam singulis coloribus, et monochromaton dictam, Plin.

monochromos.full: mŏnŏchrōmos, on, adj., = μονόχρωμος, one-colored, monochromatic, Petr. 83, 2.
monochromos.short: mŏnŏchrōmos, on, adj., = μονόχρωμος, one-colored, monochromatic, Petr.

monochronos.full: mŏnochrŏnos, on, adj., = μονόχρονος, of one time, of the same time or measure (post-class.): tempus, Mart. Cap. 9, § 982.
monochronos.short: mŏnochrŏnos, on, adj., = μονόχρονος, of one time, of the same time or measure (post-class.): tempus, Mart.

monoclonos.full: mŏnoclōnos, on, adj., = μονόκλωνος, having a single branch or shoot (postclass.): herba monoclonos, App. Herb. 10.
monoclonos.short: mŏnoclōnos, on, adj., = μονόκλωνος, having a single branch or shoot (postclass.): herba monoclonos, App.

monocnemos.full: mŏnocnēmos, i, m., = μονόκνημος, one-legged, a one-legged man, Petr. 83 dub.
monocnemos.short: mŏnocnēmos, i, m., = μονόκνημος, one-legged, a one-legged man, Petr.

monocolus.full: mŏnŏcōlus, i, m., = μονόκωλος, onelegged, epithet applied to a fabled race of giants, each with but one leg of prodigious strength (post-Aug.): hominum genus, qui monocoli vocarentur, singulis cruribus, Plin. 7, 2, 2, § 23; cf. Gell. 9, 4, 9; Sol. 52, 29.
monocolus.short: mŏnŏcōlus, i, m., = μονόκωλος, onelegged, epithet applied to a fabled race of giants, each with but one leg of prodigious strength (post-Aug.): hominum genus, qui monocoli vocarentur, singulis cruribus, Plin.

monocrepis.full: mŏnocrēpis, ĭdis, m., = μονοκρηπίς, one-shoed, he that has but one shoe (postclass.): monocrepis, id est uno pede calceatus, Hyg. Fab. 12.
monocrepis.short: mŏnocrēpis, ĭdis, m., = μονοκρηπίς, one-shoed, he that has but one shoe (postclass.): monocrepis, id est uno pede calceatus, Hyg.

monoculus.full: mŏnŏcŭlus, i, m. vox hybr. from μόνος and oculus, one-eyed, a one-eyed man (post-class.), Firm. Math. 8, 19; 8, 22; cf. Gloss. Lab. monoculus = μονόφθαλμος.

monodiaria.full: mŏnōdĭārĭa, ae, f. μονῳδία, she that sings alone, a female solo-singer, Inscr. Orell. 2633.

monodiarius.full: mŏnōdĭārĭus, ii, m. id., a solosinger, Not. Tir. p. 173.

monodium.full: mŏnōdĭum, ĭi, n., = μονῴδιον, the song of a solo-singer, Diom. p. 489.—Also called mŏnōdĭa, ae, f., = μονῳδία, Isid. Orig. 6, 19, 6.
monodium.short: mŏnōdĭum, ĭi, n., = μονῴδιον, the song of a solo-singer, Diom.

monodus.full: Mŏnŏdūs, ontos, m. μονόδους, onetoothed, a son of Prusias, who had only a solid bone instead of teeth.—So, also, Pyrrhus, king of the Epirotæ, Paul. ex Fest. p. 148 Müll.; cf. Plin. 7, 16, 15, § 69; Val. Max. 1, 8, 12 ext.

monoecus.full: Mŏnoecus, i, m., = Μόνοικος (that dwells alone), a surname of Hercules; hence, Arx Monoeci, a promontory and harbor in Liguria, the mod. Monaco: portus Herculis Monoeci, Plin. 3, 5, 7, § 47; Tac. H. 3, 42: Arx Monoeci, Verg. A. 6, 830; Luc. 1, 408; Amm. 15, 10, 9.—Called also: Saxa Monoeci, Sil. 1, 586.
monoecus.short: Mŏnoecus, i, m., = Μόνοικος (that dwells alone), a surname of Hercules;

monogamia.full: mŏnŏgămĭa, ae, f., = μονογαμία, a marrying of but one wife, monogamy (eccl. Lat.), Tert. Monog. 2 sq.; Hier. in. Jovinian. 1, 14.
monogamia.short: mŏnŏgămĭa, ae, f., = μονογαμία, a marrying of but one wife, monogamy (eccl.

monogamus.full: mŏnŏgămus, i, m., = μονόγαμος, he who has but one wife (eccl. Lat.), Hier. in. Jovinian. 1, 15; id. Ep. 69, 3.
monogamus.short: mŏnŏgămus, i, m., = μονόγαμος, he who has but one wife (eccl.

monogenes.full: mŏnŏgĕnēs, is, m. μονογενής, onlybegotten, only, Tert. adv. Valent. 7 sqq.

monogramma.full: mŏnogramma, ătis, n., = μονόγραμμα, a character consisting of several letters, a monogram (post-class.), e. g. = Christus, Paul. Nol. Carm. 26, 618.
monogramma.short: mŏnogramma, ătis, n., = μονόγραμμα, a character consisting of several letters, a monogram (post-class.), e.

monogrammus.full: mŏnogrammus or -os, -on, adj., = μονόγραμμος, lit. of pictures, that consist of lines merely, outlined, sketched; hence transf., Of incorporeal gods, shadowy: Epicurus monogrammos Deos et nihil agentes commentus est, Cic. N. D. 2, 23, 59.—Hence, as subst.: mŏnogrammus, i, m., comically, a skeleton, a shadow: monogrammi dicti sunt homines macie pertenues ac decolores: tractum a picturā, quae priusquam coloribus corporatur, umbra fingitur, Non. 37, 11 sq.; Lucil. ap. Non. l. l.— A species of jaspe

monoides.full: mŏnŏīdēs, is, adj., = μονοειδής, having a single form: luna, Firm. Math. 4 praef.
monoides.short: mŏnŏīdēs, is, adj., = μονοειδής, having a single form: luna, Firm.

monolinum.full: mŏnŏlĭnum, i, n., = μονόλινον, a necklace consisting of a string of pearls, Capitol. Max. Jun. 1, 8 (al. monolium).
monolinum.short: mŏnŏlĭnum, i, n., = μονόλινον, a necklace consisting of a string of pearls, Capitol.

monolithus.full: mŏnŏlĭthus, a, um, adj., = μονόλιθος, consisting of a single stone, monolith (ante- and post-class.): columnae, Laber. ap. Non. 544, 33: postes marmorei monolithi, Ampel. Lib. Mem. 8, 12; Inscr. Orell. 1593.
monolithus.short: mŏnŏlĭthus, a, um, adj., = μονόλιθος, consisting of a single stone, monolith (ante- and post-class.): columnae, Laber.

monoloris.full: mŏnŏlōris, e, adj. vox hybr. μόνοσ- lorum, with one thong: vestes, having a single stripe of purple, Vop. Aur. 46, 6.

monomachia.full: mŏnŏmăchĭa, ae, f., = μονομαχία, a single combat, duel (post-class.): cur ad monomachiam recurritis? Cassiod. Var. 3, 24; Serv. Verg. A. 6, 136; Cassiod. Hist. Eccl. 2, 18.
monomachia.short: mŏnŏmăchĭa, ae, f., = μονομαχία, a single combat, duel (post-class.): cur ad monomachiam recurritis? Cassiod.

monomachus.full: mŏnŏmăchus, i, m., = μονόμαχος, he who fights in single combat, Cassiod. Hist. Eccl. 1, 9; 4, 37.
monomachus.short: mŏnŏmăchus, i, m., = μονόμαχος, he who fights in single combat, Cassiod.

monometer.full: mŏnŏmĕter, tra, trum, adj., = μονόμετρος, consisting of one metre, monometer, Prisc. Metr. Ter. p. 1320 P.
monometer.short: mŏnŏmĕter, tra, trum, adj., = μονόμετρος, consisting of one metre, monometer, Prisc.

monopodium.full: mŏnŏpŏdĭum, ii, n., = μονοπόδιον, a table or stand with one foot, Liv. 39, 6 fin.; cf. Plin. 34, 3, 8, § 14.
monopodium.short: mŏnŏpŏdĭum, ii, n., = μονοπόδιον, a table or stand with one foot, Liv.

monopodius.full: mŏnŏpŏdĭus, a, um, adj., = μονοπόδιος, one-footed (post-class.), Lampr. Commod. 10.
monopodius.short: mŏnŏpŏdĭus, a, um, adj., = μονοπόδιος, one-footed (post-class.), Lampr.

monopolium.full: mŏnŏpōlĭum, ii, n., = μονοπώλιον, the exclusive privilege of dealing in or selling a thing, a monopoly (post-Aug.), Suet. Tib. 71; 30; Plin. 8, 37, 56, § 135.
monopolium.short: mŏnŏpōlĭum, ii, n., = μονοπώλιον, the exclusive privilege of dealing in or selling a thing, a monopoly (post-Aug.), Suet.

monopteros.full: mŏnoptĕros, on, adj., = μονόπτερος, of buildings, with one wing: aedes, Vitr. 4, 7.
monopteros.short: mŏnoptĕros, on, adj., = μονόπτερος, of buildings, with one wing: aedes, Vitr.

monoptota.full: mŏnoptōta, ōrum, n., = μονόπτωτα, in the later grammarians, nouns which have but one case-ending, monoptotes, Diom. p. 288 P.; Prisc. p. 672 ib. et saep.; Mart. Cap. 3, § 242 al.
monoptota.short: mŏnoptōta, ōrum, n., = μονόπτωτα, in the later grammarians, nouns which have but one case-ending, monoptotes, Diom.

monosolis.full: mŏnŏsŏlis, e, adj. vox hibr., from μόνος-solea, single-soled (post-class.), Edict. Diocl.

monostichium.full: mŏnostĭchĭum, ii, n., = μονοστίχιον, a poem consisting of a single verse (post-class.), Aus. Ecl. 7, 8.
monostichium.short: mŏnostĭchĭum, ii, n., = μονοστίχιον, a poem consisting of a single verse (post-class.), Aus.

monostichum.full: mŏnostĭchum, i, n., = μονόστιχον, a poem consisting of a single verse (postclass.), Aus. Ecl. 8, 2.
monostichum.short: mŏnostĭchum, i, n., = μονόστιχον, a poem consisting of a single verse (postclass.), Aus.

monosyllabus.full: mŏnŏsyllăbus, a, um, adj., = μονοσύλλαβος, monosyllabic (post-Aug.): VOX, Mart. Cap. 3, § 269; 5, § 520.—As subst., a monosyllable: mŏnŏsyllabon, i, n. (sc. verbum), Aus. Idyll. Lit. Monosyll. 13: monosyllaba, sc. verba, Quint. 9, 4, 42; Mart. Cap. 3, § 294.
monosyllabus.short: mŏnŏsyllăbus, a, um, adj., = μονοσύλλαβος, monosyllabic (post-Aug.): VOX, Mart.

monotriglyphus.full: mŏnotrĭglўphus, a, um, adj., = μονοτρίγλυφος, that has only one triglyph, Vitr. 4, 3, 7.
monotriglyphus.short: mŏnotrĭglўphus, a, um, adj., = μονοτρίγλυφος, that has only one triglyph, Vitr.

monotropus.full: mŏnotrŏpus, i, m., = μονότροπος, of one kind, single: nosmet inter nos ministremus monotropi, Plaut. Stich. 5, 4, 7 (v. Ritschl ad h. l.).
monotropus.short: mŏnotrŏpus, i, m., = μονότροπος, of one kind, single: nosmet inter nos ministremus monotropi, Plaut.

monoxylus.full: mŏnoxўlus, a, um, adj., = μονόξυλος, that consists of a single piece of wood (post-Aug.): linter, Plin. 6, 23, 26, § 105.
monoxylus.short: mŏnoxўlus, a, um, adj., = μονόξυλος, that consists of a single piece of wood (post-Aug.): linter, Plin.

mons.full: mons, tis (archaic abl. montei, Enn. ap. Non. 222, 33; cf. Ann. v. 420 Vahl.), m. etym. dub., perh. from the root min, whence also, emineo, mentum, minari; cf. minae; lit. a projecting body; hence, a mountain, mount. Lit.: montium altitudines, Cic. N. D. 2, 39, 98: altissimi, Caes. B. G. 3, 1: avii, Hor. C. 1, 23, 2: inaccessi, Plin. 6, 28, 32, § 144: lapidosi, Ov. M. 1, 44.—Prov.: parturiunt montes, nascetur ridiculus mus, said where much is promised but little performed, Hor. A. P. 139.— Trans

monstrabilis.full: monstrābĭlis, e, adj. monstro, worthy to be shown or noticed, conspicuous, remarkable (post-Aug.): probitate morum monstrabilis, Plin. Ep. 6, 21, 4.

monstratio.full: monstrātĭo, ōnis, f. id., a showing, direction (only in Terence and Vitruv.): defessus sum ambulando: ut, Syre, te cum tuā Monstratione magnus perdat Juppiter, direction, Ter. Ad. 4, 6, 1: solers et expedita monstratio, indication, hint, Vitr. 6, 1, 12.

monstrator.full: monstrātor, ōris, m. monstro, a shower, pointer out, introducer, inventor, teacher, informant (poet. and in post-Aug. prose): aratri, i. e. Triptolemus, Verg. G. 1, 19: sacri iniqui, an introducer of human sacrifices, Ov. Ib. 399: hospitii, Tac. G. 21; Luc. 9, 979.

monstratus1.full: monstrātus, a, um, Part. and P. a., v. monstro fin.

monstratus2.full: monstrātus, ūs (only in the abl. sing.), m. monstro, a showing (post-class.): cujus monstratu, App. M. 1, p. 112, 24: monstratu Helenae, Aus. Per. Iliad. 3.

monstrifer.full: monstrĭfer, fĕra, fĕrum, adj. monstrum-fero, monster-bearing, that produces monsters (poet. and in post-Aug. prose): campi, Val. Fl. 5, 222: novercae, i. e. Juno, who sent monsters to Hercules, id. ib. 5, 43: sinus (i. e. mare), id. ib. 2, 498: antra, Claud. Stil. 2, 110.— Monstrous, horrid, misshapen: animalium hominumque effigies monstriferas, Plin. 6, 30, 35, § 187 (but the better reading is monstrificas).

monstrificabilis.full: monstrĭfĭcābĭlis, e, adj. monstrificus, monstrous, strange (ante-class.): mirum ac monstrificabile, Lucil. ap. Non. 138, 26.

monstrificus.full: monstrĭfĭcus, a, um, adj. monstrumfacio, monstrous, strange (post-Aug.): artes, i. e. magical, Val. Fl. 6, 152: natura hyaenae, Plin. 28, 8, 27, § 92: hominum ingenia, id. 21, 5, 13, § 26: effigies, id. 2, 3, 3, § 7; and so the better reading, Plin. 6, 30, 35, § 187; 36, 13, 19, § 88.—Hence, adv.: monstrĭfĭcē, in a monstrous or strange manner (post-Aug.), Plin. 28, 11, 49, § 181.

monstrigena.full: monstrĭgĕna, ae, m. monstrumgigno, monster-bearing: monstrigenis fluctibus, Avien. Perieg. 799.

monstriger.full: monstrĭger, ĕra, ĕrum, adj. monstrum-gero, = monstrifer, II., Salv. Gub. Dei. 5, 8.

monstro.full: monstro, āvi, ātum, (archaic mostro; v. Brix ad Plaut. Trin. 2, 2, 61), 1, v. a. like monstrum, from moneo, to show, point out, to indicate, intimate, inform, advise, teach, instruct, tell any thing (in class. prose very rare, and only in the lit. signif.; in Cic. only a few times; in Cæs. and Sall. not at all; syn.: indico, significo, ostendo, exhibeo). In gen.: qui erranti comiter monstrat viam, Enn. ap. Cic. Off. 1, 16, 51 (Trag. v. 387 Vahl.); cf.: qui sibi semitam non sapiunt, alteri monstr

monstrositas.full: monstrōsĭtas, ātis, f. monstrosus, -uosus, unnaturalness, monstrosity, Aug. Civ. Dei, 7, 26.

monstrum.full: monstrum, i, n. moneo. Orig. belonging to relig. lang., a divine omen indicating misfortune, an evil omen, portent (syn.: ostentum, prodigium, portentum): quia ostendunt, portendunt, monstrant, praedicunt, ostenta, portenta, monstra, prodigia dicuntur, Cic. Div. 1, 42, 93; cf.: monstrum dictum velut monestrum, quod moneat aliquid futurum; prodigium velut praedicium, quod praedicat; portentum quod portendat; ostentum, quod ostendat, Paul. ex Fest. p. 140 and 138 Müll.; cf. id. ib. p. 157: hic est

monstruose.full: monstrŭōsē and monstrōsē, adv., v. monstruosus fin.

monstruosus.full: monstrŭōsus (post-class. mon-strōsus), a, um, adj. monstrum, strange, preternatural, monstrous (class.): monstruosissima bestia, of the ape, Cic. Div. 2, 32, 69: hominum partus monstrosi, Luc. 1, 557: ferculum longe monstruosius, Petr. 69: scriptis monstruosus, Suet. Gram. 15: libidines, unnatural, id. Calig. 16: mulier si monstrosum aliquid aut prodigiosum enixa sit, Paul. Sent. 4, 9, 3 (but in Cic. Fin. 1, 18, 61, instead of monstrosi the correct reading seems to be morosi; so B. and K.; v. Ma

montanianus.full: Montānĭānus, a, um, adj., v. 3. Montanus, II. fin.

montaniculus.full: montānĭcŭlus, a, um, adj. dim. [1. montanus], Charis. 128 P.

montanilla.full: Montanilla, ae, f., a Roman surname, Inscr. Grut. 1146, 9.
montanilla.short: Montanilla, ae, f., a Roman surname, Inscr.

montaninus.full: Montānīnus, i, m., a Roman surname, Inscr. Grut. 713, 2.
montaninus.short: Montānīnus, i, m., a Roman surname, Inscr.

montaniosus.full: montānĭōsus, a, um, adj. mons, for montanus, mountainous (post-class.): locus, Auct. Rei Agrar. p. 239 Goes.; Gromat. Vet. p. 331, 20.

montanus1.full: montānus, a, um, adj. id., of or belonging to a mountain, mountain-; full of mountains, mountainous (class.): locus montanus an planus, Quint. 5, 10, 37: ager, Varr. R. R. 1, 6: flumen, Verg. A. 2, 305: cacumina, i. e. montium, Ov. M. 1, 310: oppida, on a mountain, Plin. 5, 27, 28, § 100: loca montana et aspera, Liv. 39, 1, 5: Ligures, dwelling in the mountains, Cic. Agr. 2, 35, 95: homines asperi et montani, Caes. B. C. 1, 57, 3: uxor, Juv. 6, 5: vulgus, id. 2, 74: Dalmatia, mountainous, Ov. P.

montanus2.full: Montānus, i, m., a Roman surname. Curtius Montanus, a favorite of the emperor Tiberius, Tac. A. 16, 28 sq.; id. H. 4, 42; Ov. P. 4, 16, 11; Juv. 4, 107; 131. — Votienus Montanus, an orator of the reign of Tiberius, Tac. A. 4, 42; Sen. Contr. 4, 24, 3.—Hence, adj.: Montānĭānus, a, um, belonging to the orator Montanus, Sen. Contr. 4, 28, 17.
montanus2.short: Montānus, i, m., a Roman surname.

montensis.full: montensis, e, adj. mons, for montanus, of or belonging to mountains, mountain-: DII, Inscr. Grut. 21, 3.

monticellus.full: montĭcellus, i, m. dim. id., a small mountain, a mount (post-class.), Auct. Rei Agrar. p. 231 Goes. (Gromat. Vet. 306 sq.).

monticola.full: montĭcŏla, ae, comm. mons-colo, a dweller in the mountains, a mountaineer (poet.): monticolae Silvani, Ov. M. 1, 193.

monticulus.full: montĭcŭlus, i, m. dim. mons, a small mountain: monticulus, ὄριον, βουνός, Gloss. Philox. Donat. Art. Gram. 2, 2, 3.

montifer.full: montĭfer, fĕra, fĕrum, adj. monsfero, mountain-bearing: montiferum Titana (al. monstriferum), Sen. Herc. Oet. 1212.

montigena.full: montĭgĕna, ae, comm. mons-gigno, mountain-born: montigena, ὀρεσιγενής, Gloss. Philox. Anthol. Lat. 1, 53, 1.

montinus.full: Montīnus, i, m. mons, a mountaingod, god of the Mountains, Arn. 4, 132.

montivagus.full: montĭ-văgus, a, um, adj. mons-vagus, mountain-roaming, that wanders over mountains (mostly poet.): Diana, Stat. Ach. 1, 450: fera, Lucr. 1, 404: genus ferarum, id. 2, 597; 1081: ac silvestres cursus lustrationesque, Cic. Tusc. 5, 27, 79.

montuosus.full: montŭōsus or montōsus, a, um, adj. mons, mountainous, full of mountains (class.): regio, Cic. Planc. 9, 22: cum locis ipsis delectemur, montuosis etiam, id. Lael. 19, 68: loci, id. Part. 10, 36: frutex, Plin. 12, 13, 28, § 48.—Form montosa, Verg. A. 7, 744. —Subst.: montŭōsa, ōrum, n., mountain regions, mountainous parts: montuosa Ciliciae, Plin. 11, 53, 116, § 280; Vulg. Jer. 17, 26.
montuosus.short: montŭōsus or montōsus, a, um, adj.

monubilis.full: mŏnŭbĭlis, e, adj. moneo, reminding, admonishing (post-class.): columnae, that serve as remembrancers, Sid. Ep. 2, 2.

monumentalis.full: mŏnŭmentālis, e, adj. [monumentum, of or belonging to a monument, monumental (late Lat.): lapis, Auct. de Limit. p. 305 Goes.

monumentarius.full: mŏnŭmentārĭus (mŏnĭm-), a, um, adj. id., of or belonging to a monument or tomb (post-class.): ceraula, who played at tombs, App. Flor. p. 342, 22.

monumentum.full: mŏnŭmentum (mŏnĭm-), i, n. [moneo), that which preserves the remembrance of any thing, a memorial, a monument; esp. of buildings, statues, galleries, tombs erected to perpetuate the remembrance of a person or thing; cf. Paul. ex Fest. p. 139 Müll. Lit. (class.): statuam dare auream Solidam faciundam, quae siet factis monumentum suis, Plaut. Curc. 3, 72: monimenti causā, Cic. Rosc. Am. 50, 146: monumento ut esset, Liv. 8, 11, 16: vitiorum, Cic. Verr. 1, 4, 12: Marcelli et Africani, id. ib. 2, 1,

monuste.full: Monustē, ēs, f., one of the Danaides, who killed her husband Eurysthenes, Hyg. Fab. 170.
monuste.short: Monustē, ēs, f., one of the Danaides, who killed her husband Eurysthenes, Hyg.

monychus.full: Mōnўchus, i, m., = Μώνυχος, the name of a Centaur, Luc. 6, 388; Ov. M. 12, 499; Juv. 1, 11.
monychus.short: Mōnўchus, i, m., = Μώνυχος, the name of a Centaur, Luc.

mopsiani.full: Mopsĭāni or Mopsĭi, ōrum, m., the adherents of Mopsus, in the city of Compsa, during the second Punic war, Liv. 23, 1, 2; 3.
mopsiani.short: Mopsĭāni or Mopsĭi, ōrum, m., the adherents of Mopsus, in the city of Compsa, during the second Punic war, Liv.

mopsium.full: Mopsĭum, i, n., = Μόψιον, a hill in Thessaly, between Tempe and Larissa, Liv. 42, 61.
mopsium.short: Mopsĭum, i, n., = Μόψιον, a hill in Thessaly, between Tempe and Larissa, Liv.

mopsopius.full: Mopsŏpĭus, a, um, adj., = Μοψόπιος, of or belonging to Mopsopia (Μοψοπία, an old name of Attica), Mopsopian, Attic, Athenian (only poet.): Mopsopius juvenis, i. e. Triptolemus, Ov. M. 5, 661: muri, i. e. of Athens, id. ib. 6, 423: urbs, Athens, id. H. 8, 72.—As subst.: Mopsŏpĭa, ae, f.: Mopsopia tota, i. e. all Athens or all Attica, Sen. Hippol. 121; 1276.
mopsopius.short: Mopsŏpĭus, a, um, adj., = Μοψόπιος, of or belonging to Mopsopia (Μοψοπία, an old name of Attica), Mopsopian, Attic, Athenian (only poet.): Mopsopius juvenis, i.

mopsucrenae.full: Mopsūcrēnae, ārum, f. plur., = Μόψου κρῆναι (Mopsus-springs), a city in Cappadocia, now Mezanluk Khan, Amm. 21, 15, 2.

mopsuhestia.full: Mopsuhestĭa or Mopsuestĭa, ae, f., = Μόψου ἑστία (Mopsus-hearth), a city in Cilicia, on the river Pyramus, near the sea, also called Mopsos; now Missis, Cic. Fam. 3, 8, 10; Amm. 14, 8, 3.
mopsuhestia.short: Mopsuhestĭa or Mopsuestĭa, ae, f., = Μόψου ἑστία (Mopsus-hearth), a city in Cilicia, on the river Pyramus, near the sea, also called Mopsos;

mopsus.full: Mopsus, i, m., = Μόψος. A soothsayer in Argos, Cic. N. D. 2, 3, 7; id. Div. 1, 40, 88; id. Leg. 2, 13, 33.— A soothsayer in Thessaly, Ov. M. 12, 456; Hyg. Fab. 14; 128; 173.— Another soothsayer, the son of Manto, Val. Fl. 1, 207.— The name of a shepherd, Verg. E. 5, 1; 10; 8, 26; 29.— Another name for Mopsuhestia, q. v., Plin. 5, 27, 22, § 91.

mora1.full: mŏra, ae, f. Sanscr. smar, remember; Gr. root μερ-, μαρ-; μέρμηρα, μέριμνα, care; μάρτυρ, witness; cf. memor, memoria; perh. μέλλειν, a delay. Lit. In gen.: tarditas sententiarum, moraque rerum, Cic. Fam. 10, 22, 2: mora et sustentatio, id. Inv. 2, 49, 146: mora aut tergiversatio, id. Mil. 20, 54: moram rei alicui inferre, to delay, put off, defer, hinder, id. Inv. 1, 9, 12: moram ad insequendum intulit, Caes. B. C. 3, 75: afferre, Cic. Verr. 2, 5, 64, § 165: facere delectui, Liv. 6, 31: facere

mora2.full: mŏra, ae, f., the fish echeneis, Plin. 32, 1, 1, § 6 (al. remora).
mora2.short: mŏra, ae, f., the fish echeneis, Plin.

mora3.full: mŏra, ae, f., = μόρα, a division of the Spartan army, consisting of three, five, or seven hundred men: moram Lacedaemoniorum intercepit, the Spartan army, Nep. Iphicr. 2, 3 (but in Cic. Tusc. 2, 16, 37, the best reading is agmen, v. Klotz ad h. l.).
mora3.short: mŏra, ae, f., = μόρα, a division of the Spartan army, consisting of three, five, or seven hundred men: moram Lacedaemoniorum intercepit, the Spartan army, Nep.

moracillum.full: moracillum, dim. from moracius, Titin. ap. Paul. ex Fest. p. 139 Müll.

moracius.full: moracĭus, a, um, adj. mora, hard: nuces, Titin. ap. Paul. ex Fest. p. 139 Müll.

moralis.full: mōrālis, e, adj. mores, of or belonging to manners or morals, moral (a word formed by Cicero; cf. moratus): quia pertinet ad mores, quos ἤθη Graeci vocant, nos eam partem philosophiae de moribus appellare solemus. Sed decet augentem linguam Latinam nominare moralem, Cic. Fat. 1, 1; imitated by Seneca and Quintil.: philosophiae tres partes esse dixerunt, moralem, naturalem, et rationalem, Sen. Ep. 89, 9; Quint. 12, 2, 10: pars illa philosophiae ἠθική moralis est dicta, id. 6, 2, 8; cf. also, id.

moralitas.full: mōrālĭtas, ātis, f. moralis, manner, characteristics, character (post-class.), Macr. S. 5, 1; morality, Ambros. in Psa. 118, Serm. 3.

moramentum.full: mŏrāmentum, i, n. moror, that which causes a delay, a hinderance (postclass.), App. Flor. p. 363, 32.

moraria.full: mŏrārĭa, ae, f., a plant, called also statioron or chamaeleon, App. Herb. 25.
moraria.short: mŏrārĭa, ae, f., a plant, called also statioron or chamaeleon, App.

moratim.full: mŏrātim, adv., moror, slowly, Sol. 3, 1 dub. (al. memoratim).

moratio.full: mŏrātĭo, ōnis, f. id., a delaying, tarrying, a delay, Vitr. 9, 4: morationibus impediri, id. ib.: litoraria, delay on the coast, Cael. Aur. Tard. 3, 5, 74.

morator.full: mŏrātor, ōris, m. id.. A delayer, loiterer, malingerer: unus publici commodi, Liv. 2, 44; Curt. 4, 10, 10 (but moratorum, Liv. 21, 47, 3, and 24, 41, 5, is from morati; v. moror).— A talker against time, a sort of advocate who spoke only to gain time while his principal rested and refreshed himself, Cic. Div. in Caecil. 15, 49.— In the races, persons who strove to embarrass and delay the runners, for the amusement of the crowd, Inscr. Orell. 2597.

moratorius.full: mŏrātōrĭus, a. um, adj. morator, delaying, dilatory (post-class.): cunctatio, Dig. 26, 7, 6: appellationes, Paul. Sent. 5, 35, 2: ambages, Cod. Just. 4, 31, 14.

moratus1.full: mŏrātus, a, um, Part., from moror.
moratus1.short: mŏrātus, a, um, Part., from moror.

moratus2.full: mōrātus, a, um, adj. mos. Mannered, of morals, good or bad; constituted, conditioned, circumstanced (class.): nequiquam mulier exornata est bene, si morata est male, Plaut. Most. 1, 3, 132: condigne pater est ejus moratus moribus, id. Capt. 1, 1, 39: morata recte (puella), id. Aul. 2, 2, 62: viri bene morati, Cic. de Or. 2, 43, 184: genus hominum optime moratum, id. Agr. 2, 31, 84: melius, id. Fin. 1, 19, 63: ita haec morata est janua, is of such a nature, Plaut. As. 2, 3, 10: male moratus vente

morax.full: mŏrax, ācis, adj. moror, fond of delay, dilatory: cogitationes, Varr. ap. Non. 451, 13.

morbidus.full: morbĭdus, a, um, adj. morbus. Sickly, diseased (rare and only ante-class. and post-Aug.; syn. aeger, aegrotus): apes morbidae, Varr. R. R. 3, 16, 22: corpus, Plin. 8, 26, 40, § 96.— Sickly, unwholesome: vis, Lucr. 6, 1225: aër, id. 6, 1097: pars, id. 6, 1261.

morbifer.full: morbĭfer or morbĭfĕrus, ĕra, ĕrum, adj. morbus-fero, that brings disease (postclass.): labes, Paul. Nol. Carm. 25, 238.
morbifer.short: morbĭfer or morbĭfĕrus, ĕra, ĕrum, adj.

morbifico.full: morbĭfĭco, āre, 1, v. n. morbus-facio, to produce disease (late Lat.), Cael. Aur. Salut. Praec. 19.

morbositas.full: morbōsĭtas, ātis, f. morbosus, sickliness, unhealthiness (post-class.): si provincia, quam colimus, de morbositate suspecta est, Pall. 1, 16 (al. morbis aestate).

morbosus.full: morbōsus, a, um, adj. morbus, sickly, ailing, diseased. In gen. (only anteand post-class.): morbosum hominem morbo aliquo affectum, Paul. ex Fest. p. 139 Müll.: servus, Cato, R. R. 2: pecus, Varr. R. R. 2, 1, 21: equus, Labeo ap. Gell. 4, 2, 5; cf. ib. § 12.— In partic., diseased with lewdness, consumed by unnatural passion, Cat. 57, 6: morbosior omnibus cinaedis, Auct. Priap. 47; sick with longing or desire: in aves, Petr. 46.

morbovia.full: Morbōvĭa (or Morbōnĭa), ae, f. morbus, the land of disease, sickdom, vulg. in execrations: abire Morboviam jusserat, go to the devil, Suet. Vesp. 14.

morbus.full: morbus, i, m. Sanscr. mar-, die; Gr. βροτός (for μροτός), μαραίνω; cf. morior, marceo, a sickness, disease, disorder, distemper, ailment, illness, malady, of body or mind (class.). Corporeal: morbum appellant totius corporis corruptionem: aegrotationem morbum cum imbecillitate: vitium cum partes corporis inter se dissident: ex quo pravitas membrorum, distortio, deformitas, Cic. Tusc. 4, 13, 28: morbus est habitus cujusque corporis contra naturam, qui usum ejus facit deteriorem, Labeo ap. Gell. 4

mordacitas.full: mordācĭtas, ātis, f. mordax, the power of biting or stinging, mordacity (post-Aug.): urticarum foliis inest aculeata mordacitas, Plin. 21, 15, 54, § 91: vinosa, sharp, like sour wine, id. 21, 18, 72, § 120.— Transf., snappishness, biting severity in language, Cassiod. Hist. Eccl. 1, 12.

mordax.full: mordax, ācis, adj. mordeo, biting, given to biting, snappish (poet. and in postAug. prose). Lit.: canis, Plaut. Bacch. 5, 2, 27: equus, Labeo ap. Gell. 4, 2: asinus, App. M. 8, p. 213 init.: Memmius, Auct. ap. Cic. de Or. 2, 59, 240.—Poet.: fibula, Sid. Carm. 5, 18.— Transf., stinging, sharp, biting, pungent: urtica, stinging, Ov. A. A. 2, 417: arista mordacior hordeo, Plin. 18, 7, 10, § 61: mordacissima marga, id. 17, 8, 4, § 45: mordaci icta ferro Pinus, biting, deepcutting, Hor. C. 4, 6, 9: p

mordeo.full: mordĕo, mŏmordi (archaic memordi; v. in the foll.), morsum, 2, v. a. root smard-; Sanscr. mard-, bite; Gr. σμερδνός, σμερδαλέος; (cf. Engl. smart), to bite, to bite into (class.). Lit.: si me canis memorderit, Enn. ap. Gell. 7, 9, 3 (Sat. v. 36 Vahl.): canes mordere possunt, Cic. Rosc. Am. 20, 57: mordens pulex, biting, Mart. 14, 83: (serpens) fixum hastile momordit, bit into, Ov. M. 3, 68: mordeat ante aliquis quidquid, etc., taste, Juv. 6, 632: terram, to bite the ground, bite the dust, of exp

mordex.full: mordex, ĭcis, adj. mordeo, biting, gnawing: asini mordices, v. l., Plaut. Aul. 2, 3, 57 (better mordicus).—As subst.: Mor-dex, ĭcis, m., the biter, i. e. tooth, v. l. ap. App. M. 3, p. 140 (better mordicus, q. v.).

mordicatio.full: mordĭcātĭo, ōnis, f. mordico, a griping (post-class.): ventris mordicatio, Cael. Aur. Acut. 3, 20, 161; 2, 18, 105.

mordicativus.full: mordĭcātīvus, a, um, adj. id., biting, sharp: acetum, Cael. Aur. Tard. 3, 8, 144.

mordicitus.full: mordĭcĭtus, adv. a lengthened form for 1. mordicus, with the teeth (ante- and post-class.): asini me mordicitus scindant, Plaut. Aul. 2, 2, 57 dub. (al. mordicibus, from obsol. mordex, a bite; al. mordicus; Non. 139, 30, has mordicibus, where mordicitus is the more correct reading): mordicitus appetens (al. mordicibus), App. M. 3, p. 140, 23.

mordico.full: mordĭco, āre, v. a. mordax, to bite, sting: est acerrimae atque mordicantis qualitatis, biting, sharp, Cael. Aur. Acut. 2, 8, 34.

mordicus1.full: mordĭcus, adv. mordeo, by biting, with bites, with the teeth, ὀδάξ (class.). Lit.: mordicus arripere, Plaut. Curc. 5, 1, 7: si adbites propius, os denasabit tibi Mordicus, will bite your nose off, id. Capt. 3, 4, 73; cf. id. Men. 1, 3, 12: equus eum mordicus interfecit, Varr. R. R. 2, 7, 9: premere capita mordicus, Cic. N. D. 2, 49, 124: auriculam fortasse mordicus abstulisset, would have bitten off, id. Q. Fr. 3, 4, 2: caudā mordicus apprehensā, Plin. 8, 37, 55, § 132: calcibus feriens et mordi

mordicus2.full: mordĭcus, a, um, adj. id., biting, snappish: quem equi mordici distraxerunt (al. mordicus, al. mordicibus), Hyg. Fab. 273.

mordosus.full: mordōsus, a, um, adj. id., biting, given to biting: mordosus, δηκτικός, Gloss. Gr. Lat.

moretarius.full: mŏrētārĭus, a, um, adj. moretum, of or belonging to the dish moretum (postclass.): moretaria condimenta, Apic. 6, 4. —Subst.: mŏrētārĭum, ii, n., the dish moretum (made of garlic, rue, vinegar, oil, etc.), Don. ad Ter. Phorm. 2, 2, 4.

moretum.full: mŏrētum, i, n. from same root with mordeo, q. v.. A country dish composed of garlic, rue, vinegar, oil, etc., Ov. F. 4, 367.— Mŏrētum, i, n., the title of a small poem ascribed to Virgil; v. Heyne and Sillig in Verg. Carm. vol. iv. p. 301 sq. Wagner (acc. to Stander in Zeitschr. für Alt. Wissensch. 1853, part 4, p. 289 sq., a transl. of the Μυττωτός of Virgil's Greek teacher Parthenius).

morgetes.full: Morgētes, um, m., = Μόργητες, a people who anciently dwelt in Lucania, Plin. 3, 5, 10, § 71.
morgetes.short: Morgētes, um, m., = Μόργητες, a people who anciently dwelt in Lucania, Plin.

moribundus.full: mŏrĭbundus, a, um, adj. morior. Dying (class.): minus valet, moribundus est, Plaut. Bacch. 2, 2, 15: jacentem moribundumque vidistis, Cic. Sest. 39, 85: moribundus procubuit, Liv. 26, 15: anima, Ov. Tr. 4, 5, 3.—Transf.: vox, Stat. Th. 8, 643: membra, mortal, Verg. A. 6, 732; App. de Deo Soc. 4, p. 43 fin.: corpus, id. Mag. 50, p. 306.— Act., causing death, i. e. deadly, unwholesome (poet.): moribunda a sede Pisauri, Cat. 81, 3.

morigeratio.full: mōrĭgĕrātĭo, ōnis, f. morigeror, compliance (ante-class.), Afran. ap. Non. 2, 6 (Com. Rel. v. 381 Rib.).

morigerator.full: mōrĭgĕrātor, ōris, m. id., a complier (late Lat.), Sid.

morigeror.full: mōrĭgĕror, ātus, 1, v. dep. morigerus, to comply with, gratify, humor, endeavor to please (syn.: obsequor, obtempero; class.): nunc si servitus evenit, ei vos morigerari mos bonus est, to accommodate yourself to it, Plaut. Capt. 2, 1, 4: adulescenti, Ter. Ad. 2, 2, 9: voluptati aurium morigerari debet oratio, * Cic. Or. 48, 159. —Esp., in mal. part., ore = fellare, Suet. Tib. 44.!*? Act. collat. form, mōrĭgĕro, āre: dum mihi morigero, Plaut. Am. 3, 3, 26.

morigerus.full: mōrĭgĕrus, a, um, adj. mos-gero, complying, obsequious, obedient (ante- and post-class.): meo me aequom est morigerum patri, Plaut. Am. 3, 4, 21: male morigerus mihi est danista, id. Ep. 5, 1, 1: quando una vivis meis morigera moribus, id. Men. 1, 3, 19: dum me morigeram praebeo, Afran. ap. Non. 433, 29: imago ad omnem nutum hominis sui morigera, App. Mag. 14, p. 282, 26; id. M. 2, p. 117, 1 al.—Esp., compliant, Plaut. Cas. 5, 2, 20; cf. Lucr. 4, 1281.

morimarusa.full: Morimărūsa (Dead Sea), the Cimbric appellation of the North Sea, Plin. 4, 13, 27, § 95.
morimarusa.short: Morimărūsa (Dead Sea), the Cimbric appellation of the North Sea, Plin.

morini.full: Mŏrĭni, ōrum, m., a people of Belgic Gaul, near the channel, Caes. B. G. 2, 4; 3, 9; 4, 22; Mel. 3, 2 fin.; Plin. 4, 17, 31, § 106: extremique hominum Morini, Verg. A. 8, 727.
morini.short: Mŏrĭni, ōrum, m., a people of Belgic Gaul, near the channel, Caes.

morio1.full: mōrĭo, ōnis, m., = μωρός, an arrant fool (post-Aug.): quidam tantae sunt fatuitatis, ut non multum a pecoribus differant: quos moriones vulgo vocant, Aug. Ep. 26; Plin. Ep. 9, 17, 1 sq.; Mart. 8, 13; 14, 210 in lemm.— Transf., a monster, deformed person, Mart. 6, 39, 17.
morio1.short: mōrĭo, ōnis, m., = μωρός, an arrant fool (post-Aug.): quidam tantae sunt fatuitatis, ut non multum a pecoribus differant: quos moriones vulgo vocant, Aug.

morio2.full: mŏrĭo or mŏrĭon, a false reading for mormorion, Plin. 37, 10, 63, § 173.
morio2.short: mŏrĭo or mŏrĭon, a false reading for mormorion, Plin.

morion.full: mōrĭon, ii, n., = μώριον. A narcotic plant, nightshade, also called strychnus: alterum genus (strychni), quod halicacabon vocant ... ab aliis morion, ab aliis moly appellatum, Plin. 21, 31, 105, § 180.— — The male mandrake: album hoc (genus) alii arsena alii morion vocant, Plin. 25, 13, 94, § 148.

morior.full: mŏrĭor, mortŭus, 3 (fut. part. moriturus, a, um, Cic. Arch. 12, 30; id. Div. 2, 25, 54; 2, 47, 99; Liv. 21, 12, 4; Verg. A. 4, 308; id. ib. 2, 511 et saep.; old forms acc. to the fourth conj.: si vivimu' sive morīmur, Enn. ap. Prisc. p. 830 P.; Ann. v. 384 Vahl.; inf. moriri, Plaut. As. 1, 1, 108; id. Capt. 3, 5, 54; id. Rud. 3, 3, 12; id. Ps. 4, 7, 124 Ritschl N. cr.; Ov. M. 14, 215), v. dep. Sanscr. root mar-, die; Gr. μορ- (μρο-, βρο-), μαρ; βροτός, μαραίνω; cf.: morbus, marceo, to die (cf.:

moritasgus.full: Moritasgus, i, m. A god of the Senones, Inscr. Orell. 2028.— A male proper name among the Senones, Caes. B. G. 5, 54, 2.

moriturio.full: mŏrĭtŭrĭo, 4, v. n. desid. [morior], to desire to die, Cic. ap. Aug. de Gramm. p. 2006 P.

mormorion.full: mormorion, ōnis, f., a kind of darkbrown rock crystal, Plin. 37, 10, 63, § 173.
mormorion.short: mormorion, ōnis, f., a kind of darkbrown rock crystal, Plin.

mormyr.full: mormyr, ȳris, f., = μορμύρος, a sort of fish in Pontus: pictae mormyres, Ov. Hal. 110; cf. Plin. 32, 11, 54, § 152.
mormyr.short: mormyr, ȳris, f., = μορμύρος, a sort of fish in Pontus: pictae mormyres, Ov.

morochites.full: mŏrŏchītes (mŏrŏchthos), ae, f., a precious stone of the color of a leek, Plin. 37, 10, 63, § 173.
morochites.short: mŏrŏchītes (mŏrŏchthos), ae, f., a precious stone of the color of a leek, Plin.

morologus.full: mōrŏlŏgus, a, um, adj., = μωρολόγος, speaking foolishly, foolish (Plautinian): sermones, Plaut. Ps. 5, 1, 20.—As subst., a fool: tibi morologus fio, Plaut. Pers. 1, 1, 50.
morologus.short: mōrŏlŏgus, a, um, adj., = μωρολόγος, speaking foolishly, foolish (Plautinian): sermones, Plaut.

moror1.full: mŏror, ātus, 1, v. dep. n. and a. [mora]. Neutr., to delay, tarry, stay, wait, remain, linger, loiter (syn.: cesso, cunctor, haesito; class.); eamus ergo ad cenam: quid stas? Thr. Ubi vis: non moror, i. e. I have no objection, Ter. Eun. 3, 2, 6: Lucceius narravit, Brutum valde morari, non tergiversantem, sed exspectantem, si qui forte casus, etc., Cic. Att. 16, 5, 3: quid moror? Hor. C. 2, 17, 6: quid multis moror? why do I linger long? why make a long story of it? Ter. And. 1, 1, 87: ne multis

moror2.full: mōror, 1, v. dep. n. [μωρός], to be foolish, be a fool (post-Aug.), in the lusus verbb.: morari eum (Claudium) inter homines desiisse, productā primā syllabā, jocabatur, Suet. Ner. 33.

morositas.full: mōrōsĭtas, ātis, f. morosus. Peevishness, fretfulness, moroseness (rare but class.): si in morositatem inutilem et odiosam incidamus, Cic. Off. 1, 25, 88: morositas et ea vitia, quae dixi, habent aliquid excusationis, id. Sen. 18, 65.— Niceness, pedantry: affectatione et morositate nimiā obscurabat stilum, over-scrupulousness, too great nicety, Suet. Tib. 70.

morosus1.full: mōrōsus, a, um, adj. mos; cf. Cic. Tusc. 4, 24, 54, peevish, fretful, wayward, capricious, captious, morose (syn.: tristis, severus, gravis, difficilis; class.): usque eo difficiles ac morosi sumus, ut nobis non satisfaciat ipse Demosthenes, Cic. Or. 29, 104: at sunt morosi et anxii, et iracundi et difficiles senes, id. Sen. 18, 65: canities, Hor. C. 1, 9, 17.—Of excessive care: circa corporis curam morosior, particular, fastidious, Suet. Caes. 45.—Of things concr. and abstr.: cupressus natu mor

morosus2.full: mŏrōsus, a, um, adj. mora, lingering, slow, slow in coming (lato Lat.): cui morosum videtur quodcunque futurum est, Cassiod. in Psa. 34, 20: iter fieri morosum quod ad celeritatem est inventum, id. Var. 1, 29.

morpheus.full: Morpheus, ĕi and ĕos, m., = Μορφεύς, the son of Sleep and god of dreams: excitat Morphea, Ov. M. 11, 634; 647.
morpheus.short: Morpheus, ĕi and ĕos, m., = Μορφεύς, the son of Sleep and god of dreams: excitat Morphea, Ov.

morphnos.full: morphnos, i, m., = μορφνός, a kind of eagle that lives near lakes, Plin. 10, 3, 3, § 7.
morphnos.short: morphnos, i, m., = μορφνός, a kind of eagle that lives near lakes, Plin.

morrenas.full: Morrenas, ātis, adj. comm., of or belonging to Morrena or Morena (a country of Mysia), Inscr. Grut. 760, 4.

mors.full: mors, tis, f. root mor, v. morior (dat. morte, Varr. ap. Gell. 24), death in every form, natural or violent (syn.: letum, nex). Lit.: omnium rerum mors est extremum, Cic. Fam. 6, 21, 1: mors ultima linea rerum est, Hor. Ep. 1, 16, 79: mortem sibi consciscere, to kill one's self, Cic. Verr. 2, 3, 56, § 129: obire, to die, id. Phil. 5, 17, 48; Plaut Aul. prol. 15: nam necessest me ... cras mortem exequi, id. Ps. 4, 2, 38: certae occumbere morti, to submit to, Verg. A. 2, 62: aliquem ad mortem dare

morsicatim.full: morsĭcātim, adv. morsico, by biting, by biting the lips together (ante-class.): labellis morsicatim lusitant, Naev. ap. Non. 139, 25.

morsicatio.full: morsĭcātĭo, ōnis, f. id., a biting: ciborum, Paul. ex Fest. p. 143, 1 Müll. (al. morsitatio).

morsico.full: morsĭco, 1, v. a. mordeo. To bite continually, Paul. ex Fest. p. 68 Müll.— To bite, to press the lips together as in kissing (post-class.): ore improbo compulsat, et morsicat, App. M. 7, p. 197, 16: limis et morsicantibus oculis, winking, ogling, id. ib. 2, p. 119, 8 (al. morsito).

morsiuncula.full: morsĭuncŭla, ae, f. dim. 2. morsus, a little bite; a biting with the lips, a kissing (ante- and post - class.): formicarum, App. M. 8, p. 211, 35: teneris labellis molles morsiunculae, kisses, Plaut. Ps. 1, 1, 65.

morsum.full: morsum, i, n. mordeo, a bit, little piece, e. g. of wool (poet.): lanea morsa, Cat. 64, 316.

morsus1.full: morsus, a, um, Part., from mordeo.
morsus1.short: morsus, a, um, Part., from mordeo.

morsus2.full: morsus, ūs, m. mordeo, a biting, a bite. Lit.: contra avium minorum morsus munitur vallo aristarum. Cic. Sen. 15, 51: serpentis, id. Fat. 16, 36: morsu apprehendere, to bite, Plin. 11, 24, 28, § 84: morsibus insequi, Ov. M. 13, 568: morsu appetere, Tac. H. 4, 42: nec tu mensarum morsus horresce futuros, the eating, Verg. A. 3, 394: mucida frusta farinae ... non admittentia morsum, Juv. 5, 69: vertere morsus Exiguam in Cererem penuria adegit edendi, their bites, their teeth, id. ib. 7, 112 ; so,

morta.full: Morta, ae, f., = Μορτή, one of the Fates, Liv. Andron. ap. Gell. 3, 16, 11: tria sunt nomina Parcarum, Nona, Decima, Morta, Caesell. ib.
morta.short: Morta, ae, f., = Μορτή, one of the Fates, Liv.

mortalis.full: mortālis, e, adj. mors, subject to death, liable to die, mortal (class.). Lit.: quid in iis mortale et caducum, quid divinum aeternumque sit, Cic. Leg. 1, 23, 61: animal, id. N. D. 3, 13, 32.— Transf. Human, mortal: mucro, of human workmanship, Verg. A. 12, 740: condicio vitae, Cic. Phil. 14, 12, 33: opera, Liv. 1, 2: acta, Ov. Tr. 1, 2, 97: mortalin' decuit violari vulnere divum? from the hand of a mortal, Verg. A. 12, 797: haud tibi vultus Mortalis, id. ib. 1, 328: nec mortale sonans, like a h

mortalitas.full: mortālĭtas, ātis, f. mortalis, the state of being subject to death, mortality; a dying, death. Lit. (rare but class.): omne, quod ortum sit, mortalitas consequitur, * Cic. N. D. 1, 10, 26: metu meae mortalitatis, Quint. 6 praef. § 2: mortalitatem explere, i. e. to die, Tac. A. 6, 50: rex mortalitate interceptus, by death, Plin. Ep. 10, 50, 4: mariti, Dig. 23, 4, 2.—Of abstract things: tofus aedificiis inutilis est mortalitate, mollitia, perishableness, Plin. 36, 22, 48, § 166.— Transf., concr.,

mortariolum.full: mortārĭŏlum, i, n. dim. mortarium, a small mortar, Aem. Mac. 1, 8; Hier. Ep. 64, 9; Vulg. Num. 7, 14.

mortarium.full: mortārĭum, ii, n., a mortar (mostly ante-class. and post-Aug.). Lit.: mortarium, in quo teruntur quae solvenda sunt, Non. 543, 22; Plaut. Aul. 1, 2, 17; Cato, R. R. 74: aerea, Plin. 33, 8, 41, § 123: plumbea, id. 34, 18, 50, § 168.— Transf. A large basin or trough in which mortar is made, Vitr. 7, 3, 10; 8, 6, 14; Plin. 36, 23, 55, § 177.—Hence, Mortar: mortario caementum addatur, Vitr. 8, 7.— A hollow resembling a mortar, dug round a tree: arbori mortarium statim faciunt, Pall. 4, 8, 1.— That w
mortarium.short: mortārĭum, ii, n., a mortar (mostly ante-class.

morticinus.full: mortĭcīnus, a, um, adj. mors, dead, that has died, only of animals; hence, of or belonging to an animal that has died of itself, carrion-; as a term of abuse, carrion; and transf., dead (ante-class. and postAug.). Lit.: morticinae ovis carne vesci, Varr. R. R. 2, 9, 10: volucres aut pisces, id. ib. 3, 2, 18: in sacris ne morticinum quid adsit, id. L. L. 7, § 84 Müll.: soleae, made from the hide of an animal that has died of itself, Serv. Verg. A. 4, 518: morticine, you carrion, Plaut. Pers. 2, 4

mortifer.full: mortĭfer or (rarely) mortĭfĕrus, ĕra, ĕrum, adj. mors-fero, death-bringing, death-dealing, deadly, fatal (class.; syn.: lethalis, funestus): poculum, Cic. Tusc. 1, 29, 71: morbus, id. Div. 1, 30, 63: vulnus, id. Leg. 2, 5, 13: bellum, Verg. A. 6, 279: gravior dolor nec tamen mortiferus, Cels. 4, 2 init.; 5, 26, 22; Aug. de Util. Cred. § 36: res mortifera est inimicus pumice levis, Juv. 9, 95; 10, 10.—Neutr. plur. as subst.: mortĭfĕra, um, deadly things: cur tam multa mortifera terra mortique (de
mortifer.short: mortĭfer or (rarely) mortĭfĕrus, ĕra, ĕrum, adj.

mortificatio.full: mortĭfĭcātĭo, ōnis, f. mortifico, a killing, death (eccl. Lat.), opp. vivificatio, Tert. adv. Marc. 5, 9.

mortifico.full: mortĭfĭco, 1, v. a. mortificus, to kill, destroy (eccl. Lat.): caro mortificatur, Tert. Res. Carn. 37.—Transf., to mortify, subject, reduce to weakness: membra, Vulg. Col. 3, 5: facta carnis, id. Rom. 8, 13; cf. id. ib. 7, 4.

mortificus.full: mortĭfĭcus, a, um, adj. mors - facio, deadly, fatal (eccl. Lat.): cibus, Tert. Carm. adv. Marc. 4, 5: mortifico vulnere ictus, v. l. ap. Val. Max. 5, 6, 1 (Halm).

mortigena.full: mortĭgĕna, ae, m. mors-gen-, gigno, the producer of death, death-giver, Inscr. Grut. p. 1163.

mortualia.full: mortŭālĭa, ĭum, n. mortuus. (Sc. vestimenta.) Grave - clothes or mourningweeds (ante - class.), Naev. ap. Non. 548, 28 (Trag. Rel. v. 48 Rib.).— (Sc. carmina.) Haec sunt non nugae; non enim mortualia, funeral songs, dirges, referring to the custom at Rome of hiring women to sing absurd eulogies of the dead at funerals, Plaut. As. 4, 1, 63.

mortuarius.full: mortŭārĭus, a, um, adj. id., of or belonging to the dead (ante-class.): mortuaria glossaria, vocabularies of the dead, a term applied by Cato to the philosophers who talk of dead, and not of existing, things, Gell. 18, 7, 3.

mortuosus.full: mortŭōsus, a, um, adj. id., death-like, deadly (post-class.): vultus, Cael. Aur. Acut. 1, 3, 38.— Deadly, Cael. Aur. Acut. 1, 10, 71.

morturio.full: mortŭrĭo, ire, 4, v. n. desid. [mors], to long for death, desire to die: dictum est a Cicerone de philosophis, morturiunt, mori desiderant, Aug. de Gram. p: 2006 P. (Cic. Fragm. 50, 29, p. 146 B. and K.).

mortuus.full: mortŭus, a, um, P. a., v. morior fin.

morula.full: mŏrŭla, ae, f. dim. mora, a brief delay (post-class.): tempus nullā morulā extenditur, Aug. Conf. 11, 15; App. Fragm. M. 10, p. 71.

morulus.full: mōrŭlus, a, um, adj. dim. [2. morus], black, dark-colored (ante-class): jam pol ego illam pugnis totam faciam ut sit morula, Plaut. Poen. 5, 5, 10.

morum.full: mōrum, i, n., = μῶρον and μόρον, a mulberry; a blackberry: nigra mora, Hor. S. 2, 4, 22; cf. Plin. 15, 24, 27, § 96: in duris haerentia mora rubetis, Ov. M. 1, 105; cf. Plin. 24, 13, 73, § 117.
morum.short: mōrum, i, n., = μῶρον and μόρον, a mulberry;

morus1.full: mōrus, a, um, adj., = μωρός, foolish, silly (Plautin.). Adj.: amor mores hominum moros et morosos facit, Plaut. Trin. 3, 2, 43: ut hoc utimur more moro molestoque, id. Men. 4, 2, 1.— Subst. mōrus, i, m., a fool, simpleton: morus es, Plaut. Mil. 3, 1, 78.— mōra, ae, f., a foolish woman, Plaut. Mil. 2, 4, 17.— Hence, adv.: mōrē, foolishly (Plautin.): more hoc fit atque stulte, Plaut. Stich. 5, 1, 1.
morus1.short: mōrus, a, um, adj., = μωρός, foolish, silly (Plautin.).

morus2.full: mōrus, i, f., = μῶρα or μορέα, a mulberry-tree: arbor ibi, niveis uberrima pomis, Ardua morus erat, Ov. M. 4, 89; cf. Plin. 16, 18, 30, § 74.
morus2.short: mōrus, i, f., = μῶρα or μορέα, a mulberry-tree: arbor ibi, niveis uberrima pomis, Ardua morus erat, Ov.

morvinnicus.full: Morvinnĭcus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Morvinnus (a town of the Ædui), Inscr. Giorn. Arcad. t. 28, p. 351.
morvinnicus.short: Morvinnĭcus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Morvinnus (a town of the Ædui), Inscr.

mos.full: mos, mōris, m. etym. dub.; perh. root ma-, measure; cf.: maturus, matutinus; prop., a measuring or guiding rule of life; hence, manner, custom, way, usage, practice, fashion, wont, as determined not by the laws, but by men's will and pleasure, humor, self-will, caprice (class.; cf.: consuetudo, usus). Lit.: opsequens oboediensque'st mori atque imperiis patris, Plaut. Bacch. 3, 3, 54: huncine erat aequum ex illius more, an illum ex hujus vivere? Ter. Heaut. 1, 2, 24: alieno more vivendum est mihi

mosa.full: Mŏsa, ae, m., a river in Belgic Gaul, now the Meuse or Maas, Caes. B. G. 4, 9 fin.; 4, 10 init.; Plin. 4, 14, 28, § 100; Tac. A. 2, 6; id. H. 4, 28; 5, 23.
mosa.short: Mŏsa, ae, m., a river in Belgic Gaul, now the Meuse or Maas, Caes.

moschi.full: Moschi, ōrum, m., a people between the Black and the Caspian Seas, Mela, 1, 2, 5; 3, 5, 4; Luc. 3, 270; Plin. 6, 4, 4, § 29.— Hence, Moschĭcus, a, um, adj., Moschian, Plin. 5, 27, 27, § 99; Mela, 1, 19, 13.— Moschus, a, um, adj., Moschian, Mela, 1, 19: mons, Plin. 5, 27, 27, § 99.
moschi.short: Moschi, ōrum, m., a people between the Black and the Caspian Seas, Mela, 1, 2, 5;

moschis.full: Moschis, ĭdis, f., a female proper name, Afran. ap. Non. 318, 5; Inscr. Mur. 477, 5.
moschis.short: Moschis, ĭdis, f., a female proper name, Afran.

moschus.full: Moschus, i, m. A rhetorician of Pergamus, accused of poisoning, Hor. Ep. 1, 5, 9.— A Roman surname, Inscr. Mur. 477, 5.

moscilli.full: moscilli or moscŭli, ōrum, m. dim. mos, little customs or usages: moscillis (al. mosculis) Cato pro parvis moribus dixit, Paul. ex Fest. pp. 158 and 159 Müll.

mosella.full: Mŏsella, ae, m. and f., a river of Belgic Gaul, now the Moselle, Tac. A. 13, 53; id. H. 4, 71; 77: largus Mosella, Aus. de Clar. Urb. 4: placida Mosella, id. Idyll. 10, 73.—Also called Mŏsŭla, ae, f., Flor. 3, 10, 14.—Hence, Mŏsellēus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to the Moselle: ortus, Symm. Ep. 1, 8.

moses.full: Mōses or Mo︤︥yses, is or i, m. (in Vulg. nom. semper Mo︤︥yses; gen. Mo︤︥ysi, Lev. 8, 36; 16, 34; Num. 3, 1; 33, 1, etc.: Mosi, Sedul. 5, 274), = Μωσῆς, Μωυσῆς, Moses: Moses, Juv. 14, 102: Moyses, Tac. H. 5, 4: Moysen unum exsulum monuisse, ut, etc., id. ib. 5, 3: a Mose, Plin. 30, 1, 2, § 11: successor fuit Mosi, Lact. 4, 14: clarum videre Mŏysen, Sedul. 3, 285; Prud. Ham. 340.— Hence, Mōsēĭus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Moses (post-class.): Moseia virga, Paul. Nol. Carm. 23, 354.— Mō-sēus,
moses.short: Mōses or Mo︤︥yses, is or i, m.

mostellaria.full: Mostellārĭa, ae, f. mostellum, dim. from monstrum, The Ghost, the name of a comedy of Plautus, also called Phasma (φάσμα, ghost).

mosteni.full: Mostēni, ōrum, m., the inhabitants of Mostena or Mostene, a city of Lydia, Tac. A. 2, 47.
mosteni.short: Mostēni, ōrum, m., the inhabitants of Mostena or Mostene, a city of Lydia, Tac.

motabilis.full: mōtābĭlis, e, adj. moto, moving, that moves: anima, Vulg. Gen. 1, 21.

motacilla.full: mōtăcilla, ae, f., the white water-wagtail: motacilla, quod semper movet caudam, Varr. L. L. 5, § 76 Müll.; Plin. 37, 10, 56, § 156; Arn. 7, 223.
motacilla.short: mōtăcilla, ae, f., the white water-wagtail: motacilla, quod semper movet caudam, Varr.

motarium.full: mōtārĭum, ii, n., lint (post - class.), Cael. Aur. Tard. 3, 8, 134.
motarium.short: mōtārĭum, ii, n., lint (post - class.), Cael.

motatio.full: mōtātĭo, ōnis, f. moto, frequent motion, motion (eccl. Lat.), Tert. Anim. 45.

motator.full: mōtātor, ōris, m. id., a mover (postclass.), Tert. Anim. 12: motator sali Neptunus, Arn. 3, 118.

motio.full: mōtĭo, ōnis, f. moveo, a moving, motion; a removing (class.). Lit.: principium motionis, Cic. Fat. 19, 43: corporum, id. N. D. 2, 58, 145: ab ordine motio, a removing, Dig. 47, 20, 3.—Abstr., motion: ipsum animum ... quasi quamdam continuatam motionem, Cic. Tusc. 1, 10, 22.— In partic., in medicine, an ague-fit, Cels. 3, 5, 28.— Trop.: motiones animi, emotions or affections of the soul (old reading), Cic. Ac. 1, 8; better, notionibus.

motito.full: mōtĭto, āre, v. freq. a. moto, to move often, move about (post - class.), Gell. 9, 6, 3 dub.

motiuncula.full: mōtĭuncŭla, ae, f. dim. motio, a slight motion, shaking; in medicine, an attack of fever (post-Aug.), Sen. Ep. 53, 6: tentatus in Campaniā motiunculis levibus, Suet. Vesp. 24 init.

moto.full: mōto, āvi, ātum, 1, v. freq. a. moveo, to keep moving, move about (poet.): Zephyris motantibus, Verg. E. 5, 5; cacumina quercūs, id. ib. 6, 28: lacertos, Ov. M. 11, 674.—Pass.: fundamenta parietesque quati et motari videntur, Jul. Val. Rer. Gest. Alex. 1, 10.

motor.full: mōtor, ōris, m. id., a mover, that which keeps a thing in motion (poet.): cunarum fueras motor, Charideme, mearum, i. e. hast rocked me, Mart. 11, 39, 1.

motorius.full: mōtōrĭus, a, um, adj. motor, moving, that has motion (post-class.). Adj.: modus agendi, a stirring, bustling, noisy style of playing (opp. statarius), Don. Ter. Ad. prol. 24; id. ad argum. And.; Prisc. p. 590 P.— Subst.: mōtōrĭum, ii, n., the power of motion, Tert. Anim. 14.

motus1.full: mōtus, a, um, Part. and P. a., v. moveo fin. B.

motus2.full: mōtus, ūs, m. moveo, a moving, motion (freq. and class.). Lit. In gen.: orbes, qui versantur contrario motu, Cic. Rep. 6, 17, 17: deus motum dedit caelo, id. Univ. 6: natura omnia ciens et agitans motibus et mutationibus suis, id. N. D. 3, 11, 27: motus astrorum ignoro, Juv. 3, 42.—Poet.: futuri, departure, Verg. A. 4, 297: sub Aurorae primos excedere motus, Luc. 4, 734: crebri terrae, i. e. earthquakes, Curt. 4, 4, 20; 8, 11, 2.— In partic., artistic movement, gesticulation, dancing: haud indec

movens.full: mŏvens, entis, Part. and P. a., v. moveo fin. A.

moveo.full: mŏvĕo, mōvi, mōtum, 2 (sync., mōstis for movistis, Mart. 3, 67, 1; mōrunt for moverunt, Sil. 14, 141), v. a. and n. Sanscr. mīv, set in motion; Gr. ἀμείβω, change; cf.: momentum, mutare. Act., to move, stir, set in motion; to shake, disturb, remove, etc. (syn.: cieo, agito, ago, molior). Lit.: movit et ad certos nescia membra modos, Tib. 1, 7, 38: ut festis matrona moveri jussa diebus, to dance, Hor. A. P. 232: moveri Cyclopa, to represent a Cyclop by dancing (gesticulating), id. Ep. 2, 2, 125:
moveo.short: mŏvĕo, mōvi, mōtum, 2 (sync., mōstis for movistis, Mart.

mox.full: mox, adv. etym. dub.; cf. Sanscr. mankshu, ready, soon, soon, anon, directly, presently; mostly of the future (class.). Lit. In gen.: mox ivero, Plaut. Capt. 1, 2, 91: mox ego huc revertor, Ter. And. 3, 2, 4: jussit mihi nuntiari, mox se venturum, Cic. Att. 10, 4, 8: mox tamen ardentīs accingar dicere pugnas Caesaris, Verg. G. 3, 46; Cic. Div. 1, 23, 47.—With quam: exspectant ... quam mox emittat currus, Enn. ap. Cic. Div. 1, 48, 107 (Ann. v. 89 Vahl.); so, exspecto quam mox utatur, Cic. Rosc. C

moysiticus.full: Mŏysītĭcus, a, um, adj. Moyses, of or belonging to Moses (post-class.), Venant. Vit. S. Mart. 2, 28.

mu.full: mu, interj., = μῦ, a slight sound made with the closed lips (ante-class.): neque, ut aiunt, mu facere audent, to mutter, make a muttering, Enn. ap. Varr. L. L. 7, § 101 Müll. (Enn. p. 175, n. 10 Vahl.): nec mu facere audet, Lucil. ap. Charis. p. 213 P.: nec dico nec facio mu, Enn. ap. Don. ad Ter. And. 3, 2, 25 (Enn. p. 175, n. 8 Vahl.; but not in Plaut. Stich. 1, 3, 102, v. Ritschl ad h. l.).—* A sound of lamentation: mul perii hercle: Afer est, Plaut. Fragm. ap. Charis. p. 213 P.
mu.short: mu, interj., = μῦ, a slight sound made with the closed lips (ante-class.): neque, ut aiunt, mu facere audent, to mutter, make a muttering, Enn.

muccedo.full: muccēdo, muccĭdus, muccĭnĭ-um, muccōsus, muccŭlentus, muccus, v. mucedo, etc.
muccedo.short: muccēdo, muccĭdus, muccĭnĭ-um, muccōsus, muccŭlentus, muccus, v.

mucedo.full: mūcēdo (muccēdo), ĭnis, f. mucus, mucus of the nose (post-class.), App. Mag. p. 306 dub. (Hildebr. dulcedo).

muceo.full: mūcĕo, ui, 2, v. n. id., to be mouldy, musty (ante-class.): vinum quod neque aceat, neque muceat, Cato, R. R. 148.

mucesco.full: mūcesco, ĕre, v. inch. n. [muceo], to become mouldy or musty (post-Aug.): proprium est vino mucescere, Plin. 14, 20, 26, § 131.

muchula.full: muchula, ae, f., the Persian name of the precious stone telicardios, Plin. 37, 10, 68, § 183.
muchula.short: muchula, ae, f., the Persian name of the precious stone telicardios, Plin.

mucidus.full: mūcĭdus (mucc-), a, um, adj. mucus. Mouldy, musty: mucida panis frusta, Juv. 14, 128: vina, Mart. 8, 6, 4.— Snivelling: homo es, Qui me emunxisti mucidum, Plaut. Epid. 3, 4, 58: senex, id. Mil. 3, 1, 52.

mucilago.full: mūcĭlāgo (mucc-), ĭnis, f. muceo, a mouldy, musty juice, Theod. Prisc. 4, 1.

mucinium.full: mūcĭnĭum (mucc-), ii, n. mucus, a pocket-handkerchief, Arn. 2, 23.

mucius.full: Mūcĭus, a (Mutius, Lact. 5, 13, 13), the name of a Roman gens. The most celebrated are, C. Mucius Scaevola, who altempted to assassinate Porsena, and, on being apprehended, burned off his right hand, Liv. 2, 12; Cic. Sest. 21, 48; id. Par. 1, 2, 12; Flor. 1, 10; Sen. Ep. 24, 5; 66. 51; Sil. 8, 386; Lact. l. l.— Q. Mucius Scaevola, a governor in Asia, Cic. Caecil. 17, 57. — Q. Mucius Scaevola, an augur, the husband of Lælia, Cic. Brut. 58, 211; id. Phil. 8, 10, 31.— P. Mucius Scaevola, a friend o

mucor.full: mūcor, ōris, m. muceo. Mould, mouldiness, in bread (post-Aug.): mucorem contrahere, to become mouldy, Col. 12, 4, 4.— Mustiness, in wine, vinegar, etc.: mucor (vini), Dig. 18, 6, 4.—Also, a moisture which flows from vines, and is injurious to them: mucor, qui maxime vites infestat, Plin. 17, 15, 25, § 116.

mucosus.full: mūcōsus (mucc-), a, um, adj. mucus, slimy, mucous (post-Aug.): cruenta et mucosa ventris proluvies, Col. 1, 7, 1; 6, 7, 1; Paul. ex Fest. p. 158 Müll.: exulceratio, Cels. 5, 28, 15.— Transf., = stultus (opp. emunctae naris), Acron. ad Hor. S. 1, 4, 8.

mucro.full: mucro, ōnis, m., a sharp point or edge; esp., the point of a sword, the sword's point (class.; cf.: acies, cuspis). Lit.: mucro falcis, Col. 4, 25, 1: dentis, Plin. 8, 3, 4, § 8: folii, id. 16, 10, 16, § 38: crystalli, id. 37, 2, 9, § 26: cultri, edge, Juv. 14, 216: medio jugulaberis ensis, sword's point, Ov. M. 12, 484: coruscus, Verg. A. 2, 333.— Transf. A sword: nisi mucrones militum tremere voltis, Cic. Phil. 14, 3, 6: mortalis, Verg. A. 12, 740.— A point, extremity, end (poet. and in post-A
mucro.short: mucro, ōnis, m., a sharp point or edge;

mucronatus.full: mūcrōnātus, a, um, adj. mucro, pointed (post-Aug.): piscis mucronato rostro, Plin. 32, 2, 6, § 15: folia, id. 25, 13, 102, § 161.

muculentus.full: mūcŭlentus (mucc-), a, um, adj. mucus, snivelling (post-class.): nares, Prud. στεφ. 13, 282: munctiones, Arn. 3, 107.

mucus.full: mūcus (mucc-), i, m. mug, mungo; cf. also Sanscr. muć, solvere, dimittere, snivel, mucus of the nose: mucusque, et mala pituita nasi, Cat. 23, 17; Cels. 4, 18.

mufrius.full: mufrius, ii, m., a term of abuse: mufrius non magister, Petr. 58 fin.
mufrius.short: mufrius, ii, m., a term of abuse: mufrius non magister, Petr.

muger.full: muger dici solet a Castrensium hominibus, quasi mucosus, is, qui talis male ludit, Paul. ex Fest. p. 158, 27 Müll. (cf. Engl. smuggle; Germ. Schmuggel), a false player.
muger.short: muger dici solet a Castrensium hominibus, quasi mucosus, is, qui talis male ludit, Paul.

mugil.full: mūgil and mūgĭlis, is, m., a sea-fish; acc. to some, the mullet: mugilum natura ridetur, in metu capite abscondito, totos se occultari credentium, Plin. 9, 17, 26, § 59; 9, 42, 67, § 144; 9, 62, 88, § 185; 10, 70, 89, § 193; 32, 11, 53, § 149.—This fish was made use of in punishing adulterers: quosdam moechos et mugilis intrat, Juv. 10, 317; cf. Cat. 15, 19.
mugil.short: mūgil and mūgĭlis, is, m., a sea-fish;

mugillanus.full: Mugillānus, i, m., a Roman surname; as, e. g. Papirius Mugillanus, Liv. 4, 30.
mugillanus.short: Mugillānus, i, m., a Roman surname;

muginor.full: mūgĭnor, āri, v. dep., to dally, trifle, hesitate, delay (rare but class.): muginari est nugari et quasi tarde conari, Paul. ex Fest. p. 147 Müll.: muginamur, Lucil. ap. Non. 139, 6; Att. ib. 139, 7: dum tu muginaris, cepi consilium domesticum, Cic. Att. 16, 12, 1.—In the collat. form, mūsĭnor, āri: dum ista (ut ait M. Varro) musinamur. Plin. H. N. prooem. § 18.

mugio1.full: mūgĭo, īvi and ĭi, ītum, 4, v. n. Sanscr. root, muǵ, sonare; Gr. μυκάομαι, μύζω, to low, bellow (syn. boo). Lit.: inde cum actae boves mugissent, Liv. 1, 7. —Prov.: hic bove percusso mugire Agamemnona credit, Juv. 14, 286.—Part. pres. subst.: mugientium Prospectat errantes greges, i. e. cattle, Hor. Epod. 2, 11.— Transf., of the sound of a trumpet, to bray: Tyrrhenusque tubae mugire per aethera clangor, Verg. A. 8, 526.—Of an earthquake, to rumble: sub pedibus mugire solum, id. ib. 6, 256.—Of a
mugio1.short: mūgĭo, īvi and ĭi, ītum, 4, v.

mugio2.full: Mugĭo, ōnis, m., a Roman surname, Inscr. Grut. 339, 5.
mugio2.short: Mugĭo, ōnis, m., a Roman surname, Inscr.

mugionia.full: Mūgĭōnĭa or Mūgōnĭa, ae, or Mūgĭōnis (Mucionis), is, f. (porta), a gate of ancient Rome, which was afterwards within the city: in Palatio Mucionis a mugitu, Varr. L. L. 5, § 164 Müll.: Mugionia porta Romae dicta est a Mugio quodam. Paul. ex Fest. p. 144 Müll.; Sol. 1, 24; cf. Becker's Antiq. 1, p. 109 sq.
mugionia.short: Mūgĭōnĭa or Mūgōnĭa, ae, or Mūgĭōnis (Mucionis), is, f.

mugitor.full: mūgītor, ōris, m. 1. mugio, a bellower (poet.): mugitor Vesuvius, Val. Fl. 3, 208.

mugitus.full: mūgītus, ūs, m. id., a lowing, bellowing (class.). Lit.: mugitusque boum, Verg. G. 2, 470: edere, to utter lowings, to low, Ov. M. 7, 597: dare, id. F. 1, 560: tollere, Verg. A. 2, 223.— Transf., a bellowing, rumbling, roaring, loud noise: mugitus terrae, Cic. Div. 1, 18: nemorum, Plin. 18, 35, 86, § 360; Stat. Th. 10, 263: labyrinthi, Juv. 1, 53.

mula.full: mūla, ae (abl. plur. mulabus: data et vehicula cum mulabus ac mulionibus, Capitol. Ver. 5; Tert. Uxor. 2, 8; Prisc. p. 733 P.), f. mulus, a she-mule; also, in gen., a mule (used instead of horses for drawing carriages or bearing litters): ex asino et equā mula gignitur, Plin. 8, 44, 69, § 171; Juv. 7, 181.—She-mules bear no young, Plin. l. l. § 173. Hence: mulae partus a te prolatus est: res mirabilis propterea, quia non saepe fit, Cic. Div. 2, 22, 49; cf. id. ib. 1, 18, 36: hoc monstrum fetae c

mularis.full: mūlāris, e, adj. id., of or belonging to mules (post-Aug.): materies, the race of mules, Col. 6, 27, 1: carpentum, Lampr. Heliog. 4, 4.

mulc.full: mulc, the Persian name for the precious stone thelycardios, Plin. 37, 10, 68, § 183; al. muchala.
mulc.short: mulc, the Persian name for the precious stone thelycardios, Plin.

mulcator.full: mulcātor, ōris, m. mulco, he who handles roughly, Isid. 10, 178; Placid. Gloss. p. 483.

mulcedo.full: mulcēdo, ĭnis, f. mulceo, pleasantness, agreeableness (post-class.): Veneris atque Musae, Gell. 19, 9, 7; Sid. Ep. 5, 17.

mulceo.full: mulcĕo, si, sum (rarely mulctum), 2, v. a. Sanscr. root marc, take hold of; Gr. μάρπτω, μάρπτις; cf. mulco, to stroke; to touch or move lightly (syn. palpo; poet. and in post-Aug. prose). Lit.: manu mulcens barbam, Ov. F. 1, 259: caput, Quint. 11, 3, 158: vitulum, Ov. A. A. 2, 341: colla, id. M. 10, 118: mulcebant Zephyri flores, rustle through, id. ib. 1, 108: aura mulcet rosas, Prop. 4 (5), 7, 60. virgā mulcere capillos, to touch lightly, Ov. M. 14, 295: aristas, id. F. 5, 161: mulcere alterno

mulcetra.full: mulcētra, ae, f., a plant, called also heliotropium, App. Herb. 9.
mulcetra.short: mulcētra, ae, f., a plant, called also heliotropium, App.

mulciber.full: Mulcĭber, ēris and ĕri (gen. sync. Mulcebri, Cic. poet. Tusc. 2, 10, 23), m. mulceo; he who softens any thing; v. infra, a surname of Vulcan: Mulciber, Vulcanus, a molliendo scilicet ferro dictus: mulcere enim mollire, sive lenire est, Paul. ex Fest. p. 144 Müll.; Att. ap. Macr. S. 6, 5 (Trag. Rel. v. 558 Rib.): Mulciber, credo, arma fecit, Plaut. Ep. 1, 1, 32; Ov. A. A. 2, 562: Mulciber in Trojam, pro Troia stabat Apollo, Ov. Tr. 1, 2, 5: VOLCANO MITI SIVE MVLCIBERO L. VETT., Inscr. Orell. 1382

mulco.full: mulco († mulcto, Inscr. Grut. 155, 1), āvi, ātum, 1 (mulcassitis, for mulcaveritis, Plaut. Mil. 2, 2, 8), v. a. Sanscr. root marc, take hold of; of. Gr. μάρπτω, perh. μορφή, to beat, cudgel; to maltreat, handle roughly, injure (class.; syn.: verbero, tundo, pulso). Lit.: ipsum dominum atque omnem famibam Mulcavit usque ad mortem, Ter. Ad 1, 2, 9; Petr. S. 134: aliquem, to illtreat, Plaut. Most. 4, 2, 23: male mulcati clavis ac fustibus repelluntur, Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 43, § 94: mulcato corpore, wit

mulcta.full: mulcta, mulctātĭcĭus, mulctā-tĭo, mulcto, v. multa, etc.

mulctra.full: mulctra, ae, f. mulgeo, a milkingpail, milk-pail. Lit.: bis venit ad mulctram, Verg. E. 3, 30: e mulctrā recens caseus, Col. 8, 17, 13; cf. mulctrum.— Transf., the milk in a milk-pail, Col. 7, 8, 1; cf. mulctrum.
