mutuarius.full: mūtŭārĭus, a, um, adj. mutuus, mutual (post-class.): operae, exchanges of services, App. Mag. p. 284, 30.

mutuaticius.full: mūtŭātīcĭus or -tĭus, a, um, adj. mutuor, borrowed (post-class.): in pecuniae mutuaticiae usu (al. mutuaticae), Gell. 20, 1, 41.

mutuatio.full: mūtŭātĭo, ōnis, f. id., a borrowing (class.), Cic. Tusc. 1, 42, 100: cum multos minutis mutuationibus defraudāsset, id. Fl. 20, 47: translationes quasi mutuationes sunt, id. de Or. 3, 38, 156.

mutuatus.full: mūtŭātus, a, um, Part. Of 2. mutuo.— Of mutuor; v. h. vv.

mutucumenses.full: Mutucumenses, ĭum, m., the inhabitants of a city in Latium, Plin. 3, 5, 9, § 69 (rejected by Jahn).
mutucumenses.short: Mutucumenses, ĭum, m., the inhabitants of a city in Latium, Plin.

mutue.full: mūtŭē, adv., v. mutuus fin. B.

mutuiter.full: mūtŭĭter, adv., v. mutuus fin. C.

mutuito.full: mūtŭĭto, āre, v. a., or mūtŭĭtor, āri, v. dep. mutuo or mutuor, to seek to borrow from a person: mutuitanti, Plaut. Mere. prol. 58.

mutulus.full: mūtŭlus, i, m. In architecture, a mutule, modillion, Varr. R. R. 3, 5; Vitr. 4, 2.— A fish; v. mitulus.

mutuo1.full: mūtŭō, adv., v. mutuus fin. A.

mutuor.full: mūtŭor, ātus, 1, v. dep. a. [mutuus], to borrow something of some one (class.; opp. mutuum do, commodo, credo). Lit., to obtain a loan of money: mutuari pecunias, Caes. B. C. 3, 60: pecuniam, Gai. Inst. 4, 73.—Also without acc.: a Caelio mutuabimur, Cic. Att. 7, 3, 11: mutuari cogor, I am obliged to borrow, id. ib. 15, 15, 3.—Of other things than money: domum, Tac. Or. 9: auxilia ad bellum, Hirt. B. G. 8, 21.— Trop., to borrow, to take for one's use, to derive, obtain, get, procure: orator subti

mutus.full: mūtus, a, um, adj. root mu-, to shut; Sanscr. mūkas, dumb; Gr. μύτις, μυάω; cf. Lat. mussare, dumb, mute (class.; cf.: infans, elinguis). Lit., that does not speak, silent.—Of creatures who do not possess the faculty of speech, and can utter only inarticulate sounds: pecudes, Cic. Q. Fr. 1, 1, 8, § 24: bestiae, id. Fin. 1, 21, 71: agna, Hor. S. 2, 3, 219: armenta, Stat. Th. 5, 334: animalia, Juv. 8, 56: satius est mutum esse quam quod nemo intellegat dicere, Cic. Phil. 3, 9, 22: subjugale, anima

mutusca.full: Mŭtusca, ae, f., = Trebula Mutusca, a city in the Sabine territory: olivifera, Verg. A. 7, 711. Its inhabitants are called Trēbŭlāni Metusci, Plin. 3, 12, 17, § 107; v. Trebula.
mutusca.short: Mŭtusca, ae, f., = Trebula Mutusca, a city in the Sabine territory: olivifera, Verg.

mutuus.full: mūtŭus, a, um, adj. 1. muto, borrowed, lent (class.). Lit.: nullus est tibi, quem roges mutuom Argentum, to lend you money, Plaut. Ps. 1, 3, 60; id. Pers. 1, 1, 44: mutuum talentum dare, to lend, advance, id. Trin. 4, 3, 48: mutuum argentum quaerere, to seek to borrow money, id. Pers. 1, 1, 5: huic drachmarum argenti haec mille dederat mutuom, Ter. Heaut. 3, 3, 40: nam si mutuas (sc. minas) non potero, certumst sumam faenore, Plaut. As. 1, 3, 95: mutuas pecunias sumere ab aliquo, to borrow or ra

mutyca.full: Mŭtўca, ae, or Mŭtўcē, ēs, f., = Μοτύκα, a city in Sicily, between Camarina and Syracuse, now Modica, Sil. 14, 268.— Hence, Mŭtўcensis, e, adj., of or belonging to Mutyce: ager, Cic. Verr. 2, 3, 43, § 101; 2, 3, 51, § 120.—In plur.: Mŭtў-censes, ĭum, m., the inhabitants of Mutyca, Plin. 3, 8, 14, § 91.
mutyca.short: Mŭtўca, ae, or Mŭtўcē, ēs, f., = Μοτύκα, a city in Sicily, between Camarina and Syracuse, now Modica, Sil.

mya.full: mўa, ae, f., = μύα, a kind of mussel on the shores of the Thracian Bosporus, Plin. 9, 35, 56, § 115.
mya.short: mўa, ae, f., = μύα, a kind of mussel on the shores of the Thracian Bosporus, Plin.

myacanthos.full: mўăcanthos, i, f., or mўăcan-thon, i, n., = ὁ μυάκανθος, τὸ μυάκανθον, a plant, also called corruda, and, by the Greeks, hormenos or myacanthos, the wild asparagus, Plin. 19, 8, 42, § 151.
myacanthos.short: mўăcanthos, i, f., or mўăcan-thon, i, n., = ὁ μυάκανθος, τὸ μυάκανθον, a plant, also called corruda, and, by the Greeks, hormenos or myacanthos, the wild asparagus, Plin.

myaces.full: mўăces, um, m., = μύακες, a kind of sea-mussels, Plin. 32, 9, 31, § 95.
myaces.short: mўăces, um, m., = μύακες, a kind of sea-mussels, Plin.

myagros.full: mўăgros, i, m., = μύαγρος, a plant, otherwise unknown, Plin. 27, 12, 81, § 106.
myagros.short: mўăgros, i, m., = μύαγρος, a plant, otherwise unknown, Plin.

myax.full: mўax, ăcis, m., = μύαξ, a kind of mussel, Plin. 32, 9, 30, § 95.
myax.short: mўax, ăcis, m., = μύαξ, a kind of mussel, Plin.

mycale.full: Mўcălē, ēs, f., = Μυκάλη. A promontory and city in Ionia, opposite the Isle of Samos, Ov. M. 2, 223; Just. 2, 14, 7.— Derivv. Mўcălaeus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Mycale, Mycalean: litora, Claud. in. Eutr. 2, 264.— Mўcă-lensis, e, adj., of or belonging to Mycale: mons, Val. Max. 6, 9, 5.— A female poisoner, Ov. M. 12, 263; Sen. Herc. Oet. 525.

mycalessos.full: Mўcălessos (Mўcălēsos), i, m., = Μυκαλησσός, a mountain and city in Bœotia, Stat. Th. 7, 272; Plin. 4, 7, 12, § 25. —Hence, Mўcălēsĭus, a, um, adj., Mycalesian: cuspis, Stat. Th. 9, 281.
mycalessos.short: Mўcălessos (Mўcălēsos), i, m., = Μυκαλησσός, a mountain and city in Bœotia, Stat.

mycematias.full: mўcēmătĭas, ae, m., = μυκηματίας, an earthquake accompanied by a rumbling noise, Amm. 17, 7, 14.
mycematias.short: mўcēmătĭas, ae, m., = μυκηματίας, an earthquake accompanied by a rumbling noise, Amm.

mycenae.full: Mўcēnae, ārum, or Mўcēna, ae, and Mўcēne, ēs, f., = Μυκηναι, Μυκήνη, a celebrated city in Argolis, of which Agamemnon was king: Agamemnoniaeque Mycenae, Verg. A. 6, 838; Ov. M. 6, 414; 15, 426 al.: deprensus urbe Mycenae, Verg. A. 5, 52: Diti sacrata, Auct. Priap. 77: ante Agamemnoniam ... Mycenen, Sil. 1, 27.— Derivv. Mўcēnaeus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Mycenæ, Mycenæan: ductor, i. e. Agamemnon, Verg. A. 11, 266: teque, Mycenaeo, Phoebas, amata duci, i. e. Cassandra, beloved by Agamemnon
mycenae.short: Mўcēnae, ārum, or Mўcēna, ae, and Mўcēne, ēs, f., = Μυκηναι, Μυκήνη, a celebrated city in Argolis, of which Agamemnon was king: Agamemnoniaeque Mycenae, Verg.

mycenica.full: Mycenĭca, ae, f., a place near Argos, in the Peloponnesus, Liv. 32, 39.
mycenica.short: Mycenĭca, ae, f., a place near Argos, in the Peloponnesus, Liv.

mycenis.full: Mўcēnis, ĭdis, f., v. Mycenae, II. C.

mycetias.full: mȳcētĭas, ae, m., = μυκητίας, for mycematias, an earthquake attended with a rumbling noise, App. de Mund. p. 65, 33.
mycetias.short: mȳcētĭas, ae, m., = μυκητίας, for mycematias, an earthquake attended with a rumbling noise, App.

myconos.full: Mўcŏnos or -us, i, f., = Μύκονος, one of the Cyctades, now Mykoni, Mel. 2, 7, 11; Verg. A. 3, 76; Ov. M. 7, 463.—Hence, Mўcŏnĭus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Myconos, Myconian: vinum, Plin. 14, 7, 9, § 75.—In plur. subst.: Mўcŏnĭi, ōrum, m., the inhabitants of Myconos, the Myconians, Plin. 11, 37, 47, § 130.
myconos.short: Mўcŏnos or -us, i, f., = Μύκονος, one of the Cyctades, now Mykoni, Mel.

mydriasis.full: mydrĭăsis, is, f., = μυδρίασις, a disease of the eyes, a preternatural dilatation of the pupil, mydriasis, Cels. 6, 6, 37.
mydriasis.short: mydrĭăsis, is, f., = μυδρίασις, a disease of the eyes, a preternatural dilatation of the pupil, mydriasis, Cels.

mygale.full: mўgălē, ēs, f., = μυγαλῆ (post-class.), a small species of mouse, called in pure Lat. mus araneus, Veg. Vet. 3, 4, 33; Col. 6, 17, 1.
mygale.short: mўgălē, ēs, f., = μυγαλῆ (post-class.), a small species of mouse, called in pure Lat.

mygdones.full: Mygdŏnes, um, m., = Μυγδόνες, a people of Thrace, who afterwards took possession of a part of Phrygia, Plin. 4, 10, 17, § 35; 5, 30, 33, § 126.— Derivv. Mygdŏnĭa, ae, f., = Μυγδονία. A district in Macedonia, Plin. 4, 10, 17, § 38.— A district in Phrygia, Plin. 5, 32, 41, § 145; Sol. 40, 9.— A district in Mesopotamia, Plin. 6, 13, 16, § 42.— A district in Bithynia, Sol. 42, 1; Amm. 22, 8, 14.— Mygdŏnĭdes, ae, m., the son of Mygdon, Verg. A. 2, 342.— Mygdŏnis, ĭdis, f., a Mygdonian, Phrygian, Lydi
mygdones.short: Mygdŏnes, um, m., = Μυγδόνες, a people of Thrace, who afterwards took possession of a part of Phrygia, Plin.

myiagros.full: Mўĭăgros or -us, i, m., = Μυίαγρος or Μυἷαγρος, the fly-catcher, a deity, by invoking whom flies were destroyed; called also Myodes or Myiodes, Plin. 10, 28, 40, § 75.
myiagros.short: Mўĭăgros or -us, i, m., = Μυίαγρος or Μυἷαγρος, the fly-catcher, a deity, by invoking whom flies were destroyed;

myiodes.full: Mўiōdes, m., = μυιώδης, i. q. Myiagros, Plin. 29, 6, 34, § 106.

myiscae.full: mўiscae, ārum, f., = μυἱσκαι, small sca-mussels, Plin. 32, 9, 31, § 98; 32, 11, 53, § 149.
myiscae.short: mўiscae, ārum, f., = μυἱσκαι, small sca-mussels, Plin.

myiscus.full: mўiscus, i, m., a small sea-mussel, Plin. 32, 11, 53, § 149.
myiscus.short: mўiscus, i, m., a small sea-mussel, Plin.

mylae.full: Mȳlae, ārum (and Mȳlē, ēs, f., Sil. 14, 202), f., = Μύλαι. A city in Sicily, now Milazzo, Plin. 3, 8, 14, § 90; Vell. 2, 79, 4; Suet. Aug. 16.—Hence, Mȳlaeus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Mylæ, Mylæan: aut Pompeiani Mylaea pericula belli, Aus. Mosell. 215 (al. Milasena).— A city in Thessaly, now Dhamasi, Liv. 42, 54.— Two islands near Crete, Plin. 4, 12, 20, § 61.
mylae.short: Mȳlae, ārum (and Mȳlē, ēs, f., Sil.

mylas.full: Mylas or Myla, ae, m., a river in Sicily, now the Marcellino, Liv. 24, 30.
mylas.short: Mylas or Myla, ae, m., a river in Sicily, now the Marcellino, Liv.

mylasa.full: Mȳlăsa or Mylassa, ōrum, n., = Μύλασα, Μύλασσα, a city in Caria, now Melassa, Plin. 5, 29, 29, § 108.—Hence, Mȳlăsensis (Mylass-), e, adj., of or belonging to Mylasa, Mylasian.—In plur.: Mȳlăsenses, ĭum, m., the inhabitants of Mylasa, the Mylasians, Liv. 45, 25, 11 and 13.— Mȳlăsēnus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Mylasa, Mylasian: pericula, Aus. Idyll. 10, 215.—In plur.: Mȳlăsēni, ōrum, m., the inhabitants of Mylasa, the Mylasians, Liv. 38, 39, 9.— Mȳlăsĕus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to My
mylasa.short: Mȳlăsa or Mylassa, ōrum, n., = Μύλασα, Μύλασσα, a city in Caria, now Melassa, Plin.

mylasia.full: mylasĭa or -ĕa, ae, f., a kind of hemp, Plin. 19, 9, 56, § 174.
mylasia.short: mylasĭa or -ĕa, ae, f., a kind of hemp, Plin.

myloecus.full: mўloecus or -os, i, m., = μύλοικος, a kind of moth, which breeds in mills, Plin. 29, 6, 39, § 141.
myloecus.short: mўloecus or -os, i, m., = μύλοικος, a kind of moth, which breeds in mills, Plin.

myndus.full: Myndus or -os, i, f., = Μύνδος, a city in Caria, now Gumishlu Liman, Cic. Verr. 2, 1, 34, § 86; Liv. 37, 16, 2; Mel. 1, 16, 3.— Hence, Myndii, ōrum, m., the inhabitants of Myndus, Liv. 33, 20, 12.
myndus.short: Myndus or -os, i, f., = Μύνδος, a city in Caria, now Gumishlu Liman, Cic.

myobarbum.full: myŏbarbum, i, n. vox hibr., from μῦς-barba (mouse-beard), a rather long drinking-vessel terminating in a point, Aus. 2, 27 in lemm.

myoctonos.full: myoctŏnos, i, m., = μυοκτόνος (mouse-killer), a kind of aconitum, said to kill mice by its smell, Plin. 27, 3, 2, § 10.
myoctonos.short: myoctŏnos, i, m., = μυοκτόνος (mouse-killer), a kind of aconitum, said to kill mice by its smell, Plin.

myonnesus.full: Myonnēsus or -os, i, = Μυόννησος. Masc., a promontory in Ionia, with a city of the same name, now Ovreokastro, Liv. 37, 13; 27.— Fem., an island near Ephesus, Plin. 5, 31, 38, § 137.

myoparo.full: myŏpăro, ōnis, m., = μυοπάρων, a kind of light piratical vessel, Cic. Verr. 2, 3, 80, § 186; 2, 1, 34, § 87; Fragm. ap. Non. 534, 16; cf. Paul. ex Fest. p. 147 Müll.
myoparo.short: myŏpăro, ōnis, m., = μυοπάρων, a kind of light piratical vessel, Cic.

myophonos.full: mўŏphŏnos, i, m., or -on, i, n., = μυοφόνος (mouse-killer), a plant, perh. i. q. myoctonos, Plin. 21, 9, 30, § 54.
myophonos.short: mўŏphŏnos, i, m., or -on, i, n., = μυοφόνος (mouse-killer), a plant, perh.

myops.full: mўops, ōpis, adj., = μυώψ, near-sighted (post-class.), Dig. 21, 1, 10, § 3.
myops.short: mўops, ōpis, adj., = μυώψ, near-sighted (post-class.), Dig.

myosota.full: mўŏsōta, ae, and mўŏsōtis, ĭdis, f., = μυοσώτη, μυοσωτίς, mouse-ear, a plant, Plin. 27, 12, 80, § 105.
myosota.short: mўŏsōta, ae, and mўŏsōtis, ĭdis, f., = μυοσώτη, μυοσωτίς, mouse-ear, a plant, Plin.

myosoton.full: mўŏsōton, i, n., = μυόσωτον, the plant alsine, Plin. 27, 4, 8, § 23.
myosoton.short: mўŏsōton, i, n., = μυόσωτον, the plant alsine, Plin.

myotacismus.full: myotacismus, v. l. for moetacis-mus, the frequent repetition or recurrence of the letter m, Diom. 448 P.; Mart. Cap. 5, § 514; Cassiod. Inst. Div. Litt. 15.

myrapia.full: myrăpĭa (myrrhăpĭa) pira, = μυράπια, a kind of sweet-smelling pear, Cels. 4, 19, 20; Plin. 15, 15, 16, § 55; Col. 12, 10, 4.
myrapia.short: myrăpĭa (myrrhăpĭa) pira, = μυράπια, a kind of sweet-smelling pear, Cels.

myrice1.full: mўrīcē, ēs, or mўrīca, ae, f., = μυρίκη, the tamarisk, a kind of shrub, Plin. 13, 21, 37, § 116; 24, 9, 41, § 67.—Prov., to signify something impossible: pinguia corticibus sudent electra myricae, Verg. E. 8, 54.
myrice1.short: mўrīcē, ēs, or mўrīca, ae, f., = μυρίκη, the tamarisk, a kind of shrub, Plin.

myrice2.full: Mўrīcē, ēs, f., a nymph, from whom Hannibal's wife Imilce was said to be descended, Sil. 3, 103.
myrice2.short: Mўrīcē, ēs, f., a nymph, from whom Hannibal's wife Imilce was said to be descended, Sil.

myrina.full: Myrīna, ae, f., = Μυρίνα. A fortified seaport town of the Æolians, in Asia Minor, afterwards called Sebastopolis, Cic. Fam. 5, 20, 8; Liv. 33, 30, 3; Tac. A. 2, 47. —Hence, Myrīnus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Myrina, Mart. 9, 43, 1.— A city in the Isle of Lemnos, Plin. 4, 12, 23, § 73. — A town in Crete, Plin. 4, 12, 20, § 59.

myriogenesis.full: mȳrĭŏgĕnĕsis, is, f., = μυριογἐνεσις, multiple generation, Firm. Math. 8, 18.
myriogenesis.short: mȳrĭŏgĕnĕsis, is, f., = μυριογἐνεσις, multiple generation, Firm.

myrionymus.full: mȳrĭōnўmus, a, um, adj., = μυριώνυμος, with countless names, Inscr. Grut. 8, 3, 11.
myrionymus.short: mȳrĭōnўmus, a, um, adj., = μυριώνυμος, with countless names, Inscr.

myriophyllon.full: mȳrĭŏ-phyllon, ii, n., = μυριόφυλλον, pure Lat. millefolium, the plant milfoil, yarrow, Plin. 24, 16, 95, § 152.
myriophyllon.short: mȳrĭŏ-phyllon, ii, n., = μυριόφυλλον, pure Lat.

myrmeces.full: Myrmēcĕs Scŏpŭli, rocks in the sea, near Smyrna, Plin. 5, 29, 31, § 119.
myrmeces.short: Myrmēcĕs Scŏpŭli, rocks in the sea, near Smyrna, Plin.

myrmecias.full: myrmēcĭas, ae, m., = μυρμηκίας, a black precious stone, with protuberances like warts, Plin. 37, 10, 63, § 174.
myrmecias.short: myrmēcĭas, ae, m., = μυρμηκίας, a black precious stone, with protuberances like warts, Plin.

myrmecides.full: Myrmēcĭdes, ae, m., = Μυρμηκίδης, a celebrated sculptor, Cic. Ac. 2, 38, 120; cf. Plin. 7, 21, 21, § 85; 36, 5, 4, § 43.
myrmecides.short: Myrmēcĭdes, ae, m., = Μυρμηκίδης, a celebrated sculptor, Cic.

myrmecitis.full: myrmēcītis, ĭdis, f., = μυρμηκῖτις, a precious stone, containing something like ants, Plin. 37, 11, 72, § 187.
myrmecitis.short: myrmēcītis, ĭdis, f., = μυρμηκῖτις, a precious stone, containing something like ants, Plin.

myrmecium.full: myrmēcĭum (myrmēcĭon), ii, n., = μυρμήκιον. A kind of wart, Cels. 5, 20, 14.— A kind of spider, Plin. 29, 4, 27, § 87.

myrmidone.full: Myrmĭdŏnē, ēs, f., = Μυρμιδόνη, one of the fifty daughters of Danaüs, who killed her husband Mineus, Hyg. Fab. 170.
myrmidone.short: Myrmĭdŏnē, ēs, f., = Μυρμιδόνη, one of the fifty daughters of Danaüs, who killed her husband Mineus, Hyg.

myrmidones.full: Myrmĭdŏnes, um, m., = Μυρμιδόνες, the Myrmidons, a people of Phthiotis (Thessaly), about Phthia and Larissa Cremaste, under the sway of Achilles, Enn. ap. Non. 472, 27 (Trag. v. 222 Vahl.); Verg. A. 2, 7; Ov. M. 7, 654.—In sing. also as fem.: cruentae Vulnere Myrmidonis, Stat. Th. 5, 223.
myrmidones.short: Myrmĭdŏnes, um, m., = Μυρμιδόνες, the Myrmidons, a people of Phthiotis (Thessaly), about Phthia and Larissa Cremaste, under the sway of Achilles, Enn.

myrobalanum.full: mўrŏbălănum, i, n., = μυροβάλανον, the fruit of a palm-tree from which a balsam was made, the behen-nut; also, the balsam itself, Plin. 12, 21, 46, § 100; 12, 22, 47, § 103; Mart. 4, 57 in lemm.
myrobalanum.short: mўrŏbălănum, i, n., = μυροβάλανον, the fruit of a palm-tree from which a balsam was made, the behen-nut;

myron1.full: Myron or Myro, ōnis (Gr. gen. -ōnŏs, Mart. 4, 39, 2, etc.), m., a celebrated sculptor of Eleutheræ in Attica, who flourished about 430 B. C., Cic. Brut. 18, 70; id. de Or. 3, 7, 26; Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 60, § 135; Ov. P. 4, 1, 34; Plin. 34, 8, 19, § 57; Juv. 8, 102.

myron2.full: mўron or mўrum, i, n., = μύρον, an ointment, unguent, pure Latin, unguentum (eccl. Lat.): myro ungere caput, Hier. praef. in Libr. Reg. fin.
myron2.short: mўron or mўrum, i, n., = μύρον, an ointment, unguent, pure Latin, unguentum (eccl.

myropola.full: mўrŏ-pōla, ae, m., = μυροπώλης, a dealer in ointments, essences, balsams, etc., a perfumer (ante-class.), Naev. ap. Fulg. 565, 17; Plaut. Cas. 2, 3, 10; id. Trin. 2, 4, 7.
myropola.short: mўrŏ-pōla, ae, m., = μυροπώλης, a dealer in ointments, essences, balsams, etc., a perfumer (ante-class.), Naev.

myropolium.full: mўrŏ-pōlĭum, ii, n., = μυροπώλιον, a shop where ointments, balsams, essences, etc., were sold, a perfumer's shop (Plautin.), Plaut. Ep. 2, 2, 15; id. Am. 4, 1, 3.
myropolium.short: mўrŏ-pōlĭum, ii, n., = μυροπώλιον, a shop where ointments, balsams, essences, etc., were sold, a perfumer's shop (Plautin.), Plaut.

myrothecium.full: mўrŏthēcĭum, ii, n., = μυροθήκιον, an ointment-box, Cic. Att. 2, 1, 1.
myrothecium.short: mўrŏthēcĭum, ii, n., = μυροθήκιον, an ointment-box, Cic.

myrrha.full: myrrha, v. 1. murra.† † myrrha-, etc., v. murra-, etc.

myrrhis2.full: myrrhis, ĭdis, f., = myrtis, q. v., Plin. 26, 11, 68, § 108 al.

myrrhites.full: myrrhītes, ae, m., = μυρρίτης, a precious stone of the color of myrrh, Plin. 37, 10, 63, § 174.
myrrhites.short: myrrhītes, ae, m., = μυρρίτης, a precious stone of the color of myrrh, Plin.

myrrhiza.full: myrrhiza, ae, acc. an, f., = 2. murra, Plin. 24, 16, 97, § 154 (al. myriza).

myrsilus.full: Myrsīlus, i, m., = Μυρσῖλος. A king of Lydia, also called Candaules, Plin. 35, 8, 34, § 55.— A historian from Lesbos, Plin. 3, 7, 13, § 85; 4, 2, 22, § 65.—Also called Myrtilus, Arn. 1, 3.

myrsineum.full: myrsinĕum, i, n., a plant, also called foeniculum silvestre, Plin. 20, 23, 96, § 255.
myrsineum.short: myrsinĕum, i, n., a plant, also called foeniculum silvestre, Plin.

myrsinites.full: myrsīnītes, ae, m. A precious stone that smells like myrrh, Plin. 37, 10, 63, § 174.— A false reading for myrtites, Plin. 26, 8, 40, § 66.

myrta.full: myrta and murta, ae, f., v. myrtus.
myrta.short: myrta and murta, ae, f., v.

myrtaceus.full: myrtācĕus, a, um, adj. myrtus, of myrtle, myrtle- (post-Aug.): folium, Cels. 7, 17.

myrtale.full: Myrtălē, ēs, f., a freed-woman, a friend of Horace, Hor. C. 1, 33, 14.
myrtale.short: Myrtălē, ēs, f., a freed-woman, a friend of Horace, Hor.

myrtatus.full: myrtātus or murtātus, a, um, adj. myrtus, seasoned with myrtle or myrtleberries.—Subst.: murtātum, i, n. (sc. farcimen), a kind of pudding: murtatum a murtā, quod ea large fartum, Varr. L. L. 5, § 110 Müll.— A kind of seasoning: form myrtatum, Plin. 15, 29, 35, § 118.
myrtatus.short: myrtātus or murtātus, a, um, adj.

myrteolus.full: myrtĕŏlus (murtĕŏlus, myr-tĭŏlus), a, um, adj. dim. [myrteus], of the color of myrtle-blossoms: myrteolo modo crine viret (al. murceolo, al. murciolo), Col. poët. 10, 237.

myrtetum.full: myrtētum (murtētum), i, n. (collat. form, myrtēta, ae, f., Plaut. Fragm. ap. Prisc. p. 625 P.) [myrtus], a place full of myrtles, a myrtle-grove: quasi pineis murteta item ego vos virgis circumvinciam, Plaut. Rud. 3, 4, 27: collis vestitus oleastro ac murtetis, Sall. J. 48, 3: litora myrtetis laetissima, Verg. G. 2, 112.—In the neighborhood of Baiae there was such a myrtle-grove, where a warm, sudorific vapor rose from the earth, Cels. 2, 17; cf. id. 3, 21; Hor. Ep. 1, 15, 5.

myrteus.full: myrtĕus (murtĕus), a, um, adj. id., of or belonging to myrtles, myrtle-. Lit.: myrtea silva, Verg. A. 6, 443: corona, Val. Max. 3, 6, 5; cf.: myrtea corona (Papirius) usus est, quod Sardos in campis Myrteis superāsset, Paul. ex Fest. p. 144 Müll.: oleum, Plin. 23, 4, 45, § 88.—Also, absol.: myr-tĕum, i, n., myrtle-oil, Cels. 2, 33: vinum, Plin. 26, 11, 74, § 121.— Transf. Furnished or adorned with myrtle: coma, Tib. 3, 4, 28.— Myrtle-colored, chestnutbrown: gausapila, Petr. 21.— Olea murtea, a k

myrtidanum.full: myrtĭdănum, i, n. (sc. vinum) [id.], a wine made of wild myrtle-berries, myrtlewine, Plin. 14, 16, 19, § 104.

myrtilus.full: Myrtĭlus, i, m. A son of Mercury, slain by Pelops, Cic. N. D. 3, 38, 90; Sen. Thyest. 140; Claud. Laud. Ser. 168; cf. Hyg. Fab. 84; 224.— A Roman surname: L. Minucius Myrtilus, Liv. 38, 42.— A historian, v. Myrsilus.

myrtinus.full: myrtĭnus (murtĭnus), a, um, adj., = μύρτινος, of or belonging to myrtles, myrtle- (post-class. for myrteus): oleum, App. Herb. 121.
myrtinus.short: myrtĭnus (murtĭnus), a, um, adj., = μύρτινος, of or belonging to myrtles, myrtle- (post-class.

myrtis.full: myrtis, ĭdis, f., = μυρτίς, a kind of geranium, Plin. 26, 11, 68, § 108.
myrtis.short: myrtis, ĭdis, f., = μυρτίς, a kind of geranium, Plin.

myrtites.full: myrtītes, ae, m., = μυρτίτης οἶνος. Myrtle-wine: vinum myrtiten sic facito, Col. 12, 38: vinum myrtiten sic facies, Pall. 2, 18.— A species of the plant tithymalus, Plin. 26, 8, 40, § 66.

myrtopetalon.full: myrtŏ-pĕtălon, i, n., = μύρτοσ-πέταλον, myrtle-leaf, a plant, also called polygonon, Plin. 27, 12, 91, § 113.
myrtopetalon.short: myrtŏ-pĕtălon, i, n., = μύρτοσ-πέταλον, myrtle-leaf, a plant, also called polygonon, Plin.

myrtous.full: Myrtōus, a, um, adj., = Μυρτῶος, Myrtoan: Myrtoum mare, the Myrtoan Sea, a part of the Ægean Sea, between Crete, the Peloponnesus, and Eubœa, which derives its name from the island of Myrtos, Plin. 4, 11, 18, § 51; Hor. C. 1, 1, 14: so, pelagus, Mel. 2, 3, 3; 2, 7, 10: aqua, Ov. Ib. 372.
myrtous.short: Myrtōus, a, um, adj., = Μυρτῶος, Myrtoan: Myrtoum mare, the Myrtoan Sea, a part of the Ægean Sea, between Crete, the Peloponnesus, and Eubœa, which derives its name from the island of Myrtos, Plin.

myrtum.full: myrtum (murtum), i, n., = μύρτον, the fruit of the myrtle, a myrtle-berry: cruenta myrta, Verg. G. 1, 306; cf. Plin. 15, 29, 35, § 118.
myrtum.short: myrtum (murtum), i, n., = μύρτον, the fruit of the myrtle, a myrtle-berry: cruenta myrta, Verg.

myrtuosus.full: myrtŭōsus, a, um, adj., a false read. for montuosus, Plin. 12, 13, 28, § 48.
myrtuosus.short: myrtŭōsus, a, um, adj., a false read.

myrtus.full: myrtus (murtus), i and ūs, f., = μύρτος, a myrtle, myrtle-tree, Plin. 15, 29, 37, § 122: viridi caput impedire myrto, Hor. C. 1, 4, 9.—Poet., for a spear of myrtle-wood: et pastoralem praefixā cuspide myrtum, Verg. A. 7, 817.—Nom. plur. myrtūs, Verg. G. 2, 64.—As masc., Cato, R. R. 8.—Anteclass. also, myrta or murta, ae, f.: murta nigra, Cato, R. R. 125.—Murtus for myrtus: murti nigrae baccae, Scrib. Comp. 109.
myrtus.short: myrtus (murtus), i and ūs, f., = μύρτος, a myrtle, myrtle-tree, Plin.

myrus.full: mȳrus, i, m., = μύρρα: unxit se myro optimo, Vulg. Jud. 10, 3.—(But a false read. for zmyrus, Plin. 9, 23, 39, § 76; 32, 11, 53, § 151.)
myrus.short: mȳrus, i, m., = μύρρα: unxit se myro optimo, Vulg.

mys1.full: mys, mўos, m., = μῦς, a sea-mussel, Plin. 32, 11, 53, § 149; 9, 35, 56, § 115.
mys1.short: mys, mўos, m., = μῦς, a sea-mussel, Plin.

mys2.full: Mȳs, Mўos, m., = Μῦς, a famous artist in embossed work, Mart. 8, 51, 1; 8, 34, 1; Plin. 33, 12, 55, § 155; Prop. 3, 9, 14.
mys2.short: Mȳs, Mўos, m., = Μῦς, a famous artist in embossed work, Mart.

myscelos.full: Myscĕlŏs or -us, i, m., the founder of the city of Croton, in Italy, Ov. M. 15, 20.
myscelos.short: Myscĕlŏs or -us, i, m., the founder of the city of Croton, in Italy, Ov.

mysia.full: Mȳsĭa, ae, f., = Μυσία, a country of Asia Minor, divided into Lesser Mysia, on the Hellespont, and Greater Mysia, on the Ægean Sea, Mel. 1, 18, 1; Plin. 5, 32, 40, § 143; Cic. Or. 8, 25; Luc. 3, 203; Inscr. Orell. 2274; 3664.— Derivv. Mȳ-sĭcus, a, um, adj., for Mysius, Mysian (post-Aug.): scammonium, Plin. 26, 8, 38, § 60.— Mȳsĭus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Mysia, Mysian (class.): homo, Cic. Q. Fr. 1, 1, 6.— Mȳsus, a, um, adj., = Μυσός, of or belonging to Mysia, Mysian: Mysus juvenis, i. e
mysia.short: Mȳsĭa, ae, f., = Μυσία, a country of Asia Minor, divided into Lesser Mysia, on the Hellespont, and Greater Mysia, on the Ægean Sea, Mel.

mysta.full: mysta or mystes, ae, m., = μύστης, a priest of the secret rites of divine worship, a priest of the mysteries, Ov. F. 4, 536; Aus. Idyll. 1, 2; Inscr. Orell. 2362.
mysta.short: mysta or mystes, ae, m., = μύστης, a priest of the secret rites of divine worship, a priest of the mysteries, Ov.

mystagogica.full: mystăgōgĭca, ōn, n., = μυσταγωγικά, a treatise on initiation into the mysteries, Paul. ex Fest. p. 363, 30 Müll.
mystagogica.short: mystăgōgĭca, ōn, n., = μυσταγωγικά, a treatise on initiation into the mysteries, Paul.

mystagogus.full: mўstăgōgus, i, m., = μυσταγωγός, one who conducts a person through secret and sacred places as a guide, an initiator, a mystagogue, Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 59, § 132.— Trop.: amicitiae meae, te mystagogo usus, accessit, the founder, Symm. Ep. 5, 64.
mystagogus.short: mўstăgōgus, i, m., = μυσταγωγός, one who conducts a person through secret and sacred places as a guide, an initiator, a mystagogue, Cic.

mysterialiter.full: mystērĭālĭter, adv. mysterium, mysteriously, Vulg. Interpr. Iren. 1, 1.

mysteriarches.full: mystērĭarches, ae, m., = μυστηριάρχης, the presider over secret sacred rites (eccl. Lat.), Prud. στεφ. 2, 349.
mysteriarches.short: mystērĭarches, ae, m., = μυστηριάρχης, the presider over secret sacred rites (eccl.

mysterium.full: mystērĭum, ii, n., = μυστήριον, a secret service, secret rites, secret worship of a deity, divine mystery (class.; cf. arcanum). Lit., of the mysteries of Ceres, otherwise called sacra Eleusinia, Cic. N. D. 2, 24, 62; id. Leg. 2, 14, 35: mysteria Attica, Tert. Apol. 39: mysteria Cereris initiorum enuntiare, Just. 5, 1, 1: mysteria facere, to celebrate the sacred mysteries, Nep. Alcib. 3, 6.—Also, the festival on which these mysteries were celebrated: in quem diem Romana incidant mysteria, the fe
mysterium.short: mystērĭum, ii, n., = μυστήριον, a secret service, secret rites, secret worship of a deity, divine mystery (class.;

mysticus.full: mystĭcus, a, um, adj., = μυστικός, of or belonging to secret rites or mysteries, mystic, mystical (poet.): mystica sacra Dindymenes, Mart. 8, 81, 1: vannus Iacchi, Verg. G. 1, 166: vitis, Tib. 3, 6, 1: lampas, Stat. Th. 8, 765.—In plur. subst.: mystĭ-ca, ōrum, n., things pertaining to secret rites, Lampr. Alex. Sev. 26; Inscr. Orell. 2353.—Hence, adv.: mystĭcē, mystically (post-class.), Sol. 32; Ambros. in Luc. 7, § 9.
mysticus.short: mystĭcus, a, um, adj., = μυστικός, of or belonging to secret rites or mysteries, mystic, mystical (poet.): mystica sacra Dindymenes, Mart.

mystrum.full: mystrum, i, n., = μύστρον, the fourth part of a cyathus, Rhem. Fan. de Pond. et Mens. 77.
mystrum.short: mystrum, i, n., = μύστρον, the fourth part of a cyathus, Rhem.

mystus.full: mystus, a false read. for Nystrus, Plin. 4, 12, 19, § 53.

mysus.full: Mȳsus, a, um, adj., v. Mysia, II. C.

mytacismus.full: mўtăcismus, i. q. metacismus, q. v.

mythicus.full: mȳthĭcus, a, um, adj., = μυθικός, of or belonging to fables or myths, fabulous, mythic, mythical (post-Aug.). Adj., a false reading for mysticus, Plin. 7, 53, 54, § 184.— Subst.: mȳthĭcus, i, m., a writer of fables or myths, a mythographer, Macr. S. 1, 8.
mythicus.short: mȳthĭcus, a, um, adj., = μυθικός, of or belonging to fables or myths, fabulous, mythic, mythical (post-Aug.).

mythistoria.full: mȳthistŏrĭa, ae, f., = μυθιστορία, a fabulous narrative (post-class.), Capitol. Macr. 1.
mythistoria.short: mȳthistŏrĭa, ae, f., = μυθιστορία, a fabulous narrative (post-class.), Capitol.

mythistoricus.full: mȳthistŏrĭcus, a, um, adj., = μυθιστορικός, fabulous, mixed with fable (postclass.): volumina, Vop. Firm. 1.
mythistoricus.short: mȳthistŏrĭcus, a, um, adj., = μυθιστορικός, fabulous, mixed with fable (postclass.): volumina, Vop.

mythologia.full: mȳthŏlŏgĭa, ae, f., = μυθολογία, mythology (late Lat.): Mythologiarum liber, a work of Fulgentius, in which the origin of the myths is indicated.
mythologia.short: mȳthŏlŏgĭa, ae, f., = μυθολογία, mythology (late Lat.): Mythologiarum liber, a work of Fulgentius, in which the origin of the myths is indicated.

mythologicus.full: mȳthŏlŏgĭcus, a, um, adj., = μυθολογικός, of or belonging to mythology, mythological (late Lat.).—In plur. subst.: mȳ-thŏlŏgĭca, ōrum, n., mythological matters: Mythologicōn liber, the title of a work of Fulgentius, also called Mythologiarum liber, v. mythologia.
mythologicus.short: mȳthŏlŏgĭcus, a, um, adj., = μυθολογικός, of or belonging to mythology, mythological (late Lat.).—In plur.

mythos.full: mȳthŏs, i, m., = μῦθος, a fable, myth (late Lat. for fabula): callentes mython (gen. plur. Gr. μύθων), plasmata, Aus. ap. Prof. Carm. 21, v. 26.
mythos.short: mȳthŏs, i, m., = μῦθος, a fable, myth (late Lat.

mytilene.full: Mўtĭlēnē (in later times Mĭtўlēnē), ēs, f., and Mўtĭlēnae, ārum, f., = Μυτιλήνη, the capital of Lesbos, the birthplace of Sappho, Pittacus, Alcæus, and Diophanes, the orator, now Mytilini or Castro.— Mytilene: laudabunt alii claram Rhodon, aut Mytilenen, Hor. C. 1, 7, 1; id. Ep. 1, 11, 17 al.—In plur. form, Mytilenae: Mytilenis an Rhodi malles vivere, Cic. Agr. 2, 16, 40; id. Fam. 4, 7, 4; Suet. Caes. 2; id. Aug. 66; id. Tib. 10; Caes. B. C. 3, 102, 5.— Hence, Mўtĭlēnaeus (Mĭtў-), a, um, adj., =
mytilene.short: Mўtĭlēnē (in later times Mĭtўlēnē), ēs, f., and Mўtĭlēnae, ārum, f., = Μυτιλήνη, the capital of Lesbos, the birthplace of Sappho, Pittacus, Alcæus, and Diophanes, the orator, now Mytilini or Castro.— Mytilene: laudabunt alii claram Rhodon, aut Mytile

myus.full: Myūs, untis, f., = Μυοῦς, a city in Caria, on the southern shore of the Meander, the smallest of the cities of the Ionian League, now the ruins of Palatsha, Nep. Them. 10, 3; Vitr. 4, 1, 4; Plin. 5, 29, 31, § 113.
myus.short: Myūs, untis, f., = Μυοῦς, a city in Caria, on the southern shore of the Meander, the smallest of the cities of the Ionian League, now the ruins of Palatsha, Nep.

myxa.full: myxa, ae, f., = μύξα. A kind of plum-tree, Plin. 13, 5, 10, § 51.— = rostrum, the curved part of a lamp, nozzle, Mart. 14, 41, 2.

myxo.full: myxo or myxon, ōnis, m., = μύξων, a fish, also called bacchus, Plin. 32, 7, 25, § 77.
myxo.short: myxo or myxon, ōnis, m., = μύξων, a fish, also called bacchus, Plin.

myxos.full: myxos or myxus, a false read. for myxa, Mart. 14, 41, 2.
myxos.short: myxos or myxus, a false read.

myxum.full: myxum, i, n. myxa, the fruit of the myxa, Pall. 3, 25 fin.; Gargil. Mart. Medic. ex Rom. § 15.

n.full: N, n, had its full, pure sound only when it began a syllable; in the middle or at the end of a word it was weakened. Hence the remark of Priscian (p. 556 P.): n quoque plenior in primis sonat, et in ultimis partibus syllabarum, ut nomen, stamen; exilior in mediis, ut amnis, damnum, is not accurate, v. Corss. Ausspr. 1, p. 248 sq. Between two vowels, the single n frequently takes the place, in MSS. and inscriptions, of double n; thus: Pescenius, Porsena, conubium, conecto, conitor, coniveo. The n
n.short: N, n, had its full, pure sound only when it began a syllable;

nabataea.full: Năbătaea (Năbăthaea), ae, f., = Ναβαταια, a country in Arabia Petræa, Plin. 21, 18, 72, § 120.—Hence, Năbă-thaeus (scanned Năbătaeus, Năbāthaeus, Sid. Carm. 5, 284), a, um, adj., = Ναβαθαῖος, of or belonging to Nabathæa, Nabathœan: saltus, Juv. 11, 126.—Plur.: Năbătaei or Năbăthaei, ōrum, m., = Ναβαταῖοι or Ναβαθαῖοι, the Nabathæans, Plin. 6, 28, 32, § 144; 12, 20, 44, § 98; Auct. B. Alex. 1, 1; Tac. A. 2, 57; Amm. 14, 8, 12.— Poet., transf., for Arabian, Eastern, Oriental: Eurus ad Auroram Naba
nabataea.short: Năbătaea (Năbăthaea), ae, f., = Ναβαταια, a country in Arabia Petræa, Plin.

nabdalsa.full: Nabdalsa, ae, m., a distinguished Numidian, a general of Jugurtha, Sall. J. 70, 2.
nabdalsa.short: Nabdalsa, ae, m., a distinguished Numidian, a general of Jugurtha, Sall.

nabis.full: Nabis, idis, m., = Νάβις, a king of Sparta, about 200 B. C., Liv. 29, 12, 14; 31, 25, 3; 34, 24, 6.
nabis.short: Nabis, idis, m., = Νάβις, a king of Sparta, about 200 B.

nablio.full: nablĭo, ōnis, m., one who plays the nablium (naulium): nablio, ψάλτης, Gloss. Philox.
nablio.short: nablĭo, ōnis, m., one who plays the nablium (naulium): nablio, ψάλτης, Gloss.

nablium.full: nablĭum or nablum, i, n., a musical instrument of ten or twelve strings, played with both hands; a kind of harp, of Phœnician origin, i. q. naulium.—Form nablium, Ov. A. A. 3, 327.—Form nablum, Vulg. 1 Chron. 15, 16 sqq.; id. 1 Macc. 13, 51.
nablium.short: nablĭum or nablum, i, n., a musical instrument of ten or twelve strings, played with both hands;

nablizo.full: nablizo, 1, v. a., to play the nablium (naulium): nablizo, ψάλλω, Gloss. Philox.

nacca.full: nacca (nacta, natta), ae, m., = νάκτης (pure Lat. fullo), a fuller: naccae appellantur vulgo fullones, ut ait Curiatius, quod nauci non sint, i. e. nullius pretii. Idem sentit et Cincius. Quidam aiunt, quod omnia fere opera ex lanā nacae dicantur a Graecis, Paul. ex Fest. p. 166 Müll.; App. M. 9, p. 227, 22.
nacca.short: nacca (nacta, natta), ae, m., = νάκτης (pure Lat.

naccinus.full: naccīnus (nactīnus), a, um, adj. nacca, of or belonging to a fuller: naccina truculentia, i. e. fullonis, App. M. 9, p. 229, 36.

nacolea.full: Nacŏlēa (Nacŏlīa, Nacolĭa), ae, f., = Νακόλεια, Νακολια, a city in Great Phrygia, Amm. 26, 9, 7.
nacolea.short: Nacŏlēa (Nacŏlīa, Nacolĭa), ae, f., = Νακόλεια, Νακολια, a city in Great Phrygia, Amm.

nactus.full: nactus, a, um, Part., from nanciscor.
nactus.short: nactus, a, um, Part., from nanciscor.

nae.full: nae, vulgar form for nē (v. 3. ne), particle of assurance, verily, truly.

naevius1.full: naevĭus, a, um, adj. naevus, that has a mole on his body, Arn. 3, 108 dub. (al. naevinos).

naevius2.full: Naevĭus, a naevus; hence, prop., one born with a mole or birth-mark, name of a Roman gens. The most celebrated member of it is Cn. Naevius, a Roman epic and dramatic poet, born A. U. C. 480. He made the first Punic war, in which he had served, the subject of a poem, in which he so boldly satirized the nobility, especially the Metelli, that he was forced into exile at Utica, where he died, A. U. C. 550, Cic. Brut. 15, 60; id. Tusc. 1, 1, 3; Gell. 1, 24, 2; 17, 21, 45.—Hence, Naevĭus, a, um, adj.,

naevulus.full: naevŭlus, i, m. dim. naevus, a little mole on the body, a wart (post-Aug.), Gell. 12, 1, 7: minores aliae insulae, ut naevuli quidam, per apertas Ponti sunt sparsae regiones, App. de Mundo, p. 59, 27; cf. Fronto Ep. 1, 2 med. Mai.

naevus.full: naevus, i, m. for gnaevus, root gna-, gen-, of genus, gnatus, a mark born with one; cf.: natus, natura, etc., a mole or wart on the body. Lit.: naevus in articulo pueri... est corporis macula naevus, Cic. N. D. 1, 28, 79: egregio inspersos reprehendas corpore naevos, Hor. S. 1, 6, 67: nullus in egregio corpore naevus erit, Ov. Tr. 5, 13, 14; Plin. 22, 25, 67, § 137; 28, 4, 6, § 34.— Trop., a spot, blemish, fault (late Lat.): naevi instar est, ut frater meus, etc., Symm. 3, 34 dub.

nahanarvali.full: Nahanarvāli, ōrum, m., a Germanic people, belonging to the race of the Lygians, Tac. G. 43 (this the better read., v. Orell. ad h. l.; al. Naharvali).
nahanarvali.short: Nahanarvāli, ōrum, m., a Germanic people, belonging to the race of the Lygians, Tac.

naias.full: Nāĭăs, ădis, and more freq. Nāĭs, ĭdis and ĭdos (plur. ĭdas), f., = Ναϊάς and Ναἱς (floating, swimming, that is in the water), a water-nymph, Naiad: illum fontana petebant Numina, Naïades, Ov. M. 14, 328: Aegle Naïadum pulcherrima, Verg. E. 6, 21: Naïs Amalthēa, Ov. F. 5, 115.—Poet. of mixing wine with water: Naïda Bacchus amat, Tib. 3, 6, 57.—Adj.: puellae Naïdes, Verg. E. 10, 10.— Transf., in gen., a nymph (Hamadryad, Nereid): Naïda vulneribus succidit in arbore factis, Ov. F. 4, 231: inter Ha

nais.full: Nāĭs, idis and ĭdos, v. Naias.

nam.full: nam, conj. [acc. sing. fem. of pronom. stem na-; cf.: ἐγώ-νη, τύ-νη; Lat. ne, nae; masc. num; cf.: tum, tam; quom, quam]. To introduce a confirmation or explanation, for (always in prose beginning the sentence; cf.: enim, etenim, and v. infra C.). Introducing an explanation or fuller statement of something already said. In gen.: is pagus appellabatur Tigurinus. Nam omnis civitas Helvetia in quattuor pagos divisa est, Caes. B. G. 1, 12, 4: quibus rebus auditis ... suas quoque copias in tres parte

nama.full: nāma, ătis, n., = νᾶμα, a fluid, liquid: DEDICAVIT NAMA CVNCTIS, Inscr. Orell. 1914: NAMA SEBESIO, ib. 1915.
nama.short: nāma, ătis, n., = νᾶμα, a fluid, liquid: DEDICAVIT NAMA CVNCTIS, Inscr.

namnetes.full: Namnētes, um, m., a people in Celtic Gaul, near the site of Nantes, Caes. B. G. 3, 9, 10; Plin. 4, 18, 32, § 107.—In sing.: Namnis, Inscr. Orell. 188.— Transf., the capital of the Namnetes, the modern Nantes, Ven. Ep. 3.
namnetes.short: Namnētes, um, m., a people in Celtic Gaul, near the site of Nantes, Caes.

namque.full: nam-que (also written nanque), cong., an emphatic confirmative particle, a strengthened nam, closely resembling that particle in its uses, but introducing the reason or explanation with more assurance; Gr. και γάρ, for indeed, for truly, for (class. and freq., only before a vowel, and in Cicero and Cæsar always, like nam, beginning the proposition; rarely before a consonant, and not in Cæs., Cic. Div. 1, 30, 62; id. de Or. 3, 2, 6; id. Tusc. 3, 20, 65; Nep. Them. 6, 2; id. Ages. 2, 1; Sall. J. 4
namque.short: nam-que (also written nanque), cong., an emphatic confirmative particle, a strengthened nam, closely resembling that particle in its uses, but introducing the reason or explanation with more assurance;

nana1.full: nāna, ae, v. nanus, I. B.

nana2.full: Nana, ae, f., a nymph, daughter of Sangarius and mother of Atys, Arn. 5, p. 158.
nana2.short: Nana, ae, f., a nymph, daughter of Sangarius and mother of Atys, Arn.

nancio.full: nancĭo, īre, v. a., and nancĭor, īri, v. dep. a. [root nac-, v. nanciscor], to get, gain, obtain (post-class.): si nanciam populi desiderium, Gracch. ap. Prisc. p. 888 P.: in foedere Latino: PECVNIAM QVIS NANCITOR (i. e. nancitur) HABETO, Paul. ex Fest. p. 166 Müll.

nanciscor.full: nanciscor, nactus and nanctus (cf. Mai. ad Cic. Rep. 1, 10, 16; Drak. ad Liv. 24, 31; 25, 30; inf. nanciscier, Plaut. As. 2, 2, 59), 3, v. dep. a. [Sanscr. naç, obtain; Gr. ἐνεκ- in ἤνεγκα, etc.; cf.: ἀνάγκη, necesse] (in pass. signif, nactus, v. infra fin.), to get, obtain, receive a thing (esp. by accident or without one's co-operation), to meet with, stumble on, light on, find a thing (syn.: offendo, reperio, deprehendo): unde anulum istum nactus? Ter. Hec. 5, 3, 27: quoniam nacti te, inquit,

nanis.full: Nanis, ĭdis, f. nana, a Roman surname, Inscr. Fabr. p. 48, n. 269.

nans.full: nans, nantis, Part. and P. a., v. 1. no.

nantuates.full: Nantŭātes, um, m., a people in Gallia Narbonensis, at the foot of the Alps, Caes. B. G. 3, 1; 4, 10; Plin. 3, 20, 24, § 137.
nantuates.short: Nantŭātes, um, m., a people in Gallia Narbonensis, at the foot of the Alps, Caes.

nanus.full: nānus, i, m., = νάννος and νᾶνος (cf. Gell. 19, 13, 2 sq.); in vulg. lang., a dwarf (pure Lat. pumilio): interrogatum a quodam nano, Suet. Tib. 61; Prop. 4 (5), 8, 41; Juv. 8, 32.— In fem.: nāna, ae, a female dwarf: nanos et nanas et moriones populo donavit, Lampr. Alex. Sev. 34.— Transf. A small horse, Helv. Cinn. ap. Gell. 19, 13, 5; cf. id. ib. § 4.— A low, shallow water-vessel: vas aquarium vocant futim ... quo postea accessit nanus cum Graeco nomine, et cum Latino nomine, Graecā figurā barb
nanus.short: nānus, i, m., = νάννος and νᾶνος (cf.

napaeus.full: năpaeus, a, um, adj., = ναπαῖος, of or belonging to a wooded vale or dell: nymphae napaeae, dell-nymphs, Col. poët. 10, 264. —Hence, Subst.: Năpaeae, ārum, f., the dell-nymphs: faciles venerare Napaeas, Verg. G. 4, 535; Stat. Th. 4, 255; Nemes. Ecl. 2, 20.
napaeus.short: năpaeus, a, um, adj., = ναπαῖος, of or belonging to a wooded vale or dell: nymphae napaeae, dell-nymphs, Col.

nape.full: Năpē, ēs, f., the name of a dog, Ov. M. 3, 214.— The name of a woman, Ov. Am. 1, 12, 4.
nape.short: Năpē, ēs, f., the name of a dog, Ov.

naphtha.full: naphtha (napthas, Sall. ap. Prob. Cathol. 1465 P.), ae, f., = ἡ νάφθα (collat. form of ὁ νάφθας), naphtha: similis (maithae) est natura naphthae: ita appellatur circa Babyloniam et in Astacenis Parthiae profluens bituminis liquidi modo, Plin. 2, 105, 109, § 235; id. 24, 17, 101, § 158; 35, 15, 51, § 179; Amm. 23, 6, 38 (called oleum incendiarium, Veg. Mil. 4, 8 and 18; and: oleum vivum, Grat. Cyn. 434).

napina.full: nāpīna, ae, f. napus, a turnip-field, Col. 11, 2, 71.

napurae.full: napurae, ārum, f., straw ropes: nectere ligare significat ... pontifex minor ex stramentis napuras nectito, id est funiculos facito, quibus sues annectantur, Paul. ex Fest. s. v. nectere, p. 165 Müll.; cf. id. ib. p. 169.
napurae.short: napurae, ārum, f., straw ropes: nectere ligare significat ...

napus.full: nāpus, i, m., a kind of turnip, a navew, Col. 2, 10, 23; 12, 56, 1; Plin. 18, 13, 35, § 131; 19, 5, 25, § 75; Mart. 13, 20 in lemm.
napus.short: nāpus, i, m., a kind of turnip, a navew, Col.

napy.full: nāpy, ўŏs, n., = νᾶπυ (an old form for σίναπι), mustard: sinapi Athenienses napy appellaverunt, Plin. 19, 8, 54, § 171: alterum thlaspi aliqui Persicum napy appellaverunt, id. 27, 13, 113, § 140.
napy.short: nāpy, ўŏs, n., = νᾶπυ (an old form for σίναπι), mustard: sinapi Athenienses napy appellaverunt, Plin.

nar1.full: Nār, Nāris, m., = Νάρ, a river of Italy, which rises in the Apennines, flows through a part of the Sabine territory and Umbria, and joins the Tiber, now Nera: Nar amnis exhaurit illos (Velinos lacus) sulphureis aquis, Plin. 3, 12, 17, § 109; cf.: Solporeas posuit spiramina Naris ad undas, Enn. ap. Prisc. p. 691 P. (Ann. v. 265 Vahl.); and: audiit amnis Sulfureā Nar albus aquā fontesque Velini, Verg. A. 7, 517; cf. Aus. Idyll. 12 de deis; Ov. M. 14, 330: quod Lacus Velinus in Narem defluit, Cic.
nar1.short: Nār, Nāris, m., = Νάρ, a river of Italy, which rises in the Apennines, flows through a part of the Sabine territory and Umbria, and joins the Tiber, now Nera: Nar amnis exhaurit illos (Velinos lacus) sulphureis aquis, Plin.

nar2.full: Nar, Nartis; only plur., Nartes, ium, m., dwellers on the banks of the Nar: Interamnates, cognomine Nartes, Plin. 3, 14, 19, § 113; gen.: Interamnatium Nartium, Inscr. Grut. 407, 1.

nar3.full: Nar, Nartis, m., a river of Illyria, Mela, 2, 3, 13.
nar3.short: Nar, Nartis, m., a river of Illyria, Mela, 2, 3, 13.

narbo.full: Narbo, ōnis, m., and (late Lat.) Nar-bōna, ae, f., also with the appellation Marcius (after the consul Q. Marcius Rex, who led a colony thither A. U. C. 636), a city in Gaul, from which Gallia Narbonensis takes its name, the mod. Narbonne.—Form Narbo, Mela, 2, 5, 2; 6; Plin. 3, 4, 5, § 32; Cic. Font. 1, 3; 16, 36; Vell. 1, 15, 5; 2, 8, 1.— Form Narbona, Capitol. Max. et Balb. 5, 8; Eutr. 4, 23; Inscr. Orell. 218.—Hence, Narbōnensis, e, adj., of or belonging to Narbo, Narbonian: colonia, Cic. Bru
narbo.short: Narbo, ōnis, m., and (late Lat.) Nar-bōna, ae, f., also with the appellation Marcius (after the consul Q.

narce.full: narcē, ēs, f., = νάρκη, a numbness, torpor: a narce narcissus dictus, non a fabuloso puero, Plin. 21, 19, 75, § 128.
narce.short: narcē, ēs, f., = νάρκη, a numbness, torpor: a narce narcissus dictus, non a fabuloso puero, Plin.

narcissinus.full: narcissĭnus, a, um, adj., = ναρκίσσινος, of or from the narcissus, narcissus-: oleum, Plin. 21, 19, 75, § 129: unguentum, id. 13, 1, 2, § 6.
narcissinus.short: narcissĭnus, a, um, adj., = ναρκίσσινος, of or from the narcissus, narcissus-: oleum, Plin.

narcissitis.full: narcissītis, ĭdis, f., = ναρκισσῖτις, a precious stone, otherwise unknown, Plin. 37, 11, 73, § 188.
narcissitis.short: narcissītis, ĭdis, f., = ναρκισσῖτις, a precious stone, otherwise unknown, Plin.

narcissus1.full: narcissus, i, m., = νάρκισσος, the narcissus, Plin. 21, 5, 12, § 25; 21, 19, 75, § 128; Verg. E. 5, 38; id. G. 4, 123; 160.
narcissus1.short: narcissus, i, m., = νάρκισσος, the narcissus, Plin.

narcissus2.full: Narcissus, i, m., Narcissus, the son of Cephisus and the nymph Liriope. He was exceedingly beautiful, and fell so violently in love with himself on beholding his image in a fountain, that he wasted away with desire, until he was changed into the flower of the same name, Ov. M. 3, 407 sq. — Narcissus, a freedman of Claudius, by whose orders Messalina was put to death, Tac. A. 11, 29 sqq.; Juv. 14, 329.
narcissus2.short: Narcissus, i, m., Narcissus, the son of Cephisus and the nymph Liriope.

nardifer.full: nardĭfer, ĕra, ĕrum, adj. nardus-fero, nard-bearing Ganges, Grat. Cyn. 314.

nardinus.full: nardĭnus, a, um, adj., = νάρδινος. Of or made of nard, nard-: unguentum, Plin. 13, 1, 2, § 15.—As subst.: nardĭ-num, i, n. (sc. vinum), wine flavored with nard: deprompsit nardini amphoram cellarius, Plaut. Mil. 3, 2, 11 Brix ad loc.— Resembling nard: pira, that smell like nard, Plin. 15, 15, 16, § 55.

nardostachyon.full: nardostăchўon, ii, n., = ναρδόσταχυς, spikenard, Apic. 7, 6, § 282; 8, 2, § 347; Theod. Prisc. de Diaet. 15.
nardostachyon.short: nardostăchўon, ii, n., = ναρδόσταχυς, spikenard, Apic.

nardostatius.full: nardostatĭus, i, m., spikenard, i. q. nardostachyon, Theod. Prisc. de Diaet. 15.

nardus.full: nardus, i, f., and nardum, i, n., = νάρδος, nard, Plin. 12, 12, 26, § 42: nardus Gallicus, id. 12, 12, 26, § 46.— Transf., nard-balsam, nard-oil: Assyriāque nardo Potamus uncti, Hor. C. 2, 11, 16: Syrio madefactus tempora nardo, Tib. 3, 6, 63.
nardus.short: nardus, i, f., and nardum, i, n., = νάρδος, nard, Plin.

narinosus.full: nārĭnōsus, a, um, adj. naris, broadnosed: cum diis suis narinosis, Lact. 5, 12, 13 dub. (al. varicosis, cariosis, curiosis).

nariputens.full: nārĭpŭtens (-trens), entis narisputeo, offensive in the nose, Anthol. Lat. 5, 205, 4 (1134, 4 Burm.).
nariputens.short: nārĭpŭtens (-trens), entis narisputeo, offensive in the nose, Anthol.

naris.full: nāris, is, f. for nasis, from root na-; Sanscr. nārā, water; nāsā, nose; kindred to nasus; cf.: no, nāre, a nostril, usually in plur., nāres, ĭum, f., the nostrils, the nose. Lit. In sing. (poet. and in postclass. prose): et lati rictūs et panda loquenti Naris erat, Ov. M. 3, 675; 6, 141; 12, 253; id. A. A. 1, 520; Pers. 1, 33; Grat. Cyn. 172; Macer. ap. Charis. p. 82 P.; App. M. 8, p. 213; Tert. adv. Marc. 1, 13.— In plur.: nares, eo, quod omnis odor ad supera fertur, recte sursum sunt, Cic. N.

naristi.full: Naristi (v. l. Varisti; also Varis-tae, ārum, Capitol. Anton. Phil. 22, 1), ōrum, m., a people of Germany, part of the Suevi, near the Hermundurians, Tac. G. 42; Cap. Marc. Aur. 22.

narita.full: nārīta, ae, f., = νηρίτης, a kind of sea-snail, Plaut. ap. Paul. ex Fest. p. 166 Müll.
narita.short: nārīta, ae, f., = νηρίτης, a kind of sea-snail, Plaut.

naritas.full: nārĭtas, ātis, f. narus for gnarus; cf. gnaritas, knowledge, discernment; nares a naritate dictae sunt, Don. ad Ter. Ad. 3, 3, 43.

narnia.full: Narnĭa, ae. f., an Umbrian city on the Nar, now Narni, Liv. 10, 10; 27, 9; 29, 15; Tac. A. 3, 9.—Hence, Narnĭensis, e, adj., of or belonging to Narnia, Narnian: ager, Plin. 31, 4, 28, § 51: equites, Liv. 27, 50.—As subst.: (sc. ager), Plin. Ep. 1, 4, 1.— In plur. subst.: Narnĭenses, ĭum, m., the inhabitants of Narnia, the Narnians, Plin. 3, 14, 19, § 113.

naro.full: Năro, ōnis, m., a river in Dalmatia, Plin. 3, 22, 26, § 143.
naro.short: Năro, ōnis, m., a river in Dalmatia, Plin.

narona.full: Narōna, ae, f., a city in Dalmatia, now Opus, Mela, 2, 3, 13; Plin. 3, 22, 26, § 142; Vatin. ap. Cic. Fam. 5, 9, 2; 5, 10, 4; Cic. ib. 13, 77, 3.
narona.short: Narōna, ae, f., a city in Dalmatia, now Opus, Mela, 2, 3, 13;

narrabilis.full: narrābĭlis, e, adj. narro, that can be narrated, Ov. P. 2, 2, 61.

narratio.full: narrātĭo, ōnis, f. id., a relating, narrating, a narration, narrative. In gen.: narrationes credibiles, nec historico, sed prope cotidiano sermone explicatae dilucide, Cic. Or. 26, 124: rem narrare ita ut verisimilis narratio sit, id. de Or. 2, 19, 80: si exponenda est narratio, id. Or. 62, 210; Phaedr. 4, 5, 2.— In partic., in rhet.: narratio est rerum gestarum, aut ut gesta rum, expositio: narrationum genera sunt tria, etc., Cic. Inv. 1, 19, 27; id. de Or. 2, 19, 80; id. Part. Or. 9, 31; Auct.

narratiuncula.full: narrātĭuncŭla, ae, f. dim. narratio, a small, short narrative (post-Aug.), Quint. 1, 9, 6; Plin. Ep. 6, 33, 8.

narrative.full: narrātīvē, adv. narro, in the way of narration, Don. ad Ter. argum. And.

narrativus.full: narrātīvus, a, um, adj. id., suitable for narration, Empor. Rhet. de Loco Comm. p. 567, 2: principium (Aeneidos), Serv. Verg. A. 1, 1.

narrator.full: narrātor, ōris, m. id., a relater, narrator, historian (class.): narratores faceti, Cic. de Or. 2, 54, 219: rerum, id. ib. 2, 12, 54: disertus rerum suarum, Quint. 11, 1, 36: a narratoribus oratoribusque praecipua materia in laudem principis adsumta est, Tac. A. 16, 2.

narratum.full: narrātum, i, n., v. narro fin.

narratus1.full: narrātus, a, um, Part., v. narro.

narratus2.full: narrātus, ūs, m. narro, a narration, narrative (poet. and in post-class. prose): veniet narratibus hora Tempestiva meis, Ov. M. 5, 499; App. M. 9, p. 230, 37.

narro.full: narro, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. for gnarigo (gnarigavit, Fest. p. 95) from gnarus; Sanscr. gnā, know; Gr. γιγνώσκω; cf.: nosco (gnosco), ignoro, to tell, relate, narrate, report, recount, set forth (syn.: memoro, nuntio, trado). Lit.: quid mihi istaec narras? Ter. Hec. 5, 2, 18: ego tibi ea narro quae tu melius scis, quam ipse, qui narro, Cic. Fam. 9, 6, 6: garrula pericula, Juv. 12 82., —With acc. and inf.: mihi Philargyrus narravit, te interdum sollicitum esse vehementius, Cic. Fam. 6, 1, 6: Clitar

narseus.full: Narseus (dissyl.), ĕos, or Narses, is, m., a Persian king, Junand. Reb. Get. 21; Eutr. 9, 25.
narseus.short: Narseus (dissyl.), ĕos, or Narses, is, m., a Persian king, Junand.

narthecia.full: narthēcĭa or narthēcўa, ae, f, = ναρθηκία or ναρθηκύα, a low species of ferula, Plin. 13, 22, 42, § 123.
narthecia.short: narthēcĭa or narthēcўa, ae, f, = ναρθηκία or ναρθηκύα, a low species of ferula, Plin.

narthecium.full: narthēcĭum, ii, n., = ναρθήκιον (lit. a piece of narthex-wood which has been hollowed out for keeping ointments and medicines in; hence any vessel in which these articles are kept), an ointment-box, a medicine-chest, Mart. 14, 78, 1: jam doloris medicamenta illa Epicurea tamquam de narthecio proment, Cic. Fin. 2, 7, 22.

narthex.full: narthex, ēcis, m., = ὁ νάρθηξ, the shrub ferula, Plin. 13, 22, 42, § 123.
narthex.short: narthex, ēcis, m., = ὁ νάρθηξ, the shrub ferula, Plin.

narus.full: nārus, a, um, v. gnarus init.

narycia.full: Nārўcĭa, ae, f., the city of Locri, founded in Lower Italy by the Ozolian Locrians (from Narycion), Ov. M. 15, 705.
narycia.short: Nārўcĭa, ae, f., the city of Locri, founded in Lower Italy by the Ozolian Locrians (from Narycion), Ov.

narycion.full: Nārўcĭon, ii, n., = Ναρύκιον, Plin. 4, 17, 12, § 27; and Nāryx, ўcis, f., = Νάρυξ, a city of the Ozolian Locrians, a colony from which built the city of Locri, in Italy, Plin. 4, 17, 12, § 27 (Jan. Narycum).—Hence, Nārўcĭus, a, um, adj., = Ναρύκιος, of or belonging to the city of Narycion (the birthplace of Ajax Oïleus), Narycian: hic et Narycii posuerunt moenia Locri (cf. Narycion), Verg. A. 3, 399: pix, id. G. 2, 438: Lelex, a king of the Locrians, Ov. M. 8, 312: heros, i. e. the son of Ajax O

nasamones.full: Năsămōnes, um, m., = Νασαμῶνες, a Libyan people to the south-west of Cyrenaica, extending to the Great Syrtis, Plin. 5, 5, 5, § 33; 7, 2, 2, § 14; 13, 17, 23, § 104: tota commercia mundo Naufragiis Nasamones habent (because they plundered shipwrecked persons), Luc. 9, 443.—In sing., a Nasamonian: quas (herbas) Nasamon, gens dura, legit, Luc. 9, 439; acc. Nasamona, Sil. 6, 44.—Hence, Năsămōnĭăcus, a, um, adj., Nasamonian, Sil. 16, 630; cf. Ov. M. 5, 129.— Transf., in gen., African: rex, i. e. Han
nasamones.short: Năsămōnes, um, m., = Νασαμῶνες, a Libyan people to the south-west of Cyrenaica, extending to the Great Syrtis, Plin.

nascens.full: nascens, entis, Part. and P. a., from nascor.

nascentia1.full: nascentĭa, ae, f. nascor, birth (Vitruv.), Vitr. 9, 7.

nascentia2.full: nascentĭa, ium, n., v. nascor, II. P. a. A. 2.

nascibilis.full: nascĭbĭlis, e, adj. nascor, that can be born (post-class.), Tert. adv. Marc. 3, 19; 3, 11.

nascio.full: Nascĭo, ōnis, f., the goddess of birth; v. natio, init., I.
nascio.short: Nascĭo, ōnis, f., the goddess of birth;

nascor.full: nascor, nātus, nasci (ante-class., and in poets of the class. period also gnatus, v. under P. a. B.; part. fut. nasciturus, Pall. Jun. 7, § 8; Vulg. Judic. 13, 8), 3, v. dep. from gnascor, gnatus, root gen, whence gigno; cf. Gr. γεννάω, to be born, to be begotten (of or by male or female). Lit.; constr. with ex or de and abl., or with abl. alone; rarely with ab and abl. With ex and abl. (esp. with name or other appellation of the mother): cum ex utrāque (uxore) filius natus esset, Cic. de Or. 1,
nascor.short: nascor, nātus, nasci (ante-class., and in poets of the class.

nasica1.full: nāsīca, ae, comm. adj. [nasus], who has a large or pointed nose, Arn. 6, 196; 3, 108.

nasica2.full: Nāsīca, ae, m., a surname in the Scipio family. So P. Cornelius Scipio Nasica, who was declared to be the most virtuous man in the state, and on that account was sent to accompany the image of the Mater Idaea to Rome, Liv. 29, 14, 8; cf. Cic. Brut. 20, 79; Val. Max. 3, 7, 3.
nasica2.short: Nāsīca, ae, m., a surname in the Scipio family.

nasidianus.full: Nāsĭdĭānus, a, um, v. Nasidius fin.

nasidienus.full: Nāsīdĭēnus, i, m., a Roman surname. A wealthy upstart in the time of Horace, Hor. S. 2, 8, 1 sq.— Another person, Mart. 7, 54.
nasidienus.short: Nāsīdĭēnus, i, m., a Roman surname.

nasidius.full: Nāsĭdĭus, a, name of a Roman gens. L. Nasidius, a Roman knight, Cic. Phil. 7, 8, 24.— An adherent of Pompey, Caes. B. C. 2, 3; Cic. Att. 11, 17, 3.—Hence, Nā-sĭdĭānus, a, um, adj., Nasidian: naves, Caes. B. C. 2, 7.
nasidius.short: Nāsĭdĭus, a, name of a Roman gens.

naso.full: Nāso, ōnis, m. amplif. [nasus, largenosed], a Roman family name in the Otacilian, Octavian, Ovidian, and Voconian gentes. So esp., P. Ovidius Naso, the poet: ingenio perii Naso poëta meo, Ov. Tr. 3, 3, 74.

nasos.full: Nāsos or Nāsus, i, f., = Νᾶσος, Νῆσος (the island), a part of the city of Syracuse, Liv. 25, 30, 9 sqq.
nasos.short: Nāsos or Nāsus, i, f., = Νᾶσος, Νῆσος (the island), a part of the city of Syracuse, Liv.

nassa.full: nassa or naxa, ae, f. no, a wickerbasket with a narrow neck, for catching fish, a weel. Lit.: nassa est piscatorii vasi genus, quo, cum intravit piscis, exire non potest, Paul. ex Fest. p. 169 Müll.; Sil. 5, 47; Plin. 9, 37, 61, § 132: junci usus ad nassas marinas, id. 21, 18, 59, § 114: scarus inclusus nassis, id. 32, 2, 5, § 11: instrumento piscatoris legato, et retia et nassae ... debentur. Paul. Sent. 3, 6, 66.— Trop., of a dangerous place, a snare, net: numquam ex istā nassā escam petam, Pl

nassiterna.full: nassĭterna (nāsĭt-), ae, f. nasus, a large watering-pot with a large nose or spout: nassiterna est genus vasi aquarii ansati et patentis, quale est quo equi perfundi solent, Paul. ex Fest. p. 169 Müll.; Cato, R. R. 11; Varr. ap. Non. 546, 7; Plaut. Stich. 2, 2, 28.

nassiternatus.full: nassĭternātus, i, m. nassiterna, provided with a large-nosed watering-pot, Calp. ap. Fulg. in Expos. Serm. Antiq. p. 563, 31 Merc.

nasturtium.full: nasturtĭum, ii, n. nasi-tortium, a kind of cress: nasturtium nomen accepit a narium tormento, Plin. 19, 8, 44, § 155; cf. id. 20, 13, 50, § 127: (Persas) negat Xenophon ad panem adhibere quicquam praeter nasturtium, Cic. Tusc. 5, 34, 99; poet. in plur., Verg. M. 84; Col. poët. 10, 231.

nasus1.full: nāsus, i, m. (ante - class. nasum, i, n.: quīs oculi non sunt neque nasum, Lucil. ap. Non. 215, 4; Plaut. Am. 1, 1, 288; id. Curc. 1, 2, 18; id. Men. 1, 2, 57; id. Mil. 4, 6, 41), the nose (syn nares). Lit.: nasus ita locatus est, ut quasi murus oculis interjectus esse videatur, Cic. N. D. 2, 57, 143: abripere alicui nasum mordicus, Plaut. Men. 1, 3, 12: naso exhibere molestiam, id. Capt. 4, 2, 37: naso clamare magnum, to snore, id. Mil. 3, 2, 9: acutus, id. Capt. 3, 4, 115: collisus nasus, Sen.

nasutus.full: nāsūtus, a, um, adj. nasus, that has a large nose, large-nosed (perh. not anteAug.). Lit.: depygis, nasuta, Hor. S. 1, 2, 93: manus, the elephant's trunk, Cassiod. Var. 10, 30.— Trop., sagacious, witty, satirical, censorious: nasutus nimium cupis videri: nasutum volo, nolo polyposum, Mart. 12, 37, 1; id. 13, 2, 1: nil nasutius est, id. 2, 54, 5: homo nasutissimus, Sen. Suas. 7 med.—Hence, adv.: nāsūtē, satirically, scornfully, wittily, sarcastically: tu qui nasute scripta destringis mea, Phaedr.

nata.full: nāta, ae, f., v. natus, under nascor, P. a. B. 1.

natabilis.full: nătābĭlis, e, adj. nato, that can swim or float (post-class.): robur, Coripp. Laud. Just. 4, 43.

natabulum.full: nătābŭlum, i, n. id., a place for swimming, a swimming - place, App. Flor. p. 353, 6: natabula fluminis, Jul. Val. Res Gest. Alex. 2, 9.

natabundus.full: nătābundus, a, um, adj., swimming, Jul. Val. Res Gest. Alex. M. 2, 8 (2, 31 Mai.).
natabundus.short: nătābundus, a, um, adj., swimming, Jul.

natal.full: Natal = natale, birthday festival, the name of one of the mimes of Laberius: in mimo, qui inscribitur Natal, Gell. 16, 7, 9.
natal.short: Natal = natale, birthday festival, the name of one of the mimes of Laberius: in mimo, qui inscribitur Natal, Gell.

natalicius.full: nātālīcĭus, -tĭus, a, um, adj. 1. natalis, of or belonging to the hour or day of one's birth, birthday, natal (class.): qui haec Chaldaeorum natalicia praedicta defendunt, a casting of nativities, Cic. Div. 2, 42, 89: sidera, id. ib. 2, 43, 91: dapes, Mart. 7, 86, 1: lardum, Juv. 11, 84: sinciput, Petr. 136; Pers. 1, 16: dies natalicius, Vulg. Gen. 40, 20.—Hence, Subst. nātālīcĭ-um (-tĭum), ii, n., a birthday present: aliquid natalicii titulo tibi mittere, Censor. de Die Nat. 1.— nātālīcĭa, ae,

natalis1.full: nātālis, e, adj. natus, nascor, of or belonging to one's birth, birth-, natal: hunc emortualem facere ex natali die, Plaut. Ps. 4, 7, 139: nunc huic lenonist hodie natalis dies, id. ib. 3, 1, 9: natali die tuo scripsisti epistulam ad me, Cic. Att. 9, 5, 1; cf.: quem ego diem vere natalem hujus urbis aut certe salutarem appellare possum, Cic. Fl. 40, 102: natalis dies reditūs mei, id. Att. 3, 20, 1: scit genius natale comes qui, temperat astrum, Hor. Ep. 2, 2, 187: tempus, Ov. F. 6, 797: lux, id.

natalis2.full: Nātālis, is, m., a Roman surname, e. g. Antonius Natalis, Tac. A. 15, 50, 54 sq.; 71.
natalis2.short: Nātālis, is, m., a Roman surname, e.

natans.full: nătans, antis, Part. and P. a., v. nato fin.

nataticius.full: nătātìcĭus, a, um, adj. nato, that can swim: nataticius, νηκτικός, Gloss. Philox.

natatilis.full: nătātĭlis, e, adj. id., that can swim (post-class.): animae, Tert. adv. Herm. 33. —Subst.: nătātĭles, ĭum, m., swimming creatures: feras, volucres, reptiles, natatiles, Prud. στεφ. 10, 332; App. de Mund. 28.

natatio.full: nătātĭo, ōnis, f. id., a swimming. Lit.: habeant igitur sibi arma, sibi equos ... sibi pilam, sibi natationes atque cursus. * Cic. Sen. 16, 58: frigidae natationes, Cels. 3, 24 fin.— Transf., a place for swimming, swimming - place, Cels. 3, 27, 1; Cael. Aur. Tard. 1, 1.

natator.full: nătātor, ōris, m. id., a swimmer, Varr. L. L. 5, § 93 Müll.: pugnat in adversas ire natator aquas. Ov. R. Am. 122; id. H. 19, 70; Stat. Th. 10, 497.

natatorius.full: nătātōrĭus, a, um, adj. natator, of or belonging to a swimmer, that serves to swim with, natatory (post-class.): cortex, Isid. Orig. 17, 7, 27.— Subst.: nătātōrĭa, ae, f., and nătātōrĭum, i, n., a place for swimming, a swimming - place, a bath; a pool, Sid. Ep. 2, 2: vade ad natatoria Siloe, Vulg. Joh. 9, 7; 11.

natatura.full: nătātūra, ae, f. id., a place for swimming or bathing: natatura, κολυμβήθρα, Gloss. Philox.

natatus.full: nătātus, ūs, m. id., a swimming (postAug.), Stat. S. 1, 5, 25: piscium natatu, Pall. 1, 17, 2: fluvios natatu scindere, Claud. IV. Cons. Hon. 347; cf. id. Rapt. Pros. 3, 333.

naticidium.full: nātĭcīdĭum or † gnātĭcīdĭum, ii, n. natus-caedo, the murdering of one's son or child, child-murder: gnaticidium, τεκνοκτονία, Gloss. Philox.

natinatio.full: nătĭnātĭo, ōnis, f., a being busy, business: natinatio dicebatur negotiatio et natinatores ex eo seditiosa negotia gerentes, Paul. ex Fest. p. 166 Müll.
natinatio.short: nătĭnātĭo, ōnis, f., a being busy, business: natinatio dicebatur negotiatio et natinatores ex eo seditiosa negotia gerentes, Paul.

natinator.full: nătĭnātor, ōris, m., a rebel; v. natinatio.

natinor.full: nătĭnor, āri, v. dep., to be busy: audito tumultu Macedoniae Samnites, Lucanos inter se natinari atque factiosos esse, Cato ap. Paul. ex Fest. s. v. natinatio, p. 166 Müll.; v. h. v.

natio.full: nātĭo, ōnis, f. nascor, a being born, birth; hence, transf. Personified, Natio, the goddess of birth: Natio quoque dea putanda est, quae, quia partus matronarum tueatur, a nascentibus Natio nominata est, Cic. N. D. 3, 18, 47 (al. Nascio).— A breed, stock, kind, species, race (rare but class.; syn.: genus, stirps, familia): in hominibus emendis si natione alter est melior, emimus pluris, etc., Varr. L. L. 9, § 93 Müll.; Auct. B. Alex. 7, 3: natio optimatium, Cic. Sest. 44, 96: officiosissima cand

natis.full: nătis, is, more freq. in the plur., nă-tes, ium, f. akin to Gr. νῶτον, back; cf. νόσφι, the rump, the buttocks. Sing.: diffissā nate, Hor. S. 1, 8, 46; Auct. Priap. 77, 11; 83, 23: quod ejus natis fulmine icta erat, Paul. ex Fest. s. v. pullus, p. 244 and 245 Müll.— Plur.: nates pervellit, Plaut. Pers. 5, 2, 66: soleā pulsare nates, Juv. 6, 611; Mart. 14, 18, 2; with clunes, id. 3, 53, 3.—Of the rump of animals: nates turturum donare alicui, Mart. 3, 82, 21.

natiso.full: Natiso, ōnis, m., = Νατίσων, a small Italian river near Aquileia, now Natisone, Mel. 2, 4, 3; Plin. 3, 18, 22, § 126.
natiso.short: Natiso, ōnis, m., = Νατίσων, a small Italian river near Aquileia, now Natisone, Mel.

natito.full: nătĭto, 1, v. freq. [no], to swim (late Lat.), Anon. (Hilar.) in Job, 1, p. 98.

natiuncula.full: nātĭuncŭla, ae, f. dim. natio, a small nation: natio, natiuncula, Not. Tir. p. 79.

nativitas.full: nātīvĭtas, ātis, f. nativus, birth, nativity (post-class.; cf. ortus): municipem aut nativitas aut adoptio facit, Dig. 50, 1, 1: janua nativitatis, Tert. Anim. 39: vultum nativitatis, natural face, Vulg. Jacob. 1, 23. — Plur., Tert. Spect. 30.— A generation: usque ad quartam nativitatem, Tert. adv. Marc. 4, 27 fin.

nativitus.full: nātīvĭtus, adv. id., from birth, by birth (post-class.), Tert. Anim. 39; so id. ib. 12.

nativus.full: nātīvus, a, um, adj. nascor, that has arisen from or by birth; born (cf. naturalis). Lit. (class.): mundus, made, created, Lucr. 5, 66: animus, id. 3, 417: Anaximandri opinio est, nativos esse deos, Cic. N. D. 1, 10, 25.— Transf. Imparted by birth, inborn, innate: ut appareret, in eo nativum quendam leporem esse, non ascitum, Nep. Att. 4, 1: mulier si nativā sterilitate sit, Gell. 4, 2, 9: malum, hunger (opp. delatum), Cic. Dom. 5, 12: sensus (with domesticus), id. Har. Resp. 9, 19.— Opp. to art

nato.full: năto, āvi, ātum, 1, v. freq. n. and a. [no], to swim, to float. Lit.: qui neque in Oceano natare volueris studiosissimus homo natandi, Cic. Fam. 7, 10, 2: natant pisces aequore, Ov. P. 2, 7, 28: canis, per flumen, carnem dum ferret, natans, Phaedr. 1, 4, 2: natat uncta carina, floats, Verg. A. 4, 398: crura natantia, palmated feet, Ov. M. 14, 551; cf.: apta natando crura, id. ib. 15, 376.—Of storm-tossed or shipwrecked persons, to float about, be tossed about: naufragus natans, Cic. Inv. 2, 51,

natrix.full: nā^trix, īcis (once m.: natrix violator aquae, Luc. 9, 720; usually), f. no. A water-snake: cur deus tantam vim natricum viperarumque fecerit? Cic. Ac. 2, 38, 120.— Trop., of a dangerous person: se natricem educare, Suet. Calig. 11.— Transf., a whip, scourge, made of a watersnake's skin: natibu' natricem impressit crassam et capitatam, Lucil. ap. Non. 65, 30.— A plant: Ononis natrix, Linn.; Plin. 27, 12, 83, § 107.
natrix.short: nā^trix, īcis (once m.: natrix violator aquae, Luc.

natula.full: nātŭla, ae, f. dim. nata, a little daughter, Inscr. Gud. 335, 12.

natura.full: nātūra, ae, f. nascor, birth. Lit. (very rare): naturā tu illi pater es, consiliis ego, Ter. Ad. 1, 2, 46; cf.: naturā pater, id. ib. 5, 7, 4.— Transf. (freq. and class.; syn.: indoles, ingenium). The nature, i. e. the natural constitution, property, or quality of a thing: quod autem animal est, id motu cietur interiore et suo: nam haec est natura propria animae et vis, Cic. Rep. 6, 26, 28: ipsumque per se sua vi, sua natura, sua sponte laudabile, id. Fin. 2, 15, 50: ab ipsa natura loci, id. Agr

naturabilis.full: nātūrābĭlis, e, i. q. naturalis, App. Doct. Plat. 2, p. 19, 6.

naturalis.full: nātūrālis, e, adj. natura, natural, i. e., By birth, one's own: naturalis pater, opp. to adoptive father, Cic. Phil. 3, 6, 15: in adoptionem dato redire in familiam liceat, si pater naturalis sine liberis decesserit, Quint. 3, 6, 96: filius ( = κατὰ φύσιν υίός), Liv. 42, 52: Pauli nepos, id. 44, 44; Suet. Tib. 52; Gai. Inst. 2, 137; 3, 31: qui in avi sui naturalis potestate est, Dig. 37, 8, 1, § 2; also, natural, illegitimate ( = nothus), Dig. 40, 5, 40; 36, 1, 80, § 2; Aug. Conf. 6, 12; Inscr.

naturalitas.full: nātūrālĭtas, ātis, f. naturalis, naturainess (post-class.): somni naturalitas, Tert. Anim. 43; 16.

naturalitus.full: nātūrālĭtus, adv. naturalis, by nature (post-class.), Sid. Ep. 9, 11; App. M. 1, 12, p. 107.

naturificatus.full: nātūrĭfĭcātus, a, um, adj. naturafacio, brought into being (post-class.): animae naturificatae, Tert. adv. Valent. 23.

natus1.full: nātus, a, um, Part. and P. a., born. —Subst.: nātus, i, m., a son; v. nascor fin.

natus2.full: nātus, ūs (used only in abl. sing.), m. nascor, lit. birth; hence, * Of plants, a growing, growth: cupressus natu morosa, slow of growth, Plin. 16, 33, 60, § 139.— With esp. reference to age, birth, age, years (the class. signif. of the word): non admodum grandis natu, not very old, Cic. Sen. 4, 10: tantus natu, so old, Plaut. Bacch. 1, 2, 16: grandior natu, id. Aul. 2, 1, 37: P. Scaptius de plebe magno natu, an old man, Liv. 3, 71, 3: homo magno natu, id. 10, 38, 6: magno natu principes, id. 21

nauarchia.full: nauarchia, ae, f., = ναυαρχία, the command of a vessel, Cod. Th. 13, 5, 20.
nauarchia.short: nauarchia, ae, f., = ναυαρχία, the command of a vessel, Cod.

nauarchus.full: nauarchus, i, m. (less correctly nav-), = ναύαρχος, the master of a vessel, Cic. Verr. 2, 5, 24, § 60; Tac. A. 15, 51; Inscr. Orell. 3615; 3624; Veg. Mil. 5, 2.

naubolus.full: Naubŏlus, i, m., = Ναύβολος, a king of Phocis, father of Iphitus the Argonaut, Stat. Th. 7, 355; Hyg. Fab. 14.—Hence, Naubŏlĭdes, ae, m., the son of Naubolus, i. e. Iphitus, Val. Fl. 1, 362; cf. Stat. Th. 7, 354.
naubolus.short: Naubŏlus, i, m., = Ναύβολος, a king of Phocis, father of Iphitus the Argonaut, Stat.

nauclericus.full: nauclērĭcus, a, um, adj., = ναυκληρικός, of or belonging to a ship-owner or ship-master: facito uti venias (ornatu) ornatus huc nauclerico, in a skipper's dress, Plaut. Mil. 4, 4, 41 (MSS. nauclerioco): nauclerico ornatu, in the dress of a ship-master, id. As. 1, 1, 54 (MSS. nauclerio), for which ornatus thalassicus, id. Mil. 4, 6, 67.
nauclericus.short: nauclērĭcus, a, um, adj., = ναυκληρικός, of or belonging to a ship-owner or ship-master: facito uti venias (ornatu) ornatus huc nauclerico, in a skipper's dress, Plaut.

nauclerius.full: nauclērĭus, v. l. for nauclericus, q. v. Plaut. As. 1, 1, 54.

nauclerus.full: nauclērus, i, m., = ναύκληρος, a shipowner, a ship-master, skipper (syn.: navarchus, gubernator), Plaut. Mil. 4, 3, 17; Tert. adv. Marc. 5, 1; Vulg. Act. 27, 11; Cod. Th. 7, 16, 3; Firm. Math. 8, 20 fin.— Nauclērus, the title of a comedy of Cæcilius, Non. 12, 32; 126, 26; 506, 5; Isid. Orig. 19, 1.
nauclerus.short: nauclērus, i, m., = ναύκληρος, a shipowner, a ship-master, skipper (syn.: navarchus, gubernator), Plaut.

naucrates.full: Naucrătes, is, m., = Ναυκράτης, a Greek historian of Erythræ, a pupil of Isocrates, Cic. de Or. 2, 23, 94; 3, 44, 173; id. Or. 51, 172; Quint. 3, 6, 3.
naucrates.short: Naucrătes, is, m., = Ναυκράτης, a Greek historian of Erythræ, a pupil of Isocrates, Cic.

naucratis.full: Naucrătis, is, f., = Ναύκρατις, a town of the Delta in Egypt, now Salhadschar, Plin. 5, 10, 11, § 64; 31, 10, 46, § 111.— Hence, Naucrătītes, ae, m. adj., of Naucratis, Naucratian: nomos, Plin. 5, 9, 9, § 49.— Naucrătĭcus, a, um, adj., Naucratian: ostium Nili, Plin. 5, 10, 11, § 64.
naucratis.short: Naucrătis, is, f., = Ναύκρατις, a town of the Delta in Egypt, now Salhadschar, Plin.

naucula.full: naucŭla, ae, f. navicula, a little ship, for navicula (post-Aug.), Plin. Ep. 5, 6, 37; 9, 7, 4; Paul. Carm. 21, 247; cf.: naucula, navicella, navicula, Not. Tir. p. 177.

naucum.full: naucum, i, n., or naucus, i, m. etym. dub.; cf. nugae, something slight or trivial, a trifle: naucum ait Ateius Philologus poni pro nugis. Cincius, quod in oleae nucis, quod intus sit. Aelius Stilo omnium rerum putamen. Glossematorum autem scriptores fabae grani quod haereat in fabulo. Quidam ex Graeco quod sit ϝαὶ καὶ οὐχί, levem hominem significari. Quidam nucis juglandis, quam Verrius jugulandam vocat, medium velut dissaepimentum. Plautus in Parasito pigro: Ambo magnā laude lauti, postremo am
naucum.short: naucum, i, n., or naucus, i, m.

naufragabilis.full: naufrăgābĭlis, e, adj. naufragium, dangerous to ships (late Lat.), Caes. Ep. 2, p. 1134.

naufragalis.full: naufrăgālis, e, adj. id., where many shipwrecks occur, dangerous to ships: Capraria naufragalis, Mart. Cap. 6, § 643; cf. naufragiosus.

naufragator.full: naufrăgātor, ōris, m. naufrago, a shipwrecked person (late Lat.), Aug. Serm. in Spicil. Rom. t. 8.

naufragiosus.full: naufrăgĭōsus, a, um, adj. naufragium, full of shipwrecks, dangerous to ships: pelagus, Sid. Ep. 4, 12; Claud. Mam. de Stat. Anim. 1, 1; cf. naufragalis.

naufragium.full: naufrăgĭum, ii, n. for navifragium, from navis-frango, a shipwreck. Lit.: multi naufragia fecerunt, Cic. Fam. 16, 9, 1: naufragio perire, id. Deiot. 9, 25: naufragio interire, Caes. B. C. 3, 27: naufragio interceptus, Tac. A. 14, 3; Flor. 3, 10, 7: nullum conferri posse Naufragium velis ardentibus, Juv. 12, 22: pati, Sen. Herc. Oet. 118.—Prov.: naufragia alicujus ex terrā intueri, to behold the ruin of others from a position of safety, Cic. Att. 2, 7, 4 (cf. Lucr. 2, 1): naufragium in portu face

naufrago.full: naufrăgo, āvi, 1, v. n. naufragus, to suffer shipwreck, be wrecked: omnes naves naufragārunt, Petr. 76, 4; Sid. Ep. 4, 21; Salv. Gub. Dei, 3, p. 77.

naufragus.full: naufrăgus, a, um, adj. navis-frango, that suffers shipwreck, shipwrecked, wrecked. Lit. (class.): Marium Africa devicta expulsum et naufragum vidit, Cic. Pis. 19, 43: corpora, Verg. G. 3, 542: puppis, Ov. H. 2, 16: mulier, Tac. A. 14, 11.— Subst.: naufrăgus, i, m., a shipwrecked person: naufragus natans, Cic. Inv. 2, 51, 153: dare naufrago tabulam, Sen. Ben. 3, 9, 2: mersā rate naufragus assem Dum rogat, Juv. 14 301.. — Poet., transf., that causes shipwreck, shipwrecking: mare, Hor. C. 1, 16, 10

naulocha.full: Naulŏcha, ōrum, n. (Naulŏchus, i, m., Suet. Aug. 116), a village on the north coast of Sicily, near the promontory of Pelorus, Sil. 14, 265.

naulum.full: naulum (naulŏn), i, n., = ναῦλον, passage-money, fare: perdere naulon, Juv. 8, 97: in naulis navium, Dig. 30, 39, 1: ut naulum exsolvatur, ib. 20, 4, 6; Vulg. Jonae, 1, 3.
naulum.short: naulum (naulŏn), i, n., = ναῦλον, passage-money, fare: perdere naulon, Juv.

naumachia.full: naumăchĭa, ae, f., = ναυμαχία, the representation of a sea-fight, a mock seafight (pure Lat. navale proelium). Lit.: naumachiam commisit, Suet. Claud. 21: naumachiae spectaculum edere, id. Caes. 44: naumachiam exhibere, id. Ner. 12; Vell. 2, 56, 1; 2, 100, 2; Mart. Spect. 28, 12: voluptates naumachiae, Vopisc. Aur. 34, 6. — Transf., a place where mock seafights were exhibited: edidit et navale proelium in veteri naumachia, Suet. Tib. 7; 72; id. Dom. 5.
naumachia.short: naumăchĭa, ae, f., = ναυμαχία, the representation of a sea-fight, a mock seafight (pure Lat.

naumachiarius.full: naumăchĭārĭus, a, um, adj. naumachia, of or for a mock sea-fight: pons, Plin. 16, 39, 74, § 190.—Hence, Subst.: nau-măchĭārĭus, ii, m., a combatant in a mock sea-fight, Suet. Claud. 21.

naumachus.full: naumăchus, i, m., = ναύμαχος, a naval combatant: nauta, nauticus, naumachus, naumachia, Not. Tir. p. 77.
naumachus.short: naumăchus, i, m., = ναύμαχος, a naval combatant: nauta, nauticus, naumachus, naumachia, Not.

naupactus.full: Naupactus (-os), i, f., and Nau-pactum, i, n., = Ναύπακτος, a city of Ætolia, on the Gulf of Corinth, now Epakto or Lepanto, Caes. B. C. 3, 35; Mel. 2, 3, 5; Cic. Pis. 37, 91; Liv. 36, 30; 34 sq.; Plin. 4, 2, 3, § 6.—Hence, Naupactōus, a, um, adj., Naupactian: Naupactous Achelous, Ov. F. 2, 43.
naupactus.short: Naupactus (-os), i, f., and Nau-pactum, i, n., = Ναύπακτος, a city of Ætolia, on the Gulf of Corinth, now Epakto or Lepanto, Caes.

naupegiarius.full: naupēgĭārĭus, ii, m. naupegus, a ship-carpenter, Inscr. Spon. Miscell. p. 67.

naupegus.full: naupēgus, i, m., = ναυπηγός, a shipbuilder, shipwright, ship-carpenter: naupego in navi maritimā diurni X sexaginta, Edict. Diocl. p. 19; Dig. 50, 6, 6; Firm. Math. 4, 7 med.
naupegus.short: naupēgus, i, m., = ναυπηγός, a shipbuilder, shipwright, ship-carpenter: naupego in navi maritimā diurni X sexaginta, Edict.

nauphylax.full: nauphўlax (naufўlax, naufŭ-lax, năŏfylax), ăcis, m., = ναυφύλαξ, one who kept watch over the luggage on shipboard, Inscr. Don. 273, 2; Inscr. Maff. Mus. Ver. 125, 3.
nauphylax.short: nauphўlax (naufўlax, naufŭ-lax, năŏfylax), ăcis, m., = ναυφύλαξ, one who kept watch over the luggage on shipboard, Inscr.

naupidame.full: Naupĭdămē, ēs, f., = Ναυπιδάμη, daughter of Amphidamas, and mother of Augeas by Helios, Hyg. Fab. 14.
naupidame.short: Naupĭdămē, ēs, f., = Ναυπιδάμη, daughter of Amphidamas, and mother of Augeas by Helios, Hyg.

nauplius1.full: Nauplĭus, ii, m., = Ναύπλιος, a son of Neptune and Amymone, king of Eubœa, and father of Palamedes. To avenge his son, whom the Greeks had put to death before Troy, he made false signal-fires on the shores of Eubœa as the Greeks were returning homeward, and led them to shipwreck upon the rocks: Nauplius ultores sub noctem porrigit ignes, Prop. 4 (5), 1, 115. cf. Serv. Verg. A. 11, 260; Hyg. Fab. 116: Nauplii mala, Suet. Ner. 39.—Hence, Nauplĭădes, ae, m., = Ναυπλιάδης, the son of Nauplius, i. e.
nauplius1.short: Nauplĭus, ii, m., = Ναύπλιος, a son of Neptune and Amymone, king of Eubœa, and father of Palamedes.

nauplius2.full: nauplĭus, ii, m., = ναύπλιος, a kind of shell-fish, which sails in its shell as in a ship, Plin. 9, 30, 49, § 94; v. naviger.
nauplius2.short: nauplĭus, ii, m., = ναύπλιος, a kind of shell-fish, which sails in its shell as in a ship, Plin.

nauportum.full: Nauportum, i, n., a city in Upper Pannonia, the mod. Laybach, Tac. A. 1, 20; Vell. 2, 110, 4.—Near it is the river Nau-portus, i, m., Plin. 3, 18, 22, § 128.
nauportum.short: Nauportum, i, n., a city in Upper Pannonia, the mod.

nauscit.full: nauscit (qs. naviscit), said of a bean, which opens in the shape of a ship, Paul. ex Fest. p. 168 and 169 Müll.

nausea.full: nausĕa or nausĭa, ae, f., = ναυσία, sea-sickness. Lit.: ne nauseae molestiam suscipias aeger, Cic. Fam. 16, 11, 1: navigavimus sine timore et nauseā, id. Att. 5, 13, 1: nauseā pressus, Cels. 1, 3.— Transf., in gen., sickness, nausea; vomiting (syn. fastidium): nausea segnis, quae bilem movet nec effundit, Sen. Ep. 53, 3: cruditates, quae nauseam faciunt, Plin. 26, 11, 69, § 112: elaeomeli non sine nauseā alvum solvit, id. 23, 4, 50, § 96: nauseam fluentem coërcere. Hor. Epod. 9, 35: ubi libido v
nausea.short: nausĕa or nausĭa, ae, f., = ναυσία, sea-sickness.

nauseabilis.full: nausĕābĭlis, e, adj. nauseo, that causes nausea or vomiting, Cael. Aur. Tard. 3, 2, 18.

nauseabundus.full: nausĕābundus, a, um, adj. id., inclined to vomit, Sen. Ep. 108, 35; 47, 6.

nauseator.full: nausĕātor, ōris, m. id., one who is apt to feel nausea, who vomits easily: Ulixes nauseator erat, Sen. Ep. 53, 4.

nauseo.full: nausĕo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. n. nausea, to be sea-sick. Lit., Hor. Ep. 1, 1, 93: si sine vomitu nauseavit, Cels. 1, 3.— Transf., to be squeamish or qualmish, to vomit: quidlibet, modo ne nauseet, faciat, Cic. Phil. 2, 34, 84: ructantem et nauseantem Antonium, id. Fam. 12, 25, 4; Juv. 6, 433.— Trop. To belch forth, i. e. give vent to, utter nonsense: ista effutientem nauseare, Cic. N. D. 1, 30, 84.— To cause disgust: hoc illis dictum est, qui stultitiā nauseant, Phaedr. 4, 7, 25.

nauseola.full: nausĕŏla, ae, f. dim. id., a slight squeamishness, Cic. Att. 14, 8, 2.

nauseosus.full: nausĕōsus, a, um, adj. id., that produces nausea, nauseous: radix, Plin. 26, 8, 38, § 59.

nausicaa.full: Nausĭcăa, ae, and Nausĭcăē, ēs, f., = Ναυσικάα, the daughter of Atcinoüs, king of the Phæacians: virgo Nausicaa, Gell. 9, 9, 14; cf. Aus. Per. Odyss. 6; Hyg. Fab. 125 sq.: Nausicaë patrii horti, Mart. 12, 31, 9.
nausicaa.short: Nausĭcăa, ae, and Nausĭcăē, ēs, f., = Ναυσικάα, the daughter of Atcinoüs, king of the Phæacians: virgo Nausicaa, Gell.

nausiphanes.full: Nausĭphănes, is, m., = Ναυσιφάνης, a Grecian philosopher of Teos, instructor of Epicurus, Cic. N. D. 1, 26, 33.
nausiphanes.short: Nausĭphănes, is, m., = Ναυσιφάνης, a Grecian philosopher of Teos, instructor of Epicurus, Cic.

nausiphous.full: Nausĭphŏus, i, m., the son of Ulysses by Circe, Hyg. Fab. 125.
nausiphous.short: Nausĭphŏus, i, m., the son of Ulysses by Circe, Hyg.

nausistrata.full: Nausistrăta, ae, f., name of a woman, Ter. Phorm. 5, 7, 94 et passim.
nausistrata.short: Nausistrăta, ae, f., name of a woman, Ter.

naustathmos.full: Naustathmos, i, m., = Ναύσταθμος, a seaport in Ionia, near Phocæa, Liv. 37, 31 fin.
naustathmos.short: Naustathmos, i, m., = Ναύσταθμος, a seaport in Ionia, near Phocæa, Liv.

naustibulum.full: naustĭbŭlum, i, n. navis, a vessel shaped like a ship: naustibulum vocabant antiqui vas alvei simile, videlicet a navis similitudine, Paul. ex Fest. p. 168 and 169 Müll.

nausum.full: nausum, i, n., a kind of Gallic ship: nauso advehi, Aus. Ep. 22; id. ib. in carm.
nausum.short: nausum, i, n., a kind of Gallic ship: nauso advehi, Aus.

nauta.full: nauta (ante-class., poet., and late Lat. nāvĭta), ae, m. for navita, from navis, a sailor, seaman, mariner: ego nautas eum non putabam habiturum, Cic. Att. 9, 3, 2; id. Fam. 16, 9, 4; nautas gubernatoresque comparari jubet, Caes. B. G. 3, 9: pavidus nauta, Hor. C. 1, 1, 14: nautae = mercatores, id. S. 1, 1, 29: permixtus nautis et furibus et fugitivis, Juv. 8, 174.—Uncontracted form navita (mostly poet.): nulla est voluptas navitis major, Plaut. Men. 2, 1, 1; Cato ap. Paul. ex Fest. p. 169 Müll.

nautaca.full: Nautăca, ōrum, n., = Ναύτακα, a city of Sogdiana, near the river Oxus, probably between the mod. Samarcand and the river Amur, Curt. 8, 2, 9 (ex conject., Zumpt and Mütz. for Naura).
