octavius.full: Octāvĭus, i, m.; Octāvĭa, ae, f., the name of a Roman gens, Suet. Aug. 1 sq.; cf. Drumann, History of Rome, vol. iv. p. 218 sq. C. Octavius, the father of the emperor Augustus, Cic. Att. 2, 1, 12; id. Phil. 3, 6, 15.— Cn. Octavius, the first consul of this gens, Cic. Off. 1, 39, 138.— M. Octavius Caecina, a tribune of the people, Cic. N. D. 1, 38, 106.— Rarely of the emperor Augustus, Juv. 8, 242.— In the fem., Octavia, the name of the two sisters of the emperor Augustus, Suet. Aug. 4; 63; Tac.

octavus.full: octāvus, a, um, adj. octo, the eighth: octava pars, Cic. Att. 15, 26, 4: legio, Caes. B. G. 2, 23: marmor, the eighth mile-stone, Mart. 9, 65, 4.— Subst.: octāva, ae, f. (Sc. hora.) The eighth hour of the day, Mart. 4, 8, 5; Juv. 1, 49.— (Sc. pars.) The eighth part, as a tax, Cod. Just. 4, 65, 7; Cod. Th. 4, 12, 6; Ulp. Fragm. 6, 12 (cf. octavarius).— Adv.: octāvum, for the eighth time, Liv. 6, 36, 7.

octavusdecimus.full: octāvus-dĕcĭmus, a, um, adj., the eighteenth: pars, Vitr. 3, 3: anno aetatis, Tac. A. 13, 6.
octavusdecimus.short: octāvus-dĕcĭmus, a, um, adj., the eighteenth: pars, Vitr.

octennis.full: octennis, e, adj. octo-annus, eight years old (post-class.): puer, Amm. 18, 6, 10.

octennium.full: octennĭum, ii, n. (octo-annus), a period of eight years: tertio quoque octennio, every twenty-four years, Macr. S. 1, 13, 13.

octies.full: octĭes or octiens, adv. num. octo, eight times: septenos octies anfractus, Cic. Rep. 6, 12, 12: victor, Plin. 7, 28, 29, § 101.

octingenarius.full: octingēnārĭus, a, um, adj. octingeni, consisting of eight hundred (ante-class.): greges, Varr. R. R. 2, 10, 11; Prisc. 1355 P.

octingeni.full: octingēni and octingentēni, ae, a, distr. num. adj. [octo-centum], a hundred each, acc. to Prisc. p. 1353 P.
octingeni.short: octingēni and octingentēni, ae, a, distr.

octingentesimus.full: octingentēsĭmus (sync. octigesimus, acc. to Prisc. p. 1353 P.), a, um, ord. num. adj. [octingenti], the eight hundredth: annus, Cic. Sen. 2, 4.

octingenti.full: octingenti, ae, a (gen. plur. octingentūm, Liv. 30, 21, 4), card. num. adj. [octocentum], eight hundred, Cic. Planc 25, 60: stadia, id. Ac. 2, 25, 81.

octingenties.full: octingentĭes or -tiens, adv. num. octingenti, eight hundred times: sestertium bis mille octingenties, Vop. Tac. 10; Mart. Cap. 6, § 610.

octipes.full: octĭpēs, ĕdis, adj. octo-pes, eightfooted (poet.): Cancer, Prop. 4 (5), 1, 150. Ov. F. 1, 313.

octo.full: octŏ, num. adj. Gr. ὀκτώ; Sanscr. ashtan; Goth. ahtau; Germ. acht; Engl. eight, eight: milia militum octo, Enn. ap. Prisc. p. 556 P. (Ann. v. 336 Vahl.): milia passuum octo, Caes. B. G. 1, 21: centum et octo anni, Cic. Rep. 2, 10, 18: centuriae, id. ib. 2, 22, 39: decem et octo, Liv. 10, 21, 6: mariti, Juv. 6, 229.

octoas.full: octŏăs, ădis, f. octo, = octas, the number eight (post-class.), Tert. Praescr. 49.

october1.full: Octōber, bris, adj. id., of or belonging to the eighth (month), the eighth, October, originally the eighth month of the Roman year, reckoning from March; usually connected with mensis: mense Octobri, Vell. 2, 56; Suet. Aug. 35; id. Dom. 13 al.: Octobres Idus, Mart. 12, 67, 3: Kalendae, id. 10, 87, 1: October equus appellatur, qui in campo Martio mense Octobri immolatur quot annis Marti, bigarum victricum dexterior, Paul. ex Fest. p. 178 Müll.—Subst.: Octōber, bris, m., October, Col. 11, 3 al.

october2.full: October, a Roman surname, Inscr. Marin. Fratr. Arval. p. 564.

octodecim.full: octōdĕcim, card. num. adj. [octo-decem], eighteen (mostly post-class, for duodeviginti): tetrachma Attica centum octodecim milia, Liv. 39, 5, 14: cohortes, Front. Strat. 2, 5, 37; Eutr. 1, 1.

octodurus.full: Octōdūrus, i, m., a town of the Veragri, in Gallia Narbonensis, the modern Martigny, Caes. B. G. 3, 1.—Hence, Octō-dūrensis, e, adj., of or belonging to Octodurus; in plur.: Octōdūrenses, ĭum, m., the inhabitants of Octodurus, the Octodurians, Plin. 3, 20, 24, § 135.
octodurus.short: Octōdūrus, i, m., a town of the Veragri, in Gallia Narbonensis, the modern Martigny, Caes.

octogamus.full: octōgămus, i, m., = ὀκτώ-γάμος, that has been married eight times (eccl. Lat.), Hier. in Jovin. 1, n. 15.
octogamus.short: octōgămus, i, m., = ὀκτώ-γάμος, that has been married eight times (eccl.

octogenarius.full: octōgēnārĭus, a, um, adj. octogeni, containing eighty (post-Aug.): exheredata ab octogenario patre, who was a man of eighty, was eighty years old, Plin. Ep. 6, 33, 2; Vulg. 2 Reg. 19, 35: fistula, eighty inches broad, Vitr. 8, 7.— Subst.: octōgē-nārĭus, ĭi, m., a commander of eighty soldiers, Inscr. Orell. 3628.

octogeni.full: octōgēni, ae, a (gen. plur. octogenūm, Front. Aquaed. 58), num. distr. adj. [octo], eighty each: data ex praedā militibus aeris octogeni bini, Liv. 10, 30.— In gen., eighty: fetus, Plin. 9, 51, 75, § 165.

octogesa.full: Octogēsa, ae, f., a city in Hispania Tarraconensis, on the Iberus, near the modern La Granja, Caes. B. C. 1, 61.
octogesa.short: Octogēsa, ae, f., a city in Hispania Tarraconensis, on the Iberus, near the modern La Granja, Caes.

octogesimus.full: octōgēsĭmus, a, um, num. ord. adj. [octoginta], the eightieth: quartum annum ago et octogesimum, Cic. Sen. 10, 32; 2, 4: solstitia, Juv. 4, 92.

octogies.full: octōgĭes or -iens, num. adv. [id.], eighty times: sestertium centies et octogies, Cic. Pis. 35, 86.

octoginta.full: octōginta (octuaginta, Vitr. 10, 17), num. card. adj. [octo], eighty: qui octoginta regnaverat annos, Cic. Sen. 19, 69.

octogonos.full: octōgōnŏs (octāgōnŏs), i, adj., = ὀκτώ-γωνία, eight-cornered, octagonal: turris marmorea octogonos, Vitr. 1, 6, 4.— As subst.: octōgōnum, i, n., an octagon, Vitr. 1, 6, 4 al.
octogonos.short: octōgōnŏs (octāgōnŏs), i, adj., = ὀκτώ-γωνία, eight-cornered, octagonal: turris marmorea octogonos, Vitr.

octojugis.full: octojŭgis, e, adj. octo-jugum, eight in a team, eight together, transf., in gen., for eight: nunc jam octojuges ad imperia obtinenda ire, i. e. eight military tribunes, Liv. 5, 2, 10.— Subst., one of the œons of Valentinus, Tert. adv. Val. 36.

octolophus.full: Octolophus, i, m., or Octolophum, i, n., a city in Thessaly, Liv. 31, 36, 6; 31, 40, 9; 44, 3, 1.
octolophus.short: Octolophus, i, m., or Octolophum, i, n., a city in Thessaly, Liv.

octominutalis.full: octō-mĭnūtālis, e, adj., worth eight farthings, eight coppers (post-class.): libra, Lampr. Alex. Sev. 22, 8.
octominutalis.short: octō-mĭnūtālis, e, adj., worth eight farthings, eight coppers (post-class.): libra, Lampr.

octonalis.full: octōnālis, e, adj. octo, eight (late Lat.), Adaman Locc. Sanct. 1, 22.

octonarius.full: octōnārĭus, a, um, adj. octoni, consisting of eight: numerus, Varr. L. L. 9, § 86 Müll.: versus, an Iambic verse of eight feet, Quint. 9, 4, 72; Diom. p. 514 P.: fistula, the plate for which was eight inches broad, Front. Aquaed. 28; 42; Plin. 31, 6, 31, § 58.

octoni.full: octōni, ae, a, num. distr. adj. [octo]. Eight each, eight at a time, by eights: cum alii octonos lapides ecfodiunt, Plaut. Capt. 3, 5, 66: partes, Varr. L. L. 9, § 30 Müll.: hujus generis octoni ordines ducti, Caes. B. G. 7, 73, 8: imperat Bellovacis decem, octona Pictonibus, id. ib. 7, 75, 3: octona milia peditum praetoribus data, Liv. 32, 28.— In gen., eight: octonis iterum natalibus actis, Ov. M. 13, 753: anni, id. ib. 5, 50.— Sing.: octonus (late Lat.) numerus, the number eight, Hil. prol. i

octophoron.full: octōphŏron (octăph-), i, n., = ὀκτὠφορον, a litter carried by eight bearers: hominem portare octophoro, Cic. Q. Fr. 2, 10, 2; Suet. Calig. 43; Mart. 6, 84, 1.—Apposition: lecticā octophoro ferebatur, Cic. Verr. 2, 5, 11, § 27; cf. Becker, Gallus, 3, p. 6 (2d ed.).
octophoron.short: octōphŏron (octăph-), i, n., = ὀκτὠφορον, a litter carried by eight bearers: hominem portare octophoro, Cic.

octosyllabus.full: octōsyllăbus, a, um, adj. octo-syllaba, having eight syllables, octosyllabic (postclass.), Mar. Vict. p. 2598 P.

octotopi.full: octōtŏpi, ōrum, m., = ὀκτὼ τόποι, in astrology, eight places in the heavens. between the four cardinal points, Manil. 2, 968.
octotopi.short: octōtŏpi, ōrum, m., = ὀκτὼ τόποι, in astrology, eight places in the heavens.

octovir.full: octo-vir, ĭri, m., a member of a council of eight (usually written VIII VIR), Inscr. Orell. 3658; 3699; 3963; 3966.
octovir.short: octo-vir, ĭri, m., a member of a council of eight (usually written VIII VIR), Inscr.

octuplicatio.full: octŭplĭcātĭo, ōnis, f. octuplicatus a making eightfold, a multiplying by eight (post-class.), Mart. Cap. 7, § 796.

octuplicatus.full: octŭplĭcātus or octĭplĭcātus, a, um, Part. [octuplus], made eightfold, multiplied by eight, octupled: octuplicato censu, Liv. 4, 24, 7.
octuplicatus.short: octŭplĭcātus or octĭplĭcātus, a, um, Part.

octuplus.full: octŭplus, a, um, adj., = ὀκταπλοῦς, eightfold, octuple (class.): pars, Cic. Univ. 7, 20.—Subst.: octŭplum, i, n., the eightfold penalty, the octuple: damnare aliquem octupli, Cic. Verr. 2, 3, 11, § 28: poena octupli, id. ib.: judicium in octuplum, id. ib.
octuplus.short: octŭplus, a, um, adj., = ὀκταπλοῦς, eightfold, octuple (class.): pars, Cic.

octussis.full: octussis, is, m. octo-as, eight asses: Quanti emptae? Parvo. Quanti ergo? Octussibus, Hor. S. 2, 3, 156; cf. Charis. 58 P.

oculariarius.full: ŏcŭlārĭārĭus, a, um, adj. ocularis, of or belonging to the eyes, eye-: FABER OCVLARIARIVS, who inserted artificial eyes (of glass, silver, etc.) in statues, Inscr. Grut. 645, 1.

ocularis.full: ŏcŭlāris, e, adj. oculus, of or belonging to the eyes, eye- (post-class.): ocularis medicus, an eye-doctor, oculist, Veg. Vet. 2, 17, 2.— Subst.: ŏcŭlāre, is, n., a medicament for the eyes, eye-salve, Pelag. Vet. 30.—Adv.: ŏcŭlārĭter, with the eyes, ocularly (post class.): oculariter intueri, Sid. Ep. 7, 14 dub.

ocularius.full: ŏcŭlārĭus, a, um, adj. id., of or belonging to the eyes, eye-: CHIRVRGVS, Inscr. Grut. 400, 7: claritas, of the eyes, Sol. 24, 9: aegritudo, a disease of the eyes, id. 4, 6: ocularius medicus, an oculist, Cels. 6, 6, 8.—As subst.: ŏcŭlārĭus, i, m., an oculist, Scrib. Comp. 37.

oculata.full: ŏcŭlāta, ae, f. oculatus, a kind of fish, perh. a lamprey, Plin. 32, 11, 53, § 149; Cels. 2, 18, 25.

oculatus.full: ŏcŭlātus, a, um, adj. oculus. Lit., furnished with or having eyes, seeing (mostly ante-class. and post-Aug.): pluris est oculatus testis unus quam auriti decem, an eye-witness, Plaut. Truc. 2, 6, 8; cf. inspectio, Arn. 2, 48: Clodius male oculatus, whose sight was bad, Suet. Rhet. 5: duobus luminibus, Cassiod. Var. 1, 4: aedis patulis oculata fenestris, Ven. Fort. Carm. 3, 7, 47.—Comp.: oculatior deus, that has better sight, Tert. adv. Marc. 2, 25.— Transf., eye-shaped: oculati circuli, Sol. 17,

oculeus.full: ŏcŭlĕus, a, um, adj. id., full of eyes (ante- and post-class.). Lit.: Argus, Plaut. Aul. 3, 6, 19.— Transf., sharpsighted: oculeus totus, App. M. 2, p. 124 fin.; Mart. Cap. 8, § 810.

oculicrepida.full: ŏcŭli-crĕpĭda, ae, a false read. for collicrepidae, Plaut. Trin. 4, 3, 14; v. Ritschl ad h. l.

oculissimus.full: ŏcŭlissĭmus, a, um, adj., a comically formed sup., from oculus, dearest (cf. ocellus): oculissime homo, Plaut. Curc. 1, 2, 28: valuistin' oculissimum ostium? id. ib. 1, 1, 17; cf.: oculissimum, carissimum, Plautus: oculissimum ostium amicae, Paul. ex Fest. p. 179 Müll.
oculissimus.short: ŏcŭlissĭmus, a, um, adj., a comically formed sup., from oculus, dearest (cf.

oculitus.full: ŏcŭlĭtus, adv. oculus, as one's own eyes, i. e. most dearly: amare, Plaut. ap. Non. 147, 27 sq.; cf.: oculitus quoque dicitur, ut funditus, penitus, quo significatur tam carum esse, quam oculum, Paul. ex Fest. p. 179 Müll.

oculo.full: ŏcŭlo, 1, v. a. id.. To furnish with eyes, make to see (eccl. Lat.). Lit.: pullos, Tert. Poen. 12.— Trop., to enlighten: homines in agnitionem veritatis oculare, Tert. Apol. 2: caecos, Cypr. Idol. Van. 7, 6.— To make visible or conspicuous (eccl. Lat.): vestem purpurā, Tert. Pud. 8.

oculus.full: ŏcŭlus (sync. oclus, Prud. στεφ. 10, 592 dub.), i, m. kindr. with Sanscr. akshi and aksha, from the root ītsh, videre; Gr. ὄσσομαι, ὄσσε; Goth. augō; Germ. Auge; Engl. eye, an eye. Lit.: quae (natura) primum oculos membranis tenuissimis vestivit et saepsit ... sed lubricos oculos fecit et mobiles, Cic. N. D. 2, 57, 142; cf. Cels. 7, 7, 13; Plin. 11, 37, 52, § 139 sq.; Cic. de Or. 3, 59, 221: venusti, id. Tusc. 5, 16, 46: eminentes, prominent, id. Vatin. 2, 4: oculi tanquam speculatores, id. N. D

ocyale.full: Ōcўălē, ēs, f., one of the Amazons, Hyg. Fab. 163.
ocyale.short: Ōcўălē, ēs, f., one of the Amazons, Hyg.

ocydrome.full: Ōcўdrŏmē, ēs, f., = ὠκυδρόμη, Swiftrunner, one of Actæon's hounds, Hyg. Fab. 181.
ocydrome.short: Ōcўdrŏmē, ēs, f., = ὠκυδρόμη, Swiftrunner, one of Actæon's hounds, Hyg.

ocydromus.full: Ōcўdrŏmus, i, m., = ὠκύδρομος, Swiftrunner, one of Actæon's hounds, Hyg. Fab. 181.
ocydromus.short: Ōcўdrŏmus, i, m., = ὠκύδρομος, Swiftrunner, one of Actæon's hounds, Hyg.

ocyor.full: ōcўor, ōcyssĭmus, and ōcўus, more correctly ocior, etc.
ocyor.short: ōcўor, ōcyssĭmus, and ōcўus, more correctly ocior, etc.

ocypete.full: Ōcўpĕtē, ēs, f, = ὠκυπέτη, Swift-flier, one of the Harpies, Serv. Verg. A. 3, 209.
ocypete.short: Ōcўpĕtē, ēs, f, = ὠκυπέτη, Swift-flier, one of the Harpies, Serv.

ocypote.full: Ōcўpŏtē, ēs, f., = ὠκυπότη, Swift-flier, one of Actæon's hounds, Hyg. Fab. 181.
ocypote.short: Ōcўpŏtē, ēs, f., = ὠκυπότη, Swift-flier, one of Actæon's hounds, Hyg.

ocyrrhoe.full: Ōcyrrhŏē or Ōcўrhŏē, ēs, f., = Ὠκυρρόη, a daughter of Chiron, Ov. M. 2, 638.
ocyrrhoe.short: Ōcyrrhŏē or Ōcўrhŏē, ēs, f., = Ὠκυρρόη, a daughter of Chiron, Ov.

ocythous.full: Ōcўthŏus, i, m., = ὠκύθοος, Swiftrunner, one of Actæon's hounds, Hyg. Fab. 181.
ocythous.short: Ōcўthŏus, i, m., = ὠκύθοος, Swiftrunner, one of Actæon's hounds, Hyg.

odariarius.full: ōdărĭārĭus, ii, m. odarium, a teacher of singing: MAGISTER ODARIARIVS, Inscr. Orell. 2634.

odarium.full: ōdărĭum, ii, n., = ᾠδάριον, a song, ode (post-Aug.), Petr. 53, 11.
odarium.short: ōdărĭum, ii, n., = ᾠδάριον, a song, ode (post-Aug.), Petr.

ode.full: ōdē or ōda, ae, = ᾠδή, a song, esp. a lyric song, an ode (post-class. for carmen), Auct. Carm. Philom. 13; 25.
ode.short: ōdē or ōda, ae, = ᾠδή, a song, esp.

odefacit.full: odefăcit, dicebant pro olfacit, quae vox a Graeco ὀσμή tracta est, Paul. ex Fest. p. 179 Müll.
odefacit.short: odefăcit, dicebant pro olfacit, quae vox a Graeco ὀσμή tracta est, Paul.

odessos.full: Ŏdessos or Ŏdessus, i, f., = Ὀδησσός, a city of Lower Mœsia, on the Pontus Euxinus, now Varna, Mel. 2, 2; Plin. 4, 12, 18, § 45.—Also written ŏdyssus (-os), Amm. 32, 9.
odessos.short: Ŏdessos or Ŏdessus, i, f., = Ὀδησσός, a city of Lower Mœsia, on the Pontus Euxinus, now Varna, Mel.

odeum.full: ōdēum, i, n., = ᾠδεῖον, a public building aesigned for musical performances, an odeon, Vitr. 5, 9; Suet. Dom. 5; cf. Eutr. 7, 24; Tert. Res. Carn. 42; Amm. 16, 10, 14.
odeum.short: ōdēum, i, n., = ᾠδεῖον, a public building aesigned for musical performances, an odeon, Vitr.

odi.full: ōdi, ōdisse (old form of the pres., odio: osi sunt ab odio, declinasse antiquos testis est C. Gracchus, Paul. ex Fest. p. 201 Müll. From this are formed: odis, Ambros. in Psa. 118, 17; odiant, Arn. in Psa. 37; odiebant, id. Psa. 73; odies, Tert. adv, Marc. 4, 35; odiet, Hier. Ep. 22, 31; odivi, Vulg. Psa. 118, 104; odientes, id. Deut. 7, 10; Tert. adv. Marc. 4, 16; odiendi, App. Dogm. Plat. 3 init. —Pass. oditur, Tert. Apol. 3 fin.; Vulg. Ecclus. 20, 8: odiremur, Hier. Ep. 43, 2: oderem and oder
odi.short: ōdi, ōdisse (old form of the pres., odio: osi sunt ab odio, declinasse antiquos testis est C.

odiatus.full: ŏdiātus, a, um, adj. odium, hated, hateful: odiosus, odietas (odiatus), inodiatus, perodiatus, Not. Tir. p. 77.

odibilis.full: ŏdĭbĭlis, e, adj. odi, that deserves to be hated, hateful, odious (ante- and post-class.), Poët. ap. Prisc. p. 709 P.: improbitate ita odibilis, ut, etc., Lampr. Heliog. 18; Ambros. Ep. 33, 1: superbia, Vulg. Ecclus. 10, 7: qui procax est, id. ib. 20, 5: vita, id. 2 Macc. 6, 19: Deo, id. Rom. 1, 30.

odice.full: Ōdĭcē, ēs, f., = Ὠιδική, one of the Hours, Hyg. Fab. 183.
odice.short: Ōdĭcē, ēs, f., = Ὠιδική, one of the Hours, Hyg.

odicus.full: ōdĭcus, a, um, adj., = ᾠδικός, of or belonging to song, odic, in prosody, Mart. Vict. p. 2501 P.
odicus.short: ōdĭcus, a, um, adj., = ᾠδικός, of or belonging to song, odic, in prosody, Mart.

odinolytes.full: ōdīnŏlўtes, ae, m. ὠδινολύτης, from ὠδίς and λύω, he who or that which alleviates the pangs of childbirth (epithet of the fish called mora. Plin. 32, 1, 1, § 6).

odiosicus.full: ŏdĭōsĭcus, a, um, adj. odiosus, a comically formed word for odiosus, Plaut. Capt. 1, 1, 19.

odiosus.full: ŏdĭōsus, a, um, adj. odium, hateful, odious, vexatious, offensive, unpleasant, disagreeable, annoying, troublesome, etc. (class.; syn.: invisus, offensus). Of persons: odiosus mihi es, Plaut. Ps. 1, 1, 28: infestum et odiosum esse alicui, id. Truc. 1, 1, 65; Lucr. 4, 1165: senex, Ov. R. Am. 471. — Of things: dona odiosa ingrataque, Plaut. Truc. 4, 1, 7: odiosa et inepta amatio, id. Rud. 4, 5, 14: motus odiosiores, Cic. Off. 1, 36, 130: verbum, id. Or. 8, 25: odiosissima natio, Phaedr. 2, 5, 4: c

odites.full: Ŏdītes, ae, m. The name of a Centaur, Ov. M. 12, 457.— Another proper name, Ov. M. 5, 97.

odium1.full: ŏdĭum, ii, n. odi (syn.: simultas, inimicitia) Lit., hatred, grudge, illwill, animosity, enmity, aversion: odium (est) ira inveterata, Cic. Tusc. 4, 9, 21: in odium alicujus irruere, to become hated by him, to incur his hatred, Cic. Verr. 1, 12, 35: non publico modo sed privato etiam odio invisus atque infestus Romanis, Liv. 36, 39, 15.—Odio alicui esse, as pass. of odi (cf. odi fin.): quod viro esse odio videas, tute tibiodio habeas, to be hateful, displeasing to, Plaut. Men. 1, 2, 2: odi odioq

odium2.full: ōdīum, ii, n., i. q. odeum, q. v.

odomantes.full: Ŏdŏmantes, um, or Ŏdŏmanti, ōrum, m., = Οδομαντες, a people of Thrace, on the Strymon, Plin. 4, 11, 18, § 40.—Hence, ŏdŏmantĭcus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to the Odomantes, Liv. 45, 4.
odomantes.short: Ŏdŏmantes, um, or Ŏdŏmanti, ōrum, m., = Οδομαντες, a people of Thrace, on the Strymon, Plin.

odontitis.full: ŏdontītis, ĭdis, f., = ὀδοντῖτις, a plant good for the toothache, tooth-wort, Plin. 27. 12, 84, § 108.
odontitis.short: ŏdontītis, ĭdis, f., = ὀδοντῖτις, a plant good for the toothache, tooth-wort, Plin.

odontotyrannus.full: ŏdontŏtyrannus, i, m., = ὀδοντοτύραννος (tooth tyrant), the name of an animal, Jul. Val. Res Gest. Alex. M. 3, 33.
odontotyrannus.short: ŏdontŏtyrannus, i, m., = ὀδοντοτύραννος (tooth tyrant), the name of an animal, Jul.

odor.full: ŏdor (old form ŏdos, like arbos, labos, etc., Plaut. Capt. 4, 2, 35; id. Ps. 3, 2, 52; Sall. J. 44, 4), ōris, m. root od-; Gr. ὄζω, ὄδωδα, ὀδμή; whence oleo, olfacio, a smell, scent, odor (class.; cf. fragrantia). Lit. In gen.: omnis odor ad supera fertur, Cic. N. D. 2, 56, 141: odorem avide trahere naribus, Phaedr. 3, 1, 3: florum, Cic. Sen. 17, 59.— In partic. A pleasant odor, perfume; concr., perfumery, essences, spices (syn. odoramenta).—So mostly in plur.: sternite lectos, incendite odores,
odor.short: ŏdor (old form ŏdos, like arbos, labos, etc., Plaut.

odorabilis.full: ŏdōrābĭlis, e odoror, perceptible by smell, Ambros. Noë, 15, 22.
odorabilis.short: ŏdōrābĭlis, e odoror, perceptible by smell, Ambros.

odoramen.full: ŏdōrāmen, ĭnis, n. odoro, a perfume, spice, balsam (post-class.), Macr. S. 1 praef.

odoramentum.full: ŏdōrāmentum, i, n. id., an odoriferous substance, a perfume, spice, balsam (post-Aug.), Col. 11, 2: pretiosiora, Plin. 15, 7, 7, § 29: STATVTA EX HS., etc., Inscr. Orell. 4413: phialae plenae odoramentorum, Vulg. Apoc. 5, 8.

odorarius.full: ŏdōrārĭus, a, um, adj [odor], of or for perfuming (post-Aug.): odoraria myrrha, Plin. 12, 16, 35, § 70: MAGISTER, a vender or preparer of spices, Inscr. Rhein. cl. 11, n. 81; cf.: odorarius, ἀρωματοπώλης, Gloss. Phil.
odorarius.short: ŏdōrārĭus, a, um, adj [odor], of or for perfuming (post-Aug.): odoraria myrrha, Plin.

odoratio.full: ŏdōrātĭo, ōnis, f. odoror. Lit., a smelling, smell (very rare): qualis est haec aurium delectatio, tales sunt oculorum et tactionum et odorationum et saporum, Cic. Tusc. 4, 9, 20.— Transf., the smell, the sense of smelling: odoratio in duas nares a summo artifice divisa est, Lact. Opif. D. 10.

odorativus.full: ŏdōrātīvus, a, um, adj. odoro, fragrant, odoriferous (post-class.): semen, App. Herb. 79.

odoratus1.full: ŏdōrātus, a, um, P a., from odoro.
odoratus1.short: ŏdōrātus, a, um, P a., from odoro.

odoratus2.full: ŏdōrātus, ūs, m. odoror, a smelling, smell. Lit. (class.), eorum jucundus non gustatus solum. sed odoratus etiam, et spectatus, Cic. N. D. 2, 63, 158.— Transf. The sense of smell: nihil necesse est de gustatu et odoratu loqui, Cic. Ac. 2, 7, 20: insecta habent oculos, aliqua et odoratum, Plin. 11, 4, 3, § 10.— A smell, scent, odor which a thing gives out, Plin. 25, 13, 95, § 151.

odorifer.full: ŏdōrĭfer, ĕra, ĕrum, adj. odor-fero, bringing or spreading odors, fragrant, odoriferous (poet. and in post-Aug. prose). Lit.: panacea, Verg. A. 12, 419: flores, Sil. 16, 309.— Producing perfumes or spices: gens odorifera, i. e. Persae, Ov. M. 4, 209: Arabia, Plin. 5, 11, 12, § 65.— Prop., sweet, flattering, precious: non habemus ista odorifera, Sen. Ep. 33, 2: fructus sanctae religionis, Ambros. Spirit. Sanct. 2, 5, 40.

odorificatus.full: ŏdōrĭfĭcātus, a, um, adj. odor-facio, made to emit pleasant odor, Ambros. Ep. 8, 64.

odorisequus.full: ŏdōrĭsĕquus, a, um, adj. odor-sequor, that follows the scent (of a trail): canes, Liv. Andron. ap. Ter. Metr, p. 2426 P.; cf. Serv. Verg. A. 4, 132.

odoro.full: ŏdōro, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. odor, to give a smell or fragrance to, to perfume a thing (poet. and in post-Aug. prose; cf.: oleo, fragro): odorant aëra fumis, Ov. M. 15, 734: mella, Col. 9, 4, 4: caelum sulfure, Avien. Arat. 1430.—Hence, ŏdōrātus, a, um, P. a., that has a smell, that emits an odor; esp., sweet-smelling, fragrant: quid tibi odorato referam sudantia ligno Balsama? Verg. G. 2, 119: cedrus, id. A. 7, 13: pabula, Col. 8, 17, 1: capilli, Hor. C. 3, 20, 14: comae, Ov. A. A. 2, 734: nectar

odoror.full: ŏdōror, ātus, 1, v. dep. id., to smell at, examine by smelling (cf. olfacio). Lit.: pallam, Plaut. Men. 1, 2, 55.— Transf., to smell out, detect by the scent; to scent: ibo odorans, quasi canis venaticus, Plaut. Mil. 2, 2, 113: cibum, Hor. Epod. 6, 10: hominem, Col. 6, 2: vultures sagacius odorantur, Plin. 10, 69, 88, § 191: bellum, Vulg. Job, 39, 25.— Trop. To aspire to, aim at a thing, in a contemptuous sense; to snuff, as a dog: quos odorari hunc decemviratum suspicamini, Cic. Agr. 2, 24, 65.

odorus.full: ŏdōrus, a, um, adj. id., emitting a scent or odor, odorous (mostly poet. and in post-Aug. prose for odoratus). Lit. Sweet-smelling, fragrant: flos, Ov. M. 9, 87: arbor, i. e. myrrha, id. A. A. 1, 287: res, Varr. L. L. 6, § 83 Müll. dub.—Comp.: odorius, Plin. 20, 17, 69, § 177.—Sup.: nardum Syriacum odorissimum, Isid. 17, 9, 3.— Ill-smelling, stinking (post-class.): lumen odorum Sulfure, Claud. VI. Cons. Hon. 324. Transf., that tracks by the smell, keenscented: odora canum vis (= copia odororum c

odrysae.full: Odrўsae, ārum, m., = Ὀδρύσαι, a people of Thrace, on the Hebrus, now Rumili, Liv. 39, 53; Plin. 4, 11, 18, § 40.—Written Odrŭsae, Tac. A. 3, 38.—Hence, Odrўsĭus, a, um, adj., Odrysian, poet. for Thracian: rex, Ov. M. 6, 490: tyrannus, i. e. Tereus, id. R. Am. 459: dux, i. e. Rhesus, id. A. A. 2, 130: domus, i. e. of Tereus, king of Thrace, Sen. Thyest. 273: carmen, of Orpheus, Val. Fl. 5, 440.—Subst.: Odrўsĭus, ii, m., the Odrysian, Thracian, i. e. Orpheus, Val. Fl. 5, 100.—In plur.: Odrўsii, ōr
odrysae.short: Odrўsae, ārum, m., = Ὀδρύσαι, a people of Thrace, on the Hebrus, now Rumili, Liv.

odyssea.full: Ŏdyssēa, ae, f., = Ὀδυσσεία. The Odyssey of Homer, Ov. Tr. 2, 375.—Gr. acc. Odyssian, Varr. Sat. Men. 11, 14; Petr. 29, 4.— A poem of Livius Andronicus, Cic. Brut. 18, 71; Gell. 3, 16, 11.—Odysseae portus (Ὀδυσσεία ἄκρα, Ptol.), a promontory at the southern extremity of Sicily, Cic. Verr. 2, 5, 34, § 87

oea.full: Oea, ae, f., a town of Africa, now Tripolis, Mela. 1, 7, 5; Sil. 3, 257; App. Mag. 17. —Hence, Oeensis, e, adj., of or belonging to Œa: civitas Oeensis, Plin. 5, 4, 4, § 27; cf. Sil. 3, 257.—Plur. subst.: Oeenses, ĭum, m., the inhabitants of Œa, Plin. 5, 5, 5, § 38; Tac. H. 4, 50.
oea.short: Oea, ae, f., a town of Africa, now Tripolis, Mela.

oeagrus.full: Oeā^grus, i, m., = Οἴαγρος, a king of Thrace, the father of Orpheus, Ov Ib. 484; Hyg. Fab. 14.—Hence, Oeā^grĭus, a, um, adj., = Οἰάγριος, Œagrian, poet. for Thracian: Oeagrius Hebrus, Verg. G. 4, 524: Haemus, where Orpheus was torn in pieces, Ov. M. 2, 219: dulcius Oeagrios pulsabat pectine nervos, played on the cithara like Orpheus, Sil. 4, 463.
oeagrus.short: Oeā^grus, i, m., = Οἴαγρος, a king of Thrace, the father of Orpheus, Ov Ib.

oeanthe.full: Oeanthē, ēs, f., a city of the Ozolian Locrians, Plin. 4, 3, 4, § 7.—Called Oean-thia, Mela, 2, 3.
oeanthe.short: Oeanthē, ēs, f., a city of the Ozolian Locrians, Plin.

oebalia.full: Oebălĭa, ae, f., = Οἰβαλία, another name for Tarentum, Verg. G. 4, 125; cf. Hor. C. 2, 6, 12; Plin. 3, 11, 16, § 99.
oebalia.short: Oebălĭa, ae, f., = Οἰβαλία, another name for Tarentum, Verg.

oebalus.full: Oebălus, i, m., = Οἴβαλος, a king of Sparta, the father of Tyndarus and grandfather of Helen, under whose guidance the Parthenians went to Lower Italy and founded Tarentum, Hyg. Fab. 78.— A king of Caprea, son of Telon, Verg. A. 7, 734.—Hence, Oebălĭdes, ae, m., = Οἰβαλίδης, a male descendant of Œbalus, an Œbalide, Spartan: Oebalides puer, i. e. Hyacinthus, Ov. Ib. 590: Laberis, Oebalide, i. e. Hyacinthe, id. M. 10, 196: Oebalides, i. e. Pollux, Val. Fl. 4, 293.—In plur.: Oebă-lĭdae, ārum, m., C
oebalus.short: Oebălus, i, m., = Οἴβαλος, a king of Sparta, the father of Tyndarus and grandfather of Helen, under whose guidance the Parthenians went to Lower Italy and founded Tarentum, Hyg.

oechalia.full: Oechălĭa, ae, f., = Οἰχαλία, the name of several cities. In Eubœa, Verg. A. 8, 291; Ov. H. 9, 1; Hyg. Fab. 35.— In Messenia, Plin. 4, 5, 7, § 15. Hence, Oechălis, ĭdis, f., = Οἰχαλίς, a female Œchalian, Ov. M. 9, 331.
oechalia.short: Oechălĭa, ae, f., = Οἰχαλία, the name of several cities.

oecleus.full: Oecleus (dissyl.), ĕi and ĕos, m., = Οἰκλεύς, the father of Amphiarāus, and grandfather of Alcmœon, Hyg. Fab. 128.— Hence, Oeclīdes, ae, m., = Οἰκλείδης, the son of Œcleus, i. e. Amphiarāus, Ov. M. 8, 317.
oecleus.short: Oecleus (dissyl.), ĕi and ĕos, m., = Οἰκλεύς, the father of Amphiarāus, and grandfather of Alcmœon, Hyg.

oeclus.full: Oeclus, i, m., the name of a Centaur, Ov. M. 12, 450.
oeclus.short: Oeclus, i, m., the name of a Centaur, Ov.

oeconomia.full: oecŏnŏmĭa, ae, f., = οἰκονομία, the management of household affairs, domestic economy; hence, a proper division, arrangement, economy (of an oration, a play, etc.; post-Aug.; written as Greek, Cic. Ac. 6, 1, 1; 6, 1, 11): Hermogenes judicium, partitionem, ordinem, quaeque elocutionis sunt, subicit oeconomiae, quae, Graece appellata ex curā rerum domesticarum et hic per abusionem posita, nomine Latino caret, Quint. 3, 3, 9; 1, 8, 9.
oeconomia.short: oecŏnŏmĭa, ae, f., = οἰκονομία, the management of household affairs, domestic economy;

oeconomicus.full: oecŏnŏmĭcus, a, um, adj., = οἰκονομικός. Of or relating to domestic economy; subst.: oecŏnŏmĭcus, i, m., a work of Xenophon on domestic economy. in eo libro, qui Oeconomicus inscribitur, Cic. Off. 2, 24, 87; Gell. 15, 5, 8.— Of or belonging to a proper (oratorical) division or arrangement; orderly, methodical: oeconomica totius causae dispositio, Quint. 7, 10, 11.

oeconomus.full: oecŏnŏmus, i, m., = οἰκονόμος, a housekeeper, steward, overseer (post-class. for dispensator rei familiaris; cf. vilicus), Cod. Just. 1, 3, 33; Cod. Th. 9, 45, 3; Hier. Ep. 22, 18, § 35.† † oecūmĕnĭcus, a, um, adj., = οἰκουμενικός, of or belonging to the whole inhabited world, œcumenical (post-class.), Eckhel. D. N. t. 3, p. 336; so id. ib. p. 372.
oeconomus.short: oecŏnŏmus, i, m., = οἰκονόμος, a housekeeper, steward, overseer (post-class.

oecus.full: oecus, i, m., = οἶκος, a room in a house; a hall, saloon (only in Vitr. and Plin.): oeci magni, in quibus matresfamiliarum cum lanificis habent sessiones, Vitr. 6, 10; Plin. 36, 25, 60, § 184; cf. Becker's Gallus, 2, p. 189 (2d ed.).
oecus.short: oecus, i, m., = οἶκος, a room in a house;

oedipus.full: Oedĭpus, ŏdis and i (gen. Oedipŏdis, Cic. Fin. 5, 1, 3; acc. Oedipum, id. Sen. 7, 22; id. Fat. 13, 30; abl. Oedipŏde, id. ib. 14, 33; Stat. Th. 7, 513: Oedipo, Plaut. Poen. 1, 3, 34; plur. acc. Oedipodas, Mart. 9, 26, 10), m., = Οἰδίπους. A king of Thebes, the son of Laius and Jocasta. He unwittingly killed his father; he solved the riddle of the Sphinx, and unknowingly married his own mother, who had by him Eteocles, Polyneices, Ismene, and Antigone; when the incest was discovered, he put out h

oenanthe.full: oenanthē, ēs, f., = οἰνάνθη. The grape of the wild vine, Plin. 12, 28, 61, § 132. — A thorny plant, pimpinella-like dropwort: Oenanthe pimpinelloides, Linn.; Plin. 21, 24, 95, § 167.— A bird, called also parra, Plin. 10, 29, 45, § 87.— Œnanthe, mother of Ptolemy Epiphanes, Just. 30, 3, 3.

oenanthinus.full: oenanthĭnus, a, um, adj., = οἰνάνθινος, made from the grape of the wild vine: vinum, Plin. 14, 16, 18, § 98: oleum, id. 15, 7, 7, § 29: unguentum, id. 13, 1, 2, § 5.
oenanthinus.short: oenanthĭnus, a, um, adj., = οἰνάνθινος, made from the grape of the wild vine: vinum, Plin.

oenanthium.full: oenanthĭum, ii, n. (sc. oleum, unguentum), an ointment made from the grape of the wild vine, Lampr. Heliog. 23.

oeneus1.full: Oeneus (dissyl.), ĕi and ĕos, m., = Οινεύς, a king of Ætolia or Calydon, the husband of Althœa, and father of Meleager, Tydeus, Dejanira, Gorgo, etc., Ov. M. 8, 281 sq.; Hyg. Fab. 172; Stat. Th. 2, 165; 586; Cic. poët. Tusc. 2, 8, 20.— Hence, Oenēis, ĭdis, f., = Οἰνηΐς, the daughter of Œneus, i. e. Dejanira, Sen. Herc. Oet. 583.— Oenēĭus, a, um, adj., = Οἰνήϊος, Œnean: Oeneius heros, i. e. Tydeus, Stat. Th. 5, 661.— Oenēus (trisyl.), a, um, adj., = Οἰνήϊος, Œnean: Oeneos per agros, i. e. of Caly
oeneus1.short: Oeneus (dissyl.), ĕi and ĕos, m., = Οινεύς, a king of Ætolia or Calydon, the husband of Althœa, and father of Meleager, Tydeus, Dejanira, Gorgo, etc., Ov.

oeneus2.full: Oenēus, a, um, v. 1. Oeneus, C.

oeniadae.full: Oeniădae, ārum, m., = Οἰνιάδαι, a people of Acarnania, Liv. 38, 11; 26, 24 sq.
oeniadae.short: Oeniădae, ārum, m., = Οἰνιάδαι, a people of Acarnania, Liv.

oenigenos.full: oenĭgĕnos, unigenitos, Paul. ex Fest. p. 195 Müll.

oenobreches.full: oenŏbrĕches, = οἰνοβρεχής, a read. for onobrychis, q. v., Plin. 24, 16, 98, § 155.

oenococtus.full: oenŏcoctus, a, um, adj. vox hybr., from οἶνος-coctus, stewed in wine (post Aug.): vituli, Petr. S. 47: gallus, id. ib. 74 porcellus, Apic. 8, 7 (al. oenogaratus).

oenogaratus.full: oenŏgărātus, a, um, adj. oenogarum, cooked with wine-sauce: porcellus, Apic. 8, 7 (al. oenococtus).

oenogarum.full: oenŏgărum, i, n., = οἰνόγαρον, winesauce, Apic. 1, 31.
oenogarum.short: oenŏgărum, i, n., = οἰνόγαρον, winesauce, Apic.

oenomaus.full: Oenŏmăus, i, m., = Οἰνόμαος, a king of Elis and Pisa, the father of Hippodamia, grandfather of Atreus and Thyestes, and father-in-law of Pelops, Hyg. Fab. 8, 4; 250; Enn. ap. Cic. Tusc. 3, 12, 26 (Trag. v. 398 Vahl.); Cic. Fam. 9, 16, 4; Stat. Th. 1, 274.— The title of a tragedy of Attius: Oenomao tuo nihil utor, Cic. Fam. 9, 16, 4; cf. id. ib. § 7.
oenomaus.short: Oenŏmăus, i, m., = Οἰνόμαος, a king of Elis and Pisa, the father of Hippodamia, grandfather of Atreus and Thyestes, and father-in-law of Pelops, Hyg.

oenomeli.full: oenŏ-mĕli, ĭtos (oenŏmĕlum, Isid. 20, 3, 11), n., = οἰνόμελι, wine-honey, a kind of mead, Dig. 33, 6, 9; cf. Pall. 11, 17 init.

oenone.full: Oenōnē, ēs, f., = Ὀινώνη. A Phrygian nymph, the daughter of Cebren, beloved by Paris, but afterwards deserted by him, Ov. H. 5; Dict. Cret. 3, 21; Suet. Dom. 10.— Another name for the island of Ægina, Plin. 4, 12, 19, § 57.

oenophorium.full: oenŏphŏrĭum, ii, n., = οἰνοφόριον, a wine-basket, Paul. Sent. 3, 6, 90.
oenophorium.short: oenŏphŏrĭum, ii, n., = οἰνοφόριον, a wine-basket, Paul.

oenophorum.full: oenŏ-phŏrum, i, n., or -us, i, m., = οινοφόρος, a wine-holder, wine-basket of unknown shape, Lucil. ap. Non. 173, 16; Mart. 6, 88; Hor. S. 1, 6, 109; Juv. 6, 426; 7, 11; Pers. 5, 140; Mart. 6, 89; cf. Becker's Gallus, 3, p. 233 (2d ed.).
oenophorum.short: oenŏ-phŏrum, i, n., or -us, i, m., = οινοφόρος, a wine-holder, wine-basket of unknown shape, Lucil.

oenophorus.full: Oenŏ-phŏrus, i, f., = Ὀινοφόπος, the wine-carrier, a female statue of Praxiteles, Plin. 34, 8, 19, § 69.
oenophorus.short: Oenŏ-phŏrus, i, f., = Ὀινοφόπος, the wine-carrier, a female statue of Praxiteles, Plin.

oenopia.full: Oenŏpĭa, ae, f., = Οἰνοπία, another name for the island of Ægina, Ov. M. 7, 472 and 473 Jahn N. cr.—Hence, Oenŏ-pĭus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Œnopia, Œnopian: muri, Ov. M. 7, 490.
oenopia.short: Oenŏpĭa, ae, f., = Οἰνοπία, another name for the island of Ægina, Ov.

oenopion.full: Oenŏpĭon, ōnis, m., = Οἰνοπίων, a king of Chios, the father of Merope, Cic. Arat. 673; Germ. Arat. 656; Avien. Ar. 1182.
oenopion.short: Oenŏpĭon, ōnis, m., = Οἰνοπίων, a king of Chios, the father of Merope, Cic.

oenopius.full: Oenŏpĭus, a, um, v. Oenopia, II.

oenopolium.full: oenŏ-pōlīum, i, n., = οἰνοπωλεῖον, a wine-shop, vintry, Plaut. As. 1, 3, 48.
oenopolium.short: oenŏ-pōlīum, i, n., = οἰνοπωλεῖον, a wine-shop, vintry, Plaut.

oenothera.full: oenŏthēra, ae, f., or oenŏthēris, ĭdis, f., = οινοθήρα or οἰνοθηρίς (also ŏnŏ-thēra, onŏthūris), a plant, the juice of which, drunk in wine, produces sleep: onothera, sive onear, hilaritatem afferens in vino, Plin. 26, 11, 69, § 111; acc. onothurim, id. 24, 17. 102, § 167; 26, 14, 87, § 146.
oenothera.short: oenŏthēra, ae, f., or oenŏthēris, ĭdis, f., = οινοθήρα or οἰνοθηρίς (also ŏnŏ-thēra, onŏthūris), a plant, the juice of which, drunk in wine, produces sleep: onothera, sive onear, hilaritatem afferens in vino, Plin.

oenotria.full: Oenōtrĭa, ae, f., = Οἰνωτρία. Lit., the extreme south-eastern part of Italy, in the oldest geography of that country (afterwards the territory of the Bruttians and Lucanians): Oenotria dicta est vel a vino optimo, quod in Italiā nascitur, vel ut Varro dicit ab Oenotro rege Sabinorum. Alii Itali fratrem Oenotrum tradunt ex Arcadiā in Italiam venisse cum Pelasgis et-eam sibi cognominem fuisse, Serv. Verg. A. 1, 532.— Transf., poet., Italy, in gen., Claud. I. Cons. Stil. 2, 262; so id. ib. 146.— He

oenus1.full: oenus, a, um, an ancient form for unus, q. v.
oenus1.short: oenus, a, um, an ancient form for unus, q.

oenus2.full: Oenūs, acc. -unta, m., a river in Laconia which flows into the Eurotas, now the Kelefina, Liv 34, 28, 1.

oenusa.full: Oenūsa, ae, f., an island near Chios, Plin. 5, 31, 38, § 137; Mela, 2, 7.
oenusa.short: Oenūsa, ae, f., an island near Chios, Plin.

oenusae.full: Oenūsae, ārum, f., three islands near Messenia, Plin. 4, 12, 19, § 55.
oenusae.short: Oenūsae, ārum, f., three islands near Messenia, Plin.

oeonae.full: Oeōnae, ārum, f., fabulous islands in the north of Europe: in quīs ovis avium et avenis incolae vivant, Plin. 4, 13, 27, § 94.
oeonae.short: Oeōnae, ārum, f., fabulous islands in the north of Europe: in quīs ovis avium et avenis incolae vivant, Plin.

oeonistice.full: oeōnistĭcē, ēs, f., = οἰωνιστικη, the divination of the augurs, augury (postclass.), Mart. Cap. 9, § 894.
oeonistice.short: oeōnistĭcē, ēs, f., = οἰωνιστικη, the divination of the augurs, augury (postclass.), Mart.

oestrus.full: oestrus, i, m., = οἶστρος. Lit., a gad-fly, horse-fly, breese (pure Lat. asilus): volitans, cui nomen asilo Romanum est, oestrum Graii vertere vocantes, Verg. G. 3, 148: nascuntur in extremis favis apes grandiores, quae ceteras fugant: oestrus vocatur hoc malum, Plin. 11, 16, 16, § 47.— Transf., frenzy of a prophet or poet, inspiration, enthusiasm (in post-Aug. poets), Stat. Th. 1, 32; Nemes. Cyneg. 3; Juv. 4, 123; cf.: oestrum furor Graeco vocabulo, Paul. ex Fest. p. 195 Müll.

oesus.full: oesus, an ancient form for usus, q. v.
oesus.short: oesus, an ancient form for usus, q.

oesyma.full: Oesўma, ae, f., a city in Italy, Liv. 44, 26.
oesyma.short: Oesўma, ae, f., a city in Italy, Liv.

oesypum.full: oesўpum, i, n., = οἴσυπος, the greasy sweat and dirt of unwashed wool, Plin. 29, 2, 10, § 35; cf. id. 29, 6, 36, § 112; 30, 4, 10, § 28.—Used as a cosmetic by the Roman ladies, Ov. A. A. 3, 213; id. R. Am. 354.
oesypum.short: oesўpum, i, n., = οἴσυπος, the greasy sweat and dirt of unwashed wool, Plin.

oeta.full: Oeta, ae, or Oetē, ēs, f., = Οἴτη, the mountain range between Thessaly and Ætolia, where Hercules ascended the funeral pile, now Katavothron, Plin. 4, 7, 13, § 28; Liv. 36, 15; Luc. 8, 800; Sen. Herc. Oet. 862; Cic. Tusc. 2, 7, 19; Ov. M. 9, 165; 204; 230; id. H. 9, 147; Verg. Cul. 201.—Prov.: tibi deserit Hesperus Oeten, your wish is gratified, Verg. E. 8, 30.—Hence, Oe-taeus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Œta: in monte Oetaeo, Att. ap. Cic. N. D. 3, 16, 41: juga, Prop. 1, 13, 24: deus, i. e.
oeta.short: Oeta, ae, or Oetē, ēs, f., = Οἴτη, the mountain range between Thessaly and Ætolia, where Hercules ascended the funeral pile, now Katavothron, Plin.

oetor.full: oetor, 3, an old form for utor, q. v.
oetor.short: oetor, 3, an old form for utor, q.

oetum.full: oetum, i, n., = οἶτον, an Egyptian plant, otherwise unknown, Plin. 21, 15, 52, § 88.
oetum.short: oetum, i, n., = οἶτον, an Egyptian plant, otherwise unknown, Plin.

ofella1.full: ŏfella, ae, f. dim. offa, a bite, bit, mouthful, morsel (post-Aug.). Lit., Juv. 11, 142; Mart. 10, 48, 15; 14, 221, 1; Prud. στεφ. 10, 383.— Transf., a little piece or bit, Ser. Samm. 46, 840.

ofella2.full: Ofella, ae, m., a Roman surname: Q. Lucretius Ofella, Cic. Brut. 48, 178; Liv. Ep. 86; 88; Vell. 2, 27, 5.
ofella2.short: Ofella, ae, m., a Roman surname: Q.

ofellus.full: Ŏfellus, i, m., a Stoic, Hor. S. 2, 2, 2.
ofellus.short: Ŏfellus, i, m., a Stoic, Hor.

offa.full: offa, ae, f. Lit., a bite, bit, morsel; esp. a little ball or pellet made of flour: antiqui offam vocabant abscisum globi formā, ut manu glomeratam pultem, Paul. ex Fest. s. v. poenitam offam, p. 242 Müll.: offam eripere alicui, Enn. ap. Plin. 18, 8, 19, § 84 (Enn. p. 181 Vahl.); Varr. R. R. 3, 5: offam obicit, Verg. A. 6, 420: pultis, Cic. Div. 2, 35, 73.—Prov.: inter os et offam, = Engl. between the cup and the lip, Cato ap. Gell. 13, 18 (17), 1; cf.: vetus est proverbium inter os et offam, id

offarcinatus.full: offarcĭnātus (obf-), a, um, Part. [obfarcino], stuffed or crammed full, loaded (eccl. Lat.); with abl., Tert. adv. Marc. 4, 24.

offarius.full: offārĭus, a, um, adj. offa, dealing with morsels: cocus, a maker of minced meat (post-class.), Isid. Orig. 20, 2.

offatim.full: offātim, adv. id., in bits, by bits or little pieces (ante- and post-class.): jam hercle ego te hic hac (machaerā) offatim conficiam, Plaut. Truc. 2, 7, 52; Isid. Orig. 20, 2.

offaveo.full: offăvĕo, ēre, v. n. ob-faveo, to meet with applause, Cypr. Ep. 1.

offectio.full: offectĭo, ōnis, f. officio, a staining, coloring, dyeing (post-class.), Arn. 5, 164.

offectores.full: offectōres colorum infectores, Paul. ex Fest. p. 192 Müll.; cf.: infectores qui alienum colorem in lanam coiciunt: offectores, qui proprio colori novum officiunt, id. ib. p. 112 Müll.

offectus1.full: offectus, a um, Part., from officio.
offectus1.short: offectus, a um, Part., from officio.

offectus2.full: offectus, ūs, m. officio, a bewitching, a charm (poet.), Grat. Cyn. 406.

offendiculum.full: offendĭcŭlum, i, n. 1. offendo, a stumbling-block, obstacle, hinderance, cause of offence (post-Aug.): sunt enim in hac offendicula nonnulla. Plin. Ep. 9, 11, 1; Vulg. 1 Cor. 8, 9; id. Isa. 57, 14; Paul. Nol. Carm. 27, 96.

offendix.full: offendix, ĭcis, f. ob, and Sanscr. root bandh, to bind; Goth. binda, a tie; cf. Gr. πεῖσμα, the knot of a band, or the band itself: Titius ap. Paul. ex Fest. p. 205 Müll.: offendices dicebant ligaturae nodos, quibus apex retinebatur. Id, cum pervenisset ad mentum, dicebant offendimentum, Paul. ex Fest. p. 204: offendices nodi quibus libri signantur, Gloss. Isid.

offendo1.full: offendo, di, sum, 3, v. a. and n. obfendo. to hit, thrust, strike, or dash against something (syn.: illido, impingo; class.). Lit.: offendere caput ad fornicem, Quint. 6, 3, 67: latus vehementer, Cic. Clu. 62, 175: coxam, to hurt himself in the haunch, Col. 5, 9, 1: pedem, Auct. B. Hisp. 23; Ov. F. 2, 720: solido, against something solid, Hor. S. 2, 1, 78: in scopulis offendit puppis, strikes on, Ov. P. 4, 14, 22: in redeundo offenderunt, ran aground, Caes. B. C. 3, 8: in cornua, Sol. 40: ne que

offendo2.full: offendo, ĭnis, f. 1. offendo, an offence, Afran. ap. Non. 146, 32 (offendo, offensio, Non.).

offensa.full: offensa, ae, f. 1. offendo, like repulsa, from repello, a striking or grating against any thing. Lit. (very rare): donec cerussae similis fiat, nulla dentium offensa, and does not grit against the teeth, Plin. 34, 10, 22, § 104: sine offensis fricantium, id. 35, 15, 52, § 184.— Trop. Offence, disfavor, displeasure, hatred; enmity: quin magnā in offensā sim apud Pompeium, Cic. Att. 9, 2, a, 2: quod offensae fuerit in istā cunctatione, te subisse, to incur hatred, Cael. ap. Cic. Fam. 8, 16, 2: gra

offensaculum.full: offensācŭlum, i, n. offenso, a striking against, a tripping, stumbling (postclass.). Lit.: crebris offensaculis contusa crura, App. M. 9, p. 221, 3.— Transf., the object against which one stumbles, a stumbling-block: lapis ecce nostro fixus offensaculo est, Prud. Apoth. 45; so, adversarius nostris offensacula pedibus latenter opponit, Lact. Opt. D. 1.

offensatio.full: offensātĭo, ōnis, f. id., a hitting or striking against any thing (post-Aug.). Lit., Plin. 28, 16, 62, § 221: ut offensatione illā (hastae) commoneretur (Demosthenes), Quint. 11, 3, 130.— Trop., a stumbling, tripping; a slip, blunder: debemus patienter ferre offensationes memoriae labentis, Sen. Ben. 5, 25, 6.

offensator.full: offensātor, ōris, m. id., one who stumbles or blunders in speaking, Quint. 10, 3, 20.

offensibilis.full: offensĭbĭlĭs, e, adj. 1. offendo, liable to stumble, stumbling (eccl. Lat.): qui offensibilibus et caducis gressibus per viam mortis incedit (al. offensilibus), Lact. 4, 26, 10.

offensio.full: offensĭo, ōnis, f. 1. offendo, a striking against any thing; a tripping, stumbling (class.). Lit.: pedis offensio, Cic. Div. 2, 40, 84; in plur.: offensiones pedum, Plin. 2, 7, 5, § 24: dentium, Lact. Opif. Dei, 10, 13. —Absol.: offensione sonitūs, Vitr. 9, 8, 3.— Transf., that against which one stumbles, a stumbling-block: ut nihil offensionis haberet, Cic. Univ. 6, 15.— Trop. An offence given to any one; hence, disfavor, aversion, disgust, dislike, hatred, discredit, bad reputation, Cic. Div.

offensiuncula.full: offensĭuncŭla, ae, f. dim. offensio, II. B., a slight offence, disgust, displeasure; a slight mishap (class.): si qua offensiuncula facta est animi tui, Cic. Fam. 13, 1, 4: in istā aedilitate offensiuncula accepta, some slight check, id. Planc. 21, 51.

offenso.full: offenso, āvi, ātum, 1, v. freq. a. 1. offendo, to strike or dash against (not in Cic. or Caes.). Lit.: sponte suā offensando ut semina rerum, Lucr. 2, 1059; so id. 6, 1053: omnes offensare capita, dash their heads against the wall, Liv. 25, 37.— Trop., to stumble, trip, falter in speaking, Quint. 10, 7, 10.—(Offensatus, Quint. 10, 3, 20, is a false reading for offensator, q.v.).

offensor.full: offensor, ōris, m. id., an offender, injurer (eccl. Lat.): in gratiam suis cum offensoribus redire, Arn. 7, 216.

offensus1.full: offensus, a, um, Part. and P. a., from 1. offendo.

offensus2.full: offensus, ūs, m. 1. offendo, a striking against, a shock (poet. and in post-class. prose). Lit., Lucr. 2, 223; 4, 359; Tert. adv. Marc. 4, 39.— Transf. A lighting upon, meeting with: per offensus armorum, Stat. Th. 12, 283.— An offence, vexation, annoyance: sin vita in offensu est, Lucr. 3, 941.

offerentia.full: offĕrentĭa, ae, f. offero, a presenting, offering (eccl. Lat.): causarum, Tert. adv. Marc. 24.

offero.full: offĕro (obf-), obtŭli, oblātum, v. a. ob-fero, to bring before; to present, offer; to show, exhibit (class.; cf. obicio, ostendo). In gen.: incommode illis fors obtulerat adventum meum, Ter. Hec. 3, 3, 10; cf.: opportune te obtulisti mihi obviam, id. Ad. 3, 2, 24; id. Hec. 5, 3, 10; Cic. Att. 3, 10, 2: strictamque aciem venientibus offert, presents, opposes, Verg. A. 6, 291: speciem offerre, to present a false appearance, Cic. Div. 1, 37, 81.—In pass.: offerri, mid., to show one's self, appear;

offertor.full: offertor (obf-), ōris, m. offero, an offerer (late Lat.), Commod. Instruct. 39.

offertorium.full: offertōrĭum (obf-). ii, n. id., a place to which offerings were brought, an offertory (eccl. Lat.): offertorium tali ex causā sumpsit vocabulum. Fertum enim dicitur oblatio, quae altari offertur, et sacrificatur a pontificibus, a quo offertorium nomina tur, quasi propter fertum, Isid. Orig. 6, 19.

offerumenta1.full: offĕrŭmenta (obf-), ae, f. id., a present; comically, of a stripe, cut: offerumentas in tergo habere, Plaut. Rud. 3, 4, 48.

offerumenta2.full: offĕrŭmenta, ōrum, n. id., offerings: offerumenta dicebant quae offerebant (sc. dis), Paul. ex Fest. p. 188 Müll.

offex.full: offex, ĭcis, m. officio, a hinderer: offex, impeditor, qui officit, Gloss. Isid.

officialis.full: offĭcĭālis, e, adj. officium, of or belonging to duty, office, or service, official (post-class.). Adj.: libri officiales, which treat of duties, Lact. 6, 11, 9; 6, 18, 15: operae, official performances, Dig. 38, 1, 6.— Subst.: offĭcĭālis, is, m., a magistrate's servant or attendant, an official (for the class. apparitor), App. M. 1, p. 113 fin.: praefecti, Dig. 36, 4, 5; Paul. Sent. 5, 12, 6: universi officiales diversorum officiorum, Cod. Th. 8, 7, 2; Inscr. Orell. 2952.— In gen., a servant, a

officialitas.full: offĭcĭālĭtas, ātis, f. officialis, a body of attendants (late Lat.), Inc. Quu. ex Utroq. Test. 101.

officina.full: offĭcīna, ae, f. contr. from opificina, from opifex; the uncontracted prim. form, opĭfĭcīna, is still found in Plaut. Mil. 3, 3, 7, and Jul. Val. Res Gest. Alex. M. 3, 83 fin. Mai, a workshop, manufactory (class.; cf. fabrica). Lit.: nec enim quicquam ingenuum potest habere officina, Cic. Off. 1, 42, 150: instituit officinam Syracusis in regiā maximam, Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 24, § 54: armorum, a manufactory of arms, Caes. B. C. 1, 34; Cic. Phil. 7, 4, 13; Nep. Ages. 3, 2; for which, ferraria, Auct. B.

officinator.full: offĭcīnātor, ōris, m. officina, one who keeps a workshop, a master-workman, an artificer, artist (post-Aug.), Vitr. 6, 11: noster, App. M. 9, p. 219, 28; Inscr. Orell. 1090: OFFICINATORES ET NVMMVLARI OFFICINARVM ARGENTARIARVM, ib. 3226: OFF. and OFFIC. MONETAE, ib. 3227.

officinatrix.full: offĭcīnātrix, īcis, f. officinator, a woman that keeps a workshop, Inscr. Orell. 4257.

officio.full: offĭcĭo (obf-), ēci, ectum, 3, v. n. and a. [ob-facio], to come in the way of, to hinder, oppose, thwart, obstruct (class.; syn. obsto). Lit. Neutr.: nunc quidem paululum, inquit, a sole: offecerat videlicet apricanti, hindered him from sunning himself, stood before him so as to intercept the sunshine, Cic. Tusc. 5, 32, 92: luminibus, to obstruct one's light: jus vel altius tollendi aedes aut non tollendi, ne luminibus vicini officiatur, Gai. Inst. 2, 31; Dig. 8, 2, 2; 10; 23; 39, 1, 5 et saep.—

officiosa.full: Offĭcĭōsa, ae, f. officiosus, a Roman surname, Inscr. Malvas. Marm. Fels. p. 57.

officiositas.full: offĭcĭōsĭtas, ātis, f. officiosus, obligingness, complaisance, readiness to serve (post-class.), Sid. Carm. 23, 478.

officiosus.full: offĭcĭōsus, a, um, adj. officium. Full of courtcousness or complaisance, obliging, ready to serve (esp. towards one's superiors; class.; syn. studiosus): homo, Cic. Fam. 13, 21, 2: amicitia, id. Planc. 19, 46: sedulitas, Hor. Ep. 1, 7, 8: voluntas, Ov. P. 3, 2, 17.—Comp.: estne quisquam, qui tibi officiosior, liberaliorque videatur? Cic. Rosc. Com. 6, 18; id. Att. 13, 45, 3.—Sup.: officiosissima natio candidatorum, Cic. Pis. 23, 55; for which with summe: homines Lampsaceni summe in omnes cives R

officiperda.full: offĭcĭperda, ae, m., and offĭcĭper-dus, i, m. officium-perdo. One who makes an ill use of the favors of others, Cato, Distich. 3, 87.— One who throws away his labor, is not rewarded: officiperdi, qui sui laboris non habent remunerationem, Gloss. Isid.
officiperda.short: offĭcĭperda, ae, m., and offĭcĭper-dus, i, m.

officium.full: offĭcĭum, ii, n. for opificium, opus and facio, qs. that which one does for another, a service, whether of free will or of (external or moral) necessity (class.; cf.: studium, beneficium, meritum, munus). A voluntary service, a kindness, favor, courtesy, rendered to one whose claim to it is recognized; while beneficium is a service rendered where there is no claim: officium esse filii, uxoris, earum personarum, quas necessitudo suscitat et ferre opem jubet, Sen. Ben. 3, 18, 1. In gen.: altera se

offigo.full: offīgo (obf-), xi, xum, 3, v. a. ob-figo, to drive in, fix in, fasten (ante- and postclass.): furcas circum offigito, Cato, R. R. 48, 2; Lex Puteol. ap. Grut. 207, 1: ita densos offigunt implicantque ramos, Liv. 33, 5, 10 Drak. N. cr.: in crucem currere ... ut offigantur bis pedes, bis bracchia, Plaut. Most. 2, 1, 13: manum alicujus ad ostii tabulam grandi clavo, App. M. 4, p. 147, 3.

offilius.full: Offilĭus (Ofil-), ii, m., the name of a Roman gens.—Esp.: A. Offilius, a celebrated lawyer, a friend and at one time a creditor of Cicero, Cic. Fam. 7, 21; 16, 24, 1; id. Att. 13, 37, 4; Dig. 1, 2, 2, § 44.
offilius.short: Offilĭus (Ofil-), ii, m., the name of a Roman gens.—Esp.: A.

offirmate.full: offirmātē (obf-), adv., v. offirmo, P. a. fin.

offirmatus.full: offirmātus (obf-), a, um, Part. and P. a., from offirmo.

offirmo.full: offirmo (obf-), āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. and n. ob-firmo, to render firm, durable, or steadfast (class. only in the P. a.). Lit.: pertica, quā stabuli fores offirmari solebant, arrepta, to fasten, bolt, App. M. 7, p. 200: corium, id. ib.— Trop., to hold fast to, persevere in: certum offirmare est viam me, quam decrevi persequi, Ter. Hec. 3, 5, 4: se, to persist, be obstinate, id. Heaut. 5, 5, 8: vir impius procaciter obfirmat vultum suum, Vulg. Prov. 21, 29: faciem, id. Ezek. 4, 3: spiritus, id. Dan.

offlecto.full: offlecto (obfl-), ĕre, v. a. ob-flecto, to turn about: navem, Plaut. Rud. 4, 3, 74.

offoco.full: offōco (obf-; collat. form offuco; v. in the foll.), āre, v. a. ob-faux, to strangle, choke, suffocate (post-class.): cum oflocan das invicem fauces praebuissent (al. effo candas), Flor. 2, 11, 6; Sen. Brev. Vit. 2, 3: quicumque fluctus ejus offocant, Tert. Idol. 24: offucare aquam in fauces ad sorbendum dare, Paul. ex Fest. p. 192 Müll.

offrenatus.full: offrēnātus (obfr-), a, um, Part. [obfreno], bridled; only trop., curbed, tamed (ante- and post-class.), Plaut. Capt. 3, 5, 96: Cerberus, App. M. 6, p. 181, 8; id. Mag. p. 323, 26.

offringo.full: offringo (obfr-), ēgi, actum, 3, v. a. ob-frango, t. t. of agriculture, i. q. iterare, to plough a second time; to cross-plough: terram cum primum arant, proscindere appellant; cum iterum, offringere dicunt, to cross-plough, Varr. R. R. 1, 29; id. ib. 32: glaebas, Col. 2, 11, 3; cf.: offringi terra dicitur, cum iterum transverso sulco aratur, Paul. ex Fest. p. 199 Müll.

offucia.full: offūcĭa, ae, f. ob-fucus, a paint, wash for the face (ante- and post-class.). Lit.: pigmentum ullum, neque cerussam Melinumve neque aliam ullam offuciam, Plaut. Most. 1, 3, 107.— Trop., a trick, delusion, Plaut. Capt. 3, 4, 123: id praestigiarum atque offuciarum genus, delusions, Gell. 14, 1, 2.

offudas.full: offudas, fallacias, Paul. ex Fest. p. 192 Müll. (al. offucias; v. offucia).

offula.full: offŭla (sync. offla), ae, f. dim. offa, a little bit, a small piece (peculiar to the vulg. lang.; cf. Suet. Claud. 40): offula dicta, ut offa minima e suere, Varr. L. L. 5, § 110 Müll.: offulam cum duabus costis, id. R. R. 2, 4, 11: carnis, spisse componuntur, Col. 12, 53, 4: polentae caseatae, App. M. 1, p. 103, 34: panis, Veg. Vet. 4, 18; cf. Fall. 1, 29, 4.—Prov.: quis potest sine offulā vivere? Claud. ap. Suet. Cland. 40.—Transf., as a term of abuse applied to a bad slave: quid faciat crucis

offulcio.full: offulcĭo (obf-) (si), tum, 4, v. a. ob-fulcio, to stop up (Appul.): vulnus spongiā offulciens, App. M. 1, p. 108, 17: multis laciniis offulto vulnere, id. ib. 4, p. 147, 14.

offulgeo.full: offulgĕo (obf-), si, 2, v. n. ob-fulgeo, to shine against or upon; to appear (not ante-Aug.). Lit.: continuo nova lux oculis offulsit, Verg. A. 9, 110: dextrum offulsit conatibus omen, Sil. 13, 114: species mei amici, Ps. -Quint. Decl. 9, 7.— Trop.: lucrum, Ps. -Quint. Decl. 12, 4: ortus imperii nostri, Cod. Theod. 2, 8, 25.

offultus.full: offultus, a. um, Part., from offulcio.

offundo.full: offundo (obf-), ūdi, ūsum, 3, v. a. obundo. To pour before or around; to pour out, pour down (class.). Lit.: cibum (avibus), Plaut. As. 1, 3, 64; id. Trin. 4, 3, 84.— Transf., mid., to pour itself out; to spread, extend: ut piscibus aqua, nobis aër crassus offunditur, i. e. surrounds us, Cic. Ac. 2, 25, 81: rubor gravissimis quoque viris offunditur, Sen. Ep. 11, 3: cum ignis oculorum cum eo igne, qui est ob os offusus, se confudit, Cic. Univ. 14: asinus offunditur, tumbles down, App. M. p. 144,

offuscatio.full: offuscātĭo (obf-), ōnis, f. offusco, a darkening, obscuring; only trop., a vilifying, degrading (eccl. Lat.): deorum, Tert. ad Nat. 1, 10; id. Res Carn. 43; Vulg. Ecclus. 41, 24.

offusco.full: offusco (obf-), āre, v. a. ob-fusco, to darken, obscure; only trop., to vilify, degrade (eccl. Lat.): justitiam, Tert. adv. Marc. 2, 12: aliquem, id. Spect. 22: quoniam offuscata sum, Ambros. in Psa. 118, Serm. 2, § 9.

offusus.full: offūsus (obf-), a, um, Part., from offundo.
offusus.short: offūsus (obf-), a, um, Part., from offundo.

ogdoas.full: ogdŏas, ădis, f., = ὀγδοάς. In gen., the number eight (eccl. Lat.), Hier. Ep. 36, n. 9.— In partic., one of the œons of Valentinus, Tert. adv. Val. 7 and 20; id. Anim. 37.

oggannio.full: oggannĭo (obg-), īvi or ĭi, ītum, 4, v. n. ob-gannio, to yelp, snarl, or growl at (ante- and post-class.): ogganniunt, Enn. ap. Non. 147, 11: quin centies eadem imperem atque ogganniam, Plaut. As. 2, 4, 16: habet haec se quod, dum vivat, usque ad aurem ogganiat, Ter. Phorm. 5, 9, 41: aliquid in aurem alicujus, App. M. 2, p. 115, 16.
oggannio.short: oggannĭo (obg-), īvi or ĭi, ītum, 4, v.

oggero.full: oggĕro (obg-), ĕre, v. a. ob-gero, to proffer, bring, give (Plautin.): (amor) amarum ad satietatem oggerit, Plaut. Cist. 1, 1, 72: osculum alicui, id. Truc. 1, 2, 8; id. Ps. 3, 2, 23.

oglasa.full: Oglasa, ae, f., an island near Corsica, now Monte Christo, Plin. 3, 6, 12, § 80.
oglasa.short: Oglasa, ae, f., an island near Corsica, now Monte Christo, Plin.

ogulnius.full: Ogulnĭus, ĭi, m., a Roman proper name, Liv. 10, 6; 27, 3.
ogulnius.short: Ogulnĭus, ĭi, m., a Roman proper name, Liv.

ogyges.full: Ōgўges, is, Ōgўgus, i, and Ōgў-gĭus, ĭi, m., = Ὠγύγης, Ὤγυγος, Ὠγύγιος, the mythic founder and king of Thebes, in Bœtia, in whose reign a great deluge is said to have occurred: oppidum Thebae, quod rex Ogyges aedificarit, Varr. R. R. 2, 1, 2: ante cataclysmon Ogygi, id. ib. § 3: hoc factum Ogyge rege dicebant, Varr. Fragm. ap. Aug. Civ. Dei, 21, 8.—Form Ogygus, Paul. ex Fest. p. 179 Müll.—Form Ogygius, Aug. Civ. Dei, 18, 8.—Hence, ōgўgĭ-dae, ārum, m., the descendants of Ogyges, poet. for the The
ogyges.short: Ōgўges, is, Ōgўgus, i, and Ōgў-gĭus, ĭi, m., = Ὠγύγης, Ὤγυγος, Ὠγύγιος, the mythic founder and king of Thebes, in Bœtia, in whose reign a great deluge is said to have occurred: oppidum Thebae, quod rex Ogyges aedificarit, Varr.

ogygia.full: Ōgўgĭa, ae, f. One of the seven daughters of Amphion and Niobe. Hyg. Fab. 69.— A gate at Thebes, Hyg. Fab. 69.— An island near Italy, in which Calypso was said to have dwelt, Plin. 3, 10, 15, § 96.

ogygius.full: Ōgўgĭus, a, um, v. Ogyges, B.

oh.full: oh, interj., an expression for the most various emotions of the mind—for surprise, both joyful and painful; for great pleasure or sorrow; for earnest wishing, admiration, aversion, etc.—oh! O! ah! oh, tibi ego ut credam, furcifer? Ter. And. 3, 5, 12: oh, iniquus es, id. Heaut. 5, 3, 8: oh perii! Plaut. Cas. 2, 3, 19: oh, probus homo sum, id. Most. 1, 3, 86.—Repeated, oh, oh, oh, as an exclamation of lamentation, Plaut. Capt. 2, 1, 6: oh, oh, as an exclamation of exultation, id. Most. 1, 4, 12 (a
oh.short: oh, interj., an expression for the most various emotions of the mind—for surprise, both joyful and painful;

ohe.full: ŏhē, interj., ho! holloa! soho! ho there! ohe, inquam, si quid audis, Plaut. As. 2, 3, 4: ohe, Jam satis est, id. Stich. 5, 4, 52; Hor. S. 1, 5, 12; id. ib. 2, 5, 96; so Mart. 4, 91, 1 and 9.
ohe.short: ŏhē, interj., ho! holloa! soho! ho there! ohe, inquam, si quid audis, Plaut.

oho.full: ŏho, interj., an exclamation of surprise or joy, oho! aha! oho, amabo, quid illuc non properas? Plaut. Poen. 1, 2, 51; id. Ps. 4, 2, 32 (dub. in both passages; al. ohe).
oho.short: ŏho, interj., an exclamation of surprise or joy, oho! aha! oho, amabo, quid illuc non properas? Plaut.

oi.full: oi, interj., an exclamation of complaint, of one weeping: Ph. I intro nunc jam. Do. Oi! ei! Ter. Eun. 4, 4, 47: oi! hui! id. Phorm, 4, 3, 58.
oi.short: oi, interj., an exclamation of complaint, of one weeping: Ph.

oica.full: oica, ae, f., a precious stone, otherwise unknown, Plin. 37, 10, 65, § 176; Isid. Orig. 16, 12, 1.
oica.short: oica, ae, f., a precious stone, otherwise unknown, Plin.

oiei.full: oiei, interj., a cry of lamentation, Ter. Eun. 4, 4, 47; id. Phorm. 4, 3, 58.
oiei.short: oiei, interj., a cry of lamentation, Ter.

oileus.full: Ŏīleus (trisyl.), ĕi (ēī) and ĕŏs, m., = Ὀϊλευς. A king of Locris, father of the Ajax who violated Cassandra, and who was called, from his parentage, Ajax Oilei (to distinguish him from Ajax Telamonius), Cic. Tusc. 3, 29, 71: nec mihi Oilei proferatur Ajax, Lucil. ap. Non. 158, 12: unius ab noxam et furias Ajacis Oilei, Verg. A. 1, 41; in the form Oileos, Ov. M. 12, 622: multos, inquit Antonius, possum tuos Ajaces Oileos nominare, Cic. de Or. 2, 66, 265.—Transf., Ajax: fulmine et ponto moriens O
oileus.short: Ŏīleus (trisyl.), ĕi (ēī) and ĕŏs, m., = Ὀϊλευς.

oinos.full: oinos, a, um, an archaic orthog. for unus, q. v.
oinos.short: oinos, a, um, an archaic orthog.

olax.full: ŏlax, ācis, adj. oleo, smelling, having a smell, odorous (post-class.), Mart. Cap. 1, § 82.

olbia.full: Olbĭa, ae, f., = Ὀλβία, the name of several cities. A city in Pamphylia, Plin. 5, 27, 26, § 96.— A city in Bithynia, afterwards called Nicaea, now Izmid, Plin. 5, 32, 43, § 148.—Hence, Olbĭānus, a, um, adj.: sinus, now Golfo d' Izmid, Mela, 1, 19, 4.— A city in Gallia Narbonensis, Mela, 2, 5.— A city in Sardinia, now Terranova, Cic. Q. Fr. 2, 6, 7; 2, 8, 1; Flor. 2, 2, 6; Val. Max. 5, 1, 2.—Hence, Olbĭensis, e, adj., of or belonging to Olbia, Olbian: epistula. from Olbia, Cic. Q. Fr. 2, 3, 7: ag
olbia.short: Olbĭa, ae, f., = Ὀλβία, the name of several cities.

olbiopolis.full: Olbĭŏpŏlis, is, f., a city in Sarmatia, Plin. 4, 12, 26, § 82.—Hence. Olbĭŏpŏlī-ta, ae, adj., of or belonging to Olbiopolis or Olbia, in Sarmatia; only plur. subst., the inhabitants of that place, Capitol. Anton. 9.
olbiopolis.short: Olbĭŏpŏlis, is, f., a city in Sarmatia, Plin.

olca.full: olca, a false reading in Plin. 37, 10, 65, § 176; v. oica.
olca.short: olca, a false reading in Plin.

olcades.full: Olcădes, um, m., a people in Hispania Tarraconensis, beyond the Ebro, Liv. 21, 5.
olcades.short: Olcădes, um, m., a people in Hispania Tarraconensis, beyond the Ebro, Liv.

olciniates.full: Olcinĭātes, ium, m., the inhabitants of Olcinium, a seaport in Illyricum, the modern Dulcigno: immunes fore Olciniatas, Liv. 45, 26, 2.
olciniates.short: Olcinĭātes, ium, m., the inhabitants of Olcinium, a seaport in Illyricum, the modern Dulcigno: immunes fore Olciniatas, Liv.

olea.full: ŏlĕa, ae (dat. plur. oleabus, Gell. ap. Charis. 1, 40), = ἐλαία. Lit., an olive, olive-berry: olea ab elaea, Varr. L. L. 5, § 108 Müll.: oleas caducas, et albas condire, Cato, R. R. 58: oleam cogere, legere, stringere, verberare, id. ib. 144; cf. Plin. 15, 2, 3, § 12; Verg. G. 2, 302 al.— Transf., an olive-tree, Plaut. Stich. 5, 4, 9: agricola cum florem oleae videt, bacam quoque se visurum putat. Cic. Div. 2, 6, 16; so id. Rep. 3, 9, 15; Quint. 8, 6, 48; 8, 3, 8; 10: ure maris oleas, Ov. F. 4,

oleaceus.full: ŏlĕācĕus, a, um, adj. oleum, of the olive-tree; hence, like oil, oily (Plinian): liquor, Plin. 35, 15, 51, § 179 (al. oleique): folia oleacea (al. folia violae), id. 21, 4, 10, § 18.

oleagineus.full: ŏlĕāgĭnĕus, ŏlĕāgĭnĭus, and ŏlĕ-āgĭnus, a, um, adj. olea. Of or belonging to the olive-tree (for the class. olearius): oleagineum seminarium, Cato, R. R. 48: radix, Verg. G. 2, 31: virgulae, Nep. Thras. 4, 1: oleagineis coronis ministri triumphantium utebantur, quod Minerva dea belli esse putabatur, Paul. ex Fest. p. 192 Müll.— Resembling an olive-tree or an olive: vitis oleaginia, Col. 3, 2, 27 dub.: uva, Plin. 14, 3, 4, § 38.— Olive-colored: berylli oleagini, Plin. 37, 5, 20, § 77.
oleagineus.short: ŏlĕāgĭnĕus, ŏlĕāgĭnĭus, and ŏlĕ-āgĭnus, a, um, adj.

oleamen.full: ŏlĕāmen, ĭnis, and ŏlĕāmentum, i, n. oleum, an oil-ointment, Scrib. Comp. 222; 269.
oleamen.short: ŏlĕāmen, ĭnis, and ŏlĕāmentum, i, n.

olearis.full: ŏlĕāris, e, adj. id., of or belonging to oil, oil-: oleares cotes, i. e. which are moistened with oil, oil-stones, Plin. 34, 14, 41, § 146.

olearius.full: ŏlĕārĭus, a, um, adj. id., of or belonging to oil, oil- (class.): cella vinaria, olearia, Cato, R. R. 3; Cic. Sen. 16, 56: dolia, Plin. 15, 8, 8, § 33: mercatores, Dig. 50, 4, 5.— Subst.: ŏlĕārĭus, ii, m., an oilgrinder or oil-seller: in velabro olearii, Plaut. Capt. 3, 1, 29: diligentes, Col. 12, 50, 13.

olearos.full: Ōlĕăros (-us) or Ōlĭăros (-us), i, f., = Ὠλέαρος, Ὠλίαρος, one of the Cyclades, near Paros, now Antiparos, Mela, 2, 7, 11; Plin. 4, 12, 22, § 67; Verg. A. 3, 126.—Form Oliaros, Ov. M. 7, 469.
olearos.short: Ōlĕăros (-us) or Ōlĭăros (-us), i, f., = Ὠλέαρος, Ὠλίαρος, one of the Cyclades, near Paros, now Antiparos, Mela, 2, 7, 11;

oleastellus.full: ŏlĕastellus, i, m. dim. oleaster, a Calabrian species of olive-tree, Col. 12, 49, 3.

oleaster.full: ŏlĕaster, stri, m. olea, the wild olivetree, oleaster: oleaster, ἀγριελαία, Gloss. Philox.; Verg. G. 2, 182; 314; Ov. M. 14, 525; Plin. 17, 18, 30, § 129; 16, 44, 89, § 240; 15, 4, 5, § 19; Vulg. Rom. 11, 17 and 24.

oleastrum.full: ŏlĕastrum, i, n., i. q. oleaster, Calp.

oleatus.full: ŏlĕātus, a, um, adj. oleum, moistened with oil, put up in oil (post-class.): pultes oleatae, Cael. Aur. Acut. 2, 37, 208; Vulg. Num. 11, 8.

oleitas.full: ŏlĕĭtas, ātis, f. olea, the olive-gathering, olive-harvest (ante- and post-class.): ubi vindemia et oleitas facta erit, Cato, R. R. 68; id. ib. 144; Minuc. Fel. 17, 9; Mamert. Grat. Act. 22.

olenius2.full: Olĕnĭus, ii, m., a centurion under Drusus, Tac. A. 4, 72.
olenius2.short: Olĕnĭus, ii, m., a centurion under Drusus, Tac.

olenos1.full: Ōlĕnos or -us, i, m., = Ὤλενος, the husband of Lethœa, who was changed with her into a stone, Ov. M. 10, 69.—Hence, ōlĕnĭdes, ae, m., = Ὠλενίδης, the son of Olenus: Phoceaque Oleniden, Val. Fl. 3, 204.
olenos1.short: Ōlĕnos or -us, i, m., = Ὤλενος, the husband of Lethœa, who was changed with her into a stone, Ov.

olenos2.full: Ōlĕnos or -us, i, f., = Ὤλενος, an ancient city in Achaia, between Patrœ and Dymo, now Kato Akhaia, Plin. 4, 5, 6, § 13. — A city in Ætolia, Hyg. Astr. 2, 13; Sen. Troad. 826.—Hence, ōlĕnĭē, ēs, f. adj., Olenian; poet. for Achaian, Ætolian: capra Olenie, i. e. the goat of Amalthea, Manil. 5, 130.— ōlĕnĭus, a, um, adj., = Ὠλένιος, Olenian; poet. for Achaian, Ætolian: capella, Ov. F. 5, 113: pecus, the goat of Amalthea, id. H. 18, 188: Tydeus, of Calydon, in Ætolia, Stat. Th. 1, 402.
olenos2.short: Ōlĕnos or -us, i, f., = Ὤλενος, an ancient city in Achaia, between Patrœ and Dymo, now Kato Akhaia, Plin.

olens.full: ŏlens, entis, Part. and P. a., from oleo.

olentia.full: ŏlentĭa, ae, f. oleo, a smell, scent (eccl. Lat.), Tert. adv. Marc. 2, 22.

olentica.full: ŏlentĭca, ōrum, n. id., stinking places, Paul. ex Fest. p. 192 Müll.

olenticetum.full: ŏlentĭcētum, i, n. id., a stinking place, a dungheap, in trop. signif. (postclass.), Claud. Mam. Stat. Anim. 2, 9: olenticeta et fetutina, App. Mag. p. 278, 7.

oleo1.full: ŏlĕo, lŭi, 2 (collat. form ŏlo, ĕre; pres. subj. olat, Afran. ap. Non. 147, 2: olant, Plaut. Poen. 1, 2, 56; id. Most. 1. 3, 121; Pompon. ap. Non. 147, 5). v. n. and a. [root od-; cf. Gr. ὄζω; v. odor], to smell (class.; cf. odoro, fragro). To emit a smell, to smell of any thing. Lit., constr. absol. or with acc., less freq. with abl. of that of which any thing smells: quid (jura) olant, nescias, nisi id unum, male ut olere intellegas, Plaut. Most. 1, 3, 120 sq.; id. Truc. 2, 4, 3: rosa recens a

oleo2.full: ŏlĕo, ēre, 2 root al-; Sanscr. ar-, to rise; cf.: indoles, almus, alumnus. etc., to increase, grow, found only in the compounds: adoleo, aboleo, etc.

oleomella.full: ŏlĕŏmella, ae, f. oleum-mel, a fruittree peculiar to Syria, Isid. Orig. 17, 7, 11.

oleoselinum.full: ŏlĕŏsĕlīnum, i, n. oleum-selinon, a plant resembling parsley, Isid. Orig. 17, 11, 3.

oleosus.full: ŏlĕōsus, a, um, adj. oleum, oily, full of oil (Plin.): semen, Plin. 27, 12, 81, § 106: butyrum, id. 28, 9, 35, § 134.

olesco.full: ŏlesco, ēre, v. inch. n. [2. oleo], to grow: suboles ab olescendo, id est crescendo dictae, Paul. ex. Fest. p. 309 Müll.

oleto.full: ŏlēto, 1, v. a. 2. oletum, to foul, defile, Front. Aquaed. 97.

oletum1.full: ŏlētum, i, n. olea, a place planted with olive-trees; an olive-yard (ante-class. for the class. olivetum), Cato, R. R. 3, 5.

oletum2.full: ŏlētum, i, n. oleo, filth, dirt, excrement (very rare): oletum, stercus humanum, Paul. ex Fest. p. 203 Müll.: veto quisquam faxit oletum, Pers. 1, 112.

oleum.full: ŏlĕum, i, n., = ἔλαιον, oil, olive-oil. Lit., Cato, R. R. 64 sq.; Varr. R. R. 1, 55; Col. 12, 50; Plin. 15, 6, 6, § 21; Lex. Thor. lin. 95 Rudorff. p. 191: instillare oleum lumini, Cic. Sen. 11, 36: juventus Nudatos umeros oleo perfusa nitescit, Verg. A. 5, 135; Ov. Tr. 3, 12, 21: ungere caules oleo meliore, Hor. S. 2, 3, 125; Inscr. Orell. 748: BALNEVM CVM OLEO GRATVITO DEDIT, ib. 3738. —As a fig. of softness, gentleness: oleo tranquillior, quieter, gentler, stiller than oil, Plaut. Poen. 5, 4,
oleum.short: ŏlĕum, i, n., = ἔλαιον, oil, olive-oil.

olfacio.full: olfăcĭo, ēci, actum, 3 (uncontracted collat. form ŏlĕfăcĭo: olefacit, olefecit, olefactum, Not. Tir. p. 167), v. a. oleo-facio, to smell, scent something (class.; syn. odoror). Lit.: ea, quae gustemus, olfaciamus, tractemus, audiamus, Cic. Tusc. 5, 38, 111: unguentum, Cat. 13, 13: laurus folia trita olfactaque, smelled, Plin. 23, 8, 80, § 157: gith tusum, olfactum, id. 20, 17, 71, § 183 (olefactum, Jahn).—Absol.: delphini sagacissime olfaciunt, have a very keen scent, Plin. 11, 37, 50, § 137.— T

olfactatrix.full: olfactātrix, īcis, f. olfacto, she who scents or observes, Plin. 17, 24, 37, § 239.

olfacto.full: olfacto, āvi, ātum, 1, v. freq. a. olfacio, to smell at any thing (ante-class. and post-Aug.). Lit.: vestimentum, Plaut. Men. 1, 2, 56: membrana olfactata, Plin. 28, 16, 63, § 225 (al. olefacta): pulei ramum, id. 20, 14, 54, § 155.— Trop., to smell, snuff, detect, perceive: boves caelum olfactantes, Plin. 18, 35, 88, § 364.

olfactoria.full: olfactōrĭa, ae, f. olfacto, a nosegay, bouquet, Fronto de Orat. p. 1 Mai.

olfactoriolum.full: olfactōrĭŏlum, i, n. dim. olfactorium, a little smelling-bottle, scent-bottle (postclass.): olfactoriola vascula sunt muliebria, in quibus odoramenta gestantur, Isid. Orig. 19, 31; Vulg. Isa. 3, 20, et Hier. in loc.

olfactorium.full: olfactōrĭum, ii, n. olfacio, a nosegay or smelling-bottle (post-Aug.), Plin. 30, 11, 29, § 97; id. 20, 9, 36, § 92.

olfactrix.full: olfactrix, īcis, f., v. 1. for olfactatrix (q. v.), Plin. 17, 24, 37, § 239.

olfactus1.full: olfactus, a, um, Part., from olfacio.
olfactus1.short: olfactus, a, um, Part., from olfacio.

olfactus2.full: olfactus, ūs, m. olfacio. Lit., a smelling, smell (post-Aug.): thymi, Plin. 21, 21, 89, § 156 (al. olfacto thymo); 32, 3, 13, § 28; 35, 15, 51, § 182.— Transf., the sense of smell: delphini nec olfactūs vestigia habent, Plin. 11, 37, 50, § 137; 10, 70, 90, § 194.

olficus.full: olfĭcus, a, um, adj. olfacio, smelling, in a play on the word Alphicus, Mart. 9, 96, 1.

olidus.full: ŏlĭdus, a, um, adj. oleo, smelling, emitting a smell (mostly post-Aug.): vasa picata bene olida, Col. 12, 17: bene olidae amphorae, id. 12, 38, 4.—Of a bad smell, stinking, rank: olida capra, Hor. Ep. 1, 5, 29: praesaepia, Juv. 8, 157: senex, Suet Tib. 45: vulpes, Mart. 10, 37, 13: aures, Plin. 25, 5, 18, § 40.—Sup.: basia olidissima, Petr. 21.

oligochronius.full: ŏlĭgochrŏnĭus, a, um, adj., = ὀλιγοχρόνιος, lasting but a short time, shortlived (post-class.), Firm. Math. 3, 5.
oligochronius.short: ŏlĭgochrŏnĭus, a, um, adj., = ὀλιγοχρόνιος, lasting but a short time, shortlived (post-class.), Firm.

olim.full: ōlim, adv. ole, olle, ollus or olus, archaic for ille, with locative ending -im, = illo tempore, v. Brix ad Plaut. Trin. 523, lit., at that (sc. remote) time; hence, Of past time, some time ago, once upon a time, once, formerly, in time past, whilom, erst (freq. and class.; syn. quondam): versibu' quos olim Fauni vatesque canebant, Enn. ap. Cic. Brut. 19, 76 (Ann. v. 222 Vahl.): ut fuit olim Sisyphus, Hor. S. 1, 3, 46: sic enim olim loquebantur, Cic. de Or. 2, 43, 183: olim, vel nuper, id. Div.

olipor.full: Olipor, ōris, m. prob. from Auli puer, like Marcipor, Quintipor, a Roman surname, Inscr. Murat. 154, 2.

olisipo.full: Ŏlĭsīpo and Ŏlўsippo (Ulys-), ōnis, m., a city of Lusitania, the modern Lisbon, Plin. 4, 22, 35, § 116; 8, 42, 67, § 166: Olysippo, Varr. R. R. 2, 1, 19: Ulysippo, Mela, 3, 1, 6.—Hence, ŏlĭsīpōnensis (Olys-), e, adj., of or belonging to Olisipo: promontorium, Plin. 4, 21, 35, § 113.—Plur. subst.: ŏlĭsīpōnenses, ĭum, m., the inhabitants of Olisipo, the Olisiponians, Plin. 9, 5, 4, § 9.
olisipo.short: Ŏlĭsīpo and Ŏlўsippo (Ulys-), ōnis, m., a city of Lusitania, the modern Lisbon, Plin.

olitor.full: ŏlĭtor (better hŏlĭtor), ōris, m. holus, a kitchen-gardener, cabbage-gardener, Plaut. Trin. 2, 4, 7; Varr. L. L. 6, § 20 Müll.; Plaut. Mil. 2, 2, 38; Cic. Fam. 16, 18, 2; Col. 10, 229; 11, 1, 2; Hor. Ep. 1, 18, 36.

olitorius.full: ŏlĭtōrĭus (or, better, hŏlĭtōrĭus), a, um, adj. olitor, of or belonging to a kitchengardener or to vegetables: forum olitorium erat antiquum, macellum, ubi olerum copia, Varr. L. L. 5, § 146 Müll.; so, forum, the green-market, Liv. 21, 62: ostiola, Plin. 19, 8, 38, § 125: rotae, id. 19, 5, 23, § 64 Sillig N. cr.: horti, Dig. 50, 16, 198.
olitorius.short: ŏlĭtōrĭus (or, better, hŏlĭtōrĭus), a, um, adj.

oliva.full: ŏlīva, ae, f. ἐλαία. An olive, Col. 12, 50, 5; 2, 22, 4; Plin. 15, 3, 3, § 9; Plaut. Curc. 1, 1, 90; Afran. ap. Non. 478, 26: lecta de pinguissimis Oliva ramis arborum, Hor. Epod. 2, 56: olea duarum vel trium olivarum in summitate rami, Vulg. Isa. 17, 6.— Lit., an olive-tree: Aristaeus, qui olivae inventor dicitur, Cic. N. D. 3, 18, 45; 2, 8, 22: erum an bacis opulentet olivae, Hor. Ep. 1, 16, 2: numquam fallens, id. Epod. 16, 45: clivus Olivarum, the Mount of Olives, Vulg. 2 Reg. 15, 30: mons O

olivans.full: ŏlīvans, antis, Part. as subst. [oliva], an olive-gatherer (post-Aug.), Plin. 15, 3, 3, § 12.

olivarius.full: ŏlīvārĭus, a, um, adj. id., of or belonging to olives, olive- (post-Aug.; perh. only post-class. for olearius): olivariae metretae (al. oleariae), Col. 12, 49, 11: molae, Dig. 33, 7, 21.

oliveta.full: ŏlīvēta and ŏlīvīta, ae, f. id., the olive-harvest: olivetam dicebant ab oleis ut a vino vindemiam, Paul. ex Fest. p. 192 Müll.: olivitam antiqui dicebant, quom olea cogebantur ... quamvis quidam olivitatem eam dicant, id. ib. p. 202 Müll. N. cr.

olivetum.full: ŏlīvētum, i, n. id., a place planted with olive-trees, an olive-grove (class.): quo pluris sint nostra oliveta, Cic. Rep. 3, 9, 16: vineta, segetes, oliveta, id. N. D. 3, 36, 86; Varr. R. R. 1, 22, 3; Col. 3, 11, 3; 5, 9, 1 sq.: veteris proverbii meminisse convenit, eum qui aret olivetum, rogare fructum; qui stercoret, exorare; qui caedat, cogere, id. 5, 9, 15: facere, to plant, Calp. Fragm. 6, 16: vineta et oliveta, Vulg. Deut. 6, 11.—Hence, Mons Oliveti, the mountain of Olivet, or of the olive

olivifer.full: ŏlīvĭfer, ĕra, ĕrum, adj. oliva-fero, olive-bearing (poet.): Mutuscae, Verg. A. 7, 711: arva, i. e. Sabina, Ov. F. 3, 151: corona, of olive-branches, Mart. 12, 99, 1: Eurotas, Stat. Th. 4, 227.

olivitas.full: ŏlīvĭtas, ātis, f. oliva, the olive-gathering, olive-harvest, Varr. ap. Non. 148, 4; Col. 12, 47, 11; 12, 50, 15; 52.—In plur.: largissimis olivitatibus exuberare, Col. 1, 1, 5; cf. oliveta.

olivitor.full: ŏlīvĭtor, ōris, m. id., one who plants and tends olive-trees, an olive-dresser (postclass. for olitor): colles exercentur vinitori et olivitori, Sid. Ep. 2, 9 (App. Flor. n. 15 dub.; al. olitori).

olivum.full: ŏlīvum or ŏlīvom, i, n. id.. Lit. Oil (poet. and in post-class. prose for oleum): eme die caecā hercle olivum, id vendito oculatā die, Plaut. Ps. 1, 3, 67; id. As. 2, 4, 26; id. Ps. 1, 2, 76; Lucr. 2, 392; id. 6, 1073: inolens, id. 2, 850: pingue, Verg. E. 5, 68; Ov. M. 10, 176: perfundere pisces olivo, Hor. S. 2, 4, 50: si ex olivis meis olivum feceris, Gai. Inst. 2, 79.— Trop., the palœstra (from the use of oil to anoint wrestlers): cur olivum vitat? Hor. C. 1, 8, 8; cf. oleum.— Transf., an oi

olla.full: olla, ae (old form aula: aulas antiqui dicebant, quas nos dicimus ollas, quia nullam litteram geminabant. Itaque aulicocia exta, quae in ollis coquebantur, dicebant, id est elixa, Fest. p. 23 Müll.—Examples with aula, for olla, are found in Cato, R. R. 52, 1; 81; 85 sq.; Plaut. Aul. 2, 8, 20; 22; 3, 6, 44; 47; 4, 2, 4; 7; id. Capt. 1, 1, 21; 4, 2, 66 et saep.; Inscr. Orell. 2473; 3001; 4537 sqq.; cf. also Non. 543, 8), f. root uk-, Sanscr. ukha, pot; aula for aukula, a pot or jar: quadrilibrem a
olla.short: olla, ae (old form aula: aulas antiqui dicebant, quas nos dicimus ollas, quia nullam litteram geminabant.

ollaris.full: ollāris, e, adj. olla, of or belonging to a pot, preserved in pots, potted (post-Aug.): uvae ollares, Mart. 7, 20, 9; Col. 12, 43, 1.

ollarius.full: ollārĭus, a, um, adj. olla, of or belonging to pots, pot- (post-Aug.), Plin. 34, 9, 20, § 98: † fusor, a pot-founder, pot caster, Inscr. Grut. 630, 9.— Subst.: † ollārĭ-um, ĭi, n., the receptacle for the jars of ashes in tombs, Inscr. Fabr. p. 13, n. 60; cf. Fabr. p. 10 sq.

olle.full: olle, old form for ille, q. v.
olle.short: olle, old form for ille, q.

ollicula.full: ollĭcŭla, ae, f. dim. olla, a little pot (post-class.): ollicula aerea, Theod. Prisc. 4, 1.

ollula.full: ollŭla, ae, f. dim. id., a little pot (anteand post-class.), Varr. R. R. 1, 54, 2; App. M. 2, p. 117, 41: sub ollulā cinis, Arn. 5, 18.

ollus.full: ollus, a, um, old form for ille, q. v.
ollus.short: ollus, a, um, old form for ille, q.

olma.full: olma, ae, f., the plant ebulum, among the Dacians, App. Herb. 91.
olma.short: olma, ae, f., the plant ebulum, among the Dacians, App.

ololygon.full: ŏlŏlўgon, ŏnis, m., = ὀλολυγών, the croaking of the male frog, to attract the female, Plin. 11, 37, 65, § 172.
ololygon.short: ŏlŏlўgon, ŏnis, m., = ὀλολυγών, the croaking of the male frog, to attract the female, Plin.

olor1.full: ŏlor, ōris, m., a swan (poet. and in post-Aug. prose for cygnus): ad vada Maeandri concinit albus olor, Ov. H. 7, 2: arguti, Verg. E. 9, 36: nivei, Val. Fl. 6, 102: purpurei, Hor. C. 4, 1, 10; Plin. 10, 23, 32, § 63 et saep.: olorum morte narratur flebilis cantus, id. ib.

olor2.full: ŏlor, ōris, m. olo, oleo, a smell, odor (only ante- and post-class.): litterā commutatā dicitur odor olor, hinc olet et odorari, Varr. L. L. 6, § 83 Müll.: olore spurcissimi umoris perfusus, App. M. 1, p. 110, 2 dub.; Arn. 2, 85 (al. odores).

olorifer.full: ŏlōrĭfer, ĕra, ĕrum, adj. 1. olor-fero, swan-bearing (poet.): Padus, Claud. Ep. ad Ser. 12.

olorinus.full: ŏlōrīnus, a, um, adj. 1. olor, of or belonging to a swan or swans (poet. and in post-Aug. prose): pennae, Verg. A. 10, 187: alae, Ov. M. 10, 718: color, i. e. white, Plin. 37, 10, 59, § 163 (al. orobini): OLORINO DE IOVE, i. e. in the form of a swan, Inscr. Grut. 99, 3.

olostrae.full: Ŏlostrae, ārum, m., a people of India, Luc. 3, 249; cf. Plin. 6, 20, 23, § 76.
olostrae.short: Ŏlostrae, ārum, m., a people of India, Luc.

olus2.full: Olus, i, another form for Aulus, Inscr. Orell. 1943; 2712; cf. olipor.
olus2.short: Olus, i, another form for Aulus, Inscr.

olvatum.full: olvātum Antistius Labeo ait esse mensurae genus, Paul. ex Fest. p. 205 Müll.; v. Müll. s. v.
olvatum.short: olvātum Antistius Labeo ait esse mensurae genus, Paul.

olybrius.full: Ŏlȳbrius (Ōlўbrius, Anth. 2, p. 287), ĭi, m., the surname of several Roman consuls. To one of them, the consul Anicius Olybrius, is addressed a poem of Claudian. —Hence, Olȳbrĭăcus, a, um, adj., Olybrian: genus et nomen, Prud. ap. Symm. 1, 556.

olympeni.full: Ŏlympēni, ōrum, m., the inhabitants of the city of Olympus, in Lycia: agri Olympenorum, Cic. Agr. 1, 2, 5.
olympeni.short: Ŏlympēni, ōrum, m., the inhabitants of the city of Olympus, in Lycia: agri Olympenorum, Cic.

olympia.full: Ŏlympĭa (anciently Ŏlimpus and Ŏlumpus), ae, f., = Ὀλυμπια, a sacred region in Elis Pisatis, with an olive wood, where the Olympian games were held; there, too, were the famous temple and statue of Juppiter Olympius: cum Olympiam venisset, maximā illā quinquennali celebritate ludorum, Cic. de Or. 3, 32, 127; id. N. D. 2, 2, 6: cum uno die duo suos filios victores Olympiae vidisset, id. Tusc. 1, 46, 111; 2, 20, 46; Auct. Her. 4, 3, 4; Liv. 26, 24, 14.—Hence, ŏlympĭăcus, a, um, adj., = Ὀλυμπιακος,
olympia.short: Ŏlympĭa (anciently Ŏlimpus and Ŏlumpus), ae, f., = Ὀλυμπια, a sacred region in Elis Pisatis, with an olive wood, where the Olympian games were held;

olympiades.full: Ŏlympĭădes, um, f., v. 1. Olympus, I. B.

olympias1.full: Ŏlympĭas, ădis, f., v. Olympia, E.

olympias2.full: Ŏlympĭas, ădis, f., = Ὀλυμπιάς, the daughter of Neoptolemus, king of Epirus, consort of king Philip of Macedon and mother of Alexander the Great, Cic. Div. 1, 23; 2, 66; id. N. D. 2, 27; Curt. 5, 2 fin.
olympias2.short: Ŏlympĭas, ădis, f., = Ὀλυμπιάς, the daughter of Neoptolemus, king of Epirus, consort of king Philip of Macedon and mother of Alexander the Great, Cic.

olympias3.full: Ŏlympĭas, ădis, m., = Ὀλυμπιάς, a north-west wind, that blows on the island of Eubœa, Plin. 2, 47, 46, § 120; 17, 24, 37, § 232.
olympias3.short: Ŏlympĭas, ădis, m., = Ὀλυμπιάς, a north-west wind, that blows on the island of Eubœa, Plin.

olympicus.full: Ŏlympĭcus, a, um, v. Olympia, C.

olympio.full: Olympĭo, ōnis, m., the name of a character in Plaut. Cas.
olympio.short: Olympĭo, ōnis, m., the name of a character in Plaut.

olympiodorus.full: Ŏlympiŏdōrus, i, m., = Ὀλυμπιόδωρος, a Greek proper name. So the instructor of Epaminondas on the flute, Nep. Ep. 2, 1.
