olympiodorus.short: Ŏlympiŏdōrus, i, m., = Ὀλυμπιόδωρος, a Greek proper name.

olympionices.full: Ŏlympĭŏnīces, ae, m., = Ὀλυμπιονίκης, a victor at the Olympic games: Atyanas pugil, Olympionices, Cic. Fl. 13, 31; id. Tusc. 1, 46, 111.—As adj.: Olympionicarum equarum, Col. 3, 9, 5.
olympionices.short: Ŏlympĭŏnīces, ae, m., = Ὀλυμπιονίκης, a victor at the Olympic games: Atyanas pugil, Olympionices, Cic.

olympiscus.full: Ŏlympiscus, i, m. dim. Olympio, a caressing form for Olympio: Olympisce mi, Plaut. Cas. 3, 6, 14.

olympius.full: Ŏlympĭus, a, um, v. Olympia, D.

olympus1.full: Ŏlympus and -pos (anciently written Olĭmpus), i, m., = Ὄλυμπος. The name of several mountains, the most celebrated of which is one on the borders of Macedonia and Thessaly (now Lacha), of great height, and consequently regarded as the seat of the gods, Mel. 2, 3, 2; 4, 8, 15: Musae quae pedibus magnum pulsatis Olimpum, Enn. ap. Varr. L. L. 7, § 20 Müll.: his diis Helicona atque Olympon attribuerunt homines, Varr. R. R. 3, 16, 7: frondosus, Verg. G. 1, 282: opacus, Hor. C. 3, 4, 52: nubes excedit
olympus1.short: Ŏlympus and -pos (anciently written Olĭmpus), i, m., = Ὄλυμπος.

olympus2.full: Ŏlympus, i, f., a city in Cilicia, named from a neighboring mountain, now the ruins of Deliktash: Olympum cepit, urbem antiquam et omnibus rebus auctam, Cic. Verr. 2, 1, 21, § 56 (Zumpt N. cr.); Flor. 3, 6, 5; Eutr. 6, 3.— A city of Lycia, named from a neighboring mountain, Cic. Ac. 1, 21, 56.
olympus2.short: Ŏlympus, i, f., a city in Cilicia, named from a neighboring mountain, now the ruins of Deliktash: Olympum cepit, urbem antiquam et omnibus rebus auctam, Cic.

olympus3.full: Ŏlympus, 1, m., a famous fluteplayer, pupil of Marsyas, Ov. M. 6, 393; id. P. 3, 3, 42; Hyg. Fab. 165; Plin. 36, 5, 4, § 29.
olympus3.short: Ŏlympus, 1, m., a famous fluteplayer, pupil of Marsyas, Ov.

olynthus.full: Ŏlynthus or -os, 1, f., = Ὄλυνθος, a city of Thrace, on the borders of Macedonia, now Agia Maria, or Aio Mamas, Mel. 2, 2, 9; Plin. 4, 11, 18, § 42; Nep. Pel. 1, 2; Juv. 12, 47.—Hence, Olynthius, a, um, adj., of Olynthus, Olynthian, Curt. 8, 8, 19. —Subst. Olynthĭa, ae, f., the region about Olynthus, Varr. R. R. 1, 44.— Olynthius, ii, m., an Olynthian, Sen. Contr. 5, 10, 34.—Usually in plur.: Olyn-thii, ōrum, m., the inhabitants of Olynthus, the Olynthians, Nep. Timoth. 1, 2; Just. 8, 3, 10; 7,
olynthus.short: Ŏlynthus or -os, 1, f., = Ὄλυνθος, a city of Thrace, on the borders of Macedonia, now Agia Maria, or Aio Mamas, Mel.

olyra.full: ŏlȳra, ae, f., = ὄλυρα, a kind of grain, called also arinca, which greatly resembles spelt, Plin. 18, 10, 20. § 92; 22, 25, 57, § 121.
olyra.short: ŏlȳra, ae, f., = ὄλυρα, a kind of grain, called also arinca, which greatly resembles spelt, Plin.

omana.full: Omāna, ae, f., a town in Arabia, Plin. 6, 28, 32, § 149.—Hence, Omānus, a, um, Plin. 6, 28, 32, § 145.
omana.short: Omāna, ae, f., a town in Arabia, Plin.

omasum.full: ŏmāsum or ŏmassum, i, n. Gallic; v. infra, bullock's tripe (poet. and in post-Aug. prose): omasum βόειον κόπεον λιπαρὸν τῇ τῶν Τάλλων γλώττῃ, Gloss. Philox.: patinas cenabat omasi, Hor. Ep. 1, 15, 34; Plin. 8, 45, 70, § 180.—Transf.: pingui tentus omaso, with his fat paunch, Hor. S. 2, 5, 40.

ombria.full: ombrĭa, ae, f., = ὀμβρια, a precious stone, otherwise unknown, Plin. 37, 10, 65, § 176.
ombria.short: ombrĭa, ae, f., = ὀμβρια, a precious stone, otherwise unknown, Plin.

omen.full: ōmen (old form osmen), ĭnis, n. omen quod ex ore primum elatum est, osmen dictum, Varr. L. L. 6, § 76 Müll.; cf.: osmen, e quo s extritum, id. ib. 7, § 97: omen velut oremen, quod fit ore augurium, quod non avibus aliove modo fit, Fest. p 195 Müll.; perh. orig. osmen, for ausmen; root audio, that which is heard; hence, in gen.. Lit., any indication or action regarded as a foreboding, a foreboding, prognostic, sign, token, omen (class.; cf. prodigium): di te deaeque omnes faxint cum istoc omine,

omentatus.full: ōmentātus, a, um, adj. omentum, filled with omentum (post-class.): isicia omentata, Apic. 2, 1.

omentum.full: ōmentum, i, n., the fat-skin, adipose membrane; fat, esp. in men (post-Aug.). Lit. In gen.: ast illi tremat omento popa venter, Pers. 6, 74.— In partic. The membrane which encloses the bowels, the caul, Cels. 4, 1; Plin. 11, 37, 80, § 204.— The bowels, Pers. 2, 47: porci, Juv. 13. 116.— Transf., any skin which envelops an internal part of the body, a membrane, Macr. S. 7, 9; of the meninges, id. ib. 7, 9.
omentum.short: ōmentum, i, n., the fat-skin, adipose membrane;

ominalis.full: ōmĭnālis, e, a false read. for inominalem, Gell. 5, 17 fin.

ominatio.full: ōmĭnātĭo, ōnis, f. ominor, a foreboding, prognostic, Paul. ex Fest. p. 88 Müll.

ominator.full: ōmĭnātor, ōris, m. id., a diviner, Plaut. Am. 2, 2, 90.

ominor.full: ōmĭnor, ātus, 1, v. dep. (ante-class. act. collat. form ōmĭno, āre: ut tibi bene sit, qui ominas, Pompon. ap. Non. 474, 11) [omen], to forebode, prognosticate, to augur, presage, predict, prophesy (class.; syn.: divino, auguro, auspicor, vaticinor): malo (alienae) quam nostrae (rei publicae), ominari, Cic. Off. 2, 21, 74: melius, quaeso, ominare, id. Brut. 96, 329: felix faustumque imperium, Liv. 26, 18, 8: ac prope certā spe ominatos esse homines finem, etc., id. 44, 22, 17: vera de exitu Anton

ominosus.full: ōmĭnōsus, a, um, adj. omen, full of foreboding, portentous, ominous (post-Aug.): mons avibus obscenis ominosus, Messala ap. Gell. 13, 14, 6: res, Plin. Ep. 3, 14, 11. —Adv.: ōmĭnōsē, ominously: ominose retentus, Ps.-Quint. Decl. 6, 5.

omissio.full: ŏmissĭo, ōnis, f. omitto, an omitting, omission (post-class.): laudis, Symm. Ep. 3, 48; 10, 62.

omissus.full: ŏmissus, a, um, Part. and P. a., from omitto.

omitto.full: ŏmitto, īsi, issum, 3, v. a. ob-mitto, to let go, let loose, let fall. Lit. (rare; perh. not in Cic.; cf.: amitto, dimitto): aliquam, Plaut. Mil. 4, 3, 2; id. Stich. 2, 2, 11: mulierem, Ter. Ad. 2, 1, 18: habenas, to let go, Tac. H. 1, 86: arma, to let fall, Liv. 21, 11: animam, to give up the ghost, to die, Plaut. Am. 1, 1, 85.— Trop. (class.). In gen., to lay aside, let go, give up, dismiss, neglect, disregard: omittere tristitiam, Ter. Ad. 2, 4, 3: iracundiam, id. ib. 4, 7, 36: noxiam, to lea

ommento.full: ommento (obm-), āre, v. n., to wait anywhere, Liv. Andron. ap. Fest. p. 190 Müll.; cf.: omentat, exspectat, dictum a mantando, id est diu manendo, Placid. p. 492.

omnicanus.full: omnĭcănus, a, um, adj [omniscano], that sings everything or everywhere: oratio, App. Flor. p. 349, 24.
omnicanus.short: omnĭcănus, a, um, adj [omniscano], that sings everything or everywhere: oratio, App.

omnicarpus.full: omnĭcarpus, a, um, adj. omniscarpo, that crops everything: capra carpa, a quo scriptum Omnicarpae caprae, Varr L. L. 5, § 97 Müll.

omniciens.full: omnĭcĭens, entis omnis-cieo, all-stirring, all-exciting: sensus, Lucr. 2, 942 Bern. (dub.; Munro, omnituentes).
omniciens.short: omnĭcĭens, entis omnis-cieo, all-stirring, all-exciting: sensus, Lucr.

omnicolor.full: omnĭcŏlor, ōris, adj. omnis-color, of all colors (post-class.): pictura, Prud. στεφ. 12, 39.

omnicreans.full: omnĭcrĕans, antis omnis-creo, allcreating, Aug. Conf. 11, 13 init.

omnifarius.full: omnĭfărĭus, a, um, adj. omnis, of all sorts.—As adj. only in the gloss: omnifarius, παντοῖος, Gloss. Philox. (in Cael. Aur. Acut. 3, 16, read omnifariam).—Hence, omnĭfărĭam, adv., on all sides, on every hand, everywhere, in every way (post-class. and rare): cum Oceanus omnes terras omnifariam et undiqueversum circumfluat, Gell. 12, 13, 20; Macr. S. 7, 13 med.; Capitol. M. Aur. 11.

omnifer.full: omnĭfer, ĕra, ĕrum, adj. omnis-fero, all-bearing, all-sustaining: vultus, Ov. M. 2, 275.

omnifluentia.full: omniflŭentĭa, ae, f. omnis-fluo, superfluity of all things, Placid. ap. Auct. Class. 3, p. 118 Mai.

omniformis.full: omnĭformis, e, adj. omnis-forma, of all shapes (post-class.): mundus receptaculum omniformium specierum, App. Trism. pp. 78, 98: machina, Prud. στεφ. 10, 339.

omnigenus1.full: omnĭgĕnus, a, um, adj. omnis-genus, of all kinds (poet. and in post-class. prose): omnigenūmque deūm monstra, Verg. A. 8, 698: omnigenūm genitor deūm, Mart. Cap. 9, § 912: doctrinae, Gell. 14, 6, 1 (but in Lucr. 2, 759; 821 al. Lachm. reads omne genus).

omnigenus2.full: omnĭgĕnus, a, um, adj. omnisgigno, all-begetting, all-producing (postclass.): Pater, Prud. ap. Symm. 1, 12.

omnimedens.full: omnĭmĕdens, adj. omnis-medeor, all-healing (post-class.): Dominus, Paul. Nol. Carm. 26, 45.

omnimodis.full: omnĭmŏdīs, adv., in every way or manner, wholly, fully (= omnibus modis; cf.: multimodis, mirimodis; only Lucretian and late Lat.), Lucr. 1, 683; 2, 489; 700; 3, 406; 5, 718; 1024; App. Flor. 1, p. 342, 17.
omnimodis.short: omnĭmŏdīs, adv., in every way or manner, wholly, fully (= omnibus modis;

omnimodo.full: omnĭmŏdo (also written separate, omnī mŏdo), adv. omnis-modus, by all means, in all ways, entirely, altogether, wholly (not ante-Aug.): evitemus omnimodo, ne deliberasse videamur, Sen. Ben. 2, 1, 1: non omnimodo res ea desperationem habet, Cels. 7, 4, 3 fin.; Gell. 18, 15, 2; Dig. 29, 2, 11.
omnimodo.short: omnĭmŏdo (also written separate, omnī mŏdo), adv.

omnimodus.full: omnĭmŏdus, a, um, adj. id., of all sorts or kinds (post-class.). App. Mag. p. 306. 14: voculae, id. M. 5, p. 169, 35: gloria ejus. Vulg. Isa. 66, 11.

omnimorbia.full: omnĭmorbĭa, ae, f [omnis-morbus]. all-disease, the name of a plant regarded as a panacea: polion a Graecis, a Latinis omnimorbia, quod multis morbis subveniat, Isid. Orig. 17, 9.

omnino.full: omnīno, adv. omnis. In gen., altogether, wholly, entirely, utterly, at all (syn.: prorsus, penitus): Neoptolemus apud Ennium philosophari sibi ait necesse esse, sed paucis: nam omnino haud placere, entirely, i. e. constantly, Cic. Tusc. 2, 1, 1; v. also id. de Or. 2, 37, 156 (Enn. Trag. v. 417 Vahl.): non omnino jam perii: est reliquom quo peream magis, Plaut. As. 1, 3, 80: defensionum laboribus aut omnino aut magnā ex parte liberatus, Cic. Tusc. 1, 1, 1: ut non multum aut nihil omnino Graecis c

omninominis.full: omnĭnōmĭnis, e, adj. omnis-nomen, of every name: hunc vero innominem vel potius omninominem, siquidem sit unus et omnia, ut sit necesse aut omnia esse ejus nomine aut ipsum omnium nominibus nuncupari, App. Ascl. 20, p. 303.

omniparens.full: omnĭpărens, tis, adj. omnis-parens, all-bearing, all-producing (poet. and in post-class. prose); so, per terras omniparentes, Lucr. 2, 706: terra, Verg. A. 6, 595; App. M. 6, p. 177, 24: dea Syria, id. ib. 8, p. 213, 9 (but in id. Mund. p. 67, 12, the correct read. is omnia parentis).

omnipater.full: omnĭpăter, tris, m. omnis-pater, the father of all, the universal father (postclass.): Deus, Prud. στεφ. 3, 70.

omnipavus.full: omnĭpăvus, a, um, adj. omnis-paveo, all-fearing (post-class.): panphobi, quos nos omnipavos dicere poterimus, Cael. Aur. Acut. 3, 12, 108.

omniperitus.full: omnĭpĕrītus, a, um, adj. omnisperitus, skilled in all things, all-skilful: Aeetis sucis omniperita suis, Albinov. 2, 110.

omnipollens.full: omnĭpollens, tis, adj. omnis-polleo, all-powerful, almighty (post-class.): Deus, Prud. Apoth. praef. 31.

omnipotens.full: omnĭpŏtens, ntis, adj. omnis-potens, all-powerful, almighty, omnipotent (poet. and in post-class. prose), Enn. ap. Non. 111, 15 (Trag. v. 202 Vahl.): Juppiter, id. ap. Serv. ad Verg. A. 1, 254 (Ann. v. 446 Vahl.); Cat. 64, 171: pater, Ov. M. 1, 154.—Absol.: arcuit omnipotens, Ov. M. 2, 505; so, annuit omnipotens, id. ib. 14, 816: Neptunus, Turp. ap. Cic. Tusc. 4, 34, 73: regina, i. e. Juno, Val. Fl. 1, 81: fortuna, Verg. A. 8, 334: Juppiter, Val. Max. 1, 6, 12 init.—Comp.: nam si ideo omnipotens

omnipotentia.full: omnĭpŏtentĭa, ae, f. omnipotens, almighty power, omnipotence (post-class.), Macr. S. 1, 16.

omnis.full: omnĭs, e (omnia is freq. a dissyl. in the poets, as Verg. G. 4, 221; id. A. 6, 33; Lucr. 1, 1106 Lachm.), adj. etym. dub.; perh. akin to ambo and Gr. ἀμφί (syn.: cunctus, universus), all, every: omnium rerum, quas ad beate vivendum sapientia comparaverit, nihil esse majus amicitiā, Cic. Fin. 1, 20, 65: ego nulli omnium neque populorum neque regum ... non ausim me comparare, Liv. 37, 53, 20: nemo omnium imperatorum, qui vivunt, id. 42, 34, 7.—With sup.: cur, si cuiquam novo civi potuerit adimi ci

omniscius.full: omniscĭus, a, um, adj. omnis-scio, omniscient (eccl. Lat.), Ps.-Aug. Spec. 16.

omnisonus.full: omnĭsŏnus, a, um, adj. omnis-sono, uttering all kinds of sounds (post-class.): harmonia, Paul. Nol. Carm. 24, 81: mela, Mart. Cap. 9, § 912.

omnitenens.full: omnĭtĕnens, ntis, adj. omnis-tenens, holding all things, all-swaying (eccl. Lat.), Tert. Carm. adv. Marc. 5, 202.

omnituens.full: omnĭtŭens, entis, adj. omnis-tueor, all-seeing (poet. and in post-class. prose), Lucr. 2, 942; Val. Fl. 5, 247: sol, App. Mundo, p. 71, 23.

omnivagus.full: omnĭvăgus, a, um, adj. omnis-vagus, roving everywhere, omnivagant: Diana, Cic. N. D. 2, 27, 68; Varr. Atac. in Anth. Lat. 2, p. 337 Burm. dub. (al. omnivomus).

omnivolus.full: omnĭvŏlus, a, um, adj. omnis-volo, willing every thing: omnivoli furta Jovis, Cat. 68, 140.

omnivorus.full: omnĭvŏrus, a, um, adj. omnis-voro, all-devouring, omnivorous: boves, Plin. 25, 8, 53, § 94.

omophagia.full: ōmŏphăgĭa, ae, f., = ὠμοφαγία, the eating of raw flesh (eccl. Lat.), Arn. 5, 169.
omophagia.short: ōmŏphăgĭa, ae, f., = ὠμοφαγία, the eating of raw flesh (eccl.

omphacium.full: omphăcĭum, ii, n., = ὀμφάκιον, the oil or juice of unripe olives or grapes, Plin. 12, 27, 60, § 130; 14, 16, 18, § 98.
omphacium.short: omphăcĭum, ii, n., = ὀμφάκιον, the oil or juice of unripe olives or grapes, Plin.

omphacocarpos.full: omphăcŏcarpos, i, m., = ὀμφακόκαρπος, a plant, called also aparine, Plin. 27, 5, 15, § 32 (al. omphalocarpon).
omphacocarpos.short: omphăcŏcarpos, i, m., = ὀμφακόκαρπος, a plant, called also aparine, Plin.

omphacomel.full: omphăcŏmel, mellis, n., = ὀμφακόμελι, a sirup made of omphacium, Pall. 9, 13 lemm.
omphacomel.short: omphăcŏmel, mellis, n., = ὀμφακόμελι, a sirup made of omphacium, Pall.

omphale.full: Omphălē, ēs, f., = Ὀμφάλη, a queen of Lydia, whom Hercules served, Hyg. Fab. 32; Prop. 4, 10, 17; Ov. F. 2, 305; Stat. Th. 10, 646; cf. Preller's Gr. Mythol. 2, p. 158.
omphale.short: Omphălē, ēs, f., = Ὀμφάλη, a queen of Lydia, whom Hercules served, Hyg.

omphalos.full: omphălos, i, m., = ὀμφαλός, the navel (pure Lat. umbilicus); transf. for the centre (in post-class. poetry), Aus. Idyll. 11, 60.
omphalos.short: omphălos, i, m., = ὀμφαλός, the navel (pure Lat.

onager.full: ŏnăger and ŏnā^grus, i, m., = ὄναγρος, a wild ass, Varr. R. R. 2, 6, 3; cf. Col. 6, 37, 3; Plin. 8, 44, 69, § 174: timidi, Verg. G. 3, 409: pulcher, Mart. 13, 100, 1; Vulg. Psa. 103, 11; id. Osee, 8, 9.— Transf., a military engine for discharging large stones, Veg. Mil. 4, 22; Amm. 23, 4, 4.
onager.short: ŏnăger and ŏnā^grus, i, m., = ὄναγρος, a wild ass, Varr.

onagos.full: ŏnāgos, i, m., = ὄναγος, an ass-driver, Plaut. As. prol. 10.
onagos.short: ŏnāgos, i, m., = ὄναγος, an ass-driver, Plaut.

onchesmites.full: Onchesmītes, ae, m., = Ὀγχησμίτης, a wind blowing from Onchesmus (Ὀγχησμός), a harbor of Epirus, Cic. Att. 7, 2, 1.
onchesmites.short: Onchesmītes, ae, m., = Ὀγχησμίτης, a wind blowing from Onchesmus (Ὀγχησμός), a harbor of Epirus, Cic.

onchestius.full: Onchestĭus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to the city of Onchestus, in Bœotia, Ov. M. 10, 605.
onchestius.short: Onchestĭus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to the city of Onchestus, in Bœotia, Ov.

onchestus1.full: Onchestus, i, f., a city of Bœotia; v. Onchestius.
onchestus1.short: Onchestus, i, f., a city of Bœotia;

onchestus2.full: Onchestus, i, m., a river in Thessaly, Liv. 33, 6.
onchestus2.short: Onchestus, i, m., a river in Thessaly, Liv.

onco.full: onco, āre, v. n., to bray, like an ass: oncat asellus, Auct. Carm. Philom. 55.

oncoma.full: oncōma, ătis, n., = ὄγκωμα, a tumor (post-class.), Veg. Vet. 2, 30.
oncoma.short: oncōma, ătis, n., = ὄγκωμα, a tumor (post-class.), Veg.

onear.full: ŏnēar, ătis, n. ὄνειαρ, refreshment, a plant, the same with the onotheras, q. v., Plin. 26, 11, 69, § 111.

onerarius.full: ŏnĕrārĭus, a, um, adj. onus, of or belonging to burden, transport, or carriage; that bears a burden, carries freight (class.): jumenta, beasts of burden, Liv. 41, 4: navis, a ship of burden, Sisenn. ap. Non. 536, 5 (opp. actuaria); Caes. B. G. 4, 22; 25 al.; Liv. 22, 11, 6.—Also subst.: ŏnĕrārĭa, ae, f., a ship of burden, a merchant-vessel, a transport, Cic. Att. 10, 12, 2.

oneratus.full: ŏnĕrātus, a, um, Part. and P. a., from onero.

onero.full: ŏnĕro, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. onus. To load, lade, burden, freight with any thing (class.). Lit.: navim magnam multis mercibus, Plaut. Men. prol. 25: naves, ad celeritatem onerandi subductionesque, paulo facit humiliores, for loading expeditiously, Caes. B. G. 5, 1: jumenta, Sall. J. 75, 6: naves commeatu, etc., id. ib. 86, 1: costas aselli pomis, Verg. G. 1, 274: tauri cervix oneratur aratro, is loaded, burdened, Ov. A. A. 1, 19: aures lapillis, id. ib. 3, 129; cf.: umerum pallio, Ter. Phorm. 5, 6

onerositas.full: ŏnĕrōsĭtas, ātis, f. onerosus, burdensomeness, burden (eccl. Lat.), Tert. Cult. Fem. 7.

onerosus.full: ŏnĕrōsus, a, um, adj. onus, burdensome, heavy, oppressive (poet. and in postAug. prose; syn.: gravis, difficilis). Lit.: praeda, Verg. A. 9, 384.—Of food that is difficult of digestion and causes oppression: cibus etiam valentibus onerosus, Plin. 23, 7, 62, § 115: (ervum) capiti et stomacho onerosum, id. 22, 25, 73, § 153.— Comp.: aër est onerosior igni, Ov. M. 1, 53. — Trop., burdensome, onerous, irksome: onerosior altera sors est, Ov. M. 9, 675: donatio, Plin. Ep. 2, 4, 3: quam sit onerosum su

onesicritus.full: Ŏnēsĭcrĭtus, i, m., = Ὀνησίκριτος, an historian, a native of Ægina; he was the chief pilot (praefectus classis) of Alexander the Great, Curt. 9, 10, 3; 10, 1, 10; Gell. 9, 4, 3; Plin. 6, 22, 24, § 81.
onesicritus.short: Ŏnēsĭcrĭtus, i, m., = Ὀνησίκριτος, an historian, a native of Ægina;

onesimus.full: Ŏnēsĭmus, i, m., and -a, ae, f., = Ὀνησιμος, -η, a Roman surname, Inscr. Grut. 646, 6; Vulg. Col. 4, 9.
onesimus.short: Ŏnēsĭmus, i, m., and -a, ae, f., = Ὀνησιμος, -η, a Roman surname, Inscr.

onesipaurus.full: Ŏnēsĭpaurus, i, m., the name of a Roman slave, Inscr. Grut. 883, 1.
onesipaurus.short: Ŏnēsĭpaurus, i, m., the name of a Roman slave, Inscr.

onesiphorus.full: Ŏnēsĭphŏrus, i, m., = Ὀνησίφορος, a Roman surname, Inscr Maff. Mus. Ver. 286, 3; Vulg. 2 Tim. 1, 16.
onesiphorus.short: Ŏnēsĭphŏrus, i, m., = Ὀνησίφορος, a Roman surname, Inscr Maff.

onesis.full: Ŏnēsis, is and ĭdis, f, = Ὄνησις, a Roman surname, Inscr. Maff. Mus. Ver. 477, 4; 269, 4.
onesis.short: Ŏnēsis, is and ĭdis, f, = Ὄνησις, a Roman surname, Inscr.

onesitrophus.full: Ŏnēsitrophus, i, m., a Roman surname, Inscr Fabr p. 84, n. 144.
onesitrophus.short: Ŏnēsitrophus, i, m., a Roman surname, Inscr Fabr p.

onirocrites.full: ŏnīrocrĭtes, ae, m., = ὀνειροκρίτης, an interpreter of dreams (post-class.), Fulg. Myth. 1.
onirocrites.short: ŏnīrocrĭtes, ae, m., = ὀνειροκρίτης, an interpreter of dreams (post-class.), Fulg.

oniros.full: ŏnīros, i, m., = ὄνειρος (dream), the wild poppy, so called from its soporific qualities, App. Herb. 53.
oniros.short: ŏnīros, i, m., = ὄνειρος (dream), the wild poppy, so called from its soporific qualities, App.

oniscus.full: ŏniscus or -os, i, m., = ὀνισκος, a wood-louse, milleped, Plin. 29, 6, 39, § 136; 30, 8, 21, § 54.
oniscus.short: ŏniscus or -os, i, m., = ὀνισκος, a wood-louse, milleped, Plin.

onitis.full: ŏnītis, ĭdis, f., = ὀνῖτις, a plant, otherwise unknown; a kind of origanum, Plin. 20, 17, 67, § 175; App. Herb 122.
onitis.short: ŏnītis, ĭdis, f., = ὀνῖτις, a plant, otherwise unknown;

onitus.full: Ōnītus, i, m., = ὠνειτός (purchased), the name of a slave, Inscr. Grut. 633, 6.
onitus.short: Ōnītus, i, m., = ὠνειτός (purchased), the name of a slave, Inscr.

onoba.full: Onoba, ae, f, a city in Hispania Bœtica, Plin. 3, 1, 3, § 10; Mel. 3, 1, 3
onoba.short: Onoba, ae, f, a city in Hispania Bœtica, Plin.

onobrychis.full: ŏnŏbrўchis, ĭdis, f., = ὀνόβρυχις, a plant, called also palmes asini, Plin. 24, 16, 98, § 155 (al. oenŏbrēches).
onobrychis.short: ŏnŏbrўchis, ĭdis, f., = ὀνόβρυχις, a plant, called also palmes asini, Plin.

onocardion.full: ŏnŏcardĭon, ii, n., a plant, called also chamaeleon, App. Herb. 25.
onocardion.short: ŏnŏcardĭon, ii, n., a plant, called also chamaeleon, App.

onocentaurus.full: ŏnŏcentaurus, i, m., = ὀνοκένταυρος, an ass-centaur, a fabulous animal, Isid. Orig. 11, 3, 39: et occurrent daemonia onocentauris, Vulg. Isa. 34, 14.—Transf., of an impure person, Hier. in Isa. 6, 13, 22.
onocentaurus.short: ŏnŏcentaurus, i, m., = ὀνοκένταυρος, an ass-centaur, a fabulous animal, Isid.

onochiles.full: ŏnŏchīles, is, and ŏnŏchēlis, is, f., and ŏnŏchīlon, = ὀνοχειλές, ὀνοχειλίς, a plant, a kind of bugloss, Plin. 22, 21, 25, § 51.
onochiles.short: ŏnŏchīles, is, and ŏnŏchēlis, is, f., and ŏnŏchīlon, = ὀνοχειλές, ὀνοχειλίς, a plant, a kind of bugloss, Plin.

onocoetes.full: Ŏnŏcoetes, ae, m., = Ὀνοκοιτης, he who lies in an ass's manger, a mocking epithet applied by the heathen to Christ, Tert. Apol. 16; cf. id. ad Nat. 1, 14 (al. ŏnŏnўchītes, ae, m., = Ὀνονυχίτης, he who has an ass's hoof, likewise applied to Christ).
onocoetes.short: Ŏnŏcoetes, ae, m., = Ὀνοκοιτης, he who lies in an ass's manger, a mocking epithet applied by the heathen to Christ, Tert.

onocrotalus.full: ŏnō^crŏtălus, i, m., = ὀνοκρόταλος, the pelican, Plin. 10, 47, 66, § 131; Mart. 11, 21, 10; Vulg. Lev. 11, 18; id. Deut. 14, 18.
onocrotalus.short: ŏnō^crŏtălus, i, m., = ὀνοκρόταλος, the pelican, Plin.

onomastus.full: Ŏnŏmastus, i, m., and -a, ae, f., = Ὀνομαστός, -ή, a Roman surname, Liv. 39, 34; 40, 8; Tac. H. 1, 25; 1, 27; Inscr. Murat. 1144, 1; Inscr. Fabr. p. 751, n. 587.
onomastus.short: Ŏnŏmastus, i, m., and -a, ae, f., = Ὀνομαστός, -ή, a Roman surname, Liv.

onomatopoeia.full: ŏnŏmătŏpoeïa, ae, f., = ὀνοματοποιΐα, the forming of a word to resemble in sound the thing it signifies, onomatopée, Charis. p. 245 P.
onomatopoeia.short: ŏnŏmătŏpoeïa, ae, f., = ὀνοματοποιΐα, the forming of a word to resemble in sound the thing it signifies, onomatopée, Charis.

ononis.full: ŏnōnis (ănōnis), ĭdis, f., = ὀνωνίς, a plant, the tall rest-harrow: Ononis antiquorum, Linn.; Plin. 21, 16, 58, § 58 (better anonis).
ononis.short: ŏnōnis (ănōnis), ĭdis, f., = ὀνωνίς, a plant, the tall rest-harrow: Ononis antiquorum, Linn.;

onopordon.full: ŏnŏpordon, i, n., = ὀνόπορδον, a plant, St. Mary's thistle, Plin. 27, 12, 86, § 110 dub.; al. ŏnŏprădon.
onopordon.short: ŏnŏpordon, i, n., = ὀνόπορδον, a plant, St.

onopyxos.full: ŏnŏpyxos, i, m., a plant of the thistle kind, Plin. 21, 16, 56, § 94.
onopyxos.short: ŏnŏpyxos, i, m., a plant of the thistle kind, Plin.

onosma.full: ŏnosma, ătis, n., = ὄνοσμα, a plant, a kind of anchusa, Plin. 27, 12, 86, § 110.
onosma.short: ŏnosma, ătis, n., = ὄνοσμα, a plant, a kind of anchusa, Plin.

onotheras.full: ŏnŏthēras (-ra), ae, m., = ὀνοθηρας, a plant, also called onear, q. v., Plin. 26, 11, 69, § 111, 26, 14, 87, § 146.
onotheras.short: ŏnŏthēras (-ra), ae, m., = ὀνοθηρας, a plant, also called onear, q.

onotheris.full: ŏnŏthēris, ĭdis, f., = ὀνοθήρις, and ŏnŏthūris, a plant, the same as onotheras, Plin. 24, 17, 102, § 167.
onotheris.short: ŏnŏthēris, ĭdis, f., = ὀνοθήρις, and ŏnŏthūris, a plant, the same as onotheras, Plin.

onuris.full: ŏnūris, is, f., = ὄνουρις, a plant, called also oenothera, Plin. 26, 11, 69, § 111 (al. ŏnēar).
onuris.short: ŏnūris, is, f., = ὄνουρις, a plant, called also oenothera, Plin.

onus.full: ŏnus (in good MSS. also wr. hŏnus), ĕris, n. etym. dub.; cf. Sanscr. anas, a wagon for freight, a load, burden (cf. pondus). Lit. In gen.: oneris maximi pondus, Vitr. 10, 8: onus sustinere, Plaut. As. 3, 3, 68: cum gravius dorso subiit onus (asellus), Hor S. 1, 9, 20: tanti oneris turris, Caes. B. G. 2, 30: ad minimum redigi onus, Ov M. 14, 149.— In partic. Of goods, baggage, etc., a load, lading, freight, cargo: insula Delos, quo omnes undique cum mercibus atque oneribus commeabant, Cic. Imp. P

onusto.full: ŏnusto, āre, 1, v. a. onustus, to burden, load (only late Lat. and in Part. pass.): virgo reguli partu onustanda, Aug. Serm. 3 in Nat. Dom. 2. Verg.: nomen sollicitudinibus onustatum, Cassiod. H. E. 10, 33; Vulg. Judith, 15, 7.

onustus.full: ŏnustus (hŏnust-), a, um, adj. onus, loaded, laden, burdened, freighted, etc. (class.). Lit.: asellus onustus auro, Cic. Att. 1, 16, 12 (dub.): naves onustae frumento, id. Off. 3, 12: currus quinque liberis, Tac. A. 2, 41: magna vis camelorum onusta frumenti, id. ib. 15, 12.— Transf. Filled, full, abounding in: ager praedā onustus, Sall. J. 87, 1: pharetrae telis, Tac. A. 12, 13.— With gen.: auri, Plaut. Aul. 4, 2, 10.— Full, satisfied with food (anteclass.): quia sum onusta mei ex sententiā, Pl

onychinus.full: ŏnўchĭnus, a, um, adj., = ὀνύχινος. Of the color of the finger-nail, nail-colored: pira, Plin. 15, 15, 16, § 55: pruna, Col. 12, 10.— Of the marble called onyx: lapis, Vulg. Gen. 2, 12.—As subst.: onychinus, the onyx, Vulg. Exod. 39, 13.—Transf., resembling the onyx (poet.) of the coating of ice on rivers: tegimen onychinum, Laev ap. Gell. 19, 7 fin.—Subst.: ŏnўchĭna (sc. vasa), n. plur., vessels of onyx, Lampr. Heliog. 32.

onychipuncta.full: ŏnўchĭpuncta, ae, f., a precious stone, called also jasponyx, Plin. 37, 9, 37, § 118 (al. onychi juncta).
onychipuncta.short: ŏnўchĭpuncta, ae, f., a precious stone, called also jasponyx, Plin.

onychitinus.full: ŏnȳchītĭnus, a, um, adj., = ὀνυχίτινος, of or belonging to onyx (post-class.): crustae (al. onychintinae), Sid. Ep. 9, 7.
onychitinus.short: ŏnȳchītĭnus, a, um, adj., = ὀνυχίτινος, of or belonging to onyx (post-class.): crustae (al.

onychitis.full: ŏnўchītis, ĭdis, f., = ὀνυχῖτις, another name for onyx, Plin. 34, 10, 22, § 103.
onychitis.short: ŏnўchītis, ĭdis, f., = ὀνυχῖτις, another name for onyx, Plin.

onychius.full: ŏnўchĭus, a, um, adj. onyx, of or belonging to onyx: onychius lapis, i. e. onyx, Tert. adv. Marc. 2, 10.

onytes.full: Ŏnȳtes, is, m., the name of a Rutulian warrior, Verg. A. 12, 514.
onytes.short: Ŏnȳtes, is, m., the name of a Rutulian warrior, Verg.

onyx.full: ŏnyx, ўchis, m. and f., = ὄνυξ (a fingernail; hence, from its color). Fem., a kind of yellowish marble, onyx, of which vessels of many kinds were made; it was also used for mlaying floors, Plin. 36, 7, 12, § 59: totāque effusus in aulā Calcabatur onyx, Luc. 10, 116; calcatusque tuo sub pede lucet onyx, Mart. 12, 50, 4.— Masc., a vessel of onyx, an onyx-box: nardi parvus onyx, Hor. C. 4, 12, 17; murrheus, an ointment-box, Prop. 3, 8 (4, 9), 22; cf.: Syrio munere plenus onyx, id. 2, 10 (3, 5), 14.

oonae.full: Oönae, another form of Oeönae, q. v.
oonae.short: Oönae, another form of Oeönae, q.

opacitas.full: ŏpācĭtas, ātis, f [opacus], shadiness, shade (post-Aug.), Col. 8, 17; amoena, Plin. 6, 30, 35, § 197; noctium, id. 2, 11, 8, § 52: ramorum, id. 17, 1, 1, § 5: arborum, Tac. A. 11, 3.
opacitas.short: ŏpācĭtas, ātis, f [opacus], shadiness, shade (post-Aug.), Col.

opaco.full: ŏpāco, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. id., to cover with shade, to shade (class.; syn.: obscuro, obumbro). Lit.; platanus ad opacandum hunc locum patulis est diffusa ramis, Cic. de Or. 1, 7, 28, cf. id. Fragm. ap. Macr. S. 6, 4: ubi pinguem dives opacat Ramus humum, Verg. A. 6, 195: humum taxus opacat, Luc. 6, 645: (sol terras) modo his modo illis ex partibus opacat, Cic. N. D. 2, 19, 49.— Transf., to cover (poet.): opacat flore lanugo genas, Pac. ap. Fest. s. v. genas, p. 94 Müll.: opacat tempora pinus, S

opacus.full: ŏpācus, a, um, adj. In the shade, shaded, shady (class.): opaca vocantur umbrosa, Fest. p. 185 Müll.: ripa, Cic. Leg. 1, 5, 15: frigus, shady coolness, cool shade, Verg. E. 1, 53: vallis, Hor. Ep. 1, 16, 5.—Comp.: locus umbrā opacior, Plin. Ep. 5, 6, 25.—Sup.: opacissima nemorum pascua, Col. 6, 22.—Neutr. absol.: colores, qui in opaco clarius micant, in the shade, Plin. 10, 20, 22, § 43.—So in plur. with gen.: per opaca locorum, through shady places, Verg. A. 2, 725; 6, 633.— Transf. Darkened as

opalia.full: Ŏpālĭa, ium, n., a festival celebrated on the 19th of December, in honor of the goddess Ops, Varr. L. L. 6, § 22 Müll.; cf.: Opalia dies festi, quibus supplicatur Opi, Paul. ex Fest. p. 185 Müll.; Macr. S. 1, 10.
opalia.short: Ŏpālĭa, ium, n., a festival celebrated on the 19th of December, in honor of the goddess Ops, Varr.

opalis.full: Ŏpālis, e, adj. 2. Ops, of or belonging to Ops: Opale sacrum, i. e. the Opalia (v. Opalia), Aus. Ecl. Fer. Rom. 15 (al. Opis ante sacrum).

opalus.full: ŏpălus, i, m., a precious stone, opal, Plin. 37, 6, 21, § 80; Isid. Orig. 16, 12.
opalus.short: ŏpălus, i, m., a precious stone, opal, Plin.

opella.full: ŏpella, ae, f. dim. opera, little or light pains, labor, service (poet.): parva, Lucr. 1, 1114: forensis, Hor. Ep. 1, 7, 8.

opera.full: ŏpĕra, ae, f. opus, service, pains, exertion, work, labor (opus is used mostly of the mechanical activity of work, as that of animals, slaves, and soldiers; opera supposes a free will and desire to serve). Lit. In gen.: omnes, quorum operae, non quorum artes emuntur, Cic. Off. 1, 42, 150: sine hominum manu atque operā, id. ib. 2, 4, 14: operam exigere, id. ib. 1, 13: perdere, id. de Or. 1, 28, 126: praebere amicis, id. Brut. 47, 174: in re ponere, id. Clu. 57, 157: curamque in rebus honestis pon

operans.full: ŏpĕrans, antis, Part. and P. a., from operor.

operarius.full: ŏpĕrārĭus, a, um, adj. opera, of or belonging to labor (class.): homo, Cic. Att. 7, 2, 8: pecus, working-cattle, Col. 6, 2, 15: vinum, for working-men, Plin. 14, 10, 12, § 86.— Subst. ŏpĕrārĭus, ii, m., a laborer, workman, operative: habere oportet operarios quinque, Cato, R. R. 10, 1: operarius rusticus, the peasant as a day-laborer, Edict. Diocl. 7, 1; cf.: operarius agrarius, Vulg. Ecclus. 37, 13: quos singulos sicut operarios barbarosque contemnas, Cic. Tusc. 5, 36, 104: quidam operarii ling

operatio.full: ŏpĕrātĭo, ōnis, f. operor, a working, work, labor, operation (not in Cic. or Cæs.). In gen.: insidiantur aquantibus (apibus) ranae, quae maxima earum est operatio, cum sobolem faciunt, Plin. 11, 18, 19, § 61; 11, 24, 28, § 80; Vitr. 2, 9.— In partic. A religious performance, service, or solemnity, a bringing of offerings: operationes denicales, offerings, Fest. s. v. privatae feriae, p. 242 Müll.; Inscr. a. 286, p. Chr. ap. Orell. 2234.— In Christian authors, beneficence, charity, Lact. 6, 12; P

operativus.full: ŏpĕrātīvus, a, um, adj. id., creative, formative (eccl. Lat.), Aug. Quaest. 63.

operator.full: ŏpĕrātor, ōris, m. id., a worker, operator (post-class.), Firm. Math. 3, 9; Tert. Exhort. ad Castit. 3; id. Apol. 23 fin. al.; Lact. 6, 18, 13; Vulg. Prov. 22, 2.

operatorius.full: ŏpĕrātōrĭus, a, um, adj. id., creating, forming, Ambros. Hexaëm. 1, 1, 1; id. Fug. Saec. 2, 11.

operatrix.full: ŏpĕrātrix, īcis, f. operator, she that works, a worker, effecter, producer (eccl. Lat.): vis operatrix, Tert. Anim. 11: mortis, id. ib. 52: sapientia, creative wisdom, Ambros. Spir. Sanc. 2, 9, § 92.

operatus.full: ŏpĕrātus, a, um, P. a., v. operor fin. B.

operculo.full: ŏpercŭlo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. operculum, to furnish or cover with a lid, to cover (post-Aug.): dolia, Col. 12, 30, 1: vasa, id. 12, 15, 2: operculati favi, id. 11, 2, 50; 57.

operculum.full: ŏpercŭlum, i, n. operio, a cover, covering, lid (class.): quibus operibantur operimenta et pallia opercula dixerunt, Varr. L. L. 5, § 167 Müll.: aspera arteria tegitur quasi quodam operculo, Cic. N. D. 2, 54, 136; Col. 8, 8, 7: sorba in urceolos picatos adicito et opercula picata imponito, id. 12, 16, 4: ambulatorium, a movable cover, Plin. 21, 14, 47, § 80.—Prov.: patellae dignum operculum, like to like, Hier. Ep. 1, 7; cf. id. ib. 127 (16), n. 9.—Of the covering of walls, wainscoting, panel-wo

operimentum.full: ŏpĕrīmentum (sync. opermentum; al. oprimentum, Prud. Psych. 461), i, n. id., a covering, cover, lid (class.): quibus operibantur operimenta et pallia opercula dixerunt, Varr. L. L. 5, § 167 Müll.: operimenta decem, Cato, R. R. 10: equis paria operimenta erant, Sall. Fragm. ap. Serv. Verg. A. 11, 770: nuces gemino protectae operimento, Plin. 15, 22, 24, § 86: fulmen, quo dolia exhauriuntur intactis operimen tis, the lids, id. 2, 51, 52, § 137: oculorum, id. 8, 42, 64, § 156: testei, id. 11, 37, 5

operio.full: ŏpĕrĭo, ŭi, ertum, 4 (archaic fut. operibo: ego operibo caput, Pompon. ap. Non. 507, 33; imperf. operibat, Prop. 4, 12, 35), v. a. pario, whence the opp. aperio, to uncover; cf. paro, to cover, cover over any thing (class.; syn.: tego, velo, induo). Lit. Operire capita, Plaut. Poen. 3, 4, 34; cf.: capite operto esse, Cic. Sen. 10, 34: operiri umerum cum toto jugulo, Quint. 11, 3, 141; id. praef. § 24.—Esp., of clothing: aeger multā veste operiendus est, Cels. 3, 7 fin.; so in Vulg. Isa. 58, 7; i

opero.full: ŏpĕro, āvi, 1, v. a., post-class. collat. form of operor, q. v.

operor.full: ŏpĕror (collat. form ŏpĕro, Cassiod. Hist. Eccl. 10, 33; Commod. 30, 14), ātus, 1, v. dep. n. [opus], to work, labor, toil, take pains; to be busied (not in Cic. or Cæs.).— Constr. absol. or with dat. Lit. In gen. Absol.: seniores (apes) intus operantur, Plin. 11, 10, 10, § 21: servi, qui operari in agro consueverunt, Dig. 28, 5, 35. — With dat., to bestow pains upon a thing; to devote one's self to, be engaged in or occupied with a thing (mostly poet. and in post-Aug. prose): reipublicae, Liv.

operositas.full: ŏpĕrōsĭtas, ātis, f. operosus, excessive pains, overmuch nicety, elaborate workmanship (post-Aug.): est etiam, quae περιεργία vocatur, supervacua, ut sic dixerim, operositas, Quint. 8, 3, 55: operositas suadendi, Tert. Anim. 2 fin.: vitreorum, Vop. Tac. 11.

operosus.full: ŏpĕrōsus, a, um, adj. opera. Taking great pains, painstaking, active, busy, industrious, laborious (class.; syn.: laboriosus, industrius): senectus, opp. to languida atque iners, Cic. Sen. 8, 26: colonus, Ov. Nuce, 57: cultibus ambae, id. Am. 2, 10, 5. —Poet. with Gr. acc.: Cynthia non operosa comas (al. comis), Prop. 5, 8, 52.—Poet. with gen.: vates operose dierum, in regard to, Ov. F. 1, 101.—Sup.: Syria in hortis operosissima, exceedingly industrious in gardening, Plin. 20, 5, 16, § 33.— Tran

opertaneus.full: ŏpertānĕus, a, um, adj. opertus, concealed, secret (post-Aug.): opertanea sacra, the secret rites of the Bona Dea, Plin. 10, 56, 77, § 156: di opertanei, who dwell in the bowels of the earth, Mart. Cap. 1, § 44

operte.full: ŏpertē, adv., v. operio, P. a. fin

opertio.full: ŏpertĭo, ōnis, f. operio, a covering, a cover (for operimentum), Varr. L. L. 5, § 72 Müll.

operto.full: ŏperto, āre, v. freq. a. id., to cover (ante-class.): opertat saepe opertit, Fest. p. 191 Müll.; Enn. ap. Non. 223, 30 (Ann. v. 500 Vahl.): continuo operta denuo, Plaut. Trin. 3, 3, 75 Fleck. (Ritschl, operi).

opertorium.full: ŏpertōrĭum, ii, n. id.. In gen., a cover (post-Aug.), Sen. Ep. 87, 2; Vulg. Exod. 36, 19.—Trop.: peccati, Ambros. in Psa. 118, Serm. 7, § 31; id. Cant. Cantic. 3, § 2.— In partic. A garment, Vulg. Psa. 101, 27.— A grave (post-class.), Sid. Ep. 3, 12.

opertum.full: ŏpertum, i, n., v. operio fin.

opertus1.full: ŏpertus, a, um, Part. and P. a., from operio.

opertus2.full: ŏpertus, ūs, m. operio, a covering (post-class.), App. Mag. p. 310, 15; Macr. S. 7, 9, 26.

operula.full: ŏpĕrūla, ae, f. dim. opera, a little trouble, slight service (post-class.), Dig. 50, 14, 3.— Transf., earnings, gain (postclass.): operulas merere, App. M. 1, p. 105, 31.

opetis.full: opetis, is, f., a plant, called also aristolochia, App. Herb. 19.
opetis.short: opetis, is, f., a plant, called also aristolochia, App.

ophellius.full: Ophellĭus, ii, m., a Roman surname, Inscr. Grut. 463, 2.
ophellius.short: Ophellĭus, ii, m., a Roman surname, Inscr.

opheltes.full: Ŏpheltes, ae, m., = Ὀφέλτης, a proper name. Son of Lycurgus, king of Thrace, Stat. Th. 5, 538.— A Trojan warrior, father of Euryalus, Verg. A. 9, 201.— One of the Etruscan seamen, Ov. M. 3, 605.— A Cyzicene, Val. Fl. 3, 198.
opheltes.short: Ŏpheltes, ae, m., = Ὀφέλτης, a proper name.

ophiaca.full: Ŏphĭăca, ōrum, n. plur., = τὰ Ὀφιακά, poems or treatises on serpents, Plin. 20, 23, 96, § 258.

ophias.full: Ōphĭăs, ădis, f., the daughter of Ophius, Ov. M. 7, 383.
ophias.short: Ōphĭăs, ădis, f., the daughter of Ophius, Ov.

ophicardelos.full: ŏphĭcardēlos or -us, i, m., a precious stone, otherwise unknown; perh. a kind of onyx, Plin. 37, 10, 65, § 177.
ophicardelos.short: ŏphĭcardēlos or -us, i, m., a precious stone, otherwise unknown;

ophici.full: Ŏphĭci, ōrum, m. ὄφεις, of or belonging to snakes, Snake-men, an old name of the Capuans (because their territory abounded in snakes), Serv. Verg. A. 7, 730.

ophidion.full: ŏphĭdĭon, ii, n., = ὀφίδιον (little snake), a fish resembling the conger, Plin. 32, 9, 35, § 109; 32, 11, 53, § 149.
ophidion.short: ŏphĭdĭon, ii, n., = ὀφίδιον (little snake), a fish resembling the conger, Plin.

ophiogenes.full: Ŏphĭŏgĕnes, um, m., = Ὀφιογενεῖς, a people of Asia Minor, who cured snakebites, Varr. ap. Prisc. p. 894 P.; Plin. 7, 2, 2, § 13; 28, 3, 6, § 30.
ophiogenes.short: Ŏphĭŏgĕnes, um, m., = Ὀφιογενεῖς, a people of Asia Minor, who cured snakebites, Varr.

ophiomachus.full: ŏphĭŏmăchus, i, m., = ὀφιομάχος (fighting with serpents); hence, a kind of locust, Vulg. Lev. 11, 22.
ophiomachus.short: ŏphĭŏmăchus, i, m., = ὀφιομάχος (fighting with serpents);

ophion1.full: ŏphīon, ŏnis, m., = ὀφίων, a fabulous animal of Sardinia, Plin. 28, 9, 42, § 151; 30, 15, 52, § 146.
ophion1.short: ŏphīon, ŏnis, m., = ὀφίων, a fabulous animal of Sardinia, Plin.

ophion2.full: Ŏphīon, ŏnis, m., = Ὀφίων, a proper name. One of the giants, Claud. Rapt. Pros. 3, 348.— One of the companions of Cadmus; hence, ŏphīŏnĭus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Ophion; poet. for Theban: Ophionia caedes, i. e. of Pentheus, Sen. Oedip. 483.— The father of Amycus, the Centaur; hence, ŏphīŏnĭdes, ae, m., the son of Ophion, the Ophionide, of Amycus, Ov. M. 12, 245.
ophion2.short: Ŏphīon, ŏnis, m., = Ὀφίων, a proper name.

ophiophagi.full: Ŏphĭŏphăgi, ōrum, m., = Ὀφιοφάγοι, snake-eaters, a people of Africa, Plin. 6, 29, 34, § 169; Mel. 3, 8, 8; Sol. 33, 17.
ophiophagi.short: Ŏphĭŏphăgi, ōrum, m., = Ὀφιοφάγοι, snake-eaters, a people of Africa, Plin.

ophiostaphyle.full: ŏphĭostăphўlē (ŏphĕos-), ēs, f., = ὀφιοσταφυλη (snake-grape), a kind of caper-bush: quidam id cynosbaton vocant, alii ophiostaphylen, Plin. 13, 23, 44, § 127.
ophiostaphyle.short: ŏphĭostăphўlē (ŏphĕos-), ēs, f., = ὀφιοσταφυλη (snake-grape), a kind of caper-bush: quidam id cynosbaton vocant, alii ophiostaphylen, Plin.

ophiostaphylon.full: ŏphĭostaphўlon, i, n., = ὀφιοστάφυλον, i. q. vitis alba, the white vine, white bryony: vitis alba est, quam Graeci ampeloleucen, alii ophiostaphylon ... appellant, Plin. 23, 1, 16, § 21 (dub.; Jahn, staphylen).

ophir.full: Ophir, indecl. (= ), a region in Southern Arabia, Vulg. 3 Reg. 9, 28; id. 1 Par. 29, 4.—Hence, Ophirius, a, um, of or from Ophir, Plin. 36, 26, 66, § 193.

ophitae.full: Ŏphītae, ārum, m., = Ὀφῖται, Snakeworshippers, a sect so called, Isid. Orig. 8, 5; Tert. Praescr. 47.
ophitae.short: Ŏphītae, ārum, m., = Ὀφῖται, Snakeworshippers, a sect so called, Isid.

ophites1.full: ŏphītes, ae, m., = ὀφίτης (snakestone), a kind of marble spotted like a snake, serpentine-stone: ophites serpentium maculis similis, unde et nomen accepit, Plin. 36, 7, 11, § 55; 36, 22, 43, § 158; Mart. 6, 42, 15; Luc. 9, 714.
ophites1.short: ŏphītes, ae, m., = ὀφίτης (snakestone), a kind of marble spotted like a snake, serpentine-stone: ophites serpentium maculis similis, unde et nomen accepit, Plin.

ophites2.full: Ŏphītes, ae, m., = Ὀφίτης, a son of Hercules, Hyg. Fab. 32.
ophites2.short: Ŏphītes, ae, m., = Ὀφίτης, a son of Hercules, Hyg.

ophitis.full: ŏphītis, ĭdis, f., = ὀφῖτις, for 1. ophites.

ophiuchus.full: Ŏphĭūchus, i, m., = Ὀφιοῦχος, the Serpent-holder, a constellation: quem claro perhibent Ophiuchum nomine Graii, Cic. N. D. 2, 42, 109 ex Arat.; Manil. 1, 331.
ophiuchus.short: Ŏphĭūchus, i, m., = Ὀφιοῦχος, the Serpent-holder, a constellation: quem claro perhibent Ophiuchum nomine Graii, Cic.

ophiusa1.full: ŏphĭūsa or ŏphĭussa, ae, f., = ὀφιοῦσα or ὀφιοῦσσα, a magical herb growing on the island of Elephantine, Plin. 24, 17, 102, § 163.
ophiusa1.short: ŏphĭūsa or ŏphĭussa, ae, f., = ὀφιοῦσα or ὀφιοῦσσα, a magical herb growing on the island of Elephantine, Plin.

ophiusa2.full: Ŏphĭūsa or Ŏphĭussa, ae, f., = Ὀφιοῦσα (-οῦσσα) An ancient name of Cyprus, whence ŏphĭūsĭus, a, um, Cyprian: arva, Ov. M. 10. 229.— The name of several islands, Plin. 3, 5, 11, § 78; 5, 31, 36, § 132; 4, 12, 20, § 61; 5, 32, 44, § 151.— A town in Pontus, Plin. 4, 12, 26, § 82.
ophiusa2.short: Ŏphĭūsa or Ŏphĭussa, ae, f., = Ὀφιοῦσα (-οῦσσα) An ancient name of Cyprus, whence ŏphĭūsĭus, a, um, Cyprian: arva, Ov.

ophrys.full: ŏphrys, ўos, f., = ὀφρύς, a plant with two leaves, twiblade, bifoil, Plin. 26, 15, 93, n. 2, § 164.
ophrys.short: ŏphrys, ўos, f., = ὀφρύς, a plant with two leaves, twiblade, bifoil, Plin.

ophthalmia.full: ophthalmĭa, ae, f., = ὀφθαλμία, an inflammation of the eye, Boëth. ex Arist. Topic. 3, p. 689.
ophthalmia.short: ophthalmĭa, ae, f., = ὀφθαλμία, an inflammation of the eye, Boëth.

ophthalmias.full: ŏphthalmĭas, ae, m., = ὀφθαλμίας, a fish (in pure Lat. oculata), Plaut. Capt. 4, 2, 70.
ophthalmias.short: ŏphthalmĭas, ae, m., = ὀφθαλμίας, a fish (in pure Lat.

ophthalmicus.full: ŏphthalmĭcus, i, m., = ὀφθαλμικός, an oculist (post-Aug.), Mart. 8, 74, 1.
ophthalmicus.short: ŏphthalmĭcus, i, m., = ὀφθαλμικός, an oculist (post-Aug.), Mart.

opicerda.full: ŏpĭcerda or ŏvĭcerda, ae, f., sheep's dung, Paul. ex Fest. s. v. sucerda, p. 302 Müll. dub.
opicerda.short: ŏpĭcerda or ŏvĭcerda, ae, f., sheep's dung, Paul.

opicillum.full: ŏpĭcillum, i, n. dim. ops, a little help (ante-class.): in uxorculae opicillum, Varr. ap. Non. 83, 25.

opiconsiva.full: Ŏpĭconsīva or Ŏpĕconsīva, ōrum, n., the festival of Ops Consivia, celebrated on the 25th of August: Opeconsiva dies ab deā Ope Consivia, quojus in Regiā sacrarium, Varr. L. L. 6, § 21 Müll.; Calend. Maff. ap. Inscr. Orell. 2, p. 396 and 311.
opiconsiva.short: Ŏpĭconsīva or Ŏpĕconsīva, ōrum, n., the festival of Ops Consivia, celebrated on the 25th of August: Opeconsiva dies ab deā Ope Consivia, quojus in Regiā sacrarium, Varr.

opicus.full: ŏpĭcus, a, um, adj. a fuller form for Opsus, Obscus, and Oscus, lit. Oscan; cf. Paul. ex Fest. p. 188 Müll.; hence, transf., clownish, rude, stupid, ignorant, foolish (not in Cic.): (Graeci) nos quoque dictitant barbaros et spurcius nos quam alios opicos appellatione foedant, M. Cato ap. Plin. 29, 1, 7, § 14: ut nostri opici putaverunt, Gell. 13, 9, 4: chartae, rough, coarse, unpolished, Aus. Prof. 22: amica, Juv. 6, 454: opici mures, barbarians of mice, that gnaw books, id. 3, 207.

opifer.full: ŏpĭfer, ĕra, ĕrum, adj. ops-fero, aidbringing, helping (poet. and in post-Aug. prose): deus, Ov. M. 15, 653: FORTVNA, Inscr. Orell. 1753.—Of things: folia, Plin. 16, 13, 24, § 64: fidem opiferam sociūm advocant, Enn. ap. Non. 144, 14 (p. 109, v. 165 Vahl.).

opifex.full: ŏpĭfex, ĭcis, comm. opus-facio, one who does a work. Lit., a worker, maker, framer, fabricator (class.; cf.: faber, artifex. operarius). In gen.: opifex aedificatorque mundi deus, Cic. N. D. 1, 8, 18: rerum or aeternus, Col. 3, 10, 10; cf.: opifex natura, Plin. 31, 1, 1, § 1: calor, Lact. 2, 9, 22: sylvestres apes, Varr. R. R. 3, 16.— In partic., a workman, mechanic, artist, artisan, etc.: opifices omnes in sordidā arte versantur, Cic. Off. 1, 42, 150; cf. id. N. D. 2, 60, 150; id. Fl. 8, 18; id

opificina.full: ŏpĭfĭcīna, ae, f., v. officina init.

opificium.full: ŏpĭfĭcĭum, ii, n. opifex, a working, the doing of a work, a work (ante- and post-class), Varr. R. R. 3, 16: in opificiis opera, App. Flor. n. 9.

opigena.full: Ŏpĭgĕna, ae, f. Ops-gigno, the midwife, an epithet of Juno, as the tutelar goddess of lying-in women, Mart. Cap. 2, § 149; cf.: Opigenam Junonem matronae colebant, quod ferre eam opem in partu laborantibus credebant, Fest. p. 200 Müll.

opilio.full: ōpĭlĭo and ūpĭlĭo, ōnis, m. for ovilio, from ovis, a shepherd: etiam opilio, qui pascit alienas oves, Plaut. As. 3, 1, 36.— Form upilio, Verg. E. 10, 19; Col. 7, 3, 13; Dig. 32, 1, 60; Vulg. Gen. 38, 12.— A kind of bird, otherwise unknown, Fest. p. 191 Müll.

opilius.full: Opĭlĭus, i, m., a Roman surname. Aurelius Opilius, a grammarian and author, Suet. Gram. 6.— Another Aurelius Opilius, a physician, Plin. 28, 4, 7, § 38.— M. Opilius Severus Macrinus, emperor of Rome, A. D. 218, Eutr. 8, 21.
opilius.short: Opĭlĭus, i, m., a Roman surname.

opimatus.full: ŏpīmātus, a, um, P. a., v. opimo fin.

opimianus.full: Ŏpīmĭānus, a, um, v. Opimius, B.

opimitas.full: ŏpīmĭtas, ātis, f. opimus, plentifulness, abundance, prosperity (ante- and postclass.): opimitates maximae, Plaut. Capt. 4, 1, 2; id. As. 2, 2, 16: praedarum, Amm. 19, 11.

opimius.full: Ŏpīmĭus (old orthog. Ŏpēīmĭus, Eckh. D. N. 5, p. 264), i, m., Ŏpīmĭa, ae, f., the name of a Roman gens. L. Opimius, consul A. U. C. 633, Cic. Brut. 83, 287; id. Cat. 1, 2, 4.— Q. Opimius, consul A. U. C. 600, Cic. de Or. 2, 68, 277.—In fem.: Opimia, a Vestal, Liv. 22, 57.—Hence, adj. ŏpī-mĭus, a, um, of or belonging to an Opimius: basilica Opimia, Varr. L. L. 5, 32, § 156. — ŏpīmĭānus, a, um, of or belonging to an Opimius, Opimian: Opimianum vinum; and absol. as subst.: ŏpīmĭānum, i, n., very ce

opimo.full: ŏpīmo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. opimus, to fatten, make fat (post-Aug.). Lit.: turtures, Col. 8, 7, 5; 8, 9, 2.— Transf. Of the soil, to make fruitful, to fertilize: terram, App. de Mundo, p. 68, 6.— To enrich, to make rich or abundant, to fill, load: auctumnum, Pomona, tuum September opimat, Aus. Ecl. de Mensib. 9.— Trop., to honor, glorify: numina victimis, Mart. Cap. poët. 9, § 914.— To enrich, Aus. Ep. 15, 1.—Hence, ŏpīmātus, a, um, P. a., fat (post-class.): abdomen, Aus. Idyll. 10, 105.

opimus.full: ŏpīmus, a, um, adj. ob, and obsolete pimo, to swell, make fat; akin to Gr. πίων, πιμελή; cf. pinguis, fat, rich, plump, corpulent; of a country, etc., rich, fertile, fruitful. Lit.: regio opima et fertilis, Cic. Imp. Pomp. 6, 14: campus, Liv. 31, 41: arva, Verg. A. 2, 782: Larissa, Hor. C. 1, 7, 11: vitis, Plin. 14, 3, 4, § 36.—Of living beings: boves, Cic. Tusc. 5, 34, 100: victima, Plin. 10, 21, 24, § 49: habitus corporis, Cic. Brut. 16, 64: stabulis qualis leo saevit opimis, of fat cattle, Va

opinabilis.full: ŏpīnābĭlis, e, adj. opinor, that rests on opinion or conjecture; conjectural, imaginary (class.): hanc omnem partem rerum opinabilem appellabant, Cic. Ac. 1, 8, 31; cited ap. Non. 148, 26: artes, quae conjecturā continentur et sunt opinabiles, Cic. Div. 1, 14, 24: mediocritates, id. Tusc. 3, 31, 74 (opp. naturales): amor (opp. naturalis), Gell. 12, 1, 23.

opinatio.full: ŏpīnātĭo, ōnis, f. id., a supposing, opining; a supposition, conjecture, imagination, fancy, opinion, belief (class.): opinationem volunt esse imbecillam assensionem, Cic. Tusc. 4, 7, 15; id. Ac. 2, 25, 78: haec autem opinatio est judicatio se scire, quod nesciat, id. Tusc. 4, 11, 26; cf. the context: mordax et inepta, Val. Max. 1, 8, 8: (Tullius) quid super tali opinatione sentiret, Arn. 3, 6.

opinator.full: ŏpīnātor, ōris, m. id.. * A supposer, conjecturer: ego vero ipse et magnus quidam sum opinator, etc., Cic. Ac. 2, 20, 66.— Under the emperors, one who collected the tribute-corn in the provinces for the army, Cod. Just. 12, 38, 11; cf. Cod. Th. 7, 4, 26; 11, 7, 16.

opinatus1.full: ŏpīnātus, a, um, P. a., v. opinor fin.

opinatus2.full: ŏpīnātus, ūs, m. opinor, opinion, supposition, imagination: propter opinatus animi, Lucr. 4, 465.

opinio.full: ŏpīnĭo, ōnis, f. id., opinion, supposition, conjecture, imagination, fancy, belief (class.). In gen.: apud homines barbaros opinio plus valet saepe, quam res ipsa, Cic. Fragm. Scaur. 7: est ergo aegritudo opinio recens mali praesentis ... laetitia opinio recens boni praesentis ... metus opinio impendentis mali ... lubido opinio venturi boni, etc., id. Tusc. 4, 7, 14; cf. id. ib. 4, 11, 26: magna nobis pueris opinio fuit, L. Crassum non plus attigisse doctrinae, quam, id. de Or. 2, 1, 1: ut opini

opiniosus.full: ŏpīnĭōsus, a, um, adj. opinio, fixed or set in opinion (rare): Antipater et Archidemus opiniosissimi homines, * Cic. Ac. 2, 47, 143 dub.; Tert. adv. Marc. 4, 35.

opiniuncula.full: ŏpīnĭuncŭla, ae, f. dim. id., a slight opinion (late Lat.): tenuis opiniuncula, Salv. Avarit. 5.

opinor.full: ŏpīnor, ātus, 1, v. dep. etym. dub.; perh. akin to Gr. ὄσσεσθαι; root οπ-, to be of opinion, to suppose, imagine, conjecture, deem, believe, think, judge (freq. and class.; syn.: arbitror, reor, censeo, sentio, credo); constr. with acc., an obj.-clause, with de, or absol.: aliquid, Cic. Mur. 30, 62: quoad opinatus sum, me in provinciam exiturum, etc., id. Fam. 7, 17, 2: de vobis hic ordo opinatur non secus ac, etc., think, id. Pis. 20, 45: male de Caesare, to have a bad opinion of, to think ill

opinus.full: ŏpīnus, a, um, v. necopinus and inopinus.

opiparus.full: ŏpĭpărus, a, um (post-class. collat. form ŏpĭpăris, e), adj. ops-paro, richly furnished, rich, splendid, sumptuous (anteand post-class.): opiparum magnarum copiarum apparatum, Paul. ex Fest. p. 188 Müll.: Athenae, Plaut. Pers. 4, 4, 1: opimitates, id. Capt. 4, 1, 2: obsonia, id. Mil. 2, 1, 29: munera, App. M. 5, p. 165, 37.—In the form opiparis, App. M. 1, p. 113, 13.—Adv.: ŏpĭpărē, richly, splendidly, sumptuously (class.): instructa domus opime atque opipare, Plaut. Bacch. 3, 1, 6: apparatum co

opis1.full: Ōpis, is, f., = Ὦπις. A nymph in the train of Diana, Verg. A. 11, 836; cf. Macr. S. 5, 22.— A Naiad, Verg. G. 4, 343.

opisthodomus.full: ŏpisthŏdŏmus, i, f., = ὀπισθόδομος, the back part of a temple or house, an opisthodome, Front. Ep. ad M. Caes. 1, 8 Mai.
opisthodomus.short: ŏpisthŏdŏmus, i, f., = ὀπισθόδομος, the back part of a temple or house, an opisthodome, Front.

opisthographus.full: ŏpisthogrăphus, a, um, adj., = ὀπισθόγραφος, written on the back (as, of the paper, etc.), opisthographic (post-Aug.): commentarii, Plin. Ep. 3, 5, 17.—Subst.: ŏpisthogrăphum, i, n., that which has been written upon on the back: testari in opisthographo, Dig. 37, 11, 4.
opisthographus.short: ŏpisthogrăphus, a, um, adj., = ὀπισθόγραφος, written on the back (as, of the paper, etc.), opisthographic (post-Aug.): commentarii, Plin.

opisthotonia.full: ŏpisthŏtŏnĭa, ae, f., = ὀπισθοτονία, a disease in which the head is drawn backwards, opisthotony (post-class.); opp. emprosthotonia, in which the head is drawn forwards, Cael. Aur. Acut. 3, 6; cf. Hier. Ep. ad Ephes. 6, 4; v. opisthotonos.
opisthotonia.short: ŏpisthŏtŏnĭa, ae, f., = ὀπισθοτονία, a disease in which the head is drawn backwards, opisthotony (post-class.);

opisthotonicus.full: ŏpisthŏtŏnĭcus, a, um, adj., = ὀπισθοτονικός, laboring under opisthotony (postAug.): sanat opisthotonicos, Plin. 20, 18, 75, § 197.
opisthotonicus.short: ŏpisthŏtŏnĭcus, a, um, adj., = ὀπισθοτονικός, laboring under opisthotony (postAug.): sanat opisthotonicos, Plin.

opisthotonos.full: ŏpisthŏtŏnos, i, m., = ὀπισθότονος, a disease in which the body is violently curved backwards, a form of lock-jaw (post-Aug.), Plin. 28, 12, 52, § 192; 23, 1, 24, § 48 (written as Greek, Cels. 4, 3, § 3).— A disease that causes a person to fall backwards (eccl. Lat.), Hier. 3 Ep. ad Ephes. 6, 4.
opisthotonos.short: ŏpisthŏtŏnos, i, m., = ὀπισθότονος, a disease in which the body is violently curved backwards, a form of lock-jaw (post-Aug.), Plin.

opiter.full: Ŏpĭter, ĭtĕris and ĭtris (cf. Prisc. p. 695 P.; gen. Opetris; cf. Borghes. Framm. de' Fasti Cons. 1, p. 66), m. ob-pater, a Roman prœnomen: Opiter est, cujus pater avo vivo mortuus est, Fest. p. 184 Müll.: Opiter Verginius, Liv. 2, 17; 2, 54.

opitergium.full: Ŏpĭtergĭum, ii, n., a city of Italy, in the territory of the Veneti, now Oderzo, Plin. 3, 19, 23, § 130; Tac. H. 3, 6.—Hence, ŏpĭtergīnus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Opitergium, Opitergian, Plin. 3, 18, 22, § 126.—Plur. subst.: ŏpĭtergīni, ōrum, m., the inhabitants of Opitergium, the Opitergians, Flor. 4, 2, 33.
opitergium.short: Ŏpĭtergĭum, ii, n., a city of Italy, in the territory of the Veneti, now Oderzo, Plin.

opition.full: ŏpĭtĭon, ōnis, m., = ὀπιτίων, a bulbous root used for food, a kind of onion, Plin. 19, 5, 30, § 95.
opition.short: ŏpĭtĭon, ōnis, m., = ὀπιτίων, a bulbous root used for food, a kind of onion, Plin.

opitulatio.full: ŏpĭtŭlātĭo, ōnis, f. opitulor, a helping, assisting, help, assistance (post-class.), Arn. 4, 129; Dig. 4, 4, 1; Vulg. 1 Cor. 12. 28.

opitulator.full: ŏpĭtŭlātor (ŏpĭtŭlus), ōris, m. id., a helper, aider, succorer (post-class.): opitulus Juppiter, et opitulator dictus est, quasi opis lator, Paul. ex Fest. p. 184 Müll.: sodalis opitulator, App. Flor. 3, p. 353, 25; Hier. in Isa. 7, 17, § 10.

opitulatus.full: ŏpĭtŭlātus, ūs, m. opitulor, a helping, help, aid (post-class.): ejus opitulatu, Fulg. Myth. 3, 8.

opitulor.full: ŏpĭtŭlor, ātus, 1 (old inf. pres. opitularier; v. in the foll.), v. dep. n. [ops-tulo, whence tuli], to bring aid; to help, aid, assist, succor (class.; syn.: adjuvo, subvenio, auxilior, succurro): amanti ire opitulatum, Plaut. Mil. 3, 1, 27: amicum amico opitularier, id. Curc. 2, 3, 54: sontibus, Cic. Fam. 4, 13, 3: inopiae, to relieve, Sall. C. 33, 2: permultum ad dicendum, Cic. Inv. 2, 2, 7: frequentatio, quae conjecturalibus causis opitulatur, Auct. Her. 4, 40, 53.— With contra, to be good a

opituma.full: ŏpĭtuma, i. q. optima, Inscr.; v. bonus.

opium.full: ŏpĭum or -on, i, n., = ὄπιον, poppyjuice, opium, Plin. 20, 18, 76, § 199; 25, 10, 81, § 130.
opium.short: ŏpĭum or -on, i, n., = ὄπιον, poppyjuice, opium, Plin.

opobalsametum.full: ŏpŏbalsămētum, i, n. opobalsamum, a place planted with balsam-trees (post-class.): silva palmeto et opobalsameto distinguitur, Just. 36, 3, 3.

opobalsamum.full: ŏpŏbalsămum, i, n., = ὀποβάλσαμον, the juice of the balsam-tree, opobalsam, balsam, balm, Stat. S. 3, 2, 141; Just. 36, 3, 4; Plin. 37, 13, 78, § 204.—Used for embalming bodies, Inscr. Grut. 692, 10.— Hence, in gen., perfume: hirsuto spirant opobalsama collo Quae tibi, Juv. 2, 41.
opobalsamum.short: ŏpŏbalsămum, i, n., = ὀποβάλσαμον, the juice of the balsam-tree, opobalsam, balsam, balm, Stat.

opocarpathon.full: ŏpŏcarpăthon, i, n., = ὀποκάρπαθον, the juice of the carpathum, Plin. 28, 10, 45, § 158.
opocarpathon.short: ŏpŏcarpăthon, i, n., = ὀποκάρπαθον, the juice of the carpathum, Plin.

opopanax.full: ŏpŏpănax, ăcis, m., = ὀποπάναξ, the juice of the herb panax, Plin. 20, 24, 100, § 264.
opopanax.short: ŏpŏpănax, ăcis, m., = ὀποπάναξ, the juice of the herb panax, Plin.

oporice.full: ŏpōrĭcē, ēs, f., = ὀπωρική, a medicine prepared from tree-fruits (quinces, etc.), Plin. 24, 14, 79, § 129.
oporice.short: ŏpōrĭcē, ēs, f., = ὀπωρική, a medicine prepared from tree-fruits (quinces, etc.), Plin.

oporotheca.full: ŏpōrŏthēca, ae, or ŏpōrŏthēcē, ēs, f., = ὀπωροθήκη, a place for keeping fruits, a fruit-room, fruitery (ante-class.), Varr. R. R. 1, 59, 2; 1, 2, 10.
oporotheca.short: ŏpōrŏthēca, ae, or ŏpōrŏthēcē, ēs, f., = ὀπωροθήκη, a place for keeping fruits, a fruit-room, fruitery (ante-class.), Varr.

oportet.full: ŏportet, ŭit, 2, v. impers. [2. opus], it is necessary, needful, proper, becoming, or reasonable; it behooves; I (thou, he, etc.) must or ought (cf.: opus est, necesse est, debeo; oportet denotes the necessity of reason or duty, necesse est that of compulsion).—Constr. class. with a subject-clause, the subj., or absol.; late Lat. also with ut and subj. tamquam ita fieri non solum oporteret, sed etiam necesse esset, Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 39, § 84: hoc fieri et oportet et opus est, id. Att. 13, 25, 1:

opos.full: ŏpos, i, m., = ὀπός, juice, sap, Cael. Aur. Acut. 3, 8, 96.
opos.short: ŏpos, i, m., = ὀπός, juice, sap, Cael.

oppallesco.full: oppallesco (obp-), pallŭi, 3, v. n. inch. [ob-palleo], to turn pale (post-class.): carnifex stupore oppalluit, Prud. στεφ. 1, 92; Coripp. Joann. 6, 156.

oppando.full: oppando, pandi, pansum, or passum, 3, v. a. ob-pando, to spread or stretch out against or before, to spread out (post-class.): aliquid ad flatus helices, Grat. Cyn. 55: cornibus oppansis et summā fronte coruscum (of the cross of Christ), Prud. Psych. 410: aulaei vice oppansā, Tert. Apol. 48 fin.; Hier. Ep. ad Galat. 1, v. 11, 12; Vulg. Exod. 35, 12.—Hence, oppansum (-passum), i, n., a covering, envelope (eccl. Lat.): corporis, Tert. Anim. 53.
oppando.short: oppando, pandi, pansum, or passum, 3, v.

oppango.full: oppango (obp-), pēgi, pactum, 3, v. a. ob-pango, to fasten or fix on, to affix (anteclass. and in post-Aug. prose): ubi savium oppegit, fugit, imprinted, Plaut. Curc. 1, 1, 60: repagula, quae ... ex contrario oppanguntur, Paul. ex Fest. s. v. repagula, p. 281 Müll.

oppansum.full: oppansum, i, n., v. oppando fin.

oppansus.full: oppansus, a, um, Part., from oppando.
oppansus.short: oppansus, a, um, Part., from oppando.

oppassus.full: oppassus, a, um, Part., from oppando.
oppassus.short: oppassus, a, um, Part., from oppando.

oppecto.full: oppecto (obp-), ĕre, v. a. ob-pecto, to comb off; transf., of eating, to pluck or pick off, to pick, to eat: nimio melius oppectuntur frigida, Plaut. Pers. 1, 3, 31.

oppedo.full: oppēdo (obp-), ĕre, v. n. ob-pedo, to break wind at any one; trop. for to deride, mock, insult; with dat.: curtis Judaeis, Hor. S. 1, 9, 70.

opperior.full: oppĕrĭor (obp-), pĕrītus and pertus, 4 (arch. forms, fut. opperibor, Plaut. Truc. 1, 2, 107 al.; inf. opperirier, id. ib. 2, 3, 5; v. infra; Ter. Eun. 5, 2, 51), v. dep. n. and a. [kindred with experior, from perior, whence peritus]. Neutr., to wait (class.; syn.: exspecto, praestolor): opperiri exspectare, Fest. p. 187 Müll.: pol, quamquam domi cupio, opperiar, Plaut. Trin. 4, 1, 23: vel sex mensis opperibor, id. Ps. 1, 3, 89: non quis parumper durare opperirier? id. Truc. 2, 3, 5: aut ibidem o

oppessulatus.full: oppessŭlātus (obp-), a, um, Part., from the obs. oppessulo [ob-pessulus], bolted or barred (post-class.): januam firmiter oppessulatam pulsare, App. M. 1, p. 112, 11: januae, Amm. 31, 13, 15.
oppessulatus.short: oppessŭlātus (obp-), a, um, Part., from the obs.

oppetitus.full: oppĕtītus (obp-), a, um, Part., from oppeto.
oppetitus.short: oppĕtītus (obp-), a, um, Part., from oppeto.

oppeto.full: oppĕto (obp-), īvi and ii, ītum, 3, v. a. ob-peto, to go to meet, to encounter (an evil, esp. death; class.; syn.: obeo, occumbo, intereo): malam pestem, Enn. ap. Cic. Tusc. 2, 16, 38 (Trag. v. 15 Vahl.); so, pestem, Plaut. As. 1, 1, 7—Esp.: mortem, to encounter death, for to perish, die (only of a violent or unnatural death), Enn. ap. Non. 507, 19 (Trag. v. 235 Vahl.): cum milites pro salute populi Romani mortem oppetiverint, Cic. Phil. 14, 14, 38; cf.: clarae mortes pro patriā oppetitae, id. T
oppeto.short: oppĕto (obp-), īvi and ii, ītum, 3, v.

oppexus.full: oppexus (obp-), ūs, m. oppecto, a sombing, dressing of hair: crinium regalium, App. M. 11, p. 261, 15.

oppico.full: oppĭco (obp-), āre, v. a. ob-pico, to smear over or seal up with pitch (anteclass.): corticem oppicato, Cato, R. R. 120.

oppidaneus.full: oppĭdānĕus, a, um, adj. oppidum, of a town (post-class.), Cod. Th. 12, 1, 38 sq.

oppidanus.full: oppĭdānus, a, um, adj. id., of or in a town other than Rome (since urbanus signifies, of Rome, from the capital); sometimes in a depreciating sense, opp. to urbanus, of or belonging to a small town, provincial (class.): senex quidam oppidanus, Cic. de Or. 2, 59, 240: oppidanum et inconditum genus dicendi, id. Brut. 69, 242: lascivia, Tac. A. 14, 17.—Subst.: oppĭdānus, i, m., a townsman: oppidani domus, Liv. 29, 9, 2.—In plur.: oppĭdāni, ōrum, m., the inhabitants of a town other than Rome, townsm

oppidatim.full: oppĭdātim, adv. id., by towns, in the towns, in every town (post-Aug.): ludos oppidatim constituerunt, Suet. Aug. 59: cum oppidatim victimae caederentur, id. Galb. 18.

oppido.full: oppĭdō, adv. etym. dub.; cf. ἔμπεδον; v. oppidum, very, very much, completely, exceedingly, exactly, precisely (already obs. in the time of Quint.: oppido sunt usi paululum tempore nostro superiores, Quint. 8, 3, 25. Confined altogether to familiar discourse; we meet with no example of oppido in Cicero's orations): oppido, valde multum. Ortum est autem hoc verbum ex sermone inter se confabulantium, quantum quisque frugum faceret, utque multitudo significaretur, saepe respondebatur, Quantum vel o

oppidulum.full: oppĭdŭlum, i, n. dim. oppidum, a small town (class.), Cic. Att. 10, 7, 1; id. Q. Fr. 2, 12, 1: mansuri oppidulo, quod versu dicere non est (viz Equus Tuticus), Hor. S. 1, 5, 87.

oppidum.full: oppĭdum, i (gen. plur oppidūm, Sulp. ap. Cic. Fam. 4, 5, 4; old abl plur. oppedeis, Lex. Servil.), n. ob and pedum; Gr. πέδον; Sanscr pada-m, on or over the plain. A town (of towns other than Rome, which was called Urbs; though occasionally the term oppidum was applied to Rome) (class.): oppidum ab opi dictum, quod munitur opis causā, ubi sit: et quod opus est ad vitam gerundam, Varr. L. L. 5, § 141 Müll.; cf. Fest. p. 202: hi coetus (hominum) sedem primum certo loco domiciliorum causā constitue

oppignerator.full: oppignĕrātor (obp-), ōris, m. oppignero, one who takes a pledge, who lends on a pledge, (eccl. Lat.), Aug. Ep. 215.

oppignero.full: oppignĕro (obp-), āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. ob-pignero, to give as a pledge, to pledge, pawn (rare but class.). Lit.: libelli pro vino etiam saepe oppignerabantur, Cic. Sest. 51, 110: anulum, Mart. 2, 57, 7.— Trop.: filiam. Ter. Heaut. 4, 5, 46: verbo se oppignerare, Sen. Ben. 3, 5, 2.

oppilatio.full: oppīlātĭo (obp-), ōnis, f. oppilo, a stopping up, obstructing (post-class.): narium, Scrib. Comp. 47.

oppilo.full: oppīlo (obp-), āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. obpilo, to stop up, shut up (rare but class; syn.: obturo, obstruo, claudo): metretam novam amurcā colluito, oppilato, Cato, R. R. 100; Varr. L. L. 5, 31, 135: ostia, Lucr. 6, 725: scalis tabernae oppilatis, Cic. Phil. 2, 9: clausae portae et oppilatae, Vulg. 2 Esdr. 7, 3.

oppius.full: Oppĭus, i, m.; Oppĭa, ae, f., the name of a Roman gens. C. Oppius, a friend of Cœsar, Cic. Att. 4, 16, 14 al.— L. Oppius, a Roman knight, Cic. Fl. 13, 31.— P. Oppius, a quœstor, defended by Cicero; v. the fragm. in Orell. p. 444.—In fem.: Oppia, the wife of L. Mindius, Cic. Fam. 13, 28, 2; v. also Juv. 10, 220 Jan.; id. 10, 322. —Hence, Oppĭus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to an Oppius, Oppian: Oppia lex, proposed by the people's tribune, C. Oppius, against women's extravagance in dress, Liv. 34

oppleo.full: opplĕo (obp-), ēvi, ētum, 2, v. a. obpleo, plenus, to fill completely, to fill up, fill (class.). Lit.: saucii opplent porticūs, Enn. ap. Cic. Tusc. 2, 16, 38 (Trag. v. 16 Vahl.): ager oppletus imbrium fremitu, Enn. ap. Serv. ad Verg. G. 1, 12 (Trag. v. 196 Vahl.): oppleta tritici granaria, Plaut. Truc. 2, 6, 42: aedis spoliis, id. ib. 2, 6, 41; Varr. R. R. 1, 8, 5: nives jam omnia oppleverant, Liv. 10, 46.— Transf.: alienus odor nares opplet, Varr. R. R. 3, 4, 3.— Trop.: jam opplebit auris meas

oppletus.full: opplētus, a, um, Part., from oppleo.
oppletus.short: opplētus, a, um, Part., from oppleo.

opploro.full: opplōro (obp-), āre, v. n. ob-ploro, to cry or wail at, against, or in any thing: auribus meis, Auct. Her 4, 52, 65.

oppono.full: oppōno (obp-), pŏsŭi (in Plaut pŏsīvi), sĭtum, 3 (sync.: oppostus for oppositus, Lucr. 4, 150), v. a. ob-pono, to set or place against, to set or station before or opposite, to oppose (class., cf.: obicio, offero, adversor). Lit. In gen.: se venientibus in itinere, Caes. B. C 3, 30: huic equites, id. ib. 3, 75: turrim ad introitum portūs, id. ib. 3, 39: armatos homines ad omnes introitus. Cic. Caecin. 8, 27: Eumenem adversariis, Nep. Eum. 3, 2: (Hannibali) opposuit natura Alpemque nivemque, Juv
oppono.short: oppōno (obp-), pŏsŭi (in Plaut pŏsīvi), sĭtum, 3 (sync.: oppostus for oppositus, Lucr.

opporto.full: opporto (obp-), āre, to bring: portat, subportat, obportat, Not. Tir. p. 11.
opporto.short: opporto (obp-), āre, to bring: portat, subportat, obportat, Not.

opportunitas.full: opportūnĭtas (obp-), ātis, f. opportunus. In gen., fitness, convenience, suitableness (class.; syn. occasio; cf.: copia, facultas): loci, local advantages, Caes. B. G. 3, 14: corporis, Cic. Leg. 1, 9, 27: anuli, id. Off. 3, 9, 38: membrorum, id. N D. 1, 33, 92: aetatis, Sall. J. 6, 3.— In partic. A fit, opportune, or favorable time, a favorable opportunity: optimā opportunitate ambo autem venistis, Plaut. Merc. 5, 4, 3; so id. Ep. 2, 2, 19: scientia opportunitatis idoneorum ad agendum temporum,

opportunus.full: opportūnus (obp-), a, um, adj. obportus, lit., at or before the port; hence, In gen., fit, meet, convenient, suitable, seasonable, opportune (class.; syn.: commodus, utilis): tempus actionis opportunum, Graece εὐκαιρια, Latine appellatur occasio, Cic. Off. 1, 40, 142: aetas opportunissima, id. Fam. 7, 7, 2: nihil opportunius accidere vidi, id. ib. 10, 16, 1.—Subst.: op-portūna, ōrum, n., fit or convenient things: locorum opportuna, Tac. A. 4, 24.— In partic. Advantageous, serviceable, useful: ce

oppositio.full: oppŏsĭtĭo (obp-), ōnis, f. oppono, an opposing, opposition (class.): disparatum est id, quod ab aliquā re per oppositionem negationis separatur, hoc modo: sapere, et non sapere, Cic. Inv. 1, 28, 42; Gell. 6, 1, 4: scientiae, Vulg. 1 Tim. 6, 20.

oppositus1.full: oppŏsĭtus, a, um, Part. and P. a., from oppono.

oppositus2.full: oppŏsĭtus, ūs, m. (in sing. used only in abl.) [oppono]. A placing or setting against, an opposing; with obj.-gen.: laterum nostrorum oppositus et corporum pollicemur, Cic. Marc. 10, 32; Sil. 10, 212. —With subj.-gen.: lunae, Cic. Rep. 1, 16, 25. — A placing or laying before, an interposition, intervention: oppositu globi noctem afferente, Plin. 2, 71, 73, § 181: aedium, Gell. 4, 5, 3.— A citing or bringing forward against one: oppositu horum vocabulorum commotus, Gell. 14, 5, 4.

oppressio.full: oppressĭo (obp-), ōnis, f. opprimo. A pressing down, Vitr. 10, 3, 3; trop., force, violence (class.), Ter. Ad. 2, 2, 30.— Violent seizure: occupatio fori, oppressio curiae, Cic. Dom. 3, 5.— Oppression, overthrow: legum et libertatis, Cic. Off. 3, 21, 83.— (Late Lat.) Med. t. t., = κατάληψις, a catalepsy, Cael. Aur. Acut. 2, 10, 56; id. Tard. 2, 5, 86.

oppressiuncula.full: oppressĭuncŭla (obp-), ae, f. dim. oppressio, a slight pressing, gentle pressure: papillarum horridularum, Plaut. Ps. 1, 1, 66.

oppressor.full: oppressor, ōris, m. opprimo, a crusher, destroyer: oppressores dominationis, Brut. ap. Cic. Ep. ad Brut. 1, 16.

oppressus1.full: oppressus (obp-), a, um, Part., from opprimo.
oppressus1.short: oppressus (obp-), a, um, Part., from opprimo.

oppressus2.full: oppressus (obp-), ūs, m. opprimo, a pressing down, pressure (poet. and in post-class. prose): in oppressu valido, Lucr. 1, 851: montis, Sid. Ep. 9, 11.

opprimo.full: opprĭmo (obp-), essi, essum, 3, v. a. ob-premo, to press against, press together; to press down (class.; syn. obruo). Lit.: voluit deus ora loquentis Opprimere, to close, Ov. M. 3, 295: oculos, to press together, i. e. close the eyes, sc. of a dying person, Val. Max. 2, 6, 8: fauces manu, Suet. Calig. 12: flammam in ore, to repress, Enn. ap. Cic. de Or. 2, 54, 122 (Trag. v. 437 Vahl.).— To press down: taleam pede, to press into the ground, Cato, R. R. 45; Plaut. Ps. 5, 1, 27: opprimi ruinā concl

opprobramentum.full: opprō^brāmentum (obp-), i, n. opprobro, a reproach, disgrace (ante-class.): opprobramentum, aut flagitium muliebre, Plaut. Merc. 2, 3, 84 (420 Ritschl).

opprobratio.full: opprō^brātĭo (obp-), ōnis, f. id., a reproaching, upbraiding, (post-class.): opprobratione permotus, Gell. 12, 12, 4: reprehensionis, id. 2, 7, 13.

opprobriosus.full: opprō^brĭōsus (obp-), a, um, adj [opprobrium], opprobrious (post-class.), Cod. Just. 1, 3, 41; Ambros. Cain et Abel, 1, 4, 14.
opprobriosus.short: opprō^brĭōsus (obp-), a, um, adj [opprobrium], opprobrious (post-class.), Cod.

opprobrium.full: opprō^brĭum (obp-), i. n. opprobro, a reproach, scandal, disgrace, dishonor, opprobrium (not in Cic. or Cæs.; syn.: dedecus, probrum, infamia). vereor, ne civitati meae sit opprobrio, si, etc., lest it should be a reproach, Nep. Con. 3, 4: et turpitudo generis opprobrio multis fuit, Quint. 3, 7, 19: opprobria culpae, Hor. Ep. 1, 9, 10.— Transf. A reproach, taunt, abuse, abusive word or language: morderi opprobriis falsis, Hor Ep. 1, 16, 38: fundere, id. ib. 2, 1, 146: dicere, Ov. M. 1, 758; Insc

opprobro.full: opprō^bro (obp-), no perf., ātum, 1, v. a. ob-probrum, to reproach, taunt, upbraid (ante- and post-class.; syn.: vitupero, objurgo, reprehendo): opprobrare, probrum obicere, Fest. p. 187 Müll.: egone id exprobrem, qui mihimet cupio id opprobrarier? Plaut. Most. 1, 3, 143: rus alicui, id. Truc. 2, 2, 25: adversariis, Gell. 17, 1, 11: mollities cuidam opprobrata acerbe, id. 3, 5 in lemm.

oppugnantia.full: oppugnantĭa, ae, f. oppugno, resistance, opposition (late Lat.), Dion. Exig Epist. de Rat. Paschae, p. 513 M.

oppugnatio.full: oppugnātĭo (obp-), ōnis, f. id., a storming, assaulting, besieging; an attack, assault, siege (class.). Lit.: de oppidorum oppugnationibus, Cic. de Or. 1, 48, 210: oppugnatio Gallorum, i. e. their method of besieging, Caes. B. G. 2, 6, 2; 7, 29, 2: propulsare, Cic. Cael. 9, 20: relinquere, to raise, Tac. A. 15, 16: oppugnatione civitas cingitur, Macr. S. 3, 9, 6.— Trop., an assault, attack with words, an accusation, etc.: totum genus oppugnationis hujus propulsare debetis. Cic. Cael. 9, 20; id.

oppugnator.full: oppugnātor (obp-), ōris, m. id., an assaulter, attacker, assailant (class.). Lit.: patriae, Cic. Phil. 12, 3, 8: oppugnatores, opp. obsessi, Tac. H. 3, 71.— Trop.: meae salutis, Cic. Planc. 31, 76.

oppugnatorius.full: oppugnātōrĭus (obp-), a, um, adj. oppugnator, of or belonging to a siege (only in Vitr.): res, Vitr. 10, 22; id. 10, 19.

oppugno1.full: oppugno (obp-), āvi, ātum (old inf. fut. oppugnassere, Plaut. Am. 1, 1, 55; v. Roby, Gram. 1, 197 sq.), 1, v. a. obpugno, to fight against, to attack, assail, assault, storm, besiege, war with (class.; cf.: obsideo, occupo). Lit.: omnes Galliae civitates ad se oppugnandum venisse, Caes. B. G. 1, 44: aggeribus, vineis, turribus oppugnabam oppidum, Cic. Fam. 2, 10, 3; id. Imp. Pomp. 8, 20; id. Har. Resp. 4, 6: castra, Caes. B. G. 6, 41: locum, id. ib. 5, 21: clamor oppugnantis, Enn. ap. Fest. p. 3

oppugno2.full: oppugno (obp-), no perf., ātum, 1, v. a. ob-pugnus, to beat with fists, to buffet (Plautin.): os, Plaut. Cas. 2, 6, 56.

opputo.full: oppŭto (obp-), āre, v. a. ob-puto, to prune (post-Aug.), Plin. 17, 21, 35, § 156.

oppuvio.full: oppŭvĭo, āre, v. a., to beat, strike: oppuviat, verberat, a puviendo, id est feriendo, Fest. p. 188 Müll.

ops1.full: ops, ŏpis (nom. sing. does not occur; and the dat. perh. only in Front. Ep. ad Verr. 6 fin.; abl. ope, but opi, Varr. L. L. 5, 32, 141), f. Sanscr. ap-nas, gain; Gr. ἄφενος, wealth; cf.: opulentus. copia = co-opia. Power, might, strength, ability, in abstr.: Romani scalis summā nituntur opum vi, Enn. ap. Macr. S. 6, 1 (Ann. v. 168 Vahl.); so Verg. A. 12, 552: summā ope niti, Sall. C. 1, 1: omni ope atque operā enitar, will employ all my strength and efforts, Cic. Att. 14, 14, 5: omnibus viribus

ops2.full: Ŏps, ŏpis (nom. sing. Opis, Plaut. Pacch. 4, 8, 52; Hyg. Fab. 130), f. a personification of 1. ops, the goddess of plenty, riches, and power, the wife of Saturn, and the patroness of husbandry; identical with Terra: Jovi . . . Ope gnato, Plaut. Pers. 2, 3, 2; Varr. L. L. 5, § 57; 64 Müll.; Enn. ap. Lact. 1, 14 (Euhem. n. 3 and 4, pp. 169 and 170 Vahl.); Macr. S. 1, 10; Cic. Univ. 11; id. Phil. 1, 7, 17; Ov. M. 9, 498.

optabilis.full: optābĭlis, e, adj. opto, to be wished for, desirable (class.): quae expetenda atque optabilia videntur, Cic. de Or. 1, 51, 221: mihi pax imprimis fuit optabilis, id. Phil. 7, 3, 7: tempus, Ov. M. 9, 758: quae ut concurrant omnia, optabile est, Cic. Off. 1, 14, 33.—Comp.: bono viro optabilius, Cic. Pis. 14, 33.—Sup. seems not to occur.— Adv.: optābĭlĭter, desirably (post-class.). —Comp. optabilius, Val. Max. 5, 1, 6 ext.

optatio.full: optātĭo, ōnis, f. id., a wishing, a wish (class.). In gen.: Theseo cum tres optationes Neptunus dedisset, Cic. Off. 3, 25, 94.— Rhet. fig., the expression of a wish: optatio atque exsecratio, Cic. de Or. 3, 53, 205; cf. Quint. 9, 1, 32; 9, 2, 3.— A choosing, choice, Symm. Ep. 1, 1.

optativus.full: optātīvus, a, um, adj. id., of or belonging to a wish, expressing a wish, optative (post-class.): modus optativus, the optative, Diom. p. 330 P.: adverbia, Mart. Cap. 3, § 310.

optato.full: optātō, adv., v. opto, P. a. fin.

optatus.full: optātus, a, um, Part. and P. a., from opto.

optice.full: optĭcē, ēs, f., = ὀπτική, optics: optices non ignarus, Vitr. 1, 1, 4.
optice.short: optĭcē, ēs, f., = ὀπτική, optics: optices non ignarus, Vitr.

optimas.full: optĭmas (optŭm-), ātis, adj. optimus, of or belonging to the best or noblest, aristocratic: res publica, quae ex tribus generibus illis, regali et optumati et populari confusa modice, Cic. Rep. 2, 23, 41 (from Non. 342, 31): matronae opulentae, optimates, Enn. ap. Cic. Fam. 7, 6, 1 (Trag. v 294 Vahl.).—Hence, subst.: optĭmas (optŭm-), ātis, usually in plur.: optĭmātes (optŭm-), um and ĭum, comm., the adherents of the best men, in a political sense, i. e. the aristocratic party, the aristocrats (

optimitas.full: optĭmĭtas, ātis, f. optimus, excellence (post-class.), Mart. Cap. 4, § 369.

optio1.full: optĭo, ōnis, f. opto, choice, free choice, liberty to choose, privilege, option (class.): optio haec tua est, utram harum vis condicionem, accipe, Plaut. Cas. 2, 4, 13: nec mihi jus meum optinendi optio est, id. Cas. 2, 2, 19: utro frui malis, optio sit tua, Cic. Fat. 2, 3: vobis datur, utrum velitis, you have your choice, id. Caecin. 23, 64: potestatem optionemque facere alicui, ut eligat, to let a person have his choice, id. Div. in Caecil. 14, 45: eligendi cui patroni daretur optio, id. Brut.

optio2.full: optĭo, ōnis, m. id., a helper whom one chooses for himself, an assistant (anteand post-class.). In gen.: tibi optionem sumito Leonidam, Plaut. As. 1, 1, 88: fabricae, Dig. 50, 6, 6.— In partic., in milit. lang., an adjutant, Tac. H. 1, 21; id. A. 1, 25; Varr. L. L. 5, § 91 Müll.: in re militari optio appellatur is, quem decurio aut centurio optat sibi rerum privatarum ministrum, quo facilius obeat publica officia, Paul. ex Fest. p. 184 Müll.: optio qui nunc dicitur, antea appellabatur accensus.

optionatus.full: optĭōnātus, ūs, m. 2. optio, an adjutancy (ante-class.), Cato ap. Fest. p. 201 Müll.

optivus.full: optīvus, a, um, adj. opto, chosen (poet. and in post-class. prose): cognomen, Hor. Ep. 2, 2, 101: optivi vocantur hi (tutores) qui ex optione sumuntur, Gai. Inst. 1, 154 (opp. to dativi).

opto.full: opto, āvi, ātum, 1 (optassis for optaveris, Plaut. Mil. 3, 1, 75), v. a. root op, whence Gr. ΟΠΤΩ, ὄψομαι; qs. to look out, pick out, = legere, eligere, to choose, select (anteclass. and poet.; syn. deligo): utrum vis, opta, dum licet, Plaut. Rud. 3, 6, 14; id. Aul. prol. 11: sapientius opta, Ov. M. 2, 102: non video hic, quid magnopere optem, Lucil. ap. Non. 358, 13: inhoneste parare divitias, Ter. And. 4, 5, 2: locum tecto, Verg. A. 1, 425: locum regno, id. ib. 3, 109: externos duces, id. ib.
opto.short: opto, āvi, ātum, 1 (optassis for optaveris, Plaut.

optostrotum.full: optostrōtum, i, n. ὀπτόσ-στρωτόν, a brick pavement, Not. Tir. p. 164.

optutu.full: optūtū, quasi optuitu, a verbo, quod est tuor; et significat video, Fest. p. 186 Müll.
optutu.short: optūtū, quasi optuitu, a verbo, quod est tuor;

opulentia.full: ŏpŭlentĭa, ae, f. opulens, riches, wealth, opulence (not in Cic. or Cæs.). Lit.: habemus publice egestatem, privatim opulentiam, Sall. C. 52, 22: opulentia neglegentiam tolerabat, id. ib. 52. 9: Trojae opulentia, Verg. A. 7, 262: metallorum, Plin. 2, 93, 95, § 207.—In plur.: deos decent opulentiae et factiones, Plaut. Trin. 2, 4, 89; id. Bacch. 3, 4, 17: copiis atque opulentiis anteire, Gell. 20, 5, 8.— Transf., like opes, resources, power, of a people: invidia ex opulentiā orta est, Sall. C. 6,

opulentitas.full: ŏpŭlentĭtas, ātis, f. id., wealth, power (ante class.): quasi ejus opulentitatem reverearis, Plaut. Mil. 4, 4, 35: nostra, Caecil. ap. Non. 146, 14.

opulento.full: ŏpŭlento, āre, v. a. id., to make rich, to enrich (poet and in post-Aug. prose): erum bacis olivae, Hor. Ep. 1, 16, 2: mensam pretiosis dapibus, Col. 8, 1, 2.

opulentus.full: ŏpŭlentus, a, um (less freq. ŏpŭlens, entis, Sall. J. 69, 3; Nep. Chabr. 3, 3; App. M. 10, p. 248, 11; Aus. Idyll. 2, 7), adj. ops, cf. Varr. L. L. 5, § 92 Müll., rich, wealthy, opulent (syn.: dives, locuples; opp. inops, Cic. Lael. 13, 46; id. Off. 2, 20, 70; class.). Lit.: opulenti, terrestribus rebus copiosi, Fest. s. v opis, p. 187 Müll. Absol.: magnae gentes opulentae, Enn. ap. Fest. p. 301 Müll.; so, oppidum, id. ap. Non. 470, 4 (Trag. v. 324 Vahl.); Caes. B. C. 3, 80: opulentissima civita

opulesco.full: ŏpŭlesco, ĕre, v. inch. n. [ops], to grow rich: in patriis opulescere campis, Furius poët. ap. Gell. 18, 11, 4 (also ap. Non. 148, 17).

opulus.full: ŏpŭlus, i, f., a kind of maple-tree: in arboribus, quas vocant opulos, Varr. R. R. 1, 8; Col. 5, 6, 4; 5, 7, 1 al.; Plin. 14, 1, 3, § 12.
opulus.short: ŏpŭlus, i, f., a kind of maple-tree: in arboribus, quas vocant opulos, Varr.

opunculo.full: ŏpuncŭlo, ōnis, m. opilio, a bird that imitates the shepherd's song, Paul. ex Fest. p. 191 Müll.

opuntius.full: Ŏpuntĭus, a, um, v. 3. Opus, II.

opus1.full: ŏpus, ĕris, n. Sanscr. ap-as, work; whence apuas, gain; v. ops; cf. also Germ. üben. Lit. In gen., work, labor (cf.: labor, ars, opera): quod in opere faciundo operae consumis tuae, in doing your work, Ter. Heaut. 1, 1, 21: menses octo continuos opus hic non defuit, cum vas nullum fieret, nisi aureum, Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 24, § 54: oratio in causarum contentionibus magnum est quoddam opus, atque haud sciam, an de humanisoperibus longe maximum, id. de Or. 2, 17, 71.— Esp. Work, art, workmanship: natu

opus2.full: Ŏpūs, ūntis, f., = Ὀποῦς, a town of Locris, in Greece, now Kardhenitza, Liv. 28, 7; Ov. P. 1, 3, 73.—Hence, ŏpūn-tĭus, a, um, adj., Opuntian: sinus, Mel. 2, 3, 6; Plin. 4, 7, 12, § 27: Philodamus, of Opus, Cic. Verr. 2, 2, 44, § 109.—In plur.: ŏpūntĭi, ōrum, m., the inhabitants of Opus, the Opuntians, Liv. 28, 6 fin.
opus2.short: Ŏpūs, ūntis, f., = Ὀποῦς, a town of Locris, in Greece, now Kardhenitza, Liv.

opusculum.full: ŏpuscŭlum, i, n. dim. 1. opus, a little work (class.): Myrmecides minutorum opusculorum fabricator, Cic. Ac. 2, 38, 120: accipies igitur hoc parvum opusculum lucubratum his jam contractioribus noctibus, id. Par. prooem. § 5: Cassi Parmensis, Hor. Ep. 1, 4, 3: mea, id. ib. 1, 19, 35.

ora1.full: ōra, ae, f. kindred with Sanscr. avāra, ripa citerior fluminis, the extremity of a thing; the border, brim, edge, margin, end, boundary. Lit. In gen. (class.; syn.: limbus, fimbria, instita, margo): omnes avidi spectant ad carceris oras, at the barriers, Enn. ap. Cic. Div. 1, 48, 107 (Ann. v. 88 Vahl.): oras pocula circum, Lucr. 4, 12: (clipei), Verg. A. 10, 243: vestimentorum, Fest. p. 182 Müll.; Vulg. Exod. 26, 10; id. Hag. 2, 13: gemmae, Plin. 37, 10, 66, § 180: vulneris, Cels. 5, 26, 23: aet

ora2.full: Ŏra (Hŏra), ae, f., the name of Hersilia, as a goddess, Ov. M. 14, 851.
ora2.short: Ŏra (Hŏra), ae, f., the name of Hersilia, as a goddess, Ov.
