orabilis.full: ōrābĭlis, e, adj. oro, exorable, Not. Tir. p. 106.

oracularius.full: ōrācŭlārĭus, a, um oraculum, dealing in or uttering oracles; prophetic: habuit autem oracularios servos, qui illum pessum dederunt, Petr. S. 43.
oracularius.short: ōrācŭlārĭus, a, um oraculum, dealing in or uttering oracles;

oraculum.full: ōrācŭlum (sync. oraclum: ex oraclo, Enn. ap. Cic. Div. 1, 21, 42, or Trag. v. 65 Vahl.; plur, oracla, Att. ap. Non. 488, 2, or Trag. Rel. p. 185 Rib.; Ov. M. 1, 321), i, n. oro, a divine announcement, an oracle (class.). Lit.: oracula ex eo ipso appellata sunt, quod inest in his deorum oratio, Cic. Top. 20, 77: quid est enim oraculum? nempe voluntas divina hominis ore enuntiata, Sen. Contr. 1 praef.: edere, Cic. Tusc. 1, 48, 116: petere a Dodonā, id. Div. 1, 43, 95: quaerere, Verg. G. 4, 449: po

orarium.full: ōrārĭum, ii, n. 1. ōs, a napkin, handkerchief, Lucil. ap. Non. 539, 22: oculum ligavit orario, Aug. Civ. Dei, 22, 8, 7.—Used in signifying applause, Vop. Aur. 48 fin.

orarius.full: ōrārĭus, a, um, adj. 1. ora, of or belonging to the coast (post-Aug.): naves, coasting-vessels, coasters, Plin. Ep. 10, 15 (26); cf. naviculae, id. ib. 10, 28, 2.

orata.full: Ōrāta, ae, m., an appellation bestowed on a certain Sergius, on account of his fondness for the gilt bream (aurata, orata, v. auro, P. a. fin.), Varr. R. R. 3, 3, 10, Col. 8, 16, 5; Fest. p. 182 Müll.
orata.short: Ōrāta, ae, m., an appellation bestowed on a certain Sergius, on account of his fondness for the gilt bream (aurata, orata, v.

oratim.full: ōrātim, adv. 1. ora, coastwise, from coast to coast, Sol. 3 dub. (al. moratim).

oratio.full: ōrātĭo, ōnis, f. oro, a speaking, speech, discourse, language In gen., the connection of words to express thought: non est autem in verbo modus hic, sed in oratione, id est, in continuatione verborum, Cic. 3, 42, 167. Speech, the power or faculty of speech, the habit or use of language: quae (ferae) sunt rationis et orationis expertes, Cic. Off. 1, 16, 50: natura vi rationis hominem conciliat homini et ad orationis et ad vitae societatem, id. ib. 1, 4, 12.— Speech, language, utterance; opp. to f

oratiuncula.full: ōrātĭuncŭla, ae, f. dim. oratio, a little speech, a brief oration (class.), Cic. Brut. 19, 77; id. Att. 13, 19, 2; 15, 3, 2; Quint. 4, 3, 17: aureola, Cic. N. D. 3, 17, 43.

oratius.full: Ŏrātĭus, arch. for Horatius, v. Vahl. ad Enn. Ann. v. 164, p. 27.

orator.full: ōrātor, ōris, m. oro, one who speaks. A speaker, orator (very common in all periods and styles of writing): eum (oratorem) puto esse, qui et verbis ad audiendum jucundis et sententiis ad probandum accommodatis uti possit in causis forensibus atque communibus. Hunc ego appello oratorem, eumque esse praeterea instructum voce et actione et lepore quodam volo, Cic. de Or. 1, 49, 213: is orator erit, meā sententiā, hoc tam gravi dignus nomine, qui, quaecunque res inciderit, quae sit dictione explican

oratorius.full: ōrātōrĭus, a, um, adj. orator. Of or belonging to an orator, oratorical (class.), Cic. de Or. 1, 54, 231: ornamenta, id. Brut. 75, 261: vis dicendi, id. Ac. 1, 8, 32: ars, Quint. praef. § 17: gestus, id. 11, 3, 125: compositio, id. 1, 8, 13: virtus, id. 3, 1, 10; 6, 3, 39: ingenium, Cic. Brut. 29, 110.— Subst.: ōrātōrĭa, ae, f. (sc. ars), the oratorical art, oratory, Quint. 2, 14, 1; 2.— Of or belonging to praying; hence, subst.: ōrātōrĭum, ii. n. (sc. templum), a place of prayer, an oratory (ec

oratrix.full: ōrātrix, īcis, f. id.. She that prays or beseeches, a female suppliant (rare but class.): me oratricem haud sprevisti, Plaut. Mil. 4, 2, 80: pacis et foederis, * Cic. Rep. 2, 8, 14.— A transl. of ῥητορική, rhetoric, oratory, Quint. 2, 14, 1.

oratum.full: ōrātum, i, n. oro, a prayer, entreaty, supplication: cum orata ejus reminiscor, Ter. Hec. 3, 3, 25; 4, 1, 60.

oratus.full: ōrātus, ūs (only in abl. sing. and plur.), m. oro, a praying, entreating; a request, entreaty (very rare but class.): oratu tuo, Cic. Fl. 37, 92: illarum oratu, Plaut. Cas. 2, 2, 17; Sid. Ep. 9, 14 init.: magnis oratibus, Coripp. Laud. Just. 2, 4.

orbatio.full: orbātĭo, ōnis, f. orbo, a depriving, privation (post-Aug.), Sen. Ep. 87, 35.

orbator.full: orbātor, ōris, m. id., one who deprives others of children or parents, a bereaver (poet.): nostri orbator, Achilles, Ov. M. 13, 500.

orbefacio.full: orbĕfăcĭo, ĕre, v. a. orbus-facio, to bereave, to make an orphan: orbefacio, ὀρφανίζω, Gloss. Philox.

orbelus.full: Orbēlus (-lŏs), i, m., = Ὀρβηλός, a mountain on the borders of Macedonia and Thrace: Orbelus, Mel. 2, 2, 2; Plin. 4, 10, 17, § 35.
orbelus.short: Orbēlus (-lŏs), i, m., = Ὀρβηλός, a mountain on the borders of Macedonia and Thrace: Orbelus, Mel.

orbicularis.full: orbĭcŭlāris, e, adj. orbiculus, circular, orbicular, an appellation of a plant: herba, App. Herb. 17; cf. Marc. Emp. 4.

orbiculatim.full: orbĭcŭlātim, adv. id., circularly, in circles or rings (post-Aug.), Plin. 11, 37, 67, § 177; Macr. S. 7, 9, 3.

orbiculatus.full: orbĭcŭlātus, a, um, adj. id., circleshaped, rounded, circular, orbiculate (class.): mala, round apples, an excellent kind of apple, Varr. R. R. 1, 59; Col. 5, 10, 19; 12, 45, 5; Pall. Febr. 25, 18; Macr. S. 3, 19, 2.— Hence, transf.: malis orbiculatis pasti, i. e. well-fed, Cael. ap. Cic. Fam. 8, 15, 1: capita caulium, Plin. 27, 13, 109, § 133: ambitus foliorum, id. 24, 15, 87, § 137.

orbiculor.full: orbĭcŭlor, āri, v. dep. id., to go round in a circle: orbiculatur, κυκλεύει, Gloss. Philox.

orbiculus.full: orbĭcŭlus, i, m. dim. orbis, a small disk; a sheave, roller, pulley, etc. (anteclass. and post-Aug.), Cato, R. R. 3, 6; 22, 2; Col. 4, 30, 4; Vitr. 10, 5: radix concisa in orbiculos, cut in little disks or slices, Plin. 25, 13, 94, § 148; Inscr. Orell. 2519.— Esp., the nave of a wheel, Vitr. 10, 2, 9.

orbifico.full: orbĭfĭco, āre, v. a. orbus-facio, to bereave, make childless: orbificor liberorum leto, Att. ap. Non. 179, 26 (Trag. Rel. p. 161 Rib.).

orbile.full: orbīle, a false read. for orbis ... ligneus, Varr. R. R. 3, 5, 15.

orbilius.full: Orbĭlĭus, i, m., the name of a Roman gens. So, Orbilius, a grammarian in Rome in the time of Cicero, Hor. Ep. 2, 1, 71; Suet. Gram. 9.
orbilius.short: Orbĭlĭus, i, m., the name of a Roman gens.

orbis.full: orbis, is (nom. orbs, Ven. Carm. 8, 5. —Abl. regul. orbe; but orbi, Lucr. 5, 74: ex orbi, Varr. R. R. 3, 5, 16; Rutil. ap. Charis. p. 112 P.: orbi terrae, in the meaning in the world, Cic. Sest. 30, 66; so, orbi terrarum, Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 38, § 82 Halm; id. Dom. 10, 24; id. Fragm. ap. Charis. p. 112 P.), m. etym. dub.; perh. akin to Sanscr. dhvar, bend, twist, any thing of a circular shape, a ring, round surface, disk, hoop, orbit, orb, a circle (class.; cf.: circus, circulus, gyrus, spira). Lit

orbita.full: orbĭta, ae, f. orbis. A track or rut made in the ground by a wheel. Lit. (class.): impressa orbita, Cic. Att. 2, 21, 2; Cic. Verr. 2, 3, 3, § 6; Verg. G. 3, 293; Liv. 32, 17.— Trop., a track, course, path (ante-class. and poet.): neque id ab orbitā matrum familias instituti, quod, etc., Varr. ap. Non. 542, 28; Plin. 8, 58, 83, § 227; a beaten path, Quint. 2, 13, 16: veteris culpae, i. e. bad example, Juv. 14, 37.— An impression, mark left by a ligature: vinculi, Plin. 17, 23, 35, § 210.— A circu

orbitanium.full: Orbĭtānĭum, i, n., a city in Samnium, Liv. 24, 20.
orbitanium.short: Orbĭtānĭum, i, n., a city in Samnium, Liv.

orbitas.full: orbĭtas, ātis, f. orbus, bereavement of parents or children, of a husband or other dear person, childlessness, orphanage, widowhood (class.). Lit.: in orbitatem liberos producere, Plaut. Capt. 3, 5, 105: bonum liberi, misera orbitas, Cic. Fin. 5, 28, 84: familiaris, Liv. 26, 41, 9: mea, quod sine liberis sum, Curt. 6, 9, 12: tutorem instituere (filiorum) orbitati, Cic. de Or. 1, 53, 228: horum uxores cum viderent exsilio additam orbitatem, Just. 2, 4, 4: maximā orbitate rei publicae virorum tali

orbitosus.full: orbĭtōsus, a, um, adj. orbita, full of cart-ruts (poet.), Verg. Cat. 8, 17.

orbitudo.full: orbĭtūdo, ĭnis, f. orbus, bereavement, orphanhood (ante-class. for orbitas): miseret orbitudinis, Att. ap. Non. 146, 17; Pac. and Turp. ib. 18 sq.

orbitus.full: orbītus, a, um orbis, circular (anteand post-class.): motu, Varr. ap. Non. 148, 16; Arn. 2, 83 (others read orbico; cf. Oehler ad Varr. Sat. Menipp. p. 139).
orbitus.short: orbītus, a, um orbis, circular (anteand post-class.): motu, Varr.

orbius.full: Orbĭus clīvus, a place in Rome, Paul. ex Fest. p. 182 Müll.; the same called Urbius clivus, Liv. 1, 48, 6; cf. Becker's Antiq. 1, p. 526.
orbius.short: Orbĭus clīvus, a place in Rome, Paul.

orbo.full: orbo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. orbus, to deprive or bereave of parents, children, or other dear persons; to make fatherless, motherless, childless, etc. (class.; syn.: privo, viduo). Lit.: filio orbatus, Cic. Off. 1, 10, 30: mater orbata filio, id. Clu. 15, 45: orbatura patres fulmina, Ov. M. 2, 391.—Of animals: catulo lactente orbata leaena, Ov. M. 13, 547.— Transf., in gen., to deprive, bereave, strip of any (esp. a precious) thing: pater me lumine orbavit, Enn. ap. Charis. p. 250 P. (Trag. v. 351

orbona.full: Orbōna, ae, f. id., the tutelary goddess of parents bereft of their children, Cic. N. D. 3, 25, 63; cf. Plin. 2, 7, 5, § 16; Arn. 4, 131; Tert. ad Nat. 2, 14.

orbus.full: orbus, a, um, adj. kindr. with Gr. ὀρφανός; cf. Fest. p. 183 Müll., bereaved, bereft, of parents or children; parentless, fatherless, childless (class.; cf. pupillus). Lit.: senex, Cic. Par. 5, 2, 39; cf.: parens liberorum an orbus sit, Quint. 5, 10, 26; 7, 4, 23: filii mei, te incolumi, orbi non erunt, Cic. Q. Fr. 1, 3, 10.—With gen.: Memnonis orba mei venio, Ov. M. 13, 595.—With ab: a totidem natis orba, Ov. H. 6, 156.—Of beasts: liberis orbae oves, Plaut. Capt. 4, 2, 38.—Subst.: orba, ae, f.,

orca1.full: orca, ae, f. cf. ἄρχαὔρχα, a kind of whale, an orc, Plin. 9, 6, 5, § 12.— Transf. A large-bellied vessel, a butt, tun (cf.: seria, dolium): orca genus marinae beluae maximum dicitur: ad cujus similitudinem vasa quoque ficaria orcae dicunter: sunt enim teretes, atque uniformi specie, Fest. p. 180 Müll.: orcae in Hispaniā fervore musti ruptae, Varr. R. R. 1, 13, 6; Col. 12, 15, 2: Byzantia orca (which had contained pickled tunny-fish), Hor. S. 2, 4, 66; cf. Pers. 3, 76.— A tunnel used for throwing

orca2.full: Orca, ae, m., a Roman surname, e. g. Valerius Orca, Cic. Fam. 13, 4 sq.
orca2.short: Orca, ae, m., a Roman surname, e.

orcades.full: Orcădes, um, f., islands near Scotland, now the Orkneys, Mel. 3, 6, 7; Tac. Agr. 10; Plin. 4, 16, 30, § 103.—Acc. plur.: Orcadas, Juv. 2, 161.
orcades.short: Orcădes, um, f., islands near Scotland, now the Orkneys, Mel.

orchamus.full: Orchămus, i, m., = Ὄρχαμος, a king of Babylonia, the father of Leucothŏē, Ov. M. 4, 212.
orchamus.short: Orchămus, i, m., = Ὄρχαμος, a king of Babylonia, the father of Leucothŏē, Ov.

orchas.full: orchăs, ădis, f., a kind of edible olive of an oblong shape, Verg. G. 2, 86; cf. Macr. S. 3, 20.
orchas.short: orchăs, ădis, f., a kind of edible olive of an oblong shape, Verg.

orchesta.full: orchēsta, ae, m., = ὀρχηστής, a dancer, a pantomime (late Lat.): orchestarum loquacissimae manus, Cassiod. Var. 4, 51.
orchesta.short: orchēsta, ae, m., = ὀρχηστής, a dancer, a pantomime (late Lat.): orchestarum loquacissimae manus, Cassiod.

orchestopolarius.full: orchēstŏpŏlārĭus, ii, m., = ὀρχηστόπολος, a juggler, tumbler, dancer (postclass.), Firm. Math. 8, 15.
orchestopolarius.short: orchēstŏpŏlārĭus, ii, m., = ὀρχηστόπολος, a juggler, tumbler, dancer (postclass.), Firm.

orchestra.full: orchēstra, ae, f., = ὀρχήστρα. The place where the Senate sat in the theatre, the orchestra: in orchestrā senatorum sunt sedibus loca destinata, Vitr. 5, 6; Juv. 7, 47; Suet. Caes. 39; id. Aug. 35; 44; id. Claud. 21 et saep.— Transf., the Senate (poet.): similesque videbis Orchestram et populum, Juv. 3, 178.— Another place on the stage, acc. to Fest. p. 181 b; cf. Müll. ad h. l.

orchion.full: orchĭon, ii, n., = ὄρχις, testiculus, a plant, called also testiculata, App. Herb. 82.
orchion.short: orchĭon, ii, n., = ὄρχις, testiculus, a plant, called also testiculata, App.

orchis.full: orchis, is, f., = ὄρχις A plant, a kind of olive, Col. 5, 8, 4; id. Arb. 17, 3; Pall. Febr. 18, 4.— Another plant, so called from the shape of its roots, the orchis: mirabilis est orchis herba, sive serapias, gemina radice testiculis simili, Plin. 26, 10, 62, § 95.
orchis.short: orchis, is, f., = ὄρχις A plant, a kind of olive, Col.

orchita.full: orchīta or -es, ae, m., and orchī-tis, is, f., = ὀρχῖτις, a kind of olive of an oblong shape: albam pauseam, vel orchitam, vel radiolum, Col. 12, 49, 2; 12, 50, 1; Cato, R. R. 6, 1; 7, 4; cf. Varr. R. R. 1, 60; Paul. ex Fest. p. 180 Müll.
orchita.short: orchīta or -es, ae, m., and orchī-tis, is, f., = ὀρχῖτις, a kind of olive of an oblong shape: albam pauseam, vel orchitam, vel radiolum, Col.

orchius.full: Orchĭus, a, m. and f., the name of a Roman gens.—So, C. Orchius, a tribune of the people, 572 A.U.C., by whom the Lex Orchia was proposed, Macr. S. 3, 17, 2; Schol. Bob. ad Cic. Sest. p. 310, 32 Bait.

orchomenus.full: Orchŏmĕnus or -os, i, m. or f. (and -on or -um, i, n.), = Ὀρχόμενος. The son of Athamas and Themisto, Hyg. Fab. 1.— A city in Bœotia, Caes. B. C. 3, 55; Plin. 8, 58, 83, § 226.— A city in Thessaly: Minyius, Plin. 4, 8, 15, § 29.—Hence, Orchŏmĕnĭus, a, um, adj., = Ὀρχομένιος, Orchomenian: lacus, Plin. 16, 36, 66, § 168: calamus, id. 16, 36, 66, § 164.—Plur subst.: Orchŏmĕnii, ōrum, m., the inhabitants of Orchomenos, the Orchomenians, Nep. Lys. 3, 4; Just. 11, 3.— A city in Arcadia, Liv. 32, 5: su

orchus.full: Orchus, i, m., = Orcus: Orchi traditus thesauro, Naev. ap. Gell. 1, 24, 2.
orchus.short: Orchus, i, m., = Orcus: Orchi traditus thesauro, Naev.

orcinianus.full: Orcīnĭānus, a, um, adj. Orcus, of or belonging to Orcus or to the dead (poet.): sponda, i. e. a bier, Mart. 10, 5, 9.

orcinus.full: Orcīnus, a, um, adj. id., of or belonging to the realms of the dead: liberti, set free by the last will of their masters, Dig. 26, 4, 3, § 3; ib. 33, 8, 22; ib. 40, 5, 30, § 12 al.: senatores, who had got into the Senate by means of Cœsar's testament, Suet. Aug. 35.

orcivius.full: Orcivius, a, name of a Roman gens; esp. C. Orcivius, Cicero's colleague as prœtor, Cic. Clu. 34, 94; 53, 147; cf. id. Or. 48, 160.
orcivius.short: Orcivius, a, name of a Roman gens;

orcula.full: orcŭla, ae, f. dim. 1. orca, a small tun, a cask (ante- and post-class.): oleas in orculam calcato manibus siccis, Cato, R. R. 117; Auct. de Limit. p. 253 Goes.

orcularis.full: orcŭlāris, e, adj. orcula, of or belonging to a cask or rundlet (post-class.): termini, Auct. de Limit. p. 251 Goes.

orcus.full: Orcus, i, m. kindr. with ἕρκος and the Lat. urgeo: Orcum quem dicimus, ait Verrius ab antiquis dictum uragum, Fest. p. 202 Müll.—Hence, prop., that which impels, constrains, confines. the Lower World, the abode of the dead, Orcus: Acherunsia templa alta Orci, salvete infera, Enn. ap. Varr. L. L. 7, § 6 Müll. (Trag. v. 107 Vahl.); Lucr. 1, 115; 6, 762: Minos sedet arbiter Orci, Prop. 4, 18, 27; Verg. A. 6, 273. — Transf. The god of the infernal regions, Orcus, Pluto: Orcus recipere ad se hanc nol

orcynus.full: orcȳnus, i, m., = ὄρκυνος, a large seafish of the tunny species, Plin. 32, 11, 53, § 149.
orcynus.short: orcȳnus, i, m., = ὄρκυνος, a large seafish of the tunny species, Plin.

ordeum.full: ordĕum, and its derivv., v. hord-.

ordinalis.full: ordĭnālis, e, adj. ordo, that denotes an order of succession, ordinal: nomen, an ordinal numeral (primus, secundus, etc.), Prisc. p. 581 P. al.

ordinarius.full: ordĭnārĭus, a, um, adj. ordo, of or belonging to order, orderly; according to the usual order, usual, customary, regular, ordinary (not in Cic. or Cæs.). Of persons. In gen.: ordinarii consules, regular, elected in the usual manner at the beginning of the year (opp. suffecti), Liv. 41, 18: pugiles (with legitimi), Suet. Aug. 45; cf. consulatus, id. Galb. 6: gladiatores, Sen. Ep. 7, 3: ordinarium hominem Oppius ait dici solitum scurram et improbum ... At Aelius Stilo, qui minime ordine viveret ..

ordinate.full: ordĭnātē, adv., v. ordino, P. a. fin.

ordinatim.full: ordĭnātim, adv. ordinatus, in order or succession; in good order. Lit.: honores ordinatim petere in re publicā, Sulp. ap. Cic. Fam. 4, 5, 3: ille iit passim, ego ordinatim, in good order, with unbroken ranks, Brut. ap. Cic. Fam. 11, 13, 2.— Transf., regularly, properly: musculus ordinatim structus, Caes. B. C. 2, 10, 5.

ordinatio.full: ordĭnātĭo, ōnis, f. ordino, a setting in order, regulating, arranging; an order, arrangement, regulation (mostly postAug.). Lit.: architectura constat ex ordinatione, quae Graece τάξις dicitur, et ex dispositione. Ordinatio est modica membrorum operis commoditas separatim, universaeque proportionis ad symmetriam comparatio, Vitr. 1, 2.—Of vines, Col. 4, 29, 12.— Trop. In gen., an ordering, regulating, orderly arrangement: comitiorum, Vell. 2, 124, 3: anni, Suet. Aug. 31: vitae, Plin. Ep. 9, 28,

ordinativus.full: ordĭnātīvus, a, um, adj. id., indicating or signifying order (post-class.): principatus, Tert. adv. Herm. 19: adverbia, Prisc. p. 1022 P.

ordinator.full: ordĭnātor, ōris, m. id., an orderer, regulator, arranger (post-Aug.): litis, i. e. pleader, Sen. Ep. 109: omnium, Hilar. Trin. 4, 12, 14.— An ordainer, one authorized to ordain, Ambros. in 2 Tim. 4, 13.

ordinatrix.full: ordĭnātrix, īcis, f. ordinator, she that orders or arranges (eccl. Lat.): mens ordinatrix rerum omnium, Aug. Ep. 56.

ordinatus.full: ordĭnātus, a, um, Part. and P. a., from ordino.

ordino.full: ordĭno, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. ordo, to order, set in order, arrange, adjust, dispose, regulate. In gen. (class.; syn.: dispenso, dispono): copias, Nep. Iph. 2, 2; so, milites, Liv. 29, 1: agmina, Hor. Epod. 17, 9; and: aciem, Just. 11, 9, 8: arbusta latius sulcis, Hor. C. 3, 1, 9: vineam paribus intervallis, Col. 3, 13: res suas suo arbitrio, Sen. Ep. 9, 14: partes orationis, Cic. Inv. 1, 14, 9: litem, id. de Or. 2, 10, 43: causam, Dig. 40, 12, 24: judicium, ib. 40, 12, 25: testamentum, ib. 5, 2,

ordior.full: ordĭor, orsus, 4 (fut. ordibor for ordiar: non parvam rem ordibor, Att. ap. Non. 39, 22; part. perf. orditus, Sid. Ep. 2, 9; Vulg. Isa. 25, 7), v. dep., lit., to begin a web, to lay the warp; hence, also, in gen., to begin, undertake a thing: ordiri est rei principium facere, unde et togae vocantur exordiae, Fest. p. 185 Müll.; cf. Isid. 19, 29, 7: telam, Hier. in Isa. 9, 30, v. 1; Vulg. Isa. 25, 7. Lit., to begin to weave a web, to weave, spin: araneus orditur telas, Plin. 11, 24, 28, § 80.—So

orditus.full: ordītus, a, um, Part., from ordior.
orditus.short: ordītus, a, um, Part., from ordior.

ordo.full: ordo, ĭnis, m. from root or-; Sanscr. ar-, to go, strive upward; cf. orior, through an adj. stem ordo-; v. Corss. Krit. Beitr. p. 108, a regular row, line, or series, methodical arrangement, order (class.; syn.: series, tenor). In gen.: ordinem sic definiunt compositionem rerum aptis et accommodatis locis, Cic. Off. 1, 40, 142: vis ordinis et collocationis, id. ib. 1, 40, 142: arbores in ordinem satae, i. e. planted in a quincunx, Varr. R. R. 1, 7; cf. Cic. Caecil. 8, 22; id. Sen. 17, 59.— Esp.,

ordovices.full: Ordovices, um, m., a people of Britain, Tac. A. 12, 33; id. Agr. 18, 4.
ordovices.short: Ordovices, um, m., a people of Britain, Tac.

oreae.full: ōrĕae, ārum, f. 1. os, the bit of a bridle (ante-class.), Titin. ap. Fest. p. 182 Müll.: oreas equo detrahere, Cael. ib.

oreas.full: Ŏrēăs, ădis, f., = Ὀρειάς, a mountainnymph, Oread (poet.): quam mille secutae Hinc atque hinc glomerantur Oreades, Verg. A. 1, 500; Ov. M. 8, 787; Calp. Ecl. 4, 136; cf. Oreos.
oreas.short: Ŏrēăs, ădis, f., = Ὀρειάς, a mountainnymph, Oread (poet.): quam mille secutae Hinc atque hinc glomerantur Oreades, Verg.

oreon.full: ŏrēon or ŏrīon, i, n., = ὄρειον, a mountain-plant, a kind of polygonos, Plin. 27, 12, 91, § 115
oreon.short: ŏrēon or ŏrīon, i, n., = ὄρειον, a mountain-plant, a kind of polygonos, Plin.

oreos.full: Ŏrēos, i, m., = ὄρειος, of the mountain, i. e. Pan: Oreos Liber pater, et Oreades Nymphae appellantur, quod in montibus frequenter apparent, Fest. p. 182 Müll.
oreos.short: Ŏrēos, i, m., = ὄρειος, of the mountain, i.

oreoselinon.full: ŏrĕŏsĕlīnon (-um), i, n., = ὀρεοσέλινον, mountain-parsley, Plin. 19, 8, 37, § 124.
oreoselinon.short: ŏrĕŏsĕlīnon (-um), i, n., = ὀρεοσέλινον, mountain-parsley, Plin.

oresitrophos.full: Ŏrĕsītrŏphos (-us), i, f., = Ὀρεσίτροφος (mountain-fed), one of Actœon's hounds, Ov. M. 3, 233.
oresitrophos.short: Ŏrĕsītrŏphos (-us), i, f., = Ὀρεσίτροφος (mountain-fed), one of Actœon's hounds, Ov.

orestae.full: Ŏrestae, ārum, m., = Ὀρέσται, a people of Macedonia, Liv. 33, 34; Plin. 4, 10, 17, § 35; Curt. 4, 13, 28.
orestae.short: Ŏrestae, ārum, m., = Ὀρέσται, a people of Macedonia, Liv.

orestes.full: Ŏrestes, is and ae, m., = Ὀρέστης, the son of Agamemnon and Clytœmnestra, who avenged his father's death by slaying his mother, and, in company with his faithful friend Pylades and his sister Iphigenia, priestess of Diana in the Tauric Chersonese, carried away the image of Diana to Italy, near Aricia, Plaut. Capt. 3, 4, 30: Agamemnonius Orestes, Verg. A. 4, 471: dico vicisse Oresten, Enn. ap. Non. 306, 28 (Trag. v. 191 Vahl.): cum Pylades Orestem se esse diceret, Cic. Lael. 7, 24: clamantem nome
orestes.short: Ŏrestes, is and ae, m., = Ὀρέστης, the son of Agamemnon and Clytœmnestra, who avenged his father's death by slaying his mother, and, in company with his faithful friend Pylades and his sister Iphigenia, priestess of Diana in the Tauric Chersonese, ca

orestiades.full: Ŏrestĭădes, nymphae montium cultrices, Fest. p. 185 Müll.

orestilla.full: Orestilla, ae, f., a female surname in the gens Aurelia; esp. Aurelia Orestilla, wife of Catiline, Sall. C. 15, 2; 35, 3; 6; Cael. ap. Cic. Fam. 8, 7, 2.
orestilla.short: Orestilla, ae, f., a female surname in the gens Aurelia;

orestion.full: ŏrestĭon, ii, n., a plant, called also helenion and nectarea, Plin. 14, 16, 19, § 108.
orestion.short: ŏrestĭon, ii, n., a plant, called also helenion and nectarea, Plin.

orestis.full: Ŏrestis, ĭdis, f., a district in Macedonia, Cic. Har. Resp. 16, 35; Liv. 27, 33.
orestis.short: Ŏrestis, ĭdis, f., a district in Macedonia, Cic.

oretani.full: Ōrētāni, ōrum, m., = Ὠρητανοί, the inhabitants of Oretum in Spain, Liv. 21, 11; Plin. 3, 3, 4, § 19.
oretani.short: Ōrētāni, ōrum, m., = Ὠρητανοί, the inhabitants of Oretum in Spain, Liv.

oreus.full: Ōrēus (-os), i, f., a city in Eubœa, formerly Histiœa, Liv. 28, 5, 18; 31, 40, 10; Plin. 4, 12, 21, § 64.
oreus.short: Ōrēus (-os), i, f., a city in Eubœa, formerly Histiœa, Liv.

orexis.full: ŏrexis, is, f., = ὄρεξις, a longing, appetite (post-Aug.): rabidam facturus orexim, Juv. 6, 428: hinc surgit orexis, id. 11, 127: orexin, Lampr. Elag. 29 fin.
orexis.short: ŏrexis, is, f., = ὄρεξις, a longing, appetite (post-Aug.): rabidam facturus orexim, Juv.

organalis.full: orgănālis, e organum, belonging to the organ, organ-: fistulae, Mythogr. Lat. 3, 12.
organalis.short: orgănālis, e organum, belonging to the organ, organ-: fistulae, Mythogr.

organarius.full: orgănārĭus, ii, m. id., a musical-instrument maker (post-class.), Firm. Math. 3, 14; Amm. 28, 1, 8.

organicus.full: orgănĭcus, a, um, adj., = ὀργανικός. Of or relating to implements, mechanical: telarum organica administratio, Vitr. 10, 1, 5.— Of or belonging to musical-instruments, instrumental, musical: alterum (melos), quod vocant organicon, Cato ap. Non. 77, 9.— Subst.: orgănĭcus, i, m., a musician, Lucr. 5, 334; 3, 132; 2, 412.

organum.full: orgănum, i, n., = ὄργανον, an implement, instrument, engine of any kind (mostly post-Aug.), Col. 3, 13, 12.—Of military or architectonic engines (whereas machina denotes one of a larger size and more complicated construction), Vitr. 10, 1.—Of musical instruments, a pipe, Quint. 11, 3, 20; 9, 4, 10; Juv. 6, 3, 80; Vulg. Gen. 4, 21; id. 2 Par. 34, 12 et saep.—Of hydraulic engines, an organ, water-organ: organa hydraulica, Suet. Ner. 41: aquatica, Mythogr. Lat. 3, 12.—Of a church-organ, Cass. Expos
organum.short: orgănum, i, n., = ὄργανον, an implement, instrument, engine of any kind (mostly post-Aug.), Col.

orgessum.full: Orgessum, i, n., a castle in Macedonia, Liv. 31, 27.
orgessum.short: Orgessum, i, n., a castle in Macedonia, Liv.

orgetorix.full: Orgĕtŏrix, ĭgis, m., chief of the Helvetii, Caes. B. G. 1, 2 sq. al.
orgetorix.short: Orgĕtŏrix, ĭgis, m., chief of the Helvetii, Caes.

orgia.full: Orgĭa, ōrum, n., = Ὄργια, a nocturnal festival in honor of Bacchus, accompanied by wild bacchanalian cries, the feast or orgies of Bacchus. Lit., Verg. A. 4, 303; Ov. M. 11, 93; Verg. G. 4, 521.— Transf., in gen., secret frantic revels, orgies, Juv. 2, 91; Stat. S. 5, 5, 4.— Trop.: Itala per Graios Orgia ferre choros, the mysteries of love in the Latin tongue, Prop. 4, 1, 4: naturae, secrets, mysteries, Col. 10, 217.
orgia.short: Orgĭa, ōrum, n., = Ὄργια, a nocturnal festival in honor of Bacchus, accompanied by wild bacchanalian cries, the feast or orgies of Bacchus.

orgiophanta.full: Orgĭŏphanta, ae, m., = Ὀργιοφάντης, a presider over the orgies, an orgiophant: SACERDOTES ORGIOPHANTAE, Inscr. Grut. 66, 9.
orgiophanta.short: Orgĭŏphanta, ae, m., = Ὀργιοφάντης, a presider over the orgies, an orgiophant: SACERDOTES ORGIOPHANTAE, Inscr.

orgus.full: Orgus, i, m., a river of Upper Italy, now Orco, Ennod. Carm 1, 38
orgus.short: Orgus, i, m., a river of Upper Italy, now Orco, Ennod.

oribasus.full: Ŏrībăsus, i, m., = Ὀρείβασος (mountain-climber), one of Actœon's hounds, Ov. M. 3, 210.
oribasus.short: Ŏrībăsus, i, m., = Ὀρείβασος (mountain-climber), one of Actœon's hounds, Ov.

oribata.full: ŏrībăta, ae, m., = ὀρειβάτης, a mountain-climber (post-class.), Firm. Math. 8, 17.
oribata.short: ŏrībăta, ae, m., = ὀρειβάτης, a mountain-climber (post-class.), Firm.

orichalcum.full: ŏrĭchalcum (also erroneously written aurĭchalcum, as if from aurum), i, n., = ὀρείχαλκος, yellow copper ore, also the brass made from it. Lit., Cic. Off. 3, 23, 92; Hor. A. P. 202: album, Verg. A. 12, 87.—It was highly prized by the ancients, Plaut. Curc. 1, 3, 46; id. Mil. 3, 1, 61; id. Ps. 2, 3, 22; cf. Plin. 34, 2, 2, § 4 (al. aurichalci). — Transf., of brass implements.—So of a brazen tuba, Val. Fl. 3, 61.—Of arms of brass, Stat. Th. 10, 660.
orichalcum.short: ŏrĭchalcum (also erroneously written aurĭchalcum, as if from aurum), i, n., = ὀρείχαλκος, yellow copper ore, also the brass made from it.

oricilla.full: ōrĭcilla (aur-), ae, f. dim. auricula, auris, an ear-lap: mollior ... imula oricilla, Cat. 25, 2.

oricos.full: Ōrĭcos or Ōrĭcus, i, f., or Ōrĭcum, i, n., = Ὠρικός and Ὠρικόν, a seaport town of Illyria Grœca, now Ericho, Caes. B. C. 3, 8 sq.; Liv. 24, 40; Mel. 2, 3, 12; Prop. 1, 8, 20; Luc. 3, 187.—Hence, ōrĭcīni, ōrum, m., the inhabitants of Oricum, the Oricians: Oricinorum fines, Liv. 26, 25.— ōrĭcĭus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Oricum, Orician: Oricia terebinthus, Verg. A. 10, 136.
oricos.short: Ōrĭcos or Ōrĭcus, i, f., or Ōrĭcum, i, n., = Ὠρικός and Ὠρικόν, a seaport town of Illyria Grœca, now Ericho, Caes.

oridurius.full: ōrĭdūrĭus, a, um, adj. 1. os-durus, hard-mouthed, of horses: oridurius, σκληρόστομος, Gloss. Philox.

oriens.full: ŏrĭens, entis, Part. and P. a., v. orior.

orientalis.full: ŏrĭentālis, e, adj. oriens, of or belonging to the East, Eastern, Oriental (postclass.): periculorum et operum orientalium socii, in the East, Just. 14, 2, 8: barba ria, id. 12, 3, 3: reges, id. 38, 10, 5: venti, Gell. 2, 22, 11.— Subst. ŏrĭentā-les, ĭum, m., the Orientals, Just. 36, 3, 9.— ŏrĭentāles, ĭum, f. (sc. ferae), wild beasts designed for hunting exhibitions (as lions, tigers, panthers, etc.), Inscr. Murat. 654, 1.

orificium.full: ōrĭfĭcĭum, ii, n. 1. os-facio, an opening, orifice (post-class.): ventris sunt duo orificia, Macr. S. 7, 4: cistulae, App. M. 9, p. 236, 41; 11, p. 262, 27.

origa.full: ōrīga, ae, m., an old form for auriga, Varr. R. R. 2, 7, 8; 2, 8, 4 Schneid.
origa.short: ōrīga, ae, m., an old form for auriga, Varr.

origanitus.full: ŏrīgănītus, a, um origanum: vini sextarium origaniti, wine spiced with origanum, Cato, R. R. 127, 2.
origanitus.short: ŏrīgănītus, a, um origanum: vini sextarium origaniti, wine spiced with origanum, Cato, R.

origanum.full: ŏrīgănum and -on, i, n., and ŏrī-gănus, i, m., = ὀρείγανον, ὀρίγανον, and ὀρείγανος, or ὀρίγανος, the plant wild-marjoram, origan, Plin. 20, 17, 67, § 175; Ser. Samm. 47, 879.
origanum.short: ŏrīgănum and -on, i, n., and ŏrī-gănus, i, m., = ὀρείγανον, ὀρίγανον, and ὀρείγανος, or ὀρίγανος, the plant wild-marjoram, origan, Plin.

origenes.full: Ōrĭgĕnes, is, m., = Ὠριγένης, Origen, a famous Greek Christian writer of the early part of the third century, A.D., Hier. Ep. 100; Aug. Civ. Dei, 21, 17.—Hence, ōrĭgĕnistes, ae, m., a follower of Origen, Hier. Ep. 84, 3; id. ib. 3 in Rufin. 18.
origenes.short: Ōrĭgĕnes, is, m., = Ὠριγένης, Origen, a famous Greek Christian writer of the early part of the third century, A.D., Hier.

originalis.full: ŏrīgĭnālis, e, adj. origo, primitive, original (post-class.): Ceres frugum parens originalis, App. M. 11, p. 257: recurram ad originales libros, Hier. in Gal. 3, 10: rerum species, Macr. Somn. Scip. 1, 2: coloni, Cod. Th. 11, 1, 14.—Hence, adv.: ŏrīgĭnālĭ-ter, originally (eccl. Lat.), Aug. Trin. 3, 9; id. Retract. 1, 15.

originarius.full: ŏrīgĭnārĭus, a, um, adj. id., original (post-class.): colonus, Cod. Th. 11, 48, 7.— Subst. plur.: ŏrigĭnārii, ōrum, m., original inhabitants, aborigines, Cod. Th. 10, 38.

originatio.full: ŏrīgĭnātĭo, ōnis, f. id., the derivation of words, etymology (post-Aug.), Quint. 1, 6, 28.

originitus.full: ŏrīgĭnĭtus, adv. id., originally (postclass.): Persae, qui sunt originitus Scythae, by origin, Amm. 31, 2, 20.

origo1.full: ŏrīgo, ĭnis, f. orior, earliest beginning, commencement, source, descent, lineage, birth, origin (class.; syn. ortus). Lit. In gen.: originem rerum quaerere, Cic. Univ. 3: origo tyranni, id. Rep. 2, 29, 51: principii nulla est origo: nam e principio oriuntur omnia, id. ib. 6, 25, 27: nullius autem rei causā remotā reperiri origo potest, id. Univ. 2, 3: rerum genitalis, Lucr. 5, 176: ab origine gentem (corripiunt morbi), Verg. G. 3, 473: summi boni, Cic. Fin 2, 10, 31: omnium virtutum, id. ib. 4,

origo2.full: Ŏrīgo, ĭnis, f., a female proper name, Hor. S. 1, 2, 55.
origo2.short: Ŏrīgo, ĭnis, f., a female proper name, Hor.

orinda.full: ŏrinda, ae, f., = ὀρίνδης Ethiopian bread, Apic. 2, 2.
orinda.short: ŏrinda, ae, f., = ὀρίνδης Ethiopian bread, Apic.

orine.full: Ŏrīnē, ēs, f., Orine, = Ὀρεινή, sc. γῆ (the hill country). A region of Judea, Plin. 5, 14, 15, § 70.— A Roman surname, Inscr. Murat. 1295, 3.
orine.short: Ŏrīnē, ēs, f., Orine, = Ὀρεινή, sc.

oriola.full: ŏrĭŏla, i. q. horiola, q. v.

orion.full: Ōrīon (ŏrīōn, Verg. A. 1, 535; 4, 52), ŏnis and ōnis, m., = Ὠρίων, the constellation Orion, whose rising and setting are attended by storms; acc. to the myth, a hunter transported to heaven, Ov. F. 5, 493; Hyg. Fab. 195; Verg. A. 1, 535; 4, 52; Hor. C. 1, 28, 21; 3, 27, 18; Lact. 4, 5, 21 et saep.

orior.full: ŏrĭor, ortus, fut. part. oriturus, 4 (but with some forms of the 3d conj.: orĭtur, Enn. ap. Fest. p. 305 Müll.; Gell. 4, 17, 14; cf. Cic. Ac. 2, 28, 89; Ter. Hec. 2, 1, 26; Lucr. 3, 272; Verg. A. 2, 411; 680; Hor. S. 1, 5, 39; Ov. M. 1, 774 et saep.: oreris, id. ib. 10, 166; imperat. orere, Val. Max. 4, 7, 7: impf. subj. oreretur, Paul. Nol. Carm. 15, 59; and oreretur and orerentur are the more usual forms in the best MSS.; cf. Haase in Reisig's Vorles. p. 251; Neue, Formenl. 2, p. 418 sq.), v.

oripelargus.full: ŏrīpĕlargus, i, m., = ὀρειπελαργός, the mountain-stork, Plin. 10, 3, 3, § 8.
oripelargus.short: ŏrīpĕlargus, i, m., = ὀρειπελαργός, the mountain-stork, Plin.

oriputidus.full: ōrĭpūtĭdus, a, um, adj. 1. os-putidus, that has a stinking mouth: oriputidus, ὀζόστομος, Gloss. Philox.

oritae.full: Oritae, ārum, m., a nation of Ichthyophagi, on the borders of India, Plin. 7, 2, 2, § 30, id. 6, 23, 25, § 95.
oritae.short: Oritae, ārum, m., a nation of Ichthyophagi, on the borders of India, Plin.

orites.full: ŏrītes, ae, m., or ŏrītis, ĭdis, f., v. oritis.
orites.short: ŏrītes, ae, m., or ŏrītis, ĭdis, f., v.

orithyia.full: Ōrīthȳīa (quadrisyl.), ae, f., = Ὠρείθυια, a female proper name. A daughter of Erechtheus, king of Athens; who became by Boreas the mother of Calaïs and Zetes, Ov. M. 6, 683; Verg. G. 4, 463; id. A. 12, 83; Sil. 8, 5, 16; Cic. Leg. 1, 1, 3.— A queen of the Amazons, Just. 2, 4, 17.
orithyia.short: Ōrīthȳīa (quadrisyl.), ae, f., = Ὠρείθυια, a female proper name.

oritis.full: ŏrītis, ĭdis, f., = ὀρῖτις, a precious stone (by some called sideritis), otherwise unknown, Plin. 37, 10, 65, § 176.
oritis.short: ŏrītis, ĭdis, f., = ὀρῖτις, a precious stone (by some called sideritis), otherwise unknown, Plin.

oriundus.full: ŏrĭundus, a, um, adj. orior. Descended, sprung from any person or place (rare but class.): o sanguen dis oriundum, Enn. ap. Cic. Rep. 1, 41 (Ann. v. 117 Vahl.): Poenos Didone oriundos, id. ap. Prisc. p. 685 P. (Ann. v. 300 Vahl.): caelesti semine, Lucr. 2, 991: ab ingenuis, * Cic. Top. 6, 29: ex Etruscis, Liv. 2, 9: liberis parentibus, Col. 1, 3, 5: unde oriundi sient, Plaut. Aul. 3, 6, 6: quod inde oriundus erat, plebi carus, Liv. 2, 32.— Born, originating in, springing from: haud repudio Carth

ormenis.full: Ormĕnĭs, ĭdis, f., = Ὠρμενίς, the female descendant (granddaughter) of Ormenius, i. e. Astydamia; voc.: Ormeni nympha, Ov. H. 9, 50.
ormenis.short: Ormĕnĭs, ĭdis, f., = Ὠρμενίς, the female descendant (granddaughter) of Ormenius, i.

ormenos.full: ormĕnos, i, m., a kind of samphire, Plin. 26, 10, 61, § 94.
ormenos.short: ormĕnos, i, m., a kind of samphire, Plin.

orminalis.full: ormīnālis and hormīnālis, is, f. horminum, a plant, called also satyrion, App. Herb. 15.

orminos.full: orminos, i, m., wild asparagus, Plin. 20, 10, 43, § 110.
orminos.short: orminos, i, m., wild asparagus, Plin.

ornamen.full: ornāmen, ĭnis, n. orno, an old reading for ornamentum, Mart. Cap. 6, § 587.

ornamentarius.full: ornāmentārĭus, a, um, adj. ornamentum, adorned with the insignia of an office, without filling the office itself: DECVRIO, Inscr. Donat. 349, 1.

ornamentum.full: ornāmentum, i, n. orno. In gen., apparatus, accoutrement, equipment, furniture, trappings, etc. (class.): sine ornamentis, i. e. naked, Plaut. Ps. 1, 3, 109: ceterae copiae, ornamenta, praesidia, Cic. Cat. 2, 11, 24; Cic. Verr. 2, 5, 32, § 83: ornamenta bubus, ornamenta asinis instrata tria (collar, saddle, etc.), Cato, R. R. 11, 4: per ornamenta percussus, i. e. arms, Sen. Ep. 14, 14.—Esp of a player's wardrobe, Plaut. Trin. 4, 2, 16 sq.; id. Pers. 1, 3, 19; Plin. 2, 3, 4, § 8, as translation o

ornate.full: ornātē, adv., v. orno, P. a. fin.

ornatio.full: ornātĭo, ōnis, f. orno, an adorning, adornment, ornament (not ante-Aug., and very rare), Vitr. 5, 8, 8: ornationes templi, Inscr. Orell. 775: STATVAE, Inscr. ap. Nov. Lett. di Firenze, t. ii. p. 600.

ornator.full: ornātor, ōris, m. id.. An adorner, dresser (not ante-Aug., and very rare): deorum ornatores, Firm. Astron. 3, 6, 9: HVIVS LOCI, Inscr. Orell. 3171.— An office under the emperors: ORNATOR GLABR. (i. e. glabrorum, puerorum delicatorum), Inscr. Orell. 694.

ornatrix.full: ornātrix, īcis, f. ornator, a female adorner, a tire-woman, a slave who dressed her mistress's hair (poet. and post-Aug.; esp. freq. in inscrr.), Ov. A. A. 3, 239; id. Am. 1, 14, 16: matris meae, Suet. Claud. 40; Inscr. Orell. 2878; 2933; 4443; Schol. Juv. 6, 477.

ornatulus.full: ornātŭlus, a, um, adj. dim. [ornatus], fine, smart (Plautin.): muliercula, Plaut. Cist. Fragm. p. 19 Mai.

ornatura.full: ornātūra, ae, f. orno, ornament, trimming, esp. of the borders of a fine dress (post-class.), Edict. Diocl. p. 20.

ornatus1.full: ornātus, a, um, Part. and P. a., from orno.

ornatus2.full: ornātus, ūs (gen. ornati, Ter. And. 2, 2, 28; dat. ornatu, C. Caes. ap. Gell. 4, 16, 8), m. orno (class.; cf.: cultus, munditia), a furnishing, providing, preparing; a preparation. Lit. In gen. (very rare): in ornat bus publicis (i. e. epulis, conviviis), Varr. R. R. 3, 9, 17: in aedibus nihil ornati, no preparation (for the wed ding), Ter And. 2, 2, 28: Pompeiis emptus ornatus (trapeti), Cato, R. R. 22, 3.— In partic., an adornment, decoration, embellishment, ornament (class.): portarum, itiner

orneus1.full: ornĕus, a, um, adj. ornus, of the wild mountain-ash: frons, Col. 11, 2, 82.

orneus2.full: Ornēus, i, m., = Ὄρνειος, a Centaur at the wedding of Pirithoüs, Ov. M. 12, 302.
orneus2.short: Ornēus, i, m., = Ὄρνειος, a Centaur at the wedding of Pirithoüs, Ov.

ornithias.full: ornīthĭas, ae, m., = ὀρνιθίας, the bird-wind, a wind that blows in spring and brings with it the birds of passage: Favonium quidam a. d. VIII. Cal. Mart. Chelidoniam vocant, ab hirundinis visu: nonnulli vero Ornithian, uno et sexagesimo die post brumam, ab adventu avium, flantem per dies novem, Plin. 2, 47, 47, § 122; Vitr. 1, 6; App. Mund. p. 62; Col. 11, 2, 21.—The Etesiae are also sometimes called Ornithiae, Plin. 2, 47, 47, § 127.
ornithias.short: ornīthĭas, ae, m., = ὀρνιθίας, the bird-wind, a wind that blows in spring and brings with it the birds of passage: Favonium quidam a.

ornithogale.full: ornīthŏgălē, ēs, f., = ὀρνιθογάλη, a plant, the star of Bethlehem, Plin. 21, 17, 62, § 102.
ornithogale.short: ornīthŏgălē, ēs, f., = ὀρνιθογάλη, a plant, the star of Bethlehem, Plin.

ornithon.full: ornīthon, ōnis, m., = ὀρνιθών, a birdhouse, poultry-house (pure Lat. aviarium): ornithonas dico omnium alitum, quae intra parietes villae solent pasci, Varr. R. R. 3, 3, 1; 3, 4, 2; Col. 8, 3, 1.
ornithon.short: ornīthon, ōnis, m., = ὀρνιθών, a birdhouse, poultry-house (pure Lat.

orno.full: orno, āvi, ātum, 1 (old form of the perf. ORNAVET, Column. Rostr.; v. infra), v. a. perh. root var-, cover; Sanscr. varna-, color, to fit out, furnish, provide with necessaries; to equip, to get ready, prepare (class.; syn. exorno, concinno). In gen.: age nunc, orna te, Plaut. Ep. 2, 2, 10: prandium domi, id. Rud. 1, 2, 53: ornatur ferro Enn. ap. Gell. 16, 10 (Ann. v. 190 Vahl.): aliquem armis, Verg. A. 12, 344: decemviros apparitoribus, scribis, librariis, praeconibus, architectis, praeterea mu
orno.short: orno, āvi, ātum, 1 (old form of the perf.

ornus.full: ornus, i, f., the wild mountain-ash: steriles orni, Verg. G. 2, 111; Hor. C. 3, 27, 58; Plin. 16, 18, 30, § 73; Col. Arbor. 16; Juv. 1, 11.— Transf., a lance made of the wood of this tree: vibrabilis ornus Achilli, Aus. Ep. 24, 108.
ornus.short: ornus, i, f., the wild mountain-ash: steriles orni, Verg.

oro.full: ōro, āvi, ātum, 1 (orassis for oraveris, Plaut. Ep. 5, 2, 63), v. a. and n. 1. os, to speak: oro ab ore, Varr. L. L. 6, § 76 Müll. In gen. (so obsol.): orare antiquos dixisse pro agere testimonio est, quod oratores dicti et causarum actores et qui rei publicae mandatas causas agebant, Fest. p. 198 Müll.: bonum aequumque oras, Plaut. Most. 3, 1, 151: talibus orabat Juno, Verg. A. 10, 96.— In partic. To treat, argue, plead (as an ambassador, advocate, etc.; class., but very rare; cf. ago): REM VBI
oro.short: ōro, āvi, ātum, 1 (orassis for oraveris, Plaut.

oroanda.full: Ŏrŏanda, ae, f., a city in Pisidia, Liv. 38, 37.—Hence, ŏrŏandenses, ĭum, m., the inhabitants of Oroanda: legati Oroandensium, Liv. 38, 18.— ŏrŏandĭ-cus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Oroanda: Oroandicus ager, Cic. Agr. 2, 19, 50: tractus, Plin. 5, 32, 42, § 147.— ŏrŏ-andes, a part of the Taurus range, Plin. 5, 27, 27, § 98.
oroanda.short: Ŏrŏanda, ae, f., a city in Pisidia, Liv.

orobanche.full: ŏrŏbanchē, ēs, f., = ὀροβάγχη, a plant, broom-rape, choke-weed, Plin. 18, 17, 44, § 155.
orobanche.short: ŏrŏbanchē, ēs, f., = ὀροβάγχη, a plant, broom-rape, choke-weed, Plin.

orobethron.full: ŏrŏbēthron, i, n., another name for the plant hypocisthus, Plin. 26, 8, 31, § 49.
orobethron.short: ŏrŏbēthron, i, n., another name for the plant hypocisthus, Plin.

orobias.full: ŏrŏbĭas, ae, m., = ὀροβίας, a kind of incense, in small grains, resembling the chickpea, Plin. 12, 14, 32, § 62.
orobias.short: ŏrŏbĭas, ae, m., = ὀροβίας, a kind of incense, in small grains, resembling the chickpea, Plin.

orobinus.full: ŏrŏbĭnus, a, um, adj., = ὀρόβινος, of or resembling the chickpea: color, Plin. 37, 10, 59, § 163.
orobinus.short: ŏrŏbĭnus, a, um, adj., = ὀρόβινος, of or resembling the chickpea: color, Plin.

orobitis.full: ŏrŏbītis, is, f., = ὀροβῖτις (like the chickpea; hence, sc. chrysocolla), borax dyed of a yellowish color by means of the plant lutum, Plin. 33, 5, 27, § 89.
orobitis.short: ŏrŏbītis, is, f., = ὀροβῖτις (like the chickpea;

orobus.full: ŏrŏbus, i, m., = ὄροβος, the bitter vetch, Plin. Val. 1, 58; Cael. Aur. Acut. 2, 19, 113.
orobus.short: ŏrŏbus, i, m., = ὄροβος, the bitter vetch, Plin.

orodes.full: Ŏrōdes, is (gen. also Orodi, Cic. Att. 5, 18, 1 Orell. N. cr.; id. ib. 5, 21, 2; id. Fam. 15, 1, 2), m., = Ὀρώδης, a male proper name. A king of the Parthians, who took Crassus prisoner and put him to death, Cic. Att. 6, 1, 14; Vell. 2, 46, 4; Flor. 3, 11, 4.— Orodes, son of the former, Tac. A. 6, 35.— A king of the Colchians, Flor. 3, 5, 28. — A king of the Albanians, Eutr. 6, 11. — The name of a warrior slain by Mezentius, Verg. A. 10, 732.

oroetes.full: Ŏrŏetes, ae, m., a commander of the Medes under Darius, Cic. Fin. 5, 30, 92; Val. Max. 6, 9 fin.
oroetes.short: Ŏrŏetes, ae, m., a commander of the Medes under Darius, Cic.

oromedon.full: Ōrŏmĕdon, ontis, m., = Ὠρομέδων, one of the giants, Prop. 3, 9 (4, 8), 48.
oromedon.short: Ōrŏmĕdon, ontis, m., = Ὠρομέδων, one of the giants, Prop.

orontes.full: Ŏrontes, is or ae (gen. Oronti, Verg. A. 1, 220), m., = Ὀρόντης. The principal river of Syria, now Nahr El-Ashy, Mel. 1, 12, 5; Plin. 5, 21, 18, § 79; Prop. 2, 23 (3, 17), 21.—Hence, ŏrontēus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to the Orontes, Orontian; poet. for Syrian: Orontea myrrha, Prop. 1, 2, 3.— A chief of the Lycii and companion of Æneas, Verg. A. 1, 113; 220.

oropus.full: Ōrōpus, i, m., = Ὠρωπός, a town of Bœotia, on the borders of Attica, now Oropo, Cic. Att. 12, 23, 2; Liv. 45, 27; Plin. 4, 7, 11, § 24.
oropus.short: Ōrōpus, i, m., = Ὠρωπός, a town of Bœotia, on the borders of Attica, now Oropo, Cic.

orosius.full: Orosĭus, ii, m., an ecclesiastic of Tarragona, in Spain, who flourished A. D. 500; he wrote, by the advice of St. Augustine, and to confute the pagans, a history from the beginning of the world to his own times: Historiarum libri VII. adversus Paganos.
orosius.short: Orosĭus, ii, m., an ecclesiastic of Tarragona, in Spain, who flourished A.

orozelum.full: orozēlum, i, n., a plant, called also chamaepitys, App. Herb. 26.
orozelum.short: orozēlum, i, n., a plant, called also chamaepitys, App.

orphaicus.full: Orphăĭcus, a, um, v. Orpheus, C.

orphanotrophium.full: orphănō^trophīum, ii, n., = ὀρφανοτροφεῖον, an orphan-asylum (post-class.), Cod. Just. 1, 2, 17; 22.
orphanotrophium.short: orphănō^trophīum, ii, n., = ὀρφανοτροφεῖον, an orphan-asylum (post-class.), Cod.

orphanotrophus.full: orphănō^trŏphus, i, m., = ὀρφανοτρόφος, a bringer-up of orphans, a fosterfather of orphans, Cod. Just. 1, 3, 32; Ven. Vit. S. Mart. 2, 405.
orphanotrophus.short: orphănō^trŏphus, i, m., = ὀρφανοτρόφος, a bringer-up of orphans, a fosterfather of orphans, Cod.

orphanus.full: orphănus, i, m., = ὀρφανός, an orphan, Ven. Fort. 4, 25, 11; Ambros. Serm. 24, § 3; Vulg. Psa. 9, 34; 67, 5; id. Johan. 14, 18.
orphanus.short: orphănus, i, m., = ὀρφανός, an orphan, Ven.

orphas.full: orphas, v. l. Ov. Hal. 104 for orphus, q. v.

orpheus.full: Orpheus (dissyl.), i (Gr. dat. Orphei, Verg. E. 4, 57; Gr. acc. Orphĕă, Verg. E. 6, 30; Ov. P. 3, 3, 41: Orphēā, id. M. 10, 3; voc. Orpheu, Verg. G. 4, 494; Ov. M. 11, 44), m., = Ὀρφεύς, the famous mythic singer of Thrace, son of Œagrus and Calliope, and husband of Eurydice; after her death he led her back from the Lower World, but lost her on turning to look at her, breaking his promise to Pluto. He was one of the Argonauts, Hor. C. 1, 12, 8; Ov. M. 10, 3 sq.; 11, 5 sq.; Hyg. Fab. 164; 251; Ver

orphne.full: Orphnē, ēs, f., Orphne, = Ὄρφνη (Darkness), a nymph, Ov. M. 5, 539.
orphne.short: Orphnē, ēs, f., Orphne, = Ὄρφνη (Darkness), a nymph, Ov.

orphus.full: orphus, i, m., = ὀρφός, a sea-fish, the gilt-head, Plin. 32, 11, 54, § 152; Ov. Hal. 104.
orphus.short: orphus, i, m., = ὀρφός, a sea-fish, the gilt-head, Plin.

orrhopygium.full: orrhŏpȳgĭum, ĭi, a false read. for orthopygium, q. v.

orsa.full: orsa, ōrum, n. ordior. Beginnings, commencements, an undertaking, attempt: ut (di) orsis tanti operis successus prosperos darent, Liv. praef. fin.: Orsa juvare, Val. Fl. 1, 21.— In partic., words, speech (poet.): sic orsa vicissim Ore refert, Verg. A. 7, 435; 10, 632; 11, 124; Val. Fl. 5, 472: Menandri, i. e. carmina, Aus. Idyll. 4, 46.

orses.full: Orses, ae, m., the name of a Trojan warrior, Verg. A. 10, 748.
orses.short: Orses, ae, m., the name of a Trojan warrior, Verg.

orsiloche.full: Orsĭlŏchē, ēs, f., the name of the Tauric Diana, Amm. 22, 8.
orsiloche.short: Orsĭlŏchē, ēs, f., the name of the Tauric Diana, Amm.

orsilochus.full: Orsĭlŏchus, i, m., the name of a Trojan warrior, Verg. A. 11, 636.
orsilochus.short: Orsĭlŏchus, i, m., the name of a Trojan warrior, Verg.

orsinus.full: orsinus, i, a kind of crocus, Plin. 21, 11, 39, § 67.—Perh. an error in the MSS. for orinus, or oreinos; cf. Jan. ad loc.
orsinus.short: orsinus, i, a kind of crocus, Plin.

orsorius.full: orsōrĭus, a, um, adj. ordior, belonging to a loom: in palo orsorio, S. S. Judic. 16, 13; id. ap. Auct. de Promiss, et Praedict. Dei, 2, 22, 45 (where the Vulg. reads alia omnia).

orsus1.full: orsus, a, um, Part. and P. a., v. ordior.

orsus2.full: orsus, ūs, m., ordior, a beginning, commencement; an undertaking, attempt (poet.): pectoris, Cic. poët. Div. 2, 30, 63: tenuis, Verg. Cul. 1.
orsus2.short: orsus, ūs, m., ordior, a beginning, commencement;

orthagoriscus.full: orthăgŏriscus, i, m., = ὀρθαγορίσκος, the pig-fish, so called from the noise it was said to make when taken, Plin. 32, 2, 9, § 19.
orthagoriscus.short: orthăgŏriscus, i, m., = ὀρθαγορίσκος, the pig-fish, so called from the noise it was said to make when taken, Plin.

orthampelos.full: orthampĕlos, i, f., = ὀρθάμπελος, a straight vine, a vine that grows upright, and needs no support, Plin. 14, 3, 4, § 40.
orthampelos.short: orthampĕlos, i, f., = ὀρθάμπελος, a straight vine, a vine that grows upright, and needs no support, Plin.

orthembasis.full: orthembăsis, is, f., = ὀρθοσ-ἔμβασις, a straight step, Not. Tir. p. 152.
orthembasis.short: orthembăsis, is, f., = ὀρθοσ-ἔμβασις, a straight step, Not.

orthius.full: orthĭus, a, um, adj., = ὄρθιος, high, lofty (post-class.): carmen quod orthium dicitur (Gr. νόμος ὄρθιος), Gell. 16, 19, 14: orthius (pes), qui ex tetrasemi elatione, id est arsi, et octasemi positione constabit: ita ut duodecim tempora hic pes recepisse videatur, Mart. Cap. 9, § 985.
orthius.short: orthĭus, a, um, adj., = ὄρθιος, high, lofty (post-class.): carmen quod orthium dicitur (Gr.

orthocissos.full: orthŏcissos, i, f., = ὀρθόκισσος, a kind of tall ivy (opp. to the chamaecissos), Col. 11, 2, 30.
orthocissos.short: orthŏcissos, i, f., = ὀρθόκισσος, a kind of tall ivy (opp.

orthocolus.full: orthŏcōlus, a, um, adj., = ὀρθόκωλος, stiff in the joints (post-class.), Veg. Vet. 2, 54.
orthocolus.short: orthŏcōlus, a, um, adj., = ὀρθόκωλος, stiff in the joints (post-class.), Veg.

orthodoxus.full: orthŏdoxus, a, um, adj., = ὀρθόδοξος, orthodox (post-class.): viri, Auct. ap. Hier. Ep. 19: religio, Cod. Just. 1, 2, 12: ecclesia, ib. 1, 2, 14.—Hence, orthŏdoxē, adv., Rustic. c. Aceph. p. 1219.
orthodoxus.short: orthŏdoxus, a, um, adj., = ὀρθόδοξος, orthodox (post-class.): viri, Auct.

orthogonius.full: orthŏgōnĭus, a, um, adj., = ὀρθογώνιος, right-angled, rectangular, orthogonal: trigonum, Vitr. 10, 11: ossicla, Aus. praef. ad Idyll. 13.
orthogonius.short: orthŏgōnĭus, a, um, adj., = ὀρθογώνιος, right-angled, rectangular, orthogonal: trigonum, Vitr.

orthographia.full: orthō^grăphĭa, ae, f., = ὀρθογραφία. Orthography (post-Aug.): orthographia, id est formula ratioque scribendi a grammaticis instituta, Suet. Aug. 88; id. Gram. 19; Quint. 1, 4, 17; 1, 7, 11.— In architecture, an elevation, front view of a building, Vitr. 1, 2.

orthographus.full: orthō^grăphus, a, um, adj., = ὀρθόγραφος, orthographic (post-class.): veritas, Mart. Cap. 1, § 65.— Subst.: orthō^-grăphus, i, m., = ὀρθογράφος, an orthographer, Cassiod. Orthogr. p. 2320 P.
orthographus.short: orthō^grăphus, a, um, adj., = ὀρθόγραφος, orthographic (post-class.): veritas, Mart.

orthomastius.full: orthŏmastĭus, a, um (= ὀρθομάστιος, from ὀρθός, μαστός), high-breasted: mammarum effigie orthomastia mala, a kind of large apple, Plin. 15, 14, 15, § 51.
orthomastius.short: orthŏmastĭus, a, um (= ὀρθομάστιος, from ὀρθός, μαστός), high-breasted: mammarum effigie orthomastia mala, a kind of large apple, Plin.

orthophallicus.full: orthophallĭcus, a, um, adj., = ὀρθόσ-φαλλός, i. e. obscene, Varr. ap. Non. 101, 3 dub.
orthophallicus.short: orthophallĭcus, a, um, adj., = ὀρθόσ-φαλλός, i.

orthopnoea.full: orthopnoea, ae, f., = ὀρθόπνοια, difficulty of breathing, asthma, orthopny, Plin. 32, 4, 14, § 37; plur., id. 21, 20, 83, § 142.
orthopnoea.short: orthopnoea, ae, f., = ὀρθόπνοια, difficulty of breathing, asthma, orthopny, Plin.

orthopnoicus.full: orthopnŏĭcus, a, um, adj., = ὀρθοπνοϊκός, asthmatic, Plin. 20, 17, 73, § 193; 24, 16, 92, § 145.
orthopnoicus.short: orthopnŏĭcus, a, um, adj., = ὀρθοπνοϊκός, asthmatic, Plin.

orthopsalticus.full: orthopsaltĭcus, a, um, adj., = ὀρθοψαλτικός, with high, full playing: psalterium, Varr. ap. Non. 101, 1; cf. Oehler ad Varr. Sat. Menipp. p. 179.
orthopsalticus.short: orthopsaltĭcus, a, um, adj., = ὀρθοψαλτικός, with high, full playing: psalterium, Varr.

orthopygium.full: orthŏpȳgĭum, ĭi, n., = ὀρθοπύγιον, the rump and tail feathers of birds, Mart. 3, 93, 12 (al. orrhopygium = ὀρροπύγιον, of the same meaning).
orthopygium.short: orthŏpȳgĭum, ĭi, n., = ὀρθοπύγιον, the rump and tail feathers of birds, Mart.

orthosia.full: Orthōsĭa, ae, f., = Ὀρθωσία. A city in Phœnicia, Plin. 5, 20, 17, § 78.—By Prisc. Perieg. 856, called Orthōsis, ĭdis. — A city in Caria, on the Mœander, Liv. 45, 25; Plin. 5, 29, 29, § 108.

orthostata.full: orthostăta, ae, m., = ὀρθοστάτης (that stands upright), in archit., the facing of a wall (pure Lat. frons), Vitr. 2, 8; 10, 19 fin.
orthostata.short: orthostăta, ae, m., = ὀρθοστάτης (that stands upright), in archit., the facing of a wall (pure Lat.

orthragoriscus.full: orthrăgŏriscus, i, m., = ὀρθραγορίσκος, v. l. ap. Plin. 32, 2, 9, § 19, for orthagoriscus, q. v.)

orthrus.full: Orthrus, i, m., = Ὄρθρος. Geryon's dog, Sil. 13, 845.— A Roman surname, Inscr. Gud. 269, 2.

ortivus.full: ortīvus, a, um, adj. 2. ortus, of or belonging to rising, rising (post-class.), App. M. 3, p. 141, 23: cardo, the eastern quarter of the heavens, Manil. 3, 188.

ortona.full: Ortōna, ae, f., the capital city and port of the Frentani in Latium, now Ortona, Liv. 2, 43, 2; Plin. 3, 12, 17, § 106 (Jan. Hortona).
ortona.short: Ortōna, ae, f., the capital city and port of the Frentani in Latium, now Ortona, Liv.

ortospanum.full: Ortospanum (Hor-), i, or Orto-pana, ōrum, n., an ancient city of Bactriana; form Ortospanum, Plin. 6, 17, 21, § 61; form Ortopana, Amm. 23, 6, 70.
ortospanum.short: Ortospanum (Hor-), i, or Orto-pana, ōrum, n., an ancient city of Bactriana;

ortus1.full: ortus, a, um, Part. and P. a., from orior, q. v. fin. B.

ortus2.full: ortus, ūs, m. orior. A rising of the heavenly bodies (opp. occasus; class.): solis et lunae reliquorumque siderum ortus, obitus motusque cognoscere, Cic. Div. 1, 56, 128: primi sub lumina solis et ortus, Verg. A. 6, 255: (sol) ab ortu ad occasum commeans, from east to west, Cic. N. D. 2, 19, 49: solis, sunrise, i. e. the orient, the east, id. Cat. 3, 8: tum bis ad occasum, bis se convertit ad ortus, Ov. M. 14, 386: nitido ab ortu, id. ib. 2, 112: signorum, Verg. E. 9, 46: ortus lucis, Vulg. Sap.

ortygia1.full: ortўgĭa or ortўga, ae, f. ὄρτυξ, a quail, Hyg. Fab. 53.

ortygia2.full: Ortўgĭa, ae, or Ortўgĭē, ēs, f., = Ὀρτυγία. Another name for the isle of Delos, Serv. Verg. A. 3, 72; Ov. M. 15, 337; Fest. p. 183 Müll.—Hence, Ortў-gĭus, a, um, adj., Ortygian: dea, i. e. Diana, Ov. M. 1, 694: boves, of Apollo, bred in Delos, id. F. 5, 692.— An island which forms a part of the city of Syracuse, now Siracusa, Verg. A. 3, 694; Ov. M. 5, 499; id. F. 4, 471.
ortygia2.short: Ortўgĭa, ae, or Ortўgĭē, ēs, f., = Ὀρτυγία.

ortygometra.full: ortўgŏmētra, ae, f., = ὀρτυγομήτρα, quail-mother, a bird that leads the quails in their migrations across the sea, the landrail: ortygometrā duce, Plin. 10, 23, 33, § 66.— Transf., a quail, Tert. adv. Psych. 16; Vulg. Sap. 16, 2; 19, 12.
ortygometra.short: ortўgŏmētra, ae, f., = ὀρτυγομήτρα, quail-mother, a bird that leads the quails in their migrations across the sea, the landrail: ortygometrā duce, Plin.

ortyx.full: ortyx, ўgis, f., = ὄρτυξ, a plant, Plin. 21, 17, 61, § 101.
ortyx.short: ortyx, ўgis, f., = ὄρτυξ, a plant, Plin.

oryx.full: ŏryx, ўgis, m., = ὄρυξ, a kind of wild goat or gazelle: Gaetulus oryx, Juv. 11, 140; Mart. 13, 94, 2; Vulg. Deut. 14, 5; cf. Plin. 2, 40, 40, § 107.
oryx.short: ŏryx, ўgis, m., = ὄρυξ, a kind of wild goat or gazelle: Gaetulus oryx, Juv.

oryza.full: ŏrȳza (ŏrīza), ae, f., = ὄπνζα, rice, Hor. S. 2, 3, 155; cf. Plin. 18, 7, 13, § 71; Cels. 2, 21.
oryza.short: ŏrȳza (ŏrīza), ae, f., = ὄπνζα, rice, Hor.

os1.full: ōs, ōris (no gen. plur.), n. kindr. with Sanscr. āsya, os, vultus, facies, the mouth (syn. bucca): quam tibi ex ore orationem duriter dictis dedit, Enn. ap. Non. p. 512, 8: ex ore in ejus os inflato aquam dato palumbo, Cato, R. R. 90: ad haec omnia percipienda os est aptissimum, Cic. N. D. 2, 54, 184: oris hiatus, id. ib. 2, 47, 122: os tenerum pueri, Hor. Ep. 2, 1, 126: fetidum, Cic. Pis. 7, 13: trilingue, Hor. C. 2, 19, 31: os loquentis Opprimere, Ov. M. 3, 296: in ore omnium esse, to be in ev

os2.full: ŏs, ossis (collat. form ossum, i, Varr. ap. Charis. p. 112 P.; Att. ap. Prisc. p. 750 ib.; Tert. Carm. adv. Marc. 2, 196: ossu, u, Charis. p. 12 P.—In plur.: OSSVA for OSSA, freq. in inscrr., Inscr. Orell. 2906; 4361; 4806; Inscr. Osann. Syll. p. 497, 1; Cardin. Dipl. Imp. 2, 11: ossuum for ossium, Prud. στεφ. 5, 111), n. prop. ossis for ostis, kindred with Sanscr. asthi, os; Gr. ὀστέον; Slav. kostj, a bone (class.). Lit.: quid dicam de ossibus? Cic. N. D. 2, 55, 139: cur hunc dolorem cineri eju

osca.full: Osca, ae, f., a town in Hispania Tarraconensis, now Huesca, in Aragon, Vell. 2, 30, 1; Flor. 3, 22, 9.—Hence, Oscensis, e, adj., of or belonging to Osca, a town of Spain, Oscan: ager, Varr. R. R. 1, 57: argentum, with the Oscan stamp, Liv. 34, 10. —In plur.: Oscenses, ĭum, m., the inhabitants of Osca, the Oscans, Caes. B. C. 1, 60; Plin. 3, 3, 4, § 24.
osca.short: Osca, ae, f., a town in Hispania Tarraconensis, now Huesca, in Aragon, Vell.

oscedo.full: oscēdo, ĭnis, f. kindr. with oscito. An inclination to yawn (post-class.), Gell. 4, 20.— A sore in the mouth of children, aphthœ, Ser. Samm. 14, 216; Isid. 4, 8, 17.

oscen.full: oscen, ĭnis, m. (but f. ap. Varr. L. L. 6, 7, 67; Plin. 10, 19, 22, § 43) [obscen, from obs-cano], a singing-bird, esp. in the auspices; a divining-bird, from whose notes auguries were taken (e. g. the raven, crow, owl): aves aut oscines sunt, aut praepetes: oscines, quae ore futura praedicunt; praepetes, quae volatu augurium significant, Serv. Verg. A. 3, 361; Cic. Fam. 6, 6, 13: oscinem corvum prece suscitabo, Hor. C. 3, 27, 11; Plin. 10, 19, 22, § 43; App. de Deo Soc. p. 45, 29: Phoebeius, i.

osci.full: Osci, ōrum, m., the Oscans, a primitive people of Campania; in more ancient times called also Opici and Opsci (Obsci), Verg. A. 7, 730; cf. Paul. ex Fest. p. 198 Müll. —Hence, Oscus, a, um, adj., Oscan: ludi, Cic. Fam. 7, 1: lingua, Varr. L. L. 7, § 28 Müll.; Verg. A. 7, 730; Liv. 10, 20, 8: ludicrum, Tac. A. 4, 14.—Adv.: Oscē, in Oscan: qui Osce et Volsce fabulantur: nam Latine nesciunt, Titin. ap. Fest. p. 198 Müll.: dicere aliquid, Varr. L. L. 5, § 131 Müll.: scire, Gell. 17, 17, 1.
osci.short: Osci, ōrum, m., the Oscans, a primitive people of Campania;

oscillans.full: oscillans, antis, subst., v. oscillo fin.

oscillatio.full: oscillātĭo, ōnis, f. oscillo, a swinging (post-Aug.), Petr. 140, 9: dies festus oscillationis, a festival celebrated at Athens in honor of Erigone, Hyg. Fab. 130.

oscillo.full: oscillo, āre, v. n. 2. oscillum, to swing, swing one's self: oscillum Santra dici ait, quod oscillent, id est inclinent, praecipitesque in os ferantur, Fest. p. 194, 9 and 10 Müll.—Pass.: osculor, Mythogr. Lat. 1, 19 fin.—Hence, oscillans, antis, P. a.; as subst., a swinger: oscillantes, ait Cornificius, ab eo, quod os celare soliti personis propter verecundiam, qui eo genere lusūs utebantur, Fest. p. 194 Müll.

oscillum1.full: oscillum, i, n. dim. 1. os; lit. little mouth; hence, A little cavity in the middle of leguminous fruits, where the germ sprouts forth: oscilla lupinorum, Col. 2, 10, 3.—* A little image of the face, a little mask of Bacchus, hung from trees, so as to be easily moved by the wind: tibique (Bacche) Oscilla ex altā suspendunt mollia pinu, Verg. G. 2, 389; cf. Serv. ad loc.; Macr. S. 1, 7; 11.

oscillum2.full: oscillum, i, n. ob- or obs-cillo, a swing, Fest. p. 194 Müll.; Verg. G. 2, 389 (v. Serv. ad loc.); Tert. Pall. 1 fin.

oscitabundus.full: oscĭtābundus, a, um, adj. oscito, gaping, yawning (post-class.), Sid. Ep. 2, 2.

oscitans.full: oscĭtans, Part. and P. a., from oscito.

oscitanter.full: oscĭtanter, adv., v. oscito, P. a. fin.

oscitatio.full: oscĭtātĭo, ōnis, f. oscito, an opening of the mouth wide, a gaping. In gen.: conchas pandentes sese quādam oscitatione, a gaping, Plin. 9, 35, 54, § 107.— In partic., a gaping, yawning, Plin. 7, 6, 5, § 42; Gell. 4, 20, 9; Mart. 2, 6, 4.— Trop.: sed Bruti senis oscitationes, tediousnesses, tedious writings, Stat. S. 4, 9, 20: non ipse (judex) nostrā oscitatione solvatur, by our languid speaking, Quint. 11, 3, 3.

oscito.full: oscĭto, āre, v. n., and oscĭtor, āri, v. dep. (inf. oscitarier, Turp. ap. Non. 322, 18; or Com. Rel. v. 15 Rib.) [oscieo], to open the mouth wide, to gape. Of plants, to open, unclose: oscitat in campis caput a cervice revulsum, of the plant lion's-mouth, Enn. ap. Serv. Verg. A. 10, 396; cf. Col. 10, 260; and: (arborum) folia cotidie ad solem oscitant, turn towards the sun, Plin. 16, 24, 36, § 88.— Of living beings, to gape, yawn: ut pandiculans oscitatur, Plaut. Men. 5, 2, 80; * Lucr. 3, 1065:

osculabundus.full: oscŭlābundus, a, um, adj. osculor, kissing (post-Aug.), Suet. Vit. 2.—With acc.: manum sacerdotis, App. M. 11, 6, p. 259; id. Mag. 94, p. 333.

osculana.full: Oscŭlāna pugna in proverbio, quo significabatur, victos vincere, quia in eādem et Valerius Laevinus imperator Romanus a Pyrrho erat victus, et brevi eundem regem devicerat Sulpicius ..., Fest. p. 197 Müll. (leg. Asculana; cf. Turneb. Advers. 3, 11).
osculana.short: Oscŭlāna pugna in proverbio, quo significabatur, victos vincere, quia in eādem et Valerius Laevinus imperator Romanus a Pyrrho erat victus, et brevi eundem regem devicerat Sulpicius ..., Fest.

osculatio.full: oscŭlātĭo, ōnis, f. osculor, a kissing (rare but class.), Cic. Cael. 20, 49; Cat. 48, 5.— In med. lang.: venarum, the inosculation of blood-vessels, Gr. ὰναστόμωσις, Cael. Aur. Tard. 2, 10, 121 and 123.

osculo1.full: oscŭlo, āre, v. a. 1. os, ōris, = ἀναστομόω, to supply with a mouth or outlet, to extend a channel, e. g. the veins, Cael. Aur. Tard. 2, 10, 123.

osculo2.full: oscŭlo, āre, v. a. (old collat. form of osculor), to kiss: osculavi caput, Titin. ap. Non. 476, 32: osculato tuo capite, App. M. 2, p. 117, 23: genua sibi osculari patiebantur, Capitol. Max. Juv. 2, § 7.

osculor.full: oscŭlor, ātus, 1 (old form auscŭ-lor, Plaut. As. 5, 2, 42; id. Merc. 3, 3, 14; old inf. oscularier; v. infra), v. dep. osculum, to kiss (class.). Lit.: compellando blanditer, ausculando. Plaut. As. 1, 3, 69: eam vidisse cum alieno oscularier, kissing each other, id. Mil. 2, 2, 88: osculari atque amplexari inter se, id. ib. 5, 1, 40: ille autem me complexus atque osculans flere prohibebat, Cic. Rep. 6, 14, 14: eum complexus, osculatusque dimisit, id. Att. 16, 5, 2: simulacrum, Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 43

osculum.full: oscŭlum (auscŭlum, Plaut. Am. 2, 2, 84; osclum, id. Truc. 1, 2, 8), i, n. dim. 1. os, a little mouth, pretty mouth, sweet mouth (cf.: labium, labellum). Lit. (only poet. and in post-Aug. prose): videt oscula, quae, etc., Ov. M. 1, 499; 10, 344: delibare, to touch, i. e. to kiss, Verg. A. 12, 434; id. G. 2, 523; Mart. 11, 92, 7; Suet. Aug. 94; Petr. 126; App. M. 3, p. 137, 41.— Transf., a kiss (freq. and class.; syn.: basium, suavium): utinam continuo ad osculum Atticae possim currere, Cic. Att.

osdroena.full: Osdrŏēna, ae, f., = Ὀσδροηνή, a country in the western part of Mesopotamia, the modern Diar Mochar, Amm. 14, 3, 2; 14, 8, 7.—Its inhabitants are called Osdrŏēni, ōrum. m., Eutr. 8, 3.
osdroena.short: Osdrŏēna, ae, f., = Ὀσδροηνή, a country in the western part of Mesopotamia, the modern Diar Mochar, Amm.

osi.full: Osi, ōrum. m., a people of Germany, on the banks of the Danube, Tac. G. 28; 43.

osinius.full: Osīnĭus, ii, m., king of Clusium, and ally of Æneas, Verg. A. 10, 655.
osinius.short: Osīnĭus, ii, m., king of Clusium, and ally of Æneas, Verg.

osireostaphe.full: Ŏsīrĕostăphē, ēs, f., = Ὄσιρισ-ταφή (Osiris-grave), a plant, called also Osiritis, App. Herb. 86.
osireostaphe.short: Ŏsīrĕostăphē, ēs, f., = Ὄσιρισ-ταφή (Osiris-grave), a plant, called also Osiritis, App.

osiris.full: Ŏsīris, is and ĭdis, m., = Ὄσιρις. An Egyptian deity, the husband of Isis, Tib. 1, 7, 27; 29; 43; Ov. M. 9, 692; Hor. Ep. 1, 17, 60; Juv. 8, 29; Macr. S. 1, 21.— Name of a warrior slain by Thymbrœus, Verg. A. 12, 458.
osiris.short: Ŏsīris, is and ĭdis, m., = Ὄσιρις.

osiritis.full: Ŏsīrītis, ĭdis, f., the name of a plant, also called Osireostaphe or cynocephalea, Plin. 30, 2, 6, § 18.
osiritis.short: Ŏsīrītis, ĭdis, f., the name of a plant, also called Osireostaphe or cynocephalea, Plin.

osor.full: ōsor (ossor, Plaut. l. l. infra), ōris, m. odi, a hater (ante- and post-class.): uxoris suae ossor, Plaut. As. 5, 2, 9 Fleck. (Ussing, osor): hominum, App. de Deo Socr. p. 48, 15; Pacat. Pan. Th. 20, 5; Aus. Ep. 4, 24: mulierum, Plaut. Poen. prol. 74; cf.: osorem dixerunt, qui aliquem odisset, Paul. ex Fest. p. 196 Müll.

osphagus.full: Osphăgus, i, m., a river in Macedonia, Liv. 31, 39.
osphagus.short: Osphăgus, i, m., a river in Macedonia, Liv.

ospicor.full: ospĭcor, āri, an old orthogr. for aus-pĭcor, Quadrig. ap. Diom. p. 378 P.

ospratura.full: osprātūra, ae, f., = ὄσπριον, the purchase of pulse (post-class.), Dig. 50, 4, 18, § 19 dub. (al. hospitatura).
ospratura.short: osprātūra, ae, f., = ὄσπριον, the purchase of pulse (post-class.), Dig.

ossa.full: Ossa, ae, f. (m., Ov. M. 1, 155), = Ὄσσα, a high mountain in Thessaly, now Kissovo, Mel. 2, 3, 2; Plin. 4, 8, 15, § 30: ter sunt conati imponere Pelio Ossam, Verg. G. 1, 281: Ossan, Ov. F. 1, 307.—Hence, Ossaeus, a, um, adj., Ossean: saxa, Verg. Cir. 33: rupes, Luc. 6, 334: media, Stat. Th. 2, 82: Ossaei bimembres, i. e. the Centaurs who dwell about Ossa, id. ib. 12, 554.

osseus.full: ossĕus, a, um, adj. 2. os, of bone, bone- (post Aug.): cuneus, Col. 5, 11: cultelli, Plin. 12, 25, 54, § 115.— Like bone, hard as bone, bony: manus, Juv. 5, 53: ilex, Plin. 16, 38, 73, § 186: cutis, Cassiod. Var. 10, 30.

ossicularis.full: ossĭcŭlāris, e, adj. ossiculum, of or belonging to the small bones (post-class.): medicamentum, Veg. Vet. 4, 28.

ossiculatim.full: ossĭcŭlātim, adv. id., by bones, bone by bone (ante-class.): legere aliquem, Caecil. ap. Non. 147, 29.

ossiculum.full: ossĭcŭlum, i, n. dim. 2. os, a small bone, ossicle (post-Aug.), Plin. 11, 37, 49, § 134; Gell. 6, 1, 10: MEA (al. OSSVCVLA), Inscr. Fabr. p. 420, n. 381.

ossifragus.full: ossĭfrăgus, a, um, adj. 2. os-frango, bone-breaking, Cass. Sev. ap. Sen. Contr. 5, 33.— Subst.: ossĭfrăgus, i, m., and ossĭfrăga, ae, f., the sea-eagle, osprey, Plin. 10, 7, 8, § 20; 30, 7, 20, § 63: accipitres, atque ossifragae, Lucr. 5, 1079; cf. Isid. Orig. 12, 7, 59.

ossilago.full: ossĭlāgo, ĭnis, f. 2. os, a hardness as of bone, a bony hardness (post-class.): tumor ossilagini similis, Veg. Vet. 2, 22.— = Ossipaga, Arn. 4, p. 131.

ossilegium.full: ossĭlĕgĭum, ii, n. 2. os-lego, a bonegathering: ossilegium, ὀστολόγιον, Gloss. Philox.

ossilegus.full: ossĭlĕgus, a, um, adj. ossilegium, a bone-gatherer: ossilegus, ὀστολόγος, Gloss. Philox.

ossipaga.full: Ossĭpāga (Ossĭpanga, Ossĭpā-gĭna), ae, f. 2. os-pango, bone-fastener, the goddess who caused the bones of children to become firm and solid, Arn. 4, 1131.

ossosus.full: ossōsus, a, um, adj. 2. os, bony (late Lat.), Cael. Aur. Salut. praecc. 36.

ossuarium.full: ossŭārĭum, ii, n., v. ossuarius, II.

ossuarius.full: ossŭārĭus, a, um, adj. 2. os, of or for bones, bone- (post-class.): OLLA OSSVARIA, a vase to contain the bones of a corpse, a bone-urn, Inscr. Orell. 2896.— Subst.: ossŭārĭum (also written ossārĭum), ii, n., a receptacle for the bones of the dead, a bone-vault, charnel-house, Dig. 47, 12, 2; Inscr. Orell. 4511; 4556.

ossuosus.full: ossŭōsus, a, um, adj. 2. os, full of bones (post-class.): loci, Veg. Vet. 2, 13.

ostendo.full: ostendo, di, sum, and tum (ostensus, Varr. ap. Prisc. p. 892 P.; Luc. 2, 192: ostentus, Att. ap. Cic. Div. 1, 22, 45; Pac. and Varr. ap. Prisc. l. l.; Tac. H. 1, 78: ostensurus, Suet. Ner. 13; App. ap. Prisc. p. 892 P.: ostenturus, Cato, Or. 52, 2; v. also the apoc. form: ostende ostendam, ut permultis aliis exemplis ejus generis manifestum est, Paul. ex Fest. p. 201 Müll.; perh. used by Cato, v. Müll. ad loc., and cf. the letter E), v. a. obs-tendo, to stretch out or spread before one; hence, t
ostendo.short: ostendo, di, sum, and tum (ostensus, Varr.

ostensio.full: ostensĭo, ōnis, f. ostendo, a showing, exhibiting, manifestation (post-class.): nova ostensio, App. M. 3, p. 133, 19; Tert. adv. Marc. 5, 11: HOMINVM ARMIGERORVM, a mustering, parade, Inscr. Salm. ad Lampr. Alex. Sev. 33: si in me est iniquitas haec, da ostensionem, expose, make manifest, Vulg. 1 Reg. 14, 41: secretorum, id. Dan. 5, 12.

ostensionalis.full: ostensĭōnālis, e, adj. ostensio, that serves for parade or display (post-class.): milites, Lampr. Alex. Sev. 33.

ostensor.full: ostensor, ōris, m. ostendo, a shower, exhibiter (eccl. Lat.), Tert. Apol. 11.

ostensus.full: ostensus, a, um, Part., from ostendo.
ostensus.short: ostensus, a, um, Part., from ostendo.

ostentabilis.full: ostentābĭlis, e, adj. ostento, worth showing, worth seeing: ostentabilis, ἐπιδεικτικός, Gloss. Philox.

ostentaculum.full: ostentācŭlum, i, n. id., for ostentum, a sign, indication: ostentat, ostentaculum, Not. Tir. p. 19.

ostentamen.full: ostentāmen, ĭnis, n. id., show, display (post-class.), Prud. Psych. 203.

ostentarius.full: ostentārĭus, a, um, adj. ostentum, of or relating to prophetic indications, prophetic (post-class.): ostentaria novitas (al. ostentatoria), Mart. Cap. 2, § 151.— Subst.: ostentārĭum, ii, n., a book of prognostics: Tuscum, Macr. S. 3, 7: arborarium, id. ib. 2, 16.

ostentaticius.full: ostentātīcĭus or -tĭus, a, um, adj. ostento, that serves for display, ostentatious (post-class.): virginitas, Tert. Virg. Vel. 3.

ostentatio.full: ostentātĭo, ōnis, f. id.. In gen., a showing, exhibition, display (very rare). in armorum magis quam togarum ostentatione, Plin. Pan. 56 fin.: cognomen Imperiosi ... ab ostentatione saevitiae ascitum, from an open display, Liv. 7, 4.— In partic. An idle show, vain display, pomp, parade, ostentation (the predom. signif. of the word): vitanda etiam ingenii ostentationis suspicio, Cic. de Or. 2, 82, 333: magnifica et gloriosa, id. Fl. 22, 52: insolens, id. Par. 6, 1, 42: et gloria, id. Rab. Post. 1

ostentator.full: ostentātor, ōris, m. ostento, a vain, self-satisfied exhibiter, a displayer, parader, boaster, vaunter: ostentatores meri, Plaut. Curc. 4, 1, 15: ostentatorem pecuniae gloriosum describere, Auct. Her. 4, 50, 63: factorum, Liv. 1, 10: omnium, quae diceret, Tac. H. 2, 80: rector juveni et ceteris periculorum praemiorumque ostentator, id. A. 1, 24.

ostentatrix.full: ostentātrix, īcis, f. ostentator, she that displays or boasts (post-class.). Lit.: immodica sui ostentatrix, App. Mag. p. 323, 11.— Trop.: pompa ostentatrix vani splendoris, Prud. Psych. 439.

ostentifer.full: ostentĭfer, ĕra, ĕrum, adj. ostentumfero, portentous: ostentiferum, τερατῶδες, Vet. Gloss.

ostento.full: ostento, āvi, ātum (inf. pass. ostentarier, Plaut. Most. 1, 3, 129), 1, v. freq. a. ostendo, to present to view, to show, exhibit (class.). In gen.: alicui jugula sua pro capite alicujus, to present, offer, Cic. Att. 1, 16, 4: aliquem, Verg. A. 12, 479: campos nitentes, id. ib. 6, 678: Sidonias opes, id. ib. 4, 75: passum capillum, Caes. B. G. 7, 48: liberos, Suet. Aug. 34: quo res sapsa loco sese ostentat, Enn. ap. Fest. p. 325 Müll. (Ann. v. 372 Vahl.).— In partic. To show off with vanity or b

ostentum.full: ostentum, i, n., v. ostendo fin.

ostentus1.full: ostentus, a, um, Part. and P. a., from ostendo.

ostentus2.full: ostentus, ūs, m. ostendo. In gen., a showing, exhibiting, display (not in Cic. or Cæs.): corpora extra vallum abjecta ostentui, as a public spectacle, Tac. A. 1, 29: atrocitatis, Gell. 20, 1, 48.— In partic. Show, parade, external appearance: nova jura Cappadociae dedit bstentui magis, quam mansura, Tac. H. 1, 78.— A sign, proof: ut Jugurthae scelerum ostentui essem, Sall. J. 24, 9; also a pretence, a sign given to deceive, id. ib. 46, 6: ut ostentui esset, multum vitalis spiritūs egestum, as a

ostes.full: ostes, ae, m., = ὤστης, a kind of earthquake, App. de Mundo, p. 65, 30.
ostes.short: ostes, ae, m., = ὤστης, a kind of earthquake, App.

ostia.full: Ostĭa, ae, f., and Ostĭa, ōrum, n. ostium; cf. Engl. mouth, in Ply-mouth, Yar-mouth, etc., a seaport town in Latium, at the mouth of the Tiber, built by Ancus Marcius, still called Ostia: Ostiam urbem ad exitum Tiberis in mare fluentis Ancus Marcius rex condidisse fertur, Paul. ex Fest. p. 197 Müll.; cf.: urbs, quam secundum ostium Tiberis (Ancus Marcius) posuit, ex quo etiam Ostiam. id. s. v. Quiritium, p. 254 ib.; Enn. ap. Paul. ex Fest. s. v. quaeso, p. 258 ib. (Ann. v. 145 Vahl.): in ore Tib
ostia.short: Ostĭa, ae, f., and Ostĭa, ōrum, n.

ostiarius2.full: ostĭārĭus, a, um, adj. ostium, of or belonging to the door: ancilla, portress, Vulg. Johan. 18, 17; usu. subst. ostĭā-rĭus, ii, m., a door-keeper, porter (syn.: janitor, portitor), Varr. R. R. 1, 13; Plin. 12, 14, 32, § 64; Vulg. 1 Par. 9, 22.—By the rich they were, in early times, occasionally chained up, Suet. Rhet. 3.—In the Christian church, a sexton, Cod. Th. 1, 3, 6; 16, 2, 27.— ostĭāria, ae, f., a female doorkeeper, portress, Ambros. in Luc. 10, § 75; Vulg. 2 Reg. 4, 5; id. Johan. 18, 16.

ostiatim.full: ostĭātim, adv. id.. Lit., from door to door, from house to house (class.): ostiatim oppidum compilare, Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 24, § 53: agere crimen, to enumerate the several houses where a crime was perpetrated, id. ib. 2, 4, 22, § 48: nec scrutanda singula et velut ostiatim pulsanda, Quint. 5, 10, 112.— Transf., by particulars or details (post-class.): quicumque ostiatim cupit noscere (wishes to know the particulars), legat, Vop. Carin. 17.

ostigo.full: ostīgo, ĭnis, f., in the lang. of shepherds, a kind of eruption or scab on lambs, also called mentigo, Col. 7, 5, 21; v. mentigo.
ostigo.short: ostīgo, ĭnis, f., in the lang.

ostiolum.full: ostĭŏlum, i, n. dim. ostium, a little door (post-Aug.), Col. 8, 14, 1: ostiola olitoria, Plin. 19, 8, 38, § 125: abscondita, Vulg. Dan. 14, 20.

ostium.full: ostĭum, ii, n. kindred with Sanscr. oshtha, labium; Slav. ūsta, the same; cf. os, a door (class.; cf.: porta, janua, fores, valvae). Lit.: omnia istaec auscultavi ab ostio, Plaut. Merc. 2, 4, 9: observare, id. Mil. 2, 3, 81: rectum ostium, the front-door (cf. posticum), Plaut. Mil. 2, 3, 58 Brix ad loc.: aperire, to open, Ter. Heaut. 2, 3, 35: operire, to shut, id. Phorm. 5, 3, 33: obserare intus, to bolt, id. Eun. 4, 6, 25: obdere pessulum ostio, id. ib. 3, 5, 55: concrepuit ostium a Glycerio,

ostocopos.full: ostŏcŏpŏs, i, m., = ὀστοκόπος, boneracking, a disease (as if the bones were giving way; post-class.), Ser. Samm. 48, 892; Pelag. Vet. 3; 10.
ostocopos.short: ostŏcŏpŏs, i, m., = ὀστοκόπος, boneracking, a disease (as if the bones were giving way;

ostorius.full: Ostōrĭus, i, m., the name of several Romans. Ostorins Sabinus, a Roman knight, Tac. A. 16, 23; 16, 30: quaestor, id. ib. 16, 33.— P. Ostorius Scapula, proprœtor in Britain, Tac. A. 12, 31: bello egregius, id. Agr. 14.— M. Ostorius Scapula, son of Publius, Tac. A. 12, 31; put to death by Nero, id. ib. 16. 15.
ostorius.short: Ostōrĭus, i, m., the name of several Romans.

ostracias.full: ostrăcĭas, ae, m., and ostrăcītis, ĭdis, f., = οστρακίας, ὀστρακῖτις, a semigem, prob. hornstone or chalcedony, Plin. 37, 10, 65, § 177.
ostracias.short: ostrăcĭas, ae, m., and ostrăcītis, ĭdis, f., = οστρακίας, ὀστρακῖτις, a semigem, prob.

ostracites.full: ostrăcītes, ae, m., = ὀστρακίτης, a precious stone, otherwise unknown, Plin. 36, 19, 31, § 139.
ostracites.short: ostrăcītes, ae, m., = ὀστρακίτης, a precious stone, otherwise unknown, Plin.

ostracitis.full: ostrăcītis, ĭdis, f., = ὀστρακῖτις. Hornstone; v. ostracias.— A kind of cadmia, Plin. 34, 10, 22, § 103.

ostracium.full: ostrăcĭum or ostrăcĕum, ii, n., = ὀστράκιον, a mussel, also called onyx, Plin. 32, 10, 46, § 134.
ostracium.short: ostrăcĭum or ostrăcĕum, ii, n., = ὀστράκιον, a mussel, also called onyx, Plin.

ostrea.full: ostrĕa, ae, f., and (rarely) ostrĕum, i, n., = ὄστρεον, an oyster, mussel, sea-snail (class.). Form ostrea, Enn. Heduph. 2 (p. 166 Vahl.); Lucil. ap. Non. 216, 6; Afran.; Turp. and Varr. ib.; Plaut. Rud. 2, 1, 8; Cic. Fragm. ap. Non. 216, 14: ostrearum vivaria, Plin. 9, 54, 79, § 168.— Form ostreum: luna alit ostrea, Lucil. ap. Gell. 20, 8, 4; id. ap. Non. 216, 16; Varr. ib. 20: ostrea Circeis, Miseno oriuntur echini, Hor. S. 2, 4, 33; Ov. F. 6, 174; Juv. 4, 142. —In sing. collect.: ostrei testa
ostrea.short: ostrĕa, ae, f., and (rarely) ostrĕum, i, n., = ὄστρεον, an oyster, mussel, sea-snail (class.).

ostrearius.full: ostrĕārĭus, a, um, adj. ostrea, of or belonging to oysters, oyster- (post-Aug.): panis, oyster-bread, bread eaten with oysters, Plin. 18, 11, 27, § 105.— Subst.: ostrĕā-rĭum, ii, n., an oyster-bed, Plin. 9, 51, 74, § 160: in Baiano locare, Macr. S. 2, 11.

ostreatus.full: ostrĕātus, a, um, adj. id.; qs. covered with oyster-shells; hence, transf., rough, scabby: quasi ostreatum tergum ulceribus (i. e. verberibus), Plaut. Poen. 1, 2, 186.

ostreosus.full: ostrĕōsus, a, um, adj. id., abounding in oysters: Cyzicus ostreosa, Auct. Priap. 77; comp., Cat. 18, 4.

ostriago.full: ostrĭāgo, ĭnis, f., a plant, otherwise unknown, App. Herb. 28.
ostriago.short: ostrĭāgo, ĭnis, f., a plant, otherwise unknown, App.

ostricolor.full: ostrĭcŏlor, ōris, adj. ostrum-color, purple-colored (poet.), Sid. Carm. 5, 18.

ostrifer.full: ostrĭfĕr, ĕra, ĕrum, adj. ostrum-fero, containing or abounding in oysters (poet.): Abydos, Verg. G. 1, 207: Geraestus, Val. Fl. 1, 456: Chalcedon, Luc. 9, 959.

ostrinus.full: ostrīnus, a, um, adj. ostrum, purple (ante-class. and poet.): supparum, Varr. ap. Non. 549, 12: ricula, Turp. ib.: colores, Prop. 4, 12, 7: torus, id. 1, 14, 20: tunica, id. 3, 27, 26.

ostrogothus.full: Ostrŏgŏthus, i, or Ostrŏgŏtha, ae, m., an Ostrogoth: Ostrogothum continere, Sid. Carm. 2, 377; id. Ep. 8, 9: imperium Ostrogothae vastarent, Jornand. Reb. Get. 47; Claud. in Eutr. 2, 153.
ostrogothus.short: Ostrŏgŏthus, i, or Ostrŏgŏtha, ae, m., an Ostrogoth: Ostrogothum continere, Sid.

ostrum.full: ostrum, i, n., = ὄστρεον. Lit., the blood of the sea-snail, purple (cf.: murex, purpura): ostro Perfusae vestes, Verg. A. 5, 111; Vitr. 7, 13.— Transf. Stuff dyed with purple, a purple dress, purple covering, purple: textilibus si in picturis ostroque rubenti Jacteris, Lucr. 2, 35: stratoque super discumbitur ostro, on purple-covered couches, Verg. A. 1, 700: Sarrano dormire ostro, id. G. 2, 506: velare umeros ostro, id. A. 7, 814; 4, 134; Prop. 4 (5), 3, 51. cenae sine aulaeis et ostro, Hor. C.

ostrya.full: ostrўa, ae, and ostrys, ўos, f., = ὀστρύα, ὄστρυς, a tree with hard wood, perh. the common hornbeam, Plin. 13, 21, 37, § 117.
ostrya.short: ostrўa, ae, and ostrys, ўos, f., = ὀστρύα, ὄστρυς, a tree with hard wood, perh.

osus.full: ōsus and ōsūrus, a, um, Partt., v. odi.
osus.short: ōsus and ōsūrus, a, um, Partt., v.

osyris.full: ŏsўris, is, f., = ὄσυρις, a plant, prob. the broom-like goose-foot or summer cypress, Plin. 27, 12, 88, § 111.
osyris.short: ŏsўris, is, f., = ὄσυρις, a plant, prob.

otacilius.full: Ŏtācĭlĭus, i, m., Ŏtācĭlĭa, ae, f., the name of a Roman gens. So, Otacilius Crassus, an adherent of Pompey, Caes. B. C. 3, 28 sq.— T. Otacilius, a proprœtor, Liv. 22, 56.—In fem.: OTACILIA, Inscr. Grut. 29, 2; Eckh. D. N. 7, p. 332.—Hence, OTACILIANA VILLA, of an Otacilius, Inscr. Marin. Fratr. Arv. p. 577.
otacilius.short: Ŏtācĭlĭus, i, m., Ŏtācĭlĭa, ae, f., the name of a Roman gens.

otacustes.full: ōtăcustes, ae, m., = ὠτακουστής, a listener, eavesdropper, spy (post-class.): otacustarum relatio, App. de Mundo, p. 69, 31.
otacustes.short: ōtăcustes, ae, m., = ὠτακουστής, a listener, eavesdropper, spy (post-class.): otacustarum relatio, App.

otho.full: Ŏtho, ōnis, m., = Ὄθων, a Roman surname. L. Roscius Otho, a knight, a friend of Cicero, and author of the law that the knights should occupy the first fourteen seats in the theatre next to the orchestra, Cic. Mur. 19, 40; cf. Ascon. ad Cornel. p. 79 Orell.—Hence, sic libitum vano, qui nos distinxit, Othoni, Juv. 3, 159.— M. Salvius Otho, a Roman emperor, whose biography is given by Suetonius: mollis Otho, Mart. 6, 32, 2; Juv. 2, 99.—Hence, ŏthōnĭānus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to the emperor
otho.short: Ŏtho, ōnis, m., = Ὄθων, a Roman surname.

othonna.full: ŏthonna, ae, f., = ὄθοννα, a Syrian plant, Plin. 27, 12, 85, § 109.
othonna.short: ŏthonna, ae, f., = ὄθοννα, a Syrian plant, Plin.

othrepte.full: Othreptē, ēs, f., one of the Amazons, Hyg. Fab. 963.
othrepte.short: Othreptē, ēs, f., one of the Amazons, Hyg.

othryades.full: Othrўădes, ae, m., = Ὀθρυάδης, a male proper name. The son of Othrys, i. e. Panthus: Panthus Othryades, Verg. A. 2, 319.— A Spartan general, who, in a battle against the Argives, was the sole survivor, Ov. F. 2, 665; Val. Max. 3, 2, 4 ext.
othryades.short: Othrўădes, ae, m., = Ὀθρυάδης, a male proper name.

othrys.full: Othrys, ўos, m., = Ὄθρυς, a mountain in Thessaly, now Ierako: Homolen Othrymque nivalem Linquentes, Verg. A. 7, 675; cf. Plin. 4, 8, 15, § 30: totus, Sen. Herc. Oet. 1168.—Acc. to the later poets, situated in Thrace, Stat. Th. 4, 655; Val. Fl. 1, 24.— Hence, Othrўsĭus, a, um, adj., Othrysian; poet. for Thracian: Othrysias pruinas (al. Odrysias), Mart. 10, 7, 2: orbis (al. Odrysius), i. e. Thrace, id. 7, 8, 2.
othrys.short: Othrys, ўos, m., = Ὄθρυς, a mountain in Thessaly, now Ierako: Homolen Othrymque nivalem Linquentes, Verg.

otia.full: ōtĭa, ae, f., = ὠτίον (little ear), a kind of mussel, Plin. 32, 11, 53, § 149.
otia.short: ōtĭa, ae, f., = ὠτίον (little ear), a kind of mussel, Plin.
