otiabundus.full: ōtĭābundus, a, um, adj. otior, having or enjoying leisure, keeping holiday (postclass.). Sid. Ep. 4, 18.

otiolum.full: ōtĭŏlum, i, n. dim. otium, a little leisure: otiolum meum, my little bit of leisure, Cael. ap. Cic. Fam. 8, 3, 1.

otior.full: ōtĭor, ātus, 1, v. dep. id., to have or enjoy leisure, to be at leisure, to keep holiday (rare but class.): cum se Syracusas otiandi, non negotiandi causā contulisset, * Cic. Off. 3, 14, 58: domesticus otior, I idle about at home, Hor. S. 1, 6, 128.

otiositas.full: ōtĭōsĭtas, ātis, f. otiosus, leisure, idleness (late Lat.). Lit.: multam mahtiam docuit otiositas, Vulg. Ecclus. 33, 29. — Transf., a writing composed at leisure moments (post-class.): suas otiositates edere, the fruils of leisure, poems, Sid. Ep. 2, 10.

otiosus.full: ōtĭōsus, a, um, adj. otium, at leisure, unoccupied, disengaged, unemployed, idle (class.; cf. feriatus, immunis; opp. negotiosus). Of persons. In gen.: nimis otiosum te arbitror hominem esse, Plaut. Truc. 1, 2, 34; 40: quamvis etiam maneo otiosus hic, Ter. Ad. 2, 4, 15: cum essem otiosus domi, Cic. Brut. 3, 10: rebus humanis aliquos otiosos deos praeficere, id. N. D. 3, 39, 93.— In partic. Without official employment, free from public affairs: quo in studio hominum quoque ingeniosissimorum otios

otis.full: ōtis, ĭdis, f., = ὠτίς, a species of bustard, Plin. 10, 22, 29, § 57; 30, 14, 45, § 131.
otis.short: ōtis, ĭdis, f., = ὠτίς, a species of bustard, Plin.

otium.full: ōtĭum, ĭi, n. In gen., leisure, vacant time, freedom from business (class.; opp. negotium; cf.: immunitas, vacatio): otio qui nescit uti plus negoti habet, Quam, etc., Enn. ap. Gell. 19, 10, 12 (Trag. v. 252 Vahl.): fecero; quamquam haut otium est, Plaut. Poen. 4, 2, 36: tantumne ab re tuast oti tibi? Ter. Heaut. 1, 1, 23: clarorum virorum atque magnorum non minus otii quam negotii rationem exstare oportere, Cato ap. Cic. Planc. 27, 66: in otio de negotiis cogitare, Cic. Off. 3, 1, 1: otium iner

otopeta.full: ōtŏpĕta, ae, m., = ὠτοπετής, longear (pure Lat. auritus) poet. for hare, Petr. 35.
otopeta.short: ōtŏpĕta, ae, m., = ὠτοπετής, longear (pure Lat.

otus1.full: ōtus, i, m., = ὦτος or ὠτός, a kind of owl, the horned owl, Plin. 10, 23, 33, § 66.
otus1.short: ōtus, i, m., = ὦτος or ὠτός, a kind of owl, the horned owl, Plin.

otus2.full: Ōtus (also Ōtos, Ōthos, and Oetus), i, m., the name of a giant: immanis Otos, Verg. Cul. 233; cf. Hyg. Fab. 28.
otus2.short: Ōtus (also Ōtos, Ōthos, and Oetus), i, m., the name of a giant: immanis Otos, Verg.

oufens.full: Oufens and Oufentīnus, a, um, v. Uf-.
oufens.short: Oufens and Oufentīnus, a, um, v.

ovalis.full: ŏvālis, e, adj. ovo, of or belonging to an ovation (post-class.): ovalis corona murtea est: eā utebantur imperatores qui ovantes urbem introibant, Gell. 5, 6, 20; cf. Fest. p. 195 Müll.

ovarius.full: ōvārĭus, ii, m. ovum, an egg-keeper (who took charge of the new-laid eggs), Inscr. Collect. Ferrar. Opusc. 9, p. 179.

ovatio.full: ŏvātĭo, ōnis, f. ovo, an ovation, i. e. a lesser triumph, in which the general, after an easy, bloodless victory, or after a victory over slaves, made his public entrance into the city, not in a chariot, as in the greater triumph, but simply on horseback or on foot. The token of a bloodless victory was a wreath of myrtle around his brows; cf. Fest. p. 195 Müll.; Gell. 5, 6, 20; Plin. 15, 29, 38, § 125: fuit de servis ovatione contentus, Flor. 3, 19, 8.

ovatus1.full: ŏvātus, a, um, Part., from ovo.
ovatus1.short: ŏvātus, a, um, Part., from ovo.

ovatus2.full: ōvātus, a, um, adj. ovum. Eggshaped, ovate (post-Aug.): aliis ovata species, Plin. 15, 21, 23, § 85; App. M. 10, p. 254 med.— Having ovate spots: lapis Numidicus, Plin. 35, 1, 1, § 3.

ovatus3.full: ŏvātus, ūs, m. ovo, a shouting, rejoicing (poet.), Val. Fl. 6, 187.

oviarius.full: ŏvĭārĭus (collat. form † ŏvĭārĭcus: conductoribus gregum oviaricorum, Inscr. Momms. 4916), a, um, adj. ovis, of or belonging to sheep, sheep- (post-Aug.): pecus (al. oviaricum), Col. 7, 6, 1.— Subst.: ŏvĭārĭa, ae, f., a flock of sheep, Varr. R. R. 2 praef. § 6.

ovico.full: ōvĭco, 1, v. a. ovum, to mix with the white of an egg, Plin. Val. 1, 17.

ovicula.full: ŏvĭcŭla (ŏvĕ-). ae, f. dim. ovis, a little sheep (post-class.): ovicula, Aug. Doctr. Chr. 3, 21: ovecula. Tert. Pall. 3.—Q. Fabius Max. Cunctator Ovieula dictus est a morum clementiā, Aur. Vict. Vir. Ill. 43.

ovidius.full: Ovĭdĭus, ii, m., Ovid, the name of a Roman gens.—So esp.: P. Ovidius Naso, a celebrated Latin poet, Quint. 10, 1, 88; Sen. Ep. 79, 5; Ov. Tr. 2, 119.—A contemporary of Martial, Mart. 7, 44, 1; 7, 45, 6.
ovidius.short: Ovĭdĭus, ii, m., Ovid, the name of a Roman gens.—So esp.: P.

ovile.full: ŏvīle, is, n. ovis. A sheepfold (syn. caula). Lit.: non lupus insidias explorat ovilia circum, Verg. G. 3, 537; id. A. 9, 59; Ov. Tr. 4, 1, 79.— A fold for goats: aliis in ovilibus haedi, Ov. M. 13, 828.— Fig., the church or fold of Christ, Vulg. Johan. 10, 1, 16.— Ovile, an enclosed space in the Campus Martius, where the Romans voted at their comitia, Liv. 26, 22; Juv. 6, 528.—Plur., Luc. 2, 197; cf. Serv. Verg. E. 1, 34.

ovilio.full: ŏvīlĭo, ōnis, m. ovis, a shepherd (postclass. for opilio): pastores oviliones, Dig. 33, 7, 26.

ovilis.full: ŏvīlis, e, adj. id., of or for sheep, sheep- (ante- and post-class.): stercus, Cato, R. R. 39, 1: stabulatio, App. M. 4, p. 145, 13: grex, Dig. 7, 8, 12, § 2 al.—Hence, subst. ovile, q. v.

ovillinus.full: ŏvillīnus, a, um, adj. id., of or belonging to sheep (post-class.): lac, sheep's milk, Theod. Prisc. de Diaeta, 3: caro, mutton, id. ib. 6.

ovillus.full: ŏvillus, a, um, adj. id., of or belonging to sheep, sheep- (class.): caseus, Cato, R. R. 76, 2: grex, Liv. 22, 10: pecus, Varr. R. R. 2, 2, 6; Col. 7, 2, 6: lac, Plin. 28, 9, 33, § 124.

ovinius.full: Ŏvīnĭus, ii, m. id., a Roman surname: nomina multa habemus ab utroque pecore, a minore Porcius, Ovinius, Caprilius, Varr. R. R. 2, 1, 10.

ovinus.full: ŏvīnus, a, um, adj. id., of or belonging to sheep, sheep's (post-class.): cauda, Ser. Samm. 14, 254.

oviparus.full: ōvĭpărus, a, um, adj. ovum-pario, that lays eggs, oviparous (post-class.): vivipari et ovipari: ita enim appello, quae Graeci ζωοτόκα, καὶ ὠοτόκα, App. Mag. p. 298, 24: fetus, Fulg. Myth. 1, 12; Aus. Idyll. 10, 132.

ovis.full: ŏvis, is (acc. ovim, Plaut. Merc. 3, 1, 26; al. ovem; abl. ovi, acc. to Varr. L. L. 8, § 66 Müll.), f. (m., Varr. ap. Non. 216, 23: ovis mas, Varr. L. L. 5, 98; cf.: ovis semimas, Ov. F. 1, 588; cf. Fest. p. 195 Müll.) [kindr. with Sanscr. avi, ovis; Lith. awi-s; Slav. ovjza; Gr. ὄϊς; cf. also Goth. avistr, ovile], a sheep (class.). Lit.: oves scabrae, glabrae, Plaut. Trin. 2, 4, 140: cum fervit maxime, tam placidum quasi ovem reddo, Ter. Ad. 4, 1, 18; Cic. N. D. 2, 63, 158: multae dictione oviu

ovius.full: Ŏvĭus, a, name of a Roman gens.— Hence, ŏvĭus, Cic. Att. 16, 1, 5.— ŏvĭa, wife of L. Lollius, Cic. Att. 12, 21, 4; 12, 24, 1; 13, 22, 4.
ovius.short: Ŏvĭus, a, name of a Roman gens.— Hence, ŏvĭus, Cic.

ovo.full: ŏvo, ātum (first pers. pres. indic. and perf. forms not in use: ovet, Stat. Sil. 4, 1, 8: ovaret, id. Th. 1, 153: ovandi, Suet. Claud. 1; Gell. 5, 6: ovaturus, Sol. 45), 1, v. defect. n. [cf. Sanscr. root u-, avate, to roar; Gr. αὔω, ἀϝυω, to shout], to exult, rejoice. In gen. (mostly poet.): ovantes Horatium accipiunt, Liv. 1, 25: laetus ovat nunc laude virum, Val. Fl. 4, 342.—Of inanim. subjects: currus ovantes, Prop. 3, 7 (4, 8), 53: ovat Africus, rages, Val. Fl. 2, 506.— In partic., to celeb

ovum.full: ōvum, i, n. ὠόν, i. e. ΩϝΟΝ. Lit., an egg: ovum parere, to lay, Cic. Ac. 2, 18, 57; Varr. R. R. 3, 9, 8: edere, Col. 8, 3, 4: ponere, Ov. M. 8, 258: efferre, Verg. G. 1, 379: eniti, Col. 8, 11, 8 sq.: facere, Varr. R. R. 3, 9, 17: pullos ex ovis excuderunt, to hatch, Cic. N. D. 2, 52, 130 B. and K. (al. excluserunt): incubare ova, to sit on, brood on, hatch, Varr. R. R. 3, 9, 8; 12; for which: incubare ovis, Col. 8, 11, 14: suppovere ova, id. 8, 6, 1: an pulli rostellis ova percuderint ... nam s

oxalis.full: oxălis, ĭdis, f., = ὀξαλίς, a sort of sorrel, garden sorrel, Plin. 20, 21, 85, § 231.
oxalis.short: oxălis, ĭdis, f., = ὀξαλίς, a sort of sorrel, garden sorrel, Plin.

oxalme.full: oxalmē, ēs, f., = ὀξάλμη, a pickle or sauce made of vinegar and brine, Plin. 23, 2, 29, § 61 (al. oxyalme).
oxalme.short: oxalmē, ēs, f., = ὀξάλμη, a pickle or sauce made of vinegar and brine, Plin.

oxartes.full: Oxartes, is, m., a Persian, the father of Roxana, the wife of Alexander the Great, Curt. 10, 3, 11.
oxartes.short: Oxartes, is, m., a Persian, the father of Roxana, the wife of Alexander the Great, Curt.

oxathres.full: Oxathres, is, m., brother of the Persian king Darius Codomannus, Curt. 3, 11, 8.
oxathres.short: Oxathres, is, m., brother of the Persian king Darius Codomannus, Curt.

oximum.full: Oxĭmum, i, n., a city in Italy, also called Auximum, Liv. 41, 21.
oximum.short: Oxĭmum, i, n., a city in Italy, also called Auximum, Liv.

oxiones.full: Oxiones, um (acc. -as), m., a people in Sarmatia, Tac. G. 46, 6.

oxos.full: Oxos or -us, i, m., = Ὦξος, the Oxus, a river in Asia, which rises on the borders of Hyrcania and Sogdiana, and flows into the Caspian Sea, now the Amu or Jihon, Mel. 3, 5, 6; Plin. 6, 16, 18, § 48; Curt. 7, 4, 5.
oxos.short: Oxos or -us, i, m., = Ὦξος, the Oxus, a river in Asia, which rises on the borders of Hyrcania and Sogdiana, and flows into the Caspian Sea, now the Amu or Jihon, Mel.

oxybaphus.full: oxўbăphus, i, m., = ὀξυβάφον, lit. a vinegar-cup (pure Lat. acetabulum); hence, a liquid measure containing fifteen drachms (post-class.), Rhem. Fan. Ponder. 75; cf. Isid. Orig. 16, 26.

oxycedros.full: oxўcĕdros, i, f., = ὀξύκεδρος, a species of cedar with pointed leaves, Plin. 13, 5, 10, § 52.
oxycedros.short: oxўcĕdros, i, f., = ὀξύκεδρος, a species of cedar with pointed leaves, Plin.

oxycomina.full: oxў-cŏmĭna, ōrum, n. plur., pickled olives (al. oxycominia), Petr. 66.

oxygala.full: oxўgăla, ae, f., = ὀξύγαλα, τό (sour milk), the thick part of curdled milk, curds, Col. 12, 8.—Acc. to the Gr., as a neutr., Plin. 28, 9, 35, § 134.
oxygala.short: oxўgăla, ae, f., = ὀξύγαλα, τό (sour milk), the thick part of curdled milk, curds, Col.

oxygarum.full: oxўgărum, i, n., = ὀξύγαρον, a sauce of vinegar and garum, Mart. 3, 50, 4.
oxygarum.short: oxўgărum, i, n., = ὀξύγαρον, a sauce of vinegar and garum, Mart.

oxylapathum.full: oxўlăpăthum, i, n., = ὀξυλάπαθον, a kind of sorrel, sharp-pointed dock, Plin. 20, 21, 85, § 231.
oxylapathum.short: oxўlăpăthum, i, n., = ὀξυλάπαθον, a kind of sorrel, sharp-pointed dock, Plin.

oxymeli.full: oxўmĕli, ĭtis, and oxўmel, mellis, n., = ὀξύμελι, vinegar-honey, a mixture of vinegar and honey, oxymel, Plin. 23, 2, 29, § 60.—Also written oxymelli: brassica ex aceto oxymelli et sale sparsā (al. oxymelle, al. oxymela), Cato, R. R. 157; Col. 12, 58, 3.
oxymeli.short: oxўmĕli, ĭtis, and oxўmel, mellis, n., = ὀξύμελι, vinegar-honey, a mixture of vinegar and honey, oxymel, Plin.

oxymorus.full: oxўmōrus, a, um, adj., = ὀξύμωρος, acutely silly: oxymora verba, expressions which at first sight appear absurd, but which contain a concealed point; so especially of such apparently contradictory assertions as: cum tacent clamant, etc. (Cic. Cat. 1, 8, 21), Pseudo Ascon. ad Cic. Div. in Caecil. 1.
oxymorus.short: oxўmōrus, a, um, adj., = ὀξύμωρος, acutely silly: oxymora verba, expressions which at first sight appear absurd, but which contain a concealed point;

oxymyrsine.full: oxўmyrsīnē, ēs, f., = ὀξυμυρσινη, the plant prickly-myrtle, butcher's-broom (pure Lat. ruscus), Plin. 15, 7, 7, § 27.
oxymyrsine.short: oxўmyrsīnē, ēs, f., = ὀξυμυρσινη, the plant prickly-myrtle, butcher's-broom (pure Lat.

oxypaederotinus.full: oxўpaedĕrōtĭnus, a, um, adj., = ὀξυπαιδερώτινος, opal-colored: vestes, Vop. Aur. 46.
oxypaederotinus.short: oxўpaedĕrōtĭnus, a, um, adj., = ὀξυπαιδερώτινος, opal-colored: vestes, Vop.

oxyporus.full: oxўpŏrus, a, um, adj., = ὀξυπόρος, that passes quickly through, penetrating; of food, easily digested; of medicine, that operates quickly: moretum, Col. 12, 56; Plin. 20, 7, 26, § 65; 20, 23, 96, § 256; 24, 8, 36, § 55; Stat. S. 4, 9, 36.
oxyporus.short: oxўpŏrus, a, um, adj., = ὀξυπόρος, that passes quickly through, penetrating;

oxyrrhoe.full: Oxyrrhŏē or Oxўraē, ēs, f., = Ὀξυρρόη, one of Actœon's hounds, Hyg. Fab. 181.
oxyrrhoe.short: Oxyrrhŏē or Oxўraē, ēs, f., = Ὀξυρρόη, one of Actœon's hounds, Hyg.

oxys.full: oxys, ўos, m., = ὀξύς (sharp). Common wood-sorrel, Plin. 27, 12, 89, § 112. — A kind of sharp rush, Plin. 21, 18, 69, § 112.

oxysaccharum.full: oxўsacchărum, i, n., = ὀξυσάκχαρον, vinegar-sugar, a drink made of vinegar and sugar, Constant. Afer. 7, 1.
oxysaccharum.short: oxўsacchărum, i, n., = ὀξυσάκχαρον, vinegar-sugar, a drink made of vinegar and sugar, Constant.

oxyschoenos.full: oxyschoenos, i, m., = ὀξύσχοινος, a kind of rush, Plin. 21, 18, 69, § 112.
oxyschoenos.short: oxyschoenos, i, m., = ὀξύσχοινος, a kind of rush, Plin.

oxytonon.full: oxўtŏnon, i, n., = ὀξύτονον, wild poppy, App. Herb. 53.
oxytonon.short: oxўtŏnon, i, n., = ὀξύτονον, wild poppy, App.

oxytriphyllon.full: oxўtrĭphyllon, i, n., = ὀξυτρίφυλλον, sharp-leaved trefoil, Plin. 21, 9, 30, § 54.
oxytriphyllon.short: oxўtrĭphyllon, i, n., = ὀξυτρίφυλλον, sharp-leaved trefoil, Plin.

oxyzomus.full: oxyzōmus, a, um, adj., = ὀξύζωμος, seasoned with sour sauce (post-class.): pullus, Apic. 6, 9.
oxyzomus.short: oxyzōmus, a, um, adj., = ὀξύζωμος, seasoned with sour sauce (post-class.): pullus, Apic.

ozaena.full: ozaena, ae, f., = ὄζαινα. A kind of polypus: ozaena, dicta a gravi capitis odore, Plin. 9, 30, 48, § 89.— A polypus in the nose: narium ozaenae, Plin. 25, 13, 104, § 165.

ozaenitis.full: ozaenītis, ĭdis, f., = ὀζαινῖτις, bastard nard, Plin. 12, 12, 26, § 42.
ozaenitis.short: ozaenītis, ĭdis, f., = ὀζαινῖτις, bastard nard, Plin.

ozaenosus.full: ozaenōsus, a, um, adj. ozaena, II., affected with a polypus of the nose (late Lat.): loca, Pelag. Vet. 16.

ozogardana.full: Ozogardana, ae, f., a city of Mesopotamia, Amm. 24, 2, 3.
ozogardana.short: Ozogardana, ae, f., a city of Mesopotamia, Amm.

ozomene.full: Ozŏmĕnē, ēs, f., the wife of Thaumas and mother of the Harpies, Hyg. Fab. 14.
ozomene.short: Ozŏmĕnē, ēs, f., the wife of Thaumas and mother of the Harpies, Hyg.

p.full: P, p, the fifteenth letter of the Latin alphabet, the character for which is derived from the ancient form of the Greek II (P or P), as is shown by inscriptions and coins, which exhibit the P in these forms.The P-sound, like the K- and T-sounds, was not aspirated in the ancient language; whence the spelling TRIVMPE for triumphe, in the Song of the Arval Brothers.As an initial, P combines, in pure Latin words, only with the consonants l and r; the combinations pn, ps, and pt belong to words borro
p.short: P, p, the fifteenth letter of the Latin alphabet, the character for which is derived from the ancient form of the Greek II (P or P), as is shown by inscriptions and coins, which exhibit the P in these forms.The P-sound, like the K- and T-sounds, was

pa.full: Pa pro parte (leg. patre) et po pro potissimum positum est in Saliari carmine, Fest. p. 205 Müll.

pabillus.full: păbillus, i, m. dim. pabo, a small wheelbarrow (late Lat.), Lampr. Elag. 29.

pabo.full: păbo, ōnis, m., a one-wheeled vehicle, a wheelbarrow: pabo vehiculum unius rotae, Gloss. Isid.
pabo.short: păbo, ōnis, m., a one-wheeled vehicle, a wheelbarrow: pabo vehiculum unius rotae, Gloss.

pabularis.full: pābŭlāris, e, adj. pabulum, of or fit for fodder: vicia, Col. 2, 14, 1; Pall. 1, 6, 14; Plin. 18, 16, 41, § 142.

pabularius.full: pābŭlārĭus, a, um, adj. id., of or belonging to fodder or pasture: PABVLARIORVM COLLEGIVM, perh. the farmers of the public pastures, Inscr. Don. cl. 9, n. 3 and 20.

pabulatio.full: pābŭlātĭo, ōnis, f. pabulor, pasture. Lit., Varr. R. R. 3, 16; Col. 7, 9 fin.— Transf., in milit. language, a collecting of fodder, a foraging: omnes nostras pabulationes frumentationesque observabat, Caes. B. G. 7, 16; 1, 15: premi pabulatione, id. B. C. 1, 78: pabulatione intercludi, id. B. G. 7, 44; Hirt. B. G. 8, 7; 11.

pabulator.full: pābŭlātor, ōris, m. id.. A fodderer, a herdsman; only according to the gloss: pabulator pastor, qui bubus pabula praebet, Isid. Gloss.— In milit. lang., a forager, Caes. B. C. 1, 55; id. B. G. 5, 17; Hirt. B. G. 8, 11; Liv. 27, 43; 29, 2.

pabulatorius.full: pābŭlātōrĭus, a, um, adj. pabulator, of or for fodder: corbis, Col. 6, 3, 5; 11, 2, 99.

pabulor.full: pābŭlor, ātus, 1, v. dep. n. and a. [pabulum]. Neutr. To eat fodder, to feed, graze (syn. pascor): capella placide et lente pabulatur, Col. 7, 6, 9; 8, 15, 6: pabulantia jumenta, Front. p. 2203 P.— To seek fodder, seek for food; hence, in gen., to seek a subsistence; of fishermen: ad mare huc prodimus pabulatum, Plaut. Rud. 2, 1, 6.— In partic., in milit. lang., to forage: angustius pabulantur, Caes. B. C. 1, 29; 1, 40; Liv. 6, 30: cum Caesar pabulandi causā tres legiones misisset, Caes. B. G. 5

pabulosus.full: pābŭlōsus, a, um, adj. id., abounding in fodder (late Lat.): insula, Sol. 22, 2.

pabulum.full: pābŭlum, i, n. from the root pa, whence also pa-sco, food, nourishment. Lit. Of men (only poet.): dura mundi, Lucr. 5, 944: dira (of the human food of Polyphemus), Val. Fl. 4, 105; Stat. Th. 12, 566.— Of animals, food, fodder (very freq. and class.): bubus pabulum parare, Cato, R. R. 54, 1: pabulo pecoris student (Numidae), Sall. J. 90, 1: secare pabulum, Caes. B. G. 7, 14: supportare, id. B. C. 3, 58: consumere, id. B. G. 7, 18: conquirere, Hirt. B. G. 8, 10: comparare, Nep. Eum. 8: hirundo Pab

pacalis.full: pācālis, e, adj. pax, of or belonging to peace, peaceful (poet.): olea, Ov. M. 6, 101: laurus, peaceful, that betokens peace, id. ib. 15, 591: flammae, on the altar of the goddess of peace, id. F. 1, 719.

pacate.full: pācātē, adv., v. 2. paco, P. a. fin.

pacatio.full: pācātĭo, ōnis, f. 2. paco, a peace-making, pacification, peace, Front. Strat. praef.

pacator.full: pācātor, ōris, m. id., a peace-maker, pacificator, subjugator (post-Aug.): gentium, Sen. Ben. 5, 15, 6: terrarum, id. ib. 1, 13, 3: orbis, id. Herc. Oet. 1990: terrae Iberae, Sil. 16, 246: Nemeae, id. 2, 483: Rheni, Claud. Laud. Stil. 3, 13: orbis, Num. ap. Eckh. D. N. 7, p. 190.

pacatorius.full: pācātōrĭus, a, um, adj. pacator, peace-promoting, pacific (post-class.): judicium, Tert. adv. Marc. 4, 29.

pacatula.full: Pācātŭla, ae, f. dim. pacata, a female proper name, Hier. Ep. 128, n. 4.

pacatum.full: pācātum, i, n., v. pacatus, under 2. paco.

pacatus.full: pācātus, a, um, Part. and P. a., from 2. paco.

paccius.full: paccĭus, ii, m., a poet mentioned by Juvenal, 7, 12.
paccius.short: paccĭus, ii, m., a poet mentioned by Juvenal, 7, 12.

pacensis.full: Pācensis, e, adj. Pax Julia. Of or belonging to the city of Pax Julia (in Lusitania), the modern Beja; hence, Pā-censes, ĭum, m., the inhabitants of that city. Inscr. Grut. 199, 4.— Pacensis colonia, the city of Forum Julii, the mod. Frejus, Plin. 3, 4, 5, § 35.— The colony of Deultum, in Thrace, the mod. Derkon, Num. ap. Mionnet. Descr. des Medaill. 1, p. 383.

pachynum.full: Păchȳnum, i, n., and Păchȳnus (-os), i (Păchўnus, Avien. Perieg. 645; Prisc. Perieg. 482), m. and f., = Πάχυνος, the south-eastern promontory of Sicily, looking towards Greece, now Capo Passaro: ipsius promuntorium Pelorus vocatur vergens in Italiam, Pachynum in Graeciam, Lilybaeum in Africam, Plin. 3, 8, 14, § 87: classis Pachynum appulsa, Cic. Verr. 2, 5, 33, § 87; Liv. 25, 27: metas lustrare Pachyni, Verg. A. 3, 429; 7, 289: obversa Pachynos ad austros, Ov. M. 13, 725; voc. Pachyne, id. ib. 5
pachynum.short: Păchȳnum, i, n., and Păchȳnus (-os), i (Păchўnus, Avien.

pacidianus.full: Pācĭdĭānus, i, m., a famous gladiator, whose combat with Æserninus, the Samnite, mentioned by Lucilius, became proverbial, Lucil. ap. Non. 393, 30; Cic. Opt. Gen. Or. 6, 17; id. Tusc. 4, 21, 48; id. Q. Fr. 3, 4, 2; Hor. S. 2, 7, 97 (al. Placidianus).
pacidianus.short: Pācĭdĭānus, i, m., a famous gladiator, whose combat with Æserninus, the Samnite, mentioned by Lucilius, became proverbial, Lucil.

pacifer.full: pācĭfer, fēra, fŏrum, adj. pax-fero, peace-bringing, that makes or announces peace, peaceful, pacific (poet. and postclass.): sermo, Luc. 3, 305: oliva, Verg. A. 8, 116: laurus, Plin. 15, 30, 40, § 133; of the same: virga, Val. Fl. 4, 139.—A frequent epithet of the gods; of Mercury: Cyllenius, Ov. M. 14, 291; so Inscr. Orell. 1411; of Jupiter, Inscr. Gud. 7, 7; of Mars, Inscr. Orell. 1353; of Apollo, Inscr. Grut. 38, 7; of Hercules, ib. 49, 1; 1013, 4; of Minerva, Inscr. Rein. cl. 1, 228; of Gen

pacifero.full: pācĭfĕro, āre id., to keep peace: pacifero, εἰρήνην ἄγω, Gloss. Gr. Lat.
pacifero.short: pācĭfĕro, āre id., to keep peace: pacifero, εἰρήνην ἄγω, Gloss.

pacificatio.full: pācĭfĭcātĭo, ōnis, f. pacifico, a peacemaking, pacification (class.): spes pacificationis, Cic. Att. 7, 8, 4: opem et gratiam alicujus ad pacificationem quaerere, id. ib. 9, 11, 2; id. Fam. 10, 27, 2: ubi ista pacificatio perpetrari nequivit, Gell. 7, 3, 3.

pacificator.full: pācĭfĭcātor, ōris, m. id., a peacemaker, pacificator (class.; cf. pacator): Allobrogum, Cic. Att. 1, 13, 2: Servius pacificator, id. ib. 15, 7, 1; Liv. 27, 30, 4; Quint. 11, 3, 119: Karthaginiensium, Just. 18, 2, 4.

pacificatorius.full: pācĭfĭcātōrĭus, a, um, adj. pacificator, peace-making, pacificatory: legatio, Cic. Phil. 12, 1, 3.

pacifico.full: pācĭfĭco, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. (ante- and post-class.; also, pācĭfĭcor, ātus, v. dep.; v. in the foll., and cf. Prisc. p. 799 P.) [paxfacio], to make or conclude a peace (not in Cic. or Cæs.). Lit.: quo Metellus initio, Jugurthā pacificante, praesidium imposuerat, at the beginning of Jugurtha's negotiations for peace, Sall. J. 66, 2: legati pacificatum venerunt, Liv. 5, 23; cf. id. 7, 40; Vulg. Col. 1, 20.— As a deponent: pacificari cum altero statuit, Just. 6, 1, 2: pacificatus cum Carthaginiens

pacificus.full: pācĭfĭcus, a, um, adj. id., peacemaking, pacific, peaceable (class.): persona, * Cic. Att. 8, 12, 4: secures, the axes in the fasces of the lictors, Luc. 7, 63: Janus, Mart. 8, 66.—Plur. as subst.: beati pacifici, Vulg. Matt. 5, 9.—Esp.: victimae pacificae, peaceofferings, Vulg. Exod. 29, 28: hostiae, id. ib. 32, 6.—As subst.: pācĭfĭca, ōrum, n., peace-offerings: obtulit pacifica, Vulg. 2 Reg. 6, 17 et saep.—Hence, adv.: pācĭ-fĭcē, pacifically, peaceably (post-class.): consulere, Cypr. Ep. 41; V

pacio.full: păcĭo, ōnis, f., a contract, covenant (ante-class. for pactio): pacionem antiqui dicebant, quam nunc pactionem dicimus: unde et pacisci adhuc et paco in usu remanet, Fest. p. 250 Müll. (perh. too, ap. Fest. s. v. nuptias, p. 170, instead of ratio we should read pacio, acc. to the conject. of Dac. on the preced. passage).
pacio.short: păcĭo, ōnis, f., a contract, covenant (ante-class.

pacisco.full: păcisco, ĕre, 3, v. n. and a. [collat. form of dep. paciscor, q. v.], to agree, contract, bargain, covenant (class. only in perf. part. pass.): id quoque paciscunt, Naev. ap. Non. 474, 17: paciscit, obsides ut reddant, id. ib. 18.—Hence, pactus, a, um, in pass. signif., agreed upon, settled, determined, covenanted, stipulated (class.). In gen.: pactum pretium, Cic. Off. 3, 29, 107: pacta praemia, id. Q. Fr. 3, 3, 2: dies, id. Cat. 1, 9, 24: merces, Hor. C. 3, 3, 22: foedus, Cic. Sest. 14, 33: cu

paciscor.full: păciscor, pactus, 3, v. dep. n. and a. (act. collat. form, v. supra) [1. paco], to make a bargain, contract, or agreement with any one; to covenant, agree, stipulate, bargain, contract respecting any thing (cf.: transigo, stipulor, pango). Lit. In gen. Neutr.: pacisci cum illo paululā pecuniā potes, Plaut. Bacch. 4, 8, 24; Cic. Verr. 2, 3, 14, § 36; Ov. M. 4, 702: paciscitur magnā mercede cum Celtiberorum principibus, ut, etc., Liv. 25, 33; cf.: pacti sunt inter se, ut die statutā, Just. 1, 10,

paco1.full: păco, ĕre, prim. of paciscor and pango, to make or come to an agreement, to agree together respecting any thing: NI CVM EO PACIT TALIO ESTO, Lex XII. Tab.; cf. Dirks, Uebers. p. 516 sq.

paco2.full: pāco, ăvi, ātum, 1, v. a. pax, to bring into a state of peace and quietness, to make peaceful, to quiet, pacify, subdue, soothe (class.; cf.: pacifico, placo). Lit.: pacare Amanum, Cic. Fam. 15, 4, 8: omnem Galliam, Caes. B. C. 1, 7: qui nuper pacati erant, id. B. G. 1, 16: civitates, id. ib. 7, 65: Hispanias, id. B. C. 1, 85: bimarem Isthmon, Ov. M. 7, 405: regiones, Hirt. B. Alex. 26: Asiam, Just. 38, 7, 2: Erymanthi nemora, Verg. A. 6, 803: MARE A PRAEDONIBVS, Monum. Ancyr. fin. ap. Grut. 233

paconius.full: Pacōnĭus, i, m., the name of a Roman gens. So M. Paconius, Cic. Mil. 27, 74; another M. Paconius, Suet. Tib. 61; Tac. A. 3, 66.
paconius.short: Pacōnĭus, i, m., the name of a Roman gens.

pacorus.full: Păcŏrus, i, m. A son of Orodes, king of Parthia, the conqueror of Crassus; he was afterwards conquered by Ventidius Bassus, the legate of Antony, Cic. Att. 5, 18, 1; id. Fam. 15, 1, 2; Just. 42, 4, 6; 16.— Pacorus II., a king of the Parthians in the time of Domitian, Plin. Ep. 10, 16, 2; Mart. 9, 36, 3.— A Roman surname, Inscr. Grut. 39, 4; 102, 1.

pacta.full: pacta, ae, f., v. pactus, under pacisco fin. 1.

pacticius.full: pactīcĭus or -tĭus, a, um, adj. paciscor, agreed upon, stipulated, Gell. 1, 25, 8.

pactilis.full: pactĭlis, e, adj. pango, plaited together, wreathed: corona, Plin. 21, 3, 8, § 11 (opp. sutilis).

pactio.full: pactĭo, ōnis, f. paciscor. In gen., an agreeing, covenanting; an agreement, covenant, contract, bargain, pact (syn. pactum): est autem pactio duorum plurinmve in idem placitum et consensum, Dig. 2, 14, 1: in pactionibus faciendis legem spectare, Cic. Q. Fr. 1, 1, 12: pactionem facere de aliquā re, id. Rosc. Com. 12, 34, and 14, 40: nefarias cum multis pactiones conflare, id. Har. Resp. 20, 42: pactionem cum aliquo facere, ut, etc., id. Att. 4, 18, 2: condiciones pactionesque bellicas perturbare

pactiuncula.full: pactĭuncŭla, ae, f. dim. pactio, an agreement: pactio, pactiuncula, Not. Tir.

pactolus.full: Pactōlus, i, m., = Πακτωλός, a river in Lydia which was said to bring down golden sands, the mod. Sarabat, Verg. A. 10, 142; Plin. 5, 29, 30, § 110; Hyg. Fab. 191; Ov. M. 11, 142: Pactolus aureas undas agens, Varr. ap. Non. 243, 20.—Prov., of wealth: tibique Pactolus fluat, Hor. Epod. 15, 20; cf. Prop. 1, 14, 11; Juv. 14, 299.— Hence, Pactōlis, ĭdis, f. adj., of or belonging to the Pactolus: nymphae Pactolides, Ov. M. 6, 16.
pactolus.short: Pactōlus, i, m., = Πακτωλός, a river in Lydia which was said to bring down golden sands, the mod.

pactor.full: pactor, ōris, m. paciscor, one who makes a contract, a contractor, negotiator: societatis pactores, Cic. Verr. 2, 5, 21, § 55.

pactum.full: pactum, i, n., v. pacisco fin.

pactumejus.full: Pactŭmējus, i, m., a supposititious son of Canidia, Hor. Epod. 17, 50.
pactumejus.short: Pactŭmējus, i, m., a supposititious son of Canidia, Hor.

pactus1.full: pactus, a, um, Part. and P. a., from pacisco.

pactus2.full: pactus, a, um, Part., from pango.
pactus2.short: pactus, a, um, Part., from pango.

pactus3.full: pactus, i, m., v. pacisco fin.

pactye.full: Pactўē, ēs, and Pactўa, ae, f., = Πακτύη, a town of Thrace, now Doghan Arslan, Nep. Alc. 7, 4; Plin. 4, 11, 18, § 48.
pactye.short: Pactўē, ēs, and Pactўa, ae, f., = Πακτύη, a town of Thrace, now Doghan Arslan, Nep.

pacuvius.full: Pācŭvĭus (Pācŭus), i, m., the name of a Roman gens. So esp. Pacuvius, a celebrated Roman poet, a native of Brundisium, nephew of Ennius, and contemporary of P. Scipio Africanus, Cic. Opt. Gen. Or. 1, 1; id. Brut. 64, 229; id. Fin. 1, 2, 4; id. Or. 11, 36; Hor. Ep. 2, 1, 56; Quint. 10, 1, 97. He is also said to have distinguished himself as a painter, Plin. 35, 4, 7, § 19.—Sync. form: Pacui discipulus dicor, porro is fuit Enni, Enniu' musarum, Varr. ap. Non. 88, 4; Plin. 35, 4, 7, § 19 Jan.—Hence
pacuvius.short: Pācŭvĭus (Pācŭus), i, m., the name of a Roman gens.

padaei.full: Pădaei, ōrum, m., a people of farther India, at the mouth of the Indus. Acc. to Herodotus (3,99) they were cannibals.— Sing. collect.: vicinus Phoebo tenet arva Padaeus, Tib. 15, 1, 145.
padaei.short: Pădaei, ōrum, m., a people of farther India, at the mouth of the Indus.

padaneus.full: Pădanĕus, a, um, v. Padus, A.

padanus.full: Pădānus, a, um, v. Padus, B.

padi.full: pădi, ōrum, m. Gallic, pitch-pines, Plin. 3, 16, 20, § 117.

padus.full: Pădus, i, m., the Po, the principal river of Italy, Liv. 5, 33, 10; Mel. 2, 4, 4 sq.; Plin. 3, 16, 20, § 117: sive Padi ripis, Verg. A. 9, 680: populiferque Padus, Ov. Am. 2, 17, 32. —Hence, Pădānĕus, a, um, adj., of or on the Po: silvae, Sol. 33.— Pădā-nus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to the Po: silvae, Sol. 20: culices, Sid. Ep. 1, 8.
padus.short: Pădus, i, m., the Po, the principal river of Italy, Liv.

padusa.full: Pădūsa, ae, f., a canal running from the Po to Ravenna, now the canal of St. Alberti: piscosove amne Padusae, Verg. A. 11, 457; cf. Plin. 3, 16, 20, § 119.
padusa.short: Pădūsa, ae, f., a canal running from the Po to Ravenna, now the canal of St.

paean.full: Paean, ānis, m., = Παιάν. An appellation of Apollo, as the healing deity: signum Paeanis, Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 57, § 127: Paeana voca, Ov. M. 14, 720; Juv. 6, 172; cf. Fest. p. 222 Müll.; Macr. S. 1, 17.— Transf. A religious hymn, orig. in honor of Apollo, but also transf. to other deities, a festive hymn, hymn of triumph or praise, a pœan: conclamant socii laetum paeana secuti, Verg. A. 10, 738; id. ib. 6, 657: Herculeum paeana canunt, Stat. Th. 4, 157: paeanem citare, Cic. de Or. 1, 59, 251.—As a

paeanitis.full: Paeānītis, ĭdis, f., and Paeānītes, acc. em or en, m., a precious stone, now unknown, Plin. 37, 10, 66, § 180.—Form in -tes, Sol. 9, 22; Prisc. Perieg. 440; Isid. Orig. 14, 4, 13.
paeanitis.short: Paeānītis, ĭdis, f., and Paeānītes, acc.

paeantis.full: paeantis, ĭdis, m., a precious stone, otherwise unknown, Sol. 9; Isid. Orig. 14, 4.
paeantis.short: paeantis, ĭdis, m., a precious stone, otherwise unknown, Sol.

paedagoga.full: paedăgōga, ae, f. paedagogus, a governess, Hier. Ep. 128, n. 4.

paedagogatus.full: paedăgōgātus, ūs, m. id., education, instruction (post-class.), Tert. adv. Val. 13.

paedagogianus.full: paedăgōgĭānus, a, um, adj. paedagogium, of or belonging to the paedagogium (post-class.): puer, Amm. 26, 6, 15; 29, 3, 3: qui ministeriales et paedagogiani exsistunt, reared to serve at court, Cod. Th. 8, 7, 5.

paedagogium.full: paedăgōgīum, ii, n., = παιδαγωγεῖον, the place where boys of servile birth intended for pages were educated, the pages' hall (not ante-Aug.), Plin. Ep. 7, 27, 13.— Transf. In gen., the boys in a paedagogium: paedagogium pretiosā veste succingitur, Sen. Vit. Beat. 17, 2; id. Ep. 123, 7.— In partic., boys reared for vice: ingenuae conditionis paedagogia, Suet. Ner. 28; cf. Plin. 33, 12, 54, § 152.
paedagogium.short: paedăgōgīum, ii, n., = παιδαγωγεῖον, the place where boys of servile birth intended for pages were educated, the pages' hall (not ante-Aug.), Plin.

paedagogo.full: paedăgōgo, āre, v. a. paedagogus, to educate, instruct (ante- and post-class.): depulsum mammā paedagogandum accipit, Pac. ap. Fest. s. v. repotia, p. 281 Müll.; Fulg. Planc. Contin. Virg. fin.

paedagogus.full: paedăgōgus, i, m., = παιδαγωγός, lit. a slave who took the children to school and had the charge of them at home, a governor, preceptor, pedagogue (cf. praeceptor). Lit.: non paedagogum jam me, sed Ludum vocat, Plaut. Bacch. 1, 2, 31: nutrices et paedagogi, Cic. Lael. 20, 74: tamquam quicquam aliud sit sapiens quam humani generis paedagogus, Sen. Ep. 89, 11: de paedagogis hoc amplius, ut aut sint eruditi plane, aut se non esse eruditos sciant, Quint. 1, 1, 8; cf. id. 1, 1, 11; 1, 2, 10; 25; 1, 3

paederos.full: paedĕros, ōtis, m., = παιδέρως. A precious stone. An opal, Plin. 37, 6, 22, § 84.— An amethyst, Plin. 37, 9, 40, § 123.— A plant, a kind of bear's-foot, Plin. 22, 22, 34, § 76.

paedia.full: Paedīa, ae, f., = παιδεία (personified), a doctrine, learning, Mart. Cap. 7, 728; cf. id. 6, 578.
paedia.short: Paedīa, ae, f., = παιδεία (personified), a doctrine, learning, Mart.

paedicator.full: paedīcātor, ōris, m. 1. paedico, one given to unnatural vice, Licin. Calv. ap. Suet. Caes. 49.

paedico1.full: paedīco (pēdīco, Auct. Priap. 68), āre, v. a. παιδικός, to practise unnatural vice. Lit.: amores, Cat. 21, 4: puerum, Mart. 11, 94, 6.—Of various forms of unnatural lewdness, Mart. 11, 104, 17; id. 7, 67, 1. — Transf., of the tunic, Mart. 11, 99, 2.

paedico2.full: paedīco, ōnis, m. 1. paedico, one who practises unnatural vice, Mart. 6, 33, 1; 12, 86, 1.

paedidus.full: paedĭdus, a, um, adj. paedor, nasty, filthy, stinking: paedidos sordidos significant atque obsoletos: tractum vocabulum a Graeco, quia παῖδες, i. e. pueri, talis sint aetatis, ut nesciant a sordibus abstinere, Paul. ex Fest. p. 222 Müll.: senex, Lucil. ap. Non. 166, 13 (al. perditus, al. arthriticus): paedidissimi servi, Petr. 34, 5.

paedor.full: paedor, ōris, m. root pu-; Sanscr. pūje, to be rotten, stink; Gr. πύθομαι, πύον; cf. pus, puter, etc., nastiness, filth (syn.: illuvies, sordes). Lit.: barba paedore horrida, Poët. ap. Cic. Tusc. 3, 12, 26: membra horrida paedore, Lucr. 6, 126; plur., Cic. Tusc. 3, 26, 62: exuere paedorem, Tac. A. 6, 44: longus in carcere paedor, Luc. 2, 72; Sen. Agam. 991.— Transf., a stink, stench (post-class.): sine paedore, Aug. Civ. Dei, 14, 24.

paegniarius.full: paegnĭārĭus, a, um, adj. paegnium, of or belonging to play. Thus the name paegniarii was given to gladiators who fought only in jest, Suet. Calig. 26: APRILIS PAEGNIAR., Inscr. Orell. 2566.

paegnium.full: Paegnĭum, ii, n., = Παίγνιον (plaything), a Roman slave-name, Plaut. Pers. 5, 1, 20.
paegnium.short: Paegnĭum, ii, n., = Παίγνιον (plaything), a Roman slave-name, Plaut.

paelex.full: paelex (pēlex, and, only in inscriptions, pellex), icis, f. akin to Sanscr. pallavaka, girl; Gr. παλλακίς, concubine, a kept mistress, concubine of a married man. Lit.: antiqui proprie eam pelicem nominabant, quae uxorem habenti nubebat. Cui generi mulierum etiam poena constituta est a Numā Pompilio hāc lege: paelex aram Junonis ne tangito, etc., Paul. ex Fest. p. 222 Müll.; cf. Gell. 4, 3, 3: libro Memorialium Masurius scribit: pelicem apud antiquos eam habitam, quae, cum uxor non esset, cum al
paelex.short: paelex (pēlex, and, only in inscriptions, pellex), icis, f.

paeminosus.full: paemĭnōsus, a, um, adj. In econom. lang., full of chinks, uneven, rough: area, Varr. R. R. 1, 51 (cited Non. 163, 14).

paene.full: paene (less correctly pēne), adv. etym. dub., nearly, almost, as I may say (class.): fores paene effregisti, Plaut. Bacch. 4, 2, 4; id. Am. 4, 2, 6; id. Bacch. 4, 9, 26; id. Truc. 2, 6, 37: aliquem paene perdere, Ter. Heaut. 4, 6, 10: paene amicus, Cic. Fam. 1, 4, 1: paene communis, id. ib. 15, 1, 1: Brutum non minus amo, quam tu: paene dixi quam te, id. Att. 5, 20, 6; id. Rosc. Com. 6, 16: non solum in omnibus civitatibus, sed paene etiam in singulis domibus, factiones sunt, Caes. B. G. 6, 10:

paeninsula.full: paeninsŭla (pēn-), ae, f. paene-insula, a peninsula, Liv. 26, 42; Cat. 31, 1; Plin. 3, 10, 15, § 95.

paenitentia.full: paenĭtentĭa, ae, f. paeniteo, repentance, penitence (not in Cic.; cf. Aus. Ep. 12, 10).—Absol.: celerem paenitentiam sequi, Liv. 31, 32: nec poenā commilitonum exterriti, nec paenitentiā conversi, Tac. A. 1, 45: fidelissimus est ad honesta ex paenitentiā transitus, Sen. Q. N. 3, praef. 3.—Plur.: serae dant poenas turpes paenitentiae, Phaedr. 1, 13, 2.—With gen.: coepti, Quint. 12, 5, 3: dicti, id. 9, 2, 60: gestae rei, Plin. 17, 12, 19, § 94; 10, 23, 33, § 67: paenitentiam agere, to repent: eo u

paenitentialis.full: paenĭtentĭālis, is, m. (sc. presbyter) [paenitentia], a priest appointed to hear the confession of penitents; a confessor, Inscr. Murat. 419, 2; Cassiod. Hist. Eccl. 9, 35.

paeniteo.full: paenĭtĕo (less correctly poen-), ui, no sup., ēre, 2, v. a. and impers. [root in poena, q. v.; Gr. ποινή]. Pers. Act., to cause to repent, to displease (anteclass. and late Lat.): et me quidem haec conditio nunc non paenitet, causes me no regret, Plaut. Stich. 1, 1, 50: quod male emptum est semper paenitet, Cat. ap. Plin. 18, 5, 6, § 26: paenitemini et credite Evangelio, repent, Vulg. Marc. 1, 15; id. Act. 3, 19.— Neutr., to repent, be sorry: momenta certaminum assuefaciebant militem minus jam t
paeniteo.short: paenĭtĕo (less correctly poen-), ui, no sup., ēre, 2, v.

paeniteor.full: paenĭtĕor, ēri collat. form of paeniteo, to repent, Vulg. Marc. 1, 15; id. Act. 3, 19.

paenitudo.full: paenĭtūdo, ĭnis, f. paeniteo, repentance (ante- and post-class. for paenitentia), Pac. ap. Non. 152, 30; 169, 25; Sid. Ep. 6, 9; Hier. Ep. 84; Ambros. Laps. Virg. 8, 33.

paenula1.full: paenŭla (pēn-), ae, f., a woollen outer garment covering the whole body, a kind of cloak or mantle, worn on journeys, and also in the city in rainy weather (cf.: laena, lacerna): paenulam in caput induce, ne te noscat, Pompon. ap. Non. 537, 8; so Lucil. ib.: paenulā irretitus, Cic. Mil. 20, 54: incolumi Rhodos ... facit quod Paenula solstitio, Hor. Ep. 1, 11, 18; Plin. 8, 48, 73, § 190: non quaerenda est homini, qui habet virtutem, paenula in imbri, Varr. ap. Non. 537, 12: et multo stillaret pae
paenula1.short: paenŭla (pēn-), ae, f., a woollen outer garment covering the whole body, a kind of cloak or mantle, worn on journeys, and also in the city in rainy weather (cf.: laena, lacerna): paenulam in caput induce, ne te noscat, Pompon.

paenula2.full: Paenŭla, ae, m., a Roman surname, Liv. 25, 19, 9.
paenula2.short: Paenŭla, ae, m., a Roman surname, Liv.

paenularius.full: paenŭlārĭus, ii, m. paenula, a maker of mantles or mantillas, pœnula-maker: consequitur paenularium, Novat. ap. Non. 148, 33 (acc. to Non., paenularium is a neutr., having the sense of theca et vagina paenula, a receptacle in which the pœnula is kept): CN. COSSVTIVS PAENVLARIVS, Inscr. Grut. 646, 5.

paenulatus.full: paenŭlātus, a, um, adj. id., wearing the pœnula, Cic. Mil. 10, 28; 20, 54; Sen. Ben. 3, 28, 4; Mart. 2, 57; Sid. Ep. 8, 6.

paenuleus.full: paenŭlĕus, a, um, adj. id., of the pœnula, pœnulean, Lampr. Diadum. 2.

paenultimus.full: paenultĭmus (pēn-), a, um, adj. paene-ultimus, the last but one (post-class. for proximus a postremo, Cic. Or. 64, 217): paenultima meta November, Aus. Ecl. Quotae Cal. Sint Mens. 12.— Subst.: pae-nultĭma, ae, f. (sc. syllaba), the penultimate syllable, the penult: paenultimam circumflectere, Gell. 4, 7, 2.

paeon.full: paeon, ōnis (paean, ānis, Cic. Or. 64, 215 v. h. v.), m., = παιών, a metrical foot of four syllables, three short and one long (and which, acc. to the position of the long syllable, is called primus, secundus, tertius, quartus), Cic. de Or. 3, 47, 183; Quint. 9, 4, 47; 87; 110; Diom. p. 477 P.; Don. p. 1739 ib.; Mar. Vict. p. 1957.

paeones.full: Paeŏnes, um, m., = Παίονες, a people of Macedonia, in that part of it afterwards called Emathia, the Pœonians, Ov. P. 2, 2, 77; id. M. 5, 313.—Sing.: Paeŏn, ŏnis, m., = Παίων, a Pœonian, Liv. 42, 51, 6.— Hence, Paeŏnĭa, ae, f., = Παιονία, the country of the Pœonians, Emathia, Plin. 4, 10, 17, § 33; Liv. 40, 3.— Paeŏnis, ĭdis, f., a female Pœonian: Paeonis Euippe mater fuit, Ov. M. 5, 303.— Paeŏnĭus, a, um, adj., = Παιόνιος, of or belonging to Pœonia, Pœonian: gentes, Plin. 4, 10, 17, § 35.
paeones.short: Paeŏnes, um, m., = Παίονες, a people of Macedonia, in that part of it afterwards called Emathia, the Pœonians, Ov.

paeonia1.full: paeōnĭa, ae, f., = παιωνία, the peony, so named after its discoverer, Pæon, Plin. 25, 4, 10, § 29.
paeonia1.short: paeōnĭa, ae, f., = παιωνία, the peony, so named after its discoverer, Pæon, Plin.

paeonicus.full: paeōnĭcus, a, um, adj. paeon, of or belonging to the foot pœon, pœonic: metrum, Diom. p. 506 P.

paeonius1.full: Paeŏnĭus, a, um, v. Paeones, C.

paeonius2.full: Paeōnĭus, a, um, adj., = Παιώνιος, of or belonging to the god of medicine (Παιών), healing, medicinal (poet.): herbae, Verg. A. 7, 769: ope Paeoniā, Ov. M. 15, 535: fontes, Sil. 14, 27: unda, Claud. Apon. 67: cura, id. B. Get. 121.
paeonius2.short: Paeōnĭus, a, um, adj., = Παιώνιος, of or belonging to the god of medicine (Παιών), healing, medicinal (poet.): herbae, Verg.

paestum.full: Paestum, i, n., a city of Lucania, formerly called Posidonia, celebrated for its twice-blowing roses, now Pesti: biferique rosaria Paesti, Verg. G. 4, 119; cf. Ov. M. 15, 708; Prop. 5, 5, 61: oppidum Paestum Graecis Posidonia appellatum, Plin. 3, 5, 10, § 71.—Hence, Paestānus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Pœstum, Pœstan: sinus, Cic. Att. 16, 6, 1: rosae, Ov. P. 2, 4, 28.—In plur.: Paestāni, ōrum, m., the Pœstans, Liv. 37, 10.
paestum.short: Paestum, i, n., a city of Lucania, formerly called Posidonia, celebrated for its twice-blowing roses, now Pesti: biferique rosaria Paesti, Verg.

paetulus.full: paetŭlus, a, um, adj. dim. [paetus], having a slight cast in the eye, slightly blinkeyed: redeo ad deos: ecquos si non tam strabones, at paetulos esse arbitramur? Cic. N. D. 1, 29, 80; cf. paetus.

paetus1.full: paetus, a, um, adj. etym. dub., having leering eyes, with a cast in the eyes, blinking or winking with the eyes, blinkeyed; esp. as an epithet of Venus, prettily leering, with a pretty cast in her eyes, prettily blinking: paetus, μύωψ τοῖς ὄμμασιν, Gloss. Philox.: uni animalium homini depravantur oculi: unde Strabonum et Paetorum cognomina, Plin. 11, 37, 55, § 150; Plaut. Fragm. ap. Fest. s. v. valgos, p. 375 Müll.: strabonem Appellat paetum pater, Hor. S. 1, 3, 45.—Of Venus: non haec res de Ven

paetus2.full: Paetus, i, m., a surname. Q. Aelius Paetus, consul with M. Junius Pennus, A. U. C. 587.— P. Aelius Paetus, an augur, Liv. 27, 36.— L. Papirius Paetus, a friend of Cicero, Cic. Att. 1, 20, 7; 2, 1, 12. To him are addressed the letters of Cicero, ad Fam. 9, 15-26.

pagae.full: Pagae, arum, f., a city in Megaris, Plin. 4, 7, 11, § 23; Mel. 2, 3, 10.—Hence, Pa-gaei, ōrum, m., the people of Pagœ, Plin. 4, 7, 11, § 23.
pagae.short: Pagae, arum, f., a city in Megaris, Plin.

paganalia.full: Pāgānālĭa, ĭum, n. pagus, the festival of the pagus, celebrated in January; the country festival, rural festival, Varr. L. L. 6, § 24; cf. id. ib. 6, § 26 Müll.; Macr. S. 1, 16.

paganicus.full: pāgānĭcus, a, um, adj. id., of or belonging to the country, rural, rustic. Lit.: paganicae feriae, Varr. L. L. 6, § 26 Müll.; cf. Paganalia: IOVI PAGANICO SACR., Inscr. Orell. 1250.—Absol.: bona habere in paganico (sc. solo or agro), Cod. Just. 6, 21, 1; cf. paganus: pila paganica, a ball stuffed with down, used at first in the country, but afterwards also in the city, Mart. 7, 32, 7: pluma, id. 14, 45, 1; cf. Becker, Gall. 3, p. 94. — In eccl. Lat., heathenish, pagan, Salv. Gub. 1.

paganismus.full: pāgānismus, i, m. paganus, heathenism (eccl. Lat.), Aug. Divers. Quaest. 83, q. 83 init.

paganitas.full: pāgānĭtas, ātis f. id., heathenism, paganism (post-class.): stolidae paganitatis error, Cod. Th. 15, 5, 5.

paganus.full: pāgānus, a, um, adj. pagus. Of or belonging to the country or to a village, rustic: PORTICVS, Inscr. (A. U. C. 659) Orell. 3793: lex, Plin. 28, 2, 5, § 28: foci, Ov. F. 1, 670.— Subst.: pāgānus, i, m., a countryman, peasant, villager, rustic: nulli pagani aut montani, Cic. Dom. 28, 74: pagani vel decuriones, Cod. Th. 7, 21, 2.— Opposed to military, civil, civic: vel paganum est peculium vel castrense, Cod. Just. 3, 28, 37.—As subst.: pāgānus, i, m., a civilian, a citizen, Tac. H. 3, 24: paganoru

pagasa.full: Păgăsa, ae, and Păgăsae, ārum, f., = Παγασαί, a maritime town of Thessaly, afterwards called Demetrias, where the Argo was built: urbem Pagasam amplexus, Mel. 2, 3, 6; Prop. 1, 20, 17.—Plur., Val. Fl. 8, 451; Plin. 4, 8, 15, § 29.—Hence, Pă-găsaeus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Pagasa, Pagasœan: sinus, Mel. 2, 3, 6: colles, Ov. F. 5, 401: puppis, the Argo, id. M. 7, 1; also called carina, id. ib. 13, 24: Jason, id. ib. 8, 349: conjux Pagasaea, i. e. Alcestis, id. A. A. 3, 19.— Păgăsēĭus, a, u
pagasa.short: Păgăsa, ae, and Păgăsae, ārum, f., = Παγασαί, a maritime town of Thessaly, afterwards called Demetrias, where the Argo was built: urbem Pagasam amplexus, Mel.

pagatim.full: pāgātim, adv. pagus, by districts or villages, in every village: templa pagatim sacrata, Liv. 31, 26; 31, 30.

pagella.full: pāgella, ae, f. dim. pagina, a little page, Cic. Fam. 11, 25 fin.; Vulg. Jer. 36, 23.

pages.full: pāges, compactio, unde compages et propagare, Non. 64. 28.
pages.short: pāges, compactio, unde compages et propagare, Non.

pagidas.full: Pagĭdas or Pagĭda, ae, m. A river in Africa, Tac. A. 3, 20.— A river in Phœnicia, near Mount Carmel, also called Belus, Plin. 5, 19, 17, § 75 (Jahn, Pacida).

pagina.full: pāgĭna, ae, f. root pag-(pak-), of pango, πήγνυμι; v. pagus, a written page or leaf: paginae dictae, quod ... in illis versus panguntur, id est figuntur, Fest. p. 221 Müll. Lit.: cum hanc paginam tenerem, Cic. Q. Fr. 1, 2, 3, § 10: complere paginam, id. Att. 13, 34: tantas paginas commovere, id. Fin. 4, 19, 53; Plin. 13, 12, 24, § 80: censoriarum legum paginae, id. 8, 51, 77, § 209: millesima pagina, Juv. 7, 100.— Prov.: fortuna paginam utramque facit, fills both sides of the account, confers bo

paginalis.full: pāgĭnālis, e, adj. pagina, of or belonging to a page, pager-: stili cura, Ennod. 2, 13: commercium, id. 2, 16.

paginatus.full: pāgĭnātus, a, um, adj. id., joined together (post-class.): navis, Paul. Nol. Carm. 21, 353.

paginula.full: pāgĭnŭla, ae, f. dim. id., a little page, Cic. Att. 4, 8, 2; Not. Tir. p. 124.

pagmentum.full: pagmentum, i, n. pago, that is joined together (compactio, res compacta): qui sunt ante secundum pagmentum, Vitr. 4, 6 fin. (al. secundum antepagmentum).

pagrus.full: pagrus (phagr-) or păger (ph-), ri, m., = πάγρος (φάγρος), a fish, otherwise unknown: pagrus fluviatilis, Plin. 32, 10, 38, § 113; 9, 16, 2, § 57.
pagrus.short: pagrus (phagr-) or păger (ph-), ri, m., = πάγρος (φάγρος), a fish, otherwise unknown: pagrus fluviatilis, Plin.

pagur.full: păgur, i, m., a fish, otherwise unknown (perh. = preced.): rutilus pagur, Ov. Hal. 107.
pagur.short: păgur, i, m., a fish, otherwise unknown (perh.

pagurus.full: păgūrus, i, m., = πάγουρος, a kind of crab-fish, perh. a punger, Plin. 9, 31, 51, § 97; Pall. 1, 35.
pagurus.short: păgūrus, i, m., = πάγουρος, a kind of crab-fish, perh.

pagus.full: pāgus, i (old gen. PAGEIEI, which prob. is an error for PAGEI, Inscr. Orell. 3793), m. root pak-, pag-, to make fast or firm, whence pango, pax, pagina; Gr. πήγνυμι, πάγος, etc.; prop., a place with fixed boundaries; hence, a district, canton, province (opp. to the city), the country (cf. vicus): paganalia (feriae sunt eorum) qui sunt aliquoius pagi, Varr. L. L. 6, § 24; cf. id. ib. § 26 Müll.: Lemonia tribus a pago Lemonio appellata est, Paul. ex Fest. p. 15: pagos et compita circum, Verg. G. 2

pala.full: pāla, ae, f. contr. from pagela, from pago, pango: pala a pangendo, Varr. L. L. 5, § 134 Müll., a spade. Lit.: palas vendundas sibi ait ... ut hortum fodiat, Plaut. Poen. 5, 2, 58: sarcula VIII., palas IV., Cato, R. R. 10, 3: palae innixus, Liv. 3, 26: juncosus ager verti pala debet, Plin. 18, 6, 8, § 46: palis laxatus, id. 17, 17, 27, § 123; Col. 10, 45.— Transf. A peel for putting bread into the oven, Cato, R. R. 11 fin.— A winnowing-shovel, Tert. Praescr. 3; so Juvenc. 1, 371.— The bezel of a

palabundus.full: pālābundus, a, um, adj. palor, wandering about, struggling (post-class.): Judaei dispersi palabundi, Tert. Apol. 21: equites, Auct. Itin. Alex. 56 Mai: oves, Cypr. Ep. 42, 4.

palacrana.full: palacrāna or palacurna, ae, f. Span., an ingot of gold, Plin. 33, 4, 21, § 77.

palaemon.full: Pălaemon, ŏnis, m., = Παλαίμων. A sea-god, formerly called Melicerta, the son of Athamas and Ino: O Palaemon, sancte Neptuni comes, Plaut. Rud. 1, 2, 70; Cic. N. D. 3, 15, 39; Verg. A. 5, 823; Ov. M. 4, 542; id. H. 17, 159.—Hence, Pălae-mŏnĭus, a, um, of or belonging to the seagod Palœmon, poet. for Corinthian, Stat. Th. 2, 380: Palaemoniae coronae, won at the Isthmian games, which were celebrated in honor of Palœmon, Claud. Cons. Mall. Th. 289.— Remmius Palaemon, a Roman grammarian in the time

palaeno.full: Pălaeno, ūs or ōnis, f., one of the Danaides, Hyg. Fab. 170.
palaeno.short: Pălaeno, ūs or ōnis, f., one of the Danaides, Hyg.

palaepharsalus.full: Pălaepharsālus, i, f., Old Pharsalus, a town of Thessaly, near Pharsalus, Liv. 44, 1; Auct. B. Alex. 1; Eutr. 6, 16.
palaepharsalus.short: Pălaepharsālus, i, f., Old Pharsalus, a town of Thessaly, near Pharsalus, Liv.

palaephatius.full: Pălaephătĭus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Palœphatus (a Grecian mythographer), Palœphatian, Verg. Cir. 87.
palaephatius.short: Pălaephătĭus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Palœphatus (a Grecian mythographer), Palœphatian, Verg.

palaepolitanus.full: Pălaepŏlītānus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to the Campanian city Palœpolis, joined to Neapolis, Palœpolitan.—Subst.: Pălaepŏlītāni, ōrum, m., the inhabitants of Palœpolis, Liv. 8, 22.
palaepolitanus.short: Pălaepŏlītānus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to the Campanian city Palœpolis, joined to Neapolis, Palœpolitan.—Subst.: Pălaepŏlītāni, ōrum, m., the inhabitants of Palœpolis, Liv.

palaeste.full: Pălaestē, ēs, f., = Παλαιστή, a seaport in Epirus, Caes. B. C. 3, 6 fin. dub. (al. Pharsalia).—Hence, Pălaestīnus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Palœste or Epirus (as the entrance to the Lower World), Palœstian: Palaestinae deae, the Furies, Ov. F. 4, 236 (where Meletinas is a better reading): arenae, Luc. 5, 460.
palaeste.short: Pălaestē, ēs, f., = Παλαιστή, a seaport in Epirus, Caes.

palaestes.full: pălaestes, ae, m., = παλαιστής, a wrestler, Lampr. Alex. Sev. 27 fin.
palaestes.short: pălaestes, ae, m., = παλαιστής, a wrestler, Lampr.

palaestina.full: Pălaestīnă (Pălest-), ae, and Pă-laestīnē, ēs, f., = Παλαιστίνη, the country of Palestine, in Syria, Mel. 1, 11, 2; Plin. 5, 12, 13, § 66 sq.—Hence, Pă-laestīnus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Palestine: aqua, the Euphrates, Ov. F. 2, 464: Syrus, Tib. 1, 8, 17 (7, 18): Palaestini simul Hebraeique liquores, Stat. S. 5, 1, 213. —In plur.: Pălaestīni, ōrum, m., the inhabitants of Palestine, Ov. M. 4, 46; Hier. in Isa. 14, 29; the Philistines, Vulg. Gen. 21, 33.— Pălaestīnensis, e, adj., Palestini
palaestina.short: Pălaestīnă (Pălest-), ae, and Pă-laestīnē, ēs, f., = Παλαιστίνη, the country of Palestine, in Syria, Mel.

palaestra.full: pălaestra, ae, f., = παλαίστρα, a wrestling-school, wrestling-place, place of exercise, palœstra, where youths, with their bodies naked and anointed with oil, practised gymnastic exercises. Such palæstrae were also attached to private houses: in palaestram venire, Plaut. Bacch. 3, 3, 20; cf. id. ib. 3, 3, 27: in palaestrā atque in foro, id. Am. 4, 1, 3: statuas in palaestrā ponere, Cic. Verr. 2, 2, 14, § 36: pars in gramineis exercent membra palaestris, Verg. A. 6, 642. —Of the palæstrae in priv
palaestra.short: pălaestra, ae, f., = παλαίστρα, a wrestling-school, wrestling-place, place of exercise, palœstra, where youths, with their bodies naked and anointed with oil, practised gymnastic exercises.

palaestrice.full: palaestrĭcē and palaestrĭcōs, advv., v. palaestricus fin.

palaestricus.full: pălaestrĭcus, a, um, adj., = παλαιστρικος, of or belonging to the palœstra, palœstric: pro exercitu gymnastico et palaestrico hoc habemus, Plaut. Rud. 2, 1, 7: palaestrici motūs, the motions of a dancingmaster, Cic. Off. 1, 36, 130: magister, Quint. 2, 8, 7; cf. doctores, id. 12, 2, 12: facies decora et suci palaestrici plena, App. Mag. p. 315.—Sarcastically of Verres: palaestricus praetor, because he illegally decided a cause in favor of a company of wrestlers, Cic. Verr. 2, 2, 22, § 54.— Subst
palaestricus.short: pălaestrĭcus, a, um, adj., = παλαιστρικος, of or belonging to the palœstra, palœstric: pro exercitu gymnastico et palaestrico hoc habemus, Plaut.

palaestrita.full: pălaestrīta, ae, m., = παλαιστρίτης, the director of a wrestling-school, Cic. Verr. 2, 2, 14, § 36; 2, 2, 22, § 54: lubricus palaestrita, Mart. 3, 58, 25.— In gen., a wrestler: artifex, Amm. 15, 3, 4.
palaestrita.short: pălaestrīta, ae, m., = παλαιστρίτης, the director of a wrestling-school, Cic.

palaga.full: palaga, ae, f., an ingot of gold [Span.], Plin. 33, 4, 21, § 77 (al. palacra).
palaga.short: palaga, ae, f., an ingot of gold [Span.], Plin.

palam.full: pălam, adv. and prep. locative form; cf.: clam, perperam, etc.; root pal-, pla-; as in πλατύς, planus; cf. pellis; hence, on the surface, on the open plain, and so, openly, publicly, undisguisedly, plainly (cf.: publice, vulgo, aperte; opp.: clam, occulte, secreto, etc.; class.). Lit.: haec quae in foro palam Syracusis ... gesta sunt, Cic. Verr. 2, 2, 33, § 81: auferre argentum palam atque aperte, Plaut. Bacch. 2, 3, 68; so, non ex insidiis, sed aperte ac palam elaboratur, Cic. Or. 12, 38; and:

palamedes.full: Pălămēdes, is, m., = Παλαμήδης, son of Nauplius, king of Eubœa, who lost his life before Troy, through the artifices of Ulysses, Cic. Tusc. 1, 41, 98; id. Off. 3, 26, 98; Auct. Her. 2, 19, 28. He is said, by observing the flight of cranes, to have invented the letters Θ, Ξ, Φ, Χ, acc. to others the letters Υ and Δ, Plin. 7, 56, 57, § 192; Mart. 13, 75, 2.—Hence, Pălămēdēus, a, um, adj., Palamedean, Manil. 4, 206.— Pă-lămēdĭăcus, a, um, adj., Palamedic: Palamediaci calculi, the counters in the ga
palamedes.short: Pălămēdes, is, m., = Παλαμήδης, son of Nauplius, king of Eubœa, who lost his life before Troy, through the artifices of Ulysses, Cic.

palantieis.full: Pălantĭeis, um, m., = Παλαντιεῖς, the immigrants who accompanied Evander, Varr. L. L. 5, § 53 Müll. N. cr.
palantieis.short: Pălantĭeis, um, m., = Παλαντιεῖς, the immigrants who accompanied Evander, Varr.

palanto.full: Pălanto, ūs, f., the wife of Latinus, Varr. L. L. 5, § 53 Müll. N. cr.
palanto.short: Pălanto, ūs, f., the wife of Latinus, Varr.

palara.full: pălāra, ae, f., a bird, otherwise unknown: dulce palara sonat, quam dicunt nomine drostam, Auct. Carm. Phil. 11.
palara.short: pălāra, ae, f., a bird, otherwise unknown: dulce palara sonat, quam dicunt nomine drostam, Auct.

palaris.full: pālārĭs, e, adj. 1. palus, of or belonging to pales or stakes: silva palaris, from which pales are fetched, Dig. 7, 1, 9.— Subst.: pālārĭa, ĭum, n., the exercise of tilting against a stake; also, the place of this exercise, Veg. Mil. 1, 11; 2, 23; cf. Charis. p. 21 P.

palasea.full: pălāsĕa and plāsĕa, ae, f., the tailpiece or buttock of an ox offered for sacrifice, Arn. 7, 230.
palasea.short: pălāsĕa and plāsĕa, ae, f., the tailpiece or buttock of an ox offered for sacrifice, Arn.

palatha.full: pălătha, ae, f., = παλάθη, dried fruit, usually figs, Vulg. 2 Reg. 16, 1; id. Judith, 10, 5.
palatha.short: pălătha, ae, f., = παλάθη, dried fruit, usually figs, Vulg.

palatinus.full: Pălātīnus, a, um, v. Palatium, II.

palatio.full: pālātĭo, ōnis, f. 1. palus, a driving in of pales or stakes, Vitr. 2, 9.

palatium.full: Pălātĭum (Pāl- or Pall-, Mart. 1, 70, 5; 9, 102, 13), ĭi, n., = Παλάτιον, Παλλάντιον [root pa-, to protect, nourish; Sanscr. pala, shepherd; cf. Gr. αἰ-πόλος οἰο-πόλος; Lat. pasco], one of the seven hills of Rome, that which was first built upon, Varr. L. L. 5, § 53 Müll.; cf.: Palatium id est mons Romae, appellatus est, quod ibi pecus pascens balare consueverit, vel quod palare, id est errare, ibi pecudes solerent; alii, quod ibi Hyperborei filia Palanto habitaverit, quae ex Hercule Latinum pep

palatua.full: Pălātŭa, ae, f., the tutelary goddess of the Palatine, Varr. L. L. 7, § 45 Müll.— Hence, Pălātŭālis, e, adj., of or belonging to Palatua: flamen, Varr. L. L. 7, § 45 Müll.; cf.: Palatualis flamen constitutus est, quod in tutelā ejus deae Palatium est, Fest. p. 245 Müll.; Enn. ap. Varr. L. L. 7, § 45 ib. (Ann. v. 125 Vahl.).— Pălātŭar, āris (euphon. for Palatual), n., an offering made at Rome on the Palatine, Fest. s. v. septimontium, p. 348 Müll.
palatua.short: Pălātŭa, ae, f., the tutelary goddess of the Palatine, Varr.

palatum.full: pălātum, i, n., and (rarely) pălātus, i, m. perh. from root pa-of pasco, the palate. Lit.: suave domini, Varr. R. R. 3, 3, 7: nec enim sequitur, ut, cui cor sapiat, ei non sapiat palatus, Cic. Fin. 2, 8, 24: quae (voluptas) palato percipiatur, id. ib. 2, 10, 29: boum dare membra palato, Ov. M. 15, 141: subtile palatum, Hor. S. 2, 8, 38: nigra subest udo tantum cui lingua palato, Verg. G. 3, 388; Ov. Am. 2, 6, 47; cf.: cum balba feris annoso verba palato, Hor. S. 2, 3, 274: torpente palato, Juv.
palatum.short: pălātum, i, n., and (rarely) pălātus, i, m.

pale.full: pălē, ēs, f., = πάλη, a wrestling (in post-Aug. poets): unctā pale, Stat. Th. 6, 829: liquidam nodare (al. nudare) palen, id. Ach. 2, 441: jocos, palem, rudentem, Sid. Carm. 23, 302.
pale.short: pălē, ēs, f., = πάλη, a wrestling (in post-Aug.

palea.full: pălĕa, ae, f. kindred with Sanscr. pala, stramen; cf.: pollen, pulvis, παλύνω, chaff, Varr. R. R. 1, 50 fin.: surgentem ad Zephyrum paleae jactantur inanes, Verg. G. 3, 134; Plin. 18, 30, 72, § 297; Col. 2, 9, 15; 6, 2, 3; 7, 3, 22 al.; Vulg. Matt. 3, 12.— Transf. Dross: palea aeris, Plin. 34, 13, 36, § 134. — The wattles or gills of a cock, Varr. R. R. 3, 9, 5; Col. 8, 2, 9.— Straw, Vulg. Judic. 19, 19; id. Isa. 11, 7.

palealis.full: pălĕālis, e, adj. palea, of or belonging to chaff: uva, preserved in chaff, Cael. Aur. Acut. 2, 37, 29; 3, 21, 204.

palear.full: pălĕar, āris, n. id., the skin that hangs down from the neck of an ox, the dew-lap: Sen. Hippol. 1041.— Plur.: a collo palearibus demissis, Varr. R. R. 2, 5: palearia pendula, Ov. M. 2, 854; 7, 117: a mento palearia pendent, Verg. G. 3, 53; Col. 6, 1, 3; Plin. 8, 45, 70, § 179; Stat. Th. 3, 332.— Transf., the throat: revocat palearibus herbas, Calp. Ecl. 3, 17.

palearis.full: pălĕāris, e, adj. id., of or belonging to chaff: arista, Venant. Vit. S. Mart. 3, 284.

palearium.full: pălĕārĭum, ii, n. id., a chaff-loft, Col. 1, 6, 9.

paleatus.full: pălĕātus, a, um, adj. id., mixed with chaff: lutum, Col. 5, 6, 13; 12, 43, 1; Plin. 15, 17, 18, § 65.

pales.full: Păles, is, f. (m., Varr. ap. Serv. ad Verg. G. 3, 1; Mart. Cap. 1, § 50; Arn. 3, 113), the tutelary deity of shepherds and cattle: Pales dicebatur dea pastorum, cujus festa Palilia dicebantur; vel, ut alii volunt, dicta Parilia, quod pro partu pecoris eidem sacra fiebant, Fest. p. 222 Müll.: ipsa Pales agros ... reliquit, Verg. E. 5, 35: silvicolam tepido lacte precare Palem, Ov. F. 4, 746; Tib. 1, 1, 14 (36): fecunda, Calp. Ecl. 7, 22.

palica.full: Pălīca, ae, f., a town in Sicily.—Hence, Pălīci, ōrum, m., the Palicans, Sil. 14, 219.
palica.short: Pălīca, ae, f., a town in Sicily.—Hence, Pălīci, ōrum, m., the Palicans, Sil.

palicanus.full: Pălīcānus or Pălīkānus, i, m., a Roman surname in the gens Lollia, which sprang from the Sicilian town of Palica, Cic. Verr. 2, 2, 41, § 100; id. Att. 1, 1, 1; 1, 18, 5: M. Lollius Palicanus, Val. Max. 3, 8, n. 3.
palicanus.short: Pălīcānus or Pălīkānus, i, m., a Roman surname in the gens Lollia, which sprang from the Sicilian town of Palica, Cic.

palici1.full: Pălīci, ōrum (sing.: Pălīcus, i, m., Verg. A. 9, 585; Ov. P. 2, 10, 25), m., the sons of Jupiter and the nymph Thalia or Ætna; they were worshipped at Palica in Sicily, where were a temple and two lakes sacred to them, as enforcers of oaths, promoters of fertility, and as sea-gods, Macr. S. 5, 19; Serv. Verg. A. 9, 584: stagna Palicorum, Ov. M. 5, 406; Stat. Th. 12, 155.
palici1.short: Pălīci, ōrum (sing.: Pălīcus, i, m., Verg.

palilicius.full: Pălīlīcĭus, a, um, adj. Palilia, of or belonging to the Palilia, Palilian: Palilicium sidus, the Hyades, because they vanished in the evening twilight on the festival of the Palilia, Plin. 18, 26, 66, § 247.

palilis.full: Pălīlis, e, adj. Pales, of or belonging to Pales: flamma Palilis, a fire of straw and hay, over which the rustics leaped at the feast of Pales, Ov. F. 4, 798: festa Palilia, id. M. 14, 774; Tib. 2, 5, 87.—Also as subst.: Pălīlĭa, ĭum (euphon. collat. form Părīlĭa, Varr. R. R. 2, 1, 9; Col. 7, 3, 11; Plin. 19, 5, 24, § 69 et saep.; cf. Prob. ad Verg. G. 3 init.; Charis. p. 43 P.; Mar. Vict. p. 2470 P.), n., the feast of Pales, the shepherd festival, celebrated on the 21st of April, the anniversar

palilogia.full: pălĭlŏgĭa, ae, f., = παλιλογία, the emphatic repetition of a word or idea, Mart. Cap. 5, § 533, who cites from Cic. Cat. 1, 1, 3: nos, nos, dico aperte, nos consules desumus.
palilogia.short: pălĭlŏgĭa, ae, f., = παλιλογία, the emphatic repetition of a word or idea, Mart.

palimbacchius.full: pălimbacchīus, ii, m., = παλιμβακχεῖος, in prosody, i. q. antibacchius, an antibacchic, ¯¯˘, Quint. 9, 4, 82; Diom. pp. 461 and 476 P.
palimbacchius.short: pălimbacchīus, ii, m., = παλιμβακχεῖος, in prosody, i.

palimpissa.full: pălimpissa, ae, f., = παλίμπισσα, pitch boiled twice, Plin. 24, 7, 24, § 40.
palimpissa.short: pălimpissa, ae, f., = παλίμπισσα, pitch boiled twice, Plin.

palimpsestus.full: pălimpsestus, i, m., = παλίμψηστος, a parchment from which the old writing has been erased for the purpose of writing upon it again, a palimpsest, Cic. Fam. 7, 18, 2; Cat. 22, 5.
palimpsestus.short: pălimpsestus, i, m., = παλίμψηστος, a parchment from which the old writing has been erased for the purpose of writing upon it again, a palimpsest, Cic.

palinodia.full: pălĭnōdĭa, ae, f., = παλινῳδία, the repetition of a song. Lit., Amm. 18, 5, 4.— Transf., a recantation, palinode: palinodiam canere, to recant, Macr. S. 7, 5.
palinodia.short: pălĭnōdĭa, ae, f., = παλινῳδία, the repetition of a song.

palinurus.full: Pălĭnūrus, i, m., = Παλίνουρος, the pilot of Æneas, who fell asleep at the helm and tumbled into the sea off the coast of Lucania, whence the name of the promontory near the spot (now perh. Punta dello Spartimento), Verg. A. 5, 847; 871; 6, 337; 381; Luc. 9, 42; Mel. 2, 4, 9; Hor. C. 3, 4, 28. —In a lusus verbb. with πάλιν οὐρεῖν, iterum meiere, Mart. 3, 78, 2.
palinurus.short: Pălĭnūrus, i, m., = Παλίνουρος, the pilot of Æneas, who fell asleep at the helm and tumbled into the sea off the coast of Lucania, whence the name of the promontory near the spot (now perh.

palitans.full: pālĭtans, antis, Part., from the obsol. palito, wandering about: quom (haec oves) eunt sic a pecu palitantes, Plaut. Bacch. 5, 2, 4; v. Ritschl ad h. l.
palitans.short: pālĭtans, antis, Part., from the obsol.

paliuraeus.full: pălĭūraeus, a, um, adj. paliurus, covered with Christ's-thorn: prata, Fulg. Myth. 1 init.

paliurus.full: pălĭūrus, i, m., = παλίουρος, a plant, Christ's-thorn, Verg. E. 5, 39; cf. Plin. 24, 13, 71, § 115; 16, 30, 53, § 121; Vulg. Isa. 34, 13.
paliurus.short: pălĭūrus, i, m., = παλίουρος, a plant, Christ's-thorn, Verg.

palla.full: palla, ae, f. kindred with pellis; cf. Doed. Syn. 5, p. 211, a long and wide upper garment of the Roman ladies, held together by brooches, a robe, mantle (cf.: stola, peplum, chlamys), Plaut. As. 5, 2, 35; id. Men. 1, 2, 21; 56; id. Truc. 5, 54; Hor. S. 1, 2, 99; id. Epod. 5, 65: pro longae tegmine pallae Tigridis exuviae per dorsum a vertice pendent, Verg. A. 11, 576: palla superba, Ov. Am. 3, 13, 26: obscura, Mart. 11, 104, 7: scissā pallā, Juv. 10, 262; cf. Becker, Gall. 3, p. 144 (2d edit.).

pallaca.full: pallăca, ae, f., = παλλακή, a concubine (pure Lat. paelex), Suet. Vesp. 21; Plin. 35, 10, 36, § 86.
pallaca.short: pallăca, ae, f., = παλλακή, a concubine (pure Lat.

pallacana.full: pallăcāna, ae, f., a kind of onion, a leek, also called gethyum, Plin. 19, 6, 32, § 105.
pallacana.short: pallăcāna, ae, f., a kind of onion, a leek, also called gethyum, Plin.

palladium.full: Pallădĭum, ii, v. 1. Pallas, II. B.

palladius1.full: Pallădĭus, a, um, v. 1. Pallas, II. A.

palladius2.full: Pallădĭus, ii, m., a Roman surname. So, Palladius Rutilius Taurus Aemilianus, probably a Roman by birth, who lived in the fourth century of the Christian era, the author of a work on agriculture, in fourteen books.
palladius2.short: Pallădĭus, ii, m., a Roman surname.

pallanteum.full: Pallantēum, i, v. 2. Pallas, II. A. 2.

pallanteus.full: Pallantēus, a, um, v. 2. Pallas, II. A.

pallantias.full: Pallantĭas, ădis, v. 2. Pallas, II. B.

pallantis.full: Pallantis, ĭdis and ĭdos, v. 2. Pallas, II. C.

pallantius.full: Pallantĭus, a, um, v. 2. Pallas, II. D.

pallaris.full: pallāris, e, adj. palla, of or belonging to the palla: palla, pallaris, Not. Tir. p. 157.

pallas1.full: Pallăs, ădis and ădos, f., = Παλλάς. Surname of the Greek goddess Athene, and hence of the corresponding Minerva of the Romans, the goddess of war and wisdom; the inventress of working in wool, and of the cultivation of the olive, on which account the olive-tree was sacred to her: Pallas Minerva est dicta, quod Pallantem Gigantem interfecerit, vel, sicut putabant, quod in Pallante palude nata est, Fest. p. 220 Müll.: Pallas . . . Proeliis audax, Hor. C. 1, 12, 20; Ov. M. 5, 263: Palladis ales, t
pallas1.short: Pallăs, ădis and ădos, f., = Παλλάς.

pallas2.full: Pallas, antis (voc. Pallā, Verg. A. 10, 411 al.; also Pallas and Pallan, acc. to Prisc. p. 702), m., = Πάλλας, the name of several mythic and historical personages. Son of Pandion, the father of the fifth Minerva, Cic. N. D. 3, 23, 59; Ov. M. 7, 500.— A king of Arcadia, the great-grandfather of Evander, Verg. A. 8, 54 Serv.— Son of Evander, Verg. A. 8, 104.— One of the giants, Claud. Gigant. 94; Fest. s. v Pallas, p. 220.— A freedman of the emperor Claudius, proverbial for his wealth; slain by N

pallene.full: Pallēnē, ēs, f., = Παλλήνη, a peninsula and town of Macedonia, on the Thermaic Gulf, also called Phlegra, where the battle between the gods and the giants took place, Plin. 4, 10, 17, § 36; Ov. M. 15, 356; Val. Fl. 2, 17; Sen. Herc. Fur. 979.—Hence, Pallēnaeus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Pallene, Luc. 7, 150: triumphi, Stat. S. 4, 2, 56.— Pallēnensis, e, adj., Pallenian: ager, Liv. 44, 10: isthmus, Plin. 4, 10, 17, § 36.
pallene.short: Pallēnē, ēs, f., = Παλλήνη, a peninsula and town of Macedonia, on the Thermaic Gulf, also called Phlegra, where the battle between the gods and the giants took place, Plin.

pallens.full: pallens, entis, Part. and P. a., from palleo.

palleo.full: pallĕo, ui, 2, v. n. Sanscr. palitas, gray; Gr. πελλός, πελιδνός, πολιός; cf. pullus, to be or look pale. Lit.: sudat, pallet, Cic. Phil. 2, 34, 84: pallent amisso sanguine venae, Ov. M. 2, 824: metu sceleris futuri, id. ib. 8, 465: timore, id. F. 2, 468: mea rugosa pallebunt ora senectā, Tib. 3, 5, 25; morbo, Juv. 2, 50: fame, Mart. 3, 38, 12.— Esp. of lovers: palleat omnis amans; hic est color aptus amanti, must look pale, Ov. A. A. 1, 729; Prop. 1, 9, 17.—Also through indolence, Mart. 3, 58,

pallesco.full: pallesco, pallăi, 3, v. inch. n. [palleo], to grow or turn pale. Lit.: ut qui timent sanguine ex ore decedente pallescant, Gell. 19, 4, 4: pallescere curis, Prop. 1, 13, 7: nullā pallescere culpā, Hor. Ep. 1, 1, 61: pallescet super his, will turn pale with emotion, id. A. P. 429: umbraticā vitā pallescere, Quint. 1, 2, 18; 12, 10, 76.— Transf., to turn pale, sallow: pallescunt frondes, wither, fade, Ov. A. A. 3, 704: viso pallescit flamma veneno, Val. Fl. 7, 586; Plin. 9, 17, 30, § 66.

palliastrum.full: pallĭastrum, i, n. pallium, a ragged, sorry mantle, App. M. 1, p. 104, 28; id. Flor. p. 350.

palliatus.full: pallĭātus, a, um, adj. id., dressed in a pallium, cloaked, usually said of Greeks. Lit.: isti Graeci palliati, Plaut. Curc. 2, 3,9: Graeculus judex modo palliatus, modo togatus, Cic. Phil. 5, 5, 14; Suet. Caes. 48: Pythagoras, Val. Max. 2, 6, 10: palliata signa Phidiae, Plin. 34, 8, 19, § 54: illi palliati topiariam facere videantur, i. e. Grecian statues, Cic. Q. Fr. 3, 1, 2, § 5: fabulae palliatae, comedies in which Greek characters were introduced in the Greek dress (opp. the fabulae togatae,

pallidulus.full: pallĭdŭlus, a, um, adj. dim. [pallidus], palish, somewhat pale, Cat. 65, 6; Juv. 10, 82.

pallidus.full: pallĭdus, a, um, adj. palleo, pale, pallid (cf.: lividus, luridus). Lit.: vides ut pallidus omnis Cenā desurgat dubiā, Hor. S. 2, 2, 76: ora buxo Pallidiora, Ov. M. 4, 134; Prop. 5, 5, 72: Asturii scrutator pallidus auri, Luc. 4, 298; id. 1, 618: recto vultu et pallidus, i. e. well or sick, Juv. 10, 189: oriens, Plin. 18, 35, 78, § 342: stellae, quae sunt omnium pallidissimae, id. 2, 25, 22, § 89.—Esp. of the Lower World: pallida turba, Tib. 1, 10, 38: ditis profundi Pallida regna, Luc. 1, 456:

palliolatim.full: pallĭŏlātim, adv. pallium, dressed in a mantle very rare): palliolatim amictus, Plaut. Ps. 5, 1, 29: saltare, Front. Orat. 1 Mai.

palliolatus.full: pallĭŏlātus, a, um, adj. palliolum, covered with a cloak-cape or hood: palliolatus novo more praesedit, Suet. Claud. 2; Mart. 9, 33, 1: tunicae palliolatae, hooded mantles, Vop. Bonos. 15; cf. Dig. 34, 2, 39.

palliolum.full: pallĭŏlum, i, n. dim. pallium. Lit., a small Greek mantle or cloak: saepe est etiam sub palliolo sordido sapientia, Caecil. ap. Cic. Tusc. 3, 23, 56: palliolum in collum conice, Plaut. Ep. 2, 2, 10: ferrugineum, id. Mil. 4, 4, 42; Mart. 11, 27, 8: opertus palliolo, App. M. 1, p. 111; Mart. 11, 27, 8; Juv. 3, 95.— Transf., a covering for the head, a hood: palliolum, sicut fascias et focalia et aurium ligamenta, sola excusare potest valetudo, Quint. 11, 3, 144; Ov. A. A. 1, 734; Sen. Q. N. 4, 13,

pallium.full: pallium, i, n., a covering, cover [cf. palla]. In gen. A coverlet: et gravius justo pallia pondus habent, Ov. H. 21, 170: onerosa pallia jactat, Juv. 6, 236: tunc queror in toto non sidere pallia lecto, Prop. 5, 3, 31; Suet. Ner. 84.— A pall: arrepto pallio retexi corpora, App. M. 3, p. 133, 23; id. Flor. p. 342, 27.— A curtain: quae festis suspendam pallia portis? Prud. adv. Symm. 2, 726.— In partic., a Greek cloak or mantle, esp. as the dress of the Grecian philosophers. The Romans were accust
pallium.short: pallium, i, n., a covering, cover [cf.

pallor.full: pallor, ōris, m. palleo, pale color, paleness, wanness, pallor. Lit.: pudorem rubor, terrorem pallor et tremor consequitur, Cic. Tusc. 4, 8, 19: albus ora pallor inficit, Hor. Epod. 7, 15: luteus, id. ib. 10, 16; id. S. 2, 8, 35; 2, 18, 25: partemque coloris Luridus exsangues pallor convertit in herbas, Ov. M. 4, 267; cf.: gelidus pallor, id. Tr. 1, 4, 11: confuderat oris exsanguis notas pallor, Curt. 8, 3, 13: pallor ora occupat, Verg. A. 4, 499: femineus pallor in corpore, Plin. Pan. 48, 4: Au

pallula.full: pallŭla, ae, f. dim. palla, a little cloak or mantle: conscissa pallula est, Plaut. Truc. 1, 1, 32; 2, 2, 16; 2, 6, 55.

palma1.full: palma, ae παλάμη; Sanscr. phal, to open, f., the palm of the hand. Lit., Cic. Or. 32, 113; Cels. 8, 18: cavis undam de flumine palmis Sustulit, Verg. A. 8, 69: aliquem palmā concutere, Plin. Ep. 3, 14, 7: faciem contundere palmā, Juv. 13, 128: os hominis liberi manus suae palmā verberare, Laber. ap. Gell. 20, 1, 13. — Transf. (Pars pro toto.) The hand: compressan' palma an porrecta ferio? Plaut. Cas. 2, 6, 53: palmarum intentus, Cic. Sest. 55, 117: passis palmis salutem petere, Caes. B. C. 3, 98

palma2.full: palma, ae, a collat. form for parma, v. parma init.

palmaris.full: palmāris, e, adj. 1. palma. A hand's-breadth, or palm, in length, width, etc.: virgulae, Varr. R. R. 1, 35: spatia, Col. 8, 3; 11, 3: scrobes, Pall. 3, 24: palmarem in minutiem contrahi, Arn. 6, 204.— Of palms, full of palms, palm-: lucus, Amm. 24, 4, 7.— Trop., that merits the palm or prize, excellent (class.): statua, Cic. Phil. 6, 5, 15: sententia, id. N. D. 1, 8, 20: dea, the goddess of victory, because she is represented with a palm-branch, App. M. 2, p. 116, 2.

palmarius.full: palmārĭus, a, um, adj. id., of or belonging to palms: Insula Palmaria, the Isle of Palms in the Tyrrhenian Sea, now Palmarola, Varr. R. R. 3, 5, 7; Plin. 3, 6, 12, § 81.— Transf., subst.: palmārĭ-um, ii, n. * That which deserves the prize, a masterpiece: id vero est, quod ego mihi puto palmarium, Ter. Eun. 5, 4, 8.— The fee of a successful advocate, Dig. 50, 13, 1, § 12; cf. palmarium, ἀξιόνικον, Gloss. Philox.

palmatias.full: palmătĭas, ae, m., = παλματίας, a slight earthquake, App. de Mundo, p. 65, 20.
palmatias.short: palmătĭas, ae, m., = παλματίας, a slight earthquake, App.

palmatus.full: palmātus, a, um, Part. and P. a., from palmo.

palmensis.full: palmensis, e, adj. 1. palma, made from palms: vina, Plin. 14, 6, 8, § 67.

palmes.full: palmĕs, ĭtis, m. 1. palma, II. E., a young branch or shoot of a vine, a vinesprig, vine-sprout (syn. pampinus). Lit.: palmites vitium sarmenta appellantur, quod in modum palmarum humanarum virgulas quasi digitos edunt, Fest. p. 222 Müll.: palmitum duo genera sunt, alterum pampinarium, alterum fructuarium, Col. 5, 6, 26 sq.; id. 3, 10, 14; 4, 22, 10; Plin. 17, 22, 35, § 175; 14, 1, 3, § 10: jam laeto turgent in palmite gemmae, Verg. E. 7, 48: stratus humi palmes, Juv. 8, 78; Ov. F. 1, 152: ego su

palmetum.full: palmētum, i, n. 1. palma, a palmgrove, Hor. Ep. 2, 2, 184: Hiericus palmetis consita, Plin. 5, 14, 15, § 70; cf. Tac. H. 5, 6. —In sing., Just. 36, 3, 4.

palmeus.full: palmĕus, a, um, adj. id.. A hand'sbreadth, or palm, in length, width, etc.: orchis herba, caule palmeo, etc., Plin. 26, 10, 62, § 95.— Of or made of palms, palm-: tabulae, Vitr. 10, 20: tegetes, Col. 5, 15: vinum, Plin. 12, 17, 40, § 79: sporta, Pall. 3, 27.

palmiceus.full: palmĭcĕus and palmĭcĭus, a, um, adj. id., of or made of palms, palm-: palmicea sporta, Sulp. Sev. Dial. 1, 11 and 14.
palmiceus.short: palmĭcĕus and palmĭcĭus, a, um, adj.

palmifer.full: palmĭfer, fĕra, fĕrum, adj. 1. palmafero, palm-bearing, abounding in palms, palmiferous: Memphin palmiferamque Pharon, Ov. Am. 2, 13, 8: Thebae, Prop. 5, 5, 25: Idume, Sil. 3, 600; cf.: palmiferos Arabas, Ov. M. 10, 478.

palmiger.full: palmĭger, gĕra, gĕrum, adj. 1. palmagero, palm-bearing, holding a palm-branch: Nemea, Plin. 35, 4, 10, § 27.

palmipedalis.full: palmĭpĕdālis, e, adj. palmipes, a foot and a palm in height, breadth, etc.: limen altum palmipedale, Varr. R. R. 2, 4, 14: malleolus, Col. 3, 19, 1: cardines, Vitr. 10, 20.

palmipes1.full: palmĭpes, pĕdis, adj. 1. palma-pes, broad-footed: volucres aut palmipedum in genere sunt, uti anseres, etc., Plin. 10, 11, 13, § 29; 11, 47, 107, § 256.

palmipes2.full: palmĭpes, pĕdis, adj. palmus-pes, a foot and a palm high: palmipedi intervallo, Plin. 17, 20, 32, § 143: gradus spectaculorum ne minus alti sint palmipede (al. palmopede), Vitr. 5, 6 fin.

palmiprimus.full: palmiprīmus, a false reading for pharnuprius, Plin. 14, 16, 19, § 102.
palmiprimus.short: palmiprīmus, a false reading for pharnuprius, Plin.

palmo.full: palmo, no perf., ātum, 1, v. a. 1. palma. To make the print or mark of the palm of one's hand, Quint. Decl. 1, 12; v. in the foll. P. a.—* To tie up a vine: palmare hoc est materias alligare, Col. 11, 2, 96.—Hence, palmātus, a, um, P. a. Marked with the palm of a hand: palmatus paries, bearing the mark of a (bloody) hand, Quint. Decl. 1, 11 and 12, pp. 30 and 31 Burm.: cervi palmati, with antlers shaped like the palm of a hand, Capitol. Gord. 3 fin.— Containing the figure of a palm-tree: lapis,

palmosus.full: palmōsus, a, um, adj. 1. palma, abounding in palm-trees: palmosa Selinūs, Verg. A. 3, 705.

palmula.full: palmŭla, ae, f. dim. id., the palm of the hand. Lit., Varr. ap. Non.-372, 29: saevientes, App. M. 8, p. 105, 17; 3, p. 138, 27.— Transf. The blade of an oar, an oar: palmulae appellantur remi a similitudine manūs humanae, Fest. p. 220 Müll.; Verg. A. 5, 163.— The wing of a bird: color psittaco viridis et intimis plumulis et extimis palmulis (al. parmulis), App. Flor. p. 348, 31. — The fruit of the palm-tree, a date, Varr. R. R. 1, 67; 2, 1, 27; Cels. 2, 20; Suet. Aug. 76; Claud. 8.

palmularis.full: palmŭlāris, e, adj. palmula, of or with the palm of the hand: frictus, Mart. Cap. 8, 271, § 805.

palmus.full: palmus, i, m. 1. palma, the palm of the hand. Lit.: manūs palmum, Vitr. 2, 3: Graeci antiqui doron palmum vocabant: et ideo dora munera, quia manu darentur, Plin. 35, 14, 49, § 171.— Transf., as a measure of length, a span, or twelve digits, Varr. R. R. 3, 7: amomum frutex myrtuosus, palmi altitudine, Plin. 12, 13, 28, § 48: minor, a smaller measure, a palm, or four digits, acc. to Vitr. 3, 1, 5.

palmyra.full: Palmȳra (Palmīra), ae, f., = Παλμύρα, Παλμιρα, a city of Syria, whose ruins still remain, the seat of the empire of Odenathus and Zenobia, Plin. 5, 25, 21, § 86; 6, 28, 32, § 144.—Hence, Palmȳrēnus (Palmīr-), a, um, adj., of Palmyra: solitudines, Plin. 5, 24, 21, § 87.—Subst.: Palmȳ-rēna, ae, f., the country around Palmyra, Plin. 6, 28, 32, § 143; and Palmȳrēnus, i, m., an epithet of the emperor L. Domitius Aurelius, on account of his victory over Palmyra, Inscr. Grut. 276, 5.
palmyra.short: Palmȳra (Palmīra), ae, f., = Παλμύρα, Παλμιρα, a city of Syria, whose ruins still remain, the seat of the empire of Odenathus and Zenobia, Plin.

palo1.full: pālo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. 1. palus, to support with pales, stakes, or props; to prop up: reliquae partes vinearum nunc palandae et alligandae sunt, Col. 11, 2, 16: ut vitis paletur, id. 11, 2, 16 fin.; Pall. 12, 15.

palo2.full: pālo, āre, 1, v. n., v. palor init.

palor.full: pālor, ātus (gen. plur. part. palantūm, Sil. 5, 445), 1, v. dep. (act. collat. form pālo, āre, Sulp. Sat. 1, 43 Wernsd.; Poët. Lat. Min. 3, p. 90) [cf. Sanscr. pad, go; Gr. ποῦς, ποδός; Lat. pes], to wander up and down, to wander, wander about; to be dispersed, to straggle (not in Cic. or Cæs.; most freq. in part. pres.; syn.: vagor, erro). Lit.: palantes comites quom montes inter opacos Quaerimus et magna dispersos voce ciemus, Lucr. 4, 575; cf. id. 5, 973: vagi per agros palantur, Liv. 5, 44;

palpabilis.full: palpābĭlis, e, adj. 1. palpo, that can be touched, that may be felt, palpable (late Lat.): tenebrae crassitudine palpabiles, Oros. 1, 10: tenebrae, Hier. in Isa. 10, 32, 14.

palpamen.full: palpāmen, ĭnis, n. id., a stroking, caressing (late Lat.), Prud. Ham. 302.

palpamentum.full: palpāmentum, i, n. id., a stroking, flattering (post-class.): muliebria palpamenta, Amm. 27, 12, 6.

palpatio.full: palpātĭo, ōnis, f. id.. A stroking, flattering, flattery: aufer hinc palpationes, Plaut. Men. 4, 2, 43.— Trembling, terror (eccl. Lat.): tenebrae et palpatio, Vulg. Isa. 32, 14.

palpator.full: palpātor, ōris, m. id., a stroker; trop., a flatterer: perjurus, Plaut. Rud. 1, 2, 38; plur., id. Men. 2, 1, 35.

palpebra.full: palpē^bra, ae, f. (collat. form palpē^-brum, i, n., Non. 218, 19; Cael. Aur. Tard. 2, 1), an eyelid (usually in plur.; cf. cilium). Lit.: palpebrae sunt tegmenta oculorum ... munitaeque sunt palpebrae tamquam vallo pilorum, etc., Cic. N. D. 2, 57, 142: ipsae palpebrae, quibus mobilitas inest, et palpitatio vocabulum tribuit, etc., Lact. Opif. Dei, 10 init.; Lucr. 4, 952: Regulum resectis palpebris vigilando necaverunt, Cic. Pis. 19, 43; cf. Tubero ap. Gell. 6, 4, 3.—In sing., Cels. 5, 26, 23.— T

palpebralis.full: palpē^brālis, e, adj. palpebra, of or on the eyelids: palpebrales setae, Prud. Ham. 880.

palpebraris.full: palpē^brāris, e, adj. id., of or for the eyelids: collyria palpebraria, Cael. Aur. Tard. 4, 2 fin.

palpebratio.full: palpē^brātĭo, ōnis, f. palpebro, a blinking with the eyes, Cael. Aur. Acut. 1, 3, 36; id. Tard. 1, 5, 148.

palpebro.full: palpē^bro, āre, 1, v. n. palpebra, to wink frequently, to blink, Cael. Aur. Acut. 2, 10, 70.
