palpitatio.full: palpĭtātĭo, ōnis, f. palpito, a frequent and rapid motion, a palpitation: cordis, a palpitation of the heart, Plin. 32, 5, 18, § 49: oculorum, a blinking, id. 32, 10, 46, § 132: partium singularum, id. 11, 4, 3, § 10.

palpitatus.full: palpĭtātus, ūs (only in the abl. sing.), m. id., a frequent and rapid motion, Plin. 9, 30, 48, § 90.

palpito.full: palpĭto, āvi, ātum, 1, v. freq. n. [palpo], to move frequently and quickly, to tremble, throb, pant, palpitate. Lit.: cor palpitat, * Cic. N. D. 2, 9, 24: radix micat ultima linguae, Utque salire solet mutilatae cauda colubrae, Palpitat, Ov. M. 6, 559: cerebrum uni homini in infantiā palpitat, Plin. 11, 37, 49, § 134: in ovo gutta sanguinis salit palpitatque, id. 10, 53, 74, § 148; 11, 37, 65, § 173.—Esp. of persons or animals in the agony of death, to struggle, be convulsed: palpitat et positas

palpo1.full: palpo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a., and pal-por, ātus palpus; cf. Gr. ψάλλω, 1, v. dep. a., to stroke, to touch softly, to pat (poet. and in post-Aug. prose; syn. mulceo). Lit.: modo pectora praebet Virgineā palpanda manu, Ov. M. 2, 867 Jahn N. cr.: palpate lupos, Manil. 5, 702: cum equum permulsit quis vel palpatus est, Dig. 9, 1, 1: tamquam si manu palpetur, Schol. Juv. 6, 196: animalia blandi manu palpata magistri, Prud. στεφ. 11, 91.— Transf. To caress, coax, wheedle, flatter. Absol.: hoc sis vide u

palpo2.full: palpo, ōnis, m. 1. palpo, a flatterer, Pers. 5, 176.

palpus.full: palpus, i, m. (nom. not in use) [1. palpo], the soft palm of the hand (Plautin.): timidam palpo percutit, Plaut. Am. 1, 3, 28: palpo percutis, id. Merc. 1, 2, 42: mi obtrudere non potes palpum, id. Ps. 4, 1, 35.

paltus.full: Paltus (-tos), i, n., = Πάλτος, a city in Syria, Plin. 5, 20, 18, § 79; Mel. 1, 12, 5 (as Greek, Cass. ap. Cic. Fam. 12, 13).
paltus.short: Paltus (-tos), i, n., = Πάλτος, a city in Syria, Plin.

paluda.full: Pălūda, ae, f. (dressed in the military cloak), an epithet of Minerva, Enn. ap. Varr. L. L. 7, § 37 Müll. (Ann. v. 510 Vahl.); cf.: paluda a paludamentis, Varr. l. l.

paludamentum.full: pălūdāmentum, i, n. kindred with pallium, q. v., a military cloak, soldier's cloak. In gen. (very rare; cf.: sagum, trabea): cognito super umeros fratris paludamento sponsi, quod ipsa confecerat, Liv. 1, 26; Sall. Fragm. ap. Non. 539, 3.— In partic., a general's cloak (freq.): paludamenta (sunt) insignia atque ornamenta militaria ... quae propterea, quod conspiciuntur qui ea habent, ac fiunt palam, paludamenta dicta, Varr. L. L. 7, § 37 Müll.; cf.: omnia militaria ornamenta paludamenta dici (ait

paludatus.full: pălūdātus, a, um, adj., dressed in a military cloak (v. paludamentum). In gen. (very rare): virgines, Fest. p. 329 Müll.—Hence, a soldier: qui invident stipendia paludatis, Sid. Ep. 5, 7. — In partic., dressed in a general's cloak (class. and common): cum proficiscebamini paludati in provincias ... consules vos quisquam putavit? Cic. Pis. 13, 31; cf. id. Sest. 33, 71; id. Att. 4, 13, 2: Pansa noster paludatus a. d. III. Kalend. Jan. profectus est, Cic. Fam. 15, 17, 3: ut paludati (consules) exea
paludatus.short: pălūdātus, a, um, adj., dressed in a military cloak (v.

paludester.full: pălūdester, tris, tre, adj. 2. palus, marshy, swampy (late Lat.): illuvies, Cassiod. Var. 2, 32.

paludicola.full: pălūdĭcŏla, ae, comm. 2. palus-colo, a dweller in fens or marshes (post-class.): paludicolae Sicambri, Sid. Ep. 4, 1 fin.: Ravenna, id. ib. 7, 17.

paludifer.full: pălūdĭfer, fĕra, fĕrum, adj. 2. palusfero, marsh-making, swamp-making: aquae, Auct. Carm. Philom. 42.

paludigena.full: pălūdĭgĕna, ae, adj. gen. comm. [2. palus-gigno], marsh-born, that grows in marshes: paludigena papyrus, Poët. in Anth. Lat. 2, p. 462 Burm.

paludivagus.full: pălūdĭvăgus, a, um, adj. 2. palusvagor, wandering about or among morasses (poet.): alumni, Avien. Perieg. 312.

paludosus.full: pălūdōsus, a, um, adj. 2. palus, fenny, boggy, marshy (poet.): humus, Ov. M. 15, 268; Prop. 4 (5), 6, 77. Nilus, Stat. S. 3, 2, 108: Ravenna, Sil. 8, 602.

palumbarius.full: pălumbārĭus, ii, m. palumbes, a kind of hawk which attacks doves: palumbarius, = φασσοφόνος, Gloss. Philox.

palumbes.full: pălumbes, is, or pălumbis, is, m. and f. (collat. form pălumbus, i, m., Cato, R. R. 90; Col. 8, 8; Mart. 13, 67, 1: pălumba, ae, f., Cels. 6, 6, 39) [cf. Sanscr. kadamba, diver; Gr. κόλυμβος, columba], a woodpigeon, ring-dove: macrosque palumbes, Lucil. ap. Non. 219, 6; Pompon. ib. 9; Varr. R. R. 3, 9; Cic. poët. ap. Serv. Verg. E. 1, 58: raucae, tua cura, palumbes, Verg. E. 1, 58: aëriae palumbes, id. ib. 3, 69: fronde novā puerum palumbes Texere, Hor. C. 3, 4, 12; cf. id. S. 2, 8, 91.—Prov.: p
palumbes.short: pălumbes, is, or pălumbis, is, m.

palumbinum.full: Palumbīnum, i, n., a town of the Samnites, Liv. 10, 45.
palumbinum.short: Palumbīnum, i, n., a town of the Samnites, Liv.

palumbinus.full: pălumbīnus, a, um, adj. palumbes, of wood-pigeons: caro, Plin. 30, 12, 36, § 110: fimum, id. 30, 8, 21, § 67: ovum, Lampr. Alex. Sev. 13.

palumbulus.full: pălumbŭlus, i, m. dim. id., little wood-pigeon, little dove, as a term of endearment (post-class.): teneo te meum palumbulum, meum passerem, App. M. 10, p. 249, 16; id. ib. 8, p. 213, 33.

palumbus.full: pălumbus, i, m., v. palumbes fin.

palus1.full: pālus, i, m. (neutr. collat. form pālum, i, Varr. ap. Non. 219, 18) [for paglus (cf. dim. paxillus); root pag-; Sanscr. pācas, snare; Gr. πήγνυμι, fasten; Lat. pango; cf.: pignus, pax], a stake, prop, stay, pale. Lit. (very freq. and class.; syn.: sudes, stipes): ut figam palum in parietem, Plaut. Mil. 4, 4, 4; id. Men. 2, 3, 53: damnati ad supplicium traditi, ad palum alligati, Cic. Verr. 2, 5, 5, § 11: palis adjungere vitem, Tib. 1, 8 (7), 33; Ov. F. 1, 665: palos et ridicas dolare, Col. 11, 2

palus2.full: pălus, ūdis (nom. sing. pălŭs, Hor. A. P. 65; but usually pălūs, Verg. A. 6, 107; v. infra; gen. plur. paludum, Caes. B. G. 4, 38, 2 Oud.; rarely paludium, Liv. 21, 54, 7 Drak.; Plin. 2, 68, 68, § 174; Just. 44, 1, 10; Eum. Pan. Const. Aug. 12, 2), f. = Gr. πηλός, mud; cf. Sanscr. palvala, pool; perh. -ud of the stem = ὕδωρ, water, a swamp, marsh, morass, bog, fen, pool (cf.: stagnum, lacus). Lit.: ille paludes siccare voluit, Cic. Phil. 5, 3, 7: paludes emere, id. Agr. 2, 27, 71: palus erat non

palusca.full: palusca, ficus, a kind of fig, Cloat. ap. Macr. S. 2, 16 dub.
palusca.short: palusca, ficus, a kind of fig, Cloat.

paluster.full: păluster, tris, tre (masc. palustris, Col. 8, 14, 2), adj. 2. palus, fenny, marshy, swampy. Lit.: locus, Caes. B. G. 7, 20: ager, Liv. 36, 22; 22, 2: ulva, Verg. G. 3, 175; Col. 8, 14, 2: ranae, Hor. S. 1, 5, 14; cf. calami, Ov. M. 1, 706.—In plur. subst.: pă-lustrĭa, ĭum, n., swampy places, Plin. 14, 16, 19, § 110; Vulg. Ezech. 47, 11.— Trop.: lux, i. e., a filthy, vicious life, Pers. 5, 60.

pamisus.full: Pămīsus, i, m., = Πάμισος. A river in Messenia, Plin. 4, 3, 7, § 15; Mela, 2, 3, 9.— A river in Thrace, Plin. 4, 8, 15, § 30.

pammacharius.full: pammăchārĭus, ii, m. pammachum, the victor in the pammachum, Hier. in Psa. 36, § 5.

pammachum.full: pammachum (-chium), i, n., = παμμάχιον, an athletic contest, consisting of wrestling, boxing with the naked fists, and boxing with the cestus: in quibus (ludis) contendit pammachum (al. pammacho) quod nos pancratium vocamus, Hyg. Fab. 273; Inscr. Fabr. p. 106, n. 226.
pammachum.short: pammachum (-chium), i, n., = παμμάχιον, an athletic contest, consisting of wrestling, boxing with the naked fists, and boxing with the cestus: in quibus (ludis) contendit pammachum (al.

pammenes.full: Pammĕnes, is, m., a Greek rhetorician, instructor of Brutus, Cic. Brut. 97, 332; id. Or. 30, 105; id. Att. 5, 20, 2.—Hence, Pammĕnia, ōrum, n., of or belonging to Pammenes: Pammenia illa mihi non placent, those views of Pammenes, Cic. Att. 6, 2, 10.
pammenes.short: Pammĕnes, is, m., a Greek rhetorician, instructor of Brutus, Cic.

pamphagus.full: Pamphăgus, i, m., the name of a dog, Ov. M. 3, 210.
pamphagus.short: Pamphăgus, i, m., the name of a dog, Ov.

pamphilus.full: Pamphĭlus, i, m., = Πάμφιλος, a Greek proper name. A disciple of Plato, whom Epicurus heard, Cic. N. D. 1, 26, 72.— A celebrated painter, a native of Amphipolis, the instructor of Apelles, Plin. 35, 10, 36, § 75; 35, 11, 40, § 123.— A rhetorician, Cic. de Or. 3, 21, 81; Quint. 3, 6, 33.
pamphilus.short: Pamphĭlus, i, m., = Πάμφιλος, a Greek proper name.

pamphylia.full: Pamphȳlĭa, ae, f., = Παμφυλία, a country on the sea-coast of Asia Minor, between Lycia and Cilicia, Mela, 1, 14; Liv. 33, 41, 6; Plin. 5, 27, 26, § 96; Cic. Div. 1, 1, 2; Stat. S. 1, 4, 77.—Hence, Pam-phȳlĭus, a, um, adj., Pamphylian: teilus, Luc. 8, 249: mare, Plin. 5, 31, 35, § 129.— In plur.: Pamphȳlii, ōrum, m., the Pamphylians, Cic. Div. 1, 15, 25.
pamphylia.short: Pamphȳlĭa, ae, f., = Παμφυλία, a country on the sea-coast of Asia Minor, between Lycia and Cilicia, Mela, 1, 14;

pampinaceus.full: pampĭnācĕus, a, um, i. q. pampineus, Col. 12, 20, 5 dub.

pampinarius.full: pampĭnārĭus, a, um, adj. pampinus, of or belonging to tendrils, that has tendrils: palmitum duo genera sunt: alterum, quod, quia primo anno plerumque frondem sine fructu affert, pampinarium vocant, etc., Col. 5, 6, 29: sarmentum, id. 3, 10, 5: virga, id. 3, 10, 7: materiae, id. 4, 24, 11.— Subst.: pampĭnārĭum, ii, n., i. q. pampinarium sarmentum, a tendril-branch, leaf-branch, Plin. 17, 21, 35, § 157; 17, 22, 35, § 181.

pampinatio.full: pampĭnātĭo, ōnis, f. pampino, a breaking off of superfluous tendrils and leaves of vines, a lopping or trimming of vines: ut frequenti pampinatione supervacua detrahantur, Col. 4, 6, 1; cf. id. 4, 6, 1, § 5; 4, 7, 1; 4, 28, 1; Plin. 17, 1, 1, § 7: prima, Col. 11, 2, 38: verna, Plin. 17, 22, 35, § 190.

pampinator.full: pampĭnātor, ōris, m. id., one who plucks or lops off the superfluous tendrils and leaves of vines, a vine-trimmer, Col. 4, 10, 2: industrius, id. 4, 27, 5.

pampinatus1.full: pampĭnātus, a, um, Part., from pampino.
pampinatus1.short: pampĭnātus, a, um, Part., from pampino.

pampinatus2.full: pampĭnātus, a, um, adj. pampinus, having tendrils and leaves. Lit.: lanceam argenteam pampinatam librarum triginta, Gallien. Ep. ap. Treb. Claud. 17, 5. — Transf., tendril-shaped, tendril-like, Plin. 16, 42, 82, § 225.

pampineus.full: pampĭnĕus, a, um, adj. id., full of tendrils or vine-leaves, consisting of tendrils: uvae, Ov. P. 3, 1, 13: vites, id. ib. 3, 8, 13: umbrae, Verg. E. 7, 58: auctumnus, id. G. 2, 5: hastae, wrapped round with vine-leaves, id. A. 7, 396: habenae, id. ib. 6, 804: ratis, decked with vine-branches, Prop. 3, 15 (4, 16), 26: juga, Mart. 10, 93, 2: odor, the perfume of wine, Prop. 2, 24 (3, 31), 30: corona, of vine-leaves, Tac. A. 11, 4: ulmus, Calp. Ecl. 2, 59.

pampino.full: pampĭno, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. id., to pluck or lop off the superfluous tendrils, shoots, and leaves of vines, to trim vines. Lit.: pampinare est ex sarmento coles qui nati sunt, de iis qui plurimum valent, primum ac secundum, nonnumquam etiam tertium relinquere, reliquos decerpere, Varr. R. R. 1, 31, 2; Cato, R. R. 33, 3: pampinandi modus, Col. 5, 5, 14: vineas, Plin. 18, 27, 67, § 254; Col. Arb. 11.— Transf., in gen., to trim or prune trees: salix non minus, quam vinea pampinatur, Col. 4, 31, 2;

pampinosus.full: pampĭnōsus, a, um, adj. id., full of foliage, leafy, branchy: vitis, Col. 5, 5, 14; Plin. 23, 1, 16, § 21.

pampinus.full: pampĭnus, i, m. and f. (in fem.: circumflua pampinus, Claud. III. Cons. Stil. 366: opaca, id. Epith. Pall. et Celer. 5; cf. Donat. p. 1747 P.; Serv. Verg. E. 7, 58, acc. to whom Varro often used the word as a fem.) [root pamp-, pap-, to swell, v. pōpulus; cf. papula, pustule], a tendril or young shoot of a vine (cf. palmes). Lit., Col. 4, 22, 4: ex gemmis pampini pullulant, id. 3, 18, 4: pampinos detergere, Plin. 17, 22, 35, § 175: detrahere, id. 17, 22, 35, § 193.— A vine-leaf, the foliage of a

pan.full: Pān, Pānŏs (acc. Pāna), m., = Πάν, Pan, the god of the woods and of shepherds, the son of Mercury and Penelope, Cic. N. D. 3, 22, 56; Hyg. Fab. 224: Pan erat armenti custos, Pan numen equarum, Ov. F. 2, 277: Panos de more Lycaei, Verg. A. 8, 344. He was represented under the form of a goat; hence, semicaper Pan, Ov. M. 14, 515; cf. Sil. 13, 327. His mistress, Syrinx, was transformed, at her request, by the nymphs into a thicket of reeds, from which Pan made the shepherd's pipe (σύριγξ), Lucr. 4,

panaca.full: panăca, a kind of drinking-vessel, Mart. 14, 100 in lemm.
panaca.short: panăca, a kind of drinking-vessel, Mart.

panacea1.full: pănăcēa, ae, f., pănăces, is, n., also pănax, ăcis, m., = πανάκεια, πανακές, πάναξ. An herb to which was ascribed the power of healing all diseases, all-heal, panacea, catholicon; on the different kinds, v. Plin. 25, 4, 11, § 30 sq.: odorifera panacea, Verg. A. 12, 419: panaces ipso nomine omnium morborum remedia promittit, Plin. 25, 4, 11, § 30: panax levi et subactā terrā rarissime disseritur, Col. 11, 3, 29.— A plant, called also ligusticum silvestre: ligusticum silvestre panacem aliqui vocan
panacea1.short: pănăcēa, ae, f., pănăces, is, n., also pănax, ăcis, m., = πανάκεια, πανακές, πάναξ.

panacea2.full: Pănăcēa, ae, f., a city in Crete, Mela, 2, 7.
panacea2.short: Pănăcēa, ae, f., a city in Crete, Mela, 2, 7.

panacinus.full: pănăcĭnus, a, um, adj. panacea, made of the panacea: clyster, Cael. Aur. Tard. 4, 7, 95.

panaenus.full: Pănaenus, i, m., a famous painter, brother of the sculptor Phidias, Plin. 35, 8, 34, § 54; 35, 8, 34, § 57.
panaenus.short: Pănaenus, i, m., a famous painter, brother of the sculptor Phidias, Plin.

panaetius.full: Pănaetĭus, ii, m., = Παναίτιος, a celebrated Stoic, a native of Rhodes, the instructor and friend of Scipio Africanus the Younger, Cic. Off. 1, 26, 90; id. de Or. 1, 11, 45; id. Off. 1, 12; 3, 2, 7; id. Tusc. 1, 32, 79: Hor. C. 1, 29, 14; Vell. 1, 13, 3.
panaetius.short: Pănaetĭus, ii, m., = Παναίτιος, a celebrated Stoic, a native of Rhodes, the instructor and friend of Scipio Africanus the Younger, Cic.

panaetolicus.full: Pănaetōlĭcus, a, um, adj., = Παναιτωλικός, of or belonging to the whole of Ætolia, Panœtolian: concilium, Liv. 31, 32, 3; 35, 32, 8.
panaetolicus.short: Pănaetōlĭcus, a, um, adj., = Παναιτωλικός, of or belonging to the whole of Ætolia, Panœtolian: concilium, Liv.

panaetolium.full: Pănaetōlĭum, i, n., = Παναιτώλιον, the council of the whole of Ætolia, a general assembly or congress of the Ætolians: concilium Aetolorum quod Panaetolium vocant, Liv. 31, 29, 1; Weissenb. ad Liv. 31, 32, 3.— A very high mountain in Ætolia, now Viena, Plin. 4, 2, 3, § 6.
panaetolium.short: Pănaetōlĭum, i, n., = Παναιτώλιον, the council of the whole of Ætolia, a general assembly or congress of the Ætolians: concilium Aetolorum quod Panaetolium vocant, Liv.

panaricium.full: pănāricĭum, ii, n. corrupted from paronychium, a disease of the finger-nails, App. Herb. 42.

panariolum.full: pānārĭŏlum, i, n. dim. panarium, a small bread-basket, Mart. 5, 49, 10.

panarium.full: pānārĭum (pann-), ii, n. panis, a bread-basket: hinc panarium, ubi id (sc. panem) servabant, sicut granarium, ubi granum frumenti condebant, unde id dictum, Varr. L. L. 5, § 105 Müll.; Plin. Ep. 1, 6, 3; Suet. Calig. 18; Stat. S. 1, 6, 31.

panarius.full: pānārĭus, ii, m. id., a bread-seller: panarius, ἀρτοπώλης, Vet. Gloss.

panathenaicon.full: pănăthēnāĭcon, i, n., = παναθηναϊκόν, an ointment made in Athens, Plin. 13, 1, 2, § 6.
panathenaicon.short: pănăthēnāĭcon, i, n., = παναθηναϊκόν, an ointment made in Athens, Plin.

panathenaicus.full: Pănăthēnāĭcus, a, um, adj., = Παναθηναικός, of or belonging to the Panathenœa (a popular festival of the Athenians); hence, subst. Pănăthēnāĭca, ōrum, n. (sc. solemnia), the Panathenœa, Varr. ap. Serv. Verg. G. 3, 113.— Pănăthēnā-ĭcus, i, m. (sc. liber), a holiday oration of Isocrates pronounced at the Panathenœa, Cic. Or. 12, 38; id. Sen. 5, 13; cf. Aus. Prof. 1, 13.
panathenaicus.short: Pănăthēnāĭcus, a, um, adj., = Παναθηναικός, of or belonging to the Panathenœa (a popular festival of the Athenians);

pancarpineus.full: pancarpĭnĕus, a, um, adj. pancarpus, composed of all kinds of fruits: cibus, Varr. ap. Non. 264, 27.

pancarpius.full: pancarpĭus and pancarpus, a, um, adj., = παγκάρπιος and πάγκαρπος, consisting or composed of all kinds of fruits. Lit.: pancarpiae dicuntur coronae ex vario genere florum factae, Fest. p. 220 Müll.: Jesum cognominant Soterem et Christum ... Quam propius fuit de Atticis historiis pancarpiam vocari (alluding to the olive-branch, ornamented with all sorts of fruits, which was carried about by boys in Athens on a certain festival), Tert. ad Val. 12.— Transf., of all sorts: nomine pancarpi, qui in lu
pancarpius.short: pancarpĭus and pancarpus, a, um, adj., = παγκάρπιος and πάγκαρπος, consisting or composed of all kinds of fruits.

panchaia.full: Panchāĭa, ae, f., = Παγχαία, a fabulous island in the Erythrœan Sea, east of Arabia, rich in precious stones, incense, myrrh, etc.: totaque turiferis Panchaia pinguis arenis, Verg. G. 2, 139: (phoenicem) deferre nidum prope Panchaiam in Solis urbem, Plin. 10, 2, 2, § 4: dives, Tib. 3, 2, 23; Val. Fl. 6, 119; Claud. III. Cons. Honor. f.—Hence, Panchaeus, a, um, adj., Panchœan: odores, Lucr. 2, 417; Verg. G. 4, 379; Ov. M. 10, 478.—Plur. as subst.: Panchaei, ōrum, m., the inhabitants of Panchaia,
panchaia.short: Panchāĭa, ae, f., = Παγχαία, a fabulous island in the Erythrœan Sea, east of Arabia, rich in precious stones, incense, myrrh, etc.: totaque turiferis Panchaia pinguis arenis, Verg.

panchrestarius.full: panchrestārĭus, ii, m. panchrestus, a confectioner: coquos, panchrestarios, Arn. 2, 70.

panchrestus.full: panchrestus (panchristus), a, um, adj., = πάγχρηστος, good or useful for every thing: medicamenta, Plin. 36, 20, 38, § 146; 23, 7, 71, § 136.— Transf., ironically: cum omnes ejus comites iste sibi suo illo panchresto medicamento amicos reddidisset, by his sovereign remedy, i. e. money, Cic. Verr. 2, 3, 65, § 152.
panchrestus.short: panchrestus (panchristus), a, um, adj., = πάγχρηστος, good or useful for every thing: medicamenta, Plin.

panchromos.full: panchrōmos, i, m., = πάγχρωμος (all-colored), a plant, called also verbenaca, App. Herb. 3.
panchromos.short: panchrōmos, i, m., = πάγχρωμος (all-colored), a plant, called also verbenaca, App.

panchrus.full: panchrus, i, m., = πάγχρους (of all colors), a variegated precious stone, Plin. 37, 10, 66, § 178.
panchrus.short: panchrus, i, m., = πάγχρους (of all colors), a variegated precious stone, Plin.

panchrysos.full: Panchrȳsos, on, adj., = πάγχρυσος, all golden: Berenice urbs, quae Panchrysos cognominata est, Plin. 6, 29, 34, § 170.
panchrysos.short: Panchrȳsos, on, adj., = πάγχρυσος, all golden: Berenice urbs, quae Panchrysos cognominata est, Plin.

pancratias.full: pancrătĭas, ae, m., for pancratiastes, a pancratiast, v. l. ap. Gell. 13, 27, 3 (al. pancratiastae).
pancratias.short: pancrătĭas, ae, m., for pancratiastes, a pancratiast, v.

pancratiastes.full: pancrătĭastes, ae, m., = παγκρατιαστής, a combatant in the pancratium, a pancratiast: Diagoras tres filios adulescentes habuit, unum pugilem, alterum pancratiasten, tertium luctatorem, Gell. 3, 15, 3; Plin. 34, 8, 19, §§ 57, 59; Quint. 2, 8, 13.
pancratiastes.short: pancrătĭastes, ae, m., = παγκρατιαστής, a combatant in the pancratium, a pancratiast: Diagoras tres filios adulescentes habuit, unum pugilem, alterum pancratiasten, tertium luctatorem, Gell.

pancratice.full: pancrătĭcē, adv., after the manner of the pancratiasts: pancratice atque athletice valere, i. e. heartily, finely, Plaut. Bacch. 2, 3, 14.
pancratice.short: pancrătĭcē, adv., after the manner of the pancratiasts: pancratice atque athletice valere, i.

pancratium.full: pancrătĭum (-tion), ii, n., = παγκράτιον. A complete combat; a gymnastic contest which included both wrestling and boxing; cf. Quint. 2, 8, 13: et patitur duro volnera pancratio, Prop. 4, 13, 8; Sen. Ben. 5, 3, 1: Autolycos pancratio victor, Plin. 34, 8, 19, § 79; cf. id. 35, 11, 40, § 139; Inscr. Fabr. p. 100, n. 226.— The herb succory, Plin. 20, 8, 30, § 74.— A plant, called also scilla pusilla, Plin. 27, 12, 92, § 118.

pancratius.full: pancrătĭus, a, um, adj., = παγκράτιος, Pancratian: metrum pancratium, a trochaic metre, consisting of a monometer hypercatalectus, Serv. Centimetr. p. 1819 P.
pancratius.short: pancrătĭus, a, um, adj., = παγκράτιος, Pancratian: metrum pancratium, a trochaic metre, consisting of a monometer hypercatalectus, Serv.

panda1.full: Panda, ae, f. 2. pando, a Roman goddess; acc. to Aelius ap. Non. 44, 7, Ceres; Varro, however, distinguishes her from Ceres, Varr. ap. Gell. 13, 22, 4: quod T. Tatio, Capitolinum ut capiat collum, viam pandere atque aperire permissum est, dea Panda est appellata vel Pantica, Arn. 4, 128: Panda, εἰρήνης θεός, Gloss. Philox.

panda2.full: Panda, ae, m., a Scythian river, Tac. A. 12, 16.
panda2.short: Panda, ae, m., a Scythian river, Tac.

pandae.full: Pandae, ārum, m., a people of India: gens sola Indorum regnata feminis, Plin. 6, 20, 23, § 76.—Hence, Pandaeus, a, um, adj., of the Pandœ: gens, Sol. 52.
pandae.short: Pandae, ārum, m., a people of India: gens sola Indorum regnata feminis, Plin.

pandana.full: Pandāna, ae, f. 2. pando, one of the oldest gates of Rome, so called because it always stood open: Saturnia porta, quam Junius scribit, ibi, quam nunc vocant Pandanam, Varr. L. L. 5, § 42 Müll.; Sol. 1, 13: Pandana porta dicta est Romae, quod semper pateret, Fest. p. 220 Müll.

pandarus.full: Pandărus, i, m. A leader of the Lycians, auxiliary of the Trojans, Verg. A. 5, 496.— A son of Alcanor, companion of Æneas, slain by Turnus, Verg. A. 9, 672 sq.; 11, 396.

pandataria.full: Pandātārĭa (-ērĭa or -ōrĭa), ae, f., a small island in the Tyrrhenian Sea, a place of exile under the emperors, now the island of Vandolina, Varr. R. R. 1, 8, 5; 3, 5, 7; Plin. 3, 6, 11, § 82; Suet. Tib. 53; Tac. A. 1, 53; 14, 62; Mart. Cap. 6, § 644; Mela, 2, 7.
pandataria.short: Pandātārĭa (-ērĭa or -ōrĭa), ae, f., a small island in the Tyrrhenian Sea, a place of exile under the emperors, now the island of Vandolina, Varr.

pandatio.full: pandātĭo, ōnis, f. 1. pando, a warping of wood, Vitr. 7, 1.

pandecter.full: pandecter, ēris, m., = πανδεκτήρ (allcontaining), the title of the fourth book of the work of Apicius.
pandecter.short: pandecter, ēris, m., = πανδεκτήρ (allcontaining), the title of the fourth book of the work of Apicius.

pandectes.full: pandectes or -ta, ae, m., = πανδέκτης, a book that contains every thing, a complete repertory, an encyclopedia, a title frequently given to books; cf. Gell. 13, 9, 4; Plin. H. N. praef., § 24. In gen.: novissime Tiro in Pandecte non recte dici ait, Charis. p. 186 P.— In partic.: Pan-dectae, ārum, m., the title of the collection of Roman laws made by order of Justinian from the writings of Roman jurists; the Pandects, Just. Ep. ad Sen. § 1.
pandectes.short: pandectes or -ta, ae, m., = πανδέκτης, a book that contains every thing, a complete repertory, an encyclopedia, a title frequently given to books;

pandemus.full: pandēmus, a, um, adj., = πάνδημος, affecting all the people, public, general: lues, an epidemic, Amm. 19, 4, 7.
pandemus.short: pandēmus, a, um, adj., = πάνδημος, affecting all the people, public, general: lues, an epidemic, Amm.

pandicularis.full: pandĭcŭlāris dicebatur dies idem et communicarius, in quo omnibus diis communiter sacrificabatur, Fest. p. 220 Müll.
pandicularis.short: pandĭcŭlāris dicebatur dies idem et communicarius, in quo omnibus diis communiter sacrificabatur, Fest.

pandiculor.full: pandĭcŭlor, āri, v. dep. 2. pando, to stretch one's self: ut pandiculans oscitatur, Plaut. Men. 5, 2, 80; cf.: pandiculari dicuntur, qui toto corpore oscitantes extenduntur, eo quod pandi fiunt, Fest. p. 220 Müll.

pandion.full: Pandīon, ŏnis, m., = Πανδίων. A king of Athens, father of Progne and Philomela, Hyg. Fab. 48; Ov. M. 6, 426; 676: Pandionis populus, i. e. the Athenians, Lucr. 6, 1143: Pandione nata, i. e. Progne, Ov. M. 6, 634.—Transf., for the nightingale, Ov. P. 1, 3, 39: Cecropiae Pandionis arces, Mart. 1, 26, 3.—Hence, Pandīŏnĭus, a, um, adj., Pandionian: Pandioniae Athenae, Ov. M. 15, 430: Pandionia Orithyia, the sister of Pandion, Prop. 1, 20, 31: res Pandioniae, the Athenian state, Claud. IV. Cons. Hono

pando1.full: pando, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. and n. for spando; root spa-; Sanscr. spha-, spread, grow; Gr. σπάω; cf. spatium. Act., to bend, bow, curve any thing (cf.: flecto, curvo): pandant enim posteriora, Quint. 11, 3, 122: manus leviter pandata, id. 11, 3, 100. — Mid., to bend itself, to bend: in inferiora pandantur, Plin. 16, 42, 81, § 223; 16, 39, 74, § 189; 16, 40, 79, § 219: apes sarcinā pandatae, id. 11, 10, 10, § 21: firmiora juga sunt alliganda, ut rigorem habeant nec pandentur onere fructuum, Col. 4

pando2.full: pando pandi (acc. to Prisc. p. 891 P.), passum, and less freq. pansum (v. Neue, Formenl. 2, p. 567 sq.), 3, v. a., to spread out, extend; to unfold, expand [from the root pat of pateo, cf. πετάννυμι, q. v.] (syn.: explano, explico, extendo). Lit.: pandere palmas Ante deum delubra, Lucr. 5, 1200; so, ad solem pennas, Verg. G. 1, 398: retia, Plin. 9, 8, 9, § 29: telas in parietibus latissime, id. 29, 4, 27, § 87: aciem, to extend, deploy, = explicare, Tac. H. 2, 25; 4, 33: rupem ferro, i. e. to sp

pandora.full: Pandōra, ae (gen. Pandoras, Plin. 36, 5, 4, § 19), f. Πανδώρα, gifted by all, the first woman, made by Vulcan at Jupiter's command, and presented with gifts by all the gods, the wife of Epimetheus and mother of Pyrrha, Hyg. Fab. 142.—Prov.: Pandora Hesiodi, of a work executed by several hands, Tert. adv. Val. 12.

pandorius.full: pandōrĭus or pandūrĭus, i, m., i. q. pandura, Isid. Orig. 3, 20, 8.
pandorius.short: pandōrĭus or pandūrĭus, i, m., i.

pandosia.full: Pandōsĭa, ae, f., = Πανδωσία. A city in Epirus, on the Acheron, now Kastri, Liv. 8, 24; Plin. 4, 1, 1, § 4.— A city of the Bruttians, near the modern Mendocino, Liv. 8, 24; Just. 12, 2, 4.

pandrosos.full: Pandrŏsos, i. f., = Πάνδροσος, daughter of Cecrops and sister of Aglauros and Herse, Ov. M. 2, 559; 2, 738.

pandura.full: pandūra, ae, f., and pandūrĭum, ii, n., = πανδοῦρα, a musical instrument of three strings, invented by Pan, Isid. Orig. 3, 20: hircipedem (i. e. Pana) pandura ... Faunum tibia decuerunt, Mart. Cap. 9, § 906; 9, § 924.
pandura.short: pandūra, ae, f., and pandūrĭum, ii, n., = πανδοῦρα, a musical instrument of three strings, invented by Pan, Isid.

pandurizo.full: pandūrizo, āre, v. n. pandura, to play the pandura, Lampr. Elag. 32.

pandus.full: pandus, a, um, adj. 2. pando, bent, crooked, curved (mostly poet.; syn.: curvus, uncus): carina, Enn. ap. Vet. Schol. in Stat. Achill. 1, 558 (Ann. v. 560 Vahl.); Verg. G 2, 445: rami, Ov M. 14, 660: juga, id. Am 1, 13, 16: juvencae pandis cornibus, id. M. 10, 271: delphines, id. Tr. 3, 10, 43: rostrum, id. M. 10, 713: asellus, crook-backed, id. A. A. 1, 543: pandā urceus ansā, Mart. 14, 106, 1; Sil. 3, 277.—In prose: hominem nigrum et macrum et pandum, Quint. 6, 3, 58: cupressus et pinus habent

panegyricus.full: pănēgўrĭcus, a, um, adj., = πανηγυρικός, of or belonging to a public assembly or festival; hence, subst.: pănēgў-rĭcus, i, m., the festival oration of Isocrates, in which he eulogized the Athenians, Cic. Or. 11, 37; Quint. 10, 4, 4.— Transf., praising, laudatory, eulogistic: libelli, panegyrics, Aus. Prof. 1, 13.—More freq. subst.: pănēgўrĭcus, i, m., a eulogy, panegyric, Quint. 2, 10, 11; cf. id. 3, 4, 14: etiam malos panegyricis mendacibus adulantur, Lact. 1, 15, 13.
panegyricus.short: pănēgўrĭcus, a, um, adj., = πανηγυρικός, of or belonging to a public assembly or festival;

panegyrista.full: pănēgўrista, ae, m., = πανηγυριστής, a eulogist, panegyrist, Sid. Ep. 4, 1.
panegyrista.short: pănēgўrista, ae, m., = πανηγυριστής, a eulogist, panegyrist, Sid.

paneros.full: pănĕros, ōtis, or pănĕrastos, f., = πανέρως, a precious stone, supposed to have the property of making fruitful, Plin. 37, 10, 66, § 178.— Pănĕros, a Roman surname, Suet. Ner. 30.—As a slavename, Inscr. Marin. Fr. Arv. p. 631.
paneros.short: pănĕros, ōtis, or pănĕrastos, f., = πανέρως, a precious stone, supposed to have the property of making fruitful, Plin.

pangaeus.full: Pangaeus, i, m., and Pangaea, ōrum, n., = Πάγγαιον ὄρος, a mountain of Thrace, on the borders of Macedonia, near Philippi, now Pilaf Tepeh: Mons Pangaeus, Plin. 4, 11, 18, § 40: flerunt Rhodopeiae arces Altaque Pangaea, Verg. G. 4, 462; Luc. 1, 679.—Hence, Pangaeus, a, um, adj., Pangœan; also for Thracian (late poet.): nemora, Sil. 2, 73: juga, Val. Fl. 4, 631: arx, id. 1, 575.
pangaeus.short: Pangaeus, i, m., and Pangaea, ōrum, n., = Πάγγαιον ὄρος, a mountain of Thrace, on the borders of Macedonia, near Philippi, now Pilaf Tepeh: Mons Pangaeus, Plin.

pango.full: pango, nxi, nctum, and pēgi or pĕpĭgi, pactum (v. Neue, Formenl. 2, 474 sq.), 3, v. a. root pac-; Sanscr. pāca, band, fetter; Gr. πήγνυμι, fix; πάχνη, frost; πάσσαλος, peg, etc.; cf.: pagus, pagina, paciscor; old form paco, pago; cf.: rem ubipacunt, XII.Tab. ap. Auct. Her. 2, 13, 20; v. Prisc. 894 P., to fasten, make fast, fix; to drive in, sink in (syn.: figo, configo). Lit.: pangere, figere; unde plantae pangi dicuntur, Fest. p. 213 Müll.: clavum, Liv. 7, 3; v. clavus: tonsillam pegi laevo in
pango.short: pango, nxi, nctum, and pēgi or pĕpĭgi, pactum (v.

pangonius.full: pangōnĭus, ii, or pangōnus, m., = παγγώνιος, a precious stone, otherwise unknown, Plin. 37, 10, 66, § 178.
pangonius.short: pangōnĭus, ii, or pangōnus, m., = παγγώνιος, a precious stone, otherwise unknown, Plin.

panicellus.full: pānĭcellus, i, m. dim. panis, a little loaf, Plin. Val. 1, 6.

paniceus.full: pānĭcĕus, a, um, adj. id., made of bread: mensae, i. e. huge loaves, Serv. Verg. A. 3, 257.—As subst.: Pānĭcĕus, i, m., an inhabitant of Breadville: opus est Paniceis, milites panicei (a comic expression), Plaut. Capt. 1, 2, 59.

panicium.full: pānĭcĭum, ii, n. id.. Any thing baked, as bread, cakes, etc., Cassiod. Var. 9, 5.— = panicum, Italian panic-grass, Paul. Nol. Ep. 3 ad Sev.; Edict. Diocl. p. 27; cf. Not. Tir. p. 112.

panicoctarius.full: pānĭcoctārĭus, a, um, adj. paniscoquo, bread-making (late Lat.): mulier, Petr. Chrysol. Serm. 99.

panicula.full: pānĭcŭla (also pānŭcŭla, Paul. ex Fest. p. 220 Müll.; and contr. pānŭcla, Non. 149, 22), ae, f.; also pānĭcŭlus, i, m. dim. panus, a tuft, a panicle on plants. Lit.: tu legiones difflavisti spiritu, quasi ventus folia aut paniculum tectorium, a tuft of thatch, i. e. of reeds used for thatching, Plaut. Mil. 1, 1, 17; cf. id. Rud. 1, 2, 34; Plin. 16, 10, 19, § 49: Graecula rosa convolutis foliorum paniculis, id. 21, 4, 10, § 18: panicum a paniculis dictum, id. 18, 7, 9, § 53.— Transf., a swelling,

panicum.full: pānĭcum, i, n., Italian panic-grass: panicum Italicum, Linn.; Caes. B. C. 2, 22; cf. Plin. 18, 7, 10, § 53.
panicum.short: pānĭcum, i, n., Italian panic-grass: panicum Italicum, Linn.;

panifex.full: pānĭfex, fĭcis, m. panis-facio, a breadmaker, baker, Theod. Prisc. 4, 2; cf.: panifex, ἀρτοποιός, Gloss. Philox.

panifica.full: pānĭfĭca, ae, f. id., a female baker; plur., Vulg. 1 Reg. 8, 13.

panificium.full: pānĭfĭcĭum (pānĕf-), ĭi, n. id., the making of bread. Lit.: a pane et faciendo panificium coeptum dici, Varr. L. L. 5, § 105 Müll.— Transf., any thing baked, as bread, cakes, etc., Cels. 2, 18: verbenas coronasque et panificia libertus obtulisse ei visus est, offering-cakes, Suet. Vesp. 7.

panion.full: pānīon, ii, n., a plant, also called satyrion, App. Herb. 15.
panion.short: pānīon, ii, n., a plant, also called satyrion, App.

panionius.full: Pănĭōnĭus, a, um, adj., = Πανιώνιος, of or belonging to all Ionia, sacred to all Ionia, Panionian: regio omnibus Ionibus sacra et ideo Panionia appellata, Plin. 5, 29, 31, § 113: Apollo, Vitr. 4, 1.— Subst.: Pănĭōnĭum, ii. n., i. q. regio Panionia: ibi est Panionium, sacra regio, et ob id eo nomine appellata, quod eam communiter Iones colunt, Mel. 1, 17, 2.
panionius.short: Pănĭōnĭus, a, um, adj., = Πανιώνιος, of or belonging to all Ionia, sacred to all Ionia, Panionian: regio omnibus Ionibus sacra et ideo Panionia appellata, Plin.

panis.full: pānis, is, m. (neutr. collat. form pāne, is, Plaut. ap. Non. 218, 12, and Charis. p. 69 and 114 P.; v. infra; cf. also: non item apud vos est positum hoc pane et hic panis? etc., Arn. 1, 36.—In gen. plur., panium, acc. to Caes. ap. Charis. p. 69 and 114 P.; panuin, acc. to Prisc. p. 771 P.) [from the root pa, to feed; whence also πάομαι, pabulum, and pasco], bread, a loaf. Lit.: tunc farinam aquā sparsit et assiduā tractatione perdomuit finxitque panem, etc., Sen. Ep. 90, 23: a pistore panem pet

paniscus.full: Pāniscus, i, m., = Πανίσκος. A little Pan, a rural deity: si Nymphae, Panisci etiam et Satyri, Cic. N. D. 3, 17, 43; id. Div. 1, 13, 23; 2, 21, 48.— A Roman surname, Inscr. Gud. 172, 3.

pannarius.full: pannārĭus, a, um, adj. pannus, of or pertaining to cloth; subst.: pannāria, ōrum, n., presents of cloth, Stat. S. 1, 6, 31.

panneus.full: pannĕus, a, um, adj. id., ragged, tattered: panneus, ῥάκινος, Gloss. Philox.

pannicularius.full: pannĭcŭlārĭus, a, um, adj. panniculus, of or belonging to rags or tatters: pannicularia causa, Dig. 48, 20, 6.— Subst.: pannĭcŭlārĭa, ōrum, n., rags, tatters, ragged clothes, Dig. 48, 20, 6.

panniculus1.full: pannĭcŭlus, i, m. dim. pannus, a small piece of cloth, a rag, Cels. 7, 20; cf. id. 6, 18, 8: panniculus bombycinus, a light, short garment, Juv. 6, 258.— Pannĭ-cŭlus, i, m., the name of a mime, Mart. 2, 72, 4; 3, 86, 3; 5, 61, 12.

pannonia.full: Pannŏnĭa, ae, f., = Παννονία, a country lying between Dacia, Noricum, and Illyria, Plin. 3, 25, 28, § 147; Ov. Tr. 2, 225.— Hence, Pannŏnĭăcus, a, um, adj., Pannonian: augures, Spart. Sev. 10.— Pannŏnĭcus, a, um, adj., Pannonian: bella, Suet. Aug. 20: cattae, Mart. 13, 69, 1: Pannonicae stirpis canes, Nemes, Cyn. 126: pilei, Veg. Mil. 1, 20.— Pannŏnis, ĭdis, f. adj., Pannonian: Pannonis ursa, Luc. 6, 220.— Pannŏnĭus, a, um, adj., Pannonian; subst.: Pannŏnĭus, ii, m., a Pannonian: fallax Pannoniu
pannonia.short: Pannŏnĭa, ae, f., = Παννονία, a country lying between Dacia, Noricum, and Illyria, Plin.

pannositas.full: pannōsĭtas, ātis, f. pannosus, raggedness, flabbiness: cutis veluti ruginosa vel sulcata pannositas, quam Graeci ῥάκωσιν vocant, Cael. Aur. Acut. 1, 11, 86.

pannosus.full: pannōsus, a, um, adj. pannus, full of rags, ragged, tattered. Lit.: homines, Cic. Att. 4, 3, 5; Just. 2, 6, 19; 21, 5, 5: aedilis, Juv. 10, 102.— Transf. Rag-like, flabby, shrivelled, wrinkled: macies, Sen. Clem. 2, 6, 2: mammae, Mart. 3, 72, 3: faex aceti, that looks like rags, mothery, Pers. 4, 32.— Ragged, tattered, poor: resculae, App. M. 4, p. 148, 1.

pannuceatus.full: pannūcĕātus, a, um, adj. pannuceus, ragged, tattered: Pannuceati, the title of a comedy of Pomponius, Non. 18, 21; 31; 19, 22 et saep.

pannuceus.full: pannūcĕus and pannūcĭus, a, um, adj. pannus, ragged, tattered. Lit.: vestis, Petr. 14.—Subst.: pannūcĕa, ōrum, n., rags, Paul. Nol. Carm. 2, 12.— Transf., wrinkled, shrivelled, flabby: māla, Plin. 15, 14, 15, § 52; Cloat. ap. Macr. S. 2, 15: Baucis, Pers. 4, 21; Mart. 11, 46, 3.
pannuceus.short: pannūcĕus and pannūcĭus, a, um, adj.

pannulus.full: pannŭlus, i, m. dim. id., a small piece of cloth, a rag, Amm. 31, 2, 5.— Plur.: pannŭli, ōrum, m., rags, ragged clothes, App. M. 7, p. 190, 16.

pannuncularia.full: pannuncŭlārĭa, ōrum, n., i. q. pannicularia (v. pannicularius): pannus, pannunculus, pannuncularia, Not. Tir. p. 155.

pannunculus.full: pannuncŭlus, i, m., i. q. panniculus; v. the preced. art.

pannus.full: pannus, i, m. (neutr. collat. form pannum, i, Nov. ap. Non. 218, 27.—Dat. and abl. plur. pannibus, Enn. ap. Charis. p. 40 P.; Pompon. ap. Non. 488, 32) [πῆνος; Dor. πᾶνος], a cloth, a garment. Lit.: albo Fides Velata panno, Hor. C. 1, 35, 21; Mart. 2, 46, 9: eventus viridis panni, Juv. 11, 198. —Esp. of torn, worn-out clothes, rags, tatters: pannis annisque obsitus, Ter. Eun. 2, 2, 5; Lucr. 6, 1269; Sen. Contr. 1, 6; id. Ep. 20, 8: rara in tenui facundia panno, Juv. 7, 145; Petr. 83 fin.— Transf

pannuvellium.full: pannŭvellĭum, ii, n., the wound-up yarn of the woof, the bobbin of the shuttle, with the yarn wound upon it, Varr. L. L. 5, § 114 Müll.
pannuvellium.short: pannŭvellĭum, ii, n., the wound-up yarn of the woof, the bobbin of the shuttle, with the yarn wound upon it, Varr.

pannychismus.full: pannўchismus, i, m., = παννυχισμός, a watching all night long, Arn. 5, 173.
pannychismus.short: pannўchismus, i, m., = παννυχισμός, a watching all night long, Arn.

pannychius.full: pannўchĭus, a, um, adj., = παννύχιος, that lasts all night: negotium, Marc. Aur. ap. Front. Ep. ad M. Caes. 3, 5 Mai.
pannychius.short: pannўchĭus, a, um, adj., = παννύχιος, that lasts all night: negotium, Marc.

panomphaeus.full: Pănomphaeus, i, m., = Πανομφαῖος (the author of all oracles), an epithet of Jupiter, Ov. M. 11, 198.
panomphaeus.short: Pănomphaeus, i, m., = Πανομφαῖος (the author of all oracles), an epithet of Jupiter, Ov.

panope1.full: Pănŏpē, ēs, and Pănŏpēa, ae, f., = Πανόπη, a sea-nymph: Panopea virgo, Verg. A. 5, 240; 5, 825: Panope matertera, Albin. 1, 435.
panope1.short: Pănŏpē, ēs, and Pănŏpēa, ae, f., = Πανόπη, a sea-nymph: Panopea virgo, Verg.

panope2.full: Pănŏpē, ēs, f., a town in the south of Phocis: Panopes arva, Ov. M. 3, 19; Stat. Th. 7, 344.
panope2.short: Pănŏpē, ēs, f., a town in the south of Phocis: Panopes arva, Ov.

panopion.full: Pănōpĭon, ōnis, m. πανωπίων, all eye, a Roman surname, Val. Max. 6, 8, 6.

panormitanus.full: Pănormĭtānus (Panh-), a, um, v. Panormus, I. B.

panormus.full: Pănormus (Panh-), i, f., and Păn-ormum (Panh-), i, n., = Πάνορμος, the name of several cities. A city in Sicily, the modern Palermo: oppida Panormum, Solus, etc., Plin. 3, 8, 14, § 90: tergemino venit numero fecundo Panormus, Sil. 14, 262: judicia Panhormi, Cic. Verr. 2, 2, 26, § 63.— Hence, Pănormĭtānus (Panh-), a, um, adj., Panormitan: legati Panhormitani, Cic. Verr. 2, 2, 49, § 120: civitas, id. ib. 2, 3, 6, § 13.— A city of Samos, now Port Viskaraho, Liv. 37, 10 and 11.— A city of Crete, Pli
panormus.short: Pănormus (Panh-), i, f., and Păn-ormum (Panh-), i, n., = Πάνορμος, the name of several cities.

panosus.full: pānōsus, a, um, adj. panis, like bread: cibus panosus, Cael. Aur. Tard. 1, 4, 91; 2, 14, 203.

pansa1.full: pansa, ae, adj. pando, broad-footed, splay-foot, Plaut. Merc. 3, 4, 55.

pansa2.full: Pansa, ae, m., a Roman surname, e. g. C. Vibius Pansa, Cic. Fam. 10, 33, 3; 15, 17, 3; id. Phil. 5, 19, 53; 11, 9, 22 et saep.; cf. Plin. 11, 45, 105, § 254; Juv. 8, 96.
pansa2.short: Pansa, ae, m., a Roman surname, e.

pansebastus.full: pansĕbastus, a false read. for panerastus; v. paneros, Plin. 37, 10, 66, § 178.)

pansus.full: pansus, a, um, Part. and P. a., from 2. pando.

pantagathus.full: pantăgăthus, i, m., = πανταγαθός (all good). A bird of good omen, Lampr. Anton. Diadum. 4 fin.— A plant, also called pulegium, App. Herb. 92.

pantagias.full: Pantăgĭas, Pantăgĭes, and Pan-tăgia, ae, m., = Πανταγίης, Πανταγίας, a small river in the eastern part of Sicily, between Megaris and Syracuse, now Fiume di Porcari: ostia Pantagiae, Verg. A. 3, 689 Serv.; (acc. -ien) Ov. F. 4, 471; (acc. -iam) Claud. Rapt. Pros. 2, 58.
pantagias.short: Pantăgĭas, Pantăgĭes, and Pan-tăgia, ae, m., = Πανταγίης, Πανταγίας, a small river in the eastern part of Sicily, between Megaris and Syracuse, now Fiume di Porcari: ostia Pantagiae, Verg.

pantaleon.full: Pantălĕon, ontis, m., = Πανταλέων, a Greek proper name, Liv. 42, 15.
pantaleon.short: Pantălĕon, ontis, m., = Πανταλέων, a Greek proper name, Liv.

pantarces.full: Pantarces, is, m. πανταρκής, all-helping, a surname of Jupiter; also a proper name, Arn. 6, 199.

pantelium.full: pantĕlīum, ii, n., = παντελεῖον (allperfect), a holocaust offered in the worship of Mithras, Inscr. Marin. Fratr. Arv. p. 358.
pantelium.short: pantĕlīum, ii, n., = παντελεῖον (allperfect), a holocaust offered in the worship of Mithras, Inscr.

pantex.full: pantex, ĭcis, and usu. plur., pantĭces, um, m., the paunch, the bowels (syn.: venter, ilia): eo vos vostrosque pantices madefacitis, quom ego sim hic siccus, Plaut. Ps. 1, 2, 50: et aestuantes docte solvis pantices, i. e. sausages, Verg. Cat. 5, 31; Mart. 6, 64, 28.—In sing., Auct. Priap. 83, 19 dub.

pantheon.full: Panthē^on or -um, i, n., = Πάνθεον, Πάνθειον, the great temple of Jupiter, built by Agrippa, and restored by Hadrian, M. Aurelius, Septimius Severus, and Caracalla, now the Tempio di S. Maria Rotonda: Agrippae Pantheum, Plin. 36, 5, 4, § 38 (but id. 36, 15, 24, § 102, read tectum diribitori); 34, 3, 7, § 13; 9, 35, 58, § 121; cf. Inscr. Orell. 34; Spart. Hadr. 19; Amm. 16, 10, 14.— The statue of a god, adorned with the symbols of several other deities, Aus. Epigr. 30; Inscr. Grut. 1, 3 sq.; cf.
pantheon.short: Panthē^on or -um, i, n., = Πάνθεον, Πάνθειον, the great temple of Jupiter, built by Agrippa, and restored by Hadrian, M.

panther2.full: panther, ēris, m., = πάνθηρον, a hunting-net for catching wild beasts: rete quoddam panther, Varr. L. L. 5, § 100 Müll.
panther2.short: panther, ēris, m., = πάνθηρον, a hunting-net for catching wild beasts: rete quoddam panther, Varr.

panthera1.full: panthēra, ae, f., = πάνθηρ, like statera for στατήρ (masc. collat. form pan-ther, Auct. Carm. Phil. 50), a panther: pictarumque jacent fera corpora pantherarum, Ov. M. 3, 669; cf. Plin. 8, 17, 23, § 62: panthera imprudens olim in foveam decidit, Phaedr. 3, 2, 2.—The Romans were fond of introducing it in their combats of wild beasts, Cic. Fam. 2, 11, 2; Cael. ap. Cic. Fam. 8, 4, 5; 8, 9, 3.
panthera1.short: panthēra, ae, f., = πάνθηρ, like statera for στατήρ (masc.

panthera2.full: panthēra, ae, f., = πανθήρα, an entire capture, all that is caught at once: emere pantheram ab aucupe, Dig. 19, 1, 11, § 18.
panthera2.short: panthēra, ae, f., = πανθήρα, an entire capture, all that is caught at once: emere pantheram ab aucupe, Dig.

pantherinus.full: panthērīnus, a, um, adj. 1. panthera, of a panther or panthers. Lit.: pellis, Plin. 35, 11, 40, § 138.— Transf., spotted like a panther: mensae, Plin. 13, 15, 30, § 96.—* Trop., cunning, crafty: pantherinum genus (hominum), Plaut. Ep. 1, 1, 16.

panthius.full: Panthĭus, ii, m., one of the fifty sons of Ægyptus, Hyg. Fab. 170.
panthius.short: Panthĭus, ii, m., one of the fifty sons of Ægyptus, Hyg.

panthous.full: Panthŏus and Panthūs, i, m., = Πάνθοος (-ονς), the nephew of Hecuba and father of Euphorbus: Panthus Othryades, Verg. A. 2, 319: Panthous, Hyg. Fab. 115. —In voc. Panthu, Verg. A. 2, 322.—Hence, Panthŏĭdĕs, ae, m., the son of Panthous, Euphorbus. Pythagoras maintained that his soul animated the body of Euphorbus at the time of the Trojan war, and for this reason he was called Panthoi des: Panthoides Euphorbus eram, Ov. M. 15, 161: habentque Tartara Panthoiden iterum Orco Demissum, Hor. C. 1, 28,
panthous.short: Panthŏus and Panthūs, i, m., = Πάνθοος (-ονς), the nephew of Hecuba and father of Euphorbus: Panthus Othryades, Verg.

panticapeum.full: Panticapēum, i, n., a town on the Cimmerian Bosporus, Kertch, Plin. 4, 12, 24, § 78.
panticapeum.short: Panticapēum, i, n., a town on the Cimmerian Bosporus, Kertch, Plin.

pantolabus.full: Pantŏlăbus, i, m. παντολάβος, that takes all, the name of a parasite, Hor. S. 1, 8, 11; 2, 1, 22.

pantomima.full: pantŏmīma, ae, f. pantomimus, a female ballet-dancer, pantomime, Sen. Cons ad Helv. 12, 6.

pantomimicus.full: pantŏmīmĭcus, a, um, adj. id., of or belonging to pantomimes, pantomimic: ornamenta, Sen. Ep. 29, 12.

pantomimus.full: pantŏmīmus, i, m., = παντόμιμος, a ballet-dancer, pantomime (cf.: ludius, mimus). Lit., Suet. Aug. 45; id. Calig. 36; 55; 57 al.; Macr. S. 2, 7; Sen. Ep. 95, 56; id. Q. N. 7, 32, 3.
pantomimus.short: pantŏmīmus, i, m., = παντόμιμος, a ballet-dancer, pantomime (cf.: ludius, mimus).

panuncula.full: pānuncŭla, ae, f. dim. panus, the thread wound upon the bobbin in a shuttle, Not. Tir. p. 160.

panus.full: pānus, i, m., = πῆνος, Dor. πᾶνος, the thread wound upon the bobbin in a shuttle. Lit.: intus modo stet rectus subteminis panus, Lucil. ap. Prisc. 3 fin., and ap. Non. 149, 24; cf.: panus tramae involucrum, quem diminutive panuclam vocamus, Non. l. l.— Transf. A swelling, tumor: tumor quoque inguinum ex formae similitudine sic (sc. panus) vocatur, Non. 149, 24; Novat. ap. Non. 149, 28; Afran. ib. 25: panos aperit sevum pecudum, Plin. 30, 8, 22, § 75; 24, 11, 58, § 97; 35, 17, 57, § 195: viscum p

panyasis.full: Panyăsis, acc. sin, = Πανύασις, a Grecian poet, a relative of Herodotus, Quint. 10, 1, 54.

papa1.full: pāpa (pappa), ae, f. onomatopoeia, the word with which infants call for food: cum cibum ac potionem buas ac papas vocent, Varr. ap. Non. 81, 4.

papa2.full: pāpa, ae, m. id., a father, papa; hence, in eccl. writers, a bishop: optime papa, Prud. στεφ. 11, 127; Tert. Pudic. 13.

papa3.full: Papa, a Roman surname, Inscr. Don. Cl. 7, n. 32.

papae.full: păpae, interj., = παπαί, wonderful! how strange! indeed! papae! divitias tu quidem habuisti luculentas, Plaut. Rud. 5, 2, 33; id. Bacch. 2, 2, 29; id. Men. 5, 5, 20: papae! jugularas hominem, Ter. Eun. 2, 1, 23; 3, 1, 26; Pers. 5, 79.
papae.short: păpae, interj., = παπαί, wonderful! how strange! indeed! papae! divitias tu quidem habuisti luculentas, Plaut.

paparium.full: pāpārĭum, ii, n. 1. papa, pap, Sen. Contr. 2, 9.

papas.full: papas (pappas), ae and ătis, m., = πάππας, a governor, tutor: timidus praegustet pocula papas, Juv. 6, 632; Inscr. Murat. 1297, 11.
papas.short: papas (pappas), ae and ătis, m., = πάππας, a governor, tutor: timidus praegustet pocula papas, Juv.

papaver.full: păpāver, ĕris, n. (ante-class., m.) [etym. dub.; cf. root pa- of pasco, πέπαμαι], the poppy. Lit.: papaver Gallicanus, Cato ap. Charis. p. 64 P.: sesamum papaveremque, Plaut. Poen. 1, 2, 113; v. infra, prov.; Varr. ap. Non. 220, 11: luteum, Cat. 19, 12: spargens soporiferum papaver, Verg. A. 4, 486; id. G. 4, 131: Lethaeo perfusa papavera somno, id. ib. 1, 78: Cereale, id. ib. 1, 212: nigrum, Plin. 26, 8, 40, § 67; 20, 18, 76, § 198. —In plur.: summa papaverum capita, the heads of the tallest po

papaveratus.full: păpāvĕrātus, a, um, adj. papaver, made shining or white with poppies: toga, Plin. 8, 48, 74, § 195; cf. id. 19, 1, 4, § 21.

papaverculum.full: păpāvercŭlum, i, n. dim. id., a plant, called also leontopodion, App. Herb. 7.

papavereus.full: păpāvĕrĕus, a, um, adj. id., of poppies: comae, poppy-flowers, Ov. F. 4, 438.

paphiacus.full: Păphĭăcus, a, um, Păphĭē, ēs, and Păphĭus, a, um, v. 2. Paphos.
paphiacus.short: Păphĭăcus, a, um, Păphĭē, ēs, and Păphĭus, a, um, v.

paphlago.full: Paphlăgo (-on), ŏnis, m., = Παφλαγών, a Paphlagonian: Paphlagonum sata, Avien. Perieg. 969; Curt. 6, 11, 4.—Plur., Plaut. Pers. 3, 72.—Hence, Paphlă-gŏnĭus, a, um, adj., Paphlagonian, Plin. 6, 2, 2, § 5.—Subst.: Paphlăgŏnĭa, ae, f., the province of Paphlagonia, between Bithynia and Pontus, Cic. Agr. 1, 2, 6; Liv. 1, 1; Mel. 1, 19, 8.
paphlago.short: Paphlăgo (-on), ŏnis, m., = Παφλαγών, a Paphlagonian: Paphlagonum sata, Avien.

paphos1.full: Păphos or -us, i, m., = Πάφος, son of Pygmalion, and founder of the city of Paphos (v. 2. Paphos), Ov. M. 10, 297; Hyg. Fab. 242.
paphos1.short: Păphos or -us, i, m., = Πάφος, son of Pygmalion, and founder of the city of Paphos (v.

paphos2.full: Păphos (-us), i, f., = Πάφος, a city on the island of Cyprus, sacred to Venus, with a celebrated temple of Venus, the modern Baffo, Hor. C. 1, 30, 1; Mel. 2, 7, 5; Plin. 2, 96, 97, § 210; Tac. H. 2, 2: est celsa mihi Paphos, Verg. A. 10, 51: illa Paphon veterem linquens, Stat. Th. 5, 61: qui eum de Pharsalicā fugā Paphum persecuti sunt, Cic. Phil. 2, 15, 39.—Hence, Păphĭă-cus, a, um, adj., Paphian, Avien. Perieg. 227.— Păphĭē, ēs, f., the Paphian, i. e. Venus: sive cupis Paphien, Mart. 7, 74, 4;
paphos2.short: Păphos (-us), i, f., = Πάφος, a city on the island of Cyprus, sacred to Venus, with a celebrated temple of Venus, the modern Baffo, Hor.

papilio.full: pāpĭlĭo, ōnis, m. cf. πάλλω, brandish; palpitare, pila, a butterfly, moth. Lit.: ferali mutant cum papilione figuram, Ov. M. 15, 374; cf. Plin. 11, 19, 21, § 65; 21, 14, 47, § 81; 28, 10, 45, § 162.—Also of other winged insects, Plin. 11, 32, 37, § 112; 11, 23, 27, § 77.— Transf., a tent, pavilion: in expeditionibus apertis papilionibus prandit atque coenavit, Lampr. Alex. Sev. 51; Spart. Pescen. 11; Treb. Poll. Trig. Tyr. 16; Tert. ad Mart. 3; Vulg. Exod. 33, 8; id. Num. 16, 27; id. 2 Reg. 11,

papiliunculus.full: pāpĭlĭuncŭlus, i, m. dim. papilio, a little butlerfly, Tert. Anim. 32.

papilla.full: păpilla, ae, f. dim. papula, a nipple, teat, on the breast of human beings and of animals: papillae capitula mammarum dictae, quod papularum sint similes, Fest. p. 220 Müll.; Plaut. Rud. 2, 4, 10; Plin. 11, 37, 69, § 181: delphinum, id. 11, 40, 95, § 235: uberis, Col. 9, 11, 4; Plin. Ep. 3, 6, 2.— Transf. Poet., the breast: nudantes rejectā veste papillas, Cat. 66, 81: hasta sub exsertam donec perlata papillam Haesit, Verg. A. 11, 803: tunc nuda papillis constitit auratis, her breasts adorned wi

papillatus.full: păpillātus, a, um, adj. papilla, II. C., shaped like a bud: corymbus, Poët. ap. Anth. Lat. 1, p. 699 Burm.; so Hier. Ep. 66, n. 1.

papilus.full: Pāpĭlus, i, m., a Roman surname, Mart. 4, 48.
papilus.short: Pāpĭlus, i, m., a Roman surname, Mart.

papinianus.full: Pāpĭnĭānus, i, m., a celebrated Roman jurist under Septimius Severus, beheaded at the command of Caracalla, Spart. Sever. 21; Caracall. 4; 8.—Hence, Pā-pĭnĭānista, ae, m., a follower or admirer of Papinian, Just. in Ep. praef. Dig. 2.
papinianus.short: Pāpĭnĭānus, i, m., a celebrated Roman jurist under Septimius Severus, beheaded at the command of Caracalla, Spart.

papinus.full: Papīnus, i, m., a mountain in Cisalpine Gaul, Liv. 45, 12.
papinus.short: Papīnus, i, m., a mountain in Cisalpine Gaul, Liv.

papirius.full: Păpīrĭus, i (old form Păpīsĭus, Cic. Fam. 9, 21, 2; Paul. ex Fest. p. 23; Fest. p. 242 Müll.), m., the name of a patrician and plebeian gens, Cic. Fam. 9, 21, 2.—Thus, The dictator, L. Papirius Cursor, Liv. 8, 30; Cic. 1. 1.— C. Papirius Carbo, the friend of Ti. Gracchus, Cic. Leg. 3, 16, 35; id. Brut. 27, 43; 62, 221; id. Tusc. 1, 3, 5; Tac. Or. 34. —Hence, Păpīrĭus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to a Papirius, Papirian: Papiria lex, Plin. 33, 3, 13, § 46: tribus, one of the rural tribes, Liv. 8

papius.full: Pāpĭus, i, m., the name of a Roman gens.— C. Papius, a tribune of the people, the originator of the lex Papia de peregrinis exterminandis, Cic. Off. 3, 11, 47.— M. Papius Mutilus, a consul, who, together with his colleague, Poppaeus, passed, in the reign of Augustus, the lex Papia Poppaea, for the promotion of marriages, Tac. A. 2, 32; 3, 25; 28; suet. Claud. 23; id. Ner. 10; Aus. Epigr. 89.— Papia, wife of Oppianicus, Cic. Clu. 9, 27.—Hence, Pāpĭus, a, adj., of or belonging to the gens Papia: P
papius.short: Pāpĭus, i, m., the name of a Roman gens.— C.

pappo.full: pappo (papo), āre, v. a., to eat pap, to eat: liberto opus est quod pappet, Plaut. Ep. 5, 2, 62; Pers. 3, 17.

pappus.full: pappus, i, m., = πάππος. An old man, Varr. L. L. 7, § 30 Müll.— A grandfather, Aus. Idyll. 4, 18.— The woolly, hairy seed of certain plants, Lucr. 3, 386 Lachm.; also ap. Fest. p. 220 Müll.: semen ei lanuginis, quam pappon vocant, Plin. 21, 16, 57, § 97.— A plant, also called erigeron: quare eam Callimachus acanthida appellat, alii pappum, Plin. 25, 13, 106, § 168.

papula.full: păpŭla, ae, f. dim. root pamp-, pap, to swell; in Gr. πομφός; cf. 2. populus, a pustule, pimple, Cels. 5, 28, 18: ardentes, Verg. G. 3, 564: eruptiones papularum, Plin. 20, 7, 26, § 67: rubentes papulas sanare, id. 26, 11, 73, § 120; Vulg. Lev. 14, 56.—Prov.: papulas observatis alienas obsiti plurimis ulceribus, i. e. you see the mote in your brother's eye, but not the beam in your own, Sen. Vit. Beat. 27.

papulo.full: păpŭlo, āre, v. n. papula, to produce pustules or pimples, Cael. Aur. Tard. 2, 1, 3, 4.

papyraceus.full: păpȳrācĕus, a, um, adj. papyrus, made of papyrus: Ellychnium papyraceum, Plin. 28, 11, 47, § 168: naves, id. 6, 22, 24, § 82.

papyrifer.full: păpȳrĭfer, fĕra, fĕrum, adj. papyrusfero, papyrus-bearing, that produces papyrus: papyrifer Nilus, Ov. M. 15, 753: amnis, id. Tr. 3, 10, 27.

papyrinus.full: păpȳrĭnus, a, um, adj. papyrus, of or belonging to the papyrus plant: stilus, Varr. ap. Non. 168, 14.

papyrio.full: păpȳrĭo, ōnis, m. id., a place where papyrus grows abundantly, Vulg. Exod. 2, 5.

papyrius.full: păpȳrĭus, a, um, adj. id., of papyrus, of paper, Aus. Ep. 7, 47.

papyrus.full: păpȳrus, i, m. and f., and păpȳ-rum, i, n., = πάπυρος, the paper-reed, papyrus. Lit.: papyrum ergo nascitur in palustribus Aegypti, aut quiescentibus Nili aquis ... triangulis lateribus, decem non amplius cubitorum longitudine in gracilitatem fastigatum, Plin. 13, 11, 22, § 71: in Euphrate, id. 13, 11, 22, § 73. Ships were made of it, id. ib.; Luc. 4, 136: in vasis papyri super aquas, Vulg. Isa. 18, 2; and sails and cordage from its bark, Cels. 5, 28, 12; Col. 6, 6, 4; Pall. 3, 33; also shoes, M

par.full: pār, păris (collat. form of the nom. fem. paris, Atta ap. Prisc. p. 764 P.—Abl. pari and pare, acc. to Charis. p. 14 P.; Prisc. p. 763 ib.; the latterpoet.—Gen. plur. usu. parĭum; parum, acc. to Plin. ap. Charis. p. 110 P.), adj. cf. Sanscr. para, another, and prae, equal (cf.: aequus, similis). Lit.: par est, quod in omnes aequabile est, Cic. Inv. 2, 22, 67: par et aequalis ratio, id. Or. 36, 123: aequo et pari jure cum civibus vivere, id. Off. 1, 34, 124: vita beata ... par et similis deorum,

parabilis.full: părābĭlis, e, adj. paro, easily procured, easy to be had, of easy attainment (class.): divitiae, Cic. Fin. 1, 13, 36; cf. id. Tusc. 5, 33, 93: namque parabilem amo venerem facilemque, Hor. S. 1, 2, 119: cultus (corporis), Curt. 3, 5, 2; cf. id. 6, 2, 2; 8, 4, 14: res, Sen. Ep. 5, 4.

parabola.full: părăbŏla, ae, and părăbŏlē, ēs, f., = παραβολή, a comparison. Lit.: in omni parabole aut praecedit similitudo, res sequitur; aut praecedit res, similitude sequitur, Quint. 8, 3, 77; 6, 3, 59: qui simpliciter et demonstrandae rei causā eloquebantur, parabolis referti sunt, Sen. Ep. 59, 5.— Transf., in eccl. Lat., an allegorical relation, a parable, Tert. adv. Marc. 3, 5; Aug. quaest. Evang. 2, 45; Vulg. Job, 27, 1; id. Matt. 13, 3 et saep.— A proverb, Vulg. 3 Reg. 4, 32.— A taunting speech, Vulg.
parabola.short: părăbŏla, ae, and părăbŏlē, ēs, f., = παραβολή, a comparison.

parabolanus.full: părăbŏlānus, i, m. parabolus, lit., a reckless person, a sick-nurse, esp. in infectious diseases, Cod. Just. 1, 3, 18; cf. Cod. Th. 16, 2, 42 and 43.

parabolice.full: părăbŏlĭcē, adv. parabole, metaphorically dictare aliquid, Sid. Ep. 5, 17; Hier. in Matt. 15, 15 sq.

parabolus.full: părăbŏlus, i, m., = παράβολος, a reckless fellow, who risks his life on any thing, Cass. Hist. Trip. 11, 17.
parabolus.short: părăbŏlus, i, m., = παράβολος, a reckless fellow, who risks his life on any thing, Cass.

paracenterium.full: părăcentērĭum, ii, n., = παρακεντήριον, a surgical instrument for making a perforation, a couching-needle, Veg. Vet. 2, 18.
paracenterium.short: părăcentērĭum, ii, n., = παρακεντήριον, a surgical instrument for making a perforation, a couching-needle, Veg.

paracentesis.full: părăcentēsis, is, f., = παρακέντησις, a surgical t. t., a perforation, a couching or tapping, Plin. 25, 13, 92, § 144; Cael. Aur. Tard. 3, 8; Veg. 1, 43, 3.
paracentesis.short: părăcentēsis, is, f., = παρακέντησις, a surgical t.

paracharactes.full: părăchăractes, ae, m., = παραχαράκτης, a counterfeiter of coin, Cod. Th. 9, 21, 9.
paracharactes.short: părăchăractes, ae, m., = παραχαράκτης, a counterfeiter of coin, Cod.

paracharaximus.full: părăchăraxĭmus, a, um, adj. παραχαράκτης, counterfeit: adulterinus: adulterina nomismata et paracharaxima, Cassian. Colat. 1, 20.

parachelois.full: Părăchĕlōis, ĭdis and ĭdos, f., = Παραχελωις, a city in Thessaly, on the Achelōus, Liv. 39, 26.
parachelois.short: Părăchĕlōis, ĭdis and ĭdos, f., = Παραχελωις, a city in Thessaly, on the Achelōus, Liv.

paracletus.full: părā^clētus (ĕ scanned short, Prud. Cath. 5, 160; id. στεφ. 10, 430) or părā^clī-tus (ĭ scanned short, Prud. Perieg. 2622), i, m., = παράκλητος. An advocate, defender, helper, protector, comforter, Tert. Verg. Vel. 1; id. Anim. 55; Res. Carn. f.: Vulg. Johan. 14, 16; 15, 26.— One of the œons of Valentinian, Tert. adv. Val. 8.

paracynanche.full: părăcўnanchē, es, f., = παρακυνάγχη, an inflammation of one side of the throat, Cael. Aur. Acut. 3, 1, 3 (al. parasynanche).
paracynanche.short: părăcўnanchē, es, f., = παρακυνάγχη, an inflammation of one side of the throat, Cael.

parada.full: părăda, ae, f. perh. Celtic, a cover or an awning of a boat: subter paradas jacens, Aus. Ep. 5, 25; Sid. Ep. 8, 12.

paradiastole.full: părădĭastŏlē, ēs, f., = παραδιαστολή, a figure of speech, in which two different but similar things are put together and distinguished (pure Lat. distinctio), Rutil. Lup. Fig. Sent. 1, 4; Rufin. § 20 (written as Greek, Quint. 9, 3, 65).
paradiastole.short: părădĭastŏlē, ēs, f., = παραδιαστολή, a figure of speech, in which two different but similar things are put together and distinguished (pure Lat.

paradigma.full: părădigma, ătis, n., = παράδειγμα, in gram. and rhet. lang., an example, paradigm, Charis. p. 248 P.; Diom. p. 460 ib.; Don. Trop. p. 1779 ib. et saep.: paradigmate Platonico plenius, Tert. Anim. 43.
paradigma.short: părădigma, ătis, n., = παράδειγμα, in gram.

paradisiacus.full: părădīsĭăcus, a, um, adj. paradisus, of or belonging to Paradise, Paradisiacal: rosae, Ven. Fort. Carm. 6, 8, 1: Paradisiaca sedes, Paradise, Alc. 1, 298.

paradisicola.full: părădīsĭcŏla, ae, comm. paradisuscolo, a dweller in Paradise, i.e. in heaven, Prud. Hamart. 936.

paradisus.full: părădīsus, i, m., = παράδεισος, a park. Lit.: vivaria quae nunc vulgus, quos παραδείσους Graeci appellant, Gell. 2, 20, 4: in paradiso, hoc est in viridario, Aug. Serm. 343, n. 1; Vulg. Gen. 2, 8: malorum. an orchard, id. Cant. 4, 13.— Transf. Paradise, the dwelling-place of the first human beings, the Garden of Eden, Hier. Ep. 52, n. 5: plantatus paradisus in Eden, id. ib. 69, n. 6.— Paradise, the abode of the blessed, Tert. Apol. 47; id. Carm. Judic. Dom. 195: Vulg. Ecclus. 44, 16; id. Luc. 23
paradisus.short: părădīsus, i, m., = παράδεισος, a park.

paradoxus.full: părădoxus, a, um, adj., = παράδοξος, marvellous, strange, contrary to all expectation, paradoxical; only subst. pără-doxus, i, m., one who, contrary to expectation, has conquered both in the lucta and in the pancratium on the same day; in Gr. usu. called παραδοξονίκης (late Lat.), Aug. Princip. Rhet. n. 9. The mimes were also called paradoxi, Vet. Schol. ad Juv. 8, 184.— părădoxum or -on i, n. A figure of speech: paradoxon, sive hypomone, sustentatio vel inopinatum. Hoc schema suspendit sensum:
paradoxus.short: părădoxus, a, um, adj., = παράδοξος, marvellous, strange, contrary to all expectation, paradoxical;

paraenesis.full: păraenĕsis, is, f., = παραίνεσις, an exhortation, admonition, precept; gen. plur. paraeneseōn, Vulc. Avid. Cass. 3.
paraenesis.short: păraenĕsis, is, f., = παραίνεσις, an exhortation, admonition, precept;

paraetacene.full: Păraetăcēnē, ēs, f., = Παραιτακηνή, a district of Persia: supra Paraetacenen et Persiden, Plin. 6, 27, 31, § 131; Curt. 5, 13, 2.—Hence, Păraetăcae, ārum, m., = Παραιτάκαι, the Parœtacenes, Nep. Eum. 8; called also Păraetăcēni, Gr. Παραιτακηνοί, Plin. 6, 26, 29, § 116.
paraetacene.short: Păraetăcēnē, ēs, f., = Παραιτακηνή, a district of Persia: supra Paraetacenen et Persiden, Plin.

paraetonium.full: Păraetŏnĭum, ii, n., = Παραιτόνιον, a seaport town in Northern Africa, between Egypt and the Syrtes, now Marsa Labeit, Plin. 5, 5, 5, § 33; Ov. Am. 2, 13, 7; id. M. 9, 772.—Hence, Păraetŏnĭus, a, um, adj., Parœtonian: portus, Mela, 1, 8, 2.— Subst.: păraetŏnĭum, ii, n., a certain white and pure chalk found near Parœtonium, Parœtonium-white, Plin. 35, 6, 18, § 36; 33, 5, 27, § 90; Vitr. 7, 7.— Transf., Egyptian, African: Paraetonius Nilus, Stat. Th. 5, 12: urbs, i. e. Alexandria, Luc. 10, 9: litu
paraetonium.short: Păraetŏnĭum, ii, n., = Παραιτόνιον, a seaport town in Northern Africa, between Egypt and the Syrtes, now Marsa Labeit, Plin.

paragauda.full: părăgauda, ae, and părăgau-dis, is, f., a border, lace, worked on a garment. Lit.: auratae paragaudae, Cod. Just. 11, 8, 2; Cod. Th. 10, 21, 1.— Transf., a laced garment: interulas paragaudas duas, Val. ap. Vop. Prob. 4: paragaudem triuncem unam, id. ap. Treb. Claud. 17.
paragauda.short: părăgauda, ae, and părăgau-dis, is, f., a border, lace, worked on a garment.

paragoge.full: părăgōgē, ēs, f., = παραγωγή, in gram., a lengthening of a word, the addition of a letter or syllable to a word, paragoge (e. g. facio, facesso), Charis. p. 226 P.; Diom. p. 309 ib.
paragoge.short: părăgōgē, ēs, f., = παραγωγή, in gram., a lengthening of a word, the addition of a letter or syllable to a word, paragoge (e.

paragogia.full: părăgōgĭa, ōrum, n., = παραγώγια, aqueducts, Cod. Just. 11, 42, 10.
paragogia.short: părăgōgĭa, ōrum, n., = παραγώγια, aqueducts, Cod.

paragramma.full: păragrammă, ătis, n., = παράγραμμα, an error in writing, Hier. Ep. 71, n. 5.
paragramma.short: păragrammă, ătis, n., = παράγραμμα, an error in writing, Hier.

paralipomena.full: Părălīpŏmĕna, ōrum, n., = τὰ παραλειπόμενα (things omitted, not related), the books of the Chronicles in the Bible, Hier. Ep. 53, n. 8.
paralipomena.short: Părălīpŏmĕna, ōrum, n., = τὰ παραλειπόμενα (things omitted, not related), the books of the Chronicles in the Bible, Hier.

paralius.full: părălĭus (-os), on, adj., = παράλιος, that grows by the seaside, Plin. 20, 19, 78, § 206; 26, 8, 41, § 68.
paralius.short: părălĭus (-os), on, adj., = παράλιος, that grows by the seaside, Plin.

parallelogrammus.full: părallēlogrammus, a, um, adj., = παραλληλόγραμμος, consisting of parallel lines: mensura, Front. Colon. p. 116 and 130 Goes.
parallelogrammus.short: părallēlogrammus, a, um, adj., = παραλληλόγραμμος, consisting of parallel lines: mensura, Front.

parallelonius.full: părallēlōnĭus, a, um, adj., i. q. parallelus, parallel: terminus, Auct. Limit. p. 310 Goes.

parallelus.full: părallēlus, a, um, and părallēlos, on, adj., = παράλληλος, paraliel: parallelos linea, Vitr. 5, 8: circuli paralleli; or absol. paralleli, concentric circles on the celestial globe, parallels of latitude: nostri circulos appellavere, Graeci parallelos, Plin. 6, 33, 39, § 212; Mart. Cap. 8, § 817.
parallelus.short: părallēlus, a, um, and părallēlos, on, adj., = παράλληλος, paraliel: parallelos linea, Vitr.

paralus.full: Părălus, i, m., = Πάραλος (of or belonging to the sea), an Athenian hero whose portrait was painted by Protogenes, Plin. 35, 10, 36, § 101; 7, 58, 58, § 207; Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 60, § 135 Zumpt.
paralus.short: Părălus, i, m., = Πάραλος (of or belonging to the sea), an Athenian hero whose portrait was painted by Protogenes, Plin.

paralysis.full: părălўsis, is, f., = παράλυσις, palsy, paralysis: paralysi mederi, Plin. 20, 3, 8, § 14: paralysi periclitari, id. 20, 15, 59, § 165: adulescens, paralysin cave, Petr. 120; Vulg. 1 Macc. 9, 55.
paralysis.short: părălўsis, is, f., = παράλυσις, palsy, paralysis: paralysi mederi, Plin.

paralyticus.full: părălўtĭcus, a, um, adj., = παραλυτικός, struck with palsy, paralytic, Plin. 20, 9, 34, § 85; Petr. 131.—Esp., subst.: părălўtĭcus, i, m., a paralytic, a palsied person: graditur paralȳticus, Claud. Epigr. 49 fin.: paralyticos restringere, i. e. to heal, Tert. Apol. 21; Vulg. Matt. 4, 24; 9, 2.
paralyticus.short: părălўtĭcus, a, um, adj., = παραλυτικός, struck with palsy, paralytic, Plin.

paramese.full: părămĕsē, ēs, f., = παραμέση, the string next to the middle; hence, the next to the middle note, B b in the treble, Vitr. 5, 4. — Transf., the ring-finger; v. hypate.
paramese.short: părămĕsē, ēs, f., = παραμέση, the string next to the middle;

paranarrhinon.full: părănarrhīnon, i, n., the same as antirrhinum, Plin. 25, 10, 80, § 129.
paranarrhinon.short: părănarrhīnon, i, n., the same as antirrhinum, Plin.

paranete.full: părănētē, ēs, f., = παρανήτη, the last string but one; hence, the note next to the highest, Vitr. 6, 1; cf. id. 5, 4.
paranete.short: părănētē, ēs, f., = παρανήτη, the last string but one;

parangarius.full: părangărĭus, a, um, adj., = παράἀγγαρεία, that is done besides the service to which one is bound: praestatio, Cod. Just, 1, 3, 2.— Subst.: părangărĭa, ae, f., a service over and above that which one is bound to render, extra service, Cod. Just. 12, tit. 51; Cod. Th. 8, tit. 5.
parangarius.short: părangărĭus, a, um, adj., = παράἀγγαρεία, that is done besides the service to which one is bound: praestatio, Cod.

paranymphus.full: părănymphus, i, m., = παράνυμφος, a bridesman, Aug. Civ. Dei, 14, 18; 6, 9; Ven. Fort. Carm. 8, 5, 305.—In fem.: pără-nympha, ae, a bridesmaid, = pronuba, Isid. Orig. 9, 7.
paranymphus.short: părănymphus, i, m., = παράνυμφος, a bridesman, Aug.

parapaestus.full: părăpaestus, i, m., = παράπαιστος, a foot in poetry: anapaestus, parapaestus, Not. Tir. p. 184.
parapaestus.short: părăpaestus, i, m., = παράπαιστος, a foot in poetry: anapaestus, parapaestus, Not.

parapegma.full: părăpegma, ătis, n., = παράπηγμα (something fixed on or hung up; hence), a table of astronomical calculations, made of brass, and fixed or suspended to a pillar, Vitr. 9, 7.
parapegma.short: părăpegma, ătis, n., = παράπηγμα (something fixed on or hung up;

parapetasius.full: părăpĕtăsĭus, a, um, adj., = παραπετάσιος, covering, that serves to cover or shelter; hence, aedificia parapetasia, penthouses, sheds, Cod. Th. 15, 1, 39.
parapetasius.short: părăpĕtăsĭus, a, um, adj., = παραπετάσιος, covering, that serves to cover or shelter;

parapeteuma.full: părăpĕteuma, ătis, n., = παραπέτευμα, a ticket for which corn was received, a corn-ticket, Cod. Just. 11, 24, 2.
parapeteuma.short: părăpĕteuma, ătis, n., = παραπέτευμα, a ticket for which corn was received, a corn-ticket, Cod.

parapherna.full: părăpherna, ōrum, n., = παράφερνα, the separate possessions of a married woman, her property besides her dower, Dig. 23, 3, 9; Cod. Just. 5, 14, 8.
parapherna.short: părăpherna, ōrum, n., = παράφερνα, the separate possessions of a married woman, her property besides her dower, Dig.

paraphoros.full: părăphŏros, on, adj., = παράφορος, bad, of an inferior sort: paraphoron alumen, Plin. 35, 15, 52, § 184.
paraphoros.short: părăphŏros, on, adj., = παράφορος, bad, of an inferior sort: paraphoron alumen, Plin.

paraphrasis.full: părăphrăsis, is, f., = παράφρασις, a paraphrase: paraphrasi vertere, Quint. 1, 9, 2; 10, 5, 5.
paraphrasis.short: părăphrăsis, is, f., = παράφρασις, a paraphrase: paraphrasi vertere, Quint.

paraphrastes.full: părăphrastes, ae, m., = παραφραστής, one that paraphrases, a paraphrast, Hier. praef. ad Libr. Reg. fin.
paraphrastes.short: părăphrastes, ae, m., = παραφραστής, one that paraphrases, a paraphrast, Hier.

parapienos.full: părăpīēnos, i, m., = παρά-πιήεις, a foot in poetry (˘¯˘˘˘), Diom. p. 478 P.
parapienos.short: părăpīēnos, i, m., = παρά-πιήεις, a foot in poetry (˘¯˘˘˘), Diom.

parapotamia.full: Părăpŏtămĭa, ae, f., a district near the Tigris, Plin. 12, 28, 61, § 133.
parapotamia.short: Părăpŏtămĭa, ae, f., a district near the Tigris, Plin.

pararius1.full: părārĭus, a, um, adj. par, of or belonging to a pair: pararium aes appellabatur id, quod equitibus duplex pro binis equis dabatur, Fest. p. 221 Müll.

pararius2.full: părārĭus, ii, m. paro, an agent, factor, broker, Sen. Ben. 2, 23, 2; so of the go-between in an intrigue, id. Contr. 2, 9; 3, 15, 2.

parasanga.full: părăsanga, ae, m., = παρασάγγης, a Persian league, a parasang, containing 30 stadia, Plin. 6, 26, 30, § 124; Fest. p. 222 Müll.
parasanga.short: părăsanga, ae, m., = παρασάγγης, a Persian league, a parasang, containing 30 stadia, Plin.

parasceve.full: părăscēvē, ēs, f., = παρασκευή, the day of preparation, i. e. the day before the Sabbath, Tert. adv. Marc. 4, 12; id. adv. Psych. 14; Vulg. Matt. 27, 62; id. Luc. 23, 54.
parasceve.short: părăscēvē, ēs, f., = παρασκευή, the day of preparation, i.

parasemum.full: părăsēmum, i, n., = παράσημον, the ensign or flag of a ship, Vet. Schol. Juv. 4, 77
parasemum.short: părăsēmum, i, n., = παράσημον, the ensign or flag of a ship, Vet.

parasiopesis.full: părăsĭōpēsis, is, f., = παρασιώπησις, a figure of rhetoric, where one says he will not speak of such and such a thing, but, in the very act of so doing, suggests it: parasiopesis: hoc est, cum aliquid nos reticere dicimus et tamen tacitum intellegitur, Rutil. Lup. Fig. Sent. 2, 11.
parasiopesis.short: părăsĭōpēsis, is, f., = παρασιώπησις, a figure of rhetoric, where one says he will not speak of such and such a thing, but, in the very act of so doing, suggests it: parasiopesis: hoc est, cum aliquid nos reticere dicimus et tamen tacitum intellegitu

parasita.full: părăsīta, ae, f. parasitus, a female parasite: ciniflones, parasitae, Hor. S. 1, 2, 98.— Transf.: imitatrix avis ac parasita, Plin. 10, 23, 33, § 68.

parasitaster.full: părăsītaster, tri, m. id., a mean, sorry parasite: parasitaster parvulus, Ter. Ad. 5, 2, 4; cf. Prisc. p. 610; 618 and 628 P.

parasitatio.full: părăsītātĭo, ōnis, f. id., a playing the parasite, sponging, Plaut. Am. 1, 3, 23.

parasiticus.full: părăsītĭcus, a, um, adj. id., parasitic: perjuratiunculae, Plaut. Stich. 1, 3, 77: ars, id. Capt. 3, 1, 9: mensa, Aug. ap. Suet. Vit. Hor.

parasitor.full: părăsītor. āri, v. dep. id., to play the parasite, to sponge: parasitarier, Plaut. Stich. 4, 2, 54: parasitando pascere ventres suos, id. Pers. 1, 2, 3.

parasitus.full: părăsītus, i, m., = παράσιτος, lit. one who eats with another; hence, In gen., a guest (pure Lat. conviva): parasiti Jovis, the gods, Varr. ap. Aug. Civ. Dei, 6, 7; App. M. 10, p. 246, 35.—Hence, parasitus Phoebi, a player, actor, Mart. 9, 29, 9.— In partic., in a bad sense, one who, by flattery and buffoonery, manages to live at another's expense, a sponger, toad-eater, parasite (syn. scurra): nos parasiti planius ... Quasi mures semper edimus alienum cibum, etc., Plaut. Capt. 1, 1, 7; cf. id.

parastas.full: părastas, ădis, f., = παραστάς, a four-cornered pillar or column, a pilaster, Vitr. 10, 15; cf. parastata.
parastas.short: părastas, ădis, f., = παραστάς, a four-cornered pillar or column, a pilaster, Vitr.

parastata.full: părastăta, ae, f., = παραστάτης, a square pillar or column, a pilaster, Cato ap. Isid. Orig. 19, 2, 11: columnae habentes post se parastatas, etc., Vitr. 5, 1 (al. parastaticae).
parastata.short: părastăta, ae, f., = παραστάτης, a square pillar or column, a pilaster, Cato ap.

parastaticus.full: părastătĭcus, a, um, adj., = παραστατικός, of or belonging to pilasters, parastatic, Inscr. Fabr. p. 688, n. 100.— Subst.: părastătĭca, ae, f., = παραστατική. A square pillar or column, a pilaster: columnae atque parastaticae (al. parastatae), Plin. 33, 3, 15, § 52; Vitr. 9, 9; cf. Inscr. Labus Epigrafe Lat. Scop. ap. Egitto, p. 7.— In plur.: părastătĭ-cae, ārum, f., two bones in the knee of a horse, Veg. Vet. 4, 1.
parastaticus.short: părastătĭcus, a, um, adj., = παραστατικός, of or belonging to pilasters, parastatic, Inscr.

parastichis.full: părastĭchis, ĭdis, f., = παραστιχίς, a word formed of the initial letters of verses, an acrostic, Suet. Gram. 6 (written as Greek, Gell. 14, 6, 4).
parastichis.short: părastĭchis, ĭdis, f., = παραστιχίς, a word formed of the initial letters of verses, an acrostic, Suet.

parasynanche.full: părăsўnanchē, ēs, f., = παρασυνάγχη, v. l. Cael. Aur. Acut. 3, 1, 3; v. paracynanche.

parasynaxis.full: părăsўnaxis, is, f., = παρασύναξις, a secret, unlawful assembly: parasynaxes et conventicula, Cod. Just. 1, 5, 8, § 3.
parasynaxis.short: părăsўnaxis, is, f., = παρασύναξις, a secret, unlawful assembly: parasynaxes et conventicula, Cod.

paratarius.full: părātārĭus, a, um, adj. 1. paro, easily procured: parabilis, Apic. 8, 6 dub.

parate.full: părātē, adv., v. 1. paro, P. a. fin.

paratio.full: părātĭo, ōnis, f. 1. paro, a preparing, getting, procuring (rare for comparatio; not in Cic.): nulla inest paratio, Afran. ap. Non. 219, 27: rerum, Dig. 30, 1, 39 fin.: regni, a striving after sovereignty, Sall. J. 31, 7.

parator.full: părātor, ōris, m. id., a preparer, contriver (eccl. Lat.), Aug. c. Cresc. 1, 8.

paratragoedo.full: păratrăgoedo, āre, v. n., = παρατραγῳδέω, to express one's self in a tragic, pompous manner: ut paratragoedat carnifex, Plaut. Ps. 2, 4, 17.

paratura.full: părātūra, ae, f. 1. paro, a preparing, preparation (post-class.): materiarum, Tert. Pall. 3 fin.; id. Spect. 4; id. Cor. Mil. 1; id. Virg. Vel. 12; Vulg. 2 Par. 5, 5.

paratus1.full: părātus, a, um, Part. and P. a., from 1. paro.

paratus2.full: părātus, ūs, m. 1. paro, a preparing, fitting out, preparation, provision, = apparatus: nullum necessarium vitae cultum aut paratum requirentis, Cic. Fin. 5, 19, 53: paratu militum et armorum, Sall. Fragm. ap. Gell. 2, 27, 2; Liv. 10, 41, 3 Drak. N. cr.: proviso ante funebri paratu, Tac. A. 13, 17: natalem Vitellii diem celebravere ingenti paratu, id. H. 2, 95: mensaeque paratu Regifico, Val. Fl. 2, 652: magno cultu paratuque rerum et familiae, Gell. 19, 1, 7: lauto cenare paratu, Juv. 14, 13.—I

paraveredus.full: părăvĕrēdus, i, m. vox hibr., from παρά-veredus, a horse for extraordinary occasions, an extra post-horse, Cod. Just. 12, 51, 2; 19; id. Th. 8, 15, 7; 15 sq.; Cassiod. Var. 5, 39; 11, 14.

parazonium.full: părazōnĭum, ii, n., = παραζώνιον, a dagger, Mart. 14, 32 in lemm.
parazonium.short: părazōnĭum, ii, n., = παραζώνιον, a dagger, Mart.

parca.full: Parca, ae, f. root πλεκ-; cf. πλέκω, πλοκή; Lat. plecto, plico, one of the goddesses of Fate, whose Latin names are Nona, Decuma, and Morta, Caesell. Vindex ap. Gell. 3, 16, 11 (their Greek names are Clotho, Lachesis, and Atropos, Hyg. Fab. 171).—In sing.: Parca non mendax, Hor. C. 2, 16, 39: tenax veri, Pers. 5, 48: dura, Ov. P. 4, 15, 36.—Plur., the Fates: Parcae, Hesperides, etc.: quos omnes Erebo et Nocte natos ferunt, Cic. N. D. 3, 17, 44: Parcae fatalia nentes Stamina non ulli dissoluenda

parce.full: parcē, adv., v. parcus fin. A.

parciloquium.full: parcĭlŏquĭum, ii, n. parce-loquor, a speaking sparingly, reserve in conversation (post-class.), App. M. 5, p. 164, 34.

parcipromus.full: parcī^prōmus, i, m. parce-promo, one that gives sparingly, a niggard, curmudgeon (Plautin.): qui cum geniis suis belligerant parcipromi, Plaut. Truc. 1, 2, 81; id. Ps. 5, 1, 22.

parcitas.full: parcĭtas, ātis, f. parcus, sparingness, parsimony (post-Aug.): animadversionum, Sen. Clem. 7, 22: moderatio, parcitas, sobrietas, Macr. Somn. Scip. 1, 8: ciborum, Cael. Aur. Tard. 3, 8, 118; Pall. 1, 26, 1.— Mercy, moderation: sine ullā parcitate verberare aliquem, Cassiod. 3, Hist. Eccl. 2; id. ib. 6, 12.

parciter.full: parcĭter, adv., v. parcus fin. B.

parco.full: parco, pĕperci, less freq. parsi (the former constantly in Cic. and Cæs., the latter ante-class. and post-Aug.: parcui, Naev. ap. Non. 153, 21, or Com. 69 Rib.; part. fut. parsurus, Liv. 26, 13, 16; Suet. Tib. 62: parciturus, Hier. Ep. 14, 2), parsum, and less correctly parcĭtum, 3, v. n. and a. [for sparco; Gr. σπαρνός, rare; cf. Engl. spare; but v. also paucus, parvus], to act sparingly, be sparing with respect to a thing, to spare; constr. usually with dat. or absol.; ante-class. also with ac

parcus.full: parcus, a, um, adj., = παῦρος [v. parco], sparing in any thing, esp. in expenditure; in a good and bad sense, frugal, thrifty, economical; niggardly, penurious, parsimonious (syn.: tenax, restrictus). Lit. Absol.: detrusisti me ad senem parcissimum, Plaut. Aul. 2, 5, 9: patre parco ac tenaci, Cic. Cael. 15, 36: optimus colonus, parcissimus, modestissimus, frugalissimus, id. de Or. 2, 71, 287: parcumque genus patiensque laborum, Ov. M. 7, 656: parcā manu offerre aliquid, Hor. C. 3, 16, 43.— With

pardalianches.full: pardălĭanches, is, n., = παρδαλιαγχές, an epithet of a poisonous plant (aconitum) which chokes panthers, Plin. 27, 2, 2, § 7; 8, 27, 41, § 99; Sol. 17 fin.
pardalianches.short: pardălĭanches, is, n., = παρδαλιαγχές, an epithet of a poisonous plant (aconitum) which chokes panthers, Plin.

pardalios.full: pardălī^os, ii, m., = παρδάλειος (sc. λίθος), a precious stone spotted like a panther, jasper, Plin. 37, 11, 73, § 190.

pardalis.full: pardălis, is, f., = πάρδαλις, a female panther, Curt. 5, 1, 21.
pardalis.short: pardălis, is, f., = πάρδαλις, a female panther, Curt.

pardalium.full: pardălĭum, ii, n. pardalis, a kind of ointment that smells like a panther, Plin. 13, 1, 2, § 6.

pardus.full: pardus, i, m., = πάρδος, a male panther: nunc varias (pantheras) et pardos, qui mares sunt, appellant in eo omni genere creberrimo in Africā Syriāque, Plin. 8, 17, 23, § 63; 10, 73, 94, § 202; 11, 37, 65, § 172; Juv. 11, 123.—Prov.: si mutare potest Aethiops pellem suam, aut pardus varietates suas, Vulg. Jer. 13, 23.
pardus.short: pardus, i, m., = πάρδος, a male panther: nunc varias (pantheras) et pardos, qui mares sunt, appellant in eo omni genere creberrimo in Africā Syriāque, Plin.

pareas.full: părēas or părīas, ae, m., = παρείας, a kind of snake, Luc. 9, 721; cf.: pareas serpens, qui semper in caudā ambulat et sulcum facere videtur, Isid. Orig. 12, 4.
pareas.short: părēas or părīas, ae, m., = παρείας, a kind of snake, Luc.

parectatus.full: părectătus, a, um, adj., = παρέκτατος, grown up, marriageable (ante-class.), Lucil. and Varr. ap. Non. 67, 11 sq.
parectatus.short: părectătus, a, um, adj., = παρέκτατος, grown up, marriageable (ante-class.), Lucil.

paredros.full: părē^dros, i, m., = πάρεδρος, that sits by one's side, remains with one: paredri spiritus, familiar spirits, Tert. Anim. 28.
paredros.short: părē^dros, i, m., = πάρεδρος, that sits by one's side, remains with one: paredri spiritus, familiar spirits, Tert.

paregoria.full: părēgŏrĭa, ae, f., = παρηγορία, alleviation, ease: paregoriam praestare, App. Herb. 24.
paregoria.short: părēgŏrĭa, ae, f., = παρηγορία, alleviation, ease: paregoriam praestare, App.

paregoricus.full: părēgŏrĭcus, a, um, adj. paregoria, alleviating, assuaging: adjutoria, Theod. Prisc. 1, 9: remedium, Marc. Emp. 36.

paregorizo.full: părēgŏrizo, āvi, 1, v. a. id., to soothe, alleviate, assuage (eccl. Lat.), Aug. in Psa. 122, 11.

parelion.full: părēlĭon, i, n., = παρήλιον, a mock sun, parhelion: parelia sunt imagines solis in nube spissā et vicinā in modum speculi. Quidam parelion ita definiunt: nubes rotunda et splendida, similisque soli, Sen. Q. N. 1, 11, 2: solent et bina fieri parelia, id. ib. 1, 13, 1.
parelion.short: părēlĭon, i, n., = παρήλιον, a mock sun, parhelion: parelia sunt imagines solis in nube spissā et vicinā in modum speculi.

parens1.full: pārens, entis, Part. and P. a., from pareo.

parens2.full: părens, entis, m. and f. (gen. plur. parentum and parentium, cf. Varr. L. L. 8, § 66 Müll.; Charis. p. 111 P.; Diom. p. 282 ib.: masculino genere parentem appellabant antiqui etiam matrem, Fest. p. 151 Müll.; so, Gracchus, Charis. p. 79 P.) [pario], a procreator, a father or mother, a parent; most freq. in the plur., parents. Lit.: SI PARENTEM PVER VERBERIT ... DIVIS PARENTVM SACER ESTO, Lex regia: qui parentem aut hospitem Necasset, Enn. ap. Non. 153, 29 (Trag. v. 239 Vahl.): parens tuus, Cic.

parentalia.full: părentālĭa, ĭum, v parentalis, II. B.

parentalis.full: părentālis, e, adj. 2. parens, of or belonging to parents, parental: umbrae, of my parents, Ov.
