Tr. 4, 10, 87.— In partic., of or belonging to the festival in honor of dead parents or relatives: dies, the day of the festival in honor of the dead, Ov. F. 2, 548: mos, i. e. the annually repeated combat of the birds which rose from Memnon's funeral pile, and which were therefore regarded as his children, id. M. 13, 619 (cf. id. Am. 1, 13, 4).— Subst.: părentālĭa, ĭum, n. A festival in honor of dead

parentatio.full: părentātĭo, ōnis, f. parento, funeral obsequies for parents or near relatives (postclass.), Tert. Spect. 12.

parentela.full: părentēla, ae, f. 2. parens, relationship (post-class.), Capitol. Gord. 23.

parenticida.full: părentĭcīda, ae, m. parens-caedo, a parricide, Not. Tir. p. 79.

parento.full: părento, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. 2. parens, to offer a solemn sacrifice in honor of deceased parents or relatives (cf.: lito, sacrifico). Lit.: cujus sepulcrum usquam exstet, ubi parentetur, Cic. Phil. 1, 6, 13: parentemus Cethego, id. Fl. 38, 96: Februario mense mortuis parentari voluerunt, id. Leg. 2, 21, 54: hostiā maximā parentare, id. ib. 2, 21, 54; Cenot. Pis. in Inscr. Orell. 643: mortuis certe interdiu parentatur, Sen. Ep. 122, 3; Plin. 18, 12, 30, § 118: non sacrificamus, nec parentamus: se

pareo.full: pārĕo (parrĕo), ŭi, pārĭtum, 2, v. n. intr. form of paro, to make ready; părio, to bring forth; hence, to be ready, at hand, to come forth, appear, be visible, show one's self; to be present or at hand. Lit. (rare; not in Cic. or Cæs.): immolanti jocinera replicata paruerunt, Suet. Aug. 95: quoties paruit Hermogenes, Mart. 12, 29, 18: haec (fenestra) videt Inarimen, illi Prochyta aspera paret, Stat. S. 2, 2, 76: quae si parent simul, Quint. 1, 12, 4: caeli cui sidera parent, are open, intelligib

pareoron.full: părēŏron, i, n., = παρήορον, a plant: Pythagoras heliotropion (vocat) pareoron, App. Herb. 49.
pareoron.short: părēŏron, i, n., = παρήορον, a plant: Pythagoras heliotropion (vocat) pareoron, App.

parergon.full: părergon, i, n., = πάρεργον, an extra ornament: adjecerit parvulas naves longas in iis, quae pictores parerga appellant, Plin. 35, 10, 36, § 101; Vitr. 9, 9; Inscr. Grut. 59, 2; 77, 3 al.—Plur.: Părerga, ōn, the title of a work by Attius, Non. 61, 24.
parergon.short: părergon, i, n., = πάρεργον, an extra ornament: adjecerit parvulas naves longas in iis, quae pictores parerga appellant, Plin.

parhedrus.full: Parhĕdrus, i, m., = Πάρεδρος, a male proper name, Cic. Fam. 16, 18, 2; Inscr. Grut. 969, 7.
parhedrus.short: Parhĕdrus, i, m., = Πάρεδρος, a male proper name, Cic.

parhippus.full: părhippus, i, m., = πάριππος, an extra horse above the number allowed, demanded by a person who travels by the public post, Cod. Th. 8, 5, 14; id. Just. 12, 51, 4.
parhippus.short: părhippus, i, m., = πάριππος, an extra horse above the number allowed, demanded by a person who travels by the public post, Cod.

parhypate.full: părhўpătē, ēs, f., = παρυπάτη, the string next to the uppermost, the note next to the highest, Vitr. 5, 4.
parhypate.short: părhўpătē, ēs, f., = παρυπάτη, the string next to the uppermost, the note next to the highest, Vitr.

pariambedes.full: părĭambēdes, is, n., = παριαμβώδης, the metrical foot˘¯˘¯¯ (e. g. pĕtītĭōnēs), Diom. p. 479 P.
pariambedes.short: părĭambēdes, is, n., = παριαμβώδης, the metrical foot˘¯˘¯¯ (e.

pariambus.full: părĭambus, i, m., = παρίαμβος. A metrical foot consisting of a short and two long syllables (˘¯¯), Diom. p. 475 P.— A metrical foot consisting of a long and four short syllables (¯˘˘˘˘), Diom. p. 478 P.— A metrical foot consisting of two short syllables, commonly called a pyrrhichius, Diom. p. 471 P.; cf. Mar. Vict. p. 2486 ib.; Quint. 9, 4, 80.

parianus.full: Părĭānus, a, um, v. Parium, II.

pariatio.full: părĭātĭo, ōnis, f. 1. pario, a balancing, settling of accounts, Dig. 12, 6, 67.

pariator.full: părĭātor, ōris, m. id., a balancer, settler of an account, Dig. 35, 1, 79.

pariatoria.full: părĭātōrĭa, ae, f. id., a balancing, settling (late Lat.), Aug. in Psa. 61.

parientia.full: pārĭentĭa, ae, f. pareo, obedience (post-class: and dub.; others read patientia): parientiam accommodare, Cod. Just. 3, 4, 1: commodare, Cassiod. Var. 7, 27: monstrare, id. ib. 3, 24.

paries.full: părĭēs, ĕtis, m. (in Verg. A. 2, 442; 5, 589, pārietibus, quadrisyl.; see Carey's Lat. Prosody, § 47, p. 173) [kindr. with Sanscr. paryanta, from pari-iyanta, margo; Gr. πέρας, πεῖραρ], a wall (cf.: murus, maceria): aut permaceat paries percussus trifaci, Enn. ap. Fest. s. v. trifax, p. 367 Müll. (Ann. v. 524 Vahl.): tosti alti stant parietes, id. ap. Cic. Tusc. 3, 19, 44 (Trag. v. 116 ib.): perfodere parietem, Plaut. Mil. 2, 1, 64; id. As. 3, 2, 17: perforator parietum, a term of abuse, id. Ps.

parietalis.full: părĭĕtālis, e, adj. paries, of or belonging to walls: parietalis herba, the herb pellitory, Marc. Emp. 13; cf. parietarius, II.

parietarius.full: părĭĕtārĭus, a, um, adj. id., of or belonging to walls: structor, Firm. Math. 8, 24; Inscr. Rein. cl. 11, n. 112: pictor, Edict. Diocl. p. 19.— Subst.: părĭĕ-tārĭa, ae, f., the herb pellitory or parietary: herbam perdicalem Latini muralem et parietariam, alii vitriariam appellant, App. Herb. 81.—Acc. to Aur. Vict. Epit. 41, Constantine the Great bestowed on the emperor Trajan, on account of the numerous inscriptions which he had caused to be placed on buildings, the sobriquet of herba parietaria

parietinus.full: părĭĕtĭnus, a, um, adj. paries, of or belonging to walls: parietina forma, the shape of a wall, Tert. Pud. 20: herba, v. parietarius, II.— Subst.: părĭĕtĭnae, ārum, f., old fallen-down walls, ruins (class.): villarum, Sisenn. ap. Non. 141, 23: Corinthi, Cic. Tusc. 3, 22, 53; id. Fam. 13, 1, 3: aizoum minus in muris parietinisque nascitur, Plin. 25, 13, 102, § 161; 24, 19, 119, § 183; Vulg. Ezech. 36, 4.—Trop.: in tantis tenebris et quasi parietinis rei publicae, Cic. Fam. 4, 3, 2.

parilia.full: Părīlĭa, ium, v. Palilia, under Palilis.

parilis.full: părĭlis, e, adj. par, equal, like (anteclass. and poet.): et noctes pariles agitare diebus, Lucr. 1, 1067: aetas, Ov. M. 8, 631: vox, id. Tr. 1, 8, 26: furor, Nemes. Ecl. 4, 5 (but in Varr. L. L. 9, § 29 Müll., paria is the better reading; v. Müll. ad loc.).—Adv.: părĭlĭter, equally, Charis. p. 191 P.

parilitas.full: părĭlĭtas, ātis, f. parilis, equality (post-class.): virtutum, Gell. 14, 3, 8; so App. M. 2, p. 119, 14; Auct. Itin. Alex. 3 and 8 Mai.

parilitius.full: Părīlĭtĭus, a, um, Palilicius, q. v.

pario1.full: părĭo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. and n. par. Act. In gen., to make equal; hence, pass., with force of mid., to be equal (postclass.): pariari deo, Tert. Res. Carn. 6.— In partic., to settle, pay in full a debt: nummos alicui, Dig. 40, 1, 4: QVISQVIS MENSIB. CONTINENTER NON PARIAVERIT, has not paid his share, Inscr. Lanuv. (a. p. Chr. 136) in Momms. Collegg. et Sodalicc. Romann.— In part. perf. mid.: PARIATVS, that has paid his share, Inscr. Lanuv. in Momms. Collegg. et Sodalicc. Romann.— Neutr., to be

pario2.full: părĭo, pĕpĕri, părĭtum, and partum, 3 (fut. part. parturam, Plaut. Am. 2, 2, 86; fut. paribis for paries, Pompon. ap. Non. 508, 3; inf. parire, Enn. ap. Varr. L. L. 5, § 59 Müll., and in Diom. p. 378 P.; Plaut. Fragm. ap. Philarg. Verg. E. 2, 63), v. a. cf. Gr. root πορ- in ἔπορον, gave, πέπρωται, is fated; Lat. portio, partus, puerpera, perh. parare, to bring forth, to bear; of animals, to drop, lay, spawn, etc. (syn. gigno). Lit.: si quintum pareret mater ejus, asinum fuisse pariturum, Cic. de

pario3.full: părĭo, īre, the ground form of aperio and operio.
pario3.short: părĭo, īre, the ground form of aperio and operio.

paris.full: Păris, ĭdis, m., = Πάρις. The son of Priam and Hecuba, also called Alexandros. As soon as he was born, on account of an ominous dream of his mother, he was exposed on Mount Ida to perish; he was there reared by the shepherds, and there he decided the dispute between Juno, Pallas, and Venus in favor of the last, who promised him Helen, the most beautiful of women, as a reward; by carrying her off to Troy, he was the cause of the Trojan war, in which he fell by the arrow of Philoctetes: quapropter

parisii.full: Părīsĭi, ōrum, m., a people of Celtic Gaul, bordering on the Senones, Caes. B. G. 7, 4; 35; 75; Plin. 4, 18, 32, § 107. Their chief city, Lutetia Parisiorum (late Lat. also Parisii), stood on the isle of Paris, Caes. B. G. 6, 3; 7, 57; Amm. 20, 4, 11; 20, 5, 1.—Hence, Părīsĭăcus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to the Parisians, Parisian: arx, Ven. Vit. S. Mart. 4, 636: NAVTAE, Inscr. Murat. 1066, 5.
parisii.short: Părīsĭi, ōrum, m., a people of Celtic Gaul, bordering on the Senones, Caes.

parison.full: părĭson, i, n., = πάρισον, an even balance in the members of a sentence, Mart. Cap. 5, § 531; written as Gr., Quint. 9, 2, 76.
parison.short: părĭson, i, n., = πάρισον, an even balance in the members of a sentence, Mart.

paritas.full: părĭtas, ātis, f. par, equality, parity (post-class.): in impari paritas contineri nequit, Arn. 2, 78; Boëth. Arithm. 1, 5.

parito.full: părĭto, āre, v. freq. a. 1. paro, to prepare, get ready, be about to do a thing (Plautin.): quo nunc ire paritas? Plaut. Merc. 3, 4, 64.—With ut: ecquas viginti minas Paritas ut a med auferas? Plaut. Ps. 1, 5, 71.

paritor.full: pārĭtor, ōris, m. pareo, a servant, attendant, body-guard (post-class.), Aur. Vict. Caes. 2 fin.

parium.full: Părĭum, or -on, ĭi, n., = Πάριον, a city of Mysia, on the Propontis, now Kamares, Sall. H. Fragm. 4, 61, 14; Mel. 1, 19; Plin. 5, 32, 40, § 141; Val. Fl. 2, 622.—Hence, Părĭānus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Parium, Parian: civitas, Cic. Fam. 13, 53: colonia, i. e. Parium, Plin. 4, 11, 18, § 48: colias, a kind of fish, id. 32, 11, 53, § 146 (better read. Partianus).
parium.short: Părĭum, or -on, ĭi, n., = Πάριον, a city of Mysia, on the Propontis, now Kamares, Sall.

parius.full: Părĭus, a, um, v. Paros, II.

parma1.full: parma (or in the collat. form pal-ma, Tib. 1, 9, 82; and so many MSS. in Prop. 2, 19, 44 (3, 20, 8); 4 (5), 10, 40; Liv. 22, 1, 9), ae (old gen. parmaï, Lucr. 4, 847), f., = πάρμη, a small, round shield, a target, carried by the light infantry and the cavalry. Lit.: configunt parmam, Enn. ap. Macr. S. 6, 3 (Ann. v. 432 Vahl.); Varr. ap. Non. 552, 30: desiliunt ex equis, provolant in primum agmen et pro antesignanis parmas obiciunt, Liv. 2, 20; 2, 6, 9; 31, 35 fin.: hic miles (veles) tripedalem p

parma2.full: Parma, ae, f., the city of Parma, in Gallia Cispadana, between Cremona and Placentia, famed for its breed of sheep, Plin. 3, 15, 20, § 115; Cic. Fam. 12, 5, 2; 10, 33, 4; Liv. 39, 55: velleribus primis Apulia, Parma secundis Nobilis, Mart. 14, 155, 1; cf. id. 2, 43, 4; 5, 13, 8.—Hence, Par-mensis, e, adj., of or belonging to Parma, Parman: Cassī Parmensis opuscula, Hor. Ep. 1, 4, 3.—In plur.: Parmenses, ĭum, m., the inhabitants of Parma, the Parmans, Cic. Phil. 14, 3, 8; Brut. ap. Cic. Fam. 11,
parma2.short: Parma, ae, f., the city of Parma, in Gallia Cispadana, between Cremona and Placentia, famed for its breed of sheep, Plin.

parmatus.full: parmātus, a, um, adj. 1. parma, armed with the parma: cohors, Liv. 4, 38, 3: ut parmatis, novae cohorti hostium, locus detur, id. 4, 39, 1.

parmenides.full: Parmĕnĭdes, is, m., = Παρμενίδης, a celebrated Grecian philosopher, a native of Elea, who, with Zeno, was at the head of the Eleatic school, Cic. Ac. 2, 42, 129; 2, 37, 118; id. N. D. 1, 11, 28.
parmenides.short: Parmĕnĭdes, is, m., = Παρμενίδης, a celebrated Grecian philosopher, a native of Elea, who, with Zeno, was at the head of the Eleatic school, Cic.

parmenio.full: Parmĕnĭo (-on), ōnis, m., = Παρμενίων, general and adviser of Philip of Macedon and of Alexander the Great.—Form Parmenio, Just. 12, 1, 3.—Form Parmenion, Curt. 7, 2, 8; Val. Max. 6, 4, ext. 3; Just. 12, 5, 3.
parmenio.short: Parmĕnĭo (-on), ōnis, m., = Παρμενίων, general and adviser of Philip of Macedon and of Alexander the Great.—Form Parmenio, Just.

parmula.full: parmŭla, ae, f. dim. 1. parma, a little, round shield, a small target. Lit.: relictā non bene parmulā, Hor. C. 2, 7, 10; Fest. p. 238 Müll.— Trop.: parmulam ventilare, Front. Or. Ep. 1 Mai.

parmularius.full: parmŭlārĭus, ii, m. 1. parma, II. B.. An adherent of the party of the Threces, who were armed with the parma, a Parmularian, Suet. Dom. 10; Quint. 2, 11, 2.— A servant of the pontifices armed with the parma, Inscr. Grut. 1087, 6.

parnasus.full: Parnāsus and -os, also Parnas-sus or -os, i, m., = Παρνασός, afterwards Παρνασσός, a high mountain in Phocis with two peaks, sacred to Apollo and the Muses, at whose foot was the city of Delphi and the Castalian spring, now range of Liakhoura, Mel. 2, 3, 4; Plin. 4, 3, 4, § 7: mons ibi verticibus petit arduus astra duobus, Nomine Parnasus, Ov. M. 1, 317: biceps, id. ib. 2, 221; Pers. prol. 2: uterque, Stat. Th. 7, 346: Parnasi deserta per ardua, Verg. G. 3, 291: Parnasus gemino petit aethera col
parnasus.short: Parnāsus and -os, also Parnas-sus or -os, i, m., = Παρνασός, afterwards Παρνασσός, a high mountain in Phocis with two peaks, sacred to Apollo and the Muses, at whose foot was the city of Delphi and the Castalian spring, now range of Liakhoura, Mel.

parnes.full: Parnes, ēthis, m., = Πάρνης, -νηθος, a mountain range in Attica, on the borders of Bœotia, famous for its wine, and abounding in game, the modern Noyia: Parnesque benignus vitibus, Stat. Th. 12, 620; Sen. Hippol. 4.
parnes.short: Parnes, ēthis, m., = Πάρνης, -νηθος, a mountain range in Attica, on the borders of Bœotia, famous for its wine, and abounding in game, the modern Noyia: Parnesque benignus vitibus, Stat.

paro1.full: păro, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. cf. Sanscr. par, piparmi, to lead, to further; Gr. πόρος; Lat. porta, peritus; also -per in pauper, to make or get ready, to prepare, furnish, provide; to order, contrive, design, etc. (freq. and class.; syn.: apparo, comparo, acquiro); with personal, non-personal, and abstract objects; constr. usually with acc. or inf., rarely with ut, ne, or absol. Lit. In gen. With acc.: omne paratum est, Ut jussisti ... prandium, Plaut. Men. 2, 3, 14; cf. Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 27, § 62:

paro2.full: păro, āre, v. a. par, to make equal, esteem equal. * In gen.: eodem hercle vos pono et paro: parissumi estis iibus, Plaut. Curc. 4, 2, 20.— In partic., to bring to an agreement, arrange with any one: se paraturum cum collegā, Cic. Fam. 1, 9, 25; cf. Fest. p. 234 Müll.

paro3.full: păro, ōnis, m., = παρών, a small, light ship, Cic. poët. ap. Isid. Orig. 19, 1, 20 (ed. Orell. IV. 2, p. 572); Gell. 10, 25, 5; cf.: parones navium genus, ad cujus similitudinem myoparo vocatur, Fest. p. 222 Müll.
paro3.short: păro, ōnis, m., = παρών, a small, light ship, Cic.

parocha.full: părŏcha, ae, f., = παροχή, a supplying of necessaries to travelling public officers, purveyance (cf. parochus), Cic. Att. 13, 2, 2.
parocha.short: părŏcha, ae, f., = παροχή, a supplying of necessaries to travelling public officers, purveyance (cf.

parochensis.full: părŏchensis, e, adj. parochus, parochial (eccl. Lat.): presbyteri, Montan. Ep. 1, 4.

parochus.full: părŏchus, i, m., = πάροχος, a purveyor, a person who, for a certain sum, furnished travelling magistrates with necessaries, as beds, hay, straw, salt, etc. (pure Lat. copiarius). Lit., Cic. Att. 13, 2, 2; Hor. S. 1, 5, 46.— Transf., an entertainer, host, Hor. S. 2, 8, 36.
parochus.short: părŏchus, i, m., = πάροχος, a purveyor, a person who, for a certain sum, furnished travelling magistrates with necessaries, as beds, hay, straw, salt, etc.

parodia.full: părōdĭa, ae, f., = παρῳδία (a counter-song), a reply retaining nearly the same words or the same turn, a parody, Ps.-Ascon. Cic. Verr. 1, 10, 29.
parodia.short: părōdĭa, ae, f., = παρῳδία (a counter-song), a reply retaining nearly the same words or the same turn, a parody, Ps.-Ascon.

paroecia.full: păroecĭa, and, corrupted, părŏchĭa, ae, f., = παροικία, an ecclesiastical district, a parish: castellum ad paroeciam Hipponensis Ecclesiae pertinebat, Aug. Ep. 261; Hier. Ep. 51, n. 2: nulla in desolatis cura dioecesibus parochiisque, Sid. Ep. 7, 6 med.: tot enim Cyrus habet paroecias, Ep. Leon. 52, 4.— Transf., the place of jurisdiction of a parish: per rusticas solitudo paroecias, Sid. Ep. 7, 6 (al. parochias).
paroecia.short: păroecĭa, and, corrupted, părŏchĭa, ae, f., = παροικία, an ecclesiastical district, a parish: castellum ad paroeciam Hipponensis Ecclesiae pertinebat, Aug.

paroemia.full: păroemĭa, ae, f., = παροιμία, rhet. t. t., a proverb, Beda, Trop. 616, 15.

paronomasia.full: părŏnŏmăsĭa, ae, f., = παρονομασία, a figure of speech (pure Lat. agnominatio), Rutil. Lup. 1, 3, p. 11 Ruhnk.
paronomasia.short: părŏnŏmăsĭa, ae, f., = παρονομασία, a figure of speech (pure Lat.

paronychia.full: părōnўchĭa, ae, f., and părōnў-chĭum, i, n., = παρωνυχία, a whitlow (pure Lat. reduvia), Plin. 21, 20, 83, § 142; 23, 9, 81, § 163.—In neutr., Petr. 31: ad pa ronychia et pterygia unguium, Plin. 24, 19, 119, § 182; 28, 8, 24, § 88.
paronychia.short: părōnўchĭa, ae, f., and părōnў-chĭum, i, n., = παρωνυχία, a whitlow (pure Lat.

paropamisus.full: Parŏpamīsus (Parăp-) or Parŏ-panīsus (Parăp-), i, m., = Παροπάμισος (Παραπ-). A high mountain beyond the Caspian Sea, now Hindu-Kuh or HinduKusch, Mel. 1, 15, 2; 3, 7, 6; Plin. 6, 20, 23, § 71; Curt. 7, 4, 15.—Hence, Parŏ-pamīsădae (Parăp-), ārum, m., the inhabitants of that mountain, Curt. 7, 3, 4; 9, 8, 6.—The same: Parŏpamīsii (Parăp-), Mel. 1, 2, 5.— A river in Northern Asia, prob. the modern Obi, Plin. 4, 13, 27, § 94 (Sillig, Parapanisus).
paropamisus.short: Parŏpamīsus (Parăp-) or Parŏ-panīsus (Parăp-), i, m., = Παροπάμισος (Παραπ-).

paropsis.full: păropsis (părap-), ĭdis, f., = παροψίς (prop. a side dish), a large square dish for the dessert, a dessert-dish; also a small dish in gen., Juv. 3, 142; Mart. 11, 27, 5; Suet. Galb. 12; Isid. 16, 20, 4; Petr. 50: parapsidem proicere, id. 34; Dig. 34, 2, 20; Vulg. Matt. 23, 25; 26, 23.

paroptus.full: păroptus, a, um, adj., = πάροπτος, roasted on the outside, slightly roasted: paroptus pullus, Apic. 6, 9.
paroptus.short: păroptus, a, um, adj., = πάροπτος, roasted on the outside, slightly roasted: paroptus pullus, Apic.

parorea.full: Părōrēa and Părōrīa, ae, f., = Παρώρεια, a region in Thrace, Liv. 39, 27; 42, 51.
parorea.short: Părōrēa and Părōrīa, ae, f., = Παρώρεια, a region in Thrace, Liv.

paros.full: Păros (-us), i, f., = Πάρος, one of the Cyclades, famous for its white marble and as the birthplace of the poet Archilochus, now Paro, Mel. 2, 7, 11; Plin. 4, 12, 22, § 67; Nep. Milt. 7, 2; Liv. 31, 15: marmoreamque Paron, Ov. M. 7, 465; cf.: Olearon niveamque Paron, Verg. A. 3, 126.—Hence, Părĭus, a, um, adj., Parian: crimine Pario accusatus, with respect to Paros (the failure to capture Paros), Nep. Milt. 8, 1: Glycerae nitor Splendentis Pario marmore purius, Hor. C. 1, 19, 5: marmor, Ov. P. 4
paros.short: Păros (-us), i, f., = Πάρος, one of the Cyclades, famous for its white marble and as the birthplace of the poet Archilochus, now Paro, Mel.

parotis.full: părōtis, ĭdis, f., = παρωτίς, a tumor near the ears, a parotis: parotidas tollere, Plin. 20, 21, 84, § 229: parotidas reprimere, id. 20, 9, 36, § 95: comprimere, id. 28, 11, 48, § 177: cohibere, id. 35, 17, 57, § 195: discutere, id. 20, 15, 59, § 167: lenire, id. 28, 7, 23, § 82: sanare, id. 20, 1, 2, § 4.—In sing., Plin. 24, 5, 10, § 15 (in Cels. 5, 18, 18; 6, 16, written as Greek).— Transf., a bracket or console of a hyperthyrum, Vitr. 4, 6, 4.
parotis.short: părōtis, ĭdis, f., = παρωτίς, a tumor near the ears, a parotis: parotidas tollere, Plin.

parra1.full: parra, ae, f., a bird of ill omen, the common or barn owl; acc. to others, the green woodpecker or the lapwing: picus et cornix ab laevā, corvus, parra ab dexterā consuadent, Plaut. As. 2, 1, 12 Fleck.: impios parrae recinentis omen Ducat, etc., Hor. C. 3, 27, 1 Orell.; cf. Plin. 18, 29, 69, § 292.
parra1.short: parra, ae, f., a bird of ill omen, the common or barn owl;

parra2.full: Parra, ae, m., a Roman surname, Varr. R. R. 3, 5 fin.
parra2.short: Parra, ae, m., a Roman surname, Varr.

parrhasia.full: Parrhăsĭa (Parră-), ae, f., = Παρρασία, a town of Arcadia, Plin. 4, 6, 10, § 20.—Hence, Parrhăsis, ĭdis, f. adj., Parrhasian; poet. for Arcadian: Parrhasis ursa, the Great Bear, Ov. H. 18, 152: Arctos, id. Tr. 1, 3, 48: Parrhasides stellae, i. e. septemtriones, id. F. 4, 577.—Subst.: Parrhasis erubuit, i. e. Callisto, Ov. M. 2, 460.— Parrhăsĭus, a, um, adj., Arcadian: Parrhasius Evander, Verg. A. 11, 31: dea, i. e. Carmenta, the mother of Evander, Ov. F. 1, 618: nives, id. ib. 2, 276: virgo, i.
parrhasia.short: Parrhăsĭa (Parră-), ae, f., = Παρρασία, a town of Arcadia, Plin.

parrhasius1.full: Parrhăsĭus, a, um, v. Parrhasia, B.

parrhasius2.full: Parrhăsĭus (Parră-), ĭi, m., = Παρράσιος, a celebrated Greek painter, a native of Ephesus, Plin. 35, 10, 36, § 67 sq.; Prop. 3, 9 (4, 8), 12; Hor. C. 4, 8, 6; Sen. Contr. 5, 34.—Transf.: non multos apud nos futuros Polyclitos et Parrhasios fuisse, Cic. Tusc. 1, 2, 4.
parrhasius2.short: Parrhăsĭus (Parră-), ĭi, m., = Παρράσιος, a celebrated Greek painter, a native of Ephesus, Plin.

parrhesiastes.full: parrhēsĭastes, ae, m., = παρρησιαστής, a free-speaker, Sen. Ira, 3, 23.
parrhesiastes.short: parrhēsĭastes, ae, m., = παρρησιαστής, a free-speaker, Sen.

parricida.full: parrĭcīda (pārĭcīda; old collat. form of the nom. sing. PARICIDAS, Fragm. XII. Tab. ap. Fest. s. v. parrici, p. 221 Müll.), ae, comm. the etym. is disputed; most prob. it is for patricida, from pater-caedo, Quint. 8, 6, 35, the murderer of his or her father or parents, a parricide. Lit.: majores supplicium in parricidas singulare, Cic. Rosc. Am. 25, 70: nisi forte magis erit parricida, si qui consularem patrem quam si humilem necarit, id. Mil. 7, 17; Sen. Clem. 1, 23, 2; Suet. Aug. 34: Telegoni

parricidatus.full: parrĭcīdātus, ŭs, m. parricida, parricide, Quint. 1, 6, 42.

parricidialis.full: parrĭcīdĭālis or parrĭcīdālis (parĭc-), e, adj. id., pertaining to or producing the crime of parricide, parricidal, murderous: INSIDIATORES, Inscr. Boeckh. Corp. 2971: horror, Arn. 3, 116: manus, Prud. Ham. 14 praef.: scelus, Just. 27, 1, 10; cf. 27, 1, 2: discordiae, id. 39, 3, 1: bellum, i. e. the civil war, Flor. 3, 21: populus Judaeorum, Ambros. Cain et Abel, 1, 2, 5; Quint. Decl. 4, 19; 17, 18.— Adv.: parrĭcīdĭālĭter, murderously: perire, Lampr. Alex. Sev. 1; Aug. Ep. 168.

parricidium.full: parrĭcīdĭum, ii, n. id., the murder of one's father or parents, parricide. Lit.: patris et patrui parricidium, Cic. Phil. 3, 7, 18; id. Rosc. Am. 26, 73.— Trop., parricide: vituperare quisquam vitae parentem (philosophiam) et hoc parricidio se inquinare audet? Cic. Tusc. 5, 2, 6.— Transf. The murder of one's mother, brother, relation, etc.: matris, Suet. Ner. 34: fraternum, Cic. Clu. 11, 31: fratris, Liv. 40, 24: filii, id. 8, 11: patrui, Cic. Phil. 3, 7, 18: lege Pompeia de parricidiis tenetur,

pars.full: pars, partis (gen. sing. PARTVS, Inscr. Corp. Lat. 197, 12; acc. partim, Cic. de Or. 2, 22, 94; Liv. 26, 46, 8; 31, 36, 9; 23, 11, 11; Sall. J. 89, 1; id. H. 2, 41, 1; v. infra fin.; abl. parti, Plaut. Men. 3, 2, 14; Varr. R. R. 1, 13, 5; Lucr. 1, 1113; 4, 515; nom. plur. parteis, Varr. L. L. 5, 4, 21; gen. plur. partum, Caes. ap. Charis. p. 114 P.), f. root por; Gr. ἔπορον, gave; πέπρωται, is given, destined; Lat. portio; cf. parare, a part, piece, portion, share, etc. In gen.: ne expers partis

parsimonia.full: parsĭmōnĭa (parcĭmōnĭa), ae (collat. form, PARCIMONIVM, Inscr. Donat. 35, 4), f. parco, sparingness, frugality, thrift, parsimony. Lit.: dies noctesque estur, bibitur, neque quisquam parsimoniam adhibet, Plaut. Most. 1, 3, 78: parsimonia et duritia, id. ib. 1, 2, 75; id. Truc. 2, 2, 55; Ter. Heaut. 3, 1, 32; Cic. Verr. 2, 2, 3, § 7: res familiaris conservatur diligentiā et parsimoniā, id. Off. 2, 24, 87: non intellegunt homines, quam magnum vectigal sit parsimonia, id. Par. 6, 3, 49: instrumenti

parstrymonia.full: Parstrȳmŏnĭa, ae, f., a tract of country on the Strymon, in Thrace, Liv. 42, 51.
parstrymonia.short: Parstrȳmŏnĭa, ae, f., a tract of country on the Strymon, in Thrace, Liv.

parthaon.full: Parthāon, ŏnis, m., = Παρθάων, son of Agenor and Epicaste, king of Calydon, and father of Œneus: ego te simitu novi cum Parthaone, I know you as well as I do Parthaon, i. e. not at all, Plaut. Men. 5, 1, 45: Parthaone nate, i. e. Œneus, Ov. M. 9, 12; cf. Hyg. Fab. 175; 239 and 242.—Hence, Parthāŏnĭdes, ae, m., a descendant of Parthaon: Parthaonides dux, i. e. Tydeus, the grandson of Parthaon; acc. to others, Meleager, the brother of Tydeus, Val. Fl. 3, 705.— Parthāŏnĭus, a, um, adj., Parthaonian
parthaon.short: Parthāon, ŏnis, m., = Παρθάων, son of Agenor and Epicaste, king of Calydon, and father of Œneus: ego te simitu novi cum Parthaone, I know you as well as I do Parthaon, i.

partheni.full: Parthēni or Parthīni, ōrum, m., = Παρθεινοί or Παρθινοί, a people of Illyria, near Dyrrhachium, Plin. 3, 23, 26, § 145; Cic. Pis. 40, 96; Caes. B. C. 3, 11; 3, 41; Liv. 29, 12.— A people of Dalmatia, Plin. 3, 22, 26, § 143.
partheni.short: Parthēni or Parthīni, ōrum, m., = Παρθεινοί or Παρθινοί, a people of Illyria, near Dyrrhachium, Plin.

parthenia.full: Parthĕnĭa, ae, f., another name for the isle of Samos, because Juno dwelt there when a virgin, Plin. 5, 31, 37, § 135; Lact. 1, 17.
parthenia.short: Parthĕnĭa, ae, f., another name for the isle of Samos, because Juno dwelt there when a virgin, Plin.

partheniae.full: Parthĕnĭae, ārum, m., = Παρθενίαι (maidens' children), a name given to the colonists of illegitimate birth who emigrated with Phalantus from Sparta and founded Tarentum, the Parthenians, Just. 3, 4, 7 (= spurii, id. 20, 1, 15).
partheniae.short: Parthĕnĭae, ārum, m., = Παρθενίαι (maidens' children), a name given to the colonists of illegitimate birth who emigrated with Phalantus from Sparta and founded Tarentum, the Parthenians, Just.

parthenianus.full: Parthĕnĭānus, a, um, v. Parthenius, V.

parthenias.full: Parthĕnĭas, ae, m., = Παρθενίας (maidish). An epithet of Virgil, on account of the purity of his morals, Serv. Verg. A. praef.; Aus. Idyll. 13 fin.— A river in Asia, a tributary of the Tigris, Plin. 6, 27, 31, § 129.

parthenice.full: parthĕnĭcē, ēs, f., = παρθενική, a plant, called also parthenium, Cat. 61, 194.
parthenice.short: parthĕnĭcē, ēs, f., = παρθενική, a plant, called also parthenium, Cat.

parthenicon.full: parthĕnĭcon, i, n., = παρθενικόν, a plant, called also pulegium, App. Herb. 92.
parthenicon.short: parthĕnĭcon, i, n., = παρθενικόν, a plant, called also pulegium, App.

parthenis.full: parthĕnis, ĭdis, f., = παρθενίς, a plant, called also artemisia, Plin. 25, 7, 36, § 73.
parthenis.short: parthĕnis, ĭdis, f., = παρθενίς, a plant, called also artemisia, Plin.

parthenium.full: parthĕnĭum, ii, n., = παρθένιον, the name of several plants. A plant, called also perdicium, Plin. 22, 17, 20, § 43.— A plant, called also leucanthes or tamnacus, Plin. 21, 30, 104, § 176.— A plant, called also linozostis, hermupoa, and mer curialis, Plin. 25, 5, 18, § 38.— A plant, called also chrysocollis, q. v.
parthenium.short: parthĕnĭum, ii, n., = παρθένιον, the name of several plants.

parthenius.full: Parthĕnĭus, ĭi, m., = Παρθένιος. A mountain in Arcadia, now Partheni, Liv. 34, 26; Mel. 2, 3, 5; Plin. 4, 6, 10, § 21.— Adj.: Parthenii saltus, Verg. E. 10, 57; so, nemus, Ov. M. 9, 188; Stat. Th. 4, 285: valles, Ov. H. 9, 49: antra, Prop. 1, 1, 11.— A river in Paphlagonia, now Bartan Tchai, Mel. 1, 19; Plin. 6, 2, 2, § 5; Val. Fl. 5, 104; Ov. P. 4, 10, 49.— A Grecian erotic poet and grammarian, an instructor of Virgil, Suet. Tib. 70; Gell. 9, 9, 3; 13, 26, 1; Macr. S. 5, 17.— A silversmith, fam

parthenon.full: Parthĕnon, ōnis, m., = Παρθενών, the celebrated temple of Athene on the Acropolis of Athens, the Parthenon, Plin. 34, 8, 19, § 54.—Hence, Transf., a portico in the villa of Pomponius Atticus, Cic. Att. 13, 40, 1.
parthenon.short: Parthĕnon, ōnis, m., = Παρθενών, the celebrated temple of Athene on the Acropolis of Athens, the Parthenon, Plin.

parthenopaeus.full: Parthĕnŏpaeus, i, m., = Παρθενοπαῖος, the son of Meleager and Atalante, one of the seven who went against Thebes: inclutus armis Parthenopaeus, Verg. A. 6, 480; Stat. Th. 4, 248; cf. Hyg. Fab. 99.
parthenopaeus.short: Parthĕnŏpaeus, i, m., = Παρθενοπαῖος, the son of Meleager and Atalante, one of the seven who went against Thebes: inclutus armis Parthenopaeus, Verg.

parthenope.full: Parthĕnŏpē, ēs, f., = Παρθενόπη, one of the Sirens, who, on the departure of Ulysses, threw herself, for grief, into the sea, and was cast up on the shore where Naples afterwards stood; on this account that city was in early times called by her name, Sil. 12, 33; Verg. G. 4, 564; Ov. M. 15, 712.—Hence, Parthĕnŏpēĭus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Parthenope, i. e. to Naples, Neapolitan: moenia, Ov. M. 14, 101.
parthenope.short: Parthĕnŏpē, ēs, f., = Παρθενόπη, one of the Sirens, who, on the departure of Ulysses, threw herself, for grief, into the sea, and was cast up on the shore where Naples afterwards stood;

parthenopolis.full: Parthĕnŏpŏlis, is, f., = Παρθενόπολις, a city in Lower Mœsia, on the Euxine Sea, Plin. 4, 11, 18, § 44; Eutr. 6, 6.— A town in Bithynia, Plin. 5, 32, 43, § 148.
parthenopolis.short: Parthĕnŏpŏlis, is, f., = Παρθενόπολις, a city in Lower Mœsia, on the Euxine Sea, Plin.

parthi.full: Parthi, ōrum, m., = Πάρθοι, the Parthians, a Scythian people, situated to the north-east of the passes of the Caspian and south of Hyrcania, famed in antiquity as roving warriors and skilful archers, Just. 41, 1, 2; Cic. Att. 5, 18, 1; id. Phil. 11, 14; Verg. G. 4, 314; Hor. C. 2, 13, 18; id. S. 2, 1, 15; Ov. A. A. 1, 209: Parthis mendacior, Hor. Ep. 2, 1, 112; Tac. A. 2, 1; 6, 34; Vulg. Act. 2, 9.—In sing., Inscr. Orell. 2982.— Collect., the Parthian, Cael. ap. Cic. Fam. 8, 5, 1: ecce! fugax Pa
parthi.short: Parthi, ōrum, m., = Πάρθοι, the Parthians, a Scythian people, situated to the north-east of the passes of the Caspian and south of Hyrcania, famed in antiquity as roving warriors and skilful archers, Just.

parthus1.full: Parthus, a, um, v. Parthi, A.

parthus2.full: Parthus, i, m., a Parthian; v. Parthi.

parthus3.full: Parthus, i, f., a city in Illyria, near Dyrrachium; hence, Parthīni (Par-thēni), ōrum, m., the inhabitants of Parthus, Parthinians, Mel. 2, 3, 11; Plin. 3, 22, 26, § 143; Cic. Pis. 40, 96; Caes. B. C. 3, 11; 41; 42; Liv. 29, 12; 33, 34 fin.; Fasti Capitol. ap. Grut. 297; Marin. Frat. Arv. p. 607. —In sing.: Parthīnus, i, m. An appellation of C. Asinius Pollio, the conqueror of the Parthinians; hence, Parthina gens, of Asinius Pollio, Suet. Aug. 19.— In gen.: PARTHINVS, a surname, Inscr. Murat. 1
parthus3.short: Parthus, i, f., a city in Illyria, near Dyrrachium;

partialiter.full: partĭālĭter, adv. pars, partly (late Lat.), Cael. Aur. Tard. 2, 1, 36.

partianus.full: Partĭānus, a, um, adj., a various read. for Parianus, Plin. 32, 10, 53, § 146.
partianus.short: Partĭānus, a, um, adj., a various read.

partiarius.full: partĭārĭus, a, um, adj. pars, that shares with another; shared, that is shared with another (ante- and post-class.): colonus, who pays his rent with a part of the produce, Dig. 19, 2, 25: pecora partiaria pascenda suscipere, so that their increase is shared between the owner and the herdsman, Cod. Just. 2, 3, 8: legatarius, to whom a share of the property is left, Gai. Inst. 2, 254; 257; Ulp. Fragm. 24, 25: res, that is shared with many: honor, App. M. 4, p. 156. — Abl. adverb.: partiario, on sh

partiatim.full: partĭātim, adv. id., in different parts or places (post-class.), Cael. Aur. Acut. 1, 11.

partibilis.full: partĭbĭlis, e, adj. id., divisible (postclass.): anima, Claud. Mam. Stat. Anim. 1, 18 (al. partilis).

particeps.full: partĭceps, cipis, adj. pars-capio, sharing, partaking, participant (class.; syn.: consors, socius); constr. usually with gen., rarely also with dat. or with prepp. Adj. With gen.: fac participes nos tuae sapientiae, Plaut. Ep. 2, 2, 81: nuntii, Ter. Heaut. 3, 1, 19: esse participem leti, i. e. to be mortal, Lucr. 3, 462: animus rationis compos et particeps, Cic. Univ. 8: fortunarum omnium socius et particeps, id. Font. 17, 47: artis, id. Div. 1, 18, 34; id. Inv. 2, 30, 92: virtutes ita copulatae

participalis.full: partĭcĭpālis, e, adj. particeps, sharing, partaking, participant (ante-and postclass.): curae, Dig. 1, 11, 1 (al. principali). —In gram., participial: verba, Varr. L. L. 10, § 34 Müll.

participatio.full: partĭcĭpātĭo, ōnis, f. participo, a sharing, partaking, participation (postclass.): imperii, Spart. Jul. 6 fin.; Aug. Quaest. 83, n. 24; Vulg. 1 Cor. 10, 16.

participator.full: partĭcĭpātor, ōris, m. participo, a participator (late Lat.), Just. Imp. Fid. Conf. ap. Agapet. Pap. Ep. 1.

participatum.full: partĭcĭpātum, i, n., v. participo fin.

participatus.full: partĭcĭpātus, ūs, m. participo, a sharing, participation, partnership (post-class.), Spart. Sev. 8 fin.: ad participatum imperii Severum vocans, id. Pesc. 5: filio Diadumeno in participatum ascito, Capitol. Macr. 5; Mart. Cap. 1, § 20.

participialis.full: partĭcĭpĭālis, e, adj. participium, in gram., of the nature of a participle, participial: verba, Quint. 1, 4, 29; cf. so of supines and gerunds, Prisc. p. 808; 822 P. —Adv.: partĭcĭpĭālĭter, in the manner of a participle, participially, Fest. s. v. ostentum, p. 194 Müll.; so id. ib. s. v. torrens, p. 352 Müll.

participium.full: partĭcĭpĭum, ii, n. particeps, a sharing, partaking, participation. Lit. (post-class.): omni ad illa participio in posterum abstinere, Cod. Just. 1, 4, 34, § 3. —Far more freq., Transf., in gram., a verbal form which partakes of the functions of a noun, a participle, Varr. L. L. 8, § 58; 9, § 110 Müll.; Quint. 1, 4, 19; 27; 1, 5, 47 et saep.

participo.full: partĭcĭpo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. and n. (collat. dep. form partĭcĭpor, Dig. 4, 4, 9, § 1) [id.], to share; viz., to cause to partake of, to impart; and also, to partake of, participate in (in both senses mostly ante- and post-class.; syn.: communico, partior, impertior). To make partaker of, to give a share of, to acquaint with, make privy to, impart, inform of any thing. Lit.: aliquem sermone suo de amicā eri, Plaut. Mil. 2, 2, 108: servum sui consilii, id. Cist. 1, 3, 17: ubi sint, quid agant, e

particula.full: partĭcŭla, ae, f. dim. pars, a small part, a little bit, a particle. In gen. (class.): tenuissimae particulae, Cic. de Or. 2, 39, 162: ut ne qua particula in hoc sermone praetermissa sit, id. Rep. 1, 24, 38: caeli, id. ib. 1, 39, 179: justitiae, id. Off. 2, 11, 40: particula parva, id. Pis. 35, 85: arenae, Hor. C. 1, 28, 23: undique desectam, id. ib. 1, 16, 14: minutae rerum particulae, Quint. 3, 11, 21; cf. Val. Max. 6, 9, 7: malorum, Juv. 13, 14.— In partic. In rhet. lang., a clause of a sente

particularis.full: partĭcŭlāris, e, adj. particula, of or concerning a part, partial, particular (postclass.): propositiones aliae universales, aliae particulares, App. Dogm. Plat. 3, p. 35, 34: publicatio, Cod. Just. 9, 6, 6.—Adv.: partĭcŭlārĭter, particularly, App. Dogm. Plat. 3, p. 33, 32; so opp. generaliter, Firm. Math. 1, 5 fin.; opp. universaliter, Aug. Retract. 1, 5 fin.

particulatim.full: partĭcŭlātim, adv. id., part after part, bit by bit, one by one, piecemeal, singly, severally: si summatim, non particulatim narrabimus, by particulars, Auct. Her. 1, 9: grex particulatim facilius quam universus convalescit, Col. 7, 6, 5: quamvis fundus particulatim venerit, omnes partes servitus sequitur, Dig. 8, 3, 23; Varr. ap. Serv. Verg. G. 2, 267; opp. ubique, Lact. 2, 10, 23: hominem particulatim excarnefacere, Sen. Ep. 24, 13; Varr. R. R. 2 praef. § 2.

particulatio.full: partĭcŭlātĭo, ōnis, f. particulo, a dividing into small parts or pieces (postclass.), Mart. Cap. 9, § 953.

particulo.full: partĭcŭlo, ōnis, m. particula, a sharer, partaker, participator (ante-class.). particulones dicti sunt coheredes, quod partes patrimonii sumant, Non. 20, 6 sq.

partilis.full: partĭlis, e, adj. pars, divisible, single (post-class.): corporeum omne, quod partile, Aug. Trin. 12, 9; Cael. Aur. Tard. 2, 1, 44: Nemesis partilibus praesidens fatis, i. e. over the fate of individuals, Amm. 14, 11, 25.—Adv.: partĭlĭter, partially, in part: cum ea, quae fiant, non partiliter fiant, sed ad census summam redeant, not in favor of a part, Arn. 1, 8; 6, 192.

partio1.full: partĭo, ōnis, f. pario, a bearing, bringing forth young (ante-and post-class.): horresco misera, mentio quoties fit partionis, Plaut. Truc. 1, 2, 92; Afran. ap. Non. 217, 31: mulieris, Gell. 3, 16, 9; 12, 1, 20.— Of hens, a laying of eggs: hae (gallinae) ad partiones sunt aptiores, Varr. R. R. 3, 9, 4.

partio2.full: partĭo, ĭi or īvi, ītum, 4, v. a., and partĭor, partītus (inf. dep. partirier, Aus. Epigr. 139, 8), 4, v. dep. pars, to share, part; to divide, distribute (Cic., Cæs., and Quint. use the verb. finit. almost exclusively in the dep. form; v. infra; but the part. perf. was employed by them also in a pass. sense; syn.: communico, participo). Lit. Form partĭo, īre: tu partem laudis caperes, tu gaudia mecum Partisses, Lucil. ap. Non. 475, 23: aeternabilem divitiam partissent, Att. ib. 475, 24: praedam
partio2.short: partĭo, ĭi or īvi, ītum, 4, v.

partitio.full: partītĭo, ōnis, f. 2. partio, a sharing, parting, partition; a division, distribution. In gen.: si quā in re discrepavit ab Antonii divisione nostra partitio, Cic. de Or. 3, 30, 119: aequabilis praedae partitio, id. Off. 2, 11, 40: aerarii, id. Sest. 24, 54; esp., the division of an inheritance, id. Caecin. 5, 15; id. Leg. 2, 20, 50 sqq.: partitionem artium facere, id. de Or. 1, 6, 22; id. Fin. 1, 13, 45; Quint. 3, 4, 1: nec partitione minuitur, Aug. Civ. Dei, 10, 3 init.— In partic. In philos.

partito.full: partītō, v. 2. partio, Part. perf. fin.

partitor.full: partītor, ōris, m. partior, a divider, distributer: cum te partitorem ad partiendas merces missum putares, Cic. Vatin. 5, 12 dub. (al. portitorem); cf. partitor, μεριστής, Gloss. Philox.

partitudo.full: partĭtūdo, ĭnis, f. pario, a bearing, bringing forth young, parturition (ante-and post-class.): propinqua partitudo, Plaut. Aul. 1, 1, 36; 2, 3, 9 (both passages cited ap. Non. 217, 28 and 30); Cod. Th. 9, 42, 10; Sulp. Sev. Chron. 1, 9, 3.

partitus.full: partītus, a, um, Part., from 2. partio.

partualis.full: partŭālis, e, adj. 2. partus, of or belonging to bearing or birth: sanguis, Tert. adv. Marc. 4, 20.

partula.full: Partŭla, ae, f. id., the goddess who presides over birth, Tert. Anim. 37.

partura.full: partūra, ae, f. 2. pario, bearing, Varr. R. R. 2, 1, 26 (al. paritura).

parturibundus.full: partŭrĭbundus, a, um parturio, in travail, De Miracc. S. Steph. 2, 2, 2.
parturibundus.short: partŭrĭbundus, a, um parturio, in travail, De Miracc.

parturio.full: partŭrĭo, īvi or ĭi, 4 (imperf. parturibat, Phaedr. 4, 21, 1), v. desid. a. [2. pario], to desire to bring forth, to be in travail or labor; said of women and of animals. Lit.: vereor ne parturire intellegat, Ter. Hec. 3, 3, 53: tu (Lucina) voto parturientis ades, Ov. F. 3, 256: parturiens canis, Phaedr. 1, 18, 3.—Prov.: parturiunt montes, nascetur ridiculus mus, said of those who promise great things, but accomplish little or nothing; like the Engl. expression, great cry and little wool, Hor. A

parturitio.full: partŭrītĭo, ōnis, f. parturio, a desiring to bring forth, labor, travail (late Lat.). Lit., Hier. adv. Jovin. 1, n. 22.— Transf., a bearing or bringing forth, parturition: novae vitae, Aug. Conf. 8, 6: cordis, id. Ep. 34 (al. 31).— Any grievous pains: inferni, Capreol. Epist. ad Vital. et Const.

partus1.full: partus, a, um, Part. and P. a., from 2. pario.

partus2.full: partus, ūs (gen. parti, Pac. ap. Non. 486, 6: partuis, Varr. ib. 8; dat. sing. partu, Prop. 1, 13, 30; dat. plur. partibus, App. M. 9, 33), m. 2. pario, a bearing, bringing forth, birth (equally common in the sing. and plur.). In abstr.: propinquitas parti, Pac. ap. Non. 486, 6: cum esset gravida Auria, et jam appropinquare partus putaretur, Cic. Clu. 11, 31; cf. Ov. M. 9, 673: antequam veniret partus ejus, peperit, the time for bearing, Vulg. Isa. 66, 7: Diana adhibetur ad partus, Cic. N. D. 2,

partus3.full: partus, gen., from pars, v. pars init.

parum.full: părum, subst. indecl. and adv. (for the comp. and sup. mĭnus and mĭnĭme are used; v. h. vv. sub parvus) [akin to parvus and παῦρος: cf. parco], too little, not enough (opp. satis and nimium). Lit. Subst. With gen.: in hac enim satis erat copiae, in illā autem leporis parum, Cic. Brut. 68, 240: non parum humanitatis (= satis), id. Rosc. Com. 16, 46: satis eloquentiae, sapientiae parum, Sall. C. 5, 4: Latini sanguinis, Hor. Epod. 7, 4: splendoris, id. Ep. 2, 2, 111.— Absol.: magis offendit nimium

parumper.full: părumper, adv., with ref. to time, for a little while, for a short time, a while, a moment: parumper significat paulisper, quasi perparvum, i. e. valde parvum; refertur autem ad tempus, Fest. p. 221 Müll. (class.). Lit.: tace parumper, Plaut. Curc. 2, 3, 78: mane dum parumper, id. Bacch. 4, 6, 24; cf. Ter. And. 4, 2, 31; Liv. 4, 32: haec cum Crassus dixisset, parumper et ipse conticuit et ceteris silentium fuit, Cic. de Or. 3, 35, 143: discedo parumper a somniis, ad quae mox revertar, id. Div. 1

parunculus.full: păruncŭlus, i, m. dim. 3. paro, a small boat, a little bark, Cic. Fragm. ap. Isid. Orig. 19, 1, 20.

parus1.full: pārus i, m., a titmouse, tomtit, Auct. Carm. Phil. 9.
parus1.short: pārus i, m., a titmouse, tomtit, Auct.

parvibibulus.full: parvĭbĭbŭlus, a, um, adj. parvusbibo, that drinks little: phrenetici, Cael. Aur. Acut. 3, 15.

parvicollis.full: parvĭcollis, e, adj. parvus-collum, short-necked, a transl. of the Gr. μικροτράχηλος, Cael. Aur. Tard. 2, 12.

parvifacio.full: parvĭ-făcĭo, facĕre parvus, to make light of, to despise (as one word only anteclass.): parvifaciatur, Titin. ap. Prisc. p. 789 P.
parvifacio.short: parvĭ-făcĭo, facĕre parvus, to make light of, to despise (as one word only anteclass.): parvifaciatur, Titin.

parvipendo.full: parvĭpendo, ĕre, more correctly written separate, parvi pendo.
parvipendo.short: parvĭpendo, ĕre, more correctly written separate, parvi pendo.

parvitas.full: parvĭtas, ātis, f. parvus, smallness, littleness, slightness, insignificance (rare but class.): vincula talia quae cerni non possent propter parvitatem, * Cic. Univ. 13, 41; Plin. 2, 11, 8, § 51: parvitates et magnitudines rerum, Gell. 1, 3, 28: quaestionis, id. 7, 17, 2: mea parvitas ad favorem tuum decurrit, i. e. my humble self, Val. Max. praef.

parvulus.full: parvŭlus or parvŏlus, a, um, adj. dim. [parvus], very small, little, petty, slight, (class.): ne dum parvulum hoc consequimur, illud amittamus, quod maximum est, Cic. Inv. 2, 3, 10: parvola magni formica laboris, Hor. S. 1, 1, 33: parvula, pumilis, Lucr. 4, 1162: impulsio, Cic. Inv. 2, 8, 25: res, id. Quint. 16, 53: pecunia, id. Rosc. Com. 8: stridor, Plin. 17, 24, 37, § 221: res, Hor. Ep. 1, 18, 29: tuta et parvola laudo, id. ib. 15, 42: proelium, a skirmish, Caes. B. G. 2, 30: detrimentum, id.
parvulus.short: parvŭlus or parvŏlus, a, um, adj.

parvus.full: parvus, a, um, adj. (usual, irreg. comp. and sup.: mĭnor, mĭnĭmus.—Comp.: volantum parviores, Cael. Aur. Tard. 2, 1, 26.— Sup.: rictus parvissimus, Varr. ap. Non. 456, 10: parvissima corpora, Lucr. 1, 615; 621; 3, 199: minerrimus pro minimo dixerunt, Paul. ex Fest. p. 122 Müll.: minimissimus, Arn. 5, n. 8) [kindr. with paucus and Gr. παῦρος; cf., also, parum, parcus], little, small, petty, puny, inconsiderable (cf.: exiguus, minutus, brevis; in class. prose parvus is not used, like brevis, of st

pasargadae.full: Păsargădae, Persagădae, ārum, f., or Parsagăda, ōrum, n., = Πασαργάδαι, a citadei in Persis, inhabited by the Magi, and containing the tomb of Cyrus, now the ruins of Darabgerd. Plin. 6, 23, 26, § 99; 6, 26, 29, § 116 (al. Frasargida); Curt. 5, 6, 10.
pasargadae.short: Păsargădae, Persagădae, ārum, f., or Parsagăda, ōrum, n., = Πασαργάδαι, a citadei in Persis, inhabited by the Magi, and containing the tomb of Cyrus, now the ruins of Darabgerd.

pascalis.full: pascālis, e, adj. for pascualis, from pascuum, pasturing, grazing: pascales oves Cato posuit pro pascuales, Fest. p. 243 Müll.; cf. id. ib. p. 242: pascali pecore ac montano, Lucil. ap. Fest. s. v. Solox, p. 301 Müll.; boves pascuales, Vulg. 3 Reg. 4, 23.

pasceolus.full: pascĕŏlus, i, m. φάσκαλος, φάσκωλος, a leathern money-bag (syn.: funda, pera, marsupium): ex alutā sacculus, Non. 151, 10: pueri in ludo solent pasceolos furari, Cato ap. Non. l. l. 14; so Lucil. ib. 13: centum Philippeae minae in pasceolo, Plaut. Rud. 5, 2, 27.

pascha.full: pascha, ae, f., and ătis, n., = πάσχα (Hebr. ). The feast of the Passover, Easter: sollennibus Paschae, Tert. ad Uxor. 2, 4: lege dedit pascham, id. in Carm. adv. Marc. 2, 80: pascharum dies, Symm. Ep. 10, 77: dominicum pascha celebrare, Hier. Ep. 96, n. 20: post sanctum pascha, Aus. Ep. 10, 17: paschate vicino, Hier. in Matt. 26, 3: per tria paschata, id. in Dan. 9, 24.— The paschal lamb, Vulg. 1 Cor. 5, 7; cf. id. Marc. 14, 12.
pascha.short: pascha, ae, f., and ătis, n., = πάσχα (Hebr.

paschalis.full: paschālis, e, adj. pascha, of or belonging to the Passover or to Easter, paschal: paschale tempus, Cod. Th. 9, 35, 4: dapes, Sedul. init.: liber, that treats of the Passover, Hier. Ep. 99, n. 1.

pascito.full: pascĭto, āre, v. freq. a. pasco, to pasture, to feed: (apes), quae in silvestribus locis pascitant, Varr. R. R. 3, 16, 19 dub. (al. pastitant).

pasco.full: pasco, pāvi, pastum, 3, v. a. and n. root pa-; Sanscr. gō-pas, herdsman; Gr. πατέομαι; cf. pabulum, pastor, Pales, panis; perh. also, Penates, penum, to cause to eat, to feed, pasture. Lit. Of animals, to pasture, drive to pasture, to feed, attend to the feeding of, etc. (cf. pabulor): cum sues puer pasceret, Cic. Div. 1, 17, 31: greges armentaque pavit, Ov. M. 6, 395: non, me pascente, capellae, cytisum carpetis, Verg. E. 1, 78: turpes sub gurgite phocas, id. G. 4, 395: ut pasceret porcos, Vulg

pascor.full: pascor, pastus sum, 3, v. dep., v. pasco, I. B. 4, b., and II. 1. b.

pascua.full: pascŭa, ae, v. pascuus, II. B.

pascuosus.full: pascŭōsus, a, um, adj. pascuum, full of pasture, fit for pasture (late Lat.): herba, App. Herb. 92.

pascuus.full: pascŭus, a, um, adj. pasco, of or for pasture, grazing (class.): ager, Plaut. Truc. 1, 2, 47: agri, arvi et arbusti et pascui, Cic. Rep. 5, 2, 3: rura, Lucr. 5, 1248: silva, Dig. 50, 16, 30; cf. in the foll.— Subst. pascŭum, i, n., a pasture (usu. in plur.; cf. pabulum). Lit.: ab viridi pascuo, Varr. R. R. 2, 11, 2: ne esuriens mittatur in pascuum, Col. 8, 14, 8: rus quod pascuo caret, id. 7, 1, 1; Plin. 8, 47, 72, § 189.— Plur.: in censorum pascuis, Cic. Agr. 1, 1, 3: gregem in pascua mittere,

pasicompsa.full: Pāsĭcompsa, ae, f. πᾶσ-κομψή, alladorned, a female proper name, Plaut. Merc. 3, 1, 18 sq.

pasiphae.full: Pāsĭphăē, ēs, and Pāsĭphăa, ae, = Πασιφάη (the All-shining), daughter of Helios, sister of Circe, wife of Minos, and mother of Androgeus, Phœdra, and Ariadne, and also of the Minotaur by a beautiful bull, which Venus, out of hatred, had inspired her with a passion for, Ov. A. A. 1, 295; Cic. N. D. 3, 19, 48; id. Div. 1, 43, 96; Serv. Verg. A. 6, 14; Hyg. Fab. 40: Pasiphaen nivei solatur amore juvenci, Verg. E. 6, 46: Pasiphaae fano, Cic. Div. l. l.: Pasiphaes gener, i.e. Theseus, Ov. Ib. 90.— He
pasiphae.short: Pāsĭphăē, ēs, and Pāsĭphăa, ae, = Πασιφάη (the All-shining), daughter of Helios, sister of Circe, wife of Minos, and mother of Androgeus, Phœdra, and Ariadne, and also of the Minotaur by a beautiful bull, which Venus, out of hatred, had inspired her

pasiteles.full: Pāsĭtĕles, acc. en, m., = Πασιτέλης, a famous Greek carver in relief, who came to Rome: hanc speciem Pasiteles caelavit argento, Cic. Div. 1, 36, 79; Plin. 35, 12, 45, § 156; 36, 5, 4, § 39.

pasithea.full: Pāsĭthĕa, ae, and Pāsĭthĕē, ēs, f., = Πασιθέα, one of the three Graces: dea Pasithea, Cat. 63, 43; Sen. Ben. 1, 3, 7: Pasithee, Stat. Th. 2, 286.
pasithea.short: Pāsĭthĕa, ae, and Pāsĭthĕē, ēs, f., = Πασιθέα, one of the three Graces: dea Pasithea, Cat.

pasitigris.full: Pāsĭtīgris, ĭdis, m., = Πασιτίγρις, the river Eulœus, near the gulf, after the union of all its arms, now Kuran, Curt. 5, 3, 1.
pasitigris.short: Pāsĭtīgris, ĭdis, m., = Πασιτίγρις, the river Eulœus, near the gulf, after the union of all its arms, now Kuran, Curt.

passales.full: passales et oves et gallinae appellantur, quod passim pascuntur, Paul. ex Fest. p. 222 Müll.
passales.short: passales et oves et gallinae appellantur, quod passim pascuntur, Paul.

passarius.full: passārĭus, a, um, adj. passus, a, um, from pando, dried in the sun: ficus, Capitol. Alb. 11.

passaron.full: Passăron and Passăro, ōnis, f. = Πασσαρών, a city of Epirus, in the district of Molossis, Liv. 45, 26; 33.

passer1.full: passer, ĕris, m. for panser, from pando; cf. anser. Lit., a sparrow, Cic. Fin. 2, 23, 75; cf. Plin. 10, 36, 52, § 107; 10, 38, 54, § 111; 18, 17, 45, § 158; 30, 15, 49, § 141; Cic. Div. 2, 30, 63; 1, 33, 72; Cat. 2, 1 sq.; 3, 3 sq.; Juv. 9, 54; Mart. 11, 6, 16; Juv. 6, 8; Vulg. Lev. 14. 4.—As a term of endearment: meus pullus passer, mea columba, mi lepus, Plaut. Cas. 1, 50.— Transf. Passer marinus. an ostrich (marinus, because brought from a distance by sea), Plaut. Pers. 2, 2, 17; Aus. Ep. 11,

passer2.full: Passer, ĕris, m., a Roman surname, Varr. R. R. 3, 2, 2.
passer2.short: Passer, ĕris, m., a Roman surname, Varr.

passercula.full: passercŭla, ae, f. dim. 1. passer, a little sparrow, sparrowlet, as a term of endearment applied to a girl (perh. only in the foll. pass.), M. Aurel. ap. Front. Ep. ad M. Caes. 4. 6 Mai.

passerculus.full: passercŭlus, i, m. dim. id., a little sparrow, sparrowlet, Cic. Div. 2, 30, 65.—As a term of endearment: dic me igitur tuum passerculum, Plaut. As. 3, 3, 76.

passerinus1.full: passĕrīnus, a, um, adj. id., of or fit for a sparrow: prandium, Pomp. ap. Non. 112, 7 (Com. Rel. p. 213 Rib.).

passerinus2.full: Passĕrīnus, i, m., the name of a very fleet horse, Mart. 7, 7, 10; 12, 36, 12.— In the orthogr PASSARINVS, the name of a circus-horse, Inscr. Grut. 341.
passerinus2.short: Passĕrīnus, i, m., the name of a very fleet horse, Mart.

passernix.full: passernix, īcis Celtic, a whetstone, Plin. 36, 22, 47, § 165.
passernix.short: passernix, īcis Celtic, a whetstone, Plin.

passibilis.full: passĭbĭlis, e, adj. patior, capable of feeling or suffering, passible (post-class.), Arn. 7, 214; Prud. Apoth. 74; Tert. adv. Prax. 29; Vulg. Act. 26, 23; id. Jacob. 5, 17. —Adv.: passĭbĭlĭter, passibly, Tert. Anim. 45.

passibilitas.full: passĭbĭlĭtas, ātis, f. passibilis, capability of suffering, passibility (postclass.), Arn. 2, 62.

passienus.full: Passĭēnus, i, m., a Roman surname, Sen. Contr. 5 praef.; Inscr. Grut. 106, 4; Inscr. Murat. 1612, 13 sq.—In fem.: PASSIENA. Inscr. Murat. 1612, 12 sq.
passienus.short: Passĭēnus, i, m., a Roman surname, Sen.

passim.full: passim. adv. passus, from pando (lit., spread or scattered about; hence), at or to different places, hither and thither, in every direction, at random. Lit. (class.): ille iit passim, ego ordinatim, Brut. ap. Cic. Fam. 11, 13, 2: sive pilatim sive passim iter facere volebat, Asellio ap. Serv. Verg. A. 12, 121: Numidae quādam barbarā consuetudine nullis ordinibus passim consederant, Caes. B. C. 2, 38: Tyrii comites passim ... diversa per agros Tecta metu petiere, Verg. A. 4, 162: plurima perque v

passio.full: passĭo, ōnis, f. patior, a suffering, enduring (post-class.). Lit., Maxim. Gallus, 3, 42; Prud. στεφ. 5, 291; Tert. adv. Val 9 fin.; id. adv. Gnost. 13—Esp. (eccl. Lat.), the sufferings of Christ: demus operam, ut mereamur a Deo et ultionem passionis et praemium. Lact. 5, 23, 5: post passionem suam, Vulg. Act. 1, 3; plur., id. 2 Cor. 1, 7; id. Phil. 3, 10.— In partic., a disease, Firm. 2, 12.— Transf. An event, occurrence, phenomenon, App. Mund. p. 61, 31.— A passion, affection, a transl. of the

passionalis.full: passĭōnālis, e, adj. passio, II. B., susceptible of passion, passionate: deus, Tert. Test. Anim. 3; Cael. Aur. Tard. 1, 4, n. 83.

passivitas.full: passīvĭtas, ātis, f. 1. passivus, a scattered or confused condition, want of distinction, promiscuousness (post-class.), Tert. Pall. 4 med.; id. Apol. 9.

passivitus.full: passīvĭtus, adv., i. q. passim, everywhere, Tert. Pall. 3 fin.

passivus1.full: passīvus, a, um, adj. 2. pando. Spread about, general, common, found everywhere (post-class.): nomen dei, applied to many, common, Tert. adv. Marc. 1, 7: cupiditates, Firm. Math. 5, 1.— Promiscuous, confused: seminum passiva congeries, App. M. 6, p. 177, 14.—Hence, Subst.: passīvus, i, m., i. q. popularis: vagi Romanorum, quos passivos appellant, Aug. contr. Adamant. 24; so, populari, passivo, Schol. Juv. 8, 182.—Adv.: passīvē: crines per colla passive dispositi, dispersedly, App. M. 11 init.; T

passivus2.full: passīvus, a, um, adj. patior, capable of feeling or suffering, passible, passive (post-class.): anima passiva et interibilis, Arn. 2, 65; App. de Deo Socr. p. 49.— In partic., in gram., passive: verbum passivum . . . quod habet naturam patiendi, Quint. 1, 6, 10: verba, Charis. 2; Diom. 1; Prisc. 8 et saep.—Adv.: pas-sīvē, passively, Lucil. ap. Prisc. p. 791 P.

passum.full: passum, i, n., v. 2. pando, P. a., B. 2. b.

passus1.full: passus, a, um, Part. and P. a. of 2. pando.

passus2.full: passus, a, um, Part. of patior.

passus3.full: passus, ūs, m. from the root pat, a step, pace (cf.: gressus, gradus). Lit.: hinc campos celerl passu permensa parumper, Enn. ap. Non. 378, 20 (Ann. v. 74 Vahl.); Plaut. Bacch. 4, 7, 34; Lucr 4, 827; 877; Cic. Leg. 1, 21, 54: sequiturque patrem non passibus aequis, Verg. A. 2, 724: nec longis inter se passibus absunt, id. ib. 11, 907: rapidis ferri Passibus, id. ib. 7, 156; Ov. M. 11, 64: per litora lentis Passibus spatiari, id. ib. 2, 572: passu anili procedere, id. ib. 13, 533 et saep.: passib

pasta.full: pasta, ae, f., = πάστη, paste, Marc. Emp. 1.
pasta.short: pasta, ae, f., = πάστη, paste, Marc.

pasticus.full: pastĭcus, a, um, adj. pastus, fed, fattened: agnus, Apic. 8, 6.

pastillarius.full: pastillārĭus, ii, m. pastillus, a maker of pastils, Inscr. (Ann. p. Chr. 435) Murat. 527, 5.

pastillicans.full: pastillĭcans, antis, adj. id., having the shape of a little ball, globular, Plin. 21 8, 25, § 49.

pastillum.full: pastillum, i, n. id., a little loaf or roll of bread, Varr. ap. Charis. p. 24 P.; a little round loaf for offering: pastillum in sacris libi genus rotundi, Paul. ex Fest. p. 250 Müll.

pastillus.full: pastillus, i, m. dim. panis, a little loaf or roll: pastillus forma panis parvi utique deminutivum est a pane, Paul. ex Fest. p. 222 Müll.— Transf., medicine in the form of a round ball or cake, a lozenge, troche, trochisch, Plin. 22, 12, 14, § 29: emplastra pastillique, quos τροχίσκους Graeci vocant, Cels. 5, 17, 2; cf. id. 5, 20: sucum in sole coctum dividunt in pastillos, Plin. 13, 22, 43, § 126: digerere aliquid in pastillos, id. 12, 27, 60, § 131: in pastillos cogere, id. 20, 1, 2, § 3: den

pastinaca.full: pastĭnāca, ae, f. pastino. A parsnip, a term including also our carrot, Plin. 19, 5, 27, § 89; 25, 9, 64, § 112; Isid. Orig. 17, 10.— A fish of prey, the sting-ray, Plin. 9, 42, 67, § 144; 9, 48, 72, § 155; Cels. 6, 9.

pastinatio.full: pastĭnātĭo, ōnis, f. id., the act of preparing the soil of a vineyard, by digging and trenching it. Lit.: pastinationem suscipere, Col. 3, 12, 6; 3, 13, 4.— Transf., ground so prepared: pastinatio vitibus conserenda est, Col. 11, 2, 17; so id. 3, 15, 1; 3, 3, 15.

pastinator.full: pastĭnātor, ōris, m. id., one who digs and trenches the ground of a vineyard, Col. 3, 13, 12.

pastinatum.full: pastĭnātum, i, n., v. pastino fin.

pastinatus.full: pastĭnātus, ūs, m. pastino, the act of digging and trenching the ground of a vineyard, Plin. 17, 20, 32, § 143 (al. pastinatum, q. v.).

pastino.full: pastĭno, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. pastinum, to dig and trench the ground, to prepare the ground, for the planting of vines: pastinandi agri rationem tradere, Col. 3, 13, 6; 11, 3, 9: solum, Plin. 17, 21, 35, § 159: vineas, id. 18, 26, 65, § 240: pastinatae vineae, id. 14, 1, 3, § 14; Vulg. Marc. 12, 1.—Hence, pastĭnātum, i, n. (sc. solum), ground dug and trenched; ground prepared for planting the vine, Col. 3, 13, 7: vineam in pastinato serere, Plin. 17, 22, 35, § 172; Col. 3, 3, 11: umidum pastinatu

pastinum.full: pastĭnum, i, n., a kind of two-pronged dibble, for preparing the ground and for setting plants with: pastinum vocant agricolae ferramentum bifurcum, quo semina panguntur. Col. 3, 18. 1, and 6.— Transf. The act of digging up and trenching the ground: pastinum fieri nunc tempus est, Pall. 2, 10, 1.— In plur., ground so prepared: sed haec in pastinis vel sulcis ratio erit, Pall. 3, 9, 13: latitudo pastinorum, id. 1, 7, 2; 1, 34, 2: instituere, Dig. 24, 3, 7.
pastinum.short: pastĭnum, i, n., a kind of two-pronged dibble, for preparing the ground and for setting plants with: pastinum vocant agricolae ferramentum bifurcum, quo semina panguntur.

pastio.full: pastĭo, ōnis, f. pasco, a pasturing, grazing, feeding. Lit.: duo genera sunt pastionum, unum agreste, etc., Varr. R. R. 3, 2, 13; 3, 1, 8; 3, 2, 18: pastiones villaticae, pecuariae, Col. 8, 1, 2.— Transf., concr., a pasture, Varr. R. R. 2. 10, 2: pastiones laxae, id. ib. 1, 12, 1: magnitudine pastionis, Cic. Imp. Pomp. 6, 14.

pastophori.full: pastŏphŏri, ōrum, m., = παστοφόροι, a kind of priests who carried about the images of their deities in a little shrine for the purpose of collecting alms, App. M. 11, p. 265, 15; Inscr. Maff. Mus. Ver. 230.
pastophori.short: pastŏphŏri, ōrum, m., = παστοφόροι, a kind of priests who carried about the images of their deities in a little shrine for the purpose of collecting alms, App.

pastophorium.full: pastŏphŏrĭum, ii. n., = παστοφόριον, a little chapel in a temple where the image of a god was preserved and his servants abode, Hier. in Isa. 22, 15; Vulg. 1 Macc. 4, 38; 4, 57.

pastor.full: pastor (PAASTOR, Inscr. Orell. 3308), ōris, m. pasco, a herdsman, esp. a shepherd (syn. opilio): Mars pater ... pastores pecuaque salva servassis, Cato, R. R. 141, 3: servos pastores armat, Caes. B. C. 1, 24: jam pastor umbras ... quaerit, Hor. C. 3, 29, 21: pastor durus, Juv. 11, 151: boni pastoris esse tondere pecus, non deglubere, Suet. Tib. 32.— Trop., a shepherd: populi (transl. of the Gr. ποιμένα λαῶν, Hom. Il. 2, 243), Quint. 8, 6, 18.— Transf. A keeper: pavonum, Varr R. R. 3, 6, 5: colum

pastoralis.full: pastōrālis, e, adj. pastor, of or belonging to herdsmen or shepherds, pastoral: vita, Varr. R. R. 2, 1, 15: ille Romuli auguratus pastoralis, non urbanus fuit, Cic. Div. 1, 48, 107: habitus, Liv 9, 36: juventus, Ov. F. 2, 365: myrtus, Verg. A. 7, 817: manus, a band of shepherds, Vell. 1, 8: scientia, Col. 1 prooem.: o pastoralis Apollo, Calp. Ecl. 7, 22.—Adv.: pastōrālĭter, like a shepherd, Ven. Fort. Ep. post Carm. 8, 17.

pastoricius.full: pastōrīcĭus or -tĭus, a, um, adj. pastor, of or belonging to a shepherd, pastoral: vita, Varr. R. R. 1, 2, 16: fistula, Cic. Att. 1, 16, 11: sodalitas pastoricia atque agrestis, id. Cael. 11, 26.

pastorius.full: pastōrĭus, a, um, adj. id., of or belonging to a herdsman or shepherd: pellis, Ov. M. 2, 680: sibila, id. ib. 13, 785: virtus, Calp. Ecl. 5, 105: habitus, Flor. 1, 17, 4: sacra, the Palilia, Ov. F. 4, 723.

pastura.full: pastūra, ae. f. pasco, a pasture (postclass.), Pall. 10, 8 fin.

pastus1.full: pastus. a, um, Part., from pasco.

pastus2.full: pastus, ūs, m. pasco, pasture, fodder, food (class; equally common in sing. and plur.): animalia ad pastum accedunt, Cic. N. D. 2, 47, 122: animantia anquirunt pastum, id. Off. 1, 4, 11: pastum capessere et conficere, id. N. D. 2, 47, 121; id. Fin. 2, 13, 40: e pastu decedens, Verg. G. 1, 381.—In plur.: terra fundit ex sese pastus varios, Cic. Fin. 2, 34, 111: conatum habere ad naturalis pastus capessendos, id. N. D. 2, 47, 122.— Transf., food of men (poet. and very rare): hominum pastus pecudum

patagiarius.full: pătăgĭārĭus, ii, m. patagium, a border-maker, Plant. Aul. 3, 5, 35; Inscr. Don. cl. 8, n. 78; ct. Fest. s. v. patagium, p. 221 Müll.

patagiatus.full: pătăgīātus, a, um, adj. id., ornamented with a border: tumca, Plaut. Ep. 2, 2, 47; cf. Fest. s. v. patagium, p. 221 Müll.

patagium.full: pătăgīum, ii. n., = παταγεῖον, a gold edging or border on a Roman lady's tunic cf.: limbus, ora): patagium est, quod ad summam tunicam assui solet: quae et patagiata dicitur et patagiarii, qui ejusmodi opera faciunt, Fest. p. 221 Müll.; Naev. ap. Non. 540, 6; Tert Pall. 3; cf. Becker, Gallus, 3, p. 144 (2d ed.).— Transf., an ornarient for the kair, App. M. 2. p. 119, 2

patagus.full: pătăgus, i, m., = πάταγος, a sort of disease, Plaut Fragm ap. Macr. S. 5, 19; cf. Fest. p. 221 Müll.
patagus.short: pătăgus, i, m., = πάταγος, a sort of disease, Plaut Fragm ap.

patalene.full: Pătălēnē, Patăle, ēs, or Pătăla, f., = Παταληνη, an island at the mouth of the Indus, with a city of the same name.— Form Patalene, Mel. 3, 7, 8; Avien. Perieg. 1295.—Form Patale, Plin. 37, 9, 48, § 132.— Form Patale. Plin. 6, 20, 23, § 71.—Hence, Pătălitānus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to the island of Patalene: portus, Mart. Cap. 6, § 593 (Kopp. Patavitanus).
patalene.short: Pătălēnē, Patăle, ēs, or Pătăla, f., = Παταληνη, an island at the mouth of the Indus, with a city of the same name.— Form Patalene, Mel.

patalis.full: pătālis, e, a false reading for patulus, v. h. v.)
patalis.short: pătālis, e, a false reading for patulus, v.

patalitanns.full: Pătălītănns, a, um, v. Patalene, II.

patara.full: Pătăra, ae, f., = Παταρα, a seaport town of Lycia, with a celebrated oracle of Apollo, Mel. 1, 15, 3; Plin. 5, 27, 28, § 100; Liv. 33, 41; Vulg. Act. 21, 1; Serv Verg. A. 4, 143.—Hence, Pātăreus (trisyl.), e=i and ĕos, m., = Παταρευς, the Patarean, a surname of Apollo: Delius et Patareus Apollo, Hor. C. 3, 4, 64.— Pătăsaeus, a, um, adj., Pararœan: regia, Ov. M. 1, 516. dumeta, Stat. Th. 1, 696.— Pătărēis, īdis, f. adj., Patarœan: arx, Avien. Perieg. 684.— Pătārānus, a, um, adj., Patarœan hence,
patara.short: Pătăra, ae, f., = Παταρα, a seaport town of Lycia, with a celebrated oracle of Apollo, Mel.

patavinitas.full: Pătăvīnĭtas, ātis, f. Patavium, the mode of speaking or dialectic peculiarities of the Patavians, Patavinity (ascribed as a fault to Livy by Polliol, Quint. 1, 5, 56; 8, 1, 3.

patavium.full: Pătăvĭum, ĭi, n., an important city of Gallia Cisalpina, in the territory of the Veneti, founded by Antenor, the birthplace of Livy the historian, the modern Padua, Mel. 2, 4, 2; Plin. 3, 19, 23, § 130, Liv. 10, 2 fin.; Verg. A. 1, 247, Suet. Tib 14; Sen. Cons. ad Helv. 7 et saep.—Hence, Pă-tăvīnus, a, um, adj., atavinian. Paduan: tunicae. Mart. 14, 143, 1: volumina, i. e. Livy's Roman history, Sid. Carm. 2, 189.—In plur. subst.: Pătăvīni, ōrum, m., the inhabitants of Patavium, the Patavinians,
patavium.short: Pătăvĭum, ĭi, n., an important city of Gallia Cisalpina, in the territory of the Veneti, founded by Antenor, the birthplace of Livy the historian, the modern Padua, Mel.

patefacio.full: pătĕfăcĭo, fēci, factum, 3 (scanned pătēfēcit, Lucr. 4, 320; and in pass. pătēfīet, id. 6, 1001), v. a. pateo-facio, to make or lay open, to open, throw open (freq. and class.; syn.: pando, recludo, aperio). Lit.: iter, Cic. N. D. 2, 56, 141: patefacere et munire alicui aditum ad aliquid, id. Fam. 13, 78, 2: aures assentatoribus, id. Off. 1, 26, 91: portas, Liv. 2, 15: ordines, aciem, id. 28, 14: sulcum aratro, Ov. M. 3, 104: oculos, Plin. 11, 37, 55, § 150: patefacta triumphis Janua. Prop. 1, 1

patefactio.full: pătĕfactĭo, ōnis, f. patefacio, a laying open, disclosing, making known: patefactio quast rerum opertarum, Cic. Fin. 2, 2, 5.

patefactus.full: pătĕfactus, a, um, Part., from patefacio.
patefactus.short: pătĕfactus, a, um, Part., from patefacio.

patella1.full: pătella, ae, f. dim. patina, a small pan or dish, a plate; a vessel used in cooking, and also to serve up food in. Lit., Varr. ap. Prisc. p. 681 P.: patella esurienti posita, id. ap. Non. 543, 33; Hor. Ep. 1, 5, 2; Mart. 5, 78, 7; Juv. 10, 64: sinapi in patellis decoctum, Plin. 19, 8, 54, § 171: cicadae tostae in patellis, id. 30, 8, 21, § 68.— In partic., a vessel used in sacrifices, an offering - dish: patellae vasula parva picata sacris faciendis apta, Fest. pp. 248 and 249 Müll.: oportet bon

patella2.full: Pătella and Pătellāna (Pă-telāna), ae, f. pateo, a goddess that presiaed over the shooting of grain: Patellana numen est et Patella: ex quibus una est pateiactis, patefaciendis rebus altera praestituta, Arn. 4, 131: Patelana, Aug. Civ. Dei, 4, 8.

patellarius.full: pătellārĭus, a, um, adj. 1. patella, of or belonging to a dish or plate, patellaril di, platter-gods, i.e. the Lares (because food was set before them in a platter), Plaut. Cist. 2, 1, 46: cf. Schol. ap Pers. 3, 26

patens.full: pătens, entis, Part. and P. a., from pateo.

patenter.full: pătenter, adv. v. pateo, P a. fin.

pateo.full: păteo, ŭi, 2, v. n. root pat. (perh. orig. spat.; cf. spatium); Gr πεταννυμι, πιτνημι, to spread out; πετασμα, curtain; πεταλον, leaf; cf.: patulus, patina; also perh. pando (for pantdo)], to stand open, lie open, be open. Lit.: januae, aedes patent, Plaut. As. 1, 3, 89: facite totae plateae pateant, id. Aul. 3, 1, 2. nares semper propter necessarias utilitates patent, Cic. N. D. 2, 57, 145: omnibus haec ad visendum patebant cotidie, id. Verr 2, 4, 3, § 5: cur valvae Concordiae non patent? id. P

pater.full: păter, tris (old gen PATRVS. Inscr Corp. Lat. 1469; dat PATRE, ib 182), m. Sanscr. root pā, to nourish, protect; Lat. pasco; hence, Zend, patar, protector; Gr. πατηρ; Sanscr pitri; Engl. father; Germ. Vater, a father, sire. Lit. Aes. Ehem, pater mi, tu hic eras? De Tuus hercle vero et animo et patura pater, Ter. Ad. 5, 7, 3: patre certo nasci, Cic. Rosc. Am. 16, 46: Servius Tullius captivā Corniculanā natus, patre nullo, matre servā, i. e. by an unknown father, Liv. 4, 3: SI PATER FILIVM TER VEN

patera.full: pătĕra, ae, f. pateo, a broad, flat dish or saucer, used esp. in offerings; a libationsaucer or bowl (cf.: simpulum, simpuvium), Varr. L. L. 5, § 122 Müll.; cf. Macr. S. 5, 21: aurea, Plaut. Am. 1, 1, 104; 2, 2, 128: humani corporis sanguinem in pateris circumtulisse, Sall. C. 22, 1: Themistoclem aiunt, cum taurum immolavisset, excepisse sanguinem paterā, etc., Cic. Brut. 11, 43: vinaque marmoreas paterā fundebat in aras, Ov. M. 9, 160; Hor. S. 1, 6, 118: pateris libare et auro, golden cups, Ver

paterculus.full: Pătercŭlus, i, m. pater, a Roman surname, e. g. C. Velleius Paterculus, the historian; v. Velleius.—Hence, † Păter-cŭlārĭus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Paterculus, Not. Tir.

paternitas.full: păternĭtas, ātis, f. paternus, fatherly feeling or care (late Lat.), Aug. Ep. 232.— Collect., descendants of one father: ex quo omnis paternitas in caelis, Vulg. Eph. 3, 15.

paternus.full: păternus, a, um, adj. pater, of or belonging to a father, fatherly, paternal (said of the property, possessions, external relations, etc., of a father; while patrius is used of that which belongs essentially to his nature, dignity, or duty; hence, in good prose: patrius amor, animus, patria potestas, patrium jus; but paterni agri, liberi, servi, liberti, etc.). Lit.: injuria, against the father, Ter. Heaut. 5, 2, 39: haud paternum istuc dedisti, id. Ad. 3, 4, 4: horti, Cic. Phil. 13, 17, 34: lib

patesco.full: pătesco (-isco), pătŭi, 3, v. inch. n. [pateo], to be laid open, to be opened, to open (mostly poet. and in post-Aug. prose; not in Cic.). Lit.: atria longa patescunt, Verg. A. 2, 483: portus patescit, id. ib. 3, 530: patescens fungus, Plin. 22, 22, 46, § 95. — Transf., to stretch out, extend: paulo latior patescit campus, Liv. 22, 4: neque poterat patescere acies, Tac. H. 4, 78: civitates, in quas Germania patescit, id. G. 30; id. A. 2, 61 fin.; cf.: latius patescente imperio, Liv. 32, 27.— Tro

patetus.full: pătētus, a, um, adj., = πατητός (trodden), perhaps only as subst.: pătētae, ārum, f. (sc. caryotae), a kind of dates (which, when they burst open, look as if they had been trodden upon), Plin. 13, 4, 9, § 45; Cael. Aur. Acut. 2, 18, 108; id. Tard. 4, 8, 126.
patetus.short: pătētus, a, um, adj., = πατητός (trodden), perhaps only as subst.: pătētae, ārum, f.

patheticus.full: păthētĭcus, a, um, adj., = παθητικός, full of pathos, affecting, pathetic (postclass.): oratio, Macr. S. 4, 2, 5; 6.—Hence, adv.: păthētĭcē, pathetically: tractare aliquid, Macr. S. 4, 6.
patheticus.short: păthētĭcus, a, um, adj., = παθητικός, full of pathos, affecting, pathetic (postclass.): oratio, Macr.

pathicus.full: păthĭcus, a, um, adj., = παθικός, who submits to unnatural lust, pathic; of men: Aureli pathice et cinaede Furi, Cat. 16, 2; Juv. 2, 99: amicus, id. 9, 130; of women, Auct. Priap. 25, 41 and 76.—Sup.: pathicissimi libelli, most lascivious, Mart. 12, 96, 1.
pathicus.short: păthĭcus, a, um, adj., = παθικός, who submits to unnatural lust, pathic;

pathos.full: păthŏs, n., = πάθος, pathos, tender or passionate feeling: movere, Macr. S. 4, 6, 6; 13: permovere, id. 4, 6, 10.
pathos.short: păthŏs, n., = πάθος, pathos, tender or passionate feeling: movere, Macr.

patibilis.full: pătĭbĭlis, e, adj. patior. Pass., supportable, endurable (syn.: tolerabilis, ferendus): patibiles et dolores et labores putandi (sunt), Cic. Tusc. 4, 23, 51.— Act. Sensitive, passible: patibilem naturam habere, Cic. N. D. 3, 12, 29.— Suffering, passive: alterum elementum activum, alterum patibile, Lact. 2, 9 med.

patibulatus.full: pătĭbŭlātus, a, um, adj. patibulum, fastened to the patibulum; yoked, gibbeted, Plaut. Most. 1, 1, 53: patibulatus ferar per urbem, deinde affigar cruci, id. Fragm. ap. Non. 221, 13 (al. patibulum): exitiabili nexu patibulatum relinquens, gibbeted, App. M. 4, p. 147, 4 (al. patibulum).

patibulum.full: pătĭbŭlum, i, n. (masc. collat. form pătĭbŭlus, i, Varr. ap. Non. 221, 12; v. in the foll.) [pateo], a fork-shaped yoke, placed on the necks of criminals, and to which their hands were tied; also, a fork-shaped gibbet (syn. furca). Lit.: dispessis manibus patibulum quom habebis, Plaut. Mil. 2, 4, 7: patibulo eminens adfigebatur, Sall. Fragm. ap. Non. 4, 355 (Hist. 4, 40 Dietsch): caedes, patibula, ignes, cruces, Tac. A. 14, 33; Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 41, § 90.—Masc.: deligat ad patibulos, Varr. ap. No

patibulus1.full: pătĭbŭlus, a, um, adj. pateo, fastened to a patibulum; yoked, gibbeted, Plaut. Fragm. ap. Non. 221, 13; App. M. 4, p. 147 (in both passages al. leg. patibulatum; v. patibulatus).

paticabulum.full: pătĭcābŭlum, i, n., perhaps from pateo, in the sense of a cistern or pond, Inscr. Marin. Atti de' Fratelli Arv. p. 70.
paticabulum.short: pătĭcābŭlum, i, n., perhaps from pateo, in the sense of a cistern or pond, Inscr.

patiens.full: pătĭens, entis, Part. and P. a., from patior.

patienter.full: pătĭenter, adv., v. patior, P. a. fin.

patientia.full: pătĭentĭa, ae, f. patior, the quality of bearing, suffering, or enduring, patience, endurance. Lit. In gen.: pati entia est honestatis aut utilitatis causā rerum arduarum ac difficilium voluntaria ac diuturna perpessio, Cic. Inv. 2, 54, 163: patientia famis et frigoris, id. Cat. 1, 10, 26: hominum ea patientia, virtus frugalitasque est, Cic. Verr. 2, 2, 3, § 7: paupertatis, id. Agr. 2, 24, 64: audiendi, Quint. 11, 2, 8; 12, 9, 9.— In partic., submission to unnatural lust, pathicism, Cic. Verr. 2

patigran.full: Patigran or Patigrans, f., a city in Media, Amm. 23, 23.
patigran.short: Patigran or Patigrans, f., a city in Media, Amm.

patina1.full: pătĭna (pătĕna), ae, f. pateo, a broad, shallow dish, pan, stewpan (cf.: lanx, catinus). Lit.: ut patinae fervent, Plaut. Ps. 3, 2, 51: qui mi inter patinas exhibes argutias, id. Most. 1, 1, 2: jamdudum animus est in patinis, i. e. my belly has been crying cupboard, Ter. Eun. 4, 7, 46; Cic. Att. 4, 8, a, 1: muraena In patinā porrectā, Hor. S. 2, 8, 43; Plin. 23, 2, 33, § 68: fictiles, id. 34, 11, 25, § 109: orobanche estur et per se et in patinis, i. e. cooked, id. 22, 25, 80, § 162: patinae ob

patina2.full: Patĭna, ae, m., a Roman surname: T. Patina, Cic. Mil. 17, 46.
patina2.short: Patĭna, ae, m., a Roman surname: T.

patinarius.full: pătĭnārĭus, a, um, adj. 1. patina, of or belonging to a dish or pan: piscis. stewed in a pan with sauce, Plaut. As. 1, 3, 27: strues, a pile of dishes, id. Mer. 1, 2, 25: aliis incendiarium et patinarium vociferantibus, i. e. gormandizer, Suet. Vit. 17.— Via patinaria, a street in Rome, P. Vict. de Reg. Urb. R.

patior.full: pătĭor, passus, 3, v. dep. (act. archaic collat. form patiunto, Cic. Leg. 3, 4, 11: patias, Naev. ap. Diom. p. 395 P.) [cf. Greek ΠΑΘ, ΠΕΝΘ-, πέπονθα, πένθος], to bear, support, undergo, suffer, endure (syn.: fero, tolero). Lit. In gen. Tu fortunatu's, ego miser: patiunda sunt, Plaut. Most. 1, 1, 46; id. Am. 3, 2, 64: fortiter malum qui patitur, idem post potitur bonum, id. As. 2, 2, 58 Ussing (al. patitur bonum): o passi graviora! Naev. 1, 24; Verg. A. 1, 199; Cic. Univ. 6: belli injurias, id.

patmos.full: Patmos or -us, i, f., = Πάτμος, an island of the Ægean Sea, one of the Sporades, a place of banishment of the Romans, now Patino, Plin. 4, 12, 23, § 69; Vulg. Apoc. 1, 9.
patmos.short: Patmos or -us, i, f., = Πάτμος, an island of the Ægean Sea, one of the Sporades, a place of banishment of the Romans, now Patino, Plin.

pator.full: pător, ōris, m. pateo, an opening (postclass.), App. M. 1, p. 111, 7; 3, p. 137 et saep.: narium, Scrib. Comp. 46 and 47.

patrae.full: Pā^trae, ārum, f., = Πάτραι, a very ancient city in Achaia, on the promontory of Rhium, the mod. Patras, Cic. Fam. 7, 28, 1; 13, 17, 1; 16, 1, 2; Liv. 27, 29; Mel. 2, 3, 9; Plin. 4, 4, 5, § 11; Ov. M. 6, 417.— Hence, Pā^trensis, e, adj., of or belonging to Patrœ, Patrœan: Lyso Patrensis, of Patrœ, Cic. Fam. 13, 19, 1 sq.: bibliotheca, Gell. 18, 9, 5.—In plur.: Pătren-ses, ĭum, m., the Patrœans: Patrensium leges, Cic. Fam. 13, 19, 2.
patrae.short: Pā^trae, ārum, f., = Πάτραι, a very ancient city in Achaia, on the promontory of Rhium, the mod.

patraster.full: pătraster, tri, m. pater, a fatherin-law, Inscr. Maff. Mus. Ver. 360, 7; Inscr. Murat. 1632, 9; 1958, 6.

patratio.full: pā^trātĭo, ōnis, f. patro, an effecting, achieving, accomplishing (rare and postAug.). In gen., Vell. 2, 98, 2.— In partic., in mal. part., Schol. ad Pers. 1, 18; Theod. Prisc. 2, 11.

patrator.full: pā^trātor, ōris, m. id., an effecter, achiever, accomplisher (post-Aug.): necis, Tac. A. 14, 62: amoris, Avien. Arat. 20: illustrium operum atque signorum, Hier. in Isa. prol. init.

patratus.full: pătrātus, a, um, Part., from patro; v. patro fin.
patratus.short: pătrātus, a, um, Part., from patro;

patria.full: pā^trĭa, ae, v. 1. patrius, II. C. 1.

patriarcha.full: pătrĭarcha and pătrĭarches, ae, m., = πατριάρχης, the father or chief of a tribe, a patriarch. Lit.: secundum patriarchas et ceteros majores, Tert. Idol. 17; id. Cor. Mil. 9; Prud. Psych. 534; Vulg. 1 Par. 8, 28; id. Act. 7, 8.—Gen. plur. patriarchūm, Paul. Nol. Carm. 24, 209.— Transf., a chief bishop, a patriarch, Vop. Firm. Saturn. 8, 4.— Trop.: philosophi, patriarchae ut ita dixerim, haereticorum, Tert. Anim. 3.
patriarcha.short: pătrĭarcha and pătrĭarches, ae, m., = πατριάρχης, the father or chief of a tribe, a patriarch.

patriarchicus.full: pătrĭarchĭcus, a, um, adj. patriarcha, of or belonging to a patriarch, patriarchal: sedes, Just. Novell. 7.

patriciatus.full: pătrĭcĭātus, ūs, m. patricius, the rank or dignity of the patricians, Suet. Aug. 2.—From the time of Constantine, a high dignity at the imperial court, a rank next to that of the emperor, Cassiod. Var. 6, 2.

patricia.full: Patrĭcĭa Cŏlōnĭa, the Roman colony of Corduba, in Hispania Baetica, Plin. 3, 1, 3, § 11.—Hence, † Patrĭcĭen-sis, e, adj., of or belonging to the city of Corduba, Inscr. Grut. 432, 7; 460, 10.
patricia.short: Patrĭcĭa Cŏlōnĭa, the Roman colony of Corduba, in Hispania Baetica, Plin.

patriciolus.full: pā^trĭcĭŏlus, i, m. dim., from patricius, acc. to Prisc. p. 610 P.

patricius.full: pā^trĭcĭus (pā^trĭtĭus, Aug. Mon. Ancyr.), a, um, adj. patres, of the rank or dignity of the patres; belonging to the patricians, patrician, noble (cf. nobilis): patricii pueri, Plaut. Capt. 5, 4, 5: familia, Cic. Leg. 2, 3, 6; Vell. 2, 59, 2: gens, Juv. 10, 332: sanguis, Pers. 1, 61: ostrum, Stat. S. 1, 4, 97: Patricius Vicus Romae dictus eo, quod ibi patricii habitaverunt (the mod. Via Urbana), Fest. p. 221 Müll.— Subst.: pā^trĭcĭus, i (usu. plur., pā^trĭcĭi, ōrum), m., a patrician, a member o

patricus.full: pā^trĭcus, a, um, adj. pater, of or belonging to a father, fatherly, paternal; in gram.: patricus casus, the genitive, Varr. L. L. 8, § 66 Müll.; 8, § 67 ib.; 9, § 54 ib; 9, § 67 ib.; 9, § 85 ib.—Hence, adv.: pă-trĭcē, paternally, in the manner of a father (ante-class.): cesso magnifice patriceque ita ero meo ire advorsum? Plaut. Cas. 3, 6, 8.

patrimonialis.full: pā^trĭmōnĭālis, e, adj. patrimonium of or belonging to a patrimony, patrimonial (jurid. Lat.): munus, Dig. 50, 4, 1: fundi, Cod. Th. 11, 16, 1; 2; 9.

patrimoniolum.full: pătrĭmōnĭŏlum, i, n. dim. id., a little patrimony (late Lat.), Hier. Ep. 45, n. 15.

patrimonium.full: pā^trĭmōnĭum, ii, n. pater, an estate inherited from a father, a paternal estate, inheritance, patrimony (syn. hereditas). Lit.: lauta et copiosa, Cic. Rab. Post. 14; id. Fl. 36, 89: amplum et copiosum, id. Rosc. Am. 2, 6: expellere aliquem e patrimonio, id. ib. 50, 147: patrimonio ornatissimo spoliari, id. Sull. 20, 58: naufragium patrimonii luculentissimi, id. Phil. 12, 8, 19: patrimonia effundere, id. Off. 2, 15, 54: devorare, id. Phil. 2, 27, 67: eripere patrimonium alicui, id. Sest. 52, 111

patrimus.full: pătrīmus (quantity of the penult uncertain; v. matrimus), a, um (collat. form: MATRIMES ac PATRIMES dicuntur, quibus matres et patres adhuc vivunt, Fest. p. 126 Müll.), adj. id., that has a father living: decem ingenui, decem virgines, patrimi omnes matrimique (Gr. ἀμφιθαλεῖς), Liv. 37, 3, 6; Cic. Har. Resp. 11, 23; Tac. H. 4, 53; Gell. 1, 12, 2; Cic. Lael. ap. Macr. S. 1, 6, 13; Fest. s. v. patrimi, p. 245 Müll.; cf. Mercklin in Zeitschr. f. Alterth. Wiss. 12. Jahrg., Heft 2. pp. 97- 122. (The

patriota.full: pā^trĭōta, ae, m., = πατριώτης, a countryman, Gregor. Ep. 8, 37.
patriota.short: pā^trĭōta, ae, m., = πατριώτης, a countryman, Gregor.

patrioticus.full: pā^trĭōtĭcus, a, um (patria), of or belonging to one's native land: possessiones, Cassiod. Var. 12, 5: responsio, in the mothertongue, id. ib. 11, 1.
patrioticus.short: pā^trĭōtĭcus, a, um (patria), of or belonging to one's native land: possessiones, Cassiod.

patri.full: pā^trĭ-passĭāni, ōrum, m. paterpatior, believers in the doctrine of Noëtus, that the Supreme Father suffered in the death of Jesus, Isid. Orig. 8, 5, 41.

patrisso.full: pā^trisso (patrīzo), āre, v. n., = πατρίζω, to take after one's father (ante-class.): tene id mirari, si patrissat finus? Plaut. Ps. 1, 5, 27; Ter. Ad. 4, 2, 25.

patritus.full: pătrītus, a, um, adj. pater, like avitus from avus, of one's father or forefathers (an archaic word, which, however, in Cic. Tusc. 1, 19, 45, is suspected without sufficient cause): avito ac patrito more, Varr. ap. Non. 161, 6: secundum leges patritas, id. ib. 161, 8: patrita et avita philosophia, Cic. Tusc. 1, 19, 45: res, Cic. Verr. 1, 5, 13 (Klotz); Lex. Thor lin. 28: subleva misericordiā aetatem familiarem tibi et patritam, Front. Ep. ad Amic. 2, 6 fin.: in sedem patritam referri, Arn. 2, 87
