peltatus.full: peltātus, a, um, adj. pelta, armed with the pelta, Ov. Am. 2, 14, 2; id. H. 21, 117: Amazon, Mart. 9, 102, 5: cohors, Claud. Fescenn. de Nupt. Honor. et Mar. 33.

peltifer.full: peltĭfer, ĕra, ĕrum, adj. pelta-fero, bearing, i. e. armed with the pelta: puellae, i. e. Amazons, Stat. Th. 12, 761: maeotides, Sab. Ep. 2, 9.

pelusium.full: Pēlūsĭum, ii, n., = Πηλούσιον, an Egyptian city at the eastern mouth of the Nile, the modern Castle of Tineh, Mel. 1, 9, 9; Plin. 10, 30, 45, § 87; Caes. B. C. 3, 103; Liv. 44, 19.—Hence, Pēlūsĭăcus, a, um, adj., Pelusiac: lens, Verg. G. 1, 228: linum, Plin 19, 1, 2, § 14: ostium Nili, Mel. 1, 9, 9; Plin. 5, 10, 11, § 64: via, leading to Pelusium, id. 6, 29, 33, § 167.— Pēlū-sĭānus, a, um, adj., Pelusian: mala, Col. 5, 10, 19.— Pēlūsĭōta or Pēlūsĭō-tes, ae, m., a Pelusian: Pelusiotae caepe non e
pelusium.short: Pēlūsĭum, ii, n., = Πηλούσιον, an Egyptian city at the eastern mouth of the Nile, the modern Castle of Tineh, Mel.

pelvicula.full: pelvĭcŭla, ae, f. dim. pelvis, a small basin: pelvis, pelvicula, Not. Tir. p. 164.

pelvis.full: pelvis, is (acc. pelvim; v. in the foll., and cf. Prisc. p. 757 P.; abl. pelvi and pelve), f. Sanscr. pālavi; Gr. πελλίς, a bowl. a basin, laver; acc. pelvim, Laber. ap. Non. 543, 27; Caecil. ib. 28: patulas effundere pelves, Juv. 3, 271: tot pelves pulsari, id. 6, 441; abl. pelvi, Plin. 31, 3, 27, § 46; 28, 8, 27, § 104: unguentum in argenteā pelve, Petr. 70; Plin. 30, 2, 5, § 14; Vulg. Johan. 13, 5.

pemma.full: pemma, ătis, n., = πέμμα, pastry: panis, pemma, lucuns, Varr. ap. Non. 131, 24: vinum, pemma, lucuns, id. 131, 26.
pemma.short: pemma, ătis, n., = πέμμα, pastry: panis, pemma, lucuns, Varr.

penarius.full: pĕnārĭus, a, um, adj. penus, of or for provisions: cella, Cic. Sen. 16, 56; Cic. Verr. 2, 2, 2, § 5.—Subst.: pĕnārĭa, ae, a storehouse: a celando cellam appellarunt; penariam, ubi penus, Varr. L. L. 5, § 162 Müll.; also, pĕnārĭus, i, m., a storehouse, granary: penora dicuntur res necessariae ad victum cotidianum, et locus eorum penarius, Paul. ex Fest. p. 211 Müll.

penates.full: Pĕnātes, ĭum (Penatis singulariter Labeo Antistius posse dici putat, quia pluraliter Penates dicuntur, cum patiatur proportio etiam Penas dici, ut optimas, primas, Antias, Fest. p. 253 Müll. But the singular is never used; and for ΔΕΝΑΣ = ΠΕΝΑΣ, which some assume in Dion. Hal. 1, 68, it is probably most correct to read ΔΙΣ ΜΑΓΝΙΣ, v. Ambrosch, Studien und Andeut. vol. i. p. 231 sq.—Acc. plur. PENATEIS, perh. Tab. Bant. lin. 22), m. from the root pa, whence pascor, pabulum, pānis; also penus, and
penates.short: Pĕnātes, ĭum (Penatis singulariter Labeo Antistius posse dici putat, quia pluraliter Penates dicuntur, cum patiatur proportio etiam Penas dici, ut optimas, primas, Antias, Fest.

penatiger.full: pĕnātĭger, ĕra, ĕrum, adj. penatesgero, bearing with him his guardian gods, Ov. M. 15, 450.

penator.full: pĕnātor, ōris, m. penus, one who carries provisions, Cato ap. Fest. p. 237 Müll.; cf. Meyer Oratt. Fragmm. p. 51 ed. alt.

pendens.full: pendens, entis, Part. and P. a., from pendeo.

pendeo.full: pendĕo, pĕpendi, 2, v. n. intr. of pendo, q. v., to hang, hang down, be suspended. Lit., constr. with ab, ex, or in and abl.; also (poet.), with abl. alone, or with de: pendent peniculamenta, Enn. ap. Non. 149, 32 (Ann. v. 363 Vahl.): in candelabro pendet strigilis, Varr. ap. Non. 223, 7: in arbore, Cic. Verr. 2, 3, 23, § 57: sagittae pende, bant ab umero, id. ib. 2, 4, 34, § 74: ex arbore, id. ib. 2, 3, 26, § 66: ubera circum (pueri), Verg. A. 8, 632: horrida pendebant molles super ora capilli,

pendiculus.full: pendĭcŭlus, i, m. pendeo, a cord, noose, snare: pendiculus, ἁρπεδών, ἁρπεδώνιον, Gloss. Cyrill.

pendigo.full: pendīgo, inis, f. id., lit. an internal tumor, abscess (post-class.). Lit., Veg. Vet. 2, 44: pendiginem circumcides ad vivum, id. ib. 2, 55.— Transf., a hollow space inside of a statue: simulacri pendigines, Arn. 6, 201.

pendix.full: pendix, ĭcis, f. id., perh. i. q. pendigo: A PENDICE CEDRI, Inscr. Grut. 601, 10 and 11.

pendo.full: pendo, pĕpendi, pensum, 3 (pendissent, for pependissent, Liv. 45, 26 fin.: penderit for pependerit, Paul. Nol. Carm. 14, 122), v. a. and n. etym. dub.; cf. root σφαδ-, σφενδόνη, a sling; Lat. funda.—Lit., to cause to hang down, to suspend; esp. of scales in weighing. Act., to weigh, weigh out. Lit. (very rare: syn. penso, expendo): unumquodque verbum staterā aurariā pendere, Varr. ap. Non. 455, 21: da pensam lanam, Titin. ap. Non. 369, 21; Plin. 19, 3, 15, § 39, read repensum: aere gravi cum ute
pendo.short: pendo, pĕpendi, pensum, 3 (pendissent, for pependissent, Liv.

pendulus.full: pendŭlus, a, um, adj. pendeo, hanging, hanging down, pendent (poet. and in post-Aug. prose; syn.: pensilis). Lit.: collum, Hor. C. 3, 27, 59: libra, Ov. F. 4, 386: palearia, id. M. 7, 117: tela, id. H. 1, 10: genae (ebrii), Plin. 14, 22, 28, § 142.— Transf., of places, overhanging, Mart. 13, 112: loca et macriora, Col. 2, 18.—Of persons, hanging, swinging: putator arbustis, Col. 10, 229.—In mal. part.: Venus, App. M. 2, p. 122 med.— Trop., doubtful, uncertain, hesitating: neu fluitem dubiae spe

peneius.full: Pēnēĭus, a, um, v. Peneus, B.

peneleus.full: Pēnĕleus, ĕi and ĕos, m., son of Hippalmus and Asterope, one of Helen's suitors, Verg. A. 2, 425; Hyg. Fab. 81; Dict. Cret. 4, 17.
peneleus.short: Pēnĕleus, ĕi and ĕos, m., son of Hippalmus and Asterope, one of Helen's suitors, Verg.

penelope.full: Pēnĕlŏpē, ēs, and Pēnĕlŏpa, ae (Pēnĕlŏpēa, = Πηνελόπεια, Auct. Priap. 68, 28), f., = Πηνελόπη, daughter of Icarius and Peribœa, wife of Ulysses, and mother of Telemachus, celebrated for her chastity and constancy, Ov. H. 1; Hyg. Fab. 126; Plaut. Stich. 1, 1, 1; Cic. N. D. 3, 22, 56; id. Ac. 2, 29, 65; Hor. C. 3, 10, 11; id. S. 2, 5, 76; Juv. 2, 56: sponsi Penelopae, for sensualists, Hor. Ep. 1, 2, 28.— Transf, poet., a chaste wife, Mart. 1, 63, 6.—Hence, Pē-nĕlŏpēus, a, um, adj., of or belonging
penelope.short: Pēnĕlŏpē, ēs, and Pēnĕlŏpa, ae (Pēnĕlŏpēa, = Πηνελόπεια, Auct.

penelops.full: pēnĕlops, ŏpis, m., = πηνέλοψ, a kind of duck, also called Meleagris, Plin. 37, 2, 11, § 38.
penelops.short: pēnĕlops, ŏpis, m., = πηνέλοψ, a kind of duck, also called Meleagris, Plin.

penes.full: pĕnĕs, prep. with acc. [from the root pa- of pasco, v. Penates], with, in the possession or power of; connected only with names of persons, and freq. foll. its case (class.). Chiefly to denote possession: virtus omnia in se habet; omnia assunt bona, quem penes est virtus, Plaut. Am. 2, 2, 21; id. Capt. 2, 1, 37; cf. id. Truc. 5, 9: agri, quorum penes Cn. Pompeium omne judicium et potestas debet esse, Cic. Agr. 2, 19, 52; cf.: penes quem est potestas, id. Fam. 4, 7, 3: eloquentia non modo eos orn

penestae.full: Pĕnestae, ārum, m., = Πενέσται, a people in Grecian Illyria, Liv. 43, 21.— Pĕnestĭa, ae, f., the country of the Penestœ: in Penestiam exercitum reducit, Liv. 43, 19.—Hence, Pĕnestĭānus, a, um, adj., Penestian, Liv. 43, 16.
penestae.short: Pĕnestae, ārum, m., = Πενέσται, a people in Grecian Illyria, Liv.

penetrabilis.full: pĕnĕtrābĭlis, e, adj. penetro. Pass., that can be pierced or penetrated, penetrable (poet. and in post-Aug. prose): corpus nullo penetrabile telo, Ov. M. 12, 166: cum sit nulli penetrabilis, Sen. Const. Sap. 3: pectus ferro, Stat. Th. 2, 653: terra, Just. 4, 1, 2: caput haud penetrabile Nili, inaccessible, Stat. S. 3, 5, 21.— Act., piercing, penetrating (poet. and in post-class. prose): Boreae penetrabile frigus, Verg. G. 1, 93: telum, id. A. 10, 481: harundo, Sil. 7, 649: fulmen, Ov. M. 13, 857

penetralis.full: pĕnē^trālis, e, adj. penetro. Piercing, penetrating (ante-class.): frigus, Lucr. 1, 494: ignis, id. 1, 535: fulmineus multo penetralior ignis, id. 2, 382.— Transf., inward, inner, internal, interior, innermost (mostly poet.): tecta, Verg. G. 1, 379: aeternumque adytis effert penetralibus ignem, id. A. 2, 297: abditi ac penetrales foci, Cic. Har. Resp. 27, 57: di Penates ... ab eo, quod penitus insideret: ex quo etiam penetrales a poëtis vocantur, id. N. D. 2, 27, 68; so, per penetrales deos, Sen

penetratio.full: pĕnĕtrātĭo, ōnis, f. penetro, a piercing, penetrating (post-class.), App. Flor. p. 160, 40.

penetrator.full: pĕnē^trātor, ōris, m. id., one who penetrates, a penetrator (post-class.): domus alienae penetratores, Aug. Ep. 199; Prud. Hamart. 883; Paul. Nol. Carm. 20, 285.

penetro.full: pĕnē^tro, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. and n. root pa- of pasco; v. penates. Act. To put, place, or set any thing into any thing (ante- and post-class.; v. Brix ad Plaut. Trin. 1, 2, 109). Lit.: penetrare pedem intra aedes, Plaut. Men. 5, 2, 64; 2, 3, 49: quo illic homo foras se penetrat ex aedibus? to betake one's self, go in any direction, id. Trin. 2, 2, 1: me ad pluris penetravi, id. ib. v. 14: se in fugam, to take to flight, id. Am. 1, 1, 94: in eam (specum) me penetro et recondo, Gell. 5, 14, 18.—T

peneus.full: Pēnēus, i, m., = Πηνειός, a principal river in Thessaly, which rises in Mount Pindus, flows through the Vale of Tempe, and falls into the Gulf of Therma, the modern Selembria; in mythology, a rivergod, the father of Cyrene and Daphne, Ov. M. 1, 569 sq.; Plin. 4, 8, 15, § 31; Liv. 32, 15; Verg. G. 4, 355; Hyg. Fab. 161; 203.— Voc. Penee, Ov. Am. 3, 6, 31.—Hence, Pēnēis, ĭdis, f., = Πηνηίς, of or belonging to the Peneus, Penean (poet.): Nympha, i.e. Daphne, Ov. M. 1, 504; 1, 472.— Pē-nēĭus, a, um,
peneus.short: Pēnēus, i, m., = Πηνειός, a principal river in Thessaly, which rises in Mount Pindus, flows through the Vale of Tempe, and falls into the Gulf of Therma, the modern Selembria;

penicillum.full: pēnĭcillum, i, n., and pēnĭcillus, i, m. dim. peniculus, lit., a little tail; hence, acc. to diverse usage, A painter's brush or pencil: caudam antiqui penem vocabant, ex quo est propter similitudinem penicillus, Cic. Fam. 9, 22, 2; id. Or. 22, 74; Quint. 2, 21, 24: setae e penicillis tectoriis, Plin. 28, 17, 71, § 235; Paul. Sent. 3, 6, 63.— Transf. Painting. Plin. 35, 9, 36, § 60.— Style of composition: modo mihi date Britanniam, quam pingam coloribus tuis, penicillo meo, Cic. Q. Fr. 2, 15, 2.
penicillum.short: pēnĭcillum, i, n., and pēnĭcillus, i, m.

peniculamentum.full: pēnĭcŭlāmentum, i, n. peniculus. A tail, train, Arn. 5, 163 (11).— Transf., a train of a garment (ante-class.): pendent peniculamenta unum ad quemque pedum, Enn. Ann. ap. Non. 149, 32 (Ann. v. 363 Vahl.); Lucil. and Caecil. ap. Non. 149, 33, and 150, 3.

peniculus.full: pēnĭcŭlus, i, m. dim. penis, lit., a little tail; hence, A brush for removing dust (for which ox-tails and horse-tails were used): (a pene) peniculi, quis calciamenta tergentur, quod e codis extremis faciebant antiqui, etc., Fest. p. 230 Müll.: juventus nomen fecit Peniculo mihi, ideo quia mensam, quando edo, detergeo, Plaut. Men. 1, 1, 1; cf.: Quis iste'st Peniculus? Qui extergentur baxeae? id. ib. 2, 3, 40.— A sponge: ut peniculus novos exurgeri solet, Plaut. Rud. 4, 3, 69; Ter. Eun. 4, 7, 7;

penis.full: pēnis, is, m. (abl. peni, Naev. ap. Fest. p. 230 Müll.) [τὸ πέος], a tail. In gen. (ante-class.): caudam antiqui penem vocabant, Cic. Fam. 9, 22, 2: ... lares ludentes peni pinxit bubulo, Naev. ap. Fest. p. 230 Müll.— In partic., = membrum virile, the penis; also, by meton., for lust (class.): hodie penis est in obscenis, Cic. Fam. 9, 22, 2: ganeo, manu, ventre, pene bona patria laceraverat, Sall. C. 14, 2; Hor. Epod. 12, 8; Juv. 9, 43; Arn. 5, 18.—In a paron. with paene, Plaut. Truc. 2, 6, 37.

penite.full: pĕnĭtē, adv., v. 1. penitus fin. A.

penitus1.full: pĕnĭtus, a, um, adj. root pa- of pasco; v. penates, inward, inner, interior (ante- and post-class.): exscrea usque ex penitis faucibus, Plaut. As. 1, 1, 28: scaturigo fontis, App. M. 6, p. 178, 33: mente penitā conditum, id. ib. 11, p. 259, 38.—Comp. penitior pars domūs, App. Fragm. ap. Prisc. p. 599 P.—Sup.: advecta ex Arabiā penitissimā, Plaut. Pers. 4, 3, 53; so id. ib. 4, 3, 71: in latebras abscondas pectore penitissimo, id. Cist. 1, 1, 65: Scythae illi penitissimi, the most remote, Gell. 9,

penitus2.full: pēnītus, a, um, adj. penis, furnished with or having a tail: penitam offam Naevius appellat absegmen carnis cum codā, Fest. p. 242 Müll.; Arn. 7, 24, 230; cf. Fest. s. v. penem, p. 230 Müll.

penius.full: Pĕnĭus, ii, m., = Πενιός, a river in Colchis, Ov. P. 4, 10, 47; Plin. 6, 4, 4, § 14.
penius.short: Pĕnĭus, ii, m., = Πενιός, a river in Colchis, Ov.

penna.full: penna or pinna (old forms, pesna, petna, Fest. p. 205, 209 Müll.), f. orig. different words, penna for petna; root petor pat-; Sanscr. patāmi, to fly; Gr. πέτομαι, prop. a wing: pinna for pitna; cf. Sanscr. pitu; Gr. πίτυς, the pine-tree; Lat. pinus; cf.: spiculum, spina; prop. a sharp point or end. To a late period an effort was made to distinguish them: nec miretur (puer), cur ... fiat a pinno quod est acutum, securis utrimque habens aciem bipennis, ne illorum sequatur errorem, qui, quia a pen
penna.short: penna or pinna (old forms, pesna, petna, Fest.

pennarium.full: pennārĭum, ĭi, n. penna, a receptacle for pens, a pen-box: pennarium, καλαμοθήκη, Gloss. Philox.

pennatulus.full: pennātŭlus, a, um, adj. dim. [pennātus], provided with wings, winged (eccl. Lat.): Mercurius in calvitio pennatulus, Tert. ad Nat. 1, 10.

pennatus.full: pennātus (pinn-), a, um, adj. penna, furnished with wings, winged (poet. and in post-Aug. prose): hic Jovis altisoni subito pennata (al. pinnata) satelles, Cic. poët. Div. 1, 47, 106: apes, Plin. 11, 1, 1, § 1: serpentes, Ov. M. 7, 350: pennati equi, quos pegasos vocant, Plin. 8, 21, 30, § 72: Zephyrus, Lucr. 5, 738: ferrum, an arrow, Plin. 34, 14, 39, § 138.—Subst.: pennāta, ōrum, n. (sc. animalia), winged creatures, birds: pennatorum infecunda sunt, quae aduncos habent ungues, Plin. 10, 52, 73

pennesco.full: pennesco, ĕre, v. n. inch. [id.], to put forth feathers or wings, to become fledged (post-class.), Cassiod. Var. 1, 38.

pennifer.full: pennĭfer, ĕra, ĕrum, adj. penna-fero, feathered, winged (post-class. prose): armi, Sid. Carm. 2, 309.

penniger.full: pennĭger, ĕra, ĕrum, adj., or pinnĭ-ger penna-gero, feathered, winged. Lit. (class.): genus animantium, Cic. Univ. 10: pinniger rex apum, Plin. 11, 16, 16, § 48.— Transf. (poet.): sagittae, Sil. 3, 375.
penniger.short: pennĭger, ĕra, ĕrum, adj., or pinnĭ-ger penna-gero, feathered, winged.

penninus.full: Pennīnus (Penīnus or Poenī-nus; the latter orthog. on account of the false derivation from Poeni, because Hannibal marched over this mountain to Italy, Liv. 21, 38, 6 sqq.; Plin. 3, 17, 21, § 123), a, um, adj. from the Celtic Pen or Penn, summit, peak, of or belonging to the Pennine Alps (between the Valais and Upper Italy, the highest point of which is the Great St. Bernard), Pennine: Alpes, Plin. 3, 17, 21, § 123; Tac. H. 1, 87; called also, juga, id. ib. 1, 61: mons, i. e. the Great St. Berna

pennipes.full: pennĭpēs, ĕdis, adj. penna-pes, that has wings on his feet, wing-footed: Perseus, Cat. 55, 24.

pennipotens.full: pennĭpŏtens (pinn-; cf. Don. p. 1748 P.), entis, adj. penna-potens, able to fly, winged (poet.): pennipotentum, Lucr. 2, 878; 5, 789.

pennor.full: pennor, āri, v. dep. n. [penna], to put forth wings, become fledged, Dracont. 1, 262.

pennula.full: pennŭla, ae, f. dim. id., a little wing (rare but class.): cum pulli pennulis uti possunt, Cic. N. D. 2, 52, 129: tensa, Ven. Carm. 3, 22, 9; Hieron. adv. Pelag. 1, 14 init.; Vulg. Lev. 5, 8.

pennus1.full: pennus, a, um, adj. pinna, pointed, sharp: pennum antiqui acutum dicebant: unde et avium pennae, quia acutae, Isid. Orig. 19, 19, 11 dub. (al. pinnum).

pennus2.full: Pennus, i, m., a Roman surname: T. Quinctius Pennus, Liv. 4, 26.
pennus2.short: Pennus, i, m., a Roman surname: T.

pensa.full: pensa, ae, f. pendo, a day's provisions, a ration for a day, Edict. Diocl. p. 19.

pensabilis.full: pensābilis, e, adj. penso, reparable (post-class.): damna, Amm. 31, 13, 11.

pensatio.full: pensātĭo, ōnis, f. id.. Lit., a weighing, weighing out, a recompense, compensation (post-Aug.): multorum bonorum pensatio, Petr. 141, 6; Dig. 16, 2, 7; Quint. Decl. 2, 32; Dig. 3, 5, 7.— Trop., a weighing, pondering, consideration (postclass.), Amm. 16, 12, 33.

pense.full: pensē, adv., v. pendo, P. a. fin.

pensiculator.full: pensĭcŭlātor, ōris, m. pensiculo, a weigher, examiner: pensiculatores, ἐξετασταί, Gloss. Philox.

pensiculo.full: pensĭcŭlo, āre, v. a. pendo, to weigh, ponder, consider (post-class.): pensicula utrumque, modulareque (al. pensiculate moderateque), Gell. 13, 20, 11: scripta, App. Flor. p. 364; id. Deo. Soc. p. 103 init. —Hence, pensĭcŭlātē, adv., carefully (post-class.): pensiculate (al. pensim) scripta, Gell. 1, 3, 12.

pensilis.full: pensĭlis, e, adj. pendeo, hanging, hanging down, pendent, pensile (poet. and in post-Aug. prose; syn. pendulus). Lit.: restim volo mihi emere, qui me faciam pensilem, Plaut. Ps. 1, 1, 86: vehetur pensilibus plumis, i. e. in a bed, Juv. 1, 159: lychnuchi, Plin. 34, 3, 8, § 14: uva, which are hung up to be preserved during the winter, Hor. S. 2, 2, 121; cf. Plin. 14, 1, 3, § 15; in a double sense, alluding to the hanging of one's self, Plaut. Poen. 1, 2, 99: libertas pensilis, Plin. 19, 5, 24, § 7

pensim.full: pensim, adv., another reading for pensiculate; v. pensiculo fin.
pensim.short: pensim, adv., another reading for pensiculate;

pensio.full: pensĭo, ōnis, f. pendo; lit., a weighing, weighing out; hence, A weight (only in Vitr.), Vitr. 10, 16; 10, 8.— Transf., a paying, payment, a term of payment (class.; cf.: stipendium, pretium): pendere poenas solvere significat, ab eo, quod aere gravi cum uterentur Romani, penso eo, non numerato debitum solvebant: unde etiam pensiones dictae, Paul. ex Fest. p. 208 Müll.: nihil debetur ei, nisi ex tertiā pensione, Cic. Att. 16, 2, 1: prima, id. Fam. 6, 18, 5: altera tributi, Plin. 16, 8, 12, § 32.

pensitatio.full: pensĭtātĭo, ōnis, f. pensito. Lit., a paying, payment (post-class.), Ascon. ad Cic. Verr. 2, 2, 1, § 1; Eum. Grat. Act. ad Const. 12.— Transf. A recompense, compensation (post-Aug.), Plin. 19, 6, 32, § 103.— An expense, expenditure (late Lat.): diurna pensitatio, Sulp. Sev. Hist. Sacr. 2, 8.— That with which payment may be made, valuables: multa munera argenti et auri, et pensitationes, Vulg. 2 Par. 21, 3.

pensitator.full: pensĭtātor, ōris, m. id., one who weighs or considers, a weigher, ponderer, considerer (post-class.): verborum, Gell. 17, 1, 3.

pensito.full: pensĭto, āvi, ātum, 1, v. freq. a. penso, to weigh, weigh out. Lit.: lanam, Aur. Vict. Orig. Gent. R. 22.—Trop.: vitam aequā lance, Plin. 7, 7, 5, § 44.— Transf. To pay (rare but class.): praedia, quae pensitant, Cic. Agr. 3, 2, 9: vectigalia, id. Imp. Pomp. 6, 16.— To weigh, ponder, think over, consider (not in Cic. or Cæs.; syn.: penso, expendo, pondero): rem, Liv. 4, 41: virtutes, Gell. 1, 4, 1: aliquid morosissime, Suet. Aug. 16; id. Caes. 30; Tac. A. 12, 17: malui omnia a te pensitari quam

pensiuncula.full: pensĭuncŭla, ae, f. dim. pensio, a small payment: fenoris, Col. 10 praef. 1.

penso.full: penso, āvi, ātum, 1, v. freq. a. pendo, to weigh or weigh out carefully (not freq. till after the Aug. per.; not in Cic., for in Off. 2, 19, 68, conpensandum is the correct reading. Neither is it found in Plaut., Ter., Lucr., or Cæs.; syn.: pendo, expendo). Lit.: aurum, Liv. 38, 24; Sil. 4, 153; Col. 12, 51, 2: C. Gracchi caput auro pensatum, paid for with its weight in gold, Flor. 3, 15, 6: odores ac purpurae et auro pensanda, worth their weight in gold, Sen. Ep. 73, 5.—Prov.: pensare aliquem e

pensor.full: pensor, ōris, m. id., one who weighs or considers, a weigher, examiner (eccl. Lat.): elementorum, Aug. Conf. 5, 4 fin.; id. Civ. Dei, 15, 27.

pensum.full: pensum, i, v. pendo, P. a. B.

pensura.full: pensūra, ae, f. pendo, a weighing, Varr. L. L. 5, § 183 Müll.

pensus.full: pensus, a, um, Part. and P. a., from pendo.

pentachordus.full: pentăchordus, a, um, adj., = πεντάχορδος, five-stringed (post-class.), Mart. Cap. 9, § 962.
pentachordus.short: pentăchordus, a, um, adj., = πεντάχορδος, five-stringed (post-class.), Mart.

pentacontarchus.full: pentăcontarchus, i, m., = πεντηκόνταρχος, a commander of fifty men, pentacontarch, Vulg. 1 Macc. 3, 55.
pentacontarchus.short: pentăcontarchus, i, m., = πεντηκόνταρχος, a commander of fifty men, pentacontarch, Vulg.

pentadactylus.full: pentădactўlus, i, m., = πενταδάκτυλος, a pentadactyl, a kind of shell-fish, Plin. 32, 11, 53, § 147 Sillig N. cr.— For pentaphyllon, App. Herb. 2.
pentadactylus.short: pentădactўlus, i, m., = πενταδάκτυλος, a pentadactyl, a kind of shell-fish, Plin.

pentadoros.full: pentădōros, on, adj., = πεντάδωρος, containing five palms or hand-breadths, Vitr. 2, 3, 3; Plin. 35, 14, 49, § 170.† † pentaĕtērĭcus, a, um, adj., πενταετηρικος, of five years, Inscr. Grut. 499, 6.
pentadoros.short: pentădōros, on, adj., = πεντάδωρος, containing five palms or hand-breadths, Vitr.

pentagonius.full: pentăgōnĭus, a, um, adj., = πενταγώνιος and pentăgōnus, a, um, = πεντάγωνος, quinquangular, pentagonal.— Subst.: pentăgōnĭum, i, n., a pentagon (post-class.): pentagonii ratio, Auct. de Limit. p. 257 Goes.—pentăgōnum, i, n., for pentaphyllon, App. Herb. 2.
pentagonius.short: pentăgōnĭus, a, um, adj., = πενταγώνιος and pentăgōnus, a, um, = πεντάγωνος, quinquangular, pentagonal.— Subst.: pentăgōnĭum, i, n., a pentagon (post-class.): pentagonii ratio, Auct.

pentameter.full: pentămĕter, tri, m., = πεντάμετρος (containing five metrical feet), a pentameter: in pentametri medio, Quint. 9, 4, 98; so id. 9, 4, 109: heroicus, Diom. p. 506 P.: pentametrum elegum, id. p. 502 ib.
pentameter.short: pentămĕter, tri, m., = πεντάμετρος (containing five metrical feet), a pentameter: in pentametri medio, Quint.

pentanummus.full: pentă-nummus (-nūmus), i, m. vox hibr., from πέντε and numus, a silver coin of the value of five asses, i. q. quinarius (post-class.), Auct. de Limit. p. 265 Goes.

pentapetes.full: pentăpĕtes, is, n., = πενταπετές, five-leaf, cinque-foil: quinquefolium Graeci vocant pentapetes sive pentaphyllon, Plin. 25, 9, 62, § 109.
pentapetes.short: pentăpĕtes, is, n., = πενταπετές, five-leaf, cinque-foil: quinquefolium Graeci vocant pentapetes sive pentaphyllon, Plin.

pentapharmacum.full: pentăpharmăcum, i, n., = πενταφάρμακον, a meal consisting of five dishes (post-class.), Spart. Ael. Ver. 5.
pentapharmacum.short: pentăpharmăcum, i, n., = πενταφάρμακον, a meal consisting of five dishes (post-class.), Spart.

pentaphyllon.full: pentăphyllon, i, n., = πεντάφυλλον, i. q. quinquefolium and pentapetes, five-leaved grass, cinque-foil, Plin. 25, 9, 62, § 109; App. Herb. 2.

pentapolis.full: Pentăpŏlis, is, f., = Πεντάπολις. A district of five towns on the Dead Sea, Sol. 35; Vulg. Sap. 10, 6.— A district of Cyrene, on the Libyan Sea, Sex. Ruf. Brev. 13; Sen. Verg. A. 4, 42.—Hence, Pentă-pŏlĭtānus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Pentapolis, i. e. to Cyrene, Cyrenaic: regio, Plin. 5, 5, 5, § 31.

pentaprotia.full: pentăprōtīa, ae, f., = πενταπρωτεία, the first five men, a board or college of five superior officers (post-class.), Cod. Just. 12, 29, 2.
pentaprotia.short: pentăprōtīa, ae, f., = πενταπρωτεία, the first five men, a board or college of five superior officers (post-class.), Cod.

pentaptota.full: pentaptōta, ōrum, n., = πεντάπτωτα, in the later gramm., nouns that have five cases, pentaptotes, Diom. p. 288 P. al.
pentaptota.short: pentaptōta, ōrum, n., = πεντάπτωτα, in the later gramm., nouns that have five cases, pentaptotes, Diom.

pentas.full: pentas, ădis, f., = πεντάς, the number five, five (post-class.), Mart. Cap. 7, §§ 735 and 745.
pentas.short: pentas, ădis, f., = πεντάς, the number five, five (post-class.), Mart.

pentasemus.full: pentăsēmus, a, um, adj., = πεντάσημος, that has five marks or divisions of time (post-class.): pes, Mart. Cap. 9, § 978.
pentasemus.short: pentăsēmus, a, um, adj., = πεντάσημος, that has five marks or divisions of time (post-class.): pes, Mart.

pentaspaston.full: pentaspaston, i, n., = πεντάσπαστον, a tackle with five pulleys, two in the lower block and three in the upper, Vitr. 10, 3.
pentaspaston.short: pentaspaston, i, n., = πεντάσπαστον, a tackle with five pulleys, two in the lower block and three in the upper, Vitr.

pentasphaerus.full: pentasphaerus, a, um, adj., = πέντεσφαῖρα, folium, a kind of costly spice, Dig. 39, 4, 16, § 7.
pentasphaerus.short: pentasphaerus, a, um, adj., = πέντεσφαῖρα, folium, a kind of costly spice, Dig.

pentastichoe.full: pentastĭchoe porticus = πεντάστιχοι, having five rows of columns, Treb. Gall. 18.
pentastichoe.short: pentastĭchoe porticus = πεντάστιχοι, having five rows of columns, Treb.

pentasyllabus.full: pentăsyllăbus, a, um, adj., = πεντασύλλαβος, having five syllables, five-syllabled (post-class.): pedes, Mall. Theod. de Metr. 2.
pentasyllabus.short: pentăsyllăbus, a, um, adj., = πεντασύλλαβος, having five syllables, five-syllabled (post-class.): pedes, Mall.

pentateuchus.full: Pentăteuchus, i, m., or Pentă-teuchum, i, n., = πεντάτευχος, the five books of Moses, the Pentateuch, Tert. adv. Marc. 1, 10 et saep.; Isid. Orig. 6, 2, 2.
pentateuchus.short: Pentăteuchus, i, m., or Pentă-teuchum, i, n., = πεντάτευχος, the five books of Moses, the Pentateuch, Tert.

pentathlos.full: pentathlos or -us, i, m., = πένταθλος, one who practised the five exercises of pitching the quoit, running, leaping, wrestling, and hurling (post-Aug.), Plin. 34, 8, 19, § 57; so id. 34, 8, 19, §§ 68 and 72.† † pentathlum, i, n., = πένταθλον, the contest of the five exercises of pitching the quoit, running, leaping, wrestling, and hurling (post-class.): pentathlum antiqui quinquartium dixerunt. Id autem genus exercitationis ex his quinque artibus constat, jactu disci, cursu, saltu, jaculatione,
pentathlos.short: pentathlos or -us, i, m., = πένταθλος, one who practised the five exercises of pitching the quoit, running, leaping, wrestling, and hurling (post-Aug.), Plin.

pentatomon.full: pentătŏmon, i, n., = πεντάτομος, five-leaf, cinque-foil, i. q. quinquefolium and pentaphyllon, App. Herb. 2.
pentatomon.short: pentătŏmon, i, n., = πεντάτομος, five-leaf, cinque-foil, i.

pentecostalis.full: Pentēcostālis, e, adj. Pentecoste, of or belonging to Whitsuntide or Pentecost, Pentecostal (eccl. Lat.): festum Pentecostale, Tert. Idol. 14.

pentecoste.full: Pentēcostē, ēs, f., = πεντηκοστή (sc. ἡμέρα), the fiftieth day after Easter, WhitSunday, Pentecost (eccl. Lat.), Vulg. 2 Macc. 12, 32; id. 1 Cor. 16, 8; Tert. Idol. 14.

pentelensis.full: Pentĕlensis, e, adj., Pentelic: mons, Vitr. 2, 8; v. Pentelicus.
pentelensis.short: Pentĕlensis, e, adj., Pentelic: mons, Vitr.

pentelicus.full: Pentĕlĭcus, a, um, adj., = Πεντελικός, of or belonging to a mountain near Athens (in the demos of Πεντελή), celebrated for its while marble, Pentelie: Hermae Pentelici, of Pentelic marble, Cic. Att. 1, 8, 2.
pentelicus.short: Pentĕlĭcus, a, um, adj., = Πεντελικός, of or belonging to a mountain near Athens (in the demos of Πεντελή), celebrated for its while marble, Pentelie: Hermae Pentelici, of Pentelic marble, Cic.

penteloris.full: pentĕlōris, e, adj. vox hibr. from πέντε and lorum, having five thongs or five stripes, Vop. Aur. 46.

penteris.full: pentēris, is, f., = πεντήρης, a ship with five banks of oars, Auct. B. Alex. 47; id. B. Afr. 62 fin.
penteris.short: pentēris, is, f., = πεντήρης, a ship with five banks of oars, Auct.

pentethronicus.full: pentethronĭcus, a, um, adj., a fictitious word: pugna pentethronica, Plaut. Poen. 2, 25 dub.
pentethronicus.short: pentethronĭcus, a, um, adj., a fictitious word: pugna pentethronica, Plaut.

pentheius.full: Penthēĭus, a, um, v. Pentheus, A.

penthemimeres.full: penthēmĭmĕres or -is, is, f., = πενθημιμερής (sc. τομή; consisting of five halves, i. e. of 2 1/2 parts), a part of a verse, consisting of its first two feet and a half, esp. of a hexameter or iambic trimeter, a penthemimeris, Aus. Ep. 4, 85 and 89; Diom. 497, 8; Ter. Maur. p. 2440 P.

penthesilea.full: Penthĕsĭlēa, ae, f., = Πενθεσίλεια, a queen of the Amazons, who fought before Troy against the Greeks, and was slain by Achilles, Verg. A. 1, 491 Serv.; cf. Prop. 3, 11 (4, 10), 14; Just. 2, 4.
penthesilea.short: Penthĕsĭlēa, ae, f., = Πενθεσίλεια, a queen of the Amazons, who fought before Troy against the Greeks, and was slain by Achilles, Verg.

pentheus.full: Pentheus, ĕi and ĕos, m., = Πενθεύς, son of Echion and Agave, grandson of Cadmus, and king of Thebes; having treated with contempt the rites of Bacchus, he was torn in pieces by his mother and her sisters when under the influence of the god, Ov. M. 3, 514; Prop. 3, 17 (4, 16), 24; 3 (4), 22, 33; Ov. Tr. 5, 3, 40; Hor. Ep. 1, 16, 73; id. C. 2, 19, 14.—Hence, Penthēĭus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Pentheus, Penthean: mater, Sid. Carm. 22, 94.— Penthēus, a, um, adj., = Πενθεῖος, of or belonging
pentheus.short: Pentheus, ĕi and ĕos, m., = Πενθεύς, son of Echion and Agave, grandson of Cadmus, and king of Thebes;

pentorobon.full: pentŏrŏbon, i, n., = πεντόροβον, a plant, called also paeonia, Plin. 27, 10, 60, § 84; 25, 4, 10, § 29; App. Herb. 64.
pentorobon.short: pentŏrŏbon, i, n., = πεντόροβον, a plant, called also paeonia, Plin.

pentri.full: Pentri, ōrum, m., a Samnite people, Liv. 9, 31.
pentri.short: Pentri, ōrum, m., a Samnite people, Liv.

penuarius.full: pĕnŭārĭus, a, um, adj. penus, of or for provisions (post-class. for penarius): cellae, Dig. 33, 9, 3, § 11.

penuria.full: pēnūrĭa or paenūrĭa, ae, f. Gr. πένομαι, to toil; πένης, poor; cf. σπάνις, πεῖνα, want, need, scarcity of any thing (class.; syn.: inopia, egestas). Lit., esp. of want of the necessaries of life; constr. with or (less freq.) without a gen.: cibi, Lucr. 5, 1007: victūs, Hor. S. 1, 1, 98: edendi, Verg. A. 7, 113: aquarum, Sall. J. 17, 5: rerum necessariarum, id. ib. 23, 2: frumenti, Liv. 4, 25. —Absol.: neque enim est umquam penuria parvi, he is never in want who requires but little, Lucr. 5, 1119

penus.full: pĕnus, ūs and i, m. and f., also pĕ-num, i, and pĕnus, ŏris, n. (gen. peneris, peniteris, only acc. to Gell. 4, 1, 2; a collat. form pĕnu, Afran., acc. to Charis. p. 113 P.; cf. also Don. Ter. Eun. 2, 3, 18) [from the root pa- of pasco; Gr. πατέομαι; v. penates]. Store or provision of food provisions, victuals: est enim omne, quo vescuntur homines, penus, Cic. N. D. 2, 27, 68; cf. other and different explanations in Gell. 4, 1, and tit.: De penu legatā, Dig. 33, 9: annuus, Plaut. Ps. 1, 2, 45; T

peparethus.full: Pĕpărēthus or -os, i, f., = Πεπάρηθος, Peparethus (now Piperi), a small island in the Ægean Sea, one of the Cyclades, famous for wine and oil, with a town of the same name, now Scopelo: ferax Peparethos olivae, Ov. M. 7, 470; cf. Liv. 28, 5, 10; 31, 28, 6.—Hence, Pĕpărēthĭus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Peparethos, Peparethian: vinum, Plin. 14, 7, 9, § 76.
peparethus.short: Pĕpărēthus or -os, i, f., = Πεπάρηθος, Peparethus (now Piperi), a small island in the Ægean Sea, one of the Cyclades, famous for wine and oil, with a town of the same name, now Scopelo: ferax Peparethos olivae, Ov.

peplis.full: peplis, ĭdis, f., = πεπλίς, the name of two plants, one of which was also called porcilaca, Plin. 20, 20, 81, § 210; and the other syce, meconion, or mecon aphrodes, id. 27, 12, 93, § 119.
peplis.short: peplis, ĭdis, f., = πεπλίς, the name of two plants, one of which was also called porcilaca, Plin.

peplium.full: peplĭum, ii, n., = πέπλιον, a medicinal plant, a species of spurge, prob. the Euphorbia esula, Linn.; Cael. Aur. Acut. 2, 19, 115; id. Tard. 4, 6, 89.
peplium.short: peplĭum, ii, n., = πέπλιον, a medicinal plant, a species of spurge, prob.

peplum.full: pē^plum, i, n., and pē^plus, i, m., = πέπλον and πέπλος, the robe of state of Minerva at Athens, with which her statue was solemnly invested every five years at the Panathenaea, Plaut. Merc. prol. 67; id. Fragm. ap. Serv. Verg. A. 1, 480; Verg. Cir. 21 sq.; Stat. Th. 10, 56.— Transf. A splendid upper garment, a robe of state, either of gods or men (post-class.), Claud. Nupt. Honor. 123: imperatorium, Treb. XXX. Tyrann. 23.— Still more gen., any broad upper garment, Manil. 5, 387.— A disease of t
peplum.short: pē^plum, i, n., and pē^plus, i, m., = πέπλον and πέπλος, the robe of state of Minerva at Athens, with which her statue was solemnly invested every five years at the Panathenaea, Plaut.

pepo.full: pĕpo, ŏnis, m., = πέπων, ονος, a species of large melon, a pumpkin, Plin. 19, 5, 23, § 65; 20, 2, 6, § 11; Tert. Anim. 32; id. adv. Marc. 4, 40; Vulg. Num. 11, 5.
pepo.short: pĕpo, ŏnis, m., = πέπων, ονος, a species of large melon, a pumpkin, Plin.

pepticus.full: peptĭcus, a, um, adj., = πεπτικός, that promotes digestion, peptic (post-Aug.): medicinae, Plin. 20, 18, 76, § 201.
pepticus.short: peptĭcus, a, um, adj., = πεπτικός, that promotes digestion, peptic (post-Aug.): medicinae, Plin.

pepunculus.full: pĕpuncŭlus, i, m. dim. pepo, a small pumpkin, Not. Tir. p. 168.

pepuzitae.full: Pĕpuzītae, ārum, m., a sort of heretics (also called Montanistae), so named after the Phrygian town of Pepuza, Cod. Just. 1, 5, 5.
pepuzitae.short: Pĕpuzītae, ārum, m., a sort of heretics (also called Montanistae), so named after the Phrygian town of Pepuza, Cod.

per1.full: per, prep. with acc. (by solecism with abl. PER QVO, = whereby, Inscr. Miseni Repert. ex a. p. Chr. n. 159; Inscr. Orell. 3300) [kindr. with Gr. παρά; Sanscr. pāra, ulterior; Lith. pèr; cf.: parumper, paulisper; v. Georg Curtius Griech. Etym. p. 269], denotes, like the Gr. διά, motion through a space, or extension over it. Lit., of space, through, through the midst of, throughout, all over, all along: per amoena salicta raptare aliquem, Enn. ap. Cic. Div. 1, 20, 40 (Ann. v. 40 Vahl.): inde Fert

pera.full: pēra, ae, f., = πἠρα, a bag, wallet (syn.: mantica, loculus): peras imposuit Juppiter nobis duas, Phaedr. 4, 10, 1: cum baculo perāque senex, of a Cynic philosopher, Mart. 4, 53, 3; cf. App. Mag. p. 287, 39; Vulg. 1 Reg. 17, 40; id. Luc. 10, 4.
pera.short: pēra, ae, f., = πἠρα, a bag, wallet (syn.: mantica, loculus): peras imposuit Juppiter nobis duas, Phaedr.

perabjectus.full: pĕr-abjectus, a, um, deeply humbled, Cypr. Laud. Mart. fin.
perabjectus.short: pĕr-abjectus, a, um, deeply humbled, Cypr.

perabsurdus.full: pĕr-absurdus, a, um, adj., very absurd (class.): haec quia videntur perabsurda, etc., Cic. Part. 15, 54; id. Fin. 3, 8, 27; 3, 9, 31; 5, 11, 30.—Separated: per enim absurdum est, Dig. 22, 3, 25; v. per, II. D.
perabsurdus.short: pĕr-absurdus, a, um, adj., very absurd (class.): haec quia videntur perabsurda, etc., Cic.

peraccommodatus.full: pĕr-accommŏdātus, a, um, adj., very suitable, very convenient: per fore accommodatum tibi, si, etc., Cic. Fam. 3, 5, 3.
peraccommodatus.short: pĕr-accommŏdātus, a, um, adj., very suitable, very convenient: per fore accommodatum tibi, si, etc., Cic.

peracer.full: pĕr-ācer, ācris, ācre, adj., very sharp; trop.: judicium, Cic. Fam. 9, 16, 4 (but in Plaut. Bacch. 3, 3, 1, the correct reading is cor acre; v. Ritschl ad h. l.).
peracer.short: pĕr-ācer, ācris, ācre, adj., very sharp;

peracerbus.full: pĕr-ăcerbus, a, um, adj., very harsh to the taste. Lit.: uva peracerba gustatu, Cic. Sen. 15, 53.— Trop., very painful: mihi peracerbum fuit, quod, etc., Plin. Ep. 6, 5, 6.
peracerbus.short: pĕr-ăcerbus, a, um, adj., very harsh to the taste.

peracesco.full: pĕr-ăcesco, ăcŭi, 3, v. inch. n., to become sour through and through, thoroughly sour; hence, trop., to become vexed, to grow vexatious (Plautin.): ita mihi pectus peracuit, Plaut. Aul. 3, 4, 9: hoc, hoc est, quod peracescit: hoc est demum quod percrucior, that vexes me, id. Bacch. 5, 1, 13.

peractio.full: pĕractĭo, ōnis, f. perago, a finishing, completion. Lit.: peccati, Hilar. in Psa. 118, 4, 8.— Aetatis, transf. from the stage, qs. the last act of the drama, Cic. Sen. 23, 85 (cf. id. ib. 18, 64: fabulam aetatis peregisse, and 19, 70: peragenda fabula est).

peractus.full: pĕractus, a, um, Part., from perago.
peractus.short: pĕractus, a, um, Part., from perago.

peracutus.full: pĕr-ăcūtus, a, um, adj., very sharp. Lit.: falx, Mart. 3, 24, 5 (dub.).— Transf., of sound, very clear or penetrating: vox, Cic. Brut. 68, 241.— Trop., very keen, very acute, very penetrating: cum peracutus esset ad excogitandum, Cic. Brut. 39, 145: oratio, id. ib. 76, 264; Cic. Verr. 2, 2, 44, § 108.—Adv.: pĕrăcūtē, very sharply, very acutely, with great keenness: moveri, Cic. Ac. 1, 9, 35: peracute querebare, quod, etc., id. Fam. 3, 7, 2: reperisse, App. Mag. 34.
peracutus.short: pĕr-ăcūtus, a, um, adj., very sharp.

peradulescens.full: pĕr-ădŭlescens, entis, adj., very young: homo peradulescens, Cic. Imp. Pomp. 21, 61.
peradulescens.short: pĕr-ădŭlescens, entis, adj., very young: homo peradulescens, Cic.

peradulescentulus.full: pĕr-adŭlescentŭlus, i, m. dim., a very young man, Nep. Eum. 1, 4.

peraea1.full: Pĕraea, ae, f., = Περαία (sc. γῆ, the land beyond the sea or river; hence), A strip of land in Caria, along the coast opposite to Rhodes, and subject to the Rhodians, Liv. 32, 33; 35; 33, 18.— A part of Palestine beyond the Jordan, the capital of which was Gadara, Plin. 5, 14, 15, § 70.

peraea2.full: Pĕraea, ae, f., = Περαία. a city in Æolis, a colony of the Mityleneans, Liv. 37, 21, 4.

peraedificatus.full: pĕr-aedĭfĭcātus, a, um, adj., completely built, built up, Col. 4, 3, 1.
peraedificatus.short: pĕr-aedĭfĭcātus, a, um, adj., completely built, built up, Col.

peraequatio.full: pĕraequātĭo, ōnis, f. peraequo, a making perfectly equal (post-class.). In gen.: temporum, Sol. 1: similitudinum, Tert. adv. Marc. 4, 29.— In partic., an equalizing, equal distribution of taxes, Cod. Th. 5, 4, 3.

peraequator.full: peraequātor, ōris, m. id., an equalizer, esp. of taxes, an equal distributor (jurid. Lat.), Cod. Th. 13, tit. 11; Cod. Just. 11, tit. 57; Inscr. Grut. 361, 1.

peraeque.full: pĕr-aequē, adv., quite equally or evenly (class.): hos numquam minus, ut peraeque ducerent dena milia HS ex melle recipere esse solitos, on an average, Varr. R. R. 3, 16, 11: atque hoc peraeque in omni agro decumano reperietis, Cic. Verr. 2, 3, 52, § 121: quod cum peraeque omnes, tum acerbissime Boeotii senserunt, id. Pis. 35, 86; Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 21, § 46: terna milia peraeque in singulos menses, uniformly, Nep. Att. 13, 6.
peraeque.short: pĕr-aequē, adv., quite equally or evenly (class.): hos numquam minus, ut peraeque ducerent dena milia HS ex melle recipere esse solitos, on an average, Varr.

peraequo.full: pĕr-aequo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a., to make quite equal (post-Aug.): octogenae stirpes ...septenos culeos peraequarent, filled up, i. e. yielded, produced, Col. 3, 3, 3; 3, 3, 10: amphoras, id. 3, 9, 2: partes, Vitr. 9, 4: contracturam, id. 5, 1: iter, id. 9, 4: annum lunari computatione, Sol. 1, 37.

peraestimo.full: pĕr-aestĭmo, 1, v. a., to esteem greatly (post-class.), Cod. Th. 6, 29, 2 fin.

peragito.full: pĕr-ăgĭto, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a., to drive or hunt about greatly, to harass, disturb (not in Cic.). Lit. In gen.: vehementius peragitati ab equitatu, Caes. B. C. 1, 80: Aetna majore vi peragitata, Sen. Ben. 3, 37.— In partic., to stir up any thing, esp. a liquid: ut permisceatur medicamen rutabulo ligneo peragitare conveniet, Col. 12, 24, 4: mustum, id. 12, 19, 4.— Trop., to excite, impel: animos, Sen. Ira, 1, 7.— To complete, finish: peragitatur enim messis mense Maio, Plin. 18, 18, 47, § 169.

perago.full: pĕr-ăgo, ēgi, actum (inf. paragier, Cato, Orig. 7, p. 1), 3, v. a. To thrust through, pierce through, transfix (only poet. and in post-Aug. prose): Theseus latus ense peregit, transpierced, Ov. H. 4, 119: aliquem ardenti quercu, Val. Fl. 1, 146; cf.: externa peragi dextrā, Sil. 11, 364.—Hence, transf., to kill, slay, Mart. 5, 37, 16.— To pass through, traverse: freta, Ov. H. 15, 65: cum sol duodena peregit Signa, id. M. 13, 618.— To drive about, harass, disturb, disquiet, agitate, annoy a person

peragratio.full: pĕrā^grātĭo, ōnis, f. peragro, a wandering or travelling through, a traversing: itinerum, Cic. Phil. 2, 23, 57.

peragratrix.full: pĕrā^grātrix, īcis, f. id., she that wanders or travels through (post-class.): coelicolarum, Mart. Cap. 6, § 588.

peragro.full: pĕr-ā^gro, āvi, ātum, 1 (part. peragratus, in the dep. signif.; v. infra), v. a. per and ager, to wander or travel through or over, to go or pass through, traverse, etc. (class.; cf. percurro). Lit.: provincias, Cic. de Or. 2, 64, 258.—Of bees: saltus silvasque, Verg. G. 4, 53: loca avia, Lucr. 1, 926: in peragrandā Aegypto, Suet. Aug. 93: peragratis partibus, Vulg. Act. 19, 1.—Of sailing: litora Liburnicis, Suet. Calig. 37: eques Romanus qui et commercia ea et litora peragravit, Plin. 37, 3, 11

peragror.full: pĕrăgror, āri, v. peragro, I. β.

peralbus.full: pĕr-albus, a, um, adj., very white (postclass.): equus, App. M. 1, p. 103: avis, id. ib. 5, p. 171, 10.
peralbus.short: pĕr-albus, a, um, adj., very white (postclass.): equus, App.

peramans.full: pĕr-ămans, antis, Part. [amo], very loving, very fond: homo peramans semper nostri fuit, Cic. Att. 4, 8, b, 3.—Adv.: pĕr-ămanter, very lovingly: perofficiose et peramanter aliquem observare, Cic. Fam. 9, 20, 3.

peramarus.full: pĕr-ămārus, a, um, very bitter or hostile, Arn. in Psa. 77.
peramarus.short: pĕr-ămārus, a, um, very bitter or hostile, Arn.

perambulo.full: pĕr-ambŭlo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a., to ramble through, go through; to traverse, perambulate (poet. and in post-Aug. prose). Lit.: aedes, Plaut. Most. 3, 2, 122: multas terras, Varr. R. R. 1, 2: omnium cubilia, Cat. 29, 8: viridia, Phaedr. 2, 5, 14: rura, Hor. C. 4, 5, 17: astra, id. Epod. 17, 41: terram, Vulg. Zach. 6, 7: universam insulam, id. Act. 13, 6 et saep.—Pass.: perambulatum Romanis legionibus Niphatem, Sid. Carm. 23, 93.—Poet.: frigus perambulat artūs, runs through, Ov. H. 9, 135: recte n

peramicus.full: pĕr-ămīcus, a, um, adj., very friendly, Auct. Itin. Alex. M. 56 Mai.
peramicus.short: pĕr-ămīcus, a, um, adj., very friendly, Auct.

peramoenus.full: pĕr-ămoenus, a, um, adj., very pleasant: aestas, Tac. A. 4, 67.
peramoenus.short: pĕr-ămoenus, a, um, adj., very pleasant: aestas, Tac.

peramplus.full: pĕr-amplus, a, um, adj., very large, very ample: simulacra, Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 49, § 109 sq.: regnum, Val. Max. 5, 2, 4.
peramplus.short: pĕr-amplus, a, um, adj., very large, very ample: simulacra, Cic.

peranceps.full: pĕr-anceps, ĭpĭtis, adj., very doubtful, very uncertain, Amm. 29, 5, 37.
peranceps.short: pĕr-anceps, ĭpĭtis, adj., very doubtful, very uncertain, Amm.

perangustus.full: pĕr-angustus, a, um, adj., very narrow (good prose): fretum, Cic. Verr. 2, 5, 66, § 169: aditus, Caes. B. G. 7, 15; Curt. 3, 4, 4: via, Liv. 22, 4: semita, Curt. 7, 11, 1: termini Macedoniae, Just. 7, 1, 2.—Adv.: pĕrangustē, very narrowly, Cic. de Or. 1, 35, 163.
perangustus.short: pĕr-angustus, a, um, adj., very narrow (good prose): fretum, Cic.

peranna.full: Pĕranna, i. q. Perenna, v. Anna.

peranno.full: pĕranno, āvi, 1, v. n. per-annus, to live through a year: puella nata non perannavit, did not live a year, Suet. Vesp. 5; Macr. S. 1, 12, 6 (dub.).

perantiquus.full: pĕr-antīquus, a, um, adj., very ancient, Cic. Brut. 10, 41: testes, id. Rep. 1, 37, 58: sacrarium, Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 2, § 4: calceamenta, Vulg. Jos. 9, 5.
perantiquus.short: pĕr-antīquus, a, um, adj., very ancient, Cic.

perappositus.full: pĕr-appŏsĭtus (pĕradpŏs-), a, um, adj., very suitable or apposite: alicui, Cic. de Or. 2, 67, 274.
perappositus.short: pĕr-appŏsĭtus (pĕradpŏs-), a, um, adj., very suitable or apposite: alicui, Cic.

perardeo.full: pĕr-ardĕo, si, 2, v. n., to burn violently, Paul. Nol. Carm. 23, 404.

perarduus.full: pĕr-ardŭus, a, um, adj., very difficult: mihi autem hoc perarduum est demonstrare, Cic. Verr. 2, 3, 71, § 166.
perarduus.short: pĕr-ardŭus, a, um, adj., very difficult: mihi autem hoc perarduum est demonstrare, Cic.

peraresco.full: pĕr-āresco, ārŭi, 3, v. inch. n., to grow very dry, Varr. R. R. 1, 49, 1; Col. 4, 24, 5.

perargutus.full: pĕr-argūtus, a, um, adj. Very shrill (Appuleian): tintinnabula, App. M. 10, p. 247, 39: carmen, id. Flor. p. 349.— Very acute, very witty: homo, Cic. Brut. 45, 167.

peraridus.full: pĕr-ārĭdus, a, um, adj., very dry, very arid: frons, Cato, R. R. 5, 8: solum, Col. 3, 11, 9; 2, 19, 1.
peraridus.short: pĕr-ārĭdus, a, um, adj., very dry, very arid: frons, Cato, R.

perarmo.full: pĕr-armo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a., to arm or equip well (post-class.): perarmatus exercitus, Curt. 4, 9, 6; 23: manum gladius perarmat, Prud. Cath. 6, 85; 7, 93.

peraro.full: pĕr-ăro, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. Lit., to plough through; to traverse the sea: pontum, Sen. Med. 650.— Transf. To furrow: rugis anilibus ora, Ov. M. 14, 96; Sid. Ep. 3, 13.— To furrow or scratch over, to injure: cerebrum crebra vibice peraratum, Sid. Ep. 3, 13.— To scratch letters with the style on a waxen tablet, to write: talia perarans manus, Ov. M. 9, 563: litteram, id. A. A. 1, 455; cf. id. Tr. 3, 7, 1: peraratae tabellae, id. Am. 1, 11, 7: perarare carmina auro, Stat. S. 4, 5, 24.

perasper.full: pĕr-asper, ĕra, ĕrum, adj., very rough, Cels. 5, 28, 14: montes, Jul. Rer. Gest. Alex. 3, 51.
perasper.short: pĕr-asper, ĕra, ĕrum, adj., very rough, Cels.

per2.full: pĕr-astūtŭlus, a, um, adj., very crafty: mulier, App. M. 9, p. 219, 17.
per2.short: pĕr-astūtŭlus, a, um, adj., very crafty: mulier, App.

peraticum.full: pĕrātĭcum, i, n., = περατικόν, a species of the bdellium-tree, Plin. 12, 9, 19, § 35.
peraticum.short: pĕrātĭcum, i, n., = περατικόν, a species of the bdellium-tree, Plin.

peratim.full: pērātim, adv. pera, by bags or wallets: peratim ductare, i. e. to cheat one out of the money in his wallet, Plaut. Ep. 3, 2, 15.

perattentus.full: pĕr-attentus, a, um, adj., very attentive: animus, Cic. Verr. 2, 3, 5, § 10.—Adv.: pĕrattentē, very attentively: audire aliquem, Cic. Cael. 11, 25.
perattentus.short: pĕr-attentus, a, um, adj., very attentive: animus, Cic.

peratticus.full: pĕr-attĭcus, a, um, adj., very Attic, i. e. very elegant: philosophus, Front. Ep. ad M. Caes. 2, 1 Mai.
peratticus.short: pĕr-attĭcus, a, um, adj., very Attic, i.

peraudiendus.full: pĕr-audĭendus, a, um, false reading for perhaurienda, Plaut. Mil. 1, 1, 34.
peraudiendus.short: pĕr-audĭendus, a, um, false reading for perhaurienda, Plaut.

perbacchor.full: per-bacchor, ātus, 1, v. dep. a:, to carouse or revel through: multos dies, Cic. Phil. 2, 41, 104: annum suum in re publicā, Ps. -Cic. Decl. in Sall. 3, 10.— Transf., of fire: perbacchata domos incendia, Claud. B. G. 242.

perbasio.full: per-bāsĭo, āre, v. a., to kiss heartily, Petr. 41, 8.

perbeatus.full: per-bĕātus, a, um, adj., very fortunate, Cic. de Or. 1, 1, 1.
perbeatus.short: per-bĕātus, a, um, adj., very fortunate, Cic.

perbelle.full: per-bellē, adv., very prettily, very finely: simulare, Cic. Fam. 16, 18, 1: feceris, si, etc., id. Att. 4, 4, b, § 1.
perbelle.short: per-bellē, adv., very prettily, very finely: simulare, Cic.

perbene.full: per-bĕnĕ, adv., very well: prandi perbene, Potavi, Plaut. Men. 5, 9, 81: pol ego haud a pecuniā perbene, id. Aul. 2, 2, 9: loqui Latine, Cic. Brut. 28, 108: Fortunam fecisse, quando, etc., Liv. 45, 3, 5.
perbene.short: per-bĕnĕ, adv., very well: prandi perbene, Potavi, Plaut.

perbenemeritus.full: per - bĕnĕ-mĕrĭtus, a, um, adj., very well deserved, Inscr. Murat. 1923, 5.
perbenemeritus.short: per - bĕnĕ-mĕrĭtus, a, um, adj., very well deserved, Inscr.

perbenevolus.full: per-bĕnĕvŏlus, a, um, adj., very friendly: alicui, Cic. Fam. 14, 4, 5.
perbenevolus.short: per-bĕnĕvŏlus, a, um, adj., very friendly: alicui, Cic.

perbenigne.full: per-bĕnignē, adv., very kindly, Ter. Ad. 4, 5, 68.—Separate: per mihi benigne respondit, Cic. Q. Fr. 2, 9, 2.

perbibesia.full: Perbĭbĕsĭa, ae, a false reading for Bibesia, Plaut. Curc. 3, 74.
perbibesia.short: Perbĭbĕsĭa, ae, a false reading for Bibesia, Plaut.

perbibo.full: per-bĭbo, bĭbi, 3, v. a. (to drink much; hence), * To drink or suck up: at ego perii, cui medullam lassitudo perbibit, Plaut. Stich. 2, 2, 16.— To drink in (poet. and in post-Aug. prose). Lit., Cato, R. R. 130: lana quosdam (colores) non perbibit, Sen. Ep. 71, 31: lacrimas, Ov. M. 6, 397: medicamina, Col. 7, 4, 8.— Trop., to imbibe, receive: haec cum persuasi mihi et perbibi, Sen. Ep. 94, 11: liberalia studia, id. ib. 36, 4: nequitiam, id. Ira, 1, 16, 2: mentes eorum penitus sucum stultitiae per

perbito.full: per-bīto, ĕre, v. n. To go over to a place (ante - class.), Pac. ap. Non. 153, 24: utinam te ... malo cruciatu in Siciliam perbiteres, Plaut. Rud. 2, 6, 12.— To perish: ne fame perbitat, Liv. Andron. ap. Non. 153, 28 (Trag. Rel. p. 3 Rib.); so, fame, Caecil. ap. Non. 391, 22 (Com. Rel. p. 61 Rib.); Enn. and Titin. ap. Non. 153, 26 and 30 (cf. Enn. Trag. v. 240 Vahl.; Com. Rel. p. 117 Rib.): qui per virtutem perbitat, non interit, Plaut. Capt. 3, 5, 32 dub. (Fleck. perit, at): cruciatu maximo, id

perblandus.full: per-blandus, a, um, adj., very courteous or charming, very engaging, very bland: successor, Cic. Q. Fr. 1, 2, 3: oratio, Liv. 23, 10, 1: adulatio, Juvenc. 1, 705.— Adv.: perblandē, very winningly: aliquem salutare, Macr. S. 1, 2, 16.
perblandus.short: per-blandus, a, um, adj., very courteous or charming, very engaging, very bland: successor, Cic.

perbonus.full: per-bŏnus, a, um, adj., very good: prandium, Plaut. Most. 3, 2, 3: eam sei curabeis, perbona'st, id. Merc. 3, 1, 28: ager, Cic. Fl. 29, 71: toreumata, Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 18, § 38: perbono loco res erat, id. Att. 6, 1, 3.
perbonus.short: per-bŏnus, a, um, adj., very good: prandium, Plaut.

perbrevis.full: per-brĕvis, e, adj., very short, very brief or concise: orator perornatus et perbrevis, Cic. Brut. 43, 158: perbrevi tempore, Cic. Verr. 2, 3, 9, § 22.—Separate: altera pars per mihi brevis videtur, id. Clu. 1, 2.—In abl.: perbrevi, adverbially, in a very short time, Cic. Fam. 6, 12, 3.—Adv.: perbrĕ-vĭter, very briefly, very concisely: quid sentiam, perbreviter exponam, Cic. de Or. 2, 58, 235 al.
perbrevis.short: per-brĕvis, e, adj., very short, very brief or concise: orator perornatus et perbrevis, Cic.

perbullio.full: per-bullĭo, īvi and ii, 4, v. n., to boil thoroughly, Theod. Prisc. 4, 1.

perca.short: perca, ae, f., = πέρκη, a kind of fish, a perch, Plin.

percaedo.full: per-caedo, cĕcīdi, caesum, v. a., to cut up completely = ad internecionem caedere (post-class.): exercitum, Flor. 3, 20, 10. (dub.; al. cecidit): terga hostium, id. 4, 12, 7.

percalefacio.full: per-călĕfăcĭo, fēci, factum (also contr. percalfactum), 3, v. a.—Pass.: per-călĕfīo, factus, fieri, to make very warm, to heat thoroughly (mostly ante- and postclass.): omnia motu Percalefacta, Lucr. 6, 178: glebae a sole percalefactae, Varr. R. R. 1, 27: multo igni percalfacto cubiculo, Val. Max. 9, 12, 4: percalefieri cogit aquam, to become very warm, Vitr. 8, 3, 4.

percalesco.full: per-călesco, călŭi, 3, v. inch. n., to become very warm: inde ubi percaluit vis venti, Lucr. 6, 281; Ov. M. 1, 418.

percalleo.full: per-calleo, ŭi, ēre, v. a., to know or understand well: quinque et viginti gentium linguas, Gell. 17, 17, 2.

percallesco.full: per-callesco, callŭi, 3, v. inch. n. and a. * Neutr., to become very hardened, very callous: civitatis patientia percalluerat, Cic. Mil. 28, 76.— Act., to get a good knowledge of; in perf., to be well acquainted with, to know well, be well versed in: usum rerum, Cic. de Or. 2, 34, 137; so, disciplinas Stoicas et dialecticas, Gell. 1, 22, 7: leges, id. 20, 1, 20: quinque et viginti gentium linguas, id. 17, 17, 2.

percandefacio.full: per-candĕfăcĭo, 3, v. a., to make very hot, to heat thoroughly: terram, Vitr. 8, 3, 1.

percandidus.full: per-candĭdus, a, um, adj., very white: compositio, Cels. 5, 19, 24: gemma, Sol. 37, 20.
percandidus.short: per-candĭdus, a, um, adj., very white: compositio, Cels.

percarus.full: per-cārus, a, um, adj., very dear. Lit., very dear, very costly, Ter. Phorm. 3, 3, 25.— Trop., very dear, very much beloved: qui eis vicissim percarus et jucundus fuit, Cic. Aem. Scaur. 17, 39; Tac. A. 2, 74; Just. 12, 12, 11.
percarus.short: per-cārus, a, um, adj., very dear.

percautus.full: per-cautus, a, um, adj., very cautious, Cic. Q. Fr. 1, 1, 6, § 18.
percautus.short: per-cautus, a, um, adj., very cautious, Cic.

percedo.full: percēdo, cessi, ĕre, v. a.: cedit, cessit, percedit, percessit, Not. Tir. p. 17.

perceleber.full: per-cĕlĕber, bris, bre, adj., very famous, very celebrated or distinguished: templum vetustate et religione percelebre, Mel. 2, 3, 4.
perceleber.short: per-cĕlĕber, bris, bre, adj., very famous, very celebrated or distinguished: templum vetustate et religione percelebre, Mel.

percelebro.full: per-cĕlĕbro, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a., to practise a thing very frequently. In gen. (post-class.): ut exercerent, ut gererent, ut percelebrarent haec mala, Arn. 2, 43.— In partic., to pronounce frequently, to have often in one's mouth (class.): de quā muliere plurimi versus totā Siciliā percelebrantur, Cic. Verr. 2, 5, 31, § 81: pervulgata et percelebrata sermonibus res est, id. Cael. 29, 69.

perceler.full: per-cĕler, celĕris, adj., very quick or swift: interitus, Cic. Cael. 24, 58.—Adv.: percĕlerĭter, very quickly, very soon, Cic. Fam. 6, 12, 3.
perceler.short: per-cĕler, celĕris, adj., very quick or swift: interitus, Cic.

percello.full: per-cello, cŭli, culsum, 3 (perculsi for perculi, Amm. 17, 8, 4; 25, 8, 13), v. a. cf.: procella, celer, to beat down, throw down; to overturn, upset (class.; syn.: percutio, deicio). Lit.: ventus Cercius plaustrum oneratum percellit, Cato ap. Gell. 2, 22, 29; cf.: vento perculsam ratem, Afran. ap. Fest. p. 273 Müll. (Com. Rel. p. 154 fin. Rib.): magnas quercus, Enn. ap. Macr. S. 6, 2 (Ann. v. 194 Vahl.): abietem, Varr. ap. Non. 152, 11: alii adnutat ... alii percellit pedem, Naev. ap. Isid. Ori
percello.short: per-cello, cŭli, culsum, 3 (perculsi for perculi, Amm.

percenseo.full: per-censĕo, ŭi, 2, v. a., to go through or over a thing. Lit., to count over, reckon up, enumerate: inveniendi locos, Cic. Part. 36, 127: gentes, Liv. 33, 32; 10, 36, 15: numerum legionum, Tac. A. 4, 4: res Caesaris, Plin. 7, 26, 27, § 99.— Transf. In gen., to survey, view; lit. and trop., to review, examine: manipulos, Varr. R. R. 1, 50, 1: orationes, Liv. 32, 21: captivos, id. 6, 25: omnia vultu, Sil. 6, 648: orationem acri subtilique ingenio, Gell. 7, 3, 10.— To go over, travel through: Thess

percensio.full: percensĭo, ōnis, f. percenseo, a going over, a survey, review, Front. Orat. Ep. 3 Mai.

percepta.full: percepta, ōrum, n. plur., v. percipio, P. a. fin.

perceptibilis.full: perceptī^bĭlis, e percipio. Perceptible, Cassiod. Hist. Eccl. 5, 20.— Participating in any thing, Boëth. Dial. in Porphyr. 1, 20.

perceptio.full: perceptĭo, ōnis, f. percipio, a taking, receiving; a gathering in, collecting. Lit., Ambros. in Luc. 4, 15: frugum fruetuumque reliquorum, Cic. Off. 2, 3, 12: fructuum, Col. 1, 3, 2.— Trop., perception, comprehension (cf.: notio, cognitio): animi perceptiones, notions, ideas, Cic. Ac. 2, 7, 22: cognitio aut perceptio, aut si verbum e verbo volumus comprehensio, quam κατάληψιν illi vocant, id. ib. 2, 6, 17.

perceptor.full: perceptor, ōris, m. id., a receiver, imbiber (late Lat.): sapientiae, Aug. Soliloq. 1, 1 fin.

perceptus.full: perceptus, a, um, Part. and P. a., from percipio.

percernis.full: percernis, e, adj. per-cerno, easily visible, Inscr. Fabr. p. 615, n. 127.

percido.full: per-cīdo, cīdi, cīsum (perf. percecīdi, Flor. 4, 12, 7), 3, v. a. caedo, to beat or cut to pieces, to smash. In gen.: os alicui, Plaut. Pers. 2, 4, 12; id. Cas. 2, 6, 52; Sen. Q. N. 4, 4, 1.— Esp. To cut to pieces, rout utterly, destroy: exercitum, Flor. 3, 20, 10: terga hostium, id. 4, 12, 7.— In mal. part., i. q. paedicare, Mart. 4, 48, 1; 7, 62, 1 al.; Sen. Prov. 5, 3; Mart. 12, 35, 2; cf.: percisus, paedicatus, πεπυγισμένος, Gloss. Philox.; so, too, alicui os, i. q. irrumare, Mart. 2, 72, 3

percieo.full: per-cĭĕo, cīvi and ii, ĭtum, 2, and per-cĭo, īvi and ĭi, ītum, 4, v. a., to move or rouse greatly, to stir up, excite. In gen.: irai fax subdita percit, Lucr. 3, 303; 3, 184: crura hercle defringentur nisi istum verbum saepe unum perciet aureis Omnibus, id. 4, 563.— In partic., to attack with words, abuse, or call aloud (by an opprobrious name): aliquem impudicum percies, Plaut. As. 2, 4, 69 Ussing ad loc.— Hence, percĭtus, a, um, P. a., greatly moved, roused, stimulated, excited. Lit.: amoris c
percieo.short: per-cĭĕo, cīvi and ii, ĭtum, 2, and per-cĭo, īvi and ĭi, ītum, 4, v.

percingo.full: percingo, ĕre, v. l. for praecingere (q. v.), Col. 10, 347; Manil. 3, 325.

percipibilis.full: percĭpĭbĭlis, e, adj. percipio, perceptible: aër ictus auditu percipibilis, Mar. Vict. p. 2451 P.

percipio.full: per-cĭpĭo, cēpi, ceptum, 3 (old form of the pluperf. percepset for percepisset, Poët. ap. Cic. Off. 3, 26, 98; v. Trag. Rel. p. 207 Rib.), v. a. capio, to take wholly, to seize entirely (cf. occupo). Lit. To take possession of, to seize, occupy: mihi horror misero membra percipit dictis tuis, Plaut. Am. 5, 1, 66: priusquam percipit (eum) insania, id. Men. 5, 5, 22; id. Stich. 2, 2, 17: neque urbis odium me umquam percipit, Ter. Eun. 5, 5, 2: vitae percipit humanos odium, Lucr. 3, 80; 5, 605.— To
percipio.short: per-cĭpĭo, cēpi, ceptum, 3 (old form of the pluperf.

percis.full: percis, ĭdis, f., a false reading for pegris, Plin. 32, 11, 53, § 150.
percis.short: percis, ĭdis, f., a false reading for pegris, Plin.

percisus.full: percīsus, a, um, Part., v. percido.

percito.full: per-cĭto, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a., to excite thoroughly, strongly, vehemently (ante-class.), Pac. ap. Fest. s. v. reciprocare, p. 274 Müll.: matronae percitatae tumultu, Att. ap. Non. 467, 27.

percitus.full: percĭtus, a, um, Part. and P. a., from percieo.

percivilis.full: per-cīvīlis, e, adj., very courteous, affable, civil: sermo, Suet. Tib. 28.
percivilis.short: per-cīvīlis, e, adj., very courteous, affable, civil: sermo, Suet.

perclamo.full: per-clāmo, āre, v. a., a false reading, Plaut. Truc. 1, 1, 8; Speng. superba facta.

perclaresco.full: per-clāresco, clārŭi, 3, v. inch. n., to become very clear, very well known (postclass.), Symm. Ep. 10, 72 bis.

percludo.full: perclūdo, ĕre, a false reading for praecludo.
percludo.short: perclūdo, ĕre, a false reading for praecludo.

percnopterus.full: percnoptĕrus, i, m. (= περκνόπτερος, dusky-winged), a mountain-stork, i. q. oripelargus, Plin. 10, 3, 3, § 8.

percnos.full: percnos (-nus), i, m. (= περκνός, dusky), a kind of eagle, Plin. 10, 3, 3, § 7.

percoctus.full: percoctus, a, um, Part., from percoquo.
percoctus.short: percoctus, a, um, Part., from percoquo.

percognitus.full: percognĭtus, a, um, Part. and P. a., from percognosco.

percognosco.full: per-cognosco, nōvi, nĭtum, 3, v. a., to become perfectly acquainted with: aliquem, Plaut. Truc. 1, 2, 50 (Speng. pergnovi).— Hence, percognĭtus, a, um, P. a., well known: lex naturae non ignota, etsi nondum percognita, Plin. 2, 45, 45, § 116: Germania, id. 4, 14, 28, § 98; 37, 3, 11, § 45.

percolapho.full: per-cŏlăpho, āre, v. a., to buffet well, Petr. 44 dub.

percolatio.full: percōlātĭo, ōnis, f. 1. percolo, a straining through, a filtering, Vitr. 8, 7.

percolo1.full: per-cōlo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a., to strain through, to filter, percolate. Lit.: tum vinum percolato, polentam abicito, Cato, R. R. 108; Cels. 6, 9; Col. 12, 41, 2; Plin. 31, 6, 37, § 70.— Transf., in gen., to cause to pass through: umor per terras percolatur, passes through, Lucr. 2, 475: cibos et potiones, to pass through one, i. e. to swallow and digest, Sen. Q. N. praef. § 3: terra bibula crebros imbros percolat atque transmittit, Plin. 18, 11, 29, § 110.

percolo2.full: per-cŏlo, cŏlŭi, cultum, 3, v. a. Lit. To cultivate, of the soil; hence, to inhabit: Eleusiniam glebam, App. M. 11, 2, p. 257.— To perfect, finish: incohata percolui, Plin. Ep. 5, 6, 41.— Transf. To cleanse: os curā, App. Mag. 8.— To deck, beautify, adorn: aliquid eloquentiā, Tac. Agr. 10.— To honor greatly, to revere, reverence: si patrem percoles, Plaut. Trin. 2, 2, 4: conjugem liberosque, Tac. A. 4, 68: multos praefecturis et procurationibus, plerosque senatorii ordinis honore, id. H. 2, 82:

percolopo.full: percŏlŏpo, āre, v. a. per-colophus, to box the ears of one, to beat: larvas sic istos percolopabant, Petr. 44, 5.

percomis.full: per-cōmis, e, adj., very friendly, very courteous, Cic. Brut. 58, 212.
percomis.short: per-cōmis, e, adj., very friendly, very courteous, Cic.

percommodus.full: per-commŏdus, a, um, adj., very suitable, very convenient, very opportune: alicui rei, Liv. 22, 43, 11.—Adv.: percom-mŏdē, very suitably, very conveniently, very well: percommode accidit, quod, etc., Cic. Caecin. 27, 77: percommode factum est, quod, etc., id. Tusc. 4, 30, 64: hoc percommode cadit quod, etc., Cic. Verr. 1, 2, 5.
percommodus.short: per-commŏdus, a, um, adj., very suitable, very convenient, very opportune: alicui rei, Liv.

perconor.full: per-cōnor, āri, v. dep., to carry out an undertaking, Sen. Ep. 95, 46.

percontatio.full: percontātĭo (percunct-), ōnis, f. percontor, an asking, inquiring after any thing; a question, inquiry. In gen. (class.): tempus percontatione consumere, Cic. Univ. 1: aliquid percontationibus reperire, Caes. B. G. 5, 13: percontatio quid in senatu esset actum, Cic. Brut. 60, 218: collocutio atque percontatio, Plin. 11, 30, 36, § 110.— In partic., as a figure of speech, Cic. de Or. 3, 53, 203.

percontativus.full: percontātīvus (percunct-), a, um, adj. percontor, universally known (postclass.), Cael. Aur. Tard. 4, 8, 114.— In gram., interrogative: modus, Diom. p. 328 P.—Adv.: percontātīvē, inquiringly, Charis. p. 161 P.

percontator.full: percontātor (percunct-), ōris, m. id., an asker, inquirer, Plaut. Men. 5, 5, 31: percontatorem fugito; nam garrulus idem est, Hor. Ep. 1, 18, 69.

perconto.full: perconto (percuncto), āre, 1, v. a. and n. (ante- and post-class.) [v. percontor], to question strictly or particularly, to inquire earnestly: docte percontat, Aeneas quo pacto, etc., Naev. ap. Non. 474, 7: si percontassem, etc., Nov. ib. 474, 5: quod sedulo percontaveram, App. M. 11, p. 266, 8.— percontor, ātus, in pass. signif.: de ovium dentibus opiliones percontantur, are questioned (preceded by quae a grammatico quaerenda sunt), Gell. 16, 6, 11: percontato pretio, App. M. 1, p. 113, 14.—Hen

percontor.full: percontor (percunct-), ātus, 1 (inf. percontarier, Plaut. Am. 2, 2, 78; id. As. 2, 2, 76; id. Cas. 3, 3, 8; id. Most. 4, 2, 47 al.), v. dep. a. and n. per and root cunc-; Sanscr. canc- (canka, hesitation); cf. ὄκνος for κόκνος, to ask particularly, to question strictly, to inquire, interrogate, investigate (class.; syn.: interrogo, sciscitor).—Constr.: aliquem de aliquā re, aliquem and interrog.clause, aliquem alone; also, aliquid ab (rarely ex) aliquo and absol.; also aliquem aliquid: cocum per

percontumax.full: per-contŭmax, ācis, adj., very obstinate, very contumacious, Ter. Hec. 3, 5, 54.
percontumax.short: per-contŭmax, ācis, adj., very obstinate, very contumacious, Ter.

percooperio.full: per-cŏŏpĕrĭo, rŭi, 4, v. a., to cover entirely, Theod. Prisc. 4, 1 al.

percopiosus.full: per-cōpĭōsus, a, um, adj., very abundantly supplied; hence, very rich in expression, very copious, Plin. Ep. 9, 31, 1; Sid. Ep. 1, 1.—Adv.: percōpĭōsē, very copiously, Sid. Ep. 4, 7 fin.
percopiosus.short: per-cōpĭōsus, a, um, adj., very abundantly supplied;

percoquo.full: per-cŏquo, xi, ctum, 3, v. a., to boil or cook thoroughly, boil soft. Lit.: prandium, Plaut. Merc. 3, 3, 18: bubulas carnes, Plin. 23, 7, 64, § 127: lens non bene percocta, id. 22, 25, 70, § 142.—Prov.: In digitis hodie percoquam quod ceperit, Plaut. Rud. 4, 1, 11.— Transf. To heat: umorem, Lucr. 6, 858: terram, id. 5, 1254.— To ripen: mora percoquit uvas, Ov. R. Am. 83: sol percoquit fructus, Sen. Ben. 7, 31, 3: messem, Plin. Ep. 5, 6, 8.— To scorch, to blacken by the heat of the sun: nigra vir

percosius.full: Percōsĭus, a, um, adj., = Περκώσιος, of or belonging to Percosius, king of Cyzicus: Percosia conjux, i. e. Clyte, wife of king Percosius, Val. Fl. 3, 10.
percosius.short: Percōsĭus, a, um, adj., = Περκώσιος, of or belonging to Percosius, king of Cyzicus: Percosia conjux, i.

percote.full: Percōtē, ēs, f., = Περκώτη, a Trojan town on the coast of Mysia, now Bourgas, Plin. 5, 32, 40, § 141; Val. Fl. 2, 622.
percote.short: Percōtē, ēs, f., = Περκώτη, a Trojan town on the coast of Mysia, now Bourgas, Plin.

percrassus.full: per-crassus, a, um, adj., very thick, Cels. 5, 26, 20.
percrassus.short: per-crassus, a, um, adj., very thick, Cels.

percrebesco.full: per-crēbesco, bŭi, and per-cre-bresco, brui, 3, v. inch. n., to become very frequent or prevalent, to be spread abroad (class.): cum hoc percrebrescit, Cic. Att. 1, 1, 1: quae (opinio) apud exteras nationes omnium sermone percrebruit, Cic. Verr. 1, 1, 1; id. Div. in Caecil. 4, 12: res percrebuit; in ore atque sermone omnium coepit esse, Cic. Verr. 2, 2, 23, § 56: cum haec fama percrebuerit, id. ib. 2, 4, 30, § 68: fama percrebuit, id. ib. 2, 4, 43, § 94: quod cum percrebuisset, id. Off. 3, 14, 5
percrebesco.short: per-crēbesco, bŭi, and per-cre-bresco, brui, 3, v.

percrepo.full: per-crĕpo, ŭi, ĭtum, 1, v. a. and n. Neutr., to sound very much, to resound, ring: lucum percrepare vocibus, Cic. Verr. 2, 5, 13, § 31.— Act., to make resound, to celebrate loudly: pugnam, Lucil. ap. Non. 255, 14.

percresco.full: per-cresco, ĕre, v. n., to grow greatly, Ser. Samm. 36, 679.

percribro.full: per-crībro, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a., to sift thoroughly, Scrib. Comp. 87: res contusae et percribratae, id. ib. 289.

percrucio.full: per-crŭcĭo, āre, v. a., to torment or vex greatly: hoc est demum quod percrucior, for which I vex myself, grieve, Plaut. Bacch. 5, 1, 13.

percrudus.full: per-crūdus, a, um, adj. Lit., quite raw: coria, Vitr. 10, 20, 3.— Transf., quite unripe or crude: pruna, quite green, Col. 12, 10, 4.

percudo.full: per-cūdo, di, 3, v. a., to strike or break through: an pulli rostellis ova percuderint, Col. 8, 5, 14 (Schneid. pertuderint).

perculsus1.full: perculsus, a, um, Part., from percello.
perculsus1.short: perculsus, a, um, Part., from percello.

perculsus2.full: perculsus, ūs, m. percello, a shock, Tert. Anim. 52.

percultor.full: percultor, ōris, m. 2. percolo, an ardent adorer or reverencer: doctorum, Aur. Vict. Caes. 1, 5.

percultus.full: percultus, a, um, Part., from 2. percolo.

percumbo.full: per-cumbo, cŭbŭi, 3, v. n., mentioned as an unused form, Varr. L. L. 9, § 49 Müll.

percuncto.full: percuncto, āre, and percunctor, āri, v. percontor.
percuncto.short: percuncto, āre, and percunctor, āri, v.

percupidus.full: per-cŭpĭdus, a, um, adj., very partial to, very fond of one.—With gen.: percupidus tui, Cic. Fam. 1, 7, 2.
percupidus.short: per-cŭpĭdus, a, um, adj., very partial to, very fond of one.—With gen.: percupidus tui, Cic.

percupio.full: per-cŭpĭo, pĕre, v. a., to wish greatly, desire earnestly, to long (ante-class.): percupio obsequi gnato meo, Plaut. As. 1, 1, 61; Ter. Eun. 5, 2, 57.

percuriosus.full: per-cūrĭōsus, a, um, adj., very curious or inquisitive: servolus, percuriosus et minime mendax, Cic. Clu. 62, 175.
percuriosus.short: per-cūrĭōsus, a, um, adj., very curious or inquisitive: servolus, percuriosus et minime mendax, Cic.

percuro.full: per-cūro, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a., to heal thoroughly, cure completely (perh. not anteAug.). Lit.: percurato vulnere, Liv. 21, 57; Curt. 4, 6, 21; 7, 6, 23: tarde percurabitur, Col. 6, 12, 2: donec strumae percurentur, Plin. 32, 8, 28, § 88: desperata a medicis vitia, Sen. Q. N. 3, 1, 3.— Trop.: mentem aegram, Sen. Ep. 94, 13.

percurro.full: per-curro, percŭcurri or percurri, percursum, 3, v. a. and n. Act., to run through, hasten through; to pass through, traverse, run over, pass over or along class.; syn. peragro). Lit.: percurrere agrum Picenum, Caes. B. C. 1, 15: labro calamos, Lucr. 4, 588: rapido percurrens turbine campos, id. 1, 273: pollice chordas, Ov. Am. 2, 4, 27: conventus, Hirt. B. G. 8, 46: Tenchteros et Cattos, Flor. 4, 12: aristas, to speed over, Ov. M. 10, 655: percurrens luna fenestras, Prop. 1, 3, 31: pectine tela
percurro.short: per-curro, percŭcurri or percurri, percursum, 3, v.

percursatio.full: percursātĭo, ōnis, f. percurso, a running or travelling through, a traversing: Italiae, Cic. Phil. 2, 25, 62.—Absol., Cic. Phil. 2, 39, 100.

percursio.full: percursĭo, ōnis, f. percurro, a running through or over; trop., A rapid or hasty thinking over a thing: propter animi multarum rerum brevi tempore percursionem, Cic. Tusc. 4, 13, 31.— Rhet., a rapid or hasty passing over a subject: huic (commorationi) contraria saepe percursio est, Cic. de Or. 3, 53, 202.

percurso.full: percurso, āre, v. freq. a. and n. id.. Act., to run or range through, ramble over (perh. not ante-Aug.): ripas, Plin. Pan. 12, 11.— Neutr., to range or rove about: finibus nostris, Liv. 23, 42, 10.

percursor.full: percursor, ōris, m. id., one who runs through: viae, Lact. 6, 7 dub. (al. praecursor).

percursus.full: percursus, a, um, Part., from percurro.
percursus.short: percursus, a, um, Part., from percurro.

percussibilis.full: percussĭbĭlis, e, adj. percutio, penetrating, pervading (post-class.): odor, Cael. Aur. Acut. 1, 16, 163: virtus, id. Tard. 2, 13, 164.

percussio.full: percussĭo, ōnis, f. id., a beating, striking (class.). Lit.: capitis percussiones, beatings on the head, Cic. Tusc. 3, 26, 62: digitorum, a snapping, id. Off. 3, 19, 75. — Transf., in music and rhetoric, a beating time; hence, concr., time: percussiones numerorum, Cic. de Or. 3, 47, 182: percussionum modi, id. Or. 58, 198; Quint. 9, 4, 51; 11, 3, 108 al.

percussionalis.full: percussĭōnālis, e, adj. percutio, adapted for striking, played by striking: instrumentum musicum, Cassiod. Mus. 1.

percussor.full: percussor, ōris, m. id., a striker, stabber, shooter. In gen. (post-Aug.): leo vulneratus percussorem novit, Plin. 8, 16, 19, § 51.— In partic., a murderer, assassin, bandit (class.; syn.: sicarius, interfector), Cic. Phil. 2, 29, 74; Just. 14, 6, 9; Tac. A. 2, 31: subornatus alicui, Suet. Ner. 34; id. Caes. 83; Juv. 8, 173: nocturnus, Petr. 9.

percussura.full: percussūra, ae, f. id., a blow, stroke, thrust (post-class.): percussura ferro facta, App. Herb. 31; Veg. Vet. 2, 20, 1; Vulg. Lev. 14. 54.

percussus1.full: percussus, a, um, Part., from percutio.
percussus1.short: percussus, a, um, Part., from percutio.

percussus2.full: percussus, ūs, m. percutio, a beating, striking (poet. and in post-Aug. prose): caducis Percussu crebro saxa cavantur aquis, Ov. P. 2, 7, 40; Sen. Q. N. 2, 6, 3: venarum, Plin. 7, 51, 52, § 171: non sentire percussum, not to feel the injury deeply, Sen. Ira, 3, 25, 3: contra scorpionis percussum, App. Herb. 31, 7.

percutio.full: per-cŭtĭo, cussi, cussum, 3 (perf. contr. percusti for percussisti, Hor. S. 2, 3, 273), v. a. quatio. (With the notion of the per predominating.) To strike through and through, to thrust or pierce through (syn.: percello, transfigo). Lit.: percussus cultello, Varr. R. R. 1, 69, 2: gladio percussus, Cic. Mil. 24, 65: Mamilio pectus percussum, Liv. 2, 19, 8: coxam Aeneae, Juv. 15, 66: vena percutitur, a vein is opened, blood is let, Sen. Ep. 70, 16: fossam, to cut through, dig a trench, Front. Str

perdagatus.full: perdāgātus, a, um, Part. (from the obsol. perdāgo, like indago), explored, Claud. Mam. Stat. Anim. 2, 3 init.

perdecipio.full: per-dēcĭpĭo, cēpi, ceptum, 3, v. a., to deceive utterly (late Lat.): aurum populum ... sic specie perdecepit, ut hoc esse deum crederent, Petr. Chrys. Serm. 29.

perdecorus.full: per-dĕcōrus, a, um, adj., very comely, very pretty (post-Aug.), Plin. Ep. 3, 9, 28.
perdecorus.short: per-dĕcōrus, a, um, adj., very comely, very pretty (post-Aug.), Plin.

perdefessus.full: per-dēfessus, a, um, adj., worn out, utterly wearied: vexationibus, Petr. Chrys. Serm. 112.
perdefessus.short: per-dēfessus, a, um, adj., worn out, utterly wearied: vexationibus, Petr.

perdefleo.full: per-dēflĕo, ēre. 2, v. a., to lament: generis humani primordia perdeflenda, Petr. Chrys. Serm. 166.

perdeleo.full: per-dēlĕo, ēre, v. a., to destroy utterly, to exterminate (post-class.), Tert. adv. Jud. 11; Veg. Vet. 3, 10.

perdelirus.full: per-dēlīrus, a, um, adj., very silly or foolish (poet.), Lucr. 1, 692.
perdelirus.short: per-dēlīrus, a, um, adj., very silly or foolish (poet.), Lucr.

perdensus.full: per-densus, a, um, adj., very compact, very dense (post-Aug.): humus, Col. 3, 12, 2.
perdensus.short: per-densus, a, um, adj., very compact, very dense (post-Aug.): humus, Col.

perdeo.full: perdĕo for pereo, v. pereo init.

perdepso.full: per-depso, ŭi, 3, v. a., to knead over, to work up, in mal. part., Cat. 74, 3.

perdicalis.full: perdīcālis, e, adj. perdix, of or belonging to partridges, partridge- (postclass.): herba, App. Herb. 81.

perdiccas.full: Perdiccas and Perdicca, ae, m., = Περδίκκας. Perdiccas, a Macedonian general under Alexander the Great, Curt. 3, 9, 7; 4, 3, 1; 7, 6, 19; Cic. Tusc. 5, 12, 34; Just. 13, 2, 5; 13, 6, 6; Nep. Eum. 3, 5.— The name of three kings of Macedonia, esp. Perdiccas III., Just. 7, 4, 5; 7, 5, 6.
perdiccas.short: Perdiccas and Perdicca, ae, m., = Περδίκκας.

perdicium.full: perdīcĭum, ĭi, n., = περδίκιον. Pellitory: helxinen vocant, Plin. 22, 17, 19, § 41.— The plant parthenium, Plin. 21, 30, 104, § 176.

perdico.full: per-dīco, xi, ctum, 3, v. a., to say out, to finish saying (post-class.), Alcim. 5, 607; cf.: dicit, perdicit, perdixit, Not. Tir. p. 10.

perdifficilis.full: per-diffĭcĭlis, e, adj., very difficult (class.), Cic. Part. 24, 84: quaestio, id. N. D. 1, 1, 1: navigatio, id. Att. 3, 8, 2.—Sup.: perdifficillimus aditus, exceedingly difficult, Liv. 40, 21.—Adv.: perdiffĭcĭlĭter, with great difficulty, Cic. Ac. 2, 15, 47.
perdifficilis.short: per-diffĭcĭlis, e, adj., very difficult (class.), Cic.

perdignus.full: per-dignus, a, um, adj., very worthy; with abl.: homo perdignus tuā amicitiā, Cic. Fam. 13, 6, 4.
perdignus.short: per-dignus, a, um, adj., very worthy;

perdiligens.full: per-dīlĭgens, entis, adj., very diligent: homo, Cic. Q. Fr. 3, 5, 6.—Adv.: perdīlĭgenter, very diligently, Cic. Att. 1, 11, 1: complecti aliquid, id. Brut. 3, 14.
perdiligens.short: per-dīlĭgens, entis, adj., very diligent: homo, Cic.

perdisco.full: per-disco, dĭdĭci, 3, v. a., to learn thoroughly or completely, to get by heart (rare but class.): omnia jura belli, Cic. Balb. 20, 47: locus de moribus est oratori perdiscendus, id. de Or. 1, 15, 69: hominis speciem pingere, id. ib. 2, 16, 69: ad perdiscendum, Plaut. Truc. 1, 1, 1; cf. Cic. de Or. 3, 36, 147; id. Fam. 7, 14, 2 al.; Tib. 1, 10 (9), 65.—With object-clause: perdidici, isthaec esse vera, Plaut. As. 1, 3, 35.

perdisertus.full: per-dĭsertus, a, um, adj., very eloquent (late Lat. and rare), Gram. Vat. Praep. 5 (Class. Auct. vol. 5 Mai).—Hence, per-dĭsertē, adv., very eloquently, Cic. de Or. 1, 14, 62.
perdisertus.short: per-dĭsertus, a, um, adj., very eloquent (late Lat.

perdite.full: perdĭtē, adv., v. perdo, P. a. fin.

perditim.full: perdĭtim, adv. perditus, desperately, to desperation: aliquam amare, Afran. ap. Charis. p. 191 P. (Com. Rel. v. 354 Rib.).

perditio.full: perdĭtĭo, ōnis, f. perdo, ruin, perdition (post-class.): perditionis iter, Alcim. 4, 138; Lact. 2, 14, 11; 4, 18, 32; Vulg. Matt. 7, 13 et saep.; cf. perditio, ἀπώλεια, Gloss. Philox.

perditor.full: perdĭtor, ōris, m. id., a ruiner, destroyer (rare but class.): perditor rei publi cae, Cic. Planc. 36, 89; id. Vatin. 3, 7: vexa tor et perditor, id. Pis. 34, 84: afflictor et perditor ordinis, id. ib. 27, 64: hominum, Lact. 2, 14, 8.

perditrix.full: perdĭtrix, īcis, f. perditor, she that ruins or destroys (eccl. Lat.), Tert. Exhort. ad Cast. 13; Hier. Ep. 123, n. 8.

perditus.full: perdĭtus, a, um, Part. and P. a., from perdo.

perdiu.full: per-dĭu, adv., for a great while, very long (rare but class.), Varr. R. R. 1, 58: perdiu nihil eram auditurus, Cic. Att. 3, 22, 4; id. de Or. 1, 2, 8.
perdiu.short: per-dĭu, adv., for a great while, very long (rare but class.), Varr.

perdius.full: per-dĭus, a, um, adj. dies, all day long, the livelong day (post-class.): stare solitus Socrates dicitur, pertinaci statu perdius atque pernox, Gell. 2, 1, 1; App. M. 5, p. 161, 11; 9, p. 219, 23.

perdiuturnus.full: per-dĭŭturnus, a, um, adj., that lasts a very long time, very lingering or protracted (rare but class.), Cic. N. D. 2, 33, 85 (but Cic. Sest. 27, 58 Halm and B. and K. read diuturnum).
perdiuturnus.short: per-dĭŭturnus, a, um, adj., that lasts a very long time, very lingering or protracted (rare but class.), Cic.

perdives.full: per-dīvĕs, ĭtis, adj., very rich, Cic. Att. 6, 1, 3: mulier perdives et nobilis, Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 26, § 59.
perdives.short: per-dīvĕs, ĭtis, adj., very rich, Cic.

perdivisus.full: per-dīvīsus, a, um, adj., wholly parted from, quite apart from: marito, Petr. Chrys. Serm, 164.
perdivisus.short: per-dīvīsus, a, um, adj., wholly parted from, quite apart from: marito, Petr.

perdix1.full: perdix, īcis, comm., = πέρδιξ, a partridge, Plin. 10, 33, 51, § 100; Mart. 3, 37, 15: perdicas Boeotios, Varr. ap. Non. 218, 18: picta, Mart. 3, 58, 15; Vulg. Jer. 17, 11.
perdix1.short: perdix, īcis, comm., = πέρδιξ, a partridge, Plin.

perdix2.full: Perdix, īcis, m. In mythology, the nephew of Dœdalus, Ov. M. 8, 241 sq.; Hyg. Fab. 274.

perdo.full: per-do, dĭdi, ditum, 3 (old form of the pres. subj. perduim, Plaut. Aul. 4, 6, 6: perduis, id. Am. 2, 2, 215; id. Capt. 3, 5, 70: perduit, id. Ep. 1, 1, 64; id. Poen. 3, 4, 29; but esp. freq., perduint, Plaut. As. 2, 4, 61; id. Aul. 4, 10, 55; id. Curc. 5, 3, 41; id. Cas. 3, 5, 17; id. Most. 3, 1, 138; id. Men. 2, 2, 34; 3, 1, 6; 5, 5, 31; id. Merc. 4, 3, 11; 4, 4, 53; id. Poen. 3, 2, 33; 4, 2, 41; id. Stich. 4, 2, 15; id. Truc. 2, 3, 10; Ter. Heaut. 4, 6, 7; id. Hec. 3, 4, 27; id. Phorm. 1, 2,
perdo.short: per-do, dĭdi, ditum, 3 (old form of the pres.

perdoceo.full: per-dŏcĕo, cui, ctum, 2, v. a., to teach or instruct thoroughly (rare but class.; syn. erudio): res difficilis ad perdocendum, Cic. Sest. 44, 96: aliquem, Plaut. Capt. 3, 5, 59: quanti istuc unum me coquitare perdoces? id. Ps. 3, 2, 85: si quid Apollo Utile mortales perdocet ore meo, Ov. R. Am. 490: homines, Lucr. 5, 1438: suam stultitiam, to betray, Quint. 1, 1, 8.—With object-clause: dignam Maeoniis Phaeacida condere chartis Cum te Pierides perdocuere tuae, Ov. P. 4, 12, 28.—Hence, perdoctus,

perdoleo.full: per-dŏlĕo, ŭi, ìtum, 2, v. n., to pain or grieve greatly (ante-class.): id perdolitum est T. Manlio, Q. Claud. ap. Gell. 9, 13, 13: tandem perdoluit, Ter. Eun. 1, 2, 74.

perdolesco.full: perdŏlesco or -dŏlisco, lŭi, 3, v. inch. n. [per-doleo], to feel great pain or grief: nec perdoliscit fligi socios, Att. ap. Non. 110, 31 (Trag. Rel. p. 150 Rib.): suam virtutem irrisui fore perdoluerunt, * Caes. B. C. 2, 15.

perdolo.full: per-dŏlo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a., to hew out, to fashion with hewing (post-Aug.): cum in materiem perdolantur, Vitr. 2, 10, 2: arbor perdolata, id. 2, 9, 7: fomes perdolatus, Arn. 6, 209.

perdominor.full: per-dŏmĭnor, āri, v. dep. n., to rule or reign throughout a period of time: annum, Claud. Fesc. Nupt. Honor. 77.

perdomitor.full: perdŏmĭtor, ōris, m. perdomo, a tamer, subduer (eccl. Lat.): mortis, Prud. Cath. 4, 12.

perdomitus.full: perdŏmĭtus, a, um, Part., from perdomo.
perdomitus.short: perdŏmĭtus, a, um, Part., from perdomo.

perdomo.full: per-dŏmo, ŭi, ĭtum, āre, v. a.
