To tame or subdue thoroughly, to subjugate completely, to conquer, vanquish, overcome, etc. (Aug.; syn. subigo): ad perdomandum Latium exercitum circumducere, Liv. 8, 13: Hispaniam, id. 28, 12: Apulia perdomita, id. 9, 20: gentes, Vell. 2, 95, 2: regionem, Just. 2, 3, 15: urbes, Luc. 2, 644: serpentes, tauros feroces, to tame, subdue, Ov. H. 12, 163; id. M. 1, 447: boves, Col. 6, 2.— Transf., to work thoroughly, to knead: farinam assiduā tractatione, Sen. Ep. 90, 2

perdormisco.full: per-dormisco, 3, v. n. dormio, to sleep on: perdormiscin' tu usque ad lucem? Plaut. Men. 5, 5, 29.

perduco.full: per-dūco, xi, ctum, 3 (imper. perduce for perduc, Ser. Samm. 40, 754), v. a., lit., to lead or bring through; hence, To lead, bring, conduct, guide a person or thing to any place. In gen. (class.): filium illuc, Ter. And. 1, 1, 53: legiones ad aliquem, Cic. Fam. 12, 19, 2: comprehensos eos ad Caesarem perduxerunt, Caes. B. G. 7, 13; cf. id. B. C. 3, 28: legionem in Allobrogas, id. B. G. 3, 6: Cyrum ad angustias, Just. 1, 8, 10: nautas ad aequora, Luc. 2, 362: ad Sullam, Suet. Caes. 74: in theatr

perductio.full: perductĭo, ōnis, f. perduco, I. A. 2., a leading, conducting of water (only in Vitr.): aquarum perductiones ad habitationes, Vitr. 8, 6.

perducto.full: perducto, āre, 1, v. freq. a. perduco, to lead, conduct to or over a place (Plautin. in the double sense of perductor, q. v.): quicquid est, errabo potius, quam perductet quispiam, Plaut. Most. 3, 2, 160.

perductor.full: perductor, ōris, m. id., a leader, conductor; in partic., a pimp, pander (cf. perduco, I. B. 1.): lenonum, aleatorum, perductorum nulla mentio fiat, Cic. Verr. 2, 1, 12, § 34 (lenones sunt scortorum: perductores etiam invitarum personarum, et in quibus stupra exercita legibus vindicantur, Ascon. ad h. l.); Lact. 6, 17, 19.—* A guide, conductor, in a double sense with the preced. signif.: Si. Eho istum, puer, circumduce hasce aedes et conclavia. Th. Apage istum a me perductorem: nihil moror ducta

perductus.full: perductus, a, um, Part., from perduco.
perductus.short: perductus, a, um, Part., from perduco.

perdudum.full: per-dūdum, adv., a very long time ago: vidi edepol hominem haut perdudum, Plaut. Stich. 4, 1, 69.
perdudum.short: per-dūdum, adv., a very long time ago: vidi edepol hominem haut perdudum, Plaut.

perduellio.full: perdŭellĭo, ōnis, f. perduellis. Hostile conduct against one's country, treason, whether consisting of an attempt against the state, its institutions, and chief ruler, or of union with a foreign enemy, desertion, etc. (class.): qui perduellionis reus est, hostili animo adversus rempublicam vel principem animatus est, Dig. 48, 4, 11; Cic. Pis. 2, 4: (Clodius) actionem perduellionis intenderat (for causing the execution of the Catilinarians who were Roman citizens), id. Mil. 14, 36: perduellionis

perduellis.full: per-dŭellis, is (gen. plur. perduellūm, Att. ap. Non. 22, 15, or Trag. Rel. p. 238 Rib.; abl. perdvellibus, Enn. ap. Varr. L. L. 7, § 49 Müll., or p. 146 Vahl.), m. per-duellum, i. e. bellum, a public enemy, an enemy actually waging war against a country (mostly anteclass. for the class. hostis): quos nos hostes appellamus, eos veteres perduelles appellabant, per eam adjectionem indicantes, cum quibus bellum esset, Dig. 50, 16, 234: equidem illud etiam animadverto, quod qui proprio nomine perdue

perduis.full: perdŭis, it, etc., v. perdo init.

perdulcis.full: per-dulcis, e, adj., very sweet; sup. † PERDVLCISSIMUS, Inscr. Rein. cl. 20, n. 150.

perduro.full: per-dūro, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. and n. Act., to make hard, to harden (late Lat.): teneras plantas, Prud. Psych. 447.— Neutr., to last or hold out, to endure (poet. and in post-Aug. prose; cf.: obduro, perfero), Ter. Hec. 2, 2, 27: perdurare non posse, Suet. Ner. 24: perdurandi pervicacia, Plin. 17, 20, 34, § 147: longum probitas perdurat in aevum, Ov. Med. Fac. 49: mora perduratura, Stat. Th. 1, 142: non perdurasse in senectutem, Sen. Ben. 7, 28: cotidie unanimiter in templo, abide, continue, Vulg

perdurus.full: per-dūrus, a, um, adj., very hard (post-class.): interpretatio, Dig. 48, 3, 2.
perdurus.short: per-dūrus, a, um, adj., very hard (post-class.): interpretatio, Dig.

peredia.full: Perĕdĭa, ae, f. peredo, Gobbledom, Eating-land, a comically formed name of a country, analogous to Bibesia,. Plaut. Curc. 3, 74.

peredo1.full: pĕr-ĕdo, ēdi, ēsum, 3, v. a., to eat up, consume (poet.). Lit.: cibum, Plaut. Fragm. ap. Prisc. p. 893 P.: quinque panes et gemellos pisces, Prud. Cath. 9, 58.— Transf., to consume, devour, etc.: nec peredit Impositam celer ignis Aetnam, Hor. C. 3, 4, 75: lacrimae peredere umore exsangues genas, old poet in Cic. Tusc. 3, 12, 26 (Trag. Rel. p. 225 Rib.): vesco sale saxa peresa, Lucr. 1, 326: saxa, Tib. 1, 4, 14 (18): morbo peresa Vellera, Verg. G. 3, 561. — Trop., to consume, waste away, etc.: qu

peredo2.full: pĕr-ēdo, 3, v. a., to give forth, an old poet in Sid. Ep. 9, 14.

perefflo.full: per-efflo, āvi, 1, v. a., to breathe out entirely, breathe away (post-class.): animam, App. M. 8, p. 207, 23.

pereffluo.full: per-efflŭo, 3, v. n., to flow through.— Trop., to forget, Vulg. Heb. 2, 1 (transl. of the Gr. παραρρυῶμεν).

pereger.full: pĕrĕger (-gris), comm. per-ager, who has gone through lands, i. e., who is on a journey, abroad, away from home (postclass.): si pereger factus sit, Ulp. Reg. tit. 17, 1 (dub.; Huschke, peregrinus): nedum me peregrem composita fabulari, Aus. Ep. 17: susceptor peregrum, Ven. Carm. 4, 10, 14.—Hence, adv., in two forms, peregre and (ante- and post-class.) peregri, abroad, away from home. pĕrĕgrē, answering to the question where? whence? or whither? To the question where? qui peregre depugnavit, abr

peregregius.full: pĕr-ēgrĕgĭus, a, um, adj., very excellent (post-class.): tragoedia, App. Mag. p. 298, 6.
peregregius.short: pĕr-ēgrĕgĭus, a, um, adj., very excellent (post-class.): tragoedia, App.

peregrinabundus.full: pĕrĕgrīnābundus, a, um, adj. peregrinor, travelling about (rare): dux, Liv. 28, 18, 10; Fulg. Myth. 3, 7 fin.

peregrinatio.full: pĕrĕgrīnātĭo, ōnis, f. peregrinor, a being or living abroad, a sojourning, a travelling in foreign parts, a travelling about, travel, peregrination (class.). Lit.: perpetua, Cic. Tusc. 5, 37, 107: transmarina, Quint. 7, 3, 31; 12, 11, 18; Nep. Att. 2, 3; Plin. Ep. 3, 19, 4 al.: terra peregrinationis tuae, Vulg. Gen. 17, 8: tempus in peregrinatione consumere, Cic. Att. 16, 3, 4.—In plur., Cic. Lael. 27, 103.— Transf., of animals: bestiae peregrinatione laetantur, Cic. Fin. 2, 33, 109.—Of muscles,

peregrinator.full: pĕrĕgrīnātor, ōris, m. id., one who travels about, Cic. Fam. 6, 18, 5.

peregrinitas.full: pĕrĕgrīnĭtas, ātis, f. peregrinus. The condition of a peregrinus or foreigner, opp. to that of a Roman citizen, alienage (post-Aug.): peregrinitatis reus, Suet. Claud. 15: in peregrinitatem redigere aliquem, id. ib. 16; Dig. 2, 4, 10.— Transf. In gen., outlandish ways, foreign habits or manners (class.): cum in urbem nostram infusa est peregrinitas, Cic. Fam. 9, 15, 2.— In partic., a foreign tone or accent in speaking (post-Aug.): os, in quo nulla peregrinitas resonet, Quint. 11, 3, 30.

peregrinor.full: pĕrĕgrīnor, ātus, 1, v. dep. n. [id.], to be or live in foreign parts, to sojourn abroad, to travel about (class.; cf.: peragro, migro). Lit.: peregrinari totā Asiā, Cic. Brut. 13, 51: in alienā civitate, id. Rab. Perd. 10, 28: in terrā, Vulg. Gen. 47, 4. — Trop. To go abroad, to travel about; to roam, rove, or wander about: haec studia pernoctant nobiscum, peregrinantur, rusticantur, Cic. Arch. 7, 16: animus late longeque peregrinatur, id. N. D 1, 20, 54: in infinitatem omnem, to roam through a

peregrinulus.full: pĕrĕgrīnŭlus, a, um, adj. peregrinus, estranged (late Lat.), Ven. Fort. Vit. Germ. 64.

peregrinus.full: pĕrĕgrīnus, a, um, adj. peregre, that comes from foreign parts, strange, foreign, exotic (cf.: exter, externus). Lit. In gen. Adj.: ad portum mittunt servulos, ancillulas: peregrina navis, etc., Plaut. Men. 2, 2, 65: facies, id. Ps. 4, 2, 9: homo, id. Poen. 5, 2, 71: mulier, Hor. C. 3, 3, 20: caelum, Ov. Tr. 4, 8, 25: amnes, id. M. 8, 836: arbores, Plin. 15, 13, 12, § 43: aves, id. 9, 17, 29, § 63: morbus, id. 26, 10, 64, § 100: eluamus hodie peregrina omnia, Plaut. Stich. 5, 2, 19 (668 Ritschl)

perelegans.full: pĕr-ēlĕgans, antis, adj., very neat, fine, or elegant (class.): genus, Cic. de Or. 2, 67, 270: oratio, id. Planc. 24, 58: ingenium, Vell. 1, 7, 1.—Adv.: pĕr-ēlĕganter, very finely, very elegantly: pereleganter dicere, Cic. Brut. 52, 197.
perelegans.short: pĕr-ēlĕgans, antis, adj., very neat, fine, or elegant (class.): genus, Cic.

perelixo.full: pĕr-ēlixo, āre, 1, v. a., to boil thoroughly (post-class.): denuo eum perelixabis (al. perlaxabis), Apic. 7, 7, § 289.

pereloquens.full: pĕr-ēlŏquens, entis, adj., very eloquent: Lentulus, Cic. Brut. 70, 247.
pereloquens.short: pĕr-ēlŏquens, entis, adj., very eloquent: Lentulus, Cic.

peremensus.full: pĕr-ēmensus, a, um, adj., all measured out: permensus, peremensus, Not. Tir. p. 118.
peremensus.short: pĕr-ēmensus, a, um, adj., all measured out: permensus, peremensus, Not.

peremnis.full: pĕremnis, e, adj. per-amnis, of or belonging to crossing a river; only in augural lang., peremne auspicium, and subst., pĕremne, is, n., the auspices taken by magistrates on crossing a river or a spring: peremne dicitur auspicari, qui amnem aut aquam, quae ex sacro oritur, auspicato transit, Fest. p. 245 Müll.; p. 250 Müll.: bella nullis auspiciis administrantur: nulla peremnia servantur, nulla ex acuminibus, Cic. N. D. 2, 3, 9; cf. id. Div. 2, 36, 77.

peremptalis.full: pĕremptālis, e, adj. peremptus, of or belonging to destruction or abolition, abolishing, cancelling; only in augural lang., fulmina, lightnings that destroy the effect or portent of former lightnings: peremptalia fulgura Gracchus ait vocari, quae superiora fulgura aut portenta vi suā perimant, Fest. p. 214 Müll.: peremptalia fulmina, quibus tolluntur priorum fulminum minae, Sen. Q. N. 2, 49, 2.

peremptio.full: pĕremptĭo (pĕremtĭo), ōnis, f. perimo, a destroying, killing (eccl. Lat.), Aug. Tract. in Joann. 27 fin.

peremptor.full: pĕremptor (pĕremtor), ōris, m. id., a destroyer, slayer, murderer (postclass.): incluti regis, Sen. Oedip. 221: mariti mei cruentis, App. M. 8, p. 207, 16; cf.: puer ille peremptor meus, i. e. who has playued me almost to death, id. ib. 7, p. 198, 21.—Absol., Prud. Ham. praef. 19; Ambros. Inst. Virg. 7, 4, 9; Vulg. 2 Macc. 4, 16.

peremptorius.full: pĕremptōrĭus (pĕremtōr-), a, um, adj. id.. Lit., destructive, deadly, mortal (post-class.): venenum, App. M. 10, p. 243, 30: spiculum, Tert. Anim. 25; Sid. Ep. 8, 11.— Trop., qs. that destroys or precludes all debate, i. e. decisive, final, peremptory (jurid. Lat.): peremptorium edictum inde hoc nomen sumpsit, quod perimeret disceptationem, hoc est ultra non pateretur adversarium tergiversari, Dig. 5, 1, 70: dicuntur exceptiones aut peremptoriae aut dilatoriae. Peremptoriae sunt, quae perpetuo v

peremptrix.full: pĕremptrix (pĕremtr-), īcis, f. peremptor, she that destroys or kills (eccl. Lat.): mors peremptrix sensūs, Tert. Anim. 42.

peremptus.full: pĕremptus (pĕremtus), a, um, Part., from perimo.
peremptus.short: pĕremptus (pĕremtus), a, um, Part., from perimo.

perendie.full: pĕrendĭē, adv. Gr. πέραν-dies, on the day after to-morrow (class.): cras agito, perendie agito, Plaut. Merc. 2, 3, 41; id. Aul. 2, 1, 34; id. Stich. 4, 1, 12: scies igitur fortasse cras, summum perendie, Cic. Att. 12, 44, 3; id. Fam. 16, 17, 3.

perendinatio.full: pĕrendĭnātĭo, ōnis, f. perendinus, a putting off till the day after to-morrow (post-class.), Mart. Cap. 9, § 897.

perendinus.full: pĕrendĭnus, a, um, adj. perendie, after to-morrow (class.): tot homines tam ingeniosos, per tot annos statuere non potuisse, utrum diem tertium, an perendinum dici oporteret, Cic. Mur. 12, 27: perendino die, Caes. B. G. 5, 30.—Absol. (anteand post-class.): tu in perendinum paratus sis, against the day after to-morrow, Plaut. Trin. 5, 2, 65: dies perendini, Gell. 10, 24, 9.

perennis.full: pĕrennis († pĕremnis, Inscr. Ann. p. Chr. 341 ap. Guattani Monum. Inedit. 1, 5, p. 39), e (abl. sing. perenne, Ov. H. 8, 64; id. F. 3, 654), adj. per-annus, that lasts or continues the year through (post-Aug.): aves perennes, that remain with us all the year round, Plin. 10, 25, 36, § 73.— Transf., everlasting, never failing, unceasing, perpetual, perennial (class.; cf.: jugis, perpetuus): aquae, Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 48, § 107; cf. Liv. 1, 21, 3: fons, Caes. B. G. 8, 43: amnis, Liv. 4, 30: rivi, Pli

perenniservus.full: pĕrennĭ-servus, i, m. perennis, one who is always a slave, Plaut. Pers. 3, 3, 17.

perennitas.full: pĕrennĭtas, ātis, f. id., lastingness, continuance, perpetual duration, perpetuity (class.): fontium perennitates, Cic. N. D. 2, 39, 98: cibi, constant food, Plaut. Pers. 3, 1, 2: perennitatem conditis frumentis afferunt, Col. 1, 6, 10: vitae, Ambros. in Psa. 118, Serm. 13, 22: Perennitas, a title of the Roman emperors: vestra, your perpetuity, your perennity, Symm. Ep. 10, 45; Sex. Ruf. Brev. 2.

perenno.full: pĕrenno, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. and n. id.. Act., to keep or preserve long (post-Aug.): ea res, etiamsi non in totum perennat, certe usque in alteram vindemiam plerumque vini saporem servat, Col. 12, 20, 8 (dub.; al. perennem); 12, 19, 2.— Neutr., to last for many years, to last, continue, endure (poet. and in post-Aug. prose): arte perennat amor, Ov. A. A. 3, 42: ut diutius perennent boves, Col. 1, 9, 2; 2, 9, 18: domus, Ov. F. 1, 721: gens ultra aevi nostri terminos perennans, Sol. 52, 29.

perenticida.full: pĕrentĭcīda, ae, m., for pericida [pera-caedo], a cutpurse (a word comically formed with allusion to parenticida), Plaut. Ep. 3, 2, 13.
perenticida.short: pĕrentĭcīda, ae, m., for pericida [pera-caedo], a cutpurse (a word comically formed with allusion to parenticida), Plaut.

pereo.full: pĕr-ĕo, ĭi (īvi), ĭtum, īre (periet for peribit, Coripp. Johann. 7, 27; perf. perivit, App. M. 4, 21: perīt, Juv. 8, 85: perisset, Lact. 3, 20, 17 al.: perisse, Liv. 1, 49, 1; Ov. Am. 2, 19, 56; fut. periet, Vulg. Sap. 4, 19 al.), v. n. To pass away, come to nothing; to vanish, disappear, be lost: e patriā, Plaut. Capt. 3, 4, 5: ecqua inde perisset soror, Ter. Eun. 3, 3, 15: ne vena periret aquae, Ov. Tr. 3, 7, 16.— Esp., to pass through, leak, be absorbed (poet.): lymphae Dolium pereuntis, Hor.
pereo.short: pĕr-ĕo, ĭi (īvi), ĭtum, īre (periet for peribit, Coripp.

perequito.full: pĕr-ĕquĭto, āvi, ātum, 1, v. n. and a., to ride through, ride hither and thither, ride about; to drive about (class. but not in Cic.). Neutr.: inter duas acies perequitans, Caes. B. C. 1, 46: longe ex viā, Liv. 23, 47: per omnes partes, to drive about, Caes. B. G. 4, 33.— Act.: aciem, Liv. 5, 28: puer delphino maria perequitans, Plin. 9, 8, 8, § 27.

pererro.full: pĕr-erro, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a., to wander through, to roam or ramble over (poet. and in post-Aug. prose). Lit.: fallacem circum vespertinumque pererro Saepe forum, Hor. S. 1, 6, 113: locum, Verg. A. 5, 441: freta, Ov. H. 14, 103: saltus et fontes, Val. Fl. 3, 537: orbem, Col. praef. 1: cellas, Petr. 97: reges, to roam about from one king to another, Sen. Q. N. 3 praef. § 6.— Pass.: arva pererrantur Peligna, Ov. Am. 2, 16, 5: pererratus orbis, id. F. 1, 234; cf.: pererrato ponto, Verg. A. 2, 295.—

pereruditus.full: pĕr-ērŭdītus, a, um, adj., very learned: homo, Cic. Att. 4, 15, 2.
pereruditus.short: pĕr-ērŭdītus, a, um, adj., very learned: homo, Cic.

peresus.full: pĕrēsus, a, um, Part., from peredo.
peresus.short: pĕrēsus, a, um, Part., from peredo.

perevacuo.full: pĕr-ēvăcŭo, āre, v. a., to empty quite (late Lat.), Vit. Caes. 1, 4, 39.

perexcelsus.full: pĕr-excelsus, a, um, very high, lofty: Henna, ubi ea gesta esse memorantur, est loco perexcelso, Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 48, § 107.
perexcelsus.short: pĕr-excelsus, a, um, very high, lofty: Henna, ubi ea gesta esse memorantur, est loco perexcelso, Cic.

perexcrucio.full: pĕr-excrŭcĭo, a false read. for probe excruciavero, Plaut. Stich. 3, 1, 32; v. Ritschl ad h. l.

perexeo.full: pĕr-exĕo, īre, v. n. irr., to go out through, trop., Cassiod. Var. 11, 7.

perexiguus.full: pĕr-exĭgŭus, a, um, adj., very small, very little (class.): semen perexiguum, Cic. N. D. 2, 32, 81: dies, very short, Cic. Verr. 1, 2, 6: et perminuta bona corporis, id. Tusc. 2, 13, 30: loci spatium, Caes. B. G. 5, 15: argentum, Liv. 22, 52: ignes, Nep. Hann. 9, 3: frumentum, Caes. B. C. 3, 42.—Adv.: pĕrexĭgŭē, very little, very sparingly: perexigue et γλίσχρως praebere, Cic. Att. 16, 1, 5.
perexiguus.short: pĕr-exĭgŭus, a, um, adj., very small, very little (class.): semen perexiguum, Cic.

perexilis.full: pĕr-exīlis, e, adj., very slender (postAug.): vitis, Col. 11, 2, 60: perexile bonum est, Boëth. Cons. Phil. 2, pros. 4.
perexilis.short: pĕr-exīlis, e, adj., very slender (postAug.): vitis, Col.

perexoptatus.full: pĕr-exoptātus, a, um, adj., greatly desired, much longed for (post-class.): in tmesi: per, inquit, exoptatus venis, Gell. 18, 4, 2.
perexoptatus.short: pĕr-exoptātus, a, um, adj., greatly desired, much longed for (post-class.): in tmesi: per, inquit, exoptatus venis, Gell.

perexpeditus.full: pĕr-expĕdītus, a false read. for expedita, Cic. Fin. 3, 11, 36; v. Madv. ad h. l.

perexplicatus.full: pĕr-explĭcātus, a, um, adj., wholly completed (post-class.): sexto reditu perexplicato, Sid. Carm. 23, 385.
perexplicatus.short: pĕr-explĭcātus, a, um, adj., wholly completed (post-class.): sexto reditu perexplicato, Sid.

perexsiccatus.full: pĕr-exsiccātus, a, um, adj., quite dried up (eccl. Lat.): proluvies, Arn. 7, 230.
perexsiccatus.short: pĕr-exsiccātus, a, um, adj., quite dried up (eccl.

perextimeo.full: pĕr-ex-tĭmĕo, ŭi, 2, v. n., and † pĕr-ex-tĭmesco, timŭi, 3, v. n., to fear greatly, Not. Tir. p. 71.

perfabrico.full: per-fabrĭco, āvi, 1, v. a., to work or use up; trop., to take in, overreach, cheat (Plautin.): aliquem, Plaut. Pers. 5, 2, 4.

perfacetus.full: per-făcētus, a, um, adj., very witty, very facetious (class.).—Of persons, Cic Brut. 27, 105.—Of words: aliquid perfacetum dicere, Cic. Planc. 14, 35.—Adv.: per-făcētē, very wittily: perfacete dicta, Cic. Verr. 2, 1, 46, § 121.
perfacetus.short: per-făcētus, a, um, adj., very witty, very facetious (class.).—Of persons, Cic Brut.

perfacilis.full: per-făcĭlis, e, adj. Very easy (class.): perfacilis et expedita defensio, Cic. Fin. 3, 11, 36 Madv. N. cr.: disciplina cognitu perfacilis, id. Tusc. 4, 3, 6; id. Leg. 2, 7, 17: perfacile factu esse conata perficere, Caes. B. G. 1, 3.— In partic., very courteous (class.): perfacilis in audiendo, Cic. de Or. 1, 20, 93.—Hence, adv., in two forms: perfacile (class.) and † perfacul. perfăcĭlē. Very easily (class.): perfacile hunc hominem de medio tolli posse, Cic. Rosc. Am. 7, 20: sese tueri, Cic. Ve

perfacundus.full: per-fācundus, a, um, adj., very eloquent (post-class.): in contionibus perfacundus, Just. 22, 1, 9; App. Flor. 4, 18.
perfacundus.short: per-fācundus, a, um, adj., very eloquent (post-class.): in contionibus perfacundus, Just.

perfamiliaris.full: per-fămĭlĭāris, e, adj., very intimate, very familiar (class.): perfamiliaris Philisto, Cic. Q. Fr. 2, 11 (13), 4.—In tmesi: Phaedon Socrati per fuit familiaris, Gell. 2, 18, 1.— Subst.: perfămĭlĭāris, is, m., a very intimate or familiar friend (class.): meus, Cic. Fam. 13, 51: Epicuri, id. Fin. 5, 31, 94: M. Antonii, id. Brut. 45, 168.
perfamiliaris.short: per-fămĭlĭāris, e, adj., very intimate, very familiar (class.): perfamiliaris Philisto, Cic.

perfatuus.full: per-fătŭus, a, um, adj., very foolish, very silly: togae, Mart. 10, 18, 4 (al. fatuae); Aug. c. Duas Epp. Pelag. 2, 4, 7.
perfatuus.short: per-fătŭus, a, um, adj., very foolish, very silly: togae, Mart.

perfecte.full: perfectē, adv., v. perficio, P. a. fin.

perfectio.full: perfectĭo, ōnis, f. perficio, a finishing, completing, perfecting; perfection (class.): hanc absolutionem perfectionemque in oratore desiderans, Cic. de Or. 1, 28, 130: perfectio atque absolutio optimi, id. Brut. 36, 137: ad cumulum perfectionis accedere, Greg. M. Ep. 7, 10 fin.; Cic. Or. 29, 103; id. Fin. 3, 9, 32; Vulg. Num. 6, 21.—Plur.: operum perfectiones, Vitr. 3, 1, 4.

perfectissimatus.full: perfectissĭmātus, ūs, m. perfectus, the rank and station of a perfectissimus under the later emperors (v. perficio, P. a.), Cod. Th. 8, 4, 3.

perfector.full: perfector, ōris, m. perficio, a finisher, perfecter (rare but class.): mearum voluptatum, Ter. Eun. 5, 8, 4: dicendi, Cic. de Or. 1, 60, 257; Scip. ap. Cic. Att. 8, 11, 1.

perfectrix.full: perfectrix, īcis, f. perfector, she that finishes or perfects (very rare): philosophia beatae vitae perfectrix, Nep. ap. Lact. 3, 15, 10.

perfectus1.full: perfectus, a, um, Part. and P. a., from perficio.

perfectus2.full: perfectus, ūs, m. perficio, a finishing or perfecting; perfection (very rare), Tert. Anim. 20.—Plur., effects, Vitr. 10, 3, 1 (in Vitr. 1, 2, 6, prospectus is the true reading).

perfecundus.full: per-fēcundus (per-foec-), a, um, adj., very fruitful (post-Aug.): generatrix, Mel. 1, 9, 1.
perfecundus.short: per-fēcundus (per-foec-), a, um, adj., very fruitful (post-Aug.): generatrix, Mel.

perferens.full: perfĕrens, entis, Part. and P. a., from perfero.

perferentia.full: perfĕrentĭa, ae, f. perfero, a bearing, suffering; endurance (eccl. Lat.): malorum perferentia, Lact. 3, 11, 9.

perfero.full: per-fĕro, tŭli, lātum, ferre, v. a., to bear or carry through to a certain place or end. Lit. (poet. and in post-Aug. prose): lapis nec pertulit ictum, did not bring the blow home, did not reach the mark, Verg. A. 12, 907: hasta perlata sub papillam, id. ib. 11, 803: per arma pertulit ictum, Sil. 5, 326: partum, to go the full time, Plin. 7, 13, 11, § 58.—Pass., Plin. 7, 11, 9, § 49; cf.: ventrem perferre, Col. 6, 24, 2; 6, 27, 7: Aeneas tulit patrem per ignes, et pertulit, Sen. Ben. 3, 37, 1.—

perferus.full: per-fĕrus, a, um, adj., very wild or savage (ante-class.): boves, Varr. R. R. 2, 1, 5.
perferus.short: per-fĕrus, a, um, adj., very wild or savage (ante-class.): boves, Varr.

perfervefio.full: per-fervĕfīo, fĭĕri, v. n., to become very hot (ante-class.).—In tmesi: terra sole perferve ita fit, ut, etc., Varr. R. R. 1, 9, 2 dub. (acc. to Gesn. and Schneid. a gloss).

perferveo.full: per-fervĕo, ēre, 2, v. n., to be very hot (post-Aug.): perfervet (fons), Mel. 1, 8.

perfervidus.full: per-fervĭdus, a false read. for praefervida, Col. 5, 5.

perfica.full: Perfĭca, ae, f., v. perficus, II.

perficio.full: per-fĭcĭo, fēci, fectum, 3, v. a. facio, to achieve, execute, carry out, accomplish, perform, despatch, bring to an end or conclusion, finish, complete (class.; syn.: absolvo, conficio, exsequor). Lit.: comitiis perficiendis undecim dies tribuit, Caes. B. C. 3, 2: iis comitiis perfectis, Liv. 24, 43, 9: bellum, id. 22, 38, 7: aliquid absolvi et perfici, Cic. N. D. 2, 13, 35: multa, id. Or. 30, 105: scelus, to perpetrate, id. Clu. 68, 194: cogitata, id. Deiot. 7, 21: instituta, id. Div. 2, 5: poë

perficus.full: perfĭcus, a, um, adj. perficio, completing, perfecting (poet.): natura, Lucr. 2, 1116.— Subst.: Perfĭca, ae, f., the finishing or completing goddess, she that perfects: natura creatrix, Lucr. 2, 1116.— Of the goddess supposed to preside over sexual indulgence, Arn. 4, 131.

perfidelis.full: per-fĭdēlis, e, adj., very trusty, very faithful: homo, Cic. Att. 2, 19, 5: perfidelis in amicos, Aur. Vict. Caes. 13, 8.
perfidelis.short: per-fĭdēlis, e, adj., very trusty, very faithful: homo, Cic.

perfidens.full: per-fīdens, entis, adj., trusting greatly, confiding strongly (post-class.): pugnandi arte perfidens, Aur. Vict. Caes. 17.
perfidens.short: per-fīdens, entis, adj., trusting greatly, confiding strongly (post-class.): pugnandi arte perfidens, Aur.

perfidia.full: perfĭdĭa, ae, f. perfidus, faithlessness, dishonesty, treachery, falsehood, perfidy (class.): perfidiā deceptus, Cic. Rosc. Am. 38, 110: fraude et perfidiā aliquem fallere, id. ib. 40, 117; id. Fam. 1, 2, 3: admittere perfidiam in aliquem, Suet. Caes. 75: perfidiae tantae (fuit), ut, etc., id. Ner. 5: repens, Tac. H. 4, 25; Juv. 13, 24.—In plur., Plaut. Capt. 3, 3, 7; id. Ps. 2, 1, 6; Gell. 14, 2, 6.—Of an inanim. thing: sub ipsis positum labris in acoris perfidiam vinum repente mutari, Arn. 1,

perfidiosus.full: perfĭdĭōsus, a, um, adj. perfidia, faithless, dishonest, treacherous, false, perfidious (class.). Of persons: fallax, perfidiosus, Cic. Pis. 27, 66: perfidiosus et subdolus animo, Tac. A. 16, 32.—Sup.: omnium perfidiosissimus, Cic. N. D. 3, 32, 80.— Of inanim. and abstr. things: amor, Plaut. Cist. 1, 1, 73: nihil perfidiosum et insidiosum et fallax in amicitiā, Cic. Fam. 3, 10, 7; id. Rosc. Com. 6, 16.—Adv.: per-fĭdĭōsē, faithlessly, dishonestly, treacherously, perfidiously (rare but class.): he

perfidus.full: perfĭdus, a, um, adj. per-fides, that breaks his promise, faithless, false, dishonest, treacherous, perfidious. Lit. (class.; syn. infidus): vanum et perfidiosum esse, Cic. Quint. 6, 26: omnes, aliud agentes, aliud simulantes, perfidi, improbi, malitiosi sunt, id. Off. 3, 14, 60.— With gen. (poet.): gens perfida pacti, faithless, Sil. 1, 5.— Of inanim. and abstr. things (poet.): bella, Sil. 15, 819: nex, effected by treachery, Sen. Agam. 887: arma, Ov. F. 4, 380: verba, id. R. Am. 722.— Adverb.:

perfigo.full: perfīgo, xi, xum, 3, v. a., to pierce through, transfix (only in Lucr.): multa perfigit, 6, 350.—Elsewh. only part. perf., perfixus, a, um, transfixed, pierced: telis pavoris, Lucr. 3, 305: pectus, id. 6, 392; cf. id. 2, 360.

perfines.full: perfines, perfringas, Paul. ex Fest. p. 205 Müll.

perfingo.full: perfingo, ĕre, v. a. per-fingo, to form, represent: VARIOS AVIVM CANTVS, Inscr. Fabr. p. 685.

perfixus.full: per-fixus, a, um, Part. of perfigo, q. v.

perflabilis.full: perflābĭlis, e, adj. perflo. Pass., that can be blown through. Prop. (rare but class.): deos inducere perlucidos et perflabiles, Cic. Div. 2, 17, 40: terra, Sol. 27: lacernae, Amm. 14, 6, 9: locus, exposed to the wind, airy, App. M. 4, p. 150 med.; Pall. 1, 36, 3.— Fig., susceptible (postclass.): gentes perflabiles ad omnes dissensionum motus, Amm. 30, 7, 10.— Act., blowing through: aër, Pall. 1, 6, 9; cf.: domus perflabili tinnitu fidium resultantes, Amm. 14, 6, 18.

perflagitiosus.full: per-flāgĭtĭōsus, a, um, adj., very shameful, very flagitious.—With perturpe, Cic. Cael. 20, 50 (cf. Madv. ad Cic. Fin. p. 410).
perflagitiosus.short: per-flāgĭtĭōsus, a, um, adj., very shameful, very flagitious.—With perturpe, Cic.

perflagratus.full: per-flagrātus, a, um, Part. [flagro], blazing greatly (post-class.), Mart. Cap. 6, § 576 Kopp.

perflamen.full: perflāmen, ĭnis, n. perflo, a blowing through, a blast, breath (eccl. Lat.), Prud. Apoth. 760.

perflatilis.full: perflātĭlis, e, adj. id., that can be blown through, exposed to the wind (postclass.): pator, App. M. 3, p. 137; Ambros. Ep. 30, 5.

perflatio.full: perflātĭo, ōnis, f. id., a blowing through, a blast (post-class.), Mart. Cap. 1, § 26.

perflatus.full: perflātus, ūs, m. id., a blowing through, a draught of air: venti, Vitr. 4, 7, 4.—Concr., a wind, breeze (post-Aug.): ut perflatus aliquis accedat, Cels. 3, 19: loca perflatum non habentia, Plin. 18, 17, 44, § 154: ulmus in perflatu firma, id. 16, 40, 79, § 218.—In plur., Col. 1, 5, 8; Plin. 17, 19, 31, § 140.

perfletus.full: per-flētus, a, um, Part. [fleo], in reflex. sense. having bewailed her case to excess (post-class.): diutius usu perfleta (i. e. quae fleverat ex more), App. M. 2, p. 125.

perflo.full: per-flo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. and n., to blow through or over (not in Cæs.). Act.: cum venti nubila perflant, Lucr. 6, 132; cf. id. 6, 136, and Ov. R. Am. 369: unde (nubilarium) commodissime perflari possit, Varr. R. R. 1, 13: venti terras turbine perflant, Verg. A. 1, 83: colles, qui cum perflantur ipsi, tum adferunt umbram vallibus, Cic. Rep. 2, 6, 11: granaria perflari undique malunt, Plin. 18, 30, 73, § 302: murmura conchā, to sound by blowing through, Luc. 9, 348: perflata est terra austro,

perfluctuo.full: per-fluctŭo, āre, v. a., to flow through, to swarm over (poet.): animantum copia perfluctuat artus, Lucr. 3, 721.

perfluo.full: per-flŭo, xi, 3, v. a. and n. Act., to flow or run through (post-class.): pluvialibus nimbis perfluuntur, Arn. 6, 191.— Neutr. Lit. To flow or run through (poet. and in post-Aug. prose): per colum vina videmus Perfluere, Lucr. 2, 392; Petr. 23.— In gen., to flow: quasi in vas commoda perfluere, Lucr. 3, 937: Belus amnis in mare perfluens, Plin. 36, 26, 65, § 190.— To drip with any thing (postclass.): sudore perfluere, App. M. 1, p. 108, 1.— Of long garments, to flow or float (post-class.), App.

perfluus.full: perflŭus, a, um, adj. perfluo, flowing, undulating.—Transf., effeminate, wanton (post-class.): incessus, App. M. 11, p. 260, 36.

perfoco.full: perfōco, āre, v. a. per-fauces, to stifle, suffocate (post-class.): partum, Dig. 25, 3, 4 (al. praefocat).

perfodio.full: per-fŏdĭo, fōdi (perfodīvi, Plaut. Mil. 2, 1, 64 Ritschl N. cr.), fossum, 3, v. a. To dig through, to pierce through, transfix (class.): parietes, Plaut. As. 3, 2, 17: parietem, id. l. l.; Cic. Vatin. 5, 11; Vulg. Matt. 24, 43: montem, Varr. R. R. 3, 17, 9: Athone perfosso, Cic. Fin. 2, 34, 112: thorax perfossus, Verg. A. 11, 10: pectus, Plin. Ep. 3, 16, 6: pectora, Stat. Th. 9, 522: spinā argenteā dentes, to pick, Petr. 33.—Hence, To break into: perfodit in tenebris domos, Vulg. Job, 24, 16; id

perfoederatus.full: perfoedĕrātus, a, um, Part. [perfoedero], strongly leagued together, Not. Tir. p. 71.

perforaculum.full: perfŏrācŭlum, i, n. perforo, a borer, an auger or gimlet (post-class.), Arn. 6, 200; cf. perforaculum, τρύπανον, τέρετρον, Gloss. Philox.

performido.full: per-formīdo, no perf., ātum, 1, v. a., to fear greatly, Not. Tir. p. 71.

performidolosus.full: per-formīdŏlōsus, a, um, adj., very fearful (post-class.), Aur. Vict. Caes. 4.
performidolosus.short: per-formīdŏlōsus, a, um, adj., very fearful (post-class.), Aur.

performo.full: per-formo, 1, v. a., to form thoroughly, to form (eccl. Lat.): ad malum performantur (al. praeformantur), Tert. Apol. 1.

perforo.full: per-fŏro, āvi, ātum, 1 (in tmesi: perque forare, Lucr. 5, 126, 8), v. a., to bore through, pierce through, perforate. Lit. (class.; syn. terebro): navem, Cic. ap. Quint. 8, 6, 47: perforare ac demergere triremem, Auct. B. Alex. 25: lacernam lanceā, Vell. 2, 80, 3: duo pectora uno ictu, Ov. M. 12, 377: ense latus, id. Tr. 3, 9, 26: gladio latus, Vulg. Judith, 13, 28: Stabianum, to cut through for the sake of a prospect, Cic. Fam. 7, 1, 1: duo lumina perforata, perforated, made by boring, id. N. D
perforo.short: per-fŏro, āvi, ātum, 1 (in tmesi: perque forare, Lucr.

perfortiter.full: per-fortĭter, adv., very bravely (poet.), Ter. Ad. 4, 2, 28.

perfossio.full: perfossĭo, ōnis, f. perfodio, a digging through, perforation: perfossio, διορυγή, διορυγμός, Gloss. Philox.

perfosso.full: perfosso, āre, 1, v. a. id., to dig through: perfosso, διορύσσω, Gloss. Gr. Lat.

perfossor.full: perfossor, ōris, m. id., a digger through, breaker through (ante- and post-class.): perfossor parietum, a house-breaker, Plaut. Ps. 4, 2, 23; App. Mag. p. 295, 16.

perfossura.full: perfossūra, ae, f. id., a digging through: perfossura, διορυγή, Gloss. Gr. Lat.

perfossus.full: per-fossus, a, um, Part., from perfodio.
perfossus.short: per-fossus, a, um, Part., from perfodio.

perfoveo.full: per-fŏvĕo, 2, v. a., to warm through (post-class.): perfovet aegros, Sedul. 4, 25; cf. Not. Tir. p. 134.

perfractus.full: per-fractus, a, um, Part., from perfringo.
perfractus.short: per-fractus, a, um, Part., from perfringo.

perfragrans.full: per-fragrans, antis, adj., very fragrant (late Lat.), Fulg. Serm. 27.
perfragrans.short: per-fragrans, antis, adj., very fragrant (late Lat.), Fulg.

perfremo.full: per-frĕmo, ui, 1, v. n., to roar or snort along (ante-class.): perfremunt delphini, Att. ap. Cic. N. D. 2, 35, 89.

perfrequens.full: per-frĕquens, entis, adj., very crowded, much frequented: emporium, Liv. 41, 1.
perfrequens.short: per-frĕquens, entis, adj., very crowded, much frequented: emporium, Liv.

perfreto.full: perfrĕto, āvi, 1, v. n. per-fretum, to sail over (post-class.), Sol. 27.

perfrico.full: per-frĭco, cui, cātum, and ctum, āre, v. a. Lit., to rub all over, to rub or scratch (class.): caput unguento, Cic. Verr. 2, 3, 25, § 62: totam faciem fuligine, Petr. 22; Cels. 3, 14: totum corpus, id. 1, 3; Plin. 28, 12, 51, § 190: perfrictis oculis, App. M. 2, p. 125, 28: dentes, Ov. A. A. 3, 216: caput sinistrā manu perfricans, scratching his head, Cic. Pis. 25, 61.— Transf.: frontem, faciem, os, to rub one's forehead or face, in order to make one's blushes disappear; hence, to lay aside all
perfrico.short: per-frĭco, cui, cātum, and ctum, āre, v.

perfrictio1.full: perfrictĭo, ōnis, f. perfrigesco, a catching cold, a violent cold (post-Aug.), Plin. 20, 14, 55, § 156.—In plur., Plin. 26, 12, 76, § 124 al.; Scrib. Comp. 57, 257.

perfrictio2.full: perfrictĭo, ōnis, f. perfrico, a rubbing, abrasion (post-Aug.), Veg. 1, 35, 1; 1, 38, 3.—Plur.: perfrictionibus cum oleo mederi, Plin. 21, 18, 69, § 116 (but perh. the same word as the preced. in the same meaning).

perfrictiuncula.full: perfrictĭuncŭla, ae, f. dim. 1. perfrictio, a slight cold, M. Aur. ap. Front. Ep. ad M. Caes. 4, 6.

perfrictus.full: perfrictus, a, um, Part., from perfrico.
perfrictus.short: perfrictus, a, um, Part., from perfrico.

perfrigefacio.full: perfrīgĕfăcĭo, ĕre, v. a. per-frigefacto, to make very cold, to benumb: mihi perfrigefacit cor Surus, strikes a chill to my heart, makes me shudder with fear, Plaut. Ps. 4, 7, 117.

perfrigeo.full: per-frīgĕo, ēre, v. n., to take cold: perfrigeo, καταψύχω, Gloss. Philox.

perfrigero.full: per-frīgĕro, no perf., ātum, 1, v. a., to make cold, to cool off, to let grow cold (postclass.), Scrib. Comp. 271; Not. Tir. p. 113.

perfrigesco.full: per-frīgesco, frixi, 3, v. inch. n. Lit., to grow very cold, to catch cold: ne canes perfrigescant, Varr. R. R. 2, 9, 13; Plin. 31, 6, 33, § 66: ei, qui perfrixit, opus est in laconico sedere, donec insudet, Cels. 1, 3: si perfrixit, cantat bene, Juv. 7, 194. — Trop. (post-class.), M. Aur. ap. Front. Ep. ad M. Caes. 4, 5.

perfrigidus.full: per-frīgĭdus, a, um, adj., very cold: tempestas, Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 40, § 86: vinum, Cels. 1, 3; 4, 5.
perfrigidus.short: per-frīgĭdus, a, um, adj., very cold: tempestas, Cic.

perfringo.full: perfringo, frēgi, fractum, 3, v. a. perfrango, to break through, to break or dash in pieces, to shiver, shatter (class.). Lit. In gen.: elephanto pugno perfregisti bracchium, Plaut. Mil. 1, 1, 26: jumenta ingredientia nivem ... jactandis gravius in connitendo ungulis penitus perfringebant, broke through, Liv. 21, 36, 8: saxo perfracto capite, his skull fractured by a stroke of a stone, id. 4, 28 fin.: tempora fulvo protecta capillo, Ov. M. 12, 274: perfracto saxo sortes erupisse, Cic. Div. 2, 41

perfrio.full: per-frĭo, āre, v. a., to rub to pieces, to crumble up (post-Aug.): bacas myrti, Col. 12, 38, 5.

perfrivolus.full: per-frīvŏlus, a, um, adj., very worthless, very frivolous (post-class.), Vop. Aur. 6.
perfrivolus.short: per-frīvŏlus, a, um, adj., very worthless, very frivolous (post-class.), Vop.

perfructio.full: per-fructĭo or perfruĭtĭo, ōnis, f. perfruor, complete enjoyment or fruition (eccl. Lat.): perfructio summi et veri boni, Aug. Quant. Anim. 33: sine perfruitione, id. Trin. 6, 10.

perfructus.full: per-fructus, a, um, Part., from perfruor.
perfructus.short: per-fructus, a, um, Part., from perfruor.

perfruor.full: per-frŭor, ctus, 3, v. dep. Lit., to enjoy fully or thoroughly (class.). With abl.: his ego rebus pascor, his delector, his perfruor, Cic. Pis. 20, 45: laetitiā, id. Cat. 1, 10, 25: salvā re publicā, id. ib. 4, 6, 4: sapientiae laude, id. Brut. 2, 9: vitā modicā, id. Leg. 1, 21, 56: otio, id. Fam. 7, 1, 1: recordatione urbis, Vell. 2, 101, 3 al.: amoenitate summā perfructus est, Cic. Hort. p. 484 Orell.— In pass.: ad perfruendas voluptates, Cic. Off. 1, 8, 25.— Transf., to fulfil, perform (poet.

perfuga.full: perfŭga, ae, m. perfugio, a deserter to the enemy (class.): perfugam Gallus Aelius ait, qui liber aut servus aut hostis suā voluntate ad hostes transierit: qui idem dicitur transfuga. Quamquam sunt, qui credant, perfugam esse, non tam qui alios fugiat, quam qui ob spem commodorum ad quempiam perfugiat, Fest. p. 214 Müll.: iste, qui initio proditor fuit, deinde perfuga, Cic. Rosc. Am. 40, 117; Crass. ap. Cic. Or. 66, 223; Caes. B. G. 3, 18: perfuga ab eo (Pyrrho) venit in castra Fabricii, Cic. Of

perfugio.full: per-fŭgĭo, fūgi, 3, v. n., to flee to a place for refuge. Lit. In gen. (rare; ap. Cic. Pis. 36, 89, profugisti is the correct reading.; cf. confugio): ad aliquem, Liv. 2, 9: Corinthum, Nep. Dion. 5, 1: Bactra, Curt. 6, 6, 22: ad tribunal, Tac. A. 1, 32: in Capitolium, id. ib. 3, 36.— In partic., to go over or desert to the enemy (class.): nemo a Caesare ad Pompeium transierat, cum paene cotidie a Pompeio ad Caesarem perfugerent, Caes. B. C. 3, 61; Cic. Balb. 9, 24: servos, qui ad eos perfugissen

perfugium.full: perfŭgĭum, ii, n. perfugio, a place to flee to, a shelter, asylum, refuge (class.): perfugi sibi copiam comparare, Plaut. Cas. 3, 5, 2: si unum ostium obsideatur, aliud perfugium petat, id. Truc. 4, 4, 17 Bothe: pedibus perfugium peperit, ran off, escaped, id. Cist. 1, 3, 13: cum propter siccitates paludum, quo se reciperent, non haberent, quo perfugio superiore anno fuerant usi, Caes. B. G. 4, 38: portum ac perfugium esse, Cic. Clu. 3, 7: perfugium et praesidium salutis, id. Rab. Perd. 2, 4: pe

perfulcio.full: per-fulcĭo, fulsi, 4, v. a., to prop up, to sustain, support (post-class.): eloquio perfulcire senatum (al. permulcire), Auct. Pan. ad Pis. 86: perfulsit, Not. Tir. p. 117.

perfulgerat.full: per-fulgĕrat (fulgŭrat), impers., it flashes or gleams brightly, Not. Tir. p. 118.
perfulgerat.short: per-fulgĕrat (fulgŭrat), impers., it flashes or gleams brightly, Not.

perfunctio.full: perfunctĭo, ōnis, f. perfungor, a performing, discharging of an office (class.): honorum, Cic. de Or. 3, 2, 7: laborum, an undergoing, enduring (along with perpessio dolorum), id. Fin. 1, 15, 49.—Of things: annua fertur ei totius spatii esse perfunctio, Ambros. Hexaëm. 4, 5, 24.

perfunctorius.full: perfunctōrĭus, a, um, adj. perfunctus; despatched, i. e., done in a careless or superficial manner, slight, careless, negligent, perfunctory (jurid. Lat.): examinatio, Nov. Val. 3, Postul. 2, 11, c. l. § 1: genitus, Ambros. in Psa. 37, § 37.—Adv.: per-functōrĭē, slightly, carelessly, negligently, perfunctorily (late Lat.): me coepit non perfunctorie verberare, Petr. 11: facere aliquid, Cod. Th. 12, 3, 2; cf. ib. 14, 9, 1.

perfunctus.full: perfunctus, a, um, Part., from perfungor.
perfunctus.short: perfunctus, a, um, Part., from perfungor.

perfundo.full: per-fundo, fūdi, fūsum, 3, v. a., to pour over, to wet, moisten, bedew, besprinkle (class.; syn.: umecto, aspergo, imbuo). Lit.: aquā ferventi Philodamus perfunditur, Cic. Verr. 2, 1, 26, § 67: fluviis pecus, Verg. G. 3, 445: greges flumine, id. ib. 2, 147: perfusus liquidis odoribus, Hor. C. 1, 5, 2: postquam perfusus est, had bathed, Auct. Her. 4, 10, 14: panis perfusus aquā frigidā, Suet. Aug. 77: pisces olivo, Hor. S. 2, 4, 50: aliquem lacrimis, Ov. H. 11, 115; so, poet.: Aurorae lacrimis pe

perfungor.full: per-fungor, functus, v. dep. n. Lit., to fulfil, perform, discharge (class.). With abl.: munere quodam necessitatis, et gravi opere perfungimur, Cic. Sen. 21, 77: honoribus amplissimis et laboribus maximis, id. Fam. 1, 8, 3: rei publicae muneribus, id. de Or. 1, 45, 199: rebus amplissimis, id. Brut. 2, 8.— With acc. (post-Aug.): onera quaestoria perfunctus est, Front. Ep. ad Verum, 7.— Transf. To go through, undergo, endure; to get through with, get rid of. With abl.: pericula, quibus nos perfun

perfuro.full: per-fŭro, 3, v. a. and n., to rage through, run furiously through (poet.) Act.: Eoas domos, Stat. Th. 4, 388.— Neutr., to rage furiously, to rage on: incensus et ipse Perfurit, Verg. A. 9, 343: ita perfurit acri Cum fremitu ventus, Lucr. 1, 275.

perfuse.full: perfūsē, adv. perfundo, profusely: perfuse atque abunde sparsa vasa, Sisenn. ap. Non. 516, 31 (al. profuse).

perfusio.full: per-fūsĭo, ōnis, f. id.. In gen., a pouring over or upon, a wetting, moistening (post-Aug.). perfusio corporis ex aquā calidā, Cels. 4, 8; Plin. 18, 7, 14, § 74.—In plur.: alarum perfusiones, Plin. 23, 9, 82, § 164.— Esp., baptism, Lact. 4, 15, 1.

perfusor.full: perfūsor, ōris, m. id., one who pours water over another, a bath-servant, who poured water over the bathers (cf. Cels. 6, 24; Suet. Aug. 82), Inscr. Pompei. ap. Bullet. Napolit. II. 1843, p. 3, and v. Avellino, ib. p. 67; cf.: perfusor, περιχύτης, προσχύτης, Gloss. Cyrill.

perfusorius.full: perfūsōrĭus, a, um, adj. perfundo, merely wetting or moistening; hence, Slight, superficial (post-Aug.): tenuis et perfusoria voluptas, Sen. Ep. 23, 4.— Disturbing, wrongful (post-Aug.): assertio, Suet. Dom. 8.—Adv.: perfūsōrĭē, slightly, superficially, cursorily, indefinitely (post-class.): perfusorie dicere, aut denuntiare, Dig. 43, 24, 5: dicere, ib. 21, 2, 69.

perfusus.full: perfūsus, a, um, Part., from perfundo.
perfusus.short: perfūsus, a, um, Part., from perfundo.

pergama.full: Pergăma, ōrum, or Pergămum (Pergămon), i, n., = Πέργαμα or Πέργαμον, the citadel of Troy, poet. for Troy: Pergama, Liv. Andron. ap. Non. 512, 32 (Trag. Rel. v. 2 Rib.); Enn. ap. Macr. S. 6, 2 (Trag. v. 98 Vahl.); Lucr. 1, 476; Verg. A. 1, 651; 2, 177; 571; Ov. M. 12, 445; 591; 13, 169 et saep.: Pergamo, Enn. ap. Cic. Div. 1, 21, 42; Pac. ap. Non. 280, 27: Pergamum (acc.), Poët. ap. Auct. Her. 2, 26, 42; Plaut. Bacch. 4, 9, 2; (nom.) Sen. Agam. 419; id. Troad. 14: Pergamon, Auct. Aetn. 18.— Lavin
pergama.short: Pergăma, ōrum, or Pergămum (Pergămon), i, n., = Πέργαμα or Πέργαμον, the citadel of Troy, poet.

pergameus.full: Pergămĕus, a, um, v. Pergama, II., and 2. Pergamum, B.

pergamis.full: Pergămis, ĭdis, f., a city in Epirus, Varr. R. R. 2, 2.
pergamis.short: Pergămis, ĭdis, f., a city in Epirus, Varr.

pergamum2.full: Pergămum, i, n., a city in Mysia, on the Caystrus, the residence of the Attalian kings, with a celebrated library, now Bergamo, Plin. 5, 30, 33, § 126; Liv. 29, 11; 37, 19; 20 al.—Hence, Pergămēnus, a, um, adj., = Περγαμηνός, of or belonging to Pergamum in Mysia, Pergamean: Pergamena civitas, Cic. Fl. 30, 64: ager, Liv. 37, 21: naves, Nep. Hann. 11, 5.—Pergamena charta, or as subst.: Pergămēna (collat. form Pergămīna, Not. Tir. p. 124), ae, f., parchment, a material for writing on, prepared from
pergamum2.short: Pergămum, i, n., a city in Mysia, on the Caystrus, the residence of the Attalian kings, with a celebrated library, now Bergamo, Plin.

pergamum3.full: Pergămum, i, n., a city in Creta, founded by Agamemnon (or acc. to Verg. A. 3, 133, by Æneas), Vell. 1, 1, 2.
pergamum3.short: Pergămum, i, n., a city in Creta, founded by Agamemnon (or acc.

pergaudeo.full: per-gaudĕo, ēre, v. n., to rejoice greatly: Trebonium meum a te amari pergaudeo, Cic. Q. Fr. 3, 1, 3, § 9.

pergenitus.full: per-gĕnĭtus, a, um, adj., engendered, produced (late Lat.), Pelag. Vet. 11.
pergenitus.short: per-gĕnĭtus, a, um, adj., engendered, produced (late Lat.), Pelag.

perglisco.full: per-glisco, 3, v. n., to become quite fat (post-Aug.): gallina pergliscit, Col. 8, 7, 4.

pergnarus.full: per-gnārus, a, um, adj., that has a thorough knowledge of, that is very experienced, well versed in any thing (very rare): locorum pergnari, Sall. Fragm. ap. Non. 554, 21: colendi, App. Mag. p. 290, 34.
pergnarus.short: per-gnārus, a, um, adj., that has a thorough knowledge of, that is very experienced, well versed in any thing (very rare): locorum pergnari, Sall.

pergo.full: pergo, perrexi, perrectum, 3, v. a. and n. per-rego. Act. In gen., to go on, continue, proceed with any thing (esp. a motion), to pursue with energy, prosecute vigorously (v. Mütz. ad Curt. 3, 8, 7; rare, and in Cic. only with an obj.-clause). With acc.: pergam, quo coepi, hoc iter, Ter. Hec. 1, 2, 119: iter, Sall. J. 79, 5; Auct. B. Afr. 69; Tac. A. 4, 20; 3, 66.— With an obj.-clause: confestim ad eum ire perreximus, Cic. Ac. 1, 1, 1: perge igitur ordine quattuor mihi istas partes explicare, pr

pergracilis.full: per-grăcĭlis, e, adj., very slender (post-Aug.): caulis, Plin. 25, 13, 101, § 159.
pergracilis.short: per-grăcĭlis, e, adj., very slender (post-Aug.): caulis, Plin.

pergraecor.full: per-graecor, āri, v. dep. n., to live just like the Greeks, to play the Greek, i. e. to revel, carouse (ante-class.): ut cum solo pergraecetur milite, Plaut. Truc. 1, 1, 69; id. Most. 1, 1, 21; 64: pergraecari est epulis et potationibus inservire, Paul. ex Fest. p. 215 Müll.

pergrandesco.full: per-grandesco, ĕre, v. inch. n., to grow very large (ante-class.), Att. ap. Non. 115, 9.

pergrandis.full: per-grandis, e, adj., very large, very great (rare but class.): gemma, Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 27, § 62: vectigal, id. Agr. 1, 4, 9: lucrum, Plaut. Pers. 4, 3, 23: pergrandis natu, very old, very aged, Liv. 29, 29, 6: lapis, Vulg. Josue, 24, 26.
pergrandis.short: per-grandis, e, adj., very large, very great (rare but class.): gemma, Cic.

pergraphicus.full: per-grăphĭcus, a, um, adj., very skilful, very artful (ante-class.): sycophanta, Plaut. Trin. 5, 2, 15.
pergraphicus.short: per-grăphĭcus, a, um, adj., very skilful, very artful (ante-class.): sycophanta, Plaut.

pergratus.full: per-grātus, a, um, adj., very agreeable, very pleasant (class.): litterae, Cic. Q. Fr. 3, 1, 6, § 23: id mihi pergratum perque jucundum erit, id. ib. 3, 1, 4, § 12; id. Att. 10, 4, 1: pergratum mihi feceris, si, you would do me a great pleasure, a great favor, id. Lael. 4, 16.—In tmesi: per mihi, per, inquam, gratum feceris, si, etc., Cic. Att. 1, 20, 7.
pergratus.short: per-grātus, a, um, adj., very agreeable, very pleasant (class.): litterae, Cic.

pergravis.full: per-grăvis, e, adj., very weighty or grave, very important (class.): pergravia (haec), opp. levia, Ter. Hec. 3, 1, 12: testes, Cic. Cael. 26, 63: oratio, id. Sest. 50, 107.— Adv.: pergrăvĭter, very gravely, very seriously (class.): pergraviter offensus, Cic. Att. 1, 10, 2: reprehendere aliquem, id. de Or. 1, 53, 227.
pergravis.short: per-grăvis, e, adj., very weighty or grave, very important (class.): pergravia (haec), opp.

pergula.full: pergŭla, ae, f. pergo; cf. tegula, from tego. A projection or shed in front of a house, used as a booth, stall, shop; of an exchanger, Plin. 21, 3, 6, § 8; of a paintingroom, studio, Plin. 35, 10, 36, § 84; Lucil. ap. Lact. 1, 22.— A shop, Dig. 5, 1, 19.— A school, a lecture-room: mathematici pergula, Suet. Aug. 94: in pergulā docuit, id. Gram. 18: pergulae magistrales, Vop. Sat. 10 fin.—Transf.: cui cedere debeat omnis Pergula, the whole school, all the scholars, Juv. 11, 137.— A brothel, Plaut

pergulana.full: pergŭlāna, vitis pergula, a vine trained over an arbor, Col. 3, 2, 28.
pergulana.short: pergŭlāna, vitis pergula, a vine trained over an arbor, Col.

pergus.full: Pergus, i, m., a lake in Sicily, near the city of Enna, where Pluto is said to have carried off Proserpine, the mod. Lago Pergusa, Ov. M. 5, 386; Claud. Rapt. Pros. 2, 112.
pergus.short: Pergus, i, m., a lake in Sicily, near the city of Enna, where Pluto is said to have carried off Proserpine, the mod.

pergustus.full: per-gustus, ūs, m., taste (late Lat.): severi, Epist. Jud. Minor. Conv. p. 830, t. 41 Migne.
pergustus.short: per-gustus, ūs, m., taste (late Lat.): severi, Epist.

perhaurio.full: pĕr-haurĭo, si, stum, 4, v. a. Lit., to drain completely, to drink up: calicem uno haustu, App. M. 10, p. 246, 39; Tert. ad Nat. 1, 15.— Trop.: auribus perhauriendum'st, Plaut. Mil. 1, 1, 34.

perhaustus.full: pĕrhaustus, a, um, Part., from perhaurio.
perhaustus.short: pĕrhaustus, a, um, Part., from perhaurio.

perhibeo.full: pĕr-hĭbĕo, ui, ĭtum, 2, v. a. habeo, to hold out, extend, present, produce, bestow, grant, give, afford; to attribute, ascribe, assign, etc. In gen. (mostly ante-class. and post-Aug.; cf.: edo, exhibeo): operam rei publicae fortem atque strenuam, Cato ap. Gell. 3, 7, 19: magnanimitatis exemplum, Plin. 7, 25, 26, § 93: testimonium, to bear witness, Varr. R. R. 2, 5, 1; Col. 3, 9; Plin. 7, 30, 31, § 112; 7, 38, 39, § 127: ut testimonium perhiberet de lumine, Vulg. Joan. 1, 8; Aug. Civ. Dei, 10, 2

perhibitus.full: pĕrhĭbĭtus, a, um, Part., from perhibeo.
perhibitus.short: pĕrhĭbĭtus, a, um, Part., from perhibeo.

perhiemo.full: pĕr-hĭĕmo (pĕr-hўĕmo), āre, v. n., to winter, pass the winter; to lie or remain all winter (post-Aug.), Col. 11, 3.

perhonestus.full: pĕr-hŏnestus, a, um, adj., very honorable (post-class.), Arn. 2, 76.
perhonestus.short: pĕr-hŏnestus, a, um, adj., very honorable (post-class.), Arn.

perhonorificus.full: pĕr-hŏnōrĭfĭcus, a, um, adj. That does one much honor, very honorable: con salutatio forensis perhonorifica, Cic. Att. 2. 18, 1: discessus, id. Prov. Cons. 19, 45.— That shows much honor to another, very respectful: collega in me perhonorificus, Cic. Att. 1, 13, 2.—Adv.: pĕrhŏnōrĭfĭcē, very respectfully, Cic. Att. 14, 12, 2.

perhorreo.full: pĕr-horrĕo, ui, 2, v. a., to tremble or shudder greatly at, to have a great horror of any thing (post-class.): horum tela perhorrebimus, Jul. Val. Rer. Gest. Alex. M. 2, 9 Mai.

perhorresco.full: pĕr-horresco, rui, 3, v. inch. n. and a. Neutr., to tremble or shudder greatly (class.): toto corpore perhorresco, Cic. Div. in Caecil. 13, 41: recordatione consulatūs vestri, id. Pis. 20, 45: clamore perhorruit Aetne, trembled, shook, Ov. M. 13, 877: latumque perhorruit aequor (ventorum jactatibus), id. ib. 6, 704.— Act., to shudder greatly at, to have a great horror of any thing (class.): hanc tantam religionem non perhorrescis? Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 35, § 78: vexationem virginum Vestalium perhorre

perhorridus.full: pĕr-horrĭdus, a, um, adj., very dreadful or frightful, most horrid: stagna perhorrida situ, Liv. 22, 16, 4.
perhorridus.short: pĕr-horrĭdus, a, um, adj., very dreadful or frightful, most horrid: stagna perhorrida situ, Liv.

perhumanus.full: pĕr-hūmānus, a, um, adj., very kind, very courteous, very polite (class.): sermo, Cic. Q. Fr. 2, 6, 1: epistula, id. Att. 16, 12. —Adv.: pĕrhūmānĭter, very kindly, very politely: scribere ad aliquem, Cic. Fam. 7, 8, 1.
perhumanus.short: pĕr-hūmānus, a, um, adj., very kind, very courteous, very polite (class.): sermo, Cic.

perialogos.full: Pĕrĭălŏgos, i, m., = περιάλογος, The Very Unreasonable (sc. father), the title of a work by Orbilius, Suet. Gram. 9 dub.
perialogos.short: Pĕrĭălŏgos, i, m., = περιάλογος, The Very Unreasonable (sc.

periambus.full: pĕrĭambus, i, m. A metrical foot, consisting of two short syllaoles; usually called a pyrrhichius, Quint. 9, 4, 80.

periander.full: Pĕrĭander, dri, m., = Περίανδρος, son of Cypselus, a king of Corinth, and one of the seven wise men of Greece, Gell. 16, 19, 4; Aus. Lud. Sept. Sapient. fin.; Hyg. Fab. 221.
periander.short: Pĕrĭander, dri, m., = Περίανδρος, son of Cypselus, a king of Corinth, and one of the seven wise men of Greece, Gell.

periboetos.full: pĕrĭbŏētos, i, m. and f., = περιβόητος, cried up, i. e. celebrated, famous (post-Aug.), Plin. 34, 8, 19, § 69.

peribolus.full: pĕrĭbŏlus, i, m., = περίβολος, the circuit, enclosure: exterior, Vulg. Ezech. 42, 7: sanctorum, id. 1. Macc. 14, 48.
peribolus.short: pĕrĭbŏlus, i, m., = περίβολος, the circuit, enclosure: exterior, Vulg.

peribomius.full: Pĕrĭbōmĭus, i, m., the name of a shameless person, Juv. 2, 16.
peribomius.short: Pĕrĭbōmĭus, i, m., the name of a shameless person, Juv.

pericarpum.full: pĕrĭcarpum, i, n., = περίκαρπον, a kind of bulbous plant, Plin. 25, 10, 82, § 131.
pericarpum.short: pĕrĭcarpum, i, n., = περίκαρπον, a kind of bulbous plant, Plin.

perichristarion.full: pĕrichristārĭon, ii, n., = περίχριστος, a kind of eye-salve, Marc. Emp. 8.
perichristarion.short: pĕrichristārĭon, ii, n., = περίχριστος, a kind of eye-salve, Marc.

perichyte.full: pĕrĭchўtē, ēs, f., = περιχυτή, a kind of gladiatorial combat, an enclosing, enveloping (post-class.), Cod. Just. 3, 43, 3.
perichyte.short: pĕrĭchўtē, ēs, f., = περιχυτή, a kind of gladiatorial combat, an enclosing, enveloping (post-class.), Cod.

pericles.full: Pĕrī^cles, is and i, m., = Περικλῆς, a famous Athenian orator and statesman, Cic. Rep. 1, 16, 25; id. Brut. 15, 59; id. de Or. 3, 34, 137 et saep.; voc. Pericle, id. Off. 1, 40, 144.
pericles.short: Pĕrī^cles, is and i, m., = Περικλῆς, a famous Athenian orator and statesman, Cic.

periclitabundus.full: pĕrīclĭtābundus, a, um, adj. periclitor, trying, testing, making a trial or essay (post-class.). With acc.: puncto pollicis extremam aciem (sagittae) periclitabunda, App. M. 5, p. 168, 34: voluntatem, id. Mag. p. 308, 18.— With gen.: sui, App. M. 3, p. 138, 33.

periclitatio.full: pĕrīclĭtātĭo, ōnis, f. id., a trying, a trial, experiment: aliquid usu et periclitatione percipere, Cic. N. D. 2, 64, 161.

periclitor.full: pĕrīclĭtor, ātus, 1 (periclitatus, in pass. signif.; v. infra fin.), v. dep. a. and n. periculum. Act. In gen., to try, prove, test any thing, to make a trial of, put to the test (class.; syn.: experior, tento): periclitatus animum sum tuum, quid faceres, Plaut. Am 3, 2, 33: an periclitamini Quid animi habeam, id. ib. 2, 2, 57: belli fortunam tentare ac periclitari, Cic. Verr. 2, 5, 50, § 132: omnia, id. Quint. 31, 96: fidem alicujus. Sol. 19: in periclitandis experiundisque pueris, Cic. Div. 2,

periclymenos.full: pĕrī^clўmĕnos or -us, i, m., = περικλύμενος, a climbing plant, the woodbine or honeysuckle, also called clymenus, Plin. 27, 12, 94, § 120.
periclymenos.short: pĕrī^clўmĕnos or -us, i, m., = περικλύμενος, a climbing plant, the woodbine or honeysuckle, also called clymenus, Plin.

periclymenus.full: Pĕrī^clўmĕnus, i, m., = Περικλύμενος, son of Neleus and brother of Nestor, one of the Argonauts, who had received from Neptune the power of changing his shape at pleasure, Ov. M. 12, 556.
periclymenus.short: Pĕrī^clўmĕnus, i, m., = Περικλύμενος, son of Neleus and brother of Nestor, one of the Argonauts, who had received from Neptune the power of changing his shape at pleasure, Ov.

pericope.full: pĕrĭcŏpē, ēs, f., = περικοπή, a section of a book, etc. (eccl. Lat.), Hier. in Joel, 2,
pericope.short: pĕrĭcŏpē, ēs, f., = περικοπή, a section of a book, etc.

periculor.full: pĕrīcŭlor, ātus sum, āri, v. dep. periculum, i. q. periclitor, Cato ap. Fest. p. 242 Müll.

periculosus.full: pĕrīcŭlōsus, a, um, adj. periculum, dangerous, hazardous, perilous (class.): in nosmetipsos periculosi, incurring danger, endangering ourselves, Cic. Att. 13, 27, 1: consuetudo, id. Ac. 2, 21, 68: periculosum et grave bellum, id. Imp. Pomp. 2, 4: periculosum et infestum iter, id. Phil. 12, 10, 25: vulnera, id. ib. 14, 9, 26: curationes, id. Off. 1. 24, 83.—With dat.: populo Romano periculosum, Caes. B. G. 1, 33.—Neutr. in abl. absol.: juxta periculoso, ficta seu vera promeret, since it was equal

periculum.full: pĕrīcŭlum (contr. pĕrīclum, very freq. in the poets, e. g. Plaut. Bacch. 4, 7, 29; Ter. And. 2, 2, 13; 5, 1, 2; 5, 2, 26 al.; Lucr. 1, 580; 2, 5 et saep.; Verg. A. 2, 709; 751; 3, 711 et saep.; Juv. 6, 94), i, n. root, Sanscr. par, pi-par-mi, to conduct, guide; Gr. περάω, to pierce; πόρος. a way through, passage; Lat. porta, portus, ex - perior, per-itus; cf. Germ. fahren, Gefahr, a trial, experiment, attempt, proof, essay (class.; cf. disorimen). Lit.: fac periculum in litteris, Ter. Eun. 3, 2,

peridoneus.full: pĕr-ĭdōnĕus, a, um, adj., very fit, suitable, or proper, very well adapted to any thing (class.). With dat.: locus peridoneus castris, Caes. B. C. 2. 24: visus est peridoneus praeceptor, maxime ad poëticam tendentibus, Suet. Gram. 11: consilia, Tac. A. 4, 12.— With ad: gens ad furta belli peridonea, Sall. Fragm. ap. Non. 310, 15, and ap. Serv. Verg. A. 11, 515.— With qui and subj.: peridoneus maritus matri, cui bono periculo totam domus fortunam concrederet, App. Mag. 72.
peridoneus.short: pĕr-ĭdōnĕus, a, um, adj., very fit, suitable, or proper, very well adapted to any thing (class.).

periegesis.full: Pĕrĭēgēsis, is, f., = Περιήγησις, a leading round to exhibit whatever is worth notice; hence, a geographical description. This term is used as the title of a poem by Avienus.—Hence, pĕrĭēgētĭcus, i, m., the writer of travels: Metrodorus, Lact. ad Stat. Th. 3, 479.
periegesis.short: Pĕrĭēgēsis, is, f., = Περιήγησις, a leading round to exhibit whatever is worth notice;

perileucos.full: pĕrĭleucos, i, f., = περίλευκος (white all round), a precious stone, otherwise unknown, Plin. 37, 10, 66, § 180.
perileucos.short: pĕrĭleucos, i, f., = περίλευκος (white all round), a precious stone, otherwise unknown, Plin.

perilla.full: Pĕrilla, ae, f., a female proper name, Ov. Tr. 3, 7, 1; 2, 437; App. Mag. p. 279, 26.
perilla.short: Pĕrilla, ae, f., a female proper name, Ov.

perillus.full: Pĕrillus, i, m., = Πέριλλος, a famous Athenian worker in metal, who made a brazen bull for the tyrant Phalaris, in which criminals were to be enclosed and roasted to death, and was the first that suffered in this manner, Ov. A. A. 1, 653; Sil. 14, 212; Prop. 2, 25, 12; Plin. 34, 8, 19, § 89.—Hence, Pĕrillēus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Perillus, Perillean (poet.), Ov. Ib. 439.
perillus.short: Pĕrillus, i, m., = Πέριλλος, a famous Athenian worker in metal, who made a brazen bull for the tyrant Phalaris, in which criminals were to be enclosed and roasted to death, and was the first that suffered in this manner, Ov.

perillustris.full: pĕr-illustris, e, adj. Very brilliant, very notable: quod sub ipsā proscriptione perillustre fuit, Nep. Att. 12, 3.— Greatly distinguished, highly honored, Cic. Att. 5, 20, 1.

perimachia.full: pĕrĭmăchĭa, ae, f., = περιμαχία, an attack, hostile assault (post-class.), Sid. Ep. 1, 7.
perimachia.short: pĕrĭmăchĭa, ae, f., = περιμαχία, an attack, hostile assault (post-class.), Sid.

perimbecillus.full: pĕr-imbĕcillus, a, um, adj., very weak or feeble: collum anserum, Varr. R. R. 3, 10, 5: quod quidem est natum perimbecillum est, Cic. Att. 10, 18, 1: verbum, Sulp. Sev. Chron. 2, 17, 3.
perimbecillus.short: pĕr-imbĕcillus, a, um, adj., very weak or feeble: collum anserum, Varr.

perimedeus.full: Pĕrĭmēdēus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to the sorceress Perimede, Perimedean, magical (poet.): gramina, Prop. 2, 4, 8 (18).
perimedeus.short: Pĕrĭmēdēus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to the sorceress Perimede, Perimedean, magical (poet.): gramina, Prop.

perimele.full: Pĕrĭmēlē, ēs, f., a nymph, daughter of Hippodamas, who was changed into the island of the same name, Ov. M. 8, 590.
perimele.short: Pĕrĭmēlē, ēs, f., a nymph, daughter of Hippodamas, who was changed into the island of the same name, Ov.

perimetros.full: pĕrĭmĕtros, i, f., = περίμετρος, a circumference, perimeter, Front. Aquaed. 26; 40; Vitr. 5, 6.
perimetros.short: pĕrĭmĕtros, i, f., = περίμετρος, a circumference, perimeter, Front.

perimo.full: pĕrĭmo (orig. form pĕrĕmo, Cato ap. Fest. p. 217 Müll.), ēmi, emptum (emtum), 3, v. a. per-emo, to take away entirely, to annihilate, extinguish, destroy; to cut off, hinder, prevent. In gen. (class.; syn.: perdo, deleo): penitus materiem omnem, Lucr. 1, 226: sensu perempto, Cic. Tusc. 1, 37, 89: luna subito perempta est, was taken away, i. e. vanished, disappeared, id. poët. Div. 1, 11, 18: divum simulacra peremit fulminis ardor, id. ib. 1, 12, 19: Troja perempta, destroyed, ruined, Verg. A. 5,

perimpeditus.full: pĕr-impĕdītus, a, um, adj., very much obstructed, very difficult to pass: locus, Auct. B. Afr. 58.
perimpeditus.short: pĕr-impĕdītus, a, um, adj., very much obstructed, very difficult to pass: locus, Auct.

perimula.full: Pĕrĭmūla, ae, f., a promontory in India, Plin. 6, 20, 23, § 72.
perimula.short: Pĕrĭmūla, ae, f., a promontory in India, Plin.

perinaeon.full: pĕrĭnaeon and pĕrĭnēon, i, n., = περιναιον, περινεον, the space between the sexual parts and the fundament, the perineum (post-class.), Cael. Aur. Tard. 5, 4, 66; 68; 5, 3, 59.
perinaeon.short: pĕrĭnaeon and pĕrĭnēon, i, n., = περιναιον, περινεον, the space between the sexual parts and the fundament, the perineum (post-class.), Cael.

perincertus.full: pĕr-incertus, a, um, adj., very uncertain, Sall. Fragm. ap. Gell. 18, 4, 4.
perincertus.short: pĕr-incertus, a, um, adj., very uncertain, Sall.

perincommodus.full: pĕr-incommŏdus, a, um, adj., very inconvenient, very troublesome or annoying: alicui, Liv. 37, 41, 3.—Adv.: pĕrin-commŏdē, very inconveniently, very unfortunately: accidit perincommode, quod, etc., Cic. Att. 1, 17, 2.
perincommodus.short: pĕr-incommŏdus, a, um, adj., very inconvenient, very troublesome or annoying: alicui, Liv.

perinconsequens.full: pĕr-inconsĕquens, entis, adj., very inconsequent, very absurd (post-class.): per tmesin, Gell. 14, 1, 10.
perinconsequens.short: pĕr-inconsĕquens, entis, adj., very inconsequent, very absurd (post-class.): per tmesin, Gell.

perinde.full: pĕr-inde, adv., a particle of comparison. in the same manner, just as, quite as, equally; in like manner, just so (class.; cf. proinde, with which it is frequently confounded in MSS. and edd.). In gen.: vivendi artem tantam tamque operosam et perinde fructuosam relinquere, Cic. Fin. 1, 21, 72: si perinde cetera processissent, Liv. 8, 17 fin.: non Pyrrhum, aut Antiochum populo Romano perinde metuendos fuisse, Tac. A. 2, 63: utilissimum munus, sed non perinde populare, Plin. Ep. 1, 8, 12: Mithrida
perinde.short: pĕr-inde, adv., a particle of comparison.

perindigeo.full: pĕr-indĭgĕo, ēre, v. n., to need very much, to be in great need (eccl. Lat.), Tert. adv. Gnost. 13.

perindignus.full: pĕr-indignus, a, um, adj., very unworthy, very unbecoming, Sid. Ep. 4, 4.— Adv.: pĕrindignē, very indignantly (post-Aug.): tulit perindigne actum a senatu, ut, etc., Suet. Tib. 50.
perindignus.short: pĕr-indignus, a, um, adj., very unworthy, very unbecoming, Sid.

perindulgens.full: pĕr-indulgens, entis, adj., very indulgent, very tender: qui perindulgens in patrem, idem acerbe severus in fratrem, Cic. Off. 3, 31, 112.
perindulgens.short: pĕr-indulgens, entis, adj., very indulgent, very tender: qui perindulgens in patrem, idem acerbe severus in fratrem, Cic.

perinfamis.full: pĕr-infāmis, e, adj., very infamous (post-Aug.): vir amore libertinae perinfamis, Suet. Vit. 2.—With gen. denoting on what account, App. M. 3, p. 136, 26.
perinfamis.short: pĕr-infāmis, e, adj., very infamous (post-Aug.): vir amore libertinae perinfamis, Suet.

perinfirmus.full: pĕr-infirmus, a, um, adj., very weak or feeble: si quis perinfirmus est, Cels. 2, 14: sunt enim levia et perinfirma, quae dicebantur a te, Cic. Fin. 2, 16, 53; Cels. 2, 14 fin.
perinfirmus.short: pĕr-infirmus, a, um, adj., very weak or feeble: si quis perinfirmus est, Cels.

peringeniosus.full: pĕr-ingĕnĭōsus, a, um, adj., of good natural abilities, very clever: homines, Cic. Brut. 24, 92.
peringeniosus.short: pĕr-ingĕnĭōsus, a, um, adj., of good natural abilities, very clever: homines, Cic.

peringratus.full: pĕr-ingrātus, a, um, adj., very ungrateful (post-Aug.), Sen. Ep. 98, 11.
peringratus.short: pĕr-ingrātus, a, um, adj., very ungrateful (post-Aug.), Sen.

periniquus.full: pĕr-ĭnīquus, a, um, adj. Very unfair, very unjust: quare videant, ne sit periniquum et non ferendum, Cic. Imp. Pomp. 22, 63.— Very unwilling, very discontented: etsi periniquo patiebar animo, te a me digredi, Cic. Fam. 12, 18, 1.

perinjurius.full: pĕr-injūrĭus, a, um, adj., very unjust, very wrong (ante-class.), Cato ap. Prisc. p. 694 P.—With subject-clause, Min. Fel. 15, 1.
perinjurius.short: pĕr-injūrĭus, a, um, adj., very unjust, very wrong (ante-class.), Cato ap.

perinsignis.full: pĕr-insignis, e, adj., very remarkable, very conspicuous: corporis pravitates, Cic. Leg. 1, 19, 51.
perinsignis.short: pĕr-insignis, e, adj., very remarkable, very conspicuous: corporis pravitates, Cic.

perinsolens.full: pĕr-insŏlens, entis, adj., very unusual, Not. Tir. p. 47.
perinsolens.short: pĕr-insŏlens, entis, adj., very unusual, Not.

perinteger.full: pĕr-intĕger, gra, grum, adj., very honest, very virtuous (post-class.), Gell. 3, 5, 1.
perinteger.short: pĕr-intĕger, gra, grum, adj., very honest, very virtuous (post-class.), Gell.

perinthus.full: Pĕrinthus (-os), i, f., = Πέρινθος, a city of Thrace, afterwards called Heraclea, the modern Erekli, Mel. 2, 2, 6; Plin. 4, 11, 18, § 47; Liv. 33, 30.—Hence, Pĕrin-thĭus, a, um, adj., Perinthian (poet.): Menander fecit Andriam, et Perinthiam, the Perinthian, i. e. a comedy in which one of the principal characters was a girl from Perinthus, Ter. And. prol. 9.
perinthus.short: Pĕrinthus (-os), i, f., = Πέρινθος, a city of Thrace, afterwards called Heraclea, the modern Erekli, Mel.

perinundo.full: pĕr-ĭnundo, āre, v. a., to overflow or inundate completely (poet.), Alcim. 1, 267.

perinungo.full: pĕr-ĭnungo, ĕre, v. a., to anoint all over (ante-class.): tonsas recentes eodem die perinungunt vino et oleo (al. perungunt), Varr. R. R. 2, 11, 7.

perinvisus.full: pĕr-invīsus, a, um, Part. [invideo], much hated, very odious: homo dis ac nobilitati perinvisus, Cic. Cornel. Fragm. fin.; Sulp. Sev. Chron. 1, 32, 3.

perinvitus.full: pĕr-invītus, a, um, adj., very unwilling: ne perinvitus legerem tuas litteras, Cic. Fam. 7, 33, 2 (dub.); Liv. 40, 57, 3.
perinvitus.short: pĕr-invītus, a, um, adj., very unwilling: ne perinvitus legerem tuas litteras, Cic.

periocha.full: Pĕrĭŏcha, ae, f., = Περιοχή, a summary, compendium, the title in the MSS. of the epitomes of the books of Livy; the title of a work by Ausonius.
periocha.short: Pĕrĭŏcha, ae, f., = Περιοχή, a summary, compendium, the title in the MSS.

periodeuta.full: pĕrĭŏdeuta, ae, m., = περιοδευτής, one that goes about, a visitor, Cod. Just. 1, 3, 42.
periodeuta.short: pĕrĭŏdeuta, ae, m., = περιοδευτής, one that goes about, a visitor, Cod.

periodicus.full: pĕrĭŏdĭcus, a, um, adj., = περιοδικός, that returns at stated times, periodical (post-Aug.), Plin. 20, 3, 8, § 15: typi, Cael. Aur. Acut. 1, 14, 110.
periodicus.short: pĕrĭŏdĭcus, a, um, adj., = περιοδικός, that returns at stated times, periodical (post-Aug.), Plin.

periodus.full: pĕrĭŏdus (pĕrĭhŏdus, Fest. p. 217 Müll.), i, f., = περίοδος. A complete sentence, a period: in toto circuitu illo orationis, quem Graeci περίοδον, nos tum ambitum, tum circuitum, tum comprehensionem, aut continuationem, aut circumscriptionem dicimus, Cic. Or. 61, 204; cf. id. Brut. 8, 34; 44, 162; Quint. 9, 4, 14; Plin. Ep. 5, 20, 4.— The circuit of the four Grecian games (the Pythian, Isthmian, Nemean, and Olympian): in gymnicis certaminibus periodon vicisse dicitur, qui Pythia, Isthmia, Nemea,

periosteon.full: pĕrĭostĕon, i, n., = περιόστεον, the membrane which surrounds the bone, Cael. Aur. Tard. 5, 1, 5.
periosteon.short: pĕrĭostĕon, i, n., = περιόστεον, the membrane which surrounds the bone, Cael.

peripateticus.full: Pĕrĭpătētĭcus, a, um, adj., = Περιπατητικός, of or belonging to the Peripatetic (Aristotelian) philosophy, Peripatetic: peripatetica secta, Col. 9, 3, 1: philosophia, Gell. 1, 3, 10: disciplina, id. 19, 5, 2.—As subst.: Pĕrĭpătētĭcus, i, m., a disciple of the Peripatetic school, Gell. 2, 18, 8.— Usually in plur.: Pĕrĭpătētĭci, ōrum, m., philosophers of the Peripatetic (Aristotelian) school, Peripatetics, Cic. Ac. 1, 4, 17; id. Tusc. 4, 3, 6; Col. 1, 1, 7; Varr. R. R. 1, 1, 8. They were so called
peripateticus.short: Pĕrĭpătētĭcus, a, um, adj., = Περιπατητικός, of or belonging to the Peripatetic (Aristotelian) philosophy, Peripatetic: peripatetica secta, Col.

peripetasmata.full: pĕrĭpĕtasmăta, um, n., = περιπετάσματα, coverings, curtains, hangings, carpets (class.; syn.: aulaeum, stragulum, tapes): Attalica peripetasmata, Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 12, § 27: de peripetasmatis, id. ib. 2, 4, 12, § 28.
peripetasmata.short: pĕrĭpĕtasmăta, um, n., = περιπετάσματα, coverings, curtains, hangings, carpets (class.;

periphas.full: Pĕrĭphas, antis, m., = Περίφας. A king of Attica, Ov. M. 7, 400.— One of the companions of Pyrrhus, Verg. A. 2, 476. — One of the Lapithœ, Ov. M. 12, 449.

peripheres.full: pĕrĭphĕrēs, ĕs, = περιφερής, moving around, surrounding (pure Lat. circumstans), Mart. Cap. 9, § 958.
peripheres.short: pĕrĭphĕrēs, ĕs, = περιφερής, moving around, surrounding (pure Lat.

peripheria.full: pĕrĭphĕrīa, ae, f., = περιφέρεια, a circumference, periphery (post-class.), Mart. Cap. 8, § 827 (pure Lat.: linea circumcurrens).
peripheria.short: pĕrĭphĕrīa, ae, f., = περιφέρεια, a circumference, periphery (post-class.), Mart.

periphoretus.full: Pĕrĭphŏrētus, i, m., = περιφόρητος (carried about), an epithet of Artemon (who caused himself to be carried about in a litter), Plin. 34, 8, 19, § 56.
periphoretus.short: Pĕrĭphŏrētus, i, m., = περιφόρητος (carried about), an epithet of Artemon (who caused himself to be carried about in a litter), Plin.

periphrasis.full: pĕriphrăsis, is, f., = περίφρασις, a circumlocution, periphrase (post-Aug.), Suet. Gram. 4; Quint. 8, 3, 53; Gell. 3, 1, 6 (pure Lat.: circuitus eloquendi, ambitus verborum, circumlocutio).
periphrasis.short: pĕriphrăsis, is, f., = περίφρασις, a circumlocution, periphrase (post-Aug.), Suet.

periplus.full: pĕrĭplus, i, m., = περίπλους, a sailing round, circumnavigation, Plin. 7, 48, 48, § 155.
periplus.short: pĕrĭplus, i, m., = περίπλους, a sailing round, circumnavigation, Plin.

peripneumonia.full: pĕrĭpneumŏnĭa, ae, f., = περιπνευμονία, pulmonary consumption, peripneumonia, Cael. Aur. Acut. 2, 25, 140; 2, 26, 142; 2, 27, 143; id. Tard. 3, 1, 4.—Hence, pĕrĭ-pneumŏnĭcus (in a later corrupt form, pĕrĭpleumŏnĭcus, Veg. Vet. 1, 28; and pĕrĭpleumŏnĭăcus, Theod. Prisc. 2, 4), a, um, adj., = περιπνευμονικός, of or belonging to consumption, consumptive, peripneumonic, Cael. Aur. Acut. 2, 14, 93; Plin. 26, 7, 25, § 41 (in Cels. 4, 7, written as Greek). —As subst.: pĕrĭpneumŏnĭcus, i, m., a consumpt
peripneumonia.short: pĕrĭpneumŏnĭa, ae, f., = περιπνευμονία, pulmonary consumption, peripneumonia, Cael.

peripsema.full: pĕripsēma, ătis, n., = περίψημα, that which comes off a thing in cleaning it, offscouring, refuse, filth (post-class.), Tert. Pudic. 14; Vulg. 1 Cor. 4, 13.
peripsema.short: pĕripsēma, ătis, n., = περίψημα, that which comes off a thing in cleaning it, offscouring, refuse, filth (post-class.), Tert.

peripteros.full: pĕriptĕros, on, adj., = περίπτερος, surrounded with a row of columns on the outside: aedes, Vitr. 3, 1; 4, 7.
peripteros.short: pĕriptĕros, on, adj., = περίπτερος, surrounded with a row of columns on the outside: aedes, Vitr.

periratus.full: pĕr-īrātus, a, um, adj., very angry: alicui, Plaut. Truc. 3, 1, 11; Cic. Fam. 9, 6, 3.
periratus.short: pĕr-īrātus, a, um, adj., very angry: alicui, Plaut.

periscelis.full: pĕriscĕlis, ĭdis, f., = περισκελίς, a leg-band, anklet, worn by females: saepe periscelidem raptam sibi flentis, Hor. Ep. 1, 17, 56; v. Orell. ad h. l.; cf. Isid. Orig. 19, 31, 19; Hier. Ep. 64, 10: tortae, Petr. 67, 4; Vulg. Num. 31, 50.
periscelis.short: pĕriscĕlis, ĭdis, f., = περισκελίς, a leg-band, anklet, worn by females: saepe periscelidem raptam sibi flentis, Hor.

periscelium.full: pĕriscĕlĭum, ii, n., = περισκέλιον, i. q. periscelis, an anklet, Tert. Cult. Fem. 13.

perisseuma.full: pĕrisseuma or pĕritteuma, another reading for parapeteuma, v. h. v.
perisseuma.short: pĕrisseuma or pĕritteuma, another reading for parapeteuma, v.

perissochoregia.full: pĕrissŏchŏrēgĭa, ae, f., = περισσοχορηγία, a present over and above, an extra present, Cod. Th. 14, 26, 2.
perissochoregia.short: pĕrissŏchŏrēgĭa, ae, f., = περισσοχορηγία, a present over and above, an extra present, Cod.

perissologia.full: pĕrissŏlŏgĭa, ae, f., = περισσολογία, redundancy of expression, Serv. Verg. A. 1, 658; cf. Quint. 8, 6, 6.
perissologia.short: pĕrissŏlŏgĭa, ae, f., = περισσολογία, redundancy of expression, Serv.

perisson.full: pĕrisson, i, n., = περισσόν, the name of a plant, also called dorycnion, Plin. 21, 31, 105, § 179; App. Herb. 74.
perisson.short: pĕrisson, i, n., = περισσόν, the name of a plant, also called dorycnion, Plin.

peristasis.full: pĕristăsis, is, f., = περίστασις, a subject, theme, Petr. 48, 4.
peristasis.short: pĕristăsis, is, f., = περίστασις, a subject, theme, Petr.

peristereon.full: pĕristĕrĕon, ōnis, and pĕristĕre-os, i, m., = περιστερεών, vervain, peristereon, Plin. 25, 10, 78, § 126; 25, 9, 59, § 105; App. Herb. 3; Cael. Aur. Acut. 3, 17, 160.
peristereon.short: pĕristĕrĕon, ōnis, and pĕristĕre-os, i, m., = περιστερεών, vervain, peristereon, Plin.

peristroma.full: pĕristrōma, ătis, n., = περίστρωμα, a covering, curtain, carpet: Babylonia peristromata, Plaut. Stich. 2, 2, 54; id. Ps. 1, 2, 12: conchyliata peristromata, Cic. Phil. 2, 27, 67.
peristroma.short: pĕristrōma, ătis, n., = περίστρωμα, a covering, curtain, carpet: Babylonia peristromata, Plaut.

peristrophe.full: pĕristrŏphē, ēs, f., = περιστροφή, a turning about, the turning of an opponent's argument against himself (postclass.), Mart. Cap. 5, § 563.
peristrophe.short: pĕristrŏphē, ēs, f., = περιστροφή, a turning about, the turning of an opponent's argument against himself (postclass.), Mart.

peristylium.full: pĕristȳlĭum, ii, n., = περιστύλιον, a place surrounded with columns on the inside, a peristyle, Vitr. 3, 1; 5, 11; Plin. Ep. 10, 70, 3; 10, 71, 1; Suet. Aug. 82; cf. peristylum.
peristylium.short: pĕristȳlĭum, ii, n., = περιστύλιον, a place surrounded with columns on the inside, a peristyle, Vitr.

peristylum.full: pĕristȳlum, i, n., = περίστυλον, the part of a building enclosing the court-yard, surrounded by columns on the inside, Varr. R. R. 3, 5; Cic. Dom. 44, 116; Suet. Aug. 82; Aus. Urb. 5.
peristylum.short: pĕristȳlum, i, n., = περίστυλον, the part of a building enclosing the court-yard, surrounded by columns on the inside, Varr.

perithous.full: Pērīthŏus, i, corrupt form for Pirithous, q. v.
perithous.short: Pērīthŏus, i, corrupt form for Pirithous, q.

peritia.full: pĕrītĭa, ae, f. peritus, experience, knowledge gained by experience, practical knowledge, skill (not in Cic. or Cæs.). With gen. obj.: locorum et militiae, Sall. J. 46, 8: legum, Tac. A. 4, 58: morum, id. ib. 1, 69: futurorum, Suet. Tib. 67: castra metandi, Plin. 18, 6, 7, § 32: gratiae ac voluptatis (conciliandae), Quint. 2, 15, 24: artis pugnae, Vulg. Judith, 5, 27; Gell. 15, 31, 1.— With gen. subj.: arte servi vel peritiā uti, Dig. 7, 1, 27.— Absol.: peritiā et arte praestans, Tac. H. 4, 30:

perito.full: pĕrĭto, āre, a false read. for perit and perlit, Plaut. Capt. 3, 5, 32; Lucr. 3, 710.

peritonaeos.full: pĕrĭtŏnaeos, on, adj., = περιτόναιος, of or belonging to the peritoneum, peritoneal: membrana, Cael. Aur. Tard. 3, 4, 57; 4, 7, 93.
peritonaeos.short: pĕrĭtŏnaeos, on, adj., = περιτόναιος, of or belonging to the peritoneum, peritoneal: membrana, Cael.

peritonaeum.full: pĕrĭtŏnaeum and pĕrĭtŏnēum, i, n., = περιτόναιον and περιτόνειον, the membrane enclosing the intestines contained in the abdomen, the peritoneum, Cael. Aur. Acut. 3, 17 (in Cels. 4, 1, and 7, 4, written as Greek).
peritonaeum.short: pĕrĭtŏnaeum and pĕrĭtŏnēum, i, n., = περιτόναιον and περιτόνειον, the membrane enclosing the intestines contained in the abdomen, the peritoneum, Cael.

peritus.full: pĕrītus, a, um, adj. prop. Part. of perior (in ex-perior); root par-, per-; Gr. περάω; v. periculum, experienced, practised, practically acquainted, skilled, skilful, expert (cf.: gnarus, consultus). Lit. Absol.: nil iam mihi novi Offerri pote, quin sim peritus, Plaut. Pers. 2, 3, 19: doctos homines vel usu peritos, Cic. Off. 1, 41, 147: docti a peritis, id. ib. 3, 3, 15: ab hominibus callidis ac peritis animadversa, id. de Or. 1, 23, 109: decede peritis, Hor. Ep. 2, 2, 213: me peritus discet Ib

perixyomenos.full: pĕrixўŏmĕnos, on, adj., = περιξυόμενος, scraping himself (in the bath), the name of a statue by Antigonus, Plin. 34, 8, 19, § 26.
perixyomenos.short: pĕrixўŏmĕnos, on, adj., = περιξυόμενος, scraping himself (in the bath), the name of a statue by Antigonus, Plin.

perizoma.full: pĕrizōma, ătis, n., = περίζωμα, a girdle, Isid. Orig. 19, 22; Vulg. Gen. 3, 7.
perizoma.short: pĕrizōma, ătis, n., = περίζωμα, a girdle, Isid.

perjeratiuncula.full: perjĕrātĭuncula, ae, f. dim. perjero, a petty perjury: parasiticae, Plaut. Stich. 1, 3, 76.

perjucundus.full: per-jūcundus, a, um, adj., very agreeable, very pleasing: cui quidem litterae tuae perjucundae fuerunt, Cic. Fam. 1, 7, 3: disputatio, id. de Or. 2, 7, 26.—In tmesi: id mihi pergratum perque jucundum erit, Cic. Q. Fr. 3, 1, 4; so, pergrata perque jucunda, id. de Or. 1, 47, 205. —Adv.: per-jūcundē, very agreeably, very pleasantly: versari in aliquā re, Cic. Cael. 11, 25; id. Att. 13, 52, 1.
perjucundus.short: per-jūcundus, a, um, adj., very agreeable, very pleasing: cui quidem litterae tuae perjucundae fuerunt, Cic.

perjuriosus.full: perjūrĭōsus, a, um, adj. perjurium, full of perjury, perjured, perfidious, Plaut. Truc. 1, 2, 52.

perjurium.full: perjūrĭum, ii, n. perjurus, a false oath, perjury. Lit. (class.): perjuri caput, Plaut. Ps. 1, 1, 129: fons viti et perjuri, id. Truc. 2, 7, 50: quod ex animi tui sententiā juraris, id non facere perjurium est, Cic. Off. 3, 29, 108: perjurii poena, id. Leg. 2, 9, 22: sceleratorum hominum perjuria, id. Font. 16, 35: Deum genitor fraudem et perjuria Cercopum exosus, Ov. M. 14, 91; id. F. 5, 681: perjuras merito perjuria fallunt, id. A. A. 1, 657: luimus perjuria Trojae, Verg. G. 1, 502; cf. id. A.

perjurus.full: perjūrus, a, um, adj. per-jus. Lit., who breaks his oath, perjured (class.): quid inter perjurum et mendacem? Cic. Rosc. Com. 16, 46: perjurissimus leno, id. ib. 7, 20: perjura Troja, Verg. A. 5, 811: perjuri arte Sinonis, id. ib. 2, 195: perjuras puellas punire, Prop. 3, 8, 53: perjura fides, Hor. C. 3, 24, 59; Juv. 13, 174.— Transf., in gen., who lies under oath, false, lying (Plautin.), Plaut. Mil. 4, 2, 74. —Comp., Plaut. Mil. 1, 1, 21; id. Trin. 1, 2, 164.—Sup.: perjurissime hominum, Plaut.

perlabor.full: per-lābor, lapsus, 3 (inf. pres. perlabier, Lucr. 5, 766), v. dep. n., to slip or glide through (mostly poet.; perh. Cic. Tusc. 1, 12, 28, is also a poet. reminiscence): isque (aër) ita per nostras acies perlabitur omnes, Lucr. 4, 248; 4, 357; 5, 764 sq.: nulla nec aërias volucris perlabitur auras, Tib. 4, 1, 127; 4, 1, 155: atque rotis summas levibus perlabitur undas, glides along the surface of the waves, Verg. A. 1, 147: ad nos vix tenuis famae perlabitur aura, id. ib. 7, 646; Stat. S. 4, 6,

perlaetus.full: per-laetus, a, um, adj., very joyful or glad, full of joy: supplicatio, Liv. 10, 21.
perlaetus.short: per-laetus, a, um, adj., very joyful or glad, full of joy: supplicatio, Liv.

perlapsus.full: perlapsus, a, um, Part., from perlabor.
perlapsus.short: perlapsus, a, um, Part., from perlabor.

perlate.full: per-lātē adv., very widely, very extensively: perlate patere, Cic. de Or. 2, 4, 17.
perlate.short: per-lātē adv., very widely, very extensively: perlate patere, Cic.

perlateo.full: per-lătĕo, ŭi, ēre, v. n., to lie completely hid, lie hid always, Ov. A. A. 3, 416.

perlatio.full: perlātĭo, ōnis, f. perfero. A bearing away, a conveying, transferring (postclass.), Hyg. Astron. 1 praef.— A bearing, enduring (post-class.): malorum perlatio, Lact. 5, 22, 3.

perlator.full: perlātor, ōris, m. id., a bearer, carrier, conveyer (post-class.): litterarum, Symm. Ep. 5, 28: perlatore capto, Amm. 21, 16, 11; August. Ep. 146 et saep.

perlatrix.full: perlātrix, īcis, f. perlator, she that bears or carries: perlatrices querelarum litterae, Ennod. Ep. 1, 22.

perlatus.full: perlātus, a, um, Part., from perfero.
