perseverus.full: per-sĕvērus, a, um, adj., very strict: imperium, Tac. A. 15, 48.—Adv.: persĕ-vērē, very strictly: inquirere, Plin. Ep. 9, 5, 1.
perseverus.short: per-sĕvērus, a, um, adj., very strict: imperium, Tac.

persia.full: Persĭa, ae, v. Persae, II. A.

persianus.full: Persĭānus, a, um, v. Persius, B.

persibus.full: per-sĭbus, a, um, adj. sibus, callidus sive acutus, Fest. p. 336, very knowing, very acute, Plaut. and Naev. ap. Fest. p. 217 Müll.; cf. Naev. ap. Varr. L. L. 7, § 107 Müll.

persica.full: Persĭca, ōrum, n. v. Persae, II. B. 3.

persiccatus.full: per-siccātus, a, um, adj., quite dried, perfectly dry, Apic. 7, 6.
persiccatus.short: per-siccātus, a, um, adj., quite dried, perfectly dry, Apic.

persiccus.full: per-siccus, a, um, adj., very dry: oculi, Cels. 3, 6, 23: tempus, Fest. s. v. substillum, pp. 306 and 307 Müll.
persiccus.short: per-siccus, a, um, adj., very dry: oculi, Cels.

persice1.full: Persĭcē, adv., v. Persae, II. B. fin.

persice2.full: Persĭcē, ēs, f., v. Persae, II. B. 2.

persicus1.full: Persĭcus, a, um, v. Persae, II. B., and Perses, IV. B.

persideo.full: per-sĭdĕo, sēdi, sessum, 2, v. n. per-sedeo, to continue sitting, remain long sitting anywhere, Plin. 17, 24, 36, § 222; Curt. 9, 9, 23.

persido.full: per-sīdo, sēdi, sessum, 3, v. n., to sink or settle down, to penetrate anywhere (poet.): pestilitas fruges persidit in ipsas, Lucr. 6, 1126; 1, 307: ubi frigidus imber Altius ad vivum persedit, Verg. G. 3, 442.

persigno.full: per-signo, āre, v. a. (extremely rare; not in Cic. or Cæs.). To note down, record: uni dona, Liv. 25, 7, 5.— To mark: notis corpus, Mel. 1, 19, 20; so Firm. Math. 3, 7, 12.

persilio.full: per-sĭlĭo, īre, v. n. 2. salio, to leap through, Not. Tir. p. 146.

persimilis.full: per-sĭmĭlis, e, adj., very like or similar (class.), Cic. Part. Or. 7, 26: statuam istius persimilem deturbant, id. Pis. 38, 93: isti tabulae fore librum Persimilem, cujus, etc., Hor A. P 6 sq.
persimilis.short: per-sĭmĭlis, e, adj., very like or similar (class.), Cic.

persimplex.full: per-simplex, ĭcis, adj., very plain or simple: victus, Tac. A. 15, 45 fin.
persimplex.short: per-simplex, ĭcis, adj., very plain or simple: victus, Tac.

persis.full: Persis, ĭdis, v. Persae, II. A.

persisto.full: per-sisto, stĭti, 3, v. n., to continue steadfastly, to persist (rare): si perstiteris ad corpus ea referre, Cic. Fin. 2, 33, 107 fin.: in impudentiā, Liv. 38, 14, 11: in luxuriā, Treb. Poll. Gall. 4, 2: in oratione persistens cum lacrymis, Vulg. Tob. 3, 11: divulsusque triens prohibet persistere bessem, to remain, permanere, Aus. Ecl. 1, 22.

persites.full: persītes, ae, m., a plant, a species of tithymalus, App. Herb. 108.
persites.short: persītes, ae, m., a plant, a species of tithymalus, App.

persius.full: Persĭus, ĭi, m., a Roman surname. C. Persius, an orator, a contemporary of the Gracchi, Cic. de Or 2, 6, 25; id. Brut. 26, 99; id. Fin. 1, 3, 7.— A. Persius Flaccus, a celebrated satirist of Volaterrœ, in Etruria, who died in the reign of Nero, at the age of twenty-eight, A. D. 62, Mart. 4, 29, 7; Quint. 10, 1, 94.—Hence, Persĭānus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to the poet Persius, Persian: Persianum illud, that passage of Persius, Lact. 2, 2, 18.— A third Persius, otherwise unknown, has given h
persius.short: Persĭus, ĭi, m., a Roman surname.

persolata.full: persōlāta (persoll-), ae, f., a plant, the brown mullen: persolata, quam Graeci arcion vocant (al. persollata), Plin. 25, 9, 66, § 113; 26, 5, 12, § 24 Sillig (Jan, persollata).
persolata.short: persōlāta (persoll-), ae, f., a plant, the brown mullen: persolata, quam Graeci arcion vocant (al.

persolido.full: per-sŏlĭdo, āre, v. a., to make quite solid, Stat. Th. 1, 352.

persolitus.full: per-sŏlĭtus, a, um, adj., very usual, Not. Tir p. 46.
persolitus.short: per-sŏlĭtus, a, um, adj., very usual, Not.

persolla.full: persolla, ae, f. dim. persona, a little mask; hence, as a term of abuse, you little fright! Plaut. Curc. 1, 3, 36.

persolus.full: per-sōlus, a, um, adj., quite alone: oculum effodito persolum mihi, si, etc., my only eye, Plaut. Men. 1, 2, 46.
persolus.short: per-sōlus, a, um, adj., quite alone: oculum effodito persolum mihi, si, etc., my only eye, Plaut.

persoluta.full: persŏlūta, a corrupt read. for pesoluta, Plin. 21, 33, 108, § 184.

persolutus.full: persŏlūtus, a, um, Part., from persolvo.
persolutus.short: persŏlūtus, a, um, Part., from persolvo.

persolvo.full: per-solvo, solvi, sŏlūtum, 3, v. a., to release or discharge completely; acc. to the signif. of the simple verb. To pay, pay out: stipendium militibus, Cic. Att. 5, 14, 1: pecuniam alicui, Tac. A. 1, 37: pecuniam ab aliquo, to pay by a draft on any one, Cic. Fl. 20, 46: aes alienum alienis nominibus suis copiis, to pay the debts of others, Cat. ap. Sall. C. 35, 3; Plin. Ep. 9, 37, 2: legatā cum fide, Suet. Calig. 16: veteranis promissa praemia, id. Aug. 15.— Transf., in gen., to pay, give, show,

persona.full: persōna, ae, f [acc. to Gabius Bassus ap. Gell. 5, 7, 1 sq., from per-sŏno, to sound through, with the second syllable lengthened]. A mask, esp. that used by players, which covered the whole head, and was varied according to the different characters to be represented (syn. larva), Gell. 5, 7, 1: personam tragicam forte vulpis viderat, Phaedr. 1, 7, 1: personam capiti detrahere, Mart. 3, 43, 4: persona adicitur capiti, Plin. 12, 14, 32, § 59. The masks were usually made of clay: cretea persona, L

personalis.full: persōnālis, e, adj. persona, of or belonging to a person, personal (jurid. Lat.): usus, Dig. 8, 3, 37: tale beneficium personale est, ib. 24, 3, 13: actiones, ib. 50, 16, 178.— In gram.: verbum, a personal verb, i.e. a verb which has three persons in each number.—Adv.: persōnālĭter, personally: etiamsi personaliter ignoramus qui sint Lares, etc., Arn. 3, 124: loqui, Salv. Gub. D. 6; Ambros. Spir. Sanc. 3, 11, § 81.— In gram.. dicere, i.e. with a person expressed or implied, Gell. 15, 13, 9: adve

personata.full: persōnāta, ae, f., a kind of large burdock, said to be synonymous with persolata, Col. 6, 17, 1, App. Herb. 36; Plin. 25, 9, 58, § 104; v persolata.
personata.short: persōnāta, ae, f., a kind of large burdock, said to be synonymous with persolata, Col.

personatio.full: persŏnātĭo, ōnis, f. persono, resonance (late Lat.), Cassiod. in Psa. 150, 3.

personative.full: persōnātīvē, adv. persona, personally, Charis. p. 181, 25 Keil.

personatus.full: persōnātus, a, um, adj. id.. Lit., provided with or wearing a mask, masked: Roscius, Cic. de Or. 3, 59, 221: pater, i. e. the father in the play, Hor. S. 1, 4, 56: personata fabula (* the name of a play of Nœvius), v. Fest. p. 217 Müll.; Sen. Ep. 24; Suet. Ner. 21.— Trop., assumed, pretended, counterfeited, fictitious: personatus ambulare, in an assumed character, Cic. Att. 15, 1, 4: personata felicitas, Sen. Ep. 80, 8: personati fastus, affected, Mart. 11, 2, 3.

persono.full: per-sŏno, ŭi, ĭtum, 1 (perf. personavit, App. M. 5, p. 164, 24: personasse, Prud. στεφ. 34 praef.), v. n. and a. Neutr. To sound through and through, to resound: cum domus cantu et cymbalis personaret, Cic. Pis. 10, 22: ut cotidiano cantu vocum et nervorum et tibiarum nocturnisque conviviis tota vicinitas personet, id. Rosc. Am. 46, 134; id. Phil. 2, 41, 105: domus Molossis Personuit canibus, Hor. S. 2, 6, 114: ploratu lamentisque et planctibus tota regia personabat, Curt. 10, 5, 7: ab aetheris

personus.full: per-sŏnus, a, um, adj., resounding, ringing (post-Aug.): Io ovanti persona sistro, Val. Fl. 4, 418: verno persona cantu virgulta, Petr. 120; Mamert. Grat. Act. ad Jul. 10.
personus.short: per-sŏnus, a, um, adj., resounding, ringing (post-Aug.): Io ovanti persona sistro, Val.

persorbeo.full: per-sorbĕo, bui, 2, v. a., to suck or drink up, to absorb: spongiae persorbentes, Plin. 31, 11, 47, § 123; cf. Not. Tir. p. 168.

perspecte.full: perspectē, adv., v. perspicio, P. a. fin.

perspectio.full: perspectĭo, ōnis, f. perspicio, a seeing into, perception (post-class.): rerum caelestium, Lact. 2, 8 fin.; id. Ira Dei, 1, 4: veritatis, Aug. Civ. Dei, 8, 4.

perspecto.full: perspecto, āvi, ātum, 1, v. freq. a. id.. * To look at or behold to the end: quinquennale certamen gymnicum perspectavit, Suet. Aug. 98.— To look through, look all about: otiose perspecta aedis, ut lubet, Plaut. Most. 3, 2, 128.

perspector.full: perspector, ōris, m. id., one who understands, a discerner (eccl. Lat.): mentis perspector Jesus, Juvenc. 2, 275 (al. prospector).

perspectus1.full: perspectus, a, um, Part. and P. a., from perspicio.

perspectus2.full: perspectus, ūs, m. perspicio, a viewing thoroughly, an inspection, Luc. 8, 484 (al. prospectus).

perspeculor.full: per-spĕcŭlor, ātus, 1, v. dep., to examine or explore thoroughly, to reconnoitre well: perspeculatus locorum situs, Suet. Caes. 58: cum de vallo perspecularetur, Auct. B. Afr. 31.

perspergo.full: perspergo, ĕre, v. a. per-spargo, to besprinkle, to wet. Lit.: ligna amureā crudā perspergito, Cato, R. R. 130: unde haustā aquā templum deae perspersum est, Tac. A. 15, 44: Prusiadem urbem perspergit Hylas lacus, Sol. 42, 2.— Trop.: orationem tamquam sale, Cic. de Or. 1, 34, 159.

perspicabilis.full: perspĭcābĭlis, e, adj. perspicio, that may easily be seen, conspicuous (post-class.): urbs, Amm. 14, 8, 3; Aug. Ep. 32 ad Paul.

perspicace.full: perspĭcācē, adv. id., sharp-sightedly, acutely: quam perspicace, Afran. ap. Non. 513, 19, and 515, 31 (Com. Rel. v. 59 Rib.).

perspicacitas.full: perspĭcācĭtas, ātis, f. perspicax, sharp-sightedness, discernment, discrimination: qui nullā perspicacitate, sine innocentium sontiumque differentiā,...damnarunt, Amm. 15, 3, 2; cf.: perspicacitas, τὸ συνοπτικόν, Gloss. Lab.

perspicax.full: perspĭcax, ācis, adj. perspicio, sharp -sighted, penetrating, acute, perspicacious: perspicax prudentia, old poet ap. Cic. Off. 3, 26, 98: homo (with astutus), Ter. Heaut. 5, 1, 1: ad aliquam rem, id. ib. 2, 3, 129: sequemur et id, quod acutum et perspicax naturā est, Cic. Off. 1, 28, 100: ales oculis perspicax, unguibus pertinax, App. de Deo Soc. p. 108 Hildebr.; cf. id. Mag. 53: homo perspicacior Lynceo vel Argo et oculus totus, App. M. 2, p. 124, 38.—Adv.: perspĭcācĭter, acutely, sharp-sighte

perspicibilis.full: perspĭcĭbĭlis, e, adj. id., that may be clearly seen, bright: solis splendor, Vitr. 9, 1, 11.

perspicientia.full: perspĭcĭentĭa, ae, f. id., a full perception or knowledge of a thing: veri, Cic. Off. 1, 5, 15.

perspicio.full: perspĭcĭo, spexi, spectum, 3, v. a., to look or see through, to look into, look at. Lit.: quo non modo non intrari, sed ne perspici quidem posset, Caes. B. G. 2, 17: eas (epistulas) ego oportet perspiciam, corrigam: tum denique edentur, to look through, read through, Cic. Att. 16, 5, 5: ut prae densitate arborum perspici caelum vix posset, to look at the sky, Liv. 40, 22.— Transf., to look closely at, to view, examine, inspect: domum, Cic. Fam. 5, 6, 3: villam, id. Mil. 20, 54: operis perspicien

perspicuitas.full: perspĭcŭĭtas, ātis, f. perspicuus, transparency, clearness. Lit.: vitrea perspicuitas, Plin. 37, 10, 54, § 141; 37, 5, 20, § 79.— Trop., evidentness, clearness, perspicuity: nihil est clarius ἐναργεία, perspicuitatem, aut evidentiam nos, si placet, nominemus, Cic. Ac. 2, 6, 17: perspicuitas argumentatione elevatur, id. N. D. 3, 4, 9: perspicuitas in verbis praecipuam habet proprietatem, Quint. 8, 2, 1.

perspicuus.full: perspĭcŭus, a, um, adj. perspicio, transparent, clear (syn. tralucidus). Lit.: aquae, Ov. M. 5, 588: sal, Plin. 31, 7, 39, § 79: calix, Mart. 4, 86, 2: gemma, id. 8, 68, 5: nives, i.e. crystals, Stat. S. 3, 3, 94.— Trop., evident, clear, manifest, perspicuous (very freq. and class.; syn. evidens): quasi vero hoc perspicuum sit constetque inter omnes, Cic. N. D. 3, 4, 11: quid potest esse tam apertum, tamque perspicuum, id. ib. 2, 2, 4; id. Rosc. Am. 7, 18: adultera tenui veste perspicua, known b

perspiro.full: per-spīro, āre, v. n. To breathe everywhere, Cato, R. R. 157.— To blow constantly: venti perspirantes, Plin. 2, 45, 45, § 116.

persterno.full: per-sterno, strāvi, strātum, 3, v. a., to pave all over, to make quite even or level: viam, Liv 10, 47, 4; Vitr. 7, 1, 7.

perstillo.full: perstillo, āre, v. n., to leak, drip: tecta jugiter perstillantia, Vulg. Prov. 19, 13; 27, 15: domus, id. Ecclus. 11, 18.

perstimulo.full: per-stĭmŭlo, āre, v. a., to stimulate violently, Tac. A. 4, 12 fin.

perstipo.full: per-stīpo, āvi, 1, v. a., to crowd or press together, Cael. Aur. Acut. 3, 8, 93.

persto.full: per-sto, stĭti, stātum (fut. part. perstaturus, Liv. 8, 34, 4), 1, v. n., to stand firmly, continue standing. Lit. (rare): frenatis equis equites diem totum perstabant, Liv. 44, 33 fin.: exercitus a mane usque ad horam X. diei perstiterunt, Auct. B Afr. 61 in limine, Tib. 1, 5, 71.— Transf., to remain steadfast or constant, to last, endure: nihil est toto quod perstet in orbe: cuncta fluunt, Ov. M. 15, 177; id. H. 18, 206: laurea flaminibus, quae toto perstitit anno, Tollitur, id. F. 3, 137: rab

perstratus.full: perstrātus, a, um, Part., from persterno.
perstratus.short: perstrātus, a, um, Part., from persterno.

perstrepo.full: per-strĕpo, ŭi, ĭtum, 3, v. n. and a., to make much noise (poet. and in post-Aug. prose). Neutr., to make a great noise, to resound, echo, ring: abeunt lavatum, perstrepunt, Ter. Eun. 3, 5, 52: tellus perstrepit, Sil. 8, 430: perstrepit rumor in aulā, Stat. Achill. 2, 76: clangor buccinae, Vulg. Exod. 19, 16.— Act. To sound through, make a noise through, to make resound: turba perstrepit aedes, Claud. in Ruf. 1, 213: cubiculum jubilis suis, M. Aur. ap. Front. Ep. ad M. Caesarem, 4, 5 Mai.—In pas

perstrictio.full: perstrictĭo, ōnis, f. perstringo, a rubbing, friction (post-class.), Veg. Vet. 1, 35; so id. ib. 1, 38.— Trop., a verbal attack: de perstrictione diversae partis nihil cavetur, Paul. Sent. 5, 4, 15.

perstrictus.full: perstrictus, a, um, Part., from perstringo.
perstrictus.short: perstrictus, a, um, Part., from perstringo.

perstrido.full: per-strīdo, ĕre, v. a., to roar or whistle through: perstridunt caerula (maria) venti, German. Arat. 1, 6.

perstringo.full: per-stringo, nxi, ctum, 3, v. a. To bind tightly together; to draw together, draw up, contract: vitem, Cato, R. R. 32: stomachus nimio rigore perstrictus, Veg. Vet. 3, 53; Grat. Cyneg. 296.— To graze, graze against a thing. Lit.: femur, Verg. A. 10, 344: solum aratro, to plough slightly, Cic. Agr. 2, 25: portam vomere, to graze against, id. Phil. 2, 40 dub. (al. praestr-).— Transf., To blunt by grazing against, to make dull, to dull: minaci murmure aures, to stun, deafen, Hor. C. 2, 1, 18: juven

perstruo.full: per-strŭo, xi, ctum, 3, v. a., to build completely, build up: parietem in altitudinem, Vitr. 7, 4, 1.— Trop.: falsitatem, Hilar. Op Hist. Fragm. 2, 30.

perstudiosus.full: per-stŭdĭōsus, a, um, adj., very desirous, very fond of any thing: musicorum, Cic. Tusc. 5, 22, 63: litterarum Graecarum, id. Sen. 1 fin.—Adv.: perstŭdĭōsē, very eagerly, very fondly: audire aliquem, Cic. Brut. 56, 207.
perstudiosus.short: per-stŭdĭōsus, a, um, adj., very desirous, very fond of any thing: musicorum, Cic.

persuadeo.full: per-suādĕo, si, sum, 2, v. a., to bring over by talking, to convince of the truth of any thing, to persuade (cf. convinco). In gen., constr. absol., with an obj.-clause and dat., rarely with acc. of the person: oratoris officium est dicere ad persuadendum accommodate, Cic. de Or. 1, 31, 138: imprimis hoc volunt persuadere, non interire animas, Caes. B. G. 6, 14: velim tibi ita persuadeas, me, etc., Cic. Fam. 11, 5, 3: hoc cum mihi non modo confirmasset, sed etiam persuasisset, id. Att. 16, 5, 2:

persuasibilis.full: persuāsĭbĭlis, e, adj. persuadeo, convincing, persuasive (post-Aug.): rhetorice est vis inveniendi omnia in oratione persuasibilia, Quint. 2, 15, 13; so id. 2, 15, 17: humanae sapientiae verba, Vulg. 1 Cor. 2, 4; Hier. Ep. 65, 9.—In sing.: persuasibile, Quint. 2, 15, §§ 16 and 21.—Adv.: persuā-sĭbĭlĭter, convincingly, persuasively: dicere, Cels. ap. Quint. 2, 15, 14; 22.

persuasio.full: persuāsĭo, ōnis, f. id.. Lit., a convincing, persuading, persuasion: dicere apposite ad persuasionem, Cic. Inv. 1, 5, 6: difficilis, Just. 34, 4, 3.— Transf., conviction, persuasion, belief, opinion (postAug.): falsam sibi scientiae persuasionem induerunt, Quint. 1, 1, 8: arrogans de se persuasio, id. 2, 4, 16: persuasionis plenus cuncta fato agi, Suet. Tib. 69: persuasio est, it is a prevalent opinion, Plin. 30, 13, 39, § 115: persuasio durat in magnā parte vulgi, id. 25, 2, 5, § 10.

persuasor.full: persuāsor, ōris, m. persuadeo, a convincer, one who persuades or prevails upon, Mart. Cap. 5, § 467.

persuastrix.full: persuastrix (-itrix), īcis, f. persuasor, she that persuades, a (female) persuader. probripellecebrae et persuastrices, Plaut. Bacch. 5, 2, 47.—Collat. form persuasitrices, Mart. Cap. 5, § 514.

persuasus1.full: persuāsus, a, um, P. a., v. persuadeo fin.

persuasus2.full: persuāsus, ŭs, m. persuadeo, a persuading, persuasion: persuasu servi, Plaut. Ep. Argum. 1: hujus persuasu et inductu, Cic. ap. Quint. 5, 10, 69.

persuavis.full: per-suāvis, e, adj., very sweet, very pleasant, delightful: polus, Jul. Val. Rer. Gest. Alex. M. 3, 30 Mai.—Adv.: persuā-vĭter, very pleasantly, Aug. Music. 4, 13.
persuavis.short: per-suāvis, e, adj., very sweet, very pleasant, delightful: polus, Jul.

persubtilis.full: per-subtīlis, e, adj. Lit., very fine or delicate, very subtle: animus persubtilis atque minutis Perquam corporibus factus, Lucr. 3, 179.— Trop., very ingenious: oratio, Cic. Planc. 24, 58.

persulco.full: per-sulco, no perf., ātum, 1, v. a., to furrow through, to plough up.—Trop.: rugis persulcata genas, Claud. in Ruf. 1, 136.

persultator.full: persultātor, ōris, m. persulto, one who leaps or skips about (post-class.): litoris, Symm. Ep. 6, 23 (22).

persulto.full: per-sulto, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. and n. salto, to leap, skip, or prance about in a place (not in Cic. or Cæs.). Lit. Neutr.: in agro, Liv. 34, 20: solo stabili, id. 44, 9: ante vallum, Tac. A. 4, 47: notis vadis, id. H. 5, 15: super durata glacie stagna, Sen. Prov. 4, 12.— Act., to leap or skip through, to frisk about, range about a place: pecudes persultant pabula, Lucr. 1, 15: captam Italiam, Tac. H. 3, 49: campos exercitu, id. A. 11, 9: maria (Tritonum catervae), App. M. 4, p. 157, 2.— Transf.,

persuo.full: per-sŭo, ĕre, v. a., to sew through, sew up, Not. Tir. p. 136: persuo, διαρράπτω, Gloss. Philox.

pertabesco.full: per-tābesco, bŭi, 3, v. inch. n., to be gradually consumed, to waste away, Auct. Aetn. 472.

pertaedesco.full: pertaedesco, dŭi, 3, v. inch. n. [pertaedet], to become disgusted or wearied with any thing (ante- and post-class.): ne pertaedescat, Cato, R. R. 156: cum jam omnes pertaeduissent, Gell. 1, 2, 6.

pertaedet.full: per-taedet, taesum est, 2 (quidam pertisum volunt: quod consuetudo non probavit, Cic. Or. 48, 159; cf. Fest. pp. 216 sq.; 273, 8 Müll.; also Paul. ex Fest. p. 72, 18 Müll.), v. impers. and n., to be disgusted or wearied with any thing; to feel disgust at, be sick of. With gen.: me sermonis pertaesum est, Plaut. Most. 1, 4, 4: quem pertaesum est esse domi, Lucr. 3, 1061: pertaesum est enim (me) levitatis, Cic. Q. Fr. 1, 2, 2, § 4: pertaesum est vos injuriae, Sall. H. 3, 61, 8 Dietsch: negotii, Ne
pertaedet.short: per-taedet, taesum est, 2 (quidam pertisum volunt: quod consuetudo non probavit, Cic.

pertaesus.full: pertaesus, a, um, Part., from pertaedet.
pertaesus.short: pertaesus, a, um, Part., from pertaedet.

pertango.full: per-tango, ĕre, v. a., to touch all over, i. e. to baste well (post-class.): pullum suo sibi jure, Apic. 6, 9; 8, 8.

pertego.full: per-tĕgo, xi, ctum, 3, v. a., to cover all over (ante-class.). Lit.: villam, Plaut. Rud. 1, 2, 35: Odeum navium malis et antemnis e spoliis Persicis pertexit, Vitr. 5, 9 init. (al. pertexuit): locus pertectus, Cael. Aur. Tard. 1, 1, 18.— Trop.: benefacta benefactis pertegito, ne perpluant, Plaut. Trin. 2, 2, 41.

pertemerarius.full: per-tĕmĕrārĭus, a, um, adj., very rash; in tmesi: cum perabsurdum perque temerarium sit, Cod. Just. 12, 21, 2.
pertemerarius.short: per-tĕmĕrārĭus, a, um, adj., very rash;

pertendo.full: per-tendo, di, sum, and tum, 3, v. a., and n.—Prop., to stretch out, extend hence, transf., * Act., to carry out, go on with, perform any thing: video non licere ut coeperam hoc pertendere, Ter. Heaut. 5, 5, 9.— Neutr. Prop., to strive forward, to push on to a place; hence, to go right on, proceed to (not in Cic. or Cæs.; ap. Cic. Balb. 5, 11, the correct reading is perpendemus): pars maxima Romam pertenderunt, Liv. 5, 8: pertendit ad alteram ripam, Suet. Caes. 32; id. Vit. Plin.; id. Caes. 4.—
pertendo.short: per-tendo, di, sum, and tum, 3, v.

perteneo.full: per-tĕnĕo, ŭi, 2, v. a., to hold constantly, keep hold of, hold fast (late Lat.): utinam (me) pertinuisset, Hier. Ep. 66, n. 13.

pertento.full: per-tento, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a., to feel all over; hence, To prove, try, test any thing. Lit. (very rare): cum utrumque pugionem pertentasset, Tac. H. 2, 49: alta bipenni latera, Petr. poët. 89, v. 24.— Trop. (rare but class.): aliquem, Ter. And. 3, 4, 9: animum cohortis, Tac. H. 1, 29: rem, to consider or weigh well, Cic. Q. Fr. 1, 4, 5: omnia pertento, omnia experior, Plin. Ep. 1, 20, 15: nobilium adulescentium animos, Liv. 2, 3, 6.— To pervade, invade; to seize, affect (poet. and in postAug. p

pertenuis.full: per-tĕnŭis, e, adj., very thin, very small or fine. Lit.: sabulum pertenue, Plin. 18, 6, 7, § 34.— Trop., very slight or slender, very weak: spes salutis, Cic. Fam. 14, 3, 2: discrimen, id. Agr. 2, 32, 87: suspicio, id. Clu. 60, 168: argumentum, Cic. Verr. 1, 6, 17: ars, id. de Or. 1, 23, 107.
pertenuis.short: per-tĕnŭis, e, adj., very thin, very small or fine.

pertepidus.full: per-tĕpĭdus, a, um, adj., very lukewarm, very tepid: aqua, Vop. Carin. 17, 5.
pertepidus.short: per-tĕpĭdus, a, um, adj., very lukewarm, very tepid: aqua, Vop.

perterebro.full: per-tĕrĕbro, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a., to bore through: columnam, Cic. Div. 1, 24, 48: lapis perterebratus, Vitr. 8, 7, 8; Arn. 3, 107.

pertergeo.full: per-tergĕo, tersi, tersum, 2, and per-tergo, ĕre, v. a., to wipe off, wipe dry. Lit.: gausape purpureo mensam pertersit, Hor. S. 2, 8, 11: spongia vasa, Col. 12, 9, 2. —* Transf., to rub or touch against gently: (aër) quasi perterget pupillas, Lucr. 4, 249; so, lux oculos perterget, id. 4, 277 Lachm. N. cr.: nostros oculos perterget longior aura, id. 4, 252.
pertergeo.short: per-tergĕo, tersi, tersum, 2, and per-tergo, ĕre, v.

pertero.full: per-tĕro, no perf., trītum, 3, v. a., to rub, bruise, or pound to pieces: myrti bacam, Col. 12, 38, 7: uva pertrita, id. 8, 5, 21.

perterrefacio.full: perterrĕfăcĭo, fēci, factum, 3, v. a. perterreo-facio, to frighten or terrify thoroughly: Davum, Ter. And. 1, 1, 142.

perterrefactus.full: perterrĕfactus, a, um, Part., from perterrefacio.
perterrefactus.short: perterrĕfactus, a, um, Part., from perterrefacio.

perterreo.full: per-terrĕo, ui, ĭtum, 2, v. a., to frighten or terrify thoroughly: aliquem, Ter. Eun. 5, 3, 13: alios magnitudine poenarum, Caes. B. G. 7, 4; 50: metu perterriti, Cic. Caecin. 10, 26: obstupefactus ac perterritus, id. Cat. 2, 7, 14: maleficii conscientiā perterritus, id. Clu. 13, 38: ossa mea perterrita sunt, Vulg. Job, 4, 14 (but the true read., Cic. Caecin. 13, 37, is proterritus).

perterricrepus.full: perterrĭcrĕpus, a, um, adj. perterreo-crepo, that clatters or rattles most terribly (ante-class.); old poët. ap. Cic. Or. 49, 164: sonitus, Lucr. 6, 129.

perterrito.full: perterrĭto, āre, v. freq. a. perterreo, to frighten or terrify thoroughly (postclass.), Avien. Arat. 1169.

perterritus.full: perterrĭtus, a, um, Part., from perterreo.
perterritus.short: perterrĭtus, a, um, Part., from perterreo.

pertexo.full: per-texo, xui, xtum, 3, v. a. Lit. To weave throughout, weave entirely: palla bysso tenui pertexta, i. e. byssina, App. M. 11, p. 258, 21.— To interweave, i. e. to furnish, decorate, adorn with any thing: Odeum, quod Pericles navium malis et antennis pertexuit, Vitr. 5, 9 init. dub. (al. pertexit).— Trop., to go through with, perform, accomplish: inceptum dictis, Lucr. 6, 42: locum, Cic. Att. 1, 14, 3: pertexe modo quod exorsus es, id. de Or. 2, 33, 145.

pertextus.full: pertextus, a, um, Part., from pertexo.
pertextus.short: pertextus, a, um, Part., from pertexo.

pertica.full: pertĭca, ae, f., a pole, a long staff. In gen.: perticam habere ... quī verberarem asinos, Plaut. As. 3, 2, 43: pertica suspensos portabat longa maniplos, Ov. F. 3, 117; cf. id. Nuc. 68: perticis oleas decutere, Plin. 15, 3, 3, § 11: messis perticis flagellatur, id. 18, 30, 72, § 298; 16, 37, 68, § 174: perticae, quibus araneae deterguntur, Dig. 33, 7, 12: pertica quā stabuli fores oflirmari solebant, App. M. 7, 28, p. 200.— In partic. A set, slip, young tree; of willows, Plin. 17, 20, 32, § 141
pertica.short: pertĭca, ae, f., a pole, a long staff.

perticalis.full: pertĭcālis, e, adj. pertica, that serves for poles or stakes: salix, Col. 4, 31, 2; Plin. 17, 20, 32, § 143.

perticarius.full: pertĭcārĭus, a, um, adj. id., of or belonging to poles: negotians perticarius, Inscr. Marang. Delle Cose Gentil. p. 488.

perticatus.full: pertĭcātus, a, um, adj. id., furnished with or carrying a staff, Mart. 5, 12, 1.

pertimefacio.full: pertĭmĕfăcĭo, fēci, factum, 3, v. a. pertimeo-facio, to put in great fear, to frighten greatly: pertimefactus maerore animi, Pac. ap. Non. 467, 33 (Trag. Rel. p. 96 Rib.): te pertimefacto, Brut. ap. Cic. Fam. 11, 20, 2.

pertimeo.full: per-tĭmĕo, ŭi, 2, v. n., to fear greatly, to be very timid, Lact. 6, 17, 17: non pertimentes ullam perturbationem, Vulg. 1 Pet. 3, 6 (al. praetim).

pertimesco.full: per-tĭmesco, mŭi, 3, v. inch. a. and n., to become very much frightened, to be greatly afraid of any thing, to fear greatly: si tantam religionem non pertimescebas, etc., Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 35, § 78: id vero non mediocriter pertimesco, id. Quint. 1, 1: nomen imperii etiam in levi personā pertimescitur, id. Agr. 2, 17, 45: fames esset pertimescenda, Caes. B. G. 5, 29: non putavi famam inconstantiae mihi pertimescendam, Cic. Fam. 1, 9, 11: ne quid peccasset, pertimescebat, id. Sest. 49, 105: nec ill

pertinacia.full: pertĭnācĭa, ae, f. pertinax, perseverance, constancy, in a good sense; and (more freq.) in a bad sense, obstinacy, pertinacity (syn.: perseverantia, pervicacia): dicitur quom demonstratur in quo non debet pertendi et pertendit, pertinaciam esse; in quo oportet manere, si in eo perstet, perseverantia sit, Varr. L. L. 5, § 2 Müll.; cf.: unicuique virtuti finitimum vitium reperietur, ut pertinacia, quae perseverantiae finitima est, Cic. Inv. 2, 54, 165; v. Att. ap. Non. 432, 32 sq.: certamen instit

pertinax.full: per-tĭnax, ācis, adj. tenax, that holds fast, that clings firmly, very tenacious. Lit. (only poet. and in post-Aug. prose): digitus male pertinax, Hor. C. 1, 9, 24: ales unguibus pertinax, App. Flor. p. 366: tenaxne pater ejus est? Ph. Pater immo edepol pertinax, exceedingly avaricious, Plaut. Capt. 2, 2, 39.— Transf., that lasts long, very durable: spiritus, Plin. 10, 29, 43, § 81: siligo in Allobrogum agro pertinax, id. 18, 8, 20, § 85.— Trop., firm, constant, steadfast, persevering, unyieldin

pertineo.full: per-tĭnĕo, ŭi, 2, v. n. teneo, to stretch out, reach, extend to a place; to arrive at a place (class., esp. in the trop. signif.); constr. with ad and acc., or with advv.; very rarely with in or per and acc.; v. infra. Lit.: aspera arteria ad pulmones usque pertinet, Cic. N. D. 2, 54, 136: venae in omnes partes corporis pertinentes, id. ib. 2, 55, 137: deus pertinens per naturam cujusque rei, etc., id. ib. 2, 28, 71: Belgae pertinent ad inferiorem partem fluminis Rheni, Caes. B. G. 1, 1: rivi, q

pertingo.full: per-tingo, ĕre, v. a. tango, to stretch out, reach, extend to a certain point (rare; not in Cic.; often confounded in MSS. with pertineo). Lit.: collis in immensum pertingens, Sall. J. 48, 3 Dietsch and Kritz: montis Apennini jugum mediā curvaturā prope tangens oras maris Hadriani pertingit circumitionibus contra fretum, Vitr. 2, 10, 1: infortunatam pertingens cespite Trojam, Avien. Descr. Orb. 986: turris, cujus culmen pertingat ad caelum, Vulg. Gen. 11, 4; id. 2 Par. 28, 9 al. (but in Lucr. 4,

pertolero.full: per-tŏlĕro, āvi, 1, v. a., to bear out, endure: tormenta aetatis, Lucr. 5, 316: pertolerarem vitam, Att. Trag. Rel. v. 91 Rib.

pertono.full: per-tŏno, ŭi, 1, v. n. and a., to thunder violently (late Lat.).—Trop.: contra aliquem, to thunder away at any one, Hier. Ep. 53, n. 8: quando vero vox illa pertonuit, id. adv. Helv. 20.—Act., to proclaim aloud, thunder forth, announce: aliquem, Hier. Ep. 61, ad Pammach. 4: gloriam alicujus, Ambros. Serm. Fer. 2, Pentec.

pertorqueo.full: per-torquĕo, ēre, v. a., to twist awry, to distort: ora foedo sapore, Lucr. 2, 401.— To hurl, vent: quam senticosa verba pertorquet, Afran. ap. Fest. p. 339 Müll. and ap. Paul. ex Fest. p. 333 ib. (Com. Rel. v. 1 Rib.).

pertractatio.full: pertractātĭo and pertrectātĭo, ōnis, f. pertracto, a touching; hence trop., A handling: partium aegrarum, Gell. 5, 1, 4.— A handling, i. e. an occupying or busying one's self with any thing, application to any thing: poëtarum, Cic. de Or. 1, 42, 187: rerum publicarum, id. ib. 1, 11, 48.

pertractator.full: pertractātor, ōris, m., a handler (late Lat.), Aug. c. Faust. 3, 2.
pertractator.short: pertractātor, ōris, m., a handler (late Lat.), Aug.

pertracto.full: per-tracto (pertrecto), āvi, ātum, 1, v. a., to touch, feel, handle any thing (class.). Lit.: papillam, Plaut. As. 1, 3, 71: mullos, Cic. Par. 5, 2, 38: bestias manibus, Auct. B. afr. 72: arma, Plin. 25, 6, 30, § 66: caput dormienti, Just. 1, 9, 17: corpus hominis, App. Flor. p. 362.— Trop., to busy or occupy one's self with any thing, to handle, treat, to investigate, study any thing: mentem omni cogitatione pertractans, Cic. Fin. 2, 35, 118: sensus mentesque hominum, id. de Or. 1, 51, 222: nar

pertractus1.full: pertractus, a, um, Part., from pertraho.
pertractus1.short: pertractus, a, um, Part., from pertraho.

pertractus2.full: pertractus, ūs, m. pertraho, delay, duration (post-class.), Tert. Orat. 5.

pertraho.full: per-trăho, xi, ctum, 3, v. a., to draw or drag, to bring or conduct forcibly to a place (not in Cic. or Cæs.). Lit.: aliquem in castra, Liv. 7, 39: ratem ad ripam, id. 21, 28: pertractus ad Vitellium, Tac. H. 2, 72: mulierem Romam ad centumviros, Phaedr. 3, 10, 34: patriam suam in jus, ad aliam civitatem, Val. Max. 5, 3, 3 ext.: aliquem intra moenia vinctum, id. 7, n. 8.— To entice, allure to a place: in locum iniquum pertractus, Liv. 6, 24: hostem ad insidiarum locum, id. 21, 4, 4.— Transf., to

pertralucidus.full: per-trālūcĭdus, a, um, adj., very translucid: charta, Plin. 13, 12, 24, § 79.
pertralucidus.short: per-trālūcĭdus, a, um, adj., very translucid: charta, Plin.

pertranseo.full: per-transĕo, īvi, īre, v. n., to go or pass through (post-Aug.). Lit.: cum viridis aspectus (smaragdi), non pertransit, Plin. 37, 5, 18, § 68: terram, Vulg. Gen. 12, 6 et saep.— Transf. To go or pass by (late Lat.; not in Sen. Ep. 4, 3), Hier. in Isa. 8, 26, v. 19: Levita, cum esset secus locum et videret eum, pertransiit, Vulg. Luc. 10, 32.— To pass away: donec pertranseat indignatio, Vulg. Isa. 26, 20.

pertremisco.full: per-trĕmisco, ĕre, v. inch. a., to tremble greatly at, to be in great fear of (late Lat.); with acc.: manum domini, Hier. in Isa. 4, 10, 4; 3, 7, 2: similem sententiam, Hier. cont. Pelag. 1, 38.

pertrepidus.full: per-trĕpĭdus, a, um, adj., in great alarm or in great haste: senatus pertrepidus in aedem Concordiae concurrit, Capitol. Maxim. et Balb. 1, 1 dub. (Peter, praetrepidus).
pertrepidus.short: per-trĕpĭdus, a, um, adj., in great alarm or in great haste: senatus pertrepidus in aedem Concordiae concurrit, Capitol.

pertribuo.full: per-trĭbŭo, ŭi, 3, v. a., to give: testimonium alicui (al. retribuere), Plin. Ep. 10, 18, 2 (but ap. Plin. Pan. 95 the correct read. is perhibere).

pertricosus.full: per-trīcōsus, a, um, adj., very confused or perplexed, very strange: res pertricosa, Mart. 3, 63, 14 dub. (al. praetricosa).
pertricosus.short: per-trīcōsus, a, um, adj., very confused or perplexed, very strange: res pertricosa, Mart.

pertristis.full: per-tristis, e, adj., very sad or mournful. Lit.: carmen, Cic. poët. Div. 1, 8, 14.— Transf., very austere or morose: patruus, Cic. Cael. 11, 25.
pertristis.short: per-tristis, e, adj., very sad or mournful.

pertritus1.full: pertrītus, a, um, Part., rubbed to pieces; from pertero.
pertritus1.short: pertrītus, a, um, Part., rubbed to pieces;

pertritus2.full: per-trītus, a, um, adj., quite worn out, very hackneyed or common, very trite (post-Aug.): quaestio, Sen. Contr. 7, 18, 7: scio pertritum jam hoc esse, Sen. Ep. 63, 10.
pertritus2.short: per-trītus, a, um, adj., quite worn out, very hackneyed or common, very trite (post-Aug.): quaestio, Sen.

pertrux.full: per-trux, ŭcis, adj., very savage or terrible: bestiae, App. M. 5, p. 166, 22.
pertrux.short: per-trux, ŭcis, adj., very savage or terrible: bestiae, App.

pertumesco.full: per-tŭmesco, mŭi, 3, v. inch. n., to swell up greatly, Not. Tir. p. 115.

pertumidus.full: per-tŭmĭdus, a, um, adj., greatly swelled out: luna (Elm. protumida), App. de Deo Socr. init.
pertumidus.short: per-tŭmĭdus, a, um, adj., greatly swelled out: luna (Elm.

pertumultuose.full: per-tŭmultŭōsē, adv., in a very agitated or tumultuous manner: aliquid nunciare, Cic. Fam. 15, 4, 3.
pertumultuose.short: per-tŭmultŭōsē, adv., in a very agitated or tumultuous manner: aliquid nunciare, Cic.

pertunda.full: Pertunda, ae, f. pertundo, the goddess that presides over the loss of virginity, Arn. 4, 131; Tert. ad Nat. 2, 11; Aug. Civ. Dei, 6, 9.

pertundo.full: per-tundo, tŭdi, tūsum (tussum; pertunsus, Aur. Vict. Epit. 9, 10), 3, v. a., to beat, push, or thrust through, to make a hole through, to bore through, perforate (mostly ante-class.; not in Cic. or Cæs.): latus pertudit hasta, Enn. ap. Prisc. p. 891 P. (Ann. v. 395 Vahl.); cf.: me pertudit in latus, id. ap. Serv. ad Verg. A. 1, 81 (Ann. v. 540 ib.): terebrā vitem, Cato, R. R. 41, 3: calicem per fundum, id. ib. 52, 1: crumenam, Plaut. Ps. 1, 2, 37: guttae saxa pertundunt, Lucr. 4, 1287: tigna te

perturbate.full: perturbātē, adv., v. perturbo, P. a. fin.

perturbatio.full: perturbātĭo, ōnis, f. perturbo, confusion, disorder, disturbance. Lit.: caeli (opp. serenitas), Cic. Div. 2, 45, 94: hostium, Vulg. 2 Macc. 13, 16.— Trop. In gen., political disturbance, disorder, revolution: quid est enim aliud tumultus nisi perturbatio tanta, ut major timor oriatur? Cic. Phil. 8, 1, 3: quantas perturbationes et quantos aestus habet ratio comitiorum? id. Mur. 17, 35: cum enim omnes post interitum Caesaris novarum perturbationum causae quaeri viderentur, id. Fat. 1, 2: videtis,

perturbativus.full: perturbātīvus, a, um, adj. id., causing disturbance, Cassiod.

perturbator.full: perturbātor, ōris, m. id., a disquieter, troubler, disturber (eccl. Lat. for turbator, cf. turbo): ecclesiarum, Sulp. Sev. Hist. Sacr. 2, 49; Ambros. Spirit. Sanc. 3, 17, 121.

perturbatrix.full: perturbātrix, īcis, f. perturbator, she that disquiets or disturbs, Cic. Leg. 1, 13, 39.

perturbatus.full: perturbātus, a, um, Part. and P. a., from perturbo.

perturbidus.full: per-turbĭdus, a, um, adj., very unquiet, full of disturbance: civitas, Vop. Saturn. 7.
perturbidus.short: per-turbĭdus, a, um, adj., very unquiet, full of disturbance: civitas, Vop.

perturbo.full: per-turbo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a., to throw into confusion or disorder, to confuse, disturb (cf.: confundo, misceo). Lit.: omnia, Ter. And. 3, 4, 22: provinciam, Cic. Sull. 20, 56: aetatum ordinem, id. Brut. 62, 223: condiciones pactionesque bellicas perjurio, id. Off. 3, 29, 108: dies intermissus aut nox interposita saepe perturbat omnia, id. Mur. 17, 35: reliquos (milites) incertis ordinibus perturbaverunt, Caes. B. G. 4, 32: aciem, Sall. J. 59, 3: domum, Sen. Thyest. 83.—Pass., Plin. Pan. 76, 8.

perturpis.full: per-turpis, e, adj., very shameful, scandalous, abominable, Cic. Cael. 20, 50
perturpis.short: per-turpis, e, adj., very shameful, scandalous, abominable, Cic.

pertusio.full: pertūsĭo, ōnis, f. pertundo, a perforation (late Lat.), Ps. Soran. Quu. Medic. 230.

pertusura.full: pertūsūra, ae, f. id., a thrusting or boring through, perforation, Cael. Aur. Tard. 5, 1, 18.

pertusus.full: pertūsus, a, um, Part. and P. a., from pertundo.

perubique.full: pĕr-ŭbīquē, adv., everywhere (postclass.), Tert. Pall. 2 fin.

perula.full: pērŭla, ae, f. dim. pera, a little wallet, a pocket. Lit.: Diogenes fregit exemptum e perulā calicem, Sen. Ep. 90, 11.— Transf., comic., = uterus intumescens, App. M. 5, p. 165, 18.

perunctio.full: pĕrunctĭo, ōnis, f. perungo, a besmearing, anointing, Plin. 24, 15, 80, § 131 al.

perunctus.full: pĕrunctus, a, um, Part., from perungo.
perunctus.short: pĕrunctus, a, um, Part., from perungo.

perungo.full: pĕr-ungo or -unguo, unxi, unctum, 3, v. a., to besmear, anoint (class.): corpora oleo, Cic. Tusc. 1, 47, 113: ora manu, Ov. A. A. 3, 756: vulnera, Plin. 29, 4, 28, § 90; id. 28, 9, 37, § 141: nardo perunctus, Hor. Epod. 5, 59: faecibus ora peruncti, id. A. P. 277.

perunitus.full: pĕr-ūnītus, a, um, adj., united (eccl. Lat.), Primas in Ep. ad Cor. 15.

perurbanus.full: pĕr-urbānus, a, um, adj., very polite, pleasant, or witty. Lit.: L. Torquatus elegans in dicendo, toto genere perurbanus, Cic. Brut. 68, 239: C. Lucilius et doctus et perurbanus, id. de Or. 1, 16, 72.— Transf., with a bad accessory signif., over-fine, over-polite: cum rusticis potius quam cum his perurbanis, Cic. Att. 2, 15, 3. —Adv.: pĕrurbānē, very elegantly: respondere, Sid. Ep. 5, 17 fin.
perurbanus.short: pĕr-urbānus, a, um, adj., very polite, pleasant, or witty.

perurgeo.full: pĕr-urgĕo, ursi, 2, v. a. To press upon greatly, to oppress, distress: cum Aureolus perurgeret Illyrium, Treb. Gall. 5; Amm. 29, 1, 18: eum, Vulg. 1 Macc. 9, 7.— In gen., to press or urge greatly: aliquem ad capessendam rem publicam, Suet. Tib. 25: festinationem, Treb. Trig. Tyr. 33, 8: sacra, to take great pains with, to apply one's self earnestly to, Auct. Aetn. 226.

peruro.full: pĕr-ūro, ussi, ustum, 3, v. a., to burn through and through; hence, Lit. To burn up, consume: perussit ignis multa, Lucr. 5, 396: perusti late agri, Liv. 24, 20: vas, Plin. 34, 17, 49, § 165.—Esp., to be burned or scorched by the sun: Libyco sole perusta coma, Prop. 4 (5), 9, 46. mixti Garamante perusto, sunburned, swarthy, Luc. 4, 679: perusti Indiae populi, Sen. Med. 484: zona perusta, Macr. Somn. Scip. 2, 8.— To heat, burn, inflame: febri peruri, Plin. Ep. 7, 1, 4: sitis praecipue fatigatas p

perusia.full: Pĕrŭsĭa, ae, f., one of the twelve confederate towns of Etruria, the mod. Perugia, Liv. 9, 37, 12; Suet. Aug. 14; Vell. 2, 74, 3; Flor. 4, 5, 3.—Hence, Pĕrŭsī-nus, a, um, adj., Perusian: Perusina cohors, Liv. 23, 17: contentio, i. e. the siege of Perusia by Octavianus, Plin. 7, 45, 46. § 148; the famine produced in the town by this siege (cf. Flor. 4, 5, 3) is referred to in Perusina fames, Luc. 1, 41; Aus. Ep. 22, 42: sepulcra, Prop. 1, 22, 3.—Subst.: Pĕ-rŭsīni, ōrum, m., the Perusians, Liv. 10
perusia.short: Pĕrŭsĭa, ae, f., one of the twelve confederate towns of Etruria, the mod.

perustus.full: pĕrustus, a, um, Part., from peruro.
perustus.short: pĕrustus, a, um, Part., from peruro.

perutilis.full: pĕr-ūtĭlis, e, adj., very useful: opera, Cic. Att. 9, 17, 2.
perutilis.short: pĕr-ūtĭlis, e, adj., very useful: opera, Cic.

pervado.full: per-vādo, si, sum, 3, v. a. and n., to go or come through, to pass or press through, to spread through (class.; syn. penetro). Lit., constr. with acc. alone, or with per, ad, or in, and absol.: pervade polum, Att. ap. Varr. L. L. 7, § 13 Müll. (Trag. Rel. p. 190 Rib.): incendium per agros pervasit, Cic. Verr. 2, 3, 26, § 66: per omnis partis provinciae te tamquam aliquam calamitosam pestem tempestatemque pervasisse, id. ib. 2, 1, 38, § 96: ne cum in Siciliā quidem fuit ... pars ejus belli in Ita

pervagabilis.full: pervăgābĭlis, e, adj. pervagor, ranging or sweeping through (post-class.): cymbulae, Sid. Ep. 2, 2.

pervagatus.full: pervăgātus, a, um, Part. and P. a., from pervagor.

pervagor.full: per-văgor, ātus, 1, v. dep. n. and a., to wander or range through, to rove about, overrun (class.). Lit.: hic praedonum naviculae pervagatae sunt, Cic. Verr. 2, 5, 37, § 98: iis imperat, ut omnibus in locis pervagentur, Caes. B. G. 7, 45: natio pervagata bello prope orbem terrarum, Liv. 38, 17; 1, 29.— Trop. To spread out, extend: quod in exteris nationibus usque ad ultimas terras pervagatum est, Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 28, § 64: ardores in agris pervagantes, Vitr. 2, 6.— To spread through, pervade: ti

pervagus.full: per-văgus, a, um, adj., wandering or roaming all about: puer, Ov. A. A. 2, 18; Sabin. Ep. 1, 91.
pervagus.short: per-văgus, a, um, adj., wandering or roaming all about: puer, Ov.

pervaleo.full: per-vălĕo, a false read. for pervolat, Lucr. 6, 916 Lachm. ad h. l.)

pervalidus.full: per-vălĭdus, a, um, adj., very strong. agmina, Amm. 29, 1, 2: contritio, profound, Vulg. Isa. 30, 14.
pervalidus.short: per-vălĭdus, a, um, adj., very strong.

pervaporo.full: per-văpōro, āvi, 1, v. a., to steam, fill with vapor: solium, Petr. 73, 5 Keller (Bücheler, parabatur).

pervarius.full: per-vărĭus, a, um, adj., very various: utilitates, App. de Deo Socrat. p. 42 dub.— Adv.: pervărĭē, very variously: pervarie narrantur, Cic. de Or. 2, 80, 327.
pervarius.short: per-vărĭus, a, um, adj., very various: utilitates, App.

pervasio.full: pervāsĭo, ōnis, f. pervado, an invad ing, invasion (late Lat.): rerum alienarum pervasio, Salv. Gub. Dei, 5, 10.

pervasor.full: pervāsor, ōris, m. id., an invader (late Lat.), Cassiod. Var. 4, 20; Cod. Th. 2, 4, 5.

pervasto.full: per-vasto, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a., to lay waste, devastate: fines, Liv. 6, 4: pervastatis passim agris, id. 8, 19: pervastata Italia, Tac. A. 15, 45: Boii Laevos cum pervastassent, Liv. 33, 37, 6.

pervasus.full: pervāsus, a, um, Part., from pervado.
pervasus.short: pervāsus, a, um, Part., from pervado.

pervectio.full: pervectĭo, ōnis, f. perveho, a conveying, carrying through, Cod. Th. 11, 1, 13.

pervector.full: pervector, ōris, m. id., a bringer, conveyer (late Lat.): apicum, a letter-carrier, Symm. Ep. 4, 65.

pervectus.full: pervectus, a, um, Part., from perveho.
pervectus.short: pervectus, a, um, Part., from perveho.

perveho.full: per-vĕho, xi, ctum, 3, v. a., to bear, carry, or convey through. Lit.: commeatus, Liv 44, 6, 6.—Mid.: pervehi, to pass through, traverse: Oceanum pervehitur, Tac. A. 2, 8: volucri litora classe, Sil. 4, 51.— Transf., to carry, bring, convey to a place: virgines Caere pervexit, Liv. 5, 40: corpus...Romam usque pervexit, Suet. Tib. 7: sandaracha et ochra inde pervehuntur ad nos, Plin. 35, 6, 22, § 39: volo molliter me pervehat (sc. equus), App. de Deo Socr. p. 54 fin.; cf. id. M. 1, p. 113, 9.—Mid

pervello.full: per-vello, velli, 3, v. a., to pull or pluck hard; to pull, iwitch any thing. Lit.: nates, Plaut. Pers. 5, 2, 66: aurem, Phaedr. 5, 5, 32; also, prov., aurem, to pull one's ear, i. e. to remind one of a thing, Sen. Ben. 5, 7, 5; Val. Max. 1, 5, 8; Sen. Ep. 94, 55; id. Ben. 4, 36, 1; 5, 7, 6.— Transf., to excite, sharpen: stomachum, Hor. S. 2, 8, 9.— Trop. To twitch, pinch: fortuna pervellere te forsitan potuerit et pungere, etc., Cic. Tusc. 3, 17, 36: si te forte dolor aliquis pervellerit, id. i

pervenio.full: per-vĕnĭo, vēni, ventum, 4 (old fut. pervenibunt, Pompon. ap. Non. 508, 6; pres. subj. pervenat, Plaut. Rud. 3, 2, 12; inf. pres. pass. pervenirier, Ter. Phorm. 4, 3, 35), v. n., to come to, arrive at, reach a place. Lit.: quotumo die Sicuone huc pervenisti, Plaut. Ps. 4, 7, 78: Germani in fines Eburonum pervenerunt, Caes. B. G. 4, 6: ad portam, Cic. Pis. 25, 61: in summum montis, Ov. M. 13, 909: in portum, Quint. 2, 17, 24.— Transf., of things, to reach, become known to, come to, fall to, etc.:

pervenor.full: per-vēnor, āri, v. dep. a., to hunt through; transf., to run through or about: urbem totam pervenarier, Plaut. Merc. 4, 5, 3 (v. 818 Ritschl).

perventio.full: perventĭo, ōnis, f. pervenio, an arrival (late Lat.), Mart. Cap. 4, § 406; Aug. Conf. 6, 1.

perventor.full: perventor, ōris, m. id., a comer, arriver (post-class.), Sid. Ep. 3, 13; Aug. Cons. Evang. 2, 20.

pervenustus.full: per-vĕnustus, a, um, adj., very comely (post-class.): homo, Sid. Ep. 3, 13.
pervenustus.short: per-vĕnustus, a, um, adj., very comely (post-class.): homo, Sid.

perverse.full: perversē (pervorsē), adv., v. perverto, P. a. fin.

perversio.full: perversĭo, ōnis, f. perverto, a turning about, inversion; a wresting, perversion, Auct. Her. 4, 32, 44; Tert. adv. Marc. 4, 5.

perversitas.full: perversĭtas, ātis, f. perversus, frowardness, untowardness, perversity: quae est autem in hominibus tanta perversitas, ut, etc., Cic. Or. 9, 31: opinionum, id. Tusc. 3, 1, 2: magna perversitas, id. Off. 1, 40, 145: alicujus, id. Q. Fr. 1, 1, 13, § 38: molestissima diligentiae perversitas, Quint. 1, 6, 34: morum, Suet. Aug. 62: incredibilis hominum, Cic. Fam. 1, 7, 7.

perversus.full: perversus (pervorsus), a, um, Part. and P. a., from perverto.

perverto.full: per-verto (pervorto), ti, sum, 3, v. a., to turn around or about, to overturn, overthrow, throw down (class.). Lit.: pinus proceras pervortunt, Enn. ap. Macr. S. 6, 2 (Ann. v. 196 Vahl.): (coqui) aulas pervortunt, Plaut. Cas. 4, 1, 16: turrim ballistā, id. Bacch. 4, 4, 59: tum visam beluam immanem, quàcunque incederet, arbusta, virgulta, tecta pervertere, Cic. Div. 1, 24, 49: perversae rupes, broken, craggy rocks, Liv. 21, 33.— Esp., in wrestling or boxing, to throw down, knock down; hence: si r

pervesperi.full: per-vespĕrī, adv., very late in the evening: ad aliquem venire, Cic. Fam. 9, 2, 1.
pervesperi.short: per-vespĕrī, adv., very late in the evening: ad aliquem venire, Cic.

pervestigatio.full: pervestīgātĭo, ōnis, f. pervestigo, a searching into, examining, investigation: scientiae, Cic. de Or. 1, 3, 9.

pervestigator.full: pervestīgātor, ōris, m. id., a searcher, investigator: divinae bibliothecae, Hier. Vir. Illustr. 81.

pervestigo.full: per-vestīgo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a., to trace out, search out. Lit., of hounds; hence of spies: canes venaticos diceres, ita omnia odorabantur et pervestigabant, ut, etc., Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 13, § 31.— Trop., to seek out, examine, investigate: operam ut sumam ad pervestigandum, ubi sit illaec, Plaut. Merc. 5, 2, 94; cf. id. Rud. 1, 4, 5; Cic. de Or. 2, 34, 147: quae a me pervestigata et cognita sunt, Cic. Verr. 2, 5, 68, § 174: Locris sacrilegium pervestigatum a Q. Minucio erat, Liv. 31, 13, 1.

pervetus.full: per-vĕtus, ĕris, adj., very old: signum ligneum, Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 3, § 7: oppidum, id. ib. 2, 4, 33, § 72: amicitia, id. Fam. 13, 17: epistula sed sero allata, id. Q. Fr. 3, 1, 4, § 14: vinum non pervetus, Cels. 5, 26, 30.
pervetus.short: per-vĕtus, ĕris, adj., very old: signum ligneum, Cic.

pervetustus.full: per-vĕtustus, a, um, adj., very old: verba, Cic. de Or. 3, 52, 201: vocabulum, Varr. L. L. 6, 7, 59.
pervetustus.short: per-vĕtustus, a, um, adj., very old: verba, Cic.

perviam.full: pervĭam, adv. per-via, accessible (cf. pervius; ante-class. and post-Aug.): angulos aedium perviam facitis, i. q. pervios, Plaut. Aul. 3, 2, 24; Front. Orat. 1 fin. Mai: divus Augustus reprehendens Ti. Claudium ita loquitur: Scribis enim perviam ἀντὶ τοῦ obviam, Charis. p. 187 P.

perviaticum.full: per-vĭātĭcum, i, n., money for a journey: perviaticum publice decretum, Front. ad Amic. 2, 6 Mai.
perviaticum.short: per-vĭātĭcum, i, n., money for a journey: perviaticum publice decretum, Front.

pervicacia.full: pervĭcācĭa, ae, f. pervicax, firmness, inflexibility; in a bad sense, stubbornness, obstinacy (syn.: pertinacia, perseverantia): avaritia, ambitio, mulierositas, pervicacia, Cic. Tusc. 4, 11, 26: haec pervicacia tua et superbia coëgit me loqui, Liv. 9, 34, 24: Aegyptia, Treb. Poll. Claud. 11, 1.— Transf., in a milder signif., firmness, steadiness, steadfastness: tu pertinaciam esse, hanc praedicas, ego pervicaciam aio, Att. ap. Non. 432, 32 sq. (Trag. Rel. v. 4 Rib.; v. the entire passage under

pervicax.full: pervĭcax, ācis, adj. per and root vicof vinco, firm, determined; esp. in a bad sense, stubborn, obstinate, headstrong, wilful (not in Cic. or Cæs.): tu pertinaciam esse, Antiloche, hanc praedicas: Ego pervicaciam aio et eā me uti volo ... Nam pervicacem dici me esse et vincere Perfacile patior: pertinacem nil moror? Att. ap. Non. 432, 32 sq. (Trag. Rel. v. 8 Rib.); cf.: adversus peritos pervicax, Tac. H. 1, 26; Ter. Hec. 4, 1, 17: musa, Hor. C. 3, 3, 70: accusatio, Tac. A. 13, 33; 3, 33: pervica

pervictus.full: pervictus, a, um, Part., from pervinco.
pervictus.short: pervictus, a, um, Part., from pervinco.

pervicus.full: pervĭcus, a, um, adj. pervico for pervinco, stubborn, obstinate (ante-class. collat. form of pervicax): pervico Ajax animo atque evocabili, Att. ap. Non. 487, 15 (Trag. Rel. p. 131 Rib.); Plaut. Fragm. ap. Non. 487, 15.

pervidens.full: pervĭdens, entis, Part. and P. a., from pervideo.

pervideo.full: pervĭdĕo, vīdi, vīsum, 2, v. a., to look over, look on, overlook, survey. Lit.: sol pervidet omnia, Ov. M. 14, 375.— Transf., to look at or upon, to view: cunctaque mens oculis pervidet illa suis, Ov. P. 1, 8, 34: cum tua pervideas oculis mala lippus inunctis, Hor. S. 1, 3, 25.— Trop. To consider, examine: pervideamus, utrum, etc., Lucr. 1, 956: videbo te et pervidebo, Cic. Att. 4, 12 fin. (B. and K. promonebo).— To perceive, discern, Lucr. 2, 90 (for Cic. Att. 15, 4, 2; v. 2. pervolo): meritoru

pervigeo.full: per-vĭgĕo, gŭi, 2, v. n., to continue blooming, to bloom to the last: opibus atque honoribus perviguere, i. e. remained in constant possession of, etc., Tac. A. 4, 34.

pervigil.full: pervĭgĭl, is (collat. form pervĭgĭlis: cura, App. M. 11, p. 270, 31), adj., ever watchful (poet. and in post-Aug. prose; cf. pernox): pervigil in mediae sidera noctis eras, Ov. Am. 1, 6, 44; id. M. 10, 369: pervigilem draconem, id. ib. 7, 149; id. H. 12, 60: pervigiles et insomnes, Plin. Pan. 63: canis, Sen. Herc. Fur. 809: custodia, Luc. 4, 7: torus, Juv. 15, 43: popinae, i. e. open all night, id. 8, 158.— Transf.: nox, passed without sleep, Just. 12, 13, 7.

pervigilatio.full: pervĭgĭlātĭo, ōnis, f. pervigil, a devotional watching, a vigil: nocturnae pervigilationes, Cic. Leg. 2, 15, 37.

pervigilia.full: pervĭgĭlĭa, ae, f. id., a watching all night long: pervigiliae malum, Just. 24, 8, 14; Mart. Cap. 1, § 37; cf. Charis. p. 43 P.

pervigilium.full: pervĭgĭlĭum, ii, n. id., a watching all night, a remaining awake or sitting up all night long. In gen., Plin. 11, 53, 118, § 283: pervigilio fatigati, Just. 13, 8, 6: inter cotidiana pervigilia fessus, Sen. Ira, 3, 29, 1.— In partic., a devotional watching, a vigil: castra pervigilio neglecta, Liv 23, 35: celebrare, Tac. A. 15, 44: indicere, Suet. Calig. 54: pervigilio anniversario colere, id. Galb. 4: agere, id. Vit. 10; Plin. 18, 12, 32, § 124: Pervigilium Veneris, the name of a little Latin p

pervigilo.full: pervĭgĭlo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. n., to remain awake or watch all night; to remain awake during, to watch through any period: continuas has tris noctis pervigilavi pessume, Plaut. Am. 1, 1, 158; id. Aul. 1, 1, 33: vigilare leve est, pervigilare grave, Mart. 6, 69, 9 and 10: noctem, Cic. Rosc. Am. 35, 98: in armis, Liv. 24, 38: ad luminis ignes, Verg. G. 1, 291: nox pervigilata in mero, watched through, i. e. spent without sleep, Ov. F. 6, 326: sollicitas trivio pervigilare moras, Prop. 1, 16, 40: Ven

pervilis.full: per-vīlis, e, adj., very cheap: annona, Liv. 31, 50; Paul. Nol. Carm. 18, 219.
pervilis.short: per-vīlis, e, adj., very cheap: annona, Liv.

pervinco.full: pervinco, vīci, victum, 3, v. n. and a. Lit. Neutr., to conquer completely, gain a complete victory: pervicit Bardanes, Tac. A. 11, 10.— Act., to conquer or defeat completely, gain a complete victory over: ne nos subdolā perfidiā pervincamur, Plaut. Mil. 3, 3, 67: pervince, Theseu, quidquid alto in pectore Remanet pavoris, Sen. Herc. Fur. 654: dominae pervincere mores, Prop. 1, 17, 15.— Transf. To carry a point, maintain one's opinion: restitit ac pervicit Cato, Cic. Att. 2, 1, 8.— To surpass, o

pervincus.full: Pervincus, i, m., i. e. Achiever, a Roman surname, Inscr. Grut. 16, 7.

pervio.full: per-vĭo, āre, v. n., to go on, proceed, Auct. Itin. Alex. M. 104 Mai.

pervirens.full: per-vĭrens, entis, Part. [vireo], ever flourishing, ever green (post-class.), Paul. Nol. Carm. 7, 11.

perviridis.full: per-vĭrĭdis, e, adj., very green: campus, Mel. 2, 5, 7: color, Plin. 6, 22, 24, § 87; Sol. 53, 21; Front. Aquaed. 7 (al. praeviridis).
perviridis.short: per-vĭrĭdis, e, adj., very green: campus, Mel.

perviso.full: per-vīso, ĕre, v. a., to behold, contemplate: caelum, Manil. 4, 925.

pervivo.full: per-vīvo, xi, ctum, 3, v. n., to live on, survive to a certain time (ante-class.): pervixi usque adhuc, Att. ap. Non. 238, 2 (Trag. Rel. v. 417 Rib.): pervivo usque ad summam aetatem, Plaut. Capt. 3, 5, 84.

pervius.full: pervĭus, a, um, adj. per-via, that has a passage through; hence, Lit., that may be passed through or crossed, affording a passage through, passable, pervious (class.): aedes, Ter. Ad. 5, 7, 14: transitiones, thoroughfares, passages, Cic. N. D. 2, 27, 67: hostes saltus pervios ceperant, Liv. 9, 43: usus Tectorum inter se, Verg. A. 2, 453: Phoebo non pervia taxus, i. e. impervious to the sun's rays, Luc. 6, 645: pervius hastis, id. 2, 310: rima pervia flatibus, Ov. M. 15, 301: non ulli pervia vent

pervolaticus.full: per-vŏlātĭcus, a, um, adj., flying about, unstable, volatile (post-class.): vis vaga et pervolatica, Tert. Anim. 46.
pervolaticus.short: per-vŏlātĭcus, a, um, adj., flying about, unstable, volatile (post-class.): vis vaga et pervolatica, Tert.

pervolitantia.full: pervŏlĭtantĭa, ae, f. pervolito, a flying around, circumvolation: mundi circa terram, Vitr. 9, 7.

pervolito.full: pervŏlĭto, āre, v. freq. n. [pervolo], to fly through or around, to flit about (poet.): per dissepta domorum, Lucr. 6, 952; 2, 346: omnia loca, Verg. A. 8, 24: tecta, Val. Fl. 4, 505.—Transf.: iter, to traverse repeatedly, Vitr. 9, 1, 8.

pervolo1.full: per-vŏlo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. n. Lit. To fly through or about a place: aedes, Verg. A. 12, 473: aërium iter, Ov. F. 2, 252: rumor agitatis pervolat alis, id. ib. 6, 527: Flaminiam, Juv. 1, 61.— To fly to a place: Pegasus in nitentem pervolaturus aetheram, Poët. ap. Aug. Music. 3, 3: animus velocius in hanc sedem pervolabit, Cic. Rep. 6, 26, 29.— Transf., of swift motion in gen., to fly or dart through, to pass quickly over or through: perque volare mare ac terras (of the sun's beams), Lucr. 4, 203:

pervolo2.full: per-vŏlo, vŏlui, velle, v. n., to wish greatly, to be very desirous (rare but class.): obtunso ore nunc pervelim progredire Senem, Plaut. Cas. 5, 1, 9: scire ex te pervelim, Cic. Sull. 7, 23: quem videre pervellem, id. Att. 11, 14, 3: mihi ignosci pervelim, id. ib. 1, 1, 3.—In tmesi: ibi te quam primum per videre velim, Cic. Att. 15, 4, 2: pervelle aliquid videre, Liv. 39, 43: illud pervelim, proditum falso esse, etc., id. 8, 18, 2.

pervoluto.full: pervŏlūto, āre, v. freq. a. pervolvo, to roll over and over; hence, in partic., to turn over books, to look through, read: libros, Cic. Att. 5, 12, 2: scriptores, id. de Or. 1, 34, 158.

pervolutus.full: pervolūtus, a, um, Part., from pervolvo.
pervolutus.short: pervolūtus, a, um, Part., from pervolvo.

pervolvo.full: per-volvo, volvi, vŏlūtum, 3, v. a., to roll or tumble about (syn. voluto). Lit.: aliquem in luto, Ter. And. 4, 4, 38.—Mid., to roll one's self, to roll: in suo pervoluta sanguine, weltering, App. M. 8, p. 207, 22.— Transf., to turn over a book, to read: Smyrnam incana diu saecula pervoluent, Cat. 95, 6.— Trop., to be very busy or much engaged in any thing: ut in iis locis pervolvatur animus, Cic. de Or. 2, 35, 149.

pervulgate.full: pervulgātē, adv., v. pervulgo, P. a. fin.

pervulgatus.full: pervulgātus, a, um, Part. and P. a., from pervulgo.

pervulgo.full: pervulgo or -volgo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a., to communicate to the people, to make publicly known, to publish, spread abroad (class.; cf. publico). Lit. In gen., Lucr. 5, 1162: de re illustri et facile etiam in vulgus pervulgatā, Cic. Fin. 2, 5, 15: in re tam clarā, tam testatā, tam abs te ipso pervulgatā, Cic. Verr. 2, 2, 42, § 104: illas tabulas pervulgari atque edi populo Romano imperavi, id. Sull. 15, 42: praemia virtutis in mediocribus hominibus pervulgari, id. Inv. 2, 39, 114; Q. Cic. Pet. Con

pes.full: pēs, pĕdis, m. kindr. with Sanscr. pād, foot, from root pad, ire; Gr. ποδ-, ποῦς; Goth. fōt; old Germ. vuoz; Engl. foot, a foot of man or beast. Lit.: si pes condoluit, Cic. Tusc. 2, 22, 52: calcei apti ad pedem, id. de Or. 1, 54, 231: nec manus, nec pedes, nec alia membra, id. Univ. 6: pede tellurem pulsare, i. e. to dance, Hor. C. 1, 37, 1; cf.: alterno pede terram quatere, id. ib. 1, 4, 7; 4, 1, 27: pedis aptissima forma, Ov. Am. 3, 3, 7: aves omnes in pedes nascuntur, are born feet first, Pl

pescennius.full: Pescennĭus, i, m., name of a Roman gens. A friend of Cicero, Cic. Fam. 14, 4, 6.—Esp., Pescennius Niger, a Roman emperor; hence, Pescenniānus, a, um, adj., pertaining to the emperor Pescennius: reliquiae, Spart. Sev. 15, 4: domus, id. Pesc. Nig. 12, 4.
pescennius.short: Pescennĭus, i, m., name of a Roman gens.

pescia.full: pescia in Saliari carmine Aelius Stilo dici ait capitia ex pellibus agninis facta, quod Graeci pelles vocent pesce neutro genere pluraliter, Fest. p. 210 Müll.
pescia.short: pescia in Saliari carmine Aelius Stilo dici ait capitia ex pellibus agninis facta, quod Graeci pelles vocent pesce neutro genere pluraliter, Fest.

pesestas.full: pesestas significare videtur pestilentiam, Fest. p. 210 Müll.; cf.: pesestas dicebatur pestilentia, Paul. ex Fest. p. 211 Müll.

pesnis.full: pesnis, for pennis, acc. to Fest. p. 205 Müll.; v. penna.

pesoluta.full: pesoluta, ae, f., an Egyptian plant used for making garlands, Plin. 21, 33, 108, § 184.
pesoluta.short: pesoluta, ae, f., an Egyptian plant used for making garlands, Plin.

pessarium.full: pessārĭum, ii, n. 2. pessum, a pessary, Cael. Aur. Acut. 3, 18, 185; Theod. Prisc. 3, 5.

pessimo.full: pessĭmo, āre, v. a. pessimus, to make utterly bad, to spoil completely, to ruin (eccl. Lat.): plebem, Vulg. Ecclus. 36, 11: te ipsum pessimabis, id. ib. 38, 22.—Pass.: pessimabor, Vulg. Ecclus. 11, 26.

pessinus.full: Pessĭnūs and Pesĭnūs, untis, f. (acc. masc. Pessinuntem, Cic. Har. Resp. 13, 28), = Πεσσινοῦς and Πεσινοῦς, a very ancient town in Galatia, on the borders of Phrygia Major, celebrated for its worship of Cybele; the modern Bala Hissar, Cic. Fam. 2, 12, 2: si mater Idaea a Pessinunte Romam advecta foret, Liv. 29, 10 (in Plin. 5, 32, 42, § 146, the true read. is Pisinuus). —Hence, Pessĭnuntĭcus, a, um, adj., Pessinuntic; as subst.: Pessĭnun-tĭca, ae, f., Cybele, App. M. 11, p. 259, 7.— Pessĭnuntĭus

pessulum1.full: pessŭlum, i, n. dim. pessum, a pessary, Cael. Aur. Acut. 3, 18, 184.

pessulum2.full: pessŭlum, i, n., v. pessulus init.

pessulus.full: pessŭlus, i, m. (neutr. collat. form in plur. pessula, Paul. Nol. Carm. 18, 412) [πάσσαλος], a bolt (ante- and post-class.): occlude sis fores ambobus pessulis, Plaut. Aul. 1, 2, 25: pessuli, heus pessuli, vos saluto, id. Curc. 1, 2, 60: pessulum ostio obdo, shoot the bolt, lock the door, Ter. Eun. 3, 5, 55: foribus, id. Heaut. 2, 3, 37: pessulos inicere, to shoot the bolts, App. M. 3, p. 135, 39; 1, p. 107, 12; p. 108, 24: aperire: pessulum ostii mei aperui dilecto meo, Vulg. Cant. 5, 6.

pessum1.full: pessum, adv. prob. contr. from pedis-versum, πέξα, πέδον, towards the feet; like susum, sursum, from sub-versum; hence, in gen., to the ground, to the bottom, down (mostly ante-class. and postAug.; esp. freq. in the connection pessum ire and pessum dare). Lit.: nunc eam (cistellulam) cum navi scilicet abisse pessum in altum, Plaut. Rud. 2, 3, 64: quando abiit rete pessum, id. Truc. 1, 1, 15; and: ne pessum abeat (ratis), id. Aul. 4, 1, 12: multae per mare pessum Subsedere urbes, have gone to the

pessum2.full: pessum, i, n. (collat. form pes-sus, i, m., Plin. Val. 1, 5 fin.; Theod. Prisc. 2, 5), = πεσσόν, πεσσός, in medic. lang., a pessary, App. Herb. 121; Theod. Prisc. 3, 5 (in Cels. 5, 21, written as Greek).

pessumdo.full: pessumdo (pessun-), dăre, v. 1. pessum, II. B.

pestibilis.full: pestĭbĭlis, e, adj. pestis, pestilential, destructive, noxious (post-class.): fundus, Cod. Just. 4, 58, 4.

pestifer.full: pestĭfer and (rarely, Cels. 2, 6) pes-tĭfĕrus, ĕra, ĕrum, adj. pestis-fero. Bringing pestilence, pestilential: odor, Liv. 25, 26, 11.— In gen., that brings destruction, destructive, baleful, noxious, pernicious, pestiferous (class.): res pestiferae et nocentes, Cic. N. D. 2, 47, 120: accessus ad res salutares, a pestiferis recessus, id. ib. 2, 12, 34: acutus et pestifer morbus, Cels. 4, 1, 1: sudor, id. 2, 6: aquae, Val. Fl. 4, 594: ignis, Ov. M. 8, 477: fames, id. ib. 8, 784: fauces, Verg. A. 7

pestilens.full: pestĭlens, entis, adj. pestis, pestilential, infected, unhealthy, unwholesome (class.). Lit.: loci (opp. salubres), Cic. Fat. 4, 7: pestilens et gravis aspiratio, id. Div. 1, 57, 130: Africus, Hor. C. 3, 23, 5: aedes, Cic. Off. 3, 13, 54.—With dat.: annus urbi, Liv. 3, 6: aestas animalibus, id. 5, 16. —Comp.: fundus pestilentior, Varr. R. R. 1, 4: annus, Liv. 4, 21.—Sup.: gravissimus et pestilentissimus annus, Cic. Fam. 5, 16, 4. — Trop., pestilent, noxious, destructive (class.): homo pestilenti

pestilentia.full: pestĭlentĭa, ae, f. pestilens, an infectious or contagious disease, a plague, pest, pestilence. Lit. (class.): Massilienses gravi pestilentiā conflictati, Caes. B. C. 2, 22; Cic. Off. 2, 5, 16: pestilentia gravis incidit in urbem, Liv. 27, 23: pestilentiae contagia prohibere, Plin. 23, 8, 80, § 157; Cels. 1, 10; 2, 1; 3, 7 init.— Transf., an unwholesome atmosphere, weather, or region (class.): agrorum genus propter pestilentiam vastum atque desertum, Cic. Agr. 2, 26, 70: pestilentiae signa (opp.

pestilentiarius.full: pestĭlentĭārĭus, a, um, adj. pestilentia, pestilential (eccl. Lat.): cathedra, Tert. Spect. 27.

pestilentiosus.full: pestĭlentĭōsus, a, um, adj. id., pestilential, unhealthy (post-class.): locus, Dig. 43, 8, 2, § 29.

pestilentus.full: pestĭlentus, a, um, adj. pestis, pestilential, unhealthy (ante-class. for pestilens): loca, Laevius ap. Gell. 19, 7, 7.

pestilis.full: pestĭlis, e, adj. id., pestilential, un wholesome (eccl. Lat.): aurae, Arn. 1, 11.

pestilitas.full: pestĭlĭtas, ātis, f. pestilis, plague, pest, pestilence, for pestilentia (poet.), Lucr. 6, 1098; 1125; 1132 (the first verse also quoted by Non. 158, 2).

pestimus.full: pestĭmus, a, um, adj. pestis, plaguebringing, pestilential: λοιμοφόρος, pestimus, Gloss. Gr. Lat.

pestis.full: pestis, is, f. perh. for perd-tis, from perdo, a deadly, esp. an infectious or contagious disease, a plague, pest, pestilence; also, a noxious atmosphere, unhealthy weather (class., but rare for pestilentia; cf. contagio, lues). Lit.: hos pestis necuit, Enn. ap. Prisc. p. 861 P. (Ann. v. 549 Vahl.): ibes avertunt pestem ab Aegypto, Cic. N. D. 1, 36, 101: avertere a populo pestem, Liv. 4, 25, 3; 5, 14; 25, 26: alii aliā peste absumpti sunt, Liv. 25, 19.—Poet.: crudelem nasorum interfice pestem, i

peta.full: Pĕta, ae, f. peto, the goddess of praying or entreaty, Arn. 4, 131.† † pĕtălum, i, n., = πέταλον, a metal plate: petalum, aurea lamina in fronte pontificis, quae nomen Dei tetragrammaton Hebraicis litteris habebat scriptum, Isid. Orig. 29, 21.

petaminarius.full: pĕtămĭnārĭus, ii, m. πετάμενος, a tumbler, rope-dancer (post-class.), Firm. Math. 8, 15; Salv. Gub. D. 6, 3.

petasatus.full: pĕtăsātus, a, um, adj. petasus, with a travelling-cap on, i. e. ready for a journey (class.): petasati veniunt, Cic. Fam. 15, 17, 1; Varr. ap. Non. 4, 319; Suet. Aug. 82; Hier. prooem. in Zachar. 1, 2.

petasio.full: pĕtăsĭo and pĕtăso, ōnis, m., = πετασών, a leg or pestle of pork, esp. the shoulder (opp. perna, the ham): e Galliā apportantur Romam pernae tomacinae et taniacae, et petasiones, Varr. R. R. 2, 4, 10: pulpam dubio de petasone voras, i. e. that has already begun to turn, Mart. 3, 77, 6.
petasio.short: pĕtăsĭo and pĕtăso, ōnis, m., = πετασών, a leg or pestle of pork, esp.

petasunculus1.full: pĕtăsuncŭlus, i, m. dim. petaso, a little leg or pestle of pork: siccus petasunculus, Juv. 7, 119.

petasunculus2.full: pĕtăsuncŭlus, i, m. dim. petasus, a small travelling-cap, Arn. 6, 198.

petasus.full: pĕtăsus, i, m., = πέτασος, a travelling hat or cap, with a broad brim (cf.: pileus, cucullus). Lit., Plaut. Ps. 2, 4, 45; 4, 7, 90; id. Am. prol. 143; Arn. 6, 197.— Transf., something in the shape of a cap, placed on a building, a cap, cupola, Plin. 36, 13, 19, § 92.
petasus.short: pĕtăsus, i, m., = πέτασος, a travelling hat or cap, with a broad brim (cf.: pileus, cucullus).

petaurista.full: pĕtaurista and -es, ae, m., = πεταυριστής, a tumbler, vaulter, rope-dancer. Lit.: petauristae a veteribus dicebantur qui saltibus vel schemis levioribus moverentur, et haec proprietas a Graecā nominatione descendit, ἀπὸ τοῦ πετᾶσθαι, Non. 56, 26; Varr. ap. Non. 1. 1.; cf.: petauristas Lucilius a petauro appellatos existimare videtur. At Aelius Stilo, quod in aëre volent, Fest. p. 206 Müll.— Transf., of animals that leap very high, Plin. 11, 33, 39, § 115.
petaurista.short: pĕtaurista and -es, ae, m., = πεταυριστής, a tumbler, vaulter, rope-dancer.

petauristarius.full: pĕtauristārĭus, ii, m. petaurista, a tumbler, rope-dancer (post-Aug.), Petr. 53; 60; Firm. Math. 8, 15.

petaurum.full: pĕtaurum, i, n., = πέταυρον, a stage or spring-board used by tumblers and rope-dancers, Lucil. ap. Fest. s. v. petauristae, p. 206 Müll.; Mart. 2, 86, 8; 11, 21, 3; Juv. 14, 265; Manil. 5, 434; Petr. Fragm. 13.
petaurum.short: pĕtaurum, i, n., = πέταυρον, a stage or spring-board used by tumblers and rope-dancers, Lucil.

petax.full: pĕtax, ācis, adj. peto, catching at, striving after, greedy for any thing; with gen. (post-class.): ornatūs petax, Fulg. Myth. 2, 1: potentiae petax, id. ib. 2, 3.—Hence, adv. comp.: pĕtācĭus, more greedily, Avien. Progn. 432.

petelia.full: Pĕtēlĭa (also Pĕtīlĭa and Pĕtellĭa), ae, f., = Πετηλία A very ancient town in the Bruttian territory, north of Croton, colonized by Lucanians, near the mod. Strongoli, Liv. 23, 30; Verg. A. 3, 402; Mel. 2, 4, 8; Plin. 3, 10, 15, § 96.—Hence, Pĕtēlī-nus (Pĕtellīn-), a, um, adj., Petelian: Petelinus lucus, near Rome, Liv. 6, 20: Petelina fides, Val. Max. 6, 6 fin.—Subst.: Pĕtēlīni, ōrum, m., the inhabitants of Petelia, the Petelians, Inscr. Orell. 3678.— A city on the western coast of Lucania, bet
petelia.short: Pĕtēlĭa (also Pĕtīlĭa and Pĕtellĭa), ae, f., = Πετηλία A very ancient town in the Bruttian territory, north of Croton, colonized by Lucanians, near the mod.

petelinus.full: Pĕtēlīnus (Pĕtell-), a, um, v. Petelia, I. B. and II. B.

peteon.full: Pĕtĕōn, ōnis, f., = Πετεών, a town in Bœotia, Stat. Th. 7, 333; Plin. 4, 7, 12, § 26.
peteon.short: Pĕtĕōn, ōnis, f., = Πετεών, a town in Bœotia, Stat.

petesso.full: pĕtesso and pĕtisso, ĕre, v. intens. a. [peto], to strive after or seek for repeatedly or eagerly, to pursue; with acc. (rare but class.): petissere antiqui pro petere dicebant. Sed, ut mihi videtur, cum significabant saepius petere, Fest. p. 206 Müll.; cf.: petissere petere, Paul. ex Fest. p. 212 ib.: pugnam caedesque petessit, Lucr. 3, 648: auras petessens, id. 5, 810: laudem, Cic. Tusc. 2, 26, 62.

petibilis.full: pĕtībĭlis, e, adj. peto, capable of being demanded (eccl. Lat.), Possid. Vita, Aug.20.

petiginosus.full: pĕtīgĭnōsus, a, um, adj. petigo, full of scabs or eruptions, scabby (post-class.), Theod. Prisc. 1, 12.

petigo.full: pĕtīgo, ĭnis, f., a scab, an eruption (anteclass.): petigo genus morbi. Lucilius, lib. XXX.: illuvies, scabies . . . petigo, Non. 160, 17 sq. (others read, deque petigo; so in Cato, R. R. 157 fin., Schneid. reads depetigini).
petigo.short: pĕtīgo, ĭnis, f., a scab, an eruption (anteclass.): petigo genus morbi.

petilianus.full: Pĕtīlĭānus, a, um, v. Petilius, B.

petilium.full: pĕtīlĭum, ii, n., an autumnal flower, otherwise unknown, Plin. 21, 8, 25, § 49.
petilium.short: pĕtīlĭum, ii, n., an autumnal flower, otherwise unknown, Plin.

petilius.full: Pĕtīlĭus, a, name of a Roman gens. —Hence, Pĕtīlĭus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to a Petilius, Petilian: lex, Liv. 38, 55.— Pĕtīlĭānus, a, um, adj., Petilian: regna, i. e. the villa of a certain Petilius, otherwise unknown, Mart. 12, 57, 19.
petilius.short: Pĕtīlĭus, a, name of a Roman gens.

petilus.full: pĕtīlus, a, um, adj., thin, slender (anteclass.): petilum tenue et exile, Non. 149, 7 sq.; Lucil. and Plaut. ap. Non. 1. 1.: petilam suram, siccam et substrictam vulgo interpretantur: Scaevola ait, ungulam albam equi ita dici, Fest. p. 205 Müll.
petilus.short: pĕtīlus, a, um, adj., thin, slender (anteclass.): petilum tenue et exile, Non.

petimen.full: pĕtĭmen, ĭnis, n., perh. a sore on the shoulder of beasts of burden or draught (ante-class.): petimina in umeris jumentorum ulcera: eo nomine autem et inter duos armos suis quod est aut pectus solitum appellari, testatur Naevius, Fest. p. 209 Müll.; cf.: petimina in umeris jumentorum ulcera, Paul. ex Fest. p. 208 ib.

petina.full: Petīna, ae, f., Ælia, a wife of the emperor Claudius, whom he divorced before marrying Messalina, Suet. Claud. 26.
petina.short: Petīna, ae, f., Ælia, a wife of the emperor Claudius, whom he divorced before marrying Messalina, Suet.

petiolus.full: pĕtĭŏlus, i, m. dim. pes, a little foot, little leg (post-Aug.). Lit.: nudus, Afr. ap. Non. 160, 16; Cels. 2, 18, 31: in petiolis capitulisque haedorum et vitulorum et agnorum, id. 2, 22, 2.— Transf., a stem or stalk of fruits: petioli, quibus mala pendent, Col. Arb. 23, 2; of the olive, id. 12, 49, 8.

petisius.full: Petisĭus, a, am, adj., Petisian: mala, a small sort of apple, paradise-apples, Plin. 15, 14, 15, § 50.
petisius.short: Petisĭus, a, am, adj., Petisian: mala, a small sort of apple, paradise-apples, Plin.

petitio.full: pĕtītĭo, ōnis, f. peto. Lit., an attack, a blow, thrust, pass: tuas petiti ones effugi, Cic. Cat. 1, 6, 15; cf.: petitiones proprie dicimus impetus gladiorum, Serv. Verg. A. 9, 439.— Trop., an attack made in words before a court of justice, Cic. Or. 68, 228; or in debate, id. Cat. 1, 6, 15; cf.: novi omnis hominis petitiones rationesque dicendi, methods of attack, Cic. Div. in Caecil. 14, 44; id. de Or. 3, 54, 206.— In gen., a requesting, beseeching; a request, petition for any thing (postAug.),

petitiuncula.full: pĕtītĭuncŭla, ae, f. dim. petitio, a little petition: petitiuncula, δεησίδιον, Gloss. Philox.

petitor.full: pĕtītor, ōris, m. peto. In gen., a seeker, striver after any thing (poet.): famae, Luc. 1, 131.— In partic. Polit. t. t., an applicant or candidate for an office (very rare for candidatus; not in Cic.), Scip. Afric. ap. Macr. S. 2, 10: e petitoribus non alios adjuvare aut ad honorem pati pervenire, Suet. Caes. 23: hic generosior Descendat in campum petitor, Hor. C. 3, 1, 10.— Judicial t. t., a claimant, plaintiff, in private or civil suits (whereas he who prefers the complaint in a criminal case

petitorius.full: pĕtītōrĭus, a, um, adj. petitor. In gen., of or belonging to solicitation (post-class.): artes petitorias exercere, Mamert. Grat. Act. ad Jul. 16, 2.— In partic., of or belonging to the prosecution of a judicial claim, petitory (post-class.): judicium, Dig. 6, 1, 36: formula, Gai. Inst. 4, 91 sq.—Hence, subst.: pĕtītōrĭum, ii, n., the complaint or declaration in a private action, Cod. Th. 10, 10, 29, § 1.

petitrix.full: pĕtītrix, īcis, f. id. A female applicant or candidate for office (post-Aug.), Auct. Quint. Decl. 252.— Judicial t. t., a female claimant or plaintiff (post-class.): contra petitricem pronuntiavit, Dig. 36, 1, 74 fin.

petitum.full: pĕtītum, i, n., v. peto, II. B. 2. b.

petiturio.full: pĕtītŭrio, īre, v. desid. a. [peto], to desire to sue for office, to long to become a candidate (rare but class.): video hominem valde petiturire, Cic. Att. 1, 14, 7.

petitus1.full: pĕtītus, a, um, Part., from peto.
petitus1.short: pĕtītus, a, um, Part., from peto.

petitus2.full: pĕtītus, ūs, m. peto. An inclining towards any thing (poet.): terrae petitus, Lucr. 3, 172.— A desire, request (post-class.) jussit eum consensu petituque omnium sententiam dicere, Gell. 18, 3, 6: petitu tuo adesse, App. Mag. 45 al.

peto.full: pĕto, īvi and ĭi, ītum, 3 (perf. petīt, Verg. A. 9, 9; Ov F. 1, 109: petisti, Cic. Cat. 1, 5, 11; Verg. A. 4, 100; 12, 359: petistis, Auct. Her. 4, 15, 22: petissem, Cic. Verr. 1, 55, 145; Ov. M. 5, 26; Liv. 30, 25, 2: petisse, Cic. Quint. 11, 37; Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 63, § 140; Ov. M. 9, 623; cf. Neue, Formenl. 2, 516 sq.), v. a. Sanscr. root pat-, to fall upon, fly, find; Gr. πετ- in πίπτω (πι-πέτω), to fall; cf. Lat. impetus and in πέτομαι, to fly; cf. Lat. penna, acci-pit-er, etc.; the root of π

petoritum.full: pĕtōrĭtum or pĕtorrĭtum, i, n. Celtic petor, four, and rit, wheel, an open, four - wheeled carriage, of Gallic origin: petoritum et Gallicum vehiculum esse, et nomen ejus dictum existimant a numero quattuor rotarum: alii Osce, quod hi quoque petora quattuor vocent: alii Graece, sed αιολικῶς dictum, Fest. p. 206 Müll.; Gell. 15, 30, 1; Hor. Ep. 2, 1, 192; id. S. 1, 6, 104; cf. also Plin. 34, 17, 48, § 163; Aus. Ep. 5, 35; 8, 5.

petosiris.full: Pĕtŏsīris, ĭdis, m., = Πετόσιρις, a celebrated Egyptian mathematician and astrologer, Plin. 2, 23, 21, § 88; 7, 49, 50, § 160; Firm. Math. 4, praef.—Hence, transf., a great mathematician, astrologer, in gen., Juv. 6, 580.
petosiris.short: Pĕtŏsīris, ĭdis, m., = Πετόσιρις, a celebrated Egyptian mathematician and astrologer, Plin.

petovio.full: Petovĭo or Poetovĭo, ōnis, f., a city in Pannonia, the modern Pettau, Tac. H. 3, 1; Inscr. Orell. 3592.
petovio.short: Petovĭo or Poetovĭo, ōnis, f., a city in Pannonia, the modern Pettau, Tac.

petra1.full: pē^tra, ae, f., = πέτρα, a rock, a crag, stone (pure Lat. saxum; cf.: rupes, scopulus): petrarum genera sunt duo, quorum alterum naturale saxum prominens in mare; alterum manufactum ut docet Aelius Gallus: Petra est, qui locus dextrā ac sinistrā fornicem expletur usque ad libramentum summi fornicis, Fest. p. 206 Müll. (of the latter signif. there is no other example known): petris ingentibus tecta, Enn. ap. Fest. 1. 1. (Ann. v. 366); Sen. Herc. Oet. 804: aquam de petrā produxit, Vulg. Isa. 48, 2
petra1.short: pē^tra, ae, f., = πέτρα, a rock, a crag, stone (pure Lat.

petra2.full: Pē^tra, ae, f., = Πέτρα, the name of several cities. A city in Arabia Petrœa, now the ruins of Wadi Musa, Plin. 6, 28, 32, § 144; Vulg. Jer. 48, 28.—Hence, Pē^traeus, a, um, adj., Petrean: balanus, Plin. 12, 21, 46, § 102: hypericon, id. 12, 25, 54, § 119.— A city in Pieria, Liv. 29, 26.— A city in Thrace, Liv. 40, 22. — A city in Umbria, called Petra Pertusa, now Il Furlo, Aur. Vict. Epist. in Vespas. 17.— A hill near Dyrrachium, Caes. B. C. 3, 42.
petra2.short: Pē^tra, ae, f., = Πέτρα, the name of several cities.

petra3.full: Petra, ae, m., a Roman proper name, Tac. A. 11, 4.
petra3.short: Petra, ae, m., a Roman proper name, Tac.

petrabulum.full: petrăbŭlum, i, n., = πετρόβολον, a stone-thrower, catapult, Not. Tir. p. 179.
petrabulum.short: petrăbŭlum, i, n., = πετρόβολον, a stone-thrower, catapult, Not.

petraeus1.full: petraeus, a, um, adj., = πετραῖος, that grows among rocks, rock- (post-Aug.) brassica, Plin. 20, 9, 36, § 92.
petraeus1.short: petraeus, a, um, adj., = πετραῖος, that grows among rocks, rock- (post-Aug.) brassica, Plin.

petraeus2.full: Pĕtraeus, a, um, v. 2. Petra, I. B.

petralis.full: petrālis, e, adj. petra, stony (eccl. Lat.), Cassiod. in Psa. 39, 2.

petreius.full: Petrēĭus, i, m., name of a Roman gens. —So, esp, a lieutenant of Pompey in the civil war, Caes. B. C. 1, 38; 63; cf. Cic. Att. 8, 2, 3. He is probably the same person with M. Petrejus, lieutenant of the consul C. Antonius, who defeated the followers of Catiline at Fœsulœ, A. U. C. 692; Cic. Sest. 5, 12; Sall. C. 59, 5 sq.—Hence, Petrēius, a, um, adj., Petreian; here prob. belongs: petreia vocabatur, quae pompam praecedens in coloniis aut municipiis imitabatur anum ebriam, ab agri vitio, scilicet
petreius.short: Petrēĭus, i, m., name of a Roman gens.

petrenses.full: Petrenses, ĭum, m., the inhabitants of the city of Petra, in Sicily, Sol. 5.
petrenses.short: Petrenses, ĭum, m., the inhabitants of the city of Petra, in Sicily, Sol.

petrensis.full: petrensis, e, adj. 1. petra, found among rocks or stones (post-class.): pisces, Cael. Aur. Tard. 2, 1, 26.

petreus.full: Petrĕus, a, um, adj. 1. petra or Petrus, Petrean (eccl. Lat.): istae spinae, Petra et Petro transeunte, petreis pedibus tritae sunt, of rock or stone, or pertaining to the Apostle Peter, Aug. Serm. 297, 2 fin.

petrini.full: Petrīni, ōrum, m., the inhabitants of the city of Petra, in Sicily, the Petreans, Cic. Verr. 2, 3, 39, § 90; Plin. 3, 8, 14, § 91.
petrini.short: Petrīni, ōrum, m., the inhabitants of the city of Petra, in Sicily, the Petreans, Cic.

petrinum.full: Petrīnum, i, n., a villa near Sinuessa, in Campania, Hor. Ep. 1, 5, 5; Cic. Fam. 6, 19, 1.
petrinum.short: Petrīnum, i, n., a villa near Sinuessa, in Campania, Hor.

petrinus.full: petrĭnus, a, um, adj., = πέτρινος, of stone, stone- (eccl. Lat.): acies, Tert. adv. Marc. 3, 16.
petrinus.short: petrĭnus, a, um, adj., = πέτρινος, of stone, stone- (eccl.

petrites.full: petrītes, ae, m., = πετρίτης (οἶνος), a kind of wine, perh. from the city of Petra, in Arabia, Plin. 14, 7, 9, § 75.
petrites.short: petrītes, ae, m., = πετρίτης (οἶνος), a kind of wine, perh.

petro1.full: pē^tro, ōnis, m. 1. petra. A rustic: petrones rustici fere dicuntur, etc., Fest. p. 206, 23 Müll.; cf.: petrones rustici a petrarum asperitate et duritiā dicti, Paul. ex Fest. p. 207, 6 ib.— An old wether, whose flesh is as hard as a stone (anteclass.), Plaut. Capt. 4, 2, 40.

petro2.full: Petro, ōnis, m. 1. petra, a Roman surname, Suet. Vesp. 1.

petrocorii.full: Petrŏcŏrĭi, ōrum, m., a Gallic tribe in Aquitania, in the mod. Périgueux, Caes. B. G. 7, 75; Plin. 4, 19, 33, § 109; sing., Inscr Maff. Mus. Ver 450, 8.
petrocorii.short: Petrŏcŏrĭi, ōrum, m., a Gallic tribe in Aquitania, in the mod.

petronianus.full: Pē^trōnĭānus, a, um, adj., v. 2. Petronius, B.

petronius1.full: pē^trōnĭus, a, um, adj. 1. petra, rock-, crag-, mountain- (very rare): canes, Grat. Cyneg. 202.

petronius2.full: Pē^trōnĭus, i, m., name of a Roman gens.—So, esp.: Petronius Arbiter, a Roman knight, a favorite of the emperor Nero, perh. the same person with Petronius, the author of a Latin romance which is preserved in a fragmentary state, Tac. A. 16, 17 sq.—In fem.: Pē^trōnĭa, ae, the first wife of the emperor Vitellius, Tac. H. 2, 64; Suet. Vit. 6.—Hence, Pē^trōnĭus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to a Petronius, Petronian: Petronia amnis est in Tiberim profluens, quam magistratus auspicato transeunt, cum
petronius2.short: Pē^trōnĭus, i, m., name of a Roman gens.—So, esp.: Petronius Arbiter, a Roman knight, a favorite of the emperor Nero, perh.

petroselinon.full: petrŏsĕlīnon (-īnum), i, n., = πετροσέλινον, rock-parsley, Plin. 20, 12, 47, § 118; Pall. 5, 3.
petroselinon.short: petrŏsĕlīnon (-īnum), i, n., = πετροσέλινον, rock-parsley, Plin.
