petrosus.full: petrōsus, a, um, adj. 1. petra, full of rocks, rocky (post-Aug.): loca, Plin. 9, 31, 50, § 96.—Subst.: petrōsa, ōrum, n., rocky places: maritima, Plin. 26, 8, 29, § 46; Ambros. Laps. Virg. 7, 29: aliud cecidit super petrosa, Vulg. Marc. 4, 5; id. Matt. 13, 5.

petrotos.full: pē^trōtos, on, adj. πετρόω, stony, petrified: quae modicos calices duos quos appellabant petrotos HS. V̄Ī. venderet, Plin. 36, 26, 66, § 195 Jan. (dub.; al. pterotos).

pettalus.full: Pettălus, i, m., the mythic name of a hero who sought to attack Perseus at the court of Cepheus, Ov. M. 5, 115.
pettalus.short: Pettălus, i, m., the mythic name of a hero who sought to attack Perseus at the court of Cepheus, Ov.

petulans.full: pĕtŭlans, antis, adj. prop. part. of the obsol. petulo, from peto, qs. falling upon or assailing in jest, i. e., forward, pert, saucy, impudent, wanton, freakish, petulant. In gen. (class.; syn.: protervus, lascivus, procax): petulantes et petulci etiam appellantur, qui protervo impetu, et crebro petunt laedendi alterius gratiā, Fest. p. 206 Müll.: homo, Cic. de Or. 2, 75, 305: effuse petulans, id. Pis. 5, 10: animalia, Gell. 17, 20, 8: pictura, Plin. 35, 11, 40, § 140: petulans et furiosum genu

petulantia.full: pĕtŭlantĭa, ae, f. petulans. Lit., sauciness, freakishness, impudence, wantonness, petulance (class.; syn. lascivia): itaque a petendo petulantia, a procando, id est poscendo, procacitas nominata est, Cic. Fragm. ap. Non. 23, 18: petulantia et libido magis est adulescentium quam senum, id. Sen. 11, 36: petulantia et audacia, id. Caecin. 35, 103; cf.: te non ulla meae laesit petulantia linguae, Prop. 1, 16, 37.—In plur.: Naevius ... cum ob assiduam maledicentiam et probra in principes civitatis .

petulcus.full: pĕtulcus, a, um, adj. peto; cf. petulans init., butting, apt to butt, with the horns or head (poet. and post-Aug.). Lit.: agni, Lucr. 2, 368: haedi, Verg. G. 4, 10: caper velaries, Col. 7, 3, 5.— Transf., frisky, wanton: haedi petulci dicti ab appetendo: unde et meretrices petulcas vocamus, Serv. Verg. G. 4, 10.

peuce1.full: peucē, ēs, f., = πεύκη. The pinetree, pitch-pine-tree, Plin. 11, 35, 41, § 118.— A kind of grape, Plin. 14, 9, 9, § 74.

peuce2.full: Peucē, ēs, f. The name of an island in the Danube, Plin. 4, 12, 24, § 79; Luc. 3, 202.— In mythology, the wife of the Ister, Stat. S. 5, 2, 137; Val. Fl. 8, 217.

peucedanum.full: peucĕdănum or -on, i, n., and peucĕdănos, i, m., = πευκέδανον or -ος, the plant hog's-fennel, sulphurwort, Plin. 25, 9, 70, § 117; Luc. 9, 919: a Graecis dicitur peucedanos: Latini pinastellum vocarunt, App. Herb. 94.
peucedanum.short: peucĕdănum or -on, i, n., and peucĕdănos, i, m., = πευκέδανον or -ος, the plant hog's-fennel, sulphurwort, Plin.

peucetia.full: Peucĕtĭa, ae, f., a region in Apulia, Plin. 3, 11, 16, § 99.—Hence, Peucĕ-tĭus, a, um, adj., Peucetian: sinus, Ov. M. 14, 513; cf. Serv. Verg. A. 8, 9.
peucetia.short: Peucĕtĭa, ae, f., a region in Apulia, Plin.

peumene.full: peumĕnē, ēs, f., πευμένη, a kind of spume or scum of silver, Plin. 33, 6, 35, § 108.
peumene.short: peumĕnē, ēs, f., πευμένη, a kind of spume or scum of silver, Plin.

pexatus.full: pexātus, a, um, adj. pexus, clothed in a garment that has a nap on it (post-Aug.): pexatus pulcre rides mea, Zoile, trita, Mart. 2, 58, 1: pexatus et gausapatus, Sen. Vit. Beat. 25.

pexitas.full: pexĭtas, ātis, f. id., perh. thickness, closeness (post-Aug.); of a spider's web: telae, Plin. 11, 24, 28, § 81.

pexsus.full: Pexsus, i, m.; Pexsa, ae, f., a Roman cognomen, v. pecto, P. a.

pexus.full: pexus, a, um, Part. and P. a., from pecto.

pezicae.full: pezĭcae or pezĭtae, ārum, f., = πέζικες, πέζεαι, mushrooms without a root or without a stalk, Plin. 19, 3, 14, § 38.
pezicae.short: pezĭcae or pezĭtae, ārum, f., = πέζικες, πέζεαι, mushrooms without a root or without a stalk, Plin.

phacus.full: Phacus, i, m., = Φάκος, a fortified place near Pella in Macedonia, where the treasury of the Macedonian kings was kept, Liv. 44, 6, 2: Arx Phacus, id. 44, 46, 6.
phacus.short: Phacus, i, m., = Φάκος, a fortified place near Pella in Macedonia, where the treasury of the Macedonian kings was kept, Liv.

phaeaces.full: Phaeāces, um, m., = Φαίακες, the Phœacians, the fabled luxurious inhabitants of the isle of Scheria (in historic times, Corcyra), Cic. Brut. 18, 71; Verg. A. 3, 291; Ov. M. 13, 719; Juv. 5, 151.—In sing.: Phae-ax, ācis, m., a Phœacian; transf., of a man in good case, Hor. Ep. 1, 15, 24.—As adj.: Phaeax populus, Juv. 15, 23.—Hence, Phaeācĭa, ae, f., = Φαιακία, the country of the Phœacians, the isle of Scheria (Corcyra), in the Ionian Sea: Corcyra Homero dicta Scheria et Phaeacia, Callimacho etiam
phaeaces.short: Phaeāces, um, m., = Φαίακες, the Phœacians, the fabled luxurious inhabitants of the isle of Scheria (in historic times, Corcyra), Cic.

phaecasiani.full: phaecăsĭāni dii phaecasium, a sort of deities of whom nothing further is known (perh. shod with phaecasia), Juv. 3, 218 (al. phaecasiati).
phaecasiani.short: phaecăsĭāni dii phaecasium, a sort of deities of whom nothing further is known (perh.

phaecasiatus.full: phaecăsĭātus, a, um, adj. id., shod with phaecasia: milites, Petr. 72: quae decent phaecasiatum palliatumque, i. e. a Grecian philosopher, Sen. Ep. 113, 2.

phaecasium.full: phaecăsĭum, ii, n., and phaecă-sĭa, ae, f., = Φαικάσιον, a kind of white shoe, worn at Athens by the priests, Sen. Ben. 7, 21, 1: inauratae, Petr. 67.
phaecasium.short: phaecăsĭum, ii, n., and phaecă-sĭa, ae, f., = Φαικάσιον, a kind of white shoe, worn at Athens by the priests, Sen.

phaedo.full: Phaedo or Phaedon, ōnis, m., = Φαίδων, a disciple of Socrates and friend of Plato, after whom Plato has named his dialogue on the immortality of the soul, Cic. N. D. 1, 33, 93; Gell. 2, 18, 1; Lact. 3, 25, 15; Sid. Ep. 2, 9.
phaedo.short: Phaedo or Phaedon, ōnis, m., = Φαίδων, a disciple of Socrates and friend of Plato, after whom Plato has named his dialogue on the immortality of the soul, Cic.

phaedra.full: Phaedra, ae, f., = Φαίδρα, the daughter of king Minos, of Crete, sister of Ariadne and wife of Theseus; she slew herself for hopeless love of Hippolytus, Verg. A. 6, 445; Ov. A. A. 1, 511; id. H. 4, 74; Sen. Hippol. 434; cf. Serv. Verg. A. 6, 14; Hyg. Fab. 47; 243.
phaedra.short: Phaedra, ae, f., = Φαίδρα, the daughter of king Minos, of Crete, sister of Ariadne and wife of Theseus;

phaedrias.full: Phaedrĭas or Phaedrĭa, ae, m., a male proper name, Ter. Eun. 1, 2, 15.
phaedrias.short: Phaedrĭas or Phaedrĭa, ae, m., a male proper name, Ter.

phaedrus.full: Phaedrus (nom. PHAEDER, Inscr. Grut. 1111, 3), i, m., = Φαῖδρος. A pupil of Socrates, a native of Myrsinus, in Attica, after whom Plato named one of his dialogues, Cic. de Or. 1, 7, 28; id. Or. 4, 15; 12, 39; id. Fin. 2, 2, 4; id. Tusc. 1, 22, 53 al. — An Epicurean philosopher of Athens, an instructor of Cicero, Cic. Fam. 13, 1, 2; id. Fin. 1, 5, 16; id. N. D. 1, 33, 93; id. Phil. 5, 5, 13.— A freedman of Augustus, a Thracian by birth, and author of some well-known Latin fables.

phaenion.full: phaenĭon, ĭi, n., = φαινίον, a plant, the anemone, Plin. 21, 23, 94, § 164 (al. phrenion, v. Sillig ad h. l.).
phaenion.short: phaenĭon, ĭi, n., = φαινίον, a plant, the anemone, Plin.

phaenomenon.full: phaenŏmĕnon, i, n., = φαινόμενον, an appearance. In gen. (post-class.), Theod. Prisc. 2, 7.— In partic. phaenŏmĕna, ōrum, n. plur., = φαινόμενα, appearances in the air or sky, Lact. 2, 5, 11.— Phaenomena, the title of a poem by Aratus.
phaenomenon.short: phaenŏmĕnon, i, n., = φαινόμενον, an appearance.

phaenon.full: Phaenon, ōnis, m., = Φαίνων (shining), the planet Saturn (post-class.): quae Stilbon volvat, quae secula Phaenon, Aus. Idyll. 18, 11; Mart. Cap. 8, § 886.—In the Gr. acc. Phaenona, Mart. Cap. 8, § 851 (written as Greek, Cic. N. D. 2, 20, 52).
phaenon.short: Phaenon, ōnis, m., = Φαίνων (shining), the planet Saturn (post-class.): quae Stilbon volvat, quae secula Phaenon, Aus.

phaestum.full: Phaestum, i, n., = Φαῖστος. A town of Crete, near Cortyna, founded by Minos, Plin. 4, 12, 20, § 59.—Hence, Phae-stĭas, ădis, f., = Φαιστιάς, a female inhabitant of Phœstum, a Phœstian (poet.): inter Phaestiadas, Ov. M. 9, 715.— Phae-stĭus, a, um, adj., = Φαίστιος, of or belonging to Phœstum, Phœstian: tellus, Ov. M. 9, 668: Apollo, Plin. 4, 3, 4, § 7.— A town of Thessaly, on the Eurotas, Liv. 36, 13, 3.— A town of Locris, in Greece, Plin. 4, 3, 4, § 7.

phaethon.full: Phăĕthon (dissyl.: fulmine Phaethon, Varr. ap. Quint. 1, 5, 18), ontis, m., = Φαέθων (the shining one). Son of Helios and Clymene, who, having obtained from his father permission to drive the sun's chariot for a day, lost control of the steeds, and was struck down by a thunderbolt of Jupiter, to prevent his setting the earth on fire, Cic. Off. 3, 25, 94; id. N. D. 3, 31, 76; cf.: Phaëthontem orbi terrarum educare, Suet. Calig. 11; Ov. M. 2, 47 sq.; Verg. A. 10, 189.— An epithet of the sun (poet.

phaethusa.full: Phăĕthūsa, ae, f., = Φαέθουσα (the shining one), a sister of Phaëthon, Ov. M. 2, 346.
phaethusa.short: Phăĕthūsa, ae, f., = Φαέθουσα (the shining one), a sister of Phaëthon, Ov.

phagedaena.full: phăgĕdaena, ae, f., = φαγέδαινα (voracity). A diseased and excessive appetite, voracity, Cael. Aur. Tard. 3, 3, 46; plur., Plin. 26, 11, 68, § 110.—As a disease of bees, Col. 9, 13, 10 (written as Greek).— Hence, An eating ulcer, a cancer, Plin. 23, 7, 63, § 123.

phagedaenicus.full: phăgĕdaenĭcus, a, um, adj., = φαγεδαινικός, spreading like a cancer, can-cerous: vulnera, Plin. 24, 4, 5, § 9.— Transf., of persons, suffering from cancers, cancerous: phagedaenici, Cael. Aur. Tard. 3, 3, 47.
phagedaenicus.short: phăgĕdaenĭcus, a, um, adj., = φαγεδαινικός, spreading like a cancer, can-cerous: vulnera, Plin.

phager.full: phăger (pa-) or phăgrus (pa-), i, m., = φάγρος, a fish, Plin. 32, 11, 53, § 150; Ov. Hal. 107; plur., Plin. 9, 16, 24, § 57; 32, 10, 38, § 113.
phager.short: phăger (pa-) or phăgrus (pa-), i, m., = φάγρος, a fish, Plin.

phagita.full: Phăgīta, ae, m. φάγω, to eat, a Roman surname, Suet. Caes. 74.

phago.full: phăgo, ōnis, m., = φάγος, φαγών, a glutton, gormandizer (ante-and post-class.): edones et phagones ab edacitate, unum Latinum, aliud Graecum, Non. 48, 17 sq.; Varr. ap. Non. l. l.; Vop. Aur. 50.
phago.short: phăgo, ōnis, m., = φάγος, φαγών, a glutton, gormandizer (ante-and post-class.): edones et phagones ab edacitate, unum Latinum, aliud Graecum, Non.

phalacrine.full: Phalacrīnē, ēs, and Phalacrīna, ae, f., a town in the Sabine territory, the birthplace of the emperor Vespasian, Suet. Vesp. 2.
phalacrine.short: Phalacrīnē, ēs, and Phalacrīna, ae, f., a town in the Sabine territory, the birthplace of the emperor Vespasian, Suet.

phalacrocorax.full: phălacrŏ-cŏrax, ăcis, m., = φαλακροκόραξ, a coot or cormorant (pure Lat. corvus aquaticus): phalacrocoraces, aves Balearium insularum peculiares, Plin. 10, 48, 68, § 133; cf. id. 11, 37, 47, § 130.
phalacrocorax.short: phălacrŏ-cŏrax, ăcis, m., = φαλακροκόραξ, a coot or cormorant (pure Lat.

phalaecus.full: Phălaecus, i, m., = Φάλαικος, an ancient Greek poet, from whom a kind of verse is named Phalaecium, Phalaecum, or Phaleucium carmen. This verse is hendecasyllabic, consisting of a spondee, a dactyl, and three trochees (e. g. vidi credite per lacus Lucrinos), Aus. Ep. 4, 85; Diom. p. 509 P.; Terentian. p. 2440 ib.; Mart. Cap. 5, § 517: metrum Phalaecium, Mar. Victor. 2566 P.: carmen Phalaecum, Sulp. Sat. 4. — A tyrant of Phocœa; whence Phă-laecēus, a, um, Phalœcean, of Phalœcus: nex, Ov. Ib. 504.
phalaecus.short: Phălaecus, i, m., = Φάλαικος, an ancient Greek poet, from whom a kind of verse is named Phalaecium, Phalaecum, or Phaleucium carmen.

phalangae.full: phălangae and pălangae, ārum, f. plur., = φάλαγγες. In gen., a pole to carry burdens on, carrying-pole, Vitr. 10, 3, 7: proelium Afri contra Aegyptios primum fecere fustibus, quos vocant phalangas, Plin. 7, 56, 57, § 206; 12, 4, 8, § 17.— In partic., a wooden roller, to place under ships and military machines for the purpose of moving them along (class.), Varr. ap. Non. 163, 23 sq.; Caes. B. C. 2, 10 fin.

phalangarius1.full: phălangārĭus or pălangā-rĭus (in inscrr. also PALANCARIVS and FALANCARIVS), ii, m. phalangae, one who carries burdens with the aid of a long pole, a carrier, porter, Vitr. 10, 3, 7; Non. 163, 23 sq. (v. phalanga); Inscr. Fabr. p. 10; Inscr. Giorn. Pisan. tom. 16, p. 192; Inscr. Marin. Atti, p. 151; Inscr. Kellerm. ap. Orell. Analect. Epigr. (Index Lection. Acad. Turic. Aestiv. 1838), p. 43, 4090.

phalangarius2.full: phălangārĭus, ii, m. phalanx, a soldier belonging to a phalanx, a phalangary (post-class.), Lampr. Alex. Sev. 50, 5 (cf. phalangitae).

phalangitae.full: phălangītae, ārum, m., = φαλαγγῖται, soldiers belonging to a phalanx, phalangites, Liv. 37, 40, 1; 5; 42, 51.
phalangitae.short: phălangītae, ārum, m., = φαλαγγῖται, soldiers belonging to a phalanx, phalangites, Liv.

phalangites.full: phălangītes, ae, m., = φαλαγγίτης, spider-root: Anthericum liliastrum, Linn.; Plin. 27, 12, 98, § 124.
phalangites.short: phălangītes, ae, m., = φαλαγγίτης, spider-root: Anthericum liliastrum, Linn.;

phalangium.full: phălangĭum or -on, ii, n. (late collat. form phălangĭus, ii, m., Veg. Vet. 3, 81; Isid. 14, 6, 16), = φαλάγγιον. A kind of venomous spider, Cels. 5, 27, 9; Plin. 18, 17, 44, § 156; 8, 27, 41, § 97; 11, 24, 28, § 79. — Spider-root, anthericum, for phalangites, Plin. 27, 12, 98, § 124.

phalango.full: phălango or pălango, āre, v. a. phalanga, to carry away on a pole (anteclass.), Afran. ap. Perotti Cornucop. ad Epigr. 115. The passage is otherwise unknown.

phalannaeus.full: Phalannaeus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Phalanna, a city of Thessaly, Phalannœan: ager, Liv. 42, 65.
phalannaeus.short: Phalannaeus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Phalanna, a city of Thessaly, Phalannœan: ager, Liv.

phalantus.full: Phălantus, i, m., = Φάλαντος, a Spartan who emigrated to Italy and there founded Tarentum: et regnata petam Laconi Rura Phalanto, i.e. Tarentum, Hor. C. 2, 6, 11; Just. 3, 4, 7.—Hence, Phă-lantēus, a, um, adj., Phalantean: Phalanteum Tarentum, Sil. 11, 16.— Phă-lantīnus, a, um, adj., Phalantine, poet. for Tarentine: Phalantinus Galesus, Mart. 5, 37, 2.— Phălanthum, i, n., poetic name for the city of Tarentum, Mart. 8, 28, 3.
phalantus.short: Phălantus, i, m., = Φάλαντος, a Spartan who emigrated to Italy and there founded Tarentum: et regnata petam Laconi Rura Phalanto, i.e.

phalanx.full: phălanx (post-class. fălanx), angis, f., = φάλαγξ. In gen. Lit., a band of soldiers, a host drawn up in close order (poet.): Agamemnoniae phalanges, Verg. A. 6, 489: densae, id. ib. 12, 662: Tuscorum, id. ib. 12, 551: animosa (said of eight brothers fighting together), id. ib. 12, 277: junctae umbone phalanges, Juv. 2, 46.— Trop., a host, multitude (postclass.): culparum, Prud. Psych. 816.— In partic. Among the Athenians and Spartans, a division of an army drawn up in battle array, a battalion,

phalara.full: Phălăra, ōrum, n., = Φάλαρα, a harbor of Phthiotis, in Thessaly, on the Sinus Maliacus, now Stillida, Liv. 27, 30, 3; 12; Plin. 4, 7, 12, § 27.
phalara.short: Phălăra, ōrum, n., = Φάλαρα, a harbor of Phthiotis, in Thessaly, on the Sinus Maliacus, now Stillida, Liv.

phalaris1.full: phălăris (phălēris), ĭdis, f., = φαλαρίς or φαληρίς. The plant canarygrass (Phalaris canariensis, Linn.), Plin. 27, 12, 102, § 126.— A water-hen, coot, Varr. R. R. 3, 11 fin.; Col. 8, 15; Plin. 10, 48, 67, § 132.
phalaris1.short: phălăris (phălēris), ĭdis, f., = φαλαρίς or φαληρίς.

phalaris2.full: Phălăris, ĭdis (acc. Phalarin, Claud. B. Gild. 186), m., = Φάλαρις, a tyrant of Agrigentum, for whom Perillus made a brazen bull, in which those condemned by him were to be roasted alive. He caused Perillus to be the first to suffer by it (v. Perillus), but afterwards experienced the same punishment himself at the hands of his exasperated subjects, Cic. Off. 2, 7, 26; id. Att. 7, 20, 2; id. Rep. 1, 28, 44; id. N. D. 3, 33, 82; Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 33, § 73; Juv. 8, 81; Plin. 7, 56, 57, § 200; Ov. A.

phalasarneus.full: Phalasarnēus, a, um, adj., = Φαλασαρνεῖος, of or belonging to the Cretan city of Phalasarne, Phalasarnean, Liv. 42, 51; cf. Plin. 4, 12, 20, § 57.
phalasarneus.short: Phalasarnēus, a, um, adj., = Φαλασαρνεῖος, of or belonging to the Cretan city of Phalasarne, Phalasarnean, Liv.

phalerae.full: phălĕrae, ārum (neutr. phalera posita, Plin. 33, 1, 6, § 18; Jan. phaleras), f., = τὰ φάλαρα. Lit. A smooth, shining ornament for the breast, a metal disc or boss, worn by men, esp. as a military decoration: phalerae sunt belli ornamenta, Non. 554, 15 sq.; Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 12, § 29: phaleris et torque aliquem donare id. ib. 2, 3, 80: phaleras deponere, Liv. 9, 46; cf. Plin. 33, 1, 6, § 18: phaleris hic pectora fulget, Sil. 15, 255.—As a military mark of distinction: equites donati phaleris, Liv.

phalereus.full: Phălēreus, i, and Phălērĭcus, a, um, v. Phalerum.
phalereus.short: Phălēreus, i, and Phălērĭcus, a, um, v.

phalero.full: phălĕro, āre, v. a. phalerae, to adorn with trappings, ornament the breast (late Lat.): animalia phalerari sibi magis quam nodari gaudent, Ambros. Cant. Cantic. 1, 43.—Fig., to deck, set off, display: eloquentiae phalerandae gratiā, Ambros. Off. Min. 1, 12, 44.—Hence, phălĕrātus, a, um, adj. I. Lit., wearing an ornament for the forehead and breast: equi, Liv. 30, 17: cursor, Petr. 28: turba Mazacum atque cursorum, Suet. Ner. 30.— Trop., decorated, ornamented: phaleratis dictis aliquem ducere, wi

phalerum.full: Phălērum, i, n., = Φαληρόν, the oldest harbor of Athens, connected with the city by a long wall, with a demos of the same name belonging to it, Plin. 4, 7, 11, § 24.— Hence, Phălēreus (mostly trisyl.), ĕi and ĕos, m., = Φαληρεύς, of or from Phalerum, a Phalerian: Demetrius Phalereus, or simply Phalereus, a ruler of Athens and a famous orator, about B. C. 300, Cic. Leg. 2, 25, 64; id. Fin. 5, 19, 54; id. Div. 2, 46, 96; Nep. Milt. 6, 4.—Scanned as a quadrisyllable: Demetrius, qui dictus est Phale
phalerum.short: Phălērum, i, n., = Φαληρόν, the oldest harbor of Athens, connected with the city by a long wall, with a demos of the same name belonging to it, Plin.

phallovitrobolus.full: phallovitrobŏlus, i, m., or -vitro-bŏlum, i, n., a drinking-vessel shaped like a phallus, Capitol. Pertin. 8, 5 dub. (Momms. vitro, fundibuli).
phallovitrobolus.short: phallovitrobŏlus, i, m., or -vitro-bŏlum, i, n., a drinking-vessel shaped like a phallus, Capitol.

phallus.full: phallus, i, m., = φαλλός, a figure of an obscene shape, carried about at the festival of Bacchus, originally a symbol of the generative power of nature; a phallus, Arn. 5, 176; cf. Aug. Civ. Dei, 7, 21.
phallus.short: phallus, i, m., = φαλλός, a figure of an obscene shape, carried about at the festival of Bacchus, originally a symbol of the generative power of nature;

phanae.full: Phănae, ārum, f., = Φαναί, a harbor and promontory in the isle of Chios, noted for its wine, Liv. 36, 43, 11.—Hence, Phănaeus, a, um, adj., Phanœan: rex Phanaeus, the king of Phanœ, poet. of Phanœan wine, Verg. G. 2, 98.
phanae.short: Phănae, ārum, f., = Φαναί, a harbor and promontory in the isle of Chios, noted for its wine, Liv.

phanerosis.full: phănĕrōsis, is, f., = φανέρωσις, a manifestation, revelation (eccl. Lat.), Tert. adv. Haer. 30.
phanerosis.short: phănĕrōsis, is, f., = φανέρωσις, a manifestation, revelation (eccl.

phanote.full: Phănŏtē, ēs, and Phănŏtēa, ae, f., = Φανότη, Φανότεια, the name of several cities. A city in Epirus, with a castle, Liv. 43, 21.— A city in Phocis, also called Panope, Liv. 32, 18.
phanote.short: Phănŏtē, ēs, and Phănŏtēa, ae, f., = Φανότη, Φανότεια, the name of several cities.

phantasia.full: phantăsĭa, ae, f., = φαντασία, an idea, notion, fancy (post-Aug.): Nicetas longe disertius hanc phantasiam movit, Sen. Suas. 2, 15: cor tuum phantasias patitur, Vulg. Ecclus. 34, 6.—As a term of reproach: phantasia, non homo, a mere notion or fancy, the mere semblance of a man, Petr. 38 fin. (in Cic. Ac. 1, 11, 40; 2, 6, 8 al., written as Greek, and translated visum).— A phantom, apparition: (animus) colli-git visa nocturna, quas phantasias nos adpellamus, Amm. 14, 11, 18.
phantasia.short: phantăsĭa, ae, f., = φαντασία, an idea, notion, fancy (post-Aug.): Nicetas longe disertius hanc phantasiam movit, Sen.

phantasma.full: phantasma, ătis, n., = φάντασμα. An apparition, spectre, phantom (postAug.; cf.: idolon, imago, simulacrum): velim scire, esse phantasmata et habere figuram ... an inania, etc., Plin. Ep. 7, 27, 1: si phantasma fuit Christus, Tert. adv. Marc. 5, 7; Vulg. Matt. 14, 26; id. Marc. 6, 49.— In gen., an image, appearance, phantasm of an object (late Lat. for visum, imago, species): Alexandriam cum eloqui volo, quam nunquam vidi, praesto est apud me phantasma ejus, Aug. Trinit. 8, 6.

phantasmaticus.full: phantasmătĭcus, a, um, adj. phantasma, fantastic, imaginary, Isid. 8, 9, 7.

phantasos.full: Phantăsos, i, m., = Φάντασος, a son of Somnus, Ov. M. 11, 642.
phantasos.short: Phantăsos, i, m., = Φάντασος, a son of Somnus, Ov.

phantastice.full: phantastĭcē, adv., by the fancy (eccl. Lat.), Nebrid. ap. Aug. Ep. 8.

phantasticus.full: phantastĭcus, a, um, adj., = φανταστικός, imaginary, Cassiod. An. 2; Fulg. Myth. 3, 10.
phantasticus.short: phantastĭcus, a, um, adj., = φανταστικός, imaginary, Cassiod.

phaon.full: Phăon, ōnis, m., = Φάων. A youth of Lesbos beloved by Sappho without return, Ov. H. 15, 11; Plin. 22, 8, 9, § 20; Mart. 10, 35, 18.—As a prov. of coldness, Plaut. Mil. 4, 6, 32.— Phăon, ontis, m., a freedman of the emperor Nero, Suet. Ner. 48 and 49.

pharaeus.full: Phăraeus, a, um, adj., = Φαραῖος, of or belonging to the city of Pharœ, Pharœan: duces, Stat. Th. 2, 163.
pharaeus.short: Phăraeus, a, um, adj., = Φαραῖος, of or belonging to the city of Pharœ, Pharœan: duces, Stat.

pharanitis.full: phāranītis, ĭdis, f., pharanitis, a kind of amethyst, Plin. 37, 9, 40, § 122.
pharanitis.short: phāranītis, ĭdis, f., pharanitis, a kind of amethyst, Plin.

pharao.full: Phărăo, ōnis, m., = Φαραώ (Hebrew ), Pharaoh, the title of the Egyptian kings: Pharao nomen est non hominis, sed honoris, sicut apud nos Augusti appellantur reges, cum propriis nominibus censeantur, Isid. Orig. 7, 6; Prud. Cath. 12, 141; Vulg. Gen. 12, 15 et saep.
pharao.short: Phărăo, ōnis, m., = Φαραώ (Hebrew ), Pharaoh, the title of the Egyptian kings: Pharao nomen est non hominis, sed honoris, sicut apud nos Augusti appellantur reges, cum propriis nominibus censeantur, Isid.

pharetra.full: phărē^tra, ae, f., = φαρέτρα. Lit., a quiver for holding arrows (poet. and late Lat.): succinctam pharetrā, Verg. A. 1, 323: nec venenatis gravida sagittis, Fusce, pharetra, Hor. C. 1, 22, 3: pharetram solvere, to undo, open, Ov. M. 5, 379: venatricis puellae (Dianae), Juv. 13, 80: in pharetrā suā abscondit me, Vulg. Isa. 49, 2; Verg. G. 2, 125; Prop. 2, 9, 10; Ov. P. 4, 13, 38; id. Am. 3, 9, 7; Val. Fl. 3, 607; Stat. Th. 4, 259 al.— Transf., a kind of sundial in the form of a quiver, Vitr. 9, 8

pharetratus.full: phărē^trātus, a, um, adj. pharetra, furnished with or wearing a quiver, quivered (poet.): pharetrata Camilla, Verg. A. 11, 649: Persis, id. G. 4, 290: Geloni, Hor. C. 3, 4, 35: puer, i. e. Cupid, Ov. M. 10, 525: virgo, i.e. Diana, id. Am. 1, 1, 10: Semiramis, Juv. 2, 108.

pharetrazonium.full: phăretra-zōnĭum, ii, n., a quiverbelt, Not. Tir. p. 126.
pharetrazonium.short: phăretra-zōnĭum, ii, n., a quiverbelt, Not.

pharetriger.full: phărē^trĭger, ĕra, ĕrum, adj. pharetragero, quiver-bearing (poet.): clade pharetrigeri regis, i. e. of the Persian king Xerxes: regis, Sil. 14, 286.

pharia.full: Phărĭa ūva, a kind of grape in the neighborhood of Pisa, Plin. 14, 3, 4, § 39.
pharia.short: Phărĭa ūva, a kind of grape in the neighborhood of Pisa, Plin.

phariacus.full: Phărĭăcus, a, um, v. Pharus, A.

pharicon.full: phārĭcon or -um, i, n., = φαρικόν, a kind of poison, so named from its inventor, Pharicus, Plin. 28, 10, 41, § 158.
pharicon.short: phārĭcon or -um, i, n., = φαρικόν, a kind of poison, so named from its inventor, Pharicus, Plin.

pharis.full: Phāris, is, f., = Φᾶρις, a city in Messenia, afterwards called Pharae or Pherae, Stat. Th. 4, 226.
pharis.short: Phāris, is, f., = Φᾶρις, a city in Messenia, afterwards called Pharae or Pherae, Stat.

pharisaeus.full: Phărĭsaeus, i, m., = Φαρισαῖος, a Pharisee, a member of the Jewish sect of that name, usually in plur.: Phărĭsaei (Pharīsaei, Juvenc. 2, 574), ōrum, m., = Φαρισαῖοι, the Pharisees, a Jewish sect (eccl. Lat.), Tert. Praescr. 45; Isid. 7, 6, 40; Juvenc. 3, 221; Vulg. Marc. 2, 16 et saep.— Sing.: secundum legem Pharisaeus, Vulg. Phil. 3, 5.—Hence, Phărĭsaeus, a, um, adj., = Φαρισαῖος, Pharisœan: convivia, Sedul. 4, 66; Tert. adv. Marc. 5, 20.— Phărĭsăĭcus, a, um, adj., = Φαρισαικός, Pharisaic: sepu
pharisaeus.short: Phărĭsaeus, i, m., = Φαρισαῖος, a Pharisee, a member of the Jewish sect of that name, usually in plur.: Phărĭsaei (Pharīsaei, Juvenc.

pharitae.full: Phărītae, ārum, and Phărĭus, a, um, v. Pharus, C. and B.
pharitae.short: Phărītae, ārum, and Phărĭus, a, um, v.

pharmaceuticus.full: pharmăceutĭcus, a, um, adj., φαρμακευτικός, of or belonging to drugs, pharmaceutical, Cael. Aur. Tard. 5, 10, 126.
pharmaceuticus.short: pharmăceutĭcus, a, um, adj., φαρμακευτικός, of or belonging to drugs, pharmaceutical, Cael.

pharmaceutria.full: pharmăceutrĭa, ae, f., = φαρμακεύτρια, a sorceress (poet.), Verg. E. 8 in lemm.
pharmaceutria.short: pharmăceutrĭa, ae, f., = φαρμακεύτρια, a sorceress (poet.), Verg.

pharmacopola.full: pharmăcŏpōla, ae, m., = φαρμακοπώλης, a vender of medicines, a quack (class.), Cato ap. Gell. 1, 15, 9: circumforaneus, Cic. Clu. 14, 40; Hor. S. 1, 2, 1.
pharmacopola.short: pharmăcŏpōla, ae, m., = φαρμακοπώλης, a vender of medicines, a quack (class.), Cato ap.

pharmacus.full: pharmăcus, i, m., = φαρμακός, a poisoner, a sorcerer (post-Aug.), Petr. 107, 15.
pharmacus.short: pharmăcus, i, m., = φαρμακός, a poisoner, a sorcerer (post-Aug.), Petr.

pharmacusa.full: Pharmăcūsa, ae, f., = Φαρμακοῦσα, an island of the Ægean Sea, south-west from Miletus, where Cœsar was taken by pirates, now Farmako, Suet. Caes. 4; Plin. 4, 12, 23, § 71.
pharmacusa.short: Pharmăcūsa, ae, f., = Φαρμακοῦσα, an island of the Ægean Sea, south-west from Miletus, where Cœsar was taken by pirates, now Farmako, Suet.

pharnabazus.full: Pharnăbāzus, i, m., = Φαρνάβαζος, Pharnabazus, a Persian satrap under Darius Nothus and Artaxerxes, 412 to 377 B.C., Nep. Lys. 4, 1; Just. 5, 4, 1 al.
pharnabazus.short: Pharnăbāzus, i, m., = Φαρνάβαζος, Pharnabazus, a Persian satrap under Darius Nothus and Artaxerxes, 412 to 377 B.C., Nep.

pharnaces.full: Pharnăces, is, m., = Φαρνάκης. The name of two kings of Pontus. Grandfather of Mithridates, Just. 38, 6, 2; Plin. 33, 12, 54, § 151.— Son of Mithridates, defeated by Cœsar, Cic. Deiot. 5, 14; id. Att. 11, 21, 2; Suet. Caes. 37; Luc. 10, 476.— The name of a slave of Cicero, Cic. Att. 13, 30, 2; 13, 44, 3.

pharnacion.full: pharnăcīŏn (-ēon), ii, n., = φαρνάκειον, a species of the plant panax, named for Pharnaces, Plin. 25, 4, 14, § 33.
pharnacion.short: pharnăcīŏn (-ēon), ii, n., = φαρνάκειον, a species of the plant panax, named for Pharnaces, Plin.

pharnuprium.full: pharnuprium, i, n., a kind of figwine, Plin. 14, 16, 19, § 102 Jan.
pharnuprium.short: pharnuprium, i, n., a kind of figwine, Plin.

pharsalos.full: Pharsālos or Pharsālus, i, f., = Φάρσαλος, a city in Thessaly, where Cœsar defeated Pompey, now Fersala, Liv. 32, 33; 34, 23; 36, 14; Luc. 6, 350.—Hence, Pharsālĭcus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Pharsalus, Pharsalian: acies, Cic. Phil. 2, 29, 71: proelium, Cœsar's victory over Pompey, id. Deiot. 5, 13; 10, 29: acies, id. Lig. 3, 9: annus, Luc. 5, 391: rura, id. 7, 823.— Pharsālĭus, a, um, adj., Pharsalian: fuga, Cic. Phil. 2, 15, 39: pugna, in which Cœsar defeated Pompey, id. ib. 14, 8, 23 B
pharsalos.short: Pharsālos or Pharsālus, i, f., = Φάρσαλος, a city in Thessaly, where Cœsar defeated Pompey, now Fersala, Liv.

pharus.full: Phărus or -os, i, f. (m., Suet. Claud. 20), = Φάρος. An island near Alexandria, in Egypt, where King Ptolemy Philadelphus built a famous light-house, hence called pharus, now Faro, Mel. 2, 7, 6; Auct. B. Alex. 19.— Transf., of the lighthouse in the island of Pharos: Pharus est in insulā turris, magnā altitudine, mirificis operibus exstructa, quae nomen ab insulā accepit, Caes. B. C. 3, 112: superposuit turrem in exemplum Alexandrini Phari, Suet. Claud. 20; Juv. 6, 83; of other light-houses: phar

phascola.full: phascōla appellant Graeci, quas vulgus peras vocat, Paul. ex Fest. p. 223 Mull. ( = τὰ φάσκωλα, a wallet, scrip).
phascola.short: phascōla appellant Graeci, quas vulgus peras vocat, Paul.

phase.full: Phase, n. indecl., the Passover, a Jewish feast commemorative of the rescue of the first-born among the Jews from the destruction which visited the Egyptians: est enim Phase (id est transitus) Domini, Vulg. Exod. 12, 11: factum est Phase, id. 4 Reg. 23, 22.— Transf., the sacrifice offered at the Passover, the paschal lamb: immolare, Vulg. 2 Par. 35, 11; id. Deut. 16, 2.

phaselaria.full: phăsēlārĭa (făsēl- and făcēl-), ium, n. faselus, a dish of pickled French beans, Lampr. Elag. 20, 7.

phaselis.full: Phăsēlis, ĭdis, f., = Φασηλίς. A town in Lycia, on the borders of Pamphylia, now Tekrova, Cic. Verr 2, 4, 10, § 21; Liv. 37, 23 init.—Hence, Phăsēlītae, ārum, m., = Φασηλῖται, the inhabitants of Phaselis, the Phaselians (gen. Phaselitūm), Cic. Agr. 2, 19, 50.— A city in Judea, with a neighboring valley abounding in palmtrees, Plin. 13, 4, 9, § 44; Luc. 8, 251.—Hence, Phăsēlīnus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Phaselis, Plin. 23, 4, 49, § 95.

phaselus.full: phăsēlus (phăsell- and făs-), i, m. and f., = φάσηλος. Lit., a kind of bean with an edible pod, French beans, kidney-beans, phasel (phaseolus vulgaris of Linn.): viciamque seres vilemque phaselum, Verg. G. 1, 227: longa fasellus, Col. 10, 377; v. id. 2, 10, 4; Pall. 10, 12.— Transf., a light vessel (in the shape of a kidney-bean) made of wicker-work or papyrus, sometimes also of burned and painted clay (cf.: celox, lembus): epistulam de phaselo dare, Cic. Att. 1, 13, 1: phaselus ille quem videti

phaseolus.full: phăsĕŏlus (făsĕŏlus), i, m. dim. phaselus, I., a kind of bean with an edible pod, French beans, kidney-beans, phasel, Col. 11, 2, 72; 12, 9, 1; Plin. 24, 9, 40, § 65.

phasganion.full: phăsgănĭon, i, n., = φασγάνιον, the sword-lily, gladiole (pure Lat. gladiolus), Plin. 25, 11, 88, § 137.
phasganion.short: phăsgănĭon, i, n., = φασγάνιον, the sword-lily, gladiole (pure Lat.

phasiacus.full: Phāsĭăcus, a, um, v. 1. Phasis, B.

phasianarius.full: phāsĭānārĭus (fās-), i, m. phasiana, a pheasant-keeper (post-class.), Paul. Sent. 3, 6, 76.

phasianinus.full: phāsĭānīnus, a, um, adj. id., of or belonging to pheasants, pheasant- (postclass.): ova, Pall. 1, 29, 2.

phasianus.full: Phāsĭānus, a, um, and Phāsĭas, ădis, v. 1. Phasis, C. and D.
phasianus.short: Phāsĭānus, a, um, and Phāsĭas, ădis, v.

phasiolos.full: phāsĭŏlos (fās-), i, m., = φασίολος, a plant, also called isopyron, Plin. 27, 11, 70, § 94.
phasiolos.short: phāsĭŏlos (fās-), i, m., = φασίολος, a plant, also called isopyron, Plin.

phasis1.full: Phāsis, ĭdis or ĭdos (acc. also Phasin, Prop. 3, 22, 11; Sen. Cons. Helv. 10, 3: Phasim, Verg. G. 4, 367 al.; voc. Phasĭ, Ov. P. 4, 10, 52), m., = Φᾶσις. A river in Colchis, which empties into the Euxine Sea, now Rion, Mel. 1, 19, 12; Plin. 6, 4, 4, § 12: limosi Phasidos undae, Ov. M. 7, 6: sua jura cruentum Phasin habent, Stat. Th. 5, 457: Phasidis ales, a pheasant (v. in the foll. Phasiacus), id. S. 4, 6, 8; cf.: ultra Phasin capi volunt, quod ambitiosam popinam instruat, Sen. Cons. Helv. 10,

phasis2.full: Phāsis, ĭdis, adj., v. 1. Phasis, A.

phasma.full: phasma, ătis, n., = φάσμα, an apparition, spectre, phantom. The title of a comedy of Menander, Ter. Eun. prol. 9.— The title or principal part of a farce by a mimograph named Catullus: clamosum ut ageres phasma Catulli, Juv. 8, 186.
phasma.short: phasma, ătis, n., = φάσμα, an apparition, spectre, phantom.

phatnae.full: Phatnae, ārum, f., = Φάτναι, the Cribs, the space between two stars in the constellation Cancer (pure Lat. Praesepia), Cic. Fragm. ap. Prisc. p. 1170 P.
phatnae.short: Phatnae, ārum, f., = Φάτναι, the Cribs, the space between two stars in the constellation Cancer (pure Lat.

phaulius.full: phaulĭus, a, um, adj., = φαύλιος, bad; only in the term phauliae olivae, a bad kind of olives, Plin. 15, 3, 4, § 15 (al. babbiae); Macr. S. 2, 16, 6.
phaulius.short: phaulĭus, a, um, adj., = φαύλιος, bad;

phaunos.full: phaunos, i, m., a parasitic plant, Plin. 16, 44, 92, § 244.
phaunos.short: phaunos, i, m., a parasitic plant, Plin.

phaylleus.full: Phăyllēus, false reading for Phalaceus, q. v., Ov. Ib. 504.
phaylleus.short: Phăyllēus, false reading for Phalaceus, q.

phegeus.full: Phēgeus, i, m., = Φηγεύς, the father of Alphesibœa, Hyg. Fab. 244.—Hence, Phēgēïus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Phegeus, Phegean: Phegeius ensis, Ov. M. 9, 412.— Phēgis, ĭdis, f., = Φηγίς, daughter of Phegeus, Alphesibœa; acc. Phegida, Ov. R. Am. 455.
phegeus.short: Phēgeus, i, m., = Φηγεύς, the father of Alphesibœa, Hyg.

pheleta.full: phēlēta, ae, m., = φηλητής, a cheat, rogue, robber (post-Aug.): latrones, quos pheletas Aegyptii vocant, Sen. Ep. 51, 13.
pheleta.short: phēlēta, ae, m., = φηλητής, a cheat, rogue, robber (post-Aug.): latrones, quos pheletas Aegyptii vocant, Sen.

phellandrion.full: phellandrĭon, ii, n., = φελλάνδριον, a plant with leaves like ivy, Plin. 27, 12, 101, § 126.
phellandrion.short: phellandrĭon, ii, n., = φελλάνδριον, a plant with leaves like ivy, Plin.

phellos.full: phellos, i, m., = φέλλος, the cork-tree; transf., the part of the water-clock made from it, the cork, Vitr. 9, 8, 5.
phellos.short: phellos, i, m., = φέλλος, the cork-tree;

phemius.full: Phēmĭus, ĭi, m., = Φήμιος. A celebrated player on the cithara in Ithaca; hence, transf., of a good cithara-player, Ov. Am. 3, 7, 61.— A Roman surname, Inscr. Murat. 680, 7.

phemonoe.full: Phēmŏnŏē, ēs, f., = Φημονόη, a daughter of Apollo, priestess at Delphi, Plin. 10, 3, 3, § 7; 10, 8, 9, § 21; Isid. 8, 8, 4.—Transf., in gen., a prophetess, Lue. 5, 126; 187; Stat. S. 2, 2, 39.
phemonoe.short: Phēmŏnŏē, ēs, f., = Φημονόη, a daughter of Apollo, priestess at Delphi, Plin.

pheneos.full: Phĕnĕos or -us, i, f., = Φένεος, a town of Arcadia, with a lake of the same name, the fabled Stygian waters, Ov. M. 15, 332; Liv. 28, 7; Verg. A. 8, 165.—The city is called Phĕnĕum in Plin. 4, 6, 10, § 20.— Hence, Phĕnĕātae, ārum, m., = Φενεάται, the inhabitants of Pheneüs, the Pheneans, Cic. N. D. 3, 22, 56; Lact. 1, 6, 3.
pheneos.short: Phĕnĕos or -us, i, f., = Φένεος, a town of Arcadia, with a lake of the same name, the fabled Stygian waters, Ov.

phengites.full: phengītes, ae, m., = φεγγίτης, phengite, selenite, or erystallized gypsum, used for window-panes: in Cappadociā repertus est lapis candidus, atque translucens, ex argumento phengites appellatus, Plin. 36, 22, 46, § 163; lapis, Suet. Dom. 14.
phengites.short: phengītes, ae, m., = φεγγίτης, phengite, selenite, or erystallized gypsum, used for window-panes: in Cappadociā repertus est lapis candidus, atque translucens, ex argumento phengites appellatus, Plin.

pheos.full: phĕos, i, m., = φέως, a prickly plant, also called stoebe, Plin. 21, 15, 54, § 91 (al. phleos); 22, 11, 13, § 28.
pheos.short: phĕos, i, m., = φέως, a prickly plant, also called stoebe, Plin.

pherae.full: Phĕrae, ārum, f., = Φέραι, the name of several cities; the most celebrated are, The capital of Thessalia Pelasgiotis, the residence of Admetus, now Velestino, Plin. 4, 8, 15, § 29; Cic. Div. 1, 25, 53; Liv. 32, 13, 9.—Hence, Phĕraeus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Pherœ, Pherœan; poet., also, Thessalian: Jason, of Pherœ, Cic. N. D. 3, 28, 70; Plin. 7, 50, 51, § 166; Val. Max. 1, 8, 6: vaccae, of Admetus, Ov. H. 5, 151: duces, Thessalian, Stat. Th. 2, 16, 3: campi, Thessalian, Val. Fl. 1, 444.—
pherae.short: Phĕrae, ārum, f., = Φέραι, the name of several cities;

pherecleus.full: Phĕrē^clēus, a, um, adj., = Φερέκλειος, of or belonging to Phercelus (who built the ships with which Paris carried off Helen), Phereclean: puppis, Ov. H. 16, 22.
pherecleus.short: Phĕrē^clēus, a, um, adj., = Φερέκλειος, of or belonging to Phercelus (who built the ships with which Paris carried off Helen), Phereclean: puppis, Ov.

pherecratius.full: Phĕrecrătĭus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to the Grecian poet Pherecrates, Pherecratian: metrum dactylicum trimetrum Pherecratium constat ex spondeo, et dactylo, et spondeo, sive trocheo, ut est apud Horatium, grato, Pyrrha, sub antro, Mall. Theod. Metr. 4 (cf. Hor. C. 1, 5, 3); Sid. Ep. 9, 13 in carm.
pherecratius.short: Phĕrecrătĭus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to the Grecian poet Pherecrates, Pherecratian: metrum dactylicum trimetrum Pherecratium constat ex spondeo, et dactylo, et spondeo, sive trocheo, ut est apud Horatium, grato, Pyrrha, sub antro, Mall.

pherecydes.full: Phĕrĕcȳdes, is, m., = Φερεκύδης. A celebrated philosopher from Syros, an instructor of Pythagoras, Cic. Tusc. 1, 16, 38; id. Div. 1, 50, 112; reputed to be the inventor of prose, Plin. 7, 56, 57, § 205.—Hence, Phĕrĕcȳdēus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Pherecydes, Pherecydean: Pherecydeum illud, that saying of Pherecydes, Cic. Div. 2, 13, 31.— An Athenian chronicler, about 480 B.C., Cic. de Or. 2, 12, 53.

pheres.full: Phĕres, ētis, m., = Φέρης, the name of a Trojan; acc. Phereta, Verg. A. 10, 413.
pheres.short: Phĕres, ētis, m., = Φέρης, the name of a Trojan;

pheretiades.full: Phĕrētĭădes, ae, m., = Φερητιάδης, son of Pheres, king of Pherœ, i. e. Admetus, Ov. A. A. 3, 19.— Phĕrētĭădae (Phĕrēcўăd-), ārum, m., = Φερητιάδαι, the inhabitants of Naples, the Neapolitans; so named after Pheres, king of Pheræ: Pheretiadum muri, Sil. 12, 159.
pheretiades.short: Phĕrētĭădes, ae, m., = Φερητιάδης, son of Pheres, king of Pherœ, i.

pheretus.full: Pherētus, i, m., son of Jason and Medea, Hyg. Fab. 239.
pheretus.short: Pherētus, i, m., son of Jason and Medea, Hyg.

pherinum.full: Pherĭnum, i, n., a castle in Thessaly, Liv. 32, 14.
pherinum.short: Pherĭnum, i, n., a castle in Thessaly, Liv.

pherombros.full: phĕrombros, i, m., = φερόμβρος (rain-bringing), another name for cucumis silvaticus, App. Herb. 113.
pherombros.short: phĕrombros, i, m., = φερόμβρος (rain-bringing), another name for cucumis silvaticus, App.

pheugydros.full: pheugȳ^drŏs, ŏn, adj., = φεύγυδρος, hydrophobic, Cael. Aur. Acut. 3, 9, 98.
pheugydros.short: pheugȳ^drŏs, ŏn, adj., = φεύγυδρος, hydrophobic, Cael.

pheuxaspidion.full: pheuxaspĭdĭon, ii, n., another name of the plant polion, App. Herb. 57.
pheuxaspidion.short: pheuxaspĭdĭon, ii, n., another name of the plant polion, App.

phiala1.full: phĭăla, ae, f., = φιάλη. A broad, shallow, drinking-vessel, a saucer (cf. patera), Juv. 5, 37; Mart. 8, 33, 2; 8, 51, 1; 3, 41, 1; 14, 95 in lemm.; Plin. 33, 12, 55, § 156.— A censer, Vulg. 1 Par. 28, 17; id. Apoc. 5, 8.

phiala2.full: Phĭăla, ae, or Phĭălē, ēs, f., = Φιάλη, a companion of Diana, Ov. M. 3, 172.
phiala2.short: Phĭăla, ae, or Phĭălē, ēs, f., = Φιάλη, a companion of Diana, Ov.

phidias.full: Phīdĭas (first syll. short, Aus. Epigr 12, 1), ae, m., = Φειδίας, a famous sculptor, contemporary with Pericles, who made the celebrated statue of Jupiter Olympius, Cic. Ac. 2, 47, 146; id. Tusc. 1, 15, 34; id. Brut. 73, 257; id. Rep. 3, 32, 44; Plin. 34, 8, 19, § 49; Quint 10, 12, 8 sq.—Acc. Phidian, Cic. Fin. 2, 34, 115; Plin. 35, 8, 34, § 54.—Hence, Phīdĭăcus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Phidias, Phidian: caelum, Mart. 6, 13, 1: manus, Stat. S. 2, 2, 66: ebur, Juv. 8, 103.

phidippides.full: Phīdippĭdes or Phīlippĭdes, is, m., = Φειδιππίδης, a famous courier at Athens, Plin. 7, 20, 20, § 84; v. Sillig ad h. l. —The same called Phidippus, Nep. Milt. 4, 3.
phidippides.short: Phīdippĭdes or Phīlippĭdes, is, m., = Φειδιππίδης, a famous courier at Athens, Plin.

phidippus.full: Phīdippus, i, m., = Φείδιππος. Grandson of Hercules, one of Helen's suitors, Hyg. Fab. 80.— A famous courier, v. Phidippides.— A physician of king Deiotarus, Cic. Deiot. 6, 17.

phidon.full: Phīdon, ōnis, m., = Φείδων, a descendant of Hercules, to whom is attributed the invention of weights and measures, Plin. 7, 56, 57, § 198.
phidon.short: Phīdon, ōnis, m., = Φείδων, a descendant of Hercules, to whom is attributed the invention of weights and measures, Plin.

philadelphia.full: Phĭlădelphīa, ae, f., = Φιλαδέλφεια, an important city of Lydia, now the town and ruins of Allasher, Vulg. Apoc. 1, 11; 3, 7.—Hence, Phĭlădelphēni, ōrum, m., the inhabitants of the city of Philadelphia in Lydia, Philadelphians, Plin. 5, 29, 30, § 111; Tac. A. 2, 47.
philadelphia.short: Phĭlădelphīa, ae, f., = Φιλαδέλφεια, an important city of Lydia, now the town and ruins of Allasher, Vulg.

philadelphus.full: Phĭlădelphus, i, m., = Φιλάδελφος (loving one's brother or sister), a Grecian and Roman surname. Ptolemaeus Philadelphus, a king of Egypt, Plin. 36, 7, 14, § 67; Gell. 6, 17, 3.— Annius Philadelphus, Cic. Phil. 13, 12, 26.— Philadelphus, a slave of Atticus, Cic. Att. 1, 11, 2: L. CALPVRNIVS L. L. PHILADELPHVS, Inscr. Maff. Mus. Veron. 274, 9.
philadelphus.short: Phĭlădelphus, i, m., = Φιλάδελφος (loving one's brother or sister), a Grecian and Roman surname.

philae.full: Phĭlae, ārum, f., = αἱ Φίλαι, a small island in the Nile, south of Elephantine, with a city of the same name, now Jeziret Anas-el-Wojond, Plin. 5, 9, 10, § 59; Sen. Q. N. 4, 2, 3; Luc. 10, 313.
philae.short: Phĭlae, ārum, f., = αἱ Φίλαι, a small island in the Nile, south of Elephantine, with a city of the same name, now Jeziret Anas-el-Wojond, Plin.

philaeni.full: Phĭlaeni, ōrum (ōn), m., = Φίλαινοι, two Carthaginian brothers, who, out of love for their country, submitted to be buried alive, Sall. J. 79, 5; Val. Max. 5, 6, ext. 4; Mel. 1, 7, 6.—Philaenōn Arae, a frontier town of Cyrene named after them, the southernmost point of the Great Syrtis, Sall. J. 19, 3; called also Philaenorum Arae, Mel. 1, 7, 1; Plin. 5, 4, 4, § 28.
philaeni.short: Phĭlaeni, ōrum (ōn), m., = Φίλαινοι, two Carthaginian brothers, who, out of love for their country, submitted to be buried alive, Sall.

philammon.full: Phĭlammon, ōnis, m., = Φιλάμμων, son of Apollo, a celebrated singer, Ov. M. 11, 317; Hyg. Fab. 161.
philammon.short: Phĭlammon, ōnis, m., = Φιλάμμων, son of Apollo, a celebrated singer, Ov.

philanthropia.full: phĭlanthrōpĭa, ae, f., = φιλανθρωπία (philanthropy; hence), a benevolence, a present, gift (post-class.): philanthropiae nomine (al. philanthropii), Dig. 50, 14, 2.

philanthropos.full: phĭlanthrōpos, i, f., = φιλάνθρωπος (sc. herba), goose-grass, clivers: Galium aparine, Linn.; Plin. 24, 19, 116, § 176.

philargicus.full: phĭlargĭcus, a, um, adj., = φίλοσἀργικός, fond of ease (post-class.): philoso-phi tripartitam humanitatis voluerunt esse vitam, ex quibus primam theoreticam, secundam practicam, tertiam philargicam voluere, quas nos Latine contemplativam, activam, voluptariam nuncupamus, Fulg. Myth. 2, 1.
philargicus.short: phĭlargĭcus, a, um, adj., = φίλοσἀργικός, fond of ease (post-class.): philoso-phi tripartitam humanitatis voluerunt esse vitam, ex quibus primam theoreticam, secundam practicam, tertiam philargicam voluere, quas nos Latine contemplativam, activam, vo

philargyria.full: phĭlargўrĭa, ae, f., = φιλαργυρία, the love of money, avarice, Isid. Reg. Monach. 33.
philargyria.short: phĭlargўrĭa, ae, f., = φιλαργυρία, the love of money, avarice, Isid.

philema.full: phĭlēma, mătis, n., = φίλημα, a kiss, Lucr. 4, 1169.
philema.short: phĭlēma, mătis, n., = φίλημα, a kiss, Lucr.

philemo.full: Phĭlēmo or -on, ŏnis, m., = Φιλήμων. A Greek comic poet, a native of Soli, in Cilicia, and a contemporary of Menander, Plaut. Trin. prol. 10; cf. Quint. 10, 1, 72; Gell. 17, 4, 1; App. Flor. 3, p. 353.— An historian, Plin. 4, 13, 27, § 95.— In mythology, a pious rustic, the husband of Baucis, Ov M. 8, 631 sq.

philetaeria.full: phĭlĕtaerĭa, ae, f., and phĭlĕtae-ris, idis, f., = φιλεταίριον, a plant, called also polemonia, Plin. 25, 6, 28, § 64; 25, 8, 55, § 99.
philetaeria.short: phĭlĕtaerĭa, ae, f., and phĭlĕtae-ris, idis, f., = φιλεταίριον, a plant, called also polemonia, Plin.

philetas.full: Phĭlētas, ae, m., = Φιλήτας, a Greek elegiac poet of Cos, an instructor of Ptolemy Philadelphus, Prop. 3 (4), 1, 1; Quint. 10, 1, 58.—Hence, Phĭlētēus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Philetas, Philetean: Philetea aqua, i. e. elegiac poetry, Prop. 3, 3 (4, 2), 52: Philetei corymbi, id. 4 (5), 6, 3.
philetas.short: Phĭlētas, ae, m., = Φιλήτας, a Greek elegiac poet of Cos, an instructor of Ptolemy Philadelphus, Prop.

philippeus1.full: Phĭlippēus, a, um, v. Philippi, B.

philippeus2.full: Phĭlippēus, a, um, v. Philippus, A.

philippi.full: Phĭlippi, ōrum, m., = Φίλιπποι, a city in Macedonia, on the borders of Thrace, celebrated for the battle in which Octavianus and Antony defeated Brutus and Cassius, now Filibi, Mel. 2, 2, 9; Liv. Epit. 124; Vell. 2, 70, 1; Flor. 4, 7; Vulg. Phil 1, 1.—Hence, Phĭ-lippensis, e, adj., of or belonging to Philippi, Philippian: Philippense bellum, Suet. Aug. 9: proelium, the battle of Philippi, Plin. 7, 45, 46, § 148: Brutus, who fell at Philippi, id. 34, 8, 19, § 82.— Phĭlip-pēus, a, um, adj., of or
philippi.short: Phĭlippi, ōrum, m., = Φίλιπποι, a city in Macedonia, on the borders of Thrace, celebrated for the battle in which Octavianus and Antony defeated Brutus and Cassius, now Filibi, Mel.

philippicus1.full: Phĭlippĭcus, a, um, v. Philippi, C.

philippicus2.full: Phĭlippĭcus, a, um, v. Philippus, B.

philippopolis.full: Phĭlippŏpŏlis, ĕos (acc. -in or -im; abl. -i), f., = Φιλιππόπολις. A city of Thrace on the Hebrus, now Philippopoli, Liv. 39, 53, 13 sq.; Tac. A. 3, 38; Plin. 4, 11, 18, § 41; Amm. 26, 10, 4; 6.— A city of Palestine, perh. the ruins of Ghereyah, Aur. Vict. Caes. 28, 1.

philippus.full: Phĭlippus, i, m., = Φίλιππος, Philip, the name of several kings of Macedonia, the most celebrated of whom was the son of Amyntas, and father of Alexander the Great, Cic. Off. 1, 26, 90; Nep. Eum. 1, 4; id. Reg. 2, 1; Just. 7, 4 sq.; cf. Plaut. Aul. 4, 8, 4.— Transf., a gold coin struck by King Philip, a Philippe d'or, Plaut. Bacch. 4, 8, 27; so id. ib. 4, 8, 38; 41; 78 al.; Hor. Ep. 2, 1, 234; and, in gen., of other coins, Aus. Ep. 5, 19.— Hence, Phĭlippēus (collat. form Phĭlippĭus, Plaut. Poen.
philippus.short: Phĭlippus, i, m., = Φίλιππος, Philip, the name of several kings of Macedonia, the most celebrated of whom was the son of Amyntas, and father of Alexander the Great, Cic.

philistaea.full: Phĭlistaea (-thaea), ae, f., the southwestern portion of Canaan, Philistia; acc. to Hieronymus, another name for Palœstina, Hier. in Isa. 14, 29 and 31.
philistaea.short: Phĭlistaea (-thaea), ae, f., the southwestern portion of Canaan, Philistia;

philistaeus.full: Phĭlistaeus (-thaeus), i, m., a Philistine, Vulg. 1 Reg. 17, 8 et saep.
philistaeus.short: Phĭlistaeus (-thaeus), i, m., a Philistine, Vulg.

philistini.full: Phĭlistīni (-thīni), ōrum, and Phĭ-listhiim, indecl. m., the Philistines, the original inhabitants of Palestine, Vulg. Judic. 13, 1; id. 1 Reg. 28, 1 et saep.

philistinus.full: Phĭlistīnus, a, um, adj.: Philistinae Fossiones, the Philistine Fosses, at the mouth of the Po; and: Philistina fossa, Plin. 3, 16, 20, § 121.
philistinus.short: Phĭlistīnus, a, um, adj.: Philistinae Fossiones, the Philistine Fosses, at the mouth of the Po;

philistion.full: Phĭlistĭon, ōnis, m., = Φιλιστίων. A celebrated physician, Plin. 20, 5, 15, § 31; Gell. 17, 11, 16.— A pantomime, Mart. 2, 41, 15.

philistus.full: Philistus, i, m., = Φίλιστος, a historian in Syracuse in the reign of the tyrant Dionysius, an imitator of Thucydides, Cic. de Or. 2, 13, 57; 2, 23, 94; id. Brut. 17, 66; id. Q. Fr. 2, 13, 4; Nep. Dion. 3, 2; Quint. 10, 1, 74.
philistus.short: Philistus, i, m., = Φίλιστος, a historian in Syracuse in the reign of the tyrant Dionysius, an imitator of Thucydides, Cic.

philitia.full: phīlĭtĭa (in MSS. also phīdĭtĭa), ōrum, n., = φιλίτια (φιδίτια and φειδιτια), the public meals of the Lacedœmonians, Cic. Tusc. 5, 34, 98.

phillyrides.full: Phillўrĭdes, v. Phĭlўrĭdes, in 2. Philyra, B.

philo.full: Phĭlo or -on, ōnis, m., = Φίλων. An Academic philosopher of Athens, teacher of Cicero about A. U. C. 663, Cic. Brut. 89, 306; id. Ac. 2, 6, 17; id. Tusc. 2, 3, 9; 5, 37, 107; id. N. D. 1, 40, 113.— A celebrated architect in Athens, Cic. de Or. 1, 14, 62; Vitr. 7 praef. § 12; cf. Sillig, Catal. Artif. s. h. v.— A Greek physician, a native of Tarsus, the inventor of an eye-salve, Cels. 6, 6, 3.—Hence, adj.: Phĭlōnĭānus, a, um, of Philo: Philonianum antidotum, Marc. Emp. 20.—As subst.: Phĭlōnĭum, i

philocalia.full: phĭlŏcălĭa, ae, f., = φιλοκαλία, a love of the beautiful (eccl. Lat.), Aug. Cont. Acad. 2, 2; 2, 3.
philocalia.short: phĭlŏcălĭa, ae, f., = φιλοκαλία, a love of the beautiful (eccl.

philochares.full: phĭlŏchăres, is, n., = φιλοχαρές, a plant, called also philopaes and marrubium, Plin. 20, 22, 89, § 241.
philochares.short: phĭlŏchăres, is, n., = φιλοχαρές, a plant, called also philopaes and marrubium, Plin.

philocomasium.full: Phĭlŏcōmăsĭum, ii, n., = Φιλοκωμάσιον (tippling-friend), the name of a girl, Plaut. Mil. 2, 5, 8.
philocomasium.short: Phĭlŏcōmăsĭum, ii, n., = Φιλοκωμάσιον (tippling-friend), the name of a girl, Plaut.

philocteta.full: Phĭloctēta or Phĭloctētes, ae (corrupted form Philotes, ētis, Inscr. Grut. 42, 7), m., = Φιλοκτήτης, son of Pœas of Thessaly, celebrated as an archer, a companion of Hercules, who at his death gave him the poisoned arrows without which Troy could not be taken. On account of the stench proceeding from his wounded foot, he was left by the Greeks on the isle of Lemnos, but was afterwards taken by Ulysses to Troy, where Machaon healed his wound, and he slew Paris, Hyg. Fab. 102 Ov. M. 13, 313 sq.; C
philocteta.short: Phĭloctēta or Phĭloctētes, ae (corrupted form Philotes, ētis, Inscr.

philodemus.full: Phĭlŏdēmus, i, m., = Φιλόδημος, a famous Epicurean philosopher in the time of Cicero, the author of a work περὶ μουσικῆς, and of several epigrams, Cic. Fin. 2, 35, 119; cf. id. Pis. 29, 68, and Ascon. ad loc.
philodemus.short: Phĭlŏdēmus, i, m., = Φιλόδημος, a famous Epicurean philosopher in the time of Cicero, the author of a work περὶ μουσικῆς, and of several epigrams, Cic.

philograecus.full: phĭlograecus, a, um, adj., = φίλοσΓραικός, fond of Greek; as subst., a lover of the Greek language (ante-class.): vos philograeci, Varr. R. R. 3, 10, 1.
philograecus.short: phĭlograecus, a, um, adj., = φίλοσΓραικός, fond of Greek;

philolaus.full: Phĭlŏlāus, i, m., = Φιλόλαος, a Pythagorean philosopher of Croton, a disciple of Archytas, Cic. de Or. 3, 34, 139; id. Rep. 1, 10, 16.
philolaus.short: Phĭlŏlāus, i, m., = Φιλόλαος, a Pythagorean philosopher of Croton, a disciple of Archytas, Cic.

philologia.full: phĭlŏlŏgĭa, ae, f., = φιλολογία. In gen., love of learning or letters, literary pursuits, the study of polite literature (class.): ne et opera et oleum philologiae nostrae perierit, Cic. Att. 2, 17, 1; Vitr. 7 praef. § 4: Homerus philologiae omnis dux, id. ib.— In partic., explanation, interpretation of the writings of others, philology (post-Aug.): quae philosophia fuit, facta est philologia, Sen. Ep. 108, 24.

philologus.full: phĭlŏlŏgus, a, um, adj., = φιλόλογος. Of or belonging to learning, learned, literary: philologis et philotechnis rebus me delectans, Vitr. 6 prooem. 4: homines, Sen. Apoc. 5, 4.— Esp. of persons. Scholarly, learned, versed in history, antiquities, and literature (implying a broader culture than grammaticus, litterator; v. Krebs, Antibarb. 863 sq.): homines nobiles illi quidem, sed nullo modo philologi, Cic. Att. 13, 12, 3.—Subst.: phĭlŏlŏgus, i, m. — In gen., a person engaged in learned or liter

philomela.full: Phĭlŏmēla, ae, f., = Φιλομήλη. Lit., daughter of Pandion, king of Athens, and sister of Progne; she was violated by her brother-in-law, Tereus, and was changed into a nightingale: respondeo, Natas ex Philomelā atque ex Progne esse hirundines, Plaut. Rud. 3, 1, 12; Hyg. Fab. 45; Ov. M. 6, 424 sq.; Verg. E. 6, 79 Serv.; Mart. 14, 75, 1.— Transf., the nightingale (poet.), Verg. G. 4, 511.— The swallow: mortalium penatibus fiducialis nidos philomela suspendit, Cassiod. Var. 8, 31.— The name of a pla

philomelium.full: Phĭlŏmēlĭum, ii, n., = Φιλομήλιον, a city in Phrygia Major, now Ak Shehr, Cic. Fam. 3, 8, 15; 15, 4, 2; Cic. Verr. 2, 3, 83, § 191.—Hence, Phĭlŏmēlenses, ĭum, m., the inhabitants of Philomelium, the Philomelians, Cic. Verr. 2, 3, 83, § 191 Zumpt N. cr. (al. Philomelienses); Plin. 5, 27, 25, § 95.
philomelium.short: Phĭlŏmēlĭum, ii, n., = Φιλομήλιον, a city in Phrygia Major, now Ak Shehr, Cic.

philometor.full: Phĭlŏmētor, ŏris, m., = Φιλομήτωρ (mother-loving), an appellation of Attalus, king of Pergamus; and also of the sixth Ptolemy of Egypt, on account of his love for his mother Cleopatra, who had ruled the kingdom well during his minority, Just. 34, 2, 7 sq.; cf. of Attalus, Varr. R. R. 1, 1, 8; Plin. 18, 3, 5, § 22; Vulg. 2 Macc. 4, 21.
philometor.short: Phĭlŏmētor, ŏris, m., = Φιλομήτωρ (mother-loving), an appellation of Attalus, king of Pergamus;

philonianus.full: Phĭlōnĭānus, a, um, and Phĭlōnĭ-um, ii, v. Philo, III.
philonianus.short: Phĭlōnĭānus, a, um, and Phĭlōnĭ-um, ii, v.

philopaes.full: phĭlŏpaes, paedis, m., = φιλόπαις, a plant: marrubium nonnulli philopaeda vocant, Plin. 20, 22, 89, § 241.
philopaes.short: phĭlŏpaes, paedis, m., = φιλόπαις, a plant: marrubium nonnulli philopaeda vocant, Plin.

philopator.full: Phĭlŏpător, ŏris, m., = Φιλοπάτωρ (father-loving). An appellation of the fourth Ptolemy of Egypt, bestowed upon him in derision, because he had murdered his father and mother, Plin. 7, 56, 57, § 208; Just. 29, 1, 5; Arn. 6, 193.— A king of Cilicia, Tac. A. 2, 42.— With a Latin ending: Phĭlŏpăter, tris, a Roman surname, Inscr. Murat. 1490, 11.

philopoemen.full: Phĭlŏpoemen, ĕnis, m., = Φιλοποίυην, a celebrated general of the Achœan league, Liv. 35, 25 sqq.; 39, 49; Aus. Idyll. 12, 82; Just. 29, 4, 11.
philopoemen.short: Phĭlŏpoemen, ĕnis, m., = Φιλοποίυην, a celebrated general of the Achœan league, Liv.

philopygista.full: phĭlŏpȳgista, ae, m., = φιλοπυγιστής, an abandoned person, Schol. Juv. 9, 1.
philopygista.short: phĭlŏpȳgista, ae, m., = φιλοπυγιστής, an abandoned person, Schol.

philorhomaeus.full: Phĭlŏrhōmaeus, i, m., = Φιλορώμαιος, friend or lover of the Romans, a title given to Ariobarzanes, king of Cappadocia, Cic. Fam. 15, 2, 4.
philorhomaeus.short: Phĭlŏrhōmaeus, i, m., = Φιλορώμαιος, friend or lover of the Romans, a title given to Ariobarzanes, king of Cappadocia, Cic.

philosarca.full: phĭlŏsarca, ae, m., = φιλόσαρκος, a lover of the flesh, Auct. ap. Hier. Ep. 61.
philosarca.short: phĭlŏsarca, ae, m., = φιλόσαρκος, a lover of the flesh, Auct.

philosophaster.full: phĭlŏsŏphaster, tri, m. philosophus, a bad philosopher, a philosophaster, Aug. Civ. Dei, 2, 27 dub.

philosophia.full: phĭlŏsŏphĭa, ae, f., = φιλοσοφία, philosophy. Lit.: nec quicquam aliud est philosophia, si interpretari velis, quam studium sapientiae, Cic. Off. 2, 2, 5: omnia quae in philosophiā tractantur, id. Tusc. 5, 1, 1; id. Ac. 1, 2, 4: ars est enim philosophia vitae, id. Fin. 3, 1, 2; id. de Or 1, 15, 67; Sen. Ep. 89, 2 et saep.: videte ne quis vos decipiat per philosophiam, Vulg. Col. 2, 8.— Transf. A philosophical subject or question: circulus, in quo de philosophiā sermo habetur, Nep. Epam. 3, 3.— I

philosophicus.full: phĭlŏsŏphĭcus, a, um, adj., = φιλοσοφικός, of or belonging to philosophy, philosophic (post-class.; for the proper read., Cic. Tusc. 5, 41, 121, is philosophiae, acc. to Non. 134, 3, and 174, 18), Macr. S. 7, 1 Eyssen. (Jan. philosophis); Ambros. Off. 2, 9, 49; Sid. Ep. 4, 1.—Adv.: phĭlŏsŏphĭcē, in a philosophical manner, philosophically: vivere, Lact. 3, 14, 19.
philosophicus.short: phĭlŏsŏphĭcus, a, um, adj., = φιλοσοφικός, of or belonging to philosophy, philosophic (post-class.;

philosophor.full: phĭlŏsŏphor, ātus, 1, v. dep. n. [philosophus], to apply one's self to philosophy, to play the philosopher, to philosophize (class.): philosophatur quoque jam, non mendax modo'st, Plaut. Capt. 2, 2, 34; id. Ps. 4, 2, 18: philosophari est mihi necesse, at paucis, Enn. ap. Cic. Tusc. 2, 1, 1 (cited periphrastically ap. Cic. Rep. 1, 18, 30; id. de Or. 2, 37, 156; Gell. 5, 15 fin.; cf. Trag. Rel. v. 417 Vahl., and p. 53 Rib.); Cic. Tusc. 1, 37, 89; id. N. D. 1, 3, 6: sed jam satis est philosophatum,

philosophumenos.full: phĭlŏsŏphūmĕnos (fil-), on, adj., = φιλοσοφούμενος, philosophical: problemata, Sen. Contr. 1, 3, 8 Burs. dub.: locus, id. ib. 1, 7, 17 Burs.
philosophumenos.short: phĭlŏsŏphūmĕnos (fil-), on, adj., = φιλοσοφούμενος, philosophical: problemata, Sen.

philosophus.full: phĭlŏsŏphus, a, um, adj., = φιλόσοφος, philosophical: philosopha sententia, Pac. ap. Gell. 13, 8, 4: scriptiones, Cic. Tusc. 5, 41, 121: verbum, Macr. S. 7, 1, § 1: tractatus, id. ib. 7, 1, § 13.— Subst. phĭ-lŏsŏphus, i, m., a philosopher: philosophi denique ipsius, qui de suā vi ac sapientiā unus omnia paene profitetur, est tamen quaedam descriptio, ut is, qui studeat, omnium rerum divinarum atque humanarum vim, naturam causasque nosse et omnem bene vivendi rationem tenere et persequi, nomine h
philosophus.short: phĭlŏsŏphus, a, um, adj., = φιλόσοφος, philosophical: philosopha sententia, Pac.

philostorgus.full: phĭlostorgus, a, um, adj., = φιλόστοργος, loving tenderly, affectionate, esp. of the love of parents and children (postAug.): philostorgus, cujus rei nomen apud Romanos nullum est, Front. Ep. ad Amic. 1, 6; cf. id. ib. ad Verum, 7.— Written PHILOSTERGVS, a Roman surname, Inscr. Grut. 240, 1.
philostorgus.short: phĭlostorgus, a, um, adj., = φιλόστοργος, loving tenderly, affectionate, esp.

philotechnus.full: phĭlŏtechnus, a, um, adj., = φιλότεχνος, fond of the arts or relating to the study of the arts, philotechnic: res, Vitr. 6, prooem. § 4.
philotechnus.short: phĭlŏtechnus, a, um, adj., = φιλότεχνος, fond of the arts or relating to the study of the arts, philotechnic: res, Vitr.

philoxenus.full: Phĭloxĕnus, i, m., = Φιλόξενος (hospitable), a Roman surname: C. Avianus Philoxenus, Cic. Fam. 13, 35, 1.
philoxenus.short: Phĭloxĕnus, i, m., = Φιλόξενος (hospitable), a Roman surname: C.

philtrodotes.full: philtrŏdŏtes, ae, m., = φίλτρον-δότης. A plant, called also splenium, App. Herb. 56.— A plant, called also peristereos, App. Herb. 65.

philtrum.full: philtrum,, i, n., = φίλτρον, a love-potion, philter (poet.; only in plur.), Ov. A. A. 2, 105: philtra Thessala vendere, Juv. 6, 611.
philtrum.short: philtrum,, i, n., = φίλτρον, a love-potion, philter (poet.;

philus1.short: phĭlus, a, um, adj., = φίλος, beloved (post-Aug.

philus2.full: Philus (in MSS. also Pilus), i, m., a Roman surname: L. Furius Philus, a consul A. U. C. 618, Cic. Rep. 1, 11, 17; 1, 13, 19; id. Lael. 4, 14; 6, 21; 7, 25 sq.

philyra1.full: phĭlўra and phĭlŭra, ae, f., = φιλύρα, the linden-tree (pure Lat. tilia): rari (libri) in philyrae cortice subnotati, Mart. Cap. 2, § 136.— Transf. The inner bark of the linden-tree, of which bands for chaplets were made: displicent nexae philyris coronae, Hor. C. 1, 38, 2; Ov. F. 5, 337; Plin. 16, 14, 25, § 65; 19, 2, 9, § 31.— A sheet of the inner bark of the linden-tree prepared for writing upon, a writing-tablet, Dig. 32, 1, 52 prooem.— The skin or rind of the papyrus, Plin. 13, 11, 23, § 74
philyra1.short: phĭlўra and phĭlŭra, ae, f., = φιλύρα, the linden-tree (pure Lat.

philyra2.full: Phĭlўra, ae, f., = Φιλύρα, a nymph, daughter of Oceanus, who bore to Saturn the Centaur Chiron, and was changed into a linden-tree, Verg. G. 3, 92; Val. Fl. 5, 153; Hyg. Fab. 138.—Hence, Phĭlўrēĭus and Phĭlўrēus, a, um, adj., Philyrean: Philyreius heros, i. e. Chiron, Ov. M. 2, 676: Philyreia (al. Philyrea) tecta, i. e. of Chiron, id. ib. 7, 352.— Phĭlўrĭdes (Phill-), ae, m., Chiron, the son of Philyra, Ov. A. A. 1, 11; Prop. 2, 1, 60; Verg. G. 3, 550; Mart. 2, 14, 6 (poët. met. grat. Phīllўr-).
philyra2.short: Phĭlўra, ae, f., = Φιλύρα, a nymph, daughter of Oceanus, who bore to Saturn the Centaur Chiron, and was changed into a linden-tree, Verg.

philyrinus.full: phĭlўrĭnus, a, um, adj., = φιλύρινος, made of the inner bark of the linden-tree: liber, Serv. ad Verg. G. 3, 93.
philyrinus.short: phĭlўrĭnus, a, um, adj., = φιλύρινος, made of the inner bark of the linden-tree: liber, Serv.

phimus.full: phīmus, i, m., = φιμός, a dice-box, = fritillus: mitteret in phimum talos, Hor. S. 2, 7, 17.
phimus.short: phīmus, i, m., = φιμός, a dice-box, = fritillus: mitteret in phimum talos, Hor.

phineus.full: Phīneus, ĕi and ĕos (Gr. acc. plur. Phineas, Mart. 9, 26, 10), m., = Φινεύς. King of Salmydessus, in Thrace. He possessed the gift of prophecy, but was struck with blindness for having deprived his sons of sight, upon a false accusation made against them by Idœa, their step-mother, Ov. M. 7, 3; Val. Fl. 4, 425; Hyg. Fab. 19; Serv. Verg. A. 3, 209; Ov. A. A. 1, 339; id. R. Am. 355.— Transf., a blind man, Mart. 9, 26, 10.—Hence, Phīnēï-us and Phīnēus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Phineus, Phine

phintia.full: Phintĭa, ae, f., a city in Sicily, now Alicata or Licata, Cic. Verr. 2, 3, 83, § 192. —Hence, Phintĭenses, ĭum, m., the inhabitants of Phintia, the Phintians, Plin. 3, 8, 14, § 91.
phintia.short: Phintĭa, ae, f., a city in Sicily, now Alicata or Licata, Cic.

phintias.full: Phintĭas, ae, m., = Φιντίας, a Pythagorean, celebrated for his friendship with Damon, Cic. Off. 3, 10, 45; Val. Max. 4, 7, ext. 1.
phintias.short: Phintĭas, ae, m., = Φιντίας, a Pythagorean, celebrated for his friendship with Damon, Cic.

phlebotomia.full: phlĕbŏtŏmĭa (flĕb-), ae, f., = φλεβοτομία, blood-letting, phlebotomy: phlebotomiam adhibere, Cael. Aur. Acut. 2, 18, 104: phlebotomiā uti, Veg. Vet. 1, 14, 3.
phlebotomia.short: phlĕbŏtŏmĭa (flĕb-), ae, f., = φλεβοτομία, blood-letting, phlebotomy: phlebotomiam adhibere, Cael.

phlebotomice.full: phlĕbŏtŏmĭcē, ēs, f., = φλεβοτομική, blood-letting, phlebotomy, Cael. Aur. Acut. 1, 3, 39.
phlebotomice.short: phlĕbŏtŏmĭcē, ēs, f., = φλεβοτομική, blood-letting, phlebotomy, Cael.

phlebotomo.full: phlĕbŏtŏmo (flĕb-), āvi, ātum, 1, v. a., = φλεβοτομέω, to let blood from, to bleed, phlebotomize: aliquem, Cael. Aur. Acut. 1, 14, 111: utrum phlebotomandi necne sint aegrotantes ... non phlebotomati magno adjutorio privantur, id. Tard. 2, 13, 191; id. Acut. 2, 13, 88; Veg. Vet. 1, 24; Fulg. Myth. 3, 7.

phlebotomus.full: phlĕbŏtŏmus (flĕb-), i, m., = φλεβοτόυος, a lancet, a fleam: phlebotomo uti, Cael. Aur. Acut. 2, 19, 121: adhibendus, Theod. Prisc. 2, 21: transverso phlebotomo percutere, Veg. Vet. 1, 19, 1.
phlebotomus.short: phlĕbŏtŏmus (flĕb-), i, m., = φλεβοτόυος, a lancet, a fleam: phlebotomo uti, Cael.

phlegethon.full: Phlĕgĕthon, ontis, m., = Φλεγέθων (burning, blazing), a river in the Lower World, which ran with fire instead of water: Chaos et Phlegethon loca nocte silentia late, Verg. A. 6, 265: Tartareus, id. ib. 6, 551; Stat. Th. 4, 522: ardenti freto Phlegethon harenas igneus tostas agens, Sen. Thyest. 1018; id. Oedip. 162; id. Agam. 752. —Hence, Phlĕgĕthontēus, a, um, adj., Phlegethontian: ripa, Claud. Rapt. Pros. 1, 88.— Phlĕgĕthontis, ĭdis, f. adj., Phlegethontian: unda, Ov. M. 15, 532: lympha, id. ib
phlegethon.short: Phlĕgĕthon, ontis, m., = Φλεγέθων (burning, blazing), a river in the Lower World, which ran with fire instead of water: Chaos et Phlegethon loca nocte silentia late, Verg.

phlegma.full: phlegma (flegma), ătis, n., = φλεγμα, a clammy humor of the body, phlegm (post-class.): flegma dissolvere, Pall. 8, 6, 1; Veg. Vet. 3, 19; Hier. Ep. 52, 6; Isid. 4, 7, 29.
phlegma.short: phlegma (flegma), ătis, n., = φλεγμα, a clammy humor of the body, phlegm (post-class.): flegma dissolvere, Pall.

phlegmaticus.full: phlegmătĭcus, a, um, adj., = φλεγματικός, full of phlegm, phlegmatic: humor, Theod. Prisc. 4, 2; Isid. 4, 7, 32.
phlegmaticus.short: phlegmătĭcus, a, um, adj., = φλεγματικός, full of phlegm, phlegmatic: humor, Theod.

phlegmone.full: phlegmŏnē, ēs, f., = φλεγμονή, and phlegmōn, ŏnis, m., = φλεγμων, a burning heat or inflammation beneath the skin, Plin. 20, 4, 13, § 24.
phlegmone.short: phlegmŏnē, ēs, f., = φλεγμονή, and phlegmōn, ŏnis, m., = φλεγμων, a burning heat or inflammation beneath the skin, Plin.

phlegon.full: Phlĕgon, ontis, m., = Φλέγων (burning), one of the four horses of the sun, Ov. M. 2, 154.
phlegon.short: Phlĕgon, ontis, m., = Φλέγων (burning), one of the four horses of the sun, Ov.

phlegontis.full: phlĕgontis, ĭdis, f., = φλεγοντίς, a false reading for phlogitis, Plin. 37, 11, 73, § 189.
phlegontis.short: phlĕgontis, ĭdis, f., = φλεγοντίς, a false reading for phlogitis, Plin.

phlegra.full: Phlegra, ae, f., = Φλέγρα, a country of Macedonia, afterwards called Pallene, where the giants are fabled to have been struck with lightning when fighting with the gods, Plin. 4, 10, 17, § 36; Stat. Th. 2, 595; Val. Fl. 1, 564; Sen. Herc. Fur. 444.— As adj.: Phlegra giganteo sparsa est quo sanguine tellus, Verg. Cul. 28.—Hence, Phlegraeus, a, um, adj., Phlegrœan: Phlegraei campi, Ov. M. 10, 151: tumultus, Prop. 2, 1, 39: castra, Stat. Achill. 1, 484: pugnae, Val. Fl. 5, 693: victoria, Mart. 8, 7
phlegra.short: Phlegra, ae, f., = Φλέγρα, a country of Macedonia, afterwards called Pallene, where the giants are fabled to have been struck with lightning when fighting with the gods, Plin.

phlegraeus1.full: Phlegraeus, a, um, v. Phlegra, II.

phlegraeus2.full: Phlegraeus (-os), i, m., = Φλεγραῖος, one of the Centaurs, Ov. M. 12, 378.
phlegraeus2.short: Phlegraeus (-os), i, m., = Φλεγραῖος, one of the Centaurs, Ov.

phlegyae.full: Phlĕgўae, ārum, m., a predatory people from Thrace or Thessaly, who destroyed the temple at Delphi, Ov. M. 11, 414.
phlegyae.short: Phlĕgўae, ārum, m., a predatory people from Thrace or Thessaly, who destroyed the temple at Delphi, Ov.

phlegyas.full: Phlĕgўas, ae (acc. -an, Val. Fl. 2, 193), m., = Φλεγύας, the son of Mars, king of the Lapithœ, and father of Ixion and Coronis, Verg. A. 6, 618 Serv.; Stat. Th. 1, 713.

phliasius.full: Phlīāsĭus, a, um, adj., v. Phlius, A.

phliuntii.full: Phlīuntĭi, ōrum, m., v. Phlius fin.

phlius.full: Phlīūs, untis, m., = Φλιοῦς, a city of Peloponnesus, between Sicyon and Argolis, at the sources of the Æsopus, now Polyfengo, Liv. 28, 7, 6; Cic. Tusc. 5, 3, 8; Plin. 4, 5, 6, § 13.—Hence, Phlīāsĭus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Phlius, Phliasian: sermo, Cic. Tusc. 5, 4, 10: regna, Ov. Ib. 329.— Plur. subst. Phlīāsĭi, ōrum, m., the Phliasians, Cic. Tusc. 5, 3, 8.— Phlī-untĭi, ōrum, m., the same, Cic. Rep. 2, 4, 8. This passage Cicero afterwards corrected, and wrote Phliasii: Phliasios autem d
phlius.short: Phlīūs, untis, m., = Φλιοῦς, a city of Peloponnesus, between Sicyon and Argolis, at the sources of the Æsopus, now Polyfengo, Liv.

phloginos.full: phlŏgĭnos, i, m., = φλόγινος, a flamecolored gem, otherwise unknown, Plin. 37, 10, 66, § 179.
phloginos.short: phlŏgĭnos, i, m., = φλόγινος, a flamecolored gem, otherwise unknown, Plin.

phlogites.full: phlŏgītes, ae, m., = φλογίτης, i. q. phlogitis, Sol. 37.

phlogitis.full: phlŏgītis, ĭdis, f., = φλογῖτις, a flamecolored gem, otherwise unknown, Plin. 37, 11, 73, § 189.
phlogitis.short: phlŏgītis, ĭdis, f., = φλογῖτις, a flamecolored gem, otherwise unknown, Plin.

phlomis.full: phlŏmis, ĭdis, f., = φλομίς, mullein (pure Lat. verbascum), Plin. 25, 10, 74, § 121; cf. phlomos.
phlomis.short: phlŏmis, ĭdis, f., = φλομίς, mullein (pure Lat.

phlomos.full: phlŏmos, i, m., = φλόμος, mullein (pure Lat. verbascum), Plin. 25, 10, 73, § 120; cf. phlomis.
phlomos.short: phlŏmos, i, m., = φλόμος, mullein (pure Lat.

phlox.full: phlox, phlŏgis, f., = φλόξ (flame), a flower, otherwise unknown, Plin. 21, 11, 38, § 64.
phlox.short: phlox, phlŏgis, f., = φλόξ (flame), a flower, otherwise unknown, Plin.

phoba.full: phŏba, ae, f., = φόβη, a corymb, Plin. 18, 7, 10, § 53; v. Sillig N. cr.
phoba.short: phŏba, ae, f., = φόβη, a corymb, Plin.

phobetor.full: Phŏbētor, ŏris, m., = Φοβήτωρ, son of Morpheus, Ov. M. 11, 640.
phobetor.short: Phŏbētor, ŏris, m., = Φοβήτωρ, son of Morpheus, Ov.

phobodipsos.full: phŏbŏdipsos, i, f., = φοβόδιψος, hydrophobia, Cael. Aur. Acut. 3, 9, 98.
phobodipsos.short: phŏbŏdipsos, i, f., = φοβόδιψος, hydrophobia, Cael.

phoca.full: phōcă, ae, and phōcē, ēs, f., = φώκη, a seal, sea-dog, sea-calf (pure Lat. vitula marina), Verg. G. 4, 432: deformes phocae, Ov. M. 1, 300; so id. ib. 2, 267; Plin. 9, 7, 6, § 19. Proteus had a span of seadogs: Protea huc rexisse vias junctis super aequora phocis, Val. Fl. 2, 319. A grandson of Cephisus is fabled to have been changed by Apollo into this animal, Ov. M. 7, 388.
phoca.short: phōcă, ae, and phōcē, ēs, f., = φώκη, a seal, sea-dog, sea-calf (pure Lat.

phocaea.full: Phōcaea, ae, f., = Φωκαία, a maritime town of Ionia, a colony of the Athenians, whose inhabitants fled, to escape from Persian domination, and founded Massilia, now Fouges or Foggia, Mel. 1, 17, 3; Plin. 5, 29, 31, § 119; 5, 30, 32, § 121; Liv. 37, 31 sq.; cf. Gell. 10, 16, 4, and v. 2. Phocis, B.— Hence, Phōcaeensis, e, adj., Phocœan: Graeci, Plin. 3, 4, 5, § 35.—In plur. subst.: Phōcaeenses, ĭum, m., the Phocœans, Liv. 37, 21, 7; 38, 39, 12 Drak. ad loc.; Plin. 3, 4, 4, § 22; Just. 43, 3, 20.—
phocaea.short: Phōcaea, ae, f., = Φωκαία, a maritime town of Ionia, a colony of the Athenians, whose inhabitants fled, to escape from Persian domination, and founded Massilia, now Fouges or Foggia, Mel.

phocaicus.full: Phōcăĭcus, a, um, v. Phocaea, C., and 2. Phocis, D.

phocenses.full: Phōcenses, ĭum, v. Phocaea, E., and 2. Phocis, A.

phoceus.full: Phōcēus, a, um, v. 2. Phocis, B.

phocion.full: Phōcĭon, ōnis, m., = Φωκίων, an Athenian general, a contemporary of Demosthenes, whose life is written by Nepos.
phocion.short: Phōcĭon, ōnis, m., = Φωκίων, an Athenian general, a contemporary of Demosthenes, whose life is written by Nepos.

phocis1.full: phōcis, ĭdis, f., a kind of pear-tree on the isle of Chios, Plin. 17, 24, 37, § 237.
phocis1.short: phōcis, ĭdis, f., a kind of pear-tree on the isle of Chios, Plin.

phocis2.full: Phōcis, ĭdis, f., = Φωκίς, the country between Bœotia and Ætolia, in which were the mountains of Parnassus and Helicon, the Castalian spring, and the river Cephisus, Mel. 2, 3, 4; Plin. 4, 3, 4, § 7; Liv. 28, 5, 16; Ov. M. 1, 313; Stat. Th. 1, 64.— Transf., erroneously, in consequence of the similarity in the sound, for Phocœa: Phocide relictā, Graii, qui nunc Massiliam colunt, etc., Sen. Cons. ad Helv. 7, 8; Luc. 3, 340; 4, 256; Sid. Carm. 23, 13; Gell. 10, 16, 4.—Hence, Phōcenses, ium, m., the
phocis2.short: Phōcis, ĭdis, f., = Φωκίς, the country between Bœotia and Ætolia, in which were the mountains of Parnassus and Helicon, the Castalian spring, and the river Cephisus, Mel.

phocus.full: Phōcus, i, m., = Φῶκος, son of Æacus, who was slain by his brother Peleus, Ov. M. 7, 477; 11, 267.
phocus.short: Phōcus, i, m., = Φῶκος, son of Æacus, who was slain by his brother Peleus, Ov.

phoebe.full: Phoēbē, ēs, f., = Φοίβη. The moongoddess, sister of Phœbus, i. e. Diana, Luna, or the moon: vento semper rubet aurea Phoebe, Verg. G. 1, 431; id. A. 3, 371; 6, 18: Phoebe venantibus assit, Ov. Am. 3, 2, 51: jaculatrix Phoebe, id. H. 20, 229: innupta, id. M. 1, 476; Val. Fl. 7, 366.— Transf., night: tertia, Ov. F. 6, 235.— A daughter of Leda and sister of Helen, Ov. H. 8, 77.— Daughter of Leucippus, Ov. A. A. 1, 679; Prop. 1, 2, 15.

phoebeius.full: Phoebēĭus, a, um, v. Phoebus, A.

phoebeum.full: Phoebēum, i, n., = Φοιβεῖον, a temple of Phœbus, from which a place near Sparta received its name, Liv. 34, 38.
phoebeum.short: Phoebēum, i, n., = Φοιβεῖον, a temple of Phœbus, from which a place near Sparta received its name, Liv.

phoebeus.full: Phoebēus, a, um, v. Phoebus, B.

phoebigena.full: Phoebĭgĕna, ae, m. Phoebus-gigno, son of Phœbus, poet., an appellation of Æsculapius, Verg. A. 7, 773; Ser. Samm. 12, 186.

phoebus.full: Phoebus, i, m., = Φοῖβος (the radiant), a poetical appellation of Apollo as the god of light: quae mihi Phoebus Apollo Praedixit, Verg. A. 3, 251; Hor. C. S. 62; Prop. 1, 2, 27.—Poet. for the sun: dum rediens fugat astra Phoebus, Hor. C. 3, 21, 24: Phoebi pallidus orbis, Ov. R. Am. 256; id. M. 2, 110: tristior iccirco nox est, quam tempora Phoebi, id. R. Am. 585.—Hence, Phoe-bēĭus, a, um, adj., Phœbean, Apollinean: juvenis, i. e. Æsculapius, Stat. S. 3, 4, 6: anguis, of Æsculapius, Ov. M. 15, 74
phoebus.short: Phoebus, i, m., = Φοῖβος (the radiant), a poetical appellation of Apollo as the god of light: quae mihi Phoebus Apollo Praedixit, Verg.

phoenice1.full: Phoenīcē, ēs (Phoenīca, Cic. Fin. 4, 20, 56, v. Madv. ad loc.; Poenīcē, Vulg. 2 Macc. 4, 22 al.), f., = Φοινίκη, Phœnicia, a country of Syria, especially celebrated for the purple which came from there; its principal cities were Tyre and Sidon, Mel. 1, 12; Plin. 5, 12, 13, § 66; 5, 19, 17, § 75; 36, 26, 65, § 190; Cic. Ac. 2, 20, 66; id. Phil. 11, 13, 35; id. Fin. 4, 20, 56.—Called also Phoenīcĭa, ae, f., Mart. Cap. 6, §§ 678, 680; Serv. Verg. A. 1, 446; 3, 88.— A small island in the Ægean Sea,

phoenice2.full: phoenīcē (phoenīcĕa, ae), ēs, f., = φοινικέα, a kind of barley, mouse-barley, Plin. 22, 25, 65, § 135.
phoenice2.short: phoenīcē (phoenīcĕa, ae), ēs, f., = φοινικέα, a kind of barley, mouse-barley, Plin.

phoenicitis.full: phoenīcītis, ĭdis, f., = φοινικῖτις, a precious stone, otherwise unknown, Plin. 37, 10, 66, § 180.
phoenicitis.short: phoenīcītis, ĭdis, f., = φοινικῖτις, a precious stone, otherwise unknown, Plin.

phoenicius.full: Phoenīcĭus, a, um, v. 1. Phoenice, C.

phoenicobalanus.full: phoenīcŏbălănus, i, m., = φοινικοβάλανος, the Egyptian date, Plin. 12, 22, 47, § 103.
phoenicobalanus.short: phoenīcŏbălănus, i, m., = φοινικοβάλανος, the Egyptian date, Plin.

phoenicopterus.full: phoenīcoptĕrus, i, m., = φοινικόπτερος, the flamingo, phenicopter: phoenicopteri linguam praecipui saporis esse, Apicius docuit, Plin. 10, 48, 68, § 133; Cels. 2, 18; Sen. Ep. 110, 11; Mart. 13, 71 in lemm.; Juv. 11, 139; Lampr. Elag. 20.
phoenicopterus.short: phoenīcoptĕrus, i, m., = φοινικόπτερος, the flamingo, phenicopter: phoenicopteri linguam praecipui saporis esse, Apicius docuit, Plin.

phoenicurus.full: phoenīcūrus, i, m., = φοινίκουρος, a bird, the redtail, redstart, Plin. 10, 29, 44. § 86.
phoenicurus.short: phoenīcūrus, i, m., = φοινίκουρος, a bird, the redtail, redstart, Plin.

phoenicusa.full: Phoenīcūsa (Phoenīcussa), ae, f., = Φοινικοῦσα, one of the Æolian islands, now Filicuri, Plin, 3, 9, 14, § 94.
phoenicusa.short: Phoenīcūsa (Phoenīcussa), ae, f., = Φοινικοῦσα, one of the Æolian islands, now Filicuri, Plin, 3, 9, 14, § 94.

phoenissus.full: Phoenissus, a, um, and Phoenissa, ae, v. 1. Phoenice, D.
phoenissus.short: Phoenissus, a, um, and Phoenissa, ae, v.

phoenix1.full: Phoenix, īcis, a Phœnician; v. 1. Phoenice, A.

phoenix2.full: Phoenix, īcis, m., = Φοῖνιξ. The son of Amyntor, who was given by Peleus to Achilles as a companion in the Trojan war, Ov. M. 8, 307; id. A. A. 1, 337; Cic. de Or. 3, 15; Prop. 2, 1, 60. He brought to Peleus the news of the death of Achilles, Plaut. Bacch. 1, 2, 49.— A son of Agenor, brother of Cadmus and Europa, Hyg. Fab. 178.

phoenix3.full: phoenix, īcis (acc. Phoenica, Ov. M. 15, 393), m., the phœnix, a fabulous bird in Arabia. It was said to live 500 years, and from its ashes a young phœnix arose, Sen. Ep. 42, 1; Plin. 10, 2, 2, § 3; Tac. A. 6, 28; Aur. Vict. Caes. 4; Ov. Am. 2, 6, 54; id. M. 15, 393; Stat. S. 2, 4, 36; Claud. Laud. Stil. 2, 417.

pholoe.full: Phŏlŏē, ēs, f., = Φολόη. A forestclad mountain in Arcadia, on the borders of Elis, Plin. 4, 6, 10, § 21; Ov. F. 2, 273; Stat. Th. 10, 228.— A mountain in Thessaly, the abode of the Centaurs, Luc. 3, 198; Stat. Achill. 1, 138.—Hence, Phŏlŏē-tĭcus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Mount Pholoe, in Thessaly: monstra, i. e. the Centaurs, Sid. Carm. 5, 230.

pholus.full: Phŏlus, i, m., = Φόλος, a Centaur, son of Ixion, Verg. G. 2, 456; Ov. M. 12, 306; Luc. 6, 391; Serv. Verg. A. 8, 294; Juv. 12, 45.
pholus.short: Phŏlus, i, m., = Φόλος, a Centaur, son of Ixion, Verg.

phonascus.full: phōnascus, i, m., = φωνασκός (singing-master; hence), A teacher of singing and declamation: phonascus assum vocis suscitabulum, Varr. ap. Non. 176, 30; Suet. Ner. 23: dare operam phonasco, id. Aug. 84; Quint. 11, 3, 22.— A musical director, chorister: psalmorum hic modulator et phonascus, Sid. Ep. 4, 11.

phonema.full: phōnēma (fōn-), ătis, n., = φωνημα, a saying: Platonis fonemata, Front. Eloqu. p. 236 Mai.
phonema.short: phōnēma (fōn-), ătis, n., = φωνημα, a saying: Platonis fonemata, Front.

phonolenides.full: Phŏnōlĕnĭdes, ae, m., son of Phonolenus, a Lapitha, Ov. M. 12, 433.
phonolenides.short: Phŏnōlĕnĭdes, ae, m., son of Phonolenus, a Lapitha, Ov.

phonos.full: phŏnos (-us), i, m., = φόνος (murder), another name of the plant atractylis, Plin. 21, 16, 56, § 95.
phonos.short: phŏnos (-us), i, m., = φόνος (murder), another name of the plant atractylis, Plin.

phorbas.full: Phorbas, antis, m., = Φόρβας, the name of several mythic personages, Ov. M. 5, 74; 11, 414; 12, 322; Hyg. Fab. 14.
phorbas.short: Phorbas, antis, m., = Φόρβας, the name of several mythic personages, Ov.

phorcus1.full: phorcus, i, m., a false reading for porcus, Plin. 32, 11, 53, § 150.
phorcus1.short: phorcus, i, m., a false reading for porcus, Plin.

phorcus2.full: Phorcus, i (also Phorcys, ўos, and Phorcyn, ȳnos, acc. to Prisc. p. 690 P., but acc. to Serv., Verg. A. 5, 240, these forms are not used in Lat.), m., = Φόρκος, Φόρκυς, and Φόρκυν, son of Neptune, father of Medusa and the other Gorgons, and of the Grœœ, who was changed after death into a sea-god, Cic. Univ. 11, 35: Phorci chorus, Verg. A. 5, 240; or, Phorci exercitus, i. e. sea-gods, id. ib. 5, 824: pater Phorcys, Val. Fl. 3, 726; Luc. 9, 645.—Hence, Phorcys, ўdos (Phorcis, ĭdis), f., a female d
phorcus2.short: Phorcus, i (also Phorcys, ўos, and Phorcyn, ȳnos, acc.

phorimon.full: phŏrĭmon, i, n., = φόριμον, a kind of alum, Plin. 35, 15, 52, § 184.
phorimon.short: phŏrĭmon, i, n., = φόριμον, a kind of alum, Plin.

phorineum vinum.full: phorineum vīnum, i, n., a kind of wine, Plin. 14, 8, 10, § 79.
phorineum vinum.short: phorineum vīnum, i, n., a kind of wine, Plin.

phormio1.full: phormĭo (form-), ōnis, m., = φόρμιον, wicker-work of reeds or rushes, a mat, a straw covering, Dig. 33, 7, 12; Don. Ter. Phorm. prol. 27; 1, 2, 72.
phormio1.short: phormĭo (form-), ōnis, m., = φόρμιον, wicker-work of reeds or rushes, a mat, a straw covering, Dig.

phormio2.full: Phormĭo, ōnis, m. The name of a parasite in Terence, in a play of the same name.— A Peripatetic philosopher of Ephesus, who delivered a lecture in the presence of Hannibal on the duties of military commanders and on the art of war, Cic. de Or. 2, 18, 75; hence, transf., of a silly person, who talks about things which he does not understand: egomet in multos jam Phormiones incidi, id. ib. 2, 19, 77.— A Roman surname: Sextus Clodius Phormio, Cic. Caecin. 10, 27; id. Phil. 2, 6, 15.

phoroneus.full: Phŏrōneus (trisyll.), ĕi and ĕos, m., = Φορωνεύς, son of Inachus, king of Argos, and brother of Io, Hyg. Fab. 124; 143; 225; 274; Plin. 7, 56, 57, § 193; Stat. Th. 4, 889. —Hence, Phŏrōnēus, a, um, adj., Phoronean, poet. for Argive: Phoroneis sub antris, Stat.
