S. 3, 2, 101.— Phŏrō-nis, ĭdis, f. adj., Phoronean, poet. for Argive: Phoronides latuere venae, i. e. the river Inachus, Sen. Thyest. 115.—Subst.: Phorōnis, ĭdis, f., Io, Ov. M. 1, 668; 2, 524.
phoroneus.short: Phŏrōneus (trisyll.), ĕi and ĕos, m., = Φορωνεύς, son of Inachus, king of Argos, and brother of Io, Hyg.

phosphoreus.full: phosphŏrĕus, a, um, adj. Phosphorus, of or belonging to the morning-star, Prud. Cath. 5, 147 (al. Bosphoreum).

phosphorus.full: Phosphŏrus, i, m., = Φωσφόρος (the light-bringer). The morning-star: Phosphore, redde diem, Mart. 8, 21, 1; Mart. Cap. 8, § 851; 9, § 882.— A name of Harpocrates, Inscr. Grut. 88, 13.

photinus.full: Phōtīnus, i, m., = Φωτεινός, a male proper name. So esp., the bishop of Sirmium, founder of a Christian sect, the adherents of which are called Phōtīnĭāni, Isid. Orig. 8, 5; Cod. Just. 1, 5, 5.
photinus.short: Phōtīnus, i, m., = Φωτεινός, a male proper name.

phraates.full: Phrăātes or Phrăhātes, ae (is), m., = Φραάτης, the name of several kings of Parthia, Hor. C. 2, 2, 17; id. Ep. 1, 12, 27; Just. 41, 5, 9.
phraates.short: Phrăātes or Phrăhātes, ae (is), m., = Φραάτης, the name of several kings of Parthia, Hor.

phradmon.full: Phradmon, ŏnis, m., a celebrated statuary of Argos, Plin. 34, 8, 19, § 49.
phradmon.short: Phradmon, ŏnis, m., a celebrated statuary of Argos, Plin.

phragandae.full: Phragandae, ārum, f., a city in Thrace, Liv. 26, 25.
phragandae.short: Phragandae, ārum, f., a city in Thrace, Liv.

phragmites.full: phragmītes, is, m., = φραγμίτης, a kind of reed growing in hedges, Plin. 32, 10, 52, § 141.
phragmites.short: phragmītes, is, m., = φραγμίτης, a kind of reed growing in hedges, Plin.

phrasis.full: phrăsis, is, f., = φράσις, in rhetoric, diction (pure Lat. elocutio; post-Aug.): (in Albucio) non lexis magna, sed phrasis, Sen. Contr. 3 prooem.; acc. phrasin, Quint. 10, 1, 87 (id. 8, 1, 1, written as Greek).
phrasis.short: phrăsis, is, f., = φράσις, in rhetoric, diction (pure Lat.

phrenesis.full: phrĕnēsis, is, f., = φρένησις, madness, delirium, frenzy: phrenesis tum demum est, cum continua dementia esse incipit, etc., Cels. 3, 18 (al. phrenitis; shortly before written as Greek, φρένησις): die et phrenesin et insaniam viribus necessariam, Sen. de Ira, 1, 13, 3: manifesta, Juv. 14, 136; Ser. Samm. 7, 90; Prud. Hamart. 125.
phrenesis.short: phrĕnēsis, is, f., = φρένησις, madness, delirium, frenzy: phrenesis tum demum est, cum continua dementia esse incipit, etc., Cels.

phreneticus.full: phrĕnētĭcus (or phrĕnīt-), a, um, adj., = φρενητικός, mad, delirious, frantic, Cic. Div. 1, 38, 81: ex phreneticis alii hilares, alii tristes sunt, etc., Cels. 3, 18 (al. phreniticis); Mart. 11, 28 in lemm.—Poet., transf., of the winds, which rage, as it were, in a frantic manner, Varr. ap. Non. 46, 9.
phreneticus.short: phrĕnētĭcus (or phrĕnīt-), a, um, adj., = φρενητικός, mad, delirious, frantic, Cic.

phrenion.full: phrĕnĭon, ii, n., a plant, i. q. anemone, Plin. 21, 23, 94, § 164.
phrenion.short: phrĕnĭon, ii, n., a plant, i.

phrenitizo.full: phrĕnītīzo, āre, v. n., = φρενιτιζω, to be mad, crazy, frantic, Cael. Aur. Acut. praef.

phrixus.full: Phrixus (-os, erroneously written Phryxus), i, m., = Φρίξος, son of Athamas and Nephele, and brother of Helle, with whom he fled to Colchis on a ram with a golden fleece; he there sacrificed the ram, and hung up its golden fleece in the grove of Ares, whence it was afterwards brought back to Greece by Jason and the Argonauts, Hyg. Fab. 2; 3; 14; 21; Ov. H. 18, 143; id. A. A. 3, 175: Phrixi litora, i. e. the shores of the Hellespont, Stat. Achill. 1, 28; called also, semita Phrixi, id. ib. 1, 409
phrixus.short: Phrixus (-os, erroneously written Phryxus), i, m., = Φρίξος, son of Athamas and Nephele, and brother of Helle, with whom he fled to Colchis on a ram with a golden fleece;

phronesis.full: phrŏnēsis, is, f., = φρόνησις, understanding, good sense, prudence; personified as the mother of philology, Mart. Cap. 2, § 114.
phronesis.short: phrŏnēsis, is, f., = φρόνησις, understanding, good sense, prudence;

phryganion.full: phrygănĭon, ĭi, n., an animal, otherwise unknown, Plin. 30, 11, 50, § 103.
phryganion.short: phrygănĭon, ĭi, n., an animal, otherwise unknown, Plin.

phryges.full: Phrўges, um, m., = Φρύγες, the Phrygians, a people of Asia Minor, noted among the ancients for their indolence and stupidity, and also for their skill in embroidering in gold, Mel. 1, 2, 5; Plin. 8, 48, 74, § 196; Cic. Div. 1, 41, 92; id. Leg. 2, 13, 33.—In sing.: Phryx Aesopus, the Phrygian, Phaedr. 3 prooem. 52.—In partic., of Æneas, Prop. 4 (5), 1, 2; Ov. F. 4, 274; of Marsyas, Stat. Th. 1, 709; of a priest of Cybele (v. Gallus), Prop. 2, 22 (3, 15), 16; and with a contemptuous allusion, semi
phryges.short: Phrўges, um, m., = Φρύγες, the Phrygians, a people of Asia Minor, noted among the ancients for their indolence and stupidity, and also for their skill in embroidering in gold, Mel.

phryne.full: Phrȳnē, ēs, f., = Φρύνη. A celebrated hetœra in Athens, so wealthy that she offered to rebuild the city of Thebes after it had been destroyed by Alexander: nec quae deletas potuit componere Thebas Phryne, Prop. 2, 6, 6; cf. Quint. 2, 15, 9; Val. Max. 4, 3, ext. 3.— A Roman courtesan, Hor. Epod. 14, 16.— A procuress, Tib. 2, 6, 45.

phrynion.full: phrȳnĭon, ĭi, n., = φρύνιον, a plant, called also poterion, Plin. 27, 12, 97, § 122; 25, 10, 76, § 123.
phrynion.short: phrȳnĭon, ĭi, n., = φρύνιον, a plant, called also poterion, Plin.

phrynos.full: phrȳnos, i, m., = φρῦνος, a kind of venomous frog, living in thorn-hedges, Plin. 32, 5, 19, § 50.
phrynos.short: phrȳnos, i, m., = φρῦνος, a kind of venomous frog, living in thorn-hedges, Plin.

phryx1.full: Phryx, Phrўgis, m., = Φρύξ, a river in Ionia, rising in Lydia, and falling into the Hermus, otherwise called Hyllus, Plin. 5, 29, 31, § 119; oftener, Phrygius amnis, Liv. 37, 37, 9; 37, 38, 2; cf. Plin. 5, 29, 31, § 119; Strab. 13, 4, 5.
phryx1.short: Phryx, Phrўgis, m., = Φρύξ, a river in Ionia, rising in Lydia, and falling into the Hermus, otherwise called Hyllus, Plin.

phryx2.full: Phryx, Phrўgis, v. Phryges init. and G.

phryxianus.full: Phryxĭānus, a, um, v. Phrixus fin.

phryxonides.full: Phryxŏnĭdes nymphae, the fabled rearers of the first bees, Col. 9, 2, 3.
phryxonides.short: Phryxŏnĭdes nymphae, the fabled rearers of the first bees, Col.

phthas.full: Phthas, m., = Φθάς, the Egyplian Vulcan: secundus Vulcanus Nilo natus, Phthas, ut Aegyptii appellant, Cic. N. D. 3, 22, 55.
phthas.short: Phthas, m., = Φθάς, the Egyplian Vulcan: secundus Vulcanus Nilo natus, Phthas, ut Aegyptii appellant, Cic.

phthia.full: Phthīa, ae, f., = Φθία, a city in Thessaliotis, the birthplace of Achilles, Mel. 2, 3, 4; Verg. A. 1, 284.—Hence, Phthīas, ădis, f., a Phthian woman, Ov. H. 7, 165 (al. Phthia).— Phthīōta, ae, and Phthī-ōtes, ae, m., = Φθιώτης, a Phthiote, Cic. Tusc. 1, 10, 21.—In plur., the Phthiotes, Plin. 4, 7, 14, § 28; Liv. 33, 32; 34; 36, 15.— Phthīōtis, ĭdis, f., = Φθιῶτις, Phthiotis, a district of Thessaly, in which Phthia lay, Plin. 4, 8, 15, § 29; Liv. 28, 6.— Phthī-ōtĭcus, a, um, adj., = Φθιωτικός, of
phthia.short: Phthīa, ae, f., = Φθία, a city in Thessaliotis, the birthplace of Achilles, Mel.

phthir.full: phthīr, m., = φθείρ, louse, a sea-parasite (pure Lat. pediculus marinus), Plin. 32, 11, 53, § 150.
phthir.short: phthīr, m., = φθείρ, louse, a sea-parasite (pure Lat.

phthiriasis.full: phthīrĭăsis, is, f., = φθειρίασις, the lousy disease, phthiriasis, Plin. 26, 13, 86, § 138; 20, 6, 23, § 53; 25, 5, 25, § 61 al.
phthiriasis.short: phthīrĭăsis, is, f., = φθειρίασις, the lousy disease, phthiriasis, Plin.

phthirophagi.full: Phthīrŏphăgi, ōrum, m., = Φθειροφάγοι (lice-eaters), a people of Sarmatia, Plin. 6, 4, 4, § 14.
phthirophagi.short: Phthīrŏphăgi, ōrum, m., = Φθειροφάγοι (lice-eaters), a people of Sarmatia, Plin.

phthirophoros.full: phthīrŏphŏros, i, f., = φθειροφόρος, a kind of pine-tree that bears very small cones, Plin. 16, 10, 19, § 49.
phthirophoros.short: phthīrŏphŏros, i, f., = φθειροφόρος, a kind of pine-tree that bears very small cones, Plin.

phthisicus.full: phthĭsĭcus, a, um, adj., = φθισικός, consumptive, phthisical, Plin. 20, 6, 21, § 46; 24, 16, 19, § 28; 28, 17, 67, § 230; Vitr, 2, 9; Scrib. Comp. 186; Mart. 11, 21, 7.
phthisicus.short: phthĭsĭcus, a, um, adj., = φθισικός, consumptive, phthisical, Plin.

phthisis.full: phthĭsis, is, f., = φθίσις, consumption, phthisis: vera phthisis est, Cels. 3, 22; Sen. Ep. 91, 5; 75, 10; Plin. 26, 7, 21, § 38; 31, 6, 33, § 62; Col. 6, 14; Juv. 13, 95; Gell. 4, 2, 4.
phthisis.short: phthĭsis, is, f., = φθίσις, consumption, phthisis: vera phthisis est, Cels.

phthisisco.full: phthĭsisco, ĕre, v. inch. n. [phthisis], to become consumptive or phthisical: phthisiscentibus medicabilis piscina, Sid. Ep. 5, 14.

phthitarus.full: phthitărus, i, m., a false read. for phthir (q. v.), Plin. 32, 11, 53, § 150.
phthitarus.short: phthitărus, i, m., a false read.

phthongus.full: phthongus, i, m., = φθόγγος, a sound, tone: Saturnum dicebat Dorico moveri phthongo, Jovem Phrygio, Plin. 2, 22, 20, § 84; Fulg. Myth. 3, 2 sq.; Mart. Cap. 9, § 939 (pure Lat. sonus).
phthongus.short: phthongus, i, m., = φθόγγος, a sound, tone: Saturnum dicebat Dorico moveri phthongo, Jovem Phrygio, Plin.

phthorius.full: phthŏrĭus, a, um, adj., = φθόριος, corrupting, destructive: hoc vinum phthorium vocant, quoniam facit abortus, Plin. 14, 16, 19, § 110.
phthorius.short: phthŏrĭus, a, um, adj., = φθόριος, corrupting, destructive: hoc vinum phthorium vocant, quoniam facit abortus, Plin.

phu1.full: phū, n. indecl., or phun, = φοῦ, a kind of valerian, Plin. 12, 12, 26, § 45; Scrib. Comp. 176; 177.

phu2.full: phu or fu, interj., foh! fugh! phu in malam crucem, Plaut. Ps. 5, 2, 5 (Ritschl, fu); cf. Charis. p. 213 P.; Prisc. p. 1024 ib.
phu2.short: phu or fu, interj., foh! fugh! phu in malam crucem, Plaut.

phy.full: phy, interj., pish! tush! Ter. Ad. 3, 3, 58; cf. Prisc. p. 1024 P.

phyaces.full: Phўāces, ae, m., a king of the Getœ: nec vincet saevum Cyclops feritate Phyacen, Ov. P. 4, 10, 23.
phyaces.short: Phўāces, ae, m., a king of the Getœ: nec vincet saevum Cyclops feritate Phyacen, Ov.

phycis.full: phȳcis, ĭdis, f., = φυκίς, a fish that lives among sea-weed, and changes its color at various seasons of the year, perh. the lamprey, Plin. 9, 26, 42, § 81.
phycis.short: phȳcis, ĭdis, f., = φυκίς, a fish that lives among sea-weed, and changes its color at various seasons of the year, perh.

phycitis.full: phȳcītis, ĭdis, f., = φυκῖτις, a precious stone, otherwise unknown, Plin. 37, 10, 66, § 180.
phycitis.short: phȳcītis, ĭdis, f., = φυκῖτις, a precious stone, otherwise unknown, Plin.

phycos.full: phȳcos, i, n., = φῦκος, sea-weed, seawrack, = fucus, Plin. 13, 25, 48, § 135: phycos thalassion, rock-moss, orchil (pure Lat. fucus marinus), id. 26, 10, 66, § 103.
phycos.short: phȳcos, i, n., = φῦκος, sea-weed, seawrack, = fucus, Plin.

phycus.full: Phȳcūs, untis, m., = Φυκοῦς, a promontory in Cyrene, the mod. Ras-Sem or ElRazat, Mel. 1, 7, 5; Plin. 4, 12, 20, § 60; Luc. 9, 40.
phycus.short: Phȳcūs, untis, m., = Φυκοῦς, a promontory in Cyrene, the mod.

phylaca.full: phўlăca, ae, f., = φυλακή, a prison (pure Lat. custodia): abductus in phylacam, Plaut. Capt. 3, 5, 93.
phylaca.short: phўlăca, ae, f., = φυλακή, a prison (pure Lat.

phylace.full: Phўlăcē, ēs, f., = Φυλακή. A city of Thessaly, where Protesilaus reigned; its ruins are near the mod. Ghidek, Plin. 4, 9, 16, § 32.—Hence, Phўlăcēis, ĭdis, adj. f., Phylacian: matres Phylaceides, Ov. H. 13, 35.—Subst.: Phўlăcēis, ĭdis, f. (acc. Phylaceida), Laodamia, wife of Protesilaus, Stat. S. 5, 3, 273.— Phў-lăcēĭus, a, um, adj., Phylacian: conjux, i. e. Laodamia, Ov. Tr. 5, 14, 39.— Subst. plur.: Phўlăcaei, ōrum, m., the Phylacians, Plin. 4, 9, 16, § 34.— Phȳ^lăcĭ-des (Phyll-), ae, m., Phyl

phylacista.full: phўlăcista (phŭlă-), ae, m., = φυλακιστής, a jailer; hence, comic. transf., of a creditor who duns for his money, and makes a prisoner of the debtor by keeping a watch on his house, Plaut. Aul. 3, 5, 44.
phylacista.short: phўlăcista (phŭlă-), ae, m., = φυλακιστής, a jailer;

phylacterium.full: phўlactērĭum (fўl-), ĭi, n., = φυλακτήριον. In gen., an amulet: dolorem oculorum ut non patiaris ... de tribus cerasis lapillos pertundes et lino inserto pro phylacterio uteris, Marc. Emp. 8.— In partic. Slips of parchment worn by the Jews on the forehead and the left arm, phylacteries, Vulg. Matt. 23, 5; Hier. in Matt. 4, 23, 5.— Chains and medals worn by gladiators around their necks as tokens of victory, Vet. Schol. ad Juv. 3, 68.

phylarchus.full: phўlarchus, i, m., = φύλαρχος, the chief of a tribe, a prince, emir: phylarchus Arabum, Cic. Fam. 15, 1, 2: Saracenorum, Amm. 24, 2; Sex. Ruf. Brev. 14.
phylarchus.short: phўlarchus, i, m., = φύλαρχος, the chief of a tribe, a prince, emir: phylarchus Arabum, Cic.

phyle.full: Phȳlē, ēs, f., = Φυλή, a castle in Attica, Nep. Thras. 2, 1; Just. 5, 9, 6.
phyle.short: Phȳlē, ēs, f., = Φυλή, a castle in Attica, Nep.

phyllacides.full: Phyllăcĭdes, i. q. Phylacides, under Phylace.

phyllanthes.full: phyllanthes, is, n., = φυλλανθές, a plant with prickly leaves, Plin. 21, 16, 59, § 99.
phyllanthes.short: phyllanthes, is, n., = φυλλανθές, a plant with prickly leaves, Plin.

phylleis.full: Phyllēis, ĭdis, adj. f., = Φυλληίς, of or from the city of Phyllus, in Thessaly: matres Phylleides, i. e. Thessalian, Ov. H. 13, 35.

phylleius.full: Phyllēĭus, a, um, adj., = Φυλλήϊος, of or belonging to Phyllus in Thessaly, Phylleian: juvenis, i. e. Cœneus, Ov. M. 12, 479: mater, perh. Laodamia, id. A. A. 3, 783.
phylleius.short: Phyllēĭus, a, um, adj., = Φυλλήϊος, of or belonging to Phyllus in Thessaly, Phylleian: juvenis, i.

phyllis.full: Phyllis, ĭdis and ĭdos, f., = Φυλλίς. Daughter of King Sithon of Thrace; she was changed into an almond-tree, Ov. H. 2, 98; Hyg. Fab. 59, 243; Plin. 16, 26, 45, § 108; Serv. Verg. E. 5, 10; Pers. 1, 34.— Transf., an almond-tree, Pall. Insit. 149. — A female proper name, Verg. E. 3, 78; Hor. C. 4, 11, 3; cf. Suet. Dom. 17.
phyllis.short: Phyllis, ĭdis and ĭdos, f., = Φυλλίς.

phyllius.full: Phyllĭus, ii, m., a Bœotian who was in love with Cygnus, Ov. M. 7, 372.
phyllius.short: Phyllĭus, ii, m., a Bœotian who was in love with Cygnus, Ov.

phyllodoce.full: Phyllŏdŏcē, ēs, f., a sea-nymph, daughter of Nereus and Doris, Verg. G. 4, 336; Macr. S. 5, 17; Hyg. Fab. praef.
phyllodoce.short: Phyllŏdŏcē, ēs, f., a sea-nymph, daughter of Nereus and Doris, Verg.

phyllon.full: phyllon, i, n., = φύλλον, a plant, called also leucacantha, Plin. 22, 16, 18, § 40.
phyllon.short: phyllon, i, n., = φύλλον, a plant, called also leucacantha, Plin.

phyllos.full: Phyllos, i, f., a region in Arcadia, Stat. Th. 4, 45.
phyllos.short: Phyllos, i, f., a region in Arcadia, Stat.

phyma.full: phȳma, ătis, n., = φῦμα, a kind of boil or tumor, Cels. 5, 28; 5, 18, 23; 33.
phyma.short: phȳma, ătis, n., = φῦμα, a kind of boil or tumor, Cels.

phynon.full: phynon, ŏnis, m., a kind of eye-salve, Cels. 6, 6, 20.
phynon.short: phynon, ŏnis, m., a kind of eye-salve, Cels.

phyrama.full: phȳrāma, ătis, n., = φύραμα, the gum of the tree called metops, Plin. 12, 23, 49, § 107.
phyrama.short: phȳrāma, ătis, n., = φύραμα, the gum of the tree called metops, Plin.

physcon.full: Physcon, ōnis, m., = Φύσκων (Pot-belly, Fat-paunch), an epithet of Ptolemy Euergetes II. of Egypt, Just. 38, 8; Tert. Pall. 4.
physcon.short: Physcon, ōnis, m., = Φύσκων (Pot-belly, Fat-paunch), an epithet of Ptolemy Euergetes II.

physema.full: phȳsēma, ătis, n., = φύσημα (a bladder; hence), a hollow, empty pearl, Plin. 9, 35, 54, § 108.

physeter.full: phȳsēter, ēris, m., = φυσητήρ. A blow-pipe, blowing-tube, Pelag. Vet. fin.— Transf., a large species of whale, a cachalot, spermaceti whale, Plin. 9, 4, 3, § 8; Sen. Hippol. 1030.

physica1.full: phўsĭca, ae, and phўsĭcē, ēs, f., = φυσική, natural science, nutural philosophy, physics, Cic. Ac. 1, 7, 25; id. Fin. 3, 21, 72; 3, 22, 73.
physica1.short: phўsĭca, ae, and phўsĭcē, ēs, f., = φυσική, natural science, nutural philosophy, physics, Cic.

physica2.full: phўsĭca, ōrum, v. physicus, II. B.

physicus.full: phўsĭcus (scanned phȳsĭcus, Sid. Carm. 15, 101), a, um, adj., = φυσικός, of or belonging to natural philosophy or physics, natural, physical: quiddam physicum, something relating to physics, Cic. Div. 2, 59, 122: ratio, id. N. D. 2, 21, 54: homines, naturalists, Marc. Emp. Carm. Med. 19.— Subst. phўsĭcus, i, m., a natural philosopher, naturalist: ut ait physicus Anaxagoras, Varr. R. R. 1, 40: Democritus, id. ib. 1, 1, 8: non pudet igitur physicum, id est speculatorem venatoremque naturae, petere

physiognomon.full: phўsĭognōmon, ŏnis, m., = φυσιογνώμων (a knower of nature; hence, one who knows a person's character from his features), a physiognomist: Zopyrus physiognomon, qui se profitebatur hominum mores naturasque ex corpore, oculis, vultu, fronte pernoscere, Cic. Fat. 5, 10; cf.: naturam cujusque ex formā perspicere, id. Tusc. 4, 37, 80.
physiognomon.short: phўsĭognōmon, ŏnis, m., = φυσιογνώμων (a knower of nature;

physiologia.full: phўsĭŏlŏgĭa, ae, f., = φυσιολογία, knowledge of nature, natural philosophy, physiology, Cic. N. D. 1, 8, 20: naturae ratio, quam physiologiam Graeci appellant, id. Div. 1, 41, 90; 2, 16, 37.
physiologia.short: phўsĭŏlŏgĭa, ae, f., = φυσιολογία, knowledge of nature, natural philosophy, physiology, Cic.

physiologicus.full: phўsĭŏlŏgĭcus, a, um, adj., = φυσιολογικός, of or belonging to physiology, physiological: argumentationes, Tert. ad Nat. 2, 4; Aug. Civ. Dei, 6, 8, 1.—Adv.: phўsĭŏlŏgĭcē, naturally, physiologically: interpretari, Tert. ad Nat. 2, 12.
physiologicus.short: phўsĭŏlŏgĭcus, a, um, adj., = φυσιολογικός, of or belonging to physiology, physiological: argumentationes, Tert.

physiologus.full: phўsĭŏlŏgus, a, um, adj., = φυσιόλογος, of or belonging to physiology, physiological; hence, phўsĭŏlŏga, ōrum, n., Physiology, a work by Juba, Fulg. Myth. 2, 4.
physiologus.short: phўsĭŏlŏgus, a, um, adj., = φυσιόλογος, of or belonging to physiology, physiological;

physis.full: phўsis, is, f., = φύσις, nature. Lit.: seu cupis genitor vocari et auctor orbis aut physis ipsa Panque, Poët. in Anth. Lat. t. 2, p. 474 Burm.— In partic., partycolored precious stones which had no distinctive name, freaks of nature, Plin. 37, 12, 74, § 195.

phyteuma.full: phўteuma, ătis, n., = φύτευμα, groundsel, Plin. 27, 12, 99, § 125.
phyteuma.short: phўteuma, ătis, n., = φύτευμα, groundsel, Plin.

piabilis.full: pĭābĭlis, e, adj. pio, that may be expiated, expiable: piabile fulmen, Ov. F. 3, 289.

piacularis.full: pĭācŭlāris, e, adj. piaculum, atoning, expiatory, piacular (rare; not in Cic.): hostia, Varr. L. L. 6, § 30 Müll.: sacrificia, sinofferings, Liv. 1, 26; also absol.: ut piacularia Junoni fierent, id. 42, 3: piacularia auspicia appellabant, quae sacrificantibus tristia portendebant, cum aut hostia ab arā effugisset, aut percussa mugitum dedisset, aut in aliam partem corporis quam oporteret cecidisset, Paul. ex Fest. p. 244 Müll.: piacularis porta appellatur propter aliqua piacula, quae ibidem fie

piaculo.full: pĭācŭlo, āre, v. a. id., to appease or propitiate with an offering: Mars Pater, te hisce suovetaurilibus piaculo, Cato, R. R. 141, 4.

piaculum.full: pĭācŭlum (sync. collat. form pĭā-clum, Prud. στεφ. 14, 219), i, n. pio, a means of appeasing a deity; hence, Lit. A sin-offering, propitiatory sacrifiee: porco piaculo facito, Cato, R. R. 139; 140: porcc femina piaculum pati, to bring, Cic. Leg. 2, 22, 57: piaculum hostia caedi, Liv. 8, 10: te piacula nulla resolvent, Hor. C. 1, 28, 34: piacula manibus infert, Ov. M. 6, 569: falsi mundi, Liv. 1, 26: sed quo te, M. Tulli, piaculo taceam, i. e. how can I be justified in, etc., Plin. 7, 31, 31, § 1

piamen.full: pĭāmen, ĭnis, n. pio, a means of expiation, an atonement: Februa Romani dixere piamina patres, Ov. F. 2, 19.

piamentum.full: pĭāmentum, i, n. id., a means of expiation, an atoning sacrifice (perh. not anteAug.): terrae, Plin. 25, 9, 59, § 107; 25, 4, 11, § 30; cf.: piamenta, quibus utitur (in) expiando, Fest. s. v. piatrix, p. 213 Müll.; p. 238 ib.— Trop., Sen. Cons. ad Helv. 16; Plin. 37, 1, 2, § 3.

piatio.full: pĭātĭo, ōnis, f. id., an appeasing or propitiating of the gods by offerings (postAug.), Plin. 28, 2, 5, § 27.

piatrix.full: pĭātrix, īcis, f. piator, she that appeases the gods by a sacrifice: piatrix dicebatur sacerdos, quae expiare erat solita, quam quidam simulatricem, alii sagam, alii expiatricem vocant, Fest. p. 213 Müll. (in Plaut. Mil. 3, 1, 101, read plicatricem).

pica.full: pīca, ae, f. prob. from pingo, the variegated, spotted bird, a pie, magpie, Plin. 10, 29, 41, § 78; 10, 42, 59, § 118; Ov. M. 5, 294 sq.; Pers. prol. fin.

picanus.full: Pī^cānus, i, m., a mountain in the territory of the Picentines, Sil. 4, 304; Avien. Perieg. 500.
picanus.short: Pī^cānus, i, m., a mountain in the territory of the Picentines, Sil.

picaria.full: pĭcārĭa, ae, f. pix, a place where pitch is made, a pitch-hut, Cic. Brut. 22, 85: vectigal picariarum, Dig. 50, 16, 17.

picatus.full: pĭcātus, a, um, Part. and P. a., from pico.

picati.full: pĭcāti appellantur quidam, quorum pedes formati sunt in speciem sphingum: quod eas Dori ficas vocant, Fest. p 206 Müll.
picati.short: pĭcāti appellantur quidam, quorum pedes formati sunt in speciem sphingum: quod eas Dori ficas vocant, Fest.

picea.full: pĭcĕa, ae, f. pix, the pitch-pine: Pinus silvestris, Linn.; Verg. G. 2, 257; Ov. M. 10, 101; id. H. 12, 67; Plin. 16, 10, 18, § 40 sqq.; 16, 24, 38, § 90.

piceatus.full: pĭcĕātus, a, um, adj. id., bedaubed with pitch, pitchy; hence, of hands to which others' property seems to stick, thievish: manus, Mart. 8, 59, 4.

picentia.full: Pīcentĭa, ae, f., a city in Campania, south-east of Salernum, the mod. Vicenza, Mel. 2, 4, 9; Plin. 3, 5, 9, § 70; Sil. 8, 579.— Hence, Pīcentīnus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Picentia, Picentian: ager, Plin. 3, 5, 9, § 70.
picentia.short: Pīcentĭa, ae, f., a city in Campania, south-east of Salernum, the mod.

picentinus.full: Pīcentīnus, a, um, v. Picentia, II., and Picenum, C.

picenum.full: Pīcēnum, i, n. acc. to Fest. from picus: Picena regio in quā est Asculum, dicta, quod, Sabini cum Asculum proficiscerentur, in vexillo eorum picus consederit, Paul. ex Fest. p. 212 Müll., a district in the eastern part of Italy which produced fruits and oil of excellent quality, the territory of the mod. Ancona, Varr. R. R. 1, 50, 2; Mel. 2, 4, 6; Plin. 3, 13, 18, § 109; Cic. Att. 8, 8, 1; Caes. B. C. 1, 12; Liv. 27, 43 al.—Hence, Pīcens, entis, adj., of or belonging to Picenum, Picene: ager, Ci

piceus.full: pĭcĕus, a, um, adj. pix. Lit., of pitch, Lucr. 6, 135.— Transf., black as pitch, pitch-black: piceā crassus caligine, Verg. G. 2, 308: turbine fumans piceo, id. A. 3, 573: lumen, id. ib. 9, 75: nubes, Ov. M. 11, 549: caelum, Val. Fl. 2, 507: nimbus, id. 2, 115: oves, id. 3, 439: dentes, Mart. 2, 41, 7: imber piceus crassusque, Plin. 16, 33, 61, § 143: coacti aëris caligo picea, Ambros. in Luc. 7, 20.

picinus.full: pĭcĭnus, a, um, adj. id., pitch-black: uva, Plin. 14, 3, 4, § 42.

pico.full: pĭco, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. id., to bedaub with pitch, to pitch, to tar. Lit.: dolia picata, lacus, vinarius picatus, Cato, R. R. 25 sq.: dolia, Suet. Claud. 16: parietes, Plin. 36, 22, 48, § 166; 11, 7, 6, § 16.— Transf., to season with pitch: vinum, Col. 12, 23.— Hence, pĭcātus, a, um, P. a., pitchy: vinum picatum, wine that has naturally a pitchy taste, Plin. 23, 1, 24, § 47; 14, 2, 4, § 26; Mart. 13, 107.

picra.full: picra, ae, f., prob. a medicine made of aloes: picrae solutio, Theod. Prisc. 1, 19.

picridiae.full: picrĭdĭae, ārum, f., bitter salad, Aug. Serm. ad Catechum. de Cataclysm. 4 fin.
picridiae.short: picrĭdĭae, ārum, f., bitter salad, Aug.

picris.full: picris, ĭdis, f., = πικρίς. Bitter lettuce, a kind of salad (in Greek letters, Plin. 19, 8, 38, § 126).— A plant that blooms all the year round, Plin. 21, 17, 65, § 105.

pictacium.full: pictăcĭum, i, n., i. q. pittacium, Laber. ap. Gell. 16, 7, 9; v. pittacium.

pictavi.full: Pictāvi, ōrum, m., a later appellation of the Pictones, Amm. 15, 21; Ven. Carm. 6, 7, 215; 2, 19, 2.—Hence, Pictāva, ae, f., the capital of the Pictavi, the mod. Poictiers, Sulp. Sev. Vit. S. Mart. 5.— Pic-tāvĭcus, a, um, adj., Pictavian: rhetor, Aus. Epigr. 51, 2.
pictavi.short: Pictāvi, ōrum, m., a later appellation of the Pictones, Amm.

picti.full: Picti, ōrum, m. pingo, the painted people, a people of Britain, the Picts or ancient Caledonians (so named from their practice of tattooing themselves), Amm. 20, 1, 1; Claud. III. Cons. Hon. 54; id. Laud. Stil. 2, 254.

pictilis.full: pictĭlis, e, adj. pictus, embroidered: balteus, App. M. 10, p. 247, 38.

pictones.full: Pictŏnes, um, m., a people in Aquitanian Gaul, in the mod. Pays de Poiteau, Caes. B. G. 3, 11; Hirt. B. G. 8, 26; 27; Plin. 4, 19, 33, § 108; Luc. 1, 436.—Hence, Pictŏnĭcus, a, um, adj., Pictonic: Pictonicum litus, Aus. Ep. 9, 36.
pictones.short: Pictŏnes, um, m., a people in Aquitanian Gaul, in the mod.

pictor1.full: pictor, ōris, m. pingo. A painter, Cic. Ac. 2, 7, 20; Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 13, § 30; Hor. A. P. 9; Plin. 35, 8, 34, § 53 sq.; Juv. 3, 76; 12, 28.— Transf., an embroiderer, Coripp. Laud. Just. 2, 280.

pictor2.full: Pictor, ōris, m. id., a surname in the gens Fabia. C. Fabius Pictor, Cic. Tusc. 1, 2, 4.— Q. Fabius Pictor, an ancient Roman historian, Cic. de Or. 2, 12, 53.

pictorius.full: pictōrĭus, a, um, adj. 1. pictor, of or belonging to painters, pictorial: licentia, Tert. adv. Marc. 1, 3: operae, Dig. 38, 1, 23.

pictura.full: pictūra, ae, f. pingo, painting, the art of painting. Lit.: una est ars ratioque picturae, Cic. de Or. 3, 7, 26; 1, 16, 73; id. Brut. 18, 70; App. Mund. p. 66, 23.— In partic., a painting of the face, Plaut. Most. 1, 3, 105.— Transf., concr., a painting, picture (cf. tabula): et si qua inutilis pictura sit, eam vendat, Plaut. As. 4, 1, 10; Cic. Or. 11, 36: nego ullam picturam neque in tabulis neque textilem fuisse, quin conquisierit, Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 1, § 1: accedant statuae et picturae, Sen. Ep

picturatus.full: pictūrātus, a, um, adj. pictura, painted, pictured, i. e. Party-colored, variegated (poet.): agger floribus, Stat. Th. 6, 58: volucres, Claud. Ep. ad Ser. 3.— Embroidered: vestes, Verg. A. 3, 483.

pictus.full: pictus, a, um, Part. and P. a., from pingo.

picula.full: pĭcŭla, ae, f. dim. pix, a little pitch, App. Herb. 36; Veg. Vet. 1, 11; 2, 46.

picumnus.full: Pīcumnus, i, m., and Pīlumnus, i, m., two brother deities of the Romans; the first a personification of the woodpecker (picus), and the second a personification of the pestle (pilum); both were companions of Mars, and tutelary deities of married people and little children, Varr. ap. Non. 528, 11 sq.; id. ap. Aug. Civ. Dei, 6, 9; cf. Isid. 4, 11, 5; Aem. Mac. ap. Non. 518, 26; cf. Serv. Verg. A. 9, 4; 10, 76.—Pilumnus was the son of Daunus, husband of Danaë and ancestor of Turnus, Verg. A. 9, 4.
picumnus.short: Pīcumnus, i, m., and Pīlumnus, i, m., two brother deities of the Romans;

picus1.full: pīcus, i, m. perh. root pingo; cf. pica. A woodpecker, one of the birds used in augury, Plaut. As. 2, 1, 12: sunt et parvae aves uncorum unguium, ut pici, Martio cognomine insignes et in auspicatu magni, Plin. 10, 18, 20, § 40; 11, 37, 44, § 122; Non. 518, 24.— A fabulous bird, the griffin: picos veteres esse voluerunt, quos Graeci γρύπας appellant. Plautus Aulularia (4, 8, 1): pici divitiis, qui aureos montes colunt, Ego solus supero, Non. 152, 7 sq.

picus2.full: Pīcus, i, m., son of Saturn, grandfather of Latinus, king of the aborigines, and a prophet; he was changed by Circe, whose love he had slighted, into a woodpecker, Ov. M. 14, 320; Verg. A. 7, 189 Serv.; Juv. 8, 131.
picus2.short: Pīcus, i, m., son of Saturn, grandfather of Latinus, king of the aborigines, and a prophet;

pieria.full: Pīĕrĭa, ae, f., = Πιερία. A country of Macedonia, south of the Haliacmon, Mel. 2, 3, 2; Plin. 4, 10, 17, § 33; Liv. 39, 26.— Hence, Pīĕrĭcus, a, um, adj., Pierian: pix, Plin. 14, 20, 25, § 128.— A country of Syria, between Cilicia and Phœnicia, with a mountain of the same name, and the capital city Seleucia Pieria, Cic. Att. 11, 20, 1; Plin. 5, 12, 13, § 67; 5, 21, 18, § 79.

pieros.full: Pīĕros (-us), i, m., = Πίερος. King of Emathia, who gave to his daughters the names of the nine Muses, Ov. M. 5, 302.— A Macedonian, father of the nine Muses, Cic. N. D. 3, 21, 54; cf. Ov. Tr. 5, 3, 10.— Hence, Pīĕris, ĭdis or ĭdos, f., daughter of Pierus, a Muse, Hor. C. 4, 3, 18; Ov. F. 4, 222.—In plur.: Pīĕrĭdes, um, the Muses, Cic. N. D. 3, 21, 54; Verg. E. 8, 63; Juv. 4, 36.— Pīĕrĭus, a, um, adj., Pierian, Thessalian; sacred to the Muses, poetic: quercus, from Mount Pierus, in Thessaly, Pro

pietas1.full: pĭĕtas, ātis, f. pius, dutiful conduct towards the gods, one's parents, relatives, benefactors, country, etc., sense of duty. Lit. With respect to the gods, piety: est enim pietas justitia adversus deos, Cic. N. D. 1, 41, 115; 1, 2, 3; cf.: aequitas tripartita dicitur esse; una ad superos deos, altera ad manes, tertia ad homines pertinere. Prima pietas, secunda sanctitas, tertia justitia aut aequitas nominatur, id. Top. 23, 90: pietas adversus deos, id. Fin. 3, 22, 73: deos placatos pietas effic

pietas2.full: Pĭĕtas, ātis, f., a Roman surname, Inscr. Marin. Atti, p. 329.— Also, the name of a ship, Inscr. Orell. 3608.— Pietas Julia, a Roman colony in Istria, the mod. Pola, Plin. 3, 19, 23, § 129.
pietas2.short: Pĭĕtas, ātis, f., a Roman surname, Inscr.

pietaticultrix.full: pĭĕtātĭcultrix, īcis, f. pietas-cultrix, that practises maternal care: ciconia pietaticultrix, Petr. 55.

pigeo.full: pĭgĕo, gŭi, and pĭgĭtum est, 2, v. a. root pik-, to be angry; cf.: peccare, pejor (for pec-ior), pessimus (contr. from pējessimus); Gr. πικρός, bitter, to feel annoyance or reluctance at; to repent of a thing. As a verb. pers. (very rare): pudet quod turpe est; piget quod dolet, Donat. ap. Ter. Ad. 3, 3, 37: poscis ab invitā verba pigenda lyra, Prop. 5, 1, 74.— Piget, piguit, or pigitum est, third pers. sing. impers., it irks, troubles, displeases, chagrins, afflicts, grieves, disgusts one; I (t
pigeo.short: pĭgĕo, gŭi, and pĭgĭtum est, 2, v.

piger.full: pĭger, gra, grum (late Lat. collat. form of sup. pigrissimus, Tert. Exhort. ad Castit. 13), adj. piget. Lit., unwilling, reluctant, averse (rare): gens pigerrima ad militaria opera, Liv. 21, 25, 6: pigriores ad facinus, id. 39, 13, 11: pigriores ad cetera munia exequenda, Curt. 6, 9, 29: ad litteras scribendas pigerrimus, Cael. ap. Cic. Fam. 8, 1, 1: ad conatus magnos piger, Sen. Ira, 3, 3, 1.— Transf. Backward, slow, dull, lazy, indolent, sluggish, inactive (of persons and things). With in and

pigmentarius.full: pigmentārĭus, a, um, adj. pigmentum, of or belonging to paints or unguents: institor pigmentarius, a dealer in paints or unguents, Scrib. Larg. Comp. 22.—More freq., Subst.: pigmentārĭus, ii, m., a dealer in paints or unguents: pigmentarius, χρωματοπώλης, φαρμακοπώλης, μυροπώλης, Gloss. Philox.: Attius pigmentarius, Cic. Fam. 15, 17, 2; Dig. 48, 8, 3; Firm. Math. 8, 27 med.; Pelag. Vet. 13; Vulg. Exod. 37, 29.

pigmentatus.full: pigmentātus, a, um, adj. id., painted, colored, Tert. Cult. Fem. fin.: crinis, Prud. Ham. 316.

pigmentum.full: pigmentum, i, n. pingo, a material for coloring, a color, paint, pigment. Lit. For painting, a paint: aspersa temere pigmenta in tabulā, oris lineamenta efficere possunt, Cic. Div. 1, 13, 23: vela in cortinam pigmenti ferventis mersa, Plin. 35, 11, 42, § 150.—Jocosely: quem Apelles Zeuxisque duo pingent pigmentis ulmeis, i. e. beat black and blue, Plaut. Ep. 5, 1, 20. — For cosmetics, a paint, pigment: non istanc aetatem oportet pigmentum ullum attingere, Plaut. Most. 1, 3, 106; Plin. 16, 43, 84

pigneraticius.full: pignĕrātīcĭus (-tĭus) and pignŏ-rātīcĭus (-tĭus), a, um, adj. pignero, of or belonging to a pledge: fundus, i. e. given as a pledge, pledged, mortgaged, Dig. 13, 7, 6: creditor, who lends on a pledge, a pawnbroker, mortgagee, ib. 39, 2, 15: actio, and absol. pignĕrātīcĭa, ae, f., an action on account of a pledge, which the debtor demands back again from the creditor, ib. 13, 7, 1; 13, 9, 3; 13, 11, 2; Just. Inst. 4, 6, 28; or for a pledge which the creditor demands from the debtor, Dig. 13, 1, 3
pigneraticius.short: pignĕrātīcĭus (-tĭus) and pignŏ-rātīcĭus (-tĭus), a, um, adj.

pigneratio.full: pignĕrātĭo, ōnis, f. id., a pledging, pawning, mortgaging (jurid. Lat.): pignerationem recipere, Dig. 20, 1, 9; Cod. Just. 8, 34, 3, § 3.

pignerator.full: pignĕrātor, ōris, m. id., one who takes a pledge; a pledgee, mortgagee, Cic. Verr. 2, 3, 11, § 27.

pignero.full: pignĕro, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. pignus, to give as a pledge, to pledge, pawn, mortgage. Lit.: unionem, Suet. Vit. 7: bona tantum, quae publicari poterant, pigneranda poenae praebebant, furnished as security for the penalty, i. e. left to be confiscated, Liv. 29, 36: cujus et alveolos et laenam pignerat Atreus, which the poet Rubrenus, while he was writing the Atreus, was compelled by necessity to pawn, Juv. 7, 73: ancilla pignerata, Dig. 40, 5, 46: vestimenta pignorata, Vulg. Amos, 2, 8.— Trop. To

pigneror.full: pignĕror, ātus, 1, v. dep. a. [id.]. Lit., to take as a pledge; hence, trop., To make one's own, to appropriate (rare but class.): Mars ipse ex acie fortissimum quemque pignerari solet, Cic. Phil. 14, 12, 32: maximas ingenii, consilii partes sibi ad utilitatem suam, id. Rep. 1, 4, 8 (cited in Non. 477, 31 sq.): fidem militum praemio pigneratus, Suet. Claud. 10.— To accept as certain: quod das mihi, pigneror, omen, Ov. M. 7, 621.

pignoriscapio.full: pignŏriscăpĭo, ōnis, f. pignus-capio, a taking or seizing as a pledge, Cato ap. Gell. 7, 10, 2.

pignus.full: pignus, ŏris and ĕris (old form in plur.: pignosa pignora eodem modo quo valesii, auselii ... dicebantur, Fest. p. 213 Müll.), n. root pac-, of pango; cf. paciscor, a pledge, gage, pawn, security, mortgage (of persons as well as things). Lit.: opponere se pigneri, Plaut. Ps. 1, 1, 85: ager oppositus est pignori, Ter. Phorm. 4, 3, 56: servus, quem hic reliqueram Pignus pro me, Plaut. Capt. 5, 1, 19: quo facto pignore animos centurionum devinxit, Caes. B. C. 1, 39: rem alicujus pignori accipere, T
pignus.short: pignus, ŏris and ĕris (old form in plur.: pignosa pignora eodem modo quo valesii, auselii ...

pigredo.full: pī^grēdo, ĭnis, f. piger, sloth fulness, indolence (late Lat.), Vulg. Prov. 19, 15.

pigreo.full: pī^grĕo, ēre, v. n. id., to be slow, sluggish, reluctant (ante-class.): post aetate pigret sufferre laborem, Enn. ap. Non. 219, 12 (Ann. v. 405 Vahl.): omnes gaudent facere recte, male pigrent, Att. ap. Non. 14.

pigresco.full: pī^gresco, ĕre, v. inch. n. [pigreo], to become slow, sluggish: Nilus pigrescit, Plin. 18, 18, 47, § 168: possit pigrescere Cyllenius, Mart. Cap. 1, § 38; Ambros. Virg. 17, 110; id. in Luc. 10, § 23.

pigritas.full: pī^grĭtas, ātis, f. piger, slothfulness, indolence: pigritas, ἀργία, Gloss. Lat. Gr.

pigritia.full: pī^grĭtĭa, ae, and pī^grĭtĭes, ēi, f. id., sloth, sluggishness, laziness, indolence (cf.: desidia, socordia, inertia, segnities). Lit.: pigritiam definiunt metum consequentis laboris, Cic. Tusc. 4, 8, 18: propter pigritiam aut ignaviam, id. Off. 1, 29, 102: noli putare pigritiā me facere, quod non meā manu scribam, id. Att. 15, 15: et haesitatio, Petr. 85: nox Romanis pigritiem ad sequendum fecit, Liv. 44, 42, 9: lentae crimine pigritiae, Mart. 11, 79, 2.— Transf. Tu das ingenuae jus mihi pigrit
pigritia.short: pī^grĭtĭa, ae, and pī^grĭtĭes, ēi, f.

pigritor.full: pī^grĭtor, ātus, 1, v. freq. n. [pigror], to be slow, sluggish, tardy, Vulg. Act. 9, 38: Ὤκνησα, pigritatus sum, Gloss. Gr. Lat.

pigro.full: pī^gro, āvi, ātum, 1, v. n. piger, to be indolent, slow, dilatory (ante-class.), Lucr. 1, 410: melius pigrasse quam properasse est hoc nefas, Att. ap. Non. 154, 2 (Trag. Rel. p. 144 Rib.): cur propter haec pigrem? id. ib. 153, 32 (Trag. Rel. p. 147 Rib.).

pigror1.full: pī^gror, ātus, 1, v. dep. id., to be slow, slack, dilatory: tu scribere ne pigrere, Cic. Att. 14, 1, 2.

pigror2.full: pī^gror, ōris, m. id., sluggishness, indolence (ante-class.): obrepsit pigror torporque, Lucil. ap. Non. 219, 11.

piguus.full: pĭgŭus, a, um, adj. pigeo, indolent, acc. to Prisc. p. 635 P.

pila1.full: pīla, ae, f. perh. for pisula, from root pis-; v. pinso, piso, a mortar (syn. mortarium): pila, ubi triticum pinsant, Cato, R. R. 14; Ov. Ib. 573: zeae granum tunditur in pilā ligneā, Plin. 18, 11, 29, § 112: si contuderis stultum in pilā, Vulg. Prov. 27, 22: sal sordidum in pilā pisatum, Paul. ex Fest. p. 158 Müll.

pila2.full: pīlă, ae, f. for pigla, from root pag-, pig-, of pango, pe-pig-i, q. v., a pillar (syn. columna): pila, quae parietem sustentat, ab opponendo dicta est, Paul. ex Fest. p. 204 Müll.: locavit pilas pontis in Tiberim, Liv. 40, 51: salax taberna a pileatis nona fratribus pila, of the temple of Castor and Pollux, Cat. 37, 1: nulla taberna meos habeat neque pila libellos, i. e. they are not to be publicly sold (as the booksellers had their stalls around the pillars of public buildings), Hor. S. 1, 4,

pila3.full: pĭla, ae (gen. sing. pilaï, Lucr. 5, 713; 720; 726), f. etym. dub.; perh. akin to Gr. πάλλω, brandish; Lat. pellere, drive; v. Corss. 1, 525 sqq., a ball, playing-ball (syn. follis). Lit.: pilā expulsim ludere, Varr. ap. Non. 104, 29: di nos quasi pilas homines habent, Plaut. Capt. prol. 22; id. Most. 1, 2, 73: pilae studio teneri, Cic. de Or. 3, 23, 88; Hor. S. 1, 5, 49: cum lapsa e manibus fugit pila, Verg. Cir. 149, Prop. 3, 12 (4, 13), 5: pila cadit aut mittentis vitio, aut accipientis . . .

pilanus.full: pīlānus, i, m. pilum, a triarius, one of the soldiers forming the third rank in battle: pilani pilis pugnantes, Paul. ex Fest. p. 204 Müll.: pilani triarii quoque dicti quod in acie tertio ordine extremis subsidio deponebantur, Varr. L. L. 5, § 89 Müll.; Ov. F. 3, 129.

pilaris.full: pĭlāris, e, adj. 3. pila, of or belonging to a ball: lusio, a game of ball, Stat. S. 4 praef.

pilarium.full: pĭlārĭum, ii, n. 2. pila, a burialplace where the ashes of the dead were deposited in cylindrical vases, Inscr. Fabr. p. 13, LII.

pilarius.full: pĭlārĭus, ii, m. 3. pila, one who performs tricks with balls, a ball-thrower, juggler, Quint. 10, 7, 11; Inscr. Orell. 2590: hierosalpinctes, pilarius, Not. Tir. 173.

pilastilus.full: pilastilus, i, m., perh. a javelinmaker, Inscr. Murat. 538.

pilates.full: pilates or pellates, only in nom. [cf. πελλός, pallidus], a kind of stone: lapidis genus, cujus meminit Cato originum l. V.: lapis candidior quam pilates, Fest. p. 237 Müll.
pilates.short: pilates or pellates, only in nom.

pilatim.full: pīlātim, adv. 2. pila, pillar-wise, with pillars. Lit.: pilatim aedificia agere, Vitr. 6, 11, 4.— Transf., in milit. lang., in close bodies, in solid columns: sive pilatim, sive passim iter facere volebat, Asellio ap. Serv. ad Verg. A. 12, 121: pilatim exercitum duxi, Scaur. ib.; cf. 1. pilo, and, under it, pilatus.

pilatrix.full: pĭlātrix, īcis, f. 2. pilo, she that robs or plunders: pilatrix pallii, Tit. ap. Non. 102, 4.

pilatus1.full: pīlātus, a, um, Part. and P. a., v. 1. pilo.

pilatus2.full: pīlātus, a, um, adj. pilum, armed with javelins: agmina, Verg. A. 12, 121: cohors, Mart. 10, 48, 2.

pilatus3.full: Pīlātus, i, m., a Roman surname; esp., Pontius Pilatus, a Roman governor of Judœa, in the time of Jesus, Vulg. Matt. 27, 2 et saep.; Sedul. 5, 116.
pilatus3.short: Pīlātus, i, m., a Roman surname;

pilentum.full: pīlentum, i, n., an easy chariot or carriage, used by the Roman ladies, and in which the vessels, etc., for sacred rites were carried (cf. petorrita): pilentis et carpentis per urbem vehi matronis concessum est, quod, cum aurum non reperiretur, ex voto, quod Camillus voverat Apollini Delphico, contulerunt, Fest. p. 245 Müll.; cf. Liv. 5, 25: castae ducebant sacra per urbem Pilentis matres in mollibus, Verg. A. 8, 666; Hor. Ep. 2, 1, 192.
pilentum.short: pīlentum, i, n., an easy chariot or carriage, used by the Roman ladies, and in which the vessels, etc., for sacred rites were carried (cf.

pileo.full: pīlĕo, pīlĕus, etc., v. pilleo, pilleus, etc.

pilicrepus.full: pĭlīcrĕpus, i, m. 3. pila-crepo, a ballplayer, Sen. Ep. 56, 2; Inscr. Orell. 2591; cf. Morcell. Stil. Inscr. Lat. 1, p. 454 Patav.

pilleatus.full: pillĕātus (pīle-), a, um, adj. pilleus, covered with the pilleus or felt-cap, wearing the pilleus (this was worn in Rome at entertainments, shows, and festivals, esp. at the Saturnalia; slaves received it at their manumission as a token of freedom): pilleati aut lana alba velatis capitibus volones epulati sunt, Liv. 24, 16 fin.: rex, id. 45, 44: colonorum turba pilleatorum currum sequentium, like a general's freedmen, id. 33, 23: nec per omnia nos similes esse pilleatae turbae voluisses, i. e. t

pilleo.full: pillĕo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. id, to place the pilleus on a person's head, to bonnet him, in token of manumission: pilleari et rudem accipere possunt, Mos. et Rom. Leg. Coll. 11, 7, 4.

pilleolus.full: pillĕŏlus, i, m., and pillĕŏlum, i, n. dim. pilleus, a small felt cap, a skull-cap: ut cum pilleolo (portes) soleas conviva tribulis, Hor. Ep. 1, 13, 15; Col. Arbor. 25; Hier. Ep. 85, n. 6; 64, n. 13.
pilleolus.short: pillĕŏlus, i, m., and pillĕŏlum, i, n.

pilleus.full: pillĕus, i, m., and pillĕum, i, n. akin to Gr. πῖλος, with same signif.; also to pilus, a hair, a felt cap or hat, made to fit close, and shaped like the half of an egg. It was worn by the Romans at entertainments and festivals, esp. at the Saturnalia, and was given to a slave at his enfranchisement as a sign of freedom (cf. petasus). Lit.: pilleum quem habuit deripuit, Plaut. Fragm. ap. Non. 220, 14; id. Amph. 1, 1, 305: haec mera libertas, hanc nobis pillea donant, id. Pers. 5, 82. Free-born p
pilleus.short: pillĕus, i, m., and pillĕum, i, n.

pilo1.full: pīlo, no perf., ātum, 1, v. a., = πιλέω, qs. to ram down; hence, in gen., to thrust home (ante-class. and rare): hastam pilans prae pondere frangit, Host. ap. Serv. ad Verg. A. 12, 121 (pilans id est figens, Serv.). —Hence, pīlātus, a, um, P. a., closepressed, thick, dense = densus, pressus. Lit.: pilatum (agmen), quod sine jumentis incedit, sed inter se densum est, quo facilius per iniquiora loca tramittatur, Varr. ap. Serv. ad Verg. A. 12, 121: inde loci liquidas pilatasque aetheris oras Conte

pilo2.full: pĭlo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. n. and a. [1. pilus]. Neutr., to put forth hairs, to grow hairy: pilat pilos habere incipit, ahas pro detrahit pilos, a quo depilati, Paul. ex Fest. p. 204 Müll.: pilare dictum est, ut plumare, pilis vestiri, Non. 39, 25: corpus meum nunc pilare primum coepit, Afran. 39, 27; Nov. 39, 28.— Act. (cf. ψιλόω). Lit., to deprive of hair, make bald, depilate: nates, Mart. 6, 56, 4: uxores, id. 12, 32, 33.— Transf., to plunder, pillage (very rare, and not ante-Aug.; whereas compil

pilosus.full: pĭlōsus, a, um, adj. id., hairy, shaggy (syn.: villosus, setosus): ovis ventrem habet pilosum, Varr. R. R. 2, 2: genae, Cic. Pis. 1, 1: pilosiora folia, Plin. 20, 16, 64, § 172: ursis asperior pilosiorque, Auct. Priap. 47: nares, Juv. 14, 194: Esau, Vulg. Gen. 27, 11. —Hence, as subst.: pĭlōsus, i, m., a shaggy person or creature, esp. a satyr, Vulg. Isa. 13, 21; 34, 14.

pilula.full: pĭlŭla, ae, f. dim. 3. pila, a little ball, globule. In gen., Plin. 16, 7, 10, § 28; Pelag. Vet. 14.— In partic., in medicine, a pill, Plin. 28, 9, 37, § 138.

pilum.full: pīlum, i, n. for pis-lum, cf. piso, 1. pila, etc., a pounder, pestle of a mortar. Lit.: pilum fabarium, Cato, R. R. 10; 18: quasi tollenonem aut pilum Graecum reciproces planā viā, a pounder, in using which, one side was raised while the other was depressed, Plaut. Fragm. ap. Fest. s v. reciprocare, p. 274 Müll.: pinsente pilo praeferrato, Plin. 18, 10, 23, § 97: pilo contusum, Vulg. Exod. 27, 20.— Transf., the heavy javelin of the Roman infantry, which they hurled at the enemy at the commenceme

pilumnoe poploe.full: pilumnoe poploe in carmine Saliari Romani, velut pilis uti assueti, vel quia praecipue pellant hostes, Fest. p. 205 Müll. [the former is undoubtedly the correct derivation; the singular still occurs in Pilumnus; v. h. v. sub Picumnus].
pilumnoe poploe.short: pilumnoe poploe in carmine Saliari Romani, velut pilis uti assueti, vel quia praecipue pellant hostes, Fest.

pilus1.full: pĭlus, i, m., a hair (syn.: villus, seta). Lit.: capra pilos ministrat ad usum nauticum, Varr. R. R. 2, 11: munitae sunt palpebrae vallo pilorum, Cic. N. D. 2, 57, 143: caudae pilos equinae vellere, Hor. Ep. 2, 1, 45: duris aspera crura pilis, Ov. A. A. 3, 194: contra pilum equum fricare, Pelag. Vet. 26: in capite homini plurimus pilus, Plin. 11, 37, 47, § 130.—Prov.: non minus molestum est calvis quam comatis pilos velli, Sen. Tranq. An. 8, 2, 3: propius quidem est a sole mons quam campus aut v
pilus1.short: pĭlus, i, m., a hair (syn.: villus, seta).

pilus2.full: pīlus, i, m. pilum, regularly joined with primus: primus pilus (in the gen. written also as one word, primipili), the division of the triarii in the Roman army: P. Sextius Baculus, primi pili centurio, Caes. B. G. 3, 5; id. B. C. 1, 13: T. Balventius, qui superiore anno primum pilum duxerat, had been leader, captain of the triarii, id. B. G. 5, 35; Liv. 42, 34, 11: aliquem ad primum pilum transducere, to transfer, advance to the triarii, Caes. B. C. 3, 53, 5: primos pilos ademit, took the comman

pimpleis.full: Pimplēis (Piplēis), ĭdis and ĭdos, adj. f., = Πιμπληϊς, of or belonging to Pimpla (a place and fountain in Pieria sacred to the Muses, now Litokhoro), Pimplean; hence, as subst., The territory around Pimpla: si riguam laetis recolis Pimpleida Musis, i. e. if you devote yourself to the Muses, compose poetry, Aus. Ep. 14, 9.— (Sc. Musa.) A Muse: Musae ab terrestribus locis aliis cognominatae Libethrides, Pimpleides, Thespiades, Heliconides, Varr. L. L. 7, § 20 Müll.: Pimpleides Musae a fonte Maced

pimpleus.full: Pimplēus (Piplēus), a, um, adj., Pimplean (v. Pimpleis); hence, sacred to the Muses: mons, Cat. 105, 1: antrum, Mart. 12, 11, 3.—Subst.: Pimplēa (Pi-plēa), ae, f. A Muse: necte meo Lamiae coronam, Pimplea dulcis, Hor. C. 1, 26, 9.— The fountain of Pimpla, Stat. S. 1, 4, 25.

pimplias.full: Pimplī^ăs, ădis, f., = Πιμπλιάς, a Pimpliad (v. Pimpleis), i. e. a Muse (in later poetry for the more usual Pimpleis): hic et Pimpliadas induxerat optimus Orpheus, Sid. Carm. 10, 17; 22, 77.
pimplias.short: Pimplī^ăs, ădis, f., = Πιμπλιάς, a Pimpliad (v.

pina.full: pīna, ae, f., = πῖνα (less correctly pinna, = πίννα), the sea-pen, a kind of mussel, Cic. Fin. 3, 19, 63; id. N. D. 2, 48, 123; Plin. 9, 35, 56, § 115; 32, 11, 53, § 150.
pina.short: pīna, ae, f., = πῖνα (less correctly pinna, = πίννα), the sea-pen, a kind of mussel, Cic.

pinacotheca.full: pĭnăcŏthēca, ae, and pĭnăcŏ-thēcē, ēs, f., = πινακοθήκη, a picture-gallery: ut videant pinacothecas, Varr. R. R. 1, 2, 10: ut in pinacothece faciant, id. ib. 1, 59, 2; Vitr. 6, 5; 6, 18; Plin. 35, 2, 2, § 4: celeberrimi pictores, quorum tabulae pinacothecas implent, id. 35, 11, 40, § 148: FLAVIVS APOLLONIVS QVI FVIT A PINACOTHECIS, director of the picture-galleries, Inscr. Fabr. 724, n. 443.
pinacotheca.short: pĭnăcŏthēca, ae, and pĭnăcŏ-thēcē, ēs, f., = πινακοθήκη, a picture-gallery: ut videant pinacothecas, Varr.

pinarius.full: Pīnārĭus, i, m., the name of a Roman sacerdotal family. The Pinarii and Potitii presided at the celebration of certain sacred rites in honor of Hercules, originally instituted by Evander and re-established by Romulus. The Pinarii having on one occasion arrived after the exta were consumed, it was ordained that, as long as the family remained, they should not partake of the exta, Liv. 1, 7, 12 sqq.; 9, 29, 9 sqq.; Macr. S. 1, 12, 28; Fest. p. 237 Müll. —Hence, Pīnārĭus, a, um, adj., of or belongi
pinarius.short: Pīnārĭus, i, m., the name of a Roman sacerdotal family.

pinarus.full: Pīnărus, i, m., = Πίναρος, a river in Cilicia, now Deli Tchai, Plin. 5, 27, 22, § 91; Curt. 3, 12, 27.
pinarus.short: Pīnărus, i, m., = Πίναρος, a river in Cilicia, now Deli Tchai, Plin.

pinastellus.full: pīnastellus, i, m., and -um, i, n. pinus, a plant, also called peucedanum, App. Herb. 94.
pinastellus.short: pīnastellus, i, m., and -um, i, n.

pinaster.full: pīnaster, tri, m. id., a wild pine: pinaster nihil aliud est, quam pinus silvestris, Plin. 16, 10, 16, § 38.

pinax.full: pĭnax, ăcis, m., = πίναξ, a picture on a wooden tablet, a picture: Pinax Cebetis, the title of a work by the Theban philosopher Cebes, Tert. adv. Haeret. 39.
pinax.short: pĭnax, ăcis, m., = πίναξ, a picture on a wooden tablet, a picture: Pinax Cebetis, the title of a work by the Theban philosopher Cebes, Tert.

pincerna.full: pincerna, ae, m., = πιγκέρνης (v. Du Cange, Gloss. Graec. s. h. v.; prop. one who mixes drinks; hence, in gen.), a cupbearer, butler (post-class.), Ascon. Cic. Verr. 2, 1, 26; Lampr. Alex. Sev. 41; Hier. Quaest. in Gen. 40, 1; Inscr. Orell. 2881; Vulg. Gen. 40, 1; id. 2 Esdr. 1, 11.

pincius.full: Pincĭus, i, m., the name of a Roman gens, Grut. 352, 5. Perh. after them was named the Mons Pincius, the eighth hill of Rome, situate outside the city, but enclosed by the Aurelian wall; called, at an earlier period, Collis hortorum, now Monte Pincio. —Hence, Pincĭānus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to the Mons Pincius, Pincian: domus, Cassiod. Var. 3, 10.
pincius.short: Pincĭus, i, m., the name of a Roman gens, Grut.

pindarus.full: Pindărus, i, m., = Πίνδαρος. Pindar, a celebrated lyric poet of Thebes, contemporary with Æschylus, Hor. C. 4, 2, 1; Quint. 10, 1, 61; Cic. Fin. 2, 34, 115; Sen. Q. N. 6, 26, 3.— Hence, Pindărĕ-us, a, um, adj., Pindaric: Pindaream chelyn referre, Mart. Cap. 2, § 119.— Pin-dărĭcus, a, um, adj., Pindaric: Camenae, Hor. C. 4, 9, 6: fons, id. Ep. 1, 3, 10: Pindaricos modos, Mart. 8, 18, 6; Ov. P. 4, 16, 28: os, Prop. 3, 15, 40: Pindaricum metrum, consisting of a trimeter brachycatalectus (e. g. medi

pindenissus.full: Pindĕnissus, i, m., or -um, i, n., a fortified town in Cilicia, taken by Cicero, Cic. Att. 5, 20, 5; 6, 1, 9; id. Fam. 2, 10, 3; 15, 4, 10.—Hence, Pindĕnissae, ārum, m., the inhabitants of Pindenissus, Cic. Att. 5, 20, 1.
pindenissus.short: Pindĕnissus, i, m., or -um, i, n., a fortified town in Cilicia, taken by Cicero, Cic.

pindus.full: Pindus or -os, i, m., = Πίνδος, a lofty mountain in Thessaly, on the borders of Macedonia and Epirus, the seat of the Muses, now Mezzara, Mel. 2, 3, 4; Plin. 4, 8, 15, § 30: Othrysque Pindusque et Pindo major Olympus, Ov. M. 7, 225: juga Pindi, Verg. E. 10, 11: super Pindo, Hor. C. 1, 12, 6.
pindus.short: Pindus or -os, i, m., = Πίνδος, a lofty mountain in Thessaly, on the borders of Macedonia and Epirus, the seat of the Muses, now Mezzara, Mel.

pinetum.full: pīnētum, i, n. pinus, a pine-wood, pine-grove: cinctaque pinetis nemoris juga Nonacrini, Ov. F. 2, 275; 4, 273; Plin. 27, 8, 43, § 66.

pineus.full: pīnĕus, a, um, adj. id., of the pine, piny, pine-: pinea velamina, pine-wreaths, Lucr. 4, 587: ardor, a fire of pine-wood, Verg. A. 11, 786: silva, id. ib. 9, 85: plaga pinea, a piny tract, id. ib. 11, 320: claustra, i. e. of the wooden horse before Troy, id. ib. 2, 258: fert avidas in pinea Turnus Texta faces, i. e. into the ships, Ov. M. 14, 530; so, pinea moles, a ship, Prop. 4 (5), 6, 20. compages, Mart. 9, 76, 4: nuclei, Cels. 6, 11; 2, 22: nuces, Plin. 15, 10, 9, § 35.— Subst.: pīnĕa, ae,

pingo.full: pingo, pinxi, pictum, 3, v. a., to represent pictorially with the pencil or needle, to paint, embroider (cf.: depingo, delineo, adumbro). Lit.: quas (comas) Dione Pingitur sustinuisse manu, is represented in painting, Ov. Am. 1, 14, 34; Cic. Fam. 5, 12, 7: tabulas, id. Inv. 2, 1, 1: tabula picta, a painting, picture, id. Brut. 75: pingere hominis speciem, id. de Or. 2, 16, 69: Helenae simulacrum, id. Inv. 2, 1, 1: Nero princeps jusserat colosseum se pingi, Plin. 35, 7, 33, § 51.—Prov.: quae dicu

pinguamen.full: pinguāmen, ĭnis, n. pinguis, fat, Cypr. adv. Jud. 1, 16; cf. pinguamen, λίπος, Gloss. Gr. Lat.

pinguedo.full: pinguēdo, ĭnis, f. id., fatness, fat (post-Aug.), Plin. 12, 15, 35, § 68; Pall. 3, 29; 11, 20; Sid. Ep. 2, 2.— Transf., richness, abundance, Vulg. Gen. 27, 28; id. Job, 36, 16.— Fig., fulness, richness in expression (opp. exilitas), v. l. ap. Quint. 1, 11, 4 (al. pinguetudine).

pinguefacio.full: pinguĕfăcĭo, fēci, factum, 3, v. a. pinguis-facio, to make fat, to fatten (postAug.), Plin. 16, 44, 93, § 246: pinguefactus est, Tert. adv. Psych. 6.

pinguesco.full: pinguesco, ĕre, v. inch. n. [pinguis], to become or grow fat. Lit.: emaciatum armentum medicā (herbā) pinguescit, Col. 2, 11, 2: attilus (piscis) in Pado inertiā pinguescens, Plin. 9, 15, 17, § 44; 18, 14, 36, § 134: frumenta pinguescunt, id. 17, 2, 2, § 15: campos sanguine, grow fertile, Verg. G. 1, 492.— Transf. To grow fat, rich, or oily: vinum Maroneum vetustate pinguescit, Plin. 14, 4, 6, § 54: nuces juglandes, id. 19, 5, 30, § 95.— To become shining, like fat: achates politurā pinguescit,

pinguiarius.full: pinguĭārĭus, ii, m. id., one who likes fat, Mart. 11, 100, 6.

pinguiculus.full: pinguĭcŭlus, a, um, adj. dim. [id.], somewhat fat, fattish: plantae, Front. Ep. ad M. Caes. 4, 12 Mai.

pinguis.full: pinguis, e, adj. root pag-, pak-, of pango, q. v.; cf. Gr. παχύς, stout, = πίων, fat (opp. macer; syn.: opimus, obesus). Lit.: pingues Thebani, Cic. Fat. 4, 7: pingui tentus omaso Furius, Hor. S. 2, 5, 40: me pinguem et nitidum bene curatā cute vises, id. Ep. 1, 4, 15: Lateranus, Juv. 8, 147: pinguem facere gallinam, Col. 8, 7: pinguior agnus, Plaut. Aul. 2, 5, 5: pinguissimus haedulus, Juv. 11, 65: merum, rich, oily wine (= plenum), Hor. S. 2, 4, 65.— Subst.: pingue, is, n., fat, grease, Plin.

pinguitia.full: pinguĭtĭa, ae, and pinguĭtĭes, ēi, f. pinguis, fatness (post-class.), Arn. 7, 226; App. M. 10, p. 245, 39.
pinguitia.short: pinguĭtĭa, ae, and pinguĭtĭes, ēi, f.

pinguitudo.full: pinguĭtūdo, ĭnis, f. id., fatness, richness, coarseness, rankness. Lit.: vere sus usque adeo pinguitudine crescere solet, ut, etc., Cato ap. Varr. R. R. 2, 4; Varr. R. R. 2, 4, 6; Plin. 11, 37, 71, § 186: olei, Col. 12, 52, 17: soli, id. 4, 24, 19: palmitis, Pall. 3, 12, 2.— Transf., broadness, coarseness of pronunciation, opp. to exilitas, Quint. 1, 11, 4 (v. l. pinguedine).

pinguiusculus.full: pinguĭuscŭlus, a, um, adj. dim. [id.], somewhat fat, fattish: corpora, Sol. 11.

pinifer.full: pīnĭfer, fĕra, fĕrum, adj. pinus-fero, pine-bearing, that produces pines: Maenalus, Verg. E. 10, 14: Atlantis caput, id. A. 4, 248: Ida, Stat. S. 3, 4, 12.

piniger.full: pīnĭger, gĕra, gĕrum, adj. pinus-gero, pine-bearing: caput, Ov. F. 3, 84: Othrys, Val. Fl. 6, 393: Simois, Stat. Th. 12, 225.

pinna2.full: pinna, a kind of mussel; prop. pīnă, q. v.

pinnaculum.full: pinnācŭlum, i, n. 1. pinna, a peak, pinnacle of a building (late Lat.), Tert. adv. Jud. 8; Vulg. Matt. 4, 5.

pinnapes.full: pinnăpes, pĕdis, adj. pinna-pes, winged on the feet, having winged feet: Perseus, Cat. 55, 25.

pinnatus.full: pinnātus, a, um, adj. 1. pinna, feathered, plumed, winged. Lit.: Jovis satelles Pinnatā caudā, old poet ap. Cic. Tusc. 2, 10, 24: Musa pinnato gradu intulit se, Porc. Latro ap. Gell. 17, 21, 45: Cupido, Cic. N. D. 3, 23, 58.— Transf., feathered, pinnate: abies folio pinnato densa, feathered, i. e. having leaves that lie on each other like feathers, Plin. 16, 10, 19, § 48: fraxinus pinnata et ipsa folio, id. 16, 13, 24, § 62; 27, 9, 55, § 79.

pinnicillum.full: pinnĭcillum, i, n., for penicillum. Pall. Mart. 1.

pinniger.full: pinnĭger, gĕra, gĕrum, adj. 1. pinnagero, feather-bearing, i. e. feathered, winged. Lit.: pinnigero, non armigero in corpore tela exercentur, i. e. against birds, Att. ap. Cic. Fam. 7, 33, 1 (Trag. Rel. p. 176 Rib.): amor, Lucr. 5, 1074.— Transf, having fins, finny: piscis, Ov. M. 13, 963; Coripp. Johann. 4, 981.

pinnirapus.full: pinnĭrăpus, i, m. 1. pinna-rapio, a peak-snatcher, i. e. a gladiator, Juv. 3, 158; cf.: pinnirapos autem dicit, lanistas ex habitu gladiatorum, quia post mortem retiarii pinnam, id est manicam rapit, ut ostendat populo se vicisse, Vet. Schol. ad loc.

pinnula.full: pinnŭla, ae, f. dim. 1. pinna, a little plume or wing. Lit., Plaut. Am. prol. 143; Col. 8, 5.— Transf., a little fin, a fin, Plin. 9, 57, 83, § 175; Vulg. Lev. 11, 9; id. Deut. 14, 9.

pinophylax.full: pīnŏphўlax, ăcis, m., = πιννοφύλαξ, a species of crab, called also pinoteres, Plin. 9, 42, 66, § 142.
pinophylax.short: pīnŏphўlax, ăcis, m., = πιννοφύλαξ, a species of crab, called also pinoteres, Plin.

pinoteres.full: pīnŏtēres and pīnŏthēres (less correctly pinno-), ae, m., = πιννοτήρης or πιννοθήρης, the pinna-guard, a species of crab found in the shell of the pina, and fabled to keep watch over it, Cic. Fin. 3, 19, 63; Plin. 9, 31, 51, § 98; 32, 11, 53, § 150.
pinoteres.short: pīnŏtēres and pīnŏthēres (less correctly pinno-), ae, m., = πιννοτήρης or πιννοθήρης, the pinna-guard, a species of crab found in the shell of the pina, and fabled to keep watch over it, Cic.

pinsatio.full: pinsātĭo, ōnis, f. pinso, āre, a stamping, pounding, crushing, Vitr. 7, 1.

pinsitus.full: pinsĭtus, a, um, Part., from pinso.
pinsitus.short: pinsĭtus, a, um, Part., from pinso.

pinso.full: pinso (pīso), pinsi and pinsŭi, pinsum, pinsĭtum, and pistum (pisatum, Fest. p. 158 Müll.), 3 (also in Varr. R. R. 1, 63 fin., the reading is pinsatur; archaic form of the imperf. pinsibant, Enn. ap. Varr. L. L. 5, § 23 Müll.; v. Enn. p. 147 fin. Vahl.), v. a. [πίσσω, πτίσσω], to beat, pound, bray, crush: pinsunt terram genibus, Enn. ap. Diom. p. 370 P. (Ann. v. 354 Vahl.): flagro, to scourge, Plaut. Merc. 2, 3, 81: si communiter pisunt, Cato, R. R. 136: pilum, quod eo far pisunt: a quo ubi id f
pinso.short: pinso (pīso), pinsi and pinsŭi, pinsum, pinsĭtum, and pistum (pisatum, Fest.

pinsor.full: pinsor, ōris, m. pinso, for pistor, a baker, Varr. ap. Non. 152, 14.

pinsus.full: pinsus, a, um, Part., from pinso.
pinsus.short: pinsus, a, um, Part., from pinso.

pinus.full: pīnus, ūs and i (dat. pinu, Prop. 3, 19, 19; abl. sing. only pinu; gen. and abl. plur. pinorum and pinis), f., = πίτυς. Lit., a pine, pine-tree; a fir, fir-tree: Pinus silvestris, Linn.; Plin. 16, 20, 33, § 79; 16, 25, 40, § 95: ex altā pinu, Verg. G. 2, 389: pinos loquentes, id. E. 8, 22: evertunt actas ad sidera pinus, id. A. 11, 136: Idaeae sacro de vertice pinus, id. ib. 10, 230: gummi in cerasis, resina pinis, Plin. 37, 3, 11, § 42.— The pine was sacred to Cybele, Ov. M. 10, 103; Macr. S. 6

pio.full: pĭo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. pius. To seek to appease, to appease, propitiate by sacrifice (syn. place).— Lit.: Silvanum lacte piabant, Hor. Ep. 2, 1, 143: ossa, Verg. A. 6, 379: busta (i.e. Manes), Ov. M. 13, 515: Janus Agonali luce piandus erit, id. F. 1, 318.— Transf. To honor with religious rites, to celebrate: ubi piem Pietatem, Plaut. As. 3, 1, 3: aras ture, Prop. 3, 10 (4, 9), 19: in magicis astra piare focis, to perform sacred rites, id. 1, 1, 20.— To purify with sacred rites (syn.: procuro,

pipatio.full: pīpātĭo, ōnis, f. pipo, a piping, chirping, whimpering: pipatio clamor plorantis linguā Oscorum, Paul. ex Fest. p. 212 Müll.

pipatus.full: pīpātus, ūs, m. id., a peeping, piping, chirping: pullorum, Varr. L. L. 7, § 103 Müll.

piper.full: pĭper, pĭpĕris, n., = πέπερι (Sanscr. pippali or pippalī, the same), pepper. Lit., Plin. 12, 7, 14, § 26 sq.; Cels. 2, 27: et piper et quicquid chartis amicitur ineptis, Hor. Ep. 2, 1, 270; Ov. A. A. 2, 417; Juv. 14, 293: rugosum piper, Pers. 5, 55: sacrum piper, a term intimating that the miser is as sparing of it as if it were something sacred, id. 6, 21.— Trop., of sharp, biting speech: piper, non homo, Petr. 44; Hier. Ep. 31, n. 2.

piperatarius.full: pĭpĕrātārĭus, a, um, adj. piper, containing pepper (late Lat.): horrea piperataria, Hier. in Chron. Euseb. ad a. XCII. p. Chr. n.

piperatorium.full: pĭpĕrātōrĭum, ii, n. piper, a silver dish to hold pepper, a pepper-box: vasis argenteis legatis, continentur ... piperatoria, Paul. Sent. 3, 6, 86.

piperatus.full: pĭpĕrātus, a, um, adj. id., peppered, seasoned with pepper. Lit.: garum piperatum, Petr. 36: acetum, Col. 12, 47, 5.— Subst.: pĭpĕrātum, i, n., peppersauce, Cels. 4, 19; Apic. 3, 14.— Trop., peppery, pungent: piperata facundia, Sid. Ep. 5, 8; 8, 11.— Sharp, thievish: non fuit Autolyci tam piperata manus, Mart. 8, 59, 4.

piperitis.full: pĭpĕrītis, is and ĭdis, f., = πεπερῖτις, pepperwort, prob. Indian pepper: piperitis, quam et siliquastrum appellavimus, Plin. 20, 17, 66, § 174; 19, 12, 62, § 187.
piperitis.short: pĭpĕrītis, is and ĭdis, f., = πεπερῖτις, pepperwort, prob.

pipilo.full: pīpĭlo, āre, v. n. pipio, to peep, pip, chirp: ad solam dominam usque pipilabat (passer), Cat. 3, 10; Poët. ap. Anth. Lat. t. 2, p. 294 Burm.

pipio1.full: pīpĭo, āre, v. n., to pip, chirp, whimper: infantes pipiantes, Tert. Monog. 16: imbres pipiavit, id. adv. Valent. 15.

pipio2.full: pīpĭo, īre, v. n., to peep, pip, chirp: aviarius auscultetur, si (pulli) pipiant, Col. 8, 5, 14; Auct. Carm. Philom. 30.

pipio3.full: pīpĭo, ōnis, m., a young piping or chirping bird, a squab: servos habuit vectigales qui eos (palumbes) ex ovis et pullicenis ac pipionibus alerent, from the produce of the eggs and chickens, Lampr. Alex. Sever. 41.
pipio3.short: pīpĭo, ōnis, m., a young piping or chirping bird, a squab: servos habuit vectigales qui eos (palumbes) ex ovis et pullicenis ac pipionibus alerent, from the produce of the eggs and chickens, Lampr.

pipizo.full: pīpizo, ōnis, m. pipio, the young of the crane, Hier. Ep. 22, n. 28.

pipo.full: pīpo, āre, v. n., to peep, pip, chirp: mugit bos, balat ovis, equi hinniunt, gallina pipat, Varr. ap. Non. 156, 25; of the hawk, Auct. Carm. Philom. 24.

pipulum.full: pīpŭlum, i, n., and pīpŭlus, i, m. pipo, a peeping, piping, chirping; hence, A whimpering, crying: filioli, Front. Ep. ad Anton. 1, 3 Mai.— An outcry, upbraiding: te pipulo hic differam ante aedes, Plaut. Aul. 3, 2, 32; cf.: pipulo te differam id est convicio, declinatum a pipatu pullorum, Varr. L. L. 7, § 103 Müll.: pipulo poscere, Cn. Matius ap. Gell. 20, 9, 4.
pipulum.short: pīpŭlum, i, n., and pīpŭlus, i, m.

piracium.full: pĭrācĭum, ii, n. pirum, perry, Hier. adv. Jovin. 2, n. 5; Ven. Vit. S. Radeg. 15.

piraceus.full: Pīraceus (trisyll.) and Pīraeus, i, m., = Πειραιεύς; also Pīraea, ōrum, n. (poet.), the celebrated port of Athens, about five Roman miles from the city, with which it was connected by long walls; the Pirœus, now Porto Dracone or Porto Leone: In Piraeea cum exissem, Cic. Att. 6, 9, 1: venio ad Piraeea: in quo magis reprehendendus sum, quod homo Romanus Piraeea scripserim, non Piraeeum (sic enim omnes nostri locuti sunt), quam in quod addiderim: non enim hoc ut oppido praeposui, sed ut loco ... Se
piraceus.short: Pīraceus (trisyll.) and Pīraeus, i, m., = Πειραιεύς;

pirata.full: pīrāta, ae, m., = πειρατής (an adventurer, hence), a sea-robber, corsair, pirate (syn. praedo): nam pirata non est ex perduellium numero definitus, sed communis hostis omnium, Cic. Rosc. Am. 50, 146; id. Off. 3, 29, 107; Vell. 2, 31, 2; Luc. 3, 228; Flor. 3, 6, 11: Capito et Numitor, Piratae Cilicum, Juv. 8, 94 al.
pirata.short: pīrāta, ae, m., = πειρατής (an adventurer, hence), a sea-robber, corsair, pirate (syn.

piraticus.full: pīrātĭcus, a, um, adj., = πειρατικός, of or belonging to pirates, piratic, piratical: myoparone piratico capto, Cic. Verr. 2, 5, 28, § 73: statio, Plin. 3, 26, 30, § 152: laurea, victories over the pirates, Luc. 1, 122: bellum, Cic. Red. in Sen. 5, 11.— Subst.: pīrātĭca, ae, f., piracy: piraticam queque ut musicam fabricam dici adhuc dubitabant mei praeceptores, Quint. 8, 3, 34: piraticam facere, to practise piracy, Cic. Red. in Sen. 5; so, piraticam exercere, Just. 8, 3, 13; 22, 1, 14.
piraticus.short: pīrātĭcus, a, um, adj., = πειρατικός, of or belonging to pirates, piratic, piratical: myoparone piratico capto, Cic.

pirene.full: Pīrēnē, ēs, f., = Πειρήνη, a fountain in the citadel of Corinth (Acrocorinthus), which sprung up from a blow of the hoof of Pegasus; hence sacred to the Muses, Plin. 4, 4, 5; Plaut. Aul. 3, 6, 23; Stat. S. 1, 4, 25: Heliconidasque pallidamque Pirenen, Pers. prol. 4.—Hence, Pīrēnis, ĭdis, f. adj., = Πειρηνίς, of or belonging to Pirene, Pirenian: Ephyre, i. e. Corinth, Ov. M. 7, 391: unda, id. ib. 2, 240: Pirenida cessit ad undam (al. urbem), to Corinth, id. P. 1, 3, 75: Tantalus securus undas hau
pirene.short: Pīrēnē, ēs, f., = Πειρήνη, a fountain in the citadel of Corinth (Acrocorinthus), which sprung up from a blow of the hoof of Pegasus;

pirithous.full: Pīrĭthŏus, i, m., = Πειρίθοος, son of Ixion, king of the Lapithœ, husband of Hippodamia, and friend of Theseus. After the death of Hippodamia, he descended, in company with Theseus, to the infernal regions, to carry away Proserpine; but was, together with Theseus, seized and detained in chains. Theseus was afterwards delivered by Hercules, who vainly endeavored to save Pirithoüs also, Ov. M. 8, 302 sq.: amatorem trecentae Pirithoum cohibent catenae, Hor. C. 3, 4, 79; 4, 7, 28: Aegidae Pirithoiqu
pirithous.short: Pīrĭthŏus, i, m., = Πειρίθοος, son of Ixion, king of the Lapithœ, husband of Hippodamia, and friend of Theseus.

pirum.full: pĭrum, i, n., a pear, Cato, R. R. 7; Varr. R. R. 1, 59, 3; Col. 5, 10, 18; Plin. 15, 15, 16, § 53; Cloat. ap. Macr. S. 2, 15; Plaut. Poen. 2, 38; Juv. 11, 73: insitiva decerpens pira, Hor. Epod. 2, 19; id. Ep. 1, 7, 14; Verg. G. 2, 88.
pirum.short: pĭrum, i, n., a pear, Cato, R.

pirus.full: pĭrus, i, f., a pear-tree: insere nunc, Meliboee, piros, Verg. E. 1, 74; Plin. 16, 24, 38, § 90; 16, 26, 46, § 109; 16, 25, 42, § 103: felix arbor, Macr. S. 3, 20, 2.
pirus.short: pĭrus, i, f., a pear-tree: insere nunc, Meliboee, piros, Verg.

pirustae.full: Pīrustae, ārum, m., a people in Illyria, Caes. B. G. 5, 1; Liv. 45, 26.
pirustae.short: Pīrustae, ārum, m., a people in Illyria, Caes.

pisa2.full: Pīsa, ae, and, less freq., Pīsae, ārum, f., = Πῖσα, a city of Elis, on the Alphēus, near which the Olympic games were celebrated: aut Alphea rotis praelabi flumina Pisae, Verg. G. 3, 180: Pisa, Ov. Ib. 327; Stat. Th. 4, 238: Pisae Oenomai, Mel. 2, 3, 4.—Hence, Pīsaeus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Pisa, Pisœan: Arethusa, so called because, acc. to the myth, it rose in Elis, Ov. M. 5, 409: hasta, of Oenomăus, king of Elis, id. Am. 3, 2, 15: Pisaeā lege trementem currere et Oenomai fremitus aud
pisa2.short: Pīsa, ae, and, less freq., Pīsae, ārum, f., = Πῖσα, a city of Elis, on the Alphēus, near which the Olympic games were celebrated: aut Alphea rotis praelabi flumina Pisae, Verg.

pisae.full: Pīsae, ārum, f., a very ancient eity of Etruria, a colony of Pisa in Elis, still called Pisa: Alpheae ab origine Pisae, urbs Etrusca solo, Verg. A. 10, 179 Serv.; Just. 20, 1, 11; Luc. 2, 401; Liv. 21, 39.—Hence, Pīsānus, a, um, adj., Pisan: ager, Liv. 39, 2.—In plur.: Pīsāni, ōrum, m., the Pisans, Liv. 40, 43.— † Pīsas, ātis, adj., Pisatic, Pisan, Inscr. Orell. 4048.— Pīsātĭlis, e, adj., born at Pisa (for Pisanus), found in Naev., acc. to Fest. p. 210 Müll. (prob. Latinized from the Greek form
pisae.short: Pīsae, ārum, f., a very ancient eity of Etruria, a colony of Pisa in Elis, still called Pisa: Alpheae ab origine Pisae, urbs Etrusca solo, Verg.

pisander.full: Pīsander, dri, m., = Πείσανδρος, son of Polyctor, and one of Penelope's suitors, Ov. H. 1, 91.
pisander.short: Pīsander, dri, m., = Πείσανδρος, son of Polyctor, and one of Penelope's suitors, Ov.

pisanus.full: Pīsānus, a, um, v. Pisae, A.

pisatio.full: pīsātĭo, ōnis, f. piso, a stamping, crushing (al. spissatio), Sen. Ep. 86, 17.

pisaurum.full: Pisaurum, i, n.. a city of Umbria, at the mouth of the Pisaurus, the mod. Pesaro, Mel. 2, 4, 5; Liv. 39, 44; Vell. 1, 15, 2; Caes. B. C. 1, 11 sq.; Cic. Fam. 16, 12, 2; id. Att. 2, 7, 2 sq.—Hence, Pisaurensis, e, adj., Pisaurian: T. Accius Pisaurensis, of Pisaurum, Cic. Brut. 78, 271; Plin. 7, 39, 40, § 128.—In plur.: Pisaurenses, ĭum, m., the Pisaurians, Inscr. Grut. 276, 3; 481, 9; 1085, 12.— † Pisaurĭus, ii, m., name of a slave liberated by the city of Pisaurum, Inscr. Fabr. p. 438, n. 17.

piscarius.full: piscārĭus, a, um, adj. piscis, of or belonging to fishing or fish, fish-: copia piscaria, Plaut. Cas. 2, 8, 65: forum piscarium, the fish-market, id. Curc. 4, 1, 13: hamulus, id. Stich. 2, 1, 17.— Subst. piscārĭus, ii, m., a fish-monger: nullus in piscariā piscis erat: inter piscarios nemo vendebat, Varr. in Perott. in Cornucop.— piscārĭa, ae, f., fish-market, Varr. Fragm. v. supra; Dig. 50, 16, 17.

piscatio.full: piscātĭo, ōnis, f. piscor, a fishing, fishery: piscatio thynnaria, Dig. 8, 4, 13; 7, 1, 9; Paul. Sent. 3, 6, 41.

piscator.full: piscātor, ōris, m. id., a fisherman, fisher, Plaut. Rud. 4, 3, 48; 55: lanii, coqui, fartores, piscatores, Ter. Eun. 2, 2, 26: piscatores ad se convocat, Cic. Off. 3, 14, 58; Juv. 4, 26; Sen. Ep. 55, 6: piscatoris instrumentum, Paul. Sent. 3, 6, 66: PISCATORES PROPOLAE, Inscr. Fabr. p. 731, n. 450: PATRONVS CORPORIS PISCATORVM, Inscr. Orell. 4115.—Fig.: piscatores hominum, Vulg. Matt. 4, 19.

piscatorius.full: piscātōrĭus, a, um, adj. piscator, of or belonging to fishermen, fishing-: naves, fishing-smacks, Caes. B. C. 2, 4; Liv. 36, 27: casa, Petr. 115: harundo, a fishing-rod, Plin. 16, 36, 66, § 172: lina, of which nets were made, id. 24, 9, 40, § 65: forum, Col. 8, 17, 15: piscatorii ludi vocantur, qui quotannis mense Junio trans Tiberim fieri solent a praetore urbano pro piscatoribus Tiberinis, Fest. p. 238 Müll.; cf. Ov. F. 6, 239: piscatorium aes vetusto more appellatur, quod in monte Albano datu

piscatrix.full: piscātrix, īcis, f. id., she that fishes: rana, quae in mari piscatrix vocatur, Plin. 9, 42, 67, § 143; Inscr. Gud. 192, 8.

piscatura.full: piscātūra, ae, f. piscor, a fishing (post-class. for piscatus), Tert. adv. Marc. 4, 9.

piscatus.full: piscātus, ūs (gen. piscati, Pompon. et Turp. ap. Non. 488, 16 sq.), m. id.. Lit., a fishing, catching of fish: hamatilis et saxatilis, Plaut. Rud. 2, 1, 10; 4, 2, 6 sq.: esse et in piscatu voluptatem maxime testudinum, Plin. 6, 22, 24, § 91.—In plur.: quos venatus, aucupia, piscatusque alebant, Plin. 8, 16, 17, § 44.— Fig., a catch (of a mistress): piscatus hic tibi evenit bonus, Plaut. Bacch. 1, 1, 70.—Transf., concr., fishes, fish: parare piscatum, Plaut. Most. 1, 1, 63; 3, 2, 41: privare pisc

piscicapus.full: piscĭcăpus, i, m. piscis-capio, a fish-catcher, fisher, Inscr. Orell. 3700, c.

pisciculus1.full: piscĭcŭlus, i, m. dim. piscis, a little fish, Varr. R. R. 3, 5: minuti, Ter. And. 2, 2, 32: parvi, Cic. N. D. 2, 48, 123; Vulg. Marc. 8, 7.

pisciculus2.full: Piscĭcŭlus, i, m., a Roman surname: Junius Pisciculus, Plin. 36, 5, 4, § 39.
pisciculus2.short: Piscĭcŭlus, i, m., a Roman surname: Junius Pisciculus, Plin.

piscina.full: piscīna, ae, f. piscis, a pond in which fish are kept, a fish-pond. Lit.: piscinarum genera sunt duo, dulcium et salsarum, Varr. R. R. 3, 17, 2; 3, 3, 2; 5; 10; Col. 1, 6, 21; 8, 17: in piscinam rete qui parat, Plaut. Truc. 1, 1, 12; Cic. Par. 5, 2, 38; id. Att. 2, 1, 7.—Esp., Piscina publica, the public fish-pond at the Porta Capena: praetores tribunalia ad Piscinam publicam posuerunt, Liv. 23, 32, 4; cf. Fest. infra, II. A. — Transf. (post-Aug.). A pond for bathing or swimming, whether of warm

piscinalis.full: piscīnālis, e, adj. piscina, of or belonging to a bath: cellae, bathing-rooms, Pall. 1, 40, 4.

piscinarius.full: piscīnārĭus, a, um, adj. id., of or belonging to fish-ponds: macellum, Varr. R. R. 3, 17 ex conject. Ponted.; v. Schneid. ad loc.— Subst.: piscīnārĭus, ii, m., one fond of fish-ponds, Cic. Att. 1, 19, 6; 1, 20, 3; Macr. S. 1, 11.

piscinensis.full: piscīnensis, e, adj. id., of or belonging to fish-ponds: pugil est, Lucil. ap. Fest. s. v. piscinae, p. 213 Müll.

piscis.full: piscis, is, m. etym. dub.; cf. Angl. -Sax. fisk, Germ. Fisch, a fish. Lit.: ubi lanigerum pecus piscibus pascit, Enn. ap. Paul. ex Fest. s. v. cyprio, p. 59 Müll. (Sat. v. 42 Vahl.); id. ap. App. Mag. p. 299 (Heduph. v. 5 Vahl.); Plaut. As. 1, 3, 26; id. Truc. 2, 3, 1: pisces ut saepe minutos magnu' comest, Varr. ap. Non. 81, 11: etsi pisces ut aiunt, ova cum genuerunt, relinquunt, Cic. N. D. 2, 51, 129; Hor. C. 4, 3, 19; Juv. 4, 72.— Sing. collect.: pisce vehi quaedam (natarum videntur), Ov. M.

piscor.full: piscor, ātus, 1, v. dep. n. [piscis], to fish: ut ante suos hortulos piscarentur, Cic. Off. 3, 14, 58: piscemur, venemur, Hor. Ep. 1, 6, 57: animi laxandi causā piscabatur hamo, Suet. Aug. 83: piscatus est rete aurato, id. Ner. 30: retia in piscando durantia, Plin. 19, 1, 2, § 15: vado piscari, Vulg. Johan. 21, 3.—Prov.: piscari in aëre, to give one's self useless trouble, to labor in vain, Plaut. As. 1, 1, 86: piscari aureo hamo, to risk more than the game is worth: minima commoda non minimo se

piscosus.full: piscōsus, a, um, adj. id., full of fishes, abounding in fish (syn. pisculentus): amnes. Ov. F. 3, 581: scopuli, Verg. A. 4, 255: flumina, Sen. Ben. 6, 7, 3: Oceanus, Just. 44, 1, 7.

pisculentus.full: piscŭlentus, a, um, adj. id., full of fishes, abounding in fish (ante- and postclass.): fluvius, Cato ap. Non. 151, 7 sq.: loca, Plaut. Rud. 4, 2, 2: promuntorium omnibus mari nantibus pisculentissimum, Sol. 5, 6.— Subst.: piscŭlentum, i, n., a remedy prepared from fish, App. Mag. p. 294, 40.

pisida.full: Pī^sī^da, ae, m., a Pisidian; usually Pī^sī^dae, ārum (old orthog. Peisidae, Plebis. Therm.), m., = Πισίδαι, Pisidians, a people of Taurus, in Asia Minor, bordering on the Phrygians, Mel. 1, 2, 5; Cic. Leg. 2, 13, 33; id. Div. 1, 1, 2; 1, 15, 25; 1, 41, 92; id. Att. 6, 5, 3; Liv. 35, 13; Claud. in Eutr. 2, 241.—In sing., Cic. Div. 1, 47, 105.—Collect.: Pisida ferox, Avien. Perieg. 1023.— Hence, Pī^sī^dĭa, ae, f., = Πισιδία, the country of the Pisidians, Pisidia, Liv. 37, 54 and 56.— Pī^sī^dĭcus,

pisinnus.full: pĭsinnus, a, um, adj., small, little; only as subst.: pĭsinni, ōrum, m., little ones, children: crudum manduces Priamum Priamique pisinnos, Labeo ap. Schol. Pers. 1, 4.
pisinnus.short: pĭsinnus, a, um, adj., small, little;

pisinuus.full: Pisĭnŭus, i, f., an ancient town in Galatia, prob. the same with Pessinus (Gr. Πεσσινοῦς), q. v., Plin. 5, 32, 42, § 146.
pisinuus.short: Pisĭnŭus, i, f., an ancient town in Galatia, prob.

pisistratus.full: Pīsistrătus, i, m., = Πεισίστρατος. Pisistratus, tyrant of Athens, Cic. N. D. 3, 33, 82; id. Brut. 7, 27; id. Rep. 1, 44, 68; id. de Or. 3, 34, 137; Sen. Ira, 3, 11, 4; Phaedr. 1, 2, 5.—Hence, Pīsistrătĭdae, ārum, m., = Πεισιστρατίδαι, the Pisistratidœ, i. e. Hippias and Hipparchus, sons of Pisistratus, Liv. 31, 44, 8.— A Bœotian chief, a friend of the Romans, Liv. 33, 27 sq.

pisito.full: pīsĭto, āre, v. n., to utter the natural cry of the starling, Auct. Carm. Phil. 17.

piso1.full: pīso, āre and ĕre, v. pinso.

piso2.full: pīso, ōnis, m. pinso, piso; cf. pistor, a mortar: marmoreus, Marc. Emp. 8.

piso3.full: Pīso, ōnis, m., a Roman surname in the gens Calpurnia; v. Calpurnius, Cic. Font. 13, 39; Juv. 5, 109.—Hence, Pīsōnĭ-ānus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to a Piso, Pisonian: Pisoniana conjuratio, Suet. Ner. 36: Pisoniano vitio, cum loqui nesciret, tacere non potuit (with reference to Cic. Pis. 1, 1, where Cicero charges Piso with lack of eloquence), Hier. Ep. 69, 2.
piso3.short: Pīso, ōnis, m., a Roman surname in the gens Calpurnia;

pissasphaltus.full: pissasphaltus, i, m., = πισσάσφαλτος, earth-pitch, pissasphalt (a kind of soft bitumen), Plin. 24, 7, 25, § 41; 35, 15, 51, § 178.
pissasphaltus.short: pissasphaltus, i, m., = πισσάσφαλτος, earth-pitch, pissasphalt (a kind of soft bitumen), Plin.

pisselaeon.full: pissĕlaeon, i, n., = πισσέλαιον, an oil made from the resin of the cedar, Plin. 24, 5, 11, § 19.
pisselaeon.short: pissĕlaeon, i, n., = πισσέλαιον, an oil made from the resin of the cedar, Plin.

pissinus.full: pissĭnus, a, um, adj., = πισσινος, of pitch, pitch-: e pice fit (oleum) quod pissinum appellant, Plin. 15, 7, 7, § 31; 23, 4, 50, § 96; 25, 5, 22, § 55.
pissinus.short: pissĭnus, a, um, adj., = πισσινος, of pitch, pitch-: e pice fit (oleum) quod pissinum appellant, Plin.

pissoceros.full: pissŏcēros, i, m., = πισσόκηρος, pitch-wax, work of pitch and wax, the second foundation of the honey-comb: prima fundamenta commosin vocant periti, secunda pissoceron, tertia propolin, Plin. 11, 7, 6, § 16.
pissoceros.short: pissŏcēros, i, m., = πισσόκηρος, pitch-wax, work of pitch and wax, the second foundation of the honey-comb: prima fundamenta commosin vocant periti, secunda pissoceron, tertia propolin, Plin.

pistacia.full: pistācĭa, ae, f., = πιστακία, a pistachio-tree, Pall. 3, 25, 33.
pistacia.short: pistācĭa, ae, f., = πιστακία, a pistachio-tree, Pall.

pistacium.full: pistācĭum, ii, and pistācĕum,, i, n., = πιστάκιον, the fruit of the pistachiotree, a pistachio-nut, Plin. 13, 5, 10, § 51; Pall. 11, 12, 3; id. Insit. 157.
pistacium.short: pistācĭum, ii, and pistācĕum,, i, n., = πιστάκιον, the fruit of the pistachiotree, a pistachio-nut, Plin.

pistana.full: pistāna, ae, f., for sagitta, a plant, arrow-head, Plin. 21, 17, 68, § 111.
pistana.short: pistāna, ae, f., for sagitta, a plant, arrow-head, Plin.

pisticus.full: pistĭcus, a, um, adj., = πιστικός, pure, genuine (late Lat.), Vulg. Johan. 12, 3: unguentum, Ambros. in Luc. 6, § 34.
pisticus.short: pistĭcus, a, um, adj., = πιστικός, pure, genuine (late Lat.), Vulg.

pistillum.full: pistillum, i, n., and pistillus, i, m., a pounder, pestle of a mortar, Plaut. Aul. 1, 2, 17: semen sinapis in mortarium conicito et pistillis conterito, Col. 12, 55; Plin. 34, 18, 50, § 169: pistillum grande est, Auct. ap. Non. 221, 5 (yet pastillum appears to be the more correct reading).
pistillum.short: pistillum, i, n., and pistillus, i, m., a pounder, pestle of a mortar, Plaut.

pisto.full: pisto, āvi, ātum, 1, v. freq. a. piso, pinso, to pound (late Lat.), Veg. Vet. 1, 32: herba senecion pistatā cum axungiā, App. Herb. 75.

pistor.full: pistor, ōris, m. pinso; root in Sanscr. pish-, to crush; cf. Gr. πτίσσω, one who pounds corn in a mortar or grinds it in a hand-mill, a miller (only so in Plaut.). Lit.: nec pistorem ullum nossent, nisi eum, qui in pistrino pinseret farinam (far?), Varr. ap. Non. 152, 14; cf. id. ib. 16: pistores tantum eos qui far pinserunt nominatos, At. Cap. ap. Plin. 18, 11, 28, § 107; Plaut. Capt. 4, 2, 27; id. Trin. 2, 4, 6; Gell. 3, 3, 14.— Transf., a baker (class.): pistores Romae non fuere ad Persicum u

pistoricus.full: pistōrĭcus, a, um, a false reading for pistorius, Dig. 32, 1, 73 al.
pistoricus.short: pistōrĭcus, a, um, a false reading for pistorius, Dig.

pistorium.full: Pistōrĭum, ii, n., a city in Etruria, where Catiline was defeated and slain, the modern Pistoia, Plin. 3, 5, 8, § 52.—Hence, Pistōriensis, e, adj., of or belonging to Pistorium, Pistorian: ager. Sall. C. 57, 1: milites Pistorienses, with a play upon the word pistor, Plaut. Capt. 1, 2, 58.
pistorium.short: Pistōrĭum, ii, n., a city in Etruria, where Catiline was defeated and slain, the modern Pistoia, Plin.

pistorius.full: pistōrĭus, a, um, adj. pistor, of or belonging to a baker, baker's: opus pistorium, pastry, Cels. 2, 18; Plin. 18, 11, 27, § 105; Dig. 32, 1, 73 al.: ars, Vulg. Gen. 40, 17.

pistriger.full: pistrĭger, gĕra, gĕrum, adj. pistrisgero, whale-bearing: Triton, i. e. carrying a whale's body, ending in a whale's tail, Sid. Ep. 4, 8.

pistrilla.full: pistrilla, ae, f. dim. pistrina, a little pounding-mill, Ter. Ad. 4, 2, 45.
