pistrina.full: pistrīna, ae, f. pistor, a bakehouse, bakery, Plin. 18, 9, 20, § 86; 19, 8, 52, § 167; Varr. L. L. 5, 31, 138; Lucil. ap. Charis. p. 55 P.

pistrinalis.full: pistrīnālis, e, adj. pistrina, of or belonging to a bakery: pecus, swine fattened there, Col. 7, 9, 3.

pistrinarius.full: pistrīnārĭus, ĭi, m. pistrinum, the manager of a pounding-mill, a miller, Dig. 16, 3, 1.

pistrinensis.full: pistrīnensis, e, adj. id., of or belonging to a pounding-mill, mill-: jumenta, Suet. Calig. 39.

pistrinum.full: pistrīnum (pristrīnum, Plaut. Pers. 3, 3, 15 Ritschl; id. Ps. 5, 1, 9 Fleck.), i, n. pistor, a place where corn is pounded, a pounding-mill, mill; usually worked by horses or asses; but sometimes a lazy or otherwise bad slave was forced to perform this labor (cf. mola). Lit.: ut ferratus in pistrino aetatem conteras, Plaut. Bacch. 4, 6, 11: in pistrinum tradi, id. Most. 1, 1, 16: in pristrino credo, ut convenit fore, id. Ps. 5, 1, 9: te in pistrinum, Dave, dedam usque ad necem, Ter. And. 1, 2, 2

pistris.full: pistris or pristis, is (also pistrix or pristix, ĭcis), f., = πίστρις, πρίστις. Lit., any sea-monster; a whale, shark, sawfish: postrema immani corpore pistrix (of Scylla), Verg. A. 3, 427: in Indico mari pristes ducenum cubitorum, Plin. 9, 3, 2, § 4: jamque agmine toto Pistris adest, Val. Fl. 2, 530: marina pistrix, Flor. 3, 5, 16.— Transf. The constellation of the Whale: ad Pistricis terga, Cic. Arat. 152: Auster Pistrin agit, German. Arat. 358.— A species of swift-sailing ship, Quadrig. ap. N
pistris.short: pistris or pristis, is (also pistrix or pristix, ĭcis), f., = πίστρις, πρίστις.

pistrix.full: pistrix, īcis, f. pistor, a woman who pounds corn; hence, transf., a female baker, Lucil. ap. Varr. L. L. 5, § 138 Müll., and ap. Fest. s. v. mamphula, p. 142 Müll.

pistura.full: pistūra, ae, f. pinso, a pounding of corn, a grinding, Plin. 18, 10, 23, § 97.

pistus.full: pistus, a, um, Part., from pinso.
pistus.short: pistus, a, um, Part., from pinso.

pisum.full: pīsum, i (late Lat. collat. form pīsa, ae, f., Apic. 5, 4; Pall. 11, 14), n., = πισόν, a species of leguminous plant, pease, the pea, Col. 2, 10, 4; Plin. 18, 12, 31, § 123; 18, 12, 33, § 125.

pitane.full: Pĭtănē, ēs, f., = Πιτάνη. A city on the Æolic coast of Asia Minor, now Sandarlik, Mel. 1, 18, 1; Ov. M. 7, 357.—Hence, Pĭtănaeus, a, um, adj., of Pitane, Pitanean: Apollonius Pitanaeus, Plin. 29, 6, 38, § 117.— A town in Laconia, on the Eurotas, Plin. 4, 5, 8, § 16; Aus. Epigr. 24, 3.

pithecium1.full: pĭthēcĭum, ĭi, n., = πιθήκιον. A little ape, Plaut. Mil. 4, 1, 42.— A plant, called also antirrhinon, App. Herb. 86.

pithecium2.full: Pĭthēcĭum, ii, f., the name of an attendant, Plaut. Truc. 2, 5, 24 Speng.† † pithēcus, i, m., = πιθηκος, an ape: pithecus, cercopithecus, cercops, Not. Tir. p. 176.
pithecium2.short: Pĭthēcĭum, ii, f., the name of an attendant, Plaut.

pithecusa.full: Pĭthēcūsa, ae, and Pĭthēcūsae, ārum, f., = Πιθηκοῦσαι, an island (prop. the western and larger of two islands; whence the plur.) in the Tyrrhenian Sea, not far from Cumœ, the modern Ischia, Mel. 2, 7, 18; Plin. 3, 6, 12, § 82; Liv. 8, 22; Ov. M. 14, 90: Inarime a Graecis dicta Pithecusa, Mart. Cap. 6, § 644.
pithecusa.short: Pĭthēcūsa, ae, and Pĭthēcūsae, ārum, f., = Πιθηκοῦσαι, an island (prop.

pitheus.full: pĭtheus, ĕi and ĕos (also pĭthus, i, and pĭthĭas, ae), m., = πιθεύς, πίθος, and πιτθιας, a barrel-shaped comet, Plin. 2, 25, 22, § 90; Sen. Q. N. 1, 14, 1; App. de Mundo, p. 64.
pitheus.short: pĭtheus, ĕi and ĕos (also pĭthus, i, and pĭthĭas, ae), m., = πιθεύς, πίθος, and πιτθιας, a barrel-shaped comet, Plin.

pitpit.full: pitpit Osce quicquid, Fest. p. 212 Müll.

pittacium.full: pittăcĭum, ĭi, n., = πιττάκιον. A little leaf or slip of parchment, etc.; a ticket, label, on wine-bottles, etc.: amphorae vitreae, quarum in cervicibus pittacia erant affixa cum hoc titulo: Falernum Opimianum Annorum Centum, Petr. 34; so id. 56; Lampr. Alex. Sev. 21 fin.; Cod. Th. 7, 4, 11.— A small piece of linen or leather spread with salve, a plaster, Cels. 3, 10, 2.— A patch on a garment or shoe: calceamenta pittaciis consuta, Vulg. Josh. 9, 5.

pittacus.full: Pittăcus or -os, i, m., = Πιττακός, one of the seven wise men of Greece, from Mitylene, in Lesbos, Aus. Sept. Sap.; Cic. de Or. 3, 15, 56; id. Leg. 2, 26, 66; Nep. Thras. 4, 2; Juv. 2, 6.
pittacus.short: Pittăcus or -os, i, m., = Πιττακός, one of the seven wise men of Greece, from Mitylene, in Lesbos, Aus.

pittheus.full: Pittheus (dissyl.), ĕi and ĕos, m., = Πιτθεύς, king of Trœzen, son of Pelops, and father of Æthra, the mother of Theseus, Ov. M. 8, 622; Hyg. Fab. 37.—Hence, Pitthēus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Pittheus, Pitthean: Pitthea Troezen, ruled by Pittheus, Ov. M. 15, 296; 506.— Pit-thēïus, a, um, adj., Pitthean: Troezen, Ov. M. 6, 418; cf. regna, id. H. 4, 107.— Pitthēis, ĭdos, f., the Pittheïd, daughter of Pittheus, i. e. Æthra: Pittheidos Aethrae filius, Ov. H. 10, 131.
pittheus.short: Pittheus (dissyl.), ĕi and ĕos, m., = Πιτθεύς, king of Trœzen, son of Pelops, and father of Æthra, the mother of Theseus, Ov.

pituinus.full: pĭtŭĭnus (pĭtўĭnus), a, um, adj., = πιτύινος, of or from pines, pine- (postclass.): resina, Scrib. Comp. 202; 205; Veg. Vet. 4, 28; acc. to the Gr. orthog., resina pityina, Marc. Emp. 36.
pituinus.short: pĭtŭĭnus (pĭtўĭnus), a, um, adj., = πιτύινος, of or from pines, pine- (postclass.): resina, Scrib.

pituita.full: pītŭīta (sometimes in the poets scan. as a trisyl., Hor. S. 2, 2, 76; id. Ep. 1, 1, 108; Pers. 2, 57; cf. Santen on Ter. Maur. p. 430), ae, f. root pitu- for sputu-, from spu- of spuo, sputum; cf. Gr. πτύω, to spit, slime, clammy moisture. In the body, as diseased matter, phlegm, rheum, pituite; in fowls, the pip: cum sanguis corruptus est aut pituita redundat, Cic. Tusc. 4, 10, 23: capitis, Plin. 25, 11, 90, § 141: oris, id. 23, 1, 13, § 17: tantum bilis pituitaeque, Cato, R. R. 156, 4: adversu

pituitaria.full: pītŭītārĭa, ae, f. (sc. herba) [pituita], an herb that removes phlegm, Plin. 23, 1, 13, § 18.

pituitosus.full: pītŭītōsus, a, um, adj. id., full of phlegm, phlegmatic, pituilous: homo, Cic. Fat. 4, 7.

pitydion.full: pitydion, i, n., a reading in Plin. 15, 10, 9, § 36; v. pityis.
pitydion.short: pitydion, i, n., a reading in Plin.

pityida.full: pĭtўĭda, ae, f., = pityis (late Lat.), Cael. Aur. Acut. 2, 29, 160.
pityida.short: pĭtўĭda, ae, f., = pityis (late Lat.), Cael.

pityis.full: pĭtўis, ĭdos, f., = πιτυίς, a pine-cone, Plin. 15, 10, 9, § 36 (al. pitydion).
pityis.short: pĭtўis, ĭdos, f., = πιτυίς, a pine-cone, Plin.

pityocampa.full: pĭtўŏcampa, ae, and -ē, ēs, f., = πιτυοκάμπη, the pine-grub, pine-caterpillar, Plin. 29, 9, 4, § 95; 28, 9, 33, § 128.
pityocampa.short: pĭtўŏcampa, ae, and -ē, ēs, f., = πιτυοκάμπη, the pine-grub, pine-caterpillar, Plin.

pius.full: pĭus (written PIIVS, Inscr. Viscont. Monum. Degli Scip. tab. 6, n. 1; cf. Cic. Quint. 1, 4, 11), a, um (voc. pie: o crucifer bone, lucisator Omnipotens pie, Prud. Cath. 3, 1.—Comp. only magis pius; cf. Charis. pp. 88 and 130 P.—Sup.: piissimus, used by Antonius, and condemned by Cicero, as: verbum omnino nullum in linguā Latinā, Cic. Phil. 13, 19, 43; but freq. in the post-Aug. per., e. g. Sen. Contr. 4, 27 med.; id. Consol. ad Polyb. 26 med.; Tac. Agr. 43; Curt. 9, 6, 17; Flor. 4, 7, 15; Inscr.

pix.full: pix, pĭcis, f. akin to Gr. πικρός, bitter, πίτυς, pine; cf. πεύκη, = πίσσα, pitch: picem meminisse debemus non aliud esse quam combustae resinae fluxum, Plin. 23, 1, 24, § 47; cf. id. 16, 11, 21, § 52: postes inducti pice, Plaut. Most. 3, 2, 140: pastor junctis pice cantat avenis, Ov. Tr. 5, 10, 25: hic dies festus Corticem astrictum pice dimovebit Amphorae, Hor. C. 3, 8, 10: caelum pice nigrius, Ov. H. 18, 7.—Boiling pitch was poured on the bodies of slaves as a punishment: te Pix atra agitet a

placabilis.full: plācābĭlis, e, adj. placo. Pass., easy to be pacified, easily appeased, placable (class.): inimicis te placabilem, amicis inexorabilem praebes, Auct. Her. 4, 15, 21; 4, 45, 58: animi, Cic. Att. 1, 17, 4: ut eo placabiliorem praebeas, Anton. ap. Cic. Att. 14, 13, A fin.: omnia habuisset aequiora et placabiliora, Cic. Verr. 2, 2, 38, § 95: que quisque est major, magis est placabilis ira (al. irae), Ov. Tr. 3, 5, 31.—With ad: Hortensii tam placabile ad justas preces ingenium, Liv. 4, 42, 9.—Poet.:

placabilitas.full: plācābĭlĭtas, ātis, f. placabilis, readiness to be appeased, placable disposition, placability: nihil magno et praeclaro viro dignius placabilitate atque clementiā, Cic. Off. 1, 25, 88.

placamen.full: plācāmen, ĭnis, n. placo, a means of pacifying or appeasing, a lenitive: caelestis irae placamina, Liv. 7, 2, 3: duc praedicta sacris duro placamina Diti, Sil. 13, 415; cf. placamentum.

placamentum.full: plācāmentum, i, n. id., a means of pacifying or appeasing, a lenitive (postAug.): hoc veluti placamento terrae blandiuntur, Plin. 21, 7, 19, § 42.—In plur.: deŭm placamenta, Tac. A. 15, 44; id. H. 1, 63.

placate.full: plācātē, adv., v. placo, P. a. fin.

placatio.full: plācātĭo, ōnis, f. placo, a pacifying, appeasing, propitiating: deorum immortalium, Cic. N. D. 3, 2, 5; id. Tusc. 4, 28, 60.

placatorius.full: plācātōrĭus, a, um, adj. id., of or belonging to pacifying, appeasing, or propitiating; appeasing, placatory (post-class.): hostia, Tert. Patient. 13.

placatrix.full: plācātrix, īcis, f. id. through placator; not in use, she that appeases or propitiates (late Lat.): dei (ecclesia), Salv. Gub. D. 3, 9.

placatus.full: plācātus, a, um, Part. and P. a., from placo.

placens.full: plăcens, entis, Part. and P. a., from placeo.

placenta.full: plăcenta, ae, f., = πλακοῦς, a cake, Cato, R. R. 76; Hor. Ep. 1, 10, 11; id. S. 2, 8, 24; Juv. 11, 59; Mart. 5, 39, 3; 6, 75, 1; 9, 91, 18.—For an offering, Vulg. Jer. 7, 18.
placenta.short: plăcenta, ae, f., = πλακοῦς, a cake, Cato, R.

placentarius.full: plăcentārĭus, ĭi, m. placenta, a pastry-cook, confectioner (late Lat.): inter urbana ministeria continentur ... placentarii, Paul. Sent. 3, 6, 72; cf.: πλακουντάριος, placentarius, dulciarius, Gloss. Philox.

placentia1.full: plăcentĭa, ae, f. placeo, suavity, courteousness (post-class.), App. Dogm. Plat. 2, p. 15, 33.

placentia2.full: Plăcentĭa, ae, f., a city in Gallia Cispadana, on the Po, the modern Piacenza, Liv. 21, 25; 56 sq.; 27, 39; 31, 10 al.; Vell. 1, 14 fin.; Cic. Att. 6, 9, 5; Tac. H. 2, 17; Sil. 8, 593.—Hence, Plăcentī-nus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Placentia, Placentian, Placentine: municipium, Cic. Pis. 23, 53: calices, id. ib. 27, 67: turma, Liv. 44, 40: Tinca, from Placentia, Cic. Brut. 46, 172.—In plur. subst.: Plă-centīni, ōrum, m., the inhabitants of Placentia, the Placentines, Liv. 27, 10; 31, 21 al
placentia2.short: Plăcentĭa, ae, f., a city in Gallia Cispadana, on the Po, the modern Piacenza, Liv.

placeo.full: plăcĕo, cŭi and cĭtus, cĭtum, 2, v. n. (part. fut. pass.: dos placenda, Plaut. Trin. 5, 2, 35; v. I. A. fin.) [cf. placo], to please, to be pleasing or agreeable, to be welcome, acceptable, to satisfy (class.). Lit. In gen.: ungor ut illi placeam, Plaut. Cas. 2, 3, 11: meo neque cara'st cordi neque placet, id. Ep. 1, 2, 30: si placeo, utere, Ter. Phorm. 3, 2, 43: non placet Antonio consulatus meus: at placuit P. Servilio, Cic. Phil. 2, 5, 12; Ter. Ad. 1, 1, 34: et quae vobis placita est condicio
placeo.short: plăcĕo, cŭi and cĭtus, cĭtum, 2, v.

placibilis.full: plăcĭbĭlis, e, adj. placeo, that can please, pleasing (post-class.), Tert. Resurr. Carn. 43.

placiditas.full: plăcĭdĭtas, ātis, f. placidus, mildness, gentleness of nature or disposition, placidity (very rare): oves assumptas propter placiditatem, Varr. R. R. 2, 1; Auct. ap. Gell. 13, 22, 19.

placido.full: plăcĭdo, āvi, āre, v. a. id., to soothe, calm (late Lat.): cursus suos, Ambros. Virg. 3; id. de Cain et Abel, 1, 3, 11; id. Jac. et Vit. Beat. 2, 6, 28.

placidulus.full: plăcĭdŭlus, a, um, adj. dim. [id.], gentle, quiet, still (post-class.): cinis placidula, Aus. Parent. 27.

placidus.full: plăcĭdus, a, um, adj. placeo, qs. pleasing, mild; hence, gentle, quiet, still, calm, mild, peaceful, placid (class.; syn.: quietus, mollis, lenis). In gen. Of persons: clemens, placidus, Ter. Ad. 5, 4, 10: reddere aliquem placidum, Plaut. Curc. 4, 3, 49; Ter. Ad. 4, 1, 18; Cic. Caecin. 10.— Of things: caelum, Sil. 12, 667: placidus et serenus dies, Plin. Ep. 5, 6, 14: mare, id. ib. 9, 26: pontus, Lucr. 5, 1004: amnis, Ov. M. 1, 702: placida quietaque constantia, Cic. Tusc. 4, 5, 10: placida ac l

placitis.full: plăcītis, ĭdis, f., = πλακῖτις, a kind of calamine produced in a furnace, Plin. 34, 10, 22, § 102.
placitis.short: plăcītis, ĭdis, f., = πλακῖτις, a kind of calamine produced in a furnace, Plin.

placito.full: plăcĭto, āre, v. freq. n. [placeo], to be very pleasing: neque placitant mores, Plaut. Bacch. 4, 10, 6.

placitum.full: plăcĭtum, i, n., v. placeo, P. a. B. 2.

placitus.full: plăcĭtus, a, um, Part. and P. a., from placeo.

placivus.full: plăcīvus, a, um, adj. placeo, pleasing: ἀρεστός, placivus, Gloss. Gr. Lat.

placo.full: plāco, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. etym. dub.; cf.: placeo, planus. To reconcile; constr. alicui, aliquem (class. and freq.): agedum, fac, illa ut placetur nobis, that she be reconciled to us, Ter. Phorm. 5, 3, 1: vereor ut placari possit, id. ib. 5, 8, 72 (cf.: redigam vos in gratiam, v. 73): coeperas eum mihi placare, Cic. Att. 7, 1, 8: rogavit ut te sibi placarem, id. Fam. 13, 1, 3: his vocibus cum in se magis incitarent dictatorem quam magistro equitum placarent, Liv. 8, 33, 1: Hannibalem pater fili

placor.full: plăcor, ōris, m. placeo, contentment, approval, satisfaction (eccl. Lat.), Vulg. Ecclus. 4, 13; 39, 23; cf.: placor, ἀρέσκεια, Gloss. Cyrill.

plaetorius.full: Plaetōrĭus, i, m., the name of a Roman gens. L. Plaetorius, Cic. Clu. 60, 165.— M. Plaetorius, Cic. Clu. 45, 126; 53, 147; id. Fam. 1, 8, 1.—Hence, Plae-tōrĭus, a, um, adj., Plœtorian: lex, a law of the tribune of the people, Plœtorius, for the protection of minors, Varr. L. L. 6, 2, § 5; Censor. de Die Nat. 24.— Plae-tōrĭānus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to a Plœtorius, Plœtorian: incendium, Cic. Att. 5, 20, 8.
plaetorius.short: Plaetōrĭus, i, m., the name of a Roman gens.

plaga1.full: plāga, ae, f. cf. plango, = πληγή, a blow, stroke, wound, stripe (class.; syn.: ictus, verbera, vulnus). Lit. In gen., Cic. Verr. 2, 5, 51, § 134: (pueris) dant animos plagae, Verg. A. 7, 382; Ov. M. 12, 487; 13, 119; Gell. 5, 15, 7: plagae et vulnera, Tac. G. 7.—Of the shock of atoms striking together, Cic. Fat. 20, 48; cf. id. ib. 10, 22.— In partic., a blow which wounds or injures; a stroke, cut, thrust; a wound (class.). Absol.: plagis costae callent, Plaut. Ps. 1, 2, 4: quem irrigatum plagi

plaga2.full: plăga, ae, f. root πλακ- of Gr. πλακοῦς; cf. planca, plancus, plānus. A region, quarter, tract (mostly poet.; v. Madv. ad Cic. Fin. 2, 4, 12, where de plagis omnibus is the reading of the best MSS., but pagis of the edd.; but cf. Mütz. ad Georg Curtius p. 516 sq.; and Krebs, Antibarb. p. 869; syn.: regio, tractus, terra): aetheria, the ethereal regions, the air, Verg. A. 1, 394: caeli scrutantur plagas, Poët. ap. Cic. Div. 2, 13, 30: et si quem extenta plagarum Quattuor in medio dirimit plaga so

plaga3.full: plăga, ae, f. root plek-; Gr. πλέκω, weave, entwine; cf. plecto, plico, du-plex, a hunting-net, snare, gin (class.; syn.: retia, casses). Lit.: canes compellunt in plagas lupum, Plaut. Poen. 3, 3, 35: tendere plagas, Cic. Off. 3, 17, 68: extricata densis Cerva plagis, Hor. C. 3, 5, 32; Ov. M. 7, 768: nodosae, id. F. 6, 110: inque plagam nullo cervus agente cadit (al. plagas), id. A. A. 3, 428: aut trudit ... Apros in obstantes plagas, Hor. Epod. 2, 32.—Of the spider's web: illa difficile cernunt

plagella.full: plăgella, ae, f., v. plagula, Cael. Aur. Tard. 3, 2.

plagiarius.full: plăgĭārĭus, ii, m. plagium. A torturer, oppressor, plunderer (class.): Licinium plagiarium cum suo pullo milvino tributa exigere, Cic. Q. Fr. 1, 2, 2, § 6: inter avaros, circumscriptores, latrones, plagiarios unum esse cui noceri non possit, Sen. Tranq. 8, 4.— Esp., a man-stealer, kidnapper (post-Aug.), Dig. 21, 1, 17; 47, 2, 49; 53; 48, 15, 1; Callistr. Ib. 6; Vulg. 1 Tim. 1, 10.— Transf., a literary thief, plagiarist (one who pretends to be the author of another's book), Mart. 1, 53, 9.

plagiaticius.full: plăgĭātīcĭus, a, um, adj. plagiator, of or belonging to a plagiarist, plagiary: plagium, plagiarius, plagiaticius, Not. Tir. p. 80 (al. plagiaticus).

plagiator.full: plăgĭātor, ōris, m. plagium, same as plagiarius. A man-stealer, kidnapper (late Lat.), Tert. adv. Marc. 1, 23; Mos. et Rom. Leg. Coll. 14, 6, 6.— A seducer, corrupter of youth (late Lat.), Hier. Ep. 5, n. 3.

plagiaules.full: plăgĭaules, ae, m., = πλαγιαύλης, a player on the cross-flute: plagiaules, monaules, axaules, Not. Tir. p. 173.
plagiaules.short: plăgĭaules, ae, m., = πλαγιαύλης, a player on the cross-flute: plagiaules, monaules, axaules, Not.

plagiger.full: plāgĭger, gĕra, gĕrum, adj. 1. plagagero, stripe-bearing, born to be flogged: genera hominum, Plaut. Ps. 1, 2, 22 (Ritschl, ex conj. plagigerula; v. the foll. art.).

plagigerulus.full: plāgĭgĕrŭlus, a, um, adj. 1. plagagerulus, stripe-bearing, born to be flogged (ante-class.), Plaut. Most. 4, 1, 19; id. Ps. 1, 2, 20 Ritschl.

plagio.full: plăgĭo, āvi, 1, v. a., to steal (a person), kidnap (late Lat.): Moyses dicit, quicumque plagiaverit quemquam in Israel, etc., Mos. et Rom. Leg. Coll. 14, 1, 1.

plagiosippus.full: Plāgĭŏsippus and Plāgĭoxippus, i, m. 1. plaga -ἵππος, a fictitious name, Beater, Bruiser, Auct. Her. 4, 31 fin. dub.

plagipatida.full: plāgĭpătĭda, ae, m. 1. plaga-patior, a buffet-bearer (ante-class.), Plaut. Capt. 3, 1, 12: plagipatidae, ferritribaces viri, id. Most. 2, 1, 9.

plagium.full: plăgĭum, ii, n., man-stealing, kidnapping, the selling of freemen as slaves, Dig. 48, 15, 6; 48, 15, 1.
plagium.short: plăgĭum, ii, n., man-stealing, kidnapping, the selling of freemen as slaves, Dig.

plago.full: plāgo, āvi, āre, v. a. 1. plaga, to strike, wound (eccl. Lat.): aliquem, Aug. Civ. Dei, 21, 11; Vulg. Zach. 13, 6; Juv. Schol. 6, 655; 13, 133.

plagosus.full: plāgōsus, a, um, adj. id., full of blows. Act., fond of flogging (poet.): Orbilius, Hor. Ep. 2, 1, 70.— Pass., full of blows or wounds (post-class.): dorsum, App. M. 9, p. 222, 27: crura, id. ib. 8, p. 203, 17.

plagula.full: plăgŭla, ae, f. dim. 3. plaga, C.. A bed-curtain, a curtain (class., but not in Cic. or Cæs.): deme plagulam de lecto, Afran. ap. Non. 378, 10; Varr. ib. 86, 7: ii primum vestem stragulam pretiosam, plagulas et alia textilia Romam advexerunt, Liv. 39, 6; Suet. Tit. 10.— A part of a garment which is to be sewed to the other parts, a breadth (ante-class.), Varr. L. L. 9, § 79 Müll.— A sheet of paper (post-Aug.), Plin. 13, 12, 23, § 77.

plagusia.full: plăgūsĭa, ae, f., a kind of fish: plagusias, Plaut. Rud. 2, 1, 9.
plagusia.short: plăgūsĭa, ae, f., a kind of fish: plagusias, Plaut.

plana.full: plāna, ae, f. plano, a plane (late Lat.), Arn. 6, 200.

planaria.full: Plānārĭa, ae, f., an island in the Tyrrhenian Sea, near Elba, another name for Planasia, Plin. 3, 6, 12, § 80.
planaria.short: Plānārĭa, ae, f., an island in the Tyrrhenian Sea, near Elba, another name for Planasia, Plin.

planaris.full: plānāris, e, adj. planus, on a level surface, flat, plane (post-class.), Mart. Cap. 6, § 708.

planarius.full: plānārĭus, a, um, adj. id., on level ground, level (post-class.): conflictus, Amm. 19, 5, 2: interpellatio, which took place before the judge ascended the tribunal, Cod. Just. 3, 11, 4.

planasia.full: Planasĭa, ae, f., = Πλανασία, an island in the Tyrrhenian Sea, south of Ilva (Elba), now Pianosa, Varr. R. R. 3, 6; Plin. 3, 6, 12, § 81; Tac. A. 1, 3; Mart. Cap. 6, § 644.
planasia.short: Planasĭa, ae, f., = Πλανασία, an island in the Tyrrhenian Sea, south of Ilva (Elba), now Pianosa, Varr.

planca.full: planca, ae, f. root πλακ-; v. 2. plaga, = πλάξ, a board, slab, plank (post-Aug.): plancae tabulae planae, Paul. ex Fest. p. 231 Müll.: roboreae, Pall. 1, 21, 2.— A slab of marble, slab upon graves, Inscr. Don. 278, 3; Inscr. Murat. 1427, 4.

plancianus.full: Plancĭānus, a, um, v. 2. Plancus, II.

plancina.full: Plancīna, ae, f., wife of Cn. Calpurnius Piso, Tac. A. 2, 43; 55; 75; 6, 26.
plancina.short: Plancīna, ae, f., wife of Cn.

plancius.full: Plancĭus, i, m., the name of a Roman gens. Thus, Cn. Plancius, a friend of Cicero, and defended by him against a charge of bribery, in an oration still extant; cf. Cic. Red. in Sen. 14, 35; id. Att. 1, 12, 2.
plancius.short: Plancĭus, i, m., the name of a Roman gens.

planctus.full: planctus, ūs, m. plango. In gen., a striking or beating accompanied by a loud noise, a banging, rustling, roaring (postAug. and mostly poet.): unum omnes incessere planctibus, of the flappings of the Harpies' wings, Val. Fl. 4, 494: tremuit perterritus aether Planctibus insolitis, Petr. 136: planctus illisae cautibus undae, of the roaring of the waves, Luc. 6, 690.— In partic., a beating of the breast, arms, and face in mourning; a wailing, lamentation, lament (syn.: plangor, lamentum, ploratus)

plancus1.full: plancus, i, m., = πλάγκος, a kind of eagle, Plin. 10, 3, 3, § 7.
plancus1.short: plancus, i, m., = πλάγκος, a kind of eagle, Plin.

plancus2.full: Plancus, i, m. (flat-footed), a Roman surname: plancae tabulae planae, ob quam causam et planci appellantur qui supra modum pedibus plani sunt, Paul. ex Fest. p. 231 Müll.: vola homini tantum, exceptis quibusdam: namque et hinc cognomina inventa Planci, Plauti, Scauri, Pansae, Plin. 11, 45, 105, § 254: plancus, πλατύπους, Gloss. Cyrill.: στεγανόποδες, planci, Gloss. Gr. Lat. So, Munatius Plancus, v. Munatius.—Hence, Plancĭānus, a, um, adj., Plancian: Diana, who had a shrine in the house of the P

planeta.full: plănēta, ae (-tes, is), or plănēs, ētis, m., = πλανήτης, πλάνης, a wandering star, planet (late Lat. for the class. stellae errantes, erraticae, errones).—Only plur. form planetae, Firm. Math. 2, 2; Serv. Verg. A. 3, 284; Isid. 3, 70, 20; 19, 24, 18; Aus. Eclog. de Nomin. Sept. Dier.: Inscr. Fabr. p. 709, n. 307.—Form planetes, Gell. 14, 1, 12.
planeta.short: plănēta, ae (-tes, is), or plănēs, ētis, m., = πλανήτης, πλάνης, a wandering star, planet (late Lat.

planetarius.full: plănētārĭus, ii, m. planeta, an astrologer (eccl. Lat.): illos planetarios, quos mathematicos vocant, Aug. Conf. 4, 3 (al. planos).

planeticus.full: plănētĭcus, a, um, adj., = πλανητικός, wandering, wandering about (postclass.): sidera, Sid. Ep. 8, 11.
planeticus.short: plănētĭcus, a, um, adj., = πλανητικός, wandering, wandering about (postclass.): sidera, Sid.

plangimonium.full: plangĭmōnĭum, i, n. plango, lamentation (eccl. Lat.), Vict. Turon. Poenit. 10.

plango.full: plango, nxi, nctum, 3, v. a. from the root ΠΛΑΓ, πλήσσω; cf. Lat. plāga, to strike, beat, esp. with a noise. In gen. (poet.; cf. plaudo): fluctus plangentes saxa, Lucr. 2, 1155; 6, 115: moribundo vertice terram, Ov. M. 12, 118: humum, id. H. 16, 334: quanto planguntur litora fluctu! id. ib. 19, 121: tympana palmis, Cat. 64, 261: nunc (Boreas) ipsas alis planget stridentibus Alpes, Sil. 1, 588.—Pass., of a bird when caught: plangitur, beats with its wings, Ov. M. 11, 75.— In partic., to beat the

plangor.full: plangor, ōris, m. plango, a striking, beating, attended with noise. In gen. (poet.): (undae) leni resonant plangore cachinni, Cat. 64, 272: feminis, Auct. Her. 3, 15; Ov. M. 3, 498.— In partic., a beating the breast or face in token of grief; loud mourning, wailing, lamentation (class.): plangore et lamentatione complere forum, Cic. Or. 38, 131: feminei, Verg. A. 2, 487: dare plangorem, to make, Ov. M. 14, 421: percutit claro plangore lacertos, id. ib 4, 138: caesis plangore lacertis, id. ib. 6,

planguncula.full: planguncŭla, ae, f. dim., = πλαγγών, a little wax doll: inventae sunt quinque plangunculae matronarum (al. lagunculae or imagunculae), Cic. Att. 6, 1, 25 Orell. N. cr.

planiloquus.full: plānĭlŏquus, a, um, adj. plane-loquor, speaking clearly or intelligibly, speaking plainly (ante-class.): di immortales, ut planiloqua est! Plaut. Truc. 4, 4, 11.

planipes.full: plānĭpes, pĕdis, m. planus-pes, flatfoot, barefoot, a kind of pantomime or ballet-dancer, who performed without the comic soccus or the tragic cothurnus: exsultat planipes, Atta ap. Diom. p. 487 P.: planipedes audit Fabios, Juv. 8, 191: planipes saltans, Gell. 1, 11, 12.

planitas.full: plānĭtas, ātis, f. planus, plainness; trop., distinctness, perspicuity: sententiarum, Tac. Or. 23 fin. (al. plenitas, sanitas, gravitas).

planities.full: plānĭtĭes, ēi (collat. form plānĭtĭa, ae, very rare; Cic. Div. 1, 1, 2; Caes. B. C. 1, 43), and plur. planitiae, f. id., a flat or even surface, level ground, a plain (class.): aequata agri planities, Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 48, § 107: erat inter oppidum et collem planitia, Caes. B. C. 1, 43: planities erat inter sinistros montes, Sall. C. 59, 2; id. J. 48 fin.: speculi, Lucr. 4, 294: propter planitiem regionum, Cic. Div. 1 1: pars planitiae, Liv. 44, 6; Vitr. 7, 3: CLIVOM MARTIS IN PLANICIEM REDEGERVN

planitudo.full: plānĭtūdo, ĭnis, f. planus, evenness, levelness: planitudo, ὁμαλία, Gloss. Philox.

plano.full: plāno, āre, v. a. id., to level, make plain, flat, even, etc. (post-class.): planate vias, Coripp. Laud. Justin. 2, 223.

planta.full: planta, ae, f. for plancta; cf. plānus; root v. plango. Any vegetable production that serves to propagate the species, a sprout, shoot, twig, sprig, sucker, graft, scion, slip, cutting, Varr. R. R. 1, 55: malleoli, plantae, sarmenta, viviradices, propagines, Cic. Sen. 15, 52; Verg. G. 2, 23.— A young tree, a shrub that may be transplanted, a set, slip, Ov. R. Am. 193: plantas ex seminario transferre in aliud, Plin. 17, 11, 14, § 75: plantae sinapis primā hieme translatae, Col. 11, 3, 29: thymi n

plantago.full: plantāgo, ĭnis, f., a plantain, Plin. 25, 8, 39, § 80.
plantago.short: plantāgo, ĭnis, f., a plantain, Plin.

plantaris.full: plantāris, e, adj. planta. Of or belonging to sets; subst.: plantārĭa, ĭum, n. plur., sets, slips, or young trees, Verg. G. 2, 27: plantaria transferuntur, Plin. 21, 10, 34, § 60: non Epicurum Suspicit exigui laetum plantaribus horti, trees, plants, Juv. 13, 123.— Transf., the hair, Pers. 4, 39.— Of or belonging to the sole of the foot (poet.); of Mercury: summa pedum propere plantaribus alligat alis, Stat. Th. 1, 304.—Subst.: plantārĭa, ium, winged shoes or sandals: aërii plantaria vellet Perse

plantarium1.full: plantārĭum, ii, n. id., a nurserygarden, nursery: plantaria instituunt anniculasque transferunt, et iterum bimas, Plin. 13, 4, 8, § 37: caedua, id. 17, 20, 34, § 149.

plantarium2.full: plantārĭum, ii, n. id., the sole of the foot: quod tamen de plantario ferri orietur (statua), Vulg. Dan. 2, 41.

plantatio.full: plantātĭo, ōnis, f. planto. A setting, planting, transplanting (post-Aug.), Plin. 21, 4, 10, § 17.— A plant set out or transplanted (late Lat.), Vulg. Isa. 17, 10; id. Matt. 15, 13.

plantator.full: plantātor, ōris, m. id., a setter, planter, transplanter (late Lat.), Aug. Ep. 89; 112.

plantiger.full: plantĭger, ĕra, ĕrum, adj. plantagero, having shoots, branching (post-Aug.): siliqua, Plin. 13, 8, 16, § 59.

planto.full: planto, āre, v. a. planta. To set, plant, transplant (cf. sero): hoc modo plantantur punicae, Plin. 17, 10, 13, § 67; Pall. 4, 5: vineam, Vulg. Luc. 20, 9 et saep. — To fix in place, and hence, to form, make: qui plantavit aurem, non audiet? Vulg. Psa. 93, 9.

planula.full: plānŭla, ae, f. dim. 1. planus, a little plane: planula, ἐγκοπίς, Gloss. Philox.

planum.full: plānum, i, n., v. planus, I. B.

planus1.full: plānus, a, um, adj. for placnus; root plac-; Gr. πλακοῦς; cf. 2. plaga, planca, even, level, flat, plane (class.; cf. aequor). Lit.: facilis et plana via, Plaut. Trin. 3, 2, 19: cum duae formae praestantes sint, ex solidis globus, ex planis circulus aut orbis, Cic. N. D. 2, 18, 47: planum et aequabile corpus universitatis, id. Univ. 5: planus et aequus locus, id. Caecin. 17, 50: litus, Caes. B. G. 4, 23: carina, id. ib. 3, 13: pisces, flat-fish, Plin. 9, 20, 37, § 73: aedificia, quae plano pede

planus2.full: plănus, i, m., = πλάνος, a juggler, impostor, cheat (class.; cf. erro): ille planus improbissimus, Cic. Clu. 26, 72: fracto crure planum attollere, Hor. Ep. 1, 17, 59; Petr. 82.
planus2.short: plănus, i, m., = πλάνος, a juggler, impostor, cheat (class.;

plasma.full: plasma, ătis, n., = πλάσμα, something formed or moulded. Lit., an image, figure, a creature (eccl. Lat.): emancipator servientis plasmatis, Prud. Cath. 7, 184.— Transf., an affected modulation of the voice (post-Aug.), Pers. 1, 17: sit lectio non in canticum dissoluta, nec plasmate, ut nunc a plerisque fit, effeminata, Quint. 1, 8, 2.— Trop., a fiction (post-class.), Aus. Ep. 10, 1; Mart. Cap. 9, §§ 913, 998.
plasma.short: plasma, ătis, n., = πλάσμα, something formed or moulded.

plasmatio.full: plasmātĭo, ōnis, f. plasmo, a forming, fashioning, creating (eccl. Lat.), Hier. Ep. 22, n. 38; Ambros. Par. 1, 4, 24.

plasmator.full: plasmātor, ōris, m. id., a former, fashioner, creator (eccl. Lat.): deus hominis plasmator, Tert. adv. Jud. 2.

plasmo.full: plasmo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. plasma, to form, mould, fashion (eccl. Lat.): corporis effigiem, Prud. Apoth. 933: homo plasmatus, Tert. adv. Jud. 13 med.: me, Vulg. Psa. 118, 73: aestatem, id. ib. 73, 17.

plasso.full: plasso, āre, 1, v. a., = πλάσσω = plasmo, to form, mould, shape (post-class.), Apic. 2, 1.

plastes.full: plastes, ae, m., = πλάστης, a moulder, potter, modeller, statuary (post-Aug.; syn. fictor), Vell. 1, 17, 4: laudatissimi, Plin. 35, 12, 45, § 154; Vitr. 1, 1, 13; Tert. Idol. 3; Vulg. Isa. 41, 25.— A creator, maker (eccl. Lat.): Israel, Vulg. Isa. 45, 11: terrae, id. ib. 45, 18.
plastes.short: plastes, ae, m., = πλάστης, a moulder, potter, modeller, statuary (post-Aug.;

plasticator.full: plastĭcātor, ōris, m. plasticus, a moulder or modeller in clay (post-class.), Firm. Math. 8, 16.

plastice.full: plastĭcē, ēs, and -ca, ae, f., = πλαστική, the plastic art, statuary (post-Aug.): qui plasticen matrem statuariae scalpturaeque et caelaturae esse dixit, Plin. 35, 12, 43, § 151.—Form plastica, Tert. Cult. Fem. 2 fin. 5; id. Spect. 18.
plastice.short: plastĭcē, ēs, and -ca, ae, f., = πλαστική, the plastic art, statuary (post-Aug.): qui plasticen matrem statuariae scalpturaeque et caelaturae esse dixit, Plin.

plasticus.full: plastĭcus, a, um, adj., = πλαστικός, of or belonging to moulding or modelling, plastic: ratio, Vitr. 1, 1, 13: manus, plastic, Tert. ad Nat. 1, 12.— Subst.: pla-stĭcus, i, m., a moulder, modeller, statuary (post-class.), Firm. Math. 7, 25.
plasticus.short: plastĭcus, a, um, adj., = πλαστικός, of or belonging to moulding or modelling, plastic: ratio, Vitr.

plastus.full: plastus, a, um, adj., = πλαστός (formed); trop., fictitious, deceptive (postclass.), Fulg. Myth. praef. 1.

plataeae.full: Plătaeae, ārum, f., = Πλαταῖαι, Platœa, a city in Bœotia, celebrated for a victory of the Greeks over the Persians, now Kokla, Cic. Off. 1, 18, 61; Nep. Arist. 2, 1; id. Paus. 1, 2; Just. 2, 12, 11 al.—Hence, Plătaeenses, ĭum, m., the inhabitants of Platœa, the Platœans, Nep. Milt. 5, 1; Just. 2, 9, 9.— Plătaeēus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Platœa, Platœan: proelium, Vitr. 1, 1.
plataeae.short: Plătaeae, ārum, f., = Πλαταῖαι, Platœa, a city in Bœotia, celebrated for a victory of the Greeks over the Persians, now Kokla, Cic.

platalea.full: plătălĕa (plătĕa, Plin. 10, 40, 56, § 115), ae, f., the spoonbill, Cic. N. D. 2, 49, 124.

platanetum.full: plătănētum, i, n. platanus, a grove of plane-trees: πλατανών, platanetum, Gloss. Philox.

plataninus.full: plătănīnus, a, um, adj., = πλατανινός, of or belonging to the plane-tree, plane-, Col. 12, 16, 3.
plataninus.short: plătănīnus, a, um, adj., = πλατανινός, of or belonging to the plane-tree, plane-, Col.

platanista.full: plătănista, ae, m., = πλατανιστής, a fish in the Ganges, otherwise unknown, Plin. 9, 15, 17, § 46.
platanista.short: plătănista, ae, m., = πλατανιστής, a fish in the Ganges, otherwise unknown, Plin.

platanon.full: plătănon, ōnis, m., = πλατανών, a grove of plane-trees, Vitr. 5, 11: postero die in eundem platanona descendi, Petr. 131; Mart. 3, 19, 2 (in Plin. Ep. 1, 3, 1, written as Greek).
platanon.short: plătănon, ōnis, m., = πλατανών, a grove of plane-trees, Vitr.

platanus.full: plătănus, i (nom. plur. platanūs, Verg. Cul. 123), f., = πλάτανος, the platane or Oriental plane-tree: sub platano umbriferā, Cic. poēt. Div. 2, 30, 63; id. de Or. 1, 7, 28; Plin. 12, 1, 3, § 6: steriles platani, Verg. G. 2, 70: caelebs (because it did not, like the elm, serve to support vines), Hor. C. 2, 15, 4; 2, 11, 13; Juv. 1, 12.

platea1.full: plătēa (plătĕa, Cat. 15, 7; Hor. Ep. 2, 2, 71), ae, f., = πλατεῖα. A broad way in a city, a street (class.): quis hic est qui in plateam ingreditur? Plaut. Trin. 4, 1, 21: in hac habitasse plateă dictum est Chrysidem, Ter. And. 4, 5, 1; Caes. B. C. 1, 27: purae sunt plateae, Hor. Ep. 2, 2, 71.— An open space in a house, an area, court-yard (post-class.), Lampr. Elag. 24.

platea2.full: plătĕa, the spoonbill, Plin. 10, 40, 56, § 115; v. platalea.

platessa.full: plătessa, ae, f., a flatfish, plaice, Aus. Ep. 4, 58.
platessa.short: plătessa, ae, f., a flatfish, plaice, Aus.

platice2.full: plătĭcē, ēs, f., = πλατική, general or summary instruction, a general plan or scheme (post-class.): nunc ad platicen revertamur, Firm. Math. 2, 16.
platice2.short: plătĭcē, ēs, f., = πλατική, general or summary instruction, a general plan or scheme (post-class.): nunc ad platicen revertamur, Firm.

platicus.full: plătĭcus, a, um, adj., = πλατικός, general, compendious, summary (post-class.): dispositio, Firm. Math. 3, 2.—Adv.: plă-tĭcē, in general, generally (post-class.): platice institui, Firm. Math. 2, 16.
platicus.short: plătĭcus, a, um, adj., = πλατικός, general, compendious, summary (post-class.): dispositio, Firm.

plato.full: Plăto or Plăton, ōnis, = Πλάτων. A celebrated Grecian philosopher, the disciple of Socrates, the instructor of Aristotle, and founder of the Academic philosophy, Cic. Leg. 3, 1, 1; id. Brut. 31, 121; id. Tusc. 1, 17, 39; id. Or. 3, 12: Plato divinus auctor, id. Opt. Gen. Or. 6; Sen. Ep. 6, 6, 13.—In Greek acc.: doctum Platona, Hor. S. 2, 4, 3; Petr. 2, 5.—Hence, Plătōnĭcus, a, um, adj., = Πλατωνικός, of or belonging to Plato, Platonic: sublimitas, Plin. Ep. 1, 10, 5: philosophus, Gell. 15, 2, 1:

platyceros.full: plătўcĕros, ōtis, adj., = πλατύκερως (broad-horn), having spreading horns, broadhorned; acc. plur. platycerotas, Plin. 11, 37, 45, § 123.
platyceros.short: plătўcĕros, ōtis, adj., = πλατύκερως (broad-horn), having spreading horns, broadhorned;

platycoriasis.full: plătўcŏrĭăsis, is, f., = πλατυκορίασις, an excessive dilatation of the pupil of the eye, Veg. Vet. 2, 16.
platycoriasis.short: plătўcŏrĭăsis, is, f., = πλατυκορίασις, an excessive dilatation of the pupil of the eye, Veg.

platyophthalmus.full: plătўophthalmus, i, m., = πλατυόφθαλμος (eye-dilator), a name for antimony, because it was supposed to enlarge and beautify the eye, Plin. 33, 6, 34, § 102.
platyophthalmus.short: plătўophthalmus, i, m., = πλατυόφθαλμος (eye-dilator), a name for antimony, because it was supposed to enlarge and beautify the eye, Plin.

platyphyllon.full: plătўphyllon, i, n., = πλατύφυλλον (broad-leaf), a broad-leaved species of the plant tithymalus, Plin. 26, 8, 44, § 70.
platyphyllon.short: plătўphyllon, i, n., = πλατύφυλλον (broad-leaf), a broad-leaved species of the plant tithymalus, Plin.

platys.full: plătys, ўos, adj., = πλατύς, broad (post-Aug.; found only in nom. sing.): nervus, qui platys appellatur, Plin. 26, 8, 58, § 90.

plaudo.full: plaudo (plōdo, Varr. ap. Non. 478, 5, and Quint. 6, 1, 52), si, sum, 3, v. a. and n. Act., to clap, strike, beat any thing (poet.; cf. plango), Verg. Cir. 179: pectora manu, Ov. M. 2, 866: clipeum pectore, Stat. Th. 7, 134: aquas, id. S. 1, 3, 74: choreas pedibus, to execute a choral dance, stamping with the feet, Verg. A. 6, 644: plausis alis, Ov. M. 14, 507; 14, 577.— Neutr., to clap, strike, beat (of two bodies striking together). In gen. (poet. and in postAug. prose): alis Plaudentem figit s

plaumoratum.full: plaumŏrātum, i, n. (Rætian), a kind of plough, Plin. 18, 18, 48, § 172; v. Sillig ad h. 1.

plausibilis.full: plausĭbĭlis, e, adj. plaudo, deserving applause, praiseworthy, acceptable, pleasing (class.): censorium nomen (with populare), Cic. Div. in Caecil. 3, 8: oratio, Sen. Ep. 5, 9: locus, Quint. 4, 3, 1.—Hence, adv.: plau-sĭbĭlĭter, with applause (post-class.): ingenium plausibilius manifestare, with more applause, Sid. Ep. 8, 10.

plausilis.full: plausĭlis, e, adj. id., that claps applause, applauding, plausive (post-class.): plausilibus ulnis (al. plausibilibus), Sid. Ep. 9, 14; cf.: plausilis, plausibilis, Not. Tir. p. 172.

plausio.full: plausĭo, ōnis, f. id., applause (late Lat.), Cassiod. Hist. Tripart. 2, 1.

plausito.full: plausĭto, āre, v. freq. n. [id.], to clap (poet.): plausitat arborea clamans de fronde palumbes, i. e. flaps its wings, Auct. Carm. Philom. 21.

plausor.full: plausor (plōsor, Sid. Ep. 9, 3; id. Carm. 9, 300), ōris, m. id., one who claps applause, an applauder (poet. and in post-Aug. prose): in vacuo laetus sessor plausorque theatro, Hor. Ep. 2, 2, 130; Petr. 5; Suet. Ner. 25.

plaustrarius.full: plaustrārĭus (plostr-), a, um, adj. plaustrum, plostrum, of or belonging to a wagon, wagon-: asini, Cato, R. R. 11, 1: juga duo, id. ib. 2.— Subst.: plau-strārĭus (plostr-), ii, m. A wagon - maker, wheelwright: plaustrariorum vectigal, Lampr. Alex. Sev. 24.— A wagon - driver, wagoner: si Aquiliae actione plaustrarium (al. plostrarium) teneri placet, Dig. 9, 2, 27 fin.

plaustrilucus.full: plaustrĭlūcus, a, um, adj. plaustrum-luceo, shining like Charles's Wain, brilliant (post-class.), Mart. Cap. 9, § 912.

plaustrix.full: plaustrix, īcis, f. plausor, a female applauder, acc. to Non. 150, 29.

plaustrum.full: plaustrum (plostrum, Cato, R. R. 2, 10; 62; Varr. R. R. 1, 22, 3; cf. Suet. Vesp. 22: plaustra, ae, f., v. infra), i, n. Sanscr. plavas, ship; prop., that which sways hither and thither; root plu-; Gr. πλέω, πλύνω, a vehicle for carrying heavy loads, a wagon, wain, cart. Lit. (class.): vendat plostrum vetus, Cato, R. R. 2, 7; Plaut. Aul. 3, 5, 31: in plaustrum conici, Cic. Div. 1, 27, 57: stridentia plaustra, Ov. Tr. 3, 10, 59; id. M. 2, 177: sicut stridet plaustrum onustum foeno, Vulg. Amos, 2,

plausus1.full: plausus, a, um, Part., from plaudo.
plausus1.short: plausus, a, um, Part., from plaudo.

plausus3.full: plausus (plōsus, Macr. S. 6, 1), ūs (a later collat. form, plausus, i, Cod. Th. 15, 9, 2), m. plaudo, a clapping sound, the noise that arises from the beating or striking together of two bodies. In gen. (poet. and in post-Aug. prose): it eques et plausu cava concutit ungula terram, Enn. ap. Macr. S. 6, 1 (Ann. v. 419 Vahl.),—Of cocks: plausu premunt alas, Enn. ap. Cic. Div. 2, 26, 57 (Trag. v. 251 Vahl.).—Of doves: plausumque exterrita pennis Dat tecto ingentem, Verg. A. 5, 215: laterum, Plin. 1

plautianus.full: Plautĭānus, a, um, v. Plautius, B.

plautinus.full: Plautīnus, a, um, v. 2. Plautus, II.

plautius.full: Plautĭus (Plōt-), i, m., name of a Roman gens. M. Plautius Hypsaeus, a consul A. U. C. 630, Cic. de Or. 1, 36, 166.— M. Plautius Silvanus, a tribune of the people A. U. C. 666, Ascon. Cic. Corn. p. 79.— L. Plotius Gallus, a rhetorician in the time of Marius, Suet. Rhet. 2.— L. Plotius, a poet who celebrated the Mithridatic war, Cic. Arch. 9, 20.—Hence, Plautĭus (Plōt-), a, um, adj., of or pertaining to a Plautius (Plotius), Plautian, Plotian: Plautia lex, of the tribune of the people M. Plautius
plautius.short: Plautĭus (Plōt-), i, m., name of a Roman gens.

plautus1.full: plautus (plōt-), a, um, adj. Flat, broad: plauti appellantur canes, quorum aures languidae sunt ac flaccidae et latius videntur patere, Paul. ex Fest. p. 231 Müll.: conchae plautiores, Tert. Pall. 3.— Among the Umbrians, flat-footed: (plotos appellant) Umbri pedibus planis (natos . . . unde et Maccius) poëta, quia Umber Sarsinas erat, a pedum planitie initio Plotus, postea Plautus coeptus est dici, Fest. p. 238 Müll.; cf. Paul. ex Fest. p. 239 ib.

plautus2.full: Plautus, i, m. flat-foot, v. 1. plautus, an Umbrian surname.—So, T. Maccius (or Maccus) Plautus, a celebrated Roman comic poet, a native of the Umbrian village Sarsina.—(On the name Maccius, instead of the earlier reading Accius or Attius, v. Ritschl, De Plauti poëtae nominibus, in his Parergon Plautinorum I. pp. 3-43; and respecting his life and writings, id. ib. pp. 47 - 579), Cic. Brut. 15, 60; Quint. 10, 1, 99.— Transf., the works of Plautus, a comedy of Plautus: adporto vobis Plautum linguā

plebecula.full: plēbēcŭla (plēbĭcŭla, Jul. Val. Rer. Gest. Alex. M. 2, 36), ae, f. dim. plebs, the common people, the populace, the mob, rabble (class.): misera ac jejuna, Cic. Att. 1, 16; Hor. Ep. 2, 1, 186; Pers. 4, 6; Suet. Vesp. 18.

plebeius.full: plēbēĭus (-ējus), a, um, adj. id.. Of or belonging to the common people or commonalty, plebeian (opp. to patricius), Liv. 4, 4, 11; Cic. Fam. 9, 21: familia, id. Mur. 7, 15: consul, Liv. 6, 40; 10, 23: Pudicitia, the goddess of Chastity of the plebeians, as there was also a Pudicitia patricia, id. ib.; cf. Fest. p. 237 Müll.: ludi, popular sports, shows instituted by the commonalty, Liv. 29, 38 fin.: fatum (opp. divitibus responsa data), Juv. 6, 588: Deciorum animae, id. 8, 254.—Subst.: plēbēĭus

plebes.full: plēbes, is and ĕi, v. plebs.

plebicola.full: plēbĭcŏla, ae, comm. plebs-colo, one who courts the favor of the common people, a friend of the people (class.): ab hoc plebicolā tribuno plebis eicitur, Cic. Agr. 2, 31, 84; id. Sest. 52, 110; Liv. 3, 33.

plebiscitum.full: plēbiscītum (also separately plēbi scītum, Plaut. Ps. 2, 4, 58), i. n. (abl. plebis scitu, Decret. ap. Cic. Att. 4, 2, 3) [plebs-scitum], a decree or ordinance of the people (opp.: senatus consultum), Cic. Dom. 17, 44; Just. Inst. 1, 2, 4: plebis scitum igitur est secundum eum Capitonem lex quam plebes, non populus, accipit, Gell. 10, 20, 6; cf. plebs, I., and scitum, s. v. scisco, P. a.

plebitas.full: plēbĭtas, ātis, f. plebs, the rank of a common citizen, plebeian rank or condition (ante-class.): propter tenuitatem, et plebitatem, Cato ap. Non. 149, 4: Hemina, id. ib. 149, 5 (plebitatem, ignobilitatem, Non.).

plebs.full: plebs (in inscriptions often PLEPS), -bis, and archaic plēbēs († plēbis), is and ĕi (plebium, Prud. στεφ. 10, 709: plebibus, Aug. Ep. 166), f. root ple-, fill; whence Gr. πίμπλημι, πλήρης; cf. πλῆ θος, multitude. Lit., the common people, the commons or commonalty, the plebeians (opp. the patricians, senators, and knights; whereas populus signifies the collective people, including, therefore, the Senate), Cic. Leg. 3, 3, 10: plebes in hoc regi antistat loco, licet Lacrumare plebi, regi honeste no
plebs.short: plebs (in inscriptions often PLEPS), -bis, and archaic plēbēs († plēbis), is and ĕi (plebium, Prud.

plecta.full: plecta, ae, f. 1. plecto, archit. t. t., a border of interwoven lines in relief, Vulg. 3 Reg. 7, 29.

plectibilis.full: plectĭbĭlis, e, adj. 2. plecto. Pass., deserving punishment (post-class.): invidia, Sid. Ep. 4, 6: usurpatio, Cod. Th. 14, 3, 16.— Act., penal: severitas, Cod. Th. 12, 1, 161.

plectilis.full: plectĭlis, e, adj. 1. plecto, plaited. Lit. (ante-class.): corona plectilis, Plaut. Bacch. 1, 1, 37.— Trop., complicated, involved, intricate (post-class.): syllogismi, Prud. Apoth. praef. 2, 36.

plecto1.full: plĕcto, xi and xŭi, xum, 3, v. a. root plek-; Gr. πλέκω, πλοκή; Lat. plicin sim-plic-is, im-plic-o, etc.; cf. 3. plaga. To plait, braid, interweave (rare; mostly in the part. perf. and poet.; not in Cic. or Cæs.; syn.: plico, flecto, necto]. Lit.: crines plexueris, Vulg. Judic. 16, 13: coronam de spinis, id. Matt. 27, 29: plexa colligata significat ex Graeco, cui nos etiam praepositionem adicimus, cum dicimus perplexa, Fest. p. 230 Müll.: plexae coronae, Lucr. 5, 1399: flores plexi, Cat. 64, 284
plecto1.short: plĕcto, xi and xŭi, xum, 3, v.

plecto2.full: plēcto, ĕre, v. a. πλήττω, to beat, punish; in class. lang. usually in pass., to be punished, suffer punishment, be beaten. Act. (post-class; syn. punio): capite aliquem plectere, Cod. Just. 9, 20, 7: quae sibi ignoscunt et plectunt deum, Aus. Idyll. 6 praef.— Pass. Lit.: Venusinae Plectantur silvae, Hor. C. 1, 28, 26: ego plectar pendens, Ter. Phorm. 1, 4, 43: tergo plecti, Hor. S. 2, 7, 105; id. Ep. 1, 2, 14. ut in suo vitio quisque plectatur, Cic. Leg. 3, 20, 46: ut in judiciis culpa plectatu

plectrifer.full: plectrĭfer, ĕra, ĕrum, adj. plectrumfero, carrying the plectrum (late Lat.), Dracont. Carm. 10, 285 Duhn.

plectripotens.full: plectrĭpŏtens, entis, adj. plectrumpotens, master of or skilful with the plectrum, great in lyric poetry (post-class.), Sid. Ep. 9, 13.

plectrum.full: plēctrum, i, n., = πλῆκτρον (an instrument to strike with; esp.), A little stick with which the player struck the chords of a stringed instrument, a quill, plectrum: itaque plectri similem linguam nostri solent dicere, chordarum dentis, naris cornibus illis qui resonant, etc., Cic. N. D. 2, 59, 149; Ov. M. 11, 168: plectra movere, id. H. 3, 113.— Poet., transf., a lyre or lute; also a lyric poem, lyric poetry: plectro modulatus eburno, Tib. 3, 4, 39: et te sonantem plenius aureo, Alcaee, plectro
plectrum.short: plēctrum, i, n., = πλῆκτρον (an instrument to strike with;

pleias.full: Plēïas and Plējas (dissyl.), (Plī^as), ădis, f., = Πληϊάς and Πλειάς. One of the Seven Stars, a Pleiad; usually in plur.: Pleiades (Pliades) = Πλειάδες, the constellation of the Seven Stars, the Pleiades or Pleiads (pure Lat. Vergiliae), acc. to the myth, the seven daughters of Atlas and Pleione (Electra, Halcyone, Celaeno, Maia, Sterope, Taygete, and Merope): Pleïas enixa est, Ov. M. 1, 670: Plias, Stat. S. 1, 6, 22; Ov. F. 3, 105: Plĭadum nivosum Sidus, Stat. S. 1, 3, 95.— Poet., transf., a st
pleias.short: Plēïas and Plējas (dissyl.), (Plī^as), ădis, f., = Πληϊάς and Πλειάς.

pleione.full: Plēĭŏnē, ēs, f., = Πληϊόνη. A daughter of Oceanus and Tethys, wife of Atlas and mother of the Pleiades: hinc sata Pleione cum caelifero Atlante, Ov. F. 5, 83; Hyg. Astr. 2, 21: Pleiones nepos, i.e. Mercury, son of Maia, Ov. H. 16, 62; Val. Fl. 1, 738.— The constellation of the Pleiades, Val. Fl. 2, 67.

plemmyrium.full: Plemmўrĭum (Plēmўrĭ), ii, n., = Πλημμύριον, a promontory of Sicily, near Syracuse, now Punta di Gigante: undosum, Verg. A. 3, 693.
plemmyrium.short: Plemmўrĭum (Plēmўrĭ), ii, n., = Πλημμύριον, a promontory of Sicily, near Syracuse, now Punta di Gigante: undosum, Verg.

plenilunium.full: plēnĭlūnĭum, ii, n. (sc. tempus) [plenus-luna], the full moon (post-Aug. for luna plena), Col. 11, 2, 85: cum vero occidente sole orietur ex adverso, ita ut pariter aspiciantur; tunc erit plenilunium, Plin. 18, 32, 75, § 323; in plur., id. 9, 15, 20, § 53.

plenitas.full: plēnĭtas, ātis, f. plenus, a being full, fulness, repletion (post-Aug.). Lit.: nubes propter plenitatem et gravitatem liquescendo disperguntur, Vitr. 8, 2, 2; 5, 9, 5.— Transf., abundance, copiousness: humoris plenitas, Vitr. 6, 1, 3.

plenitudo.full: plēnĭtūdo, ĭnis, f. id., a being full, fulness, plenitude (generally post-Aug.). Completeness: plenitudo syllabarum, Auct. Her. 4, 20, 28.— Fulness, abundance: terrae (i.e. frugum), Vulg. Deut. 33, 16 al.— Thickness, stoutness, e. g. of a rod, of a man (post-Aug.), Col. 4, 30, 4; Plin. 11, 37, 87, § 216.

plenus.full: plēnus, a, um, adj. from the root ple-; Sanscr. prā-, to fill; Gr. πλα- in πίμπλημι, πλήθω; Lat. plerus, plebs, populus, etc.; whence compleo, expleo, suppleo, full, filled with any thing (class.; cf.: refertus, oppletus). Lit. In gen., with gen.: rimarum, Ter. Eun. 1, 2, 25: corpus suci, id. ib. 2, 3, 27: Gallia est plena civium Romanorum, Cic. Font. 1, 11: domus plena caelati argenti, Cic. Verr. 2, 2, 14. § 35: vini, somni, id. Red. in Sen. 6, 13: stellarum, id. Rep. 6, 11, 11.—With abl.: plen

pleo.full: plĕo, ēre, v. n., to fill, to fulfil, the root of plenus, q. v., compleo, expleo, suppleo: plentur antiqui etiam sine praepositionibus dicebant, Fest. p. 230 Müll.

pleonasmus.full: plĕŏnasmus, i, m., = πλεονασμός, in gram., a pleonasm, Mart. Cap. 5, § 537 al.
pleonasmus.short: plĕŏnasmus, i, m., = πλεονασμός, in gram., a pleonasm, Mart.

pleroma.full: plērōma, ătis, n., = πλήρωμα, fulness (eccl. Lat.), Tert. Praescr. 49.

pleromarius.full: plērōmārĭus, ii, m. pleroma, a seaman in large ships of burden or of war (opp. to lenuncularius), Inscr. Orell. 4104.

pleroticus.full: plērōtĭcus, a, um, adj., = πληρωτικός, serving to fill out, complemental (postclass.): termini plerotici, Front. Colon. p. 131 Goes.
pleroticus.short: plērōtĭcus, a, um, adj., = πληρωτικός, serving to fill out, complemental (postclass.): termini plerotici, Front.

plerus.full: plērus, a, um, adj. root ple-, v. plenus, very many, a very great part, most (anteclass. prim. form, for the class. plerusque, plerique): ager, campestris plerus, for the most part, Cato ap. Prisc. p. 668 P.: pater Achaeos in Caphareis saxis pleros perdidit, Pac. ib.: plera pars, id. ib. and ap. Fest. p. 230 Müll.: minores magistratus partiti iuris ploeres in ploera sunto, Cic. Leg. 3, 3, 6.—Neutr. adverb.: plerum (like plerumque, v. plerusque), for the most part, mostly, commonly: fieri solet p

plerusque.full: plērusque, răque, rumque, adj. a strengthened form from plerus, very many, a very great part, the most, most (rare in sing., and only in Sall. and post-class. writers; but in plur. freq. in all periods and styles). Plur.: habent hunc morem plerique argentarii, Plaut. Curc. 3, 7: pleraeque hae (meretrices) sub vestimentis secum habebant retia, id. Ep. 2, 2, 32; Ter. Eun. 1, 2, 38: multi nihil prodesse philosophiam, plerique etiam obesse arbitrantur, Cic. Inv. 1, 36, 65: ut plerique meministis, id

plestina.full: Plestina, ae, f., a town of the Marsi, Liv. 10, 3, 5.
plestina.short: Plestina, ae, f., a town of the Marsi, Liv.

pletura.full: plētūra, ae, f. pleo. Lit., fulness, a filling (post-class.), Paul. Nol. Carm. 21, 47.— Transf., fulness of blood, excess of blood, plethora (post-class.), Veg. Vet. 1, 35.

pleumosii.full: Pleumosĭi or Pleumoxĭi, ōrum, m., a people of Belgic Gaul, Caes. B. G. 5, 39.
pleumosii.short: Pleumosĭi or Pleumoxĭi, ōrum, m., a people of Belgic Gaul, Caes.

pleuricus.full: pleurĭcus, a, um, adj., = πλευρικός, at or on the side, lateral (post-class.): termini, Front. Colon. p. 117 Goes.
pleuricus.short: pleurĭcus, a, um, adj., = πλευρικός, at or on the side, lateral (post-class.): termini, Front.

pleurisis.full: pleurĭsis, is, f., for pleuritis, pleurisy (post-class.), Prud. στεφ. 10, 484; Isid. 4, 6, 8.
pleurisis.short: pleurĭsis, is, f., for pleuritis, pleurisy (post-class.), Prud.

pleuriticus.full: pleurītĭcus, a, um, adj., = πλευριτικός, affected with pleurisy, pleuritic (postAug.): medentur pleuriticis, Plin. 27, 4, 3, § 12: passio, Cael. Aur. Acut. 2, 16, 100; Isid. 4, 6, 8.—Plur. as subst.: pleurītĭci, pleuritic patients, Plin. 20, 5, 15, § 31; Cael. Aur. Acut. 2, 16, 100; 2, 17, 102.
pleuriticus.short: pleurītĭcus, a, um, adj., = πλευριτικός, affected with pleurisy, pleuritic (postAug.): medentur pleuriticis, Plin.

pleuritis.full: pleurītis, ĭdis, f., = πλευρῖτις. A sharp pain in the side, pleurisy (pure Lat. dolor lateris): arthritis, tussis, pleuritis, phthisis, Vitr. 1, 6.— The register in a hydraulic organ, Vitr. 10, 13 dub. (al. plinthis).

pleuron.full: Pleuron, ōnis, f., = Πλευρών, a city in Ætolia, now Castle of Irene, Plin. 4, 2, 3, § 6; Stat. Th. 2, 727; Ov. M. 7, 382.— Hence, Pleurōnĭus, a, um, adj., = Πλευρώνιος, of or belonging to Pleuron, Pleuronian: Pleuronius Acmon, Ov. M. 14, 494. —Subst.: Pleurōnĭa, ae, f., Ætolia, or that part of Ætolia in which Pleuron is situated, Aus. Epit. 10.
pleuron.short: Pleuron, ōnis, f., = Πλευρών, a city in Ætolia, now Castle of Irene, Plin.

plexippus.full: Plexippus, i, m., = Πλήξιππος. One of the fifty sons of Ægyptus, Hyg. Fab. 170.— A son of Thestius, Hyg. Fab. 173.

plexus1.full: plexus, a, um, Part. and P. a., from 1. plecto.

plexus2.full: plexus, ūs, m. 1. plecto, a twining, plaiting, braid (poet.), Manil. 5, 147 dub. (al. flexum, fluctum).

plicatilis.full: plĭcātĭlis, e, adj. plico, that may be folded together or doubled up, flexible, pliable (post-Aug.): upupae crista, Plin. 10, 29, 44, § 86: naves, id. 5, 9, 10, § 59.

plicatrix.full: plĭcātrix, īcis, f. plicator, she who folds clothes, Plaut. Mil. 3, 1, 101.

plicatura.full: plĭcātūra, ae, f. plico, a folding or doubling, a fold, plicature (post-Aug.): vestis, Plin. 7, 51, 52, § 171.

plicitus.full: plĭcĭtus, a, um, Part., from plico.
plicitus.short: plĭcĭtus, a, um, Part., from plico.

plico.full: plĭco (plĭcāvi, plĭcui, acc. to Prisc. p. 680 P.), plĭcātum and plĭcĭtum, āre, v. a. root plic-; Gr. πλέκω; v. plecto, to fold, to lay or wind together, to fold up, double up (poet. and in post-class. prose; cf.: complico, plecto, necto, flecto), Lucr. 4, 828: quaedam plicata, id. 6, 1086: chartam, Mart. 4, 83, 7: seque in sua membra plicantem (anguem), winding or coiling himself up, Verg. A. 5, 279; Gell. 17, 9, 9: decas plena his quattuor numeris gradatim plicatis integratur, folded together,

plinius.full: Plīnĭus, i, m., Pliny, name of a Roman gens. The most celebrated are, C. Plinius Secundus, also called Major (the Elder), author of an encyclopedical work in 37 books, who lost his life in an eruption of Vesuvius, A. D. 79.— His nephew, C. Plinius Caecilius, also called Junior (the Younger), author of Letters and a Pane gyric on the emperor Trajan: facundus, Mart. 10, 19, 3.— Plinius Valerianus, a physician in the time of the emperor Constantine.—Hence, Plīnĭānus, a, um, adj., belonging to or na
plinius.short: Plīnĭus, i, m., Pliny, name of a Roman gens.

plinthis.full: plinthis, ĭdis, f., = πλινθίς (a square tile). A square; in architect., a square base, a plinth, for plinthus, Vitr. 3, 3, 2; in land-surveying, for plinthus, Hyg. Condit. Agror. p. 210 Goes.— Plur.: plinthĭ-des, a register in the hydraulic organ, Vitr. 10, 8, 8; v. pleuritis.
plinthis.short: plinthis, ĭdis, f., = πλινθίς (a square tile).

plinthium.full: plinthĭum, ii, n., = πλίνθιον, a hollow square figure, a kind of sundial, Vitr. 9, 9.
plinthium.short: plinthĭum, ii, n., = πλίνθιον, a hollow square figure, a kind of sundial, Vitr.

plinthus.full: plinthus (-os), i, m. and f., = πλίνθος (a tile). In archit., the large flat member under the inferior moulding of a column, the base, plinth, Vitr. 3, 3; 4, 7, 3.— In land-surveying, a tile-shaped figure, containing a hundred acres of land: quae centuriae nunc appellantur plinthi, id est laterculi, Hyg. Condit. Agror. p. 205 Goes.

plisima.full: plisĭma, sup. form for plurima; v. plurimus, under multus, III.

plisthenes.full: Plisthĕnes, is, m., = Πλεισθένης. The son of Pelops, brother of Atreus and Thyestes, and the father of Agamemnon and Menelaus, who were brought up by his brother Atreus (whence they are called Atridae), Serv. Verg. A. 1, 458; acc. to others, the son of Atreus, Hyg. Fab. 86 and 97.—Hence, Plisthĕnĭdes, ae, m., = Πλεισθενίδης, a male descendant of Plisthenes, a Plisthenide: felix Plisthenide, i. e. Menelaus, Sabin. Ep. 1, 107.— Plisthĕ-nĭus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Plisthenes, Plisthenian:

plistia.full: Plistĭa, ae, f., a city of the Samnites, Liv. 9, 21; 22.
plistia.short: Plistĭa, ae, f., a city of the Samnites, Liv.

plistolochia.full: plistŏlŏchĭa, ae, f., a plant facilitaling parturition, Plin. 25, 8, 54, § 96 (al. pistolochia); 25, 8, 55, § 101.— A plant, = althaea, Plin. 20, 21, 84, § 222.
plistolochia.short: plistŏlŏchĭa, ae, f., a plant facilitaling parturition, Plin.

plistonices.full: Plistŏnīces, ae, m., an epithet of Apion the grammarian, Gell. 5, 14, 1; Plin. 37, 5, 19, § 75.
plistonices.short: Plistŏnīces, ae, m., an epithet of Apion the grammarian, Gell.

plitendum.full: Plitendum, i, n., a town of Asia, Liv. 38, 18, 3.
plitendum.short: Plitendum, i, n., a town of Asia, Liv.

ploce.full: plŏcē, ēs, f., = πλοκή. In rhetoric, a repeating of the same word with a different meaning, Mart. Cap. 5, § 532; Jul. Rufin. p. 236 Ruhnk. (ad Quint. 9, 3, 41, written as Greek).— In music, a combining of different tones together, Mart. Cap. 9, §§ 936, 958.

ploeres.full: ploeres, ploera, archaic for plures, plura, Cic. Leg. 3, 3, 6 B. and K.
ploeres.short: ploeres, ploera, archaic for plures, plura, Cic.

plorabilis.full: plōrābĭlis, e, adj. ploro, lamentable, deplorable (poet.): plorabile si quid Eliquat, Pers. 1, 34: plorabile quiddam, Claud. in Eutr. 1, 261.

ploratio.full: plōrātĭo, ōnis, f. id., a wailing, weeping, lamentation (late Lat.): a convalle plorationis, Aug. Serm. S. S. 17.

plorator.full: plōrātor, ōris, m. id., a wailer, lamenter, mourner (poet.), Mart. 14, 54, 1.

ploratus.full: plōrātus, ūs, m. id., a wailing, weeping, lamenting. Lit.: virginalem ploratum edere, Cic. poët. Tusc. 2, 9, 21: ploratum infantis cohibere, Plin. 36, 5, 4, § 29: vox ploratūs, Vulg. Matt. 2, 18.—In plur.: omnia mulierum ploratibus sonant, Liv. 29, 17.— Transf., of the weeping or bleeding of a tree, Plin. 12, 25, 54, § 116.

ploro.full: plōro, āvi, ātum, 1, v. n. and a. [etym. dub.; cf. pluo]. To cry out, to cry aloud = clamare: SI PARENTEM PVER VERBERIT. AST OLLE PLORASSIT, and he cry out, Lex. Serv. Tull. ap. Fest. p. 230 Müll.— To wail, lament, to weep aloud. Neutr. (class.; syn.: lugeo, fleo): ego hercle faciam plorantem illum, Plaut. Poen. 1, 2, 164: ne plora, id. Merc. 3, 1, 3; id. Ps. 4, 4, 1: eam plorare, Ter. Phorm. prol. 8: plorando fessus sum, Cic. Att. 15, 9: date puero panem, ne ploret, Auct. ap. Quint. 6, 1, 47: l

plostellum.full: plostellum, i, n. dim. plostrum, plaustrum, a small wagon or cart: plostellum Poenicum, Varr. R. R. 1, 52: plostello adjungere mures, Hor. S. 2, 3, 247; Aug. Civ. Dei, 7, 21.

plotae.full: Plōtae, ārum, f., an ancient name of the Strophades, Mel. 2, 7; Plin. 4, 12, 19, § 55.
plotae.short: Plōtae, ārum, f., an ancient name of the Strophades, Mel.

plotinus.full: Plōtīnus, i, m., = Πλωτῖνος, a famous philosopher of the Eclectic school, who flourished in the third century A. D., Amm. 21, 14, 5.
plotinus.short: Plōtīnus, i, m., = Πλωτῖνος, a famous philosopher of the Eclectic school, who flourished in the third century A.

ploxemum.full: ploxĕmum, ploxĭmum, or plo-xĕnum, i, n. Gallic, a wagon-box: gingivas vero ploxemi habet veteris, Cat. 97, 6 (quoted ap. Quint. 1, 5, 8, and ap. Fest. p. 230 Müll.).
ploxemum.short: ploxĕmum, ploxĭmum, or plo-xĕnum, i, n.

pluma.full: plūma, ae, f., a small, soft feather; in plur., fine, soft feathers, down. Lit. (clas.; syn. penna): (animantium) pluma alias, alias squamā videmus obductas, Cic. N. D. 2, 47, 121: plumae versicolores, id. Fin. 3, 5, 18: mollis, Verg. A. 10, 192: in plumis delituisse Jovem, i. e. in the form of a swan, Ov. H. 8, 68.—They were used esp. for stuffing pillows and the beds of litters: dormit in plumā, Mart. 12, 17, 8: pensilibus plumis vehi, i. e. in litters, Juv. 1, 159: in plumā paternā dormire, i
pluma.short: plūma, ae, f., a small, soft feather;

plumacium.full: plūmācĭum, i, n. pluma, a feather pillow, down pillow (eccl. Lat.), Ambros. Ep. 26, n. 12; Cassiod. Hist. Eccl. 7, 16.

plumalis.full: plūmālis, e, adj. id., feathered (poet.). —Of Leda: plumalem de Jove fecit avem (Jupiter, who, for love of her, changed himself into a swan), Poët. in Anthol. Lat. 3, 275, 58.

plumarius.full: plūmārĭus, a, um, adj. id., of or belonging to soft feathers; transf., embroidered with feathers: vestes plumariā arte contextae, the art of embroidering, Hier. Ep. 29, n. 6; Adelh. Laud. Virg. 15: ars, embroidery, Vulg. Exod. 39, 28.— Subst.: plūmārĭus, ii, m., an embroiderer, Varr. ap. Non. 162, 27: plumariorum textrinae, Vitr. 6, 7; Firm. Math. 3, 13, 10; Vulg. Exod. 35, 35; Inscr. Grut. 649, 8; Inscr. Rein. cl. 11, n. 114.

plumatile.full: plūmātĭle, is, n. (sc. vestimentum) [from pluma; embroidered like feathers], an embroidered garment: cumatile aut plumatile, Plaut. Ep. 2, 2, 49.

plumatus.full: plūmātus, a, um, Part. and P.a., from plumo, q. v.

plumbago.full: plumbāgo, ĭnis, f. plumbum. A species of lead ore, black-lead, plumbago, also called molybdaena, Plin. 34, 18, 50, § 168.— Transf., a leaden color in gems, Plin. 37, 5, 18, § 68.— A plant, also called molybdaena, leadwort, fleawort, Plin. 25, 13, 97, § 155.

plumbarius.full: plumbārĭus, a, um, adj. id., of or belonging to lead, lead-: artifices plumbarii, workers in lead, plumbers, Vitr. 8, 7: officinae, plumbers' shops, Plin. 34, 18, 54, § 175: metallum, a lead-mine, id. 33, 7, 40, § 119.— Subst. plumbārĭus, ii, m. (sc. artifex), a plumber; plur., Dig. 50, 6, 6.— plumbārĭum, ii, n., a place to keep leaden vessels in: plumbum, plumbeus, plumbarium, Not. Tir. p. 164.

plumbatae.full: plumbātae, ārum, v. plumbo, II. B.

plumbatura.full: plumbātūra, ae, f. plumbo, a soldering with lead (post-class.), Dig. 6, 1, 23, § 5.

plumbeus.full: plumbĕus, a, um, adj. plumbum, of or belonging to lead, made of lead, leaden, lead-. Lit.: plumbea glans, Lucr. 6, 306: pistillum, Plin. 34, 18, 50, § 169: vas, id. 33, 6, 35, § 109: ictus, blows given with a scourge to which a leaden ball is attached, Prud. στεφ. 10, 122.—Subst. plum-bĕum, i, n., a leaden vessel, Cato, R. R. 105: Nicerotiana, Mart. 6, 55, 3.— plum-bĕa, ae, f., a leaden ball: ut mortuus ictu plumbeae crederetur, Spart. Sever. 11, 2. — Transf. Leaden, blunt, dull (class.): plumbe

plumbo.full: plumbo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. id.. To lead, to solder with lead (ante-class. and post-Aug.): modiolos indet et plumbet, Cato, R. R. 21: argentum, Plin. 34, 17, 48, § 161: scyphum alieno plumbo, Dig. 41, 1, 27.— To make a thing of lead; hence, plumbātus, a, um, Part., leaden (postAug.): plumbatae sagittae, Plin. 10, 33, 50, § 97: jacula, Sol. 3, 3: canales, Front. Aquaed. 124: tabulae, Val. Max. 3, 7, n. 2. — Subst.: plumbātae, ārum, f. Leaden balls, Veg. Mil. 1, 17.— Scourges to which leaden balls

plumbosus.full: plumbōsus, a, um, adj. id., full of lead, having much lead mixed with it (postAug.): plumbosa molybdaena, Plin. 34, 18, 53, § 173.—Sup.: faex plumbosissima, Plin. 33, 6, 34, § 103.

plumbum.full: plumbum, i, n. for mlumbum; Gr. μόλμβος, μόλυβδος, lead. Lit. In gen.: dolia plumbo vincito, Cato, R. R. 39: plumbum album, tin, Lucr. 6, 1079; Caes. B. G. 5, 12; called also candidum, Plin. 34, 16, 47, § 157; but plumbum nigrum, lead, id. 34, 16, 47, § 159.— In partic. A leaden ball or bullet (poet.): Balearica plumbum Funda jacit, Ov. M. 2, 727; Verg. A. 9, 587.— Leaden pipes (poet.): purior in vicis aqua tendit rumpere plumbum, Hor. Ep. 1, 10, 20.— A scourge with a leaden ball at the end of i

plumella.full: plūmella, ae, f. dim. pluma, a small feather: pluma, plumella, Not. Tir. p. 171.

plumesco.full: plūmesco, ĕre, v. inch. n. [id.], to begin to have or get feathers, to become fledged (post-Aug.), Plin. 10, 53, 74, § 149; Hier. in Matt. 24, § 28.

plumeus.full: plūmĕus, a, um, adj. id.. Lit., downy, covered or filled with down, down- (class.): culcita plumea, Cic. Tusc. 3, 19, 46: aures, Plin. 10, 23, 33, § 68.— Transf. Downy, like down, i. e. light, soft, delicate (poet. and post-class.): plumea pondera, Mart. 4, 19, 7: nives, Arn. 2, 84: plumea et lactea cutis, App. M. 3, p. 135, 26.— Embroidered: indumenta, Prud. Ham. 295.

plumiger.full: plūmĭger, ĕra, ĕrum, adj. pluma-gero, feather-bearing, feathered (post-Aug.): plumigeri anseres, Plin. 10, 22, 27, § 53: series, i. e. pennae, Prud. Cath. 3, 44.

plumipes.full: plūmĭpes, ĕdis, adj. pluma-pes, feather-footed, with feathered feet (poet.): adde huc plumipedas, Cat. 55, 27.

plumo.full: plūmo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. and n. pluma. Act. To cover with feathers, to feather (poet. and post-Aug.): plumato corpore corvus, Cic. poët. N. D. 2, 44, 114: molli plumatā lanugine, Plin. 8, 32, 50, § 117: plumare se in avem, i. e. to transform, App. M. 3, p. 138, 18.— To embroider (poet. and post-class.): pars auro plumata nitet, pars ignea cocco, Luc. 10, 123; Vop. Carin. 20: plumato amictus aureo Babylonico, Petr. Poet. 55, 6.— To cover with scales (post-class.): loricae plumatae, Just. 41, 2,

plumosus.full: plūmōsus, a, um, adj. id., full of down or feathers, covered with feathers, feathered. Lit.: aucupium, Prop. 4 (5), 2, 34.— Transf.: folia, downy, Plin. 25, 6, 29, § 65.

plumula.full: plūmŭla, ae, f. dim. id., a little downfeather, a little feather (post-Aug.), Col. 8, 5, 19; App. Flor. p. 348 fin.

pluo.full: plŭo, plui (or plūvi in Plaut. and Liv.; cf. Prisc. p. 881 P.; Varr. L. L. 9, § 104 Müll.), 3, v. n., usu. impers. (ante-class. and late Lat. also pers.; v. infra) [root plu-, to swim; Gr. πλύνω, to wash; cf.: πλέω, πλεύσω, to sail; cf. ploro], to rain; constr. absol., or with abl. or acc. Lit.: pluet credo hercle hodie, Plaut. Curc. 1, 2, 42: ut multum pluverat, id. Men. prol. 63: has Graeci stellas Hyadas vocitare suerunt, a pluendo: ὕειν enim est pluere, Cic. N. D. 2, 43, 111: aqua, quae plue

pluor.full: plŭor, ōris, m. pluo, rain (ante-class.): pluor, Laber. ap. Non. 220, 33.

pluralis.full: plūrālis, e, adj. plus, belonging or relating to more than one, relating to many (post-Aug.). In gen. Pluralis elocutio testium, Dig. 22, 5, 12.— Plural, consisting of more than one: deitas, Arn. in Psa. 67.— In partic., a gram. t. t., plural: praeterea numeros, in quibus nos singularem ac pluralem habemus, Graeci et δυικον, Quint. 1, 5, 42: genitivus, of the plural, id. 1, 6, 26.—Absol.: cum singulari pluralis subjungitur, the plural, Quint. 9, 3, 8: singularia pluralibus miscet, id. 9, 3, 63;

pluralitas.full: plūrālĭtas, ātis, f. pluralis. Plurality (opp. to unitas), Ambros. in Psa. 118, prol. § 2; plur., Boëth. Arithm. 1, 4.— Gram. t. t., the plural number, Charis. p. 50 P.

plurativus.full: plūrātīvus, a, um, adj. plus, plural, gram. t. t. (post-class.): plurativus numerus, Gell. 19, 8, 4.—Subst.: plūrātīvum, i, n., the plural number, the plural (postclass.): mei interrogandi casus est, et ab eo declinatur, quod est ego. Hujus deinde plurativum est nos, Gell. 20, 6, 8.

plures.full: plūres, v. plus, under multus, II.

pluries.full: plūrĭes (-ens), adv. plus, often, oftentimes, frequently (post-class.; cf.: saepius, identidem), Treb. Poll. Gall. 1 (but in Caes. B. C. 1, 79, 1, the correct read. is pluresque).

plurifariam.full: plūrĭfārĭam, adv. id., in many parts or places (post-Aug.), Suet. Aug. 46; 80; id. Tib. 43; id. Calig. 54; id. Ner. 24; id. Vit. 9: gladiatoria munera plurifariam exhibuit, id. Claud. 21 (al. plurifaria).— In many ways, manifoldly, variously (post-class.), App. Flor. p. 357, 37; p. 178 Bip.: mons Taurus pro gentium ac linguarum varietate plurifariam nominatus, Sol. 38.

pluriformis.full: plūrĭformis, e, adj. plures-forma, having many forms, manifold, varied (postclass.): pluriformi modo, App. Flor. p. 341, 14; Mart. Cap. 7, § 729.

plurilaterus.full: plūrĭlătĕrus, a, um, adj. plus-latus, having several sides (post-class.), Front. Expos. Form. p. 35 Goes.

plurimus.full: plūrĭmus, a, um, v. multus, III.

plurivocus.full: plūrĭvŏcus, a, um, adj. plus-vox, having several or many significations: quaeritur quid sit aequivocum, quid univocum, quid, ut ita dicam, plurivocum, Mart. Cap. 4, §§ 339, 357.

plusculum.full: pluscŭlum, adv., v. the foll. art.

plusculus.full: pluscŭlus, a, um, adj. dim. [plus], somewhat more, a little more; rather many (only as subst. class.): tum pluscula Supellectile opus est, Ter. Phorm. 4, 3, 60: sal, Col. 12, 50, 12: ad cujus noctis exemplar similes adstruximus plusculas, several nights, App. M. 2, p. 122, 25: pyxides, id. ib. 3, p. 138, 25.—Neutr. subst., a somewhat larger amount: plusculum etiam, quam concedit veritas, amori nostro largiare, Cic. Fam. 5, 12, 3.—With gen.: plusculum negotii, Cic. de Or. 2, 24: ut plusculum sibi

plusimus.full: plūsĭmus, for plurimus, Varr. L. L. 6, § 27 Müll.; v. multus, III.

plutearius.full: plŭtĕārĭus or plŭtĭārĭus, ii, m. pluteus, a maker of balustrades, Inscr. Don. 417, 9.

pluteus.full: plŭtĕus, i, m., less freq. plŭtĕum, i, n. A penthouse, shed, or mantlet, made of hurdles covered with raw hides, and used to protect besiegers (cf. vineae): plutei crates corio crudo intentae, quae solebant opponi militibus opus facientibus, et appellabantur militares. Nunc etiam tabulae, quibus quid praesepitur, eodem nomine dicuntur, Paul. ex Fest. p. 231 Müll.; cf. Veg. Mil. 4, 15: pluteos praeferre, Amm. 21, 12, 6; so Caes. B. C. 2, 9; Liv. 21, 61, 10 al.—Transf.: ad aliquem vineam pluteosqu

pluto.full: Plūto or Plūton, ōnis, m., = Πλούτων, the king of the Lower World, the husband of Proserpine, and brother of Jupiter and Neptune, Cic. N. D. 2, 26, 66; Hyg. praef.; Verg. A. 7, 327; Juv. 13, 50.—Acc. Gr. Plutona, Hor. C. 2, 14, 7.—Hence, Plūtōnĭus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Pluto, Plutonian: et domus exilis Plutonia, i. e. the realms. of death, the Lower Regions, Hor. C. 1, 4, 17.—Subst.: Plūtō-nĭa, ōrum, n. plur., a pestilential district in Asia, Cic. Div. 1, 36, 79.
pluto.short: Plūto or Plūton, ōnis, m., = Πλούτων, the king of the Lower World, the husband of Proserpine, and brother of Jupiter and Neptune, Cic.

plutor.full: plūtor, ōris, m. pluo, the rainer, he who sends rain (eccl. Lat.), Aug. Serm. Divers. 8, 3.

plutus.full: Plūtus, i, m., = Πλοῦτος, Plutus, the god of riches, Phaedr. 4, 12, 5.
plutus.short: Plūtus, i, m., = Πλοῦτος, Plutus, the god of riches, Phaedr.

pluvia.full: plŭvĭa, ae, f. (sc. aqua) [pluvius]. Rain (class.; cf. imber): pluvias metuo, Cic. Att. 15, 16: tenues, Verg. G. 1, 92: in gens, id. ib. 325: a pluviā tueri, Juv. 3, 202: de pluviis loqui, id. 4, 87: pluviarum signa, Sen. Q. N. 1, 9, 1: qui aufert stillas pluviae, Vulg. Job, 36, 27.— Transf., a fall or shower of any thing (post-class.; cf. pluo); of blossoms, Claud. Nupt. Honor. 298: pluvia ignea, Aug. Quaest. in Num. 4, 27; id. Serm. 105, 7.— Rain-water (post-Aug.): admixtā pluviā, Plin. 33, 6,

pluvialia.full: Plŭvĭālĭa, ae, f. (sc. insula), one of the Fortunate Isles, Plin. 6, 32, 37, § 202.

pluvialis.full: plŭvĭālis, e, adj. pluvia, of or belonging to rain, rainy, rain-: Auster, rainbringing, Verg. G. 3, 429: Haedi, id. A. 9, 668: sidus, Ov. M. 3, 594: fungi, which are produced by rain, id. ib. 7, 393: aqua, rainwater, Sen. Q. N. 3, 7, 4: dies, Col. 2, 13: imbres, Tac. H. 5, 23.

pluviaticus.full: plŭvĭātĭcus, a, um, adj. id., of or belonging to rain, rain- (post-class.): aqua, Marc. Emp. 8.

pluviatilis.full: plŭvĭātĭlis, e, adj. id., of or belonging to rain, rain- (post-Aug.): aqua, Cels. 4, 12 fin.; 7, 3; Col. 9, 1, 2.

pluviosus.full: plŭvĭōsus, a, um, adj. id., full of rain, rainy (post-Aug.): hiems, Plin. 18, 25, 60, § 225.

pluvius.full: plŭvĭus, a, um, adj. pluo, rainy, causing or bringing rain, rain- (class.): SI AQVA PLVVIA NOCET, rain-water, Fragm. XII. Tab.; cf. aquae, Cic. Mur. 9, 22; id. Top. 9, 38: tempestates, Cato, R. R. 2, 3: caelum, Varr. R. R. 1, 13, 2: Hyades, rain-bringing, Verg. A. 3, 516: venti, Hor. C. 1, 17, 4: rores, rain, id. ib. 3, 3, 56: arcus, rainbow, id. A. P. 18: Juppiter, who dispenses rain, Tib. 1, 8 (7), 26 (cf.: Juppiter uvidus, Verg. G. 1, 418, and Ζεὺς ἰκμαῖος): dies, Col. 2, 15: caeli status, id

pneumaticus.full: pneumătĭcus, a, um, adj., = πνευματικός, of or belonging to air or to wind, air-, wind-, pneumatic; of machines that are driven by the force of air: Ctesibius, qui pneumaticas res invenit, Vitr. 9, 9: organa, Plin. 19, 4, 20, § 60: ratio, id. 7, 37, 38, § 125.
pneumaticus.short: pneumătĭcus, a, um, adj., = πνευματικός, of or belonging to air or to wind, air-, wind-, pneumatic;

pneumatomachi.full: Pneumătŏmăchi, ōrum, m., = Πνευματομάχοι (fighters with the Spirit), a sect of heretics, Cod. Just. 1, 5, 5.
pneumatomachi.short: Pneumătŏmăchi, ōrum, m., = Πνευματομάχοι (fighters with the Spirit), a sect of heretics, Cod.

pnigeus.full: pnīgeus (dissyl.), ei, m., = πνιγεύς, a cover or damper, which keeps down the rising air in the hydraulic organ, Vitr. 10, 13.
pnigeus.short: pnīgeus (dissyl.), ei, m., = πνιγεύς, a cover or damper, which keeps down the rising air in the hydraulic organ, Vitr.

pnigitis.full: pnīgītis, ĭdis, f., = πνιγῖτις, a kind of potter's clay, Plin. 35, 16, 56, § 194.
pnigitis.short: pnīgītis, ĭdis, f., = πνιγῖτις, a kind of potter's clay, Plin.

pnytagoras.full: Pnўtăgŏras, ae, m., a king of Cyprus, an ally of Alexander the Great, Curt. 4, 8, 9.
pnytagoras.short: Pnўtăgŏras, ae, m., a king of Cyprus, an ally of Alexander the Great, Curt.

po'.full: po', an old form of post; as, po' meridiem, mentioned by Quint. 9, 4, 39.
po'.short: po', an old form of post;

po.full: po, insep. prep. (cf. ποτί, πρός), a prefix denoting power or possession, or that renders emphatic the meaning of a verb; as in polleo, polliceor, pono. † po pro potissimum positum est in Saliari carmine, Fest. p. 205 Müll.

poblilia.full: Poblĭlĭa or Publĭlĭa tribus (also, Publĭa, Publĭcĭa, Popĭlĭa, Popĭl-lĭa), one of the rustic tribes, Liv. 7, 15, fin.; Inscr. Grut. 568, 1; Inscr. Don. cl. 6, n. 112; Inscr. Maff. Ver. Illustr. 1; cf. Fest. p. 233 Müll.; cf.: Popillia tribus a progenitrice traxit vocabulum, Paul. ex Fest. p. 232 Müll.
poblilia.short: Poblĭlĭa or Publĭlĭa tribus (also, Publĭa, Publĭcĭa, Popĭlĭa, Popĭl-lĭa), one of the rustic tribes, Liv.

pocillator.full: pōcillātor, ōris, m. pocillum, a cupbearer (post-class.): quo, Jovi pocillatorem Phrygium sustulerat, i. e. Ganymede, App. M. 6, p. 179, 16; so id. ib. 10, p. 247.

pocillum.full: pōcillum, i, n. dim. poculum, a little cup: pocillum fictile, Cato, R. R. 156: mulsi, Liv. 10, 42 fin.; cf. Plin. 14, 13, 14, § 91: argenteum, Suet. Vesp. 2.

poculentus.full: pōcŭlentus (poscŭl-, pōtŭl-), a, um, adj. id., drinkable, potable: penus est quod esculentum aut poculentum est, etc., Q. Scaevola ap. Gell. 4, 1, 17.— Of vessels, fit for use in drinking: a poculento argento vascularius, Inscr. Grut. 643, 3.

poculum.full: pōcŭlum (contr. pōclum, Plaut. Curc. 2, 3, 80; 89; Arn. 5, 175), i, n. from root po-, pot; Gr. πίνω, v. potus. Lit., a drinking-vessel, a cup, goblet, bowl, beaker (class.; syn.: calix, cyathus): et nobis idem Alcimedon duo pocula fecit, Verg. E: 3, 44: poculum grande, Plaut. Curc. 2, 3, 89: magnis poculis aliquem invitare, id. Rud. 2, 3, 32: exhaurire poculum, to empty, Cic. Clu. 11, 31; so, ducere, Hor. C. 1, 17, 21: siccare, Petr. 92: poscunt majoribus poculis (sc. bibere), out of goblets, Ci

podager.full: pŏdăger, gri, m., = ποδαγρός, one who has the gout, a gouty man (ante- and postclass. for podagricus): numquam poetor nisi si podager, Enn. ap. Prisc. p. 829 P. (Sat. v. 8 Vahl.); Claud. Epigr. 29.
podager.short: pŏdăger, gri, m., = ποδαγρός, one who has the gout, a gouty man (ante- and postclass.

podagra.full: pŏdā^gra, ae, f., = ποδάγρα, the gout in the feet: doloribus podagrae cruciari, Cic. Tusc. 2, 19, 45: cum arderet podagrae doloribus, id. Fin. 5, 31, 94: nodosa, Ov. P. 1, 3, 23; cf. Plin. 26, 10, 64, § 100: locuples, Juv. 13, 96.—In plur., Cels. 5, 18.
podagra.short: pŏdā^gra, ae, f., = ποδάγρα, the gout in the feet: doloribus podagrae cruciari, Cic.

podagricus.full: pŏdā^grĭcus, a, um, adj., = ποδαγρικός, gouty, podagric: cum tot feminae podagricae calvaeque sint, Sen. Ep. 15, 3, 21. — Subst.: pŏdā^grĭcus, i, m., a gouty person, Cels. 4, 24: podagrici pedibus suis maledicunt, chiragrici manibus, Petr. 132.
podagricus.short: pŏdā^grĭcus, a, um, adj., = ποδαγρικός, gouty, podagric: cum tot feminae podagricae calvaeque sint, Sen.

podagrosus.full: pŏdā^grōsus, a, um, adj. podagra, having the gout, gouty (ante-class.): deformis senex, arthriticus ac podagrosus, Lucil. ap. Non. 166, 14: podagrosi estis ac vicistis cochleam tarditudine, Plaut. Poen. 3, 1, 28: pedes, id. Merc. 3, 4, 8.

podalirius.full: Pŏdălīrĭus, ii, m., = Ποδαλείριος. Son of Æsculapius, a celebrated physician, Ov. Tr. 5, 6, 11; id. A. A. 2, 735.— A Trojan who followed Æneas to Italy, Verg. A. 12, 304.— A Roman surname: C. PETRONIVS PODALIRIVS, Inscr. Amaduzzi Anecd. Litter. t. l. p. 463.

poderes.full: pŏdēres or pŏdēris, is, m., = ποδήρης, a long garment descending to the ankle, worn by the priests, Tert. adv. Jud. 11; cf. Isid. Orig. 19, 21: in veste poderis quam habebat totus erat orbis, Vulg. Sap. 18, 24.
poderes.short: pŏdēres or pŏdēris, is, m., = ποδήρης, a long garment descending to the ankle, worn by the priests, Tert.

podex.full: pōdex, ĭcis, m. perh. for pordex, from pedo, ere, the fundament, anus, Hor. Epod. 8, 6: lēvis, Juv. 2, 12.

podia.full: pŏdĭa, ae, f., a rope fastened to one of the lower corners of a sail, for the purpose of setting it to the wind; in Engl. nautical lang., a sheet, Serv. Verg. A. 5, 830 (al. podium).
podia.short: pŏdĭa, ae, f., a rope fastened to one of the lower corners of a sail, for the purpose of setting it to the wind;

podiarius.full: pŏdĭārĭus, i, m. podium, one who performs mimes on the stage, a mime, Not. Tir. p. 174: podiarius, inter mimos, Gloss. Isid.

podicus.full: pŏdĭcus, a, um, adj. ποῦς, of or belonging to a foot (post-class.): sed temporum alia simplicia sunt, quae podica etiam perhibentur. Pes veri est numeri prima progressio, Mart. Cap. 9, § 974.

podismatus.full: pŏdismātus, a, um, adj. podismus, measured out by feet (post-class.): ager, Front. Colon. p. 132 Goes.

podismus.full: pŏdismus, i, m., = ποδισμός, a measuring out by feet, foot-measure (post-class.): ad podismum dimetiri loca, Veg. Mil. 2, 7 fin.; 3, 15; Front. Colon. p. 130 Goes.; Inscr. Orell. 4570.
podismus.short: pŏdismus, i, m., = ποδισμός, a measuring out by feet, foot-measure (post-class.): ad podismum dimetiri loca, Veg.

podium.full: pŏdĭum, ii, n., = πόδιον, an elevated place, a height. In gen. (post-class.): podia ternis alta pedibus fabricantur, Pall. 1, 38.— In partic. A projection in a building, a jutty, balcony, podium (postAug.), Plin. Ep. 5, 6, 22; Vitr. 3, 3; 5, 7; 7, 4, 4; Dig. 33, 7, 12, § 22.— A projecting part in the circus or amphitheatre, a parapet or balcony next to the arena, where the emperor and other distinguished persons sat, Suet. Ner. 12; cf. Plin. 37, 3, 11, § 45: omnes ad podium spectantes, Juv. 2, 1
podium.short: pŏdĭum, ii, n., = πόδιον, an elevated place, a height.

poeas.full: Poeas (Paeas), antis, m., = Ποίας, the father of Philoctetes, Ov. M. 9, 233; Sen. Herc. Oet. 1603; Hyg. Fab. 14.—Hence, Poeantĭădes (Paeant-), ae, m., the son of Pœas, i. e. Philoctetes, Ov. M. 13, 313. — Poeantĭus (Paeant-), a, um, adj., of or belonging to Pœas, Pœantian: Poeantia proles, i. e. Philoctetes, Ov. M. 13, 45; also: heros, id. R. Am. 111; and absol. Poeantius, id. Tr. 5, 1, 61.
poeas.short: Poeas (Paeas), antis, m., = Ποίας, the father of Philoctetes, Ov.

poecile.full: Poecĭle, ēs, f., = Ποικίλη (variegated). The picture-gallery, a celebrated hall or portico in the market-place at Athens: in porticu, quae Poecile vocatur, Nep. Milt. 6, 3; cf. Plin. 35, 9, 35, § 59.— A gallery in the Athenian style at the Tiburtine villa of the emperor Hadrian, Spart. Hadr. 26.

poeeessa.full: Poeēessa or Poeessa, ae, f., = Ποιήεσσα. An ancient name of the island of Rhodes, Plin. 5, 31, 36, § 132.— An ancient town of Cea, Plin. 4, 12, 20, § 62.
poeeessa.short: Poeēessa or Poeessa, ae, f., = Ποιήεσσα.

poema.full: pŏēma, ătis (gen. plur. poëmatorum, Afran. ap. Non. 493, 9; cf. Charis. p. 114 P.: poëmatum, Suet. Gram. 23; Spart. Hadr. 14; dat. and abl. plur. usually poëmatis, Cic. Off. 3, 3, 15; Plaut. As. 1, 3, 22; Auct. Her. 4, 2, 3; but also poëmatibus, Suet.
