Tit. 3; App. Mag. 5), n., = ποίημα, a composition in verse, a poem (freq. and class.; syn. carmen): pars est parva poëma, proinde ut epistola quaevis. Illa poësis opus totum, ut tota Ilias una Est θέσις, annalesque Enni: atque istoc opus unum Est m

poematium.full: pŏēmătĭum, ĭi, n., = ποιημάτιον, a little or short poem (post-Aug.), Plin. Ep. 4, 14; so id. ib. 4, 27; Aus. Idyll. 7.
poematium.short: pŏēmătĭum, ĭi, n., = ποιημάτιον, a little or short poem (post-Aug.), Plin.

poemenis.full: Poemĕnis, ĭdis, f., the name of a dog, Ov. M. 3, 215; Hyg. Fab. 181.
poemenis.short: Poemĕnis, ĭdis, f., the name of a dog, Ov.

poena.full: poena, ae, f. Gr. ποινή, ἄποινα, quitmoney, fine; Lat. pūnio, poenitet, indemnification, compensation, satisfaction, expiation, punishment, penalty (cf. mulcta). Lit.: SI INIVRIAM FAXIT ALTERI VIGINTI QVINQVE AERIS POENAE SVNTO, Fragm. XII. Tab.: mi calido das sanguine poenas, Enn. ap. Macr. S. 6, 1 (Ann. v. 101 Vahl.); imitated by Virgil: tu tamen interea calido mihi sanguine poenas Persolves amborum, Verg. A. 9, 422 Serv.: poenas justas et debitas solvere, Cic. Mil. 31, 85: poenas pendere, Pla

poenalis.full: poenālis, e, adj. poena, of or belonging to punishment, penal (post-Aug.; esp. freq. in the jurists): opera, Plin. 18, 11, 29, § 112: poenalis aquae dirisque genitae, in the infernal regions, id. 4, 8, 15, § 31: ex lege poenali aquā et igne interdici, by the penal law, Gai. Inst. 1, § 128: actio, Dig. 40, 12, 21: causa, ib. 46, 3, 7: conditio, ib. 22, 2, 5: stipulatio, ib. 19, 2, 54 et saep.— Absol.: poenāles, ĭum, m., men subject to punishment, criminals: carcer poenalium, Cod. Just. 10, 19, 2.

poenarius.full: poenārĭus, a, um, adj. id., of or belonging to punishment, penal, criminal (post-Aug.): actiones, Quint. 4, 3, 9; 7, 4, 20.

poeni.full: Poeni, ōrum, m., the Phœnicians, i. e. the Carthaginians (descended from the Phœnicians): Poeni stipendia pendunt, Enn. ap. Varr. L. L. 5, § 182 Müll. (Ann. v. 269 Vahl.); id. ap. Fest. p. 249 ib. (Ann. v. 278 Vahl.); Cic. Rep. 2, 4, 9: Poeni foedifragi, id. Off. 1, 12, 38: Poenorum crudelitas, id. N. D. 3, 32, 80: ponuntque ferocia Poeni Corda, Verg. A. 1, 302.—Gen. plur.: Poenūm, Sil. 7, 714; 17, 311.—In sing.: Poenus, i, m., a Carthaginian: Poenus plane est, he is a true Carthaginian, i. e. f
poeni.short: Poeni, ōrum, m., the Phœnicians, i.

poenice.full: Poenĭcē, adv., v. Poeni, B. fin.

poenicus.full: Poenĭcus, a, um, v. Poeni, B.

poenitens.full: poenĭtens, entis, Part. and P. a., from poeniteo.

poenitenter.full: poenĭtenter, adv., v. poeniteo, P. a. A. fin.

poenosus.full: poenŏsus, a, um, adj. poena, painful (eccl. Lat.), Ps.-Aug. ad Fratr. Erem. Serm. 48.

poenulus.full: Poenŭlus, i, m. dim. Poeni, The Young Carthaginian, the title of a comedy of Plautus.

poenus2.full: Poenus, a, um, v. Poeni, A.

poesis.full: pŏēsis (pŏĕsis, Prud. ap. Symm. 2, 52), is, f., = ποίησις. The art of composing poems, poetry, poesy (rarely so used), Quint. 12, 11, 26.— A poem, poetry (class.): ut pictura, poësis erit: quae, si propius stes, Te capiat magis, etc., Hor. A. P. 361; Cic. de Or. 3, 25, 100: Anacreontis tota poësis est amatoria, id. Tusc. 4, 33, 71.

poeta.full: pŏēta, ae (POETES, Inscr. Orell. 1163), m., = ποιητής. In gen., a maker, producer (ante-class.): nec fallaciam Astutiorem ullus fecit poëta, a contriver, trickster, Plaut. Cas. 5, 1, 7: tu poëta es prorsus ad eam rem unicus, you are just fit for it, id. As. 4, 1, 3.— In partic., a poet (class.; syn. vates): visus Homerus adesse poëta, Enn. ap. Cic. Ac. 2, 16, 51 (Ann. v. 6 Vahl.); Cic. de Or. 2, 46, 194: oratores et poëtae, id. ib. 3, 10, 39: versificator quam poëta melior, Quint. 10, 1, 89: pic

poetelius.full: Poetelĭus, i, m., name of a Roman gens: M. Petelius, a consul, Liv. 9, 24.
poetelius.short: Poetelĭus, i, m., name of a Roman gens: M.

poeticus.full: pŏētĭcus, a, um, adj., = ποιητικός, poetic, poetical: verbum, Cic. de Or. 3, 38, 153: non poëtico sed quodam oratorio numero et modo, id. ib. 1, 33, 151: di, represented by the poets, id. N. D. 3, 31, 151: quadrigae, id. Q. Fr. 2, 15, 2: mella, Hor. Ep. 1, 19, 44. —Adv.: pŏētĭcē, after the manner of poets, poetically: loqui (perh. not anteAug., since the words ut poëtice loquar, Cic. Fin. 5, 4, 9, seem not to be genuine), Plin. Ep. 8, 4, 1; 2, 5, 5: poëtice vel oratorie, Quint. 9, 1, 13; Lact. 2
poeticus.short: pŏētĭcus, a, um, adj., = ποιητικός, poetic, poetical: verbum, Cic.

poetilla.full: pŏētilla, a false read. for post illum, Plaut. Truc. 2, 6, 4.

poetneum.full: Poetneum, i, n., a fortress of Athamania, Liv. 39, 25.
poetneum.short: Poetneum, i, n., a fortress of Athamania, Liv.

poetor.full: pŏētor, āri, v. dep. poëta, to be a poet, to write poetry, to poetize (ante- and postclass.): numquam poëtor nisi si podager, Enn. ap. Prisc. p. 829 P. (Sat. v. 8 Vahl.): ineptia poëtandi, Aus. Idyll. 6 praef.—In an active collat. form: priusquam poëtare incipio, Verus ap. Front. Ep. ad Caes. 2, 8 Mai.

poetria.full: pŏētrĭa, ae, f., = ποιήτρια, a poetess: fabularum poëtria, Cic. Cael. 27, 64; Ov. H. 15, 183; Mart. Cap. 8, § 809.
poetria.short: pŏētrĭa, ae, f., = ποιήτρια, a poetess: fabularum poëtria, Cic.

poetris.full: pŏētris, ĭdis or ĭdos, f., = ποιητρίς, a poetess, Pers. prol. 13 (al. poëtrias).
poetris.short: pŏētris, ĭdis or ĭdos, f., = ποιητρίς, a poetess, Pers.

pogonias.full: pōgōnĭas, ae, m., = πωγωνίας (bearded), a kind of comet, Sen. Q. N. 1, 15, 4; Plin. 2, 25, 22, § 89.
pogonias.short: pōgōnĭas, ae, m., = πωγωνίας (bearded), a kind of comet, Sen.

pogonus.full: Pogonus, i, m., a harbor in Argolis, Mel. 2, 3.
pogonus.short: Pogonus, i, m., a harbor in Argolis, Mel.

pola.full: Pola, ae, f., a maritime town of Istria, Mel. 2, 3; Plin. 3, 19, 23, § 129.
pola.short: Pola, ae, f., a maritime town of Istria, Mel.

polea.full: pōlĕa, ae, f., = πωλίον, the dung of an ass's foal, Plin. 28, 13, 57, § 200.
polea.short: pōlĕa, ae, f., = πωλίον, the dung of an ass's foal, Plin.

polemo.full: Pŏlĕmo or -mon, ōnis, m., = Πολέμων. A Grecian philosopher at Athens, a disciple of Xenocrates and teacher of Zeno and Arcesilaus, Cic. Ac. 1, 9, 34; id. de Or. 3, 18, 67; id. Fin. 4, 6, 14; Hor. S. 2, 3, 254; Val. Max. 6, 9, 1 ext.—Hence, Pŏlĕ-mōnēus, a, um, adj., Polemonian: P. Stoicus, Cic. Ac. 2, 43, 132.— A king of Pontus after Mithridates, Suet. Ner. 18; Eutr. 7, 14.—Hence, Pŏlĕmōnĭăcus, a, um, adj., Polemonian: Pontus, Aur. Vict. Caes. 15; Vop. Aur. 21 fin.; Eutr. 7, 14.

polemonia.full: pŏlĕmōnĭa, ae, f., = πολεμώνιον, Greek valerian, otherwise called philaeteria, Plin. 25, 6, 28, § 64.
polemonia.short: pŏlĕmōnĭa, ae, f., = πολεμώνιον, Greek valerian, otherwise called philaeteria, Plin.

polemoniacus.full: Pŏlĕmōnĭăcus, a, um, v. Polemo, II. B.

polenta.full: pŏlenta, ae, f. (collat. form pŏlen-tum, i, n., Cael. Aur. Tard. 3, 2; so plur.: pŏlenta, ōrum, Macr. S. 7, 15) [perh. from πάλη = pollen], peeled barley, pearl-barley: homines, qui polentam pinsitant, Plaut. As. 1, 1, 17; Cato, R. R. 168; Col. 6, 17, 18; Plin. 18, 7, 14, § 72; 24, 1, 1, § 3; 27, 8, 37, § 59; Ov. M. 5, 450; Pers. 3, 55; Vulg. Lev. 23, 14.

polentarius.full: pŏlentārĭus, a, um, adj. polenta, of or belonging to pearl-barley: crepitus, caused by eating pearl-barley, Plaut. Curc. 2, 3, 16: damnum, the loss of a mouthful of pearl-barley, App. M. 6, p. 181, 2.

polia1.full: pŏlĭa, ae, f., = πολιά, a precious stone of a gray color, otherwise unknown, Plin. 37, 11, 73, § 191.
polia1.short: pŏlĭa, ae, f., = πολιά, a precious stone of a gray color, otherwise unknown, Plin.

polia2.full: pōlīa, ae, f., = πωλεία, a stud of horses, Dig. 21, 1, 38 fin.
polia2.short: pōlīa, ae, f., = πωλεία, a stud of horses, Dig.

polimen.full: pŏlīmen, ĭnis, n. 1. polio. Polish, brightness (post-class.). baltei polimina, App. de Deo Socr. p. 54, 30.— poli-mina, um, n., the testicles, Arn. 7, 230.

polimenta.full: pŏlīmenta, ōrum, n. id., the testicles: porcina, Plaut. Men. 1, 3, 28 (dub.; Ritschl, sincipitamenta); cf. Fest. p. 234 Müll.

polindrum.full: polindrum, i, a false read. for cepolindrum, Plaut. Ps. 3, 2, 43; v. Ritschl ad h. l.

polio1.full: pŏlĭo, īvi and ĭi, ītum, 4 (imperf polibant, Verg. A. 8, 436), v. a. root par, in parēre, appārere; cf. pulcher, to smooth, furbish, polish (class.; syn.: limo, levigo). Lit.: ROGVM ASCIA NE POLITO, Fragm. XII. Tab. ap. Cic. Leg. 2, 23, 59: parietem tectorio, Col. 8, 8, 3: daedala signa, Lucr. 5, 1451: gemmas cotibus, Plin. 37, 8, 32, § 109: ligna squatinae piscis cute, id. 32, 9, 34, § 108. marmora, id. 36, 6, 9, § 52: scabritiam ferri hircorum sanguine, id. 28, 9, 41, § 148: lapis politus, Vul
polio1.short: pŏlĭo, īvi and ĭi, ītum, 4 (imperf polibant, Verg.

polio3.full: Pōlio (Pollio), ōnis, m., the name of a music-teacher, Juv. 7, 176.
polio3.short: Pōlio (Pollio), ōnis, m., the name of a music-teacher, Juv.

polion.full: pŏlĭon or -ĭum, ĭi, n., = πόλιον, a strong-smelling plant, perh. the poley-germander: Teucrium polium, Linn.; Plin. 21, 7, 21, § 44; 21, 20, 84, § 145; Scrib. Comp. 83.
polion.short: pŏlĭon or -ĭum, ĭi, n., = πόλιον, a strong-smelling plant, perh.

poliorcetes.full: Pŏlĭorcētes, ae, m., = Πολιορκητής (the besieger or stormer of cities), a surname of Demetrius, king of Macedonia (cf.: Demetrius expugnator), Plin. 7, 38, 39, § 126; Sen. Ep. 9, 15; Vitr. 10, 22; Amm. 23, 4, 10; 24, 2, 18.
poliorcetes.short: Pŏlĭorcētes, ae, m., = Πολιορκητής (the besieger or stormer of cities), a surname of Demetrius, king of Macedonia (cf.: Demetrius expugnator), Plin.

polite.full: pŏlītē, adv., v. 1. polio, P. a. fin.

polites.full: Pŏlītes, ae, m., = Πολίτης, a son of Priam, killed by Pyrrhus, Verg. A. 2, 526; 5, 564.
polites.short: Pŏlītes, ae, m., = Πολίτης, a son of Priam, killed by Pyrrhus, Verg.

politia.full: pŏlītīa, ae, f., = πολιτεία. The State, the name of one of Plato's works, Cic. Div. 1, 29, 60; 2, 27, 59.— The administration of the Commonwealth (late Lat.), Ambros. Hexaëm. 5, 15, 52; Cassiod. Var. 9, 2.

politicus.full: pŏlītĭcus, a, um, adj., = πολιτικός, of or belonging to civil polity or to the State, political, civil: libri, Cael. ap. Cic. Fam. 8, 1, 5: philosophi, Cic. de Or. 3, 28, 109: virtutes, Macr. Somn. Scip. 1, 8.
politicus.short: pŏlītĭcus, a, um, adj., = πολιτικός, of or belonging to civil polity or to the State, political, civil: libri, Cael.

politio.full: pŏlītĭo, ōnis, f. 1. polio, a smoothing, a furbishing, polishing. Lit. (post-Aug.): speculi, Vitr. 7, 3.—Of smoothing or plastering a wall, Vitr. 7, 4.— Transf., an improving, cultivating: agrorum, Cato, R. R. 136.

politor.full: pŏlītor, ōris, m. id., one who furbishes or polishes, a polisher. Lit.: gemmarum, Firm. Math. 4, 7 fin.— Transf., a cultivator, improver: agri, Cato, R. R. 5, 136; Dig. 17, 2, 52.

politorium.full: Politorĭum, ii, n., a town of Latium, the modern La Giostra, Liv. 1, 33; Plin. 3, 5, 9, § 68.
politorium.short: Politorĭum, ii, n., a town of Latium, the modern La Giostra, Liv.

politura.full: pŏlītūra, ae, f. 1. polio, a furbishing, polishing, smoothing, working at, etc. (postAug.): chartae, Plin. 13, 12, 25, § 81: marmoris, id. 36, 6, 9, § 53: gemmarum (of the vine), id. 17, 26, 39, § 246: laevitas et politura corporum, Sen. Q. N. 7, 31, 4.—Of a cobweb, Plin. 11, 24, 28, § 84.—In plur., Vitr. 7, 1.— Transf., of literary composition: videbimus quid parum recisum sit, quid non hujus recentis politurae, Sen. Ep. 100, 5.

politus.full: pŏlītus, a, um, Part. and P. a., from polio.

polla.full: Polla, ae, f. another form for Paulla, Paula, a female proper name. The wife of D. Brutus, Cic. Fam. 11, 8, 1.— The wife of the poet Lucan, Stat. S. 2, 7, 62; 82; Mart. 7, 21, 2; 7, 23, 3; 10, 64, 1.

pollen.full: pollen, ĭnis, n., and pollis, ĭnis, m. and f [πάλη]. Lit., fine flour, milldust, Cato, R. R. 156; 157; Plin. 13, 12, 26, § 82; 18, 9, 20, § 87; Ter. Ad. 5, 3, 60.— Transf., fine dust of other things: piperis, Cels. 4, 4: turis, Col. 6, 30, 6; Plin. 29, 3, 11, § 39: aliquid in pollinem tundere, id. 19, 5, 29, § 91.
pollen.short: pollen, ĭnis, n., and pollis, ĭnis, m.

pollens.full: pollens, entis, Part. and P. a., from polleo.

pollenter.full: pollenter, adv., v. polleo, P. a. fin.

pollentia1.full: pollentĭa, ae, f. polleo, might, power (ante-class.): impiorum, Plaut. Rud. 3, 2, 4; id. Cas. 4, 4, 3.—Personified, the goddess of power or of victory, Liv. 39, 7, 8.

pollentia2.full: Pollentĭa (Pōlent-), ae, f. A city in Picenum, now Monte Moline, Cic. Phil. 11, 6, 14; id. Fam. 11, 13, 3.—Hence, Pollentīni, ōrum, m., the Pollentians, Plin. 3, 13, 18, § 111.— A city in Liguria, now Pollenza, Col. 7, 2, 4; Mart. 14, 157; Sil. 8, 598.—Hence, Pollentī-nus (Pōlent-), a, um, adj., of or belonging to Pollentia, Pollentian: plebs, Suet. Tib. 37.

polleo.full: pollĕo (polet, pollet: quia nondum geminabant antiqui consonantes, Fest. p. 205 Müll.), ēre, v. n. potis-valeo. Lit. In gen., to be strong, powerful, or potent, to be able, to prevail, avail (class.; cf.: valeo, possum): QVANTO MAGIS POTES POLLESQVE, an old formula in Liv. 1, 24, 8: potest polletque (populus), Liv. 8, 33; Plaut. As. 3, 3, 46: qui plus pollet potiorque est patre, old poet ap. Cic. Tusc. 4, 32, 69: pollere, regnare, dominari, Cic. Rep. 3, 12, 21: qui in republicā tum plurimum poll
polleo.short: pollĕo (polet, pollet: quia nondum geminabant antiqui consonantes, Fest.

pollex1.full: pollex, ĭcis, m. polleo; cf.: pollex nomen ab eo, quod pollet, accepit, Atei. Cap'to ap. Macr. S. 7, 13, 11. Lit. The thumb: hominis digiti articulos habent ternos, pollex binos et digitis adversus universis flectitur, per se vero in obliquum porrigitur, crassior ceteris, huic minimus mensura par est, Plin. 11, 43, 99, § 244; Cic. Off. 3, 11, 46; Hor. Epod. 5, 48; id. C. 4, 6, 36; Ov. M. 4, 36; 8, 198; Verg. A. 11, 68.—Connected with digitus (as a measure), Cato, R. R. 20: clavi digiti pollicis

pollex2.full: Pollex, ĭcis, m., the name of a slave of Cicero, Cic. Fam. 14, 6, 1; id. Att. 8, 5, 1; 13, 47, 1.—A lusus verbb. with 1. pollex, Cic. Att. 13, 46, 1.
pollex2.short: Pollex, ĭcis, m., the name of a slave of Cicero, Cic.

pollia.full: Pollĭa trĭbus, one of the Roman tribes, Liv. 8, 37; 29, 37; Inscr. Grut. 400, 1.
pollia.short: Pollĭa trĭbus, one of the Roman tribes, Liv.

pollicaris.full: pollĭcāris, e, adj. 1. pollex, of or belonging to a thumb (post-Aug.): frutex pollicari crassitudine, of the thickness of a thumb, Plin. 13, 23, 45, § 128: latitudine, id. 15, 24, 26, § 95: amplitudine, id. 27, 9, 49, § 73.

polliceor.full: pollĭcĕor, ĭtus (act. form polliceres, Varr. Sat. Menip. 8, 5), 2, v. dep. a. and n. from an old prep. por or port (= Gr. πορτί, προτί, or πρός; cf. pro) and liceor. To hold forth, offer, promise any thing (freq. and class.; syn.: promitto, spondeo): neque minus prolixe de tuā voluntate promisi, quam eram solitus de meā polliceri, Cic. Fam. 7, 5, 1; id. Planc. 42, 101; cf.: alicui studium, id. Fam. 5, 8, 4; cf.: mirandum in modum profitentur, offerunt se, pollicentur, id. Q. Fr. 1, 2, 5: id omne

pollicitatio.full: pollĭcĭtātĭo, ōnis, f. pollicitor, a promising, a promise (class. but not in Cic., who uses promissio, promissum; usu. plur.): vereor ne istaec pollicitatio Te in crimen populo ponat, Plaut. Trin. 3, 3, 10: hinc pollicitationes aufer, Ter. Phorm. 5, 6, 18: huic magnis praemiis pollicitationibusque persuadet, ut, etc., Caes. B. G. 3, 18; 3, 26; 7, 1; id. B. C. 3, 108; Sall. J. 61, 4; Sen. Ben. 3, 19, 3; Plin. Ep. 10, 33, 3; Auct. B. Afr. 35; Dig. 50, 12, 1 sqq.—In sing.: cum (legionem) ad se arce

pollicitator.full: pollĭcĭtātor, ōris, m. id., a promiser (eccl. Lat.), Tert. adv. Jud. 1.

pollicitatrix.full: pollĭcĭtātrix, īcis, f. pollicitator, she that promises (eccl. Lat.), Tert. Apol. 23.

pollicitor.full: pollĭcĭtor, ātus, 1, v. freq. a. and n. polliceor, to promise (mostly ante- and post-class.; not in Cic. or Cæs.): pro capite argentum, Plaut. Rud. 4, 2, 24: operam suam alicui, id. Mil. 3, 3, 6; Dig. 50, 12, 6. —Absol.: ego te complures menses tuli Pollicitantem, nihil ferentem, Ter. Phorm. 3, 2, 36: sollicitando et pollicitando, id. And. 5, 4, 9: largiundo atque pollicitando magis incendere, Sall. C. 38, 1; id. J. 8, 1.

pollicitum.full: pollĭcĭtum, i, n., v. polliceor fin.

pollicitus.full: pollĭcĭtus, a, um, Part., from polliceor.
pollicitus.short: pollĭcĭtus, a, um, Part., from polliceor.

pollinaris.full: pollĭnāris, e, adj. pollen, of or belonging to fine flour, flour-, meal-: pollinare cribrum, γυριστήριον κόσκινον, Gloss. Cyril.; v. pollinarius.

pollinarius.full: pollĭnārĭus, a, um, adj. id., of or belonging to fine flour, flour-, meal-: cribrum, a bolting-sieve, Plaut. Poen. 3, 1, 10; Plin. 18, 11, 28, § 108.

pollinctor.full: pollinctor (or pollictor), ōris, m. pollingo, one who washes corpses and prepares them for burning, an undertaker: pollinctores sunt, qui mortuos curant, Non. 157, 20; cf.: pollinctores dicti sunt, qui funera morientium accurant, Fulg. p. 559, 9; Plaut. Poen. prol. 63; id. As. 5, 2, 60; Varr. ap. Non. 157, 21 sq.; Mart. 10, 97, 3; Dig. 14, 3, 5; Sid. Ep. 3, 13; of buriers, Vulg. Ezech. 39, 15.

pollinctus.full: pollinctus, a, um, Part., from pollingo.
pollinctus.short: pollinctus, a, um, Part., from pollingo.

pollingo.full: pollingo, nxi, nctum, 3, v. a., to wash a corpse, and prepare it for the funeral pile (ante- and post-class.): pollingo, περιστέλλω νεκρόν, σιροπλόκω, ταριχεύω, ἐνταφιάζω, Gloss. Philox.: quia mihi pollinctor dixit, qui eum pollinxerat, Plaut. Poen. prol. 63; App. Flor. p. 362, 27: figmenta hominum mortuorum curate pollincta, Amm. 19, 1, 10.—Transf., of an old man near his grave: pollinctum corpus, Val. Max. 7, 7, 4; cf.: voluptas fucata aut medicamentis pollincta, Sen. Vit. Beat. 7, 2.

pollio1.full: pollĭo, īre: pollit, pila ludit, Paul. ex Fest. p. 243 Müll.
pollio1.short: pollĭo, īre: pollit, pila ludit, Paul.

pollio2.full: Pollĭo (Pōlĭo, v. Lucr. p. 33 Lachm.), ōnis, m., a Roman surname. So esp., Asinius Pollio, v. Asinius.— Trebellius Pollio, v. Trebellius.— The name of a bad actor, Plaut. Bacch. 2, 2, 37. — v. Polio.

pollubrum.full: pollūbrum (pōlūbr-), i, n. polluo, a wash-basin, laver: polubrum pelluvium vas, quod nos pelvem vocamus, Paul. ex Fest. p. 247 Müll.: polubrum quod Graeci χέρνιβα, nos trulleum vocamus. Livius: argenteo polubro (acc. to Hom. Od. 1, 136); Fabius Pictor, lib. xvi.: polubrum sinistrā manu teneto, Non. 544, 22 sq.

polluceo.full: pollūcĕo, xi, ctum, 2, v. a. old prep. port = Gr. προτί, πρός, and liceor; root licof linquo; Gr. λειπω; cf. licet. Lit., in relig. lang., to place upon the altar as a sacrifice to the deity, to offer, offer up: Jovi dapali culignam vini quantumvis polluceto ... cum pollucere oportebit, sic facies, etc., Cato, R. R. 132: polluxi tibi iam publicando epulo Herculis decumas, Naev. ap. Prisc. p. 874 P. (Com. Rel. p. 9 Rib.): decumam partem Herculi, Plaut. Stich. 1, 3, 80: pisces, Cass. Hem. ap. Plin

pollucibilis.full: pollūcĭbĭlis, e, adj. polluceo, bountifully distributed; hence, in gen., sumptuous, rich, magnificent (post-class.): cena, Macr. S. 2, 13 fin.: victus, Symm. Ep. 6, 71. —Comp.: obsonandi pollucibilior, Tert. Jejun. 17.—Adv.: pollūcĭbĭlĭter, sumptuously, magnificently (ante-class.): obsonate, Plaut. Most. 1, 1, 23: pergraecamini, id. Fragm. ap. Fulg. Myth. 1, 2.

pollucibilitas.full: pollūcĭbĭlĭtas, ātis, f. pollucibilis, magnificence, excellence, Fulg. Myth. 1, 2.

pollucte.full: polluctē, adv., and polluctum, i, n., v. polluceo fin.
pollucte.short: polluctē, adv., and polluctum, i, n., v.

polluctura.full: polluctūra, ae, f. polluceo, a sumptuous entertainment, a feast, banquet, Plaut. Stich. 5, 4, 6.

polluctus.full: polluctus, a, um, Part., from polluceo.
polluctus.short: polluctus, a, um, Part., from polluceo.

polluo.full: pollŭo, ŭi, ūtum, 3, v. a. cf.: adluo, diluo; Gr. λούω, to wash; λῦμα, λύμη, λυμαίνω, to cleanse, ruin, to soil, defile, pollute. Lit. (very rare): ore dapes, Verg. A. 3, 234: ora cruore, Ov. M. 15, 98: pollui cuncta sanie, odore, contactu, Tac. A. 4, 49: usu tegmina, id. ib. 13, 57: vina deciduo immundiore lapsu, Plin. 14, 19, 23, § 119: polluta mensa cruore, Sil. 7, 183.— Trop. In gen., to defile morally, to pollute, contaminate, violate, dishonor, desecrate, etc. (class.; syn.: inquino, conta

pollutio.full: pollūtĭo, ōnis, f. polluo, defilement, contamination, pollution, Pall. 9, 10: peccati, Vulg. Judith, 13, 20.

pollutrix.full: pollūtrix, īcis, f. id., a polluter (late Lat.), Jul. ap. Aug. c. Sec. Resp. Jul. 6, 5.

pollux.full: Pollux, ūcis (collat. form of nom. Pol-lūces, Plaut. Bacch. 4, 8, 53; cf. Varr. L. L. 5, § 73 Müll.—Voc. pol, edepol, v. infra), m., = Πολυδεύκης, a famous pugilist, son of Tyndarus and Leda, and brother of Castor, in connection with whom, as the constellation of the Twins (Gemini, v. 2. Castor), he serves as a guide to mariners, Cic. N. D. 3, 21, 53; id. Leg. 2, 8, 19; Hyg. Fab. 14; 173: ita me ... Castor, Polluces ... dique omnes ament, Plaut. Bacch. 4, 8, 53; Aug. Civ. Dei, 4, 27.—Poet.: gemi

polose.full: pŏlōsē, adv. polus, going through the poles (post-class.): obliqua decussata polose, Mart. Cap. 1, § 37 (al. oblique decussatos polos).

polteo.full: poltĕo, pro ulteriore, Fest. p. 205 Müll.

polulus.full: pōlŭlus (poll-), a, um, adj. a rustic form for paululus, little (only in the two foll. pass.): labellum, Cato, R. R. 10, 2: sublaminae, id. ib. 21, 3.

polus1.full: pŏlus, i, m., = πόλος. Lit., the end of an axis, a pole (poet. and postAug.): terra a verticibus duobus, quos appellaverunt polos, centrum caeli est, nec non Signiferi oblique inter eos siti, Plin. 2, 15, 13, § 63; 2, 70, 71, § 179; Ov. M. 2, 75; id. P. 2, 7, 64: polus glacialis, the north pole, id. M. 2, 173; or, gelidus, id. H. 18, 152; also absol., the north pole, id. Tr. 4, 3, 15: polus australis, id. M. 2, 131; or, austrinus, the south pole, Plin. 5, 9, 10, § 56.— Transf. The polar star, Vi

polus2.full: Pŏlus, i, m., a celebrated Greek tragic actor, Gell. 7, 5, 2.
polus2.short: Pŏlus, i, m., a celebrated Greek tragic actor, Gell.

polusca.full: Polusca, ae, f., a small and very ancient town in Latium, Liv. 2, 33; 39; cf. Mann. Ital. 1, p. 645.
polusca.short: Polusca, ae, f., a small and very ancient town in Latium, Liv.

polyacanthos.full: pŏlўăcanthos, i, m., = πολυάκανθος, a kind of thistle, Plin. 21, 16, 56, § 94.
polyacanthos.short: pŏlўăcanthos, i, m., = πολυάκανθος, a kind of thistle, Plin.

polyaegos.full: Pŏlўaegos, i, f., = Πολύαιγος, an island of the Ægean Sea, Mel. 2, 7; Plin. 4, 12, 23, § 70.
polyaegos.short: Pŏlўaegos, i, f., = Πολύαιγος, an island of the Ægean Sea, Mel.

polyaenus.full: Pŏlўaenus, i, m., = Πολύαινος, a mathematician, a friend and follower of Epicurus, Cic. Fin. 1, 6, 20; id. Ac. 2, 33, 106.
polyaenus.short: Pŏlўaenus, i, m., = Πολύαινος, a mathematician, a friend and follower of Epicurus, Cic.

polyandrion.full: pŏlўandrĭon, ĭi, n., = πολυάνδριον, a common burial-place, graveyard, cemetery, Lact. Epit. 72, 17; Arn. 6, p. 194.
polyandrion.short: pŏlўandrĭon, ĭi, n., = πολυάνδριον, a common burial-place, graveyard, cemetery, Lact.

polyanthemum.full: pŏlўanthĕmum, i, n., = πολυάνθεμον (pure Lat. ranunculus), a caustic plant, otherwise called batrachion (perh. Ranunculus polyanthemos, Linn., many-flowered, crowfoot), Plin. 27, 12, 90, § 112.

polyarchion.full: pŏlўarchĭon (-cўon), i, n., = πολυαρχίον, a kind of soothing ointment, Cael. Aur. Acut. 2, 24, 136.
polyarchion.short: pŏlўarchĭon (-cўon), i, n., = πολυαρχίον, a kind of soothing ointment, Cael.

polybe.full: Polўbē, ēs, f., one of the fifty daughters of Danaüs, Hyg. Fab. 170.
polybe.short: Polўbē, ēs, f., one of the fifty daughters of Danaüs, Hyg.

polybius.full: Pŏlўbĭus, ii, m., = Πολύβιος, a celebrated Greek historian from Megalopolis, in Arcadia, the son of Lycortas and friend of the younger Scipio Africanus, Cic. Rep. 1, 21, 34; 2, 14, 27; 4, 3, 3; id. Off. 3, 32, 113; Liv. 30, 45.
polybius.short: Pŏlўbĭus, ii, m., = Πολύβιος, a celebrated Greek historian from Megalopolis, in Arcadia, the son of Lycortas and friend of the younger Scipio Africanus, Cic.

polybus.full: Pŏlўbus, i, m., = Πόλυβος. A king of Corinth, at whose court Œdipus was brought up, Stat. Th. 1, 64; Hyg. Fab. 66; 67; Sen. Oedip. 12.— One of Penelope's suitors, Ov. H. 1, 91.

polycarpos.full: pŏlўcarpos, i, f., = πολύκαρπος, a plant, also called polygonus, App. Herb. 18.
polycarpos.short: pŏlўcarpos, i, f., = πολύκαρπος, a plant, also called polygonus, App.

polychronius.full: pŏlychrŏnĭus, a, um, adj., = πολυχρόνιος, long-lived (late Lat.), Firm. Math. 8, 28 med.
polychronius.short: pŏlychrŏnĭus, a, um, adj., = πολυχρόνιος, long-lived (late Lat.), Firm.

polyclitus.full: Pŏlўclītus (Pŏlŭ-, -ētus) (ĕ scanned short, Prud. στεφ. 10, 269), i, m., = Πολύκλειτος, a celebrated Grecian sculptor from Argos or Sicyon, contemporary with Pericles.—Form Polyclitus, Plin. 34, 8, 19 § 55; Cic. Brut. 18, 70; 86, 296; id. de Or. 2, 16, 70; 3, 7, 26; Juv. 8, 103; Mart. 8, 51, 2. —Form POLYCLETVS, Inscr. Orell. 3245.— Hence, Pŏlyclētēus (-īus), a, um, adj., Polycletean: caelum, Auct. Her. 4, 6, 9; Stat. S. 2, 2, 67.

polycnemon.full: pŏlycnēmon, i, n., = πολύκνημον, a plant, otherwise unknown, Plin. 26, 14, 88, § 148.
polycnemon.short: pŏlycnēmon, i, n., = πολύκνημον, a plant, otherwise unknown, Plin.

polycrates.full: Pŏlycrătes, is, m., = Πολυκράτης, a prince of Samos, and friend of Amasis, celebrated for his good fortune, but at last crucified by the Persian governor Orœtes, Cic. Fin. 5, 30, 92; Val. Max. 6, 9, 5 ext.— Gr. acc. in -en, Quint. 2, 17, 4.
polycrates.short: Pŏlycrătes, is, m., = Πολυκράτης, a prince of Samos, and friend of Amasis, celebrated for his good fortune, but at last crucified by the Persian governor Orœtes, Cic.

polycratia.full: Pŏlycrătĭa, ae, f., wife of the Achœan chief Aratus, Liv. 27, 31.
polycratia.short: Pŏlycrătĭa, ae, f., wife of the Achœan chief Aratus, Liv.

polydaemon.full: Pŏlўdaemon, ŏnis, m., a descendant of Semiramis, slain by Perseus, Ov. M. 5, 85.
polydaemon.short: Pŏlўdaemon, ŏnis, m., a descendant of Semiramis, slain by Perseus, Ov.

polydamas.full: Pō^lўdămas (the o made long by the requirements of the verse), antis, m., = Πολυδάμας. A Trojan, son of Panthous and friend of Hector, Ov. M. 12, 547; id. H. 5, 94.—Hence, Pō^lўdămantēus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Polydamas: arma, Sil. 12, 212.— A famous athlete, Val. Max. 9, 12, 10 ext.
polydamas.short: Pō^lўdămas (the o made long by the requirements of the verse), antis, m., = Πολυδάμας.

polydectes.full: Pŏlўdectes or -ta, ae, m., = Πολυδέκτης, a king of Seriphus, who brought up Perseus, Ov. M. 5, 242; Hyg. Fab. 273; id. Astr. 2, 12.
polydectes.short: Pŏlўdectes or -ta, ae, m., = Πολυδέκτης, a king of Seriphus, who brought up Perseus, Ov.

polydector.full: Pŏlўdector, ŏris, m., one of the fifty sons of Ægyptus, Hyg. Fab. 170.
polydector.short: Pŏlўdector, ŏris, m., one of the fifty sons of Ægyptus, Hyg.

polydorus.full: Pŏlўdōrus, i, m., = Πολύδωρος, a son of Priam and Hecuba, killed by the Thracian Polymnestor, Cic. poët. de Or. 3, 58, 219; Verg. A. 3, 45 Serv.; Ov. M. 13, 432 sq. —Hence, Pŏlўdōrēus, a, um, adj., of Polydorus, Polydorean: sanguis, Ov. M. 13, 629.
polydorus.short: Pŏlўdōrus, i, m., = Πολύδωρος, a son of Priam and Hecuba, killed by the Thracian Polymnestor, Cic.

polygala.full: pŏlўgăla, ae, f., = πολύγαλον, the herb milkwort, Plin. 27, 12, 96, § 121.
polygala.short: pŏlўgăla, ae, f., = πολύγαλον, the herb milkwort, Plin.

polygnotus.full: Pŏlygnōtus, i, m., = Πολύγνωτος, a celebrated Grecian painter and statuary of Thasus, contemporary with Socrates, Plin. 35, 6, 25; Cic. Brut. 18, 70.
polygnotus.short: Pŏlygnōtus, i, m., = Πολύγνωτος, a celebrated Grecian painter and statuary of Thasus, contemporary with Socrates, Plin.

polygonaton.full: pŏlўgŏnăton, i, n., = πολυγόνατον. The plant called Solomon's seal: Convallaria polygonatum (Linn.), Plin. 27, 12, 91, § 113.— Another name for leucacantha, Plin. 22, 17, 18, § 40.

polygonius.full: pŏlygōnĭus, a, um, adj., = πολυγώνιος, having many angles, polygonal: turres, Vitr. 1, 5.
polygonius.short: pŏlygōnĭus, a, um, adj., = πολυγώνιος, having many angles, polygonal: turres, Vitr.

polygonoides.full: pŏlўgŏnŏīdes, is, f., = πολυγονοειδής, a species of the plant clematis, Plin. 24, 15, 90, § 141.
polygonoides.short: pŏlўgŏnŏīdes, is, f., = πολυγονοειδής, a species of the plant clematis, Plin.

polygonos.full: pŏlўgŏnos or -us, i, f., or pŏlў-gŏnon, i (pŏlўgŏnĭum, ĭi, Scrib. Comp. 193), n., = πολύγονος or -ον, a plant (called in pure Lat. herba sanguinalis or sanguinaria), knotgrass, Plin. 27, 12, 91, § 113; 26, 15, 90, § 158.
polygonos.short: pŏlўgŏnos or -us, i, f., or pŏlў-gŏnon, i (pŏlўgŏnĭum, ĭi, Scrib.

polygonum.full: pŏlўgōnum, i, n., = πολύγωνον, a polygon, Censor. de Die Nat. 8 med.
polygonum.short: pŏlўgōnum, i, n., = πολύγωνον, a polygon, Censor.

polygrammos.full: pŏlygrammos, i, f., = πολύγραμμος, a sort of jasper, with many white streaks, Plin. 37, 9, 37, § 118.
polygrammos.short: pŏlygrammos, i, f., = πολύγραμμος, a sort of jasper, with many white streaks, Plin.

polygynaecon.full: pŏlўgўnaecon, i, a false reading for syngenicon, Plin. 35, 11, 40, § 134; v. Sillig ad h. l.
polygynaecon.short: pŏlўgўnaecon, i, a false reading for syngenicon, Plin.

polyhistor.full: Pŏlўhistor, ŏris, m., = Πολυίστωρ (the much-knowing or learned man). The title of the natural history written by C. Julius Solinus.— A surname of the grammarian Cornelius Alexander, Suet. Gram. 20; Plin. 9, 35, 56, § 115.
polyhistor.short: Pŏlўhistor, ŏris, m., = Πολυίστωρ (the much-knowing or learned man).

polyhymnia.full: Pŏlўhymnĭa (Pŏlymnĭa, Poët. ap. Anth. Lat. 1, p. 51 Burm.), ae, f., = Πολυμνία (she of many hymns), one of the Muses, Hor. C. 1, 1, 33; Ov. F. 5, 9; Mart. 4, 31, 7; Aus. Idyll. 20.

polyidus.full: Pŏlўĭdus, i, m., = Πολύϊδος, a soothsayer, native of Corinth, Cic. Div. 1, 40, 89; id. Leg. 2, 13, 33.
polyidus.short: Pŏlўĭdus, i, m., = Πολύϊδος, a soothsayer, native of Corinth, Cic.

polymachaeroplagides.full: Pŏlўmăchaerŏplăgĭdes, ae, m. πολύσ-μάχαιρα-plaga, a fictitious name of a soldier, Plaut. Ps. 4, 2, 31.

polymitarius.full: pŏlўmĭtārĭus, a, um, polymitus, of damask, highly wrought or finished: opus, Vulg. Exod. 36, 35.—Hence, subst.: pŏlў-mĭtārĭus, ii, m., a damask-weaver, Ven. Carm. 5, 6 praef.; Vulg. Exod. 35, 35; 38, 23.
polymitarius.short: pŏlўmĭtārĭus, a, um, polymitus, of damask, highly wrought or finished: opus, Vulg.

polymitus.full: pŏlўmĭtus, a, um, adj., = πολύμιτος, wrought with many treads: alicula, Petr. 40: ars, the art of weaving, Hier. Ep. 64, 12: tunica, Vulg. Gen. 37, 3.—Subst.: pŏlў-mĭta, ōrum, n., damask, Plin. 8, 48, 74, § 198; also sing. pŏlўmĭtum, i, Vulg. Ezech. 16, 13.
polymitus.short: pŏlўmĭtus, a, um, adj., = πολύμιτος, wrought with many treads: alicula, Petr.

polymnestor.full: Pŏlymnēstor and Pŏlўmēstor, ŏris, m., = Πολυμνήστωρ and Πολυμήστωρ, a king of Thrace, the husband of Ilione, daughter of Priam; he killed his brotherin-law Polydorus, who had been intrusted to his charge, Ov. M. 13, 536; Hyg. Fab. 109; Mythogr. Lat. 2, 209; Serv. Verg. A. 3, 6; 3, 15.
polymnestor.short: Pŏlymnēstor and Pŏlўmēstor, ŏris, m., = Πολυμνήστωρ and Πολυμήστωρ, a king of Thrace, the husband of Ilione, daughter of Priam;

polymyxos.full: pŏlўmyxos, i, adj. f., = πολύμυξος, having many wicks: lucerna, Mart. 14, 41 in lemm.

polyneuron.full: pŏlўneuron, i, n., = πολύνευρον, a plant (pure Lat. plantago major), great plantain, App. Herb. 1.
polyneuron.short: pŏlўneuron, i, n., = πολύνευρον, a plant (pure Lat.

polynices.full: Pŏlȳnīces, is, m., = Πολυνείκης, son of Œdipus and Jocasta, brother of Eteocles, and son-in-law of Adrastus, Stat. Th. 7, 689; Hyg. Fab. 68; 72; Quint. 5, 10, 31; Plin. 35, 11, 40, § 144.
polynices.short: Pŏlȳnīces, is, m., = Πολυνείκης, son of Œdipus and Jocasta, brother of Eteocles, and son-in-law of Adrastus, Stat.

polyonymos.full: pŏlўōnўmos, i, f., = πολυώνυμος, a plant (pure Lat. perdicium), parietary, App. Herb. 81.
polyonymos.short: pŏlўōnўmos, i, f., = πολυώνυμος, a plant (pure Lat.

polyphagus.full: pŏlўphăgus, i, m., = πολυφάγος, a glutton, gormandizer, Suet. Ner. 37.
polyphagus.short: pŏlўphăgus, i, m., = πολυφάγος, a glutton, gormandizer, Suet.

polyphemus.full: Pŏlўphēmus (-os), i, m., = Πολύφημος. The one-eyed Cyclops in Sicily, son of Neptune, who was blinded by Ulysses, Cic. Tusc. 5, 39, 115; Ov. M. 13, 772; 14, 167; Mart. 4, 49, 6; Juv. 14, 20; 9, 64; Hyg. Fab. 125; cf. Verg. A. 3, 618 sq.— One of the Argonauts, Hyg. Fab. 14.

polyplusius.full: Pŏlўplūsĭus, a, adj., = πολυπλούσιος (very rich), a fictitious name of a gens, Plaut. Capt. 2, 2, 27.
polyplusius.short: Pŏlўplūsĭus, a, adj., = πολυπλούσιος (very rich), a fictitious name of a gens, Plaut.

polypodium.full: pŏlўpŏdĭum (-ĭon), ii, n., = πολυπόδιον, a kind of fern, polypody, Plin. 16, 44, 92, § 244; 26, 12, 75, § 122.
polypodium.short: pŏlўpŏdĭum (-ĭon), ii, n., = πολυπόδιον, a kind of fern, polypody, Plin.

polyposus.full: pŏlўpōsus, a, um, adj. polypus, having a polypus in the nose, Mart. 12, 37, 2; Dig. 21, 1, 12.

polyptoton.full: pŏlyptōton, i, n., = πολύπτωτον, a figure of speech, when several cases of the same word stand together, as homo homini, Mart. Cap. 5, § 535.
polyptoton.short: pŏlyptōton, i, n., = πολύπτωτον, a figure of speech, when several cases of the same word stand together, as homo homini, Mart.

polyptycha.full: pŏlyptўcha, ōrum, n., = πολύπτυχα (that has many folds or leaves), accountbooks, registers (post-class.), Veg. Mil. 2, 19; Cod. Th. 1, 26, 2; 1, 28, 13.
polyptycha.short: pŏlyptўcha, ōrum, n., = πολύπτυχα (that has many folds or leaves), accountbooks, registers (post-class.), Veg.

polypus.full: pō^lўpŭs, i, m. (fem., Lucil. ap. Non. 220, 4), = πολύπους (many-footed; Dor. and Æol. πωλύπος), a polypus. An aquatic animal, sea-polypus: Sepia octopodia, Linn.: piscis polypus, Plaut. Rud. 4, 3, 71; Plin. 9, 12, 14, § 40; 9, 19, 35, § 71 al. (Jahn, polybi); Lucil. l. l.; Enn. ap. App. Mag. p. 299 (Heduph. v. 10 Vahl.); Ov. M. 4, 366; id. Hal. 31 (with the o long).—Transf., of rapacious men, Plaut. Aul. 2, 2, 21.— A polypus in the nose, Cels. 6, 8, 2; 6, 7, 10; Plin. 24, 16, 92, § 146; Hor. S.

polyrrhizos.full: pŏlyrrhīzos, on, adj., = πολύρριζος. Having many roots, an appellation of several plants, Plin. 25, 8, 54, §§ 96, 98 al.— Subst.: pŏlyrrhīzon, i, n., a plant, otherwise unknown, Plin. 27, 12, 103, § 126.

polysemus.full: pŏlўsēmus, a, um, adj., = πολύσημος, having many significations (postclass.): sermo, Serv. Verg. A. 1, 1.
polysemus.short: pŏlўsēmus, a, um, adj., = πολύσημος, having many significations (postclass.): sermo, Serv.

polysigma.full: pŏlўsigma πολύ-σίγμα, a too frequent repetition of the letter s: ubi s littera crebrius geminatur: Sosia in Solario soleas sarciebat suas, Mart. Cap. 5, § 514.
polysigma.short: pŏlўsigma πολύ-σίγμα, a too frequent repetition of the letter s: ubi s littera crebrius geminatur: Sosia in Solario soleas sarciebat suas, Mart.

polyspaston.full: pŏlyspaston, i, n., = πολύσπαστον, a hoisting-tackle with many pulleys, Vitr. 10, 5, and 16.
polyspaston.short: pŏlyspaston, i, n., = πολύσπαστον, a hoisting-tackle with many pulleys, Vitr.

polytimetus.full: Pŏlўtīmētus, i, m., a river of Sogdiana, now Koi, near Bokhara, Curt. 7, 10, 2.
polytimetus.short: Pŏlўtīmētus, i, m., a river of Sogdiana, now Koi, near Bokhara, Curt.

polytrichon.full: pŏlўtrĭchon, i, n., = πολύτριχον. The herb golden-hair, Venus's-hair, Plin. 22, 21, 30, § 63; called also pŏlythrix, trĭchos, f., πολύθριξ, Plin. 26, 14, 87, § 147. — A precious stone, otherwise unknown, Plin. 37, 11, 73, § 190.

polyxena.full: Pŏlyxĕna, ae, f., = Πολυξένη, a daughter of Priam, whom Pyrrhus, the son of Achilles, sacrificed at his father's grave, Ov. M. 13, 448; Juv. 10, 262; Sen. Troad. 368; Hyg. Fab. 110; cf. Verg. A. 3, 321.— Hence, Pŏlyxĕnĭus, a, um, adj., of Polyxena, Polyxenian: caedes, Cat. 64, 369.
polyxena.short: Pŏlyxĕna, ae, f., = Πολυξένη, a daughter of Priam, whom Pyrrhus, the son of Achilles, sacrificed at his father's grave, Ov.

polyxo.full: Pŏlyxo, ūs, f., = Πολυξώ. A prophetess in Lemnos, Stat. Th. 5, 90 sq.; Val. Fl. 2, 316 sq.— One of the Hyades, Hyg. Fab. 191.

polyzonos.full: pŏlyzōnos, i, f., = πολύζωνος, a kind of black precious stone with many stripes, otherwise unknown, Plin. 37, 11, 73, § 189.
polyzonos.short: pŏlyzōnos, i, f., = πολύζωνος, a kind of black precious stone with many stripes, otherwise unknown, Plin.

pomarius.full: pōmārĭus, a, um, adj. pomum, of or belonging to fruit or fruit-trees, fruit-: seminarium, Cato, R. R. 48.— Subst. pōmārĭus, ii, m., a fruit-seller, fruiterer, Hor. S. 2, 3, 227; Lampr. Elag. 27; Inscr. Grut. 651, 11.— pōmārĭum, ii, n. A fruit-garden, orchard, Varr. R. R. 1, 2, 6; Col. 5, 10; id. Arb. 8; Cic. Sen. 15, 54; Sen. Ep. 122, 8; Hor. C. 1, 7, 14; Ov. de Nuce, 111; Vulg. Dan. 13, 4.— A store-room for fruit, a fruit-loft, fruitery, Varr. R. R. 1, 2; Plin. 15, 16, 18, § 59 (acc. to Charis.

pomeridianus.full: pōmĕrīdĭānus (postm-), a, um, adj. post-meridianus, in the afternoon, post-meridian: impetratum est a consuetudine, ut peccare suavitatis causā liceret, et pomeridianus quadrigas quam postmeridianus libentius dixerim, Cic. Or. 47, 157: pomeridianum tempus, id. de Or. 3, 5, 17; also: postmeridianum tempus, id. Tusc. 3, 3, 7: dies, Sen. Ep. 7, 3, 1: horae, Suet. Gram. 24: gnomonis umbra, Vitr. 1, 6: pomeridiana sessio (opp. ambulatio antemeridiana), Cic. de Or. 3, 30, 121: litterae, id. Att. 12, 5

pomerium.full: pōmērĭum and pōmoerĭum (the first is most freq. in inscrr., the latter in MSS.; but the better manuscripts have also, Varr. R. R. 1, 2, 13, and Tac. A. 12, 23 and 24, pomerium. A third form, post-moerium, Varr. L. L. 5, § 143 Müll., seems merely to have been assumed from the etymology; a fourth archaic form is posi-merium, pontificale pomoerium, qui auspicato olim quidem omnem urbem ambiebat praeter Aventinum ... estque prosimerium quasi proxi-murium, pontifices auspicabantur, Paul. ex Fest. p.
pomerium.short: pōmērĭum and pōmoerĭum (the first is most freq.

pometia.full: Pōmētĭa, ae, f. (collat. form Pōmē tii, ōrum, m., Verg. A. 6, 775), a very old town of the Volsci, in Latium, also called Suessa Pometia; perh. the mod. Torre Petrara or Mesa, Cic. Rep. 2, 24, 45; Liv. 1, 53; 2, 16; 2, 25 al.—Hence, Pōmētīnus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Pometia, Pometian: manubiae, Liv. 1, 55.

pometum.full: pōmētum, i, n. pomus, a place planted with fruit-trees, an orchard (post-class. for pomarium), Pall. 1, 36, 3.

pomifer.full: pōmĭfer, ĕra, ĕrum, adj. pomum-fero, fruit-bearing, fruit-bringing (poet. and in post-Aug. prose): arbor, Plin. 12, 3, 7, § 15; Mel. 2, 2, 1: rami, Sen. Herc. Fur. 700: auctumnus, Hor. C. 4, 7, 11: annus, id. ib. 3, 23, 8: lignum, tree, Vulg. Gen. 1, 11: SVLVANVS, Inscr. Murat. 70, 6.—Hence, subst.: pōmĭ-ferae, ārum, f., fruit-trees, Plin. 17, 27, 43, § 253.

pomona.full: Pōmōna, ae, f. pomum. The goddess of fruit and fruit-trees, Pomona, Varr. L. L. 7, § 45 Müll.; Ov. M. 14, 623; Serv. Verg. A. 7, 190; Arn. 3, p. 118.— Transf., fruit-trees, fruit (post-Aug.), Plin. 23 prooem. 1, § 1: Thyle larga et diutina Pomona copiosa est, Sol. 22 med.— Derivv. † Pōmōnal, ālis, n., the temple of Pomona, Fest. p. 250 Müll.— Pōmōnālis, e, adj., of or belonging to Pomona, Pomonal: flamen, Varr. L. L. 7, § 45 Müll.; cf. Fest. s. v. maximae dignationis, pp. 154 and 155 Müll.

pomosus.full: pōmōsus, a, um, adj. id., full of or abounding in fruit (poet.): horti, Tib. 1, 1, 21 (25): arva, Prop. 4 (5), 7, 81. cf.: pomosi Tiburis arva, Col. poët. 10, 138: corona, a chaplet of fruits, Prop. 4 (5), 2, 17.

pompa.full: pompa, ae, f., = πομπή, a solemn procession, a public procession of any kind (at public festivals, games, triumphs, marriages, funerals, etc.). Lit. In gen.: in pompā cum magna vis auri argentique ferretur, Cic. Tusc. 5, 32, 91: per Dionysia pompam ducere, Plaut. Cist. 1, 1, 92: sollemnes ordine pompas Exequi, Verg. A. 5, 53: sollemnes ducere pompas Ad delubra juvat, id. G. 3, 22: Pontico triumpho inter pompae fercula trium verborum protulit titulum: veni, vidi, vici, Suet. Caes. 37; so, pompa I
pompa.short: pompa, ae, f., = πομπή, a solemn procession, a public procession of any kind (at public festivals, games, triumphs, marriages, funerals, etc.).

pompabilis.full: pompābĭlis, e, adj. pompa, pompous, splendid (post-class.); comp.: nihil pompabilius, Treb. XXX. Tyrann. 30.

pompalis.full: pompālis, e, adj. pompa, showy, pompous, splendid (post-class.): vultus, Capitol. Gord. 6.—Adv.: pompālĭter, splendidly, pompously, etc.: ornatus, Treb. Gallien. 8 (al. pompabiliter).

pompalitas.full: pompālĭtas, ātis, f. pompalis, splendor, brilliancy of style (post-class.), Prisc. p. 1320 P.

pompaticus.full: pompātĭcus, a, um, adj. pompa, showy, pompous, splendid (post-class.): femina, Tert. Cult. Fem. 9: genus vehiculi, for state occasions, Isid. 20, 12, 3.—Hence, adv.: pompātĭcē, with display, pompously, Vulg. Amos, 6, 1; Jul. Vict. Rhet. 10, p. 233: favor, App. M. 10, p. 253, 11.

pompatilis.full: pompātĭlis, e, adj., = pompalis (eccl. Lat.): fastus, Aug. Alterc. Eccl. et Synag. p. 1132.

pompejanus.full: Pompējānus, a, um, v. Pompeji, II., and Pompejus, B.

pompeji.full: Pompēji, ōrum, m., a maritime city in the south of Campania, overwhelmed, together with Herculaneum and Stabiœ, by an eruption of Vesuvius, A. D. 79, Mel. 2, 4, 9; Liv. 9, 38; Sen. Q. N. 6, 1, 1.—Hence, Pompējānus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Pompeii, Pompeian: regio, Sen. Q. N. 6, 27, 1: Sarnus, Stat. S. 1, 2, 265: vinum, Plin. 14, 6, 8, § 70: brassica, id. 19, 8, 41, § 140.— Subst. Pom-pējānum, i, n., a villa of Cicero, near Pompeii, Cic. Fam. 7, 3, 1; 7, 4 al.— Pompējāni, ōrum, m., the in
pompeji.short: Pompēji, ōrum, m., a maritime city in the south of Campania, overwhelmed, together with Herculaneum and Stabiœ, by an eruption of Vesuvius, A.

pompejopolis.full: Pompējŏpŏlis, is, f. A city of Cilicia, formerly called Soli, now Mezetli, Mel. 1, 13, 2; Plin. 5, 27, 22, § 92; Tac. A. 2, 58.— A city of Paphlagonia, now Tash Kupri, Plin. 6, 2, 2, § 7.

pompejus.full: Pompējus (trisyl.) or Pompēïus (quadrisyl.), i, m., and Pompēja, ae, f., name of a Roman gens. So the famous Cn. Pompejus Magnus, the triumvir, Caes. B. C. 3, 86; Cic. Fam. 3, 4, 2; 13, 41, 1; id. Imp. Pomp. 1 sqq. et saep.—In fem., Pompeja, his sister, Cic. Fam. 5, 11, 2; another, his daughter, Hirt. B. Afr. 95, 3; a third, daughter of Q. Pompeius, wife of Julius Cœsar, divorced from him, Suet. Caes. 6; 74.— Hence, Pompējus (Pompēïus), a, um, adj., of or belonging to a Pompey, Pompeian: domus,
pompejus.short: Pompējus (trisyl.) or Pompēïus (quadrisyl.), i, m., and Pompēja, ae, f., name of a Roman gens.

pompeum.full: Pompēum, i, n., a building at Athens, Plin. 35, 11, 40, § 132.
pompeum.short: Pompēum, i, n., a building at Athens, Plin.

pompholyx.full: pomphŏlyx, ўgis, f., = πομφόλυξ, a substance deposited from the smoke of smelting-furnaces, pompholyx, Plin. 34, 13, 33, § 128.
pompholyx.short: pomphŏlyx, ўgis, f., = πομφόλυξ, a substance deposited from the smoke of smelting-furnaces, pompholyx, Plin.

pompilius.full: Pompĭlĭus, a, name of a Roman gens. The most celebrated is Numa Pompilius, the second king of Rome, Hor. C. 1, 12, 34; Ov. F. 2, 69; Liv. 1, 18.—Hence, Pom-pĭlĭus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Pompilius, Pompilian: sanguis, i.e. descendants of Numa Pompilius, Hor. A. P. 292.— Pompĭlĭānus, a, um, adj., Pompilian: curia, built by Numa, Vop. Aur. 41: indigitamenta, Arn. 2, 95.
pompilius.short: Pompĭlĭus, a, name of a Roman gens.

pompilus.full: pompī^lus, i, m., = πομπίλος, a seafish (that follows ships), the pilot-fish, rudder-fish (Gasterosteus ductor, Linn.), Ov. Hal. 101; Plin. 32, 11, 54, § 153; 9, 15, 20, § 51.—This name was applied by some to the nautilus, Plin. 9, 29, 47, § 88.
pompilus.short: pompī^lus, i, m., = πομπίλος, a seafish (that follows ships), the pilot-fish, rudder-fish (Gasterosteus ductor, Linn.), Ov.

pompo.full: pompo, no perf., ātum, 1, v. a., to make or do any thing with pomp (post-class.): grandisonis pompare modis, Sedul. 1, 2.— Hence, pompātus, a, um, P. a., magnificently ordered, pompous, splendid: pompatior suggestus, Tert. Spect. 7.

pomponius.full: Pompōnĭus, i, m., and Pompōnĭa, ae, f., name of a Roman gens. L. Pomponius, an Atellane poet of Bononia, Gell. 12, 10, 7.— T. Pomponius Atticus, a friend of Cicero, whose life is written by Nepos, Cic. Att. 1, 5; Nep. Att. 1 sqq.— P. Pomponius Secundus, a tragedian, Quint. 8, 3, 31; 10, 1, 98.— Sex. Pomponius, a lawyer, Lampr. Alex. Sev. 68.— M. Pomponius Matho, a prœtor, Liv. 22, 7; and augur, id. 29, 38.— Pomponius Mela, a geographer of the first century, author of a treatise De Situ Orbis.—In
pomponius.short: Pompōnĭus, i, m., and Pompōnĭa, ae, f., name of a Roman gens.

pomposus.full: pompōsus, a, um, adj. pompa, pompous, stately, solemn (post-class.): incessus, i.e. dignified, slow, Sid. Ep. 4, 9; Ven. Fort. Carm. 3, 23, 7.— Rich, Cael. Aur. Acut. 2, 34, 182; id. Tard. 5, 10, 92: poëmata, Ven. Carm. 3, 23, 7.—Adv.: pompōsē, pompously, etc.: scribere, Sid. Ep. 9, 9 med.

pomptinus.full: Pomptīnus (Pontīn-), a, um, adj., Pomptine, an appellation given to a district in Latium, near Pometia: ager, Liv. 6, 5; Flor. 1, 13, 20: palus, Juv. 3, 307; and freq. in the plur. paludes, the extensive marshy district exposed to the inundations of the Amasenus and Ufens, still called the Pomptine (Pontine) Marshes, Plin. 3, 5, 9, § 59; 26, 4, 9, § 19; Suet. Caes. 47; Mart. 10, 74; Luc. 3, 85.— Subst.: Pomptī-num, i, n., the Pomptine district, Liv. 2, 34: inde Pomptinum sumam, Cic. Att. 7, 5, 3
pomptinus.short: Pomptīnus (Pontīn-), a, um, adj., Pomptine, an appellation given to a district in Latium, near Pometia: ager, Liv.

pomulum.full: pōmŭlum, i, n. pomum, a little apple, Jul. ap. Aug. c. Sec. Resp. Jul. 6, 20.

pomum.full: pōmum, i, n. root pa- of pasco, q. v.. Lit., fruit of any kind (apples, cherries, nuts, berries, figs, dates, etc.), Varr. R. R. 1, 31; Plin. 15, 18, 20, § 74; 15, 24, 30, § 104; 16, 26, 49, § 113; 17, 26, 39, § 247; Cic. ap. Macr. S. 2, 16: poma, fruit, Verg. E. 7, 54; Ov. M. 13, 812; cf. Macr. S. 2, 6, 1.—Of truffles, Mart. 13, 50, 2.—Of grapes, Dig. 50, 16, 205; Nemes. Ecl. 3, 38: et pomis arbores replebuntur, Vulg. Lev. 26, 4.— Transf., for pomus, a fruit-tree, Cato, R. R. 28; Verg. G. 2, 42

pomus.full: pōmus, i, f. Lit., a fruit-tree of any kind (v. pomum init.), Tib. 2, 1, 43; Vulg. Cant. 5, 1.— Transf., for pomum, fruit, Cato ap. Plin. 15, 18, 20, § 74.

pomusculum.full: pōmuscŭlum, i, n. dim. pomum, small fruit, fruit, Poët. in Anthol. Lat. 1, p. 461 Burm.

ponderabilis.full: pondĕrābĭlis, e, adj. pondero, that can be weighed, ponderable (post-class.): corpora, Claud. Mam. Stat. Anim. 2, 4.— Hence, adv.: pondĕrābĭlĭter, ponderably, Aug. Spec. 20.

ponderale.full: pondĕrāle, is, n. pondus, the public scales, Inscr. Rein. cl. 7, n. 15; v. ponderarium.

ponderans.full: pondĕrans, antis, Part. and P. a., from pondero.

ponderarium.full: pondĕrārĭum, ii, n. pondero, the place where public weights are kept and things are weighed, the public scales, Inscr. Orell. 144 and 4344.

ponderatio.full: pondĕrātĭo, ōnis, f. pondus, a weighing, poising (post-Aug.); plur., Vitr. 10, 3, 7: aequā ponderatione confici, Theod. Prisc. 1, 13; Vulg. Ecclus, 6, 15.

ponderator.full: pondĕrātor, ōris, m. pondero, a weigher (post-class.): De ponderatoribus, Cod. Th. 7, 12; Cod. Just. 71, 10: ponderator spirituum Dominus, Vulg. Prov. 16, 2; cf.: ponderator, σταθμιστὴς ἢ ζυγοστάτης, Gloss. Lat. Gr.

ponderatura.full: pondĕrātūra, ae, f. id., a weighing: σταθμός, ponderatura, Gloss. Gr. Lat.

ponderatus.full: pondĕrātus, a, um, Part. and P. a., from pondero.

ponderitas.full: pondĕrĭtas, ātis, f. pondus, weight: hominis (or nominis), Att. ap. Non. 156, 6.

pondero.full: pondĕro, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. id., to weigh a thing (syn. examino). Lit.: granum, Plin. 18, 7, 12, § 66: semper amatorum ponderat illa sinus, Prop. 2, 13 (3, 8), 12: pugnos, Plaut. Am. 1, 1, 156: in unum omnia ponderata confunduntur, Scrib. Comp. 106.— Trop., to weigh in the mind, to ponder, consider, reflect upon (class.): imprimis, quo quisque animo fecerit, ponderandum est, Cic. Off. 1, 15, 49: momento suo unamquamque rem ponderandam, id. Font. 6, 21: verborum delectum aurium judicio, id. de O

ponderosus.full: pondĕrōsus, a, um, adj. id., of great weight, weighty, heavy, ponderous. Lit.: compedes, Plaut. Capt. 3, 5, 64: frumentum, Varr. R. R. 1, 52 fin.: verbera, Val. Max. 1, 8 fin.—Comp.: lana ponderosior, Varr. R. R. 2, 11; Plin. 21, 17, 67, § 107.—Sup.: ponderosissimi lapides, Plin. 36, 19, 30, § 138.— Trop.: ponderosa epistola, weighty, significant, Cic. Att. 2, 11, 1: vox, weighty, imposing, Val. Max. 6, 4, 1 ext.

pondiculum.full: pondĭcŭlum, i, n. dim. pondus, a small weight (late Lat.), Claud. Mam. Stat. Anim. 2, 4.

pondo.full: pondo, adv. abl. from pondus, by weight, in weight. In gen.: neque piscium ullam unciam hodie pondo cepi, an ounce weight, Plaut. Rud. 4, 2, 8: ut exercitus coronam auream dictatori libram pondo decreverit, a pound in weight, weighing a pound, Liv. 3, 29; 4, 20: vettonicae tusae pondo libra, Plin. 26, 7, 19, § 33: pretium in pondo libras denarii duo, id. 33, 12, 56, § 158: styracis, resinae terebinthinae pondo sextantes, Cels. 5, 25, 16: sextarium aquae cum dodrante pondo mellis diluunt, Col. 12

pondus.full: pondus, ĕris, n. pendo, a weight. Lit. In gen., a weight used in a scale, Cic. Tusc. 5, 24, 69: pondera ab Gallis allata iniqua, Liv. 5, 48 fin.: utuntur taleis ferreis ad certum pondus examinatis pro numo, Caes. B. G. 5, 12; Dig. 19, 1, 32: pondera publica, Paul. ex Fest. p. 246 Müll.— In partic., the weight of a pound, a pound (very rare for the usual pondo): dupondius a duobus ponderibus, quod unum pondus assipondium dicebatur. Id ideo, quod as erat libra pondus, Varr. L. L. 5, § 169 Müll.: a

pondusculum.full: ponduscŭlum, i, n. dim. pondus, a small weight (post-Aug.): saxi, Col. 12, 51: si cooriatur procella, apprehensi pondusculo lapilli (apes) se librant, Plin. 11, 10, 10, § 24.

pone.full: pōne, adv. and prep. for posine, posne; cf. Gr. πύματος, the last, and v. post. Adv., after, behind, back, = post, a tergo (opp. ante, before; rare and mostly poet.; by Quint., 8, 3, 25, considered as archaic; cf. also: pone gravi sono antiqui utebantur pro loci significatione, Fest. p. 249 Müll.; Plaut. Cas. 5, 1, 16): (moveri) et ante et pone, ad laevam et ad dextram, Cic. Univ. 13 fin.: (remiges) Pone petunt, exim referunt ad pectora tonsas, Enn. ap. Fest. s. v. tonsam, p. 356 Müll. (Ann. v.

pono.full: pōno, pŏsŭi (Plaut. posīvi), pŏsĭtum, 3 (old form of perf. POSEIVEI, Inscr. Orell. 3308: posivi, Plaut. Ps. 5, 1, 35: posivimus, id. Fragm. ap. Prisc. p. 898 P.: posiverunt, Cato, R. R. praef. 1: posiveris, id. ib. 4, 1; Plaut. Trin. 1, 2, 108: POSIERunt, Inscr. Orell. 5061: POSIT, contr. from posivit, ib. 71; 732; 1475; 3087 al.; part. perf. sync. postus, a, um, Lucr. 1, 1059; 3, 87; 6, 965), v. a. for posno, posino, from old prep. port, = προτί, πρός, and sino; cf.: porricio, pollingo, etc., a

pons1.full: pons, ntis, m. kindred with Sanscr. pathi, a path; Gr. πάτος; old Germ. phat, pfat; mod. Germ. Pfad; Angl.-Sax. padh; hence prop. a board across a ditch, brook, etc., a bridge across a river, ditch, or marsh, between towers, etc. In gen.: pars oppidi mari disjuncta angusto, ponte rursus adjungitur et continetur, Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 52, § 117: pontem in Arare faciendum curat, to throw a bridge over the stream, Caes. B. G. 1, 13: in Isarā, flumine maximo, ponte uno die facto, Planc. ap. Cic. Fam. 10,

pons2.full: Pons, ntis, m., a geographical proper name. Pons Argenteus, the modern Argens, Lepid. ap. Cic. Fam. 10, 34, 2; 10, 35.— Pons Campanus, Hor. S. 1, 5, 45; Plin. 14, 6, 8, § 62.— Aureoli, the modern Pontiruolo, Trebell. XXX. Tyr. Aureol. al.
pons2.short: Pons, ntis, m., a geographical proper name.

pontia1.full: Pontĭa, ae, f., a woman notorious as the poisoner of her own children, Juv. 6, 638; Mart. 2, 34, 6; 4, 43, 5; 6, 75, 3 sq.
pontia1.short: Pontĭa, ae, f., a woman notorious as the poisoner of her own children, Juv.

pontia2.full: Pontia, ae, f., = Ποντία, an island in the Tuscan Sea, now Ponza, Suet. Tib. 54. —Plur.: Pontiae, ārum, the group of little islands which includes Ponza, Liv. 9, 28; Mel. 2, 7; Plin. 3, 6, 12, § 81; Varr. L. L. 3, 5, 7.
pontia2.short: Pontia, ae, f., = Ποντία, an island in the Tuscan Sea, now Ponza, Suet.

ponticulus.full: pontĭcŭlus, i, m. dim. 1. pons, a little bridge, Cic. Tusc. 5, 20, 59; Cat. 17, 3; Col. 2, 2, 11; Suet. Caes. 31; Inscr. Murat. 598.

ponticus1.full: Pontĭcus, a, um, v. 2. Pontus, II.

ponticus2.full: Pontĭcus, i, m., a poet, contemporary with Propertius, Prop. 1, 7, 1; Ov. Trist. 4, 10, 47; cf. id. P. 4, 16, 21 sq.; Prop. 1, 9, 9 sqq.
ponticus2.short: Pontĭcus, i, m., a poet, contemporary with Propertius, Prop.

pontifex.full: pontĭfex (pontŭ-), fĭcis doubtless from pons-facio; but the original meaning is obscure, m., a Roman high-priest, a pontiff, pontifex (cf.: antistes, sacerdos): pontifices, ut Q. Scaevola pontifex maximus dicebat, a posse et facere, Varr. L. L. 5, § 83 Müll.; Cic. Leg. 2, 8, 20, on the laws of the Twelve Tables; id. de Or. 3, 19, 73; id. Rep. 2, 14, 26; Liv. 1, 20; Ov. F. 6, 454; Hor. C. 3, 30, 9; 2, 14, 28; 3, 23, 12; id. Ep. 2, 1, 26; Juv. 6, 604. Their chief or president was called Pontifex M

pontificalis.full: pontĭfĭcālis, e, adj. pontifex, of or belonging to a pontifex, pontifical: insignia, Liv. 10, 7: auctoritas, Cic. Leg. 2, 21, 52: honos, of the Pontifex Maximus, Ov. F. 3, 420: ludi, given by the Pontifex Maximus on his entrance into office, Suet. Aug. 44: lectio, Macr. S. 7, 13, 11.

pontificatus.full: pontĭfĭcātus, ūs, m. pontifex, the office or dignity of a pontifex, the pontificate, Cic. Har. Resp. 9, 18; Vell. 2, 59, 3; Tac. H. 1, 77; Suet. Calig. 12: pontificatus maximus. the office of a Pontifex Maximus, id. Caes. 13; 46; id. Aug. 31; id. Vitell. 11; id. Tit. 9.

pontificius.full: pontĭfĭcĭus, a, um, adj. id., of or belonging to a pontifex, pontifical: libri, Cic. N. D. 1, 30, 84; id. Rep. 2, 31, 54: jus, id. Fragm. ap. Non. 174, 7; Cic. Dom. 14. — Subst. pontĭfĭcĭi, ōrum, m. (sc. libri), the pontifical books, Amm. 17, 7, 10.— pontĭfĭcĭum, ii, n. Lit., the dignity of a pontiff or of a bishop (post-class.), Sol. 16 fin.; Cod. Th. 16, 5, 13.— Transf., the power or right of doing any thing: is, cujus negotium id pontificiumque esset, Gell. 1, 13, 3; Cod. Th. 8, 18, 1; Symm.

pontilis.full: pontīlis, e, adj. 1. pons, of or belonging to a bridge, bridge- (post-class.): stratus, perh. a wooden floor, Veg. Vet. 1, 56; 2, 58 Schneid.

pontius.full: Pontĭus, i, m., the name of a gens, originally Samnite, afterwards Roman. So, C. Pontius, a leader of the Samnites, who surrounded the Romans in the Caudine Pass, Cic. Off. 2, 21, 75; Liv. 9, 1; Flor. 1, 16, 10.— L. Pontius Aquila, one of the assassins of Cœsar, Cic. Phil. 11, 6, 14; Asin. Poll. ap. Cic. Fam. 10, 33, 4; Suet. Caes. 78. — Pontius Pilatus, governor of Judœa in the time of Christ, Tac. A. 15, 44; Tert. Apol. 21; Lact. 4, 18; Sed. Carm. 5, 116.
pontius.short: Pontĭus, i, m., the name of a gens, originally Samnite, afterwards Roman.

pontivagus.full: pontĭvăgus, a, um, adj. 1. pontusvagor, roaming over the sea; subst., one who sails over the sea, a voyager, navigator, Poët. ap. Anthol. Lat. 1, p. 487.

ponto.full: ponto, ōnis, m. 1. pons. A kind of Gallic transport, a punt, Caes. B. C. 3, 29.— A floating bridge, a pontoon, Aus. Idyll. 12, 10; Dig. 8, 3, 38; Gell. 10, 25, 5.

pontonium.full: pontonĭum, ĭi, n. dim. ponto, a small punt, acc. to Isid. Orig. 19, 1.

pontus1.full: pontus, i, m., = πόντος. Lit., the sea (poet. for mare): mulserat huc navem pontus, Enn. ap. Prisc. p. 870 P. (Ann. v. 257 Vahl.): placidus, Lucr. 2, 559: pontus Libyae, Verg. A. 1, 556: caelum undique et undique pontus, id. ib. 3, 193 al.: aequora ponti, Lucr. 1, 8; 2, 772; Verg. G. 1, 469; cf.: freta ponti, id. ib. 1, 356.— Poet., transf. * The deep: maris, Verg. A. 10, 377 (a poetic pleonasm, like the Homer. πόντος ἁλὸς πολιῆς, Il. 21, 59).—* A wave of the sea, sea-wave: ingens a vertice pont

pontus2.full: Pontus, i, m., = Πόντος. Lit., the Black Sea, called in full Pontus Euxinus, Mel. 1, 1, 5; 1, 3, 1; Plin. 4, 12, 24, § 75; Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 58, § 129; id. Tusc. 1, 20, 45; 1, 39, 94; Val. Fl. 8, 180 al.— Transf., the region about the Black Sea: Medea ex eodem Ponto profugisse, Cic. Imp. Pomp. 9, 22; Ov. Tr. 5, 10, 1.— In partic., Pontus, a district in Asia Minor, between Bithynia and Armenia, the kingdom of Mithridates, afterwards a Roman province, Verg. G. 1, 58; Cic. Agr. 1, 2, 6; 2, 19, 5; id

popa.full: pŏpa, ae, m. A Roman inferior priest, a priest's assistant or minister, who brought the victim to the altar and felled it with an axe, Suet. Calig. 32 fin.; Prop. 4 (5), 3, 62; Cic. Mil. 24, 65; Serv. Verg. A. 12, 120. Alluding to the corpulence of such priests: popa venter, a fat paunch, glutton, Pers. 6, 74.—* In fem.: PHILEMA POPA DE INSVLA, perh. = she who sells animals for sacrifice, Inscr. Orell. 2457.

popanum.full: pŏpănum, i, n., = πόπανον, a sacrificial cake, Juv. 6, 541.
popanum.short: pŏpănum, i, n., = πόπανον, a sacrificial cake, Juv.

popellus.full: pŏpellus, i, m. dim. populus, the rabble, mob, populace, Hor. Ep. 1, 7, 65; Pers. 4, 15.

popilius.full: Popĭlĭus (Popill-), i, m., and Popi-lĭa (Popill-), ae, f., the name of a Roman gens. So esp., M. Popillius Laenas, a consul A. U.C. 395, Cic. Brut. 14, 56.— C. Popilius Laenas, the assassin of Cicero, Liv. Epit. 120; Sen. Suas. 7.— In fem.: Popilia, the wife of Q. Catulus, Cic. de Or. 2, 11, 44.— Hence, Popĭlĭus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to a Popilius, Popilian: gens, Cic. Leg. 2, 22, 55.
popilius.short: Popĭlĭus (Popill-), i, m., and Popi-lĭa (Popill-), ae, f., the name of a Roman gens.

popina.full: pŏpīna, ae, f. πέπω, πέπτω, to cook, a cook-shop, victualling-house, eating-house (syn.: caupona, taberna): bibitur, estur, quasi in popinā, Plaut. Poen. 4, 2, 13; Cic. Phil. 2, 28, 69; 13, 11, 24; Suet. Tib. 34; id. Ner. 16; Hor. S. 2, 4, 62; id. Ep. 1, 14, 21; Mart. 1, 42, 10; 5, 70, 3; Juv. 8, 172; 11, 81. — Transf., the food sold at a cookshop: si epulae potius quam popinae nominandae sunt, Cic. Phil. 3, 8, 20: taeterrimam popinam inhalare, id. Pis. 6, 13.

popinalis.full: pŏpīnālis, e, adj. popina, of or belonging to a cook-shop: deliciae, Col. 8, 16, 5: luxuria, App. M. 8, p. 201, 13.

popinarius.full: pŏpīnārĭus, ĭi, m. id., a cook, victualler (post-class.), Lampr. Alex. Sev. 49 fin.; Firm. Math. 4, 15.

popinator.full: pŏpīnātor, ōris, m. id., a frequenter of cook-shops, a gormandizer, Macr. S. 7, 14; cf. popino.

popino.full: pŏpīno, ōnis, m. id., a frequenter of eating - houses, a gormandizer, Lucil. and Varr. ap. Non. 161, 16 sq.; Hor. S. 2, 7, 39; Suet. Gram. 15.

popinor.full: pŏpīnor, āri, v. dep. n. [id.], to frequent eating-houses, to gormandize (post-class.): dum Gallienus popinatur, Trebell. XXX. Tyr. 29.

poples.full: poplĕs, ĭtis, m. Lit.: the ham of the knee, the hough (cf. suffrago): genua poplitesque et crura, Col. 6, 12, 3: succisis feminibus poplitibusque, Liv. 22, 51, 7: succiso poplite, Verg. A. 9, 762; cf. Liv. 22, 48, 4; Hor. C. 3, 2, 16: elephas poplites intus flectit hominis modo, Plin. 11, 45, 101, § 248; 28, 6, 17, § 59.— Transf., in gen., the knee, Luc. 9, 771; Lucr. 4, 953: duplicato poplite, i. e. with bended knee, Verg. A. 12, 927: se collegit in arma poplite subsidens, id. ib. 12, 492: cont

poplicula.full: Poplĭcŭla (Poplĭcŏla) or Publĭ-cŏla (the very ancient inscr. in Orell. 547 has POPLICVLA, the palimpsest of Cic. Rep. 2, 31, 53; 55, twice Publicola), ae, m. 1. populus-colo (a favorer or friend of the people), a surname of P. Valerius, and of his descendants, Inscr. Orell. 547: inde cognomen factum Publicolae est, Liv. 2, 8: Poplicola, ingentis Volesi Spartana propago, Sil. 2, 8; Inscr. Grut. 480, 5: Poplicola atque Corvinus, Hor. S. 1, 10, 28.—Poet., in plur., as an appellative, Sid. Carm. 23,
poplicula.short: Poplĭcŭla (Poplĭcŏla) or Publĭ-cŏla (the very ancient inscr.

poplifugia.full: Pŏplĭfŭgĭa (Pŏpŭ-), ōrum, n. 1. populus-fugio, a festival in memory of the people's flight to the rescue of the Latins, celebrated on the nones of July, POPLIF. NP., Calend. Maff. ap. Inscr. Orell. 2, p. 394; cf. Varr. L. L. 6, 3, § 18; Piso ap. Macr. S. 3, 2.

poplus.full: poplus and pŏpŏlus, i, v. 1. populus init.

poppaeus.full: Poppaeus, i, m.; Poppaea, ae, f., the name of a Roman gens. Masc., Poppaeus Sabinus, Tac. A. 1, 80; 4, 46; 5, 10; 6, 39: Poppaeus Silvanus, id. H. 2, 86; 3, 50.— Fem.: Poppaea (on inscrr. also Poppea and Poppaia) Sabina, wife of the emperor Nero, Suet. Oth. 3; id. Ner. 35; Tac. A. 13, 45 sq.; id. H. 1, 13; 78; Inscr. Orell. 731; 733; Inscr. Fratr. Arval. ap. Marin. tab. XVII. b, p. 123.—Hence, Poppaeā-nus, a, um, adj., named after Poppœa, Poppœan: pinguia, a species of cosmetic (bread-dough mixe

poppysma.full: poppysma, ătis, n., and poppys-mus, i, m., = πόππυσμα and ποππυσμός, a smacking or clucking with the tongue, as a sign of approbation, Juv. 6, 584; on occasion of lightning, as a religious ceremony, Plin. 28, 2, 5, § 25; of a similar sound, Mart. 7, 18, 11.
poppysma.short: poppysma, ătis, n., and poppys-mus, i, m., = πόππυσμα and ποππυσμός, a smacking or clucking with the tongue, as a sign of approbation, Juv.

poppyzon.full: poppȳzon, ontis, m., = ποππύζων, one who clucks with the tongue: cum pingeret poppyzonta retinentem equum, Plin. 35, 10, 36, § 104.
poppyzon.short: poppȳzon, ontis, m., = ποππύζων, one who clucks with the tongue: cum pingeret poppyzonta retinentem equum, Plin.

populabilis.full: pŏpŭlābĭlis, e, adj. populor, that may be laid waste or ravaged, destructible (poet.): quodcunque fuit populabile flammae, Ov. M. 9, 262.

populabundus.full: pŏpŭlābundus, a, um, adj. id., laying waste, ravaging (rare): agros populabundus, Sisenn. ap. Non. 471, 23; cf.Gell. 11, 15, 7: in fines Romanos excurrerunt populabundi, Liv. 1, 15, 1: vagari populandum, id. 2, 60, 2: consul per agrum populabundus ierat, id. 3, 3, 10.

popularia.full: pŏpŭlārĭa, ĭum, v. popularis, I. B.

popularis.full: pŏpŭlāris (sync. poplāris, Plaut. Rud. 3, 4, 36), e, adj. 1. populus, of or belonging to the people, proceeding from or designed for the people. In gen.: populares leges, i. e. laws instituted by the people, Cic. Leg. 2, 4, 9: accessus, id. Q. Fr. 1, 1, 8, § 25: coetus, id. Ac. 2, 2, 6: munus, a donation to the people, id. Off. 2, 16, 56: popularia verba usitata, id. ib. 2, 10, 35; cf.: ad usum popularem atque civilem disserere, id. Leg. 3, 6, 14: dictio ad vulgarem popularemque sensum accommoda

popularitas.full: pŏpŭlārĭtas, ātis, f. popularis. * (Acc. to popularis, II. A.) A being of the same country, fellow-citizenship: popularitatis causa, Plaut. Poen. 5, 2, 81.— (Acc. to popularis, II. B.) Popularity, but only subjectively, an effort to please the people, a courting of popular favor, popular bearing (post-Aug.): ne quid popularitatis praetermitteret, Suet. Tit. 8; id. Calig. 15; id. Ner. 53: quanto rarior apud Tiberium popularitas, tanto, etc., Tac. A. 3, 69: gratus popularitate, Stat. S. 2, 7, 69.—

populatim.full: pŏpŭlātim, adv. 1. populus, from people to people, among all nations, everywhere, universally (ante-class.): poëta placuit populatim omnibus, Pompon. ap. Non. 150, 20; Caecil. ap. ib. 154, 14; Arn. 3, 5.

populatio1.full: pŏpŭlātĭo, ōnis, f. populor, a laying waste, ravaging, plundering, spoiling, devastation, etc. (not in Cic.). Lit.: populationem effuse facere, Liv. 2, 64.—In plur.: populationibus incursionibusque, Liv. 3, 3 fin.: hostem rapinis, pabulationibus populationibusque prohibere, Caes. B. G. 1, 15.— Transf. Concr., things plundered, plunder, booty: Veientes pleni populationum, Liv. 2, 43.— A ravaging, destroying done by animals: a populatione murium formicarumque frumenta defendere, Col. 2, 20; so, vo

populatio2.full: pŏpŭlātĭo, ōnis, f. 1. populus, population; concr., a people, a multitude (late Lat.): flebat populatio praesens, Sedul. 4, 275.

populator.full: pŏpŭlātor, ōris, m. populor, a devastator, destroyer, ravager, spoiler, plunderer (perh. not ante-Aug.). Lit.: agrorum, Liv. 3, 68 fin.: Trojae (Atrides), Ov. M. 13, 655.—Poet., transf.: Tuscae glandis aper, Mart. 7, 27, 1: Calabri arvi Sirius, Val. Fl. 1, 683.— Trop., a destroyer, consumer: luxus populator opum, Claud. in Ruf. 1, 35: civitatis, Quint. Decl. 12, 24 fin.; Luc. 4, 92.

populatrix.full: pŏpŭlātrix, īcis, f. populator, she that wastes or destroys (poet.): Siculi populatrix virgo profundi, i. e. Scylla, Stat. S. 3, 2, 86: catervae, Claud. Rapt. Pros. 3, 167.— Poet., transf.: populatrix Hymetti, apis, a rifler, Mart. 13, 104.

populatus.full: pŏpŭlātus, ūs, m. populor, a laying waste, a devastating, devastation (poet.), Luc. 2, 634: squalent populatibus agri, Claud. in Eutr. 1, 244: coërcere populatibus, Sid. Ep. 3, 3, p. 181, 40.

populetum.full: pōpŭlētum, i, n. 2. populus, a poplar wood, Plin. 14, 6, 8, § 61.

populeus.full: pōpŭlĕus, a, um, adj. id., of or belonging to poplars, poplar-: frus, Enn. ap. Aus. Idyll. 5, 160 (Ann. v. 562 Vahl.): frondes, Verg. A. 8, 32; 10, 190; cf. Cato ap. Plin. 16, 21, 38: corona, Hor. C. 1, 7, 23: umbra, Verg. G. 4, 511: silva, Sen. Herc. Oet. 1641.

populifer.full: pōpŭlĭfer, ĕra, ĕrum, adj. 2. populusfero, poplar-bearing (poet.): Padus, whose banks abound with poplars, Ov. Am. 2, 17, 32: Spercheos, id. M. 1, 579.

populiscitum.full: pŏpŭliscītum, i, n., or better written separately, pŏpŭli scītum, a decree of the people: Athenienses nihil nisi populi scitis ac decretis agebant, Cic. Rep. 1, 27, 43; id. Opt. Gen. 7, 19: populiscito in patriam restitutus est, Nep. Arist. 1, 5: scitum populi, Liv. 45, 25.
populiscitum.short: pŏpŭliscītum, i, n., or better written separately, pŏpŭli scītum, a decree of the people: Athenienses nihil nisi populi scitis ac decretis agebant, Cic.

populito.full: pŏpŭlĭto, āre, v. freq. a. populor, to lay waste, to plunder: fructus agrorum, Dig. 49, 1, 21 fin. (al. popularentur).

populneus.full: pōpulnĕus, a, um, adj. 2. populus, of poplars, poplar-: frons, Cato, R. R. 5, 8; Col. 6, 3, 7: scobis, Col. 12, 43, 4; cf. populeus.

populnus.full: pōpulnus, a, um, adj. id., of poplars, poplar-: sors, Plaut. Cas. 2, 6, 32.

populonia1.full: Pŏpŭlōnĭa, ae, f. populor (she who protects against devastation), a surname of Juno, Macr. S. 3, 11; Arn. 3, 118; Mart. Cap. 2, § 149; Sen. ap. Aug. Civ. Dei, 6, 10 fin.

populonia2.full: Pŏpŭlōnĭa, ae, f., also Pŏpŭlō-nĭum, ĭi, n., and Pŏpŭlōnĭi, ōrum, m., a town on the coast of Etruria, now the ruins of Poplonia, near Piombino.—Form Populonia, Verg. A. 10, 172; Mel. 2, 4, 9: Populonium, Plin. 3, 5, 8, § 50: Populonii, Liv. 30, 39, 2.—Hence, Pŏpŭlōnĭen-ses, ĭum, m., the inhabitants of Populonia, the Populonians, Liv. 28, 45.
populonia2.short: Pŏpŭlōnĭa, ae, f., also Pŏpŭlō-nĭum, ĭi, n., and Pŏpŭlōnĭi, ōrum, m., a town on the coast of Etruria, now the ruins of Poplonia, near Piombino.—Form Populonia, Verg.

populor.full: pŏpŭlor, ātus, 1. v. dep., and pŏpŭlo, āre, v. a. 1. populus; prop. to spread or pour out in a multitude over a region; hence, transf. to the result, to lay waste, ravage, devastate, desolate; to spoil, plunder, pillage (class.; syn.: vasto, vexo, diripio). Lit. Form populor: Romanus exercitus insulam integram urit, populatur, vastat, Naev. ap. Non. 90, 29: noctu populabatur agros, Cic. Off. 1, 10, 33: Remorum agros, Caes. B. G. 5, 56: arva ferro populatur et igni, Luc. 2, 445; so, omnia igni fe

populositas.full: pŏpŭlōsĭtas, ātis. f. populosus, a multitude (post-class.): deorum, Arn. 3, p. 102: luminum Argi, Fulg. Myth. 1, 24; Sid. Ep. 1, 6.

populosus.full: pŏpŭlōsus, a, um, adj. 1. populus, abounding in people, populous, numerous (post-class.): gens populosa, App. Flor. p. 342: familia, id. M. 5, p. 162: Briareus populoso corpore, Sid. Carm. 15, 27.—Comp.: populosior globus, Veg.Mil. 3, 19 fin.—Sup.: insula populosissima, Sol. 52.

populus1.full: pŏpŭlus (contr. POPLVS, Inscr. Column. Rostr. in Corp. Inscr. Lat. 195, 17, Plaut. Am. prol. 101; 1, 1, 103; id. Aul. 2, 4, 6; id. Cas. 3, 2, 6 et saep.—Also written POPOLVS, Corp. Inscr. Lat. 197, 15 al.; nom. plur. poploe, Carm. Sal. ap. Fest. p. 205 Müll.; v. pilumnoe) [from root pleof pleo; v. plenus], i, m., a people, the people. Lit. In gen. (cf.: gens, natio): res publica res populi: populus autem non omnis hominum coetus quoquo modo congregatus, sed coetus multitudinis juris consensu et

populus2.full: pōpŭlus, i, f. root pamp-, pap-, to swell; Lat. papula, papilla, pampinus, a poplar, poplar-tree, Plin. 16, 23, 35, § 85; 16, 18, 31, § 77; 17, 11, 15, § 78; Ov. H. 5, 27; sacred to Hercules, Verg. E. 7, 61; Ov. H. 9, 64; Plin. 12, 1, 2, § 3: alba, the silver-poplar, Hor. C. 2, 3, 9.

por.full: por, for puer, i. e. servus; e. g. Marcipor, Lucipor, etc., i. e. servus Marci, etc., Prisc. 6.—Thus also pora for puera, i. e. serva, Inscr. Rein. Class. 17, n. 180.

porca1.full: porca, ae, f. porcus, a female swine, a sow, Cato, R. R. 134; Pall. 3, 26.— By poet. license for a male swine, a boar, Verg. A. 8, 641 Serv.; cf. Quint. 8, 3, 19: tenera, Juv. 2, 86.

porca2.full: porca, ae, f. cf. O. H. Germ. furh; Germ. Furche; Engl. furrow, the ridge between two furrows, a balk (cf. lira), Varr. L. L. 5, § 39 Müll.; id. R. R. 1, 29; Col. 11, 3, 44.— In Spain, a measure of land, Col. 5, 1, 5.

porcarius.full: porcārĭus, a, um, adj. porcus, porca, of or belonging to a swine, swine-: vulva, that has farrowed properly, Plin. 11, 37, 84, § 210.— Subst.: porcārĭus, ĭi, m., a swine-herd, Firm. Math. 3, 6, 6.

porcastrum.full: porcastrum, i, n., a plant, also called portulaca, purslain, App. Herb. 103.
porcastrum.short: porcastrum, i, n., a plant, also called portulaca, purslain, App.

porcella.full: porcella, i, f. dim. porcula, a little female pig, Plaut. Mil. 4, 2, 68; Theod. Prisc. 4, 1.

porcellinus.full: porcellīnus, a, um, adj. porcellus, of young swine, pig-: glandulae, Apic. 4, 3: caro, Theod. Prisc. de Diaeta, 6.

porcellio.full: porcellĭo, ōnis, m., a cheslip, woodlouse, sowbug, Cael. Aur. Tard. 1, 4, 119; Pelag. Vet. 5.
porcellio.short: porcellĭo, ōnis, m., a cheslip, woodlouse, sowbug, Cael.

porcellus.full: porcellus, i, m. dim. porculus, a little pig, Varr. R. R. 2, 4, 14; Suet. Ner. 33; Plin. 30, 6, 16, § 47.—Plur., the litter of a wild sow, Phaedr. 2, 4, 15.

porceo.full: porceo (PORXI, acc. to Charis. p. 217 P., without any example). 2, v. a. porro-arceo, to keep off, keep back, to hinder, restrain (ante-class.): porcet quoque dictum ab antiquis quasi porro arcet, Paul. ex Fest. p. 15 Müll.: porcet significat prohibet, Non. 159, 33: non te porro procedere porcent, Lucil. ap. Non. 160, 9: civium porcet pudor, Enn. ap. ib. 160, 6 (Trag. v. 369 Vahl.); Varr. ap. ib. 160, 8; Pac. and Att. ap. ib. 160, 2 and 5.

porcetra.full: porcē^tra, ae, f. porca, a sow that has once littered, Meliss. ap. Gell. 18, 6, 4.

porcilaca.full: porcĭlāca or porcillāca, ae, f., for portulaca, purslain, Plin. 20, 20, 81, § 210.
porcilaca.short: porcĭlāca or porcillāca, ae, f., for portulaca, purslain, Plin.

porcilia.full: porcilĭa, ae, f. porca, a young sow, Inscr. Fratr. Arv. ap. Marin. n. 41, lin. 22; cf. Not. Tir. p. 167.

porciliaris.full: porcilĭāris, e, adj. porcilia, of or belonging to a young sow: extae, Inscr. Fratr. Arv. ap. Marin. n. 41, lin. 18.

porcinarium.full: porcīnārĭum, ĭi, n. porcus, a pigsty: ὑοφορβεῖον, porcinarium, Gloss. Gr. Lat.

porcinarius.full: porcīnārĭus, ĭi, m. id., a porkseller, Plaut. Capt. 4, 3, 5.

porcinus.full: porcīnus, a, um, adj. id.. Lit., of a hog, hog's, swine's: polimenta, Plaut. Men. 1, 3, 28: vox, Sen. Ira, 2, 12: numen, Petr. Frag. 35: caro, porcina, Vulg. 2 Macc. 6, 18.— Subst.: porcīna, ae, f. (sc. caro), swine's flesh, pork, Plaut. Capt. 4, 2, 69; Cael. Aur. Acut. 1, 11, 95.— Transf., in milit. lang.: porcinum caput, a swine's head, a wedge-shaped order of battle, Veg. Mil. 3, 19 fin.

porcius.full: Porcius, i, m.; Porcia, ae, f., the name of a Roman gens. The most celebrated are, M. Porcius Cato Censorinus, or Major, the severe censor, whose life was written by Nepos, and for whom Cicero named his Essay on Old Age, Nep. Cato, 1 sqq.; Cic. Rep. 1, 1.— M. Porcius Cato, the younger, called Uticensis, because of his famous death at Utica, Sall. Cat. 52, 1; Cic. Att. 12, 12, 1.— In fem., Porcia, a sister of the younger Cato, wife of Domitius Ahenobarbus, Cic. Att. 13, 37; 3, 48.—Hence, Porcĭus,

porcula.full: porcŭla, ae, f. dim. porca, a little sow, v. l. for porcella, Plaut. Mil. 4, 2, 68.

porculatio.full: porcŭlātĭo, ōnis, f. porculus, swinebreeding, Varr. R. R. 2, 4, 13.

porculator.full: porcŭlātor, ōris, m. id., one who rears young swine, a swine-breeder, Varr. R. R. 2, 4, 1; Col. 1 praef. § 26; 7, 9, 12.

porculetum.full: porcŭlētum, i, n. porca, II., a field divided into beds, Plin. 17, 22, 35, § 171.

porculus.full: porcŭlus, i, m. dim. porcus. Lit., a young swine, young pig, a porker, porkling, Plaut. Men. 2, 2, 36; id. Rud. 4, 4, 126; Gell. 4, 11, 6.— Transf. Porculus marinus, a sea-hog, porpoise, Plin. 9, 15, 17, § 45.— A hook in a wine- or oil-press, Cato, R. R. 19, 2.

porcus.full: porcus, i, m. cf. Gr. πόρκος, Varr. L. L. 5, § 97 Müll.; Umbr. purka, O. H. Germ. farah. Lit., a tame swine, a hog, pig: sunt domi agni, et porci sacres, Plaut. Rud. 4, 6, 4: villa abundat porco, haedo, agno, gallinā, etc., Cic. Sen. 16, 56; Mart. 8, 22, 1: Scrofa alat suos porcos, her pigs, Varr. R. R. 2, 4, 13: porcus femina, a female swine, sow, Cato, R. R. 134; Cic. Leg. 2, 22, 57.—Of a glutton, as a term of reproach, hog, Hor. Ep. 1, 4, 16; Cat. 39, 11.— Transf. Porcus marinus, the sea-hog,

porphyreticus.full: porphўrētĭcus, a, um, adj. πορφύρα, purple-red, porphyretic: marmor, Suet. Ner. 50: saxa, Lampr. Elag. 24: porticus, Vop. Prob. 2: columnae, Capitol. in Anton. Pio, 11: tabulae, Ambros. Ep. 53, 4.

porphyrio.full: porphўrĭo, ōnis, m., = πορφυρίων, a species of water-fowl, the sultana-hen, porphyrton (Fulica porphyrio, Linn.), Plin. 10, 16, 63, § 129; Vulg. Lev. 11, 18.
porphyrio.short: porphўrĭo, ōnis, m., = πορφυρίων, a species of water-fowl, the sultana-hen, porphyrton (Fulica porphyrio, Linn.), Plin.

porphyrion.full: Porphўrĭon, ōnis, m., = Πορφυρίων. One of the giants, Hor. C. 3, 4, 54; Mart. 13, 78, 2; Claud. Gigant. 35; 115.— An ancient commentator on Horace, Charis. p. 196 P.

porphyrites.full: porphўrītes, ae, m., = πορφυρίτης, a purple-colored precious stone in Egypt, porphyry, Plin. 36, 7, 11, § 57; 36, 13, 19, § 88.
porphyrites.short: porphўrītes, ae, m., = πορφυρίτης, a purple-colored precious stone in Egypt, porphyry, Plin.

porphyritis.full: porphўrītis, ĭdis, adj. f., = πορφυρῖτις, purple-colored: ficus, Plin. 15, 18, 19, § 71.

porraceus.full: porrācĕus, a, um, adj. porrum. Of leeks: folia, Plin. 21, 18, 70, § 117.— Like leeks, leek-green: color, Plin. 37, 10, 58, § 160; 24, 4, 6, § 11.

porrecte.full: porrectē, adv., v. 1. porrigo, P. a. fin.

porrectio.full: porrectĭo, ōnis, f. 1. porrigo, a stretching out, extending, extension: digitorum (opp. contractio), Cic. N. D. 2, 60, 150: bracchii, Auct. Her. 3, 15, 27.— Concr., a straight line (opp. circinatio), Vitr. 10, 3, 8.

porrectus.full: porrectus, a, um, Part. and P. a., from 1. porrigo.

porriciae.full: porrĭcĭae, ārum, f. porricio, the parts of the victim consecrated to the gods, sacrificial pieces, Arn. 2, p. 231; Sol. 5 med. (al. prosiciae).

porricio.full: porrĭcĭo (porĭ-), ēci, ectum, 3, v. a. old prep. port (v. pōno) and root ric-, to extend; cf. rica, a flowing veil. Lit., to lay before, to offer sacrifice to the gods: exta porriciunto, diis danto in altaria, Veran. ap. Macr. S. 3, 2: atrocia porriciunt exta ministratores, Naev. ap. Non. 76, 6; Plaut. Ps. 1, 3, 32: cruda exta in mare porricit, Liv. 29, 27; cf.: extaque salsos Porriciam in fluctus, Verg. A. 5, 238 and 776; Fenest. ap. Non. 154, 21.—Prov.: inter caesa et porrecta ut aiunt, betwee

porriginosus.full: porrīgĭnōsus, a, um, adj. 2. porrigo, full of dandruff, scurvy: caput, Plin. Val. 1, 4.

porrigo1.full: porrĭgo, rexi, rectum, 3 (contr. form porgo, porgite, Enn. ap. Serv. ad Verg. A. 1, 26, and Verg. A. 8, 274: porge, Plaut. Ps. 2, 4, 18; Aus. Idyll. 4, 37: porgebat, Sil 9, 458: porgens, Val. Fl. 2, 656: porgi, Stat. Th. 8, 755: porxit, id. S. 2, 1, 204; cf.: antiqui etiam porgam dixerunt pro porrigam, Fest. p. 218 Müll.—Acc. to Lachmann, Hor. S. 2, 6, 59, instead of perditur, we should read porgitur; v. perdo init.), v. a. por, = pro, and rego, to stretch or spread out before one's self, to put

porrigo2.full: porrīgo, ĭnis, f., the scurf, dandruff on the head, Cels. 6, 2; Plin. 20, 6, 23, § 53; 20, 6, 27, § 69; 28, 11, 46, § 163; 32, 4, 14, § 35; Hor. S. 2, 3, 126.—Also of other hairy parts of the body, Scrib. Larg. 243.—Of animals, perhaps the mange: porci, Juv. 2, 80.
porrigo2.short: porrīgo, ĭnis, f., the scurf, dandruff on the head, Cels.

porrima.full: Porrĭma, ae, f., a Roman goddess worshipped by women, perh. another name for Carmentis, Ov. F. 1, 633; cf. Hartung, Rel. d. Röm. 2, p. 199.
porrima.short: Porrĭma, ae, f., a Roman goddess worshipped by women, perh.

porrina.full: porrīna, ae, f. porrum, a bed of leeks, Cato, R. R. 47; Arn. 2, 85; Dig. 7, 1, 58.

porrixo.full: porrixo, āre, v. freq. a. 1. porrigo, to stretch out strongly, App. M. Fragm. p. 717 Oud.

porro.full: porro, adv. root pra-; Sanscr. prathamus, primus; Lat. prae, pro, prior; cf. Gr. πόρρω, πρόσω, forward, onward, farther on, to a distance, at a distance, after off, far. Lit., in space, with verbs both of motion and of rest (rare and mostly anteclass.), Ter. Hec. 3, 1, 18: porro agere armentum, Liv. 1, 7, 6: ire, id. 9, 2.—So ellipt.: porro Quirites, on! hither! ye Romans! Laber. ap. Macr. S. 2, 7; Tert. adv. Val. 13 (al. proh).—With verbs of rest: habitare, Plaut. Rud. 4, 3, 95: inscius Aeneas,

porrum.full: porrum, i, n., and porrus, i, m. πράσον, a leek, scallion; of two kinds, capitatum and sectile, the latter our chives, Col. 8, 11, 14; Plin. 19, 6, 33, § 108; Mart. 3, 47, 8; 3, 13, 18; 19; Juv. 3, 293; 14, 133.
porrum.short: porrum, i, n., and porrus, i, m.

porsena.full: Porsĕna and Porsenna (also Por-sina), ae, m., a king of Etruria, who made war on Rome on account of the banished Tarquins, Liv. 2, 9 sq.; Cic. Att. 9, 10, 3; id. Sest. 21; id. Par. 1, 2, 12: Etrusca Porsĕnae manus, Hor. Epod. 16, 4; scanned Porsĕna also Sil. 8, 391; 480; 10, 484; 502; Mart. 1, 22, 6: nec non Tarquinium ejectum Porsenna jubebat, Verg. A. 8, 646 Serv.—Prov.: bona Porsenae vendere, to sell Porsena's goods, i. e. to sell goods at auction, Liv. 2, 14.
porsena.short: Porsĕna and Porsenna (also Por-sina), ae, m., a king of Etruria, who made war on Rome on account of the banished Tarquins, Liv.

porta.full: porta, ae (portabus for portis, Cn. Gell. ap. Charis. p. 40 P.), f. from root par-, to pierce, pass through; Gr. περάω, πείρω, πόρος, ford; Lat.: peritus, ex-perior, and v. periculum, a city-gate, a gate. Lit.: hic (miles) portas frangit, at ille (amans) fores, Ov. Am. 1, 9, 20: rectā portā invadam extemplo in oppidum antiquom et vetus, Plaut. Bacch. 4, 4, 60; id. Ps. 2, 2, 3: si Hannibal ad portas venisset, Cic. Fin. 4, 9, 22: pedem portā efferre, id. Att. 8, 2, 4; 7, 2, 6; Verg. A. 4, 130: ad

portabilis.full: portābĭlis, e, adj. porto, that can be carried or borne, portable (post-class.), Sid. Ep. 8, 11 med.—Comp.: onus portabilius, Aug. Ep. 34.

portarius.full: portārĭus, ii, m. porta, a door-keeper, porter, Vulg. Reg. 4, 7, 11; id. 1 Par. 16, 42.
