prospicientia.full: prōspĭcĭentĭa, ae, f. prospicio. Foresight, forethought, precaution: vigilia et prospicientia, Cic. Phil. 7, 7, 19; Ambros. Off. 1, 21: Creatoris, id. Hexaëm. 3, 9.—* A view; hence, an appearance, shape, form, Tert. adv. Val. 26.

prospicio.full: prō-spĭcĭo, exi, ectum, 3, v. n. and a. [specio]. Neutr., to look forward or into the distance, to look out, to look, see (class.). In gen.: neque post respiciens, neque ante prospiciens, Varr. ap. Non. 443, 2: parum prospiciunt oculi, do not see well, Ter. Phorm. 5, 1, 8; Plaut. Curc. 2, 3, 38: grues volant ad prospiciendum alte, Plin. 10, 23, 30, § 58: ex superioribus locis prospicere in urbem, Caes. B. C. 2, 5: multum, to have an extensive prospect, Cic. Fam. 7, 20, 1: per umbram, Verg. A. 2,

prospicus.full: prōspĭcus, a, um, adj. prospicio, taking care: hac sibi prospicā, hac despicā, Naev. ap. Non. 155, 25 (Com. Rel. p. 8 Rib.).

prospicuus.full: prōspĭcŭus, a, um, adj. id.. * That may be seen afar off, conspicuous: turris, Stat. Th. 12, 15.— Looking forward, looking into the future: turris illa prospicua vaticinationis munus explicuit, App. M. 6, p. 181, 20.—Adv.: prōspĭcuē, providently, cautiously, carefully, App. M. 1, p. 112, 8.

prospiro.full: prō-spīro, āvi, 1, v. n., to breathe forth, exhale, App. Mag. p. 306, 12.

prostas.full: prostas, ădis, f., = προστάς, a porch, vestibule, Vitr. 6, 10.
prostas.short: prostas, ădis, f., = προστάς, a porch, vestibule, Vitr.

prosterno.full: prō-sterno, strāvi, strātum, 3, v. a., to strew in front of, to strew before one; also, to throw to the ground, throw down, overthrow, prostrate (syn.: fundo, profligo, provolvo). Lit.: eo prosternebant folia farferi, Plaut. Poen. 2, 31 (al. praesternebant): ceteros ruerem ... et prosternerem, Ter. Ad. 3, 2, 21: pondere silvam, Ov. M. 8, 776: prostraturus humi corpus, Curt. 8, 5, 6; cf. Liv. 9, 6: se ad pedes alicujus, Cic. Phil. 2, 18, 45; so, prosternere se et supplicare alicui, id. Planc. 20,

prosthesis.full: prosthĕsis, is, f., = πρόσθεσις, and prŏthĕsis, is, f., = πρόθεσις, a grammatical figure consisting in the prefixing of a letter or syllable to a word, prosthesis; as gnatus for natus, tetuli for tuli, Charis. 4; Diom. 2.
prosthesis.short: prosthĕsis, is, f., = πρόσθεσις, and prŏthĕsis, is, f., = πρόθεσις, a grammatical figure consisting in the prefixing of a letter or syllable to a word, prosthesis;

prostibilis.full: prōstĭbĭlis, is, f. prosto, a harlot, prostitute, Plaut. Pers. 5, 2, 56.

prostibula.full: prōstĭbŭla, ae, f. id., a prostitute, Plaut. ap. Non. 423, 18; Tert. Apol. 6.

prostibulum.full: prōstĭbŭlum, i, n. id.. A prostitute, Plaut. Aul. 2, 4, 6; Vulg. Lev. 21, 7.— Transf., a male who prostitutes himself, Arn. 6, 199.— A brothel, Isid. Orig. 18, 42, 2; Vulg. Ezech. 16, 24; also, in transf. signif., id. Joel, 3, 3.

prostituo.full: prō-stĭtŭo, ŭi, ūtum, 3, v. a. statuo. To place before or in front, Arn. 5, 177. — To expose publicly to prostitution, to prostitute: cras populo prostituam vos, Plaut. Ps. 1, 2, 45; Sen. Contr. 1, 2: quae (meretrix) sese toto corpore prostituit, Cat. 110, 8: pudicitiam suam, Suet. Ner. 29; Lact. 3, 21, 6: formam, Petr. 126: faciem suam lucro, Ov. Am. 1, 10, 42: corpora libidinibus, Lact. 5, 9, 16; 1, 20, 15: virgines, Just. 21, 3, 2.— Transf.: famam alicujus, to prostitute, dishonor, sully, Cat

prostitutio.full: prōstĭtūtĭo, ōnis, f. prostituo. Prostitution, Arn. 2, 53; Tert. Pudic. 6; Aug. in Psa. 128, 6.—Plur.: mulierum, Lact. 5, 8, 7.— In gen., a dishonoring, profaning: imaginum, Tert. Apol. 27.

prostitutor.full: prōstĭtūtor, ōris, m. id.. A prostitutor, pander, Tert. Cult. Fem. 9.— In gen., one who dishonors, a violator: Christiani sacramenti, Tert. Pudic. 10; id. Cult. Fem. 2, 10.

prostitutus.full: prōstĭtūtus, a, um, Part. and P. a., from prostituo.

prosto.full: prō-sto, stĭti, stātum, 1, v. n. * To stand forth, stand out, project: angellis prostantibus, Lucr. 2, 428.— To stand in a public place. Of a seller, to offer one's wares for sale, carry on one's business (cf. propono): hi (lenones) saltem in occultis locis prostant, vos in foro ipso, Plaut. Curc. 4, 2, 21.— Of wares, to be set out or exposed for sale: liber prostat, Hor. Ep. 1, 20, 2.— In partic., to sell one's body, prostitute one's self: si mater tua prostitisset, Sen. Contr. 1, 2; Juv. 1, 47

prostomis.full: prostŏmis, ĭdis, f., = προστομίς, an instrument to hold a horse by the nose, a barnacle, twitch, beak; trop., a drinkingvessel, Lucil. ap. Non. 1, n. 84 (others read postomis, q. v.).
prostomis.short: prostŏmis, ĭdis, f., = προστομίς, an instrument to hold a horse by the nose, a barnacle, twitch, beak;

prostratio.full: prostrātĭo, ōnis, f. prosterno, an overthrowing, subverting, prostration (postclass.): disciplinae, Tert. Praescr. 41.

prostrator.full: prōstrātor, ōris, m. id., an overthrower, prostrator (late Lat.): hostium, Jul. Firm. Err. Prof. Relig. 21 fin.

prostratus.full: prōstrātus, a, um, Part., from prosterno.
prostratus.short: prōstrātus, a, um, Part., from prosterno.

prostylos.full: prostȳlos, on, adj., = πρόστυλος, having pillars in front: aedes, Vitr. 3, 1; 7 praef. fin.
prostylos.short: prostȳlos, on, adj., = πρόστυλος, having pillars in front: aedes, Vitr.

prostypum.full: prostўpum, i, n., = πρόστυπον, a pattern, model, Plin. 35, 12, 43, § 152; v. Sillig N. cr.
prostypum.short: prostўpum, i, n., = πρόστυπον, a pattern, model, Plin.

prosubigo.full: prō-sŭbĭgo, ĕre, v. a. * To dig up, cast up: terram, Verg. G. 3, 256.—* To fashion beforehand, prepare: fulmina Cyclops Prosubigit, Val. Fl. 4, 288.—* To tear down, trample on: molam pede, Prud. στεφ. 3, 130.

prosum1.full: prō-sum, fŭi, prōdesse, v. n., to be useful or of use, to do good, benefit, profit. In gen., constr. with dat., a subjectclause, or absol., rarely with ad or in and acc.: sibi prodesse, Enn. ap. Cic. Fam. 7, 6, 2 (Trag. v. 310 Vahl.); cf.: qui nec sibi nec alteri prosunt, Cic. Off. 2, 10, 36: multis, id. Lael. 1, 4: nihil tibi litterae meae proderunt, id. Fam. 2, 17, 7.—With subj.-clause: multum prodest ea quae metuuntur ipsa contemnere, Cic. Tusc. 4, 30, 64: iis carum et jucundum esse maxime pr

prosumia.full: prōsūmĭa, ae, f., a small kind of vessel for reconnoitring, a spy - boat, Caecil. ap. Non. 536, 11 sq. (Com. Rel. pp. 29 and 45 Rib.); cf.: prosumia genus navigii speculatorium parvum, Paul. ex Fest. p. 226 Müll.
prosumia.short: prōsūmĭa, ae, f., a small kind of vessel for reconnoitring, a spy - boat, Caecil.

prosumnus.full: Prosumnus, i, m., the name of a lewd favorite of Bacchus, who showed the latter the way to the infernal regions, Arn. 5, 176.
prosumnus.short: Prosumnus, i, m., the name of a lewd favorite of Bacchus, who showed the latter the way to the infernal regions, Arn.

prosumo.full: pro-sūmo, prosumpserit, a false read. for praesumpserit, Plaut. Trin. 5, 2, 6; v. Ritschl ad h. l.

prosurgo.full: prosurgo, ĕre, 3, v. n., to rise up (late Lat.), Fulg. Serm. 11.

prosymna.full: Prŏsymna, ae, or Prŏsymnē, ēs, f., = Προσυμνα, a country or town of Argolis, Stat. Th. 1, 383; 3, 325.
prosymna.short: Prŏsymna, ae, or Prŏsymnē, ēs, f., = Προσυμνα, a country or town of Argolis, Stat.

protagion.full: prōtăgĭon, ĭi, n., a good kind of wine, Plin. 14, 7, 9, § 76.
protagion.short: prōtăgĭon, ĭi, n., a good kind of wine, Plin.

protagoras.full: Prōtăgŏras, ae, m., = Πρωταγόρας, a celebrated sophist of Abdera, a disciple of Democritus, and an older contemporary of Socrates; he was banished from Athens on a suspicion of atheism, Cic. N. D. 1, 1, 2; 1, 23, 63; id. Ac. 2, 46, 142; id. Brut. 8, 30; 12, 46; Gell. 5, 3, 1 sqq.—Hence, Prōtăgŏrīon, ĭi, n., = Πρωταγόρειον, a dictum or maxim of Protagoras, Gell. 5, 11, 1.
protagoras.short: Prōtăgŏras, ae, m., = Πρωταγόρας, a celebrated sophist of Abdera, a disciple of Democritus, and an older contemporary of Socrates;

protasis.full: prŏtăsis, is, f., = πρότασις. An assertion, proposition (pure Lat. effatum), App. Dogm. Plat. p. 29.— The beginning or first part of a play, Don. Ter. And. praef.

protaticus.full: prŏtătĭcus, a, um, adj., = προτατικός, appearing in the first part of a play: persona, Don. Ter. And. praef.
protaticus.short: prŏtătĭcus, a, um, adj., = προτατικός, appearing in the first part of a play: persona, Don.

prote.full: Prōtē, ēs, f. One of the Stœchades, islands on the southern coast of Gaul, now Porquerolles, Plin. 3, 5, 11, § 79.— An island of the Ionian Sea, now Proti, Mel. 2, 7.

protectio.full: prōtectĭo, ōnis, f. protego, a covering over; trop., a protecting, protection (postclass.): fidei, Tert. Fug. in Persec. 2: armorum, Ambros. Serm. 8: Dei, Vulg. Psa. 90, 1.

protector.full: prōtector, ōris, m. id.. In gen., a coverer; trop., a protector (post-class.): legum protectores, Tert. Apol. 6; Vulg. Psa. 17, 3.— In partic., one of the lifeguard or body - guard (post - class.): inter protectores suos, Spart. Carac. 7; Amm. 14, 7, 9; Cod. Th. 6, 24; Inscr. Grut. 1028, 2 al.

protectorius.full: prōtectōrĭus, a, um, adj. protector, II., of or belonging to the life-guard or body-guard: dignitas, Cod. Th. 7, 20, 5; Cod. Just. 12, 47, 2.

protectum.full: prōtectum, i, n. protego, I. B., the projecting part of a roof, the eaves (postAug.), Dig. 9, 2, 29; 47, 7, 6; 43, 25, 15; Inscr. Maff. Mus. Veron. 448, 2: vinearum, Plin. 17, 12, 18, § 89.

protectus1.full: prōtectus, a, um, Part., from protego.
protectus1.short: prōtectus, a, um, Part., from protego.

protectus2.full: prōtectus, ūs, m. protego, a covering (post-class.): tignorum, Dig. 8, 2, 41.

protego.full: prō-tĕgo, xi, ctum, 3, v. a., to cover before or in front, to cover over, cover, protect (class.; syn.: defendo, tutor). Lit.: tabernacula protecta hederā, Caes. B. C. 3, 96: rates cratibus ac pluteis, id. ib. 1, 25 fin.: aedes, to furnish with a projecting roof, Cic. Top. 4, 24: hunc scutis protegunt hostes, to cover, protect, Caes. B. G. 5, 43: se umbone, Just. 33, 2, 4: caput contra solem, Plin. 31, 11, 47, § 131: scutis protecti corpora longis, Verg. A. 8, 662: protegendi corporis memor, Liv

protelo.full: prō-tēlo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. telum, to drive forth or forwards, to drive away, put to flight, repulse, remove (only ante- and post-class.). Lit.: protelare longe propellere, ex Graeco videlicet τῆλε, quod significat longe, Paul. ex Fest. p. 235 Müll.: equites, Sisenn. ap. Non. 363, 18: Romanos impetu suo protelant, id. ib. 363, 4: aliquem patriā, Turp. ib. 363, 16 (Com. Rel. p. 83 Rib.): aliquem saevidicis dictis, Ter. Phorm. 1, 4, 36: hanc cladem de vestris manibus, App. M. 8, p. 209, 36; p. 1

protelum.full: prōtēlum, i, n. A row of oxen, etc., harnessed together for draught, a team: protelo trini boves unum aratrum ducent, Cato ap. Non. 363, 10; Lucil. ib. 363, 7 and 8: boum, Plin. 9, 15, 17, § 45: bina ternaque, id. 18, 18, 48, § 173; cf.: protelum, ἔξαμπρον, Gloss. Philox.— Transf., a line, row, succession (ante-class. and poet.): protelo plagarum continuato, Lucr. 2, 531; 4, 190.

protendo.full: prō-tendo, di, sum and tum, 3, v. a., to stretch forth or out, to extend (not in Cic.; syn. porrigo). Lit.: hastas, Verg. A. 11, 606 Wagn.: bracchia in mare, Ov. M. 14, 191: supinas manus ad genua alicujus, Petr. 17 fin.: aciem (oculorum) in aestus pelagi, Cat. 64, 127: cervicem fortiter, Tac. A. 15, 67: cochleae bina ceu cornua protendentes contrahentesque, Plin. 9, 32, 51, § 101: protentis hastis, Tac. A. 14, 37: pedes temo protentus in octo, Verg. G. 1, 171: consanguineam protendere dextram,
protendo.short: prō-tendo, di, sum and tum, 3, v.

protensio.full: prōtensĭo, ōnis, f. protendo. Lit., a stretching out: manus, Hier. Ep. 29.— As a lit. transl. of πρότασις, a proposition, App. Dogm. Plat. 3, p. 36.

protentatus.full: prō-tentātus, a, um, Part. [tento], tried, tested: protentatā manu, Avien. Arat. 85.

protentus.full: prōtentus, a, um, Part. and P.a., from protendo.

protermino.full: prō-termĭno, āre, v. a., to more forward, to widen, extend the boundaries (postclass.): fines usque et usque, App. M. 9, p. 235, 11: possessionis metas in Rhodanum, Sid. Ep. 3, 1 fin.

protero.full: prō-tĕro, trīvi, trītum, 3, v. a. * To drive forth, drive away: ver proterit aestas Interitura, i. e. supplants, Hor. C. 4, 7, 9.— To tread under foot, trample down, wear away, crush, bruise (class.; syn. proculco). Lit.: aliquem pedibus, Plaut. Truc. 2, 2, 13: homines elephantis proterendos substravit, Val. Max. 2, 7, 14: januam limā, i. e. to destroy, Plaut. Men. 1, 1, 9: equitatus aversos proterere incipit, Caes. B. C. 2, 41: agmina curru, Verg. A. 12, 330: florentia arva, Ov. M. 2, 791: adve

proterreo.full: prō-terrĕo, ŭi, ĭtum, 2, to frighten or scare away, to drive away by terror, to affright, terrify (rare but class.): filium Proterruisti hinc, Ter. Heaut. 3, 1, 37: aliquem adverso equo, Verg. A. 12, 291: aliquem jaculo parmāque, Stat. Th. 2, 645: feras ardentibus facibus, App. M. 8, p. 208, 39; Plaut. Trin. 3, 2, 77: patriā pulsus atque proterritus, Cic. Rep. 1, 3, 5: tu a tuis aedibus vi atque armis proterritus, id. Caecin. 13, 37; 9, 24; 11, 31: proterritis hostibus atque in fugam conjectis,
proterreo.short: prō-terrĕo, ŭi, ĭtum, 2, to frighten or scare away, to drive away by terror, to affright, terrify (rare but class.): filium Proterruisti hinc, Ter.

proterritus.full: prōterrĭtus, a, um, Part., from proterreo.
proterritus.short: prōterrĭtus, a, um, Part., from proterreo.

proterve.full: prŏtervē, adv., v. protervus fin. A.

protervia.full: prŏtervĭa, ae, f. protervus, wantonness, impudence (post-class.), Aus. Idyll. 10, 172: procorum, id. Per. 22; Ambros. Interp. Job, 3, 2, 5.

protervio.full: prŏtervĭo, īre, v. n. id., to be bold, shameless, impudent (post-class.), Tert. Patient. 12 fin.

protervitas.full: prŏtervĭtas, ātis, f. id., pertness, sauciness, boldness, impudence (class.): protervitas levior est quaedam contumelia, procacitas major, petulantia maxima, Don. Ter. Heaut. 4, 6, 10: coërcere protervitatem, Pac. ap. Non. 121, 15 (protervitates, acc. to Fest. s. v. redhostire, p. 270 Müll.); Ter. Heaut. 4, 6, 10; Cic. Cael. 12, 29: urit me Glycerae nitor, Urit grata protervitas, forwardness, wantonness, Hor. C. 1, 19, 7.

proterviter.full: prŏtervĭter, adv., v. protervus fin. B.

protervus.full: prŏtervus, a, um, adj. protero; qs. trampling on every thing; hence, violent, vehement. Lit. (poet.): venti, Hor. C. 1, 26, 2: Africus, id. Epod. 16, 22: Eurus, Ov. H. 11, 14: stella canis, scorching, oppressive, id. Am. 2, 16, 4.— Trop., forward, bold, pert, wanton, shameless, impudent (class.; generally milder than procax and petulans; v. protervitas): petulans protervo animo sum, Plaut. Bacch. 4, 3, 1: homo, Cic. Fin. 5, 12, 35; 1, 18, 61: dictum aut factum, id. ib. 2, 14, 47: vidua, id. Cael

protesilaus.full: Prōtĕsĭlāus, i, m., = Πρωτεσίλαος, a son of Iphiclus, a native of Phylace in Thessaly, the husband of Laodamia, and the leader of the Thessalians against Troy, where he was the first man killed, Ov. M. 12, 68; Prop. 1, 19, 7; Mel. 2, 2; Hyg. Fab. 103 sq.—Hence, Prōtĕsĭlāēus, a, um, adj., Protesilœan: domus, Cat. 68, 74.
protesilaus.short: Prōtĕsĭlāus, i, m., = Πρωτεσίλαος, a son of Iphiclus, a native of Phylace in Thessaly, the husband of Laodamia, and the leader of the Thessalians against Troy, where he was the first man killed, Ov.

protestatio.full: prōtestātĭo, ōnis, f. protestor, a declaration, protestation (post-class.): amoris, Symm. Ep. 1, 56: veritatis suae, Hilar. Trin. 1, 27; Vulg. 2 Macc. 7, 6.

protestor.full: prō-testor, ātus, 1, v. dep. a. (act. collat. form prōtesto, āre, acc. to Prisc. p. 799), to declare in public, to bear witness, testify, protest (post-Aug.): praedico, protestor, non ego parricidium faciam, Quint. Decl. 4, 21: quae mihi conscius sum, protestabor, Front. Nep. Am. 2 Mai: floris species florem rerum protestatur, Macr. S. 1, 17 fin.: mulier magno fidem praesidis protestata clamore, App. M. 10, p. 252; Vulg. Act. 20, 23; Just. Inst. prooem. 1.—With object-clause: quippe protestantur

proteus.full: Prōteus (dissyl.), ĕi and ĕos, m., = Πρωτεύς, a sea-god who often changed his form; he was in the service of Neptune, and kept his sea-calves, Ov. M. 8, 731; 2, 9; id. A. A. 1, 761; Hor. C. 1, 2, 7; Verg. G. 4, 388; Ov. F. 1, 367: Protei columnae, i. e. the boundary of Egypt, Verg. A. 11, 262.— Transf., of a fickle person: Protea tenere, Hor. Ep. 1, 1, 90; of a cunning person, id. S. 2, 3, 71; cf. Amm. 29, 1, 39.
proteus.short: Prōteus (dissyl.), ĕi and ĕos, m., = Πρωτεύς, a sea-god who often changed his form;

protheorema.full: prŏthĕōrēma, ătis, n., = προθεώρημα, a considering beforehand, preconsideration, Mart. Cap. 2, § 138.
protheorema.short: prŏthĕōrēma, ătis, n., = προθεώρημα, a considering beforehand, preconsideration, Mart.

prothoenor.full: Prŏthŏēnor, ŏris, m., a hero at the wedding of Perseus, Ov. M. 5, 98.
prothoenor.short: Prŏthŏēnor, ŏris, m., a hero at the wedding of Perseus, Ov.

prothyme.full: prŏthȳmē, adv., = προθύμως, willingly, gladly, with pleasure; only Plaut. Ps. 5, 1, 23.
prothyme.short: prŏthȳmē, adv., = προθύμως, willingly, gladly, with pleasure;

prothymia.full: prŏthȳmĭa, ae, f., = προθυμία, readiness, willingness, inclination, Plaut. Stich. 4, 2, 53; 5, 2, 11; Marc. Aur. ap. Front. Ep. 2, 5 Mai.
prothymia.short: prŏthȳmĭa, ae, f., = προθυμία, readiness, willingness, inclination, Plaut.

prothyra.full: prŏthўra, ōrum, n., = πρόθυρα. In a Grecian house, the space before the door, the vestibule, Vitr. 6, 10.— In a Roman house, a railing or wicket before the door, the Gr. διάθυρα, Vitr. 6, 10.

prothyris.full: prŏthўris, ĭdis, f., = προθυρίς, an ornament over a door or pillars, called also ancon, Vitr. 4, 6 dub.
prothyris.short: prŏthўris, ĭdis, f., = προθυρίς, an ornament over a door or pillars, called also ancon, Vitr.

protinam.full: prōtĭnam (prōtĕnam), adv. protinus, forthwith, immediately (ante-class.): protinam a protinus, continuitatem significans, Varr. L. L. 7, § 107 Müll.: exinde me illico protinam dedi, Plaut. Curc. 2, 3, 84; cf. id. Bacch. 3, 1, 7; id. Cas. 5, 3, 13; id. Pers. 4, 5, 8; Ter. Phorm. 1, 4, 13; Naev. ap. Non. 376, 13 (Com. Rel. p. 12 Rib.).

protinis.full: prōtĭnis (prōtĕnis), adv. id., forthwith, immediately (ante-class.). Afran. ap. Non. 376, 6 (Com. Rel. p. 178 Rib.).

protinus.full: prō-tĭnus (less properly prō-tĕnus), adv. tenus, before one's self, forward, farther on, onward. Lit. (rare but class.; syn.: statim, continuo, actutum): praecepisse, ut pergeret protinus, quid retro atque a tergo fieret, ne laboraret, Cic. Div. 1, 24, 49: ipse capellas Protinus aeger ago, drive along before me, Verg. E. 1, 13: quā (voce) protinus omne Contremuit nemus, far and wide, id. A. 7, 513.— Transf. Right on, continuously, constantly, uninterruptedly (rare; not in Cic.). In space, Plin.

protocomium.full: prōtŏcŏmĭum, i, n., = πρωτοκόμιον, the place where the hair begins, Veg. Vet. 2, 11 dub. (al. procomion).
protocomium.short: prōtŏcŏmĭum, i, n., = πρωτοκόμιον, the place where the hair begins, Veg.

protogenes.full: Prōtŏgĕnes, is, m., = Πρωτογένης, a celebrated Grecian painter of Caunus, on the coast of Caria, Cic. Brut. 18; id. Att. 2, 21, 4; Plin. 35, 10, 36, § 104; Gell. 15, 31 fin.
protogenes.short: Prōtŏgĕnes, is, m., = Πρωτογένης, a celebrated Grecian painter of Caunus, on the coast of Caria, Cic.

protollo.full: prō-tollo, ĕre, v. a. To stretch forth or out, to bring forth (ante- and post-class.): manum, Plaut. Ps. 3, 2, 71: Pleiadas, Avien. Arat. 567.— Trop. To prolong, protract, put off, defer, Lucil. ap. Non. 159, 23: vitam in crastinum, Plaut. Cas. 3, 5, 43: mortem sibi, id. ib. 2, 8, 11: feturam mulierum non ultra decimum mensem, Gell. 3, 16, 15.— To elevate, raise: vox a minore solita ad majorem protolli, Amm. 31, 7, 11.

protomedia.full: prōtŏmēdĭa, ae, f., = πρωτομηδία, an herb, otherwise unknown, Plin. 24, 17, 102, § 185.
protomedia.short: prōtŏmēdĭa, ae, f., = πρωτομηδία, an herb, otherwise unknown, Plin.

protomysta.full: prōtŏmysta, ae, m., = πρωτομύστης, a chief priest in mystic ceremonies, Sid. Ep. 2, 9.
protomysta.short: prōtŏmysta, ae, m., = πρωτομύστης, a chief priest in mystic ceremonies, Sid.

protono.full: pro-tŏno, āre, v. a., to thunder forth: tali protonat ira, Val. Fl. 4, 205.

protoplastus.full: prōtŏ_plastus (prŏtoplastus, Alcim. 2, 35), i, m., = πρωτοπλαστός (first-formed), the first man; in plur., the first men, Tert. Exhort. ad Castit. 2 fin.; id. adv. Jud. 13; Alcim. 2, 35.

protopraxia.full: prōtopraxĭa, ae, f., = πρωτοπραξία, the privilege of being preferred to other creditors, = jus primae exactionis, Plin. Ep. 10, 109.
protopraxia.short: prōtopraxĭa, ae, f., = πρωτοπραξία, the privilege of being preferred to other creditors, = jus primae exactionis, Plin.

protosedeo.full: prōtŏsĕdĕo, ēre, v. n. πρῶτος-sedeo, to sit in the first place, Tert. Cor. Mil. 15.

protostasia.full: prōtostăsĭa, ae, f., = πρωτοστασία, the office of chief collector of taxes in the municipia, the chief collectorship, Cod. Th. 11, 23, 2; Cod. Just. 8, 10, 41.
protostasia.short: prōtostăsĭa, ae, f., = πρωτοστασία, the office of chief collector of taxes in the municipia, the chief collectorship, Cod.

prototomus.full: prōtŏtŏmus, a, um, adj., = πρωτότομος, that is cut off first, of the first cutting: caules, the earliest cabbage - sprouts, Col. 10, 369 (cf. Plin. 19, 8, 41, § 137); so, coliculi, Mart. 14, 101.— As subst.: prō-tŏtŏmi, ōrum, m., cabbages of the first cutting, Mart. 10, 48, 16.
prototomus.short: prōtŏtŏmus, a, um, adj., = πρωτότομος, that is cut off first, of the first cutting: caules, the earliest cabbage - sprouts, Col.

prototypia.full: prōtŏtўpĭa, ae, f., = πρωτοτυπία, the office of one who has charge of the commutation for recruits, Cod. Th. 6, 35; 11, 23.
prototypia.short: prōtŏtўpĭa, ae, f., = πρωτοτυπία, the office of one who has charge of the commutation for recruits, Cod.

prototypus.full: prōtŏtўpus, a, um, adj., = πρωτότυπος, original, primitive (post-class.): metra, standard metre, Mar. Vict. p. 2552 P.
prototypus.short: prōtŏtўpus, a, um, adj., = πρωτότυπος, original, primitive (post-class.): metra, standard metre, Mar.

protracte.full: prōtractē, adv. protractus, with the time dragged (late Lat.; music. t. t.), Pauli et Steph. Reg. ad Mon. 7.

protractio.full: prōtractĭo, ōnis, f. protraho, a drawing out, lengthening, protraction (postclass.), Macr. Somn. Scip. 1, 12.

protractus1.full: prōtractus, a, um, Part., from protraho.
protractus1.short: prōtractus, a, um, Part., from protraho.

protractus2.full: prōtractus, ūs, m. protraho, a prolonging, protraction: LONGI, Inscr. Amadut. Anecd. Litt. 2, p. 480.

protraho.full: prō-trăho, xi, ctum, 3 (sync. form protraxtis for protraxistis, Sil. 16, 84.—Inf. protraxe for protraxisse, Lucr. 5, 1159), v. a., to draw or drag forth, to bring forth or out, pull out, to draw to a place (class.; cf.: promo, profero). Lit., Cels. 7, 12, 1: aliquem e tentorio, Tac. H. 4, 27: me istam capillo protracturum in viam, Plaut. Merc. 4, 4, 58: aliquem hinc in convivium, Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 10, § 24: Calchanta in medios, Verg. A. 2, 123: aliquem in medium manibus suis, Suet. Ner. 53: ad op

protrepticon.full: protreptĭcon or -um, i, n., = προτρεπτικόν, an exhortation, a hortatory or protreptical discourse, Treb. Pol. 2; Stat. S. 5, 2 in lemm.; Aus. Idyll. 4 praef.; Sid. Ep. 1, 25.
protrepticon.short: protreptĭcon or -um, i, n., = προτρεπτικόν, an exhortation, a hortatory or protreptical discourse, Treb.

protrico.full: pro-trīco, āre, v. n., to make difficulties beforehand, Not. Tir. p. 150.

protrimentum.full: prōtrīmentum, i, n. protero, a dish composed of various ingredients hashed together, a ragout, App. M. 8, p. 216.

protritus.full: prōtrītus, a, um, Part. and P. a., from protero.

protropum.full: prŏtrŏpum, i, n., = πρότροπον, the first new wine that runs from the grapes before pressing, Plin. 14, 9, 11, § 85; Vitr. 8, 3, 12: Cnidium, a kind of wine, Plin. 14, 7, 9, § 75.
protropum.short: prŏtrŏpum, i, n., = πρότροπον, the first new wine that runs from the grapes before pressing, Plin.

protrudo.full: prō-trūdo, si, sum, 3, v. a., to thrust or push forwards, to thrust forth, push out (class.; syn.: proturbo, propello). Lit.: moles protruditur, Lucr. 4, 891; 4, 246 and 280: cylindrum, Cic. Fat. 19, 43: is . . . domo atque nostrā familiā protruditur, Afran. ap. Don. Ter. 3, 4, 34 (Com. Rel. p. 174 Rib.; cf. Lachm. ad Lucr. II. p. 121); so, protrudi penatibus, to be thrust out of doors, Amm. 29, 1, 21.— Trop., of time, to put off, defer: comitia in Januarium mensem, Cic. Fam. 10, 26, 3.

protubero.full: prō-tūbĕro, āre, v. n., to swell or bulge out, to grow forth (late Lat.), Sol. 45: poma, id. 46 fin.— Trop.: densa ne supra modum protuberent, Aus. Idyll. 13, praef. § 8; cf. id. ib. 16, 10.

protumidus.full: prō-tŭmĭdus, a, um, adj., swollen in front, protuberant, gibbous: luna, App. de Deo Socr. p. 42, 1.
protumidus.short: prō-tŭmĭdus, a, um, adj., swollen in front, protuberant, gibbous: luna, App.

proturbo.full: prō-turbo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a., to drive on or forward, to drive forth or away, to repel, repulse (mostly post-Aug.; not in Cic.). Lit.: his facile pulsis ac proturbatis, Caes. B. G. 2, 19 fin.: hostes telis, Liv. 5, 47: apes pigras et ignavas, Plin. 11, 19, 21, § 67: extra tecta proturbantur, Col. 9, 15, 2: aliquem de domo, App. M. 9, p. 230, 20: aliquem laribus, Claud. in Eutr. 2, 513; Tac. H. 2, 85: hostem Missilibus, Verg. A. 10, 801: hostes hinc comminus, id. 9, 441: in exsilium proturbatus

protutela.full: prō-tūtēla, ae, f., a vice-guardianship, vice-tutelage, Dig. 27, 5, 1; 8, 3, 24.
protutela.short: prō-tūtēla, ae, f., a vice-guardianship, vice-tutelage, Dig.

protypum.full: prŏtўpum, i, a false read. for prostypum, Plin. 35, 12, 43, § 152.

protyrum.full: prŏtўrum, i, n., a kind of wine made in the island of Lesbos, Vitr. 8, 3.
protyrum.short: prŏtўrum, i, n., a kind of wine made in the island of Lesbos, Vitr.

provectibilis.full: prōvectĭbĭlis, e, adj. proveho, capable of progress (post-class.), Fulg. Cont. Virg. p. 747 Stav.

provectio.full: prōvectĭo, ōnis, f. id., an advancement, promotion (post - class.): dignitatis, Lact. 5, 11, 8.

provector.full: prōvector, ōris, m. id., a promoter (eccl. Lat.), Jul. ap. Aug. c. Sec. Resp. Jul. 6, 17.

provectus1.full: prōvectus, a, um, Part. and P. a., from proveho.

provectus2.full: prōvectus, ūs, m. proveho (postclass.). Advancement, promotion to places of honor: honestiorum, Aur. Vict. Caes. 39 fin.— Progress, increase, furtherance: aetatis, Sid. Ep. 4, 4: praesentia domini provectus est agri, Pall. 1, 6, 1.—Plur., Amm. 28, 4, 20.

provegeo.full: prō-vĕgĕo, ēre, a false read. for probito.

proveho.full: prō-vĕho, xi, ctum, 3, v. a., to carry or conduct forwards, to carry or convey along, to conduct, convey, transport, etc., to a place; and freq. pass. in mid. signif., to go, proceed, advance, move, drive, ride, sail, etc., to a place (freq. and class.). Lit.: eam pol provexi: avehere non quivi, I took her on board the ship, Plaut. Rud. 3, 6, 24: alvos apum mulis, Plin. 21, 13, 43, § 74: aër a tergo quasi provehat atque propellat, Lucr. 6, 1026.—Mid.: cum classe freto provehi, Caes. B. C. 2, 3;

provendo.full: prō-vendo, ĕre, a false read. for protruditur, Afran. ap. Don. ad Ter. Ad. 3, 4, 34; cf. Com. Rel. p. 174 Rib.; Lachm. Lucr. 2, p. 121; and v. protrudo.

provenio.full: prō-vĕnĭo, vēni, ventum, 4, v. n., to come forth, appear (not in Cic.; syn. appareo). Lit. In gen. (mostly anteclass.): proveniebant oratores novi, Naev. ap. Cic. Sen. 6, 20 (Com. Rel. p. 14 Rib.): scriptorum magna ingenia, Sall. C. 8, 3: in scenam, Plaut. Ps. 1, 5, 155: quibus feminis menstrua non proveniunt, Cels. 2, 7.— In partic. To come forth, be brought forth, be born; to originate, arise, be produced (post-Aug.; cf. progigno): deductis olim, quique mox provenere, haec patria est, were bor

proventus.full: prōventus, ūs, m. provenio, a coming forth, growing up, growth, increase; produce, yield, crop (not in Cic.; syn. reditus). Lit.: proventu oneret sulcos, Verg. G. 2, 518: papilionis, Plin. 18, 25, 57, § 209: rosarum, id. 21, 5, 11, § 22: olei, id. 17, 21, 19, § 93: lactis, id. 20, 12, 48, § 122: uberi vinearum proventu, Suet. Claud. 16 fin.: ficus trifero proventu, Plin. 15, 18, 19, § 71; Amm. 22, 8, 32; Sen. Ben. 4, 33, 2; id. Ep. 114, 1; cf.: equinus proventus, Sol. 45, 5.— In plur.: frugum, C

proverbialis.full: prōverbĭālis, e, adj. proverbium, proverbial (post-class.): versus, Gell. 2, 22, 24.—Adv.: prōverbĭālĭter, proverbially, Amm. 29, 2, 25; Sid. Ep. 7, 9; Don. ad Ter. Eun. 2, 2, 37.

proverbium.full: prōverbĭum, ĭi, n. pro-verbum. An old saying, a saw, maxim, adage, proverb (class.; syn. adagium): ex quo illud factum est jam tritum sermone proverbium, etc., Cic. Off. 1, 10, 33; cf. id. ib. 3, 19, 77: in proverbii consuetudinem venire, id. ib. 2, 15, 55: illud in proverbium venit, Liv. 40, 46: quod est Graecis hominibus in proverbio, Cic. Verr. 2, 1, 20, § 53; id. Or. 70, 235: quod proverbii loco dici solet, id. Phil. 13, 12, 27: proverbii locum obtinere, id. Tusc. 4, 16, 36: vulgare, id. Fam

proversus.full: prōversus, a, um, Part., from proverto.
proversus.short: prōversus, a, um, Part., from proverto.

proverto.full: prō-verto (-vorto), no perf., sum, 3, v. a., to turn forwards (ante-class.): ut transversus, non proversus cedit, quasi cancer solet, turned forwards, i. e. straightforwards, Plaut. ap. Varr. L. L. 7, § 81 Müll.: provorsum fulgur appellatur, quod ignoratur noc tu an interdiu sit factum, etc., Fest. p. 229 Müll.

providens.full: prōvĭdens, entis, Part. and P.a., from provideo.

providenter.full: prōvĭdenter, adv., v. provideo, P. a. A. fin.

providentia.full: prōvĭdentĭa, ae, f. provideo. Foresight, foreknowledge: providentia est, per quam futurum aliquid videtur ante quam factum sit, Cic. Inv. 2, 53, 160: timoris tormentum memoria reducit, providentia anticipat, Sen. Ep. 5, 9.— Foresight, forethought, forecast, precaution, providence (cf. prudentia): deorum providentiā mundum administrari, Cic. Div. 1, 51, 117; cf. id. N. D. 1, 8, 18; 2, 22, 58; Quint. 11, 1, 23: alterum ex providentiā timorem afferre solet, Sall. J. 7, 5: plurimum tibi et usus et p

provideo.full: prō-vĭdĕo, vīdi, vīsum, 2, v. n. and a. Neutr. Lit., to see forwards or before one's self, to see in the distance, to discern, descry (very rare): ubi, quid petatur, procul provideri nequeat, Liv. 44, 35, 12.— Trop. To be provident or cautious, to act with foresight, to take care (rare but class.; syn. praecaveo): actum de te est, nisi provides. Cic. Fam. 9, 18, 4; id. Rab. Post. 1, 1: nisi providisses, tibi ipsi pereundum fuisset, Cic. Verr. 2, 1, 61, § 157.— To see to, look after, care for; to

providus.full: prōvĭdus, a, um, adj. provideo. Foreseeing: mens provida rerum futurarum, Cic. Div. 2, 57, 117: nec eum provida futuri, fefellit opinio, Liv. 23, 36: fati, Tib. 2, 5, 12: veri providus augur, Ov. M. 12, 18: nec futuri providus est nec praeteriti memor, Sen. Ep. 66, 35.— Cautious, circumspect, provident, prudent (syn.: cautus, consideratus): homines parum cauti providique, Cic. Rosc. Am. 40, 117: animal hoc providum, sagax ... quem vocamus hominem, id. Leg. 1, 7, 22: orator prudens et providus, i

provincia.full: prōvincĭa, ae (old gen. PROVINCIAI, Inscr. Grut. 376, 6) [etym. dub.; perh. contr. for pro-noventia (cf. nuntius), the charge or government of a legate]. A province, i. e. a territory out of Italy, acquired by the Romans (chiefly by conquest), and brought under Roman government; freq., also, to be rendered provincial administration, employment, etc.: Sicilia prima omnium provincia est appellata, Cic. Verr. 2, 2, 1, § 2: defendo provinciam Siciliam, id. Div. in Caecil. 2, 5: provincia Syria, id.

provincialis.full: prōvincĭālis, e, adj. provincia, of or belonging to a province, provincial: administratio, Cic. Q. Fr. 1, 1, 15, § 43: scientia, the administration of a province, id. ib. 1, 1, 7, § 20: edictum, belonging to a province, Cic. Verr. 2, 1, 46, § 118: molestia, arising from the administration of a province, id. Fam. 2, 7, 4: abstinentia, observed in the administration of a province, id. Sest. 3, 7: integritas, id. ib. 5, 13: ornamenta et commoda, id. Red. in Sen. 14, 34: parsimonia, Tac. Agr. 4: bel

provinciatim.full: prōvincĭātim, adv. id., through the provinces, province by province: legiones provinciatim distribuit, Suet. Aug. 49; Amm. 31, 4, 4.

provinco.full: prō-vinco, vīci, victum, 3, v. a., to conquer before, Paul. ex Fest. s. v. Provinciae, p. 226 Müll.

provindemiator.full: prō-vindēmĭātor, ōris, m., a star over the right shoulder of Virgo, which rises just before the vintage; called also Vindemiatrix, Vindemiator, Vindemitor, the Gr. προτρυγητής, Vitr. 9, 4, 1 Schneid. N. cr. (al. provindemia).
provindemiator.short: prō-vindēmĭātor, ōris, m., a star over the right shoulder of Virgo, which rises just before the vintage;

provisio.full: prōvīsĭo, ōnis, f. provideo. A foreseeing, foreknowing: provisio animi, Cic. Tusc. 3, 14, 30.— Foresight, providence: genus longā animi provisione fugiendum, Cic. Or. 56, 189.— Forethought, precaution for a thing: posteri temporis, Cic. Part. 20, 69: annonaria, i. e. a providing with provisions, purveying, Treb. XXX. Tyrann. 18.— Hindrance, prevention of a thing: horum incommodorum una cautio est atque una provisio, ut, etc., Cic. Lael. 21, 78.

proviso1.full: prōvīsō, adv., v. provideo fin. B.

proviso2.full: prō-vīso, ĕre, v. n. and a., to go or come forth to see (ante-class.): proviso, quid agat Pamphilus, Ter. And. 5, 5, 1: huc proviso, ut, ubi tempus siet, Deducam, id. Eun. 3, 1, 4; id. Ad. 5, 6, 1 (proviso duas res significat: procedo et video, Don.).—With acc.: si quem hominem exspectant, eum solent provisere, to be on the lookout for him, Plaut. Stich. 5, 1, 2.

provisor.full: prōvīsor, ōris, m. provideo. * A foreseer: ingruentium dominationum, Tac. A. 12, 4.— A provider: utilium tardus, Hor. A. P. 164: PROVISORI. EIVSDEM. PROVINCIAE, Inscr. Orell. 105: ORDINIS (decurionum), ib. 3766: civitatis, Vulg. 2 Macc. 4, 2.

provisus1.full: prōvīsus, a, um, Part., from provideo.
provisus1.short: prōvīsus, a, um, Part., from provideo.

provisus2.full: prōvīsus, ūs (only in abl. sing.), m. provideo (Tacitean). * A looking before, looking into the distance: ne oculi quidem provisu juvabant, Tac. H. 3, 22.— Trop. * A foreseeing: periculi, Tac. A. 1, 27.— A caring for or furnishing beforehand, precaution, providing, providence: deūm, Tac. A. 12, 6: dispositu provisuque civilium rerum peritus, id. H. 2, 5: rei frumentariae, id. A. 15, 8: curā, provisu deinde agere ac si hostis ingrueret, id. ib. 12, 12.

provivo.full: prō-vīvo, ĕre, v. n., to live on: quam spe sustentatam provixisse reor, Tac. A. 6, 25.

provocabilis.full: prōvŏcābĭlis, e, adj. provoco, easily aroused, excitable (post-class.): motus liquidorum, Cael. Aur. Acut. 3, 21, 198.

provocabulum.full: prō-vŏcābŭlum, i, n., a word that is used for another, a pronoun, Auct. ap. Varr. L. L. 8, § 45 Müll.
provocabulum.short: prō-vŏcābŭlum, i, n., a word that is used for another, a pronoun, Auct.

provocaticius.full: prōvŏcātīcĭus, a, um, adj. provoco, called forth, excited (post-class.): animatio, Tert. adv. Marc. 2, 3.

provocatio.full: prōvŏcātĭo, ōnis, f. id.. A calling out, summoning, challenging to combat (post-Aug.): ex provocatione hostem interemit, Vell. 1, 12, 4; Plin. 7, 20, 19, § 81; 7, 28, 29, § 101; 33, 1, 4, § 12.— A stimulus, provocation, encouragement (late Lat.): in provocationem caritatis, Vulg. Heb. 10, 24. — A citation before a higher tribunal, an appeal (freq. and class.): ad populum provocatio esto, Cic. Leg. 3, 3, 6; cf.: Publicola legem ad populum tulit ... ne quis magistratus civem Romanum adversus provo

provocativus.full: prōvŏcātīvus, a, um, adj. id., called forth, elicited (post-class.). Pass.: crementa animae, Tert. Anim. 37 ext.— Act., calling forth, eliciting: unguenta, Cael. Aur. Acut. 3, 4, 40.

provocator.full: prōvŏcātor, ōris, m. id.. In gen., a challenger to combat, Liv. Epit. 48 med.; Just. 10, 3, 3; 33, 4, 12; Gell. 9, 13, 4; Flor. 2, 17, 11.— In partic., a kind of gladiator, Cic. Sest. 64, 134; Inscr. Orell. 2566 and 2568.

provocatorius.full: prōvŏcātōrĭus, a, um, adj. provocator, of or belonging to challenging, provocatory: dona, given to one who had challenged and slain an enemy, Gell. 2, 11, 3.

provocatrix.full: prōvŏcātrix, īcis, f. id., she that entices (post-class.): improbitas, Lact. 6, 18 med.; Vulg. Soph. 3, 1.

provoco.full: prō-vŏco, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. and n., to call forth, call out. Lit. In gen. (very rare): aliquem, Plaut. Ps. 2, 2, 43: ut ubi illaec prodeat, me provoces, id. Mil. 4, 3, 28; id. Bacch. 3, 3, 40: mandant, ut ad se provocet Simonidem, Phaedr. 4, 23, 25: dum rota Luciferi provocet orta diem, lead up, call forth, Tib. 1, 9, 62: Memnonis mater roseo provocet ore diem, Ov. P. 1, 4, 58; cf. id. F. 1, 456: provocare et elicere novas radiculas, Col. 3, 15, 5.— In partic. To call out, challenge, invite on

provolo.full: prō-vŏlo, āvi, 1, v. n., to fly forth. Lit., Plin. 10, 58, 79, § 159: apes, id. 11, 18, 19, § 62.— Transf., to hurry or hasten forth, to rush out (class.): capillo passo in viam provolarunt, Quadrig. ap. Gell. 2, 19, 8: subito omnibus copiis provolaverunt, Caes. B. G. 2, 19, 6: in primum infestis hastis provolant duo Fabii, Liv. 2, 46 fin.; cf. id. 3, 62 fin.: ad primores provolat, id. 1, 12: formicae provolant, Plin. 11, 31, 36, § 111.— Of things: sonitus provolat ictu, flies forth or out, Lucr

provolvo.full: prō-volvo, volvi, vŏlūtum, 3, v. a. Lit. In gen., to roll or tumble forwards, to roll along, roll over and over, roll away (class., but not in Cic.): aliquem in viam mediam, Ter. And. 4, 4, 37: corpora, Lucr. 6, 1264: ubi glaeba e terrā provolvitur ingens, id. 6, 553: cupas ardentes in opera, Hirt. B. G. 8, 42: congestas lapidum moles, Tac. A. 4, 51: Galba projectus e sellā ac provolutus est, id. H. 1, 41; Verg. A. 12, 533; 10, 556.— In partic., with se or mid., to cast one's self down, fall dow

provomo.full: prō-vŏmo, ĕre, v. a., to vomit forth: vim turbinis atque procellae, Lucr. 6, 447.

provorsus.full: prōvorsus, a, um, Part., from proverto (-vorto).
provorsus.short: prōvorsus, a, um, Part., from proverto (-vorto).

provulgo.full: pro-vulgo (-volgo), āvi, ātum, 1, v. a., to make publicly known, to publish, divulge (post-Aug.): conjurationibus provulgatis, Suet. Ner. 36: operam, Sid. Ep. 9, 11: eas litteras, App. Mag. 84, p. 327, 20: facti miraculum, Sulp. Sev. Chron. 2, 5, 4; Tert. adv. Marc. 4, 21.

prox.full: prox (bona vox, Fest. p. 253 Müll.; cf.: prox, bona vox, ut aestimo, quasi proba vox, Paul. ex Fest. p. 252 Müll.), interj., by your leave, Plaut. Ps. 5, 1, 33 Fleck.

proxeneta.full: proxĕnēta, ae, m., = προξενητής, a negotiator, factor, broker, agent, Sen. Ep. 119; Mart. 10, 3, 4; Dig. 50, 14, 2.
proxeneta.short: proxĕnēta, ae, m., = προξενητής, a negotiator, factor, broker, agent, Sen.

proxeneticum.full: proxĕnētĭcum, i, n., = προξενητικόν, brokerage, factorage, Dig. 50, 14, 1; 3.
proxeneticum.short: proxĕnētĭcum, i, n., = προξενητικόν, brokerage, factorage, Dig.

proximatus.full: proxĭmātus, ūs, m. proximus, the next place after that of the magister scriniorum, the proximate, Cod. Th. 6, 26, 11 and 17.

proxime.full: proxĭmē (proxŭmē), adv., v. propior, II. fin.

proximitas.full: proxĭmĭtas, ātis, f. proximus, nearness, vicinity, proximity. Lit., Vitr. 2, 9 med.; Ov. de Nuce, 56.— Trop. Near relationship, Ov. M. 10, 340; 13, 154; Quint. 3, 6, 95.— Similarity, resemblance: et lateat vitium proximitate boni, Ov. A. A. 2, 662; Ap. Asclep. p. 79, 2.— Connection, union, App. Dogm. Plat. 2, p. 20, 15.

proximo1.full: proxĭmō, adv. id., very lately, Cic. Att. 4, 17, 3.

proximo2.full: proxĭmo, āre, v. n. and a. [id.], to come or draw near, to approach, be near (only post - class.; for in Cic. N. D. 2, 44, 112, we should read proxima): dum in vicum proximamus, App. M. 2, p. 169 Oud.; p. 179 Bip.: alicui, Sol. 48: foribus, App. M. 6, p. 389 Oud.: ripam maris, id. ib. 11, p. 785 Oud.: luce proximante, id. ib. 5, p. 332 Oud.: per quam proximamus ad Deum, Vulg. Heb. 7, 19.

proximus.full: proxĭmus (proxŭmus), a, um, v. propior, II.

prudens.full: prūdens, entis, adj. contr. from providens. Foreseeing, foreknowing (very rare); constr. with an objective clause, or absol.: ille contra urinam spargit, prudens, hanc quoque leoni exitialem, Plin. 8, 38, 57, § 136: quos prudentis possumus dicere, id est providentis, Cic. Div. 1, 49, 111: de futuro satis callidus satisque prudens, Ps.-Sall. ap. Cic. init.— Transf. Knowing, skilled, experienced, versed, practised in a thing (class.; syn.: peritus, consultus); constr. with gen. or in; poet. and po

prudentia.full: prūdentĭa, ae, f. prudens. A foreseeing (very rare): id enim est sapientis providere: ex quo sapientia est appellata prudentia, Cic. Fragm. ap. Non. 41, 31: futurorum, id. Sen. 21, 78.— Acquaintance with a thing, knowledge of a matter, skill in a matter: juris publici, Cic. de Or. 1, 60, 256: juris civilis, Nep. Cim. 2, 1: legum, Cic. Rep. 2, 36, 61; cf. id. Mur. 13, 28: physicorum, id. Div. 2, 4, 11: cani rectoris, Juv. 12, 32; 10, 48.— Esp., = juris prudentia, Just. Inst. praef. § 2.— Sagacity

prudentius.full: Prūdentĭus, ĭi, m., Aurelius Prudentius Clemens, a Christian poet of Calagurris, in Spain, who lived in the latter half of the fourth century, Sid. Ep. 2, 9; Alcim. Avit. ad Fascin. Sor. 416.
prudentius.short: Prūdentĭus, ĭi, m., Aurelius Prudentius Clemens, a Christian poet of Calagurris, in Spain, who lived in the latter half of the fourth century, Sid.

prugnum.full: prugnum, pro privignum, Paul. ex Fest. p. 226 Müll.

pruina.full: prŭīna, ae, f. for provina; root pra-, prae; cf. Gr. πρωΐ, early, hoar-frost, rime (cf.: glacies, gelu), Cic. N. D. 2, 10, 26; Sen. Q. N. 4, 3 fin.; Plin. 2, 60, 61, § 152; Varr. R. R. 2, 2; Lucr. 2, 431 et saep.—In plur.: pruinae ac nives, Cic. Cat. 2, 10, 23; Hor. C. 1, 4, 4: matutinae, Ov. M. 3, 488; Val. Fl. 2, 287 al.— Transf. Snow (poet. and in post-class. prose): nix concreta pruinā, Lucr. 3, 20: gelidae, Verg. G. 2, 263; 3, 368; Val. Fl. 8, 210; Gell. 12, 5, 11.— Ad medias sementem exten

pruinosus.full: prŭīnōsus, a, um, adj. pruina. Full of hoar-frost, frosty, rimy: herbae, Ov. M. 4, 82: nox, id. Am. 2, 19, 22: axis (Aurorae), id. ib. 1, 6, 65; 1, 13, 2: equi Noctis, id. P. 1, 2, 56: caeli status, Col. 4, 23, 2. —* Transf.: panni, cold, i. e. affording no warmth, Petr. 83 fin.

pruna.full: prūna root in Gr. πῦρ, fire, ae, f., a burning coal, live coal (cf. carbo): medium per ignem multā premimus vestigia prunā, Verg. A. 11, 788 Serv.; 5, 103: latum clavum prunaeque batillum, Hor. S. 1, 5, 36; Plin. 20, 6, 23, § 54; 29, 3, 11, § 45 al.

prunitius.full: prūnĭtĭus (or -cĭus), a, um, adj. prunus, of or from plum-tree wood: torris, Ov. M. 12, 272.

prunulum.full: prūnŭlum, i, n. dim. prunum, a little plum, Front. de Or. 1 Mai.

prunum.full: prūnum, i, n. prunus, a plum: cerea, Verg. E. 2, 53: cereola, Col. 10, 404; 12, 10, 2; Plin. 15, 13, 13, § 44: spini jam pruna ferentes, Verg. G. 4, 145; Ov. M. 13, 817; Mart. 13, 29, 1.

prunus.full: prūnus, i, f., = προύνη, a plum-tree, Verg. G. 2, 34; Plin. 13, 10, 19, § 65; Pall. Nov. 7, 14; id. Feb. 25, 32.—Esp.: prunus silvestris, the blackthorn, sloe-tree, Col. 2, 2, 20; Plin. 18, 6, 7, § 34.
prunus.short: prūnus, i, f., = προύνη, a plum-tree, Verg.

pruriginosus.full: prūrīgĭnōsus, a, um, adj. prurigo. Having the itch, scabby, pruriginous, Dig. 21, 1, 3.— Lecherous, lascivious, Auct. Priap. 64.

prurigo.full: prūrīgo, ĭnis, f. prurio. An itching, the itch, Cels. 2, 8; Plin. 23, 8, 80, § 154 (al. porriginem); 25, 11, 87, § 136; 27, 4, 5, § 18; Mart. 14, 23, 1.— A lecherous itching, lasciviousness, Mart. 4, 48, 3; 11, 73, 3; Aus. Epigr. 108, 5.

prurio.full: prūrĭo, īre, v. n. etym. dub.; cf. pruna, to itch. Lit.: si prurit frictus ocelli angulus, Juv. 6, 578: os prurit, Scrib. Comp. 193.— Transf., to itch or long for a thing. For blows, stripes, etc., Plaut. Poen. 5, 5, 36; id. Am. 1, 1, 139; id. Bacch. 5, 2, 75; id. Mil. 2, 4, 44: vitulus prurit in pugnam, is eager for the combat, Mart. 3, 58, 11.— For pleasure, to be wanton, Plaut. Pers. 1, 1, 32; id. Stich. 5, 5, 15; Cat. 88, 2; Mart. 3, 93, 20; 6, 37, 3; 9, 91, 8: incipiant prurire choro puella

pruriosus.full: prūrĭōsus, a, um, adj. prurio. That causes itching: bulbus, Cael. Aur. Tard. 2, 1, 33.— Excited by desire: puella, Priap. 63, 18.

pruritivus.full: prūrītīvus, a, um, adj. pruritus, that causes itching, itching: ulcera, Plin. 19, 8, 45, § 157.

pruritus.full: prūrītus, ūs, m. prurio, an itching, the itch, Plin. 9, 45, 68, § 146; 23, 1, 16, § 26; 24, 6, 14, § 23; 27, 7, 28, § 51; 30, 3, 8, § 26; Ser. Samm. 6, 87.— Esp., of sensual desire, Mart. Cap. 1, § 7.

prusa.full: Prūsa, ae, f., a town of Bithynia, near Mount Olympus, now Brussa, Plin. 5, 32, 43, § 148.—Hence, Prūsenses, ĭum, m., the inhabitants of Prusa, Plin. Ep. 10, 66, 3 al.
prusa.short: Prūsa, ae, f., a town of Bithynia, near Mount Olympus, now Brussa, Plin.

prusias.full: Prūsĭas, ae, and Prūsĭa, ae, m., = Προυσίας, a king of Bithynia, who hospitably received Hannibal, but afterwards betrayed him to the Romans, Cic. Div. 2, 24, 52; Nep. Hann. 10, 1; Just. 32, 4, 2; Liv. 37, 25; Val. Max. 3, 7, 6 ext.—Form Prusia, Liv. 29, 12, 14.—Hence, Prūsĭăcus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Prusias, Prusiacan: orae, i. e. his kingdom, Sil. 13, 888.— Prūsĭădes, ae, m., a male descendant of (an older) Prusias, a Prusiade, applied to king Prusias himself, Varr. ap. Non. 345, 23
prusias.short: Prūsĭas, ae, and Prūsĭa, ae, m., = Προυσίας, a king of Bithynia, who hospitably received Hannibal, but afterwards betrayed him to the Romans, Cic.

prusinius.full: prūsĭnĭus, a, um, adj., a kind of grape, Plin. 14, 3, 7, § 39.
prusinius.short: prūsĭnĭus, a, um, adj., a kind of grape, Plin.

prymnesius.full: prymnēsĭus, a, um, adj., = πρυμνήσιος, belonging to the stern of a ship: funis, Isid. 19, 4, 6: palus, Paul. ex Fest. p. 224, 16 Müll.
prymnesius.short: prymnēsĭus, a, um, adj., = πρυμνήσιος, belonging to the stern of a ship: funis, Isid.

prytanes.full: prўtănes or prўtănis, is, m., = πρύτανις, one of the chief magistrates in some of the Grecian States, Sen. Tranq. 4, 5; acc. prytanin, Liv. 42, 45, 4.
prytanes.short: prўtănes or prўtănis, is, m., = πρύτανις, one of the chief magistrates in some of the Grecian States, Sen.

prytaneum.full: prўtănēum, i, n., = πρυτανεῖον, the town-hall, a public building in some of the Grecian states, where the Prytanes assembled and dined, and where those who had done special service to the State were entertained at the public expense, Cic. de Or. 1, 54, 232; Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 53, § 119; Liv. 41, 20.—Also in RHEGIVM, Inscr. Orell. 3838; in Cyzicum, Plin. 36, 15, 23, § 99.
prytaneum.short: prўtănēum, i, n., = πρυτανεῖον, the town-hall, a public building in some of the Grecian states, where the Prytanes assembled and dined, and where those who had done special service to the State were entertained at the public expense, Cic.

psacae.full: Psacae, ārum, m., a people of Scythia, near the river Imaus, Plin. 6, 17, 19, § 50.
psacae.short: Psacae, ārum, m., a people of Scythia, near the river Imaus, Plin.

psallo.full: psallo, i, 3, v. n., = ψάλλω. In gen., to play upon a stringed instrument; esp., to play upon the cithara, to sing to the cithara: psallere saltare elegantius, Sall. C. 25, 2 (but in Cic. Cat. 2, 10, 23 the correct read. is saltare et cantare; v. Halm ad h. l.): qui canerent voce et qui psallerent, Gell. 19, 9, 3; cf.: cantare et psallere jucunde, Suet. Tit. 3; Aur. Vict. Epit. 14: docta psallere Chia, Hor. C. 4, 13, 7; id. Ep. 2, 1, 33. —Of singing to the cithara: Calliope princeps sapienti psa

psalma.full: psalma, ătis, n., = ψάλμα, a song sung to the accompaniment of stringed instruments, a psalm (eccl. Lat.). Aug. in Psa. 4; Hier. Ep. 28; Isid. Orig. 6, 19.
psalma.short: psalma, ătis, n., = ψάλμα, a song sung to the accompaniment of stringed instruments, a psalm (eccl.

psalmicen.full: psalmĭcen, ĭnis, m. psalmus-cano, a psalm-singer (eccl. Lat.), Sid. Ep. 5, 17.

psalmidicus.full: psalmĭdĭcus, i, m. psalma-dico, the psalmist (eccl. Lat.), Aug. Alterc. Eccl. et Synag. p. 1137.

psalmisonus.full: psalmĭsŏnus, i, m. psalma-sono, a psalm-singer, Alcim. Homil. Fragm. 7.

psalmista.full: psalmista, ae, m., = ψαλμιστής, a composer or singer of psalms, a psalm-writer, psalm-singer, psalmist (eccl. Lat.), Hier. adv. Pelag. 1, 2; 3, 2; Ambros. Poen. 2, 8, 72.
psalmista.short: psalmista, ae, m., = ψαλμιστής, a composer or singer of psalms, a psalm-writer, psalm-singer, psalmist (eccl.

psalmographus.full: psalmogrăphus, i, m., = ψαλμογράφος, a psalm - writer, psalmographer (eccl. Lat.), Tert. Carm. adv. Marc. 3, 130; Sid. in Conc. post Ep. 7, 9.
psalmographus.short: psalmogrăphus, i, m., = ψαλμογράφος, a psalm - writer, psalmographer (eccl.

psalmus.full: psalmus, i, m., = ψαλμός, i. q. psalma, a psalm (eccl. Lat.; cf.: carmen, hymnus), Tert. adv. Prax. 11; Lact. 4, 8, 14; 4, 12, 7; Vulg. Isa. 38, 20.—Esp., the Psalms of David, Vulg. Luc. 20, 42; id. Act. 13, 33 et saep.

psalterium.full: psaltērĭum, ĭi, n., = ψαλτήριον (e scanned short, Ven. Fort. 2, 19, 43). A stringed instrument of the lute kind, a psaltery, Varr. ap. Non. 215, 16; Cic. Har. Resp. 21, 44; Verg. Cir. 178; Quint. 1, 10, 31; Arn. 6, 209; Aug. in Psa. 32; 70; Tert. Cor. Mil. 9; Vulg. 1 Par. 13, 8; id. Psa. 56, 8.— Transf., a song sung to the psaltery. A satire, Varr. ap. Non. 101, 3; Paul. Sent. 5, 4, 16.— The songs of David, the Psalms, Hier. Ep. 53, 8; 125, 11 et saep.
psalterium.short: psaltērĭum, ĭi, n., = ψαλτήριον (e scanned short, Ven.

psaltes.full: psaltes, ae, m., = ψαλτής, a player on the cithara, a musician, minstrel, Quint. 1, 10, 18; Mart. Cap. 9, § 924; Sid. Ep. 8, 9; Inscr. Grut. 331, 2; Vulg. 2 Reg. 23, 1.
psaltes.short: psaltes, ae, m., = ψαλτής, a player on the cithara, a musician, minstrel, Quint.

psaltria.full: psaltrĭa, ae, f., = ψάλτρια, a female player on the cithara, a lutist, Ter. Ad. 3, 3, 34; 51; 4, 7, 41 et saep.; Cic. Sest. 54, 116; id. Fragm. ap. Non. 465, 16; Juv. 6, 336; Aur. Vict. Epit. 76; Macr. S. 2, 1.
psaltria.short: psaltrĭa, ae, f., = ψάλτρια, a female player on the cithara, a lutist, Ter.

psamathe.full: Psămăthē, ēs, f., = Ψαμάθη. Daughter of Crotopus, king of Argos, Ov. Ib. 575.— A sea-nymph, mother of Phocus, Ov. M. 11, 398.— A fountain in Laconia, near Psamathus, Plin. 4, 5, 9, § 17; Val. Fl. 1, 365.

psamathus.full: Psamăthūs (Psamm-), untis, f., = Ψαμμαθοῦς, a town and harbor of Laconia, Plin. 4, 5, 8, § 16.
psamathus.short: Psamăthūs (Psamm-), untis, f., = Ψαμμαθοῦς, a town and harbor of Laconia, Plin.

psammetichus.full: Psammĕtĭchus, i, m., = Ψαμμέτιχος, a king of Egypt, who is said to have been the designer of the labyrinth, Plin. 36, 13, 19, § 84; Mel. 1, 9, 5.
psammetichus.short: Psammĕtĭchus, i, m., = Ψαμμέτιχος, a king of Egypt, who is said to have been the designer of the labyrinth, Plin.

psaranus.full: psārānus or psārōnĭus, ĭi, m., = ψαρώνιος, a precious stone, otherwise unknown, Plin. 36, 22, 43, § 157.
psaranus.short: psārānus or psārōnĭus, ĭi, m., = ψαρώνιος, a precious stone, otherwise unknown, Plin.

psecas1.full: psĕcas, ădis, f., = ψεκάς (drizzle), a female slave who perfumed her mistress's hair, Juv. 6, 489: psecade natus, a phrase denoting a man of humble birth, Cael. ap. Cic. Fam. 8, 15, 2.
psecas1.short: psĕcas, ădis, f., = ψεκάς (drizzle), a female slave who perfumed her mistress's hair, Juv.

psecas2.full: Psĕcăs, ădis, f., the name of an attendant of Diana, Ov. M. 3, 172.
psecas2.short: Psĕcăs, ădis, f., the name of an attendant of Diana, Ov.

psegma.full: psēgma, ătis, a false read. for smegma, Plin. 34, 13, 36, § 134.

pselcis.full: Pselcis, ĭdis, f., = Ψέλκις, a town of Ethiopia, now Dakke, Plin. 6, 29, 35, § 181.
pselcis.short: Pselcis, ĭdis, f., = Ψέλκις, a town of Ethiopia, now Dakke, Plin.

psephisma.full: psēphisma, ătis, n., = ψήφισμα, an ordinance of the people among the Greeks = the plebiscitum of the Romans, Cic. Fl. 6, 15; 7, 17; 8, 19; 10, 23; Plin. Ep. 10, 52, 1.
psephisma.short: psēphisma, ătis, n., = ψήφισμα, an ordinance of the people among the Greeks = the plebiscitum of the Romans, Cic.

psephopaectes.full: psēphŏpaectes, ae, m., = ψηφοπαίκτης, a juggler (pure Lat. praestigiator), Jul. Firm.
psephopaectes.short: psēphŏpaectes, ae, m., = ψηφοπαίκτης, a juggler (pure Lat.

psesii.full: Psēsĭi or Psessĭi, ōrum, m., = Ψήσιοι, an Asiatic tribe near the Mœotic Lake, Plin. 6, 7, 7, § 19 (al. Gnissi).
psesii.short: Psēsĭi or Psessĭi, ōrum, m., = Ψήσιοι, an Asiatic tribe near the Mœotic Lake, Plin.

psetta.full: psetta or psitta, ae, f., = ψῆττα, a species of plaice or sole, called also rhombus, Plin. 9, 16, 24, § 57.
psetta.short: psetta or psitta, ae, f., = ψῆττα, a species of plaice or sole, called also rhombus, Plin.

pseudanchusa.full: pseudanchūsa or pseudoan-chūsa, ae, f., = ψευδάγχουσα, a plant, bastard-anchusa, alkanet, oxtongue, bugloss, Plin. 22, 20, 24, § 50.
pseudanchusa.short: pseudanchūsa or pseudoan-chūsa, ae, f., = ψευδάγχουσα, a plant, bastard-anchusa, alkanet, oxtongue, bugloss, Plin.

pseudapostolus.full: pseudăpostŏlus, i, m., = ψευδαπόστολος, a false apostle, Tert. Praescr. 4; id. Res. Carn. 24; Vulg. 2 Cor. 11, 13.
pseudapostolus.short: pseudăpostŏlus, i, m., = ψευδαπόστολος, a false apostle, Tert.

pseudenedrus.full: pseudĕnĕdrus, i, m., = ψευδένεδρος, a feigned lier-in-wait, Firm. Math. 3, 8, 7 fin.
pseudenedrus.short: pseudĕnĕdrus, i, m., = ψευδένεδρος, a feigned lier-in-wait, Firm.

pseudisodomos.full: pseudīsŏdŏmos, i, m., = ψευδισόδομος, a disproportionate building, Vitr. 2, 8; Plin. 36, 22, 51, § 171.
pseudisodomos.short: pseudīsŏdŏmos, i, m., = ψευδισόδομος, a disproportionate building, Vitr.

pseudoantoninus.full: Pseudŏ-antōnīnus, i, m., the false Antoninus, Pseudo - Antoninus, Lampr. Elag. 8.
pseudoantoninus.short: Pseudŏ-antōnīnus, i, m., the false Antoninus, Pseudo - Antoninus, Lampr.

pseudobunion.full: pseudŏbūnĭon, ĭi, n., = ψευδοβούνιον, a plant, bastard-bunion, Plin. 24, 16, 96, § 153.
pseudobunion.short: pseudŏbūnĭon, ĭi, n., = ψευδοβούνιον, a plant, bastard-bunion, Plin.

pseudocato.full: Pseudŏ-căto, ōnis, m., a sham Cato, Pseudo-Cato, Cic. Att. 1, 14, 6.
pseudocato.short: Pseudŏ-căto, ōnis, m., a sham Cato, Pseudo-Cato, Cic.

pseudochristus.full: Pseudŏ-christus, i, m., a false Christ, Pseudo-Christ, Tert. adv. Marc. 3, 3; Vulg. Matt. 24, 24.
pseudochristus.short: Pseudŏ-christus, i, m., a false Christ, Pseudo-Christ, Tert.

pseudocyperus.full: pseudŏcўpērus or pseudŏcў-prus, i, f., = ψευδοκύπειρος, a plant, falsecyperus, Plin. 17, 13, 20, § 95.
pseudocyperus.short: pseudŏcўpērus or pseudŏcў-prus, i, f., = ψευδοκύπειρος, a plant, falsecyperus, Plin.

pseudodamasippus.full: Pseudŏ-dămăsippus, i, m., falseDamasippus, Pseudo - Damasippus, Cic. Fam. 7, 23, 3.
pseudodamasippus.short: Pseudŏ-dămăsippus, i, m., falseDamasippus, Pseudo - Damasippus, Cic.

pseudodecimiana.full: pseudŏ-dĕcĭmiāna pĭra, pears similar to the decimiana pira, Plin. 15, 15, 16, § 54.
pseudodecimiana.short: pseudŏ-dĕcĭmiāna pĭra, pears similar to the decimiana pira, Plin.

pseudodiaconus.full: pseudŏ-dĭācŏnus, i, m., = ψευδοδιάκονος, a false deacon, Hier. Ep. 143, 2.
pseudodiaconus.short: pseudŏ-dĭācŏnus, i, m., = ψευδοδιάκονος, a false deacon, Hier.

pseudodictamnum.full: pseudŏdictamnum, i, n., and pseudŏdictamnos, i, f., = ψευδοδίκταμνον, bastard-dittany, Plin. 25, 8, 53, § 93; 26, 15, 90, § 154; App. Herb. 62.
pseudodictamnum.short: pseudŏdictamnum, i, n., and pseudŏdictamnos, i, f., = ψευδοδίκταμνον, bastard-dittany, Plin.

pseudodipteros.full: pseudŏdiptĕros, on, adj., = ψευδοδίπτερος, that appears to have two rows of columns, pseudodipteral: aedes, Vitr. 3, 1; 2.
pseudodipteros.short: pseudŏdiptĕros, on, adj., = ψευδοδίπτερος, that appears to have two rows of columns, pseudodipteral: aedes, Vitr.

pseudoepiscopus.full: pseudŏ-ĕpiscŏpus, i, m., = ψευδεπίσκοπος, a false bishop, Cyprian. Ep. 55.
pseudoepiscopus.short: pseudŏ-ĕpiscŏpus, i, m., = ψευδεπίσκοπος, a false bishop, Cyprian.

pseudoflavus.full: pseudŏ-flāvus, a, um, adj., not exactly yellow, yellowish: color, Marc. Emp. 8.
pseudoflavus.short: pseudŏ-flāvus, a, um, adj., not exactly yellow, yellowish: color, Marc.

pseudographus.full: pseudŏ-grăphus, a, um, adj., = ψευδογράφος, having a false superscription or title, Cassiod. Inst. Litt. 5.
pseudographus.short: pseudŏ-grăphus, a, um, adj., = ψευδογράφος, having a false superscription or title, Cassiod.

pseudoliquidus.full: pseudŏ-lĭquĭdus, a, um, adj., apparently liquid: mel, Marc. Emp. 16.
pseudoliquidus.short: pseudŏ-lĭquĭdus, a, um, adj., apparently liquid: mel, Marc.

pseudolus.full: Pseudŏlus, i, m., = ψευδής (lying), The Liar, the title of a comedy of Plautus, Cic. Lael. 14, 50.
pseudolus.short: Pseudŏlus, i, m., = ψευδής (lying), The Liar, the title of a comedy of Plautus, Cic.

pseudomenos.full: pseudŏmĕnos or -us, i, m., = ψευδόμενος; in logic, a false, sophistical species of syllogism, Cic. Ac. 2, 48, 147; id. Fragm. ap. Non. 329, 19 (as Greek, Cic. Div. 2, 4, 11; Sen. Ep. 45, 10).

pseudonardus.full: pseudŏnardus, i, f., = ψευδόναρδος, bastard-nard, Plin. 12, 12, 26, § 43.
pseudonardus.short: pseudŏnardus, i, f., = ψευδόναρδος, bastard-nard, Plin.

pseudonedrus.full: pseudŏnedrus, i, m., = ψευδόνεδρος, a secret lier-in-wait, Firm. Math. 3, 8.
pseudonedrus.short: pseudŏnedrus, i, m., = ψευδόνεδρος, a secret lier-in-wait, Firm.

pseudopastor.full: pseudŏpastor, ōris, m. ψευδής - pastor, a false pastor (eccl. Lat.), Hier. in Eph. 2, 4, 11.

pseudopatum.full: pseudŏpătum, i, n., = ψευδόπατον, a false floor (in a house), Cod. Just. 8, 10, 12.
pseudopatum.short: pseudŏpătum, i, n., = ψευδόπατον, a false floor (in a house), Cod.

pseudoperipteros.full: pseudŏpĕriptĕros, on, adj., = ψευδοπερίπτερος, that seems to have columns all round, Vitr. 4, 7 fin.
pseudoperipteros.short: pseudŏpĕriptĕros, on, adj., = ψευδοπερίπτερος, that seems to have columns all round, Vitr.

pseudophilippus.full: Pseudŏ-phĭlippus, i, m., the false Philip, Pseudo-Philip, i. e. Andriscus, who gave himself out to be Philip, son of King Perseus, Cic. Agr. 2, 33, 90; Liv. Epit. 49; Vell. 1, 11, 1; Flor. 2, 14, 3; Val. Max. 7, 5, 4.
pseudophilippus.short: Pseudŏ-phĭlippus, i, m., the false Philip, Pseudo-Philip, i.

pseudopropheta.full: pseudŏprŏphēta, ae, m., = ψευδοπροφήτης, a false prophet, Tert. adv. Haer. 4; Vulg. Zach. 13, 2; id. Luc. 6, 26.
pseudopropheta.short: pseudŏprŏphēta, ae, m., = ψευδοπροφήτης, a false prophet, Tert.

pseudoprophetia.full: pseudŏprŏphētīa, ae, f., = ψευδοπροφητεία, a false prophecy, Tert. Jejun. 11.
pseudoprophetia.short: pseudŏprŏphētīa, ae, f., = ψευδοπροφητεία, a false prophecy, Tert.

pseudopropheticus.full: pseudŏprŏphētĭcus, a, um, adj., = ψευδοπροφητικός, prophesying falsely, pseudo-prophetic: spiritus, Tert. Pudic. 21.
pseudopropheticus.short: pseudŏprŏphētĭcus, a, um, adj., = ψευδοπροφητικός, prophesying falsely, pseudo-prophetic: spiritus, Tert.

pseudoprophetis.full: pseudŏprŏphētis, ĭdis, f., = ψευδοπροφῆτις, a false prophetess, Tert. Anim. 57.
pseudoprophetis.short: pseudŏprŏphētis, ĭdis, f., = ψευδοπροφῆτις, a false prophetess, Tert.

pseudopylae.full: Pseudŏpўlae, ārum, f., = ψευδόπυλαι (false doors), the name of two islands in the Arabian Gulf, near Ethiopia, Plin. 6, 29, 34, § 174.
pseudopylae.short: Pseudŏpўlae, ārum, f., = ψευδόπυλαι (false doors), the name of two islands in the Arabian Gulf, near Ethiopia, Plin.

pseudoselinum.full: pseudŏsĕlīnum, i, n., = ψευδοσέλινον, a plant, bastard-selinum, App. Herb. 2.
pseudoselinum.short: pseudŏsĕlīnum, i, n., = ψευδοσέλινον, a plant, bastard-selinum, App.

pseudosmaragdus.full: pseudŏsmăragdus, i, m., = ψευδοσμάραγδος, a false emerald, Plin. 37, 5, 19, § 75.
pseudosmaragdus.short: pseudŏsmăragdus, i, m., = ψευδοσμάραγδος, a false emerald, Plin.

pseudosphex.full: pseudosphex, ēcis, f., = ψευδόσφηξ, a false wasp, Plin. 30, 11, 30, § 98.
pseudosphex.short: pseudosphex, ēcis, f., = ψευδόσφηξ, a false wasp, Plin.

pseudothyrum.full: pseudŏthўrum, i, n., = ψευδόθυρον. Lit., a backdoor, private entrance, postern-gate: palatii, Amm. 14, 1, 3; Oros. 7, 6 fin.— Trop., a secret manner: (nummi) per pseudothyrum revertantur, Cic. Verr. 2, 2, 20, § 50: non janua receptis, sed pseudothyro intromissis voluptatibus, id. Red. in Sen. 6, 14.

pseudourbanus.full: pseudŏ-urbānus, a, um, adj., imitating the fashion of towns: aedificia, Vitr. 6, 8 fin.
pseudourbanus.short: pseudŏ-urbānus, a, um, adj., imitating the fashion of towns: aedificia, Vitr.

psiathium.full: psĭathĭum, ĭi, n., = ψιάθιον, a little rush mat, Hier. praef. in Reg. S. Pachom. 4.
psiathium.short: psĭathĭum, ĭi, n., = ψιάθιον, a little rush mat, Hier.

psila.full: psīla, ae, f. (sc. vestis), = ψιλή, a covering shaggy on one side, a shaggy covering, Lucil. ap. Non. 540, 26.

psile.full: Psilē, ēs, f., a small island in the Ægean Sea, near Samos, Plin. 5, 31, 38, § 137.
psile.short: Psilē, ēs, f., a small island in the Ægean Sea, near Samos, Plin.

psilocitharista.full: psīlŏcĭthărista, ae, m., = ψιλοκιθαριστής, one who plays on the cithara without singing to it, a citkara-player, Suet. Dom. 4.
psilocitharista.short: psīlŏcĭthărista, ae, m., = ψιλοκιθαριστής, one who plays on the cithara without singing to it, a citkara-player, Suet.

psilothrum.full: psīlōthrum (-trum), i, n., = ψίλωθρον. An unguent for removing the hair and making the skin smooth, a depilatory, Plin. 24, 10, 47, § 79; 24, 9, 37, § 58; 32, 9, 47, § 135; Sen. Contr. 3, praef. 3; Mart. 6, 93, 9.— A plant, called also ampeloleuce, Plin. 23, 1, 16, § 21.

psimmythium.full: psimmȳthĭum or psimithĭum, ĭi, n., = ψιμμύθιον, white-lead, ceruse, = cerussa, Plin. 34, 18, 54, § 175.
psimmythium.short: psimmȳthĭum or psimithĭum, ĭi, n., = ψιμμύθιον, white-lead, ceruse, = cerussa, Plin.

psittacinus.full: psittăcīnus, a, um, adj. psittacus, of or belonging to a parrot: collyrium, parrot - colored, Scrib. Comp. 27; Marc. Emp. 8.

psittacus.full: psittăcus, i, m., = ψίττακος, a parrot, Plin. 10, 42, 58, § 117; Pers. prol. 8; Ov. Am. 2, 6, 1; Stat. S. 2, 4, 25; App. Flor. 2, p. 348.
psittacus.short: psittăcus, i, m., = ψίττακος, a parrot, Plin.

psoadicus.full: psŏădĭcus, a, um, adj., = ψοαδικός, having pains in the buttocks or loins, Cael. Aur. Tard. 5, 1.
psoadicus.short: psŏădĭcus, a, um, adj., = ψοαδικός, having pains in the buttocks or loins, Cael.

psoleos.full: psōlĕos, i, m., the penis, Auct. Priap. 68.
psoleos.short: psōlĕos, i, m., the penis, Auct.

psophis.full: Psōphis, ī^dis, f., = Ψωφίς, a city in Arcadia, west of the chain of Erymanthus, now Tripotamo, Mel. 2, 3, 5; Plin. 4, 6, 10, § 20; Ov. M. 5, 607; Stat. Th. 4, 296.— Hence, Psōphidĭus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Psophis, Plin. 7, 46, 47, § 151; Val. Max. 7, 1, 2.
psophis.short: Psōphis, ī^dis, f., = Ψωφίς, a city in Arcadia, west of the chain of Erymanthus, now Tripotamo, Mel.

psophodees.full: Psŏphŏdĕes, is, m., = Ψοφοδεής, The Bashful Man, the title of a comedy of Menander, Quint. 10, 1, 70.
psophodees.short: Psŏphŏdĕes, is, m., = Ψοφοδεής, The Bashful Man, the title of a comedy of Menander, Quint.

psora.full: psōra, ae, f., = ψώρα, the itch, mange (pure Lat. scabies), Plin. 20, 1, 2, § 4; 20, 5, 20, § 41; 22, 22, 32, § 72.
psora.short: psōra, ae, f., = ψώρα, the itch, mange (pure Lat.

psoranthemis.full: psōranthĕmis, ĭdis, f., = ψωράνθεμις, a barren kind of rosemary, App. Herb. 79.
psoranthemis.short: psōranthĕmis, ĭdis, f., = ψωράνθεμις, a barren kind of rosemary, App.

psoricus.full: psōrĭcus, a, um, adj., = ψωρικός, of or for the itch or mange: medicamentum, good for the itch, Plin. 34, 12, 29, § 119: collyrium, Scrib. Comp. 32.—As subst.: psō-rĭcum, i, n., a remedy for the itch, Cels. 6, 6, 31.
psoricus.short: psōrĭcus, a, um, adj., = ψωρικός, of or for the itch or mange: medicamentum, good for the itch, Plin.

psyche.full: Psȳchē, ēs, f., = Ψυχή, Psyche, a maiden beloved by Cupid, made immortal by Jupiter, App. M. 4, p. 155 sqq.
psyche.short: Psȳchē, ēs, f., = Ψυχή, Psyche, a maiden beloved by Cupid, made immortal by Jupiter, App.

psychicus.full: psȳchĭcus, a, um, adj., = ψυχικός (opp. πνευματικός), animal, carnal, carnally inclined, Tert. Monog. 1.

psychomachia.full: psȳchŏmăchĭa, ae, f., = ψυχομαχία, The Contest of the Soul, the title of a poem by Prudentius.
psychomachia.short: psȳchŏmăchĭa, ae, f., = ψυχομαχία, The Contest of the Soul, the title of a poem by Prudentius.

psychomantium.full: psȳchŏmantīum or -ēum, i, n., = ψυχομαντεῖον, a place where the spirits of the dead were interrogated, a place of necromancy, Cic. Tusc. 1, 48, 115.—Plur., Cic. Div. 1, 58, 132.
psychomantium.short: psȳchŏmantīum or -ēum, i, n., = ψυχομαντεῖον, a place where the spirits of the dead were interrogated, a place of necromancy, Cic.

psychophthoros.full: psȳchŏphthŏros, i, m., = ψυχοφθόρος, the Soul-destroyer, an epithet of Apollinarius, who denied the existence of a human soul in Christ, Cod. Just. 1, 1, 6 fin.
psychophthoros.short: psȳchŏphthŏros, i, m., = ψυχοφθόρος, the Soul-destroyer, an epithet of Apollinarius, who denied the existence of a human soul in Christ, Cod.

psychotrophon.full: psȳchŏtrŏphon, i, n., = ψυχότροφον, a plant, betony, Plin. 25, 8, 46, § 84.
psychotrophon.short: psȳchŏtrŏphon, i, n., = ψυχότροφον, a plant, betony, Plin.

psychrolusia.full: psȳchrŏlūsĭa, ae, f., = ψυχρολουσία, a cold bathing, Cael. Aur. Acut. 1, 14, 112; id. Tard. 1, 1, 47.
psychrolusia.short: psȳchrŏlūsĭa, ae, f., = ψυχρολουσία, a cold bathing, Cael.

psychroluta.full: psȳchrŏlūta and -tes, ae, m., = ψυχρολούτης, one who bathes in cold water, Sen. Ep. 53, 3; 83, 5.
psychroluta.short: psȳchrŏlūta and -tes, ae, m., = ψυχρολούτης, one who bathes in cold water, Sen.

psylli.full: Psylli, ōrum, m., = Ψύλλοι, an African people south-west of the Syrtis Major, celebrated as serpent-charmers: qui Psylli nominantur, Cels. 5, 27, 3; Plin. 7, 2, 2, § 14; 8, 25, 38, § 93; Suet. Aug. 17; Luc. 9, 893.—Sing.: exemplum Psylli secutus, Cels. 5, 27, 3.
psylli.short: Psylli, ōrum, m., = Ψύλλοι, an African people south-west of the Syrtis Major, celebrated as serpent-charmers: qui Psylli nominantur, Cels.

psyllion.full: psyllĭon, ĭi, n., = ψύλλιον, a plant, fleabane, fleawort, Plin. 25, 11, 90, § 140; Cael. Aur. Acut. 3, 8, 97.
psyllion.short: psyllĭon, ĭi, n., = ψύλλιον, a plant, fleabane, fleawort, Plin.

psythius.full: psўthĭus or psĭthĭus, a, um, adj., = ψύθιος (ψιθ-), psythian, a designation of a species of vine: vitis, Verg. G. 4, 269; Col. 3, 2, 24.—Called also simply psўthĭa, ae, f., Verg. G. 2, 93; and in plur.: psythiae (sc. uvae), Stat. S. 4, 9, 38.—Neutr. subst.: psўthĭum, ii, a kind of raisin - wine, Plin. 14, 9, 11, § 80.
psythius.short: psўthĭus or psĭthĭus, a, um, adj., = ψύθιος (ψιθ-), psythian, a designation of a species of vine: vitis, Verg.

psyttalia.full: Psyttălĭa or Psittălīa, ae, f., = Ψυτταλία or Ψυττάλεια, a small island in the Saronic Gulf, near Salamis, Plin. 4, 12, 20, § 62.
psyttalia.short: Psyttălĭa or Psittălīa, ae, f., = Ψυτταλία or Ψυττάλεια, a small island in the Saronic Gulf, near Salamis, Plin.

ptarmicus.full: ptarmĭcus, a, um, = πταρμικός, causing to sneeze, Theod. Prisc. 2, 3; Cael. Aur. Tard. 3, 5, 71.—Hence, as subst.: ptarmĭ-cum, i, n., that which causes sneezing, Cael. Aur. Acut. 1, 15, 138.—Plur., Cael. Aur. Tard. 3, 2, 42.
ptarmicus.short: ptarmĭcus, a, um, = πταρμικός, causing to sneeze, Theod.

pte.full: -ptĕ, a pronominal suffix appended to adjective and (more rarely) to substantive personal pronouns, esp. in the ablative; the Engl. self, own: meopte ingenio, Plaut. Ps. 3, 2, 14. With adj. pron.: meāpte malitiā, Plaut. Truc. 2, 5, 18: tuopte ingenio, id. Capt. 2, 3, 11; Tac. H. 2, 63: suopte pondere, Cic. N. D. 1, 25, 69: suāpte manu, id. de Or. 3, 3, 10: nostrāpte culpā, Ter. Phorm. 5, 2, 1.— With subst. pron.: mepte fieri servum, Plaut. Men. 5, 8, 10: suumpte amicum, id. Mil. 2, 4, 38.
pte.short: -ptĕ, a pronominal suffix appended to adjective and (more rarely) to substantive personal pronouns, esp.

pteleum.full: Ptĕlĕum or -on, i, n., and Ptĕlĕŏs, i, f., = Πτελεόν. A port in Thessaly, over against Eubœa, now Pteleo, Mel. 2, 3, 6; Liv. 35, 43; 42, 67.—Form Pteleos, Luc. 6, 352.— A city in Messenia, Plin. 4, 5, 7, § 15.— A city in Ionia, Plin. 5, 29, 31, § 115 (al. Ptelea).
pteleum.short: Ptĕlĕum or -on, i, n., and Ptĕlĕŏs, i, f., = Πτελεόν.

ptenethu.full: Ptĕnĕthu, indecl. n., a district of Lower Egypt, Plin. 5, 9, 9, § 49 (Jan. Ptenethum).

pterelas.full: Ptĕrĕlas, ae, m., = Πτερέλας. A prince of Taphus, Ov. Ib. 364.— One of Actœon's hounds, Ov. M. 3, 212.

pteris.full: ptĕris, ĭdis, f., = πτερίς, a species of fern, Plin. 27, 9, 55, § 78.
pteris.short: ptĕris, ĭdis, f., = πτερίς, a species of fern, Plin.

pternix.full: pternix, ĭcis, f., = πτέρνιξ, the straight stem of a plant, Plin. 21, 16, 57, § 97.
pternix.short: pternix, ĭcis, f., = πτέρνιξ, the straight stem of a plant, Plin.

pteroma.full: ptĕrōma, ătis, n., = πτέρωμα, the colonnade on the two sides of a Grecian temple, Vitr. 3, 2; 4, 4; 7.
pteroma.short: ptĕrōma, ătis, n., = πτέρωμα, the colonnade on the two sides of a Grecian temple, Vitr.

pteron.full: ptĕron, i, n., = πτερόν, the side walls of a building, Plin. 36, 5, 4, § 30; 36, 13, 19, § 88.
pteron.short: ptĕron, i, n., = πτερόν, the side walls of a building, Plin.

pterophoros.full: Ptĕrŏphŏros, i, f., = πτεροφόρος (winged), a country near the Riphœan Mountains, Plin. 4, 12, 26, § 88.—Hence, Ptĕrŏphŏrītae, ārum, m., the inhabitants of Pterophoros, Mel. 1, 2.
pterophoros.short: Ptĕrŏphŏros, i, f., = πτεροφόρος (winged), a country near the Riphœan Mountains, Plin.

pterotos.full: ptĕrōtos, on, adj., = πτερωτός, winged, with handles: calix, Plin. 36, 26, 66, § 195 (al. petrotos).
pterotos.short: ptĕrōtos, on, adj., = πτερωτός, winged, with handles: calix, Plin.

pterygium.full: ptĕrўgĭum, ĭi, n., = πτερύγιον. A film that grows over the eye, a pearl, web, or haw, Cels. 7, 7, 4; Plin. 32, 7, 24. § 72; 34, 10, 23, § 105.— A growth of flesh over the nails, Plin. 24, 4, 5, § 9; 26, 5, 14, § 26; 27, 4, 5, § 20; 30, 12, 37, § 111; cf. Cels. 6, 19, 1.— A cloudy spot in the beryl, Plin. 37, 5, 20, § 79.

pterygoma.full: ptĕrўgōma, ătis, n., = πτερύγωμα, something shaped like a wing, a wing of a ballista, Vitr. 10, 17 dub.
pterygoma.short: ptĕrўgōma, ătis, n., = πτερύγωμα, something shaped like a wing, a wing of a ballista, Vitr.

ptisana.full: ptĭsăna, ae, f., = πτισάνη (al. tisana). Barley crushed and cleaned from the hulls, barley-groats, pearl-barley, Cels. 2, 18, 24; Mart. 12, 72, 5; Scrib. Comp. 93; Vulg. Prov. 27, 22.— Transf., a drink made from barley-groats, barley-water, ptisan, Varr. ap. Non. 550, 19; Plin. 18, 7, 15, § 74.

ptisanarium.full: ptĭsănārĭum, ii, n. ptisana, a decoction of barley-groats, or, transf., of rice: oryzae, Hor. S. 2, 3, 155; cf. Plin. 18, 7, 13, § 71.

ptocheum.full: ptōchēum or -īum,, i, n., = πτωχεῖον, a poor-house, Cod. Just. 1, 2, 15; 19.
ptocheum.short: ptōchēum or -īum,, i, n., = πτωχεῖον, a poor-house, Cod.

ptochotropheum.full: ptōchŏtrŏphēum or -īum, i, n., = πτωχοτροφεῖον, a poor-house, Cod. Just. 1, 3, 35.
ptochotropheum.short: ptōchŏtrŏphēum or -īum, i, n., = πτωχοτροφεῖον, a poor-house, Cod.

ptochotrophus.full: ptōchŏtrŏphus, i, m., = πτωχοτρόφος, an overseer of the poor, Cod. Just. 1, 3 in lemm.
ptochotrophus.short: ptōchŏtrŏphus, i, m., = πτωχοτρόφος, an overseer of the poor, Cod.

ptolemaeus.full: Ptŏlĕmaeus, i, m., = Πτολεμαῖος. Ptolemy, the name of the kings of Egypt after Alexander the Great, Curt. 9, 8, 22; Just. 13, 4, 10; Sil. 11, 383.—Hence, in plur.: Ptolemaeorum manes, Luc. 8, 696.— Hence, Ptŏlĕmaeēus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Ptolemy, Ptolemœan, Egyptian: Pharus, Prop. 2, 1, 30.— Ptŏlĕ-maeus (-maeius), a, um, adj., Ptolemœan, Ptolemaic: gymnasium, Cic. Fin. 5, 1, 1.—Subst.: Ptŏlĕmaeum, i, n., the tomb of the Ptolemies, Suet. Aug. 18.— Ptŏ-lĕmāïs, ĭdis, f. adj., Ptolemœan,

ptyas.full: ptўas, ădis, f., = πτυάς, a kind of serpent, said to spit venom into the eyes of men, Plin. 28, 6, 18, § 65; 31, 6, 33, § 65.
ptyas.short: ptўas, ădis, f., = πτυάς, a kind of serpent, said to spit venom into the eyes of men, Plin.

ptychia.full: Ptўchĭa, ae, f., = Πτυχία, an island near Corfu, now Vido, Plin. 4, 12, 19, § 53.
ptychia.short: Ptўchĭa, ae, f., = Πτυχία, an island near Corfu, now Vido, Plin.

pubeda.full: pūbēda, ae, m. pubes, a youth arrived at the age of puberty, Mart. Cap. 1, § 31; 9, § 908 (dub.; al. bupaeda).

pubens.full: pūbens, entis, adj. id., arrived at the age of puberty, pubescent (poet.). Lit.: frater, Claud. Cons. Prob. et Olybr. 142: anni, Aus. Idyll. ap. Monos. Membr. 12, 2.— Transf., of plants, in full vigor, juicy, flourishing, exuberant: herbae, Verg. G. 3, 126; id. A. 4, 514: frondes salicum, Aus. Ep. 2, 14: gramina, id. Idyll. 10, 203: rosae, Stat. S. 3, 3, 129.

pubertas.full: pūbertas, ātis, f. puber, the age of manhood or maturity, puberty. Lit.: primis pubertatis annis, Just. 9, 6, 5: ab initio pubertatis, id. 23, 1, 8; 35, 2, 2; and: circa pubertatem, Plin. 25, 13, 95, § 154: pubertatis et primae adulescentiae tempus, Suet. Dom. 1; cf. Macr. S. 7, 7: differetur quaestio in tempus pubertatis, Dig. 37, 10, 1, § 11; 37, 10, 7, § 3.— Transf. The signs of puberty, the beard, etc., Cic. N. D. 2, 33, 86; Plin. 7, 16, 17, § 76; 21, 26, 97, § 170.— Of plants, soft down, pu

pubes1.full: pūbes and pūber (cf. Prisc. p. 707 P.; also pūbis, ĕris, Caes. ib.), ĕris, adj. root pu-, to beget; in Sanscr. putras, son; pumans, man; cf.: puer, pūpa, putus, etc., that is grown up, of ripe age, adult, pubescent. Lit. (class.): pubes et puber qui generare potest: is incipit esse a quattuordecim annis: femina a duodecim viri potens, sive patiens, ut quidam putant, Fest. p. 250 Müll.; Crass. ap. Cic. de Or. 2, 55, 224: filii, Cic. Off. 1, 35, 129: priusquam pubes esset, Nep. Dion, 4, 4: ad pube

pubes2.full: pūbes (nom. pubis, Prud. Cath. 7, 162), is, f. 1. pubes, the signs of manhood, i. e. the hair which appears on the body at the age of puberty, Gr. ἥβη. Lit.: si inguen jam pube contegitur, Cels. 7, 19: capillus et pubes, Plin. 34, 8, 19, § 58.— Transf. The hair in gen.: ciliorum, Mart. Cap. 2, § 132.— The private parts, Verg. A. 3, 427; Ov. Am. 3, 12, 22; Plin. 11, 37, 83, § 208; 28, 15, 60, § 215; App. M. 10, p. 254, 3.— Collect., grown-up males, youth, young men (class.): omnem Italiae pubem,

pubesco.full: pūbesco, bŭi, 3, v. inch. n. [id.], to reach the age of puberty, become pubescent. Lit. (class.; syn. adulesco): molli pubescere veste, to put on the down of puberty, Lucr. 5, 672: flore novo, Sil. 3, 79: Herculem, cum primum pubesceret, etc., Cic. Off. 1, 32, 118: flos juvenum pubescentium ad militiam, Liv. 8, 8: puer vix pubescente juventā, Sil. 16, 678: et nunc aequali tecum pubesceret aevo, Verg. A. 3, 491: pubescere bello, Sil. 4, 429: dehinc pubescens (Tiberius), Suet. Tib. 6: pubescunt du

publicanus.full: pūblĭcānus, a, um, adj. publicus. Of or belonging to the public revenue, or to the farming of the revenue: muliercula, the wife of a farmer-general (with an odious secondary meaning), Cic. Verr. 2, 3, 34, § 78. — Subst.: pūblĭcānus, i, m. A farmer-general of the Roman revenues, usually from the equestrian order (freq. and class.; syn.: manceps, redemptor), Cic. Planc. 9, 23; id. Rab. Post. 2, 3; id. Q. Fr. 1, 1, 11, § 32; Liv. 43, 16; 25, 3; 39, 44: quod publicanus ejus publici nomine vi ademeri

publicarius.full: pūblĭcārĭus, a, um, adj. id., that makes public (post-class.), Firm. Math. 3, 8.

publicatio.full: pūblĭcātĭo, ōnis, f. publico, an adjudging to the public treasury, confiscation, Cic. Cat. 4, 5, 10; id. Planc. 41, 97.

publicater.full: pūblĭcāter, ōris, m. id., one who makes known, a publisher, proclaimer (postclass.): occulti, Sid. Ep. 3, 13.

publicatrix.full: pūblĭcātrix, īcis, f. publicator, she that publishes or exposes (post-class.), Arn. 1, 20.

publicianus.full: Publĭcĭānus, a, um, v. Publicius, B.

publicitus.full: pūblĭcĭtus, adv. publicus. On the public account, at the public expense, by or for the State (ante-class.): publicitus aurum praebere, Lucil. ap. Non. 513, 4: dare publicitus cibaria, Pompon. ib. 10: proletarius publicitus scutis Ornatur, Enn. ap. Gell. 16, 10, 1 (Ann. v. 189 Vahl.): hospitio accipi, i. e. into imprisonment, Plaut. Am. 1, 1, 8; 4, 2, 7: aurum in aede Dianae publicitus servant, id. Bacch. 2, 3, 79; Ter. Phorm. 5, 7, 85; Treb. Pol. XXX. Tyr. 18: quae (peccata) prohibere publicitus

publicius.full: Pūblĭcĭus, i, m., the name of a Roman gens; esp. the brothers L. and M. Publicius Malleolus, œdiles, Varr. L. L. 5, 32 fin.; Ov. F. 5, 288.—Hence, Pūblĭcĭus, a, um, adj., Publician: Clivus Publicius, a hill in Rome, Liv. 26, 10, 6; 27, 37 fin.; Ov. F. 5, 294.— Publĭcĭānus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to a Publicius, Publician: locus, prob. the Clivus Publicius (v. supra), Cic. Att. 12, 38, 4: actio, so called after a prætor named Publicius, Dig. 6, tit. 6; cf. Just. Inst. 4, 6, 4.
publicius.short: Pūblĭcĭus, i, m., the name of a Roman gens;

publico.full: pūblĭco, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. publicus. To make public property, to seize and adjudge to the public use, to confiscate (class.; cf. proscribo): regnum Jubae, Caes. B. C. 2, 25: bona Cingetorigis, id. B. G. 5, 54; 7, 43: privata, Cic. Agr. 2, 21, 57: bona, id. Cat. 4, 4, 8: Ptolemaeum, id. Dom. 8, 20: censeo publicandas eorum pecunias, Sall. C. 51, 43; Nep. Thras. 1, 5; Liv. 3, 58; 29, 19; Plin. Ep. 4, 11, 13: aurarias, Tac. A. 6, 19.— To show or tell to the people, to impart to the public, make p

publicus.full: pūblĭcus (in inscrr. also POBLICVS and POPLICVS), a, um, adj. contr. from populicus, from populus, of or belonging to the people, State, or community; that is done for the sake or at the expense of the State; public, common. Lit.: multi suam rem bene gessere et publicam patriā procul, the business of the State, Enn. ap. Cic. Fam. 7, 6, 1 (Trag. v. 295 Vahl.): publica magnificentia (opp. privata luxuria), Cic. Mur. 36, 76: sacrificia publica ac privata, Caes. B. G. 6, 12: injuriae, done to the St

publilius.full: Pūblĭlĭus, a, the name of a Roman gens, of whom the best known are, Publilius, brother of Publilia, second wife of Cicero, Cic. Att. 12, 32, 1.— Volero Publilius, who secured to the plebs the election of the tribunes, A. U. C. 282, Liv. 2, 55 sqq. — Publilius Syrus, a famous composer and actor of mimes, at the beginning of the eighth century A. U. C., Plin. 35, 17, 58, § 199; Macr. S. 2, 7, 6 sqq.; Sen. Ep. 8, 8; less correctly called Publius Syrus, Gell. 17, 14, 1; Sen. Tranq. 11, 8 al.; v. Wöl
publilius.short: Pūblĭlĭus, a, the name of a Roman gens, of whom the best known are, Publilius, brother of Publilia, second wife of Cicero, Cic.

publipor.full: Pūblĭpor, ŏris, m. Publius-puer, the slave of Publius. The name of a slave, Quint. 1, 4, 26.— A proper name, Sall. ap. Prisc. p. 700 P.

publius.full: Publius, ĭi, m., a Roman prœnomen; in writing, abbrev. P.; e. g. P. Lentulus, to whom are addressed the letters, Cic. Fam. 1, 1 sqq.; v. also Publilius, III.—Hence, Publĭānus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to a Publius: sententia, i. e. of Publius Syrus, Sen. Contr. 7, 18, 8 (where the better reading is Publilianae).
publius.short: Publius, ĭi, m., a Roman prœnomen;

pucinum.full: Pūcīnum, i, n., = Πούκινον, a town in Illyria, now Proseck, Plin. 3, 18, 22, § 127. —Hence, Pūcīnus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Pucinum: vinum, Plin. 14, 6, 8, § 60.
pucinum.short: Pūcīnum, i, n., = Πούκινον, a town in Illyria, now Proseck, Plin.

pudefactus.full: pŭdēfactus, a, um, Part. [pudeo-facio], ashamed: pudefactus oris deformitate, Gell. 15, 17, 1.
