Herc. Fur. 561.—Hence,
pylus.short: Pўlus and Pўlos, i, f., = Πύλος, the name of three cities of the Peloponnesus, of which one was in Arcadia;

pyra.full: pўra, ae, f., = πυρά. A funeral pile, pyre (pure Lat. rogus), Verg. A. 6, 215; 11, 185; Ov. F. 2, 534; id. Ib. 36; Auct. B. Afr. 91; Vulg. Ezech. 24, 9.— A fire, Vulg. Act. 28, 2.— Pўra, ae, f., the name of the place on Mount Œta where Hercules is said to have burned himself, Liv. 36, 30.

pyracmon.full: Pўracmon, ŏnis, m., = Πυράκμων, a Cyclops, a servant of Vulcan, Verg. A. 8, 425; Claud. Rapt. Pros. 1, 238; id. Cons. Hon. 3, 195.
pyracmon.short: Pўracmon, ŏnis, m., = Πυράκμων, a Cyclops, a servant of Vulcan, Verg.

pyracmos.full: Pўracmos, i, m., a Centaur who was present at the marriage of Pirithoüs, Ov. M. 12, 460.
pyracmos.short: Pўracmos, i, m., a Centaur who was present at the marriage of Pirithoüs, Ov.

pyrae.full: Pyrae, ārum, f., an ancient town of Latium, Plin. 3, 5, 9, § 59.
pyrae.short: Pyrae, ārum, f., an ancient town of Latium, Plin.

pyraei.full: Pyraei, ōrum, m., a people of Illyria, Plin. 3, 22, 26, § 144; Mel. 2, 3.
pyraei.short: Pyraei, ōrum, m., a people of Illyria, Plin.

pyralis.full: pўrălis (-allis), ĭdis, f., = πυραλίς, a winged insect that was supposed to live in fire, called also pyrausta = πυραύστης, or pyrota, Plin. 11, 36, 42, § 119; 10, 74, 95, § 204.
pyralis.short: pўrălis (-allis), ĭdis, f., = πυραλίς, a winged insect that was supposed to live in fire, called also pyrausta = πυραύστης, or pyrota, Plin.

pyrameus.full: Pȳrămĕus, a, um, v. 1. Pyramus, II.

pyramidatus.full: pȳrămĭdātus, a, um, adj. pyramis, pyramidal: corpuscula, a gloss ap. Cic. N. D. 1, 24, 66; formerly received into the text.)

pyramis.full: pȳrămis, ĭdis, f., = πυραμις (prob. Egyptian), a pyramid, Cic. N. D. 2, 18, 47; Prop. 3 1, 55; Mart. Spect. 1, 1; Tac. A. 2, 61; Plin. 36, 12, 16, § 75: pyramidas regum miramur, id. 36, 15, 24, § 103; Mel. 1, 9; Luc. 9, 155; Tac. A. 2, 61.— Transf., a geometrical solid figure, a pyramid, Boëth. Arith. 2, 21 sqq.

pyramus1.full: Pȳrămus, i, m., = Πύραμος, the lover of Thisbe, who, on account of her supposed death, stabbed himself under a mulberry-tree, Ov. M. 4, 55 sq. — Hence, Pȳrămĕus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Pyramus, Pyramian: arbor, i. e. the mulberry-tree, Ser. Samm. 29, 553.
pyramus1.short: Pȳrămus, i, m., = Πύραμος, the lover of Thisbe, who, on account of her supposed death, stabbed himself under a mulberry-tree, Ov.

pyramus2.full: Pȳrămus, i, m., = Πύραμος, a river in Cilicia, now the Jaihān, Mel. 1, 13, 1; Plin. 5, 27, 22, § 91; Cic. Fam. 3, 1, 1; Curt. 3, 4, 7; 3, 7, 5.
pyramus2.short: Pȳrămus, i, m., = Πύραμος, a river in Cilicia, now the Jaihān, Mel.

pyren.full: pȳrēn, ēnis, f., = πυρήν, a precious stone, otherwise unknown, Plin. 37, 11, 73, § 188.
pyren.short: pȳrēn, ēnis, f., = πυρήν, a precious stone, otherwise unknown, Plin.

pyrenaeus.full: Pȳrēnaeus, a, um, and Pȳrēnāĭ-cus, a, um, v. Pyrene.
pyrenaeus.short: Pȳrēnaeus, a, um, and Pȳrēnāĭ-cus, a, um, v.

pyrene.full: Pȳrēnē (y scanned short, Tib. 1, 7, 10), ēs, f., = Πυρηνη. One of the fifty daughters of Danaüs, Hyg. Fab. 170.— Daughter of Bebryx, beloved by Hercules, and buried upon the mountains called after her name; cf. Sil. 3, 420 sq.— Transf. The Pyrenæan Mountains, the Pyrenees, Tib. 1, 7, 9; Luc. 1, 689; Sil. 1, 487: Pyrenes promunturium, Liv. 26, 19.— Spain, Sil. 15, 451; 16, 247: Pyrenes populi, id. 1, 190.—Hence, Pȳrēnaeus (y scanned short, Luc. 4, 83), a, um, adj. Of or belonging to Pyrene, Pyren

pyreneus.full: Pўrēneus (trisyl.), ĕi and ĕos, m., = Πυρηνεύς, a king of Thrace, Ov. M. 5, 274 sq.
pyreneus.short: Pўrēneus (trisyl.), ĕi and ĕos, m., = Πυρηνεύς, a king of Thrace, Ov.

pyrethrum.full: pўrē^thrum or -on, i, n., = πύρεθρον, a plant, Spanish chamomile, pellitory: Anthemis pyrethrum, Linn.; Plin. 28, 9, 42, § 151; Cels. 5, 4; 19; Scrib. Comp. 9; 55; Ov. A. A. 2, 418.
pyrethrum.short: pўrē^thrum or -on, i, n., = πύρεθρον, a plant, Spanish chamomile, pellitory: Anthemis pyrethrum, Linn.;

pyretus.full: Pўrētus, i, m., one of the Centaurs, Ov. M. 12, 449.
pyretus.short: Pўrētus, i, m., one of the Centaurs, Ov.

pyreum.full: pȳrēum, i, n., = πυρεῖον, the sanctuary of Vesta, Cassiod. H. E. 30.
pyreum.short: pȳrēum, i, n., = πυρεῖον, the sanctuary of Vesta, Cassiod.

pyrgi.full: Pyrgi, ōrum, m., = Πύργοι, a colony in Etruria, now the village of S. Severa, Mel. 2, 4, 9; Plin. 3, 5, 8, § 51; Liv 36, 3, 6; Verg. A. 10, 184; Suet. Ner. 5; Mart. 12, 2, 1; cf. Müll. Etrusk. 1, p. 296 sq. — Hence, Pyrgensis, e, adj., of or belonging to Pyrgi, Pyrgan: scorta, Lucil. ap. Serv. Verg. A. 10, 184: Antistius, of Pyrgi, Cic. de Or. 2, 71, 287: publicanus, Liv. 25, 3.
pyrgi.short: Pyrgi, ōrum, m., = Πύργοι, a colony in Etruria, now the village of S.

pyrgis.full: pyrgis, is, f., a plant, dog's-tongue, App. Herb. 96.
pyrgis.short: pyrgis, is, f., a plant, dog's-tongue, App.

pyrgo.full: Pyrgo, ūs, f., the nurse of Priam's children, Verg. A. 5, 645.
pyrgo.short: Pyrgo, ūs, f., the nurse of Priam's children, Verg.

pyrgopolinices.full: Pyrgŏpŏlĭnīces, is, m., Tower-towntaker, the name of the hero in Plautus's Miles Gloriosus, 1, 1, 56; 4, 2, 9; Sid. Ep. 1, 9.
pyrgopolinices.short: Pyrgŏpŏlĭnīces, is, m., Tower-towntaker, the name of the hero in Plautus's Miles Gloriosus, 1, 1, 56;

pyrgoteles.full: Pyrgŏtĕles, is, m., = Πυργοτέλης, a sculptor of the time of Alexander the Great, Plin. 7, 37, 55, § 125; 37, 1, 4, § 8.
pyrgoteles.short: Pyrgŏtĕles, is, m., = Πυργοτέλης, a sculptor of the time of Alexander the Great, Plin.

pyrgus1.full: pyrgus, i, m., = πύργος, a little wooden tower on the side of a gaming-board, hollow and having steps inside, through which the dice were thrown upon the board (pure Lat. turricula), Sid. Ep. 8, 12 (in Hor. S. 2, 7, 17, called phimus; v. phimus).
pyrgus1.short: pyrgus, i, m., = πύργος, a little wooden tower on the side of a gaming-board, hollow and having steps inside, through which the dice were thrown upon the board (pure Lat.

pyrgus2.full: Pyrgus, i, m., = Πύργος, a castle in Elis, Liv. 27, 32; Rutil. Itin. 223.
pyrgus2.short: Pyrgus, i, m., = Πύργος, a castle in Elis, Liv.

pyriphlegethon.full: Pўrĭphlĕgĕthon, ontis, m., = Πυριφλεγέθων, a river in the Infernal Regions, usually called Phlegethon, Cic. N. D. 3, 17, 43 dub.; Tert. Apol. 47 fin.; Arn. 2, 52.
pyriphlegethon.short: Pўrĭphlĕgĕthon, ontis, m., = Πυριφλεγέθων, a river in the Infernal Regions, usually called Phlegethon, Cic.

pyrites.full: pўrītes, ae, m., = πυρίτης. Flint, Plin. 36, 19, 30, § 138. — A millstone, Plin. 36, 19, 30, § 137.— Iron pyrites, sulphuret of iron, marcasite, Plin. 36, 19, 30, § 137.

pyritis.full: pўrītis, ĭdis, f., = πυρῖτις, a precious stone of a black color, otherwise unknown, Plin. 37, 11, 73, § 189.
pyritis.short: pўrītis, ĭdis, f., = πυρῖτις, a precious stone of a black color, otherwise unknown, Plin.

pyrodes.full: Pyrōdes, is, m., = Πυρώδης, the discoverer of the art of kindling fire: ignem e silice Pyrodes Cilicis filius (invenit), Plin. 7, 56, 57, § 198.
pyrodes.short: Pyrōdes, is, m., = Πυρώδης, the discoverer of the art of kindling fire: ignem e silice Pyrodes Cilicis filius (invenit), Plin.

pyrois.full: Pўrŏis and Pўrŏeis, entis, m., = Πυρόεις (fiery). The planet Mars, Col. poët. 10, 290; Aus. Idyll. 18, 12; App. de Mundo, p. 171; Mart. Cap. 8, § 851 (in Cic. N. D. 2, 20, 53, written as Greek).— One of the horses of the sun, Ov. M. 2, 153; Val. Fl. 5, 432; Hyg. Fab. 182.
pyrois.short: Pўrŏis and Pўrŏeis, entis, m., = Πυρόεις (fiery).

pyropoecilos.full: pўrŏpoecĭlos lapis, = πυροποίκιλος, or pyrrhŏpoecĭlos, = πυρροποίκιλος, a kind of porphyry, Plin. 36, 8, 13, § 63; 36, 22, 43, § 157.
pyropoecilos.short: pўrŏpoecĭlos lapis, = πυροποίκιλος, or pyrrhŏpoecĭlos, = πυρροποίκιλος, a kind of porphyry, Plin.

pyropus.full: pўrōpus, i, m., = πυρωπός (fire-colored), a metallic mixture, gold - bronze, bronze, Plin. 34, 8, 20, § 94; Lucr. 2, 803; Prop. 4 (5), 10, 21; Ov. M. 2, 2.
pyropus.short: pўrōpus, i, m., = πυρωπός (fire-colored), a metallic mixture, gold - bronze, bronze, Plin.

pyrrha.full: Pyrrha, ae, and Pyrrhē, ēs, f., = Πύρρα. Daughter of Epimetheus, and wife of Deucalion, Ov. M. 1, 350 sq.; Hor. C. 1, 2, 6; Hyg. Fab. 153; Sen. Troad. 1039. — Hence, Pyrrhaeus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Pyrrha, Pyrrhæan: saxa, which Pyrrha and Deucalion flung behind them, Stat. Th. 8, 305. — The name borne by Achilles when clothed as a girl, Hyg. Fab. 96; Sid. Carm. 9, 138.— A city in Lesbos, with a harbor, now called Caloni, Mel. 2, 7, 4; Plin. 2, 92, 94, § 206; 5, 31, 39, § 139.
pyrrha.short: Pyrrha, ae, and Pyrrhē, ēs, f., = Πύρρα.

pyrrheum.full: Pyrrhēum, i, n., a place in Ambracia, Liv. 38, 5.
pyrrheum.short: Pyrrhēum, i, n., a place in Ambracia, Liv.

pyrrhia.full: Pyrrhĭa, ae, f., name of a thievish female slave, in a comedy of Titinnius, Hor. Ep. 1, 13, 14 Schol. Cruq. ad loc.
pyrrhia.short: Pyrrhĭa, ae, f., name of a thievish female slave, in a comedy of Titinnius, Hor.

pyrrhias1.full: Pyrrhĭas, ae, m., = Πυρρίας, commander of the Ætolians, Liv. 27, 30.
pyrrhias1.short: Pyrrhĭas, ae, m., = Πυρρίας, commander of the Ætolians, Liv.

pyrrhias2.full: Pyrrhĭăs, ădis, adj. f., = Πυρριάς, of the city of Pyrrha in Lesbos, Pyrrhian: puellae, Ov. H. 15, 15.

pyrrhicha.full: pyrrhĭcha, ae, and pyrrhĭchē, ēs, f., = πυρριχη, a dance in armor, the Pyrrhic dance, Plin. 7, 56, 57, § 204: elephas lasciviente pyrrhiche conludere, id. 8, 2, 2, § 5; Suet. Caes. 39; id. Ner. 12; Spart. Hadr 19; App. M. 10, p. 253, 18.—As adj.: ars pyrrhicha, Sid. Ep. 9, 15, 7.
pyrrhicha.short: pyrrhĭcha, ae, and pyrrhĭchē, ēs, f., = πυρριχη, a dance in armor, the Pyrrhic dance, Plin.

pyrrhicharius.full: pyrrhĭchārĭus (purrhĭch-), ĭi, m. pyrrhicha, one who performs the Pyrrhic dance, a Pyrrhichist, Dig. 48, 19, 8 fin.

pyrrhichius.full: pyrrhĭchĭus, a, um, adj., = πυρρίχιος; in prosody, pes, or simply pyrrhichius, a poetical foot consisting of two short syllables, a pyrrhic, Quint. 9, 4, 80; 106; 101; 140 al.; Mart. Cap. 9, § 975.

pyrrhidae.full: Pyrrhĭdae, ārum, v. Pyrrhus, I. B.

pyrrho.full: Pyrrho, ōnis, m., = Πύρρων, a philosopher of Elis, contemporary with Aristotle, and founder of the sceptical school, Cic. Fin. 2, 11, 35; 4, 16, 43; 4, 18, 49; 4, 22, 60; 5, 8, 23; id. Ac. 2, 42, 130; id. Off. 1, 2, 6; id. Tusc. 2, 6, 15; Quint. 12, 2, 24.— Hence, Pyrrhōnĕi (-ōnĭi), ōrum, m., the followers of Pyrrho, Pyrrhonists, Cic. de Or. 3, 17, 62.— As adj.: Pyrrhonii philosophi, Gell. 11, 5, 1; 6.
pyrrho.short: Pyrrho, ōnis, m., = Πύρρων, a philosopher of Elis, contemporary with Aristotle, and founder of the sceptical school, Cic.

pyrrhocorax.full: pyrrhŏcŏrax, ăcis, m., = πυρροκόραξ, a kind of crow with a reddish beak, the Alpine-crow, hermit-crow: Corvus pyrrhocorax, Linn.; Plin. 10, 48, 68, § 133 (al. pyrocorax).
pyrrhocorax.short: pyrrhŏcŏrax, ăcis, m., = πυρροκόραξ, a kind of crow with a reddish beak, the Alpine-crow, hermit-crow: Corvus pyrrhocorax, Linn.;

pyrrhus.full: Pyrrhus, i, m., = Πύρρος. Son of Achilles and Deïdamia (otherwise called Neoptolemus), founder of a kingdom in Epirus, slain at Delphi by Orestes, Just. 17, 3, 18; Verg. A. 2, 469; 526 sq.; Ov. H. 8, 3; Hyg. Fab. 97; 123; Dict. Cret. 4, 15. — Pyrrhi Castra, a place in Laconia, Liv. 35, 27; in Triphylia, id. 32, 13. — Hence, Pyrrhĭdae, ārum, m., the inhabitants of the kingdom founded in Epirus by Pyrrhus, Just. 17, 3, 3. — King of Epirus, about 280 B.C., an enemy of the Romans; on account of his

pyrum.full: pўrum and pўrus, v. pirum and pirus.

pysma.full: pysma, ătis, n., = πύσμα; in rhet., a question, Aquila Rom. p. 152 Ruhnk.

pythagoras.full: Pȳthăgŏras, ae, m., = Πυθαγόρας, a celebrated philosopher of Samos, about 550 B.C.; he taught in Lower Italy (Croton and Metapontum), and was the founder of the Pythagorean philosophy, which received its name from him, Cic. Tusc. 1, 10, 20; 1, 16, 38; 4, 1, 2; id. Fin. 5, 2, 4; id. Div. 1, 3, 5; Hor. S. 2, 6, 63; Ov. M. 15, 60; Liv. 1, 18.— The Greek letter γ (called littera Pythagorae), with its two divergent arms, was used by Pythagoras as a symbol of the two diverse paths of life, that of vir
pythagoras.short: Pȳthăgŏras, ae, m., = Πυθαγόρας, a celebrated philosopher of Samos, about 550 B.C.;

pythagorisso.full: pȳthăgŏrisso, āre, v. n., = Πυθαγορίζω, to imitate Pythagoras, to pythagorize: noster Plato pythagorissat, App. Flor. 2, p. 352.

pytharatus.full: Pytharātus, i, m., = Πυθάρατος, an archon at Athens, B.C. 270, Cic. Fat. 9, 19.
pytharatus.short: Pytharātus, i, m., = Πυθάρατος, an archon at Athens, B.C.

pythaules.full: pȳthaules, ae, m., = πυθαύλης. One who plays upon the flute the song of the combat between the Pythian Apollo and the dragon Python, Hyg. Fab. 273.— Transf., in gen., one who plays upon the flute an accompaniment to the canticum (solo) of an actor, Varr. ap. Non. 166, 11; Sen. Ep. 76, 3; Vop. Carin. 19 Obr.

pythaulicus.full: pȳthaulĭcus, a, um, adj. pythaules, II., of or belonging to a pythaules, pythaulic: in canticis pythaulicis responsabat, Diom. p. 489 P.

pytheas.full: Pythĕas, ae, m., a geographer, a native of Marseilles, contemporary with Ptolemy Philadelphus, Plin. 2, 75, 77, § 187; 2, 97, 99, § 217.
pytheas.short: Pythĕas, ae, m., a geographer, a native of Marseilles, contemporary with Ptolemy Philadelphus, Plin.

pythia.full: Pȳthĭa, ae and ōrum, v. Pythius, sub Python, II. B. 1. and 2.

pythias1.full: Pythias, ae, m., a false reading for Phintias, v. h. v.
pythias1.short: Pythias, ae, m., a false reading for Phintias, v.

pythias2.full: Pȳthiăs, ădis, f., name of a female slave, Ter. Eun. 3, 2, 47 al.; also in a comedy of Caecilius, Hor. A. P. 238 Schol. Cruq and Orell.; Turp. ap. Non. p. 281, 26.
pythias2.short: Pȳthiăs, ădis, f., name of a female slave, Ter.

pythion.full: pȳthĭon, ĭi, n., = πυθίων, a kind of bulbous plant, otherwise unknown, Plin 19, 5, 30, § 95 (the correct reading is opitiona).
pythion.short: pȳthĭon, ĭi, n., = πυθίων, a kind of bulbous plant, otherwise unknown, Plin 19, 5, 30, § 95 (the correct reading is opitiona).

pythium.full: Pythĭum, i, n., = Πύθιον, a town of Thessaly, Liv. 42, 53; 44, 2.
pythium.short: Pythĭum, i, n., = Πύθιον, a town of Thessaly, Liv.

pythius.full: Pȳthĭus, a, um, v. Python, II.

pytho1.full: Pȳtho, ūs, f., = Πυθώ, the former name of Delphi and its environs, Tib. 2, 3, 27 (Python, Müll.); Luc. 5, 134.—Hence, Pȳthĭcus, a, um, adj., = Πυθικός, another form for Pythius, Pythian: Apollo, Liv. 5, 21: oraculum, id. 5, 15: sortes, id. 5, 23: divinatio, Val. Max. 1, 8, 10: agon, Tert. adv. Gnost. 6.— Pȳthĭus, a, um, adj., = Πύθιος, Pythian, Delphic, Apollonian: Delphis prognatus Pythius Apollo, Naev B. P. 2, 20; so, Apollo, Cic. Off. 2, 22, 77; also incola, Hor. C. 1, 16, 6; and deus, Prop.
pytho1.short: Pȳtho, ūs, f., = Πυθώ, the former name of Delphi and its environs, Tib.

pytho2.full: Pȳtho, ōnis, m., a masculine proper name, Liv. 44, 12.
pytho2.short: Pȳtho, ōnis, m., a masculine proper name, Liv.

pytho3.full: Pȳtho, ōnis, m., a familiar spirit, the demon possessing a soothsayer (late Lat.), Vulg. Deut. 18, 11: puella habens spiritum pythonem, id. Act. 16, 16: fecit pythonas, et aruspices multiplicavit, id. 4 Reg. 21, 6.
pytho3.short: Pȳtho, ōnis, m., a familiar spirit, the demon possessing a soothsayer (late Lat.), Vulg.

python.full: Pȳthon, ōnis, m., = Πύθων, the serpent slain, according to the myth, near Delphi by Apollo, who was fabled to have been called Pythius in commemoration of this victory, Ov. M. 1, 438; 460; Claud. in Rufin. 1, 1.
python.short: Pȳthon, ōnis, m., = Πύθων, the serpent slain, according to the myth, near Delphi by Apollo, who was fabled to have been called Pythius in commemoration of this victory, Ov.

pythonicus.full: pȳthōnĭcus, a, um, adj., = πυθωνικός, prophetic, magical: spiritus, Tert. Anim. 28 fin.; Vulg. Lev. 20, 27.
pythonicus.short: pȳthōnĭcus, a, um, adj., = πυθωνικός, prophetic, magical: spiritus, Tert.

pythonion.full: pȳthōnĭon, ĭi, n., = πυθώνιον, a plant, dragon-wort, App. Herb. 4; 14.
pythonion.short: pȳthōnĭon, ĭi, n., = πυθώνιον, a plant, dragon-wort, App.

pythonissa.full: pȳthōnissa, ae 3. pytho, a possessed woman, a sorceress, Vulg. 1 Par. 10, 13.

pytisma.full: pȳtisma, ătis, n., = πύτισμα, that which is spit or spirted out through the lips in tasting wine, Vitr. 7, 4 fin.; Juv. 11, 173, 1.
pytisma.short: pȳtisma, ătis, n., = πύτισμα, that which is spit or spirted out through the lips in tasting wine, Vitr.

pytisso.full: pȳtisso, āre, v. n., = πυτίζω, to spit or spirt out wine in tasting: pytissando modo mihi Quid vini absumpsit, Ter. Heaut. 3, 1, 48 Don.; cf. Diom. 417 P.

pyxacanthus.full: pyxăcanthus or os, i, comm., = πυξάκανθα, a plant, boxthorn, buckthorn, Plin. 12, 7, 15, § 31; 24, 14, 77, § 125.
pyxacanthus.short: pyxăcanthus or os, i, comm., = πυξάκανθα, a plant, boxthorn, buckthorn, Plin.

pyxagathus.full: pyxăgăthus or os, i, m., = πυξἀγαθός, a skilful boxer, Mart. 7, 57, 2.
pyxagathus.short: pyxăgăthus or os, i, m., = πυξἀγαθός, a skilful boxer, Mart.

pyxidatus.full: pyxĭdātus, a, um, adj. pyxis, made like a box, box-like: commissurae, Plin. 31, 6, 31, § 57.

pyxidicula.full: pyxĭdĭcŭla, ae, f. dim. id., a small box, Cels. 6, 6, 5.

pyxinum.full: pyxĭnum, i, n. (sc. collyrium), = πύξινον, an unguent kept in boxes made of boxwood, box-salve, Cels. 6, 6, 25.

pyxis.full: pyxis (puxis, Juv. 13, 25; Scrib. Comp. 228), ĭdis, f., = πυξίς. Lit., a box, a small box, esp. for unguents, medicines, etc. — Orig., of boxes made of boxwood, then of those of any kind of wood, and finally, also, of metallic boxes: veneni, Cic. Cael. 25, 61: aurea, Suet. Ner. 47; cf. id. ib. 12: cornea, Plin. 21, 20, 81, § 137: plumbea, id. 32, 10, 47, § 135.—Belonging to the toilet of women, Petr. 110; Paul. Sent. 3, 6, 83 (al. buxides).— Transf.: ferrea, an iron cap fitted to the lower end o

q.full: Q, q, the sixteenth letter of the Latin alphabet (in which i and j were reckoned as one), concerning the origin of which the ancients were in doubt, some correctly supposing it to be the Greek Koppa (?*!), transferred from the Dorian alphabet of Cumæ, Quint. 1, 4, 9; Ter. Maur. p. 2253 P.; Mar. Victor. p. 2459 and 2468 ib.; while others erroneously explained it as a mere graphical contraction of C and V, Vel. Long. p. 2218 P.; Ter. Maur. p. 2399 ib.; cf. Diom. p. 420 ib.; Mart. Cap. 3, § 255; Is
q.short: Q, q, the sixteenth letter of the Latin alphabet (in which i and j were reckoned as one), concerning the origin of which the ancients were in doubt, some correctly supposing it to be the Greek Koppa (?*!), transferred from the Dorian alphabet of Cumæ

qua.full: quā, adv. abl. fem. from qui, on which side, at or in which place, in what direction, where, by what way (class.). Lit., of place: orasque Italicas omnis, quā adgreditur mare, sumus circumvecti, Plaut. Men. 2, 1, 12: fumus si quā exit foras, id. Aul. 2, 4, 22: jubet persequi, si quā queat reperire quae sustulerit, id. Cist. 1, 3, 35: regna mihi liquit Pelops, quā ponto ab Helles urgetur Isthmos, Poët. ap. Sen. Ep. 80, 7; cf. Cic. Or. 49, 163: ad omnes introitus, quā adiri poterat, id. Caecin. 8,

quacumque.full: quā-cumquē (-cunque) (in tmesi: quā porro cumque, Lucr. 1, 508: quā se cunque tulit, Verg. A. 11, 762), adv. By whatever way, wherever, wheresoever (class.): quācumque iter fecit, Cic. Verr. 2, 1, 16, § 44; id. Clu. 68, 193: quācunque ingredimur, id. Fin. 5, 2, 5: quācumque custodiant, Liv. 24, 2: quācumque equo invectus est, Liv. 8, 9, 12.— Transf. Whencesoever, from what side soever: hujus erat Minerva spectantem aspectans, quācumque aspiceretur, Plin. 35, 10, 37, § 120.— Whithersoever: quācum
quacumque.short: quā-cumquē (-cunque) (in tmesi: quā porro cumque, Lucr.

quadantenus.full: quādantĕnus or quādamtĕnus (in tmesi, Hor.; v. infra), adv. quidam-tenus. To a certain point or limit, so far (poet. and in post-Aug. prose): est quadam prodire tenus, si non datur ultra, Hor. Ep. 1, 1, 32.— Transf., to a certain extent, in some measure, somewhat: citreis odor acerrimus, quadantenus et cotoneis, Plin. 15, 28, 33, § 110: rubens, id. 24, 14, 76, § 124: quae fuerit origo gemmarum diximus quadantenus, id. 37, prooem. 1. § 2: ut noctes nostrae quadamtenus his historiae floscuculis as

quadi.full: Quādi, ōrum, m., a German people in the modern Moravia, Tac. G. 42; 43; Eutr. 8, 6; 9, 6; Capitol. Anton. Phil. 14, 3.
quadi.short: Quādi, ōrum, m., a German people in the modern Moravia, Tac.

quadra1.full: quā^dra, ae, f., a square. In gen.: qui locus gradibus in quadram formatus est, Fest. s. v. Romanam, p. 262 Müll.— In partic. In arch. The lowest and largest member of the base of a pedestal, the foundation-stone, socle, plinth, Vitr. 3, 3.— Any small member for the separation of larger ones, a platband, list, fillet, Vitr. 3, 3; 10, 2.— A table to eat from, a dining-table (as these were usually square; cf. Varr. L. L. 5, § 118 Müll.): patulis nec parcere quadris, of the pieces of bread used as

quadra2.full: Quā^dra, ae, m., a Roman surname, e. g. Hostius Quadratus, Sen. Q. N. 1, 16, 1.
quadra2.short: Quā^dra, ae, m., a Roman surname, e.

quadragenarius.full: quā^drāgēnārĭus, a, um, adj. quadrageni, of or belonging to the number forty, consisting of forty, of forty: dolium, perh. holding forty congii, Cato, R. R. 105, 1: fistula, a forty-inch pipe, i. e. made of a plate forty inches in width, Vitr. 8, 7: numerum, Vulg. Deut. 25, 3: pupillus, of forty, i. e. forty years old, Sen. Ep. 25, 1.—As subst.: quā^drāgēnārĭus, i, m., a man forty years of age: quadragenarium istum ad te voca, Arn. 2, 60.

quadrageni.full: quā^drāgēni, ae, a (gen. quadragenūm, Caes. B. G. 4, 17; Liv. 38, 38), num. distrib. adj. [quadraginta]. Forty each: columnae singulae sestertiis quadragenis milibus locatae, Cic. Verr. 2, 1, 56, § 147; id. Att. 4, 18, 2: octoginta confecit centurias, quadragenas seniorum et juniorum, Liv. 1, 43: pyramides complures quadragenarum ulnarum, Plin. 36, 13, 19, § 87; Liv. 38, 38: septuagies centeni quadrageni fiunt novem milia et octingenti, forty each time, Col. 5, 2, 8.—Plur. fem. quadragenae (supp

quadragesimus.full: quā^drāgēsĭmus (old form † quā^-drāgensŭmus, Num. ap. Eckh. D. N. 6, p. 296), a, um, adj. quadraginta. The fortieth: pars quadragesima, Cato, R. R. 23, 2: nono et quadragesimo die, Varr. ap. Gell. 3, 10, 7: anno fere centesimo et quadragesimo, Cic. Rep. 2, 15, 29; id. Fam. 10, 33, 5: pars quadragesima octava, Col. 5, 1, 9; Plin. 2, 8, 6, § 37.— Subst.: quā^-drāgēsĭma, ae, f. (sc. pars), the fortieth part, a fortieth: quadragesima summae, Suet. Calig. 40.— In partic. As a tax, the fortieth part,

quadragies.full: quā^drāgĭes (old orthogr. QVA DRAGIENS, Monum. Ancyr. ap. Grut. 230), adv. num. id., forty times: quadragies quater accusatus, Aur. Vict. Vir. Illustr. 47: sestertium ter et quadragies, the 4,300,000 sesterces, Cic. Fl. 13, 30; Liv. 38, 55, 9 and 12.

quadraginta.full: quā^drāgintā, num. adj. quattuor, forty: quattuor quadraginta minae, Plaut. Most. 3, 1, 102: annos natus, Cic. Rosc. Am. 14, 39; id. Rep. 2, 30, 52: jugera arvi, Cat. 115, 2; Col. 5, 2, 10; 5, 1, 13.

quadrangulatus.full: quā^drangŭlātus, a, um, adj. quadrangulus, quadrangular (eccl. Lat.): quadrangulata turris, Tert. Anim. 17: ligna, Vulg. 3 Reg. 7, 5.

quadrangulum.full: quā^drangŭlum, i, n. quattuor-angulus, a quadrangle: quadrangulum, τετράγωνον, Gloss. Lat. Gr.; Mart. Cap. 7, § 754 (dub.; al. quadriangulo).

quadrans.full: quā^drans, antis (gen. plur. quadrantūm, Front. Aquaed. 24), m. quattuor. A fourth part, a fourth, a quarter: operae, Col. 2, 4, 8: diei noctisque, Plin. 18, 25, 57, § 207. — In partic. A fourth part, a fourth of a whole: creditoribus quadrantem solvi, Vell. 2, 23, 2: heres ex quadrante, of the fourth part of the inheritance, Suet. Caes. 83; cf. Plin. Ep. 5, 7, 1; Dig. 44, 4, 17, § 2; Ulp. Frag. 24, 32.— The fourth part of an as (as a coin), three unciae: nota in triente et quadrante rates (fuit

quadrantal.full: quā^drantal, ālis, n. quadrantalis. A liquid measure containing eight congii, a quadrantal, Cato ap. Fest. p. 258, 20 Müll.; id. R. R. 57, 2; Plaut. Curc. 1, 2, 15; Plin. 14, 14, 16, § 95.— A die, cube, Gell. 1, 20, 3.

quadrantalis.full: quā^drantālis, e, adj. quadrans, containing the fourth part of a measure (postAug.): mensa crassitudine quadrantali, of a quarter of a foot, Plin. 13, 15, 29, § 93.

quadrantarius.full: quā^drantārĭus, a, um, adj. id.. Prop., of or belonging to a quarter, relating to a fourth part: in tabulis quadrantariis, quas ait ab Hirtuleio institutas, i. e. new accounts reducing all debts to one fourth, Cic. Font. 1, 2.— In partic., relating to a quarter of an as (as a coin), that costs a quarter of an as, etc.: res quadrantaria, i. e. a bath (because a quarter of an as was the price of a bath; v. quadrans, II. B), Sen. Ep. 86, 8: mulier, of Clodia, wife of Metellus, who sold herself for

quadratarius.full: quā^drātārĭus, a, um, adj. quadratus, of or belonging to work with the square, i. e. to the work of the stone-cutter: OPVS, perh. a stone monument, Inscr. Murat. 2012, 2.— As subst.: quā^drātārĭus, ĭi, m., a stonecutter (post-class.), interchanged with lapidicida, Sid. Ep. 3, 12; Cod. Just. 10, 64, 1; Auct. Limit. p. 294 Goes.

quadrate.full: quā^drātē, adv., v. quadro, P. a. fin.

quadratilla.full: Quā^drātilla, ae, f., a Roman female name, e. g. Ummilia, Plin. Ep. 7, 24, 7; cf. Inscr Murat. 3, 27, 5.
quadratilla.short: Quā^drātilla, ae, f., a Roman female name, e.

quadratim.full: quā^drātim, adv. quadratus, fourfold, acc. to Charis. p. 168 P.

quadratio.full: quā^drātĭo, ōnis, f. id., a square, quadrate: agatur linea rotundationis, quae quadrationis angulos tangat, Vitr. 4, 3, 9.

quadrator.full: quā^drātor, ōris, m. quadro, a stonecutter: marmorum, Cassiod. Ep. 2, 7.

quadratum.full: quā^drātum, i, n., v. quadro fin.

quadratura.full: quā^drātūra, ae, f. quadro. A making square, squaring, quadrature (postclass.): circuli quadratura, the squaring or quadrature of the circle, App. Dogm. Plat. 3, p. 37, 11.— Transf., a square: vitreae, Vop. Firm. 3.

quadratus1.full: quā^drātus, a, um, Part. and P. a., v. quadro.

quadratus2.full: quā^drātus, i, m., v. quadro fin.

quadratus3.full: Quadrātus, i, m., a Roman surname, e. g. Ummilius Quadratus, Plin. Ep. 6, 11, 1; 7, 24, 6.
quadratus3.short: Quadrātus, i, m., a Roman surname, e.

quadriangulus.full: quā^drĭangŭlus, a, um, adj. quattuor-angulus, four-cornered, quadrangular (post-Aug.); figura, Plin. 13, 22, 38, § 118: herba quadriangulo caule, id. 25, 6, 27, § 63: membrum, Aus. Epigr. 128. — As subst.: quădrĭangŭlum, i, n., a quadrilateral figure, quadrangle, Prisc. Fig. Num. p. 417; cf. quadrangulum.

quadribaccium.full: quā^drĭbaccĭum and † quā^drĭ-bacĭum, ii, n. quattuor-bacca, fourbeads, four-pearls, an ornament composed of four pearls, Inscr. Murat. 139, 1.

quadriburgium.full: Quā^drĭburgĭum, ii, n., a fortified town in Gallia Belgica, Amm. 18, 2, 4; Inscr. Orell. 2090.
quadriburgium.short: Quā^drĭburgĭum, ii, n., a fortified town in Gallia Belgica, Amm.

quadridens.full: quā^drĭdens, entis, adj. quattuordens, four - toothed, having four teeth (ante - class.): rastri quadridentes, Cato, R. R. 10, 3; 11, 4.

quadriduanus.full: quā^drĭdŭānus (quā^trĭd-), a, um, adj. quadriduum, of four days, for the space of four days: Lazarus mortuus, Hier. Ep. 108, n. 24; Vulg. Joan. 11, 39.

quadriduum.full: quā^drĭdŭum (quā^trĭd-), ĭi, n. quattuor-dies, a space of four days, four days (class.): in hoc triduo aut quadriduo, Plaut. Pers. 1, 1, 37; so Cato, R. R. 65, 2; 113, 2; Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 3, § 6; id. Tusc. 5, 4, 11; 4, 38, 82; Liv. 3, 3; Curt. 4, 7, 15: quadriduo quo haec gesta sunt, four days after, Cic. Rosc. Am. 7, 20: quadriduum per vastas solitudines absumptum est, Plin. 6, 22, 24, § 86.

quadriennis.full: quā^drĭennis, e, adj. quattuor-annus, of four years, four years old (post-class.): homo, Aur. Vict. Epit. 45.

quadriennium.full: quā^drĭennĭum, ii, n. quadriennis, a space or period of four years (class.), Cic. Caecin. 7, 19; id. Opt. Gen. 7, 22; id. Sen. 4, 10; Cic. Verr. 2, 3, 18, § 47; Flor. 2, 6.

quadrieris.full: quā^drĭēris (quā^t-), is, f. vox hibr. from quattuor and ἄρω, analog. to τριήρης, a vessel having four banks of oars, a quadrireme (post-class.): EX CLASS. PR. MIS. QVADRIERE FIDE, Inscr. Murat. 876, 3: quatrieris, Not. Tir. p. 177.

quadrifariam.full: quā^drĭfārĭam, adv. quattuor. Fourfold, into four parts (class.; not in Cic. or Cæs.): quadrifariam aliquid dispertire, Varr. ap. Non. 92, 15: conjurati quadrifariam se diviserunt, Liv. 38, 1: quadrifariam diviso exercitu, id. 4, 22, 5; Suet. Vit. 13.— In a fourfold manner, Dig. 38, 10, 10, § 16; cf. quadrifariter.

quadrifariter.full: quā^drĭfārĭter, adv., in a fourfold manner, in four ways (post-class.), Dig. 38, 10, 10, § 14; cf. quadrifariam.
quadrifariter.short: quā^drĭfārĭter, adv., in a fourfold manner, in four ways (post-class.), Dig.

quadrifarius.full: quā^drĭfārĭus, a, um, adj. quattuor, fourfold (post-class.): divisio, Cassiod. Var. 3, 51; 1, 45; Arn. in Psa. 108.

quadrifidus.full: quā^drĭfĭdus, a, um, adj. quattuorfindo, four-cleft, split into four parts, quadrifid (poet.). Lit.: quadrifidas sudes, Verg. G. 2, 25: quadrifidam quercum Scindebat, was cleaving in four, id. A. 7, 509: quadrifidā trabe fingere tela Jovis, Val. Fl. 1, 663: ridicae, Col. 4, 33, 4.— Transf., in gen., divided into four parts: labor, Claud. Cons. Prob. et Olybr. 268.

quadrifinalis.full: quā^drĭfīnālis, e, adj. quadrifinium, bordering on four places, or marking four boundaries (post-class.): arca, Innocent. de Casis Litterar. p. 222 Goes.

quadrifinium.full: quā^drĭfīnĭum, ii, n. quattuor-finis, a place where four boundaries meet (postclass.), Innocent. p. 221 and 227 Goes.; Isid. 15, 14, 5.

quadrifluus.full: quā^drĭflŭus, a, um, adj. quattuorfluo, having four streams, flowing into four parts (eccl. Lat.): amnis, Prud. Cath. 3, 103.

quadrifluvium.full: quā^drĭflŭvĭum, ii, n. quattuor-fluvius, a flowing into four parts, in four directions: ima abietis pars, cum excisa quadrifluviis disparatur, i. e. into four parts, according to the course of the veins, Vitr. 2, 9, 7.

quadriforis.full: quā^drĭfŏris, e, adj. quattuor-fores, four-doored, i.e. having four doors or four doorways (openings) (post-Aug.): nidi, Plin. 11, 21, 24, § 74: januae, having four leaves, divided crosswise, Vitr. 4, 6, 5.

quadriformis.full: quā^drĭformis, e, adj. quattuor-forma, four-formed, quadriform, Macr. S. 1, 9, 13; Not. Tir. p. 110.

quadrifrons.full: quā^drĭfrons, tis, adj. quattuor-frons, four-fronted, having four foreheads, or four faces: Janus, Aug. Civ. Dei, 7, 4; Serv. ad Verg. A. 7, 607.

quadriga.full: quā^drīga, ae, f., v. quadrigae, I. fin.

quadrigae.full: quā^drīgae, ārum (collat. form in the sing. v. infra), f. contr. from quadrijugae, a set or team of four, a four-abreast, fourin-hand, four together (class.). Lit. Of horses, applied to the animals with or without the car or vehicle, rarely to the car or chariot alone: quadrigarum currus duplici temone olim erant, perpetuoque, et qui omnibus equis iniceretur jugo. Primus Clisthenes Sicyonius tantum medios jugavit, eosque singulos ex utrāque parte simplici vinculo applicuit, quos Graeci σειραφόρο

quadrigalis.full: quā^drīgālis, e, adj. quadrigae, of or belonging to a team of four: equi, Paul. ex Fest. s. v. curules, p. 49 Müll.

quadrigamus.full: quā^drĭgămus, i, m. vox hibr. from quattuor-γάμος, one who has married four times, a husband for the fourth time (eccl. Lat.), Hier. adv. Jovin. 1, n. 15.

quadrigarius1.full: quā^drīgārĭus, a, um, adj. quadrigae, of or belonging to a four-horse (racing) chariot (post-Aug.): quadrigario habitu, in the dress of the driver of a quadriga, Suet. Calig. 17: pulvis, for the race-horses, Veg. Vet. 1, 56; 2, 28, 19: FAMILIA, slaves who took care of the race-horses, Inscr. Grut. 339, 5.— Hence, as subst.: quā^drīgārĭus, ii, m., one who drives a four-horse chariot in the circus, a chariot-racer (class.), Varr. R. R. 2, 7: in victoriā, Cic. Fragm. Or. in Toga Cand. ap. Ascon.; S

quadrigarius2.full: Quā^drīgārĭus, ii, m., a Roman surname. Thus, Q. Claudius Quadrigarius, an old Roman historian, Vell. 2, 9, 6; Gell. 1, 7, 9; called simply Claudius, Liv. 8, 19, 13.
quadrigarius2.short: Quā^drīgārĭus, ii, m., a Roman surname.

quadrigatus.full: quā^drīgātus, a, um, adj. quadrigae, marked or stamped with the figure of a quadriga (a coin), Liv. 22, 58, 4; cf.: nota argenti fuere bigae, atque quadrigae, et inde bigati et quadrigati dicti, Plin. 33, 3, 13, § 46; Paul. ex Fest. p. 98, 3 Müll.

quadrigeminus.full: quā^drĭgĕmĭnus, a, um, adj. quattuor-geminus, fourfold, four (post-Aug.): cornicula, four, Plin. 8, 23, 35, § 85; cf. Sol. 27, 28.

quadrigonus.full: quā^drĭgōnus, a, um, adj. quadrus, γῶνος, having four angles: figura, Claud. Mam. Ep. 1 med.

quadrigulae.full: quā^drīgŭlae, ārum, f dim. [quadrigae], a little four-horse team (class.), Cic. Fat. 3, 5.—In sing., Plin. 34, 8, 19, § 83.

quadrigularius.full: quā^drīgŭlārĭus, a, um, adj. quadrigulae, of or belonging to a little fourhorse team (post-class.): PICTOR, who painted little four-horse teams, Inscr. Don. 317, 6; Inscr. Orell. 4262.

quadrijugis.full: quā^drĭjŭgis, e, adj. quattuor-jugum, of or belonging to a team of four (poet. and post-Aug.): equi, Verg. A. 10, 571: currus, App. Flor. 3, p. 356, 14.

quadrijugus.full: quā^drĭjŭgus, a, um, adj. id., of or belonging to a team of four (poet.): curru, Enn. ap. Cic. Tusc. 1, 44, 105 (Trag. v. 129 Vahl.); Verg. A. 12, 162; id. G. 3, 18; Plin. Pan. 22, 1: equi, Ov. Am. 3, 2, 66; id. Tr. 4, 2, 54: certamen, with four-horse chariots, Stat. Th. 6, 370.— Subst.: quā^drĭjŭgi, ōrum, m., a four-horse team: ruunt tritumque relinquunt Quadrijugi spatium, Ov. M. 2, 167; Sil. 4, 441; Stat. Th. 12, 533.

quadrilaterus.full: quā^drĭlătĕrus, a, um, adj. quattuorlatus, four-sided, quadrilateral, Front. p. 35 Goes.; Boëth. Art. Geom. p. 375, 16 (Friedl.): figura, Isid. Orig. 3, 3, 12.

quadrilibris.full: quā^drĭlībris, e, adj. quattuor-libra, that weighs four pounds (ante-class.), Plaut. Aul. 5, 2.

quadrimanus.full: quā^drĭmănus, a, um, and quā^drĭ-mănis, e, adj. quattuor-manus, fourhanded, having four hands (post-class.): puella biceps, quadripes, quadrimana, Jul. Obseq. Prodig. 111: pueri quadrupedes et quadrimanes, id. ib. 73.
quadrimanus.short: quā^drĭmănus, a, um, and quā^drĭ-mănis, e, adj.

quadrimatus.full: quā^drīmātus, ūs, m. quadrimus, the age of four years (post-Aug.): extra quadrimatum, Plin. 19, 11, 58, § 181: ante quadrimatum, id. 8, 45, 70, § 176: dum quadrimatum agant, Col. 7, 9, 2; 9, 1, 7.

quadrimembris.full: quā^drĭmembris, e, adj. quattuormembrum, four-limbed or four-footed, going on all fours (post-class.), Mart. Cap. poët. 8, § 805 dub. (al. hiantimembrem).

quadrimenstruus.full: quā^drĭmenstrŭus, a, um, adj. quattuor-mensis, of four months (late Lat.), Cod. Just. 1, 32, 1; Cod. Th. 12, 6, 27, § 1.

quadrimestris.full: quā^drĭmestris, e, adj. id., of four months (ante-class. and post-Aug.): agni, Varr. R. R. 2, 2, 17: consulatus, Suet. Ner. 14: indutiae, Cod. 7, 54, 3, pr. § 1.

quadrimulus.full: quā^drīmŭlus, a, um, adj. dim. [quadrimus], of four years, four years old (Plautin.): parvulus, Plaut. Capt. 5, 3, 4: altera, id. Poen. prol. 85.

quadrimus.full: quā^drīmus, a, um, adj. quattuor and root ghim-, him-, of Sanscr. himas, snow; cf. Gr. χιών, χεῖμα; Lat. hiems, hibernus; hence, of four winters, of four years, four years old (class.): de quadrimo Catone, of Cato of Utica, when four years old, Cic. Fam. 16, 22, 1; cf.: infantem natum esse quadrimo parem, Liv. 27, 37: boves, Varr. R. R. 1, 20, 5: merum, Hor. C. 1, 9, 7: vitis, Col. 4, 16, 1: dies, a term of four years, Dig. 23, 4, 19: equae, Plin. 8, 44, 69, § 171.

quadringenarius.full: quā^dringēnārĭus, a, um, adj. quadringeni, of four hundred each (class.): cohortes, each consisting of four hundred men, Cic. Att. 6, 1, 14: quadringenariae cohortes (al. quadringentariae), Liv. 7, 7, 4: IVDEX, who possessed an equestrian fortune of four hundred thousand sesterces, Inscr. Murat. 1048, 4; Inscr. Grut. 431, 7.

quadringeni.full: quā^dringēni, ae, a (quā^drigēni, Varr. R. R. 2, 8, 3), num. distrib. adj. [quadringenti], four hundred each, Liv. 8, 11 fin.; 45, 16, 3: milia nummūm, Suet. Vit. 13.

quadringenteni.full: quā^dringentēni, a false read. for quadringenti, q. v.

quadringentesimus.full: quā^dringentēsĭmus, a, um, adj. quadringenti, the four hundredth: annus, Liv. 5, 45, 4; so Plin. 8, 6, 6, § 16.

quadringenti.full: quā^dringenti, ae, a, adj. quattuorcentum, four hundred: anni, Cic. Rep. 1, 37, 58; so id. Pis. 5, 10: talis quadringentis jactis, id. Div. 2, 21, 48: (sestertia), Juv. 1, 105; Vitr. 10, 9, 4: pantheres, Plin. 8, 17, 24, § 64.

quadringenties.full: quā^dringentĭes, adv. quadringenti, four hundred times: HS quadringenties, forty millions of sesterces, Cic. Verr. 2, 2, 10, § 26; id. Phil. 2, 37, 93; id. Rab. Post. 8, 21.

quadrini.full: quā^drīni, ae, a, num. distrib. adj. [quattuor], four each, four (ante-class. and postAug.): ab uno uni, a tribus trini, a quattuor quadrini, Varr. L. L. 8, § 55 Müll.: si haberem quadrinas molas, Pompon. ap. Non. 483, 24: dies, Plin. 11, 36, 43, § 120: febris quadrini circuitūs, a quartan fever, id. 7, 50, 51, § 170: cardines, Arn. 6, 192: temporum vices, App. Dogm. Plat. 1, p. 7, 16.

quadrinoctium.full: quā^drĭnoctĭum, ii, n. quattuornox, a space or period of four nights, acc. to Prisc. p. 1357 P.

quadripartio.full: quā^drĭ-partĭo, no perf., ītum, 4, v. a., and quā^drĭ-pertĭor, īri, 4, v. dep. quattuor-partio, to divide into four parts (in the verb. finit. post-class.): quadripartitur exercitus, Dict. Cret. 1, 19.— Dep.: quadripartiretur, Not. Tir. p. 109.— Hence, quā^-drĭpartītus (quā^drĭpert-), a, um, P. a., divided into four parts, consisting of four parts, fourfold, quadripartite (class.): distributio accusationis, Cic. Verr. 2, 1, 12, § 33: commutationes temporum, fourfold, four, id. Tusc. 1, 28, 68: d

quadri.full: quā^drĭ-partītĭo, ōnis, f. quadripartio, a division into four parts, quadripartition (only in Varro), Varr. L. L. 5, § 1, and 7, § 5 Müll.

quadripartito.full: quā^drĭpartītō, adv., v. quadripartio, P. a. fin.

quadripartitus.full: quā^drĭpartītus, a, um, P. a., from quadripartio.

quadripertitus.full: quā^drĭpertītus, a, um, v. quadripartio, P. a.

quadriplatores.full: quā^drĭplātōres dicebantur, qui eo quaestu se tuebantur, ut eas res persequerentur, quarum ex legibus quadrupli erat actio, Fest. p. 259, 3 Müll.; v. quadruplator.
quadriplatores.short: quā^drĭplātōres dicebantur, qui eo quaestu se tuebantur, ut eas res persequerentur, quarum ex legibus quadrupli erat actio, Fest.

quadriremis.full: quā^drĭ-rēmĭs, e (quā^trĭrēmis, Not. Tir. p. 177), adj. quattuor-remus, having four banks of oars: machina, Paul. Nol. Carm. 21, 73.— Hence, subst.: quā^drĭ-rēmis, is, f., a vessel having four banks of oars, a quadrireme (class.): egreditur Centuripinā quadriremi e portu, Cic. Verr. 2, 5, 33, § 86; 2, 5, 34, § 88: quinque, Caes. B. C. 3, 24; Liv. 24, 33; Plin. 7, 56, 57, § 207; Inscr. Orell. 2671; 3629.— As adj., Paul. Nol. Carm. 21, 73.

quadrisemus.full: quā^drĭ-sēmus, a, um, adj. vox hibr. from quattuor-σῆμα, sign, quadrisyllabic, containing four morae or prosodial times (gram. term): numerus, Mart. Cap. 9, § 981.

quadrisomus.full: quā^drĭ-sōmus, a, um, adj. vox hibr. from quadrus, σῶμα, containing four bodies: SEPVLCRVM, Inscr. Rein. col. 2, 40; 43 al.

quadrivium.full: quā^drĭvĭum, ii, n. quattuor-via. Lit., a place where four ways meet, a crossway, cross-road: in quadriviis et angiportis, Cat. 58, 4; so Juv. 1, 63: DII, the tutelar gods of cross-roads, Inscr. Grut. 84, 5; 1015, 1; Inscr. Rein. col. 1, n. 14.— Transf., the assemblage of the four mathematical sciences (arithmetic, music, geometry, and astronomy), Boëth. Arithmet. 1, 1.

quadrivius.full: quā^drĭvĭus, a, um, adj. quadrusvia, of the cross-roads, only in the phrase DIS or LARIBVS QVADRIVIIS (sometimes QVADRIBIS), Inscr. Orell. 389; 1664; 2103 sqq.

quadro.full: quā^dro, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. and n. quadrus. Act., to make four-cornered, to square, make square: abies atque populus ad unguem quadrantur, Col. 11, 2, 13: lapides, Vulg. 3 Reg. 5, 17.— Transf., to put in proper order, to join properly together, to complete, perfect: quadrandae orationis industria, in properly arranging, Cic. Or. 58, 197: quae pars quadrat acervum, Hor. Ep. 1, 6, 35 Orell. ad loc. — Neutr. (to be square, said of squared stones for building, which fit well together; hence), trans

quadrula.full: quā^drŭla, ae, f. dim. quadra, a little square (post-class.), Sol. 37.

quadrum.full: quā^drum, i, n. quattuor, something square, a square, quadrate (class.). Lit.: perticae dolantur in quadrum, Col. 8, 3, 7: per quadrum singulos habens cubitos, Vulg. Exod. 37, 25. — Transf., a being squared or fitted together, fitness, proper order, arrangement: in quadrum redigere sententias, Cic. Or. 61, 208; 70, 233.

quadrupedans.full: quā^drŭ-pĕdans, antis, Part., from the obsol. quadrupedo [quadrupes]. Going on four feet, galloping (poet. and postAug.): canterius, Plaut. Capt. 4, 2, 34: equo juxta quadrupedante, galloping close by on horseback, Plin. 8, 45, 70, § 182: sonitus, of a horse galloping, Verg. A. 8, 596.— Subst., a galloping horse, a steed, courser (poet.): quadrupedantum Pectora, Verg. A. 11, 614.
quadrupedans.short: quā^drŭ-pĕdans, antis, Part., from the obsol.

quadrupedatim.full: quā^drŭpĕdātim, adv. quattuorpes, in the manner of a quadruped, acc. to Charis. p. 163 P.

quadrupedius.full: quā^drŭpĕdĭus, a, um, adj. id.,fourfooted, quadruped, Jul. Val. Rer. Gest. Alex. M. 3, 36.

quadrupedus.full: quā^drŭpĕdus (quā^drĭpĕdus, Front. ad M. Anton. Or. 1), a, um, adj. quadrupes, going on four feet, galloping (postAug.): quadrupedo gradu repentes, on all fours, Amm. 14, 2, 2: quadripedo cursu, on a gallop, Front. 1, 1.— Absol.: quadrupedo currere, to gallop, Front. Ep. ad M. Caes. 2, 1.

quadrupes.full: quā^drŭpēs (quā^drĭpes), pĕdis (gen. plur. quadrupedium, Capitol. Ver. 5, 2), adj. quattuor-pes, having four feet, going on four feet; esp., Galloping (post-Aug.): ecus, Enn. ap. Gell. 18, 5, 4; cf. Macr. S. 6, 9, 10: equestri celeritate, quadrupedi cursu solum replaudens, App. M. 6, p. 185, 7.— Transf.: dum certum flectit in orbem Quadrupedis cursus, Ov. M. 6, 226.— Of persons, on all fours, creeping, going on hands and feet: atque audin? quadrupedem constringito, so that he can only move on al

quadruplaris.full: quā^drŭplāris, e, adj. quadruplus, fourfold, quadruple (post-class.): numerus duplaris, triplaris, quadruplaris (al. quadruplus), Macr. Somn. Scip. 1, 19, 21.

quadruplator1.full: quā^drŭplātor (quadrĭplātor, Fest. p. 259 Müll. v. h. v.: quădrŭpŭlā-tor, Plaut. Pers. 1, 2, 18), ōris, m. quadruplo. One who multiplies by four, a quadrupler, App. Mag. p. 330, 20. — Transf., a multiplier, magnifier, exaggerator: beneficiorum suorum, Sen. Ben. 7, 25, 1. — One who farmed the tolls, of which he received a fourth part, Sid. Ep. 5, 7.

quadruplator2.full: quā^drū^plātor (quā^drī^-), ōris, m. quadruplor, a public informer, who received a fourth part of the thing informed against (acc. to others, against one who committed an offence punishable with a fourfold penalty; cf. sector); also, in gen., a trickster, chicaner, Plaut. Pers. 1, 2, 18: deterrimus, Cic. Verr. 2, 2, 7, § 21; 2, 2, 8, § 22; Liv. 3, 72; cf. Paul. ex Fest. p. 259, 3 Müll.; Cic. Div. in Caecil. 7, 24; 21, 68.

quadruplex.full: quā^drŭplex, ĭcis, adj. quattuor-plico. Fourfold, quadruple: pecunia, Plaut. Curc. 5, 2, 21: ordo, Liv. 30, 10: quadruplici radice, Plin. 27, 8, 38, § 60.—* Poet., in gen., four: stellae, Cic. Arat. 92.— As subst.: quā^drŭplex, ĭcis, n., a fourfold amount: gubernatoribus duplex, magistris quadruplex dedit, Liv. 45, 42, 1.

quadruplicatio.full: quā^drŭ-plĭcātĭo, ōnis, f. quadruplico, a making fourfold, quadruplication (post-class.): numeri, Mart. Cap. 7, § 750; so Dig. 44, 1, 2.

quadruplico.full: quā^drŭplĭco, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. quadruplex, to multiply by four, make fourfold, quadruplicate: rem suam, one's property, Plaut. Stich. 3, 1, 4: numerum, Dig. 38, 10, 10.— Hence, adv.: quădrŭplĭcā-tō, four times as much, quadruply (postAug.), Plin. 2, 17, 14, § 76: emptis vineis, id. 14, 4, 5, § 51.

quadruplo.full: quā^drŭplo, no perf., ātum, 1, v. a. quadruplus, to multiply by four, make fourfold, quadruple (post-class.), Dig. 4, 2, 14, §§ 1, 7: numerus quadruplatus, ib. 38, 10, 10, § 17; 47, 2, 50 pr.; Ambros. Apol. Dav. 5, 22.

quadruplor.full: quā^drŭplor, āri, v. dep. id., to be an informer, cheater, trickster, chicaner: neque quadruplari me volo, Plaut. Pers. 1, 2, 10 (al. quadrupulari).

quadruplus.full: quā^drŭplus (quā^drŭpŭlus, Plaut. Truc. 4, 2, 49 Fleck.), a, um, adj. quattuor, fourfold, quadruple (rare as adj.): strena, Suet. Tib. 34: numerus, Macr. Somn. Scip. 1, 19, 21; 2, 1, 19.— Subst.: quā^drŭplum, i, n., a fourfold amount, four times as much, quadruple (class.): furem dupli condemnari, feneratorem quadrupli, to a fourfold penalty, Cato, R. R. prooem.: judicium in aratorem in quadruplum dare, to sentence the cultivator, who did not deliver the quantity of grain fixed by law, to pay fo

quadrurbem.full: quadrurbem Athenas Attius appellavit, quod scilicet ex quattuor urbibus in unam domicilia contulerunt, Braurone, Eleusine, Piraeeo, Sunio, Fest. p. 258 Müll. (transl. of τετράπολις).
quadrurbem.short: quadrurbem Athenas Attius appellavit, quod scilicet ex quattuor urbibus in unam domicilia contulerunt, Braurone, Eleusine, Piraeeo, Sunio, Fest.

quadrus.full: quā^drus, a, um, adj. for quatrus, from quattuor, square (post-class.): quadrus terminus, Auct. Limit. p. 281 Goes.: cella, Pall. 1, 40: lapides, Vulg. Isa. 9, 10.

quadruus.full: quā^drŭus, a, um, adj. quattuor, fourcornered or fourfold (post-class.): errabam riguis per quadrua compita in hortis, i. e. laid out in squares, Aus. Idyll. 14, 5: vis, fourfold, Prud. Psych. 842.

quaerito.full: quaerĭto, āvi, ātum, 1, v. freq. a. quaero, to seek, search, or look for earnestly (ante-class.). In gen.: hominem inter vivos quaeritamus mortuum, Plaut. Men. 2, 1, 15: defessus sum quaeritando, id. Am. 4, 1, 4; id. Cist. 4, 2, 19: aliquem mari terrāque, id. Poen. prol. 105: te ipsum, Ter. Ad. 2, 4, 2: hospitium ab aliquo, Plaut. Poen. 3, 3, 77: lanā ac telā victum, to earn, Ter. And. 1, 1, 48: multis languoribus peresus essem te quaeritando, Cat. 58, 15.—Prov.: hujus sermo haud cinerem quaerit

quaero.full: quaero (old orthogr. QVAIRO, Epitaphs of the Scipios, 6; for the original form and etym. quaeso, ĕre, v. quaeso), sīvi or sĭi, sītum, 3, v. a., to seek. Lit. In gen.: aliquem, Enn. ap. Cic. Div. 1, 20, 40 (Ann. v. 43 Vahl.); Plaut. Mil. 2, 3, 3: te ipsum quaerebam, Ter. Heaut. 4, 8, 3: escam in sterquilinio, Phaedr. 3, 12 init.— In partic. To seek to get or procure, to seek or search for a thing, Ter. Heaut. 3, 1, 38: rem mercaturis faciendis, Cic. Par. 6, 2, 46.—Absol.: contrivi in quaerendo vi

quaesitio.full: quaesītĭo, ōnis, f. quaero, a seeking or searching after (post-Aug.). In gen.: Psyche quaesitioni Cupidinis intenta, populos circuibat, App. M. 5, p. 171, 8.— In partic., a questioning by torture, the question, inquisition: cum postero ad quaesitionem retraheretur, proripuit se custodibus, Tac. A. 4, 45; Inscr. Bertol. Antiq. Aquilei. p. 300, n. 419.

quaesitor.full: quaesītor, ōris, m. id., a seeker, searcher (post-class.). In gen., as for gold, connected with scrutator, Pacat. Pan. Th. 28.— In partic., an investigator. In judicial (esp. in criminal) matters, an examiner, inquisitor: quid mihi opus est sapiente judice? quid aequo quaesitore? Cic. Font. 6, 11; id. Sull. 28, 78; Cic. Verr. 1, 10, 29: quaesitorem edere, id. Planc. 17, 43: quaesitor Minos, Verg. A. 6, 432: tres, Sall. J. 40, 4.— Of Cicero, as the investigator of the Catilinarian conspiracy, Cic

quaesitum.full: quaesītum, i, v. quaero, P. a. C.

quaesitura.full: quaesītūra, ae, a false read. for quaestura, Tac. A. 3, 29.

quaesitus1.full: quaesītus, a, um, Part. and P. a., from quaero.

quaesitus2.full: quaesītus, ūs (only in abl. sing.), m. quaero. A seeking, searching (postAug.), Plin. 5, 9, 10, § 51 (al. quae situs).— Investigation: (rem) semper quaesitu dignam putavi, Macr. S. 7, 8, 9.

quaeso.full: quaeso, īvi or ĭi, 3, v. a. old form of quaero; root kis-; Sanscr. cish-, to hunt out. To seek, to seek to obtain any thing (ante-class.): quaeso, ut significat idem, quod rogo, ita quaesere ponitur ab antiquis pro quaerere, Fest. p. 258 Müll.: nautisque mari quaesentibus vitam, Enn. ap. Fest. l. l: quaese adveniente morbo nunc medicum tibi, Plaut. ap. Non. 44, 30. — To beg, pray, beseech, entreat (class.; mostly in first pers. sing.; syn.: rogo, oro, obsecro, peto, precor). With ut: Mars pater,

quaesticulus.full: quaestĭcŭlus, i, m. dim. quaestus, a small profit, slight gain (class.), Cic. Div. 2, 15, 34; id. Fam. 9, 16, 7; App. M. 11, p. 272, 1.

quaestio.full: quaestĭo, ōnis, f. quaero, a seeking. In gen. (Plautin.): cave, fuas mi in quaestione, lest you suffer yourself to be to seek, lest I have to look after you, Plaut. Pers. 1, 1, 52: tibi ne in quaestione essemus, id. Capt. 2, 2, 3; id. Ps. 2, 2, 68.— In partic., an inquiry, investigation, a questioning, question, subject of inquiry: quaestio est appetitio cognitionis, quaestionisque finis inventio, Cic. Ac. 2, 8, 26; 2, 36, 115: quae veri simillima (sententia sit), magna quaestio est, id. Tusc. 1

quaestionaliter.full: quaestĭōnālĭter, adv. quaestio, by way of question, in the form of a question (post-class.): propositio quaestionaliter posita, Fulg. Prisc. Serm. 16.

quaestionarius.full: quaestĭōnārĭus, ii, m. id., a torturer, executioner (post-class.), Cod. Th. 16, 12, 3; Hier. in Joel. 2, 21; Schol. Juv. 6, 480; Inscr. Grut. 545, 6.

quaestiono.full: quaestĭōno, āvi, 1, v. a. id., put to the question, i. e. put to the torture, put to the rack (eccl. Lat. and rare): omnes quaestionari, Fragm. Jur. Civ. Ante-Just. p. 109 Mai: tot confessores quaestionati et torti, Cypr. Ep. 69, n. 6.

quaestiuncula.full: quaestĭuncŭla, ae, f. dim. id., a little or trifling question (class.): quaestiunculam alicui ponere, Cic. de Or. 1, 22, 102; Sen. Ep. 117, 1: multae, Cic. Leg. 2, 20, 51; Quint. 1, 3, 11; Suet. Gram. 24 fin.

quaestor.full: quaestor (old orthogr., QVAISTOR, Epit. of the Scipios, et saep.), ōris, m. contr. from quaesitor, from quaero, a quætor, the title of a class of Roman magistrates, some of whom had charge of the pecuniary affairs of the State, while others conducted certain criminal trials (but only, it would seem, as delegates or commissioners of the people): quaestores a quaerendo, qui conquirerent publicas pecunias et maleficia, quae triumviri capitales nunc conquirunt: ab his postea, qui quaestionum judicia

quaestoricius.full: quaestōrīcĭus or -tĭus, a, um, adj. quaestor, of or belonging to a quæstor, quæstorian: QVAESTORICII, who had been quæstors, Tab. Canusin. ap. Inscr. Orell. 3721.

quaestorius.full: quaestōrĭus, a, um, adj. id., of or belonging to a quæstor, quæstorian (quite class.): officium quaestorium, the duty of a quæstor, Cic. Fam. 2, 17, 6: scelus, perpetrated in the quæstorship or by a quæstor, Cic. Verr. 1, 1, 4: aetas, the age requisite for the quæstorship, Quint. 12, 6, 1; cf.: adulescentes jam aetate quaestorios, Cic. Rep. 1, 12, 18: scribae, of the quæstor, Suet. Dom. 10: scriptum quaestorium comparavit, acted as secretary to a quæstor, id. Vit. Hor.: munera, i. e. gladiatoria

quaestuarius.full: quaestŭārĭus, a, um, adj. quaestus, of or belonging to gain, money-making, mercenary (post-Aug.): quaestuaria mancipia, Dig. 3, 2, 4, § 2: mulier, a prostitute for hire, ib. 23, 2, 43, § 7: majestas, Tert. Apol. 13.— Subst.: quaestuaria, ae, f., a prostitute: ex adulterā in quaestuariam versa, Sen. Ben. 6, 32, 1.

quaestuosus.full: quaestŭōsus, a, um, adj. quaestus. Gainful, profitable, advantageous, lucrative, productive (class.; syn. lucrosus): ager, productive, fruitful, Cato, R. R. 1, 6: mercatura, Cic. Tusc. 5, 31, 86; id. Fin. 5, 30, 91: quaestuosissima officina, id. Phil. 2, 14, 35: res Verri, Cic. Verr. 2, 2, 19, § 46: uberrimus et quaestuosissimus annus, id. ib. 1, 14, 40: hoc multo est quaestuosius, quam, etc., id. Agr. 2, 25, 67: benignitas quaestuosior, id. ib. 1, 4, 10: edictum quaestuosissimum, Cic. Verr. 2,

quaestura.full: quaestūra, ae, f. quaestor, the office of quæstor, the quæstorship (class.): quaestura primus gradus honoris, Cic. Verr. 1, 4, 11: quaesturam petere, id. Mur. 8, 18; Tac. A. 3, 29: ex quaesturā consulatum petere, Liv. 32, 7: gerere, Suet. Calig. 1. — Transf., the quæstor's chest: translator quaesturae, an embezzler of the public chest, Cic. Verr. 2, 5, 58, § 152.

quaestus.full: quaestus, ūs (archaic gen. quaesti, Plaut. Aul. 1, 2, 5; id. Poen. prol. 95; Ter. Hec. 5, 3, 38; Titin., Nov., Turp., and Caecil. ap. Non. 483, 19 sq.; Varr. ib. 492, 20.— Gen. quaestuis, Varr. ap. Non. 483, 32), m. quaero, a gaining, acquiring; gain, acquisition, profit, advantage (quite class.; syn.: lucrum, emolimentum). Lit.: quaestus pecuniae, Caes. B. G. 6, 17, 1: emendi aut vendendi quaestu et lucro duci, Cic. Tusc. 5, 3, 9: pauperes homines, quibus nec quaestus est, nec, etc., Plaut. Rud

qualibescit.full: quā-lĭbescit, adv., for qualibet, everywhere, in every way, Not. Tir. p. 35.
qualibescit.short: quā-lĭbescit, adv., for qualibet, everywhere, in every way, Not.

qualibet.full: quālĭbet (-lŭbet, abl. from quilibet), where it pleases, i. e. Where you will, everywhere: qualibet perambula aedes, Plaut. Most. 3, 2, 122; id. Aul. 4, 4, 19: quisquis amore tenetur, eat tutusque sacerque qualibet, Tib. 1, 2, 27: transitum praebent (flumina), Quint. 5, 13, 13.— As you please, anyhow, in any way: qualubet esse notus optas? Cat. 40, 6; 76, 13.

qualis.full: quālis, e, pron. adj. quis; kindr. with Gr. πη-λίκος; Goth. huc-leik; Germ. welcher, how constituted, of what sort, kind, or nature, what kind of a (class.). Interrog.: qualine amico mea commendavi bona? Call. Probo, et fideli, et fido, Plaut. Trin. 4, 4, 3: qualis oratoris et quanti hominis in dicendo putas esse historiam scribere? Cic. de Or. 2, 12, 51: quali fide, quali pietate existimatis eos esse, qui, etc., Cic. Font. 10, 21: qualis est istorum oratio? what kind of a speech is that? id. Ac

qualiscumque.full: quālis-cumque, quale-cumque, or -cunque (separated: quale id cumque est, Cic. N. D. 2, 30, 76; Ov. P. 4, 13, 6), adj. qualis. Rel., of what quality soever, of whatever kind (class.). With verb: licet videre, qualescumque summi civitatis viri fuerunt, talem civitatem fuisse, Cic. Leg. 3, 14, 31: sed homines benevolos, qualescumque sunt, grave est insequi contumeliā, be they as they may, id. Att. 14, 14, 5. — Absol. by ellipsis of verb, in emphatic expressions (v. Zumpt, § 706): qualicumque urbis
qualiscumque.short: quālis-cumque, quale-cumque, or -cunque (separated: quale id cumque est, Cic.

qualislibet.full: quālis-lĭbet, quale-libet, pron. indef., of what quality it pleases, of what sort you will (post-class.): pisces, Apic. 4, 2, § 143; Aug. Ep. 48; Claud. Mam. Stat. Anim. 1, 21 (in Cic. N. D. 2, 37, 93, written separately).

qualisnam.full: quālis-nam, pron. rel., of what quality, what sort of a (post-class.): qualisnam accusatio futura esset, App. Mag. p. 274, 21.

qualisqualis.full: quālis-quālis, quālequāle, adj., i. q. qualiscumque, of what quality soever, of whatever kind (post-class.), Dig. 4, 9, 7, § 4; 25, 4, 1, § 13; 43, 8, 2, § 11; 50, 14, 3 al.

qualitas.full: quālĭtas, ātis, f. qualis, III., a quality, property, nature, state, condition (class.; a word formed by Cicero as the translation of Gr. ποιότης; freq. only in postclass. prose), Cic. Ac. 1, 6, 24; cf.: qualitates igitur appellavi, quas ποιότητας Graeci vocant: quod ipsum apud Graecos non est vulgi verbum, sed philosophorum, id. ib. 1, 7, 25 sq.; cf. id. N. D. 2, 37, 94: litoris nostri, Col. 8, 17, 8; so, caeli, Quint. 5, 9, 15: facti, id. 7, 4, 16 et saep.— In plur.: qualitatium differentia, P

qualum.full: quālum, i, n., and quālus, i, m., a wicker basket or hamper, for various purposes; a fruit-hamper, wool-basket, winestrainer, etc. (cf. colum). Neutr.: quala satoria, Cato, R. R. 11, 5; so, quala, id. ib. 23, 1: mundissima, Col. 7, 3, 9.— Masc.: in qualos pertusos propagari, Cato, R. R. 52, 1: spisso vimine qualos, Verg. G. 2, 241 Serv.; so Hor. C. 3, 12, 4: saligneus, Col. 9, 15, 12; 8, 3, 4: vindemiatorii, Dig. 33, 7, 8 pr.; Pall. 4, 10.
qualum.short: quālum, i, n., and quālus, i, m., a wicker basket or hamper, for various purposes;

quam.full: quam (archaic form quamde or quande: quamde pro quam usos esse antiquos, cum multi veteres testimonio sunt, tum Ennius ... et Lucretius (1, 640), Fest. p. 261 Müll.; cf. Enn. Ann. v. 29, and v. 139 Vahl. So, too, Naev. ap. Fest. s. v. topper, p. 352 Müll.), adv. qui, in what manner, how, how much, as much as: quam nihil praetermittis in consilio dando! quam nihil tamen, quod tibi placeat, explicas! Cic. Att. 9, 2, A, 1: ut se accusari nolunt! quam cupiunt laudari! id. Fin. 5, 22, 61: quam multa,
quam.short: quam (archaic form quamde or quande: quamde pro quam usos esse antiquos, cum multi veteres testimonio sunt, tum Ennius ...

quamdiu.full: quam-dĭu, less freq. quandĭu (mostly as two words, sometimes separated: quam voluit diu, Cic. Q. Fr. 1, 1, 7), adv. Interrog., how long ago? how long? quamdiu id factum est? Plaut. Capt. 5, 3, 3: quandiu apud vos ero, Vulg. Marc. 9, 18.— Rel. Of time, as long as, until, during (class.): quamdiu potuit, tacuit, Caes. B. G. 1, 17: disces, quamdiu voles, Cic. Off. 1, 1, 2; Col. 12, 52, 13.— Until (very rare): jubebat, ut semper id comesset, quamdiu tamen melius invenisset, Lampr. Elag. 29, 7.— Comp

quamdiutinus.full: quamdĭūtĭnus, a, um, adj. quamdiu, lasting how long, of how long duration, Not. Tir. p. 35.

quamdudum.full: quamdūdum, more correctly as two words, quam dūdum.
quamdudum.short: quamdūdum, more correctly as two words, quam dūdum.

quamlibet.full: quam-lĭbet (-lŭbet), adv. As it pleases, as you (they, etc.) will, at pleasure: quamlubet esto unica res, Lucr. 2, 541: lambe otio, Phaedr. 1, 24, 6.— In gen., how much soever, ever so much, howsoever: quodvis quamlibet tenue munusculum, Cael. ap. Cic. Fam. 8, 10, 3: occupat egressas quamlibet ante rates, Ov. Tr. 1, 10, 5: infirmae manus, howsoever weak, id. Am. 1, 7, 66: quamlibet parum sit, however inconsiderable it may be, Quint. 1, 1, 18; 1, 12, 5; 5, 13, 56; 12, 1, 29: specularis lapis find

quamobrem.full: quămobrem (or quăm ob rem), adv. quam-ob-rem (class.). Interrog., for what reason? on what account? wherefore? why? Am. Scelestissumum te arbitror. So. Nam quamobrem? Am. Quia, etc., Plaut. Am. 2, 1, 2: quem ad finem? ... quamobrem? quam ob causam? Cic. Verr. 2, 5, 29, § 75; id. Fin. 1, 5, 15.— In indirect questions: cum quaereret quam ob rem Ariovistus non decertaret. Caes. B. G. 1, 50. — Rel., from which cause or reason, wherefore, why: hoc est homini, quamobrem vitam amet, Plaut. Ps. 5, 1, 11

quamplures.full: quamplūres, a (or quam plūres), adj. quam-plus, very many (ante-class. and post-Aug. for complures): curiosi sunt hic quamplures mali, Plaut. Stich. 1, 3, 44: palaestritae, Petr. 21.— Sup.: quamplūrĭ-mus (quam plūrĭmus), a, um; commonly in plur., very many: colles, Caes. B. C. 3, 45: radices, Cato ap. Plin. 17, 18, 29, § 126.—Hence, subst.: quamplūrĭmum, i, n., very much: quam plurimo vendere, Cic. Off. 3, 12, 50: quam plurimum brassicae, Cato, R. R. 157, 8.

quamprimum.full: quam-prīmum (or quam prī-mum), forthwith, as soon as possible (class.): hominem istum quam primum absolvitote, Ter. Ad. 2, 4, 18: huic mandat, ut ad se quamprimum revertatur, Caes. B. G. 4, 21; Cic. Fam. 2, 6, 1: invisam quaerens quam primum abrumpere lucem, Verg. A. 4, 631.—With posse: ut quamprimum possis, redeas, Plaut. Capt. 2, 3, 88: sed recipe te, quam primum potes, id. Pers. 1, 1, 52.
quamprimum.short: quam-prīmum (or quam prī-mum), forthwith, as soon as possible (class.): hominem istum quam primum absolvitote, Ter.

quamquam.full: quam-quam (quan-), conj., though, although, albeit; ante-class. always, and in class. prose regularly joined with indic.; by Cic. rarely with the subj., and usu. when the general idea would demand the subj. (as potential, conditional, consecutive, etc.; cf. Zumpt, Gram. § 574; Madv. § 361, A, 3; and v. esp. Fischer, Gram. 2, p. 696 sq.). With indic.: quamquam blandā voce vocabam, Enn. ap. Cic. Div. 1, 20, 41 (Ann. v. 50 Vahl.): quamquam libenter escis alienis studes, Plaut. Pers. 3, 1, 8; id. Mi

quamvis.full: quam-vīs, adv. and conj. Adv., as you will, as much as you will or like, ever so much, ever so; hence, to designate a very high degree, as much as possible, very much, exceedingly (class.): quamvis multos nominatim proferre, as many as you will, very many, Cic. Rosc. Am. 16, 47: esse quamvis facetum atque salsum, id. de Or. 2, 56, 228: quamvis callide, quamvis audacter, quamvis impudenter, Cic. Verr. 2, 2, 54, § 134: quamvis subito, id. Lael. 5, 17: et praeter eos quamvis enumeres multos licet,

quanam.full: quā-nam, adv. Where indeed, where (very rare): quanam in alium orbem transirent, Liv. 5, 34.— How then, how: delphini quanam audiant, mirum, Plin. 11, 37, 50, § 137.

quando.full: quando (old form quandod, acc. to Fest. p. 258 b Müll.), adv. and conj. Adv. Interrog., at what time? when? Do. Venit Chaerea. Ph. Quando? Do. Hodie. Ph. Quamdudum? Do. Modo, Ter. Eun. 4, 4, 30; id. Heaut. 2, 2, 9; Cic. de Or. 1, 22, 102; id. Pis. 21, 49: o rus, quando ego te aspiciam? quandoque licebit? etc., Hor. S. 2, 6, 60; id. Epod. 9, 1; id. C. 1, 24, 8: dic mihi cras istud, Postume, quando venit? Mart. 5, 58, 2.— Rel., at what time, when: non intellegitur, quando obrepat senectus, Cic. Se

quandocumque.full: quandō-cumquē or -cunquē (quandŏ - cumque, Ter. Maur. p. 2404 P.; separated: quando consumet cumque, Hor. S. 1, 9, 33), adv. Rel., at what time soever, at whatever time, whenever, as often as, as soon as (mostly poet.). With indic.: quandocumque ista gens suas litteras dabit, Cato ap. Plin. 29, 1, 7, § 14: quandocumque igitur vitam mea fata reposcant, Prop. 2, 1, 71: quandocumque trahunt invisa negotia Romam, Hor. Ep. 1, 14, 17; cf. id. ib. 1, 16, 58: quandocunque fors obtulerat, Auct. B. Alex.

quandolibet.full: quandō-lĭbet, adv., at some time or other, in due time (eccl. Lat.): necesse est, ut mortem recipiat quandolibet, Lact. Opif. Dei, 4, 7.
quandolibet.short: quandō-lĭbet, adv., at some time or other, in due time (eccl.

quandone.full: quandōnē, adv., for quandocumque, as soon as, when: QVANDONE EGO ESSE DESIERO, Inscr. Grut. 607, 1 dub.
quandone.short: quandōnē, adv., for quandocumque, as soon as, when: QVANDONE EGO ESSE DESIERO, Inscr.

quandoque1.full: quandō-quē, adv. Rel. Temp., at what time soever, whenever, whensoever, as often as (class.): QVANDOQVE SARPTA DONEC DEMPTA ERVNT, Lex XII. Tabularum: quandoque ab eādem parte sol eodemque tempore iterum defecerit, tum, etc., Cic. Rep. 6, 22, 24: ut, quan doque idem prodigium nuntiaretur, feriae per novem dies agerentur, Liv. 1, 31, 4: reddituros, quandoque recepisset, Curt. 7, 10, 9; Liv. 27, 10, 5: indignor, quandoque bonus dormitat Homerus, Hor. A. P. 359: quandoque trahet feroces Per sacrum

quandoquidem.full: quandō-quĭdem (o scanned short, Verg. E. 3, 55; Lucr. 2, 980), adv., since indeed, since, seeing that (class.): quandoquidem tam iners, tam nulli consili sum, Ter. And. 3, 5, 2; 3, 2, 7; id. Ad. 5, 8, 33; id. Eun. 2, 3, 82: quandoquidem tu istos oratores tantopere laudas, Cic. Brut. 44, 163: quandoquidem id tale esse debet, ut, etc., id. Fin. 5, 13, 37; 5, 23, 66; Liv. 8, 33: haec detur cura censoribus, quandoquidem eos in re publicā semper volumus esse, Cic. Leg. 3, 20, 47; id. Or. 31, 112; id.

quantillus.full: quantillus, a, um, adj. dim. [quantulus], how small a deal, i. e. how little, how small, how diminutive (Plautin.). Interrog.: huic debet Philolaches paulum. Then. Quantillum? Tra. Quasi quadraginta minas, Plaut. Most. 3, 1, 95; id. Ps. 4, 7, 95; id. Curc. 1, 2, 14.— In exclamations: haecine sunt meae filiae? Quantae e quantillis jam sunt factae! Plaut. Poen. 5, 3, 47; id. Truc. 2, 8, 7.— Rel.: subducam ratiunculam, quantillum argenti mihi apud trapezitam siet, Plaut. Capt. 1, 2, 90.

quantisper.full: quantisper, adv. [quantum, how much), how long (ante-class.). Interrog.: velim paulisper opperiri te. Quantisper? Non plus triduum, Caecil. ap. Non. 511, 30.— Rel.: possum exorare te, ut recedas a me paulisper modo? Quantisper sat habes, as long as, Pompon. ap. Non. 511, 33.

quantitas.full: quantĭtas, ātis, f. quantus. In gen., greatness, extent, quantity (perh. only post-Aug.): quantitas est modulorum ex ipsius operis sumptione, singulisque membrorum partibus, universi operis conveniens effectus, Vitr. 1, 2: umoris, Plin. 17, 24, 37, § 219: modi seu numeri, Quint. 7, 4, 3: vocis, strength, id. 11, 3, 14: quantitas et qualitas, id. 7, 2, 6: pretii, App. Mag. p. 239, 11.— In partic. A sum, amount (post-class.): si non corpus sit legatum, sed quantitas, Dig. 30, 1, 34, § 3; 12, 1, 6.

quantitudo.full: quantĭtūdo, ĭnis, f. id., quantity, degree, Cael. Aur. Salat. Praec. 10.

quanto.full: quantō, adv., v. quantus fin. B.

quantocius.full: quant-ōcĭus, adv. quanto-ocius, the sooner the better, as quickly as possible (post-class.): ut quantocius ad ea perveniat oratio, Mamert. Grat. Act. ad Julian. 2: discede quantocius, ne, Sulp. Sev. Dial. 3, 4; Licin. ap. Lact. Mort. Pers. 48, 10; Vulg. Gen. 45, 19.

quantopere.full: quant-ŏpĕrē (contr. form, for which, in recent editions, the MS. form quantō ŏpĕre is restored), adv., how greatly, how much (class.): dici non potest, quanto opere gaudeant, Cic. Att. 14, 6, 2; id. Tusc. 3, 3, 6. —After tanto opere, as: neque enim tanto opere hanc a Crasso disputationem desiderabam, quanto opere, etc., Cic. de Or. 1, 35, 164; v. quantus.

quantulus1.full: quantŭlus, a, um, adj. dim. [quantus], how little, how small, how trifling (class.): nescio quantulum attulerit: verum haud permultum attulit, Plaut. Bacch. 2, 3, 86: corpora, Lucr. 3, 378: quantulum visum est, as much as seems good to him, Cic. Div. in Caecil. 17, 57: quantulus (sol) nobis videtur! Cic. Ac. 2, 26, 82: id autem quantulum est? how small? id. Leg. 2, 19, 47: quantula sint hominum corpuscula, Juv. 10, 172; Plin. 11, 5, 4, § 12: quantulum est mihi memoriae, as much as I remember, i.

quantuluscumque.full: quantŭlus-cumque (or-cunque), ăcumque, umcumque, adj., however small, how little soever (class.): de hac meā, quantulacumque est, facultate quaeritis, Cic. de Or. 1, 30, 135: adfectus quantulicumque sunt, Sen. Ep. 85, 8: occasio, Juv. 13, 183: umor, Col. 2, 11, 7. — Neutr. as subst.: quantŭlumcumque, however small, however insignificant a thing: quicumque eramus, et quantulumcumque dicebamus, Cic. Or. 30, 106.— Separated: quantulum id cumque est, Cic. de Or. 2, 23, 97. — With gen.: quantulumcunq
quantuluscumque.short: quantŭlus-cumque (or-cunque), ăcumque, umcumque, adj., however small, how little soever (class.): de hac meā, quantulacumque est, facultate quaeritis, Cic.

quantulus2.full: quantŭlus-lĭbet, lălĭbet, lumlĭbet, adj., how little soever (post-class.): febricula, Dig. 21, 1, 4.
quantulus2.short: quantŭlus-lĭbet, lălĭbet, lumlĭbet, adj., how little soever (post-class.): febricula, Dig.

quantulusquisque.full: quantŭlus-quisque, lăquaeque, lumquodque, adj., how small soever (post-class.), Gell. praef. § 24.
quantulusquisque.short: quantŭlus-quisque, lăquaeque, lumquodque, adj., how small soever (post-class.), Gell.

quantus.full: quantus, a, um, adj. quam, how great. Bellum, Nep. Dat. 5, 1: calamitates, Cic. Tusc. 1, 35, 86: homo in dicendo, id. de Or. 2, 12, 51: gravitas, Vell. 2, 129, 2.—Corresp. with tantus: videre mihi videor tantam dimicationem, quanta numquam fuit, Cic. Att. 7, 1, 2.—With sup.: tanta est inter eos, quanta maxima esse potest, morum studiorumque distantia, the greatest possible difference, Cic. Lael. 20, 74.—Without tantus: quantus non unquam antea, exercitus venit, Liv. 9, 37, 2: quanta maxime poter

quantuscumque.full: quantus-cumque, tăcumque, tumcumque, adj., how great soever, of whatever size (class.): quantuscumque sum ad judicandum, Cic. de Or. 2, 28, 122: bona, quantacumque erant, id. Phil. 5, 8, 22: adfectus, quantuscumque est, Sen. Ep. 85, 8: quantaecumquae de Romanis tamen, victoriae fama, however small, Liv. 27, 31, 3: unum quantumcunque ex insperato gaudium, id. 30, 10, 20 Weissenb. ad loc.: quanticumque, at whatsoever price, Sen. Ep. 80, 4.—To denote indefiniteness in number, how many soever: naves
quantuscumque.short: quantus-cumque, tăcumque, tumcumque, adj., how great soever, of whatever size (class.): quantuscumque sum ad judicandum, Cic.

quantuslibet.full: quantus-lĭbet, tălibet, tumlĭbet, adj., as great as you please, how great soever, ever so great (poet. and in post - Aug. prose): quantolibet ordine dignus, Ov. F. 6, 669: saevitia hiemis, Col. 8, 17, 11: facilitas, Tac. Agr. 6: quantālibet lassitudine recreari defessos, Plin. 27, 12, 104, § 127.— Neutr. adverb.: quantum-lĭbet, how much soever, ever so much: quantumlibet intersit, Liv. 39, 37, 14; Quint. 12, 6, 4: te quantumlibet oderint hostes, Eum. Pan. Const. 10.
quantuslibet.short: quantus-lĭbet, tălibet, tumlĭbet, adj., as great as you please, how great soever, ever so great (poet.

quantusvis.full: quantus-vīs, tăvis, tumvis, adj., as much as you will, as great as you please, however great, ever so great (class.): et manus una regit quantovis impete euntem (navem), Lucr. 4, 903; 4, 1171: quantasvis magnas copias sustineri posse, Caes. B. G. 5, 28: portum satis amplum quantaevis classi, for any fleet, be it ever so large, Liv. 26, 42: cum faciem videas, videtur esse quantivis pretii, Ter. And. 5, 2, 15: ingenium hominis, Gell. 4, 1, 2.— Neutr. subst.: quantum-vīs, however great an amount, a
quantusvis.short: quantus-vīs, tăvis, tumvis, adj., as much as you will, as great as you please, however great, ever so great (class.): et manus una regit quantovis impete euntem (navem), Lucr.

quapropter.full: quă-propter (in tmesi: qua me propter adduxi, Ter. Hec. 3, 3, 4), adv. qui-propter, for what, wherefore, why. Interrog. (ante- and post-class.): quapropter id vos factum suspicamini? Plaut. Most. 2, 2, 52: Tra. Quāpropter? Theo. Quia, etc., id. ib. 3, 2, 140: parumper opperire me hic: My. Quapropter? Ter. And. 4, 2, 31.— Indirect: sed quid est quapropter nobis vos malum minitamini? Plaut. Bacch. 5, 4, 25: credo te non nihil mirari, Quid sit, quapropter te huc foras puerum evocare jussi, Ter. Hec
quapropter.short: quă-propter (in tmesi: qua me propter adduxi, Ter.

quaqua.full: quāquā, adv. prop. abl. of quisquis, wheresoever, whithersoever (ante- and postclass.): quaqua incedit, Plaut. Mil. 2, 1, 14: tangit, id. Ep. 5, 2, 9; App. M. 2, p. 116, 2; cf. id. ib. 11, p. 258, 30: quaqua versus, to all sides, id. ib. 4, p. 145, 6.

quaquam.full: quāquam, a false read. for quoquam, Lucr. 1, 428.

quaque.full: quāquē, adv. prop. abl. of quisque, wheresoever, whithersoever (poet.): quaque iverit, Manil. 5, 313.

quare.full: quā-rē (or separately, quā rē), adv. quae-res. Interrog., by what means? how? Ter. Eun. 2, 3, 78.— Rel., by which means, whereby (rare but class.): multas res novas in edictum addidit, quare luxuria reprimeretur, Nep. Cat. 2, 3: permulta sunt, quae dici possunt, quare intellegatur, etc., Cic. Rosc. Am. 33, 94.— From what cause, on what account, wherefore, why. Interrog.: quare ausus? Plaut. Mil. 5, 12: quare negasti illud te fuisse laturum? Cic. de Or. 1, 16, 71: quā re enim primum ille adesse n

quarta.full: quartă-dĕcŭmāni, ōrum, m. adj. quartus-decumanus, of or belonging to the fourteenth legion; subst., the soldiers of the fourteenth legion, Tac. H. 2, 11.

quartanarius.full: quartānārĭus, a, um, adj. quartus. Amounting to or containing a fourth (post-class.): tabula, Pall. 2, 11.— That has a quartan ague, Schol. Juv. 9, 16.

quartanus.full: quartānus, a, um, adj. id., of or belonging to the fourth; esp., Of or occurring on the fourth day, quartan: febris, Cic. N. D. 3, 10, 24; Plin. 7, 50, 51, § 166; Mart. 10, 77, 3.— Hence, as subst.: quar-tāna, ae, f. (sc. febris), an ague occurring every fourth day, a quartan ague (class.): in quartanam conversa vis est morbi, Cic. Fam. 16, 11, 1; cf. Cels. 2, 1, 20; Plin. 22, 25, 72, § 150: frigida, Hor. S. 2, 3, 290.— Of or belonging to the fourth legion; plur. as subst.: quartāni, m., the sol

quartarius.full: quartārĭus, ii, m. id.. A fourth part, quarter of any measure, esp. of a sextarius, a quartern, gill: sumito bituminis tertiarium, et sulphuris quartarium, Cato, R. R. 95, 1: vini, Liv. 5, 47: mellis, Col. 12, 5, 1: farris, Plin. 18, 3, 3, § 9.— A mule-driver, muleteer, who received a fourth part of the profits, Lucil. ap. Fest. p. 258 Müll.

quartato.full: quartātō, adv. id., for the fourth time: tertiato et quartato dicere, Cato ap. Serv. ad Verg. A. 3, 314.

quarticeps.full: quartĭceps, cĭpĭtis, adj.,four-peaked: collis, an old formula, Varr. L. L. 5, § 52 Müll.; so id. ib. 5, § 50 and 47.
quarticeps.short: quartĭceps, cĭpĭtis, adj.,four-peaked: collis, an old formula, Varr.

quartocerius.full: quartōcērĭus, a, um, adj. quartus-cera, that is of the fourth rank, Cod. Just. 12, 24, 7.

quartum.full: quartum, adv., v. quartus, A. fin.

quartus.full: quartus, a, um, num. adj. for quatertus from quattuor, kindr. with Gr. τέτϝαρτος and Sanscr. caturtha, the fourth, the fourth: perfidia, et peculatus ex urbe et avaritiā si exsulant, quarta invidia, quinta ambitio, Plaut. Pers. 4, 4, 7: pars copiarum, Caes. B. G. 1, 12: quartus ab Arcesilā, the fourth from Arcesilas, Cic. Ac. 2, 6: pater, i. e. abavus, Verg. A. 10, 619: quartus decimus, the fourteenth, Tac. A. 13, 15: die quarto, on the fourth day, four days ago: nuper die quarto, ut recordor, C

quartusdecimus.full: quartus-dĕcĭmus, a, um, num. adj., the fourteenth: pars, Vitr. 4, 6: legio, Tac. A. 1, 70; 13, 15.

quasi.full: quăsĭ (old form QVăSEI, Tab. Bantin. lin. 10; Inscr. Orell. 2488), adv. quamsi. Lit., as if, just as, as it were (cf.: veluti, sicuti, tamquam): modo introii. Si. Quasi ego, quam dudum, rogem, as if I asked, Ter. And. 5, 2, 9: quasi vero venire debuerint, just as though they ought to have come, Cic. Fam. 3, 7, 3: quasi vero ille factum id esse defendat, id. Off. 3, 9, 39: philosophia laudatarum artium omnium quasi parens, id. de Or. 1, 3, 9; cf.: quasi decursus temporis, id. Fam. 3, 2, 2.— After

quasillaria.full: quăsillārĭa, ae, f. quasilla, a basketwench, spinning-girl (post-Aug.), Petr. 132; Inscr. Grut. 648, 5.

quasillum.full: quăsillum, i, n., and quăsillus, i, m. dim. qualum, a small basket for various purposes; esp., a wool-basket (class.), Cato, R. R. 133.—Of wool-baskets: inter quasilla pendebatur aurum, in the spinning-room, Cic. Phil. 3, 4, 10: pressumque quasillo Scortum, who must spin, i. e. low, mean, Tib. 4, 10, 3; Prop. 4 (5), 7, 37.
quasillum.short: quăsillum, i, n., and quăsillus, i, m.

quassabilis.full: quassābĭlis, e, adj. quasso, that may be shaken (post-Aug.): munimen quassabile ferro, Luc. 6, 22.

quassabundus.full: quassābundus, a, um, adj. id., tottering, of a drunkard, Macr. S. 5, 21.

quassatio.full: quassātĭo, ōnis, f. id., a shaking: capitum, Liv. 22, 17, 3: cymbalorum, a striking together, beating, Arn. 7, 237: quassationes, shakings of the body, Macr. S. 7, 15, 9. — A disturbance, affliction: cessavit quassatio, Vulg. Psa. 105, 30.

quassati.full: quassātĭ-pennae, ārum, f. quatio-penna, feather-shaking, an epithet of geese: anates, Varr. ap. Non. 460, 8 dub.

quassatura.full: quassātūra, ae, f. quasso, a shaking; hence, transf., An injury occasioned by shaking: quassaturas fovere, Plin. Val. 4, 5.— A part injured by shaking, Veg. Vet. 1, 28, 5.

quasso.full: quasso (old form casso, Plaut. Bacch. 2, 3, 71 Ritschl), āvi, ātum, 1, v. freq. a. and n. quatio. Act., to shake or toss violently (class.). Lit.: ecus saepe jubam quassat, Enn. ap. Macr. S. 6, 3 (Ann. v. 506 Vahl.): caput, Plaut. Merc. 3, 4, 15; Verg. A. 7, 292; Val. Fl. 1, 526: Etruscam pinum, Verg. A. 9, 521: hastam, id. ib. 12, 94; Ov. A. A. 1, 696: monumenta, Plin. Ep. 8, 17, 5: lampade, of the Furies, Sil. 2, 611; cf. lampada, Verg. A. 6, 587.—Pass., in mid. force, tremble: quassantur memb

quassus1.full: quassus, a, um, Part. and P. a., from quatio.

quassus2.full: quassus, ūs, m. quatio, a shaking, Pac. ap. Cic. Tusc. 2, 21, 50.

quatefacio.full: quătĕ-făcĭo, fēci, factum, 3, v. a. quatio-facio, to shake; trop., to cause to waver, to weaken: quatefeci Antonium, Cic. Ep. ad Brut. 1, 10, 4.

quatenus.full: quā-tĕnus (quātĭnus, quātĕnos; cf. Fest. p. 258 fin. Müll.), adv. Lit. (only in indirect questions; cf. quī), until where, how far: in omnibus rebus videndum est, quatenus, Cic. Or. 22, 73: quatenus progredi debeat, id. Lael. 11, 36.— Transf. How far, to what extent: quatenus sint ridicula tractanda oratori, perquam diligenter videndum est, Cic. de Or. 2, 58, 237: quatenus quaque fini dari venia amicitiae debeat, Gell. 1, 3, 16.—Ellipt.: nulla cognitio finium, ut ullā in re statuere possimus, qu

quater.full: quăter, adv. num. quattuor, four times: quater in anno pariunt, Varr. R. R. 3, 10; Verg. A. 2, 242; Hor. S. 2, 3, 1.—With other numerals: quater quinis minis, Plaut. Ps. 1, 3, 111: quater deni, forty, Ov. M. 7, 293: quater decies, fourteen times, Cic. Verr. 2, 1, 39, § 100: quater centies, Vitr. 10, 14. —Freq. in phrase: ter et quater, ter aut quater, or terque quaterque, three and (or) four times, i. e. over and over again, often, extremely: ter et quater Anno revisens aequor, Hor. C. 1, 31, 13

quaternarius.full: quăternārĭus, a, um, adj. quaterni, consisting of four each, containing four, quaternary (post-Aug.): scrobes quaternarii, hoc est quoquoversus pedum quattuor, four feet square, Col. 11, 2, 28: numerus, the number four, the quaternary, Plin. 28, 6, 17, § 64: formae, of coins, Lampr. Alex. Sev. 38.

quaterni.full: quăterni, ae, a (gen. plur. quaternūm, Liv. 6, 22, 7; Col. 5, 5, 2; Plin. 9, 3, 2, § 4), adj. plur. [quattuor]. Four each, by fours, four at a time: quaternos denarios in singulas vini amphoras exegisse, Cic. Font. 5, 9: primam aciem quaternae cohortes ex V. legionibus tenebant, i. e. four from each legion, Caes. B. C. 1, 83: saepe tribus lectis videas cenare quaternos, Hor. S. 1, 4, 86.— Four together, four at once: propter bis quaternas causas, Varr. L. L. 5, 1, 6; Aus. ldyll. 10, 60; Sedul. 2

quaternio.full: quăternĭo, ōnis, m. quaterni, the number four, a quaternion, Mart. Cap. 7, § 767.— Esp., On dice, a quatre (postclass.), Isid. 18, 65.— A body of four soldiers, a quaternion, Vulg. Act. 12, 4.

quatio.full: quătĭo, no perf., quassum, 3, v. a. Sanscr. root, cyu-, to move, set in motion; cf. Gr. σκεῦος, instrument; σκευάζω, to prepare, to shake (class.; syn.: concutio, convello). Lit. In gen., Fest. p. 261 Müll.: cum equus magnā vi caput quateret, Liv. 8, 7: alas, Verg. A. 3, 226: pennas, Ov. M. 4, 676; Hor. C. 3, 29, 53: aquas, to agitate, disturb, Ov. H. 18, 48: cymbala, Verg. G. 4, 64: catenas, Plin. Ep. 7, 27, 5: caput. Ov. F. 6, 400: comas, id. H. 14, 40: quercum huc illuc, id. M. 12, 329.— Of e

quatrio.full: quā^trĭo, ōnis, m. quattuor, the number four, esp. on dice, a four, a quatre: jactus quisque apud lusores veteres a numero vocabatur, ut unio, binio, trio, quatrio, quinio, senio. Postea appellatio singulorum mutata est, et unionem canem, trionem suppum, quatrionem planum vocabant, Isid. Orig. 18, 65.

quatrisextium.full: quā^trĭsextĭum, ii, n. quattuorsextus, four times sixfold, Not. Tir. p. 147.
