resex.full: rĕsex, ĕcis (only resecem and reseces occur), m. reseco, the stump of a vinebranch left in pruning, = pollex, Col. 4, 21, 3; 3, 10, 15; 4, 24, 17; 5, 5, 11.
resex.short: rĕsex, ĕcis (only resecem and reseces occur), m.

resibilo.full: rĕ-sībĭlo, āre, v. n., to hiss at, Sid. Carm. 9, 83.

resideo.full: rĕ-sĭdĕo, sēdi, 2, v. n. and a. [sedeo], to sit back, remain sitting anywhere (cf. resisto); to remain behind, to remain, rest, linger, tarry, abide, reside (syn. remaneo; class.). Lit.: sine mente animoque nequit residere per artus pars ulla animai, Lucr. 3, 398: piger pandi tergo residebat aselli, Ov. F. 3, 749: in tergo, id. M. 10, 124; cf.: Acidis in gremio (latitans), resting, id. ib. 13, 787: in hoc facto de cautibus antro, residing, id. ib. 1, 575; cf.: Erycina Monte suo residens, id. ib.

resido.full: rĕ-sīdo, sēdi (in some MSS. also rĕsīdi), 3, v. n., to sit down, to settle anywhere (class.). Lit.: residamus, si placet, Cic. Fin. 3, 2, 9 Madv. N. cr.: in ripă inambulantes, tum vero residentes, id. Leg. 1, 5, 15: (aves) plurimum volant ... cetera genera residunt et insistunt, Plin. 10, 39, 55, § 114: mediis residunt Aedibus, Verg. A. 8, 467: Siculis arvis, id. ib. 5, 702: residunt In partem, quae peste caret, id. ib. 9, 539: loci amoenitate captos in iisdem terris cum virgine resedisse, Just.

residuus.full: rĕsĭdŭus, a, um, adj. resideo, that is left behind, that remains over and above, remaining, residuary; subst., the remainder, residue, rest (class.; cf.: reliquus, superstes): odium, Cic. Fam. 1, 9, 20: sollicitudo, Planc. ap. Cic. Fam. 10, 11, 3: ex residuā vetere simultate, Liv. 29, 37; cf. Suet. Calig. 15: irae bellorum, Liv. 1, 30; cf. bellum, Suet. Ner. 13: nomen libertatis (with reliqua umbra), Plin. Ep. 8, 24, 4: residuae integraeque etiam nunc (copiae), Suet. Oth. 9; cf.: manus Spartaci

resignaculum.full: rĕsignācŭlum, i, n. resigno, an unsealing; trop., a disclosure: similitudinis, Tert. adv. Marc. 2, 10.

resignatrix.full: rĕsignātrix, īcis, f. resignator, she that unseals or opens: arboris Eva, Tert. Hab. Mul. 1.

resigno.full: rĕ-signo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. To unseal, open (class.). Lit.: litteras, Plaut. Trin. 3, 3, 65; Cic. Att. 11, 9, 2: testamenta, Hor. Ep. 1, 7, 9; Dig. 28, 1, 23; 29, 3, 6: loculos, Plin. 14, 13, 14, § 89.—Poet.: perjuria Graia resignat, breaks through the faithless band, Sil. 17, 426: (Mercurius) lumina morte resignat, opens the eyes of the dead whom he is about to conduct to Orcus, Verg. A. 4, 244.— Trop. To annul, cancel, invalidate, rescind, destroy (syn.: rescindere, dissolvere): tabularum fi

resilio.full: rĕ-sĭlĭo, ŭi (resiliit, Quadrig. ap. Prisc. p. 906 P.; resilivi, Sen. Contr. 1, 3, 4), 4, v. n., to leap or spring back (rare but class.). Lit.: (exit in terram) in Indiae fluminibus certum genus piscium, ac deinde resilit, Plin. 9, 19, 35, § 71: recedere sensim datur (oratoribus): Quidam et resiliunt, quod est plane ridiculum, Quint. 11, 3, 127: (ranae) saepe In gelidos resilire lacus, Ov. M. 6, 374: piratae in aquas suas, Flor. 3, 6, 6: velites ad manipulos, Liv. 30, 33 fin.: a taetro veneno,

resimplicatus.full: rĕ-simplĭcātus, a, um, Part. [simplico], doubled, Cael. Aur. Tard. 5, 1, 20.

resimus.full: rĕ-sīmus, a, um, adj., turned up, bent back: nares (boum, simiarum), Col. 6, 1, 3; Ov. M. 14, 95: rostrum hippopotami, Plin. 8, 25, 39, § 95: labra canis, Varr. R. R. 2, 9, 3: renes, Cels. 4, 1: lamina, id. 8, 3: plaga, id. 7, 26, 2.
resimus.short: rĕ-sīmus, a, um, adj., turned up, bent back: nares (boum, simiarum), Col.

resina.full: rēsīna, ae, f. perh. kindr. with ῥητίνη, resin, rosin, Auct. B. Hisp. 33; Plin. 16, 11, 22, § 53; 24, 6, 19, § 28; 24, 6, 22, § 32; Cato, R. R. 23, 3; Pall. 3, 25, 23; Mart. 3, 74, 4; 12, 32, 21: vinum quod resinā conditum est, Cels. 4, 5, 29: resina terebintha, turpentine, Col. 12, 20, 3.

resinaceus.full: rēsīnācĕus, a, um, adj. resina, resinous, resinaceous: semen (rosmarini), Plin. 24, 11, 59, § 99.

resinalis.full: rēsīnālis, e, adj. id., resinous, Cael. Aur. Tard. 2, 13, 178; 2, 14, 207.

resinatus.full: rēsīnātus, a, um, adj. id., resined: vinum, seasoned or flavored with resin, Mart. 3, 77, 8; Plin 23, 1, 24, § 46; Cels. 2, 24, 11; 2, 28, 5: juventus, smeared with resin (to remove the hair and make the skin smooth), Juv. 8, 114.

resinosus.full: rēsīnōsus, a, um, adj. id., full of resin, gummy, resinous: medicamina, Col. 12, 20, 3: ladanum, Plin. 26, 8, 30, § 48: lentor, id. 13, 6, 12, § 54: odor, id. 27, 4, 10, § 26.—Sup.: pix Brutia (with pinguissima), Plin. 15, 7, 7, § 31; 24, 7, 23, § 37.

resinula.full: rēsīnŭla, ae, f. dim. id., a little bit of gum, as frankincense, Arn. 7, 233.

resipio.full: rĕ-sĭpĭo, ĕre, v. a. sapio, to savor, taste, or smack of something; to have a savor or flavor of something (class.). Lit.: mustum resipit ferrum, Varr. R. R. 1, 54, 3; cf. picem (uva), Plin. 14, 1, 3, § 18: quicquam (aqua), id. 31, 3, 22, § 37: quam minimum amaritudinis (taleolae), Col. 12, 48, 2.— Trop., to smack of, savor of: Epicurus homo non aptissimus ad jocandum, minimeque resipiens patriam, Cic. N. D. 2, 17, 46: istae (comoediae) resipiunt stilum Plautinum, Gell. 3, 3, 13. — * Pregn., to

resipiscentia.full: rĕsĭpiscentĭa, ae, f. resipisco, a transl. of μετάνοια, a change of mind, reformation, repentance, Lact. 6, 24, 6.

resipisco.full: rĕsĭpisco, īvi or ĭi (resipui, Cic. Att. 4, 5, 1; Afran. ap. Prisc. 897 P.; or Com. Rel. v. 16 Rib.; resipisti, Plaut. Mil. 4, 8, 34; resipisset, Cic. Sest. 38, 80; resipiit, Suet. Ner. 42), 3, v. inch. n. [resipio], to recover one's senses, come to one's self again; to revive, recover (class.): afferte aquam ... dum resipiscit ... Jam resipisti? Plaut. Mil. 4, 8, 24, and 35; Ter. And. 4, 2, 15; Suet. Tib. 73; id. Ner. 42; Plin. 30, 10, 24, § 84: multo omnium nunc me fortunatissimum Factum puto

resistentia.full: rĕsistentia, ae, f. resisto, resistance, opposition (late Lat. for repugnantia), Aug. de Pecc. Mer. 2, 22.

re3.full: rĕ-sisto, stĭti, 3, v. n. To stand back, remain standing anywhere (cf. resideo); to stand still, halt, stop, stay; to stay behind, remain, continue (class.; less freq. than consistere). Lit.: dabo μέγα κακόν, nisi resistis ... Mane ... Mane atque asta, Plaut. Cas. 3, 6, 10; cf. id. Truc. 4, 2, 38; 41: Resiste! Stop! Halt! Ter. And. 2, 2, 7; id. Phorm. 5, 6, 10; Poët. ap. Sen. Ep. 89, 6: quaeso ubinam illic restitit miles modo? Plaut. Poen. 2, 22; cf.: ubi restiteras? id. Ps. 4, 1, 9: heus! heus!

resociandus.full: rĕsŏcĭandus, a, um, Part. [re-socius], to be reunited (eccl. Lat.), Auct. Hypogn. 3, 9, 14.

resolubilis.full: rĕsŏlūbĭlis, e, adj. resolvo, that may be dissolved again, resoluble (post-class.): caementum, Prud. Apoth. 581: corpus, id. Cath. 10, 157: homines luti corruptione resolubiles, Ambros. in Psa. 118, Serm. 13, § 20.

resolute.full: rĕsŏlūtē, adv., v. resolvo, P. a. fin.

resolutio.full: rĕsŏlūtĭo, ōnis, f. resolvo, an untying, unbinding, loosening (not ante-Aug.). Lit., a slackening, relaxing; a laxness, looseness, weakness: lori, Gell. 17, 9, 12: ventris, stomachi, nervorum, oculorum, Cels. 2, 6; 4, 5; 2, 1; 3, 27, 1; 6, 6, 36.— Trop. A making void, a cancelling: venditionis, Dig. 41, 2, 13.— A solution: sophismatis, an explanation, Gell. 18, 2, 10 (dub.). — A release, escape (late Lat.), Vulg. 2 Tim. 4, 6.

resolutus.full: rĕsŏlūtus, a, um, Part. and P. a. of resolvo.

resolvo.full: rĕ-solvo, solvi, sŏlūtum, 3, v. a., to untie, unfasten, unbind; to loose, loosen, release, open (not freq. till after the Aug. per.; cf.: relaxo, resero, recludo, libero). Lit. In gen.: equos, to unyoke, Ov. F. 4, 180; cf.: juncta juga leonibus, Cat. 63, 76: quem suā sponte vinxerit, non resolvat, etc., Col. 1, 8, 16; 11, 1, 22: cinctas vestes, Ov. M. 1, 382; cf. nodum, Cels. 7, 4, 4: fila, to loose, separate, Ov. M. 2, 654: vulnera, to unbind, Quint. 6, 1, 30; 49: oras, to cast loose from the s

resonabilis.full: rĕsŏnābĭlis, e, adj. resono, resounding; a poet. epithet of Echo, Ov. M. 3, 358; Aus. Epigr. 99, 1.

resonantia.full: rĕsŏnantĭa, ae, f. id., an echo, Vitr. 5, 3.

resonatio.full: rĕsŏnātĭo, ōnis, f. id., resonance (late Lat.), Cassiod. in Psa. 150, 4.

resono.full: rĕ-sŏno, āvi, 1 (ante-class. collat. form, acc. to the 3d conj., resonit, Pac. and Att. ap. Non. 504, 30 sq.: resonunt, Enn. and Att. ap. Prisc. p. 838 P.; of the perf. only resonavit, Manil. 5, 567), v. n. and a., to sound or ring again, to resound, re-echo (freq. and class.). Neutr. Lit.: tum clupei resonunt, Enn. l. l. (Ann. v. 364 Vahl.): valvae resonunt regiae, Att. l. l.: theatrum naturā ita resonans, ut, etc., Cic. Q. Fr. 1, 1, 14, § 42: venenum sic e poculo ejecit, ut id resonaret, id. T

resonus1.full: rĕsŏnus, a, um, adj. resono, resounding, re-echoing (poet.): voces, Ov. M. 3, 496: valles, Luc. 7, 480: ictus, Val. Fl. 1, 618: ripae, Sil. 6, 285: resonas plaudere caetras, id. 3, 348.

resonus2.full: rĕ-sŏnus, ūs, m., resonance; a resounding (late Lat.), Cael. Aur. Tard. 3, 8, 105.

resopio.full: rĕ-sōpĭo, īre, 4, v. a., to put to sleep: Tricerberum mellitis resopit offulis, Fulg. Cont. Virg. p. 156 Munk.

resorbeo.full: rĕ-sorbĕo, ēre, v. a., to suck back, swallow again (poet. and in post-Aug. prose): quaeque vomit fluctus totidem totidemque resorbet, Ov. H. 12, 125; so, saxa (pontus), Verg. A. 11, 627 Wagn.: mare in se resorberi videbamus, Plin. Ep. 6, 20, 9: mare accrescere aut resorberi, Tac. Agr. 10 fin.: te rursus in bellum resorbens Unda fretis tulit aestuosis, Hor. C. 2, 7, 15: hamum (opp. egerunt), Plin. 9, 43, 67, § 145: (lapidis aestus) respuit ab se Atque per aes agitat, sine eo quod saepe resorbet,

respectio.full: respectĭo, ōnis, f. respicio, a review, survey, inspection: animarum sanctarum, i. e. the judgment, Vulg. Sap. 3, 13.

respecto.full: respecto, āre, v. freq. n. and a. [id.], to look back, look round or behind repeatedly or intently, to look or gaze about; to look at any thing (class.). Lit. Neutr. absol.: quid respectas? nihil pericli est, Ter. Ad. 2, 1, 3: ubi respectantes hostium antesignanos vidit, Liv. 8, 39; Quint. 12, 3, 2; Verg. A. 11, 630: respectans abit, Sil. 12, 729; Stat. Th. 3, 377: ad tribunal, Liv. 3, 48: respecto identidem, ne senex, etc., Plaut. Cas. 5, 2, 13; so, identidem, ne, id. Men. 1, 2, 51. — Poet.: le

respectus1.full: respectus, a, um, Part. of respicio.

respectus2.full: respectus, ūs, m. respicio, a looking back or about (class.). Lit.: fugientibus miserabilem respectum incendiorum fore, Cic. Div. 1, 32, 68: sine respiratione ac respectu pugnabant, Liv. 8, 38: effuse ac sine respectu fugit, id. 32, 12: sine respectu mea fata relinquens, Verg. Cul. 226. — Meton., a refuge, retreat, asylum: ad Romanos, Liv. 42, 46: respectum pulcherrimum et praesidium firmissimum adimit rei publicae, Cic. Phil. 10, 4, 9; 11, 11, 26; Liv. 21, 44; cf.: omnium rerum respectum praete

respergo1.full: rē-spergo, si, sum, 3, v. a., to sprinkle over any thing; to besprinkle, bestrew (rare but class.). Lit.: praetoris oculos, Cic. Verr. 2, 5, 38, § 100: manus, os, simulacrum sanguine, id. Rosc. Am. 24, 68: morientium sanguine os uxoris respersum, id. Phil. 3, 2, 4; id. de Or. 3, 3, 10; cf.: aliquem cruore, Liv. 21, 63: sanguine dextram, Cat. 64, 230; Curt. 8, 3, 11: comae respersae sanguine, Ov. F. 3, 452: caede fraternā juvenis respersus, Cat 64, 181; Suet. Ner. 12; id. Calig. 57: se sanguine n

respergo2.full: rēspergo, ĭnis, f. 1. respergo, a besprinkling (late Lat.): marmoris, Prud. adv. Symm. 1, 503.

respersio.full: rēspersĭo, ōnis, f. id., a sprinkling over, besprinkling (Ciceron.): pigmentorum, Cic. Div. 2, 21, 48: ne sumptuosa respersio, a sprinkling of the funeral pile with wine, id. Leg. 2, 24, 60; v. 1. respergo, I.

respersus1.full: rēspersus, a, um, Part. of 1. respergo.

respersus2.full: rēspersus, ūs, m. 1. respergo, a sprinkling over, besprinkling (only in abl. sing.): pinnarum, Plin. 10, 3, 3, § 9: urinae, id. 24, 17, 102, § 163 dub. (Jan.: urinā adspersā).

respiciens.full: rēspĭcĭens, entis, Part., P. a., and subst.; v. respicio.

respicio.full: rē-spĭcĭo, spexi, spectum, 3 (old form of subj. perf. respexis, Plaut. Aul. 1, 1, 19; id. Most. 2, 2, 90; id. Rud. 3, 3, 16), v. n. and a., to look back or behind, to look about, look; to see behind one; to look back upon, to look at, look to or for any thing (very freq. and class.). Lit. Neutr.: respicere quasi retro aspicere, Varro Manio: sedens ... neque post respiciens, neque ante prospiciens, Non. p. 442, 31 sq. (cf. infra, β): longe retro respicere non possunt, Cic. Tusc. 5, 2, 6; Liv. 21,
respicio.short: rē-spĭcĭo, spexi, spectum, 3 (old form of subj.

respiraculum.full: rēspīrācŭlum, i, n. respiro, breathing, respiration (late Lat.), Claud. Mam. Stat. An. 2, 12.

respiramen.full: rēspīrāmen, ĭnis, n. id., the windpipe (Ovid.): respiramen iterque Eripiunt animae, Ov. M. 12, 142; plur.: respiramina claudere, id. ib. 2, 828.

respiramentum.full: rēspīrāmentum, i, n. id. II., relief, comfort (late Lat.), Aug. Conf. 7, 7 fin.; Serm. Temp. 144 fin.

respiratio.full: rēspīrātĭo, ōnis, f. respiro. Lit., a breathing out, exhaling; hence, in gen., breathing, respiration, Cic. Univ. 6; Plin. 9, 7, 6, § 18; Quint. 9, 4, 67 (with spiritus); 11, 3, 39; 53; 63; Cael. Aur. Acut. 2, 3, 16; 2, 32, 167.—* Transf., exhalation: aquarum, Cic. N. D. 2, 10, 27.— Trop., a breathing in the course of an action, i. e. a taking breath, resting; an intermission, pause: in suo quisque gradu obnixi sine respiratione ac respectu pugnabant, Liv. 8, 38.—So of a pause in speaking: morae

respiratus.full: rēspīrātus, ūs, m. id., a drawing breath, inhaling, inspiration; only Cic. N. D. 2, 55, 136 (dub. Orell. N. cr.; Bait. intrante spiritu), and App. M. 4, p. 149, 28.

respiro.full: rē-spīro, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. and n. Lit., to blow or breathe back; to breathe out, exhale (class.; esp. in the trop. signif.): quod nisi respirent venti, vis nulla refrenet Res ... nunc quia respirant, etc., Lucr. 6, 568 sq.: cum aspera arteria ad pulmones usque pertineat excipiatque animam eam, quae ducta sit spiritu eandemque a pulmonibus respiret et reddat, Cic. N. D. 2, 54, 136: ex eā pars redditur respirando, id. ib. 2, 55, 138: malignum aëra, to exhale, send forth, Stat. S. 2, 2, 78; cf.

resplendentia.full: rēsplendentĭa, ae, f. resplendeo, splendor, resplendence: veritatis, Aug. Ep. ad Maced. 55.

resplendeo.full: rē-splendĕo, ēre, v. n., to shine brightly; to glitter, be resplendent (poet.): fulvā resplendent fragmina harenā, Verg. A. 12, 741; Sil. 12, 732; Sen. Q. N. 1, 13, 2; Claud. Rapt. Pros. 3, 446; Sen. Agam. 543: sidera, Manil. 5, 719: facies, Vulg. Matt. 17, 2.— Trop.: resplendet gloria Martis, Claud. Laud. Stil. 1, 16.

respondeo.full: rē-spondĕo, di, sum, 2, v. a. Lit., to promise a thing in return for something else; to offer or present in return. So, only in a few examples, the phrase par pari (dat.) respondere, to return like for like: par pari respondes dicto, you return tit for tat with your tongue (syn. refero), Plaut. Pers. 2, 2, 41; cf.: istuc serva; et verbum verbo par pari ut respondeas, Ter Phorm. 1, 4, 35; and: paria paribus respondimus, Cic. Att. 6, 1, 23.— Pass.: provide, si cui quid debetur, ut sit, unde par pa

responsio.full: rēsponsĭo, ōnis, f. respondeo. An answer, reply; a refutation (rare but class.; syn. responsum): in quo erat accusatoris interpretatio indigna responsione, Cic. Balb. 16, 36; Gell. 12, 12, 1: responsio mollis frangit iram, Vulg. Prov. 15, 1.— In plur., Plaut. Most. 3, 1, 63.— In rhet.: sibi ipsi responsio, a replying to one's own argument, Cic. de Or. 3, 54, 207; Quint. 9, 1, 35; 9, 3, 90 (cf.: ut quasi ad interrogata sibi ipse respondeat, Cic. Or. 40, 137).

responsito.full: rēsponsĭto, āvi, 1, v. freq. a. respondeo, II. A. 2. a.; of lawyers, to give an answer, opinion, advice, Cic. Rep. 5, 3, 5; id. Leg. 1, 4, 14 Mos. N. cr.; Gell. 13, 10, 1; Dig. 3, 1, 1.

responsive.full: rēsponsīvē, adv. respondeo, responsively, Ascon. Ped. ad Cic. Verr. 2, 1, 56, § 148.

responsivus.full: rēsponsīvus, a, um, adj. id., answering, responsive: sententia, Jul. Rufin. Fig. Sent. 19; Isid. 2, 21, 18 (dub.): verba, Prisc. 574 P.

responso.full: rēsponso, āre, v. freq. a. id., to return an answer, to answer, reply, respond (poet.). Lit.: neu quisquam responset, quando hasce aedes pultabit senex, Plaut. Most. 2, 1, 56: pro me responsa tibi, id. Cist. 2, 1, 40; id. Mil. 4, 1, 17: num ancillae aut servi tibi Responsant? answer you back, id. Men. 4, 2, 57.— Trop.: exoritur clamor, ripaeque lacusque Responsant circa, re-echo, Verg. A. 12, 757; Val. Fl. 3, 597; 4, 286; Claud. in Eutr. 2, 162: ne gallina malum responset dura palato, ill suit h

responsor.full: rēsponsor, ōris, m. id., one that answers or replies, Plaut. Rud. 1, 4, 7.

responsoria.full: rēsponsōria, ōrum, n. id., repetitions in vocal worship, responses, Ambros. Hexaem. 3, 5, 23.

responsus1.full: rēsponsus, a, um, Part. of respondeo.

responsus2.full: rēsponsus, ūs, m. respondeo, II. B.. An answer, reply (opp. interrogatio), Dig. 44, 7, 1, § 7.— Correspondence of parts, harmony, symmetry, Vitr. 1, 2; 3, 1.

respuo.full: rē-spŭo, ŭi, 3, v. a., to spit back or out; to discharge by spitting; to cast out, cast off, eject, expel, etc. (class.; esp. freq. in the trop. signif.). Lit.: quin etiam gustatus, quam cito id, quod valde dulce est, aspernatur ac respuit, Cic. de Or. 3, 25, 99: quas natura respuerit, id. N. D. 2, 9, 24: lumen per cornum transit, at imber respuitur, Lucr. 2, 389; cf. Quint. 1, 2, 28: liquorem ab se, Vitr. 7, 4; cf.: ferrum ab se (opp. resorbere), Lucr. 6, 1054; 2, 197; cf. Plin. 2, 103, 106, §

restagnatio.full: rēstagnātĭo, ōnis, f. restagno, an overflowing, inundation: Euphratis, Plin. 6, 28, 32, § 146; cf. id. 2, 67, 67, § 168: alvi, a rising, id. 11, 37, 66, § 176.

restagno.full: rē-stagno, āre, v. n., to run over, overflow; of bodies of water: paludes restagnantes, Liv. 44, 46, 5: ostium amnis, id. 44, 6, 15; Plin. 5, 5, 5, § 34: restagnantis fecit maris unda paludem, Ov. M. 11, 364: flumen, Luc. 4, 89: palus, Sil. 8, 382; Col. 2, 12, 5; 8, 15, 3.—Transf., of the inundated place: late is locus restagnat, is overflowed, Caes. B. C. 2, 24 fin.; cf.: arva palude, Sil. 4, 752.

restauratio.full: rēstaurātĭo, ōnis, f. restauro, a restoration, renewal (jurid. Lat.): servitutis, Dig. 23, 5, 7: eremodicii, ib. 4, 4, 7 fin.

restaurator.full: rēstaurātor, ōris, m. id., a renovator, Inscr. Fabr. 3, 297 al.

restauro.full: rē-stauro, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a., to restore, repair, rebuild (perh. only post-Aug.; for in Liv. 5, 52, 9, and 27, 21, instaurare is the better read.; v. Drak. N. cr.; cf. instauro, reficio, restituo, sarcio). Lit.: restaurare theatrum igne fortuito haustum, Tac. A. 3, 72: aedem Veneris, id. ib. 4, 43: navem iisdem tabulis, Dig. 7, 4, 10: in pristinum statum, ib. 43, 21, 1, § 6.— Trop., to renew, repeat (syn. redintegro): bellum, Just. 2, 10, 1; 3, 5, 2; 20, 5, 6; 31, 3, 8: accusationem, Dig. 48,

restiarius.full: restĭārĭus, ii, m. restis, a ropemaker, Fronto, p. 2201 P.

restibilio.full: rēstĭbĭlĭo, īre, v. a. restibilis, to reestablish, restore: Teucrum regi sapsa res restibiliet, Pac. ap. Fest. p. 325 Müll. (Trag. Rel. p. 99 Rib.).

restibilis.full: rē-stĭbĭlis, e, adj. stabilis; hence, that is made to stand again. Lit., in econom. lang.. that is restored or renewed: ager, that is sown or tilled every year (opp. novalis, which lies fallow), Varr. L. L. 5, § 39 Müll.; id. R. R. 1, 44, 2 and 3; so, locus, Cato, R. R. 35, 2: vinetum, Col. 3, 18, 1; 11, 4: segetes, Varr. R. R. 1, 9, 6; Plin. 18, 17, 45, § 162: platanus restibilis facta, flourishing again, id. 16, 32, 57, § 133. — Subst.. restĭbĭle, is, n., fallow land, Col. 2, 10, 6.— Transf.:

resticula.full: restĭcŭla, ae, f. dim. restis, a small rope, a cord, line, Cato, R. R. 110; Varr. R. R. 1, 41, 5; Cic. Scaur. Fragm. p. 261 fin. Orell.; Amm. 14, 7, 15; Vulg. 3 Reg. 7, 23.

resticulum.full: restĭcŭlum or -us, a false read. for reticulum, Dig. 9, 3, 5, § 12.

restillo.full: rē-stillo, āvi, 1, v. n. and a., to drop back; to fall back in drops. * Neutr., Prud. adv. Symm. 2, 287.—* Act.: quae (tuae litterae) mihi quiddam quasi animulae restillarunt, have instilled again, Cic. Att. 9, 7, 1 Orell. N. cr. dub. (B. and K. stillarunt).

restinctio.full: rēstinctio, ōnis, f. restinguo, a quenching (of thirst): voluptas ipsius retinctionis in motu est (after restincta siti), Cic. Fin. 2, 3, 9.

restinctus.full: rēstinctus, a, um, Part. of restinguo.

restinguo.full: rē-stinguo, nxi, nctum, 3, v. a., to put out, quench, extinguish (class.). Lit.: ignem restinguunt aquā, Plaut. Cas. 4, 1, 16; so, ignem, Cic. Rosc. Com. 6, 17 (with refrigerare); id. Cat. 3, 1, 2; id. Top. 12, 52; Verg. A. 2, 686; Plin. 20, praef. 1, § 1; Ov. R. Am. 807 al.: flammam, Lucr. 4, 1087; Cic. Sull. 30, 83; Liv. 28, 23: incendium, Catil. ap. Sall. C. 31, 9; id ap. Cic. Mur. 25, 51; Liv. 28, 42: restincto aggere, Caes. B. G. 7, 25 fin.; Hirt. B. G. 8, 43: aes accensum, Plin. 33, 3, 20,

restio.full: restĭo, ōnis, m. restis. A ropemaker, rope-seller, Suet. Aug. 2 fin.; cf. Fronto, p. 2201 P.— Transf., in a comic lusus verbb., with bucaeda, for one who is scourged with ropes, Plaut. Most. 4, 2, 2. — The title of a poem by Laberius, Gell. 10, 17, 2.

restipulatio.full: rēstĭpŭlātĭo, ōnis, f. restipulor, a counter-engagement, counter-obligation, Cic. Rosc. Com. 13, 37 sq.; Gai. Inst. 4, 18, p. 259 Goes.

restipulor.full: rē-stĭpŭlor, āri, v. dep. a., to stipulate, promise, or engage in return (syn.: recipio, despondeo), Cic. Rosc. Com. 13, 38; App. Mag. p. 338, 25; Val. Max. 2, 8, 2.

restis.full: restis, is (acc. more freq. restim, Plaut. Cas. 2, 7, 2; id. Ps. 1, 1, 86; id. Poen. 1, 2, 184; id. Pers. 5, 2, 34; id. Rud. 2, 3, 37; Ter. Ad. 4, 7, 34; id. Phorm. 4, 4, 5; Caecil. ap. Non. 200, 21; Cato, R. R. 77; App. M. 1, p. 109: restem, Plaut. Rud. 4, 3, 97; Mart. 4, 70, 1; Juv. 10, 58; Petr. 45, 4; Inscr. Grut. 715, 10; but abl. usually reste, Juv. 3, 226; 14, 274; Liv. 1, 26, 6; 8, 16, 9; 27, 37, 14; Val. Max. 7, 8, 5; Plin. 17, 10, 11, § 62; Mart. 5, 62, 6: resti, Don. 2, 10, 3, p. 1751

restito.full: rēstĭto, āre, v. freq. n. [resto], to stay behind, to loiter, tarry, hesitate (ante-class., and several times in Liv. and Pliny the Elder): restitant, occurrunt, obstant, etc., Enn. ap. Non. 147, 10 (Sat. 5 Vahl.): me miserum restitando reddiderunt, Plaut. Capt. 3, 2, 3: at enim restitas, Ter. Eun. 4, 4, 1; Liv. 7, 39 fin. Drak.; 10, 19; 30, 31; Plin. 18, 16, 19, § 50: Menelaus me objurgat? id meis rebus regimen restitat, Enn. ap. Rufin. Fig. § 11, p. 205 Ruhnk. (Trag. v. 264 Vahl.).

restitrix.full: rēstĭtrix, īcis, f. resisto, she that stays behind: ego hic restitrix, Plaut. Truc. 4, 2, 5.

restituo.full: rē-stĭtŭo, ŭi, ūtum, 3, v. a. statuo, to put or set up again, i. e. either to replace in its former position, or (more freq.) to restore to its former condition, to rebuild, revive, etc. (freq. and class.; syn.: restauro, renovo, reficio). In gen. Lit.: senatus decrevit, ut Minerva nostra, quam turbo dejecerat, restitueretur, Cic. Fam. 12, 25, a, 1: arborem, Verg. G. 2, 272: luxatum femur ex toto, Cels. 8, 20: aedes (with reficere), Cic. Top. 3, 15: domum a Clodio disjectam, i. e. to rebuild, Ve

restitutio.full: rēstĭtūtĭo, ōnis, f. restituo, a restoring, restoration. In gen.: domus incendio absumptae, i. e. a rebuilding, Suet. Aug. 57: Capitolii, id. Vesp. 8: theatri, id. Tib. 47: urbis in majus, Just. 2, 14, 2: afflictarum civitatum, Suet. Tit. 8.—Trop.: omnis pristinae fortunae, Suet. Ner. 40: libertatis, Val. Max. 4, 1, ext. 4: lunae, Arn. 6, 196. — In partic. A giving back, restitution (in jurid. Lat.), Dig. 50, 16, 22; 36, 1, 1, § 14; 36, 1, 6, § 3.— The act of replacing, reinstating one condemned

restitutor.full: rēstĭtūtor, ōris, m. id., a restorer, rebuilder. Lit.: templorum omnium, Liv. 4, 20: urbium, Inscr. Orell. 1103.— Trop.: salutis meae, Cic. Mil. 15, 39; cf. Quint. 7, 1, 43 and 61: reipublicae, Eum. Grat. Act. ad Constant. 4: Galliarum, Vop. Aur. 9: tanti operis restitutor deus, App. Herm. Trism. p. 92.

restitutorius.full: rēstĭtūtōrĭus, a, um, adj. id. II., of or relating to restitution, restitutory (jurid. Lat.): interdictum, Dig. 43, 1, 1: judicium, ib. 3, 3, 46: actio, ib. 2, 10, 3.—As subst.: in restitutorio agendo (i. e. judicio), Dig. 27, 6, 7.

restitutrix.full: rēstĭtūtrix, īcis, f. restitutor, she that gives back, a restorer: omnium generum, quae accipit (terra, with receptrix), App. Trism. p. 77, 31.

restitutus1.full: rēstĭtūtus, a, um, Part. of restituo.

restitutus2.full: Restĭtūtus, i, m., a Roman surname, e. g. Claudius Restitutus, a friend of Pliny the younger, Plin. Ep. 3, 9, 16; 6, 17; Mart. 10, 87.
restitutus2.short: Restĭtūtus, i, m., a Roman surname, e.

resto.full: rē-sto, stĭti, 1 (perf. subj. restaverit, Prop. 2, 34, 53), v. n. To stop behind, keep back, stand still (very rare and only poet., whereas resisto is class.). Lit.: si resto, pergit, ut eam: si ire conor, prohibet betere, Pac. ap. Non. 77, 25. — Trop.: impetus haut longe mediis regionibus restat, Enn. ap. Fest. p. 285 Müll. (Ann. v. 475 Vahl.): nullo dominae teritur molimine amator Restat et immerita sustinet aure minas, stands firm, holds out, Prop. 2, 25 (3, 20), 18. — To withstand, resist, o

restricte.full: rēstrictē, adv., v. restringo, P. a. fin.

restrictim.full: rēstrictim, adv. restringo, closely, carefully: restrictim cogitata, Afran. ap. Non. 516, 9.

restrictio.full: rēstrictĭo, ōnis, f. id., a restriction, limitation (eccl. Lat.): epularum, Aug. Mor. Eccl. Cath. 31.

restrictus.full: rēstrictus, a, um, Part. and P. a. of restringo.

restringo.full: rēstringo, inxi, ictum, 3, v. a. To draw back tightly; to bind back, bind fast, tighten, etc. (in the verb. finit. not anteAug., but in the P. a. class.; syn. religo). Lit.: laevam, Quint. 11, 3, 131: restrictis ad terga manibus, Plin. 35, 10, 36, § 93: manus, Petr. 73, 4: lacertos, Hor. C. 3, 5, 35; cf.: restringitur vinculis, Tac. A. 14, 64; and: si manus manicis restringantur, App. Flor. 17, p. 357, 29; cf. also: Prometheus quondam silici restrictus membra catenā, Cat. 64, 297: vinclo fasciae

restruo.full: rē-strŭo, xi, ctum, 3, v. a., to erect again (eccl. Lat.). Lit.: aras, Tert. Apol. 6 fin.: statuas dejectas, id. ad Nat. 1, 10.— Trop., to restore: Deus eam restruebat fidem, quam populus destruebat, Tert. Res. Carn. 31.

resudatio.full: rĕsūdātĭo, ōnis, f. resudo, exudation (late Lat.), Cael. Aur. Signif. 79.

resudo.full: rĕ-sūdo, āre, v. n. and a., to sweat, sweat out, exude (post-class.). Neutr., Curt. 5, 1, 2; 7, 10, 3.— Act.: congeriem ventris, Prud. Apoth. 787; id. Cath. 10, 105.

resulco.full: rĕ-sulco, āre, v. a., to furrow or plough again (poet.): vulnera, to scratch open, Prud. στεφ. 5, 141.

resultatio.full: rĕsultātĭo, ōnis, f. resulto, a reverberation, echo: grata et consona, Ambros. Hexaëm. 3, 5, 11: laetitiae, id. in Psa. praef. § 9: blanda, Cassiod. Var. 2, 40.— Trop., a resistance, refusal, Cassiod. Var. 2, 24.

resultator.full: rĕsultātor, ōris, m. id., one who resists or denies (late Lat.), Cassiod. in Psa. 9, 27.

resulto.full: rĕsulto, no perf., ātum, 1, v. freq. n. and a. [resilio], to spring or leap back, to rebound (poet. and in post-Aug. prose; only of inanimate or abstract subjects). Lit.: (corpora) conflicta resultant, etc., Lucr. 2, 98 and 101: tela irrita galeā clipeoque, Verg. A. 10, 330: aqua objectu lapillorum, Quint. 12, 2, 11; cf.: unda scissa, Petr. poët. Sat. 89, 2, 31: illisum caput scopulis resultat, Sen. Hippol. 1064.— Of animals: resultabunt canes ululantibus lupis, Amm 31, 1, 2.— In partic., of sou

resum.full: rĕ-sum = resideo, assumed as pres. for the var. l. l. resit, Cic. Scaur. 8, 14, where B. and K. read residet; and reesset, Cic. Verr. 2, 2, 58, § 143, B. and K. esset.

resumo.full: rĕ-sūmo, mpsi, mptum, 3, v. a., to take up again, take back, resume (poet. and in post-Aug. prose). Lit. (terra) gentes omnis peperit et resumit denuo, Enn. ap. Varr. L. L. 5, § 64 Müll. (Epich. v. 4 Vahl. p. 168): positas (tabellas) resumit, Ov. M. 9, 524: tela, id. Am. 2, 9, 34: librum perlectum utique ex integro, Quint. 10, 1, 20: librum in manus, id. 10, 4, 3: pugillares, Plin. Ep. 7, 9, 16: cito elapsum baculum, Suet. Ner 24: fuscinam, id. Calig. 30: arma, id. ib. 48; Tac. H. 2, 44; 4, 76 f

resumptio.full: rĕsumptĭo, ōnis, f. resumo, a restoration, recovery of a sick person, Cael. Aur. Acut. 2, 37 fin.

resumptivus.full: rĕsumptīvus, a, um, adj. id., restorative: odoramenta, Cael. Aur. Tard. 4, 3, 75: cyclus, id. ib. 2, 1, 47.

resumptorius.full: rĕsumptōrĭus, a, um, adj. id., restorative: adjutoria, Cael. Aur. Acut. 3, 8 fin.

resumptus.full: rĕsumptus, a, um, Part., from resumo.
resumptus.short: rĕsumptus, a, um, Part., from resumo.

resupino.full: rĕ-sŭpīno, no perf., ātum, 1, v. a., to bend or turn back (rare; not in Cic.). Lit.: puer ad me accurrit, Pone apprehendit pallio, resupinat, Ter. Phorm. 5, 6, 23: assurgentem ibi regem umbone resupinat, Liv. 4, 19: hominem, Cels. 7, 16: nares planā manu, to bend back, Quint. 11, 3, 80: colla (turtures, cum bibunt), Plin. 10, 34, 52, § 105; cf.: caput (aves bibentes), id. 10, 46, 63, § 129: valvas, to beat in, break down, Prop. 4 (5), 8, 51. resupinati cessantia tympana Galli, i. e. prostrate fr

resupinus.full: rĕ-sŭpīnus, a, um, adj., bent back or backwards, lying on one's back or with the face upwards, supine (not in Cic.). Lit.: resupinum in caelo contueri, i. e. lying on one's back, face upwards, supine, Att. ap. Cic. Div. 1, 22, 44: fertur equis curruque haeret resupinus inani, Verg. A. 1, 476: eque tuo pendet resupino spiritus ore, Lucr. 1, 37; Ov. H. 16, 255; id. M. 2, 267: jacuit resupinus humi, id. ib. 4, 121; 12, 324: hunc ego resupinum fudi, id. ib. 13, 86 al.: retro lentas tendo resupinus h
resupinus.short: rĕ-sŭpīnus, a, um, adj., bent back or backwards, lying on one's back or with the face upwards, supine (not in Cic.).

resurgo.full: rĕ-surgo, surrexi, surrectum, 3, v. n., to rise or raise one's self again, to appear again (poet. and post-Aug.; once in Liv. with velut; v. infra). Lit.: pugnat resurgere saepe, Ov. M. 5, 349: si resurgat centimanus Gyges, Hor. C. 2, 17, 14; Tac. A. 3, 46; cf., of convalescent persons: resurgam, Ov. Tr. 3, 3, 23.— Esp., to rise again, rise from the grave (eccl. Lat.): ab inferis, Lact. 4, 19, 6; 4, 26, 3; Vulg. Marc. 9, 8; id. Luc. 7, 22.—Of things: cupressus arbor repente prociderat ac postero

resurrectio.full: rĕsurrectĭo, ōnis, f. resurgo, in eccl. Lat., a rising again from the dead, resurrection, Tert. Res. Carn. 1; Aug. Civ. Dei, 22, 28; Vulg. Matt. 22, 23; id. Rom. 3, 4; Lact. 4, 19, 9; 4, 20, 4: dominica (i. e. Domini), Sulp. Sev. Chron. 2, 33, 5.

resuscitatio.full: rĕsuscĭtātĭo, ōnis, f. resuscito, in eccl. Lat., a raising again from the dead, resuscitation, Tert. Res. Carn. 30.

resuscitator.full: rĕsuscĭtātor, ōris, m. id., in eccl. Lat., one who raises again from the dead, a resuscitator, Tert. Res. Carn. 12.

resuscito.full: rĕ-suscĭto, āre, v. a., to raise up again, rebuild: templum, Lact. 4, 18, 5.— To rouse again, revive, resuscitate, freq. in the Christian writers, of the resurrection of the dead, Hier. in Psa. 33, 5; id. Ep. 103; Tert. Res. Carn. 38; Prud. στεφ. 6, 136; Vulg. Act. 2, 32; id. Johan. 6, 39.— Trop. (very rare): positam iram, to revive, resuscitate, Ov. M. 8, 474: veterem iram, id. ib. 14, 495: legatum, to renew, Dig. 34, 4, 27, § 1: gratiam Dei, Vulg. 2 Tim. 1, 6.

resutus.full: rĕ-sūtus, a, um, Part. [suo], ripped open: tunica ex utrāque parte, Suet. Aug. 94.

retae.full: rētae, ārum, f., trees standing on the bank or in the bed of a stream, acc. to Gabius ap. Gell. 11, 17, 4.— From this is said to come the verb retare, to clear, free from obstructions, in an old edict: flumina retanda; v. Gell. l. l.
retae.short: rētae, ārum, f., trees standing on the bank or in the bed of a stream, acc.

retalio.full: rĕ-tālĭo, āre, v. a., to retaliate: quod imprudentiā factum est, retaliari per imprudentiam debet, Gell. 20, 1, 16.

retango.full: rĕ-tango, ĕre, 3, v. a., to touch again or repeatedly: faciem spongiā, Cael. Aur. Tard. 2, 13, 156.

retardatio.full: rĕtardātĭo, ōnis, f. retardo, a hindering, delaying, retarding, Cic. Phil. 5, 11, 30 (with mora).— In plur., Vitr. 9, 1, 6.

retardo.full: rĕ-tardo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. and n. Act., to keep back, hinder, delay, detain, impede, retard (class.; a favorite word with Cic., esp. in the trop. signif.; syn. moror). Lit.: quarum (stellarum vagarum) motus tum incitantur, tum retardantur, saepe etiam insistunt, Cic. N. D. 2, 40, 103: aliquem in viā, id. Phil. 10, 5, 11: itinere devio per ignorantiam locorum retardati, Suet. Galb. 20: flumina retardant equos, Verg. G. 3, 253: boves retinere ac retardare, Col. 2, 2, 26: instantia ora retardat

retaxo.full: rĕ-taxo, āre, v. a., to censure, reprove, Suet. Vesp. 13.

rete.full: rēte, is, n. (abl. reti, Plaut. Rud. 4, 4, 27; id. Truc. 1, 1, 17; more freq. rete, id. Pers. 1, 2, 22; id. Rud. 4, 2, 9; 4, 3, 81; 4, 4, 124; Varr. R. R. 3, 5, 8; 3, 11, 3; id. L. L. 5, 29, § 130 Müll.; Col. 8, 10, 1; Suet. Ner. 30; Ov. F. 5, 371; id. Hal. 22; Plin. 11, 24, 28, § 81; Sen. Octav. 412 al.—Collat. form, acc. retem, Plaut. Rud. 4, 3, 45; Varr. R. R. 3, 5, 11; 14.— As fem.: tecta porticus sit rete cannabina, Varr. R. R. 3, 5, 11; cf. in plur.: in retes meas incidisti, Charis. p. 20

retectus.full: rĕtectus, a, um, Part. of retego.

retego.full: rĕ-tĕgo, xi, ctum, 3, v. a. To uncover, bare, open (not freq. till after the Aug. period; syn.: nudo, exuo). Lit.: thecam nummariam, Cic. Att. 4, 7, 2: (area) retecta, unroofed, Varr. R. R. 1, 51, 2: vultus scisso velamine, Luc. 8, 669: caput pallio, Petr. 17, 3: caput, Caes. ap. Plin. Ep. 3, 12, 13: jugulum simul pectusque, Ov. M. 13, 459: pedes, Suet. Aug. 78: dentes, Pers. 3, 101: ensem, Luc. 9, 830: sacra, to throw open, make accessible, Prop. 5, 9, 26: solum hiatu, to open, Ov. M. 5, 357 (w

retendo.full: rĕ-tendo, di, tum, or sum, 3, v. a., to release from tension, to unbend, slacken, relax (very rare; syn.: relaxo, resolvo). Lit.: lentos arcus, to unbend, Ov. M. 2, 419; Stat. S. 4, 4, 30; in the part. perf.: arcus retentus, Ov. M. 3, 166: arcus retensus, Phaedr. 3, 14, 5.— * Trop.: ea quoque, quae sensu et animā carent, velut alternā quiete retenduntur, i. e. unbend, relax (shortly before, remissio), Quint. 1, 3, 8.
retendo.short: rĕ-tendo, di, tum, or sum, 3, v.

retensus.full: rĕtensus, a, um, Part. of retendo.

retentator.full: rĕtentātor, ōris, m. 1. retento, a detainer, retainer, Cassiod. Var. 2, 10.

retentatrix.full: rĕtentātrix, īcis, f. retentator, she that retains, Macr. S. 7, 4.

retentio.full: rĕtentĭo, ōnis, f. retineo, a keeping back, i. e., A holding back, holding in: aurigae, Cic. Att. 13, 21, 3; 13, 25, 1.—Trop., a withholding: assensionis (as a transl. of the Gr. ἐποχή), Cic. Ac. 2, 18, 59, and 2, 24, 78.— A keeping back, retaining (postclass.): dotis, Dig. 31, 1, 79; 5, 3, 19; 10, 1, 30: urinae, retention, Cael. Aur. Tard. 3, 8. — Preservation, maintenance: societatis, Lact. 6, 10 fin.: veteris disciplinae, Tert. adv. Marc. 5, 3: delicti, i. e. not to forgive, id. ib. 4, 28.—In

retento1.full: rĕtento, āvi, ātum, 1, v. freq. a. id., to hold back firmly, to keep back, to hold fast (rare; not in Cic.). Lit.: cur me retentas? Plaut. As. 3, 3, 1; id. Rud. 3, 6, 39; cf. agmen, Liv. 10, 5: legiones, Tac. H. 4, 13: fugientes, id. ib. 5, 21: admissos equos, Ov. A. A. 2, 434; cf. frena, id. Am. 2, 9, 30: puppes, Tac. H. 2, 35; Luc. 3, 586: vires regni, id. 4, 723: pecuniam, calones, sarcinas, Tac. H. 4, 60: caelum a terris, i. e. to hold apart, Lucr. 2, 729: iste qui retentat sese tacitus, quo

retento2.full: rĕ-tento (-tempto), āvi, ātum, 1, v. a., to try or attempt again, to reattempt (a poet. word of the Aug. per.): timide verba intermissa retentat, Ov. M. 1, 746: preces, id. ib. 14, 382: fila lyrae, id. ib. 5, 117: referoque manus iterumque retento, id. H.10,11: viam leti, id. M. 11, 792: studium fatale, id. Tr. 5, 12, 51: arma, Luc. 2, 514: memoriam meam, Sen. Ep. 72, 1: nec audent ea retentare, quorum vitia retractando patescunt, id. Brev. Vit. 10, 2: nec vana retentet spes Minyas, move or affe

retentor.full: rĕtentor, ōris, m. retineo, one that holds back; a detainer, retainer (post-class.), App. Flor. p. 343, 10.

retentorius.full: rĕtentōrĭus, a, um, adj. retentor, fitted to hold back, checking, restraining (late Lat.): virtus animae, Cassiod. Anim. 6.

retentus1.full: rĕtentus, a, um. Part. of retendo.— Part. of retineo.

retentus2.full: rĕtentus, ūs, m. retineo, a holding fast, grasping: vivosque imitata retentus (manūus), Claud. in Rufin. 2, 438.

retergeo.full: rĕ-tergeo, si, 2, v. a., to wipe out, cleanse, clear (late Lat.). Lit.: vulnera, Cael. Aur. Tard. 2, 14, 107.— Transf.: fossas ruderibus obrutas, Amm. 29, 6, 11.

retexo.full: rĕ-texo, xui (retexi, Manil. 4, 214 dub.), xtum, 3, v. a. To unweave, unravel what has been woven (class.). Lit.: quasi Penelope telam retexens, Cic. Ac. 2, 29, 95: tela retexta dolo, Ov. Am. 3, 9, 30: telas, Stat. S. 3, 5, 9.— Poet., transf., of other things: nec (corpora possunt) retexi, be decomposed, Lucr. 1, 529; so, umorem maris (sol), id. 5, 267: luna quater plenum tenuata retexuit orbem, i. e. lessened or diminished again, Ov. M. 7, 531.— Trop., to break up, cancel, annul, reverse (cf.:

retextus.full: rĕtextus, a, um, Part. of retexo.

retiarius.full: rētĭārĭus, ii, m. rete, one who fights with a net, a net-fighter (a kind of gladiator, who endeavored to hold his adversary by throwing a net over his head), Quint. 6, 3, 61; Suet. Calig. 30; id. Claud. 34; Val. Max. 1, 7, 8; Inscr. Orell. 2566; 2578; 4273; cf. Juv. 8, 204 sqq.; v. Dict. of Antiq.; and cf. mirmillo.—Prov.: contra retiarium ferula, to fight with feeble weapons against one well equipped, or, as we might say, to parry a lance with a bodkin, Mart. 2 praef.

reticentia.full: rĕtĭcentĭa, ae, f. reticeo, a keeping silent, silence (rare but good prose): quid taces? enicas me miserum tuā reticentiā, Plaut. Merc. 5, 2, 52; Pac. ap. Non. 1, 31 (Trag. Rel. p. 94 Rib.): posterorum, Cic. Phil. 14, 12, 33: a jurisconsultis etiam reticentiae poena est constituta (viz. as to a defect in a thing sold), id. Off. 3, 16, 65.— In rhetor.,= aposiopesis, a pause in the midst of a speech, Cic. de Or. 3, 53, 205; Quint. 9, 1, 31; 9, 2, 54; 57.

reticeo.full: rĕ-tĭcĕo, cŭi, 2, v. n. and a. Neutr., to be silent, keep silence (class.; syn.: sileo, obmutesco): cum Sulpicius reticuisset, etc., Cic. de Or. 2, 57, 232: de Chelidone reticuit, quoad potuit, Cic. Verr. 2, 1, 53, § 139: de utriusque vestrum errore, id. Phil. 1, 12, 29: non placuit reticere, Sall. J. 85, 26: ne retice, ne verere, Ter. Heaut. 1, 1, 33: de adversis, Tac. A. 1, 67: velut vinculis ori impositis reticentes, Amm. 30, 4, 11. — Poet.: lyra, quae reticet, Claud. IV. Cons. Hon. 223: Peli

reticulatus.full: rētĭcŭlātus, a, um, adj. reticulum, made like a net, net-like, reticulated: fenestra, Varr. R. R. 3, 7, 3: structura parietum, Vitr. 2, 8; Plin. 36, 22, 51, § 172: distinctio concharum, id. 9, 33, 52, § 103.

reticulum.full: rētĭcŭlum, i, n. (collat. form rētĭ-cŭlus, i, m., Varr. R. R. 3, 5, 13; Fenest. ap. Non. 221, 33; Petr. 67, 6; Plin. 12, 14, 32, § 59; also rētĭācŭlum, i, Vulg. Exod. 38, 5 et saep.), dim. rete, a little net, a cloth made like a net, a net-work bag for carrying or keeping any thing in, a reticule, Cic. Verr. 2, 5, 11, § 27; Hor. S. 1, 1, 47; Juv. 12, 60; a fishing-net: venari reticulo in medio mari, Plaut. As. 1, 1, 87; a strainer, colander, Sen. Q. N. 7, 19, 1; a net used in playing ball, Ov. A

reticulus.full: rētĭcŭlus, i, m., v. reticulum init.

retifex.full: rētĭfex, fĭcis, m. rete-facio, a netmaker (late Lat.), Alcim. Homil. Fragm. 3.

retinaculum.full: rĕtĭnācŭlum (sync. retinaclum, Prud. ap. Symm. 2, 147), i, n. retineo, I., that which holds back or binds; a holdfast, band, tether, halter, halser, rope, cable (only in plur.; but the sing. occurs as v. l. Amm. 30, 4, 4). Lit., Cato, R. R. 63; 135, 5; Liv. 21, 28; Col. 4, 13, 1; 6, 2, 4; Vitr. 10, 5; Verg. G. 1, 265; 513; id. A. 4, 580; Hor. S. 1, 5, 18; Ov. M. 8, 102; 11, 712; 14, 547; Stat. S. 3, 2, 32.— Trop., a bond, chain, tie: vita abrupit, Plin. Ep. 1, 12, 8: desiderii, App. M. 11, p. 26

retinax.full: rĕtĭnax, ācis, adj. id., holding back: arbor, Symm. Ep. 1, 41.

retinens.full: rĕtĭnens, entis, Part. and P. a. of retineo.

retinentia.full: rĕtĭnentĭa, ae, f. retineo, II., a retaining in the memory, recollection: actarum rerum, Lucr. 3, 675: nostri, id. 3, 851.

retineo.full: rĕ-tĭnĕo, ŭi, tentum, 2, v. a. teneo. (With the signif. of the re predominating.) To hold or keep back, not let go; to detain, retain; to restrain (class.; cf. restringo). Lit.: Ep. Asta, abire hinc non sinam. Th. Quid nunc me retines? Plaut. Ep. 1, 1, 61: quotiens foras ego ire volo, me retines, revocas, id. Men. 1, 2, 5: quid, malum, astas? Quin retines altrinsecus? id. Mil. 2, 5, 36; id. Stich. 2, 3, 11: te dexterā retinens manu Opsecro, id. Capt. 2, 3, 82: si magis vis, eam omittam. Py. Nolo

retinnio.full: rĕ-tinnĭo, īre, v. n., to ring again, resound, Varr. R. R. 2, praef. § 2: in vocibus nostrorum oratorum retinnit quiddam et resonat urbanius, Cic. Brut. 46, 171.

retiolum.full: rētĭŏlum, i, n. dim. rete, a little net (post-class.), App. M. 8, p. 202, 33; Aug. Ep. 109, 10; Serv. Verg. A. 4, 138.

retollo.full: rĕ-tollo, ĕre, 3, v. a., to take away again: triumphos, Coripp. Johan. 2, 329: signa, id. ib. 4, 1154.

retono.full: rĕ-tŏno, āre, v. n., to thunder back, resound: loca fremitu, Cat. 63, 82.

retonsus.full: rĕ-tonsus, a, um, Part. [tondeo], cut down, mown: segetes, Plin. 18, 17, 45, § 161.

retorpesco.full: rĕ-torpesco, ĕre, v. inch. n., to become torpid (late Lat.): pristini sensus, Tert. adv. Gnost. 1 med.

retorqueo.full: rĕ-torquĕo, si, tum, 2, v. a., to twist or bend back; to turn or cast back (class.; cf. reflecto). Lit.: caput in sua terga (anguis), Ov. M. 3, 68: ora, id. ib. 4, 715: ora ad os Phoebi, id. ib. 11, 163: oculos saepe ad hanc urbem, * Cic. Cat. 2, 1, 2: oculos, Ov. M. 10, 696: omnium oculos in se, Quint. Decl. 8, 8: tergo bracchia, Hor. C. 3, 5, 22; cf.: manibus retortis, id. Ep. 2, 1, 191: cervices, Plin. Pan. 34, 3: ferocis equi colla, Ov. H. 4, 79: pantherae terga, to wrap about, cast about, V

retorresco.full: rĕ-torresco, ĕre, v. inch. n., to parch or dry up, to wither: sata, Col. 3, 3, 4; 3, 5, 1; 3, 17, 4.

retorridus.full: rĕ-torrĭdus, a, um, adj., parched up, burned up, dried up (mostly post-Aug.; not in Cic.). Lit.: rami platani, Sen. Ep. 12, 2; 86, 18: manus Mucii, id. ib. 66, 51: retorrida et muscosa prata, Varr. R. R. 1, 9, 5: plantae, Col. 3, 12, 2: frons, id. 11, 2, 87: fructus, Plin. 17, 22, 35, § 176: myrtus, id. 15, 29, 36, § 121: (herba) spinis retorrida, id. 27, 12, 97, § 122: mus, dried up, wizen, wrinkled, Phaedr. 4, 2, 27. — Trop.: detriti et retorridi ad litterarum disciplinas serius adeunt, Gell.
retorridus.short: rĕ-torrĭdus, a, um, adj., parched up, burned up, dried up (mostly post-Aug.;

retortus.full: rĕtortus, a, um, Part. of retorqueo.

retostus.full: rĕ-tostus, a, um, Part. [torreo], roasted, Plin. 13, 4, 9, § 48.

retractatio.full: rē^tractātĭo, ōnis, f. retracto. A taking in hand again; a retouching, revision, correction; so only Retractationes, the title of a work of Augustine.— Reconsideration, remembrance: eorum qui fuerunt retractatio non sine acerbitate quādam juvat, Sen. Ep. 63, 6.— Hesitation, refusal (only in connection with sine): sine ullā retractatione, Cic. Phil. 14, 14, 38; id. Att. 13, 25 (with dubitatio); id. Tusc. 5, 29, 82; Liv. 6, 28: absque retractatione morietur, surely, certainly, Vulg. 1 Reg. 14, 39.

retractator.full: rē^tractātor, ōris, m. id., a refuser: officii, Tert. Jejun. 15 dub.

retractatus1.full: rē^tractātus, a, um, Part. and P.a. of retracto.

retractatus2.full: rē^tractātus, ūs, m. retracto, Tertullian; v. retractatio. A repetition, Tert. Praescr. 7. — Hesitation, doubt: sine retractatu, Tert. Apol. 4; id. adv. Marc. 1, 1 fin.; in plur., id. Spect. 3.

retractio.full: rē^tractĭo, ōnis, f. retraho. A drawing back, retreating: graduum, i. e. the breadth, Vitr. 3, 4, 4.— Trop. A diminishing: dierum (opp. auctio), Macr. S. 1, 14.— Hesitation, refusal: sine ullā retractione, Arn. 5, 162.

retracto.full: rē^-tracto (in many MSS. also written rē^trecto), āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. id.. To take hold of or handle again; to take in hand again, undertake anew, etc. (class.; esp. in the trop. sense). Lit. (mostly poet.): arma, Liv. 2, 30: ferrum, Verg. A. 7, 694; 10, 396: gladios, Petr. poët. 89, 61: vulnera, to feel again, Ov. Tr. 3, 11, 19; 4, 4, 41; cf.: manu sua vota (i. e. the image), id. M. 10, 288: pedamenta, to go over again, retouch, Col. 4, 26, 1: agrum, to look over again, examine again, id. 1, 4,

retractus1.full: rē^tractus, a, um, Part. and P. a. of retraho.

retractus2.full: rē^tractus, ūs, m. retraho, a drawing back: machinae bellicae, Tert. adv. Gnost. 1.

retrado.full: rē^-trādo, ĕre, v. a., to deliver up again, restore (jurid. Lat.), Dig. 4, 2, 9; 19, 1, 6; 24, 3, 58 al.

retraho.full: rē^-trăho, xi, ctum, 3, v. a. To draw back, withdraw; to call back (class.). Lit.: me retrahis, Plaut. Rud. 4, 3, 8; aliquem, Cic. Sen. 23, 83; Liv. 30, 20; 21, 63 (in the last two passages with revocare); 10, 25: bos domitus et procurrentem (bovem) retrahit, et cunctantem producit, holds back, Col. 6, 2, 10: aliquem hinc, Lucceius ap. Cic. Fam. 5, 14, 1: Hannibalem in Africam (Scipio), Cic. Fin. 2, 17, 56: aliquem in urbem, Caes. B. C. 1, 9: manum, Cic. Cael. 26, 63: pedem, Verg. A. 10, 307: qu

retribuo.full: rē^-trĭbŭo, ŭi, ūtum, 3, v. a., to give back, return, restore, repay (class., but freq. only in eccl. Lat.; syn. remuneror). Lit.: corpora retribuat rebus recreetque fluentes, Lucr. 5, 275: populo pecuniam acceptam, Liv. 2, 41, 8: fructum quem meruerunt, Cic. Rosc. Com. 15, 44: aliena suis, Paul. Nol. Carm. 32, 514: quodcunque aliud acceperis, potes cum libuit retribuere, App. Mag. p. 332, 24.— Trop.: vicem alicui, to repay, requite, Lact. 6, 18, 22: retributionem gentibus, Vulg. 1 Macc. 2, 68:

retributio.full: rē^trĭbūtĭo, ōnis, f. retribuo, recompense, repayment, retribution (eccl. Lat.): mali pro bono, Aug. Civ. Dei, 22, 23: vitae aeternae, Tert. Apol. 18: meritorum, Sid. Ep. 4, 11: contumeliae, Lact. 6, 18, 27; Vulg. Psa. 136, 8.

retributor.full: rē^trĭbūtor, ōris, m. id., a recompenser, requiter, retributer (eccl. Lat.), Tert. adv. Marc. 4, 29; 5, 16: gratia retributoris, Paul. Nol. Ep. 2, 4.

retricibus.full: retricibus cum ait Cato, aquam eo nomine significat, quā horti irrigantur, Fest. pp. 282 and 283 Müll. (a canal, aqueduct; perh. kindr. with ῥέεθρον, ῥεῖθρον).
retricibus.short: retricibus cum ait Cato, aquam eo nomine significat, quā horti irrigantur, Fest.

retrimentum.full: rē^-trīmentum, i, n. tero, the dregs, refuse, sediment of pressed olives, Varr. R. R. 1, 64; of metals, dross, Cels. 5, 15; 5, 19, 26; of food and drink, refuse, waste (i. e. excrement, urine), Varr. ap. Non. 217, 23; Macr. S. 7, 4; 7, 15.

retrituro.full: rē^-trītūro, āre, v. a., to thresh over, to thresh (eccl. Lat.), Aug. Ep. ad Macr. 255, 3.

retritus.full: rē^-trītus, a, um, adj., worn down: rutabulum, Naev. ap. Fest. p. 262 Müll.: retritis pilis, Sen. Ep. 47, 5.
retritus.short: rē^-trītus, a, um, adj., worn down: rutabulum, Naev.

retro.full: rē^trō, adv. from re and the pronominal suffix ter, as in citro, ultro, intro, etc.. Lit., of place, backwards, back; on the back side, behind. Denoting tendency, direction, with verbs or nouns of motion: multa videbis retro repulsa revorti, Lucr. 2, 130; so very often with redire, regredi, repetere, remittere, respicere, reverti, revocare, etc., v. h. vv., and cf. Drak. ad Liv. 22, 6, 7, and 27, 28, 6: vestigia retro sequor, Verg. A. 2, 753; 9, 392; 11, 405: dare lintea retro, id. ib. 3, 686: o

retroago.full: rē^trŏ-ăgo, ēgi, actum, 3, v. a., to drive back, to turn back, etc. (post - Aug.; esp. freq. in Quint.). Lit.: capillos a fronte contra naturam, to push back, Quint. 11, 3, 160: vasta flumina, Mel. 3, 1, 1.— Trop.: honores, Plin. 7, 44, 45, § 145: rursus litteras (opp. recto contextu), to go through or repeat backwards, Quint. 1, 1, 25: ordinem, to reverse, id. 12, 2, 10: expositionem, id. 2, 4, 15: iram, to turn aside, Sen. Ira, 1, 16, 10: huic (dactylo) temporibus parem sed retroactum, appella

retrocedo.full: rē^trō-cēdo (or separate, rē^tro cēdo), ĕre, v. n., to go back, retire, recede, Liv. 8, 8, 9 (Weissenb. retro cedentes); Curt. 3, 8, 17; 7, 4, 4.
retrocedo.short: rē^trō-cēdo (or separate, rē^tro cēdo), ĕre, v.

retrocessio.full: retrōcessio, ōnis, f., = retrocessus, Aug. Quant. Anim. 37.

retrocessus.full: rē^trō-cessus, ūs, m. cedo, a going back or backwards, retrocession (opp. processus), App. Dogm. Plat. 1, p. 5 fin.

retroduco.full: retrō-dūco, xi, ctum, 3, v. a., to bring or draw back, Vitr. 10, 6 fin.; Dig. 34, 5, 16.

retroeo.full: rē^trŏ-ĕo, īre, v. n., to go back or backwards, to recede, retire, Sen. Q. N. 7, 21, 1; Plin. 2, 16, 13, § 70.

retroflecto.full: rē^trō-flecto, xi, 3, v. a., to bend or turn back (post-Aug.): capillos, Petr. 126, 15.

retrogradatio.full: rē^trōgrădātĭo, ōnis, f. retrogradior, a going back, retrograding (late Lat.), Mart. Cap. 8, § 881: stellarum, Isid. Orig. 3, p. 83.

retrogradior.full: rē^trō-grădĭor, di, v. dep. n. (collat. form rē^trōgrădo, āre, v. n., Mart. Cap. 8, § 887), to go back or backwards, to retrograde, Plin. 8, 15, 16, § 39; of the retrograde motion of the stars, id. 2, 15, 12, § 61; 2, 17, 14, § 76; Mart. Cap. 8, § 883.

retrogradus.full: rē^trōgrădus, a, um (collat. form rē^-trōgrădis, e, App. M. 4, p. 151), adj. retrogradior, going back or backwards, retrograde; usually of the stars, Sen. Q. N. 7, 25; Plin. 2, 17, 15, § 77; Sid. Ep. 8, 11: carmen retrogradum (i. e. reciprocum), Aug. Civ. Dei, 17, 15: retrogradis fuga, App. l. l.

retrogressus.full: rē^trōgressus, ūs, m. id., a retrograde movement, retrogression of the sun (post-class.), Macr. S. 1, 17.

retropendulus.full: rē^trō-pendŭlus, a, um, adj., hanging back or backwards: crinium globi (opp. antependuli), App. M. 5, p. 168, 22.
retropendulus.short: rē^trō-pendŭlus, a, um, adj., hanging back or backwards: crinium globi (opp.

retrospicio.full: rē^trō-spĭcĭo, cĕre, v. a. specio, to look back at: orbem lunae (sol), Vitr. 9, 4.

retroversim.full: rē^trōversim, adv. retroversus, backwards: cedentes radii, Claud. Mam. Stat. An. 1, 7.

retroversus.full: rē^trō-versus or -sum (-vorsus, and sync. rē^trōrsus, -sum, also rē^-trōsus, Tert. Apol. 19), a, um, adj. verto, turned back or backwards (adj. very rare, but freq. as adv.; v. infra). Form rē^-trōversus: Medusae Ipse retroversus squalentia prodidit ora, Ov. M. 4, 655: retroversi ortus omen, Sol. 4. — Trop.: argumentum, confuted, Lact. 1, 16 fin.— Form rē^trōrsus: retrorsā manu, Plin. 26, 9, 60, § 93: denique saepe retrorsa respiciens (mulier) substitit, App. M. 2, 6 Hild. p. 101 Oud. (retrorsus

retrudo.full: rē^-trūdo, no perf., sum, 3, v. a., to thrust back (in the verb. finit. only anteand post-class.): quasi retruderet hominum me vis invitum, Plaut. Ep. 2, 2, 64: in metallum retrudendus, Cod. Th. 1, 5, 1: in carcerem, Vulg. Gen. 41, 10. — Hence, rē^-trūsus, a, um, P. a., removed, concealed; several times in Cic. with abditus: simulacra deorum, Cic. Verr. 2, 1, 3, § 7.—Trop.: voluntas, Q. Cic. Petit. Cons. 11, 44: haec in philosophiā, Cic. de Or. 1, 19, 87.

retundo.full: rĕ-tundo, tŭdi (also rettŭdi, Phaedr. 4, 22, 21 Orell. N. cr.), tūsum (retunsus, Plaut. Ps. 1, 2, 27; 4, 4, 8), 3, v. a., to beat or pound back any thing sharp, i. e. to blunt, dull (class.). Lit.: ferrum, Cic. Sull. 30, 83: in Massagetas ferrum, Hor. C. 1, 35, 39: gladios in rem publicam destrictos, Cic. Cat. 3, 1, 2: ascias (tilia), Plin. 16, 40, 76, § 207: hamata tela, Ov. Am. 2, 9, 13; cf.: conjurationis nefaria tela, Cic. Dom. 24, 63. — Trop., to blunt, dull, deaden, weaken, restrain, check

retunsus.full: rĕtunsus, a, um, Part. and P. a. of retundo.

returo.full: rĕ-tūro, āre, v. a. turo, whence also obturo, to open, unstop (only in the two foll. passages): obscenis verbis novae nuptae aures returare, Varr. ap. Non. 167, 6: ora coarticulare mutorum, surdorum auriculas returare, Arn. 1, 31.

retusus.full: rĕtūsus, a, um, Part. and P. a. of retundo.

reudigni.full: Reudigni, ōrum, m. Gothic; root rinds, venerable, a people of northern Germany, on the right bank of the Albis, north of the Longobards, Tac. G. 40.

reunctor.full: rĕ-unctor, ōris, m. ungo, an anointer (a physician's assistant, who rubbed the patient with ointments), Plin. 29, 1, 2, § 4.

reus.full: rĕus, i, m., and rĕa, ae, f. res, jurid. t. t. Originally, a party to an action (res), either plaintiff or defendant; afterwards restricted to the party accused, defendant, prisoner, etc.: reos appello non eos modo, qui arguuntur, sed omnes, quorum de re disceptatur. Sic enim olim loquebantur, Cic. de Or. 2, 43, 183; cf.: reos appello, quorum res est, id. ib. 2, 79, 321: reus nunc dicitur, qui causam dicit: et item qui quid promisit spoponditve ac debet. At Gallus Aelius, lib. II. Significationu
reus.short: rĕus, i, m., and rĕa, ae, f.

revalesco.full: rĕ-vălesco, lŭi, 3, v. inch. n., to grow well again; to regain one's former strength, state, or condition; to recover (poet. and post-Aug. for convalesco, reficior). Lit., Ov. H. 21, 231: ex capitali morbo, Gell. 16, 13, 5: interibi revalesco, App. Mag. p. 320, 29: te significasti jam revalescere coepisse, Ambros. Ep. 79, 1. — Trop.: Laodicea (tremore terrae prolapsa), revaluit, Tac. A. 14, 27: diplomata Othonis, quae neglegebantur, revalescerent, regain their force or authority, id. H. 2, 54: a

revecto.full: rĕ-vecto, āre, 1, v. a., to carry back again: ad Macedoniam corpus alicujus, Jul. Val. Res Gest. Alex. 3, 42.

reveho.full: rĕ-vĕho, xi, ctum, 3, v. a., to carry or bring back, to convey back (class.; syn.: reporto, refero, reddo). Lit.: Diana Segestam Carthagine revecta, Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 35, § 77; so, praedam inde, Liv. 1, 35: tela ad Graios, Ov. M. 13, 402: aliquem domum (mater), Plaut. Bacch. 1, 1, 9; 10; Hor. Epod. 13, 16: Promethea (satelles Orci), id. C. 2, 18, 36: arma, Stat. Th. 2, 734: exsequias Romam, Eutr. 9, 2: revehunt vitrea, et aëna, vestis, fibulas, Plin. 12, 19, 42, § 88.— Pass., in mid. force, to dr

revelatio.full: rĕvēlātĭo, ōnis, f. revelo, an uncovering, laying bare (eccl. Lat.). Lit.: pudendorum, Arn. 5, 182. — Trop.: imaginariae revelationes, Aug. Conf. 9, 10: filii sui, a revelation, Tert. adv. Marc. 5, 4; Vulg. 1 Cor. 1, 7. — Esp., the Revelation of St. John, Lact. Inst. Epit. 42, 8.

revelator.full: rĕvēlātor, ōris, m. id., a revealer (eccl. Lat.), Tert. adv. Marc. 4, 25.

revelatorius.full: rĕvēlātōrĭus, a, um, adj. id., of or belonging to revelation (eccl. Lat.), Tert. Anim. 47.

revello.full: rĕ-vello, velli, vulsum or volsum, 3, v. a., to pluck or pull away, to pull or tear out, to tear off or away (freq. and class.). Lit.: tela de corpore, Cic. Pis. 11, 25: nascentis equi de fronte revolsus amor, Verg. A. 4, 515: titulum de fronte, Ov. P. 4, 13, 7: telum altā ab radice, Verg. A. 12, 787: caput a cervice, id. G. 4, 523; cf.: cornu a fronte, Ov. M. 9, 86: saxum e monte, id. ib. 12, 341: partem e monte, id. ib. 13, 882: a silvis silvas et ab arvis arva, id. ib. 8, 584: ab aliquo morte
revello.short: rĕ-vello, velli, vulsum or volsum, 3, v.

revelo.full: rĕ-vēlo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a., to unveil, uncover, lay bare (not ante-Aug.; syn.: patefacio, aperio, nudo, retego). Lit.: caput (opp. involvere), Suet. Galb. 7: frontem, Tac. G. 31: os, Ov. F. 6, 619: pectus, Flor. 4, 2, 71: carpenta (opp. contegere), App. M. 10, p. 247: sacra, Ov. H. 11, 73. — Trop., to disclose, reveal: fraudes (with detegere), App. M. 9, p. 229: omnia (tempus), Tert. Apol. 7 fin.: justitiam et salutem Domini cunctis gentibus, Hier. in Isa. 15, 56, 2; Vulg. Psa. 28, 9; id. Matt

revendo.full: rĕ-vendo, dĭdĭ, 3, v. a., to sell again: operas liberto, etc., Dig. 38, 2, 37.

reveneo.full: rĕ-vēnĕo, ii, 4, v. n., to be sold again: si fundus revenisset, Dig. 18, 3, 5.

revenio.full: rĕ-vĕnĭo, vēni, ventum, 4, v. n., to come again, come back, to return (class.; cf.: redeo, revertor). Lit., absol.: reveni, ut illum persequar, Plaut. Merc. 4, 1, 3; so id. Men. 5, 3, 4; Tac. A. 12, 59: domum, Plaut. Am. 1, 1, 33; 2, 2, 13; id. Bacch. 4, 9, 125; Cic. de Or. 1, 38, 175; 1, 40, 181 sq.; id. Balb. 11, 28; cf.: domum de hippodromo, Plaut. Bacch. 3, 3, 27: in urbem, Tac. A. 4, 74 fin.: huc, Plaut. Bacch. 4, 9, 143; id. Most. 1, 1, 54; id. Mil. 3, 2, 49; id. Trin. 1, 2, 119 al.: ex lo

reventilo.full: rĕ-ventĭlo, āre, to produce again, = proferre: nihil phantasiarum, Claud. Mam. Stat. An. 1, 24.
reventilo.short: rĕ-ventĭlo, āre, to produce again, = proferre: nihil phantasiarum, Claud.

revento.full: rĕvento, āre, a false read. for reverto, Lucr. 3, 1061; v. Lachm. ad h. l.

reventus.full: rĕventus, ūs, m. revenio, a return, Suevius ap. Macr. S. 2, 14 fin.

reverbero.full: rĕ-verbĕro, āre, 1, v. a., to strike back, repel, cause to rebound (post-Aug.): sic veneficiis corpus induruit, ut saxa reverberet, Sen. Contr. 1, 3, 11: Indus saxis saepe impeditus quīs crebro reverberatur, Curt. 8, 9, 7: reverberato lapide, Amm. 24, 4, 28: ut humus molliter cedat nec incrementa duritiā suā reverberet, Col. 3, 13, 7: usque adeo ut radios omnis nostri tuoris splendore reverberent, App. de Deo Socr. p. 48, 3: hinc vi reverberante ventorum, Amm. 22, 15, 7. — Trop.: iram Fortunae,

reverecunditer.full: rĕ-vĕrēcundĭter, adv., respectfully, Enn. ap. Prisc. p. 1010 P. (Enn. p. 180 Vahl.); Pompon. ap. Non. 516, 22 (Com. Rel. p. 200 Rib.).

reverendus.full: rĕvĕrendus, a, um, Part. and P. a. of revereor.

reverens.full: rĕvĕrens, entis, Part. and P. a. of revereor.

reverenter.full: rĕvĕrenter, adv., v. revereor, P. a. A. fin.

reverentia.full: rĕvĕrentĭa, ae, f. revereor, timidity arising from high respect or (more rarely) from fear, respect, regard, fear, awe, reverence (not freq. till after the post-Aug. per.): adhibenda est quaedam reverentia adversus homines, et optimi cujusque et reliquorum: nam neglegere, quid de se quisque sentiat, non solum arrogantis est, sed omnino dissoluti, Cic. Off. 1, 28, 99: personae, Quint. 9, 2, 76: judicum, id. 11, 1, 29: senatus, Plin. Pan. 69, 4: nulla superiorum, Tac. Or. 40: sacramenti, id. H. 1,

revereor.full: rĕ-vĕrĕor, ĭtus. 2, v. dep. a. (act. collat. form rĕvĕrĕo, acc. to Prisc. p. 799 P.), to stand in awe or fear of; to regard, respect, honor; to fear, be afraid of; to reverence, revere (ante-class. and post-Aug.; syn. veneror): Ap. Quid est quod pudendum siet, genere natam bono pauperem Ducere uxorem? Pe. Revereor filium, Plaut. Ep. 2, 1, 5 (cf. infra, the passage, Ter. Phorm. 2, 1, 3): observantia, per quam aetate aut sapientiā aut honore ... antecedentis reveremur et colimus, Cic. Inv. 2, 22,

revergo.full: rĕ-vergo, ĕre, v. n., to incline towards any thing; trop.: in aliorum commoda, to tend, conduce (late Lat.), Claud. Mam. Ep. ad Sid. 4, 2.

reverro.full: rĕ-verro (rĕvorro), ĕre, v. a., to sweep back again, to scatter again: revorram hercle hoc, quod convorri modo, Plaut. Stich. 2, 2, 64 (cf. id. ib. 2, 2, 27 and 51).

reversio.full: rĕversĭo (rĕvors-), ōnis, f. reverto. A turning back before reaching one's destination (differing from reditus, a coming back, return): quam valde ille reditu vel potius reversione meă laetatus, Cic. Att. 16, 7, 5: exponam vobis breviter consilium et profectionis et reversionis meae, id. Phil. 1, 1, 1: reversionem ut ad me faceret denuo, Plaut. Truo. 2, 4, 45; id. Bacch. 2, 3, 62; Varr. ap. Non. 222, 19; 245, 14. — Of things in gen., a returning, return: febrium, Cic. N. D. 3, 10, 24: annua (sol

reverso.full: rĕverso, āre, v. freq. a. id., to turn round (late Lat.): versa et reversa in tergum et in latera, Aug. Conf. 6 fin.: panis qui non reversatur, Vulg. Os. 7, 8: subcinericius panis est cinere coctus et reversatus, Isid. 20, 2, 15.— Mid.: reversatur ejus ex talis, Veg. 3, 11.— Pass. reversatus, turned back: palpebra ejus, Plin. Val. 1, 23.

reversus.full: rĕversus, a, um, Part. of revertor.

reverticulum.full: rĕvertĭcŭlum, i, n. reverto, a return: annua solis, App. M. 3, p. 134; id. Flor. 4, p. 361, 9.

reverto.full: rĕ-verto (-vort-) and rĕ-vertor (-vort-), versus (-vors-) (inf. paragog. revertier, Phaedr. 4, 18, 14), 3 (the authors of the ante-Aug. per. make the perfect forms, with the exception of the part. reversus, only from the active root, reverti, reverteram, revertisse, etc., Plaut. Am. 3, 2, 28: Cic. Fam. 10, 28, 1; id. Att. 8, 3, 7; id. Phil. 2, 24, 59; id. Div. 1, 15, 27; id. Phil. 8, 10, 28; id. Tusc. 5, 37, 107; Caes. B. G. 1, 8; 1, 31, 2, 29; 2, 14; Sall. C. 37, 11 et saep.: reversus, Cic. Phi

revestio.full: rĕ-vestĭo, īvi or ĭi, ītum, 4, v. a., to clothe again (late Lat.), Tert. adv. Marc. 5, 129; id. Res. Carn. 42 fin.; trop., Dracont. Hexaëm. 1, 629.
revestio.short: rĕ-vestĭo, īvi or ĭi, ītum, 4, v.

revibratio.full: rĕvī^brātĭo, ōnis, f. revibro, a reflection of light (late Lat.), Hyg. Astr. 4, 14.

revibratus.full: rĕvī^brātus, ūs, m. id. (only in abl. sing.), a reflection of light, Mart. Cap. 2, § 110.

revibro.full: rĕ-vī^bro, āvi, 1, v. a. and n. Act., to cast back, reflect: radios, Mart. Cap. 2, § 169.— Neutr., to send back a reflection: ipsa caeli contextio lucis fulgoribus revibravit, Mart. Cap. 8, § 810.

revictio.full: rĕvictĭo, ōnis, f. revinco, a refuting, refutation (post-class.), App. Dogm Plat. 3, p. 31, 39.

revictus.full: rĕvictus, a, um, Part. of revinco.

revideo.full: rĕ-vĭdĕo, ēre, v. n., to see again, go to see again: nunc ad eram revidebo, Plaut. Truc. 2, 2, 65: aspectus alicujus, Cassiod. Complex. Act. Apos. 51.

revigesco.full: rĕ-vĭgesco, ĕre, v. inch. n., to begin to flourish again, Juvenc. 2, 204.

revilesco.full: rĕ-vīlesco, ĕre, v. inch. n., to become vile or contemptible: virtus admota oculis, Sen. Tranq. 17, 2.

revimentum.full: rĕ-vīmentum, i, n. vieo, a lappet; an edging, fringe (syn. lacinia): (in oratione) omnia, ut in tenui veste, oris detexta et revimentis sint vincta, Fronto Laud. fumi (a little after, laciniam aliquam porrigat).

revincibilis.full: rĕvincĭbĭlis, e, adj. revinco, that may be disproved or refuted (eccl. Lat.): materiae iisdem litteris, Tert. Res. Carn. 13 fin.

revincio.full: rĕ-vincĭo, vinxi, vinctum, 4, v. a. To bind back or backwards; to bind around, bind fast, fasten (class.; not in Cic.). Lit.: nisi esset (terra) caelo revincta, Lucr. 5, 553: ancorae pro funibus ferreis catenis revinctae, Caes. B. G. 3, 13: tignis in contrariam partem revinctis, id. ib. 4, 17; cf.: trabes introrsus, id. ib. 7, 23: stipites demissi et ab infimo revincti, id. ib. 7, 73: navigium (with religare), Plin. Pan. 82, 2: aliquem ad saxa, to bind fast, Ov. M. 11, 212; cf.: zonam de poste,

revinco.full: rĕ-vinco, vīci, victum, 3, v. a., to conquer, subdue. Lit. (only poet., and in Tac.): victrices catervae Consiliis juvenis revictae, Hor. C. 4, 4, 24; cf.: revicta conjuratio, repressed, checked, Tac. A. 15, 73: primordia rerum aliquā ratione, Lucr. 1, 593: vires (ignis), id. 5, 410.— Trop., to convict; to refute, disprove (class.; syn.: convinco, refuto), Lucr. 4, 488: numquam hic neque suo neque amicorum judicio revincetur, * Cic. Arch. 6, 11: aliquem, Tac. A. 6, 5: aliquem in mendacio, Dig. 2

revinctus.full: rĕ-vinctus, a, um, Part. of revincio.

revindico.full: rĕ-vindĭco, āre, 1, v. a., to exact retribution from (late Lat.), Primas in Gal. Ad. c. 5.

revireo.full: rĕ-vĭrĕo, ēre, v. n., to be green again, be covered again with verdure: arbores, Albin. 2, 113.

reviresco.full: rĕ-vĭresco, rŭi, 3, v. inch. n., to become or grow green again; to recover its verdure. Lit. (rare): laesae silvae, Ov. M. 2, 408: arbor Ruminalis in novos fetus, Tac. A. 13, 58: caepe revirescit decedente lunā, contra autem inarescit adulescente, Gell. 20, 8, 17.— Poet., transf., of an old man, to become young again: spes est virginibus subjecta, Arte suum parili revirescere posse parentem, Ov. M. 7, 305: pars credunt torvos patriā revirescere vultus, Sil. 15, 134.— Trop., to grow strong or vig

revisceratio.full: rĕ-viscĕrātĭo, ōnis, f., a restoring of the flesh (eccl. Lat.): revisceratio et respiratio ossium, Tert. Res. Carn. 30.
revisceratio.short: rĕ-viscĕrātĭo, ōnis, f., a restoring of the flesh (eccl.

revisio.full: rĕvīsĭo, ōnis, f. revideo, a seeing again, Claud. Mam. Ep. ad Sid. 4, 2.

revisito.full: rĕ-vīsĭto, āre, v. a., to visit again, revisit: urbem nundinis, Plin. 18, 3, 3, § 13.

reviso.full: rĕ-vīso, ĕre, v. n. and a. Neutr., to look back on a thing, come back or again to see (cf. respicio); to pay a visit again (ante- and post-class.): ut ad me revisas, Plaut. Truc. 2, 4, 79: ad me, Gell. 13, 30, 10: ad stabulum, Lucr. 2, 359.— Poet.: signa ad lunam, Lucr. 5, 636: reviso quid agant, aut quid captent consili, Ter. And. 2, 4, 1; id. Eun. 5, 4, 1: inde redit rabies eadem et furor ille revisit, i. e. comes back, returns, Lucr. 4, 1117.— Act., to go or come to see again; to revisit: tu

revivificatus.full: rĕ-vīvĭfĭcātus, a, um, Part. [vivifico], restored to life (eccl. Lat.), Tert. Res. Carn. 19.

revivisco.full: rĕ-vīvisco (rĕvīvesco; v. Orell. Cic. Fam. 6, 10, 5), vixi, 3, v. inch. n., to come to life again, to be restored to life, to revive (class.; a favorite word with Cic., esp. in the trop. signif.). Lit.: reviviscat M'. Curius aut eorum aliquis, etc., Cic. Par. 5, 2, 38; id. Fin. 4, 22, 61; id. Mil. 29, 79; id. Pis. 27, 67; id. N. D. 2, 38, 96: ille reviviscet jam nunquam, Ter. Hec. 3, 5, 15: apes, Varr. R. R. 3, 16, 38: ut revixisse aut renatum sibi quisque Scipionem imperatorem dicat, Liv. 26, 4

revivo.full: rĕ-vīvo, no perf., victum, 3, v. n., to live again (post-class.), Sen. Med. 477; Paul. Nol. Carm. 35, 563.

revocabilis.full: rĕvŏcābĭlis, e, adj. revoco, that may be recalled or revoked, revocable (mostly poet.): poenae leves et revocabiles, Sen. Ira, 1, 5, 6.—Hence, with a negative, for irrevocable: colus Parcarum, Sen. Herc. Fur. 559: telum, Ov. M. 6, 264: carmen fatorum, Prop. 4 (5), 7, 51. aliquis (sc. mortuus), Albin. 1, 427: damnum, Claud. in Eutr. 2, 488: non revocabile verum, Stat. Th. 1, 291.

revocamen.full: rĕvŏcāmen, ĭnis, n. id., a calling back or away, a recall (Ovidian), Ov. F. 1, 561.—Plur., Ov. M. 2, 596.

revocatio.full: rĕvŏcātĭo, ōnis, f. id., a calling back or away, a recalling (rare but good prose). Lit.: a bello (with receptui signum), Cic. Phil. 13, 7, 15.— Transf., in plur.: revocationes lunae a sole, Vitr. 9, 4 fin.— Trop.: revocatio ad contemplandas voluptates, Cic. Tusc. 3, 15, 33. — Ejusdem verbi crebrius positi quaedam distinctio et revocatio, i.e. qualification and withdrawal, as a fig. of speech, Cic. de Or. 3, 54, 206; Quint. 9, 1, 33.— As law t. t., the right of one absent from home to appeal to

revocator.full: rĕvŏcātor, ōris, m. revoco, a recaller: animarum (magus), one who restores to life, Quint. Decl. 10, 19.

revocatorius.full: rĕvŏcātōrĭus, a, um, adj. id., for calling or drawing back, revocatory (postclass.): emplastrum, Theod. Prisc. 2, 32.— Subst.: rĕvŏcātōrĭa, ae, f. (sc. epistula), a letter of recall, Cod. Just. 12, 1, 18.

revoco.full: rĕ-vŏco, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. To call back, recall (class. and freq., esp. in the trop. sense). Lit. In gen.: quotiens foras ire volo, me retines, revocas, Plaut. Men. 1, 2, 5; cf. Suet. Claud. 15 fin.: de meo cursu rei publicae sum voce revocatus, Cic. Fam. 10, 1, 1: aliquem ex itinere, id. Div. 2, 8, 20; Suet. Aug. 98; id. Tib. 21: revocatus de exsilio Camillus, Liv. 5, 46: revocatum ex provinciā, Suet. Claud. 1: Caesar in Italiam revocabatur, Caes. B. C. 2, 18 fin.: spes Campanae defectionis S

revolo.full: rĕ-vŏlo, āre, v. n., to fly back (rare but class.). Lit.: turdi quotannis in Italiam trans mare advolant et eodem revolant, Varr. R. R. 3, 5, 7: grus, Cic. N. D. 2, 49, 125: mergi, Verg. G. 1, 361: Daedalus ceratis alis, Ov. M. 9, 741: apis ut nulla intro revolet, Col. 9, 12, 1.— Transf.: telum, Ov. M. 7, 684: sol, to hasten back, Manil. 2, 193: ad aliquem, Vell. 2, 123, 2.

revolsus.full: rĕvolsus, a, um, Part. of revello, q. v.

revolubilis.full: rĕvŏlūbĭlis, e, adj. revolvo, that may be rolled back (poet.): pondus (i. e. saxum), Ov. Ib. 193: unda, Sil. 15, 237: orbita, Aus. Ecl. Nomin. Sept. Dier. 12.—Fig.: juro ego Fatorum nulli revolubile carmen, Prop. 4 (5), 7, 51. saxum, Sil. 11, 476.

revolutio.full: rĕvŏlūtĭo, ōnis, f. id., a revolving, revolution (late Lat. for conversio), Aug. Civ. Dei, 22, 12; id. Trin. 12, 24; Mart. Cap. 9, § 922.

revolutus.full: rĕvŏlūtus, a, um, Part. of revolvo.

revolvo.full: rĕ-volvo, volvi, vŏlūtum, 3, v. a., to roll back; to unroll, unwind; to revolve, return (class.; esp. freq. since the Aug. per.). Lit. In gen.: Draco revolvens Sese, Cic. poët. N. D. 2, 42, 106: (pelagus) gelidum ab imo fluctum revolvit in partem superiorem, Col. 8, 17, 1: fluctus (hibernus auster), Tac. A. 6, 33: retro Aestum (ventus), Sen. Agam. 487: retro sua fila (Sorores), id. Herc. Fur. 182; cf.: inmites scis nulla revolvere Parcas Stamina, Stat. Th. 7, 774: lapidem, Vulg. Matt. 28, 2. — P

revomo.full: rĕ-vŏmo, ŭi, 3, v. a., to spew or vomit forth again; to vomit up, disgorge (poet. and in post-Aug. prose). Lit.: salsos pectore fluctus, Verg. A. 5, 182: plumam avibus devoratis (dracones), Plin. 10, 72, 92, § 197: haustum mare (Charybdis), Sen. Thyest. 581; cf. Sil. 2, 308; and of the same: vorat haec raptas revomitque carinas, Ov. M. 13, 731; cf.: umorque aquae sursum revomit atque remittit (tigna), Lucr. 2, 199: spolia assidue mota ventis maria revomebant, cast up again, Flor. 4, 11, 7: at mi

revulsio.full: rĕvulsĭo (rĕvols-), ōnis, f. revello, a tearing off or away (post-Aug.): unius schedae, Plin. 13, 12, 24, § 80.

revulsus.full: rĕvulsus, a, um, Part. of revello.

rex1.full: rex, rēgis (gen. plur regerum, Gell. ap. Charis p. 40 P.), m. rego, a ruler of a country, a king. Lit.: omnis res publica, quae ut dixi populi res est, consilio quodam regenda est, ut diuturna sit. Id autem consilium aut uni tribuendum est aut delectis quibusdam, etc. Cum penes unum est omnium summa rerum, regem illum unum vocamus et regnum ejus rei publicae statum, etc., Cic. Rep. 1, 26, 41; cf. id. ib. 2, 23, 43; 1, 42, 65: simulatque se inflexit hic rex in dominatum injustiorem, fit continuo

rex2.full: Rex, rēgis, m., a surname in the gens Marcia, e. g. Q. Marcius Rex, consul A. U. C. 686, Sall. C. 30, 3: Q. (Marcius) Rex, brotherin-law of Clodius, Cic. Att. 1, 16, 10 (in a lusus verbb. with rex, a tyrant, despot); cf. Hor. S. 1, 7, 35: P. Marcius Rex, Liv. 43, 1 al.; cf. Suet. Caes. 6.
rex2.short: Rex, rēgis, m., a surname in the gens Marcia, e.

rha.full: Rha, indecl., = Ῥᾶ, the Wolga, on whose banks grew the radix pontica, Rha ponticum, rhubarb (Rheum Rhaponticum, Linn.), which thence received its name, Amm. 22, 8, 28 (cf. Cels. 5, 23 fin.).
rha.short: Rha, indecl., = Ῥᾶ, the Wolga, on whose banks grew the radix pontica, Rha ponticum, rhubarb (Rheum Rhaponticum, Linn.), which thence received its name, Amm.

rhabdos.full: rhabdŏs, i, f., = ῥάβδος (a rod), a sort of meteor, App. de Mundo, p. 64, 14.
rhabdos.short: rhabdŏs, i, f., = ῥάβδος (a rod), a sort of meteor, App.

rhacoma.full: rhacŏma or rhecŏma, ae, f., a root, perh. i. q. rha, rhubarb, Plin. 27, 12, 105, § 128.
rhacoma.short: rhacŏma or rhecŏma, ae, f., a root, perh.

rhacotes.full: Rhacōtes, ae, or Rhacōtis, is, f., an ancient name of the site of Alexandria in Egypt, form Rhacotes, Plin. 5, 10, 11, § 62; form Rhacotis, Tac. H. 4, 84.
rhacotes.short: Rhacōtes, ae, or Rhacōtis, is, f., an ancient name of the site of Alexandria in Egypt, form Rhacotes, Plin.

rhadamanthus.full: Rhădămanthus, i, m., = Ῥαδάμανθος, a son of Jupiter and Europa, brother of Minos, a judge in the infernal regions, Cic. Tusc. 1, 5, 10; 1, 41, 98; Ov. M. 9, 435; 439; Verg. A. 6, 566; Claud. in Rufin. 2, 480.
rhadamanthus.short: Rhădămanthus, i, m., = Ῥαδάμανθος, a son of Jupiter and Europa, brother of Minos, a judge in the infernal regions, Cic.

rhadamas.full: Rhădămas, antis, m., a fictitious name in Plaut. Trin. 4, 2, 83.
rhadamas.short: Rhădămas, antis, m., a fictitious name in Plaut.

rhaeti.full: Rhaeti, Rhaetĭa, Rhaetĭcus, Rhaetus, v. Raeti, etc.

rhagades.full: rhăgădes, um, f., and rhăgădia, ōrum, n., = ῥαγάδες and ῥαγάδια, a kind of sores or chaps on various parts of the body, Plin. 23, 4, 44, § 87; 23 7 64. § 129; 24, 7, 23, § 39; 28. 6, 18, § 66 (in Cels. 6, 18, 7, written as Greek).
rhagades.short: rhăgădes, um, f., and rhăgădia, ōrum, n., = ῥαγάδες and ῥαγάδια, a kind of sores or chaps on various parts of the body, Plin.

rhagion.full: rhăgĭon, ii, n., = ῥάγιον, a small spider Plin. 29, 4, 27. § 86.
rhagion.short: rhăgĭon, ii, n., = ῥάγιον, a small spider Plin.

rhamnos.full: rhamnos, i, m., = ῥάμνος, buckthorn, Christ's-thorn: Rhamnus, Linn.; Plin. 24, 14, 76, § 124, Veg. 5, 74.
rhamnos.short: rhamnos, i, m., = ῥάμνος, buckthorn, Christ's-thorn: Rhamnus, Linn.;

rhamnus.full: Rhamnūs, untis, f., = Ῥαμνοῦς, the northernmost town of Attica, famed for an ancient temple of Themis, and in later times for a statue of Nemesis, the mod. Ovriokastro, Plin. 4, 7, 11, § 24; 36, 5, 4, § 17; Luc. 5, 233.— Hence, Rhamnūsĭus, a, um, adj., Rhamnusian Rhamnusium se aiebat esse, from Rhamnus, Ter. And. 5, 4, 27: Antiphon, Cic. Brut. 12, 47: virgo, i. e. Nemesis, Cat. 66, 71; also called dea, Claud. B. Get. 631; and simply Rhamnūsia, ae, f., Ov. M. 3, 406; id. Tr. 5, 8, 9; Stat S. 3, 5
rhamnus.short: Rhamnūs, untis, f., = Ῥαμνοῦς, the northernmost town of Attica, famed for an ancient temple of Themis, and in later times for a statue of Nemesis, the mod.

rhamses.full: Rhamses, is (or ae), m., an ancient and powerful king of Egypt, Tac. A. 2, 60, Plin. 36, 8, 14, § 65 (al. Ramises).
rhamses.short: Rhamses, is (or ae), m., an ancient and powerful king of Egypt, Tac.

rhanis.full: Rhănis, ĭdis. f., a nymph in the train of Diana, Ov. M. 3, 171.

rhapeion.full: † rhăpēĭon, ii, n., = ῥαπήϊον, a plant, also called leontopetaion, Plin. 27, 11, 72, § 96 (al. rhaphanidion).
rhapeion.short: † rhăpēĭon, ii, n., = ῥαπήϊον, a plant, also called leontopetaion, Plin.

rhapisma.full: † rhăpisma, ătis, n., = ῥάπισμα, a blow with the palm of the hand, Cod. Just. 8, 49, 6.
rhapisma.short: † rhăpisma, ătis, n., = ῥάπισμα, a blow with the palm of the hand, Cod.

rhapsodia.full: † rhapsōdĭa, ae, f., = ῥαψῳδία, a rhapsody: secunda, i. e. the second book of the Iliad, Nep. Dion, 6, 4.
rhapsodia.short: † rhapsōdĭa, ae, f., = ῥαψῳδία, a rhapsody: secunda, i.

rhea1.full: Rhēa, ae, f., an old Italian name. Thus, Rhea Silvia, daughter of Numitor and mother of Romulus and Remus, Liv. 1, 3; Flor. 1, 1, 1; Prud. adv. Symm. 1, 174 (cf. Verg. A. 1, 276).—Hence comes the name of the fabled priestess Rhea in Verg. A. 7, 659.
rhea1.short: Rhēa, ae, f., an old Italian name.

rhea2.full: Rhĕa, ae, f., = Ῥέα, another name for Cybele, Ov. F. 4, 201: Rhea, quae Latiis Ops, Aus. Idyll. 12 de Deis, 2.
rhea2.short: Rhĕa, ae, f., = Ῥέα, another name for Cybele, Ov.

rhectae.full: † rhēctae, ārum, m., = ῥῆκται, a kind of earthquake, App. de Mundo, p. 65, 26.
rhectae.short: † rhēctae, ārum, m., = ῥῆκται, a kind of earthquake, App.

rhedones.full: Rhēdŏnes (Rēd-), um, m., a people in Gallia Lugdunensis, in the neighborhood of the modern Rennes, in Bretagne, Caes. B. G. 2, 34; 7, 75; Plin. 4, 18, 32, § 107.
rhedones.short: Rhēdŏnes (Rēd-), um, m., a people in Gallia Lugdunensis, in the neighborhood of the modern Rennes, in Bretagne, Caes.

rhegium.full: Rhēgĭum and Rhēgīnus, incorrect spelling for Regium and Reginus, q. v.
rhegium.short: Rhēgĭum and Rhēgīnus, incorrect spelling for Regium and Reginus, q.

rhene.full: Rhēnē, ēs, f., = Ῥήνη, an island in the Ægean Sea, one of the Cyclades, Plin. 4, 12, 22, § 67; Mel. 2, 7.
rhene.short: Rhēnē, ēs, f., = Ῥήνη, an island in the Ægean Sea, one of the Cyclades, Plin.

rhenus.full: Rhēnus, i, m. The Rhine, the river which divided Gaul from Germany, Caes. B. G. 1, 1; 4, 10; 4, 17; 6, 9; Tac. G. 1; id. A. 1, 63; 2, 6; Mel. 3, 2 sq.; Plin. 4, 14, 28, § 100; Cic. Pis. 33, 81; Verg. A. 8, 727; id. E. 10, 47; Hor. S. 1, 10, 37; id. A. P. 18; Ov. M. 2, 258; id. P. 3, 4, 88.—Hence, Rhē-nānus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to the Rhine, Rhenish: terrae, Sid. Ep. 4, 17 (but in Mart. 9, 35, 4, Rhenigenam is the better reading).—; Meton., the dwellers on the Rhine, the Germans, Ov. F.

rhesus.full: Rhēsus, i, m., = Ῥῆσος, the son of a Muse, a king in Thrace, who was robbed of his horses and killed by Diomede and Ulysses before Troy, Cic. N. D. 3, 18, 45; Verg. A. 1, 469; Ov. M. 13, 249 sq. al.
rhesus.short: Rhēsus, i, m., = Ῥῆσος, the son of a Muse, a king in Thrace, who was robbed of his horses and killed by Diomede and Ulysses before Troy, Cic.

rhetenor.full: Rhētēnor, ŏris, m., a companion of Diomede, Ov. M. 14, 504.
rhetenor.short: Rhētēnor, ŏris, m., a companion of Diomede, Ov.

rhetico.full: Rhetĭco, ōnis, m., a mountain range in Germany, now the Siebengebirge, near Bonn, Mel. 3, 3, 3.
rhetico.short: Rhetĭco, ōnis, m., a mountain range in Germany, now the Siebengebirge, near Bonn, Mel.

rhetor.full: rhētor, ŏris, m., = ῥήτωρ, a teacher of oratory or rhetoric, a rhetorician: eos, qui rhetores nominarentur et qui dicendi praecepta traderent, nihil plane tenere, Cic. de Or. 1, 18, 84; cf. Quint. 2, 2, 1: in rhetorum scholis, id. 10, 5, 14; 12, 2, 23: rhetorum artes, Cic. Fin. 3, 1: rhetorum epilogus, id. Tusc. 1, 47, 112; 2, 3, 9: (pueri) priusquam tradantur rhetori, Quint. 1, 10, 1; Mart. 2, 64, 1; Tac. Dial. 30 and 35; Macr. S. 5, 2, 1.— * After the Greek manner, an orator; but with contempt
rhetor.short: rhētor, ŏris, m., = ῥήτωρ, a teacher of oratory or rhetoric, a rhetorician: eos, qui rhetores nominarentur et qui dicendi praecepta traderent, nihil plane tenere, Cic.

rhetorica.full: rhētŏrĭca, ae, and rhētŏrĭcē, ēs, v. rhetoricus.
rhetorica.short: rhētŏrĭca, ae, and rhētŏrĭcē, ēs, v.

rhetorico.full: rhētŏrĭco, āvi, 1 (ante-class.), and rhētŏrĭcor, āri, v. dep. (post-class.) [rhetoricus], to speak rhetorically or like an orator, Novat. ap. Non. 476, 6 (Com. Rel. p. 216 Rib.); act. form, Tert. Res. Carn. 5.
rhetorico.short: rhētŏrĭco, āvi, 1 (ante-class.), and rhētŏrĭcor, āri, v.

rhetoricoteros.full: rhētŏrĭcōtĕros, i, adj., = ῥητορικώτερος, more oratorical, Lucil. ap. Cic. de Or. 3, 43, 171.
rhetoricoteros.short: rhētŏrĭcōtĕros, i, adj., = ῥητορικώτερος, more oratorical, Lucil.

rhetoricus.full: rhētŏrĭcus, a, um, adj., = ῥητορικός, of or belonging to a rhetorician, rhetorical. Adj.: nostro more aliquando, non rhetorico loquamur, Cic. de Or. 1, 29, 133: ars, i. e. a treatise on rhetoric, id. Fin. 4, 3, 7: rhetorici doctores, i. e. teachers of rhetoric, Cic. de Or. 1, 19, 86: syllogismus, Quint. 5, 10, 3; 9, 4, 57: libri, books on rhetoric, Cic. de Or. 2, 3, 10. — Hence, Substt. rhētŏrĭca, ae, or rhētŏrĭcē, ēs, f. (the first form in Cic., the latter in Quint.), the art of oratory, rhetor
rhetoricus.short: rhētŏrĭcus, a, um, adj., = ῥητορικός, of or belonging to a rhetorician, rhetorical.

rhetoriscus.full: rhētŏriscus, i, m. dim. rhetor, a little rhetorician, Gell. 17, 20, 4.

rhetorisso.full: rhētŏrisso, āre, v. n., = ῥητορίζω, to speak rhetorically, Pompon. ap. Non. 166, 3 (Com. Rel. p. 201 Rib.).

rhetra.full: rhētra, ae, f., = ῥήτρα, a saying, maxim, law: quas (leges) ex rhetris Lycurgi reparavit Sylla, Amm. 16, 5, 1.
rhetra.short: rhētra, ae, f., = ῥήτρα, a saying, maxim, law: quas (leges) ex rhetris Lycurgi reparavit Sylla, Amm.

rheuma.full: rheuma, ătis, n., = ῥεῦμα. A flow, flood: maris (i. e. aestus), Veg. Mil. 5, 12.— A catarrh, rheum, Hier. Ep. 122, 1.
