C. 2, 37; Liv. 1, 33; Col. 2, 2, 15 sq. al.: Salinae Romanae, the salt-works established by Ancus Martius at Ostia, near Rome, Liv. 7, 19 fin.; cf. id. 1, 33; also called simply Salinae, id. 5, 45; 24, 47: Herculeae, near Herculaneum, Col. poët. 10, 135.—In a play upon the meaning of this word and that of sal, II.: quod parum diligenter possessio salin

salinarius.full: sălīnārĭus, a, um, adj. salinae, of or belonging to salt-works: areae, Vitr. 8, 3.

salinator1.full: sălīnātor, ōris, m. id., a dealer in salt, a salter, Arn. 2, 70; Inscr. Orell. 749: aerarii, a farmer of the salt-revenue, Cato ap. Serv. Verg. A. 4, 244.

salinator2.full: Sălīnātor, ōris, m. 1. salinator, a Roman surname, Cic. Sen. 3, 7; 4, 11; id. de Or. 2, 67, 273; Liv. 29, 37; 35, 24 al.

salinum.full: sălīnum, i, n. sal (sc. vas; masc. collat. form, plur., sălīni, Varr. ap. Non. 546, 14), a salt-cellar, Plaut. Pers. 2, 3, 15; Hor. C. 2, 16, 14; Pers. 3, 25; 5, 138; also used at sacrifices, Liv. 26, 36; Val. Max. 4, 4, 3; Arn. 2, 91.—Prov.: salinum cum sale obsignare, Plaut. Pers. 2, 3, 15.

salio1.full: sălĭo (sall-), no perf., ītum, 4 (collat. form sălo or sallo, no perf., salsum, 3: salunt, Varr. ap. Diom. p. 372 P.: salerent, Sall. Fragm. ap. Prisc. p. 909: salere, Lucil. ib.: salsurus, Mummius ap. Prisc. p. 910 P.; part. salsus, v. infra P. a.), v. a. id.. To salt down, to salt: pernas, Cato ap. Varr. R. R. 1, 2 fin.: oleas caducas, Cato, R. R. 23, 1: pisces, Sisenn. ap. Prisc. p. 909 P.; Cels. 2, 18: saliturus istaec mittam salem, Naev. ap. Prisc. p. 910 P.: saliti pumiliones, Corn. Sev. i

salio2.full: sălĭo, ŭi (cf. Diom. p. 371 P.; Prisc. p. 906 P.; Serv. Verg. A. 3, 416: salii, Stat. S. 1, 2, 210; id. Th. 9, 132; Aug. Doctr. Chr. 2, 20, § 31: salivi, Serv. Verg. G. 2, 384), saltum, 4 (gen. plur. part. pres. salientum, Lucr. 4, 1200), v. n. and a. [kindr. with Sanscr. sar-, sal-, to go, and Gr. ἅλλομαι; cf. salax]. Neutr., to leap, spring, bound, jump (cf. tripudio), hop. Lit. (class.): ambulant aliquae (aves), ut cornices: saliunt aliae, ut passeres, merulae, etc., Plin. 10, 38, 54, § 111:

salipotens.full: sălĭ-pŏtens, entis, adj., he that rules the salt sea: frater Jovis, i. e. Neptune, Plaut. Trin. 4, 1, 1 Ritschl N. cr.
salipotens.short: sălĭ-pŏtens, entis, adj., he that rules the salt sea: frater Jovis, i.

salisatio.full: sălĭsātĭo (salissātĭo), ōnis, f. saliso, whence also salisator, a leaping: cordis (with pulsus), a beating, palpitating, Marc. Emp. 21 fin.; cf.: salisatio, παλμός, Gloss. Philox.

salisatores.full: sălĭsātōres vocati sunt, quia dum eis membrorum quaecumque partes salierint, aliquid sibi exinde prosperum seu triste significari praedicunt, Isid. Orig. 8, 9, 26 (v. Theocriti Idyll. 3, 37, and Plaut. Ps. 1, 1, 105) [saliso, whence also salisatio].
salisatores.short: sălĭsātōres vocati sunt, quia dum eis membrorum quaecumque partes salierint, aliquid sibi exinde prosperum seu triste significari praedicunt, Isid.

salisubsuli.full: Sălĭsubsŭli, ōrum, m. Salii-subsilio, a word comically formed by Cat., to signify the dancing priests of Mars (v. Salii), Cat. 17, 6.

salitio.full: sălītĭo, ōnis, f. 2. salio, a leaping: equorum, on horseback, Veg. Mil. 1, 18.

salitura.full: sălītūra, ae, f. 1. salio, a salting down, salting, Col. 12, 21, 3.

salitus.full: sălītus, a, um, Part. of 1. salio.

saliunca.full: sălĭunca, ae, f., an odoriferous plant, the wild or Celtic nard: Valeriana Celtica, Linn.; Plin. 21, 7, 20, § 43; Verg. E. 5, 17; Scrib. Comp. 195; 258; Vulg. Isa. 55, 13.
saliunca.short: sălĭunca, ae, f., an odoriferous plant, the wild or Celtic nard: Valeriana Celtica, Linn.;

saliuncula.full: sălĭuncŭla, ae, f. dim. of saliunca, an odoriferous plant, Hier. in Isa. 15, 55; v. 12 and 13. † Sălĭus, ii, v. 1. Salii.

saliva.full: sălīva, ae, f. kindr. with σίαλον, spittle, saliva (in gen., while sputum is that already spit out; equally used in sing. and plur.). Lit., sing., Cat. 23, 16; 78, 8; 99, 10; Juv. 6, 623; Sen. Ira, 3, 38, 2; Plin. 27, 6, 24, § 41; 28, 12, 53, § 193: in manum ingerere, id. 28, 4, 7, § 37 al.—Plur., Lucr. 4, 638; 4, 1108; Col. 6, 9, 3: unā salivā, without interruption, Hier. ad Pam. 61, 4.— Transf., a spittle-like moisture, slime: cochlearum, slime, Plin. 30, 15, 47, § 136; cf. ostrearum, id, 32,

salivarius.full: sălīvārĭus, a, um, adj. saliva, I. B., slimy, clammy: lentor (muricum), Plin. 9, 51, 74, § 160.

salivatio.full: sălīvātĭo, ōnis, f. salivo, II., in the later med. lang., salivation, Cael. Aur. Acut. 3, 2 al.

salivo.full: sălīvo, no perf., ātum, 1, v. a. saliva. * To spit out, discharge, yield: lentorem cujusdam cerae (purpurae), Plin. 9, 36, 60, § 125.— In veterinary lang., to salivate, cure by salivation: aegrotum pecus, vaccam, admissarium, Col. 6, 5, 2; 6, 7, 9; 5, 24, 5; 6, 37, 9; pass., Pall. Apr. 7.—Hence, să-līvātum, i, n. (acc. to II.), a medicine employed to excite the flow of saliva, Col. 6, 10, 1; Plin. 27, 11, 76, § 101; Veg. 3, 2, 25.

salivosus.full: sălīvōsus, a, um, adj. id.. Full of spittle, slavering: labia, App. Mag. p. 313: aegrotans, Cael. Aur. Acut. 2, 2 fin.— Slimy, clammy: umor (corticis ulmorum), Plin. 16, 38, 72, § 181.

salix.full: sălix, ĭcis, f. Lit., a willow-tree, willow, sallow, Cato, R. R. 6, 4; Varr. R. R. 1, 24, 4; Col. 4, 30, 4; Plin. 16, 37, 68, § 174; 24, 9, 37, § 56; Lucr. 2, 361; Verg. E. 3, 65; 83; 5, 16 et saep.—* Meton., a willowbranch, withy, osier, Prud. στεΦ. 10, 703.

sallo.full: sallo and sălo, ĕre, v. 1. salio.

sallustianus.full: Sallustĭānus, a, um, v. Sallustius, I. and III.

sallustius.full: Sallustĭus or Salustĭus, ii, m., Sallust, a Roman name. C. Sallustius Crispus, the celebrated Roman historian, Tac. A. 3, 30; Quint. 2, 5, 19; 10, 1, 101.—Hence, Sallustĭānus (Salust-), a, um, adj., of or like Sallust, Sallustian: illa brevitas, Quint. 4, 2, 45; 10, 1, 32: lectio, Gell. 18, 4, 1.—Subst.: Sallustĭānus, i, m., an imitator of Sallust, Sen. Ep. 114, 17: Sallustianum illud, that expression of Sallust, Gell. 10, 26, 9.—Hence, adv.: Sallustĭā-nē, in the manner of Sallust, Prisc. 1022 P
sallustius.short: Sallustĭus or Salustĭus, ii, m., Sallust, a Roman name.

salluvii.full: Salluvĭi (Saluv-), ōrum, or Sal-ўes, um, m., a Celtic or Ligurian tribe in Gallia, Liv. 5, 34, 7; 5, 35, 2; 21, 26, 3; Plin. 3, 4, 5, § 36.
salluvii.short: Salluvĭi (Saluv-), ōrum, or Sal-ўes, um, m., a Celtic or Ligurian tribe in Gallia, Liv.

salmacidus.full: salmăcĭdus, a, um, adj. contr. from salgama, salma, and acidus, of water, having a salt and sour taste, salso-acid: salmacidum ἁλμυρόν, salmacidus ἁλμυρός, ἁλώδης, Gloss. Philox. (post-Aug.): aquae (with nitrosae), Plin. 31, 3, 22, § 36: aqua (opp. dulcis), Plin. Val. 5, 41 fin.: fluvii, Flor. 4, 10, 8.

salmacis.full: Salmăcis, ĭdis, f. A very cleat fountain in Caria, much used, and fabled to render soft and effeminate all who drank of it, Ov. M. 4, 286; Vitr. 2, 8; Stat. S. 1, 5, 21.—Personified, the nymph of this fountain, Ov. M. 4, 337; 4, 347; voc. Salmaci, id. ib. 4, 306; cf. Fest. p. 329 Müll.— Transf., a weak, effeminate person, Enn. ap. Cic. Off. 1, 18, 61 (Trag. v. 36 Vahl.; cf. Trag. Rel. p. 53 Rib.).

salmo.full: salmo, ōnis, m., a salmon, Plin. 9, 18, 32, § 68; Aus. Idyll. 10, 97.
salmo.short: salmo, ōnis, m., a salmon, Plin.

salmoneus.full: Salmōneus (trisyl.), ĕos, m., = Σαλμωνεύς, a son of Æolus, brother of Sisyphus, who imitated lightning with burning torches, and was on that account hurled into Tartarus by a thunderbolt from Jupiter, Hyg. Fab. 60; 61; 250; Verg. A. 6, 585 Serv.; Claud. in Rufin. 2, 514; Epigr. ap. Sphaer. Archim. 18.—Hence, Salmōnis, ĭdis, f., = Σαλμωνίς, Tyro, a daughter of Salmoneus, mother of Neleus and Pelias by Neptune, who assumed the form of Enipeus, Prop. 3, 19 (4, 18), 13; 1, 13, 21; Ov. Am. 3, 6, 43;
salmoneus.short: Salmōneus (trisyl.), ĕos, m., = Σαλμωνεύς, a son of Æolus, brother of Sisyphus, who imitated lightning with burning torches, and was on that account hurled into Tartarus by a thunderbolt from Jupiter, Hyg.

salo2.full: Sălo, ōnis, m., a river of Hispania Tarraconensis, near the town of Bilbilis, now the Xalon, Mart. 10, 103, 2; 10, 104, 6; called also Bilbilis, Just. 44, 3, 8.
salo2.short: Sălo, ōnis, m., a river of Hispania Tarraconensis, near the town of Bilbilis, now the Xalon, Mart.

salomon.full: Sălŏmon (Sŏlŏmon), ōnis, m., = Σαλωμών, Σαλομών, Σολομών [], Solomon, son of David, Prud. Hamart. 581; Juvenc. 2, 717; Alcim. 6, 387; Lact. 4, 16. —Hence, Sălŏmōnĭus (Sŏlŏm-), a, um, adj., of or belonging to Solomon, Solomon's: templum, Lact. 4, 13 fin.; also called saxa, Prud. Apoth. 512.— Să-lŏmōnĭăcus, a, um, adj. (poet.), of Solomon, Solomon's: templum, Sid. poët. Ep. 4, 18; Ven. Carm. 1, 11, 1.
salomon.short: Sălŏmon (Sŏlŏmon), ōnis, m., = Σαλωμών, Σαλομών, Σολομών [], Solomon, son of David, Prud.

salonae.full: Sălōnae, ārum (Sălōna, ae, Mel. 2, 3, 13; Plin. 3, 22, 26, § 141; Auct. B. Alex. 43), f., a maritime town in Dalmatia, still called Salona, Caes. B. C. 3, 8 and 9.

salor.full: sălor, ōris, m. salum, the color of the sea, sea-green (late Lat.), Mart. Cap. 1, § 16.

salpa.full: salpa, ae, f., a kind of stock-fish, Plin. 9, 18, 32, § 68; Ov. Hal. 121.
salpa.short: salpa, ae, f., a kind of stock-fish, Plin.

salpicta.full: salpicta (collat. form salpista, Vop. Carin. 19), ae, m., = σαλπιγκτής (σαλπιστής), a trumpeter, Firm. Math. 8, 21; Arn. 7, 239 (v. Orell. N. cr. p. 440).

salpinates.full: Salpīnātes, um, m., a people of Etruria, Liv. 5, 31, 5; 5, 32, 2.—Sing. as adj.: Salpīnas, belonging to the Salpinates: ager, Liv. 5, 32, 4.
salpinates.short: Salpīnātes, um, m., a people of Etruria, Liv.

salsamen.full: salsāmen, ĭnis, n. salsus, for salsamentum, salted food, any thing pickled in brine (late Lat.), Arn. 7, 230.

salsamentarius.full: salsāmentārĭus, a, um, adj. salsamentum, of or belonging to salted fish: vasa, Col. 2, 10, 16: cadi, Plin. 18, 30, 73, § 308: testa, id. 28, 9, 37, § 140: NEGOTIANS, a dealer in salted fish, Inscr. Orell. 4249.— As subst.: salsāmentārĭus, ii, m., a dealer in salted fish, Auct. Her. 4, 54, 67; Suet. Vit. Hor. init.

salsamentum.full: salsāmentum, i, n. salsus. * Fish-pickle, brine, * Cic. Div. 2, 57, 117.— Salted or pickled fish (usu. in plur.): salsamenta Fac macerentur, Ter. Ad. 3, 3, 26; Varr. R. R. 3, 17, 7; Col. 8, 17, 12; Plin. 32, 2, 9, § 18; 32, 7, 26, § 79; 32, 9, 34, § 106 al.—Sing., Col. 12, 55, 4; Gell. 2, 24, 7.

salse.full: salsē, adv., v. 1. salio, P. a. fin.

salsedo.full: salsēdo, ĭnis, f. salsus, a salt taste, saltness, Pall. Oct. 14, 2.

salsipotens.full: Salsĭ-pŏtens, entis, a false reading for salipotenti, Plaut. Trin. 4, 1, 1.
salsipotens.short: Salsĭ-pŏtens, entis, a false reading for salipotenti, Plaut.

salsitas.full: salsĭtas, ātis, f. salsus, saltness (late Lat.). Lit.: liquoris, Jul. Val. Rer. Gest. Alex. 3, 29.— Trop., wit: Sardorum, Hier. adv. Luc. 14.

salsitudo.full: salsĭtūdo, ĭnis, f. id., saltness, brackishness, Vitr. 1, 4 fin.—Plur., Plin. 20, 14, 54, § 154.

salsiusculus.full: salsĭuscŭlus, a, um, adj. dim. [salsius, from salsus], rather salt (late Lat.): quaedam salsiuscula comedunt ebriosi, Aug. Conf. 8, 3.

salsugo.full: salsūgo (collat. form salsĭlāgo, Plin. 31, 7, 42, § 92; 18, 12, 32, § 124), ĭnis, f. salsus, saltness, brackishness, Vitr. 1, 4; Plin. 36, 23, 55, § 176; 19, 5, 26, § 84 al.: terra salsuginis, i. e. a desert, Vulg. Job, 39, 6; id. Jer. 17, 6.— Transf., salt-water, brine, Plin. 19, 5, 26, § 85; 31, 7, 42, § 92.

salsula.full: Salsŭla, ae, f., a Roman female name, Amm. 28, 4, 28; Inscr. Murat. 1456, 6.
salsula.short: Salsŭla, ae, f., a Roman female name, Amm.

salsulae.full: Salsŭlae, ārum, f. (sc. aquae), a saltspring in Gallia Narbonensis, now La Fontaine des Salses, Mel. 2, 5, 7.— A city near the salt-spring, now Salses, ltin. Anton. 389, 7.

salsura.full: salsūra, ae, f. salsus. Abstr. A salting, pickling: de sucidiā et salsurā faciendā, Col. 12, 55, 1.—* Transf., in comic lang.: ita meae animae salsura evenit, i. e. I am in such an ill-humor, Plaut. Stich. 1, 2, 35.— Concr. Brine, pickle, Varr. R. R. 2, 4, 18; Col. 12, 48, 5.— Pickled or salted fish (syn. salsamentum): pabula salsurae, Col. 8, 17, 13.

salsus.full: salsus, a, um, P. a., from 1. salio.

saltabundus.full: saltābundus, a, um, adj. salto, dancing (post-class.): saltabundi canebant, quae nunc stantes canunt, Gell 20, 3, 2.

saltatim.full: saltātim, adv. id., by leaps: singulis cruribus saltatim currere, Gell. 9, 4, 9.

saltatio.full: saltātĭo, ōnis, f. id., a dancing; concr., a dance, Quint. 1, 11, 18 sq.; 2, 18, 1; Scipio Afric. ap. Macr. S. 2, 10: multarum deliciarum comes est extrema saltatio, Cic. Mur. 6, 13; id. Brut. 62, 225; id. Fin. 3, 7, 24; Quint. 11, 3, 128; Suet. Tit. 7 al.—Plur., Plaut. Stich. 5, 2, 11.

saltatiuncula.full: saltātĭuncŭla, ae, f. dim. saltatio, a little dance (late Lat.), Vop. Aur. 6.

saltator.full: saltātor, ōris, m. salto, a dancer (generally among the Romans with an accessory contemptuous signif.), Cic. Off. 1, 42, 150; id. Mur. 6, 13; id. Deiot. 10, 28; id. Fin. 3, 7, 24; Quint. 1, 12, 14; 11, 3, 89; Suet. Calig. 54; id. Ner. 6; Macr. S. 2, 10 al.

saltatorius.full: saltātōrĭus, a, um, adj. salto, of or belonging to dancing, dancing-, saltatory (class.): ludus, a dancing-school, Scipio Afric. ap. Macr. S. 2, 10, § 7; cf. Macr. S. 2, 10, 4: orbis, a dancing in a ring, Cic. Pis. 10, 30; Arn. 2, 73.—* Adv.: saltātōrĭē, like a dancer, in a dancing attitude: procurrens, App. M. 10, p. 253, 36.

saltatricula.full: saltātrīcŭla, ae, f. dim. saltatrix, a little dancing-girl (post-class.), Gell. 1, 5 fin.

saltatrix.full: saltātrix, īcis, f. saltator, a female dancer, dancing-girl, Cic. Pis. 8, 18; Plin. 10, 23, 33, § 68; Macr. S. 2, 10, 1; Vulg. Ecclus. 9, 4.

saltatus.full: saltātus, ūs, m. salto, a (religious) dance (not ante-Aug., and very rare): (Numa Salios) per urbem ire canentes carmina cum tripudiis sollennique saltatu jussit, Liv. 1, 20; so Sen. Troad. 786; Lact. 1, 21 fin.—Plur.: saltatibus apta juventus, Ov. M. 14, 637.

saltem.full: saltem (sometimes in MSS. saltim; cf. Aus. Ep. 7, 23; and Prisc. p. 1013 P.), adv. old acc. form, from salvus, salus. prop., saved, reserved (salvā re; compare Engl. save, except). It serves to point out that which still remains or holds good, in spite of or by way of exception to something opposed to it; and accordingly is used (like certe, II.) as a restrictive particle, at least, at the least, at all events, anyhow. Affirmatively (class.). With a statement of the opposite: si illud non licet,

salticus.full: saltĭcus, a, um, adj. saltus, dancing (late Lat.): puella, Tert. adv. Gnost. 8.

saltito.full: saltĭto, āre, v. freq. n. [salto], to dance much or vigorously (post-Aug. and very rare), Quint. 9, 4, 142; Macr. S. 2, 4, 14; 2, 10 fin.; Arn. 2, 73.

salto.full: salto (once salĭto, Varr. L. L. 5, § 85 Müll., Salii a salitando), āvi, ātum, 1, v. freq. n. and a. [2. salio], to dance (in the widest signif. of the word, including pantomime and gesticulation; mostly with a contemptuous accessory signif.). Neutr.: vidi in his unum puerum bullatum, non minorem annis duodecim, cum crotalis saltare, quam saltationem impudicus servulus honeste saltare non posset, Scipio Afric. ap. Macr. S. 2, 10 (v. the whole chapter on this subject); cf. Cic. Pis. 10, 22; id. De

saltuarius.full: saltŭārĭus, ii, m. 2. saltus, one who has the care of a forest or of an estate, a forester, ranger; a steward, bailiff (postAug.), Dig. 32, 1, 58 fin.; 7, 8, 16; 33, 7, 15; Petr. 53, 9; Inscr. Orell. 6294: VIRTVTIS, keeper of the grove of Virtue, ib. 1599.

saltuatim.full: saltŭātim, adv. 1. saltus. Lit., by leaps or hops: currere singulis cruribus, Gell. 9, 4, 9.— Trop., of a written narrative, in a skipping or desultory manner: vellicatim ac saltuatim scribere, Sisenn. ap. Gell. 12, 15, 2, and ap. Non. 168, 11: dum ex loco subinde saltuatim redire festinamus, Amm. 26, 5, 15 al.

saltuensis.full: saltŭensis, e, adj. 2. saltus, of or belonging to a forest (jurid. Lat.): fundi, forest-pastures, Cod. Just. 11, 62, 13: coloni, ib. 11, 64, 1.

saltuosus.full: saltŭōsus, a, um, adj. id., full of woods or forests, well-wooded, woody: loca, Sall. J. 38, 1; Liv. 27, 12; Tac. A. 4, 45; 6, 34: convalles, Plin. 6, 7, 7, § 19: per saltuosos tramites, Amm. 19, 9, 5.

saltus1.full: saltus, ūs, m. 2. salio, a leaping, leap, spring, bound (class.), Sen. Ep. 15, 4: saltu uti, * Cic. Sen. 6, 19: cum alacribus saltu, cum velocibus cursu certabat, Sall. Fragm. ap. Veg. Mil. 1, 9 fin.: saltu pernici tollere corpus, Lucr. 5, 559; cf.: (monocoli) mirae pernicitatis ad saltum, Plin. 7, 2, 2, § 23: corpora saltu Subiciunt in equos, Verg. A. 12, 287: saltu Emicat in currum, id. ib. 12, 326; 9, 553: saltu superare viam, id. G. 3, 141: saltum dare, to make a leap, Ov. M. 4, 551; so in p

saltus2.full: saltus, ūs (gen. salti, Att. ap. Non. 486, 1), m. etym. dub.; perh. akin to Sanscr. sar-, sal-, to go; v. Corss. Ausspr. 2, 71, a woody district, uncultivated but used for pasture, a forest-pasture, woodland-pasture, woodland (level or mountainous); freq. and class.; cf.: silva, nemus, lucus). Lit.: saltus est, ubi silvae et pastiones sunt, quarum causā casae quoque. Si qua particula in eo saltu pastorum aut custodum causā aratur ea res non peremit nomen saltui, non magis quam fundi, qui est in

salubris.full: sălūbris, e (masc. collat. form sălū-ber, Varr. R. R. 1, 2, 8; Ov. R. Am. 704; but salubris, m., Cic. Div. 1, 57, 130; Cels. 1, 3; 2, 1; 3, 6; abl. salubri, v. Neue, Formenl. 2, p. 30), adj. salus, health-giving, promoting health, healthful, wholesome, salubrious; salutary, serviceable, advantageous, beneficial (v. salutaris init.). Lit. (freq. and class.) Absol.: saluber locus, Varr. R. R. 1, 2, 8; so Cic. Fat. 4, 7 (opp. pestilens); id. Rep. 2, 6, 11 (opp. pestilens regio); 1, 1, 1; id. de Or.

salubritas.full: sălūbrĭtas, ātis, f. salubris. Healthfulness, wholesomeness, salubrity (class.): hostiarum exta, quorum ex habitu atque ex colore tum salubritatis, tum pestilentiae signa percipi, Cic. Div. 1, 57, 131: amoenitatem hanc (sc. hujus loci) et salubritatem sequor, id. Leg. 2, 1, 3; so of places, id. Agr. 2, 35, 95; Varr. R. R. 1, 4, 3 sq.; Suet. Tib. 11; Auct. B. G. 8, 52; cf.: aquarum, Liv. 42, 54 fin.; Tac. A. 12, 66; Plin. 5, 16, 15, § 72: nemorum, id. 37, 10, 77, § 201: caeli, Col. 1, 3, 1; Plin.

salum.full: sălum, i, n. (masc. collat. form, corresp. to the Gr. acc., undantem salum, Enn. ap. Non. 223, 24, or Trag. v. 226 Vahl.), = σάλος, the open sea, the high sea, the main, the deep; opp. to the sea near the coast or in a port (occurring only in sing., and mostly in the acc. and abl.). Lit. (rare but class.), Cic. Caecin. 30, 88: in salum nave evectus, Liv. 29, 14: paucas (naves) ante portum in salo habiturum, id. 37, 10: pars (classis) in salo ad ostium portūs in ancoris stetit, id. 37, 13 (cf. th

salus.full: sălūs, ūtis (archaic gen. SALVTES, on a clay vessel, v. Ritschl de Fictilibus Litteratis, Berol, 1853, p. 18, n. 5; cf. APOLONES, from Apollo; dat. SALVTEI, Corp. Inscr. Lat. 587), f. root sar, to guard, whence servus, servare, salvus, sollus; cf. Gr. ὅλος, entire, a being safe and sound; a sound or whole condition, health, welfare, prosperity, preservation, safety, deliverance, etc. (very freq. and class.: cf.: valetudo, sanitas). Lit. In gen.: Mars pater te precor, pastores pecuaque salva serv

salutabundus.full: sălūtābundus, a, um, adj. saluto, greeting, saluting (late Lat.): Jovem, Mart. Cap. 7, § 729.

salutaris.full: sălūtāris, e, adj. salus, of or belonging to well-being, healthful, wholesome, salutary, serviceable, beneficial, advantageous (in the most general sense, while the predominant meaning of salubris, in class. lang., is healthy in a medical sense; very freq. and class.). In gen. Absol.: ut quae mala perniciosaque sunt, habeantur pro bonis ac salutaribus, Cic. Leg. 1, 16, 44: pro salutaribus mortifera conscribere, id. ib. 2, 5, 13: res salutares (opp. pestiferae), id. N. D. 2, 12, 34: res utiles et

salutatio.full: sălūtātĭo, ōnis, f. saluto, a greeting. saluting, salutation (rare but good prose). In gen.: quis te aditu, quis ullo honore, quis denique communi salutatione dignum putet? Cic. Pis. 40, 96: salutationem facere, Liv. 1, 1 fin.: salutationem reddere, Tac. A. 4, 61: salutatione acceptā ac redditā, Macr. S. 1, 6: mutuā salutatione factā, Curt. 10, 8, 23.—Of performing devotions: uti praetereuntes possint respicere (aedificia deorum) et in conspectu salutationes facere, Vitr. 4, 5.—Rarely of a writt

salutator.full: sălūtātor, ōris, m. id., one who greets; a greeter, saluter. In gen.: salutator regum, Stat. S. 2, 4, 29.— In partic. (cf. salutatio, II.), one who makes complimentary visits, who pays his respects to another, a visitor; also (in the time of the emperors), one who appears at court, a courtier, Q. Cic. Petit. Cons. 9, 34; Col. praef. § 9; Mart. 1, 71, 18; 10, 74, 2; Suet. Claud. 35; Juv. 5, 15.

salutatorius.full: sălūtātōrĭus, a, um, adj. id. (postAug.). Of or belonging to visiting or paying court: cubilia, an audience-chamber, Plin. 15, 11, 10, § 38.—As subst.: să-lūtātōrĭum, i, n., the audience-chamber, Cassiod. Hist. Eccl. 9, 30.— In gram.. salutatorius casus, i. e. the vocative, acc. to Prisc. p. 671 P.

salutatrix.full: sălūtātrix, īcis, f. salutator (postAug.), she that salutes; occurring only in apposition. In gen.: pica, Mart. 7, 87, 6: charta, i. e. a letter of greeting, id. 9, 99, 2.— In partic., she that makes complimentary visits, that pays court: turba, i. e. the crowd of clients who come to salute their patron in the morning, Juv. 5, 21.

salutifer.full: sălūtĭfer, fĕra, fĕrum, adj. salus-fero (poet. for salubris), health-bringing, healing, salubrious: totique salutifer orbi Cresce, puer, dicit, Ov. M. 2, 642; so, anguis Urbi, id. ib. 15, 744; 15, 632: herbae animantibus, Stat. Achill. 1, 117: aquae, Mart. 5, 1, 6; Ov. H. 21, 174: salutiferā potione pestem veneni exstinguere, App. M. 10, p. 251, 29; Aug. in Psa. 118, Serm. 26, 4: verba, Alcim. 4, 225.

salutificator.full: sălūtĭfĭcātor, ōris, m. salus-facio, a bringer of safety, a savior (eccl. Lat.), Tert. Res. Carn. 47; id. Carn. Chr. 14 (al. salvificator).

salutiger.full: sălūtĭger, gĕra, gĕrum, adj. salusgero (post-class.). Health-bringing: Juppiter, Aus. Idyll. 8, 26 (cf. salutaris, II. fin.): ortus, Prud. στεφ. 11, 235.— That brings a greeting, salutatory: libelli, Aus. Ep. 25, 4.—Hence, subst.: sălūtĭger, gĕri, m., one who delivers a greeting; a messenger, servant, App. de Deo Socr. p. 45, 24.

salutigerulus.full: sălūtĭgĕrŭlus, a, um, adj. id., that carries salutations or messages: pueri, errand-boys, pages, Plaut. Aul. 3, 5, 28.

salutio.full: Sălūtĭo, or Salvitto, ōnis, m., a Roman surname of one Scipio, Suet. Caes. 59; Plin. 7, 12, 10, § 54; 35, 2, 2, § 8; v. Sillig ad h. l.
salutio.short: Sălūtĭo, or Salvitto, ōnis, m., a Roman surname of one Scipio, Suet.

saluto.full: sălūto, āvi, ātum (gen. plur. salutantum, Lucr. 1, 318; Verg. G. 2, 462; Ov. M. 5, 295), 1, v. a. salus. * (Acc. to salus, I. A.) To keep safe, to preserve: sequenti anno palmites salutentur pro viribus matris singuli aut gemini, Plin. 17, 22, 35, § 177. — (Acc. to salus, I. B.) To greet, wish health to, pay one's respects to, salute any one (freq. in all periods and kinds of composition; cf.: salvere jubeo). In gen.: Charmidem Lysiteles salutat, greets, bids good-day, Plaut. Trin. 5, 2, 29: Ly.

salvamentum.full: salvāmentum, i, n. salvo, salvation (eccl. Lat.), Ven. v. Alb. 9.

salvatio.full: salvātĭo, ōnis, f. id., deliverance, salvation (late Lat.), Boëth. Duab. Nat. p. 953; Vulg. Joel, 2, 32.—Plur., Vulg. Psa. 27, 8.

salvator.full: salvātor, ōris, m. id.. In gen., a saviour, preserver (late Lat.; class. servator): Cicero Soterem salvatorem noluit nominare, Mart. Cap. 5, § 510; Vulg. Isa. 17, 10: IOVI SALVATORI, Inscr. Grut. 19.— In partic., in the Vulg. and Christian fathers, as a transl. of σωτήρ and Jesus (Heb. ), the Saviour, Redeemer: Christus Jesus, id est Christus Salvator: hoc est enim Latine Jesus ... Salus Latinum nomen est: salvare et salvator non fuerunt haec Latina, antequam veniret Salvator, etc., Aug. Serm. 2

salveo.full: salvĕo, ēre, v. n. salvus. To be well, or in good health; so in the verb. finit. only once in a lusus verbb. with the foll.; v. II. 1. fin.— In partic., as a term of salutation. Salve, salveto, salvete, God save you; how are you? I hope you are well; and, salvere jubeo, I bid you good-day, goodday, welcome, etc. (very freq. and class.; cf.: haveo, valeo): Ly. Charmidem Lysiteles salutat. Ca. Non ego sum salutis dignus? Ly. Immo salve, Callicles, Plaut. Trin. 5, 2, 29: Ph. Curculio exoptate, salv

salvia.full: salvĭa, ae, f., the herb sage, Plin. 22, 25, 71, § 147; 26, 6, 17, § 31.
salvia.short: salvĭa, ae, f., the herb sage, Plin.

salvianus.full: Salvĭānus, a, um, adj., of or named from one Salvius, Salvian: interdictum, Dig. 43, 33, 5.
salvianus.short: Salvĭānus, a, um, adj., of or named from one Salvius, Salvian: interdictum, Dig.

salvifico.full: salvĭfĭco, āre, v. a. salvus-facio, to save, deliver (late Lat.): pater istā memet ab horā Salvifica, Sedul. 5, 7: me, Vulg. Johan. 12, 27: mundum, id. ib. 12, 47.

salvificus.full: salvĭfĭcus, a, um, adj. id., saving: corpus Christi, Alcim. Avit. ad Sor. 180.

salvo.full: salvo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. salvus, to save (late Lat.; opp. perdere; syn.: servo, conservo), Veg. Vet. 3, 23, 3; Lact. de Ira Dei, 5, 7; Hier. Ep. 20, 4; Vulg. Isa. 4, 2; id. Amos, 2, 14; Sedul. 1, 109.

salvus.full: salvus (ante-class. -vos), a, um, adj. root sar, sal; v. salus, saved, preserved, unharmed, safe, unhurt, uninjured, well, sound, etc. In gen. (very freq. and class.; syn.: sospes, sanus, incolumis): Mars pater, te precor, pastores pecuaque salva servassis duisque bonam salutem valetudinemque mihi, etc., an ancient form of praver in Cato, R. R. 141, 3; cf.: si respublica populi Romani Quiritium ad quinquennium proximum salva servata erit hisce duellis, datum donum duit, etc., an ancient formula

samaei.full: Sămaei, ōrum, v. Same, II. fin.

samarabriae.full: Samarabrĭae, ārum, m., a people of India, Plin. 6, 20, 23, § 78.
samarabriae.short: Samarabrĭae, ārum, m., a people of India, Plin.

samardacus.full: sămardăcus, i, m. African, a juggler (late Lat.), Aug. cont. Acad. 3, 15; cf. Schol. Cruq. ad Hor. S. 1, 6, 113 (al. sarmadacus).

samaria.full: Sămărīa, ae, f., = Σαμάρεια (orig. Heb. ), the middle district of Palestine, Plin. 5, 13, 14, § 68.—Hence, Să-mărītae, ārum, m., the inhabitants of Samaria, the Samaritans, Tac. A. 12, 54; Vulg. 4 Reg. 17, 29.—In sing.: Sămărī-tes, ae, m., a Samaritan, Hadr. ap. Vop. Sat. 8.— Sămărītis, ĭdis, f., a Samaritan woman, Juvenc. 2, 246; 252; Alcim. 3, 405.— Sămărītānus, a, um, adj., Samaritan: via, Sedul. 4, 222.—In plur., the Samaritans, Vulg. 2 Esd. 4, 2.— Sămărītĭcus, a, um, adj., Samaritan: mulier

samarobriva.full: Sămărŏbrīva (SAMARABRIVA, Inscr. Orell. 5236), ae, f., a town of Gallia Belgica, in the country of the Ambiani, now Amiens, Caes. B. G. 5, 24; 5, 47; 5, 53; Cic. Fam. 7, 11, 2; 7, 12, 1; 7, 16, 3.

sambraceni.full: Sambracēni, ōrum, m., a people of India, Plin. 6, 20, 23, § 78.
sambraceni.short: Sambracēni, ōrum, m., a people of India, Plin.

sambrachate.full: Sambrachatē, ēs, f., an island on the Arabian coast; also a city upon it, Plin. 6, 28, 32, § 151.
sambrachate.short: Sambrachatē, ēs, f., an island on the Arabian coast;

sambuca.full: sambūca, ae, f., = σαμβύκη. A triangular stringed-instrument of a very sharp, shrill tone (and hence of slight esteem), Plaut. Stich. 2, 2, 57; Scipio Afric. ap. Mácr. S. 2, 10; Pers. 5, 95; Spart. Hadr. 26; cf. Fest. pp. 324 and 325 Müll.; Isid. 3, 20, 7; Vulg. Dan. 3, 5.— Transf., a machine of like form used by besiegers; a sort of bridge for storming walls, Veg. Mil. 4, 21; Vitr. 10, 22; cf. Fest. 1. c.

sambuceus.full: sambūcĕus, a, um, adj. sambucus, of elder, elder-: arbor, Plin. 29, 4, 14, § 57 (Jahn, sabuceus): baculum, Aur. Vict. Vir. Ill. 10.

sambucina.full: sambūcĭna, ae, f. sambuca-cano, a female player on the sambuca (with fidicina, tibicina), Plaut. Stich. 2, 2, 57; cf. sambucistria.

sambucistria.full: sambūcistrĭa (sambȳc-), ae, f., = σαμβυκίστρια, a woman that plays on the sambuca (with psaltria), Liv. 39, 6; Arn. 2, n. 42; cf. Fest. pp. 324 and 325 Müll., and v. sambucina.
sambucistria.short: sambūcistrĭa (sambȳc-), ae, f., = σαμβυκίστρια, a woman that plays on the sambuca (with psaltria), Liv.

sambucus1.full: sambūcus, i, m. sambuca, he who plays on the sambuca, Mart. Cap. 9, § 924.

sambucus2.full: sambūcus (săbūcus, ap. Ser. Samm.), i, f., an elder-tree, Plin. 16, 18, 30, § 74; 17, 20, 34, § 151 al.; Ser. Samm. 7, 100; 19, 337; 27, 503 al.—Hence, sambū-cum, i, n., the fruit of the elder, elder-berries, Scrib. Comp. 160.

same.full: Sămē, ēs (collat. form Sămŏs, acc. to the Homeric Σάμος, Ov. M. 13, 711 Jahn and Bach N. cr.; Aus. Per. Odyss. 4), f., = Σάμη. An earlier name for the island of Cephalenia, in the Ionian Sea, the mod. Cephalonia, Verg. A. 3, 271; Ov. Tr. 1, 5, 67; Sil. 15, 303; Liv. 26, 42 (acc. to Mel. 2, 7, 10, and Plin. 4, 12, 19, § 54, another neighboring island).— The principal town of the island of Cephalenia, Liv. 38, 29.—Hence, Sămaei, ōrum, m., the inhabitants of Same, Liv. 38, 28 and 29.

samiator.full: sămĭātor, ōris, m. samio, a polisher, furbisher (late Lat.), Edict. Diocl. p. 20; Gloss. Philox.

samio.full: sămĭo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. Samius, to polish or furbish with Samian stone (late Lat.): loricas, cataphractas, Veg. Mil. 2, 14: ferramenta, Aur. ap. Vop. Aur. 7.

samiolus.full: Sămĭŏlus, a, um, adj. dim. [id.], Samian: poterium, i.e. of Samian cīay, Plaut. Stich. 5, 4, 12.

samius.full: Sămĭus, a, um, v. Samus, I.

sammonium.full: Sammonĭum (Samon-) promontorium, a promontory of Crete, Plin. 4, 12, 20, § 58; Mel. 2, 7.
sammonium.short: Sammonĭum (Samon-) promontorium, a promontory of Crete, Plin.

samnium.full: Samnĭum, ii, n. contr. from Sabinium, from Sabini: ab Sabinis orti Samnites, Varr. L. L. 7, § 29 Müll., an ancient country of Italy, in the neighborhood of Latium, whose inhabitants were an offshoot from the Sabines, Liv. 7, 32; Cic. Clu. 69, 197; id. Att. 14, 20, 2; 16, 11, 6; id. Rep. 3, 7 al.—Hence, Samnīs (collat. form of the nom. Samnītis, Cato ap. Prisc. p. 762; Prud. adv. Symm. 2, 515), ītis, adj., of or belonging to Samnium, Samnite: ager, Liv. 24, 20: exercitus, id. 10, 16 fin.: bellum,

samolus.full: samŏlus, i, m. Celtic, a plant, supposed to be the Anemone pulsatilla (Linn.), but, acc. to Sprengel, the Samolus valerandi, Linn.; or brook-weed, Plin. 24, 11, 63, § 104.

samosata.full: Samŏsăta, ōrum, n., = τὰ Σαμόσατα, the capital of Commagene, on the western shore of the Euphrates, now Samosat, Plin. 2, 104, 108, § 235; 5, 24, 20, § 85; 5, 24, 21, § 86.—Also Samŏsăta, ae, f., Amm. 14, 8, 7; 18, 4, 7.—Hence, Sămŏsătēnus, a, um, of Samosata, a Samosatene: Paulus, Ambros. de Fide, 5, 8, § 105; Incarn. Dom. Sac. 2, § 8.
samosata.short: Samŏsăta, ōrum, n., = τὰ Σαμόσατα, the capital of Commagene, on the western shore of the Euphrates, now Samosat, Plin.

samothracia.full: Sămŏthrācĭa, ae, f., Samothrace, an island near the coast of Thrace, famous for the mystic worship of the Cabiri, now Samothraki, Cic. N. D. 1, 42, 119; 3, 37, 87; id. Pis. 36, 89; Varr. L. L. 5, § 58 Müll.; Verg. A. 7, 208.—Also called Sămŏthrācē, ēs, f., Varr. R. R. 2, 1, 5; Mel. 2, 7, 8; Plin. 4, 12, 23, § 73; Sămŏthrāca, ae, f., Liv. 42, 25; 44, 45; 44, 46; and Thrēïcĭa Să-mus or Sămos, after the Gr. θρηϊκίη Σάμος, Verg. A. 7, 208; Ov. Tr. 1, 10, 20.— Hence, Sămŏthrācĭus, a, um, adj., Samoth
samothracia.short: Sămŏthrācĭa, ae, f., Samothrace, an island near the coast of Thrace, famous for the mystic worship of the Cabiri, now Samothraki, Cic.

sampsa.full: sampsa, ae, f., the pulp of olives, Col. 12, 49 in lemm.; 12, 51, 2; 12, 52, 10.
sampsa.short: sampsa, ae, f., the pulp of olives, Col.

sampsiceramus.full: Sampsĭcĕrămus, i, m., a humorous designation of Pompey in Cicero's letters (after a petty king of Emesa conquered by him), Cic. Att. 2, 14, 1; 2, 16, 2; 2, 17, 2.
sampsiceramus.short: Sampsĭcĕrămus, i, m., a humorous designation of Pompey in Cicero's letters (after a petty king of Emesa conquered by him), Cic.

sampsuchinus.full: sampsūchĭnus, a, um, adj., = σαμψύχιυος, of marjoram: oleum, Plin. 21, 22, 93, § 163.
sampsuchinus.short: sampsūchĭnus, a, um, adj., = σαμψύχιυος, of marjoram: oleum, Plin.

sampsuchum.full: sampsūchum (-sūchus, m., Cels. 5, 11: sampsūcum, Col. 10, 171), i, n., = σάμψυχον, marjoram: Origanum majorana, Linn.; Plin. 21, 11, 35, § 61; 21, 22, 93, § 163; Col. 10, 171.

samus.full: Sămus or Sămos, i, f., = Σάμος. An island on the coast of Asia Minor opposite Ephesus, famed as the birthplace of Pythagoras, as also for its earth and the vessels made from it, the mod. Samo, Mel. 2, 7, 4; Verg. A. 1, 16; Hor. Ep. 1, 11, 2; 1, 11, 21; Ov. M. 8, 221; acc. Samum, Cic. Imp. Pomp. 12, 33; id. Q. Fr. 1, 1, 8, § 25; Liv. 37, 10 fin. sq.; Suet. Aug. 17; Lact. 1, 15, 9; cf.: Threïciam Samon (i. e. Samothraciam), Verg. A. 7, 208; Ov. M. 15, 61; id. F. 6, 48; id. Tr. 1, 10, 20.—Hence, Să
samus.short: Sămus or Sămos, i, f., = Σάμος.

sanabilis.full: sānābĭlis, e, adj. sano, that can be healed, curable, remediable (rare but class.); of the body: vulnus, Ov. P. 2, 2, 59; id. R. Am. 101: dolor sanabilior, Cels. 2, 8; of the mind, * Cic. Tusc. 4, 37, 80; Sen. Ep. 108, 3. —Sup. and adv. do not occur.

sanates.full: Sanates dicti sunt, qui supra infraque Romam habitaverunt: quod nomen ideo his est inditum, quia cum defecissent a Romanis, brevi post in amicitiam quasi sanatā mente redierunt, Fest. p. 326 Müll. —The word occurred in the laws of the Twelve Tables, acc. to Gell. 16, 10, 8, and Fest. l. l.
sanates.short: Sanates dicti sunt, qui supra infraque Romam habitaverunt: quod nomen ideo his est inditum, quia cum defecissent a Romanis, brevi post in amicitiam quasi sanatā mente redierunt, Fest.

sanatio.full: sānātĭo, ōnis, f. sano, a healing, curing (Ciceron.): corporum, Cic. Tusc. 3, 3, 5: malorum, id. ib. 4, 15, 35; cf.: certa et propria (perturbationis animi), id. ib. 4, 28, 60. —Absol., Tert. Fug. ap. Pers. 3.

sanator.full: sānātor, ōris, m. id., a healer, curer (late Lat.), Paul. Nol. Carm. 26, 294; 27, 272.

sanatorius.full: sānātōrĭus, a, um, adj. id., giving health (late Lat.), Cassiod. Hist. Trip. 12, 2.

sanchromaton.full: sanchrōmăton, i, n., a plant, otherwise called dracontea, App. Herb. 14.
sanchromaton.short: sanchrōmăton, i, n., a plant, otherwise called dracontea, App.

sancio.full: sancĭo, xi, ctum, 4 (pluperf. sancierat, Pompon. ap. Diom. p. 368 P.; id. ap. Prisc. p. 904 ib.: sancivi, Prisc. 904; Diom. 368; part. perf. sancitum, Lucr. 1, 587; Cass. Sev. ap. Diom. l. l.), v. a. Sanscr. root sac, sak, to accompany, honor (cf. sequor); whence also sacer; cf. Gr. ἉΓ, ἅγιος, ἁγνός, to render sacred or inviolable by a religious act; to appoint as sacred or inviolable. Lit., mostly of legal ordinances or other public proceedings, to fix unalterably; to establish, appoint, decree

sancte.full: sanctē, adv., v. sancio, P. a. fin.

sanctesco.full: sanctesco, ĕre, v. inch. n. [sanctus], to become sacred: per nos sanctescat genus (Pelopidarum), Att. ap. Non. 143, 23 (Trag. Rel. p. 163 Rib.).

sanctificatio.full: sanctĭfĭcātĭo, ōnis, f. sanctifico, sanctification (eccl. Lat.), Tert. Exhort. ad Cast. 1; Sid. Ep. 8, 14; Vulg. 1 Cor. 1, 30 et saep.

sanctificator.full: sanctĭfĭcātor, ōris, m. id., a sanctifier (eccl. Lat.), Tert. ap. Prax. 2; Aug. Conf. 10, 34; Vulg. Ezech. 37, 28.

sanctificium.full: sanctĭfĭcĭum, ii, n. id., sanctification; meton., a sanctuary (eccl. Lat.), Tert. Res. Carn. 47 (from Paul. ad Rom. 6, 19); Vulg. Psa. 77, 69.

sanctifico.full: sanctĭfĭco, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. sanctusfacio, to make holy or treat as holy, to sanctify, consecrate, dedicate (eccl. Lat.), Tert. Or. 3; id. Exhort. ad Cast. 7; Prud. Cath. 3, 15; Vulg. Gen. 2, 3 et saep.

sanctificus.full: sanctĭfĭcus, a, um, adj. sanctifico, sanctifying (eccl. Lat.): auctor Spiritus, Juvenc. praef. 1 fin.

sanctiloquus.full: sanctĭlŏquus, a, um, adj. sanctus-loquor, speaking holily (eccl. Lat.): Lucas, Prud. Apoth. 1070: propheta, Paul. Nol. Carm. 23, 228.

sanctimonia.full: sanctĭmōnĭa, ae, f. sanctus; cf.: acrimonia, parsimonia, etc., sacredness, sanctity, moral purity, virtuousness, chastity, etc. (rare but class.): ad deorum religionem et sanctimoniam demigrasse, Cic. Rab. Perd. 10, 30: habere domum clausam pudori et sanctimoniae, patentem cupiditati et voluptatibus, id. Quint. 30, 93: summa sanctimonia, id. ib. 17, 55: priscae sanctimoniae virgo, Tac. A. 3, 69 fin.; cf. id. ib. 2, 86: femina sanctimoniā insignis, id. ib. 12, 6: nuptiarum, Auct. Her. 4, 33, 44:

sanctimonialis.full: sanctĭmōnĭālis, e, adj. sanctimonia, holy; of Christians, pious, religious (late Lat.): vita, i. e. a monastic life, Cod. Just. 1, 3, 56: mulier, i. e. a nun, ib. 1, 2, 13. —As subst.: sanctĭmōnĭālis, is, f., a nun, Aug. Ep. 169; id. Retract. 2, 22.—Adv.: sanctĭmōnĭālĭter, holily, piously: degere, i. e. in a cloister, Cod. Just. 1, 3, 56.

sanctio.full: sanctĭo, ōnis, f. sancio, an establishing, ordaining, or decreeing as inviolable under penalty of a curse; a decree, ordinance, sanction: sanctiones sacrandae sunt ...poenā, cum caput ejus qui contra fecerit consecratur, Cic. Balb. 14, 33; 16, 36; cf.: legis sanctio poenaque, Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 66, § 149: sanctio legum, quae novissime certam poenam irrogat iis, qui praeceptis legis non obtemperaverint, Dig. 48, 19, 41; cf.: interdum in sanctionibus adicitur, ut qui ibi aliquid commisit, capite pun

sanctitas.full: sanctĭtas, ātis, f. sanctus. Inviolability, sacredness, sanctity: tribunatūs, Cic. Sest. 37, 79: regum, Caes. ap. Suet. Caes. 6; cf.: regii nominis, Sall. Fragm. ap. Serv. Verg. G. 4, 211: sanctitas templi insulaeque, Liv. 44, 29: templo sanctitatem tribuere, Tac. A. 3, 62 fin.; cf.: augusti atque inviolati soli, Liv. 45, 5: fori, Quint. 11, 3, 58: mecum deorum et hominum sanctitates omnes et religiones afuerunt, Cic. Red. in Sen. 14, 34: propter sanctitatem aliquam, Massur. Sabin. ap. Gell. 4,

sanctitudo.full: sanctĭtūdo, ĭnis, f. sanctus. Mostly ante-class. for sanctitas, sacredness, sanctity: Jovis, Att. ap. Non. 173, 33: Apollinis, Turp. ib. 174, 5: nominis matronae sanctitudinem, Afran. ib. 174, 9: fani, Quadrig. ap. Gell. 17, 2, 19 sq.: sepulturae, Cic. Rep. Fragm. ap. Non. 174, 7 (4, 8 Mos.).—In plur., Att. ap. Non. 174, 2.— In the postclass. per., transf., uprightness, purity, Capitol. Ver. 8: domum tuam decet sanctitudo, Domine, Vulg. Psa. 92, 5.

sanctor.full: sanctor, ōris, m. sancio, an establisher, ordainer: legum, Tac. A. 3, 26 fin.

sanctuarium.full: sanctŭārĭum, ii, n. sanctus (postAug. for sacrarium). A place for keeping sacred things, a shrine, sanctuary, Aggen. Limit. p. 61 Goes.; Vulg. Dan. 8, 13 et saep.— The private cabinet of a prince: Mithridatis, Plin. 23, 8, 77, § 149; Sicul. Fl. p. 16 Goes.; Inscr. Orell. 2388.

sanctus.full: sanctus, a, um, Part. and P. a. of sancio.

sancus.full: Sancus, i, m., a deity of the Sabines, also worshipped at Rome; the same as Dius Fidius and Semo, Varr. L. L. 5, § 66 Müll.; Ov. F. 6, 213 sq.; Liv. 8, 20; 32, 1; Prop. 4 (5), 9, 74 (Müll. sanctus); Sil. 8, 422; Fest. s. v. praedia, p. 238 Müll.; id. s. v. propter, p. 229 ib.; Lact. 1, 15, 8; Aug. Civ. Dei, 18, 19; and v. Semo.
sancus.short: Sancus, i, m., a deity of the Sabines, also worshipped at Rome;

sandala.full: sandăla, ae, f., a very white kind of corn, Plin. 18, 7, 11, § 62 (v. l. scandala); also called scandŭla, Edict. Diocl. 27; Isid. Orig. 17, 3, 11.
sandala.short: sandăla, ae, f., a very white kind of corn, Plin.

sandaliarius.full: sandălĭārĭus, a, um, adj. sandalium, of or belonging to sandals: Apollo Sandaliarius, who had a statue in the Sandal-street (in the fourth region of Rome), Suet. Aug. 57.—Subst.: Sandălĭārĭus, ii, m. (sc. vicus), Sandal-street, Shoemakers'-street: in Sandaliario forte apud librarios fuimus, Gell. 18, 4, 1; cf. VICVS, Inscr. Grut. p. 79, 5.—Sandaliarius signifies also a sandal-maker in Inscr. Spon. Miscell. Ant. p. 114 (perh. in Plaut. Aul. 3, 5, 39, sandaliarii sutores should be read instead of

sandaligerulae.full: sandălĭgĕrŭlae, ārum, f. sandalium-gerulus, maids who carried their mistresses' slippers, sandal-bearers, slipper-carriers, Plaut. Trin. 2, 1, 22.

sandalios.full: Sandălĭos, ii, f., an island near Samos, Plin. 31, 5, 37, § 135.
sandalios.short: Sandălĭos, ii, f., an island near Samos, Plin.

sandaliotis.full: Sandălĭōtis, ĭdis, f., = Σανδαλιῶτις, an ancient name of Sardinia; acc. Sandaliotim, Plin. 3, 7, 13, § 85.
sandaliotis.short: Sandălĭōtis, ĭdis, f., = Σανδαλιῶτις, an ancient name of Sardinia;

sandalis.full: sandălis, ĭdis, f., a kind of palm-tree, Plin. 13, 4, 9, § 43.
sandalis.short: sandălis, ĭdis, f., a kind of palm-tree, Plin.

sandalium.full: sandălĭum, ii, n. (plur. scanned sandālĭa, Albin. 2, 65), = σανδάλιον, a slipper, sandal, Turp. ap. Non. 427, 28; Ter. Eun. 5, 7, 4; Vulg. Judith, 10, 3

sandapila.full: sandăpĭla, ae, f., a common kind of bier for people of the lower classes (persons of rank were borne on a lectica), Suet. Dom. 17 fin.; Mart. 8, 75, 14; 2, 81, 2; 9, 3, 12; Juv. 8, 175; Suet. Dom. 17; cf. Fulg. Expos. Serm. Ant. p. 558.
sandapila.short: sandăpĭla, ae, f., a common kind of bier for people of the lower classes (persons of rank were borne on a lectica), Suet.

sandapilarius.full: sandăpĭlārĭus, ii, m. sandapila, one that carries a sandapila, a corpse-bearer, Sid. Ep. 2, 8.

sandaraca.full: sandărăca (sandĕrăca and san-dărăcha), ae, f., = σανδαράκη (σανδαράχη). Sandarach, a red coloring matter, Plin. 34, 18, 56, § 178; 35, 6, 22, § 39; Vitr. 7, 12; 12, 8, 3; Paul. ex Fest. p. 324 Müll.— Bee-bread, also called cerinthus and erithace. Plin. 11, 7, 7, § 17.
sandaraca.short: sandărăca (sandĕrăca and san-dărăcha), ae, f., = σανδαράκη (σανδαράχη).

sandaracatus.full: sandărăcātus, a, um, adj. sandaraca, I., mixed with sandarach: acetum, Plin. 35, 15, 50, § 177.

sandaraceus.full: sandărăcĕus, a, um, adj. id., of sandarach: color, Labeo ap. Fulg. 559, 19.

sandaracinus.full: sandărăcīnus (sandĕr-), a, um, adj., = σανδαράκινος, of the color of sandarach: os (merulae), Naev. ap. Fest. p. 324 Müll. (Com. Rel. p. 24 Rib.).
sandaracinus.short: sandărăcīnus (sandĕr-), a, um, adj., = σανδαράκινος, of the color of sandarach: os (merulae), Naev.

sandaresus.full: sandarēsus, i, f., a precious stone found in India and Arabia, a kind of onyx, Plin. 37, 7, 28, § 102 (also, sandrastos, sandaresius, sandarestos).
sandaresus.short: sandarēsus, i, f., a precious stone found in India and Arabia, a kind of onyx, Plin.

sandix.full: sandix (sandyx), ï¯cis (long, Prop. 2, 25 (3, 20), 45; short, Grat. Cyn. 86), f., = σάνδυξ (σάνδιξ), vermilion or a color like vermilion, Plin. 35, 6, 12, § 30; 35, 6, 23, § 40; 35, 6, 26, § 45; Verg. E. 4, 45; Prop. l. l.; Grat. l. l.; Vop. Aur. 29.

sanesco.full: sānesco, ĕre, v. inch. n. [sanus], to become sound, get well, heal (post-Aug.): insanientes sub somno sanescunt, Cels. 3, 18: corpus, id. 2, 8: ulcera, id. 3, 22; Plin. 17, 23, 35, § 214: vulnera, Col. 6, 7, 4: cutis, Cels. 8, 4 et saep.

sanguiculus.full: sanguĭcŭlus, i, m. dim. sanguis, a blood-pudding, black-pudding, Plin. 28, 14, 58, § 209.

sanguinarius.full: sanguĭnārĭus, a, um (also late Lat. sanguĭnāris, e, Vulg. Ecclus. 42, 5), adj. sanguis, of or belonging to blood, blood-, Lit.: herba, an herb that stanches blood, the Gr. πολύγονον, Col. 7, 5, 19; also called sanguinaria alone, Plin. 27, 12, 91, § 113, and sanguinalis herba, Col. 6, 12 fin.; Cels. 2, 33; 3, 22 fin.: latus sanguinare, covered with blood, Vulg. Ecclus. 42, 5.— Trop., blood-thirsty, bloody, sanguinary (rare but class.): juventus, Cic. Att. 2, 7, 3: Claudius (with saevus), Suet. Cl

sanguinatio.full: sanguĭnātĭo, ōnis, f. sanguino, a bleeding (late Lat.), Cael. Aur. Tard. 4, 6, 87.

sanguineus.full: sanguĭnĕus, a, um, adj. sanguis. Lit., of blood, consisting of blood, bloody, blood- (class.; a favorite word of the Aug. poets): imber, * Cic. Div. 2, 28, 60: guttae, Ov. M. 2, 360; 14, 408: dapes, Tib. 1, 5, 49: manus, Ov. M. 1, 143: lingua, id. ib. 3, 57: humus, id. H. 16, 334; cf. mater, id. M. 3, 125: hasta, Stat. Th. 8, 436: pulmo, Sen. Agam. 760; Plin. 11, 37, 72, § 188: caedes, Ov. M. 13, 85: rixae, Hor. C. 1, 27, 4: bellum, Val. Fl. 5, 308; 6, 134: crines, Stat. Th. 10, 173: leo, Val. F

sanguino.full: sanguĭno, āre, v. n. id.. Lit., to be bloody; to bleed, run with blood (postAug. and very rare): femina sanguinans (in menstruation), Tert. adv. Marc. 4, 20: lacertos sanguinantes porrigere, Quint. Decl. 10, 8; 10, 18.— Transf., to be of a blood-color: unda purpureis profundis, Sol. poët. in Anthol. Lat. II. p. 384 Burm. (234 Meyer): colubrum veneno noxio colla sanguinantem, App. M. 5, p. 160, 20 (cf.: sanguineae jubae anguium, Verg. A. 2, 207). —* Trop., to be blood-thirsty, sanguinary: sanguin

sanguinolentia.full: sanguĭnŏlentia, ae, f. sanguinolentus, a congestion, a blood-shot condition: oculorum, Cael. Aur. Acut. 1, 1, 10.

sanguinolentus.full: sanguĭnŏlentus (collat. form san-guĭlentus, Scrib. Comp. 182), a, um, adj. sanguis Lit., full of blood, bloody (class., but, like sanguineus, mostly poet.; not in Cic.): torques, Quadrig. ap. Gell. 9, 13, 18; so, soror, Tib. 2, 6, 40: pectora, Ov. H. 3, 50: ille, id. F. 4, 844: Erinys, id. H. 6, 46: (Curetes) inter se armis Ludunt in numerumque exsultant sanguinolenti, Lucr. 2, 631; v. Lachm. ad h. l.: Allia...vulneribus Latiis, Ov. A. A. 1, 414: seditiones, Varr. ap. Non. 465, 33.— Transf., blo

sanguinosus.full: sanguĭnōsus, a, um, adj. id.; in late medic. lang., sanguineous, plethoric, Cael. Aur. Acut. 3, 4.

sanguis.full: sanguis, ĭnis (acc. SANGVEM, Inscr. Fratr. Arval. tab. 41, 22; Inscr. Orell. 2270 and 5054; cf. ex-sanguis, acc. -em.—Neutr. collat. form sanguen, ante-class., Enn. ap. Non. 224; id.ap.Cic.Rep. 1, 41, 64; id.ap.Cic. Fin. 5, 11, 31; Cic. de Or. 3, 58, 218; id. ap. Prisc. p. 708 P.; Cato ap. Gell. 3, 7, 19; Att. and Varr. ap. Non. l. l.; Lucr. 1, 837; 1, 860; Petr. 59, 1; Arn. 1, 36), m. etym. dub.; prob. root sak-, sag-, to drop, flow; cf. Angl.-Sax. sūc-an; Germ. saugen, blood (class. only in th

sanguisuga.full: sanguĭsūga, ae, f. sanguis-sugo, a blood-sucker, leech (called also hirudo), Cels. 5, 27, 16; Plin. 8, 10, 10, § 29; 32, 10, 42, § 123; Vulg. Prov. 30, 15.

sanies.full: sănĭes, em, e, f. a weakened form of sanguis. Diseased or corrupted blood, bloody matter, sanies (cf.: pus, tabes): ex his (vulneribus ulceribusque) exit sanguis, sanies, pus. Sanguis omnibus notus est: sanies est tenuior hoc, varie crassa et glutinosa et colorata: pus crassissimum albidissimumque, glutinosius et sanguine et sanie, etc., Cels. 5, 26, 20: saxa spargens tabo, sanie et sanguine atro, Enn. ap. Cic. Tusc. 1, 44, 107, and id. ap. Cic. Pis. 19 (Trag. v. 414 Vahl.); Cato, R. R. 157, 3;

sanifer.full: sānĭfer, fĕra, fĕrum, adj. sanus-fero, health-bringing, healing: virtus (dextrae), Paul. Nol. Carm. 20, 218.

saniosus.full: sănĭōsus, a, um, adj [sanies], full of bloody matter, sanious: partus, Plin. (perh. Nigid. ap. Plin.) 7, 15, 13, § 66.
saniosus.short: sănĭōsus, a, um, adj [sanies], full of bloody matter, sanious: partus, Plin.

sanitas.full: sānĭtas, ātis, f. sanus, soundness of body, health (class., = valetudo bona; opp. valetudo mala, imbecillitas; cf. also salus): est enim corporis temperatio, cum ea congruunt inter se, e quibus constamus, sanitas: sic animi dicitur, cum ejus judicia opinionesque concordant, Cic. Tusc. 4, 13, 30; cf. id. ib. 3, 5, 10. Lit.: Apollo, quaeso te, ut des Salutem et sanitatem nostrae familiae, Plaut. Merc. 4, 1, 13 (for which, in the old formula of prayer in Cato, R. R. 141, 3: duis bonam salutem valet

saniter.full: sānĭter, adv., v. sanus, adv. A.

sanna.full: sanna, ae, f. δάννας, a mimicking grimace, esp. in mockery, derision, Pers. 1, 62; 5, 91; Juv. 6, 306.

sannat.full: sannat, χλευάζει, Gloss. Philox. (cf.: sanna, sannio, and †sannator).

sannator.full: sannātor, χλευαστής, Gloss. Philox. (cf.: †sannat, sanna, and sannio).

sanni.full: Sanni, ōrum, m., a people in Pontus, Plin. 6, 4, 4, § 12; 21, 15, 45, § 77.
sanni.short: Sanni, ōrum, m., a people in Pontus, Plin.

sannigae.full: Sannigae, ārum, m., a people in Pontus, Plin. 6, 4, 4, § 14.
sannigae.short: Sannigae, ārum, m., a people in Pontus, Plin.

sannio.full: sannĭo, ōnis, m. sanna, one who makes mimicking grimaces, a buffoon (cf. scurra), Cic. de Or. 2, 61, 251; id. Fam. 9, 16, 10; Amm. 14, 6, 16.

sano.full: sāno, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. sanus, to make sound, to heal, cure, restore to health (freq. and class.; syn.: curo, medeor, medico). Lit.: quam (vomicam) sanare medici non potuerant, Cic. N. D. 3, 28, 70: Ptolemaeum, id. Div. 2, 66, 135; so, aliquem, id. Phil. 2, 39, 101 Orell. N. cr.: oculorum tumor sanatur, id. Tusc. 4, 37, 81: tumores, Plin. 20, 6, 23, § 55: volnera, Cic. Rep. 1, 3, 5; Cic. Verr. 2, 5, 46, § 121; id. Fin. 4, 24, 66; id. Att. 5, 17, 6; Ov. M. 14, 23 (with mederi); Quint. 5, 13, 3:

sanqualis.full: Sanquālis (Sanguālis), e, adj. Sancus; cf. arquatus, from arcus, of or belonging to Sancus: avis, a bird sacred to Sancus, the ospray (ossifragus), Plin. 10, 7, 8, § 20; Liv. 41, 13; cf. Fest. p. 317 Müll.: sanqualis porta appellatur proxima aedi Sanci, Fest. p. 343, 34, and Paul. ex Fest. p. 345, 2 Müll.

santerna.full: santerna ae, f., borax or mountaingreen, prepared for soldering gold, Plin. 33, 5, 29, § 93; 34, 12, 28, § 116.
santerna.short: santerna ae, f., borax or mountaingreen, prepared for soldering gold, Plin.

santoni.full: Santŏni, ōrum (collat. form Santŏ-nes, Plin. 4, 19, 33, § 108 (Jahn, Santoni); cf. in sing., Santo, acc. to Prob. II., p. 1450 P.), m., a people of Aquitania, about the mouth of the Garumna, opposite to Burdigala, now Saintes, in the Départ. Charente Inférieure: Santones, Caes. B. G. 1, 11 fin.: Santonis, id. ib. 3, 11 fin.; 7, 75, 3; Mel. 3, 2, 7; Tac. A. 6, 7; Aus. Ep. 11 fin.—Gen. Santonum, Caes. B. G. 1, 10; Plin. 9, 5, 4, § 10: Santonorum, Aus. Ep. 15, 11.—In sing.: Santŏnus, Luc. 1, 422 Co

santra.full: Santra, ae, m., a famous grammarian, Quint. 12, 10, 16; Suet. Vit. Ter. 4; Paul. ex Fest. p 68 Müll.
santra.short: Santra, ae, m., a famous grammarian, Quint.

sanus.full: sānus, a, um (sanun', for sanusne, Plaut. Bacch. 3, 6, 37; id. Men. 5, 2, 66; id. Mere. 2, 2, 21; 2, 4, 21; id. Rud. 3, 2, 19; id. Truc. 2, 4, 13; cf. sanan', id. Am. 3, 2, 48; id. Cure. 5, 2, 54; id. Cist. 4, 1, 14; id. Ep. 5, 1, 42; id. Men. 2, 3, 43; and sanin', id. Ps. 4, 7, 83), adj. kindr. with ΣΑ, σῶς, sound, whole, healthy, physically or mentally (cf.: integer, incolumis, sospes, salvus). Lit., sound in body, whole, healthy, well: pars corporis, Cic. Sest. 65, 135: sensus si sani sunt et
sanus.short: sānus, a, um (sanun', for sanusne, Plaut.

saoces.full: Săōces, is, m., a mountain in Samothrace, Plin. 4, 12, 23, § 73.
saoces.short: Săōces, is, m., a mountain in Samothrace, Plin.

sapa.full: săpa, ae, f. cf. Germ. Saft; Engl sap, must or new wine boiled thick, Varr. ap. Non. 551, 23; 551, 18; Col. 12, 19, 1; Plin. 14, 9, 11, § 80; 14, 19, 24, § 121; Ov. F. 4, 780; Mart. 7, 53, 6; Fest. s. v. burranica, p. 30.

sapaei.full: Săpaei, ōrum, m., = σαπαῖοι, a Thracian people on the Propontis, Plin. 4, 11, 18, § 40; Ov. F. 1, 389.
sapaei.short: Săpaei, ōrum, m., = σαπαῖοι, a Thracian people on the Propontis, Plin.

sape.full: Sapē, ēs, f., a city in Ethiopia on the Arabian gulf, Plin. 6, 30, 35, § 191.
sape.short: Sapē, ēs, f., a city in Ethiopia on the Arabian gulf, Plin.

sapenos.full: sapenos, i, m. Indian, a bright hyacinth-colored amethyst found in India, Plin. 37, 9, 40, § 122; v. sacondios.

saperda.full: sāperda, ae, m., = σαπέρδης, an inferior kind of salt fish from the Black Sea, a herring or sardine, Pers. 5, 134; cf.: saperda genus pessimi piscis, Fest. pp. 324 and 325 Müll.—Hence, transf.: omnes videmur nobis esse belli, festivi, saperdae cum simus σαπροί, rotten sardines, Varr. ap. Non. 176, 20 sq. (Sat. Men. 56, 2); cf.: saperdae quasi sapientes, Non. 1. 1., and Fest. p. 325 Müll.
saperda.short: sāperda, ae, m., = σαπέρδης, an inferior kind of salt fish from the Black Sea, a herring or sardine, Pers.

saphon.full: saphōn, ōnis, m., a ship's cable, Isid. 19, 4, 5.
saphon.short: saphōn, ōnis, m., a ship's cable, Isid.

sapidus.full: săpĭdus, a, um, adj. sapio (post-class.). Lit., well-tasted, relishing, savory: tucetum perquam sapidissimum, App. M. 2, p. 117, 32; 10, p. 344, 32: avis sapidior, Apic. 6, 6.—* Trop., wise, prudent: puellae, Alcim. 6 prooem.—* Adv.: să-pĭdē, savorily: femur sapidissime percoctum, App. M. 8 fin.

sapiens.full: săpĭens, entis, Part. and P. a., from sapio.

sapienter.full: săpĭenter, adv., v. sapio, P. a. fin.

sapientia.full: săpĭentĭa, ae, f. sapiens. (Acc. to sapiens, A.) Prop., good taste, i. e. good sense, discernment, discretion, prudence, intelligence (class.; syn. prudentia): pellitur e medio sapientia, vi geritur res, Enn. ap. Gell. 20, 10, 4 (Ann. v. 272 Vahl.): non aetate verum ingenio adipiscitur sapientia, Plaut. Trin. 2, 2, 88; id. Mil. 4, 6, 36: fac participes nos tuae sapientiae, id. Ep. 2, 2, 73; cf.: neque habet (erus meus) plus sapientiae quam lapis, id. Mil. 2, 2, 81; id. Capt. 2, 3, 53; cf. id. ib

sapientialis.full: săpĭentĭālis, e, adj. sapientia, of or belonging to wisdom: summus in animā gradus vitalis et sapientialis, etc., Tert. Anim. 15.

sapientipotens.full: săpĭentĭ-pŏtens, entis, adj. sapiens, mighty in wisdom: bellipotentes sunt magis quam sapientipotentes, Enn. ap. Cic. Div. 2, 56, 116 (Ann. v. 188 Vahl.).

sapineus1.full: sapīnĕus (sapp-), a, um, adj. sapinus, of or belonging to the sapinus: nuces, Col. 12, 5, 2.

sapinus.full: sapīnus (sapp-), i, f. Lit., a kind of fir- or pine-tree, Cato ap. Plin. 16, 39, 75, § 193; Varr. R. R. 1, 6, 4; Plin. 16, 12, 23, § 61; cf. id. 15, 10, 9, § 36 (al. sappium).— Transf., the lower, smooth part of the fir-tree, Vitr. 1, 2, 8; 1, 2, 9; Plin. 16, 39, 76, § 196.

sapio.full: săpĭo, īvi or ĭi (sapui, Aug. Civ. Dei, 1, 10; id. Ep. 102, 10; but sapivi, Nov. ap. Prisc. p. 879 P.; id. ap. Non. 508, 21: saPisti, Mart. 9, 6, 7: sapisset, Plaut. Rud. 4, 1, 8), 3, v. n. and a. [kindr. with ὀπός, σαφής, and σοφός], to taste, savor; to taste, smack, or savor of, to have a taste or flavor of a thing (cf. gusto). Lit. (so only in a few examples). Of things eaten or drunk: oleum male sapiet, Cato, R. R. 66, 1: occisam saepe sapere plus multo suem, Plaut. Mil. 2, 6, 104: quin case

sapis.full: Sāpis, is, m., a river in Cisalpine Gaul and Umbria, between Ravenna and Ariminum, now the Savio, Plin. 3, 15, 20, § 115; Sil. 8, 450; Luc. 2, 406 (al. Isapis).—Hence, Sāpĭnĭus, a, um, adj., of the Sapis, Sapinian: tribus, Liv. 31, 2, 6; 33, 37, 1.
sapis.short: Sāpis, is, m., a river in Cisalpine Gaul and Umbria, between Ravenna and Ariminum, now the Savio, Plin.

sapo.full: sāpo, ōnis, m. Germ., soap, Plin. 28, 12, 51, § 191; Mart. 14, 26 in lemm.; Ser. Samm. 11, 157.

saponatum.full: sāpōnātum, i, n. sapo, soap-water, suds, Theod. Prisc. 1, 16.

sapor.full: săpor, ōris, m. sapio, I.. Lit., a taste, relish, flavor, savor (objectively of the taste inherent in a thing; whereas gustatus is used subjectively, of the taste experienced by him who eats or drinks; class.), Lucr. 2, 679; cf.: si quem forte inveneritis, qui aspernetur oculis pulchritudinem rerum, non odore ullo, non tactu, non sapore capiatur, excludat auribus omnem suavitatem, Cic. Cael. 17, 42: ut mel, suo proprio genere saporis, dulce esse sentitur, id. Fin. 3, 10, 34: in os salsi venit um

saporatus.full: săpōrātus, a, um, adj. sapor, seasoned, savory (post-Aug.): offa medicatis frugibus, Petr. poët. Fragm. 19 (dub.): pulmenta, Tert. Spect. 27: cibi, Amm. 31, 2, 3. —Comp.: sanguis, Arn. 5, 164 (dub.).

saporosus.full: săpōrōsus, a, um, adj. id., of good flavor (late Lat.), Ps.-Aug. ad Fratr. Erem. Serm. 69.

saporus.full: săpōrus, a, um, adj., that relishes well, savory (post - class.): merces, Lact. 3, 16, 15; Prud. Cath. 4, 94; id. Ham. 751.
saporus.short: săpōrus, a, um, adj., that relishes well, savory (post - class.): merces, Lact.

sapphar.full: Sapphar (perh. n. indecl.), a city in Arabia Felix, Plin. 6, 23, 26 § 104.

sapphiratus.full: sapphīrātus, a, um, adj. sapphirus, adorned or set with sapphires: lapillos, Sid. poët. Ep. 2, 10 in carm. v. 14.

sapphirinus.full: sapphīrĭnus, a, um, adj., = σαπφείρινος, of sapphire, sapphirine: lapis, i. e. a sapphire, Plin. 37, 9, 38, § 119 (Jahn, sappir); Vulg. Exod. 24, 10.
sapphirinus.short: sapphīrĭnus, a, um, adj., = σαπφείρινος, of sapphire, sapphirine: lapis, i.

sapphirus.full: sapphīrus, sapphir, sappir, i (i short, Ven. Carm. 6, 2), f., = σάπφειρος, a sapphire, Plin. 37, 9, 39, § 120; Vulg. Apoc. 21, 19; id. Isa. 54, 11.—Form sappir, Plin. 37, 9, 38, § 119.—Form sapphir, Tert. adv. Marc. 2, 10; Vulg. Exod. 28, 18; Hier. in Isa. 15, 54, v. 11 (as m., Isid. 16, 9, 2).
sapphirus.short: sapphīrus, sapphir, sappir, i (i short, Ven.

sappho.full: Sapphō, ūs, f., = Σαπφώ, a celebrated poetess, born at Mytilene, in the island of Lesbos, who, on account of her hopeless love for Phaon, threw herself from the Leucadian rock into the sea. Under her name Ovid composed the fifteenth epistle of his Heroides, Sappho Phaoni; nom. Sapphō, Hor. Ep. 1, 19, 28; Stat. S. 5, 3, 155; Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 57, § 125; gen. Sapphūs, Ov. H. 15, 3; acc. Sapphō, Hor. C. 2, 13, 25; abl. Sappho, Plin. 22, 8, 9, § 20.—Hence, Sap-phĭcus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to
sappho.short: Sapphō, ūs, f., = Σαπφώ, a celebrated poetess, born at Mytilene, in the island of Lesbos, who, on account of her hopeless love for Phaon, threw herself from the Leucadian rock into the sea.

sapriportus.full: Sapriportus, ūs, m., a harbor between Sybaris and Tarentum, Liv. 26, 39.
sapriportus.short: Sapriportus, ūs, m., a harbor between Sybaris and Tarentum, Liv.

saprophago.full: saprŏphăgo, ĕre, v. n., = σαπροφαγεῖν, to eat putrid meat, Mart. 3, 77, 3 (sometimes written as Greek).

sapros.full: sapros, on, adj., = σαπρός, rotten, putrid: caseus, Plin. 28, 9, 34, § 132.
sapros.short: sapros, on, adj., = σαπρός, rotten, putrid: caseus, Plin.

sapsa.full: sapsa, pron. [contr. from sa-, i. e. suaipsa; cf.: sam, sas; v. suus init.], his (her, its) own (ante-class. only in the two foll. passages): quo res sapsa loco sese ostentatque jubetque, Enn. ap. Fest. s. v. sas, p. 325 Müll.; so, sapsa res, Pac. ap. ib. p. 325 ib. (Trag. Rel. p. 99 Rib.).

sarabara.full: sărăbāra, ōrum (collat. form sără-balla, Hier. Ep. 1, 9), n., or ae, f. Persian; cf. Gesen. under ], wide trowsers, such as are worn in the East, Tert. Pall. 4; id. Res. Carn. 58; Hier. ad Dan. 3, 21; cf. Isid. Orig. 19, 23, 2.—Form sarabala, Vulg. Dan. 3, 94.

saraceni.full: Saracēni, ōrum, m., the Saracens, a people of Arabia Felix, Amm. 14, 4, 1; Hier. in Isa. 42, 4; 60, 7.
saraceni.short: Saracēni, ōrum, m., the Saracens, a people of Arabia Felix, Amm.

sarcasmos.full: sarcasmos, i, m., = σαρκασμός, a keen or bitter jest, a taunt, gibe, sarcasm, a figure of speech, Charis. p. 247 P. (in Quint. 8, 6, 57, and Diom. p. 458 P., written as Greek).
sarcasmos.short: sarcasmos, i, m., = σαρκασμός, a keen or bitter jest, a taunt, gibe, sarcasm, a figure of speech, Charis.

sarcimen.full: sarcīmen, ĭnis, n. sarcio, a seam, suture, App. M. 4, p. 149, 24.

sarcina.full: sarcĭna, ae, f. id.. Lit., a package, bundle, burden, load, pack; more freq. in the plur., luggage (class. only in the plur.; not in Cic.); sing.: quid ego nunc agam? nisi uti sarcinam constringam et clipeum ad dorsum accommodem, Plaut. Trin. 3, 2, 93; 2, 4, 195: sarcinam inponam seni, id. Most. 2, 1, 83: essem militiae sarcina fida tuae, Prop. 4 (5), 3, 46. gravis, Hor. Ep. 1, 13, 6; Petr. 117, 11.—In plur.: sarcinas colligere, Sall. J. 97, 4; Varr. R. R. 1, 1, 1; Caes. B. G. 3, 24; 7, 18; id.

sarcinalis.full: sarcĭnālis, e, adj. sarcina (postclass. for sarcinarius), of or belonging to burdens or baggage, pack-, baggage-: jumenta, Amm. 15, 5, 3; 29, 5, 55.

sarcinarius.full: sarcĭnārĭus, a, um, adj. id., of or belonging to burdens or baggage, pack-, baggage-: jumenta, Caes. B. C. 1, 81 fin.

sarcinator.full: sarcĭnātor, ōris, m. sarcio, a patcher, botcher, mender of old garments (anteand post-class.), Lucil. ap. Non. 175, 33; Plaut. Aul. 3, 5, 41; Dig. 4, 4, 5; 47, 2, 82; 14, 4, 1; cf. Serv. ad Verg. A. 12, 13.

sarcinatrix.full: sarcĭnātrix, īcis, f. sarcinator, she that mends or patches (ante- and postclass.), Varr. ap. Non. 56, 25; Dig. 15, 1, 27; Inscr. Orell. 645.

sarcinatus.full: sarcĭnātus, a, um, adj. sarcina, laden, burdened (ante- and post-class.): homines, Plaut. Poen. 5, 2, 19; id. Nol. Carm. 21, 911.

sarcinosus.full: sarcĭnōsus, a, um, adj. id., heavily burdened, heavy laden: lupi vastis corporibus, App. M. 8, p. 208, 8.

sarcinula.full: sarcĭnŭla, ae, f. dim. id., a little pack, bundle, or fardel (mostly post-Aug. and in plur.); sing., Gell. 19, 1, 14.—Plur.: sarcinulas expedire, Cat. 28, 2; Petr. 10, 4: colligere, id. 81, 1: alligare, Plin. Ep. 4, 1, 2; Juv. 6, 146; Vulg. Judic. 19, 17 al.—Poet.: puellae, i. e. the wealth she brings her husband, her marriage-portion, dowry, Juv. 3, 160.

sarcio.full: sarcĭo, sarsi, sartum, 4, v. a. etym. dub.; cf. Gr. ῥάπτω, to patch, botch, mend, repair, restore, etc.: sarcire est integrum facere, Paul. ex Fest. s. v. sarte, p. 323 Müll. (class.; cf.: renovo, instauro, redintegro). Lit.: funes veteres, centones, cuculiones, Cato, R. R. 2, 3; cf.: in vestimento sartum quod comprehensum, Varr. L. L. 6, § 64 Müll.: corbulas, Cato, R. R. 23, 1; 31, 1: dolia, id. ib. 39, 1 sq.; Plin. 18, 26, 64, § 236: aedes, Plaut. Most. 1, 2, 68; 1, 2, 34: seminaria, Plin. 18,

sarcion.full: sarcĭon, ii, n., = σαρκίον, a fault or defect in emeralds, Plin. 37, 5, 18, § 73.
sarcion.short: sarcĭon, ii, n., = σαρκίον, a fault or defect in emeralds, Plin.

sarcites.full: sarcītes, is, f., = σαρκίτης, a precious stone, otherwise unknown, Plin. 37, 10, 67, § 181.
sarcites.short: sarcītes, is, f., = σαρκίτης, a precious stone, otherwise unknown, Plin.

sarcocolla.full: sarcŏcolla, ae, f., = σαρκοκόλλα, a Persian gum, Plin. 13, 11, 20, § 67; 24, 14, 78, § 128.
sarcocolla.short: sarcŏcolla, ae, f., = σαρκοκόλλα, a Persian gum, Plin.

sarcophagus.full: sarcŏphăgus, a, um, adj., = σαρκοφἅγος (flesh-devouring, carnivorous): sarcophagus lapis, a kind of limestone used for coffins (so called because the corpses were quickly consumed by it), Plin. 2, 96, 98, § 211; 36, 17, 27, § 161.—In medicine, Plin. 28, 9, 37, § 140.— Transf., subst.: sarcŏphăgus, i, m. († sarcŏphă-gum, i, n., Inscr. Don. 7, 8), a grave, sepulchre (post-Aug.), Juv. 10, 172; Dig. 11, 7, 37; 34, 1, 18 fin.; Prud. Cath. 3, 203; Inscr. Orell. 194; 4432; 4554 al.
sarcophagus.short: sarcŏphăgus, a, um, adj., = σαρκοφἅγος (flesh-devouring, carnivorous): sarcophagus lapis, a kind of limestone used for coffins (so called because the corpses were quickly consumed by it), Plin.

sarcosis.full: sarcōsis, is, f., = σάρκωσις, a swelling in the flesh of animals, Veg. 5, 25, 1.
sarcosis.short: sarcōsis, is, f., = σάρκωσις, a swelling in the flesh of animals, Veg.

sarculatio.full: sarcŭlātĭo, ōnis, f. sarculo, a hoeing, Plin. 18, 21, 50, § 184; Pall. Febr. 24, 6.

sarculo.full: sarcŭlo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. sarculum, to hoe: frumenta, segetes, etc., Pall. Jan. 9, 1; id. Oct. 11, 2: nata in hortis sarculatis, Prud. στεφ. 10, 264.

sarculum.full: sarcŭlum, i, n. (masc. collat. form, acc. plur., sarculos, Pall. 1, 43, 3) [sario = sarrio], an implement for loosening the soil, weeding, etc., a light hoe (cf.: ligo, pastinum), Cato, R. R. 10, 3; 155, 1; Varr. L. L. 5, § 134 Muüll.; Col. 2, 11, 10; Plin. 18, 7, 18, § 79 (Jahn, sacculo); 19, 6, 33, § 109; Ov. M. 11, 36; id. F. 1, 699; Hor. C. 1, 1, 11; Vulg. Isa. 7, 25.

sarda1.full: sarda, ae, f. A kind of fish that was pickled or salted, perh. sardine, Plin. 32, 11, 53, § 151; 32, 5, 17, § 46.—Also called sardina, Col. 8, 17, 12.— A kind of precious stone, perh. carnelian, Plin. 37, 7, 31, § 105.

sarda2.full: Sarda, ae, f., a Sardinian woman, Cic. Scaur. 4, 5.—In a lusus verbb. with 1. sarda: quamvis salsa ista Sarda fuerit, Cic. Scaur. 4, 6.
sarda2.short: Sarda, ae, f., a Sardinian woman, Cic.

sardachates.full: sardăchātes, ae, m., = σαρδαχάτης, sardachate, carnelian-agate, Plin. 37, 10, 54, § 139 (Jahn, zmaragdachates).
sardachates.short: sardăchātes, ae, m., = σαρδαχάτης, sardachate, carnelian-agate, Plin.

sardanapalus.full: Sardănăpālus (-pallus), i, m., = Σαρδανάπαλος, a celebrated effeminate king of Assyria, who at last burned himself, together with his treasures, Vell. 1, 6, 2; Just. 1, 3, 1; Cic. Tusc. 5, 35, 101; Juv. 10, 362; Ov. Ib. 313; Val. Max. 4, 7 pr.—Poet., as a designation for a weak, effeminate person, Mart. 11, 11, 6.—Hence, Sardănăpā-lĭcus, a, um, adj., of or pertaining to Sardanapalus: Sardanapalicum in morem prandere, Sid. Ep. 2, 13 med.
sardanapalus.short: Sardănăpālus (-pallus), i, m., = Σαρδανάπαλος, a celebrated effeminate king of Assyria, who at last burned himself, together with his treasures, Vell.

sardi.full: Sardi, ōrum, m. from Σαρδώ, Sardinia, the inhabitants of the island of Sardinia, the Sardinians, Cic. Div. in Caecil. 19, 63; id. Off. 2, 14, 50; id. Balb. 18, 41; noted for their faithlessness, id. Scaur. 19, 42 sq.; hence, prov.: Sardi venales, alius alio nequior, id. Fam. 7, 24, 2; Fest. p. 322 Müll.; Varr. Sat. Men. 78; Aur. Vict. Vir. Ill. 57, 2. —Hence, Sardus, a, um, adj., Sardinian: Tigellius, of Sardinia, Hor. S. 1, 3, 3: mel, id. A. P. 375 (Sardum mel pessimi saporis, Schol.): triticum

sardinianus.full: Sardĭnĭānus, a, um, v. Sardi, D.

sardinus.full: sardīnus, a, um, v. sardius fin.

sardis.full: Sardīs (Sardes), ĭum (cf.: hae Sardis, has Sardis, Prisc. p. 775 P.; Freund, Annott. ad Cic. Mil. p. 14), f., = Σάρδεις, Sardis (now Sart), the very ancient capital of Lydia, on the Pactolus, the residence of Crœsus; nom. Sardis, Plin. 6, 34, 39, § 215; Hor. Ep. 1, 11, 2.—Gen. Sardium, Curt. 5, 1, 45.—Acc. Sardis, Just. 14, 1, 7; Cic. Sen. 17, 59; Nep. Milt. 4, 1; id. Ages. 3, 5; Sen. Ben. 6, 31, 9; Curt. 3, 12, 6.—Dat. and abl. Sardibus, Liv. 33, 19, 10; 37, 18, 6; Ov. M. 11, 137; Plin. 5, 29,
sardis.short: Sardīs (Sardes), ĭum (cf.: hae Sardis, has Sardis, Prisc.

sardius.full: sardĭus, a, um, adj. cf. 1. sarda, II., sardian, carnelian (late Lat.): lapis, Vulg. Exod. 28, 17.—Hence, subst.: sardĭus, ii, m., the carnelian, a precious stone, Vulg. Exod. 39, 10; id. Apoc. 21, 20; Tert. adv. Marc. 2, 10; called lapis sardinus, Vulg. Apoc. 4, 3; cf. Hier. in Isa. 15, 54, v. 11 sq.

sardo.full: sardo, āre, v. a., to understand: sardare intellegere. Naevius. Quod bruti nec satis sardare queunt, Fest. p. 322 Müll.

sardonia.full: Sardŏnĭa herba, v. Sardi, B. fin.

sardonychatus.full: sardŏnўchātus, a, um, adj. sardonyx, adorned with a sardonyx: manus, Mart. 2, 29, 2.

sardonyx.full: sardŏnyx, ўchis, m. and f., = σαρδόνυξ, a precious stone, sardonyx; fem., Plin. 37, 6, 23, § 85; Pers. 1, 16; Juv. 7, 144. —Masc., Juv. 6, 382; Mart. 4, 28, 4; 4, 61, 6. —Gen. plur. sardonychum, Juv. 13, 139.— Hence, adj.: sardŏnĭchus, a, um, of sardonyx: lapis, Vulg. Job, 28, 16.

sardous.full: Sardōus, a, um, v. Sardi, B.

sardus.full: Sardus, a, um, v. Sardi, A.

sare.full: Sarē, ēs, f., a village in Thrace, Liv. 38, 41, 8.
sare.short: Sarē, ēs, f., a village in Thrace, Liv.

sargus.full: sargus, i, m., = σάργος, a kind of sea-fish esteemed by the Romans, Plin. 9, 17, 30, § 65; 9, 51, 74, § 162; Lucil. ap. Fest. p. 322 Müll.; Enn. ap. App. Mag. p. 299; Ov. Hal. 105.
sargus.short: sargus, i, m., = σάργος, a kind of sea-fish esteemed by the Romans, Plin.

sari.full: sari, n., = σάρι, or saripha, ae, f., a shrub growing on the banks of the Nile, Plin. 13, 23, 45, § 128.
sari.short: sari, n., = σάρι, or saripha, ae, f., a shrub growing on the banks of the Nile, Plin.

sarisa.full: sarīsa (-issa), ae, f., = σάρισα. A long Macedonian lance, Liv. 9, 19; 37, 42; 38, 7 fin.; Curt. 7, 4, 36; 9, 7, 19; Ov. M. 12, 466; 12, 479 al.; cf. Fest. pp. 145 and 251.— Poet., in gen., for Macedonians, Luc. 8, 298; 10, 47; cf.: denominatio est ...si quis Macedonas appellarit hoc modo: Non tam cito sarissae Graecia potiti sunt, Auct. Her. 4, 32, 43.

sarisophoros.full: sarīsŏphŏros (sarissŏ-), i, m., = σαρισοφόρος, a Macedonian lancer, Liv. 36, 18; Curt. 4, 15, 13.
sarisophoros.short: sarīsŏphŏros (sarissŏ-), i, m., = σαρισοφόρος, a Macedonian lancer, Liv.

sarmata.full: Sarmăta, ae, m., = Σαρμάτης, a Sarmatian, Luc. 1, 430; Mart. Spect. 3, 4; Juv. 3, 79; Claud. Laud. Stil. 1, 111.—Plur.: Sarmătae (Gr. collat. form Saurŏ-mătae, Ov. Tr. 2, 198; 3, 3, 6; 3, 10, 5; 4, 1, 94; 5, 1, 74; Val. Fl. 7, 235; Mel. 1, 2, 6; 2, 1, 2; Plin. 6, 13, 15, § 38; cf. id. 4, 12, 25, § 80; v. also in the foll.), ārum, m., = Σαυρομάται, the Sarmatians, a great Slavic people, dwelling from the Vistula to the Don, in the mod. Poland and Russia, Mel. 1, 3, 5; 3, 6, 8; Plin. 4, 12, 25, §
sarmata.short: Sarmăta, ae, m., = Σαρμάτης, a Sarmatian, Luc.

sarmatia.full: Sarmătĭa, Sarmătĭcē, Sarmă-tĭcus, and Sarmătis, v. Sarmata.
sarmatia.short: Sarmătĭa, Sarmătĭcē, Sarmă-tĭcus, and Sarmătis, v.

sarmen.full: sarmen, ĭnis, n. sarpo (for the usu. sarmentum), twigs, brushwood, Plaut. Most. 5, 1, 65.

sarmenticius.full: sarmentīcĭus or -tĭus, a, um, adj. sarmentum, of or belonging to twigs, cuttings, or brushwood: cinis, Col. 6, 26, 3.— In plur. subst.: sarmentīcĭi, ōrum, m., the Christians, who were burned with fagots, Tert. Apol. 50.

sarmentosus.full: sarmentōsus, a, um, adj. id., full of twigs or little branches: psyllion, Plin. 25, 11, 90, § 140.

sarmentum.full: sarmentum, i, n. sarpo, twigs, light branches, brushwood; a fagot, fascine (class.; usu. in plur.; only so in Cic. and Cæs.; cf.: lignum, materia); sing., Varr. R. R. 1, 31, 2; Col. 3, 10, 1; Sil. 7, 314.— Plur., Col. 4, 24, 7; 5, 5, 16; Cic. Sen. 15, 52 and 53; id. de Or. 2, 21, 88; Cic. Verr. 2, 1, 27, § 69; * Caes. B. G. 3, 18 fin.; Liv. 22, 16 fin.; Quint. 2, 17, 19; Plin. 12, 25, 54, § 118; 22, 25, 72, § 150 al.

sarnus.full: Sarnus, i, m., a river in Campania, near Pompeii, now the Sarno, Plin. 3, 5, 9, § 62; Verg. A. 7, 738; Sil. 8, 539; Stat. S. 1, 2, 265.
sarnus.short: Sarnus, i, m., a river in Campania, near Pompeii, now the Sarno, Plin.

saronicus.full: Sărōnĭcus sĭnus, the Saronic Gulf; a gulf of the Ægean Sea, between Attica and Peloponnesus, now Gulf of Egina, Plin. 4, 4, 5, § 10; 4, 5, 9, § 18.

sarpedon.full: Sarpēdōn, ŏnis, m., = Σαρπηδών, a son of Jupiter and Europa, king of Lycia, who was killed by Patroclus before Troy, Hyg. Fab. 106; 112; Verg. A. 1, 100; Serv. 9, 697; 10, 471; Ov. M. 13, 255; Cic. Div. 2, 10, 25; Gr. acc. Sarpedona, Gell. 15, 21, 1.— A promontory in Cilicia, now Lissan el Kahpe, Liv. 38, 38, 9; Mel. 1, 13, 5; Plin. 5, 27, 22, § 92.
sarpedon.short: Sarpēdōn, ŏnis, m., = Σαρπηδών, a son of Jupiter and Europa, king of Lycia, who was killed by Patroclus before Troy, Hyg.

sarpo.full: sarpo, no perf., sarptum, 3, v. a. root sarp-; Gr. ἁρπάζω; in agricult. lang., to cut off, trim, prune, clean: sarpta vinea putata, id est pura facta: unde et virgulae abscisae sarmenta. Sarpere enim antiqui pro purgare ponebant, Fest. p. 322 Müll.

sarptus.full: sarptus, a, um, Part., v. sarpo.

sarra.full: Sarra (Sara, Plaut. Truc. 2, 6, 58), ae, f., Heb. Zor. The city of Tyre, in Phœnicia, celebrated for its purple dye: Poenos Sarrā oriundos, Enn. ap. Prob. Verg. G. 2, 506; cf. Serv. ad loc., and Gell. 14, 6, 4: purpuram ex Sarā tibi Attuli, Plaut. l. l.— Hence, Sarrānus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Sarra, i. e., Tyrian: gens, Sil. 1, 72: Leptis, built by the Tyrians, id. 3, 256: ostrum, Verg. G. 2, 506; Col. poët. 10, 287; cf. murex, Sil. 15, 205: aulaea, Juv. 10, 38: violae, purple-red, Col

sarracius.full: sarrācĭus, a, um, adj. serra, sawshaped, serrate (late Lat.): lactuca, Dynam. 2, 52.

sarracum.full: sarrācum (serrā-), i, n. A kind of wagon or cart (acc. to Quint. 8, 3, 21, belonging to vulgar lang.), Sisenn. ap. Non. 195, 29; Cic. Pis. Fragm. ap. Quint. l. l.; Vitr. 10, 1 fin.; Juv. 3, 255; Capitol. M. Aurel. 13; Amm. 31, 2, 18.— Transf., the Wain, a constellation: frigida Bootae, Juv. 5, 23.

sarrastes.full: Sarrastes, um, m., a people of Campania, near the Sarnus, Verg. A. 7, 738; Sil. 8, 538.
sarrastes.short: Sarrastes, um, m., a people of Campania, near the Sarnus, Verg.

sarrio.full: sarrio (sario), ŭi and īvi (the former in Cato, R. R. 161, 2; the latter in Col. 11, 2, 10), ītum, 4, v. a.; in agricult. lang., to hoe the soil, plants, etc., for the purpose of destroying weeds; to weed, Cato, R. R. 161, 1 and 2; Varr. R. R. 1, 18, 8; 1, 29, 1; Col. 2, 11, 4; 11, 2, 9 sq.; Plaut. Capt. 3, 5, 5; Plin. 18, 21, 50, § 184; 18, 17, 45, § 158; Mart. 3, 93, 20; Vulg. Isa. 7, 25.
sarrio.short: sarrio (sario), ŭi and īvi (the former in Cato, R.

sarritio.full: sarrītĭo (sarītĭo, sartĭo), ōnis, f. sarrio, a hoeing, weeding, Col. 2, 12, 1; 11, 2, 9; Serv. Verg. G. 1, 21.

sarritor.full: sarrītor (collat. form sartor), ōris, m. id.. A hoer, weeder, Varr. R. R. 1, 29, 2; Col. 2, 13, 1.—* Trop.: sator sartorque scelerum et messor maxime, i. e. cultivator, Plaut. Capt. 3, 5, 3.

sarritorius.full: sarrītōrĭus (sarīt-), a, um, adj. id., of or belonging to hoeing or weeding: opera, Col. 2, 13, 2.

sarritura.full: sarrītūra (sarīt-), ae, f., a hoeing, a weeding, Col. 11, 2, 27; also sartūra, Plin. 18, 27, 67, § 254; cf.: sarritor and sarritio.
sarritura.short: sarrītūra (sarīt-), ae, f., a hoeing, a weeding, Col.

sarritus.full: sarrītus, a, um, Part., from sarrio.
sarritus.short: sarrītus, a, um, Part., from sarrio.

sarsina.full: Sarsĭna (Sassĭna), ae, f. An ancient town in Umbria, the birthplace of Plautus, still called Sarsina, Mart. 9, 59, 4; Sil. 8, 463.—Hence, Sarsĭnātis, e (collat. form Sassĭnas, Inscr. Orell. 4404; v. infra), adj., of or belonging to Sarsina: Sassinate de silvā, Mart. 3, 58, 35.—In a lusus verbb., Plaut. Most. 3, 2, 83.—In plur. subst.: Sarsĭnātes (Sass-), ĭum, m., the inhabitants of Sarsina, Plin. 3, 14, 19, § 114.

sarsurius.full: sarsūrĭus, a, um, adj. sartor, mending, patching (late Lat.), Caes. Arch. Reg. ad Virg. 42.

sartago.full: sartāgo, ĭnis, f. A frying-pan, baking-pan (post-Aug.), Plin. 16, 11, 22, § 55; Juv. 10, 63; Ambros. Ep. 100, § 9; Vulg. Lev. 7, 9.—* Trop.: sartago loquendi, a hotchpotch, mixture, medley, Pers. 1, 80.

sarte.full: sartē, adv., v. sarcio, P. a. init.

sartor1.full: sartor, ōris, m. sarcio, a patcher, botcher, mender, Non. 7, 28: sartoris arte se pascere, Aug. Civ. Dei, 22, 8, n. 10.

sartrix.full: sartrix, īcis, f. sartor, she who patches or mends, Cael. Aur. Acut. 3, 9, 100.

sartura1.full: sartūra, ae, f. sarcio, a patching, mending, Col. 4, 26, 2: sarturae veteris lintei, Sen. Vit. Beat. 25, 2.

sartus.full: sartus, a, um, Part. and P. a. of sarcio.

saserna.full: Saserna, ae, m., a friend of Antony, Cic. Phil. 13, 13, 28; id. Att. 15, 2, 3.— Sasernae, father and son, Latin writers on agriculture, Varr. R. R. 1, 16, 5; 1, 18, 2; 5, 2, 22; Col. 1, 1, 12.
saserna.short: Saserna, ae, m., a friend of Antony, Cic.

saso.full: Sāso (Sāson), ōnis, f., = Σάσων, Σάσω, a small island near the promontory Acroceraunia, on the coast of Illyria, now Saseno, Plin. 3, 26, 30, § 152; Luc. 2, 627; 5, 650; Sil. 7, 480.
saso.short: Sāso (Sāson), ōnis, f., = Σάσων, Σάσω, a small island near the promontory Acroceraunia, on the coast of Illyria, now Saseno, Plin.

sassius.full: Sassĭus, a, the name of a Roman gens. —Sassĭa, ae, f., the name of the mother of Cluentius, Cic. Clu. 5, 12 sq.; 62, 175 sq.
sassius.short: Sassĭus, a, the name of a Roman gens.

sassula.full: Sassŭla, ae, f., a town of Latium, in the neighborhood of Tibur, Liv. 7, 19.
sassula.short: Sassŭla, ae, f., a town of Latium, in the neighborhood of Tibur, Liv.

sata.full: săta, ōrum, n., v. 1. sero, I. A.

satagito.full: sătăgĭto, āre, v. satis, II. A.

satagius.full: sătăgĭus, a, um, adj. satago, that troubles or vexes himself, over-anxious: ut istos satagios ac sibi molestos describam tibi, Sen. Ep. 98, 8.

satago.full: sătăgo, ĕre, v. satis, II. B.

satanaria herba.full: satanaria herba, a plant, also called peucedanos, sulphurwort, hog's-fennel, App. Herb. 94.
satanaria herba.short: satanaria herba, a plant, also called peucedanos, sulphurwort, hog's-fennel, App.

satanas.full: Sătănas, ae, and Sătan, indecl. m., = Σατανᾶς or Σατᾶν (Heb. ), an adversary, Satan, the Devil, Tert. Apol. 22 init.; id. adv. Marc. 3, 20; Vulg. Matt. 4, 10 et saep.; form Satan, id. 2 Reg. 19, 22 et saep.

satelles.full: sătellĕs, ĭtis, comm., an attendant upon a distinguished person, esp. a prince, a lifeguard; in plur., attendants, escort, train, retinue (class.; syn.: stipator, apparitor, accensus). Lit.: regii satellites, Liv. 2, 12; 34, 36 fin.; cf. Quint. 7, 2, 54: administri et satellites Sex. Naevii, Cic. Quint. 25, 80 (cf. infra, II.): habet sectatores vel potius satellites, qui, etc., Tac. A. 16, 22: contumeliosum foret, si equites Romani satellites Numidae traderentur, Sall. J. 65, 2: Sullae, id. H. 1
satelles.short: sătellĕs, ĭtis, comm., an attendant upon a distinguished person, esp.

satellitium.full: sătellĭtĭum, ii, n. satelles, an escort, convoy, Jul. Val. Rer. Gest. Alex. 1, 17.— Trop., a guard, protection (eccl. Lat.): scripturarum, Aug. Doctr. Chr. 3, 18.

satias.full: sătĭas, ātis (collat. form sătĭes, Juvenc. 1, 637: ad satiem, id. 3, 216; abl. satie, Plin. 8, 51, 77, § 209), f. satis, a sufficiency, abundance, plentifulness. In gen. (mostly ante- and post-class.; not found in Cic. or Cæs.; commonly used only in nom. sing., the other cases being taken from satietas): quorum crudelitatem numquam ulla explet satias sanguinis, Att. ap. Non. 172, 7 (Trag. Rel. p. 133 Rib.); cf. id. ap. Cic. N. D. 3, 38, 90 (v. Charis. p. 70 P., and l. l. p. 188 Rib.): fessus sat

satiate.full: sătĭātē, adv., v. satio fin. adv. b.

saticula.full: Sătīcŭla, ae, f., a town of Samnium, on the frontiers of Campania, now S. Agata dei Goti, Liv. 7, 32; 9, 21; 23, 39; Vell. 1, 14, 4.—Hence, Sătīcŭlānus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Saticula: ager, Liv. 23, 14 fin.—Plur. subst.: Sătīcŭlā-ni, ōrum, m., the inhabitants of Saticula, the Saticulans, Liv. 27, 10.— Sătīcŭ-lus, i, m., a Saticulan: asper (collectively), Verg. A. 7, 729.
saticula.short: Sătīcŭla, ae, f., a town of Samnium, on the frontiers of Campania, now S.

saties.full: sătĭes, ēi, f., v. satias init.

satietas.full: sătĭĕtas, ātis, f. satis, a sufficiency, abundance (syn. saturitas). In gen. (very rare): neque ulla ornandi satis satietas est, Plaut. Poen. 1, 2, 6.—Plur.: quercus terrenis principiorum satietatibus abundans, parumque habens umoris et aëris, Vitr. 2, 9, 8; 2, 9, 9.— In partic., subject., the state of being glutted or sated; a loathing, disgust, satiety (class. and very freq., esp. in the trop. sense and with Cicero; syn. fastidium). Lit.: cibi satietas et fastidium, Cic. Inv. 1, 17, 25: amarum

satin'.full: sătĭn' and sătĭne for satisne; v. satis init.

satio1.full: sătĭo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. satis, to fill, satisfy; to sate, satiate with food (class.; esp. freq. in the trop. sense; syn. saturo). Lit.: satiat semimodius cibi in diebus singulis vicenos et centenos turtures, Col. 8, 9, 3: se (orca), Plin. 9, 6, 5, § 14: desideria naturae, to satisfy, appease, Cic. Fin. 2, 8, 25: sitim, Mart. 6, 35, 5: famem, Ov. M. 11, 371.—In part. perf.: satiati agm ludunt, Lucr. 2, 320: canes sanguine erili, Ov. M. 3, 140: vultur humano cadavere, Plin. 30, 10, 27, § 92.— T
