satio2.full: sătĭo, ōnis, f. 1. sero, a sowing, a planting (syn. sementis), Cic. Verr. 2, 3, 47, § 112; Varr. R. R. 1, 39, 1; Col. 2, 9, 6; 3, 14, 2; 11, 2, 80; Liv. 32, 34; Verg. G. 2, 319 al.—In plur., sowed fields, cultivated lands, Cic. Verr. 2, 3, 15, § 38; Vulg.Ecclus. 40, 22.

satira.full: sătĭra, ae, v. satur fin. B.

satiricus.full: sătĭrĭcus (on account of the confusion of the Roman Satira with the Greek Satyros, often erroneously written Sătўrĭcus; hence in the neutr. even with a Greek ending, Sătўrĭcon; cf. satirographus), a, um, adj. satira, of or belonging to (Roman) satire, satiric, satirical: satirici carminis scriptor, Lact. 2, 4, 3; so, materia, Sid. Ep. 8, 11; Schol. Juv. 1, 168.—Substt. să-tĭrĭcus, i, m., a writer of satires, a satirist, Sid. Ep. 1, 11; 4, 1.— Sătĭrĭcon, i, n., the title of a work of Petronius.
satiricus.short: sătĭrĭcus (on account of the confusion of the Roman Satira with the Greek Satyros, often erroneously written Sătўrĭcus;

satirographus.full: sătĭrŏgrăphus (sătўrŏgr-; v. satiricus init.), i, m., = σατυρογράφος, a writer of satires, a satirist, Sid. Ep. 1, 11.

satis.full: sătis, and abbreviated, săt (cf. the letter S.: satin', contr. for satisne; v.the foll.), adv. root in Gr. ἄδην, ἅδην, orig. a comp. form, weakened from satius; cf.: magis, nimis, etc., enough, sufficiently (objectively, so that one needs nothing more; whereas affatim subjectively, so that one wishes nothing more). Posit. Adject., enough, sufficient, satisfactory. Form sătis: quod (faenum et pabulum) bubus satis siet, qui illic sient, Cato, R. R. 137: cui, si conjuret populus, vix totu' satis si

satisacceptio.full: sătĭsacceptĭo (or separately, sătĭs acceptĭo), ōnis, f. satis-accipio; v. satis, II. C., a taking of security, admitting to bail, Dig. 45, 1, 5.
satisacceptio.short: sătĭsacceptĭo (or separately, sătĭs acceptĭo), ōnis, f.

satisdatio.full: sătisdătĭo (or separately, sătis dă-tĭo), ōnis, f. satis-do; v. satis, II. C.. The satisfaction of a creditor, Dig. 46, 3, 49. — A giving of bail or security, Dig. 2, 8, 1; 4, 6, 28; 46, 5, 1; 50, 16, 61; Cic. Att. 5, 1, 2; Gai. Inst. 1, 200.—Transf.: capitalis, i. e. a pledging of or answering with one's life, Plin. 36, 5, 4, § 29.
satisdatio.short: sătisdătĭo (or separately, sătis dă-tĭo), ōnis, f.

satisdator.full: sătisdător, ōris, m. satis-do; v. satis, II. C., one who gives security; a surety, bail (late Lat.), Sid. Ep. 4, 24 fin.; Ps.-Ascon. Cic. Verr. 2, 1, 45.

satisfactio.full: sătisfactio, ōnis, f. satisfacio; v. satis, II. D.. * A satisfying of a creditor by security; a giving security or bail: satisfactio pro solutione est, Dig. 46, 3, 52.— An excuse, apology, plea, explanation (class.): (Caesar) Ubiorum satisfactionem accepit, Caes. B. G. 6, 9 fin.; cf. id. ib. 1, 41: hic tu me etiam insimulas, nec satisfactionem meam accipis, Cic. Fam. 7, 13, 1: ne aliquid satisfactio levitatis habere videatur, id. Att. 4, 6, 3: satisfactionem ex nullā conscientiā de culpā propone

satisfactionalis.full: sătisfactĭōnālis, e, adj. satisfactio, making amends, apologetic (late Lat.): liber (with apologeticus), Cassiod. Hist. Eccl. 9, 23.

sativus.full: sătīvus, a, um, adj. 1. sero, that is sown or planted (opp. agrestis, silvestris, etc., that grows wild; very rare), Varr. ap. Gell. 17, 3, 4: morus, Plin. 24, 13, 73, § 120: corna, id. 32, 2, 11, § 22.—Neutr. plur.: sativa (opp. silvestria), Plin. 19, 12, 60, § 185.

sator.full: sător, ōris, m. id.. Lit., a sower, planter, Varr. R. R. 1, 45, 3; Lucr. 2, 1168; Cic. N. D. 2, 34; Col. 3, 15, 3; Plin. 15, 1, 1, § 3; Vulg. Jer. 50, 16.— Poet., transf., a begetter, father, creator: caelestum sator, i. e. Jupiter, Cic. poët. Tusc. 2, 9, 21; also termed hominum sator atque deorum, Verg. A. 1, 254; 11, 725: hominum (with deorum genitor), Phaedr. 3, 17, 10: rerum, Sil. 4, 432: aevi, id. 9, 306: verus Alcidae sator, Sen. Herc. Fur. 357: annorum nitidique mundi, i. e. Janus, Mart.

satorius.full: sătōrĭus, a, um, adj. id., of or belonging to sowing or planting: quala, Cato, R. R. 11 fin.: trimodia, Col. 2, 9, 9; 12, 52, 8.

satrapes.full: sătrăpes, sătraps, is, and sătră-pa, ae (plur. satrapae), m., = σατράπης [Persian; cf. Gesenius, under ], a governor of a province, a viceroy among the Persians, a satrap; nom. satrapes, Nep. Paus. 1, 2; id. Alcib. 10, 3; Curt. 8, 4, 21: satrapa, Ter. Heaut. 3, 1, 43; Curt. 3, 13, 1; Amm. 18, 6, 20: satraps, Sid. Carm. 2, 78; Alcim. 6, 392.—Gen. satrapis, Nep. Lys. 4, 1.—Acc. satrapen, Nep. Con. 2, 1: satrapam, Curt. 3, 13, 1.—Plur. nom. satrapae, Nep. Dat. 3, 1; id. Ages. 2, 2; Vulg. Dan. 6, 6:
satrapes.short: sătrăpes, sătraps, is, and sătră-pa, ae (plur.

satricum.full: Satrĭcum, i, n., an ancient town in Latium, on the Appian Way, near Antium, now Casale di Conca, Cic. Q. Fr. 3, 1, 2, § 4; Liv. 2, 39; 6, 8; 6, 22; 9, 16.—Hence, Sa-trĭcāni, ōrum, m., the inhabitants of Satricum, Liv. 9, 12; 28, 11.
satricum.short: Satrĭcum, i, n., an ancient town in Latium, on the Appian Way, near Antium, now Casale di Conca, Cic.

satricus.full: Sătrĭcus, i, m., the name of a warrior, Sil. 9, 68 sq.
satricus.short: Sătrĭcus, i, m., the name of a warrior, Sil.

satullo.full: sătullo, āre, v. a. satullus, to satisfy, satiate: cibis corpora, Varr. ap. Non. 171, 16.

satullus.full: sătullus, a, um, adj. dim. [satur], filled with food, satisfied: agni satulli lacte, Varr. R. R. 2, 2, 15.

satum.full: satum, i, n., = σάτον, a Hebrew measure of corn, etc., containing about a modius and a half (eccl. Lat.), Vulg. Gen. 18, 6; id. Matt. 13, 33; id. Luc. 13, 21.
satum.short: satum, i, n., = σάτον, a Hebrew measure of corn, etc., containing about a modius and a half (eccl.

satur.full: sătur, ŭra, ŭrum, adj. satis, full of food, sated, that has eaten enough (class.). Lit.: ubi satur sum (opp. quando esurio), Plaut. Men. 5, 5, 27; so (opp. esurientes) id. Poen. prol. 6 sq.: sopor quem satur aut lassus capias, Lucr. 4, 957: esurientibus pullis res geri poterit; saturis nihil geretur, Cic. Div. 1, 35, 77: postquam isti a mensā surgunt saturi, poti, Plaut. Ps. 1, 3, 62: cum tu satura atque ebria eris, puer ut satur sit facito, Ter. Hec. 5, 2, 3; so (with ebrius and crudus), Quint.

satura.full: sătŭra, ae, f., v. satur fin. B.

saturae.full: Sătŭrae pălūs, a lake in Latium, otherwise unknown; perh. a part of the Pontine Marshes, Verg. A. 7, 801; Sil. 8, 382.
saturae.short: Sătŭrae pălūs, a lake in Latium, otherwise unknown;

saturamen.full: sătŭrāmen, ĭnis, n. saturo, a filling, satisfying (late Lat.): inopum, Paul. Nol. Carm. 27, 194.

saturanter.full: sătŭranter, adv. id., sufficiently, to satiety, Fulg. Virg. Cont. p. 149 Munk.— Comp.: saturantius, Fulg. Pathol. 3, 6 med.

saturatio.full: sătŭrātĭo, ōnis, f. saturo, a filling, satisfying, Aug. Tract. in Joann. 24.

saturator.full: sătŭrātor, ōris, m. id., a filler, satisfier, Aug. Ep. 120, 25 dub.

saturatus.full: sătŭrātus, a, um, Part. and P. a. of saturo.

satureia.full: sătŭrēia, ae, f. (neutr. collat. form in plur. sătŭrēia (quadrisyl.), ōrum, Ov. A. A. 2, 415; Mart. 3, 75, 4; though this is perh. another plant), the common name for the pot-herb cunila, savory, Col. 9, 4, 2; 9, 4, 6; 9, 10 (poet.), 233; 11, 3, 57; Plin. 19, 8, 50, § 165; Pall. Febr. 24, 2.

satureianus.full: Sătŭrēiānus, a, um, adj., the appellation of a region in Appulia; hence, poet. for Appulian: caballus, Hor. S. 1, 6, 59 (Schol. Porphyr.); Serv. Verg. G. 2, 197; 4, 335.
satureianus.short: Sătŭrēiānus, a, um, adj., the appellation of a region in Appulia;

saturio.full: Sătŭrĭo, ōnis, m. satur. The name of a lost comedy of Plautus, Gell. 3, 3, 14.— The name of a parasite in the Persa of Plautus; hence, in a lusus verbb.: Essurio venio, non advenio saturio, Plaut. Pers. 1, 3, 23.

saturitas.full: sătŭrĭtas, ātis, f. id., fulness, repletion, satiety (mostly ante-class. and postAug. for the class. satietas; perh. only once in Cic.). Lit.: aperitur ostium, unde saturitate saepe ego exii ebrius, Plaut. Capt. 1, 1, 35; 4, 1, 4; 4, 2, 85; Aur. Vict. Epit. 45 fin.: quid causae est quin virgis te usque ad saturitatem sauciem? till you have enough, Plaut. Rud. 3, 4, 53 (for which usu. ad satietatem; v. satietas); Vulg. Exod. 16, 3.— Humorously personified as the goddess of a parasite, Plaut. Capt

saturnalia.full: Sāturnālĭa, ĭum; Sāturnālĭcĭus or -tĭus, a, um; Sāturnālis, e; Sā-turnĭa, ae; v. Saturnus.

saturnigena.full: Sāturnĭgĕna, ae, m. Saturnus-gigno, offspring of Saturn (poet. and late Lat.); of Jupiter, Aus. Idyll. 15, 22; Sid. Carm. 9, 131.

saturninus.full: Sāturnīnus, i, m., a Roman surname. So esp. L. Appuleius Saturninus, a tribune of the people A.U.C. 654; who, with C. Servilius Glaucia, was pronounced guilty of treason and put to death, Cic. Rab. Perd. 6, 18; id. Brut. 62, 224; id. Cat. 1, 2, 4; id. Mil. 5, 14; Suet. Aug. 27; id. Calig. 38; Mart. 4, 11, 2.
saturninus.short: Sāturnīnus, i, m., a Roman surname.

saturnius.full: Sāturnĭus, a, um.— Sātur-nĭus, ii, v. Saturnus, A.
saturnius.short: Sāturnĭus, a, um.— Sātur-nĭus, ii, v.

saturnus.full: Sāturnus (old collat. form Sāteur-nus, Fest. pp. 323 and 325 Müll., and SAETVRNVS, on a vase; v. Ritschl, de Fictil. Litteratis, and Schweizer, Zeitschr. für vergl. Sprachf. 4, p. 65 sq.), i, m. 1. sero; ab satu est dictus Saturnus, Varr. L. L. 5, § 64 Müll., Saturn; according to the myth, the most ancient king of Latium, who came to Italy in the reign of Janus; afterwards honored as the god of agriculture and of civilization in general; hence early identified with the Κρόνος of the Greeks: qui

saturo.full: sătŭro, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. satur, to fill, glut, cloy, satiate (rare but class.; syn. satio). Lit.: animalia duce naturā mammas appetunt earumque ubertate saturantur, Cic. N. D. 2, 51, 128: armenta, Verg. A. 8, 213: nec cytiso saturantur apes, id. E. 10, 30: caede leones, Ov. M. 10, 541; id. Am. 2, 16, 25: testudines, Plin. 9, 10, 12, § 36: saturabat glebula talis Patrem ipsum, Juv. 14, 166: famem, i. e. to satisfy, appease, Claud. Phoen. 13; Vulg. Deut. 14, 29 et saep. — Transf., in gen., to f

satus1.full: sătus, a, um, Part. of 1. sero.

satus2.full: sătus, ūs, m. 1. sero, a sowing, planting (several times in Cic.; elsewhere rare). Lit.: satui semen dederit nemini, Cato, R. R. 5, 3: herbam asperam, credo (sc. exstitisse), avium congestu, non humano satu, Cic. Div. 2, 32, 68: quid ergo vitium ortus, satus, incrementa commemorem? id. Sen. 15, 52.— Transf., a begetting, producing; origin, stock, race: a primo satu, quo a procreatoribus nati diliguntur, Cic. Fin. 5, 23, 65; cf.: genitalis, Lucr. 4, 1229: me ut credam ex tuo esse conceptum satu,

satyriasis.full: sătўrĭăsis, is, f., = σατυρίασις, excessive sexual excitement, lascivious madness, priapism, Cael. Aur. Acut. 3, 18; Theod. Prisc. 2, 11.
satyriasis.short: sătўrĭăsis, is, f., = σατυρίασις, excessive sexual excitement, lascivious madness, priapism, Cael.

satyricus1.full: sătўrĭcus, a, um, adj., = σατυρικός. Of or belonging to Satyrs, like Satyrs: signa, i. e. misshapen figures resembling Satyrs, Plin. 19, 4. 19, § 50.— Of or belonging to (Greek) satire, satiric (cf. satiricus, with which the word is often confounded): genus scenarum (with tragicum and comicum), Vitr. 5, 6, 9.— Trop., heating, exciting: medicamenta, Cael. Aur. Acut. 2, 18.

satyricus2.full: sătўrĭcus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to (Roman) satire, satiric, satirical; v. satiricus init.
satyricus2.short: sătўrĭcus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to (Roman) satire, satiric, satirical;

satyrion.full: sătўrĭon, ii, n. (sătўrĭos, ii, f., Plin. 26, 10, 62, § 96), = σατύριον, a plant that excited lust, ragwort, satyrion, Plin. 26, 10, 63, §§ 97, 99; also, a drink prepared from it, Petr. 8, 4; 21, 1.

satyriscus.full: Sătўriscus, i, m. dim., = Σατυρίσκος, a little Satyr, Cic. Div. 1, 20, 39.

satyrus.full: sătўrus, i, m., = σάτυρος. A kind of ape, Plin. 7, 2, 2, § 24; 5, 8, 8, § 44; 10, 72, 93, § 199; Sol. 27 fin.— A Satyr, one of the satyri, a kind of wood-deities resembling apes, with two goat's feet, and very lascivious; sing., Ov. M. 6, 110; 6, 383; Hor. Ep. 2, 2, 125; Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 60, § 135; Sil. 3 103. —Commonly plur.: capripedes Satyros, Lucr. 4, 580; Hor. C. 2, 19, 4; 1, 1, 31; id. Ep. 1, 19, 4; id. A. P. 221 sq.; Ov. F. 1, 397; id. M. 1, 193; 1, 692; 4, 25; Cic. N. D. 3, 17, 43 al.— L

saucaptis.full: saucaptis, ĭdis, f., a fictitious spice, Plaut. Ps. 3, 2, 43 Ritschl (al. sancaptis).
saucaptis.short: saucaptis, ĭdis, f., a fictitious spice, Plaut.

sauciatio.full: saucĭātĭo, ōnis, f. saucio, a wounding, Cic. Caecin. 15, 43.

saucietas.full: saucĭĕtas, ātis, f. saucius, a hurting, hurt, Cael. Aur. Tard. 2, 13.

saucio.full: saucĭo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. id., to wound, hurt. Lit. (class. but rare; not in Cæs.; syn.: vulnero, laedo): Rubrius in turbā sauciatur, Cic. Verr. 2, 1, 26, § 67; id. Vatin. 5, 13: ut ictu tragulae sauciaretur, Sall. Fragm. ap. Non. 398, 8 (Hist. 2, 19 Dietsch): aliquem virgis, Plaut. Rud. 3, 4, 53: ungue genas, Ov. A. A. 3, 708: radices, Cato ap. Plin. 17, 22, 35, § 198: sive quis sauciatus in opere noxam ceperit, Col. 11, 1, 18.—* In partic., pregn., to kill: meus discipulus valde amat illum,

saucius.full: saucĭus, a, um, adj., wounded, hurt. Lit.: omnes saucios Convisit, Att. ap. Non. 398, 4: multis civibus sauciis, Varr. ib. 398, 13: videmus ex acie efferri saepe saucios, Cic. Tusc. 2, 16, 38; so, too, in milit. lang., Caes. B. G. 3, 4 fin.; 5, 36; id. B. C. 3, 75; 3, 78 al.; cf. humorously: saucius factus sum in Veneris proelio: Sagittā Cupido cor meum transfixit, * Plaut. Pers. 1, 1, 24: taurus, Verg. A. 2, 223: funesto saucia morsu, Ov. M. 11, 373: bracchia direptā saucia fecit acu, id. Am. 1
saucius.short: saucĭus, a, um, adj., wounded, hurt.

saufeius.full: Saufēius, i, m.; Saufēia, ae, f., the name of a Roman gens. C. Saufeius, Cic. Rab. Perd. 7, 20.— L. Saufeius, Cic. Att. 1, 3, 1; 4, 6, 1.

saul.full: Săūl, ūlis, or indecl. m., the first king of the Jews, Alcim. ad Sor. 435; Paul. Nol. Carm. 13, 601; Vulg. 1 Reg. 9, 2; id. Act. 13, 21; gen. Saulis, id. Isa. 10, 29; dat. Sauli, id. Psa. 51, 1; acc. Saulem, id. 1 Reg. 15, 35.

saulus.full: Saulus, i, m., Saul, the name of St. Paul before his conversion, Prud. Ench. 186; Arat. A. Ap. 1, 709; Vulg. Act. 9, 1 et saep.
saulus.short: Saulus, i, m., Saul, the name of St.

saumarius.full: saumārĭus, a late form for sagmā-rĭus, Ven. Fort. v. Germ. 3.
saumarius.short: saumārĭus, a late form for sagmā-rĭus, Ven.

saurea.full: Saurea, ae, m., the name of a slave, Plaut. As. 2, 1, 16.
saurea.short: Saurea, ae, m., the name of a slave, Plaut.

saurion.full: saurĭon, i, n., = σαύριον, mustard, Plin. 19, 8, 54, § 171.
saurion.short: saurĭon, i, n., = σαύριον, mustard, Plin.

sauritis.full: saurītis, is, f., = σαυρῖτις (lizardstone), a precious stone, otherwise unknown, Plin. 37, 10, 67, § 181.
sauritis.short: saurītis, is, f., = σαυρῖτις (lizardstone), a precious stone, otherwise unknown, Plin.

sauroctonos.full: Saūroctŏnos, i, m., = Σαυροκτόνος, the lizard-killer, an epithet of Apollo; hence, Apollo Sauroctonos, a statue by Praxiteles, Plin. 34, 8, 19, § 70; cf. Corinthius, Mart. 14, 172 in lemm.
sauroctonos.short: Saūroctŏnos, i, m., = Σαυροκτόνος, the lizard-killer, an epithet of Apollo;

sauromatae.full: Saurŏmătae, ārum, and Saurŏ-mătes, ae, v. Sarmatae.
sauromatae.short: Saurŏmătae, ārum, and Saurŏ-mătes, ae, v.

savillum.full: savillum, i, n. suavis, a cheese-cake, Cato, R. R. 84.

savio.full: sāvĭo, sāvĭŏlum, sāvĭor, sāvĭ-um, v. suav-.

savus.full: Sāvus (Saus), i, m., = Σαοῦος, a river in Pannonia, a tributary of the Danube, now the Save, Claud. Laud. Stil. 2, 192; Just. 32, 3, 8; Sex. Ruf. Brev. 7 fin.—Form Saus, Plin. 3, 25, 28, § 147.—Hence, adj.: Sā-vensis, e, lying upon or adjoining the Save: regis, Sex. Ruf. Brev. 7 fin.
savus.short: Sāvus (Saus), i, m., = Σαοῦος, a river in Pannonia, a tributary of the Danube, now the Save, Claud.

saxa.full: Saxa, ae, m., a surname of L. Decidius, a partisan of Cœsar, Caes. B. C. 1, 66; Cic. Phil. 10, 10, 22; 11, 5, 12; 12, 8, 20.
saxa.short: Saxa, ae, m., a surname of L.

saxa rubra.full: Saxa Rubra, the name of a place, v. ruber, II. B.
saxa rubra.short: Saxa Rubra, the name of a place, v.

saxatilis.full: saxātĭlis, e, adj. saxum, that dwells or is found among rocks, saxatile: columbae, i. e. which inhabit towers, Varr. R. R. 3, 7, 1: pisces, that frequent rocks, Col. 8, 16, 8: piscatus (opp. hamatilis), Plaut. Rud. 2, 1, 10.—As subst.: saxātĭles, fishes that frequent rocks, Cels. 2, 18; Plin. 9, 15, 20, § 52; 32, 9, 31, § 94; Ov. Hal. 109.

saxetum.full: saxētum, i, n. saxum, a rocky place (very rare): asperum saxetum, * Cic. Agr. 2, 25, 67.—In plur., Col. 5, 10, 9 Schneid. N. cr. (al. saxosa).

saxeus.full: saxĕus, a, um, adj. id.. Lit., of rock, of stone, rocky, stony: saxea est verruca in summo montis vertice, Auct. ap. Quint. 8, 3, 48: moles, Att. ap. Cic. N. D. 2, 35, 89; Ov. M. 12, 283: scopulus, id. ib. 14, 73: saepta, Lucr. 4, 699: strata viarum, id. 1, 315: tecta, id. 5, 984; Ov. H. 10, 128: crepido, Plin. 12, 1, 5, § 9: effigies bacchantis, Cat. 64, 61: umbra, of the rocks, Verg. G. 3, 145 et saep.: mater ad auditas stupuit ceu saxea voces, Ov. M. 5, 509: Niobe saxea facta, id. P. 1, 2, 32

saxialis.full: saxĭālis, e, adj. id., of rock or stone, stone- (late Lat.): termini, Front. Colon. p. 132 Goes.

saxifer.full: saxĭfer, fĕra, fĕrum, adj. saxum-fero, stone-bearing: habenae, i. e. that hurl stones, Val. Fl. 5, 608.

saxificus.full: saxĭfĭcus, a, um, adj. saxum-facio, that turns into stone, petrifying (poet.): Medusa, Ov. Ib. 555; Sil. 10, 178; Luc. 9, 670; cf.: vultus Medusae, Ov. M. 5, 217: os (Medusae), Sen. Herc. Fur. 901.

saxifragus.full: saxĭfrăgus, a, um, adj. saxum-frango, stone-breaking, stone-crushing: undae maris, Enn. ap. Cic. de Or. 3, 42, 167 (Ann. v. 564 Vahl.): adiantum, so called because it breaks or dissolves the stone in the bladder, Plin. 22, 21, 30, § 64; also, herba, Ser. Samm. 32, 602; App. Herb. 67.—Absol. (sc. herba), Veg. 1, 13, 5; 6, 11, 1 al.

saxigenus.full: saxĭgĕnus, a, um, adj. saxum-gigno, born or sprung from stone: semen, Prud. Cath. 5, 7.

saxiperium.full: saxĭpērĭum, i, n. saxum-pero, a bag to hold stones for slinging (late Lat.), Fulg. Serm. 74 (cf. Vulg. 1 Reg. 17, 40).

saxitas.full: saxĭtas, ātis, f. saxum, stony nature, stoniness (late Lat.), Cael. Aur. Tard. 3, 4; 3, 8, n. 109; cf. saxositas.

saxo.full: Saxo, ŏnis, m., a Saxon; acc. Saxona, Claud. Laud. Stil. 2, 255; id. Epith. Pallad. et Cel. 89; abl. Saxone, id. IV. Cons. Hon. 31; id. Nupt. Hon. et Mar. 219; id. in Eutr. 1, 392.—Usu. plur.: Saxŏnes, the Saxons, Amm. 27, 8, 5; Salv. Gub. Dei, 7, 15; Eutr. 9, 21.—Hence, Saxŏnia, ae, f., the country of the Saxons, Saxony, Ven. Fort. 7, 16, 47.

saxositas.full: saxōsĭtas, ātis, f. saxosus, stony nature, stoniness, Cael. Aur. Tard. 3, 6, 82; cf. saxitas.

saxosus.full: saxōsus (collat. form saxŭōsus, Sicul. Fl. p. 11 Goes.), a, um, adj. saxum, full of rocks or stones, rocky, stony: montes, Verg. G. 2, 111: valles, id. E. 5, 84: loca, Col. Arb. 21, 1: mare, id. ib. 8, 16, 8: Hypanis, Verg. G. 4, 370: Euphrates, Plin. 5, 24, 20, § 84: frutex, growing among stones, id. 15, 7, 7: Phlegethon saxosa incendia torquet, Sil. 13, 565.—As subst.: saxōsa, ōrum, n., rocky or stony places: piscium genera alia planis gaudent, alia saxosis, Quint. 5, 10, 21 (cf.: saxatiles pi

saxulum.full: saxŭlum, i, n. dim. id., a little rock: in asperrimis saxulis, Cic. de Or. 1, 44, 196.

saxum.full: saxum (in inscrr. also SAKSVM; from collat. form saxus; a vocative SAXE, Inscr. Orell. 2982), i, n. root sak-; Sanscr. ska; cf. secare, any large, rough stone; a detached fragment of rock; a rock (in gen.; whereas rupes is a steep rock, crag, cliff). In gen., Lucr. 4, 266 sq.; cf. id. 1, 882: non est e saxo sculptus, Cic. Ac. 2, 31, 100: pars ludicre saxa Jactant, inter se licitantur, Enn. ap. Non. 134, 13 (Ann. v. 76 Vahl.): (Sisyphum) adverso nixantem trudere monte Saxum, etc., Lucr. 3, 1001:

saxuosus.full: saxŭōsus, a, um, v. saxosus init.

scabellum.full: scăbellum (scăbillum), i, n. dim. scamnum; cf. Quint. 1, 4, 12. A low stool, footstool, cricket, Varr. L. L. 5, 35, 46 fin.; Cato, R. R. 10, 4; Vulg. Psa. 98, 5; id. Isa. 66, 1.— Transf., an instrument of the nature of the castanet, played on by the foot, esp. used in dramatic representations, Cic. Cael. 27, 65; Suet. Calig. 54; Arn. 2, 73; Aug. Mus. 3 init.

scaber.full: scăber, bra, brum, adj., rough, scurfy, scabrous (esp. from uncleanness). Lit. In gen. (poet. and in post-Aug. prose): pectus illuvie scabrum, Poët. ap. Cic. Tusc. 3, 12, 26: manus, Ov. F. 4, 921: rubigine dentes, id. M. 8, 802: scabros nigrae morsu rubiginis enses, Luc. 1, 243; Suet. Aug. 79: unguis, Ov. A. A. 3, 276; Cels. 6, 19 fin.: scaber intonsusque homo, Hor. Ep. 1, 7, 90: tophus, Verg. G. 2, 214; Ov. H. 15, 141: robigo (pilorum), Verg. G. 1, 495 (cf.: scabies et robigo ferri, id. ib. 2,
scaber.short: scăber, bra, brum, adj., rough, scurfy, scabrous (esp.

scabidus.full: scăbĭdus, a, um, adj. scabies, scabby, mangy, itchy (post-class.). Lit.: palpebrae, Marc. Emp. 8.— Trop.: concupiscentia, Tert. Anim. 38.

scabies.full: scăbĭes, em, ē, f. scabo, a roughness, scurf. Lit. In gen. (very rare): ferri (with robigo), Verg. G. 2, 220 (cf.: scabra robigo pilorum, id. ib. 1, 495): mali, Juv. 5, 153: vetusta cariosae testae, filth, App. M. 9, p. 220, 11; cf. Vulg. Lev. 13, 6.— In partic., as a disease, the scab, mange, itch, Cels. 5, 28, 16; Lucil. ap. Non. 160, 21; Cato, R. R. 5, 7; Col. 6, 13, 1; 6, 31, 2; 7, 5, 5; Verg. G. 3, 441; Juv. 2, 80; 8, 34; Hor. A. P. 453 et saep.—Of plants, Plin. 17, 24, 37, § 225; 19, 10, 5

scabillarii.full: scăbillārĭi, ōrum, m. scabillum, players on the scabellum, Inscr. Orell. 2643; so ib. 4117.

scabiola.full: scăbĭŏla, ae, f. dim. scabies, the scab, the itch, Aug. adv. Julian. 4, 13.

scabiosus.full: scăbĭōsus, a, um, adj. id. (post-Aug.). Rough, scurfy: coralium, Plin. 32, 2, 11, § 22: far, old, spoiled, Pers. 5, 74.— Scabby, mangy: boves, Col.11,2,83: (homo), Pers. 2, 13: anguli (oculorum), Plin. 29, 2, 10, § 36: macies mulorum, App. M. 9, p. 223.

scabitudo.full: scăbĭtūdo, ĭnis, f. [scabies, II.), an itching, irritation.—Trop., of anger: omnem scabitudinem animi delere, sine cicatrice, Petr. 99, 2.

scabo.full: scăbo, scābi (no sup.), 3, v. a. root skap-, skamp; Gr. σκάπτω, to dig; κάπετος, ditch; Lat. scaber, scabies, to scratch, to scrape (syn. rado): caput, Lucil. ap. Non. 472, 6; Hor. S. 1, 10, 71: scaberat ut porcus contritis arbore costis, Lucil. ap. Prisc. p. 884 P.: aures pedibus posterioribus, Plin. 11, 48, 108, § 260: se, id. 8, 27, 41, § 99; 10, 74, 95, § 204: tellurem, id. 10, 71, 91, § 196: laminas (doliorum), id. 18, 26, 64, § 236.—Prov.: mutuum scabere, i. e. to praise one another, Symm.

scabratus.full: scă_brātus, a, um, adj. scaber, made rough, roughened: vitis, i. e. jagged by pruning it with a dull knife, Col. 4, 24, 22.

scabredo.full: scă_brēdo, ĭnis, f. scaber, I. B., a roughness of the skin, scabbiness, itch, mange, App. Herb. 73; Coripp. 4, 48; Hier. Vit. Hil. init.

scabreo.full: scă_brĕo, ēre, v. n. scabo, to be scurfy, scabby, Enn. ap. Non. 169, 21 (Trag. Rel. p. 23 Rib.; Vahl. ad Enn. l. l. p. 106, reads scaprent); Pac. ap. Non. 152, 29 (l. l. p. 97 Rib.).

scabres.full: scă_bres, is, f. id., the scab, the itch, Varr. ap. Non. 168, 20.

scabridus.full: scă_brĭdus, a, um, adj. scaber, rough, rugged: lingua robigine, Ven. Carm. 2, 13, 7.

scabritia.full: scă_brĭtĭa, ae, and scă_brĭtĭes, em, ē (in both forms post-Aug.; esp. freq. in Plin.), f. id.. In gen., roughness, ruggedness: digitorum, Plin. 34, 13, 34, § 131: unguium, id. 28, 9, 37, § 139: linguae, id. 31, 9, 45, § 100: chartae levigatur dente, id. 13, 12, 25, § 81: corticis, id. 21, 4, 10, § 17: ferramentorum, id. 28, 9, 41, § 148: arteriae, id. 27, 12, 105, § 130 et saep.—* The scab, the itch, Col. 7, 5, 8.
scabritia.short: scă_brĭtĭa, ae, and scă_brĭtĭes, em, ē (in both forms post-Aug.;

scabrosus.full: scă_brōsus, a, um, adj. id., rough, scabrous: sorde, Prud. Psych. 106.

scaea porta.full: Scaea porta, ae, f., = Σκαιαὶ πύλαι, the Scœan (western, σκαιός) gate of Troy; Verg. A. 3, 351; Sil. 13, 73; also, acc. to the Greek, in the plur.: Scaeae portae, Verg. A. 2, 612. —As subst.: Scaeae, the Scœan gate: Astyanax Scaeis dejectus ab altis, Aus. Epit. Her. 15, 3.
scaea porta.short: Scaea porta, ae, f., = Σκαιαὶ πύλαι, the Scœan (western, σκαιός) gate of Troy;

scaena.full: scaena, ae (falsely scēna, v. Prol. in Verg. p. 387 Rib.), f., = σκηνή. Lit., the stage, boards, scene of a theatre: dum histrio in scaenă siet, Plaut. Poen. prol. 20: in scaenă esse Roscium intellegat, Cic. Brut. 84, 290: foris hic extra scaenam fient proelia, Plaut. Capt. prol. 60: cum scaena croco Cilici perfusa recens est, Lucr. 2, 416: scaenaique simul varios splendere decores, id. 4, 983: scaenae magnificentia, Cic. Mur. 19, 38: nec vero scaena solum referta est his sceleribus, id. N. D. 3

scaenalis.full: scaenālis, e, adj. scaena, of or belonging to the stage, scenic, theatrical (very rare for scaenicus): species, Lucr. 4, 77: frondes, Poët. ap. Anth. Lat. 2, p. 48 Burm.

scaenarius.full: scaenārĭus, a, um, adj. id., of or belonging to the stage, scenic, dramatic, theatrical (late Lat. for scaenicus): artifices, i. e. players, Amm. 28, 4, 32: PICTOR, i. e. a scenepainter, Inscr. Murat. 948, 4.

scaenaticus.full: scaenātĭcus, i, m. id., a stageplayer: ut comici, cinaedici, scaenatici, Varr. ap. Non. 176, 19.

scaenatilis.full: scaenātĭlis, e, adj. id., for scenicus, of or belonging to the stage, Varr. ap Non. 176, 18 (an unintelligible passage).

scaenicus.full: scaenĭcus (scen-), a, um, adj., = σκηνικός, of or belonging to the stage, scenic, dramatic, theatrical (class.). Lit.: poëtae, dramatic poets, Varr. L. L. 9, § 17 Müll.: artifices, players, actors, Cic. Arch. 5, 10; Suet. Caes. 84: actores, Quint. 6, 1, 26; 11, 3, 4: ludi, stage-plays, theatrical representations, in a gen. sense (opp. to games of wrestling, racing, etc.), Liv. 7, 2; 31, 4; 34, 54; Ter. Hec. prol. alt. 37; Suet. Calig. 26; id. Ner. 11; cf. operae (with gladiatoriae), id. Aug. 43:
scaenicus.short: scaenĭcus (scen-), a, um, adj., = σκηνικός, of or belonging to the stage, scenic, dramatic, theatrical (class.).

scaenographia.full: scaenŏgrăphĭ_a, ae, f., = σκηνογραφία, a drawing in perspective: scaenographia est frontis et laterum abscedentium adumbratio ad circinique centrum omnium linearum responsus, Vitr. 1, 2, 2 Rode. (Others read scĭāgrăphĭ_a, σκιᾶγραφία, in the same signif.)
scaenographia.short: scaenŏgrăphĭ_a, ae, f., = σκηνογραφία, a drawing in perspective: scaenographia est frontis et laterum abscedentium adumbratio ad circinique centrum omnium linearum responsus, Vitr.

scaeva2.full: scaeva, ae, m. scaevus, a lefthanded person, Dig. 21, 1, 12; cf. Scaevola.

scaeva3.full: Scaeva, ae, m. 2. scaeva, a Roman surname, e. g. D. Junius Brutus Scaeva, consul A. U. C. 429, Liv. 10, 43; 10, 47: Cassius Scaeva, a partisan of Cœsar, Caes. B. C. 3, 53; Cic. Att. 13, 23, 3.

scaevitas.full: scaevĭtas, ātis, f. scaevus, II. (postclass.). Awkwardness, perverseness, unskilfulness, Gell. praef., § 20; 6, 2, 8: artium, Amm. 30, 4, 10.— A mischance, misfortune, App. M. 3, p. 135, 27: fortunae, id. ib. 7, p. 189, 4: indignae rei, id. ib. 9, p. 221, 21.

scaevola.full: Scaevŏla (in the Fast. Capit. also written Scaevŭla), ae, m. prop. a dim. of 3. Scaeva, the Left-handed. A surname of C. Mucius, who made his way into the camp of Porsenna to kill him, and, on being discovered, burned off his own right hand, Liv. 2, 12 sq.; Flor. 1, 10; Cic. Sest. 21, 48; Sil. 8, 386 al.— After his time, a frequent surname in the gens Mucia; so, P. Mucius Scaevola, consul A. U. C. 621, a friend of Tiberius Gracchus, Cic. Ac. 2, 5, 13 (cf. id. de Or. 2, 70, 285); id. Planc. 36, 8

scaevus.full: scaevus, a, um, adj. kindred with Sanscr. savya, laevus, sinister, as the Gr. σκαιός and the Germ. schief, oblique, left, that is on the left, towards the left side (rare; most freq. in Appul.; syn. laevus, sinister). Lit.: itinera portarum, i. e. running from right to left, Vitr. 1, 5, 2: iter, Serv. Verg. A. 3, 351.— Trop. Awkward, perverse, stupid, silly: scaevus profecto et caecus animi forem, si, etc., Gell. 12, 13, 4: mulier, App. M. 9, p. 223, 22: scaevus iste Romulus, Sall. H. Fragm. 1,

scala.full: scāla, ae (acc. to the ancient grammarians, not used in sing.; cf. Varr. L. L. 9, §§ 63 and 68; 10, § 54 Müll.; Quint. 1, 5, 16 Spald.; Charis. p. 20 P. p. 72 ib.; Diom. p. 315 ib. al.; but v. infra), f. for scandla, from scando; cf. mala, from mando, mostly plur.: scālae, ārum, a flight of steps or stairs, a staircase; a ladder, scaling-ladder. Plur. Lit.: scalas dare alicui utendas, Plaut. Rud. 3, 1, 10: scalarum gradus, the rounds of a ladder, Caecin. ap. Cic. Fam. 6, 7, 3: Romani scalis summ

scalarii.full: scālārĭi, ōrum, m. scalae, stairmakers, Inscr. Orell. 4071.

scalaris.full: scālāris, e, adj. id., of or belonging to a flight of steps or a ladder: forma, Vitr. 5, 6 fin.; STRVCTIO, Inscr. Orell. 4570.—As subst.: scālārĭa, ĭum, n., a flight of stairs or steps, a staircase, Vitr. 5, 6, 3; also in the sing.: SCALARE, is, Inscr. Orell. 4750.

scaldis.full: Scaldis, is, m., the Scheldt, a river of Gallia Belgica; acc. Scaldem, Caes. B. G. 6, 33 Oud. N. cr.: Scaldim, Plin. 4, 14, 28, § 98; abl. Scalde, id. 4, 17, 31, or Scaldi, ib.
scaldis.short: Scaldis, is, m., the Scheldt, a river of Gallia Belgica;

scalenus.full: scălēnus, a, um, adj., = σκαληνός; in mathematics, of a triangle, of unequal sides, scalene: figura geometrica, Aus. Idyll. 13, prooem. § 7.

scalmus.full: scalmus, i, m., = σκαλμός, a peg to which an oar was strapped; a thole, tholepin, Vitr. 10, 8 med.; Cic. Brut. 53, 197; id. de Or. 1, 38, 174; Vell. 2, 43, 1: venit (Canius) mature: scalmum nullum videt, not even a thole-pin, i. e. no trace of a boat, Cic. Off. 3, 14, 59.
scalmus.short: scalmus, i, m., = σκαλμός, a peg to which an oar was strapped;

scalpellum.full: scalpellum, i, n. (collat. form scal-pellus, i, m., Cels. 2, 10 twice), dim. scalprum, a small surgical knife, a scalpel, a lancet: scalpellum adhibere, Cic. Sest. 65, 135; id. Div. 2, 46, 96; Col. 6, 32, 3; Plin. 28, 8, 28, § 110; Veg. Vet. 1, 26, 2; Sen. Ira, 2, 27, 4: scribae, a penknife, Vulg. Jer. 36, 23.

scalpo.full: scalpo, psi, ptum, 3, v. a. root skalp-; Gr. σκάλοψ, mole; Lat. talpa; cf. scalprum; also Gr. γλύφω. To cut, carve, scrape, scratch, engrave (class.; syn. caelo), said of surface work, = ξέειν; sculpo, of deeper work, high relief, or statuary, = γλύφω: ad pingendum, ad fingendum, ad scalpendum apta manus est, Cic. N. D. 2, 60, 150: Phidiam tradunt scalpsisse marmora, Plin. 36, 5, 4, § 15: marmora ac scyphos, id. 35, 11, 40, § 128 (Sillig, sculpsit): gemmas, id. 37, 10, 65, § 177: flores et acant

scalpratus.full: scalprātus, a, um, adj. scalprum, having a sharp or cutting edge: ferramentum, Col. 9, 15, 9.

scalprum.full: scalprum, i, n. (collat. form scalper, ri, m., Cels. 8, 3) [scalpo], a sharp cutting instrument; a chisel, knife, etc., of sculptors, husbandmen, shoemakers, surgeons, etc., Liv. 27, 49; Col. 4, 25, 1; Hor. S. 2, 3, 106; Cels. 8, 3 sq.; Sen. Ep. 65, 13.—A penknife, Tac. A. 5, 8; Suet. Vit. 2.—Of a pruning-knife, Plin. 17, 16, 26, § 119.

scalptor.full: scalptor, ōris, m. id., a cutter, graver in metal or stone (cf. sculptor), Vell. 1, 17, 4; Plin. 20, 13, 51, § 134; 36, 6, 5, § 44; 37, 4, 15, § 60.

scalptorium.full: scalptōrĭum, ii, n. id., an instrument for scratching one's self, in the form of a hand, Mart. 14, 83 in lemm.

scalptura.full: scalptūra, ae, f. id.. A cutting, carving, or graving in stone: gemmarum, Plin. 37, 7, 30, § 104; Suet. Galb. 10.—Plur., Plin. 37, 10, 63, § 173.— Concr., a graved figure, a sculpture: Zophori scalpturis ornati, Vitr. 4, 1, 2; 2, 9, 9; 3, 3, 10.

scalpturigo.full: scalptŭrīgo (scalpŭrīgo), ĭnis, f. scalpturio, a scratching, Sol. 32 med.

scalpturio.full: scalptūrĭo (scalpūrĭo, Non. 171, 32), īre, v. desid. n. [scalpo], to scratch, claw: occoepit (gallus) ibi scalpturire ungulis circumcirca, Plaut. Aul. 3, 4, 8.

scamander.full: Scămander, dri, m., = Σκάμανδρος. A river in Troas, the Scamander, now the Bunar-bashi Tchai, Mel. 1, 18, 3; Plin. 5, 30, 33, § 124; Enn. ap. Non. 467, 31 (Trag. v. 214 Vahl.); Hor. Epod. 13, 14 al.; Cat. 64, 357.—Called Xanthus, from its red color, Verg. A. 1, 473; Ov. M. 2, 245.—Hence, adj.: Scămandrĭus, a, um, of or belonging to the river Scamander: unda, Att. ap. Non. p. 192, 1 (Trag. Fragm. v. 322 Rib.).— A freedman of the Fabricii, Cic. Clu. 16, 47; Quint. 11, 1, 74.—Hence, Scămandrĭa, ae,

scambus.full: scambus, a, um, adj., = σκαμβός, bow-legged, bandy-legged (pure Lat. varus), Suet. Oth. 12.
scambus.short: scambus, a, um, adj., = σκαμβός, bow-legged, bandy-legged (pure Lat.

scamillus.full: scămillus, i, m. (acc. to Prisc. p. 615 P., scămellum, i, n.) dim. scamnum, a little bench or stool: impares, i. e. unequal projections or steps on the pedestals of columns, Vitr. 3, 4, 5; 5, 9, 4; App. 615 P.

scamma.full: scamma, ătis, n., = σκάμμα, a wrestling-place in the Palaestra. Lit. (late Lat.), Cael. Aur. Tard. 2, 1 fin.; Hier. Joann. Hieros. 16; id. Ep. 61, 5; Ambros. Off. 1, 16. —* Trop., a wrestling, a contest, Tert. adv. Martyr. 3; cf. harena. II.
scamma.short: scamma, ătis, n., = σκάμμα, a wrestling-place in the Palaestra.

scammonea.full: scammōnĕa, ae, f., = σκαμμωνία, scammony, Cic. Div. 1, 10, 16; Plin. 25, 5, 22, § 54.—Also scammōnĕum, i, n., Cato, R. R. 157, 12: scammōnĭa, ae, f., Plin. 26, 8, 58, § 90; 26, 9, 60, § 93; Veg. 3, 6, 9; Scrib. Comp. 140: scammōnĭum, i, n., Plin. 26, 8, 38, § 59.
scammonea.short: scammōnĕa, ae, f., = σκαμμωνία, scammony, Cic.

scammonites.full: scammōnītes, ae, m., = σκαμμωνίτης (SC. οἶνος), wine seasoned with scammony, Plin. 14, 16, 19, § 110.

scamnatus.full: scamnātus, a, um, adj. scamnum, II. B.; in the agrimensores: ager, a field whose breadth (or measurement from east to west) is greater than its length, Aggen. p. 46 Goes.

scamnum.full: scamnum, i, n. for scap-num; root skap-; Gr. σκήπτω, to support; cf.: scabellum, scapus, scipio, a bench, stool, step, etc. In gen.: quă simplici scansione scandebant in lectum non altum, scabellum; in altiorem, scamnum, Varr. L. L. 5, § 168 Müll.; Ov. A. A. 2, 211; 1, 162: longis considere scamnis, id. F. 6, 305; Cels. 2, 15: sedere in scamnis equitum, Mart. 5, 41, 7.— Of horizontal branches of trees serving as seats, Plin. 12, 1, 5, § 10: ramorum, id. 17, 23, 35, § 201.—Poet., a throne: regni

scandalizo.full: scandălizo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a., = σκανδαλιζω, to cause to stumble, tempt to evil (eccl. Lat.), Tert. Virg. Vel. 3; id. Cor. Mil. 14; id. adv. Marc. 15, 18 fin.; Vulg. Mal. 2, 8; id. Matt. 5, 30.

scandalum.full: scandălum, i, n., = σκάνδαλον, that which causes one to stumble, a stumblingblock (eccl. Lat.). * Lit., Prud. Apoth. 47 praef.— Trop., an inducement to sin, a temptation, cause of offence, Tert. Virg. Vel. 3; id. adv. Jud. 14; id. adv. Marc. 3, 1; Vulg. Psa. 118, 165; id. 1 Johan. 2, 10.
scandalum.short: scandălum, i, n., = σκάνδαλον, that which causes one to stumble, a stumblingblock (eccl.

scandianus.full: Scandĭānus, a, um, adj., named from one Scandius: mala, Col. 5, 10, 19; Plin. 15, 14, 15, § 50; Cels. 4, 19.
scandianus.short: Scandĭānus, a, um, adj., named from one Scandius: mala, Col.

scandila.full: Scandila, ae, or -ē, ēs, f., an island near Eubœa, now Skantzoura, Plin. 4, 12, 23, § 72 (al. Scandira); Mel. 2, 7.
scandila.short: Scandila, ae, or -ē, ēs, f., an island near Eubœa, now Skantzoura, Plin.

scandinavia.full: Scandĭnāvĭa, ae, f., a large and fruitful island in Northern Europe; acc. to some, Zealand; acc. to others, Schonen, Mel. 3, 6, 7; Plin. 4, 13, 27, § 96; 8, 15, 16, § 39.—Also called Scandĭa, Plin. 4, 16, 30, § 104.
scandinavia.short: Scandĭnāvĭa, ae, f., a large and fruitful island in Northern Europe;

scandix.full: scandix, īcis, f., = σκάνδιξ, the herb chervil: Scandix caerefolium, Linn.; Plin. 21, 15, 52, § 89; 22, 22, 38, § 81.
scandix.short: scandix, īcis, f., = σκάνδιξ, the herb chervil: Scandix caerefolium, Linn.;

scando.full: scando (no perf. or sup.; cf.: ascendo, descendo, etc.), 3, v. a. and n. Sanscr. root skand-, to climb; cf. Gr. σκάνδαλον, σκανδάληθρον. Act., to climb, mount, clamber or get up; to ascend. Lit. (rare but class.): cum alii malos scandant, alii per foros cursent, etc., * Cic. Sen. 6, 17: arcem et Capitolium, Liv. 3, 68, 7; 4, 2 fin.; cf.: in curru Capitolium (of a triumphal entry), id. 45, 39: curru Capitolia, Luc. 9, 600: moenia, Liv. 22, 14 Drak. N. cr.: muros, id. 5, 21: tectum scalis, Plin. 1

scandula.full: scandŭla (later form scindŭla, as if from scindo), ae, f. dim. scando, a shingle for a roof (so named from their rising, like steps, one above the other); mostly plur., Hirt. B. G. 8, 42 init.; Plin. 16, 10, 15, § 36; 16, 10, 18, § 42; Col. 8, 3, 6; Vitr. 2, 1; Isid. 19, 19, 7; Pall. 1, 22.
scandula.short: scandŭla (later form scindŭla, as if from scindo), ae, f.

scandulaca.full: scandulaca genus herbae frugibus inimicae, quod eas velut hedera implicando necat, Fest. p. 330.
scandulaca.short: scandulaca genus herbae frugibus inimicae, quod eas velut hedera implicando necat, Fest.

scandularis.full: scandŭlāris, e, adj. scandula, shingled, shingle-: tectum, App. M. 3, p. 137, 2.

scandularius.full: scandŭlārĭus, ii, m. id., a shingler, Dig. 50, 6, 6.

scansilis.full: scansĭlis, e, adj. scando, that may be climbed. Lit.: ficus, Plin. 17, 11, 16, § 84: gradus superiores scansiles, Schol. Juv. 7, 45; Amm. 16, 10, 14.—* Trop.: lex annorum, i. e. the law of critical years (placed at certain distances or steps from each other) or climacterics, Plin. 7, 49, 50, § 161.

scansio.full: scansĭo, ōnis, f. scando, a climbing up (very rare). * Lit.: quā simplici scansione scandebant in lectum, Varr. L. L. 5, § 168 Müll.— Trop.: sonorum, a rising or elevation of tones of the voice, Vitr. 6, 1. —In gram., a metrical reading or scanning of verse, scansion, Beda, p. 2368 P.; Diom. 494 sq. P.

scansorius.full: scansōrĭus, a, um, adj. id., of or for climbing: genus machinarum, Vitr. 10, 1.

scantianus.full: Scantĭānus, a, um, v. Scantius, B.

scantinius.full: Scantīnĭus (Scātīnĭus), i, m., a Roman name. P. Scantinius, a pontifex, Liv. 23, 21 fin.—b. C. Scantinius Capitolinus, a tribune of the people, Val. Max. 6, 1, 7.—Hence, adj.: Scantīnĭus (Scātīn-), a, um, the Lex Scantinia (Scātīnĭa) de nefandă Venere is named after one Scantinius, a tribune of the people, otherwise unknown, Cael. ap. Cic. Fam. 8, 12, 3; 8, 14, 4; Suet. Dom. 8; Juv. 2, 44; Tert. Monog. 12; Prud. στεφ. 10, 203.—Form Scatinia, Aus. Epigr. 89, 4.
scantinius.short: Scantīnĭus (Scātīnĭus), i, m., a Roman name.

scantius.full: Scantĭus, a, name of a Roman gens. So, Scantia, a woman abused by Clodius, Cic. Mil. 27, 75.—Hence, Scantĭus, a, um, adj., Scantian: silva, in Campania, Cic. Agr. 1, 1, 3; 3, 4, 15: aquae, perh. in the same place, Plin. 2, 107, 111, § 240.— Scantĭānus, a, um, adj., Scantian: mala, Cato, R. R. 7, 3; 7, 143 fin.; Varr. R. R. 1, 59, 1; Plin. 15, 14, 15, § 50 (Jahn, Scandianus): vitis, Varr. ap. Plin. 14, 4, 5, § 47.
scantius.short: Scantĭus, a, name of a Roman gens.

scapha.full: scăpha, ae, f. = σκάφη; cf. scabo, a light boat, a skiff (cf.: lembus, cymba): de navi timidae desiluerunt in scapham, Plaut. Rud. prol. 75; 1, 2, 74; 1, 2, 76; 1, 2, 84; 2, 3, 36; 2, 3, 38; Cic. Inv. 2, 51, 154; Auct. Her. 1, 11, 19; Sall. Fragm. ap. Non. 535, 11; Liv. 44, 42: biremis, * Hor. C. 3, 29, 62: piscatoria, Just. 2, 13, 9 et saep.; Vulg. Act. 27, 16.

scaphe.full: scăphē, ēs, f., = σκάφη, a concave sundial, Vitr. 9, 9.
scaphe.short: scăphē, ēs, f., = σκάφη, a concave sundial, Vitr.

scaphium.full: scăphĭum (scăpĭum), ii, n., = σκάφιον. In gen., a concave vessel or basin in the form of a boat (cf. cymbium), Lucr. 6, 1046; Vitr. 8, 1 med.— In partic. A drinking-vessel in the form of a boat, Plaut. Stich. 5, 4, 11; id. Bacch. 1, 1, 37; Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 17, § 37; 2, 4, 24, § 54.— A chamber-pot, Mart. 11, 11, 6; Juv. 6, 264; Dig. 34, 2, 27 fin.— A concave sundial, Mart. Cap. 6, § 597.— The reservoir of a water -clock, Vitr. 9, 8, 5.

scaphula.full: scăphŭla, ae, f. dim. scapha, a little boat or skiff, Veg. Mil. 3, 7; Paul. Nol. Ep. 49, 1.—Used as a bath-tub, Cael. Aur. Acut. 1, 11, 95; 2, 40, 232.

scaptesula.full: Scaptēsŭla (Scaptensŭla), ae, f., = Σκαπτησύλη, a town in Thrace, celebrated for its silver mines, Lucr. 6, 810; cf. Fest. p. 330 Müll.
scaptesula.short: Scaptēsŭla (Scaptensŭla), ae, f., = Σκαπτησύλη, a town in Thrace, celebrated for its silver mines, Lucr.

scaptia.full: Scaptĭa, ae, f., a very ancient town in Latium, now Passerano, Plin. 3, 5, 9, § 68. —Hence, Scaptĭus, a, um, adj., of Scaptia, Scaptian: tribus, Liv. 8, 17 fin.—Hence, Scaptĭensis, e, adj., of the Scaptian tribe: tribules, Suet. Aug. 40.
scaptia.short: Scaptĭa, ae, f., a very ancient town in Latium, now Passerano, Plin.

scapula1.full: Scăpŭla, ae, m., a Roman surname. A partisan of Pompey, the main instigator of the Spanish war, Auct. B. Hisp. 33; Cic. Fam. 9, 13, 1.— A usurer in the time of Cicero, Cic. Quint. 4, 17.—Hence, Scă-pŭlānus, a, um, adj., named after one Scapula: horti, Cic. Att. 12, 40, 4.
scapula1.short: Scăpŭla, ae, m., a Roman surname.

scapula2.full: scăpŭla, ae, f., a kind of vine, = vennucula, q. v., Plin. 14, 2, 6, § 34.
scapula2.short: scăpŭla, ae, f., a kind of vine, = vennucula, q.

scapula3.full: scăpŭla, ae, f., v. scapulae fin.

scapulae.full: scăpŭlae, ārum, f., the shoulder-blades, in men and animals. Lit., Cels. 8, 1 med.; Plin. 21, 21, 89, § 155; 30, 14, 43, § 125; Ov. A. A. 3, 273; Varr. R. R. 2, 7, 5; Plin. 11, 29, 35, § 107 al.— Transf. The shoulders, back, in gen.: qui saepe ante in nostras scapulas cicatrices indiderunt, have cut me over the shoulders, Plaut. As. 3, 2, 7; 2, 2, 49; id. Cas. 5, 3, 14; id. Ep. 1, 2, 22; id. Poen. 1, 1, 25; id. Pers. 1, 1, 32; id. Trin. 4, 3, 2; id. Truc. 4, 3, 19; Ter. Phorm. 1, 2, 26; Sen. Ira
scapulae.short: scăpŭlae, ārum, f., the shoulder-blades, in men and animals.

scapus.full: scapus, i, m. root skap-; Gr. σκήπτω, to prop, σκῆπτρον; Doric, σκᾶπος; cf.: scipio, scamnum, scopus; Engl. shaft, a shaft, stem, stalk, trunk, etc. In gen., Varr. R. R. 1, 31, 5; Col. 9, 4, 4; Plin. 18, 10, 21, § 95; Sen. Ep. 86, 17.— In partic. A cylinder on which sheets of paper or leaves of papyrus were rolled, Plin. 13, 12, 23, § 77.— A sheet of paper: aliquid papyri illinere scapo, Varr. ap. Non. 168, 14.— A weaver's yarn-beam, Lucr. 5, 1353.— The shaft of a column, Vitr. 3, 2 sq.— The sha

scarabaeus.full: scărăbaeus, i, m., = σκαράβειος σκάραβος), a beetle, scarab, scarabee, Plin. 11, 28, 34, § 97; 30, 11, 30, § 99; Aus. Epigr. 70, 10.
scarabaeus.short: scărăbaeus, i, m., = σκαράβειος σκάραβος), a beetle, scarab, scarabee, Plin.

scardia.full: scardĭa, ae, f., a plant, also called aristolochia, App. Herb. 19.
scardia.short: scardĭa, ae, f., a plant, also called aristolochia, App.

scardus.full: Scardus (Scordus), i, m., a mountain in Illyria, now Sharradagh or Tchardagh, Liv. 43, 20.
scardus.short: Scardus (Scordus), i, m., a mountain in Illyria, now Sharradagh or Tchardagh, Liv.

scarifatio.full: scărīfātĭo (scărīphātĭo; later collat. form scărīfĭcātĭo, Veg. 4, 21, 1), ōnis, f. scarifo, a scratching open; of the skin, a scarifying, Col. 6, 12, 1; 6, 17, 1; 6, 17, 4; Veg. 4, 21, 1.—Of the bark of a tree, Plin. 17, 27, 42, § 251.—Of the ground for planting, Plin. 18, 16, 39, § 140.

scarifo.full: scărīfo (-īpho; later collat. form scă-rīfĭco, Pall. 4, 10, 28; cf. pass. scarifio, Scrib. 262 dub.), āvi, ātum, 1, v. a., = σκα^ρῖφάομαι, to scratch open, scarify: gingivas, Plin. 32, 7, 26, § 79: truncum arboris, Pall. Mart. 10, 28: sinapi compressum, Col. 12, 57, 1: dentes, Plin. 28, 11, 49, § 179; cf. id. 30, 3, 8, § 21.

scaritis.full: scărītis, ĭdis, f., = σκαρῖτις, a precious stone, resembling in color the fish scarus, Plin. 37, 11, 72, § 187.
scaritis.short: scărītis, ĭdis, f., = σκαρῖτις, a precious stone, resembling in color the fish scarus, Plin.

scarphea.full: Scarphēa (-ĭ_a), ae, f. A town of Locris, near Thermopylœ, Liv. 32, 3; 36, 20; Plin. 4, 7, 12, § 27.— An island of the Ægean Sea, Plin. 4, 12, 20, § 62.

scarus.full: scărus (scārus, Enn. ap. App. Mag. p. 299), i, m., = σκάρος, scar, a kind of seafish much esteemed by the Romans; acc. to some, a species of wrasse: Labrus scarus, Linn.; Plin. 9, 17, 29, § 62; Ov. Hal. 9; 119; Col. 8, 16, 1 and 9; Enn. l. l.; Hor. S. 2, 2, 22; id. Epod. 2, 50; Mart. 13, 84; Fest. s. v. pollucere, p. 253: scarorum jocinora, Suet. Vit. 13.

scatebra.full: scătĕ_bra, ae, f. scateo, a bubbling or gushing up of water (not ante-Aug., and very rare): fontium, Plin. 5, 1, 1, § 6: fonticuli, id. 31, 10, 46, § 108.— Transf.: (unda) scatebris arentia temperat arva, spring - water, bubbling water, Verg. G. 1, 110; cf. scaturex and scaturigines.

scateo.full: scăteo, ēre (ante-class. also scatit, Lucr. 5, 40; 6, 891; and scatĕre, Enn. ap. Cic. Tusc. 1, 28, 69, or Trag. v. 196 Vahl.; Lucr. 5, 598; 5, 952; 6, 896; perf. and sup. wanting), v. n. etym. dub.; cf. Lith. skas-, leap, to bubble, gush, well, spring, or flow forth (poet.; not before the Aug. period in prose). Lit.: fontes scatere, Enn. l. l.; cf.: fons dulcis aquaï qui scatit et salsas circum se dimovet undas, Lucr. 6, 891 sq.; and (with erumpere) id. 5, 952; 5, 598.— Transf., = abundo. To be

scaturex.full: scătūrex, igis, m. scaturio, a bubbling or gushing spring, Varr, ap. Non. 172, 27; cf. scaturigines and scatebra.

scaturigines.full: scătūrīgĭnes, um, f. id., gushing or bubbling waters, spring-water, Liv. 44, 33; Front. Aquaed. 10: in nigrā (terrā) scaturigines perennes, Plin. 31, 3, 28, § 47.— Transf., of other fluids: sanguinis, Amm. 19, 1, 9.

scaturiginosus.full: scătūrīgĭnōsus, a, um, adj. scaturigines, full of or abounding in springs, springy: terra, i. e. boggy, marshy, Col. 5, 8, 6.

scaturio.full: scătūrĭo, īre (imperf. scaturribat, App. M. 4, p. 145, 8), v. n. scateo, to stream, flow, or gush out (not before the Aug. period, and very rare). Lit.: scaturiens aqua, Pall. 1, 33 fin.: de summo vertice fons scaturribat (i. e. -riebat), App. M. 4, 6, p. 145, 8: oleum de terrā, Ampel. Lib. Mem. 8, § 5.— Transf., like scateo. To come forth in great numbers, to swarm, abound: vermiculi, Auct. Priap. 4, 6 fin.: vermes, Vulg. 2 Macc. 9, 9.— To be full of, filled with, abound in a thing. Lit.: solum

scaurianus.full: Scaurĭānus, a, um, v. 2. Scaurus. † scaurus, a, um, adj., = σκαῦρος [cf. σκαιός], with large and swollen ankles, having the ankles bunching out (cf.: varus, valgus), Plin. 11, 45, 105, § 254: illum Balbutit scaurum pravis fultum male talis, Hor. S. 1, 3, 48.

scaurus.full: Scaurus, i, m. 1. scaurus, a frequent surname in the gens Aemilia and Aurelia. So, M. Aemilius Scaurus, whom Cicero defended in an oration, part of which is still extant.—Hence, Scaurĭānus, a, um, adj., relating to Scaurus: oratio, Mart. Cap. 5, § 441.

scazon.full: scāzon, ontis, m., = σκάζων (limping), an iambic trimeter, with a spondee or trochee in the last foot, Plin. Ep. 5, 11, 2; cf. Mart. 1, 97, 1; 7, 25, 1.
scazon.short: scāzon, ontis, m., = σκάζων (limping), an iambic trimeter, with a spondee or trochee in the last foot, Plin.

scelerate.full: scĕlĕrātē, adv., v. scelero, P. a. fin.

scelerator.full: scĕlĕrātor, is, m. scelero, an evil doer, a wretch (late Lat.), Adaman. Columb. 3, 7.

sceleratus.full: scĕlĕrātus, a, um, Part. and P. a. of scelero.

sceleritas.full: scĕlĕrĭtas, ātis, f. scelus, guilt, wickedness, criminality (late Lat.): facti, Dig. 48, 21, 3.

scelero.full: scĕlĕro, no perf., ātum, 1, v. a. id., to pollute, defile, contaminate, desecrate (in the verb. finit. rare, and only poet.; syn.: temero, polluo): impia non verita est divos scelerare parentes, Cat. 64, 405; cf. Stat. Th. 2, 663: sanguine fauces, id. ib. 8, 761: parce pias scelerare manus, Verg. A. 3, 42: Cererem, Juv. 9, 25: animum, Sil. 16, 122; cf.: dextram sanguine, Stat. Th. 9, 666. —Hence, scĕlĕrātus, a, um, P. a., polluted, profaned by crime. Lit. (appellatively; only in the poets): terr

scelerosus.full: scĕlĕrōsus, a, um, adj. scelus, full of wickedness, vicious, abominable, accursed (ante- and post-class.): ubi ego illum scelerosum et impium inveniam? Ter. Eun. 4, 3, 1: scelerosa et polluta mulier, App. M. 10, p. 253, 2: scelerosa atque impia facta, Lucr. 1, 82: o diem scelerosum et indignum, Afr. ap. Non. 174, 29.—As subst.: scĕlĕrōsus, i, m., a wicked or vicious person, a wretch, Lucil. ap. Non. 174, 27.

scelerus.full: scĕlĕrus, a, um, adj. id., wicked, abominable: sinapis, Plaut. Ps. 3, 2, 28: caput, id. ib. 5, 1, 3; cf. Serv Verg. A. 9, 486.

scelestus.full: scĕlestus, a, um, adj. scelus; like funestus, from funus, wicked, villanous, infamous, accursed, abominable; knavish, roguish; and subst., a wicked person, a knave, rogue, scoundrel, miscreant (freq. ante-class. in Plaut. and Ter.; after the class. per. sceleratus is more freq.; by Cic. not used of persons). Lit., of persons: ego sum malus, Ego sum sacer, scelestus, Plaut. Bacch. 4, 6, 14: eheu, scelestus galeam in navi perdidi, id. Rud. 3, 5, 22: perjuravisti, sceleste, id. Ps. 1, 3, 120 sq.: o

sceletus.full: scĕlĕtus, i, m., = σκελετός, a skeleton: eviscerata forma diri cadaveris, App. Mag. pp. 313, 35, and 315, 9 sq.
sceletus.short: scĕlĕtus, i, m., = σκελετός, a skeleton: eviscerata forma diri cadaveris, App.

scelio.full: scĕlĭo, ōnis, m. scelus, a wicked man, scoundrel: magnus scelio, Petr. 50, 5.

scelotyrbe.full: scĕlŏtyrbē, ēs, f., = σκελοτύρβη, a lameness in the ankles or in the knees, Plin. 25, 3, 6, § 20.
scelotyrbe.short: scĕlŏtyrbē, ēs, f., = σκελοτύρβη, a lameness in the ankles or in the knees, Plin.

scelus.full: scĕlus, ĕris, n. Sanscr. root skhal, to fall, akin to khal-, to deceive; cf. Goth. skal, to owe, an evil deed; a wicked, heinous, or impious action; a crime, sin, enormity, wickedness (the strongest general term for a morally bad act or quality; very freq. both in sing. and plur.; cf. nefas). Lit. Absol.: facinus est vincire civem Romanum, scelus verberare, prope parricidium necare, Cic. Verr. 2, 5, 66, § 170; cf. so (opp. to flagitia and delicta) Tac. G. 12: majus in sese scelus concipere nefar

scena2.full: scēna ab aliis, a quibusdam sacena appellatur, dolabra pontificalis, Fest. pp. 330 and 319 Müll.
scena2.short: scēna ab aliis, a quibusdam sacena appellatur, dolabra pontificalis, Fest.

scenarius.full: scēnārĭus, scēnĭcus, etc., v. scaenarius, scaenicus, etc.

scenites.full: scēnītes, ae, m., = σκηνίτης, one who dwells in a tent, one of a nomadic race: Nomades, Plin. 6, 28, 32, § 143: Sabaei, id. 6, 28, 32, § 151: Arabes, id. 5, 24, 21, § 87.
scenites.short: scēnītes, ae, m., = σκηνίτης, one who dwells in a tent, one of a nomadic race: Nomades, Plin.

scenofactorius.full: scēnŏfactōrĭus, a, um, adj. σκῆνος -facio, of or belonging to the making of tents: ars, the business of tent-making, Vulg. Act. 18, 3.

scenopegia.full: scēnŏpēgĭa, ae, f., = σκηνοπηγία, the Jewish Feast of Tabernacles (eccl. Lat.), Vulg. 1 Macc. 10, 21; id. 2 Macc. 1, 18; id. Johan. 7, 2.
scenopegia.short: scēnŏpēgĭa, ae, f., = σκηνοπηγία, the Jewish Feast of Tabernacles (eccl.

scepsis.full: Scēpsis, is, f., = Σκῆψις, a town in Mysia, Plin. 5, 30, 32, § 122.—Hence, Scēp-sĭus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Scepsis: Metrodorus, of Scepsis, Cic. Tusc. 1, 24, 59; Plin. 34, 7, 16, § 34; also called simply Scepsius, Ov. P. 4, 14, 38.
scepsis.short: Scēpsis, is, f., = Σκῆψις, a town in Mysia, Plin.

sceptici.full: Sceptĭci, ōrum, m., = Σκεπτικοί, the Sceptics, the disciples of Pyrrho, Quint. 10, 1, 124.
sceptici.short: Sceptĭci, ōrum, m., = Σκεπτικοί, the Sceptics, the disciples of Pyrrho, Quint.

sceptos.full: scēptos, i, m., = σκηπτός, a gust, squall, storm, that rushes from above, App. de Mundo, p. 64, 5.
sceptos.short: scēptos, i, m., = σκηπτός, a gust, squall, storm, that rushes from above, App.

sceptrifer.full: scēptrĭfer, fĕra, fĕrum, adj. sceptrum-fero, sceptre-bearing (poet.): manus Servi, Ov. F. 6, 480: Tonantes, i.e. Jupiter and Juno, Sen. Med. 59.

sceptriger.full: scēptrĭger, ĕra, ĕrum, adj. sceptrumgero, sceptre-bearing (poet. and post-Aug.): Laii, Stat. Th. 11, 636: rex, Sil. 16, 245.

sceptrum.full: scēptrum, i (less correctly scaep-trum), n., = σκῆπτρον, a royal staff, a sceptre. Lit.: (rex Ptolemaeus) sedens cum purpurā et sceptro et illis insignibus regiis, Cic. Sest. 26, 57; Quint. 9, 3, 57; 11, 3, 158; Suet. Aug. 94: Augusti, id. Galb. 1; Verg. A. 7, 247: dextrā sceptrum gerebat, id. ib. 12, 206; Ov. M. 7, 103; 1, 178; 2, 847; 5, 422. Also borne by a king's daughter, Verg. A. 1, 653 Heyne: exitiale, Stat. Th. 1, 34; of a triumphant general, Liv. 5, 41; Juv. 10, 43.—Poet., in the plur.,
sceptrum.short: scēptrum, i (less correctly scaep-trum), n., = σκῆπτρον, a royal staff, a sceptre.

sceptuchus.full: scēptūchus, i, m., = σκηπτοῦχος, a sceptre-bearer, a high officer of state in the East, Tac. A. 6, 33.
sceptuchus.short: scēptūchus, i, m., = σκηπτοῦχος, a sceptre-bearer, a high officer of state in the East, Tac.

schedius.full: schĕdĭus, a, um, adj., = σχέδιος, made suddenly or off-hand; hastily put or thrown together; hence, as in the Greek subst., schĕdĭa, ae, f., = σχεδία (sc. ναῦς), a raft, float, constructed in haste, Dig. 14, 1, 1, § 6; cf. Fest. pp. 334 and 335 Müll.— schĕdĭum, ii, n. (sc. carmen), an extemporaneous poem: Lucilianae humilitatis, Petr. 4 fin.; App. de Deo Socr. p. 364, 34; Aus. Idyll. 7 praef.; Sid. Ep. 8, 3; cf. Fest. l. l.
schedius.short: schĕdĭus, a, um, adj., = σχέδιος, made suddenly or off-hand;

schedula.full: schĕdŭla (scĭdŭla), ae, f. dim. scheda or scida, a small leaf of paper, Hier. in Ruf. 3, 2.

schema.full: schēma, ae, f. (cf.: diadema, dogma, etc., Prisc. p. 679 P.), and (mostly post-Aug.) ătis, n. (dat. and abl. plur. schemasin, Varr. ap. Charis. p. 38; but schematibus, Lampr. Heliog. 19), = σχῆμα. In gen., a shape, figure, form, fashion, manner, posture, attitude, etc. (so mostly ante-class.; not in Cic.). Fem.: quod processi huc cum servili schemā, Plaut. Am. prol. 117; cf. Caecil. ap. Prisc. p. 679 P.: Tiara ut lepidam lepide condecorat schemam, Plaut. Pers. 4, 2, 2 Ritschl; cf. Prisc. l. l.;

schematismos.full: schēmătismos, i, m., = σχηματισμός, a figurative or florid manner of speaking, Quint. 1, 8, 14.
schematismos.short: schēmătismos, i, m., = σχηματισμός, a figurative or florid manner of speaking, Quint.

schidia.full: schĭdĭa, ae, f., = σχίδαι or σχίδια, a chip, splinter of wood, Vitr. 2, 1; 7, 10.
schidia.short: schĭdĭa, ae, f., = σχίδαι or σχίδια, a chip, splinter of wood, Vitr.

schinus.full: schīnus, i, f., = σχῖνος, the mastic-tree (pure Lat. lentiscus), Vulg. Dan. 13, 54.
schinus.short: schīnus, i, f., = σχῖνος, the mastic-tree (pure Lat.

schisma.full: schisma, ătis, n., = σχίσμα, a split, separation, disunion, schism (eccl. Lat.), Tert. Praescr. 5; Prud. στεφ. 11, 19; 11, 30; Vulg. Johan. 9, 16.
schisma.short: schisma, ătis, n., = σχίσμα, a split, separation, disunion, schism (eccl.

schismaticus.full: schismătĭcus, i, m., = σχισματικός, a separatist, seceder, schismatic (eccl. Lat.): schismaticos non fides diversa facit, sed communionis disrupta societas, Aug. Quaest. in Matt. 11.
schismaticus.short: schismătĭcus, i, m., = σχισματικός, a separatist, seceder, schismatic (eccl.

schistos.full: schistos, a, on, adj., = σχιστός, split, cleft, divided; a t. t. in Pliny the Elder: lapis, that easily cleaves or cracks, fissile, schistose, a name given to a kind of red oxide of iron, Plin. 29, 6, 38, § 124; 33, 4, 25, § 84; 36, 20, 37, § 144: lac, i. e. curdled, id. 28, 9, 33, § 126: caepa, a peculiar kind, id. 19, 6, 32, § 101: alumen, id. 31, 7, 39, § 79.
schistos.short: schistos, a, on, adj., = σχιστός, split, cleft, divided;

schoeneus.full: Schoeneus, ei, m., = Σχοινεύς, a king of Bœotia, father of Atalanta, Hyg. Fab. 244; 246.—Hence, Schoenēïs, ĭdis, f., the daughter of Schœneus, Atalanta, Ov. H. (15) 16, 263; id. Am. 1, 7, 13.— Schoe-nēïus, a, um, adj., of or pertaining to Schœneus: virgo, i. e. Atalanta, Ov. M. 10, 660; id. Tr. 2, 399; and absol.: Schoe-nēïa, ae, f., Atalanta, id. M. 10, 609.— Schoenis, ĭdis, f., Atalanta, Sid. Carm. 14, 14.
schoeneus.short: Schoeneus, ei, m., = Σχοινεύς, a king of Bœotia, father of Atalanta, Hyg.

schoeniculae.full: schoenĭcŭlae, ārum, f. schoenum, prostitutes anointed with schoenum, Plaut. ap. Varr. L. L. 7, § 64 Müll.; id. ap. Fest. pp. 328 and 329 ib.

schoenobates.full: schoenŏbătes, ae, m., = σχοινοβάτης, a rope-dancer, Juv. 3, 77.
schoenobates.short: schoenŏbătes, ae, m., = σχοινοβάτης, a rope-dancer, Juv.

schoenus.full: schoenus, i, m. (neutr. collat. form schoenum, Col. 12, 20, 2 and 5, somewhat dub.), = σχοῖνος, ὁ. A rush, of an aromatic kind (pure Lat. juncus), used by the Romans to season wine, Cato, R. R. 105, 2; 113, 1; Col. 12, 20, 2; 12, 20, 5; 12, 53, 2; low women anointed themselves with a perfume made from it: schoeno delibutae, Plaut. Poen. 1, 2, 55 (where others read caeno delibutae); cf. also schoeniculae.— A measure of distance among the Persians (= 40 stadia), Plin. 6, 26, 30, § 124; 12, 14, 30,

schola.full: schŏla (scŏla), ae, f., = σχολή (spare time, leisure; hence, in partic.), Leisure given to learning, a learned conversation or debate, a disputation, lecture, dissertation, etc.: in quam exercitationem (disputandi) ita nos studiose operam dedimus, ut jam etiam scholas Graecorum more habere auderemus ... Itaque dierum quinque scholas, ut Graeci appellant, in totidem libros contuli, Cic. Tusc. 1, 4, 7; 8: separatim certae scholae sunt de exsilio, de interitu patriae, etc. ... Haec Graeci in singul
schola.short: schŏla (scŏla), ae, f., = σχολή (spare time, leisure;

scholaris.full: schŏlāris, e, adj. schola. Of or belonging to a school (late Lat.): incohamenta, Mart. Cap. 3, § 326: murmur, Prud. στεφ. 9, 16: declamatio, Hier. Ep. 36, 14.— (Acc. to schola, I. B. 2. b.) Subst.: schŏlāres, ĭum, m., the imperial guard, Cod. Th. 11, 18, 1; 7, 4, 34; Cod. Just. 12, 38, 14.

scholasticus.full: schŏlastĭcus, a, um. Adj. = σχολαστικός, of or belonging to a school, scholastic (post-Aug., and in gen. referring to the schools of rhetoric): controversiae, Quint. 4, 2, 92; 4, 2, 97; Tac. Or. 14 fin.: materia, Quint. 11, 1, 82: declamationes, Gell. 15, 1, 1: scholasticae atque umbraticae litterae, Plin. Ep. 9, 2, 3: lex, id. ib. 2, 20, 9.— As subst.: schŏlastĭca, ōrum, n. plur., school-exercises: in scholasticis nonnumquam evenit, ut pro narratione sit propositio, Quint. 4, 2, 30; 7, 1, 14.—

scholicus.full: schŏlĭcus, a, um, adj., = σχολικός, of or belonging to a school, school- (anteand post-class.): dape, Varr. ap. Non. 452, 1: quaedam nugalia, Gell. 4, 1, 1: axioma, Mart. Cap. 4, § 327.
scholicus.short: schŏlĭcus, a, um, adj., = σχολικός, of or belonging to a school, school- (anteand post-class.): dape, Varr.

sciadeus.full: scĭădeus, ĕi, m., and scĭaena, ae, f., = σκιαδεύς and σκίαινα, the male and female of a sea-fish; perh. a kind of grayling or ombre: Salmo thymallus, Linn.; Plin. 32, 11, 53, § 151.
sciadeus.short: scĭădeus, ĕi, m., and scĭaena, ae, f., = σκιαδεύς and σκίαινα, the male and female of a sea-fish;

sciapodes.full: Sciāpŏdes (Scĭŏpŏdes), um, m., = Σκιάποσες, a fabulous people in Libya, with monstrously large soles to their feet, which they were said to turn up and use as umbrellas, Plin. 7, 2, 2, § 23; Tert. Apol. 8; Aug. Civ. Dei, 16, 8.
sciapodes.short: Sciāpŏdes (Scĭŏpŏdes), um, m., = Σκιάποσες, a fabulous people in Libya, with monstrously large soles to their feet, which they were said to turn up and use as umbrellas, Plin.

sciathos.full: Scĭăthos (-us), i, f., = Σκίαθος, a small island in the Sinus Thermaicus, with a town of the same name, now still Skiatho, Mel. 2, 7; Plin. 4, 12, 23, § 72; Liv. 31, 28; 31, 45; 44, 13; Val. Fl. 2, 8.
sciathos.short: Scĭăthos (-us), i, f., = Σκίαθος, a small island in the Sinus Thermaicus, with a town of the same name, now still Skiatho, Mel.

scibilis.full: scībĭlis, e, adj. scio, that can be known, knowable, discernible (post-class.): Deus non omnibus scibilis, Tert. adv. Marc. 5, 16: scientia rei, Mart. Cap. 4, § 375.

scida.full: scĭda or schĕda, ae, f., = σχίδν, σχέδη, a strip of papyrus bark, Plin. 13, 12, 23, § 77.—Form scheda, a leaf or sheet of paper, Cic. Att. 1, 20, 7; id. Fam. 15, 16, 1; Quint. 1, 8, 19; Mart. 4, 89, 4 (form scheda; al. scida).
scida.short: scĭda or schĕda, ae, f., = σχίδν, σχέδη, a strip of papyrus bark, Plin.

sciens.full: scĭens, entis, Part. and P. a., from scio.

scienter.full: scĭenter, adv., v. scio, P. a. fin.

scientia.full: scĭentĭa, ae, f. (plur. only Vitr. 1, 1, 18; 3, praef. 1) [sciens], a knowing or being skilled in any thing, knowledge, science, skill, expertness, = cognitio, eruditio (freq. and class.). Absol.: aut scire istarum rerum nihil, aut, etiamsi maxime sciemus, nec meliores ob eam scientiam nec beatiores esse possumus, Cic. Rep. 1, 19, 32: se a scientiae delectatione ad efficiendi utilitatem referre, id. ib. 5, 3, 5: Antiochus ingenio scientiāque putatur excellere, id. Ac. 2, 2, 4: omnes trahimur ad

scientiola.full: scĭentĭŏla, ae, f. dim. scientia, a little knowledge, a smattering, Aug. Civ. Dei, 11, 31: parvas concinnavit scientiolas artium, Arn. 2, 56.

scilicet.full: scīlĭcet, adv. contr. from sci- (root of scire) licet; cf. vide-licet, i-licet, or scīre lĭcet, as it is freq. written in Lucr. and in archaic lang. in Liv., and sometimes in Cels.; prop., you may understand or know, = Gr. δηλονότι, and serving to imply that a statement is in itself obviously true, and is not overlooked by the speaker (cf. Madv. ad Cic. Fin. 5, 1, 3). Lit., it is evident, clear, plain, or manifest; of course, naturally, evidently, certainly, undoubtedly, etc. (freq. and class.;

scilla.full: scĭlla (squilla), ae, f., = σκίλλα. A sea-onion, sea-leek, squill: Scilla maritima, Linn.; Plin. 19, 5, 30, § 93; 20, 9, 39, § 97; 21, 17, 66, § 106; Varr. R. R. 2, 7, 8; Col. 12, 33; 12, 34; Pall. Febr. 29, 2; id. Mart. 10, 4; id. Jul. 8, 1 al.— A small fish of the lobster kind, which defends the pinna, a prawn, shrimp: Cancer squilla, Linn.; in this sense more usually written squilla, Cic. N. D. 2, 48, 123; Plin. 9, 42, 66, § 142; Lucil. ap. Cic. Fin. 2, 8, 24; Hor. S. 2, 4, 58; 2, 8, 42; Mart

scillinus.full: scillĭnus, a, um, adj., = σκίλλινος, of sea-onions or squills: acetum, vinegar flavored with squills, Plin. 23, 2, 28, § 59; also called acetum scilliticum (σκιλλιτικόν), Cels. 5, 19, 19; Col. 12, 34; Plin. 32, 10, 47, § 135; Ser. Samm. 510.
scillinus.short: scillĭnus, a, um, adj., = σκίλλινος, of sea-onions or squills: acetum, vinegar flavored with squills, Plin.

scillites.full: scillītes, ae, m., = σκιλλίτης (οἶνος), wine seasoned with squills, Col. 12, 33; Pall. Jul. 6.—Hence, also, acetum scillites, Plin. 26, 8, 48, § 77; Aus. Ep. 4, 69.
scillites.short: scillītes, ae, m., = σκιλλίτης (οἶνος), wine seasoned with squills, Col.

scimpodion.full: scimpŏdĭon, ii, n., = σκιμπόδιον, a small bed or couch (syn. grabatus): Graeciense, Gell. 19, 10, 1.
scimpodion.short: scimpŏdĭon, ii, n., = σκιμπόδιον, a small bed or couch (syn.

scin'.full: scīn' for scisne, v. scio init.

scincos.full: scincos or -us, i, m., = σκίγκος, a kind of lizard common in Asia and Africa, Plin. 8, 25, 38, § 91; 28, 8, 30, § 119; 32, 5, 16, § 43.
scincos.short: scincos or -us, i, m., = σκίγκος, a kind of lizard common in Asia and Africa, Plin.

scindo.full: scindo, scĭdi, scissum, 3 (old perf. redupl. scicidi, Enn., Naev., Att, and Afran. ap. Prisc. p. 890 P.; or Enn. p. 133 Vanl.; Com. Rel. pp. 19 and 164 Rib.; cf. also, sciciderat. Gell 6, 9, 16), v. a. akin to Gr. σχίζω, to split; cf. Germ. scheiden, and Lat. scio, to cut, tear, rend, or break asunder; to split, cleave, divide, or separate by force, etc. (freq. and class.; but in tempp.perf.ante-class.and postAug.; syn.: findo, rumpo). Lit.: quom saxum scisciderit, Enn. ap. Prisc. l. l.: non erg

scindula.full: scindŭla, ae, f. scindo, a split piece of wood, a shingle; later form of scandula, q. v.

scintilla.full: scintilla, ae, f. dim. kindr. with σπινθήρ, a spark (class.). Lit.; sing.: videmus Accedere ex unā scintillā incendia passim, Lucr. 5, 609; 4, 606; Verg. A. 1, 174; Ov. M. 7, 80; Liv. 38, 7 al.: parva saepe scintilla contempta excitavit incendium, Curt. 6, 3, 11.—Plur., Lucr. 2, 675; 6, 163; Verg. A. 12, 102; Quint. 8, 5, 29 al.— Transf., a bright, sparkling point: nullis ut in auro lucentibus scintillis, Plin. 33, 6, 31, § 95.— Trop., a spark, glimmer, faint trace: scintilla ingenii, Cic. Rep.

scintillatio.full: scintillātĭo, ōnis, f. scintillo, a sparkling: oculorum, as a disease, Plin. 20, 9, 33, § 80.

scintillo.full: scintillo, āvi, 1, v. n. scintilla, to sparkle, glitter, glow, gleam, flash (poet. and in post-Aug. prose; cf. fulguro). Lit.: templa caeli, Lucr. 6, 644: fulgetra, Plin. 2, 43, 43, § 113: clipeus ardens, id. 2, 34, 34, § 100: testā ardente oleum, Verg. G. 1, 392: oculi, Plaut. Men. 5, 2, 77: carbunculi contra radios solis, Plin. 37, 7, 25, § 95: cristae, Sil. 7, 593.— Trop.: scintillavit cruentis Ira genis, Sil. 9, 562: tunc Venus et calidi scintillat fervor amoris, Calp. 5, 22: cupiditatis ard

scintillula.full: scintillŭla, ae, f. dim. id., a little spark, sparklet (rare): eas in pueris virtutum quasi scintillulas videmus, e quibus accendi philosophi ratio debet, Cic. Fin. 5, 15, 43: vitae, Tert. Anim. 23: animae, Plaut. Trin. 2, 4, 91 Fleck.

scio.full: scĭo, īvi, ītum, 4 (old imperf. scibam, Plaut. As. 2, 2, 34; 2, 4, 89; id. Ps. 1, 5, 84; 1, 5, 86; Ter. Heaut. 2, 3, 68; id. Phorm. 4, 1, 16: scibas, Plaut. Aul. 4, 10, 24; id. Ps. 1, 5, 85: scibat, id. Am. prol. 22; Lucr. 5, 934: scibatis, Plaut. Rud. 2, 3, 47: scibant, Lucr. 5, 949; 5, 953; Cat. 68, 85.—Fut. scibo, Plaut. As. 1, 1, 13; id. Most. 4, 3, 5; id. Men. 2, 3, 35; 5, 2, 57; id. Ps. 1, 2, 41; 1, 5, 65; id. Truc. 2, 6, 69; Ter. Eun. 4, 4, 58; id. Ad. 3, 3, 7; 5, 2, 5; id. Hec. 2, 2, 4:

sciolus.full: scĭŏlus, i, m. scius, a smatterer, sciolist, Arn. 2, 86 dub.; Hier. Ep. 48, 18; 58, 5; 125, 16.

sciothericon.full: scĭŏthērĭcon, i, n., = σκιοθηρικόν, a sun-dial, Plin. 2, 76, 78, § 187.—Also called scĭŏthērum (σκιόθηρον), Hyg. Limit. p. 175 Goes.
sciothericon.short: scĭŏthērĭcon, i, n., = σκιοθηρικόν, a sun-dial, Plin.

scipio1.full: scīpĭo, ōnis, m. root skap-; Gr. σκήπτω, to support, σκίπων, = σκῆπτρον, a staff; cf.: scāpus, scopio, scamnum, a staff (carried by persons of wealth, rank, high official station, etc.): unde ornatu hoc advenis? quid fecisti scipione? Plaut. Cas. 5, 4, 6; id. Am. 1, 3, 22; id. As. 1, 1, 111; id. Men. 5, 2, 103; Cat. 37, 10; Plin. 28, 2, 4, § 15: eburneus, carried by the viri triumphales, Liv. 5, 41 fin.; cf. Val. Max. 4, 4, 5; in the time of the emperors, also by the consuls, Val. Imp. ap. Vop.

scipio2.full: Scīpĭo, ōnis, m. 1. scipio, the name of a celebrated family in the gens Cornelia, the most famous members of which were the two conquerors of the Carthaginians, P. Cornelius Scipio Africanus major, in the second, and P. Cornelius Scipio Aemilianus Africanus minor, in the third Punic war. —In hexameter verse scanned nom. Scīpĭŏ, Luc. 4, 658; Sil. 8, 548; 10, 427; 13, 386; 13, 449 al.; cf., in the foll., 3. init.—Hence, Scīpĭōnĕus, a, um, adj., of the Scipios (late Lat.), Fab. Cl. Gord. Fulg. Act.

scirerytis.full: scīrĕrўtis, ĭdis, f., a sort of silver dross, Plin. 33, 6, 35, § 108.
scirerytis.short: scīrĕrўtis, ĭdis, f., a sort of silver dross, Plin.

sciron1.full: Scīron, ōnis, m., = Σκίρων (Σκείρων). A noted robber on the rocky coast between Megaris and Attica, destroyed by Theseus, Ov. M. 7, 444 sq.; Stat. Th. 1, 333; Mel. 2, 3, 7; Gell. 15, 21, 1; Claud. in Rufin. 1, 253. —Hence, Scīrōnĭus, a, um, adj., of Sciron, Scironic: saxa, Mel. 2, 3, 7; so Plin. 4, 7, 11, § 23; Sen. Hippol. 1225; and, rupes, Claud. B. Get. 188 (cf. also: infames Scirone petras, Stat. Th. 1, 333).— Scī-rōnis, ĭdis, adj. f., Scironic: petrae, Sen. Hippol. 1023.—Hence, A north-west

sciron2.full: Scīron, ōnis, m., an Epicurean philosopher in Cicero's time: omnia meminit Sciron Epicuri dogmata, Cic. Ac. 2, 33, 106.
sciron2.short: Scīron, ōnis, m., an Epicurean philosopher in Cicero's time: omnia meminit Sciron Epicuri dogmata, Cic.

scirpeus.full: scirpĕus (sirp-), a, um scirpus. Adj., of rushes, rush-: ratis, Plaut. Aul. 4, 1, 9: clava, Nov. ap. Fest. s. v. scirpus, p. 330 Müll.: simulacra, i. e. images of men made of rushes, which were thrown into the Tiber annually, Ov. F. 5, 622 (v. Argei); also imago, id. ib. 5, 659: fila, a rush-wick of wax tapers, Prud. Cath. 5, 15: fiscella, Vulg. Exod. 2, 3.— Subst.: scirpĕa (sirp-), ae, f., a basket-work of rushes to form the body of a wagon (generally used for carrying manure), Varr. L. L. 5, §

scirpiculus.full: scirpĭcŭlus (sirp- and surp-), a, um id.. Adj., of or made of rushes. So with falces (their use is unknown), Cato, R. R. 11, 4; Varr. R. R. 1, 22, 5; id. L. L. 5, § 137 Müll.: fiscella, Vulg. Exod. 2, 3.—More freq., Subst.: scirpĭcŭlus (sirp-, surp-), i, m., a basket made of rushes, a rush-basket: surpiculi olerorum, Lucil. ap. Non. 490, 24; Varr. R. R. 2, 2, 10; Col. poët. 10, 305; Prop. 4 (5), 2, 40. piscarii, wears, weels, Plaut. Capt. 4, 2, 36.
scirpiculus.short: scirpĭcŭlus (sirp- and surp-), a, um id..

scirpo.full: scirpo (sirpo), no perf., ātum, 1, v. a. id., to plait of rushes, Varr. L. L. 5, § 137 sq.; id. ap. Non. 83, 24.

scirpula.full: scirpŭla vitis, a kind of vine, otherwise unknown, Plin. 14, 3, 4, § 41; so, uva, Col. 3, 2, 27; Plin. 14, 9, 11, § 81.
scirpula.short: scirpŭla vitis, a kind of vine, otherwise unknown, Plin.

scirpus.full: scirpus (sometimes sirpus), i, m. A rush, bulrush, Plin. 16, 37, 70, § 178; 7, 56, 57, § 206; Fest. p. 330 Müll.; Plaut. Rud. 2, 6, 39; Vulg. Job, 8, 11. — Prov.: nodum in scirpo quaerere, to seek a knot in a bulrush, to find a difficulty where there is none: quaerunt in scirpo, soliti quod dicere, nodum, Enn. ap. Fest. p. 330 (Sat. v. 46 Vahl.); so, in scirpo nodum quaeris, Plaut. Men. 2, 1, 22; and: nodum in scirpo quaeris, Ter. And. 5, 4, 38.— Transf., deriving the idea of intricacy from plai

scirros.full: scirros, i, m., = σκίρρος, a hard swelling or tumor, Plin. 7, 15, 13, § 63.
scirros.short: scirros, i, m., = σκίρρος, a hard swelling or tumor, Plin.

scirrosis.full: scirrōsis, is, f., = σκίρρωσις, a hardening in the flesh, = saxitas, Cael. Aur. Tard. 3, 4, 49.
scirrosis.short: scirrōsis, is, f., = σκίρρωσις, a hardening in the flesh, = saxitas, Cael.

sciscitatio.full: sciscĭtātĭo, ōnis, f. sciscitor, an asking, inquiry: diligentissima sciscitatio, Petr. 24, 5.

sciscitator.full: sciscĭtātor, ōris, m. id., an inquirer, examiner, investigator (post-Aug.): urinae, Mart. 3, 82, 16; Prud. Cath. 7, 193: minutissimus artium, Amm. 22, 16, 16.

sciscitor.full: sciscĭtor, ātus, 1, v. dep. a. [scisco], to inform one's self; to ask, inquire, question, examine, interrogate, etc. (class.; syn.: percontor, interrogo); constr. regularly, ex (ab) aliquo aliquid, de aliquā re, with a rel.clause or absol.; also (post-Aug.) with aliquem quid. With acc. rei: Epicuri ex Velleio sciscitabar sententiam, Cic. N. D. 1, 7, 17: sententiam ex aliquo (with requirere), id. de Or. 1, 23, 105: id sciscitari, id. Or. 16, 52: consulis voluntatem, Liv. 7, 26. consilium ejus, Ta

scisco.full: scisco, scīvi, scītum, 3 (dep. collat. form sciscor, acc. to Prisc. p. 799 P.), v. inch. a. [scio], to seek to know; to search, inquire. Lit. (ante-class. and very rare; cf., on the other hand, the deriv. sciscitor): praefestinamus, quae sit causa, sciscere, Afran. ap. Charis. p. 186 P.: ibo ad eam, ut sciscam, quid velint, Att. ap. Non. 505, 12; cf. Plaut. Am. 5, 1, 17.— Transf. Publicists' t. t., of the people, after inquiry or examination, to accept, approve, assent to something proposed; hen

scissilis.full: scissĭlis, e, adj. scindo. That may easily be split, cleft, or rent: alumen, Cels. 5, 2; 6, 11: lapis, id. 6, 6, 30.— (Postclass.) scissus, a, um, rent, torn: palliastrum, App. M. 1, p. 104, 27; cf. centunculus, id. 9, p. 222, 27: fasciae, Veg. 3, 47, 3.

scissim.full: scissim, adv. id., by rending, cleaving, or dividing (late Lat.), Prud. Enchir. Vet. Test. 9.

scissio.full: scissĭo, ōnis, f. id., a cleaving, dividing, scission of a number (late Lat.), Macr. Somn. Scip. 1, 6; Vulg. Amos, 6, 12.

scissis.full: Scissis, is, f., a town of Hispania Tarraconensis, probably in the territory of the Lacetani, Liv. 21, 60 fin.
scissis.short: Scissis, is, f., a town of Hispania Tarraconensis, probably in the territory of the Lacetani, Liv.

scissor.full: scissor, ōris, m. scinde. One who cleaves or divides, a carver, Petr. 36, 6.— A kind of gladiator, Inscr. Orell. 2569.

scissura.full: scissūra, ae, f. id., a tearing, rending, dividing; a rent, cleft, scissure (postAug.). Lit., Sen. Q. N. 6, 2: ad scissuram Nili, Plin. 5, 9, 9, § 50; 11, 28, 34, § 100: sal rectis scissuris, id. 31, 7, 39, § 79; Pall. Mai, 12; Vulg. Matt. 9, 16.— Trop.: domestica turbat rem populi, Prud. Psych. 756: audio scissuras esse inter vos, Vulg. 1 Cor. 11, 18.

scissus1.full: scissus, a, um, Part. and P. a. of scindo.

scissus2.full: scissus = σχίσμα, a rent, cleft, Gloss. Philox.
scissus2.short: scissus = σχίσμα, a rent, cleft, Gloss.

scitamenta.full: scītāmenta, ōrum, n. 1. scitus, A. 2.. Delicate food, dainties (ante- and postclass.), Plaut. Men. 1, 3, 26: Matius ap. Gell. 20, 9, 3; Macr. S. 7, 14; App. M. 10, p. 245. —* Trop., of figures of speech, niceties, prettinesses: 'Ομοιοτέλευτα ... καὶ ὁμοιόπτωτα ceteraque hujusmodi scitamenta, Gell. 18, 8, 1.

scitatio.full: scītātĭo, ōnis, f. scitor, an asking, inquiring: indefessa scitatio, Amm. 18, 5, 1.

scite.full: scītē, adv., v. scisco, P. a. fin.

scitor.full: scītor, ātus, 1 (old inf. scitarier, Ov. M. 2, 741), v. freq. dep. a. [scio], to seek to know; to ask, inquire (poet. and late Lat.; in Cic. Or. 16, 52, read sciscitari; cf.: interrogo, percunctor): scitari et quaerere causas, Verg. A. 2, 105: causam viae, Ov. M. 2, 511: causam adventūs, id. ib. 2, 741: omnia, id. ib. 2, 548: digna relatu, id. ib. 4, 793: scitanti deus huic de conjuge dixit, id. ib. 10, 564: quid veniat, scitatur, id. ib. 11, 622: Eurypylum scitatum oracula Phoebi Mittimus, i. e

scitulus.full: scītŭlus, a, um, adj. dim. [1. scitus, A. 2.], handsome, pretty, neat, trim, elegant (ante- and post-class.): facies, Plaut. Rud. 2, 7, 7: forma atque aetatula, id. ib. 4, 1, 3; App. M. 2, 113, 19: juvenem formulae scitulae, id. ib. 3, 136, 13: caupona, id. ib. 1, p. 105, 23: pusiones, Arn. 5, 179.—Adv.: scītŭlē, elegantly, gracefully, App. M. 2, p. 123, 8; 7, p. 192, 35; 10, p. 253, 38.

scitum.full: scītum, i, n., v. scisco, P. a., A. 1. and B.

scitus1.full: scītus, a, um, Part. and P. a. of scisco.

scitus2.full: scītus, ūs, m. scisco, with plebi, for the more usual plebiscitum, a decree or ordinance of the people: neque populi jussu neque plebi scitu, Vet. Decr. ap. Cic. Att. 4, 2, 3: comitia deinde de senatūs sententiā plebique scitu sunt habita, Liv. 25, 7, 5.

sciurus.full: scĭūrus, i, m., = σκίουρος, a squirrel, Plin. 8, 38, 58, § 138; 11, 43, 99, § 245; Mart. 5, 37, 13.
sciurus.short: scĭūrus, i, m., = σκίουρος, a squirrel, Plin.

scius.full: scĭus, a, um, adj. scio, knowing, having knowledge of a thing (mostly ante- and post-class., and rare for sciens, gnarus, peritus). Absol.: neque quemquam invenit scium, Pac. ap. Prisc. p. 634: mulieres plus sciae, Petr. 63, 9: puto eos prudentes et scios mendacia defendenda suscipere, knowingly, wittingly, Lact. 3, 24 fin.; Vulg. Ecclus. 21, 18.— With gen.: rerum, Lact. 2, 14, 6: Latinae linguae, Macr. S. 6, 9 fin.

scobina.full: scŏbīna, ae, f. scobis, a rasp, Varr. L. L. 7, § 68; Plaut. Fragm. ib.; Plin. 11, 37, 68, § 180; Tert. Apol. 12.

scobis.full: scŏbis (collat. form scobs, only acc. to Prisc. p. 751 P.; but scobis is found in Cels. 5, 5; 8, 2; Col. 4, 29, 15; 7, 10, 4; cf. scrobis init.), is, f. (m., Vitr. 8, 3; Pall. Febr. 17, 6) [scabo], powder or dust produced by sawing, rasping, etc.; sawdust, scrapings, filings, etc., Cels. 1. 1.; Col. 1. 1.; Hor. S. 2, 4, 81; Plin. 34, 11, 26, § 111; Juv. 14, 67 al.: citreus, i. e. grated lemon-peel, Vitr. 8, 3, 8: cutis, scurf, etc., Plin. 30, 4, 10, § 28.

scodra.full: Scodra, ae, f., a town of Dalmatia, now Scutari, on Lake Labeatis, Liv. 44, 31; 44, 32; 45, 26; Plin. 3, 22, 26, § 144.—Hence, Scodrenses, ium, m., the inhabitants of Scodra, Liv. 45, 26.
scodra.short: Scodra, ae, f., a town of Dalmatia, now Scutari, on Lake Labeatis, Liv.

scolecion.full: scōlēcĭon, ii, n., = σκωλήκιον, a kind of scarlet berry (which is apt to be wormeaten), Plin. 24, 4, 4, § 8.
scolecion.short: scōlēcĭon, ii, n., = σκωλήκιον, a kind of scarlet berry (which is apt to be wormeaten), Plin.

scolex.full: scōlex, lēcis, m., = σκώληξ, a kind of copper rust with the appearance of being worm-eaten, Plin. 34, 12, 28, § 116.
scolex.short: scōlex, lēcis, m., = σκώληξ, a kind of copper rust with the appearance of being worm-eaten, Plin.

scolibrochon.full: scŏlĭbrŏchon, i, n., = σκολίβροχον, a plant, also called callitrichos, scolopendrion, and Capillus Veneris, App. Herb. 47.
scolibrochon.short: scŏlĭbrŏchon, i, n., = σκολίβροχον, a plant, also called callitrichos, scolopendrion, and Capillus Veneris, App.

scolopax.full: scŏlōpax, ăcis, f., = σκολώπαξ, a snipe, woodcock, Nemes. Fragm. Aucup. 2, 3.
scolopax.short: scŏlōpax, ăcis, f., = σκολώπαξ, a snipe, woodcock, Nemes.

scolopendra.full: scŏlŏpendra, ae, f., = σκολόπενδρα. A kind of multipede, a scolopendra, Plin. 8, 29, 43, § 104.— A kind of sea-fish, Plin. 9, 43, 67, § 143.

scolopendrion.full: scŏlŏpendrĭon, ii, n., = σκολοπένδριον, a plant, also called callitrochon and scolibrochon, App. Herb. 57.
scolopendrion.short: scŏlŏpendrĭon, ii, n., = σκολοπένδριον, a plant, also called callitrochon and scolibrochon, App.

scolos.full: Scōlos, i, f., = Σκῶλος, a city of Bœotia, Plin. 4, 7, 12, § 26; Stat. Th. 7, 266.
scolos.short: Scōlos, i, f., = Σκῶλος, a city of Bœotia, Plin.

scolymos.full: scŏlўmos, i, m., = σκόλυμος, an edible kind of thistle, carāoon: Cynara cardunculus, Linn.; Plin. 20, 23, 99, § 262; 21, 16, 56, § 94; 22, 22, 43, § 86.
scolymos.short: scŏlўmos, i, m., = σκόλυμος, an edible kind of thistle, carāoon: Cynara cardunculus, Linn.;

scomber.full: scomber, bri, m., = σκόμβρος, a kind of tunny, a mackerel: Scomber scomber, Linn.; Plin. 9, 15, 19, § 49; 31, 8, 43, § 94; 32, 11, 53, § 151; Col. 8, 17, 12; Plaut. Capt. 4, 2, 71; Cat. 95, 8; Pers. 1, 43; Mart. 3, 50, 9; 4, 87, 8; 13, 102, 2.
scomber.short: scomber, bri, m., = σκόμβρος, a kind of tunny, a mackerel: Scomber scomber, Linn.;

scomma.full: scomma, ătis, n., = σκῶμμα, a teasing, taunting expression; a taunt,jeer, scoff, cavil (late Lat. for convicium, maledictum), Macr. S. 7, 3.
scomma.short: scomma, ătis, n., = σκῶμμα, a teasing, taunting expression;

scopa1.full: scōpa, ae, and plur.: scōpae, ārum (cf. on plur., Varr. L. L. 8, § 7 Müll.; 10, § 24 ib.; Quint. 1, 5, 16; Charis. p. 20 P.; 72 ib.; Diom. p. 315 ib.; sing., v. infra, B.), f. root skap-, to support; cf.: scipio, scamnum. Lit., thin branches, twigs, shoots (rare), Cato, R. R. 152; Pall. 3, 24, 8; 4, 9, 12; Auct. B. Afr. 47, 5; Plin. 20, 22, 89, § 241; 22, 18, 21, § 46 al.— In partic.: scō-pa rēgĭa, a plant, a species of the goosefoot: Chenopodium scoparia, Linn.; Plin. 21, 6, 15, § 28; 25, 5, 19
scopa1.short: scōpa, ae, and plur.: scōpae, ārum (cf.

scopa2.full: scŏpa, ae, f., = σκοπή, a speculation, theory, Mart. Cap. 8, § 812.
scopa2.short: scŏpa, ae, f., = σκοπή, a speculation, theory, Mart.
