selago.full: selāgo, ĭnis, f., a plant resembling the savin-tree: Lycopodium selago, Linn.; Plin. 24, 11, 62, § 103.
selago.short: selāgo, ĭnis, f., a plant resembling the savin-tree: Lycopodium selago, Linn.;

selas.full: sĕlas, plur. sela, n., = σέλας, a kind of fiery meteor, Sen. Q. N. 1, 15, 1; App. Mund. p. 64, 20.

selectio.full: sēlectĭo, ōnis, f. seligo, a choosing out, choice, selection (Ciceron.): cum virtutis hoc proprium sit, earum rerum, quae secundum naturam sint, habere delectum: qui omnia sic exaequaverunt, ut in utramque partem ita paria redderent, uti nullā selectione uterentur, virtutem ipsam sustulerunt, Cic. Fin. 3, 4, 12; cf.: virtutem rerum selectione exspoliare, id. ib. 2, 13, 43; 3, 6, 20: vitiorum, id. Leg. 3, 10, 23.

selector.full: sēlector, ōris, m. id., a chooser, selecter, Aug. Civ. Dei, 7, 3.

selectus.full: sēlectus, a, um, Part. of seligo.

selene.full: Sĕlēnē, ēs, f., = Σελήνη, daughter of Ptolemy Physco, and mother of Antiochus and Seleucus of Syria, Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 27, § 61 Zumpt; Just. 39, 4, 1.
selene.short: Sĕlēnē, ēs, f., = Σελήνη, daughter of Ptolemy Physco, and mother of Antiochus and Seleucus of Syria, Cic.

selenion.full: sĕlēnĭon, ii, n., = σελήνιον, a plant, the peony, App. Herb. 64; called also selenogonon, id. ib. 64.
selenion.short: sĕlēnĭon, ii, n., = σελήνιον, a plant, the peony, App.

selenitis.full: sĕlēnītis, ĭdis, f., or sĕlēnītes, ae, m., = σεληνῖτις, crystalline gypsum, selenite. Form selenitis, Plin. 37, 10, 67, § 181; form selenites, Sol. 37, 31; Aug. Civ. Dei, 21, 5; Isid. 16, 4, 6.
selenitis.short: sĕlēnītis, ĭdis, f., or sĕlēnītes, ae, m., = σεληνῖτις, crystalline gypsum, selenite.

selenitium.full: sĕlēnītĭum, ii, n., a kind of ivy, Plin. 16, 34, 62, § 146 (al. Silenicis).
selenitium.short: sĕlēnītĭum, ii, n., a kind of ivy, Plin.

seleucia.full: Sĕleucĭ_a (also written Sĕleucĕ_a), ae, f., = Σελεύκεια, the name of several cities in Asia. Pieria, a city in Syria, on the Orontes, now Kepse, Plin. 5, 12, 13, § 67; Cic. Att. 11, 20 init.— A celebrated city in Babylonia, near the river Tigris, now ElModain, Sall. Ep. Mithrid. 19; called Seleucia Parthorum, Plin. 10, 48, 67, § 132; form Seleucea, Cael. ap. Cic. Fam. 8, 14, 1. — Seleucia Trachēa = Σελεύκεια ἡ τραχει?͂ α, a city of Cilicia, Plin. 5, 27, 22, § 93; Amm. 14, 2, 14.
seleucia.short: Sĕleucĭ_a (also written Sĕleucĕ_a), ae, f., = Σελεύκεια, the name of several cities in Asia.

seleucis.full: Sĕleucis, ĭdis, f., a kind of bird on Mount Casius, Plin. 10, 27, 39, § 75.
seleucis.short: Sĕleucis, ĭdis, f., a kind of bird on Mount Casius, Plin.

seleucus.full: Sĕleucus, i, m., = Σέλευκος. The name of several kings of Syria; their ancestor, Seleucus Nicator, a general of Alexander the Great after the latter's death founded the kingdom of the Seleucidae, Just. 13, 4, 17; 15, 4, 1.— Name of a servant of Q. Lepta, Cic. Fam. 6, 18, 1.— Name of a player on the cithern, Juv. 10, 24.

selgiticus.full: Selgĭtĭcus (Selgĭcus), a, um, adj., of or belonging to the city of Selga, in Pisidia: (oleum) Plin. 15, 7, 7, § 31; 23, 4, 49, § 95
selgiticus.short: Selgĭtĭcus (Selgĭcus), a, um, adj., of or belonging to the city of Selga, in Pisidia: (oleum) Plin.

selibra.full: sē-libra (e short, Mart. 4, 46, 7; 10, 57 1), ae, f. semi, a half-pound, Cato, R. R. 84, 1; Varr. L. L. 5, § 171 Müll.; Col. 12, 5; Liv. 5, 47; Plin. 14, 16. 19, § 108; Mart. 1. 1.

seligo.full: sē-lĭgo, lēgi. lectum, 3, v. a. se-lego. In gen. separate by culling out; to choose out, cul select (rare but class.; syn.: eligo, deligo), nec vero utetur imprudenter hac copia (communium locorum), sed omnia expendet et seliget, Cic. Or. 15, 47: exempla, id. ib. 29, 103; id. Fin. 3, 6, 22 Orell. and Otto N. cr.: ex quo (commentario) tu, quae digna sunt, selige, Cael. ap. Cic. Fam. 8, 11, 4; Ov. Am. 3, 11, 49; App. M. 10, p. 245, 10: selectae sententiae, Cic. N. D. 1, 30, 85: (Romulus) selecta p

selinas.full: sĕlīnas (acc. Gr. -ada), ādis, f., a kind of cabbage resembling parsley, Plin. 20, 9, 33, § 79.

selinon.full: sĕlīnon, i, n., = σέλινον, pure Lat. apium, parsley, App. Herb. 8; 116; 118.
selinon.short: sĕlīnon, i, n., = σέλινον, pure Lat.

selinus.full: Sĕlīnūs, untis, f., = Σελινοῦς. A town on the coast of Sicily, near Lilybœum, now Pileri: palmosa, Verg. A. 3, 705; Sil. 14, 201.—Hence, Sĕlīnūsĭus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Selinus, Selinusian: creta, Vitr. 7, 14; Plin. 35, 6, 27, § 46; 35, 16, 56, § 194.— Sĕlīnuntĭi, ōrum, m., the inhabitants of Selinus, Plin. 3, 8, 14, § 91.— A town on the coast of Cilicia, now Selinty, Plin. 5, 27, 22, § 92; Liv. 33, 20, 5.—Also, a river near it of the same name, Luc. 8, 260.

seliquastrum.full: sēlĭquastrum, i, n., a kind of seat or stool: ab sedendo appellatae sedes, sedile, solium, sellae, seliquastrum, Varr. L. L. 5, § 128 Müll.; cf.: seliquastra sedilia antiqui generis appellantur D littera in L conversa, ut etiam in sellā factum est et subsellio et solio, quae non minus a sedendo dicta sunt, Fest. p. 340 ib.; Hyg. Astr. 2, 10; 3, 9.
seliquastrum.short: sēlĭquastrum, i, n., a kind of seat or stool: ab sedendo appellatae sedes, sedile, solium, sellae, seliquastrum, Varr.

sella.full: sella (ancient collat. form sedda, acc. to Scaur. p. 2252 P.), ae, f. dim. for sedla; root sed-; .sedes, a seat, settle, chair, stool (syn.: sedile, scamnum): viden' ut expalluit! datin' isti sellam, ubi assidat cito, Plaut. Curc. 2, 3, 32; id. Bacch. 3, 3, 28; id. Poen. 1, 2, 56: scabilla, sellas, solia, Cato, R. R. 10, 4; 157, 11: in sellā sedere, Cic. Div. 1, 46, 104 (corresp. to sedes): fracta est patris sella, Petr. 136: altā deducere sellā, Juv. 3, 136 al.— Esp. Of a mechanic's work-stool:

sellaria.full: sellārĭa, ae, f. sella, a room furnished with seats or settles; a sitting-room, drawing-room, Plin. 34, 8, 19, § 84; 36, 15, 24, § 111; used by Tiberius for debauchery, Suet. Tib. 43; cf. sellarius.— A public courtesan, Vet. Schol. Juv. 3, 136.

sellariolus.full: sellārĭŏlus, a, um, adj. sellaria, of or for sitting: popinae, as a resort for idlers and debauchees, Mart. 5, 70, 3.

sellaris.full: sellāris, e, adj. sella, of or belonging to a seat (post-class.): gestatio, in a sedan, Cael. Aur. Tard. 1, 4, 92: jumenta, furnished with saddles, used for riding, Veg. 2, 28, 34; 6, 7, 5.—Subst.: sellāris, is, m., a saddlehorse, Vit. Caes. Arel. 2, 2, 20.

sellarius.full: sellārĭus, ii, m. sellaria, one that practises lewdness upon a settle (a word invented by the emperor Tiberius), Tac. A. 6, 1; v. sellaria.

sellasia.full: Sellasĭa, ae, f., = Σελλασία, a town of Laconia, on the river Œnus, now St. Saranda, Liv. 34, 28.
sellasia.short: Sellasĭa, ae, f., = Σελλασία, a town of Laconia, on the river Œnus, now St.

sellisternia.full: sellĭsternĭa, ōrum, n. sella-sterno; cf. lectisternium, religious banquets offered to female deities (because, at table, the women sat upon sellae, while the men reclined upon lecti, whence lectisternium), Tac. A. 15, 44; Fest. s. v. solla, pp. 298 and 299 Müll.; Serv. Verg. A. 8, 176; cf.: Juno et Minerva in sellas ad cenam invitantur, Val. Max. 2, 1, 2: sellisternium = σελλάστρωσις, Gloss. Cyrill.

sellula.full: sellŭla, ae, f. dim. sella, a little seat or stool; also, a sedan (post-Aug.; but cf. sellularius), Arn. 2, 23; Tac. H. 3, 84; Fronto Ep. ad M. Caes. 5, 44.

sellularius.full: sellŭlārĭus, a, um, adj. sellula, of or belonging to a chair: quaestus, sedentary occupations or trades, Gell. 3, 1, 10; so, artes, App. Flor. p. 346, 34: artifex, a mechanic, id. ib. p. 351, 21.—As subst.: sel-lŭlārĭus, ii, m., a mechanic: de plebeiā faece sellulariorum, Cic. ap. Aug. adv. Pelag. 2, 37; cf.: opificum vulgus et sellularii, minime militiae idoneum genus, Liv. 8, 20.

selymbria.full: Sēlymbrĭa, ae, f., = Σηλυμβρία, a town of Thrace, on the Propontis, Liv. 33, 39; Mel. 2, 3; Plin. 4, 11, 18, § 47.
selymbria.short: Sēlymbrĭa, ae, f., = Σηλυμβρία, a town of Thrace, on the Propontis, Liv.

semanticus.full: sēmantĭcus, a, um, adj., = σημαντικός, designating, having an indicative force, Mart. Cap. 9, §§ 985, 988.
semanticus.short: sēmantĭcus, a, um, adj., = σημαντικός, designating, having an indicative force, Mart.

sembella.full: sembella, ae, f. contr. from semi and libella, a half-libella (a coin): sembella quod libellae dimidium, quod semis assis, Varr. L. L. 5, § 174 Müll.: eandem rationem habere assem ad semissem, quam habet in argento libella ad sembellam, id. ib. 10, § 38 ib.

semel.full: sĕmĕl, adv. num. root sam-, one; Sanscr. sa-, sam-, with, together; Gr. ἅμα, ἅπαξ; cf.: sem-per, sim-ilis, sim-plex, sin-gulus, etc.. Lit., once, a single time: ter sub armis malim vitam cernere, Quam semel modo parere, Enn. ap. Varr. L. L. 6, § 81 Müll.; and ap. Non. 261, 9 (Trag. v. 298 Vahl.); so, potin' ut semel modo huc respicias? Plaut. Ps. 1, 3, 30: satis sum semel deceptus, id. Capt. 3, 5, 99: semel fugiendi si data est occasio, Satis est, id. ib. 1, 2, 8; so, semel si, id. As. 1, 3, 66

semele.full: Sĕmĕlē, ēs (Sĕmĕla, ae, pure Lat. collat. form in the cass. obll.), f., = Σεμέλη, a daughter of Cadmus, and mother of Bacchus by Jupiter; nom. Semele, Ov. M. 3, 293; id. F. 6, 485; id. Tr. 4, 3, 67; id. Am. 3, 3, 37; Hyg. Fab. 167 and 179; gen. Semelae, Ov. F. 6, 503: Semeles, Hor. C. 1, 19, 2; Tib. 3, 4, 45; Ov. M. 3, 274; 3, 278; dat. Semelae, Prop. 2, 28 (3, 24), 27; acc. Semelen, Ov. M. 3, 261; id. F. 3, 715: Semelam, Macr. S. 1, 12; abl. Semelā, Cic. Tusc. 1, 12, 28; id. N. D. 2, 24, 62; Pr

semen.full: sēmen, ĭnis, n. root sa-, sē-; cf.: sero, sevi; Saturnus, sator, etc.. Seed. Of plants, Cato, R. R. 17; 27; 31 fin.; 34; Varr. R. R. 1, 40 sq.: semen manu spargere, Cic. Rosc. Am. 18, 50: terra semen excepit, id. Sen. 15, 51; id. N. D. 2, 32, 81; Ov. M. 1, 108; 7, 623 et saep.— Of men, animals, etc., Plaut. Am. 5, 2, 9; Varr. R. R. 2, 2, 4; 2, 3, 4; 3, 7, 10 al.; Lucr. 4, 1031; 4, 1034 sq.; Cels. 4, 19; Ov. M. 1, 748; 15, 760 et saep.— Poet., of the elements of other bodies (of fire, water, ston

sementatio.full: sēmentātĭo, ōnis, f. semento, a sowing, the seed sown, Tert. Spect. 8.

sementifer.full: sēmentĭfer, fĕra, fĕrum, adj. sementis-fero, seed-bearing, fruitful: Seriphus, Verg. Cir. 476.

sementis.full: sēmentis, is (acc. sementim, Cic. N. D. 3, 30, 75 B. and K.; Cato, R. R. 17, 2; 17, 27; 17, 30; 17, 61 fin. al.; Col. 11, 2, 81, with the var. lect. sementem, a form which appears also in Plaut. Men. 5, 7, 23; Varr. L. L. 5, § 37; Cic. Att. 9, 8, 1; id. de Or. 2, 65, 281; Liv. 23, 48; Col. 2, 15, 1; 11, 2, 90; abl. semente, Cic. Verr. 2, 3, 54, § 125; Ov. F. 1, 667; Pall. Nov. 1, 1: sementi, Col. 2, 9, 15; 2, 10, 8; 2, 11, 1; 11, 2, 82; gen. plur. sementium, Plaut. Poen. 5, 5, 33 dub.), f. semen

sementivus.full: sēmentīvus, a, um, adj. sementis, of or belonging to seed or sowing: feriae, that occur at seed-time, Varr. R. R. 1, 2, 1; cf. id. L. L. 6, § 26 Müll.; Macr. S. 1, 16; Fest. p. 337 Müll.; called also sementiva dies, Ov. F. 1, 658: pira, perh., that are not ripe till late in autumn, late pears, frost-pears, Cato, R. R. 7, 3; Varr. R. R. 1, 59, 3; Plin. 15, 15, 16, § 56: pirum sementivum serum, Cloat. ap. Macr. S. 2, 15 fin.: genera frumenti, that are sown in autumn (opp. verna): sementiva autem (

semento.full: sēmento, āre, v. n. id., to bear seed, to run to seed: herbae sementaturae, Plin. 18, 28, 67, § 259.

semestris1.full: sēmestris, e, adj. sex-mensis. Of six months, half-yearly, semi-annual: dies, nox, lasting six months (far in the north), Varr. R. R. 1, 2, 5: regnum, Cic. Att. 10, 8, 7: imperium, Caes. B. C. 1, 9: dux, Liv. 21, 43, 15: consulatus, Suet. Ner. 14: tribunatus (militaris), Plin. Ep. 4, 4, 2; hence also, aurum, the ring of the tribunes (worn for six months): semestri vatum digitos circumligat auro, Juv. 7, 89; cf. also, consilia, Suet. Aug. 35: spatium, Plin. 18, 29, 69, § 280: filius, six months o

semestris2.full: sēmestris, e, adj. semi-mensis, semi-monthly: luna, i. e. the full moon, App. M. 11, p. 258, 29: species (lunae), Amm. 20, 3, 1; cf. semestrium.

semestrium.full: sēmestrĭum, ii, n. id., a half month, a fortnight, Col. 11, 2, 6.

semesus.full: sēmēsus (sēmiēsus (trisyl.), Verg. A. 3, 244; and 8, 297; cf. Wagn. ib. 3, 578), a, um, adj. semi-edo, half-eaten, half-devoured, half-consumed (not ante-Aug.): praeda, Verg. A. 3, 244: ossa, id. ib. 8, 297: pisces, Hor. S. 1, 3, 81: lardi frusta, id. ib. 2, 6, 85: serpentes, Ov. M. 2, 771: lepus, Juv. 5, 167: obsonia, Suet. Tib. 34; id. Vit. 13 fin.: corpora liberorum, Petr. 141, 11: cibi, Flor. 4, 2, 69.

semetra.full: sē-mĕtra, ōrum, n. metrum, irregular, inharmonious: dissona, Prud. Psych. 826.

semi.full: sēmi- (also, before vowels, merely sēm-, and before libra, mestris, from mensis, and modius, sē-), an inseparable particle [Sanscr. sāmi; Gr. ἡμι-, ἥμισυς; cf. semis], half, demi-, semi-; as, semestris, semi-monthly; semesus, half-eaten; semideus, demigod, etc.; hence, also, for small, thin, light, etc.; as, semicinctium, semifunium, semipiscina, semispatha, al.—Only a very few of these compounds are ante-Aug.; most of them, indeed, belong only to the post-class. per.
semi.short: sēmi- (also, before vowels, merely sēm-, and before libra, mestris, from mensis, and modius, sē-), an inseparable particle [Sanscr.

semiacerbus.full: sēmĭ-ăcerbus, a, um, adj., halfsour, half-ripe: uvae, Pall. Aug. 13.
semiacerbus.short: sēmĭ-ăcerbus, a, um, adj., halfsour, half-ripe: uvae, Pall.

semiadapertus.full: sēmĭ-ădăpertus (quinquesyl.), a, um, adj. adaperio, half-opened: janua, Ov. Am. 1, 6, 4.

semiadopertulus.full: sēmĭ-ăd-ŏpertŭlus, a, um, adj. operio, half-shut, half-closed: oculi, App. M. 3, 135, 34.

semiagrestis.full: sēmĭ-ăgrestis, e, adj., half-rustic, somewhat boorish: Maximianus, Aur. Vict. Caes. 39 med.
semiagrestis.short: sēmĭ-ăgrestis, e, adj., half-rustic, somewhat boorish: Maximianus, Aur.

semiambustus.full: sēmĭ-ambustus, a, um, adj. amburo, half-burned, half-consumed (post-Aug.): cadaver, Suet. Calig. 59: turba, Sil. 2, 681: saxa, id. 14, 63.

semiamictus.full: sēmĭ-ămictus, a, um, adj. amicio, half-clad, half-naked (Appuleian), App. M. 1, p. 104, 28; 7, p. 189, 37.

semiamputatus.full: sēmĭ-ampŭtātus, a, um, adj. amputo, half cut off, half-trimmed, lopped, or pruned: ramuli, App. M. 1, p. 104, 5.

semianimis.full: sēmĭ-ănĭmis (in verse, per synizesin, read as a quadrisyl.; and in some editions also written sēmănĭmis), e anima, and less freq. sēmĭ-ănĭmus, a, um, adj. animus, half-alive, half-dead (mostly poet. and in post-Aug. prose; syn.: semivivus, seminex). Form semianimis: semianimes micant oculi, Enn. ap. Serv. ad Verg. A. 10, 396 (Ann. v. 463 Vahl.): semianimesque micant digiti, Verg. A. 10, 396; 10, 404; 4, 686; 11, 635; 12, 356; Luc. 4, 339; Sil. 9, 123 al.; Nep. Paus. 5, 4; Liv. 3, 13, 2; 3, 57, 4
semianimis.short: sēmĭ-ănĭmis (in verse, per synizesin, read as a quadrisyl.;

semiannuus.full: sēmĭ-annŭus, a, um, adj., of or lasting half a year: nox (in insulā Thule), Mart. Cap. 6, § 595.
semiannuus.short: sēmĭ-annŭus, a, um, adj., of or lasting half a year: nox (in insulā Thule), Mart.

semiapertus.full: sēmĭ-ăpertus, a, um, adj. aperio, half-opened, half-open: fores portarum, Liv. 26, 39 fin.

semiatratus.full: sēmĭ-ătrātus, a, um, adj., clothed in half-black, in half-mourning, Varr. ap. Non. 107, 6.
semiatratus.short: sēmĭ-ătrātus, a, um, adj., clothed in half-black, in half-mourning, Varr.

semiaxius.full: sēmĭ-axĭus, ii, m. axis, an appellation of the early Christians, derived from the manner of their martyrdom: licet nunc sarmentitios et semiaxios appelletis, quia ad stipitem dimidii axis revincti, sarmentorum ambitu uriemur, Tert. Apol. 50.

semibarbarus.full: sēmĭ-barbărus, a, um, adj., semibarbarous (post-Aug.): Galli, Suet. Caes. 76: homo, Capitol. Max. 2: urbs Leptis, Hier. adv. Jovin. 1, 48.
semibarbarus.short: sēmĭ-barbărus, a, um, adj., semibarbarous (post-Aug.): Galli, Suet.

semibos.full: sēmĭ-bōs, bŏvis, m., a half-ox (Ovidian): vir, i. e. the Minotaur, Ov. A. A. 2, 24; id. Tr. 4, 7, 18.
semibos.short: sēmĭ-bōs, bŏvis, m., a half-ox (Ovidian): vir, i.

semicanaliculus.full: sēmĭ-cănālĭcŭlus, i, m., the halfchannel or groove on the edge of a triglyph, Vitr. 4, 3, 5.
semicanaliculus.short: sēmĭ-cănālĭcŭlus, i, m., the halfchannel or groove on the edge of a triglyph, Vitr.

semicanis.full: sēmĭ-cănis, e, a half-dog: semicanes dei, the Egyptian god Anubis, Luc. 8, 832 Weise.
semicanis.short: sēmĭ-cănis, e, a half-dog: semicanes dei, the Egyptian god Anubis, Luc.

semicanus.full: sēmĭ-cānus, a, um, adj., half-gray, grizzled (Appuleian): comae, App. M. 9, p. 231, 5: cincinni, id. ib. 8, p. 212, 27.
semicanus.short: sēmĭ-cānus, a, um, adj., half-gray, grizzled (Appuleian): comae, App.

semicaper.full: sēmĭ-căper, pri, m., a half-goat (Ovidian), an epithet of Pan, Ov. M. 14, 515; of a Faun, id. F. 5, 101.
semicaper.short: sēmĭ-căper, pri, m., a half-goat (Ovidian), an epithet of Pan, Ov.

semicentesima.full: sēmĭ-centēsĭma, ae, f., one-half per cent., as an impost, Cod. Th. 13, 9, 3.
semicentesima.short: sēmĭ-centēsĭma, ae, f., one-half per cent., as an impost, Cod.

semichristianus.full: Sēmĭ-christĭānus, i, m., a half-Christian, Hier. Gal. 3, 14.
semichristianus.short: Sēmĭ-christĭānus, i, m., a half-Christian, Hier.

semicinctium.full: sēmĭ-cinctĭum, ii, n., a semi-girdle, a narrow girdle or apron, Mart. 14, 153 in lemm.; Petr. 94, 8 (al. hemicyclo); Isid. Orig. 19, 33; Vulg. Act. 19, 12; cf. semifunium.
semicinctium.short: sēmĭ-cinctĭum, ii, n., a semi-girdle, a narrow girdle or apron, Mart.

semicirculatus.full: sēmĭcircŭlātus, a, um, adj. semicirculus, semicircular: ferramentum, Cels. 7, 26, 2.

semicirculus.full: sēmĭ-circŭlus, a, um, adj., semicircular: ager, Col. 5, 2, 8.—Hence, subst.: sēmĭ-circŭlus, i, m., a half-circle, semicircle (syn. semiorbis): uncus in semicirculi speciem, Cels. 7, 26, 2: ager, i. e. semicircular, Col. 5, 2, 8.
semicirculus.short: sēmĭ-circŭlus, a, um, adj., semicircular: ager, Col.

semiclausus.full: sēmĭ-clausus (-clūsus), a, um, adj. claudo, half-shut, half-closed: os, App. M. 10, p. 243: postica, Amm. 18, 6, 11: SILVANE SEMICLVSE FRAXINO (because only half was visible), Inscr. Orell. 1613.

semicoctus.full: sēmĭ-coctus, a, um, adj. coquo, halfcooked, half-done, Col. 8, 5, 2; Plin. 18, 11, 29, § 116; 22, 25, 70, § 145; Pall. 1, 27, 1.

semicombustus.full: sēmĭ-combustus, a, um, adj. comburo, half-burned, half-consumed, Prud. στεΦ. 10, 859; Sid. Ep. 3, 13.

semiconfectus.full: sēmĭ-confectus, a, um, adj. conficio, half-made: caespes, Sid. Ep. 6, 10.

semiconspicuus.full: sēmĭ-conspĭcŭus, a, um, adj. conspicio, half-visible: nonnulli per fenestras, App. M. 3, p. 130, 14.

semicorporalis.full: sēmĭ-corpŏrālis, e, adj. corpus, half-bodied, having but half its body visible: signum (Aries), Firm. Math. 2, 12; cf. semicorporeus.

semicorporeus.full: sēmĭ-corpŏrĕus, a, um, adj. id., having but half its body visible: signum (Cancer), Firm. Math. 2, 12; cf. semicorporalis.

semicorporis.full: sēmĭ-corpŏris, e, adj. id., having half a body (late Lat.), Cassiod. Hist. Eccl. 8, 1.

semicorrectus.full: sēmĭ-correctus, a, um, adj. corrigo, half-corrected (late Lat.), Aug. c. Mend. 3, 6.

semicrematus.full: sēmĭ-crĕmātus, a, um, adj. cremo, half-burned: membra, Ov. Ib. 636: tura, Mart. 11, 54, 2; cf. semicremus.

semicremus.full: sēmĭ-crĕmus, a, um, adj. id., halfburned: stipes, Ov. M. 12, 287.

semicrudus.full: sēmĭ-crūdus, a, um, adj. Halfraw: caro, Front. Strat. 2, 5, 13: exta, Suet. Aug. 1: lupinum, Col. 6, 25.—* That has but half-digested, Stat. S. 4, 9, 48.

semicubitalis.full: sēmĭ-cŭbĭtālis, e, adj. cubitum, a half-cubit long: hastile, Liv. 42, 65, 9.

semicupae.full: sēmĭ-cūpae, ārum, m. cupa, a halftun; as a term of reproach, i. q. pot-belly, fat-paunch, Amm. 28, 4, 28.

semideus.full: sēmĭ-dĕus, a, um, adj., half-divine: heroes, i. e. the Argonauts, Stat. Th. 5, 373; called also, reges, id. ib. 3, 518; id. Acnill. 2, 363: parentes, id. Th. 9, 376: Manes, Luc. 9, 7: canes, i. e. Anubis, id. 8, 832 (al. semicanes dei): Dryades, Ov. H. 4, 49: Nymphae semideumque genus, id. Ib. 82; cf.: Silvanus arbiter umbrae Semideumque pecus, i. e. the Pans, Stat. Th. 6, 112.— Hence, subst. sēmĭ-dĕus, i, m., a demigod: semideique deique, Ov. M. 14, 673; 1, 192.— sēmĭ-dĕa, ae, f., a demigoddess
semideus.short: sēmĭ-dĕus, a, um, adj., half-divine: heroes, i.

semidies.full: sēmĭ-dĭes, ēi, m., a half-day, Aus. Ecl. Rat. Dier. 5, and Rat. Solst. 2.
semidies.short: sēmĭ-dĭes, ēi, m., a half-day, Aus.

semidigitalis.full: sēmĭ-dĭgĭtālis, e, adj , of the size of half a finger, half a digit in diameter: foramen, Vitr. 10, 22.
semidigitalis.short: sēmĭ-dĭgĭtālis, e, adj , of the size of half a finger, half a digit in diameter: foramen, Vitr.

semidivinus.full: sēmĭ-dīvīnus, a, um, adj., half-divine, semi-divine: locus ex oratione tuā, M. Aur. ap. Front. Ep ad Caes. 1, 5.
semidivinus.short: sēmĭ-dīvīnus, a, um, adj., half-divine, semi-divine: locus ex oratione tuā, M.

semidoctus.full: sēmĭ-doctus, a, um, adj., half-taught, half-learned: discipulus, Plaut. As. 1, 3, 74: haec ut et properans et apud doctos et semidoctus ipse percurro, Cic. de Or. 2, 42, 178: grammaticus, Gell. 15, 9, 6: manus villici, Mart. 10, 92, 5.
semidoctus.short: sēmĭ-doctus, a, um, adj., half-taught, half-learned: discipulus, Plaut.

semiermis.full: sēmĭ-ermis (sēmerm-, v. Liv. 27, 1, 15 Drak.; cf. semesus), e (in Liv.), and sēmĭ-ermus (sēmerm-), a, um (in Tac.), adj. arma, half-armed, badly or indifferently armed: mille semermes per agros palati sunt, Liv. 39, 31: multitudo, id. 22, 50; 23, 5: exercitus, id. 25, 19; 27, 1 fin.: cum sex milibus semiermium, id. 28, 16; 30, 28; 31, 41; 40, 58: hosti et paucos ac semermos cogitanti, Tac. A. 1, 68; 3, 39 and 45.

semifactus.full: sēmĭ-factus, a, um, adj. facio, halfmade, half-finished: opera, Tac. A. 15, 7: portae valli, Auct. B. Afr. 83, 3.

semifastigium.full: sēmĭ-fastīgĭum, i, n., a half-pediment, Vitr. 7, 5 med.
semifastigium.short: sēmĭ-fastīgĭum, i, n., a half-pediment, Vitr.

semifer.full: sēmĭ-fer, fĕra, fĕrum, adj. ferus, halfbestial, half man and half beast. Lit.: semifer interea divinae stirpis alumno Laetus erat, i. e. the Centaur Chiron, Ov. M. 2, 633; so of the Centaurs, id. ib. 12, 406; Stat. Th. 9, 220; Luc. 6, 386: caput Panis, Lucr. 4, 587: pectus (Tritonis), Verg. A. 10, 212: corpus Capricorni (because half goat and half fish), Cic. Arat. 59 Orell. N. cr.: species hominum (with portenta), Lucr. 2, 702 et saep.— Trop., half-wild, half-savage: (Cacus), Verg. A. 8, 267 (f

semiformis.full: sēmĭ-formis, e, adj. forma, halfformed: pulli, Col. 8, 5, 12: luna, a halfmoon, id. 4, 25, 1.

semifultus.full: sēmĭ-fultus, a, um, adj. fulcio, half-propped, Mart. 5, 14, 9.

semifumans.full: sēmĭ-fūmans, antis, adj. fumo, halfsmoking; trop.: dignitas praefecturae, i. e. still warm or fresh, Sid. Ep. 1, 7.

semifunium.full: sēmĭ-fūnĭum, ii, n. funis, a halfrope, i. e. a slender line or cord, Cato, R. R. 135, 5; cf. semicinctium.

semigaetulus.full: Sēmĭ-gaetūlus, i, m., a half-Gœtulian, semi-Gœtulian, App. Mag. p. 289, 11.
semigaetulus.short: Sēmĭ-gaetūlus, i, m., a half-Gœtulian, semi-Gœtulian, App.

semigermanus.full: Sēmĭ-germānus, a, um, adj., halfGerman, semi-German: gentes, Liv. 21, 38 fin.
semigermanus.short: Sēmĭ-germānus, a, um, adj., halfGerman, semi-German: gentes, Liv.

semigraeculus.full: Sēmĭgraecŭlus, i, m. dim. semigraecus, a little half-Greek, Hier. Ep. 50, 2.

semigraecus.full: Sēmĭ-graecus, a, um, adj., halfGreek, semi-Grecian: pastores, Varr. R. R. 2, 1, 2: poëtae et oratores, Suet. Gram. 1: civitas (Tarentum), Flor. 1, 18, 6.—* Adv.: Sēmĭgraecē, half in the Greek manner: quod dicimus, Lucil. ap. Vel. Long. p. 2214 P.
semigraecus.short: Sēmĭ-graecus, a, um, adj., halfGreek, semi-Grecian: pastores, Varr.

semigravis.full: sēmĭ-grăvis, e, adj., half-overcome: vino, i. e. half-drunken, Liv. 25, 24, 2 Weissenb. ad loc.
semigravis.short: sēmĭ-grăvis, e, adj., half-overcome: vino, i.

semigro.full: sē-mĭ_gro, āvi, 1, v. n., to go away, remove from any one: a patre, Cic. Cael. 7, 18.

semihians.full: sēmĭ-hĭans, antis, adj. hio, halfopened, half-open: labellum, Cat. 61, 220; cf. labiae, App. M: 10, p. 252, 32; cf. semihiulcus.

semihiulcus.full: sēmĭ-hĭulcus, a, um, adj., half-opened, half-open: savium, Poët. ap. Gell. 19, 11, 4; Macr. S. 2, 2, 17; cf. semihians.
semihiulcus.short: sēmĭ-hĭulcus, a, um, adj., half-opened, half-open: savium, Poët.

semihomo.full: sēmĭ-hŏmo, ĭnis, m., a half-man, i. e. half man and half beast. Lit.: Centauri, Ov. M. 12, 536 (for which, semiferi, id. ib. 12, 406 al.; v. semifer, I.): mandragoras (because formed below like a man), Col. poët. 10, 19.— Trop., half-human, i. e. half-wild, half-savage, = semifer, II.: Cacus, Verg. A. 8, 194 (for which, semifer, id. ib. 8, 267): Nasamones, Sil. 11, 180.
semihomo.short: sēmĭ-hŏmo, ĭnis, m., a half-man, i.

semihora.full: sēmĭ-hōra, ae, f., a half-hour, half an hour, Cic. Rab. Perd. 2, 6; Cels. 3, 21; Petr. 69, 4; Auct. B. Afr. 38.
semihora.short: sēmĭ-hōra, ae, f., a half-hour, half an hour, Cic.

semiinanis.full: sēmĭ-ĭnānis (sēmĭn-), e, adj., halfempty, but half-full: orbis (lunae), Plin. 2, 18, 16, § 80.
semiinanis.short: sēmĭ-ĭnānis (sēmĭn-), e, adj., halfempty, but half-full: orbis (lunae), Plin.

semiinteger.full: sēmĭ-intĕger, gra, grum, adj., halfwhole, half-uninjured, Amm. 20, 5, 4.
semiinteger.short: sēmĭ-intĕger, gra, grum, adj., halfwhole, half-uninjured, Amm.

semijejunia.full: sēmĭ-jējūnĭa, ōrum, n., half-fasts, Tert. adv. Psych. 13.

semijudaeus.full: Sēmĭ-jūdaeus, i, m., a half-Jew, half a Jew, Hier. in Isa. 1, 2, 20; 15, 54, 12.
semijudaeus.short: Sēmĭ-jūdaeus, i, m., a half-Jew, half a Jew, Hier.

semijugerum.full: sēmĭ-jūgĕrum, i, n., a half-juger, quarter-acre, Col. 4, 18, 1; 5, 1, 6.
semijugerum.short: sēmĭ-jūgĕrum, i, n., a half-juger, quarter-acre, Col.

semilacer.full: sēmĭ-lăcer, ĕra, ĕrum, adj., half-lacerated, half-mangled, Ov. M. 7, 344.
semilacer.short: sēmĭ-lăcer, ĕra, ĕrum, adj., half-lacerated, half-mangled, Ov.

semilater.full: sēmĭ-lăter (or sēmĭ-lătĕrĭum, ii, n.), ĕris, m., = ἡμιπλίνθιον, a half-brick, Vitr. 2, 3, 4.
semilater.short: sēmĭ-lăter (or sēmĭ-lătĕrĭum, ii, n.), ĕris, m., = ἡμιπλίνθιον, a half-brick, Vitr.

semilautus.full: sēmĭ-lautus, a, um, adj., halfwashed: crura, Cat. 54, 2.
semilautus.short: sēmĭ-lautus, a, um, adj., halfwashed: crura, Cat.

semiliber.full: sēmĭ-līber, ĕra, ĕrum, adj., half-free: semiliberi saltem simus, Cic. Att. 13, 31, 3; id. ap. Sen. Brev. Vit. 5, 2.
semiliber.short: sēmĭ-līber, ĕra, ĕrum, adj., half-free: semiliberi saltem simus, Cic.

semilibra.full: sēmĭ-lībra, ae, f., a half-pound, half a pound, App. Herb. 99.
semilibra.short: sēmĭ-lībra, ae, f., a half-pound, half a pound, App.

semilixa.full: sēmĭ-lixa, ae, m., half a sutler, one little better than a sutler, as a term of reproach, Liv. 28, 28, 4; 30, 28, 3.
semilixa.short: sēmĭ-lixa, ae, m., half a sutler, one little better than a sutler, as a term of reproach, Liv.

semilixula.full: sēmĭ-lixŭla, a half-lixula, acc. to Varr. L. L. 5, § 107 Müll.

semilunaticus.full: sēmĭ-lūnātĭcus, i, m., half-lunatic, Firm. Math. 7, 3 fin.

semimadidus.full: sēmĭ-mădĭdus, a, um, adj., halfwet, moist, damp: ager, Col. 2, 4, 5.
semimadidus.short: sēmĭ-mădĭdus, a, um, adj., halfwet, moist, damp: ager, Col.

semimarinus.full: sēmĭ-mărīnus, a, um, adj., half in the sea: corpora (Seyllarum), Lucr. 5, 892.
semimarinus.short: sēmĭ-mărīnus, a, um, adj., half in the sea: corpora (Seyllarum), Lucr.

semimas.full: sēmĭ-mās, măris, m. Lit., a halfmale, hermaphrodite, Ov. M. 4, 381; 12, 506; Liv. 31, 12 fin.— Transf., adj., unmanned, emasculated: capri, Varr. R. R. 3, 9, 3: semimares capi (appellantur), cum sint castrati, Col. 8, 2, 3: ovis, Ov. F. 1, 588: Galli (the priests of Cybele), id. ib. 4, 183.

semimasculus.full: sēmĭ-mascŭlus, i, adj. m., = semimas, II.: Attis, Fulg. Myth. 3, 5.

semimaturus.full: sēmĭ-mātūrus, a, um, adj., half-ripe, Pall. Mart. 10, 22; id. Jun. 12.
semimaturus.short: sēmĭ-mātūrus, a, um, adj., half-ripe, Pall.

semimedus.full: Sēmĭ-mēdus, i, m., a half-Mede, half a Mede, App. Mag. p. 289, 13.
semimedus.short: Sēmĭ-mēdus, i, m., a half-Mede, half a Mede, App.

semimetopia.full: sēmĭ-mĕtōpĭa, ōrum, n. metopa, half-metopes, Vitr. 4, 3, 5.

semimitra.full: sēmĭ-mitra, ae, f., a half-turban, Dig. 34, 2, 25, § 10.
semimitra.short: sēmĭ-mitra, ae, f., a half-turban, Dig.

semimortuus.full: sēmĭ-mortŭus, a, um, adj., half-dead (cf.: semivivus, seminecis), Cat. 50, 15; App. M. 6, p. 184, 23.
semimortuus.short: sēmĭ-mortŭus, a, um, adj., half-dead (cf.: semivivus, seminecis), Cat.

seminalis.full: sēmĭnālis, e, adj [semen], of or belonging to seed, good for seed, seminal (late Lat.): vicia, Col. 11, 2, 76: membrum, Auct. Priap. 26, 2; cf. venae, Lact. Opif. Dei, 12: viae, Cael. Aur. Acut. 3, 18, 180: vascula, Theod. Prisc. 4, 2: vita, vegetable, Claud. Mam. Stat. Anim. 1, 21.—Plur. subst.: sē-mĭnālia, n., standing crops, Tert. adv. Marc. 13 fin.
seminalis.short: sēmĭnālis, e, adj [semen], of or belonging to seed, good for seed, seminal (late Lat.): vicia, Col.

seminarius.full: sēmĭnārĭus, a, um. Adj. semen, of or belonging to seed: seminarium pilum, for bruising seed, Cato, R. R. 10, 5.— Subst.: sēmĭnārĭum, ii, n., a nursery, nursery-garden, seed-plot, seminary. Lit., Plin. 18, 27, 71, § 295; Cato, R. R. 46; 48; Varr. R. R. 1, 29; Col. 5, 6, 1; 11, 2, 16; 11, 2, 30; id. Arb. 1, 3; 2, 1 et saep.— Trop. (class.): seminarium rei publicae, Cic. Off. 1, 17, 54: fons et seminarium triumphorum, id. Pis. 40, 97: Catilinarium, id. Cat. 2, 10, 23; so, judicum (veterani), id. Ph

seminatio.full: sēmĭnātĭo, ōnis, f. semino, a breeding, propagation, Varr. R. R. 2, 6, 3; Ambros. de Noë, 29, 107.

seminator.full: sēmĭnātor, ōris, m. id., an originator, producer, author (Ciceronian). Lit.: seminator et sator et parens omnium rerum (mundus), Cic. N. D. 2, 34, 86.— Trop.: omnium malorum, Cic. N. D. 3, 26, 66: tamquam fallaciae seminatores, Lact. 5, 2, 17.

seminecis.full: sēmĭ-nĕcis, is (nom. does not occur), adj. nex, half-dead (not ante-Aug.; syn. semivivus): alicui semineci rapere arma, Verg. A. 10, 462: seminecem eum ad Cannas in acervo caesorum corporum inventum, Liv. 23, 15; so, seminecem, id. 29, 2 fin.; Verg. A. 5, 275; Ov. Tr. 5, 9, 19: vita, Sil. 10, 456: semineces, Verg. A. 9, 455; 12, 329: artus, Ov. M. 1, 228: crines, Val. Fl. 6, 176; Tac. Agr. 36; id. H. 3, 28: seminecum, Sil. 4, 164; 6, 11.

seminium.full: sēmĭnĭum, ii, n. semen, a begetting (of animals), procreation (ante-class.), Plaut. Mil. 4, 2, 68; Varr. R. R. 2, 6, 1.— Transf., a race, stock, breed (of animals), Varr. R. R. 2, 1, 14; 2, 3, 3; 3, 9, 6; Lucr. 3, 742; 3, 746; 4, 1005.

seminiverbius.full: sēmĭnĭverbĭus, a, um semino-verbum, scattering words, babbling (for Gr. σπερμολόγος), Vulg. Act. 17, 18.
seminiverbius.short: sēmĭnĭverbĭus, a, um semino-verbum, scattering words, babbling (for Gr.

semino.full: sēmĭno, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. semen, to sow (rare; not in Cic.; syn.: sero, planto). Lit.: adoreum, triticum, hordeum, etc., Col. 2, 8, 1; 2, 8, 3; 2, 9, 15; 2, 9, 16: agrum, id. 2, 4 fin.— Transf. To beget, engender, procreate: alter decumo post mense nascetur puer quam seminatus est, Plaut. Am. 1, 2, 20: armenta, Col. 6, 24, 1; 6, 24, 3; 6, 37, 4 sq.—* Of plants, to bring forth, produce: viscum quod non sua seminat arbos, Verg. A. 6, 206.— Trop.: cultum dei per terram, to plant, propagate, disse

seminosus.full: sēmĭnōsus, a, um, adj. id., full of seeds: cucurbitae, Auct. Priap. 51, 17.

seminudus.full: sēmĭ-nūdus, a, um, adj., half-naked (not ante-Aug.). Lit.: consules, prope seminudi sub jugum missi, Liv. 9, 6; 24, 40; Suet. Vit. 17; Front. Princ. Hist. p. 318.—As subst.: ille seminudus, Sen. Ep. 6, 2, 2.— Transf., half-unarmed, almost defenceless: pedes vagus et prope seminudus, Liv. 31, 35, 6.— Trop.: sententiae, Front. Ep. ad Anton. 1, 2.
seminudus.short: sēmĭ-nūdus, a, um, adj., half-naked (not ante-Aug.).

seminumida.full: Sēmĭ-nŭmĭda, ae, m., a half-Numidian, half a Numidian, App. Mag. p. 289, 11.
seminumida.short: Sēmĭ-nŭmĭda, ae, m., a half-Numidian, half a Numidian, App.

semiobolus.full: sēmĭ-ŏbŏlus, i, m., a half-obolus, Rhem. Fan. Pond. 8; Isid. 16, 25, 10.
semiobolus.short: sēmĭ-ŏbŏlus, i, m., a half-obolus, Rhem.

semiobrutus.full: sēmĭ-obrŭtus, a, um, adj. obruo, half-covered: dolium, App. M. 9, p. 219, 18.

semionustus.full: sēmĭ-ŏnustus, a, um, adj., halfladen: naves, Sisenn. ap. Prisc. p. 909 P.
semionustus.short: sēmĭ-ŏnustus, a, um, adj., halfladen: naves, Sisenn.

semiorbis.full: sēmĭ-orbis, is, m., a half-circle, semicircle, Sen. Q. N. 1, 8, 4; Amm. 20, 3, 10; 22, 8, 5.
semiorbis.short: sēmĭ-orbis, is, m., a half-circle, semicircle, Sen.

semipaganus.full: sēmĭ-pāgānus, i, m., a half-rustic, half a clown, Pers. prol. 6.
semipaganus.short: sēmĭ-pāgānus, i, m., a half-rustic, half a clown, Pers.

semipatens.full: sēmĭ-pătens, entis, adj. pateo, standing half-open, half-open: vestibula, Sid. Ep. 7, 6.

semipedalis.full: sēmĭ-pĕdālis, e, adj., a half-foot in size, half a foot long, broad, etc.: apertura, Vitr. 10, 19; Col. 11, 3, 21: spatium, id. 12, 52, 4: altitudo, Plin. 26, 8, 42, § 69: truncus, id. 13, 4, 8, § 37: pisciculus, id. 32, 1, 1, § 3; cf. the foll. art.
semipedalis.short: sēmĭ-pĕdālis, e, adj., a half-foot in size, half a foot long, broad, etc.: apertura, Vitr.

semipedaneus.full: sēmĭ-pĕdānĕus, a, um, adj., a halffoot in size, half a foot long, broad, etc.: terra, Col. 4, 1, 4.
semipedaneus.short: sēmĭ-pĕdānĕus, a, um, adj., a halffoot in size, half a foot long, broad, etc.: terra, Col.

semiperactus.full: sēmĭ-pĕractus, a, um, adj. perago, half-finished: homo, Paul. Nol. Carm. 20, 299.

semiperemptus.full: sēmĭ-pĕremptus, a, um, adj. perimo, half-destroyed: jugera, Tert. Carm. Sodom. 133.

semiperfectus.full: sēmĭ-perfectus, a, um, adj. perficio, half-finished. Lit.: opera absolvit, Suet. Calig. 21; Ambros. Spirit. Sanc. 3, 14, 18.— Trop.: virtutes, half-perfect, incomplete, App. Dogm. Plat. 2, p. 17, 24.

semiperitus.full: sēmĭ-pĕrītus, a, um, adj., halfskilled (with semidoctus), Front. Ep. ad M. Caes. 4, 3.
semiperitus.short: sēmĭ-pĕrītus, a, um, adj., halfskilled (with semidoctus), Front.

semipersa.full: Sēmĭ-persa, ae, m., a half-Persian, half a Persian, App. Mag. p. 289, 13.
semipersa.short: Sēmĭ-persa, ae, m., a half-Persian, half a Persian, App.

semipes.full: sēmĭ-pēs, pĕdis, m. A half-foot, half a foot. As a measure of length, Cato, R. R. 123; Varr. R. R. 3, 5, 15: latum semipede, Vitr. 2, 3: minimi semipedum mensura, Plin. 9, 5, 4, § 11: non altiores quino semipede, id. 17, 11, 16, § 80: intervallo duum pedum et semipedis, id. 17, 20, 33, § 144.— A half-foot in verse, Varr. ap. Gell. 18, 15, 2; Aus. Ep. 4, 86; Aug. de Musica, 5, 11.— Half-lame: crure trunco semipes, Prud. στεΦ. 2, 150.

semiphalarica.full: sēmĭ-phălārĭca, ae, f., a small phalarica, Gell. 10, 25, 2.
semiphalarica.short: sēmĭ-phălārĭca, ae, f., a small phalarica, Gell.

semipiscina.full: sēmĭ-piscīna, ae, f., a small fishpond, Varr. R. R. 1, 13, 3.
semipiscina.short: sēmĭ-piscīna, ae, f., a small fishpond, Varr.

semiplacentinus.full: Sēmĭ-plăcentīnus, i, m., a half-Placentine, half a Placentine, Cic. Pis. 6, 14.
semiplacentinus.short: Sēmĭ-plăcentīnus, i, m., a half-Placentine, half a Placentine, Cic.

semiplenus.full: sēmĭ-plēnus, a, um, adj., half-full (class.): naves, Cic. Verr. 2, 5, 25, § 63: scrobes, Col. 5, 5, 4: favi, id. 9, 15, 4: vas, Pall. Febr. 32: stationes, only half-filled, half-manned, Liv. 25, 30 fin.; cf. legiones, Vell. 2, 80, 1; 2, 112, 2.—* Adv.: sēmĭ-plēnē, half in full, incompletely, in part: dicuntur praesentia, Sid. Ep. 4, 22 med.
semiplenus.short: sēmĭ-plēnus, a, um, adj., half-full (class.): naves, Cic.

semiplotia.full: sēmiplotĭa, soleae dimidiatae appellantur, quibus utebantur in venando, quo planius pedem ponerent, Fest. s. v. ploti, p. 238 Müll.
semiplotia.short: sēmiplotĭa, soleae dimidiatae appellantur, quibus utebantur in venando, quo planius pedem ponerent, Fest.

semipuella.full: sēmĭ-pŭella, ae, f., a half-maiden, as a designation of the Sirens, who were half girl and half bird, Aus. Idyll. 11, 21.
semipuella.short: sēmĭ-pŭella, ae, f., a half-maiden, as a designation of the Sirens, who were half girl and half bird, Aus.

semipullatus.full: sēmĭ-pullātus, a, um, adj., clothed in half-black: accusatores, Sid. Ep. 1, 7.
semipullatus.short: sēmĭ-pullātus, a, um, adj., clothed in half-black: accusatores, Sid.

semiputatus.full: sēmĭ-pŭtātus, a, um, adj. puto, halfpruned: vitis, Verg. E. 2, 70; Ambros. Ep. 37, 42.

semiramis.full: Sĕmīrămis (Sămērămis, in good MSS. and Schol., Juv. 2, 108), is or ĭdis, f., = Σεμίραμις, the celebrated queen of Assyria, consort and successor of Ninus, Just. 1, 1, 9; Curt. 5, 1, 24; Ov. M. 4, 58; Juv. 2, 108.—Acc. Semiramin, Curt. 7, 6, 20; Amm. 28, 4, 9.—Abl. Semirami, Just. 36, 2, 1: Semiramide, id. 1, 1, 10.—So Cicero sarcastically calls the profligate A. Gabinius, Cic. Prov. Cons. 4, 9.—Hence, Sĕmīrămĭus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Semiramis, Semiramian: Semiramio sanguine cretus Po

semirasus.full: sēmĭ-rāsus, a, um, adj. rado, halfshaven: ustor, Cat. 59, 5: homines, App. M. 9, p. 222, 30.

semireductus.full: sēmĭ-rĕductus, a, um, adj. reduco, half bent back: Venus, Ov. A. A. 2, 614.

semirefectus.full: sēmĭ-rĕfectus, a, um, adj. reficio, half-repaired: laniata classis, Ov. H. 7, 176.

semirosus.full: sēmĭ-rōsus, a, um, adj. rodo, halfgnawed: panis, Arn. 6, 202.

semirotundus.full: sēmĭ-rŏtundus, a, um, adj., half-round, semicircular (Appuleian): subterraneum, App. M. 11, p. 260, 2: suggestus, id. ib. 5, p. 160, 2.
semirotundus.short: sēmĭ-rŏtundus, a, um, adj., half-round, semicircular (Appuleian): subterraneum, App.

semirutus.full: sēmĭ-rŭtus, a, um, adj. ruo, halfpulled down, half-overthrown, half-demolished, half-destroyed, half-ruined (not anteAug.; freq. in the historians, esp. in Liv.): murus, Liv. 31, 26; 32, 17: tecta, id. 10, 4; Luc. 1, 24: vallum, Tac. A. 1, 61: castella, Liv. 28, 44; Tac. A. 4, 25: urbs, Liv. 5, 49; 31, 24: plus negotii fuit cum semirutā Karthagine quam cum integrā, Flor. 2, 15, 13: patria, Liv. 26, 32 et saep.: telae confuso stamine, half-torn, Claud. Rapt. Pros. 3, 155. —Neutr. plur. as subst.:

semis.full: sēmis, issis (in Vitr., Front., and Pall. indecl., e.g. duo semis pedes, Pall. Febr. 9, 10: duobus semis pedibus, id. Jan. 10, 3; 13, 7: diametros octo semis, Vitr. 4, 1: passuum milium et semis, Front. Aquaed. 7; cf.: habere duos et semis cubitos, Vulg. Exod. 25, 10 al.), m. cf. semi-; Gr. ἡμι-, ἥμισυ, a half, half-unity, a semi-unit (v. as, I.). In gen. (very rare for the usual dimidium): sex domini semissem Africae possidebant, Plin. 18, 6, 7, § 35: patrimonii, Dig. 36, 1, 78, § 7: e libertor
semis.short: sēmis, issis (in Vitr., Front., and Pall.

semisaucius.full: sēmĭ-saucĭus, a, um, adj., halfwounded; trop.: voluntas, Aug. Conf. 8, 8.

semisenex.full: sēmĭ-sĕnex, sĕnis, m., an oldish or elderly man, Plaut. Mil. 3, 1, 53 (dub.).
semisenex.short: sēmĭ-sĕnex, sĕnis, m., an oldish or elderly man, Plaut.

semisepultus.full: sēmĭ-sĕpultus, a, um, adj. sepelio, half-buried: ossa, Ov. H. 1, 55.

semisermo.full: sēmĭ-sermo, ōnis, m., a half-speech, a jargon: barbarus, Hier. Ep. 7, 2.
semisermo.short: sēmĭ-sermo, ōnis, m., a half-speech, a jargon: barbarus, Hier.

semisiccus.full: sēmĭ-siccus, a, um, adj., half-dry: thalli, Pall. Febr. 24, 4.
semisiccus.short: sēmĭ-siccus, a, um, adj., half-dry: thalli, Pall.

semisomnus.full: sēmĭ-somnus, a, um, and sēmĭ-somnis, e, adj. somnus, half-asleep, sleepy, drowsy (class.): tibi siccae semisomnae, Plaut. Curc. 1, 2, 22; Cic. Fam. 7, 1, 1; Cic. Verr. 2, 5, 36, § 95 Zumpt N. cr.; Sall. J. 21, 2; Liv. 9, 24; 9, 37; 25, 39 Drak.; 30, 5 fin.; 37, 20; 40, 15; Tac. A. 1, 51; 4, 25; id. H. 5, 22: sopor, Cael. ap. Quint. 4, 2, 124: cor, Phaedr. 4, 14, 13.—Form semisomnis, Sen. Brev. Vit. 14, 4.
semisomnus.short: sēmĭ-somnus, a, um, and sēmĭ-somnis, e, adj.

semisonans.full: sēmĭ-sŏnans, antis, adj. sono, halfsounding, semi-vocal: littera, i. e. a semivowel, App. de Mundo, 16, 29; Ter. Carm. Her. p. 2406 P.; Isid. 1, 4, 4.

semisopitus.full: sēmĭ-sōpītus, a, um, adj. sopio, half-asleep, sleepy, drowsy (for the class. semisomnus), App. M. 1, p. 109, 9.

semisoporus.full: sēmĭ-sŏpōrus, a, um, adj. sopor, half-asleep, sleepy, drowsy (for the class. semisomnus), Sid. Carm. 11, 59.

semispatha.full: sēmĭ-spătha, ae, f., a little spatha, Veg. Mil. 2, 15; 2, 16.
semispatha.short: sēmĭ-spătha, ae, f., a little spatha, Veg.

semissalis.full: sēmissālis, e, adj. semis, of or belonging to a half-as: usurae, i.e. a half-as a month (six per cent. a year), Dig. 50, 12, 10.

semissarius.full: sēmissārĭus, a, um, adj. id., of or belonging to a half-as: coheres, i.e. who inherits one half, Dig. 30, 1, 116.

semisso.full: sēmisso, āre, v. a. semis, II. C. 2., to fire or cauterize one half of a horse's foot: pedes equorum, Veg. 1, 26, 4; 2, 10, 9.

semisupinus.full: sēmĭ-sŭpīnus, a, um, adj., half bent backwards, half-supine (poet.): jacet in dextrum semisupina latus, Ov. A. A. 3, 788; id. Am. 1, 14, 20: manus, id. H. 10, 10; Mart. 6, 35, 4.
semisupinus.short: sēmĭ-sŭpīnus, a, um, adj., half bent backwards, half-supine (poet.): jacet in dextrum semisupina latus, Ov.

semita.full: sēmĭta, ae,f.se-(=sed-), i.e. aside; and root mi-, to go; cf.: meo, trames, a narrow way, a path, foot - path, lane, by - way, etc. (opp. via, a highway; cf.: callis, trames): quā ibant, ab itu iter appellarunt; quā id anguste, semita ut semiter, dictum, Varr. L. L. 5, § 35 Müll. Lit. (freq. and class.): angustissimae semitae, Cic. Agr. 2, 35, 96; cf. Mart. 7, 61, 4: aut viam aut semitam monstrare, Plaut. Rud. 1, 3, 30: decedam ego illi de viā, de semitā, id. Trin. 2, 4, 80; cf. id. Curc. 2, 3,

semitactus.full: sēmĭ-tactus, a, um, adj. tango, half-touched, Mart. 6, 74, 2.

semitalis.full: sēmĭtālis, e, adj. semita, of or be longing to foot-paths or by-ways: dei, whose statues are placed in by-ways, ἐνοδιοι, Verg. Cat. 8, 20.

semitarius.full: sēmĭtārĭus, a, um, adj. id., of or belonging to lanes or by-ways: moechi, Cat. 37, 16.

semitatim.full: sēmĭtātim, adv. id., through byways: semitatim fugere, Titin. ap. Charis. p. 194 P. (Com. Rel. p. 117 Rib.).

semitectus.full: sēmĭ-tectus, a, um, adj. tego, halfcovered (post-Aug.): nudis scapulis aut semitectis, Sen. Vit. Beat. 25, 2 fin.: capuli, App. M. 4, p. 150, 27: femora (Dianae), Arn. 6, 209: exercitus, Amm 19, 11 fin.

semitonium.full: sēmĭ-tŏnĭum, i, n. tonus, a halftone, semitone, Macr. Somn. Scip. 2, 1 fin.

semitractatus.full: sēmĭ-tractātus, a, um, adj. tracto, half-treated: materia, Tert. Fug. in Persec. 1.

semitrepidus.full: sēmĭ-trĕpĭdus, a, um, adj., halftrembling, App. M. 7, p. 191, 13.
semitrepidus.short: sēmĭ-trĕpĭdus, a, um, adj., halftrembling, App.

semitritus.full: sēmĭ-trītus, a, um, adj. tero, halfthrashed: frumenta, Col. 1, 6, 24; Pall. 1, 36, 2.

semivietus.full: sēmĭ-vĭētus, a, um, adj., half-shrivelled, half-withered: uvae, Col. 12, 16, 3.
semivietus.short: sēmĭ-vĭētus, a, um, adj., half-shrivelled, half-withered: uvae, Col.

semivigil.full: sēmĭ-vĭgil, adj., half-awake, Vict. Fur. Poen. 13.

semivir.full: sēmĭ-vĭr, vĭri, m. adj., a half-man, i. q. semihomo and semimas (not anteAug.). Lit. Half man and half beast, e. g. the Centaur Chiron. Ov. F. 5, 380; the Minotaur, id. A. A. 2, 24 (cf. semibos): Nessus, id. H. 9, 141.— An hermaphrodite, Ov. M. 4, 386; Plin. 11, 49, 110, § 263.— Transf., emasculated. Lit., of a priest of Cybele (cf. semimas), Juv. 6, 513: semiviri chori, Sil. 17, 20: formosum adulescentem semivirum reddidit, Lact. 1, 17, 7. — Trop., unmanly, womanish, effeminate: et nunc ille Pa

semivivus.full: sēmĭ-vīvus, a, um, adj., half-alive, half-dead, almost dead (class.; syn. semianimis). Lit.: ibi hominem fumo excruciatum, semivivum reliquit, Cic. Verr. 2, 1, 17, § 45: Bibulum semivivum reliquerunt, id. Att. 7, 2, 8; id. Pis. 14, 31; Sen. Brev. Vit. 13; Nep. Eum. 4, 4; Vulg. Luc. 10, 30.— Trop.: cum erat reclamatum semivivis mercenariorum vocibus, with half-expiring words, Cic. Sest. 59, 126.
semivivus.short: sēmĭ-vīvus, a, um, adj., half-alive, half-dead, almost dead (class.;

semivocalis.full: sēmĭ-vŏcālĭs, e, adj. Half-sounding, half-talking, semi-vocal: instrumentum rusticum, i. e. cattle (distinguished from vocale, slaves, and mutum, i. e. carts), Varr. R. R. 1, 17, 1.—In like manner: signum militare, i. e. horns, trumpets, etc. (distinguished from vocale, words, and mutum, banners), Veg. Mil. 3, 5.— In gram., as subst., a semi - vowel (of which there were, acc. to the old grammarians, the foll. seven: f, l, m, n, r, s, x), Quint. 1, 4, 6; 1, 7, 14; Prisc. p. 540 sq. P.; 564 ib. al

semivolucris.full: sēmĭ-vŏlucris, e, adj., half-winged: puellae, i. e. the Sirens, Symm. Ep. 1, 41.
semivolucris.short: sēmĭ-vŏlucris, e, adj., half-winged: puellae, i.

semivulsus.full: sēmĭ-vulsus, a, um, adj. vello, half torn to pieces: vittae, Mart. Cap. 1, § 10.

semizonarius.full: sēmĭ-zōnārĭus, ii, m., a maker of small girdles, Plaut. Aul. 3, 5, 42; cf. semicinctium.
semizonarius.short: sēmĭ-zōnārĭus, ii, m., a maker of small girdles, Plaut.

semnion.full: semnion, i, n., a plant of great virtue, = theobrotion, Plin. 24, 17, 102, § 162.
semnion.short: semnion, i, n., a plant of great virtue, = theobrotion, Plin.

semnones.full: Semnŏ_nes, um, m., = Σέμνωνες, Strab.; Σέμνονες, Ptol., a people of Northern Germany, in the territory of the mod. Brandenburg, Tac. G. 39; id. A. 2, 45; Vell. 2, 106, 2.

semo.full: Sēmo, ōnis, m. probably from sēmen, an ancient god that presided over the crops: SEMVNIS ALTERNEI ADVOCAPIT CONCTOS, song of the Fratres Arvales, Inscr. Orell. 2270.—As an epithet of Sancus, Ov. F. 6, 214; Liv. 8, 20; Inscr. Orell. 1860; 6999.

semodialis.full: sēmŏdĭālis, e, adj. semodius, containing a half-peck: placenta, Cato, R. R. 76, 5: olla, Marc. Emp. 16 med.

semodius.full: sē-mŏdĭus, ii, m. semi-, a half-peck, Cato, R. R. 11, 3; Col. 2, 10 fin.; 6, 3, 5; Mart. 7, 53, 5; Juv. 14, 67.

semonia.full: Sēmōnĭa, ae, f. semen; cf. Semo, a goddess of the Romans that presided over the crops, Macr. S. 1, 16.

semote.full: sēmōtē, adv., v. semoveo, P. a. fin.

semotus.full: sēmōtus, a, um, Part. and P. a., from semoveo.

semoveo.full: sē-mŏvĕo, mōvi, mōtum, 2, v. a., to move apart, to put aside, remove, separate (rare but class.; syn.: sepono, sejungo). Lit.: vos semotae, nos soli, Ter. And. 1, 5, 50: qui ante voce praeconis a liberis semovebantur, Cic. Har. Resp. 12, 26.— Trop., to part, separate, remove: Strato ab eā disciplinā omnino semovendus est, Cic. Ac. 1, 9, 34: omnes sententias eorum omnino a philosophiā, id. Fin. 2, 13, 39: te a curis, Lucr. 1, 51; for which, also: curā metuque, id. 2, 19: egestatem ab dulci vitā,

semper.full: semper, adv. root sam-; Gr. ἁμ-; v. semel and -per = παρά; cf. tantisper, ever, always, at all times, forever (cf. usque). In gen.: nequiter factum illud apud vos semper manebit, Cato ap. Gell. 16, 1: locus hic apud nos semper liber est, Plaut. Bacch. 1, 1, 49: semper occant priusquam sarriunt rustici, id. Capt. 3, 5, 5: sat habet favitorum semper, qui recte facit, Plaut. Am. prol. 79: quod improbis semper aliqui scrupus in animis haereat, semper iis ante oculos judicia et supplicia versentur: n

semperflorium.full: semper-flōrĭum, ii, n. flos, = sempervivum, evergreen, houseleek, App. Herb. 123.

sempervivus.full: semper-vīvus, a, um, adj., ever-living: res (Spiritus sanctus), Prud. Ham. 164: herba, the plant called also aizoon, evergreen, houseleek, App. Herb. 123.—Also, subst.: sempervīva, ae,f., Pall. 1, 35, 3. —And in analogy with aizoon (Gr. ἀείζωον), sempervīvum, i, n., Plin. 25, 13, 102, § 160 (not in Jahn).
sempervivus.short: semper-vīvus, a, um, adj., ever-living: res (Spiritus sanctus), Prud.

sempiterne.full: sempĭternē, adv., v. sempiternus fin. c.

sempiternitas.full: sempĭternĭtas, ātis,f. sempiternus, perpetuity, eternal duration, eternity (postclass.): stabilis mundi, App. Trism. p. 94, 30; Claud. Mam. Stat. An. 1, 3; 2, 1.

sempiterno.full: sempĭternō, adv., v. sempiternus fin. b.

sempiternum.full: sempĭternum, adv., v. sempiternus fin. a.

sempiternus.full: sempĭternus, a, um, adj. semper; like hesternus and aeternus, from heri and aevum, everlasting, ever-during, perpetual, continual, imperishable, eternal, sempiternal (cf. aeternus init.; very freq. and class.): fragile corpus animus sempiternus movet, etc., Cic. Rep. 6, 24, 26; cf. id. N. D. 3, 12, 29: immortalis memoria et sempiterna, Plaut. Mil. 3, 3, 15: deorum vita sempiterna, Ter. And. 5, 5, 3; cf.: aevo sempiterno frui, Cic. Rep. 6, 13, 13: ignes, id. ib. 6, 15, 15; cf.: cursus stellarum,

sempronius.full: Semprōnĭus, i, m.; Semprōnĭa, ae, f., the name of a Roman gens. Its most celebrated members were Ti. and C. Sempronius Gracchus, after whom are named the leges Semproniae (v. infra, A.); fem. Sempronia, wife of D. Junius Brutus, and sharer in Catiline's conspiracy, Sall. C. 25 and 40, 5.—Hence, Semprōnĭus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to a Sempronius: lex frumentaria, Cic. Brut. 62, 222; id. Dom. 9, 24; id. Fam. 1, 7, 10: leges, Cic. Verr. 2, 5, 63, § 163; id. Phil. 1, 8, 18 et saep.: Sempronia

semuncia.full: sēm-uncĭa, ae, f. semi; semuncia quod dimidia pars unciae, Varr. L. L. 5, § 171 Müll., a half-ounce, i. e. the twenty-fourth part of an as. In gen., a twenty-fourth part of any whole: facit heredem ex deunce et semunciā Caecinam, Cic. Caecin. 6, 17: semunciae horarum, Plin. 2, 14, 11, § 58. —Hence, transf., a trifle: bona ejus propter alieni aeris magnitudinem semunciā venierunt, for a trifling sum, qs. for a mere song, Ascon. ad Cic. Mil. fin. p. 54 Orell.— Trop.: brevis semuncia recti, Pers. 5

semuncialis.full: sēmuncĭālis, e, adj. semuncia, amounting to a half-ounce: asses, the twenty-fourth part of a pound in weight, Plin. 33, 3, 13, § 46 (Jahn, semiunciarius).

semunciarius.full: sēmuncĭārĭus, a, um, adj. id., amounting to a half-ounce (one twentyfourth of an as): semunciarium tantum ex unciario faenus factum, one twenty-fourth of an as upon each as, for a year of ten months, or, acc. to our mode of computation, five per cent. for a full year, Liv. 7, 27, 3; cf. id. 7, 16, 1: asses, weighing half an ounce, Plin. 33, 3, 13, § 46 Jahn.

semurium.full: Semurĭum, ii, n., a field near Rome, where was a temple of Apollo, Cic. Phil. 6, 5, 14; Macr. S. 1, 10.
semurium.short: Semurĭum, ii, n., a field near Rome, where was a temple of Apollo, Cic.

semustulo.full: sēmustŭlo (sēmĭ-ustŭlo, -tĭlo, v. Beier ad Cic. Tull. p. 33, a.; Cod. Erf. has semiustilo, Cic. Mil. 13, 33), no perf., ātum, 1, v. a. (only in part. perf. and fut.), to half burn, to burn in part: infelicissimis lignis semustulatus, Cic. Mil. 13, 33: faces mcendisti, quibus semustulatus ille est, id. Phil 2, 36, 91: semustulatus effugit, id. Tull. 18, 33; Varr. ap. Non. 263, 21: pauci semustulati venere in potestatem, Curt. 6, 6, 32: corpus in amphitheatro semustulandum, Suet. Tib. 75 fin.; cf.

semustus.full: sēmustus (sēmĭ-ustus), a, um, adj. uro, half-burned (not ante-Aug.). Lit.: Enceladi semustum fulmine corpus. Verg. A. 3, 578: robora, id. ib. 5, 697: facem, Ov. F. 4, 167; Sil. 3, 16; Stat. Th. 12, 439 al.: forum, Liv. 26, 27: simulacra, id. 31, 30; Vell. 2, 119, 6: tectorum vestigia lacera et semusta, Tac. A. 15, 40; Suet. Dom. 15 al.— Trop.: se populare incendium priore consulatu semustum effugisse, Liv. 22, 40, 3.

sena.full: Sēna, ae, f. A town on the coast of Umbria, where Hasdrubal was defeated by M. Livius Salinator (547 A.U.C.), now Sinigaglia, Liv 27, 46 sq.; Eutr. 3, 10.—Hence, Sēnānus, a, um, adj., of Sena: aquae, Cael. Aur. Tard. 2, 1, 48.— Sēnensis, e, adj., of or belonging to Sena: populus, Liv. 27, 38: proelium, in which Hasdrubal was defeated, Cic. Brut. 18, 73.— A river near the town of Sena, now Cesano, Sil. 8, 455; 15, 555; Luc. 2, 407.

senaculum.full: sĕnācŭlum, i, n. senatus. Orig., an open place on the Forum, near the Grœcostasis, serving for the meetings of the Senate: senaculum supra Graecostasim, ubi aedis Concordiae et basilica Opimia. Senaculum vocatum, ubi senatus aut ubi seniores consisterent, dictum ut gerusia apud Graecos, Varr. L. L. 5, § 156 Müll.; so Val. Max. 2, 2, 6; Liv. 41, 27, 7.— Later, in gen., for any council-hall of the Senate (including the curiae): senacula tria fuisse Romae, in quibus senatus haberi solitus sit, memo

senariolus.full: sēnārĭŏlus, i, m. senarius, a little, insignificant senarius, or verse of six feet, Cic. Tusc. 5, 23, 64.

senarius.full: sēnārĭus, a, um, adj. seni. In gen., consisting of six each; fistula, six quarter-digits (quadrantes) in diameter, Front. Aquaed. 25: numerus, the number six, Macr. Somn. Scip. 1, 6.— In partic.: versus, a verse consisting of six feet (usu. iambics), Quint. 9, 4, 125; Phaedr. 1, prol. 2.—More freq. as subst.: sēnārĭus, ii, m., Cic. Or. 55, 184; 56, 189; Quint. 9, 4, 72; 9, 4, 140 al.

senator.full: sĕnātor, ōris, m. senex, a senator, a member of the Roman Senate, a body consisting originally of one hundred eminent citizens, selected by Romulus for their age, wisdom, and experience, out of the noblest families, to be his council in the government. When the Sabines were incorporated with Rome, the number was doubled; and Tarquin the Elder raised it to three hundred; Sulla to four hundred; Julius Cæsar to nine hundred, while Augustus reduced it to six hundred. Originally, patricians alone wer

senatorius.full: sĕnātōrĭus, a, um, adj. senator, of or belonging to a senator, senatorial: cujus aetas a senatorio gradu longe abesset, Cic. Imp. Pomp. 21, 61; cf. ordo, Caes. B. C. 1, 23; 3, 33; Cic. Fl. 18, 43; Sall. C. 17, 3; id. J. 62, 4; 104, 1: dignitas, Suet. Claud. 24: locus, Gell. 12, 1, 2: subsellia, Cic. Corn. 1, p. 449 Orell.: consilium, the deliberations of the Senate, Cic. Verr. 2, 1, 2, § 4: munera, id. Tusc. 1, 1, 1; Suet. Aug. 35: litterae, speeches made in the Senate, Cic. Off. 2, 1, 3: album,

senatrix.full: sĕnātrix, trīcis, f. id., a female senator, Prisc. 638 P.

senatus.full: sĕnātus, ūs (gen. senati, Plaut. Cas. 3, 2, 6; id. Ep. 2, 2, 5; Sisenn. ap. Non. 484, 18; Cic. Div. in Caecil. 5, 19; also cited ap. Charis. p. 116 P.; Sall. C. 30, 3; 36, 5; 53, 1. acc. to Non. 484, 15; Charis. p. 10 P.; Don. Ter. Hec. 3, 2, 21; Prisc. p. 712 P.; id. Fragm. ap. Don. Ter. And. 2, 2, 28; also Cic. Fam. 2, 7, 4, acc. to the pr. man. of the Cod. Medic.; cf. Quint. 1, 6, 27.—Another form of the gen. senatuis, C. Fann. ap. Charis. p. 116 P.; Sisenn. ap. Non. 484, 19; also, as it seem

senatusconsultum.full: sĕnātusconsultum, i, v. consulo, P. a. III.

seneca.full: Sĕnĕca, ae, m., a surname (cognomen) in the gens Annaea. The most famous are, M. Annaeus Seneca, a native of Corduba (in Hispania Baetica), a celebrated rhetorician in the time of Augustus and Tiberius, whose writings (Controversiae and Suasoriae) are now extant only in fragments, Quint. 9, 2, 42; 9, 2, 98; v. Teuffel, Röm. Lit. § 264.— His son, L. Annaeus Seneca, a Stoic philosopher, instructor of Nero; of whom are extant, in prose, philosophical treatises, letters, and a satire upon the Empero
seneca.short: Sĕnĕca, ae, m., a surname (cognomen) in the gens Annaea.

senecio1.full: sĕnĕcĭo, ōnis, m. senex, an old man, Afran. ap. Prisc. p. 618 P.

senecio2.full: Sĕnĕcĭo, ōnis, m. id., a Roman surname, Tac. Agr. 2; 45; id. A. 13, 12; 15, 50; 15, 56 sq.; Plin. Ep. 3, 11, 3.

senecio3.full: sĕnĕcĭo, ōnis, m., a plant, called also erigeron, groundsel, Plin. 25, 13, 106, § 167; App. Herb. 75.
senecio3.short: sĕnĕcĭo, ōnis, m., a plant, called also erigeron, groundsel, Plin.

senectus1.full: sĕnectus, a, um, adj. senex, aged, very old. Adj. (rare, and mostly anteclass.): senecta aetas, Plaut. Am. 4, 2, 12; id. Trin. 1, 2, 5; id. Aul. 2, 2, 75; id. Cas. 2, 3, 23; 2, 3, 41; id. Merc. 5, 4, 25; Lucr. 5, 886; 5, 896; Sall. Fragm. ap. Serv. Verg. A. 11, 165: membris exire senectis, Lucr. 3, 772: corpus, Sall. ap. Prisc. p. 869 (H. 4, 63 Dietsch): aetas, id. ap. Serv. Verg. A. 11, 165 (H. inc. lib. 115 Dietsch).— Subst.: sĕ-necta, ae, f., old age, extreme age, senility (freq., though most

senectus2.full: sĕnectūs, ūtis,f. senex. Old age, extreme age, senility (freq. and class.; only in sing.): adulescentia (tua) senectuti dedecoramentum (fuit), senectus rei publicae flagitium, C. Gracch. ap. Isid. Orig. 2, 21, 4; cf.: quasi qui adulescentiam florem aetatis, senectutem occasum vitae velit definire, Cic. Top. 7, 32: ut in Catone Majore, qui est scriptus ad te de senectute ... ut tum ad senem senex de senectute, sic, etc., id. Lael. 1, 4 sq.; cf. id. Sen. 1 sqq.: T. Aufidius, qui vixit ad summam se

seneo.full: sĕneo, ēre, v. n. v. senex. Lit., to be old (very rare; perh. only in the foll. examples): quamquam aetas senet, Pac. ap. Prisc. p. 887; Cat. 4, 26.— Transf., to be weak, feeble: corpus meum tali maerore, errore, macore senet, Pac. ap. Non. 137, 1; (with languere) Att. ap. Prisc. p. 887 P.

senesco.full: sĕnesco, nŭi, 3 (gerundive: senescendi homines, Varr. L. L. 6, § 11 Müll. N. cr.), v. inch. n. [seneo], to grow old, become aged; to grow hoary. Lit. (rare): ita sensim aetas senescit, Cic. Sen. 11, 38; cf.: tempora labuntur tacitisque senescimus annis, Ov. F. 6, 771: senescente jam Graeciā, Cic. Rep. 1, 37, 58: solve senescentem mature equum, Hor. Ep. 1, 1, 8: arbores senescunt, Plin. 16, 27, 50, § 116: Solon significat se cottidie aliquid addiscentem senescere. Val. Max. 8, 7, 14.—In perf.: av

senex.full: sĕnex, sĕnis (nom. and acc. of the neutr. plur. in the posit. and of the neutr. sing. in the comp. do not occur; orig. gen. sĕnicis, Plaut. Fragm. ap. Prisc. p. 724 P.), adj. Sanscr. sana-s, old; Gr. ἕνος, ἕνη, old; cf.: senium, senesco, senatus, senilis, senectus, Seneca (comp. senior), old, aged, advanced in years; and subst., an aged person, an old man, old woman (from the latter half of the fortieth year onward; v. infra the passages from Gell. 10, 28, 1, and from Liv. 30, 30; cf.: annosus,

seni.full: sēni, ae, a (gen. plur. senūm, Cic. Verr. 2, 49, 122; Caes. B. C. 2, 15), num. distrib. [sex]. Lit., six each: cum in sex partes divisus exercitus Romanus senis horis in orbem succederet proelio, Liv. 6, 4: senos viros singuli currus vehebant, Curt. 8, 14, 3: ut tribuni militum seni deni (by many written in one word, senideni) in quattuor legiones crearentur, Liv. 9, 30; so, sena dena (or senadena) stipendia, Tac. A. 1, 36 fin.: senūm pedum crassitudo, Caes. B. C. 2, 15; cf.: pueri annorum senūm

seniae.full: Seniae, ārum, f.: balneae, the name of a public bath at Rome, Cic. Cael. 25, 62 (this the correct read., not Xeniae).
seniae.short: Seniae, ārum, f.: balneae, the name of a public bath at Rome, Cic.

senica.full: sĕnĭca, ae, m. or f. senicus; whence senex, an aged person, an old man, old woman, only Pompon. ap. Non. 17, 20, and 21.

seniculus.full: sĕnĭcŭlus, i, m. dim. senex, a little old man, only App. M. 1, p. 113, 32.

seniensis.full: Sēnĭensis (Colonia), a town of Etruria, now Siena, Plin. 3, 5, 8, § 51; Tac. H. 4, 45.—Hence, Sēnĭenses, ium, m., the inhabitants of Sena, Tac. l. l.
seniensis.short: Sēnĭensis (Colonia), a town of Etruria, now Siena, Plin.

senilis.full: sĕnīlis, e, adj. senex, of or belonging to old people, aged, senile (freq. and class.): Tages puerili specie dicitur visus, sed senili fuisse prudentiā, Cic. Div. 2, 23, 50; cf. partes (opp. viriles), Hor. A. P. 176: senile aliquid (opp. adulescentis aliquid), Cic. Sen. 11, 38: corpus, id. Sest. 22, 50: artus, Ov. M. 7, 250: vultus, id. ib. 8, 528: genae, id. ib. 8, 210: guttur, Hor. Epod. 3, 2: ruga, Ov. F. 5, 58: statua incurva, of an old man, Cic. Verr. 2, 2, 35, § 87: anni, Ov. M. 7, 163; 13

senio.full: sēnĭo, ōnis, m. seni, the number six, a sice upon dice: talis jactatis, ut quisque canem aut senionem miserat, August. ap. Suet. Aug. 71; Pers. 3, 48; Mart. 13, 1, 6.

senipes.full: sēnĭ-pēs, pĕdis, adj., six-footed, senarian (late Lat.): stilus, Sid. Carm. 23, 131; 12, 10.
senipes.short: sēnĭ-pēs, pĕdis, adj., six-footed, senarian (late Lat.): stilus, Sid.

senium.full: sĕnĭum, ii, n. seneo, II.. Lit., the feebleness of age, decline, decay, debility (cf. senectus; class.): tardigemulo senio oppressum, Laev. ap. Gell. 19, 7, 3: opus perfectum, quod omni morbo seniove careret, Cic. Univ. 5 fin.; (with aegritudo) id. Tusc. 3, 12, 27; cf.: senio debilis, Phaedr. 3, epil. 16: senio vel aliquā corporis labe insignes, Suet. Aug. 38: senio confectos gladiatores, id. Calig. 26 fin.: senium Galbae et juventa Othonis, Tac. H. 1, 22: principis, id. ib. 2, 1: curvata senio

senones.full: Sĕnŏnes or Sēnōnes, um, m., = Σένονες or Σήνωνες. A people in Gallia Lugdunensis, whose chief city was Agendicum, now Sens, Caes. B. G. 5, 54; 5, 56; 6, 2 sq.; 6, 44; 7, 4 al.; Plin. 4, 18, 32, § 107; Juv. 8, 234; Sil. 4, 160; Eutr. 10, 7.—In sing.: Sĕno, ŏnis, m., one of the Senones: Drappeten Senonem, Hirt. B. G. 8, 30.— A people in Gallia Cisalpina, sprung from the above, Liv. 5, 35; 10, 26; Plin. 3, 15, 20, § 116.—Hence, Sĕnŏnĭcus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to the Senones: bellum, Gell. 1
senones.short: Sĕnŏnes or Sēnōnes, um, m., = Σένονες or Σήνωνες.

sensatus.full: sensātus, a, um, adj. 2. sensus, gifted with sense, intelligent: homines (with callidi and astuti), Firm. Math. 3, 10; 5, 12; Vulg. Ecclus. 7, 27.—Adv.: sensātē, intelligently, sensibly: loqui, Vulg. Ecclus. 13, 27.

sensibilis.full: sensĭbĭlis, e, adj. id., that can be perceived by the senses, sensible (post-Aug. and very rare): vox auditui, perceptible, Vitr. 5, 3: (voluptatem) sensibile judicant bonum: nos contra intellegibile, Sen. Ep. 124, 2.— Act., endowed with feeling, capable of perceiving: simulacrum, Lact. 2, 10, 3; 2, 8, 33; 7, 4, 12.—Adv.: sensĭbĭlĭter, by the senses, sensibly: commovere deos nidore, Arn. 7, 234.

sensibilitas.full: sensĭbĭlĭtas, ātis, f. sensibilis. The sense or meaning of words, Non. 173, 14; 526. 22.— Sensibility, Fulg. Cont. Verg. p. 750 Stav.

sensiculus.full: sensĭcŭlus, i, m. dim. 2. sensus, II. B. 2. b., a little sentence: minuti corruptique sensiculi, Quint. 8, 5, 14.

sensifer.full: sensĭfer, fĕra, fĕrum, adj. 2. sensusfero, producing sensation (Lucret.): motus, Lucr. 3, 240; 3, 245; 3, 272.

sensificator.full: sensĭfĭcātor, ōris, m. sensifico, that produces sensation, an explanation of Sentinus, Aug. Civ. Dei, 7, 3.

sensifico.full: sensĭfĭco, āre, v. a. 2. sensus-facio, to make sensible, endow with sensation (late Lat.): rupes tonis (Musica), Mart. Cap. 9, § 908: corpus, Claud. Mam. Stat. An. 1, 17; 3, 2.

sensificus.full: sensĭfĭcus, a, um, adj. id., producing sensation (late Lat.): spiramentum (cerebri), Macr. S. 7, 9.

sensilis.full: sensĭlis, e, adj. 2. sensus, sensitive, sensible, i. e. endowed with sensation (Lucret.): ex insensilibus ne credas sensile gigni, Lucr. 2, 888; so id. 2, 893; 2, 895; 2, 902.

sensim.full: sensim, adv. sentio (prop. sensibly, i. e. perceptibly, observably, visibly; hence, as opp. to what is unforeseen, unexpected, sudden), slowly, gently, soflly, gradually (freq. and class.; syn.: paulatim, pedetemptim; opp. repente): sensim tardeve potius quasi nosmet ipsos cognoscimus, Cic. Fin. 5, 15, 41: sensim et pedetemptim, Lucil. ap. Non. 29, 7; cf.: sensim et pedetemptim progrediens extenuatur dolor, Cic. Tusc. 3, 22, 54: sensim pedetemptimque ... sensim dissuere amicitias, id. Off. 1, 33

sensorium.full: sensōrĭum, ii, n. id., the seat or organ of sensation, Boëth. Arist. Top. 8, 5, p. 732.

sensualis.full: sensŭālis, e, adj. 2. sensus, endowed with feeling or sensation, sensitive, sensual (post-class.), App. Trism. p. 80, 16; Tert. Anim. 43; Prud. στεφ. 10, 346.—Adv.: sensŭālĭter, in a sensual manner, carnally, Claud. Mam. Stat. An. 2, 12.

sensualitas.full: sensŭālĭtas, ātis, f. sensualis, the capacity for sensation, sensibility (postclass.), Tert. Anim. 17; 38 fin.

sensus1.full: sensus, a, um, Part. of sentio.

sensus2.full: sensus, ūs, m. sentio, the faculty or power of perceiving, perception, feeling, sensation, sense, etc. Corporeal, perception, feeling, sensation: omne animal sensus habet: sentit igitur et calida et frigida et dulcia et amara, nec potest ullo sensu jucunda accipere et non accipere contraria: si igitur voluptatis sensum capit, doloris etiam capit. etc., Cic. N. D. 3, 13, 32: moriendi sensum celeritas abstulit, id. Lael. 3, 12: si quis est sensus in morte, id. Phil. 9, 6, 13: (Niobe) posuit sensum

senta.full: Senta, ae, f., a place in Dalmatia, noted for a curious cavern, Plin. 2, 45, 44, § 115.
senta.short: Senta, ae, f., a place in Dalmatia, noted for a curious cavern, Plin.

sententia.full: sententĭa, ae, f. for sentientia, from sentio, a way of thinking, opinion, judgment, sentiment; a purpose, determination, decision, will, etc. Lit. (cf.: opinio, voluntas, studium). In gen.: quoniam sententiae atque opinionis meae voluistis esse participes, nihil occultabo et quoad potero, vobis exponam, quid de quāque re sentiam, Cic. de Or. 1, 37, 172: sententia et opinio mea, id. ib. 2, 34, 146: senis sententia de nuptiis, Ter. And. 1, 3, 2: de aliquā re, id. Ad. 3, 5, 5; id. Phorm. 2, 4, 4;

sententialis.full: sententĭālis, e, adj. sententia, = Gr. γνωμικός, in the form of a sentence, sententious, Cassiod. Rhet. 13, p. 499, 22; Isid. 2, 9, 11.—Hence, adv.: sententĭālĭter, in the form of maxims or axioms, sententiously (post-class.): et alia plurima, quae sententialiter proferuntur: nec haec apud Vergilium frustra desideraveris (Ecl. 8, 63): Non omnia possumus omnes, etc., Macr. S. 5, 16; so Tert. Carn. Chr. 18 med.

sententiola.full: sententĭŏla, ae, f. dim. id., a short or little sentence, maxim, or aphorism: sententiolas edicti cujusdam memoriae mandavi, * Cic. Phil. 3, 9, 21; Quint. 5, 13, 37; 9, 2, 98; 11, 1, 52; 12, 10, 73; Petr. 118, 2; Gell. 17, 12, 4.

sententiosus.full: sententĭōsus, a, um, adj. sententia, II. B. 2., full of meaning, pithy, sententious (rare but Ciceron.): sententiosum et argutum genus dictionis, Cic. Brut. 95, 325.— Adv.: sententĭōsē. Full of meaning, suggestively: sententiose (dicere) sine verborum et ordine et modo (opp. composite) et apte sine sententiis, Cic. Or. 71, 236: oratione habitā graviter et sententiose, id. Inv. 1, 55, 106.— Sententiously: saepe sententiose ridicula dicuntur, Cic. de Or. 2, 71, 286.

senticetum.full: sentĭcētum, i, n. sentis, a thicket of briers, thorn-brake, Plaut. Capt. 4, 2, 80; App. Flor. p. 348, 21.

senticosus.full: sentĭcōsus, a, um, adj. id., full of briers or thorns, thorny, briery (ante- and post-class.); trop.: verba, Afr. ap. Fest. s. v. sentes, p. 339 Müll.: merces (with aspera), App. Flor. p. 361, 1.

sentifico.full: sentĭfĭco, āre, v. a. sentio-facio, to endow with feeling or sensation (late Lat.): corpus, Claud. Mam. Stat. An. 1, 17: oculum, id. ib. 3, 2.

sentina.full: sentīna, ae, f. Lit., the filthy water that collects in the bottom of a ship, bilgewater: cum alii malos scandant, alii per foros cursent, alii sentinam exhauriant, Cic. Sen. 6, 17; * Caes. B. C. 3, 28: in nave, quae sentinam trahit, Sen. Ep. 30, 2: pisces sentinae navium odorem procul fugiunt, Plin. 10, 70, 90, § 194 al.; Gell. 19, 1, 3: mersamque vitiis suis, quasi sentinā, rempublicam pessum dedere, Flor. 3, 12, 7. — Transf., the bottom of a ship where the bilge-water is, the hold: hi Romam s

sentinaculum.full: sentīnācŭlum, i, n. sentino, an instrument for bailing out the bilge-water of a ship, a scoop, Paul. Nol. Ep. 36, 3.

sentinas.full: Sentīnas, ātis, adj., of or belonging to Sentinum (Sentis ap. Front. Colon. p. 124 Goes.; Σέντινον in Ptol. and Polyb.), a town of Umbria: ager, Liv. 10, 27, 1; 10, 30, 4; 10, 31, 12; for which, absol.: in Sentinate, Front. Strat. 1, 8, 3 Oud. N. cr.—Plur. subst.: Sentīnātes, um, m., the inhabitants of Sentinum, Plin. 3, 14, 19, § 114.
sentinas.short: Sentīnas, ātis, adj., of or belonging to Sentinum (Sentis ap.

sentinator.full: sentīnātor, ōris, m. sentino, one who bails out the bilge-water, from a ship (late Lat.), Paul. Nol. Ep. 36, 12.

sentino.full: sentīno, āre, v. n. sentina. Lit., to bail or pump out the bilge-water from a ship (late Lat.), Paul. Nol. Ep. 36 init.; Aug. Homil. 42.—* Trop., to be in difficulty or danger: sentinare, satagere, dictum a sentinā, quia multum aquae navis cum recipit periclitatur, Fest. p. 339 Müll.; Caecil. ib.

sentinosus.full: sentīnōsus, a, um, adj. id., full of bilge-water: naves, Cato ap. Non. 152, 25.

sentinus.full: Sentīnus, i, m. sentio, the deity who gives sensation to new-born infants, Varr. in Aug. Civ. Dei, 7, 2 fin.; Tert. ad Nat. 2, 11; cf. Becker, Antiq. 4, p. 10.

sentio.full: sentĭo, si, sum, 4 (perf. sync. sensti, Ter. And. 5, 3, 11), v. a. Physically. In gen., to discern by the senses; to feel, hear, see, etc.; to perceive, be sensible of (syn. percipio). With acc.: calorem et frigus, Lucr. 1, 496; cf.: duritiem saxi, id. 4, 268; 3, 381 sq.: feram nare sagaci (venaticā), Enn. ap. Fest. p. 177 Müll. (Ann. v. 346 Vahl.): varios rerum odores, Lucr. 1, 298: sucum in ore, id. 4, 617 sq.: suavitatem cibi, Cic. Phil. 2, 45, 115: varios rerum colores, Lucr. 4, 492: sonitum

sentis1.full: sentis, is (acc. sentim, Col. 11, 3, 4), m. (fem.: et rubus et sentes tantummodo natae, Ov. de Nuce, 113: tenerae fruticum sentes, Verg. Cul. 55). A thorn, thornbush, brier, bramble (usually in plur., and mostly poet.; not in Cic.; but. cf. vepris). Plur.: arbores, vites, vepres, sentes, S. C. ap. Front. Aquaed. 129: He. Asper meus victus sane est. Er. Sentesne esitas? Plaut. Capt. 1, 2, 85; Lucr. 5, 207; Verg. E. 4, 29; id. G. 2, 411; id. A. 2, 379; 9, 382; Ov. M. 1, 509; 2, 799; *Caes. B. G. 2

sentisco.full: sentisco, ĕre, v. inch. n. [sentio, II.], to perceive, note, observe (Lucretian), Lucr. 3, 392; 4, 586.

sentius.full: Sentius, i, m., the name of a Roman gens. Sentius Saturninus, a proprœtor in Macedonia, A. U.C. 671, Cic. Verr. 2, 3, 93, § 217; id. Pis. 34, 84.— Cn. Sentius, a governor of Syria, Tac. A. 2, 74; 3, 7.
sentius.short: Sentius, i, m., the name of a Roman gens.

sentix.full: sentix, ĭcis, m. sentis, the plant cynosbatos or sentis canis, dog rose, wildbrier, App. Herb. 87, Isid. Orig. 17, 7, 59 sq.

sentosus.full: sentōsus (-tŭōsus), a, um, adj. id., full of thorns, thorny (late Lat.), Paul. Nol. Carm. 6,310; Fulg. Myth. prol.— Trop., form sentuosus: stricto et sentuoso brevitatis vinculo, Boëth. in Porphyr. Dial. 1, p. 12.

sentus.full: sentus, a, um, adj. id., Lit., thorny, rough, rugged (poet. and very rare): loca senta situ, * Verg. A. 6, 462; Ov. M. 4, 436: vepres, Prud. in Symm. 2, 1039: rubus, id. Apoth. 123.—* Transf.: video sentum, squalidum, aegrum, pannis annisque obsitum (hominem), bristly, Ter. Eun. 2, 2, 5.

seorsus.full: sĕorsus, a, um, adj. abbrev. from sevorsus, from se-vorto, sundered, separate, apart (syn. separatus). Adj. (so only ante- and post-class.): seorsum atque diversum pretium, Cato ap. Fest. s. v. optionatus, p. 201 Müll.: vocabulum, id. ap. Gell. 7, 10, 2: syllabae, Ter. Maur. p. 2398 P.: seorsa quae (videor tractasse), id. p. 2439 fin. ib.; cf. studia, Aus. Idyll. 17, 5.—Hence, Adv.: sĕorsum (often erroneously written sĕorsim; collat. form sĕor-sus, Plaut. Rud. 5, 2, 27; Afran. ap. Charis, p. 195

separ.full: sē-pār, păris (perh. only in abl. sing.), adj., separate, different (syn. dispar; postAug. and mostly poet.)' ossa separe urnā contegere, Val. Fl. 5, 58; separe coetu, Stat. Th. 4, 481: separe ductu, Prud. Apoth. 311: duo flumina naturā separi, Sol. 7 fin.

separabilis.full: sēpărābĭlis, e, adj. separo, that may be separated, separable: nec (eam vim) separabilem a corpore esse, Cic. Tusc. 1, 10, 21; a veritate unius Dei, Hilar Trin. 1, 16 fin.

separate.full: sēpărātē, adv., v. separo, P a. fin.

separatim.full: sēpărātim, adv. separo, asunder, apart, separately (freq. and good prose; syn. seorsum) With ab: (di) separatim ab universis singulos diligunt, Cic. N D. 2, 66, 165: nihil accidet ei separatim a reliquis civibus, id. Fam. 2, 16, 5: separatim a reliquis consilium capere, Caes. B. C. 1, 76: separatim eos ab illis consulturos, Liv. 40, 47, 4.— Absol. (so most freq.): hoc sejungi potest separatimque perscribi, Cic. Phil. 13, 21, 50: unā in re separatim elaborare, id. de Or. 1, 3, 9: separatim singul

separatio.full: sēpărātĭo, ōnis, f. id., a sundering, severing, separation (rare, but good prose): sui facti ab illā definitione separatio, Cic. Inv. 2, 18, 55: distributione partium ac separatione, id. de Or. 3, 33, 132: congregatio criminum accusantem adjuvat, separatio defendentem, Quint. 7, 1, 31: nominum idem significantium (opp. congregare, and corresp. to disjunctio), id. 9, 3, 45: animi et corporis in morte, Gell. 2, 8, 7: tamquam eā separatione ad caedem destinarentur, Tac. H. 4, 46.— Esp., rhet. t. t.

separativus.full: sēpărātīvus, a, um, adj. separo, of or belonging to separation, disjunctive, separative (late Lat.): conjunctio, Diom. p. 412 P.; Prisc. 1002 P.

separator.full: sēpărātor, ōris, m. id., he that separates, a separator (late Lat.), Tert. Praescr. 30 med.; Vulg. Zach. 9, 6.

separatrix.full: sēpărātrix, īcis, f. separator, she that separates (late Lat.): voluntas conjunctrix ac separatrix hujuscemodi rerum, Aug. Trin. 11, 10.

separatus1.full: sēpărātus, a, um, Part. and P. a. of separo.

separatus2.full: sēpărātus, ūs, m. separo, a parting, separating: parili (crinis), App. Flor. p. 350, 40.

separo.full: sē-păro, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. 2. paro, to disjoin, sever, part, divide, separate (class. and freq., esp. in the trop. sense; cf.: divido, dirimo, disjungo, secludo). Lit. With ab: senatoria subsellia a populari consessu, Cic. Corn. Fragm. 12, p. 449 Orell.: separat Aonios Oetaeis Phocis ab arvis, Ov. M. 1, 313: Asiam ab Europā, Plin. 4, 12, 26, § 87: separandos a cetero exercitu ratus, Curt. 7, 2, 35.— With abl. (poet.): Seston Abydenā separat urbe fretum, Ov. Tr. 1, 10, 28: separat (spatium) aet

sepelibilis.full: sĕpĕlībĭlis, e, adj. sepelio, that may be buried; hence, trop., that may be hidden or concealed (a word formed by Plaut.): stultitia, Plaut. Cist. 1, 1, 64.

sepelio.full: sĕpĕlĭo, pelīvi or ii, pultum, 4 (perf. sepeli, Pers. 3, 97; part. perf. sepelitus, Cato ap. Prisc. p. 909 P.; fut. sepelibis, Aus. Ep 25, 61; perf. sepelisset, Prop. 1, 17, 19; Quint. 8, 5, 16), v. a., to bury, inter (class.): sepultus intellegitur quoquo modo conditus, humatus vero humo contectus, Plin. 7, 54, 55, § 187 (cf. also condo). Lit.: hominem mortuum, inquit lex in XII., in urbe ne sepelito neve urito. Credo vel propter ignis periculum. Quod autem addit, neve urito, indicat, non qui u

sepes1.full: sē-pēs, pĕdis, adj. sex, six-footed: populi (formicae), App. M. 6, p. 177, 26.

sepia.full: sēpĭa, ae, f., = σηπία, the cuttle-fish, having a black, inky liquid, Cic. N. D. 2, 50, 127; Plin. 9, 29, 45, § 84; Plaut. Rud. 3, 2, 45; Col. 6, 17, 7.—This liquid was used for ink, Pers. 3, 13; hence, transf., ink: furva, Aus. Ep. 4, 76.
sepia.short: sēpĭa, ae, f., = σηπία, the cuttle-fish, having a black, inky liquid, Cic.

sepias.full: Sēpĭăs, ădis, f., = Σηπιὰς ἄκρα, a promontory of Magnesia, Plin. 4, 9, 16, § 32; Mel. 2, 3; Val. Fl. 2, 9.
sepias.short: Sēpĭăs, ădis, f., = Σηπιὰς ἄκρα, a promontory of Magnesia, Plin.

sepiola.full: sēpĭŏla, ae, f. dim. sepia, a little cuttle-fish, Plaut. Cas. 2, 8, 57.

seplasia.full: Sēplā^sĭa (ă, Aus. Epigr 123; ā, Marcell. Medic. 66), ae, f. (Sēplā^sĭa, ōrum, n., Varr. ap. Non. 226, 16), a street in Capua, where unguents were sold: Seplasia platea Capuae, in quā unguentarii negotiari sunt soliti, Ascon. Cic. Pis. 11, 24, p. 10 Orell.; so Varr. ap. Non. 226, 18; Cic. Pis. 11, 24; id. Agr. 2, 34, 94; id. Sest. 8, 19; Plin. 16, 10, 18, § 40; 33, 13, 57, § 164: fraus Seplasiae, i. e. ointments adulterated in the Seplasia, id. 34, 11, 25, § 108; Val. Max. 9, 1, 1 ext.—In plur.,

sepono.full: sē-pōno, pŏsŭi, pŏsĭtum, 3 (part. perf. sync. sepostus, Sil. 8, 378; 17, 281; but, sepositus, Hor. S. 2, 6, 84), v. a., to lay apart or aside; to put by, separate, pick out, select, etc. (class.; not in Cæs.; syn.: sejungo, segrego, recondo). Lit. In gen.: seponi et occultari, Cic. Att. 11, 24, 2; cf.: aliquid habere sepositum et reconditum, Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 10, § 23; so (with conditus) id. Div. 2, 54, 112; cf.: ornamenta seposita (for which, just before, recondita), id. de Or. 1, 35, 162: id eg

sepositio.full: sēpŏsĭtĭo, ōnis, f. sepono, a laying aside, setting apart, hoarding: pecuniae, Veg. Mil. 2, 20.— A separation (postclass.): si forte qui decimam vovit decesserit ante sepositionem (for which, just before, separata), Dig. 50, 12, 2, § 2.

sepositus.full: sēpŏsĭtus, a, um, Part. and P. a. of sepono.

seps1.full: seps, sēpis, comm., = σήψ. A venomous serpent, whose bite occasioned putrefaction, Luc. 9, 764 sq.; 9, 723.—Acc. sing. sepa, Plin. 29, 5, 32, § 102.—Acc. Plur. sepas, Plin. 23, 2, 29, § 61; Tert. Carm. adv. Marc. 1, 1 fin.; Aus. Idyll. Grammat. 12, 14.— An insect, perh. the wood-louse, milleped, Plin. 20, 2, 6, § 12; 29, 6, 39, § 137.

sepse.full: sepse, pron. reflex. fem. [se - ipse], one's self. quae (virtus) omnes magis quam sepse diligit, Cic. Rep. 3, 8 (also cited by Sen. Ep. 108, 32).

septa.full: septa, ōrum, n., v. saepio fin.

septages.full: septages, ae, f. Indian, = ψίττακος, a parrot, Plin. 10, 41, 58, § 117.

septas.full: septăs, ădis, f. ἑπτάς, the number seven, acc. to Macr. Somn. Scip. 1, 6 med.

septejugis.full: septĕjŭgis, is, m. (sc. currus) [septem-jugum; cf. 1. sejugis], a team of seven, Inscr. Grut. 337, 8.

septem.full: septem, num. adj. indecl. [Sanscr. saptan; Gr. ἑπτά; Goth. sibun; Germ. sieben; Engl. seven], seven: septem menses sunt, quom, etc., Plaut. Most. 2, 2, 39: septem milia, id. Mil. 1, 1, 46: dis, quibus septem placuere colles, Hor. C. S. 7: septem et decem, Plaut. Cist. 4, 2, 89: decem et septem, Liv. 33, 21, 8; Plin. Ep. 2, 17, 2: decem septemque, Nep. Cato, 1, 2: decem septem, Liv. 24, 15, 2 Weissenb.; cf. Prisc. p. 1170 P.; v. also septendecim: septem et viginti minae, Plaut. Merc. 2, 3, 94: se

september.full: September, bris, m. septem; as, October, Novem-ber, Decem-ber; cf. Varr. L. L. 6, § 34 Müll., the seventh month of the Roman year, reckoning from March, i. e. our ninth, September (consisting, as now, of thirty days); usually with mensis: mense Septembri, Cic. Att. 1, 1, 2; Suet. Aug. 31; 35; id. Tib. 26; id. Calig. 15; id. Dom. 13 fin.—Without mensis, Aus. Ecl. de Mens. Monos. 9; so id. ib. Dist. 18; id. ib. Quot. Kal. 8 al.—As adj., with other substantives, of September, September-: Kalendis S

septemchordis.full: septem-chordis (-cordis), e, adj. chorda, with seven strings: cithara, Isid. Or. 3, 21, 4.

septemfluus.full: septem-flŭus, a, um, adj. fluo, sevenfold-flowing, an Ovidian epithet of the Nile (as having seven mouths): Nilus, Ov. M. 1, 422: flumina Nili, id. ib. 15, 753 (cf. the foll. art. and septemplex).

septemgeminus.full: septem-gĕmĭnus, a, um, adj., sevenfold (poet.): Nilus (as having seven mouths), Cat. 11, 7; Verg. A. 6, 800 (cf. the preced. art. and septemplex): Roma (the city of seven hills), Stat. S. 1, 2, 191: septemgemino Roma jugo, id. ib. 4, 1, 6.
septemgeminus.short: septem-gĕmĭnus, a, um, adj., sevenfold (poet.): Nilus (as having seven mouths), Cat.

septemmestris.full: septem-mestris (septĭmestris), e, adj. mensis, of seven months (late Lat.): infans, Censor. de Die Nat. 8, § 10: septimestris partus, id. ib. 11, § 2.

septemnerva.full: septem-nerva, ae, f. septem-nervus, an herb, called also plantago, App. Herb. 1.

septempedalis.full: septem-pĕdālis, e, adj., of seven feet, seven feet high: statua, Plaut. Curc. 3, 71.
septempedalis.short: septem-pĕdālis, e, adj., of seven feet, seven feet high: statua, Plaut.
