Inv. 1, 24, 35; cf.: natus ambiguo inter marem ac feminam sexu infans, Liv. 27, 11; and: mare et femineum sexus, App de Mundo, c. 20, p. 66 med.: feminarum sexus, Plin. 7, 52, 53, § 175: virilis

si.full: sī (orig. and ante-class. form seī), conj. [from a pronominal stem = Gr. ἑ; Sanscr. sva-, self; cf. Corss. Ausspr. 1, 778; Georg Curtius Gr. Etym. 396], a conditional particle, if. Prop. With indic.; so in gen., in conditions which are assumed to be true, with the verb in pres. or perf.; less freq. in imperf or pluperf.; and in conditions which may probably become true, with the verb in fut. or fut. perf. (Madv. Gram. § 332; Zumpt, Gram. § 517). Pres.: SI IN IVS VOCAT, Fragm. XII. Tab. ap. Gell.

siagones.full: sĭāgŏnes, um, m., = σιαγόνες, the muscles which support the jaw, the maxillary muscles; acc. siagonas, Cael. Aur. Tard. 1, 1, 37; 1, 4, 90.—Called also sĭāgŏnītae, ārum, m., = σιαγονῖται, Cael. Aur. Acut. 2, 10, 59; 2, 3, 6; 2, 3, 8.
siagones.short: sĭāgŏnes, um, m., = σιαγόνες, the muscles which support the jaw, the maxillary muscles;

sibe.full: sĭbĕ, for sibi, Quint. 1, 7, 24; v. sibi, under sui.

sibilatio.full: sībĭlātĭo (collat. form sĭfĭlātĭo, Non. 531, 4), ōnis, f. sibilo, a sibilation, hissing (late Lat.): serpentium, Vulg. Sap. 17, 9: vel stridor, Cael. Aur. Tard. 2, 14, 198.

sibilatrix.full: sībĭlātrix, īcis, adj. f. [sibilator], hissing, whistling: fistula sibilatrix, Mart. Cap. 9, § 906.

sibilatus.full: sībĭlātus, ūs, m. sibilo, a hissing whistling, Cael. Aur. Acut. 2, 27, 144.

sibilo.full: sībĭlo (collat. form sīfĭlo, Non. 531, 2), āre, v. n. and a. [sibilus] (class. but rare). Neutr., to hiss, to whistle: imitationis hoc modo, ut majores rudere et vagire et mugire et murmurare et sibilare appellaverunt, Auct. Her. 4, 31, 42: (serpens) sibilat ore, * Verg. A. 11, 754; so of a serpent, Prop. 4 (5), 7, 54. Ov M. 4, 588.—Of gossips: contemplent, conspiciant omnes, nutent, nictent, sibilent, * Plaut. Merc. 2, 3, 72.—Of things: illud (ferrum igne rubens) Stridet et in trepidā submersum

sibilus1.full: sībĭlus, i (collat. form, abl., sibilu, Sisenn. ap. Prisc. p. 715 P.—In plur. in the poets, prob. merely for the sake of the metre: sībĭla, ōrum; cf. 2. sibilus init.; but in Cic. sibili), m. cf. σιφνός, σιβλός, hollow; Angl. S. and Engl. sipan, sip; O. H. Germ. sip, Germ. Sieb, a sieve; regarded by the ancients as imitation of a natural sound; cf. Quint. 8, 6, 31; Auct. Her. 4, 31, 42, a hissing, a whistling (class.) In gen. Sing., of men: sibilo dare signum, Liv. 25, 8 fin.—Of cattle: (boves)

sibilus2.full: sībĭlus, a, um, adj. 1. sibilus, hissing, whistling (poet.; occurring, on account of the metre, only in the form sibila; cf. 1. sibilus init.): colla (colubrae), Verg. G. 3, 421; id. A. 5, 277; cf. ora (anguium), id. ib. 2, 211: coma torvae frontis (Panis), Val. Fl. 3, 50.

sibina.full: sĭbĭna or sĭbўna, ae, f., = σιβύνη, a kind of hunting-spear, Enn. ap. Paul. ex Fest. p. 336 Müll. (Ann. v. 496 Vahl.); Tert. adv. Marc. 1, 1, as a transl. of , Isa. 2, 4 (for which the Vulg. has lanceae).
sibina.short: sĭbĭna or sĭbўna, ae, f., = σιβύνη, a kind of hunting-spear, Enn.

sibus.full: sibus, callidus sive acutus, Fest. p. 336 Vahl.; cf. persibus.

sibuzates.full: Sibuzātes, a people in Aquitania (the mod. Sobusse on the Adour, between Dax and Bayonne), Caes. B. G. 3, 27.
sibuzates.short: Sibuzātes, a people in Aquitania (the mod.

sibylla.full: Sĭbylla (in many MSS. and edd. Sĭbul-la, e. g. Tac. A. 6, 18 Ritter), ae, f.,= Σίβυλλα, a female soothsayer, a prophetess, Sibyl, Varr. ap. Lact. 1, 6, 7; Aug. Civ. Dei, 18, 23; Lact. 2, 8, 48; Verg. A. 5, 735: has (litteras), credo, nisi Sibylla legerit, Interpretari alium potesse neminem, Plaut. Ps. 1, 1, 23: terrae vis Pythiam Delphis incitabat: naturae Sibyllam. Cic. Div. 1, 36, 79; cf. id. ib. 1, 18, 34.—In Roman mythology, the most celebrated is the Sibyl at Cumae, in the service of Apollo

sic.full: sīc (old form sīce, Plaut. Rud. 2, 4, 12; also seic, C. I. L. 818), adv. for si - ce; si, locat. form of pron. stem sa- = Gr. ὁ, ἁ, or ἡ, and demonstr. -ce; v. Corss. Ausspr. 1, 777, so, thus, in this or that manner, in such a manner, in the same way or manner, in like manner, likewise, to this or that extent or degree, to such a degree, in this or that state or condition, in such a condition (syn. ita); sic refers, I. To a previous fact, description, or assumption.—II. To a subsequent independe

sica.full: sīca, ae, f. A curved dagger, a poniard, Enn. ap. Paul. ex Fest. p. 336 Müll. (Ann. v. 496 Vahl.); Cic. Cat. 1, 6, 16; 2, 10, 23; cf. id. ib. 2, 1, 1; Suet. Calig. 32; Mart. 3, 16, 2; Val. Max. 3, 2, 12 al.: tum haec cottidiana, sicae, veneni, peculatus, i. e. for stabbing, Cic. N. D. 3, 30, 74: hinc sicae, hinc venena, hinc falsa testamenta nascuntur, id. Off. 3, 8, 36.— Transf., the edge of a boar's tusk: cum arbore et saxo apri exacuant dentium sicas, Plin. 18, 1, 1, § 2.—Of wit: sicam ingeni

sicani.full: Sĭcāni, ōrum, m., = Σῖκα^νοί, a very ancient people of Italy on the Tiber, a portion of whom afterwards migrated to Sicily, Verg. A. 5, 293; 7, 795; 11, 317; Sil. 14, 34. —Hence, Sĭcānus (scanned Sīcănŭs, in analogy with the Greek, Sil. 10, 314; 14, 258: Sīcānŭs, Aus. Griph. 46), a, um, adj., = Σικανός. * Of or belonging to the Sicani, Sicanian: gentes, i. q. Sicani, Verg. A. 8, 328.—More freq., Poet., Siculian, Sicilian: fluctus, Verg. E. 10, 4: portus, id. A. 5, 24: fines, id. ib. 11, 317: mon
sicani.short: Sĭcāni, ōrum, m., = Σῖκα^νοί, a very ancient people of Italy on the Tiber, a portion of whom afterwards migrated to Sicily, Verg.

sicarius.full: sīcārĭus, i, m. sica, an assassin, murderer (syn.: percussor, homicida): per abusionem sicarios etiam omnes vocamus, qui caedem telo quocumque commiserint, Quint. 10, 1, 12: vetus, Cic. Rosc. Am. 14, 39; * Hor. S. 1, 4, 4; Cic. Rosc. Am. 3, 8; Cic. Verr. 2, 1, 3, § 9; Suet. Caes. 72: jam sexcenti sunt, qui inter sicarios et de veneficiis accusabant, of assassination, Cic. Rosc. Am. 32, 90; so, quaestio inter sicarios, id. Clu. 53, 147; id. Fin. 2, 16, 54; and: inter sicarios defendere, id. Phil.

sicca.full: Sicca, ae, f., a border-town on the east of Numidia, with a temple of Venus, now Kef, Plin. 5, 3, 2, § 22; Sall. J. 56, 3; Val. Max. 2, 6, 15.—Hence, Siccenses, ĭum, m., the inhabitants of Sicca, Sall. J. 56, 4 sq.
sicca.short: Sicca, ae, f., a border-town on the east of Numidia, with a temple of Venus, now Kef, Plin.

siccabilis.full: siccābĭlis, e, adj. sicco, that makes dry, drying, Cael. Aur. Tard. 3, 8, 138 sq.

siccaneus.full: siccānĕus, a, um, adj. siccus (a technical word of Columella); of soil, dry, of a dry nature: genus prati (opp. riguum), Col. 2, 16, 3: locus (opp. riguus), id. 4, 30, 5; 11, 2, 71.—Neutr. plur. absol.: de siccaneis et riguis non comperimus, dry places, Col. 2, 2, 4.

siccanus.full: siccānus, a, um, adj. id. (a technical word of the elder Pliny); of plants, dry, of a dry nature: ulmi (opp. riguae), Plin. 16, 17, 29, § 72: olus, Pelag. Vet. 7.

siccarius.full: siccārĭus, a, um, adj. id., of or for drying or keeping dry: canistra, stands for wine-cups (used for keeping the table or the clothes from being wet), acc. to Serv. Verg. A. 1, 706.

siccatio.full: siccātĭo, ōnis, f. sicco, a drying, Plin. 34, 13, 33, § 129; Vulg. Ezech. 26, 5.

siccativus.full: siccātīvus, a, um, adj. id., that makes dry, drying, siccative: malagma, Cael. Aur. Tard. 4, 3, 71: aquae, Casslod. Var. 10, 29.

siccatorius.full: siccātōrĭus, a, um, adj. sicco, that makes dry, drying: origanum, Theod. Prisc. Diaet. 10.

sicce1.full: sicce, adv., a false read. for sic, Plaut. Rud. 2, 4, 12.)

siccesco.full: siccesco, ĕre, v. inch. n. [siccus], to grow or become dry, to dry up (not anteAug.), Cels. 7, 7, 15; Vitr. 2, 10; Col. 12, 28; Plin. 18, 34, 77, § 339.

siccificus.full: siccĭfĭcus, a, um, adj. siccus-facio, that makes dry, drying: vis aeris, Macr. S. 7, 16 fin.

siccitas.full: siccĭtas, ātis (gen. plur. siccitatium, Plin. 17, 24, 37, § 222), f. siccus, dryness, siccity (freq. and class.; used alike in sing. and plur.). Lit. In gen.: ab lippitudine usque siccitas ut sit tibi, * Plaut. Rud. 3, 2, 18: uvae, Plin. 18, 31, 74, § 315: palmarum, id. 13, 4, 9, § 47.— In partic. Of places, dryness: in Sipontinā siccitate, Cic. Agr. 2, 27, 71: siccitates paludum, Caes. B. G. 4, 38.— Of the weather, dryness, drought: siccitate et inopiā frugum insignis annus fuit: sex menses num

sicco.full: sicco, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. and n. id.. Act., to make dry, to dry, to dry up. In gen. (freq. and class.): venti et sol siccare prius confidunt omnia posse, Lucr. 5, 390; cf.: sol siccaverat herbas, Ov. M. 4, 82: siccabat rorantes capillos, id. F. 4, 141: sole capillos, id. M. 11, 770; Plin. 27, 9, 55, § 79: aliquid in sole, Col. 12, 46, 5; Plin. 12, 13, 27, § 47: aliquid ad lunam, id. 21, 11, 36, § 62: lina madentia, Ov. M. 13, 931: retia litore, id. ib. 11, 362: vellera, Verg. E. 3, 95: veste cr

siccoculus.full: siccŏcŭlus, a, um, adj. siccus-oculus, having dry eyes, dry-eyed: genus nostrum semper siccoculum fuit, Plaut. Ps. 1, 1, 75.

siccus.full: siccus, a, um, adj. cf. Sanscr. cush, to dry up; Gr. αὔω, dry. Lit. In gen. (mostly poet. and in post-Aug. prose; cf. aridus): arena, Verg. G. 1, 389: fauces fluminum, id. ib. 4, 427: siccāque in rupe resedit, id. A. 5, 180: litus, id. ib. 6, 162: siccum et sine umore ullo solum, Quint. 2, 4, 8: glebae, Hor. Epod. 16, 55: agri, id. S. 2, 4, 15: lacus, Prop. 2, 14 (3, 6), 11: regio, Curt. 9, 10, 2: via (opp. palustris), Dig. 43, 8, 2, § 32 et saep.—Sup.: horreum siccissimum, Col. 12, 15, 2: oculi

sicelicon.full: sĭcĕlĭcon, i, n., = σικελικόν, a plant, called also psyllion, fleawort, fleabane, Plin. 25, 11, 90, § 140.
sicelicon.short: sĭcĕlĭcon, i, n., = σικελικόν, a plant, called also psyllion, fleawort, fleabane, Plin.

sicera.full: sīcĕra, n., = σίκερα [from the Heb. ], a kind of spirituous, intoxicating drink (eccl. Lat.), Ter. adv. Psych. 9, from Vulg. Lev. 10, 9; Hier. Ep. 52, 1; cf. Isid. Orig. 20, 3, 16.

sicilicula.full: sīcīlĭcŭla, ae, f. dim. sicilis, a little cutting instrument, a small sickle, Plaut. Rud. 4, 4, 125.

sicilicus.full: sīcīlĭcus (sīcīlĭquus, and in inscrr. also designated by , Inscr. Orell. 2537), i, m. id.. Lit. In gen., the fourth part of an uncia, and consequently the forty-eight part of an as: cum noverca universae hereditatis habeat dodrantem semunciam et sicilicum, Dig. 33, 1, 21, § 2. — In partic. As a measure of length, a quarter of an inch, Front. Aquaed. 28; Plin. 13, 15, 29, § 94; 31, 6, 31, § 57.— As a measure of land, one forty-eighth of a jugerum, Col. 5, 1, 9; 5, 2, 5.— As a weight, two drachms,

sicilimenta.full: sīcīlīmenta, ōrum, n. sicilis, what is cut or mown with the sickle (sc. after the first crop has been taken off), the aftermath, Cato, R. R. 5 fin.

sicilio.full: sīcīlĭo, īre, v. a. id., to cut or mow with the sickle, after the first crop has been taken off: prata, Varr. R. R. 1, 49, 2; Col. 2, 22, 3; Plin. 18, 28, 67, § 259.

sicilis.full: sīcīlis, is, f. sica, a cutting instrument, sickle (cf. falx): incedit veles vulgo sicilibus latis, Enn. ap. Paul. ex Fest. p. 337 Müll. (Ann. v. 499 Vahl.): sicilis similitudo, Plin. 6, 13, 15, § 38.

sicilisso.full: sĭcĭlisso or sĭcĕlisso, āre, v. n. Siculi, to imitate Sicilian manners: hoc argumentum graecissat: tamen Non atticissat, verum sicelissat, Plaut. Men. prol. 8; v. Ritschl ad h. l.

sicimina.full: Sicimina, ae, a mountain in Gallia Cisalpina, Liv. 45, 12.
sicimina.short: Sicimina, ae, a mountain in Gallia Cisalpina, Liv.

sicine.full: sīcĭnē (less correctly, siccĭne), adv. sice, orig. form of sic, q. v., and the interrog. particle ne, so, thus; in interrog. and exclamatory sentences always beginning the sentence (once in Cic.; twice in Liv.; not in Cæs. or Sall.; freq. in the comic writers; sometimes in the other poets). Like sic, it refers either to a previous statement, or δεικτικῶς to something pointed out by the speaker (cf. sic, I. and III.). It almost always implies reproach; sometimes self-reproach (v. infra, 3.). Refe

sicinius.full: Sicinĭus, i, m., the name of a Roman gens. C. Sicinius, Cic. Brut. 76, 263.— Cn. Sicinius, Cic. Brut. 60, 216 et saep.
sicinius.short: Sicinĭus, i, m., the name of a Roman gens.

sicinnista.full: sĭcinnista, ae, m., = σικιννιστής, one who performs the sicinnis (a dance of Satyrs), a sicinnis-dancer, Att. ap. Gell. 20, 3, 1 sq., where Gellius calls the dance itself sicinnium (Gr. σίκιννις).
sicinnista.short: sĭcinnista, ae, m., = σικιννιστής, one who performs the sicinnis (a dance of Satyrs), a sicinnis-dancer, Att.

siclus.full: siclus, i, m. Heb. , a shekel (a Hebrew coin), Hier. in Ezech. 1, 4, 9; Vulg. Exod. 21, 32 et saep.; cf. Isid. Orig. 16, 25, 18.

sicoris.full: Sĭcŏris, is, m., a tributary of the Iberus, near Ilerda, in Hispania Tarraconensis, now Segre, Caes. B. C. 1, 40; 1, 48; 1, 62; Plin. 3, 3, 4, § 24; Luc. 4, 14 sq.; 4, 130; 4, 335; Aus. Ep. 25, 58.
sicoris.short: Sĭcŏris, is, m., a tributary of the Iberus, near Ilerda, in Hispania Tarraconensis, now Segre, Caes.

sicubi.full: sīcŭbi, adv. si-ubi; cf. sicunde, from si-unde, if in any place, if anywhere, wheresoever (rare but class.), Ter. Eun. 3, 1, 13: sicubi nactus eris, Cic. Tusc. 1, 43, 103: sicubi inciderit, id. Att. 15, 29, 1: sicubi aderit Gellius, id. Sest. 51, 110: sicubi est certamen, scutis magis quam gladiis geritur res, Liv. 9, 41 fin.: sicubi loco cessum, si terga data hosti, tamen, etc., id. 7, 13: sicubi artiora erant, Tac. Agr. 37: ubi est igitur exceptum foedere Gaditano? etc. ... Nusquam. Ac sicubi

sicula.full: sīcŭla, ae, f. dim. sica, a little dagger; transf., = membrum virile, Cat. 67, 21.

siculi.full: Sĭcŭli, ōrum, m., = Σικελοί. The Siculians or Sicilians, an ancient Italian people on the Tiber, a portion of whom, driven thence, migrated to the island of Sicily, which derived its name from them, Plin. 3, 5, 9, § 56; 3, 5, 10, § 71; Varr. L. L. 5, § 101 Müll.; Col. 1, 3, 6.—Hence, in the class. per., The inhabitants of Sicily, Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 43, § 95; id. Brut. 12, 46; id. de Or. 2, 54, 217; id. Att. 14, 12, 1 al.—Gen. plur. Siculūm, Lucr. 6, 642.—In the sing.: Sĭcŭlus, i, m., a Sicilian, P

siculus.full: Sĭcŭlus, a, um, v. Siculi, A.

sicunde.full: sīcundē adv. si-unde; cf. sicubi, from si-ubi, if from anywhere (rare but class.): sicunde potes, erues, qui decem legati Mummio fuerint, Cic. Att. 13, 30, 3: sicunde spes aliqua se ostendisset, Liv. 26, 38: sicunde hostis appareat, Suet. Calig. 51: sicunde discederet, id. ib. 4.

sicut.full: sīc-ut and (far less. freq. but class.) sīc-ŭti, adv., so as, just as, as. Lit. With a separate clause. Form sicut: sicut dixi, faciam, Plaut. Trin. 3, 2, 59: clanculum, sicut praecepi, id. ib. 3, 3, 76: nempe sicut dicis (shortly after: ita ut dicis), id. Aul. 2, 4, 15; so, sicut dicis, id. Bacch. 4, 4, 67; id. Men. prol. 74: hae sunt, sicut praedico, id. Most. 3, 2, 84; cf. id. Bacch. 3, 6, 20: stultitia magna est, Hominem amatorem ad forum procedere, etc. ... sicut ego feci stultus, id. Cas.

sicyon.full: Sĭcўon, ōnis (abl. e, rarely i), f. (but masc. Cic. Att. 1, 13, 1), = Σικυών, the capital of the territory of Sicyonia in the Peloponnesus (now Vasiliko), near the isthmus, sometimes considered as belonging to Achaia, abounding in olive-trees, the birthplace of Aratus, Mel. 2, 3, 10; Plin. 4, 5, 6, § 12; Cic. Off. 2, 23, 81; id. Fam. 13, 21; id. Att. 1, 13, 1; Ov. Ib. 315; id. P. 4, 15, 10; Plaut. Curc. 3, 25; id. Merc. 3, 4, 62 al.—Abl. Sicyoni, Plaut. Cist. 1, 3, 8; 1, 3, 42; id. Ps. 4, 2, 38;

sicyos.full: sĭcўos agrĭos, = σίκυος ἄγριος, wildcucumber, App. Herb. 113.
sicyos.short: sĭcўos agrĭos, = σίκυος ἄγριος, wildcucumber, App.

sida.full: Sīda, ae (collat. form Sīdē, ēs, Plin. 5, 27, 26, § 96), f., = Σίδη, a town in Pamphylia, now Eski Adalia, Mel. 1, 14 sq.; Cic. Fam. 3, 6, 1; 3, 12, 4; 12, 15, 5; Liv. 35, 13; 37, 23 al.—Hence, Sīdētae, ārum, m., = Σιδῆται, the inhabitants of Sida, Liv. 35, 48, 6 Drak. N. cr.

sideralis.full: sīdĕrālis, e, adj. sidus, of or belonging to the stars, sidereal (Plinian): scientia, Plin. 7, 49, 50, § 160; cf. difficultas, astronomy, id. 18, 24, 56, § 206.

sideraticius.full: sīdĕrātīcĭus or -tĭus, a, um, adj. sideratio, planet-struck, blasted, palsied (late Lat.): jumenta, Veg. 5, 34; cf. sideror.

sideratio.full: sīdĕrātĭo, ōnis, f. sideror. * A grouping or configuration of stars, a constellation, Firm. Math. 4, 13 fin.— A disease produced by a constellation, a blast, sideration; of plants, a blast, a blight, Plin. 17, 24, 37, § 222 sq.; of animals, a numbness, palsy, Macr. Emp. 20 med.; Scrib. Larg. 101 med.

sidereus.full: sīdĕrĕus, a, um, adj. sidus. Of or belonging to the constellations or to the stars, starry (poet.; esp. freq. in Ov.): caelum, Ov. M. 10, 140; for which: arx mundi, id. Am. 3, 10, 21: sedes, id. A. A. 2, 39; Verg. A. 10, 3: caput (Noctis), Ov. M. 15, 31: dea, i. e. the moon, Prop. 3 (4), 20, 18. aethra, Verg. A. 3, 586: ignes, i. e. the stars, Ov. M. 15, 665; cf. Canis, id. F. 4, 941: conjux, i. e. Ceyx (as the son of Lucifer), id. M. 11, 445: Pedo, who discoursed of the stars, id. P. 4, 16, 6:

siderion.full: sĭdērĭon, ii, n., = σιδήριον, the plant ironwort, vervain, Plin. 25, 4, 15, § 34; 26, 14, 87, § 140.
siderion.short: sĭdērĭon, ii, n., = σιδήριον, the plant ironwort, vervain, Plin.

siderites.full: sĭdērītes, ae, m., = σιδηρίτης. A loadstone, magnet, Plin. 36, 16, 25, § 127 (Jan. sideritis).— A kind of diamond, Plin. 37, 4, 16, § 58.

sideritesis.full: sĭdērītĕsis, is, f. σιδηρῖτις, a plant, also called heliotropium, App. Herb. 49 (al. sideritis).

sideritis.full: sĭdērītis, is, f., = σιδηρῖτις. Ironwort, vervain, Plin. 25, 5, 19, § 42; 26, 14, 88, § 148.— A precious stone, Plin. 37, 10, 67, § 182. A variety of it, found in Æthiopia, is called sĭdērŏpoecĭlos, = σιδηροποίκιλος, id. 37, 10, 67, § 182.— The loadstone, magnet, Plin. 36, 16, 25, § 127 Jan.

sideropoecilos.full: sĭdērŏpoecĭlos, i, m., v. sideritis, II.

sideror.full: sīdĕror, ātus, 1, v. dep. n. [sidus, II. E.], to be blasted or palsied by a constellation, to be planet-struck, to be sunstruck, = sidere afflari, ἀστροβολεῖσθαι: fluviatilium silurus Caniculae exortu sideratur, Plin. 9, 16, 25, § 58: siderati, id. 28, 16, 63, § 226: sideratum jumentum, Veg. 3, 39, 1.

sidicini.full: Sĭdĭcīni, ōrum, m., a people in Campania, whose chief town was Teanum, on the north-eastern side of Mount Massicus, Liv. 7, 29; 8, 1 sq.; 8, 15 sq.; Cic. Phil. 2, 41, 107.—Sing.: de Egnatii Sidicini nomine, Cic. Att. 6, 1, 23.—Hence, Sĭdĭcīnus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to the Sidicini, Sidicinian: ager, Liv 10, 14; 26, 9: aequora, Verg. A. 7, 727: cohors, Sil. 5, 551: olivae, Plin. 15, 3, 4, § 16.
sidicini.short: Sĭdĭcīni, ōrum, m., a people in Campania, whose chief town was Teanum, on the north-eastern side of Mount Massicus, Liv.

sido1.full: sīdo, sīdi, 3, v. n. cf. sedeo; Gr. ἵζω, to seat one's self, sit down; to settle, alight (poet. and in post-Aug. prose; usu. of things) In gen.: quaesitisque diu terris, ubi sidere detur, Ov. M. 1, 307; cf.: (columbae) super arbore sidunt, Verg. A. 6, 203: canes sidentes, sitting down, Plin. 10, 63, 83, § 177.— Of things, to sink down, settle: sidebant campi (shortly after: subsidere saxa), Lucr. 5, 493: nec membris incussam sidere cretam, id. 3, 382; cf. Col. 12, 24, 2: in tepidā aquā gutta (ba

sido2.full: Sido, ōnis, m., a chief of the Suevi about the middle of the first century, Tac. H. 3, 5; 3, 21; id. A. 12, 29 sq.
sido2.short: Sido, ōnis, m., a chief of the Suevi about the middle of the first century, Tac.

sidon.full: Sīdon, ō^nis (usu. ō, as in Greek; but in the derivatives common. A later collat. form Sīdōnĭa, ae, Just. 11, 10, 8; cf.: Babylonia, Lacedaemonia, etc.), f, = Σιδών, ῶνος and όνος, Heb. and Phoen. a very ancient and celebrated Phœnician city, the mother-city of Tyre, now Saida, Mel. 1, 12, 2; Plin. 5, 19, 17, § 76; Just. 18, 3, 4; Cic. Att. 9, 9, 2; Luc. 3, 217 al.; abl. Sidone, Lucr. 6, 585; Ov. M. 4, 571; cf. acc. Sīdōna Verg A. 1, 619; abl. Sīdŏne, Sil. 8 438 .—Hence, Sīdŏ_nĭus, a, um, adj. O

sidonius1.full: Sīdŏnĭus, i, m., a proper name; so, C. Sollius Sidonius Apollinaris, a Christian writer in the middle of the fifth century, whose Carmina and Epistolae are still extant; v. Bähr, Röm. Lit. § 291.
sidonius1.short: Sīdŏnĭus, i, m., a proper name;

sidonius2.full: Sīdō^nĭus, a, um, v. Sidon, A.

sidus.full: sīdus, ĕris, n. cf. Sanscr. svid, to sweat, melt; Gr. σίδηρος (molten) iron; Lat. sudo. Stars united in a figure, a group of stars, a constellation (and hence mostly plur.; only so ap. Cic., Cæs., and Quint.): sunt stellae quidem singulares, ut erraticae quinque et ceterae, quae non admixtae aliis solae feruntur: sidera vero, quae in aliquod signum stellarum plurium compositione formantur, ut Aries, Taurus, Andromeda, Perseus, vel Corona et quaecumque variarum genera formarum in caelum recepta c

siem.full: siem, sies, etc., v. sum init.

sifilum.full: sīfĭlum, i, n., collat. form of sibilum, q. v.

sigalion.full: Sīgălĭon, ōnis, m. σιγάω, to be silent, the god of Silence among the Egyptians, Aus. Ep. 25, 27.

sigambri.full: Sĭgambri (also Sĭcambri, Sў-gambri, and Sŭgambri), ōrum, m., = Σύγαμβροι, Ptol. Dio Cass.; Σούγαμβροι, Strabo, a powerful people of Germany, between the Sieg and the Ruhr, and as far as the Lippe (the mod. Cleve, Berg, and Recklingshausen), Caes. B. G. 4, 16; 4, 18 sq.; 6, 35; Hor. C. 4, 2, 36; 4, 14, 51; Tac. A. 2, 26; 12, 39; Suet. Aug. 21; Mart. Spect. 3, 9.—Hence, Sĭgamber, bra, brum, adj., of or belonging to the Sigambri, Sigambrian: cohors, Tac. A. 4, 47 fin.— Subst.: Sĭgambra, ae, f., a S
sigambri.short: Sĭgambri (also Sĭcambri, Sў-gambri, and Sŭgambri), ōrum, m., = Σύγαμβροι, Ptol.

sigeum.full: Sīgēum, i, n., = Σίγειον, a promontory in Troas, and a town of the same name, where Achilles was buried, now Yenishehr, Mel. 1, 18, 3; Plin. 5, 30, 33, § 124; Cic. Arch. 10, 24; id. Fam. 5, 12, 7; Liv. 44, 28, 6.—Hence, Sīgēus (collat. form Sīgēïa tellus, Ov. H. 1, 33: Sigeïa litora, id. M. 13, 3), a, um, adj., of or belonging to Sigeum, Sigean: litora, Mel. 2, 7, 4; Ov. M. 12, 71: freta, Verg. A. 2, 312: campi, id. ib. 7, 294: profundum, Ov. M. 11, 197. Poet. transf., Trojan: natum Sigeo in pul
sigeum.short: Sīgēum, i, n., = Σίγειον, a promontory in Troas, and a town of the same name, where Achilles was buried, now Yenishehr, Mel.

sigilla.full: sĭgilla, ōrum (sing.: SIGILLVM VOLKANI, Inscr. Marin. Fratr. Arv. p. 357; v. also infra, II.), n. dim. signum. Little figures or images: apposuit patellam, in quā sigilla erant egregia, Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 22, § 48: Tyrrhena sigilla, Hor. Ep. 2, 2, 180: parva, Lact. 2, 4, 19: perparvula, Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 43, § 85; Plin. 36, 24, 59, § 183; Ov. A. A. 1, 407: quattuor certamina brevibus distincta sigillis, woven or wrought in, id. M. 6, 86.— Of the figures on seal-rings: sigilla anulo imprimere, Cic.

sigillaria.full: Sĭgillārĭa, ōrum, ibus and iis, n. sigilla. The last days of the Saturnalia, in which people made each other presents, especially of little images; the feast of images, Macr. S. 1, 10 fin.; 1, 11; Tiber. ap. Suet. Claud. 5; Spart. Carac. 1 fin. (called by Aus. Eclog. Fer. Rom. 52, festa sigillorum; and by Lucil. ap. Porph. Hor. S. 1, 5, 87, Servorum festus).— Transf. The little images presented on the Sigillaria: alicui sigillaria afferre, Sen. Ep. 12, 3 (called sigillaricia, Spart. Hadr. 17).—
sigillaria.short: Sĭgillārĭa, ōrum, ibus and iis, n.

sigillariarius.full: sĭgillārĭārĭus, ii, m. Sigiliaria, II. A., a maker of images, Inscr. Orell. 4280. —Also called SIGILLARIVS, Inscr. Orell. 4279; and SIGILLATOR FIGVLVS, ib. 4191.

sigillaricius.full: sĭgillārīcĭus (-tĭus), a, um, adj. sigilla. * Of or belonging to sealing: anulus, a seal-ring, signet-ring, Vop. Aur. 50.— Subst.: sĭgillārīcĭa, ōrum, n., little images; v. Sigillaria, II. A. 1.

sigillatus.full: sĭgillātus, a, um, adj. sigilla, furnished or adorned with little images or figures: scyphi, Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 14, § 32: putealia, id. Att. 1, 10, 3: tentoria, Treb. XXX. Tyr. 16: serica, Cod. Th. 15, 7, 11: sal, the pillar of salt into which Lot's wife was changed, Prud. Ham. 707.

sigilliola.full: sĭgillĭŏla, ōrum, n. dim. id., little figures or images, Arn. 6, 197; 6, 204.

sigillum.full: sĭgillum, i, n. dim., v. sigilla.

sigimerus.full: Sigimerus (Seg-), i, m., a prince of the Cherusci, the father of Arminius and brother of Segestes, Vell. 2, 118, 2.—Segimerus, Tac. A. 1, 71.
sigimerus.short: Sigimerus (Seg-), i, m., a prince of the Cherusci, the father of Arminius and brother of Segestes, Vell.

sigla.full: sigla, ōrum, n. contr. from sigilla, signs of abbreviation, abbreviations (late Lat.): sigla in libris ponere, Just. Ep. ad Antecess. § 8: leges per siglorum obscuritates conscribere, Cod. Just. 1, 17, 2, § 22.

sigma.full: sigma, ătis, n., = σίγμα (the Greek letter sigma; hence, from its more ancient form, C). A semicircular couch for reclining at meals, Mart. 10, 48, 6; 14, 87, 2; Lampr. Heliog. 25.— A bathing-tub of the same shape, Sid. Ep. 2, 2 med.; id. Carm. 17, 6.
sigma.short: sigma, ătis, n., = σίγμα (the Greek letter sigma;

signaculum.full: signācŭlum, i, n. signo. In gen., a mark, a sign (post-class.): corporis, i.e. circumcision, Tert. Apol. 21: frontis inscripta oleo, i.e. the sign of the cross, Prud. Psych. 360.— In partic., a seal, signet, App. Flor. 2, p. 346; Dig. 16, 3, 1, § 36; Novat. Th. 2, tit. 16, c. 1, § 5.

signanter.full: signanter, adv., v. signo fin. A.

signarius.full: signārĭus, ii, m. signum, a sculptor: ARTIFEX, Inscr. Orell. 4282.

signate.full: signātē, adv., v. signo, P. a. B. fin.

signatio.full: signātĭo, ōnis, f. signo, a marking, signing: furtiva (crucis), Tert. ad Uxor. 2, 9.

signator.full: signātor, ōris, m. id.. A sealer, signer. One who attests a will by sealing it, a witness to a will (mostly postAug.; not in Cic.): ex illis testes signatoresque falsos commodare, Sall. C. 16, 2: signator falso, a forger, Juv. 1, 67; Suet. Aug. 33; id. Tib. 23; Val. Max. 7, 7, 2; Dig. 18, 3, 8; Vulg. 2, Esd. 10, 1.— One who affixes his seal as witness to a marriage-contract, a witness to a marriage, Juv. 10, 336. — One who stamps money, a coiner, Inscr. Grut. 1066, 5; 1070, 1; Inscr. Orell. 3229

signatorius.full: signātōrĭus, a, um, adj. id., of or belonging to sealing: anulus, a seal-ring, Val. Max. 8, 14, 4; Dig. 50, 16, 74; 34, 2, 25, § 10.—Subst.: signātōrĭum, ii, n., a sealing, Alcim. Ep. 78.

signatus.full: signātus, a, um, Part. and P. a. of signo.

signia.full: Signĭa, ae, f., an ancient town in Latium which produced an astringent wine, now Segni, Liv. 1, 56; 2, 21 fin.; 8, 3; 32, 2; Plin. 14, 6. 8, § 65; Sil. 8, 380.—Hence, Signīnus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Signia, Signian: vinum, Cels. 4, 5; 4, 19 fin.; Mart. 13, 116: pira, Col. 5, 10, 18; Plin. 15, 15, 16, § 55; Juv. 11, 73 al.: opus, a kind of plaster for walls and pavements, made of potsherds and lime, Vitr. 2, 4; 7, 11; 8, 7; Col. 1, 6, 12; 8, 15, 3; 8, 17, 1.—As subst. Signīnum, i, n., =
signia.short: Signĭa, ae, f., an ancient town in Latium which produced an astringent wine, now Segni, Liv.

signias.full: Signĭas, ae, m., = Σιγνίας, a mountain in Greater Phrygia, Plin. 5, 29, 29, § 106.
signias.short: Signĭas, ae, m., = Σιγνίας, a mountain in Greater Phrygia, Plin.

signifer.full: signĭfer, fĕra, fĕrum, adj. signumfero. In gen., sign-bearing, imagebearing, i.e. bearing signs, figures, or images (poet.): puppis, i.e. adorned or painted with images, Luc. 3, 558; so, crater, Val. Fl. 1, 337: manus, giving signals, Amm. 27, 9, 7.— In partic. (class.). Bearing the heavenly signs or constellations, starry: aether, Lucr. 6, 481: caelum, Luc. 7, 363; 8, 172: orbis, qui Graece ζωδιακὸς dicitur, the zodiac, Cic. Div. 2, 42, 89; so, orbis, Lucr. 5, 691; Sen. Q. N. 7, 11, 8; for whic

signifex.full: signĭfex, fĭcis, m. signum-facio, an image-maker, carver, statuary (post-class.), App. M. 2, p. 116, 13; Arn. 6, 199; Mart. Cap. 1, § 36; Sid. Ep. 6, 12.

significabilis.full: signĭfĭcābĭlis, e, adj. significo, that has meaning, significative: vox, Varr. L. L. 6, § 52 Müll.

significans.full: signĭfĭcans, antis, Part. and P. a. of significo.

significanter.full: signĭfĭcanter, adv., v. significo, P. a. fin.

significantia.full: signĭfĭcantĭa, ae, f. significo (postAug.). * Force, energy, significancy of words: verborum, Quint. 10, 1, 121.— In gen., meaning, import, signification, Tert. Res. Carn. 21; Arn. 7, 230; Lact. 4, 26.

significatio.full: signĭfĭcātĭo, ōnis, f. id.. A pointing out, indicating, denoting, signifying; an expression, indication, mark, sign, token, = indicium, signum, ἐπισημασία, etc. (freq. and class.). Absol.: gestus sententiam non demonstratione sed significatione declarans, Cic. de Or. 3, 59, 220: aliquem nutu significationeque appellare, id. Fam. 1, 9, 20: ignibus significatione factā. Caes. B. G. 2, 33: significatione per castella fumo factā, id. B. C. 3, 65; id. B. G. 7, 81.—With subj. gen.: ex significatione G

significativus.full: signĭfĭcātīvus, a, um, adj. significo, denoting, signifying, significative (jurid. Lat.); with gen.: enuntiatio et quantitatis et aestimationis significativa, Dig. 50, 16, 232; 45, 1, 75, § 2.

significatorius.full: signĭfĭcātōrĭus, a, um, adj. id., denoting, signifying, significatory (late Lat.); with gen. (like significativus): verbum factitationis significatorium, Tert. adv. Herm. 32; Ambros. Incarn. Dom. Sacr. § 98.

significatum.full: signĭfĭcātum, σημασία, δήλωσις, Gloss. Lat. Gr.

significatus.full: signĭfĭcātus, ūs, m. significo (postAug. for significatio, II. B. and D.). A sign, token, prognostic of coming changes of weather: tempestatum significatus. Vitr. 9, 7 fin.; Plin. 18, 25, 59, § 221; 18, 31, 74, § 310.— Lit., meaning, import, signification of a word (syn. vis): ve particula duplicem significatum capit, Gell. 5, 12, 9. — Transf., a name, appellation: bellis significatum dare, Arn. 1, 3.

significo.full: signĭfĭco, āvi, ātum, 1 (dep. collat. form signĭfĭcor, acc. to Gell. 18, 12, 10, without an example), v. a. signum-facio. In gen., to show by signs; to show, point out, express, publish, make known, indicate; to intimate, notify, signify, etc. (freq. and class.; syn.: monstro, declaro, indico). With acc.: aliquid alicui, Plaut. Rud. 4, 1, 5: hoc mihi significasse et annuisse visus est, Cic. Verr. 2, 3, 91, § 213: quae significari ac declarari volemus, id. de Or. 3, 13, 49: gratulationem, id. Att

signitenens.full: signĭtĕnens, entis, Part. [signumteneo], constellation-bearing, starry: bigae, Enn. ap. Varr. L. L. 5, § 19 Müll. (Trag. v. 132 Vahl.); cf. signifer.

signo.full: signo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. signum, to set a mark upon, to mark, mark out, designate (syn.: noto, designo). Lit. In gen. (mostly poet. and in post-Aug. prose): discrimen non facit neque signat linea alba, Lucil. ap. Non. 405, 17: signata sanguine pluma est, Ov. M. 6, 670: ne signare quidem aut partiri limite campum Fas erat, Verg. G. 1, 126: humum limite mensor, Ov. M. 1, 136; id. Am. 3, 8, 42: moenia aratro, id. F. 4, 819: pede certo humum, to print, press, Hor. A. P. 159; cf.: vestigia summo pu

signum.full: signum, i, n. perh. Sanscr. sag-, to cling to, adhere; cf. sigilla. In gen., a mark, token, sign, indication (very frequent in all styles and periods; cf. insigne): meo patri torulus inerit aureus Sub petaso: id signum Amphitruoni non erit, Plaut. Am. prol. 145 sq.: ut eam (nutricem) adducam et signa ostendam haec, i. e. crepundia, Ter. Eun. 4, 7, 38; 5, 3, 5: ut fures earum rerum, quas ceperunt, signa commutant, etc., Cic. Fin. 5, 25, 74; so (with notae) id. de Or. 2, 41, 174; id. Lael. 17, 62;

sil1.full: sil, silis, n., a kind of yellowish earth, yellow ochre, Plin. 33, 12, 56, § 158; Vitr. 7, 11; Veg. 5, 26; 5, 39; 6, 28 fin.; Aus. Idyll. 12, Gram. 8.
sil1.short: sil, silis, n., a kind of yellowish earth, yellow ochre, Plin.

sila.full: Sīla, ae, f., a large forest in the country of the Bruttii, which yielded great quantities of pitch, Cic. Brut. 22, 85; Sall. Fragm. ap. Serv. Verg. A. 12, 715 (H. 4, 7 Dietsch); Plin. 3, 5, 10, § 74; Verg. G. 3, 219; id. A. 12, 715.—Hence, Sīlānus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to the forest of Sila: caseus, Cassiod. Var. 12, 12.
sila.short: Sīla, ae, f., a large forest in the country of the Bruttii, which yielded great quantities of pitch, Cic.

silaceus.full: silācĕus or silācĭus, a, um, adj. 1. sil, like ochre, of ochre: color, Plin. 35, 7, 32, § 50: cunei, Vitr. 7, 4; 7, 5.
silaceus.short: silācĕus or silācĭus, a, um, adj.

silana.full: Silana, ae, f., a town of Thessaly, Liv. 36, 13.
silana.short: Silana, ae, f., a town of Thessaly, Liv.

silanio.full: Silanĭo or Silanĭion, ōnis, m., a celebrated statuary, Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 57, § 126; Plin. 34, 8, 19, § 51; Vitr. 7, praef.
silanio.short: Silanĭo or Silanĭion, ōnis, m., a celebrated statuary, Cic.

silanus1.full: Sīlānus, i, m., a Roman surname in the Julian gens, Liv. 23, 15; 25, 2. D. Junius Silanus, Cic. Fin. 1, 7, 24; id. Off. 2, 16, 57; id. Cat. 4, 4, 7; Sall. C. 50, 4; 51, 16. — M. Silanus, Cic. Brut. 35, 135; id. Fan 10, 30. 1.—Hence, Sīlānĭānus, a, um, adj., of or named from one Silanus: senatusconsultum, Dig. 29, 5, 1, §§ 7 and 21.
silanus1.short: Sīlānus, i, m., a Roman surname in the Julian gens, Liv.

silanus2.full: sīlānus, i, m., = σιληνός, Doric σιλανός, a fountain or jet of water (usually spirting from a head of Silenus). Lucr. 6, 1265; Cels. 3, 18 med.; Fest. s. v. tullios, p. 352 Müll.; Inscr. Orell. 3321; Hyg. Fab. 169.
silanus2.short: sīlānus, i, m., = σιληνός, Doric σιλανός, a fountain or jet of water (usually spirting from a head of Silenus).

silarus.full: Sĭlărus, i, m., = Σίλαρις, a river forming the boundary between Lucania and Campania, now Sele, Plin. 3, 5, 9, § 70 (al. Silerus) sq.; 2, 103, 106, § 226; Verg. G. 3, 146; Sil. 8, 582.—Also called Silerus, Mel. 2, 4, 9; and Siler, Luc. 2, 426; Col. poët. 10, 136.
silarus.short: Sĭlărus, i, m., = Σίλαρις, a river forming the boundary between Lucania and Campania, now Sele, Plin.

silatum.full: silatum antiqui pro eo, quod nunc jentaculum dicimus, appellabant, quia jejuni vinum sili conditum ante meridiem absorbebant, Fest. p. 347 Müll.
silatum.short: silatum antiqui pro eo, quod nunc jentaculum dicimus, appellabant, quia jejuni vinum sili conditum ante meridiem absorbebant, Fest.

silaus.full: silaus, i, m., a kind of parsley, smallage: Apium graveolens, Linn.; Plin. 26, 8, 56, § 88.
silaus.short: silaus, i, m., a kind of parsley, smallage: Apium graveolens, Linn.;

silenicus.full: Sīlēnĭcus, a, um, adj. Silenus, of or sacred to Silenus: racemi (hederae), a species of ivy, Plin. 16, 34, 62, § 146.

silens.full: sĭlens, entis, Part. and P. a. of sileo.

silenter.full: sĭlenter, adv., v. sileo, P. a. fin.

silentiarius.full: sĭlentĭārĭus, ii, m. silentium. A confidential domestic servant (orig. watching for the domestic silence; cf. Sen. Ep. 47, 3), Salv. Gub. Dei, 4, 3; Inscr. Orell. 2956; 3193; cf. Becker, Gallus, 2, p. 99 (2d. ed.).— In the later imperial period, a certain high officer at court, a privy-councillor, Cod. Just. 3, 28, 30 fin.; 15, 62, 25; Inscr. Orell. 3194.

silentiosus.full: sĭlentĭōsus, a, um, adj. silentium, perfectly still or silent: nactus opacae noctis silentiosa secreta, App. M. 11 init.—Adv.: sĭlentĭōsē, stilly, silently: silentiose geritur publicum bonum, Cassiod. Var. 11, 1 med.

silentium.full: sĭlentĭum, ii, n. sileo. Lit. In gen., a being still or silent, noiselessness, stillness, silence (freq. and class.; cf. taciturnitas): otium et silentium est, Ter. Hec. prol. alt. 35: et ipse conticuit et ceteris silentium fuit, Cic. de Or. 3, 35, 143; cf. id. ib. 1, 35, 160; id. Rep. 2, 38, 64: auditus est magno silentio, id. Q. Fr. 2, 1, 1: silentio auditus, Caes. B. C. 3, 19, 3: huic facietis Fabulae silentium, Plaut. Am. prol. 15: fac silentium, id. Pers. 4, 3, 50; cf. Cic. Div. 1, 28, 59:

silentus.full: sĭlentus, a, um, adj. sileo, silent, quiet: loca, Laev. ap. Gell. 19, 7, 7.

silenus.full: Sīlēnus, i, m., = Σειληνός. Silenus, the tutor and constant attendant of Bacchus; represented as baldheaded, with short horns and a flat nose, as drunken, lascivious, and mounted on an ass, Hor. A. P. 239; Verg. E. 6, 14; Ov. A. A. 1, 543; id. F. 1, 399; 1, 413; 6, 339; id. M. 11, 90; 11, 99; Cic. Tusc. 1, 48, 114; Hyg. Fab. 191.—Plur.: Sīlēni, gods of the woods, satyrs, Cat. 64, 252; Plin. 35, 10, 36, § 110; cf. Serv. Verg. E. 6, 14.— A Greek historian, Cic. Div. 1, 24, 49; Liv. 26, 49; Nep. Ha

sileo.full: sĭlĕo, ŭi (perf. pass. silitum est, Aug. Civ. Dei, 16, 2), 2, v. n. and a. [cf. Goth. silan, ana-silan, to be silent; Germ. seltsam, selten], to be noiseless, still, or silent, to keep silence; act., not to speak of, to keep silent respecting a thing (class.; stronger than tacere). Lit. Absol.: silete et tacete atque animum advortite, Plaut. Poen. prol. 3; id. Capt. 3, 1, 20: optimum quemque silere, Liv. 39, 27 fin.: muta silet virgo, Ov. M. 10, 389: lingua, sile, id. P. 2, 2, 61: sedentibus ac

siler1.full: sīler, ĕris, n., a kind of brook-willow, Plin. 16, 18, 31, § 77; 24, 10, 44, § 73; Verg. G. 2, 12 Serv.
siler1.short: sīler, ĕris, n., a kind of brook-willow, Plin.

silesco.full: sĭlesco, ĕre, v. inch. n. [sileo], to become still, silent, calm, or quiet (rare; not in Cic.; syn. obmutesco): dum hae silescunt turbae, Ter. Ad. 5, 2, 10: deum domus alta silescit, Verg. A. 10, 101: caeli furor aequinoctialis Zephyri silescit auris, Cat. 46, 3: venti silescunt, Ov. Tr. 2, 151.

silex.full: sĭlex, ĭcis, m. (poet. and late Lat.; also fem., Verg. E. 1, 15; id. A. 6, 471; 6, 602; 8, 233; Ov. M. 9, 225; 9, 304; 9, 613; Amm. 14, 6, 16; cf. Quint. 1, 6, 2; gen. plur. silicum, Lucr. 6, 683; Luc. 4, 304) [root sar-, to be firm; cf.: solum, solidus]. Any hard stone found in fields, a pebble-stone, a flint, flint-stone: silicem caedere, Cic. Div. 2, 41, 85: silice vias sternere, Liv. 41, 27; cf. id. 41, 27, § 7: silici scintillam excudere, Verg. A. 1, 174: gravem medios silicem jaculatus in

silicarius.full: sĭlĭcārĭus, ii, m. silex, one that paves roads with pebble-stones, a pavior, Front. Aquaed. 117; Inscr. Grut. 645.

silicernium.full: sĭlĭcernĭum, ii, n. A funeral feast, Caecil. ap. Fest. p. 294 Müll.; Varr. ap. Non. 48, 9; Mart. Cap. 8, § 805; cf. Becker, Gallus, vol. 3, p. 296 (2d ed.).—Hence, a term of abuse applied to an old man: te exercebo hodie, silicernium, drybones, Ter. Ad. 4, 2, 48; for which, in masc.: sĭlĭcernĭus, Cinc. ap. Fulg. 560, 21.— A kind of sausage, Arn. 7, 229.

silices.full: Silĭces, um, m., a mountain-tribe in Asia: montani, Plin. 6, 26, 30, § 118.
silices.short: Silĭces, um, m., a mountain-tribe in Asia: montani, Plin.

siliceus.full: sĭlĭcĕus, a, um, adj. silex, of flint or limestone, silicious: saxa, Vitr. 8, 3 fin.: lapides, Cato, R. R. 18, 3.—Trop.: cor, Laev. ap. Gell. 19, 7, 10.

silicia.full: sĭlĭcĭa, ae, f., a plant, also called faenum Graecum, fenugreek, Plin. 18, 16, 39, § 140; 24, 19, 120, § 184; called also siliqua, Col. 2, 10, 33; 11, 2, 71.
silicia.short: sĭlĭcĭa, ae, f., a plant, also called faenum Graecum, fenugreek, Plin.

silicula.full: sĭlĭcŭla, ae, f. dim. siliqua, a little husk or pod, a silicle, Varr. R. R. 1, 23, 3.

siliginarius.full: sĭlīgĭnārĭus, ii, m. siligo, a baker of wheat-flour, Dig. 47, 2, 52, § 11; Inscr. Orell. 1810; Inscr. Rein. cl. 1, n. 254; Inscr. Don. cl. 9, n. 11.

siligineus.full: sĭlīgĭnĕus (late form sĭlīgnus, Dynam. 1, 7), adj. id., of wheat, wheaten: farina, Cato, R. R. 121; Plin. 18, 9, 20, § 88: panis, Varr. ap. Non. 88, 14; Sen. Ep. 123, 2; Vop. Aurel. 35: cunni, i. e. wheaten loaves of obscene form, Mart. 9, 3, 3; cf. Priapus, id. 14, 69 in lemm.

siligo.full: sĭlīgo, ĭnis, f. A kind of very white wheat, winter-wheat: Triticum hibernum, Linn.; Cato, R. R. 35, 1?? Varr. R. R. 1, 23, 2; Cels. 2, 19; Col. 2, 6, 2; 2, 9, 5; 2, 9, 13; Plin. 18, 8, 20, § 85; 18, 7, 10, § 61.— Transf., fine wheaten flour, Plin. 18, 9, 20, § 85; Juv. 5, 70; 6, 472.

siliqua.full: sĭlĭqua, ae, f. Lit., a pod or husk of leguminous plants, Varr. R. R. 1, 23, 3; Plin. 18, 12, 30, § 120; Verg. G. 1, 74.— Transf.: sĭlĭquae, ārum, pulse, Hor. Ep. 2, 1, 123; Pers. 3, 55; Juv. 11, 58.— Siliqua Graeca, the carob-tree, a carob, St. John's bread, Col. 5, 10, 20; 7, 9, 6; id. Arb. 25, 1; also simply siliqua, Plin. 15, 24, 26, § 95; 23, 8, 79, § 151; Pall. Febr. 25, 27; id. Insit. 117.—A variety of the same is called siliqua Syriaca, Plin. 23, 8, 79, § 151; Scrib. Comp. 121.— The same

siliquastrum.full: sĭlĭquastrum, i, n., a plant, also called piperitis, pepperwort, Plin. 19, 12, 62, § 187; 20, 17, 66, § 174.
siliquastrum.short: sĭlĭquastrum, i, n., a plant, also called piperitis, pepperwort, Plin.

siliquor.full: sĭlĭquor, āri, v. dep. siliqua, I., to put forth or get pods, Plin. 17, 9, 6, § 54; 18, 7, 10, § 59.

silis.full: Silis, is, m., the name of several rivers. I. q. Jaxartes, Plin. 6, 16, 18, § 49.— I. q. Tanais, the Don, Plin. 6, 7, 7, § 20.— A river in the Venetian territories, Plin. 3, 18, 22, § 126.
silis.short: Silis, is, m., the name of several rivers.

silius.full: Sīlĭus, i, m., the name of a Roman gens. P. Silius Nerva, a proprœtor in Bithynia and Pontus, to whom are addressed the letters Cic. Fam. 13, 47, and 61 sqq.; cf. id. Att. 10, 13, 3.— T. Silius, a military tribune under Cœsar, Caes. B. G. 3, 7 fin.— C. Silius Italicus, a celebrated Roman poet in the latter half of the first century of the Christian era, author of a poem still extant, called Punica, Plin. Ep. 3, 7; Mart. 4, 14, 1; v. Bähr, Röm. Lit. 9, § 63 sq.—Hence, Sīlĭānus, a, um, adj., of or
silius.short: Sīlĭus, i, m., the name of a Roman gens.

sillographus.full: sillŏgrăphus, i, m., = σιλλογράφος, a writer of lampoons or satires, Amm. 22, 16, 16.
sillographus.short: sillŏgrăphus, i, m., = σιλλογράφος, a writer of lampoons or satires, Amm.

sillybus.full: sillўbus, i, m., = σίλλυβον, a kind of thistle, Plin. 22, 22, 42, § 85; 26, 7, 25, § 40 (but the true reading, Cic. Att. 4, 5, 3; 4, 8, a, 2, is sittybus, q. v.).
sillybus.short: sillўbus, i, m., = σίλλυβον, a kind of thistle, Plin.

silphium.full: silphĭum, ii, n., = σίλφιον, a plant, called in pure Latin laserpitium, Cato, R. R. 157, 7; Plin. 19, 3, 15, § 38; 22, 23, 48, § 100 (Col. 6, 17, 7; 12, 7, 4, written as Greek).
silphium.short: silphĭum, ii, n., = σίλφιον, a plant, called in pure Latin laserpitium, Cato, R.

silpia.full: Silpia, ae, f., a city of Hispania Baetica, prob. Linares, Liv. 28, 12.
silpia.short: Silpia, ae, f., a city of Hispania Baetica, prob.

silures.full: Silŭres, um, m., = Σίλυρες, a warlike people of Britain, Plin. 4, 16, 30, § 103; Tac. A. 12, 32; id. Agr. 11 and 17; cf. Mannert, Britan. p. 53 sq.
silures.short: Silŭres, um, m., = Σίλυρες, a warlike people of Britain, Plin.

silurus.full: sĭlūrus, i, m., = σίλουρος, a riverfish, prob. the sheat-fish: Silurus glanis, Linn.; Plin. 9, 15, 17, § 44; 32, 9, 33, § 104; Lucil. ap. Varr. L. L. 7, § 47 Müll; Juv. 4, 33; 14, 132; Aus. Mos. 135.
silurus.short: sĭlūrus, i, m., = σίλουρος, a riverfish, prob.

silus1.full: sĭlus, a, um, adj., having a broad, turned-up nose, pug-nosed, snub-nosed, σιμός (cf. simus): ecquos (deos arbitramur) silos, flaccos, frontones? etc., Cic. N. D. 1, 29, 80; ante-class. collat. form sīlo, ōnis, m., Plaut. Rud. 2, 2, 11; Varr. ap. Non. 25, 25.
silus1.short: sĭlus, a, um, adj., having a broad, turned-up nose, pug-nosed, snub-nosed, σιμός (cf.

silus2.full: Sĭlus, i, or Sīlo, ōnis, m. 1. silus, a Roman surname, esp. of the gens Sergia. M. Sergius Orata Silus, Cic. de Or. 2, 70, 285.— M. Sergius Silus, Liv. 32, 27, 7; Eckhel. D. N. 5, p. 306.— Domitius Silus, Tac. A. 15, 59 fin. al.— In the form Silo: Arruntius Silo, Dig. 48, 19, 27; cf. Plin. 11, 37, 59, § 158.
silus2.short: Sĭlus, i, or Sīlo, ōnis, m.

silva.full: silva (less correctly sylva), ae (old gen. silvaï; silua as trisyl., Hor. C. 1, 23, 4; id. Epod. 13, 2; cf. Prisc. p. 546 P.), f. cf. Gr. ὕλη,, a wood, forest, woodland (syn.: saltus, nemus, lucus). Lit.: (lupus) Conicit in silvam sese, Enn. ap. Non. 378, 19 (Ann. v. 75 Vahl.): omne sonabat Arbustum fremitu silvaï frondosaï, id. ap. Macr. S. 6, 2 (Ann. v. 197 ib.): (ignes) Conficerent silvas, Lucr. 1, 906: per silvas profundas, id. 5, 41; so id. 5, 992: densa et aspera, Cic. Att. 12, 15; id. Div

silvanae.full: Silvānae, ārum (dat. Silvanabus), f. silva, female wood-deities, Inscr. Orell. 2103.

silvanus.full: Silvānus (Sylv-), i, m. id.. Silvanus, a deity presiding over woods and all places planted with trees, the god of woods, the rural Mars, Cato, R. R. 83; Verg. E. 10, 24; id. A. 8, 600; id. G. 1, 20; Hor. Ep. 2, 1, 143; id. C. 3, 29, 23; id. Epod. 2, 22; Ov. M. 14, 639; Plaut. Aul. 4, 6, 8; 4, 6, 10; Cic. N. D. 2, 35, 89; Inscr. Orell. 276; 328; 333; 882; 1587 sq. al.— Transf., plur., the gods of woods and fields, sylvan deities, sylvans, Ov. M. 1, 193; Luc. 3, 403; Inscr. Orell. 1616.— A Roman p

silvaticus.full: silvātĭcus (sylv-), a, um, adj. id.. Of or belonging to a wood or to trees, wood-: falces, Cato, R. R. 11, 4; Varr. R. R. 1, 22, 5.— Transf., of plants and animals, growing or running wild, wild: laurus, mala, pirus. etc., Cato, R. R. 8, 2; 143, 3: pirus, Varr. R. R. 1, 40, 5: sus, id. ap. Non. 555, 31; Pall. Aug. 8, 5: mus, Plin. 30, 8, 22, § 70.

silvesco.full: silvesco (sylv-), ĕre, v. inch. n. [id.], of the grape-vine, to grow or run wild, to run to wood: (vitis) ne silvescat sarmentis, Cic. Sen. 15, 52: nec pati vitem silvescere, Col. 4, 11, 2.— Transf.: capilli silvescentium crinium velleribus involuti, Arn. 3, p. 109.

silvestris.full: silvestris (silvester, Plin. 14, 16, 19, § 110; Col. 1, praef. 25; Sen. Hippol. 460; also written sylv-), e (collat. form, dat. SILVANO SILVESTRO, Inscr. Orell. 4990; gen. plur. sync. silvestrum, Att. Trag. Rel. v. 256 Rib.), adj. silva. Of or belonging to a wood or forest, overgrown with woods, wooded, woody (class.; syn. saltuosus): collis silvestris, Caes. B. G. 2, 18: mons, Varr. R. R. 1, 12, 1; Cic. N. D. 2, 53, 132: locus, id. Lael. 19, 68; Caes. B. G. 5, 19; 6, 34; 7, 35; Liv. 27, 26, 7:

silvicola.full: silvĭcŏla (sylv-), ae, comm. silvacolo, inhabiting woods, sylvan (poet.): silvicolae homones, Naev. B. Pun. 2, 17: viri, Prop. 3, 13 (4, 12), 34: Faunus, Verg. A. 10, 551: Pales, Ov. F. 4, 746.

silvicultrix.full: silvĭ-cultrix (sylv-), īcis, adj. f. [silva], living in the woods: cerva, Cat. 63, 72.

silvifragus.full: silvĭfrăgus (sylv-), a, um, adj. silva-frango, breaking or crushing the forest or trees: flabra venti, Lucr. 1, 275.

silviger.full: silvĭger (sylv-), gĕra, gĕrum, adj. silva-gero, bearing woods, wooded, woody (very rare): montes, Plin. 31, 3, 26, § 43: DEVS, a sylvan deity, Inscr. Orell. 1488 (perhaps spurious).

silvini.full: Silvīni, ōrum, m., a people of Apulia, Plin. 3, 11, 16, § 105.
silvini.short: Silvīni, ōrum, m., a people of Apulia, Plin.

silvius.full: Silvĭus, ii, m., the name of several kings of Alba Longa, Liv. 1, 3; Verg. A. 6, 769; Ov. M. 14, 610.—Hence the fem. Silvia; v. 1. Rhea.
silvius.short: Silvĭus, ii, m., the name of several kings of Alba Longa, Liv.

silvosus.full: silvōsus, a, um, adj. silva, full of woods or trees, woody: saltus, Liv. 9, 2, 7: rami emicant silvosā multitudine, forestlike, Plin. 12, 5, 11, § 23; so, crebrae arbores et silvosae, Vitr. 8, 1 fin.

silvula.full: silvŭla, ae, f. dim. id., a little wood, a copse (very rare), Col. 8, 15, 4; Sid. Carm. 9, 229.

silybum.full: sīlўbum, i, n., = sillybus, q v.
silybum.short: sīlўbum, i, n., = sillybus, q v.

sima.full: sīma, ae, f.; in architecture, a moulding, the ogee, Vitr. 3, 3 fin.; Inscr. Grut. 207, col. 1.

simbruvium.full: Simbrŭvĭum, ii, n., a district in Latium, abounding in hills and springs of water, Sil. 8, 371.—Hence, Simbrŭīnus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Simbruvium: colles, Tac. A. 11, 13: stagna, id. ib. 14, 22.
simbruvium.short: Simbrŭvĭum, ii, n., a district in Latium, abounding in hills and springs of water, Sil.

simia.full: sīmĭa, ae, f. (rarely m.), or sīmĭus, ii, m. etym. dub.; perh. akin with similis. An ape, Plin. 8, 54, 80, § 215; 11, 44, 100, § 246; Enn. ap. Cic. N. D. 1, 35, 97 (Sat. v. 45 Vahl.); Cic. Div. 1, 34, 76; 2, 32, 69; Plaut. Mil. 2, 2, 7; 2, 2, 23; 2, 2, 106; id. Rud. 3, 1, 6 sq.; 3, 4, 66; Quint. 5, 11, 30 al. —Form simius, Phaedr. 1, 10, 6; 1, 10, 8; Mart. 14, 202; Claud. in Eutr. 1, 303.— Esp. As a term of abuse (hence even simia in the masc.): quis hic est simia, qui, etc., Afran. ap. Charis.

simila.full: sĭmĭla, ae, f. root si, to sift; cf. Gr. ἱμαλιά; Germ. Semmel, the finest wheat flour, Cels. 2, 18 med.; 2, 30; Mart. 13, 10 in lemm.; Hier. Ep. 52, 6; 54, 11.—Called also, sĭmĭlāgo, Plin. 18, 10, 20, § 89; Ambros. in Luc. 8, § 49; Vulg. Num. 7, 13 et saep.

similagineus.full: sĭmĭlāgĭnĕus, a, um, adj. similago, made of fine wheat flour: panis, Vulg. Ecclus. 39, 31.

similigenus.full: sĭmĭlĭgĕnus, a, um, adj. similisgigno, of a like kind, Cael. Aur. Acut. 2, 19.

similis.full: sĭmĭlis, e, adj. Sanscr. samā, together; Gr. ἅμα, ομοῖος; Lat. simul, simulare; cf. simia, like, resembling, similar (cf. par); constr. with gen. (so usu. in ante-Aug. Lat.), with dat. (rare in Cic., except with neuter nouns), with inter, atque, and absol. With gen. (mostly ante - Aug.; so always in Plaut. and Ter.; cf. Brix ad Plaut. Capt. 1, 2, 7; but in Cic. almost exclusively of living beings; yet always veri simile; v. Madv. ad Cic. Fin. 5, 5, 12); of persons: similes avorum, Lucr. 4, 1218:

similitas.full: sĭmĭlĭtas, ātis, f. similis a rare form for similitudo, likeness, resemblance, similarity: morum, Caecil. ap. Non. 177, 2 (Com. Rel. v. 216 Rib.).—Plur.: naturae rerum similitates, Vitr. 2, 9 med.

similitudo.full: sĭmĭlĭtūdo, ĭnis, f. similis. In gen., likeness, resemblance, similitude (class.). With gen.: id ex similitudine floris lilium appellabant, Caes. B. G. 7, 73: id ad similitudinem panis efficiebant, id. B. C. 3, 48; cf.: umor ex hordeo aut frumento in quandam similitudinem vini corruptus, Tac. G. 23: armorum, Caes. B. G. 7, 50: coronae, Cic. N. D. 1, 11, 28: similitudo speciesque sapientium, id. Off. 3, 4, 16: studiorum societas similitudoque, id. Phil. 7, 2, 6: artis imago et similitudo. id. de

simininus.full: sīmĭnīnus, a, um, adj. simia, of or belonging to apes: herba, App. Herb. 86: caput, Jul. Obs. Prod. 103.

simiolus.full: sīmĭŏlus, i, m. dim. simius, a little ape, as a term of abuse, Cic. Fam. 7, 2, 3.

simitu.full: sĭmītu (collat. form sĭmītur, Inscr. Orell 2863; Inscr. Neap. ap. Momms. 423; v. Corss. Krit. Beitr. p. 400), adv. Sanscr. sama; Gr. ὁμο-; old Lat. semo, together; cf.: semul, semper, similis, etc. (ante-class. form of simul), at once, at the same time, together: gratia habetur utrisque illisque sibique simitu, Lucil. ap. Non. 175, 16: ita opertis oculis simitu manducatur ac molit, Pompon. ap. Non. 477, 4 (Com. Rel. v. 100 Rib.): multas res simitu in meo corde vorso, Plaut. Trin. 2, 1, 1 Brix ad

simo1.full: sīmo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. simus, to press flat, to flatten (only in the foll. passages): simavit taxim ad nares, Lucil. ap. Non. 169, 31: simataeque jacent pando sinuamine nares, Sulp. Luperc. ap. Anthol. Lat. 1, p. 516 Burm.: projecturas simaverunt, Vitr. 4, 2, 3.

simo2.full: Sĭmo, ōnis, m. id., a proper name, Plaut. Most.; id. Ps.; Ter. And.; Hor. A. P. 238; Plin. 11, 37, 59, § 158; cf. id. 9, 8, 7, § 23.

simodo.full: sī-mŏdo, v. modo, B. b.; and si, I. α.

simois.full: Sĭmŏīs, entis, m., = Σιμόεις, a small river in Troas that falls into the Scamander, now Mendere Tchai, Mel. 1, 18, 3; Plin. 5, 30, 33, § 124; Verg. A. 1, 100; 1, 618; 6, 88; Hor. Epod. 13, 14; Ov. M. 13, 324; Prop. 2, 9, 12.
simois.short: Sĭmŏīs, entis, m., = Σιμόεις, a small river in Troas that falls into the Scamander, now Mendere Tchai, Mel.

simon1.full: Sĭmon or Sĭmo, ōnis, m., = Συμεών (Heb. ). A chief of the Jews, Tac. H. 5, 9; 5, 12.— Simon Petrus, Vulg. Matt. 5, 8 al.; Juvenc. 4, 584: Sĭmŏnem, id. 1, 423.— Simon Magus, or the sorcerer, Vulg. Act. 8, 18 sq.— An Athenian writer on horsemanship, Plin. 34, 8, 19, § 76 (Jan. Semonem).— A sculptor, Plin. 34, 8, 19, § 90 (scanned Sīmōn, Prud. Sym. 742).
simon1.short: Sĭmon or Sĭmo, ōnis, m., = Συμεών (Heb.

simon2.full: Sĭmon, ōnis, m., = Σίμων, a famous statuary, Plin. 34, 8, 19, § 90.
simon2.short: Sĭmon, ōnis, m., = Σίμων, a famous statuary, Plin.

simonides.full: Sĭmōnĭdes, is, m., = Σιμωνίδης, a celebrated lyric poet of Cos, Cic. Rep. 2, 10, 20; id. Tusc. 1, 42, 101; 1, 24, 59; id. N. D. 1, 22, 60; id. Div. 1, 27, 56; Quint. 10, 1, 64; 11, 2, 11 al.—Hence, Sĭmōnĭdēus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to simonides: lacrimae, i. e. poems of Simonides that moved the reader to tears, Cat. 38, 8 (cf. Hor. C. 2, 1, 38; Quint. 10, 1, 64).
simonides.short: Sĭmōnĭdes, is, m., = Σιμωνίδης, a celebrated lyric poet of Cos, Cic.

simpla.full: simpla, ae, v. simplus, II. B.

simplaris.full: simplāris, e, adj. simplus; milit. t. t., that receives a single ration (cf. duplaris): armaturae, Veg. Mil. 2, 7: candidati, id. ib. 2, 7.

simplarius.full: simplārĭus, a, um, adj. id., simple: venditiones, Dig. 21, 1, 48, § 8.

simplex.full: simplex, ĭcis (abl., regul. simplici; simplice, Lucr. 1, 1013), adj. sim-; cf. Sanscr. sam, Gr. ἅμα, with Lat. sin-guli, semel, sem-per; and plico. In gen., simple, plain, uncompounded, unmixed, = ἁπλοῦς (cf.: sincerus, purus): aut simplex est natura animantis, ut vel terrena sit, vel ignea, etc. ... aut concreta est ex pluribus naturis, Cic. N. D. 3, 14, 34: natura (opp. mixta, conexa, etc.), Lucr. 3, 231; Cic. N. D. 2, 11, 29; id. Sen. 21, 78: si unum ac simplex (genus inperii) probandum sit,

simplicabilis.full: simplĭcābĭlis, e, adj. simplico, simple (late Lat.), Cassiod. An. 12.

simplicitas.full: simplĭcĭtas, ātis, f. simplex. In gen., simpleness, simplicity (not freq. till after the Aug. period, esp. in the signif. II.; not found in Cic.; cf.: candor, sinceritas): sunt solida primordia simplicitate, Lucr. 1, 609 sq.; so id. 1, 574; 2, 157: indigesta (ligni), i. e. plainness, straightness of grain, Plin. 13, 15, 30, § 97.— In partic., in a moral sense, plainness, frankness, openness, artlessness, innocence, honesty, candor, simplicity, directness, ingenuousness, naturalness, etc.: juveni

simplico.full: simplĭco, āre, v. a. simplex, to make single or simple: radicem, to strike a single root, Pall. Jan. 15, 15.

simplo.full: simplo, āre, 1, v. a. id., to make simple, simplify (late Lat.), Sedul. 1, 281.

simpludiarea.full: simplŭdĭārĕa funera sunt, quibus adhibentur duntaxat ludi, Fest. p. 334; Paul. ex Fest. p. 335 Müll. [contr. from simplus-ludus].
simpludiarea.short: simplŭdĭārĕa funera sunt, quibus adhibentur duntaxat ludi, Fest.

simplus.full: simplus, a, um. Adj. kindr. with simplex, simple; as adj. only post-class.: mors, Prud. στεφ. 10, 878.—More freq., Substt. simplum, i, n., that which is single or simple, the simple sum or number (opp. to the double): duplum simplum, Cic. Top. 11, 49: simplum solvere, Plaut. Poen. 5, 6, 25 (opp. duplum, id. ib. 5, 6, 14): si simplum imperetur, Liv. 29, 15; Dig. 49, 14, 5.— simpla, ae, f. (sc. pecunia), the simple purchase-money, Varr. R. R. 2, 10, 5; Dig. 21, 2, 60.

simpulariarius.full: simpŭlārĭārĭus, ii, m. simpulum, a maker of simpula, Inscr. Orell. 4283.

simpulum.full: simpŭlum, i, n. sim-; root sam-; cf.: simul, simplex, and pul-; cf. Gr. πολύς, plenus; v. Corss. Ausspr. 2, 74, a small ladle: simpulum vas parvulum non dissimile cyatho, quo vinum in sacrificiis libabatur; unde et mulieres rebus divinis deditae simpulatrices dicuntur, Fest. p. 337 Müll.; cf. Varr. L. L. 5, § 124 ib.; App. Mag. p. 285, and v. Becker, Gallus, 2, p. 280; 3, p. 221 (2d edit.).—Prov.: excitare fluctus in simpulo, i. e. to make much ado about nothing, to raise a tempest in a teapot,

simpuvium.full: simpŭvĭum, ii, n., a vessel for offering liquids, esp. wine, in sacrifices, a sacrificial bowl (cf.: patera, poculum), Varr. ap. Non. 544, 30; Cic. Rep. 6, 2, 11; Plin. 35, 12, 46, § 158 (Jahn, simpuis); Juv. 6, 343; Arn. 7, 235; cf. Becker, Gallus, 2, p. 280 (2d edit.).
simpuvium.short: simpŭvĭum, ii, n., a vessel for offering liquids, esp.

simul.full: sĭmŭl (ante-class. also sĕmŭl, Plaut. Trin. prol. p. 97 Ritschl; v. infra; and sĕ-mŏl, C. I. L. 1175 fin.; cf. Lorenz ad Plaut. Most. 96; cf. also simitu. The final l of simul was scarcely pronounced in the vulg. lang., and in comic poetry does not make position with an initial consonant following; v. Corss. Ausspr. 2, p. 643 sq.; Lorenz ad Plaut. Ps. 567), adv. Sanscr. sama-; Gr. ἅμα, ὅμος; cf. semel, = eodem tempore, unā, at the same time, together, at once, as soon as. Referring, as temporal

simulacrum.full: sĭmŭlācrum, i, n. simulo, an image formed in the likeness of a thing, a likeness, image, form, representation, semblance (class.; syn.: imago, effigies, signum). Lit., of images formed by art, reflected in a mirror, or seen in a dream; of apparitions, visions, etc. (the latter mostly poet. and in post-Aug. prose). Of images formed by art, esp. of statues of the gods, an image, figure, portrait, effigy, statue, etc.: alicujus effigiem simulacrumque servare, Cic. Verr. 2, 2, 65, § 159; cf.: statua

simulamen.full: sĭmŭlāmen, ĭnis, n. simulo, a copy, an imitation (poet. and very rare), Ov. M. 10, 727; Aus. Idyll. 10, 228.

simulamentum.full: sĭmŭlāmentum, i, n. id., a deception; with astu, Gell. 15, 22.

simulans.full: sĭmŭlans, antis, Part. and P. a. of simulo.

simulanter.full: sĭmŭlanter and sĭmŭlātē, advv., v. simulo fin. A. and B.

simulatilis.full: sĭmŭlātĭlis, e, adj. simulo, feigned, fictitious: umbra, Ven. Vit. S. Mart. 2, 276.

simulatio.full: sĭmŭlātĭo, ōnis, f. simulo, II., a falsely assumed appearance, a false show, feigning, shamming, pretence, feint, insincerity, deceit, hypocrisy, simulation, etc. (class. and very freq.; cf. imitatio). With gen.: simulatio insaniae, Cic. Off. 3, 26, 97: stultitiae, id. Brut. 14, 53: imitatio simulatioque virtutis, id. Ac. 2, 46, 140; id. Att. 7, 1, 6: omnium rerum, id. Lael. 25, 92: timoris, Caes. B. G. 5, 50 fin.; id. B. C. 2, 40: itineris, id. B. G. 6, 8: deditionis, id. B. C. 3, 28: vulnerum,

simulator.full: sĭmŭlātor, ōris, m. simulo. A copier, imitator (poet. and very rare): excitat artificem simulatoremque figurae Morphea, Ov. M. 11, 634: humani qualis simulator simius oris, Claud. in Eutr. 1, 303.— A feigner, pretender, counterfeit, hypocrite, simulator, etc. (the class. signif. of the word). With gen.: animus cujus rei libet simulator ac dissimulator, Sall. C. 5, 4: segnitiae, Tac. A. 14, 57: belli, Luc. 4, 722.— Absol.: in omni oratione simulatorem, quem εἴρωνα Graeci nominarunt, Socratem acce

simulatrix.full: sĭmŭlātrix, īcis, f. simulator, a (female) transformer; of Circe, who transformed men into beasts, Stat. Th. 5, 551.

simulo.full: sĭmŭlo (less correctly sĭmĭlo; v. assimulo fin.), āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. similis. In gen., to make a thing like another; to imitate, copy, represent a thing (mostly poet.; syn. imitor): corpora igni simulata, made like, like, Lucr. 1, 687: nimbos et non imitabile fulmen simulare, Verg. A. 6, 591: simulet Catonem, Hor. Ep. 1, 19, 13: cum sint crura tibi, simulent quae cornua lunae, Mart. 2, 35, 1: furias Bacchi, Ov. M. 6, 596: equam (sonus), id. ib. 2, 668: artem (natura), id. ib. 3, 158: anum, to a

simultas.full: sĭmultas, ātis (gen. plur. simultatium, Liv. 1, 60, 2; 3, 66, 4; 9, 38, 12; 28, 18, 12; 39, 5, 2; 39, 44, 9; Val. Max. 4, 2, 2; Auct. B. Alex. 49, 2: simultatum, Cic. Fl. 35, 87; Capitol. Ver. 9, 2), f. simul; therefore, orig., a coming together, encounter of two persons or parties; hence, A hostile encounter of two persons or parties, dissension, enmity, rivalry, jealousy, grudge, hatred, animosity (class.; syn.: aemulatio, odium, inimicitia; on account of the idea of reciprocity, most freq. in

simulter.full: sĭmulter, adv., v. similis fin. A.

simulus1.full: sīmŭlus, a, um, dim. adj. [simus], flat-nosed, pug-nosed, Lucr. 4, 1169.

simulus2.full: Sīmŭlus, i, m. 1. simulus, a proper name, Ter. Ad. 3, 4, 19.

simus.full: sīmus, a, um, adj., = σιμός, flat-nosed, snub-nosed (cf. silus). Lit.: avibus, serpentibus, piscibus, foramina tantum ad olfactus sine naribus, et hinc cognomina Simorum, Plin. 11, 37, 59, § 158: pecus Nerei, i. e. dolphins, Liv. Andron. ap. Non. 335, 22 (Trag. Rel. p. 1 Rib.); cf.: rostrum delphini, Plin. 9, 8, 7, § 23: capellae, Verg. E. 10, 7: puer simā nare, Mart. 6, 39, 8; Cels. 8, 10, 7.— Trop., Verg. M. 107.
simus.short: sīmus, a, um, adj., = σιμός, flat-nosed, snub-nosed (cf.

sin.full: sīn, conj. [apocop. from si-ne], an adversative conditional particle, if however, if on the contrary, but if (good prose). With a preceding si, nisi, quando, dum. After si. In gen.: si domi sum, foris est animus: sin foris sum, animus domi est, Plaut. Merc. 3, 4, 2; cf. id. ib. 3, 4, 7: hunc mihi timorem eripe: si est verus, ne opprimar; sin falsus, ut, etc., Cic. Cat. 1, 7, 18 fin.: si optimates ... sin populus, etc., id. Rep. 1, 42, 65: quos si boni oppresserunt ... sin audaces, id. ib. 1, 44,

sinapi.full: sĭnāpi (sĭnāpe, Apic. 6, 4; 8, 7), is, n. (collat. form sĭnāpis, is, f., Plaut. Ps. 3, 2, 28; Col. poët. 10, 122; acc. sinapim, Pall. Oct. 11, 2), = σίναπι, mustard, Col. 11, 3, 29; Plin. 19, 8, 54, § 170; 20, 22, 87, § 236; Enn. ap. Macr. S. 6, 5; Cels. 2, 21; 2, 22; 2, 31; Petr. 66, 7.—Gen. sinapis, Col. 11, 3, 29; Plin. 21, 12, 41, § 71.—Abl. sinapi, Plaut. Truc. 2, 2, 60: sinape, Varr. R. R. 1, 59, 4.

sinapismus.full: sĭnāpismus, i, m., = σιναπισμός, a mustard - plaster or poultice, a sinapism, Cael. Aur. Tard. 3, 8, 112.
sinapismus.short: sĭnāpismus, i, m., = σιναπισμός, a mustard - plaster or poultice, a sinapism, Cael.

sinapizo.full: sĭnāpīzo, āre, v. a., = σιναπίζω, to poultice with mustard, to cover with a mustara-plaster: partem corporis, Veg. 3, 6, 11; 3, 5, 33; Cael. Aur. Tard. 5, 2.

sincerasco.full: sincērasco, rāvi, 1, v. inch. n. [sincerus], to begin to clear, grow clear (late Lat.): aer sinceravit, mundumque efficitur caelum, Fulg. Serm. 16.

sincere.full: sincērē, adv., v. sincerus fin. a.

sinceritas.full: sincērĭtas, ātis, f. sincerus, cleanness, purity, soundness, wholeness (not anteAug.). Lit.: pura (olei), Plin. 15, 6, 6, § 22: firma capitis, Pall. 1, 3: corporis, Val. Max. 2, 6, 8: alia convertenda, quae sinceritatem habent, Col. 4, 26.— Trop.: nec summum bonum habebit sinceritatem suam, si, etc., Sen. Vit. Beat. 15: summa vitae, moral purity, Val. Max. 5, 3, 2 ext.: ad perniciem solet agi sinceritas, uprightness, honesty, integrity, sincerity (with recte loqui), Phaedr. 4, 13, 3; so (with pr

sinceriter.full: sincērĭter, adv., v. sincerus fin. b.

sincero.full: sincēro, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. sincerus, to make clean or pure, Diom. 361 P.

sincerus.full: sincērus, a, um, adj. sin- = sim-, v. simplex; root in Sanscr. sama, whole, together; and root skir-, Sanscr. kir-, pour out, clean, pure, sound, not spoiled, uninjured, whole, entire, real, natural, genuine, sincere (class.; esp. freq. in the trop. sense; cf.: simplex, verus, incorruptus). Lit.: omnia fucata et simulata a sinceris atque veris (internoscere), Cic. Lael. 25, 95: aliquem ab omni incommodo, detrimento, molestiā sincerum integrumque conservare, unharmed, unhurt, id. Fam. 13, 50, 2:

sincinium.full: sincĭnĭum, ii, n. sin- = sim- (cf. simplex) and cano, the song of a single person, a solo, = μονῳδία (late Lat.), Isid. Orig. 6, 19, 6.

sincipitamentum.full: sincĭpĭtāmentum, i, n. sinciput, = ἡμικεφάλαιον, a half - head: sincipitamenta porcina, Plaut. Men. 1, 3, 28 Ritschl, Brix.

sinciput.full: sincĭput, pĭtis, n. semi - caput; cf.: sinciput ἡμικεφάλιον, ἡμίκρανον, ἡμικέφαλον, Gloss. Philox.. Half a head; of the smoked cheek, jowl of a hog, Plaut. Men. 1, 3, 28 (Ritschl, sincipitamenta); Plin. 8, 51, 77, § 209; Pers. 6, 70; Juv. 13, 85.— Transf. The brain: non tibi Sanum est, adulescens, sinciput, Plaut. Men. 3, 2, 41: sanum, id. ib. 4, 2, 69.—* The head, in gen.: miserabile sinciput, Sid. Carm. 5, 419.

sindenses.full: Sindenses, ĭum, m., the inhabitants of Sinda (Σινδα), a town of Pisidia, near Cibyra and the river Caularis, Liv. 38, 15.
sindenses.short: Sindenses, ĭum, m., the inhabitants of Sinda (Σινδα), a town of Pisidia, near Cibyra and the river Caularis, Liv.

sindes.full: Sindes, is, m.; acc. sinden, a river in Asia, Tac. A. 11, 10 Ritter (al. Gyndes).

sindica.full: Sindica, ae, f., a part of Scythia on the Black Sea, Plin. 4, 12, 26, § 84.
sindica.short: Sindica, ae, f., a part of Scythia on the Black Sea, Plin.

sindon.full: sindon, ŏnis, f., = σινδών, a kind of fine cotton stuff, muslin, Mart. 4, 19, 12; 11, 1, 2; Aus. Ephem. in Parecb. 2; Vulg. Matt. 27, 59; id. Marc. 14, 52; id. Luc. 23, 53.
sindon.short: sindon, ŏnis, f., = σινδών, a kind of fine cotton stuff, muslin, Mart.

sindos.full: Sindŏs, i, f., a city of Scythia, on the Cimmerian Bosporus, Mel. 1, 19.—Hence, Sindŏnes, um, m., the inhabitants of Sindos, Mel. 1, 19; cf. Sindica.
sindos.short: Sindŏs, i, f., a city of Scythia, on the Cimmerian Bosporus, Mel.

sindus.full: Sindus, i, m., an Indian name of the river Indus, Plin. 6, 20, 23, § 71.
sindus.short: Sindus, i, m., an Indian name of the river Indus, Plin.

sine.full: sĭne (old form sē or sēd; v. the foll.), prep. with abl. [si and ne; si, the demonstrative instrumental, and the negative ne; hence, nesi was also found, Fest. p. 165; cf. Rib. Beiträge, p. 15; Corss. Ausspr. 1, 201; 1, 778]. Without. Form se (sed): socordia compositum videtur ex se, quod est sine, et corde, Fest. pp. 292 and 293 Müll.: sed pro sine inveniuntur posuisse antiqui, id. p. 336 ib.: SI PLVS MINVSVE SECVERVNT SE FRAVDE ESTO, Fragm. XII. Tab. ap. Gell. 20, 1, 49: IM CVM ILLO SEPELIREI

singania.full: Singanĭa, ae, m., a river of Pontus, Plin. 6, 4, 4, § 14.
singania.short: Singanĭa, ae, m., a river of Pontus, Plin.

singara.full: Singăra, ōrum, n., a city of Mesopotamia, the capital of the Arabes Prætavi, Plin. 5, 24, 21, § 86.—Hence, adj.: Singărē-nus, a, um, of or belonging to Singara: congressiones, Sext. Ruf. Brev. 27.
singara.short: Singăra, ōrum, n., a city of Mesopotamia, the capital of the Arabes Prætavi, Plin.

singentiana.full: Singentĭāna rādix, a plant, = acoros, App. Herb. 6.
singentiana.short: Singentĭāna rādix, a plant, = acoros, App.

singidonensis.full: Singidonensis, e, adj., of or belonging to the town Singido in Pannonia, Aur. Vict. Epit. 44.
singidonensis.short: Singidonensis, e, adj., of or belonging to the town Singido in Pannonia, Aur.

singili.full: Singĭli, ōrum, m., a city in Hispania Bætica, Plin. 3, 1, 3, § 10.
singili.short: Singĭli, ōrum, m., a city in Hispania Bætica, Plin.

singilio.full: singĭlĭo, ōnis, m., perh. a plain, short garment, Gallien. ap. Treb. Claud. 17 dub.

singillarius.full: singillārĭus, a, um, adj. singularis, single, simple (post - class.): motus, Tert. Anim. 6: ductus, id. adv. Valent. 18.

singillatim.full: singillātim or singŭlātim (in many MSS. also sigillātim; contr. collat. form singultim), adv. singuli, one by one, singly (class.): sic singillatim nostrum unusquisque movetur, Lucil. ap. Non. 176, 11: singillatim potius quam generatim atque universe loqui, Cic. Verr. 2, 5, 55, § 143: singillatim de uno quoque genere dicere, id. Inv. 1, 30, 49; Ter. Phorm. 5, 8 (9), 43; Lucr. 2, 153; 4, 105; Caecil. and Cael. ap. Non. 176, 8 sq.; Cic. Mil. 1, 52, 98 and 99; 1, 55, 107; id. Tusc. 5, 33, 94; id. P

singos.full: Singos or Siggos, i, f., = Σίγγος, a city of Chalcidice, on the Ægean Sea, Plin. 4, 10, 17, § 37.
singos.short: Singos or Siggos, i, f., = Σίγγος, a city of Chalcidice, on the Ægean Sea, Plin.

singularis.full: singŭlāris, e, adj. singuli. Lit. In gen., one by one, one at a time, alone, single, solitary; alone of its kind, singular (class.; syn.: unus, unicus): non singulare nec solivagum genus (sc. homines), i. e. solitary, Cic. Rep. 1, 25, 39: hostes ubi ex litore aliquos singulares ex navi egredientes conspexerant, Caes. B. G. 4, 26: homo, id. ib. 7, 8, 3; so, homo (with privatus, and opp. isti conquisiti coloni), Cic. Agr. 2, 35, 97: singularis mundus atque unigena, id. Univ. 4 med.: praeconium Dei

singularitas.full: singŭlārĭtas, ātis, f. singularis. In gen., a being alone or single, singleness (post-class.), Tert. adv. Valent. 37; id. Anim. 13; id. Exhort. ad Cast. 1; Salv. Cont. Avar. 7, p. 70.— In partic., in gram., the singular number, Charis. p. 72 P.— In arithmetic, unity, the number one: singularitas omnibus mensura communis, Mart. Cap. 7, §§ 750 and 774.

singularius.full: sĭngŭlārĭus, a, um, adj. singularis. Lit., single, separate, alone of its kind, peculiar (ante- and post-class. for the class. singularis; but cf. infra, adv.): homo unicā est naturā ac singulariā, Turp. ap. Non. 491, 2: litterae, i. e. abbreviations (syn. sigla), Gell. 17, 9, 2: catenae, perh. of a single ply, = simplices (or of a pound weight, i. e. light; opp. istas majores, v. 4; cf.: centenariae ballistae), Plaut. Capt. 1, 2, 3.—* Remarkable, extraordinary, singular: homines singulariae vel

singuli.full: singŭli, ae, a (in sing. only ante- and post-class.; v. infra), num. distr. adj. [cf. simul, v. simplex]. One to each, separate, single (opp. universi; for syn. cf.: privus, unusquisque): vini in culleos singulos quadragenae et singulae urnae dabuntur, Cato, R. R. 148, 1: ut ad denas capras singulos parent hircos, Varr. R. R. 2, 3 fin.: binae singulis quae datae nobis ancillae, Plaut. Poen. 1, 2, 12: describebat censores binos in singulas civitates, Cic. Verr. 2, 2, 53, § 133: duodena describit

singultim.full: singultim. adv. from singultus; cf.: furtim, partim, etc., sobbingly: μετά λυγμοῦ, Hor. S. 1, 6, 56 (others less correctly make it = singulatim, singillatim, singly): lamentabiles questus singultim instrepebat, App. M p. 127, 36.

singultio.full: singultĭo, īre, v. n. singultus. To hiccup: aut bilem vomunt aut singultiunt, Cels. 5, 26, 19; Plin. 23, 1, 24, § 48; to sob, App. M. 3, p. 133, 40.—* Transf., of a hen, to cluck, Col. 8, 11, 15.—* Transf., to throb with pleasure: vena, Pers. 6, 72.

singulto.full: singulto, no perf., ātum, 1, v. n. and a. [id.]. Neutr., to hiccup; to sob: singultantium modo, Quint. 10, 7, 10.— Transf., poet., of persons dying, to rattle in the throat, Verg. A. 9, 333; Sil. 2, 362; 1, 388; Val. Fl. 2, 211.—Of speech interrupted with sobs: verba singultantia, Stat. S. 5, 5, 26; Calp. Ecl. 6, 22.—Of water flowing from an orifice, to gurgle, Sid. Ep. 2, 2 med.— Act.: animam, to breathe out with sobs, to gasp away with short sobs or rattling in the throat, Ov. M. 5, 134: in li

singultus.full: singultus, ūs, m. singuli, and hence, an uttering of single sounds. Lit., a sobbing, speech interrupted by sobs (class.); sing.: multas lacrimas et fletum cum singultu videre potuisti, Cic. Planc. 31, 76; Lucr. 6, 1160; Ov. M. 11, 420; id. Tr. 1, 3, 42; Tac. H. 3, 10 al.—Plur., Cat. 64, 131; Ov. M. 6, 509; Hor. C. 3, 27, 74.—As a disease, hiccups, Sen. Ep. 47, 3; Plin. 20, 17, 73, § 189; 21, 18, 72, § 120; 23, 1, 27, § 54 al.— Transf., a rattling in the throat of dying persons, Verg. A. 9, 415;

sinis.full: Sĭnis, is, m., = Σίνις, a mythical robber on the Isthmus of Corinth, who bound travellers to the tops of pine-trees which he had bent to the ground, and then, by letting go his hold, hurled them into the air; he was killed at last by Theseus, Prop. 3 (4), 22, 37; Ov. M. 7, 440; id. H. 2, 70; Stat. Th. 12, 576.
sinis.short: Sĭnis, is, m., = Σίνις, a mythical robber on the Isthmus of Corinth, who bound travellers to the tops of pine-trees which he had bent to the ground, and then, by letting go his hold, hurled them into the air;

sinister.full: sĭnister, tra, trum (comp. sinisterior; sup. sinistimus, Prisc. pp. 605 and 607 P.; Fest. s. v. dextimum, p. 74; and s. v. sinistrae, p. 339 Müll.), adj. etym. dub.; perh. from sinus (i. e. togae); cf. Pott, Etym. Forsch. 2, 555; the ending is a double comp. -is and -ter; cf.: magister, minister. Left, on the left, on the left hand or side (syn.: laevus, scaevus): manus sinistra (opp. dextra), Quint. 11, 3, 114: manus, Nep. Dat. 3; Quint. 11, 3, 159: bracchium, id. 11, 3, 141: latus, id. 11, 3,

sinisteritas.full: sĭnistĕrĭtas, ātis, f. sinister, II. A., awkwardness, untowardness, perversity (cf. the opp. dexteritas); perh. only in Plin. Ep. 6, 17, 3; 9, 5, 2.

sinistre.full: sĭnistrē, adv., v. sinister, II. C. fin.

sinistrorsus.full: sĭnistrorsus (collat. form sĭnis-trorsum, Hor. Epod. 9, 20; id. S. 2, 3, 50; and not contr. sĭnistrōversus, Lact. 3, 6, 4), adv. contr. from sinistrovorsus, from sinister-vorto, towards the left side, to the left: hinc (Hercynia silva) se flectit sinistrorsus, Caes. B. G. 6, 25; Suet. Galb. 4; Front. Aquaed. 5: portu latent Puppes sinistrorsum citae, Hor. Epod. 9, 20: ille sinistrorsum, hic dextrorsum abit, id. S. 2, 3, 50: dextro aut sinistroversus, Lact. 3, 6, 4.

sinnius.full: Sinnĭus, ia, the name of a Roman gens, e. g. Sinnius Capito, a Roman grammarian, Gell. 5, 21, 9.—Hence, Sinnĭānus, a, um, adj., of Sinnius: opinio, Gell. 5, 21, 14.
sinnius.short: Sinnĭus, ia, the name of a Roman gens, e.

sino.full: sĭno, sīvi, sĭtum, 3 (sinit, as archaic subj. pres. formerly stood, Plaut. Curc. 1, 1, 27; Verg. Cir. 239; but in the former passage has been corrected to sierit, Fleck.; and in the latter the clause is spurious.— Perf. sii, Varr. ap. Diom. p. 371 P.: siit, Ter. Ad. 1, 2, 24, acc. to Diom. l. l.; another old form of the perf. sini, Scaur. ap. Diom. l. l.; so, too, pluperf. sinisset, Rutil. ib.— Sync. perf. sisti, Plaut. Mil. 4, 2, 80: sistis, Att. ap. Cic. Sest. 57, 122.—Subj. sieris or siris, P
sino.short: sĭno, sīvi, sĭtum, 3 (sinit, as archaic subj.

sinon2.full: Sĭnon, ōnis, m., son of Æsimus, through whose perfidy the Trojans were induced to take the wooden horse within their city, Verg. A. 2, 79 sq.; Hyg. Fab. 108; Dict. Cret. 5, 12; Plin. 7, 56, 57, § 202.
sinon2.short: Sĭnon, ōnis, m., son of Æsimus, through whose perfidy the Trojans were induced to take the wooden horse within their city, Verg.

sinonia.full: Sinōnĭa, ae, f., an island in the Tyrrhenian Sea, now Sanone, Mel. 2, 7; Plin. 3, 6, 12, § 81.
sinonia.short: Sinōnĭa, ae, f., an island in the Tyrrhenian Sea, now Sanone, Mel.

sinope.full: Sĭnōpē, ēs (or -a, ae; cf. Zumpt ad Cic. Verr. 2, 1, 34, § 87, p. 166), f., = Σινώπη. A famous Greek colony in Paphlagonia, on the Euxine, the birthplace of Diogenes the Cynic and residence of Mithridates, now Sinoub, Mel. 1, 19, 9; Plin. 6, 2, 2, § 6; Cic. Verr. 2, 1, 34, § 87; id. Imp. Pomp. 8, 21; Tac. H. 4, 83 sq. al.: Sinopae, Cic. Agr. 2, 20, 53.—Hence, Sĭnōpensis, e, adj., of or belonging to Sinope: colonia, Dig. 50, 15, 1 fin.—Plur. subst.: Sĭnōpenses, ĭum, m., the inhabitants of Sinope,

sinti.full: Sinti or Sintii, ōrum, m., a people of Macedonia: Heraclea ex Sintiis, Liv. 42, 51, 7.—Hence, Sintĭcus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to the Sintii, Sintian: Heraclea Sintica, Plin. 4, 10, 17, § 35; or, Sintice Heraclea, Liv. 45, 29, 6 and 7.
sinti.short: Sinti or Sintii, ōrum, m., a people of Macedonia: Heraclea ex Sintiis, Liv.

sinuamen.full: sĭnŭāmen, ĭnis, n. sinuo, a bending, turning, winding (post-class.), Prud. Psych. 870; Juvenc. 1, 87; 3, 56; Sid. Carm. 22, 151.

sinuatio.full: sĭnŭātĭo, ōnis, f. id., a bending, bend, curve: corniculata lunae, Fulg. Myth. praef.

sinuessa.full: Sĭnŭessa, ae, f., a colony of the Latins, formerly called Sinope, in Campania, now ruins near Monte Dragone, Mel. 2, 4, 9. Plin. 3, 5, 9, § 59; Liv. 10, 21, 8; Cic. Att. 9, 15, A, 6; 9, 16, 1; Ov. M. 15, 715.—Hence, Sĭnŭessuānus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Sinuessa: deversoriolum, Cic. Fam. 12, 20; id. Att. 14, 8, 1.—Absol.: mansi in Sinuessano, the Sinuessan estate, Cic. Att. 15, 1, B, 1: aquae, Plin. 31, 2, 4, § 8: ager, id. 2, 93, 94, § 208; cf. lacus, Mart. 11, 7, 12; 13, 11, 1: Petrinu
sinuessa.short: Sĭnŭessa, ae, f., a colony of the Latins, formerly called Sinope, in Campania, now ruins near Monte Dragone, Mel.

sinum.full: sīnum, i, n. (masc. collat. form sīnus, Plaut. Curc. 1, 1, 82; id. Rud. 5, 2, 31; for the form of the abl., sinu, Varr. ap. Non. 547, 23, we should perh. substitute sino; cf. Prisc. p. 714 P.) [1. sinus], a large, round drinking-vessel with swelling sides (like our bowls), esp. for wine (cf. Cic. Fragm. ap. Schol. Veron. ad Verg. E. 7, 33), Varr. L. L. 5, § 123 Müll.; id. ap. Non. 547, 23; Plaut. Curc. 1, 1, 75; 1, 1, 82; id. Rud. 5, 2, 32; Atta ap. Serv. Verg. E. 7, 33; Valgius ap. Philarg. Ver

sinuo.full: sĭnŭo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. id.. Lit., to bend, wind, curve; to bow, to swell out in curves (perh. not ante-Aug.; most freq. in the poets; syn.: curvo, flecto): (anguis) sinuat immensa volumine terga, Verg. A. 2, 208; cf.: flexos corpus in orbes (anguis), Ov. M. 9, 64: (equus) sinuet alterna volumina crurum, Verg. G. 3, 192: imposito patulos calamo sinuaverat arcus, i. e. had bent, stretched, Ov. M. 8, 30; so, arcum, id. ib. 8, 381: nervum, Sen. Herc. Fur. 1198: Euphraten immensum attolli et in m

sinuosus.full: sĭnŭōsus, a, um, adj. 1. sinus, full of bendings, windings, or curves; full of folds, bent, winding, sinuous (poet. and in postAug. prose; syn. tortuosus). Lit.: flexus anguis, Verg. G. 1, 244: volumina (serpentis), id. A. 11, 753: Maeander flexibus, Plin. 5, 29, 31, § 113: arcus, Ov. Am. 1, 1, 23: vela, Prop. 4 (5), 1, 15. Ov. H. 8, 23: vestis, id. M. 5, 68: folia lateribus, Plin. 16, 6, 8, § 19 et saep.— Trop. Of style, full of digressions, diffuse: ratio narrandi, * Quint. 2, 4, 3: quaestio,

sinus1.full: sĭnus, ūs, m. In gen., a bent surface (raised or depressed), a curve, fold, a hollow, etc. (so mostly poet. and in postAug. prose): draco ... conficiens sinus e corpore flexos, folds, coils, Cic. poët. N. D. 2, 42, 106; so Ov. M. 15, 689; 15, 721: sinu ex togā facto, Liv. 21, 18 fin.—Of the bag of a fishing-net: quando abiit rete pessum, tum adducit sinum (piscator), Plaut. Truc. 1, 1, 15; so Juv. 4, 41; and of a hunter's net, Mart. 13, 100; Grat. Cyn. 29; also of a spider's web, Plin. 11, 24, 2

sion1.full: sĭon, ii, n., = σίον, water - parsley: Sium latifolium, Linn.; Plin. 26, 8, 56, § 88; 22, 22, 41, § 84.
sion1.short: sĭon, ii, n., = σίον, water - parsley: Sium latifolium, Linn.;

sion2.full: Sīon, ōnis (or indecl.), m., f., or n., a hill of Jerusalem, and, by meton., Jerusalem, Prud. Ham. 459; Vulg. Matt. 21, 5: facta est deserta Sion, id. Isa. 64, 10.
sion2.short: Sīon, ōnis (or indecl.), m., f., or n., a hill of Jerusalem, and, by meton., Jerusalem, Prud.

siparium.full: sīpărĭum, ii, n. kindr. with supparum, from σίπαρος, orig. a little sail; hence, transf., The smaller curtain in a theatre (drawn up between the scenes of a comedy; cf. aulaeum, the main curtain): aulaeo subducto et complicitis sipariis, scena disponitur, App. M. 10, p. 253, 23; 1, p. 106, 4: post siparium, i. e. behind the scenes, Cic. Prov. Cons. 6, 14; Juv. 8, 186.— Meton., comedy (opp. cothurnus, tragedy): (verba) cothurno, non tantum sipario fortiora, Sen. Tranq. 11, 6.— A curtain or screen

siphae.full: Siphae, ārum, f., a city of Bœotia, on the borders of Phocis, Plin. 4, 3, 4, § 8.
siphae.short: Siphae, ārum, f., a city of Bœotia, on the borders of Phocis, Plin.

siphnus.full: Siphnus (-os), i, f., one of the Cyclades, now Sifano, Mel. 2, 7; Plin. 4, 12, 22, § 66; 36, 22, 44, § 159.—Hence, Siphnĭus, a, um, adj., Siphnian: lapis, Plin. 36, 22, 44, § 159.
siphnus.short: Siphnus (-os), i, f., one of the Cyclades, now Sifano, Mel.

sipho.full: sīpho (-on; in many MSS. also written sīfo), ōnis, m., = σίφων (a small pipe). A siphon (called also diabetes): sipho, quem diabeten vocant mechanici, Col. 3, 10, 2; 9, 14, 15; Lucil. ap. Cic. Fin. 2, 8, 23; Sen. Q.
