N. 2, 16; Plin. 2, 65, 66, § 166; 32, 10, 42, § 124; Luc. 7, 156; Juv. 6, 310.— A little pipe to suck drinks through, a drinking-tube, Cels. 1, 8 fin.— A kind of fireengine, Dig. 33, 7, 12, § 18; Plin. Ep. 10, 42, 2; Isid. 20, 6, 9.

siphunculus.full: sīphuncŭlus, i, m. dim. sipho, a little pipe from which water springs forth, Plin. Ep. 5, 6, 23; 5, 6, 36.—Also written without the aspirate, sīpuncŭlus, Fronto, Or. 1 med.

sipontum.full: Sīpontum, i, n., = Σιποῦς (cf. Cic. Att. 6, 2, 3), an important maritime town in Appulia, now S. Maria di Siponto, Mel. 2, 4, 7; Plin. 3, 11, 16, § 103; Cic. Att. 9, 15, 1; 10, 7, 1; Liv. 34, 45, 3; 39, 23, 3 al. (in Liv. 8, 24, 4 dub., v. Weissenb. ad h.l.).—In a Greek form, Sīpūs, Sil. 8, 635; Luc. 5, 377: Sipontum, aut ut Graii dixere, Sipus, Mel. 2, 4, 7.—Hence, Sīpontīnus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Sipontum, Sipontian: siccitas, Cic. Agr. 2, 27, 71: POPVLVS, Inscr. Murat. p. 1081, 6.

siptachora.full: siptachŏra, ae, f. Indian, a tree in India that yields amber; in Ctesias, σιπταχόρα, Plin. 37, 2, 11, § 39.

sipyleius.full: Sĭpўlēïus a, um, and Sĭpўlēus, a, um, and Sĭpўlensis, e, v. Sipylus.
sipyleius.short: Sĭpўlēïus a, um, and Sĭpўlēus, a, um, and Sĭpўlensis, e, v.

sipylus.full: Sĭpўlus, i, m., = Σίπυλος. A mountain on the frontiers of Lydia and Phrygia, on which Niobe was changed into stone, the modern Manisa Dagh, Prop. 2, 20 (3, 13), 8; Ov. M. 6, 149; Cic. Q. Fr. 2, 11, 3; Sen. Herc. Oet. 184; id. Agam. 374.—Hence, Sĭpўlē-us, a, um, adj., of Sipylus: genitrix Sipylea, i. e. Niobe, Stat. S. 5, 1, 33; also called Sipyleïa cautes, Aus. Epit. 27.—Sĭpўlen-sis, e: mater deorum, Ulp. Fragm. 22, 6.— A son of Niobe, Ov. M. 6, 231.

siquando.full: sīquandō (better separate, sī quan-dō), adv., if ever, Cic. Lael. 15, 52; Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 64, § 142; id. Rep. 1, 38, 59; Liv. 8, 4; Verg. G. 3, 98; id. A. 12. 851 al.—Absol., Ov. A. A. 2, 15; Stat. Achill. 1, 509 al.
siquando.short: sīquandō (better separate, sī quan-dō), adv., if ever, Cic.

siquidem.full: sīquĭdem (or separate, sī quĭdem; in poets, sĭquĭdem, Ov. M. 10, 104; 11, 219; id. Am. 3, 7, 17), adv., = εἴπερ. If only, if indeed (class.): actumst, siquidem haec vera praedicat, Ter. And. 3, 1, 7; cf.: gratulor Baiis nostris, si quidem, ut scribis, salubres repente factae sunt, Cic. Fam. 9, 12, 1: robur et suboles militum interiit, si quidem quae nuntiantur ullā ea parte vera sunt, Asin. ap. Cic. Fam. 10, 33, 1: Sy. Quid aliud tibi vis? Cl. Siquidem hoc fit. Sy. Siquidem? experiundo scies, Te

siquis.full: sī-quis or sī-qui, sīqua, sīquid or sīquod, or separately, sī quis, etc., indef. pron. (v. Zumpt, Gr. § 740), if any, if any one: si quis recte Tractaret, Ter. Heaut. 1, 1, 100: si qui (filius) natus esset, Cic. Clu. 12, 33: si qua tui Corydonis habet te cura, Verg. E. 7, 40.—Adverb.: si qui and si qua, if in any way, if by any means: si qui, Liv. 3, 64 fin.; Plaut. Trin. 1, 2, 83: si qua, id. Cist. 1, 3, 35; Verg. A. 1, 18; Hor. C. 3, 14, 19: si quo, if any whither, Cic. Att. 8, 2, 1; also, if
siquis.short: sī-quis or sī-qui, sīqua, sīquid or sīquod, or separately, sī quis, etc., indef.

siraci.full: Siraci, ōrum, m., a people of Asiatic Sarmatia, Plin. 4, 12, 26, § 83; Tac. 12, 15 and 16.
siraci.short: Siraci, ōrum, m., a people of Asiatic Sarmatia, Plin.

sirae.full: Sirae, ārum, f., a town of the Odomantic region in Thrace, Liv. 45, 4.
sirae.short: Sirae, ārum, f., a town of the Odomantic region in Thrace, Liv.

siraeum.full: sĭraeum, i, n., = σίραιον, new wine boiled down (pure Lat. sapa), Plin. 14, 9, 11, § 80.
siraeum.short: sĭraeum, i, n., = σίραιον, new wine boiled down (pure Lat.

sirbenus.full: sirbēnus, a, um, adj., = συρβηνός, speaking confusedly: virgo, Fronto, Or. 3.
sirbenus.short: sirbēnus, a, um, adj., = συρβηνός, speaking confusedly: virgo, Fronto, Or.

sirbitum.full: Sirbitum, i, n., a city in Ethiopia, Plin. 6, 30, 35, § 194 al.
sirbitum.short: Sirbitum, i, n., a city in Ethiopia, Plin.

sirbonis.full: Sirbonis lacus, a lake on the borders of Palestine, Plin. 5, 13, 14, § 68.
sirbonis.short: Sirbonis lacus, a lake on the borders of Palestine, Plin.

sircitula.full: sircitŭla, ae, f., a kind of grape, Col. 12, 45, 1.
sircitula.short: sircitŭla, ae, f., a kind of grape, Col.

sircula.full: sircŭla, ae, f., a kind of grape, Plin. 14, 2, 4, § 34.
sircula.short: sircŭla, ae, f., a kind of grape, Plin.

siredones.full: Sīrēdŏnes, um, f., = Sirenes, the Sirens, Aus. Idyll. 11, 20.
siredones.short: Sīrēdŏnes, um, f., = Sirenes, the Sirens, Aus.

siremps.full: sĭremps (sĭrempse, Plaut. Am. prol. 73), adj. acc. to Fest. pp. 344 and 345 Müll., contr. from similis re ipsā, qs. simrepsa, simrepse, and by transposition, sirempse; but prob. from si-, loc. form from pronom. stem sa-, cf. sic; rem is acc. of reference, cf. prope-diem, pri-dem; -pe is the intens. part., as in nem-pe, etc., and becomes pse, with enclit. se, as in ipse, etc., v. Corss. Ausspr. 2, 846 sq.; publicists' t. t., of a like application of laws, like, the same: sirempse legem jussit ess

siren.full: Sīrēn, ēnis, f., = Σειρήν, a Siren. Lit., usu. plur.: Sīrēnes, um, = Σειρῆνες, the Sirens, who, according to the myth, were birds with the faces of virgins. They dwelt on the southern coast of Italy, where, with their sweet voices, they enticed ashore those who were sailing by, and then killed them, Ov. M. 5, 555; Hyg. Fab. 125; 141; Serv. Verg. A. 5, 864; Cic. Fin. 5, 18, 49; Prop. 3, 12 (4, 11), 34; Hor. Ep. 1, 2, 23; Mart. 3, 64, 1; Ov. R. Am. 789; Plin. 10, 49, 70, § 136 al.—Sing.: Siren, Si
siren.short: Sīrēn, ēnis, f., = Σειρήν, a Siren.

sirena.full: Sīrēna, ae, f., later collat. form of Siren, q. v.; abl. Sirenā, Phil. ad Verg. G. 4, 564; plur., Hier. Ep. 22 (18), 6; 18; Schol. Juv. 9, 150: mortifera Sirenarum carmina, Hier. Ep. 54 (47), 13: cantus Sirenarum, Ambros. de Jac. et Vit. Beat. 2, 12, 56: scopuli Sirenarum, Mart. Cap. 6, § 641: Cyclopum et Sirenarum ora, Tert. Apol. 7 (Oehl. Sirenum).

sirenaeus.full: Sīrēnaeus, a, um, v. Sirenes, I. B.

siriacus.full: sīrĭăcus, a, um, adj., = σειριακός, of or belonging to the dog-star: calor, Avien. Arat. 285.
siriacus.short: sīrĭăcus, a, um, adj., = σειριακός, of or belonging to the dog-star: calor, Avien.

siriasis.full: sīrĭăsis, is, f., = σειρίασις, an inflammatory disease of children, siriasis, occasioned by excessive heat of the sun, Plin. 30, 15, 47, § 135; 32, 10, 48, § 138; 22, 21, 29, § 59.
siriasis.short: sīrĭăsis, is, f., = σειρίασις, an inflammatory disease of children, siriasis, occasioned by excessive heat of the sun, Plin.

siris1.full: siris, sirit, etc., v. sino init.

siris2.full: Sīris, is, m., = Σίρις. The name of a branch of the Nile in Ethiopia, Plin. 5, 9, 10, § 54; Prisc. Perieg. 212.— A river in Italy, Plin. 3, 11, 15, § 97.— A name for Heraclea in Magna Graecia, Plin. 3, 11, 15, § 97.

sirium.full: sīrĭum, ii, n., a plant, called also artemisia and serpyllum majus, mugwort, App. Herb. 10.
sirium.short: sīrĭum, ii, n., a plant, called also artemisia and serpyllum majus, mugwort, App.

sirius.full: Sīrĭus, ii, m., = σείριος, the dog-star, Sirius, Hyg. Astr. 3, 34; 2, 35; Verg. G. 4, 425; id. A. 3, 141; Tib. 1, 7, 21; Luc. 10, 211 al.—Adj.: ardor, of Sirius, Verg. A. 10, 273; Col. poët. 10, 289: vapor, Prud. Cath. 12, 22.
sirius.short: Sīrĭus, ii, m., = σείριος, the dog-star, Sirius, Hyg.

sirmio.full: Sirmio, ōnis, m., a peninsula on the shores of the Lacus Benacus, in Upper Italy, now Sermione, Cat. 32, 1.
sirmio.short: Sirmio, ōnis, m., a peninsula on the shores of the Lacus Benacus, in Upper Italy, now Sermione, Cat.

sirmium.full: Sirmium, ii, n., an important city of Pannonia Inferior, now Mitrovitz, Sid. Pan. 774; Aus. Ep. 26, 1.
sirmium.short: Sirmium, ii, n., an important city of Pannonia Inferior, now Mitrovitz, Sid.

siromastes.full: sīromastes, ae, m., = σειρομάστης, a pit-searcher, an instrument used by taxgatherers in probing corn-pits, etc. (late Lat.), Hier. Ep. 109, 3; 147, 9.
siromastes.short: sīromastes, ae, m., = σειρομάστης, a pit-searcher, an instrument used by taxgatherers in probing corn-pits, etc.

sirona.full: Sĭrōna, ae, f., name of a goddess among the Gauls, coupled with APOLLO, Inscr. Orell. 2001; 2047 sq.
sirona.short: Sĭrōna, ae, f., name of a goddess among the Gauls, coupled with APOLLO, Inscr.

sirpe.full: sirpe, is, n. σίλφιον, a plant, called also silphium and laser, asafœtida, Plaut. Rud. 3, 2, 16; Sol. 27, § 48.

sirpicus.full: sirpĭcus, a, um, adj. sirpe, of or belonging to the plant sirpe: lac, Sol. 27, § 49.

sirus.full: sīrus, i, m., = σιρός, a pit to keep corn in, an underground granary (cf. cumera), Plin. 18, 30, 73, § 306; Col. 1, 6, 15; Curt. 7, 4, 24; cf. Auct. B. Afr. 65; Vitr. 6, 8 (Varr. R. R. 1, 57 and 63, written as Greek).
sirus.short: sīrus, i, m., = σιρός, a pit to keep corn in, an underground granary (cf.

sis.full: sīs. Subj. of sum.— Contr. from si vis; v. volo init.— I. q. suis, v. suus init.

sisapo.full: Sisăpo, ōnis, f., a small town in Hispania Baetica, rich in mines of cinnabar, now Almaden in the Sierra Morena, Plin. 3, 1, 3, § 14; Cic. Phil. 2, 19, 48.—Hence, Sisăpōnensis, e, adj., of or belonging to Sisapo, Sisaponian: regio, Plin. 33, 7, 40, § 121: minarii, id. 33, 7, 40, § 121.
sisapo.short: Sisăpo, ōnis, f., a small town in Hispania Baetica, rich in mines of cinnabar, now Almaden in the Sierra Morena, Plin.

sisara.full: sisăra, ae, f., a name among the Eubœans for the plant erice, heath, sweetbroom, Plin. 11, 16, 15, § 42; Varr. R. R. 3, 16. 26.
sisara.short: sisăra, ae, f., a name among the Eubœans for the plant erice, heath, sweetbroom, Plin.

siscia.full: Siscia, ae, f., a city of Pannonia, now Siszek, Vell. 2, 113; Plin. 3, 25, 28, § 147; Prud. στεφ. 7, 3.
siscia.short: Siscia, ae, f., a city of Pannonia, now Siszek, Vell.

sisenna.full: Sīsenna, ae, m., a Roman surname. L. Cornehus, a celebrated Roman historian, born about A.U.C. 635, author of a Roman history (Historiae). He preceded Sallust, who took him as a model, Cic. Brut. 64, 228; id. Leg. 1, 2, 7; Sall. J. 95, 2; Ov. Tr. 2, 443; v. the fragments, Krause, Vit. et Fragm. Hist. Rom. p. 303 sq.— The name of a notorious slanderer in Rome, Hor. S. 1, 7, 8.
sisenna.short: Sīsenna, ae, m., a Roman surname.

siser.full: sĭser, ĕris, n. (masc. in plur. siseres, Plin. 20, 5, 17, § 35) [σίσαρον], a plant with an esculent root, skirwort or skirret: Sium sisarum, Linn.; Plin. 19, 5, 28, § 90; 20, 5, 17, § 35; Col. 11, 3, 18; 11, 3, 35; 12, 58, 3; 10, 114.

sisichthon.full: Sīsichthon, ŏnis, m., = Σεισίχθων, Earth-shaker, an epithet of Neptune, Amm. 17, 7, 12.
sisichthon.short: Sīsichthon, ŏnis, m., = Σεισίχθων, Earth-shaker, an epithet of Neptune, Amm.

sison agrion.full: sison agrion, i, n., a plant, also called peucedanos and pinastellus, App. Herb. 94.
sison agrion.short: sison agrion, i, n., a plant, also called peucedanos and pinastellus, App.

sisto.full: sisto, stĭti (Charis. p. 220, and Diom. p. 369, give steti for both sisto and sto, confining stiti to the compounds of both. But steti, as perfect of sisto, is late jurid. Lat., and perh. dub.; for steterant, Verg. A. 3, 110; steterint, id. ib. 3, 403; Liv. 8, 32, 12, belong to stare; cf. also Gell. 2, 14, 1 sqq.; and v. Neue, Formenl. 2, 461 sq.), stătum [root stă, strengthened by reduplication; cf. ἵστημι], used in two general senses, I. To cause to stand, place, = colloco, pono; II. To stand,

sistratus.full: sistrātus, a, um, adj. sistrum, having or bearing a sistrum: turba, i. e. priests of Isis, Mart. 12, 29, 19.

sistrum.full: sīstrum, i, n., = σεῖστρον, a metallic rattle which was used by the Egyptians in celebrating the rites of Isis, and in other lascivious festivals, Ov. Am. 2, 13, 11; id. P. 1, 1, 38; id. M. 9, 692; 9, 777; 9, 783; id. A. A. 3, 635; Mart. 14, 54, 2; Juv. 13, 93; Stat. S. 3, 2, 102; App. M. 2, p. 127; 11, p. 258; 11, p. 261 al.—By the Jews, Vulg. 1 Reg. 18, 6.—Hence sarcastically, as if used for a war - trumpet by the wanton Cleopatra, Verg. A. 8, 696; Prop. 3, 11 (4, 10), 43; Luc. 10, 63; Isid. O
sistrum.short: sīstrum, i, n., = σεῖστρον, a metallic rattle which was used by the Egyptians in celebrating the rites of Isis, and in other lascivious festivals, Ov.

sisura.full: sĭsura or sĭsurna, ae, f., = σίσυρα, σίσυρνα, a shaggy outer garment, a coverlet of skins, Plaut. Pers. 1, 3, 17; Amm. 16, 5, 5.
sisura.short: sĭsura or sĭsurna, ae, f., = σίσυρα, σίσυρνα, a shaggy outer garment, a coverlet of skins, Plaut.

sisygambis.full: Sisygambis, is, f., a Persian female name; esp., the mother of Darius, Curt. 3, 3, 22; 5, 2, 18.
sisygambis.short: Sisygambis, is, f., a Persian female name;

sisymbrium.full: sĭsymbrĭum, ii, n., = σισύμβριον, a fragrant herb sacred to Venus, perh. wildthyme or mint, Plin. 20, 22, 91, § 247; 19, 8, 55, § 172; 19, 10, 57, § 176; Ov. F. 4, 869.
sisymbrium.short: sĭsymbrĭum, ii, n., = σισύμβριον, a fragrant herb sacred to Venus, perh.

sisyphus.full: Sīsўphus (anciently Sīsŭpus and Sīsĭpus; the last in Inscr. R. N. 4472 Momms.; cf. Ritschl, Monum. Epigr. Tria, p. 26), i, m., = Σίσυφος. Son of Æolus, king of Corinth, famous for his cunning and robberies. He was killed by Theseus. His punishment in the infernal regions was to roll a stone up hill which constantly rolled back again, Hyg. Fab. 60; Serv. Verg. A. 6, 616; Poët. ap. Cic. Tusc. 1, 5, 10; Ov. M. 4, 459; 4, 465; 13, 26; Prop. 4 (5), 11, 23; Hor. C. 2, 14, 20; id. Epod. 17, 68 al.: Uli

sisyrinchion.full: sisyrinchĭon, ii, n., = σισυρίγχιον, a kind of bulbous plant, Plin. 19, 5, 30, § 95.
sisyrinchion.short: sisyrinchĭon, ii, n., = σισυρίγχιον, a kind of bulbous plant, Plin.

sisyrus.full: sisyrus, i, m., a plant, also called erice, Plin. 11, 16, 15, § 42.
sisyrus.short: sisyrus, i, m., a plant, also called erice, Plin.

sitanius.full: sītănĭus, a, um, adj., = σητάνιος, of this year, this year's: panis, of summer wheat, Plin. 22, 25, 68, § 139.
sitanius.short: sītănĭus, a, um, adj., = σητάνιος, of this year, this year's: panis, of summer wheat, Plin.

sitarchia.full: sītarchĭa, ae, f., = σιταρχία. Provisions for a journey, App. M. 2, p. 119, 29; Hier. Comment. in Matt. med.; Vit. Malch. 10; Schol. Juv. 12, 61.— Meton., a receptacle for such provisions, a scrip, Vulg. 1 Reg. 9, 7; Isid. 20, 9, 6.

sitella.full: sĭtella, ae, f. dim. situla, a kind of urn used in drawing lots. It was made narrow at the top, so that but one lot at a time could be on the surface of the water with which it was partly filled, Plaut. Cas. 2, 4, 17; 2, 5, 34; 2, 5, 43; 2, 6, 11; 2, 6, 44: sitellam detulit, Auct. Her. 1, 12, 21: de M. Octavio deferre sitellam, Cic. N. D. 1, 38, 106: sitella lata est, ut sortirentur, Liv. 25, 3, 16 Weissenb. ad loc.; 41, 18, 8.

sitellitergus.full: Sĭtellĭtergus, i, m. situla-tergo, the cleaner of buckets, the title of a comedy by Plautus, Varr. L. L. 7, § 66 Müll. N. cr.; cf. Ritschl, Parerga Plaut. p. 15; corrupted into Silitergo, Fest. p. 375 Müll.; and (from the writing siti litergus) into Lipargus ap. Prisc. p. 893 P.; cf. Freund, Rhein. Mus. Neue Folge 10, p. 445 sq.

sithone.full: Sīthōnē, ēs, f., a city of Macedonia, Plin. 4, 10, 17, § 38.
sithone.short: Sīthōnē, ēs, f., a city of Macedonia, Plin.

sithonii.full: Sīthŏnĭi, ōrum, m., = Σιθόνιοι, a Thracian people; hence, poet., in gen., the Thracians, Plin. 4, 11, 18, § 41; Hor. C. 1, 18. 9.—Hence, Sīthŏnĭus, a, um, adj., Sithonian, Thracian: agri, Ov. M. 13, 571: nives, Verg. E. 10, 66; Hor. C. 3, 26, 10: Aquilo, Ov. H. 11, 13: nurus, id. M. 6, 588: rex, id. P. 4, 7, 25.— Sīthon, ŏnis, adj., Sithonian, Thracian: Sithones et Scythici triumphi, Ov. F. 3, 719.— Sī-thŏnis, ĭdis, adj. f., Sithonian, Thracian: unda, Ov. H. 2, 6.—Subst., a Thracian woman, Ov. R
sithonii.short: Sīthŏnĭi, ōrum, m., = Σιθόνιοι, a Thracian people;

sitibundus.full: sĭtĭbundus, a, um, adj., thirsty (late Lat.), Ven. Fort. Vit. Rhadeg. 21.
sitibundus.short: sĭtĭbundus, a, um, adj., thirsty (late Lat.), Ven.

siticines.full: sĭtĭcĭnes, um, m. 1. situs-cano, musicians at funerals, Cato ap. Gell. 20, 2; Non. 54, 26 sq.

siticulosus.full: sĭtīcŭlōsus, a, um, adj. sitis (not ante-Aug.). Thirsty. Lit.: quidam, Sid. Ep. 2, 2 med.: corvus, Auct. Priap. 61, 12.— Transf., of things, very dry, parched, arid: Appulia, Hor. Epod. 3, 16: siticulosum et peraridum solum, Col. 3, 11 fin.; Pall. Jan. 13, 4: calx, Vitr. 7, 2: aestas, Auct. Priap. 64, 3.— Act., producing thirst: melimela, Plin. 23, 6, 55, § 104.

sitiens.full: sĭtĭens, entis, Part. and P. a., v. sitio.

sitienter.full: sĭtĭenter, adv., v. sitio, P. a. fin.

sitio.full: sĭtĭo, īvi or ĭi, 4, v. n. and a. [sitis]. Neutr., to thirst, be thirsty (class.). Lit.: ego esurio et sitio, Plaut. Cas. 3, 6, 6; 4, 3, 4: sitit haec anus, id. Curc. 1, 2, 14: in medio sitit flumine potans, Lucr. 4, 1100: ne homines sitirent, Suet. Aug. 42.—With gen.: cochleae cum sitiunt aëris, Symm. Ep. 1, 27.—Prov.: sitire mediis in undis, i. e. to be poor in the midst of wealth, Ov. M. 9, 760.— Transf. (esp. in the lang. of country people), of things (the earth, plants, etc.), to be dried u

sitiogagus.full: Sitiogagus, i, m., a river of Asia, Plin. 6, 23, 26, § 99.
sitiogagus.short: Sitiogagus, i, m., a river of Asia, Plin.

sitis.full: sĭtis, is (abl. site, Ven. Carm. 2, 13, 3; acc. sitem, Prud. στεφ. 2, 250), f. etym. dub.; perh. akin with siccus, thirst (class.; used only in sing.). Lit.: demum fodere puteum, ubi sitis fauces tenet, Plaut. Most. 2, 1, 33; cf.: tibi cum fauces urit sitis, Hor. S. 1, 2, 114: siti sicca sum, Plaut. Curc. 1, 2, 26: anum interfecero siti fameque atque algu, id. Most. 1, 3, 36; id. Rud. 2, 2, 7; cf.: cum cibo et potione fames sitisque depulsa est, Cic. Fin. 1, 11, 37: explere diuturnam sitim, id.

sitistus.full: sītistus, a, um, adj., = σιτιστός, fed, fattened (pure Lat. altilis), Plin. 29, 3, 11, § 45.
sitistus.short: sītistus, a, um, adj., = σιτιστός, fed, fattened (pure Lat.

sitites.full: sītītes, ae, m., = σιτίτης, a kind of precious stone, Plin. 37, 7, 25, § 43 (Jahn, syrtites).
sitites.short: sītītes, ae, m., = σιτίτης, a kind of precious stone, Plin.

sititor.full: sĭtītor, ōris, m. sitio, a thirster after any thing (post-Aug.). * Lit.: aquae, Mart. 12, 3, 12.— Trop.: sanguinis, Mart. Cap. 1, § 82: novitatis, App. M. 1, p. 103, 17.

sitona.full: sītōna, ae, m., = σιτώνης, a purchaser of grain, a commissary, purveyor, Dig. 50, 8, 9, § 6.
sitona.short: sītōna, ae, m., = σιτώνης, a purchaser of grain, a commissary, purveyor, Dig.

sitones.full: Sitones, um, m., a people of northern Germany, in the neighborhood of the Suiones, Tac. G. 45 fin.
sitones.short: Sitones, um, m., a people of northern Germany, in the neighborhood of the Suiones, Tac.

sitonia.full: sītōnĭa, ae, f., = σιτωνία, the office of a sitona, commissariat, purveyance, Dig. 50, 5, 2 init.
sitonia.short: sītōnĭa, ae, f., = σιτωνία, the office of a sitona, commissariat, purveyance, Dig.

sittace.full: sittăcē, ēs, f. Indian, a parrot, Plin. 10, 42, 58, § 117 dub. (Jan. septages).

sittius.full: Sittĭus, a, the name of a Roman gens, e. g. P Sittius, a friend of Cicero, Cic. Sull. 56; Sall. C. 21, 3; Auct. B. Afr. 25; 30. To him is addressed the letter, Cic. Fam. 5, 17; cf. id. ib. 15, 17, 1.—Hence, Sittĭānus, a, um, adj., of Sittius: syngrapha, Cic. Fam. 8, 2, 2; 8, 4, 5: negotium, id. ib. 8, 11, 4.— After him was named Sittianorum colonia = Cirta, Mel. 1, 6, 1; Plin. 5, 2, 3, § 22.
sittius.short: Sittĭus, a, the name of a Roman gens, e.

sittybus.full: sittўbus, i, m., a strip of parchment, attached to a roll or book, bearing the title and the author's name, Cic. Att. 4, 5, 3; 4, 8, a, 2 B. and K. (in some editions sillybus; cf. σιλλύβους, id. ib. 4, 4, b, 1).
sittybus.short: sittўbus, i, m., a strip of parchment, attached to a roll or book, bearing the title and the author's name, Cic.

situatus.full: sĭtŭātus, a, um, adj., situated (late Lat.), Ps.-Aug. ad Fr. Erem. Serm. 37.
situatus.short: sĭtŭātus, a, um, adj., situated (late Lat.), Ps.-Aug.

situla.full: sĭtŭla, ae, f. (masc. collat. form sĭtŭ-lus, Cato, R. R. 10, 2; 11, 3; Vitr. 10, 9 fin.; Fest. s. v. nanum, pp. 176 and 177 Müll.; Paul. Sent. 3, 7 fin.). A bucket for drawing water, Plaut. Am. 2, 2, 39; Dig. 18, 1, 40 fin.; Poët. ap. Anthol. Burm. 1, p. 493; Non. s. v. creterra, p. 375, 6 Gerl.; cf. Becker, Gallus, 2, p. 268 (2d edit.).— An urn, used in drawing lots (instead of the usual sitella), Plaut. Cas. 2, 6, 7.

situs1.full: sĭtus, a, um, Part. and P. a. of sino.

situs2.full: sĭtus, ūs, m. sino. (Sino, 1. situs, A.; prop. a being laid or placed, a lying; hence, by meton.) The manner of lying, the situation, local position, site of a thing (class. in sing. and plur.; mostly of localities; syn. positus). Sing.: terrae, Cic. Tusc. 1, 20, 45: urbem Syracusas elegerat, cujus hic situs esse dicitur, Cic. Verr. 2, 5, 10, § 26: loci, id. Ac. 2, 19, 61: urbis, id. Rep. 2, 11, 22; Caes. B. G. 7, 68; 7, 36; Liv. 9, 24, 2: locorum, Curt. 3, 4, 11; 7, 6, 12: Messana, quae situ mo

sive.full: sīve (old orthog. SEIVE, Tab. Bantin. l. 6; and hence, by apocope, like neu, from neve, NEIVE). seu (the latter form very rare in Cic.; more freq. in Cæs.; as freq. as sive in the poets), conj. [si-ve], a disjunctive conditional particle, or if = vel si. Put once, preserving the conditional signif. of the si (cf., on the other hand, infra, II. B. 2.). After a preceding si (mostly ante-class.): si vivimus sive morimur, Enn. ap. Prisc. p. 880 P. (Ann. v. 384 Vahl.): si media nox est, sive est prim

smaragdinus.full: smăragdĭnus (zmăr-; smar- with long a, Prud. Psych. 862), a, um, adj., = σμαράγδινος, of or belonging to the emerald, smaragdine: emplastrum (on account of its green color), Cels. 5, 19, 4; cf. prata, Prud. l. l.: lapis, Vulg. Esth. 1, 6.—Postclass. collat. form smăragdĭnĕus, a, um, adj.: viriditas, Mart. Cap. 1, § 66: postis, Ven. Carm. 8, 8, 18.

smaragdites.full: Smăragdītes (Zmăr-), ae, m. (sc. mons), a mountain on which the smaragdus was found, Plin. 37, 5, 18, § 74.

smaragdus.full: smăragdus (in many MSS. written also zmăr-: smărăgdus, Mart. 5, 11, 1), i, comm. (m., Plin. 37, 5, 16, § 62; Luc. 10, 121; f., Mart. 4, 28, 4; Claud. VI. Cons. Hon. 563), = σμάραγδός, a transparent precious stone of a bright green color; including not only our emerald, but also the beryl, jasper, malachite, etc., Plin. 37, 5, 16, § 62; 37, 5, 18, § 73; Lucr. 2, 805; 4, 1126; Tib. 1, 1, 51; 2, 4, 27; Ov. M. 2, 24; Stat. Th. 2, 276 al.

smaris.full: smăris (zmăris), ĭdis, f., = σμαρίς, a small sea-fish of inferior quality, Ov. Hal. 120; Plin. 32, 9, 34, § 106; 32, 10, 45, § 128; 32, 11, 53, § 151.
smaris.short: smăris (zmăris), ĭdis, f., = σμαρίς, a small sea-fish of inferior quality, Ov.

smecticus.full: smectĭcus, a, um, adj., = σμηκτικός, cleansing, abstersive: vis, Plin. 30, 4, 10, § 29.
smecticus.short: smectĭcus, a, um, adj., = σμηκτικός, cleansing, abstersive: vis, Plin.

smegma.full: smegma (smigma and zmeg-ma), ătis (dat. plur. smegmatis, Plin. 31, 7, 42, § 92), n., = σμῆγμα, a cleansing medicine, a detergent, Plin. 22, 25, 74, § 156; 34, 13, 36, § 134.—For making the skin smooth, Plin. 24, 7, 28, § 43; cf. Becker, Gallus, 3, p. 64 (2d edit.): afferte mihi smigmata, Vulg. Dan. 13, 17.

smerdaleos.full: smerdălĕos, a, um, adj., = σμερδαλέος, terrible, Auct. Priap. 69 sq.
smerdaleos.short: smerdălĕos, a, um, adj., = σμερδαλέος, terrible, Auct.

smerdis.full: Smerdis, is, m. A brother of Cambyses, king of Persia, by whom he was put to death, Just. 1, 9, 4.— An impostor named Oropastes, who assumed the name of Smerdis after the death of Cambyses, Just. 1, 9, §§ 9, 10.

smila.full: smīla, ae, f., = σμίλη, a knife (syn. scalprum), Arn. 5, 172 Orell. N. cr.
smila.short: smīla, ae, f., = σμίλη, a knife (syn.

smilax.full: smīlax, ăcis, f., = σμῖλαξ. Bindweed, withwind, rough smilax: Smilax aspera, Linn.; Plin. 16, 35, 63, § 153; 24, 10, 49, § 82.—Hence Smilax personified, a maiden who was changed into this herb, Ov. M. 4, 283.— The yew-tree, Plin. 16, 10, 20, § 51. — A kind of oak, Plin. 16, 6, 8, § 19.

smilion.full: smīlĭon, ii, n., = σμιλίον, a kind of medicinal salve, Marc. Emp. 35 fin.
smilion.short: smīlĭon, ii, n., = σμιλίον, a kind of medicinal salve, Marc.

smintheus.full: Smintheus or Zmin- (dissyl.), ĕi, m., = Σμινθεύς, an epithet of Apollo (from the Cretan σμίνθος, mouse, i. e. the mousekiller; or, as Aristarchus asserts, from Smintha (Σμίνθη), a town in the Troad, the Sminthean, Lact. 1, 7, 9; Ov. F. 6, 425; acc. Sminthea, id. M. 12, 585.—Hence, Sminthēus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Smintheus: spolia, i. e. Astynome, daughter of Chryses, priest of Apollo, Sen. Agam. 176.— Sminthius (Zmin-), a, um, adj., of Smintheus: mures (acc. to the myth, killed by Apo
smintheus.short: Smintheus or Zmin- (dissyl.), ĕi, m., = Σμινθεύς, an epithet of Apollo (from the Cretan σμίνθος, mouse, i.

smyrna1.full: smyrna, ae, f., = σμύρνα, myrrh, Lucr. 2, 504; Dig. 39, 4, 16, § 7.
smyrna1.short: smyrna, ae, f., = σμύρνα, myrrh, Lucr.

smyrna2.full: Smyrna (in the best MSS. Zmyr-na), ae, f., = Σμύρνα, a celebrated maritime city of Ionia; according to some, the birthplace of Homer, still called Smyrna, Cic. Fl. 29, 71; id. Agr. 2, 15, 39; id. Att. 9, 9, 2; Liv. 33, 36; 37, 35; Stat. S. 4, 2, 9 al.— Hence, Smyrnaeus (Zmyr-), a, um, adj., of or belonging to Smyrna, Smyrnean: sinus, Mel. 1, 17, 3: conventus, Plin. 5, 29, 31, § 120: vates, i. e. Homer, Luc. 9, 984; cf. of the same, plectra, Sil. 8, 595; and, tubae, Sid. Carm. 23, 131.—Plur. subs

smyrnion.full: smyrnĭon or zmyrnĭum, ii, n., = σμυρνίον, a kind of herb like myrrh, common Alexanders: Smyrnium olus atrum, Linn.; Plin. 27, 13, 109, § 133; 19, 8, 48, § 162.
smyrnion.short: smyrnĭon or zmyrnĭum, ii, n., = σμυρνίον, a kind of herb like myrrh, common Alexanders: Smyrnium olus atrum, Linn.;

smyrrhiza.full: smyrrhīza, ae, f., = σμυρριξα, a plant, called also myrrha and myrrhis, Plin. 24, 16, 97, § 154 (Jahn, myrrhiza).
smyrrhiza.short: smyrrhīza, ae, f., = σμυρριξα, a plant, called also myrrha and myrrhis, Plin.

smyrus.full: smyrus or zmyr-, i, m., = σμῦρος, a kind of fish, otherwise unknown, Plin. 32, 11, 53, § 151.
smyrus.short: smyrus or zmyr-, i, m., = σμῦρος, a kind of fish, otherwise unknown, Plin.

sobriefactus.full: sōbrĭĕfactus, a, um, Part. [sobrius, II., -facio], made reasonable, sobered: sobriefactus sermone, App. M. 8, p. 205, 34.

sobrietas.full: sōbrĭĕtas, ātis, f. sobrius, sobriety (post-Aug.). Lit., temperance in drinking, Sen. Tranq. 15, 16; Val. Max. 6, 3, 9.— Hence Sobrietas personified, the enemy of Venus, App. M. 5, p. 172, 20; Prud. Psych. 450.— In gen., moderation, temperance, continence (cf.: modestas, temperantia): vitae, Dig. 1, 7, 17 fin.; Vulg. 1 Tim. 2, 9.— Trop., reasonableness, prudence: consiliorum, Amm. 31, 10, 19.

sobrinus.full: sōbrīnus, i, m., and sōbrīna, ae, f. contr. for sororinus from soror, and therefore prop. an appellation for the children of sisters; hence, in gen., a cousin-german, cousin by the mother's side, Fest. p. 297 Müll.; Dig. 38, 10, 3; Just. Inst. 3, 6. Masc., Ter. And. 4, 5, 6; id. Phorm. 2, 3, 37; Cic. Off. 1, 17, 54; Dig. 38, 10, 1; 38, 10, 10. — Fem., Plaut. Poen. 5, 2, 108; Tac. A. 12, 6 and 64; Dig. 38, 10, 10.
sobrinus.short: sōbrīnus, i, m., and sōbrīna, ae, f.

sobrio.full: sōbrĭo, āre, v. a. sobrius, to sober, make sober (late Lat.), Paul. Nol. Carm. 21, 685; 24, 106.

sobrius.full: sōbrĭus (sōbrĕus), a, um (comp. sobrior, Laber. ap. Charis. p. 64; elsewhere not compared), adj. cf. Gr. σώφρων, σάος; Lat. sanus, not drunk, sober (freq. and class.). Lit., opp. vinolentus, Cic. Ac. 2, 17, 52; so id. Or. 28, 99; opp. vino madens, Plaut. Truc. 4, 4, 2; opp. madidus, id. Am. 3, 4, 18; cf. Hor. S. 2, 3, 5; Cato Utic. ap. Suet. Caes. 53; and ap. Quint. 8, 2, 9; opp. ebrius, Sen. Ep. 18, 4 (with siccus); Mart. 3, 16, 3; opp. temulentus, Tac. A. 13, 15 et saep.: male sobrius, i. e. e

soccatus.full: soccātus, a, um, adj. soccus, furnished with or wearing socci, Sen. Ben. 2, 12, 2.

soccifer.full: soccĭfer, fĕra, fĕrum, adj. soccus-fero, sock-wearing: Menander, Sid. Carm. 9, 215; v. soccus.

socculus.full: soccŭlus, i, m. dim. soccus, a small soccus, Sen. Ben. 2, 12, 1; Suet. Vit. 2 fin.; Plin. 9, 35, 56, § 114.—Of the sock worn by comic actors (v. soccus, II.), Plin. Ep. 9, 7, 3; Quint. 10, 2, 22.

soccus.full: soccus, i, m. A kind of low-heeled, light shoe, worn by the Greeks; a slipper, sock, Plaut. Trin. 3, 2, 94; id. Ep. 5, 2, 60; id. Bacch. 2, 3, 98; id. Pers. 1, 3, 44; id. Cist. 4, 2, 29: soccos, quibus indutus esset, Cic. de Or. 3, 32, 127; id. Rab. Post. 10, 27; Cat. 61, 10 et saep.—When worn by Romans they were a sign of effeminacy, Suet. Calig. 52; Sen. Ben. 2, 12, 1; Plin. 37, 2, 6, § 17.—The soccus was worn especially by comic actors (the cothurnus, on the contrary, by tragic actors).—Hence

socer.full: sŏcer (nom. socerus, Plaut. Cas. 4, 2, 18; id. Men. 5, 5, 54; with socer, id. ib. 5, 7, 56), ĕri, m. Gr. ἑκυρός. A father-in-law, Plaut. Stich. 4, 1, 22; id. Trin. 5, 2, 27; Cic. Off. 1, 35, 129; id. Lael. 1, 1 and 5; Caes. B. G. 1, 12 fin.; Ov. M. 1, 145; Hor. C. 3, 11, 39; id. Ep. 1, 19, 30 al.; v. also socrus.—Plur. soceri, parents-in-law, Verg. A. 2, 457; 10, 79; Ov. M. 3, 132.— Transf., for consocer, a son's father-in-law, Ter. Hec. 5, 2, 4: magnus, grandfather-in-law, i. e. one's husband's

sociabilis.full: sŏcĭābĭlis, e, adj. socio, that may be easily united or joined together, sociable (not ante-Aug., and very rare): natura nos sociabiles fecit, Sen. Ep. 95, 52: consortio inter reges, Liv. 40, 8: abies maxime sociabilis glutino, Plin. 16, 42, 82, § 225.—Hence, adv.: sŏcĭābĭlĭter, connectedly, Aug. Mus. 5, 15.

socialis.full: sŏcĭālis, e, adj. socius, of or belonging to companionship. In gen., companionable, sociable, social (so not ante-Aug.): homo sociale animal, Sen. Ben. 7, 1, 8: beneficium dare socialis res est, id. ib. 5, 11, 4: amicitiae, App. M. 5, p. 171, 20.— In partic. Of or belonging to allies or confederates, allied, confederate (the class. signif. of the word): lex, Cic. Div. in Caecil. 5, 18: lex judiciumque, Cic. Verr. 2, 2, 6, § 15: foedus, Liv. 34, 57: exercitus, i. e. of the allies, id. 31, 21: coe

socialitas.full: sŏcĭālĭtas, ātis, f. socialis, fellowship, sociableness, sociality (very rare), Plin. Pan. 49, 4.

sociatio.full: sŏcĭātĭo, ōnis, f. socio, union: rata inter eos (post-class.), Mart. Cap. 2, § 109.

sociatrix.full: sŏcĭātrix, īcis, f. id., she who associates or unites, Val. Fl. 5, 500.

sociennus.full: sŏcĭennus, i, m. socius, a fellow, comrade: tuos, Plaut. Aul. 4, 4, 32.

societas.full: sŏcĭĕtas, ātis, f. id., fellowship, association, union, community, society (implying union for a common purpose; cf.: conjunctio, consociatio; and not a mere assembly; cf.: circulus, coetus; conventus, sodalitas; freq. and class.). In gen.: hominum inter ipsos societas conjunctioque, Cic. Leg. 1, 10, 28: (nos) natos esse ad societatem communitatemque generis humani, id. Fin. 4, 2, 4: societas generis humani, quam conciliavit ipsa natura, id. Lael. 5, 20: fides et societas generis humani, id. N.

socio.full: sŏcĭo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. id., to join or unite together, to associate; to do or hold in common, to share a thing with another, etc. (freq. and class.; in Cic. mostly with inanimate objects; syn. jungo): coetus utilitatis communione sociatus, Cic. Rep. 1, 25, 39: concilia coetusque hominum jure sociati, id. ib. 6, 13, 13: omne genus hominum sociatum inter se esse, id. Leg. 1, 11, 32: (Romulus) regnum suum cum illorum (Sabinorum) rege sociavit, id. Rep. 2, 7, 13; cf.: quae nos domo socias, Verg.

sociofraudus.full: sŏcĭŏfraudus, i, m. socius-fraudo, one that deceives his comrades, Plaut. Ps. 1, 3, 128.

socius.full: sŏcĭus, a, um, adj. root sec- of sequor, sharing, joining in, partaking, united, associated, kindred, allied, fellow (mostly poet. and in post-Aug. prose; cf. subst. infra): hic (Augustus) socium cum Jove nomen habet, Ov. F. 1, 608: aurea possedit socio Capitolia templo Mater, i. e. in common with Jupiter, id. ib. 6, 73: regnum, id. M. 5, 378: classis, id. ib. 13, 352: sepulcrum, id. H. 11, 123: lectus, id. A. A. 2, 377: ignes, id. M. 9, 795: anni, id. H. 2, 33: linguae, id. Tr. 5, 10, 35: dei,

socordia.full: sōcordĭa (o short, Prud. Apoth. 194; cf. socors; sometimes, on account of the etymology, written also sēcordĭa), ae, f. socors, dulness of mind, i. e., Weakmindedness, silliness, folly, stupidity (very rare; syn.: insipientia, stoliditas): socordiam quidam pro ignaviā posuerunt (v. II.); Cato pro stultitiā posuit, Fest. pp. 292 and 293 Müll.: si quem socordiae argueret, stultiorem aiebat filio suo Claudio, Suet. Claud. 3; Tac. A. 4, 35.— Carelessness, negligence, sloth, laziness, indolence, inac

socors.full: sōcors (o short, Prud. Cath. 1, 33; cf. socordia), cordis, adj. se, = sine, and cor(d)s, mentally dull, i. e., Narrow-minded, silly, foolish, blockish, stupid, thoughtless, senseless, etc. (rare but class.; syn.: stultus, stolidus, ineptus, insipiens, insulsus): socors naturā neglegensque, Cic. Brut. 68, 239: homines non socordes ad veri investigandi cupiditatem excitare, id. N. D. 1, 2, 4: stolidi ac socordes, Liv. 9, 34: socors ingenium, Tac. A. 13, 47: animus, id. H. 3, 36: Tiberius callidior

socrates.full: Sōcrătes, is, m., = Σωκράτης. The celebrated Greek philosopher: parens philosophiae, Cic. Fin. 2, 1, 1: fons et caput philosophiae, id. de Or. 1, 10, 42: ab Apolline omnium sapientissimus dictus, id. Ac. 1, 4, 16; Plaut. Ps. 1, 5, 50.—Voc. Socrate, bis, Cic. Fragm. p. 477 Orell.—As an appellative, in the plur.: ut exsistant ... Socratae simul et Antisthenae et Platones multi, Gell. 14, 1, 29; cf. Lachm. ad Lucr. 2, p. 50. —Hence, Sōcrătĭcus, a, um, adj., = Σωκρατικός, of or belonging to Socrates

socrualis.full: socrŭālis, e, adj. socrus, of or belonging to a mother-in-law: munificentia, Sid. Ep. 7, 2 med.: hereditas, id. ib. 8, 9.

socrus.full: socrus, ūs (orig. comm.; v. infra), f. a collat. form of socer; Gr.ἑκυρός, orig.also m., either a father-in-law or a mother-in-law; but of the first signif. we have only two examples in ancient poets: praemia erepta a socru suo, Att. ap. Prisc. p. 698 P. (Trag. Rel. p. 136 Rib.); and: a socru, Oenomao rege, Poët. ap. Cic. Tusc. 3, 12, 26 (Rib. l. l. p. 213).—The signif. mother-in-law was the prevailing one through all periods of the language: uno animo omnes socrus oderunt nurus, Ter. Hec. 2, 1,

sodaliciarius.full: sŏdālĭcĭārĭus (sŏdālĭt-), a, um, adj. sodalicium, of or belonging to an associalion or fellowship, only as subst. sŏdālĭcĭārĭus, ii, m., one who is bound to another by fellowship, a comrade, bosomfriend, Inscr. Orell. 4794.— sŏdālĭcĭ-ārĭa, ae, f.: SODALICIARIA CONSILII BONI, a companion, Inscr. Orell. 4644.

sodalicium.full: sŏdālĭcĭum (-tĭum), ii, v. the foll. art., II.

sodalicius.full: sŏdālĭcĭus (-tĭus), a, um, adj. sodalis. Of or belonging to a sodalis; of or belonging to fellowship or companionship (as adj. very rare): jure sodalicio mihi junctus, Ov. Tr. 4, 10, 46 (al. sodalicii); Just. 20, 4, 14: Druidae sodaliciis astricti consortiis, Amm. 15, 9, 8.— In a bad sense, secret: collegia sodalicia, pertaining to an unlawful secret association, Dig. 47, 22, 1.— Subst.: sŏdālĭcĭum (-tĭum), ii, n. Lit., a fellowship, friendly intercourse or intimacy, brotherhood, companionship,

sodalis.full: sŏdālis, is (abl., regularly, sodali; sodale, Mart. 1, 86, 5; Plin. Ep. 2, 13, 6), comm. cf. Sanscr. svadhā, will, power; Gr. ἔθος, custom; v. Georg Curtius Gr. Etym. p. 251. In gen., a mate, fellow, intimate, comrade, crony, boon-companion, etc. (freq.and class.; a favorite word with Plautus; cf.: socius, familiaris): tuos amicus et sodalis, Plaut. Merc. 2, 4, 7: hic sodalis tuos amicus optimus, id. Cas. 3, 3, 18; so (with amicus) id. Bacch. 3, 3, 71: sodalem me esse scis gnato tuo, id. Most. 5

sodalitas.full: sŏdālĭtas, ātis, f. sodalis. Lit., fellowship, companionship, brotherhood, friendship, intimacy; abstr. and concr. (class.; cf. societas): sodalitas familiaritasque, Cic. Verr. 2, 1, 37, § 94: summā nobilitate homo, cognatione, sodalitate, collegio, id. Brut. 45, 166: intima sodalitas, Tac. A. 15, 68.—Concr.: nunc ego de sodalitate solus sum orator datus, Plaut. Most. 5, 2, 5. —Plur.: aliquem a sodalitatibus abducere, Gell. 20, 4, 3.— Transf. A society, association of any kind, esp. for religiou

sodalitium.full: sŏdālĭtĭum and sŏdālĭtĭus, a, um, v. sodalicius.
sodalitium.short: sŏdālĭtĭum and sŏdālĭtĭus, a, um, v.

sodanus.full: Sodanus, i, m., a river of Gedrosia, Plin. 6, 23, 25, § 94.
sodanus.short: Sodanus, i, m., a river of Gedrosia, Plin.

sodes.full: sōdes contr. from si audes, for audies, Cic. Or. 45, 154; cf.: dic mihi si audes, quis ea est, etc., Plaut. Fragm. ap. Prisc. p. 960; in colloq. lang. (esp. freq. with an imper.), if you will, if you please, with your leave, prithee, pray. With imper.: dic sodes mihi, Bellan' videtur specie mulier? Plaut. Bacch. 4, 7, 39; so, dic sodes (mihi), id. Trin. 2, 4, 161; Ter. And. 1, 1, 58; id. Heaut. 4, 5, 22; id. Ad. 4, 5, 9; Hor. Ep. 1, 1, 62; 1, 16, 31: emitte sodes, ne enices fame, sine ire pastum

sodii.full: Sodii, ōrum, m., an Iberian people in Asia, Plin. 6, 10, 11, § 29.
sodii.short: Sodii, ōrum, m., an Iberian people in Asia, Plin.

sodoma.full: Sŏdŏma, ōrum, n., = Σόδομα (Heb. ), the city of Sodom in Palestine, Tert. Apol. 40; Vulg. Gen. 14, 2.—Called also Sŏdŏma, ae, f., Sulp. Sev. Hist. Sacr. 1, 6; Sedul. 1, 105; Vulg. Gen. 10, 19; also Sŏdŏmum, i, n., Sol. 35; and Sŏdŏmi, ōrum, m., Tert. Carm. Sodom. 127 and 163. —Hence, Sŏdŏmītae, ārum, m., = Σοδομῖται, the inhabitants of Sodom, the Sodomites, Prud. Apoth. 384.—In the sing., adject.: Sodomita libido, of Sodom, Prud. Psych. 42; so, cinis, id. στεφ. 5, 195.— Sŏdŏmītĭcus, a, um, adj.,

sogdiana.full: Sogdĭāna rĕgĭo, a district in Asia between the Jaxartes and the Oxus, Curt. 7, 10, 1 sqq.—Hence, Sogdĭāni, ōrum, m., the inhabitants of Sogdiana, Curt. 7, 4, 5; 9, 2, 24; Plin. 6, 16, 18, § 49; called also Sugdĭāni, Mel. 1, 2, 5; 3, 5, 6.
sogdiana.short: Sogdĭāna rĕgĭo, a district in Asia between the Jaxartes and the Oxus, Curt.

sogionti.full: Sogĭonti, ōrum, m., an Alpine people, whose name appeared upon a triumphal arch in honor of Augustus, Plin. 3, 20, 24, § 136.
sogionti.short: Sogĭonti, ōrum, m., an Alpine people, whose name appeared upon a triumphal arch in honor of Augustus, Plin.

sol.full: sōl, sōlis, m. Sanscr. svar, shine; cf. Gr. Σείριος, σείρ, σέλας, Ἑλένη; and Lat. serenus. Sing., the sun, as a heavenly body. In gen.: tempora duorum generum sunt, unum annale, quod sol circuitu suo finit, Varr. R. R. 1, 27: solis cursus lunaeque meatus, Lucr. 5, 77: annum ad cursum solis accommodavit, Suet. Caes. 40: liquidi fons luminis aetherius sol, Lucr. 5, 282: quid potest esse sole majus? Cic. Ac. 2, 26, 82: illud dubium esse nulli potest quin arcus imago solis sit, Sen. Q. N. 1, 3, 11.—

solaciolum.full: sōlācĭŏlum (sōlāt-), i, n. dim. solacium, a little comfort or solace: sui doloris, Cat. 2, 7.

solacium.full: sōlācĭum (sōlāt-), ii, n. solor, a soothing, assuaging; a comfort, relief, consolation, solace (class.; used equally in sing. and plur.): et vigilantibus hinc aderant solacia somni, Lucr. 5, 1405: permulcent animos solacia vitae, id. 5, 21; 6, 4: haec sunt solacia, haec fomenta summorum dolorum, Cic. Tusc. 2, 24, 59: oblectamenta et solacia servitutis, Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 60, § 134: perfugium ac solacium praebere, id. Arch. 7, 16: praebere solacia, Ov. Tr. 4, 10, 117: id solacio est, Plaut. Am. 2,

solago.full: sōlāgo, ĭnis, f. sol, a plant, called also heliotropium, App. Herb. 49 and 63.

solamen.full: sōlāmen, ĭnis solor, a comfort, relief, solace, consolation (poet. for the class. solacium): solamen mali, Verg. A. 3, 661; 10, 493; 10, 859; Luc. 7, 181; Val. Fl. 3, 319; 4, 443; Sen. Med. 539; id. Herc. Fur. 1090.
solamen.short: sōlāmen, ĭnis solor, a comfort, relief, solace, consolation (poet.

solamentum.full: sōlāmentum, i, n. id., a relief, consolation, mitigation (late Lat.), Paul. Nol. Carm. 18, 343.

solanum.full: sōlānum, i, n., a plant, called also strychnos, nightshade, Plin. 27, 13, 108, § 132; Cels. 2, 33; 3, 18; 5, 26.
solanum.short: sōlānum, i, n., a plant, called also strychnos, nightshade, Plin.

solanus.full: Sōlānus, i (sc. ventus), m. sol, the east wind, Vitr. 1, 6 med.; usually called Subsolanus, q. v.

solaris.full: sōlāris, e, adj. id., of or belonging to the sun, sun-, solar (not ante-Aug.): lumen, Ov. Tr. 5, 9, 37: arcus solares lunaresque sunt, Sen. Q. N. 1, 10 fin.: circulus, Plin. 2, 23, 21, § 86: pars piceae, sunny, towards the sun, id. 16, 12, 23, § 57: herba, i.e. a plant, called also heliotropium, Cels. 5, 27, 5.

solarium1.full: sōlārĭum, ii, n. id.. (Sc. horologium, which is expressed in Plin. 7, 60, 60, § 213.) A sundial: solarium dictum id, in quo horae in sole inspiciebantur, etc., Varr. L. L. 6, § 4 Müll.: ut illum Di perdant, primus qui horas repperit, Quique adeo primus statuit hic solarium, Plaut. Fragm. ap. Gell. 3, 3, 5; cf. Becker, Gallus, 2, p. 301 sq. (2d ed.): venter erat solarium, Aquil. ib. 3, 3, 4.— Transf. Ad solarium, a much-frequented place in the Forum where the sundial stood, Cic. Quint. 18, 59; Au

solarium2.full: sŏlārium, ii (sc. vectigal), n. solum, a ground-rent, Dig. 43, 8, 2, § 17; 7, 1, 7, § 2; 13, 7, 17; 30, 1, 39, § 5; Inscr. Orell. 39; cf. Becker, Antiq. 3, 2, p. 121, n. 614.

solarius.full: sōlārĭus, a, um, adj., v. 1. solarium init.

solator.full: sōlātor, ōris, m. solor, a comforter, consoler (poet. and very rare): ipse ego solator, Tib. 1, 3, 15: mitis lugentum, Stat. S. 5, 5, 40.

solatus.full: sōlātus, a, um, adj. sol, sunburned, sunstruck; subst. masc.: solatis, id est sole correptis, prosunt, Plin. 29, 6, 38, § 118; cf. neutr.: solatum, genus morbi maxime a rusticantibus dicitur, cujus meminit etiam Afranius, a sunstroke, Fest. pp. 300 and 301 Müll.

soldurii.full: soldūrĭi, ōrum, m. Celtic, retainers or vassals of a chieftain: devoti, Caes. B. G. 3, 22.

soldus.full: soldus, a, um, v. solidus init.

solea.full: sŏlĕa, ae, f. solum. A slipper consisting of a sole fastened on by a strap across the instep, a sandal: omnia ferme id genus, quibus plantarum calces tantum infimae teguntur, cetera prope nuda et teretibus habenis vincta sunt, soleas dixerunt, nonnumquam voce Graecā crepidulas, Gell. 13, 21, 5 (worn by men in the house only: considered as a mark of effeminacy if worn out of doors): NEIVE QVIS IN POPLICO LVCI PRAETEXTAM NEIVE SOLEAS HABETO, Lex in Marin. Fratr. Arv. p. 569; cf. Hor. S. 1, 3, 128;

solearis.full: sŏlĕāris, e, adj. solea, like a sole or sandal, sandal-shaped: cella, Spart. Car. 9.

solearius.full: sŏlĕārĭus, ii, m. id., a sandal-maker, Plaut. Aul. 3, 5, 40; Inscr. Orell. 4085.

soleatus.full: sŏlĕātus, a, um, adj. id., wearing sandals, having sandals on (if of a man and in public, a mark of effeminacy; v. solea): stetit soleatus praetor populi Romani cum pallio purpureo tunicāque talari, mulierculā nixus, Cic. Verr. 2, 5, 33, § 86; cf. id. Pis. 6, 13; Castric. ap. Gell. 13, 21, 1; Afran. ap. Non. 207, 32; Sen. Ira, 3, 18, 3; Petr. 27, 2; Mart. 12, 83, 6.

solen.full: sōlēn, ēnis, m., = σωλήν, a kind of seamussel, the razor-fish: Solen, Linn.; Plin. 32, 11, 53, § 151; 10, 69, 88, § 192; 11, 37, 52, § 139.
solen.short: sōlēn, ēnis, m., = σωλήν, a kind of seamussel, the razor-fish: Solen, Linn.;

soleo.full: sŏlĕo, ĭtus, 2 (pres. solinunt, for solent, acc. to Fest. s. v. nequinunt, p. 162 Müll.; perf. solui, Cato and Enn. acc. to Varr. L.L. 9, § 107: soluerint, Cael. ap. Non. 509, 2: soluerat, Sall. Fragm. ap. Prisc. p. 872 P.; or H. 2, 55 Dietsch; no fut., v. Neue, Formenl. 2, 591; 609), v. n. cf. suesco. In gen., to use, be wont, be accustomed (cf. assuesco). With inf. (so most freq.); act.: qui mentiri solet, pejerare consuevit, Cic. Rosc. Com. 16, 46: ruri crebro esse soleo, Ter. Hec. 2, 1, 18:

solers.full: sōlers, sōlerter, and sōlertĭa, v. sollers, etc.

soletum.full: Soletum, i, n., a town in Calabria, Plin. 3, 11, 16, § 101.
soletum.short: Soletum, i, n., a town in Calabria, Plin.

soli.full: Sŏli (collat. form Soloe, Mel. 1, 13, 2; Plin. 5, 27, 22, § 92), ōrum, m., = Σόλοι. A town of Cilicia, afterwards called Pompeiopolis, now Mezetli, Cic. Leg. 2, 16, 41; Liv. 33, 20, 4; 37, 56, 8.—Hence, Sŏleus, ei, m., = Σολεύς, of Soli: Milon, Plin. 35, 11, 40, § 146.— A town of Cyprus, now Solia, Plin. 5, 31, 35, § 130 (Jan. Soloe).

soliar.full: sŏlĭar, āris, n. solium, a covering for the feet, Varr. ap. Non. 3, 25; Fest. s. v. solla, pp. 298 and 299 Müll.

solicanus.full: sōlĭcănus, a, um, adj. solus-cano, singing alone: Musae, Mart. Cap. 2, § 127.

solicatio.full: sōlĭcātĭo, ōnis, f. sol, a sunning, a transl. of the Gr. ἡλίωσις (late Lat.), Cael. Aur. Tard. 4, 2, 18.

solicitatio.full: sōlĭcĭtātio, sōlĭcĭto, sōlĭcĭtus, etc., v. soll-.

solidamen.full: sŏlĭdāmen, ĭnis, n. solido, that which makes firm or solid, a strengthener (late Lat.), Ven. Carm. 6, 2, 115.

solidamentum.full: sŏlĭdāmentum, i, n. id., that which makes firm or solid, a strengthener (late Lat.): corporis (ossa), Lact. Opif. Dei, 7 init.

solidatio.full: sŏlĭdātĭo, ōnis, f. id., a making firm or solid; a fastening, strengthening, Vitr. 5, 3, 3; 7, 1, 7.

solidatrix.full: sŏlĭdātrix, īcis, f. solidator, she that makes firm or solid, a strengthener: ossium, Arn. 4, 131.

solidesco.full: sŏlĭdesco, ĕre, v. inch. n. [solidus], to become firm, solid, whole (post - Aug. and very rare): moles sub aquā, Vitr. 2, 6, 1: rupta cartilago, to unite, grow together, Plin. 11, 37, 87, § 216.

solidipes.full: sŏlĭdĭ-pēs, pĕdis, adj. id.; of animals whose feet are not cloven, solid-footed, whole-hoofed, Plin. 10, 65, 84, § 184; 10, 73, 93, § 199; 11, 37, 45, § 128.

soliditas.full: sŏlĭdĭtas, ātis, f. id.. Lit., solidness, solidity (good prose), Cic. Fin. 1, 6, 17; id. N. D. 1, 19, 49; 1, 38, 105; id. Univ. 5, 13; Pall. Mai, 9, 1.— Transf. (post-Aug.). Thickness, Pall. 1, 6, 9; id. Febr. 17, 5. — Solidity, firmness, Vitr. 2, 6; 2, 8.— Hence, plur. concr.: soliditates, firm or solid masses, Vitr. 7, 3, 7.— In jurid. Lat., the whole, entirety (opp. a share, part): possessionis, etc., Cod. Just. 4, 52, 2; 11, 35, 2; App. Trism. p. 288 Bip.: hereditas universorum soliditas sin

solido.full: sŏlĭdo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. id., to make firm, dense, or solid; to make whole or sound; to strengthen, fasten together (not ante-Aug., and for the most part only in the pass.; cf.: compono, reficio, stabilio). Lit.: (area) cretā solidanda, Verg. G. 1, 179: locus fistucationibus solidetur, Vitr. 7, 1: terra aëre, id. 2, 3 fin.: aedificia sine trabibus, Tac. A. 15, 43; cf. muri, id. H. 2, 19: ossa fracta, Plin. 28, 16, 65, § 227; Plin. Ep. 8, 20, 4; cf.: hi (nervi) incisi solidantur, Plin. 11, 37,

solidus.full: sŏlĭdus, a, um (contr. collat. form sol-dus, a, um, Hor. S. 1, 2, 113; 2, 5, 65), adj. Sanscr. sarvas, all; Gr. ὅλος, whole; old Lat. sollus; cf. sollistimus, firm, dense, compact, not hollow, solid (class.). Lit.: individua et solida corpora (sc. ἀτόμοι), Cic. Fin. 1, 6, 18; cf. id. Div. 2, 67, 98: terra solida et globosa, id. N. D. 2, 39, 137: columna aurea (opp. extrinsecus inaurata), id. Div. 1, 24, 48; cf. cornua (opp. cava), Plin. 11, 37, 45, § 127: lapides, Sen. Q. N. 3, 25, 6: corpus, Te

solifer.full: sōlĭfĕr, fĕra, fĕrum, adj. sol-fero, sun-bringing, of the east: plaga, Sen. Herc. Oet. 159.

solifundium.full: sŏlĭfundĭum, ii, n. solum-fundus, perh. landed property, Front. Princ. Hist. Fragm. 7 Mai.

soligena.full: sōlĭgĕna, ae, comm. sol-gigno, a child of the Sun: Aeetes, Val. Fl. 5, 317.

soliloquium.full: sōlĭlŏquĭum, ii, n. solus-loquor, a talking to one's self, a soliloquy, a word formed by Augustin, Aug. Solil. 2, 7 fin.

solino.full: solino = consulo, acc. to Fest. pp. 350 and 351 Müll. [prob. the lengthened form from solo, the ground form to con-sul and con-sulo; different from solinunt-solent; v. soleo init.].

solinus.full: Sōlīnus, i, m. C. Julius, a Roman writer of the third century of the Christian era, author of a work entitled Polyhistor, mostly taken from Pliny's Historia Naturalis.

solipuga.full: sŏlĭpūga, ae, f., a kind of venomous ant (or, acc. to Solinus, a kind of venomous spider), Plin. 29, 4, 29, § 92; 22, 25, 81, § 163. —Called also solpūga, Luc. 9, 837; soli-pugna, acc. to Fest. pp. 300 and 301 Müll.; sŏlĭfūga, Sol. 4, 3 and 6; and salpūga, Plin. 29, 4, 29, § 92.
solipuga.short: sŏlĭpūga, ae, f., a kind of venomous ant (or, acc.

solitaneus1.full: sŏlĭtānĕus, a, um, adj. solitus, from soleo, usual, customary, ordinary: dolores, Marc. Emp 20 med.

solitaneus2.full: sōlĭtānĕus, a, um, adj. solus, separate, distinct: libellum confeci, Theod. Prisc. 3 praef.

solitanus.full: sōlĭtānus, a, um, adj. sol, the appellation of a species of African snail, perh. named from the Promunturium Solis (Plin. 5, 1, 1, § 9); Varr. R. R. 3, 14, 4; Plin. 9, 56, 82, § 174.

solitarius.full: sōlĭtārĭus, a, um, adj. solus, alone, by itself, lonely, solitary (class.; syn. singularis): natura solitarium nihil amat, Cic. Lael. 23, 88: quoniam solitaria non posset virtus ad ea, quae summa sunt, pervenire, conjuncta et consociata cum alterā perveniret, id. ib. 22, 83: quae (natura) non solitaria sit neque simplex, sed cum alio juncta atque conexa, id. N. D. 2, 11, 29: deus desertus ac solitarius, Lact. 1, 7, 4; Min. Fel. 10, 3: hae apes non sunt solitaria natura, ut aquilae, sed ut homine

solitas.full: sōlĭtas, ātis, f. solus, a being alone, loneliness, solitude (ante- and post-class. for solitudo): tuam solitatem memorans, Att. ap. Non. 173, 28 (Trag. Rel. p. 153 Rib.); App. M. 9, p. 225, 14; id. Mag. p. 288, 5; Tert. adv. Val. 37.

solitatim.full: sōlĭtātim, adv. solitas, solitarily, Front. Eloqu. p. 235 Mai.

solito.full: sŏlĭto, āvi, 1, v. freq. n. [soleo], to be much accustomed or wont: Scipionem Africanum solitavisse in Capitolium ventitare, Gell. 7, 1, 6.

solitudo.full: sōlĭtūdo, ĭnis, f. solus, a being alone or solitary, loneliness, solitariness, solitude (of a person or place); a lonely place, desert, wilderness (class. in sing. and plur.; cf.: secretum, secessus). In gen.: ampla domus dedecori saepe domino fit, si est in eā solitudo, Cic. Off. 1, 39, 139: si aliquis nos deus ex hac hominum frequentiā tolleret et in solitudine uspiam collocaret, id. Lael. 23, 87; so (opp. frequentia) id. Pis. 22, 53; opp. celebritas, id. Inv. 1, 26, 38; Plin. Pan. 49, 2: audi

solitus.full: sŏlĭtus, a, um, Part. and P. a., from soleo.

solium.full: sŏlĭum, ii, n. from the root sol, kindr. with sed, sedeo, a seat. Most usu. of gods, kings, or other distinguished personages. Lit., a seat, chair of state, throne (cf.: thronus, tribunal): regali in solio sedens, Cic. Fin. 2, 21, 69: domus regia et in domo regale solium, Liv. 1, 47, 4; cf.: solio rex infit ab alto, Verg. A. 11, 301: solio tum Juppiter aureo Surgit, id. ib. 10, 116; so, Jovis, Hor. Ep. 1, 17, 34; Suet. Calig. 57: divinum, Cic. Rep. 3, 8, 12: deorum solia, id. Har. Resp. 27, 57:

solivagus.full: sōlĭvăgus, a, um, adj. solus - vagor (Ciceron.). Lit., wandering or roving alone; of animals that lead a solitary life: earum (bestiarum) partim solivagas, partim congregatas, Cic. Tusc. 5, 13, 38.—Of persons: non est enim singulare nec solivagum genus hoc (hominum), id. Rep. 1, 25, 39: (elephanti) minume ex omnibus solivagi, Plin. 8, 7, 7, § 23; v. solitarius.— Transf., alone, by itself, single, solitary (rare): caelo solivago et volubili et in orbem incitato, Cic. Univ. 6, 18: solivaga, cognit

sollemnis.full: sollemnis (less correctly sōlemnis, sollennis, sōlennis, sollempnis), e, adj. sollus, i. e. totus-annus, prop. that takes place every year; in relig. lang. of solemnities, yearly, annual; hence, in gen., Lit., stated, established, appointed: sollemne, quod omnibus annis praestari debet, Fest. p. 298 Müll. (cf. anniversarius): sollemnia sacra dicuntur, quae certis temporibus annisque fleri solent, id. p. 344 ib.: sacra stata, sollemnia, Cato ap. Fest. s. v. stata, p. 344 ib.; so, ad sollemne et s
sollemnis.short: sollemnis (less correctly sōlemnis, sollennis, sōlennis, sollempnis), e, adj.

sollemnitas.full: sollemnĭtas (sollenn-, solenn-, and solemn-), ātis, f. sollemnis (postclass.; cf.: sollemne, celebratio). A solemnity, festival, celebration of a day: dierum variae sollemnitates, Gell. 2, 24, 15: pristina (ludorum Isthmiorum), Sol. 7: condendi honoris, Aus. Grat. Act. 36: sacrorum sollemnitate prisco more completa, Amm. 23, 3, 7; Vulg. Deut. 16, 16 et saep.— A usage, formality: juris, Dig. 26, 8, 19; 1, 7, 25.
sollemnitas.short: sollemnĭtas (sollenn-, solenn-, and solemn-), ātis, f.

sollemnitus.full: sollemnĭtus (sollenn-, sōlenn-, sōlemn-), adv. sollemnis, solemnly, Liv. Andron. ap. Non. 176, 14.

sollers.full: sollers (sōlers), tis (abl. regularly sollerti; sollerte, Ov. P. 4, 14, 35), adj. sollus, i. e. totus - ars, and therefore qs. all art; hence, in gen., skilled, skilful, clever, dexterous, adroit, expert (class.; syn.; sagax, subtilis, expertus). Of persons: quae liberum Scire aequom est adulescentem, solertem dabo, to make ready, accomplished, Ter. Eun. 3, 2, 25: vigilans ac sollers, sicca, sana, sobria sum, Afran. ap. Non. 21, 33: in omni vel officio vel sermone sollers, Cic. Rep. 2, 21, 37: p

sollertia.full: sollertĭa (sōlert-), ae, f. sollers, skill, shrewdness, quickness of mind, ingenuity, dexterity, adroitness, expertness, etc. (class.; syn.: acumen, subtilitas, scientia): data est quibusdam bestiis machinatio quaedam atque sollertia, Cic. N. D. 2, 48, 123: nulla ars imitari sollertiam naturae potest, id. ib. 1, 33, 92: Chaldaei sollertiā ingeniorum antecellunt, id. Div. 1, 41, 91; cf.: est genus (Gallorum) summae sollertiae, Caes. B. G. 7, 22: hominum adhibita sollertia, id. B. C. 2, 8 fin.: in

sollicitatio.full: sollĭcĭtātĭo (sōlĭc-), ōnis, f. sollicito. Vexation, anxiety: nuptiarum, i. e. on account of, Ter. And. 1, 5, 26.— An inciting, instigating, instigation (good prose): omnium, Planc. ap. Cic. Fam. 10, 24, 2: Allobrogum, Cic. Cat. 3, 9, 22: Diogenis, id. Clu. 19, 53.—Plur.: sollicitationibus expugnari, seductions, allurements, Sen. Contr. 2, 15 med.: sollicitationibus periclitari, to find by trial, Caes. B. G. 2, 8 (dub.).

sollicitator.full: sollĭcĭtātor (sōlic-), ōris, m. id., a tempter, seducer (post - Aug.): alienarum nuptiarum, Dig. 47, 11, 1; 11, 3, 14 fin.; Sen. Contr. 2, 15 med.: servi, Dig. 11, 3, 11; 11, 3, 14.

sollicito.full: sollĭcĭto (sōlĭ-), āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. sollicitus, to disturb, stir, agitate, move; to distress, harass, make uneasy, vex, solicit, tempt, seduce, attract, induce. Lit., to stir, put in lively motion, move violently, disturb, shake, exercise (poet. and in post-Aug. prose). Histri tela manu jacientes sollicitabant, Enn. ap. Macr. S. 6, 3 (Ann. v. 438 Vahl.): myropolas omnes sollicito; ubicumque unguentum est, ungor, keep them busy, Plaut. Cas. 2, 3, 10: nec fas esse, quod sit fundatum perpetuo ae

sollicitudo.full: sollĭcĭtūdo (sōlic-), ĭnis, f. sollicitus, II., uneasiness of mind, care, disquiet, anxiety, solicitude (class.; used equally in sing. and plur.; syn.: aegritudo, dolor, anxietas): sollicitudo aegritudo cum cogitatione, Cic. Tusc. 4, 8, 18: quibus nunc me esse experior summae sollicitudini, Plaut. Mil. 3, 1, 77: istaec mihi res sollicitudini'st, Ter. Phorm. 4, 1, 22: aliquem afficere curā et sollicitudine, id. ib. 2, 4, 1: vita vacua metu, curā, sollicitudine, Cic. Rep. 3, 16, 26; id. Tusc. 1, 4

sollicitus.full: sollĭcĭtus (sōlĭcĭtus), a, um, adj. sollus-cieo; cf. sollicito, thoroughly moved, agitated, disturbed. Of physical motion (poet. and rare). As attrib. of motus, restless, unceasing: quae sollicito motu carerent, referring to the elements in constant motion, as air, water, etc., Lucr. 1, 343: sic igitur penitus qui in ferro'st abditus aër Sollicito motu semper jactatur, i. e. an unceasing air-current within the iron, to explain its attraction by the magnet, id. 6, 1038.— Of the sea agitated by st

sollicuria.full: sollĭcūrĭa in omni re curiosa, Fest. s. v. sollo, p. 298 Müll.
sollicuria.short: sollĭcūrĭa in omni re curiosa, Fest.

solliferreum.full: sollĭferreum (sōlĭf-), i, n. (sc. telum) [sollus-, i. e. totus-ferrum], a missile weapon made wholly of iron, an iron javelin, Liv. 34, 14 fin.; Gell. 10, 25, 2; cf. Fest. s. v. sollo, p. 298 Müll.; Paul. ex Fest. p. 299 ib.; and s. v. solitaurilia, p. 293 ib.

sollistimus.full: sollistĭmus (sōlist-), a, um, adj. old sup. form of sollus = salvus; v. Corss. Krit. Beitr. p. 313 sq., most perfect, only in the expression tripudium sollistimum, in augural lang.; the most favorable omen, when the chickens ate so greedily that the corn fell from their bills to the ground, Fest. p. 298 Müll.; Cic. Div. 1, 15, 28; 2, 34, 72; Liv. 10, 40; cf. Becker, Antiq. II. pt. 3, p. 79; and Lange, Antiq. I. p. 257.

sollus.full: sollus, a, um, adj. cf. Sanscr. sarva, entire; Gr. ὅλος; Lat. salvus; v. Corss. Krit. Beitr. p. 313, whole, entire, unbroken: vasa quoque omnino redimit non solla dupundi, Lucil. ap. Fest. p. 298 (Sat. v. 38 Gerl.): sollum Osce totum et solitum significat, unde tela quaedam solliferrea vocantur tota ferrea, et homo bonarum artium sollers, etc., Fest. s. v. solitaurilia, p. 293 Müll.; cf. Paul. ex Fest. s. v. sollo, p. 298 ib. (v. also the com. pounds sollennis, sollers, sollistimus, and sollicit

solo1.full: sōlo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. solus, to make lonely or desolate; to lay waste, desolate (only a few times in the post-Aug. poets): urbes populis, Stat. Th. 4, 36: domos, id. ib. 5, 149; Sen. Oedip. 4.

soloe.full: Sŏloe (dissyl.), v. Soli, I. and II.

soloecismus.full: sŏloecismus (sŏlĭcismus, Aus. Epigr. 138), i, m., = σολοικισμός. Lit., a grammatical fault in the construction of a sentence, a solecism (cf. stribligo): vitia in sermone, quo minus is Latinus sit, duo possunt esse: soloecismus et barbarismus. Soloecismus est, cum in verbis pluribus consequens verbum superiori non accommodatur. Barbarismus est, cum verbum aliquod vitiose effertur, Auct. Her. 4, 12, 17; cf. Sinn. Capito ap. Gell. 5, 20, 1 (who called it, in pure Latin, imparilitas); Quint. 1, 5,

soloecista.full: sŏloecista, ae, m., = σολοικιστής, one that speaks faultily, that commits solecisms, Hier. in Ruf. 3, 6.
soloecista.short: sŏloecista, ae, m., = σολοικιστής, one that speaks faultily, that commits solecisms, Hier.

soloecophanes.full: sŏloecŏphănĕs, is, n., = σολοικοφανές, that which appears to be a solecism, Cassiod. Or. 6.
soloecophanes.short: sŏloecŏphănĕs, is, n., = σολοικοφανές, that which appears to be a solecism, Cassiod.

soloecum.full: sŏloecum, i, n., = σόλοικον, = soloecismus, Auct. ap. Gell. 5, 20, 6; Gell. 17, 2, 11.
soloecum.short: sŏloecum, i, n., = σόλοικον, = soloecismus, Auct.

solon1.full: Sŏlon or Sŏlo (the latter in Cic. Rep. 2, 1, 2), ōnis, m., = Σόλων. A famous legislator of the Athenians, one of the seven sages of Greece, Cic. Brut. 7, 27; 10, 39; id. de Or. 1, 44, 197; id. Leg. 2, 23, 59; 2, 25, 64; Liv. 3, 31 fin.; Juv. 10, 274.—Plur.: aerumnosi Solones, i. e. philosophers, Pers. 3, 79 al.— A commander in Pydna, Liv. 44, 45.
solon1.short: Sŏlon or Sŏlo (the latter in Cic.

solon2.full: Sŏlōn, ōnis, m., = Σολώνιον, a city of the Allobroges, in Gallia Narbonensis, north-west of the Rhodanus, perh. near the modern Sortie, Liv. Epit. 103.
solon2.short: Sŏlōn, ōnis, m., = Σολώνιον, a city of the Allobroges, in Gallia Narbonensis, north-west of the Rhodanus, perh.

solonates.full: Sŏlonātes, ĭum, m., a Gallic tribe in Gallia Cisalpina, south-west of Forum Julii, now probably Torre di Sole, Plin. 3, 15, 20, § 116; Inscr. Orell. 5124.
solonates.short: Sŏlonātes, ĭum, m., a Gallic tribe in Gallia Cisalpina, south-west of Forum Julii, now probably Torre di Sole, Plin.

solonium.full: Solonĭum, ii, n., a district near Lanuvium, on the Via Ostiensis, Cic. Div. 1, 36, 79; 2, 31, 66; id. Att. 2, 3, 3.—Called also Solonius ager, Liv. 8, 12; Fest. s. v. pomonal, p. 250, b. Müll.
solonium.short: Solonĭum, ii, n., a district near Lanuvium, on the Via Ostiensis, Cic.

solor.full: sōlor, ātus, 1, v. dep. a. To comfort, console, solace (poet. and in post-Aug. prose; while consolor is class.): diffidentem verbis solatur suis, Plaut. Ep. 1, 2, 9: lenire dolentem Solando cupit, Verg. A. 4, 394: quos bonus Aeneas dictis solatur amicis, id. ib. 5, 770; Ov. F. 5, 237: inopem et aegrum, Hor. Ep. 2, 1, 131; Verg. A. 9, 290; Cat. 38, 5: solantia tollite verba! your words of comfort, Ov. M. 11, 685: solandus cum simul ipse fores, id. Tr. 5, 4, 42: et Caesar quamvis posthabitam decie

solorius.full: Solorius, ii, m., a mountain in Hispania Tarraconensis, Plin. 3, 1, 2, § 6.
solorius.short: Solorius, ii, m., a mountain in Hispania Tarraconensis, Plin.

solox.full: sŏlox, ōcis, adj. (cf.: salvus, solidus; v. Corss. Ausspr. 1, 486; ante- and post-class.). Lit., of raw, unwrought wool, of a coarse staple, coarse, harsh, bristly: solox, lana crassa, et pecus, quod passim pascitur non tectum, Fest. p. 301 Müll.: lana, Titin. ap. Fest. 1. 1.: pecore hirto atque soloce, Lucil. ap. Fest. 1. 1.; cf. Paul. ex Fest. p. 300 Müll.: solox, ἔριον παχύ, Gloss. Philox.: pallium philosophorum soloci lana, Fronto Eloq. p. 228 Mai.—* Transf., subst.: solox, ōcis, f. (sc. ves

solsequium.full: solsequĭum, ii, n., a plant, also called heliotropium, App. Herb. 49.
solsequium.short: solsequĭum, ii, n., a plant, also called heliotropium, App.

solstitialis.full: solstĭtĭālis, e, adj. solstitium. Lit., of or belonging to the summer solstice, solstitial (opp. brumalis): (sol) Brumales adeat flexus, atque inde revortens Cancri se ut vortat metas ad solstitiales, Lucr. 5, 617: dies, the day on which the sun enters Cancer, the longest day, Cic. Tusc. 1, 39, 94: tempus, Ov. F. 6, 790; Vitr. 9, 5: nox, i. e. the shortest, Ov. P. 2, 4, 26: ortus sideris, Just. 13, 7, 10: circulus, the tropic of Cancer, Varr. L. L. 9, § 24 Müll.; Plin. 2, 11, 8, § 50.—Called als

solstitium.full: solstĭtĭum, ii, n. sol-sisto. In gen., the time when the sun seems to stand still, either in Cancer or in Capricorn, the (summer or winter) solstice (so in gen. not till after the Aug. period): solstitium aestivum ... hibernum, Col. 7, 3, 11: aestivum, Plin. 2, 103, 106, § 229: brumale, Col. 11, 2, 94: solstitia et aequinoctia, id. 9, 14, 12.— In partic., the summer solstice, the longest day of the year (opp. bruma, the prevalent signif. of the word): alter motus solis est ... a brumā ad solstit

solubilis.full: sŏlūbĭlis, e, adj. solvo (post-class.). Pass., that may be loosed or taken apart, dissolvable: pons, Amm. 16, 8, 10: mundus, Min. Oct. 34: caro, Prud. στεφ. 10, 506. —* Act., loosening, relaxing: aër, Cael. Aur. Acut. 2, 37, 192.

solum1.full: sŏlum, i, (collat. form sŏlus, ūs, m., acc. to Varr. L. L. 6, 1, 2), n. root sar-, to guard, make whole; Sanscr. Sarva, entire; cf.: solea, solidus, sollus, the lowest part of a thing, the bottom, ground, base, foundation. Lit., the floor or pavement of a room; the bottom of a ditch or trench; the foundation of a building or the ground, site, on which it stands, etc.; ground, earth, land, soil; the sole of the foot or of a shoe, etc.: aurata tecta in villis et sola marmorea, Cic. Par. 6, 3, 49:

solus1.full: sōlus, a, um (gen. regular. solius; dat. soli; gen. m. soli, Cato ap. Prisc. p. 694 P.; dat. m. SOLO, Inscr. Orell. 2627; f. solae, Plaut. Mil. 4, 2, 28; Ter. Eun. 5, 6, 3), adj. orig. the same with sollus, q. v.; cf. salus. By Pott referred to sui, Kühn. Zeitschr. 5, 242. Lit. In gen., alone, only, single, sole (syn.: unus, unicus, singularis): quod egomet solus feci, nec quisquam alius affuit, Plaut. Am. 1, 1, 269: cum omnibus potius quam soli perire voluerunt, Cic. Cat. 4, 7, 14: cum visum es

solus2.full: Sŏlūs, untis, f., = Σολοῦς, a town on the northern coast of Sicily, now Castello di Solanto, Plin. 3, 8, 14, § 90.—Hence, Sŏ-luntīni, ōrum, m., the inhabitants of Solus, Cic. Verr. 2, 3, 43, § 103; sing., id. ib. 2, 2, 42, § 102.
solus2.short: Sŏlūs, untis, f., = Σολοῦς, a town on the northern coast of Sicily, now Castello di Solanto, Plin.

solus3.full: sŏlus, ūs, m., v. solum init.

solute.full: sŏlūtē, adv., v. solvo, P. a. fin.

solutilis.full: sŏlūtĭlis, e, adj. solvo, that is easily loosed or taken apart: navis, Suet. Ner. 34.

solutim.full: sŏlūtim, adv. id., loosely, = solute, Tert. Pall. 5.

solutio.full: sŏlūtĭo, ōnis, f. id., a loosing, unloosing, dissolution (rare but class.). Lit. In gen.: linguae, Cic. de Or. 1, 25, 114: totius hominis, id. Tusc. 3, 25, 61.—Plur.: ventris et stomachi solutiones, looseness, weakness, Plin. 23, 6, 60, § 112; cf.: stomachi solutio, Cels. 4, 5.— In partic., payment: solutio rerum creditarum, Cic. Off. 2, 24, 84: legatorum, id. Clu. 12, 34: justi crediti, Liv. 42, 5: nummorum, Dig. 46, 3, 54: Romae solutione impeditā fides concidit, Cic. Imp. Pomp. 7, 19: solutio

solutor.full: sŏlūtor, ōris, m. id. (post-class.). A looser, an opener: signaculi, Aug. Mor. Manich. 2, 13 fin.— A payer, Tert. adv. Marc. 4, 17.

solutrix.full: sŏlūtrix, īcis, f. solutor, she that looses or sets free: malorum, Diom. p. 484 P.

solutus.full: sŏlūtus, a, um, Part. and P. a. of solvo.

solva.full: Solva, ae, f., a city of Noricum, Inscr. Grut. 537, 1.—Hence, Solvensis, e, adj., of or belonging to Solva: Flavium Solvense (sc. oppidum), Plin. 3, 24, 27, § 146.
solva.short: Solva, ae, f., a city of Noricum, Inscr.

solvo.full: solvo, solvi, solūtum, 3, v. a. (perf. soluit, trisyll., Cat. 2, 13: soluisse, Tib. 4, 5, 16) [for se-luo; cf. socors for se-cords], to loosen an object from any thing, to release or to loose, remove any thing which binds or restrains another. To loose an object bound, to release, set free, disengage, dissolve, take apart. In a corporeal sense. Outwardly, to release. From fetters or custody, to free, set free, release; absol.: solvite istas, i. e. from fetters, Plaut. Truc. 4, 3, 64: solvite ist

solyma.full: Sŏlўma, ōrum and ae, Sŏlўmi, ōrum, and Sŏlўmus, a, um, v. Hierosolyma.
solyma.short: Sŏlўma, ōrum and ae, Sŏlўmi, ōrum, and Sŏlўmus, a, um, v.

solymus.full: Sŏlўmus or Sŏlĭmus (-os), i, m., a Trojan, the founder of Sulmo, Ov. F. 4, 79; Sil. 9, 72.
solymus.short: Sŏlўmus or Sŏlĭmus (-os), i, m., a Trojan, the founder of Sulmo, Ov.

somnialis.full: somnĭālis, is, adj. somnium, dreambringing, an epithet of Hercules, Inscr. Fabr. p. 692, 130; Inscr. Rein. cl. 10, 4.— Hence, adv.: somnĭālĭter, in a dream (late Lat.), Fulg. Myth. 2, 17 dub.

somniator.full: somnĭātor, ōris, m. somnio, one who has faith in dreams; a dreamer, Sen. Contr. 3, 22, 15.—Of Joseph, Tert. adv. Gnost. 2 med.; Vulg. Gen. 37, 19; id. Zech. 10, 2.

somniculosus.full: somnĭcŭlōsus, a, um, adj. somnus, full of sleep, i. e. Pass., inclined to sleep, drowsy, dozy, sleepy, sluggish, slothful (rare but class.; cf. sopitus): quae vitia non sunt senectutis, sed inertis, ignavae, somniculosae senectutis, Cic. Sen. 11, 36: villicus, Col. 11, 1, 13: genus mancipiorum (with socors), id. 1, 8, 2: glires, Mart. 3, 58, 36: Etesiae, Sen. Q. N. 5, 11, 1.— Act., making sleepy, drowsy, or sluggish: aspis, i. e. causing torpor or numbness, palsying, deadly (cf. somnifer and som

somnifer.full: somnĭfer, ĕra, ĕrum, adj. somnus-fero, sleep-bringing, soporific, somniferous (poet. and in post-Aug. prose): vis papaveris, Plin. 18, 25, 61, § 229: virga (Mercurii), Ov. M. 1, 672: aspis, causing torpidity, deadly, Luc. 9, 701; so, venenum (aspidis), Ov. M. 9, 693: strychnos, App. Flor. 74; cf. somniculosus, II., and somnificus.

somnificus.full: somnĭfĭcus, a, um, adj. somnus-facio, causing sleep, narcotic (Plinian): crater, Mart. Cap. 1, § 82: medicamentum, Plin. 37, 10, 57, § 158: vis aspidum, id. 24, 4, 17, § 63.

somniger.full: somnĭger, gĕra, gĕrum, adj. somnusgero, sleep-bringing (very rare for somnifer): cornua Lunae, Dracont. 1, 212.

somnio.full: somnĭo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. (dep. collat. form: hic aedes non somniatur, Petr. 74, 14) [somnium], to dream; to dream of or see in a dream (freq. and class.). Lit.: mirum atque inscitum somniavi somnium, Plaut. Rud. 3, 1, 5; so, somnium, id. Mil. 2, 4, 28; 2, 4, 47: aliquid (in somnis), id. Rud. 3, 4, 68; id. Curc. 2, 1, 32; 2, 2, 4; Ter. And. 5, 6, 7; Cic. Div. 2, 59, 121 al.; cf. aurum, Plaut. Stich. 5, 2, 18: ovum, Cic. Div. 2, 65, 134: speciem fortunae querentis, Suet. Galb. 18 al.; cf.: me s

somniosus.full: somnĭōsus, a, um, adj. somnus, sleepy, overcome by sleep, Cael. Aur. Acut. 3, 5, 51.

somnium.full: somnĭum, ii, n. id.. Lit., a dream, Cic. Div. 1, 20, 39; 2, 58, 119; Plin. 10, 75, 98, § 211; Macr. Somn. Scip. 1, 3; Lact. Opif. Dei, 18: rex Priamus somnio perculsus, Enn. ap. Cic. Div. 1, 21, 42 (Trag. v. 59 Vahl.): dum huic conicio somnium, interpret, Plaut. Curc. 2, 2, 3; cf. id. Rud. 3, 1, 19: interpretes somniorum, Cic. Div. 1, 58, 132: jucundissima somnia, id. Fin. 5, 20, 55: per somnia loquentes, talking in their sleep, Lucr. 5, 1158; cf.: quae somnio visa fuerant, Liv. 8, 6, 11 Weissen

somnulentia.full: somnŭlentĭa (somnŏl-), ae, f., somnulentus, sleepiness, drowsiness, somnolence (late Lat.), Sid. Ep. 2, 2 med.
somnulentia.short: somnŭlentĭa (somnŏl-), ae, f., somnulentus, sleepiness, drowsiness, somnolence (late Lat.), Sid.

somnulentus.full: somnŭlentus (somnŏl-), a, um, adj. somnus, full of sleep, i. e. sleepy, drowsy, dozy, somnolent (post-Aug.), App. M. 1 fin.; 10, p. 251, 37.—Hence, adv.: somnŏlen-ter, sleepily, Hier. in Psa. 118; Sol. 20, 7.

somnurnus.full: somnurnus, a, um, adj. id.; in analogy with nocturnus, diurnus, of or belonging to sleep: imagines, seen in sleep, Varr. ap. Non. 172, 3.

somnus.full: somnus, i, m. Sanscr. svap-nas; Gr. ὕπνος; som-nus for sop-nus; cf.: sopor, sopio. Lit., sleep: hostes vino domiti somnoque sepulti, Enn. ap. Macr. S. 6 (Ann. v. 291 Vahl.); Lucr. 1, 133: vix aegro cum corde meo me somnus reliquit, Enn. ap. Cic. Div. 1, 20, 40 (Ann. v. 52 Vahl.); cf., on the contrary: pandite sulti' genas et corde relinquite somnum, id. ap. Fest. p. 343 Müll. (Ann. v. 521 Vahl.): somnum capere, Plaut. Mil. 3, 1, 115; cf. Cic. Tusc. 4, 19, 44: somnum videre, Ter. Heaut. 3, 1, 82:

sonabilis.full: sŏnābĭlis, e, adj. sono, sounding, noisy: sistrum, Ov. M. 9, 784.

sonans.full: sŏnans, antis, Part. and P. a. of sono.

sonax.full: sŏnax, ācis, adj. sono, sounding, noisy (poet. and in post - Aug. prose): concha, App. M. 4, p. 157, 3: dentium attritus, id. ib. 8, p. 202, 30.

sonchus.full: sonchus, i, m., = σόγχος, the herb sow-thistle: Sonchus oleraceus, Linn.; Plin. 22, 22, 44, § 88.
sonchus.short: sonchus, i, m., = σόγχος, the herb sow-thistle: Sonchus oleraceus, Linn.;

sonipes.full: sŏnĭ-pēs (sŏnŭpēs), pĕdis, adj. sonus, with sounding feet, noisy-footed (poet.): turba (in Isidis sacris), Grat. Cyn. 43.—As subst., noisy-foot, i. e. a horse, a prancer, steed: fremit aequore toto Insultans sonipes et pressis pugnat habenis, Verg. A. 11, 600; Cat. 63, 41; Sil. 1, 222; Val. Fl. 3, 334; Stat. Th. 5, 3 al. (in Cic., sonipedes is cited as an example of a fourth pæon, de Or. 3, 47, 183).

sonito.full: sŏnĭto, āre, v. freq. n. [sono], to make a noise: cicadae, Sol. 2, § 40 dub. (al. so nant).

sonitus.full: sŏnĭtus, ūs (gen. soniti, Pac. and Cae cil. ap. Non. 491, 24 sq.), m. id., a noise, sound, din, etc. (class.; in sing. and plur.): at tuba terribili sonitu taratantara dixit, Enn. ap. Prisc. p. 842 P. (Ann. v. 452 Vahl.); cf.: lituus sonitus effudit acutos, id. ap. Paul. ex Fest. p. 116 Müll. (Ann. v. 522 Vahl.): summo sonitu quatit ungula terram, id. ap. Macr. S. 6, 1 (Ann. v. 281 Vahl.); imitated by Virg. A. 8, 596: ungularum, Plaut. Men. 5, 2, 113: tumultuosus, id. Trin. 5, 2, 52; cf. id. Bac

sonivius.full: sŏnĭvĭus, a, um, adj. sonus, noisy (cf. solistimum), only in the phrase sonivium tripudium, of the rattling of the corn upon the ground as it fell from the mouths of the sacred chickens, Cic. Fam. 6, 6, 7; Plin. 15, 22, 24, § 86; cf. Fest. pp. 290, 291, and 297 Müll.

sono.full: sŏno, ŭi, ĭtum, 1 (ante-class. collat. form acc. to the 3d conj., sonit, Enn. and Att. ap. Non. 504, 32 sq.; sonunt, Enn. and Att. ib. 505, 11 sq.; Enn. ap. Prisc. p. 863 P.; inf. sonĕre, Att. ap. Non. 505; Lucr. 3, 156; part. fut. sonaturum, Hor. S. 1, 4, 44; perf. sonaverint, Tert. ad Scap. 3; gen. plur. sonantum, Cat. 34, 12), v. n. and a. [Sanscr. svan-, to sound; cf. O. H. Germ. svana; Engl. swan]. Neutr., to make a noise, to sound, resound: aes sonit, the trumpet sounds, Enn. ap. Non. 504,

sonor.full: sŏnor, ōris, m. sono, a noise, sound, din (poet. and in post-Aug. prose for sonitus and sonus); sing., Lucr. 1, 644; 4, 567; 4, 570; Verg. G. 3, 199; id. A. 7, 462; Tac. A. 1, 65; 4, 48; App. M. 11, p. 258 fin.— Plur., Lucr. 5, 334; 6, 1185; Verg. A. 9, 651; Val. Fl. 5, 306; Tac. A. 14, 36; App. Dogm. Plat. 1, p. 9, 28; id. Flor. 3, p. 357, 4.

sonoritas.full: sŏnōrĭtas, ātis, f. sonorus, = εὐφωνία, fulness of sound, melodiousness, Prisc. 541; 1220 P; Sarisb. 1, 16.

sonorus.full: sŏnōrus, a, um (collat. form sŏnōris, e, Diom. 497 and 498), adj. sonor, noisy, loud, sounding, resounding, sonorous (poet. and in post-Aug. prose for the class. sonans): cithara, Tib. 3, 4, 69: aes, Claud. IV. Cons. Hon. 149: arcus, id. in Ruf. 2, 80: tempestates sonoras, Verg. A. 1, 53: tonitru, Claud. Laud. Stil. 2, 26: pelage, Lucr. 5, 35 Lachm.: flumina, Verg. A. 12, 139: nemus, Stat. Th. 4, 34: Phocis (on account of the Delphic oracle), id. ib. 11, 281: insula fluctibus, Claud. B. Gild. 51

sons.full: sons, sontis, adj. (nom. sing., Fest. p. 297; Aus. Idyll. 12) [Part. from root as-, es-; Sanscr. as-mi; Gr. εὶμί; Lat. esum, sum; cf. Gr. ἐτεός, ἐτήτυμος; prop. he who was it, the real person, the guilty one]. Guilty, criminal; subst., a guilty person, an offender, malefactor, criminal (freq. and class., esp. as subst.; syn.: reus, nocens): anima, Verg. A. 10, 854; Ov. M. 6, 618: ulni, id. ib. 7, 847: di, Stat. Th. 5, 610: manus foedata sanguine sonti (poet. for sontis), Ov. M. 13, 563: morae ab

sontiates.full: Sontĭātes, um, m., a powerful tribe in Aquitania, Caes. B. G. 3, 20 sq.
sontiates.short: Sontĭātes, um, m., a powerful tribe in Aquitania, Caes.

sonticus.full: sontĭcus, a, um, adj. sons. Lit., dangerous, serious, critical, in the connection morbus sonticus, of a serious disorder that excuses one from duty, etc., Fragm. XII. Tab. ap. Fest. p. 290 Müll.; cf. Gell. 20, 1, 27; Dig. 21, 1, 65; 42, 1, 60; 2, 11, 2; 5, 1, 46; Plin. 36, 19, 34, § 142; Cincius ap. Gell. 16, 4, 4.— Transf.: sontica causa, arising from a morbus sonticus; hence, in gen., serious, weighty, important, Cato ap. Fest. p. 344 Müll.; Naev. ib. p. 290; Tib. 1, 8, 51.

sontini.full: Sontini, ōrum, m., a people of Lucania, Plin. 3, 11, 15, § 98.
sontini.short: Sontini, ōrum, m., a people of Lucania, Plin.

sontius.full: Sontĭus, ii, m., a river in Carinthia, now the Lisonzo, Cassiod. Ep. 1, 18; Jornand. Get. 57.
sontius.short: Sontĭus, ii, m., a river in Carinthia, now the Lisonzo, Cassiod.

sonus1.full: sŏnus, i (collat. form sŏnus, ūs, in gen., Amm. 20, 4, 14; abl. sonu, Sisenn. ap. Non. p. 491, 27; App. M. 8, p. 216, 7; nom. plur., Amm. 22, 9, 15), m. sono, a noise, sound (syn. fragor): et pereunte viro raucum sonus aere cucurrit, Enn. ap. Lact. ap. Stat. Th. 11, 56 (Ann. v. 509 Vahl.): tympana raucis Obstrepuere sonis, Ov. M. 4, 392: non exaudito tubae sono, Caes. B. G. 7, 47: signorum sonus, id. B. C. 3, 105; cf.: cum ingenti sono fluminis, Liv. 21, 28: olli respondit suavis sonus Egeriai,

sonus2.full: sōnus, a, um, adj. id., sounding, resounding, Isid. Orig. 1, 4, 4.

sonus3.full: Sōnus, i, m., = Σῶνος, a river of India, a branch of the Ganges, Plin. 6, 18, 22, § 65.
sonus3.short: Sōnus, i, m., = Σῶνος, a river of India, a branch of the Ganges, Plin.

sopater.full: Sōpăter, tri, m., = Σώπατρος, a Greek proper name, e. g. a victim of Verres: Halicyensis, Cic. Verr. 2, 2, 28, § 68.—Another, a witness against Verres, Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 39, § 85.
sopater.short: Sōpăter, tri, m., = Σώπατρος, a Greek proper name, e.

sophene.full: Sōphēnē, ēs, f., = Σωφηνή, a district in Armenia, Mel. 1, 11; Luc. 2, 592; Plin. 5, 12, 13, § 66.
sophene.short: Sōphēnē, ēs, f., = Σωφηνή, a district in Armenia, Mel.

sopheni.full: Sōphēni, ōrum, m., a people of Asia, Plin. 6, 9, 10, § 28.
sopheni.short: Sōphēni, ōrum, m., a people of Asia, Plin.

sophia.full: sŏphĭa (i long, Prud. Sym. 122; id. Cath. 1613; Fortun. Suppl. 2, 62), ae, f., = σοφία, wisdom (pure Lat. sapientia): sophiam, sapientia quae perhibetur, Enn. ap. Fest. p. 325 Müll. (Ann. v. 227 Vahl.); Afran. ap. Gell. 13, 8, 3; Mart. 1, 112, 1; cf. Sen. Ep. 89, 6; Lact. 3, 16, 10 (in Cic. Off. 1, 43, 153, written as Greek).

sophisma.full: sŏphisma, ătis, n., = σόφισμα, a false conclusion, fallacy, sophism (pure Lat. captio), Sen. Ep. 45, 8; Gell. 18, 13, 2 (in Cic. Ac. 2, 24, 75, written as Greek, and explained by fallaces conclusiunculae; cf. also Sen. Ep. 111, 1).
sophisma.short: sŏphisma, ătis, n., = σόφισμα, a false conclusion, fallacy, sophism (pure Lat.

sophismatius.full: sŏphismătĭus, a, um, adj. sophisma, sophistical: dialecticus, Gell. 18, 13 in lemm.

sophistes.full: sŏphistes or sŏphista, ae, m., = σοφιστής, a sophist: quis hic est? num sophistes? sic enim appellabantur hi, qui ostentationis aut quaestus causā philosophabantur, Cic. Ac. 2, 23, 72; cf. id. Fin. 2, 1, 1; id. Or. 11, 37: Protagoras, sophistes maximus, id. N. D. 1, 23, 63.—Form sophista, Gell. 17, 5, 3; voc.: insulse sophista, Lucil. ap. Don. Ter. Eun. 2, 3, 10.
sophistes.short: sŏphistes or sŏphista, ae, m., = σοφιστής, a sophist: quis hic est? num sophistes? sic enim appellabantur hi, qui ostentationis aut quaestus causā philosophabantur, Cic.

sophistice2.full: sŏphistĭcē, ēs, f., = σοφιστική (τέχνη), false reasoning, sophistry, App. Dogm. Plat. 2, p. 17, 10.
sophistice2.short: sŏphistĭcē, ēs, f., = σοφιστική (τέχνη), false reasoning, sophistry, App.

sophisticus.full: sŏphistĭcus, a, um, adj., = σοφιστικός, sophistic, sophistical; res admodum insidiosa et sophistica, neque ad veritates magis quam ad captiones reperta, Tiro Tullius ap. Gell. 7, 3, 35: captio, Gell. 18, 2, 6: ostentatio, Arn. 1, 36: ut concidant sophistica, Prud. Apoth. 2, 41.—Adv.: sŏphi-stĭcē, sophistically: interpretari legem et cavillari, Cod. Just. 8, 10, 12, § 3; Vulg. Ecclus. 37, 23.
sophisticus.short: sŏphistĭcus, a, um, adj., = σοφιστικός, sophistic, sophistical;

sophocles.full: Sŏphŏcles, is and i, m., = Σοφοκλῆς, a celebrated Greek tragic poet, Cic. Fin. 5, 1, 3; id. Sen. 7, 22; 14, 47; id. Div. 1, 25, 54; id. Off. 1, 40, 144; Hor. Ep. 2, 1, 163; Quint. 10, 1, 67 sq.; Sen. Q. N. 4, 2, 17; Vell. 1, 16, 3; gen. Sophocli, Gell. 12, 11, 6; 13, 18, 3; voc. Sophocle (like Socrate), Cic. Off. 1, 40, 144.—Hence, Sŏphō^clēus, a, um, adj., of or in the manner of Sophocles: an pangis aliquid Sophocleum? Cic. Fam. 16, 18, 3: cothurnus, Verg. E. 8, 10; Ov. Am. 1, 15, 15.
sophocles.short: Sŏphŏcles, is and i, m., = Σοφοκλῆς, a celebrated Greek tragic poet, Cic.

sophoclidisca.full: Sŏphō^clĭdisca, ae, f., the name of a woman, Plaut. Pers. 2, 2, 23.
sophoclidisca.short: Sŏphō^clĭdisca, ae, f., the name of a woman, Plaut.

sophoniba.full: Sŏphŏnība, ae, f., wife of Syphax and daughter of Hasdrubal, Liv. 30, 12, 11; 30, 15, 4.
sophoniba.short: Sŏphŏnība, ae, f., wife of Syphax and daughter of Hasdrubal, Liv.

sophos1.full: sŏphos or sŏphus, i, m., = σοφός, a wise man, sage: te sophos omnis amat, Mart. 7, 32, 4.—Adjectively, wise, shrewd: victor sophus, Phaedr. 3, 14, 9: factus periclo tum gubernator sophus, id. 4, 15, 8.
sophos1.short: sŏphos or sŏphus, i, m., = σοφός, a wise man, sage: te sophos omnis amat, Mart.
