spodos.full: spŏdos, i, f., = σποδός, dross, slag, scoria, Plin. 34, 13, 33, § 128 sqq.
spodos.short: spŏdos, i, f., = σποδός, dross, slag, scoria, Plin.

spoletium.full: Spōlētĭum (afterwards called also Spōlētum; cf. Prisc. p. 592 P.; but whether so as early as the class. period is doubtful, owing to the uncertainty of the readings in the MSS. of Livy, Suetonius, and Florus; cf. Duk. ad Flor. 3, 21, 27), ii, n., a city of Umbria, now Spoleto, Liv. 22, 9; 24, 10; 45, 43; id. Epit. 20; Vell. 1, 14 fin.; Flor. 3, 21, 27; Suet. Vesp. 1; id. Gram. 21; Aur. Vict. Ep. 31.—Hence, Spōlē-tīnus, a um, adj., of or belonging to Spoletium: populus, Cic. Balb. 21, 48: Spoleti

spoliabilis.full: spŏlĭābĭlis, e, adj. spolio, that can be stripped off (late Lat.), Mar. Mercat. Nestor Serm. 12, 2.

spoliarium.full: spŏlĭārĭum, ii, n. spolium (postAug.). Lit., a place in the amphitheatre where the clothes were stripped from the slain gladiators who were dragged thither, Sen. Ep. 93, 10; Lampr. Commod. 18, 3; 19, 3.— Transf., a den of robbers or murderers, a cutthroat place, Sen. Prov. 3, 7; id. Contr. 5, 33; Plin. Pan. 36, 1.

spoliatio.full: spŏlĭātĭo, ōnis, f. spolio, a pillaging, robbing, plundering, spoliation (class.). Lit.: in tantā spoliatione omnium rerum, Cic. Sest. 21, 47: sacrorum, Liv. 29, 8, 9.— Plur.: spoliationes fanorum atque oppidorum, Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 59, § 132; id. Agr. 1, 3, 9. — Trop.: consulatūs, Cic. Mur. 40, 87: dignitatis, id. Phil. 2, 11, 27.

spoliator.full: spŏlĭātor, ōris, m. id., a robber, pillager, plunderer, spoiler (rare but class.): eorum (monumentorum), * Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 36, § 80: templi, Liv. 29, 18, 15: pupilli, Juv. 1, 46.

spoliatrix.full: spŏlĭātrix, īcis, f. spoliator, she that robs, pillages, or spoils: Venus spoliatrix, * Cic. Cael. 21, 52: amica, Mart. 4, 29, 5.

spoliatus.full: spŏlĭātus, a, um, Part. and P. a. of spolio.

spolio.full: spŏlĭo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. spolium, to strip, to deprive of covering, rob of clothing. In gen. (rare but class.; syn. exuo): Phalarim vestitu spoliare, Cic. Off. 3, 6, 29: consules spoliari hominem et virgas expediri jubent, Liv. 2, 55 Drak.; cf. Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 40, § 86: Papirius spoliari magistrum equitum ac virgas et secures expediri jussit, Liv. 8, 32; cf. also, Val. Max. 2, 7, 8: corpus caesi hostis, Liv. 7, 26: cadaver, Luc. 7, 627: Gallum caesum torque, Liv. 6, 42: corpus jacentis uno t

spolium.full: spŏlĭum, ii, n. root spal- (skal-); cf.: populor, calamitas, calvus. Lit., the spoil of an animal, i. e. the skin or hide of an animal stripped off (so only poet. and very rare): pelles et spolia ferarum, Lucr. 5, 954: serpentum, id. 4, 62: leonis, Ov. M. 9, 113; 3, 81: apri, id. ib. 8, 426; id. H. 4, 100: pecudis (i. e. arietis Phrixei), id. ib. 6, 13; cf. id. M. 7, 156: viperei monstri (i. e. Medusae), id. ib. 4, 615.— Transf., the arms or armor stripped from a defeated enemy; hence, in gen.,

sponda.full: sponda, ae, f. Lit., the frame of a bedstead, sofa, etc., Ov. M. 8, 657; Petr. 97, 4; 94, 8.— Transf. A bed, couch, sofa (syn. lectus), Verg. A. 1, 698; Hor. Epod. 3, 22; Ov. F. 2, 345; Mart. 3, 91, 9; Suet. Caes. 49.— A bier, Mart. 10, 5, 9.

spondalium.full: spondālĭum or spondaulĭum (the form is uncertain), ii, n., a sacrificial hymn, accompanied by the flute: spondalium canere, Diom. p. 472 fin. P.: spondalia dicens, etc., Cic. de Or. 2, 46, 193 Orell. N. cr.
spondalium.short: spondālĭum or spondaulĭum (the form is uncertain), ii, n., a sacrificial hymn, accompanied by the flute: spondalium canere, Diom.

spondeo.full: spondĕo, spŏpondi, sponsum, 2 (perf. spepondi, Cic., Caes., and Val. Antias ap. Gell. 7, 9, 12 sq.; Inscr. Orell. 4358; without redup. sponderat, Tert. Carm. adv. Mart. 3, 135; subj. sponsis = spoponderis, an ancient formula of prayer in Fest. p. 351 Müll.), v. a. akin with σπένδω, to pour out, = libare; cf. σπονδαί, league. Jurid. and publicists' t. t. In bargains, covenants, treaties, etc., to promise solemnly, to bind, engage, or pledge one's self (class.; syn.: recipio, stipulor, promitto; c

spondeus.full: spondēus (spondīus; sometimes incorrectly written spondaeus), i, m., = σπονδεῖος, of or belonging to libations; hence, substt. spondēum, i, n., a vessel used in making libations, App. M. 11, p. 266, 26.— (Because of its prolonged, solemn character.) A spondee (metrical foot), Cic. Or. 64, 216; Quint. 9, 4, 80 sq.; Hor. A. P. 256; Aus. Ep. 21, 42.

spondiacus.full: spondīăcus (less correctly spondă-ĭcus), a, um, adj., = σπονδειακός, consisting of spondees, spondaic: versus, Diom. p. 494 P.: tractus, Terentian. ap. Prisc. Metr. p. 1321 P.
spondiacus.short: spondīăcus (less correctly spondă-ĭcus), a, um, adj., = σπονδειακός, consisting of spondees, spondaic: versus, Diom.

spondyle.full: spondўlē (sphond-), ēs, f., = σπονδύλη, an insect that lives in the ground, and gnaws the roots of trees, Plin. 27, 13, 118, § 143.
spondyle.short: spondўlē (sphond-), ēs, f., = σπονδύλη, an insect that lives in the ground, and gnaws the roots of trees, Plin.

spondylion.full: spondўlĭon (sphond-) or -ĭum, ii, n., = σπονδύλιον (σφονδύλιον), the herb bear's-foot, bear's-wort, spicknel: Heracleum sphondylium, Linn.; Plin. 12, 26, 58, § 128; 24, 6, 16, § 25; Scrib. Comp. 2 and 5.
spondylion.short: spondўlĭon (sphond-) or -ĭum, ii, n., = σπονδύλιον (σφονδύλιον), the herb bear's-foot, bear's-wort, spicknel: Heracleum sphondylium, Linn.;

spondylus.full: spondўlus (sphond-), i, m., = σπόνδυλος (σφόνδυλος). A joint of the spine, a vertebra, spondyle, Plin. 29, 4, 20, § 67; 32, 10, 38, § 116; Veg. Vet. 6, 1, 1.— The hard white or muscle of an oyster or other bivalve, Plin. 32, 6, 21, § 60; 32, 11, 54, § 154.— A kind of muscle: Spondylus gaederopus, Linn.; Metell. ap. Macr. S. 2, 9; Mart. 7, 20, 14; Sen. Ep. 95, 26 and 28; Col. 8, 16, 7; Plin. 32, 11, 53, § 151.

spongia1.full: spongĭa or spongĕa, ae, f., = σπογγιά. Lit., a sponge, Plin. 9, 45, 69, § 148; 31, 11, 47, § 123; Lucr. 4, 618; Cic. N. D. 2, 55, 136; id. Sest. 35, 77; Varr. ap. Non. 96, 14; Mart. 12, 48, 7; 14, 144, 1; Sen. Ep. 70, 20; id. Ira, 3, 19, 3; Suet. Vesp. 16. — Transf., of things resembling a sponge. An open-worked coat of mail, Liv. 9, 40, 3: retiariorum, Tert. Spect. 25. —In a double sense, with the signif. I.: Ajax in spongeam incubuit, Aug. ap. Macr. S. 2, 4; cf. Suet. Aug. 85.— The root of som
spongia1.short: spongĭa or spongĕa, ae, f., = σπογγιά.

spongia2.full: Spongĭa, ae, m., a proper name, perh. fictitious, in contempt, Cic. Att. 1, 16, 6.
spongia2.short: Spongĭa, ae, m., a proper name, perh.

spongio.full: spongĭo, āre, v. a. spongia, to wipe off with a sponge, to sponge (late Lat.), perh. only Apic. 1, 26, and 8, 1.

spongiola.full: spongĭŏla, ae, f. dim. id.. A rosegall, a spongy substance growing upon the wild rose-bush, Plin. 25, 2, 6, § 18.— The small roots of the asparagus, Col. 11, 3, 44.

spongiolus.full: spongĭŏlus, i, m. dim. id., a kind of small fungus or mushroom, Apic. 2, 1; 5, 1; 3, 20.

spongiosus.full: spongĭōsus or spongĕōsus, a, um, adj. id., spongy, porous (post-Aug.): pulmo, Cels. 4, 1; Plin. 11, 37, 72, § 188: pumices, id. 36, 21, 42, § 155: panis, id. 18, 11, 27, § 105.
spongiosus.short: spongĭōsus or spongĕōsus, a, um, adj.

spongitis.full: spongītis, ĭdis, f., = σπογγῖτις [id.] (sponge - stone), a kind of precious stone, Plin. 37, 10, 67, § 182.
spongitis.short: spongītis, ĭdis, f., = σπογγῖτις [id.] (sponge - stone), a kind of precious stone, Plin.

spongius.full: spongĭus, a, um, adj. id., spongy (late Lat.): lignum, Cassiod. Var. 11, 38.

spongizo.full: spongīzo, āre, v. a., = σπογγίζω, to wipe off with a sponge, to sponge, Apic. 7, 16; 8, 7.

spongos.full: spongos, i, m., a sponge (late Lat.), Juvenc. 4, 696.
spongos.short: spongos, i, m., a sponge (late Lat.), Juvenc.

sponsa.full: sponsa, ae, v. spondeo, P. a., E.

sponsalicius.full: sponsālīcĭus or -tĭus, a, um, adj. sponsalia, of or belonging to betrothal, spousal (post-class.): arrha, Cod. Just. 5, 1, 5; 5, 2, 1: donatio, Sid. Ep. 7, 2 med.

sponsalis.full: sponsālis, e, adj. 3. sponsus. Of or belonging to betrothal or espousal, spousal, sponsal (class.): quo die sponsum erat, sponsalis, Varr. L. L. 6, § 70 Müll.: tabulae, Hier. Ep. 54, 15: largitas, Cod. Th. 3, 16, 2. — Substt. sponsālĭa, ĭum (gen. sponsaliorum, Sen. Ben. 1, 9, 4; Suet. Aug. 53), n. A betrothal, espousal: sponsalia dicta sunt a spondendo. Nam moris fuit veteribus stipulari et spondere sibi uxores futuras, Dig. 23, 1, 2; where v. the whole section: De sponsalibus; and cf. Sulp. ap.

sponsio.full: sponsĭo, ōnis, f. spondeo, jurid. and publicists' t. t., a solemn promise or engagement to some performance (in bargains, covenants, treaties, etc.); a promise, guarantee, security, sponsion for any one (freq. and class.; cf.: pactio, foedus). In gen.: sponsio appellatur omnis stipulatio promissioque, Dig. 50, 16, 7: voti sponsio, quā obligamur deo, Cic. Leg. 2, 16, 41: Scandilium cogis sponsionem acceptam facere, Cic. Verr. 2, 3, 60, § 139: per inducias sponsionem faciunt, uti, etc., made an ag

sponsiuncula.full: sponsĭuncŭla, ae, f. dim. sponsio, a little engagement or stipulation, Petr. 58, 8.

sponso.full: sponso, āre, v. a. sponsus, to betroth, affiance, espouse (post-class.). Lit.: aliquam, Dig. 23, 2, 38; Tert. Vel. Virg. 11.— Trop.: animam, Paul. Nol. Carm. 18, 43: et sponsabo te mihi in sempiternum, Vulg. Osee, 2, 19; 2, 20.

sponsor.full: sponsor, ōris, m. spondeo, one who becomes answerable for another. Lit., a bondsman, surety (cf.: vas; gen. vadis, praes, vindex): de tuo negotio, quod sponsor es pro Pompeio, si Galba consponsor tuus redierit, non desinam cum illo communicare, Cic. Fam. 6, 18, 3: sponsores et creditores L. Trebellii, id. Phil. 6, 4, 11; cf. id. Quint. 23, 73: sponsor promissorum alicujus, id. Att. 15, 15, 2; 1, 10, 6; cf. id. ib. 1, 8, 2: si Pompeius mihi testis de voluntate Caesaris et sponsor est illi de meā,

sponsum.full: sponsum, i, v. spondeo, P. a., C.

sponsus1.full: sponsus, a, um, Part. and P. a. of spondeo.

sponsus2.full: sponsus, i, v. spondeo, P. a., A.

sponsus3.full: sponsus, ūs, m. spondeo, an engagement, betrothal; bail, suretyship (rare but class.): quod sponsu erat alligatus, Varr. L. L. 6, § 71 sq. Müll.: de sponsu si quid perspexeris, Cic. Att. 12, 19, 2: agere cum aliquo ex sponsu, Varr. 1. 1.: sponsu locare, Phaedr. 1, 16, 1; Sulp. ap. Gell. 4, 4, 2: lex Furia de sponsu adversus eum, qui, etc., Gai. Inst. 4, 22.

spontalis.full: spontālis, e, adj. sponte, voluntary (post-class.): parricidium, App. M. 4, p. 147, 25: sobrietas, id. ib. 11, p. 272, 30.—* Adv.: spontālĭter, voluntarily: facere (opp. coactus), Sid. Ep. 8, 9.

spontaneus.full: spontānĕus, a, um, adj. sponte, of one's free will, voluntary, spontaneous (late Lat.): mors, Macr. Somn. Scip. 2, 22: voluntas, free will, Cod. Just. 2, 3, 2: benignitates numinum, Arn. 3, p. 114.—Adv.: spontānĕē, voluntarily, willingly, of one's own mind: apparere tumores, Theod. Prisc. 1, 8; Vulg. 1 Pet. 5, 2; Hier. Ep. 52, n. 7.

sponte.full: sponte, abl., and spontis, gen. (perh. the only cases in use of a noun spons, assumed by Charis. p. 34 P., and Aus. Idyll. 12, 8, 11, as nom. But ad spontem is Müller's reading, Varr. L. L. 6, 7, 72, for a sponte), f. spondeo; prop. a pledging of one's self to a thing; hence, opp. to external necessity or inducement, of free will, of one's own accord. Sponte, in good prose always joined with meā, tuā, suā (poet. and in post-Aug. prose; also absol. or with gen.), of free will, of one's own accord

sporades.full: Spŏrădes, um, f., = Σποράδες, islands in the Ægean Sea, between the Cyclades and Crete, Mel. 2, 7, 11; Plin. 4, 12, 23, § 63.—Acc. Sporadas, Prisc. Perieg. 550.
sporades.short: Spŏrădes, um, f., = Σποράδες, islands in the Ægean Sea, between the Cyclades and Crete, Mel.

sporta.full: sporta, ae, f. cf. Gr. σπυρίς, basket σπάρτον, σπεῖρα, a plaited basket or ham per, Cato, R. R. 11, 4; Varr. and Sall. ap. Non. 177, 22 sq.; Col. 8, 7, 1; 12, 6, 1.— A sieve, Plin. 18, 7, 17, § 77; Mart. 10, 37, 17; Dig. 33, 9, 3; Vulg. Matt. 15, 37; Inscr. Grut. 440, 8.

sportella.full: sportella, ae, f. dim. sporta, a little basket, a fruit-basket, Cic. Fam. 9, 20, 2; Petr. 40, 3; Suet. Dom. 4.

sportula.full: sportŭla, ae, f. dim. id.. Lit., a little basket: sportulam cape atque argentum, Plaut. Men. 1, 4, 1; id. Curc. 2, 3, 10; id. Stich. 2, 1, 17; App. M. 1, p. 113, 39; Ascon. ad Cic. Verr. 1, 8.—In such little baskets it was customary for a great man to distribute presents of food or money to the mass of his clients, Juv. 1, 95; 3, 249; Suet. Ner. 16; Mart. 3, 14, 3; 14, 125, 2; 10, 27, 3.—Hence, the emperor Claudius called the brief games which he gave to the people sportulae, acc. to Suet. Claud

sportulo.full: sportŭlo, āvi, 1, v. n., to take the dole of a patron (late Lat.), Cypr. Ep. 6, 6.

sporus.full: Spŏrus, i, m., a eunuch, a favorite of Nero, Suet. Ner. 28; 46 al.
sporus.short: Spŏrus, i, m., a eunuch, a favorite of Nero, Suet.

spretio.full: sprētĭo, ōnis, f. sperno, a despising, disdain, scorn, contempt: Romanorum, Liv. 40, 5 dub.; Ambros. Enarr. in Psa. 43, § 54.

spretor.full: sprētor, ōris, m. id., a despiser, disdainer, scorner, contemner (poet. and very rare): deorum, Ov. M. 8, 613: morarum, Nemes. Cyn. 79: matronalium amplexuum, App. M. 3, p. 137, 39.

spretus1.full: sprētus, a, um, Part. of sperno.

spretus2.full: sprētus, ūs, m. sperno, a despising, disdain, scorn, contempt (post-class. and very rare): insolentissimo spretu deos neglegit, App. de Deo Socr. p. 43, 3: spretui maximc est judiciis, Sid. Ep. 3, 14 fin.

spuma.full: spūma, ae, f. spuo. In gen., foam, froth, scum, spume from the mouth; of the sea; in boiling, etc. (class.; used alike in sing. and plur.): spiritus (equi) ex animā calidā spumas agit albas, foams, Enn. ap. Macr. 6, 3 (Ann. v. 507 Vahl.): vi morbi coactus Concidit et spumas agit, Lucr. 3, 489; cf.: cum spumas ageret in ore, Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 66, § 148; Ov. M. 3, 74: per armos Spuma (apri) fluit, id. ib. 8, 288: Venus altera spuma procreata, Cic. N. D. 3, 23, 59; cf. Ov. M. 4, 538: spumas salis ae

spumabundus.full: spūmābundus, a, um, adj. spumo, foaming, frothing, App. Mag. p. 303, 1.

spumatio.full: spūmātĭo, ōnis, f. id., a foaming, Cael. Aur. Acut. 3, 2, 8.

spumatus.full: spūmātus, ūs, m. id., a foaming, frothing, foam, froth: anguis abundat spumatu, Stat. S. 1, 4, 103.

spumesco.full: spūmesco, ĕre, v. inch. n. [spuma], to grow foamy or frothy, to begin to foam or froth: aequora remo, Ov. H. 2, 87.

spumeus.full: spūmĕus, a, um, adj. id., foaming, frothy (poet. and in post-Aug. prose): Nereus, Verg. A. 2, 419: amnis, id. ib. 2, 496: unda, id. ib. 10, 212: torrens, Ov. M. 3, 571: aper, Mart. 14, 221, 2: cumulus undarum, Luc. 9, 798: Rhodanus, Amm. 15, 11, 18: rabies per ora effluit, Luc. 5, 190; cf.: salivae hominis, Prud. στεφ. 1, 101: sucus malorum, Plin. 15, 28, 33, § 109: semen heraclii, id. 20, 19, 79, § 207: color equorum, foamlike, i. e. dappled, Pall. Mart. 13, 4.

spumidus.full: spūmĭdus, a, um, adj. id., foaming, frothy (Appuleian): umor, App. Mag. p. 306: tabes, id. ib. p. 306.

spumifer.full: spūmĭfer, ĕra, ĕrum, adj. spuma-fero, foam-bearing, foaming (poet.): amnis, Ov. Am. 3, 6, 46: fons, id. M. 11, 140: fluctus, Stat. Achill. 1, 59.

spumigena.full: spūmĭgĕna, ae, f. spuma-gigno, foam-born, an epithet of Venus, Mart. Cap. 9, § 915.

spumiger.full: spūmĭger, gĕra, gĕrum, adj. spumagero, making foam, foaming: sus, Lucr. 5, 985: lupi, Manil. 5, 74.

spumo.full: spūmo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. n. and a. [spuma]. Neutr., to foam, froth (poet. and in post-Aug. prose): caeruleum spumat sale, Enn. ap. Gell. 2, 26 (Ann. v. 378 Vahl.): maria salsa spumant sanguine, id. Non. 183, 19 (Trag. v. 145 ib.): fluctu spumabant caerula cano, Verg. A. 8, 672: adductis spumant freta versa lacertis, id. ib. 5, 141; cf. Lucr. 3, 493: spumans aper, Verg. A. 4, 158; Claud. Rapt. Pros. 2, 243: Amasenus spumabat, Verg. A. 11, 548: equus spumat habenis, Luc. 6, 399: pocula bina novo sp

spumosus.full: spūmōsus, a, um, adj. spuma. Lit., full of foam, foaming (poet. and in postAug. prose): unda, Verg. A. 6, 174: litora, Cat. 64, 121: undae, Ov. M. 1, 570: aequor, Luc. 2, 627: morsus equi, Claud. IV. Cons. Hon. 548: spumosus nec sanguineus (pulmo), Plin. 11, 37, 72, § 188.—Comp.: Addua, Claud. VI. Cons. Hon. 458.—* Trop.: carmen, frothy, bombastic, Pers. 1, 96.

spuo.full: spŭo, ui, ūtum, 3, v. n. and a. [Sanscr. shtiv.; Gr. πτύω; Germ. speien; Engl. spit], to spit, to spit out, spew (very rare; not in Cic.). Neutr.: Antoniam Drusi non spuisse percelebre est, Sol. 1, § 74: ex toto spuere desisse, Cels. 2, 8, § 77: in faciem alicujus, Vulg. Num. 12, 14.—Esp., as a charm against fascination, etc. (cf. conspuo, I. fin.): veniam a deis petimus spuendo in sinum, Plin. 28, 4, 7, § 35; cf.: qui sputatur morbus, Plaut. Capt. 3, 4, 18 sqq. Brix ad loc.; Schol. Juv. 7, 112

spurcalia.full: spurcālĭa, ĭum, n. plur. [spurco], pollutions (late Lat.), Aldh. Laud. Virg. 25.

spurcamen.full: spurcāmen, ĭnis, n. id., dirt, filth, Prud. Cath. 9, 56.

spurcidicus.full: spurcĭdĭcus, a, um, adj. spurcusdico, using filthy language, smutty, obscene: versus, Plaut. Capt. prol. 56.

spurcificus.full: spurcĭfĭcus, a, um, adj. spurcusfacio, making filthy, smutty, obscene, Plaut. Trin. 4, 1, 7.

spurciloquium.full: spurcĭlŏquĭum, ii, n. spurcus-loquor, filthy or smutty language, obscenity, Tert. Res. Carn. 4 fin.

spurcitia.full: spurcĭtĭa, ae (nom. collat. form spur-cĭtĭes, Lucr. 6, 977; abl. spurcitie, App. M. 8, p. 214, 33), f. spurcus, filth, dirt, smut, dung (rare; not in Cic.). Lit., Col. 1, 5, 8; 12, 17, 2; Plin. 33, 4, 21, § 69; plur., Varr. R. R. 3, 16, 17: spurcitias suum laudant, Plin. 17, 9, 6, § 52.— Trop.: alicujus, Afran. ap. Non. 393, 33: patris, id. ib. 394, 4.

spurco.full: spurco, no perf., ātum, 1, v. a. id., to make filthy, to befoul, defile (rare; syn.: polluo, contamino). Lit.: si quis fimo aliquem pertuderit, luto oblinierit, aquā spurcaverit, Dig. 47, 11, 1: vinum, ib. 9, 2, 27: ex istoc loco spurcatur nasum odore inlutili, Plaut. Men. 1, 2, 57.—* Trop.: senectus Spurcata impuris moribus, Cat. 108, 2.—P. a.: spurcātus, a, um, sup.: helluo spurcatissimus, most foul, Cic. Dom. 10, 25 B. and K.

spurcus.full: spurcus, a, um, adj. cf. spargo, dirty, unclean, impure (class.; syn.: immundus, impurus, obscenus). Lit.: res, Lucr. 6, 782; cf.: rem spurcissimam gustare, Varr. ap. Non. 394, 11: quaeque aspectu sunt spurca et odore, Lucil. ib. 394, 25: saliva, Cat. 78, 8; 99, 10: ager, Col. 1, praef. § 25: spurcum atque pollutum vas, Gell. 17, 19, 4; App. M. 1, p. 108, 21: si quid est urinā spurcius, Gell. 17, 19, 4: tempestas spurcissima, Cic. Fragm. ap. Non. 394, 9: spurcatissimis tempestatibus, Suet. Caes.

spurinna.full: Spūrinna, ae, m. Etruscan, the surname of several Romans. The haruspex who warned Cœsar to beware of the Ides of March, Cic. Div. 1, 52, 119; id. Fam. 9, 24, 2; Suet. Caes. 81; Val. Max. 1, 6, 13; 8, 11, 2.— Vestricius Spurinna, a lyric poet, the leader of the Othonian party, Tac. H. 2, 11; 2, 18; 2, 36; Plin. Ep. 2, 7, 1; 3, 1, 1.

spurium.full: spŭrĭum, ii, n. σπορά, generation. = pudendum muliebre, acc. to Isid. Orig. 9, 5, 24; cf. Plut. Quaest. Rom. 103.— Transf., a marine animal of a similar shape, App. Mag. p. 297, 11.

spurius1.full: spŭrĭus, i, m. root spar-; cf. σπείρω, σπορά, and sperno, adj. Lit., of illegitimate birth; subst., an illegitimate or spurious child, a bastard (only post-class.; esp. among jurists): si quis nefarias atque incestas nuptias contraxerit, neque uxorem habere videtur neque liberos. Hi enim, qui ex eo coitu nascuntur, matrem quidem habere videntur, patrem vero non utique, etc. ... Unde solent spurii filii appeliari, vel a Graecā voce, quasi σποράδην concepti vel quasi sine patre filii, Gai. Inst. 1

spurius2.full: Spŭrĭus (abbrev. Sp.), a Roman prœnomen; e. g. Spurius Cassius, Spurius Maelius, Cic. Rep. 2, 27, 50; Liv. 2, 41; 4, 13.

sputamen.full: spūtāmen, inis, n. sputo, spittle (late Lat.), Prud. Apoth. 744; Tert. adv. Gnost. 10; plur., Cael. Aur. Tard. 2, 14, 199.

sputamentum.full: spūtāmentum, i, n. id., spittle (late Lat.), Jul. Val Rer. Gest. Alex. 1, 2; Tert. Spect. 30.

sputatilicus.full: spūtātĭlĭcus, a, um, adj. id., that deserves to be spit at, abominable, detestable (a word coined by Sisenna): crimina ejus, Sisenn. ap. Cic. Brut. 75, 260 (= κατάπτυστα).

sputator.full: spūtātor, ōris, m. id., one who spits much, a spitter, Plaut. Mil. 3, 1, 52.

sputo.full: spūto, āre, v. freq. a. spuo, to spit, spit out (mostly ante-class.): sanguinem, Plaut. Merc. 1, 2, 30: morbus, qui sputatur, that disease before which one spits, i. e. the epilepsy, id. Capt. 3, 4, 18 (cf. Plin. 10, 23, 33, § 69; 28, 4, 7, § 35): mixtos sputantem sanguine dentes, Ov. M. 12, 256.

sputum.full: spūtum, i, n., v. spuo fin.

sputus.full: spūtus, ūs, m. spuo, a spitting (late Lat.), Cael. Aur. Tard. 4, 4, 80; 3, 2, 18; Auct. ap. Lact. 4, 18; Aug. Civ. Dei, 18, 23.

squalefacio.full: squālĕfăcĭo, ĕre, 3, v. a. squalidusfacio, to make squalid (late Lat.), Petr. Chrysol. Serm. 164.

squalentia.full: squālentĭa, ae, f. squaleo, dirt, filth, Tert. Exh. ad Cast. 10.

squaleo.full: squālĕo, ŭi, 2, v. n. squalor, to be stiff or rough with any thing, etc. (mostly poet. and in post-Aug. prose; cf. sordeo). Lit. In gen.: squalentes infode conchas, i. e. rough, Verg. G. 2, 348: per tunicam squalentem auro, id. A. 10, 314; cf.: auro squalens lorica, id. ib. 12, 87: maculis auro squalentibus, id. G. 4, 91; Sil. 2, 585: picti squalentia terga lacerti, Verg. G. 4, 13: squalentia tela venenis, Ov. F. 5, 397.— In partic. To be stiff or rough from dryness or drought, to be dry, parche

squales.full: squāles, is, f. squaleo, II., filth, dirt: ager periret squale, Varr. ap. Non. 226, 5; 125, 33; 168, 20: squale scabieque, Pac. ib. 152, 29 (Trag. Rel. v. 314 Rib.).

squaliditas.full: squālĭdĭtas, ātis, f. squalidus, filth, dirt, squalidity; trop., neglect, disorder (late Lat.): omnia confundentes squaliditate, Amm. 26, 5, 15.

squalidus.full: squālĭdus, a, um, adj. squaleo. (Acc. to squaleo, I.) In gen., stiff, rough (ante-class.): corpora, Lucr. 2, 469: membra, id. 5, 956: serpentis squamae squalido auro et purpurā praetextae, Att. ap. Gell. 2, 6, 23; id. ap. Non. 452, 28 (Trag. Fragm. v. 517 Rib.).— (Acc. to squaleo, II.) In partic. Stiff with dirt, dirty, foul, filthy, neglected, squalid (poet. and in post-Aug. prose): stola, Enn. ap. Non. 537, 26 (Trag. v. 373 Vahl.): homo horridus et squalidus, Plaut. Truc. 5, 41 sq.; Ter. Eun.

squalitas.full: squālĭtas, ātis, f. id., dirt, filth, Att. and Lucil. ap. Non. 226, 4 sq. (Att. Trag. Fragm. v. 617 Rib.).

squalitudo.full: squālĭtūdo, ĭnis, f. squalidus, dirt, filth, Att. ap. Non. 226, 2 (Trag. Rel. v. 340 Rib.).

squalor.full: squālor, ōris, m. Sanscr. kālas, black; Gr. κελαινός, κηλίς. In gen., stiffness, roughness: quaecumque (res) aspera constat, Non aliquo sine materiae squalore reperta est (opp. lēvor), Lucr. 2, 425.— In partic., stiffness from dirt, dirtiness, filthiness, foulness, squalor (the predom. signif. of the word; syn.: sordes, illuvies). Lit. In gen.: immundas fortunas aequum est squalorem sequi, Plaut. Cist. 1, 1, 115: squaloris plenus ac pulveris (opp. unguentis oblitus), Cic. Verr. 2, 3, 12, § 31: o

squalus1.full: squālus, a, um, adj. squales, dirty, filthy, squalid, = squalidus: lavere lacrimis vestem squalam et sordidam, Enn. ap. Non. 172, 20 (Trag. v. 370 Vahl.).

squalus2.full: squălus, i, m., a kind of sea-fish, Varr. R. R. 3, 3, 9 Schneid. N. cr.; Plin. 9, 24, 40, § 78; 9, 51, 74, § 162; Ov. Hal. 123.
squalus2.short: squălus, i, m., a kind of sea-fish, Varr.

squama.full: squāma, ae, f., a scale (of a fish, serpent, etc.). Lit.: alias (animantes) squamis obductas, Cic. N. D. 2, 47, 121.—Of a serpent: tractu squamae crepitantis harenam Sulcat, Ov. M. 15, 725: hydri, Verg. G. 3, 545; id. A. 5, 88; 11, 754; Ov. M. 3, 63; 4, 577.—Of a fish: alia integuntur squamis ut pisces, Plin. 9, 12, 14, § 114; Claud. in Eutr. 1, 295.—Of bees: rutilis clarus squamis, Verg. G. 4, 93.— Transf. * Poet., a fish, Juv. 4, 25.— Of scaleshaped things (poet. and in post-Aug. prose). Scale
squama.short: squāma, ae, f., a scale (of a fish, serpent, etc.).

squamatim.full: squāmātim, adv. squama, like scales: compacta nucamenta, Plin. 16, 10, 19, § 49.

squamatus.full: squāmātus, a, um, adj. id., scaly, Tert. Apol. 21: lorica squamata, Vulg. 1 Reg. 17, 5.

squameus.full: squāmĕus, a, um, adj. id., scaly (poet.). Lit.: anguis, Verg. G. 2, 154: terga (anguium), id. A. 2, 218: membrana chelydri, Ov. M. 7, 272.—* Transf.: clipeatus et auro Squameus, in golden scales (of a coat of mail), Claud. IV. Cons. Hon. 522.

squamifer.full: squāmĭfer, fĕra, fĕrum, adj. squamafero, scale - bearing, scaly (poet.): orbes, Luc. 9, 709: turba (anguium), Sen. Med. 685.

squamiger.full: squāmĭger, gĕra, gĕrum, adj. squamagero, scale-bearing, scaly (poet. and in postAug. prose): pisces, Cic. Arat. 328 (574): cervices (anguis), Ov. M. 4, 717.—Subst.: squāmĭgĕri, ōrum, m., fishes, Lucr. 1, 162; 1, 370 sq.; 2, 343; 2, 1083; Plin. 11, 37, 50, § 137.

squamosus.full: squāmōsus (-mossus), a, um, adj. squama, full of or covered with scales, scaly, squamous (poet. and in post - Aug. prose). Lit.: pecus (i. e. pisces), Plaut. Rud. 4, 3, 5: soleamne esse avis squamossas? id. Men. 5, 5, 19: draco, Verg. G. 4, 408; cf.: venter cerastae, Prop. 3 (4), 22, 27. orbes (anguis), Ov. M. 3, 41: greges (piscium), Col. 8, 17, 2: agmina, Prud. στεφ. 5, 144: belua, Sen. Hippol. 1048: pellis, Claud. Laud. Stil. 1, 263.— Transf.: thorax, Prud. Ham. 423: smaragdi, Plin. 37, 5, 18

squamula.full: squāmŭla, ae, f. dim. id., a little scale, Cels. 7, 26, 3; 5, 28, 17; 5, 6, 2.

squarrosus.full: squarrōsus, a, um, adj. (perh. scurfy, scabby, scalled): squarrosi a squamarum similitudine dicti, quorum cutis exsurgit ob assiduam illuviem, Fest. pp. 328 and 329 Muüll.; Lucil. ap. Fest. l. l.

squatina.full: squātĭna, ae, f. cf. Gr. κῆτος, a species of shark, the angel-fish, skate: Squalus squatina, Linn.; Plin. 9, 12, 14, § 40; 9, 51, 74, § 162.—Called also squātus; cf. Isid. Orig. 12, 6, 37; Plin. 32, 11, 53, § 150; and: squatus ῥίνα, εἶδος ἰχθύος, Gloss. Philox.

st.full: st, interj., hist! whist! hush! st, tale verbum cave faxis, Naev. ap. Charis. p. 214 P.: st, st, tacete, Plaut. Ep. 2, 2, 1: st, tacete, quid hoc clamoris? Poët. ap. Cic. de Or. 2, 64, 257: st, litteras tuas exspecto, Cic. Fam. 16, 24, 2; Plaut. Bacch. 5, 2, 37; id. Most. 2, 2, 58; 2, 2, 74; 3, 2, 163 sq. al.; Ter. And. 4, 1, 59; id. Heaut. 3, 3, 36; id. Phorm. 2, 3, 3; 5, 1, 16.
st.short: st, interj., hist! whist! hush! st, tale verbum cave faxis, Naev.

'st.full: 'st, abbrev. for est, v. sum init.

staberius.full: Stăbĕrĭus, ii, m., the name of a Latin grammarian, Suet. Gram. 13; Plin. 35, 7, 58, § 199.
staberius.short: Stăbĕrĭus, ii, m., the name of a Latin grammarian, Suet.

stabiae.full: Stăbĭae, ārum, f., a small town on the coast of Campania near Pompeii, celebrated for its medicinal springs. It was partially destroyed by Sylla during the Social War, and was finally overwhelmed at the same time with Herculaneum and Pompeii, Plin. 3, 5, 9, § 70; Ov. M. 15, 711; Col. poët. 10, 133; Plin. Ep. 6, 16, 12.—Hence, Stăbĭā-nus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Stabiœ, Stabian: litus, Sen. Q. N. 6, 1, 1.—Subst.: Stăbĭānum, i, n. The Stabian territory: in Stabiano, Plin. 31, 2, 5, § 9.— A
stabiae.short: Stăbĭae, ārum, f., a small town on the coast of Campania near Pompeii, celebrated for its medicinal springs.

stabilimen.full: stăbĭlīmen, ĭnis, n. stabilio, a stay, support, stabiliment: regni stabilimen, Att. ap. Cic. poët. N. D. 3, 26, 68 (Fragm. Trag. v. 210 Rib.).

stabilimentum.full: stăbĭlīmentum, i, n. id., a stay, support, stabiliment (very rare; not in Cic.). Lit.: haec sunt ventris stabilimenta, pane et assa bubula, Poclum grande, Plaut. Curc. 2, 3, 88: favorum, Plin. 11, 7, 6, § 16. —* Trop.: Sicilia et Sardinia stabilimenta bellorum, Val. Max. 7, 6, 1 fin.

stabilio.full: stăbĭlĭo, īvi, ītum (sync. imperf. stabilibat, Enn. Ann. 44), 4, v. a. stabilis, to make firm, steadfast, or stable; to fix, stay, establish (class.; esp. in the trop. sense). Lit.: semita nulla pedem stabilibat, Enn. ap. Cic. Div. 1, 20, 40 (Ann. v. 44 Vahl.): eo stabilita magis sunt, Lucr. 3, 202; cf.: confirmandi et stabiliendi causā singuli ab infimo solo pedes terrā exculcabantur, * Caes. B. G. 7, 73: vineas, Col. 4, 33, 1: loligini pedes duo, quibus se velut ancoris stabiliunt, Plin. 9, 28

stabilis.full: stăbĭlis, e, adj. sto, prop. where one can stand; hence, pregn., that stands firm; firm, steadfast, steady, stable (class.; esp. in the trop. sense; syn.: firmus, constans). Lit.: via plana et stabilis (opp. praeceps et lubrica), Cic. Fl. 42, 105: locus ad insistendum, Liv. 44, 5, 10: solum, id. 44, 9, 7: stabulum, Plaut. Aul. 2, 2, 56: domus, id. Merc. 3, 4, 68: medio sedet insula ponto, Ov. F. 4, 303: per stabilem ratem tamquam viam, Liv. 21, 28, 8: elephanti pondere ipso stabiles, id. 21, 28,

stabilitas.full: stăbĭlĭtas, ātis, f. stabilis, a standing fast or firm, steadfastness, firmness, durability, immovability, stability (class.). Lit.: ita mobilitatem equitum, stabilitatem peditum in proeliis praestant, * Caes. B. G. 4, 33: stirpes stabilitatem dant iis, quae sustinent, Cic. N. D. 2, 47, 120: dentium, Plin. 23, 3, 37, § 74.— Trop.: qui poterit aut corporis firmitate aut fortunae stabilitate confidere? Cic. Tusc. 5, 14, 40: benevolentiam non stabilitate et constantiā judicare, id. Off. 1, 15, 47;

stabilitor.full: stăbĭlītor, ōris, m. stabilio, an establisher (post-Aug.): Deus, quod stant beneficio ejus omnia, stator stabilitorque est, Sen. Ben. 4, 7, 2.

stabularius.full: stăbŭlārĭus, a, um, adj. stabulum, of or belonging to a stopping-place or stable (post - Aug.): stabularia mulier, a hostess, landlady, Aug. Civ. Dei, 18, 18.—As subst.: stăbŭlārĭus, i, m. * A stable - boy, hostler, Col. 6, 23 fin.— A host, landlord of the lowest kind of inn; a tavern-keeper, stable-keeper, Sen. Ben. 1, 14, 1; Dig. 4, 9, 5; 47, 5, 1; App. M. 1, p. 110, 9; Vulg. Luc. 10, 35.

stabulatio.full: stăbŭlātĭo, ōnis, f. stabulor, a place where cattle stand or are housed: hiberna, Col. 6, 3, 1.

stabulo.full: stăbŭlo, āre, v. stabulor, I. β, and II.

stabulor.full: stăbŭlor, ātus, 1, v. dep. n. (collat. form stăbŭlo, āre; v. in the foll.) [stabulum] (mostly poet. and post-Aug.; not in Cic.). Neutr., to have an abode anywhere; to stable, kennel, harbor, roost, etc. (mostly of animals). Dep. form: aviaria, in quibus stabulentur turdi ac pavones, Varr. R. R. 3, 3, 7: bos sicce, Col. 6, 12, 2: pecudes multae in antris, Ov. M. 13, 822: pisces in petris, Col. 8, 16, 8: serpens in illis locis, Gell. 6, 3, 1: ut permittat jumenta apud eum stabulari, Dig. 4, 9, 5.—

stabulum.full: stăbŭlum, i, n. sto, a standing-place, abode, habitation, dwelling. In gen. (very rare; perh. only in the foll. passages): stabile stabulum, Plaut. Aul. 2, 2, 56; cf.: nusquam stabulum est confidentiae, id. Most. 2, 1, 3: DOMESTICORVM ET STABVLI SACRI, Inscr. Orell. 1134.— A stoppingplace or abode for animals or persons of the lower class (freq. and class.). For animals, a stall, stable, enclosure of any kind (cf. praesepe): ovium, Varr. R. R. 2, 2, 19: pecudum, boum, etc., Col. 1, 6, 4; 6, 23,

stachys.full: stăchys, ўos, f., = στάχυς, a plant, horsemint, Plin. 24, 15, 86, § 136.
stachys.short: stăchys, ўos, f., = στάχυς, a plant, horsemint, Plin.

stacta.full: stacta, ae, or stactē, ēs, f., = στακτή, myrrh-oil. Stacta, Lucr. 2, 847; Plaut. Truc. 2, 5, 23; id. Most. 1, 3, 151; Plin. 12, 15, 35, § 70.— Stacte, Plaut. Curc. 1, 2, 5; Plin. 13, 1, 2, § 17.—Also, myrrha stacta (stacte), Scrib. Comp. 125; 145; Plin. 12, 15, 35, § 68.—Plur., Col. poët. 10, 173.
stacta.short: stacta, ae, or stactē, ēs, f., = στακτή, myrrh-oil.

stacton.full: stacton, i, n., = στακτόν, a kind of eye-salve, Scrib. Comp. 34.
stacton.short: stacton, i, n., = στακτόν, a kind of eye-salve, Scrib.

stacula.full: stacŭla, ae, f., a kind of vine, also called sircula, Plin. 14, 2, 4, § 34 (Jahn, scapula).
stacula.short: stacŭla, ae, f., a kind of vine, also called sircula, Plin.

stadia.full: Stadia, ae, f., an ancient name of the town of Cnidus in Caria, Plin. 5, 28, 29, § 104.
stadia.short: Stadia, ae, f., an ancient name of the town of Cnidus in Caria, Plin.

stadialis.full: stădĭālis, e, adj. stadium, of or containing a stadium: ager, Auct. Grom. ap. Goes. p. 321.

stadiatus.full: stădĭātus, a, um, adj. id., furnished with a race-course: porticus, Vitr. 5, 11 med.

stadiodromos.full: stădĭŏdrŏmos, i, m., = σταδιόδρομος, a runner in a foot-race, Firm. Math. 8, 8.—A statue of Astylon, Plin. 34, 8, 19, § 59; Censor. 14, 5.
stadiodromos.short: stădĭŏdrŏmos, i, m., = σταδιόδρομος, a runner in a foot-race, Firm.

stadios.full: Stadĭos, i, m., a Greek painter, Plin. 35, 11, 42, § 146.
stadios.short: Stadĭos, i, m., a Greek painter, Plin.

stadisis.full: Stadisis, is, f., a town in Ethiopia, Plin. 6, 29, 35, § 81.
stadisis.short: Stadisis, is, f., a town in Ethiopia, Plin.

stadium.full: stădĭum, ii, n. (masc. collat. form, acc. plur. stadios, Macr. Somn. Scip. 1, 15 med.; gen. plur. usu. stadium; but stadiorum, Plin. 2, 108, 112, § 247; 4, 1, 2, § 5; 4, 12, 24, § 75), = στάδιον. In gen., a stade, stadium, a distance of 125 paces, or 625 Roman feet, equal to 606 feet 9 inches English; it was an eighth part of a milliarium, or somewhat less than an eighth of an English mile, Plin. 2, 23, 21, § 85; Col. 5, 1, 6; Censor. de Die Nat. 13; Cic. Fin. 5, 1, 1; id. Ac. 2, 31, 100; id. Fa

stadius.full: Stadius, ii, m., the name of a man, Pers. 6, 65.
stadius.short: Stadius, ii, m., the name of a man, Pers.

stagira.full: Stăgīra, ōrum, n., = Στάγειρα, a town in Macedonia, the birthplace of Aristotle, Plin. 4, 10, 17, § 38; Amm. 27, 4, 8.—Hence, Stăgīrītes, ae, m., = Σταγειρίτης, the Stagirite, i. e. Aristotle, Cic. Ac. 1, 4, 17; also written Stăgērītes, Varr. R. R. 2, 1, 3.
stagira.short: Stăgīra, ōrum, n., = Στάγειρα, a town in Macedonia, the birthplace of Aristotle, Plin.

stagnatilis.full: stagnātĭlis, e, adj. stagnum, of or belonging to ponds or pools: pisces, Plin. Val. 5, 42.

stagnensis.full: stagnensis, e, adj. stagnum. of or belonging to ponds or pools: aves, Aug. in Psa. 1, 103.

stagninus.full: stagnīnus, a, um, adj. stagnum, resembling stagnant water: color perviridis, Front. Aquaed. 7 dub.

stagno1.full: stagno, āvi, ātum, 1, v. n. and a. [id.]. Neutr. Lit., to form a pool of standing water, to stagnate, be stagnant (mostly poet. and in post-Aug. prose; not in Cic.; cf. redundo): stagnans Nilus, Verg. G. 4, 288: ubi mollius solum reperit (Indus) stagnat insulasque molitur, Curt. 8, 9, 7: nam flumen, quo latius fusum est, hoc placidius stagnat, id. 9, 2, 17: aquae stagnantes, id. 8, 13, 9: stagnantibus undis, Sil. 5, 95: Nili aquae, ubi evagatae stagnant, Plin. 13, 11, 22, § 71; 31, 3, 21, § 31:

stagno2.full: stagno, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. stagnum = stannum; cf. stagneus, s. v. stanneus. Lit., to overlay or plate with stannum (post-class.), Plin. Val. 1, 31 med.; 3, 4 med. — Trop., to make fast, strengthen, fortify: se adversus insidias, Just. 37, 2, 6: potionibus stagnata animalia, strengthened, invigorated, Veg. 1, 18 fin.; 3, 2, 5.

stagnosus.full: stagnōsus, a, um, adj. stagnum, full of standing waters or pools (post-Aug.): Liternum, Sil. 6, 653: loca, App. Herb. 8.— Absol.: stagnosa et referta salicibus, places full of pools, Amm. 17, 13, 4.

stagnum1.full: stagnum, i, n. cf. Gr. τέναγος = vadum. Lit., a piece of standing water (whether permanent or formed by the overflowing of a stream], a pool, pond, swamp, fen, etc. (cf.: lacus, palus): propter stagna, ubi lanigerum pecus piscibus pascit, Enn. ap. Paul. ex Fest. p. 59 Müll. (Sat. v. 42 Vahl.): super ripas Tiberis effusus lenibus stagnis, Liv. 1, 4, 4; cf. Varr. ap. Non. 217, 2 (as an example for stativae aquae); Cic. poët. Div. 1, 9; Auct. ap. Cic. Agr. 3, 2, 7; Tib. 1, 3, 77; Verg. A. 6, 323: u

stagnum2.full: stagnum, = stannum, whence 2. stagno, and the orthog. stagneus, for stanneus.

stagonias.full: stăgŏnĭas, ae, m., = σταγονίας (dropping), a kind of frankincense, Plin. 12, 14, 32, § 62.
stagonias.short: stăgŏnĭas, ae, m., = σταγονίας (dropping), a kind of frankincense, Plin.

stagonitis.full: stăgŏnītis, ĭdis, f., = σταγονῖτις, gum galbanum, Plin. 12, 25, 56, § 126.
stagonitis.short: stăgŏnītis, ĭdis, f., = σταγονῖτις, gum galbanum, Plin.

staienus.full: Stāiēnus, i, m., a Roman surname, e. g. C. Aelius Paetus Staienus, a judge, Cic. Clu. 20, 55; 24, 64; cf. as a proverb of bad oratory: Staieni et Autronii, id. Brut. 69, 244; 72, 251.
staienus.short: Stāiēnus, i, m., a Roman surname, e.

stalagmias.full: stălagmĭas, ae, m., = σταλαγμίας, a natural vitriol, which distils in drops, Plin. 34, 12, 32, § 124.
stalagmias.short: stălagmĭas, ae, m., = σταλαγμίας, a natural vitriol, which distils in drops, Plin.

stalagmium.full: stălagmĭum, ii, n., = σταλάγμιον, an ear-drop, pendant, Plaut. Men. 3, 3, 18; Caecil. ap. Fest. p. 317 Müll. (Com. Rel. p. 45 Rib.).
stalagmium.short: stălagmĭum, ii, n., = σταλάγμιον, an ear-drop, pendant, Plaut.

stalagmus.full: Stālagmus, i, m., the name of a slave, Plaut. Capt. 4, 2, 95.
stalagmus.short: Stālagmus, i, m., the name of a slave, Plaut.

stamen.full: stāmen, ĭnis, n. sto, the warp in the upright loom of the ancients (cf.: trama, subtemen). Lit., Varr. L. L. 5, § 113 Müll.; Tib. 1, 3, 86; Ov. M. 6, 54 sq.; 6, 576; 4, 275; 4, 397 al.— Transf., in gen. A thread hanging from the distaff: aut ducunt lanas aut stamina pollice versant, Ov. M. 4, 34; 4, 179; 4, 221; 12, 475: operoso stamine, id. A. A. 1, 695: et minuent plenas stamina nostra colos, id. H. 3, 76: deducere plenā stamina longa colu, Tib. 1, 3, 86; 1, 6, 78: digitis dum torques stamina

staminatus.full: stāmĭnātus, a, um, adj. stamen, consisting of threads, Petr. 41 fin. dub.

stamineus.full: stāmĭnĕus, a, um, adj. id., consisting of threads, full of threads, thready: rota rhombi, Prop. 3, 6 (4, 5), 26: vena ligni, i. e. fibrous, Plin. 16, 43, 83, § 226.

stannatio.full: stannātĭo, ōnis, f., a trowel (late Lat.): stannatio sive trulla caementarii, Hier. in Amos, 3, 7.
stannatio.short: stannātĭo, ōnis, f., a trowel (late Lat.): stannatio sive trulla caementarii, Hier.

stannatura.full: stannātūra, ae, f., plastering, varnishing (late Lat.), Hier. in Amos, 3, 7.
stannatura.short: stannātūra, ae, f., plastering, varnishing (late Lat.), Hier.

stanneus.full: stannĕus (stagnĕus), a, um, adj. stannum, made of stannum: vasa, Plaut. Fragm. ap. Fest. s. v. narica, p. 166 Müll.; Plin. 30, 7, 19, § 38: cacabus, Col. 12, 42, 1: pyxis, Plin. 29, 2, 10, § 35; 30, 5, 12, § 38: nummi, Dig. 48, 10, 9.

stannum.full: stannum (perh. also stagnum; hence 2. stagno and stagneus, v. stanneus), i, n., an alloy of silver and lead, Plin. 34, 16, 47, § 159; 33, 9, 45, § 130; Suet. Vit. 5 fin.— Tin (late Lat. for plumbum album or candidum), Hier. in Zach. 1, 4, 10; Isid. Orig. 16, 22.

staphis.full: stăphis, ĭdis, f., = σταφίς, a plant, perh. licebane, staves - acre, Plin. 23, 1, 13, § 17; Pall. 1, 27, 2.
staphis.short: stăphis, ĭdis, f., = σταφίς, a plant, perh.

staphyla.full: Stăphўla, ae, and Stăphўlē, ēs, f., = σταφυλή, the name of a woman, Plaut. Aul. 2, 3, 2.
staphyla.short: Stăphўla, ae, and Stăphўlē, ēs, f., = σταφυλή, the name of a woman, Plaut.

staphylinus.full: staphўlīnus or -os, i, f., = σταφυλῖνος, a kind of parsnip, Plin. 19, 5, 27, § 88; 25, 9, 64, § 112; Col. 10, 168.
staphylinus.short: staphўlīnus or -os, i, f., = σταφυλῖνος, a kind of parsnip, Plin.

staphylodendron.full: stăphўlŏdendron, i, n., = σταφυλόδενδρον, the pistachio - tree: Staphylea pinnata, Linn.; Plin. 16, 16, 27, § 69.
staphylodendron.short: stăphўlŏdendron, i, n., = σταφυλόδενδρον, the pistachio - tree: Staphylea pinnata, Linn.;

staphyloma.full: staphўlōma, ătis, n., = σταφύλωμα, a blemish in the eye shaped like a grape. stone, Veg. 3, 19, 1.
staphyloma.short: staphўlōma, ătis, n., = σταφύλωμα, a blemish in the eye shaped like a grape.

staphylus.full: Staphўlus, i, m., a son of Silenus, who taught the art of mixing wine with water, Sall. H. 1, 87 Dietsch; Plin. 7, 56, 57, § 199.
staphylus.short: Staphўlus, i, m., a son of Silenus, who taught the art of mixing wine with water, Sall.

staseas.full: Stasĕas, ae, m., a Peripatetic philosopher of Neapolis, Cic. Or. 1, 22, 104; id. Fin. 5, 3, 8; 5, 25, 75.
staseas.short: Stasĕas, ae, m., a Peripatetic philosopher of Neapolis, Cic.

stasiastae.full: Stăsĭastae, ārum, m., = Στασιασταί, the name of a tragedy of Attius, v. the Fragments, Non. 20, 25 al.; Trag. Rel. p. 214 sqq. Rib.
stasiastae.short: Stăsĭastae, ārum, m., = Στασιασταί, the name of a tragedy of Attius, v.

stasimum.full: stăsĭmum, i, n., = στάσιμον, that part of a poem which was sung standing, Mar. Vict. 2, p. 2522 P.
stasimum.short: stăsĭmum, i, n., = στάσιμον, that part of a poem which was sung standing, Mar.

stasimus.full: Stăsĭmus, i, m., the name of a slave, Plaut. Trin. 2, 4, 3 al.
stasimus.short: Stăsĭmus, i, m., the name of a slave, Plaut.

statae.full: stătae mātris simulacrum in foro colebatur, identical with that of Vesta, Fest. p. 317 Müll.; Cic. Leg. 2, 11, 28; Inscr. Orell. 1386 sq.
statae.short: stătae mātris simulacrum in foro colebatur, identical with that of Vesta, Fest.

statanum.full: stătānum vīnum, an excellent kind of wine in Campania, Plin. 14, 6, 8, § 65; 23, 1, 21, § 36.
statanum.short: stătānum vīnum, an excellent kind of wine in Campania, Plin.

statanus.full: Stătānus and Stătŭlīnus, i, m. sto, the deity who presided over the standing of children, Varr. ap. Non. 532, 24 sq.; Aug. Civ. Dei, 4, 21.—As a female deity, called Stătīna, Tert. Anim. 39.

statarius.full: stătārĭus, a, um, adj. sto, of or belonging to standing or standing fast, standing, standing firm, stationary, steady (very rare; usually stabilis). In gen.: statarius miles, Liv. 9, 19: hostis, id. 22, 18: retia, i. e. that remain long in the water, Sid. Ep. 2, 2 med.: prandium, eaten standing, Mamert. Grat. Act. ad Jul. 11 fin.: congressio, i. e. a battle in the open field, Amm. 14, 2, 8.— Transf., calm, tranquil; of an orator: C. Piso, statarius et sermonis plenus orator, Cic. Brut. 68, 239.—

stater.full: stăter, ēris, m., = στατήρ, a small silver coin of the Jews, of the value of four drachmae, Hier. in Matt. 3, 17, 26; Vulg. 1 Reg. 9, 8; id. Matt. 17, 27.
stater.short: stăter, ēris, m., = στατήρ, a small silver coin of the Jews, of the value of four drachmae, Hier.

statera.full: stătēra, ae, f. perhaps kindred with στάθμη, a rule, a steelyard; also, a balance (syn.: libra, trutina). Lit., Vitr. 10, 8; Petr. 35; Suet. Vesp. 25; Plin. 31, 3, 23, § 38; Stat. S. 4, 9, 46: auraria, a goldsmith's scales, Varr. ap. Non. 455, 20; called also aurificis, Cic. de Or. 2, 38, 159.— Transf., of any thing of a similar shape. * The pole-bar of a chariot, Stat. S. 4, 3, 35.—* A kind of platter, so called from its resemblance to the scale of a steelyard or balance, Nep. ap. Plin. 33, 11,

statianus.full: Stătĭānus, i, m., the name of a lieutenant of Antony, Vell. 2, 82, 2.
statianus.short: Stătĭānus, i, m., the name of a lieutenant of Antony, Vell.

statice.full: stătĭcē, ēs, f., = στατική, an herb of an astringent quality: Statice armeria, Linn.; Plin. 26, 8, 33, § 51.
statice.short: stătĭcē, ēs, f., = στατική, an herb of an astringent quality: Statice armeria, Linn.;

staticulum.full: stătĭcŭlum, i, n. statua. A little statue or image, a statuette, Plin. 34, 17, 48, § 163; 37, 10, 54, § 140.— Of images of the gods, idols, as a transl. of the Heb. , Tert. adv. Gnost. 2 ex Deut. 12, 3; id. ib. fin. ex Lev. 26, 1.

staticulus.full: stătĭcŭlus, i, m., a kind of gentle dance, Cato ap. Macr. S. 2, 10 med.; Plaut. Pers. 5, 2, 43.
staticulus.short: stătĭcŭlus, i, m., a kind of gentle dance, Cato ap.

statielli.full: Statielli (Statelli), ōrum, m., a people of Liguria, Plin. 3, 5, 7, § 47; Liv. 42, 21.—Their chief town was called Aquae Statiellorum, Plin. l. l.; or Statĭellae, ārum, f., id. 31, 2, 2, § 4.—Hence, Sta-tiellas, ātis, adj., of or belonging to the Statielli: ager, Liv. 42, 7.—Subst.: Sta-tiellātes, ĭum, m., Liv. 42, 8; 42, 21.— Statiellenses, ĭum, m., the inhabitants of Aquae Statiellorum, Brut. ap. Cic. Fam. 11, 11, 2.
statielli.short: Statielli (Statelli), ōrum, m., a people of Liguria, Plin.

statilius.full: Stătĭlĭus, ii, m., a Roman name. L. Statilius, a fellow-conspirator with Catiline, Cic. Cat. 3, 3, 6; Sall. C. 17, 4; 43, 2; 46, 3; 55, 6.— L. Statilius, an augur, Cic. Att. 12, 13 and 14.— An indifferent actor, Cic. Rosc. Com. 10, 30.— Statilius Taurus, Varr. R. R. 2, 1, 10; cf. Inscr. Orell. 2725 sq.
statilius.short: Stătĭlĭus, ii, m., a Roman name.

statim.full: stătim (a scanned long, Avien. Arat. 397; Alcim. 2, 180), adv. sto. Firmly, steadily, steadfastly, unyieldingly (so only ante-class.): nemo recedit loco, quin statim rem gerat, Plaut. Am. 1, 1, 84; so, qui rem cum Achivis gesserunt statim, Enn. ap. Non. 393, 14 (Trag. v. 39 Vahl.); cf.: statim stant signa, Plaut. Am. 1, 1, 120: vectigalia legerunt vestra et servantur statim, steadily, regularly, Att. ap. Charis. p. 195 P. (statute et ordinate, Charis.); cf.: ex his praediis talenta argenti bina

statio.full: stătĭo, ōnis, f. sto, a standing, a standing still. Lit. (so very rare; not in Cic.): navis, quae manet in statione, remains standing, stands still, does not move, Lucr. 4, 388; so, manere in statione, id. 4, 396; 5, 478; 5, 518: in statione locata nubila, id. 6, 193: varas In statione manus et pugnae membra paravi, in a firm posture (for fighting), Ov. M. 9, 34: numquam id (sidus) stationem facere, stands still, Plin. 2, 17, 15, § 77: stationes matutinas facere, id. 2, 15, 12, § 59: solus immob

stationalis.full: stătĭōnālis, e, adj. statio, I., standing still, stationary, fixed: stella, Plin. 2, 15, 12, § 60.

stationarius.full: stătĭōnārĭus, a, um, adj. statio, II., of or belonging to a post or station (jurid. Lat.): stationarii milites, soldiers stationed at a post, a kind of gendarmery instituted by Augustus for suppressing the grassatores, Suet. Aug. 32; Dig. 11, 4, 1; 11, 4, 4; 1, 12, 1 fin.—As subst.: stătĭōnārĭus, i, m. A postman, postmaster at a post - station, Cod. Th. 8, 5, 1.— A police-officer, Cod. 12, 23, 1; 12, 58, 1; Cod. Th. 6, 29, 1; 8, 4, 2.

statius.full: Stātĭus, ii, m. Orig., a name for slaves, acc. to Gell. 4, 20, 12.—A slave of Cicero was thus named, Cic. Fam. 16, 16, 2; id. Att. 6, 2, 1; id. Q. Fr. 1, 2, 1, § 1.—Also a prœnomen of freemen, e. g. Statius Albius Oppianicus, Cic. Clu. 4, 9.— A surname (cognomen or agnomen). Caecilius Statius, of Insubria, a comic poet, a younger contemporary of Ennius, who died A. U. C. 586, Cic. Opt. Gen. 1, 2; id. Att. 7, 3, 10; Vell. 1, 17, 1.— P. Papinius Statius, a poet under Domitian, author of the Silvae

stativus.full: stătīvus, a, um, adj. sto, standing still, stationary. In gen. (very rare): de stativis aquis, ut sunt lacus et stagna et putea et maria, standing waters, Varr. ap. Non. 217, 2: tarditas, Firm. Math. 1, 2 fin.—Of a light (transl. of Gr. στηριγμός), App. de Mundo, 16, p. 64, 24.— In partic. In milit. lang., of or belonging to posts, stations, or quarters (the predom. signif. of the word): praesidium stativum, appointed post or station = statio, Cic. Phil. 12, 10, 24; Liv. 41, 1, 6; 44, 40, 6: cas

statones.full: Statones, um, m., the people of Statonia in Southern Etruria, celebrated for its vines and stone-quarries, Plin. 3, 5, 8, § 52. —Hence, Statonĭensis, e, adj., of or belonging to Statonia: ager, Plin. 2, 95, 96, § 209: vina, id. 14, 6, 8, § 67: lacus, Sen. Q. N. 3, 25, 8.—As subst.: Statonĭensis, is, m. (sc. ager), Plin. 36, 22, 49, § 168; Varr. R. R. 3, 12. 1.
statones.short: Statones, um, m., the people of Statonia in Southern Etruria, celebrated for its vines and stone-quarries, Plin.

stator1.full: stător, ōris, m. sto, a magistrate's attendant, servant, messenger, orderly-man (since Augustus there were centuriae statorum Augusti): statores mittere, Cic. Fam. 2, 19, 2; Planc. ib. 10, 21, 2; Dig. 4, 6, 10; 1, 16, 4; Inscr. Orell. 2780; 3422; 3524; cf. Kellerm. Vigil. App. 40; 199 sq.; Jahn, Spec. Epigr. p. 28, n. 1; p. 49.

stator2.full: Stător, ōris, m. sisto, one who causes any thing to stand fast, a stayer, supporter, an epithet of Jupiter, Liv. 1, 12, 6; Cic. Cat. 1, 5, 11; 1, 13, 31; id. Fin. 3, 20, 66; Sen. Ben. 4, 7, 1; Ov. F. 6, 793; Vell. 2, 131.—Plur., Plin. 2, 53, 54, § 140.—Also, of Mars, Vell. 2, 131, 1.

statorius.full: Statorĭus, i, m., the name of a Roman gens: Q. Statorius, Liv. 24, 48.
statorius.short: Statorĭus, i, m., the name of a Roman gens: Q.

statua.full: stătŭa, ae, f. statuo, an image, statue (syn.: signum, effigies, imago) (commonly made of metal, Quint. 2, 21, 10); rarely of the gods: statuae deorum, Cato ap. Prisc. p. 782 P.; Plin. 34, 7, 18, § 47; Sen. Q. N. 2, 42, 1.—But freq. and class. of men: statuam dare auream Solidam faciundam, Plaut. Curc. 3, 80: statuae et imagines, non animorum simulacra sed corporum, Cic. Arch. 12, 30: statua istius persimilis, id. Pis. 38, 93: statua equestris inaurata, id. Phil. 5, 15, 41; cf. id. ib. 9, 7, 16;

statualis.full: stătŭālis, is, m. statua, = STATVARIVS, a sculptor, Inscr. Murat. 937, 1.

statuarius.full: stătŭārĭus, a, um, adj. id., of or belonging to statues (post-Aug.): ars, the art of making statues, statuary, Plin. 34, 7, 16, § 33; 36, 5, 4, § 37: temperatura (aeris), id. 34, 9, 20, § 97.—As substt. stătŭ-ārĭa, ae, f., the art of statuary, Plin. 35, 12, 45, § 156; 36, 5, 4, § 15 (= ars fingendi). — stătŭārĭus, ii, m., a maker of statues, a statuary (syn. sculptor), Quint. 2, 21, 1; Sen. Ep. 88, 15; Plin. 35, 8, 34, § 54.

statuliber.full: stătūlīber (also separate, stătū lī-ber), bĕri, m. prob. instead of statuto liber; v. infra, a slave to whom liberty is granted under a certain condition or from a certain time, generally by testament: statuliber est qui statutam et destinatam in tempus vel condicionem libertatem habet, Dig. 40, 7, 1: qui sub condicione testamento liber esse jussus est, statu liber appellatur, Ulp. Fragm. 2, 1; cf. Titin. 2 passim: statuliber est qui testamento certā condicione propositā jubetur esse liber, Fest
statuliber.short: stătūlīber (also separate, stătū lī-ber), bĕri, m.

statumaria.full: stătūmārĭa, ae, f., a plant, also called proserpinaca, App. Herb. 18.
statumaria.short: stătūmārĭa, ae, f., a plant, also called proserpinaca, App.

statumen.full: stătūmen, īnis, n. statuo, that upon which any thing rests, a support, stay, prop, Col. 4, 2, 1; 4, 16, 2; 5, 5, 18; Vitr. 7, 1, 1; Plin. 13, 12, 24, § 79.— Esp., a rib of a ship, Caes. B. C. 1, 54.

statuminatio.full: stătūmĭnātĭo, ōnis, f. statumino, an underpropping, foundation, Vitr. 7, 1 med.

statumino.full: stătūmĭno, āre, v. a. statumen, to prop up, to underprop, support (post-Aug.): oras fossarum, Plin. 18, 6, 8, § 47: aliquid saxo, Vitr. 7, 1.

statunculum.full: stătuncŭlum, i, n. dim. statua, a little statue, statuette, Petr. 50, 6.

statuo.full: stătŭo, ŭi, ūtum, 3, v. a. stătum, sup. of sto, to cause to stand (cf.: colloco, pono). Corporeally. To cause to stand, set up, set, station, fix in an upright position. To set up, set in the ground, erect: ibi arbores pedicino in lapide statuito, Cato, R. R. 18: inter parietes arbores ubi statues, id. ib.: stipites statuito, id. ib.: palis statutis crebris, Varr. R. R. 1, 14 init.: pedamenta jacentia statuenda, are to be raised, Col. 4, 26: pedamentum inter duas vitis, Plin. 17, 22, 21, § 194:

statura.full: stătūra, ae, f. status, from sto; prop. a standing upright, an upright posture; hence, height or size of the body, stature. Lit. (class.): (vir) commodā staturā, Plaut. As. 2, 3, 21: staturā haud magnā, id. Poen. 5, 2, 152: pro facie, pro staturā, Lucil. ap. Non. 226, 25: velim mihi dicas, L. Turselius quā facie fuerit, quā staturā, etc., Cic. Phil. 2, 16, 41: corporis nostri partes totaque figura et forma et statura, quam apta ad naturam sit, apparet, id. Fin. 5, 12, 35; so, corporis (corresp.

staturosus.full: stătūrōsus, a, um statura, of great stature, gigantic, Aug. Civ. Dei, 15, 23 fin.
staturosus.short: stătūrōsus, a, um statura, of great stature, gigantic, Aug.

status2.full: stătus, ūs, m. sto and sisto. In a corporeal sense. Mode or way of standing, of holding one's body (at rest), posture, position, attitude, station, carriage; sing. and plur.: Ps. Statur hic ad hunc modum. Si. Statum vide hominis, Callipho, quasi basilicum, look at the way he stands, Plaut. Ps. 1, 5, 41: stat in statu senex ut adoriatur moechum, in an attitude of attack, ready, id. Mil. 4, 9, 12: concrepuit digitis, laborat; crebro conmutat status, his posture, id. ib. 2, 2, 51: qui esset status

statutio.full: stătūtĭo, ōnis, f. statuo, a placing, setting up, erecting: tigni, Vitr. 10, 5 med.

statutus.full: stătūtus, a, um, Part. and P. a., from statuo.

staures.full: Staures, um, m., a people on the Caspian Sea, Plin. 6, 16, 18, § 46.
staures.short: Staures, um, m., a people on the Caspian Sea, Plin.

steatitis.full: stĕătītis, ĭdis, f., = στεατῖτις, a precious stone, otherwise unknown; perhaps soapstone, steatite, Plin. 37, 11, 71, § 186.
steatitis.short: stĕătītis, ĭdis, f., = στεατῖτις, a precious stone, otherwise unknown;

steatoma.full: stĕătōma, ătis, n., = στεάτωμα, a kind of fatty tumor, Plin. 26, 14, 87, § 144; Veg. 3, 30, 1 (in Cels. 7, 6, written in Greek).
steatoma.short: stĕătōma, ătis, n., = στεάτωμα, a kind of fatty tumor, Plin.

stega.full: stĕga, ae, f., = στέγη, the deck of a ship, Plaut. Bacch. 2, 3, 44; id. Stich. 3, 1, 12.
stega.short: stĕga, ae, f., = στέγη, the deck of a ship, Plaut.

steganos.full: Stĕgănos, i, m., = Στεγανός, one of the channels by which the city of Alexandria had access to the sea. Plin. 5, 31, 34, § 128.
steganos.short: Stĕgănos, i, m., = Στεγανός, one of the channels by which the city of Alexandria had access to the sea.

stegnus.full: stegnus, a, um, adj., = στεγνός, making close, drawing together, costive: febres, Plin. 23, 7, 63, § 120.
stegnus.short: stegnus, a, um, adj., = στεγνός, making close, drawing together, costive: febres, Plin.

stela.full: stēla, ae, f., = στήλη, a pillar, column, stele, Plin. 6, 28, 32, § 150; 6, 29, 34, § 174; Mart. Cap. 2, § 137.
stela.short: stēla, ae, f., = στήλη, a pillar, column, stele, Plin.

stelephuros.full: stĕlĕphūros, i, f., = στελεφοῦρος, a plant, perh. Ravenna sugar-cane: Saccharum Ravennae, Linn.; Plin. 21, 17, 61, § 101.
stelephuros.short: stĕlĕphūros, i, f., = στελεφοῦρος, a plant, perh.

stelis.full: stĕlis, ĭdis, f., = στελίς, a mistletoe that grows upon firs and larches, Plin. 16, 44, 93, § 245.
stelis.short: stĕlis, ĭdis, f., = στελίς, a mistletoe that grows upon firs and larches, Plin.

stella.full: stella, ae, f. for sterula; cf. Sanscr. staras; cf. Gr. ἀστήρ; Germ. Stern; Engl. star; perh. root ster- of sterno; Gr. στορέννυμι. Lit., a star (whereas sidus denotes a group of stars, a constellation; v. sidus; cf. also astrum): ignes, quae sidera et stellas vocatis, Cic. Rep. 6, 15, 15: sunt stellae naturā flammeae, id. N. D. 2, 46, 118: o magna templa caelitum commixta stellis splendidis Enn. ap. Varr. L. L. 7, § 6 Müll. (Trag. v. 227 Vahl.); cf.: caelum stellis fulgentibus aptum, id. ap. Ma

stellaris.full: stellāris, e, adj. stella, of or belonging to a star, starry (post-class.): essentia, Macr. Somn. Scip. 1, 14 med.

stellatis ager.full: Stellātis ăger or campus, a district in Southern Campania, near Cales, Cic. Agr. 2, 31, 85; 1, 7, 20; Liv. 9, 44, 5; 10, 31, 5; 22, 13, 6; Suet. Caes. 20; Sil. 11, 268. —Hence, Stellātīnus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to the ager Stellatis: tribus, Liv. 6, 5, 8; cf. Fest. p. 343; Inscr. Grut. 35, 3; 484, 3.
stellatis ager.short: Stellātis ăger or campus, a district in Southern Campania, near Cales, Cic.

stellatura.full: stellātūra, ae, f., a deduction from the soldiers' rations granted to the military tribunes (late Lat.), Spart. Pescenn. 3; Lamprid. Alex. Sev. 15 med.; Cod. Th. 7, 4, 28, § 1 al.
stellatura.short: stellātūra, ae, f., a deduction from the soldiers' rations granted to the military tribunes (late Lat.), Spart.

stellatus.full: stellātus, a, um, v. stello, II.

stellifer.full: stellĭfer, fĕra, fĕrum, adj. stella-fero, star-bearing, starry (very rare): caeli stellifer cursus, * Cic. Rep. 6, 18, 18: polus, Sen. Hippol. 785: sphaera, Macr. Somn. Scip. 2, 1, § 1.

stelliger.full: stellĭger, gĕra, gĕrum, adj. stella-gero, star-bearing, starry (mostly poet.): viae stelligerae aetheris, Varr. ap. Non. 299, 32: orbes, Cic. Arat. 238 (482): polus, Stat. Th. 12, 565: axis, id. S. 3, 3, 77: Olympus, Sen. Herc. Oet. 1907: apex, Sil. 13, 863.

stellimicans.full: stellĭmĭcans, antis, adj. stellamico, glittering with stars: signa, Varr. ap. Prob. Verg. E. 6, 31.

stellio1.full: stellĭo (stēlĭo), ōnis, m. stella. A newt, stellion (having star-like spots on its back): Lacerto gecko, Linn.; Plin. 29, 4, 28, § 90; 11, 26, 31, § 91; Verg. G. 4, 243; Col. 9, 7, 5.— Transf., a crafty, knavish person, Plin. 30, 10, 27, § 89; App. M. 5, p. 172, 19; cf. stellionatus.

stellio2.full: Stellio, ōnis, m. 1. stellio, a Roman surname, e. g. C. Afranius Stellio, Liv. 39, 23, 2.

stellionatus.full: stellĭōnātus, ūs, m. 1. stellio, B., cozenage, trickery, cheating, stellionate (jurid. Lat.): stellionatum obici posse his, qui dolo quid fecerunt sciendum est, scilicet si aliud crimen non sit, quod obiciatur; quod enim in privatis judiciis est de dolo actio, hoc in criminibus stellionatus persecutio. Ubicumque igitur titulus criminis deficit, illic stellionatum obiciemus, etc., Dig. 47, 20, 3 sq.; 13, 7, 36; 17, 1, 29 fin.; 40, 7, 9.

stello.full: stello, no perf., ātum, 1, v. n. and a. [stella]. Neutr., to be set or covered with stars. So only in the part. pres. stellans, antis, bestarred, starry (poet.): caelo stellante, Lucr. 4, 212; so, caelum, Verg. A. 7, 210: tecta summi patris, Val. Fl. 5, 623: Olympus, Cic. poët. Div. 1, 12, 19: nox, id. ib. 1, 11, 18: ora Tauri, Ov. F. 5, 603.— Transf.: gemmis caudam (pavonis) stellantibus implet, glittering, shining, Ov. M. 1, 723: tegmina (i. e. vestes), gleaming, Val. Fl. 3, 98: lumina (i. e.

stellula.full: stellŭla, ae, f. dim. id., a little star, asterisk, as a mark in writing; the Lat. word for asteriscus (late Lat.), Hier. Ep. 112, 19.

stemma.full: stemma, ătis, n., = στέμμα. In gen., a garland, wreath (post-class.), Prud. στεφ. 10, 908; Firm. Math. 3, 8.— In partic., a garland hung upon an ancestral image (post-Aug.), Sen. Ben. 3, 28, 1; Plin. 35, 2, 2, § 6.— Transf., a pedigree, genealogical table, genealogical tree, Sen. Ep. 44, 1; Suet. Ner. 37; id. Galb. 2; Stat. S. 3, 3, 43; Pers. 3, 28; Juv. 8, 1; Mart. 5, 35, 4.— Trop., nobility, high value: argenti fumosa sui stemmata narrare, Mart. 8, 6, 3: referre prisci jejunii, the great antiq

stena.full: Stĕna, ōrum, n., = Στενά, a narrow defile near Antigonea, in Chaonia, Liv. 32, 5.
stena.short: Stĕna, ōrum, n., = Στενά, a narrow defile near Antigonea, in Chaonia, Liv.

stenocoriasis.full: stĕnŏcŏrĭăsis, is, f., = στενοκορίασις, a contraction of the pupil, a disease of the eyes of horses, Veg. 3, 16.
stenocoriasis.short: stĕnŏcŏrĭăsis, is, f., = στενοκορίασις, a contraction of the pupil, a disease of the eyes of horses, Veg.

stentor.full: Stentor, ŏris, m., = Στέντωρ, a Greek warrior in the army before Troy, celebrated for the strength of his lungs, Juv. 13, 112. —Hence, Stentŏrĕus, a, um, adj., Stentorian, i. e. loud-sounding: vagitus, Arn. 2, 97.
stentor.short: Stentor, ŏris, m., = Στέντωρ, a Greek warrior in the army before Troy, celebrated for the strength of his lungs, Juv.

stephane1.full: Stĕphănē, ēs, f., = Στεφάνη. Ancient name of the island of Samos, Plin. 5, 31, 37, § 135.— Another name of the city of Prœneste, Plin. 3, 5, 9, § 64.

stephane2.full: Stĕphănē, ēs, m., = Στεφάνη, a mountain in Thessaly, Plin. 4, 8, 15, § 29.
stephane2.short: Stĕphănē, ēs, m., = Στεφάνη, a mountain in Thessaly, Plin.

stephaneplocos.full: Stĕphănēplŏcos, i, f., = Στεφανηπλόκος, the Chaplet-wreather, a picture by Pausias, Plin. 35, 11, 40, § 125; 21, 2, 3, § 4.— Called also, Stĕphănŏpōlĭs, is, f., = Στεφανόπωλις, the Chaplet-seller, Plin. 35, 11, 40, § 125.
stephaneplocos.short: Stĕphănēplŏcos, i, f., = Στεφανηπλόκος, the Chaplet-wreather, a picture by Pausias, Plin.

stephanio.full: Stĕphănĭo, ōnis, m., a mime of the time of Augustus, Plin. 7, 48, 49, § 159.
stephanio.short: Stĕphănĭo, ōnis, m., a mime of the time of Augustus, Plin.

stephanitis.full: stĕphănītis, ĭdis, f., = στεφανῖτις, a kind of vine, which winds about in the shape of garlands, Plin. 14, 3, 4, § 42; Macr. S. 2, 16 fin.—Called also, stĕphănītes, ae, m., = στεφανίτης, Col. 3, 2, 2; Isid. Orig. 17, 5.
stephanitis.short: stĕphănītis, ĭdis, f., = στεφανῖτις, a kind of vine, which winds about in the shape of garlands, Plin.

stephanium.full: Stĕphănĭum, ii, f. dim. of Stephane, a character in the Stichus of Plautus, Plaut. Stich. 5, 4, 54 al.—Called also, Stĕphă-niscĭdĭum, ii, f., Plaut. Stich. 5, 4, 57.

stephanomelis.full: stĕphănŏmĕlis, is, f., a plant which checks bleeding at the nose, Plin. 26, 13, 84, § 136.
stephanomelis.short: stĕphănŏmĕlis, is, f., a plant which checks bleeding at the nose, Plin.

stephanos.full: stĕphănos, i, m., = στέφανος (garland), the name of several plants: Alexandri, Plin. 15, 30, 39, § 132: Aphrodites, App. Herb. 105.
stephanos.short: stĕphănos, i, m., = στέφανος (garland), the name of several plants: Alexandri, Plin.

stephanus.full: Stĕphănus, i, m., = Στέφανος, a Grecian sculptor, Plin. 36, 5, 4, § 33.
stephanus.short: Stĕphănus, i, m., = Στέφανος, a Grecian sculptor, Plin.

stephanusa.full: Stephănūsa, ae, f., = Στεφανοῦσα, the female Chaplet-wreather, a little statue of Praxiteles, Plin. 34, 8, 19, § 70 Jan. and Sillig. (al. Stephusa, of the same meaning).
stephanusa.short: Stephănūsa, ae, f., = Στεφανοῦσα, the female Chaplet-wreather, a little statue of Praxiteles, Plin.

sterceia.full: stercēia, ae, f. stercus, a maidservant who cleans the excrements from children, Tert. adv. Val. 8.—As a nickname, Petr. 75, 9 (al. sterteja).

stercorarius.full: stercŏrārĭus, a, um, adj. id., of or belonging to dung: crates, Varr. R. R. 1, 22, 3: porta, a gate in the temple of Vesta (v. stercus), Fest. p. 344 Müll.; cf. Bunsen's Rome, 3, p. 12.

stercoratio.full: stercŏrātĭo, ōnis, f. stercoro, a dunging, manuring, Varr. R. R. 2, 2, 12; Col. 2, 1 fin.; 2, 16, 2; Plin. 18, 23, 53, § 192.

stercoratus.full: stercŏrātus, a, um, Part. and P. a., v. stercoro.

stercoreus.full: stercŏrĕus, a, um, adj. stercus, dungy, stinking: miles, as a term of abuse, Plaut. Mil. 2, 1, 12.

stercoro.full: stercŏro, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. id.. To dung, manure with dung, to muck: loca, Varr. R. R. 1, 38; Cic. Sen. 15, 54: agrum, Mart. Cap. 3, § 305; Col. 2, 16, 2; Plin. 17, 9, 6, § 50.— To cleanse from dung: latrinas, Dig. 7, 1, 15: stercorata colluvies, dungheap, Col. 1, 6, 24.—Hence, stercŏ-rātus, a, um, P. a., dunged, mucked, manured: locus stercoratissimus, Col. 11, 2, 85; 2, 11, 8.

stercorosus.full: stercŏrōsus, a, um, adj. id., full of excrements or dung, well manured: aqua, full of filth, impure, Col. 8, 3, 8; cf. Sen. Q. N. 3, 26, 6: solum, Col. 11, 3, 43: herbae, id. 9, 4, 7.—Sup.: locus, Cato, R. R. 46.

sterculius.full: Stercŭlĭus, ii, m. stercus, the deity that presides over manuring, Tert. Apol. 25; Macr. S. 1, 7; Lact. 1, 20 fin.; 1, 36; Serv. Verg. G. 1, 21.—Called also, Stercŭ-lus, Prud. στεφ. 2, 450; Stercŭtus or Stercŭtĭus, Plin. 17, 9, 6, § 50; Lact. 1, 20, 36; and, Stercenĭus, Serv. Verg. A. 11, 850; cf. Aug. Civ. Dei, 18, 15; and Becker, Ant. 4, p. 16.

stercus.full: stercus, ŏris, n. Gr. σκώρ; gen. σκατός, dung; Sanscr. cakrt = sakart. Lit., dung, excrements, ordure (syn.: fimus, merda), Varr. R. R. 1, 38; Col. 2, 15; Cato, R. R. 29; 37; Cic. Div. 1, 27, 57; Hor. Epod. 12, 11 al.; Fest. p. 344 Müll.; cf. Varr. L. L. 6, § 32 ib., and Fest. s. v. Quando stercus, pp. 258 and 259 ib.; Juv. 14, 64.—Prov.: aurum in stercore quaerere, Cassiod. Inst. Div. Lit. 1, p. 510.— As a term of abuse: nolo stercus curiae dici Glauciam, Cic. de Or. 3, 41, 164.— Transf.: ferri

sterelytis.full: sterelȳtis, ĭdis, f., a sort of scum or litharge of silver, Plin. 33, 6, 35, § 108.
sterelytis.short: sterelȳtis, ĭdis, f., a sort of scum or litharge of silver, Plin.

stereobata.full: stĕrĕŏbăta, ae, f., = στερεοβάτης, a pedestal of a column or row of columns, Vitr. 3, 3.
stereobata.short: stĕrĕŏbăta, ae, f., = στερεοβάτης, a pedestal of a column or row of columns, Vitr.

stergethron.full: stergēthron, i, n., = στέργηθρον, a plant, great houseleek, Plin. 25, 13, 102, § 160; App. Herb. 123.
stergethron.short: stergēthron, i, n., = στέργηθρον, a plant, great houseleek, Plin.

steria.full: Stēria, ae, f., = Στειρία, a town in Attica, Plin. 4, 7, 11, § 24.
steria.short: Stēria, ae, f., = Στειρία, a town in Attica, Plin.

stericula.full: stērĭcŭla, ae. f. dim., the uterus of a sow that has not yet farrowed, Petr. 35, 3.

sterigmos.full: stērigmos, i, m., = στηριγμός, the standing-still of a planet (pure Lat. stativa lux), App. de Mundo, p. 64, 25.
sterigmos.short: stērigmos, i, m., = στηριγμός, the standing-still of a planet (pure Lat.

sterilefio.full: stĕrĭlĕfīo, fĭĕri, v. n. sterilis-facio, to become unfruitful, barren, or sterile: leaenae sterilefiunt in aeternum, Sol. 27 med. dub. (al. steriles fiunt).

sterilesco.full: stĕrĭlesco, ĕre, v. inch. n. [sterilis], to grow unfruitful, barren, or sterile. Lit.: leaenae, Plin. 8, 16, 17, § 45: caprae pinguitudine, id. 8, 50, 76, § 200: amygdalae, id. 17, 10, 11, § 63: mamma (suis), id. 11, 40, 95, § 234.—* Trop.: gaudia, Val. Cato, Dir. 9.

sterilicula.full: stĕrĭlĭcŭla, ae, f., = vulva sterilis, the womb of a sow that has never borne young, Petr. 35, 3.
sterilicula.short: stĕrĭlĭcŭla, ae, f., = vulva sterilis, the womb of a sow that has never borne young, Petr.

sterilis.full: stĕrĭlis, e (collat. form, acc. sing. fem sterilam sterilem, Fest. p. 316 Müll.; neutr. plur. sterila, Lucr. 2, 845; abl. sterile, Apic. 7, 1, § 258), adj. Gr. στερεός, hard; στερίφη, στεῖρα, barren; Sanscr. starī, vacca sterilis, unfruitful, barren, sterile, of plants and animals (class. and very freq.; syn infecundus): steriles nascuntur avenae, Verg. E. 5, 37; so, ulvae, Ov. M. 4, 299: herba, id. Am. 3, 7, 31; Curt. 4, 1, 21: platani, Verg. G. 2, 70: agri, id. ib. 1, 84; id. A. 3, 141: tellus

sterilitas.full: stĕrĭlĭtas, ātis, f. sterilis, unfruitfulness, barrenness, sterility (class.). Lit.: quae sit vel sterilitas agrorum vel fertilitas futura, Cic. Div. 1, 57, 131; id. Agr. 2, 26, 70: frugum, Vell. 1, 1 fin.: arborum, Plin. 16, 26, 47, § 111: annonae, Col. 2, 10, 1: vitium, id. 3, 10, 15: terrae, Vulg. Thren. 4, 9: fetus exstitit in sterilitate naturae, Cic. Div. 1, 18, 36: mulierum, Plin. 28, 8, 27, § 97: in sterilitatem castrare, id. 18, 14, 36, § 136.—Plur., Suet. Claud. 18: continuae, Plin. Ep

sterilus.full: stĕrĭlus, a, um, v. sterilis init.

sternax.full: sternax, ācis, adj. sterno, that throws to the ground (poet.): equus, that throws his rider, Verg. A. 12, 364; Sil. 1, 261: cives, that fall prostrate, Sid. Ep. 5, 14 fin.; so of a suppliant, id. ib. 4, 12 fin.

sterno.full: sterno, strāvi, strātum, 3 (pluperf. sync. strarat, Manil. 1, 774: strasset, Varr. ap. Non. 86, 8), v. a. Gr. root ΣΤΟΡ, στορέννυμι, to spread; στρατός, camp; Sanscr. star- strnāmi = sterno; cf.: strages, struo, torus, and lātus, adj., old Lat. stlatus, to spread out, spread abroad; to stretch out, extend. Lit. (mostly poet. and in postAug. prose; in Cic. only in the part. perf.; cf.: effundo, extendo, subicio, subdo): vestes, Ov. M. 8, 658: in duro vellus solo, id. F. 4, 654: bubulos utres pont

sternumentum.full: sternūmentum, i, n. sternuo, a sneezing (class.; but cf. sternutamentum). Lit., Cic. Div. 2, 40, 84; Plin. 2, 7, 5, § 24; 21, 22, 93, § 163; 25, 5, 21, § 52; 28, 6, 15, § 57; Gell. 12, 5, 11; Cels. 3, 20; 8, 4; 8, 9.— Transf., a means of provoking sneezing, sneezing-powder, Cels. 6, 7, 9; Plin. 25, 11, 86, § 135; 25, 13, 109, § 173.

sternuo.full: sternŭo, ŭi, 3, v. n. and a. [cf. Gr. πτάρνυσθαι, v. Georg Curtius Griech. Etym. p. 696]. Neutr., to sneeze: adorare aliquem, cum sternuerit, Plin. 2, 40, 40, § 107; 28, 6, 15, § 57; 19, 3, 15, § 40 (al. sternuto); Col. 7, 5, 18 Schneid. N. cr.—* Transf., of a light, to sputter, crackle: sternuit et lumen ... sternuit, et nobis prospera signa dedit, Ov. H. 19, 151 sq.— Act., to sneeze out, give by sneezing: omen, Prop. 2, 3, 24; so, approbationem, Cat. 45, 9 and 18.

sternutamentum.full: sternūtāmentum, i, n. sternuto, a sneezing (post-Aug.): sternutamenta erunt observanda, Sen. Ira, 2, 25, 4; Scrib. 10 (in Cic. Div. 2, 40, 84, the better reading is sternumenta).

sternutatio.full: sternūtātĭo, ōnis, f. id., a sneezing, sternutation (post-class. and rare for sternumentum), App. M. 9, p. 228, 24; Scrib. Comp. 10 fin.; Front. Ep. ad M. Caes. 4, 5 fin.

sternuto.full: sternūto, āvi, 1, v. freq. n. [sternuo], to sneeze, Petr. 98, 4; 102, 10; Plin. 19, 3, 15, § 40.

sterope.full: Stĕrŏpē, ēs, f., = Στερόπη. One of the Pleiades, Att. ap. Serv. Verg. A. 8, 130 (Trag. Rel. p. 135 Rib.); Ov. F. 4, 172; id. Tr. 1, 11, 14.— One of the horses of the sun, Hyg. Fab. 183.

steropes.full: Stĕrŏpes, is, m., = Στερόπης, one of the Cyclops in Vulcan's smithy, Verg. A. 8, 425; Ov. F. 4, 288; Claud. III. Cons. Hon. 195; id. Rapt. Pros. 1, 239; acc. Steropem, Stat. S. 1, 1, 4.
steropes.short: Stĕrŏpes, is, m., = Στερόπης, one of the Cyclops in Vulcan's smithy, Verg.

sterquilinium.full: sterquĭlīnĭum (in MSS. also written stercŭl- and stercĭl-, Plaut. Pers. 3, 3, 3; Ter. Phorm. 3, 2, 41; Dig. 19, 1, 17, § 2), ii, n. (collat. form sterquĭlīnum, i, Phaedr. 3, 12, 1) [stercus], a dung-pit, laystall, mixen, Cato, R. R. 2, 3; Varr. 1, 13, 4; 1, 38, 3; Col. 1, 6, 21; 7, 5, 8; Phaedr. l. l. —As a term of reproach, Plaut. Pers. 3, 3, 3; id. Cas. 1, 26; Ter. Phorm. 3, 2, 41.

stertinius.full: Stertĭnĭus, ii, m., a Stoic philosopher, Hor. S. 2, 3, 33; 2, 3, 296.—Adj.: Stertĭ-nĭus, a, um, of Stertinius: acumen, Hor. Ep. 1, 12, 20.
stertinius.short: Stertĭnĭus, ii, m., a Stoic philosopher, Hor.

sterto.full: sterto, ŭi (acc. to Prisc. p. 903 P.; cf. desterto), 3, v. n. cf.: δέρθω, δαρθάνω, to snore: noctem totam stertere, Plaut. As. 5, 2, 22; id. Mil. 3, 2, 7: stertit noctes et dies, Ter. Eun. 5, 8, 49; Hor. Ep. 2, 2, 27: Marcellus ita stertebat, ut ego vicinus audirem, Cic. 4, 3, 5; id. Ac. 2, 29, 93: diem totum stertebat, Hor. S. 1, 3, 18: qui vigilans stertis, Lucr. 3, 1048; Pers. 3, 3; 5, 132: vigilanti stertere naso, Juv. 1, 57: altiore stertitur somno, Amm. 27, 12, 8.— Trop.: qui stertit aesta

stesichorus.full: Stēsĭchŏrus, i, m., = Στησίχορος, a Greek lyric poet of Himera: Stesichori graves Camenae, Hor. C. 4, 9, 8; cf. Quint. 10, 1, 62; Cic. Sen. 7, 23; Cic. Verr. 2, 2, 35, § 87; Stat. S. 5, 3, 154.
stesichorus.short: Stēsĭchŏrus, i, m., = Στησίχορος, a Greek lyric poet of Himera: Stesichori graves Camenae, Hor.

stheneboea.full: Sthĕnĕboea or Sthĕnŏboea, ae, f., = Σθενέβοια, Σθενόβοια, daughter of Iobates, king of Lycia, Juv. 10, 327; Hyg. Fab. 57 and 243.—Hence, adj.: Sthĕnĕ-boeïus, a, um, of or belonging to Sthenebœa: heros, i. e. Bellerophon, whom Sthenebœa loved, Sid. Carm. 11, 74.
stheneboea.short: Sthĕnĕboea or Sthĕnŏboea, ae, f., = Σθενέβοια, Σθενόβοια, daughter of Iobates, king of Lycia, Juv.

sthenelus.full: Sthĕnĕlus, i, m., = Σθένελος. King of Mycenœ, son of Perseus, and father of Eurystheus, Hyg. Fab. 244.— King of the Ligurians, father of Cycnus, who was changed into a swan, and who, from his father, is called proles Stheneleïa, Ov. M. 2, 367; cf. sqq.— One of the Epigoni, charioteer of Diomede at the siege of Troy, and one of those shut up in the wooden horse, Verg. A. 2, 261; Hor. C. 1, 15, 24; 4, 9, 20.— A Rutulian, slain by Pallas, Verg. A. 10, 388.—Hence. Sthĕnĕlēĭus, a, um, adj., Sthenelei

sthenius.full: Sthĕnĭus, ii, m., a Thermitan, Cic. Verr. 2, 2, 34, § 83 sqq.
sthenius.short: Sthĕnĭus, ii, m., a Thermitan, Cic.

sthennis.full: Sthennis, ĭdis, m., = Σθένις, a sculptor of Olynthus, Plin. 34, 8, 19, § 90.
sthennis.short: Sthennis, ĭdis, m., = Σθένις, a sculptor of Olynthus, Plin.

stheno.full: Sthĕno, ūs, f., = Σθενώ, a daughter of Phorcus and Ceto, sister of Medusa, Hyg. Fab. praef.
stheno.short: Sthĕno, ūs, f., = Σθενώ, a daughter of Phorcus and Ceto, sister of Medusa, Hyg.

stibadium.full: stĭbădĭum, ii, n., = στιβάδιον, a semicircular seat or couch, Plin. Ep. 5, 6, 36; Serv. Verg. A. 1, 698; Sid. Ep. 1, 11 med.; 2, 2 med.; Mart. 14, 87 in lemm.; Inscr. Orell. 2358.
stibadium.short: stĭbădĭum, ii, n., = στιβάδιον, a semicircular seat or couch, Plin.

stibinus.full: stĭbĭnus, a, um, adj. stibium, antimonial, of antimony: lapides, Vulg. 1 Par. 29, 2.

stibium.full: stĭbĭum, ii, n.; also called stĭbi, is, and stimmi = στίβι, στιμμι, antimony, a sulphuret of antimony, stibium, used by women, in the form of powder, to color their eyebrows and eyelashes black; and in medicine, as an eye-salve, Plin. 33, 6, 33, § 101; 29, 6, 37, § 115; Cels. 6, 6, 6; 6, 6, 8; 6, 6, 12 sq.; Scrib. Comp. 27; 34 al.; Vulg. 4 Reg. 9, 30.

sticha.full: stĭcha, ae, f., = στίχη, a kind of vine (pure Lat. apiana), Plin. 14, 9, 11, § 81.
sticha.short: stĭcha, ae, f., = στίχη, a kind of vine (pure Lat.

stichus.full: Stĭchus, i, m., the name of a slave, Gai. Inst. 2, 193; 2, 199; 4, 55; Dig. 2, 14, 27, § 7 al.—Hence, Title of a comedy of Plautus.
stichus.short: Stĭchus, i, m., the name of a slave, Gai.

sticte.full: Stictē, ēs, f., one of Actœon's hounds, Ov. M. 3, 217; Hyg. Fab. 181.
sticte.short: Stictē, ēs, f., one of Actœon's hounds, Ov.

sticula.full: stĭcŭla, ae, f. dim., a kind of grape, Col. 3, 2, 27.

stigma.full: stigma, ătis, n. (fem. collat. form, acc. stigmam, Petr. 45, 9; 69, 1), = στίγμα, a prick, puncture (post-Aug.). A mark burned in, a brand impressed upon slaves or others, as a mark of disgrace. Lit., Petr. 103, 2; 105, 11: inscribere, Sen. Ben. 4, 37, 4: stigmata fugitivo scribere, Quint. 7, 4, 14; Suet. Calig. 27; Plin. 30, 4, 10, § 30: stigmate dignus, Juv. 10, 183; Mart. 10, 56, 6 al.; or as a mark of ownership, Vulg. Gal. 6, 17.— Trop., a mark of disgrace, a stigma, Suet. Caes. 73; Mart. 6,

stigmatias.full: stigmătĭas, ae, m., = στιγματίας. One who is branded, of a slave, Cic. Off. 2, 7, 25.— Title of a comedy of Nœvius, Varr. L. L. 7, § 107 Müll.; v. Com. Rel. p. 19 Rib.

stigmo.full: stigmo, āvi, 1, v. a. stigma, to brand, stigmatize (late Lat.), Prud. στεφ. 10, 1079.

stigmosus.full: stigmōsus, a, um, adj. id., full of brand-marks, branded, Petr. 109, 8; Regul. ap. Plin. Ep. 1, 5, 2.

stilbon.full: Stilbon, ōnis, m., = Στίλβων (the shining, glittering), a name of the planet Mercury, Aus. Idyll. 18, 11; Mart. Cap. 8, § 851; Hyg. Astr. 2, 42 fin. (as Greek, Cic. N. D. 2, 20, 53).— One of Actœon's hounds, Hyg. Fab. 181.
stilbon.short: Stilbon, ōnis, m., = Στίλβων (the shining, glittering), a name of the planet Mercury, Aus.

stilicho.full: Stilicho (written STELICHO, Inscr. Orell. 4999), ōnis, m., the famous general and father-in-law of the emperor Honorius, celebrated by Claudian in his poem De laudibus Stilichonis; cf. also Oros. 7, 37 sq.—Hence, adj.: Stĭlĭchōnĭus, a, um, of or belonging to Stilicho: virgo, i. e. Maria, daughter of Stilicho and wife of Honorius, Claud. Nupt. Hon. et Mar. 177.

stilla.full: stilla, ae, f. dim. of stĭria; cf. Fest. s. v. stiricipium, p. 345 Müll.; Corss. 1, p. 518, a drop (a dense, viscous, gummy, fatty drop; whereas gutta is a natural, liquid drop: gutta imbrium est, stilla olei vel aceti, Suet. Fragm. p. 319, 27 Roth). Lit. (rare but class.): stilla muriae, * Cic. Fin. 3, 14, 45; Plin. 29, 4, 21, § 70: sicca et sine stillis arbor, Vitr. 2, 9, 3; Serv. Verg. A. 3, 366: olei, App. M. 5, p. 169: stilla saeva (arborum), Plin. 17, 12, 19, § 92.— Transf., a drop, i. e.

stillanter.full: stillanter, adv. stillo, drop by drop, Ambros. Ep. 41, 14.

stillarium.full: stillārĭum, ii, n. stilla, an added drop, a trifling addition, Sen. Ep. 97, 2.

stillaticius.full: stillātīcĭus, a, um, adj. stillo, dropping, dripping, stillatitious: resina, Plin. 16, 11, 22, § 54.

stillatim.full: stillātim, adv. stilla, by drops, drop by drop: stillatim cadere, Varr. L. L. 5, § 27 Müll.

stillatio.full: stillātĭo, ōnis, f. stillo, a dropping down, falling in drops (late Lat.): pluviae, Hier. in Mich. 1, 2, 6.

stillativus.full: stillātīvus, a, um, adj. id., dropping, dripping (late Lat.): mel, Plin. Val. 1, 18.

stillicidium.full: stillĭcĭdĭum (also written stilĭcĭd-; v. Lachm. ad Lucr. p. 33), ii, n. stilla-cado, a liquid which falls drop by drop, a dripping moisture, stillicide: stillicidium eo quod stillatim cadat, Varr. L. L. 5, § 27 Müll. In gen. (poet. and in post-Aug. prose): stillicidi casus lapidem cavat, Lucr. 1, 313: grandinis, Sen. Q. N. 4, 3, 2: urinae, Plin. 30, 8, 21, § 66; cf. vesicae, id. 28, 8, 32, § 122: arborum, id. 17, 12, 18, § 89: mellis, Tert. Spect. 27 fin.: raritas nubium stillicidia dispergit, A

stillo.full: stillo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. n. and a [stilla]. Neutr., to drop, drip, trickle, distil (mostly poet.; syn. roro). Lit.: vas, unde stillet lente aqua, Varr. R. R. 1, 41, 2: gutta (dulcedinis) in cor, Lucr. 4, 1060: umorem, quasi igni cera super calido tabescens multa liquescat, id. 6, 515: cruor ferro, Prop. 2, 8, 26 (2, 8 b, 26 (10)): unguenta capillo, Tib. 1, 7, 51: de viridi ilice mella, Ov. M. 1, 112: ros, id. ib. 11, 57: hammoniaci lacrima stillat m harenis, Plin. 12, 23, 49, § 107.— Transf., of

stilo1.full: stĭlo, āvi, 1, v. n. stilus, I., to get stalks, Col. 4, 33, 3.

stilo2.full: Stĭlo, ōnis, m., a surname of L. Aelius Praeconinus, Plin. 33, 1, 7, § 29; Suet. Gram. 3; cf. v. Hensde, Disquis. de L. Aelio Stilone; and Ritschl, Parerga, p. 239.
stilo2.short: Stĭlo, ōnis, m., a surname of L.

stilpo.full: Stilpo or Stilpon, ōnis, m., = Στίλπων. A proper name, Ter. ap. Cic. Or. 47, 157.— Esp., a philosopher of Megara, Cic. Fat. 5, 10; id. Ac. 2, 24, 75; Sen. Ep. 9, 1.
stilpo.short: Stilpo or Stilpon, ōnis, m., = Στίλπων.

stilus.full: stĭlus (not stylus), i, m. for stiglus; Gr. στίζω, to stick, puncture; στίγμα, mark, point; Sanscr. tig, to be sharp; tigmas, sharp; cf. Engl. stick, sting; Lat. stimulus; not connected with στῦλος. In gen., a stake, pale: extra vallum stili caeci, concealed stakes, Auct. B. Afr. 31, 5; cf. Sil. 10, 415 (for which stimuli, Caes. B. G. 7, 73 fin.): ligneus, Amm. 23, 4, 5; 15, 10, 5.—In agriculture, a pointed instrument for freeing plants from worms or from shoots which grow too rankly, etc., Col.

stimula.full: Stĭmŭla (Sĭmĭla, Liv. 39, 12), ae, f. stimulus, the goddess who pricks on, excites, stimulates to action or pleasure, Aug. Civ Del, 4, 11; 4, 16; perh. for Semele, Ov. F. 6, 503; Schol. Juv. 2, 3; cf. Müller, Etrusk. 2, 77.

stimulatio.full: stĭmŭlātĭo, ōnis, f. stimulo, a pricking on, incitement, stimulation (post-Aug.): ingens, Plin. 35, 2, 2, § 7: privata cuique, Tac. H. 1, 90 fin.

stimulator.full: stĭmŭlātor, ōris, m. id., a pricker-on, instigator, stimulator, Claud. ap. Ruf. 2, 501; Mamert. Grat. Act. ad Iul. 5 (in Cic. Dom. 5, 11, Orell. and B. and K. read instimulator); Vulg. Jer. 46, 20.

stimulatrix.full: stĭmŭlātrix, īcis, f. stimulator, she that pricks on, instigates, or stimulates, Plaut. Most. 1, 3, 46; 1, 3, 62.

stimuleus.full: stĭmŭlĕus, a, um, adj. stimulus, consisting of prickles or goads: supplicium, Plaut. Mil. 2, 6, 31.

stimulo.full: stĭmŭlo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. id., to prick with a goad, to prick or goad on, to urge on (syn. pungo). Lit.
