Cic. N. D. 2, 64, 160: (muriatica) Sine omni lepore et sine suavitate, Plaut. Poen. 1, 2, 33: cibi, Cic. Phil. 2, 45, 115: odorum, id. Sen. 17, 59: coloris, id. Opt. Gen. 3, 8: me tuus sonus et suavitas ista delectat: omitto verborum ... sed hanc dico suavitatem, quae erit ex ore, id. de Or. 3, 11, 42: villa mirific

suavitudo.full: suāvĭtūdo, ĭnis, f. suavis, sweetness, pleasantness, agreeableness, delight (very rare for the class. suavitas): cor meum, spes mea, mel meum, suavitudo, cibus, gaudium, my sweet, Plaut. Fragm. ap. Non. 173, 3; id. Stich. 5, 5, 14; Turp. ap. Non. 173, 5 (Com. Fragm. v. 110): pronuntiationis, Auct. Her. 3, 12, 22.—Plur.: suavitudinum mollitie capti, Lact. 6, 22, 5.

suavium.full: suāvĭum (sāvĭum), ii, n. id.. A mouth puckered up to be kissed (anteclass. and very rare; syn. osculum): dum semihiulco savio meo puellum savior, Poët. ap. Gell. 19, 11, 4; Plaut. Mil. 2, 1, 16; cf. id. As. 4, 1, 53; App M. 3, p. 135, 35.— Transf., a kiss, a love-kiss, φίλημα (mostly ante-class.; esp. freq. in Plaut.; syn.: osculum, basium; cf.: sciendum osculum religionis esse, savium voluptatis; quamvis quidam osculum filiis dari, uxori basium, scorto savium dicant, Serv. Verg. A. 1, 260): qui

sub.full: sŭb (on the form sus from subs v. infra, III.), prep. with acc. and abl. [perh. for es-ub, ens-ub, = ἐνς (εις) and ὑπό; Sanscr. upa; cf. Georg Curtius Gr. Etym. p. 290], under. With abl., to point out the object under which a thing is situated or takes place (Gr. ὑπό, with dat. or gen.), under, below, beneath, underneath. Of space: si essent, qui sub terrā semper habitavissent ... nec tamen exissent umquam supra terram, Cic. N. D. 2, 37, 95; Plaut. Capt. 3, 5, 72: sub aquā, id. Cas. 2, 6, 28: su
sub.short: sŭb (on the form sus from subs v.

subabsurdus.full: sŭb-absurdus, a, um, adj., somewhat or rather absurd (Ciceronian): sunt illa subabsurda, Cic. de Or. 2, 67, 274: subabsurda dicere, id. ib. 2, 71, 289: tempus discessūs, id. Att. 16, 3, 4: incompositus, reconditus et, quo Cicero utitur, subabsurdus, Quint. 1, 5, 65; cf. id. 6, 3, 23; 6, 3, 99.—Adv.: sŭbabsurdē, somewhat absurdly: aliquid subabsurde dicere, Cic. de Or. 2, 68, 275.
subabsurdus.short: sŭb-absurdus, a, um, adj., somewhat or rather absurd (Ciceronian): sunt illa subabsurda, Cic.

subaccuso.full: sŭb-accūso, āre, v. a., to blame or accuse somewhat (Ciceronian): alicujus discessum, Cic. Planc. 35, 86; id. Att. 16, 7, 1: subaccusa quaeso Vestorium, id. ib. 13, 46, 2.

subacer.full: sub-ăcĕr, acris, acre, adj., somewhat sharp (late Lat.): gustus, Isid. 17, 10, 8.
subacer.short: sub-ăcĕr, acris, acre, adj., somewhat sharp (late Lat.): gustus, Isid.

subacidus.full: sŭb-ăcĭdus, a, um, adj., somewhat sour, sourish: vinum, Cato, R. R. 108, 2: sucus, Plin. 12, 25, 54, § 120.
subacidus.short: sŭb-ăcĭdus, a, um, adj., somewhat sour, sourish: vinum, Cato, R.

subactio.full: sŭbactĭo, ōnis, f. subigo. Lit., a working through, working up, preparing (rare): harena fluviatica bacillorum subactionibus in tectorio recipit soliditatem, Vitr. 2, 4 fin.: subactiones ciborum, Arn. 3, 107.—* Trop., preparation, discipline: subacto mihi ingenio opus est ... subactio autem est usus, auditio, lectio, litterae, Cic. de Or. 2, 30, 131.

subactor.full: sŭbactor, ōris, m. id., a debaucher, polluter (syn. paedico; post-class.), Lampr. Heliog. 31; 5; id. Commod. 3.

subactus1.full: sŭbactus, a, um, Part. of subigo.

subactus2.full: sŭbactus, ūs, m. subigo, a working up, kneading, Plin. 18, 7, 12, § 67.

subadjuva.full: sŭb-adjŭva, ae, m. adjuvo, an assistant (post-class.), Cod. Th. 6, 27, 3 fin.; Cod. Just. 12, 20, 4.

subadmiratio.full: sŭb-admīrātio, ōnis, f., admiration (late Lat.), Dion. Exeg. Greg. Nyss. Creat. Hom. 10.
subadmiratio.short: sŭb-admīrātio, ōnis, f., admiration (late Lat.), Dion.

subadmoveo.full: sŭb-admŏvĕo, ēre, 2, v. a., to bring close, Col. 6, 36, 4 (dub.).

subaduno.full: sŭb-ădūno, are, 1, v. a., to unite (late Lat.), Cassiod. in Psa. 134, 4.

subaemulatio.full: sŭb-aemŭlātio, ōnis, f. subaemulor, secret rivalry, Ambros. in Psa. 36, § 10.

subaemulor.full: sŭb-aemŭlor, āri, 1, v. dep., to accumulate secretly, Ambros. in. Psa. 36, § 10.

subaeratus.full: sŭb-aerātus, a, um, adj., that has copper underneath, i. e. inside: aurum, Pers. 5, 106.
subaeratus.short: sŭb-aerātus, a, um, adj., that has copper underneath, i.

subagitatio.full: sŭbăgĭtātĭo, sŭbăgĭtātrix, sŭb-ăgĭto, v. subigitatio, etc.

subagrestis.full: sŭb-ăgrestis, e, adj., somewhat rustic, rather boorish (Ciceronian): subagreste quiddam planeque subrusticum, Cic. Brut. 74, 259: consilium, id. Rep. 2, 7, 12: ingenium, Amm. 14, 11, 11.
subagrestis.short: sŭb-ăgrestis, e, adj., somewhat rustic, rather boorish (Ciceronian): subagreste quiddam planeque subrusticum, Cic.

subalaris.full: sŭb-ālāris, e, adj., that is under the arms, placed or carried under the arms: telum, Nep. Alcib. 10, 5: culcitae, Lampr. Heliog. 19 fin.—As substt. sŭbālāres, ĭum, f. plur., the feathers under the wing, Vulg. 4 Esd. 11, 25.— sŭbālāre, is, n., an under-girdle, Edict. Diocl. p. 25; cf. Isid. Orig. 19, 33.
subalaris.short: sŭb-ālāris, e, adj., that is under the arms, placed or carried under the arms: telum, Nep.

subalbens.full: sŭb-albens, entis, adj., somewhat white, whitish: prasinus, Cassiod. Var. 5, 34.
subalbens.short: sŭb-albens, entis, adj., somewhat white, whitish: prasinus, Cassiod.

subalbicans.full: sŭb-albĭcans, antis, adj., somewhat white, whitish: palea rubra, Varr. R. R. 3, 9, 5.
subalbicans.short: sŭb-albĭcans, antis, adj., somewhat white, whitish: palea rubra, Varr.

subalbidus.full: sŭb-albĭdus, a, um, adj., rather whitish: pars corrupta, Cels. 5, 28, 8: folia, Plin. 21, 25, 96, § 168; Isid. 12, 1, 50.
subalbidus.short: sŭb-albĭdus, a, um, adj., rather whitish: pars corrupta, Cels.

subalbus.full: sŭb-albus, a, um, adj., rather white, whitish: sabulo, Varr. R. R. 1, 9, 5.
subalbus.short: sŭb-albus, a, um, adj., rather white, whitish: sabulo, Varr.

subalpinus.full: sŭb-alpīnus, a, um, adj., lying near the Alps, sub-Alpine: montes, Plin. 25, 7, 34, § 71: Italia, Plin. 16, 11, 22, § 55.
subalpinus.short: sŭb-alpīnus, a, um, adj., lying near the Alps, sub-Alpine: montes, Plin.

subalternicum.full: sŭbalternĭcum, i, n., a kind of reddish amber, Plin. 37, 2, 11, § 33.
subalternicum.short: sŭbalternĭcum, i, n., a kind of reddish amber, Plin.

subamarus.full: sŭb-ămārus, a, um, adj., somewhat bitter, bitterish (Ciceronian), Cic. Fat. 4, 8. —Adverb.: subamarum arridens, somewhat bitterly, Amm. 27, 11, 5.
subamarus.short: sŭb-ămārus, a, um, adj., somewhat bitter, bitterish (Ciceronian), Cic.

subaperio.full: sŭb-ăpĕrĭo, īre, v. a., to open from within (post-class.): nivem, Arn. 2, 84: auriculam sub cutem, Apic. 8, 7, § 372.

subaquaneus.full: sŭb-ăquānĕus, a, um, adj. aqua, that is or belongs under water, sub-aqueous: subterraneum et subaquaneum viventia carent haustu aëris, Tert. Anim. 32.

subaquilus.full: sŭb-ăquĭlus, a, um, adj., somewhat dusky, brownish, tawny (ante- and postclass.): corpus. Plaut. Rud. 2, 4, 9: vultus, Trebell. XXX. Tyr. 30.
subaquilus.short: sŭb-ăquĭlus, a, um, adj., somewhat dusky, brownish, tawny (ante- and postclass.): corpus.

subarator.full: sŭb-ărātor, ōris, m., one who ploughs close to any thing, Plin. 17, 24, 37, § 227.
subarator.short: sŭb-ărātor, ōris, m., one who ploughs close to any thing, Plin.

subarescens.full: sŭb-ārescens, entis, adj. aresco, growing somewhat dry: trullissatio, Vitr. 7, 3 med.

subargutulus.full: sŭb-argūtŭlus, a, um, adj., somewhat subtle, tolerably keen, Gell. 15, 30, 1.
subargutulus.short: sŭb-argūtŭlus, a, um, adj., somewhat subtle, tolerably keen, Gell.

subarmalis.full: sŭb-armālis, e, adj. armus, passing under the arms (post-class.): vestis (perh. thrown back under the arm), Mart. Cap. 5, § 426.—As subst.: sŭbarmāle, is n., = subarmalis vestis, Valer. ap. Treb. Claud. 14; Spart. Sever. 6 fin.; Vop. Aur. 13; cf. subalaris.

subaro.full: sŭb-ăro, no perf., ātum, 1, v. a., to plough close to any thing (Plinian), Plin. 16, 27, 50, § 116: subarata ocius senescunt, id. 16, 29, 51, § 119.

subarroganter.full: sŭb-arrŏganter, adv., somewhat proudly or arrogantly: facere, Cic. Ac. 2, 36, 114.
subarroganter.short: sŭb-arrŏganter, adv., somewhat proudly or arrogantly: facere, Cic.

subasper.full: sŭb-asper, ĕra, ĕrum, adj., rather rough, roughish: ἀλφός, Cels. 5, 28, 19.
subasper.short: sŭb-asper, ĕra, ĕrum, adj., rather rough, roughish: ἀλφός, Cels.

subassentiens.full: sŭb-assentĭens, a, um, P. a. assentio, assenting or yielding a little: manus subassentientibus umeris movetur, Quint. 11, 3, 100.

subasso.full: sŭb-asso, no perf., ātum, 1, v. a., to roast a little, Apic. 4, 2; 7, 2; 7, 5; 8, 8: squilla, Cael. Aur. Tard. 4, 3, 6.

subatio.full: sŭbātĭo, ōnis, f. subo, the heat, brimming of swine, Plin. 8, 51, 77, § 205; Fulg. Prisc. Serm. 46.

subaudio.full: sŭb-audĭo, ii, ītum, 4, v. n. (postclass.). To understand, supply a word omitted: subaudito jubeo, Dig. 28, 5, 1; Aug. Civ. Dei, 15, 7; 17, 11; Greg. M. in Job, 33, 17.— To hear a little: nocturnis subaudiens vocibus, App. M. 5, p. 167, 4.

subauditio.full: sŭbaudītĭo, ōnis, f. subaudio, an understanding, supplying a word omitted (post-class.), Serv. Verg. A. 10, 80; Hier. Quaest. Hebr. in Reg. 2, 3, 13.

subauratus.full: sŭb-aurātus, a, um, adj., slightly gilt: anulus, Petr. 32, 3: tabellae, Schol. Juv. 7, 23: STATVA, Inscr. Orell. 1126.
subauratus.short: sŭb-aurātus, a, um, adj., slightly gilt: anulus, Petr.

subausculto.full: sŭb-ausculto, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a., to listen secretly, to eavesdrop (rare but class.): subauscultando excipere voces, Cic. de Or. 2, 36, 153: opprime os: is est, etiam subauscultemus, Plaut. As. 3, 2, 40: tace, subauscultemus, ecquid de me fiat mentio, id. Mil. 4, 2, 3: videntur subauscultare quae loquor, Cic. Att. 10, 18, 1: viris subauscultantibus pariete interposito, id. Top. 20, 75.

subausterus.full: sŭb-austērus, a, um, adj., rather harsh: vinum austerum vel certe subausterum, Cels. 3, 6, § 61; 6, 6. 8, § 68.
subausterus.short: sŭb-austērus, a, um, adj., rather harsh: vinum austerum vel certe subausterum, Cels.

subbalbe.full: sub-balbē, adv. balbus, somewhat stammeringly: canorus, Spart. Get. 5, § 1.

subballio.full: Sub-ballĭo, ōnis, m., Under - Ballio, Sub - Ballio; a comically - formed name: Ha. Tune es Ballio? Ps. Immo vero ego ejus sum Subballio, Plaut. Ps. 2, 2, 13.
subballio.short: Sub-ballĭo, ōnis, m., Under - Ballio, Sub - Ballio;

subbasilicanus.full: sub-băsĭlĭcānus, i, m. basilica, one who lounges around the basilicas, a lounger: quorum odos subbasilicanos omnes abigit, Plaut. Capt. 4, 2, 35 Brix ad loc.

subbibo.full: sub-bĭbo, bĭbi, 3, v. a., to drink a little, to tipple (very rare), * Plaut. Truc. 4, 3, 58 (dub.; Speng. si urnas bibit): si paulum subbibisset, * Suet. Ner. 20.

subblandior.full: sub-blandĭor, īri (fut. subblandibitur, Plaut. Bacch. 3, 4, 19; inf. subblandirier, id. Cas. 3, 3, 22), v. dep. n., to caress or fondle a little (ante-class.): subblanditur, palpatur, Lucil. ap. Non. 472, 6; Plaut. As. 1, 3, 33: viris alienis, id. Cas. 3, 3, 22: mihi inani atque inopi, id. Bacch. 3, 4, 19; 4, 8, 35; id. Most. 1, 3, 64.

subbrevis.full: sub-brĕvis, e, adj., rather short: folium (saliuncae), Plin. 21, 7, 20, § 43.
subbrevis.short: sub-brĕvis, e, adj., rather short: folium (saliuncae), Plin.

subbullio.full: sub-bullĭo, īre, 4, v. n., to foam or bubble slightly, Cassiod. Hist. Eccl. 7, 2; Plin. Val. 1, 11.

subdealbo.full: sub-dĕalbo, āre, v. a., to whiten a little, make whilish, Varr. ap. Non. 72, 11.

subdebilis.full: sub-dēbĭlis, e, adj., somewhat weak or enfeebled: femur, Suet. Vit. 17.
subdebilis.short: sub-dēbĭlis, e, adj., somewhat weak or enfeebled: femur, Suet.

subdebilitatus.full: sub-dēbĭlĭtātus, a, um, adj. debilito, somewhat enfeebled or debilitated; trop., somewhat discouraged, rather spiritless, Cic. Att. 11, 5, 1 (dub.; better: subitā re quasi debilitatum, B. and K.).

subdefectio.full: subdēfectĭo, ōnis, f. sub - deficio, a slight failure: fidei, Aug. Quaest. in Heptat. 6, 30.

subdeficio.full: sub-dēfĭcĭo, ĕre, v. n., to become more and more feeble, to fail somewhat (postAug.), Curt. 7, 7, 10: in labore, Aug. Serm. 343 fin.

subdeligo.full: subdēlĭgo, ĕre, 3, v. a. sub-deligo, to choose (late Lat.), Aug. Categ. 6.

subdescendo.full: subdescendo, ĕre, 3, v. n. sub-descendo, to descend lower (late Lat.), Mar. Merc. Commonit. 4, 6.

subdiaconus.full: sub-dĭăcŏnus, i, m., a sub - deacon, Cod. Just. 1, 3, 6; Aug. Ep. 53; 63; Isid. 7, 12, 23.
subdiaconus.short: sub-dĭăcŏnus, i, m., a sub - deacon, Cod.

subdialis.full: sub-dĭālis (subdīvālis, Amm. 19, 11, 4), e, adj. dius, that is in the open air (post-Aug.): inambulationes, Plin. 14, 1, 3, § 11: petrae, id. 34, 12, 29, § 117.—As subst.: subdĭālĭa, ĭum, n., open galleries or terraces; a transl. of the Gr. ὑπαίθρια, ὕπαιθρα, Plin. 36, 25, 62, § 186.—Also in sing.: subdival domus, Tert. adv. Jud. 11.

subdifficilis.full: sub-diffĭcĭlis, e, adj., somewhat difficult: quaestio, Cic. Lael. 19, 67.
subdifficilis.short: sub-diffĭcĭlis, e, adj., somewhat difficult: quaestio, Cic.

subdiffido.full: sub-diffīdo, ĕre, v. n., to be somewhat distrustful, Cic. Att. 15, 20, 2.

subdimidius.full: sub-dīmĭdĭus, a, um, adj., of a number, half as much less, less by one half of itself (i. e. that bears to another the ratio of 2 to 3): numerus (opp. superdimidius), Mart. Cap. 7, § 761.
subdimidius.short: sub-dīmĭdĭus, a, um, adj., of a number, half as much less, less by one half of itself (i.

subdisjunctio.full: sub-disjunctĭo, ōnis, gram. t. t., a minor stop, colon, Diom. p. 432 P.

subdisjunctivus.full: sub-disjunctīvus, a, um, adj., subdisjunctive; said of two statements opposed to each other in such a way that neither of them may hold good (postclass.): haec verba: ille aut ille, non solum disjunctiva sed etiam subdisjunctivae orationis sunt, etc., Dig. 50, 16, 124: conjunctiones, Prisc. p. 1029 P.

subdistinguo.full: sub-distinguo, xi, ctum, 3, v. a., to make a smaller interpunction (perh. a colon), Ascon. ad Cic. Verr. 2, 2, 13 fin.

subditicius.full: subdĭtīcĭus (later -tĭus), a, um, adj. subdo, substituted, supposititious, spurious, counterfeit (perh. only ante- and postclass., since the correct read. in Cic. Verr. 2, 5, 27, § 69, is subditivum; and in Quint. 1, 4, 3, subditos): servus, Plaut. Ps. 2, 4, 62: Antonius, Lampr. Heliog. 17; Amm. 14, 6, 15.

subditivus.full: subdĭtīvus, a, um, adj. id., substituted, supposititious, spurious, counterfeit (rare but class.): de illo subditivo Sosia mirum nimis est, Plaut. Am. 2, 2, 198; 1, 2, 35: archipirata, Cic. Verr. 2, 5, 27, § 69: fratrem ut subditivum arguere, Suet. Ner. 7. —Subst.: Subdĭtīvus, i, m., the title of a comedy of Cœcilius, Gell. 15, 9, 1 (Com. Rel. p. 39 sq. Rib.).

subdito.full: subdĭto, āre, a false read., Lucr. 6, 604; v. Lachm. ad h. l.
subdito.short: subdĭto, āre, a false read., Lucr.

subditus.full: subdĭtus, a, um, Part., from subdo.
subditus.short: subdĭtus, a, um, Part., from subdo.

subdiu.full: sub-diū, adv., by day, Plaut. Most. 3, 2, 78.

subdivido.full: sub-dīvĭdo, īsi, īsum, 3, v. a., to subdivide (late Lat.): libros, Aug. Civ. Dei, 6, 3 med.: deinde subdivisimus, id. Trin. 3 prooem.: hebdomades, Tert. adv. Jud. 11 fin.

subdivisio.full: subdīvīsĭo, ōnis, f. subdivido, a subdivision (post-class.), Cod. Just. 3, 28, 37; 6, 2, 22; Hier. Ep. 58, 5 al.

subdivisus.full: subdīvīsus, a, um, Part. of subdivido.

subdo.full: sub-do, dĭdi, dĭtum, 3, v. a. To put, place, set, or lay under (syn.: suppono, sterno). Lit. (class.). In gen.: ego puerum interead ancillae subdam lactantem meae, Liv. Andron. ap. Non. p. 153, 26 (Trag. Rel. v. 26 Rib.): ignem subdito, Cato, R. R. 105, 1; so, ignem, id. ib. 38, 4; Cic. N. D. 2, 10, 27; Liv. 8, 30 al.: faces, Lucr. 6, 1285: lapidem magnetem, id. 6, 1046: manum oculo uni, id. 4, 447; cf.: rem oculorum visu, id. 5, 101: furcas vitibus, Plin. 14, 2, 4, § 32: pugionem pulvino, Suet.

subdoceo.full: sub-dŏcĕo, ēre, v. a. and n., to teach as an assistant, to act as an assistant-teacher for a person (very rare): aliquem, Cic. Att. 8, 4, 1: subdocere grammatico, Aug. Conf. 8, 6.

subdoctor.full: sub-doctor, ōris, m., an underteacher, assistant-instructor, Aus. Prof. 22.
subdoctor.short: sub-doctor, ōris, m., an underteacher, assistant-instructor, Aus.

subdolens.full: sub-dŏlens, entis, adj. sub - doleo, somewhat painful: faucium sensus, Cael. Aur. Acut. 3, 2, 7.

subdolositas.full: subdŏlōsĭtas, ātis, f. sub - dolosus, craft, cunning, Isid. 10, n. 229.

subdolosus.full: subdŏlōsus, a, um, adj. id., crafty (late Lat.), Cassiod. in Psa. 106, 34.

subdolus.full: sub-dŏlus, a, um, adj., somewhat crafty, cunning, sly, subtle, deceptive, or deceitful (mostly ante - class. and post - Aug.; syn.: fallax, astutus): homo et sycophanta et subdolus, Plaut. Poen. 5, 2, 72; id. Mil. 2, 4, 2; id. Men. 3, 2, 24; id. Aul. 2, 5, 8; id. Poen. 5, 2, 129: ut viro subdola sies, memento, id. Cas. 4, 4, 5: subdola adversus senem, id. Ep. 2, 3, 13: jugurtha, cognitā vanitate legati, subdolus ejus augere amentiam, Sall. J. 38, 1: occultus ac subdolus fingendis virtutibus, Tac
subdolus.short: sub-dŏlus, a, um, adj., somewhat crafty, cunning, sly, subtle, deceptive, or deceitful (mostly ante - class.

subdomo.full: sub-dŏmo, āre, v. a., to subject by taming, to tame, subdue, Plaut. As. 3, 3, 112.

subdubito.full: sub-dŭbĭto, āre, v. n., to be a little doubtful or undecided, to have some hesitation (Ciceron.): antea subdubitabam, Cic. Att. 14, 15, 2: significabant tuae litterae, te subdubitare, quā essem erga illum voluntate, id. Fam. 2, 13, 2.

subduco.full: sub-dūco, xi, ctum, 3 (perf. sync. subduxti, Ter. Eun. 4, 7, 25; inf. subduxe, Poët. ap. Varr. R. R. 2, 1, 6), v. a., to draw from under or from below. Without the idea of removal. In gen., to draw or pull up; to lift up, raise (rare): brassicam ad nasum admoveto: ita subducito susum animam, quam plurimum poteris, Cato, R. R. 157, 15: aliquid sursum, Plaut. Aul. 2, 7, 4: cataractam funibus, Liv. 27, 28, 10: subductis (tunicis) usque ad inguen, pulled up (opp. demissis), Hor. S. 1, 2, 26: superci

subductarius.full: subductārĭus, a, um, adj. subduco, I., that serves for drawing up: funes, hoisting-ropes, lifts, Cato, R. R. 12; 68; 135, 3.

subductio.full: subductĭo, ōnis, f. id.. (Acc. to subduco, I. B. 1.) Naut. t. t., a hauling ashore of a ship: ad celeritatem onerandi subductionesque paulo facit humiliores (naves), * Caes. B. G. 5, 1: navium, Vitr. 10, 2, 10.—* (Acc. to subduco, II. B.) A reckoning, Cic. Or. 2, 30, 132.

subductus.full: sub-ductus, a, um, Part. and P. a., v. subduco.

subdulcis.full: sub-dulcis, e, adj., somewhat sweet, sweetish (Plinian): radix, Plin. 26, 8, 37, § 58; 26, 10, 63, § 98.
subdulcis.short: sub-dulcis, e, adj., somewhat sweet, sweetish (Plinian): radix, Plin.

subdurus.full: sub-dūrus, a, um, adj., somewhat hard, hardish. * Lit.: (genus verrucae) subdurum, Cels. 5, 28, 14.—* Trop., Q. Cic. Petit. Cons. 12, 46.
subdurus.short: sub-dūrus, a, um, adj., somewhat hard, hardish.

subedo.full: sŭb-ĕdo, ēdi, 3, v. a., to eat, waste, or wear away below: e scopulo, quem rauca subederat unda, Ov. M. 11, 783; Hier. in Jer. 1, 2, 37.

subelectio.full: sŭbēlectĭo, ōnis, f. sub-eligo, a further selection (late Lat.): subelectio est quando de bonis electis eliguntur meliores, Ps.Aug. ad Frater. Erem. Serm. 39.

subeligo.full: sŭbēlĭgo, ĕre, 3, v. a., to choose further (late Lat.), Ps.-Aug. ad Fratr. Serm. 39.

subenarro.full: sŭb-ēnarro, āre, 1, v. a., to relate (late Lat.), Anon. [Hilar.] in Job, 2, p. 174.

subeo.full: sŭb-ĕo, ĭi, ĭtum, īre (perf. subīvit, Ov. F. 1, 314; Stat. S. 2, 1, 155: subivimus, Claud. ap. Tac. A. 11, 24 dub.), v. n. and a., to come or go under any thing; to come or go up to, to approach, draw near, advance or proceed to a place; to come or go on; to follow, succeed; to go down, sink; to come up, spring up (cf. succedo). Neutr. Lit. In gen.: subire sub falas, Plaut. Most. 2, 1, 10: in nemoris latebras, Ov. M. 4, 601; cf.: in aliquem locum, to enter, Auct. B. Alex. 74, 4: in adversum Roma

suber.full: sūber, ĕris, n., the cork-oak, cork-tree: Quercus suber, Linn.; Plin. 16, 8, 13, § 34; 16, 25, 41, § 98; Col. 4, 26, 1; 9, 6, 1; Verg. A. 7, 742.— Transf., cork: silvestre, Verg. A. 11, 554; cf.: ut ramale vetus vegrandi subere coctum, i. e. a thick bark, like that of the cork-tree, Pers. 1, 97.—The tree is called sūbĕrĭes, ēi, f., Lucil. ap. Fest. p. 294 Müll.; cf. Isid. Orig. 17, 7, 27.
suber.short: sūber, ĕris, n., the cork-oak, cork-tree: Quercus suber, Linn.;

suberectus.full: sŭbērectus, a, um, Part. of suberigo.

subereus.full: sūbĕrĕus, a, um, adj. suber, of the cork-tree, cork-: cortex, Ser. Samm. 34, 649: robur, Col. 9, 1, 3 Schneid. N. cr.

suberigo.full: sub-ērĭgo, no perf., ectum, 3, v. a., to raise up from below (post-Aug.): Isthmon curvata sublime suberigit unda, Sil. 15, 155: effultus in cubitum suberectusque, App. M. 2, p. 123 fin.; Marc. Emp. 20.

suberinus1.full: sūbĕrīnus, a, um, adj. suber, of the cork-tree, cork- (syn. subereus): cortices, Sid. Ep. 2, 2 med.

suberinus2.full: Sūbĕrīnus, i, m. 1. suberinus, a Roman surname, Plin. Ep. 6, 33, 6.

suberro.full: sŭb-erro, āre, v. n., to wander about under any thing: fluvii Italis suberrant Montibus, Claud. Cons. Prob. et Olybr. 254.

subertani.full: Subertāni, ōrum, m., a people of Etruria, the inhabitants of Subertum, the modern Sovretto in Tuscany, Plin. 3, 5, 8, § 52. —Hence, Subertānus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to the Subertani: forum, Liv. 26, 23, 5.
subertani.short: Subertāni, ōrum, m., a people of Etruria, the inhabitants of Subertum, the modern Sovretto in Tuscany, Plin.

subexcuso.full: sŭb-excūso, āre, 1, v. a., to excuse in part, Salv. Gub. Dei, 4, 3.

subexhibeo.full: sŭb-exhĭbĕo, ēre, v. a., to exhibit under any thing, Arn. 6, 195.

subexplicans.full: sŭb-explĭcans, antis, Part. [explico], unfolding below (late Lat.): non pedibus se ferens neque suas subexplicans itiones, Arn. 7, 251.

subhaereo.full: sŭb-haerĕo, ēre, v. n., to stick under or behind; to cleave, adhere to a thing, Val. Max. 6, 3, 10.

subhastarius.full: sŭbhastārĭus, a, um, adj. sub-hasta, that is sold by public auction (jurid. Lat.): possessiones, Cod. Th. 13, 6, 9.

subhastatio.full: sŭbhastātĭo, ōnis, f. subhasto, a sale by public auction (late Lat. for venditio palam habita), Cod. Just. 4, 44, 16; Cod. Th. 10, 17, 3.

subhasto.full: sŭb-hasto, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. sub-hasta, to sell by public auction (jurid. Lat. for hastae subicio, palam vendo): res pignori datas. Cod. Just. 7, 53, 3; Sol. 10, 4.

subheres.full: sŭb-hēres (-haeres), ēdis, m., the next or second heir (syn.: heres secundus), Inscr. Orell. 3612.
subheres.short: sŭb-hēres (-haeres), ēdis, m., the next or second heir (syn.: heres secundus), Inscr.

subhorresco.full: sŭb-horresco, ĕre, v. inch. n., to become rough or stormy from below, to boil up: subito mare subhorrescere, Sisenn. ap. Non. 423, 9.

subhorridus.full: sŭb-horrĭdus, a, um, adj., somewhat rough, roughish: subhorridus atque incultus, Cic. Sest. 9, 21.
subhorridus.short: sŭb-horrĭdus, a, um, adj., somewhat rough, roughish: subhorridus atque incultus, Cic.

subi.full: Subi, m. indecl., a river of Spain, Plin. 3, 3, 4, § 21.—Called also Subis, is, m., Mel. 2, 6.

subices.full: sŭbĭces, um, f. subicio, underlayers, supports: Ennius in tragoediā, quae Achilles inscribitur, pro aëre alto ponit, qui caelo subjectus est, in his versibus: per ego deum sublimas subices umidas, Unde oritur imber, sonitu saevo et strepitu, Gell. 4, 17, 14; cf. Fest. p. 305 Müll., and Non. 168, 33 (Trag. v. 5 Vahl.).

subicio.full: sūb-ĭcĭo (less correctly subjĭcĭo; post-Aug. sometimes sŭb-), jēci, jectum, 3, v. a. sub-jacio. Lit., to throw, lay, place, or bring under or near (cf. subdo); in all senses construed with acc. and dat., or with acc. and sub and acc.; not with sub and abl. (v. Madvig. ad Cic. Fin. 2, 15, 48; cf. II. B. 2. infra). In gen.: si parum habet lactis mater, ut subiciat (agnum) sub alterius mammam. Varr. R. R. 2, 1, 20: manum ventri et sub femina (boum), Col. 6, 2, 6: nonnulli inter carros rotasque mata

subiculum.full: sŭbĭcŭlum, a false read., Plaut. Pers. 3, 3, 14; v. Ritschl ad h. l.

subidus.full: sŭbĭdus, a, um, adj, knowing, sensible, Poët. ap. Gell. 19, 9, 11 (dub.; Hertz, subitus).
subidus.short: sŭbĭdus, a, um, adj, knowing, sensible, Poët.

subigitatio.full: sŭbĭgĭtātĭo (sŭbăgĭt-), ōnis, f. subigito, illicit intercourse, Plaut. Capt. cat. 2.

subigitatrix.full: sŭbĭgĭtātrix (sŭbăgĭt-), īcis, f. id., she that indulges in illicit intercourse, a lascivious woman, Plaut. Pers. 2, 2, 45.

subigito.full: sŭbĭgĭto (sŭbăgĭto), āre, v. freq. a. sub-agito. Lit., to lie with illicitly (ante-class.): scortum, Plaut. Mil. 3, 1, 53 (649 Ritschl): aliquam, id. ib. 5, 9; id. Cas. 5, 4, 2 (al. subicitare); id. Merc. 1, 2, 91; Ter. Heaut. 3, 3, 6.— Trop., to work upon, incite to any thing (post-class.): aliquem, M. Aurel. ap. Front. Ep. ad M. Caes. 4, 5: mulierem blanditiis, App. Mag. p. 329, 3.

subigo.full: sŭbĭgo, ēgi, actum, 3 (sūbĭgĭt, scanned with u long, Cic. poët. Div. 1, 47, 106), v. a. sub-ago, to bring under, get under; bring or get up, or up to any place. Lit. (mostly poet.): sues antequam aestus incipiat, subigunt in umbrosum locum, Varr. R. R. 2, 4, 6: qui adverso flumine lembum Remigiis subigit, i. e. rows up stream, Verg. G. 1, 202: naves ad castellum, Liv. 26, 7: classem ad moenia, Sil. 15, 218: saxum contra ardua montis, id. 13, 610: frondosum apicem ad sidera, id. 17, 641 et saep.:
subigo.short: sŭbĭgo, ēgi, actum, 3 (sūbĭgĭt, scanned with u long, Cic.

subigus.full: Sŭbĭgus, i, m. subigo, I., the tutelary god of the wedding-night, Aug. Civ. Dei, 6, 9.

subimpleo.full: sŭbimplĕo, ēre, 2, v. a. sub-impleo, to fill up, Aug. c. Epist. Manich. 22, 24.

subimpudens.full: sŭb-impŭdens, entis, adj., somewhat shameless or impudent: saepe, Cic. Fam. 7, 17, 1.
subimpudens.short: sŭb-impŭdens, entis, adj., somewhat shameless or impudent: saepe, Cic.

subinanis.full: sŭb-ĭnānis, e, adj., somewhat empty or vain: quod est subinane in nobis, Cic. Att. 2, 17, 2.
subinanis.short: sŭb-ĭnānis, e, adj., somewhat empty or vain: quod est subinane in nobis, Cic.

subinde.full: sŭb-inde, adv., a particle of time. In gen., immediately after, just after, presently, forthwith, thereupon (not ante-Aug.): primum gaudere, subinde Praeceptum auriculis hoc instillare memento, Hor. Ep. 1, 8, 15: ager primum aretur ultimā parte mensis Augusti, subinde Septembri sit iteratus, Col. 2, 4, 11: primo auctumno arandi et subinde conserendi, id. 11, 2, 8; Tac. Agr. 14: sparge subinde, Hor. S. 2, 5, 103: aliud subinde bellum cum alterius orae Graecis ortum, Liv. 8, 27; cf. id. 28, 25, 1
subinde.short: sŭb-inde, adv., a particle of time.

subindico.full: sŭb-indĭco, āre, 1, v. a., to indicate slightly, to hint at (late Lat.), Mar. Marc. Cyril. Incarn. Unigen. 31.

subindo.full: sŭb-indo, ĕre, 3, v. a., to subjoin, add, Aur. Vict. Orig. Rom. 3, § 7.

subinfero.full: sŭb-infĕro, tŭli, ferre, irreg. v. a., to subjoin, add, Aug. Genes. Litt. 3, 24; Rutil. Lup. 1, 1; Vulg. 2 Pet. 1, 5.

subinflo.full: sŭb-inflo, āre, 1, v. a., to puff up somewhat; pass. subinflari, Cael. Aur. Tard. 2, 4, 71.—Rare, except in part., somewhat puffed up or inflated (late Lat.): vultus, Cael. Aur. Acut. 1, 2 sq.: pulsus, id. ib. 1, 6: pectus, Arn. 2, 46.

subinfluo.full: sŭb-inflŭo, a false read. for subterfluant, Sen. Q. N. 3, 30, 4.

subinjectus.full: sŭb-injectus, a, um, Part. [inicio], laid down upon: subinjectā manu, Sen. Contr. 3, 13 init.

subinscribo.full: sŭb-inscrībo, ĕre, 3, v. a., = παρεγγράφω, to subjoin, Rustic. c. Aceph. p. 1208 B.

subinsulsus.full: sŭb-insulsus, a, um, adj., somewhat tasteless or insipid: si quid absurdum ... aut subinsulsum est, Cic. Opt. Gen. 3, 7.
subinsulsus.short: sŭb-insulsus, a, um, adj., somewhat tasteless or insipid: si quid absurdum ...

subintellego.full: sŭb-intellĕgo, ĕre, v. a., to understand or perceive a little (late Lat.), Tert. adv. Marc. 5, 3; Hier. Ep. 145 med.— To supply in thought, understand in addition, Aug. Trin. 6, 4; id. Serm. 104, 3 fin.; Greg. M. in Job, 33, 7 al.

subintro.full: sŭb-intro, āvi, ātum, 1, v. n., to go into secretly, to enter by stealth, steal into (late Lat.); trop.: populo bellicoso ludorum scenicorum subintravit insania, Aug. Civ. Dei, 1, 32; so Tert. adv. Marc. 5, 3 al.

subintroduco.full: sŭb-intrōdūco, ĕre, v. a., to introduce in secret (late Lat.): eum, Aug. Ep. 137: fratres, Vulg. Gal. 2, 4.

subintroeo.full: sŭb-intrŏĕo, īre, v. a., to go into, enter: subintroire speciem alicujus, Arn. 6, 198; Vulg. Gal. 2, 4.

subintromitto.full: sŭbintrōmitto, ĕre, 3, v. a. sub-intromitto, introduced temporarily, Facund. Defens. 9, 1 (probably an error for subintermitto).

subinvideo.full: sŭb-invĭdĕo, no perf., sum, 2, v. a. To envy a little or slightly, to be somewhat envious of (Ciceronian): subinvideo tibi, ultro te etiam arcessitum ab eo, Cic. Fam. 7, 10, 1.—* Part. perf., a little disliked, somewhat odious: subinvisum apud malevolos Postumi nomen, Cic. Rab. Post. 14, 40.

subinvito.full: sŭb-invīto, āvi, 1, v. a., to invite slightly: aliquem, ut ad se scriberet, Cic. Fam. 7, 1, 6.

subirascor.full: sŭb-īrascor, ātus, 3, v. dep. n., to be somewhat angry (Ciceronian): interdum soleo subirasci, Cic. Fin. 2, 4, 12: brevitati litterarum, id. Fam. 11, 24, 1: in Epirum quod me non invitas, subirascor, id. Att. 9, 7, 7.—Hence, sŭbīrātus, a, um, P. a., somewhat angry: tibi, Cic. de Or. 1, 16, 72; id. Fam. 3, 9, 1: anus subiratior, App. M. 4, p. 154 (dub. al. iratior).

subis1.full: subis, is, f., a kind of bird that breaks eagles' eggs, otherwise unknown, Nigid. ap. Plin. 10, 14, 17, § 37.
subis1.short: subis, is, f., a kind of bird that breaks eagles' eggs, otherwise unknown, Nigid.

subitaneus.full: sŭbĭtānĕus, a, um, adj. subitus, sudden: imber, Col. 1, 6, 24; 2, 4, 4; Sen. Q. N. 7, 22, 1; Vulg. Sap. 17, 6; 17, 14; 19, 16.

subitarius.full: sŭbĭtārĭus, a, um, adj. id., done suddenly or in haste, sudden, hasty: ad eum exercitum explendum Latini Hernicique dare Quintio subitarios milites (ita tum repentina auxilia appellabant) jussi, Liv. 3, 4, 11; so, milites (corresp. to tumultuarii), id. 40, 26, 6: exercitus, id. 3, 30, 3; 31, 2, 6; 41, 17, 9: res, Plaut. Mil. 2, 2, 70: aedificia, Tac. A. 15, 39: gradus theatri (with scena in tempus structa), id. ib. 14, 20: dictio, a speaking extempore, Gell. 9, 15, 5: consilium, App. M. 9, p. 22

subitatio.full: sŭbĭtātĭo, ōnis, f. id., suddenness (late Lat.), Vulg. Sap. 5, 2.

subito.full: sŭbĭtō, adv., v. subeo, P. a. fin.

subitum.full: sŭbĭtum, i, n., v. subitus, 2. s. v. subeo fin.

subitus.full: sŭbĭtus, a, um, v. subeo, P. a.

subjacentia.full: subjăcentia, ae, f. sub-jaceo, the being a subject (philos. t. t., = τὸ ὑποκεῖσθαι): omni qualitate remotā ipsum subjacentiae solius punctum contuetur, absolute objectiveness, Rufin. Orig. Princ. 4, 1.

subjaceo.full: sub-jăcĕo, cŭi, 2, v. n., to lie under or near any thing (post-Aug.). Lit.: feles coeunt mare stante, feminā subjacente, Plin. 10, 63, 83, § 174: frumentum si tegulis subjaceat, id. 18, 30, 73, § 301: fenestris subjacet vestibulum villae, Plin. Ep. 2, 17, 15; cf.: subjacentes petrae, Curt. 5, 3, 18: campus aedificio subjacet, adjoins, lies close to the building, Col. 1, 2, 3; so, monti, Plin. Ep. 5, 6, 2: fenestra subjacens, id. ib. 2, 17, 6.— Trop., to be under, subject to any thing; to belong

subjecte.full: subjectē, adv., v. subicio, P. a. fin.

subjectibilis.full: subjectĭbĭlis, e, adj. subicio, submissive, Vulg. Baruch, 1, 18.

subjectio.full: subjectĭo, ōnis, f. id., a laying, putting, or placing under. Lit. In gen.: rerum sub aspectum paene subjectio, Cic. de Or. 3, 53, 202: totius rei sub oculos subjectio, Gell. 10, 3, 7; Quint. 9, 2, 40.— In partic. A representation, Vitr. 9, 8; 9, 9.— A substituting, forging: testamentorum, Liv. 39, 18.— A subjugation, reduction to obedience: provinciarum, Oros. 3, 14 fin.: mentium, Ambros. in Psa. 118, Serm. 12, § 27: in omni subjectione, in all submissiveness, Vulg. 1 Tim. 2, 11; the state of s

subjectivus.full: subjectīvus, a, um, adj. subjectus, of or belonging to the subject of a proposition, subjective: pars, i. e. the subject, App. Dogm. Plat. 3, p. 30, 30; Mart. Cap. 4, § 393; Tert. Virg. Vel. 4 fin.—Adv.: subjectīvē, subjectively, Mart. Cap. 4, § 393.

subjecto.full: subjecto (also written subjacto, Varr. R. R. 1, 52, 2), āre, v. freq. a. subicio, to lay, place, or put under; to throw out from below (mostly poet.; not in Cic.): manus, Ov. M. 4, 359: acres Subjectat lasso stimulos, Hor. S. 2, 7, 94: saxa, Lucr. 6, 700: nigram alte harenam, to cast up from its depths, Verg. G. 3, 241; so, grana e terrā, Varr. R. R. 1, 52, 2.

subjector.full: subjector, ōris, m. id., one who substitutes, a substitutor, forger: testamentorum, Cic. Cat. 2, 4, 7.

subjectum.full: subjectum, i, v. subicio, II. C.

subjectus1.full: subjectus, a, um, Part. and P. a., from subicio.

subjectus2.full: subjectus, ūs, m. subicio, a laying under (post-Aug. and very rare), Plin. 26, 15, 90, § 154.

subjugalis.full: sub-jŭgālis, e, adj., accustomed to the yoke: subjugales beluae, Prud. στεφ. 10, 333.—Subst., a beast of burden, Vulg. Matt. 21, 5.
subjugalis.short: sub-jŭgālis, e, adj., accustomed to the yoke: subjugales beluae, Prud.

subjugator.full: subjŭgātor, ōris, m. subjugo, one who brings under the yoke, a conqueror, subjugator (post-Aug.): ORBIS TERRARVM, Inscr. Orell. 838: malorum, App. Dogm. Plat. 2, pp. 16, 17.

subjugius.full: subjŭgĭus, a, um, adj. sub-jugum, of or belonging to the yoke, that is attached to the yoke: lora, Cato, R. R. 135, 5; Vitr. 10, 3, 3 Schneid. N. cr.—Subst.: subjŭ-gĭa, ōrum, n. plur. (sc. lora), yoke-straps, Cato, R. R. 63.

subjugo.full: subjŭgo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. id. (postclass.) To bring under the yoke: decus publicum, Arn. 4, p. 129: exercitum, Eutr. 4, 17.— In gen., to subject, subjugate: ORBEM TERRAE ROMANO NOMINI, Inscr. Grut. 281, 2: hostes, Claud. VI. Cons. Hon. 249: provinciam, Ps.-Ascon. ad Cic. Verr. 1, 21: multi periculo subjugati sunt, Lact. Mort. Pers. 34.—With dat.: aliquem poenae, Dig 4, 8, 43: aliquem personali muneri, ib. 50 4, 18, § 9: ingratum populum legi, Lact. 4, 10, 10: totum hominem alienae dicioni, id

subjugus.full: subjŭgus, a, um, adj. id. * That is attached to the yoke, yoked: molae machinariae subjugum aliquem dare, App. M. 7, p. 194, 29.— subjŭgum, i, n., the name of an unknown animal: eïdem auctores subjugum, quod nec quale esset animal, nec ubi nasceretur, tradiderunt, Plin. 30, 15, 52, § 146.

subjunctivus.full: subjunctīvus, a, um, adj. subjungo, of or belonging to binding together, connecting; in the later gram. lang., modus, the subjunctive mood, Diom. p. 331 P.; Prisc. p. 820 ib. al.: conjunctiones, e. g. si, cum, antequam, etc., Charis. p. 200 sq. P.: vocales, Prisc. 561 ib.

subjunctorium.full: subjunctōrĭum, ii, n. id., a carriage drawn by animals, Cod. Th. 8, 5, 10.— = ὑποζύγιον, a beast used for draught, Ambros. Interp. Job et Dav. 2, 5, § 20.

subjunctus.full: subjunctus, a, um, Part. of subjungo.

subjungo.full: sub-jungo, xi, ctum, 3 (inf. pass. subjungier, Prud. ap. Symm. 2, 586), v. a., to yoke, harness (rare): curru subjungere tigres, Verg. E. 5, 29: (juvencos) plostro, Col. 6, 2, 8: carpento suo equas, Plin. 11, 49, 109, § 262.— Transf., in gen. To join or add to, to annex, affix, subjoin. * Lit.: Aeneia puppis ... rostro Phrygios subjuncta leones, having affixed, Verg. A. 10, 157.— Trop., to bring under, make subject, subordinate, subjoin (class.): aliquid sub suom judicium, Naev. 1, 5: tu fac utr

sublabium.full: sublăbĭum, ii, n. sub-labium, a plant, dog's-tongue, App. Herb. 96.

sublabor.full: sub-lābor, lapsus, 3, v. dep. n., to fall, glide, or sink under or down, to sink (poet. and in post-Aug. prose). Lit.: imperfecta necesse est labent et modo prodeant, modo sublabantur aut succidant, Sen. Ep. 71, § 34: aedificia vetustate sublapsa, Plin. Ep. 10, 75, 1; cf. poet. transf.: annis sublapsa vetustas, Verg. A. 12, 686.—* In partic., to slip down, glide away: lues udo sublapsa veneno Pertentat sensus, Verg. A. 7, 354.— Trop.: retro sublapsa Spes, Verg. A. 2, 169: memoria senum, Sen. Oed

sublabro.full: sub-lăbro, āre, v. a. labrum, to put into the mouth, Nov. ap. Non. 170, 8.

sublacrimans.full: sub-lăcrĭmans, antis, P. a. lacrimo, weeping a little: oculi, Veg. Vet. 1, 30.

sublamina.full: sub-lāmĭna, ae, f. an under-plate, Cato, R. R. 21, 3.

sublapsus.full: sublapsus, a, um, P. a. of sublabor.

sublaqueum.full: Sublăquĕum, i, n., a little town of the Æqui, in Latium, near which Nero had a country-seat, now Subiaco, Plin. 3, 12, 17, § 109; Tac. A. 14, 22.—Hence, Sublăcen-sis, e, adj., of or belonging to Sublaqueum: villa, that of Nero, near Sublaqueum, Front. Aquaed. 93: viae, constructed there by him, id. ib. 7; 14; 15.
sublaqueum.short: Sublăquĕum, i, n., a little town of the Æqui, in Latium, near which Nero had a country-seat, now Subiaco, Plin.

sublate.full: sublātē, adv., v. tollo, P. a. fin.

sublatio.full: sublātĭo, ōnis, f. [tollo), a lifting up, raising, elevation. Lit.: a sublatione (soni) ad positionem, an upward beat in marking time, Quint. 9, 4, 48; so (opp. positio) id. 9, 4, 48, § 55.— Trop. * In gen., an elevation, exaltation: animi, Cic. Fin. 2, 4, 13.— In partic., a removal: furtiva, Ambros. in Luc. 5, § 112.— An abrogation, annulling: judicii, Quint. 7, 1, 60.

sublatus.full: sublātus, a, um, Part. of tollo; as P. a., v. tollo fin.

sublavo.full: sub-lăvo, āre, v. a., to wash from beneath (post-Aug. and rare): os vulvae vino, Cels. 6, 18, 10: se, Capitol. M. Aur. 19; App. Herb. 79.

sublectio.full: sublectĭo, ōnis, f. sublego, a gleaning, leasing (post-class.), Tert. adv. Marc. 4, 31 med.

sublecto.full: sublecto, āre, v. freq. a. sub-lacio, to wheedle, cajole: os, Plaut. Mil. 4, 2, 74.

sublectus.full: sublectus, a, um, Part. of sublego.

sublego.full: sub-lĕgo, lēgi, lectum, 3, v. a. To gather from below, to gather or search for underneath, to gather up: (puer) sublegit quodcumque jaceret inutile quodque Posset cenantes offendere, Hor. S. 2, 8, 12: baca tempestatibus in terram decidit et necesse est eam sublegere, Col. 12, 52, 1: ficum viridem, id. 12, 17, 1.— In partic., to catch up secretly or by stealth. Lit.: liberos, to kidnap, Plaut. Rud. 3, 4, 44.— Trop.: clam alicujus sermonem, to overhear, Plaut. Mil. 4, 2, 98; so, sermonem hinc, Tur

sublestus.full: sublestus, a, um, adj. acc. to Döderl. Synon. 2, p. 101 sq., perh. from sublevo; and hence, light, slight, trifling, trivial (ante-class.): sublesta antiqui dicebant infirma et tenuia, Plaut. Pers. 3, 1, 20: fides sublestior, id est, infirmior. Idem in Nervolaria vinum ait sublestissimum, quia infirmos faciat vel corpore vel animo, Fest. pp. 294 and 295 Müll.; cf.: sublestum est leve, frivolum, Non. 177, 11: sublestus infirmus, tristis, Gloss. Isid.: fides, Plaut. Bacch. 3, 6, 13.

sublevatio.full: sublĕvātĭo, ōnis, f. sublevo, II. B., a lightening, alleviation; trop.: sublevatio et medicina, Cic. Rep. 2, 34, 59.

sublevo.full: sub-lĕvo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a., to lift up from beneath, to raise up, hold up, support (class.: esp. freq. in the trop. sense; syn.: extollo, erigo). Lit.: qui nos sibi quondam ad pedes stratos ne sublevabat quidem, Cic. Att. 10, 4, 3: in ascensu sublevati, Caes. B. C. 2, 34; id. B. G. 7, 47: alterni innixi sublevantesque invicem et trahentes alii alios, Liv. 5, 47, 2; 28, 20, 5; cf.: jubis equorum sublevati, Caes. B. G. 1, 48: erigere se aut sublevare, id. ib. 6, 27: terrā sublevat ipsum, Verg.

sublica.full: sublĭca, ae, f., a stake or pile driven into the ground, a palisade (cf.: palus, sudes, stipes), Caes. B. C. 3, 49; Liv. 23, 37; Vitr. 3, 3.—Esp., of the piles for a bridge, Caes. B. G. 4, 17; 7, 35; Liv. 1, 37.—In the form sublices, Sall. H. Fragm. 4, 77; cf. Gloss. Labb.
sublica.short: sublĭca, ae, f., a stake or pile driven into the ground, a palisade (cf.: palus, sudes, stipes), Caes.

sublicius.full: sublĭcĭus, a, um, adj. sublica, consisting of or resting upon piles: Pons Sublicius, the pile-bridge, a wooden bridge across the Tiber, built by Ancus Marcius, Liv. 1, 33; 2, 10; Sen. Vit. Beat. 25, 1; Plin. 36, 15, 23, § 100; Tac. H. 1, 86; Varr. L. L. 5, § 83, and 6, § 44 Müll.; Fest. p. 293 ib.; cf. Becker, Antiq. 1, p. 693 sq.—As the place where beggars sat, Sen. Vit. Beat. 25.

sublido.full: sublīdo, ĕre, v. a. sub-laedo, to press out: murmur voce, Prud. Apoth. 915.— To injure by degrees, Vitr. 6, 8 (12), 2 dub.

subligaculum.full: sublĭgācŭlum, i, n. subligo, a waistband, breech - cloth, Cic. Off. 1, 35, 129; cf. Non. 19, 21.—Called subsequently sublĭ-gar, āris, n., Mart. 3, 87, 4; Juv. 6, 70; Plin. 12, 14, 32, § 59; and sublĭgātūra, ae, f., Theod. Prisc. 1, 26.

subligatio.full: sublĭgātĭo, ōnis, f. id., a binding or tying below: uvarum, Pall. 1, 6, 10.

subligo.full: sub-lĭgo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a., to bind or tie below, to bind on (mostly poet.; not in Cic.; syn. subnecto): vites, Cato, R. R. 33, 4; Plin. 17, 22, 35, § 197: lateri atque umeris ensem, Verg. A. 8, 459: clipeum sinistrae, id. ib. 11, 11: arma, Val. Fl. 5, 445; cf. poet., transf.: quem (virum) balteus asper Subligat, girds, id. 5, 579: tiaram extremā cervice, id. 6, 700 et saep.: subligata ludit, trussed up, tucked up, Mart. 7, 67, 4.

sublimatio.full: sublīmātĭo, ōnis, f. sublimo, a lifting up, deliverance, Alcim. Ep. 2.

sublimator.full: sublīmātor, ōris, m. id., an elevator, exalter (late Lat.): Deus est Abrahami sublimator, Salv. Gub. Dei, 1, 8.

sublimen.full: sub-līmen, adv. acc. to Ritschl, Opusc. 2, p. 464, = sublimen superum, referring to the hanging up of slaves for punishment; but acc. to Ussing ad Plaut. As. v. 859 from sublimis, on high, upwards (mostly anteclass.): facite illic homo jam in medicinam ablatus sublimen siet, Plaut. Men. 5, 7, 3 Ritschl: jam sublimen raptum oportuit, id. ib. 5, 7, 6 ib.: sublimen ferre, id. ib. 5, 7, 13 ib.; 5, 8, 3 ib. (in all these passages Brix reads sublimis, sublimem); cf.: illum jubes ancillas rapere sublim

sublimis.full: sublīmis, e (collat. form sublīmus, a, um: ex sublimo vertice, Cic. poët. Tusc. 2, 7, 19; Enn. ap. Non. 169; Att. and Sall. ib. 489, 8 sq.; Lucr. 1, 340), adj. etym. dub.; perh. sub-limen, up to the lintel; cf. sublimen (sublimem est in altitudinem elatum, Fest. p. 306 Müll.), uplifted, high, lofty, exalted, elevated (mostly poet. and in postAug. prose; not in Cic. or Cæs.; syn.: editus, arduus, celsus, altus). Lit. In gen., high, lofty: hic vertex nobis semper sublimis, Verg. G. 1, 242; cf. Hor

sublimitas.full: sublīmĭtas, ātis, f. sublimis, height, loftiness (post-Aug.; cf. altitudo). Lit.: corporis, Quint. 12, 5, 5: cellarum, Col. 8, 3, 3: cucurbitarum, Plin. 19, 5, 24, § 69.—In plur.: lunae, Plin. 2, 16, 13, § 68.— Trop. In gen.: sublimitas incomparabilis invicti animi, Plin. 7, 25, 26, § 94: in picturā, id. 35, 10, 36, § 67.— In partic., of language, loftiness, elevation, sublimity (while elevatio means disparagement): heroici carminis, Quint. 1, 8, 5; cf.: ab his (poëtis) in verbis sublimitas peti

sublimitus.full: sublīmĭtus, adv. sublimis, up high, high: pauci militum equum sublimitus insilire, Fronto Ep. ad Ver. 1 med. Mai.

sublimo.full: sublīmo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. id., to lift up on high, to raise, elevate (ante- and postclass.). Lit.: facem (sol), Enn. ap. Non. 170, 11 (Trag. v. 319 Vahl.): se nubium tenus, App. Flor. p. 340, 38; cf. mid.: sublimata in altum, id. M. 3, p. 138, 34; Vitr. 6, 6, 4; Vulg. 1 Reg. 2, 10.— Trop.: sublimavit dixit (Cato), id est in altum extulit, Originum, l. II.: in maximum decus atque in excelsissimam claritudinem sublimavit, Fest. p. 306 Müll.: aliquem, Macr. S. 1, 24 med.: Pallas praetoriis ornam

sublimus.full: sublīmus, a, um, v. sublimis init.

sublingio.full: sublingĭo, ōnis, m. sub-lingo, a lick-dish, under-scullion: coqui, Plaut. Ps. 3, 2, 103.

sublinguium.full: sublinguĭum, ii, n. id., the epiglottis, Isid. 11, 1, 59.

sublino.full: sub-lĭno, lēvi, lĭtum, 3, v. a., to besmear or anoint beneath, to lay on as a groundcolor, to prime with any thing (ante-class. and post-Aug.). Lit.: chrysocollam atramento, Plin. 33, 5, 27, § 90: caeruleum, id. 35, 6, 26, § 45: argentum vivum, id. 33, 6, 32, § 100: sanguinem lacertae, id. 30, 9, 23, § 80.— Transf. To put underneath, underlay (syn. substerno): maceriam calce, Cato, R. R. 15, 1: tertium (genus sardonychis) argenteis bracteis sublinitur, etc., Plin. 37, 7, 31, § 105.— Sublinere os

sublitus.full: sublĭtus, a, um, Part. of sublino.

sublividus.full: sub-līvĭdus, a, um, adj., somewhat blue, bluish (very rare): pustulae, Cels. 5, 28, 1 and 11 med.
sublividus.short: sub-līvĭdus, a, um, adj., somewhat blue, bluish (very rare): pustulae, Cels.

sublucanus.full: sub-lūcānus, a, um, adj. lux, towards day, towards morning: temporibus, Plin. 11, 12, 12, § 30.

subluceo.full: sub-lūcĕo, ēre, v. n., to shine a little, to gleam faintly, to glimmer (poet. and in post - Aug. prose): aries sublucet corpore totus, Cic. Arat. 289: crepuscula sublucent, Ov. Am. 1, 5, 5: si fragmenta (picis), subluceant, Plin. 14, 20, 25, § 127: (liquor) nigrantis rosae colore sublucens, id. 9, 36, 60, § 126: violae sublucet purpura nigrae, Verg. G. 4, 275; cf.: candida nec mixto sublucent ora rubore, Ov. H. 21, 217.

sublucidus.full: sub-lūcĭdus, a, um, adj., somewhat light, lightish: lucus, App. M. 6, p. 174, 24.
sublucidus.short: sub-lūcĭdus, a, um, adj., somewhat light, lightish: lucus, App.

subluco.full: sub-lūco, āre, 1, v. a. lux, to trim, cut away, thin out the branches of a tree, to admit light: sublucare arbores est ramos earum supputare, et veluti subtus lucem mittere, Fest. p. 348 Müll.: arbor ... nisi a domino sublucari non potest, isque conveniendus est ut eam sublucet, Paul. Sent. 5, 6, 13; cf. colluco.

sublugeo.full: sub-lūgĕo, ēre, v. n., to lament a little, Inscr. Cenot. Pis. ap. Orell. 643.

subluo.full: sub-lŭo, no perf., lūtum, ĕre, v. a., to wash or bathe underneath (very rare; not in Cic.). Lit.: aliquid aquā calidā, Cels. 4, 15; Col. 6, 32, 1: inguina, Mart. 6, 81, 2: subluto podice, id. 2, 42, 1.— Transf., of rivers, to flow along the base of, to wash the foot of: hunc montem flumen subluebat, Caes. B. C. 3, 97: radices collis (flumina), id. B. G. 7, 69.—Pass.: Asia, quā Hellesponto, quā rubro mari subluitur, Curt. 9, 6, 20.
subluo.short: sub-lŭo, no perf., lūtum, ĕre, v.

sublustris.full: sublustris, e, adj. sub-lux, giving some light, having a faint light, glimmering (not ante-Aug., and very rare). Lit.: nox, Hor. C. 3, 27, 31; Liv. 5, 47: umbra (noctis), Verg. A. 9, 373; Val. Fl. 3, 141.— * Trop.: eloquentiae Latinae lumina, Gell. 13, 24, 12.

subluteus.full: sub-lūtĕus, a, um, adj., somewhat yellow, yellowish (post-class.): color, App. Flor. p. 348, 29: color purpurei luminis suffectione subluteus, Arn. 5, 164.
subluteus.short: sub-lūtĕus, a, um, adj., somewhat yellow, yellowish (post-class.): color, App.

sublutus.full: sublūtus, a, um, Part. of subluo.

subluvies.full: sublŭvĭes, em, e, f. subluo, that which is washed off, filth, dirt (post-Aug.). In gen.: via subluvie caenosā lubrica, App. M. 9, p. 221, 2: limosa, Amm. 15, 4.— In partic., a disease in the feet of sheep, the foul, Col. 7, 5, 11; so in the feet of men, Plin. 30, 9, 23, § 80.—Called also sublŭvĭum, ii, n., Marc. Emp. 18 fin.

subnascor.full: sub-nascor, nātus, 3, v. dep. n., to grow up under, out of, or after; to follow after, succeed (not ante-Aug.): num vada subnatis imo viridentur ab herbis, Ov. Hal. 90: qui (cortex) subnascente alio expellitur, Plin. 17, 24, 37, § 234; so, folia, id. 16, 22, 34, § 84: poma, id. 12, 3, 7, § 15: castaneae, id. 17, 20, 34, § 148: pilus, id. 11, 39, 94, § 230: plumae, id. 11, 23, 27, § 78: ulcera, Sen. Brev. Vit. 5, 5: aqua, id. Ira, 2, 10, 5: ignis, Sil. 14, 65.

subnato.full: sub-năto, āre, v. n., to swim beneath (post-Aug. and very rare): pars subnatat unda Membrorum, pars exstat aquis, Sil. 14, 482: currus bijuges alii subnatant, App. M. 4, p. 157, 6.

subnatus.full: subnātus, a, um, Part. of subnascor.

subnavigo.full: sub-nāvĭgo, āvi, āre, v. a., to sail under the lee: Cyprum, Vulg. Act. 27, 4 (transl. of the Gr. ὑπεπλεύσαμεν).

subnecto.full: sub-necto, nexui, xum, ĕre, v. a., to bind or tie under, bind on beneath (poet. and in post-Aug. prose; syn. subligo). Lit.: antennis velum, Ov. M. 11, 483: cingula mammae, Verg. A. 1, 492: tenui de vimine circlos Cervici, id. G. 3, 167: subnectit fibula vestem, id. A. 4, 139: fragmentum clavi collo, Plin. 28, 4, 11, § 46: specieque comam subnexus utrāque, wreathed, garlanded, Stat. S. 5, 3, 113 et saep.— Trop., to add, subjoin in speaking: ut inventioni judicium subnecterent, Quint. 3, 3, 5 Spa

subnego.full: sub-nĕgo, āvi, 1, v. a., to half deny or refuse: quod praesenti tibi prope subnegāram, Cic. Fam. 7, 19 init.

subnero.full: Subnĕro, ōnis, m. sub-Nero, the second Nero, an appellation given to the emperor Domitian, on account of his crimes, Tert. Pall. 4 (cf. of the same: calvus Nero, Juv. 4, 37).

subnervo.full: subnervo, āvi, 1, v. a. sub-nervus, to cut the sinew beneath, to hamstring, hough (post-class.). Taurum, Tert. adv. Jud. 10 med.: equos, Vulg. Jos. 11, 6: jugales, id. 2 Reg. 8, 4.—* Trop., to invalidate, refute: calumnias, App. Mag. p. 327.

subnexus.full: subnexus, a, um, Part. of subnecto.

subniger.full: sub-nĭger, gra, grum, adj., somewhat black, blackish: ventriosus, subniger, Plaut. Ps. 4, 7, 120: oculis, id. Merc. 3, 4, 55: labris (canum), Varr. R. R. 2, 9, 3: color (cutis), Cels. 5, 28, 4.
subniger.short: sub-nĭger, gra, grum, adj., somewhat black, blackish: ventriosus, subniger, Plaut.

subnixus.full: sub-nixus (-nīsus), a, um, Part. [nitor], supported from beneath, under-propped, propped up, supported by, resting or leaning upon any thing, etc. (class., esp. in the trop. sense; cf. suffultus). Lit.: (duos circulos) caeli verticibus ipsis ex utrāque parte subnixos vides, Cic. Rep. 6, 20, 21: solioque alte subnixa resedit, Verg. A. 1, 506: parva Philoctetae subnixa Petelia muro, supported, i. e. defended by, id. ib. 3, 402: subnixae nubibus altis, id. Cir. 195: cubito subnixa, id. ib. 348: Cae

subnotatio.full: subnŏtātĭo, ōnis, f. subnoto, a signing underneath, subscription (post-class.), Cod. Just. 1, 23, 6; Cod. Th. 8, 5, 22; Hier. Ep. 123.

subnoto.full: sub-nŏto, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. (post-Aug.). To mark, note, or write underneath (cf. subscribo): in inferiori lineā particulares propositiones subnotentur, App. Dogm. Plat. 3, p. 31, 27: nomina palam, to write down, Suet. Calig. 41.—Transf.: libellos, to subscribe, Plin. Ep. 1, 10, 9.— To note secretly, to mark, watch, observe: et non sobria verba subnotasti, Mart. 1, 28, 5: aliquem vultu digitoque, id. 6, 82, 3.

subnuba.full: subnŭba, ae, f. sub-nubo, a rival: lecti subnuba nostri, Ov. H. 6, 153.

subnubilus.full: sub-nūbĭlus, a, um, adj., somewhat cloudy or overcast, rather gloomy: nox, * Caes. B. C. 3, 54: limes, Ov. R. Am. 599.
subnubilus.short: sub-nūbĭlus, a, um, adj., somewhat cloudy or overcast, rather gloomy: nox, * Caes.

subo.full: sŭbo, āre, v. n., to be in heat. Prop. of sows, Plin. 10, 63, 83, § 181.— Transf. Of other animals, Lucr. 4, 1199; App. Mag. p. 298, 22.— Of women, Hor. Epod. 12, 11; Tert. Apol. 46; 14; Hier. ap. Jovin. 1, 38; 2, 36.

subobscenus.full: sŭb-obscēnus (-caenus), a, um, adj., somewhat smutty or obscene: ridiculum, Cic. Or. 26, 88.
subobscenus.short: sŭb-obscēnus (-caenus), a, um, adj., somewhat smutty or obscene: ridiculum, Cic.

subobscurus.full: sŭb-obscūrus, a, um, adj., somewhat obscure; trop., of language: breves et ob eam ipsam causam interdum subobscuri, Cic. Brut. 7, 29: ingressio, id. Or. 3, 11: cicatrix, Vulg. Lev. 13, 21.—Adv.: sŭbob-scūrē, somewhat obscurely: dixit, Gell. 10, 1, 7: explicat, id. 3, 14, 6.
subobscurus.short: sŭb-obscūrus, a, um, adj., somewhat obscure;

subocrini.full: Sub-ocrīni, ōrum, m., an Alpine people, Plin. 3, 20, 24, § 133.
subocrini.short: Sub-ocrīni, ōrum, m., an Alpine people, Plin.

subocularis.full: sŭb-ŏcŭlāris, e, adj., that is beneath the eye, subocular: venae, Veg. Vet. 4, 4.
subocularis.short: sŭb-ŏcŭlāris, e, adj., that is beneath the eye, subocular: venae, Veg.

subodiosus.full: sŭb-ŏdĭōsus, a, um, adj., somewhat vexatious or odious, Cic. Att. 1, 5, 4.
subodiosus.short: sŭb-ŏdĭōsus, a, um, adj., somewhat vexatious or odious, Cic.

suboffendo.full: sub-offendo, ĕre, v. n., to give some offence: apud faecem populi, Cic. Q. Fr. 2, 6, 5.

suboleo.full: sŭb-ŏlĕo (-ŏlo, pres. subj. subolat, Ter. Heaut. 5, 1, 26; cf. oleo init.), ēre, v. n. (prop. to emit a smell; only trop. and in third pers. sing.): hoc subolet alicui, or impers. subolet (alicui), to smell, scent, perceive any thing; I (thou, etc.), perceive, detect, etc. (ante-class.): id jam pridem sensi et subolet mihi, Plaut. Ps. 1, 5, 7; id. Cas. 2, 3, 59; 3, 2, 24; Ter. Phorm. 3, 1, 10: propemodum quod illic festinet, sentio et subolet mihi, Plaut. Trin. 3, 1, 14 Brix ad loc.: scio equide

suboles.full: sŭbŏles (less correctly sŏbŏles), is, f. sub- 2. oleo, olesco, a sprout, shoot, offshoot, twig, spray: suboles ab olescendo, id est crescendo, ut adulescentes quoque et adultae et indoles dicitur, Fest. p. 309 Müll. Lit. (very rare; syn. surculus), of plants: ulmum serere ex subolibus, Col. 5, 6, 2: caepa, quae non habuit suboles adhaerentes, id. 12, 10; Plin. 17, 10, 12, § 65 et saep. —Of the hair: ex subolibus parvuli (capilli) demittebantur, Varr. ap. Non. 456, 7: cum capillus frequenti subol

subolesco.full: sŭb-ŏlesco, ĕre, v. inch. n., to grow up (very rare): juventus subolescens, Liv. 29, 3: subolescere imperio adultos ejus filios, Amm. 14, 11, 3.

subolfacio.full: sŭb-olfăcĭo, cĕre, v. a., to smell out, perceive by the scent: subolfacio, quod nobis epulum daturus est Mammea, Petr. 45, 10.

suborior.full: sŭb-ŏrĭor, īri, v. dep. n., to spring up, arise, proceed (very rare), Lucr. 1, 1036; 1, 1049; 2, 1138: metallorum opulentia tot saeculis suboriens, Plin. 2, 93, 95, § 207; Arn. 3, 9.

subornator.full: sŭbornātor, ōris, m. suborno, an instigator, abettor, suborner (post-class.): subornatores ac delatores puniuntur, Paul. Sent. 5, 13: servorum, Lampr. Commod. 19 fin.: subornatore et conscio praefecto praetorio, Amm. 15, 5 med.

suborno.full: sŭb-orno, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. With the idea of the verb predominating, to fit out, furnish, provide, equip, adorn (class.; syn. instruo): aliquem pecuniā, Anton. ap. Cic. Phil. 13, 16, 32: vigilanter nervoseque nos, qui stamus in acie, subornes, Planc. ap. Cic. Fam. 10, 23, 6: paenulati isti in militum cultum subornati, Sen. Ben. 3, 28, 4: praeturae insignia invasit, praecedentibus in modum lictorum subornatis, Val. Max. 7, 3, 10: qui se ipse norit, intelliget, quemadmodum a naturā subornatus in

subortus.full: sŭbortus, ūs, m. suborior, a rising or springing up, Lucr. 5, 303.

subostendo.full: sŭb-ostendo, di, sum, 3, v. a., to point out secretly, to show indirectly (post-class.): aliquid, Tert. adv. Marc. 4, 38 med.; id. adv. Valent. 1: spes adventus Domini subostensa, id. Bapt. 19; id. Anim. 12.

subostensus.full: subostensus, a, um, Part. of subostendo.

subota.full: Subota, ōrum, n., an island of the Ægean Sea, Liv. 44, 28, 6.
subota.short: Subota, ōrum, n., an island of the Ægean Sea, Liv.

subquartus.full: sub-quartus, a, um, adj., = ὑποτέταρτος, one fourth less (late Lat.), Mart. Cap. 7, § 761.
subquartus.short: sub-quartus, a, um, adj., = ὑποτέταρτος, one fourth less (late Lat.), Mart.

subsalsus.full: sub-salsus, a, um, adj., somewhat salt, brackish: aqua, Cels. 5, 12: herba, Plin. 21, 29, 103, § 175.
subsalsus.short: sub-salsus, a, um, adj., somewhat salt, brackish: aqua, Cels.

subsannatio.full: sub-sannātĭo, ōnis, f. subsanno, mockery by gestures, derision in pantomime, Vulg. Psa. 34, 16; 43, 14.

subsannator.full: subsannātor, ōris, m. id., one who insults or mocks by gestures, Vulg. Ecclus. 33, 6.

subsanno.full: sub-sanno, āre, v. a. sanna, to insult by derisive gestures, to deride, mock (late Lat.): ecce ipsi quasi subsannantes, Tert. adv. Jud. 11 med.; Hier. Ep. 40, 2; Vulg. Psa. 34, 16; id. Isa. 37, 22.

subsarcino.full: subsarcĭno, āre, 1, v. a., to repair, heal (late Lat.), Victor Funon. Poenit. 29.

subscalpo.full: sub-scalpo, ĕre, v. a., to scratch or rub underneath, Mart. Cap. 1, § 7.

subscribendarius.full: sub-scrībendārĭus, ii, m. scribo, an under-secretary (late Lat.), Cod. Th. 7, 4, 1; 7, 84, 8 al.

subscribo.full: sub-scrībo, psi, ptum, 3, v. a. To write underneath or below (class.; cf. subnoto). In gen.: statuis inauratis ... subscripsit, Reges ab se in gratiam esse reductos, Cic. Clu. 36, 101; cf.: subscripsere quidam L. Bruti statuae: utinam viveres, etc., Suet. Caes. 80: si quaeret Pater Urbium Subscribi statuis, Hor. C. 3, 24, 28; cf.: meo subscribi causa sepulcro, Ov. M. 9, 563: quarum (litterarum) exemplum subscripsi, Balb. ap. Cic. Att. 9, 13, A, § 1; Treb. ap. Cic. Fam. 12, 16, 3; cf.: seminaria

subscriptio.full: subscriptĭo, ōnis, f. subscribo. Any thing written underneath, a subscription (class.). In gen.: Serapionis subscriptio, Cic. Att. 6, 1, 17.— In partic. Jurid. t. t., a subscription to an accusation: si cui crimen obiciatur, praecedere debet in crimen subscriptio, quae res ad id inventa est, ne facile quis prosiliat ad accusationem, cum sciat inultam sibi non futuram, Dig. 48, 2, 7: componere, Sen. Ben. 3, 26, 2: consecratur subscriptio, id. Cons. ad Marc. 22, 5: edere, id. Lud. Mort. Claud. 14,

subscriptor.full: subscriptor, ōris, m. id.. (Acc. to subscribo, I. B. 1.) A signer or joint-signer of an accusation, Cic. Div. in Caecil. 15, 47; 16, 51: venalis scriptor et subscriptor tuus, id. Dom. 19, 49: accusatore Lentulo subscriptoribusque ejus, id. Q. Fr. 3, 4, 1: sine ullo subscriptore descendit, Cael. ap. Cic. Fam. 8, 8, 1.— (Acc. to subscribo, I. B. 3. b.) One who subscribes or assents to any thing, a favorer, approver (post-class.): sententiae legisque fundus subscriptorque, Gell. 19, 8, 12: subscrip

subscriptus.full: subscriptus, a, um, Part. of subscribo.

subscruposus.full: sub-scrūpōsus, a, um, adj. (late Lat.), somewhat sharp or critical: examinator meritorum, Amm. 21, 16, 3.

subscus.full: subscūs, ūdis, f. sub-cudo, the tongue or tenon of a dovetail: subscudes appellantur cuneatae tabellae, quibus tabulae inter se configuntur, quia, quo eae immittuntur, succuditur, Fest. p. 306 Müll.: nec ulla subscus cohibet compagem alvei, Pac. ap. Fest. l. l. (Trag. Rel. v. 250 Rib.): terebratus multum sit et subscudes additae, Plaut. ib.; Cato, R. R. 18, 9; Vitr. 4, 7; 10, 6; 10, 10.—Plur.: subscudibus et catenis uncis retentari, Arn. 6, 16.—Collat. form of plur. subscudines, Aug. Civ. Dei, 1

subseco.full: sub-sĕco, cui, ctum, 1, v. a., to cut under, cut away below; to clip, pare (rare; not in Cic.): stramentum et manipulum falce, Varr. R. R. 1, 50, 1: herbam. id. ib. 1, 49, 1: legumina, id. ib. 1, 23, 3: radices, Col. 2, 9, 10: partes, unde creatus erat (Saturnus), Ov. Ib. 276: ungues ferro, id. F. 6, 230: papavereas ungue comas, id. ib. 4, 438; Cels. 7, 33.

subsectus.full: subsectus, a, um, Part. of subseco.

subsecundarius.full: sub-sĕcundārĭus, a, um, adj., that comes afterwards, additional: tempora, spare time, leisure moments (with subseciva), Gell. N. A. praef. § 23.
subsecundarius.short: sub-sĕcundārĭus, a, um, adj., that comes afterwards, additional: tempora, spare time, leisure moments (with subseciva), Gell.

subsellium.full: subsellĭum, ii, n. sub-sella, a low bench (quod non plane erat sella, subsellium, Varr. L. L. 5, § 128 Müll.); hence, transf., a bench for sitting upon, a seat of any kind (in a house, the theatre, the curia, a court, etc.; syn.: scamnum, sedile). In gen., Plaut. Stich. 5, 4, 21; 1, 2, 36; id. Capt. 3, 1, 11; Suet. Ter. 2; cf. Cels. 7, 26, 1.—Of places in the theatre: ut conquisitores singuli in subsellia Eant per totam caveam, etc., Plaut. Am. prol. 65; id. Poen. prol. 5; Cic. Corn. Fragm. med.

subsentator.full: subsentātor, ōris, m. sub-sentio, formed after the analogy of assentator, a flatterer, fawner: subdoli, Plaut. Fragm. ap. Front. Ep. ad M. Caes. 2, 13, p. 62 Nieb.

subsentio.full: sub-sentĭo, si, 4, v. a., to notice or perceive secretly, to smell out: etsi subsensi id quoque, Illos ibi esse, Ter. Heaut. 3, 1, 62.

subsequium.full: subsĕquĭum, i, n. sub-sequor, the sequel, what follows after (late Lat.), Cassiod. in Psa. 9, 5.

subsequor.full: sub-sĕquor, cūtus, 3, v. n. and a., to follow close after or immediately; to follow, succeed, ensue (class.). Lit. With acc.: subsequor te, Plaut. Am. 2, 1, 1; cf. id. ib. 1, 3, 52; id. Bacch. 4, 4, 72: has (cohortes) subsidiariae ternae subsequebantur, Caes. B. C. 1, 83: signa, id. B. G. 4, 26: ancillam, Ov. H. 20, 131: senem, id. F. 4, 528. — Absol.: quom verba facis, subsequere, Plaut. Most. 3, 2, 116: Caesar equitatu praemisso sequebatur omnibus copiis, Caes. B. G. 2, 19; cf. id. ib. 2, 11;

subsequus.full: subsĕquus or subsĭcŭus, a, um, adj. subsequor, following, succeeding (late Lat.); form subsequus: probatio, Oros. 1, 1; form subsicuus: metus, Jul. Val. Rer. Gest. Alex. 2, 21 fin.
subsequus.short: subsĕquus or subsĭcŭus, a, um, adj.

subsericus.full: sub-sērĭcus, a, um, adj., half-silken: vestis, Lampr. Heliog. 26; Gall. ap. Treb. Claud. 17; Vop. Aur. 15, 4.
subsericus.short: sub-sērĭcus, a, um, adj., half-silken: vestis, Lampr.

subsero1.full: sub-sĕro, ĕre, v. a., to sow or plant after, Col. 4, 15, 1; Dig. 7, 1, 13.— Trop., to plant or distribute secretly: nutrimenta fictis criminibus, Amm. 14, 11, 3.

subsero2.full: sub-sĕro, no perf., sertum, 3, v. a., to put or insert under (late Lat.). * Lit.: subsertis manibus, App. M. 7, p. 200, 23.— Trop.: res monuit super Eutherio pauca subserere, to add, subjoin, Amm. 16, 7, 4; 14, 11, 3.

subsertus.full: subsertus, a, um, Part. of 2. subsero.

subservio.full: sub-servĭo, īre, v. n., to be subject to, to serve (ante-class.). Lit.: istaec, quae viros subservire Sibi postulant, Plaut. Men. 5, 2, 14; Naev. ap. Front. Ep. 2, 13, p. 62 Nieb. (Com. Rel. p. 22 Rib.).—* Trop., to comply with, humor, accommodate one's self to: orationi, Ter. And. 4, 3, 20.

subsessa.full: subsessa, ae, f. subsido, an ambush, ambuscade (post-class.): subsessas occultius collocare, Veg. Mil. 3, 6 med.: in subsessā esse, id. ib. 3, 22; cf.: hostium dolos subsessas vocamus, Serv. Verg. A. 11, 268.

subsessor.full: subsessor, ōris, m. id., a waylayer, lier-in-wait (post-Aug.). Lit.: subsessores vocantur, qui occisuri aliquem delitescunt, Serv. Verg. A. 11, 268; cf. id. ib. 5, 498: subsessores cum venabulis, Petr. 40, 1.— Trop.: alieni matrimonii, Val. Max. 2, 1, 5; 7, 2, ext. 1; cf.: subsessoris et adulteri persona, Arn. 4, p. 142.

subsicivus.full: subsĭcīvus, less correctly subsĕcī-vus (also transp. subcĭsīvus or suc-cĭsīvus), a, um, adj. [sub-seco). Lit., as t. t. of the agrimensores, that is cut off and left remaining, in surveying lands.— Subst.: subsĭcīvum, i, n., a remainder or small patch of land, etc.: subsiciva, quae divisis per veteranos agris carptim superfuerunt, etc., Suet. Dom. 9 fin.; Auct. Rei Agr. ap. Goes. p. 17; 23; 39: mensores nonnumquam dicunt in subsicivum esse unciam agri, etc., Varr. R. R. 1, 10, 2.— Transf., of ti

subsidentia.full: subsīdentĭa, ae, f. subsido, a sinking down, subsidence; concr., a settling, sediment: aquarum, Vitr. 8, 3 med.

subsidialis.full: subsĭdĭālis, e, adj. subsidium, of or belonging to a reserve, subsidiary (late Lat. for the class. subsidiarius): acies, Amm. 14, 6, 17: manus, id. 27, 10, 15.

subsidiarius.full: subsĭdĭārĭus, a, um, adj. id.; in milit. lang., of or belonging to a reserve, reserve-, subsidiary. Lit. Adj. (class.): cohortes, Caes. B. C. 1, 83; Liv. 9, 27; Tac. A. 1, 63: acies, Auct. B. Afr. 59, 2: naves, Auct. B. Alex. 14, 3.— Subst.: subsĭdĭ-ārĭi, ōrum, m., the reserve, body of reserve, Liv. 5, 38; 6, 8; 9, 32.— Transf., in gen., out of the military sphere, serving for support, subsidiary: palmes, = resex, Col. 4, 24, 13 and 16.— Esp.: actio, jurid. t. t., a form of action by which the w

subsidior.full: subsĭdĭor, āri, v. dep. n. [id.], to act as a reserve, stand in reserve, Hirt. B. G. 8, 13, 2.

subsidium.full: subsĭdĭum, ii, n. subsideo. Milit. t. t. Orig., the troops stationed in reserve in the third line of battle (behind the principes), the line of reserve, reserve-ranks, triarii: subsidium dicebatur, quando milites subsidebant in extremā acie labentique aciei succurrebant. Quod genus militum constabat ex iis, qui emeruerant stipendia, locum tamen retinebant in exercitu: quae erat tertia acies triariorum, Fest. p. 306 Müll.; cf.: subsidium, quod postpositum est ad subveniendum laborantibus, id. p.

subsido.full: sub-sīdo, sēdi, sessum, 3 (collat. form acc. to 2d conj., subsīdent, Luc. 1, 646; Amm. 28, 4, 22), v. n. and a. Neutr., to sit down, crouch down, squat; to set one's self down, settle down, sink down (class.). Lit. In gen.: agite nunc, subsidite omnes, quasi solent triarii, Plaut. ap. Varr. L. L. 5, § 89 Müll.; and ap. Fest. p. 306 ib.; cf.: subsidunt Hispani adversus emissa tela ab hoste, inde ad mittenda ipsi consurgunt, Liv. 28, 2: partem militum subsidere in subsidiis jussit, id. 1, 14; cf.:

subsiduus.full: subsĭdŭus, a, um, adj. subsideo, sinking down, settling: fraces, Grat. Cyn. 474.

subsignanus.full: subsignānus, a, um, adj. sub-signum, that is or serves under the standard: miles, a kind of legionary soldiers kept in reserve to strengthen the centre, Tac. H. 1, 70 fin.; 4, 33; Amm. 29, 5, 23.

subsignatio.full: subsignātĭo, ōnis, f. subsigno, a subscription, signature. * Lit.: veteres subsignationis verbo pro subscriptione uti solebant, Dig. 50, 16, 39.—* Trop., a firm promise, assurance: poenitentiae, Tert. Poen. 2 med.

subsigno.full: sub-signo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a., to mark or write beneath, to undersign, subscribe (mostly post - Aug.; syn. subscribo). Lit.: traditas notas subsignabimus Catonis maxime verbis, Plin. 18, 6, 7, § 33: Ciceronis sententiam ipsius verbis, id. 18, 25, 61, § 228: subsignatum dicitur quod ab aliquo subscriptum est, Dig. 50, 16, 39; cf.: adhuc subsignare dicimus pro subscribere, Fest. p. 281 Müll.— Transf. * To set down, enter, register on a list: subsignari apud aerarium (praedia), Cic. Fl. 32, 80. —

subsilio.full: sub-sĭlĭo, lŭi, 4, v. n. salio, to spring upwards, leap up (mostly poet.; not in Cic.). Lit.: decido de lecto praeceps, subsilit, Plaut. Cas. 5, 2, 50; cf. id. Curc. 1, 2, 64: non subsilis ac plaudis? Varr. ap. Non. 135, 28: semper damnosi subsiluere canes, Prop. 4 (5), 8, 46. Pegasus adusque caelum subsilit ac resultat, App. M. 8, p. 208, 33: subsiliunt ignes ad tecta domorum, Lucr. 2, 191.—* Trop.: subsiluisti et acrior constitisti, Sen. Ep. 13, 3.— To leap into: jamdudum flammis dexteram obje

subsilles.full: subsilles dicebantur quaedam lamellae sacrificiis necessariae, Paul. ex Fest. p. 307 Müll.; cf. Fest. p. 306 ib.
subsilles.short: subsilles dicebantur quaedam lamellae sacrificiis necessariae, Paul.

subsimilis.full: sub-sĭmĭlis, e, adj., somewhat like, partly similar (very rare): Μελίκηρα melli albo subsimilis, Cels. 5, 26, 20: subsimile aliquid, Dig. 35, 3, 1 med.
subsimilis.short: sub-sĭmĭlis, e, adj., somewhat like, partly similar (very rare): Μελίκηρα melli albo subsimilis, Cels.

subsimus.full: sub-sīmus, a, um, adj., with a nose slightly turned up, somewhat snub-nosed or pug-nosed: boves, Varr. R. R. 2, 5, 7.
subsimus.short: sub-sīmus, a, um, adj., with a nose slightly turned up, somewhat snub-nosed or pug-nosed: boves, Varr.

subsipere.full: subsĭpĕre quod non plane sapit, Varr. L. L. 5, § 128 Müll.
subsipere.short: subsĭpĕre quod non plane sapit, Varr.

subsistentia.full: subsistentia, ae, f. subsisto, = ὑπὀστασις, the substance, reality, Cassiod. Hist. Eccl. 5, 38; 9, 3; 12, 4 fin.; Boëth. Duab. Nat. p. 950.

subsisto.full: sub-sisto, stĭti, 3, v. n. and a. Neutr., to take a stand or position, to stand still, remain standing; to stop, halt. Lit. In gen.: reliqui in itinere substiterant, Caes. B. C. 2, 41: in locis campestribus, id. ib. 1, 79: in eodem loco, Hirt. B. G. 8, 16: ad insulam Tauridem, Auct. B. Alex. 45, 1: circa ima (opp. ad summa niti), Quint. prooem. § 20.—Absol.: quo proelio sublati Helvetii audacius subsistere ... coeperunt, Caes. B. G. 1, 15: substitit Aeneas et se collegit in arma, Verg. A. 12, 49

subsitus.full: sub-sĭtus, a, um, adj., lying or situated below: convallis, App. M. 6, p. 174, 24.
subsitus.short: sub-sĭtus, a, um, adj., lying or situated below: convallis, App.

subsolaneus.full: subsŏlānĕŭs, a, um, adj. sub-solum, underground, from under the earth: subsolaneae res, Fest. p. 306 Müll.

subsolanus.full: sub-sōlānus, a, um, adj., lying beneath the sun, eastern, oriental (post-Aug.): montes, Plin. 7, 2, 2, § 24.—As subst.: subsō-lānus, i, m. (sc. ventus), the east wind, Sen. Q. N. 5, 16, 4; Plin. 2, 47, 46, § 119; Gell. 2, 22, 8; plur.: salubriores septentrionales quam subsolani vel austri sunt, Cels. 2, 1.
subsolanus.short: sub-sōlānus, a, um, adj., lying beneath the sun, eastern, oriental (post-Aug.): montes, Plin.

subsono.full: sub-sŏno, āre, v. a., to express secretly, to hint, intimate: quanti pretii (dentur), Sisenn. ap. Charis. p. 175 P.

subsortior.full: sub-sortĭor, tītus, 4, v. a., jurid. t. t., to choose by lot as a substitute, sc. a judge in place of one rejected by the parties: judicem, Cic. Clu. 35, 96.—Absol.: subsortiemur etiam in M. Metelli locum, Cic. Verr. 1, 10, 30.—Part. in pass. sense: si ex lege subsortitus non erat Junius, Cic. Clu. 34, 92.

subsortitio.full: subsortītĭo, ōnis, f. subsortior, a choosing of substitutes by lot, sc. of other judges in place of those rejected by the parties, Cic. Verr. 2, 1, 61, § 157; id. Clu. 33, 91; a selection of citizens to receive corn in place of those who had died: subsortitio a praetore fieret, Suet. Caes. 41 fin.

subspargo.full: sub-spargo, ĕre, v. n., to scatter under: semina versutiis haereticorum, Tert. Res. Carn. 63 fin.

subspissus.full: subspissus, a, um, adj. sub-spissus, thickish, medic. t. t.: pleureticorum pulsus, Ps.-Soran. Puls. p. 279.

substamen.full: sub-stāmen, ĭnis, n., the woof or weft in weaving (late Lat.), Vet. Schol. Juv. 2, 66.
substamen.short: sub-stāmen, ĭnis, n., the woof or weft in weaving (late Lat.), Vet.

substantia.full: substantĭa, ae, f. substo, that of which a thing consists, the being, essence, contents, material, substance (post - Aug.): hominis, Quint. 7, 2, 5: rerum, id. 2, 21, 1: placidae et altae mentis, id. 6, prooem. § 7: rhetorices, id. 2, 15, 34: de substantiā aut de qualitate, id. 3, 6, 38: singula animalia singulas habere debent substantias, Sen. Ep. 113, 4: esse diversae substantiae, Front. Strat. 4 praef.: earum rerum pretium non in substantiā, sed in arte positum est, in the material, Dig. 50,

substantialis.full: substantĭālis, e, adj. substantia. Lit., of or belonging to the essence or substance, essential, substantial (post - class.): differentia, Tert. Res. Carn. 45 fin.— Transf., substantial, substantive: potestates, i. e. spirits, Amm. 21, 1, 8.—Adv.: sub-stantĭālĭter, essentially, substantially, Tert. adv. Valent. 7, 4; id. adv. Marc. 35 fin.

substantialitas.full: substantĭālĭtas, ātis, f. substantialis, the quality of being substantial or essential, Hier. in Didym. Spir. Sanc. 15; Cassiod. Hist. Eccl. 7, 14.

substantiola.full: substantĭŏla, ae, f. dim. substantia, a little substance, a small property (late Lat.): paterna et materna, Hier. Ep. 108, 26: tenuis, id. ib. 125, 16.

substantivalis.full: substantīvālis, e, adj. substantivus, substantive, substantial: forma, Tert. adv. Val. 27 fin.

substantivus.full: substantīvus, a, um, adj. substantia, self-existent, substantive (post - class.). In gen.: res, Tert. adv. Prax. 26; id. adv. Hermog. 26.— In gram.: substantivum verbum, the substantive verb, i.e. sum (a transl. of the Gr. ὑπαρκτικόν), Prisc. p. 812 fin. P.

substerno.full: sub-sterno, strāvi, strātum, 3, v. a., to strew, scatter, spread, or lay under or beneath (class.; cf. subicio). Lit.: segetem ovibus, Cato, R. R. 37, 2: verbenas, Ter. And. 4, 3, 12: casias et nardi lenis aristas, Ov. M. 15, 398; Plin. 20, 14, 56, § 158: folia, id. 20, 21, 84, § 226: semina hordei, Col. 5, 9, 9: fucum marinum, to spread underneath, lay as a ground - color, Plin. 26, 10, 66, § 103 (syn. sublino): se (mulier), to submit, in mal. part., Cat. 64, 403: substratus Numida mortuo Roman

substillus.full: substillus, a, um, adj. sub - stillo (ante- and post - class.), slightly dropping, dribbling. Adj.: lotium, i. e. strangury, Cato, R. R. 156, 6.— Subst.: substil-lum, i, n., a slight dropping, a sprinkling: substillum tempus ante pluviam jam paene uvidum et post pluviam non persiccum, quod jam stillaret, aut nondum desisset, Fest. pp. 306 and 307 Müll.: dehinc substillum et denuo sudum, Tert. Pall. 2.

substituo.full: sub-stĭtŭo, ŭi, ūtum, 3, v. a. statuo. To set, put, place, or lay under, to set or place next to any thing (so rare and mostly post - Aug.). Lit.: lapides plantae, Pall. Mart. 10, 22: post elephantos armaturas leves, Hirt. B. Afr. 59, 3.— Trop.: substituerat animo speciem corporis amplam ac magnificam, had presented to his imagination, figured to himself, Liv. 28, 35; cf.: funera fratrum Debueras oculis substituisse tuis, Ov. R. Am. 574: substituebantur crimini, were subjected to the charge, wer

substitutio.full: substĭtūtĭo, ōnis, f. substituo, II.. In gen., a putting in the place of another, substitution, Arn. 3, p. 104.— In partic., in jurid. lang., the appointment of a second or alternate heir, Gai. Inst. 2, § 174 sq.; Dig. 28, tit. 6.

substitutivus.full: substĭtūtīvus, a, um, adj. substituo, conditional: propositio, App. Dogm. Plat. 3, p. 29, 36.

substitutus.full: substĭtūtus, a, um, Part. of substituo.

substo.full: sub-sto, āre, v. n. To stand or be under or among, to be present (very rare; not in Cic.): si pure substante non rumpuntur hi tumores, Cels. 6, 10 med.: nullo dolore substante, id. 2, 7 med.; 2, 12, 2.— * To stand firm, hold out, = subsisto: metuo, ut substet hospes, Ter. And. 5, 4, 11.

substomachans.full: sub-stŏmăchans, antis, Part. [stomachor], somewhat angry or vexed: taedio, Aug. Conf. 3, 12.

substramen.full: substrāmen, ĭnis, n. substerno, what is strewn under, litter: molle, Varr. R. R. 3, 10, 4; 3, 6, 5; 3, 9, 8.— Transf., supports: lubrica roboreis aderant substramina plaustris, i. e. rollers, Sil. 12, 444.

substramentum.full: substrāmentum, i, n. id., litter, = substramen, Cato, R. R. 161, 2 (al. sub stramentis).

substratus1.full: substrātus, a, um, Part. of substerno.

substratus2.full: substrātus, ūs, m. substerno, a spreading or laying under; only in abl. sing., Plin. 24, 9, 38, § 61.

substrepens.full: sub-strĕpens, entis, Part. [strepo], just sounding, just uttering, gasping: verba, App. M. 5, p. 166 fin.

substrictus.full: sub-strictus, a, um, Part. and P. a. of substringo.

substridens.full: sub-strīdens, entis, Part. [strido], grating or gnashing somewhat, Amm. 16, 4, 2.

substringo.full: sub-stringo, nxi, ctum, 3, v. a., to bind beneath; to bind, tie, or draw up (poet. and in post-Aug. prose; syn. subligo). Lit.: crinem nodo, Tac. G. 38: ligatas auro comas, Luc. 3, 281: sinus, Sen. Troad. 88: lintea malo, Sil. 1, 689: caput equi loro, Nep. Eum. 5, 5: carnem fasciā, Suet. Galb. 21.— Transf., to bind or draw together; to draw up, contract, check: aurem, i. e. to point or prick the ear, Hor. S. 2, 5, 95: lacrimas, Marc. Emp. 8: bilem, Juv. 6, 433. — Trop., to check, restrain, etc.:

substructio.full: substructĭo, ōnis, f. substruo, an under - building, foundation, substructure, Vitr. 1, 5: maxima debet esse cura substructionum, id. 6, 11: maximae, Caes. B. C. 2, 25: insanae, Cic. Mil. 20, 53; 31, 85; Liv. 38, 28; Front. Aquaed. 3, 5 sq.; Col. 1, 5, 9; v. substruo fin.

substructus.full: substructus, a, um, Part. of substruo.

substruo.full: sub-strŭo, xi, ctum, 3, v. a., to build beneath, to underbuild, lay; lit.: fundamentum, Plaut. Most. 1, 2, 40: intervalla montium, Vitr. 8, 7 med.; cf.: intervalla substructis canalibus junguntur, Plin. 33, 4, 21, § 74: locus substructus, Varr. L. L. 5, § 155 Müll.: Capitolium saxo quadrato, Liv. 6, 4: substruendo iter facere, Dig. 8, 1, 10: vias glareā, i. e. to lay, to pave, Liv. 41, 27.—Absol.: non alte substruitur, the foundation is not laid deeply, Vitr. 8, 6, 5. —P. a. as subst.: substruct

subsultim.full: subsultim, adv. subsilio, with leaps or jumps. decurrere, Suet. Aug. 83.

subsulto.full: subsulto, āre, v. freq. n. [id.], to spring up, to leap, jump, hop (rare; not in Cic.). Lit., Plaut. Cas. 2, 7, 10: tu subsultas, ego miser vix asto, id. Capt. 3, 4, 104.— Trop.: ne sermo subsultet imparibus spatiis, Quint. 11, 3, 43: compositio multis clausulis concisa, id. 9, 4, 42.

subsum.full: sub-sum, no perf., esse, v. n., to be under, among, or behind; to be near, close, or at hand (class.): ubi non subest, quo praecipitet ac decidat, there is nothing underneath, Cic. Rep. 1, 45, 69; Lucr. 3, 873; cf. id. 4, 1082: si quid intra cutem subest ulceris, Planc. ap. Cic. Fam. 10, 18, 3: subucula subest tunicae, Hor. Ep. 1, 1, 96: nigra subest lingua palato, Verg. G. 3, 388: suberat Pan ilicis umbrae Tib. 2, 5, 27: cum sol Oceano subest, Hor. C. 4, 5, 40.— To be near, to be at hand, of pl

subsummo.full: sub-summo, āre, 1, v. a. sub-summa, to sum up, to multiply (late Lat.), Primas in Apoc. V. 21.

subsurdus.full: sub-surdus, a, um, adj., somewhat deaf: vox, indistinct, Quint. 11, 3, 32 Halm. (al. surda).
subsurdus.short: sub-surdus, a, um, adj., somewhat deaf: vox, indistinct, Quint.

subsutura.full: subsūtūra, ae, f. sub-suo, the hem of a garment, Edict. Diocl. 7, n. c. 49.

subsutus.full: sub-sūtus, a, um, Part. [suo], sewn beneath or at the lower part: vestis, trimmed, edged, or fringed at the bottom, Hor. S. 1, 2, 29.

subtabidus.full: sub-tābĭdus, a, um, adj., somewhat shrunken: stetit subtabidus, Amm. 26, 6, 15.
subtabidus.short: sub-tābĭdus, a, um, adj., somewhat shrunken: stetit subtabidus, Amm.

subtacitus.full: sub-tăcĭtus, a, um, adj., somewhat still, silent: secta, Prud. Ham. 174.
subtacitus.short: sub-tăcĭtus, a, um, adj., somewhat still, silent: secta, Prud.

subtalaris.full: sub-tālāris, e, adj. sub-talus, lying under the heel: calcei, Isid. Orig. 19, 34, 7.

subtectio.full: subtectĭo, ōnis, f. sub-tego, a covering (late Lat.), Aug. Quaest. in Heptat. 2, 177, 15.

subtego.full: sub-tĕgo, xi, ĕre, v. a., to cover underneath: caelum, Amm. 19, 7, 3 (al. sub-texunt); Vitr. 9, 9: aëra ipsum subtexisse jaculis, Jul. Val. Rer. Gest. Alex. 2, 4: sub avis caudā pedes equi sunt subtecti, Vitr. 9, 9: subtecto nubibus caelo, Hilar. in Psa. 146, 7; Aug. Quaest. in Heptat. 2, 177, 14.

subtegulaneus.full: sub-tĕgŭlānĕus, a, um, adj. tegula, that is under the roof, = in-doors: pavimenta, Plin. 36, 25, 61, § 185.

subtel.full: subtel, τὸ κοῖλον τοῦ ποδός, the hollow of the foot, Prisc. p. 644 P. [sub-talus].
subtel.short: subtel, τὸ κοῖλον τοῦ ποδός, the hollow of the foot, Prisc.

subtemen.full: subtēmen (subtegmen), ĭnis, n. contr. from subteximen, subtecmen, from sub-texo, that which is wrought or woven in, the woof, weft of a web: inseritur medium radiis subtemen acutis, etc., Ov. M. 6, 56; Varr. L. L. 5, § 113 Müll.; Verg. A. 3, 483; Vitr. 10, 1 med.; Plin. 11, 24, 28, § 81; 13, 12, 24, § 79.— Meton. (pars pro toto), any thing spun, thread, yarn (rare, and mostly poet.): subtemen tenue nere, Plaut. Merc. 3, 1, 20: nere, Ter. Heaut. 2, 3, 52; Front. Nep. Am. 2 med.: Tyrium, Tib. 4, 1

subtendo.full: sub-tendo, no perf., tum, 3, v. a. and n. Act., to stretch underneath: lectos loris, Cato, R. R. 10, 5; 10, 25.—* Neutr., to extend underneath: linea, Front. Expos. Form. p. 32 Goes.
