subteneo.full: sub-tĕnĕo, ēre, v. a., to hold underneath: vinaceos lectos cestibus subtento (contr. for subteneto), Cato, R. R. 25 Schneid. N. cr.

subtentus.full: subtentus, a, um, Part., from subtendo.
subtentus.short: subtentus, a, um, Part., from subtendo.

subtenuis.full: sub-tĕnŭis, e, adj., rather thin, thinnish: setae, Varr. R. R. 2, 7, 5.
subtenuis.short: sub-tĕnŭis, e, adj., rather thin, thinnish: setae, Varr.

subter.full: subter (also supter), adv. and prep. sub. Adv., below, beneath, underneath: navem in fugam transdunt subter saxa, Att. ap. Non. 155, 8 (Trag. Rel. v. 630 Rib.): terram fac ut esse rearis Subter item, ut supera, Lucr. 6, 537: partim quod supter per terras diditur omnis, id. 5, 268: aliam naturam supter habere, id. 5, 536: omnia haec, quae supra et subter, unum esse, Cic. de Or. 3, 5, 20; id. poët. N. D. 2, 42, 106: anulus subter adhaerens, Lucr. 6, 914: oculum subter premere, id. 4, 447: subter m

subteractus.full: subtĕr-actus, a, um, Part. [ago], driven below or underneath: subteractis quasi radicibus, Cels. 5, 28, 1.

subteranhelo.full: subter-ănhēlo, āre, v. n., to pant or gasp beneath, Stat. S. 1, 1, 56.

subtercavatus.full: subter-căvātus, a, um, Part. [cavo], hollowed out underneath, Sol. 2 fin.

subtercurrens.full: subter-currens, entis, Part., moving underneath: basim Vergiliarum, Vitr. 9, 6.
subtercurrens.short: subter-currens, entis, Part., moving underneath: basim Vergiliarum, Vitr.

subtercutaneus.full: subter-cŭtānĕus, a, um, adj. cutis, that is beneath the skin, subcutaneous (post-class.): morbus, the dropsy, Aur. Vict. Epit. 14 fin.: umor, Veg. Vet. 3, 2, 18.

subterduco.full: subter-dūco, xi, 3, v. a., to carry off secretly, to steal away any thing (Plautin.): ne tibi clam se subterducat istinc, Plaut. Mil. 2, 3, 72: si huic occasioni tempus sese subterduxerit, id. As. 2, 2, 12.

subterfluo.full: subter-flŭo, ĕre, v. n., to flow beneath (post-Aug. and very rare). Lit.: amnis sub montes subterfluens, Vitr. 8, 2 med.: torrente subterfluente, Plin. 8, 50, 76, § 201: aquae, Sen. Q. N. 3, 30, 4, acc. to Fickert and Haase (not subinfluo).— Trop.: eos felicitas ingrata subterfluit, Eum. Pan. Const. 15.

subterfugio.full: subter-fŭgĭo, fūgi, 3, v. n. and a. Neutr., to flee secretly or by stealth, to get off (so very rare): subterfugisse sic mihi hodie Chrysalum, Plaut. Bacch. 4, 6, 2; Dig. 42, 6, 20.— Act., to escape, evade, avoid, shun (class.; a favorite word of Cic.): mare, Plaut. Merc. 1, 2, 83: vim criminum, Cic. Verr. 1, 3, 8: imprudentiam, id. ib. 1, 4, 13: militiam, id. Off. 3, 26, 97: poenam aut calamitatem, id. Caecin. 34, 100: periculum, id. Fam. 15, 1, 4: omnia quasi fata, id. Lael. 10, 35: tempestate

subterfugium.full: subterfŭgĭum, i, n. subterfugio, a subterfuge: Nestorianorum, Facund. Defens. 1, 3.

subterfundo.full: subter-fundo, āre, v. a., to found or establish beneath: terram, Lact. 2, 8, 52.

subterinsero.full: subtĕr-insĕro, ĕre, 3, v. a., to insert, Aldh. Sept. col. 219, t. 89 med.

subterintendo.full: subtĕr-intendo, ĕre, 3, v. a., to look askance, = ὑποβλέπειν (Appul.), Polem. Physiogn. p. 126.

subterior.full: subtĕrĭor, us, comp. [subter], that is farther beneath, lower, = inferior (late Lat.): termini, Innoc. Cas. Lit. p. 232 Goes.: per subteriora, Aem. Mac. 2, 13.—Hence, adv.: subtĕrĭus, lower, farther down: subterius nigro, superius mineo, Isid. Orig. 16, 8, 4.

subterjaceo.full: subter-jăcĕo, ēre, v. n., to lie under any thing: hic gens ardentem caeli subterjacet axem, Alcim. 1, 196.

subterjacio.full: subter-jăcĭo, cĕre, v. a., to throw under any thing: hordei grana, Pall. Febr. 18, 1.

subterlabor.full: subter-lābor, lābi, v. dep. n. Lit., to glide or flow under (mostly poet.): fluctus Sicanos, Verg. E. 10, 4: flumina subterlabentia muros, flowing close by, id. G. 2, 157: subterlabens Mosella, Aus. Idyll. 10, 21.— Transf., to slip away, escape: celeritate subterlabentem, Liv. 30, 25 (dub.).

subterlino.full: subter-lĭno, ĕre, v. a., to anoint underneath: plantas aegri, Plin. 28, 7, 23, § 83.

subterluo.full: subter-lŭo, ĕre, v. a., to wash beneath, flow underneath: gurgite sidereo subterluit Oriona, Claud. VI. Cons. Hon. 177.

subterluvio.full: subterlŭvĭo, ōnis, f. subterluo, a washing beneath, washing away: loca umoris assidui subterluvione cadentia, Claud. Mam. Stat. An. 1, 2.

subtermeo.full: subter-mĕo, āre, v. n., to pass beneath: pontes rapido aestu, Claud. Idyll. 6, 61.

subtermitto.full: subter-mitto, ĕre, v. a., to place underneath, Aug. Quaest. in Heptat. 2, 177, 14.

subtermoveo.full: subter-mŏvĕo, ēre, v. a., to push under, Isid. 16, 4, 2.

subternatans.full: subter-nătans, antis, Part. [nato], swimming under any thing, Sol. 32, 26.

subternus.full: subternus, a, um, adj. subter, that is underneath, lower, = infernus (post-class.): antra, Prud. adv. Symm. 1, 392: nox, id. Hamart. 930.

subtero.full: sub-tĕro, trīvi, trītum, 3, v. a., to rub off or wear away underneath; to rub, bruise, or grind to pieces (rare; not in Cic.): boves ne pedes subterant, Cato, R. R. 72; so, pedes, Col. 6, 15, 2; Plin. 28, 16, 62, § 221: ungulas, Plaut. As. 2, 2, 73: jumenta cito subteruntur, Sen. Ep. 51, 9: salis sextarium subterito, et subtritum, etc., pound, triturate, Col. 12, 5, 1: caepam aridam, id. 12, 5, 56; 2, 10, 25; Plin. 20, 20, 82, § 218; 30, 9, 23, § 80.

subterpendens.full: subter-pendens, entis, Part. [pendeo], hanging down: mala, Pall. Mart. 10, 8.

subterraneus.full: sub-terrānĕus, a, um, adj. terra, underground, subterranean (class.): specus, Cic. Att. 15, 26, 4; cf.: supterraneos specus aperire, Tac. G. 16: ergastulum, Col. 1, 6, 3: structura, Plin. 36, 22, 50, § 170: regna, Juv. 2, 149: animalia, Pall. Sept. 3, 2: mures, Sen. Q. N. 3, 16, 3: subterraneis venis in mare defluunt, Plin. 9, 15, 20, § 53: domus, id. 36, 13, 19, § 88: cubiculum, Plin. Ep. 4, 11, 9: subterraneis dolis peractum urbis excidium, Flor. 1, 12 fin.—Subst.: sub-terrānĕum, i, n., a subt

subterrenus.full: sub-terrēnus, a, um, adj. id., underground, subterrene, = subterraneus: plagae orbis, App. M. 9, p. 227, 27.

subterreus.full: sub-terrĕus, a, um, adj. id., underground, subterranean, = subterraneus: divi, Arn. 7, 226.

subterseco.full: subter-sĕco, āre, v. a., to cut, divide, separate underneath: medium Capricornum, Cic. Arat. 273.

subtersterno.full: subter-sterno, strāvi, strātum, 3, v. a., to spread under, strew under: aëra jaculis et sagittis, Jul. Val. Rer. Gest. Alex. 2, 17.

subtertenuo.full: subter-tĕnŭo, āre, v. a., to make thin below or at the lower part: anulum, Lucr. 1, 312 (Lachm. subter tenuatur).

subtertius.full: sub-tertĭus, a, um, adj., of a number, less by a third of itself (i. e. that bears to another the ratio of 3 to 4), a transl. of the Gr. ὑπότριτος: numerus, Mart. Cap. 7, § 761.
subtertius.short: sub-tertĭus, a, um, adj., of a number, less by a third of itself (i.

subtervacans.full: subter-văcans, antis, Part. [vaco], empty below; locus, Sen. Q. N. 6, 25, 1.

subtervolo.full: subter-vŏlo, āre, v. n., to fly beneath: fragor subtervolat astra, Stat. Th. 3, 669 (al. subter volat).

subtexo.full: sub-texo, xŭi, xtum, 3, v. a., to weave under or below any thing; hence, to join on, fasten, affix (mostly poet. and in post-Aug. prose; not in Cic.). Lit. (very rare): lunam alutae, Juv. 7, 192.—Poet.: patrio capiti nubes, i. e. soli, to draw before, veil, Ov. M. 14, 368; cf.: nox subtexta polo, Luc. 4, 104: sol diem subtexit Olympo, spreads around Olympus, Val. Fl. 5, 414.—To cover, hide, darken, obscure, conceal, with acc. of thing concealed: subtexunt nubila caelum, Lucr. 5, 466: caerula nim

subtextus.full: subtextus, a, um, Part. of subtexo.

subtililoquentia.full: subtīlĭlŏquentĭa, ae, f. subtililoquus, fine or elegant language, Tert. adv. Marc. 5, 19 med.

subtililoquus.full: subtīlĭlŏquus, a, um, adj. subtilisloquor, speaking finely or elegantly, Tert. adv. Marc. 5, 19 med.

subtilis.full: subtīlis, e, adj. sub-tela; and therefore, prop., woven fine; hence, fine, not thick or coarse, thin, slender, minute (syn. tenuis). Lit. (mostly poet. and in postAug. prose; not in Cic.): quae vulgo volitant subtili praedita filo, Lucr. 4, 88: ventus subtili corpore tenuis, id. 4, 901; cf. id. 3, 195; Cat. 54, 3: acies gladii, Sen. Ep. 76, 14: farina, Plin. 18, 7, 14, § 74: mitra, Cat. 64, 63: ignis, Lucr. 6, 225: subtilia et minuta primordia rerum, id. 4, 122; 4, 114.— Subst.: subtīlĭa, ĭum, n

subtilitas.full: subtīlĭtas (supt-), ātis, f. subtilis, fineness, thinness, slenderness, minuteness (syn. tenuitas). Lit. (mostly post-Aug.; not in Cic.): linearum, Plin. 35, 10, 36, § 82: ferramentorum, the keen edge, sharpness, id. 28, 9, 41, § 148: inenarrabilis florum, id. 21, 1, 1, § 1: muliebris, Vitr. 4, 1 med.: immensa animalium, Plin. 11, prooem. 1. § 1: caelandi fingendique ac tingendi, id. 35, prooem. § 1: umoris, id. 2, 65, 65, § 163. — Trop. In gen., keenness, acuteness, penetration, definiteness, e

subtimeo.full: sub-tĭmĕo, ēre, v. n., to be somewhat afraid, to fear a little: numquid subtimes, ne? etc., Cic. Phil. 2, 14, 36.

subtinnio.full: sub-tinnĭo, īre, v. n., to sound a little, to tinkle, Tert. Pall. 4 med.

subtitubo.full: sub-tĭtŭbo, āre, v. n., to stagger, totter, or waver a little (late Lat.). Lit.: pede subtitubo, Ven. Vit. S. Mart. 2, 475. — Trop.: subtitubante fide, Prud. Apoth. 651.

subtractio.full: subtractĭo, ōnis, f. subtraho, a drawing back, Vulg. Ep. ad Hebr. 10, 39 (transl. of the Gr. ὑποστολή).

subtractus.full: subtractus, a, um, Part. of subtraho.

subtraho.full: sub-trăho, xi, ctum, 3, v. a., to draw away from underneath or by stealth; also, in gen., to draw off, carry off, withdraw, take away, remove, etc. (class.; syn. subduco). Lit.: subtractus Numida mortuo superincubanti Romano vivus, Liv. 22, 51, 9 (Weissenb. substratus): pedibus raptim tellus subtracta, Lucr. 6, 605: effracto colla jugo, Ov. Tr. 5, 2, 40: viro (peculium), Plaut. Cas. 2, 2, 28: (impedimenta) clandestinā fugā, Hirt. B. G. 8, 33: aggerem cuniculis, Caes. B. G. 7, 22: si dediticii su

subtremulus.full: sub-trĕmŭlus, a, um, adj., somewhat tremulous, Ps.-Soran. 280.
subtremulus.short: sub-trĕmŭlus, a, um, adj., somewhat tremulous, Ps.-Soran.

subtriplus.full: sub-triplus, a, um, adj., contained three times in a larger number, Boëth. Inst. Arith. 1, 23.
subtriplus.short: sub-triplus, a, um, adj., contained three times in a larger number, Boëth.

subtristis.full: sub-tristis, e, adj., somewhat sad or sorrowful (ante- and post-class.): subtristis visus est mihi, Ter. And. 2, 6, 16; Hier. Ep. 107, 9.—Comp.: cera subtristior, Hier. Ep. 60, 1.
subtristis.short: sub-tristis, e, adj., somewhat sad or sorrowful (ante- and post-class.): subtristis visus est mihi, Ter.

subtritus.full: subtrītus, a, um, Part. of subtero.

subtunicalis.full: subtŭnĭcālis, is, f. sub-tunica, = ὑποδύτης, the under-garment of a Jewish priest, Hier. Ep. 29, 4.

subturpiculus.full: sub-turpĭcŭlus, a, um, adj., somewhat mean or disgraceful, Cic. Att. 4, 5, 1.
subturpiculus.short: sub-turpĭcŭlus, a, um, adj., somewhat mean or disgraceful, Cic.

subturpis.full: sub-turpis, e, adj., somewhat mean or disgraceful: quae sint, quod ridiculi proprium est, subturpia, Cic. de Or. 2, 66, 264.
subturpis.short: sub-turpis, e, adj., somewhat mean or disgraceful: quae sint, quod ridiculi proprium est, subturpia, Cic.

subtus.full: subtus, adv. from sub; like intus, from in, below, beneath, underneath (mostly ante-class.; not in Cic. or Cæs.): subtus ambulare, Cato, R. R. 48, 2: labra subtus pendula, Varr. R. R. 2, 9, 3: Romani aggere et vineis et omnibus supra terram operibus, subtus Macedones cuniculis oppugnabant, Liv. 36, 25; cf. Plaut. Cas. 5, 2, 26; Varr. L. L. 5, § 131 Müll.

subtussio.full: sub-tussĭo, īre, v. n., to cough slightly, Veg. Vet. 3, 25 dub.

subtusus.full: sub-tūsus, a, um, Part. [tundo], somewhat bruised: flet teneras subtusa genas, Tib. 1, 10, 55: angulus, an obtuse angle, Boëth. Geom. 1, p. 1180.

subtutus.full: sub-tūtus, a, um, adj., moderately safe, Commod. Instr. 30, 18.
subtutus.short: sub-tūtus, a, um, adj., moderately safe, Commod.

subucula.full: sŭbūcŭla, ae, f. sub - UO; whence exuo. A man's under-garment, a shirt: postea quam binas tunicas habere coeperunt, instituerunt vocare subuculam et indusium, Varr. ap. Non. 542, 24; id. L. L. 5, § 131 Müll.; Hor. Ep. 1, 1, 95; Suet. Aug. 82. — Of the priest's dress, Vulg. Lev. 8, 7. — Subuculam Aelius Stilo et Cloatius iisdem fere verbis demonstrant vocari, quod dis detur ex alicā et oleo et melle. Nam de tunicae genere notum est omnibus, Fest. pp. 308 and 309 Müll.

subula.full: sūbŭla, ae, f. Lit., an awl, Mart. 3, 16, 2: aënea, Col. 6, 5, 4; Pall. Jun. 14, 3: perforabit aurem ejus subulā, Vulg. Exod. 21, 6; id. Deut. 15, 17. — Transf., a very small weapon: subulā armatus, Sen. Ep. 85, 1; cf. prov.: subulā leonem excipis, id. ib. 82, 25.

subulcus.full: sŭbulcus, i, m. from sus; formed in analogy with bubulcus, a swine-herd, Varr. R. R. 2, 4, 14 and 20; Mart. 10, 98, 10; Verg. E. 10, 19 Wagn. (al. bubulci).

subulo1.full: sūbŭlo, ōnis, m. A flute-player, the Tuscan name for tibicen: subulo Tusce tibicen dicitur. Itaque Ennius: Subulo quondam marinas propter astabat plagas, Fest. p. 309 Müll.; cf. Varr. L. L. 7, § 35 ib. (Sat. v. 41 Vahl.).— A kind of hart with pointed horns, Plin. 11, 37, 45, § 213; 28, 17, 67, § 231. — Perh. i. q. paedico, Aus. Epigr. 70.

subulo2.full: Sūbŭlo, ōnis, m. 1. subulo, a Roman surname; e. g. P. Decius Subulo, Liv. 43, 17.

subumbilicus.full: sŭb-umbĭlīcus, i, n., the parts below the navel, Hier. in Zach. 1 ad 2, 18.
subumbilicus.short: sŭb-umbĭlīcus, i, n., the parts below the navel, Hier.

subumidus.full: sŭb-ūmĭdus, a, um, adj., somewhat moist: oculi, Cels. 3, 6, 23.
subumidus.short: sŭb-ūmĭdus, a, um, adj., somewhat moist: oculi, Cels.

subunctio.full: sŭb-unctĭo, ōnis, f., a rubbing in: faucium, Cael. Aur. Acut. 3, 3, 22.
subunctio.short: sŭb-unctĭo, ōnis, f., a rubbing in: faucium, Cael.

subur.full: Sŭbur, f., a town in Spain, on the river Rubricatus, perh. the mod. Villa Nuova, in Castile, Mel. 2, 6; Plin. 3, 3, 4, § 21.—Hence, Sŭbūrĭtāni, ōrum, m., the inhabitants of Subur, Inscr. Grut. 414, 3.
subur.short: Sŭbur, f., a town in Spain, on the river Rubricatus, perh.

subura.full: Sŭbūra, ae (abbrev. SVG.; v. infra), f., a quarter in Rome, in the second region, between the Esquiline, Viminal, and Quirinal, where provisions were sold, and where many prostitutes dwelt: Subura Junius scribit ab eo, quod fuerit sub antiquā Urbe: quoi testimonium potest esse, quod subest ei loco, qui Terreus murus vocatur. Sed ego a pago potius Succusano dictam puto Succusam, quod in notā etiam nunc scribitur tertia littera C, non B, Varr. L. L. 5, § 48 Müll.; cf.: Subura cum tribus litteris n

suburbanitas.full: sŭburbānĭtas, ātis, f. suburbanus, nearness to the city of Rome: suburbanitas hujusce provinciae (Siciliae), * Cic. Verr. 2, 2, 3, § 7; Symm. Ep. 2, 22; Sid. Ep. 7, 2 med.

suburbanus.full: sŭb-urbānus, a, um, adj., situated near the city of Rome, suburban. Adj.: rus suburbanum, Cic. Rosc. Am. 46, 133: fundus, id. Q. Fr. 3, 1, 3, § 9: ager, id. Div. 2, 32, 69: gymnasium, id. de Or. 1, 21, 98: regio Italiae, Col. 11, 2, 61; cf. Italia, Plin. 26, 4, 9, § 19: caulis, Hor. S. 2, 4, 15: peregrinatio, Tac. A. 3, 47: crimina, id. ib. 13, 43 et saep. — Substt. sŭburbā-num, i, n. (sc. praedium), an estate near Rome, a suburban villa: malo esse in Tusculano aut uspiam in suburbano, Cic. Att.
suburbanus.short: sŭb-urbānus, a, um, adj., situated near the city of Rome, suburban.

suburbicarius.full: sŭb-urbĭcārĭus, a, um, adj., late jurid. Lat. for suburbanus, situated near Rome, suburban: regiones, Cod. Th. 11, 1, 9; 11, 28, 12; 11, 16, 12: mare, Schol. Juv. 5, 94.
suburbicarius.short: sŭb-urbĭcārĭus, a, um, adj., late jurid.

suburbium.full: sub-urbĭum, ii, n. urbs, a suburb: in suburbium ire, Cic. Phil. 12, 10, 24.

suburgeo.full: sŭb-urgĕo (also written sŭbur-guĕo), ēre, v. a., to drive or urge close to: proram ad saxa, Verg. A. 5, 202.

suburo.full: sŭb-ūro, no perf., ustum, v. a., to burn slightly, to singe, scorch: crura nuce ardenti, Suet. Aug. 68: subustum corpus, Paul. Nol. Carm. 7, 37.

subustio.full: sŭbustĭo, ōnis, f. suburo, a heating from below: thermarum, Cod. Th. 15, 1, 32.

subustus.full: sŭbustus, a, um, Part. from suburo.

subvades.full: subvădes, um, m. sub-vas, sub-sureties, i. e. those who give surety for the bail, Auct. ap. Gell. 16, 10, 8.

subvectio.full: subvectĭo, ōnis, f. subveho, a carrying, transporting, conveying, conveyance: frumenti, Liv. 44, 8; Tac. A. 13, 51 fin.— Plur.: durae subvectiones, Caes. B. G. 7, 10: marinae, Vitr. 1, 5, 1.

subvecto.full: subvecto, āvi, ātum, 1, v. freq. a. id., to bring up from below (on the shoulder, by ship, etc.), to bring, carry, convey, transport to a place (poet. and in post-Aug. prose): asini, qui tibi subvectabant rure huc virgas ulmeas, Plaut. As. 2, 2, 74: saxa umeris, Verg. A. 11, 131: saxa, Sil. 4, 21: onera, Col. 6, praef. 3: panaria candidasque mappas, Stat. S. 1, 6, 32: corpora cymbā, Verg. A. 6, 303: naves, quae frumentum Tiberi subvectassent, Tac. A. 15, 43.

subvector.full: subvector, ōris, m. subveho, a bearer, carrier, conveyer: Bosporus Inachiae subvector virginis olim, Avien. Perieg. 199.

subvectus1.full: subvectus, a, um, Part. of subveho.

subvectus2.full: subvectus, ūs, m. subveho, a carrying, conveying, conveyance, Tac. A. 15, 4; Cassiod. Hist. Eccl. 5, 17.

subveho.full: sub-vĕho, vexi, vectum, 3, v. a., to bring up from below (on the shoulder, by ship, etc.), to bring, carry, convey, conduct to a place, to bring or carry up stream, etc. (not freq. till after the Aug. per.; not in Cic.): ast alium (aërem fluere) subter, contra qui subvehat orbem, Lucr. 5, 515: frumentum flumine Arari navibus, * Caes. B. G. 1, 16: adversum remis superes subvectus ut amnem, Verg. A. 8, 58: subvecta ponto Barbara agmina, Ov. M. 6, 423: matris fratrisque cineres Romam Tiberi, Suet.

subvello.full: sub-vello, no perf., vulsum (volsum), 3, v. a., to pluck up, pull out (only in the two foll. passages): rador, subvellor, desquamor, Lucil. ap. Non. 95, 15: qui barba volsa feminibusque subvolsis ambulet, Scip. Afric. ap. Gell. 7, 12, 5.

subvelo.full: sub-vēlo, āre, 1, v. a., to overshadow, Aug. Lib. Arb. 2, 38.

subvenio.full: sub-vĕnĭo, vēni, ventum, 4 (old fut. subvenibo, Plaut. Men. 5, 7, 20), v. n., to come up or advance to one's assistance (the figure taken from the advance of a military reserve; v. subsidium), to come to one's assistance, to aid, assist, relieve, succor; to obviate, remedy, heal, cure a disease, an evil, etc. (freq. and class.; syn.: adjuvo, succurro, sublevo). With dat. (so most freq.): quibus (equitibus) celeriter subveniunt levis armaturae pedites, Hirt. B. G. 8, 19: Lucanius circumvento fili

subventio.full: subventĭo, ōnis, f. subvenio, a rendering aid, assistance, Cassiod. Var. 12, 28.

subvento.full: subvento, āre, v. freq. n. [id.], to come with assistance to one: spes bona, opsecro, subventa mihi, Plaut. Rud. 1, 4, 11.

subventor.full: subventor, ōris, m. id., one who comes in aid, a helper: CIVIVM, Inscr. Orell. 6: POPVLI, ib. 3766.

subventralis.full: subventrālis, e, adj. sub-venter, subventral, med. t. t., Ps. - Soran. Quaest. Med. 235.

subventrile.full: sub-ventrīle, is, n. id., the lower belly, the abdomen (late Lat.), Marc. Emp. 28 fin.; cf.: ὑποκοίλιον, sumen, subventrile, Gloss. Philox.

subverbustus.full: subverbustus, a, um, adj. perhaps contr. from sub verubus ustus, branded under the spear, an epithet of a male or female slave (ante- and post-class.): subverbustam veribus ustam significat Plautus cum ait: ulcerosam, compeditam, subverbustam, sordidam, Fest. p. 309 Müll.; Tert. Pall. 4 med.

subvereor.full: sub-vĕrĕor, ēri, v. dep. n., to be somewhat fearful or apprehensive: subvereri ne te delectet, etc., Cic. Fam. 4, 10, 1.

subversio.full: subversĭo, ōnis, f. subverto, an overturn, overthrow, ruin, destruction (late Lat.): humani generis, Arn. 1, 7: urbium, Vulg. Gen. 19, 29.—Plur.: animorum, Arn. 5, 165.

subverso.full: subverso (-vorso), āre, v. freq. a. id., to overturn, overthrow, ruin, Plaut. Curc. 4, 1, 23.

subversor.full: subversor, ōris, m. id., an overturner, overthrower, subverter (very rare): legum (opp. auctor), Tac. A. 3, 28: naturae (diabolus), Alcim. 2, 75.

subversus.full: subversus, a, um, Part. of subverto.

subverto.full: sub-verto (-vorto), ti, sum, 3, v. a., to turn upside down; to upset, overturn, overthrow (not in Cic. or Cæs.). Lit.: lupinum aratro, Col. 11, 2, 44: mensam, Suet. Ner. 47: statuas, id. Calig. 34: tantas operum moles, Ov. F. 6, 645: silvam, Luc. 3, 436: subversi montes, Sall. C. 13, 1: Arisbe terrarum motu subversa, Plin. 5, 31, 39, § 139: Silvani simulacrum, id. 15, 18, 20, § 77: obices portarum, Tac. A. 13, 39. — Absol., Quadrig. ap. Gell. 9, 13, 17: calceus olim Si pede major erit, subvertet

subvespertinus.full: sub-vespertīnus ventus, the southwest wind, Veg. Mil. 5, 8.
subvespertinus.short: sub-vespertīnus ventus, the southwest wind, Veg.

subvesperus.full: sub-vespĕrus, i, m. (sc. ventus), the southwest-by-west wind, Vitr. 1, 6, 10.

subvestio.full: sub-vestĭo, īre, 4, v. a., to clothe from beneath, clothe by degrees: et nova subvestit reparatas pluma volucres, Dracont. 1, 642.

subvexus.full: subvexus, a, um, adj. subveho, sloping upwards (opp. devexus): omnia fastigio leni subvexa, Liv. 25, 36.

subvilicus.full: sub-vīlĭcus, i, m., an under-steward: HORTORVM, Inscr. Orell. 2860.
subvilicus.short: sub-vīlĭcus, i, m., an under-steward: HORTORVM, Inscr.

subviridis.full: sub-vĭrĭdis, e, adj., somewhat green, greenish: folia, Plin. 25, 9, 65, § 113: balanitae, id. 37, 10, 55, § 149: emplastrum, Scrib. Comp. 201 and 202.
subviridis.short: sub-vĭrĭdis, e, adj., somewhat green, greenish: folia, Plin.

subvolo.full: sub-vŏlo, āre, v. n., to fly up or upwards (rare but class.): hae (partes corporum) sursum in caelestem locum subvo lent, Cic. Tusc. 1, 17, 40: avis, Ov. M. 11, 790: ex agmine, id. ib. 14, 507: praepes, id. ib. 14, 577: ad capita, Aug. Civ. Dei, 18, 16 fin.: alte, Aur. Vict. Vir. Ill. 6, 3.

subvolsus.full: subvolsus or subvulsus, a, um, Part. of subvello.
subvolsus.short: subvolsus or subvulsus, a, um, Part.

subvolvo.full: sub-volvo, ĕre, v. a., to roll up or along: manibus saxa, Verg. A. 1, 424.

subvulturius.full: sub-vultŭrĭus, a, um, adj., somewhat vulture-like, a facetiously formed word: corpus, Plaut. Rud. 2, 4, 9.
subvulturius.short: sub-vultŭrĭus, a, um, adj., somewhat vulture-like, a facetiously formed word: corpus, Plaut.

sucasini.full: Sucasīni (Succas-), ōrum, m., a surname of the Interamnates on the Liris in Latium, Plin. 3, 5, 9, § 64.
sucasini.short: Sucasīni (Succas-), ōrum, m., a surname of the Interamnates on the Liris in Latium, Plin.

succabar.full: Succabar, f., a town in Mauritania, Plin. 5, 2, 1, § 21.
succabar.short: Succabar, f., a town in Mauritania, Plin.

succaelestis.full: suc-caelestis (subc-), e, adj., that which is under the heavens, subcelestial, sublunary: hebdomas, Tert. adv. Val. 31.
succaelestis.short: suc-caelestis (subc-), e, adj., that which is under the heavens, subcelestial, sublunary: hebdomas, Tert.

succaeruleus.full: suc-caerŭlĕus (subc-), a, um, adj., somewhat blue, bluish: creta, Cels. 6, 5 fin.
succaeruleus.short: suc-caerŭlĕus (subc-), a, um, adj., somewhat blue, bluish: creta, Cels.

succandidus.full: suc-candĭdus (subc-), a, um, adj., somewhat white, whitish (Plinian): folia, Plin. 27, 8, 39, § 61; 27, 12, 94, § 120.
succandidus.short: suc-candĭdus (subc-), a, um, adj., somewhat white, whitish (Plinian): folia, Plin.

succasses.full: Succasses, ĭum, m., a people of Gaul, Plin. 4, 19, 33, § 108.
succasses.short: Succasses, ĭum, m., a people of Gaul, Plin.

succavus.full: suc-căvus (subc-), a, um, adj., hollow below or underneath (ante- and postclass.): areae, Cato, R. R. 151, 3: loca, Lucr. 6, 557; Auct. Limit. pp. 252, 260, 303 Goes.: natura Aetnae, Lucr. 6, 682.
succavus.short: suc-căvus (subc-), a, um, adj., hollow below or underneath (ante- and postclass.): areae, Cato, R.

succedaneus.full: succēdānĕus or succīdāneus (on the latter very ancient orthog. cf. Gell. 4, 6, 4 sq.), a, um, adj. succedo, that follows after or succeeds to something, that supplies the place of something, substituted, succedaneous: hostia, quae ad aras adducta est immolanda, si casu effugeret, effugia vocari veteri more solet: in cujus locum quae supposita fuerat, succidanea, Serv. Verg. A. 2, 140; cf. Gell. l. l.; and Fest. p. 302 Müll.: si quid succidaneis opus esset, robus succederet, S. C. ap. Gell. 4, 6,
succedaneus.short: succēdānĕus or succīdāneus (on the latter very ancient orthog.

succedo.full: suc-cēdo, cessi, cessum, 3, v. n. and a. [sub]. To go below or under (so mostly poet.; syn. subeo). Lit. In gen., to enter, go under, come under: simul ac primum nubes succedere soli Coepere, to go under the sun, Lucr. 5, 286; cf. id. 6, 402: tectum, cui imbris vitandi causā succederet, Cic. Dom. 44, 116: maestae Succedunt ramis volucres, Val. Fl. 6, 505: succedere tectis, Ov. M. 2, 766; so, tectis, id. ib. 8, 549; Verg. A. 1, 627: rex jussae succedit aquae, Ov. M. 11, 142: tecto et umbrae, Verg

succendo.full: suc-cendo, di, sum, 3, v. a. sub-candeo; v. accendo, to kindle or set on fire from below (syn. inflammo). Lit. (class.): (sapiens) etiamsi in Phalaridis tauro inclusus succensis ignibus torreatur, Cic. Pis. 18, 42: aggerem cuniculo hostes succenderant, Caes. B. G. 7, 24: arma cumulata in ingentem acervum ipse imperator face subditā succendit, Liv. 45, 33; cf. Quadrig. ap. Gell. 15, 1, 7; Caes. B. G. 5, 43: rogum, Liv. 28, 23: pontem, id. 1, 37: pinus duabus manibus, Ov. M. 5, 442: urbem suis man

succeno.full: suc-cēno (subc-, succoe-), āre, 1, v. a., to eat below, dine underneath: Galba de piscibus, qui cum pridie ex parte adesi et versati postero die appositi essent, Festinemus, alii subscenant, inquit, Quint. 6, 3, 90 Spald. N. cr.

succenseo.full: succensĕo and suscensĕo, sŭi, sum, 2, v. n. succensus, from succendo, to be inflamed with anger, to be angry, irritated, enraged (class.; syn.: irascor, indignor). With dat.: hominibus irasci et succensere, Cic. Rosc. Com. 16, 46: neque illi sum iratus neque quicquam succenseo, Plaut. Most. 5, 2, 41: id tibi suscensui, Quia, etc., id. Pers. 3, 3, 26: nil succenseo Nec tibi nec huic, Ter. Heaut. 5, 2, 23: ne tu illi succenseas, ne tibi illum succensere aliquid suspicere, Cic. Deiot. 13, 35: nec v
succenseo.short: succensĕo and suscensĕo, sŭi, sum, 2, v.

succensio1.full: succensĭo, ōnis, f. succendo, a setting on fire, kindling (late Lat.): lavacri, i. e. a heating, Amm. 31, 1, 2: prunarum nimia, id. 25, 10, 13: matutina succensio, Tert. Res. Carn. 12.

succensio2.full: succensĭo, ōnis, f. succenseo, anger, irritation, indignation: memoriam succensionis obliterare, Symm. Ep. 5, 35.

succensus.full: succensus, a, um. Part. from succendo.— Part. from succenseo.

succentivus.full: succentīvus, a, um, adj. succino, sounding to, accompanying: tibia, Varr. R. R. 1, 2, 15.

succentor.full: succentor, ōris, m. id., an accompanier in singing, Aug. Enarr. in Psa. 87, 1; Isid. 7, 12, 26.— Trop., a furtherer, promoter: fabularum, Amm. 19, 12, 13; Isid. Orig. 6, 19, 13.

succenturio1.full: suc-centŭrĭo (subc-), no perf., ātum, 1, v. a., to receive as a recruit into a centuria; hence, transf., to put in the place of another, receive as a substitute (very rare): succenturiare est explendae centuriae gratiā supplere, subicere, Plaut. ap. Saturione: succenturia, centum require, qui te delectent domi, Fest. p. 306 Müll.: nunc prior adito tu, ego in insidiis hic ere Succenturiatus, si quid deficies, as a reserve, Ter. Phorm. 1, 4, 55; cf.: tota metaphora de re militari est. Succenturiat

succenturio2.full: suc-centŭrĭo (subc-), ōnis, m., an under-officer, sub-centurion, Liv. 8, 8.
succenturio2.short: suc-centŭrĭo (subc-), ōnis, m., an under-officer, sub-centurion, Liv.

succentus.full: succentus, ūs, m. succino, an accompanying, accompaniment, Mart. Cap. 1, § 11.

succerno.full: suc-cerno (subc-), crēvi, crētum, 3, v. a., to sift through, to sift. Lit.: vinaceos cottidie recentes succernito, Cato, R. R. 25; 10, 5; 18, 7; 151, 3; Plin. 18, 11, 29, § 115; Vitr. 2, 5.—Comically: iste gradus succretu'st cribro pollinario, Plaut. Poen. 3, 1, 10.—* Transf., to shake up, agitate, Sev. Aetna, 492.

successio.full: successĭo, ōnis, f. succedo, II.. A coming into the place of another, a following after, succeeding, succession in office, possession, etc. (mostly post-Aug.): si merces Antonii oppressi poscitur in Antonii locum successio, Brut. ap. Cic. Ep. ad Brut. 1, 17, 2: Neronis principis successio, Plin. 7, 13, 11, § 58: quorum non dubia, Tac. A. 4, 12; Suet. Tib. 15; 25; 55: ad spem successionis admoveri, id. Calig. 12; id. Oth. 4 fin.: regni, Just. 9, 2; App. M. 8, p. 210, 33; Lact. 6, 23, 17.—Plur.: m

successivus.full: successīvus, a false read. for succissiva, Lact. Opif. Dei, 12, 15 Bünem. ad loc.

successor.full: successor, ōris, m. succedo, II., a follower, successor in office, possession, time, etc. (class.; cf. vicarius): conjunctissimus, Cic. Fam. 3, 3, 1; cf.: successori decessor invidit, id. Scaur. Fragm. 33; id. Prov. Cons. 15, 37; id. Fl. 14, 33; id. Fam. 3, 6, 2: successorem alicui mittere, to remove from office, Liv. 23, 27, 12; cf. id. 32, 28, 1: legato eum consulari successorem dedisse, Suet. Aug. 88; id. Dom. 1: successorem accipere, to be removed, Plin. Ep. 8, 13, 23: successores Alexandri,

successorius.full: successōrĭus, a, um, adj. successor, of or belonging to succession, successory (post-class.; esp. freq. in jurid. Lat.): de successorio edicto, Dig. 38, 9, 1 pr.: ex successorio capite, ib. 22, 6, 1, § 3: successorio jure aliquid tenere, Amm. 14, 8, 5.

successus1.full: successus, a, um, Part. of succedo.

successus2.full: successus, ūs, m. succedo. (Acc. to succedo, I.) An advance, approach (very rare). Lit.: successus et incursus hostium, Caes. B. G. 2, 20: equorum, Verg. A. 12, 616.— Transf. (post-class.), a place which one goes down into, a cavern: terrarum, Arn. 5, 173; 7, 251.— (Acc. to succedo, II.) A succession of time, continuance (post-class.): continuo totius temporis successu, Just. 1, 8, 14: ex successu continuae felicitatis obliviscitur se hominem, id. 16, 5, 8.— Trop., a happy issue, good result, su

succi.full: Succi, ōrum, m., a people of Thrace, Amm. 26, 7, 12.
succi.short: Succi, ōrum, m., a people of Thrace, Amm.

succidaneus.full: succīdānĕus, a, um, v. succedaneus, init.

succidia.full: succīdĭa, ae, f. 2. succido. A leg or side of meat cut off, esp. of pork; a leg of pork, flitch of bacon, Varr. L.L. 5, § 110 Müll.; id. R. R. 2, 4, 3: jam hortum ipsi agricolae succidiam alteram appellant, their second flitch, Cic. Sen. 16, 56. — * Transf., a slaughtering: succidias humanas facere, Cato ap. Gell. 13, 24, 12.

succido1.full: suc-cĭdo, ĭdi, 3, v. n. sub-cado, to fall under any thing. * In gen.: lorica quod e loris de corio crudo pectoralia faciebant: postea succidit Gallica e ferro sub id vocabulum, i. e. were comprehended under the word, Varr. L. L. 5, § 116 Müll.— Pregn., to sink under one's self, sink down, sink (poet. and in post-Aug. prose). Lit.: genua inedia succidunt, Plaut. Curc. 2, 3, 30; so, artus, Lucr. 3, 156: omnia fragore, id. 5, 109: terra repente, id. 5, 482: in mediis conatibus aegri Succidimus, Ver

succido2.full: suc-cīdo, cīdi, cīsum, 3, v. a. sub-caedo, to cut off or away below, cut from below, to cut through, cut off, cut down, fell (rare but class.; not in Cic.): is pernas succidit iniquā superbiā Poeni, Enn. ap. Fest. pp. 304 and 305 Müll. (Ann. v. 279 Vahl.); cf.: vivos Succisis feminibus poplitibusque invenerunt, Liv. 22, 51, 7: poplitem, Verg. A. 10, 700: crura equis (with suffodere ilia), Liv. 42, 59, 3: nervos equorum, id. 44, 28, 14: arbores, Caes. B. G. 5, 9; Liv. 23, 24; Col. 2, 2, 11; 11, 2

succiduus.full: succĭdŭus, a, um, adj. 1. succido, sinking down, sinking, failing (poet.). Lit.: genu, Ov. H. 13, 24: poples, id. M. 10, 458: gradus, Stat. Th. 4, 661: flammae, id. ib. 10, 116 et saep.— Trop.: benedictio, faltering, trembling, Sid. Ep. 7, 6 fin.— = succidaneus (late Lat.), Ven. Misc. 4, 25, 10.

succincte.full: succinctē, adv., v. succingo, P. a. fin.

succinctim.full: succinctim, adv. succingo, briefly, succinctly: denotare, Claud. Mam. Stat. Anim. praef.

succinctio.full: succinctĭo, ōnis,f. id., a girding about (late Lat.), Aug. c. Jul. 2, 6.

succinctorium.full: succinctōrĭum, ii, n. id., an apron (late Lat.), Aug. Gen. adv. Manich. 2. 15 fin.; id. Serm. Verb. Dom. 10 fin.; id. Civ. Dei, 14, 17 al.

succinctulus.full: succinctŭlus, a, um, adj. dim. [succinctus], girded, girt: fasciola, App. M. 2, p. 117, 34.

succinctus.full: succinctus, a, um, Part. and P. a. of succingo.

succinerarius.full: suc-cĭnĕrārĭus (subc-), a, um, adj. sub-cinis, = succinericius, panis, Hier. in Hos. 2, 8, 7 al.

succinericius.full: suc-cinĕrīcius (subc-), a, um, adj. id., prepared under the ashes (late Lat.): panis, baked under the ashes, Vulg. Gen. 18, 6; id. Exod. 12, 39; id. Osee, 7, 8 al.; cf. Isid. Orig. 20, 21.

succingo.full: suc-cingo (subc-), nxi, nctum, 3, v. a., to gird below or from below, to tuck up, gird, gird about, girdle (mostly poet. and in postAug. prose; cf. subligo). Lit.: crure tenus medio tunicas, Juv. 6, 455: astricti succingant ilia ventres, Grat. Cyn. 271; cf.: Virginem et Leonem Anguis intortus succingit, Vitr. 9, 5 (7), 1: illa (Scylla) feris atram canibus succingitur alvum, Ov. M. 13, 732; cf. Lucr. 5, 892; Tib. 3, 4, 89: eāpse sic succincta, tucked up, Plaut. Rud. 2, 3, 80: amicus, Mart. 2, 46,

succingulum.full: succingŭlum (subc-), i, n. succingo, an under-girdle, lower girdle, Plaut. Men. 1, 3, 17; cf. Fest. p. 302 Müll.

succino.full: suc-cĭno (subc-; also succăno, Varr. L. L. 6, § 75 Müll.), ĕre, v. a. and n. cano, to sing to, accompany (rare). Lit.: tubicines imitatus est succinente Habinnā, Petr. 69, 4: cantibus iste tuis alterno succinet ore, Calp. Ecl. 4, 79.— Transf., to accord, agree: (agricultura) succinit pastorali, Varr. R. R. 1, 2, 16: clamat: Victum date. Succinit alter: Et mihi, etc., another chimes in, Hor. Ep. 1, 17, 48.

succisio.full: succīsĭo, ōnis, f. 2. succido, a cutting off or away: cottidiana pilorum, Sid. Ep. 1, 2.

succisor.full: succīsor, ōris, m. 2. succido, one who cuts or prunes (late Lat.): quam (silvam) nec si serā succisor falce repurget, Alcim. Ep. 4, 48.

succisus.full: succīsus, a, um, Part. of 2. succido.

succlamatio.full: succlāmātĭo, ōnis, f. succlamo, a calling or crying out, a shouting, acclamation after any thing (rare; perh. not anteAug.); only plur.: ultro territuri succlamationibus, Liv. 28, 26, 12; 40, 36, 4; 42, 28, 2; Suet. Ner. 24.

succlamo.full: suc-clāmo (subc-), āvi, ātum, 1, v. a., to call or cry out, to shout, exclaim after or in reply to any thing (not in Cic. or Cæs.); with obj.-clause: haec Virginio vociferanti succlamabat multitudo, nec illius dolori nec suae libertati se defuturos, Liv. 3, 50, 10: quidam ausi sunt mediā ex contione succlamare: Abite hinc, ne, etc., id. 44, 45; cf.: si esset libera haec civitas, non tibi succlamassent, id. 6, 40: cum centuria fre quens succlamasset, nihil se mutare sententiae, etc., id. 26, 22,

succlausus.full: succlausus, a, um, adj. sub-claudo, half-closed [Appul.], Polem. Physiogn. p. 128.

succlino.full: succlīno, āre, 1, v. n. sub-clino, to bend or incline somewhat, Ven. Fort. Ep. Praem. Carm. 5, lib. 6.

succollo.full: suc-collo (subc-), āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. collum, to take upon the neck or shoulder, to shoulder (very rare): apes fessum (regem) sublevant, et si nequit volare, succollant, Varr. R. R. 3, 16, 8 (for which: attollunt umeris, Verg. G. 4, 217): vicissim succollantibus (lecticam), Suet. Claud. 10 med.: succollatus et a praesente comitatu imperator consalutatus, id. Oth. 6 med.; Plin. 35, 10, 37, § 117.

succonditor.full: suc-condĭtor (subc-), ōris, m., an inferior officer in the Circensian games, Inscr. Grut. 339, 5, and 340, 3.
succonditor.short: suc-condĭtor (subc-), ōris, m., an inferior officer in the Circensian games, Inscr.

succontumeliose.full: suc-contŭmēlĭōsē (subc-), adv., somewhat insolently or contumeliously: tractari, Cic. Att. 2, 7, 3.
succontumeliose.short: suc-contŭmēlĭōsē (subc-), adv., somewhat insolently or contumeliously: tractari, Cic.

succoquo.full: suc-cŏquo (subc-), ĕre, v. a., to cook a little: omnia igni, Marc. Emp. 36 med.

succoriatio.full: succŏrĭātĭo, ōnis, f. sub-corium; med. t. t., an operating beneath the skin (late Lat.), Ps.-Soran. Quaest. Medic. 245.

succornicularius.full: suc-cornĭcŭlārĭus (subc-), ii, m., a sub-adjutant, second adjutant, Inscr. Orell. 3490.
succornicularius.short: suc-cornĭcŭlārĭus (subc-), ii, m., a sub-adjutant, second adjutant, Inscr.

succortex.full: suc-cortex (subc-), ĭcis, m., the under or inner bark, Veg. 4, 28.
succortex.short: suc-cortex (subc-), ĭcis, m., the under or inner bark, Veg.

succrassulus.full: suc-crassŭlus (subc-), a, um, adj. dim. [crassus], somewhat thick, thickish: corporis qualitate succrassulus, Capitol. Gord. 6.

succrepo.full: suc-crĕpo (subc-), āre, 1, v. n., to crackle beneath (late Lat.), Aug. Vit. Beat. 3.

succresco.full: suc-cresco (subc-), ĕre, v. inch. n., to grow under or from under any thing; to grow up (very rare). Lit.: sub ordine naturali pilorum (in palpebris) alius ordo succrescit, Cels. 7, 7, 8: succrescit ab imo, Ov. M. 9, 352: ne patiantur herbam succrescere, Col. 4, 14, 2; cf.: mores mali, Quasi herba irrigua, succrevere uberrime, Plaut. Trin. 1, 1, 9.— Transf., to grow up to any thing: toties haustum cratera repleri Sponte suā, per seque vident succrescere vina, to spring up, or be supplied anew, O

succretus.full: succrētus, a, um, Part. of succerno.

succrispus.full: suc-crispus (subc-), a, um, adj., somewhat curled, frizzled, or crisped: capillus, Cic. Verr. 2, 2, 44, § 108: juba equi, Varr. R. R. 2, 7, 5: pars inferior caudae, id. ib. 2, 5, 8.
succrispus.short: suc-crispus (subc-), a, um, adj., somewhat curled, frizzled, or crisped: capillus, Cic.

succrotillus.full: suc-crotillus (subc-), a, um, adj., thin, slender, delicate (ante-class.): succrotilla vox tenuis et alta. Titinnius: femina fabulare succrotillā voculā. Afranius in epistulā: loquebatur succrotillā voce serio. Plautus in describendis mulierum cruribus gracilibus in Syro: cum extortis talis, cum succrotillis crusculis, Fest. p. 301 Müll.
succrotillus.short: suc-crotillus (subc-), a, um, adj., thin, slender, delicate (ante-class.): succrotilla vox tenuis et alta.

succrudus.full: suc-crūdus (subc-), a, um, adj., somewhat raw, half raw: brassica, parboiled, Cato, R. R. 156, 7: succrudum incidendum ne, etc., not fully ripe, Cels. 6, 13; 7, 2.
succrudus.short: suc-crūdus (subc-), a, um, adj., somewhat raw, half raw: brassica, parboiled, Cato, R.

succruentus.full: suc-crŭentus (subc-), a, um, adj., somewhat bloody: livor facie contusā, Cels. 5, 18, 24; 4, 18.
succruentus.short: suc-crŭentus (subc-), a, um, adj., somewhat bloody: livor facie contusā, Cels.

succuba.full: succŭba (subc-), ae, comm. 1. succubo. One who lies under; hence, in mal. part., a lecher or strumpet (post-class.): florulentus, Prud. στεφ. 10, 192; cf. 2. succubo.— Transf., a supplanter, rival: formae, App. M. 5, p. 171, 31: tori, id. ib. 10, p. 250, 18.

succubo1.full: suc-cŭbo (subc-), āre, v. n., to lie under (very rare): grabatulo succubans, App. M. 1, p. 107, 39: alveum, id. ib. 9, p. 229, 30.

succubo2.full: suc-cŭbo (subc-), ōnis, m. cubo, one who lies under; hence, a lecher, Titin. ap. Non. 224, 22 (but Com. Fragm. v. 92 Rib. reads: quam arbitrer Illarum subcuboneam esse, i. e. succubam).

succultro.full: suc-cultro (subc-), no perf., ātum, 1, v. a. culter, to cut up with a knife, to chop up, mince (late Lat.): pulpas, Apic. 4, 2: thymum, id. 8, 8 med.

succumbo.full: suc-cumbo (subc-), cŭbŭi, cŭbĭtum, 3, v. n., to lay or put one's self under any thing; to fall down, lie, or sink down. Lit. (rare; not in Cic.; cf. subsido). In gen.: ancipiti succumbens victima ferro, Cat. 64, 370: vidit Cyllenius omnes Succubuisse oculos, had sunk in sleep, i. e. had closed, Ov. M. 1, 714: (Augustus) Nolae succubuit, took to his bed, Suet. Aug. 98 fin.: non succumbentibus causis operis, Plin. 36, 15, 24, § 106; Arn. 6, 16 Hildebr.— In partic. Of a woman, to lie down to a man,

succumbus.full: succumbus (subc-), i, m., a boundary-stone, Auct. Limit. pp. 265 and 302 Goes.
succumbus.short: succumbus (subc-), i, m., a boundary-stone, Auct.

succuneatus.full: suc-cŭnĕātus (subc-), a, um, Part. [cuneo], wedged underneath, supported with wedges: postes, Vitr. 6, 2.

succurator.full: suc-cūrātor (subc-), ōris, m., a subcurator (post-class.), Dig. 3, 5, 29.
succurator.short: suc-cūrātor (subc-), ōris, m., a subcurator (post-class.), Dig.

succurro.full: suc-curro (subc-), curri, cursum, 3, v. n., to run under. Lit. In gen.: tempore eodem aliud nequeat succurrere lunae Corpus, * Lucr. 5, 763; cf.: pagus Succusanus, quod succurrit Carinis, runs, i. e. lies under or behind, Varr. L. L. 5, § 48 Müll.— In partic., to run or hasten to the aid or assistance of one; to help, aid, assist, succor (the predom. and class, signif.; syn.: subvenio, adjuvo, sublevo): ut laborantibus succurrat, Cic. de Or. 1, 37, 169: saluti fortunisque communibus, id. Rab. Pe

succursor.full: succursor (subc-), ōris, m. succurro, perh. a helper, succorer, who comes to the aid of the bestiarius, in the combats with beasts in the circus, Inscr. Orell. 2530.

succurvus.full: suc-curvus (subc-), a, um, adj., somewhat curved, Amm. 26, 9, 11.
succurvus.short: suc-curvus (subc-), a, um, adj., somewhat curved, Amm.

succussator.full: succussātor, ōris, m. succusso, a jolter: caballus, a jolting horse, Lucil. ap. Non. 16, 30; cf. succussor.

succussatura.full: succussātūra (subc-), ae, f. id., the jolting of a hard-going horse, Non. 17, 23.

succussio.full: succussĭo (subc-), ōnis, f. succutio, a shaking, quaking: succussio est, cum terra quatitur et sursum ac deorsum movetur, Sen. Q. N. 6, 21, 2.

succusso.full: succusso (subc-), āre, v. freq. a. id., to shake or jerk up and down, to jolt (as a hard-going horse does his rider), Att. ap. Non. 16, 29 (Trag. Rel. 568 Rib.).

succussor.full: succussor (subc-), ōris, m. id., a jolter, said of a horse: sonipes, Lucil. ap. Non. 16, 31; cf. succussator.

succussus1.full: succussus, a, um, Part. of succutio.

succussus2.full: succussus (subc-), ūs, m. succutio, a shaking, jolting, Pac. ap. Cic. Tusc. 2, 21, 48 (Trag. Rel. 257 Rib.): membra tremulo succussu quatit, App. M. 3, p. 138, 29. —Plur., Tert. Anim. 49 init.

succustos.full: suc-custos (subc-), ōdis, m., an under-keeper, assistant-overseer, Plaut. Mil. 3, 2, 54.
succustos.short: suc-custos (subc-), ōdis, m., an under-keeper, assistant-overseer, Plaut.

succutio.full: suc-cŭtĭo (subc-), ussi, ussum, 3, v. a. sub-quatio, to fling up from below, fling aloft, toss up (poet. and in post-Aug. prose). Lit.: orbes rotarum, Lucr. 6, 551: currus alte, Ov. M. 2, 166: mare, Sen. Q. N. 5, 1, 1: vasculum, App. M. 2, p. 166: caput, id. Mag. p. 333 et saep.—* Trop.: vultūs succussus, Val. Max. 6, 9 ext. 5.

sucerda.full: sucerda, ae, f. sus and root skar-; Gr. σκώρ; cf. stercus, the dung of swine, Lucil. ap. Non. 175, 14; Titin. ap. Fest. p. 302 Müll. (Com. Rel. v. 178 Rib.; cf. excerno, 2).

suche.full: Suchē, ēs, f., a town in Egypt, Plin. 6, 29, 34, § 172.
suche.short: Suchē, ēs, f., a town in Egypt, Plin.

sucido.full: sūcĭdo, āre, 1, v. a. sucus, to make fresh or juicy: cyminum, Plin. Val. 2, 9.

sucidus.full: sūcĭdus (succ-), a, um, adj. id., juicy, sappy; fresh (very rare; not in Cic.): solum, App. Mag. p. 289: tonsurae tempus inter aequinoctium vernum et solstitium, cum sudare inceperunt oves; a quo sudore recens lana tonsa sucida appellata est, Varr. R. R. 2, 11, 6: lana, Mart. 11, 27, 8; Juv. 5, 24; Fest. p. 118 Müll.; such wool was much used in medicine, Cels. 8, 3 fin.; Plin. 29, 2, 9, § 30; and was called sucidae sordes, id. 29, 2, 10, § 35: (puella) fresh, plump, Plaut. Mil. 3, 1, 192.

sucinacius.full: sūcĭnācĭus, a, um, adj. sucinum, amber-colored, Isid. 20, 3, 5.

sucineus.full: sūcĭnĕus (succ-), a, um, adj. id., of amber: novaculae, with amber handles, Plin. 22, 23, 47, § 99 (al. sucinas).

sucinum.full: sūcĭnum (succ-), i, n. sucus, amber, usu. called electrum, Plin. 37, 2, 11, § 30; Mart. 3, 65, 5; 5, 37, 11; Juv. 6, 573 al.

sucinus.full: sūcĭnus (succ-), a, um, adj. sucinum, of amber: gutta, Mart. 6, 15, 2: gemma, id. 4, 59, 2: novacula, Plin. 22, 23, 47, § 99.

suco.full: sūco (succ-), ōnis, m. sugo, a sucker; of a usurer, Att. ap. Cic. Att. 7, 13, b, § 5.

sucositas.full: sūcōsĭtas, ātis, f. sucosus, juici ness, Cael. Aur. Acut. 2, 29, 151.

sucosus.full: sūcōsus (succ-), a, um, adj. sucus, full of juice or moisture, juicy, sappy, succulent. Lit. (post-Aug.): poma, Cels. 2, 18: solum, Col. 2, 16, 3: resina, Plin. 24, 6, 22, § 33: radix, id. 25, 9, 70, § 117: folia, id. 25, 13, 102, § 161: vinum, id. 14, 6, 8, § 68: lana, i. e. sucida, Ser. Samm. 60, 1054.— Comp.: liber (stirpium), Col. 4, 29, 1.—* Transf., rich in money, Petr. 38, 6.

sucro.full: Sucro, ōnis, m. A river of Hispania Tarraconensis, now the Xucar, Mel. 2, 6; Plin. 3, 3, 4, § 20.— A town at the mouth of this river, now Sueca, Plin. 3, 3, 4, § 20; Liv. 28, 24; 28, 26; 28, 29; Sen. Ben. 5, 24, 1; Flor. 3, 22, 7. — Hence, Sucrō-nensis, e, adj., of or pertaining to Sucro: proelium, Cic. Balb. 2: sinus, Mel. 2, 6, 7; 2, 7, 21.— An island near the coast of Spain, Plin. 3, 5, 11, § 76.— The name of a Rutulian, Verg. A. 12, 505.

suctus1.full: suctus, a, um, Part. of sugo.

sucula1.full: sŭcŭla, ae, f. dim. perh. root σεύω, to drive, a kind of machine for drawing or lifting, a winch, windlass, capstan, Cato, R. R. 19, 2; Vitr. 10, 2; Plaut. Rud. 4, 4, 126; of a wine- or oil-press, Cato, R. R. 12; 18, 2; Dig. 19, 2, 19.

sucula2.full: sŭcŭla, ae, f. dim. sus, a little pig, only in paronom. with 1. sucula, Plaut. Rud. 4, 4, 126.

sucula3.full: sŭcŭla, ae, f. cf. ὕω, to rain, mostly plur. suculae, the constellation Hyades, a transl. of the Gr. ὑάδες, Tiro ap. Gell. 13, 9, 4; Plin. 2, 39, 39, § 106: nostri a similitudine cognominis Graeci propter sues impositum arbitrantes imperitiā appellavere suculas, id. 18, 26, 66, § 247; cf. Cic. N. D. 2, 43, 111; Col. 2, 2, 4; 2, 2, 34; 2, 2, 36; 2, 2, 89.

suculentus.full: sūcŭlentus (succ-), a, um, adj. sucus, full of juice or sap, sappy, succulent (post-class.). Lit.: gracilitas, App. M. 2, p. 115, 22: arvina, id. ib. 10, 245: corpus, Paul. Nol. Carm. 21, 631. — * Trop., vigorous: furores, Prud. Ham. 57 praef.

suculus.full: sŭcŭlus, i, m. dim. sus, a little boar, Just. Inst. 2, 1, 37.

sucus.full: sūcus (succus), i (collat. form, gen. sing. sucūs, Isid. 17, 9, 28; gen. plur. sucuum, App. M. 10, p. 244, 32), m. sugo, juice, moisture, sap (class.; cf.: liquor, latex). Lit. In gen.: stirpes ex terrā sucum trahunt, Cic. N. D. 2, 47, 120: sucus ex intestinis et alvo secretus a reliquo cibo, id. ib. 2, 55, 137: cochleae suo sibi suco vivunt, Plaut. Capt. 1, 1, 13: ambrosiae suco saturi (equi solis), Ov. M. 2, 120; so, ambrosiae, Verg. A. 12, 419: uvae, Tib. 1, 10, 47; 4, 2, 16: sucus nuci expre

sudabundus.full: sūdābundus, a, um, adj. sudo, sweating: turba, Auct. Carm. ad Pis. 176.

sudariolum.full: sūdārĭŏlum, i, n. dim. sudarium, a little handkerchief, Hier. Ep. 52, 5; App. Mag. p. 307, 37 al.

sudarium.full: sūdārĭum, ii, n. sudor, a cloth for wiping off perspiration, a handkerchief, Cat. 12, 14; 25, 7; Mart. 11, 39, 3; Petr. 67: sudario candido tergere frontem, Quint. 6, 3, 60; 11, 3, 148; Suet. Ner. 25; 48; 51; Val. Max. 9, 12, 7; App. Mag. p. 309, 28.

sudatilis.full: sūdātĭlis, e, adj. sudo, flowing like sweat, fluid (late Lat.): metallum, Cassiod. Var. 5, 2.

sudatio.full: sūdātĭo, ōnis, f. id.. Lit., a sweating, perspiration, sudation (post-Aug.): multa, Sen. Ep. 86, 5.—Plur., Cels. 3, 2 med. —* Transf., in concr., a sweatingroom, sudatory: concamerata, Vitr. 5, 11 med.

sudator.full: sūdātor, ōris, m. id., one that perspires easily or copiously, Plin. 23, 1, 23, § 43.

sudatorius.full: sūdātōrĭus, a, um, adj. sudo, belonging to or serving for sweating, sudatory. Adj.: unctiones, Plaut. Stich. 1, 3, 73: qualitas, Cassiod. Var. 2, 39 med. — Subst.: sūdātōrĭum, ii, n., a sweatingbath, sweating-room, a sudatory: circa balinea ac sudatoria, Sen. Vit. Beat. 7, 2; id. Ep. 51, 6.

sudatrix.full: sūdātrix, īcis, f. sudator, she that sweats or causes sweating: toga, Mart. 12, 18, 5.

sudiculum.full: sūdĭcŭlum (sūdŭc-), i, n. sudor, producing sweat, a kind of whip or scourge, Plaut. Pers. 3, 3, 14; cf. Fest. p. 336 Müll.

sudines.full: Sudīnes, is, m., a writer on precious stones, Plin. 9, 35, 56, § 115; 36, 7, 12, § 59; 37, 8, 35, § 114 al.
sudines.short: Sudīnes, is, m., a writer on precious stones, Plin.

sudis.full: sŭdis (nom. sing. only, Plin. 32, 10, 54, § 154 infra), is, f., a stake, pile (syn.: palus, sublica). Lit., plur.: sudes stipitesque, Caes. B. C. 1, 27; id. B. G. 5, 18; 5, 40; Verg. A. 7, 524: quadrifidae, id. G. 2, 25: fraxineae, id. ib. 2, 359; Sil. 6, 559: quominus putrescerent sudes, Plin. 17, 14, 24 § 101 al. — In sing., Ov. M. 12, 299 sq.; Luc. 6, 174.—As a weapon: multa vulnera sudibus facta, Liv. 40, 6, 6; Tib. 1, 10, 65; cf.: sudes in terga erectae, bristles, spines, Juv. 4, 128: densa

sudo.full: sūdo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. n. and a. [Gr. root ἰδ-; ἶδος, ἱδρός, sweat; Germ. Schweisz]. Neutr. (class.), to sweat, perspire. Lit. Absol.: qui sudat, Plaut. As. 2, 2, 23: sine causā sudare, Cic. de Or. 2, 55, 223: sudavit et alsit, Hor. A. P. 413: juvenum sudantibus lacertis, Ov. M. 4, 707: quid cum Cumis Apollo sudavit, Cic. Div. 1, 43, 98; cf.: deorum sudasse simulacra nuntiatum est, id. ib. 2, 27, 58: bibere et sudare vita cardiaci est, Sen. Ep. 15, 3: in montes sudantes conscendimus, Petr. 116.—

sudor.full: sūdor, ōris, m. [sudo). Lit., sweat, perspiration: manat ex omni corpore sudor, Enn. ap. Macr. S. 6, 1 (Ann. v. 399 Vahl.); Lucr. 6, 944: sudor e corpore, Cic. Div. 2, 27, 58; cf.: totum sudor habet corpus, Enn. ap. Macr. S. 6, 3 (Ann. v. 436 Vahl.): sudorem multum consecutum esse audiebamus, Cic. de Or. 3, 2, 6: Herculis simulacrum multo sudore manavit, id. Div. 1, 34, 74: sudor fluit undique rivis, Verg. A. 5, 200: salsusque per artus Sudor iit, id. ib. 2, 174: gelidus toto manabat corpore sud

sudorifer.full: sūdōrĭfer, fĕra, fĕrum sudor-fero, sudorific: vapores, Cael. Aur. Acut. 3, 21, 206.
sudorifer.short: sūdōrĭfer, fĕra, fĕrum sudor-fero, sudorific: vapores, Cael.

sudorus.full: sūdōrus, a, um, adj. sudor, dripping with sweat, sweaty: corpus, App. Flor. p. 354, 27.

suduculum.full: sūdŭcŭlum, i, n. dim. sudes, a kind of whip, scourge: flagri, Plaut. Pers. 3, 3, 14 Ritschl N. cr. (cf. sudiculum).

sudus.full: sūdus, a, um, adj. se-udus; cf.: sudum siccum quasi seudum id est sine udo, Fest. pp. 294 and 295 Müll., without moisture, dry; and of the weather, cloudless, bright, clear (class.; cf. serenus). Adj.: ventorum flamina suda, Lucil. ap. Non. 31, 19: flamen venti, Varr. ib. 234, 7: ver, Verg. G. 4, 77: tempestas, App. de Deo Socr. p. 42, 27: splendor luminis, id. M. 11, p. 260, 30: cuncta specula vel uda vel suda videre, id. Mag. p. 283, 37.—Adverb.: sudum, brightly, Prud. Cath. 7, 79.— Subst.: sū

sue.full: Suē, ēs, f., a town in Assyria, Plin. 6, 26, 30, § 118.
sue.short: Suē, ēs, f., a town in Assyria, Plin.

suebri.full: Suebri, ōrum, m., a people of Gaul, Plin. 3, 4, 5, § 35.
suebri.short: Suebri, ōrum, m., a people of Gaul, Plin.

suel.full: Suël, f., a town in Spain, Plin. 3, 1, 3, § 8; Mel. 2, 6.
suel.short: Suël, f., a town in Spain, Plin.

suelleni.full: Suellēni, ōrum, m., a people of Arabia, Plin. 6, 28, 32, § 157.
suelleni.short: Suellēni, ōrum, m., a people of Arabia, Plin.

suelteri.full: Suelteri, ōrum, m., a people of Gallia Narbonensis, Plin. 3, 4, 5, § 35.
suelteri.short: Suelteri, ōrum, m., a people of Gallia Narbonensis, Plin.

sueo.full: sŭĕo, ēre assumed as a stem for the form sŭēmus, which is probably a contracted perf., = suevimus from suesco; cf. consuesco and the Gr. εἰώθαμεν, to be wont, used, or accustomed: appellare suemus, Lucr. 1, 60: cernere suemus (dissyl.), id. 1, 301: perhibere suemus, id. 4, 369.
sueo.short: sŭĕo, ēre assumed as a stem for the form sŭēmus, which is probably a contracted perf., = suevimus from suesco;

suesco.full: sŭesco, sŭēvi, sŭētum (dissyl. suēvi, suētum; sync. forms, suesti, suerunt, suesse, etc.; v. in the foll., and cf. also the preced. art.), 3, v. inch. n. and a. [Sanscr. svadhā, will, might, custom; Gr. ἔθος, ἦθος]. Neutr., to become used or accustomed; in the tempp. perff., to have accustomed one's self; hence, to be wont, used, or accustomed (rare). Tempp. press.: Drusus in Illyricum missus est, ut suesceret militiae, Tac. A. 2, 44; 2, 52; Aus. Ep. 16, 91.— Tempp. perff.: has Graeci stellas Hy

suessa.full: Suessa, ae, f., = Σύεσσα. A city of Latium, five miles south of the Liris and eight from the sea, founded B. C. 337 by the Aurunci, and afterwards made their capital. It was often called Suessa Aurunca, now Sessa, Liv. 8, 15; 9, 28; Vell. 1, 14; Liv. 27, 9; 29, 15; Cic. Phil. 3, 4, 10; 4, 2, 4; 13, 8, 18; it was the birthplace of the satiric poet Lucilius, cf. Juv. 1, 20; Aus. Ep. 15, 9.— A very ancient city of Latium, a colony of Alba, conquered by Tarquinius Superbus, usually called Suessa Pom

suessetani.full: Suessetāni, ōrum, m., a people of Hispania Tarraconensis, Liv. 25, 34; 34, 20; 39, 42.—Hence, adj.: Suessetānus, a, um: ager, Liv. 28, 24.
suessetani.short: Suessetāni, ōrum, m., a people of Hispania Tarraconensis, Liv.

suessiones.full: Sŭessĭōnes (Sŭessōnes, trisyl., Luc. 1, 423), um, m., a people in Gaul, in the neighborhood of the modern Soissons, Caes, B. G. 2, 3; 2, 12; 2, 13; Hirt. B. G. 8, 6; Plin. 4, 17, 31, § 106.

suessula.full: Suessŭla, ae, f., a town of Campania, now Castel di Sessola, Liv. 7, 37; 8, 14; 23, 14; 23, 17; 23, 32; 24, 46.—Hence, Sues-sŭlāni, ōrum, m., the inhabitants of Suessula, Liv. 8, 14; Plin. 3, 5, 9, § 64; Inscr. Orell. 130; 2369.
suessula.short: Suessŭla, ae, f., a town of Campania, now Castel di Sessola, Liv.

suetonius.full: Suētōnĭus, ii, m., the name of a Roman gens. So, C. Suetonius Paulinus (Lenis), father of the foll., Tac. A. 14, 29; id. H. 2, 23; 2, 31; id. Agr. 5; 14, 16; Suet. Oth. 10.— C. Suetonius Tranquillus, a contemporary and friend of the younger Pliny, author of the biographies of the first twelve Roman emperors, Plin. Ep. 1, 24, 1 sq.; Spart. Hadr. 11, 3. See, concerning him, Bähr's Röm. Lit. Gesch. § 216 sq.
suetonius.short: Suētōnĭus, ii, m., the name of a Roman gens.

suetri.full: Suetri, ōrum, m., an Alpine people, Plin. 3, 20, 24, § 137.
suetri.short: Suetri, ōrum, m., an Alpine people, Plin.

suetudo.full: suētūdo, ĭnis, f. suesco, custom, habit (late Lat.): blanda, Paul. Pell. Euchar. 179; 271.

suetus.full: suētus, a, um, Part. of suesco.

suevi.full: Suēvi or Suēbi (in inscrr. always; but most MSS. have Suevi), ōrum, m., the Suevi, a powerful people in the north-eastern part of Germany, Caes. B. G. 4, 1; Tac. G. 38; Luc. 2, 51.—Hence, Suēvus or Suē-bus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to the Suevi, Suevan: natio, Caes. B. G. 1, 53: crinis, worn in the manner of the Suevi, Sil. 5, 134. — Subst.: Suēvus, i, m., one of the Suevi (poet.), Claud. Cons. Hon. 4, 655.— Suē-vĭa or Suēbĭa, ae, f., the country of the Suevi, Tac. G. 43 init. and 45 fin.— S

suevius.full: Suēvĭus, ii, m., a poet, otherwise unknown, Macr. S. 2, 14.
suevius.short: Suēvĭus, ii, m., a poet, otherwise unknown, Macr.

sufes.full: sūfes (suffes), ĕtis, m. Phoen. , a judge, the chief magistrate of the Carthaginians, corresponding to the Roman consul, a sufet, Liv. 28, 37; 30, 7; 34, 61; Sen. Tranq. 4, 5; Inscr. Orell. 3056 sq. —Plur., Liv. 34, 61; cf. Fest. p. 309 Müll., and Gesen. Script. Phoenic. Monum. p. 394.

sufetula.full: Sufetŭla, ae, f., a town in Africa, Aug. c. Donat. 6, 26.
sufetula.short: Sufetŭla, ae, f., a town in Africa, Aug.

suffarcino.full: suf-farcĭno (subf-), āvi, ātum, 1, v. a., to stuff full, to cram (ante- and postclass.). Lit.: incedunt suffarcinati cum libris, Plaut. Curc. 2, 3, 10: vidi Cantharam Suffarcinatam, stuffed out, i. e. with a bundle under her dress, Ter. And. 4, 4, 31: bellule suffarcinatus, crammed full, gorged with food, App. M. 10, p. 246, 23: aliquem multis muneribus, id. ib. 9, p. 230, 26.— Transf., to deck, adorn, enrich: auro et argento et veste, Cassiod. Inst. Div. Litt. 28.

suffarraneus.full: suffarrānĕus or suffarrānĭus, a false read. for furnariae, Plin. 7, 43, 44, § 135 Sillig ad h. l.)
suffarraneus.short: suffarrānĕus or suffarrānĭus, a false read.

suffectio.full: suffectĭo (subf-), ōnis, f. sufficio (post-class.). An adding: unguentorum, Arn. 5, 166: macularum, id. 7, 251.— A supplying, substituting: animarum alterna mortuorum atque viventium suffectio, Tert. Anim. 28; cf. suffectura.

suffectura.full: suffectūra (subf-), ae, f. id., a supplying, supplement (post-class.): suffectura est quodammodo spiritus animae, Tert. adv. Marc. 1, 28 med.

suffectus.full: suffectus, a, um, Part. of sufficio.

suffenates.full: Suffēnātes, ĭum, m., the inhabitants of Nebula Suffena, a town in the Sabine territory, Plin. 3, 12, 17, § 107.
suffenates.short: Suffēnātes, ĭum, m., the inhabitants of Nebula Suffena, a town in the Sabine territory, Plin.

suffenus.full: Suffēnus, i, m., a bad poet, ridiculed by Catullus, Cat. 14, 19; 22, 1 sqq.
suffenus.short: Suffēnus, i, m., a bad poet, ridiculed by Catullus, Cat.

sufferentia.full: suffĕrentĭa (subf-), ae, f. suffero, a bearing, enduring, toleration, sufferance (post-class.), Tert. adv. Marc. 4, 15; id. Or. 4 med.; Vulg. Jacob. 5, 11; id. Ecclus. 16, 14.

suffermentatus.full: suf-fermentātus (subf-), a, um, Part. [fermento], somewhat fermented (postclass.), Tert. adv. Valent. 17.

suffero.full: suf-fĕro (subf-), sustŭli, sublātum, sufferre, v. a. To carry under, to put or lay under (very rare; syn. subicio): corium, Plaut. Poen. 4, 2, 33: tergum, id. Fragm. ap. Non. 397, 1.— In gen. To offer, proffer: neque mater potest sufferre lac, Varr. R. R. 2, 4, 19.—T. t. in jurid. Lat.: litis aestimationem, to tender, Dig. 30, 1, 69 fin.; 21, 2, 21.— To hold up, bear, support, sustain (very rare; syn. sustineo): an axis eum (mundum) sustineat an ipse se potius vi propriā sufferat, Arn. 2, 83: co

suffertus.full: suffertus (sufferctus, Lucil. ap. Gell. 4, 17, 3), a, um, adj. sub - farcio, crammed full, full (very rare): subicit suffectus posteriorem, Lucil. l. l.: aliquid se sufferti tinniturum, something full-sounding, sonorous, Suet. Ner. 20.

suffervefacio.full: suf-fervēfăcĭo (subf-), no perf., factum, 3, v. a., to heat or warm from below (Plinian), Plin. 18, 11, 26, § 104: affirmant, lapillos, qui sufferveflant, rumpi, id. 27, 9, 51, § 75: aceti heminis quinque suffervefactis, id. 14, 17, 21, § 114: semuncia amyli cum ovo, id. 22, 25, 67, § 137; 37, 10, 54, § 142.

sufferveo.full: suf-fervĕo (subf-), ēre, v. n., to boil or seethe gently, App. Herb. 115.

suffibulum.full: suffībŭlum, i, n. sub-fibula, a white four-cornered veil, worn on the head by priests and priestesses, Varr. L. L. 6, § 21 Müll.; cf. Fest. pp. 348 and 349 ib.

sufficienter.full: suffĭcĭenter, adv. sufficio, sufficiently, enough, Dig. 7, 1, 15; Vulg. Nah. 2, 12; Plin. Ep. 10, 18 (29), 3 dub.

sufficientia.full: suffĭcĭentĭa, ae, f. id., a sufficiency (post-class.), Tert. ad Uxor. 1, 4 fin.; Sid. Ep. 6, 12 fin.; Vulg. 2 Cor. 3, 5; 9, 8.

sufficio.full: suf-fĭcĭo (subf-), fēci, fectum, 3, v. a. and n. facio. Act. To put under or among. Of a building, to lay the foundation for: opus. Curt. 5, 1, 29 Zumpt. — Esp., to put into, dip in, dye, impregnate, imbue, tinge, lanam medicamentis, to impregnate, imbue, tinge, Cic. ap. Non. 386, 10, and 521, 19: (angues) ardentes oculos suffecti sanguine et igni, suffused, colored, Verg. A. 2, 210: maculis suffecta genas, Val. Fl. 2, 105: suffecta leto lumina, id. 1, 822; cf.: nubes sole suffecta, i. e. shone

suffigo.full: suf-fīgo (subf-), xi, xum, 3, v. a., to fasten beneath or below, to fasten or fix on, to affix (rare but class.): ecce aedificat: columnam mento suffigit suo, Plaut. Mil. 2, 2, 54 Ritschl N. cr.: antennae suffixit lintea, Luc. 9, 328: aureis clavis crepidas, Plin. 33, 3, 14, § 50: janua suffixa tigillo, Cat. 67, 39: trabes multo auro, Sen. Hippol. 497: cruci suffixus, * Cic. Pis. 18, 42: aliquem cruci, Vell. 2, 42 fin.; Suet. Caes. 74; Paul. Sent. 5, 23, 15: patibulo, Just. 22, 7, 8: patibulis,

suffimen.full: suffīmen, ĭnis, n. suffio, fumigation, incense (poet. for suffimentum), Ov. F. 4, 731 sq.

suffimento.full: suffīmento, āre, v. a. suffimentum, to fumigate: totum bovem, Veg. 3, 2 fin.

suffimentum.full: suffīmentum, i, n. suffio, fumigation, incense (cf.: odor, fragrantia): in iis sine illius suffimentis expiati sumus, Cic. Leg. 1, 14, 40: quia suffimentum sit (laurus) caedis hostium et purgatio, Plin. 15, 30, 40, § 135; cf. Fest. pp. 348 and 349 Müll.— Plur., Veg. Vet. 1, 19 sq.; 4, 12.

suffio.full: suf-fĭo (subf-), īvi or ĭi, ītum, 4, v. a. fio = θύω, to fumigate, perfume, scent (mostly poet. and in post-Aug. prose; not in Cic.; but cf. suffimentum; cf.: vaporo, fumigo): (testam) suffito sertā et schoeno et palmā, Cato, R. R. 113, 1: thymo, Verg. G. 4, 241: bonis odoribus, Col. 12, 18, 3: locum, Prop. 4 (5), 8, 84. suffire et purgare domos, Plin. 25, 5, 21, § 49: tecta, id. 12, 17, 40, § 81: se taetris odoribus, Lucr. 4, 1175: oculos jocinore decocto, Plin. 28, 11, 47, § 171: urnā suffitā
suffio.short: suf-fĭo (subf-), īvi or ĭi, ītum, 4, v.

suffiscus.full: suffiscus dicebatur folliculus testium arietinorum, quo utebantur pro marsupio, forsitan dictus a fisci similitudine, Fest. pp. 308 and 309 Müll.
suffiscus.short: suffiscus dicebatur folliculus testium arietinorum, quo utebantur pro marsupio, forsitan dictus a fisci similitudine, Fest.

suffitio.full: suffītĭo, ōnis, f. suffio, a fumigating, fumigation, perfuming: nimia, Col. 1, 6, 20: suffitionem doliorum facere, id. 12, 50, 16: suffitiones commendavere, Plin. 25, 2, 5, § 12: verbenarum, Arn. 5, 3: funus prosecuti redeuntes ignem supergradiebantur aquā aspersi: quod purgationis genus vocabant suffitionem, Fest. p. 3 Müll.; cf. id. s. v. laureati, p. 117.

suffitor.full: suffītor, ōris, m. id., a fumigator: puerum suffitorem fecit, Plin. 34, 8, 19, § 79.

suffitus1.full: suffītus, a, um, Part. of suffio.

suffitus2.full: suffītus, ūs, m. suffio. A fumigating, fumigation (Plinian): suffitu necare cimices, Plin. 32, 10, 42, § 142; 37, 10, 54, § 142: crebrior, id. 22, 23, 48, § 100.— Plur., Plin. 24, 11, 61, § 102.— In concr., the smoke produced by fumigation: herbae, Plin. 21, 18, 69, § 116.

suffixus.full: suffixus, a, um, Part. of suffigo.

sufflabilis.full: sufflābĭlis, e, adj. sufflo, that can be breathed, breathable (post-class.): animae, Prud. Apoth. 906.

sufflamen.full: sufflāmen, ĭnis, n. id., a clog, break, drag-chain, to check the motion of a wheel. Lit.: rotam astringit multo sufflamine, Juv. 8, 148: tardat sufflamine currum, Prud. Psych. 417.— Trop., a clog, hinderance, impediment (post-class.): nec res atteritur longo sufflamine litis, Juv. 16, 50; Inscr. Grut. 180, 3.

sufflamino.full: sufflāmĭno, āre, v. a. sufflamen, to hold back by a clog, to clog, check. * Lit.: rotam Ixionis, Sen. Lud. Mort. Claud. (Apocol.) 14, 3.—* Trop., to stay, check, repress in speaking: tanta illi erat velocitas orationis, ut vitium fieret. Itaque D. Augustus optime dixit, Aterius noster sufflaminandus est, Sen. Exc. Contr. 4, praef. § 7.

sufflammo.full: suf-flammo (subfl-), āre, v. a., to kindle, inflame: calumniam invidiā, Sid. Ep. 5, 6 fin.

sufflatio.full: sufflātĭo (subfl-), ōnis, f. sufflo, a blowing or puffing up, inflation (Plinian): bullantium aquarum, Plin. 9, 7, 6, § 18: praedurum est sufflatione viventibus, id. 9, 29, 46, § 86.

sufflatorium.full: sufflātōrĭum, i, n. id., the bellows, Vulg. Jer. 6, 29.

sufflatus1.full: sufflātus (subfl-), ūs, a false read. for si afflavit, Sen. Clem. 1, 25, 4.

sufflatus2.full: sufflātus, a, um, Part. and P. a., v. sufflo.

sufflavus.full: suf-flāvus (subfl-), a, um, adj., yellowish, light blonde: capillus, Suet. Aug. 79.
sufflavus.short: suf-flāvus (subfl-), a, um, adj., yellowish, light blonde: capillus, Suet.

sufflo.full: suf-flo (subflo), āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. and n. (rare; not in Cic. or Cæs.). Act., to blow forth from below; to blow up, puff out, inflate. Lit.: age, tibicen, refer ad labeas tibias, Suffla celeriter tibi buccas, quasi proserpens bestia, Plaut. Stich. 5, 4, 42: venae ubi sufflatae sunt ex cibo, Cato, R. R. 157, 7: sufflata cutis, Plin. 8, 38, 57, § 138.— To blow upon: ignes, Plin. 34, 8, 19, § 79: gladiatores decrepiti, quos si sufflasses, cecidissent, Petr. 45, 11: prunas, Vulg. Isa. 54, 16.—* Tr

suffocabilis.full: suffōcābĭlis (subf-), e, adj. suffoco, suffocating: parvus locus, Cael. Aur. Acut. 1, 9.

suffocatio.full: suffōcātĭo (subf-), ōnis, f. id., a choking, stifling, suffocating, Sen. Ep. 54, 2; hence, mulierum, suffocation of the womb, hysterical passion, Plin. 20, 5, 15, § 30; 26, 15, 90, § 158; v. suffoco, I.

suffoco.full: suf-fōco (subf-), āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. faux, to choke, stifle, strangle, suffocate by compressing the throat (rare but class.; syn.: strangulo, elido). Lit.: patrem, Cic. Mur. 29, 61: quem crassior saliva suffocat, Sen. Q. N. 6, 2, 4: in melle situm suffocari, to be suffocated, Lucr. 3, 891: vox suffocatur saepe, Quint. 11, 3, 51: suffocatae (mulieres), hysterical, Plin. 20, 22, 87, § 238; cf. suffocatio.— Transf.: injuriā suffocante vitem, that chokes, kills, Plin. 17, 23, 35, § 209: urbem et It

suffodio.full: suf-fŏdĭo (subf-), fōdi, fossum, 3, v. a., to dig or pierce underneath; to pierce or bore through; to dig under, sap, undermine (class.; not in Cic.): ilia equis suffodere, Liv. 42, 59: inguina, Suet. Dom. 17: equos, to stab in the belly, Caes. B. G. 4, 12; Tac. A. 1, 65; 2, 11: suffosso equo, Verg. A. 11, 671; Liv. 42, 59; Curt. 4, 13, 33: radices frumenti, Plin. 18, 21, 50, § 184: montes, Vell. 2, 33, 4; Plin. 36, 15, 24, § 104; cf.: vineas expediunt suffodiendis muris, Tac. H. 2, 21: Alexandr

suffossio.full: suffossĭo (subf-), ōnis, f. suffodio, a digging under, undermining, Vulg. Jer. 51, 58.—Transf., in plur., concr., mines, Vitr. 1, 5, 5 (dub.): cum ipsum solum subfossionibus tremeret, Sen. Ep. 49, 8.

suffossus.full: suffossus (subf-), a, um, Part. of suffodio.

suffragatio.full: suffrāgātĭo (subf-), ōnis, f. suffragor, a voting for one or in one's favor, interest, favor, support, suffrage (class.): suffragationem, observantiam, et gratiam tollere, Cic. Planc. 18, 44; cf.: sublata sunt studia, exstinctae suffragationes, id. ib. 6, 15: in consule declarando multum etiam apud universum populum Romanum auctoritatis habet suffragatio militaris, id. Mur. 18, 38: urbana, id. ib. 19, 38; cf. Planc. ap. Cic. Fam. 10, 9, 2: justa, Liv. 10, 13, 13: nec potestas nec suffragatio hor

suffragator.full: suffrāgātor (subf-), ōris, m. id., one who votes for another, a supporter, partisan, suffragator (class.): suffragatorum comparatio, Cic. Mur. 21, 44: historicis notior, suffragatoribus obscurior, id. ib. 7, 16: ex fucosis firmi suffragatores evadunt, Q. Cic. Pet. Cons. 9, 35: meus in petendis honoribus, Plin. Ep. 4, 17, 6; id. Pan. 92, 3: competitoris sui suffragatorem agere, Val. Max. 4, 5, 3: candidati laborare desiimus: suffragatores incipimus, Sen. Brev. Vit. 17, 5.—With gen.-obj.: quaestur

suffragatorius.full: suffrāgātōrĭus, a, um, adj. id., of or belonging to the support of a candidate, recommendatory, suffragatory: non brevis et suffragatoria, sed firma et perpetua amicitia, Q. Cic. Pet. Cons. 7, 26.

suffragatrix.full: suffrāgātrix, īcis, f. suffragator, a (female) favorer, supporter (late Lat.): nec adfuit (Minerva) suffragatricibus suis, Aug. Civ. Dei, 18, 9 fin.; 18, 10 fin.

suffraginosus.full: suffrāgĭnōsus, a, um, adj. suffrago, diseased in the hough or pastern: mula, Col. 6, 38, 2.

suffragium.full: suffrāgĭum, ii, n. perh. kindr. with suffrago, and therefore, prop., the pasternbone; cf. Wunder, Var. Lect. p. 169; hence, transf., publicists' and jurid. t. t., a votingtablet, a ballot (syn. tabella), and in gen., a vote, voice, suffrage (freq. and class.). Lit.: dicam et versabor in re difficili, suffragia magistratu mandando aut reo judicando clam an palam ferre melius esset ... Ego in istā sum sententia, quā te fuisse semper scio, nihil ut fuerit in suffragiis voce melius, Cic. Leg. 3, 15,

suffrago1.full: suffrāgo, ĭnis, f. sub-frag, frango. Lit., the ham or hough, hock of a quadruped's hind leg (opp. armus): articulum suffraginis contingere (cf. poples), Plin. 8, 45, 70, § 183: suffraginum artus in aversum flectunt, id. 11, 45, 101, § 248; Col. 6, 15, 2. —Rarely of birds: aves ut quadripedes alas in priora curvant, suffraginem in posteriora, Plin. 11, 45, 102, § 249: aquilae pedes evellunt in aversum a suffragine, id. 30, 6, 18, § 54. — Transf., a shoot, spray of a vine: suboles, quam rustici su

suffrago2.full: suffrāgo, āvi, 1, v. a., = suffragor. In gen., to favor, support, vote for, Sisenn. ap. Non. 468, 12.— Absol. To agree with, Pomp. ap. Non. 468, 7 (Com. Fragm. 106 Rib.).— To proceed favorably: opera, Vulg. 3 Esd. 6, 10.

suffragor.full: suffrāgor, ātus, 1, v. dep. n. [suffragium], publicists' t. t., to vote for, to support with one's vote and interest. Lit.: si nihil erit praeter ipsorum suffragium, tenue est; si, ut suffragantur, nihil valent gratiā, Cic. Mur. 34, 71: suffragandi libido, id. Leg. 3, 15, 34: convenerant undique, non suffragandi modo sed etiam spectandi causā P. Scipionis, Liv. 28, 38, 8.— Transf., in gen., to be favorable, to favor, recommend, support (class.; syn.: faveo, studeo). With dat.: domus suffragata d

suffrenatio.full: suf-frēnātĭo (subf-, also suffraen-), ōnis, f. freno, a binding down fast, cementing: lapidis, Plin. 36, 22, 49, § 169: globus multā suffrenatione devinctus, Isid. Orig. 19, 10.

suffrendens.full: suf-frendens (subf-), entis, Part. [frendo], gnashing a little: uxor inflatā cervice, Amm. 15, 12, 1.

suffrico.full: suf-frĭco (subf-), āre, v. a., to rub underneath, to rub down, rub or wipe off, Col. 12, 23, 2: vasa, id. 12, 25, 4; 12, 30, 2: seriam, id. 12, 38, 4: palpebras medicamentis, Cels. 6, 6, 26.

suffrigidus.full: suf-frīgĭdus (subf-), a, um, adj., rather cold or frigid (post-class. and very rare); trop.: argumentum, Amm. 17, 11, 4. —Adv.: suffrīgĭdē, rather coldly or frigidly: nimis minute ac prope etiam suffrigide, Gell. 2, 9, 4.
suffrigidus.short: suf-frīgĭdus (subf-), a, um, adj., rather cold or frigid (post-class.

suffringo.full: suf-fringo (subf-), ĕre, v. a. frango, to break below, to break (rare but class.): talos alicui, Plaut. Rud. 4, 4, 15; id. Truc. 2, 8, 8: crura alicui, * Cic. Rosc. Am. 20, 56: ossa ejus, Lact. 4, 26, 32.

suffrondeo.full: suf-frondĕo (subf-), ēre, 2, v. n., to put forth leaves (late Lat.), Aug. Serm. Mai, 3.

suffugio.full: suf-fŭgĭo (subf-), fūgi, 3, v. n. and a., to flee away (rare; not in Cic.). Neutr.: custodes vigilesque suffugere in tecta coëgit (imber), Liv. 24, 46.— Act., to flee from, to shun, avoid, escape a person or thing: manuum tactum et ictum, Lucr. 5, 150: sensum, id. 4, 360: consularem orare conantem, Suet. Tib. 27.

suffugium.full: suffŭgĭum (subf-), ii, n. suffugio, a place beneath which one flies for shelter from rain, etc., a shelter, covert (not anteAug.). Lit.: quid nisi suffugium nimbos vitantibus essem? Ov. de Nuce, 119: subterranei specus suffugium hiemi, Tac. G. 16: propinqua suffugia, id. A. 4, 47; 3, 74: suffugia adversus perpetuum caeli rigorem, Sen. Ira, 1, 11, 3: suffugium nullum aut imbris aut solis, Plin. Ep. 9, 39, 2: ferarum imbriumque, Tac. G. 46.— Trop., a refuge, remedy: haec deverticula suffugia sunt

suffulcio.full: suf-fulcĭo (subf-), fulsi, fultum, 4, v. a., to prop underneath, to underprop, prop up, support (mostly ante- and post-class.; not in Cic.). Lit.: porticus paribus suffulta columnis, Lucr. 4, 427: maxillas et cervices pulvillis, App. M. 10, p. 248, 26: lectica Syris suffulta, i. e. borne, carried, Mart. 9, 3, 11.—Absol.: nisi suffulcis firmiter, Non potes subsistere, Plaut. Ep. 1, 1, 77: vestis imum tegat suffulta latus, lying on it, Sen. Troad. 105.— Trop.: propterea capitur cibus, ut suffulcia

suffulgeo.full: suf-fulgĕo (subf-), ēre, 2, v. n., to gleam or shine beneath: tum fit ut umor aquae suffulgeat, Poët. in Anthol. Lat. 2, p. 311 Burm.

suffultura.full: suffultūra, ae, f. suffulcio, a propping, support (late Lat.): columnae suffulturae solacio nudatae, Cassiod. Hist. Eccl. 34.

suffultus.full: suffultus, a, um, Part. of suffulcio.

suffumigatio.full: suf-fūmĭgātĭo (sūbf-), ōnis, f. suffumigo, a fumigating from below, Veg. Vet. 3, 23 fin.

suffumigo.full: suf-fūmĭgo (subf-), āre, v. a., to fumigate from below, to suffumigate: si ex alvo apes minus frequentes evadunt, suffumigandum, Varr. R. R. 3, 16, 6: vulvam sulphure, Cels. 4, 20 med.: vulnus, id. 5, 27, 5: vasa rore marino vel lauro vel myrto, Col. 12, 25, 4: dolia albā cerā, id. 12, 52, 16.— Absol.: suffumigare expedit, Cels. 6, 6, 35.

suffumo.full: suf-fūmo (subf-), āre, v. n., to smoke or reek a little; trop., Hier. Ep. 29, 1.

suffundatus.full: suf-fundātus (subf-), a, um, Part. [2. fundo], built under, laid as a foundation: lapidibus suffundatis, Varr. ap. Non. 48, 15.

suffundo.full: suf-fundo (subf-), fūdi, fūsum, 3, v. a., to pour below or underneath; to pour into or among; to pour over or upon; to overspread, suffuse (mostly ante-class. and postAug.). Lit. In gen.: animum esse cordi suffusum sanguinem, Cic. Tusc. 1, 9, 19: aqua suffunditur, flows underneath, diffuses itself, Sen. Q. N. 3, 26, 1 (al. adfunditur): intumuit suffusā venter ab undā, i. e. from dropsy, Ov. F. 1, 215: mane suffundam aquolam, Plaut. Curc. 1, 3, 3: mare (i. e. aquam marinam) vinis, id. Rud. 2, 7,

suffuror.full: suf-fūror (subf-), āri, v. dep. n., to steal secretly, to steal away, filch: suffuror, suppilo, Plaut. Truc. 2, 7, 15.

suffuscens.full: suffuscens, false read. for suffundens, Lucr. 3, 39.

suffusculus.full: suffuscŭlus (subf-), a, um, adj. dim. [suffuscus], somewhat brown, brownish (postclass.): homines Aegyptii, Amm. 22, 16, 23; so App. M. 2, p. 120, 18.

suffuscus.full: suf-fuscus (subf-), a, um, adj., somewhat brown, brownish, dusky: margarita, Tac. Agr. 12 fin.
suffuscus.short: suf-fuscus (subf-), a, um, adj., somewhat brown, brownish, dusky: margarita, Tac.

suffusio.full: suff-ūsĭo (subf-), ōnis, f. suffundo, a pouring or spreading into or among, a pouring over, a suffusion (post-Aug.). In gen.: vini, an infusion, Apic. 1, 1; so, cucumeris, Pall. 1, 35, 9.— Esp., of diseases. A spreading: fellis, i. e. the jaundice, Plin. 22, 23, 49, § 104.— Suffusio oculorum (oculi); and often absol. suffusio, opacity of the cornea, cataract, Cels. 7, 7, 14; 6, 6, 35; Plin. 28, 1, 2, § 7; 32, 4, 14, § 33; 34, 11, 27, § 114. — Suffusio pedis, a disease of the feet of animals, Veg

suffusorium.full: suffūsōrĭum, ii, n. id., a vessel for pouring, a pitcher, Hier. in Isa. 2, 4, 1; Vulg. Zach. 4, 12; cf.: suffusorium ἐπίχυσις, Gloss. Philox.

suffusus.full: suffūsus (subf-), a, um, Part. and P. a., from suffundo.

suggero.full: sug-gĕro (subg-), gessi, gestum, 3, v. a., to carry, bring, put or lay under, etc. (class., esp. in the trop. sense). Lit.: flammam costis aëni, Verg. A. 7, 463: ignem fornace succensā, Pall. 1, 20, 2. — To heap up, raise, erect, build: humo, Prop. 4 (5), 4, 8. cf.: celsis suggesta theatra columnis, Sil. 14, 644.— To furnish, afford, supply ( = praebeo, suppedito, ministro): cur tu his rebus sumptum suggeris? Ter. Ad. 1, 1, 37: tela mihi, Verg. A. 10, 333: omnium rerum apparatus, Auct. B. Alex.

suggestio.full: suggestĭo (subg-), ōnis, f. suggero. * Lit., an adding to, addition: potus suggestione auctus, Cael. Aur. Tard. 2, 13, 182.— Trop. * A rhet. fig., where the orator puts a question and answers it himself, a suggestion: quod schema quidam per suggestionem vocant, i. e. per subjectionem, Quint. 9, 2, 15.— A hint, intimation, suggestion (late Lat.), Vop. Aur. 14; 19; Symm. Ep. 9, 20; Inscr. Orell. 2.

suggestum.full: suggestum, i, n. id., a raised place, height, mound: ex suggesto faleris prodeunt anates in stagnum, Varr. R. R. 3, 5, 16.— Esp., a platform, stage, tribune for a speaker: cum in communibus suggestis consistere non auderet, Cic. Tusc. 5, 20, 59: illud suggestum, in quo causam dixerat, ascendens, id. Div. 1, 54, 124.

suggestus1.full: suggestus, a, um, Part., from suggero.
suggestus1.short: suggestus, a, um, Part., from suggero.

suggestus2.full: suggestus (subg-), ūs, m., and suggestum, i, n. suggero. (Acc. to suggero, I.) An elevated place made of materials poured out; hence, a raised place, a height, elevation (cf. pulpitum). Lit. In gen.: labrum in suggestu inter dolia positum, Cato, R. R. 154: lapideus, Col. 9, 7: insulae, Plin. 12, 10, 21, § 38: suggestus in orchestrā, a raised seat, Suet. Caes. 76; Flor. 4, 2, 91 Duk.; cf. Plin. Pan. 51, 4: comae, i. e. a lofty head-dress, Stat. S. 1, 2, 113: montium, Amm. 15, 10, 1.— In partic.,
suggestus2.short: suggestus (subg-), ūs, m., and suggestum, i, n.

sugglutio.full: sug-glūtĭo (subg-), īre, v. n., to hiccup a little, Veg. Vet. 3, 60.

suggrandis.full: sug-grandis (subg-), e, adj., rather large: cubiculum, Cic. Q. Fr. 3, 1, 1, § 2.
suggrandis.short: sug-grandis (subg-), e, adj., rather large: cubiculum, Cic.

suggredior.full: sug-grĕdĭor (subg-), gressus, 3, v. dep. n. and a. [gradior], to go or come up to, to approach (Tacitean). Neutr.: caesis qui barbarorum propius suggrediebantur, Tac. A. 15, 11: suggressi propius speculatores, id. ib. 2, 12; so, propius, id. ib. 13, 57; 14, 37.— Act., to attack: quos dux Romanus acie suggressus, Tac. A. 4, 47; Sall. H. Fragm. 4, 68.

suggrunda.full: sug-grunda (subg-), ae, f. cf. grando; Sanscr. hrāduni, storm; Gr. χάλαζα, hail, the lower border of a roof, the eaves, Varr. R. R. 3, 3, 5; Vitr. 10, 21; Dig. 9, 3, 5, § 6; 50, 16, 242, § 1.—Called also sug-grundium, Vitr. 2, 9, 16; Plin. 25, 13, 102, § 160; and suggrundātio, Vitr. 4, 2.

suggrundarium.full: suggrundārĭum (subg-), ii, n. suggrunda, the grave of a child less than forty days old (which was a niche in a wall, covered by a projecting roof or eaves; cf. columbarium, 2. d.): suggrundaria antiqui dicebant sepulcra infantium, qui necdum XL dies implessent, quia nec busta dici poterant, quia ossa quae comburerentur non erant, nec tanta cadaveris immanitas, quā locus tumesceret. Unde Rutilius Geminus Astyanacte ait: Melius suggrundarium misero quaereres quam sepulcrum, Fulg. Expos. Serm. Ant.

suggrundatio.full: suggrundātĭo (subg-), ōnis, and suggrundium, i, v. suggrunda.
suggrundatio.short: suggrundātĭo (subg-), ōnis, and suggrundium, i, v.

suggrunnio.full: sug-grunnĭo (subgr-), īre, v. n., to grunt a little: sus, Paul. Nol. Carm. 27, 345.

sugillatio.full: sūgillātĭo, ōnis, f. sugillo, a blackand-blue mark, a livid spot (made by a blow, bruise, etc.; not ante-Aug.). Lit.: sugillationem rapere, Plin. 32, 7, 24, § 74.— Trop., an affronting, insulting: consulum, Liv. 43, 14, 5: domini, Dig. 47, 10, 15: foeda majestatis ejus, Plin. 7, 45, 46, § 150: ipsius gloriae, Val. Max. 2, 3, 1: amara, id. 6, 9, 12: admonitionis, Sen. Ben. 5, 22, 3.

sugillatiuncula.full: sūgillātĭuncŭla, ae, f. dim. sugillatio, a small livid spot, Claud. Mam. Stat. Anim. 2, 9 dub.

sugillatus.full: sūgillātus, ūs, m. sugillo, post-class. for sugillatio, Tert. adv. Marc. 4, 34.
