synemmenon.short: sўnēmmĕnon, i, n., = συνημμένον (conjoined), the name of a certain series of musical sounds, Vitr.

synephebi.full: Sўnĕphēbi, ōrum, m., = Συνέφηβοι, The Fellow-youths, the title of a comedy by Statius Caecilius, Cic. Fin. 1, 2, 4; id. Sen. 7, 24; id. Opt. Gen. 6, 18.
synephebi.short: Sўnĕphēbi, ōrum, m., = Συνέφηβοι, The Fellow-youths, the title of a comedy by Statius Caecilius, Cic.

synesis.full: sўnĕsis, is, f., = σύνεσις, understanding, one of the Æons, Tert. adv. Val. 8.
synesis.short: sўnĕsis, is, f., = σύνεσις, understanding, one of the Æons, Tert.

syngenicos.full: syngĕnĭcos, on, adj., = συγγενικός, belonging to one's family or race, Plin. 35, 11, 40, § 134.
syngenicos.short: syngĕnĭcos, on, adj., = συγγενικός, belonging to one's family or race, Plin.

syngrapha.full: syngrăpha, ae, f., = συγγραφή, a written agreement to pay, a promissory note, bond (cf. chirographum), Cic. Fam. 7, 17, 1; id. Att. 5, 21, 11 sq.; id. Phil. 2, 37, 95; Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 13, § 30: ex syngraphā agere, id. Mur. 17, 35; Amm. 26, 3, 4.
syngrapha.short: syngrăpha, ae, f., = συγγραφή, a written agreement to pay, a promissory note, bond (cf.

syngraphus.full: syngrăphus (sungr-), i, m., = σύγγραφος. A written contract, Plaut. As. 4, 1, 1; 4, 1, 57.— A passport, pass, Plaut. Capt. 2, 3, 90; 3, 2, 6.

synhietae.full: Synhiētae, ārum, m., a people of Asia, Plin. 6, 7, 7, § 22.
synhietae.short: Synhiētae, ārum, m., a people of Asia, Plin.

synicense.full: Synicense Castellum, a fortress in Numidia, Aug. Civ. Dei, 22, 8.
synicense.short: Synicense Castellum, a fortress in Numidia, Aug.

synizesis.full: sўnīzēsis, is, f., = συνίζησις, a contraction of two vowels into one syllable, Serv. Verg. A. 1, 698.
synizesis.short: sўnīzēsis, is, f., = συνίζησις, a contraction of two vowels into one syllable, Serv.

synnada.full: Synnăda, ōrum, n., a town in Phrygia Major, famous for its marble, now Afioum Karahissar, Cic. Fam. 3, 8, 3 sq.; 15, 4, 2; id. Att. 5, 20, 1.—Also called Synnăda, ae, f., Claud. in Eutr. 2, 273; and Syn-nas, ădis, Mart. 9, 76, 8; Stat. S. 1, 5, 37; 2, 2, 87; Plin. 5, 29, 29, § 105.—Hence, Synnădensis, e, adj., of or belonging to Synnada: forum, Cic. Att. 5, 21, 9.— Synnădĭcus, a, um, adj., Synnadic: lapis, Plin. 35, 1, 1, § 3.— Synnas, ădis, adj. f., Synnadic: columnae, of Synnadic marble, Capit
synnada.short: Synnăda, ōrum, n., a town in Phrygia Major, famous for its marble, now Afioum Karahissar, Cic.

synnephitis.full: synnĕphītis, ĭdis, f., another name for the gem galactitis, Plin. 37, 10, 59, § 162 (al. synophites).
synnephitis.short: synnĕphītis, ĭdis, f., another name for the gem galactitis, Plin.

synochitis.full: synŏchītis, ĭdis, f., = συνοχῖτις, a kind of precious stone now unknown, Plin. 37, 11, 73, § 192.
synochitis.short: synŏchītis, ĭdis, f., = συνοχῖτις, a kind of precious stone now unknown, Plin.

synodalis.full: sўnŏdālis, e, adj. synodus, of or belonging to a synod, synodal: Nemausum, Ven. Vit. S. Mart. 3, 415.—Subst.: sўnŏ-dālĭa, ĭum, n., constitutions of a synod, synodals, Ven. Vit. S. Mart. 3, 423.

synodicus.full: sўnŏdĭcus, a, um, adj., = συνοδικός, going or coming together, synodical: luna, i. e. when in conjunction with the sun, Firm. Math. 3, 6; 4 praef. fin.— According to the decrees of the synod, Cassiod. Hist. Eccl. 4, 21; 9, 13.—Hence, adv.: sўnŏdĭcē, in accordance with the synod's decrees, Cassiod. Hist. Eccl. 4, 25.
synodicus.short: sўnŏdĭcus, a, um, adj., = συνοδικός, going or coming together, synodical: luna, i.

synoditae.full: sўnŏdītae, ārum, m., = συνοδῖται, fellow-travellers, companions, a kind of monks, Cod. Just. 1, 4, 6; Cod. Th. 11, 30, 57.
synoditae.short: sўnŏdītae, ārum, m., = συνοδῖται, fellow-travellers, companions, a kind of monks, Cod.

synodontitis.full: sўnŏdontītis, ĭdis, f., = συνοδοντῖτις, a precious stone found in the brain of the fish synodus, Plin. 37, 10, 67, § 182.
synodontitis.short: sўnŏdontītis, ĭdis, f., = συνοδοντῖτις, a precious stone found in the brain of the fish synodus, Plin.

synodus1.full: sўnŏdus (in inscrr. written also SYNHODVS; v. Inscr. Orell. 2160; 2627), i, f., = σύνοδος. A college of priests: ARCHIEREVS SYNHODI, Inscr. Orell. l. l.— An ecclesiastical assembly or council, a synod, Cod. Just. 1, 3, 23; Amm. 15, 7, 7.

synodus2.full: sўnŏdūs, ontis, m., = συνόδους, a fish of the bream genus: Sparus, Linn.; Ov. Hal. 107; Plin. 37, 10, 67, § 182.
synodus2.short: sўnŏdūs, ontis, m., = συνόδους, a fish of the bream genus: Sparus, Linn.;

synoecium.full: sўnoecĭum, ii, n., = συνοίκιον, a room where several persons dwell together, Petr. 93.
synoecium.short: sўnoecĭum, ii, n., = συνοίκιον, a room where several persons dwell together, Petr.

synoneton.full: sўnōnēton, i, n., = συνώνητον, a buying up, a collecting by purchase, Cod. Th. 11, 15, 1.
synoneton.short: sўnōnēton, i, n., = συνώνητον, a buying up, a collecting by purchase, Cod.

synonymia.full: sўnōnўmĭa, ae, f., = συνωνυμία, a sameness of meaning in words, synonymy, Mart. Cap. 5, § 535 (Quint. 8, 3, 16, written as Greek).
synonymia.short: sўnōnўmĭa, ae, f., = συνωνυμία, a sameness of meaning in words, synonymy, Mart.

synonymum.full: sўnōnўmum, i, n., = συνώνυμον, a word having the same meaning with another, a synonym, Front. Eloqu. p. 237; Prisc. 579 P.; Serv. Verg. A. 2, 128.
synonymum.short: sўnōnўmum, i, n., = συνώνυμον, a word having the same meaning with another, a synonym, Front.

synophites.full: sўnŏphītes, ae, m., a read. in Plin. 37, 10, 59, § 162 for synnephitis.

synopsis.full: sўnopsis, is, f., = σύνοψις, a general view, a list, synopsis: pupillarium bonorum, Dig. 27, 9, 5, § 11.
synopsis.short: sўnopsis, is, f., = σύνοψις, a general view, a list, synopsis: pupillarium bonorum, Dig.

synoris.full: sўnōris, ĭdis, f., = συνωρίς, a yoke, pair, Hier. Ep. 130, n. 7.
synoris.short: sўnōris, ĭdis, f., = συνωρίς, a yoke, pair, Hier.

syntaxis.full: syntaxis, is, f., = σύνταξις, the connection of words, Prisc. 17, 1, 1.
syntaxis.short: syntaxis, is, f., = σύνταξις, the connection of words, Prisc.

syntecticus.full: syntēctĭcus, a, um, adj., = συντηκτικός, ill of consumption, consumptive, syntectic, Plin. 22, 23, 49, § 105; 28, 8, 24, § 88; 28, 9, 33, § 125; Veg. 1, 38.
syntecticus.short: syntēctĭcus, a, um, adj., = συντηκτικός, ill of consumption, consumptive, syntectic, Plin.

syntexis.full: syntēxis, is, f., = σύντηξις (a melting away of strength), a decline, consumption, Plin. 22, 25, 61, § 120; Cael. Aur. Tard. 3, 7, 90; Theod. Prisc. 2, 1.
syntexis.short: syntēxis, is, f., = σύντηξις (a melting away of strength), a decline, consumption, Plin.

synthema.full: synthē^ma, ătis, n., = σύνθημα or σύνθεμα (a token agreed upon), a passport, Hier. Ep. 118, 1.
synthema.short: synthē^ma, ătis, n., = σύνθημα or σύνθεμα (a token agreed upon), a passport, Hier.

synthesinus.full: synthĕsĭnus, a, um, adj., = συνθέσινος, pertaining to a dressing-gown: vestis, i. e. a dressing-gown, Suet. Ner. 51 (v. the commentators ad loc.).
synthesinus.short: synthĕsĭnus, a, um, adj., = συνθέσινος, pertaining to a dressing-gown: vestis, i.

synthesis.full: synthĕsis, is, f., = σύνθεσις (a putting together). In medicine, a mixture, compound, Ser. Samm. 30, 578; 61, 1069. — A set or service of plate, Mart. 4, 46, 15; Stat. S. 4, 9, 44.— Lit., a set of wearing-apparel, suit of clothes, Dig. 34, 2, 39; Mart. 2, 46, 4.— Transf., a kind of loose, easy garment worn at table, a loose gown, dressing-gown, Mart. 5, 79, 2; 1, 1, 1 (Suet. Ner. 52: synthesina vestis); cf. Becker, Antiq. vol. 3, p. 124 sq.
synthesis.short: synthĕsis, is, f., = σύνθεσις (a putting together).

syntonum.full: syntŏnum (-non), i, n., = σύντονον (accordant, harmonious), a kind of musical instrument: syntonorum modis saltitantes, Quint. 9, 4, 142 Spald.
syntonum.short: syntŏnum (-non), i, n., = σύντονον (accordant, harmonious), a kind of musical instrument: syntonorum modis saltitantes, Quint.

syntrophium.full: syntrŏphĭum, ii, n., = συντρόφιον, a bramble-bush, App. Herb. 87.
syntrophium.short: syntrŏphĭum, ii, n., = συντρόφιον, a bramble-bush, App.

syntrophus.full: syntrŏphus, i, m., = σύντροφος, that has been brought up with another, Tert. adv. Valent. 8.
syntrophus.short: syntrŏphus, i, m., = σύντροφος, that has been brought up with another, Tert.

syphax.full: Sўphax, ācis (acc. scanned Sўphăcēn, Claud. B. Gild. 90), m., = Σύφαξ, a king of Numidia at the time of the second Punic war, Sall. J. 5, 4; Liv. 24, 48 sq.; 29, 23 sq.; 30, 5 sq.; Sil. 17, 62 sq.; Prop. 3, 11 (4, 10), 59; Ov. F. 6, 769; Juv. 6, 169 al.

sypheum.full: Syphēum, i, n., a town of the Bruttii, now Montalto, Liv. 30, 19.
sypheum.short: Syphēum, i, n., a town of the Bruttii, now Montalto, Liv.

syra.full: Syra, ae, f., the name of a slave, Plaut. Merc. 4, 5, 18; 2, 3, 79.
syra.short: Syra, ae, f., the name of a slave, Plaut.

syracusae.full: Sўrācūsae, ārum (scanned Sўrăcūsae, Aus. Clar. Urb. 10, 1), f., = Συράκουσαι, the city of Syracuse in Sicily, now Siragossa, Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 52, § 115 sqq.; Liv. 24, 3 sq.; Ov. F. 4, 873; Sil. 14, 277; Nep. Timol. 3; Vell. 2, 15; Plin. 3, 8, 14, § 89.—Hence, Sўrācūsānus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Syracuse, Syracusan: lautumiae, Cic. Verr. 2, 5, 27, § 68: conventus, id. ib. 2, 3, 13, § 32: mensae, id. Fin. 2, 28, 92: esne tu Syracusanus? from Syracuse, Plaut. Men. 5, 9, 50. — Subst.: Sўrāc

syrbotae.full: Syrbotae, ārum, m., a people of Ethiopia remarkable for stature, Plin. 6, 30, 35, § 190; 7, 2, 2, § 31.
syrbotae.short: Syrbotae, ārum, m., a people of Ethiopia remarkable for stature, Plin.

syreon.full: syrĕon, i, n., = σύρεον, a plant, called also tordylion, Plin. 24, 19, 117, § 177.
syreon.short: syrĕon, i, n., = σύρεον, a plant, called also tordylion, Plin.

syria.full: Sȳrĭa (also written Sĭrĭa and Sŭ-rĭa), ae, f., = Συρία, a country in Asia, on the Mediterranean Sea, Mel. 1, 11; Plin. 5, 12, 13, § 67; Cic. Div. 1, 41, 91; id. Agr. 2, 29, 80; id. Imp. Pomp. 22, 64; Manil. 4, 622. —Transf., for Assyria, Cic. Tusc. 5, 35, 101; Suet. Caes. 22 Oud.—Plur., Cat. 45, 22; Dig. 48, 22, 7, § 7; 50, 15, 3 proöem.— Hence, Sўrĭus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Syria, Syrian: triticum, Plin. 18, 7, 12, § 63: oleum, id. 23, 4, 49, § 95: pira, Verg. G. 2, 88: ros, i. e. nar
syria.short: Sȳrĭa (also written Sĭrĭa and Sŭ-rĭa), ae, f., = Συρία, a country in Asia, on the Mediterranean Sea, Mel.

syriarcha.full: Sўrĭarcha, ae, m., = Συριάρχης, the chief priest in Syria, Cod. Th. 15, 9, 2; called Sўrĭarchus, Just. Nov. 89, 15.— His office is called Sўrĭarchĭa, ae, f., = Συριαρχία, Cod. Th. 12, 1, 103.
syriarcha.short: Sўrĭarcha, ae, m., = Συριάρχης, the chief priest in Syria, Cod.

syriaticus.full: Sўrĭātĭcus, a, um, v. Syria, E.

syricus.full: Sўrĭcus, a, um, v. Syria, D.

syrie.full: Syrĭē, ēs, f., an island near Ephesus, Plin. 2, 89, 91, § 204; cf. id. 5, 29, 31, § 115.
syrie.short: Syrĭē, ēs, f., an island near Ephesus, Plin.

syringias.full: sȳringĭas, ae, m., = συριγγίας, a kind of reed or cane good for pipes, Plin. 16, 36, 66, § 164.
syringias.short: sȳringĭas, ae, m., = συριγγίας, a kind of reed or cane good for pipes, Plin.

syringitis.full: sȳringītis, ĭdis, f., = συριγγῖτις, an unknown kind of precious stone, Plin. 37, 10, 67, § 182.
syringitis.short: sȳringītis, ĭdis, f., = συριγγῖτις, an unknown kind of precious stone, Plin.

syringnatus.full: sȳringnātus (sȳringiānus), a, um, adj. syrinx, hollowed out like a pipe: haedus, Apic. 8, 6.

syringotomium.full: sȳringŏtŏmĭum, ii, n., = συριγγοτόμιον, a surgical instrument for cutting fistulas, Veg. Vet. 2, 27, 2.
syringotomium.short: sȳringŏtŏmĭum, ii, n., = συριγγοτόμιον, a surgical instrument for cutting fistulas, Veg.

syrinx.full: Sȳrinx, ingis (also Sȳringa, ae, Serv. Verg. E. 2, 31; 10, 26), f., = Σύριγξ. A nymph changed into a reed, Ov. M. 1, 691 sq.— sȳringes, um, f., caverns or subterraneous passages, Amm. 22, 15, 30; 17, 7, 11 al.

syriscus.full: Sўriscus, a, um, v. Syria, F.

syrites.full: sȳrītes, ae, m., = συρίτης, a stone found in the bladder of the wolf, Plin. 11, 37, 83, § 208.
syrites.short: sȳrītes, ae, m., = συρίτης, a stone found in the bladder of the wolf, Plin.

syrius1.full: Sȳrĭus, a, um, v. Syria, A.

syrma.full: syrma, ae, f. (neutr., Juv. 8, 229; Sen. Herc. Fur. 474), = σύρμα. A robe with a train, Sen. Oed. 423; Prud. Psych. 362; worn esp. by trag. actors, Juv. 8, 229; Val. ap. Prisc. p. 679 P.; Sid. poët. Ep. 8, 11.— Transf., tragedy, Mart. 12, 95, 4; 4, 49, 8; Juv. 15, 30.

syrmatae.full: Syrmătae, ārum, m., a people of Asia, Plin. 6, 16, 18, § 48.
syrmatae.short: Syrmătae, ārum, m., a people of Asia, Plin.

syrmaticus.full: syrmătĭcus, a, um, adj., = συρματικός, dragging or trailing along: jumentum, limping, Veg. Vet. 3, 22.
syrmaticus.short: syrmătĭcus, a, um, adj., = συρματικός, dragging or trailing along: jumentum, limping, Veg.

syrnos.full: Syrnos, i, f., an island in the Ægean Sea, one of the Sporades, Plin. 4, 12, 23, § 69.
syrnos.short: Syrnos, i, f., an island in the Ægean Sea, one of the Sporades, Plin.

syron.full: syron, i, n., another name for the plant molon, Plin. 26, 7, 19, § 33.
syron.short: syron, i, n., another name for the plant molon, Plin.

syrophoenix.full: Sўrŏphoenix, īcis, m., = Συροφοίνιξ, a Syrophœnician (on the borders of Syria and Phœnicia), Lucil. ap. Non. 397, 27; Juv. 8, 159 sq.—Hence, Sўrŏphoenissa, ae, f., Hier. in Isa. 5, 23, 12.
syrophoenix.short: Sўrŏphoenix, īcis, m., = Συροφοίνιξ, a Syrophœnician (on the borders of Syria and Phœnicia), Lucil.

syros.full: Sȳros, i, f., = Σῦρος, one of the Cyclades, between Delos and Paros, now Syra, Mel. 2, 7; Plin. 14, 12, 22, § 67; Ov. M. 13, 175.—Hence, Sȳrĭus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Syros, Plin. 33, 12, 56, § 158.
syros.short: Sȳros, i, f., = Σῦρος, one of the Cyclades, between Delos and Paros, now Syra, Mel.

syrtis.full: Syrtis, is (gen. Syrtidos, Luc. 9, 710), f., = Σύρτις, a sand-bank in the sea; esp. on the northern coast of Africa, Syrtis Major, near Cyrenaica, now Gulf of Sidra; and Syrtis minor, near Byzacene, now Gulf of Cabes, Sall. J. 78, 2; Mel. 2, 7; Plin. 5, 4, 4, § 26; Liv. 29, 33; 34, 62; Tib. 3, 4, 91; Prop. 2, 9, 33; Ov. M. 8, 120; Verg. A. 1, 111; 1, 146; 4, 41; Luc. 9, 303; 9, 861; Hor. C. 1, 22, 5; 2, 6, 3; 2, 20, 15; id. Epod. 9, 31; Prud. Apoth. 511.— Trop.: videndum est, ne longe simile sit

syrus1.full: syrus, i, m., a broom, besom, Varr. ap. Non. 46, 10.
syrus1.short: syrus, i, m., a broom, besom, Varr.

syrus2.full: Syrus, a, um, v. Syria, B.

syrus3.full: Sўrus, i, m., the name of a slave, Ter. Ad. 2, 2, 41; id. Heaut. 2, 3, 69.—Of a dog of Actæon, Hyg. Fab. 187.
syrus3.short: Sўrus, i, m., the name of a slave, Ter.

systalticus.full: systaltĭcus, a, um, adj., = συσταλτικός, drawing together: tropi in rhythmopoeia, Mart. Cap. 9, § 994.
systalticus.short: systaltĭcus, a, um, adj., = συσταλτικός, drawing together: tropi in rhythmopoeia, Mart.

systema.full: systēma, ătis, n., = σύστημα, a whole consisting of several parts, a complex whole, a system, Mart. Cap. 9, §§ 947, 953; Fulg. Myth. 3, 9.
systema.short: systēma, ătis, n., = σύστημα, a whole consisting of several parts, a complex whole, a system, Mart.

systylos.full: systȳlos, i, m., = σύστυλος (closecolumned); in architecture, an arrangement of columns at a distance from each other of twice their thickness, a systyle, Vitr. 3, 2.

syzygia.full: sȳzўgĭa, ae, f., = συζυγία (pure Lat. conjugatio), a joining together or conjunction, a syzygy, Tert. Praescr. 46.

t.full: T, t. indecl. n. or (to agree with littera) f., the nineteenth letter of the Lat. alphabet (i and j being counted as one), = Gr. T (ταῦ). It is very freq. as a final letter, esp. in verbal endings of the third person. As an initial, it is, in pure Lat. words, followed by no consonant except r: traho, tremo, tribuo, etc.; the combinations tl and tm are found only in words borrowed from the Greek: Tlepolemus, tmesis, Tmolus. Hence an initial t occurring in the ancient language before l (like an in

tabae.full: Tabae, ārum, f. A town of Caria, on the boundaries of Phrygia, now Damas, Liv. 38, 13, 11.— A city in the inner part of Sicily, Sil. 14, 272.— A city of Parœtacene, between Persis and Media, Curt. 5, 1, 13.

tabanus.full: tăbānus, i, m., a gad-fly, horse-fly, oxfly, breese; called also asilus, Varr. R. R. 2, 5, 14; Plin. 11, 28, 34, § 100; 11, 33, 38, § 113; 30, 11, 30, § 101.
tabanus.short: tăbānus, i, m., a gad-fly, horse-fly, oxfly, breese;

tabefacio.full: tābĕfăcĭo, fēci, 3, v. a. tabes-facio, to melt, dissolve.—Trop.: tabefac audaciam virtutis eorum, Vulg. 1 Macc. 4, 32: vigilia honestatis tabefaciet carnes, subdue, id. Ecclus. 31, 1.—Hence, Part.: tābē^factus, a, um, melted, dissolved (post-class.): tabefactis nivibus, Sol. 2 med.: cadaver in suo sanguine, Vulg. Jud. 14, 14.

tabefio.full: tābĕfīo, factus sum, v. n. irr. dep., to be melted or dissolved (late Lat.), Cassiod. in Psa. 38, 13.

tabella.full: tăbella, ae (nom. plur. TABELAI, S. C. de Bacch. Corp. I. R. 196). f. dim. tabula. In gen., a small board, a little table or tablet (rare and mostly poet. and in post-Aug. prose): liminis, i. e. the door-sill, Cat. 32, 5: tabella aerea, a brass plate, Plin. 33, 1, 6, § 19: hos (libellos) eme, quos artat brevibus membrana tabellis, little tablets, i. e. small pages, Mart. 1, 3, 3: parva tabella capit ternos utrimque lapillos, small gamingboards, Ov. A. A. 3, 365; id. Tr. 2. 481: pistor multiplice

tabellarius.full: tăbellārĭus, a, um, adj. tabella, of or belonging to tablets, i. e., (Acc. to tabella, II.A.) Of or pertaining to writing or to letters. Adj.: naves, vessels to carry letters, packet-boats, Sen. Ep. 77, 1. — Hence, Subst.: tăbellārĭus, ii, m., a lettercarrier, courier: epistulam, quam attulerat Phileros tabellarius, Cic. Fam. 9, 15, 1; 10, 31, 4; 15, 18, 2; id. Phil. 2, 31, 77; id. Prov. Cons. 7, 15; Cass. ap. Cic. Fam. 12, 12, 1; Liv. 45, 1, 6 al.— (Acc. to tabella, II. B.) Of or relating to vo

tabellio.full: tăbellĭo, ōnis, m. tabella, II. A., one who draws up written instruments, such as contracts, wills, etc., a notary, scrivener, Dig. 48, 19, 9; Capitol. Macr. 4; Firm. Math. 4, 5; Cod. Th. 9, 19, 1.

tabeo.full: tābĕo, ēre, v. n. tabes, to melt, melt down or away, to waste away, consume (poet.). Lit.: aliis rebus concrescunt semina membris, Atque aliis extenuantur tabentque vicissim, Lucr. 4, 1262: corpora tabent, Ov. M. 7, 541: tabentes genae, Verg. A. 12, 221: tabens sanies, Stat. Th. 4, 364: sale tabentes artus in litore ponunt, dripping, Verg. A. 1, 173.— Trop., to waste away, vanish: seditio tabetne an numeros augificat suos? Enn. ap. Non. 76, 2 (Trag. v. 105 Vahl.).

taberna.full: tăberna, ae, f. root ta (tan); Gr. τείνω, perf. τέτακα; cf.: tabula, tenus, a hut, shed, booth, stall, shop constructed of boards. Hence, in gen., any slight structure used for a dwelling, a hut or cottage (very rare): tabernae appellatio declarat omne utile ad habitandum aedificium, non ex eo, quod tabulis cluditur, Dig. 50, 16, 183: pauperum tabernae, Hor. C. 1, 4, 13; so, obscurae, id. A. P. 229.—Of stalls in the circus: qui in circo totas tabernas tribulium causā compararunt, Cic. Mur. 35, 7

tabernacularius.full: tăbernācŭlārĭus, ii, m. tabernaculum, a tent-maker, Inscr. Grut. p. 642, 8.

tabernaculum.full: tăbernācŭlum, i, n. taberna, a tent (syn. tentorium): tabernacula dicuntur a similitudine tabernarum, quae ipsae, quod ex tabulis olim fiebant, dictae sunt, non, ut quidam putant, quod tabulis cludantur, Fest. p. 356 Müll.; cf.: unde (sc. a tabernis) et tabernacula sunt dicta, licet ex tentoriis pellibus fiant, id. s. v. contubernales, p. 38 ib. In gen.: tabernaculo in litore posito, Cic. Verr. 2, 5, 33, § 87: in ipso aditu portus tabernacula carbaseis intenta velis collocabat, id. ib. 2, 5, 12,

tabernarius.full: tăbernārĭus, a, um, adj. id., of or belonging to booths or shops, used to denote any thing low, common: blanditiae, App. Mag. p. 229, 3: fabulae, a low kind of comedy, Diom. p. 487 P.; Fest. s. v. togatarum, p. 352 Müll. — Hence, subst. tă-bernārĭi, ōrum, m., shopkeepers, small dealers, Inscr. Orell. 1368: opifices et tabernarios atque illam omnem faecem civitatum quid est negotii concitare? Cic. Fl. 8, 18: concitator tabernariorum, id. Dom. 5, 13; (with aquarii) Cael. ap. Cic. Fam. 8, 6, 4. — t

tabernula.full: tăbernŭla (tăbernŏla, Varr. L. L. 5, §§ 47 and 50 Müll.), ae, f. dim. id., a small booth or shop, a little tavern, Suet. Ner. 26; Dig. 5, 1, 19; App. M. 7, p. 190. 30; 9, p. 236, 40; id. Mag. p. 314, 27.— Tă-bernŏla, ae, f., a place in Rome, Varr. l. l.

tabes.full: tābes, is, f. root in Gr. τήκω, ἐτάκην, to melt; suffix as in plebes, pubes, a wasting away, melting, dwindling, consumption corruption, putrefaction; a wasting disease, consumption, decline; plague, pestilence. Lit. (class.; syn. lues): aegritudo (habet) tabem, cruciatum, afflictationem, foeditatem, Cic. Tusc. 3, 13, 27: fames lenta nos consumit tabe, Plin. 2, 63, 63, § 156: atrox hiems seu parum provisi commeatus et orta ex utroque tabes, Tac. A. 12, 50: orta per Aegyptum, id. H. 5, 3: per tab

tabesco.full: tābesco, bŭi, 3, v. inch. n. [tabes], to melt gradually, to be dissolved or consumed; to waste, pine, or dwindle away; to decay, decline, languish (class.). Lit.: frigoribus durescit umor: et idem vicissim mollitur tepefactus et tabescit calore, Cic. N. D. 2, 10, 26; cf. Lucr. 6, 516; so, nives radiis (solis), id. 6, 964; 3, 581: cerae, Ov. A. A. 2, 89: sal, Cato, R. R. 88, 1; Plin. 31, 8, 44, § 95: calore Corpora, Ov. M. 15, 363.— Trop.: crescere itemque dies licet et tabescere noctes, Lucr. 5,

tabidosus.full: tābĭdōsus, a, um, adj. tabidus, corrupting, putrefying, decaying, Tert. Apol. 13 fin.; id. Pudic. 14 med. (al. tabiosus).

tabidulus.full: tābĭdŭlus, a, um, adj. dim. [id.], consuming: mors, Verg. Cir. 182.

tabidus.full: tābĭdus, a, um, adj. tabeo, melting or wasting away, dissolving, decaying, consuming, putrefying, pining away, languishing (perh. not ante-Aug.). Lit.: nix, Liv. 21, 36: corruptum et tabidum corpus, Suet. Tib. 51: ferae, id. Calig. 26: juvenci, Sen. Oedip. 147: jecur, id. ib. 358: mens, Ov. P. 1, 1, 67: tabidus erro, i. e. pining for love, Calp. Ecl. 3, 50.— Transf., act., wasting, consuming, corrupting, infectious: venenum, Tac. A. 12, 66: vetustas, Ov. P. 4, 8, 49: pestis, Mart. 1, 79, 1: lues

tabificabilis.full: tābĭfĭcābĭlis, e, adj. tabificus, wasting, consuming: letum liberorum, Att. ap. Non. 179, 27 (Trag. Rel. v. 421 Rib.).

tabificatio.full: tābĭfĭcātĭo, ōnis, f. tabifico, decay (late Lat.), Aug. in Psa. 122, 6.

tabifico.full: tābĭfĭco, āre, 1, v. a. tabes-facio, to waste, consume (late Lat.), Cassiod. in Psa. 37, 5; Aug. c. Jul. 5, 15, 54.

tabificus.full: tābĭfĭcus, a, um, adj. id., melting, dissolving, wasting, infectious, corroding: radii (solis), Lucr. 6, 737: venenum lentum atque tabificum, Suet. Tib. 73; so, seps, Luc. 9, 723: aër, id. 5, 911: urina, Plin. 8, 37, 56, § 134: sanies, Sil. 6, 276: caeli vitia, Sen. Oedip. 79: terram edisse his tabificum est, Plin. 8, 10, 10, § 29: tabificae mentis perturbationes, * Cic. Tusc. 4, 16, 36.

tabifluus.full: tābĭflŭus, a, um, adj. tabes-fluo (late Lat.). * Neutr., wasting away, decaying: corpus, Prud. Apoth. 958.—* Act., consuming: morbus, Ven. Vit. S. Mart. 4, 430.

tabis.full: Tabis, is, m., a mountain of Eastern Asia, Plin. 17, 17, 29, § 53; Mel. 3, 7, 1.
tabis.short: Tabis, is, m., a mountain of Eastern Asia, Plin.

tabitudo.full: tābĭtūdo, ĭnis, f. tabidus, consumption, decline: morbo ad tabitudinem redactus, Plin. 22, 25, 61, § 129; Vulg. Ecclus. 28, 7.

tablinum.full: tablīnum, i, v. tabulinum.† † tablisso, āre, v. n., = ταβλίζω, to play dice, acc. to Diom. pp. 417 and 421 P.

tabraca.full: Tābrăca (Thābrăca), ae, f., a town of Numidia, on the Mediterranean Sea, now Tabarkah, Mel. 1, 7; Plin. 5, 3, 2, § 22; Juv. 10, 194; Sil. 3, 256.
tabraca.short: Tābrăca (Thābrăca), ae, f., a town of Numidia, on the Mediterranean Sea, now Tabarkah, Mel.

tabula.full: tăbŭla, ae, f. root ta-, tab; whence also taberna, q. v., a board, plank. In gen.: si tabulam de naufragio stultus arripuerit, Cic. Off. 3, 23, 89; cf. id. Att. 4, 18, 3; Verg. A. 1, 119: laceras tabulas in litore vidi, Ov. M. 11, 428: tabula navis, Juv. 14, 289; Verg. A. 9, 537: inauratae, Plin. 36, 15, 24, § 114: latera (fossarum) cluduntur tabulis, id. 33, 4, 21, § 76: perforatae, Col. 7, 4, 5.—Esp., a board to play on, Ov. de Nuce, 77; Sen. Tranq. An. 14, 7; Juv. 1, 90.— In partic. A writing

tabulamentum.full: tăbŭlāmentum, i, n. tabula, a boarding, flooring, Front. Strat. 1, 7; Inscr. Murat. 587, 1.

tabularis.full: tăbŭlāris, e, adj. tabula, of or relating to boards of wood or plates of metal. Adj. (post-Aug. and very rare): aeris temperatura statuaria eademque tabularia, Plin. 34, 9, 20, § 97: clavus, Petr. 75. — Substt. * tăbŭlārĭa, ĭum, n., plates, Sen. Ira, 3, 19, 1. — * Tabulare palati, the roof of the mouth, Veg. Vet. 2, 11 fin.

tabularius1.full: tăbŭlārĭus, a, um, adj. tabula, II. A., of or belonging to written documents; used only substt. tăbŭlārĭus, ii, m., a keeper of archives, a registrar, a public notary, scrivener, etc., Sen. Ep. 88, 9; Dig. 11, 1, 6 fin.; 50, 4, 18; 50, 13, 1 med.; 43, 5, 3; Inscr. Orell. 2348; 2962; 3246 sq. al.— tăbŭlārĭa, ae, f. A place where records were kept, a record-office (for the more usual tabularium), Claud. Aug. ap. Non. 208, 29.— The office of a registrar or public notary, Cod. Just. 7, 9, 3.— tăbŭlā

tabulatim.full: tăbŭlātim, adv. tabula, II. K., in rows or divisions: disponere genera vitium, Pall. Febr. 9, 11.

tabulatio.full: tăbŭlātĭo, ōnis, f. tabula, a planking or flooring over; a floor or story: ne tela tabulationem perfringerent, Caes. B. C. 2, 9: complures theatrorum ligneorum, Vitr. 5, 5 fin.

tabulatus.full: tăbŭlātus, a, um tabula, boarded, floored. Adj.: transitus, Plin. Ep. 2, 17, 9: gentes quae tabulatis habitant aedificiis, Fest. s. v. adtubernalis, p. 12 Müll.— More freq., Subst. tăbŭlātum, i, n., board-work, a flooring, floor, story (cf. contignatio): turris tabulatorum quattuor, Caes. B. G. 6, 29; cf. Verg. A. 2, 464; 12, 672; Liv. 28, 6, 2: summa tabulata conceperant, ignem, Curt. 4, 3, 4; 8, 10, 26: exstruere, Caes. B. C. 2, 9: fiunt tabulata falaeque, Enn. ap. Non. 114, 7 (Ann. v. 389 Vah
tabulatus.short: tăbŭlātus, a, um tabula, boarded, floored.

tabulinum.full: tăbŭlīnum (also contr. tăblīnum), i, n. id.. A balcony, terrace, or other floored place in the open air: (cenitabant) rure in corte, in urbe in tabulino, Varr. ap. Non. 83, 21.— A place where family records were kept, archives (for the usual tabularium), Vitr. 6, 4; 6, 8; Plin. 35, 2, 2, § 7; cf. Fest. p. 356 Müll.; cf. Becker, Gallus, 2, p. 178 sq. — A picture-gallery, App. Flor. p. 364, 14.

tabum.full: tābum, i, o, um, n. (masc.: tabum fluentem, Sen. Herc. Oet. 520; cf. Charis. p. 19 P.) [tabes]. Lit., corrupt moisture, matter, corruption, putrid gore, etc. (poet. and in post-Aug. prose): saxa spargens tabo, sanie et sanguine atro, Enn. ap. Cic. Pis. 19, 43; id. Tusc. 1, 44, 107 (Trag. v. 414 Vahl.); Verg. A. 3, 29; 3, 626; 8, 487; Ov. M. 2, 760; 6, 646; 14, 190; Hor. Epod. 5, 65; Tac. H. 2, 70.—Gen. tabi, Luc. 6, 547. — * Poet., like sanies, of the liquor of the purple-fish, Stat. S. 1, 2, 12

taburnus.full: Tăburnus, i, m., a small mountainchain south of Caudium, between Samnium and Campania, abounding in olives, now Monte Taburno, Verg. G. 2, 38; Grat. Cyn. 509.
taburnus.short: Tăburnus, i, m., a small mountainchain south of Caudium, between Samnium and Campania, abounding in olives, now Monte Taburno, Verg.

taceo.full: tăcĕo, cŭi, cĭtum, 2, v. n. and a. [etym. dub.; perh. root tak-, tvak-, to be or make quiet, content; Sanscr. tucyati, to satisfy; v. Fick, Vergl. Wört. s. v. § 73; 362]. Neutr., to be silent, i. e. not to speak, to say nothing, hold one's peace (therefore more limited in signif. than silere, to be still, to make no noise): qui dicta loquive tacereve possit, Enn. ap. Gell. 12, 4 (Ann. v. 255 Vahl.); so, tacere ac fabulari, id. ap. Non. 475, 2 (Trag. v. 182 ib.): Ag. Ne obturba ac tace. Mil. Tace

tacite.full: tăcĭtē, adv., v. 1. taceo, P. a. fin.

tacito.full: tăcĭtō = tacite, adv. (very rare): Elissa fugam tacito molitur, Just. 18, 4.

tacitulus.full: tăcĭtŭlus, a, um, adj. dim. [1. tacitus], silent, without speaking (only in the two foll. passages), Varr. ap. Non. 47, 27; 550, 18.

taciturio.full: tăcĭtūrĭo, īre, v. desid. n. [taceo], to desire or try to keep silence: taciturire jam deliberavimus, Sid. Ep. 8, 16.

taciturnitas.full: tăcĭturnĭtas, ātis, f. taciturnus, a being or keeping silent, silence, taciturnity (class.; opp. oratio), Cic. Sest. 18: taciturnitatem alicujus experiri, id. Brut. 65, 231: curiae taciturnitas annua, id. Pis. 14, 32: vocis exspectas contumeliam, cum sis gravissimo judicio taciturnitatis oppressus? id. Cat. 1, 7, 16: taciturnitas testium, id. Rosc. Com. 5, 14: taciturnitas imitatur confessionem, id. Inv. 1, 32, 54: suspitionem mihi majorem tua taciturnitas attulerat, id. Att. 7, 8, 1: taciturnit

taciturnus.full: tăcĭturnus, a, um, adj. 1. tacitus, not talkative, of few words, quiet, still, taciturn, silent, noiseless (mostly poet., but cf. taciturnitas): quia tristem semper, quia taciturnum videbant, * Cic. Sest. 9, 21: silentia, Lucr. 4, 583; Ov. A. A. 2, 505; id. M. 8, 84: obstinatio, Nep. Att. 22: deserta loca et taciturna, Prop. 1, 18, 1: ripa, Hor. C. 3, 29, 24: tineas pasces (liber) taciturnus inertes, silent, i. e. unread, id. Ep. 1, 20, 12: Liris taciturnus amnis, id. C. 1, 31, 8: vestigia, Ov.

tacitus1.full: tăcĭtus, a, um, Part. and P. a. of taceo.

tacitus2.full: Tăcĭtus, i, m. v. taceo, P. a., C., a Roman proper name; esp., Cornelius Tacitus, the greatest Roman historian of the imperial epoch, born between A. D. 50 and A. D. 60; flourished under Trajan, and was a friend of the younger Pliny, Plin. Ep. 2, 1, 6; 2, 11, 2; Sid. Ep. 4, 14; 4, 22.— M. Claudius Tacitus, Roman emperor A. D. 275, Vop. Tac. 1 sqq.; Eutr. 9, 16; Aur. Vict. Caes. 36.

tacompsos.full: Tacompsos (-on), i, f., a town of Ethiopia, upon an island of the Nile, Plin. 6, 29, 35, §§ 178 and 180.
tacompsos.short: Tacompsos (-on), i, f., a town of Ethiopia, upon an island of the Nile, Plin.

tactilis.full: tactĭlis, e, adj. tango, that may be touched, tangible, Lucr. 5, 151.

tactio.full: tactĭo, ōnis, f. id.. Lit., a touching, touch (Plautin.), as a verbal noun with acc.: quid tibi hanc digito tactio est? Plaut. Poen. 5, 5, 29; id. Aul. 3, 2, 9; 4, 10, 14; id. Cas. 2, 6, 56; id. Curc. 5, 2, 27. — * Transf., the sense of touch, feeling: oculorum et tactionum et odorationum et saporum (voluptates), Cic. Tusc. 4, 9, 20.

tactor.full: tactor, ōris, m. id., a toucher (late Lat.), Aug. in Psa. 95, 6.

tactus1.full: tactus, a, um, Part. of tango.

tactus2.full: tactus, ūs, m. tango, a touching, touch, handling (class.). Lit.: salutantum tactu praeterque meantum, Lucr. 1, 318: quae (chordae) ad quemque tactum respondeant, Cic. de Or. 3, 57, 216: leo asper tactu, Hor. C. 3, 2, 11; Verg. A. 2, 683; 7, 618; id. G. 3, 416; 3, 502: tactus Assilientis aquae, Ov. M. 6, 106: tactuque viriles Virgineo removete manus, id. ib. 13, 466; so, viriles, id. ib. 10, 434.—Prov.: membra reformidant mollem quoque saucia tactum, Ov. P. 2, 7, 13.— Transf. Influence, effect,

tader.full: Tader, eris, m., a river in Spain, Plin. 3, 1, 3, § 9; 3, 3, 4, § 19.
tader.short: Tader, eris, m., a river in Spain, Plin.

tadiates.full: Tadĭātes, um, m., an extinct tribe of Central Italy, Plin. 3, 12, 17, § 108.
tadiates.short: Tadĭātes, um, m., an extinct tribe of Central Italy, Plin.

tadinates.full: Tadinātes, um, m., a people of Umbria, Plin. 3, 14, 19 § 114.
tadinates.short: Tadinātes, um, m., a people of Umbria, Plin.

tadius.full: Tadius, ii, m., a painter of the Age of Augustus, Plin. 35, 10, 37, § 116.
tadius.short: Tadius, ii, m., a painter of the Age of Augustus, Plin.

tadu.full: Tadu, f., an island near Meroë in Ethiopia, Plin. 6, 29, 33, § 185 Jan. (al. Tado).
tadu.short: Tadu, f., an island near Meroë in Ethiopia, Plin.

taeda.full: taeda (tēda), ae (gen. taedaï, Lucr. 6, 897), f. etym. dub.; cf. taedet, a resinous species of pine-tree, the pitch-pine tree (syn. fax): Pinus combra, Linn. Lit., Plin. 16, 10, 19, § 44; 16, 11, 21, § 52; 37, 3, 11, § 43; 35, 6, 25, § 41: ceu flamma per taedas equitavit, Hor. C. 4, 4, 43. — Transf. Resinous fir or pine wood, pitch-pine: cupas taedā ac pice refertas incendunt, Caes. B. C. 2, 11; 3, 101: pyrā erectā taedis atque ilice sectā, Verg. A. 4, 505: schedias taedā comburere, Vitr. 7, 10.

taedescit.full: taedescit, ĕre, v. impers. inch. [taedet], it disgusts: quos prius taedescit impudicitiae suae quam pudescit, who are disgusted, Min. Oct. 28 fin.

taedet.full: taedet, dŭit or sum est, 2, v. impers. [perh. root tau-; Sanscr. tu-, to be strong; tiv-, to grow fat; cf. tumeo]. It disgusts, offends, wearies one; I (thou, he, etc.) am disgusted, offended, tired, weary of, I loathe, etc.; with acc. of the person and gen. of the thing; or with inf. (cf. piget): sunt homines, quos libidinis infamiaeque suae neque pudeat neque taedeat, Cic. Verr. 1, 12, 35: eos vitae, id. Att. 5, 16, 2: vos talium civium, id. Fl. 42, 105; cf.: ita me ibi male convivii sermonisq
taedet.short: taedet, dŭit or sum est, 2, v.

taedifer.full: taedĭfer, fĕra, fĕrum, adj. taedafero, torch-bearing: dea, i. e. Ceres, who kindled a pine-torch on Mount Ætna, in order to search for Proserpine, Ov. H. 2, 42.

taedio.full: taedĭo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. n. taedium, to feel loathing or disgust, to be weary (postclass.): neque umquam taediavit, Lampr. Alex. Sev. 29: cor taedians, Tert. adv. Jud. 11 med.: animal taedians, loathing its food, Veg. Vet. 1, 17; 3, 2; 3, 68.

taediose.full: taedĭōsē, adv. taediosus, wearily, tediously, irksomely, App. de Deo Socr. p. 51, 4; cf. Gram. ap. Mai. Auct. Class. 8, p. 3.

taediosus.full: taedĭōsus, a, um, adj. taedium, wearisome, irksome, tedious: sarcina lucis, Firm. Math. 1, 3 fin.

taedium.full: taedĭum, ii, n. taedet, weariness, irksomeness, tediousness; loathing, disgust (not freq. till after the Aug. period; perh. not at all in Cic. or Cæs.). Subject. With gen.: rerum adversarum, Sall. J. 62, 9: belli, Liv. 8, 2, 2: confectus taedio puellae, Auct. B. Alex. 23: taedio curarum fessus, Tac. A. 12, 39: taedium movere sui, id. ib. 13, 2: laboris, Quint. 2, 2, 6; 12, 3, 11: lucis, id. 1, 3, 16: capere taedium vitae, Gell. 7, 18, 11: educationis taedium suscipere libenter, Plin. Ep. 1, 8, 1

taedulum.full: taedŭlum antiqui interdum pro fastidioso; interdum, quod omnibus taedio esset, ponere soliti sunt, Fest. p. 360 Müll.

taenarus.full: Taenărus (-os), i, comm., and Tae-nărum (-on), i, n., = Ταίναρος and Ταίναρον, a promontory and town in Laconia; on the promontory (now Cape Matapan) was a temple of Neptune, and near it a cavern, the fabled entrance to the infernal regions; it was also famous for its black marble, Mel. 2, 3, 8; Plin. 4, 5, 8, § 16; Liv. Andron. ap. Fest. p. 181 Müll. (Trag. Rel. p. 4 Rib.); Sen. Herc. Fur. 662; Luc. 9, 36; Stat. Th. 2, 32 sq.; Tib. 3, 3, 14; Serv. Verg. G. 4, 467.— Poet., for the infernal regio
taenarus.short: Taenărus (-os), i, comm., and Tae-nărum (-on), i, n., = Ταίναρος and Ταίναρον, a promontory and town in Laconia;

taenia.full: taenĭa, ae (abl. plur. taeniis; dissyl., Verg. A. 5, 269), f., = ταινία, a band, ribbon, fillet; a head-band, hair-band, bandeau (syn. vitta). Lit. (only poet.): taenias Graecam vocem sic interpretatur Verrius, ut dicat ornamentum esse laneum capitis honorati, ut sit apud Caecilium in Androgyno: sepulcrum plenum taeniarum, ita ut solet, et alias: dum taeniam, qui volnus vinciret, petit. Ennius in Alexandro: volans de caelo cum coronā et taeniis (Trag. Rel. v. 33 Rib.): Attius in Neoptolemo: (tum

taeniensis.full: taenĭensis, e, v. taenia, II. E.

taeniola.full: taenĭŏla, ae, f. dim. taenia, a little band or ribbon, Col. 11, 3, 23.

taeter.full: taeter (less correctly tēter), tra, trum, adj. perh. from taedet. Physically, offensive, foul, noisome, shocking, hideous, loathsome (class.; syn.: foedus, putidus). Absol.: taetra et immanis belua, Cic. Tusc. 4, 20, 45: odor ex multitudine cadaverum, Caes. B. C. 3, 49: cadavera, Lucr. 2, 415: aut foedā specie taetri turpesque videntur, id. 2, 421: sapor, id. 6, 22: absinthia, id. 1, 936: ulcera, id. 5, 995; 5, 1126; 4, 172; 6, 976: cruor, Verg. A. 10, 727: spiritus, Hor. C. 3, 11, 19; Luc. 1, 6
taeter.short: taeter (less correctly tēter), tra, trum, adj.

taetricitas.full: taetrĭcĭtas (tētr-), ātis, f. taetricus, a grave or serious expression; gravity, seriousness: habitus oris taetricitate decorus, Auct. Pan. ad Pis. 90.

taetricus.full: taetrĭcus (tētr-), a, um, adj. taeter, forbidding, harsh, crabbed, gloomy, sour, stern, severe (perh. not ante-Aug.; cf.: tristis, severus): puella, Ov. A. A. 1, 721: Sabinae, id. Am. 3, 8, 61: taetricus et asper censor udorum, Mart. 12, 70, 4: lector, id. 11, 2, 7: deae, i. e. the Fates, id. 4, 73, 6; 7, 96, 4: taetrica ac tristis disciplina Sabinorum, Liv. 1, 18, 4: animus (ccupled with horridus), Sen. Ep. 36, 3: febres, Mart. 6, 70, 8: tubae, fierce, warlike, id. 7, 80, 2.

taetritudo.full: taetrĭtūdo (tētr-), ĭnis, f. teter, I., loathsomeness, hideousness, Att. ap. Non. 179, 33 (Trag. Rel. v. 556 Rib.).

taetro.full: taetro (tētr-) (perf. and sup. perh. not found), āre, 1, v. a. id., to render foul, Pac. ap. Non. 178, 7 (Trag. Rel. v. 303 Rib.).

tagaste.full: Tagastē, ēs, f., a city in Numidia, south-east of Hippo Regius, the birthplace of St. Augustine, now the ruins of Tagilt, Itin. Anton. p. 44, 6.—Hence, Tagasten-sis, e, adj., of Tagaste: oppidum, Plin. 5, 4, 4, § 30: municeps, Aug. Conf. 2, 3.
tagaste.short: Tagastē, ēs, f., a city in Numidia, south-east of Hippo Regius, the birthplace of St.

tagax.full: tăgax, ācis, adj. tago, that is apt to touch any thing; pregn., light - fingered, thievish (very rare): tagax furunculus a tangendo, Fest. p. 359 Müll.; cf. Non. 408, 33: manus, Lucil. ap. Fest. l. l. (Sat. Fragm. 30; 86): levis, libidinosus, tagax, * Cic. Att. 6, 3, 1.

tages.full: Tăges, is, m., an Etrurian divinity, grandson of Jupiter; he sprang from the ploughed earth in the form of a boy, and taught the Etrurians the art of divination, Cic. Div. 2, 23, 50; Ov. M. 15, 558; Amm. 21, 1, 10; Stat. S. 5, 2, 1; Luc. 1, 637; Col. 10, 345; Serv. ad Verg. A. 8, 398; Censor. de Die Nat. 4.—Hence, Tăgētĭcus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Tages: sacra, Carmin. ap. Macr. S. 5, 19 med.
tages.short: Tăges, is, m., an Etrurian divinity, grandson of Jupiter;

tagrus.full: Tagrus, i, m., a mountain in Lusitania, Varr. R. R. 2, 1, 19.
tagrus.short: Tagrus, i, m., a mountain in Lusitania, Varr.

tagus.full: Tăgus, i, m., a river in Lusitania, celebrated for its golden sands, now Tajo or Tagus, Liv. 21, 5, 8; Mel. 3, 1, 6; Plin. 4, 22, 35, § 115; Ov. Am. 1, 15, 34; id. M. 2, 251; Luc. 7, 755; Sil. 1, 155; 16, 559; Mart. 1, 50, 15; 10, 96, 3.
tagus.short: Tăgus, i, m., a river in Lusitania, celebrated for its golden sands, now Tajo or Tagus, Liv.

talabarrio.full: talabarrĭo, ōnis, and talabarrĭ-unculus, i, dim., collat. form used by Laberius; words of unknown meaning, Gell. 16, 7, 6.
talabarrio.short: talabarrĭo, ōnis, and talabarrĭ-unculus, i, dim., collat.

talaria.full: tālārĭa, ĭum, v. talaris, I. B.

talaris.full: tālāris, e, adj. talus. Of or belonging to the ankles. Adj.: tunica, i. e. reaching to the ankles, long, Cic. Verr. 2, 5, 13, § 31; 2, 5, 33, § 86; id. Cat. 2, 10, 22; Lact. 4, 14, 8; Vulg. Gen. 37, 23.— Subst.: tā-lārĭa, ĭum, n. * The ankles or parts about the ankles, Sen. Ep. 53, 7.— (Sc. calceamenta.) Winged shoes or sandals fastened to the ankles.—Of Mercury, Verg. A. 4, 239; Ov. M. 2, 736.—Of Perseus, Ov. M. 4, 667; 4, 730.—Of the fifth Minerva: cui pinnarum talaria adfigunt, Cic. N. D. 3,

talarius.full: tālārĭus, a, um, adj. talus, II., of or belonging to dice: ludus, Cic. Off. 1, 42, 150: consessus in ludo talario, a gaming-house for dice-playing, id. Att. 1, 16, 3: lex, relating to dice-playing, Plaut. Mil. 2, 2, 9 (dub.; Ritschl, alearia).

talasio.full: Tălasĭo (Tălassĭo), ōnis, or Tă-lassĭus (Thăl-), ii, m., a congratulatory exclamation to a bride, in use from the time of Romulus, like the Gr. Ὑμὴν ὦ ὑμέναιε. Its meaning was unknown to the ancient writers themselves, but it was probably the name of the god of marriage, Liv. 1, 9, 12; Serv. Verg. A. 1, 651; Fest. pp. 351 and 350 Müll.; Cat. 61, 134; Mart. 1, 36, 6; 12, 42, 4; cf. Becker, Gallus, 2, p. 17 (2d ed.).— In mal. part., Mart. 12, 96, 5.
talasio.short: Tălasĭo (Tălassĭo), ōnis, or Tă-lassĭus (Thăl-), ii, m., a congratulatory exclamation to a bride, in use from the time of Romulus, like the Gr.

talaus.full: Tălăus, i, m., = Ταλαός, an Argonaut, the father of Adrastus and Eriphyle, Ov. Ib. 356.—Hence, Tălăīŏnĭdes, ae, m., one sprung from Talaus, the offspring of Talaus, of Adrastus, Stat. Th. 5, 18; 2, 140; of Eriphyle, Ov. A. A. 3, 13.
talaus.short: Tălăus, i, m., = Ταλαός, an Argonaut, the father of Adrastus and Eriphyle, Ov.

talea.full: tālĕa, ae, f., a slender staff, a rod, stick, stake, bar (syn.: virga, stipes). In gen.: taleae pedem longae ferreis hamis infixis totae in terram infodiebantur, Caes. B. G. 7, 73: ferreae, iron rods, used as money by the Britons, id. ib. 5, 12; Plin. 16, 6, 8, § 23. — In partic. In agricult., A cutting, set, layer for planting, Cato, R. R. 45; Varr. R. R. 1, 40, 4; Col. 4, 31, 2; 4, 33, 4; Pall. Mart. 10, 11; Plin. 17, 10, 11, § 61. — * Transf., a scion, twig, sprig, Ser. Samm. 12, 167.— In arc
talea.short: tālĕa, ae, f., a slender staff, a rod, stick, stake, bar (syn.: virga, stipes).

talentarius.full: tălentārĭus, a, um, adj. talentum, of or belonging to a talent (in weight): balistae, throwing stones of a talent in weight, Sisenn. ap. Non. 555, 27.

talentum.full: tălentum, i (gen. plur. talentum, Cic. Rab. Post. 8, 21; Liv. 30, 16, 12 et saep.; rarely talentorum, Suet. Caes. 54), n. τάλαντον, a thing weighed, a weight; hence, a talent, i. e., A Grecian weight, varying in different states, usually about half a hundred-weight (very rare): auri eborisque talenta, Verg. A. 11, 333: thynni, Plin. 9, 15, 17, § 44: turis, id. 12, 17, 40, § 80.— A sum of money, likewise varying in amount. The Attic talent, which is most usually meant, contained sixty minæ, i. e.

taleola.full: tālĕŏla, ae, f. dim. talea, a small slip, shoot, or set for planting, Col. 3, 17, 1; 12, 33, 1; 12, 48, 2.

talge.full: Talgē, ēs, f., a small island in the Caspian Sea, Mel. 3, 6, 10.
talge.short: Talgē, ēs, f., a small island in the Caspian Sea, Mel.

talio.full: tālĭo, ōnis, f. (masc., Tert. adv. Marc. 4, 16) [talis]; in jurid. lang., a punishment similar and equal to the injury sustained, like for like, retaliation in kind: talionis mentionem fieri in XII. ait Verrius hoc modo: si membrum rupit, ni cum eo pacit, talio esto, neque id, quid significet, indicat, puto, quia notum est. Permittit enim lex parem vindictam, Fest. p. 363 Müll.; Cato ap. Prisc. p. 710 P.; Gell. 20, 1, 33 sq.; 20, 1, 38; Cic. ap. Aug. Civ. Dei, 21, 11; Plin. 7, 54, 55, § 187; Ter

talipedo.full: tālĭpĕdo, āre (prop. to walk on the ankles), to be weak in the feet, to totter: talipedare antiqui dicebant pro vacillare pedibus lassitudine, quasi qui trahit pedes, ut talis videatur insistere aut identidem tollere pedes, Fest. p. 359 Müll.

talis.full: tālis, e, adj. demonstr. stem to-, cf. Gr. τηλίκος, such, of such a kind, nature, or quality, such like; with a corresp. qualis, atque, ut, qui, or absol. Ingen. With correlatives. With qualis: talis est quaeque res publica, qualis ejus aut natura aut voluntas, qui illam regit, Cic. Rep. 1, 31, 47: ut facillime, quales simus, tales esse videamur, id. Off. 2, 13, 44: cum esset talis, qualem te esse video, id. Mur. 14, 32; id. Rep. 1, 26, 41: quale solet viscum virere ... Talis erat species, Verg.

taliscumque.full: tālis-cumque, talecumque, adj., of about such a nature, about such, nearly so: quale fuit malum . . . taliacumque, etc., Auct. Priap. 16.
taliscumque.short: tālis-cumque, talecumque, adj., of about such a nature, about such, nearly so: quale fuit malum .

talitrum.full: tālitrum, i, n. perh. from talus, a rap or fillip with the finger: caput talitro vulnerare, Suet. Tib. 68 init.

talla.full: talla, ae, f., a peel or coat of an onion, Lucil. ap. Non. 201, 2; cf.: talla κρομμύου λέπυρον, Gloss. Philox.
talla.short: talla, ae, f., a peel or coat of an onion, Lucil.

talpa.full: talpa, ae, f. (masc., Verg. G. 1, 183) [root scalp-; Gr. σκάλοψ; cf. Lat.: scalpo, scalprum], a mole, Cic. Ac. 2, 25, 81; Plin. 9, 7, 6, § 17; 10, 69, 88, § 191; 30, 5, 12, § 38; Sen. Q. N. 3, 16, 5; Isid. Orig. 12, 3.

talpinus.full: talpīnus, a, um, adj. talpa, like a mole, mole-like: animal, Cassiod. Var. 9, 3.

talpona.full: talpōna, ae, f., a kind of grape-vine, Plin. 14, 3, 4, § 36.
talpona.short: talpōna, ae, f., a kind of grape-vine, Plin.

talthybius.full: Talthўbĭus, i, m., = Ταλθύβιος, a herald of Agamemnon, Plaut. Stich. 2, 1, 33; Ov. H. 3, 9.
talthybius.short: Talthўbĭus, i, m., = Ταλθύβιος, a herald of Agamemnon, Plaut.

talus.full: tālus, i, m. from tax-lus; root tak-, tvak-; cf. Gr. τάσσω, whence taxus; cf. taxillus, the ankle, ankle-bone; of animals, the pastern-bone, knuckle-bone (syn. calx). Lit., Ov. M. 4, 343; Cels. 8, 1 fin.; 8, 7 fin.; 8, 22; Plin. 11, 46, 106, § 253; Ov. M. 8, 808: talum expellere, to dislocate, Mart. 8, 75, 3: extorsisse, Sen. Ben. 5, 24, 1.— Transf. The heel: purpura ad talos demissa, Cic. Clu. 40, 111; Hor. S. 1, 2, 29 and 99; cf. id. ib. 1, 9, 11: talos a vertice pulcher ad imos, id. Ep. 2, 2,

talutatium.full: talutatium, ii, n.; mining t. t., the superficial indication of the presence of gold under the earth: cum ita inventum est in summo caespite, talutatium vocant, si et aurosa tellus subest, Plin. 33, 4, 21, § 67 (Sillig, talutium).

tam.full: tam, adv. orig. acc. fem. of the demonstrative root ta-; cf.: tum, tamen, correlative of quam, so, so much, as. As comparative adverb, demonstrative with correlative quam, introducing comparative clauses of like intensity. As adjunct of adjectives or participles the intensity of which is expressed by a comparative clause, tam ... quam = as ... as; negatively, non (neque, nihil, etc.) tam ... quam = not so ... as. In comparison between two adjj.: tam esse clemens tyrannus quam rex importunus pote

tama.full: tăma, ae, f., a kind of swelling of the feet and legs: tama dicitur, cum labore viae sanguis in crura descendit et tumorem facit, Fest. p. 360 Müll.; Lucil. ap. Fest. l. l.
tama.short: tăma, ae, f., a kind of swelling of the feet and legs: tama dicitur, cum labore viae sanguis in crura descendit et tumorem facit, Fest.

tamarici.full: Tamarici, ōrum, m., a people of Hispania Tarraconensis, on the river Tamaris, Plin. 4, 20, 34, § 111; Mel. 3, 1, 8; cf. Plin. 31, 2, 18, § 23.
tamarici.short: Tamarici, ōrum, m., a people of Hispania Tarraconensis, on the river Tamaris, Plin.

tamarix.full: tămărix, īcis, f., a tamarisk, tamariskshrub, Col. 8, 15, 4; Luc. 9, 916.—Called also tămărīcē, Plin. 13, 21, 37, § 116; 24, 9, 41, § 67; and tămăriscus, Pail. Nov. 8, 1.
tamarix.short: tămărix, īcis, f., a tamarisk, tamariskshrub, Col.

tamasos.full: Tămăsŏs, i, f., = Τάμασος, an ancient city of Cyprus, Plin. 5, 31, 35, § 130.—Hence, Tămăsēus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Tamasus: ager, Ov. M. 10, 644.
tamasos.short: Tămăsŏs, i, f., = Τάμασος, an ancient city of Cyprus, Plin.

tamdiu.full: tam-dĭū (also separately, tam diu; and less correctly, tandiu), adv., so long, for so long a time. With comp.-clause understood (cf. tam, II. B.): quid illaec nunc tam diu intus Remoratur? as long as she does, Plaut. Cas. 4, 3, 10: haud quidquam est quod cupiam tam diu, id. Curc. 1, 3, 15: quid tam intus fuisse te dicam diu? id. Mil. 4, 5, 2: quid illic tam diu restitisti? id. Most. 3, 2, 100: credo ego miseram fuisse Penelopam quae tam diu viro suo caruit, id. Stich. 1, 1, 2: sed quid haec hic

tamen.full: tămen, adv. perh. from tam and en, Corss. Ausspr. 1, 842; but cf. Rib. Lat. Part. p. 27 sqq., notwithstanding, nevertheless, for all that, however, yet, still, etc. In gen. With a corresp. concessive or conditional particle (quamquam, quamvis, etsi, etiamsi, tametsi, licet, si, ut, cum, etc.; tamen stands at the beginning of the clause or after a prominent word; cf.: certe, nihilo minus). With quamquam: verumtamen, quamquam abest a culpā, suspitione tamen non caret, Cic. Rosc. Am. 20, 55: quamqu

tamesis.full: Tămĕsis, is, m., a river in Britain, now the Thames, Caes. B. G. 5, 11; 5, 18.— Called also Tămĕsa, ae, Tac. A. 14, 32.
tamesis.short: Tămĕsis, is, m., a river in Britain, now the Thames, Caes.

tametsi.full: tămetsi, conj. [contr. from tamen etsi, which is freq. written in full, tamenetsi, as Plaut. Mil. 4, 5, 10 sq.; Enn. ap. Cic. de Or. 3, 42, 168, or Ann. v. 512 Vahl.; Pac. ap. Non. 378, 6, or ap. Trag. Rel. p. 68 Rib.; Cic. Fam. 13, 71; Caes. B. G. 5, 34; Cat. 68, 135], notwithstanding that, although, though (class. and freq.). In gen. With indic. (so most freq.): Ca. Da mihi igitur operam. Co. Tametsi non novi, dabo, Plaut. Curc. 2, 2, 9: age, loquere, quid vis, tametsi tibi succenseo, id. Ps.

tamfana.full: Tamfana, ae, f., the name of a deity worshipped by the Marsi, Tac. A. 1, 51.
tamfana.short: Tamfana, ae, f., the name of a deity worshipped by the Marsi, Tac.

tamiacus.full: tămĭăcus, a, um, adj., = ταμιακός, of or belonging to the imperial treasury or fisc. Adj.: praedia, crown-lands, imperial domains, Cod. Just. 11, 68: fundi tamiaci juris, ib. 1, 2.— Subst.: tămĭăcus, i, m., an occupant of crown-lands, Cod. Just. 11, 68, 1.
tamiacus.short: tămĭăcus, a, um, adj., = ταμιακός, of or belonging to the imperial treasury or fisc.

taminare.full: tāmĭnāre violare: hinc contaminare dictum, Fest. p. 363 Müll.
taminare.short: tāmĭnāre violare: hinc contaminare dictum, Fest.

taminia uva.full: taminia uva, a kind of wild grape, Cels. 3, 21; Plin. 23, 1, 13, § 17; cf. Fest. p. 359 Müll.—The vine on which it grew was called tamnus, Col. 10, 373; Plin. 21, 15, 50, § 86.
taminia uva.short: taminia uva, a kind of wild grape, Cels.

tammodo.full: tammŏdo (or in two words, tam mŏdo), adv., a Prænestine provincial form for modo, just now, a moment since, Plaut. Trin. 3, 1, 8 Brix ad loc.; cf.: tammodo antiqui ponebant pro modo, ut Attius, tammodo inquit Praenestinus, Fest. p. 359 Müll.; v. Ritschl ad Plaut. l. l.
tammodo.short: tammŏdo (or in two words, tam mŏdo), adv., a Prænestine provincial form for modo, just now, a moment since, Plaut.

tamphilus.full: Tamphĭlus, i, m., a Roman surname. Cn. Baebius Tamphilus, Liv. 31, 49 fin.; Nep. Hann. 13, 1.— Baebius Tamphilus, Liv. 21, 6.— Hence, Tamphĭlĭānus, a, um, adj., belonging to Tamphilus: domus, Nep. Att. 13, 2.
tamphilus.short: Tamphĭlus, i, m., a Roman surname.

tamquam.full: tam-quam and tanquam, adv., as much as, so as, just as, like as, as if, as it were, so to speak, etc. In gen.: Sa. Esne tu huic amicus? To. Tamquam di omnes, qui caelum colunt, Plaut. Pers. 4, 4, 32: Cu. Serva me. Ph. Tamquam me et genium meum, id. Curc. 5, 2, 29: Ge. Nostin' ejus natum Phaedriam? Da. Tamquam te, Ter. Phorm. 1, 2, 14: quod video tibi etiam novum accidisse tamquam mihi, Cic. Att. 6, 1, 5: tenebrae ibi erant tamquam nox, Plaut. Cas. 5, 2, 8: Si. Quālibet perambula aedes oppido tam
tamquam.short: tam-quam and tanquam, adv., as much as, so as, just as, like as, as if, as it were, so to speak, etc.

tana.full: Tana or Tanas, ae, m., a river of Numidia, between Lares and Capsa, Sall. J. 90 fin.
tana.short: Tana or Tanas, ae, m., a river of Numidia, between Lares and Capsa, Sall.

tanager.full: Tănăger, gri, m., a small river in Lucania, now Negro or Tangro, Verg. G. 3, 151.
tanager.short: Tănăger, gri, m., a small river in Lucania, now Negro or Tangro, Verg.

tanagra.full: Tānā^gra, ae, f., = Τάναγρα, a town of Bœotia, now Grimadha, Cic. Dom. 43, 111; Plin. 4, 7, 12, § 26; Liv. 33, 28; 35, 51. —Hence, Tānā^graeus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Tanagra: meretrix, Cic. Dom. 43, 111: Choroebus, Stat. Th. 9, 745.— Tānā^grĭcus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Tanagra: galli, Varr. R. R. 3, 9, 6; Col. 8, 2, 4 and 13.
tanagra.short: Tānā^gra, ae, f., = Τάναγρα, a town of Bœotia, now Grimadha, Cic.

tanais.full: Tănăis, is, m., = Τάναϊς. The river Tanais, now the Don, Mel. 1, 1, 6; 1, 2, 1; 1, 2, 6 al.; Plin. 4, 12, 24, § 78; 6, 7, 7, § 19; Hor. C. 3, 10, 1; 3, 29, 28; 4, 15, 24 et saep.: Tanaimque nivalem, Verg. G. 4, 517; Liv. 38, 38.—Hence, Tănăītae, ārum, m., the inhabitants of the country near the Don, Plin. 6, 7, 7, § 22; Amm. 31, 3, 1.— Tă-năītis, ĭdis, f., she that lives by the Don, i. e. an Amazon, Sen. Hippol. 399.— A river in Numidia, Sall. J. 90, 2.— Tă-năītĭcus, a, um, adj., of or belonging

tanaquil.full: Tănăquil, īlis, f., the proud, imperious wife of the elder Tarquin, Liv. 1, 34; Plin. 36, 27, 70, § 204.—Hence, as an appellative, for a domineering, ambitious woman, Juv. 6, 566; Aus. Ep. 23, 31.
tanaquil.short: Tănăquil, īlis, f., the proud, imperious wife of the elder Tarquin, Liv.

tandem.full: tandem, adv. tam and the demonstr. termination dem; prop. just so far; hence, transf. to time, after so long, after a long time, implying the end of long delay or expectation, at length, at last, in the end, finally (cf.: denique, postremo). Lit. In gen. Alone: Juppiter tibi summe tandem male re gestā gratulor, Enn. ap. Non. 116, 29 (Trag. v. 242 Vahl.): ne navigarem tandem hoc aetatis senex, Plaut. Bacch. 2, 3, 109: haec illic est pugnata pugna usque a mane ad vesperum ... Sed proelium id tande

tanetum.full: Tanētum or Tannētum, i, n., a village of Upper Italy, now Taneto, Liv. 21, 25; 21, 26; 30, 19.—Hence, Tannētāni (Tanē-), ōrum, m., the inhabitants of Tanetum, Plin. 3, 15, 20, § 116.
tanetum.short: Tanētum or Tannētum, i, n., a village of Upper Italy, now Taneto, Liv.

tanfana.full: Tanfana, a false read. for Tamfana.

tangibilis.full: tangĭbĭlis, e, adj. tango, that may be touched, tangible (post-class.): quae tangibilia sunt manu, Lact. 7, 11, 9; 7, 12, 3; Hier. Ep. 61, 9.

tango.full: tango, tĕtĭgi, tactum, 3 (old collat. form tago, xi, 3: tagit Pacuvius in Teucro: ut ego, si quisquam me tagit. Et tagam idem in Hermiona: aut non cernam, nisi tagam: sine dubio antiquā consuetudine usurpavit. Nam nunc ea sine praepositionibus non dicuntur, ut contigit, attigit, Fest. p. 356 Müll.: PELLEX ARAM IVNONIS NE TANGITO, Lex Numae ap. Fest. p. 222 ib.: sed o Petruelle, ne meum taxis librum, Varr. ap. Non. 176, 18, and 180, 8), v. a. root tag-; Gr. τε-ταγ-ών, grasping; τῆ, take; Lat. tag

taniacae.full: tanĭăcae, ārum, f., long strips of pork, Varr. R. R. 2, 4, 10.
taniacae.short: tanĭăcae, ārum, f., long strips of pork, Varr.

tanos.full: tanos, i, m., a precious stone, otherwise unknown, Plin. 37, 5, 19, § 74.
tanos.short: tanos, i, m., a precious stone, otherwise unknown, Plin.

tantalus.full: Tantălus (-los), i (Greek collat. form of dat. Tantaleo, after the form Τανταλεύς), m., = Τάνταλος, a king of Phrygia, son of Jupiter, and father of Pelops and Niobe. He was admitted by Jupiter to the feasts of the gods; but, having disclosed their secrets, he was sent for punishment to the infernal regions, where he stood up to his chin in water under an overhanging fruittree, both of which retreated whenever he attempted to satisfy the hunger and thirst that tormented him. A rock also hung ove

tantillus.full: tantillus, a, um, adj. dim. [tantulus], so little, so small; in neutr. subst., so little a thing, such a little thing (mostly anteclass.; not in Cic.). With correl.-clause: febrem tantillam esse, ut, etc., Cels. 2, 8: tantillum loci, ubi catellus cubet, id mihi sat est loci, Plaut. Stich. 4, 2, 40: si hercle tantillum peccassis, etc., id. Rud. 4, 4, 106.— Absol.: quem ego modo puerum tantillum in manibus gestavi meis, * Ter. Ad. 4, 2, 24: monstrum mulieris! tantilla tanta verba funditat, Plaut.

tantisper.full: tantis-per, adv. tantus, for so long a time, so long; in the mean time, meanwhile. With dum (class.): ego hic tantisper, dum exis, te opperiar foris, Plaut. Most. 3, 1, 153: meretrix tantisper blanditur, dum illud, quod rapiat, videt, id. Men. 1, 3, 11: tantisper volo, Dum facies, Ter. Heaut. 1, 1, 54: ut ibi esset tantisper, dum culeus compararetur, Cic. Inv. 2, 50, 149: latendum tantisper ibidem, dum defervescat haec gratulatio, id. Fam. 9, 2, 4.— With quoad (post-class.): ut viveret tantisper

tantulus.full: tantŭlus, a, um, adj. dim. [tantus], so little, so small; in neutr. subst., so little, such a trifle, ever so little (class.; a favorite word with Cic.): non tantulum Usquam intermittit tempus, quin eum nominet, Plaut. Bacch. 2, 2, 31: omitto vim, quae ex fici tantulo grano ... tantos truncos ramosque procreet, Cic. Sen. 15, 52: homines tantulae staturae, Caes. B. G. 2, 30 fin.: tantularum rerum occupationes, id. ib. 4, 22: tantulo spatio interjecto, id. ib. 7, 19: tantula causa, Cic. Att. 4, 8,

tantummodo.full: tantummŏdo, v. tantus, II. B. b.

tantus.full: tantus, a, um, adj. perh. for tavantus; cf. Sanscr. tāvant, so great; Gr. τέως, i. e. τεϝως. Of such size or measure, so great in amount, extent, value, degree, etc. (as some standard expressed or understood); usually with a foll. quantus, ut, qui, or absol.; rarely quam. With quantus: nullam (contionem) umquam vidi tantam, quanta nunc vestrum est, Cic. Phil. 6, 7, 18: quae tanta sunt in hoc uno, quanta in omnibus reliquis imperatoribus, id. Imp. Pomp. 11, 29: est alienum tanto viro, quantus es

tantusdem.full: tantus-dem, tantădem, tantundem, adj., just so great or large, as great (as an adj. rare, but freq. and class. in the neutr. as a subst.). Adj.: malo bene facere tantundem est periculum, Quantum bono male facere, Plaut. Poen. 3, 3, 20: cum ita legatum esset: Titia uxor mea tantandem partem habeat, quantulam unus heres, Dig. 32, 1, 29: quia forte tantandem pecuniam Titio debuit, ib. 2, 14, 30; so, si postea tantandem summam a domino mutuatus sit, ib. 15, 3, 10 fin.: tantidem ponderis petitio est,
tantusdem.short: tantus-dem, tantădem, tantundem, adj., just so great or large, as great (as an adj.

tanusius.full: Tanūsius, ii, m., the name of a Roman gens: Tanusiorum capita demere, Q. Cic. Pet. Cons. 2, 9.— Esp.: Tanusius Geminus, a Latin historian: annales Tanusii scis quam ponderosi sint, Sen. Ep. 93, 11; Suet. Caes. 9.
tanusius.short: Tanūsius, ii, m., the name of a Roman gens: Tanusiorum capita demere, Q.

taos.full: tăos, i, m., = ταώς, a kind of precious stone of the colors of the peacock, otherwise unknown, Plin. 37, 11, 72, § 187.
taos.short: tăos, i, m., = ταώς, a kind of precious stone of the colors of the peacock, otherwise unknown, Plin.

tapanta.full: tăpanta = τὰ πάντα, all things, all: in caelum abiit et Trimalchionis tapanta est, the all in all, Petr. 37.
tapanta.short: tăpanta = τὰ πάντα, all things, all: in caelum abiit et Trimalchionis tapanta est, the all in all, Petr.

tapete.full: tăpēte, is, n. (sing. acc. m. tapeta fulgentem, Sil. 4, 270; plur. tapetia, Plaut. Ps. 1, 2, 14; id. Stich. 2, 2, 54; Vulg. 2 Reg. 17, 28; but nom. tapeta, from unused tapetum, Lucil. ap. Prob. p. 130: tapetae, Enn. ap. Fest. p. 351 Müll.; Placid. Gloss.; acc. m. tapetas pulcros, Verg. A. 9, 358; abl. tapetibus, id. ib. 9, 325; Liv. 40, 24, 7; Ov. M. 13, 638; Varr ap. Non. 542, 15: tapetis, Verg. A. 7, 277 Serv. ad loc.; Mart. 14, 147, 1; cf. the Gr. forms from τάπης, and v. Neue, Formenl. 2, 57

taphrae.full: Taphrae, ārum, f., = Τάφραι. The isthmus of the Tauric Chersonese, Mel. 2, 1; Plin. 4, 12, 26, § 87.— A town upon this isthmus, Plin. 4, 12, 26, § 85.

tapinoma.full: tăpīnōma, ătis, n., = ταπείνωμα, a low or humble expression, Sid. Ep. 4, 3.
tapinoma.short: tăpīnōma, ătis, n., = ταπείνωμα, a low or humble expression, Sid.

tapinosis.full: tăpīnōsis, is, f., = ταπείνωσις, a depreciation, Serv. ad Verg. A. 1, 118.
tapinosis.short: tăpīnōsis, is, f., = ταπείνωσις, a depreciation, Serv.

taposiris.full: Taposiris, is, f., a town in Egypt, Plin. 27, 7, 29, § 53; 32, 9, 31, § 100.
taposiris.short: Taposiris, is, f., a town in Egypt, Plin.

tappulus.full: Tappŭlus, i, m., a Roman cognomen: L. Villius Tappulus, Liv. 31, 49 fin.
tappulus.short: Tappŭlus, i, m., a Roman cognomen: L.

taprobane.full: Tāprŏbănē, ēs, f., = Ταπροβάνη, an island in the Indian Ocean, now Ceylon, Mel. 3, 7, 7; Plin. 6, 22, 24, § 81; Ov. P. 1, 5, 80; Avien. Perieg. 777.—Also written Tā-prŏbăna, App. de Mundo, p. 60, 16.
taprobane.short: Tāprŏbănē, ēs, f., = Ταπροβάνη, an island in the Indian Ocean, now Ceylon, Mel.

tapullam.full: tapullam legem convivalem ficto nomine conscripsit jocoso carmine Valerius Valentinus, cujus meminit Lucilius hoc modo: tapullam rident legem congerrae optimi, Fest. p. 363 Müll.
tapullam.short: tapullam legem convivalem ficto nomine conscripsit jocoso carmine Valerius Valentinus, cujus meminit Lucilius hoc modo: tapullam rident legem congerrae optimi, Fest.

tarandrus.full: tărandrus, i, m., an animal found in northern countries; acc. to Cuvier, the reindeer, Plin. 8, 34, 52, § 124; Sol. 30 med.
tarandrus.short: tărandrus, i, m., an animal found in northern countries;

taranis.full: Tărănis, is, m., the name of Jupiter among the Gauls, Luc. 1, 446; and so perh. TANARVS, Inscr. Orell. 2054.
taranis.short: Tărănis, is, m., the name of Jupiter among the Gauls, Luc.

taranucnus.full: Taranucnus, i, m., the name of a German deity, Inscr. Orell. 2055 sq.; Cod. Inscr. 50 Steiner.
taranucnus.short: Taranucnus, i, m., the name of a German deity, Inscr.

taras.full: Tăras, antis, m., = Τάρας. A son of Neptune, and founder of the city of Tarentum, Stat. S. 1, 1, 103.— The city of Tarentum, Luc. 5, 376.

taratalla.full: Tărătalla, a humorous name of a cook, taken from Homer (Il. 1, 465): Μίστυλλον τʼ ἄρα τʼ ἄλλα: si tibi Mistyllus cocus, Aemiliane, vocatur, Dicetur quare non Taratalla mihi? Mart. 1, 51, 2.
taratalla.short: Tărătalla, a humorous name of a cook, taken from Homer (Il.

taratantara.full: tărătantără, an onomatopee, representing the sound of the tuba: at tuba terribili sonitu taratantara dixit, Enn. ap. Prisc. p. 842 P. (Ann. v. 452 Vahl.).
taratantara.short: tărătantără, an onomatopee, representing the sound of the tuba: at tuba terribili sonitu taratantara dixit, Enn.

tarbelli.full: Tarbelli, ōrum, m., a people in Aquitanian Gaul, extending southwards from Burdigala to the Pyrenees, in the neighborhood of the mod. Dax, Caes. B. G. 3, 27; Plin. 4, 19, 33, § 108; 31, 2, 2, § 4.—Hence, Tarbellus, a, um, adj., Tarbellian: Pyrene, Tib. 1, 7, 9: mater, Aus. Parent. 2, 2. — Tarbellĭus, a, um, adj., Tarbellian: aequor, Luc. 1, 421.— Tar-bellĭcus, a, um, adj., Tarbellian: Aturus, i. e. the river Adour, Aus. Mos. 468: arva, id. Ep. 24, 125: origo, id. Prof. 16, 7.
tarbelli.short: Tarbelli, ōrum, m., a people in Aquitanian Gaul, extending southwards from Burdigala to the Pyrenees, in the neighborhood of the mod.

tarcho.full: Tarcho or Tarchon, ōnis or ontis, m., a noble Etrurian who assisted Æneas against Turnus, Verg. A. 8, 506; 8, 603; 11, 727; Sil. 8, 474.
tarcho.short: Tarcho or Tarchon, ōnis or ontis, m., a noble Etrurian who assisted Æneas against Turnus, Verg.

tarcondimotus.full: Tarcondimotus, i, m., a Cilician prince and faithful ally of the Romans, Cic. Fam. 15, 1, 2.
tarcondimotus.short: Tarcondimotus, i, m., a Cilician prince and faithful ally of the Romans, Cic.

tardabilis.full: tardābĭlis, e, adj. tardo, that renders slow: rigor, Tert. Anim. 43.

tardatio.full: tardātĭo, ōnis, f. id., slowness, sluggishness, Cael. Aur. Tard. 2, 1, 28.

tardesco.full: tardesco, ĕre, v. inch. n., to become slow: tardescit lingua, grows sluggish, hesitates, stammers, Lucr. 3, 479; Tib. 1, 4, 27.

tardicors.full: tardĭcors, cordis, adj. tardus-cor, slow-minded, i. e. of a dull, heavy disposition, stupid, stolid: ingeniosos, tardicordes, fatuos, Aug. Enchir. 103.

tardigemulus.full: tardĭgĕmŭlus (tardĭng-), a, um, adj. tardus-gemo, slow-moaning: tardingemulo senio oppressus, Laev. ap. Gell. 19, 7, 3: tardigenulo, i. e. tardigrado (cf.: tarda trementi Genua labant, Verg. A. 5, 431).

tardigradus.full: tardĭgrădus, a, um, adj. tardusgradior, slow-paced, tardy-paced: quadrupes, Pac. ap. Cic. Div. 2, 64, 133 (Trag. v. 2 Rib.).

tardiloquus.full: tardĭlŏquus, a, um, adj. tardus-loquor, slow-speaking, slow of speech, Sen. Ep. 40, 14.

tardipes.full: tardĭ-pēs, pĕdis, adj. tardus-pes, slowfooted, tardy-footed; hence, poet. transf., limping, halting, an epithet of Vulcan: deus, Cat. 36, 7; and of the same, absol.: quin et Tardipedi sacris jam rite solutis, of slow-foot, tardy-foot, Col. 10, 419.

tarditas.full: tardĭtas, ātis, f. id., slowness, tardiness (class.). Lit., of motion or action: celeritati tarditas, non debilitas (contraria est), Cic. Top. 11, 47: pedum, id. Rab. Perd. 7, 21: cursu corrigam tarditatem tum equis tum quadrigis, id. Q. Fr. 2, 13, 2: vehiculis tarditati, id. Rep. 3, 2, 3: navium, Caes. B. C. 1, 58: onerariae navis, Tac. A. 2, 39: mula effrenis et tarditatis indomitae, Plin. 8, 44, 69, § 171: occasionis, Cic. Phil. 2, 46, 118; cf.: moram et tarditatem afferre bello, id. ib. 5, 9

tardities.full: tardĭtĭes, ēi, f. id., slowness, tardiness (ante-class. form for tarditas): multa amittuntur tarditie et socordiā, Att. ap. Non. 181, 21 (Trag. Rel. v. 278 Rib.).

tarditudo.full: tardĭtūdo, ĭnis, f. id., slowness, tardiness (ante-class. form for tarditas): podagrosi estis ac vicistis cochleam tarditudine, * Plaut. Poen. 3, 1, 29: segnes somno et tarditudine, Att. ap. Non. 181, 20 (Trag. Rel. v. 69 Rib.).

tardiuscule.full: tardĭuscŭlē, adv. tardiusculus, somewhat slowly: venire, M. Aurel. ap. Front. Ep. ad M. Caes. 5, 7.

tardiusculus.full: tardĭuscŭlus, a, um, adj. dim. [tardus], somewhat slow, slowish (ante- and postclass.): mulier, Plaut. Fragm. ap. Non. 198, 26: servus, Ter. Heaut. 3, 2, 4.

tardo.full: tardo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. and n. id.. Act., to make slow, to hinder, delay, retard, impede, prevent (freq. and class.; syn.: remoror, impedio): aut impedire profectionem aut certe tardare, Cic. Fam. 7, 5, 1: cursum, id. Tusc. 1, 31, 75: pedes (alta harena), Ov. H. 10, 20: alas, Hor. C. 2, 17, 25: at non tardatus casu neque territus heros, Verg. A. 5, 453: tardante sagittā Interdum genua impediunt, id. ib. 12, 746: nos Etesiae vehementissime tardarunt, Cic. Att. 6, 8, 4: celeritatem insequendi,

tardor.full: tardor, ōris, m. tardus, slowness (anteclass. form for tarditas): versuum, Varr. ap. Non. 229, 22.

tardus.full: tardus, a, um, adj., slow, not swift, sluggish, tardy (freq. and class.; syn.: lentus, languidus). Lit., of motion or action: velox an tardus sit, Cic. Inv. 1, 24, 35: tardi sumus nos, Plaut. Poen. 3, 1, 66: aetate tardiores, id. ib. 3, 1, 6; cf. id. ib. 1 and 4: fatuus est, insulsus, tardus, stertit noctes et dies, Ter. Eun. 5, 8, 49: redemptor non inertiā aut inopiā tardior fuit, Cic. Div. 2, 21, 47: qualem existimas, qui in adulterio deprehenditur? tardum, id. de Or. 2, 68, 275: nemo erat ade
tardus.short: tardus, a, um, adj., slow, not swift, sluggish, tardy (freq.

tarentum.full: Tărentum, i, n. (poet. collat. form Tărentus, i, m., Sil. 12, 434; Sid. Carm. 5, 430), = Τάρας, a town of Lower Italy, founded by the Spartan Parthenians, now Taranto, Mel. 2, 4, 8; Flor. 1, 18; Cic. Sen. 4, 11 sq.; id. Brut. 18, 72; Hor. C. 3, 5, 56; id. S. 2, 4, 34; Ov. M. 15, 50 al.—Hence, Tărentīnus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Tarentum, Tarentine: juventus, Liv. 24, 13, 2: juvenes, id. 25, 8, 3: sinus, Mel. 2, 4, 8: portus, Plin. 3, 11, 16, § 101: ager, Varr. R. R. 1, 14, 4: lanae, id.

targines.full: Targines, is, m., a river of Magna Graecia, Plin. 3, 10, 15, § 96 (al. Thagines or Thargines).
targines.short: Targines, is, m., a river of Magna Graecia, Plin.

tarichea.full: Tarichēa, ae, f., the sea or lake of Galilee, Plin. 5, 15, 15, § 71.
tarichea.short: Tarichēa, ae, f., the sea or lake of Galilee, Plin.

taricheae.full: Tarichē^ae, ārum, f., a town of Galilee, near Tiberias, now El-Kerak, Cassiod. ap. Cic. Fam. 12, 11, 2.—Called also Tari-chēa or Tarichaea, ae, Plin. 5, 15, 15, § 71; Suet. Tib. 4.
taricheae.short: Tarichē^ae, ārum, f., a town of Galilee, near Tiberias, now El-Kerak, Cassiod.

tarinates.full: Tarinātes, um, m., a people in the Sabine country, Plin. 3, 12, 17, § 107.
tarinates.short: Tarinātes, um, m., a people in the Sabine country, Plin.

tariotae.full: Tariotae, ārum, m., a people of Dalmatia, Plin. 3, 22, 26, § 141.
tariotae.short: Tariotae, ārum, m., a people of Dalmatia, Plin.

tarmes.full: tarmĕs, ĭtis, m. root tero; Gr. τείρω, to bore, a worm that eats wood, a woodworm, Plaut. Most. 3, 2, 140.—Written also termes, Isid. Orig. 12, 5, 10; Serv. Verg. G. 1, 256.

tarnis.full: Tarnis, is, m., a river of Gaul falling into the Garonne, now the Tarn, Aus. in Mos. 465; Plin. 4, 19, 33, § 109; Sid. 24, 44.
tarnis.short: Tarnis, is, m., a river of Gaul falling into the Garonne, now the Tarn, Aus.

tarpeius.full: Tarpēius, i, m.; Tarpēia, ae, f., a Roman proper name; so esp., Sp. Tarpeius, the father of Tarpeia, who opened the citadel to the Sabines, Liv. 1, 11; Val. Max. 9, 6, 1.— Tarpeia, a Roman maiden, who treacherously opened the citadel to the Sabines, and for her reward was killed by the weight of their arms, which they cast upon her, Flor. 1, 1; Aur. Vict. Vir. Ill. 2; cf. Liv. 1, 11, 6 sqq.; Ov. M. 14, 776.—Hence, Tarpēius, a, um, adj., Tarpeian: mons, the Tarpeian Rock, the name of a rock on th

tarpessita.full: tarpessīta, ae, m., = trapezita, q. v.

tarquinii.full: Tarquĭnĭi, ōrum, m., a very ancient and important town of Etruria, now Trachina, Liv. 1, 34; 1, 47; 2, 4; 26, 3; 27, 4; Cic. Rep. 2, 19, 34.—Hence, Tarquĭ-nĭus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Tarquinii, Tarquinian.—As subst.: Tarquĭ-nĭus, ii, m., Tarquin, the name of the fifth king of Rome, who came from Tarquinii, Cic. Rep. 2, 20, 35 sq.; Liv. 1, 34 sq.; and of his descendants, esp. the last Roman king, Cic. Rep. 2, 25, 46; 2, 29, 51; Liv. 1, 46 sq.; Ov. F. 2, 687; Hor. C. 1, 12, 35; id. S. 1,
tarquinii.short: Tarquĭnĭi, ōrum, m., a very ancient and important town of Etruria, now Trachina, Liv.

tarquitius.full: Tarquĭtĭus, ii, m., an Etruscan proper name; so esp. the Etruscan Tarquitius, who wrote on divination, Macr. S. 3, 7, 2; Lact. 1, 10, 2; Plin. ind. libri 2.—Hence, Tar-quĭtĭānus, a, um, adj., of Tarquitius: libri, Amm. 25, 2, 7.
tarquitius.short: Tarquĭtĭus, ii, m., an Etruscan proper name;

tarracina.full: Tarrăcīna (less correctly Terr-), ae, f., = Ταρρακινα and Τραχίνη (cf. Trachas, Ov. M. 15, 717; the first a in Tarracina inserted like the u in Alcumena, Aesculapius, etc.), a town in Latium, formerly called Anxur, now Terracina, Mel. 2, 4 fin.; Plin. 3, 5, 9, § 59; Cic. Att. 7, 5, 3; id. de Or. 2, 59, 240; id. Fam. 7, 23, 3 al.—Also called Tarrăcīnae, ārum, Liv. 4, 59.—Hence, Tarrăcĭnensis (Terr-), e, adj., of or belonging to Tarracina, Tarracinian: Ceparius, Sall. C. 46, 3.—As subst.: Tarră-cĭ
tarracina.short: Tarrăcīna (less correctly Terr-), ae, f., = Ταρρακινα and Τραχίνη (cf.

tarraco.full: Tarrăco or Tarracon, ōnis, f., a town in Spain, now Tarragona, Plin. 3, 3, 4, § 21; Cic. Balb. 11, 28; Liv. 22, 22. — Hence, Tarrăcōnensis, e, adj., of or belonging to Tarraco, Tarraconian: conventus, Liv. 26, 19: colonia, Tac. A. 1, 78: Hispania, Plin. 3, 1, 2, § 6; cf. provincia, id. 3, 1, 3, § 9: vinum, id. 14, 6, 8, § 71.
tarraco.short: Tarrăco or Tarracon, ōnis, f., a town in Spain, now Tarragona, Plin.

tarragenses.full: Tarrăgenses, ĭum, m., a people of Hispania Tarraconensis, Plin. 3, 3, 4, § 24.
tarragenses.short: Tarrăgenses, ĭum, m., a people of Hispania Tarraconensis, Plin.

tarsatica.full: Tarsatica, ae, f., a city of Illyria, Plin. 3, 21, 25, § 140.
tarsatica.short: Tarsatica, ae, f., a city of Illyria, Plin.

tarsus.full: Tarsus, i, f., the capital of Cilicia, now Tersoos, Cic. Fam. 2, 17, 1; id. Att. 5, 20, 3; Luc. 3, 225; Auct. B. Alex. 66. — Hence, Tarsensis, e, adj., of or belonging to Tarsus: pelagus, Col. 8, 16 fin.— Subst.: Tarsenses, ium, m., the inhabitants of Tarsus, Cic. Fam. 12, 13, 4; id. Att. 5, 21, 7.
tarsus.short: Tarsus, i, f., the capital of Cilicia, now Tersoos, Cic.

tartarus1.full: Tartărus or -os, i, m., in plur. (on prosodial grounds): Tartăra, ōrum, n., = Τάρταρος, plur. Τάρταρα, the infernal regions, Tartarus (poet.; in prose, inferi); sing., Lucr. 3, 1012; Verg. A. 6, 577; Hor. C. 3, 7, 17; Stat. S. 2, 7, 116; plur., Lucr. 3, 42; 3, 966; 5, 1126; Verg. A. 4, 243; 6, 135; Hor. C. 1, 28, 10; Ov. M. 1, 113; 5, 371; 5, 423; 10, 21 et saep. al.—Personified: Tartarus pater, i. e. Pluto, Val. Fl. 4, 258.—Hence, Tartărĕus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to the infernal regions,
tartarus1.short: Tartărus or -os, i, m., in plur.

tartarus2.full: Tartărus, i, m., a river of Italy, now Tariaro, Tac. H. 3, 9.
tartarus2.short: Tartărus, i, m., a river of Italy, now Tariaro, Tac.

tartessus.full: Tartessus (Tartēsus), or -os, i, f., a very ancient maritime town of Spain, now El Rocadillo, near S. Roque, Mel. 2, 6, 9; Plin. 3, 1, 3, § 7; Sil. 3, 399; 5, 399.—Hence, Tartessĭus (Tartēsĭus), a, um, adj., of or belonging to Tartessus, Tartessian: litora, Ov. M. 14, 416: stagna, Sil. 10, 538: muraena, Varr. ap. Gell. 7, 16, 5.— Poet. for Spanish: tellus, Sil. 13, 673; 15, 5. —Subst.: Tartessĭi, ōrum, plur., the inhabitants of Tartessus, Plin. 7, 48, 49, § 154.— Tartessĭăcus (Tartēsĭăcus), a, u
tartessus.short: Tartessus (Tartēsus), or -os, i, f., a very ancient maritime town of Spain, now El Rocadillo, near S.

tarusates.full: Tarusātes, ĭum, m., a people of Aquitanian Gaul, Caes. B. G. 3, 23; 3, 27; Plin. 4, 19, 33, § 108.
tarusates.short: Tarusātes, ĭum, m., a people of Aquitanian Gaul, Caes.

tarutius.full: Tarutius, ii, m., a Roman proper name: L. Tarutius Firmanus, a celebrated astrologer, Cic. Div. 2, 47, 98.
tarutius.short: Tarutius, ii, m., a Roman proper name: L.

tasconium.full: tasconĭum, ii, n., a white, clayey kind of earth, Plin. 33, 4, 21, § 69.
tasconium.short: tasconĭum, ii, n., a white, clayey kind of earth, Plin.

tasgetius.full: Tasgetĭus, ii, m., a prince of the Carnutes, Caes. B. G. 5, 25.
tasgetius.short: Tasgetĭus, ii, m., a prince of the Carnutes, Caes.

tasis.full: tăsis, is, f., = τάσις, a straining, tension, exertion: vocis = intentio, Mart. Cap. 9, 939.
tasis.short: tăsis, is, f., = τάσις, a straining, tension, exertion: vocis = intentio, Mart.

tat.full: tăt, interj., an exlamation of surprise, what! strange! Tat! ecquis est? Plaut. Truc. 3, 1, 18; cf. tatae.
tat.short: tăt, interj., an exlamation of surprise, what! strange! Tat! ecquis est? Plaut.

tata.full: tăta, ae, m. Gr. τέττα; Sanscr. tātas, = papa. A name by which young children, speaking imperfectly, call their father, as with us, dad, daddy, Varr. ap. Non. 81, 5; Inscr. Orell. 2813 sq.; 4943.— A bringer up, rearer, analog. to mamma, Mart. 1, 101, 1.

tatae.full: tatae, interj., an exclamation of surprise, so! the deuce! Sa. Fac tu hoc modo. St. At tu hoc modo. Sa. Babae! St. Tatae! Sa. Papae! St. Pax! Plaut. Stich. 5, 5, 31; cf. tat.
tatae.short: tatae, interj., an exclamation of surprise, so! the deuce! Sa.

tatius.full: Tătĭus, ii, m., T., a king of the Sabines, who afterwards reigned jointly with Romulus, Enn. ap. Prisc. p. 947 P. (Ann. v. 113 Vahl.); Cic. Rep. 2, 7, 13; Liv. 1, 10 sq.; Prop. 4 (5), 2, 52. — Hence, Tătĭus, a, um, adj., of Tatius: turma, Prop. 4, 4, 31. — Tătĭenses (sometimes also called, after his praenomen Titus, Titienses), ĭum, m., one of the three Roman centuries of cavalry, Varr. L. L. 5, 9, 17; Cic. Rep. 2, 20, 36; Liv. 1, 13; Aur. Vict. Vir. Ill. 2; Ov. F. 3, 131.
tatius.short: Tătĭus, ii, m., T., a king of the Sabines, who afterwards reigned jointly with Romulus, Enn.

tattaeus.full: Tattaeus, i, m.: sal, the name of a marsh in Phrygia, Plin. 31, 7, 41, § 84; 31, 9, 45, § 99.
tattaeus.short: Tattaeus, i, m.: sal, the name of a marsh in Phrygia, Plin.

tatula.full: tătŭla, ae, m. dim. tata, daddy, Inscr. Donat. 4, 68.

tau1.full: tau, n. indecl., a Celtic word of unknown meaning, Verg. Cat. ap. Quint. 8, 3, 28; cf. Aus. Idyll. 12, 6.

tau2.full: tau, n. indecl., the name of the Greek T, Aus. Idyll. Lit. Monos. 18: et signa tau super frontes virorum gementium, Vulg. Ezech. 9, 4 (al. thau).

taulantii.full: Taulantĭi, ōrum, m., a people of Illyria, Mel. 2, 3, 11; Plin. 3, 22, 26, § 144; Liv. 45, 26, 14.—Hence, Taulantĭus, a, um, adj., Taulantian: incola, Sil. 15, 294; Luc. 6, 16.
taulantii.short: Taulantĭi, ōrum, m., a people of Illyria, Mel.

taum.full: Taum, i, n., an arm of the sea in Britain, now the Firth of Tay, Tac. Agr. 22.
taum.short: Taum, i, n., an arm of the sea in Britain, now the Firth of Tay, Tac.

taunus.full: Taunus, i, m., a mountain range in Western Germany (between Frankfort and Mayence), now called Taunus, or the Höhe, Mel. 3, 3, 3; Tac. A. 1, 56; 12, 28.
taunus.short: Taunus, i, m., a mountain range in Western Germany (between Frankfort and Mayence), now called Taunus, or the Höhe, Mel.

taura.full: taura, ae, f., = ταῦρα, a barren, hybrid cow, a free-martin, Varr. R. R. 2, 5, 6; Col. 6, 22, 1; cf. Fest. pp. 352 and 353.
taura.short: taura, ae, f., = ταῦρα, a barren, hybrid cow, a free-martin, Varr.

taureus.full: taurĕus, a, um, adj. taurus, of a bull or ox, of oxen, taurine (mostly poet.). Adj.: vincla, i. e. taurean bands (a poet. expression to denote glue), Lucr. 6, 1071: terga, bulls' hides, Verg. A. 9, 706; also, meton., for a drum, Ov. F. 4, 342.— Subst.: taurĕa, ae, f. A whip of bull's hide, Juv. 6, 492; Tert. ad Mart. 5.— = taura, Serv. Verg. A. 2, 140.

tauri.full: Tauri, ōrum, m., the Taurians, a Thracian people, living in what is now Crimea, who sacrificed foreigners to Diana, Mel. 2, 1, 11; Cic. Rep. 3, 9, 15; Ov. P. 3, 2, 45.— Hence, Taurĭcus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to the Taurians, Taurian, Tauric: Chersonesus, Plin. 4, 12, 26, § 85: terra, Ov. P. 1, 2, 80: sacra, id. Ib. 386: ara, id. Tr. 4, 4, 63.
tauri.short: Tauri, ōrum, m., the Taurians, a Thracian people, living in what is now Crimea, who sacrificed foreigners to Diana, Mel.

taurianum.full: Taurĭānum, i, n., a town in Bruttia, Mel. 2, 4, 8.
taurianum.short: Taurĭānum, i, n., a town in Bruttia, Mel.

tauricornis.full: taurĭcornis, e, adj. taurus-cornu, bull-horned, tauricornous, an epithet of Jupiter, Prud. στεφ. 10, 222.

taurifer.full: taurĭfer, fĕra, fĕrum, adj. taurusfero, bull-bearing, i. e. bearing, feeding, or supporting bulls: campi, Luc. 1, 473.

tauriformis.full: taurĭformis, e, adj. taurus-forma, bull-shaped, tauriform, an epithet of the river Aufidus, Hor. C. 4, 14, 25.

taurigenus.full: taurĭgĕnus, a, um, adj. taurus-gigno, bull-born, i. e. begotten by or proceeding from a bull, Att. ap. Macr. S. 6, 5 fin. (Trag. Fragm. v. 463 Rib.).

taurii.full: Taurĭi lūdi, games at Rome in the Circus Flaminius, held in honor of the infernal gods, Varr. L. L. 5, § 154 Müll.; Liv. 39, 22; Fest. pp. 350 and 351 Müll.; Serv. Verg. A. 2, 140.—Hence, Taurium aes, quod in ludos Taurios consumitur, Fest. p. 360 Müll.
taurii.short: Taurĭi lūdi, games at Rome in the Circus Flaminius, held in honor of the infernal gods, Varr.

taurini.full: Taurīni, ōrum, m., a people of Northern Italy, near the modern Turin (Augusta Taurinorum), Plin. 3, 17, 21, § 123; Liv. 21, 38 sq.; Tac. H. 2, 66.—Hence, Taurīnus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to the Taurini, Taurine: saltus, Liv. 5, 34: campi, Sil. 3, 646.
taurini.short: Taurīni, ōrum, m., a people of Northern Italy, near the modern Turin (Augusta Taurinorum), Plin.

taurinus1.full: taurīnus, a, um, adj. taurus, of or belonging to bulls or oxen, bull's-, taurine (mostly poet.): vultus (Eridani), Verg. G. 4, 371: frons, Ov.
