termino.full: termĭno, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. terminus, to set bounds to, mark off by boundaries, to bound, limit (class.; syn.: finio, definio). Lit.: terra mare et contra mare terras terminat omnes, Lucr. 1, 1000: fines, Cic. Off. 1, 10, 33; cf.: quorum alter fines vestri imperii non terrae sed caeli regionibus terminaret, id. Cat. 3, 11, 26: locus, quem oleae terminabant, id. Caecin. 8, 22: quo (lituo) regiones vineae terminavit, id. N. D. 2, 3, 9: fana, Liv. 5, 50, 2: stomachus palato extremo atque intimo te

terminus.full: termĭnus, i, m. (collat. form termo, ōnis, Enn. ap. Fest. p. 363 Müll., or Ann. v. 470 and 471 Vahl.; and termen, ĭnis, n., acc. to Varr. L. L. 5, § 21 Müll.; so, (BTERMINA DVO STANT, Inscr. Orell. 3121) [Sanscr. root tar-, overcome; tīrain, shore, edge; Gr. τέρμα, goal; τέρμων, border; cf. trans, in-trare], a boundary-line, boundary, bound, limit (syn.: finis, limes, meta). Lit., of local boundaries: contentio de terminis, Cic. Ac. 2, 43, 132: agrorum, Plin. 18, 2, 2, § 8; Hor. C. 2, 18, 24: te

termiteus.full: termĭtĕus, a, um, adj. termes, of or belonging to an olive-branch: ramus, an olive-branch, Grat. Cyn. 446.

ternarius.full: ternārĭus, a, um, adj. terni, containing or consisting of three, ternary. Adj.: scrobes, i. e. of three feet, Col. 11, 2, 28: numerus, Aus. Idyll. 11 praef. — Subst.: ternārĭus, ii, m., for triens, a third of an as, Pelag. Vet. 16.

terni.full: terni, ae, a, num. distr. adj. [ter]. Lit., three each: ea partes habet novem discretas, ter ternas, Varr. R. R. 2, 1, 12; so, terni ter cyathi, Hor. C. 3, 19, 14: ut in jugera singula ternis medimnis decidere liceret, Cic. Verr. 2, 3, 48, § 114; so id. Balb. 21, 48; Caes. B. G. 3, 15 al.: ternae sunt utriusque partes, Cic. Or. 60, 201: muneraque in naves ternos optare juvencos, Verg. A. 5, 247: ternūm pedum longitudo, Plin. 11, 29, 35, § 103: ternūm digitorum, id. 20, 17, 73, § 190: cubitorum,

ternideni.full: terni-dēni, ae, a, num. distr. adj., thirteen each: ternadena ova subicito aestate totā, Plin. 18, 26, 62, § 231.

ternio.full: ternĭo, ōnis, m. terni, the number three, a ternion, τριάς, Gell. 1, 20, 6; Mart. Cap. 7, § 775; Isid. Orig. 18, 65.

ternox.full: ter-nox, noctis, f., a threefold night: Herculea, in which Hercules was begotten, Stat. Th. 12, 301.
ternox.short: ter-nox, noctis, f., a threefold night: Herculea, in which Hercules was begotten, Stat.

tero.full: tĕro, trīvi, trītum, 3 (perf. terii, acc. to Charis. p. 220 P.; perf. sync. tristi, Cat. 66, 30), v. a. root ter; Gr. τείρω, τρύω, τρίβω, to rub; cf. Lat. tribulare, triticum; akin to τέρην, tender, Lat. teres, to rub, rub to pieces; to bruise, grind, bray, triturate (syn.: frico, tundo, pinso). Lit. (mostly poet. and in post-Aug. prose). In gen.: num me illuc ducis, ubi lapis lapidem terit? (i. e. into a mill), Plaut. As. 1, 1, 16: lacrimulam oculos terendo vix vi exprimere, Ter. Eun. 1, 1, 23:

terpsichore.full: Terpsĭchŏrē, ēs, f., = Τερψιχόρη, the Muse of dancing, Aus. Idyll. 20, 5; hence, in gen., for Muse, poetry: Terpsichoren odit, Juv. 7, 35; Sid. Ep. 8, 16.
terpsichore.short: Terpsĭchŏrē, ēs, f., = Τερψιχόρη, the Muse of dancing, Aus.

terra.full: terra (archaic tera, Varr. L. L. 5, 4, 21), ae (gen. terras, Naev. ap. Prisc. p. 679 P.: terraï, Enn. ap. Charis. p. 7 ib. (Ann. v. 479 Vahl.); Lucr. 1, 212; 1, 251; 2, 1063; 3, 989 et saep.), f. perh. Sanscr. root tarsh-, to be dry, thirsty; Lat. torreo, torris; Germ Durst; Engl. thirst; prop. the dry land, the earth, opp. to the heavens, the sea, the air, etc.; land, ground, soil (cf.: tellus, solum). In gen.: principio terra universa cernatur, locata in mediā sede mundi, solida et globosa et

terralis herba.full: terrālis herba, a plant, also called sisymbrium, water-cresses, App. Herb. 105.
terralis herba.short: terrālis herba, a plant, also called sisymbrium, water-cresses, App.

terrenus.full: terrēnus, a, um, adj. terra. Consisting of earth, earthy, earthen (class.). Adj.: tumulus, Caes. B. G. 1, 43: agger, Verg. A. 11, 850; Suet. Calig. 19: colles, Liv. 38, 20, 1: campus, id. 33, 17, 8: fornax, Ov. M. 7, 107: via, Dig. 43, 11, 1: vasa, Plin. 35, 12, 46, § 160 et saep.—Hence, Subst.. terrēnum, i. n., land, ground, Liv. 23, 19, 14; Col. 2, 2, 1; 3, 11, 8; Plin. 9, 51, 74, § 164. — Of or belonging to the globe or to the earth, earthly, terrestrial, terrene (class.): terrena concretaque

terreo.full: terrĕo, ŭi, ĭtum, 2, v. a. Sanscr. root tras-, trasāmi, tremble; Gr. τρέω, to frighten, affright, put in fear or dread, to alarm, terrify. Lit. (class. and very freq.): nec me ista terrent, Cic. Fam. 2, 16, 4: adversarios, id. de Or. 1, 20, 90: qui urbem totam . . . caede incendiisque terreret, id. Har. Resp. 4, 6: eum hominem istis mortis aut exsilii minis, id. Par. 2, 17: suae malae cogitationes terrent, id. Rosc. Am. 24, 67: maris subita tempestas terret navigantes, id. Tusc. 3, 22, 52: milit

terrestris.full: terrestris, e (nom. masc. terrester, Flor 2, 2, 4; v. infra), adj. terra, of or belonging to the earth or to the land, earth-, land-, terrestrial: erant animantium genera quattuor, quorum unum divinum atque caeleste, alterum pennigerum et aërium, tertium aquatile, terrestre quartum, Cic. Univ. 10: pecudes, Plaut. Ps. 3, 2, 46: admiratio rerum caelestium atque terrestrium, Cic. N. D. 2, 30, 75: in Capitolio, hoc est in terrestri domicilio Jovis, Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 58, § 129: terrestris coepulonus,

terreus.full: terrĕus, a, um, adj. id., of earth, earthen: terrea progenies duris caput extulit arvis, Verg. G. 2, 341 (al. ferrea, Rib.): fossa et terreus agger, a dam or dike of earth, Varr. R. R. 1, 14, 2: murus, id. L. L. 5, § 48 Müll.

terribilis.full: terrĭbĭlis, e, adj. terreo, frightful, dreadful, terrible (class.; syn.: dirus, horribilis, torvus). Lit.: quam terribilis aspectu! Cic. Sest. 8, 19; cf.: jam ipsi urbi terribilis erat, Liv. 44, 10, 6: furiis accensus et irā terribilis, Verg. A. 12, 947: terribilis cunctis et invisus, Suet. Dom. 12: noverca, Ov. M. 1, 147: fera, id. H. 9, 34: tyrannus affatu, Stat. S. 3, 3, 73: visu formae, Verg. A. 6, 277: vultus, Ov. M. 1, 265: squalor Charontis, Verg. A. 6, 299; cf.: incultu, tenebris, odore

terribilitas.full: terrĭbĭlĭtas, ātis, f. terribilis, the quality of inspiring terror, horrible aspect, Jornand, Get. 24.

terricola.full: terrĭcŏla, ae, comm. terra-colo, a dweller upon earth, a terrestrial (ante- and post-class.): terricolae Lamiae, Lucil. ap. Lact. 1, 22: inter terricolas caelicolasque, App. de Deo Socr. 45, 21.

terricrepus.full: terrĭcrĕpus, a, um, adj. terror-crepo, frightfully thundering, Aug. Conf. 8, 2.

terricula.full: terrĭcŭla, ōrum, n. (collat. form ter-rĭcŭla, ae, f.) [terreo], means of exciting terror, a fright, scarecrow, bugbear (very rare; not in Cic. or Cæs.). Neutr.: proinde ista haec tua aufer terricula, Att. ap. Non. 227, 31 (Trag. Fragm. v. 324, 623): nullis minis, nullis terriculis se motos, Liv. 34, 11, 7: sine tribuniciae potestatis terriculis, id. 5, 9, 7.— Fem. (ante- and post-class.): pertimuistis cassam terriculam adversari, Afran. ap. Non. 352, 26 (Com. Fragm. v. 270 Rib.): terriculas tyra

terriculamenta.full: terrĭcŭlāmenta, ōrum, n. terricula, things that excite terror, frights, terrors (post-class.): sepulchrorum, App. Mag. 315, 27: prodigiorum, Sid. Ep. 7, 1.—Sing.: inane terriculamentum bonis hominibus, App. de Deo Socr. p. 50, 16.

terrifagus.full: terrĭfăgus, a, um, adj. terra, φάγω, eating dust (eccl. Lat.): serpens, Jul. ap. Aug. c. Sec. Resp. Jul. 6, 28.

terrificatio.full: terrĭfĭcātĭo, ōnis, f. terrifico, a frightening, terrifying, terror: imaginum, Non. 135, 15.

terrifico.full: terrĭfĭco, āre, v. a. terrificus, to make afraid, to frighten, alarm, terrify (poet. and very rare), Lucr. 1, 134: caecique in nubibus ignes Terrificant animos, Verg. A. 4, 210: viros, Stat. Th. 7, 678.

terrificus.full: terrĭfĭcus, a, um, adj. terreo-facio, that causes terror, frightful, terrific (poet.): (Curetes) cristae, Lucr. 2, 632; 5, 1314: caesaries capitis, Ov. M. 1, 179: vates, Verg. A. 5, 524: sacrum, Val. Fl. 1, 785: vaticinationes, Plin. Ep. 6, 20, 19.

terrigena.full: terrĭgĕna, ae, comm. (neutr. plur. adj.: terrigena animalia, Tert. adv. Marc. 2, 12) [terra-gigno], born of or from the earth, earth-born; a poet. epithet of the first men, Lucr. 5, 1411; 5, 1427; Amm. 19, 8, 11.—Of the men who sprang up from the dragon's teeth which had been sown, Ov. M. 3, 118; 7, 141; id. H. 6, 35; 12, 99, Val. Fl. 7, 505.— Of Typhoeus, Ov. M. 5, 325.—Of the giants, Val. Fl. 2, 18; Sil. 9, 306.—Of the serpent, Sil. 6, 254; Stat. Th. 5, 506.—Of the snail, Poët. ap. Cic. Div. 2

terrigenus.full: terrĭgĕnus, a, um, v. terrigena init.

terriloquus.full: terrĭlŏquus, a, um, adj. terreo-loquor, fear-speaking, fear-inspiring: dicta vatum, Lucr. 1, 103.

terrisonus.full: terrĭsŏnus, a, um, adj. terreo-sono, sounding terribly: stridor venientis Alani, Claud. Laud. Stil. 1, 109.

territio.full: terrĭtĭo, ōnis, f. terreo, a frightening, alarming, terrifying: levis, Dig. 47, 10, 15, § 41.

territo.full: terrĭto, āre, v. freq. a. id., to put in terror, to frighten, affright, alarm, terrify (class., but perh. not in Cic.): aliquem verbis, Plaut. Most. 3, 1, 80: aliquem morte, id. Bacch. 4, 8, 44: pavor territat mentem animi, id. Ep. 1, 1, 4: aliquem territare metu, Caes. B. G. 5, 6: aliquem supplicio, id. ib. 7, 63: audacter territas, humiliter placas, * Auct. Her. 4, 20, 28: alias (civitates) territando ... alias cohortando, Caes B. G. 5, 54: magnas territat urbes, Verg. A. 4, 187; cf. Plaut. Ca

territorialis.full: terrĭtōrĭālis, e, adj. territorium, of or belonging to territory, territorial: termini, Front. Limit. p. 47 Goes.

territorium.full: terrĭtōrĭum, ii, n. terra, the land round a town, a domain, district, territory: colonis locus communis, qui prope oppidum relinquitur, territorium, Varr. L. L. 5, § 21 Müll.; cf.: territorium est universitas agrorum intra fines cujusque civitatis, Dig. 50, 16, 239 fin.: florentis coloniae territorium, Cic. Phil. 2, 40, 102; so, Neapolitanum, Pall. Mart. 10, 16: extra territorium abire, Plin. 29, 6, 34, § 106: territoria earum (civitatum) habitare, Amm. 16, 2, 12.

territus.full: terrĭtus, a, um, Part. of terreo.

terror.full: terror, ōris, m. terreo, great fear, affright, dread, alarm, terror (syn.: pavor, trepidatio, metus). Lit.: definiunt terrorem metum concutientem: ex quo fit, ut pudorem rubor, terrorem pallor et tremor et dentium crepitus consequatur, Cic. Tusc. 4, 8, 19: eadem nos formido timidas terrore impulit, Plaut. Am. 5, 1, 27; cf.: terrorem alicui inicere, Cic. Prov. Cons. 18, 43: ferae, injecto terrore mortis horrescunt, id. Fin. 5, 11, 31: aliquem terrore periculoque mortis repellere, id. Caecin. 12,

terrosus.full: terrōsus, a, um, adj. terra, full of earth, earthy (very rare): harena, Vitr. 2, 4: montes, id. 2, 6 fin.

terrula.full: terrŭla, ae, f. dim. id., a small piece of land, a field (late Lat.): alienae, other men's fields, Cod. Just. 10, 15, 1; 11, 24, 6; cf. Prisc. p. 615 P.

terrulentus.full: terrŭlentus, a, um, adj. terra, of or belonging to the earth, earthly (late Lat.): quod terrulentum ac sordidum, etc., Prud. στεφ. 2, 196: hic (Cain) terrulentis, ille (Abel) vivis fungitur, i. e. fruits of the earth, id. Hamart. 5 praef.—Adv.: terrŭlentē in an earthly manner: quaerere rem spiritalem, Prud. στεφ. 10, 378.

tersus1.full: tersus, a, um, Part. of tergeo.

tersus2.full: tersus, ūs, m. tergeo, a wiping off, cleansing (Appuleian): lintea tersui profer, App. M. 1, p. 113, 2: tersui dentium petere aliquid, i.e. for tooth-powder, id. Mag. p. 277, 2.

tertia.full: Tertia, ae, f., v. tertius, a, um, II. B.

tertiadecimani.full: tertĭa-dĕcĭmāni, ōrum, m. (sc. milites) [tertius], soldiers of the thirteenth legion, Tac. H. 3, 27.

tertianus.full: tertĭānus, a, um, adj. id., of or belonging to the third, tertian. Adj.: tertianae febres, i.e. the tertian fever, Cic. N. D. 3, 10, 24.— Substt. tertĭāna, ae, f. (sc. febris), the tertian fever, Cels. 3, 5; Petr. 17; Plin. 24, 19, 107, § 170: tertianis et quartanis remedium, id. 21, 23, 94, § 166; 22, 25, 72, § 150.— tertĭāni, ōrum, m. (sc. milites), soldiers of the third legion, Tac. A. 13, 38; id. H. 3, 24.

tertiarius.full: tertĭārĭus, a, um, adj. id., containing a third part. Adj.: stannum, that contains one part of white and two of black lead, Plin. 34, 17, 48, § 160. — Subst.: tertĭārĭum, ii, n., a third part, a third, Cato, R. R. 95, 1; Vitr. 4, 7, 5.

tertiatio.full: tertĭātĭo, ōnis, f. tertiatus, a doing a thing the third time; concr., that which is produced by a third operation: miscere tertiationem cum primā pressurā, the oil produced by the third pressure, Col. 12, 52, 11.

terticeps.full: tertĭceps, ĭpis, adj. tertius, the third: mons, the third hill (of Rome), an old formula in Varr. L. L. 5, § 50 Müll.

tertio1.full: tertĭō, adv., v. tertius fin. A.

tertio2.full: tertĭo, no perf., ātum, 1, v. a. tertius, to do for the third time (very rare): jugerum, to plough for the third time, Col. 2, 4, 8: campos, id. 2, 4, 4: colles iterandi tertiandique, id. 2, 4, 9: agrum, Pall. Sept. 1, 1: tertiata verba, thrice repeated, i. e. stammered out, App. M. 5, p. 166 fin.— Hence, for the third time, thrice: verba tertiato et quartato dicere, Cato ap. Serv. Verg. A. 3, 314.—* Part.: tertĭātus, a, um, greater by a third: castra, whose length is one third greater than its

tertiocerius.full: tertĭōcērĭus, ii, m. tertius-cera, a functionary of the third rank, Cod. Just. 12, 21, 1; 12, 24, 7.

tertium.full: tertĭum, adv., v. tertius, B. fin.

tertius.full: tertĭus, a, um, num. ord. adj. [ter], the third. Adj.: vos duo eritis, atque amica tua erit tecum tertia, Plaut. Bacch. 4, 4, 66: tres video sententias ferri: unam, etc. ... alteram, etc. ... tertiam ut, etc., Cic. Lael. 16, 56; cf. Caes. B. G. 1, 1; Varr. R. R. 1, 2, 26: sic disserunt: si quod sit in obscenitate flagitium, id aut in re esse aut in verbo: nihil esse tertium, Cic. Fam. 9, 22, 1; cf. id. Phil. 2, 13, 31: annus, id. Rep. 2, 37, 62: tertio illo anno, id. ib. 3, 32, 44: mancipia veni

tertiusdecimus.full: tertĭus-dĕcĭmus (-dĕcŭmus), a, um, num. ord. adj., the thirteenth: dies, Cels. 3, 4 med.: mense, Col. 6, 36, 2; Plin. 8, 44, 69, § 171: tertiadecuma legio, Tac. A. 1, 37.

tertullianus.full: Tertullĭānus, i, m. Q. Septimius Florens, Tertullian, a learned father of the Church, a native of Carthage, in the first half of the third century of the Christian era, Lact. 5, 1, 23; 5, 4, 3; Isid. 8, 5, 60.— A celebrated jurist under Septimius Severus, Dig. 29, 2, 30, § 6; 28, 5, 3, § 2.

tertus.full: tertus, a, um, Part. of tergeo.

teruncius.full: ter-uncĭus, ii, m. (sc. nummus) [uncia]. Lit., three twelfths of an as, a quarter - as, Varr. L. L. 5, § 174 Müll.; Plin. 33, 3, 13, § 45.— Transf., a trifle: sic in provinciā nos gerimus, ut nullus teruncius insumatur in quemquam, i. q. not a farthing, not a cent, Cic. Att. 5, 17, 2; 6, 2, 4; id. Fam. 2, 17, 4; id. Fin. 3, 14, 45: non jam teruncii faciunt, Plaut. Capt. 3, 1, 17; App. Mag. p. 323, 14.— Of inheritances, the fourth part: Curius fecit palam te (heredem) ex libellā, me ex teruncio,

terveneficus.full: ter-vĕnēfĭcus, i, m., thrice poisoner, i. q. triple-dyed scoundrel, thorough knave, as a term of abuse, Plaut. Bacch. 4, 7, 15.
terveneficus.short: ter-vĕnēfĭcus, i, m., thrice poisoner, i.

tesca.full: tesca (tesqua), ōrum (the sing. v. in foll.), n., rough or wild regions, wastes, deserts: tesqua sive tescua κατάκρημνοι καὶ ῥάχεις καὶ ἔρημοι τόποι, Gloss. Philox.: deserta et tesca loca, Att. ap. Varr. L. L. 7, § 11 Müll.; v. Varr. in loc.: loca aspera, saxea tesca tuor, Cic. poët. ap. Fest. pp. 356 and 357 Müll.; so, deserta et inhospita tesca, Hor. Ep. 1, 14, 19: nemorosa, Luc. 6, 41: remota, App. Flor. p. 358, 22; cf. id. ib. p. 348, 22. Such places were sacred to the gods: loca quaedam agr

tessaracoste.full: tessărăcostē, ēs, f., = τεσσαρακοστή, the fortieth day, Ambros. in Luc. 3, § 16.
tessaracoste.short: tessărăcostē, ēs, f., = τεσσαρακοστή, the fortieth day, Ambros.

tessella.full: tessella, ae, f. dim. tessera, a small square piece of stone, a little cube, for pavements, etc., Sen. Q. N. 6, 31, 2; Juv. 11, 132; Plin. 37, 10, 54, § 144; 17, 16, 26, § 120; Inscr. Oreil. 4316.

tessellarius.full: tessellārĭus, ii, m. tessella, one who makes tessellae, for pavements or for playing, Cod. Th. 13, 4, 2; Inscr. Orell. 4289.

tessellatim.full: tessellātim, adv. id., in a checkered or tesselated form (late Lat.): concidere spathulam porcinam, Apic. 4, 3: incidere pernam, id. 7, 9.

tessellatus.full: tessellātus, a, um, adj. id., of small square stones, checkered, tesselated: pavimenta, Suet. Caes. 46.

tessera.full: tessĕra, ae, f., = τέσσερες, α (lon. for τέσσαρες, α, four), a square, square piece of stone, wood, etc., for various purposes. Most freq., a die for playing, numbered on all the six sides (while the tali, prop. pastern-bones, were marked only on four sides; v. talus; syn. alea): ludere tesseris, Ter. Ad. 4, 7, 21: ut homines ad pilam se aut ad talos aut ad tesseras conferunt, Cic. de Or. 3, 15, 58: tesseras jacere, id. Div. 2, 41, 85; id. Sen. 16, 58: in tesserarum prospero jactu, Liv. 4, 17, 3

tesserarius.full: tessĕrārĭus, a, um, adj. tessera, of or belonging to tesserae. Adj.: ars, the art of dice-playing, Amm. 14, 6, 14; 28, 4, 21.— Subst.: tessĕrārĭus, ii, m. A dice-thrower, dice-player, Amm. 28, 4, 21; Inscr. Grut. 624, 8.— He who receives and distributes the watchword from the commander (v. tessera, II.), Tac. H. 1, 25; Veg. Mil. 2, 7; Inscr. Orell. 3462; 3471; 3480.

tesserula.full: tesserŭla, ae, f. dim. id., a little tessera. * A square bit of stone for paving, Lucil. ap. Cic. Or. 44, 149.—* A votingtablet, = a ballot, Varr. R. R. 3, 5, 18.— A small tally or counter, Gell. 10, 27, 5.—Esp., a ticket for the distribution of corn, Pers. 5, 74.— A die used in play, Gell. 18, 13, 2.

testa.full: testa, ae, f. = tosta, from torreo, a piece of burned clay, a brick, tile, ὄστρακον. Lit., Cic. Dom. 23, 61; Cato, R. R. 18, 7; 18, 110; Varr. R. R. 2, 3, 6; Vitr. 2, 8 fin.; 7, 1; 7, 4; Aus. Parent. 11, 9.— Transf. A piece of baked earthen-ware, an earthen pot, pitcher, jug, urn, etc. (cf. testu): si Prometheus ... a vicinis cum testā ambulans carbunculos corrogaret, Auct. Her. 4, 6, 9: testā cum ardente viderent Scintillare oleum, a lamp, Verg. G. 1, 391: quo semel est imbuta recens, servabit

testabilis.full: testābĭlis, e, adj. testor, that has a right to give testimony, Gell. 6, 7, 2.

testaceus.full: testācĕus (TESTACIVS, Inscr. Orell. 4353), a, um, adj. testa. Consisting of bricks or tiles, brick-, tile-: structura, Vitr. 2, 8 fin.: pavimentum, id., 7, 4, fin.: Col. 1, 6, 13: opus, Plin. Ep. 10, 37, 2; 10, 39, 4: MONVMENTVM, Inscr. Orell. 4354. — Subst.: testācĕum, i, n., a kind of brick, Plin. 36, 23, 55, § 176; Pall. Mai. 11, 3.— Covered with a shell, testaceous: omnia, shell fish, testacea, Plin. 32, 5, 20, § 58; cf. operimentum, id. 11, 37, 55, § 153 (Jahn, testeus).— Brick-colored: gem

testamen.full: testāmen, ĭnis, n. testor, evidence, proof, testimony, Tert. adv. Marc. 3, 99.

testamentalis.full: testāmentālis, e, adj. testamentum, of or belonging to a last will (late Lat.): vox, Jornand. Get. 59.

testamentarius.full: testāmentārĭus, a, um, adj. id., of or belonging to wills, testamentary. Adj.: (lex) Cornelia, Cic. Verr. 2, 1, 42, § 108: adoptio, by will, Plin. 35, 2, 2, § 8: hereditates, Dig. 50, 16, 130.— Subst.: testā-mentārĭus, ii, m. Ingen., one who draws up a will: si testamentarius contra voluntatem testatoris condicionem detraxit. Dig. 28, 5, 9, §§ 3 and 6; 29, 6, 1; 36, 1, 3 fin.— In a bad sense, one who forges a will, Cic. Sest. 17, 39; id. Off. 3, 18, 73.

testamentum.full: testāmentum, i, n. testor, the publication of a last will or testament; a will, testament (cf. codicilli). In gen., Gell. 7 ($3), 12, 1 sqq.: testamentum est voluntatis nostrae justa sententia de eo, quod quis post mortem suam fieri velit, Dig. 28, 1, 1: testamentum legere ... obsignare ... facere, Cic. Mil. 18, 48; Cic. Verr. 2, 1, 43, § 111; cf.: testamenti factio, id. Top. 11, 50: testamenti factionem habere, id. Fam. 7, 21: testamentum conscribere, id. Har. Resp. 20, 42: obsignare, id. Clu.

testatim.full: testātim, adv. testa, like sherds, in bits or fragments (ante-class.): comminuere, Pompon. ap. Non. 178, 25: caput alicui, Inv. ap. Charis. p. 196 P.

testatio.full: testātĭo, ōnis. f. testor. A bearing witness (whether orally or in writing), a giving testimony, attesting, testifying (not in Cic., but cf. testificatio), Dig. 22, 4, 4; 3, 2, 21; 48, 19, 9; 48, 10, 1; Quint. 5, 7, 32; 5, 13, 49; 12, 3, 5 al.— A calling to witness, invoking as witness: inter foederum ruptorum testationem, i.e. during an invocation of the gods as witnesses, Liv. 8, 6, 3 (cf. id. 8, 6, 1).

testator.full: testātor, ōris, m. testor. One who bears witness or testifies to a thing, a witness (very rare), Prud. Cath. 12, 85.— One who makes a will or testament, a testator (the predom. jurid. signif. of the word, but not in Cic.), Dig. 28, 3, 17; 31, 1, 89; Suet. Ner. 17; Lact. 4, 20 al.

testatrix.full: testātrix, īcis, f. testator, II., she that makes a will or testament, a testatrix, Dig. 31, 1, 30; 31, 1, 35; 31, 1, 89 fin.; 36, 3, 18, § 1.

testatus.full: testātus, a, um, Part. and P. a. of testor.

testeus.full: testĕus, a, um, adj. testa, of earthen materials, earthy, earthen (late Lat.): testea terrenaque corpora, Macr. S. 7, 15 med.: indumentum animi (corpus), id. Somn. Scip. 1, 11 fin.: fragmen, Prud. στεφ. 5, 553: vasa, Vulg. Thren. 4, 2.

testiculari.full: testĭcŭlāri est jumentis maribus feminas vel mares feminis admovere, licet alii dicant testilari, Fest. p. 366 Müll. [testiculus; v. 2. testis].
testiculari.short: testĭcŭlāri est jumentis maribus feminas vel mares feminis admovere, licet alii dicant testilari, Fest.

testiculatus.full: testĭcŭlātus, a, um, adj. testiculus, having testicles. Adj.: equi (opp. spadones), Veg. Vet. 4, 7.— Subst.: testĭcŭ-lata, ae, f. (sc. herba), a plant, called also mercurialis and orchion, App. Herb. 82.

testiculus.full: testĭcŭlus, i, m. dim. 2. testis, a testicle. Lit., Auct. Her. 3, 20, 33; Juv. 6, 339; Mart. 3, 24, 5; Cels. 7, 18.— Transf., as a designation of manly vigor, manliness: haec fierent, si testiculi vena ulla paterni Viveret in nobis? Pers. 1, 103.— The name of a plant, App. Herb. 15.

testificatio.full: testĭfĭcātĭo, ōnis, f. testificor, a bearing witness, giving testimony, testifying, testification (Ciceron.; whereas testatio is found in the jurists and in Quint.; v. testatio, I.). Lit.: si ejus rei testificatio tolleretur, Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 42, § 92; 2, 5, 39, § 102.—In plur., Cic. Mur. 24, 49; id. Brut. 80, 277.— Transf., a giving evidence, attestation, proof, evidence: egit causam tuam . . . cum summā testificatione tuorum in se officiorum et amoris erga te sui, Cic. Fam. 1, 1, 2: sempiterna

testificor.full: testĭfĭcor, ātus, 1, v. dep. a. [1. testisfacio].— To bear witness, give evidence, attest, testify (class.; esp. freq. in Cic.; cf. testor). Lit.: haec cum maxime testificaretur, in vincula conjectus est, Cic. Verr. 2, 5, 7, § 17.—With obj.-clause: testificantur illi Quinctium non stitisse, Cic. Quint. 6. 25; testificor, denuntio, ante praedico, nihil M. Antonium, etc., id. Phil. 6, 3, 5; id. de Or. 2, 55, 224; id. Or. 10, 35: licet Te memorem dominae testificere tuae, Ov. A. A. 2, 270.—With rel

testimonialis.full: testĭmōnĭālis, e, adj. testimonium, of, belonging to, or serving for evidence, testimonial (late Lat.). Adj.: comparatio, Tert. adv. Psych. 16 fin.— Subst.: te-stĭmōnĭāles, ĭum, f. (sc. litterae), testimonials, Cod. Th. 7, 20, 12; 7, 21, 4; Veg. Mil. 3, 2.

testimonium.full: testĭmōnĭum, ii, n. testor, witness, evidence, attestation, testimony (oral or written): qui falsas lites falsis testimoniis Petunt, Plaut. Rud. prol. 13: testimonii dictio, Ter. Phorm. 2, 1, 63: quorum egregiam fuisse virtutem testimonio Ciceronis cognoverat, Caes. B. G. 5, 52: testimonium in aliquem dicere, Cic. Rosc. Am. 36, 102; testimonium dicere de conjuratione, id. Sull. 30, 83: testimonium dicere contra deos, id. N. D. 3, 34, 83; cf.: dicere aliquid pro testimonio, Plaut. Poen. 3, 2, 19;

testis1.full: testis, is, comm. (neutr. form: caelum teste vocat, Alcim. 6, 576), one who attests any thing (orally or in writing), a witness (cf. superstes): testes vinctos attines, Plaut. Truc. 4, 3, 63: pluris est oculatus testis unus quam auriti decem, id. ib. 2, 6, 8: deos absentes testes memoras, id. Merc. 3, 4, 42: vosque, dii, testes facio, Liv. 1, 59, 1: deos hominesque se testes facere, id. 34, 11, 8: deūm, quos testes foederum invocabant consules, id. 8, 6, 1: ut manus ad caelum tendens deos testes

testis2.full: testis, is, m., a testicle, Plaut. Mil. 5, 28; 5, 33: dexter asini testis in vino potus, Plin. 28, 19, 80, § 261: testes pecori ad crura decidui, id. 11, 49, 110, § 263; so in plur., Lucil. ap. Non. 235, 5; Hor. S. 1, 2, 45.—In a pun, with 1. testis: quod amas, amato testibus praesentibus, Plaut. Curc. 1, 1, 31: magnis testibus ista res agetur, Auct. Priap. 2: cf. integritatis, Phaedr. 3, 11, 5.
testis2.short: testis, is, m., a testicle, Plaut.

testitrahus.full: testĭtrăhus, a, um, adj. 2. testistraho, that drags his testicles: aries, Laber. ap. Tert. Pall. 1 (Com. Rel. xx. Rib.).

testor.full: testor, ātus, 1, v. a. 1. testis. To be a witness, speak as witness, to bear witness, give evidence, depose, testify, attest any thing. Lit. (very rare, and not in Cic.; cf. testificor): confiteor: testere licet: signate Quirites, thou canst attest it, Ov. P. 4, 15, 11: quasi inclamaret aut testaretur locutus est, Quint. 11, 3, 172.— Transf., in gen., to make known, show, prove, demonstrate; to give to understand, to declare, aver, assert, bear witness to, etc. (class and very freq.): ego quod f

testu.full: testu or testum, i, n. testa, a vessel or lid which was placed over food, etc., to be cooked, and then covered with hot coals, usually of earthenware. Lit.: in foco caldo sub testu coquito leniter, Cato, R. R. 75: sub testu, id. ib. 74; cf.: et fumant testu pressus uterque suo, Ov. F. 5, 510: fimo ovium sub testo calefacto, Plin. 30, 13, 39, § 114: unguito focum, ubi coquas, colfacito bene et testum, Cato, R. R. 76, 2.—Abl. testo, Cato, R. R. 76, 4; 84, 2; Verg. M. 51.— Afterwards of metal: rana

testuatium.full: testŭātĭum, ii, n. testu, a cake baked in an earthen cup, cup-cake, Varr. L. L. 5, § 106 Müll.

testudineatus.full: testūdĭnĕātus and testūdĭnātus, a, um, adj. testudo, II. B., arched, vaulted: tectum, Col. 12, 15; Vitr. 2, 1 med.: cavaedium, id. 6, 3.
testudineatus.short: testūdĭnĕātus and testūdĭnātus, a, um, adj.

testudineus.full: testūdĭnĕus, a, um, adj. testudo, I. and-II., of or belonging to a tortoise; made of tortoise-shell: gradus, a tortoise-pace, snail's pace, Plaut. Aul. 1, 1, 10: lyra, made of or overlaid with tortoise-shell, Prop. 4 (5), 6, 32; Tib. 4, 2, 22: conopeum, Juv. 6, 80: hexaclinon, Mart. 9, 60, 9.—As subst.: cui testudinea legata essent, ei lectos testudineos pedibus inargentatos deberi, Dig. 32, 1, 100, § 4.

testudo.full: testūdo, ĭnis, f. testa, a tortoise. Lit., Pac. ap. Cic. Div. 2, 64, 133; Plin. 9, 10, 12, § 35; 32, 4, 14, § 32; Cic. N. D. 2, 48, 124; 2, 52, 129; Liv. 36, 32, 6; Sen. Ep. 121, 9; Phaedr. 2, 6, 5 al.—Prov.: testudo volat, of any thing impossible, Claud. in Eutr. 1, 352.— Transf., tortoise-shell. Used for overlaying or veneering, Cic. N. D. 2, 57, 144; Verg. G. 2, 463; Ov. M. 2, 737; Mart. 12, 66, 5; Luc. 10, 120; Juv. 14, 308. — From the arched shape of a tortoise-shell. Of any stringed instru

testula.full: testŭla, ae, f. dim. id., a small potsherd. Lit., Col. 11, 3, 3.— Transf. An earthen lamp, Ser. ap. Diom. p. 511 P. — A voting-tablet used by the Athenians, Nep. Arist. 1, 2 (cf. testa, II. C.).

teta.full: teta, ae, f., a kind of dove: columbae, quas vulgus tetas vocat, Serv. Verg. E. 1, 58.
teta.short: teta, ae, f., a kind of dove: columbae, quas vulgus tetas vocat, Serv.

tetanicus.full: tĕtănĭcus, i, m., = τετανικός, one affected with tetanus (cramp in the neck), Plin. 20, 22, 87, § 239; 26, 12, 81, § 130; 32, 10, 41, § 120.
tetanicus.short: tĕtănĭcus, i, m., = τετανικός, one affected with tetanus (cramp in the neck), Plin.

tetanothrum.full: tĕtănōthrum, i, n., = τετάνωθρον, a cosmetic for removing wrinkles (pure Lat. tentipellium), Plin. 32, 7, 24, § 73 (dub.; Jahn, et tetanis).
tetanothrum.short: tĕtănōthrum, i, n., = τετάνωθρον, a cosmetic for removing wrinkles (pure Lat.

tetanus.full: tĕtănus, i, m., = τέτανος, a stiffness or spasm of the neck, tetanus, Plin. 23, 1, 24, § 48; 31, 10, 46, § 122; Scrib. Comp. 101 (in Cels. 4, 3, written as Greek).
tetanus.short: tĕtănus, i, m., = τέτανος, a stiffness or spasm of the neck, tetanus, Plin.

tetartemoria.full: tĕtartēmŏrĭa, ae, f., = τεταρτημοπία, a fourth in music, Mart. Cap. 9, §§ 930 and 959.
tetartemoria.short: tĕtartēmŏrĭa, ae, f., = τεταρτημοπία, a fourth in music, Mart.

tetartemorion.full: tĕtartēmŏrĭon, ii, n., = τεταρτημόριον, a fourth of the zodiac, Plin. 7, 49, 50, § 160; Hyg. Limit. p. 173 Goes.
tetartemorion.short: tĕtartēmŏrĭon, ii, n., = τεταρτημόριον, a fourth of the zodiac, Plin.

tethalassomenon.full: tĕthălassōmĕnon, i, n. (sc. vinum), = τεθαλασσωμένον, wine mixed with sea-water, Plin. 14, 8, 10, § 78.

tethea.full: tēthĕa, ae, f., = τήθεα, a kind of sponge, Plin. 32, 9, 31, § 99; 32, 9, 30, § 42, 32, 10, 39, § 117.
tethea.short: tēthĕa, ae, f., = τήθεα, a kind of sponge, Plin.

tethys.full: Tēthys, ўos, f., = Τηθύς, a sea-goddess, wife of Oceanus, and mother of the seanymphs and river - gods; acc. Tethyn, Ov. F. 5, 81: Tethyos neptes, id. ib. 5, 168; Verg. G. 1, 31; Cat. 64, 29; 66, 70.— Transf., the sea, Ov. M. 2, 69; 2, 509; Luc. 1, 413; Sil. 3, 60; Mart. Spect. 3, 6; Sen. Herc. Fur. 886.
tethys.short: Tēthys, ўos, f., = Τηθύς, a sea-goddess, wife of Oceanus, and mother of the seanymphs and river - gods;

tetrachordos.full: tē^trăchordos, on, adj., = τετράχορδος, ον, having four strings or notes. Adj.: machina, a water-organ, Vitr. 10, 13. — Subst. tē^trăchordon (-dum), i, n., a chord of four notes, a tetrachord. Lit., Vitr. 5, 4; Mart. Cap. 9, §§ 935 and 941; Macr. S. 1, 19 med.— Trop.: anni, i. e. the four seasons, Varr ap. Non. 71, 16.
tetrachordos.short: tē^trăchordos, on, adj., = τετράχορδος, ον, having four strings or notes.

tetracolon.full: tē^trăcōlon, i, n., = τετράκωλον, a period consisting of four members, Sen. Contr. 4, 25 fin.; 5 praef. med.
tetracolon.short: tē^trăcōlon, i, n., = τετράκωλον, a period consisting of four members, Sen.

tetradice.full: tē^trădĭcē, ēs, f., a plant, Plin. 11, 16, 15, § 42.
tetradice.short: tē^trădĭcē, ēs, f., a plant, Plin.

tetradium.full: tē^trădĭum, ii, n., = τετράδιον, the number four, a quaternion, tetrad, Col. 3, 20, 3; Sen. Contr. 5 praef.
tetradium.short: tē^trădĭum, ii, n., = τετράδιον, the number four, a quaternion, tetrad, Col.

tetradoros.full: tē^trădōros, on, adj., = τετράδωρος, ον, of four palms or hand-breadths, Plin. 35, 14, 49, § 170; Vitr. 2, 3.
tetradoros.short: tē^trădōros, on, adj., = τετράδωρος, ον, of four palms or hand-breadths, Plin.

tetradrachmum.full: tē^trădrachmum and tē^trach-mum, i, n., = τετράδραχμον, a silver coin of four drachmas among the Greeks, Cass. ap. Cic. Fam. 12, 13, 4.—Form tetrachmum, Liv 34, 52, 6; 37, 58, 4; 37, 46, 3; 39, 7, 1 Weissenb.
tetradrachmum.short: tē^trădrachmum and tē^trach-mum, i, n., = τετράδραχμον, a silver coin of four drachmas among the Greeks, Cass.

tetragnathius.full: tē^trăgnăthĭus, ii, m., = τετράγναθος (having four jaws), a kind of poisonous spider, Plin. 29, 4, 27, § 87.
tetragnathius.short: tē^trăgnăthĭus, ii, m., = τετράγναθος (having four jaws), a kind of poisonous spider, Plin.

tetragonis.full: Tetragŏnis, ĭdis, f., a town in Asia, near the Caucasus, Plin. 6, 24, 25, § 92.
tetragonis.short: Tetragŏnis, ĭdis, f., a town in Asia, near the Caucasus, Plin.

tetragonum.full: tē^trăgōnum, i, n., = τετράγωνον, a quadrangle, tetragon, Aus. Ecl. de Ratione Puerp. 21 and fin.; Mart. Cap. 6, § 712.
tetragonum.short: tē^trăgōnum, i, n., = τετράγωνον, a quadrangle, tetragon, Aus.

tetralix.full: tē^trălix, ĭcis, f., = τετράλιξ, a plant, heath, = erice, sisara, Plin. 11, 16, 15, § 42 (al. tetradice); 21, 16, 56, § 95.
tetralix.short: tē^trălix, ĭcis, f., = τετράλιξ, a plant, heath, = erice, sisara, Plin.

tetrametrus.full: tē^trămĕtrus, i, m., = τετράμετρος, a verse of four metrical feet, a tetrameter, Ter. Maur. p. 2430 P.; Diom. p. 506 ib. al.
tetrametrus.short: tē^trămĕtrus, i, m., = τετράμετρος, a verse of four metrical feet, a tetrameter, Ter.

tetrans.full: tē^trans, antis (gen. plur., heterocl., tetrantorum, Vitr. 3, 3 med.), m., = τετρᾶς. A fourth part, a quarter: columnarum, Vitr. 4, 2; 4, 3: circini, a quadrant, id. 10, 11.— Among surveyors, the place where two lines meet, Hyg. Limit. pp. 160, 164 and 181 Goes.; Front. Limit. p. 132 al.

tetrao.full: tē^trăo, ōnis, m., = τετράων, a heath-cock, moor-fowl, Plin. 10, 22, 29, § 56; Suet. Calig. 22 med.; Tert. adv. Marc. 1, 13 fin.
tetrao.short: tē^trăo, ōnis, m., = τετράων, a heath-cock, moor-fowl, Plin.

tetrapharmacum.full: tē^trăpharmăcum, i, n., = τετραφάρμακον. A plaster composed of four ingredients, Veg. Vet. 4, 28 med. (in Cels. 5, 19, 9; 5, 26, 35, and Scrib. Comp. 211, written as Greek).— A mess of four kinds of food, Spart. Hadr. 21; Ael. Ver. 5; Lampr. Alex. Sev. 30.

tetraphoros.full: tē^trăphŏros, on, adj., = τετράφορος, of four bearers: tetraphori phalangarii, four bearers carrying any thing together, Vitr 10, 8, 7.
tetraphoros.short: tē^trăphŏros, on, adj., = τετράφορος, of four bearers: tetraphori phalangarii, four bearers carrying any thing together, Vitr 10, 8, 7.

tetraphylia.full: Tē^traphȳlĭa, ae, f., a town of Athamania in Epirus, Liv. 38, 1.
tetraphylia.short: Tē^traphȳlĭa, ae, f., a town of Athamania in Epirus, Liv.

tetraplasius.full: tē^trăplăsĭus, a, um, adj., = τετραπλάσιος, fourfold: ratio, Mart. Cap. 9, § 953.
tetraplasius.short: tē^trăplăsĭus, a, um, adj., = τετραπλάσιος, fourfold: ratio, Mart.

tetraptota.full: tē^traptōta, ōrum, n., = τετράπτωτα, words which occur in only four cases, tetraptotes, Diom. 1; Prisc. 5; Isid. 1, 6, 43.
tetraptota.short: tē^traptōta, ōrum, n., = τετράπτωτα, words which occur in only four cases, tetraptotes, Diom.

tetrapus.full: Tē^trăpūs, pŏdis, m., = τετράπους (four-footed), the title of the eighth book of Apicius, which treats of the dishes prepared from quadrupeds.
tetrapus.short: Tē^trăpūs, pŏdis, m., = τετράπους (four-footed), the title of the eighth book of Apicius, which treats of the dishes prepared from quadrupeds.

tetrarches.full: tē^trarches, ae, m., = τετράρχης, a ruler who governed the fourth part of a country, a tetrarch; in gen., the title of a petty prince, Cic. Att. 2, 9, 1; id. Phil. 11, 12, 31; id. Balb. 5, 13; id. Mil. 28, 76; id. Deiot. 9, 27; Caes. B. C. 3, 3; Sall. C. 20, 7; Vell. 2, 51; Tac. A. 15, 25; Hor. S. 1, 3, 12; Luc. 7, 227; Sid. Ep. 5, 7.—Also tē^trar-cha, Vulg. Matt. 14, 1; id. Luc. 3, 19.
tetrarches.short: tē^trarches, ae, m., = τετράρχης, a ruler who governed the fourth part of a country, a tetrarch;

tetrarchia.full: tē^trarchĭa, ae, f., = τετραρχία, the dominions of a tetrarch, a tetrarchy, Cic. Deiot. 15, 42; id. Div. 1, 15, 27; Auct. B. Alex. 78, 3.
tetrarchia.short: tē^trarchĭa, ae, f., = τετραρχία, the dominions of a tetrarch, a tetrarchy, Cic.

tetras.full: tē^tras, ădis, f., = τετράς, the number four, a quaternion, tetrad, Tert. adv. Val. 7; 8; Mart. Cap. 7, § 734.
tetras.short: tē^tras, ădis, f., = τετράς, the number four, a quaternion, tetrad, Tert.

tetrasemus.full: tē^trăsēmus, a, um, adj., = τετράσημος, of four syllables, quadrisyllabic: pes, a poetical foot of four syllables, Mart. Cap. 9, § 987.
tetrasemus.short: tē^trăsēmus, a, um, adj., = τετράσημος, of four syllables, quadrisyllabic: pes, a poetical foot of four syllables, Mart.

tetrastichos.full: tē^trastĭchos, on, adj., = τετράστιχος, containing four rows or lines. Adj.: porticus, Treb. Gall. 18. — Subst.: tē^-trastĭchon, i, n., a poem of four verses, a tetrastich, Quint. 6, 3, 96 Spald. N. cr.; Mart. 7, 85, 1.
tetrastichos.short: tē^trastĭchos, on, adj., = τετράστιχος, containing four rows or lines.

tetrastylos.full: tē^trastȳlos, on, adj., = τετράστυλος, having four columns. Adj.: frons loci, Vitr. 3, 2: cava aedium, id. 6, 3.— Subst.: tē^trastȳlon, i, n., a building with four columns, a tetrastyle, Capitol. Gord. 32; Inscr. Orell. 2270.
tetrastylos.short: tē^trastȳlos, on, adj., = τετράστυλος, having four columns.

tetrica.full: Tĕtrĭca, ae, f., a rocky mountain in the Sabine territory, abounding in wild goats, Varr. R. R. 2, 1, 5; Verg. A. 7, 713; called Tetrica rupes, Sil. 8, 419.
tetrica.short: Tĕtrĭca, ae, f., a rocky mountain in the Sabine territory, abounding in wild goats, Varr.

tetrinnio.full: tē^trinnĭo, īre, v. n., to utter the natural cry of the duck, to quack, Auct. Carm. Philom. 22.

tettigometra.full: tettīgŏmētra, ae, f., = τεττιγομήτρα, the larva or matrix of the cicada, Plin. 11, 26, 32, § 93.
tettigometra.short: tettīgŏmētra, ae, f., = τεττιγομήτρα, the larva or matrix of the cicada, Plin.

tettigonia.full: tettīgŏnĭa, ae, f., = τεττιγόνια, a kind of small cicada, Plin. 11, 26, 32, § 92.
tettigonia.short: tettīgŏnĭa, ae, f., = τεττιγόνια, a kind of small cicada, Plin.

teucer.full: Teucer, cri (nom. Teucrus, Verg. A. 3, 108; Lact. 1, 21, 1), m., = Τεῦκρος. Son of Telamon, king of Salamis, and brother of Ajax, Hor. C. 1, 7, 21; 1, 7, 27; 1, 15, 24; 4, 9, 17; id. S. 2, 3, 204; Ov. M. 13, 157; 14, 698; Auct. Her. 1, 11, 18.— Son of Scamander of Crete, son-in-law of Dardanus, and afterwards king of Troy, Ov. M. 13, 705; Verg. A. 3, 108. — Hence, Teu-crus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Teu cer; poet. transf. for Trojan: carinae, Ov. M. 14, 72: sanguis, Cat. 64, 345.—As subst.

teuchites.full: teuchītes, ae, m., = τευχίτης, a kind of fragrant rush, Plin. 21, 18, 72, § 120.
teuchites.short: teuchītes, ae, m., = τευχίτης, a kind of fragrant rush, Plin.

teucri.full: Teucri, ōrum, and Teucrĭa, ae, v. Teucer, II. 1. and 2. b.
teucri.short: Teucri, ōrum, and Teucrĭa, ae, v.

teucrion.full: teucrĭon, ĭi, n., = τεύκριον. A plant, the germander: Teucrium chamaedrys, Linn.; Plin. 24, 15, 80, § 130 (al. Teucria).— The herb spleenwort: Teucrium flavium, Linn.; Plin. 25, 5, 20, § 45.—Called also teucrĭa, Plin. 26, 7, 19, § 35.

teucris.full: Teucris, ĭdis; Teucrĭus, a, um, and Teucrus, i, v. Teucer.

teuta.full: Teuta, ae, f., a queen of Illyria, Plin. 34, 6, 11, § 24. — Called also Teutāna, Flor. 2, 5, 2.
teuta.short: Teuta, ae, f., a queen of Illyria, Plin.

teutani.full: Teutāni, ōrum, m., a people of the Peloponnesus, Plin. 3, 5, 8, § 50.
teutani.short: Teutāni, ōrum, m., a people of the Peloponnesus, Plin.

teutates.full: Teutātes, ae, m., a deity of the Gauls, to whom human sacrifices were offered, Luc. 1, 445; Lact. 1, 21, 3.
teutates.short: Teutātes, ae, m., a deity of the Gauls, to whom human sacrifices were offered, Luc.

teuthalis.full: teuthălis, ĭdis, f., = τευθαλίς, a plant, called also sanguinaria and polygonos. Plin. 27, 12, 91, § 113.
teuthalis.short: teuthălis, ĭdis, f., = τευθαλίς, a plant, called also sanguinaria and polygonos.

teuthras.full: Teuthras, antis, m., = Τεύθρας. A king of Mysia, father of Thespius, Hyg. Fab. 99 and 100.—Hence, Teuthran-tēus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Teuthras; poet. for Mysian: Caicus, Ov. M. 2, 243. — Teuthrantĭus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Teuthras: turba, the daughters of Thespius, a son of Teuthras, Ov. H. 9, 51.— Teuthrānĭa (Teu-thrānĭē), ae, f., the territory in Mysia ruled by Teuthras, Plin. 2, 85, 87, § 201; 5, 30, 33, § 125 sq.— A river in Campania, Prop. 1, 11, 11.— The name of a Tro

teuticus.full: Teutĭcus, i, m., an Illyrian chief, Liv. 44, 31, 9.
teuticus.short: Teutĭcus, i, m., an Illyrian chief, Liv.

teutobodiaci.full: Teutobodiaci, ōrum, m., a people of Galatia, Plin. 5, 32, 42, § 146.
teutobodiaci.short: Teutobodiaci, ōrum, m., a people of Galatia, Plin.

teutoburgiensis.full: Teutoburgiensis, e, adj., of or belonging to the citadel of the Teutones: saltus, a forest of Western Germany in which Varus was defeated A. D. 9, Tac. A. 1, 60.
teutoburgiensis.short: Teutoburgiensis, e, adj., of or belonging to the citadel of the Teutones: saltus, a forest of Western Germany in which Varus was defeated A.

teutomatus.full: Teutomatus, i, m., a king of the Nitiobriges, Caes. B. G. 7, 31; 7, 46.
teutomatus.short: Teutomatus, i, m., a king of the Nitiobriges, Caes.

teutoni.full: Teutŏni, ōrum (collat. form Teutŏ-nes, um, Caes. B. G. 7, 77 fin.; Vell. 2, 12, 4; Aur. Vict. Vir. Ill. 67; Eutr. 5, 1 sq.), m., the Teutons, a people of Germany, Mel. 3, 3, 4; 3, 6, 7; Cic. Imp. Pomp. 20, 60; Caes. B. G. 1, 33; Liv. Ep. 67 fin.; Suet. Caes. 11; Sen. Ep. 94, 66 al.—Poet., in sing.: Cantaber exiguis aut longis Teutonus armis, Luc. 6, 259. — Hence, Teutŏnĭcus, a, um, adj., Teutonic; or, poet. for Germanic, German: opes, Prop. 3, 3 (4, 2), 44: militia, Vell. 2, 120, 1: furor, Luc.

teutria.full: Teutrĭa, ae, f., an island in the Ionian Sea, Plin. 3, 26, 30, § 151.
teutria.short: Teutrĭa, ae, f., an island in the Ionian Sea, Plin.

texo.full: texo, xui, xtum (inf. paragog. texier, Plaut. Trin. 3, 3, 69), 3, v. a. root tek-; Gr. ἔτεκον, τίκτω, to beget; Sanscr. takman, child; taksh, to make, to weave (class.; syn. neo). Lit.: texens telam, Ter. Heaut. 2, 3, 44: vestes, Tib. 2, 3, 54: tegumenta corporum vel texta vel suta, Cic. N. D. 2, 60, 150: in araneolis aliae quasi rete texunt, id. ib. 2, 48, 123: tenuem texens sublimis aranea telam, Cat. 68, 49: in vacuo texetur aranea lecto, Prop. 3, 6 (4, 5), 33: chlamydem, Val. Fl. 2, 499.—Abs

textilis.full: textĭlis, e, adj. texo, woven, wrought, textile. Lit. (class.) Adj.: tegmen, Lucr. 5, 1350: stragulum, Cic. Tusc. 5, 21, 61: dona, Verg. A. 3, 485: aurum, Plin. 33, 3, 19, § 63; Sen. Med. 372: picturae, Lucr. 2, 35; cf.: tabernacula textilibus signis adornata, Val. Max. 9, 1, ext. 4.—Poet.: pestis, i. e. a garment steeped in poison, Cic. poët. Tusc. 2, 8, 20: induere nuptam ventum textilem, i.e. a very thin garment, Petr 55 fin. — Subst.: textĭle, is, n. (sc. opus), a web, stuff, fabric, piece o

textor.full: textor, ōris, m. texo, a weaver, Plaut. Aul. 3, 5, 45; Hor. Ep. 1, 19, 13; Mart. 12, 59, 6; Juv. 9, 30: textorum et textricum cibaria, Dig. 33, 9, 3, § 6.

textorius.full: textōrĭus, a, um, adj. id., of or belonging to weaving, plaiting, or braiding, textorial (post-Aug. and very rare). Lit.: alvearia opere textorio salicibus connectentur, plaited work, Col. 9, 6, 1.— Trop.: textorium, inquis, totum mehercule istud est, i. e. entangled, entangling, Sen. Ep. 113, 25.

textricula.full: textrīcŭla, ae, f. dim. textrix, a little (female) weaver; in apposition: puellae, Arn. 5, 166.

textrinus.full: textrīnus, a. um, adj. contr. from textorinus, from textor. Of or belonging to weaving, textrine. Adj.: ars, the art of weaving, Firm. Error. Prof. Relig. 17: opus, Vulg. Tob. 2, 19. — More freq., Substt. textrīnum, i, n. (sc. opus), weaving, Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 26, § 58; 2, 4, 46, § 103; Sen. Ep. 90, 20; Suet. Gram. 23.— Collect.: juxta vehiculi frontem omne textrinum incedit ( = omnes textores), Amm. 14, 6, 17.— textrīna, ae, f. (sc. officina), a weaver's shop, Vitr. 6, 7 fin.; cf. App. Flor 2, p

textrix.full: textrix, īcis,f. textor, a female weaver, Mart. 4, 19, 1; Inscr. Rein. cl. 9, n. 77; Dig. 33, 9, 3, § 6; Tib. 2, 1, 65; App. M. 6, p. 181, 25. — In apposition: anus, i. e. the Fates, App. M. 6, p. 180, 39.

textura.full: textūra, ae, f. texo, a web, texture (very rare). Lit.: aranearum, Plaut. Stich. 2, 2, 24: Minervae, Prop. 4 (5), 5, 23. Sen. Ep. 121, 22.— Transf., a construction, structure: quam tenui constet texturā (animi natura), Lucr. 3, 209; Luc. 9, 777.

textus1.full: textus, a, um, Part. of texo.

textus2.full: textus, ūs, m. texo, I. B., texture, tissue, structure (poet. and in post - Aug. prose). Lit.: haec sunt tenuia textu, Lucr. 4, 728: capiuntur purpurae parvulis rarique textu, Plin. 9, 37, 61, § 132; 18, 7, 10, § 60.— Trop., of language, construction, combination, connection, context, Quint. 9, 4, 13; 8, 6, 57: rem brevi textu percurram, Amm. 15, 7, 6: ut ostendit textus superior, id. 15, 8, 1: quod contra foederum textum juvarentur Armeniae, id. 27, 12, 18: gestorum, id. 27, 12, 11; Manil. 3, 2

thabena.full: Thabēna, ae, f., a city of Numidia, Auct. B. Afr 77; its inhabitants are called Thabēnenses, ium, m., id. ib. 77
thabena.short: Thabēna, ae, f., a city of Numidia, Auct.

thabraca.full: Thabraca, ae, f., a city of Numidia on the coast of the Mediterranean, Mel. 1, 7, 1; Juv 10, 194, Plin. 5, 3, 2, § 22.
thabraca.short: Thabraca, ae, f., a city of Numidia on the coast of the Mediterranean, Mel.

thais.full: Thāis, ĭdis, f., = Θαΐς, a celebrated courtesan of Athens, Prop. 2, 6, 3; 4 (5), 5, 43; Ov. A. A. 3, 604; id. R. Am. 383 sq.— Another at Rome, Mart. 3, 8; 4, 12.— A courtesan in the Eunuchus of Terence, Ter. Eun. 1, 2, 11; 2, 1, 25.
thais.short: Thāis, ĭdis, f., = Θαΐς, a celebrated courtesan of Athens, Prop.

thala.full: Thala, ae, f., = Θάλα, an important town of Numidia, Sall. J. 75, 1 sq.; Tac. A. 3, 21; Flor. 3, 1.
thala.short: Thala, ae, f., = Θάλα, an important town of Numidia, Sall.

thalamegus.full: thălămēgus, i, f., = θαλαμηγός, a state-barge fitted up with cabins, Suet. Caes. 52 (called navis cubiculata, Sen. Ben. 7, 20, 3).
thalamegus.short: thălămēgus, i, f., = θαλαμηγός, a state-barge fitted up with cabins, Suet.

thalamus.full: thălămus, i, m., = θάλαμος, an inner room, chamber, apartment (poet.). Lit In gen.: Pars secreta domus ... Tres habuit thalamos, quorum tu, Pandrose, dextrum, Aglauros laevum, medium possederat Herse, Ov. M. 2, 738: ferreique Eumenidum thalami, Verg. A. 6, 280; cf.: delubra ei gemina, quae vocant thalamos, Plin. 8, 46, 71, § 185; and of bees: ubi jam thalamis se conposuere, Verg. G. 4, 189.— Esp., a sleeping-room, bedchamber (cf.: cubiculum, dormitorium, cubile), Verg. A. 6, 623; Ov. M. 10, 456;
thalamus.short: thălămus, i, m., = θάλαμος, an inner room, chamber, apartment (poet.).

thalassa.full: Thălassa, ae, f., = θάλασσα (the sea), the title of the ninth book of Apicius, which treats of sea-fish.
thalassa.short: Thălassa, ae, f., = θάλασσα (the sea), the title of the ninth book of Apicius, which treats of sea-fish.

thalassegle.full: thălassēglē, ēs, f., a plant, called also potamantis, Plin. 24, 17, 102, § 164.
thalassegle.short: thălassēglē, ēs, f., a plant, called also potamantis, Plin.

thalassicus.full: thălassĭcus, a, um, adj., = θαλασσικός, of or like the sea, sea-colored, sea-green: colos (pallioli), Plaut. Mil. 4, 4, 43; cf. ornatus, id. ib. 4, 6, 67; v. thalassinus.
thalassicus.short: thălassĭcus, a, um, adj., = θαλασσικός, of or like the sea, sea-colored, sea-green: colos (pallioli), Plaut.

thalassinus.full: thălassĭnus, a, um, adj., = θαλάσσινος, sea-colored, sea-green: vestis, Lucr. 4, 1127; cf. thalassicus.
thalassinus.short: thălassĭnus, a, um, adj., = θαλάσσινος, sea-colored, sea-green: vestis, Lucr.

thalassion.full: thălassĭon phȳcos, = θαλάσσιον φῦκος, archil or orchil (a sea-plant which produces a reddish dye): Lichen roccella, Linn.; Plin. 26, 10, 66, § 103.
thalassion.short: thălassĭon phȳcos, = θαλάσσιον φῦκος, archil or orchil (a sea-plant which produces a reddish dye): Lichen roccella, Linn.;

thalassites.full: thălassītes, ae, m., = θαλασσίτης, sea-wine, i. e. wine which has been ripened by sinking it in the sea, Plin. 14, 8, 10, § 78.
thalassites.short: thălassītes, ae, m., = θαλασσίτης, sea-wine, i.

thalassomeli.full: thălassŏmĕli, n., = θαλασσόμελι, sea-water mixed with honey, used as a beverage, Plin. 31, 6, 35, § 68; Ser. Samm. 28, 537.
thalassomeli.short: thălassŏmĕli, n., = θαλασσόμελι, sea-water mixed with honey, used as a beverage, Plin.

thales.full: Thăles, is and lētis (gen. Thaletis, Mel. 1, 17; Juv 13, 184; dat. Thaleti, Val. Max. 4, 1, ext. 7), m., = Θαλῆς, a celebrated Greek philosopher of Miletus, one of the seven wise men, and founder of the Ionic sect, Varr. R. R. 2, 1, 3; Cic. N. D. 1, 10, 25; 1, 33, 91; id. Ac. 2, 37, 118; id. Leg. 2, 11, 26; Sen. Q. N. 3, 13, 1; Min. Fel. 19, 4; Aug. Civ Dei, 18, 25.—Gen. Thalis, Prob. Cath. 1466 P.: Thaletis, Mel. 1, 17, 1; Sen. Q. N. 3, 14, 1; Juv. 13, 184.—Dat. Thali, App. Flor. 4, n. 18: Thal

thalia.full: Thălīa (written Thălēa, acc. to Fest. p. 359 Müll., and Serv. Verg. E. 6, 2; so Rib.), ae, f., = Θάλεια. One of the Muses; the Muse of Comedy, Verg. E. 6, 2; Ov. A. A. 1, 264; of Lyric poetry, Hor. C. 4, 6, 25.— One of the Graces, Sen. Ben. 1, 3, 6; 1, 3, 10.— A sea-nymph, Verg. A. 5, 826.

thaliarchus.full: Thălĭarchus, i, m., = Θαλίαρχος, the name given by Horace to the friend to whom is addressed C. 1, 9.
thaliarchus.short: Thălĭarchus, i, m., = Θαλίαρχος, the name given by Horace to the friend to whom is addressed C.

thalictrum.full: thălictrum or thălitruum, i, n., a plant, meadow-rue, Plin. 27, 13, 112, § 138.
thalictrum.short: thălictrum or thălitruum, i, n., a plant, meadow-rue, Plin.

thalli.full: Thalli, ōrum, m., a people on the Caspian Sea, Plin. 6, 5, 5, § 17.
thalli.short: Thalli, ōrum, m., a people on the Caspian Sea, Plin.

thallumetus.full: Thallumētus, i, m., a slave of Atticus, Cic. Att. 5, 12, 2.
thallumetus.short: Thallumētus, i, m., a slave of Atticus, Cic.

thallus.full: thallus, i, m., = θαλλός, a green stalk, green bough: cepae, Col. 11, 3, 58; Pall. Febr. 24, 4: Amyclaeus, perh. a myrtlebough, Verg. Cir. 376; Vulg. 2 Macc. 14, 4.
thallus.short: thallus, i, m., = θαλλός, a green stalk, green bough: cepae, Col.

thalna.full: Thalna, ae, m., a Roman surname of the Juventian gens, Liv. 39, 31.
thalna.short: Thalna, ae, m., a Roman surname of the Juventian gens, Liv.

thamyras.full: Thămўras, ae, m., a Thracian poet who entered into a contest with the Muses, and, being vanquished, was deprived of his eyes, Prop. 2, 22 (3, 15), 19; Ov. Am. 3, 7, 62; id. A. A. 3, 399; id. Ib. 274; Plin. 7, 56, 57, § 204.—Called Thămўris, ĭdis, Stat. Th. 4, 183.
thamyras.short: Thămўras, ae, m., a Thracian poet who entered into a contest with the Muses, and, being vanquished, was deprived of his eyes, Prop.

thannum.full: thannum (thamnum), i, n., = θάμνος, a shrub, otherwise unknown, Col. 12, 7, 1; Tert. Anim. 32.
thannum.short: thannum (thamnum), i, n., = θάμνος, a shrub, otherwise unknown, Col.

thapsacus.full: Thapsăcus, i, f., = Θάψακος, a town of Syria, on the Euphrates, now El-Hammam, Plin. 5, 24, 21, § 87.
thapsacus.short: Thapsăcus, i, f., = Θάψακος, a town of Syria, on the Euphrates, now El-Hammam, Plin.

thapsia.full: thapsĭa, ae, f., = θαψία, a poisonous shrub: Thapsia Asclepium, Linn.; Plin. 13, 22, 43, § 124.—Called thapsos, Luc. 9, 919.
thapsia.short: thapsĭa, ae, f., = θαψία, a poisonous shrub: Thapsia Asclepium, Linn.;

thapsus.full: Thapsus or -os, i, f., = Θάψος. A peninsula and city in Sicily, now Magnisi, Ov. F. 4, 477; Verg. A. 3, 689; Sil. 14, 206.— A city in Africa Propria, famed for Cæsar's victory over the partisans of Pompey, now Baltah, Plin. 5, 4, 3, § 25; Liv. 33, 48; Auct. B. Afr. 28, 1; 44, 1; 46, 4; 79, 3; 80, 2.—Hence, Thapsĭtāni, ōrum, m., the inhabitants of Thapsus, Auct. B. Afr. 97, 2.

thasus.full: Thăsus or -os, i, f., = Θάσος, an island in the north of the Ægean Sea, off the coast of Thrace, now Thaso, Mel. 2, 7, 8; Plin. 4, 12, 23, § 73; Cic. Pis. 36, 89; Auct. Her. 4, 54, 68; Liv 33, 30; 33, 35; Stat. S. 1, 5, 34; 2, 2, 92 al.—Hence, Thăsĭus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Thasus, Thasian: nuces, Varr. ap. Gell. 7, 16, 5; Plin. 15, 22, 24, § 90: vinum, Poët. ap. Plin. 14, 14, 16, § 95: vites, Verg. G. 2, 91: lapis, Sen. Ep. 86, 5.
thasus.short: Thăsus or -os, i, f., = Θάσος, an island in the north of the Ægean Sea, off the coast of Thrace, now Thaso, Mel.

thaumaci.full: Thaumăci, ōrum, m., a people of Thessaly, now Dhomoko, Plin. 4, 9, 16, § 32; Liv. 32, 4, 1; 36, 14, 12; inhabiting the town called Thaumăcĭē, ēs, f.
thaumaci.short: Thaumăci, ōrum, m., a people of Thessaly, now Dhomoko, Plin.

thaumas.full: Thaumas, antis, m., = Θαύμας, the father of Iris, Cic. N. D. 3, 20, 51.—Hence, Thaumantēus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Thaumas, Thaumantian: virgo, i. e. Iris, Ov. M. 14, 845.— Thauman-tĭăs, ădis, f., daughter of Thaumas: Iris, Ov. M. 4, 480; called also simply Thaumantias, Verg. A. 9, 5; Val. Fl. 8, 115.— Thau-mantis, ĭdis, f., the daughter of Thaumas: Iris, Ov. M. 11, 647.
thaumas.short: Thaumas, antis, m., = Θαύμας, the father of Iris, Cic.

theamedes.full: theamēdes, is, m., an Ethiopian stone that repels iron; acc. to some, the tourmaline, Plin. 36, 16, 25, § 130.
theamedes.short: theamēdes, is, m., an Ethiopian stone that repels iron;

theangelis.full: theangelis, ĭdis, f., a kind of plant growing on Libanus, Plin. 24, 17, 102, § 164.
theangelis.short: theangelis, ĭdis, f., a kind of plant growing on Libanus, Plin.

theatralis.full: thĕātrālis, e, adj. theatrum, of or belonging to the theatre, theatrical: theatrales gladiatoriique consessus, Cic. Sest. 54, 115: operae, Tac. A. 1, 16: lascivia populi, id. ib. 11, 13: ad theatrales artes degeneravisse, id. ib. 14, 21: licentia, Suet. Dom. 8: lex, concerning the order of sitting in the theatre, Plin. 7, 30, 31, § 117; 33, 2, 8, § 32; Quint. 3, 6, 19: humanitas, i. e. feigned, spurious, id. 2, 2, 10: sermones, i. e. low, vulgar, Sid. Ep. 3, 13 fin.: omnes (montes) theatrali mod

theatricus.full: thĕātrĭcus, a, um, adj., = θεατρικός, of or belonging to the theatre, theatric (late Lat. for the class. theatralis): nugae, Aug. Doctr. Chabr. 2, 18: turpitudines, id. Civ. Dei, 6, 6: operarii, id. Mus. 2, 5.
theatricus.short: thĕātrĭcus, a, um, adj., = θεατρικός, of or belonging to the theatre, theatric (late Lat.

theatrum.full: thĕātrum, i, n., = θέατρον, a playhouse, theatre (cf.: scena, spectaculum, ludus). Lit.: num theatrum, gymnasia, porticus, etc. ... rem publicam efficiebat? Cic. Rep. 3, 32, 44: theatrum ut commune sit, id. Fin. 3, 20, 67: castra munita ... alterā (ex parte) a theatro, quod est ante oppidum, Caes. B. C. 2, 25; Nep. Reg. 2, 1: populi sensus maxime theatro et spectaculis perspectus est, Cic. Att. 2, 19, 3: aliquid totius theatri clamore dicere, id. ib.: consessus theatri, id. Tusc. 1, 16, 37: in v
theatrum.short: thĕātrum, i, n., = θέατρον, a playhouse, theatre (cf.: scena, spectaculum, ludus).

thebae.full: Thēbae, ārum (collat. form Thēbē, ēs, Juv. 15, 6; Plin. 5, 9, 11, § 60), f., = Θῆβαι (or Θήβη), Thebes, the name of several cities of antiquity.—The most considerable were, The city of the hundred gates, in Upper Egypt, now Karnak, etc., Mel. 1, 9, 9; Plin. 5, 9, 11, § 60; 36, 7, 11, § 58; 36, 8, 12, § 60; 36, 13, 20, § 94 al.—Hence, Thēbae-us, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Thebes, Theban: mons, in the Thebaid, Claud. Idyll. 1, 91.— Thēbāĭcus, a, um, adj., Theban: palmae, Plin. 23, 4, 51, § 97

thebagenes.full: Thēbāgĕnes (MSS. Thēbŏgĕnes), is, adj. Thebae-gigno, born at Thebes: Ismenias, Varr. ap. Non. 172, 26.

thebe2.full: Thēbē, ēs,f., a female name. A nymph, daughter of the river-god Asopus, Ov. Am. 3, 6, 33.— Wife of the tyrant Alexander of Pheræ, Cic. Inv. 2, 49, 144; id. Off. 2, 7, 25.

thebes.full: Thēbes, a city in Samaria, Vulg. Judic. 9, 50; id. 2 Sam. 11, 21.
thebes.short: Thēbes, a city in Samaria, Vulg.

theca.full: thēca, ae, f., = θήκη, that in which any thing is enclosed, an envelope, hull, cover, case, sheath, etc. (syn. vagina): grani, Varr. R. R. 1, 48, 1: efferri sine thecis vasa, Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 23, § 52; id. Att. 4, 7, 2; Quint. 6, 3, 61: calamaria, Suet. Claud. 35; Mart. 14, 19, 1; Amm. 28, 4, 13.
theca.short: thēca, ae, f., = θήκη, that in which any thing is enclosed, an envelope, hull, cover, case, sheath, etc.

thecatus.full: thēcātus, a, um, adj. theca, placed in a case or cover, encased: arcus, Sid. Ep. 1, 2 med.

theium.full: Theium, ii, n., a town of Athamania, Liv. 38, 1.
theium.short: Theium, ii, n., a town of Athamania, Liv.

thelxinoe.full: Thelxĭnŏē, ēs, f., one of the first four Muses, Cic. N. D. 3, 21, 54.
thelxinoe.short: Thelxĭnŏē, ēs, f., one of the first four Muses, Cic.

thelygonon.full: thēlўgŏnon, i, n., = θηλυγόνον (producing females). A species of the plant phyllum, Plin. 26, 15, 91, § 162.— A species of the Satyrion, Plin. 26, 10, 63, § 99.— A species of the crataeogonos, Plin. 27, 8, 40, § 62.

thelyphonon.full: thēlўphŏnon, i, n., = θηλυφόνον, another name of the aconitum, Plin. 25, 10, 75, § 122; 27, 3, 2, § 9.
thelyphonon.short: thēlўphŏnon, i, n., = θηλυφόνον, another name of the aconitum, Plin.

thelypteris.full: thēlyptĕris, is, f., = θηλύπτερις, the female plant of the filix (fern, polypody), Plin. 27, 9, 55, § 78.
thelypteris.short: thēlyptĕris, is, f., = θηλύπτερις, the female plant of the filix (fern, polypody), Plin.

thema.full: thĕma, ătis, n., = θέμα. A subject or topic treated of, a theme (post-Aug.): Scholastici exempla cum dixerunt, volunt et illa ad aliquod controversiae thema redigere, Sen. Contr. 3, 20 fin.; so id. ib. 3, 28 med.; Quint. 4, 2, 28; 4, 2, 91; 7, 2, 54; 9, 2, 85 al.— The position of the celestial signs at one's birth, a nativity, horoscope, Suet. Aug. 94 fin.

themis.full: Thĕmis, ĭdis, f., = Θέμις, the goddess of justice and of prophecy, Cat. 68, 153; Ov. M. 1, 321; 1, 379; 4, 643; 7, 762; 9, 403; 9, 419; Luc. 5, 81; Claud. Rapt. Pros. 1, 107; Mart. Cap. 2, § 174; Schol. Juv. 1, 82.— The daughter of Ilus and mother of Anchises, Hyg. Fab. 94; 270.
themis.short: Thĕmis, ĭdis, f., = Θέμις, the goddess of justice and of prophecy, Cat.

themiscyra.full: Thĕmiscȳra, ae, f., = Θεμίσκυρα, a town in Pontus, on the Thermodon, Plin. 6, 3, 4, § 10.—Hence, Thĕmiscȳrae-us, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Themiscyra: luci, Amm. 22, 8, 14.— Thĕmi-scȳrēnus, a, um, adj., the same, Plin. 6, 3, 3, § 9; 24, 17, 102, § 165.
themiscyra.short: Thĕmiscȳra, ae, f., = Θεμίσκυρα, a town in Pontus, on the Thermodon, Plin.

themison.full: Thĕmĭson, ōnis, m., = Θεμίσων, a celebrated physician of Laodicea in Syria, Juv. 10, 221; Cels. Praef. al.; Plin. 29, 1, 5, § 6; Sen. Ep. 95, 9.
themison.short: Thĕmĭson, ōnis, m., = Θεμίσων, a celebrated physician of Laodicea in Syria, Juv.

themista.full: Thĕmista, ae, f., a female Epicurean philosopher of Lampsacus, Cic. Fin. 2, 21, 68; id. Pis. 26, 63; Lact. 3, 25, 15.
themista.short: Thĕmista, ae, f., a female Epicurean philosopher of Lampsacus, Cic.

themistocles.full: Thĕmistŏcles, i and is, m., = Θεμιστοκλῆς, a celebrated Athenian commander, whose life is written by Nepos; cf. Cic. de Or. 2, 74, 300; 2, 86, 351; 3, 16, 59; id. Rep. 1, 3, 5; id. Att. 7, 11, 3; id. Tusc. 4, 19, 44; id. Fin. 3, 32, 104; Nep. Them. 1, 1 sqq.— Hence, Thĕmistŏclēus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Themistocles: consilium, Cic. Att. 10, 8, 4: exsilium, id. ib. 10, 8, 7.
themistocles.short: Thĕmistŏcles, i and is, m., = Θεμιστοκλῆς, a celebrated Athenian commander, whose life is written by Nepos;

theocritus.full: Thĕō^crĭtus, i, m., = Θεόκριτος, a celebrated Grecian idyllic poet, Quint. 10, 1, 55; Macr. S. 5, 2, 4; Suet. Vit. Verg. p. 53.
theocritus.short: Thĕō^crĭtus, i, m., = Θεόκριτος, a celebrated Grecian idyllic poet, Quint.

theodamas.full: Thēŏdămas, antis, m., = Θειοδάμας, king of the Dryopes, and father of Hylas, Hyg. Fab. 14; 271. — Hence, Thēŏdă-mantēus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Theodamas, Theodamantean: Hylas, i. e. the son of Theodamas, Prop. 1, 20, 6 (Thiodamanteus, Müll.).
theodamas.short: Thēŏdămas, antis, m., = Θειοδάμας, king of the Dryopes, and father of Hylas, Hyg.

theodectes.full: Thĕŏdectes, is, m., = Θεοδέκτης, a Greek orator of Cilicia, a disciple of Plato, Isocrates, and Aristotle, Cic. Or. 51, 172; 57, 195; 64, 218; id. Tusc. 1, 24, 59; Quint. 11, 2, 51; Val. Max. 8, 14, ext. 3.
theodectes.short: Thĕŏdectes, is, m., = Θεοδέκτης, a Greek orator of Cilicia, a disciple of Plato, Isocrates, and Aristotle, Cic.

theodorus.full: Thĕŏdōrus, i, m., = Θεόδωρος. A Greek sophist of Byzantium, Cic. Brut. 12, 48; Quint. 3, 1, 11.— A Greek atheist of Cyrene, Cic. N. D. 1, 1, 2; id. Tusc. 1, 43, 102; 5, 40, 117; Sen. Tranq. 14, 3.— A celebrated rhetorician of Gadara, Quint. 3, 1, 17; 3, 11, 26; Suet. Tib. 57.—Hence, Thĕ-ŏdōrēus, i, m., a pupil and follower of Theodorus, Quint. 2, 11, 2.—Plur., Quint. 4, 2, 32; 3, 1, 18.

theodosia.full: Thĕŏdŏsia, ae, f., a town of the Tauric Chersonese, now Caffa or Feodosia, Mel. 2, 1; Plin. 4, 12, 26, § 86.
theodosia.short: Thĕŏdŏsia, ae, f., a town of the Tauric Chersonese, now Caffa or Feodosia, Mel.

theognis.full: Thĕognis, ĭdis, m., = Θέογνις, an ancient Greek poet; hence, as a designation of a very ancient period: etiam priusquam Theognis nasceretur, Lucil. ap. Gell. 1, 3, 19.
theognis.short: Thĕognis, ĭdis, m., = Θέογνις, an ancient Greek poet;

theogonia.full: Thĕŏgŏnĭa, ae, f., = θεογονία (the Origin of the Gods), the title of a poem by Hesiod, Cic. N. D. 1, 14, 36.
theogonia.short: Thĕŏgŏnĭa, ae, f., = θεογονία (the Origin of the Gods), the title of a poem by Hesiod, Cic.

theologia.full: thĕŏlŏgĭa, ae, f., = θεολογία, theology, Varr. ap. Aug. Civ. Dei, 6, 5.
theologia.short: thĕŏlŏgĭa, ae, f., = θεολογία, theology, Varr.

theologicus.full: thĕŏlŏgĭcus, a, um, adj., = θεολογικός, of or belonging to theology, theological: doctrina, Amm. 16, 5, 5: metrum, heroic verse, Plot. 2629 P.
theologicus.short: thĕŏlŏgĭcus, a, um, adj., = θεολογικός, of or belonging to theology, theological: doctrina, Amm.

theologumena.full: Thĕŏlŏgūmĕna, ōn, n., = Θεολογούμενα, speculations on divine things, the title of a work by Aristotle, Macr. S. 1, 18, 1.
theologumena.short: Thĕŏlŏgūmĕna, ōn, n., = Θεολογούμενα, speculations on divine things, the title of a work by Aristotle, Macr.

theologus.full: thĕŏlŏgus, i, m., = θεολόγος, one who treats of the deity and of divine things, a theologian, Cic. N. D. 3, 21, 53 sq.; Arn. 3, 106.
theologus.short: thĕŏlŏgus, i, m., = θεολόγος, one who treats of the deity and of divine things, a theologian, Cic.

theombrotios.full: thĕombrōtĭos, ii, f., = θεωμβρώτιον, a plant, Plin. 24, 17, 102, § 166.
theombrotios.short: thĕombrōtĭos, ii, f., = θεωμβρώτιον, a plant, Plin.

theon.full: Thĕon, ōnis, m. A satirical poet.— Hence, Thĕōnīnus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Theon: dens, Hor. Ep. 1, 18, 82. — A celebrated Samian painter, Quint. 12, 10, 6; Plin. 35, 11, 40, § 144.

theophane.full: Thĕŏphănē, ēs, f., = Θεοφάνη, a daughter of Bisaltes, loved by Poseidon, Hyg. Fab. 188; cf. Ov. M. 6, 117.
theophane.short: Thĕŏphănē, ēs, f., = Θεοφάνη, a daughter of Bisaltes, loved by Poseidon, Hyg.

theophanes.full: Thĕŏphănes, is, m., = Θεοφανής, a Greek historian of Mitylene, a friend of Pompey, Cic. Arch. 10, 24; id. Att. 5, 11, 3; Caes. B. C. 3, 18; Tac. A. 6, 18 fin.
theophanes.short: Thĕŏphănes, is, m., = Θεοφανής, a Greek historian of Mitylene, a friend of Pompey, Cic.

theophilus.full: Thĕŏphĭlus, i, m., = Θεόφιλος, a freedman of M. Marcellus, Cic. Fam. 4, 9, 1; 4, 10, 1.
theophilus.short: Thĕŏphĭlus, i, m., = Θεόφιλος, a freedman of M.

theophrastus.full: Thĕophrastus, i, m., = Θεόφραστος, a Greek philosopher of Eressus, a disciple of Plato and Aristotle, Cic. Or. 19, 62; id. Brut. 31, 121; id. Tusc. 3, 28, 69; id. Att. 2, 16, 3.
theophrastus.short: Thĕophrastus, i, m., = Θεόφραστος, a Greek philosopher of Eressus, a disciple of Plato and Aristotle, Cic.

theopompos.full: Thĕŏpompos, i, m., = Θεόπομπος, a Greek historian and orator, a pupil of Isocrates, Cic. de Or. 2, 13, 57; 2, 23, 94; 3, 9, 36; Nep. Alcib. 11, 1. — Hence, Thĕŏ-pompēus or -īnus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Theopompus, Theopompean: Theopompino genere (dicendi), Cic. Att. 2, 6, 2: Theopompeo more, id. Or. 61, 207.
theopompos.short: Thĕŏpompos, i, m., = Θεόπομπος, a Greek historian and orator, a pupil of Isocrates, Cic.

theorema.full: thĕōrēma, ătis, n., = θεώρημα, a proposition to be proved, a theorem, Gell. 17, 19, 3; Mart. Cap. 3, § 230. — Dat. plur. theorematis, Gell. 1, 2, 6.
theorema.short: thĕōrēma, ătis, n., = θεώρημα, a proposition to be proved, a theorem, Gell.

theoremation.full: thĕōrēmătĭon, ii, n. dim., = θεωρημάτιον, a little theorem, Gell. 1, 13, 9.

theoreticus.full: thĕōrētĭcus, a, um, adj., = θεωρητικός, contemplative, speculative (pure Lat. contemplativus; opp. practicus), Fulg. Myth. 2, 1; Ambros. Hexaem. 1, 5, 17.
theoreticus.short: thĕōrētĭcus, a, um, adj., = θεωρητικός, contemplative, speculative (pure Lat.

theoria.full: thĕōrĭa, ae, f., = θεωρία, a philosophic speculation, theory, Hier. in Ezech. 12, 40, 4 (in Cic. Att. 12, 6, 1, written as Greek).
theoria.short: thĕōrĭa, ae, f., = θεωρία, a philosophic speculation, theory, Hier.

theorice.full: thĕōrĭcē, ēs, f., = θεωρική, a philosophic speculation, Hier. Ep. 30, 1.
theorice.short: thĕōrĭcē, ēs, f., = θεωρική, a philosophic speculation, Hier.

theotocos.full: thĕŏtŏcos, i, f., = θεοτόκος, Godbearing, mother of God: theotocos virgo Maria, Cod. Just. 1, 1, 6.
theotocos.short: thĕŏtŏcos, i, f., = θεοτόκος, Godbearing, mother of God: theotocos virgo Maria, Cod.

thera.full: Thēra, ae (Thērē, ēs), f., = Θήρα, an island in the Ægean Sea, the chief of the Sporades, now Santorin, Mel. 2, 7, 11; Plin. 2, 87, 89, § 202; 4, 12, 23, § 70; Sen. Q. N. 6, 21, 1.—Hence, Thēraeus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Thera: colonus, Tib. 4, 1, 139: cyperos, Plin. 21, 18, 70, § 117.—Plur. subst.: Thēraei, ōn, m., the Theræans, Sall. J. 19, 3.
thera.short: Thēra, ae (Thērē, ēs), f., = Θήρα, an island in the Ægean Sea, the chief of the Sporades, now Santorin, Mel.

theramenes.full: Thērāmĕnes, ae, m., = Θηραμένης, one of the thirty tyrants of Athens, who was put to death for resisting the oppressive measures of his associates, Cic. Tusc. 1, 40, 96.
theramenes.short: Thērāmĕnes, ae, m., = Θηραμένης, one of the thirty tyrants of Athens, who was put to death for resisting the oppressive measures of his associates, Cic.

therapnae.full: Thĕrapnae (Thĕramnae), ārum, = Θεράπναι, or -ē, ēs, f., = Θεράπνη, a small town in Laconia, the birthplace of Helen, Mel. 2, 3, 4; Stat. S. 4, 8, 53.—Hence, Thĕ-rapnaeus (Thĕramn-), a, um, adj., of or belonging to Therapnæ, Therapnæan; in the poets for Laconian, Spartan: rus, Ov. H. 15 (16), 196: marita, i. e. Helen, id. A. A. 3, 49: fratres, i. e. Castor and Pollux, Stat. Th. 7, 793; cf.: membra Therapnaea resolutus gymnade Pollux, id. S. 4, 2, 48: Amyclae, Mart. 9, 104, 5.—And, as the Tarentin
therapnae.short: Thĕrapnae (Thĕramnae), ārum, = Θεράπναι, or -ē, ēs, f., = Θεράπνη, a small town in Laconia, the birthplace of Helen, Mel.

therasia.full: Thērăsĭa, ae, f., = Θηρασία, a small island in the Ægean Sea, opposite to Thea, westward, still called Therasia, Plin. 2, 87, 89, § 202; 4, 12, 23, § 70; Sen. Q. N. 6, 21, 1. — One of the Lipari islands near Sicily, now Vulcanello, Plin. 3, 9, 14, § 93; Mart. Cap. 6, § 648.
therasia.short: Thērăsĭa, ae, f., = Θηρασία, a small island in the Ægean Sea, opposite to Thea, westward, still called Therasia, Plin.

theriacus.full: thērĭăcus, a, um, adj., = θηριακός, good against the poison of animals, esp. against the bite of serpents. Adj.: pastilli, Plin. 29, 4, 21, § 70: vitis, Pall. Febr. 28, 1.— Subst.: thērĭăca, ae, or -ē, ēs, f., an antidote against the bite of serpents, or against poison in gen., Plin. 20, 24, 100, § 264; 29, 1, 8, § 24; Scrib. Comp. 163; Tert. Anim. 24; Hier. adv. Jovin. 2, 6.
theriacus.short: thērĭăcus, a, um, adj., = θηριακός, good against the poison of animals, esp.

thericles.full: Thēricles, is, m., = Θηρικλῆς, a famous potter of Grecian antiquity, Plin. 16, 40, 76, § 205 (from Theophr. Hist. Plant. 5, 4).—Hence, Thēriclēus or -īus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Thericles, Thericlean: pocula, Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 18, § 38.
thericles.short: Thēricles, is, m., = Θηρικλῆς, a famous potter of Grecian antiquity, Plin.

therionarca.full: thērĭŏnarca, ae, f., = θηριονάρκη, a plant which benumbs serpents, Plin. 24, 17, 102, § 163; 25, 9, 65, § 113.
therionarca.short: thērĭŏnarca, ae, f., = θηριονάρκη, a plant which benumbs serpents, Plin.

theristrum.full: thĕristrum, i, n., = θέριστρον, a summer garment. Lit. (late Lat.), Hier. in Isa. 2, 3, 23; Vulg. Gen. 38, 14.— Trop., a garment, covering: theristrum pudicitiae, Hier. Ep. 107, 7.
theristrum.short: thĕristrum, i, n., = θέριστρον, a summer garment.

thermae.full: thermae, ārum, f. (sc. aquae), = θερμὰ ὕδατα, warm springs, warm baths (natural or artificial; cf.: tepula aqua): Agrippae, Plin. 34, 8, 19, § 62; 35, 4, 9, § 26; 36, 25, 64, § 189: Neronianae, Mart. 7, 34, 5; 12, 84, 5; cf. Sen. Ep. 122, 8.— = thermopolium, q. v. Juv. 8, 168.— As nom. prop.: Thermae, = Θέρμαι, a town in Sicily, near Himera, now Termini, Mel. 2, 7, 16; Plin. 3, 8, 14, § 90; Cic. Verr. 2, 2, 34, § 85 sq.; Sil. 14, 232.—Hence, Thermitānus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Thermæ, T

thermanticus.full: thermantĭcus, a, um, adj., = θερμαντικός, that serves for warming, warming: virtus, App. Herb. 120: unctiones, Pelag. Vet. 16 med.
thermanticus.short: thermantĭcus, a, um, adj., = θερμαντικός, that serves for warming, warming: virtus, App.

thermapalus.full: thermăpălus, a, um, adj., = θερμάπαλος ( θερμόσ-ἁπαλός ), warm and soft: ova, Theod. Prisc. 2, 10.
thermapalus.short: thermăpălus, a, um, adj., = θερμάπαλος ( θερμόσ-ἁπαλός ), warm and soft: ova, Theod.

therme.full: Thermē, ēs, f., = Θέρμη, a town in Macedonia, afterwards Thessalonica, Plin. 4, 10, 17, § 36.—Hence, adjj. Ther-maeus, a, um, of Therme: sinus, the Thermaic Gulf, now il Golfo di Salonichi, Tac. A. 5, 10.— Thermăĭcus, a, um, = Θερμαϊκός, of Therme: sinus, the same, Mel. 2, 3, 1; Plin. 4, 10, 17, § 35.
therme.short: Thermē, ēs, f., = Θέρμη, a town in Macedonia, afterwards Thessalonica, Plin.

therminus.full: thermĭnus, a, um, adj., = θέρμινος, made of lupines (horse-beans): oleum, Plin. 23, 4, 49, § 94.
therminus.short: thermĭnus, a, um, adj., = θέρμινος, made of lupines (horse-beans): oleum, Plin.

termitanus.full: Termitānus, a, um, v. thermae, II.

thermodon.full: Thermōdon, ontis, m., = Θερμώδων, a river of Pontus, on which dwelt the Amazons, now Termeh Tchai, Mel. 1, 19, 9; Plin. 6, 3, 4, § 10; Verg. A. 11, 659; Prop. 4 (5), 4, 71; Ov. M. 2, 249; id. P. 4, 10, 51; Sil. 8, 432; Just. 2, 4, 2.—Hence, Thermōdon-tēus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to the Thermodon, Thermodontean; poet. for Amazonian: agri, Prop. 3, 14 (4, 13), 14 (Müll. Thermodontiacis).— Thermōdontĭ-ăcus, a, um, adj., the same: turmae, Stat. S. 1, 6, 56: bipennis, i. e. of Penthesilea, the
thermodon.short: Thermōdon, ontis, m., = Θερμώδων, a river of Pontus, on which dwelt the Amazons, now Termeh Tchai, Mel.

thermopolium.full: thermŏpōlĭum, ii, n., = θερμοπώλιον, a place where warm drinks were sold, a pothouse, tap-house, tavern, Plaut. Curc. 2, 3, 13; id. Trin. 4, 3, 6; id. Rud. 2, 6, 45; id. Ps. 2, 4, 52.
thermopolium.short: thermŏpōlĭum, ii, n., = θερμοπώλιον, a place where warm drinks were sold, a pothouse, tap-house, tavern, Plaut.

thermopoto.full: thermŏpōto, āvi, āre, v. a. vox hibrida, θερμός-poto, to refresh with warm potations: gutturem, Plaut. Trin. 4, 3, 7.

thermopylae.full: Thermŏpўlae, ārum, f., = Θερμοπύλαι, the famous defile of Œta, where Leonidas fell, Mel. 2, 3, 6: saltus Thermopylarum, Liv. 36, 15, 5; 37, 58, 7; Cic. Off. 1, 18, 61; id. Tusc. 1, 42, 101; id. Sen. 10, 32; id. Fin. 2, 30, 97; Just. 2, 11, 2; Cat. 68, 54; Flor. 2, 8, 11; Nep. Them. 3, 4.
thermopylae.short: Thermŏpўlae, ārum, f., = Θερμοπύλαι, the famous defile of Œta, where Leonidas fell, Mel.

thermospodium.full: thermospŏdĭum, ii, n., = θερμοσπόδιον, hot, glowing ashes, embers, Apic. 4, 2 med.
thermospodium.short: thermospŏdĭum, ii, n., = θερμοσπόδιον, hot, glowing ashes, embers, Apic.

thermulae.full: thermŭlae, ārum, f. dim. thermae, a little warm bath, Mart. 6, 42, 1.

thermus.full: Thermus, i, m., a Roman cognomen in the Minucian gens: Q. Minucius Thermus, Cic. Fam. 2, 17, 6; 2, 17, 18; 2, 13, 53.
thermus.short: Thermus, i, m., a Roman cognomen in the Minucian gens: Q.

therodamas.full: Thērŏdămas, antis, m., = Θηροδἀμας (beast-feeder), a Scythian king, who fed lions with human flesh, Ov. P. 1, 2, 121.—Hence, Thērŏdămantēus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Therodamas, Therodamantean: leones, Ov. Ib. 385 (others read, in both places, Theromedon, Theromedonteus.)
therodamas.short: Thērŏdămas, antis, m., = Θηροδἀμας (beast-feeder), a Scythian king, who fed lions with human flesh, Ov.

thersites.full: Thersītes, ae, m., = Θερσίτης, a Greek before Troy, famous for his ugliness and scurrility, Ov. M. 13, 233; id. P. 3, 9, 10; Juv. 11, 31.—Hence, a contemptible person, Juv. 8, 269; and for a calumniator, reviler, Sen. Ira, 3, 23, 3.
thersites.short: Thersītes, ae, m., = Θερσίτης, a Greek before Troy, famous for his ugliness and scurrility, Ov.

thesaurarius.full: thēsaurārĭus, a, um, adj. thesaurus, of or belonging to treasure: fures, treasure-thieves, Plaut. Aul. 2, 8, 25.—Subst.: thēsaurārĭum, i, n., treasure (late Lat.), Cassiod. in Psa. 21, 31.

thesaurensis.full: thēsaurensis, is, m. id., a treasure-keeper, treasurer, Cod. Just. 12, 24, 2.

thesaurizator.full: thēsaurizātor, ōris, m. thesaurizo, one who lays up treasure (late Lat.), Hier. Interp. Orig. in Jer. Hom. 5.

thesaurizo.full: thēsaurizo, āre, v. n. and a. [thesaurus], to gather or lay up treasure (late Lat.). Lit., Vulg. Bar. 3, 18; Aug. Civ. Dei, 1, 10; Salv. adv. Avar. 1, 2; 1, 4 al.— Trop., to treasure up: disciplinam, Salv. adv. Avar. 3, 12: iram, id. Gub. Dei, 5, 9; Vulg. Jacob. 5, 3.

thesaurochrysonicochrysides.full: Thēsaurŏchrȳsŏnīcochrȳsĭdes (Thens-), ae, m., a facetiously-formed proper name, Plaut. Capt. 2, 2, 35.
thesaurochrysonicochrysides.short: Thēsaurŏchrȳsŏnīcochrȳsĭdes (Thens-), ae, m., a facetiously-formed proper name, Plaut.

thesaurus.full: thēsaurus (old form thensaurus, Plaut. Trin. prol. p. ciii. Ritschl; cf. Marin. Fratr. Arv. p. 590; collat. form thensau-rum, n., Petr. 46, 8), i, m., = θησαυρός. Any thing laid or stored up, a hoard, treasure, provision, store. Lit.: TABVLARIVS THENSAVRORVM, Inscr. Orell. 3247: thensaurum effodere, Plaut. Trin. 3, 3, 53; 4, 4, 8; id. Ps. 2, 2, 33; id. Aul. prol. 7: thesaurum defodere ... invenire, Cic. Div. 2, 65, 134: nec vero quemquam senem audivi oblitum, quo loco thesaurum obruisset, id. Se

theseus.full: Thēseus (dissyl.), -ĕï;, and -ĕos, m., = Θησεύς, a king of Athens, son of Ægeus (acc. to others, of Neptune) and Æthra; husband of Ariadne, and afterwards of Phædra; father of Hippolytus, by the Amazon Hippolyte; friend of Pirithoüs; conqueror of the highway-robbers Periphetes, Sinnis, etc., and of the Minotaur, Ov. M. 7, 433 sq.; id. H. 10, 3; Stat. Th. 12, 576; Cic. N. D. 3, 18, 45; 3, 31, 76; id. Fin. 1, 20, 65; Prop. 2, 14 (3, 6), 7; Ov. F. 6, 737; Verg. A. 6, 618; Hor. C. 4, 7, 27 al.—Hence
theseus.short: Thēseus (dissyl.), -ĕï;, and -ĕos, m., = Θησεύς, a king of Athens, son of Ægeus (acc.

thesion.full: thēsīon or -īum, ii, n., = θησεῖον, a plant, bastard toad - flax: Thesium linophyllum, Linn.; Plin. 21, 17, 67, § 107; 22, 22, 31, § 66.
thesion.short: thēsīon or -īum, ii, n., = θησεῖον, a plant, bastard toad - flax: Thesium linophyllum, Linn.;

thesis.full: thĕsis, is, f., = θέσις, in rhetoric, a proposition, thesis (pure Lat. propositum), Quint. 3, 5, 11; 3, 5, 14; 2, 4, 24; 7, 10, 5; 12, 2, 25; Sen. Contr. prooem.— In prosody, the falling of the voice, the thesis (opp. arsis), Mart. Cap. 9, §§ 974 and 985.
thesis.short: thĕsis, is, f., = θέσις, in rhetoric, a proposition, thesis (pure Lat.

thesmophoria.full: thesmŏphŏrĭa, ōrum, n., = θεσμοφόρια, τά, the festival of Demeter or Ceres (as lawgiver) among the Greeks, Plin. 24, 9, 38, § 59; Arn. 5, 173; Macr. S. 3, 12; Hyg. Fab. 147.
thesmophoria.short: thesmŏphŏrĭa, ōrum, n., = θεσμοφόρια, τά, the festival of Demeter or Ceres (as lawgiver) among the Greeks, Plin.

thespiae.full: Thespĭae, ārum, f., = Θεσπιαί, a town in Bœotia, at the south-eastern foot of Helicon, now the village of Lefka, near Rimokastro, Plin. 4, 7, 12, § 25; 36, 5, 4, § 22; Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 2, § 4; 2, 4, 60, § 135; id. Fam. 13, 22, 1; Liv. 42, 43 al.—Hence, The-spĭus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Thespiæ, Thespian; moenia, Val. Fl. 1, 478.— Plur.: Thespĭi, ōrum, m., the inhabitants of Thespiæ, Arn. 6, p. 196.— The-spienses, ĭum, m., the inhabitants of Thespiæ, Cic. Verr. 2,4,60, § 135.— Thespĭă-cu
thespiae.short: Thespĭae, ārum, f., = Θεσπιαί, a town in Bœotia, at the south-eastern foot of Helicon, now the village of Lefka, near Rimokastro, Plin.

thespis.full: Thespis, is, m., = Θέσπις, the founder of the Greek drama, Hor. A. P. 276; id. Ep. 2, 1, 163.
thespis.short: Thespis, is, m., = Θέσπις, the founder of the Greek drama, Hor.

thesproti.full: Thesprōti, ōrum, m., = Θεσπρωτοί, a people in the south-western part of Epirus, Luc. 3, 179; Liv. 43, 21, 4.—Their land was called Thesprōtĭa, ae, f., = Θεσπρωτία, Plin. 4, 1, 1, § 4; Cic. Att. 6, 3, 2.—Hence, Thesprōtĭus, a, um, adj., Thesprotian: sinus, Liv. 8, 24: arva, Sil. 15, 297.— Thesprōtis, ĭdis, adj. f., Thesprotian: terra, i. e. Thesprotia, Avien. Arat. 384.
thesproti.short: Thesprōti, ōrum, m., = Θεσπρωτοί, a people in the south-western part of Epirus, Luc.

thesprotus.full: Thesprōtus, i, m., = Θεσπρωτός, a king of the region about Puteoli, Hyg. Fab. 88; hence, Regnum Thesproti, i. e. Puteoli, Prop. 1, 11, 3 (al. Protei regnum).
thesprotus.short: Thesprōtus, i, m., = Θεσπρωτός, a king of the region about Puteoli, Hyg.

thessalia.full: Thessălĭa, ae, f., = Θεσσαλία, the country of Thessaly, Mel. 2, 3, 4; Plin. 4, 8, 15, § 29; Luc. 6, 333 sq.; Cat. 64, 10; 64, 26; Prop. 1, 5, 28; Cic. Pis. 40, 96; id. Fl. 26, 63. — Hence, Thessălĭus, a, um, adj. (poet. and late Lat.), of or belonging to Thessaly, Thessalian: regio, App. M. 1, p. 113: decus, Grat. Cyn. 228.— Thessălĭcus, a, um, adj., of Thessaly, Thessalian (class.): juga, Ov. H. 9, 100: Tempe, Plin. 16, 44, 92, § 244: equi, Varr. R. R. 2, 7, 6: dux, i. e. Jason, Val. Fl. 5, 219
thessalia.short: Thessălĭa, ae, f., = Θεσσαλία, the country of Thessaly, Mel.

thessalonica.full: Thessălŏnīca, ae, or -ē, ēs, f., = Θεσσαλονίκη, a city of Macedonia, on the Sinus Thermaicus, now Saloniki, Mel. 2, 3, 1; Plin. 4, 10, 17, § 36; Cic. Planc. 41, 99; id. Q. Fr. 1, 4, 2; Liv. 39, 27 al. — Hence, Thessălŏnīcenses, ium, m., the inhabitants of Thessalonica, Cic. Prov. Cons. 2, 4; id. Pis. 34, 84.
thessalonica.short: Thessălŏnīca, ae, or -ē, ēs, f., = Θεσσαλονίκη, a city of Macedonia, on the Sinus Thermaicus, now Saloniki, Mel.

thessalonice.full: Thessălŏnīcē, ēs, f., a daughter of Philip, king of Macedon, Just. 14, 6, 3; 14, 6, 13; 16, 1, 1.
thessalonice.short: Thessălŏnīcē, ēs, f., a daughter of Philip, king of Macedon, Just.

thessalus.full: Thessălus, a, um, v. Thessalia, C.

thestius.full: Thestĭus, ii, m., = Θέστιος, a king of Ætolia, father of Leda and Althæa, and of Plexippus and Toxeus, Ov. M. 8, 487; Hyg. Fab. 77; 155; 174.—Hence, Thestĭă-des, ae, m., a (male) descendant of Thestius: duo, i. e. Plexippus and Toxeus, Ov. M. 8, 304 and 434: respice Thestiaden, i. e. Meleager, son of Althæa, id. F. 5, 305. — Thestĭas, ădis, f., the daughter of Thestius, i. e. Althæa, Ov. M. 8, 452; 8, 473; id. Tr. 1, 7, 18.
thestius.short: Thestĭus, ii, m., = Θέστιος, a king of Ætolia, father of Leda and Althæa, and of Plexippus and Toxeus, Ov.

thestor.full: Thestor, ŏris, m., = Θέστωρ, the father of the soothsayer Calchas, Hyg. Fab. 128.— Hence, Thestŏrĭdes, ae, m., the son of Thestor, i. e. Calchas, Ov. M. 12, 19; 12, 27; Stat. Achill. 1, 496.
thestor.short: Thestor, ŏris, m., = Θέστωρ, the father of the soothsayer Calchas, Hyg.
