theta.full: thēta, indecl. n., = θῆτα, the Greek letter θ; as the initial letter of the word θάνατος (death), written by the Greeks upon their voting-tablets in sign of condemnation, Mart. 7, 37, 2; Aus. Epigr. 128 (cf. Pers. 4, 13).—Upon Latin epitaphs, = OBIIT, MORTVVS EST, Inscr. Orell. 4472 sq.; cf. Marin. Fratr. Arv. p. 610.—Appended to a passage as a critical mark of censure, Sid. Carm. 9, 335.

thetidium.full: Thĕtĭdĭum, ii, n., = Θετίδιον, a town of Thessaly, Liv. 33, 6 and 7.
thetidium.short: Thĕtĭdĭum, ii, n., = Θετίδιον, a town of Thessaly, Liv.

thetis.full: Thĕtis, ĭdis, or ĭdos (abl. also Theti; v. the foll.; ante-class. collat. form Thĕlis, Enn. ap. Varr. L. L. 7, § 87 Müll., or Trag. v. 431 Vahl.; cf.: antiqui ut Thetin Thelim dicebant, sic Medicam Melicam vocabant, Varr. R. R. 3, 9, 19), f., = Θέτις, a sea-nymph, daughter of Nereus and Doris, wife of Peleus, and mother of Achilles, Plaut. Truc. 4, 2, 17; Hyg. Fab. 54; 244; Ov. M. 11, 221 sq.; 11, 400; Cat. 64, 21; Hor. C. 1, 8, 14; 4, 6, 6 al.; abl. Thetide, Hor. Epod. 13, 12: Theti, Plaut. Ep.

theudoria.full: Theudorĭa, ae, f., a town of Athamania, now Thodhoriana, Liv. 38, 1.
theudoria.short: Theudorĭa, ae, f., a town of Athamania, now Thodhoriana, Liv.

theuma.full: Theuma, n., a village of Thessaly, Liv. 32, 13 fin.
theuma.short: Theuma, n., a village of Thessaly, Liv.

theumesus.full: Theumēsus, i, m., a mountain of Bœotia, near Thebes, Stat. Th. 4, 372. — Hence, Theumēsius, a, um, adj., Theban, amnis, i. e. Ismenus, Stat. Th. 8, 462: arva, id. ib. 2, 383: juvenis, i. e. Polynices, id. ib. 2, 331.
theumesus.short: Theumēsus, i, m., a mountain of Bœotia, near Thebes, Stat.

theurgia.full: thĕurgĭa, ae, f., = θεουργία, a summoning of spirits, magic, theurgy, Aug. Civ. Dei, 10, 9 and 10.
theurgia.short: thĕurgĭa, ae, f., = θεουργία, a summoning of spirits, magic, theurgy, Aug.

theurgicus.full: thĕurgĭcus, a, um, adj., = θεουργικός, spirit-summoning, magic, theurgic: ars, Aug. Civ. Dei, 10, 10: consecratio, id. ib. 10, 9.
theurgicus.short: thĕurgĭcus, a, um, adj., = θεουργικός, spirit-summoning, magic, theurgic: ars, Aug.

theurgus.full: thĕurgus, i, m., = θεουργός, one who summons spirits, a magician, theurgist, Aug. Civ. Dei, 10, 10.
theurgus.short: thĕurgus, i, m., = θεουργός, one who summons spirits, a magician, theurgist, Aug.

thia.full: Thīa, ae, f., = Θεία. The wife of Hyperion, and mother of Sol, Cat. 66, 44.— An island near Crete, Mel. 2, 7; Plin. 4, 12, 23, § 70; 2, 87, 89, § 202.

thiasus.full: thĭăsus (thўăsus), i, m., = θίασος, the Bacchic dance, a dance performed in honor of Bacchus, Verg. E. 5, 30; id. A. 7, 581; Stat. S. 3, 1, 41; Cat. 63, 28; 64, 253.
thiasus.short: thĭăsus (thўăsus), i, m., = θίασος, the Bacchic dance, a dance performed in honor of Bacchus, Verg.

thiatis.full: Thĭătis, is, m. Egypt., the name of one of the Egyptian months, answering to August, Plin. 27, 12, 80, § 105 (al. Thoti).

thibii.full: Thibii, ōrum, m., a fabulous people of Pontus, Plin. 7, 2, 2, § 17.
thibii.short: Thibii, ōrum, m., a fabulous people of Pontus, Plin.

thieldones.full: thieldones, um, m. Span., a kind of Spanish horse, Plin. 8, 42, 67, § 166.

thimanli.full: Thimanli, ōrum, m., a people of Arabia, Plin. 6, 28, 32, § 157.
thimanli.short: Thimanli, ōrum, m., a people of Arabia, Plin.

thirmida.full: Thirmida, ae, f., a town of Numidia, Sall. J. 12, 3.
thirmida.short: Thirmida, ae, f., a town of Numidia, Sall.

thisbe.full: Thisbē, ēs, f., = Θίσβη. A little town on the coast of Bœotia, celebrated for its wild doves, now Kakosia, Plin. 4, 7, 12, § 26; Stat. Th. 7, 261; 9, 768.—Hence, This-baeus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Thisbe, Thisbæan: columbae, Ov. M. 11, 300.— A maiden beloved by Pyramus, Ov. M. 4, 55 sq.

thlasias.full: thlasĭas, ae, m., = θλασίας (the crushed), one made a eunuch by bruising; called also thlibĭas, = θλιβίας (the pressed), Dig. 50, 16, 128; 48, 8, 5.
thlasias.short: thlasĭas, ae, m., = θλασίας (the crushed), one made a eunuch by bruising;

thlaspi.full: thlaspi, is, n., = θλάσπι, a kind of cress, Plin. 27, 13, 113, § 139; Cels. 5, 23, 3; Scrib. Comp. 170.
thlaspi.short: thlaspi, is, n., = θλάσπι, a kind of cress, Plin.

thoas.full: Thŏas, antis, m., = Θόας. A king of the Chersonesus Taurica, under whom Iphigenia was priestess of the Tauric Diana; he was slain by Orestes, Ov. P. 3, 2, 59; id. Tr. 1, 9, 28; 4, 4, 66.—Hence, Thŏantēus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Thoas; poet. for Tauric: Diana, Val. Fl. 8, 208; Sil. 14, 260; called also dea, Ov. Ib. 386. — A king of Lemnos, father of Hypsipyle, by whom he was conveyed to Chios, when the women of Lemnos slew all the men there, Hyg. Fab. 15; Ov. H. 6, 135; id. M. 13, 399; S

thocum.full: thōcum genus sellae habetur apud Plautum, Fest. p. 367 Müll. [ = θῶκος].
thocum.short: thōcum genus sellae habetur apud Plautum, Fest.

tholus.full: thŏlus, i, m., = θόλος, a dome, cupola, a rotunda (syn.: fornix, testudo), Varr. R. R. 3, 5, 12; id. ap. Non. 448, 22; Vitr. 4, 7; 7, 5 med.; Ov. F. 6, 282; 6, 296; Mart. 2, 59, 2. — In the tholi of the temple the votive gifts were suspended, Verg. A. 9, 408; Stat. S. 1, 4, 32; id. Th. 2, 734; Val. Fl. 1, 56.
tholus.short: thŏlus, i, m., = θόλος, a dome, cupola, a rotunda (syn.: fornix, testudo), Varr.

thomix.full: thōmix (thōmex, tōmex, and tō-mix), icis, f., = θώμιξ, a cord, string, line, thread, Lucil. ap. Fest. pp. 356 and 357 Müll.; Vitr. 7, 3; Col. 12, 32; Plin. 17, 10, 11, § 62; Pall. 1, 13, 1.
thomix.short: thōmix (thōmex, tōmex, and tō-mix), icis, f., = θώμιξ, a cord, string, line, thread, Lucil.

thoracatus.full: thōrācātus, a, um, adj. thorax, armed with a breastplate or corselet (Plinian): navarchus, Plin. 35, 10, 36, § 69: effigies Neronis, id. 37, 9, 37, § 118.

thoraciculus.full: thōrācĭcŭlus, i, m. (dim. of thorax), a little bust (late Lat.), Aldh. Laud. Virg. 14.

thorax.full: thōrax, ācis, m. (but f. Treb. Poll. Claud. 3, 3), = θώραξ, the breast, chest, thorax. Lit., in anatomy, Cels. 5, 25, 8; Plin. 27, 7, 28, § 49.— Transf. A defence, armor, or covering for the breast, a breastplate, corselet, cuirass; a doublet, stomacher (syn. lorica), Liv. 4, 20, 7; Suet. Aug. 82; Verg. A. 10, 337; Mart. 7, 1, 1.— Dat. thoracibus, Val. Fl. 3, 87.—Gen. thoracum, Claud. in Ruf. 2, 260.— A bust, Treb. Claud. Goth. 3.

thorius.full: Thŏrĭus, i, m., the name of a Roman gens; thus, Sp. Thorius Balbus, a tribune of the people, author of the agrarian law, called, after him, Lex Thoria, Cic. Brut. 36, 136; id. de Or. 2, 70, 284; cf. Orell. Index Legg. s. h. v.—Another Thorius, Flor. 3, 22, 6.
thorius.short: Thŏrĭus, i, m., the name of a Roman gens;

thos.full: thōs, ōïs, m., = θώς, a kind of wolf, Plin. 8, 34, 52, § 123; 10, 74, 95, § 206; Grat. Cyn. 253; Sol. 30, 28.
thos.short: thōs, ōïs, m., = θώς, a kind of wolf, Plin.

thoth.full: Thoth, indecl. Egypt., the Egyptian name of the fifth Mercury, Cic. N. D. 3, 22, 56; Lact. 1, 6, 3.

thraca.full: Thrāca, ae, and Thrācē, ēs, v. Thracia.
thraca.short: Thrāca, ae, and Thrācē, ēs, v.

thracia.full: Thrācĭa and Thrēcĭa, ae, f., = Θρᾴκη, Thrace, Mel. 2, 2, 3; Plin. 4, 11, 18, § 40; Varr. R. R. 1, 57, 2; 2, 1, 5; Liv. 44, 27; Ov. M. 6, 435; Luc. 2, 162.—Called also, after the Greek, Thrācē, ēs, Cic. Rep. 2, 4, 9; Ov. F. 5, 257; id. P. 4, 5, 5; Hor. C. 2, 16, 5; 3, 25, 11; and, Latinized, Thrāca, ae, Verg. A. 12, 335; Hor. Ep. 1, 3, 3; 1, 16, 13; Cic. Fragm. ap. Serv. Verg. l. l. (but the Cod. palimps. Rep. 2, 4, 9, has in this passage Thracia).—After the Greek form Θρῄκη, also Thrēcē, ēs, Ov.
thracia.short: Thrācĭa and Thrēcĭa, ae, f., = Θρᾴκη, Thrace, Mel.

thranis.full: thranis, is, m., = θράνις, a fish, called also xiphias, Plin. 32, 11, 53, § 151.
thranis.short: thranis, is, m., = θράνις, a fish, called also xiphias, Plin.

thrascias.full: Thrascĭas, ae, m., = θρασκίας, the north-by-a-third-northwest wind, Vitr. 1, 6 med.; Plin. 2, 47, 46, § 120; cf. Sen. Q. N. 5, 16, 6.
thrascias.short: Thrascĭas, ae, m., = θρασκίας, the north-by-a-third-northwest wind, Vitr.

thrasea.full: Thrasĕa, ae, m., a Roman name, esp. P. Thrasea Paetus, a Stoic philosopher, put to death by Nero, Tac. H. 2, 5; 2, 7; id. Agr. 2; id. A. 13, 49; 14, 12; Juv. 5, 36; Mart. 1, 9; Suet. Ner. 37; id. Dom. 10; Plin. Ep. 8, 22, 3.
thrasea.short: Thrasĕa, ae, m., a Roman name, esp.

thraso.full: Thrăso, ōnis, m., = Θράσων. The name of a braggart soldier in Terence's Eunuch; hence, Thrăsōnĭānus, a, um, adj., Thrasonian, i. e. bragging, vainglorious, Sid. Ep. 1, 9 fin.— A friend of Hieronymus, king of Syracuse, Liv. 24, 5.

thrasybulus.full: Thrăsўbūlus, i, m., = Θρασύβουλος, the liberator of Athens, his native city, from the thirty tyrants. His life is written by Cornelius Nepos; cf. also Cic. Att. 8, 3, 6; Val. Max. 4, 1, ext. 4; 5, 6, ext. 2.
thrasybulus.short: Thrăsўbūlus, i, m., = Θρασύβουλος, the liberator of Athens, his native city, from the thirty tyrants.

thrasyllus.full: Thrăsyllus, i, m., = Θράσυλλος, the court astrologer of Tiberius, Juv. 6, 576.
thrasyllus.short: Thrăsyllus, i, m., = Θράσυλλος, the court astrologer of Tiberius, Juv.

thrasymachus.full: Thrăsўmăchus, i, m., = Θρασύμαχος, a celebrated Grecian sophist of Chalcedon, Cic. de Or. 3, 16, 59; 3, 32, 128; id. Or. 12, 39; 13, 40; id. Brut. 8, 30; Quint. 3, 1, 10; 3, 3, 4; Juv. 7, 204 (where Ritschl, in Rhein. Mus. Neue Folge, 9, p. 480, reads Tharsymachi; many MSS. have Thresimachi).
thrasymachus.short: Thrăsўmăchus, i, m., = Θρασύμαχος, a celebrated Grecian sophist of Chalcedon, Cic.

thrausi.full: Thrausi, ōrum, m., a Thracian people, Liv. 38, 41.
thrausi.short: Thrausi, ōrum, m., a Thracian people, Liv.

thrauston.full: thrauston, i, n., = θραυστόν, a kind of metopion (gum), Plin. 12, 23, 49, § 107.
thrauston.short: thrauston, i, n., = θραυστόν, a kind of metopion (gum), Plin.

threcicus.full: Thrēcĭcus, a, um, v. Thracia, C.

threcidicus.full: Thrēcĭdĭcus, a, um, v. Thracia, E. 2. b.

threicius.full: Thrēĭcĭus, a, um, v. Thracia, D.

threissa.full: Thrēïssa, ae, or Thressa, ae, v. Thracia, F.
threissa.short: Thrēïssa, ae, or Thressa, ae, v.

threnus.full: thrēnus, i, m., = θρῆνος, a song of mourning, a lamentation, dirge, elegy (syn. planctus), Aus. Prof. 5, 3; 7, 3; 14, 5.
threnus.short: thrēnus, i, m., = θρῆνος, a song of mourning, a lamentation, dirge, elegy (syn.

thridax.full: thrĭdax, ăcis, f., = θρίδαξ, wild lettuce, Ser. Samm. 24, 448; App. Herb. 30.
thridax.short: thrĭdax, ăcis, f., = θρίδαξ, wild lettuce, Ser.

thrips.full: thrips, ĭpis, m., = θρίψ, a wood-worm. Lit., Plin. 16, 41, 80, § 220.— Transf., trifles, worthless things, = quisquiliae, Mart. Cap. 2, § 164 (al. thriptes).
thrips.short: thrips, ĭpis, m., = θρίψ, a wood-worm.

thronium.full: Thrŏnĭum (-on), ii, n., a town of the Locri Epicnemidii on the Boagrius, Liv. 32, 36; 33, 3; 35, 37; Plin. 4, 7, 12, § 27.
thronium.short: Thrŏnĭum (-on), ii, n., a town of the Locri Epicnemidii on the Boagrius, Liv.

thronus.full: thrŏnus, i, m., = θρόνος, an elevated seat, a throne (syn. solium): Jovis, Plin. 35, 9, 36, § 63; Poët. ap. Suet. Aug. 70: dei, Prud. Hamart. 10 praef.; Auct. Pervig. Ven. 7: Thronos Caesaris, one of the constellations, Plin. 2, 70, 71, § 178.— An angelic order: sive throni, sive dominationes, Vulg. Col. 1, 16.
thronus.short: thrŏnus, i, m., = θρόνος, an elevated seat, a throne (syn.

thryallis.full: thryallis, ĭdis, f., = θρυαλλίς, the name of two different plants. A plant, called also lychnitis, Plin. 25, 10, 74, § 121. — An ear-shaped plant, Plin. 21, 17, 61, § 101.
thryallis.short: thryallis, ĭdis, f., = θρυαλλίς, the name of two different plants.

thucydides.full: Thūcȳdĭdes, is, m., = Θουκυδίδης, a celebrated Greek historian, Cic. Or. 9, 30 sq.; 65, 219; id. Brut. 83, 287 sq.; id. de Or. 2, 13, 56; Quint. 10, 1, 73. — Hence, Thūcȳdĭdīus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Thucydides, Thucydidian: genus (orationis), Cic. Opt. Gen. 6, 16. — Subst. plur.: Thūcȳdĭdĭi, ŏrum, m., imitators of Thucydides, Cic. Or. 9, 30.
thucydides.short: Thūcȳdĭdes, is, m., = Θουκυδίδης, a celebrated Greek historian, Cic.

thule.full: Thūlē (Thȳlē), ēs, f., = Θούλη or Θύλη, an island in the extreme nortl of Europe; acc. to some, Iceland; acc. to others, Mainland (the largest of the Shetland lslands), Mel. 3, 6, 9; Plin. 2, 75, 77, § 187; 4, 16, 30, § 104; 6, 34, 39, § 220; Tac. Agr. 10; Stat. S. 3, 5, 20; 4, 4, 62; Claud. III. Cons. Hon. 53.
thule.short: Thūlē (Thȳlē), ēs, f., = Θούλη or Θύλη, an island in the extreme nortl of Europe;

thunnarius.full: thunnārĭus (thynn-), a, um, adj. thunnus, of or belonging to the tunny, tunny-: piscatio, Dig. 8, 4, 13.

thunnus.full: thunnus (thynnus), i, m., = θύννος, the tunny or tunny - fish: Scomber thynnus, Linn.; Plin. 9, 15, 17, § 44 sq.; Hor. S. 2, 5, 44; Ov. Hal. 98; Mart. 10, 48, 12.
thunnus.short: thunnus (thynnus), i, m., = θύννος, the tunny or tunny - fish: Scomber thynnus, Linn.;

thuralis.full: thūrālis, thūrārĭus, thūrĕus, thūrĭbŭlum, etc., v. tur-.
thuralis.short: thūrālis, thūrārĭus, thūrĕus, thūrĭbŭlum, etc., v.

thuriae.full: Thūrĭae, ārum, f., = Θουπίαι, a town in Calabria, in the territory of the Salentines, Liv. 10, 2; 25, 15; 27, 1.
thuriae.short: Thūrĭae, ārum, f., = Θουπίαι, a town in Calabria, in the territory of the Salentines, Liv.

thurii.full: Thūrĭi, ōrum, m., = Θούριοι, a city of Lucania, on the Tarentine Gulf, built upon the site of the ancient Sybaris, Varr. R. R. 1, 7, 6; Cic. Att. 9, 19, 3 (and perh., also, id. ib. 9, 3, 5); Caes. B. C. 3, 22; Tac. A. 14, 21; Suet. Aug. 2; Liv. 25, 15, 9. — Called also Thūrĭum, ii, n., = Θούριον, Mel. 2, 4, 8; Plin. 3, 11, 15, § 67; Cic. Att. 3, 5 (Thurii, where, perh., Turiis should be read).— Hence, Thūrīnus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Thurii, Thurine: ager, Cic. Tull. 14; Caes. B. C. 3,
thurii.short: Thūrĭi, ōrum, m., = Θούριοι, a city of Lucania, on the Tarentine Gulf, built upon the site of the ancient Sybaris, Varr.

thya.full: thȳa or thȳia, ae, f., = θύα or θυΐα, the Greek name for the citrus-tree, Plin. 13, 16, 30, § 100; Prop. 3, 7 (4, 6), 49.
thya.short: thȳa or thȳia, ae, f., = θύα or θυΐα, the Greek name for the citrus-tree, Plin.

thyamis.full: Thўămis, is, m., = Θύαμις, a river in Epirus, now the Calamas, Plin. 4, 1, 1, § 4; Cic. Att. 7, 2, 3; id. Leg. 2, 3, 7.
thyamis.short: Thўămis, is, m., = Θύαμις, a river in Epirus, now the Calamas, Plin.

thyatira.full: Thyatīra, ae, f., = Θυάτειρα, a town of Lydia, now Ak-hissar, Liv. 37, 44, 4; Plin. 5, 29, 31, § 115; also, Thyatīra, ōrum, n., Liv. 37, 8, 7. — Hence, Thyatīrēni, ōrum, m., the inhabitants of Thyatira, Plin. 5, 30, 33, § 126.
thyatira.short: Thyatīra, ae, f., = Θυάτειρα, a town of Lydia, now Ak-hissar, Liv.

thyene.full: Thўēnē, ēs, f., one of the Hyades who nursed Jupiter and Bacchus, Ov. F. 6, 711.
thyene.short: Thўēnē, ēs, f., one of the Hyades who nursed Jupiter and Bacchus, Ov.

thyestes.full: Thўestes, ae, m., = Θυέστης, son of Pelops and brother of Atreus, who set before him for food the flesh of his own son; he was the father of Ægisthus, Hyg. Fab. 88; Plaut. Rud. 2, 6, 25; Cic. Tusc. 3, 12, 26; Hor. A. P. 91; id. C. 1, 16, 17; Pers. 5, 8.— Hence, Thўestēus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Thyestes, Thyestean: Mycenae, Luc. 1, 544: mensa, Ov. P. 4, 6, 47; id. M. 15, 462: exsecratio, Cic. Pis. 19, 43; cf. preces, Hor. Epod. 5, 86: more furere, Sen. Contr. 1, 1 med.— Thўestĭădes, ae,
thyestes.short: Thўestes, ae, m., = Θυέστης, son of Pelops and brother of Atreus, who set before him for food the flesh of his own son;

thyias.full: Thȳiăs (dissyl.) or Thȳăs, ădis, f., = Θυιάς or Θυάς, a Bacchante, Verg. A. 4, 302; Hor. C. 3, 15, 10; Stat. Th. 5, 92.—More freq. in plur.: Thȳiădes or Thȳădes, um, Bacchantes, Cat. 64, 392; Hor. C. 2, 19, 9; Ov. F. 6, 514; Stat. Th. 12, 791.
thyias.short: Thȳiăs (dissyl.) or Thȳăs, ădis, f., = Θυιάς or Θυάς, a Bacchante, Verg.

thyinus.full: thȳĭnus, a, um, adj., = θύϊνος, made of the citrus-tree, Vulg. 3 Reg. 10, 11; id. Apoc. 18, 12.
thyinus.short: thȳĭnus, a, um, adj., = θύϊνος, made of the citrus-tree, Vulg.

thymbra1.full: thymbra, ae, f., = θύμβρα, a plant, savory: Satureia hortensis, Linn.; Plin. 19, 8, 50, § 165; Col. 9, 4, 6; 9, 10, 233; Verg. G. 4, 31; Stat. S. 1, 2, 21; Petr. 135.
thymbra1.short: thymbra, ae, f., = θύμβρα, a plant, savory: Satureia hortensis, Linn.;

thymbra2.full: Thymbra, ae, or Thymbrē, ēs, f., = Θύμβρη, a city in Troas, with a temple of Apollo, Plin. 5, 30, 33, § 126 (dub.; al. Cambre); Stat. S. 4, 7, 22.—Hence, Thym-braeus, i, m., the Thymbræan, an epithet of Apollo, Verg. A. 3, 85; cf. Macr. S. 1, 17, and Fest. p. 356 Müll.— thymbrae-um, i, n., another name for the sisymbrium silvestre, Plin. 20, 22, 91, § 247.
thymbra2.short: Thymbra, ae, or Thymbrē, ēs, f., = Θύμβρη, a city in Troas, with a temple of Apollo, Plin.

thymela.full: thўmĕla, ae, and thўmĕlē, ēs, f., = θυμέλη, an elevation in the centre of the orchestra of a Greek theatre, in the form of an altar, upon which stood the leader of the chorus, Sid. Ep. 9, 13; Cod. Th. 8, 7, 21; Inscr. Spon. Miscell. Ant. p. 148.
thymela.short: thўmĕla, ae, and thўmĕlē, ēs, f., = θυμέλη, an elevation in the centre of the orchestra of a Greek theatre, in the form of an altar, upon which stood the leader of the chorus, Sid.

thymelaea.full: thўmĕlaea, ae, f., = θυμέλαια, a plant, the flax - leaved daphne: Daphne Gnidium, Linn.; Plin. 13, 21, 35, § 114.
thymelaea.short: thўmĕlaea, ae, f., = θυμέλαια, a plant, the flax - leaved daphne: Daphne Gnidium, Linn.;

thymele.full: Thўmĕlē, ēs, f., a celebrated female dancer, Juv. 1, 36; 8, 197; Mart. 1, 5, 5.
thymele.short: Thўmĕlē, ēs, f., a celebrated female dancer, Juv.

thymelicus.full: thўmĕlĭcus, a, um, adj., = θυμελικός. Lit., of or belonging to the thymele or to the orchestra; hence, subst.: thў-mĕlĭci, ōrum, m., theatrical musicians (opp. scaenici, actors), Vitr. 5, 8; Dig. 3, 2, 4 init.— Transf., in gen., = scaenicus, of or belonging to the theatre: choragium, App. Mag. p. 282: Thymelica obscenitas, Aug. Civ. Dei, 6, 7 fin. — Substt. thў-mĕlĭcus, i, m., an actor, Cod. Th. 15, 7, 12; Inscr. Orell. 2589. — thўmĕlĭca, ae, f., an actress, Cod. Th. 15, 7, 5.

thymiama.full: thȳmĭāma, ătis, n., = θυμίαμα, a composition for fumigating, incense, Cels. 5, 18, 7 sq.; 6, 6, 25; Vulg. Exod. 25, 6.
thymiama.short: thȳmĭāma, ătis, n., = θυμίαμα, a composition for fumigating, incense, Cels.

thymiamaterium.full: thȳmĭāmătērĭum, ii, n. thymiama, a censer, a vessel for incense, Vulg. Jer. 52, 19.—Called also thȳmātērĭum, Ambros. Ep. 5, 3; Vulg. 2 Par. 4, 22.

thymiamus.full: thўmĭămus, a, um, a false read. in Plaut. Bacch. 5, 2, 10; v. Ritschl ad h. l.
thymiamus.short: thўmĭămus, a, um, a false read.

thyminus.full: thўmĭnus, a, um, adj., = θύμινος, of thyme, made of thyme: mel, Col. 6, 33, 2; cf. thymosus.
thyminus.short: thўmĭnus, a, um, adj., = θύμινος, of thyme, made of thyme: mel, Col.

thymion.full: thўmĭon, ii, n., = θύμιον, a kind of wart, Plin. 32, 10, 45, § 128.
thymion.short: thўmĭon, ii, n., = θύμιον, a kind of wart, Plin.

thymites.full: thўmītes, ae, m., = θυμίτης (οἶνος), thyme-wine, Col. 12, 35, 1.
thymites.short: thўmītes, ae, m., = θυμίτης (οἶνος), thyme-wine, Col.

thymosus.full: thўmōsus, a, um, adj. thymum, full of thyme, thymy: mel, Plin. 11, 15, 15, § 39; cf. thyminus.

thymum.full: thўmum, i, n., = θύμον, thyme (both the common or Roman, Thymus vulgaris, Linn., and the Cretan or Greek, Satureia capitata, ib.), Plin. 21, 21, 89, § 154; Quint. 12, 10, 25; Verg. E. 7, 37; id. A. 1, 436; Hor. C. 1, 17, 6; 4, 2, 29; id. Ep. 1, 3, 21; Ov. M. 15, 80.—In plur., Ov. F. 5, 272; id. A. A. 1, 96; Mart. 11, 42, 4 al.
thymum.short: thўmum, i, n., = θύμον, thyme (both the common or Roman, Thymus vulgaris, Linn., and the Cretan or Greek, Satureia capitata, ib.), Plin.

thyni.full: Thȳni, ōrum, m., = Θυνοί, a Thracian people, who emigrated to Bithynia, Plin. 4, 11, 18, § 41; 5, 32, 43, § 150; Cat. 25, 7.— Hence, Thȳnus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to the Thyni, Thynian; poet. for Bithynian: merx, Hor. C. 3, 7, 3 (for which: Bithyna negotia, id. Ep. 1, 6, 33).— Thȳ-nĭa, ae, f., the seat of the Thyni in Bithynia, Cat. 31, 5.— Thȳnĭăcus, a, um, adj., Thyniac: sinus, i. e. of the Euxine in Thrace, Ov. Tr. 1, 10, 35.— Thȳnĭăs, ădis, adj. f., Thynian; poet. for Bithynian: grata
thyni.short: Thȳni, ōrum, m., = Θυνοί, a Thracian people, who emigrated to Bithynia, Plin.

thynus.full: Thȳnus, a, um, v. Thyni, A.

thyone.full: Thўōnē, ēs, f., = Θυώνη, the mother of the fifth Bacchus, enumerated in Cic. N. D. 3, 23, 58.—Hence, Thўōneus, ĕi, m., the son of Thyone, i. e. Bacchus: indetonsus, Ov. M. 4, 13: Semeleius, Hor. C. 1, 17, 23.— Thўōnĭānus, i, m., the son of Thyone, i. e. Bacchus, Aus. Idyll. 13 praef. —Meton., for wine, Cat. 27, 8.
thyone.short: Thўōnē, ēs, f., = Θυώνη, the mother of the fifth Bacchus, enumerated in Cic.

thyotes.full: thўōtes, ae, m., = θυώτης, a sacrificer: sacerdos, Val. Fl. 2, 438 (perh. as nom. prop.).
thyotes.short: thўōtes, ae, m., = θυώτης, a sacrificer: sacerdos, Val.

thyraeus.full: thўraeus, a, um, adj., = θυραῖος, of or belonging to a door, a gate: Apollo, the god of the entrance, Tert. Mil. 13 fin.
thyraeus.short: thўraeus, a, um, adj., = θυραῖος, of or belonging to a door, a gate: Apollo, the god of the entrance, Tert.

thyre.full: Thўrē, ēs, f., = Θύρη, a little town in the Peloponnesus, the possession of which was contested by the Argives and the Lacedæmonians, Stat. Th. 4, 48.—Hence, Thў-rĕātis, ĭdis, adj. f., Thyreatic: terra, the region of Thyre, Ov. F. 2, 663.
thyre.short: Thўrē, ēs, f., = Θύρη, a little town in the Peloponnesus, the possession of which was contested by the Argives and the Lacedæmonians, Stat.

thyreum.full: Thyrĕum or Thyrĭum, ii, n., a town in Acarnania, near Leucas, Cic. Fam. 16, 5, 1; Liv. 36, 11; 36, 12; 38, 9.—Hence, Thyrĭenses, ĭum, m., the inhabitants of Thyreum, Liv. 36, 12.
thyreum.short: Thyrĕum or Thyrĭum, ii, n., a town in Acarnania, near Leucas, Cic.

thyroma.full: thўrōma, ătis, n., = θύρωμα, a door, Vitr. 4, 6.
thyroma.short: thўrōma, ătis, n., = θύρωμα, a door, Vitr.

thyrsagetae.full: Thyrsăgĕtae, Thyssăgĕtae, or Thussăgĕtae, ārum, m., a people of Asiatic Sarmatia, on the Wolga, Val. Fl. 6, 140; Mel. 1, 19, 19; Plin. 4, 12, 26, § 88.— Sing.: Thyrsagĕtes, ae, m., Val. Fl. 6, 135.
thyrsagetae.short: Thyrsăgĕtae, Thyssăgĕtae, or Thussăgĕtae, ārum, m., a people of Asiatic Sarmatia, on the Wolga, Val.

thyrsiculus.full: thyrsĭcŭlus, i, m. dim. thyrsus, a little stalk, App. Herb. 68.

thyrsiger.full: thyrsĭger, gĕra, gĕrum, adj. thyrsusgero, bearing the thyrsus or Bacchic staff: Lyaeus, Sen. Med. 110: India, id. Hippol. 753: Bacchus, Pall. Insit. 87.

thyrsis.full: Thyrsis, ĭdis, m., = Θύρσις, the name of a shepherd, Verg. E. 7, 2.
thyrsis.short: Thyrsis, ĭdis, m., = Θύρσις, the name of a shepherd, Verg.

thyrsus.full: thyrsus, i, m., = θύρσος, a stalk, stem of a plant. Lit., Plin. 19, 8, 39, § 129; 25, 8, 41, § 81; 26, 8, 33, § 51; Suet. Aug. 77; Col. 10, 370.— Transf. A staff twined round with ivy and vine-shoots, borne by Bacchus and the Bacchantes; the Bacchic staff, thyrsus, Hor. C. 2, 19, 8; Ov. M. 3, 542; 3, 712; 4, 7; 9, 641; 11, 28; Stat. Th. 9, 614; Sen. Herc. Fur. 904; id. Oedip. 628 al. — Hence, poet. transf., A thorn, goad: acri Percussit thyrso laudis spes magna meum cor, Lucr. 1, 923; Ov. Tr. 4,
thyrsus.short: thyrsus, i, m., = θύρσος, a stalk, stem of a plant.

tiara.full: tĭāra, ae, f., or tĭāras, ae, m., = τιάρα or τιάρας, the head-dress of the Orientals, a turban, tiara: rectam capite tiaram gerens, Sen. Ben. 6, 31, 8: sceptrumque sacerque tiaras, Verg. A. 7, 247; cf. Plaut. Pers. 4, 2, 2; Ov. M. 11, 181; Val. Fl. 6, 700; Juv. 6, 516; 10, 267; Just. 1, 2, 3; App. M. 10, p. 253, 30.
tiara.short: tĭāra, ae, f., or tĭāras, ae, m., = τιάρα or τιάρας, the head-dress of the Orientals, a turban, tiara: rectam capite tiaram gerens, Sen.

tiaratus.full: tĭārātus, a, um, adj. tiara, wearing a turban, turbaned: reges, Sid. Ep. 8, 3 fin.

tibarani.full: Tibarāni, ōrum, m., a people in Cili, cia, upon Mount Amanus, Cic. Fam. 15, 4, 10.
tibarani.short: Tibarāni, ōrum, m., a people in Cili, cia, upon Mount Amanus, Cic.

tibareni.full: Tĭbărēni, ōrum or ūm, m., = Τιβαρηνοί, a people of Asia, on the Black Sea, Mel. 1, 2, 5; 1, 19, 10; Val. Fl. 5, 148.
tibareni.short: Tĭbărēni, ōrum or ūm, m., = Τιβαρηνοί, a people of Asia, on the Black Sea, Mel.

tibereius.full: Tĭbĕrēĭus, a, um, v. Tiberius, II. 3.

tiberianus.full: Tĭbĕrĭānus, a, um, v. Tiberius, II. 2.

tiberinis.full: Tĭbĕrīnis, ĭdis, v. Tiberis, I. B.

tiberis.full: Tĭbĕris, is, also contr., Tibris (Ty-bris), is or ĭdis, m. The river Tiber, now Tevere: Tiberis antea Tybris appellatus et prius Albula, Plin. 3, 5, 9, § 53; cf. Liv. 1, 3. Form Tiberis, Mel. 2, 4, 9; Plin. 3, 5, 9, § 53; Enn. ap. Macr. S. 6, 4 (Ann. v. 453 Vahl.); Cic. Att. 13, 33, 4; 12, 19, 1; id. Rosc. Am. 35, 100; id. Mil. 15, 41; Liv. 1, 7; 5, 13; 24, 9; 30, 38; Hor. C. 1, 2, 13; 1, 29, 12; 2, 3, 18; id. S. 1, 9, 18; 2, 1, 8; 2, 3, 292; id. Ep. 1, 11, 19. — Form Tibris (Tybris; only in the
tiberis.short: Tĭbĕris, is, also contr., Tibris (Ty-bris), is or ĭdis, m.

tiberius.full: Tĭbĕrĭus, ii, m. In gen., a Roman prænomen (abbrev. Ti.); as, Ti. Sempronius Gracchus, Ti. Claudius Asellus, Ti. Claudius Nero.— In partic., the emperor Tiberius (whose full name is Ti. Claudius, Ti. F. Nero).—Hence, Tĭbĕ-rĭus (-rĕus), a, um, adj., of or belonging to the emperor Tiberius, Tiberian: marmor, Plin. 36, 7, 11, § 55. — Tĭbĕrĭā-nus, a, um, adj., of Tiberius, Tiberian: domus, Suet. Vit. 15: scorta, id. ib. 3: tempora, Tert. adv. Marc. 4, 7: vetus S. C., Sid. Ep. 1, 7 fin.: pira, a kind

tibia.full: tībĭa, ae, f., the large shin-bone, tibia (cf. sura). Lit.: alterum (os) a priore parte positum, cui tibiae nomen est, Cels. 8, 1 fin.: et in crure (recedit) tibia a surā, id. 8, 11.— In gen., the shin-bone, shin, leg: posse fieri ut genu esset aut tibia aut talus, Plin. Ep. 1, 20, 15: sinistram fregit tibiam, Phaedr. 5, 7, 8. — Transf., a pipe, flute (orig. made of bone; syn. fistula): age tibicen, refer ad labias tibias, Plaut. Stich. 5, 4, 41: si tibiae inflatae non referant sonum, Cic. Brut.
tibia.short: tībĭa, ae, f., the large shin-bone, tibia (cf.

tibialis.full: tībĭālis, e, adj. tibia. Of or belonging to the shin-bone or tibia, tibial; hence, subst.: tībĭāle, is, n., a warm wrappage about the shins, a kind of stockings or leggings: hieme feminalibus et tibialibus muniebatur, Suet. Aug. 82: si miles tibiale vel umerale alienavit, Dig. 49, 16, 14, § 1.— Of or belonging to the flute, flute-: harundo tibialis calami, used for flutes, Plin. 16, 36, 66, § 168: tibialis aura gemit, Sid. Ep. 9, 13 in carm. 2 med.

tibiarius.full: tībĭārĭus, ii, m. id., a pipe-maker, flute-maker, Inscr. Orell. 4292.

tibicen.full: tībīcen, ĭnis, m. contr. from tībĭĭcen, from tibia-cano, a piper, flute-player, flutist. Lit.: age, tibicen, refer ad labias tibias, suffla celeriter tibi buccas, Plaut. Stich. 5, 4, 41: si tibiae non referant sonum, abiciendas sibi tibicen putat, Cic. Brut. 51, 192: tibicen sine tibiis canere non potest, id. de Or. 2, 83, 338; id Leg. 2, 24, 62; id. Ac. 2, 7, 20; id. Dom. 47 123; id. Agr. 2, 34, 93; Hor. Ep. 2, 1, 98; id. A. P. 415: tibicines abierunt, Liv. 9, 30, 5: funus celebratum ... praece

tibicina.full: tībīcĭna, ae, f. tibicen, a female fluteplayer, Enn. ap. Varr. L. L. 7, § 104 Müll. (p. 175 Vahl.); Plaut. Stich. 4, 1, 36 sq.; 2, 2, 56; id Most. 4, 3, 2 al.; Ter. Ad. 5, 7, 7 sq.; Hor. Ep. 1, 14, 25; Ov. F. 6, 687; Juv. 2, 90; Mart. 14, 64, 1; Gell. 1, 11, 7.

tibicinium.full: tībīcĭnĭum, ii, n. tibicen, a playing upon the pipe or flute, a piping, fluting (class.): tibicinii scientia, Cic. N. D. 2, 8, 22; id. Or. 58, 198; App. Flor. p. 341, 28; 342, 20; Gell. 4, 13, 2.

tibicino.full: tībīcĭno, āre, v. a. id.. * To play upon the pipe or flute: ordo tibicinantium, Fulg. Myth. 3, 9.— To prop up, support any thing, Tert. Anim. 38; Schol. Juv. 3, 193.

tibigensis.full: Tibigensis, e, adj., of or belonging to the town Tibiga, in Numidia: oppidum, Plin. 5, 4, 4, § 29.
tibigensis.short: Tibigensis, e, adj., of or belonging to the town Tibiga, in Numidia: oppidum, Plin.

tibilis.full: Tibilis, is, f., a town in Numidia, Aug. Ep. 128. — Hence, adj.: Tibilitā-nus, a, um, of Tibilis: aquae, Aug. Civ. Dei, 22, 8.
tibilis.short: Tibilis, is, f., a town in Numidia, Aug.

tibinus.full: tībĭnus, a, um, adj. tibia, of or belonging to the pipe or flute: modi, Varr. ap. Non. 49, 23.

tibricola.full: Tibrĭcŏla, ae, m. Tibris-colo, a dweller by the Tiber, Prud. στεφ. 4, 174.

tibrinus.full: Tībrīnus, a, um, v. Tiberis, I. A.

tibris.full: Tibris, is and idis, v. Tiberis.

tibullus.full: Tĭbullus, i, m., Albius, a celebrated Roman elegiac poet, born about 700 A. U. C., died about 735, a contemporary and friend of Ovid and Horace, Quint. 10, 1, 93; Ov. Am. 1, 15, 28; id. Tr. 4, 10, 51; Vell. 2, 36 fin. al.; cf. Hor. C. 1, 33, 1; id. Ep. 1, 4, 1.
tibullus.short: Tĭbullus, i, m., Albius, a celebrated Roman elegiac poet, born about 700 A.

tibulus.full: tībŭlus, i, f., a kind of pine-tree, Plin. 16, 10, 17, § 39.
tibulus.short: tībŭlus, i, f., a kind of pine-tree, Plin.

tibur.full: Tībur, ŭris, n., an ancient town of Latium on both sides of the Anio, now Tivoli: Tiburque superbum, Verg. A. 7, 630; Hor. C. 2, 6, 5: supinum, id. ib. 3, 4, 23: udum, id. ib. 3, 29, 6; id. Ep. 1, 8, 12; 2, 2, 3: pronum, Juv. 3, 192: vacuum, quiet, Mart. 1, 13, 1; 4, 64, 32. — Hence, Tīburs, urtis, adj., of or belonging to Tibur, Tiburtine: populus, Liv. 8, 12; cf.: SENATVS POPVLVSQVE TIBVRS, Inscr. Orell. 113 and 3728: hostis, Liv. 7, 11, 4: via, Hor. S. 1, 6, 108: moenia, Verg. A. 7, 670: poma
tibur.short: Tībur, ŭris, n., an ancient town of Latium on both sides of the Anio, now Tivoli: Tiburque superbum, Verg.

tiburtus.full: Tīburtus, i, m., the founder of the town of Tibur, Verg. A. 7, 671; 11, 519; Plin. 16, 44, 87, § 237 (al. in each passage Tiburnus).
tiburtus.short: Tīburtus, i, m., the founder of the town of Tibur, Verg.

tichius.full: Tichĭūs, untis, m., one of the summits of Mount Œta, Liv. 36, 16; 36, 17; 36, 19.
tichius.short: Tichĭūs, untis, m., one of the summits of Mount Œta, Liv.

tichobates.full: tīchŏbătes, ae, m., = τειχοβάτης, a wall-climber, Vop. Carin. 18.
tichobates.short: tīchŏbătes, ae, m., = τειχοβάτης, a wall-climber, Vop.

ticida.full: Tĭcĭda or Tĭcĭdas, ae, m., an obscene Latin poet, Ov. Tr. 2, 433; Suet. Gram. 11; App. Mag. p. 279, 26. — A knight of Cæsar's party, Auct. B. Afr. 44; 46.
ticida.short: Tĭcĭda or Tĭcĭdas, ae, m., an obscene Latin poet, Ov.

ticinum.full: Tīcīnum, i, n., a city in Gallia Cisalpina, on the river Ticinus, now Pavia, Plin. 3, 17, 21, § 124; Tac. A. 3, 5; id. H. 2, 17; 2, 68.
ticinum.short: Tīcīnum, i, n., a city in Gallia Cisalpina, on the river Ticinus, now Pavia, Plin.

ticinus.full: Tīcīnus (scanned Tĭcīnus, Sid. Carm. 7, 552), i, m., the river Ticinus, in Gallia Cisalpina, celebrated for the victory of Hannibal over the Romans, now Ticino, Plin. 2, 103, 106, § 224; 3, 16, 20, § 118; Liv. 5, 34, 9; 21, 39, 10; 21, 45, 1; Sil. 4, 81 sq.; 6, 706; 7, 31; Claud. Cons. Hon. 6, 195; Flor. 2, 6, 10. — Hence, Tīcīnus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to the Ticinus, Ticinian: fluenta, Sil. 12, 548. — Tīcī-nensis, e, adj., Ticinian: campi, lying on the Ticinus, Aur. Vict. Epit. 35.

tifata1.full: Tīfāta, ōrum, n., a mountain ridge north of Capua, now Monte Maddaloni, Liv. 7, 29, 6; 23, 36, 1; 26, 5, 4; Vell. 2, 25, 4; Sil. 12, 487; 13, 219; cf. Fest. p. 366. — Hence, † Tīfātīnus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Tifata, Tifatinian: DIANA, Inscr. Rein. cl. 6, n. 91; Inscr. Murat. 446, 4.
tifata1.short: Tīfāta, ōrum, n., a mountain ridge north of Capua, now Monte Maddaloni, Liv.

tifata2.full: Tīfāta iliceta. Romae autem Tifata curia, Fest. p. 366 Müll. N. cr.

tifernum.full: Tifernum, i, n., the name of three towns of Italy. A town in Umbria, on the Tiber, called also Tifernum Tiberinum, near the mod. Citta di Castello, Plin. 3, 5, 9, § 53; Plin. Ep. 4, 1, 4; 10, 24.—Its inhabitants are called Tifernates Tiberini, Plin. 3, 14, 19, § 114.— A second town in Umbria, on the Metaurus, now S. Angelo in Vado, whose inhabitants, to distinguish them from the preceding, are called Tifernates Metaurenses, Plin. 3, 14, 19, § 114.— A town in Samnium, on the mountain and river Ti
tifernum.short: Tifernum, i, n., the name of three towns of Italy.

tifernus.full: Tĭfernus, i, m. A mountain in Samnium, upon which was the town of Tifernum, now Monte Matese, Liv. 10, 30, 7. — A river flowing by it, now Biferno, Mel. 2, 4, 6; Plin. 3, 11, 16, § 103.

tigellinus.full: Tĭgellīnus (Tĭgil-), i, m.; in full: Tofonius Tigellinus, a favorite of Nero, Tac. A. 14, 48 sqq.; 14, 57; 15, 50; 16, 17; Suet. Galb. 15; Juv. 1, 155; he committed suicide, Tac. H. 1, 72.

tigellius.full: Tĭgellĭus, ii, m., the name of two musicians. The more ancient, Tigellius Sardus, a contemporary of Cicero, Cic. Att. 13, 49, 1; id. Fam. 7, 24, 1; Hor. S. 1, 2, 3; 1, 3, 4. — The more modern, Tigellius Hermogenes, a censurer of Horace, Hor. S. 1, 3, 129; 1, 4, 72; 1, 9, 25; 1, 10, 18; 1, 10, 80; 1, 10, 90; cf. Schol. Cruq. ad Hor. S. 1, 2, 2.
tigellius.short: Tĭgellĭus, ii, m., the name of two musicians.

tigillum.full: tĭgillum, i, n. dim. tignum. A small piece of wood: clamat suam rem perisse ... de suo tigillo fumus si qua exit foras, i. e. if the least bit of wood is burned in his house, Plaut. Aul. 2, 4, 21. — Esp., a little beam, Liv. 1, 26, 13; Cat. 67, 39; Tib. 2, 1, 39; Phaedr. 1, 2, 14; Juv. 7, 46; App. M. 1, p. 109. — Sororium Tigillum; v. sororius, II.

tigillus.full: Tĭgillus, i, m. tigillum, an epithet of Jupiter, who sustains and holds the world like a beam, Aug. Civ. Dei, 7, 11.

tignarius.full: tignārĭus, a, um, adj. tignum, of or belonging to beams: faber, a carpenter, builder, Cic. Rep. 2, 22, 39; id. Brut. 73, 257; Inscr. Orell. 4087 sq.; cf.: Fabros tignarios dicimus non eos duntaxat, qui tigna dolant, sed omnes, qui aedificant, Dig. 50, 16, 235; Vulg. 4 Reg. 22, 6.

tignum.full: tignum, i, n. (masc. collat. form, plur. tigni, Liv. 44, 5, 4; but Weissenb. reads tigno) [root tek-; Gr. ἔτεκον, τίκτω, whence τέχνη, τέκτων, texo], building-stuff, building-materials (syn. trabs). In gen. (ante-class. and in jurid. lang.): tigni appellatione in lege duodecim tabularum omne genus materiae, ex quā aedificia constant, significatur, Dig. 50, 16, 62; cf.: tigni autem appellatione continetur omnis materia, ex quā aedificium constat vineaeque necessaria. Unde quidam aiunt, tegulam qu

tigranes.full: Tī^grānes, is, m. A king of Armenia, son-in-law of Mithridates, Cic. Imp. Pomp. 9, 23; 15, 45; id. Sest. 27, 58; id. Att. 2, 4, 2; Sall. H. 4, 61, 3 Dietsch; Flor. 3, 5, 27; 4, 12, 43. — His son, Cic. Att. 3, 8, 3; cf. Ascon. Cic. Mil. p. 47 Orell.; Schol. Bob. Cic. Mil. p. 284 ib.

tigranocerta.full: Tī^grānŏcerta, ae, f., and ōrum, n., the capital city of Greater Armenia, built by Tigranes during the Mithridatic war; fem., Plin. 6, 9, 10, § 26 sq.; neutr., Tac. A. 12, 50; 14, 24; 15, 4 sq.
tigranocerta.short: Tī^grānŏcerta, ae, f., and ōrum, n., the capital city of Greater Armenia, built by Tigranes during the Mithridatic war;

tigrifer.full: tī^grĭfer, fĕra, fĕrum, adj. tigris-fero, tiger-bearing, producing tigers: Niphates, Sid. Carm. 2, 444.

tigrinus.full: tī^grīnus, a, um, adj. tigris, tigerlike, barred or spotted like a tiger, Plin. 13, 15, 30, § 96.

tigris1.full: tī^gris, is or ĭdis (gen. tigris, Verg. Cir. 136: tigridis, id. A. 11, 577; Ov. M. 11, 245; Val. Fl. 5, 590; 6, 148; acc. tigrim, Verg. A. 9, 730; Manil. 5, 708; Sen. Ep. 85, 35; Plin. 8, 17, 25, § 65; 8, 18, 25, § 66; Sil. 5, 148; Suet. Aug. 43: tigrin, Val. Fl. 6, 704; Stat. Th. 6, 722; abl. tigri, Plin. 6, 20, 23, § 73: tigride, Ov. M. 7, 32; 9, 612; Luc. 5, 405; Sil. 5, 280; Mart. 8, 26, 8; Juv. 15, 163; plur. tigres, Verg. G. 2, 151; id. A. 4, 367; Hor. C. 3, 3, 14; 3, 11, 13; id. A. P. 393

tigris2.full: Tī^gris, ĭdis, m., = Τίγρις, the river Tigris (qs. arrowy, so called from its rapidity), Varr. L. L. 5, § 100 Müll.; Mel. 1, 11, 2; 3, 8, 32; Plin. 6, 27, 31, § 127; Hor. C. 4, 14, 46; Luc. 3, 256; 3, 261 sq.; 8, 370; Curt. 4, 9, 16; Sen. Herc. Fur. 1324.
tigris2.short: Tī^gris, ĭdis, m., = Τίγρις, the river Tigris (qs.

tigurinus.full: Tigŭrīnus pāgus, a district in Helvetia, perh. the mod. Zurich, Caes. B. G. 1, 12; Inscr. Orell. 366. — Its inhabitants are called Tigŭrīni, ōrum, m., Caes. B. G. 1, 12; Liv. Ep. 65.
tigurinus.short: Tigŭrīnus pāgus, a district in Helvetia, perh.

tilia.full: tĭlĭa, ae, f., the linden or lime-tree. Lit., Plin. 16, 14, 25, § 65; Verg. G. 1, 173; 2, 449; 4, 183; Ov. M. 8, 620; 10, 92. — Transf., the inner bark of the linden, barkbands, Plin. 16, 14, 25, § 65; cf. of the elm: corticis interior tilia lepras sedat, id. 24, 8, 33, § 48.
tilia.short: tĭlĭa, ae, f., the linden or lime-tree.

tiliaceus.full: tĭlĭācĕus, a, um, adj. tilia, of linden-wood, linden-: tabulae, Capitol. Anton. P. 13; cf. tiliagineus.

tiliagineus.full: tĭlĭāgĭnĕus, a, um, adj. id., of linden-wood, linden-: arculae, Col. 12, 47, 5; cf. tiliaceus.

tiliaris.full: tĭlĭāris, e, adj. id., of linden-wood, linden-: tabula, Cael. Aur. Tard. 5, 1, 20; cf. tiliaceus and tiliagineus.

tillius.full: Tillĭus, ii, m., a senator and tribune, reproached by Horace for rudeness, Hor. S. 1, 6, 107; cf. Sen. Ira, 3, 30, 5; id. Ep. 83, 12.
tillius.short: Tillĭus, ii, m., a senator and tribune, reproached by Horace for rudeness, Hor.

timaeus.full: Tīmaeus, i, m., = Τίμαιος. A Greek historian of Sicily, under Agathocles, Cic. de Or. 2, 14, 58; id. N. D. 2, 27, 69; id. Fam. 5, 12, 2; id. Rep. 3, 31, 43; id. Brut. 16, 63; Nep. Alcib. 11, 1.— A Pythagorean philosopher, a contemporary of Plato, Cic. Fin. 5, 29. 87; id. Rep. 1, 10, 16. — After him was named the Platonic dialogue Timaeus, which Cicero translated into Latin, Cic. Tusc. 1, 25, 63; id. N. D. 1, 8, 18; id. Ac. 2, 39, 123; id. Fin. 2, 5, 15; v. the fragment of this translation (Timae

timagenes.full: Tīmāgĕnes, is, m., = Τιμαγένης, a learned and plain-speaking rhetorician of the time of Augustus, Sen. Contr. 34; Sen. Ira, 3, 23, 3; id. Ep. 91, 13; Hor. Ep. 1, 19, 15 Schmid; Quint. 1, 10, 10; 10, 1, 75.
timagenes.short: Tīmāgĕnes, is, m., = Τιμαγένης, a learned and plain-speaking rhetorician of the time of Augustus, Sen.

timanthes.full: Tīmanthes, is, m., = Τιμάνθης, a celebrated Greek painter, contemporary with Parrhasius, Plin. 35, 9, 36, § 64; 35, 10, 36, § 65; Cic. Brut. 18, 70; Quint. 2, 13, 13 Spald. (cf. also Cic. Or. 22, 74).
timanthes.short: Tīmanthes, is, m., = Τιμάνθης, a celebrated Greek painter, contemporary with Parrhasius, Plin.

timarchides.full: Tīmarchĭdes, is, m., a sculptor, Plin. 34, 8, 19, § 91.
timarchides.short: Tīmarchĭdes, is, m., a sculptor, Plin.

timarchus.full: Tīmarchus, i, m., a sculptor, Plin. 34, 8, 19, § 51.
timarchus.short: Tīmarchus, i, m., a sculptor, Plin.

timarete.full: Tīmărĕtē, ēs, f., = Τιμαρέτη, a female painter, Plin. 35, 9, 35, § 59; 35, 11, 43, § 147.
timarete.short: Tīmărĕtē, ēs, f., = Τιμαρέτη, a female painter, Plin.

timavus.full: Tĭmāvus (better -vos), i, m., a river in Istria, between Aquileia and Trieste, Mel. 2, 4, 3; Plin. 2, 103, 106, § 229; 3, 18, 22, § 127; Verg. A. 1, 244; Luc. 7, 194; Stat. S. 4, 7, 55; Sil. 12, 215; Claud. Cons. Hon. 6, 197; Mart. 4, 25, 5.
timavus.short: Tĭmāvus (better -vos), i, m., a river in Istria, between Aquileia and Trieste, Mel.

timefactus.full: tĭmĕfactus, a, um, adj. timeo-facio, made afraid, frightened, alarmed, intimidated (very rare): timefactae religiones, Lucr. 2, 44: timefacta libertas, Cic. Off. 2, 7, 24.

timeo.full: tĭmĕo, ŭi, 2, v. a. and n. root tam-; Sanscr. tam-yati, to be stupefied; tamas, darkness; cf. temulentus, to fear, be afraid of, to dread, apprehend; to be afraid or in fear, to be fearful, apprehensive, or anxious; constr. with acc., rel.-clause, inf., ne or ut, and absol. With acc. (class.; syn.: vereor, metuo, paveo): quamquam omnia sunt metuenda, nihil magis quam perfidiam timemus, Cic. Fam. 1, 5, a, 2: timeo meos, Plaut. Truc. 5, 63; cf.: quos aliquamdiu inermes timuissent, Caes. B. G. 1, 4

timescens.full: tĭmescens, entis, Part. inch. [timeo], lecoming fearful of, fearing: Athanaricus paria timescens abscessit, Amm. 31, 4, 13.

timiditas.full: tĭmĭdĭtas, ātis, f. timidus, fearfulness, cowardice, timidity (a favorite word of Cic.): formido, timiditas, pavor, ignavia, etc., Cic. Tusc. 5, 18, 52: ecfare, quae cor tuom timiditas territet, Pac. ap. Non. 228, 18: ex rebus timiditas, non ex vocabulis nascitur, Cic. Fin. 4. 19, 53; id. Rep. 2, 41, 68; id. Tusc. 3, 7, 14; id. Clu. 46, 129; id. Cael. 15, 36; id. Phil. 2, 29, 71; id. de Or. 2, 3, 10; 2, 74, 300; Plin. Ep. 2, 10, 8; Suet. Aug. 67; id. Calig. 45. — In plur.: quantae timiditates, C

timidule.full: tĭmĭdŭlē, adv. dim. [timidus], somewhat timidly: reptare per balneas, App. M. 4, p. 146, 16.

timidus.full: tĭmĭdus, a, um, adj. timeo, fearful, afraid, faint-hearted, cowardly, timid (opp. audax; cf.: pavidus, trepidus, iners, ignavus): timido metu refugere, Enn. ap. Cic. de Or. 3, 58, 218; id. ap. Fin. 5, 11, 31 (Trag. v. 46 Vahl.); cf.: nimium me timidum fuisse confiteor, Cic. Sest. 16, 36: se timidum atque ignavum judicari, id. Fam. 11, 18, 1: timidus ac tremens, id. Pis. 30, 74: imbelles timidique, id. Off. 1, 24, 83: timidus imperitusque, id. Caecin. 7, 18: timidus in labore militari, id. Fam. 1

timochares.full: Tīmŏchăres, is, m., a courtier of Pyrrhus, who proposed to Fabricius, for a reward, to kill the king his master, Gell. 3, 8, 3.
timochares.short: Tīmŏchăres, is, m., a courtier of Pyrrhus, who proposed to Fabricius, for a reward, to kill the king his master, Gell.

timocrates.full: Tīmŏcrătes, ae, m., = Τιμοκράτης, an Epicurean philosopher of the third century B. C., Cic. Fin. 2, 31, 101; id. N. D. 1, 33, 93.
timocrates.short: Tīmŏcrătes, ae, m., = Τιμοκράτης, an Epicurean philosopher of the third century B.

timoleon.full: Tīmŏlĕon, ontis, m., = Τιμολέων, a Corinthian general, whose life was written by Nepos, Cic. Fam. 5, 12, 7.—Hence, Tīmŏ-lĕontēus, a, um, adj., of or named from Timoleon: gymnasium, Nep. Tim. 5, 4.
timoleon.short: Tīmŏlĕon, ontis, m., = Τιμολέων, a Corinthian general, whose life was written by Nepos, Cic.

timomachus.full: Tīmŏmăchus, i, m., = Τιμόμαχος, an eminent painter of Byzantium, of the time of Julius Cæsar, Plin. 7, 38, 39, § 126; Aus. Epigr. 121 sq.
timomachus.short: Tīmŏmăchus, i, m., = Τιμόμαχος, an eminent painter of Byzantium, of the time of Julius Cæsar, Plin.

timon.full: Tīmon, ōnis, m., = Τίμων, a celebrated misanthrope of Athens, Cic. Lael. 23, 87; id. Tusc. 4, 11, 25 and 27.
timon.short: Tīmon, ōnis, m., = Τίμων, a celebrated misanthrope of Athens, Cic.

timor.full: tĭmor (tĭmos, Naev. ap. Non. 487, 6), ōris, m. timeo. Lit., fear, dread, apprehension, alarm, anxiety (cf.: metus, horror, formido, timiditas, pavor): definiunt timorem metum mali appropinquantis, Cic. Tusc. 4, 8, 19: metus ac timor, Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 19, § 41: timor praepedit dicta linguae, Plaut. Cas. 3, 5, 25: timore torpeo, id. Truc. 4, 3, 50: prae timore in genua concidit, id. Rud. 1, 2, 85; id. Cist. 4, 2, 45: in timorem dabo militarem advenam, id. Ps. 4, 1, 19: animus timore Obstipuit, Ter

timoratus.full: tĭmōrātus, a, um, adj. timor, full of reverence towards God, devout, Vulg. Luc. 2, 25 (transl. of the Gr. εὐλαβής); id. Act. 8, 2; Hier. in Isa. 14, 50, 10.

timotheus.full: Tīmŏthĕus, ĕi, m., = Τιμόθεος. Son of Conon, leader of the Athenians, and restorer of the walls of Athens; his life is written by Nepos; cf. also Cic. Off. 1, 32, 116; id. de Or. 3, 34, 139; id. Tusc. 5, 35, 100; Nep. Con. 1 sqq.— A musician, a native of Miletus, Cic. Leg. 2, 15, 39; Quint. 2, 3, 3; Macr. S. 5, 22.

tina.full: tīna, ae, f., a wine-vessel, Varr. ap. Non. 544, 6; cf.: tinia vasa vinaria, Fest. p. 365 Müll.; and: canava, cavea, tinum, Not. Tir.
tina.short: tīna, ae, f., a wine-vessel, Varr.

tinca.full: tinca, ae, f., a small fish, perh. the tench: Cyprinus tinca, Linn.; Aus. Idyll. 10, 125.
tinca.short: tinca, ae, f., a small fish, perh.

tinctilis.full: tinctĭlis, e, adj. tingo, in which something is dipped: volucri ferro tinctile virus inest, Ov. Tr. 3, 10, 63.

tinctor.full: tinctor, ōris, m. id., a dyer, Inscr. Marin. Papir. Dipl. 251; cf.: tinctor, βαφεύς, Gloss. (but not Vitr. 7, 14, where tectores is the true reading).

tinctorius.full: tinctōrĭus, a, um, adj. id., of or belonging to plunging in or dyeing; trop.: mens, i. e. bloodthirsty, Plin. 7, 7, 5, § 44.

tinctura.full: tinctūra, ae, f. id., a dyeing, Plin. 37, 9, 38, § 119.—In plur., Plin. 31, 10, 46, § 110.

tinctus1.full: tinctus, a, um, Part. of tingo.

tinctus2.full: tinctus, ūs, m. tingo, a dipping into, a dyeing; meton., a sauce into which something is dipped: avis croceo tinctu cibis gratissima, i. e. saffron-sauce, Plin. 10, 48, 68, § 134.

tinea.full: tĭnĕa, ae, f. tan-, root of tondeo; cf. Gr. τέμνω. In gen., a gnawing worm, in clothes, books, etc., a moth, bookworm, etc.: Phalaena tinea, Linn.; Cato, R. R. 98, 1; Hor. S. 2, 3, 119; id. Ep. 1, 20, 12; Ov. P. 1, 1, 72; Mart. 11, 1, 14; Plin. 11, 35, 41, § 117.— In partic. Of the moth that flutters about a light, Lact. Phoen. 107.— Of the wood-worm, Vitr. 5, 12 fin.— Of worms in beehives, Verg. G. 4, 246; Col. 9, 14, 2.— Of worms in fig-trees, Col. 5, 10, 9.— Of worms in the human body, Plin.

tineo.full: tĭnĕo, āre, 1, v. n. tinea, to be infested by moths, Vulg. Bar. 6, 71.

tineola.full: tĭnĕŏla, ae, f. dim. id., a little worm, Veg. Vet. 1, 4.

tineosus.full: tĭnĕōsus, a, um, adj. id., full of worms, wormy, Col. 9, 14, 20.

tinge.full: Tingē or Tingi, f., a town of Mauritania, now Tangiers, Mel. 1, 5, 2; Plin. 5, 1, 1, § 4.—Hence, Tingĭtānus, a, um, adj., of or pertaining to Tingi: litus, Mamert. Gen. Max. 16 fin.
tinge.short: Tingē or Tingi, f., a town of Mauritania, now Tangiers, Mel.

tingo.full: tingo (less correctly, tinguo), nxi, nctum, 3, v. a. root tvak-, to wet; Sanscr. tuc-; Gr. τέγγω, to wet, moisten, bathe with or in any liquid (class.; cf.: aspergo, irroro, imbuo). Lit.: tunica sanguine centauri tincta, Cic. N. D. 3, 28, 70: Lydia Pactoli tingit arata liquor, Prop. 1, 6, 32: in amne comas, id. 4 (5), 4, 24: tinget pavimentum mero, Hor. C. 2, 14, 27: Arctos Oceani metuentis aequore tingi, Verg. G. 1, 246: stridentia Aera lacu, id. ib. 4, 172: gemmam lacrimis, Ov. M. 9, 567: in u
tingo.short: tingo (less correctly, tinguo), nxi, nctum, 3, v.

tiniaria.full: tĭnĭārĭa, ae, f. tinea, a plant, mothmullein: Teucrium polium, Linn.; Scrib. Comp. 83.

tinnimentum.full: tinnīmentum, i, n. tinnio, a tingling: illud quidem edepol tinnimentum est auribus, Plaut. Rud. 3, 5, 26.

tinnio.full: tinnĭo (tīnĭo), īvi or ĭi, ītum, 4, v. n. and a. [root tan-; cf.: tono, tonitru], to ring, chink, clink, jingle, tinkle, tingle. Lit.: tinniit tintinnabulum, Plaut. Trin. 4, 2, 162: tinnit hastilibus umbo, Enn. ap. Macr. S. 6, 3 (Ann. v. 432 Vahl.): apes tinniendo aere perterritas perducet, Varr. R. R. 3, 16, 30: (Graeci) n (litteram) jucundam et in fine praecipue quasi tinnientem illius (m litterae) loco ponunt, Quint. 12, 10, 31 (cf. retinnit, Cic. Brut. 46, 171): nec tibi dubito in foro diu t
tinnio.short: tinnĭo (tīnĭo), īvi or ĭi, ītum, 4, v.

tinnito.full: tinnĭto, āre, v. freq. n. [tinnio], to sing: parus enim quamvis per noctem tinnitet omnem, Auct. Carm. de Philom. 9 (al. tinniat): in trivio tinnitare, i. e. to boast in public, Commod. Fratr. 64.

tinnitus.full: tinnītus, ūs, m. id., a ringing, jingling, tingling (poet. and in post-Aug. prose). Lit.: tinnitusque cie et Matris quate cymbala circum, Verg. G. 4, 64: strepit assiduo Tinnitu galea, id. A. 9, 809: sonuit tinnitibus ensis acutis, Ov. M. 5, 204; 6, 589; 14, 536: aera tinnitus repulsa dabunt, id. F. 4, 184; Sil. 13, 146; Quint. 11, 3, 31: ad tinnitum aeris, Sen. Ira, 3, 35, 3; Plin. 34, 8, 19, § 76; 19, 1, 2, § 9: cuminum silvestre auribus instillatur ad sonitus atque tinnitus, a ringing in the

tinnulus.full: tinnŭlus, a, um, adj. id., ringing, tinkling, shrill-sounding (poet. and in post-Aug. prose). Lit.: sistra, Ov. P. 1, 1, 38: aera, id. M. 4, 393: chordae, Sen. Troad. 833: fistula, Calp. Ecl. 4, 74: vox, Cat. 61, 13; Pompon. ap. Macr. S. 6, 4 (with tenuis): illic cymbala tinnulaeque Gades, i. e. the shrill noise of the Gaditan maidens, Stat. S. 1, 6, 71 (cf. Juv. 11, 162).— Transf., of speakers: (rhetores) tumidi et corrupti et tinnuli, jingling, Quint. 2, 3, 9: verba, Hier. Ep. 143, 2; cf. tinn

tinnunculus.full: tinnunculus, i, m., a kind of hawk, the kestrel: Falco tinnunculus, Linn.; Plin. 10, 37, 52, § 109; Col. 8, 8, 7.
tinnunculus.short: tinnunculus, i, m., a kind of hawk, the kestrel: Falco tinnunculus, Linn.;

tintinnabulatus.full: tintinnābŭlātus, a, um, adj. tintinnabulum, belled, i. e. wearing a bell or bells: greges, Sid. Ep. 2, 2.

tintinnabulum.full: tintinnābŭlum, i, n. tintinno, a bell, signal-bell, e. g. on a door to summon the attendant, on the necks of cattle, etc., Plaut. Trin. 4, 2, 162; id. Ps. 1, 3, 98; Suet. Aug. 91; Plin. 36, 13, 19, § 92; Juv. 6, 441; Mart. 14, 163 in lemm.; Paul. Nol. Carm. 18, 336.

tintinnaculus.full: tintinnācŭlus, a, um, adj. id., tinkling, clinking, clanking: educi ad tintinnaculos, i. e. to the manacled malefactors, Plaut. Truc. 4, 3, 8 Spengel ad loc. (acc. to others, the executioners who fastened the chains).

tintinno.full: tintinno (tintĭno), āre, and tintin-nĭo, īre, v. n. reduplicated from tinnio, to ring, clink, clank, to jingle, tingle (anteclass.): tintinnabant compedes, Naev. ap. Fest. p. 364 Müll.; Nigid. ap. Non. 40, 16: tintinnire janitoris impedimenta (i. e. catenas) audio, Afran. ap. Non. 40, 14; id. apFest. p. 364 Müll. N. cr.: sonitu suopte Tintĭnant aures, Cat. 51, 11.
tintinno.short: tintinno (tintĭno), āre, and tintin-nĭo, īre, v.

tintinnum.full: tintinnum, i, n. tintinno, a jingling, tinkling, Ven. Carm. 2, 20, 49.

tinus.full: tīnus, i, m., a plant: Viburnum tinus, Linn.; Plin. 15, 30, 39, § 128; 17, 10, 11, § 60: bacis caerula, Ov. M. 10, 98.
tinus.short: tīnus, i, m., a plant: Viburnum tinus, Linn.;

tiphe.full: tiphē, ēs, f., = τίφη, a kind of grain, acc. to Sprengel, Peter's-corn, one-grained wheat: Triticum monococcon, Linn.; Plin. 18, 8, 19, § 81; 18, 10, 20, § 93.
tiphe.short: tiphē, ēs, f., = τίφη, a kind of grain, acc.

tiphyon.full: tiphўon, i, n., = τίφυον, a kind of narcissus, Plin. 21, 11, 39, § 67 (dub.; Jahn, iphyon).
tiphyon.short: tiphўon, i, n., = τίφυον, a kind of narcissus, Plin.

tiphys.full: Tīphys, ўos (voc. Tiphy), m., = Τῖφυς, the pilot of the Argo, Verg. E. 4, 34; Ov. H. 6, 48; id. Tr. 4, 3, 77; id. P. 1, 4, 37; Poët. ap. Charis. p. 243 P.

tippula.full: tippŭla (tip-), ae, f., an insect that runs swiftly over the water, the water-spider, water - spinner, Varr. ap. Non. 180, 11. — Transf., of any very light object: neque tippulai leonis pondu'st quam fides lenonia, Plaut. Pers. 2, 2, 62; v. Ritschl ad h. l.
tippula.short: tippŭla (tip-), ae, f., an insect that runs swiftly over the water, the water-spider, water - spinner, Varr.

tirenus pons.full: Tirēnus pons, a bridge at Minturnæ, Cic. Att. 16, 13.
tirenus pons.short: Tirēnus pons, a bridge at Minturnæ, Cic.

tiresias.full: Tīrĕsĭas, ae, m., = Τειρεσίας. A celebrated blind soothsayer of Thebes, Hyg. Fab. 68; 75; Cic. Tusc. 5, 39, 115; id. Div. 1, 40, 88; 2, 3, 9; id. N. D. 2, 3, 7; Ov. M. 3, 323; 6, 157; Hor. S. 2, 5, 1; Stat. Th. 10, 589.— Transf., for a blind man, Juv. 13, 249.

tiridates.full: Tīrĭdātes, ae, m., the name of several kings of Armenia, Hor. C. 1, 26, 5; Suet. Ner. 13; 30; Just. 42, 5; Tac. A. 6, 32 sqq.; Plin. 7, 39, 40, § 129; 30, 2, 6, § 16.
tiridates.short: Tīrĭdātes, ae, m., the name of several kings of Armenia, Hor.

tiro1.full: tīro, ōnis, m.; in milit. lang., a newly-levied soldier, a young soldier, recruit. Lit.: aetas tironum, Cic. Tusc. 2, 16, 38: legio tironum, Caes. B. C. 3, 28; 3, 29; 3, 34; Auct. B. Afr. 31, 7; Suet. Tib. 42; id. Ner. 19; id. Vit. 15.—Trop.: multaque tironi non patienda feret (opp. vetus miles), Ov. A. A. 3, 566.—Esp., in appos. like an adj.: tirones milites (opp. veterani), Cic. Phil. 11, 15, 39: miles, Auct. B. Afr. 16, 1: exercitus, Cic. Fam. 7, 3, 2; Liv. 21, 39, 3; 21, 43, 14.— Transf., in

tiro2.full: Tīro, ōnis, m., a Roman proper name. So esp., M. Tullius Tiro, the learned freedman of Cicero, Cic. Fam. 16, 10; id. Att. 6, 7, 2; 9, 17, 2 (to him are addressed the letters id. Fam. 16, 3-10; 16, 12-15); Gell. 7, 3, 8; 13, 9, 1 sq.—Hence, Tīrōnĭ-ānus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Tiro: liber, Gell. 13, 20, 16: Tironiana cura, id. 1, 7, 1.
tiro2.short: Tīro, ōnis, m., a Roman proper name.

tirocinium.full: tīrōcĭnĭum, ii, n. tiro. Lit. In milit. lang., the first military service or first campaign of a young soldier, military rawness or inexperience, = rudimentum (perh. not ante-Aug.): juvenis, Liv. 39, 47, 3: propter exercitūs paucitatem et tirocinium, Auct. B. Afr. 31, 6: aetatis infirmitas aut militiae tirocinium, Val. Max. 5, 4, 2: tirocinii rudimenta deponere, Just. 9, 1, 8. —In plur.: si non solum tirocinia, verum et incunabula in ipsis castris posuissent, Just. 12, 4, 6; Flor. 2, 3.— Concr.,

tironatus.full: tīrōnātus, ūs, m. id., the state or condition of a recruit (late Lat.), Cod. Th. 7, 13, 21.

tirunculus.full: tīruncŭlus, i, m. dim. tiro, a young beginner, little tiro (post-Aug.): ut probarem tibi, quam vehementes haberent tirunculi impetus primos ad optima quaeque, Sen. Ep. 108, 23: servitia sic tirunculum (vilicum) contemnunt ut senem, Col. 11, 1, 3: quod me quamquam tirunculum sollicitavit ad Emendum, Plin. Ep. 3, 6, 4: nec frustum capreae Novit noster tirunculus, Juv. 11, 143. — In apposition: miles, Suet. Ner. 21 fin.—In fem.: tīruncŭla, ae, a female beginner: saluta Blaesillam et Eustochium, tir

tiryns.full: Tīryns, nthis or nthos, f., = Τίρυνς, a very ancient town in Argolis, where Hercules was brought up, Plin. 4, 5, 9, § 17; Stat. Th. 4, 147; Serv. Verg. A. 7, 662.—Hence, Tīrynthĭus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Tiryns, Tirynthian; and poet., also, of or belonging to Hercules, Herculean: heros, i. e. Hercules, Ov. M. 7, 410; id. F. 2, 349; called also juvenis, id. ib. 2, 305: hospes, id. ib. 1, 547: Tirynthius heros, Chromis, the son of Hercules, Stat. Th. 6, 489; and Q. Fabius Maximus (becaus
tiryns.short: Tīryns, nthis or nthos, f., = Τίρυνς, a very ancient town in Argolis, where Hercules was brought up, Plin.

tis.full: tis, i. e. tui, Plaut. Mil. 4, 2, 42; v. tu.

tisaeus.full: Tīsaeus, i, m., or Tīsaeum, i, n., = Τισαῖον, a mountain of Thessaly, now Bardjora, Liv. 28, 5, 17; Val. Fl. 2, 7.
tisaeus.short: Tīsaeus, i, m., or Tīsaeum, i, n., = Τισαῖον, a mountain of Thessaly, now Bardjora, Liv.

tisagoras.full: Tīsăgŏras, ae, m., = Τισαγόρας, a brother of Miltiades, Nep. Milt. 7, 5.
tisagoras.short: Tīsăgŏras, ae, m., = Τισαγόρας, a brother of Miltiades, Nep.

tisamenus.full: Tīsămĕnus, i, m., = Τισαμενός, a son of Orestes, and king of Argos, Ov. Ib. 346; Hyg. Fab. 124.
tisamenus.short: Tīsămĕnus, i, m., = Τισαμενός, a son of Orestes, and king of Argos, Ov.

tisanusa.full: Tisanūsa, ae, f., a town and harbor of Caria, Plin. 5, 28, 29, § 104; Mel. 1, 16.
tisanusa.short: Tisanūsa, ae, f., a town and harbor of Caria, Plin.

tisias.full: Tīsĭas, ae, m., = Τισίας, a Sicilian who wrote on oratory, Cic. Brut. 12, 46; id. Inv. 2, 2, 6; id. de Or. 1, 20; Quint. 2, 16, 3; 3, 1, 8.
tisias.short: Tīsĭas, ae, m., = Τισίας, a Sicilian who wrote on oratory, Cic.

tisicrates.full: Tīsicrătes, is, m., = Τισικράτης, a sculptor of Sicyon, father of the painter Arcesilas, Plin. 34, 8, 19, § 67; 35, 11, 40, § 146.
tisicrates.short: Tīsicrătes, is, m., = Τισικράτης, a sculptor of Sicyon, father of the painter Arcesilas, Plin.

tisiphone.full: Tīsĭphŏnē, ēs, f., = Τισιφόνη (avenger of murder), one of the Furies, Verg. A. 6, 571; 10, 761; Prop. 3, 5 (4, 4), 40; Ov. M. 4, 481; id. H. 2, 117; Hor. S. 1, 8, 34; Juv. 6, 29; Sen. Herc. Fur. 984. — Hence, Tīsĭ-phŏnēus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Tisiphone Tisiphonean: tempora, i. e. deserving of punishment, guilty, criminal, Ov. Tr. 4, 9, 6.
tisiphone.short: Tīsĭphŏnē, ēs, f., = Τισιφόνη (avenger of murder), one of the Furies, Verg.

tisse.full: Tissē, ēs, f., a little town in Sicily, now Randazzo, Sil. 14, 267.—Hence, Tis-senses, ĭum, m., the inhabitants of Tisse, Cic. Verr. 2, 3, 38, § 86; for which: Tis-sinenses, Plin. 3, 8, 14, § 91.
tisse.short: Tissē, ēs, f., a little town in Sicily, now Randazzo, Sil.

titan.full: Tītan, ānis (collat. form Tītānus, i, v. in the foll.), m., = Τιτάν. Son of Cœlus and Vesta, elder brother of Saturn, and ancestor of the Titans, called Tītāni or Tītānes, who contended with Saturn for the sovereignty of heaven, and were, by the thunderbolts of his son Jupiter, precipitated into Tartarus: quasi Titani cum dis belligerem? Plaut. Pers. 1, 1, 26.—Dat. Titanis, Cic. N. D. 2, 28, 70.—Gen. genus Titanum, Cic. Leg. 3, 2, 5: Titanum suboles, id. poët. Tusc. 2, 10, 23.—Acc. Titanas, Hor.

titanomachia.full: Tītānŏmăchĭa, ae, f., = Τιτανομαχία, the battle with the Titans, Hyg. Fab. 150 in lemm.
titanomachia.short: Tītānŏmăchĭa, ae, f., = Τιτανομαχία, the battle with the Titans, Hyg.

titarisos.full: Titarīsos, i, m., a river of Thessaly, Luc. 6, 376.
titarisos.short: Titarīsos, i, m., a river of Thessaly, Luc.

tithoes.full: Tithoës, is, m., an Egyptian king, builder of the labyrinth, Plin. 36, 13, 19, § 84.
tithoes.short: Tithoës, is, m., an Egyptian king, builder of the labyrinth, Plin.

tithonus.full: Tīthōnus or -nos, i, m., = Τιθωνός, son of Laomedon, consort of Aurora, and father of Memnon; endowed with immortality, and changed at last, after reaching a decrepit old age, into a cicada, Cic. Sen. 1, 3; Verg. A. 4, 585; Ov. F. 6, 473; Hor. C. 2, 16, 30; 1, 28, 8: Tithoni conjux, Ov. H. 17 (18), 111.—Hence, Tīthōnĭus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Tithonus, Tithonian: conjux, i. e. Aurora, Ov. F. 3, 403.—Called also, absol.: Tīthōnia, Ov. F. 4, 943; Val. Fl. 1, 311; 3, 1; Stat. Th. 12, 3: s
tithonus.short: Tīthōnus or -nos, i, m., = Τιθωνός, son of Laomedon, consort of Aurora, and father of Memnon;

tithymalis.full: tĭthўmălis, ĭdis, v. the foll. art.

tithymalus.full: tĭthўmălus (tĭthўmallus), i, m., = τιθύμαλος, a plant with a milklike sap, spurge (Euphorbia, Linn.), of many species, Plin. 26, 8, 39, § 62; App. Herb. 108; Ser. Samm. 46, 841; 64, 1106.—A female species, called tĭthўmălis, ĭdis, sea-spurge: Euphorbia paralias, Linn.; Plin. 26, 8, 41, § 68.
tithymalus.short: tĭthўmălus (tĭthўmallus), i, m., = τιθύμαλος, a plant with a milklike sap, spurge (Euphorbia, Linn.), of many species, Plin.

titianus.full: Tĭtĭānus, a, um, v. Titius, II. B.

titienses.full: Tĭtĭenses, ĭum, v. Titius, II. C.

titiens.full: Tĭtĭens, ĭum, v. Titius, II. C. fin.

titillamentum.full: tītillāmentum, i, n. titillo, a tickling, for titillatio, Fulg. Myth. 2, 18.

titillatio.full: tītillātĭo, ōnis, f. id., a tickling, titillation: voluptates, quibus quasi titillatic sensibus adhibetur, Cic. N. D. 1, 40, 113: non est voluptatum tanta quasi titillatio in senibus, id. Sen. 14, 47; Hier. Ep. 52, 3: corporis, Sen. Ep. 92, 6.

titillatus.full: tītillātus, ūs, m. id., a tickling, for titillatio, Plin. 11, 37, 77, § 198; Cael. Aur. Acut. 2, 6, 26; id. Tard. 2, 11, 129.

titillo.full: tītillo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a., to tickle, titillate. Lit.: sensus, Lucr. 2, 429: voluptas, quae quasi titillaret sensus, Cic. Fin. 1, 11, 39; cf. carnem, Tert. Pud. 22 med.: multitudinis levitatem voluptate quasi titillantes, Cic. Off. 2, 18, 63. — Trop.: ne vos titillet gloria, Hor. S. 2, 3, 179: maerorem, Sen. Ep. 99, 7: appetentia cum titillatur, Macr. S. 7, 5, 30: titillata voluptas, Aus. Epigr. 108, 15: femina nulla prorsus invidia titillata, Mart. Cap. 2, § 172: his blandimentis titillat an

titillus.full: tītillus, i, m. titillo, a tickling, for titillatio, Cod. Th. 8, 5, 2.

titinius.full: Tĭtĭnĭus (Tĭtinnĭus), ii, m., a Roman comic poet of the ante-class. period; see the fragments of his writings in Com. Rel. pp. 115-137 Rib.; Varr. ap. Charis. p. 215 P.
titinius.short: Tĭtĭnĭus (Tĭtinnĭus), ii, m., a Roman comic poet of the ante-class.

titio.full: tĭtĭo, ōnis, m., a burning brand, firebrand (syn.: taeda, fax), Varr. ap. Non. 182, 21; 302, 7; Cels. 2, 17; Hyg. Fab. 171 al.; cf.: titionem vulgus appellat extractum foco torrem semiustum et exstinctum, Lact. 4, 14 med.
titio.short: tĭtĭo, ōnis, m., a burning brand, firebrand (syn.: taeda, fax), Varr.

titius.full: Tĭtĭus, i, m.; Tĭtĭa, ae, f., the name of a Roman gens; e. g. Sex. Titius, a tribune of the people, whose motions so much resembled dancing that a certain dance was named Titius after him, Cic. Brut. 62, 225; id. de Or. 2, 11, 48.— Titius Septimius, to whom is addressed Hor. C. 2, 6; cf. id. Ep. 1, 9, 1. — Hence, Tĭtĭus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to a Titius, Titian: lex, Cic. Mur. 8, 18; id. Leg. 2, 6, 14; Val. Max. 8, 1, 3; Dig. 11, 5, 3: atrium, Liv. 39, 44, 7: sodales, appointed for the S

titivillitium.full: tītivillitĭum, ĭi, n., a very small trifle, a bagatelle: non ego istuc verbum empsitem (empsiculem, Müll.) titivillitio, Plaut. Cas. 2, 5, 39; cf. Fest. p. 366 Müll. N. cr., and Fulg. Prisc. Serm. 562.
titivillitium.short: tītivillitĭum, ĭi, n., a very small trifle, a bagatelle: non ego istuc verbum empsitem (empsiculem, Müll.) titivillitio, Plaut.

titubantia.full: tĭtŭbantĭa, ae, f. titubo, a staggering, wavering (very rare): linguae, i. e. stammering, Suet. Claud. 30; so too, oris, id. Vit. 6; cf. the foll. art., I.

titubatio.full: tĭtŭbātĭo, ōnis, f. id., a staggering, wavering. Lit.: in ipsā ebrietate, Sen. Ep. 95, 16: linguae, i. e. stammering, Macr. S. 7, 6 med.; cf. the preced. art.— Trop.: titubatio aut offensio, Auct. Her. 2, 8, 12; Cic. Inv. 2, 12, 41; Hier. de Cain et Abel, 1, 5, 19.

titubo.full: tĭtŭbo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. n. and a., to stagger, totter, reel. Lit. (rare; cf.: vacillo, labo); of drunken persons: Silenus titubans annisque meroque, Ov. M. 11, 90: mero somnoque gravis titubare videtur, id. ib. 3, 608; 4, 26; 15, 331; cf.: titubans pes, Phaedr. 4, 14, 12: vestigia titubata, tottering, Verg. A. 5, 332: titubat lingua, stammers, stutters, Ov. A. A. 1, 598.— Trop., to hesitate, falter, waver, be in suspense, be embarrassed or perplexed (class.): Licinius titubans, Cic. Cael. 28, 6

titulo.full: tĭtŭlo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. titulus, to give a title to, to call, name, entitle (postclass.): magos quoque Samaritanorum appellatione titulavit, Tert. adv. Jud. 9 med.; id. Anim. 13; Carm. Judic. Dom. 2; Mart. Cap. 1, § 41.

titulus.full: tĭtŭlus, i (collat. form, n.: HOC TITVLVM, Inscr. Fabr. 8, 47; Inscr. Cardin. Dipl. 22), m. root ti- of τίνω, τιμάω, a superscription, inscription, label, litle; a ticket, bill, placard, notice that a thing is to be sold or let (syn. index). Lit. (esp. freq. after the Aug. per.): aram condidit dedicavitque cum ingenti rerum ab se gestarum titulo, Liv. 28, 46, 16: virtutes in aevum Per titulos memoresque fastos Aeternet, Hor. C. 4, 14, 4: dant munera templis; Addunt et titulum: titulus breve carm

titurius.full: Titūrĭus, ii, m., a legate of Cæsar in the Gallic war, Caes. B. G. 5, 27; 5, 29; 5, 33; Suet. Caes. 25. — Hence, Tĭtūrĭā-nus, a, um, adj., of Titurius, Titurian: clades, Suet. Caes. 67.
titurius.short: Titūrĭus, ii, m., a legate of Cæsar in the Gallic war, Caes.

titurnius.full: Titurnĭus, i, m., the name of a Roman gens, Cic. Fam. 13, 39.
titurnius.short: Titurnĭus, i, m., the name of a Roman gens, Cic.

titus.full: Tĭtus, i, m., a Roman prænomen, abbreviated T.
titus.short: Tĭtus, i, m., a Roman prænomen, abbreviated T.

tityos.full: Tĭtўos, ўi, m., = Τιτυός, a giant, son of Jupiter, slain by Apollo with arrows for his attempt on the chastity of Latona; and, as a further punishment, as he lay in the infernal regions stretched out over a space of nine jugera, a vulture kept feeding on his liver, which was as constantly reproduced, Lucr. 3, 992 sq.; Verg. A. 6, 595; Prop. 3, 5, 44; Tib. 1, 3, 75; Ov. M. 4, 457; id. P. 1, 2, 41; Hor. C. 4, 6, 2; 3, 11, 21.
tityos.short: Tĭtўos, ўi, m., = Τιτυός, a giant, son of Jupiter, slain by Apollo with arrows for his attempt on the chastity of Latona;

tityrus.full: Tītўrus, i, m. Lit., the name of a shepherd in Virgil's Eclogues, Verg. E. 1.— Transf. For a shepherd in gen., Verg. E. 8, 55.— As a designation of Virgil's Eclogues, Ov. Am. 1, 15, 25. — As a designation of Virgil himself, Prop. 2, 34 (3, 32), 72.

tityus.full: Titўus, i, m., a river of Illyria, Plin. 3, 21, 25, § 139; Flor. 2, 5.
tityus.short: Titўus, i, m., a river of Illyria, Plin.

tlepolemus.full: Tlēpŏlĕmus, i, m., = Τληπόλεμος, a son of Hercules, leader of the Rhodians before Troy, Hyg. Fab. 81, 97; Ov. M. 12, 537.
tlepolemus.short: Tlēpŏlĕmus, i, m., = Τληπόλεμος, a son of Hercules, leader of the Rhodians before Troy, Hyg.

tmaros.full: Tmărŏs or -us, i, m., a mountain in Epirus, Verg. E. 8, 44.—Called also Tŏ-mărus, Plin. 4, 2, 3, § 6.—Hence, Tmă-rĭus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Tmaros, Tmarian: Juppiter, Claud. B. Get. 18.
tmaros.short: Tmărŏs or -us, i, m., a mountain in Epirus, Verg.

tmesis.full: tmēsis, is, f., = τμῆσις, in grammar, the separation of a word, tmesis (as, Saxo cere comminuit brum; v. cerebrum init.), Serv. Verg. A. 1, 412.
tmesis.short: tmēsis, is, f., = τμῆσις, in grammar, the separation of a word, tmesis (as, Saxo cere comminuit brum;

tmolus.full: Tmōlus and Tĭmōlus, i, m., = Τμῶλος, a mountain of Lydia in which the Pactolus rises, producing excellent wines, now Kisilja Mousa Dagh, Plin. 5, 29, 30, § 110; Verg. G. 1, 56; Ov. M. 2, 217; 11, 151 sq.— Form Timolus, Ov. M. 6, 15; 11, 86.— A town near Mount Tmolus, Tac. A. 2, 47.— A small river flowing from Mount Tmolus, Plin. 33, 8, 43, § 126. — Hence, Tmōlĭus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Tmolus, Tmolian: terra, Ov. P. 4, 15, 9.— Subst.: Tmōlĭus, ii, m. (sc. mons), Mount Tmolus, Verg. G.
tmolus.short: Tmōlus and Tĭmōlus, i, m., = Τμῶλος, a mountain of Lydia in which the Pactolus rises, producing excellent wines, now Kisilja Mousa Dagh, Plin.

toculio.full: tŏcŭlĭo or tŏcullĭo, ōnis, m. τόκος, usury, a usurer: neque te in toculionibus habebam, Cic. Att. 2, 1, 12.

todi.full: todi, ōrum, m.: todi genus avium parvarum. Plautus: cum todillis crusculis, Fest. pp. 352 and 353 Müll.
todi.short: todi, ōrum, m.: todi genus avium parvarum.

toecharchus.full: toecharchus, i, m., = τοίχαρχος, the commander of the rowers, Hyg. Fab. 14 fin.
toecharchus.short: toecharchus, i, m., = τοίχαρχος, the commander of the rowers, Hyg.

tofaceus.full: tōfācĕus or -ĭus, a, um, adj. tofus, of tufa, tufaceous: argilla, Plin. 17, 7, 4, § 43: lapis, Pall. Aug. 9, 2.

toficius.full: tōfĭcĭus, a, um, adj. id., like tufa, tufaceous: lapides, Capitol. Max. 6.

tofinus.full: tōfīnus, a, um, adj. id., of tufa: metae (circi), Suet. Claud. 21.

tofosus.full: tōfōsus, a, um, adj. id., like tufa, tufaceous, porous: verruca umore, Sid. Ep. 3, 13.

tofus.full: tōfus (tōphus), i, m., tufa or tuff; Ital. tufo, Plin. 17, 4, 3, § 29; 36, 22, 48, § 166; Vitr. 2, 7; Front. Aquaed. 122; Verg. G. 2, 214; Ov. M. 3, 160; 8, 562; Stat. S. 4, 3, 52.
tofus.short: tōfus (tōphus), i, m., tufa or tuff;

toga.full: tŏga, ae, f. tego, a covering, garment. In gen. (ante-class. and rare): praeterea quod in lecto togas ante habebant; ante enim olim fuit commune vestimentum et diurnum et nocturnum et muliebre et virile, Varr. ap. Non. 541, 2: incinctā togā, Afran. ib. 540, 33; cf. comic.: ne toga cordylis, ne paenula desit olivis, Mart. 13, 1, 1. —* A roofing, roof: (toga) dicitur et tectum, Non. 406, 21. — In partic., the outer garment of a Roman citizen in time of peace, long, broad, and flowing, and consisti

togatarius.full: tŏgātārĭus, ii, m. togatus, an actor in the Fabula togata, Suet. Aug. 45 (al. togatarum).

togatulus.full: tŏgātŭlus, i, m. dim. toga, II. B. 2., a man of humble station, a little client, Mart. 10, 74, 3; 11, 24, 11.

togatus.full: tŏgātus, a, um, adj. toga, wearing the toga, clad in the toga, gowned: fovebit Romanos, rerum dominos, gentemque togatam, Verg. A. 1, 282: ut togatus mandata senatus audiret, Liv. 3, 26, 9.— Transf., of a private station: sportula turbae rapienda togatae, by the crowd of clients (cf. toga, II. B. 2.), Juv. 1, 96: opera, the service of a client, Mart. 3, 46, 1. — Hence, subst. tŏgātus, i, m., lit., a Roman citizen, opp. to a foreigner or to a Roman soldier: judex modo palliatus modo togatus, Cic.

togula.full: tŏgŭla, ae, f. dim. id., a little toga: togulae lictoribus praesto fuerunt, Cic. Pis. 23, 55: picta, id. Att. 1, 18, 6: trita quidem nobis togula est, Mart. 9, 101, 5.

tolerabilis.full: tŏlĕrābĭlis, e, adj. tolero. Pass., that may be borne, bearable, supportable, endurable, passable, tolerable (class.): amicitiae si tolerabiles erunt, ferendae sunt, Cic. Lael. 21, 78: tolerabilis conditio servitutis, id. Cat. 4, 8, 16: genus rei publicae, id. Rep. 1, 26, 42: fenus, id. Att. 6, 1, 16: hoc utcumque tolerabile: gravius illud quod, etc., Plin. Ep. 5, 5, 2: regi tolerabili, aut, si vultis, etiam amabili, Cic. Rep. 1, 28, 44; cf. orator, id. Brut. 48, 178: oratores, id. de Or. 1, 2,

tolerans.full: tŏlĕrans, antis, Part. and P. a. of tolero.

tolerantia.full: tŏlĕrantĭa, ae, f. tolero, a bearing, supporting, endurance (very rare): rerum humanarum, Cic. Par. 4, 1, 27: pax vel incuriā vel tolerantiā priorum timebatur, Tac. Agr. 20; Sen. Ep. 67, 5: doloris, Quint. 2, 20, 10: malorum, id. 5, 10, 33; Vulg. 2 Cor. 1, 6.

toleratio.full: tŏlĕrātĭo, ōnis, f. id., a bearing, supporting, enduring: dolorum, Cic. Fin. 2, 29, 94.

tolerator.full: tŏlĕrātor, ōris, m. tolero, one who endures (late Lat.), Aug. in Psa. 99, 11.

toleratus.full: tŏlĕrātus, a, um, Part. and P. a. of tolero.

tolero.full: tŏlĕro, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. (dep. collat. form tŏlĕror, āri, acc. to Prisc. p. 800 P.) [lengthened form of the root tol, whence tollo and tuli, kindr. with the Gr. ΤΛΑΩ], to bear, support, sustain (syn.: fero, patior, sustineo, sino). Lit. (rare and mostly post-class.): aquilae ipsae non tolerantes pondus apprehensum una merguntur, Plin. 10, 3, 3, § 10; cf. id. 35, 14, 49, § 173: aliquem sinu, App. M. 3, p. 132, 29: gremio suo, id. ib. 4, p. 154, 23: mensula cenae totius honestas reliquias toler

toletum.full: Tŏlētum, i, n., a town of Spain, now Toledo, Liv. 35, 7; 39, 30. — Hence, adj.: Tŏlētānus, a, um, of Toletum: culter, Grat. Cyn. 34. — As subst.: Tŏlētāni, ōrum, m., the inhabitants of Toletum, Liv. 35, 22; Plin. 3, 3, 4, § 25.
toletum.short: Tŏlētum, i, n., a town of Spain, now Toledo, Liv.

tolistobogii.full: Tolistobogii (Tolost-), ōrum, m., a people of Galatia, whose precise home is unknown, Liv. 38, 15, 15 (Weissenb. Tolostobogiorum); Plin. 5, 32, 42, § 146; Flor. 2, 11, 5.
tolistobogii.short: Tolistobogii (Tolost-), ōrum, m., a people of Galatia, whose precise home is unknown, Liv.

tolleno.full: tollēno, ōnis, m. tollo, in mechanic. and milit. lang., a swing-beam, a swipe or swape, e. g. to raise a water-bucket from a well, or to raise a body of men to a level with the enemy's ramparts, Plin. 19, 4, 20, § 60; Plaut. Fragm. ap. Fest. s. v. reciprocare, p. 274 Müll.; Veg. Mil. 4, 21; Liv. 24, 34, 10; 38, 5, 4; Sil. 14, 320 sq.; cf. Fest. p. 356 Müll.

tollo.full: tollo, sustŭli, sublātum, 3, v. a. (perf. tollit, Pers. 4, 2: tollisse, Dig. 46, 4, 13) [root Sanscr. tul-, tulajāmi, lift up, weigh; Gr. ταλ-, τελ, in τλῆναι, τάλαντον; cf.: tuli, tlātus (latus), tolerare], to lift or take up, to raise, always with the predom. idea of motion upwards or of removal from a former situation. To lift up, raise up, elevate, exalt, etc. (syn.: effero, elevo). Lit. In gen.: unus erit quem tu tolles in caerula caeli templa, Enn. ap. Varr. L. L. 7, § 6 Müll. (Ann. v. 66

tolosa.full: Tŏlōsa, ae, f., a city in Gallia Narbonensis, now Toulouse, Mel. 2, 5, 2; Caes. B. G. 3, 20; Cic. Font. 5, 9; Mart. 9, 100, 3.— Hence, Tŏlōsānus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Tolosa, Tolosan: aurum, plundered by the consul Q. Servilius from Tolosa, Cic. N. D. 3, 30, 74; Gell. 3, 9, 7 sq.; Just. 32, 3.—In plur.: Tŏlōsāni, ōrum, m., the inhabitants of Tolosa, Tolosans, Plin. 4, 19, 33, § 109.— Tŏlōsas, ātis, adj., of Tolosa, Tolosan: caseus, Mart. 12, 32, 18: cathedra, Sid. Ep. 9, 16. — In plur
tolosa.short: Tŏlōsa, ae, f., a city in Gallia Narbonensis, now Toulouse, Mel.

tolumnius.full: Tŏlumnĭus, ii, m. A king of the Veientes, Liv. 4, 17.— A Rutulian soothsayer, Verg. A. 11, 429; 12, 258.

tolutarius.full: tŏlūtārĭus, a, um, adj. tolutim, going on a trot, trotting: equus, Sen. Ep. 87, 9.— Collat. form tŏlūtāris, e, in the trop. sense: sententiae tolutares, Front. Or. 1.

tolutilis.full: tŏlūtĭlis, e, adj. id., going on a trot, trotting: gradu vectus, Varr. ap. Non. 17, 26.

tolutiloquentia.full: tŏlūtĭlŏquentĭa, ae, f. tolutim-loquor, a talking on a trot, volubility: o pestifera . . . trux tolutiloquentia, Nov. ap. Nen. 4, 7 (Com. Rel. p. 220 Rib.).

tolutim.full: tŏlūtim, adv. from the root tol, whence tollo, tolero, tŭli; Gr. ΤΛΑΩ; prop. lifting up the feet; hence, pregn., on a trot, full trot (mostly ante - class.): cedit citu', celsu' tolutim, Varr. ap. Non. 4, 20; so of horses, id. ib. 4, 16; Lucil. ib. 4, 11; Plin. 8, 42, 67, § 166: ire tolutim, Nov. ap. Non. 4, 9: ni tolutim badizas, Plaut. As. 3, 3, 116.

tomacina.full: tŏmācĭna, ae, f. τομή, a cutting up, a kind of sausage, Varr. R. R. 2, 4, 10; cf. tomaculum.

tomaculum.full: tŏmācŭlum, or, contr., tŏmā-clum, i, n. τομή, a cutting in pieces, a kind of sausage, probably similar to our brain- or liver-sausage, Juv. 10, 355; Mart. 1, 42, 9; Petr. 31 fin.; 39 fin.; v. the preced. art., and cf. Becker, Gallus, 3, p. 193 (2d edit.).
tomaculum.short: tŏmācŭlum, or, contr., tŏmā-clum, i, n.

tome.full: tŏmē, ēs, f., = τομή, a cut, separation; in metre, the cæsura, Ter. Maur. p. 2440 P.; Aus. Ep. 4, 90.
tome.short: tŏmē, ēs, f., = τομή, a cut, separation;

tomentum.full: tōmentum, i, n., a stuffing for cushions (e. g. of wool. hair, feathers, straw, etc.), cushioning, Plin. 8, 48, 73, § 192; 19, 1, 2, § 13; 27, 10, 61, § 88; Varr. L. L. 5, § 167 Müll.; Suet. Tib. 54; Tac. A. 6, 23 med.; Mart. 14, 159 in lemm.; 14, 160 in lemm.; 14, 162; App. Mag. p. 276, 14; cf. Becker, Gallus, 2, p. 240 (2d edit.).
tomentum.short: tōmentum, i, n., a stuffing for cushions (e.

tomis.full: Tŏmis, is, f., or Tŏmi, ōrum, m., = Τόμις or Τόμοι, a town of Mœsia, on the Pontus Euxinus, famous as the place to which Ovid was banished.—Form Tomis, Ov. P. 4, 14, 59; id. Tr. 3, 9, 33.—Form Tŏmi, ōrum, m., Stat. S. 1, 2, 254; Claud. Epith. Pall. et Celer. 70; Sid. Carm. 23, 159.—And after the Greek orthog., Tŏmoe, Mel. 2, 2, 5. — Hence, Tŏmītae, ārum, m., the inhabitants of Tomis, Ov. Tr. 1, 2, 85.— Tŏmītānus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Tomis, Tomitan: terra, Ov. P. 1, 1, 1: harena, id.
tomis.short: Tŏmis, is, f., or Tŏmi, ōrum, m., = Τόμις or Τόμοι, a town of Mœsia, on the Pontus Euxinus, famous as the place to which Ovid was banished.—Form Tomis, Ov.

tomus.full: tŏmus, i, m., = τόμος. In gen., a cut, piece, bit: vilis, a cheap piece, i. e. roll of paper, Mart. 1, 67, 3. — In partic. A part, book, tome of a larger work: feci excerpta ex libris sexaginta in quinque tomis, M. Aurel. ap. Front, Ep. ad Caes. 2, 13. — Transf., a book, in gen.: accipe tibi tomum magnum novum, Hier. Ep. 22, 38.

tomyris.full: Tŏmўris, is, f., = Τόμυπις, a Scythian queen, by whom the elder Cyrus was defeated and slain, Just. 1, 8; Tib. 4, 1, 143; Val. Max. 9, 10, ext. 1.—Called also Tămўris or Tămĭris, Front. Strat. 2, 5; and Thămўris, Val. Max. 9, 10.
tomyris.short: Tŏmўris, is, f., = Τόμυπις, a Scythian queen, by whom the elder Cyrus was defeated and slain, Just.

tondeo.full: tondĕo, tŏtondi, tonsum, 2 (collat. form acc. to the third conj.: OVES TONDVNTVR, Calend. ap. Grut. 138), v. a. for tomdeo; root in Gr. τέμνω, to cut, to shear, clip, crop, to shave, etc. Lit.: barbam et capillum, Cic. Tusc. 5, 20, 58; so, barbam, Mart. 11, 39, 3: capillum, Ov. M. 8, 151: cutem, Hor. Ep. 1, 18, 7: os, Cat. 61, 139: ovem, Plaut. Merc. 3, 1, 28; Hor. Epod. 2, 16; Verg. G. 3, 443; Plin. 18, 27, 67, § 257; cf. lanam, Hor. C. 3, 15, 14: naevos in facie, Plin. 28, 4, 6, § 34: saltatri

tonesco.full: tŏnesco, ĕre, v. inch. n. [tono], to resound: caelitum altum tonitribus templum tonescit, Varr. ap. Non. 180, 15.

tongere.full: tongēre Aelius Stilo ait noscere esse, quod Praenestini tongitionem dicant pro notione. Ennius: alii rhetoricam tongent, Fest. p. 356 Müll. (Sota, v. 4 Vahl. p. 165).
tongere.short: tongēre Aelius Stilo ait noscere esse, quod Praenestini tongitionem dicant pro notione.

tonitralis.full: tŏnĭtrālis, e, a false read. for penetralia, Lucr. 1, 1105.

tonitrualis.full: tŏnĭtrŭālis, e, adj. tonitrus, thundering, an epithet of Jupiter, App. de Mundo, p. 75, 6.

tonitruo.full: tŏnī^trŭo, āre, 1, v. a., to thunder: Deus tonitruat, Hier. in Psa. 76.

tonitrus.full: tŏnī^trus, ūs, m., or tŏnī^trŭum, ii (gen. tonitrui, Vulg. Marc. 3, 17), n. tono, thunder. Sing.: tonitrum auribus accipiamus, Lucr. 6, 164; 6, 171: tonitrum audire, Plin. 2, 54, 55, § 142: tonitruum terribile exsistit, id. 36, 13, 19, § 88; Sen. Q. N. 2, 54, 1; 2, 56, 1: auditum praeterea tonitruum, Treb. Gall. 5; Tert. adv. Marc. 3, 6: veri tonitrūs similitudinem imitari, Fest. s. v. Claudiana, p. 57 Müll.: caelum tonitru contremit, Poët. ap. Cic. de Or. 3, 39, 157: tonitru caelum omne ciebo,
tonitrus.short: tŏnī^trus, ūs, m., or tŏnī^trŭum, ii (gen.

tono.full: tŏno, ŭi, 1 (collat. form of third conj.: tonimus, Varr. ap. Non. 49, 21), v. n. and a. [root in Sanscr. tan-, to stretch, extend; Gr. τείνω; whence teneo, tendo, tenus; cf. O. H. Germ. donar; Engl. thunder], to thunder. Lit.: ingens Porta tonat caeli, Enn. ap. Vet. Gram. ap. Col. (Ann. v. 597 Vahl.); imitated by Verg. G. 3, 261: cum tonuit laevum bene tempestate serenā, Enn. ap. Cic. Div. 2, 39, 82 (Ann. v. 517 Vahl.): ut valide tonuit! Plaut. Am. 5, 1, 10; so id. ib. 5, 1, 78: si fulserit, si

tonor.full: tŏnŏr, ōris, m., old form of tenor, Quint. 1, 5, 23.
tonor.short: tŏnŏr, ōris, m., old form of tenor, Quint.

tonsa.full: tonsa, ae, f. perh. from tundo, an oar (poet.; mostly in plur.; syn. remus). Sing.: in mari magno tenere tonsam, Enn. ap. Fest. p. 356 Müll. (Sota, v. 3 Vahl. p. 164): valida tonsa, Val. Fl. 1, 369. — Plur., Enn. ap. Fest. p. 356 Müll. (Ann. v. 232; 235; 236 Vahl.); Lucr. 2, 554; Verg. A. 7, 28; 10, 299; Luc. 3, 527; 5, 448; Sil. 11, 492; Sen. Agam. 443 al.

tonsicula.full: tonsĭcŭla, ae, f. dim. tonsa, the name of a small fish, Cassiod. Var. 12, 4.

tonsilis.full: tonsĭlis, e, adj. tondeo, that may be shorn, cut, or clipped. Lit.: villus, Plin. 8, 50, 76, § 203: facilitas piceae, id. 16, 10, 18, § 40. — Transf., for tonsus, shorn, clipped, cut, lopped: tapetes, Matius ap. Gell. 20, 9, 3: nemora, Plin. 12, 2, 6, § 13; cf. buxetum, Mart. 3, 58, 3.

tonsilla.full: tonsilla (tosilla), ae, f. A sharppointed pole which was stuck in the ground to fasten vessels to the shore, Pac. and Att. ap. Fest. p. 356 Müll. (Pac. Trag. Fragm. v. 218; Att. Trag. Fragm. v. 517 Rib.). — In plur.: tonsillae, ārum, f., the tonsils in the throat, Cic. N. D. 2, 54, 135; Cels. 6, 10; 7, 12, 2; Plin. 11, 37, 66, § 175.

tonsio.full: tonsĭo, ōnis, f. tondeo, a shearing (late Lat.): lanae ex ovium tonsione, Vulg. Deut. 18, 4; id. Amos, 7, 1.

tonsito.full: tonsĭto, āre, v. freq. a. id., to shear: oves, Plaut. Bacch. 5, 2, 9.

tonsor.full: tonsor (TOSOR, Inscr. Fabr. p. 214, n. 546), ōris, m. id.. A shearer, clipper, shaver of the hair, beard, nails, etc., a hair-cutter, barber, Varr. R. R. 2, 11, 10; Cic.
