triplus.full: trĭplus, a, um, adj. num., = τριπλοῦς, threefold, triple: pars, Cic. Univ. 7 med.— In neutr. absol.: triplo plus scortorum, three times as many, Plaut. Truc. 1, 1, 70.

tripodatio.full: trĭpŏdātĭo, ōnis, f. † tripodo, a solemn, measured stamping with the feet of the Arval brothers, Inscr. Frat. Arv. Orell. 2271; cf. trĭpŭdĭātĭo, χορεία ἱερέως περὶ τὸν βωμόν, Gloss. Philox.

tripodius.full: trĭpŏdius, a, um, adj., = τριπόδιος, consisting of three feet: pes, a metrical foot, = Bacchius.
tripodius.short: trĭpŏdius, a, um, adj., = τριπόδιος, consisting of three feet: pes, a metrical foot, = Bacchius.

tripolis.full: Trĭpŏlis, is, f., = Τρίπολις (prop. threetown), the name of several districts of country and of towns. A district of Thessaly, Liv. 42, 53, 6.—Hence, Trĭpŏlĭtānus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Tripolis: ager, Liv. 36, 10, 5.— A country of Africa, Sol. 27.—Hence, Trĭpŏlĭtānus, a, um, adj., of Tripolis, Eutr. 8, 10.— A town of Phœnicia, Mel. 1, 12, 3; Plin. 5, 20, 17, § 78— A district of Laconia, near Tegea, including the cities of Belmina, Carystus, and Pellene, Liv. 35, 27, 9. — Hence, Trĭpŏl

tripolium.full: trĭpŏlĭum, ii, n., = τριπόλιον, a plant growing on cliffs, Plin. 26, 7, 22, § 39.
tripolium.short: trĭpŏlĭum, ii, n., = τριπόλιον, a plant growing on cliffs, Plin.

triportentum.full: trĭ-portentum, i, n. ter, an extraordinary omen or portent: deūm triportenta. Pac. ap. Varr. L. L. 7, § 59 Müll. (Trag. Rel. v. 381 Rib.).

triporticus.full: Trĭportĭcus, ūs, f., a triple porch (late Lat.), Aug. Quaest. in Heptat. 2, 177, 22.
triporticus.short: Trĭportĭcus, ūs, f., a triple porch (late Lat.), Aug.

triptolemus.full: Triptŏlĕmus, i, m., = Τριπτόλεμος, a son of Celeus, king of Eleusis and of Metanira; he was the inventor of agriculture, and became a judge in the infernal regions, Ov. F. 4, 507 sq.; id. Tr. 3, 8, 1; id. M. 5, 646 sq.; Auct. Her. 4, 6, 9; Cic. Tusc. 1, 41, 98; Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 49, § 110; Stat. S. 4, 2, 36; Hyg. Fab. 147.—Prov.: Triptolemo fruges dare, like the Engl. to carry coals to Newcastle, Ov. P. 4, 2, 10. — Hence, Triptŏlĕmĭcus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Triptolemus, i. e. to husban
triptolemus.short: Triptŏlĕmus, i, m., = Τριπτόλεμος, a son of Celeus, king of Eleusis and of Metanira;

triptota.full: triptōta, ōrum, n., = τρίπτωτα, nouns that have only three cases, triptotes, Diom. p. 288 P.
triptota.short: triptōta, ōrum, n., = τρίπτωτα, nouns that have only three cases, triptotes, Diom.

tripudiatio.full: trĭpŭdĭātĭo, ōnis, f., v. tripodatio fin.

tripudio.full: trĭpŭdio, āvi, 1 (collat. form trĭpŏdo, āre; v. the foll.), v. n. tripudium; in relig. lang., to beat the ground with the feet, to leap, jump, dance, as a relig. exercise (syn.: salio, salto). Lit.: CARMEN DESCINDENTES TRIPODAVERVNT IN VERBA HAEC: ENOS LASES, etc., Inscr. Frat. Arv. Orell. 2271: sacro tripudiare gradu, Ven. Carm. 8, 4, 4: qui in honesto saltatu tripudiant, Lact. 1, 21, 45; Liv. 23, 26, 9.— Transf., in gen., to leap, spring, dance, caper: virilem in modum, Sen. Tranq. 17, 4; id.

tripudium.full: trĭpŭdĭum, ii, n. acc. to Cic. Div. 2, 34, 72, contr. from terripavium, terripudium, but prob. from ter and pes; cf. the old form tripodare, whence tripodatio; in relig. lang., Lit., a measured stamping, a leaping, jumping, dancing in relig. solemnities, a solemn religious dance: Salios ancilia ferre ac per urbem ire canentes carmina, cum tripudiis sollemnique saltatu jussit, Liv. 1, 20, 4; cf. tripudio and † tripodatio.— Transf., in gen., a dance: citatis celerare tripudiis, Cat. 63, 26: tripud

tripus.full: trĭpūs, pŏdis (abl. tripodi, Lucr. 1, 739), m., = τρίπους, a three-footed seat, a tripod. In gen.: donarem tripodas, praemia fortium Graiorum, Hor. C. 4, 8, 3; Verg. A. 5, 110; Sid. Ep. 4, 24; Sulp. Sev. Dial. 2, 1. — In partic. Lit., the tripod of Pythia, the priestess of Apollo, at Delphi, Cic. N. D. 3, 16, 42; Verg. A. 3, 360; Ov. A. A. 3, 789; Luc. 5, 121; Sen. Med. 86.— Transf. The oracle at Delphi: mittitur ad tripodas, Ov. F. 3, 855.— An oracle, in gen.: salve, prisca fides tripodum, Stat

triquetrus.full: trĭquē^trus, a, um, adj., having three corners, three-cornered, triangular. In gen.: triquetra aliis, aliis quadrata, Lucr. 4, 653: ager (opp. quadratus), Col. 5, 2, 1: figura (opp. quadrata), Plin. 2, 25, 23, § 93: (Britannia) insula naturā triquetra, Caes. B. G. 5, 13: Martis sidus numquam stationem facere Jovis sidere triquetro, i. e. distant by a third of the zodiac, Plin. 2, 17, 15, § 77; also as subst.: trĭquē^trum, i, n., the trinal aspect, that in which a planet's longitude differs by on
triquetrus.short: trĭquē^trus, a, um, adj., having three corners, three-cornered, triangular.

triremis.full: trĭ-rēmis, e, adj. ter-remus, having three banks of oars. Adj.: naves, Caes. B. C. 2, 6; 3, 24; Nep. Dion, 9, 2; cf. Front. Ep. ad M. Caes. 4, 3 fin.— Subst.: trĭ-rēmis, is, f., a vessel with three banks of oars, a trireme, Caes. B. C. 2, 23; 3, 101; Cic. Verr. 2, 5, 17, § 44; Hor. C. 3, 1, 39; id. Ep. 1, 1, 93; Liv. 31, 22, 5; Plin. 7, 56, 57, § 207,

trisaeclisenex.full: trĭsaeclĭsĕnex, is, m. tres-saeculumsenex, the old man of three generations, a surname of Nestor, Laev. ap. Gell. 19, 7, 13.

trischoenus.full: trĭschoenus, a, um, adj., = τρίσχοινος, containing three schoeni: mensura. Plin. 5, 24, 20, § 85.
trischoenus.short: trĭschoenus, a, um, adj., = τρίσχοινος, containing three schoeni: mensura.

triscurrium.full: triscurrĭum, i, n. ter-scurra, gross buffoonery, Prisc. 2, 480, 10; Juv. 8, 190.

trisemus.full: trĭsēmus, a, um, adj., = τρίσημος, containing three syllabic times, i. e. one long and one short syllable: pes, Mart. Cap. 9, § 978.
trisemus.short: trĭsēmus, a, um, adj., = τρίσημος, containing three syllabic times, i.

trismegistus.full: Trismĕgistus, i, m., = Τρισμέγιστος (thrice-greatest), an epithet of Mercury, Lact. 1, 6, 3; 6, 25, 10.
trismegistus.short: Trismĕgistus, i, m., = Τρισμέγιστος (thrice-greatest), an epithet of Mercury, Lact.

trispastos.full: trispastos, i, f. (sc. machina), = τρίσπαστος, a hoisting-tackle with three pulleys, two in the upper and one in the lower block, a trispast, Vitr. 10, 3.

trispithami.full: Trispĭthămi, ōrum, m., = Τρισπιθαμοί (three spans high), a race of dwarfs beyond India, Plin. 7, 2, 2, § 26.
trispithami.short: Trispĭthămi, ōrum, m., = Τρισπιθαμοί (three spans high), a race of dwarfs beyond India, Plin.

trisso.full: trisso, āre, v. n., of the note of the swallow, to twitter, Auct. Carm. Philom. 26 (al. trinsat).

tristatae.full: Tristătae, ārum, m., = Τριστάται, the three highest nobles of a country next to the king, Hier. in Ezech. 7, 23, 23.
tristatae.short: Tristătae, ārum, m., = Τριστάται, the three highest nobles of a country next to the king, Hier.

tristega.full: tristĕga, ōrum, n., = τρίστεγα, third stories or floors, Hier. in Ezech. 12, 41, 7; Alcim. Avit. 4, 244; Vulg. Gen. 6, 16; id. Ezech. 42, 6.
tristega.short: tristĕga, ōrum, n., = τρίστεγα, third stories or floors, Hier.

tristiculus.full: tristĭcŭlus, a, um, adj. dim. [tristis], somewhat sorrowful, rather sad: filiola, * Cic. Div. 1, 46, 103; M. Aur. ap. Front. Ep. 3, 17.

tristificus.full: tristĭfĭcus, a, um, adj. tristis-facio, making sad, saddening: voces, Cic. poët. Div. 1, 7, 13: tyrannus, Prud. Cath. 4, 76: acetum acore, Macr. S. 7, 12, § 30.

tristimonia.full: tristĭmōnĭa, ae, f. tristis, sadness, sorrowfulness, = tristitia (very rare): tristimoniā sollicitari, Auct. B. Afr. 10, 3: tristimoniam Ex animo deturbavit, Novat. ap. Fest. p. 372 M. (Com. Rel. v. 40 Rib.).—Collat. form tristĭmōnĭum, i, n.: esse in tristimonio, Petr. 63.

tristis.full: tristis, e, adj. etym. dub.; cf. Sanscr. trastas, frightened; and Lat. terreo, sad, sorrowful, mournful, dejected, melancholy, disconsolate, trist (syn.: maestus, severus, austerus, luctuosus). In gen.: maesti tristesque, Plaut. Bacch. 4, 4, 18: cum maestus errares, quaerere ex te, quid tristis esses, Cic. Div. 1, 28, 59: tristis et conturbatus, Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 14, § 32: tristis, demissus, id. Mur. 21, 45: sic tristes affatus amicos, Hor. C. 1, 7, 24: Sequanos tristes, capite demisso, terram in

tristitas.full: tristĭtas, ātis, f. tristis, sadness (anteclass.), Pac. ap. Non. 182, 2; so Turp. ib. 182, 4.

tristitia.full: tristĭtĭa, ae, f. id., sadness, mournfulness, sorrow, grief, melancholy, gloominess, dejection (class.; syn. maestitia). In gen. Of living beings: tum ad tristitiam, tum ad laetitiam est contorquendus, Cic. de Or. 2, 17, 72: ex summā laetitiā atque lasciviā repente omnes tristitia invasit, Sall. C. 31, 1: in eādem tristitiā permanere, Caes. B. G. 1, 32: magno metu ac tristitiā sollicitari, Auct. B. Afr. 10: lacrimis ac tristitiā te tradidisti, Luccei. ap. Cic. Fam. 5, 14, 2: tu sapiens finire me

tristities.full: tristĭtĭes, ēi id., = tristitia, sadness, mournfulness, sorrow, grief (ante- and postclass.): vultum alligat quae tristities? Pac. ap. Non. 182, 2 (Trag. Rel. v. 59 Rib.): tristitiem, Tac. A. 2, 4, 3: tristitie, Turp. ap. Non. l. l. (Com. Rel. v. 126 Rib.); App. M. 4, p. 155, 13; 9, p. 231, 2; 10, p. 239, 18.— Personified, Tristĭtĭes, the name of a maid of Psyche, App. M. 6, p. 176, 36.
tristities.short: tristĭtĭes, ēi id., = tristitia, sadness, mournfulness, sorrow, grief (ante- and postclass.): vultum alligat quae tristities? Pac.

tristitudo.full: tristĭtūdo, ĭnis, f. id., sadness, sorrow, grief, melancholy, dejection (post-class.): omnem de tuo pectore tristitudinem mitte, App. M. 3, p. 134; so id. Mag. p. 295, 19; Sid. Ep. 8, 11 fin.

tristor.full: tristor, āri, v. dep. n. [id.], to be sad, grieved, or downcast (very rare): numquam flere, numquam tristari, Sen. Prov. 2, 3; id. Ira, 2, 7, 1.

trisulcus.full: trĭ-sulcus, a, um (form trĭsulcis, e, Fulg. Rusp. Ep. 9), adj. ter (having three furrows), three-cleft, three-forked, threepointed; threefold, triple (poet.): lingua (serpentis), Verg. A. 2, 475; Plin. 11, 37, 65, § 171: sermo, of the serpent in Paradise, Prud. Ham. 203: ordine trisulco quatit ora fragor, of the teeth, Val. Fl. 2, 500: fulmen, Varr. ap. Non. 448, 20; cf. Fest. p. 352; also called Jovis telum trisulcum, Ov. Ib. 467: ignes, id. M. 2, 848: Sicilia, Claud. Rapt. Pros. 1, 145: fores,
trisulcus.short: trĭ-sulcus, a, um (form trĭsulcis, e, Fulg.

trisyllabus.full: trĭsyllăbus, a, um, adj., = τρισύλλαβος, of three syllables, trisyllabic: verbum, Varr. L. L. 9, § 91 Müll.; Mart. Cap. 5, § 522; 3, § 169.
trisyllabus.short: trĭsyllăbus, a, um, adj., = τρισύλλαβος, of three syllables, trisyllabic: verbum, Varr.

trit.full: trit, indecl., the cry of a mouse, a squeak, Naev. ap. Charis. p. 213 P. (Com. Rel. p. 11 Rib.).
trit.short: trit, indecl., the cry of a mouse, a squeak, Naev.

tritannus.full: Tritannus or Tributanus, i, m., a gladiator famous for his bodily strength, Plin. 7, 20, 19, § 81; Lucil. ap. Cic. Fin. 1, 3, 9.
tritannus.short: Tritannus or Tributanus, i, m., a gladiator famous for his bodily strength, Plin.

tritavia.full: trĭtăvĭa, ae, f. tritavus, the mother of an atavus or atavia, Dig. 58, 10, 3; 58, 10, 10.

tritavus.full: trĭtăvus (old sibilated collat. form strĭtăvus, acc. to Fest. p. 314 Müll.), i, m. teravus, the father of an atavus or atavia. Lit., Dig. 58, 10, 3; 58, 10, 10; Plaut. Pers. 1, 2, 5; Fest. l. l.—* Transf., in gen., remote ancestors, Varr. R. R. 3, 3, 2.

trite.full: trĭtē, ēs, f., = τρίτη; in music, the third string or tone in the musical scale, Vitr. 5, 4.

tritemoria.full: trĭtēmŏrĭa, ae, f., = τριτημορία; in music, a third, Mart. Cap. 9, § 930; 9, § 959.

trithales.full: trĭthăles, is, n., = τριθαλές, i. q. erithales, wall-pepper, the lesser houseleek, Plin. 25, 13, 102, § 160.

tritia.full: Trītīa or Trītaea, ae, f., = Τριταία, an inland town of Achaia, near the confines of Elis, now Kastritzi, Cic. Att. 6, 2, 3.— Hence, Trittenses or Trītienses, ium, m., the inhabitants of Tritia, Plin. 4, 6, 10, § 22.
tritia.short: Trītīa or Trītaea, ae, f., = Τριταία, an inland town of Achaia, near the confines of Elis, now Kastritzi, Cic.

triticeus.full: trītĭcĕus (collat. form trītĭcēĭus, Plaut. Cas. 2, 8, 58), a, um, adj. triticum, of wheat, wheaten, wheat-: messis, Verg. G. 1, 219; Ov. M. 5, 486: fetus, id. F. 1, 693: frumentum, Mart. 13, 12 in lemm.: paleae, Cato, R. R. 54, 2: furfures, Varr. R. R. 2, 5, 17: far, Col. 8, 5, 23.

triticiarius.full: trītĭcĭārĭus, a, um, adj. id., of or relating to wheat (jurid. Lat.): condictio, Dig. 13, tit. 13.

triticinus.full: trītĭcĭnus, a, um, adj. id., of wheat, wheaten, wheat-: amylum, Plin. Val. 5, 31.

triticum.full: trītĭcum, i, n. from tritus, from tero, Varr. L. L. 5, § 106 Müll., wheat, Col. 2, 6, 1; Plin. 18, 7, 12, § 63 sq.; Plaut. Curc. 4, 4, 30; id. Poen. 1, 2, 113; id. Truc. 1, 1, 12; Cic. Div. 1, 36, 78; 2, 31, 66; Cic. Verr. 2, 3, 73, § 170; Caes. B. C. 2, 18.

tritomus.full: trĭtŏmus, i, m., = τρίτομος, a kind of sea-fish, Plin. 32, 11, 53, § 151.
tritomus.short: trĭtŏmus, i, m., = τρίτομος, a kind of sea-fish, Plin.

triton.full: Trītōn, ōnis or ōnŏs, m., = Τρίτων. Lit., a son of Neptune and the nymph Salacia, a sea-god, who, at the bidding of Neptune, blows through a shell to calm or rouse the sea, Ov. M. 2, 8; 1, 333 sq.; 13, 919; Cic. N. D. 1, 28, 78; 2, 35, 89; Luc. 9, 348; Hyg. Astr. 2, 23 fin.—Plur.: Tritones, sea-gods that serve the other gods, Verg. A. 5, 824; Plin. 36, 5, 4, § 26.— Transf. A humorous designation of a lover of fish-ponds: piscinarum Tritones, qs. fish-pond gods, Cic. Att. 2, 9, 1.— A sea-fish of
triton.short: Trītōn, ōnis or ōnŏs, m., = Τρίτων.

tritopatreus.full: Tritopătreus (quadrisyl.), ĕi, m., a son of Jupiter by Proserpine, Cic. N. D. 3, 21, 53 B. and K. (al. Tritopatores).
tritopatreus.short: Tritopătreus (quadrisyl.), ĕi, m., a son of Jupiter by Proserpine, Cic.

tritor.full: trītor, ōris, m. tero, a rubber, grinder, chafer: colorum, a grinder of colors, Plin. 35, 11, 40, § 145: compedium, a chain-rubber, a term of reproach applied to a chained slave, Plaut. Pers. 3, 3, 15: stimulorum, of one who is often scourged, id. ib. 5, 2, 17: ARGENTARIVS, i. e. caelator, Inscr. Rein. cl. 11, n. 97.

tritura.full: trītūra, ae, f. id., a rubbing, wearing off, chafing. * In gen.: muli pectora copulae sparteae triturā continuā exulcerati, App. M. 9, p. 222, 39.— In partic., a threshing, of grain, Varr. L. L. 5, § 21 Müll.; Verg. G. 1, 190; Col. 2, 19, 1; 1, 6, 23.

trituratio.full: trītŭrātĭo, ōnis, f. trituro, a threshing (late Lat.), Aug. Tract. in Joan. 27 fin.

triturator.full: trītūrātor, ōris, m. id., a thresher (late Lat.), Aug. ad Don. 10.

trituro.full: trītūro, āre, v. a. tritura, II., to thresh (late Lat.): bos triturans, Vulg. 1 Cor. 9, 9: paleam areae, Aug. Tract. in Johan. 4, § 2: fruges, Isid. 15, 13, 16.—Trop.: passionum flagellis triturari, Sid. Ep. 7, 6 med.

tritus1.full: trītus, a, um, Part. and P.a. of tero.

tritus2.full: trītus, ūs (found only in abl. sing.), m. tero, a rubbing or wearing: lapidum conflictu atque tritu, * Cic. N. D. 2, 9, 25; cf. Plin. 33, 4, 21, § 66 (al. attritu); 34, 12, 30, § 120 (dub.); Lact. 6, 4, 6.

triumphalis.full: trĭumphālis, e, adj. triumpho, of or be longing to a triumph, triumphal: provincia, i. e. the conquest of which entitled the general to a triumph, Cic. Pis. 19, 44: porta, through which the triumphing general entered Rome, id. ib. 23, 55; Suet. Aug. 100: pictā Veste triumphales senes, Ov. F. 6, 364: currus, a triumphal chariot, Plin. 7, 26, 27, § 96: corona, which the triumphant person wore, id. 22, 3, 4, § 6; cf. vestes, id. 8, 48, 74, § 195: statua, Plin. Ep. 2, 7, 1: ornamenta (usually consis

triumphator.full: trĭumphātor, ōris, m. id., one who triumphs, a triumpher, conqueror, vanquisher (post-class.). Lit.: de Samnitibus triumphator, App. Mag. p. 285, 12; Vulg. 1 Reg. 15, 29.— Triumphator, an epithet of Jupiter, App. de Mundo, 75, 10.— Of Hercules, Inscr. Orell. 1042.—Of the Roman emperors, Inscr. Orell. 2.— Trop.: erroris, Min. Fel. Oct. 37.

triumphatorius.full: trĭumphātōrĭus, a, um, adj. triumphator, of or belonging to one who triumphs, triumphing, triumphant (post-class.): verbum, Tert. adv. Marc. 5, 10 fin.

triumphatrix.full: Trĭumphātrix, īcis, f. id. (she that triumphs), the Triumphant, a name given to the ninth legion, because they triumphed over the younger Pompey in Spain, Labus. ap. Gazzett. di Venez. ann. 1833, n. 56.

triumpho.full: trĭumpho, āvi, ātum, 1, v. n. and a. [triumphus]. Neutr., to make a triumphal procession, to hold or celebrate a triumph, to triumph (cf. ovo). Lit.: triumphare appellatum, quod cum imperatore milites redeuntes clamitant per urbem in Capitolium eunti Io triumphe: id a θριάμβῳ Graeco Liberi cognomento potest dictum, Varr. L. L. 6, § 68 Müll.: ex praeturā triumphare, Cic. Mur. 7, 15: commissi sunt iis magistratus, in quibus re bene gestā triumpharent, id. Planc. 25, 61: Africanus, qui de Numantini

triumphus.full: triumphus (in the earliest per. written triumpus; v. the foll.; and cf. Cic. Or. 48, 160; Quint. 1, 5, 20; and the letter P), i, m. cf. θρίαμβος, a hymn in honor of Bacchus. TRIVMPE, an exclamation used in the solemn processions of the Arval brothers: ENOS MARMOR IVVATO. TRIVMPE, TRIVMPE, TRIVMPE, Carm. Fratr. Arv. ap. Inscr. Orell. 2270.— A solemn and magnificent entrance of a general into Rome after having obtained an important victory, a triumphal procession, triumph (cf. Smith, Antiq. 1163 s

triumviralis.full: trĭumvĭrālis, e, adj. triumviri, of or belonging to the triumvirs, triumviral: sectus flagellis triumviralibus, i. e. of the superintendents of prisons, Hor. Epod. 4, 11: supplicium, Tac. A. 5, 9 fin.: proscriptio, i. e. of the triumvirorum reipublicae constituendae, Sen. Ben. 2, 11, 1; Lact. 2, 4, 36.

triumviratus.full: trĭumvĭrātus, ūs, m. id., the office or dignity of a triumvir, the triumvirate: triumviratus (coloniae deducendae), * Cic. Brut. 31, 117; cf.: tribunatu ante gesto triumviratibusque, Liv. 9, 46, 3: ne triumviratu suo (reipublicae constituendae) nimis superbiat Antonius, Plin. 9, 35, 59, § 122: nullo more triumviratus invaditur, Flor. 4, 6, 3: reipublicae constituendae, Suet. Aug. 27: senatūs legendi, id. ib. 37.

triumviri.full: triumvĭri (also written tresvĭri, and IIIvĭri), ōrum or ūm, m. tres-vir, three men holding an office together or associated in public business, a board of three, three joint commissioners appointed for various purposes, a triumvirate. So, Triumviri coloniae deducendae or agro dando, for leading out a colony and distributing the land among its members, Liv. 3, 1, 6; 4, 11, 5; 6, 21, 4; 8, 16, 14 al.—In sing.: nobilitas ... Gaium Gracchum ... triumvirum coloniis deducundis ferro necaverat, Sall. J
triumviri.short: triumvĭri (also written tresvĭri, and IIIvĭri), ōrum or ūm, m.

triuncis.full: trĭuncis, e, adj. ter-uncia, of three unciae: paragaudis, Gall. ap. Treb. Claud. 17.

trivenefica.full: trĭvĕnēfĭca, ae, f. ter-veneficus, an arrant poison-mixer, a thorough hag, witch, or sorceress, Plaut. Aul. 1, 2, 8.

trivialis.full: trĭvĭālis, e, adj. trivium; prop. that is in or belongs to the cross-roads or public streets; hence, transf., that may be found everywhere, common, commonplace, vulgar, ordinary, trivial (post-Aug.): trivialis scientia, Quint. 1, 4, 27: verba (opp. splendide atque adornate declamare), Suet. Rhet. 6: ludii ex circo, id. Aug. 74: carmen, Juv. 7, 55: mos, Calp. Ecl. 1, 28.

trivialiter.full: trĭvĭālĭter, adv. trivialis, in a common manner: trivialiter et populariter instituti infantes, Arn. 7, 242.

triviatim.full: trĭvĭātim, adv. trivium, in the public streets: dissultare, Mart. Cap. 1, § 3.

trivicum.full: Trĭvīcum, i, n., a small town in the mountains between Samnium and Apulia, near the mod. Trevico, Hor. S. 1, 5, 79.
trivicum.short: Trĭvīcum, i, n., a small town in the mountains between Samnium and Apulia, near the mod.

trivium.full: trĭvĭum, i, n. ter-via. Lit., a place where three roads meet, a fork in the roads, cross-road: ut ventum est in trivium, Cic. Div. 1, 54, 123.— Transf., in gen., a public square, the public street, highway; plur.: in triviis aut in compitis, Cic. Agr. 1, 3, 7: nocturnisque Hecate triviis ululata per urbes, Verg. A. 4, 609; Lucr. 4, 1203: occurram in triviis, Hor. S. 1, 9, 59; id. Ep. 1, 16, 64; 1, 17, 58; id. A. P. 245.— Sing.: pueros in trivio docere, Just. 21, 5; Tib. 1, 1, 12 (22).—Prov.: arr

trivius.full: trĭvĭus, a, um (gen. fem. Triviaï, Lucr. 1, 84), adj. trivium, an epithet of those deities whose temples were often erected where three ways met: DI, Inscr. Grut. 84, 5; 1015, 1: virgo, i. e. Diana or Hecate, Lucr. 1, 84; also called: Trivia dea, Prop. 2, 32 (3, 30), 10.—More freq. absol.: Trĭ-vĭa, ae, f., Diana, Enn. ap. Varr. L. L. 7, § 16 Müll. (Trag. v. 318 Vahl.); Cat. 34, 15; 66, 5; Tib. 1, 5, 16; Verg. A. 6, 35; Ov. F. 1, 389; id. M. 2, 416 al.—Hence, Lăcus Trĭvĭae (the Lake of Diana), a

trixago.full: trixāgo or trissāgo, ĭnis, f., a plant, called also chamaedrys, germander: Teucrium chamaedrys, Linn.; Plin. 24, 15, 80, § 130; Veg. Vet. 1, 17; 1, 42 al.
trixago.short: trixāgo or trissāgo, ĭnis, f., a plant, called also chamaedrys, germander: Teucrium chamaedrys, Linn.;

trochaeides.full: trŏchaeīdes, is, adj., = τροχαιειδής, like a trochee: numerus, Mart. Cap. 9, § 992.
trochaeides.short: trŏchaeīdes, is, adj., = τροχαιειδής, like a trochee: numerus, Mart.

trochaeus.full: trŏchaeus, i, m., = τροχαῖος (cf. Mart. Cap. 9, § 988). A metrical foot of two syllables, a long and a short (— ˘), a trochee, Cic. de Or. 3, 47, 182; Quint. 9, 4, 80; Prud. στεφ. 8 praef.— Another name for the tribrachys, a metrical foot of three short syllables (˘ ˘ ˘), a tribrach, Cic. Or. 57, 193; Quint. 9, 4, 82.

trochaicus.full: trŏchăĭcus, a, um, adj., = τροχαϊκός, consisting of trochees, trochaic: versus, Quint. 9, 4, 140; Ter. Maur. p. 2437 P.; Diom. pp. 504 and 508 ib.
trochaicus.short: trŏchăĭcus, a, um, adj., = τροχαϊκός, consisting of trochees, trochaic: versus, Quint.

trochilus.full: trŏchĭlus, i, m., = τρόχιλος. A very small bird, perh. the golden-crested wren, trochil, Plin. 10, 74, 95, § 203; 8, 25, 37, § 90.— In architecture, a semicircular hollow running round the base of a column, a casement, scotia, trochil, Vitr. 3, 3 med.

trochiscus.full: trŏchiscus, i, m., = τροχίσκος, a small, round ball; in medicine, a pill, troche, trochisk, Cael. Aur. Tard. 2, 7, 104; Veg. Vet. 2, 9 fin. (in Cels. 5, 17, written as Greek).
trochiscus.short: trŏchiscus, i, m., = τροχίσκος, a small, round ball;

trochlea.full: trochlĕa or troclĕa, ae, f. contr. from τροχαλία, a mechanical contrivance for raising weights, a case or sheaf containing one or more pulleys, a block, Vitr. 10, 2; Cato, R. R. 3, 5; Lucr. 4, 905.—Prov.: trochleis pituitam adducere, q. s. to draw up phlegm with a hoisting-tackle, i. e. to hawk violently, Quint. 11, 3, 56.

trochleatim.full: trochlĕātim, adv. trochlea, with a block: erecto fune, Sid. Ep. 5, 17 med.

trochus.full: trŏchus, i, m., = τροχός, an iron hoop set round with small rings, a trundling-hoop for children, Hor. C. 3, 24, 57; id. A. P. 380; Prop. 3, 14 (4, 13), 6; Ov. A. A. 3, 383; id. Tr. 2, 486; Mart. 14, 168, 2; 14, 169, 2 al.
trochus.short: trŏchus, i, m., = τροχός, an iron hoop set round with small rings, a trundling-hoop for children, Hor.

trocmi.full: Trocmi, ōrum, m., a people of Galatia, Liv. 38, 16; called also Trogmi, Cic. Div. 2, 37, 79; Plin. 5, 32, 42, § 146.
trocmi.short: Trocmi, ōrum, m., a people of Galatia, Liv.

troezen.full: Troezēn, ēnis, f., = Τροιζήν, a very ancient city of Argolis, where Pittheus, the maternal grandfather of Theseus, reigned, near the mod. village of Damala, Mel. 2, 3, 8; Plin. 4, 5, 9, § 18; Cic. Off. 3, 11, 48; Ov. M. 6, 418: prope Troezena, id. ib. 15, 296; 15, 506; id. P. 4, 16, 15; Stat. Th. 4, 81.— Hence, Troezēnĭus, a, um, adj., of or beionging to Trœzen: ager, Plin. 4, 12, 19, § 56: litus, Mel. 2, 7, 10: vinum, Plin. 14, 18, 22, § 116: carbunculi, id. 37, 7, 25, § 97: heros, i. e. Lelex,
troezen.short: Troezēn, ēnis, f., = Τροιζήν, a very ancient city of Argolis, where Pittheus, the maternal grandfather of Theseus, reigned, near the mod.

trogini.full: Trogini, ōrum, m., a people of Galatia, Cic. Div. 2, 37.
trogini.short: Trogini, ōrum, m., a people of Galatia, Cic.

troglodytae.full: Trōglŏdўtae or Trōgŏdўtae, ārum, m., = Τρωγλοδύται, a people of Ethiopia who dwelt in caves, the Troglodytes, Mel. 1, 4, 4; 1, 8, 6; Plin. 2, 73, 75, § 183; 5, 8, 8, § 34; 6, 29, 33, § 168; Cic. Div. 2, 44, 93.—Hence, Trōglŏdўtĭcus or Trōgŏdўtĭcus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to the Troglodytes, Troglodytic: myrrha, Plin. 12, 16, 35, § 69: balanus, id. 12, 21, 46, § 101.—Subst.: Trōglŏdў-tĭcē or Trōgŏdўtĭcē, ae, f., the country of the Trogiodytes, Plin. 2, 70, 71, § 178, 2, 74, 76, § 185; 6, 29
troglodytae.short: Trōglŏdўtae or Trōgŏdўtae, ārum, m., = Τρωγλοδύται, a people of Ethiopia who dwelt in caves, the Troglodytes, Mel.

trogus pompeius.full: Trogus Pompēĭus, a Roman historian in the time of Augustus, whose work was abridged by Justin, Just. praef.; id. 38, 3; 43, 1 and 5 fin.; Plin. 11, 15, 114, § 274; v. Teuffel, Rö. Lit. 253.
trogus pompeius.short: Trogus Pompēĭus, a Roman historian in the time of Augustus, whose work was abridged by Justin, Just.

troicus.full: Trōĭcus, a, um, v. 1. Tros, B. 3.

troilus.full: Trōĭlus, i, m., = Τρώϊλος, a son of Priam, slain by Achilles, Verg. A. 1, 474; Plaut. Bacch. 4, 9, 30; 4, 9, 36; Hor. C. 2, 9, 16; Dict. Cret. 4, 9.
troilus.short: Trōĭlus, i, m., = Τρώϊλος, a son of Priam, slain by Achilles, Verg.

troius.full: Trōĭus, a, um, v. 1. Tros, B. 1.

trojanus.full: Trōjānus, a, um, v. 1. Tros, B. 2.

trojugena.full: Trōjŭgĕna, ae, comm. Troja-gigno, Troy-born, born in Troy, of Trojan descent, Trojan (poet.): gentes, Lucr. 1, 465: Romanus, descended from Trojans, Vet. Carm. ap. Liv. 25, 12, 5.—Subst. m. A Trojan, Cat. 64, 356; Verg. A. 8, 117; 3, 359.— A Roman, Juv. 1, 100; 11, 95.

tromentina tribus.full: Tromentīna trĭbus, one of the tribus rusticae, Liv. 6, 5, 8; Inscr. Grut. 1109, 8; cf. Fest. p. 367 Müll.
tromentina tribus.short: Tromentīna trĭbus, one of the tribus rusticae, Liv.

tropa1.full: trŏpa, ae, f., = τροπή, the tropic solstice: CHIMERINA, Kal. Vet. ap. Inscr. Orell. II. p. 381.
tropa1.short: trŏpa, ae, f., = τροπή, the tropic solstice: CHIMERINA, Kal.

tropa2.full: trŏpa, adv., turning; Gr. τρόπα (v. Lidd. and Scott, s. v.): et ludit tropa nequiore talo, i. e. at a game played by throwing dice, etc., Mart. 4, 14, 9.

tropaeatus.full: trŏpaeātus, a, um, adj. tropaeum, trophied, adorned with trophies (late Lat.): victores et tropaeati, Amm. 23, 5, 17.

tropaeophorus.full: Trŏpaeŏphŏrus, i, m., = Τροπαιοφόρος, The Tropny-bearer, an epithet of Jupiter, App. de Mundo, p. 75, 11.
tropaeophorus.short: Trŏpaeŏphŏrus, i, m., = Τροπαιοφόρος, The Tropny-bearer, an epithet of Jupiter, App.

tropaeum.full: trŏpaeum or trŏphaeum, i, n., = τροπαιον. Lit., a sign and memorial of victory, a trophy; orig. a trunk of a tree, on which were fixed the arms, shields, helmets, etc., taken from the enemy; afterwards made of stone and ornamented in the same manner, Cic. Pis. 38, 92: statuere, id. Inv. 2, 23, 69: devictis Hispanis tropaea in jugis constituit, Sall. H. 4, 29 Dietsch: in modum tropaeorum arma imposuit, Tac. A. 2, 18 fin.: sistere Romae tropaea de Parthis, id. ib. 15, 18; Suet. Caes. 11; id. Claud
tropaeum.short: trŏpaeum or trŏphaeum, i, n., = τροπαιον.

tropaeus.full: trŏpaeus, a, um, adj., = τροπαῖος, turning back, returning: venti, blowing from the sea towards the land, sea-breezes, Plin. 2, 43, 44, § 114.
tropaeus.short: trŏpaeus, a, um, adj., = τροπαῖος, turning back, returning: venti, blowing from the sea towards the land, sea-breezes, Plin.

trophonius.full: Trŏphōnĭus, ii, m., = Τροφώνιος. A brother of Agamedes, in conjunction with whom he built the temple of Apollo at Delphi, Cic. Tusc. 1, 47, 114.— A deity that imparted oracles in a cave near Lebadia, in Bœotia; sometimes called also Juppiter Trophonius, Cic. Div. 1, 34, 74; id. N. D. 3, 19, 49; Liv. 45, 27, 8; Plin. 34, 8, 19, § 66; 31, 2, 11, § 15.—Hence, Trŏphōnĭānus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Trophonius, Trophonian: narratio Chaeronis, of a certain Chœron, who descended into Trophonius'

tropicus.full: trŏpĭcus, a, um, adj., = τροπικός. Lit., of or belonging to a turn or turning, tropical: Capricornus, i. e. where the sun turns back, Aus. Idyll. 16, 7; cf. id. Ecl. de Ratione Diei Anni, 2; Manil. 3, 614.— Trop. * trŏpĭca, ōrum, n., changes, alterations: pecuniae cupiditas haec tropica instituit, Petr. 88.— In the later rhet. lang., figurative, metaphorical, tropical (late Lat.): figura, Gell. 13, 24, 31: locutiones, Aug. contra Mendac. 10.—Adv.: trŏpĭcē, figuratively: loqui maluit, Aug. Genes.

tropis.full: trŏpis, is, f., = τρόπις, the lees of wine, Mart. 12, 83, 11.
tropis.short: trŏpis, is, f., = τρόπις, the lees of wine, Mart.

tropologia.full: trŏpŏlŏgĭa, ae, f., = τροπολογία, a figurative manner of speaking, a metaphorical or tropical style, tropology, Hier. in Joel, 2, 18.
tropologia.short: trŏpŏlŏgĭa, ae, f., = τροπολογία, a figurative manner of speaking, a metaphorical or tropical style, tropology, Hier.

tropologicus.full: trŏpŏlŏgĭcus, a, um, adj., = τροπολογικός, figurative, tropical, tropological (late Lat.): tropologicum et figuratum genus, Sid. Ep. 9, 3 med.: interpretatio, Hier. adv. Joan. Hierosol. 7.—Adv.: trŏpŏlŏ-gĭcē, figuratively, metaphorically: exponere aliquid, Hier. in Soph. 1, 8; id. in Ezech. 1, 6, 2.
tropologicus.short: trŏpŏlŏgĭcus, a, um, adj., = τροπολογικός, figurative, tropical, tropological (late Lat.): tropologicum et figuratum genus, Sid.

tropus.full: trŏpus, i, m., = τρόπος. In rhet., a figurative use of a word, a trope (postAug. for translatio, verborum immutatio), Quint. 9, 1, 4 sq.; 9, 2, 44 sq.; 9, 3, 20 al.— A manner of singing, a song, Ven. Carm. 10, 10, 54; 10, 10, 60; 10, 12, 4.

tros1.full: Trōs, Trōis, m., = Τρώς, a king of Phrygia, after whom Troy was named; he was the son of Erichthonius and grandson of Dardanus, Verg. G. 3, 36; Ov. F. 4, 33; Sil. 11, 297; Aus. Idyll. 12, 19.—Hence, Trōja or Trōia, ae, f., Troy, a city of Phrygia, Mel. 2, 3, 6; Liv. 1, 1; Verg. A. 1, 1; 3, 3; Ov. M. 11, 199 sq.; 13, 404 sq.— Transf. A place founded by Æneas in the Laurentine territory in Italy, Liv. 1, 1, 3.— A place settled by Helenus in Epirus, Ov. M. 13, 721; Verg. A. 3, 349.— A Roman game pl
tros1.short: Trōs, Trōis, m., = Τρώς, a king of Phrygia, after whom Troy was named;

tros2.full: Trōs, ōis, m., v. 1. Tros, B. 4.

trosmis.full: Trosmis, is, f., = Τροσμίς, a town of Lower Mœsia, on the Ister, Ov. P. 4, 9, 79.
trosmis.short: Trosmis, is, f., = Τροσμίς, a town of Lower Mœsia, on the Ister, Ov.

trossuli.full: Trossŭli, ōrum, m., a name given to the Roman cavalry, from Trossulum, a town of Etruria, which was conquered by them, Varr. ap. Non. 49, 3; cf.: Junius Gracchanus in Plin. 33, 2, 9, § 36; Fest. p. 367 Müll.— In sing., Pers. 1, 82 Schol.—In the Aug. per., a name used in contempt for fops, coxcombs, Sen. Ep. 87, 9; so id. ib. 76, 2.
trossuli.short: Trossŭli, ōrum, m., a name given to the Roman cavalry, from Trossulum, a town of Etruria, which was conquered by them, Varr.

troxalis.full: troxălis, ĭdis, f., = τροξαλίς, an insect resembling a grasshopper, perhaps a cricket, Plin. 30, 6, 16, § 49.
troxalis.short: troxălis, ĭdis, f., = τροξαλίς, an insect resembling a grasshopper, perhaps a cricket, Plin.

trua.full: trŭa, ae, f. A stirring-spoon, skimmer, ladle, Titin. and Pompon. ap. Non. 19, 17 sq.; cf. Varr. L. L. 5, § 118 Müll.— Perh. a drain, gutter, spout, acc. to Varr. l. l.

trucidatio.full: trŭcīdātĭo, ōnis, f. trucido, a slaughtering, massacring, butchery. Lit.: inde non jam pugna, sed trucidatio velut pecorum fleri, Liv. 28, 16, 6: civium, Cic. Phil. 4, 5, 11.—In plur. absol.: tantas trucidationes facis, Cato ap. Gell. 13, 24, 12.— Transf., a cutting to pieces, cutting up, cutting off, Cels. praef. med.: arborum, a lopping, trimming, Plin. 17, 27, 45, § 257.

trucidator.full: trŭcīdātor, ōris, m. id., a slaughterer, murderer (late Lat.), Aug. Civ. Dei, 1, 1; id. Ep. 105 med.

trucido.full: trŭcīdo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. perh. for truci-cidare, i. e. truncum caedere, to cut to pieces, to slay or kill cruelly, to slaughter, butcher, massacre (class.; syn.: obtrunco, jugulo, perimo). Lit.: cavete neu capti sicut pecora trucidemini, Sall. C. 58, 21; cf.: pecus diripi, trucidari, Auct. B. Afr. 20, 6: cives Romanos necandos trucidandosque curavit, Cic. Imp. Pomp. 3, 7: ne hic ibidem ante oculos vestros trucidetur, id. Rosc. Am. 5, 13: trucidando occidere, Liv. 29, 18, 14: quos ferro truci

tructa.full: tructa, ae, f., = τρώκτης, a kind of trout, Isid. Orig. 12, 6.—Also called truc-tus, i, m., Plin. Val. 5, 43.
tructa.short: tructa, ae, f., = τρώκτης, a kind of trout, Isid.

truculentia.full: trŭcŭlentĭa, ae, f. truculentus, savageness, ferocity, roughness, harshness, truculence (very rare): tua, Plaut. Truc. 3, 2, 7: caeli, harshness, inclemency, Tac. A. 2, 24.

truculentus.full: trŭcŭlentus, a, um, adj. trux, savage, fierce, ferocious, stern, grim, harsh, cruel, fell (mostly poet. and in post-Aug. prose; syn.: saevus, crudelis, trux). Lit.: agrestis, saevus, tristis, parcus, truculentus, tenax, Ter. Ad. 5, 4, 12; cf.: quam taeter incedebat! quam truculentus! quam terribilis aspectu, Cic. Sest. 8, 19: truculentus atque saevus, Plaut. Bacch. 4, 5, 3; id. Truc. 2, 2, 10 sq.; 3, 2, 6; Quint. 11, 3, 73; Ov. M. 13, 558: tigris etiam feris ceteris truculenta, Plin. 8, 4, 5, §

trudis.full: trŭdis, is, f. trudo, a pointed pole, a pike: ferratae, Verg. A. 5, 208; cf.: trudes hastae sunt cum lunato ferro, Isid. Orig. 18, 7.

trudo.full: trūdo, si, sum, 3, v. a. cf. Sanscr, tard-, to split, to thrust, push, shove; to crowd or shove forward; to press on, drive, impel (class.; syn.: pello, expello). Lit. In gen.: vis haec quidem hercle est et trahi et trudi simul, Plaut. Capt. 3, 5, 92: quas mihi tenebras trudis? id. Ep. 3, 4, 40: trudit et impellit, Lucr. 6, 1032: adverso trudere monte saxum, id. 3, 1000: montem pectore, Verg. G. 3, 373: (hostes) trudunt adversos, Tac. A. 2, 11: glaciem cum flumina trudunt, Verg. G. 1, 310: ille

truentum.full: Trŭentum, i, n., a town of Picenum, on the river Truentus (now Tronto), Plin. 3, 13, 18, § 110.—Hence, Trŭentīnus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Truentum, Truentine: Castrum, another name for Truentum, Pompon. ap. Cic. Att. 8, 12, B, 1: turres, Sil. 8, 435.—Plur. subst.: Trŭentī-ni, ōrum, m., the inhabitants of Truentum, the Truentines, Plin. 3, 15, 20, § 116.
truentum.short: Trŭentum, i, n., a town of Picenum, on the river Truentus (now Tronto), Plin.

trugonus.full: trūgŏnus, i, m., = trygon, the stingray, Plaut. Capt. 4, 2, 71.
trugonus.short: trūgŏnus, i, m., = trygon, the stingray, Plaut.

trulla.full: trulla, ae, f. dim. trua. Lit., a small ladle, dipper, or scoop (esp. for dipping wine from the crater into the drinking-cups), Varr. L. L. 5, § 118; Cato, R. R. 13, 2 sq.; Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 27, § 62 sq.; Hor. S. 2, 3, 144; Mart. 9, 97, 1; Plin. 37, 2, 7. § 20; Dig. 34, 2, 36 al.— Transf. A scoop-shaped fire-pan, Liv. 37, 11, 13.— A mason's trowel, Pall. 1, 15; 1, 13, 2.— = trulleum, a basin, wash-basin, Juv. 3, 108.

trulleum.full: trullĕum (trullĭum), i, n. trulla, a basin, wash-basin, Varr. L. L. 5, 25, 34; id. ap. Non. 547, 6; Cato, R. R. 10, 2.—Called also trullĕus, i, m., Plin. 34, 2, 3, § 7; and trullĭo, ōnis, m., Plin. Val. 3, 38.

trullissatio.full: trullissātĭo, ōnis, f. trullisso, a trowelling, i. e. rough casting, plastering, Vitr. 7, 3; 7, 4.

trullisso.full: trullisso, āre, v. a. trulla, II. B., to plaster, rough-cast: parietes, Vitr. 7, 3; 7, 4; 5, 10.

truncatio.full: truncātĭo, ōnis, f. trunco, a maiming or mutilating by cutting off: digitorum, Cod. Th. 7, 13, 5.

trunco.full: trunco, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. 2. truncus, to maim, mutilate, mangle, or shorten by cutting off, to cut off (mostly poet. and in post-Aug. prose; syn.: mutilo, amputo): truncata simulacra deum, Liv. 31, 30, 7: statuis regis truncatis, id. 31, 23, 10: truncat olus foliis, strips, cuts off the leaves, Ov. M. 8, 647: truncato ex vulneribus corpore, Tac. A. 1, 17; cf. id. H. 3, 33: truncatā corporis parte, partem corporis, Just. 11, 14, 11; 15, 3, 4: cadavera, Luc. 6, 584: caput, id. 6, 566: lacertos,

trunculus.full: truncŭlus, i, m. dim. 1. truncus, a small piece cut off from the body, a bit, tip: suum, pigs' trotters, pettitoes, Cels. 2, 20; 2, 22; 4, 7 fin.

truncus1.full: truncus, a, um, adj [root tark-, truc-, to break, tear; cf. torqueo], maimed, mutilated, mangled, dismembered, disfigured, deprived of some of its parts (mostly poet. and perh. not ante-Aug.; syn.: mutilus, mancus). Lit.: trunca manu pinus regit (Polyphemum), i. e. the trunk of a pinetree, Verg. A. 3, 659: trunca illa et retorrida manus Mucii, Sen. Ep. 66, 51: nemora, i. e. trees stripped of their branches, Stat. Th. 4, 455: truncas mhonesto vulnere nares, Verg. A. 6, 497: vultus naribus auribus
truncus1.short: truncus, a, um, adj [root tark-, truc-, to break, tear;

truncus2.full: truncus, i, m., the stem, stock, bole, or trunk of a tree (without regard to its branches). Lit.: cibus ... Per truncos ac per ramos diffunditur omnes, Lucr. 1, 353: quid? in arboribus, in quibus non truncus, non rami, non folia sunt denique, nisi, etc., Cic. de Or. 3, 46, 179; cf. id. Sen. 15, 52; id. N. D. 2, 47, 120; id. Lael. 13, 48; Caes. B. G. 4, 17; 7, 73, Verg. G. 2, 78; 3, 233; Hor S. 1, 8, 1; id. C. 2, 17, 27; 3, 4, 55; Ov. M. 2, 358; 8, 346; id. H. 9, 93; Col. Arb. 17, 1; Sen. Ep. 86,
truncus2.short: truncus, i, m., the stem, stock, bole, or trunk of a tree (without regard to its branches).

truo.full: trŭo, ōnis, m., = avis onocrotalus: Caecilius irridens magnitudinem nasi: pro di immortales, unde prorepsit truo? Fest. p. 367 Müll.
truo.short: trŭo, ōnis, m., = avis onocrotalus: Caecilius irridens magnitudinem nasi: pro di immortales, unde prorepsit truo? Fest.

trusatilis.full: trūsātĭlis, e, adj. truso, that is or may be pushed: mola, a hand-mill, Cato, R. R. 10, 4; 11, 4; Gell. 3, 3, 14.

trusito.full: trūsĭto, āre, v. freq. a. id., to push or thrust often: mulum trusitant, Phaedr. 2, 7, 8 (al. trucidant).

truso.full: trūso, āre, v. freq. a. trudo, to push often or strongly, Cat. 56, 6.

trusus.full: trūsus, a, um, Part. of trudo.

trutina.full: trŭtĭna, ae, f. τρυτάνη, a balance, pair of scales (cf.: lanx, statera). Lit., Varr. L. L. 5, § 183 Müll.; id. ap. Non. 180, 32: ex trutinis quae staterae dicuntur, Vitr. 10, 8.— Trop.: ad ea probanda quae non aurificis staterā, sed quādam populari trutinā examinantur, * Cic. de Or. 2, 38, 159: Romani pensantur eādem Scriptores trutinā, Hor. Ep. 2, 1, 30; id. S. 1, 3, 72: aliā parte in trutinā suspendit Homerum, Juv. 6, 437: examenve inprobum in illā castiges trutinā, Pers. 1, 7.

trutinator.full: trŭtĭnātor, ōris, m. trutinor, a weigher; only trop., one who examines, judges: ut civilia negotia aequus trutinator examines, Cassiod. Var. 6, 23; Ennod. Epigr. 1, 1; 2, 19.

trutino.full: trŭtĭno, āre, 1, v. a., and trŭtĭnor, ātus, 1, v. dep. a. [trutina] Dep. form, to weigh, balance (syn. pensito).—Trop.: verba, Pers. 3, 82.— Act., Hier. Ep. 36, 14: diu trutinandus est, cui traduntur examina, Cassiod. Var. 5, 40.— trŭtĭnā-tus, a, um, in a pass. signif., Sid. Ep. 7, 9.

trux.full: trux, ŭcis (abl. usually truci, but truce in Cic. Agr. 2, 25; Ov. Tr. 4, 7, 14), adj. perh. τρύξ, new, unfermented wine; hence, trop., wild, rough, hard, harsh, savage, fierce, ferocious, grim, stern (mostly poet.; cf.; truculentus, torvus). Of living beings: horridus ac trux tribunus plebis, Cic. Agr. 2, 25, 65: M. Catonem oratorem non solum gravem sed interdum etiam trucem esse scimus, Liv. 34, 5, 6: insectator, id. 3, 33, 7: puer, i. e. Achilles, Sen. Troad. 832: puellae, i. e. Amazons, id. O

tryblium.full: tryblĭum, ii, n., = τρύβλιον, a plate, salver, Plaut. Stich. 5, 4, 9; cf. Varr. L. L. 5, § 120 Müll.
tryblium.short: tryblĭum, ii, n., = τρύβλιον, a plate, salver, Plaut.

tryga.full: tryga antiqui vinum appellabant. unde trygetus adhuc dicitur, Fest. p. 366 Müll. [τρύξ, τρυγητός].

tryginon.full: trўgĭnon, i, n., = τρύγινον, a black coloring matter made from the lees of wine, Plin. 35, 6, 25, § 42.
tryginon.short: trўgĭnon, i, n., = τρύγινον, a black coloring matter made from the lees of wine, Plin.

trygon.full: trȳgōn, ōnis, m., = τρυγών, a stingray: Raia pastinaca, Linn.; Plin. 9, 48, 72, § 155; Aus. Ep. 4, 60.
trygon.short: trȳgōn, ōnis, m., = τρυγών, a stingray: Raia pastinaca, Linn.;

trygona.full: trȳgŏna, ae, f., a bird, otherwise unknown. Plin. 10, 16, 18, § 38.
trygona.short: trȳgŏna, ae, f., a bird, otherwise unknown.

trypherus.full: Trўphĕrus, i, m., a Roman skilled in caroing, Juv. 11, 137.
trypherus.short: Trўphĕrus, i, m., a Roman skilled in caroing, Juv.

tryphon.full: Tryphon, ōnis, m. A surgeon, Cels. 6, 5; 7 praef.— A king in Syria, Just. 36, 1, 7; 38, 9, 3; 39, 1, 3.— A surname of Ptolemy Philopator, Plin. 7, 56, 57, § 208. — A publisher of Rome, Quint. ad Tryph. 1 sqq.; Mart. 4, 72, 2; 13, 3, 4.

tu.full: tū (old form of the gen. sing. tis, Plaut. Mil. 4, 2, 42; id. Trin. 2, 2, 62; id. Bacch. 5, 2, 87; id. Ps. 1, 1, 6; acc. ted, id. As. 2, 2, 33 et saep.; gen. plur. vestrorum or vostrorum, Pac. ap. Non. 85, 5; Plaut. Most. 1, 3, 123; fem. vostrarum, Ter. Heaut. 2, 4, 6; v. ego init.), pers. pron. [Sanscr. tva, tvam; Gr. σύ; Dor. τύ; Goth. thu; Germ. du; Engl. thou, etc.], thou. In gen.: nec pol homo quisquam faciet impune animatus Hoc nisi tu, Enn. ap. Macr. S. 6, 1 (Ann. v. 101 Vahl.); imitated

tuatim.full: tŭātim, adv. tuus, after your manner: eccere, jam tuatim facis, ut, etc., Plaut. Am. 2, 1, 4; cf. Non. 179, 31; and Charis. p. 196 P.

tuba.full: tŭba, ae, f. kindr. with tubus, a tube, a trumpet, esp. a war-trumpet (straight, while the cornu was curved, Acron ad Hor. C. 1, 1, 23). Lit.: ille arma misit, cornua, tubas, falces, Cic. Sull. 5, 17: tubae et signa militaria, id. Cat. 2, 6, 13: at tuba terribili sonitu taratantara dixit, Enn. ap. Prisc. p. 842 P. (Ann. v. 452 Vahl.); imitated by Verg. A. 9, 503: tubae utrimque canunt, Plaut. Am. 1, 1, 73: signum tubā dare, Caes. B. G. 2, 20; so id. ib. 7, 81; id. B. C. 3, 46; 3, 90; Liv. 29, 27

tubantes.full: Tubantes, um, m., a people of Germany, between the Rhine and the Elbe, Tac. A. 1, 51; 13, 55 sq.; cf. Ukert, Germ. p. 363.
tubantes.short: Tubantes, um, m., a people of Germany, between the Rhine and the Elbe, Tac.

tubarius.full: tūbārĭus, ii, m. tuba, a trumpetmaker, Dig. 50, 6, 6.

tuber1.full: tūber, ĕris, n. from root tum, tumeo, a hump, bump, swelling, tumor, protuberance on animal bodies, whether natural or caused by disease. Lit.: cameli, Plin. 8, 18, 26, § 67: boum, id. 8, 45, 70, § 179: tubera ... anserino adipe curantur, tumors, id. 30, 12, 33, § 107; so id. 22, 24, 50, § 107; 26, 14, 87, § 139 al.; cf.: colaphis tuber est totum caput, is one boil, i. e. is full of boils, Ter. Ad. 2, 2, 37.—Prov.: ubi uber, ibi tuber, there are no roses without thorns, App. Flor. p. 359, 29: qu

tuber2.full: tŭber, ĕris, m. and f. Fem., a kind of apple-tree, Plin. 16, 25, 42, § 103; Col. 11, 2, 11; Pall. Jan. 15, 20; id. Sept. 14, 1.— Masc., the fruit of this tree, Plin. 15, 14, 14, § 47; Mart. 13, 42, 1; 13, 43, 2; Suet. Dom. 16.

tuberans.full: tūbĕrans, antis, adj. 1. tuber, swelling out, swelling: sinus, App. M. 2, p. 121, 22.

tuberatus.full: tūbĕrātus, a, um, adj. id., covered with knobs or bosses = tuberosus: ocreae, Fest. s. v. ocrem, p. 181 Müll.

tuberculum.full: tūbercŭlum, i, n. dim. id., a small swelling, bump, or protuberance; a boil, pimple, tubercle: in gingivis, Cels. 6, 13: in capite, id. 7, 6: fabae, an excrescence, Plin. 22, 22, 45, § 91; 11, 11, 12, § 29.

tubero.full: Tūbĕro, ōnis, m., a surname in the gens Aelia; e. g. Q. Aelius Tubero, a Stoic, an opponent of Tiberius Gracchus, Cic. brut. 31, 117; id. Lael. 11, 37; 27, 101; id. de Or. 3, 23, 87.— L. Tubero, lieutenant of Q. Cicern in Asia, an historian, Caes. B. C. 1, 31; Cic. Q. Fr. 1, 1, 3, § 10; Gell. 6, 3, 4.— Q. Aelius Tubero, son of the preceding, a relative (according to some, the brother-in-law) of Cicero, and the accuser of Ligarius, Cic. Lig. 1, 1; 3, 9 al.; Quint. 11, 1, 80; Suet. Caes. 83.
tubero.short: Tūbĕro, ōnis, m., a surname in the gens Aelia;

tuberosus.full: tūbĕrōsus, a, um, adj. tuber, full of humps, lumps, or protuberances (very rare): campus, Varr. R. R. 1, 49, 2: tuberosissima frons, Petr. 15.

tubertus.full: Tūbertus, i, m., a Roman cognomen in the gens Postumius, Cic. Leg. 2, 23, 58; Ov. F. 6, 723; Liv. 4, 29.
tubertus.short: Tūbertus, i, m., a Roman cognomen in the gens Postumius, Cic.

tubicen.full: tŭbĭcen, cĭnis, m. tuba-cano, a trumpeter; esp. in war: cornicines tubicinesque canere jubet, Liv. 2, 64, 10; Auct. B. Afr. 82, 3; Ov. M. 3, 705; Sen. Ep. 78, 16; 76, 4.—At sacrifices: sacrorum, Varr. L. L. 5, § 91 Müll.—At funerals, Atei. Capito ap. Gell. 20, 2, 3; Petr. 129.— Tubicines etiam hi appellantur, qui sacerdotes viri speciosi publice sacra faciunt tubarum lustrandarum gratia, Fest. p. 352 Müll.

tubilustrium.full: tŭbĭlustrĭum or tŭbŭlustrĭum, ii, n. tuba-lustro, a festival held on the 23d of March and 23d of May, when the trumpets used at sacrifices were purified, the feast of trumpets: dies tubulustrium appellatur, quod eo die in atrio sutorio sacrorum tubae lustrantur, Varr. L. L. 6, § 14 Müll. (cf. Ov. F. 3, 849).—Also plur.: tubilustria, Ov. F. 5, 725; cf. Fest. p. 352 Müll.

tubula.full: tŭbŭla, ae, f. dim. tuba, a small trumpet, Sen. Ep. 56, 4.

tubulatio.full: tŭbŭlātĭo, ōnis, f. tubulus, a hollowing into a tube, tubulation: ligulae, App. Flor. p. 346, 28; Arn. 3, 108 (al. incumulatio).

tubulatus.full: tŭbŭlātus, a, um, adj. id., formed like a pipe, tubular, tubulated: rostrum, Plin. 9, 36, 61, § 130; Plin. Ep. 2, 17, 9.

tubulus1.full: tŭbŭlus, i, m. dim. tubus, a small pipe or tube, a water-pipe. Lit., Varr. R. R. 1, 8, 4; Vitr. 8, 7; Plin. 35, 12, 46, § 159.—A smoke - pipe, Dig. 8, 2, 13.— Transf., a bar of metal, a pig, ingot, Plin. 33, 6, 35, § 106.

tubulus2.full: Tŭbŭlus, i, m., a Roman cognomen in the gens Hostilia: L. Hostilius Tubulus, a prœtor A. U. C. 611, Lucil. ap. Cic. N. D. 1, 23, 63; Cic. Att. 12, 5, 3; id. Fin. 4, 28, 77; 5, 22, 62.
tubulus2.short: Tŭbŭlus, i, m., a Roman cognomen in the gens Hostilia: L.

tuburcinabundus.full: tuburcĭnābundus (tuburchĭn-), a, um, adj. tuburcinor, greedily eating or devouring, gobbling (cf. lurcus), Cato ap. Quint. 1, 6, 42 Spald.

tuburcinor.full: tuburcĭnor, ātus, 1, v. dep. a., to eat greedily, gobble up, devour (syn. voro): raptim manducare, Non. 179, 21 (ante- and postclass.): de suo, Plaut. Pers. 1, 3, 42; Titin. and Turp. ap. Non. 1. 1.!*? tuburcĭnātus, a, um, in a pass. signif.: prandio raptim tuburcinato, App. M. 6, p. 183, 30.

tubus.full: tŭbus, i, m., a pipe, tube. Lit., for conducting water, Col. 1, 5, 2; Plin. 16, 42, 81, § 224; 5, 31, 34, § 128.—For wine, Pall. 1, 18, 1.—For heating baths, Sen. Ep. 90, 25.— Transf. For tuba, a trumpet used at sacrifices, acc. to Varr. L. L. 5, § 117 Müll., and Verr. Kalend. Praenest. s. 23 Mart. (Inscr. Orell. II. p. 386).— Transf.: per omnes viscerum tubos, Mart. 11, 61, 6.
tubus.short: tŭbus, i, m., a pipe, tube.

tuccetum.full: tuccētum or tūcētum, i, n., a kind of sausage or haggis: tuceta crassa, Pers. 2, 43 Schol.: sapidissimum, App. M. 2, p. 117; 7, p. 192; 9, p. 227; Arn. 2, 73.
tuccetum.short: tuccētum or tūcētum, i, n., a kind of sausage or haggis: tuceta crassa, Pers.

tuccius.full: Tuccĭus, i, m.; Tuccĭa, ae, f., the name of a Roman gens. M. Tuccius, Liv. 35, 41; Cael. ap. Cic. Fam. 8, 8.— L. Tuccius Valla, a physician, Plin. 7, 53, 54, § 183.— Tuccia, a celebrated vestal, Val. Max. 8, 1, 5; Plin. 28, 2, 3, § 12.

tuder.full: Tŭder, ĕris, n., a town in Umbria, near the Tiber, now Todi, Plin. 3, 14, 19, § 113; Sil. 6, 645.—Hence, Tŭders, ertis, adj. m., of or belonging to Tuder; as subst., an inhabitant of Tuder, Sil. 4, 222; 8, 464; Inscr. Orell. 1228 and 3726.— Tŭder-nis, is, adj. f., of or belonging to Tuder: vitis, Plin. 14, 3, 4, § 36.
tuder.short: Tŭder, ĕris, n., a town in Umbria, near the Tiber, now Todi, Plin.

tudes.full: tŭdes, is (ĭtis, acc. to Fest. p. 253 Müll.), m. root tud, tundo; Sanscr. tud-, to thrust, a hammer, mallet: tudites malleos appellant antiqui a tundendo, Fest. p. 352 sq. Müll.: fabriles operae tudibus contundere massas Festinant, Auct. Aetnae, 659.

tudicius.full: Tudicĭus, i, m., the name of a Roman gens: Cn. Tudicius, a Roman senator, Cic. Clu. 70.
tudicius.short: Tudicĭus, i, m., the name of a Roman gens: Cn.

tudicula.full: tŭdĭcŭla, ae, f. dim. tudes, a small machine for bruising olives, Col. 12, 52, 7.

tudiculo.full: tŭdĭcŭlo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. tudicula, to stir, stir about (ante- and post-class.), Varr. ap. Non. 178, 30: cum bene ferbuerit, tudiculabis, Apic. 5, 2.

tuditans.full: tŭdĭtans, antis, Part. [tud, tundo], striking or beating often (ante-class.). Lit., Lucr. 3, 394: corpora, id. 2, 1142.— Trop., pushing or driving on: tuditantes significat negotium tundentes, id est agentes, Fest. pp. 352 and 353 Müll.: haec inter sese tum (certabant) tuditantes, Enn. ib. (Ann. v. 138 Vahl.).

tuditanus.full: Tŭdĭtānus, i, m., a surname in the gens Sempronia, Enn. ap. Cic. Brut. 15, 58 (Ann. v. 305 Vahl.); Cic. Sen. 4, 10; 14, 50 al.; cf. Fest. p. 252 Müll.
tuditanus.short: Tŭdĭtānus, i, m., a surname in the gens Sempronia, Enn.

tueor.full: tŭĕor, tuĭtus, 2 (perf. only post-Aug., Quint. 5, 13, 35; Plin. Ep. 6, 29, 10; collat. form tūtus, in the part., rare, Sall. J. 74, 3; Front. Strat. 2, 12, 13; but constantly in the P. a.; inf. parag. tuerier, Plaut. Rud. 1, 4, 35; collat. form acc. to the 3d conj. tŭor, Cat. 20, 5; Stat. Th. 3, 151: tuĕris, Plaut. Trin. 3, 2, 82: tuimur, Lucr. 1, 300; 4, 224; 4, 449; 6, 934: tuamur, id. 4, 361: tuantur, id. 4, 1004; imper. tuĕre, id. 5, 318), v. dep. a. [etym. dub.], orig., to see, to look or g

tufa.full: tūfa, ae, f., a kind of helmet-crest; or, acc. to others, a kind of military standard, Veg. Mil. 3, 5; cf. Lyd. Magistr. 1, 8 (hence the Fr. toupet).
tufa.short: tūfa, ae, f., a kind of helmet-crest;

tugio.full: Tugĭo, ōnis, m., a jurist in the time of Cicero, Cic. Balb. 20, 45.
tugio.short: Tugĭo, ōnis, m., a jurist in the time of Cicero, Cic.

tuguriolum.full: tŭgŭrĭŏlum, i, n. dim. tugurium, a little hut or cottage, App. M. 4, p. 147, 34; Arn. 6, 191; Hier. Ep. 112, 5.

tugurium.full: tŭgŭrĭum (TEGVRIVM and TIGVRIVM in inscrr.; cf. Inscr. Orell. 1773; and ib. Labus), ii, n. tego, a hut, cot, cottage of shepherds, peasants, etc., Varr. R. R. 3, 1, 3; Afran. and Caecil. ap. Fest. p. 355 Müll.; Cic. Sest. 43, 93; Verg. E. 1, 69; Col. 12, 15, 1; Plin. 16, 9, 14, § 35; Val. Max. 5, 4, 1; 5, 3, ext. 3; 7, 1, 2; Dig. 50, 16, 180.

tuguriunculum.full: tŭgŭrĭuncŭlum, i, n. dim. tugurium, a little hut or cottage, Hier. Vit. Hil. 9.

tuisco.full: Tuisco, ōnis, m., the progenitor of the Germans, honored by them as a god, Tac. G. 2; cf. Grimm, Myth. pp. 176 and 318 (2d ed.).
tuisco.short: Tuisco, ōnis, m., the progenitor of the Germans, honored by them as a god, Tac.

tuitio.full: tŭĭtĭo, ōnis, f. tueor, II., a taking care of, keeping, guarding, preserving, defense, protection, preservation; with gen. subj. praetoris, Dig. 7, 4, 1 pr.; with gen. obj.: tuitio sui, Cic. Top. 23, 90: pudoris, Macr. S. 2, 2 med.; Dig. 37, 11, 2; 7, 9, 9: militaris, Cod. Just. 1, 46, 1: aedium, Hier. in Isa. 16, 57, 7.

tuitus.full: tŭĭtus, a, um, Part. of tueor.

tulingi.full: Tulingi, ōrum, m., a German or Helvetic tribe on the Rhine, Caes. B. G. 1, 5.
tulingi.short: Tulingi, ōrum, m., a German or Helvetic tribe on the Rhine, Caes.

tulliola.full: Tullĭŏla, ae, f. dim. Tullia, a pet name for Tullia, the daughter of Cicero, Cic. Att. 1, 3, 3; 1, 8, 3; 1, 10, 6 et saep.

tullius.full: Tullĭus, i, m.; Tullĭa, ae, f., the name of a Roman gens. Esp., Servius Tullius, the sixth king of Rome, Liv. 1, 41 sqq. — M. Tullius Cicero, the renowned statesman and orator.— Q. Tullius Cicero, his brother.— M. Tullius Tiro, a freedman of M. Cicero.— Fem. Tullia, a daughter of king Servius Tullius, and wife of Tarquinius Superbus.—Also, A daughter of M. Tullius Cicero.—Hence, Tullĭā-nus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to a Tullius, Tullian: semis, Cic. Att. 15, 29, 1: caput, id. ib. 15, 26, 4:

tullus.full: Tullus, i, m., a Roman prœnomen, e.g. Tullus Hostilius, the third king of Rome, Liv. 1, 22 sqq.; Val. Max. 3, 4, 1; 9, 12, 1: Tullus Cluilius, a Roman ambassador, Cic. Phil. 9, 2, 5 al.
tullus.short: Tullus, i, m., a Roman prœnomen, e.g.

tulo.full: tulo, tĕtŭli (tŭli), 3, v. a. akin with tollo; Gr. τλάω, ante-class. collat. form of fero, to bring, bear, lift up: nisi quid tua facultas nobis tulat opem, peream, Att. ap. Macr. Diff. et Soc. Gr. et Lat. Verb. 6, 14 (Trag. Frag. v. 102 Rib.); cf. Non. 178, 16; and v. fero init.

tum.full: tum, adv. demonstr., of time [pronom. demonstr. stems to-, ta-; Gr. το, seen in ita, tam, etc.; cf. quom or cum], then. Absol. Referring to a time previously specified. To a definite past time. To a period of time in which something was or happened (opp. later periods) = illis temporibus: is dictu'st ollis popularibus olim Qui tum vivebant homines, Enn. Ann. v. 308 Vahl.: quod tum erat res in pecore et locorum possessionibus, i. e. Romuli temporibus, Cic. Rep. 2, 9, 16: cum illi male dicerent, q

tumba.full: tumba, ae, f., = τύμβα (τύμβος), a sepulchral mound, a sepulchre, tomb, Prud. στεφ. 11, 9.
tumba.short: tumba, ae, f., = τύμβα (τύμβος), a sepulchral mound, a sepulchre, tomb, Prud.

tumbula.full: tumbŭla, ae, f. tumba, a little tomb (late Lat.), Aldhelm. Carm. Virg. 889.

tumefacio.full: tŭmĕ-făcĭo, fēci, factum, 3, v. a. tumeo, to cause to swell, to tumefy (poet.). Lit.: vis fera ventorum ... Extentam tumefecit humum, Ov. M. 15, 303: tumefactus pontus, id. ib. 11, 518.— Trop., to swell or puff up, to inflate with pride, etc.: num me laetitiā tumefactum fallis inani? Prop. 3, 6 (4, 5), 3: ut nostris tumefacta superbiat Umbria libris, id. 4 (5), 1, 63: dum nimium vano tumefactus nomine gaudes, Mart. 4, 11, 1.

tumentia.full: tŭmentĭa, ae, f. id., a swelling (late Lat.): capitis, Cael. Aur. Acut. 1, 10, 74; 3, 8, 92.

tumeo.full: tŭmĕo, ēre, v. n. Sanscr. tu-, taumi, tavīmi, to be strong; Gr. τύλος, τύλη, lump; Lat. tuber, tumulus, tumor, etc.; cf. O. H. Germ. dūmo; Germ. Daumen; Engl. thumb, to swell, be swollen or tumid, to be puffed out or inflated (mostly poet. and in postAug. prose; cf. turgeo). Lit.: So. Quid hoc in collo tibi tumet? Sa. Vomica'st: pressare parce, Plaut. Pers. 2, 5, 11: corpus tumet omne veneno, Ov. M. 3, 33: guttura plenis venis, id. ib. 3, 73: lumina fletu, Tib. 1, 8, 68 (al. timet): pedes, Verg.

tumesco.full: tŭmesco, mŭi, 3, v. inch. n. [tumeo], to begin to swell, to swell up (poet. and in postAug. prose). Lit.: inflatum mare cum subito penitusque tumescit, Cic. poët. Div. 1, 7, 13: vi maria, Verg. G. 2, 479: freta ventis, Ov. M. 1, 36: inflata colla, id. ib. 6, 377: vulnera, Tac. H. 2, 77: fluvius tabe nivis, Luc. 10, 244: suco herba, Sen. Herc. Fur. 936: matura virginitas, Claud. Epith. 125.— Trop., to swell up, become swollen with passionate excitement, to become excited, violent, ready to burst

tumicla.full: tūmicla, ae, f. dim. contracted from tomicula, from tomix. a little rope, a cord: spartea, App. M. 8, p. 213 (p. 575 Oud.).

tumiditas.full: tŭmĭdĭtās, ātis, f. tumidus, a swelling, tumor (late Lat.): ventris, Firm. Math. 8, 29 med.; Hier. Ep. 53, 11.

tumido.full: tŭmĭdo, āre, 1, v. a. id., to cause to swell (late Lat.), Aug. Spec. 30.

tumidosus.full: tŭmĭdōsus, a, um, adj. id., high-swelling: colles, Amm. 21, 10, 3 (al. tumulosi; cf., however, Ov. Am. 2, 16, 51, and Tac. A. 2, 23 s. v. tumidus; v. also tumor).

tumidulus.full: tŭmĭdŭlus, a, um, adj. dim. [tumidus], swollen, tumid: gingivula, App. Mag. p. 277, 12.

tumidus.full: tŭmĭdus, a, um, adj. tumeo, swollen, swelling, rising high, protuberant, tumid (class.). Lit.: membrum tumidum ac turgidum, Cic. Tusc. 3, 9, 19: serpens inflato collo, tumidis cervicibus, id. Vatin. 2, 4: Python, Ov. M. 1, 460: Echidnae, id. ib. 10, 313: venter, id. Am. 2, 14, 15: papillae, id. R. Am. 338: virginitas, i. e. with swelling breasts, Stat. Th. 2, 204: mare, Verg. A. 8, 671: aequor, id. ib. 3, 157; Ov. M. 14, 544: fluctus, id. ib. 11, 480: Nilus, Hor. C. 3, 3, 48: vela, id. Ep. 2, 2,

tumor.full: tŭmor, ōris, m. id., the state of being swollen or tumid; a swelling, tumor (class.; syn. tuber). Lit.: oculorum tumor, Cic. Tusc. 4, 37, 81; so of a tumor, id. ib. 3, 9, 19; Auct. Her. 2, 27, 44.—In plur.: tumores ardentes, Plin. 20, 25, 96, § 257: tollere, id. 21, 21, 89, § 157: discutere, id. 24, 4, 6, § 11: vetat Chrysippus ad recentes quasi tumores animi remedium adhibere. Cic. Tusc. 4, 29, 63: turpia cum faceret Palladis ora tumor, inflation of the cheeks from blowing the tibia, Prop. 2, 3

tumorosus.full: tŭmōrōsus, a, um, adj. tumor, inflated, bloated (late Lat.), Ps.-Aug. ad Fr. Erem. Serm. 12.

tumulamen.full: tŭmŭlāmen, ĭnis, n. tumulus, a sepulchral mound, tumulus, Inscr. Fabr. 634, 290.

tumulo.full: tŭmŭlo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. id., to cover with a mound, to bury, inter, entomb (poet.; syn. humo): neque injectā tumulabor mortua terrā, Cat. 64, 153: neu sim tumulandus ab illā, Ov. M. 8, 710; 15, 716; id. P. 1, 6, 49; Mart. 11, 91, 1.

tumulosus.full: tŭmŭlōsus, a, um, adj. id., full of hills, hilly: locus, Sall. J. 91, 3.

tumultuarius.full: tŭmultŭārĭus, a, um, adj. tumultus, of or belonging to bustle, hurry, or tumult; in milit. lang., of troops brought hurriedly together, raised hastily or suddenly (not ante-Aug., but esp. freq. in Livy). Lit.: tumultuario exercitu raptim ducto, Liv. 5, 37, 7; so, milites, id. 35, 2, 7; 35, 23, 8; Auct. B. Alex. 34, 5: manus, Curt. 4, 16, 24: militia, Gell. 16, 10, 13.— Transf., that is done or happens in a hurry, hurried, hasty, sudden, confused, irregular, disorderly, tumultuary: pugna, Liv. 21

tumultuatim.full: tŭmultŭātim, adv. id., in haste, hastily, Sid. Ep. 4, 11.

tumultuatio.full: tŭmultŭātĭo, ōnis, f. tumultuor. A bustling, hurrying, bustle, confusion, tumult (very rare), Liv. 38, 2, 8.— The irregular swearing of the milites tumultuarii, acc. to Isid. Orig. 9, 3, 55.

tumultuor.full: tŭmultŭor, ātus, 1, v. dep. n. [tumultus], to make a bustle or disturbance, to be in great agitation or confusion, be in an uproar, raise a tumult: in otio tumultuaris, in tumultu es otiosus, Auct. Her. 4, 15, 21: non decet tumultuari, Plaut. Poen. 3, 1, 22: saepe et sine causā, Cic. Agr. 2, 37, 101: quid tumultuaris, soror? quid insanis? id. Cael. 15, 36: fortis et constantis est, non perturbari in rebus asperis nec tumultuantem de gradu deici, confused, agitated, id. Off. 1, 23, 80; Petr. 79:

tumultuosus.full: tŭmultŭōsus, a, um, adj. tumultus, full of bustle, confusion, or tumult, restless, turbulent, tumultuous (class.): qui homo tam tumultuoso sonitu me excivit foras? Plaut. Trin. 5, 2, 52: seditiosa ac tumultuosa vita, Cic. Inv. 1, 3, 4: contiones, id. Fam. 2, 12, 1: actio, Quint. 11, 1, 29: nuntius, Liv. 2, 24, 1: turba, id. 6, 14, 6: multitudo, id. 24, 29, 1: genus pugnae, id. 1, 14, 7; 28, 15, 5: proelia, id. 27, 2, 11: excursiones, id. 30, 8, 4: somnia, Cels. 1, 2; 8, 4: mare, Hor. C. 3, 1, 26

tumultus.full: tŭmultus, ūs (gen. tumulti, Enn., Att., Afran., Turp., and Pompon. ap. Non. 489, 29 sq.; Plaut. Cas. 3, 5, 22; id. Poen. 1, 1, 79; Ter. And. 2, 2, 28; id. Hec. 3, 2, 21; Sall. C. 59, 5), m. Sanscr. tumalas, tumulas, disturbing; cf. tumeo, an uproar, bustle, violent commotion, disturbance, tumult (freq. and class.; cf.: turba, perturbatio). Lit. In gen.: quid hoc hic clamoris, quid hoc hic tumulti est? Enn. ap. Non. 489, 29 (Trag. v. 204 Vahl.): quis sonitu ac tumultu tanto nomine nominat me atqu

tumulus.full: tŭmŭlus, i, m. (late Lat. in the neutr.: HOC TVMVLVM, Inscr. Rein. cl. 20, 197) [tumeo; cf. also tumor and tumidus], a raised heap of earth, a mound, hill, hillock (freq. and class.; cf.: agger, moles). In gen.: terrenus, Caes. B. G. 1, 43: ignis e speculā sublatus aut tumulo, Cic. Verr. 2, 5, 35, § 93: coacervatis cadaveribus, qui superessent ut ex tumulo tela in nostros conicerent, Caes. B. G. 2, 27: quaeris, utrum magis tumulis prospectuque an ambulatione delecter, Cic. Att. 14, 13, 1: cum tu

tunc.full: tunc, adv. demonstr., of time [tum, and demonstr. suffix -ce], then, at that time; but in ante-class. and class. prose tunc is always emphatic, and generally refers to a point of time. In post-Aug. style tunc freq. occurs without emphasis, and is freely used of periods of time. Tunc = deinde occurs first in the class. per. and rarely in prose; but is very freq. after the Aug. per. Tunc in mere co-ordinative use is very rare and not ante-class. (v. I. C.). Tunc coupled with an emphatic or tempora

tundo.full: tundo, tŭtŭdi, tunsum, tūssum, and tusum (v. Neue, Formenl. II. 568), 3 (old collat. form of the perf. tuserunt, Naev. 1, 1: tunsi, acc. to Diom. p. 369 P.; inf. tundier, Lucr. 4, 934), v. a. Sanscr. tu-dāmi, thrust; cf. Gr. Τυδεύς, Τυνδάρεος, to beat, strike, thump, buffet with repeated strokes. Lit. In gen. (class.; cf.: verbero, pulso, ico, impello, cudo): oculos converso bacillo, Cic. Verr. 2, 5, 54, § 142: pectus palo, Plaut. Rud. 5, 2, 3: pectora manu, Ov. Am. 3, 9, 10; id. M. 8, 535; Verg
tundo.short: tundo, tŭtŭdi, tunsum, tūssum, and tusum (v.

tunes.full: Tūnēs, ētis, m., a maritime town of Africa Propria, now Tunis: Scipio occupat relictum Tuneta, Liv. 30, 9, 16.—Acc. Tunetem, Liv. 30, 36, 6.
tunes.short: Tūnēs, ētis, m., a maritime town of Africa Propria, now Tunis: Scipio occupat relictum Tuneta, Liv.

tungri.full: Tungri, ōrum, m., a people of Gallia Belgica, near the modern Tongres, Plin. 4, 17, 31, § 106; 31, 2, 8, § 12; Tac. G. 2; id. H. 2, 14 sq.; 4, 16, 55; Amm. 15, 11, 7; Inscr. Orell. 3399.—In sing.: Tunger, Sil. 7, 682; Inscr. Grut. 334, 3.
tungri.short: Tungri, ōrum, m., a people of Gallia Belgica, near the modern Tongres, Plin.

tunica.full: tŭnĭca, ae, f. perh. for tog-nica, from tego, an under-garment of the Romans worn by both sexes, a tunic. Lit., Plaut. Ep. 2, 2, 46; 5, 2, 60; id. Mil. 3, 1, 93; 5, 30; id. Pers. 1, 3, 75; Cic. Tusc. 5, 20, 60; id. de Or. 2, 47, 195; Hor. S. 1, 2, 132; id. Ep. 1, 1, 96; 1, 18, 33.—A tunic with long sleeves was thought effeminate, Plaut. Ps. 2, 4, 48; Cic. Cat. 2, 10, 22; Suet. Calig. 52; Gell. 7, 12, 4: et tunicae manicas habent, Verg. A. 9, 616: manicata, Curt. 3, 3, 13; cf. Plin. 8, 48, 74, §

tunico.full: tŭnĭco, no perf., ātum, 1, v. a. tunica, to clothe with a tunic. In the verb. finit. only once: tunicare homulum, Varr. ap. Non. 182, 17.— In part. perf. (freq. and class.): tŭnĭcātus, a, um, clothed with a tunic, Cic. Cael. 5, 11; cf. in poet. transf., of life in the country: o tunicata quies! Mart. 10, 51, 6.—Of the common people, who went clothed simply with the tunic: novistin' tu illunc tunicatum hominem? Plaut. Poen. 5, 3, 2: qui metus erat tunicatorum illorum? Cic. Agr. 2, 34, 94: popellu

tunicopallium.full: tŭnĭcopallĭum, ĭi, n. tunica-pallium, a garment uniting in one the tunic and the pallium, Serv. Verg. A. 1, 648; ad Hor. S. 1, 2, 99; cf. Non. 537, 33.

tunicula.full: tŭnĭcŭla, ae, f. dim. tunica. A little tunic, Plaut. Rud. 2, 6, 65; Turp. ap. Non. 538, 10; Varr. ib. 228, 27.— A little coat, skin, or membrane: oculorum, Plin. 26, 12, 76, § 123; 29, 6, 38, § 124: stellionis, id. 30, 10, 27, § 88: hordei, Fest. s. v. gluma, p. 98 Müll.

tunsus.full: tunsus, a, um, Part. of tundo.

tuor2.full: tŭor, ōris, m. 1. tuor, = tueor, the sight, vision: radios omnis nostri tuoris raritate transmittunt, App. de Deo Socr. p. 48.

turalis.full: tūrālis (thūr-), e, adj. tus, of or belonging to incense, incense-: arca, Serv. Verg. A. 5, 745.

turarius.full: tūrārĭus (thūr-), a, um, adj. id., of or belonging to frankincense. In gen. Adj.: tibiae, incense-flutes, i. e. flutes played upon while the incense was burned at sacrifices, Sol. 5 med. (called also tibiae sacrificae Tuscorum, Plin. 16, 36, 66, § 172; cf. Verg. G. 2, 193).— Subst.: tūrārĭus, ii, m., a dealer in frankincense, Firm. Math. 8, 25 fin.; Tert. Idol. 11; Inscr. Orell. 4291; cf. Marini, Fratr. Arv. p. 338.— Vicus Turarius, a street in Rome, in the eighth region, Ascon. Cic. Verr. 2, 1,

turba.full: turba, ae, f. = τύρβη; cf. Sanscr. turāmi, to hasten; turas, hasty; Lat. turma, a turmoil, hubbub, uproar, disorder, tumult, commotion, disturbance, of a crowd of people (syn. tumultus): praetor ait: cujus dolo malo in turbā damnum quod factum esse dicetur ... Turbam appellatam Labeo ait ex genere tumultūs, idque verbum ex Graeco tractum ἀπὸ τοῦ θορυβεῖν. Turbam autem ex quo numero admittimus? Si duo rixam commiserint, utique non accipiemus in turbā id factum, quia duo turba non proprie dicentur

turbamentum.full: turbāmentum, i, n. turbo, a means of disturbance (very rare): turbamenta reipublicae, Sall. Or. Lepid. 11: turbamenta vulgi, Tac. H. 1, 23.

turbate.full: turbātē, adv., v. 1. turbo, P. a. fin.

turbatio.full: turbātĭo, ōnis, f. 1. turbo, confusion, disorder, disturbance (perh. not ante-Aug.; cf.: conturbatio, perturbatio): turbam multitudinis hominum esse turbationem et coetum, rixam etiam duorum, Dig. 48, 8, 4 (v. turba init.): rerum, Liv. 24, 28, 1: reipublicae, Flor. 4, 6, 2: coloris et vultūs, Gell. 19, 1, 6: non sine magnā turbatione, App. M. 11, p. 271, 30.

turbator.full: turbātor, ōris, m. id., a troubler, disquieter, disturber (not ante-Aug.): turbatores vulgi erant tribuni plebis, Liv. 4, 48, 1; so, vulgi, id. 4, 2, 7: plebis (Gracchi et Saturnini), Tac. A. 3, 27: Germaniae (Arminius), id. ib. 1, 55; cf. id. ib. 1, 30: otii, Sen. Contr. 3, 17 fin.—Plur.: turbatores belli, stirrers up of war, Liv. 2, 16, 4.

turbatrix.full: turbātrix, īcis, f. turbator, she that troubles, disquiets, or disturbs (poet. and very rare): turbatrix fama, Stat. Th. 4, 369: pacis, Prud. Psych. 668.

turbatus.full: turbātus, a, um, Part. and P. a. of 1. turbo.

turbellae.full: turbellae or turbēlae, ārum, f. dim. turba. A bustle, stir, row (only in vulg. lang.): tantas turbellas facio, Plaut. Bacch. 4, 9, 134; so id. Ps. 1, 1, 108; App. de Deo Socr. p. 48, 20.—* A little crowd, multitude: populi circumfluentis, App. M. 4, p. 151, 39 al.

turbido.full: turbĭdo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. turbidus, to trouble, to make turbid, to disturb, obscure (post-class.). Lit.: aquam, Sol. 49 fin.: aër turbidatus, Mart. Cap. 2, § 165. — Trop.: laetitiam, Mart. Cap. 1, § 67; cf.: serenitatem animae, Sid. Ep. 6, 2.

turbidulus.full: turbĭdŭlus, a, um, adj. dim. [id.], somewhat disturbed or confused: sensus, Prud. Apoth. 276.

turbidus.full: turbĭdus, a, um, adj. turba, full of confusion or disorder, wild, confused, disordered (class.; cf.: agitatus, tumultuosus). Lit.: turbida tempestas heri fuit, wild, stormy, Plaut. Rud. 4, 3, 3: tempestas, Lucr. 4, 169; 6, 376; Cic. Inv 1, 3, 4; Caes. B. C. 2, 22; Suet. Calig. 15: tempestas telorum, Verg. A. 12, 283: Auster, Hor. C. 3, 3, 5: aequora ponti, Lucr. 5, 1000: scaturiges, Liv. 44, 33, 3: nubila, Verg. A. 4, 245: caelum inmite ac turbidum, Plin. Ep. 8, 17, 1: imber, Verg. A. 12, 685: c

turbinatio.full: turbĭnātĭo, ōnis, f. turbinatus, a pointing in the form of a cone: piri, Plin. 15, 21, 23, § 85.

turbinatus.full: turbĭnātus, a, um, adj. 2. turbo, coneshaped, pointed like a cone, conical. In gen.: adamas ... turbinatus in mucronem, Plin. 37, 4, 15, § 56; 11, 37, 69, § 181. —Comp.: turbinatior piris figura, Plin. 15, 15, 17, § 58.— As adj. propr.: lapis Turbinatus, Inscr. Orell. 3304 and 6616.

turbineus.full: turbĭnĕus, a, um, adj. id., shaped like a top, cone-shaped: vortex, Ov. M. 8, 556.

turbo1.full: turbo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. (fut. perf. turbassit, for turbaverit, Cic. Leg. 3, 4; al. turbassitur) [turba], to disturb, agitate, confuse, disorder; to throw into disorder or confusion (freq. and class.; syn.: confundo, misceo, agito). Lit.: ventorum vi agitari atque turbari mare, Cic. Clu. 49, 138: aequora ventis, Lucr. 2, 1: hibernum mare, Hor. Epod. 15, 8; Ov. M. 7, 154; 14, 545 al.: eversae turbant convivia mensae, id. ib. 12, 222; cf. in a poet. transf.: ancipiti quoniam bello turbatur utrim

turbo2.full: turbo, ĭnis, m. (collat. form tur-ben, ĭnis, n., Tib. 1, 5, 3; id. ap. Charis. p. 118 P.; gen. turbonis, Caes. ib.) [1. turbo], that which spins or twirls round (cf. vertex). A whirlwind, hurricane, tornado: ventus circumactus et eundem ambiens locum et se ipse vertigine concitans turbo est. Qui si pugnacior est ac diutius volutatur, inflammatur, et efficit, quem πρηστῆρα Graeci vocant: hic est igneus turbo, Sen. Q. N. 5, 13, 3: falsum est faces et trabes turbine exprimi, id. ib. 7, 5, 1; 2, 22,

turbo3.full: Turbo, ōnis, m., the name of a gladiator, Hor. S. 2, 3, 310.
turbo3.short: Turbo, ōnis, m., the name of a gladiator, Hor.

turbor.full: turbor, ōris, m. 1. turbo, restlessness, unquietness, disturbance, tumult (late Lat.), Cael. Aur. Acut. 1, 15, n. 149; 2, 1 med.

turbula.full: turbŭla, ae, f. dim. turba, a disorderly group, a little crowd of people (Appuleian): turbulae complent totas plateas, App. M. 11, p. 260, 16; 11, p. 159, 27; 4, p. 151, 39.

turbulenter.full: turbŭlenter, adv. turbulentus, in a turbulent manner, confusedly, tumultuously, etc.: nihil turbulenter, nihil temere facere, Cic. Fam. 2, 16, 7.

turbulentia.full: turbŭlentĭa, ae, f. id., trouble, disquiet, turbulence (post-class.), Tert. adv. Prax. 29 fin.; id. adv. Herm. 41.

turbulento.full: turbŭlento, āre, v. a. id., to trouble, disturb (post-class.): me strepitu turbulentant, App. M. 9, p. 222, 16; 2, p. 120, 9.

turbulentus.full: turbŭlentus, a, um, adj. turba, full of trouble or commotion. Pass., restless, agitated, confused, disturbed, boisterous, stormy, tempestuous (class.; syn. tumultuosus): tempestas, stormy, Cic. Verr. 2, 5, 10, § 26; Plaut. Rud. 4, 4, 143; Auct. B. Alex. 45, 2: loci Neptunii, Plaut. Mil. 2, 5, 3: aqua, turbid, muddy, Phaedr. 1, 1, 5: atomorum turbulenta concursio, confused, Cic. Fin. 1, 6, 20: est igitur quiddam turbulentum in hominibus singulis, id. Rep. 3, 35, 49 (Non. 301, 6): res publica, id.

turbystum.full: turbystum or turbistum, i, n., a drug used by painters to facilitate the reception of a color, a mordant: scytatum atque turbystum, Plin. 33, 5, 26, § 88.
turbystum.short: turbystum or turbistum, i, n., a drug used by painters to facilitate the reception of a color, a mordant: scytatum atque turbystum, Plin.

turdarium.full: turdārĭum, ii, n. turdus, a place where thrushes are kept, Varr. L. L. 6, § 2 Müll.

turdelix.full: turdelix, icis; of uncertain signif., Varr. L. L. 6, § 2 Müll.

turdetani.full: Turdētāni, ōrum, m., a people of Hispania Baetica, near the mod. Seville, Liv. 21, 6, 1; 34, 17, 2.—In a comic lusus verbb. with turdus (a thrush), Plaut. Capt. 1, 2, 60. —Hence, Turdētānia, ae, f., the country of the Turdetani, Turdetania: in Turdetaniam proficiscitur, Liv. 34, 17, 1; 28, 39, 11.
turdetani.short: Turdētāni, ōrum, m., a people of Hispania Baetica, near the mod.

turduli.full: Turdŭli, ōrum, m., a people in Bœtica, living to the east of the Turdetani, Varr. R. R. 2, 10, 4; Liv. 28, 39, 8.—Hence, Tur-dŭlus, a, um, adj., of or relating to the Turduli: bellum, Liv. 34, 20, 2.
turduli.short: Turdŭli, ōrum, m., a people in Bœtica, living to the east of the Turdetani, Varr.

turdus.full: turdus, i, m. (collat. form turda, ae, f., Pers. 6, 24; denied by Varr. L. L. 9, § 55 Müll.; cf. id. R. R. 3, 5, 6) [cf. O. H. Germ. trosca; Angl. Sax. throsle; Engl. thrush]. Lit., a thrush, a fieldfare, Plin. 10, 25, 36, § 73; Varr. R. R. 3, 2, 15; 3, 5, 1 sq.; Col. 8, 10; Hor. Ep. 1, 15, 41; id. Epod. 2, 34; id. S. 2, 2, 74; 2, 5, 10; Mart. 13, 92, 1 al.— Transf., a kind of fish, a seacarp, Plin. 32, 11, 53, § 151; Col. 8, 16, 8; 8, 17, 8; cf. Varr. L. L. 5, 12, 23; Quint. 8, 2, 8.

tureus.full: tūrĕus (thūrĕus), a, um, adj. tus, of frankincense: solis est turea virga Sabaeis, the frankincense-shrub, Verg. G. 2, 117; so, virga, Ov. M. 4, 255: planta, Col. 3, 8, 4: grana, Ov. F. 4, 410: dona, Verg. A. 6, 225: altaria, on which incense is burned, Stat. Th. 4, 412.

turgeo.full: turgĕo, rsi, gēre, v. n. cf. Gr. σπαργάω, to swell; σφριγάω, to be full; perh. Sanscr. root ūrgā, succulence; Gr. ὀργάω, to swell, etc., to swell out, be swollen or tumid (mostly poet.; not in Cic.; cf. tumeo). Lit.: si lienes turgent, Cato, R. R. 157, 7: Cyclopis venter turserat alte, Enn. ap. Prisc. p. 870 P. (Ann. v. 326 Vahl.): ora (ab ictu), Ov. F. 3, 757: lumina gemitu, Prop. 1, 21, 3: mammae, Plin. 20, 13, 51, § 141: rana, Prop. 3, 6 (4, 5), 27: laeto in palmite gemmae, Verg. E. 7, 48: fr

turgesco.full: turgesco, ĕre, v. inch. n. [turgeo], to begin to swell, to swell up, swell. Lit.: ne aqua in eorum corpore turgescat, Varr. R. R. 8, 9, 13: hoc (umore) aetas illa (puerilis) turgescit, Quint. 11, 3, 28: prima Ceres docuit turgescere semen in agris, Ov. Am. 3, 10, 11: brassica valido caule, Col. poët. 10, 325: virgulta, Plin. 8, 50, 76, § 200: hic satur irriguo mavult turgescere somno, i. e. to grow fat or stout, Pers. 5, 56: bullatis nugis Pagina turgescit, i. e. is full, id. 5, 18.— Trop. To sw

turgidulus.full: turgĭdŭlus, a, um, adj. dim. [turgidus], swollen: ocelli flendo, Cat. 3, 18.

turgidus.full: turgĭdus, a, um, adj. turgeo, swollen, inflated, distended, turgid (class.; syn. tumidus). Lit.: membrum tumidum ac turgidum, Cic. Tusc. 3, 9, 19: oculi, Plaut. Mil. 4, 3, 15: labra, Mart. 6, 39, 8: venter, App. M. 6, p. 176, 40; cf.: aqua subter cutem fusa turgidus, Plin. 7, 45, 46, § 148: haedus, Cui frons turgida cornibus, Hor. C. 3, 13, 4: loca semine, Lucr. 4, 1034: mare, Hor. C. 1, 3, 19; cf.: fluvii hibernā nive, id. ib. 4, 12, 4: vento vela, id. ib. 2, 10, 24; Ov. Am. 2, 11, 42: (femina)

turgor.full: turgor, ōris, m. id., a swelling, turgidity (post-class.), Mart. Cap. 2, § 135; 5, § 566.

turia.full: Tūrĭa, ae, m., a river in Hispania Tarraconensis, now the Turia or Guadalaviar, Mel. 2, 6, 6; Sall. H. 2, 96, 6 Dietsch; 2, 18 ib.—Called also Tūrĭum, ii, n., Plin. 3, 3, 4, § 20.—Hence, Tūrĭensis, e, adj., of or pertaining to Turia: proelium (in the Sertorian war), Cic. Balb. 2, 5.
turia.short: Tūrĭa, ae, m., a river in Hispania Tarraconensis, now the Turia or Guadalaviar, Mel.

turibulum.full: tūrĭbŭlum (thūr-), i, n. tus. Lit., a vessel to burn incense in, a censer, Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 21, § 46; Liv. 29, 14, 13; Curt. 8, 9, 23; Val. Max. 3, 3, ext. 1; Aus. Idyll. 12, 104; Prud. Apoth. 479.— Transf., a constellation, otherwise called Ara, German. Arat. 390; Vitr. 9, 7.

turicremus.full: tūrĭcrĕmus (thūr-), a, um, adj. tuscremo, incense-burning, for burning incense (poet.): arae, Lucr. 2, 353; Verg. A. 4, 453: foci, Ov. H. 2, 18: ignes, Luc. 9, 989.

turifer.full: tūrĭfĕr (thūr-), fĕra, fĕrum, adj. tusfero, incense-bearing, that bears, yields, or produces incense: Indus, Ov. F. 3, 720: regio, Plin. 6, 23, 26, § 104: Sabaei, Val. Fl. 6, 138; cf. Arabes, Claud. III. Cons. Hon. 71: silvae, id. Rapt. Pros. 2, 81: grex, that offers frankincense, i. e. idolaters, heathen, Prud. Apoth. 359.

turificator.full: tūrĭfĭcātor (thūr-), ōris, m. turifico, one that offers incense to the gods, i. e. an idolater, Aug. contr. Liter. Petil. c. 103.

turifico.full: tūrĭfĭco, āvi, 1, v. n. tus-facio, to burn incense, offer incense (eccl. Lat.), Aug. Ep. 87, 2.—Hence, subst.: tūrĭfĭcātus (thūr-), i, m., one that offers incense (to the gods), a term applied to those Christians who sacrificed to the heathen gods in time of persecution, Cyprian. Ep. 55.

turilegus.full: tūrĭlĕgus, a, um, adj. tus-lego, incense-gathering: Arabes, Ov. F. 4, 569.

turio.full: turĭo, ōnis, m., a shoot, sprout, tendril, young branch of a tree, Col. 12, 50, 5; Apic. 8, 1.
turio.short: turĭo, ōnis, m., a shoot, sprout, tendril, young branch of a tree, Col.

turius.full: Tŭrĭus, i, m., the name of a Roman gens. Q. Turius, Cic. Fam. 12, 26, 1.— C. Turius, Hor. S. 2, 1, 49.—Hence, Tŭrĭ-ānus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to a Turius, Turian: hereditas, of Q. Turius, Cic Fam. 12, 26, 2: cassia, a peculiar kind so called, Dig. 39, 4, 16, § 7.
turius.short: Tŭrĭus, i, m., the name of a Roman gens.

turma.full: turma, ae, f. Sanscr. root tvar-, tur-, hasten; v. turba, a division of Roman cav alry, the tenth part of an ala, consisting at first of thirty, and afterwards of thirty-two men; a troop, squadron of horse. Lit., Varr. L. L. 5, 16, 26; Veg. Mil. 2, 14; Fest p. 355; Caes. B. G. 4, 33; 6, 8; 7, 45; 7, 80, 7, 88; Hirt. B. G. 8, 19; Cic. Att. 5, 21, 10; id. Fam. 15, 4, 7; Hor. C. 2, 16, 22; id. Ep. 2, 1, 190 al.; cf. Becker, Antiq. 3, 2, p. 258 sq.— Transf., in gen., a troop, crowd, throng, band, bo

turmalis.full: turmālis, e, adj. turma, of or belong ing to a troop or squadron. Lit., as subst.: turmāles, ium, m.: T. Manlius cum suis turmalibus evasit, i. e. with those of his squadron or troop, Liv. 8, 7, 1; 25, 18, 11.— Transf.: non sanguine cretus Turmali trabeāque Remi, i. e. of the equestrian order, Stat. S. 5, 2, 17: buccina, a cav alry-trumpet, Claud. B. Gild. 447.—In a pun Scipio ille major Corinthiis statuam pollicentibus eo loco, ubi aliorum essent impe ratorum, turmales dixit displicere, i. e ho

turmarii.full: turmārĭi, ōrum, m. id., recruiting officers of cavalry, Cod. Th. 6, 35, 3.

turmatim.full: turmātim, adv. id.. Lit., by troops or squadrons: equites se turmatim explicare coeperunt, Caes. B. C. 3, 93: nostri turmatim in eum devenerunt, Hirt. B. G. 8, 18: vagantibus circa moenia turmatim barbaris, Liv. 5, 39, 5: abire, id. 28, 13, 9 al.— Transf., in gen., in troops, in bands: corpora turmatim certantia, Lucr. 2, 118.

turnus.full: Turnus, i, m. A king of the Rutuli, killed by Æneas, Liv. 1, 2, 3; Verg. A. 7, 344 sq.; Ov. M. 14, 451 sq.; Tib. 2, 5, 48; Suet. Ner. 54: Turni lacus, i. e. lacus Juturnae, Col. 10, 138.— Turnus Herdonius, a Latin, the enemy of Tarquinius Superbus, Liv. 1, 50 sqq.

turones.full: Tŭrŏnes, um, m., a people in Gallia Lugdunensis, on the Liger, near the site of the mod. Tours, Caes. B. G. 2, 35; 7, 4; Plin. 4, 18, 32, § 107.—Called afterwards Tŭrŏ-ni or Tŭrŏnĭi, ōrum, Tac. A. 3, 41; Caes. B. G. 7, 75; Hirt. B. G. 8, 46; Amm. 15, 11, 12.—Hence, Tŭrŏnĭcus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to the Turones, Turonic: ecclesiae episcopatus, of Tours, Sulp. Sev. Vit. S. Mart. 9.—Tŭrŏnĭcensis, e, Ven. Misc. 8, 21.
turones.short: Tŭrŏnes, um, m., a people in Gallia Lugdunensis, on the Liger, near the site of the mod.

turpiculus.full: turpĭcŭlus, a, um, adj. dim. [turpis], ugly, foul, deformed. Lit.: nasus, Cat. 41, 3: res, Varr. L. L. 7, § 97 Müll.—* Trop.: jocus in (rebus) turpiculis et quasi deformibus ponitur, Cic. de Or. 2, 61, 248.

turpido.full: turpīdo, ĭnis, f. contr. from turpidudo, baseness, etc., Tert. Cor. Mil. 14; Cic. Rep. 1, 2, 2 MSS. (B. and K. turpitudinis; cf. Osann ad loc.).

turpificatus.full: turpĭfĭcātus, a, um, adj. turpisfacio, made foul or filthy, debased, deformed, corrupted; trop.: foeditas turpificati animi. Cic. Off. 3, 29, 105.

turpilius.full: Turpĭlĭus, i, m.; Turpĭlĭa, ae, f., the name of a Roman gens. So, Sex. Turpilius, a Roman comic poet, a contemporary and friend of Terence, Cic. Fam. 9, 22, 1; cf. id. Tusc. 4, 34, 72.—Fem. Turpilia, Cic. Fam. 7, 21.

turpiloquium.full: turpĭlŏquĭum, ii, n. turpis-loquor, obscene or immodest speech, Tert. Pud. 17 fin.; Ambros. Fid. 5, 10, § 110.

turpilucricupidus.full: turpĭlŭcrī^cŭpĭdus, i, adj. m. [turpis-lucrum-cupidus], = αισχροκερδής, covetous of base or dishonest gain, as a term of abuse, Plaut Trin. 1, 2, 63.

turpilucrus.full: turpĭlŭcrus, i, adj. m. [turpis-iucrum], making dishonest gain, Aug. Op. Mon. 13.
