vulgaris.full: vulgāris (volg-), e (ante- and postclass. collat. form vulgārius, a, um, Afran., Nov., and Turp. ap. Non. p. 488, 26 sq.; Gell. 1, 22, 2; 3, 16, 18; 12, 10, 6; 16, 5, 1), adj. vulgus, of or belonging to the great mass or multitude, general, usual, ordinary, every-day, common, commonplace, vulgar (freq. and class.): in omni arte, cujus usus vulgaris communisque non sit, Cic. Fin. 3, 1, 3: in communi vitā et vulgari hominum consuetudine, id. de Or. 1, 58, 248: vulgaris popularisque sensus, id. ib.

vulgaritas.full: vulgārĭtas (volg-), ātis, m. vulgaris, the great mass, the multitude (postclass.), Arn. 3, 123 and 155.

vulgarius.full: vulgārĭus, a, um, v. vulgaris init.

vulgate.full: vulgātē (volg-), adv., v. 2. vulgo, P. a. fin.

vulgator.full: vulgātor (volg-), ōris, m. 2. vulgo, one that makes a thing generally known, a publisher. divulger: taciti, i. e. Tantalus, who divulged the secrets of the gods, Ov. Am. 3, 7, 51.

vulgatus1.full: vulgātus (volg-), a, um, Part. and P. a. of 2. vulgo.

vulgatus2.full: vulgātus, ūs, m. 2. vulgo, a making generally known, a publishing, divulging (late Lat.), Sid. Ep. 8, 1.

vulgivagus.full: vulgĭvăgus (volg-), a, um, adj. vulgus-vagor, that wanders about everywhere, roving, rambling, vagrant; inconstant (Lucretian): mos ferarum, Lucr. 5, 932: Venus, id. 4, 1071.

vulgo2.full: vulgo (volg-), āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. vulgus, to spread among the multitude; to make general, common, or universal; to put forth to the world, publish (cf. publico). In gen.: morbos, Liv. 3, 6, 3: contagium in alios, Curt. 9, 10, 1: rem, i. e. to let all share in, Liv. 2, 29, 7: librum, to publish, Quint. 1, prooem. § 7; Suet. Gram. 8.— Mid.: vulgari cum privatis, i. e. to confound one's self with, put one's self on a level with, Liv. 3, 35, 6.— In partic. To make known to all by words, to spread a

vulgus.full: vulgus (volg-), i, n. (masc., Att., Sisenn., and Varr. ap. Non. p. 230, 27 sq.; Verg. A. 2, 99; Phaedr. 4, 14; Liv. 6, 34, 5; 24, 32, 1; Lucr. 2, 920 et saep.) [Sanscr. várga, a group], the great mass, the multitude, the people, public (class.; cf.: plebs, turba). In gen.: non est consilium in vulgo, non ratio, etc., Cic. Planc. 4, 9; Sall. J. 66, 2; Verg. A. 2, 39: quod in vulgus gratum esse sentimus, with the people, with the public, generally, Cic. Att. 2, 22, 3: in vulgus notus, id. ib. 9, 5

vulnerabilis.full: vulnĕrābĭlis (voln-), e, adj. vulnero, wounding, injurious (late Lat.): materia, Cael. Aur. Acut. 3, 17, § 171.

vulnerarius.full: vulnĕrārĭus (voln-), a, um, adj. vulnus, of or belonging to wounds. Adj.: emplastrum, a plaster for wounds, Plin. 23, 4, 40, § 81; 34, 11, 27, § 114.— Subst.: vulnĕrārĭus, ii, m., a surgeon, Plin. 29, 1, 6, § 13.

vulneratio.full: vulnĕrātĭo (voln-), ōnis, f. vulnero, a wounding, wound. Lit., Cic. Caecin. 16, 47; Hirt. B. G. 8, 47; Cael. Aur. Tard. 2, 1, 27.— Trop., an injuring, injury: famae, salutis, Cic. Pis. 20, 47.

vulnerator.full: vulnĕrātor (voln-), ōris, m. id., a wounder; trop., an injurer (late Lat.): gentium, Hier. in Isa. 14, 12.

vulnero.full: vulnĕro (voln-), āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. vulnus, to wound, to hurt, or injure by a wound (syn.: saucio, ferio). Lit.: neu quis quem prius vulneret, quam illum interfectum viderit, Caes. B. G. 5, 58: L. Cotta legatus in adversum os fundā vulneratur, id. ib. 5, 35 fin.: plerosque jacula tormentis aut manu emissa vulnerabant, Sall. J. 57, 6: acie ipsā et ferri viribus vulnerari, Cic. Sest. 10, 24: corpus vulneratum ferro, id. Red. in Sen. 3, 7: (aper) vulnerat armentum, Ov. M. 11, 372.—With acc. of par

vulnifer.full: vulnĭfer (voln-), ĕra, ĕrum, adj. vulnus-fero, wound-bringing (post-class.), Prud. Psych. 173; Maxim. Gall. 5, 98.

vulnifico.full: vulnĭfĭco, āre, 1, v. a. id., to wound (late Lat.), Ven. Fort. Misc. 10, 2.

vulnificus.full: vulnĭfĭcus (voln-), a, um, adj. vulnus-facio, wound-making, wound-inflicting, wounding (poet.): sus, Ov. M. 8, 359: telum, id. ib. 2, 504: chalybs, Verg. A. 8, 446: plumbum (i. e. caestus), Val. Fl. 1, 420: Apollo, Mart. Cap. 1, § 13.

vulnus.full: vulnus (voln-), ĕris, n. root vul-; cf. vultur; akin to vello, a wound (cf.: ictus, cicatrix). Lit.: cave faxit volnus tibi jam, Plaut. Truc. 5, 51: qui abstergerem volnera? Ter. Eun. 4, 7, 9: vulnus in latere, Cic. Mil. 24, 65: multis et illatis et acceptis vulneribus, Caes. B. G. 1, 50; so, inferre, id. B. C. 2, 6: accipere, id. B. G. 1, 48: claudicare ex vulnere ob rem publicam accepto, Cic. de Or. 2, 61, 249: sustinere, Caes. B. C. 1, 45: excipere, Cic. Sest. 10, 23: alicui infligere, id. Ph

vulnusculum.full: vulnusculum (voln-), i, n. dim. vulnus, a little or slight wound, Dig. 21, 1, 1, § 8; Hier. Ep. 112, 13.

vulpecula.full: vulpēcŭla, ae, f. dim. vulpes, a little fox, Cic. N. D. 1, 31, 88; id. Off. 1, 13, 41; Auct. Carm. Phil. 59: tum vulpecula evasit puteo, Phaedr. 4, 9, 10.

vulpes.full: vulpes (volp-), is (collat. form, nom. vulpis, Petr. 58; Avien. 40, 7), f. cf. Gr. ἀλώπηξ, a fox. Lit., Plin. 28, 11, 46, § 165; Hor. S. 2, 3, 186; id. Ep. 1, 1, 73; id. C. 3, 27, 4 al.— Trop., cunning, craftiness: animi sub vulpe latentes, Hor. A. P. 437; Pers. 5, 117.—Prov. Jungere vulpes, for any absurd or impossible undertaking, Verg. E. 3, 91.— Vulpes pilum mutat, non mores, Suet. Vesp. 16.— Tam facile, quam pirum vulpes comest, Plaut. Most. 3, 1, 32.— Transf.: vulpes marina, a kind of shar

vulpinor.full: vulpīnor (volp-), āri, v. dep. n. [vulpinus], to play the fox, be sly as a fox (anteand post-class.), Varr. ap. Non. p. 46, 26; App. M. 3, p. 139, 5.

vulpinus.full: vulpīnus (volp-), a, um, adj. vulpes, of or belonging to a fox: lingua, Plin. 28, 11, 47, § 172: jecur, id. 28, 13, 55, § 197: sanguis, id. 32, 5, 16, § 44.

vulpio.full: vulpĭo (volp-), ōnis, m. id., one cunning as a fox, a sly fox, App. Mag. p. 328, 32.

vulsio.full: vulsĭo, ōnis, f. vello, a plucking, Veg. 3, 65.

vulso.full: Vulso (Vols-), ōnis, m., a cognomen in the Manlian gens: Manlius Vulso, Liv. 22, 35; 40, 59.
vulso.short: Vulso (Vols-), ōnis, m., a cognomen in the Manlian gens: Manlius Vulso, Liv.

vulsura.full: vulsūra (vols-), ae, f. vello, a plucking, pulling, Varr. R. R. 2, 11, 9.

vulsus.full: vulsus, a, um, Part. and P. a. of vello.

vulticulus.full: vultĭcŭlus (volt-), i, m. dim. vultus, a look, mien, air: non te Bruti nostri vulticulus ab istā oratione deterret? i. e. severe look, Cic. Att. 14, 20, 5.

vultuosus.full: vultŭōsus (volt-), a, um, adj. vultus, of an expressive countenance, full of expression, full of airs or grimaces, grimacing, affected: homo, Prud. στεφ. 10, 171: frons, App. M. 3, p. 135, 9: ne quid ineptum aut vultuosum sit (in oratione), Cic. Or. 18, 60; cf. pronuntiatio, Quint. 11, 3, 183.

vultur1.full: vultur (volt-), ŭris (ante-class. collat. form of the nom. sing. vultŭrus (volt-), Enn. ap. Charis. p. 120 P.; id. ap. Prisc. p. 683 ib.; and id. ap. Serv. Verg. A. 6, 597, or Ann. v. 141 Vahl.), m., a vulture. Lit., Plin. 10, 6, 7, § 19; Liv. 41, 21; Verg. A. 6, 597.—As a bird of omen, Liv. 1, 7, 1. —Prov.: vultur profert cornua, for something impossible, Claud. in Eutr. 1, 352.— Transf., a designation of a grasping, avaricious person, Sen. Ep. 95, 43; Mart. 6, 62, 4.

vultur2.full: Vultur (Volt-), ŭris, m., a mountain in Apulia, near Venusia, now Monle Vulture, Hor. C. 3, 4, 9; Luc. 9, 185.—Hence, Vulturnus (Volt-), a, um, adj., of or belonging to Vultur: ventus, a southeastby-one-third-south wind, Plin. 2, 47, 46, § 119; Sen. Q. N. 5, 16, 3; Col. 5, 5, 15; 11, 2, 65; Gell. 2, 22, 11; App. de Mundo, p. 63, 14.
vultur2.short: Vultur (Volt-), ŭris, m., a mountain in Apulia, near Venusia, now Monle Vulture, Hor.

vulturcius.full: Vulturcĭus (Volt-), i, m., one of the fellow-conspirators of Catiline, Cic. Cat. 3, 2 sq.; Sall. C. 44, 4.
vulturcius.short: Vulturcĭus (Volt-), i, m., one of the fellow-conspirators of Catiline, Cic.

vulturinus.full: vultŭrīnus (volt-), a, um, adj. 1. vultur, of or belonging to a vulture, vulture-like, vulturine: fel, Plin. 29, 6, 38, § 123: sanguis, id. 30, 4, 10, § 30: collum, Mart. 9, 28, 2: species, the form of a vulture, Plin. 10, 3, 3, § 8.

vulturius.full: vultŭrĭus (volt-), ii, m. id., a vulture, bird of prey. Lit., Plaut. Truc. 2, 3, 16; id. Most. 3, 2, 146 sqq.; Lucr. 4, 680; Liv. 27, 23, 3; 27, 11, 4; 41, 21, 7.— Transf. A vulture; a designation for a rapacious or covetous person, an extortioner, and the like: sunt alii qui te volturium vocant, Plaut. Trin. 1, 2, 64: vulturius illius provinciae imperator, Cic. Pis. 16, 38; Cat. 68, 124.— An unlucky throw at dice: jacit vulturios quattuor. Talos arripio: jacto basilicum, Plaut. Curc. 2, 3, 78.

vulturnalis.full: Vulturnālis (Volt-), e, adj., of or belonging to the god Vulturnus (perh. the same as Vertumnus). Adj.: flamen, Enn. ap. Varr. L. L. 7, § 45 Müll. (Ann. v. 125 Vahl.).— Subst.: Vulturnālia, ĭum, n., the festival of Vulturnus, acc. to Fest. p. 379 Müll.
vulturnalis.short: Vulturnālis (Volt-), e, adj., of or belonging to the god Vulturnus (perh.

vulturnum.full: Vulturnum (Volt-), i, n., a town in Campania, on the river Vulturnus, now Castel Volturno, Liv. 25, 20; 34, 45.
vulturnum.short: Vulturnum (Volt-), i, n., a town in Campania, on the river Vulturnus, now Castel Volturno, Liv.

vulturnus.full: Vulturnus (Volt-), i, m., a river in Campania, the mod. Volturno, Liv. 8, 11; Verg. A. 7, 729 al.—Hence, Vulturnus (Volt-), a, um, adj., of or belonging to the Vulturnus, Vulturnian: vada, Sil. 12, 521: amnis, Plin. 36, 26, 66, § 194: oppidum, id. 3, 5, 9, § 61.
vulturnus.short: Vulturnus (Volt-), i, m., a river in Campania, the mod.

vulturnus ventus.full: Vulturnus ventus, v. 2. Vultur. † Vulturnus, i, m., the god Vulturnus; v. Vulturnalis.

vultus.full: vultus (volt-), ūs, m. (neutr. collat. form, plur. volta, Enn. ap. Non. p. 230, 15, or Ann. v. 536 Vahl.; Lucr. 4, 1213) [etym. dub.; cf. Goth. vulthus, glory], an expression of countenance, the countenance, visage, as to features and expression; hence, often to be translated by features, looks, air, mien, expression, aspect (syn. aspectus). Lit. In gen., sing.: nam et oculi nimis arguti, quemadmodum animo affecti sumus, loquuntur, et is qui appellatur vultus, qui nullo in animante esse praeter

x.full: X, x, a character probably derived from the Greek Ξ (this form of that letter being found in some few Greek inscriptions). Though not introduced instead of the characters for the two separate sounds till after the adoption of the alphabet, the letter x is certainly older than the Latin inscriptions known to us; for we find in the Columna rostr., EXEMET MAXIMOS, EXFOCIONT; in the fifth Epitaph of the Scipios, SAXSVM; and in the S. C. de Bacch., EXDEICENDVM, EXDEICATIS. EXTRAD, etc.The sound of X
x.short: X, x, a character probably derived from the Greek Ξ (this form of that letter being found in some few Greek inscriptions).

xanthicus.full: Xanthĭcus, a, um, adj. (sc. mensis), the Macedonian name of a month which corresponded to the Roman Aprilis, Cassiod. Hist. Eccl. 9, 38.

xanthippe.full: Xanthippē, ēs, f., = Ξανθίππη, the wife of Socrates, Cic. Tusc. 3, 15, 31; Gell. 1, 17, 1.
xanthippe.short: Xanthippē, ēs, f., = Ξανθίππη, the wife of Socrates, Cic.

xanthippus.full: Xanthippus, i, m., = Ξάνθιππος. The father of Pericles, Cic. Brut. 11, 44.— A Lacedœmonian, who took Regulus prisoner, Cic. Off. 3, 26, 99.

xantho.full: Xantho, ūs, f., = Ξανθώ, a sea-nymph, daughter of Nereus and Doris, Verg. G. 4, 336.
xantho.short: Xantho, ūs, f., = Ξανθώ, a sea-nymph, daughter of Nereus and Doris, Verg.

xanthos.full: xanthos, i, m., = ξάνθος, a precious stone of a golden color, otherwise unknown, Plin. 37, 10, 60, § 169.
xanthos.short: xanthos, i, m., = ξάνθος, a precious stone of a golden color, otherwise unknown, Plin.

xanthus.full: Xanthus, i, m., = Ξάνθος, the name of several rivers. A river of Troas, confounded by many with the Scamander, Plin. 5, 30, 33, § 124; 2, 103, 106, § 230; Verg. A. 1, 473; 5, 634 al.; Ov. M. 2, 245; 9, 646; Vitr. 8, 3 med.— A river in Lycia, near a town of the same name, now Essenide, Mel. 1, 15, 3; Verg. A. 4, 143; id. Cul. 14; Hor. C. 4, 6, 26; Plin. 5, 27, 28, § 100; 6, 34, 39, § 214.— A small stream in Epirus, Verg. A. 3, 350.
xanthus.short: Xanthus, i, m., = Ξάνθος, the name of several rivers.

xeniades.full: Xĕniădes, is, m., = Ξενιάδης, a Corinthian who purchased and liberated Diogenes the Cynic, Gell. 2, 18, 9.
xeniades.short: Xĕniădes, is, m., = Ξενιάδης, a Corinthian who purchased and liberated Diogenes the Cynic, Gell.

xeniolum.full: xĕnĭŏlum, i, n. dim. xenium, a small gift or present, App. M. 2, p. 119, 24; Dig. 1, 16, 6.

xenium.full: xĕnĭum, ii, n., = ξένιον, a gift or present made to a guest (pure Lat. lautia). Lit., Plin. Ep. 6, 31, 14; Vitr. 6, 10.—Hence, Xenia, the title of the thirteenth book of Martial's epigrams, because treating of such things as were usually presented to guests, Mart. 13, 3, 1.— Transf., in gen., a gift. present, Plin. Ep. 5, 14, 8; Dig. 1, 16, 6; Vulg. Ecclus. 20, 31.
xenium.short: xĕnĭum, ii, n., = ξένιον, a gift or present made to a guest (pure Lat.

xeno.full: Xĕno, ōnis, m., = Ξένων, an Epicurean philosopher, a native of Athens, Cic. Att. 5, 10, 5; 5, 11, 6; 7, 1, 1; 13, 37, 1.
xeno.short: Xĕno, ōnis, m., = Ξένων, an Epicurean philosopher, a native of Athens, Cic.

xenocles.full: Xĕnocles, is, m., = Ξενοκλῆς, a rhetorician of Adramytteum, Cic. Brut. 91, 316.
xenocles.short: Xĕnocles, is, m., = Ξενοκλῆς, a rhetorician of Adramytteum, Cic.

xenocrates.full: Xĕnŏcrătes, is, m., = Ξενοκράτης, a disciple of Plato, born at Chalcedon in the 95th Olympiad, B. C. 400, Cic. Ac. 1, 4, 17; id. Tusc. 5, 18, 51; id. Off. 1, 30, 109; id. Rep. 1, 2, 3.— A sculptor, a pupil of Tisicrates, and author of works on sculpture, Plin. 34, 8, 19, § 83.— A writer on the art of painting, Plin. 35, 10, 36, § 68.
xenocrates.short: Xĕnŏcrătes, is, m., = Ξενοκράτης, a disciple of Plato, born at Chalcedon in the 95th Olympiad, B.

xenodochium.full: xĕnŏdŏchīum or -ēum, i, n., = ξενοδοχεῖον, a public building for the reception of strangers, a caravansary, a stranger's hospital (syn. deversorium), Hier. Ep. 66, 11; Cod. Just. 1, 2, 17; 1, 3, 33; 1, 3, 35. —Called also xĕnōn, ōnis, Cod. Just. 1, 2, 19 al.
xenodochium.short: xĕnŏdŏchīum or -ēum, i, n., = ξενοδοχεῖον, a public building for the reception of strangers, a caravansary, a stranger's hospital (syn.

xenodochus.full: xĕnŏdŏchus, i, m., = ξενοδόχος, one who receives strangers, a superintendent of the stranger's hospital, Cod. Just. 1, 8, 33 fin.
xenodochus.short: xĕnŏdŏchus, i, m., = ξενοδόχος, one who receives strangers, a superintendent of the stranger's hospital, Cod.

xenoparochus.full: xĕnŏpărŏchus, i, m., = ξενοπάροχος, one who attends to or provides for strangers, Dig. 5, 4, 18.
xenoparochus.short: xĕnŏpărŏchus, i, m., = ξενοπάροχος, one who attends to or provides for strangers, Dig.

xenophanes.full: Xĕnŏphănes, is, m., = Ξενοφάνης, a celebrated Greek philosopher of Colophon, born about B. C. 556, a disciple of Archelous, Cic. Ac. 2, 37, 118; id. N. D. 1, 11, 28; id. Div. 1, 3, 5; 1, 39, 87; Lact. 3, 23, 11.
xenophanes.short: Xĕnŏphănes, is, m., = Ξενοφάνης, a celebrated Greek philosopher of Colophon, born about B.

xenophilus.full: Xĕnŏphĭlus, i, m., = Ξενόφιλος, a Pythagorean philosopher and musician, Val. Max. 8, 13, ext. 2; Plin. 7, 50, 51 § 168.
xenophilus.short: Xĕnŏphĭlus, i, m., = Ξενόφιλος, a Pythagorean philosopher and musician, Val.

xenophon.full: Xĕnŏphon, ontis, m., = Ξενοφῶν, a celebratea Greek historian and philosopher, born B. C. 445, a pupil of Socrates and a leader of the Greeks in the army of Cyrus the younger, Cic. Div. 1, 25, 52; id. Tusc. 5, 34, 99; id. Sen. 9, 30; id. Leg. 2, 22, 56; Varr. R. R. 1, 1, 8.—Hence, Xĕnŏphontēus or -īus, a, um, adj., = Ξενοφόντειος, of or belonging to Xenophon, Xenophontian: genus sermonis, Cic. Brut. 35, 132: Hercules, i. e. mentioned in his writings, id. Fam. 5, 12, 3.
xenophon.short: Xĕnŏphon, ontis, m., = Ξενοφῶν, a celebratea Greek historian and philosopher, born B.

xerampelinae.full: xērampĕlĭnae, ārum. f. (sc. vestes), = ξηραμπελιναι (of the color of dry vineleaves), dark-red or dark-colored clothes, Juv. 6, 519.

xeranticus.full: xērantĭcus, a, um, adj., = ξηραντικός, drying: decoctio, Macer, 1, 88; Theod. Prisc. 2, 3.
xeranticus.short: xērantĭcus, a, um, adj., = ξηραντικός, drying: decoctio, Macer, 1, 88;

xerocollyrium.full: xērŏcollȳrĭum, ii, n., = ξηροκολλύριον, a dry salve, Marc. Emp. 8, 3.
xerocollyrium.short: xērŏcollȳrĭum, ii, n., = ξηροκολλύριον, a dry salve, Marc.

xerolophus.full: Xērŏlŏphus, i, m., = Ξηρόλοφος (prop. Dry Hill), the name of a place in Byzantium, Just. Inst. 4, 18, 5; Prisc. p. 347 P.

xeromyrrha.full: xērŏmyrrha, ae, f. (ξηρόσ-μύρρα), dry myrrh, Sedul. Hymn. 2, 81.

xerophagia.full: xērŏphăgĭa, ae, f., = ξηροφαγία, the eating of dry food: xerophagias observare, Tert. adv Psych. 1 fin.
xerophagia.short: xērŏphăgĭa, ae, f., = ξηροφαγία, the eating of dry food: xerophagias observare, Tert.

xerophthalmia.full: xērophthalmĭa, ae, f., = ξηροφθαλμία, a dry soreness of the eyes, an inflammation of the eyes, Marc. Emp. 8, 3 (in Cels. 6, 6, 29, written as Greek).
xerophthalmia.short: xērophthalmĭa, ae, f., = ξηροφθαλμία, a dry soreness of the eyes, an inflammation of the eyes, Marc.

xerxes.full: Xerxes (Xerses, Cic. Leg. 2, 10, 26), is (i, Nep. Reg. 1), m., = Ξέρξης, the celebrated king of Persia, son of Darius Hystaspis, vanquished by the Greeks at Salamis, Cic. Tusc. 5, 7, 20; id. N. D. 1, 41, 115.

xiphias.full: xĭphĭas, ae, m., = ξιφίας (swordshaped). A sword-fish: Xiphias gladius, Linn.; Plin. 32, 2, 6, § 15; Ov. Hal. 97. — A sword-shaped comet, Plin. 2, 25, 22, § 89.

xiphion.full: xĭphĭon, ii, n., = ξιφίον, sword-flag, gladiole, Plin. 25, 11, 88, § 137.
xiphion.short: xĭphĭon, ii, n., = ξιφίον, sword-flag, gladiole, Plin.

xuthus.full: Xūthus, i, m., = Ξοῦθος, a son of Helen, grandson of Deucalion, and father of a branch of the Hellenic nation, T. Mam. Syll. 884.
xuthus.short: Xūthus, i, m., = Ξοῦθος, a son of Helen, grandson of Deucalion, and father of a branch of the Hellenic nation, T.

xyline.full: Xўlĭnē, ēs, f. (ξυλίνη): Xyline come, a village in Pamphylia, Liv. 38, 15.

xylinum.full: xўlĭnum, i, n., = ξύλινον, cotton, Plin. 19, 1, 2, § 14.
xylinum.short: xўlĭnum, i, n., = ξύλινον, cotton, Plin.

xylobalsamum.full: xўlŏbalsămum, i, n., = ξυλοβάλσαμον, balsam-wood, the wood of the balsamtree, Plin. 12, 25, 54, § 118; 13, 1, 2, §§ 13, 15; 29, 3, 13, § 56.
xylobalsamum.short: xўlŏbalsămum, i, n., = ξυλοβάλσαμον, balsam-wood, the wood of the balsamtree, Plin.

xylocassia.full: xўlŏcassĭa, ae, f., = ξυλοκασσία, the wood of the cassia, cassia-wood, Dig. 39, 4, 16, § 7.
xylocassia.short: xўlŏcassĭa, ae, f., = ξυλοκασσία, the wood of the cassia, cassia-wood, Dig.

xylocinnamomum.full: xўlŏcinnămōmum, i, n., = ξυλοκιννάμωμον, the wood of the cinnamonshrub, cinnamon-wood, Plin. 12, 19, 42, § 91; Dig. 39, 4, 16, § 7.—Also contracted, xylŏ-cinnămum, i, n., Scrib. Comp. 271.
xylocinnamomum.short: xўlŏcinnămōmum, i, n., = ξυλοκιννάμωμον, the wood of the cinnamonshrub, cinnamon-wood, Plin.

xylon.full: xўlon, i, n., = ξύλον (wood; in partic.), the cotton-tree, Plin. 19, 1, 2, § 14.

xylophytum.full: xўlŏphўtum (-on), i, n., = ξυλόφυτον, a kind of herb, comfrey, App. Herb. 59.
xylophytum.short: xўlŏphўtum (-on), i, n., = ξυλόφυτον, a kind of herb, comfrey, App.

xyniae.full: Xȳnĭae, ārum, f., a town of Thessaly, Liv. 32, 13, 14; 33, 3, 8; 39, 26, 2.
xyniae.short: Xȳnĭae, ārum, f., a town of Thessaly, Liv.

xyris.full: xўris, ĭdis, f., = ξυρίς, wild iris, Plin. 21, 20, 83, § 143.
xyris.short: xўris, ĭdis, f., = ξυρίς, wild iris, Plin.

xystarches.full: xystarches, ae, m., = ξυστάρχης, the master, director, or manager of a xystus, Amm. 21, 1, 4; Tert. ad Mart. 3.
xystarches.short: xystarches, ae, m., = ξυστάρχης, the master, director, or manager of a xystus, Amm.

xystiani.full: Xystĭāni, ōrum, m., a people of Caria, Plin. 5, 29, 29, § 109.
xystiani.short: Xystĭāni, ōrum, m., a people of Caria, Plin.

xysticus.full: xystĭcus, a, um, adj., = ξυστικός, of or belonging to a xystus. Adj.: vanitas, i. e. of the athletes, Tert. Pud. 7 med.— Subst.: xystĭci, ōrum, m., athletes, Suet. Aug. 45; Dig. 3, 2, 4; Inscr. Grut. 332, 6.
xysticus.short: xystĭcus, a, um, adj., = ξυστικός, of or belonging to a xystus.

xystilis.full: Xystĭlis, is, f., the name of a woman, Plaut. Ps. 1, 2, 81.
xystilis.short: Xystĭlis, is, f., the name of a woman, Plaut.

xystus.full: xystus, i, m., or xystum, i, n., = ξυστός or ξυστόν. Among the Greeks, a covered portico or gallery, where the athletes exercised in winter, Vitr. 5, 11, 4; 6, 10, 5; Tert. Apol. 38.— Among the Romans, an open colonnade or portico, or a walk planted with trees, etc., for recreation, conversation, philosophic discussion, etc., Cic. Att. 1, 8, 2; id. Brut. 3, 10; id. Ac. 2, 3, 9; Sen. Ira. 3, 18, 3; Plin. Ep. 2, 17, 17; 5, 6, 19; 9, 7, 4; 9, 36, 3; Suet. Aug. 72; Phaedr. 2, 5, 18.
xystus.short: xystus, i, m., or xystum, i, n., = ξυστός or ξυστόν.

y.full: Y, y, a Greek letter introduced at a late period for words borrowed from the Greek, the place of the Greek Υ being previously filled by U (i. e. V, which graphically originated from Υ; v. the letters U and V). Thus, according to the express testimony of Cicero (Or. 48, 160), Ennius always wrote Burrus for Pyrrhus, and Bruges for Phryges; and so the words which were identical in Greek and Latin in the oldest period of the language have either preserved u where the Greek has υ, as bucina and βυκάν
y.short: Y, y, a Greek letter introduced at a late period for words borrowed from the Greek, the place of the Greek Υ being previously filled by U (i.

z.full: Z, z, was perhaps a letter of the original Latin alphabet, since it is found in the Carmen Saliare, Varr. L. L. 7, § 26 Müll.; and in a Latin record of an Oscan law of the time of the Gracchi, C. I. L. 1, 197; but it had long disappeared, when, in Cicero's time, it again came into use, but only in transcribing Greek names, to represent the Greek Ζ, ζ, which had previously been represented, when initial, by s, as in Saguntum for Ζάκυνθος, Sethus, sona, etc.; and by ss when medial, as in Atticisso
z.short: Z, z, was perhaps a letter of the original Latin alphabet, since it is found in the Carmen Saliare, Varr.

zabulon.full: Zăbŭlōn, ōnis, m., = Ζαβουλών, one of the tribes of Israel, Juvenc. 1, 441; cf. Vulg. Apoc. 7, 8.
zabulon.short: Zăbŭlōn, ōnis, m., = Ζαβουλών, one of the tribes of Israel, Juvenc.

zabulus.full: Zābŭlus or Zābŏlus, i, m., = Ζάβολος (collat. form of Διάβολος; cf. the letter D init.), the Devil, Lact. Mort. Pers. 16.
zabulus.short: Zābŭlus or Zābŏlus, i, m., = Ζάβολος (collat.

zacharias.full: Zachărīas, ae, m. (i short, Juvenc. 1, 29; Paul. Nol. 5, 27; Sid. Carm. 16, 36), = Ζαχαρίας, Zacharias, the father of St. John the Baptist, Vulg. Luc. 1, 5; 1, 12; 1, 13; 3, 2; Lact. 4, 14, 6.

zacynthus.full: Zăcynthus or -ŏs, i, f., = Ζάκυνθος, an island in the Ionian Sea, now Zante or Zacyntho, Mel. 2, 7, 10; Plin. 4, 12, 19, § 54; Liv. 21, 7; 26, 24; Verg. A. 3, 270; Plaut. Merc. 3, 4, 62; Ov. H. 1, 87 al.—Hence, Zăcynthĭus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Zacynthus, Zacynthian: Calchas, Plaut. Merc. 5, 2, 104: bitumen, Plin. 35, 15, 51, § 178.
zacynthus.short: Zăcynthus or -ŏs, i, f., = Ζάκυνθος, an island in the Ionian Sea, now Zante or Zacyntho, Mel.

zaleucus.full: Zăleucus, i, m., = Ζάλευκος, a lawgiver of the Locrians, Cic. Att. 6, 1, 18; id. Leg. 1, 22, 57; 2, 6, 14; Sen. Ep. 90, 5.
zaleucus.short: Zăleucus, i, m., = Ζάλευκος, a lawgiver of the Locrians, Cic.

zama.full: Zăma, ae, f., = Ζάμα. A small town in Numidia (now Zamra), celebrated for the victory gained there by Scipio over Hannibal, Liv. 30, 29; Sil. 3, 261 al.— Another town in Numidia, also, with the addition regia, the residence of Juba, now Jama, Sall. J. 57 sq.; Auct. B. Afr. 91; Inscr. Grut. 364, 1.—Hence, Zămensis, e, adj., of or belonging to Zama: oppidum, i. e. Zama, Plin. 5, 4, 4, § 30 (al. Ziamensis). —As subst.: Zămenses, ĭum, m., the inhabitants of Zama, Auct. B. Afr. 92.

zamia.full: zāmĭa (sāmĭa; cf. Fleck. Ep. Crit. 12), ae, f., = ζημία, hurt, damage, loss (cf. detrimentum), Plaut. Aul. 2, 2, 20.

zamolxis.full: Zămolxis, is, m., = Ζάμολξις, a Thracian philosopher, App. Mag. p. 290, 9.
zamolxis.short: Zămolxis, is, m., = Ζάμολξις, a Thracian philosopher, App.

zancha.full: zancha, zanca, or zanga, ae, f., a kind of soft Parthian shoe, Gallien. ap. Treb. Claud. 17; Cod. Th. 14, 10, 2.
zancha.short: zancha, zanca, or zanga, ae, f., a kind of soft Parthian shoe, Gallien.

zancle.full: Zanclē, ēs, f., = Ζάγκλη, an older name of the city of Messana (Messina), in Sicily, Ov. M. 14, 5; 15, 290; Sil. 1, 662.—Hence, Zanclaeus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Zancle, Zanclean: harena, i. e. Sicily, Ov. M. 13, 729.— Zanclēĭus, a, um, adj., of Zancle, Zanclean: moenia, i. e. Messana, Sil. 14, 48: saxa, Ov. M. 14, 47.
zancle.short: Zanclē, ēs, f., = Ζάγκλη, an older name of the city of Messana (Messina), in Sicily, Ov.

zanthenes.full: zanthenes, is, m., a yellow gem, Plin. 37, 10, 70, § 185.
zanthenes.short: zanthenes, is, m., a yellow gem, Plin.

zaplutus.full: zāplūtus, a, um, adj., = ζάπλουτος, very rich, Petr. 37.
zaplutus.short: zāplūtus, a, um, adj., = ζάπλουτος, very rich, Petr.

zea.full: zēa, ae, f., = ζειἀ. A kind of grain, spelt: Triticum spelta, Linn. (pure Lat. alica); Plin. 18, 8, 19, § 81 sq.; Hier. in Isa. 9, 28, 25; id. in Ezech. 4, 9.— A kind of rosemary, App. Herb. 97.

zelanter.full: zēlanter, adv. zelo, zealously (late Lat.), Ven. Fort. Vit. Patern. 3.

zelator.full: zēlātor, ōris, m. id., a zealous person, a zealot, Ven. Carm. 5, 6, 12; Ambros. in Psa. 51, 15.

zelivira.full: zēlĭvĭra, ae, f., a false read. for caelibi, Tert. Exhort. Cast. 9.
zelivira.short: zēlĭvĭra, ae, f., a false read.

zelo.full: zēlo, āre, v. a., = ζηλόω. To love with zeal or ardently (eccl. Lat.): populum summo pietatis amore, Tert. Carm. adv. Marc. 4, 36; Aug. Conf. 1, 7.— To be jealous of: non zeles mulierem sinus tui, Vulg. Ecclus. 9, 1.— To be zealous for: zelat zelum legis, Vulg. 1 Macc. 2, 58.—Also in dep. form: zelatus est legem. Vulg. 1 Macc. 2, 26.—Absol.: zelatus est pro Deo suo, Vulg. Num. 25, 13.

zelotes.full: zēlōtes, ae, m., = ζηλωτής, one that loves with jealousy, one that is jealous (eccl. Lat.); of God, Tert. adv. Marc. 1, 28; 4, 25; Vulg. Exod. 20, 5 al.
zelotes.short: zēlōtes, ae, m., = ζηλωτής, one that loves with jealousy, one that is jealous (eccl.

zelotypia.full: zēlŏtўpĭa, ae, f., = ζηλοτυπία, jealousy, Plin. 25, 7, 37, § 75; Vulg. Num. 5, 14 (in Cic. Tusc. 4, 8, 18, and Att. 10, 8, A, 1, written as Greek).
zelotypia.short: zēlŏtўpĭa, ae, f., = ζηλοτυπία, jealousy, Plin.

zelotypus.full: zēlŏtўpus, a, um, adj., = ζηλότυπος, jealous: larba, Juv. 5, 45: moechae, id. 6, 278.—As substt. zēlŏtўpus, i, m., a jealous man, Petr. 45; Quint. 4, 2, 30; Mart. 1, 93, 13.— zēlŏtўpa, ae, f., a jealous woman, Petr. 69.
zelotypus.short: zēlŏtўpus, a, um, adj., = ζηλότυπος, jealous: larba, Juv.

zelus.full: zēlus, i, m., = ζῆλος, zeal, emulation; jealousy, Vitr. 7 praef.; Prud. Ham. 188; Aus. Epigr. 77; Hier. in Gal. 2, 4, vv. 17, 18; Vulg. Num. 25, 11.
zelus.short: zēlus, i, m., = ζῆλος, zeal, emulation;

zema.full: zĕma or zŭma, ătis, n., = ζέμα, a cooking utensil, a saucepan, Apic. 8, 1 fin.; Val. ap. Treb. Claud. 14; Serv. ad Verg. A. 3, 466.
zema.short: zĕma or zŭma, ătis, n., = ζέμα, a cooking utensil, a saucepan, Apic.

zeno.full: Zēno or Zēnon, ōnis, m., = Ζἠνων, the name of several Greek philosophers. The founder of the Stoic school, a native of Cittium in Cyprus; form Zeno, Varr. R. R. 2, 1, 3; Cic. Fin. 3, 2, 5; 3, 4, 15; id. N. D. 2, 22, 57; Sen. Ben. 4, 39, 1; Quint. 2, 20, 7; form Zenon, Cic. Tusc. 5, 9, 27 B. and K.; Sen. Ep. 33, 7.— An Eleatic philosopher of Elea, in Magna Grœcia, Cic. Ac. 2, 42, 129; id. Tusc. 2, 22, 52; id. N. D. 3, 33, 82.— An Epicurean philosopher, the teacher of Cicero and Atticus, Cic. Fin.
zeno.short: Zēno or Zēnon, ōnis, m., = Ζἠνων, the name of several Greek philosophers.

zenobia.full: Zēnŏbĭa, ae, f., = Ζηνοβία, a queen of Palmyrene, wife of Odenatus, conquered by Aurelian, Treb. Poll. XXX. Tyrann. 14, 23; 14, 29; Vop. Aurel. 22 sq.; Eutr. 9, 9.— Daughter of Mithridates, king of Armenia, Tac. A. 12, 44; 13, 6; 13, 37.
zenobia.short: Zēnŏbĭa, ae, f., = Ζηνοβία, a queen of Palmyrene, wife of Odenatus, conquered by Aurelian, Treb.

zephyre.full: Zĕphўrē, ēs, f., an island near Crete, Mel. 2, 7; Plin. 4, 12, 20, § 61.
zephyre.short: Zĕphўrē, ēs, f., an island near Crete, Mel.

zephyritis.full: Zĕphўrītis, ĭdis, f., = Ζεφυρῖτις, the Zephyritide, an appellation of Arsinoë, wife of Ptolemaeus Philadelphus, who was honored as a goddess, Cat. 66, 57 (cf. Plin. 34, 14, 42, § 148).
zephyritis.short: Zĕphўrītis, ĭdis, f., = Ζεφυρῖτις, the Zephyritide, an appellation of Arsinoë, wife of Ptolemaeus Philadelphus, who was honored as a goddess, Cat.

zephyrius.full: zĕphўrĭus, a, um, adj., = ζεφύριος, of or belonging to a zephyr or to the west wind: ova, i. e. wind-eggs, addle-eggs, Plin. 10, 60, 80, § 167.
zephyrius.short: zĕphўrĭus, a, um, adj., = ζεφύριος, of or belonging to a zephyr or to the west wind: ova, i.

zephyrus.full: Zĕphўrus, i, m., = Ζέφυρος, a gentle west wind, the western breeze, zephyr (pure Lat. Favonius); personified, son of Astrœus and Aurora. Lit., Plin. 18, 34, 77, § 337; Hor. C. 3, 1, 24; 4, 7, 9; id. Ep. 1, 7, 13; Verg. G. 1, 44; id. A. 4, 223; Ov. M. 1, 64; 1, 108; cf. Sen. Q. N. 5, 16, 5.— Poet., in gen., wind, Verg. A. 4, 562.
zephyrus.short: Zĕphўrus, i, m., = Ζέφυρος, a gentle west wind, the western breeze, zephyr (pure Lat.

zeros.full: zeros, i, m., a precious stone, otherwise unknown, Plin. 37, 9, 53, § 138 (al. leros).
zeros.short: zeros, i, m., a precious stone, otherwise unknown, Plin.

zerynthius.full: Zērynthĭus, a, um, adj., = Ζηρύνθιος, of or belonging to the Thracian town of Zerynthus, Zerynthian: litora, Ov. Tr. 1, 10, 19: Apollo, Liv. 38, 41.
zerynthius.short: Zērynthĭus, a, um, adj., = Ζηρύνθιος, of or belonging to the Thracian town of Zerynthus, Zerynthian: litora, Ov.

zeta1.full: zēta, ae, f., v. diaeta init.

zeta2.full: zēta, indecl. n., = ζῆτα, the Greek letter zeta, Aus. Idyll. Lit. Monos. 12, 11.

zetarius.full: zētārĭus, a, um, = diaetarius, Paul. Sent. 3, 6, 58.

zetes.full: Zētes, ae, m., = Ζήτης, a brother of Calăis and son of Boreas, one of the Argonauts, Ov. M. 6, 716; Prop. 1, 20, 26.—Collat. form Zētus, i, n., Serv. ad Verg. A. 10, 350.
zetes.short: Zētes, ae, m., = Ζήτης, a brother of Calăis and son of Boreas, one of the Argonauts, Ov.

zethus.full: Zēthus, i, m., = Ζῆθος, a son of Jupiter by Antiopa, and brother of Amphion, Cic. de Or. 2, 37, 155; id. Rep. 1, 18, 30; Auct. Her. 2, 27, 43; Hor. Ep. 1, 18, 42; Hyg. Fab. 76 and 155.
zethus.short: Zēthus, i, m., = Ζῆθος, a son of Jupiter by Antiopa, and brother of Amphion, Cic.

zeugitana.full: Zeugĭtāna rĕgio = ἡ Ζευγιτανή, a very fruitful district in Africa, now the northern part of Tunis, Plin. 5, 4, 3, § 23; Mart. Cap. 6, § 669.—Called Zeugis, Isid. 14, 5, 8.
zeugitana.short: Zeugĭtāna rĕgio = ἡ Ζευγιτανή, a very fruitful district in Africa, now the northern part of Tunis, Plin.

zeugites.full: zeugītes, ae, m., = ζευγίτης, a kind of reed, Plin. 16, 36, 66, § 169.
zeugites.short: zeugītes, ae, m., = ζευγίτης, a kind of reed, Plin.

zeugma1.full: zeugma, ătis, n., = ζεῦγμα, a grammatical figure, according to which two nouns or two infinitives are united to a verb which is applicable to only one of them, Ascon. ad Cic. Verr. 1, 18.
zeugma1.short: zeugma, ătis, n., = ζεῦγμα, a grammatical figure, according to which two nouns or two infinitives are united to a verb which is applicable to only one of them, Ascon.

zeugma2.full: Zeugma, ătis, n., = Ζεῦγμα, a town in Syria, on the Euphrates, now Rumkaleh, Plin. 5, 12, 13, § 67; 5, 24, 21, § 86; 34, 15, 43, § 150; Tac. A. 12, 12; Luc. 8, 237; Stat. S. 3, 2, 137.
zeugma2.short: Zeugma, ătis, n., = Ζεῦγμα, a town in Syria, on the Euphrates, now Rumkaleh, Plin.

zeus.full: zēus, i m., = ζαιός, a kind of fish (pure Lat. faber), Col. 8, 16, 9; Plin. 9, 18, 32, § 68.
zeus.short: zēus, i m., = ζαιός, a kind of fish (pure Lat.

zeuxis.full: Zeuxis, is and ĭdis (acc. -im or -in), m., = Ξεῦξις. A famous Greek painter of Heraclea, Plin. 35, 10, 36, § 65 sq.; Cic. Brut. 18, 70; id. de Or. 3, 7, 26; acc. Zeuxin, id. Inv. 2, 1, 1.— Zeuxis Blandenius (a native of Blandos, a city of Phrygia), a matricide, Cic. Q. Fr. 1, 2, 2, § 4 sq.

zingiberi.full: zingĭbĕri or zimpĭbĕri, indecl. n., = ζιγγίβερι, ginger: Amomum zingiber, Linn.; Plin. 12, 7, 14, § 27.—Also zingĭ-ber, ĕris, n., Cels. 5, 23 fin.; Pall. Oct. 20, 2; Apic. 2, 2.

zinzala.full: zinzăla, ae, f., a kind of gnat (rustic Lat.; cf. Span. zenzalo; Ital. zanzara), Cassiod. in Psa. 104, 31.
zinzala.short: zinzăla, ae, f., a kind of gnat (rustic Lat.;

zinzilulo.full: zinzĭlŭlo, āre, v. n., the natural cry of certain birds, to chirp (of the regulus, merops, and progne), Auct. Carm. Phil. 43.

zirbus.full: zirbus, i, m., = omentum, the caul, omentum, Apic. 8, 6 fin.
zirbus.short: zirbus, i, m., = omentum, the caul, omentum, Apic.

zizania.full: zīzā^nĭa, ōrum, n., = ζιζάνια, darnel, cockle, tares (eccl. Lat.), Prud. Apoth. 6, 8; Vulg. Matt. 13, 25; 13, 26 sq.; Ambros. in Luc. 8, 49.
zizania.short: zīzā^nĭa, ōrum, n., = ζιζάνια, darnel, cockle, tares (eccl.

zizyphum.full: zīzўphum or zīzĭphum, i, n., = ζίζυφον, the jujube. Plin. 15, 14, 14, § 47; 17, 10, 14, § 74; 21, 9, 27, § 51.
zizyphum.short: zīzўphum or zīzĭphum, i, n., = ζίζυφον, the jujube.

zizyphus.full: zīzўphus, i, m., = ζίζυφος, the jujube-tree, Col. 9, 4, 3; Pall. 5, 4.
zizyphus.short: zīzўphus, i, m., = ζίζυφος, the jujube-tree, Col.

zmilampis.full: zmilampis, is, m., a precious stone, otherwise unknown, Plin. 37, 10, 70, § 185.
zmilampis.short: zmilampis, is, m., a precious stone, otherwise unknown, Plin.

zmintha.full: zmintha, ae, f., an aromatic plant, a kind of mint, Plin. 19, 10, 57, § 176.
zmintha.short: zmintha, ae, f., an aromatic plant, a kind of mint, Plin.

zmyrna.full: Zmyrna and Zmyrnaeus, a, um, v. Smyrn-.
zmyrna.short: Zmyrna and Zmyrnaeus, a, um, v.

zodiacus.full: zōdĭăcus, i, m., = ζωδιακός, the zodiac (pure Lat. orbis signifer), Cic. Arat. 317; Gell. 13, 9, 6.—Hence, zōdĭăcus, a, um, adj., of the zodiac: zodiacum diastema, Sid. Ep. 8, 11: zodiacus tractus, Mart. Cap. 1, § 44: zodiaca hospitia, id. ib. 1, § 5.
zodiacus.short: zōdĭăcus, i, m., = ζωδιακός, the zodiac (pure Lat.

zoe.full: Zōē, ēs, f., = ζωή (life), one of the Æons of Valentinus, Tert. adv. Valent. 12.
zoe.short: Zōē, ēs, f., = ζωή (life), one of the Æons of Valentinus, Tert.

zoilus.full: Zōĭlus, i, m., = Ζώιλος, a severe critic in the time of Ptolemaeus Philadelphus, a censurer of Homer (hence called Ὁμηρομάστιξ, Homeromastix), Vitr. 7 praef.— Transf., of a censorious person, Ov. R. Am. 366; Mart. 11, 37, 1.
zoilus.short: Zōĭlus, i, m., = Ζώιλος, a severe critic in the time of Ptolemaeus Philadelphus, a censurer of Homer (hence called Ὁμηρομάστιξ, Homeromastix), Vitr.

zomoteganite.full: zōmŏtēgănītē, ēs, f. ζωμόσ-τήγανον, a dish of fish stewed in their own liquor, Apic. 4, 2, § 147 dub.

zona.full: zōna (sōna, Plaut. Merc. 5, 2, 85 Ritschl), ae, f., = ζώνη, a belt, girdle, zone, worn about the loins by women (cf. cingulum). Lit., Cat. 2, 13; Ov. F. 2, 320; id. H. 2, 116; id. M. 5, 470; 10, 379; id. R. Am. 602; id. Am. 1, 7, 48 al.— Transf. A girdle worn by men for containing money, a money-belt (cf. crumena), C. Gracch. ap. Gell. 15, 12 fin.; Hor. Ep. 2, 2, 40.— The girdle or belt of Orion, a constellation, Ov. F. 6, 787.— A line running around the edge of a gem, a girdle, Plin. 37, 6, 24,

zonalis.full: zōnālis, e, adj. zona, II. D., of or belonging to a zone (of the earth): ambitus, Macr. Somn. Scip. 2, 5 med.

zonarius.full: zōnārĭus (sōnārĭus), a, um, adj. zona, of or belonging to a belt or girdle. Adj.: sector, a cutpurse, Plaut. Trin. 4, 2, 20.— Subst.: zōnārĭus, ii, m., a maker of girdles, Cic. Fl. 7, 17; Lucil. ap. Non. p. 2, 379 (Sat. Fr. 30, 16).

zonatim.full: zōnātim, adv. zona, round about, in a circle, Lucil. ap. Non. p. 189, 33.

zone.full: Zōnē, ēs, f., a promontory of Thrace, opposite to Thasos, Mel. 2, 2; Plin. 4, 11, 18, § 43.
zone.short: Zōnē, ēs, f., a promontory of Thrace, opposite to Thasos, Mel.

zonula.full: zōnŭla, ae, f. dim. zona, a little girdle, Cat. 61, 53; Seren. ap. Non. p. 539, 19; Lampr. Alex. Sev. 52.

zoophorus.full: zōophŏrus, i, m., = ζωοφόρος. the frieze of a column (between the epistylium and the coronis), Vitr. 3, 5, 10; 4, 1, 2.

zoophthalmos.full: zōophthalmos, i, m., = ζωόφθαλμος, great houseleek, called also aizoum majus, Plin. 25, 13, 102, § 160.
zoophthalmos.short: zōophthalmos, i, m., = ζωόφθαλμος, great houseleek, called also aizoum majus, Plin.

zopissa.full: zōpissa, ae, f., = ζώπισσα, pitch mixed with wax, which was scraped off from ships, Plin. 16, 12, 23, § 56; 24, 7, 26, § 41.
zopissa.short: zōpissa, ae, f., = ζώπισσα, pitch mixed with wax, which was scraped off from ships, Plin.

zopyron.full: zōpўron, i, n., = ζωπυρόν, a plant, called also clinopodion, Plin. 24, 15, 87, § 137.
zopyron.short: zōpўron, i, n., = ζωπυρόν, a plant, called also clinopodion, Plin.

zopyrus.full: Zōpўrus, i, m., = Ζώπυρος. A celebrated physiognomist, Cic. Fat. 5, 10; id. Tusc. 4, 37, 80.— A Persian noble, who mutilated himself and thereby helped to conquer Babylon, Just. 1, 10, 15.— A rhetorician, Quint. 3, 6, 3.—Hence, perh., Zōpўrion, Lucil. ap. Non. p. 210, 28.— Zōpўriātim, adv., in the manner of Zopyrus, Lucil. ap. Non. p. 455, 17.

zoranisceos.full: zoranisceos, i, m., a precious stone, otherwise unknown, Plin. 37, 10, 70, § 185.
zoranisceos.short: zoranisceos, i, m., a precious stone, otherwise unknown, Plin.

zoroastres.full: Zōrŏastres, is, m., Zoroaster, a lawgiver of the Medes, Just. 1, 1, 9; Plin. 30, 1, 2, § 3; App. Mag. p. 291.—Hence, Zōrŏ-astrēus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Zoroaster, Zoroastrian: susurri, i. e. magical, Prud. Apoth. 494 (where Zŏr-, by solecism).
zoroastres.short: Zōrŏastres, is, m., Zoroaster, a lawgiver of the Medes, Just.

zoster1.full: zoster, ēris, m., = ζωστήρ (a girdle). A kind of herpes, the shingles (cf. zona, II. E.), Plin. 26, 11, 74, § 121.— A kind of sca shrub (called also prason), Plin. 13, 25, 48, § 135.

zoster2.full: Zoster, ēris, m., a promontory, town, and harbor of Attica; the promontory is now called C. Lombarda, Cic. Att. 5, 12 init.
zoster2.short: Zoster, ēris, m., a promontory, town, and harbor of Attica;

zotheca.full: zōthēca, ae, f., = ζωθήκη. A little private chamber, closet, or cabinet, for reposing in by day (cf. conclave), Plin. Ep. 2, 17, 21; cf. zothecula.— A recess, niche, for religious purposes, Inscr. Orell. 1368; 2006; 3889.

zothecula.full: zōthēcŭla, ae, f. dim. zotheca, I., a little closet or cabinet, Plin. Ep. 5, 6, 38; Sid. Ep. 8, 16; 9, 11.

zura.full: zura, ae, f. African, the seed of the Christ's-thorn (paliurus), Plin. 24, 13, 71, § 115.

zygia1.full: zўgĭa, ae, f., = ζυγία (prop. an adj. from ζύγιος, belonging to or fit for yokes). A tree, called also carpinus, horn-beam: Carpinus betulus, Linn.; Plin. 16, 15, 26, § 67.— Zygia tibia, a nuptial or marriage flute, App. M. 4, p. 157, 37.

zygia2.full: Zygia, ae, f., a name of Juno, as the goddess of marriage, App. M. 6, p. 174, 38.
zygia2.short: Zygia, ae, f., a name of Juno, as the goddess of marriage, App.

zygis.full: zўgis, ĭdis, f., = ζυγίς, wild thyme, App. Herb. 99.
zygis.short: zўgis, ĭdis, f., = ζυγίς, wild thyme, App.

zygostasium.full: zўgostăsĭum, ii, n., = ζυγόστασις, the office of a weigh-master, Cod. Th. 15, 26, 1.
zygostasium.short: zўgostăsĭum, ii, n., = ζυγόστασις, the office of a weigh-master, Cod.

zygostates.full: zўgostătes, ae, m., = ζυγοστάτης, a master of the weights, weigh-master, Cod. Th. 12, 7, 2; Cod. Just. 10, 71, 2.
zygostates.short: zўgostătes, ae, m., = ζυγοστάτης, a master of the weights, weigh-master, Cod.

zythum.full: zythum, i, n., = ζῦθος, a kind of malt-liquor among the Egyptians, Plin. 22, 25, 82, § 164; Col. 10, 116; Dig. 33, 6, 9 praef.
zythum.short: zythum, i, n., = ζῦθος, a kind of malt-liquor among the Egyptians, Plin.
